## 1:1 Introduction: J. N. J. The Bible of the Old Testament Illustrated. In Which the Emphases of the Words an
J. N. J. THE BIBLE OF THE OLD TESTAMENT ILLUSTRATED. In which the emphases of the words and the genuine meaning of the sayings are elicited from the sources, the context, and the analogy of Scripture: II. The principal versions are compared with the Hebrew text, the sincerity of which is vindicated everywhere: III. The expositions of both ancient and more recent interpreters are weighed, the truer ones of the Fathers themselves, of B. Luther, and of other theologians are established in their own words: IV. The more difficult and doubtful textual, historical, chronological, topographical, and other passages are explained: V. Apparent contradictions are discussed: VI. Various theoretical and practical questions are solved: VII. Prophetic oracles concerning CHRIST and his kingdom, and whatever else makes for the confirmation of the Evangelical faith, are brought forward by design: VIII. The corruptions of the Jews and heretics, especially modern ones, are clearly refuted: IX. Grotian depravations and ψευδερμηνεῖαι (false interpretations) are subjected to a just examination and exploded. AND SO IT IS ESPECIALLY AND DILIGENTLY SOUGHT THAT THE SINGLE LITERAL SENSE OF SCRIPTURE BE ASSERTED AND CONFIRMED ON ALL SIDES. With necessary preliminaries prefixed, also a SACRED CHRONICLE, a treatise on Coins, Weights, and Measures, and maps of the Holy Land; as well as prefaces and divisions of the individual books, and also suitable summaries of any chapters, with the addition, according to the wish of the learned, of ALL THE ANNOTATIONS OF GROTIUS, whether they contribute to the understanding of Scripture, or deserve observation, or have been recalled for censure. Finally, with a very rich fivefold Index added at the end. By the work and study of D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, PRIMARY PROFESSOR IN THE ACADEMY OF WITTENBERG, AND GENERAL SUPERINTENDENT OF THE ELECTORATE OF SAXONY. Second edition. DRESDEN & LEIPZIG, at the expense of Johann Christoph Zimmermann. RUDOLSTADT, PRINTED BY HENR. URBAN & BALTHASAR PENSOLD, IN THE YEAR 1719.

BIBLES OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT FROM GREEK AND LATIN INTO THE GERMAN LANGUAGE TRANSLATED, AND WITH THE UTMOST DILIGENCE REVISED ACCORDING TO THE TRUTH OF THE GREEK TEXT, THE HEBREW LANGUAGE, AND THE ANCIENT INTERPRETERS, AND ILLUSTRATED WITH ANNOTATIONS.

THE WORK OF D. ABRAHAMI CALOVII, P. P. PRIMARY PROFESSOR IN THE ACADEMY OF WITTENBERG AND COUNSELOR TO THE ELECTOR OF SAXONY.

TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST POWERFUL PRINCE AND LORD, LORD JOHANN GEORG I, DUKE OF SAXONY, JULICH, CLEVES AND BERG, ARCH-MARSHAL AND ELECTOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE, LANDGRAVE OF THURINGIA, MARGRAVE OF MEISSEN, AS ALSO OF BOTH LUSATIAS, BURGGRAVE OF MAGDEBURG, COUNT OF THE MARK AND RAVENSBERG, LORD IN RAVENSTEIN, ETC. ETC., MY MOST CLEMENT LORD,

GRACE, PEACE, SALVATION, AND WHATEVER ARE THE DESIRES OF A PIOUS PRINCE, WHATEVER PROMISES HAVE BEEN MADE IN THE HOLY SCRIPTURES TO A PIOUS PRINCE, I PRAY FOR WITH ALL MY HEART.

MOST POWERFUL ELECTOR.

The twenty-second year is now passing since your parent, of glorious memory, most clemently called me, unworthy as I am, to this illustrious Electoral University, famous throughout the whole world. Following the divine nod, having left my most dear fatherland, in which I had taught theology publicly for over thirteen years, first at the Königsberg Academy, and then indeed in the Church and Athenaeum of Danzig, I betook myself hither, relying on the assistance of Him whose calling I revered, spurning the dictates of flesh and blood. Which I have also experienced to be not ineffective in the pious performance of the parts of sacred duties, the more serious of which were subsequently committed to my trust. However, that nothing has been earlier or more ancient, nothing more sacred to me, than that the heavenly deposit of saving faith should be kept undefiled in this Zion and elsewhere, I trust in the Lord, to whom alone be the glory, that my actions, counsels, and writings, published both in a public and private name, will bear witness along with the ordinary parts of my office.

Although indeed I have had the necessity to experience that twin Davidic enthymeme, I believed, therefore have I spoken, I was greatly afflicted, and what the same man after God's own heart complained of elsewhere, I was peaceable with them that hated peace. When I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause. Princes also did sit and speak against me, both in my fatherland and in foreign shores, yet there was not lacking either the Davidic Spirit (for we have the same Spirit of faith, as St. Paul says to Timothy), or the divine protection, provided also through You, LORD, the vicar of GOD in these lands; nay, it is permitted even now to proclaim with the Prophet: But thy servant was exercised in thy justifications: The sinners have laid a snare for me: but I erred not from thy commandments. Thy testimonies have I acquired as an inheritance for ever; because they are the joy of my heart.

I presented a monument of joyful confidence in the Lord, no less than of my studies and labors, to your Most Serene sight twenty years ago and more, when I presented the first volume of my Theological System: in which I began to explain our faith from the Holy Scriptures, to assert it, and to defend it against the manifold enemies of the truth. Now may it be permitted to bring forth a similar specimen into your august sight, the first volume, nay even the second and third, of the illustrated Bibles of the Old Testament. Which is directed toward the same goal, namely the propagation of a purer faith, which is to be drawn solely from the clearest fountains of Israel. For most rightly did St. Augustine write concerning the divine Scriptures: Whatever a man has learned outside of them, if it is harmful, it is condemned there; if it is useful, it is found there. And when everyone has found there all things which he has learned usefully, he will find much more abundantly those things which are learned nowhere at all elsewhere, but only in the wonderful height and wonderful humility of those Scriptures. And truly with Athenagoras our churches can boast: We have as witnesses of our opinion and faith the Prophets, who discoursed by the divine Spirit concerning GOD and divine things. For we ought, as Origen warns, to bring forward for the testimony of all the words which we utter in doctrine the sense of Scripture, as if confirming the sense which we are expounding. For just as all gold, whatever it may be outside the temple, is not sanctified; so every sense which is outside the divine Scripture, however admirable it may seem to some, is not holy, because is not contained by the sense of Scripture, which is accustomed to sanctify that sense alone which it has in itself, just as the temple sanctifies the gold. Nor indeed is there any other source of errors than ignorance of Holy Scripture, as Christ testifies: You err, not knowing the Scripture and the power of God. Hence, says St. Chrysostom, infinite evils have been stirred up, namely from this very ignorance of the Holy Scriptures: hence the plague of many heresies has sprouted, hence the rite has been neglected in many things, hence useless and profitless labors. For just as those who are deprived of the use of this light can by no means walk straight, so those who do not direct their eyes to the rays of the divine Scriptures necessarily fall into many errors, just as if they were walking about in most dangerous darkness.

Which is entirely the reason why heretics flee the light of Scripture as much as they can: and when they are refuted from the Scriptures, as St. Irenaeus teaches, they turn to accusing the Scriptures, as if they were not correct, nor of authority: and because they are spoken in various ways, and because the truth cannot be found from them by those who do not know the tradition: for that was not handed down through letters, but through the living voice. In which words, indeed, the Roman Catholics and their advocate Hugo Grotius might seem to be depicted to the life, as there is nothing more frequent for them than to argue against the Scriptures, either that they are not correct (in the original sources), or that they are of no authority, or no more authority than Aesop's fables, without the authority of the Church, or that they are ambiguous and can be taken in various ways, so that their genuine meaning must be sought solely from the shrine of the Papal breast as an infallible Judge, or that the truth concerning those things which must be believed cannot at all be had from the Scriptures alone without the tradition of the Church as the unwritten word of God. Known to the world are the insults publicly hurled against Scripture and its followers: by which they harass these as Bibliasts, Scripturarians, Word-Deists, ink-stained theologians, and the former as the subject of a dispute, a mute witness, a lifeless judge, a dead letter, cobbler's ink, torn rags, a Lesbian or leaden rule, a wax nose, and other such gibes of this bran, not only common monks, but Jesuits, even Bishops, and Cardinals in the Roman Church, Costerus, Bailius, Melchior Canus, Piggius, Hosius, and others. Who nevertheless, being convinced in their conscience of the divine majesty and efficacy of Scripture, strive therefore to extort it from the hands of the laity, as they call them, and even of Princes themselves, and have not feared to argue against Blessed Luther (which we know was done by Alfonso Virves, Cardinal Hosius, and others) because he made the mysteries of the Holy Scriptures common, that the holy is given to dogs, and pearls are scattered among swine, and as the Jesuit Stapleton says, to entrust swords and knives to the foolish and to little ones.

How this tyranny was established by the most recent Papal Council, the Fourth Rule of the Index of prohibited books, prepared by the deputation of the Tridentine Synod, teaches not obscurely: Whoever shall presume to read or possess Bibles without permission (granted by the Prelates), unless he has first returned the Bibles to the Ordinary, cannot receive absolution of sins. And the observation to the same is far more tyrannical, delivered through the office of the Roman Inquisition: It must be noted concerning the above-written fourth rule of the Index of happy memory. of Pope Pius IV, that by this printing and edition no new power is granted to Bishops, or Inquisitors, or superiors of Regulars, to grant license to buy, read, or retain Bibles published in the vulgar tongue, since hitherto by the mandate and usage of the holy Roman and universal inquisition the power of granting such licenses to read or retain vulgar Bibles, or other parts of Holy Scripture of both the Old and New Testament, published in any vulgar tongue, has been taken away from them; and furthermore summaries and compendia, even historical, of the same Bibles, or books of Holy Scripture, written in any vulgar idiom: which indeed is to be kept INVIOLATE. Although Grotius asserted that this is neglected in France and elsewhere, he was nevertheless warned by Rivet: that this is true only of some, who reports this memorable thing: I know that the greatest part of the French, who are called Catholics, so abstain from the reading of the Bibles, that I have seen and heard many who gave thanks to God that they had never touched those books, and protested that they would diligently take care in the future not to do so, even with an oath added: moved by no other reason than the Roman prohibition, and the fear of danger, which was struck into them by their preachers and confessors. Johannes Molanus, a Louvain Theologian, says, we deny that the study of the Scriptures is required of Christian Laymen, nay rather we say it is wholesome that they be kept from the reading of the Scriptures. But Alphonsus a Castro even dares to call the translation of Holy Scripture into the vulgar tongue the parent and origin of heresies, and says that it was, among others, no small occasion that almost the whole populace adhered to Luther. Andradius, defender of the Council of Trent, asserts that nothing can be expected from it but the destruction of piety, the ruin of religion, and the destruction of the faith.

How clearly these agree with the previous admonitions of St. Chrysostom and other ancient Doctors is in the open. This is that, says again that golden mouth of Christian eloquence, which corrupts all things with one plague, that you think the reading of the Scriptures pertains to monks alone. Therefore the holy martyr Cyprian warned that the faithful Christian should apply himself to the sacred Scriptures. Origen, as Claudius Espencaeus praises, observes that John writes to four ages: children, adolescents, young men, and parents. Jerome, who is also cited by Espencaeus, distinguishes between philosophers and apostles thus: that Plato wrote certain things but for few of the people; but the apostles did not write for a few, but for the universal people. Likewise, St. Jerome frequently exhorted not only men, but also virgins and widows to the frequent reading of sacred literature; as witnessed by his letters to Laeta, to Algasia, to Marcella, to Principia, etc., and he praised Pamphilus the martyr because he handed down the Scriptures to be read not only to men, but also to women. Cornelius Agrippa commends the decree of the Council of Nicaea, that no Christian should lack the Biblical Code. He whom I praised a little before, a doctor equally most learned and, above others among the Romanists, candid, Claudius Espencaeus, appeals not only to the ancient custom of the Jews, but also to the practice of the primitive Christian Church in this cause. Some, he says, think that the Scriptures are too difficult to be worn out by the hands of the laity. But it seemed otherwise to the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments. The Jews adapted their five-year-old children to the Holy Bibles, and attributed the first place to instructing boys in sacred literature, from which they began, which Eusebius writes that the Jews preserved from ANCIENT custom to his own times. Let Christians therefore be ashamed to be alien to this care. And again, he says, it is manifest,

from the Apostle in Colossians 3 and the practice of the ancient Church, that the public use of reading the Scriptures was granted to the people. Concerning the first Alexandrian Christians, Cornelius à Lapide the Jesuit reports from Eusebius that they applied themselves to reading sacred literature from dawn until night. Concerning which Tertullian also testified that all Christians once gathered for the reading of divine literature. A twin zeal for piety of John

observed in the time of Cantacuzenus about three hundred years ago. Christians, he says, already gathered in churches, and now individuals read the Bibles daily in their own homes. And at that time, the length of time, the continuous reading, and the diligent investigation manifest and teach the truth. Jodocus Coccius, Book 6, Part 1 of the Catholic Treasury, commends the Fourth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the year 540, because in chapter 24 it says: Ignorance, the mother of all errors, is especially to be avoided in the priests of God, who have undertaken the office of teaching the people. For Paul frequently admonishes priests to read the Holy Scriptures. He also commends Julianus Pomerius, Book 1 against the Jews, similarly warning: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. He also commends Rabanus Maurus, who in the year 850 wrote to a certain Abbot: The divine wisdom which shines forth in sacred Scripture is a wholesome medicine to all: as much to the powerful as to the weak, as much to the wise as to the foolish, if they have understood it rightly and have duly obeyed it. It is the illumination of the soul, it is the correction of life, it is the path of justice, in it is the acquisition of eternal glory: it consoles the grieving in labor, and exercises them in the virtue of patience, it promises a crown in the reception of the reward: and therefore both the greater and the lesser need its support, and have need of its teaching. For may its assiduity in reading console you, most beloved, foster you with exhortations, and comfort you with examples. The Gregories who were Popes were even more pious than Pius IV, not only the Great, so called by his own merit, who abhorred the name of universal Bishop or Priest as a mark of the Anti-Christ, but also the Ninth and the Thirteenth of that name: of whom THE FORMER exhorted Theodore, although a physician by profession, thus: The Emperor of heaven, the Lord of men and Angels, has transmitted his letters to you for your life, and yet you neglect to read them ardently: Study therefore, I ask, and meditate daily on the words of your Creator; learn the heart of God in the words of God, so that you may sigh more ardently for eternal things. THE LATTER, according to Matthew Paris in

“To Henry III. Since, he says, according to the testimony of the Truth, ignorance of the Scriptures is an occasion of error, it is expedient for all to read or hear them. He indeed held as valid the opinion of St. Chrysostom included in the Canon Law, and did not expunge or remove it: C. Nolite, Causa XI, question 3. Just as a priest is a debtor to preach freely the truth which he has heard from GOD, so a layman is a debtor to defend confidently the truth which he has heard from priests, provided it is proven in the Scriptures; for if he does not do so, he is a traitor to the truth. But how can it be defended with confidence, unless he has searched the Scriptures with the Beroeans to see if it agrees with them? And, as St. John and Christ himself command, has examined the same from Scripture? These things undoubtedly moved Erasmus, the beloved son of Leo X, to write to this effect

“to write: I do not see why the unlearned should be removed from the evangelical writings in particular, as the profane are from the sacred, which are equally for the learned and the unlearned, for Greeks as well as Scythians, for slaves just as for the free, for women as well as men, for the common people no less and have been set forth for Kings: What they teach pertains equally to all, what they promise pertains equally to all: And they have been so set forth that they are more quickly understood by a pious and modest unlearned person than by an arrogant Philosopher. Which evidence of truth also drew this eulogy of Scripture from Francisco Ruiz: Scripture calls us to the heavenly fatherland, it changes the heart of the reader with eternal desires for embracing heavenly things: it is set before the eyes of the mind like a certain mirror, so that our internal face may be seen in it, there we feel how much we progress, there we see how far we are from the perfect. Nor should it be rashly omitted that GROTIUS, the defender

of the Roman Church was forced to confess concerning those Papal decrees, that DECREES, if any were ever made, that Scripture should not be read by the people, are AGAINST SCRIPTURE & against the Canons; and therefore DESERVE to be NEGLECTED in France & elsewhere:

But while the Roman Pope decrees against Scripture, while he prohibits Scripture from being read by the people, in what place his authority, and holiness, and infallibility should be held is not at all obscure. And does the Roman Pontiff not thus sufficiently show himself to be not a successor of the doctrine and apostleship of Peter, but a destroyer, not a vicar of Christ, but a true ANTICHRIST, not a servant of GOD, but the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called GOD? For PETER did not prohibit the Scriptures to the people, but proposed them to be read by them; saying, You do well to attend to the prophetic word. CHRIST did not ordain that the Scriptures should not be read without permission, but commanded all to search the Holy Scriptures: concerning which St. Chrysostom says: Christ relegated the Jews not to a simple and rude reading of the Scriptures, but to a very diligent investigation. He did not say, read the Scriptures, but search. For divine things require the greatest diligence. Therefore he commands us to dig deeper, so that we may find what lies hidden high up: we do not dig for a thing placed on the surface and in plain sight, but for that which is hidden deep like a treasure. No one is kept away from the Holy Scriptures by GOD, but all are invited, stirred up, and warned by the most serious commands to the reading and meditation of the Holy Scriptures; inasmuch as He destined, commended, and enjoined Scripture to all for that end, and promised a salutary fruit from it to all. You shall tell these words, says the Lord, to your children, and you shall meditate on them, sitting in your house, and walking on the way, sleeping, and rising: and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be and shall move between your eyes, and you shall write them on the threshold of your door. Whence St. Chrysostom in a far different

moved by a spirit other than the Papal, he says, I always exhort, and I will not cease to exhort, that you do not attend to what is said only here in the temple, but also when you are at home, you should assiduously devote yourselves to the reading of the divine Scriptures. For let no one say to me: I am tied to legal cases, I conduct public business, I practice a craft, I have a wife, I feed children, I take care of a household, I am a worldly man, it is not for me to read the Scriptures, but for those who have said farewell to the world, who have occupied the mountain tops, who live such a life continuously. What are you saying, man? Is it not your business to unfold the Scriptures, because you are distracted by countless cares? On the contrary, it is more yours than theirs. For they do not need the protection of the Scriptures as much as you do, who are tossed in the midst of the waves of business. The Holy Father therefore adds a most serious exhortation: Let us not neglect our salvation, beloved, all these things were written for our sake, for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The reading of the Scriptures is a great fortification against sin. A great precipice, a deep abyss is the ignorance of the Scriptures; it is a great loss of salvation to know nothing of the divine laws. This matter has both brought forth heresies and introduced a corrupt life: this has turned everything upside down. For it CANNOT happen, it cannot, I say, happen that anyone should depart without fruit who enjoys the assiduous and attentive reading of the Scriptures. Regarding this fruit of the reading of Scripture, Basil the Great, his foster-brother, also deserves to be heard: Every Scripture, he says, divinely inspired and useful, is established as having been written by the Holy Spirit for this one reason, that from it, just as from some COMMON DISPENSARY for the healing of souls, EVERYONE may be able to select a remedy that is salutary and suitable for his own disease.

But concerning Kings and Princes, even if they are laymen and not clerics, as the Papacy considers them—being far removed from St. Peter in that regard as well—the King of Kings and Lord of Lords, certainly not like that masked SERVANT OF SERVANTS, but in this very tenor defined, not indeed from the Roman chair, to which the Lord will never be joined, as David testifies, but from heaven and the seat of His majesty He defined: But after the King (or Prince) has sat on the throne of his Kingdom, he shall DESCRIBE for himself a copy of this law in a volume, taking an exemplar from the Priests of the Levitical tribe, and he shall have it with “and he shall read it ALL THE DAYS OF HIS LIFE, that he may learn to fear the Lord his GOD, and to keep his words, and his ceremonies, which are commanded in the law. That his heart be not lifted up with pride over his brethren, nor decline to the RIGHT or to the LEFT, that he may reign a long time, he and his children over Israel. Which divine decree, when Joshua was being invested with the Israelite leadership by the divine hand, so to speak, the Lord inculcated again: Be comforted therefore, and be very robust, that you may keep and do all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you: do not decline from it to the right or to the left, that you may understand all that you do. Let the VOLUME of this law not depart from YOUR MOUTH; but you shall meditate on it DAYS and NIGHTS, that you may keep and do all things that are written in it; then you shall direct your way, and you shall understand it. Regarding the commandment about transcribing the law, although Lyranus, Azorius, and Pineda think it could be done by another hand, Bonfrerius the Jesuit, however, following Philo, affirms that it ought to have been done by the King of Israel's own hand, adding the reason for the same, namely that divine precepts are more fixed in the mind through writing, which easily flow away with bare reading: but Oleaster and Grotius, with the Rabbis, assert that the King was to have a double copy of the law transcribed by his own hand: one which he would have transcribed for himself as a private individual; another which was to be transcribed for him once established on the Royal throne. Some Hebrews also, as Fagius observes, warn: that if the King had not previously had the law transcribed, when he had been raised to the Royal throne, he was required to transcribe two copies of the law; one, which he would store in his treasury; the other, which he should keep constantly with him, whether he goes out to war, or sits in judgment, or is at a banquet, etc.

How holy, how religious that commandment of the divine Majesty was to YOU, MOST SERENE ELECTOR, those who were divinely appointed to care for your soul were able to testify from the truth: I speak of B. Weller, from whom I have heard more than once with pleasure, with what zeal he turned the pages of the Holy Bible of Your Serene Highness, not only by day, but also by night, so much so that if any daily task could not be completed due to other intervening matters, he would even rise in the middle of the night and meditate on the law of the Lord: AND WITH HIS OWN HAND in the STERNIAN Bibles, after they had made the Wittenberg collection their own, he extracted several hundred typographical errors: And also his most worthy successor Dn. D. Geier; who celebrated the holy inclination of Your Serene Highness toward the Holy Scriptures with a public eulogy, because he has always labored so afflictedly and assiduously at reading them, and still labors, so that posterity will one day have something to ADMIRE and IMITATE; and how many cares he has expended up to this point regarding the most corrected edition of the German Bibles, how greatly he still labors on the same task, how exactly he knows the location of almost every saying and Biblical history, how accurately he has compared the differing editions themselves, and indeed has even recorded these variant readings with his own hand, an ἀξιόπισον (trustworthy) witness has testified. To which end, I remember, it was most graciously entrusted to my insignificance ten years ago, that I should preside over the two Theologians of this Electoral Academy as they instituted a collation of the German Bibles with the more exact editions of Megalandrus, and that I should direct those sacred labors, and that a copy from the Electoral Wittenberg Library of Your Serene Highness, which was judged by the opinion of Your Serene Highness to be more corrected, was sent here, so that for the good of the Church the HOLY BIBLES might be more accurately disseminated thereafter, and as far as it can be done, just as they came forth from the very hand of B. LUTHER. What praise for You, MOST SERENE ELECTOR, proper and perpetual, altogether worthy of SO GREAT AN ELECTOR!

Cornelius à Lapide praises the Emperor Charlemagne, he praises Robert of Sicily and Alfonso King of Aragon, because they assiduously read the Holy Scriptures; And Claudius Espensæus reports of Alfonso from his own testimony, that he read through the Holy Bible with commentaries and glosses fourteen times, and he not undeservedly opposes this to the Papists; let them see, therefore, he says, those who keep Christian princes from the reading of the Scriptures as if they were PROFANE, whether they would prefer to be like ALPHONSUS or the DONATISTS. For Augustine once charged the heretical Donatists that they feared that the Kings of the age might know the eloquence of the sacred Codices. But, without doubt, S. T. C. turned the pages of the Holy Bible more frequently, and turned them in such a way that he did not have much need for such glosses as may have happened to be at hand for Alphonsus, but by more frequent and more accurate reading he found Scripture to be its own interpreter, much more certain and more solid than such glosses: concerning which, in the midst of the Papacy, Johannes de Wesfalia, a preacher of Worms, taught openly that the Word of God must be illustrated by mutual comparison, and that one must believe only the Word of God, not the Gloss or the Fathers; and Josephus Acosta confesses: nothing seems to me to open the Scriptures in the same way as Scripture itself, and therefore diligent, attentive, and frequent reading, as well as meditation and comparison of the Scriptures, is the supreme rule for understanding the Scriptures that has always seemed so to me. For from other Scriptures others are best understood, since the phrase itself and the spirit are familiar, so that the understanding lies open to discourses already accustomed.

For which reason it seemed that these meditations on the entire Bible of the Old Testament, and on writings both Canonical and Apocryphal, could be consecrated to no PRINCE more worthy than Your Serene Electoral Highness, and I am entirely sustained by the confidence that it will not be ungrateful to Your Serene Electoral Highness that I have devoted my efforts to this task in your Electoral University rather than to another, for I am certain by the judgment of Your Serene Electoral Highness yourself that no work can be treated more fruitfully for the benefit of either the Church or the studious youth devoted to sacred letters: nor do I despair that these labors of mine, however slight, will be admitted with a more serene countenance, since I prefer to conclude in my own mind that whatever is lacking in these lucubrations due to the insignificance of the author can easily be supplied, partly by the dignity of the subject matter, and partly by the most religious inclination of Your Serene Electoral Highness toward sacred letters. Furthermore, concerning the disposition of Your Serene Electoral Highness toward the theologians of the Augsburg [Confession]. sincerely devoted to the Unaltered Confession, and being secure of the most clement affection toward me, the least of them: which, even to my own insignificance, has been declared more than once by both most gracious letters and by a voice truly ELECTORAL, and most worthy of such great eminence (which is an INCREDIBLE kindness of Your Serene Electoral Highness, to be celebrated with ETERNAL MEMORY), I venerate, and shall venerate, with the devotion that is due, as long as the Spirit shall rule these limbs, or rather, as long as the Holy Spirit of God shall rule this mind. I pass over in silence the public care for the Lutheran Church, which Your Electoral Highness has demonstrated by the Electoral solicitude for averting the danger of a most destructive Schism, by the general visitation of Academies and Churches, by the annual festival in memory of the most holy work of the Reformation, by the Eucharistic solemnities for the benefit of peace obtained from the Muslims and others, by axiomatic intercessions for those afflicted in the faith who are our kin, by the Electoral munificence for building temples, Schools, and towns, and by supporting the converted, the exiles, the captives, and those exhausted by the flames of fire and war with diplomas and many other most illustrious documents. These things, therefore, for the praising of which I acknowledge that not only I, but even some Chrysostom reborn would be far unequal, I nevertheless had to set forth as an example for PRINCES and SUPREME HEADS. While I do this, and humbly lay these meditations of mine, which have sprung up under the rule, protection, and nourishment of Your Serene Electoral Highness, at the feet of Your Serene Electoral Highness, I most submissively commend myself, my own, and my studies to the Electoral grace, adoring God, the fountain of all grace, with bended knee, that He may deign to bless Your Serene Electoral Highness with increments of every blessing and happiness for the perpetual splendor of the kingdom of Christ, the vigor of the Holy Roman Empire, and the flourishing of the Saxon Court!

Your Serene Electoral Highness.

Most humble servant and tireless intercessor before God

Abraham Calovius, Doctor.

Latin:

J. N. J. BIBLIA TESTAM. VETERIS ILLUSTRATA. In Quibus Emphases vocum ac mens dictorum genuina e fontibus, con- textu, & analogia Scripturæ eruuntur: II. Versiones præcipuę cum Ebræo textu, vindicata ubique hujus sinceritate, conferuntur: III. Expositiones cum veterum tum recentiorum Interpretum expenduntur, veriores Patrum ipsorummet, B. Lu- theri, & aliorum Theologorum propriis verbis stabiliuntur: IV. Loca difficiliora & dubia textua- lia, Historica, Chronologica, Topographica & alia expediuntur: V. Contradictiones apparen- tes discutiuntur: VI. Quæstiones variæ Theoreticæ & Practicæ solvuntur: VII. Oracula Pro- phetica de CHRISTO, ejusque regno, & quæcunque omnino ad fidei Evangelicæ confirmationem faciunt, ex instituto adferuntur: VIII. Corruptelæ Judæorum & Hæreticorum, maxime modernorum, luculenter retunduntur: IX. Grotianæ depravationes, & ψευδερμηνεῖαι justo examini sistuntur & exploduntur. ADEOQUE ID IMPRIMIS SEDULO AGITUR UT UNICUS LITERALIS SCRIPTURÆ SENSUS UNDIQUAQUE ADSERATUR ET CONFIRMETUR. Præmissis necessariis præliminaribus, CHRONICO item SACRO, Tractatu de Nummis, Ponderibus, & Mensuris, & Tabulis terræ Sanctæ; ut & librorum singulorum præloquiis ac partitionibus, nec non ca- pitum quorumvis summariis convenientibus, insertis etiam ex voto Eruditorum ANNOTA- TIS GROTII VNIVERSIS, utpote vel ad intelligentiam Scripturæ facientibus, vel animadversionem merentibus, vel sub censuram revocatis. Adjecto denique sub finem Indice quintuplici locupletissimo. Opera & Studio D. ABRAHAM CALOVII, P. P. IN ACAD. WITEBERG. PRIMARII, ET ELECT. SAX. SUPERINT. GENERALIS. Editio secunda. DRESDÆ & LIPSIÆ, Sumptibus Johannis Christophori Zimmermanni. RUDOLSTADII, IMPRIMEBANT HENR. URBAN & BALTHASAR PENSOLD, ANNO M DCC XIX.

BIBLIA TESTAMENTI VETERIS ET NOVI E GRAECO ET LATINO IN GERMANICAM LINGUAM TRANSLATA, ET AD VERITATEM GRAECI TEXTUS, HEBRAICAE LINGUAE, ET VETERUM INTERPRETUM SUMMA DILIGENTIA RECOGNITA, ET ADNOTATIONIBUS ILLUSTRATA.

OPERA D. ABRAHAMI CALOVII, P. P. IN ACAD. WITTEBERG. PRIMARII ET ELES. SAX. CONSILIARII.

SERENISSIMO, ET POTENTISSIMO PRINCIPI, AC DOMINO DOMINO JOHANNI GEORGIO I. DUCI SAXONIAE, JULIÆ CLIVIÆ AC MONTIUM, SACRI ROMANI IMPERII ARCHIMAR- SCHALLO ET ELECTORI, LANDGRAFIO THURINGIÆ, MARCHIONI MISNIÆ, NEC NON UTRIUSQVE LUSATIÆ, BURGGRAFIO MAGDEBURGENSI, COMITI DE MARCA, ET RAVENSBERG, DYNASTÆ IN RAVENSTEIN, ETC. ETC. DOMINO MEO CLEMENTISSIMO,

GRATIAM, PACEM, SALUTEM, ET QVÆCUNQVE SUNT PII PRINCIPIS DESIDERIA, QVÆCUNQVE IN SCRIPTU- RIS SACRIS FACTA SUNT PRINCIPI PIO PROMISSA TOTO ANIMO PRECOR.

ELECTOR POTEN- TISSIME.

ANnus jam agitur secundus & vigesimus, ex quo Parens Tuus, Gloriosæ recordationis, me indignum ad in- clutam, totoque orbe celeberrimam hanc Electora- lem Universitatem clementissimè vocavit. Sequu- tus nutum divinum, relictâ Patriâ charissimâ, in quâ ultra tredecim annos publicè Theologiam, primùm in Academia Regiomontana, dehinc verò in Ecclesiâ, & Athenæo Gedanensi docueram, huc me contuli, Ejus- dem fretus assistentiâ, cujus vocationem spreto carnis & sanguinis dictamine, venerabar. Quam etiam in partibus sacrorum munerum, quorum subinde graviora fidei meæ commissa, piè obeundis expertus sum non inefficacem. Nihil autem mihi prius, aut antiquius, nihil sanctius fuisse, quam ut cœleste fidei salvificæ depositum intemeratum in hac Sione & alibi custodiretur, actiones, consilia, & scripta varià tùm publico, tùm privato edita nomine, cum or- dinariis officii partibus testimonium latura, in Domino, cui soli sit gloria, confido.

Quanquam verò geminum illud Davidicum Enthymema, Credidi, propterea loquu- tus sum, Ego autem afflictus sum nimis, & quod idem Vir secundum Cor Dei alibi que- stus est, Cum his, qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus. Cum loquebar illis, impugnabant me gratis. Etiam Principes sederunt, & adversùs me loquebantur, cùm in Patria, tùm in exteris oris experiri necessum habuerim, non defuit tamen vel Davidicus Spiritus, (habemus enim eundem Spiritum fidei, S. Paulo & Timotheo dicente;) vel præsidium divinum, per Te etiam, DOMINE, DEI in hisce terris vicarium, præstitum; quin cum Propheta etiamnum prædicare liceat: Servus autem tuus exercebatur in justifi- cationibus tuis: Posuerunt peccatores laqueum mihi: at de mandatis tuis non erravi. Hæ- reditas mea testimonia tua in æternum; quia exultatio cordis mei sunt.

Exposui lætæ in Domino fiduciæ non minùs, quàm studiorum & laborum monumentum aliquod Serenissimo Tuo conspectui, ante quatuor lustra, & quod ex- currit, cum Systematis Theologici Tomum primum sisterem: quo fidem nostram è S. literis explicare, asserere, & adversus hostes veritatis multivarios defendere oc- cœpi. Jam liceat in augustum Conspectum simile specimen producere, Tomum pri- mum, imò & alterum, tertiumque Bibliorum Veteris Testamenti illustratorum. Quod ad Eundem pariter scopum, fidei nempe purioris, quæ è limpidissimis Israëlisfon- tibus haurienda unicè est, propagationem directum. De divinis enim Scriptu- ris rectissimè S. Augustinus scripsit: Quicquid homo extra didicerit, si noxium est, ibi damnatur, si utile est, ibi invenitur. Et cum ibiquisque invenerit omnia, quæ utiliter di- dicit, multò abundantius inveniet ea, quæ nusquam omninò alibi, sed in illarum tantummodò Scripturarum mirabili altitudine, & mirabili humilitate discuntur. Et verè cum Athe- nagorâ Ecclesiæ nostræ gloriari possunt: Nos sententiæ fideique nostræ testes habemus Prophetas, qui Spiritu divino de DEO, & rebus divinis disseruerunt. Debemus namque monente Origene, ad testimonium omnium verborum, quæ proferimus in doctrinâ, profer- re sensum Scripturæ, quasi confirmantem, quem exponimus sensum. Sicut enim omne au- rum, quotquot fuerit extra templum, non est sanctificatum; sic omnis sensus, qui fuerit ex- tra divinam Scripturam, quamvis admirabilis videatur quibusdam, non est sanctus, quia non continetur a sensu Scripturæ, quæ solet eum solum sensum sanctificare, quem habet in se, sicut templum proprium aurum. Neque vero alia errorum scaturigo est, quam Scripturæ S. ignorantia, teste Christo: Erratis nescientes Scripturam & virtutem DEI. Hinc infinita, inquit S. Chrysostomus, excitata sunt mala, ab ipsa videlicet S. Scripturarum ignoratione: hinc multa hæreseon lues pullulavit, hinc ritus in multis neglectus, hinc inutiles & lucro carentes labores. Nam quemadmodum qui luminis hujus usura sunt privati, nequaquam recte ingredi possunt; ita qui ad divinarum Scripturarum radios oculos non intendunt, necessario in multa errata incurrunt, perinde ac si in tenebris periculosissimis obambularent.

Quæ omnino causa est, cur hæretici Scripturæ lucem, qua possunt, defugiant: & cum ex Scripturis arguuntur, S. Irenæo docente, in accusationem convertantur Scripturarum, quasi non recte habeant, neque sint ex autoritate: & quia varie sint dictæ, & quia non possit ex his inveniri veritas ab iis, qui nesciunt traditionem: non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem. Quibus sane verbis ad vivum depicti videri possint Romano Catholici, & Advocatus eorum Hugo Grotius, utpote quibus nihil frequentius, quam Scripturas arguere, vel quod non recte sese (in fontibus) habeant, vel quod nullius, aut non majoris, quam fabulæ Æsopi, autoritatis sint sine autoritate Ecclesiæ, vel quod ambiguæ sint, varieque accipi possint, ut germana earum mens e scrinio pectoris Papalis ceu Judicis infallibilis unice petenda sit, vel quod veritas de his, quæ credenda sunt, e solis scripturis citra traditionem Ecclesiæ ceu verbum Dei non scriptum haberi minime possit. Orbi nota sunt in Scripturam, ejusque cultores publice jactata convitia: quibus hos quidem ut Bibliistas, Scripturarios, Verbi-Deistas, Theologos atramentales, illam vero ut materiam litis, testem mutum, Judicem exanimem, literam mortuam, atramentum sutorium, laceros panniculos, regulam Lesbiam, sive plumbeam, nasum cereum, & quæ hujus furfuris alia sunt fcommata, exagitant, non Monachi tantum vulgares, sed Jesuitæ, etiam Episcopi, atque Cardinales in Romana Ecclesia, Costerus, Bailius, Melch. Canus, piggius, Hosius, aliique. Qui tamen in conscientia de divina Scripturæ majestate & efficacia convicti, extorquere eam ideo satagunt e Laicorum, quos vocant, ipsorum etiam Principum manibus, nec veriti sunt B. Lutherum arguere (quod ab Alphonso Virvesio, Cardinali Hosio, aliisque factum novimus) quod liberum fecerit sanctarum Scripturarum vulgari mysteria, sanctum dari canibus, & spargi margaritas inter porcos, & ut Jesuita Stapletonus loquitur, stultis & parvulis enses ac cultros committere.

Quæ tyrannis quomodo per novissimum Papale Concilium stabilita fuerit, non obscure docet Quarta Regula Indicis librorum prohibitorum a deputatione Tridentinæ Synodi adornati: Qui absque facultate (a Prælatis concessa) Biblia legere seu habere præsumpserit, nisi prius Bibliis Ordinario redditis peccatorum absolutionem percipere non possit. Et observatio ad eandem longe magis tyrannica, per officium inquisitionis Romanæ tradita: Animadvertendum est circa suprascriptam quartam regulam Indicis fel. rec. Pii Papæ IV. nullam per hanc impressionem, & editionem de novo tribui facultatem Episcopis, vel Inquisitoribus, aut Regularium superioribus, concedendi licentiam emendi, legendi aut retinendi Biblia vulgari lingua edita, cum hactenus mandato, & usu sanctæ Romanæ & universalis inquisitionis sublata eis fuerit facultas concedendi bujusmodi licentias legendi, vel retinendi Biblia vulgaria, aut alias Sacræ Scripturæ tam veteris, quam Nov. Testamenti partes, quavis vulgari lingua editas; ac insuper summaria & compendia etiam historica eorundem Bibliorum, seu librorum Sacræ Scripturæ, quocunque vulgari idiomate conscripta: quod quidem INVIOLATE servandum est. Quod etsi in Galliis & alibi negligi "asseruerit Grotius, a Riveto tamen monitus fuit: de nonnullis id tantum verum esse, "qui hoc memorabile refert: Scio maximam partem Gallorum, qui appellantur "Catholici, ita abstinere a Bibliorum lectione, ut multos viderim & audiverim, "qui Deo gratias agerent, quod libros illos nunquam contigissent, & se id diligen- "ter inposterum curaturos, ne id facerent, etiam juramento adhibito protesta- "rentur: non alia ratione permoti, quam Romana prohibitione, & periculi me- "tu, quod eis a suis concionatoribus & confessoribus incutiebatur. Johannes Molanus, Theologus Lovaniensis, negamus, inquit, a Laicis Christianis requiri studium Scripturarum, imo salubriter dicimus, eos a lectione Scripturarum arceri. Alphonsus vero a Castro etiam hæresium parentem & originem audet dicere S. literarum in linguam vulgarem translationem, eamque occasionem inter alias non parvam fuisse, ait, ut Luthero totus pene populus adhæreret. Andradius Conc. Trident. defensor nihil inde nisi pietatis interitum, religionis exitium fideique perniciem sperari posse asserit.

Quam præclare hæc superioribus S. Chrysostomi, aliorumque veterum Doctorum monitis conveniant, in aprico est. Hoc illud est, ait iterum aureum Elo- quentiæ Christianæ os, quod omnia una q. peste corrumpit, quod lectionem Scripturarum putatis ad solos Monachos pertinere. Sanctus ergo Martyr Cyprianus monuit, Scri- pturis sacris incumbat Christianus fidelis. Origenes, laudante Cl. Espensæo, observat Johannem quatuor ætatibus scribere, pueris, adolescentibus, juvenibus, parentibus. Hierony- mus, quod etiam ab Espensæo adducitur, inter Philosophos & Apostolos sic distinguit, quod Plato scripsit quædam sed paucis de populo; at Apostoli non scripserunt paucis, sed uni- verso populo. Item S. Hieronymus non viros modo, sed virgines etiam atque viduas frequenter ad S. literarum lectionem crebro hortatus est; testibus Epistolis ad Lætam ad Algasiam, ad Marcellam, ad Principiam, &c. laudavitque Pamphi- lum Martyrem, quod Scripturas legendas tradiderit non viris tantum, sed & fœmi- nis. Cornelius Agrippa decretum Concilii Niceni, ne quis Christianus Codice Biblico careat, commendat. Is quem paulo ante laudavi eruditissimus pariter, & præ aliis inter Romanenses candidus Doctor, Claudius Espensæus non ad priscam tantum Judæorum consuetudinem, sed etiam ad praxin Ecclesiæ Christianæ primitivæ in „hac causa provocat. Aliqui, inquit, existimant, Scripturas difficiliores esse, „quam ut debeant Laicorum manibus conteri. Sed aliter visum est Patribus Vet. „& Nov. Test. Judæi filios suos quinquennes ad S. Biblia adaptabant, & primum „locum informandis pueris sacris literis, unde auspicabantur, tribuebant, quod ex „PRISCA consuetudine Judæos ad sua tempora servasse, Eusebius scribit. Pudeat „igitur Christianos ab hac cura alienos esse. Et rursus, manifestum est, inquit,

„ex Apostolo Col. III. & Ecclesiæ antiquæ praxi, quod usus Scripturarum legen- „darum publicus populo concedebatur, De Christianis primis Alexandrinis perhibet Cornelius à Lapide Jesuita ex Eusebio, quod ab aurora in noctem S. literis le- gendis incubuerint. Quo de testatus etiam est Tertullianus, omnes olim Christianos ad lectionem divinarum literarum convenisse. Geminum pietatis studium Johannis

Contacuzeni tempore ante trecentos circiter annos observatum. Christiani, in- „quit ille, jam in Ecclesiis congregati, jam singuli domui suæ quotidie legunt Bi- „blia. Atque tum temporis diuturnitas, tum continua lectio, tum diligens inve- „stigatio manifestat, docetque veritatem. Jodocus Coccius l. VI. part. I. Thesaur. Cathol. Concilium Quartum Toletanum anno 540. celebratum commendat, quod c. 24. Ignorantia, inquit, mater cunctorum errorum, maxime in Sacerdotibus DEI vitanda est, qui docendi officium in populis susceperunt. Sacerdotes enim legere S. Scripturas frequen- ter admonet Paulus. Commendat & Julianum Pomerium l. 1. contr. Jud. similiter mo- nentem: Ignorantia Scripturarum est ignorantia Christi. Commendat & Rabanum Maurum, qui anno 850. ad Abbat. quendam scripsit: Sapientia divina quæ in sacra Scriptura elucet omnibus: tam potentibus, quam infirmis: tam sapientibus, quam insipien- tibus, si eam recte intenderint, & ei rite obedierint, medicina salubris est. Ipsa est illumi- natio animæ, ipsa correctio vitæ, ipsa semita justitiæ, in ipsa acquisitio sempiternæ gloriæ: ipsa mærentes consolatur in labore, & exercet in virtute patientiæ, promittit coronam in præ- mii perceptione: & ideo magis majores atque minores ejus adminiculo indigent, ejusque magisterio opus habent. Hujus enim assiduitas in lectione te amantissime consoletur, ex- hortamentis foveat, atque exemplis confortet. Magis etiam pii quam Pius IV. fuere Gregorii Pontifices non tantum Magnus, merito suo ita nuncupatus, qui nomen universalis Episcopi vel Sacerdotis, ceu notam Anti-Christi, abhorruit, sed etiam No- nus & Decimus Tertius ejus nominis: quorum ILLE Theodorum licet professione Me- „dicum sic hortatus est: Imperator cæli, Dominus hominum & Angelorum „pro vita tua tibi suas Epistolas transmisit, & tamen easdem ardenter legere ne- „gligis: Stude ergo quæso, & quotidie Creatoris tui verba meditare; Disce cor „DEI in verbis DEI, ut ardentius ad æterna suspiras. ISTE apud Matth. Paris in

„Henrico III. Cum, inquit, juxta testimonium veritatis occasio sit erroris igno- „rantia Scripturarum, cunctis expedit illas legere, vel audire. HIC vero Jure Ca- nonico comprehensam S. Chrysostomi sententiam ratam habuit, non expurgavit, „aut sustulit: C. Nolite Causa XI. quæst. 3. Sicut Sacerdos debitor est, ut veri- „tatem, quam audivit à DEO, libere prædicet, sic Laicus debitor est, ut veritatem „quam audivit quidem à Sacerdotibus probatam in Scripturis defendat fiduciali- „ter; Quod si non fecerit, proditor est veritatis. Quomodo vero defendi cum fiducia poterit, nisi Scripturis eam congruere cum Berrœensibus scrutatus fuerit? & S. Johanne, ipsaque Christo jubente è Scriptura eandem examinaverit? Quæ mo- verunt procul dubio Erasmum dilectum Leonis X. filium, ut in hanc sententiam

„scriberet: Non video cur idiotæ sint ab Evangelicis præcipue literis, ceu profa- „ni à sacris submovendi, quæ doctis pariter & indoctis, quæ Græcis æque ac Scy- „this, servis itidem ut liberis, quæ fœminis simul ac viris, quæ plebejis non mi- „nus atque Regibus proditæ sunt: Quod docent, æque ad omnes pertinet, quod „pollicentur, pariter ad omnes pertinet: Et ita proditæ sunt, ut citius intelligan- „tur ab idiota pio modestoque, quam ab arrogante Philosopho. Quæ veritatis evi- dentia etiam Francisco Ruizio hoc Scripturæ elogium expressit: Scriptura ad cæle- „lestem patriam vocat, æternis desideriis ad superna amplectenda cor legentis „immutat: mentis oculis quasi quoddam speculum opponitur, ut interna nostra „facies in ipsa videatur, ibi sentimus quantum proficimus, ibi à perfecto quantum distamus. Neque temere prætermittendum, quod GROTIUS hyperaspistes

„Romanæ Ecclesiæ fateri de illis decretis Papalibus coactus fuerit, DECRETA, „si quæ usquam facta sunt, ne Scriptura legatur à populo, ea esse CONTRA „SCRIPTURAM & contra Canones; & propterea MERITO in Galliis & alibi „NEGLIGI:

Dum autem contra Scripturam decernit Romanus Papa, dum Scripturam legi à po- pulo prohibet, quo loco habenda sit ejus autoritas, & sanctitas, & infallibilitas, mini- me obscurum est. Et annon ita satis prodit Pontifex Romanus se non doctrinæ & Apostolatus Petri successorem, sed destructorem, non Christi vicarium, sed verum ANTI- CHRISTUM, non servum DEI, sed hominem peccati, filium perditionis esse, qui adver- satur & extollitur supra omne, quod dicitur DEUS? PETRUS enim non prohibuit Scri- pturas populo, sed legendas ipsi proposuit; Bene facitis, inquiens, attendentes ser- moni Prophetico. CHRISTUS non ordinavit, ne sine concessione legerentur Scri- pturæ, sed omnes jussit Scripturas S. scrutari: de quo S. Chrysostomus: Christus Judæos ad Scripturarum non simplicem, & rudem lectionem, sed ad investigationem perquam dili- gentem relegavit. Non dixit, legite Scripturas, sed scrutamini. Divina enim summa indigent diligentia. Idcirco effodere profundius jubet, ut quæ alte delitescunt, invenire possimus: rem in superficie, & in promptu positam non effodimus, sed quæ tanquam thesau- rus profunde reconditur. A DEO non arcentur ulli à S. literis, sed invitantur, ex- citantur, & mandatis gravissimis monentur omnes ad lectionem & meditatio- nem S. literarum; utpote qui omnibus eo fine Scripturam destinavit, commen- davit, & injunxit, omnibus fructum inde salutarem promisit. Narrabis verba hæc, inquit Dominus, filiis tuis, & meditaberis ea, sedens in domo tua, & ambulans in itinere, dormiens, atque consurgens: & ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque & movebun- tur inter oculos tuos, scribesque ea in limine ostii tui. Unde S. Chrysostomus longe alio

„quam Papali agitatus Spiritu, semper, inquit hortor, exhortari non desinam, ut „non hic tantum in templo attendatis iis, quæ dicuntur, verum etiam cum do- „mi fueritis, assidue divinarum Scripturarum lectioni vacetis. Ne quis enim „mihi dixerit: Ego forensibus causis affixus sum, publica gero negotia, artificium „exerceo, uxorem habeo, alo liberos, familiæ curam gero, mundanus homo sum, „non est meum legere Scripturas, sed eorum, qui mundo dixerunt vale, qui „montium vertices occuparunt, qui vitam ejusmodi continenter agunt. Quid „ais homo? Non est tui negotii Scripturas evolvere, quoniam innumeris curis „distraheris? imo tuum magis est, quam illorum. Neque enim illi perinde Scri- „pturarum egent præsidio, atque vos in mediis negotiorum undis jactati. Sub- „jungit ergo gravissimam adhortationem Sanctus Pater: Ne neglexerimus sa- „lutem nostram, dilecti, hæc omnia scripta sunt propter nos, ad correctionem no- „stram, in quos fines seculorum inciderunt. Magna adversus peccatum muni- „tio est Scripturarum lectio. Magnum præcipitium, profundum barathrum „Scripturarum ignoratio, magna salutis perditio nihil scire ex divinis legibus. „Ea res & hæreses peperit, & vitam corruptam invexit: hoc sursum deorsum „miscuit omnia. Nam fieri NON POTEST, non potest, inquam, fieri, ut quis „sine fructu discedat, qui assidua attentaque Scripturarum lectione fruatur. De quo lectionis Scripturæ fructu audiri etiam meretur Basilius M. ei collacteus: Scri- ptura omnis, inquit, divinitus inspirata & utilis hac una ratione à Spiritu S. conscripta ad- struitur, ut ex ea haut secus, atque è COMMUNI quapiam curandarum animarum OFFICINA medelam suo QUISQUE morbo salutarem & accommodam queat seligere.

De Regibus autem & Principibus etsi laici sint, non clerici, ut Papatus eos æsti- mat, longe à S. Petro in eo etiam dissonus, Rex Regum & Dominus Dominantium, non certe ut larvatus ille SERVUS SERVORUM, sed in hunc omnino tenorem definivit, non de cathedra quidem Romana, cui nunquam sociabitur Dominus, Davide „teste, sed de cælo & sede majestatis suæ definivit: Postquam autem sederit Rex „(vel Princeps) in solio Regni sui, DESCRIBET sibi Deuteronomium legis hujus „in volumine, accipiens exemplar à Sacerdotibus Leviticæ tribus, & habebit se- „cum, LEGETQVE illud OMNIBUS DIEBUS VITÆ SUÆ, ut discat timere Do- „minum DEUM suum, & custodire verba, & ceremonias ejus, quæ in lege præ- „cepta sunt. Nec elevetur cor ejus in superbiam super fratres suos, neque decli- „net in partem DEXTERAM vel SINISTRAM, ut longo tempore regnet ipse, „& filii ejus super Israël. Quod decretum divinum JOSUÆ cum ad Ducatum Israëliticum divina manu, ut ita dicam, investiretur, iterum inculcavit Dominus: Confortare igitur, & esto robustus valde, ut custodias & facias omnem legem, quam præcepit tibi Moses servus meus: ne declines ab ea ad dexteram vel ad sinistram, ut intelligas cuncta quæ agis. Non recedat VOLUMEN legis hujus ab ORE TUO; sed meditaberis in eo DIEBUS ac NOCTIBUS, ut custodias & facias omnia, quæ scripta sunt in eo; tunc diriges viam tuam, & intelliges eam. Quod de describenda lege præceptum, etsi Lyranus, Azorius, Pineda aliena manu fieri posse existiment, Bonfrerius tamen Jesuita Philonem sequutus ma- nu propria à Rege Israëlis fieri debuisse affirmat, addita ejusdem ratione, ut nempe divina præcepta magis per scriptionem animo infigantur, quæ nuda lectione facile effluunt: Oleaster vero & Grotius cum Rabbinis duplex exemplar legis Regi habendum propria descriptum manu asserunt: unum quod ipse, ut privatus sibi descripsisset; alterum quod ipsi in throno Regio constituto describendum erat. Ebræi etiam nonnulli, observante Fagio, monent: Regem si antea non habuerit descriptam legem, cum ad solium Regale evečtus fuerit, debuisse duo legis exemplaria describere; alterum, quod reponeret in thesauro suo; alterum quod jugiter secum habeat, sive egrediatur ad bellum, sive sedeat in judicio, sive in convivio, &c.

Quod divinæ Majestatis mandatum quam sanctum, quam religiosum TIBI fuerit, ELECTOR SERENISSIME, testari ex vero potuere, qui curandæ animæ diuinitus præfečti fuerunt: B. WELLERUM dico, ex quo non semel cum prolu- bio accepi, quanto studio, non diurna tantum, sed nocturna etiam manu evolve- rit S. T. C. Sacra Biblia, adeo ut si qua pensum quotidianum per alia interveni- entia absolvi nequiverit, vel media nočte surrexerit, & in lege Domini meditata fuerit: PROPRIAQVE MANU in Bibliis STERNIANIS, postquam illi peculium Witebergense suum fecerant, aliquot centena errata typographica excerpserit: Nec non successorem ejus dignissimum Dn. D. GEIERUM; Qui sanctam Serenissi- mæ Celsitudinis Tuæ in S. literas propensionem, publico mactavit elogio, quod afflictim adeo atque assidue his pellegendis insudarit semper, & adhuc insudet, ut posteritas habitura sit aliquando, quod MIRETUR ac IMITETUR; & quantas bucusque curas impenderit, circa emendatissimam Bibliorum Germanicorum editionem, quantopere circa idem adhuc negotium laboret, quam exacte cujusvis ferme dičti, historiæque Biblicæ calleat sedem, quam accurate contulerit ipsamet editiones discrepantes, imo & variantes hasce lectiones propria consigna- rit manu, testimonium perhibuit ἀξιόπισον. Qua fini, recordor, gratiosissime meæ tenuitati ante decennium demandatum, ut binis hujus Electoralis Academiæ Theo- logis Bibliorum Germanicorum collationem cum exactioribus Megalandri edi- tionibus instituentibus præessem, operasque illas sacras dirigerem, eque S. T. C. Bibliotheca Witebergense exemplar, quod judicio S. T. C. emendatius censebatur, huc missum fuisse, quo Ecclesiæ bono accuratius deinceps divulgarentur S. BI- BLIA, & quoad ejus fieri potest, prout ab ipsa B. LUTHERI prodiere manu. Quæ laus Tibi ELECTOR SERENISSIME, propria & perpetua, TANTO ELE- CTORE omnino digna!

Laudat Cornelius à Lapide Carolum M. Imperatorem, laudat Robertum Siciliæ & Alphonsum Arragonum Regem, quod assidue lectitarint S. literas; Ac de Alphonso refert Claudius Espensæus è proprio ejus testimonio, quod S. Biblia cum Commentariis & glossis quater & decies perlegerit, idque non immerito Pontificiis opponit; videant igitur, inquiens, qui Christianos principes à lectione Scripturarum ceu PROFANOS arcent, ALPHONSINe an DONATI similes esse malint. Nam Donatistis hæreticis olim impegit Au- gustinus, quod timerent, ne seculi Reges sacrorum Codicum eloquia nossent. At, fine du- bio, frequentius evolvit S. T. C. Sacra Biblia, & ita evolvit, ut non multum glossis talibus, quæ Alphonso forte ad manus fuere, opus habuerit, sed frequentiori & accuratiori lectione Scripturam sui ipsius interpretem invenerit, glossis ejusmo- di multo certiorem, & solidiorem: quo de in medio Papatu Johannes de Wesfalia Concionator Wormatiensis palam docuit, Verbum Dei per collationem mutuam illu- strandum esse, tantum Verbo Dei credendum non Glossæ aut Patribus; & Josephus Acosta faretur: nihil perinde mihi videtur Scripturas aperire, atque ipsa Scriptura, itaque dili- gens, attenta, frequensque lectio, tum meditatio & collatio Scripturarum omnium summa regula ad intelligendas Scripturas mihi semper visa est. Nam ex aliis Scripturis aliæ opti- me intelliguntur, cum phrasis ipsa & spiritus familiaris sit, ut assuetis jam sermonibus in- telligentia pateat.

Quo nomine nec digniori PRINCIPI hæc in universa Biblia Veteris Testamenti, & scripta tum Canonica, tum Apocrypha meletemata consecranda videbantur, quam S. T. C. & fiducia ea omnino sustentor, non ingratum fore S. T. C. quod in Electorali ejus Universitate hanc potius, quam aliam operam occuparim, qua nullam fructuosius tractari posse ex usu sive Ecclesiæ, sive studiosæ, sacrisque li- teris deditæ juventutis, arbitrio ipsiusmet S. C. T. certus sum: neque etiam de- spero, sereniori vultu meos hosce, licet perexiguos labores, admissum iri, quum ita potius apud animum meum statuam, quicquid ob autoris tenuitatem hisce lucu- brationibus decedit, id omne partim à materiæ dignitate, partim à religiosissima S. T. C. in sacras literas propensione facile suppleri posse. De cætero, de S. T. C. erga Theologos August. Confessioni invariatæ sincere addictos, meque eorum minimum clementissimo affectu securus: quem meæ etiam vilitati cum literis gratiosisissimis, tum voce vere ELECTORALI, tantoque fastigio dignissima, plus vice simplici, (quæ INCREDIBILIS, & ÆTERNA MEMORIA celebranda est S. T. C. comitas,) declaratum, ea qua par est, devotione, veneror, & venerabor, dum Spiritus hos reget artus, vel potius, dum Sanctus Dei Spiritus hanc reget mentem. Taceo publicam de Ecclessia Lutherana curam, quam solicitudine Electorali de avertendo Schismatis exitiosissimi periculo, visitatione Academiarum & Ecclesiarum genera- li, festivitate annua in memoriam sanctissimi Reformationis operis, Eucharisticis pro pacis à Muselmannis, aliisque obtentæ beneficio solemnibus, intercessionibus axiomaticis pro affli- ctis in fide consanguineis, munificentia Electoralis pro templis, Scholis, oppidis exstruendis, conversis, exulibus, captivis, ignis bellique flammis exhaustis sustentandis diplomatibus, & aliis plurimis perquam illustribus documentis demonstravit. Hæc ergo, quibus deprædicandis non me tantum, sed vel Chrysostomum aliquem redivivum longe imparem agnosco, in exemplum tamen PRINCIPUM & CAPITUM SUMMO- RUM sistere debui. Quod dum facio, atque ista meletemata mea, sub S. T. C. regi- mine, præsidio, & nutricatu enata, ad pedes S. T. C. humillime depono, gratiæ Electo- rali me, & meos, ac studia mea subjectissime commendo, Deum omnis gratiæ fontem, poplite flexo, adorans, ut S. T. C. omnis benedictionis & felicitatis incre- mentis ad perpetuum regni Christi splendorem, S. R. Imperii vigorem, Aulæ Saxonicæ virorem beare dignetur!

S. T. C.

Servus humillimus & intercessor ad Deum indefessus

Abraham Calovius D.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus
In the name of Jesus.

Benevolent reader.

Before I admit you to the reading of these commentaries, I will detain you at the very threshold, if you please, for a few moments, and perhaps not without profit. I present the ILLUSTRATED BIBLE OF THE OLD TESTAMENT. Not that the Bible, whether of the Old or New Testament, has need of light other than that which was divinely implanted in it. For they shine with their own light, and whatever light we have, we have it from no other source than this light of Scripture, outside of which there is nothing but smoke and darkness. The Holy Scriptures are a light, which St. Peter proclaims concerning the prophetic writings themselves, shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the Morning Star rises in our hearts. If you listen to the Papists, with Pistorio in his Hodegeticon, chapter 3, as interpreter, the Church—that is, according to the final analysis, the Roman Pontiff—brings light to Scripture, without which it is entirely obscure and dark. But St. Peter, whom they make the first Pontiff, does not call SCRIPTURE obscure and dark, but a light shining in a dark place: without which there is nothing but gloom, nothing but darkness. He does not say that he brings light to the prophetic Scripture, even though he was among those to whom Christ had said, 'You are the light of the world,' and, being illuminated by the Holy Spirit, he brought much light to the prophetic Scriptures; but he celebrates with a grateful mind that the day dawns for him, and the Morning Star rises in his heart through the light of Scripture. Indeed, he was not bringing light to the prophetic Scriptures, but with the Holy Spirit illuminating his heart, and the darkness that had been cast upon Scripture from elsewhere being dispelled, he was bringing forth the light innate to it and producing it into the open. For the prophetic Word was already a lamp to the feet of the faithful in the Old Testament and a light to their paths, as David testifies in Psalm 119:105, 114; the testimonies of the Lord were clear, enlightening their eyes, Psalm 19:9. The commandment was a lamp, and the law was a light to them, as Solomon testifies in Proverbs 6:23, and the reproof of discipline is the way of life. For since they were destitute of the light of the New Testament, the writings of the Old Testament must have shone for them, unless we wish to believe that all the faithful under the Old Testament were illuminated through immediate flashes of light and enthusiasm. But what the Bishop, once Roman, who attained the title of 'the Great'—I mean Gregory—attributes to the prophetic Scriptures, when in his Pastoral Care, chapter 44, he calls the Scripture of the prophetic discourse a lamp in the darkness of the present life, and a light for the journey. Genebrardus, however, explains this in parts, regarding what is to be believed, done, and hoped for, in Psalm 119: The Word of God is a light, a lamp, a luminary: because it directs one to God in things to be done, believed, hoped for, and loved, and provides guidance, lest we stumble anywhere and fall in the darkness of this life, and lest we wander from that way which leads to the blessed life. For it is the rule of faith and life, showing the way in the darkness of the world to eternal life. And how could the Apostle have openly protested before small and great that he was sent to open eyes and to convert men from darkness to light, yet having said nothing outside of those things which Moses and the Prophets said would come to pass, Acts 26:18, 22, unless the writings of Moses and the Prophets had been endowed with such and so great a light, which would have sufficed to illuminate the eyes of the mind and to convert hearts from darkness to light? Therefore, a foreign light was not to be brought into the Scripture of the Old Testament, but the innate light was to be brought forth through diligent reading, through the investigation of words and phrases, in which the light is sometimes hidden, through the pious observation of the scope and context, and also of the meanings which shine forth through the torch lit in the New Testament, and through holy meditation, by which that Spirit, by whom the holy Men of God spoke and wrote as θεόπνευστοι, reveals the mysteries and sentences that lie hidden in the letters: when we pray devoutly, with David leading the way: Open my eyes and I will consider the wonders of your law, Ps. CXIX, 34. Alphonsus Salmero, Disp. X. c. 1. on the Epistle to the Romans, acknowledged that this is the best rule for understanding and explaining more obscure passages, if similar passages, which differ concerning the same matter, are compared among themselves: for one is accustomed to illustrate another: Joseph à Costa also acknowledged this, l. 2. de Christo revel. c. 5. He who reads, he says, with a pure mind can understand more about the Holy Scriptures than one surrounded by a great abundance of commentaries could attain. This I hold to be most true, if it concerns that knowledge which does not puff up. Indeed, I have seen men who were entirely illiterate and scarcely knew Latin draw so much from the Scriptures, and bring forth such meanings, that I was thoroughly amazed, and I would not have doubted that men learn nothing of the sort during a long time spent in a Biblical Gymnasium: for the spiritual man judges all things. In the judgment of Andrzej Frycz, l. IV. de Eccl. c. 7., it is also absurd that God should have wished to deal with us in such a way that His words were not understood. Nor does Sixtus of Siena deny this, l. VI. Biblioth. S. annot. CLII., praising this opinion of Chrysostom concerning the amanuenses of the Holy Scriptures: They composed these things not for empty glory, as the heathens did, but for the salvation of their hearers. Philosophers, not seeking what is for the common good, but looking to this, that they themselves might be in admiration, even if they said anything useful, the obscurity customary to them hid this also in a certain darkness of wisdom: but the Apostles and Prophets did the opposite, they produced all things manifest and clear, they explained them to all, like common teachers of the world, so that each person might be able to learn by himself the things that are said, from reading alone.

If, however, the Papists absolutely wish Scripture to be obscure and dark, unless it receives light from the Roman Pontiff, as the sole authentic and infallible interpreter, let them explain, I pray, why the Jesuits and other Doctors sweat with such effort over the interpretation of the sacred letters, and over the meaning, from the observation of the emphasis of words and the phraseology of the Holy Spirit, from the investigation of antecedents and consequents, from the comparison of parallel passages, whether regarding words or sentences, from the interpreters of various others, who are nevertheless fallible, in their collation, when, in their own judgment, all those things cannot render the meaning infallible, unless the ratification of the Roman Pontiff, who alone is believed to be infallible, is added, just as all Roman Catholic Doctors and interpreters submit their writings and interpretations to the judgment of this one man, as the supreme Pastor and infallible heir of the Chair of Peter, and wish whatever he rejects to be held as unsaid, as can be seen from Bellarmine, l. IV. de Eccl. 10. l. 1. de Euchar. c. 5. Why do they not use a shortcut, and beseech the Roman Pontiffs with hand-made petitions, that they might produce some Catholic and perpetual gloss or interpretation of Scripture through that infallible Spirit of theirs, which the Church could enjoy everywhere and always? Thus, not only will the Jesuits and other Doctors be able to dispense with all these labors, but there will be no need for such expense and such vigils to unfold their huge volumes, from which, however, an infallible interpretation, even if they were all exhausted in their entirety, cannot be had, especially because, by the authority of Cardinal Hosius, if anyone has the interpretation of the Roman Church concerning some passage of Scripture, even if he neither knows nor understands whether or how it agrees with the words, he nevertheless has the most true word of God, and Scripture in itself is not that true word of God unless it is expounded according to the sense of the Church. It is a principle known even to boys τῇ Φύσει: What can be done by few, and indeed EQUALLY WELL, nay FAR BETTER, ought not to be done by many. But let them see to that themselves.

When I said illustrated BIBLES, let no one judge me of such rashness or confidence or rather arrogance, that I would have presumed to illustrate all things whatsoever that are found in the Bibles of the O. T.: for there is no need that all things be illustrated, but concerning many things that saying of Augustine holds true, l. XIIX. de civ. Dei c. 28. If we wish to expound this further, the flavor of the Prophetic eloquence will be blunted, which is not rarely observed in such perpetual glosses (let the Ordinary and Interlinear gloss be a witness), nor is it the task of one man, even if he were more diligent than Origen τῶ χαλκεντέρῳ, and much more instructed in every kind of apparatus of erudition and languages than Jerome himself, who in the Preface to l. III. of his commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians professed: it is my duty to discuss the obscure, to touch upon the manifest, and to dwell on the doubtful. For however much that most learned interpreter of the Holy Scriptures attempted this, he did not nevertheless achieve it, nor will anyone rashly presume to achieve it. Here it is helpful to hear our Blessed Luther, who towards the end of his Operations on the Psalms

T. III. Witteberg. Latin. f. 367. This, he says, I have learned: that Scripture is that which surpasses the genius, the erudition, the diligence, and the holiness of no one in many parts, and deceives them, and is exposed even to all little ones to the point of satiety, yet it is always more set aside for hunger. So that Gregory most truly and wisely said that Scripture is a river in which a lamb walks and an elephant swims, nor have any erred more foully or more perniciously in it than those who presumed that they had not erred at all in it. Nor have any progressed more happily and healthily in it than those who feared that they erred in all things. For it is wisdom, whose beginning is the fear of God, which gives understanding to little ones, and rejects the wisdom of the wise. Thus far Megalander.

It was therefore enough for me if, in some places, yet through all the books of the Old Testament, as well Apocryphal as Canonical, and through all the chapters of the books, the Bible was illustrated to some extent, or rather liberated from the obscurity which others had poured upon it, and restored to its own light. And that not entirely by my own efforts: but by the studies and labors of the best of any who were at hand, Interpreters and Doctors, both ancient and modern, as well those who expressly, as they say, commented on the sacred books, as those who illustrated either the Old Testament or books or some particles of it with Scholias or Disputations or observations, whether those were Theologians or Philologists and Critics, and whomever I saw could contribute something to the illustration of the sacred texts, or rather, whom it was permitted to contribute in the straits of time and among other scattered and concatenated labors. Of whom, so far from being ungrateful, but as I hope, with ready willingness, I have mostly retained their very words, not with the names of the authors—whose diligence entirely deserved it—silenced, but praised, so that to each his own might be attributed, and so that nowhere, which can easily happen sometimes with even one word, when the mind of others is rendered with the words of others, a sense alien to them might be brought in, or believed to be brought in, which I sincerely testify was nowhere done by me out of zeal, and especially because a certain δεινότης and efficacy is wont to underlie most things that are produced αὐτολεξεὶ, and because it is more approved, and more pleasing, and more useful to the reader to hear the authors themselves.

Therefore, I did not think that the ANNOTATIONS of him whose censure I had undertaken should be neglected, but rather, as was desired by MANY most illustrious men, especially because those copies are handled by few among us and are not easily found in the shops of booksellers, I decided to insert them ENTIRE, each in its own place, but in a different and smaller typeface. For even those, although in most places they deserved animadversion or censure, in not a few seemed to contribute to the ILLUSTRATION of the sacred text. Indeed, concerning that man of his own name, Maresius himself, his sharp antagonist in the Preface. Concordiæ discordis, seu Anti-Christi revelati, as a witness, it may deservedly be used, what was once said of Origen, where he is good, no one is better, where he is bad, no one is worse, of whom however I would not wish to pronounce entirely that which the same said of him, provided he himself had not turned into such an Ecebolius in religion: He could, he says, be considered a Theologian if he had written nothing on Theology, and had been mindful of that warning of Epictetus: ἐὰν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀναλάβῃς τὶ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἐν τύτῳ ἠσχημόνησας, καὶ ὃ ἠδύνασο ἐκπληρῶσαι, παρέλιπες; If you take on a person that exceeds your strength, you will both bear it indecorously, and you will neglect that which you could fulfill.

For I do not believe that Grotius lapsed so frequently from there, that he took on a person that exceeded his strength, since from that huge store of multivarious erudition, a man of great judgment and most capacious genius could have contributed much to the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures themselves, and indeed did contribute not a few things, even though he often plowed with another's heifer in those things which are still of good quality, but because he was of too ample, or rather of no religion, and strove to reconcile almost all sects; to whom it was quite easy to reconcile the Council of Trent with the Augsburg Confession, so much so that in the collections by which he wished to indicate the way to Ecclesiastical peace, he inserted both the Augsburg Confession, and yet gave the first place in them to the Bull of Pius IV on the form of the oath of the profession of faith, in which he added twelve new articles of faith to the Apostolic Creed, and unheard of in the ancient Church. Which the defender of his Discussion of the Apologetic for true peace of the Church against the deceitful Mediators, the author, excused against Andr. Rivetus, because Grotius thought, namely, that the Augsburg Confession could be reconciled with the Tridentine canons, provided they were accepted CONVENIENTLY.

But Rivetus rightly answered him in the Διαλύσει: It would be necessary for that, if taken conveniently, to be aided by various far-fetched inventions and marvelous glosses, and yet Grotius would not have supporters on either side. But he was a strange man in this, who could have proven with equal industry and even greater ease that fire and water, white and black, and similar things, do not conflict with one another in any way. Yet he gained no other thanks from the Papists than that the Inquisition [placed] him among

LETTER TO THE READER.

he has placed CONDEMNED AUTHORS, concerning whose Annotations I am pleased to add the judgment of the same Rivet: Whether he followed the Rule of the Council of Trent in his glosses, or whether he did not almost everywhere skip over it, I willingly appeal to the judgment of those who follow the decrees of the Council of Trent: And time will show whether those volumes of Grotius's explanations pleased the Sacred congregation, as they call it, in all and principal matters. Future indexes will indicate that. Certainly, although they were published in Paris, they were produced without any privilege, and fortified or commended by no approval.

And indeed he wished to please not only the Papists, or others whitewashed with the Christian name, such as the Arminians and Socinians, but even the Jews themselves, whom he follows with a bias not only in explaining words or phrases—which has been done by others also with discernment, but by this man of ours out of a certain blind affection for the Rabbis, not rarely—but also in corrupting the oracles and predictions of Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets, and in depriving them of their genuine sense, which both the prophetic text renders and the Holy Apostles in the New Testament have elicited; whence he seemed to Maresius to have the name of the Evangelicals, the Pelagianism of the Remonstrants, the Photinianism of the Socinians, and the Anti-Christianism of the Papists, which I demonstrated about the same man succinctly in the Preface to the Apostolic Roman Theology twenty-five years ago in Danzig. Moreover, the Judaism of the new Rabbis must be added to these, which I showed in the year 1658, as it were in a summary, in a preliminary dissertation. This was also revealed more fully later by the public disputations that followed for a decade, opposed to Grotius in this Academy, and by the refutations of his Annotations. Concerning which I append the judgment of a man of the highest merit and honors of office, a polymath and incomparable jurist, JOHANN OTTO TABOR, written to me eleven years ago, which, along with other exhortations of great men, added a spur to me to continue the work undertaken for the vindication of the heavenly truth against more than Rabbinical corruptions. The entire letter, because it is uniquely consecrated to the present argument, seemed worthy to be read here. In which, however, kind reader, I would have you recall that saying of Plutarch: ἐρῶσιν ὥσπερ νοσᾶσι συγγνώμην ἔχειν εὐθιμον. It reads thus:
