The letter was indeed very welcome to me, most Reverend, Most Amplified, and Most Excellent Sir, Patron, and most cherished Friend, which was written at Wittenberg on the Kalends of September and was finally delivered to me toward the end of the previous month by a certain friend from Lübeck, together with the most learned Anti-Grotian annotations, in which I both kissed the constancy of your love and perceived the counsel of the Holy Spirit. For a long time now, the Church of GOD has desired such work from its defenders. I have indeed in my circles that which wearies me to the point of exhaustion, and I judge those who are busy with many things to be little short of impiety; for they boast that they can perform more than the reason of the office committed to them demands of them. Indeed, since the cause of religion ought to be both common and principal, I could not without a sense of pain know, face to face and more clearly, how greatly the reputation of a man, certainly ingenious, has prevailed in corrupting and inclining the minds of men toward atheism; and not only of the younger ones, but also of the veterans. There was a time when this Megalander embraced me with the greatest love, and while I was staying in Paris in the year 1629, soothed me with clearly familiar services: Nor did I try to produce proofs of a grateful mind with a lagging devotion: Nor was I deterred by the little words of some who thought that something demonic lay hidden in that demon of a man: (although many experiences taught me that a mad pursuit of glory drives even the foolish to this very crime and company). But after I perceived long ago from the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures themselves that the man, great in talent, was striving with greater impiety to erase our Christ from all the Prophets, as much as was in him; I seriously detested the crime, as was fitting, and many years ago in a certain solemn Disputation I said that he was Judaizing; because, indeed, the salvation of the students who had been entrusted to me then seemed to demand it entirely. He was bitterly attacking the pronouncement of a certain Academic thesis, which he ought not to have done at all. But let them sleep, if I have my way, in peace, who are now about to render an account of their words and deeds. But you, most religious prelate, do not doubt that this distinguished labor of yours, as it is necessary for the Church, so it will be pleasing to the Lord of the Church, as it will come to pass, who will abundantly repay You and Yours for what the ungrateful world, rushing its own pursuits into every impiety, may perhaps have looked upon with an envious eye (for I know some of those in the very neighborhood) the importance of the excellent work performed. I humbly beseech His divine goodness that He may preserve You, most religious Prelate, surviving for a very long time for the consolation of His Church. But if it should be permitted to add anything further from my own, I ask You, greatest of men, not to overwhelm the divine strength of Your mind too much with labors, but through pleasant interludes, becoming cheerful and vigorous in spirit, to preserve it prudently for great works worthy of Your genius. May GOD so will it: so I vow and pray,

Given at Giessen, the Kalends of November, in the year 1660. As the least,

Of Your Most Reverend Amplitude

Most devoted and observant with a sincere heart

Johann Otto Tabor.

But let these things concerning Grotius suffice for the present; but to return to where I digressed, in the arrangement of this Biblical work I judged that not only the Orthodox, but also Interpreters of other parties and various writers should be employed, because they too, regarding τὰ ἔξω τῆς συῤῥάξεως κείμενα and matters concerning the faith, have left behind some things here and there which seemed to contribute to the illustration of the Holy Scriptures: and not only the Reformed, but also learned Papists and Jesuits: indeed, even Rabbis were sometimes to be heard. For as Hesiod says, πολλάκι καὶ κοιπαρὸς ἀνὴρ μάλα καίρια εἶπε, Often even a gardener has spoken very opportunely.

The testimonies of all of whom, however, since they rendered them to the truth even against their will, were not to be neglected, but the corruptions which they attempted to introduce had to be discussed by design: and those especially by which they gratified heterodox and heretical dogmas, or which were brought into Scripture from preconceived opinions. So that, namely, the true meaning of Scripture might be vindicated, and the light of the Holy Scriptures might shine openly once the mists of errors were dispersed.

To which end both principal versions and diverse expositions were also brought in: not regarding all passages: for that is more laborious than fruitful, and already occupied by others, especially in the recent Synopsis of Critics and Interpreters edited by Matth. Polo as far as the Poetical books, but regarding the more important ones, and in which such a collation contributed to the illustration of Scripture, or to the dissipation of the darkness brought upon them. For it must be admitted that sometimes by versions, but more frequently by various expositions, more darkness has been brought upon the original text, which shines like light, than light itself.

Whose sincerity, therefore, because it is greatly undermined no less by the Innovators Capellus, Grotius, and others, than by professed Papists, had to be asserted here and there, especially because some incautious persons, from the oversights and elaborations of interpreters, call the authentic text into question, or at the very least imagine it to be subject to diverse readings. Which is also to be observed in Brian Walton, editor of the Polyglot Bibles, who, incautiously seduced by Grotius, seduces many others with a long catalog of diverse readings which rely on no Hebrew codex.

In proposing the genuine meaning of Scripture, we have devoted our efforts primarily to ensuring that the literal sense—which, having dismissed the mystical sense and having disposed of it in the prolegomena to GENESIS, we believe to be uniquely intended by the Holy Spirit—might be piously and carefully elicited, consistent no less with the perpetual mind of Scripture, both Prophetic and Apostolic, and the analogy of faith, than with the intention and words of any given passage. For not less correctly than brilliantly, St. Augustine says against Faustus, book XIII: We, he says, read the Prophetic and Apostolic books for the commemoration of our faith, for the consolation of our hope, and for the exhortation of our charity, sounding in harmony with one another, and by that harmony, as if by a heavenly trumpet, both rousing us from the torpor of mortal life and stretching us toward the palm of the heavenly calling. But it cannot be said with how much damage to the true meaning of Scripture the plurality of meanings has bewitched some interpreters of Scripture. has bewitched some, by which, beyond a single literal and historical [sense], if not other literal ones, at least spiritual and mystical ones, or diverse ones, for instance allegorical, tropological, and anagogical, have been introduced into the Scriptures, or even to the same passage and the same words in certain sayings of Scripture a double sense, namely literal and mystical, has been assigned. This bad habit prevailed first among the Rabbis, then Origen and those like him, and furthermore most especially among the Papists, as we explained in the cited passage.

Moreover, since by the Apostle's warning in 1 Thess. V, 20, prophecies are not to be despised, or the interpretations of others who have rightly used hermeneutical means in investigating the literal sense, we have not infrequently called into use the venerable gray hairs of the Fathers and the ἐξηγήσεις of blessed Luther and other theologians of our own, and for the reasons already stated we have not been reluctant to adduce them in their own words, even if they are sometimes rather prolix: whence in quite a few places a kind of chain of interpreters has arisen; but with a selection of authors, which was required for illustrating, not obscuring, the Scriptures. However, in the so-called classic passages, which make for the confirmation of the Evangelical faith, and in the prophecies concerning Christ and His Kingdom and benefits, we had to labor more exquisitely, both on account of others and especially on account of Grotius, who leaves all others who στρεβλῶσι τὰς γραφὰς far behind him, so that they might be solidly asserted. In which, what has been achieved by divine gift, we entrust to your, kind Reader, sensible judgment. Nor, however, have other more difficult passages and textual, historical, chronological, or topographical doubts, or even apparent contradictions, been neglected, but rather those were resolved and these were discussed. And where Grotius could be of use with his annotations, whether he received them from others, which he perpetually conceals, when he followed our own or the Reformed, naming almost only Rabbis and exotic writers, or whether he observed them by his own industry, we have approved them either tacitly or expressly, and we have applied stricter warnings or observations to them only where, in our judgment, they needed them, although even that was not always or too scrupulously done, both because, as is commonly said, the praetor does not care about trifles, and because we had to take care that the work did not grow too much. Nor indeed was it safe to leave those notes without notes, since not all readers are of the same judgment, and often the author, as if doing something else, has inserted dangerous glosses or comments sometimes improvidently adduced by some, or approved without more accurate discussion. But those things which were present from profane writers, especially poets, because they neither helped the interpretation of the sense of Scripture, but easily delayed the reader panting for the same, nor did it seem that poetic things should be mixed with prophetic ones, we have indicated not so much by mere citations as by the very beginnings of the words in their proper places, or to be inquired into at the end of our work, if it should be opportune.

But when I noticed in chronological matters that not only Grotius, but others who are held in great esteem, had stumbled in various ways against the truth of Scripture, and that the standard of Scripture regarding coins, weights, and measures had not been observed equally by all, I wished to communicate here with a liberal hand the diligence I have applied to these matters. To which, on account of the double topography, I thought it right to add the map of Arias Montanus, which seemed worthy of the Royal work. Furthermore, those more minute details observed by critics or philologists, if they could bring any light to the words or phrases of the Holy Spirit, did not seem to be things to be overlooked, in which, however, proper moderation had to be applied, lest these sacred things be disturbed or overwhelmed rather than adorned or illustrated by excessive variety and by trifles, nonsense, and useless things no less unbecoming to sacred commentaries (with which the sons of grammarians and critics are often wonderfully delighted): indeed, I judged that observations or corollaries and documents which pertain to commonplaces are more suitable for complete commentaries than for these illustrative notes; and therefore they will appear here more rarely, and almost only ὥς ἐν ῥοαδινῶς [as if in passing]. Nevertheless, I did not wish to pass over theoretical and practical questions which either occurred among the interpreters or arose spontaneously from the text. But I have resolved not a few of the more noble ones, not so much by pursuing everything that pertains to theological commonplaces, or to polemical or moral theology—for this was foreign to my purpose—as by selecting especially those which are raised by commentators and pertain to exegetical matters, or which had to be defended from the abuse of heretics and others, unless perhaps ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ [as if in passing] some things from ecclesiastical antiquity also had to be touched upon.

But as for those things which had already been treated in our other writings, so that we might not do what has already been done, nor bring them in here unless necessity required it; for many things would have had to be repeated, which could have contributed some ἐπιβάλλον μέρος [fitting part] toward bringing light to quite a few passages of Scripture, toward amending versions, toward discussing corruptions, and toward asserting testimonies of the faith against the enemies of the truth: all the places which were handed down in the Critico Sacro, and which would have had to be inserted in their own places, would have had to be transferred here: whose dissertations on the Canonical Scriptures, on the authority of Scripture, on the original text, on the Hebrew letters, on those same contemporary points, on the exotic words occurring in the Bibles, on the purity of the fountains, and on the various versions, especially of the Old Testament, on the edition of the LXX Interpreters. & on other Greek versions, on the Vulgate Version, (such as most of those things which are prefixed to the English polyglot Work, and which are wont to be prefixed by Papist Interpreters, but from their own sense, and for the use and convenience not so much of the truth as of Papistic hypotheses) I had almost decided to insert, having made a revision and some addition, because I saw that it was desired by some on account of the lack of copies of the Critico Sacro; But I changed my plan, both because the Preliminaries have already grown sufficiently in this Biblical work, and because others have persuaded a new edition of the CRITICI SACRI, and have offered their own effort in promoting it. Nor are there few things, which concerning natural knowledge of GOD, concerning the divine Hebrew names and concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity from the Code of the Old Testament, either κατασκευαστικῶς [constructively] or ἀνασκευαστικῶς [destructively] in natural and revealed Theology, which in IV. Volumes of the Theological System concerning the matters treated there from the Scriptures of the O.T., which were sought out from dissertations on demonstrating the plurality of divine persons from the O.T., on the προϋπάρξει [pre-existence] of the Son of God before his temporal birth, on the faith of the antediluvians, and similar singular dissertations; which concerning the Satisfaction of Christ, and other articles of faith in the refuted Socinianism, which have been handed down against other heretics and Syncretists in our various treatises, could have had both their place and use here, but because most of those writings have already been recalled under the hammer, or perhaps will have to be recalled hereafter, and can easily be compared with these Annotations through indices of Scripture passages, there was no need to repeat them here again.

Nor let anyone think that those things which have been annotated in the Commentary on GENESIS, whether regarding the τὰ προλεγόμενα [preliminary matters], or regarding the elucidation of the text or the treatment of documents, have been proposed here again: The collation itself will teach what was handed down there and omitted here, and what occurs here is sought in vain there; whence it happened that these annotations on GENESIS are not as prolix as those observed on EXODUS: because, namely, those things which pertained there can be read in the separate commentary, which, as not having been elaborated with a common effort, I did not doubt would be used by the cultivators of Holy letters together with these. But those things which were either observed by us on Exodus, or even proposed in a private College to the listeners of the Lord, even if they could have easily completed a just commentary, with documents or commonplaces added, it pleased me to insert into this work, lest those efforts perish, yet with a prior just recognition and with additions added to what was to be added. Also some Academic Programs treating illustrious passages of the O.T., which were published either in the College of the Theological Faculty, or in the name of the Academic Rector according to solemn custom, have found their place somewhere, as they are in the hands of few, and yet were judged to contribute to illustrating certain divine oracles.

Finally, since a work on the entire Old Testament, not only regarding the Canonical books, but also the Apocryphal, seemed to be desired in our Church, because besides the Osiandrian and Ernestine Paraphrase (which some call the Weimar and Nuremberg), none could be found, so that I might satisfy the vows and desires of many, as much as my insignificance allows, and divine kindness grants, I not only added Annotations to the Apocryphal books, which were entirely required on account of the GROTIAN annotations, so that those might be had whole according to the wish of the Learned, and on account of conformity with other Anti-Grotian and other Biblical observations, and also on account of the lack of Annotations of the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession to the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament; but I also prefixed PARTITIONS to individual books and sections and summaries of chapters throughout the entire Bible of the O.T., which little work of mine I trust will be neither ungrateful nor useless to students of Holy Theology. And since the first ἀπορμὴ [occasion] of this work were our Anti-Grotian [writings] publicly proposed in this university, which indeed, because they were continued for an entire decade, and exhibited by way of Disputations,

LETTER TO THE READER.

they are possessed in their entirety by few, but were desired by many, so much so that they were desired in foreign kingdoms and provinces—in Denmark, Sweden, Pannonia, Prussia, indeed even in Belgium and by the British, who are separated from the whole world—and they deserved a revision and a just addition: having compared the interpretations of others, I finally took this counsel, that it would be for the benefit of our Church if the entire work, such as is now seen here by the grace of God, were adorned for the whole Bible of the Old Testament, and if more rigorous notes and other observations were added to the Grotian and Anti-Grotian annotations, and then also those of new interpreters who often seek various mysteries where they should not be sought, and introduce a marvelous kind of commentary, such as has never been heard of in the Christian world, and which they could not prove even to the men of their own sect—such as, among others, Johannes Cocceius and Balthasar Willius—might be noted as discoveries according to the occasion, and all those things which we have already mentioned might be taken into account. But as for those things which were to be added in place of Biblical Apparatus and prolegomena, which you see added or rather placed first here for your convenience and use, BENEVOLENT READER, I address you in particular, you who are called a student of Holy Theology. Although we all, as many as call ourselves students of Holy Scripture, in this earthly university at least, hardly deserve a more sublime name. For we are and remain students of the Sacred letters only, while we are here; nor do we turn out to be Doctors, even if we are called Doctors. For we must always be learning: there is always something that we may learn occurring in these letters; Scripture, as Augustine says in Book XV of The City of God, ch. 25, both terrifies the proud, and excites the negligent, and exercises those who seek, and nourishes those who understand. And just as aromatics—which is a comparison of St. Chrysostom in Homily XIII on Genesis—the more they are rubbed by the fingers, the greater fragrance they give off by their nature, so it happens with the Scriptures, that the more familiar one is with them, the more one is able to see the treasure hidden in them, and the more fruits of infallible riches. So great is, says St. Augustine again in Epistle III to Volusianus, the depth of the Christian letters, that I would be making progress in them daily if I were to try to learn them alone from early childhood until decrepit old age with the greatest leisure, the highest study, and the best talent: not that such difficulty is encountered in them regarding those things which are necessary for salvation, but when anyone has held the faith there, without which one does not live piously and rightly, so many things, and things so obscured by the multiple shadows of mysteries, remain to be understood by those who are progressing, and such a height of wisdom lies hidden not only in the words in which these things are said, that it happens to the most aged, the most acute, and the most burning with the desire to speak, what the same Scripture has in a certain place: When a man has finished, then he begins. If, therefore, it is not permitted to define the matter everywhere in all things, one must consider that we are ignorant of many things in the Scriptures, and that regarding many things it is necessary to apply that rule of St. Augustine in Book II of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 27. When from the words of the same Scripture not one thing or several are perceived, even if it lies hidden what he who wrote it may have thought, there is no danger if any of them can be taught to be consistent with the truth from other places of the Holy Scriptures. Regarding which, however, St. Augustine in Book XI of The City of God, ch. 33, opportunely warns: If we are unable to investigate the intention of the author, we shall nevertheless not stray from the rule of faith, which is known to the faithful through other holy letters of the same authority.

We have certainly applied diligence, if not as much as is required, yet not an ordinary amount in most things. For Scripture is a rock, which is not accustomed to pour forth the water of doctrine immediately unless we strike it repeatedly by reading, meditating, and praying. But since so many things are required for the investigation of Scripture, who here would dare to arrogate everything to himself? St. Augustine touched upon some things in Book III of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 1. A man fearing God diligently seeks His will in the Holy Scriptures. And that he may not love contentions, being gentle in piety, being also forearmed with the knowledge of languages, so that he may not stick at unknown words and expressions, being also forearmed with the knowledge of certain necessary things, so that he may not be ignorant of the force or nature of those things which are used for the sake of comparison, with the truth of the codices also helping, which the skillful diligence of emendation has provided, let him come thus instructed to discuss and solve the ambiguities of the Scriptures. Basil the Great, in the preface to his exposition on Isaiah, expressed these two things as added requirements. Namely, purity of mind and diligent exercise: The purity of life, he says, is required so that it may pertain to the exercise of moral virtue to judge what is wrapped up in the Scriptures. But besides purity of life, assiduous exercise in the Scriptures is required, so that the majesty and the secret of the divine words may be imprinted on the mind by perpetual meditation. But it must also be observed accurately what St. Jerome warned in Matthew, ch. XXV. I always advise the prudent reader, he says, not to acquiesce in superstitious interpretations, and those which are said according to the whim of those who invent them, but to consider the preceding, the middle, and the following parts, and to connect for himself all things that are written. Which rule heretics are accustomed to disregard, and those who distort the Scriptures to perverse dogmas, concerning whom St. Irenaeus [writes] most elegantly in book 1, chapter 1: 'Indeed, overstepping the order and text of the Scriptures, and as far as in them lies, dissolving the members of the truth. They transfer and transpose, and making one thing out of another, they seduce many of those whom they fit out with a poorly composed phantasm from the Lord's utterances.' Just as if someone, having diligently fashioned a good image of a king from precious gems by a wise craftsman, should dissolve the underlying figure of a man, transfer those gems, and by reshaping them make from them the form of a dog or a fox, and then arrange this poorly disposed [figure] and say that this is that good image of the king which the wise craftsman fashioned, showing the gems which were indeed well composed by the first craftsman in the image of the king, but were truly poorly transferred by the later one into the figure of a dog, and by the phantasy of the gems they deceive the unlearned, who do not have a comprehension of the royal form, and persuade them that this base figure of a fox is that good image of the King. Furthermore, as Chrysostom warns in Homily XIII on Genesis, we must reach for the very scope of Scripture, which interprets itself. For when Holy Scripture wishes to teach us something, it explains itself and does not allow the hearer to err. For just as a building is weak without a foundation, so Scripture is useless unless the scope is found, as Chrysostom has again in Psalm II. Furthermore, St. Anselm piously suggests in his Epistle on the Faith to Urban, chapter 2: 'If anyone can understand, let him give thanks to God; if he cannot, let him not thrust his horns to ventilate, but let him bow his head to venerate.'

All of which, although they have always been before my eyes, if it has not always been permitted to hit the mark, I ask that this be ascribed to our imperfection and to my meager equipment, which I do not deny, but not to a voluntary aberration, and with St. Augustine in book XV of the Trinity, the last chapter, I pray:

LORD GOD, whatever I have said that is Yours, may Yours recognize; if anything is of my own, do You forgive, and may Yours [forgive] also.

ACCLAMATIONS.

Ajax, trusting in his own wit and laughing at those who pray, do not wonder why he errs so often: the Spirit himself, who brought forth the oracle, alone also explains this to the one who prays. Thus the Little One is preferred to the wise man. The monuments of HUGO will teach this sufficiently, as our CALOVIUS shows exactly. May GOD further preserve him, that he may vindicate and reveal whatever has been in the dark until now! O GOD, hear!

Thus MARTIN GEJER, D., prayed at Dresden.

On the BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA of my dearest brother, Mr. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, etc., etc., etc.

If that book lives which has seemed to have genius, if fame comes to the author by his own labor, by what reason should the HOLY BIBLE, the Word which is handed down eternally to them, fear destruction for itself? GOD is the founder of genius, and GOD himself is the AUTHOR; they are the same, full of the divinity of their own genius. Shall the ages not survive, nor the fame endure, of those who devoted effort with a true mind for GOD? With what great investigation do you unearth this, with how much study, dexterity, and faithfulness do you illustrate it? Truly, the BIBLE will live by its genius, and your fame will live as long as they themselves live. LIVE, AND MY BROTHER, may the Fates come to you late one day, and may your labor flow in its accustomed stream. We are prevented by a sweet embrace, divided by wide tracts; affection strikes our separated hearts. Here, weary, I drink from the PRÆGEL; the ELBE helps you, the brave one; here and there, the LOVE which BLOOD gave burns.

FABIAN Kalaw vom Hofe, Councilor to the Most Serene ELECTOR PRINCE of Brandenburg, sends his own from Prussia, July 3, 1671.

Latin:

I. N. J.

LECTOR BENEVOLE.

PRiusquam ad lectionem harum commentationum te admittam, in limine ipso, si ita lubet, paucis, nec for- te circa fructum, te morabor. BIBLIA exhibeo VE- TERIS TESTAMENTI ILLUSTRATA. Non quod Biblia seu Veteris seu Novi Testamenti aliena, quam quæ divinitus ipsis indita, opus habeant luce. Lucent enim ipsa luce propria, nec aliunde nobis est, quicquid habemus lucis, quam ab hac Scripturæ luce, extra quam meræ fumus tenebræ. Lumen sunt Scripturæ S. quod de ipsis Propheticis literis S. Petrus prædicat, lucens in loco caliginoso, donec dies illucescat & Phophorus oriatur in cordibus nostris. Pontificios si audias, Pistorio in Ho- deget. c. 3. interprete, Ecclesia, id est, juxta ultimam analysin, Romanus Pontifex, infert Scripturæ lucem, sine qua tota est obscura & tenebricosa. At S. Petrus, quem pri- mum faciunt Pontificem, non obscuram & tenebricosam dicit SCRIPTURAM, sed lumen in loco caliginoso lucens: sine quo nil nisi caligo, nil nisi tenebræ: non se dicit lumen inferre Scripturæ Propheticæ, etsi ex iis erat, quibus Christus dixerat, vos estis lux mundi, & illuminatus à Spiritu S. multum lucis Scripturis Propheticis attulerit: sed diem sibi illucescere, & in corde suo Phosphorus oriri per lucem Scripturæ grata mente cele- brat. Nimirum non inferebat Scripturis Propheticis lucem, sed Spiritu Sancto cor illuminante, tenebris, aliunde Scripturæ affusis, discussis, lucem eidem in- fitam efferebat, & in apricum producebat. Lucerna enim erat Verbum Prophe- ticum jam pedibus fidelium in V. T. & lumen semitis ipsorum teste Davide Ps. CXIX. 105. 114. luculenta erant testimonia Domini, oculos eorum illustrantia Ps. XIX, 9. Man- datum lucerna, & lex ipsis erat lux Salomone teste Prov. VI, 23. & via vitæ increpatio disciplinæ. Quum enim illi luce Novi Testamenti destituti fuerint, Veteris Test. scripta illis luxisse oportet, nisi per immediatas ἐκλάμψεις & ἐνθουσιασμὸς omnes fide- les sub V. T. illuminatos credere velimus. Quod vero Scripturis Propheticis tribuit Episcopus quondam Romanus Magni elogium adeptus, Gregorium intelligo, cum in Pastorali c. XLIV. Scripturam Prophetici Sermonis in tenebris vitæ præsentis fa- ctam dicit lucernam, & lumen itineris. Genebrardus vero id per partes, quoad creden- da, agenda, speranda explicat in Ps. CXIX. Verbum Dei est lux, lucerna, lumen: Quo- niam ad Deum dirigit in agendis, credendis, sperandis, amandis, & ducatum præstat, ne u- spiam offendamus, & labamur in hujus vitæ tenebris, neve aberremus ab ea via, quæ ducit ad beatam vitam. Est enim fidei & vitæ regula, monstrans viam in tenebris mundi ad vitam æternam. Et quomodo coram parvis & magnis palam protestari potuisset Aposto- lus, se esse missum ad aperiendum oculos, & convertendum homines à tenebris ad lucem, ni- hil tamen extra ea, quæ Moses & Prophetæ dixerunt futura, dixisse Act. XXVI, 18. 22. nisi Mosis & Prophetarum scripta luce tali & tanta prædita fuissent, quæ ad illumi- nandum mentis oculos, & convertendum corda è tenebris ad lucem suffecisset? Non ergo aliena inferenda erat lux Scripturæ Veteris Testamenti, sed lux con- genita efferenda per sedulam lectionem, vocum & phræsium, in quibus lux quando- que recondita, indagationem, scopi & contextus, nec non sensuum, qui per facem in Novo Testam. accensam emicant, piam observationem, sanctamque meditationem, per quam Spiritus ille, quo θεόπνευστοι loquuti sunt & scripserunt sancti Dei Homines, revelat mysteria, & sententias, quæ in literis latent : cùm devote, Davide præ- eunte, oramus: Revela oculos meos & considerabo mirabilia de lege tua, Psal. CXIX, 34. Agnovit id Alphonsus Salmero Disp. X. c. 1. Epist. Rom. optimam illam regulam esse ad locos obscuriores intelligendos, & explicandos, si loci similes, qui de eadem re differunt, inter se conferantur: nam unus solet alterum illustrare: Agnovit & Joseph. à Costa l. 2. de Christo revel. c. 5. Legens, inquit, mente pura plura intelligere de S. Scripturis potest, quam magna vallatus commentariorum copia assequi posset. Quod ego sane verissimum te- neo, si de ea scientia agatur, quæ non inflat. Equidem vidi viros prorsus illiteratos ac vix La- tine scientes ex Scripturis tanta depromere, sensusque eos afferre, ut penitus miratus sim, neque dubitaverim, longo Gymnasii Biblici terendi tempore nihil tale homines discere: spiri- tualis enim omnia dijudicat. Andreæ vero Fricii judicio l. IV. de Eccl. c. 7. absurdum etiam est, Deum ita agere nobiscum voluisse, ut verba ejus non intelligerentur. Nec abnuit Sixtus Senensis l. VI. Biblioth. S. annot. CLII. hanc de amanuensibus S. S. laudans Chrysostomi sententiam : Non ad inanem gloriam, quemadmodum Ethnici, sed ad audi- entium salutem hæc composuerunt. Philosophi non quod in commune conducit quærentes, sed illud spectantes, ut ipsi sint in admiratione, etiamsi quid utile dixerint, hoc quoque in ca- ligine quadam sapientiæ, consuetà illis occultavit obscuritas : Apostoli vero & Prophetæ con- tra fecerunt omnia manifesta, claraque prodiderunt, exposuerunt omnibus, veluti communes orbis doctores, ut per se quisque discere possit ea, quæ dicuntur, è sola lectione.

Si tamen omnino velint Pontificii Scripturam obscuram esse & tenebricosam, nisi lumen accipiat à Pontifice Romano, ceu solo authentico & infallibili inter- prete, edisserant quæso, cur Jesuitæ, aliique Doctores tanto studio insudent sacra- rum literarum interpretationi, & sensui, è vocum emphasī & Phrasēologias Spiritus S. ob- servatione, ex antecedentium & consequentium indagatione, ex locorum parallelorum, seu qua voces, seu qua sententias, comparatione, ex interpp. variorum, qui tamen fallibiles sunt, collatione, quum, ipsorum judicio, ea omnia non possint sensum reddere infallibi- lem, nisi accedat Romani Pontificis, qui solus creditur infallibilis, ratihabitio, quemadmodum omnes Doctores & interpretes Romano-Catholici scripta & in- terpretationes suas hujus unius, ceu summi Pastoris & Cathedræ Petri infallibilis hæredis submittunt judicio, & quicquid ille reprobat, pro indicto haberi velint, ut è Bellarm. l. IV. de Eccl. 10. l. 1. de Euchar. c. 5. videre est. Cur non compendio utuntur, & Romanos Pontifices manu facta exorant, ut Scripturæ Catholicam ali- quam & perpetuam glossam vel interpretationem per illum Spiritum suum infallibilem con- ficiant, qua ubique & semper frui possit Ecclesia ? Sic non modo omnibus istis labori- bus supersedere poterunt Jesuitæ, & Doctores cæteri, sed nec opus erit tanto sum- ptu, tantisque vigiliis ingentia ipsorum volumina, è quibus tamen infallibilis in- terpretatio, etiamsi omnes in universum exhauriantur, haberi nequit, evolvere, imprimis quia Hosio Cardinali autore, si quis habet interpretationem Romanæ Ecclesiæ, de loco aliquo scripturæ, etiamsi nec sciat, nec intelligat, an aut quomodo cum verbis conve- niat, habeat tamen verissimum Dei verbum, & scriptura in se ipsa non sit verum il- lud Dei verbum, nisi juxta sensum Ecclesiæ exponatur. Principium est vel pueris no- tum τῇ Φύσει : Quod potest fieri per pauca, & quidem ÆQVE BENE imo LONGE MELIVS, non debet fieri per plura. Sed de eo ipsi viderint.

Illustrata cum dixi BIBLIA, nemo ejus temeritatis vel confidentiæ aut arro- gantiæ potius me censeat, qui omnia, quæcunque in Bibliis V. T. inveniuntur, il- lustrare præsumserim : nam nec opus est, ut illustrentur omnia, sed de multis va- let illud Augustini, l. XIIX. de civ. Dei c. 28. Hoc si velimus exponere adhuc, eloquii Pro- phetici obtundetur sapor, quod in glosfis ejusmodi perpetuis non raro observatur, (testis sit glossa & Ordinaria & Interlinearis) nec unius hominis est, etiamsi diligen- tior Origene τῶ χαλκεντέρῳ sit, & multo instructior omnigeno eruditionis & lingua- rum apparatu ipso met Hieronymo, qui Proœm. l. III. commentar. in Epist. ad Gal. profitebatur : officii mei est obscura differere, manifesta perstringere, & in dubiis immo- rari. Nam quantumcunque hoc conatus eruditissimus ille S. literarum inter- pres fuerit, non præstitit tamen id, nec præstare quisquam temere præsumet. Au- dire hic juvat B. Lutherum nostrum, qui sub finem Operationum suarum in Psalmos

T. III. Witteberg. Latin. f. 367. Hoc, inquit, didici Scripturam esse eam, quæ nullius inge- nium, nullius eruditionem, nullius diligentiam, nullius sanctimoniam, non in multis partibus & superet, fallat atque cum omnibus etiam parvulis sit exposita ad satietatem usque, magis tamen semper seposita est ad esuriem. Vt verissime & sapientissime dixerit Gregorius, Scriptu- ram esse fluvium, in quo agnus peditat, & elephas natat, nec in ea fœdius nec perniciosius er- raverunt, quam qui se nihit in ea errasse præsumserunt. Nec felicius & salubrius in ea pro- fecerunt, quam qui timuerunt se in omnibus errare. Sapientia enim est, cujus principium ti- mor Dei, quæ intellectum dat parvulis, & sapientiam Sapientum reprobat. Hactenus Mega- lander.

Satis ergo mihi fuit, si in locis aliquibus, per omnes tamen libros Veteris Testam. tam Apocryphos, quam Canonicos & per omnia librorum capita quadantenus illustrata sint Biblia, vel potius ab obscuritate, quam affuderunt alii, liberata, suæque luci reddita. Nec id meis omnino operis: sed optimorum quorumvis, qui ad manus erant, Interpretum & Doctorum, cum veterum tum recentiorum, studiis & labo- ribus, tum qui ex professo, quod ajunt, in libros sacros commentati sunt, tum qui Scholiis aut Disputationibus, aut observationibus sive Vet. Testamentum sive li- bros, aut particulas aliquas ejusdem illustrarunt, sive Theologi illi fuerint, sive Phi- lologi & Critici, & quoscunque videbam aliquid conferre posse ad textuum sacro- rum illustrationem, aut potius, quos in angustia temporum, & inter alios diffu- sos & concatenatos labores conferre licebat. Quorum adeo non ingratiis, sed ut spero, prompta lubentia ipsa plerumque eorum verba retinui, non tacitis, sed lau- datis authorum, quorum id omnino merebatur diligentia, nominibus, ut suum cuique tribueretur, & ne alicubi, quod vel uno verbo facile quandoque fieri pot- est, cum aliis verbis aliorum mens redditur, sensus ab ipsis alienus afferretur, aut afferri crederetur, quod nuspiam studio abs me factum esse, sincere testor, & im- primis, quod δεινότης & efficacia, nescio quæ plerumque in iis, quæ αὐτολεξεὶ produ- cuntur, subesse soleat, quodque probatius, & gratius atque utilius lectori sit auto- res ipsos audire.

Ideo nec ejus ANNOTATA, cujus censuram susceperam, negligenda duxi, quin, quod à MULTIS clarissimis viris desiderabatur, imprimis, quia illa paucorum ma- nibus penes nos teruntur, nec in officinis Bibliopolarum facile reperiuntur, IN- TEGRA eadem suis quæque locis, at diverso & minutiori literarum Charactere, inse- rerem. Nam & illa, quamvis in plerisque animadversionem vel censuram mere- rentur, in non paucis ad ILLUSTRATIONEM textus sacri facere videbantur. Siquidem de viro illo sui nominis, ipsomet Maresio, acri ejus antagonista in Præfat. Concordiæ discordis, seu Anti-Christi revelati, teste, usurpari merito possit, quod de Origene dictum olim fuit, ubi bene, nemo melius, ubi male, nemo pejus, de quo tamen nollem id omnino, quod idem de ipso, pronunciare, modo ipse in tantum in religione Ecebo- lium non evasisset: Poterat, inquit, & Theologus censeri, si nihil ad Theologiam scripsisset, memorque fuisset moniti illius Epicteti: ἐὰν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀναλάβῃς τὶ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἐν τύ- τῳ ἠσχημόνησας, καὶ ὃ ἠδύνασο ἐκπληρῶσαι, παρέλιπες; Si quam personam, quæ vires tuas su- peret, indueris, tum eam indecore geres, tum eam, quam sustinere posses, negliges.

Non e- nim inde credo Grotium tam frequenter lapsum, quod eam, personam induerit, quæ vires ejus superarit, siquidem ex ingenti illa eruditionis multivariæ suppellectile vir magni judicii, & ingenii capacissimi, multa conferre potuerit ad ipsarum etiam Sa- crar. literarum interpretationem, & contulerit etiam nonnulla, tametsi aliorum non raro in iis, quæ boni adhuc commatis sunt, ararit vitula, sed quod amplæ nimis, vel potius nullius esset religionis, omnesque propemodum sectas conciliare fatage- ret; cui facile admodum fuit, Concilium Tridentinum cum Augustana Confessione conciliare, adeo ut collectaneis, quibus viam ad pacem Ecclesiasticam indicare voluit, & Augustanam inseruerit Confessionem, & primum tamen locum in illis Bullæ Pii IV. super forma juramenti professionis fidei dederit, in qua Symbolo Apostolico addidit duode- cim fidei articulos novos, & in veteri Ecclesia inauditos. Quod contra Andr. Ri- vetum ita excusavit hyperaspistes Discussionis Apologetici ejus pro vera pace Ecclesiæ con- tra subdolos Mediatores autor, quod putarit nempe Grotius, Augustanam Confessionem conciliari posse cum Tridentinis canonibus, modo illi COMMODE acciperentur.

Sed recte ei respondit in Διαλύσει Rivetus: Oporteret illud commode acceptum variis excogita- tis commentis & mirabilibus glosis juvari, nec tamen ab alterutra parte haberet Grotius suffraganeos. Sed mirus in eo fuit homo, qui ignem & aquam, album & nigrum & similia pari industria atque etiam faciliori potuisset evincere, nulla ratione inter se pugnare. Qui vero non aliam à Pontificiis reportavit gratiam, quam quod Inquisitio eum inter

EPISTOLA AD LECTOREM.

AUTORES DAMNATOS locarit, de cujus Annotatis addere placet ejusdem Ri- veti judicium: An Regulam Concilii Tridentini in suis glossis sequutus fuerit, annon ubi- que fere eam transilierit, libenter appello judicium eorum, qui Tridentini Concilii decreta se- quuntur: Et tempus indicabit, an in omnibus & præcipuis placuerint Sacræ, quam vocant, congregationi volumina illa explicationum Grotianarum. Id indicabunt futuri indices. Certe quamvis Lutetiæ fuerint edita, nullo tamen privilegio, nulla approbatione munita vel commendata prodierunt.

Nec vero Pontificiis solum placere voluit, aut aliis Christiano nomine dealba- tis, Arminianis puta & Socinianis, sed ipsis etiam Judæis, quos pronus sequitur non modo in exponendis vocibus aut phrasibus, quod ab aliis quoque cum delectu, ab hoc autem nostro e cæco quodam in Rabbinos affectu non raro factum, sed etiam in oraculis & prædictionibus Mosis, Psalmorum & Prophetarum depravandis, & sensu suo genuino, quem & textus Prophetici reddunt, & S. Apostoli in Novo Testamento eruerunt, privandis, unde Maresio visus est Evangelicorum nomen habere, Remonstran- tium Pelagianismum, Photinianismum Socinianorum, Anti-Christianismum Papistarum, quod de eodem succincte in Præfatione ad Theologiam Apostolicam Romanam ante ipsos 25. annos Dantisi demonstravi. Addendum autem hisce Judaismum novorum Rabbinorum Anno cIɔ Iɔc LIIX. veluti per saturam, in præliminari dissertatione osten- di. Quod etiam patefecerunt postea uberius, quæ per decennium sequutæ sunt, disputationes publicæ Grotio in hac Academia oppositæ, Annotatorum ejusdem E- lencticæ. De quo judicium Viri & meritis & munerum honoribus summi, Polyhistoris ac juris Consulti incomparabilis, JOHANNIS OTTONIS TABORIS, ante undecim annos ad me perscriptum subjungo, quod cum aliis magnorum Virorum κελεύσμασι, calcar mihi addidit ad pergendum opus, pro vindicanda adversus corruptelas plusquam Rabbinicas cœlesti veritate susceptum. Epistola integra, quia Argu- mento præsenti unice consecrata, digna visa est, quæ hic legeretur. In qua tamen, Lector benevole, recolas, velim, illud Plutarchi: ἐρῶσιν ὥσπερ νοσᾶσι συγγνώμην ἔχειν εὐθιμον. Ita autem habet:

FUit mihi sane perquam grata Epistola, Vir plurimum Reve- rende, Amplissime & Excellentissime, Domine Fautor, & Amice colendissime, quæ Calend. Septembr. Witebergæ scripta sub fi- nem demum superioris mensis ab amico quodam Lubecensi, una cum doctissimis annotatis Anti-Grotianis mihi reddita fuit, in quibus & constantiam amoris exosculatus sum, & consilium Spiri- tus Sancti deprehendi. Jamdudum enim Ecclesia DEI operam talem a suis parastatis desiderabat. Habeo equidem in meis circulis, quod me ad lassitudinem usque defatiget, & multarum rerum satagentes, parum ab impietate abesse censeo; quippe qui plura se præstare posse nugentur, quam officii commissi ratio ab ipsis exigat. Enimvero cum religionis causa & communis ac præcipua esse debeat, non potui sine doloris sen- su coram & liquidius cognoscere, quantopere viri, ingeniosi sane, exi- stimatio evaluerit in corrumpendis & ad atheismum inclinandis homi- num animis; nec juniorum tantum, sed & veteranorum. Fuit, cum Megalander iste, summo me amore complecteretur, & Lutetiæ Anno 1629. hærentem, familiaribus plane officiis demulceret: Neque ego seguidore cultu grati animi documenta edere conatus sum: Nec me ab- sterruerunt quorundam voculæ, qui in Dæmonio isto hominis, Dæmo- niacum quid latitare arbitrarentur: (quanquam multa me experimenta docuerint, insanum gloriæ aucupium etiam ad hoc usque facinus & con- fortium væcordes impellere) At postquam ex ipsa S. S. interpretatione jamdudum deprehendi, Hominem ingenio magnum, majore impietate id moliri, ut Christum nostrum ex omnibus Prophetis, quantum in ipso fuit, expungeret; facinus, ut decebat, serio detestatus sum, & plures ante annos in Disputatione quadam solenni ἴσψι judaizare dixi; quia nempe salus studiosorum, qui mihi tum commendati fuerant, id omni- no exigere videbatur. Id theseos cujusdam Academicæ pronunciatum acriter impugnabat, qui id facere debebat minime. Sed dormiant, me volente, in pace, qui jam dictorum suorum factorumque rationem red- dituri sunt. Tu vero, præsul religiosissime, ne dubites quin insignis iste labor Tuus, ut Ecclesiæ necessarius, ita Domino Ecclesiæ gratus futurus fit, qui Tibi Tuisque prolixe rependet, quod ingratus orbis ac in o- mnem impietatem studia sua præcipitans, livido forsan oculo aspexerit (novi enim quosdam ex illis in ipsa vicinia) præclaræ operæ navatæ momentum. Cujus divinam bonitatem supplex obtestor, ut Te, Præ- sul Religiosissime, Ecclesiæ suæ solatio diutissime superstitem servet. Quod si de meo aliquid præterea licuerit addere, rogo Te, Vir maxime, ne divinam animi Tui vim nimis laboribus obruas, sed per jucundas in- tercalationes Spiritus hilarescentes & vegetos, magnis ac ingenio tuo æquis operibus, prudenter conserves. Ita velit DEUS: ita ego voveo rogoque,

Dab. Giessæ Kal. Novembr. An. 1660. ὡς ἑλάχιστος,

Plurimum Reverendæ Amplitudinis Tuæ

Sincero pectore studiosissimus atque observantiss.

Johann Otto Tabor.

Sed hæc de Grotio in præsenti sufficiant, ut autem eo revertar, unde digres- sus sum, in operis hujus Biblici concinnatione non Orthodoxos tantum, sed et- iam aliarum partium Interpretes, & scriptores varios adhibendos censui, quod & illi, quoad τὰ ἔξω τῆς συῤῥάξεως κείμενα & fidem concernentia nonnulla passim reli- querint, quæ ad illustrationem S. literarum facere videbantur: nec Reformatos solum, sed eruditos quoque Pontificios & Jesuitas: imo audiendi etiam quandoque & Rab- bini fuere. Nam quod Hesiodus ait, πολλάκι καὶ κοιπαρὸς ἀνὴρ μάλα καίρια εἶπε, Sæpe etiam est olitor valde opportuna loquutus.

Quorum vero omnium testimonia, cum vel inviti ea veritati reddidere, haud ne- gligenda, corruptelæ autem, quas invehere conati sunt, ex instituto discutiendæ e- rant: & illæ quidem maxime, quibus gratificati sunt heterodoxis & hæreticis dogma- tibus, vel quæ è præconceptis opinionibus in Scripturam illatæ sunt. Ut scil. vera Scripturæ sententia vindicaretur, & discussis errorum nebulis lux S. literarum palam effulgeret.

Qua fini etiam adductæ sunt cum versiones præcipuæ, tum expositiones diversæ: non quoad omnia loca: id enim magis operosum, quam fructuosum, & ab aliis jam occupatum, maxime in nupera Criticorum & Interpp. Synopsi à Matth. Polo usque ad libros Poëticos edita, sed quoad potiora, & in quibus talis collatio ad illustratio- nem Scripturæ faciebat, aut ad caliginis illis inductæ profligationem. Fateri enim oportet, interdum versionibus, frequentius autem expositionibus variis plus te- nebrarum textui primigenio instar lucis coruscanti, quam luminis conciliatum.

Cujus proinde sinceritas, quia non minus à Novatoribus Capello, Grotio, & aliis, quam à Papicolis professis valde labefactatur, passim asserenda fuit, imprimis quia incauti nonnulli ex interpretum παροράμασι, & exarationibus textum authenti- cum in partes vocant, vel ad minimum diversis lectionibus obnoxium comminis- cuntur. Quod etiam in Briano Waltono Bibliorum πολυγλώττων editore observare est, qui prolixo diversarum lectionum, quæ nullo Ebræo nituntur codice, catalogo à Grotio improvide seductus plures alios seducit.

In genuina autem Scripturæ sententia proponenda id operæ dedimus impri- mis, ut sensus literalis, quem misso, & in prolegomenis ad GENESIN profligato sensu mystico, unice à Spiritu Sancto intendi credimus, pie ac solicite erueretur, perpetuæ Scripturæ cum Propheticæ tum Apostolicæ menti & fidei analogiæ non mi- nus quam intentioni, & verbis loci cujusvis consentaneus. Non enim recte mi- nus quam præclare S. Augustinus contra Faustum l. XIII. Nos, inquit, ad commemora- tionem fidei nostræ, & ad consolationem spei nostræ, & ad exhortationem charitatis nostræ li- bros Propheticos & Apostolicos legimus, alterutris vocibus sibimet concinentes, atque ea conci- nentia, tanquam cœlesti tuba, & à torpore mortalis vitæ nos excitantes, & ad palmam su- pernæ vocationis extendentes. Dici autem non potest, quanto cum damno veri Scri- pturæ sensus pluralitas sensuum Scripturæ Interpp. nonnullos fascinarit, quo præter literalem ac historicum unicum, si non alii literales, spirituales saltem & mystici, vel diver- si, allegoricus puta, tropologicus, & anagogicus in Scripturas invecti sunt, vel etiam ei- dem loco, iisdemque verbis in quibusdam Scripturæ dictis geminus, literalis nem- pe & mysticus sensus assignatus est. Quod cacoëthes penes Rabbinos primum, dein- de Origenem, eique geminos, porro vel maxime penes Pontificios obtinuit, ut loco laudato exposuimus.

Cæterum quum Apostolo monente 1. Thess. V, 20. non spernendæ sint Prophetiæ, vel interpretationes aliorum, qui mediis hermeneuticis recte usi sunt, in literali sensu indagando, in usum non raro vocavimus venerandam Patrum canitiem, & B. Lutheri aliorumque nostratium Theologorum ἐξηγήσεις, easque ob causas jam dictas propriis ipsorum verbis, etsi aliquando prolixiuscula sint, adducere mini- me piguit: unde in locis plusculis catena veluti aliqua Interpp. enata; sed cum au- torum delectu, qui ad illustrandas, non obscurandas Scripturas requirebatur. In lo- cis autem classicis, quæ vocantur, quæ ad fidei Evangelicæ confirmationem faciunt, & in vaticiniis de Christo ejusque Regno, & beneficiis exquisitius tum ob alios, tum maxi- me ob Grotium, alios omnes qui στρεβλῶσι τὰς γραφὰς longo post se intervallo relin- quentem, laborandum fuit, ut ea solide assereretur. In quo quid, divino munere, præstitum sit, Tuo, Lector benevole, cordato arbitrio committimus. Nec tamen posthabita sunt alia loca difficiliora, ac dubia textualia, Historica, Chronologica, Topogra- phica, aut contradictiones etiam apparentes, quin expedirentur illa, hæ vero discute- rentur. Et ubi Grotius suis annotatis usui esse potuit, sive ab aliis ea acceperit, quod perpetuo dissimulat, cum nostros, aut Reformatos sequutus est, Rabbinis fere tantum nominatis, & exoticis Scriptoribus, sive propria industria observarit, ea aut tacite, aut expresse approbavimus, atque illis solum monita strictiora, vel animadver- siones adhibuimus, ubi iis opus, nostro judicio, habebant, quanquam nec id semper, aut scrupulose nimis factum, tum quia ut vulgo dici solet, minima non curat prætor, tum quia cavendum erat, ne excresceret nimis opus. Nec vero tutum fuit, sine no- tis notas illas relinquere, quum non omnes lectores ejusdem sint judicii, & sæ- pe velut aliud agendo ingesserit autor periculosa gloffemata, aut commenta a nonnullis improvide quandoque adducta, vel sine accuratiori discussione, proba- ta. Quæ vero e prophanis scriptoribus, Poëtis præcipue affuit, quia nec interpreta- tionem sensus Scripturæ juvabant, lectorem autem eandem anhelantem facile morabantur, nec Propheticis commiscenda videbantur Poëtica, non tam meris cita- tionibus, quam initiis ipsis verborum indicavimus in propriis sedibus, aut sub cal- cem operis nostri, si opportunum fuerit, inquirenda.

In Chronologicis vero quum non Grotium solum, sed alios, qui in magno habentur pretio, multivariam in Scripturæ veritatem impegisse, animadverterem, nec cir- ca nummos, pondera, & mensuras amusss Scripturæ ab omnibus ex æquo observata fuerit, quæ diligentia mediocri de hisce confignavi, liberali manu hic communicare volui. Quibus ob Topographiam geminam Ariæmontani tabellam, quæ opere Re- gio digna visa est, adjiciendam duxi. Porro nec minutiora illa Criticis vel Philolo- gis observata, si qua lucem aliquam adferre poterant verbis aut phrasibus Spiri- tus S. insuper habenda videbantur, in quibus tamen justam adhibendam modera- tionem, ne varietate nimia, & tricis, apinisque atque inutilibus non minus, quam commentationes sacras indecentibus, (quibus Grammaticorum & Criticorum fi- lii mirum quantum sæpe oblectantur) turbarentur potius, aut obruerentur hæc sacra, quam ornarentur aut illustrarentur: Observationes vero vel porismata & documenta, quæ ad locos communes spectant, commentariis integris magis conveni- re, quam hisce notis illustratoriis censui; ideoque rarius hic comparebunt, & fe- re solum ὥς ἐν ῥοαδινῶς. Quæstiones tamen & Theoreticas & Practicas, quæ vel penes interpp. occurrebant, vel e textu sponte nascebantur, præterire nolui. Sed no- biliores non paucas expedivi, non tam omnia consectando, quæ ad Locos Theolo- gicos, seu Theologiam vel Polemicam vel Moralem faciunt, hoc enim a scopo alie- num erat, quam ea potissimum seligendo, quæ a commentatoribus moven- tur, & ad Exegetica spectant, vel ab hæreticorum aliorumque abusu vindicanda erant, nisi forte ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ nonnulla etiam ex antiquitate Ecclesiastica attin- genda fuerint.

Quæ vero in aliis scriptis nostris jam tractata erant, ne actum ageremus, nec nisi requirente necessitate hic adducta; Repetenda enim multa fuissent, quæ ad lucem conciliandam plusculis Scripturæ locis ad versiones emendandas, ad corruptelas discutiendas, ad testimonia fidei contra hostes veritatis adserenda aliquod ἐπιβάλλον μέρος conferre poterant: Transferenda huc vel maxime loca omnia, quæ in Critico Sacro tradita, & quæque suis sedibus inserenda fuissent: cujus dissertatio- nes de Scripturis Canonicis, de authoritate Scripturæ, de textu originali, de literis Ebrais, de punctis iisdem coævis, de vocibus exoticis in Bibliis occurrentibus, de puritate fontium, & versionibus variis, Veteris imprimis Testamenti, de editione LXX. Interpp. & aliis Græcis versionibus, de Versione vulgata, (qualia pleraque sunt, quæ Operi Ang- licano πολυγλώττῳ præmissa, quæque à Pontificiis Interpretibus, sed ex sensu ipso- rum, & prousu & commodo non tam veritatis, quam hypothefium Papisticarum præmitti solent) facta revisione & accessione aliqua inferere pene constitueram, quia à nonnullis id ob defectum exemplarium Critici Sacri desiderari videbam; Sed mutavi consilium, tum quod Præliminaria jam satis excreverint in hoc opere Biblico, tum quod CRITICI SACRI novam editionem alii suaferint, operamq; suam in ea provehenda obtulerint. Neque pauca, quæ de Cognitione DEInaturali, de no- minibus divinis Ebræis & circa mysterium S. Trinitatis è Codice Vet. Test. vel κατασκευαστικῶς vel ἀνασκευαστικῶς in Theologia naturali & revelata, quæ in IV. Systematis Theologici Tomis circa materias ibi è Scripturis V. T. tractatas, quæ de pluralitate per- sonarum divinarum è V. T. demonstranda, de προϋπάρξει Filii Dei ante nativitatem tempo- ralem, de fide antediluvianorum, & similibus dissertationibus singularibus expetita; quæ de Satisfactione Christi, aliisque articulis fidei in Socinismo profligato, quæ adversus alios hæreticos & Syncretistas in variis tractatibus nostris tradita sunt, hic suum habere poterant & locum & usum, sed quia pleraque illa scripta iterum sub incu- dem vel revocata jam sunt, aut fortassis deinceps revocanda erunt, & per indices locorum Scripturæ facile cum Annotatis hisce conferri poterunt, non opus erat hic denuo ea repetere.

Nec arbitretur quispiam, ea quæ in Commentario in GENESIN seu quoad τὰ προλεγόμενα, seu quoad dilucidationem textus aut documentorum tractationem annotata sunt, hic iterum proposita esse: Collatio ipsa docebit, quæ illic tradita, hic prætermissa esse, & quæ hic occurrunt, illic frustra quæri; unde factum, quod hæc in GENESIN annotata non tam prolixa sint, quam quæ ad EXODUM ob- servata: quod nempe quæ illuc pertinebant in Commentario peculiari legi pos- sint, quem utpote non proletario studio elaboratum una cum hisce adhibitum iri à S. literarum cultoribus non dubitavi. Quæ vero in Exodum vel observata no- bis, vel in Collegio etiam privato Dn. auditoribus proposita, etsi justum commenta- rium, accedentibus documentis, vel locis communibus facile absolvissent, huic operi, ne operæ illæ perirent, prævia tamen justa recognitione additisque adden- dis inferere placuit. Programrnata etiam nonnulla Academica loca illustria V. T. tractantia, quæ vel in Collegio Facultatis Theologicæ, vel nomine Academici Rectoris pro more solenni publicata sunt, alicubi sedem suam invenerunt, utpote quæ in pau- corum manibus versantur, & conducere tamen illustrandis quibusdam oraculis divinis censebantur.

Denique quum opus super integrum Vetus testamentum, non solum quoad libros Canonicos, sed etiam Apocryphos desiderari in nostrate Ecclesia videbatur, quod præter Osiandrinam & Ernestinam Paraphrasin (quæ Vinariensis & Noribergen- sis nonnullis dicta,) nullum inveniretur, ut multorum votis atque desideriis, quantum mea fert tenuitas, & divina largitur benignitas, satisfacerem, non ad- jeci tantum Annotata ad libros Apocryphos, quæ ob annotata GROTIANA, ut integra illa è voto Eruditorum haberentur, & ob conformitatem cum aliis Anti-Grotianis, cæterisque observationibus Biblicis, nec non ob defectum Annotationum Theo- logorum Aug. Confess. ad libros Apocryphos Vet. Testamenti, omnino require- bantur; sed præmisi etiam PARTITIONES singulis libris & sectionibus & summa- ria capitum per universa Biblia V. T. quam opellam meam Studiosis S. Theologiæ nec ingratam, nec inutilem futuram confido. Et cum prima ἀπορμὴ hujus ope- ris fuerint Anti-Grotiana nostra in hac universitate publice proposita, quæ vero, quia per integrum decennium continuata, & per modum Disputationum exhibita,

EPISTOLA AD LECTOREM.

a paucis habentur integra, à multis autem desiderabantur, adeo ut in exoticis regnis & provinciis in Dania, Svecia, Pannonia, Prussia, imo in Belgio quoque & à toto divisis orbe Britannis desiderarentur, & revisionem, ac προσθήκην justam merebantur: collatis aliorum interpretationibus tandem id consilii cepi, è re fore Ecclesiæ nostratis, si opus integrum, quale nunc divina gratia concedente hic visitur, in universa Biblia Vet. Test. adornaretur, & Annotatis Grotianis & Anti-Grotianis strictiora hypomnemata & observationes aliæ accederent, tum novorum etiam Interpp. qui varia sæpe mysteria quærunt, ubi quærenda non sunt, & mirabile commentandi genus invehunt, quale nunquam in orbe Christiano auditum est, quodque ne suæ quidem sectæ hominibus probare potuerunt, quales inter alios sunt Johannes Coccejus, & Balthasar Willius, ἐυρήματα pro re nata notarentur, ac ea omnia, quæ jam diximus, in censum venirent. Quibus vero Apparatus Biblici & προλεγομένων loco addenda erant, quæ hic ex commodo & usu tuo addita vel potius præmissa vides, LECTOR BENEVOLE. Te imprimis compello, qui S. Theologiæ Studiosus diceris. Quanquam nos omnes, quotquot S. literis vocamus, in hac quidem terrena universitate, sublimius nomen haud mereamur. Sumus enim & manemus studiosi solum literarum Sacrarum, dum hic sumus: nec evadimus Doctores, etsi Doctores dicamur. Semper enim nobis discendum est: Semper, quod discamus, in his literis occurrit; Scriptura, dicente Augustino l. XV. de Civ. DEI c. 25, & perterret superbientes, & excitat negligentes, & exercet quærentes, & alit intelligentes. Et sicut aromata, quod simile est S. Chrysostomi Hom. XIII. in Genes. quanto magis digitis teruntur, tanto majorem natura sua fragrantiam reddunt, ita & Scripturis usu venit, ut quanto quis illis est familiarior, tanto magis videre possit latentem in illis thesaurum, pluresque infallibilium divitiarum fructus. Tanta est, inquit iterum S. Augustinus Epist. III. ad Volus. Christianarum profunditas literarum, ut in eis quotidie proficerem, si eas solas ab ineunte pueritia usque ad decrepitam senectutem maximo otio, summo studio, meliori ingenio conarer addiscere: Non quod ad ea, quæ necessaria sunt saluti, tanta in eis perveniatur difficultate, sed cum quisque ibi fidem tenuerit, sine qua pie recteque non vivitur, tam multa, tamque multiplicibus mysteriorum umbraculis opaca intelligenda proficientibus restant, tantaque non solum in verbis, quibus ista dicta sunt, latet altitudo sapientiæ, ut annosissimis, acutissimis, flagrantissimis cupiditate dicendi hoc contingat, quod eadem Scriptura quodam loco habet: Cum consummaverit homo, tunc incipit. Si ergo ubique in omnibus rem definire non liceat, cogitandum est, quod multa in Scripturis ignoremus, & de multis valere oporteat illam S. Augustini regulam l. II. de doctr. Christ. c. 27. Quando ex ejusdem Scripturæ verbis non unum aliquod vel plura sentiuntur, etiamsi latet, quid senserit ille, qui scripserit, nihil periculi est, si quodlibet eorum congruere veritati ex aliis locis sanctarum Scripturarum doceri potest. De quo vero S. Augustinus l. XI. de civ. DEI. c. 33, opportune monet: Si voluntatem autoris indagare nequimus, à regula tamen fidei, quæ per alias ejusdem autoritatis sacras literas fidelibus nota est, non aberrabimus.

Diligentiam certe, si non tantam, quanta requiritur, non vulgarem tamen in plerisque adhibuimus. Petra enim est Scriptura, quæ non statim consvevit aquam doctrinæ fundere nisi aliquoties legendo, meditando, & orando eam percutiamus. Sed quum multa adeo requirantur ad Scripturæ indagationem, ecquis unus hic sibi arrogare ausit omnia? Attigit nonnulla S. Augustinus libr. III. de doctr. Christ. c. 1. Homo timens Deum, voluntatem ejus in Scripturis Sanctis diligenter inquirit. Et ne amet certamina pietate mansvetus, præmunitus etiam scientia linguarum, ne in verbis locutionibusque ignotis hæreat, præmunitus etiam cognitione quarundam rerum necessariarum, ne vim naturamve earum, quæ propter similitudinem adhibentur, ignoret, adjuvante etiam codicum veritate, quam solers emendationis diligentia procuravit, veniat ita instructus ad ambigua scripturarum discutienda atque solvenda. Basilius M. præfat. exposit. in Es. duo hæc expressit προσκείμενα. Puritatem nempe mentis & exercitationem diligentem: Vitæ, inquit, puritas requiritur, ut ad moralis virtutis exercitationem pertineat, quod in Scripturis obvolutum est, dijudicare. Requiritur autem præter vitæ puritatem assidua in Scripturis exercitatio, ut majestas, atque arcanum divinorum verborum perpetua meditatione animo imprimatur. Sed & observandum accurate, quod S. Hieronymus monuit in Matth. c. XXV. Prudentem, inquit, semper admoneo lectorem, ne superstitiosis acquiescat interpretationibus, & quæ commatice pro fingentium dicuntur arbitrio: sed consideret priora, media & sequentia, & nectat sibi universa quæ scripta sunt. Quam regulam posthabere solent hæretici, & qui Scripturas ad dogmata perversa detorquent, de quibus S. Irenæus elegantissime l. 1. c. 1. Ordinem quidem & textum Scripturarum supergradientes, & quantum in ipsis est solventes membra veritatis. Transferunt autem & transfigunt, & alterum ex altero facientes, seducunt multos ex iis, quæ aptant ex domi- nicis eloquiis male composito phantasmati. Quomodo si quis regis imaginem bonam fabrica- tam diligenter ex gemmis pretiosis à sapiente artifice, solvens subjacentem hominis figuram, transferat gemmas illas, & reformans faciat ex iis formam canis, vel vulpeculæ, & hanc ma- le dispositam dehinc conformet & dicat, hanc esse regis illam imaginem bonam, quam sapi- ens artifex fabricavit, ostendens gemmas, quæ bene quidem à primo artifice in regis imagi- ne compositæ erant, male verò à posteriore in canis figuram translatæ sunt, & per gemma- rum phantasiam decipiant idiotas, qui comprehensionem regalis formæ non habeant, & sua- deant, quoniam hæc turpis vulpeculæ figura, illa est bona Regis imago. Porro Chrysostomo in Genes. Hom. XIII. monente, ad ipsum Scripturæ scopum pertendamus oportet, quæ seipsam interpretatur. Sacra enim Scriptura cum nos quippiam docere vult, seipsam expo- nit, & auditorem errare non sinit. Vt enim absque fundamento imbecillis est ædificatio, ita nisi invento scopo Scriptura est inutilis, ut iterum habet Chrysostomus in Ps. II. De cætero pie suggerit S. Anshelmus in Epist. de fid. ad Urban. c. 2. Si quis potest intelligere, Deo gratias agat, si non potest, non immittat cornua ad ventilandum, sed submittat caput ad venerandum.

Quæ omnia, quamvis præ oculis fuerint semper, si tamen acu rem non semper attingere licuit, imperfectioni nostræ id adscribi peto, & curtæ suppellecti- li, quam non diffiteor, non vero voluntariæ aberrationi, & cum S. Augustino l. XV. de Trin. c. ult. precor:

DOMINE DEUS, quæcunque dixi de Tuo, agnoscant & tui; si quæ de meo, & tu ignosce, & tui.

ΕΥΦΗΜΙ'ΑΙ.

AJax ingenio fisus, ridensque precantes, Cur toties erret, noli mirarier: ipse Spiritus, oraculum qui protulit, hoc quoque solus Oranti solvit. Præfertur sic sapienti Parvulus. HUGONIS satis hoc monumenta docebunt, Noster ut exacte monstrat CALOVIUS. Ipsum Servet porro DEUS, quo vindicet atque recludat, Quicquid in obscuro fuit hactenus! o DEUS audi!

Ita Dresdæ apprecabatur MARTINUS GEJER, D.

In Fratris Charissimi DN. ABRAHAM CALOVI, S. S. TH. D. &c. &c. &c. BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA.

SI liber is vivet genium qui visus habere, Si venit Auctori fama labore sua, Traditur æternum queis Verbum, BIBLIA SACRA, Interitum timeant qua ratione sibi? CONDITOR est genii DEUS, AUCTOR & est Deus ipse, Sunt eadem genii Numine plena sui. Secula nec superent, nec fama perennet EORUM, Qui pro vera operam mente dedere DEI? Eruis hanc quanta solers indagine, quanto Illustras studio, dexteritate, fide? Næ genio victura sunt BIBLIA, vivet, Ipsa quoad vivent, & Tua fama simul. VIVE &, MI FRATER, veniant Tibi serius olim Fata, Tuus solito flumine eatque labor. Amplexu dulci prohibemur tractibus amplis Divisi, Affectus dissita corda ferit. PRÆGORIN hic fessus bibo, fortem Te juvat ALBIS, Hic & ibi, SANGUIS quem dedit, ardet AMOR.

Serenissimo PRINCIPI ELECTORI Brandenburgico a Consiliis FABIAN Kalaw vom Hofe/ Sen. sua mittit e Prussia V. Non Julii, CIO. IOC. LXXI.

## 1:1 Introduction: On the Portrait
ON THE PORTRAIT.

From the origin of CALOVIUS, where the victor knight, bound with the Pisan olive, will soon bear twelve-fold rewards, is this brow given in small bronze, VISTULA, PRÆGEL, ELBE, by which the renowned rivers carry a great name? F. K. v. H. S.

That he struck down the giant Goliath in a notable battle was a glory worthy of the great-souled David. As much as the Gittite surpassed all others in the bulk of his body, so much did Grotius surpass them in genius. Would it not, therefore, be a glory worthy of another David to drive this enemy from the holy camp? Our Abramus accomplishes this, and the victor brings back praise and honor greater than that great man from the enemy. Therefore, just as the grateful tribe of Judah once sang songs of victory for the brave deeds of the son of Jesse, now let the grateful Church likewise sing of the brave deeds of Abramus with joyful applause.

He acclaims the venerable and most celebrated theologian HAPPILY, and prays for many more victories for him over the enemies of the truth.

PHILIPPUS JACOBUS SPENERUS, Doctor, Pastor of the Church of Frankfurt-am-Main and Senior of the Ministry there.

Latin:

IN EFFIGIEM.

ORtu a CALOVII, Pisæa ubi vinctus oliva Mox bis-sena feret, præmia victor eques, Ære datur parvo hoc frons, VISTULA, PRÆGORIS, ALBIS Inclyta quo nomen flumina grande vehunt? F. K. v. H. S.

GOliathum insigni pugna stravifse gigantem, Gloria magnanimo digna Davide fuit. Quantum mole sui superavit corporis omnes Gethæus, tantum Grotius ingenio. Hunc ergo sanctis hostem depellere castris, Nonne Davide alio gloria digna foret? Præstat id Abramus noster, laudemque decusque Magno illo major victor ab hoste refert. Ergo ut Jessæi gratans Epinicia quondam Juda sui gestis fortibus accinuit. Nunc etiam Abrami lætis Ecclesia grata Plausibus haud aliter fortia facta canat.

Venerando & Celeberrimo Theologo FELICITER acclamat, & à veritatis hostibus multas adhuc victorias precatur

PHILIPPUS JACOBUS SPENERUS D. Pastor Eccles. Mœno-Francofurt. & Minist. ibi- dem Senior.

## 1:1 Introduction: On the Portrait
ON THE PORTRAIT.

You, whoever you are, who see the venerable face of the great CALOVIUS, which the learned hand of the artist has fashioned in bronze: believe that the ethereal Pallas hides herself in this countenance, believe that the whole goddess lies hidden beneath this brow: whether she brandishes certain spears against untamed enemies, or whether she is diligently occupied with divine books. She lies hidden in these spoils. If you desire to know her herself, turn the pages that you see lying written around. Here, because the sculptor could not represent the native [spirit] of the MAN, the Muse herself has revealed his glory with her pen.

Desiring that a monument of respect should exist for an incomparable theologian and teacher, [he] made [this].

SAMUEL BENEDICTUS CARPZOVIUS, Public Professor in the Academy of Wittenberg.

POEMS SENT LATE.

Let Rome boast of its Stone; that Cornelius is unequal to such a burden, a greater Abraham is present. Grotius senses this, he is lesser, we see greater things; nothing will be a busybody, but the polymath rejoices. Here wisdom is joined, and the sacred acumen of the man of Hippo; let fame speak of one work for all.

With these things I offer thanks to this most eminent theologian for his incomparable completed labor. Halle, Saxony. Johannes Olearius, D., Councilor of the Most Serene Duke of Saxony Augustus, Ecclesiastical Counselor, and General Superintendent.

)0(

Dedication, in which to the most Reverend, most Amplified, and most Excellent Lord, Dr. Abraham Calovius, a Theologian who has served and still serves the Church of Christ most excellently, Primary and most celebrated Professor in the renowned Wittenberg Academy, likewise most vigilant General Superintendent, etc., his Patron, Friend, Kinsman, and Brother most united in Christ, and most highly to be honored, concerning his Anti-Grotian labors, happily brought to an end and now being sent forth into the public light, from Rev. 3:12, in this manner:

While Calovius, standing with unbroken spirit and firm arms as an athlete, yielding to no battle thus far, strives to continue the holy wars with the new victorious arms of Jehovah, having fiercely attacked the Grotian entanglements and laboring to show the Fountain of Truth to the followers of Christ, and to spread the thrice-great Honor of Christ, as the head to be worshipped with a devoted mind: Truly the worthy victor deserves solid and ever-green praise; may he remain, flashing with splendor, who is a perennial pillar in the Temple of the Lord and King; from which the names of God may hang written for eternity; from which the celestial Glory, to be celebrated by the Word, may shine forth, fixedly impressed; at the same time for whom the Names of Christ may remain inscribed, who takes the Throne with the Father, after He redeemed us with His saving Death, from whence holy Joys flow in a beatific stream.

With a votive and sincere mind, Peter Haberkorn, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Public Professor, and Superintendent of Giessen, wished to offer congratulations.

To the most Reverend, Magnificent, and Excellent Lord Abraham Calovius, most deserving of the Church of Christ, Lord, Brother in Christ, and his most honored Patron, who is publishing the Biblia Illustrata.

It pleases you, Great Man, to have undertaken Herculean labors, by which divine glory and the republic grow. Long ago the Papist felt the arms of the victor, and the cohort of Calvin complained of wounds inflicted upon themselves; those who desire to join fighting Religions confess themselves prostrated by the sword of Calovius. The ambiguous Grotius introduced opaque shadows into Holy Scripture, which you dispel with a favorable star, and thus you fight the wars of JEHOVAH brilliantly. Peace follows wars, the beaked trophies receive the battle, and victorious garlands encircle your head; may you depart late to the heavens, and joyfully, while you are among fleeting things, may you happily teach the Youth; finally dismissed, may you enjoy the hoped-for peace!

Sent to Wittenberg from Altenburg on the 40th of March in the year 1662 by J. Christfried Sagittarius, Doctor in the Duchy of Altenburg, General Superintendent, First Court Preacher, and Assessor of the Consistory.

Bring forth, Calovius, the fires of your fruitful breast; thus the divine Work, which you explain well, radiates; thus, while we admire the other tasks of your praise, the Interpreter of sacred things has what he may contemplate; that Work will endure for every age, so I augur, and equal glory and honor will ennoble the same.

As a testimony of honor and observance, Balthasar Mentzer, Doctor, appended this.

GROTIUS was GREAT by name, and at the same time GREAT by omen, had he known how to keep his own sphere. But the Civil Doctor rushed into sacred orbs; thus GROTIUS is the LEAST in the kingdom of heaven. NO ONE WOULD HAVE LIVED EQUAL FROM APOSTOLIC TIMES, Slichting I (a) if there were any faith in his words: BUT A VERTUMNUS GREATER FROM APOSTOLIC TIMES HAS SCARCELY EXISTED IN APOSTOLIC RELIGION. Indeed, he disturbed the whole BIBLE with his filth, the source of which was purer than any river. Demonstrating this solidly to the world, GREAT CALOVIUS, you are GREATEST in pen and in spirit compared to GROTIUS. For the sake of observance and sincere protestation in the Catholic faith, I, JOH. AD. Scherzer, S. S. Theol. D. & Prof. Primar. Fac. Th. Senior, Canon of the noble Prelacy of Meissen, Assessor of the Electoral and Ducal Saxon Consistory, hastened this at Leipzig to my venerable Father and Patron in Christ, with a prayer for a long life and for the integrity of his bodily and mental powers.

A CERTAIN EPIGRAM Although it was consecrated to another writing thirty years ago, it seemed good to append it here because of the grateful memory of a Theologian and best Friend, now triumphing ἐν ἁγίοις, and the analogy of the work.

ABRAM CALOVIUS, most excellent Doctor, highest glory of the choir of holy Theologians: The Church of Christ fighting rightly praises you, and the Lyceums and the Thrones of the Pierides cherish you. How clearly it is evident that you have taught for many years with voice and pen, with zeal and vigilant care! And with what things you unfold the mysteries of the invincible Faith; and the clever and deadly deceits of heresy! The University of Rostock is a rich witness, which knows you privately and itself publicly! The Pregelan Lyceum speaks of this more, all things, with you teaching the holy Way for six years! The Pope Triumphed, Calvin, and Socinus himself, cannot have diminished your Praise! As they are to whom your divinely-inspired writings, which your genius produces with God breathing, are a most certain terror! Which give to the world the light of true Piety by the rule, and the same give endless cross to heretics! There was scarcely any work of our August Religion more useful, scarcely any more accurate! Therefore, continue to help the flock of Christ so dexterously, as you do, and rightly show the way of salvation! Endure and persist, CALOVIUS, for behold, He who gave you gifts will be about to give you the CROWN! Live, Doctor, for the Choir, remain and live as a survivor for the Forum, and live and fare well for a long time as a pillar for the Bed. M. ZACHARIAS L. KLINGIUS, a Swede from Närke, Candidate of S. S. Theology and student of the most illustrious Chancellor of the Kingdom of Sweden, later Doctor of S. S. Theology and finally Bishop of Strängnäs, wished to congratulate his best Teacher and Host at Königsberg and Danzig reverently with these lines.

Latin:

IN EFFIGIEM.

TU quisquis veneranda vides summi ora CALOVI, Quæ docta artificis finxit in ære manus: Crede, hoc ætheream se condere Pallada vultu, Fronte sub hac totam crede latere deam: Seu certa indomitos hastilia vibrat in hostes, Sedula divinis seu vacat illa libris. His latet exuviis. Ipsam si noscere gestis, Volvito, quæ circum scripta jacere vides. Hic, quia non poterat nativum sistere sculptor, Musa VIRI calamo prodidit ipsa decus.

Theologo ac præceptori incomparabili observantiæ monu- mentum extare cupiens f.

ABRAHAMO CALOVIO, Theologo de Ecclesia Christi optime merito & adhuc merenti, Professori in incly- ta Wittenbergensi Academia Primario & celeberrimo, Superintendenti itidem Generali Vigilantissimo, &c. Dn. Fautori, Amico, Affini, & Fratri suo in Christo uni- tiffimo, & perquam Honorando, De laboribus Anti Grotianis, feliciter ad finem perductis & nunc in lucem publicam emittendis Ex Apoc. III. vers. 12. Hunc in modum:

DUm sacra bella novis Jhovæ victricibus armis, Stans animo infracto, & firmis Athleta lacertis, Haud pugnæ cedens huc usque Calovius ulli, Continuare studet, Grotianas acer adortus Tricas, & Veri Fontem monstrare laborat Christicolis, ac ter magnum diffundere Honorem Christi, ceu capitis devota mente colendi: Næ solidam laudem semper viridemque meretur Victor condignus; maneat splendore corusca Qui in Templo Domini Regisque columna perenni; Nomina scripta Dei de qua pendantur in ævum; Ex qua cœlestis celebranda reluceat Verbis Gloria, fixe impressa; simul cui Nomina Christi Permaneant inscripta, Thronum capientis Eundem Cum Patre, salvifica postquam nos Morte redemit, Unde beatifico manant sacra Gaudiarivo.

Votivo & candido animo gratulari volebat PETRUS Haberkorn, S. Theol. D. Prof. P. & Superint. Gissensis.

Ad VIRUM Maxime Reverendum, Magnificum & Excellentissimum Dn. ABRAHAMUM CALOVIUM, de Ecclesia Christi bene merentissi- mum, Dominum, in Christo Fratrem, atque Fautorem suum colendiss. BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA edentem.

HErculeos, Vir Magne, placet subiisse labores, Gloria quis divina, quibus respublica crescit. Jamdudum Victoris senserat arma Papæus, Calvinique cohors questa est sibi vulnera fixa, Pugnantes qui optant conjungere Relligiones, CALOVII sese prostratos ense fatentur. Grotius ambiguus tenebras induxit opacas Scripturæ sacræ, quas pellis sidere fausto, Et sic præclare depugnas bella JEHOVÆ. Bella quies sequitur, pugnam rostrata trophæa Excipiunt, cinguntque caput victricia serta, In cœlos abeas serus, lætusque caducis Interfis rebus, felix doceasque Juventam; Dimissus tandem sperata pace fruaris!

Wittebergam Alteburgo XL. Martiis Anno cIɔ. Iɔc. LXII. missum à J. CHRISTFRIED SAGITTARIO, D. in Ducatu Alteburg. Superint. Gener. Concion. aulic. prim. & Consistor. Assessore.

PRome Tuos CALOVI fœcundi pectoris ignes, Sic radiat Dium, quod bene pandis, Opus; Sic, dum pensa Tuæ miramur cætera laudis, Sacrorum Interpres, quæ meditetur, habet, Ætatem feret illud Opus, sic auguror, omnem, Gloria parque decus nobilitabit idem.

Honoris & observantiæ test. app. BALTHASAR MENTZERUS D.

NOmine MAGNUS erat GROTIUS, simul omine MAGNUS, Scivisset sphæram si retinere suam. Irruit ast sacros Doctor Civilis in orbes, Cœlorum in regno sic MINIMUS GROTIUS. PAR AB APOSTOLICO VIXISSET TEMPORE NEMO, Slichting I (a) verbis si foret ulla fides: AST AB APOSTOLICO VERTUMNUS TEMPORE MAJOR VIX IN APOSTOLICA RELLIGIONE FUIT. Imo tota suo turbavit BIBLIA cæno, Quorum fons omni purior amne fuit. Hoc orbi solide demonstrans, MAGNE CALOVI, Præ GROTIO es calamo MAXIMUS, ac animo. Observantiæ, ac sinceræ, in Catholica fide, contestationis ergo, meo in Christo Patri ac Patrono venerando, cum voto prolixæ vitæ, & in- tegrarum corporis animique virium deproperabam Lipsiæ JOH. AD.
