Scherzer, S. S. Theol. D. & Prof. Primar. Fac. Th. Senior, Ingenui Præsulatus Misn. Canonicus, Consistorii Electoral. & Ducal. Saxon. Assessor.

EPIGRAMMA QVODDAM Etsi alii Scripto ante triginta ipsos annos consecratum, ob Theologi & Amici optimi, jam ἐν ἁγίοις triumphantis, gratam memoriam, ope- risque analogiam, his subjungere visum fuit.

ABRAM CALOVI Præcellentissime Doctor, Sancti Theologum, Gloria summa, Chori: Te merito Christi pugnans Ecclesia laudat, Teque Lycea colunt, Pieridumque Throni. Quæ voce, & calamo, zelo, & cura vigilante, Annos per multos Te docuisse patet! Et quibus invictæ Fidei mysteria pandis; Hæresis argutos mortiferosque dolos! Est testis locuples Academia Rostochiensis, Quæ Te privatim novit, & ipsa palam! Hæc magis eloquitur Pregelanum, cuncta, Lyceum, Sexenni sanctam Te profitente Viam! Papa Triumphatus, Calvinus, & Ipse Socinus, Non possunt Laudem diminuisse tuam! Utpote queis terror certissimus Enthea scripta, Quæ parit ingenium, Numine flante, tuum! Orbi quæ lumen veræ Pietatis Amussim, Hæreticis eadem dant sine fine crucem! Vix fuit utilius, vix accuratius ullum, Augustæ nostræ Religionis opus! Ergo Gregem Christi fic dextre perge juvare, Ut facis, & monstra rite salutis iter! Perfer & obdura CALOVI, namque CORONAM, Ecce daturus erit, qui Tibi dona dedit! Vive Choro Doctor, remaneto Foroque superstes, Atque Toro columen vive valeque diu. Regiomonti, ac Gedani Præceptori & Hospiti suo Optimo, hisce reverenter gratulari voluit M. ZACHARIAS L. KLINGIUS, Nericius Svecus, S. S. Theol. Cand. & Illustrissimi R. Svec. Cancellarii Alumnus, Postea S. S. Theol. Doctor & denique Episcopus Strignicensis.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface to the Books
PREFACE TO THE BOOKS

Those who have interpreted the Holy Scriptures have for the most part prefixed some prolegomena concerning Holy Scripture and its interpretation, and certain things necessary for the same. But because we have already dispatched such things in other writings, lest we do what is already done, it pleases us here to digest the same as if in a miscellany, and to refer to the writings hitherto published most of the things which need to be advised in advance. For almost entire volumes would have to be repeated if all those things which might be read here with utility were transcribed here with the same diligence. These, however, are the things which chiefly come to be tasted beforehand: I. The names of the Holy Code: such as these generally occur: τὰ Βιβλία, or Biblia, among the Greeks and Latins, ספר יהוה the book of the Lord, Isa. 36:16. ἡ γραφή Scripture, 2 Tim. 3:16, and τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα v. 15. מקרא Reading Neh. 8:8. תורה Doctrine Psalm 19 and 119. מגלה volume Psalm 40:8. and among the Hebrews מקדש sanctuary, among Christians the Old and New Testament; concerning all of which see the Commentary on Genesis in the Prolegomena, ch. 1, following.

II. Divine authority, which Holy Scripture has not from the Church, but from divine inspiration, which we asserted against the Papists in the Sacred Critic, p. 274, following; in the System of Theology, Vol. I, part 458, 583, following; whence Scripture is truly ἀξιόπιστος, and αὐτόπιστος, to which one must simply believe on account of itself, not on account of the Church, as shown in the System of Theology, p. 600; and indeed αὐτόπιστος both simply, so that for that reason alone, because Scripture asserts something, faith is owed to it; and in all things, whatsoever are in any way held in Scripture, whether they pertain to saving faith or not, as demonstrated in the same place, p. 604, 606.

III. Θεοπνευστία (God-breathedness), that the letters, syllables, and words and the whole context in the Holy Scriptures are of divine origin, not only the sense of Scripture: concerning which see the same place, p. 554, 561.

IV. The perfection of Holy Scripture regarding all things necessary to be known and believed for salvation delivered in it, asserted p. 467, 609.

V. The perspicuity of Scripture, and its faculty of interpreting itself is asserted p. 467, 469, 630, following.

VI. Normal use, and judicial power, that Holy Scripture is the sole norm and judge of religious controversies is proven p. 467. 681. et seqq.

VII. Canon of Scripture: concerning which in Genesis p. 3. Critico S. p. 234. et seqq. and the distinction of Canonical books from Apocryphal T. I. Syst. Theol. p. 92. sqq. p. 778.

VIII. Integrity and perpetual preservation of the Canon of Scripture, Syst. Theol. T. I, p. 482. 718. Comm. in Gen. p. 18. et seqq.

IX. Scope and end of Holy Scripture, saving instruction, conversion, sanctification, and eternal salvation, as also

the intrinsic power and efficacy of Scripture for producing these effects, T. I. Syst. p. 454. 478. 692. et seqq.

X. Object of Scripture to whom, which are all men, to whom it is granted without distinction of status or sex, and therefore it is to be permitted to be read by all, as an Epistle of God Almighty sent to all, V. Syst. Theol. T. I. p. 457. 643. et seqq. Whence it is in itself by no means harmful, but useful, nay even necessary, that Scripture be translated into vulgar languages, concerning which see l. c. p. 650.

XI. The object of Scripture, ὗ, or that for whose sake all things are delivered in the Scriptures, is Christ, the end of the Law, Romans 10:4, and the kernel of the Gospel, John 20:31, to whom as to a goal and center all things in the Holy Literature of the Old and New Testament are referred, Psalm 40:8, John 5:39, Acts 13:19, 24, ch. 10:43, Hebrews 10:5, seq., and who is the Epitome and Sum of the entire Scripture, Isaiah 53, Jeremiah 23:6, ch. 33:15, 1 Corinthians 2:2, Galatians 3:21, ch. 6:13, 2 Timothy 3:15, to whom the Sum of the whole Holy Scripture is to be referred, namely of the books of the Old and New Testament, prefixed to the Zurich Bibles, and those edited by Robert Stephanus under the name of Vatablus.

XII. Distribution of Holy Scripture into Old and New Testament, concerning which see Volume I of the System of Theology, p. 492, seqq.

Furthermore, how the books are called τῆς διαθήκης or Testament, whether Old or New, has been explained at the beginning of the annotations on the New Testament on Matthew, against Grotius: Namely, not in the sense in which διαθήκη denotes law, as not only Papists call the New Testament a new law, but also the Jews תוֹרָה חֲדָשָׁה, because no new or other moral laws were delivered in the New Testament than in the Old, as indeed

the Socinians and Pontificians contend, and the Jews are accustomed to cavil: nor in that sense only, in which it is generally called a Testament, by which someone makes his will known, especially that by which a certain collection of goods is conferred upon someone, so that no relation to a properly called Testament is introduced: but in the special meaning of the word, which the Apostle urges, Hebrews 9:17, because it exhibits the evangelical will of Christ the Testator concerning the remission of sins, grace, and salvation, both sanctioned and confirmed by the death of the testator himself, which is proposed not only in the books of the New Testament, but also in the books of the Old Testament. Compare Acts 15:10, 2 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 13:8, Revelation 13:18. Therefore it is called the Old and New Testament from 2 Corinthians 3:14, not because there are two different Testaments properly so called, because as there is a single testator, a single inheritance, so there is a single Testament, since the inheritance of eternal salvation and those spiritual and heavenly legacies which Christ the testator himself acquired for us by his death have been sanctioned in Christ: nor are they called two because of the very matter of the saving doctrine being one and then another; but because of the different manner of delivering this matter, as we explained in the place cited. meanwhile it is not incorrectly asserted that the books of the Old Testament are so named because they contain most things pertaining to the legal covenant: but the New [Testament], because most things pertain to the Evangelical covenant, since the former are occupied for the most part with the antecedents, concomitants, and consequents of the old legal covenant, while the latter are occupied with the history of the New covenant and matters pertaining thereto. In which sense the German Preface of the blessed Luther to the books of the Old Testament explains it. Yet the Testament properly so called remains unique, as far as concerns the matter, contents, testator, legacies, inheritance, and indeed the object, or the heirs constituted, who are the faithful, and the condition, if we may so speak, of entering upon the inheritance, which is but one: faith in Christ the Testator: even if the mode of proposing it is different in the books which we call the Old Testament. and in the books of the New Testament, because in this not only the Testator and the legacies and the condition of entering upon the inheritance are described and expressed more clearly and lucidly, but also the mode by which that inheritance was procured for us, namely through the obedience of the Testator himself, both active and passive, and the history of that obedience and satisfaction, i.e., the life and death of Christ, is distinctly, orderly, and most lucidly set forth, which in those [books] was partly only predicted by Prophetic oracles and partly prefigured by types, in the knowledge of which, however, that faith is situated which is required for entering upon the inheritance. Add that something peculiar occurs in that divine disposition and dispensation, which has been historically set forth and frequently inculcated by Moses and the Prophets, described with certain limits, distinct from that disposition and dispensation which is both historically described by the Evangelists and Apostles and, indeed, primarily set forth more lucidly. In which manner our Theologians distinguish between religion itself or faith and the doctrine which is about Christ the Testator and his legacies, comprised in both Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture, and which was one and the same at all times, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13:8, and between the divine disposition, which, concerning the dispensation of that religion, was one thing or another according to the diversity of times by divine good pleasure, which is called a Testament in the general signification of the word, yet not without reflection upon those things which pertain to a testament properly so called. For thus they say that a Testament is nothing other than a divine disposition concerning the legitimate dispensation of religion itself and the government of the people of God, or the Church, instituted to the end that it might be contained within a certain Polity distinct from all peoples: in which sense the O.T. is that ancient solemn disposition by which God, after the Israelite people were led out of Egypt, delivered to them amidst thunders and lightnings the entire administration of both religion and Polity, described in a certain form of constitution, on Mount Sinai: concerning which the books of Moses and the Prophets are occupied, and are called the books of the O. Testament. But the New Testament is a new and solemn disposition by which God, the former Old Testament having been abrogated, announced to his people the universal promulgation of the Gospel and its most clear propagation into the whole world from Zion and Jerusalem, and instituted and ordained a new administration of Evangelical doctrine through two Sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Concerning which the Evangelical and Apostolic books are occupied, and thus the books are called those of the New Testament.

But since in that divine disposition the Gospel and the Evangelical covenant, which also has the nature of a Testament properly so called, is contained as the chief κειμήλιον, therefore the notion of neither the pact or covenant, nor of the Testament properly so called, is to be entirely sequestered or excluded here, especially because Scripture itself, when it speaks not indeed of the Prophetic and Apostolic books, but of the twofold divine covenant, old and new, Jerem. XXXI:31 seqq., 2 Cor. II:8, describes it in such a way that it comprises in the former the legal pact, entered into on Mount Sinai between God and the Israelite people, which under the condition of perfect obedience promises temporal and eternal goods, denouncing punishment to the disobedient in this and the future age, and was dedicated with the blood of bulls and calves: but in the latter (i.e., the new Covenant) it comprises at the same time the gracious pact of the remission of sins, of righteousness, and of eternal life in Christ, by whose death it was both acquired and confirmed. Although the books of Moses and the Prophets are for the most part occupied with the legal covenant, and the Evangelical and Apostolic books with the Evangelical one, and for that reason the books are called by some those of the Old and New Covenant, yet that explanation is without doubt more accurate and fuller, by which the Old Testament designates not so much the law itself and the legal covenant, as that divine dispensation concerning the arrangement of the religion and polity of the Israelite people: the New signifies not the covenant of grace itself, but the divine dispensation concerning the new administration and promulgation of the Evangelical doctrine throughout the whole world, sanctioned by new sacraments. Because as the legal covenant, so also the covenant of grace is the same and immutable, nor can it partake of the nature of oldness or newness: nor has the legal covenant been antiqued, but rather it had need of the fulfillment of the same performed by Christ, which can by no means be held for abrogation or antiquation. Therefore, in order that the nature of Oldness and Newness in those two Testaments, which the holy Apostle so strongly urges from Jeremiah ch. XXXI, 31, Heb. 8, 6, ch. 9, 15, ch. 7, 22, ch. 12, 24, and Gal. 4, 24, 2 Cor. 3, 6, may be clear, it must be observed that, just as the Jewish people was other and plainly different from the Christian people, so God by a most wise counsel willed that there be one dispensation of religion and another of the form of polity itself among the Jewish people, whom He had then chosen before all peoples, Deut. 7, 6, and had enclosed in a certain ecclesiastical, civil, and economic polity, which would endure so long as a new face of the ages should approach, namely that, when the Messiah having been exhibited in the flesh, that polity having been abrogated, He would introduce another form and polity of living and acting. And this is the solid foundation, as the blessed Hutter learnedly teaches in the cited passages, from which the diversity of the two Testaments, distinct in appearance, emerges and depends, indeed in such a way that the former is called the Old, but the latter the New Testament. That Old one did not have the image of the things itself, or the future goods, but only the shadow or type, Heb. X, 1. The New one, however, has the body itself, Christ, Col. II, 17. The Old, by reason of the law, whose solemn promulgation was the chief part of the O.T., was inscribed on tables of stone: the New, however, by reason of the Gospel, whose universal preaching is likewise the primary part of the N.T., is written in the hearts of men, Jerem. 31, 34, 2 Cor. 3, 6. That old Mosaic polity was in itself most burdensome, since it consisted of almost infinite rites and ceremonies, serving chiefly for restraining and curbing the old man; but this public and universal and most clear promulgation of the Gospel contributes most to the forming of the new man. Since, therefore, the Old and New covenant and pact are comprehended in both these dispensations in a certain respect, although it is not the Old or New covenant or pact itself, the same is called both a federal and a testamentary dispensation. Nor is such a dispensation improperly called a testament, by which it is provided by the Testator, in what way to the heirs, in what order, with what distinction by the will of the Testator goods ought to come: Wherefore this arrangement also, by which God, in the cause of the heavenly inheritance, instituted a different mode of religion for the diversity of peoples and times according to the counsel of divine wisdom, although the doctrine of salvation is always the same, is not undeservedly called a Testament, nor quite improperly. Moreover, the tables of the Testament, or federal ones, which are the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, come under the name of the Old and New Testament by metonymy 2 Cor. 3, 14. just as the promise made to Abraham is called a Testament synecdochically: because it is a part of the covenant comprised in the Testament, Gal. 3, 17. as also is circumcision Acts 7, 8.

Lyranus distinguishes the Old and New Testament in such a way that the former is principally about God as Creator and governor, the latter about God as redeemer and glorifier. But neither is the benefit of redemption and glorification passed over in silence in the O. T., or, as not a few Scholastics wish, only implicitly revealed, nor is the treatment of the work of divine creation and governance interrupted in the N. T. Such distinctions are dangerous, as has been established by the disputes of subsequent times, although this dichotomy seems to have been handed down by the author in no bad sense. St. Augustine and other ancients more correctly say that the Old Testament deals with Christ to be exhibited, the New with Christ exhibited, and that the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

XIII. The authentic dignity, which belongs only to the Hebrew text in the O. T. and the Greek in the N. T.: concerning which see Syst. Theol. Vol. I. p. 485. Because, namely, the Hebrew text alone in the O. T. is θεόπνευστος, which God employed, inasmuch as He spoke to the Israelite people in Hebrew through the Prophets, with the exception only of those places where there was need for the Chaldean language, such as when Laban named the heap of witness in his own language, Gen. 31, 47. when Jeremiah warned what the Jews ought to answer the Chaldeans soliciting them to idolatry c. X, 11. and in the books written after the Babylonian captivity, when the letters or speeches of the Chaldeans are reported in their own language c. IV. Ezra v. 8. up to c. VI, 19. and c. VII, 10. up to v. 27. as well as Dan. II 4. up to the end of c. VII. We have explained more prolixly the causes of the Hebrew language being employed in the O. T. in Crit. Sacr. p. 311. because it was consecrated to the Old Testament on account of its antiquity, dignity, the end of the Scripture of the O. T., the condition of the Prophets, and the nature of the language, which is most divine, the matrix of all others, most natural, purest, most luminous, and most eminent in the praise of the propriety of speech and the expression of all things: where we have also discoursed more fully concerning Chaldean words, and Chaldaisms and Arabisms, as well as Egyptian, Persian, and Greek words in the O. T.: and also concerning the original text of the N. T., why the Greek was employed, and that the Greek text is entirely authentic in all books of the N. T. page 439. as also concerning the Hellenistic idiom, p. 452. seqq.

XIV. The versions of Holy Scripture were dealt with in Vol. I. of Syst. Theol. p. 485. seqq. and in Comment. in Genes. prol. cap. VII, p. 26.

Moreover, it must still be said primarily concerning the versions of the whole Scripture, both Latin and German. Among the Latin ones, the Vulgate stands out on account of its antiquity and authority in the Church. Which name, however, is ambiguous: for formerly the Vulgate was called a certain ancient Latin version of uncertain authorship translated from the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters as far as the O. T. is concerned, which Augustine called the Itala, and Jerome called the Vulgate. But now the Vulgate is called that which is translated from the Hebrew text and ascribed to Jerome: which we always designate by this name absolutely, the former one being now lost. Erasmus, however, amended it in the N. T. in many places according to the Greek truth, with the permission of Leo X. Another version made from the sources is that of Sebastian Münster, published in the year 1525, 34, 39, and 46, which Matthew Poole acknowledges was made with no common learning and the highest acumen, and that the Hebrew is rendered in it very faithfully in most places, and no less perspicuously. Moreover, the amendment of the Vulgate was undertaken among the Pontificians in the year 1540 by Isidorus Clarius, Bishop of Foligno, according to the Hebrew and Greek truth: concerning whom see Possevinus in Appar. in the third part; to which Clarius, Matthew Poole in the preface to Synops. Crit. p. 2, attributes the eulogy of a lazy and manifest plagiarist, who for the most part copied not only the sentiments but even the very individual words from Münster, so much so that if he had lived in that Republic where, with impunity granted to ingenious thieves, the penalty of death was established only for the unskilled and lazy, he would undoubtedly have been condemned to the gallows. Then among our own, as will be said later, Lucas Osiander. Which therefore can be held as a Fourth Latin version, even though it is not new, but likewise recalls the Vulgate to the norm of the Original text. The fifth, therefore, is that of Sante Pagnini of Lucca, of the Order of Preachers, published in the year 1528, whom Sixtus of Siena calls a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and most skilled in the three languages, but especially in Hebrew, and testifies that, with Leo X encouraging and providing the expenses, he gave the whole O. T. to the Latin tongue from the Hebrew truth with the greatest diligence and fidelity he could, and with no less praise translated the N. T. according to the Greek faith, which work he dedicated to Clement VIII. The theologians of Louvain commend that version as most convenient, as do the Parisians in the Royal Bibles, as excelling all (the Vulgate excepted) both in the purity of speech and in the propriety of words, sought with discernment from the very sources, Laurentius Beyerlingk in the preface to Bibl. var. Interpret. Our B. Franzius in De Interp. Script. declares it to be held by solidly learned and pious men as a thousand times dearer and more certain than the old (Vulgate). Matthew Polus says that almost all learned men agree that that version, in which that great man labored for more or less 25 years, is most literal, as far as could conveniently be done, faithful, and prepared with singular judgment and skill. Regarding Munster and Pagninus, B. Luther, in Vol. VIII of the Jena German edition, on the Schem-hamphor, judges thus toward the end: That those two men, Sanctes and Munster, translated the Bible with incredible study and inimitable diligence, and did much good with it, but the Rabbis were somewhat too powerful for them, so that they also failed in the Analogy of faith, and hung too much upon the glosses of the Rabbis. The sixth is that of Benedict Arias Montanus of Seville, although it is not a new version, because he merely transferred Pagninus's edition into an interlinear Bible and amended it according to the language of the sources, with his own version in the places he corrected written in small letters, and Pagninus's relegated to the margin, which was also done in the New Testament with the words of the Vulgate retained or amended: regarding which version, both the preface of Montanus and also that of our father-in-law, the learned Dr. Hulsemann, prefixed to the new Leipzig edition, should be compared. Matthew Polus, however, criticizes Montanus, along with some others, because he rashly moved Pagninus's version from its place and replaced Pagninus's good words with his own corrupt, inept, and barbarous vocabulary. But Brian Walton's judgment in the preface to his English work is different. regarding this version, that although it may seem somewhere barbarous and not to express the sense as conveniently as Pagninus, it may nevertheless deserve pardon in this, that he changed Pagninus's version for the use of beginners, not for the elegance of the Latin language, but to express the force of the Hebrew word. The seventh is called the Tigurine version, which at Zurich in Switzerland by LEO JUDA was begun, and completed up to the last eight chapters of Ezekiel, the whole of Daniel, the book of Job, the last 40 Psalms, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, continued by Theodor Bibliander and Conrad Pellican, finished by Peter Cholin and Rudolf Gualther, published at Zurich in the year 1544. The latter (Cholin and Gualther) at least interpolated the Erasmian version of the New Testament and recalled it in their own way to the Greek text: Cholin also translated the Apocryphal books. Afterwards, with the names of the authors suppressed not without cause, it was published by Robert Estienne in the year 1545 at Paris, with the addition of the Vulgate Latin version and the Annotations of François Vatable: and again in the same place in the year 1547, with the annotations of both Sante Pagnini and Vatable, which Bertin had taken down from his own mouth, the New Testament, with the addition of Beza's interpretation with the Author's Notes: upon which John Bois at London in the year 1655 published a collation with the old (Vulgate) interpreter on the four Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles, and attempted to prove that it departed from the Old without just cause, unlike other more recent ones. But which version was subsequently published by the Papists at Lyons in the year 1584 under the name of Franc. Vatable, even though he is not the author of the translation, as Genebrard acknowledges in book IV of his Chronology and Possevin in his Apparatus, and as De Thou teaches in book XXXVI for the year 1564, as also at Salamanca in only four places, and those indeed slightly changed (which Matthew Poole claims to have learned from a most learned man who compared both editions with each other, vehemently commending it for its erudition, judgment, faithful interpretation of the sense, and likewise for the propriety and purity of its language). The Reformed also published at Hanau in the year 1605 that old and New translation with the Annotations of Franc. Vatable, just as it had first appeared at Paris in the year 1545. However, there are held in the Wolfenbüttel Library under the name of Fr. Vatable Bibles already published at Lyons in the years 1515, 1518, and also 1528.

The eighth version is that of Sebastian Castellio at Basel in the year 1545, whom De Thou, however, observes in book XXXVI for the year 1563 to be a man who brought impure hands to the handling of sacred things and was most unprepared in matters necessary for such a great work, and whom Sixtus of Siena criticizes in book VIII of his Bibliotheca Sancta, because he suffers nothing that smacks of Hebraism, nor does he think he speaks truly in Latin unless he speaks most effeminately, and, devoid of all the majesty of divine Scripture, paints every single sentence with makeup in the manner of harlots and curls them with curling irons, luxuriating in a certain wanton abundance of soft words. Senensis illustrates this with examples brought forward. Yet Matthew Poole affirms that the sense is expressed clearly, purely, elegantly, and faithfully in that version in very many places, and that great difficulties are not rarely solved happily by it, led no doubt by his own experience.

The ninth is that of Immanuel Tremellius, a converted Jew, and Francis Junius, first published in the year 1574, and afterwards set forth by the care of Junius in a second, third, and even fourth edition, and illustrated with various annotations both for explaining Hebraisms and for elucidating the text. In the New Testament, however, Tremellius translated only the Syriac version into the Latin language, with that Greek translation of the text retained which Theodore Beza adorned, with annotations added from both Beza, Junius, and Loselerius Villerius from the larger annotations of Beza, and notes of Joach. Camerarius excerpted, as well as those of Joh. Cherpuntius and others. If the Calvinists in Belgium had approved of this version, they would not have departed from it so much in their own new version, which is to be observed in countless places. Not to mention anything about the overly Hebraizing language and about the many words inserted into the text too boldly for the sake of supplying the sense. Rivetus noted excessive license and liberty in this translation. Leusden says it was conformed more to the elegance of Latinity than to an accurate agreement with the original text in his Philologus Hebræo-Græcus, p. 66, the contrary of which, however, seems rather to be said. I would not, however, approve the censure of Joh. Drusius, which could be approved by neither Gomarus nor Fullon, passed upon his Francis Junius. As he had learned these letters (Hebrew) most unhappily, so he taught them most unhappily. His learned writings deserved something else and a kinder judgment. But to grammaticasters, to mark that kind of men with a barbarous word (for Drusius was a pure and simple grammarian), all things are permitted. Matthew Poole teaches that that version was received with great applause of the Reformed Churches, both from the judgments of famous men and from its many editions, although he burdens it with excessive praises more than he adorns it. Which Piscator first used, with his own Scholia added, and many things corrected not without judgment and handed down more clearly, but afterwards he observes that he adorned a new one, printed at Herborn in the year 1646.

But we shall speak of the work of Piscator later. We add here only the judgment of Poole concerning the English and French version: The French, he says, which is also called the Genevan by Louis de Dieu and others, because it was made by the Genevan Pastors around the year of the Lord (if I am not mistaken) 1560. But that version has no small praise for doctrine, judgment, and faith. Concerning the English, however: I understand and follow here that which was prepared by the order of the most Serene and most Learned King JAMES, but by the counsel and labors of Bishops and other learned men chosen for this work, in the year of the Lord 1611, in which occur many specimens of great erudition and skill in the original languages, and of acumen and judgment more than ordinary; and which was to me not rarely of the greatest help and use in the most difficult texts.

Germanic versions before Dr. Luther's translation were adorned with a less elegant idiom, such as those which appeared at Augsburg in the year 1447, as also in the year 1477, at Nuremberg in the year 1477 and in the year 1483, and also at Lübeck in the year 1494, and again at Augsburg in the year 1518. Which last copy I possess. So that it may be clear what the idiom is like, and a comparison with Luther's version can be made, I shall excerpt one or two passages: Gen. 3, 15. She will crush your head, and you will secretly bear envy to her footprint, v. 16. I will multiply your misery, and your conception, c. 8, 21. The LORD tastes the taste of sweetness. Ex. 34, 29. and he knew not that his face was horned by reason of the fellowship of the word of GOD (exactly as in the Vulgate, and he did not know that his face was horned from the fellowship of the word of the Lord) Ps. 1, 1. Blessed is the man who did not depart in the counsel of the ungodly: and did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the chair of pestilence. But his will is in the law of the LORD: and in his law he will meditate day and night. To the second Psalm this summary is prefixed, by which the genuine sense concerning Christ is plainly overturned: David makes this Psalm, when he was to fight against Amalek, and against the heathen Philistines. V. 1. it is rendered thus: Why do the heathen grumble, and the peoples have meditated vain things. v. last. So his anger burns in a short time, they are all blessed who trust in him. Similarly the meaning of the eighth Psalm is perverted by the prefixed argument: David makes this Psalm, and it was sung by the prophets, whom David consecrated, to the honor of GOD. Psalm 23 is referred to in the Summary to David's inauguration in Hebron. The first verse is rendered thus: The LORD rules me, and I lack nothing, and in the place of the pasture there he has grasped me. He has led me upon the water of restoration. v. 7. you have fattened my head with oil, and my cup makes me drunk as pure as it is. However, the Summaries interpret many Psalms concerning Christ, which are commonly not explained in that way by the Papists, as we shall perhaps mention in their proper place. Michael Beringer, J.U.D. and Professor of the Hebrew language in the Academy of Tübingen, in the Rescue of the German Biblical Translation of Dr. Martin Luther, brought forward an ancient German version, and from its comparison with the version of the blessed Luther, he taught how highly this is esteemed: p. 62. This first verse (Ps. 1.) I find translated in an old Psalter thus: Blessed is the man who has not walked the way of the ungentle, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the master-seat of the scoundrels. From which it is not difficult to gather that not only years ago the Psalter, indeed the whole Bible, was so poorly translated that almost neither German, nor Hebrew, nor Greek remained much in it, but also how much more blessed our time is. For the faithful GOD has let a truly German, understandable translation of his holy Bible happen to us Germans through Dr. Luther, as a German Cicero. And this version of our blessed Luther, not like other German versions from the Latin Vulgate translation, such as is also that of Joh. Dietenberger, and the German translation of Caspar Ullenberger, as also the German version produced in the year 1661 by the authority of the Elector of Mainz and the work of certain Jesuits, which although it flows more purely as regards the German idiom than others approved by the Papists, yet it is not adorned from anything but the Latin Vulgate text, but was undertaken from the authentic and original text itself: and therefore it appeared first in parts: And indeed the translation of the New Testament published here in Wittenberg in folio is in the German language in the year 1522, but in the year 1523 in the idiom proper to Lower Saxony. In which he used the work of Phil. Melanchthon at the same time, concerning whom let Epist. I to Camerarius be consulted. In the year 1524 it appeared in this place in quarto, illuminated, as they call it. In the year 1528 it was published in Wittenberg in the idiom of both Saxonies, namely the upper and the lower. The German N.T. also appeared in Basel in the year 1523 in quarto, in Augsburg in the year 1524. & in Strasbourg in the year 1527 in folio. In Dresden in the year 1527 in folio. But that the Dresden copy did not appear under Luther's name, indeed by the order of the Prince prefixed to the same, Luther's translation was forbidden, but this one was commended; although this itself was Luther's translation: concerning which the blessed Luther in the year 1530, Tom. V. Jen. Germ. in the Ep. on Translating p. 141. We have indeed seen the scribbler at Dresden, who has mastered my New Testament, (I will no longer name his name in my books, for he now has his judge, and is otherwise well known) who confesses that my German is sweet and good, and saw well that he could not do it better, and yet wanted to bring it to shame, went ahead, and took my New Testament, almost word for word, as I have made it, and took my preface, gloss, and name away from it, wrote his name, preface, and gloss to it, and thus sells my New Testament under his name. When, dear children, how it pained me then, when his territorial Prince with a horrible preface condemned and forbade reading Luther's New Testament, which is yet the very same that Luther made. The author was Hieronymus Emser the Swabian: whom therefore how rashly Anton. Possevinus in Appar. under the Title Bible, that passage of the blessed Luther, and the collation itself, showing the plagiarism of the man clearly, will teach. What Possevinus says, that this Bock Emser, as he is wont to be called by the blessed Luther, observed three hundred depravations of Luther in the N.T., concerning that Megalander replied in a few words, but sufficiently, in the l.c.: Take both Testaments before you / Luther's and the scribbler's / hold them against each other / then you will see / who in both is the translator / for what he has patched and changed in a few places, (although not everything pleases me) so I can still well tolerate it, and it harms me especially nothing / as far as it concerns the text / therefore I have also never wanted to write against it / but have had to laugh at the great wisdom / that one has so horribly blasphemed, condemned, and forbidden my New Testament / because it has gone out under my name: But yet they must read it, because it has gone out under another's name,

As for the Old Testament, he published the Pentateuch in Wittenberg in the year 1523, and the second part, containing the Historical books, and the third, the Poetical, he published in Wittenberg in 1524, fortified with the seal of his customary symbol: yet the Psalter of David tastes of Hebraisms in many places, which he later adapted more to the German idiom in a revision, he published Isaiah here in the year 1529, but in the year 1523 he published all the Prophets in German in this place by the types of Joh. Lufft, of which translation and edition I have some pages written by the hand of the blessed Luther, and by comparing them with that edition I observe that the printer used the same papers; but especially I discover not without admiration and veneration of the highest study of Megalander, with what accuracy he labored, so that he might render the Hebrew text both emphatically and purely in German; since he corrected words and phrases from time to time, until he found those with which he was satisfied. Which parts, collected into one body in the year 1534, amended, and rendered even more clear as to their meaning, yet with a new, more German version of the Psalter substituted, were published. This was the first edition of Luther's Bible; to which, however, a second, begun to be revised in the year 1541 and completed in the year 1542, succeeded as the author's second effort: which was subsequently reprinted so frequently in various places, and translated into diverse idioms, into Dutch, English, Bohemian, Polish, Lithuanian: so that I would dare to affirm that no work has ever been sent out into the world by the press so often, and in such a great multitude of copies. What is more, not only did Emser from the Papists publish the N.T. translation, peddling it as his own, but also the Calvinists of Neustadt published Luther's Bible in the year 1588 with new, albeit marginal, doctrinal summaries added, not without the poison of their heresy (which the blessed Jac. Andreae) and the Herborners in the year 1595 with similar various falsifications (concerning which the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg warned in the year 1598), as also Paul Tossanus in the year 1618, whose impostures Mr. Dr. Joh. Winckelmannus exposed. Which, however, the Reformed brought forward again in the year 1665, augmented with some annotations. The Crypto-Calvinists of Wittenberg also attempted something of the sort in the previous century, but the work was hindered when barely half of the edition was completed. But how this man of God undertook this version, and what he achieved in his translation, George, Prince of Anhalt, in Ps. 16, German Works, fol. 100, Joh. Matthesius, sermon 13 on Luther, year 1540, p. 142, Tilemannus Heshusius in the Preface to Ps. 4, and our theological faculty in the preface prefixed to the Wustian Wittenberg editions have taught. D. Mich. Beringerus, B. D. Gerhardus, D. Groshain, B. Waltherus, D. D. Müllerus, and others have abundantly satisfied on various occasions the accusations of Bellarmine, Pistorius, Ulenberg, Tanner, Melch. Zanger, the Jesuit Holzai, Keckermann, and others against this work, which can never be praised enough. Joh. Leusden recently caviled in his Phil. Ebræo-mixta that Luther's version was composed in a time of tumult and abounds with many faults: but when it came to the demonstration of that matter, he appealed only to his Bucer in the Dialogue with Melanchthon, and to Philipp Marnix in his Epistle to Drusius as witnesses of the house, and while he calumniates the former as a Vertumnus and a forger, and the latter as openly abusive, [claiming] that no version admitted by the Reformed Church differs so far from the authentic text as the German version of Luther, and to Melch. Zanger (whom, however, he never saw, but praises by the testimony of Baudartius), whose mouth Mich. Beringerus stopped as an impious calumniator, and from him B. D. Maukisch in the Preface to the Notar. Philolog. Theolog. Nor does he bring forward more than two examples, Gen. 1:20 and ch. 23:2, because there Luther rendered 'under the firmament' not 'above,' and here 'Haupt-Stadt' for the city of Arba: But the former was dealt with in our Commentary on Genesis; as for the latter, a marginal gloss could have informed Aristarchus more correctly. If Luther's translation is so faulty, how does it happen, I ask, that the Calvinists have edited it so often, and as it were claimed it for themselves and made it their own, even setting aside their own translations, as is evident not only from the examples of the Wittenbergers, Neostadians, Herborners, and Tossanus, but recently also in the year 1665 at Basel with the Privilege of the Vicariate of the Empire of the Most Serene Elector Palatine, they edited the version of B. Luther, with the notes of D. Paul Tossanus, adding excerpts from the Annotations attached to the new Belgian version, and the writings of other theologians? For even if they say that in this edition Luther's edition is recalled to the source by means of some notes, they could have, nay, they ought rather to have applied their Piscator or even the Belgian version to the German translation, if Luther's translation abounds with such great faults and departs so far from the authentic text, as Leusden cavils with Marnix: or why did they not apply the Tigurine versions, which they once held in high regard, as they were translated into the German idiom and appeared at Zurich in the Helvetic language in 1540 in folio and 1548 in quarto, and in Latin in 1531 in folio and 1544 in quarto, or the German version published at Zurich in octavo in 1530, to the Tossanian or even the modern notes? Not to mention the work of Tremellius, which is excessively praised by some. Indeed, Joh. Piscator of Herborn did adorn a new version published in 1604, but they understood without a doubt that the judgment of our theologians was not for nothing, who argued that he translated many things not only childishly and ineptly, and in a Vandalic rather than a German manner, and that, as B. Mænzer teaches in Vol. III, Giess. disput. XV, that translation, made according to the prescription of the Latin Junio-Tremellian version, abounds with infinite faults, blasphemies, and errors. Paulus Röder in a special writing and D. Petrus Piscator, a theologian of Jena, dealt with this version at greater length and exposed its corruptions, errors, and faults.

The States of the United Netherlands certainly did not acquiesce in the Piscatorian version of the Bible, or the version of the New Testament by Amandus Polanus, any more than in the German Bibles of B. Luther and the old Belgian version translated from them; because by a decree made in the Synod of Dordrecht, held in the year 1618, they sanctioned that another Belgian translation should be adorned; which, as it had various authors and also various revisers, whose opinions were as many as their heads, so it cannot but be considered varied, whether you look at the metaphrase itself or the diverse notes added to it; which, however, we do not deprive of its due praise. For there are many things in that work to be preferred by long distances to the inventions of others, even those who were leaders in the Reformed Church, which have been not infrequently observed and praised in their proper places in these our meletemata. In vain were the aforementioned Marnix, Arnoldus Cornelius, and Wernerus Helmichius once appointed to that task, having died before they could seriously undertake it. Those chosen by the Synod of Dordrecht for the interpretation of the O. T. are reported to be Joh. Bogerman, Wilhelmus Baudartius, and Gerson Bucerus, to whom were added D. Ant. Thysius, Jac. Rolandus, and Herman. Fauckelius: for the New Testament, the same Rolandus and Fauckelius, with Petrus Cornelii: to whom were added D. Fest. Hommius, D. Ant. Walæus, and Jodocus Hoingius; but because of the intervening death of others, Leusden (l. c. p. 80) reports that Rolandus, Walæus, and Hommius were added as interpreters of the N. T. The revisers of the O. T. deputed by the Synod were D. Ant. Thysius, D. Joh. Polyander, Petrus Plancius, to whom Rolandus succeeded after his death, just as D. Abdias Widmarius succeeded the latter; likewise Jacobus Larenus, D. Sibrandus Lubbertus, Bernhardus Fullenius, D. Jacobus Revius, D. Franciscus Gomarus, and Arnoldus Teckmannus: In the revision of the New Testament, however, were employed D. Sebast. Damman, D. Festus Hommius (in whose place succeeded Johan. Arnoldi, Lindanus), D. Gosvinus Geldorphius (to whom succeeded Wilhelmus Nieuhusius), D. Carolus Dematius, Bernhard. Fullenius, D. Cass. Sibelius, Ubbo Emmius, D. Henric. Altingius, D. Ludovicus Gerhardus à Keneffe. The Dordracene Synodals, however, ordered that this version should be so adorned that from the old version (translated from B. Luther) all those things should be retained which, in their judgment, could be preserved without prejudice to the truth and the purity and propriety of the Belgian language. Matth. Polus commends that version coldly Polus, and adds nothing about the annotations, except that he calls them brief little annotations: That version, he says, responds not insignificantly to the Hebrew text, and exhibits the sense clearly, faithfully, and solidly in most places: and although it is named in the last place, it is not to be named among the LAST. Yet he dismissed hardly any of those he mentioned with a slighter eulogy. He certainly celebrated the Junio-Tremellian [version] far more magnificently: Although some versions may be closer to the Hebrews in certain places, and some even render the sense more clearly and elegantly; yet when all things required for an accurate Version have been considered and put together, [such as] agreement with the authentic text even to the very accents, which others for the most part neglect, the sense having been elicited with no small sharpness and rendered with the greatest fidelity, the words, if not always the most polished, yet for the most part proper and suitable, the difficult passages having been more diligently weighed and more learnedly and solidly explained; this Version will perhaps claim the first place for itself, and will carry it off before fair judges.

Moreover, among the Papists after B. Luther, Dietenberger also undertook a translation, which appeared at Mainz in the year 1534, but since it neither agrees with the original text, nor is adorned with sufficiently refined, nay rather, [is adorned with] horrid language, another German Biblical [version] was recently procured by the authority of the Elector of Mainz, namely in the year 1661, which, however, as the comparison teaches, can in no way come into comparison with the Bibles of B. Luther, inasmuch as they are no less distant from the source than the Vulgate itself, from which the same were formed.

The Papists did indeed vehemently insult the blessed Luther’s version, especially both Zangers, namely Melchior in the year 1605 in his so-called wahrhafftigen und augenscheinlichen Erweisung/ welchergestalt Martinus Luther die H. Schrifft den Haupt-Sprachen/ und der gantzen Catholischen Kirchen Theologischem Verstand zuwider an unterschiedenen Orten ungleich verdolmetschet: by which writing he did not hesitate to discredit Luther’s version and exalt his own Dietenberger; and Georgius, who published that at Mainz, and in the dedication most gravely accused Luther: but how futile and vain that attempt was, D. Beringerus sufficiently demonstrated in the aforementioned vindications, to such an extent that the Papists were even reduced to silence.

Let us see certain examples of the version of Dietenberger and the criticism of Zanger, so that a judgment may be made whether Luther's version is to be preferred, and what is to be thought of Dietenberger's translation and Zanger's attempts?

I. Gen. 4, v. last. Dietenberger rendered it with the Vulgate: 'This one began to call upon the name of the Lord.' Wrongly. For was the name of God not invoked before? More correctly the Blessed Luther: 'At that same time one began to preach of the name of the Lord.' Marcus Marinus in 'Arca Noae' under the word קרא and Mercer in 'Thesaurus Pagnini' agree.

II. Gen. 23, 3. The version of the Blessed Luther has it very well: 'After that he stood up from his corpse'; yet he is refuted by Zanger, and it is amended thus: 'And when he had stood up from the office of the dead corpse.' But in the Hebrew there is nothing about an office, from which he attempts to carve out Mass and vigils: but as Pagninus explained it with Luther. 'And Abraham stood up from the face of his dead,' so also the Chaldean, as well as the LXX Interpreters.

III. Gen. 48, 16. Dietenberger translated it: 'That my name and the name of my fathers may be called upon them,' whereas in the Hebrew it is held, as Pagninus translates, 'and let my name be called in them, and the name of my fathers,' which the Blessed Luther translated likewise: 'That they may be named after my name and after the name of my fathers.'

IV. Deut. 2, 34. Dietenberger renders it, 'and slew all the inhabitants'; but more correctly the Blessed Luther, whom Zanger ignorantly criticizes: 'And banned all the cities'; with which Pagninus agrees: 'And we anathematized every city.'

V. 1 Sam. 20, 6. Dietenberger wrongly: 'For it is a glorious sacrifice there.' But the Blessed Luther correctly, according to the sources: 'For it is a yearly sacrifice there,' as Pagninus, because it is a sacrifice of days, or annual, there.

VI. 2 Sam. 23, 8. Dietenberg, having followed the Vulgate ineptly, inserted 'ein zartes Holtwürmlein' [a tender wood-worm]: Pagninus and Rabbi David, as also the Belgians, take the Hebrew עדינו העצנו as a proper name. Junius and Tremellius render it, 'it was pleasing to this spearman,' consonant (as to the sense) with the version of Luther and Osiander. Thus also in the notes of the Basel Bible, Luther-Toilan: 'Dem kam eine Lust an/ seinen Spieß (auffzuheben) 2c.' [A desire came upon him / his spear (to lift up) etc.]

VII. Job 33, 27. Dietenberg translated it inconveniently: 'Aber noch nicht gefangen' [But not yet captured]: Luther, on the contrary, [translated it] conveniently to the Hebrew text, as it is also explained by Pagninus: 'Et non profuit mihi' [And it did not profit me]: 'Aber es hat mir nichts genutzet' [But it has profited me nothing].

VIII. Job 36, 36. Dietenberg [translated it] irrelevantly: 'Wer sein Freund ist/ dem verkündiget er/ daß er sein Erbe sey/ und daß er mỏge darzu kommen' [Whoever is his friend, to him he declares that he is his heir, and that he may come to it]. Sanctes Pagninus rendered the Hebrew: 'Tonitruus erit in urbe' [There will be thunder in the city]. Luther.

Davon zeuget sein Geselle, nemlich des Donners Zorn in Wolcken [Of this his companion testifies, namely the wrath of the thunder in the clouds]. In the context there is nothing about a citation or the division of an inheritance, but about clouds, lightning, and thunder.

IX. Psalm 1, 1. B. Luther. Dietenberger and Zanger could not disapprove of the version, yet for the sake of the Vulgate translation, the name of 'pestilence' was preferred over Luther's word 'scoffers' [Spötter], even though this corresponds to the Hebrew לצים: 'Und ist nicht gesessen auff dem Stul der Pestilentz' [And has not sat in the seat of the pestilence].

X. Psalm 6, 7. Dietenberger translated: 'Mein Auge ist betrübet für deinem Zorn, und bin alt worden zwischen allen meinen Feinden' [My eye is troubled because of your wrath, and I have become old among all my enemies]: Much more congruently to the Hebrew text, with the approval of Pagninus, and more elegantly, B. Luther: 'Meine Gestalt ist verfallen für Trauren, und ist alt worden, daß ich allenthalben geängstiget werde' [My form has wasted away from sorrow, and has become old, so that I am distressed on every side].

XI. Psalm 18, 2. B. Luth. translated: 'Hertzlich lieb habe ich dich' [I love you heartily]: Dietenberg: 'Ich will dich lieben' [I will love you]: The former's version is consonant with the Hebrew verb, because רחם is, according to Marcus Marinus, to love vehemently, as if you were to say, if it were permitted to speak so in Latin, to 'inviscerate,' to enclose within the bowels.

XII. Psalm 37, 31. B. Luther's translation has, 'Bleib fromm, und halte dich recht, denn solchen wirds zulezt wohlgehen' [Remain pious, and keep yourself right, for to such it will go well in the end]. Which agrees with the Hebrew text, as Arias Montanus does not deny, 'custodi integrum, & vide rectum, quia novissimum viro pax' [keep the upright, and see the right, for the end for the man is peace]. And yet Luther is beaten by Zanger, who renders it so incongruously: 'Bewahre die Unschuld, und suche die Gerechtigkeit, denn es sind die überbliebene den friedsamen Menschen' [Preserve innocence, and seek justice, for they are the survivors of the peaceful man].

XIII. Psalm 37, 3. Dietenb. Hearken, all ye people, attend to all who live in this world: All children of the earth and children of men, both rich and poor together. Zangerus here censures Luther because he rendered it both common man and lords, but he did not understand the nature of the Hebrew language, as D. Beringer rightly answered him, according to which sons of man are plebeians, sons of a man are famous ones, as noted by Mercer in Thes. Pagn. & Marco Marin. in arc. Noæ, which is also to be observed in Is. 2, 9, where the Blessed Luther, rendering it excellently, 'the rabble bows down, the nobles humble themselves,' is wrongly corrected: 'The man bows down, the man humbles himself.'

XIV. Is. 24, 16. The convenient version of the Blessed Luther, 'But how lean am I,' which Mercer and Marc. Marin. likewise favor, is ineptly corrected: 'I keep my secret to myself': Cf. also Forster in the word רזי & Schindl. in Lexic. Pentagl.

XV. Is. 26, 18. Incongruously with Dietenberg, Zanger, nay foolishly: 'We have become pregnant, and have lain as in birth pangs, and have brought forth the spirit of salvation,' not attending to the accent Athnah, which brings the word ישועות to what follows. Conveniently the Blessed Luther: 'There we are also pregnant, and we are anxious, so that we can hardly catch our breath, nor can we help the land.' Ariasmont. in this manner: We have conceived, we have been in pain as if we brought forth the Spirit. Salvations have not been made in the earth.

XVI. Is. 27, 11. The Blessed Luther rightly has: 'Their branches will break for dryness, so that the women will come and make fire with them.' Which exactly agree with the Hebrew truth, and are approved by Marc. Mar. in the word קציר. Dietenberg, however, wrongly: 'In the dryness of their harvest the women who come to her will perish, and they will teach her.' Cf. again Forster & Schindler, as also Mercer. The versions of Pagnini, Münster, Vatablus, Tigurina, Castalio, Junius & Tremellius, Piscator, and the Belgian versions agree with Luther's version.

XVII. Is. 31, 8. Luth. according to the Heb. text rendered: And yet he will flee from the sword, is poorly emended by Zanger to the erroneous vulgate, He will not flee from the sword. Pagninus & Montanus adhere to the source with Luther, And he shall flee from the faces of the sword.

XVIII. Isa. 34, 7. Blessed Luther had rendered it well, And the bullocks together with the fattened oxen. It is corrected, however, in this way: And the animals together with the strong ones. In Hebrew it is: And the bullocks with the bulls. Who does not see that Luther's translation is correct, which Mercerus, Marinus, & others in the Lexicon support?

XIX. Isa. 41, 14. Luther explained it conveniently according to the sense: So fear not, you little worm Jacob, you poor crowd of Israel: Zanger criticizes Luther, & not understanding the word מתי which signifies mortals, not dead men, he ineptly rendered it: O you little worm of Jacob, and you dead little people of Israel, fear not.

XX. Jerem. 16, 5. Luther rightly: You shall not go to the house of mourning. Which agrees with the Hebrew text, and is approved by Marcus Marinus: but it is poorly emended by Dietenberger and Zanger, you shall not go into a drinking-house.

XXI. Jerem. 23, 11. The version of blessed Luther: For both prophet and priest are knaves, is poorly emended in this way: the prophets and priests are unclean. Marcus Marinus also noted that the Hebrew חנף means to act impiously, to be impious. The same reason applies to the passage Jerem. XXIII, 15.

XXII. Jerem. 25, 38. Dietenberger very ineptly rendered it according to the Latin Vulgate, for their land is devastated before the wrath of the dove; Whereas in the Hebrew it is, as Pagninus & Arias Montanus explained, and also in the Arca Noae Marcus Marinus at the word יונה with blessed Luther: For their land has been rendered desolate because of the fury of the oppressor, or the one pressing hard. The Chaldean also agrees with Luther, along with the LXX Interpreters.

XXIII. Jerem. 31, 20. The version of blessed Luther is unskillfully carped at by Zanger. Megalander rendered it: Is not Ephraim my dear son, and my beloved child? But here he corrects it thus: Ephraim is my legitimate son and my tender child. Marcus Marinus stands for Luther, as does Pagninus.

XXIV. Hos. VIII, 9. Luther explained it not inappropriately, like a wild animal in the wilderness. Dietenberger: Ephraim is like a solitary wild ass. The word Ephraim in the authentic text is to be separated, by force of the accentuation. Marcus Marinus & Forster interpret it, A wild animal to itself, which according to the sense easily agrees with the version of blessed Luther.

XXV. Malach. 3, 2. Luther interpreted it well, for he is like the fire of a goldsmith, and like the soap of the washers. Ineptly, and without cause, Zanger emends it: for he rages like a fire, and like soap-wort. Marcus Marinus stands for Luther, rendering it: He is like the fire of the refiner (goldsmith) & like the cleansing (soap, or detergent) of the fullers. Compare Forster, Mercer, & Pagninus, as also Schindler in the Lexicon at the word צרף & בורית. And let these suffice for the present. More can be sought from Mr. Beringer himself. The version of blessed Luther is praised also by the most diligent and most learned English author among the Reformed, Matthew Poole, in his Synopsis Criticorum Interpretum. with the eulogy of the same Osiander brought forward: that it is the best and most clear version, elaborated with incredible labor, most exquisite judgment, and admirable dexterity, and such a work, than which the sun has seen nothing more perfect in this kind: whence in the correction of the Vulgate, Osiander did not so much need to add his own emendation as to employ the German Version of B. Luther.

XV. On the authority of the Vulgate Latin Version, which

the Papists sell as authentic, we have treated specially and of set purpose, and we have detected even six hundred of its errors in Crit. Sacr. from p. 502 to p. 691, and also in Tom. I. Syst. Theol. p. 642.

XVI. On the sense of Scripture, which we have shown not to be diverse, much less fourfold—literal, tropological, allegorical, and anagogical—but in one and the same text to be ONLY ONE, and that the LITERAL one intended by the Holy Spirit, more succinctly in Tom. I. System. Theol. p. 622: but we have proven it expressly, as they say, in our Commentary on Genesis, p. 64 up to 98, and we have refuted the various senses of Scripture asserted both by Papists and by others in c. VIII of the prolegomena of that Commentary, which we wish to be considered as repeated here in its entirety.

XVII. On Biblical interpreters, and the diverse method of commenting, treated in the same place, c. 8.

Furthermore, those who have contributed some effort from the Fathers to the illustration of the whole of Scripture are generally these: (I.) Origen, called Adamantius for his labor, around the year of Christ 260, who, because of his excessive zeal for allegories and various errors, is to be read with judgment. (II.) Diodorus of Tarsus, according to Sozomen l. 8. Hist. Eccl. c. 2. and Nicephorus l. 13. Hist. Eccles., explained most books of both Testaments according to the letter in the year 350, to whom must be joined (III.) John, Archbishop of the Church of Constantinople, a disciple of Diodorus, Bishop of Tarsus, who wrote on almost all Biblical books, called Chrysostom for his golden eloquence in the year 400. (IV.) Jerome in the year 420, who leaves all others far behind him in antiquity, especially in the explanation of the books of the O.T., as being almost the only one skilled in the Hebrew language and most versed in the humanities. (V.) St. Augustine of Hippo Bishop in the year 422. (VI.) Theodoret, a follower of Chrysostom, in the year 450. (VII.) Paterius in the year of Christ 600 collected annotations from Gregory the Great. (IIX.) The Venerable Bede in the year 734 undertook to write on the whole of Scripture Rhapsodies on mystical expositions, Questions, Homilies, and Commentaries. (IX.) Oecumenius in the year 800 compiled a catena on almost the whole of Scripture, especially on the New Testament, from the Greek Fathers. (X.) Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, in the year 834 adorned brief Commentaries, and those more Allegorical and Anagogical. (XI.) Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, compiled Commentaries on the whole of Scripture in 172 books from the Latin Fathers from Jerome to Bede according to the sense of the letter and spiritual understanding in the year 840, whom (XII.) Strabus, formerly his auditor and scribe, author of the Ordinary Gloss, imitated in the year 844. (XIII.) Remigius, Bishop of Auxerre, wrote on most books of the O. and N. Testament in the year 880. (XIV.) Anselm of Laon was the author of the interlinear gloss in the year 1110. (XV.) Rupert of Deutz in the year 1124 collected Commentaries of various senses, mostly from the Fathers. To these, from the Scholastic and Papist writers, were added those who follow: (XVI.) Hugh of St. Victor, or Victorinus, a Saxon by nation, from the reading of the ancient Fathers and especially St. Augustine, from whose emulation he was called THE TONGUE OF AUGUSTINE, compiled a great number of opuscula on the whole of Scripture, distributed into five parts, into Annotations, Questions, Homilies, Commentaries, and Miscellanea, around the year of Christ 1130. (XVII.) Peter the Chanter, Bishop of Paris, wrote a Scholastic Gloss on the whole Bible around the year of Christ 1200. At which time also (XVIII.) Pontius Carbonellus interpreted both Testaments. (XIX.) Alexander of Hales, a Briton, called THE FOUNTAIN OF LIFE, completed a Postil on the whole Bible (so he titled it) in the year 1240. (XX.) Peter Berchorius of Poitiers, at about the same time, explained Scripture tropologically, as the Papists love to speak, i.e., morally under various titles: Morale Reductorium, Repertorium & Inductorium. (XXI.) Hugo of Saint-Cher, Cardinal, interpreted Scripture according to a fourfold sense, who also first adorned the Latin Concordances about the year 1245. (XXII) Albert the Great, Archbishop of Regensburg, illustrated the whole of Scripture with a scholastic type of explanation in the year 1280. (XXIII.) Franciscus Mayron, a disciple of John Duns Scotus, in the year 1320 published Postils of Annotations on the whole of Scripture. (XXIV.) Nicholas of Lyra, from a town in Brabant, a converted Jew, who in the judgment of Sixtus of Siena had no equal of his time in explaining the Scriptures, compiled on the books of the Old and New Testament 85 Scholastic Postils, in the first 50 of which he brought out the literal sense of Scripture, which is, as Senensis says, more excellent and equally more difficult than the other senses of divine Scripture, having brought forward the opinions of both the Rabbis and the Fathers; in the remaining ones he pursued a moral exposition in the year 1320. Papists boast about Lyranus to the hatred and contempt of Luther: Unless Lyra had played the lyre, Luther would not have danced. But let them compare, I beg, those things which B. Luther published on the Biblical books and the sentences of Scripture with those which occur in the Postils of Lyranus, and let them show where Luther dances to the lyre of Lyra: They will certainly never teach that which they indicate with a shameful taunt, namely that Luther could not have found the sense of Scripture without Lyra; but they will find it more true that Lyranus very often raves, whereas on the contrary B. Luther wisely observed the concert of the Prophets and Apostles and the perennial harmony of the whole of Scripture. But where Lyra agrees with Scripture in literal exposition, it would have been desirable that the Papists had danced according to his measures, and not played with mystical and foreign senses in Scripture, disturbed the harmony of the letter, and raved, which he who compares the exposition of Lyra with more recent Papist interpreters will not rarely discover. For Luther does not detract from the praise due to Lyranus; indeed, in the preface to the Explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians, he commends the labor of Lyra, saying that his exposition would not be to be rejected if only it were amended and perfected, Vol. VI. Altenburg German f. 1073; that he interprets the Old Testament excellently when he opposes the Jews and follows the lead of the New Testament, not so when he follows his Rabbi Solomon, preface to the explanation of the words of the Last Days of David, Vol. VIII. Altenburg German p. 305; and he prefers him to all others because he presses the literal sense closely and adheres to it, Commentary on Genesis Ch. IX. (XXV.) Paul of Burgos, Bishop, a converted Jew likewise, wrote some censures against Lyranus in the year 1430. (XXVI.) Diego Deza, Archbishop of Seville, called back into consideration places explained by Lyranus otherwise than was done by Thomas, in the year 1500. (XXVII.) Matthew Döring, a Saxon, adorned replies against Paul of Burgos for Lyranus in the year 1440. Whence (XXVIII.) the Douay Glossed Bibles, published in the year 1617, exhibited the Ordinary Gloss of Strabus of Fulda, but enriched with new explanations of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, as well as the interlinear gloss of Anselm of Laon, and the Commentaries of Lyranus, together with the Additions of Burgensis and the Replies of Döring. (XXIX.) Peter Paludanus, Patriarch of Jerusalem, adorned a Postil according to a triple sense, Literal, Moral, and Allegorical, on the entire Bible in the year 1330. (XXX.) Nicholas Trivet, an Englishman, made a chain from the Fathers on the entire Bible in the year 1360, but not, as Sixtus of Siena says, 400.

whose error Antonio Possevino observed in his Apparatus. (XXXI.) Nicholas Gorran in the year 1390 compiled brief Scholastic Commentaries on the whole of Scripture. (XXXII.) James, surnamed Magnus, of Toledo, illustrated the entire Bible with Annotations in the year 1400. (XXXIII.) Bartholomew of Urbino, Bishop, in the year 1410 interpreted all the books of Scripture from the volumes of Augustine. At which time also (XXXIV.) Peter Brunnquellus is said to have published Scholastic lectures on the whole Bible. (XXXV.) Albert of Sideberg wrote Commentaries on both Testaments in the year 1450. (XXXVI.) Dionysius the Carthusian, a German from the town of Rickel (by which name he is also wont to be called simply), in the year 1472 explained the whole of Scripture according to a triple sense from the Fathers and Scholastics, Hugo, Bonaventure, Thomas, as also Lyranus. (XXXVII.) Godofredus Tilemannus collected Allegories and Tropologies from more than thirty authors on selected passages of both Testaments in the year 1550.

(XXXVIII.) Antonius Medicis, who collected Annotations on the Bible from Lyranus in the year 1490, compiled more concise notes on Holy Scripture after Apollinaris the Younger, Bishop of Laodicea, praised by St. Jerome in the year 380. (XXXIX.) Bernardinus Galdolus in the year 1496 compiled a work of Annotations on all the books of the Bible. (XL.) Johannes Benedictus of Paris collected very brief scholia on the entire Scripture in the year 1550. (XLI.) Franciscus Lucas Brugensis wrote annotations on the Holy Bible in the year 1560, as did (XLII.) Emanuel Saa, who explains primarily Hebrew and Greek idioms, and also (XLIII.) Basilius Zanchius, who, according to Possevinus, compiled annotations on both Testaments around the same time. (XLIV.) Joh. Mariana subsequently wrote brief annotations or scholia of the same kind, which, augmented and corrected with the annotations of Eman. Saa, with the addition of Petr. Lansselius the Jesuit's supplement, (as the title states for the sake of argument) were published at Antwerp from the Plantin press together with the text of the Vulgate edition of Sixtus V in the year 1624, under the title, albeit a very vain one, of a perpetual commentary. Although neither Saa's nor Mariana's notes are to be despised. (XLV.) Franciscus Haræus, however, added his scholia of little use on the Sacred Books to the Vulgate text edited by himself. (XLVI.) Guilhelmus Estius, a professor at Douai, published in the year 1622 annotations, which he too gloriously calls golden, on the principal and more difficult passages of Holy Scripture. Furthermore, (XLVII.) Jac. Tirinus the Jesuit adorned certain observations with summaries for individual chapters, published at Brussels in the year 1645 under the title of Commentaries, reduced into an epitome from various authors: which, however, and which controversial passages, and the index of Articles of faith subjoined, Samuel Maresius of the Reformed Church corrected in his Anti-Tirinus. (XLVIII.) Joh. Stephanus Menochius the Jesuit published a brief explanation of the literal sense with the text of the Vulgate edition at Cologne in the year 1630. From these, namely Guilhelmus Estius, Emanuel Saa, Jacobus Tirinus, and Joh. Steph. Menochius, with the addition of the explanations of Joh. Gagnæus on the New Testament, were born.

(XLIX.) THE GREAT BIBLE, comprised in 5 volumes, published at Paris in the year 1644 under the care of Johannes de la Haye, Royal Preacher, to serve the literal sense, in which, however, the Latin Vulgate is often corrected from the Hebrew text, especially by Emanuel Saa. Which (L.) subsequently in the year 1660 the same Johannes de la Haye, with only the annotations of Nicolaus de Lyra the Minorite prefixed, under the title THE GREATEST BIBLE, of versions from several Oriental languages, from sacred manuscript codices, almost countless sacred and ancient Fathers and Orthodox Interpreters, and their harmony with the Vulgate (which, of what kind, and how great it may be, the learned know), published at Paris. Matthew Poole notes the untrustworthy faith of that Johannes de la Haye with a brand, but a most deserved one, because Münster's version in the Biblia Maxima, but always calls it the Venetian, fearing perhaps that the name of the heretic Münster might defile that most celebrated work. However, Cornelius Cornelii à Lapide easily returns the ambiguous palm to all those Papist Interpreters (LI.), who in this century illustrated most Biblical Books with brilliant Commentaries, in his own way. In his own way, I say. For on account of the hypothesis of various senses of Scripture, the true literal sense is often more obscured, and for the sake of the fabricated authenticity of the Latin Vulgate, many things were rashly, many things falsely and against the original text asserted, and in moral matters, frequently fabulous stories, with which the Papacy abounds, were mixed with true ones. Matthew Poole professes concerning Cornelius’s Commentaries that among many things alien to the matter, he found not a few things written with more than ordinary learning and acumen. Such a eulogy he could hardly, and even then barely, attribute to his own Calvin. For his commentaries are not so much Critical, by his own judgment, as they are Practical, nor do they so much elucidate words and phrases as they treat Theological matters; yet he argues against his own [followers] who wrote after Calvin, because they plucked most things from him, and adorned their books with his interpretations, even those who assail their author and Master with insults.

But we can supersede the reviewing of those commentaries of the Reformers here, since there do not occur so many who, besides Critical [works] and strict annotations, or Commentaries added to new versions, have published on the entire Bible, and each in their own place, or in special Biblical books, others may be more conveniently mentioned, as we have already said a good part about those. Nor does Poole find any from the Reformed to mention, except Fr. Junius and Joh. Piscator; he praises the former’s Scholia, because they are brief indeed, but polished with multifarious erudition and the highest judgment, and because even a few words equal the volumes of others, and he therefore brings forward the judgment of Grotius, who did not think the labors of Junius were to be despised, which indeed he himself judges to be highly esteemed and placed in the first benches of Interpreters: concerning these, see. (Piscator’s) annotations he judges thus: that his Critical Scholia, in which he also calls the version of Junius and Tremellius to examination, and draws out the force and sense of the words and phrases of the Sacred books, from which you may gather that Piscator is preferred in his judgment to Junius, whose version also, although he follows the Junian in most things, he pronounces not rarely more accurate and agreeable to the Hebrew truth, and handed down with greater perspicuity, when yet he had said a little before that he perhaps claimed the first place for himself, and carried it off before fair judges. But we leave these things to be reconciled by the Reformed or the author himself: Nor do we deprive either Junius or Piscator of their praises, but we judge that they can be usefully employed and compared, provided that it be done with judgment, and in Piscator especially, the Calvinian heterodoxies are avoided. But the work of this Matthew deserves no ordinary praise in this, that with great study he compared various notes, and Commentators of no last rank, and especially reduced Critical [matters] diligently and compendiously into order, and exhibited them in this synopsis as if in one view, without vain repetitions, and hair-splitting or trifles, such as he says occur in great numbers of no weight or use in the works of Drusius; and that he took pains to illustrate the entire Biblical text indeed, yet to watch more diligently over some places, as being doubtful, obscure, and difficult to understand, even neglected by the crowd of Commentators; which he entirely intends, but how he has achieved it, the investigation will teach in many things. Nor can it be displeasing that he sometimes exhibits various versions and expositions in those places or matters in which it is permitted without great danger to embrace this or that opinion: but that the author wished to waver rather than establish anything certain even in those things which make for the confirmation of the faith, that indeed is not to be approved. For that excuse will not suffice for sensible men: that contrary opinions are left to the judgment of the sagacious reader, and that the mind had to be kept uncorrupted by party spirit: because the sense of Scripture must be certain, and everyone ought to be fully convinced in his own mind, Rom. XIV, 5. And there is given between those two, namely, bringing one’s own senses into Scripture, and only expounding the opinions of others, a third, namely, to draw out the proper sense of Scripture, and to bring it forth from the Scriptures according to the warning of hermeneutics. For the best reader, as Hilary says in book 1 de Trinit., is he who expects the understanding of what is said from the things said rather than imports it, and has reported rather than brought in. Finally, in all the Reformed Interpreters who do not stick only to Critical [matters], it is deservedly desired that, fascinated by preconceived opinions which make both pages in the vanity of the Calvinian religion, they depart from the propriety of the letter of the text, and indulge in their own tropes and figures, sometimes even clearly new ones, and unused in all the schools of rhetoricians, which will be evident in these annotations of ours by countless examples. For that is a sound sense, as Irenaeus says in book II against heresies, ch. 46, and without danger, which is placed openly and without ambiguity in the very expressions in the Scriptures.

Our Paraphrasts, therefore, and Interpreters, whose sole care it was to search the original text, and to investigate the literal sense, and not to depart rashly from the propriety of words, have handled the Holy Code with far purer hands: whose commentaries, therefore, as well as annotations, after the labors of the Holy Fathers, Jerome, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Augustine, and other Ancients, are to be held in value, and are deservedly preferred to the inventions of the Scholastics and Papists as well as the Calvinians, as making as much as possible for the genuine sense of the Holy Spirit, and holily guarding the deposit of heavenly truth and the analogy of faith. However, they contribute not a little to the phrase and rites, and the circumstances of places, times, and persons, as the Jews and the Rabbis themselves, so also the more learned, and those more skilled in languages among the Papists: nay, they are also not rarely of use for the more correct understanding of divine oracles: in all of which, indeed, the Reformed, along with the Orthodox, deserve more praise, where they are not carried away by preconceived opinions. Therefore, we do not doubt to assign the chief place to our great man and god-man B.
