LUTHER, of whom Philip Melanchthon in the preface to Vol. III of the Latin Works of Luther testifies: that Erasmus was accustomed to say that there is no interpreter more skillful among all the writings that exist since the Apostles, and that the same was the judgment of wise and serious men understanding the doctrine of the Church, nor is it an obscure matter to one applying judgment and candor in reading: And D. Nic. Ambsdorfius in the Preface to Vol. I of the Latin. But if the truth, he says, is to be explained ingenuously and openly, the very comparison of the expositions leads me to this opinion, that I think all the ancient and recent Commentators, even if they were melted into one mass, and that which is best were culled from them, yet not even then with this man's writings can be compared and collated. But he who, besides the German version made from the Hebrew and Greek source with most useful scholia—which, as the blessed Johann Bugenhagen of Pomerania testifies, can in most places serve in place of a great commentary and is clearer than all versions—not only in many books of Scripture which are above all praise, interpreted the Scriptures so thoroughly that from them, by the benefit of the Index attached to our Theological Encyclopedia and the Altenburg Tomes, commentaries on the entire Holy Scripture worthy of cedar could be collected: which most useful labor our blessed Walther vehemently desired and diligently commended to the most powerful King of the Danes and Norwegians, CHRISTIAN IV, of most glorious memory, at the dedication of the Biblical workshop.

Johann Brentz rightfully claims for himself the place next to the blessed Luther, who compiled eight tomes of commentaries on the books of the Old and New Testament, published at Tübingen in the year 1576: whom Luther himself vehemently commended in a letter to Johann Brentz.

prefixed to his preface to Amos. I preach not Brentz, he says, but the Spirit, who in you is sweeter, calmer, quieter; furthermore, instructed in the arts of speaking, he flows more purely, clearly, and elegantly: therefore he affects and delights more. Nor without merit did the Theological Faculty of Tübingen, in the edition of the works of the blessed Brentz, comparing the blessed Luther with Elijah and Brentz with Elisha, judge for a certain reason that these commentaries should be preferred to the writings and expositions of the Fathers: whose judgment, as it stands verbatim, it is pleasing to submit here, so that others may be invited to the reading of these truly inspired writers, whom we have frequently wished to cite for this reason in these our annotations and commentary on Genesis. Nor indeed, say the masters of Tübingen, while we praise these heroes, do we snatch away their praise from the holy Fathers (for they too labored diligently in the vineyard of the Lord, and indeed with the eternal fame of their name), but we see that they rather tasted many theological disputes than treated them. For they were mostly attentive to those occasions for defending the Church which then seemed necessary: and to defeating those enemies who, with all their might, wished to strip the Son of God of His eternal divinity and reduce Him to the order of men. While they labored with all their might in this matter, they left behind excellent monuments of their own study, diligence, and faith for posterity. In other matters they were not so occupied, because at that time controversies had not yet been stirred up about those things. For to speak of the chief head of our faith, that of justification, although there are excellent γνῶμαι (maxims) scattered here and there in the Fathers, yet there is no one who does not notice that all those Doctors (except for St. Augustine, who, while refuting the heresy of the Pelagians, performed excellent work, above all other Fathers) spoke more succinctly, and sometimes even quite inconveniently, because they did not have adversaries in that part. Sometimes also, in the heat of their genius, while treating those materials about which they were accustomed to declaim, they indulged themselves too much, and being carried too far, did not always attain the native meaning of the Scriptures. There was also lacking in most of them a knowledge of languages, wherefore it came about that while the Latins followed that old translation, and the Greeks their Seventy, they brought in and mixed in many things not only irrelevantly, but even against the mind of the Prophets and Apostles. But in the disputes of Luther and Brentz, not only this article, but the others also are built up from the Prophetic and Apostolic sources, so that the whole body of heavenly doctrine may be seen. Moreover, testimonies are so repeated from that truly learned and holy antiquity, and accommodated to the purpose, that there is no one who, when he has added attention and study to the reading of those writers, does not perceive that there is an invincible demonstration of truth in them, which, with explored hope of victory, we can oppose to all the enemies of the Church. There was, moreover, in both an excellent eloquence, fidelity in teaching, sweetness in consoling, sharpness in disputing, and dexterity in refuting opinions. To all these ornaments was added that which must be placed in the citadel of praise, that in those things which served the benefits of the Church, they labored with such great diligence, tireless study, perpetual desire, incredible care, and incomparable love, and so dedicated themselves entirely to this commentary, that those who are of sound mind understand that these Doctors were born by a singular benefit of the Lord for the purging and adorning of the Church. This is the Theological Faculty of Tübingen. It is also helpful to add that comparison which it institutes there between the blessed Luther and the blessed Brentz; further submitting this: Just as roses and little flowers, while they are wonderfully powerful for refreshing human spirits, yet have a pleasant variety in fragrance and a manifold difference in shape and colors: so, while all things were at their highest in both these heroes, and each labored with great contention of mind and strength for the greatest benefits of the Church, yet each had something peculiar which would come into the admiration of all. Luther was more vehement in his disputes, and was as it were a certain sword, which enemies would fear: for according to the measure of his gifts, times, and adversaries, he had to fight more than teach. Brentz was calmer; while Luther was alive, he preferred to teach rather than to fight, and could be seen as a certain shield if one had to engage with an enemy. And so there exist more of his works undertaken for the sake of disputing than for teaching. And just as Elijah, carried to heaven in a chariot of fire, is famous, so Luther, more vehement, with his divine and burning zeal, inveighed against the Papists and Sectarians, and from here happily departed. Brentius, however, while he lived, was as a disciple a spectator of Luther's praises in this regard, and prayed that he might feel in his own breast a double flame of that Spirit which his Preceptor had possessed. In speaking, the former was more abundant, like another Chrysostom: the latter imitated the brevity of either Basil or Nazianzen, in which, however, a most pleasing πυκνότης of subject matter lay hidden. An excellent genius had armed the former for all things, but especially for a more abundant and diffuse manner of speaking, which an outstanding learning also aided: the latter was promoted both by the gifts of nature, and there was added a more accurate method of invention and disposition in speaking, in imitation of the ancients. And so, while he indeed had very many who admired the elegance and copiousness of his oratory, and few who imitated it: the latter, however, since he accommodated everything to the popular grasp, although he had no equal in that matter, nevertheless invited everyone to the methods of learned brevity. The German language pleased the former, upon whose elegance he labored so much that he is rightly called the German and Christian Cicero: the latter followed in his speaking a Latinity which would not exercise the talents even of beginners: and yet he proposed the most serious matters in a proper and native style of speaking. Many things must be passed over on purpose, lest we make this long. And we have certainly not said these things because we prefer Brentius to Luther, or because we measure and divide their merits toward the Church of God as equal. For Brentius always both acknowledged and called Luther his Preceptor with a preface of honor. And that which Cyprian was accustomed to say about Tertullian: I worship the Master: he both felt and said the same about the writings of Luther: and he himself testified with a clearly generous spirit that he was the most skillful interpreter of all whose letters exist after the Apostles: but that we may show how much in both for the purification of the Church the Lord may have bestowed gifts. This [is the] Theological Faculty of Tübingen.

The blessed Lucas Osiander happily followed the blessed Luther and Brentius in his never-sufficiently-praised Paraphrase, in which, alongside the emendation of the Vulgate version instituted from the original text, he expressed the literal sense almost everywhere, and exhibited it with vigorous brevity, having also inserted, but succinctly, the principal Commonplaces: whence we have frequently used this work of his in these annotations not without significant profit. But in order that it may be understood what the blessed Osiander achieved in that work, and that the cultivators of Holy Scripture may be the more attracted to its use, it will be worth the effort to hear the author himself here: both regarding the plan of emending the Vulgate, and regarding the paraphrase and the unfolding of the literal sense according to the guidance of the blessed Luther, and

Brentius. Regarding the former, he says, it is better known than to require proof, that that old Latin translation is worn out by daily use in the Church, especially among students of theology, and is utilized, and thus still obtains public authority. For although the German version of the Bible, elaborated by Dr. Luther, of holy memory, with incredible labor, most exquisite judgment, and admirable dexterity, is such a work as the sun has seen nothing more absolute of its kind: yet, because that Latin translation (whether of Jerome, or of another, whoever he may have been) has nevertheless been retained until now in schools and theological exercises by reason of its antiquity and recommendation: and those who are destitute of the knowledge of the German language cannot enjoy the most wholesome labor of Luther: it seemed good to devote my effort to that old translation, both to correct it and to illustrate it, to the best of my ability. For it cannot be denied by learned and good men that in that very Latin version many things occur which are either corrupted by the carelessness of scribes or the rashness of sciolists, or translated so thoughtlessly by the interpreter that they do not correspond to the Hebrew truth. Often, even though the interpreter did not think he should depart from the Hebrew phrase, but rendered word for word: yet such obscurity, and sometimes ambiguity, was left that you cannot even guess what the interpreter intended for himself. Then indeed, in some places, the things themselves are obscure by their very nature (even where the translation cannot be accused) and have great need of some explanation.

Regarding the latter, he holds as follows: And I willingly confess that in this undertaken labor I was so aided by the commentaries of most illustrious men, Dr. Luther and Brentius, of holy memory, that without them I would by no means have dared to enter upon this journey: and the attentive reader will recognize their matters and words throughout. For I ought not, nor do I wish, to steal the labors and industry of others and claim them for myself. It remains that I should also answer in a few words and lovingly those who perhaps are going to find some things lacking in this plan of mine. Others will perhaps wonder that in more obscure places, where many differing, and often even conflicting, opinions are alleged by other interpreters, I have recited only one opinion. That was done by me not without grave cause, even though the diverse interpretations did not escape me. For I did not wish to disturb the reader with a variety of opinions, lest those who are not equipped with such sharp judgment that they can choose the best from many opinions should be dismissed by me more uncertain than they had approached this reading. Wherefore, from many, I have proposed that which I, having carefully weighed the circumstances, judged to be the truest. For this labor of mine is not destined for Doctors of Theology, but for students. For that reason, I also thought that unnecessary questions, and those tending more to satisfy curiosity than to the true knowledge of God or piety, should be studiously cut off, so that I might keep the reader occupied in considering matters more serious and useful for salvation. Furthermore, in those allegories which Scripture does not point out with a finger, it seemed best to spend almost no effort, because although some are neatly applied to theological matters, they are nevertheless little firm. And curious minds otherwise take too much delight in them; for which reason Scripture is often twisted into a foreign sense, not without great danger to the truth. But the most putrid trifles of the Jews, and their more than old-womanish fables, and the most monstrous interpretations of Scripture which they invent, I judged to be entirely unworthy of being touched upon even by a single word. For I do not value their judgments concerning the meaning of Scripture any more than those pronounced by a blind man concerning colors. For that kind of men has been so impure, by the just judgment of God, that it was blinded long ago, so that it stumbles in the very midday as if in the densest darkness. Thus Osiander: whom the Dean and Faculty of Theological Study at the University of Tübingen rightly judged to have carried every point in this paraphrase. They put forward these causes for this judgment concerning this golden work, which they call so by its own right. For he neither rejects that old translation, which is pleasing by the name of antiquity: nor yet, if there are any errors in that version, does he hide them, but explains the more obscure ones: he points his finger to the principal theological places: so that true and solid consolation may be sought from there. And although he is excellently learned in Hebrew and Chaldean, yet he is not so addicted to the commentaries of the Hebrews that he does not judge the explanations of the Fathers and the moderns, who brought the knowledge of Christ to the interpretation of the sacred letters, to be preferable. He himself brings forward many things thought out with the highest industry and elaborated by his genius, for the sake of his excellent learning, to illustrate the Biblical texts: finally, in all things he follows a brevity that is not so much pleasant as it is useful. And since one and the same work aims at this, that it may restore those old Latin Bibles to their own splendor, explain Hebraisms, unfold obscure things, establish the best and briefest Commentaries, and help the learned and unlearned alike; yet let nothing in all these be troublesome, disjointed, or idle. Therefore, what Flaccus thought was joined with the greatest difficulty, D. D. Osiander has achieved quite happily: that both abundance in brevity and brevity in abundance, and in both, a clear and pleasing explanation of the highest and best things may be discerned. So far he. We add to this judgment the judgment which Urbanus Regius added after the distinguished praises of B. Luther: This judgment did not flow from love, but love from judgment. For which reason our blessed Lord Dr. Weller has deserved very well indeed of the Church, while he was the author and advocate that the Osiandrian Paraphrase, translated into the German language by M. David Fortner, should be published together with the text of the version of B. Luther—to which Joh. Sturmius, a primary Calvinist rhetorician, professed that the others of the Greeks, Latins, and others yield in perspicuity, purity, propriety, and similarity to the Hebrew origin, to such an extent that he testified that, just as no one is read to have surpassed Apelles among painters, so no one among writers will surpass the translation of Luther—and with the most useful scholia of the Great Man, in most elegant type, with notes placed separately from the text, in the year 1650 at Lüneburg. Matth. Polus, from among the Reformed, also praises Osiander in his Synopsis Criticorum. This author, he says, is not prolix, but solid: indeed, the Theological Faculty of Tübingen does not obscurely approve the judgment concerning Osiander's work.

For the significant good and benefit of the Church, a German Paraphrase has also been adorned in this century, which they are accustomed to call now the Nuremberg [Paraphrase] from the place of publication, now the Weimar [Paraphrase], because it was promoted under the auspices of the Illustrious Dukes of the Weimar line of Saxony, and especially by the most praiseworthy care of the Most Serene Duke of Saxony, ERNEST, who is also celebrated as the author of most of the added tables, whence it is also deservedly called the ERNESTINE; it was elaborated by principal theologians of great name, which, compared with the Osiandrian, not rarely is better than entire Commentaries: and on account of the diligent collation of parallel passages it does much for elucidating the sense of Scripture. The authors of the work, as far as fame has reached us, were these: The blessed Dr. Joh. Gerhard worked out Genesis, Daniel, and the Apocalypse: The blessed Dr. Olsner, P.P. Erfurt, Leviticus: the Historical books partly the blessed Dr. Joh. Himmelius, partly the blessed Hubmeier, Superintendent of Heldburg, namely the books of Kings and Chronicles, partly M. Paul Schlevogt, such as Ezra and Nehemiah: M. Dillher, Job: but the Psalter and the books of Solomon the blessed Dr. Sal. Glassius, the blessed Dr. Weber, Superintendent of Ordruf, Isaiah: the blessed Dr. Andr. Kesler, Ezekiel: as also the Apocryphal books, except for Sirach, which the blessed Dr. Mengering is said to have illustrated: the blessed Dr. Groshein, Professor of Erfurt, expounded Matthew: M. Prætorius, Superintendent of Schleusingen, Mark and Luke: M. Mylius, court preacher of Cranichfeld, John: the blessed Joh. Major, Superintendent of Jena, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistles of John: the blessed Joh. Himmelius the Epistles to the Romans, and to the Corinthians, Dr. Nic. Zapfius, Superintendent, the minor Pauline Epistles: M. Neander, Pastor of Lobested, the Epistle to the Hebrews. Concerning the remaining Biblical books it is not certain by whom they were worked out, which perhaps was done by the Revisers of the Work; but we have received that these were that Johannine trio, the blessed Gerhard, the blessed Major, and the blessed Himmelius, as also the blessed Glassius; from whom, however, we know the principal works and direction were given to the German Adamant, our blessed Gerhard, the incomparable Theologian, from the preface of the work exhibiting the scope, contents, and use, given at Jena on June 25, in the year 1640.

To these principal works on the whole of Scripture add from ours the Annotations of the blessed Dr. Andr. Osiander on the Vulgate Latin edition in the year 1612, which are more Didactic-Elenctic, and those of the blessed Dr. Daniel Cramer on the version of the blessed Luther, which look especially to moral and homiletic use. From the Reformed, on the same version of the blessed Luther, those of the Neustadians in the year 1588 (whose frauds, however, the blessed Jac. Andreæ exposed), those of the Herbornians in the year 1595, concerning whose impostures our Theological Faculty warned in the year 1598, those of Dr. Paul Tossanus in the year 1617 (concerning whose insidious attempts the blessed Menzer in Catholischen New-Jahr q. XI. and the blessed Winckelm. T. VII. Giess. Disp. XVII. treated), as also the new Annotations on the German version compiled from diverse authors: To the new German translation the Scholia of Joh. Piscator, in the year 1604, concerning which Paulus Röder, and Dr. Petrus Piscator: to the new Belgian translation, instituted by public authority from the sources, annotations added by the authors, in the year 1642. To the new Latin translation adorned by themselves, the notes of Imman. Tremellius and Franc. Junius in the year 1585, with Beza on the N.T. in the year 1596 and the year 1610. Likewise the notes of Sebastian Castellio added to his own version (which are of the same bran as the version itself, and of little value) in the year 1551, 1555, 1573. Finally, from the Pontificals, the Scholia of Isidorus Clarius, Bishop of Foligno, added to the new Latin version adorned by himself from the Hebrew at Venice in the year 1542, which, because it did not please the Pontificals, his version was rejected; but with the Scholia, preface, and prolegomena cut away, it appeared again by the authority of the Synod of Trent in the year 1564, as Anton. Possevinus and Sixtus Senensis note.

Separately, and apart from the Biblical text, have appeared Exegetical Annotations born from the nature of the oriental languages, and the phrases and idioms of the original text, on the Old and New Testament by Ludovicus de Dieu; as also by Joh. Drusius, who however not rarely attributes too much to the Hebrews, and especially that Work which recently appeared in LONDON by the labor of MATTHEW Poole of London, namely in the year 1669, under the title SYNOPSIS CRITICORUM, and of other INTERPRETERS of HOLY SCRIPTURE: who besides others from the Critical Library now to be enumerated and the principal Interpreters of Scripture, employed not a few from the Reformed, Lud. de Dieu, Samuel Bochart in his Sacred Geography and Hierozoicon, the Criticism and Anti-Criticism of Lud. Capellus, Buxtorf, the Cinnum, Adversaria and unpublished Annotations of Thomas Gattaker, also those written in the English language by Jos. Mede, Lightfoot, Carver on Paradise, etc., and from ours one, Dr. D. Glassius, and his Philologia Sacra alone. This work is almost like a chain, and akin to the exposition of the N.T. by Augustinus Marloratus, except that this one has also employed Critics and particular Writings; and that it has not so much rendered the true sense as it has collected various senses. Also useful are observations of a different kind collected from various authors, which sometimes also serve for the elucidation of the text, such as those of the blessed Dr. Quistorpius the Elder; and also Elenctic ones, for example those of Dr. Jac. Grossius the Calvinist, which he entitled Theatrum Biblicum, for the most part collected from the writings of Amandus Polanus: But what kind of vindications and exegeses, if anyone wished to collect them from the writings of our Theologians, with the help of an index of Scriptural passages, without doubt a much more exquisite work on almost the whole of Scripture, certainly on the places which are called classical against the Pontificals and Calvinists, even from the Loci Communes of our one blessed Gerhard and his Confessio Catholica he would compile; to which, on account of the Socinians, Arminians, and Calixtines, those things which we have set forth in our System, Socinianism, Arminianism, Calixtine-heretical Harmony, and various Anti-Socinian Disputations and others, might perhaps not uselessly be added. Compare what we have said in Pædia Theol. art. post. c. II. Can. IIX. To the idioms of the original text, however, besides the Philologia Sacra of the blessed Glassius and the Clavis Scripturæ of Flacius, those contribute which we designated from the Critics in the Commentary on Genesis 1, p. 103, and Pæd. l. c. Can. IX. from which, if particular treatises and Biblical Disputations treating of the passages were added, notes could be adorned which would be most conducive and very useful for the understanding of the phraseology of the Scripture of the Old and New Testament. To difficult passages, and the phrase and sense of the Holy Spirit, those things which have been gathered in the BIBLIOTHECA CRITICO-SACRA in London also sometimes contribute not a little, if they are employed with judgment: which work is distributed into nine volumes, and in the first five presents the perpetual annotations of S. Münster, F. Vatablus, S. Castalio, Is. Clarius, Joh. Drusius, & H. Grotius on the Old Testament, with the singular notes and commentaries of P. Fagius, A. Masius, P. Codurcus, F. Forerius, C. Badwell, Ed. Liveley, & D. Heschelius: In the sixth and seventh volumes are contained the annotations of L. Valla, D. Erasmus, F. Vatablus, S. Castalio, Is. Clarius, N. Zeger, Joh. Drusius, & H. Grotius on the New Testament, with the scattered notes of H. Stephanus, J. Scaliger, Is. Casaubon, Joh. Cameron, Lud. Capellus, & the particular notes of S. Münster, Jac. Capellus & Sc. Gentilis: The eighth and ninth contain very many books and treatises previously published separately, and not easily obtainable, which serve for the explanation of Holy Scripture. Such as Christ. Helvicus's Desire of Eve, and the Paradisiacal Proto-Evangelium, Joh. Buteo on Noah's Ark, Matthaeus Hostus on the construction of Noah's Ark. Mart. Helvicus on the Prophecy of Jacob, Gen. XLIX. v. 10. P. Pithaeus's collation of Mosaic and Roman laws, Georg. Rittershusius on the Right of Asylum. Mat. Hostus on the single combat of David and Goliath, 1 Sam. XVII. Mich. Rothardus's Samuel Revived, and Saul αὐτόχειρ. Leo Allatius's Syntagma on the Engastrimythus. Gasp. Varrerius on A dissertation on the region of Ophir. William Schickard on the feast of Purim. Benedict Arias Montanus's book of Jewish Antiquities. Bonaventura Cornelius Bertram on the Republic of the Jews. The same author's Francktal Lucubrations, or a Specimen of Expositions on the most difficult passages of both Testaments. Peter Cunaeus on the Republic of the Hebrews, Gaspar Waser on ancient Hebrew coins and measures. Antonio de Nebrija's Quinquagena, or an explanation of fifty passages of Holy Scripture. John Drusius's various works; namely, Animadversions, Notes on the Sacred Parallels, Sacred Observations, Hebrew Questions, Proverbs, Miscellanies of sacred locutions, on questions by letter, on the name Elohim. From the eighth volume. Also from the ninth volume of Critical Treatises, Nicholas Fuller's Sacred Miscellanies. Samuel Petit's Various readings on Holy Scripture. Simon de Muis's Sacred Miscellanies woven together from various Rabbis. John. Gregory's Notes and Observations on some passages of Holy Scripture, Paul Fagius's collation of the principal translations of the Old Testament. Christopher Cartwright's Hebrew Mellificium, or observations taken from the monuments of the ancient Hebrews. Lucas Brugensis's Notations on the variant passages of the Holy Bible. John Cloppenburg's Sacred Critical Collations by letters with Ludovicus de Dieu. Franciscus Moncaeius's Aaron Purgatus, or on the Golden Calf. Hugo Grotius on the Truth of the Christian Religion, etc. For the emendation of the versions of the Seventy Interpreters, the Vulgate Latin, and others, and for the assertion of Hebrew sincerity in countless places, those things which John Buxtorf did in his Anti-Critic against Ludovicus Capellus, in his Antibarbarus and Censure of the Vulgate version, as also the Biblical Conference of Sixtinus Amama, in the Collation to the New Testament, Laurentius Valla, in Phil. Sacred part I. B. Glassius observed, and those things which have been observed in our Sacred Critic, where we have amended several hundred passages of the version of the Seventy Interpreters and the Vulgate Latin, and have vindicated the original text from the suspicion of corruptions against John Morin and other Papists, as well as Theodore Beza and others: Which has been done most frequently in these Annotations against Grotius (and those like him); whose suspicions concerning the diverse readings and corruptions of the original text, I would wonder that they were not only held as valid by Brian Walton, the author of the English Polyglot work, but also added to that illustrious work, were it not that other distinguished men had long since noted this man's remarkable lack of judgment in other matters as well, and especially in the fact that he makes the Samaritan text authentic, and that he was found to have bestowed the same honor upon that most inept of critics, Ludovicus Capellus himself. The Philological-Theological notes of Theodore Hackspan also deserve praise, where he is not carried away by a desire for singularity or Calixtine novelty. Our blessed Franzius also rightly expounded many oracles in his treatise on the Interpretation of Scripture, many in his vindications the blessed D. Helvicus and the blessed D. Georg Koenig, many the blessed Walther in his Officina, Spongia, Harmonia, Exercitationibus, many the blessed Glassius in the Exegetical notes added to the Gospels and Epistles, the Onomatologia Messiae, Christologia; to say nothing of others now.

To this end contribute those who have recalled passages that are seemingly contradictory to harmony, which, besides Richard of Cluny, who wrote questions on the 'antikeimena' or contraries in the year 1160, and Seraphinus Cumarinus, who compiled two volumes on contrary passages in the Old and New Testaments under the title Conciliation of Scripture passages in the year 1566 from the Fathers, was done likewise from the Fathers by Hermann Badius, and also by the blessed Althammer, and the blessed D. Walther, as also in part by Franciscus Junius in his Sacred Parallels. Antonio Possevino also refers to Gerard of Bergamo, Bishop of Saronno, who adorned the Concordances of the New with the Old Testament.

Finally, those who have compiled Biblical compendia must not be passed over: such as Richard of St. Victor, who published an epitome of the whole Scripture in the year 1140. Petrus Verbelius, surnamed Aureolus, who wrote a Breviary of the Bible in the year 1317. Of our own, Vitus Dietericus adorned the summaries of the Biblical chapters, prefixed to Luther's Bibles. There also appeared John Brenz's arguments and summaries on the books of the Old and New Testaments at Hall in Swabia in the year 1548. Lucas Loffius's Epitome of the Bibles in the year 1599 at Frankfurt. D. Aegidius Hunnius's Biblical Epitome at Wittenberg in 1593. An Enchiridion of Biblical chapters from the Commentaries of Lucas Osiander at Tübingen in 1601. Wilhelm Alard's Biblical Epitome at Rostock in 1596. The summaries of D. Leonhard Hutter, D. Daniel Cramer, and M. John Saubert are prefixed to various Biblical editions of the blessed Luther. Vitus Albinus's Epitome contains summaries with more notable sayings, Erfurt, in the year 1592.

These things concerning the Interpreters of Scripture: Those who have written on individual books of the Old Testament will be presented next. A catalog of authors who have written on the Holy Bible, increased by more than 400 authors after the edition of G. Theophilus, appeared at Wittenberg in the year 1579. There also exists Jacob Zanach's Theological Library, both of authors who have written on the Holy Bible and of subjects, published in the year 1592: as well as Peter Besodner's Theological Library, or an index of the principal Bibles and their Hebrew, Greek, and Latin interpreters, both ancient and modern, published at Frankfurt in the year 1609.

XIX. The causes to be observed here of oversights, false interpretations, deviations from the Holy text and the sense of the Holy Spirit, corruptions, and even ineptitudes, and absurd and fabulous interpretations of Scripture, which occur among very many interpreters. Of which these are the most important. I. Ignorance of the original language: which flourished greatly in previous centuries, but especially regarding the Hebrew idiom: whence even the ancient Fathers frequently hallucinated, most of whom, if you except Origen, Theodoret, and Jerome among the interpreters of Scripture, were entirely ignorant of the Holy Language: but the Doctors of later centuries, and the Scholastics especially on account of their ignorance of both the Greek and Hebrew languages, and the barbarism dominating even in the Latin itself, produced everywhere not only inconvenient and false, but even inept and absurd expositions, as noted by Sixtinus Amama in the Anti-Barbarus Biblicus, and others. Which indeed is not so surprising regarding them: since that ignorance even prevailed among the Clergy around the beginnings of the Reformation, so that, as the famous Espencæus testifies in 2 Tim. III, to know Greek was suspicious: to know Hebrew was almost heretical: and that Arias Montanus, on account of the effort spent on the translation of the Bibles and the Royal work, was accused of various heresies before the Roman Pontiff, as his Apology has taught, as Amama observes in the Prolegomena to the Censure of the Vulgate Version. Guilhelmus Raynerius in the preface to the Apology for the Roman Church, published at Paris in 1615, slanders Hebrew and Greek letters as the assertors of depraved opinions, and says that in our age, since those have prevailed, depraved dogmas have been brought in by starving little Greeks as if they were new oracles fallen from heaven. But I cannot wonder enough that even now there are found among the Evangelicals themselves those who do not so much require knowledge of the Hebrew language for Holy Theology, a point which we have corrected in Dr. Georg Calixt, in the preface to his Isagoge Theologica, as was fitting, and in Dr. Hermann Conring, Dr. Wasmuth has expressed his detestation in his Anti-Conring.

II. The authority of the Greek Version of the LXX Interpreters, which, just as it was great among those who could not compare the sources, so, as it departed from the Hebrew truth—which it does in countless places—those who used it were bound to err much more, since they did not always grasp its meaning, and the Greek copies also varied greatly. See what we have said about these things in the Critica Sacra.

III. The manifold errors of the Latin Vulgate: those who used it alone, which was done by many, or who held it as authentic after the definition of the Council of Trent, could not but diverge from the true sense. For we have shown in the Critica Sacra, p. 567, through eight classes, with how many errors it teems, namely that even after the Clementine revision there occur in it errors that are ἀντοφατικὰ (contradictory), contradicting the sources of truth, ἀριθμητικὰ (arithmetical), ἐλλειπτικὰ (elliptical), πλεοναστικὰ (pleonastic), γραφικὰ (scribal), διαιρετικὰ (divisional), ὀνομαστικὰ (nominal), and others; indeed, that it impinges upon the faith not only by contradicting, adding to, or taking away from the Word of God, by changing the words and the sense of Scripture, and by varying the circumstances, but also by approving fables, encrusting it with false opinions, inverting divine constitutions, establishing foundations for a false faith, changing sacred maxims and sentences, enervating the loci of faith, and above all by patronizing heretical opinions. Compare Sixtus Amama’s Censure of the Vulgate Version on the Pentateuch. Amama’s Censure of the Vulgate Version on the Pentateuch.

IV. The lack of concordances. For, being destitute of these—since they were only invented four centuries ago—they could not compare the passages of Scripture as is fitting, for the more successful eliciting of the sense of Scripture: just as today this can be done with great fruit, since not only Latin, German, and Greek, but also Hebrew concordances exist. See what Conr. Kirchner, author of the Greek Concordances of the LXX Interpreters, wrote about the use of concordances, and compare Pæd. Theol. c. II. Can. II.

V. The hypothesis concerning the manifold sense of Scripture, which the Scholastics and Papists especially fostered and still foster, because of which it happened that the single, true, and genuine sense was obscured everywhere, or even neglected by investigating senses which they called mystical—allegorical, anagogical, tropological—or at least a double literal sense was introduced: whence things were rendered ambiguous and obscure which are not so at all, and which, by the intention of the Holy Spirit, ought not to have been. How this was sinned against in part even by the Fathers, especially by Origen, who explained things allegorically—Jerome saying that he did whatever he could, and for that reason was called allegorical κατ' ἀντονομασίαν (by antonomasia), Sidon. Apollin. l. IX. Epist. 2—(inasmuch as, according to Theophilus of Alexandria, he destroyed the truth of Scripture with the shadows and empty images of allegory): but far more gravely by the Rabbis with their mystical and Cabbalistic senses, and most gravely of all by the Papists, who in some things are worse than the Rabbis themselves, we have shown in our Prolegomena to Genesis, c. IIX. We have warned, however, that some of the Calvinists follow them, and especially Lud. Capellus, l. c. p. 69; and we are about to warn the same concerning Grotius in his proper place. Nor can what Dr. Hackspan says in his Prolegomena to Not. Phil. Theol. p. 4 be approved: Let the philologist presuppose that there is one literal sense of one passage, except for a few places in the Old Testament that share a double sense, and which is intended by the Holy Spirit and applied and explained by Him in the New Testament: we have abundantly refuted that in the aforementioned place.

VI. Various methods of interpreting Scripture: which Sixtus of Siena in his art of expounding Scripture in book III of his Bibliotheca Sacra distributed into XXIV classes,

and multiplies them so much under these distributions that they exceed LX, boasting that no one before him had written out this art. If anyone reads them through, he will recognize them as astonishing even by their very names, and I well know he will marvel that it was of such great concern to the dark Scholastics and Papists to cast darkness upon the Scriptures. For there is in them not only Stigmatic, Syllabic, and the Notariaca of the Hebrews, but Rhapsody, and even Hagiographic, Ecclesiastical (and the same Anonymous, Proonymous), Ethnic (chain, and cento), Scholastic, Dictionarial, Lectural, Pandestical, Meditative, lowly, sublime, to say nothing of others. Behold a certain specimen of the Dictionarial Method, produced by Sixtus on p. 218 from the Dictionary of Peter Berchorius the Frenchman! Exposition on the letter A, or concerning the letter A: FIRST we can note that this letter, or syllable A, can be taken in three ways. For it is taken for an initiatory letter, for an interjection of grieving and lamenting, and for an ablative preposition; by the first I can understand the initiator of all things: by the second I can accept the miserable man and traveler: but by the third the impious man and sinner. For in the first way, A is the first letter of the Alphabet, signifying Him who is first in the order of things, namely GOD, who says of Himself in the first chapter of the Apocalypse: I am the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end. For Alpha in Greek is the same as A in Latin. In the second way, A is an interjection of one grieving: and thus it can signify the human condition, which is, namely, tearful and empty, whence this is that first voice which a child, coming to this misery, immediately cries out, saying A, A, as if grieving for the misery into which he has entered. Concerning which it is written in Wisdom chapter 7, I being born received the air, and emitted the first voice like others, weeping. In the third way A is an Ablative preposition, serving the Ablative, that is, the princes of the world: and thus it can signify to me proud men, who always wish to be preferred to others, and especially those in charge and bailiffs, who serve the ablative, that is, the princes of the world; who do not cease to take away the goods of their subjects. 2 Cor. XI. The governor of the people under Aretas the king at DAMASCUS, sought to apprehend me &c. Whence concerning such an A, that which is written in Psalm CXXXIX can be said: Deliver me from the wicked MAN. Concerning the first A again, the initiatory, whatever is said about God, or even about the beginning, can be said. Concerning the second A, the lamentative, everything that is said about human misery can be said: But concerning the third A, whatever is said about evil princes can be said, &c. What is it to defile the Holy Scriptures, if this is not? Add if you please from the Compendium of Aureolus the distribution of Scripture, which Sixtus brought forward as an example of the Scholastic Method on p. 221. and you will marvel that these futile things were a delight to this great Librarian and censor of ours, which could not but be a mockery to our novices. The same Senensis designated the diverse classes of Interpreters, listing according to alphabetical order Abbreviators, Annotators, Accumulators, Collectors, (Rhapsodists, Centonists), Compendiaries, Chronographers, Dialogists, Dictionarians, Disputers and Questioners, Eclogists, Epistolarians, Geographers, Harmonists, Homiliasts, and Enarrators, Isagogics, Indicists, Meditators, Paraphrasts, Partitors, Poets, Sciographics, Scholastics, Thematics, Translators: of which the order of Scholastics, by whom the sacred books have been most defiled, is the most numerous, and alone exhibits CXXIII authors.

VII. Aberration from the true scope and object of Scripture: That they have not sought Christ, who is the A & Ω of the Holy Scriptures, in the Scriptures, but any other things whatsoever. Which as it is to be lamented in the Jews, so much the more in those who from

They derive their name from Christ: most especially, however, those who wish to be considered Evangelical; e.g., in Calvin, whom the blessed Hunnius showed to Judaize; in Grotius, whom these writings of ours will show to be worse than the Jews. Petrus Cunaeus, in book III of his Republic of the Hebrews, ch. 9, imagines that even if the multitude of the Jews had known nothing of the Messiah, nonetheless heavenly blessedness could not have been denied to them on account of the Patriarchs, who beheld the Messiah in their minds and received the promise of the covenant: I will be YOUR GOD and that of your seed. But this is true atheism, to promise salvation without knowledge and faith in the Messiah. But then, if the Messiah is set forth in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, as he himself testifies to the Jews in John 5:39, how could they have been ignorant of him?

VIII. Excessive veneration of the Hebrews: After Hebrew letters began to be cultivated, it happened to some, who prided themselves on their knowledge of Grammar alone and the reading of Hebrew writers, that they slipped into the other extreme, attributing too much to the commentaries and other writings of the Hebrews, which had once been utterly neglected alongside the Hebrew sources. The blessed Johann Forster complained gravely about this in his Preface to his Lexicon: I have seen, he says, for many years now, since the restoration of the doctrine of the Gospel, the commentaries of the Rabbis reigning in the schools of Christians no less in the translation and interpretation of Holy Scripture than in the synagogues of the Jews themselves, and their פרושים [Pharisees] being cultivated and adored by all with the highest reverence and religion as if they were the sacrosanct mysteries of God. Hence it has come about that you could by no means attain the certain sense of Holy Scripture. And afterwards: And I have often vehemently wondered at the dullness of our countrymen (if I may say so with all respect to them), who, without any judgment, preferred to embrace the Commentaries of the Jews—in which there is no light, no knowledge of God, no Spirit, no true and solid knowledge of any discipline or art, no knowledge of languages, and not even of the Hebrew language itself—rather than to consider the words and their meanings themselves. What, I ask, could the Jews understand, whose hearts (as our Apostle Paul testifies) remain covered by the veil of Moses in the reading of the Old Testament to this very day, and whose senses are blinded so that they cannot look to the end of the law? But those who do not see or acknowledge the end of the law, the Son of God, born according to the flesh of a virgin, the true Messiah, mediator, victim, and liberator of the human race, and who are ignorant that he is the subject and scope of the entire Scripture; furthermore, who dream that his kingdom is only external, corporal, and temporal, and do not believe it to be spiritual or eternal, nor distinguish between the promises of the law and the Gospel concerning the free remission of sins on account of Christ the Mediator: what and how could they teach others about Moses and the Prophets? Wherefore Christ rightly called them blind and leaders of the blind, not to mention in the meantime their virulence and the hatred with which they burn against Christ, so that you find few prophecies about Christ whose words or entire meaning they have not most wickedly corrupted. They were therefore of no use, except that, like librarians, they merely supplied us Christians with the sacred books (which we call the Bible) and a few grammars; but as far as the understanding of Holy Scripture (as I have already said) and even the knowledge of the Hebrew language is concerned, they provided absolutely nothing that deserves praise. For their Dictionaries and Commentaries have brought more obscurity and error into the Church of Christ than light and truth. This can be seen in the Commentaries of our countrymen; when (as it seems to them) an ambiguous word or a more obscure sentence occurs, they cite a few Rabbis, and as they have explained it in various ways (for they rarely or never agree among themselves), they report it and afterwards leave the reader in doubt; but they do not indicate at all which of them sensed it correctly and whom one ought to follow; or if they do indicate it, because they are ignorant of the force of the words, they easily embrace the false for the true, so that not only do they err and are deceived themselves, but they also deceive the reader, and thus, according to Christ's saying, it happens that if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the pit. These are the words of the blessed Forster.

Therefore, those things which Theodorus Hackspan has in the cited prolegomena, p. 6, cannot be simply approved: It will be useful, nay almost necessary, for an Interpreter to consult the Rabbis concerning the true meaning of words, even where they occur more frequently. For usage is not always and everywhere one and the same. Moreover, the Rabbis have preserved the usage and skill of many words for many centuries; but Christians only attained the knowledge of this language from the Jewish teachers themselves in the last century. If, therefore, we see a dispute arise, as we often see happen between Avenarius and Schindler, we safely recur to the Jews and seek the end of the controversy from them, even if it is not appropriate to follow them in the exposition of mysteries. Distinguished philologists clash here on the opposite front, and standing on the side not of our Forster, whose pronouncement against the commentaries of the Jews he declares sufficiently harsh, but of Hackspan, whom Hottinger praises in Thesaurus Phil. p. 244, appealing to Münster in the preface to the Bible translated by him, who denies that anyone can interpret Holy Scripture correctly without the aid of the Rabbis. Whom Joh. Leusden also cites for this purpose in Philologo Hebræo-mixto, (agreeing with those who have praised the Rabbinic commentators almost to the skies, and establishing that they are not only useful for Christians to read for a good understanding of Holy Scripture, but in a certain way necessary) p. 114 seqq. But in truth, Münster did not absolutely deny this; at least he asserted that the Hebrews are often monitors of the truth, and that some have been hallucinating who have attempted to interpret the Hebrew text in our age without the aid of the Hebrews: nor is it among the impossibilities to draw the true sense from the Hebrew Scripture without employing the commentaries of the Rabbis: But neither does Forster exclude the grammar of the Hebrews, which he acknowledges they themselves have supplied to us Christians: nor the explanation of words handed down by the Hebrews: at least that they contribute something besides, WHICH DESERVES PRAISE, to a solid understanding of Scripture, without having heaped MORE obscurity and error (he speaks in a comparative sense) into the Church of Christ than light and truth: nor does he wish that we should depend AS MUCH on the authority of the Rabbis AS we should lean on the foundation of Scripture, which are again said comparatively; and he renders this reason for his undertaking: Moved therefore by pious zeal, I decided to compile a Dictionary, in which the true and certain meaning of Hebrew words would be indicated from Moses and the Prophets, so that students of this language would not be troubled by that most confused Babylon and variety of meanings which they have hitherto attributed to a single theme, nor depend so much on the authority of the Rabbis as lean on the solid foundation of Holy Scripture. And Forster did not only say this, but he also proved it at length in that golden preface, and in the whole Dictionary, truly incomparable, which was of the greatest use to Marco Marini in his Arca Noæ, although he (which is ingratitude) kept silent the name of the Author, and concealed from whom he had profited. I could mention, he says, more than a thousand themes, the true and genuine meaning of which neither their Dictionaries nor their Commentaries show, but rather miserably lead the student of that language away from the truth. Let their entire Synagogue tell me, with all their books brought together, what the name תרף properly signifies, and what its etymology is. Similarly, what is the etymology and meaning of the name ישרון? &c. I am not ignorant of what the most learned Schickard retorted against our Forster in Behinat Happerushim p. 107. But he, captured by an excessive love of the Rabbis, treated in unworthy ways a man who has deserved exceedingly well

of Hebrew literature, so that he deservedly begged pardon for his fault—may his blessed shades forgive me! Christopher Cartwright of York also strongly attacks Forster in his Electa Thargumico-Rabbinica on Genesis, in the preface, and thunders against his pride and insolence, even though he protests that he wishes to detract nothing from his labor and reputation. But with what bile he rose up against him, and how much he attempted to detract not from the blessed Forster's work, which he rashly attributes to him, but from his erudition and skill in Hebrew literature, that preface will testify. But in what place, and in how much esteem, Forster's Lexicon and his Hebrew erudition ought to be held, the blessed Dr. Mauckisch at length and with clear documents in his Philological-Theological Notes defends Forster, who was noted and attacked by Mercer in France in the notes added to Pagnini's Thesaurus, and in Italy by Marco Marini in the Arca Noae, although his name was suppressed. He not so much affirms as demonstrates with evident examples that this is the source and fountain of the lexicons which have appeared since his death, from which Mercer's notes on Pagnini's Thesaurus flowed, and from this thesaurus into Marco Marini's Arca Noae. But if from this a lack of skill in Hebrew literature and ignorance of Rabbinic writers is certainly concluded, because Forster sometimes cited Rabbinic writings from the allegations of others, what is to be thought of this Aristarchus, who frequently alleges the same things in such a way, and immediately at the beginning of his Annotations cited R. David Kimchi in no other way than that Fagius testifies that he explains the first Biblical verse in the Roots, etc. Moreover, if Cartwright is unwilling to lend an ear to the blessed Lutheran Forster, let him hear Marco Marini, who in the preface to his Arca, giving the reason why he did not wish to explain the ambiguous meanings of words from the opinions of the Rabbis (as was done by some), but rather by the collation of Scripture itself and by conjectures, adds: 'I avoid the opinions of the Rabbis, and especially the older ones, all the more willingly because I see that they have lost all skill in the Hebrew language, as you can discover from the words of Kimchi himself, etc.' Let him hear Theodore Beza from his own school, who in his Icones of illustrious men highly commends Forster's Lexicon along with the author himself, because it testifies that he was born for the whole Church, in which, just as in the things themselves, so also in his wishes, he contends that the Hebrew grammarians often blundered, etc. We add what the excellent Christian Rabbi added in place of a conclusion from his own experience: 'If there is anyone,' he says, 'who has poured out his resources on the Rabbis, who has spent a long time in their synagogues, who has supported the teachers themselves at home at his own expense, who has studiously unrolled their commentaries, it is Forster, and yet (I call God and my conscience to witness) I have brought back nothing excellent, and which would be worthy of singular praise. I was initially addicted to them as anyone else, but the more addicted I was to them once, the more hostile I have become now, because I confess truly, but not without pain, that I have wasted all my labor and oil. And although I sometimes bring forward the interpretations of words by the Rabbis, I do it partly so that the sciolists may see that I have also read their writings, and partly to show their ineptitude and ignorance, if ever I allege several opinions dissenting among themselves.' But I never or very rarely cite them to rely on their authority, but to convince those who are more addicted to the Rabbis, so that they may the more easily agree with my exposition: knowing very well that those who are blind (as indeed all Jews are) cannot testify to the truth, nor should faith be placed in them. Thus Forster. With whom the blessed Luther agrees in the preface to the exposition of the last words of David, Vol. VIII, Altenburg German, p. 305, gravely warning that one should not labor to force the sense of the Rabbis upon Christians, since it creeps in of its own accord and insinuates itself, even when we wish to avoid it as much as possible: 'It sticks of itself anyway like pitch and glue, even when one wants to guard against it on purpose.' Such things occur here and there in Luther: In the tract 'On the Schemhamphoras', Vol. VIII. Jena, fol. 147: 'If, over such judgment and condemnation of the Jews, a Christian wants to seek understanding in the Scripture from the Jews, what does he do other than seek sight from a blind man, wisdom from the raving, life from the dead, grace and truth from the devil? It serves him right if he also becomes insane, blind, and raving, as his masters are condemned by God.' But this by no means prevents the Hebrews from being urged from the Rabbis or their teachers, or Rabbis being opposed to Rabbis, according to human capacity; or when the matter concerns institutions, rites, and ceremonies, the Hebrews may be heard where they do not dissent from the Scriptures, nor inculcate their own secondary traditions; nor does it prohibit, I think, that when some hapax legomenon occurs, or whose root is unusual and not found in the Code, its sense may sometimes be sought from the writings of the Rabbis, which use John Mercer teaches in Joel. 1, 17, since in that case it is also permitted to turn to related languages, Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic. Although even in historical matters, laws, and rites, we are hardly safely guided by the traditions and writings of the Hebrews: nor can we add our vote here to the opinion of Hackspan in the place cited: 'No one will explain the history of idols, and likewise the laws proper to the Hebrew people, and also various rites, more correctly than a Jew, and as for the laws which they kept secret from other nations, and they did not care about them: nor shall we less consult the Jews about those laws, which are a great part of the Old Testament, than we consult the Romans about the Twelve Tables, the Athenians about the Athenians: and we learn the laws of the Mohammedans from the Mohammedans.' Without the aid of these, there is mere darkness for Christian interpreters. Such is almost the judgment of John Lightfoot, Doctor of the Cambridge Academy, in his Hebrew and Talmudic Hours on the Gospels, concerning the writings of the New Testament. Matth. in the preface, who does not hesitate to defend this paradox, that the interpreters have no clearer text of the Gospel than the Jews. We do not deny, of course, that the writings of the Rabbis can be compared in such matters, but only so that they may be tested against Scripture; in which, if there is MERE DARKNESS without the aid of the traditions of the Rabbis, how is the law celebrated for its clarity in Scripture and compared to a light and a lamp, how could the Israelites, without such an aid, have obtained the true sense of the laws from the law, as it proceeded from God and was recorded by Moses, and from where shall we be made certain that the genuine sense of the laws has been propagated down to those Rabbis who are now handled by our hands, or to which of them, where they disagree among themselves, should trust be given, and that there are not mixed in by the same, even in those matters on which they perhaps agree, δευτερώσεις, such as were disapproved by Christ? The example of the Roman and Athenian laws, therefore, is different, which have been preserved in writing, though perhaps the laws and customs of the ancients will not be learned safely enough from the more recent Athenians or modern Romans. But it is well known how much the Muhammadans themselves contend about the sense of their laws, and indeed the Rabbanite and Karaite Jews, since the latter, having rejected traditions, adhere only to the texts of Scripture, and do not observe the statutes of the Rabbis, e.g., concerning degrees of consanguinity, divorces, purifications of women, forbidden and permitted foods, and maintain that all Israelites from the beginning were קראים Karaites, but that the degenerate Rabbanites fell away from the institutions of their ancestors, or indeed of God, or from the rest of the Ancient Hebrews also, See Comment. in Gen. p. 555. while the former are carried away into various divorces of opinions. Whence it cannot be rashly approved that, without a more accurate examination, those things which concerning rites and laws this one, or that one among the Rabbis, or even the Talmud itself hands down, should therefore be accepted, and applied to the interpretation of the Mosaic laws: when rather their meaning should be sought from a diligent scrutiny of Holy Scripture itself. And Isaac Casaubon, to whom Hottinger appeals along with Hackspan, spoke more cautiously about these matters, in Exerc. XIV. on Baronius's Annals, ch. VII. p. 402. Where the Hebrew language is concerned, he says, and the propriety of some word, or some TALMUDIC INSTITUTION (but where are TALMUDIC INSTITUTIONS held in the Hebrew Code? Casaubon deals with these, not with Mosaic laws and their meaning), no small amount is deservedly attributed by Christians: but when one comes from words TO THINGS, or TO HISTORY, or to the explanation OF THE ANCIENT THINGS of the old people (such as rites and customs, or divine laws), unless we wish TO BE DECEIVED and misled, NO faith at all should be placed in them. Which are clearly different from Hackspan's assertion, if not diametrically opposed to it. The judgment of Joh. Buxtorf, easily the Prince of Christian Rabbis, in the dedicatory preface to his Philological and Theological Dissertations, is also more moderate. When Maro was reading Ennius, he is said to have remarked: That he was gathering gold from a dunghill. And St. Jerome, speaking somewhere of the Apocrypha, says: It is a matter of great prudence to seek gold in the mud. The same can be said of the books and readers of the Hebrews. It is enough, therefore, if some gold lies hidden in those otherwise impure veins, and can be found: let us not regret the labor and effort: but judgment must be applied, the dross must be separated and rejected, and, to use a phrase, one must attend to how much bronze differs from lupines. Nor should this study be considered as alien to us Christians as is commonly held, we who are the successors and descendants of the Jews, as Lactantius writes, and we dwell in the Tabernacles of Shem, that is, as Jerome interprets it, we are occupied in the erudition and knowledge of the Scriptures, Israel having been cast out. For the rest, the judgment of Blessed Luther, Vol. III. on Genesis ch. XXV. f. 10, is pleasing. We acknowledge indeed that it is a great benefit that we received the language from the Jews: But one must beware of the dung of the Rabbis, who have made of Holy Scripture a kind of latrine, into which they might cast their filth and most foolish opinions. I warn of this because many of our own theologians today attribute too much to the Rabbis in explaining the meaning of Scripture. In grammar I easily tolerate them, but they lack true sense and understanding, according to that saying in Isaiah XXIX: The wisdom of the wise shall perish, and the understanding of the prudent shall be hidden. This sentence testifies that there will be no understanding of Scripture among the Jews. But that book of Holy Scripture is closed and sealed to them; it speaks to that people in another language, Isaiah XXIX. Nor do they know anything other than mere blasphemies against the Christian religion. These are the words of that man of divine judgment, Blessed Luther. Similar things are found in the Tract on the Schemhamphoras, Vol. IIX. Jena, German, f. 147: that one learns the language and grammar from them, that is fine and well done, just as they also do, they learn the German language from us, the Romance language from the Walloons, and wherever they are, they learn the language of the land, but they do not learn our faith and the understanding of Scripture, etc. Meanwhile, we do not disapprove in a certain respect of Schickard's distinction between those commentaries which the Rabbis call Midrashim, and those which they call Perushim: for he himself acknowledges that the former wander further afield and soothe the reader with fabulous narratives: but he prefers the latter, because they follow the text more closely, examine individual words, and explain the idioms of the language: which, however, we believe should also be used with a grain of salt. What, moreover, Christoph. Cartwright brought forward concerning the fruits of Rabbinic writings, are either peripheral, as for instance concerning certain passages of the Old Testament explained regarding the Messiah, or concerning the preserved sincerity of the Old Testament, or very doubtful, as for instance concerning proverbial sentences contributing to the understanding of the New Testament, or likewise concerning certain rites: and concerning difficult passages of Scripture: concerning all of which we doubt not that a more certain remedy can be prepared from the Scriptures themselves than from blind Jews, and as the occasion arises we show this throughout, even though for the rest we not infrequently cite the Rabbis also for the sake of comparison, or humanly speaking.

IX. The untimely comparison of Pagan writers. Sixtus of Siena praises a certain method of interpreting Scripture, Pagan Rhapsody, which he defines as an exposition described word for word from the sayings and sentences of Gentile authors. Not unlike this was the study of those who, when they have been exercised in the reading of Exotic writers, or imbued with certain opinions of the same, mix them into the interpretation of Holy letters; which one may observe even in the Fathers, or from the sentences or histories, rites, and laws of the Pagans, both poets and others, whether to show off their polymathy, or to enrich their commentaries, they drew out many things which would have been more correctly omitted in exegetical works, or proposed in another place; not infrequently they even serve more to obscure or pervert the meaning of Holy Scripture, and they detract from the authority, dignity, and efficacy of Scripture rather than serve it, and sometimes they are not so much analogous as heterogeneous and alien, indeed they can be compared not without impiety, which we have often observed in Grotius: or finally, they judge the sacred amanuenses of God by the word and phrase of Exotic writers, with their own importunate, officious, or untimely judgment; which we detect in theological critics who, often little grounded in sacred things, assume to themselves the authority to interpret the Scriptures without a calling, and who relying solely on their confidence in languages, undertake this, when they know neither the context, nor the rest of the analogies of Scripture, and sometimes not even the analogy of faith, and having discovered a similar phrase, or as it seems to them, the same use of the meaning of a word, they immediately exclaim eureka, eureka, and it is wonderful how much they triumph in their interpretations. Which is what those are doing now, who spend all their oil and effort to strip the New Testament of that custom of speaking and those idioms which are found among the Hellenists, as we call them, the LXX Interpreters. as they were also among writers contemporary with the Apostles and in use in their own time: and so that nothing of the sort is left in the Scriptures of the N. T., they examine all Greek writers, of the most diverse ages and furthermore of the most diverse dialects, both prose and metric, and even to them, though they are anything but that, they make the sacred expressions analogous: who would undoubtedly do better if, instead of profane authors, they would institute Ecclesiastical Doctors, equally skilled in the language and in sacred matters, and instead of pagan parallelisms, a more diligent collation of the Sacred Writers, both those who wrote by the same Spirit, and those who, led by the Holy Spirit himself, are not rarely in the N. T. as regards phrase and sentiments, that is, if they would more frequently employ the concordances of the N. T. and also those of Kirchner compiled from the LXX Interpreters of the Old Testament, and from the same would evaluate the sacred ῥεύσεις. Nor undeservedly does he here praise not only his own Martinius (Preface in Technol.) concerning the books of the N. T. Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barb. p. 138, because they are so Greek that while the individual words are indeed Greek, the conjunction and phrase, as coming from Hebrew men, is recognized as mostly Hebrew, whence the idiom of the N. T. can be called Hebrew-Greek: But also our blessed Martinius, preface in the Syriac New Testament, Trost, and others, Philip Melanchthon, Orations, Vol. IV, p. 475, ὁμοψήφως: Although (this brings forward the words of the late Dr. Jacob Martini) the phrase of the New Testament can be said to be originally Greek, it does not flow purely, but is mixed with the flavor of the Hebrew and Syriac language. Wherefore, although a reader of the New Testament may be most skillfully instructed and informed in the Greek language, he will nevertheless be most unhappily occupied in the reading of it if he is ignorant of the Hebrew and Syriac languages. These are supported (says Amama) by Illyricus, Clavis, part 1, p. 664, Calvin, Beza, Piscator, Scultetus, Drusius, Fuller, Scaliger, Buxtorf, Pareus, and other doctors, both Catholic and Protestant, everywhere. Indeed, Beza also gives the reasons for this matter, at Acts 10, in his digression on the gift of tongues. And yet you may still find such headstrong men who, in order to draw the youth away from the study of the most holy language—as if it were a thing of nothing and a subject upon which generous and subtle minds, if it pleases the GODS, should be ashamed to be occupied—deny that there are Hebraisms in the New Testament. These men, I think, should be sent to the Anticyrae, either to the rudiments of the Hebrew language, or to the great Heinsius’s Aristarchus Sacrus, or if not even the clear demonstrations of the latter can tame their obstinacy. Compare what we have said about Hebraisms in the Critico Sacro, in the Annotations to Genesis, prolegomena, ch. VII, p. 27, and what men no less learned in Greek than in Hebrew have observed everywhere, especially Grotius and B. Glassius, as well as expressly Georg Pasor in his Greek Grammar, and Caspar Wyssius in his Dialectologia, Section XIII, assigning the classes of New Testament Hebraisms, of which indeed Johann Vorstius established 31 in his work on New Testament Hebraisms, and Johann approved his opinion. Leusden in his Philologus Hebraeo-Graecus, p. 95 and following, illustrating the same with various examples, and refuting Sebastian Pfochen, who rashly denies Hebraisms in the New Testament: which was also done by Thomas Gataker in his dissertation on the style of the New Testament. Leusden certainly does not hesitate, in the place cited, p. 10, to maintain that if Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Isocrates, and other profane Greek authors were to come back to life, they would not understand the Greek of the New Testament well, because it does not consist of such a Greek language as was once used by those authors: just as someone, however well-versed in the ancient writings of the Greeks and in the writings of the Apostles, would not understand the modern Greek language accepted by the modern Greeks themselves; whence it was arranged by the States of Belgium, for the sake of the modern Greeks, that the New Testament be adorned in the modern Greek language, and the Greek text of the Evangelists and Apostles was added to it side by side. One may add Ludovicus Capellus in his Spicilegium, John. Lightfoot, in Hebrew Hours, on Matthew.

X. Preconceived errors: which, just as they carry away Jewish interpreters, so too do they carry away Catholics, Calvinists, and indeed even Socinians and Arminians to glosses that conform to them; since the eyes of their minds are so fascinated by them that they cannot see the true light of Scripture. Therefore, they bring a meaning into the words of the Scriptures, they do not bring it out of them. Whereas, on the contrary, as Hilary warns in Book I of De Trinitate, the best reader is he who expects the understanding of the things said from the things themselves rather than bringing it to them, and who reports rather than imports, and does not force it to seem that what he had presumed to understand before reading is contained in the words. And since every prophecy ought to be in accordance with the analogy of faith, as the Apostle teaches in Romans XII, 6, how can those who are occupied with errors that overturn the analogy of faith render a genuine prophecy or interpretation of Scripture?

XI. The bad habit of multiplying questions. For when interpreters seek difficulties where there are no difficulties, they invent contradictions where none occur, and devote effort to devising questions without end or number—just as Sixtus of Siena praises Alphonsus Tostatus because he pursued his exposition with so many and such great Scholastic questions that he often brought forward over 170 Scholastic questions in the explanation of only one or a short chapter—they often obscure the Scripture more than they illustrate it, and they diverge too much from its simple sense and understanding.

XII. Excessive love of, if I may say so, Patristic and Scholastic theology. For after Peter Lombard had reduced the opinions of the Fathers into a compendium, and Thomas Aquinas had offered his Summa Theologiae to the world, the Holy Scriptures were held in low esteem compared to the study of the Fathers and the Scholastics, and everything resounded with Lombardian and Thomistic contentions, so much so that even those who dealt with the Bible did not seem to have fulfilled their duty unless they mixed in that Scholastic and Lombardian material everywhere. Thus, those two patchworks, says Sixtus Amama in his Oration on Barbarism, the Book of Sentences and the Summa of Thomas, were introduced into the pulpits as if they were two Testaments. These filled both pages in the theological schools. Let the example be what Sixtus of Siena has in his Scholastic reading on Psalm 117, in the Bibliotheca. S. p. 220, where he treats that Psalm, which he calls by the barbarous term Hallelujatic and laudatory, not only most ineptly according to the four causes—which he explains in a completely magisterial way from Isaiah ch. X, according to that saying, 'The Lord made a shortened word upon the earth,' illustrating the material cause by THE WORD, the formal by SHORTENED, the Agent by MADE, and the Final by upon the earth, indeed!—but he also pours darkness over this most bright Psalm from Scholastic disputation, raising and resolving a doubt in this manner: 'But a difficulty arises, whether God is to be praised? And it seems that he is not. For the Philosopher says in the first book of the Ethics that praise is not for the best things, but something greater and better: but God is above all best things: therefore praise is not owed to God, but something greater than praise, whence it is said in Ecclesiasticus 43 that God is greater than all praise.' But the contrary is that which is said here in Ps. Praise the Lord, all nations. I answer, it must be said, that we can speak of God in two ways: in one way, regarding his essence: and thus, since he is incomprehensible and ineffable, he is greater than all praise. However, reverence and the honor of latria are owed to him according to this comparison. In another way, according to his effects, which are ordered for our benefit, such as mercy and justice: and according to these, God is to be praised, and in fact is praised in the present Psalm, etc. Thus far Sixtus of Siena. This, forsooth, is to interpret Scripture! Many such things could be noted, were it not tiresome to stir up that stench. Although the study of the Holy Fathers contributes more to the explanation of Scripture, when discernment is applied and the laws of good interpretation are observed: yet it is shown by the crowd of many interpreters that this was sinned against most greatly in previous centuries under Papistic darkness, both by those who sometimes made chains without judgment, or rather patched together quilts from the Fathers, and also by those who mixed in various interpretations and opinions of the Fathers without proper examination. For it is evident even from Sixtus of Siena that the commentaries of these men teem with not a few errors, who spent two whole books on collecting the same, although while he notes the errors of others, he himself not rarely falls into errors.

XIII. The neglect of divine mysteries in Scripture when they occur, or the superfluous investigation where none are held. For in both ways it is no light sin. Thus not only the Jews, and some Scholastics, and Papists, but even Calvin and fools among the Reformed [treat] the mysteries of the Trinity and the incarnation and the Redemption of the Son of God in Scripture

They despise the oracles of the Old Testament, and are unwilling to see: indeed, Calixtus with his followers argues at length, having been seduced by certain Scholastics, that the Holy Trinity was not revealed in the books of the O.T., nor the incarnation of the Son of God, the second Person of the Deity, and other mysteries of the faith, to which Theod. Hackspan also sometimes pours cold water in his Philological and Theological Notes. But on the other side, some of the Reformed investigate and point out mysteries everywhere, even in those places in which no one could see them, or even now, with them pointing them out, can see them, not even excepting their own associates in the faith, and indeed they even claim as mysteries things which rest on no foundation of Scripture, which we have noted especially in Joh. Cocceius, the Reformed theologian, again and again in these Annotations, who did not hesitate to introduce—or rather, to intrude—the various periods and aspects of the N.T. Church into the Johannine Apocalypse, and indeed into those places where he does not deliver prophecies but proposes historical matters, such as chapters II and III, which had been introduced by Ludovicus Crocius or other teachers of his, into the prophets Isaiah and Zechariah—what more? into the Song of Solomon, and indeed even into Moses and his final words—and to scrutinize, investigate, and find in Moses, Solomon, Isaiah, Zechariah, and others, prophecies which not even the most sharp-sighted of the Fathers or theologians ever saw in the history of the Apocalypse itself, and to penetrate with the sharpness of his vision the prophecies of these men as an interpretation of the history of the Apocalypse, or at least to perceive that this was a certain exegesis of those. Whence forced, twisted, violent, and tangled interpretations shine through his writings everywhere.

XIV. Departure from the literal sense of words in Scripture to figurative interpretations: Where, namely, no necessity compels it. Which one may observe especially in the Calvinists, who wrap the clearest passages of Scripture in their figures and tropes, and often attribute different tropes to one and the same word. Some even among the Rabbis themselves reject figurative senses when the literal is neglected. R. Isaac Abarbenel on the standing still of the Sun says: Although, he says, allegorical explanations may be sought, yet Scripture must be explained conveniently according to its literal sense; our wise men have warned us, and have taught us this FOUNDATION.

XV. Less accurate observation of the context of Scripture. Which has been the cause of very many errors. Concerning which one should compare the blessed Franzius on the Interpretation of Scripture, precept II, no. 48 et seqq., illustrating this with more than a hundred examples or oracles.

XVI. Comparison of words and phrases from very different places. Which is especially frequent among the Socinians and Calvinists. To be sure, parallel passages are indeed rightly compared, so that Scripture may be its own interpreter, since it is not of private interpretation. But in the first and primary place, both the literal text of the words and the connection of the context must be taken into account: nor are the passages which are considered parallel always such, but often treat of far different things, and are most alien to the passages being dealt with.
