AGGÆUS, fe- stivus & lætus, qui seminavit in lacrymis, ut in gau- dio meteret, destructum templum ædificat, De- umque patrem inducit loquentem, Adhuc unum modicum, & ego commovebo cœlum & terram, & mare, & aridam, & movebo omnes gentes, & veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus.

ZACHARIAS me- mor Domini sui, multiplex in prophetia, Jesum ve- stibus sordidis indutum & lapidem oculorum se- ptem; candelabrumq; aureum cum totidem lucer- nis quot oculis; duas quoque olivas a sinistris lam- padis cernit & dextris: ut post equos nigros, rufos, albos, & varios, & dissipatas quadrigas ex Ephraim, & equum de Jerusalem, pauperem regem vaticine- tur, & prædicet, sedentem super pullum filium asi- næ subjugalis.

MALACHIAS aperte, & in fine omnium Prophetarum, de abjectione Israël, & vo- catione Gentium, Non est mihi, ait, voluntas in vo- bis, dicit Dominus exercituum: & munus non susci- piam de manu vestra. Ab ortu enim Solis usque ad oc- casum, magnum est nomen meum in gentibus: & in omni loco sacrificatur, & offertur nomini meo obla- tio munda.

ISAIAM, JEREMIAM, EZECHIE- LEM & DANIELEM, quis potest vel intelligere vel exponere? Quorum primus non prophetiam mihi videtur texere, sed Evangelium. Secun- dus virgam nuceam, & ollam succensam a facie a- quilonis, & pardum spoliatum suis coloribus, & quadruplex diversis metris nectit Alphabetum. Tertius principia & finem tantis habet obscurita- tibus involuta, ut apud Hebræos istæ partes cum exordio Geneseos ante annos triginta non legan- tur. Quartus vero, qui & extremus inter quatuor Prophetas, temporum conscius, & totius mundi Φιλίσωρ, lapidem præcisum de monte sine manibus, & regna omnia subvertentem, claro sermone pro- nunciat. DAVID Simonides noster, Pindarus & Alcæus, Flaccus quoque, Catullus, atque Serenus, Christum Lyra personat, & in decachordo Psalte- rio, ab inferis excitat resurgentem. SALO- MON pacificus, & amabilis Domini, mores cor- rigit, naturam docet, Ecclesiam jungit & Chri- stum, sanctarumque nuptiarum dulce canit epitha- lamium. ESTHER in Ecclesiæ typo, populum liberat de periculo; & interfecto Aman, qui inter- pretatur iniquitas, partes convivii, & diem cele- brem mittit in posteros. PARALIPOMENON liber, id est Instrumenti Veteris ἐπιτομὴ tantus ac talis est, ut absque illo si quis scientiam Scriptura- rum sibi voluerit arrogare, seipsum irrideat. Per singula quippe nomina juncturasque verborum, & prætermissæ in Regum libris tanguntur historiæ, & innumerabiles explicantur Evangelii quæstiones.

ESDRAS & NEHEMIAS, adjutor videlicet, & consolator a Domino, in unum volumen coartan- tur, instaurant templum, muros extruunt civitatis: omnisque illa turba populi redeuntis in patriam, & descriptio Sacerdotum, Levitarum, Israëlis, prose- lytorum, ac per singulas familias murorum ac tur- rium opera divisa: aliud in cortice præferunt, aliud retinent in medulla. Cernis me Scripturarum a- more raptum, excessisse modum epistolæ, & tamen non implesse, quod volui. Audivimus tantum, quid nosse, quid cupere debeamus, ut & nos quoque possimus dicere: Concupivit anima mea desiderare justificationes tuas in omni tempore. ## 1:1 Introduction: Preface to the Old Tes
PREFACE TO THE OLD TES

As regards the books of the Old Testament in particular, to which these Annotations pertain, these things in particular can be observed in advance. I. Concerning the HEBREW language as the original and authentic one, and its own proper letters, we have said some things in the Critico S. p. 510, 325, as also in T. I. Syst. Theol. p. 721, and likewise in Comment. in Genes. prolegom. c. VI. p. 16, 17, and c. V. p. 18, seqq. But it will be worth the effort, here on account of the Hebrews and modern Bible-scourgers, untimely critics, Ludovicus Cappellus, Brian Walton, and others, who while they wish to appear to deserve well of the Holy Scripture, deserve very ill, to pursue some things more accurately. And first indeed, it is almost the common opinion that the Hebrew language, named after Eber, remained in the family of Eber after the γλωττοσύγχυσιν [confusion of tongues]. Scaliger, however, in Epist. ad Rich. Thons. and Ubertus, out of a mere desire for novelty, which was proper and perpetual to him, dared to contend that the Hebrew language is falsely called by that name, since it is Phoenician, and that the Hebrew language had to be learned by Abraham only in the land of Canaan, but that in Canaan among the Phoenicians, the descendants of Ham, the primeval language had been preserved pure: whom Erpenius followed in Orat. de lingua Ebræa (although contradicting himself, since in Orat. de lingua Arab.

LUCAS, and JOHN, the chariot of the Lord, and the true Cherubim, which is interpreted as a multitude of knowledge, are full of eyes throughout the whole body, sparks flash, lightnings run to and fro, they have feet straight and tending on high, backs feathered and flying everywhere, they hold one another, and are entangled with themselves, and as it were a wheel is turned in the middle of a wheel, and they go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit has led them. PAUL the Apostle writes to seven Churches: for the eighth, to the Hebrews, is placed by most outside the number. He instructs Timothy and Titus, and pleads with Philemon for the fugitive servant. Concerning which I think it better to be silent than to write a few things. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES seem indeed to sound a bare history, and to weave the infancy of the nascent Church: but if we know that their writer Luke is a physician, whose praise is in the Gospel, we shall perceive that all his words are likewise a medicine for the languishing soul. JAMES, PETER, JOHN, JUDE, published seven Epistles, as mystical as they are succinct, and equally short and long: short in words, long in meanings: so that he is rare who does not grow blind in the reading of them. THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN has as many Sacraments as it has words. I have said little, and for the merit of the volume all praise is inferior. In individual words, multiple intelligences lie hidden. I pray you, dearest brother, to live among these, to meditate on these, to know nothing else, to seek nothing else. Does it not seem to you already here on earth to be a dwelling place of the heavenly kingdom? I do not want you to be offended in the holy Scriptures by the simplicity, and as it were the vileness of the words, which were brought forth thus either by the fault of the interpreters, or on purpose, so that they might more easily instruct the rustic congregation, and that in one and the same meaning the learned might hear one thing, the unlearned another. I am not so petulant and dull as to promise that I know these things, and to take the fruit of those whose roots are fixed in heaven: But I confess I wish to. I prefer myself to the one sitting, refusing the master, I pledge myself as a companion. To the one asking it is given, to the one knocking it is opened, the one seeking finds. Let us learn on earth those things whose knowledge may persevere for us in heaven.

asserted that the Chaldean and Arabic languages arose in the family of Ham) as also M. Johannes Vorstius in Exerc. de lingua omnium prima, arguing that the family of Canaan retained the ancient language, when others were losing the use of the primeval language entirely, and had transported the same into those lands which it occupied, but that the descendants of Eber used a language other than Hebrew until Abraham: inasmuch as when Abraham migrated from his Fatherland Mesopotamia into the seats of the Canaanites, he spoke not the Hebrew language, but the Chaldean, or Syriac, which Laban is said to have used as his native language in Gen. XXXI, 46, and that he finally learned Hebrew in Canaan, whence it began to be called the Hebrew language, because Abraham and his descendants, as being sprung from Eber, used the same, and it was rather called the Hebrew language afterwards than the Canaanite, because the Hebrews prevailed over the Canaanites and were much more famous than them. But could not the Hebrew language have flourished first in the family of Eber, from which Abraham descended, even down to Abraham himself, although Abraham remained in Ur of the Chaldeans and was only called from there into Canaan? Could not the Hebrew language have been the vernacular of Terah, even though afterwards, when Nahor learned the Syriac language in Mesopotamia, that language, being proper to that region, was adopted in his family, and thus

would have been the vernacular of his son Laban? Since two almost entire centuries had intervened from the time when Abraham departed from Ur of the Chaldeans and from Haran, at which time a change of language, as well as of religion, could easily have occurred in the family of Nahor. Nor is it in doubt that Abraham was a Chaldean by nation, even if he was called forth from Ur Kasdim or of the Chaldeans: because it is asserted that the city of Charran, in Syria (which name this region has from the name of the fifth son of Shem, Gen. 10:22, whence it is called Aramia Syria—Aramus, says Josephus, Antiq. book 1, ch. 7, held those whom the Greeks prefer to call Syrians), was the birthplace of Abraham, Gen. 24:4, 10. Which is called Aram Naharaim, Syria of the two rivers, because it is encompassed between the two rivers, the Euphrates and the Chiddekel or Tigris: by the Greeks, Syria Mesopotamia or the land between the rivers: by the Chaldeans, Aram di al Perat, Syria which is near or beyond the Euphrates (which is the boundary of the land of Israel) is called; as it is also named in John 24:23, 'beyond the river.' Compare 2 Sam. 10:16, 1 Chron. 19:16, as also 1 Kings 4:24. It is also called Padan Aram, Syria of the plains, from the Ishmaelite language, or as some prefer, 'yoked,' as if placed under the yoke of the two rivers, Gen. 29:5, within which space of those two rivers, i.e., Mesopotamia, Chaldea was not included; but was conterminous; and Aramia had fallen to the sons of Shem in the dispersion of the peoples, as had Assyria, but Chaldea to the sons of Ham, from whom Abraham certainly was not. Wherefore R. Moses Nachmanides or Gerundensis maintains that Abraham's parent Terah was from Charran, but that he went with Abraham into the land of the Chaldeans before Haran was born, and that Haran was both born and died there for him, Gen. 11:28. But in this opinion Abarbenel rightly desires that which is said outside of Scripture, nay, against the Scripture of Josh. 24, where they are said to have dwelt in the land beyond the river 'from of old'; which would not be true if they had dwelt in Chaldea for many years. Wherefore Abarbenel thus maintains that Abraham was both born and dwelt in Aram Naharaim or Syria Mesopotamia before he came into the land of Canaan, and that the city of Ur, his birthplace, was situated not in Chaldea, but in Mesopotamia; and that it is called Ur of the Chaldeans not by reason of its site and location, but either because the Chaldeans began and occupied it and poured themselves out that far, or because the Chaldeans worshipped fire there: but that Charan was the city in which they dwelt when they journeyed from the city of Ur into Canaan. Which opinion is greatly approved by Buxtorf in his Dissertation on the Hebrew language after the confusion, preservation, and propagation. (which is the third in his Philological-Theological Dissertations) p. 137, namely, that the native land of the Hebrew fathers was Mesopotamia or Perataea, the region beyond the Euphrates, the birthplace of Abraham, Ur in Mesopotamia, but occupied by the Chaldeans and defiled by idolatrous worship, and thence called Ur of the Chaldeans, just as in Gen. 40:50, the land of Canaan, or the part of it, Hebron, where they were commemorated, is called the land of the Hebrews, because it was inhabited by Hebrews; and thus Acts 7:2, God is said to have appeared to Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, namely in that Ur of the Chaldeans, before he dwelt in Charran: and that he went out from the land of the Chaldeans, that is, the city and field, or that valley in which Ur was situated; or also that Stephen spoke in this way from current usage, because in later times Mesopotamia was included under Chaldea. Whence he concludes that the seat of the family of Eber was in Aramia or Syria, and consequently that this was also the same place in which the Hebrew language was preserved from the confusion of tongues and the dispersion of the peoples until Abraham's departure from it: which opinion was also that of Elias Levita in the preface to his Meturgeman, although not correctly understood by Genebrard and certain others. We do not indeed deny that the Chaldean or Assyrian language flourished in those regions of Aramia or Syria and Assyria, or that Abraham was skilled in it, but we only deny that he knew only that language, and that it alone so prevailed there that no family had the use of the pure Hebrew language. That the Hebrew language remained after the confusion of tongues not in Canaan, but in Aramia in the family of Eber, the great-grandson of Shem, is a common opinion not only of Christians but also of the Hebrews, which can hardly be rashly denied. See Augustine. book 16, On the City of God, ch. 11, book 18, ch. 39. Chrysostom in Gen. Hom. 30. Eucherius book 2 in Gen. 2. Joh. Mercer in Gen. Bened. Perer. Commentary on Gen. book 5. Theod. Bibliander in Commentary on the best manner of explaining Hebrew, p. 29. Valentin. Schindler in the Pentaglot Lexicon. Guid. Fabricius Boderianus in the Preface to the Syriac New Testament in the Royal Bibles, although, he says, the notations of proper names are Hebrew, yet Philo calls them Chaldean both because of the great affinity between the two languages; and because Abraham used the Hebrew speech in the middle of Chaldea, and had received it through the hands of his ancestors from the times of Eber, the grandson of Shem, from whom it is called Hebrew, for the reason that in the confusion of tongues that first lip of the whole earth was preserved purely in the family of Eber alone. Among the Hebrews, the author of the book Cosri, part 2, § 68, is cited for this opinion. For it is certain, he says, that this was the same language of Eber: and that it was called Hebrew on his account, because it remained with him at the time of the division of the earth and the confusion of tongues, Elias Levita in the preface to the book Meturgeman. For without doubt Abraham himself and his fathers spoke in the holy language, just as they received it from Adam down to Noah, one from another. Add Abarbenel on Genesis, fol. 49. Abrah. de Balnis in the preface to his Grammar, Samuel Arcuvolti, and those who acknowledge the Hebrew language to be named after Eber: which is likewise the common opinion of the Hebrews, R. Nehemiah in Bereshith Rabba, Aben Ezra on Ex. 1:46, R. David Kimchi, R. Gedaliah, Obadiah Sforno on the Law, etc., which is favored by the form of the gentilic names in the word עברי, with the places of Scripture, Gen. 10:21, Num. 24:24. See Buxtorf, loc. cit., p. 149. B. Luther on Gen. ch. 11. Calvin on Gen. 10:21, Junius, Oration on the Hebrew language.

Reasons that the language was preserved in the family of Eber after the Babylonian confusion, and not among the Canaanites, are these: 1. That the family of Shem did not consent to the impious plan of the tower-builders, whence Augustine, in the place cited, says that the trace of divine justice appeared especially in this, that while other nations were punished by the mutation of languages, such a punishment did not reach the family of Eber alone. 2. That those architects were from the family of Ham, whose leader was Nimrod, Gen. 10:9-10. Cf. Josephus, Book I, ch. 5, whence it is in no way likely that the primeval language remained among the Canaanites, as descendants of Ham, if indeed the family of Ham was to be punished most of all for that impious undertaking by the confusion of language. Shall we believe that the authors of this faction obtained the benefit of having the primeval language preserved among them, when the languages of others were confused by God because of that crime? 3. Since Eber lived long after the confusion of languages, indeed Sala his parent also, Arphaxad his grandfather, and Shem his great-grandfather, who, I ask, will be persuaded that the holy language remained uncorrupted not in the blessed family of Shem, but in the cursed family of Ham? See Gen. 9:26. Did the holy language therefore perish for those most holy patriarchs, while the impious Canaanites received and retained it uncorrupted? By what fault, or by what chance, shall we believe that Shem and Arphaxad, and indeed the others as well, lost their mother tongue and vernacular, by which some of them used for several centuries before the confusion of tongues. 4. But do not the names of the Patriarchs, such as Eber, Peleg, Abram, Sarah, along with the proper names of places, sufficiently testify that they used the holy language, and not the Chaldean? 5. Add that from Eber his descendants were named sons of Eber and Hebrews, as Moses testifies in Gen. 10:21. Concerning which Augustine, Book XVI of The City of God, ch. 11, when it is read that there was originally one language for all, and before all the sons of Shem, Heber is commended, although he arises from him as the fifth (according to the LXX, the fourth according to the Hebrew text), and thence the language is called Hebrew, which the authority of the Prophets and Patriarchs preserved not only in their sermons but also in the sacred letters: truly, when it is asked in the division of languages where that language could have remained which was previously common: which without any doubt remained where that punishment which was brought about by the change of languages did not exist: what else occurs, except that it remained in the nation of him from whose name it received its name? And what else, I ask, is indicated by those Mosaic words: The father of all the sons of Eber, than that he is the father of the Hebrews? For thus the sons of Israel are Israelites, the sons of Judah are Jews, the sons of Moab are Moabites, thus Ham is the father of the Canaanites, Gen. 9:18, 22. Thus the father of Moab, ch. 19:37, the father of the sons of Ammon, or the Ammonites, v. 38, are called, and specifically Shem is called the father of the sons of Eber, even though he was also the father of many others, because Eber was the סגלה (segullah), the peculiar treasure of Shem, as the Hebrews say, i.e., the chief of his sons, into whom not only the family but also the paternal blessing, Gen. 9:26, passed, from which line through Peleg, Abraham, the father of believers, arose, into whom also the language and religion divinely handed down by Shem were propagated and preserved: just as R. Judah Hallevi in the book Cosri, part I, § 47, calls Shem, Eber, and Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses the heart of Adam and his peculiar treasure. And § 49 in the same book Cosri it is read thus: Abraham our father himself was in the age of the division, and he remained with his relatives in the language of Eber his ancestor, whence he was also called a Hebrew. Add also § 95, where he says Abraham was the peculiar treasure of Eber, and his disciple: and the author of the book Arugas Habbosem says that the Hebrew language was preserved among the singular ones of the peculiar treasure: concerning which again Augustine, l. c. Nor in vain did he transmit that language, i.e., which Abraham held, not to all his sons, but only to those who, propagated through Jacob, and coalescing more notably and eminently into the people of God, were able to have the testaments of God and the stock of Christ. Nor did Heber himself pour the same language into his entire progeny; but only into that one whose generations are led to Abraham. Add what St. Augustine has in the following chapter. There was therefore one house of Terah, from which Abraham was born, in which the worship of the one true God, and as far as is credible, in which the Hebrew language alone had already remained. Joh. Mercer, Comment. in Gen. 14. From Heber, he says, the great-grandson of Shem, the Hebrew nation was named, which remained especially in Abraham, whence those who descended from him were called Hebrews, not the others who were dispersed here and there from his sons through the Orient as far as India, in whose families the purity of that primordial language did not remain, as it did in the family of Abraham. In that family of (Heber) alone, in a straight line, that is, in those only in whom some form of the Church and the worship of the true God remained, the Hebrew language also persisted and was preserved pure and inviolate. For Ishmael and Esau, and others descending from the Ishmaelites and the Fathers, just as they degenerated from the pure worship of God, so also they departed from that pure and native language to their own, each one, which was already in other families and nations. Which are read in duplicate also in August. Steuchus in Gen. 14 and most other commentators, and no less in our B. Luther in Gen. 1.

This virtue of his (Heber) merited that the Church of the holy Patriarch Shem should take its name from him, and that they should be called Hebrews who retained the doctrine and faith of the holy Father Heber. And this appellation of the Church remained until the time of Christ.

Although Abraham undoubtedly spoke Syriac in Ur of the Chaldeans, which language was in common use there, he nevertheless did not ignore or had not forgotten Hebrew: for Shem, Arphaxad, Salah, and Heber were still living with him after the confusion of tongues, whom no one would say had lost their primordial language. Nor was it in any way likely that the Canaanites, a cursed people, dedicated to anathema, and subsequently extirpated, had retained the purity of the holy language rather than Shem, Eber, and Abraham, among whom the knowledge of God, true holiness, and the seed of the Church were preserved. Nor indeed is the Hebrew language called the language of Canaan in Isa. 19:18 because the Canaanites, the descendants of the cursed Ham, from whom the Egyptians also came, used it: but because the inhabitants of the land of Canaan used it, first indeed the Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, then the Israelites, after the Canaanites and Phoenicians were ejected, as Bibliander notes in his treatise on the method. Communi omnium ling. p. 20. Whence some Rabbis observe that, after the Canaanites learned the language of the Hebrews themselves through association, in distinction to their own vulgar language, that primordial and most ancient one, which they had learned, was called the holy language: which nevertheless was also called the language of Canaan, because some use of it existed among the Canaanites, and they themselves had become accustomed to it; afterwards the language of the Canaanites came under the name of the Hebrew (עברי), inasmuch as the Hebrews inhabited Canaan, and the land of Canaan became the land of the Hebrews after the ancient inhabitants were extirpated.

But if the nature of the language of the Canaanites is unknown, as the great Buxtorf judges in the place cited, p. 153, no one ought to be surprised, since very many other languages are unknown from the Babylonian Confusion; but to whom it is probable that the Canaanites, as neighbors to the Syrians, also received a language akin to Hebrew; which Jerome, Book VII, Commentary on Isaiah 19:18, says was intermediate between Egyptian and Hebrew, and in great part akin to Hebrew, and in Book V on the same place, he declares the Canaanite language to be Syrian. Indeed, the Punic language, which Fuller in Book IV, Misc. c. 4, and others make the same as the Canaanite, Laurentius Valla in Vol. Epist. p. 351, Galeottus Martius de doctr. promisc. c. 6, Gesner in Mithridates, Schindler in Lex. Pentagl. c. 1614, Drusius in Book II, q. Ebr. 44, Megiserus in thef. 6, Polygl. tab. 1, make Arabic. But Erpenius, Oration II on the Hebrew language and Arabic, says that those who interpret the Punic language as having been Arabic are mistaken; and that it is rather Syrian, the ἰσόψηφα of the Punic language of Thomas Reinesius teach, or at least very akin to the Syrian language, which he proves from Augustine, tract. XV on John IV, Sermon XXXV on the Words of the Lord, to St. Luke, Ep. XLIII to Maximus Madaurensis, showing in c. VIII that Punic words are aptly derived from the Hebrew and Syriac language, not from the Arabic: Sixtinus Amama says that the Egyptian, Punic, and Arabic languages are dialects of the Hebrew mother, in Cens. Vulgat. in Pentat. on Gen. 41:45. Compare what we have said on Gen. 11:1.

Furthermore, not only in Syria and Canaan did Abraham preserve the primeval language, namely Hebrew, uncorrupted, but in Egypt it was also preserved by Jacob and his sons and descendants, without mixture, even though they were oppressed there for over two hundred years and served hard bondage. Whence the Rabbis celebrate this as a miracle, that the Israelites did not change their language, in Tanchuma on the book of Numbers, section Balack, and in Schir Haschirim Rabbati on Cant. IV, 12. But after the exodus from Egypt, and the occupation of the land of Canaan, the Canaanite idiom was extirpated by the Israelites, and their own proper Hebrew language was so introduced that it became the vernacular in that land, and began to be called the language of Canaan, which also alone remained uncorrupted there until the Babylonian captivity: concerning which R. Asarias in Meor Enajim c. 57. After the Israelites entered into the land of Canaan in the time of Joshua, it is credible that all, even those of the common order among them, always spoke the holy language: Which he proves from Jud. XII, 6. c. XV, 15. 16. 2. Reg. XIIX, 26. Dan. I, 4., as also from the proper names of persons and places, Gilgal, Jerubbaal, Ramath, Lechi, Noomi, Schemuel, Jedidjah, Obed, which, although they were translated into other languages in history, remained unchanged. Furthermore, in the Babylonian captivity they became accustomed to the Chaldean language, such as was then in use there, whence they also began to interpret the law in Chaldean. Nevertheless, both the divine law and the Hebrew language were preserved, especially in the heart of the Priests and Judges, as is held in the book Cosri part III. §. 15., so that they might teach the judgments of justice: until the law was purged by Ezra from various corruptions, and the Hebrew language was in some way recalled again into use: which, however, since it was for the most part accustomed to the Chaldean idiom among the people, could not be so restored that there was no need for a Chaldean interpretation of the divine law: whence at length arose the Chaldean Paraphrases. Conf. Neh. XIII, 23. 24. and by that also, the Hebrew language having been removed from common use in speaking and writing, the matter at length reached the point that outside of the Sacred Codex the pure and uncontaminated Hebrew language remained nowhere. Concerning which R. Dav. Kimchi in the preface of the book Michlol. From the time that our Fathers were deported into a foreign land, and among those nations learned their language, and forgot the holy language, until their sons and daughters became accustomed to this very day to speak a foreign language and a strange lip, each one, namely, according to the language of the place of his captivity or exile, and of his people, nothing is found in Hebrew in our hands except the XXIV sacred books etc.

II. Concerning the ancient and genuine character of Hebrew letters. That this is entirely the same as that which is seen in the Hebrew Bibles, and is frequented in common use, and that no other was received from GOD on the tables of the law, or used by Moses and the Prophets in the original sacred Codices, we doubt not at all: even though some Innovators, Scaliger especially in Animadvers. ad Chron. Euseb., Capellus in Arc. Pæct. Reisch. l. I. c. 16., Morinus in Exercit. in Pentat. Exercit. II. c. 1., most confidently go in all other directions, contending tooth and nail that the law was handed down in Samaritan letters, which remained among the Samaritans, and that all the books of the Old Testament were described by the sacred amanuenses of GOD in them, but that these figures of letters which we now have are Chaldean or Assyrian, and that Ezra described the whole Old Testament Canon in them after his return from the Babylonian captivity, and left them to posterity. Drusius ad diffic. loc. Exod. c. 56., Isaac. Casaubon. in Exerc. Contr. Baron., from the Pontificals Bened. Arias Montanus, Genebrardus, Andr. Masius, Guil. Fabricius, Vilalpand. Bellarm. & others agree.

They can be seen to be led by the authority of Jerome and Eusebius: but the latter asserts nothing else in his Chron. at the year M. 4710 than that it is AFFIRMED that Ezra composed the divine Scriptures from memory, and that he changed the Jewish letters so that they would not be mixed with the Samaritans, which, however, he himself does not affirm, and he could have said it from the mind of the Samaritans, of whom there was a great number in Caesarea, although it can also be understood concerning that change by which he left the common letters used among the Hebrews to the Samaritans, and restored the ancient ones for the use of the Jews. Jerome, however, in the preface to the book of Kings, says: It is certain that Ezra the scribe and doctor of the law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, found other letters, which we use now, whereas up to that time the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were the same, which Guilh. Postellus explains it thus: that Ezra publicly brought forth, proposed, and recalled into use the ancient sacred Hebrew characters that were hidden, which to the people, who commonly did not know them, seemed no otherwise than if he had found new ones. But what he says, that up to that time the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were the same, can be accepted concerning common copies, and letters received in common use and civil business. That these letters which we use today were newly found and devised by Ezra, not even those who oppose the truth here would say: for then these would not be the characters of the Assyrians, as most say, but clearly novel; and why would Ezra have devised new letters from his own brain? Why would God have entrusted to the impious Samaritans, to whom the oracles of God were not entrusted, the letters with which He Himself wrote the tables of the law, and Moses and the Prophets consigned the sacred Scriptures; but to the Jews, to whom those were entrusted, have taken away those ancient letters, and allowed newly devised ones, or even those accepted from profane nations, to be thrust upon them for the preservation of His oracles and the sacred canon? And who has ever heard it said that the books of any of those Prophets who wrote before the captivity were seen to be written by the Prophets in the Samaritan character? They are also accustomed to appeal to Bede:

but he, regarding Ezra ch. IX, only reports the tradition of certain Hebrews: THEY REPORT also, he says, the Hebrews.

But concerning the Hebrews, Buxtorf teaches excellently that almost all the Hebrews (a few excepted, and those later ones, whose opinion nevertheless is either inconsistent or can be explained in different ways) stand for the antiquity of the modern letters. So that what these bring forward from the contrary, or in the first place from R. Jos. in the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin ch. II, that the script had been changed, can be understood as the change by which the old and true Scripture, having been abolished for a long time in common use among the Jews, was restored by Ezra. What Mar Sutra says, that the Assyrian script was given to the Israelites, and therefore the Hebrew was left to these Cutheans, is explained by the common answer of the Hebrews: namely, that the Jews formerly had a twofold script, sacred and profane; the former called Assyrian, which is still in use; the latter Hebrew, because it was in common use among the Hebrews, since it was not pleasing to use the former commonly on account of its singular holiness and veneration; but it was permitted by Ezra after the Babylonian captivity promiscuously, or rather joined, while the latter was left to the Samaritans, as apostates. Let us hear one from many, namely Rabbi Gedaliah in the book Schalscheleth hakkabalah, f. 89: The law was given in that script in which we write the book of the law today, which is called Assyrian. But this figure was guarded and preserved among the magnates of Israel, just like the oral law. For the common people used the figure of the Samaritan Hebrew letters: but when Ezra had come, and had permitted them to transcribe the written law, so that the law might not be consigned to oblivion among the Israelites, he permitted them also to write in the figure of the letters in which the law was given. They called it Assyrian, however, because the magnates of Israel brought it with them, or carried it, from Assyria. For it was among them by Kabbalah and tradition, and they had it secretly, because it was a holy script. But concerning the more recent Hebrews, Buxtorf testifies: Of all whom it has so far been my lot to see and read, I have found only one, R. Joseph Albo in the book Ikkarim, Orat. III, ch. 16, who expressly and clearly undertook to defend and champion this opinion concerning the novelty of the Hebrew letters and their change into Assyrian, but what is one against many? Whom, however, R. Jacob accurately refutes in En Israel, fol. 142.

Moreover, that great champion of Hebrew literature, Buxtorf, carefully observed that that opinion concerning the double Scripture of the Jews, sacred and profane, was not only widespread among the Rabbis, whose many testimonies he adduced, but was also approved by very many Christians, such as Guil. Postellus in his book on the origin of Etruria, pp. 113, 246; Joh. Boulese in the preface to the Hebrew Alphabet; Augustino Pantheo Veneto under the word Sadumia; Theod. Bibliander in his book on the method of learning all languages, p. 62; Nic. Fuller in book IV of his Miscellanies, ch. 4, from which Postellus concludes that this double kind of Scripture was already in use in the times of the first fathers before Abraham, and that Abraham indeed had, before he came into the land of Canaan, as the holy language, so also the holy character received from his grandfather Eber, with which God later inscribed the law on the Tablets: but that he also used in Ur of the Chaldeans the Chaldean or Syrian language, which was then common and vernacular in Assyria, and along with this the common character, which they hold to be the Samaritan today, or at least that of which this is the offshoot: to which opinion Buxtorf adds his support, confirming that the letters we call Samaritan reached the Samaritans when they were made participants in the law and Scripture of the Jews (2 Kings 17:25; from Pirke R. Eleazar, ch. 38): because they would not have wanted to communicate the holy character to a people so vile and abject, but since the Samaritans were excommunicated by Ezra (Conf. Syr. L, 27, 28), so that it was decreed that the Israelites should have no commerce with them, and that the Israelites should no longer use that common and vulgar character, which was also the Samaritans', but only the holy one, which they called Assyrian. Which, since it was known to few before, but ignored by the greater part, all and everyone learned it in Assyria partly from Daniel, and partly and especially from Ezra, and from then on and further used it alone, for which reason R. Joseph said that this writing ascended with the Israelites from Assyria: the occasion for publishing which in Assyria he thinks was given by an Angel, when he wrote those symbolic words on the wall before Belshazzar, Dan. 5, Mene Mene Tekel Upharsin, as is taught in En Israel from R. Joseph. If this Angelic writing was Assyrian in this sense, that it had always been the Assyrians', how did it happen that no one among all the wise men of the King of Babylon could read it? Whence it is concluded rather that it was then entirely new, unusual, and foreign to the Babylonians and Assyrians, and not common to the Jews, but known only to a few, such as Daniel, Ezra, and their companions. And from this time some think the Assyrians and Chaldeans used these letters, and they give this as the reason why the Hebrew and Chaldean languages are written with the same characters today. Although others wish it to be called Assyrian from Abraham and the other Fathers who came from Assyria into Canaan and used that method of writing: which pleases August. Sebast. Nouzenus in his book on the primary Hebrew language and Petrus Cevallerius in his Annotations to the Grammar, ch. 1.

But that this Assyrian writing, as they call it, which is accepted today in Hebrew Codices, was the primeval, most ancient, and holy one, with which God once inscribed the law on stone tablets, can be proved: (1) From the Hebrew Scripture itself, Isa. 9:7, where the closed or final Mem in the word לםרבה, by the consensus of Jews and Christians, including F. Ludovicus, S. Franciscus Lusitanus Olyssiponensis in his Globe of Canons and Mysteries of the Holy and Divine Scripture (who otherwise opposes the antiquity of the Hebrew letters), hints at some mystery: which, however, would have no place if Isaiah had used Samaritan letters: since the Samaritans lack final letters. (2) From the words of Christ, Matt. 5:17, that not one iota or one apex should perish from the law. For in the Samaritan character, Yod is not a letter of the smallest figure, but it is in the Assyrian, as they call it. Then if the sacred books no longer exist in the old and original character, not only one iota has perished from the law, but the whole law or Scripture of the O.T., which, in the judgment of Christ, is among the impossibilities. (3) The Hebrew characters are simpler than the Samaritan, and thus they savor of greater majesty and authority. On which see Wilh. Schickard in Bechinath Happenischim, p. 82. What of the fact that the Merubba itself, i.e., the square depiction of the letters, being consistent, uniform, easy, and capable of being joined into a graceful line, moreover reflecting the form of the voice with the disposition of the organs in a certain way, and thus by its very appearance bearing a certain hidden majesty, seems to suit the most wise Legislator better than this gaping, deformed, rough, laborious, and difficult-to-write, and thus, as appears from all circumstances, fictitious one. (4) Since the Jews were very religious in preserving Scripture, it is in no way likely that they would have allowed the genuine and ancient Scripture either to perish or to pass to the cursed Samaritan people, which they held as sacrosanct and divine, and venerated: as being used by GOD himself on the tablets of the law. (5) That the Cuthites, says Schickard, have the ancient Scripture remaining, I never believe; for just as in religion the Samaritans fell away from the Jews, not the Jews from them; so also in writing, the holy people of God are to be judged to have retained the ancient figures; but the schismatics, so that they might differ in all things, are deservedly thought to have changed the characters of the letters, or rather, as it seems to us, that the common characters were left to those schismatics, so that the Jews might separate themselves from them even by the figures of the letters, and have nothing in common with them. (6) Theodor. Bibliander, on the best kind of Grammar. Hebr. p. 77. He proposes for his adversaries to consider how Ezra could have changed the Scripture among the people of God, in which God had inscribed His law with His fingers, or how he could have wished to, he who did not suffer that children should speak in the Ashdodite, Ammonite, and Moabite dialect (Neh. XIII, 23, 24, 25), not because the old speech of the Ammonites and Moabites was different from the Hebrew, but because those who had succeeded into the place of the Ammonites and Moabites then had a different speech, and were called Ammonites and Moabites, just as the Samaritans who inhabited Samaria, when they were Cuthites and Medes, and gathered from other regions of the East. It was not fitting, therefore, for Ezra or Nehemiah, or other most holy men of those times, that they should have wished to abolish the characters of the native language or the speech. (7.) Buxtorf also urges this in the same place, §. 36. How could Ezra have easily abrogated all the copies of the old Scripture which existed everywhere among the Jews? The Jews were then already dispersed into various parts of the world. And both in Babylonia, where they had schools and academies, and in Palestine, there remained without doubt very many copies publicly and privately among them. To these (8.) is added that Theod. Bibliander in the book de rat. commun. omnium lingv. p. 62. shows that the letters of all peoples and nations were derived from the letters of the Hebrews. (9.) And that the Cabbalistic mysteries (which is an argument κατ' ἄνθρωπον) have no small place in these letters, which do not at all suit the Samaritans. Which Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola urges in his Epistle to Ignatius; to which he adds that of R. Schemuel Arcuvolti in the book Aragashabbosem: In general we have received from those standing in the secret of the Lord (the Cabbalists) that in these holy letters, both in their figure and in their names, there is a certain occult spirituality and life. And what is held in the book Cosri part IV. n. 25. And therefore it is said (by the Cabbalists) concerning the (Hebrew) Scripture that the figures of its letters are not such without intention, or by accident, but because of a signification convenient with that which each letter is intended to mean. However vain, says Buxtorf, l. c. §. 19. the Jews may be in finding and devising frivolous minutiae and quibbles, it is nevertheless hardly credible that they would have sought holy mysteries in letters that are in their opinion human, especially those of profane nations hostile to them. Therefore, these also fight for the antiquity of the Hebrew letters. For if this change of letters by Ezra is admitted, a great part of Cabbalistic Theology will collapse. (10.) R. Abraham Harophe in שלטי הגבורים thus rises up against the Rabbi, the defender of the innovated Scripture: My heart is astonished at this, how could that have ascended into the mind of Mar Sutra, or Mar Ukba? Is God like a man, that He should change anything concerning the Scripture of the Law, just as it was given by Himself publicly in the eyes of all Israel on Mount Sinai, or that He should repent of that language proper to the Jews, which He gave as a gift to Abraham, so that He did not preserve all that for those ascending from Babylon, the very same Scripture and language in which He gave it to all Israel by the hand of Moses, or that He should send a bill of divorce to it, and hand it into its hand, and dismiss it from His house, by prevaricating against it, and changing it into a foreign Scripture at the time of Ezra? Furthermore, how did the foolish men not notice that if it is not permitted even to any Prophet to innovate anything in the Law, how much less was it permitted to Ezra, or to Israel, to choose the Assyrian Scripture, and to abolish the Hebrew (i.e., the holy one) in which the Tables and the book of Moses were written? (11.) Add now the testimonies of the Hebrews, both the Ancients and the תנאים TANNAIM, who are the deuterotists, the Mishnaic Doctors, the Authors of the Talmudic text (such as R. Jehudah Hakkadosch in the Babylonian Talmud Gemara, Sanhedrim c. 11. & R. Schimeon, and the two Eleazars, as also R. Eliezer Hakkahir) and the אמוראים Amoraim, who are the authors of the Gemara, or the Talmudic complement, such as Rafchasda, and also R. Jeremia in the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Megill. c. 1. as well as R. Matthia and R. Levi in the Jerusalem Talmud. Likewise the Baaletosephos, who are the authors of the Talmudic additions, and especially R. Jom Tof Bar Abraham, or ריטבא Ritba in En Israël c. 1.) and furthermore the נאוני, who have been considered excellent above others, (concerning whose consensus R. Afarias has handed down in Meor Enajim c. 58.) and finally the Cabbalists; then also the more recent ones R. Aben-Ezra, R. Solomon, R. Moses Ben Maimon, or Rambam, R. Obadiah of Bartenora, R. Ephodei, R. Jacob. bar Schelomo ben Gharif in En Israël, R. Samuel Arcuvolthi, R. Afarias in Meor Enajim c. 58. R. Gedalia, Abraham Harophi, Abraham de Balmis in c. 1. Gram. Elie the Grammarian, etc. (12.) Testimonies of the Christians, such as Mirandulanus, Marcus Marinus, Theodorus Bibliander, Franciscus Junius, Nicolaus Fullerus, Caesar Baronius Ann. T. II. p. 293. Nouzenus, Brugtbonus, Schickardus, and indeed even S. Jerome, who in his Epistle to Fabiola says that the name of God was inscribed on the golden plate of the high priest's turban (not in Samaritan, but) in the 4 Hebrew letters יהוה. (13.) Testimonies of ancient coins, especially Shekels, which are marked with Hebrew letters: See Schickardus dissert. de nummis Hebr. (14.) Testimonies of ancient monuments, in R. Benjamin in Itiner., concerning all of which see Buxtorf l. c. and what Mr. D. Wasmuth has argued against Walton in his vindications.

III. Concerning the vowel points of the Hebrews, that they are contemporary with the letters, we have dealt against Ludovicus Capellus and other Innovators both κατασκευασικῶς and ἀνασκευαστικῶς in the Critica Sacra from p. 326 to 379. Johannes Buxtorf the Son also treated accurately of the same matter afterwards against the same Capellus in a special writing on the origin, antiquity, and authority of the points and accents in the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament. Conf. T. I. Syst. Th. p. 728.

IV. The antiquity of the accents, as also of the letters and vowels, was asserted by the excellently praised Mr. D. Wasmuth in his vindications for the Holy Hebrew text against Capellus and Walton, as also in the Anti-Conringius Apologeticus, which the Theological College of our Academy fortified with an approving judgment, which was later added to the same by the author of the Vindications.

V. Concerning the whole System of the Hebrew Codex of the Old Testament as well as its sincerity, it was dealt with in the Critica Sacra p. 370 and following, especially against Johannes Morinus and other Papists: which argument was later treated at length against his companion in faith Ludovicus Capellus the Critic by Johannes Buxtorf the Younger in his Anti-Criticus or Vindications of the Hebrew truth, and we treat it subsequently in our Anti-Grotianus.

VI. The catalog of the books of the Old Testament and the Canon of the Hebrews in Crit. S. p. 235 et seqq. was asserted, and was especially recorded by S. JEROME in his PROLOGUS GALEATUS. Which, because the Vulgate Versions, and the Commentaries on the same, as well as the Parisian Bibles, and also some versions of the Reformers place it at the beginning, it has pleased us to append it here likewise, since the τὰ προλεγόμενα in the Old Testament have been dispatched.

VII. Concerning the Distribution of the O.T. according to the Hebrews into the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa (concerning which R. Isaac Abarbenel wears himself out to no purpose in his treatise on the division of the Biblical books, added to the Philological and Theological Dissertations of Joh. Buxtorf) and according to the Christians into Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets: likewise into Historical, Poetical, and Prophetical, we have treated in Vol. I of the System of Theology, p. 469, and in the Commentary on Genesis, p. 7.

VIII. Concerning the poetry of the Hebrews, it was treated in the Prolegomena prefixed to the Commentary on Genesis, ch. III, p. 10, et seqq.

IX. The distribution of the Hebrews according to sections, expedited by Parashot and Haftarot, is primarily by Laurentius Fabricius in his work on the partitions of the Hebrew Codex. There is also an Index added to the end in Hebrew Codices, the explanation of which we shall subsequently present with certain notes illustrating the same. Concerning the distribution according to chapters and verses, see Joh. Leusden, Philol. Ebr. Disp. III.

X. Regarding the Masoretic annotations of the Hebrew Codex, and those things which are particularly to be observed in the same, the Masoretic Commentary of Johan. Buxtorf the Elder is especially relevant, which is to be consulted here. Joh. Leusden reduced it to a compendium for the most part in his Philologus Hebraeus, Disp. XXII and following.

XI. Concerning the sum and the principal scope of the books of the O.T., which is CHRIST JESUS, we have discoursed in the preface to the Major Prophets and the Davidic Psalms; to which must be added what is in Vol. I of the System of Theology, ch. IV, quest. XXXIX and following, concerning the same value of the writings of the O.T. regarding the faith and worship of Christians as the writings of the N.T., and concerning the utility of them for the purpose of convincing the Jews, and we have treated of the mysteries of the Christian Religion contained in the same. Which matter I have elsewhere also treated of at large against the Arminians and the Calixtine Innovators, and as far as concerns the examples and special sayings of Scripture against the Jews, Grotius, Calvin, Arminius, and the Calixtines, we have in these Annotations defended them here and there.

XII. As for the versions of the Old Testament, the most ancient of all was the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters, as was shown in the Commentary on Genesis, prolegomena, chapter VII, page 26. It is called in the Talmudic Tract Sopherim, chapter I, section 7, the work of five Elders, whence Johannes Leusden in his Philologus Hebraeo-mixtus thinks that Eleazar the High Priest sent five Elders from the great Sanhedrin to King Ptolemy, page 12, who adorned this version, and it is so named from the LXX men of the Sanhedrin, by whom they were deputed, the LXX Interpreters, as it is commonly wont to be called. Which version, indeed, although it is by no means to be held as divine—in which part we stopped the mouth of the foolish Morin in his Critica Sacra and his Exercitations, which Christ. Cartwright in the preface to his Electa Targumica [showed] that no one had touched Rabb. says, we have destroyed thirty years ago, who attempted to attribute divine authority to the version of the LXX men: yet it is of the greatest authority, because it was used by Christ and the Apostles, and frequented by the use of the Church for many centuries, and infinitely, as Augustine testifies in book II of De Doctrina Christiana, chapter II, transferred into the Latin idiom: which [version], only in the Pentateuch adorned by the LXX Elders, and furthermore another [version] on Moses and the Prophets together composed under Cleopatra and celebrated under the name of the LXX Elders, Jacob Ussher taught with great but vain effort in a special Syntagma (as we demonstrated in the aforementioned place, page 30 et seqq.), imagining besides a twin Cleopatrine [version], a genuine one and a vulgar one, of which we spoke in the aforementioned place, page 39 et seqq. Although indeed perhaps another Greek version of an uncertain author preceded this one truly called the LXX Interpreters, concerning which Aristobulus [writes] in Eusebius, book XIII of the Praeparatio Evangelica, chapter 7, yet it does not surpass it any longer. See Critica Sacra, page 693. Under the last Ptolemy also some Greek version appeared, but neither does that exist any longer. See Critica Sacra, page 697.

After the birth of Christ, therefore, arose the version of Aquila, which is the second, and furthermore the third of Symmachus, as well as the fourth of Theodotion, as also the fifth and sixth, which are so called by Origen, of an uncertain author; from which Origen composed first the tetrapla, then the hexapla, and after that the octapla, with the addition of Hebrew editions partly in the Hebrew character, partly in Greek letters, as we taught in the aforementioned place, and proved against Morin; where we also warned what is to be held concerning the Lucianic and likewise the Hesychian edition, namely that they are not peculiar versions, but emendations of the vulgar Greek, page 705, such as the Origenian [edition] also was, page 706.

Next in age to the Greek version of the LXX men was the Chaldaic [version] of Onkelos on the Pentateuch, and of Jonathan on the former and latter Prophets, to which was added that of R. Joseph the Blind on the Hagiographa of the Psalter, Job, and Proverbs, and of an uncertain author on the five Festival scrolls, the Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther, as also the Jerusalem Targum on the principal places of the Pentateuch. But Onkelos the Jew, who wrote a Chaldaic Paraphrase before Christ was born, is wrongly confused by some with Aquila the Christian, who adorned a Greek version: and with Akila the proselyte, who wrote a Targum, but which perished. The Targum on the Pentateuch is also attributed to Jonathan ben Uzziel, a disciple of the great Hillel, who adorned a Paraphrase on the Prophets: but the style and

the manner of the Paraphrase show a different author, and the contents show a later [author] than that Jonathan; who indeed is uncertain, just as the author of the other Targum is, nay, as both are on the book of Esther: For besides the Targum of him who adorned the paraphrase on the festival scrolls, there is another Targum on Esther almost three times larger than the Hebrew text, both of which Francis Taylor rendered into Latin in the year 1655 at London. On the book of Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles there exists no Chaldaic Paraphrase.

To these paraphrases was added the Syriac and Arabic Version, as also the Samaritan, concerning which we spoke in Comment. on Gen. p. 41. Hottinger makes the Syriac twofold: the Simple, if not made before Christ, certainly made in the time of the Apostle Thaddaeus from the Hebrew: the other made after the coming of Christ from the LXX Interpreters. He teaches, moreover, that the Arabic is later than the age of Muhammad. See his Analecta Hist. Theol. Diss. 11. But the authority of the Samaritan text, which Morinus and Walton rashly make divine, he discussed in Exercit. Anti-Morin., as also in the cited dissertation p. 129.

From these translations, therefore, joined with the original text, notable editions of the Bibles have arisen, such as (1.) the Octapla of Augustinus Nebiensis, Bishop in Corsica, who with a new and huge undertaking, as Senensis writes, was the first of all to reduce both instruments of the sacred law into one body, primarily in five languages, Hebrew, Chaldean, Greek, Latin, and Arabic, having arranged eight columns on individual pages, in the first of which he proposed the Hebrew edition, in the second a Latin one responding word for word, in the third the Latin Vulgate, in the fourth the Greek, in the fifth the Arabic, in the sixth the Chaldean Paraphrase, in the seventh a Latin translation responding to the Chaldean, in the eighth short scholia or annotations, by which he refutes the errors of the Jews especially, in the year 1516.

(2.) The Complutensian Bible by the author Cardinal Franc. Ximenius in the year 1517, in which the Pentateuch is held according to the Hebrew text, the Chaldean version of Onkelos, and the Greek of the LXX Interpreters, to which the Latin Vulgate responds, added to the Hebrew as well as the Chaldean, and also a Latin interlinear interpretation of the Greek. The Hagiographa and Prophetic books, however, are exhibited in Hebrew and Greek text with a double Latin translation. The Apocryphal books have only the Greek Scripture with a double translation, the Vulgate, and an interlinear one made word for word. The New Testament, however, exhibits the Greek text with the version of Jerome.

(3.) The Antwerp Bible or Royal Work, printed at the expense of Philip II, King of the Spains, in Hebrew with an interlinear version, in Chaldean with an interpretation (exhibiting not only the paraphrases of Onkelos on the Pentateuch, but also of Jonathan on the Prophets, and of Joseph the Blind or others on the Hagiographa), in Greek with an exposition, and in Latin: in the N.T. also in Syriac with a translation, in IX Volumes in the year 1572, by the work especially of Benedictus Arias Montanus of Seville, who in the last Volume in the Sacred Apparatus added seven books on Hebrew idioms, on the arcane language, on action or habit, on sacred weights and measures, on sacred fabrics, on ages and times: and he rendered the Psalter of David in Latin verse. By which Arias Montanus the interlinear version of Sanctes Pagninus was also amended.

(4.) The Parisian work inscribed Parisian Heptapla, which appeared in this century in ten Volumes, 1. the Hebrew text, 2. the Samaritan, 3. the Samaritan version, 4. the Latin interpretation of this, 5. the Chaldean text, 6. the Greek of the LXX Interpreters, 7. the Latin of Jerome, 8. the Syriac of the ancient version made from the Hebrew text, which the simple the Syrians call it. 9. It exhibits the Arabic from an ancient Arabic exemplar copied in Egypt three centuries ago, with Latin translations of the Syriac and Arabic versions.

(5.) The English polyglot Bible in the Pentateuch presents 1. the Hebrew text, 2. the Samaritan, and the ancient Samaritan version, and the Latin translation of both, 3. the Greek of the LXX Interpreters according to the Vatican exemplar, with a collation of the most ancient Alexandrian MS, 4. the Old Vulgate Latin expressed from the LXX Interpreters, 5. the Latin of Sixtus and Clement, which is now commonly called the Vulgate. 6. The Chaldean Paraphrase, from the work of Buxtorf, as also the Jerusalem Targum of the Pentateuch and that of Jonathan, with a Latin interpretation, 7. the Persian Paraphrase of Jacob Tufensis, or Tawosi, with a Latin interpretation. In the Psalter, the Song of Songs, and the N.T., the Ethiopic version is exhibited with a Latin interpretation. The Persian Gospels are also presented with a Latin version. Finally, the Syriac version from various MSS, as also the Arabic translation, are contained in this work. Which work appeared in the year 1657. Of which versions, on account of their antiquity and sincerity, Hottinger in his dissertation on the Parisian Heptapla commends the Syriac above all, as following the Hebrew text almost word for word. He shows, however, on p. 85, that the Arabic is much more recent, and approaches very closely to the version of the excellent R. Saadia Haggon, who lived in the ninth century. Added to the polyglot work is an apparatus containing I. A chronology from the creation of the world until the destruction of the second temple by S. Scripture alone, by Lud. Capellus; II. A description of the Holy Land with a Chronographical Table, with a delineation of ancient Syria. III. A table of ancient Jerusalem according to the exemplar of Villalpando. IV. The Trisagion of Capellus, or a triple delineation of the Temple of Jerusalem from the Scriptures (according to Villalpando), from Josephus, and from the Talmud. V. The treatises of Brerewood and Tirinus on coins, weights, and measures, as also the Prolegomena of Brian Walton, the author of this work, on the nature of languages, characters, the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Persian languages, and the various editions and versions of the Bibles. Most of which stand in need of great emendation.

XIII. A Sacred Chronicle of the years from the creation of the world until the end of the seventy weeks of Daniel, to illustrate especially the writings of the O.T., elaborated with no common care, we shall afterwards prefix even to these Annotations, just as was done by Jac. Tirinus in his Annotations, which was also observed in the Great and Maximum Parisian Bibles of de la Haye, with only the Chronicle of Tirinus repeated.

XIV. A treatise on coins, serving likewise for the understanding of various places of the O.T., will be prefixed equally to the special annotations, with an appendix on weights and measures.

XV. Commentators on the books of the O.T. Besides those who, from among the Christians, have illustrated the whole Holy Scripture or most of the books of both Testaments with commentaries or annotations, from among the Hebrews are Raschi, or R. Solomon Jarchi, R. Abraham Ezra, R. David Kimchi, Rambam, or R. Moses Ben Nachman, Ralbag or R. Levi Ben Gerson, R. Saadia, R. Isaac Abarbenel, etc. Sixtus Senensis also lists Joseph Kimchi, the father of David Kimchi, who wrote Commentaries on the Pentateuch, Psalms, and Prophets in the year 1360. But of the Christians who wrote not indeed on the whole O.T., but on the Octateuch, Sixtus Senensis cites, besides Theodoret, Procopius of Gaza, Gregory the Great, Oecumenius, and Claudius the Monk, a disciple of the Venerable Bede. The same Senensis teaches that Stephen the Englishman recorded moral expositions not only on the Pentateuch but also on the Prophets at Paris in the year 1200; and that a certain James Martin, a Frenchman, published the Tropologies and Allegories of Origen on the Heptateuch in the year 1536. Alphonsus Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, completed the historical books of the O.T. up to Ezra and Matthew in the N.T. with prolix commentaries. Thomas de Vio, a native of Gaeta, Cardinal Cajetan, wrote commentaries on all the books of Scripture except the Prophetical ones and the Song of Songs in the year 1530, expounding the literal sense, from which later writers have drawn not a few things: to which Antonius Lusitanus a Fonseca added his own Annotations on the Pentateuch, but Ambrosius Catharinus, Archbishop of Conza, opposed Cajetan with invective refutations. Thomas Malvenda, a Spaniard, compiled various versions and interpretations of difficult passages in particular in Holy Scripture from Genesis to Ezekiel from diverse authors, though for the most part concealing their names; he also added his own version, literal indeed, but with affected and absurd words, in place of which he substituted other more suitable words of his own, existing either in the margin or in the Commentaries; it has its own praise and a use not to be despised at all, in the judgment of Matthew Poole. It was published at Lyon in the year 1650. On the first eight biblical books, Jacques Bonfrère wrote quite prolixly but excellently and learnedly, which commentaries, where he does not sail in favor of his Pope and the Vulgate, can be usefully employed.

XVI. Since it seemed convenient and useful, not only to us but even more so to others, to insert the Annotations on Grotius into this volume for many reasons, his preface, and what we have observed in that προπυλαίῳ (vestibule) by way of introduction, must absolutely be placed first, before the Annotations themselves and our own observations follow. Now there seems to be added

ST. JEROME'S HELMETED PROLOGUE.

That there are twenty-two letters among the Hebrews, the language of the Syrians and Chaldeans also testifies, which is for the most part akin to Hebrew. For they too have twenty-two elements with the same sound, but with different characters. The Samaritans also write the Pentateuch of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in shapes and points. And it is certain that Ezra the scribe, and doctor of the law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, found other letters, which we use now: since up to that time the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were the same. In the book of Numbers also this same calculation, under the census of the Levites and priests, is mystically shown. And the tetragrammaton name of the Lord, in certain Greek volumes, we find even today expressed in ancient letters. But also the thirty-sixth, and the hundred and tenth, and the hundred and eleventh, and the hundred and eighteenth, and the hundred and forty-fourth Psalms, although they are written in different meter, are nevertheless woven with the Alphabet of the same number. And the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and his prayer: also the Proverbs of Solomon at the end, from the place where he says, 'Who shall find a valiant woman?' are calculated by the same Alphabets or divisions. Furthermore, there are five double letters among the Hebrews, Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, Sade: for they are written differently at the beginnings and middles of words, otherwise the boundaries. Whence also five books are reckoned by most as double: Samuel, Melachim, Dibre hajamim, Esdras, Jeremias, with Cinoth, that is, his lamentations. Just as therefore there are twenty-two elements, through which we write everything that we speak in Hebrew, and by whose beginnings the human voice is comprehended; so twenty-two volumes are calculated, by which, as if by letters and rudiments, the tender and still suckling infancy of a just man is instructed in the doctrine of GOD.

The first book among them is called בראשית Beresith: which we call Genesis. The second, ואלה שמות Veelle semoth: which is called Exodus. The third, ויקרא Vajicra, that is, Leviticus. The fourth, וידבר Vajedabber, which we call Numbers. The fifth, אלה הדברים Elle haddebarim, which is entitled Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which they properly call תורה Thora, that is, the Law. They make the second order of the Prophets: and they begin from Jesus the son of Nave: who among them is called יהושע בן נון Josue ben Nun. Then they subjoin שפטים Sophetim, that is, the book of Judges. And they bind Ruth into the same: because its history is narrated in the days of the Judges. The third follows שמואל Samuel, which we call the first and second of Kings. The fourth, מלכים Melachim, that is, of Kings, which is contained in the third and fourth volume of Kings. And it is much better to say מלכים Melachim, that is, of Kings, than ממלכות Mamlachot, that is, of kingdoms. For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but of one Israelite people, which is contained by twelve tribes. The fifth is ישעיה Isaias. The sixth, ירמיה Jeremias. The seventh, יחזקאל Ezechiel. The eighth, the book of the twelve Prophets: which among them is called תרי עשר There asar. The third order possesses the Hagiographa. And the first book begins from איוב Job. The second from דוד David: which they comprehend in five divisions and one volume of Psalms. The third is שלמה Salomon, having three books: Proverbs, which they call משלי Misle, that is, Parables. The fourth, Ecclesiastes, that is, קהלת Coheleth. The fifth, the Song of Songs, which they entitle with the title שיר השירים Sir hassirim. The sixth is דניאל Daniel. The seventh, דברי הימים Dibre hajamim, that is, Words of days: which we can more significantly call the Chronicle of all divine history, which book is inscribed among us as the first and second of Paralipomenon. The eighth, עזרא Esdras: who himself also is similarly divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins. The ninth, אסתר Esther.

And thus the twenty-two books of the Old Law end equally: that is, five of Moses, and eight of the Prophets, and nine of the Hagiographa. Although some write that Ruth and Cinoth are among the Hagiographa, and think that these books should be reckoned in their number: and by this there are twenty-four books of the ancient law: which the Apocalypse of John introduces under the number of the twenty-four Elders worshipping the Lamb, and offering their crowns with prostrate faces: while there stand before them four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind, that is, looking into the past and into the future, and crying with an indefatigable voice, Holy, holy, holy Lord, God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come. This prologue, as a helmeted beginning of the Scriptures, can be suitable for all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin: so that we may be able to know that whatever is outside of these is to be placed among the apocrypha. Therefore Wisdom, which is commonly inscribed as Solomon's, and the book of Jesus the son of Syrach, and Judith, and Tobias, and the Shepherd, are not in the canon. The first book of Maccabees I found in Hebrew. The second is Greek: which can be proven from the very phrasing itself. Since these things are so, I beseech you, Reader, do not think my labor to be a disparagement of the ancients. In the temple of God everyone offers what he can: some offer gold, silver, and precious stones: others offer fine linen and purple and scarlet and hyacinth: it goes well with us if we have offered skins and goats' hair. And yet the Apostle judges our more contemptible things to be more necessary. Whence also all that beauty of the tabernacle, and the distinction of the present and future Church through individual species, is covered with skins and haircloth, and those things which are viler prevent the heat of the sun and the injury of the rains. Read therefore the first Samuel, and my Melachim: mine, I say, mine. For whatever we have both learned and hold by translating more frequently and correcting more solicitously, is ours. And when you have understood what you did not know before, consider me an interpreter, if you are grateful, or a Paraphrast, if ungrateful, although I am not at all conscious to myself that I have changed anything from the Hebrew truth. Certainly if you are incredulous, read the Greek codices, and the Latin, and compare them with those little works which we have recently corrected: and wherever you see them to differ among themselves; ask any of the Hebrews, to whom you ought to give more credence: and if he confirms our work, I think that you will not consider him a guesser, as if he had divined in the same place similarly with me. But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ (who anoint the head of the reclining Lord with the most precious myrrh of faith, who by no means seek the Savior in the sepulcher, to whom Christ has already ascended to the Father) that you oppose the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs, who rage against me with a rabid mouth, and go around the city, and think themselves learned in this, if they disparage others. I, knowing my humility, will always remember that sentence, I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood against me. I was dumb: and I was humbled, and I kept silence from good things.

The Helmeted [Prologue] of S. JEROME. There follows the interpretation of the Index usually added to the end of Bibles from the Hebrews.

NOTES ILLUSTRATING THE INDEX.

II. NOTES ILLUSTRATING THE INDEX.

This index teaches in order what the Parashot and Haftarot of the holidays are among the Jews, both the weekly and ordinary ones, and those falling between these. פָרָשָׁה explanation, סִדְרָה ordinary reading. Legal and Prophetic readings are attributed to the Sabbaths. The legal ones are called Parashot, of which there are as many as there are Sabbaths in a year. For they divided the whole law of Moses, comprised in five books, into 54 sections or Parashot, and assigned them to individual Sabbaths. But the fact that in the present לוח only 53 Parashot are numbered, and the last one וזאת הַבְּרָכָה is omitted, which is from chapter 33 of Deuteronomy to the end, appears from this, that this one is accustomed to be joined with the preceding Parashah, and to have one haftarah with it.

To the Sabbath texts of Moses they added others taken from the Prophets here and there; these they call הַפְטָרוֹת cessation. But which haftarot have been assigned to which Parashot, this Luach teaches, which similarly shows which haftarot are appropriate for holidays other than the Sabbath.

Other holidays that occur have their own haftarot, which are subjoined after the weekly readings; namely, from number 53 to the end of the Table.

The distinction of the Parashot of the Law is everywhere the same among the Jews of the nations. In the Haftarot, however, they sometimes vary according to nations. For to one Parashah, the Spanish Jews (הַסְפָרַדִים) formerly assigned one haftarah, and the German Jews (הָאַשְׁכְּנַזִים) assigned another to the same Parashah.

That the distinction of the Parashot is very ancient is gathered 1. from Nehemiah ch. VIII, 9, where it is ordered that mourning be deferred in the σκηνοπηγίᾳ until the twenty-fourth. During the whole time of the Feast of Tabernacles, the law was read for seven days, v. 18. The weeping was deferred to the 24th day of the 7th month, so that the twenty-third day, which was one of great joy, might pass. 2. From Luke XVI, 9, Acts XV, 21, that Moses is read every Sabbath in the Synagogues, namely a certain part or Parashah. Whence it is undoubted that the use of such particular readings destined for certain Sabbaths existed already in the time of Christ. When this was so ordained, we do not know, because we lack histories noting that time when the Parashot began.

This Index is divided into 4 columns. The first shows the names of the Parashot on weekly holidays: but on other festivals it represents the names of the festivals. The second contains the beginnings of the haftarot corresponding to any Parashah or festival. In the third column, the chapter of the Prophet from which the Haftarah is taken is assigned. In the fourth, the diversity of the haftarot according to the Spaniards and Germans and others is shown.

† l. 2. & 49. The same haftarah is assigned to a double Parashah, namely from Isaiah ch. 54, as can also be seen in the text.

† A. l. 23. The haftarah does not seem to be correctly noted by the word Vaijaas. Otherwise, one haftarah would serve two Parashot, Vayakhel and Pekude.

† B. l. 25. In the text, the beginning of this haftarah is omitted in the margin, which this haftarah has in common with many.

† C. l. 38. No mention of this haftarah is made in the margin of the text. But the words assigned in the לוח exist in the cited verse.

† D. l. 42. This haftarah is also joined to the Parashah Elleh Shemot by the custom of the Spanish Jews.

† E. l. 53. This parashah has two haphtarot: The beginning of the first is: Return, O Israel; of the second: Blow the trumpet in Zion.

† F. l. 57. Nor was the beginning of this one noted in the margin of the texts.

† G. l. 62. The weekday of the Sabbath during a festival. What this is, the marginal haphtara in Ezekiel, ch. 36, explains. It is the haphtara for the Sabbath בְּחוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד שֶׁל פֶּסַח. It is, namely, the haphtara of the Sabbath on the weekday of the solemnity, which is during Pesach.

† H. l. 74. This is stated more explicitly in Ezekiel ch. 38, in the margin, הַפְטָרַת חוֹל וְשֶׁל מוֹעֵד שֶׁל סֻכּוֹת the haphtara of the weekday, which is of the festival of tabernacles.

The use of the Parashot and Sidrot is evident in Deut. V, 20, where the letter פ is placed between the ninth and last commandment.

Et primo quidem Ebræam linguam ab Ebero dictam, in familia Eberi post γλωττοσύγχυσιν man- sisse communis fere est sententia. Scaliger vero in Epist. ad Rich. Thons. & Ubert. mero novitatis stu- dio, quod ipsi proprium & perpetuum fuit, linguam Ebræam falso eo nomine appellari, quum sit Phœni- cia, & Abrahamo demum in terra Canaan lin- guam Ebræam discendam fuisse, in Canaan vero apud Phœnices Chami posteros puram conservatam fuis- se primævam linguam, contendere ausus est: quem secutus est Erpenius in Orat. de lingua Ebræa (etsi sibi ipsi adversus, quum Orat. de lingua Arab.

CAS, & JOHANNES, quadriga Domini, & ve- rum Cherubim, quod interpretatur scientiæ mul- titudo, per totum corpus oculati sunt, scintillæ e- micant, discurrunt fulgura, pedes habent rectos, & in sublime tendentes, terga pennata & ubique voli- tantia, tenent se mutuo, sibiq; perplexi sunt, & quasi rota in rota volvuntur, & pergunt quocunque eos flatus Spiritus S. perduxerit. PAULUS Aposto- lus ad septem scribit Ecclesias: octava enim ad He- bræos, a plerisque extra numerum ponitur. Timo- theum instruit ac Titum, & Philemonem pro fugi- tivo famulo deprecatur. Super quo melius tace- re puto, quam pauca scribere. ACTUS APOSTO- LORUM nudam quidem sonare videntur histo- riam, & nascentis Ecclesiæ infantiam texere: sed si noverimus Scriptorem eorum Lucam esse medi- cum, cujus laus est in Evangelio, animadvertemus pariter omnia verba illius animæ languentis esse medicinam. JACOBUS, PETRUS, JOHANNES, JUDAS, septem Epistolas ediderunt, tam mysticas, quam succinctas, & breves pariter & longas: breves in verbis, longas in sententiis: ut rarus sit, qui non in earum lectione cœcutiat. APOCALYPSIS JO- ANNIS tot habet Sacramenta, quot verba. Pa- rum dixi, & pro merito voluminis laus omnis infe- rior est. In verbis singulis multiplices latent intel- ligentiæ. Oro te, frater carissime, inter hæc vive- re, ista meditari, nihil aliud nosse, nihil quærere. Nonne tibi videtur jam hic in terris regni cœlestis habitaculum? Nolo offendaris in Scripturis sanctis simplicitate, & quasi vilitate verborum, quæ vel vitio interpretum, vel de industria sic prolata sunt, ut rusticam concionem facilius instruerent, & in u- na eademque sententia aliter doctus, aliter audiret indoctus. Non sum tam petulans, & hebes, ut hæc me nosse pollicear, & eorum fructus capere, quo- rum radices in cœlo fixæ sunt: Sed velle fateor. Se- denti me præfero, magistrum renuens, comitem spondeo. Petenti datur, pulsanti aperitur, quærens invenit. Discamus in terris, quorum scientia nobis perseveret in cœlo.
