D. ABRAHAM AND THE ABOVE IN THE CHRONIC GENEALOGY

SECTION I. ON THE PRINCIPAL EPOCHS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT IN GENERAL.

It is especially useful and necessary to observe diligently the epochs which comprise years succeeding one another, up to the end of the weeks of Daniel, by which the times of the Old Testament are terminated, as far as concerns the completion of the prophetic predictions about Christ. For as the primary scope of the Holy Scriptures is Christ, for whose coming the τὸ πλήρωμα τẽ χρόνẽ (fullness of time) was defined in the mystery of the Holy Trinity, Gal. 4:4, concerning which the prophets inquired and searched, εἰς τίνα ἢ ποῖον καιρὸν ἐδήλꙋ τὸ ἐν ἀυτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστẽ (searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify), when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glories that should follow, 1 Pet. 1:11, so we ought to be solicitous in our searching of the prophetic Scripture concerning those times most of all. For the other times are indicated on account of that πλήρωμα τẽ χρόνꙋ (fullness of time), or they pertain to the kingdom of Christ, to the divine glory of Him exalted on the throne of Majesty, and concern His state under the New Testament. But those things which are less clear, as long as they are not yet illuminated by the light of completion—such as those designated in Daniel, which indeed receive some light from the Apocalypse handed down by the Son of God to the most beloved disciple—those words are nevertheless closed and sealed until the predetermined time of completion, Dan. 12:9, as regards a full, solid, and certain understanding.

Moreover, of those epochs which cohere with one another toward the blessed seed, the true MESSIAH, CHRIST JESUS, and His passion, resurrection, ascension, and the sending forth of His scepter to the nations, seven are found to be most illustrious.

The first is from the Proto-Evangelium, concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the infernal serpent—namely CHRIST JESUS, the God-man, the Redeemer of the world—promulgated by the Son of God immediately after the creation of the world and the fall of the protoplasts, up to the flood, by which the first world, incredulous to Noah the herald of the righteousness of Christ, perished with the exception of a few, namely eight souls, that faithful servant of God having been saved with his family in the ark, on account of that blessed Seed, for the sake of which the new world was also to be established through those remnants of the first world. Which comprises 1656 years.

The second period of years, or Epoch, begins from the repetition and confirmation of the Proto-Evangelium in the new world after the flood, concerning the grace to be shown to man—even though he is only prone to evil from his youth—on account of the sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savor, through which alone we are rendered propitious to God; namely, that God would not wish to curse the earth further, and that for the sake of Adam, or that one man in whom grace reaches all, Gen. 8:21, Rom. 5:15, and that for the sake of the same He deigned to bless the mortals of Noah and his sons anew, with the covenant of grace established with the human race and confirmed by the illustrious sign of the Rainbow, Gen. 9:1, 11, seqq. The terminus of the epoch is the promise made to Abraham, the father of believers, concerning the blessed seed, when he was called in Ur of the Chaldeans and journeyed from Haran into Canaan, Gen. 11:31, c. 12:1, 2, 3, 4. The whole period is 427 years, namely 222 from the flood up to Terah, 130 up to Abraham, and 75 to the Ἐπαγγελίαν (promise) made to Abraham, Gen. 12:4, which was afterwards sealed to the same patriarch by the Sacrament of Circumcision, Gen. 17.

The third epoch began from the said promise made to Abraham and his pilgrimage; and it ended at the Exodus, namely the leading out from Egypt, when the sacrament of the Paschal lamb was instituted, and furthermore the Law was delivered, not that the promise might be made void, but that it might be a tutor unto Christ. Which comprises 430 years, as the Apostle testifies in Gal. 3:17, and Moses himself in Exod. 12:40.

The fourth flowed from the Exodus to the construction of Solomon's Temple, which was a type of the temple of Christ's body, and in which the doctrine concerning the Messiah was propagated, both by the preaching of the Word and by the foreshadowing of figures, such as the priesthood, sacrifices, altars, the ark of the covenant, and other things of that kind. This was of 480 years, 1 Kings 6:1.

The fifth is from the construction of Solomon's Temple to the indulgence of the people's liberty and the building of the new temple by Cyrus, after the 70 years of Babylonian servitude and the total destruction of the former temple, granted by divine gift: since the Messiah was to perform his office in the promised land and the later temple. And this was of 424 years up to the destruction of the former Temple, to which are added furthermore 52 years up to the indulgence of liberty under the Monarchy of Cyrus, so that this whole period is of 476 years.

The sixth epoch extends from the released Babylonian captivity up to the beginning of the 70 weeks of Daniel, or the going forth of the word concerning the restoring of the sacred things and the rebuilding of the city, into the certainty of the coming of the Messiah, that is, up to the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus. Which comprises 78 years.

The seventh is of the 70 weeks of Daniel. In the sixty-fifth current week of which falls the birth of Christ, in the beginning of the last the start of Christ's office, in the middle his passion, death, resurrection, and ascension, in the end the calling of the Gentiles, and the new name of the faithful, which they received from Christ, being called Christians: where the Old Testament properly ceased, the New fully began. This whole is of 490 years. But 483 up to Christ's ministry, 453 to his birth.

Thus, therefore, the epochs up to Christ from the foundation of the world, or the promulgation of the Proto-Evangelium, will stand:

I. From the foundation of the world (which was followed shortly after by the paradisiacal promise of the seed of the woman) up to the flood, 1656 years.

II. From the renewal of the promise of grace made to Noah, up to the calling of Abraham 427

III. From the ἐπαγγελίᾳ of Abraham concerning the blessed seed, up to the exodus from Egypt 430

IV. From there to the construction of Solomon's Temple 480

V. From there to the liberty of building the new Temple 476

VI. From there to the beginning of the weeks of Daniel 78

VII. From there to the Advent of Christ 453

To the Baptism of Christ, therefore, 4030 years have flowed from the foundation of the world. Since this falls in the 30th year of Christ's age, the year of Christ's birth will be the year of the World 4000. And by adding to the year of Christ's baptism from the foundation of the world the 7 years of the final week of Daniel, there will emerge 4037 years, namely from the foundation of the world, until the end of the 70 weeks.

QUESTION I. Whether the night was prior to the day in the Creation?

Philoponus, Marius Victorinus, as also Procopius of Gaza, make the day prior; but the history of the Creation teaches the contrary, because it testifies that darkness was first upon the face of the abyss, the primordial mass having been created, which we commonly call Chaos, which primordial darkness lasted for twelve hours before the light was created, and constituted the first night; but when light was created by God, the first morning arose, and the light being diffused through the remaining hours of the νυχθημερινꙋ, and its motion having been completed until the darkness returned, the first day was constituted. Petavius indeed denies that the primordial darkness was the first night, but because no other things preceded the primordial light, those certainly constituted the first night, even if it was not merely a privation of light, as in the following days, but a mere negation, and therefore Moses makes the evening prior to the dawn in the description of the Hexaemeron: And there was evening, and there was morning, Gen. 1, 5.

Whence the Jews also make the beginning of the day from the evening, who received it from nowhere else than from the Patriarchs and Adam. Conf. Exod. 12, 18. which custom was received by other nations and peoples also from ancient times. Gellius, book III, ch. 2, reports the same also of the Athenians, disciples of the Phoenicians in many things. Concerning the Numidians, Nicolaus of Damascus says: The Numidians in Libya compute their times not by days, but by nights. Concerning the Druids, Pliny, book XVI of Natural History, last chapter. The moon which makes the beginnings of the months and years here. Caesar also teaches that the Gauls once had this in use, book VI of the Gallic War: They measure the spaces of all time, not by the number of days, but of nights; which Tacitus also noted concerning the ancient Germans: They do not compute the number of days as we do, but of nights: thus they appoint, thus they agree, the night seems to lead the day. Grotius observed somewhere that the Bohemians and Poles still observe this custom even now.

QUESTION II. Whether the seventh day was consecrated to divine worship from the divine Sabbath of the Creation?

That the sanctification of the Sabbath was not instituted immediately from creation, but only around the promulgation of the law, is contended by Franciscus Gomarus, following Tostatus of Avila, along with John Prideaux and Robert Loc; but that it must be derived from the first creation is clear, first from the very history of Creation in Gen. 2, 2. 3: God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, where neither a hysteron proteron nor a parenthesis has a place; for it would be most absurd that Moses should have joined in that simple and clear history things which were separated by a very great interval of time. Which is then also confirmed from the Apostolic passage Heb. 4, 9, which derives the rest of the Sabbath day from the perfection of the works of God within the hexaemeron. Furthermore, from the very law concerning the gathering of Manna, Exod. 16, 27, the same is proved not obscurely, because the sanctification of the Sabbath was required there, with the law not yet promulgated, not as a new thing, but as one already instituted long ago. Furthermore, it is inconvenient that the Patriarchs either had no set day for divine worship, or defined some day for themselves out of mere will-worship. Finally, it was not only among the Hebrews that it was beyond doubt that the Sabbath had been instituted when God rested on the seventh day of the world, as Philo, book III on the Life of Moses, says that the Sabbath day has a privilege from nature, from the time the world was born. (Add also Josephus, book I, Antiquities, ch. 2.) But other nations also observed a revolution of seven days from every age, the origin of which Andreas Rivetus, in his Appendix to the Explanation of the Decalogue, concludes could be none other than the inveterate opinion that the world was created in six days and that work ceased on the seventh, and thus the remaining ones were numbered from this first week. Salmasius observes from the Chronological works of Georgius Syncellus that the most ancient peoples, before the method of calculating by years and months prevailed among them, distinguished spaces of time by weeks. Josephus, against Apion, says there is no city, Greek or barbarian, which the custom of the seventh day, on which the Jews rest, has not pervaded. Philo, on the seventh day, says: It is a feast day, not for one city or region, but for the universe. To which add what Eusebius brings forward from Aristobulus, book XIII of Evangelical Preparation, ch. 12; what Clement of Alexandria brings from Hesiod, Homer, and Callimachus, book V of the Stromata; and what Dio Cassius, book 33, teaches, that the custom of calculating time by seven days flowed from the Egyptians to the whole human race; that this was most ancient is evident from Herodotus, book II.

Nor was there any doubt, either among the Fathers—see Chrysostom, Homily IX on chapter II of Genesis; Tertullian, book IV against the Jews and against Marcion, book IV, chapter 12; Theodoret on Genesis 2; Augustine to Casalanus—or among the Papists (if you except Abulensis)—see Catharinus, Genebrardus, Salianus, Emanuel Saá, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus—or among the Reformed, who, besides those three modern triumvirs, all affirm it with a common voice: Zwingli, Calvin, Beza, Martyr, Pelican, Bullinger, Gualther, Zanchius, Aretius, Ursinus, Bucanus, Junius, Bertram, Paraeus, Zepper, Martinius, Alsted, etc., or among our own people, who unanimously agree here, concerning the fact that the Sabbath was instituted from the beginning of the world. See those things which Rivetus and Walaeus opposed to Gomarus. Finally, it is evident from Menasseh Ben-Israel, problem 8 on creation, that even some modern Jews admit that the Sabbath was observed before Abraham and the other Patriarchs; he confirms this opinion, among other things, from Schemoth Rabba, which states that Moses requested from Pharaoh in Egypt that he allow the afflicted people to cease from labors for one day in the week, and having obtained this, he chose the Sabbath by tradition.

But as for the fact that Abulensis and Gomarus appeal to Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Eusebius, and Damascenus, who seem to derive the Sabbath from the Mosaic law, it must be observed that they are either speaking of the rigor sanctioned in the law, or certainly are looking not at the novelty of the sanctification of the Sabbath, but only at its innovation under Moses.

QUESTION III. Whether the years designated by the Holy Spirit, both before and after the flood, are of the same quantity?

There have not been wanting those who thought that the years designated by Moses in the lives of the Patriarchs before the flood were not equal to the rest, but much smaller, so that they would not have to admit the unusual longevity of those Patriarchs. But it is evident from very many places in Scripture that the Mosaic years had 12 months, and it is in no way to be believed that the Holy Spirit established some years in one place and other years in different places of Scripture; for thus all things would be rendered uncertain in the sacred calculation, and all reasons for chronology would be easily overturned. Furthermore, since the years of the later Patriarchs cannot be understood as months or quarters, inasmuch as Abraham at 100 and Jacob at 130 years of age are introduced as decrepit old men, and most of the sons of Jacob are said to have begotten children before their 20th year; but since in the former [cases] no trace of distinction or diversity appears, it would be the height of rashness to understand the former years otherwise, and to invent some distinction of years beyond Scripture. And how absurd that monthly examples: e.g., when we read that Mahalaleel and Enoch begat [children] in the 65th year of their age, if monthly years are understood, it must be said that they begat them in the sixth solar year; if bimonthly, in the tenth; if trimonthly, in the fifteenth. Finally, lest any doubt remain as to what kind of years are understood by Moses, Moses himself in the description of the flood defined the year with its months, when he made mention of the 150 days of the year of the flood, Gen. 7, 24, which completed five months, from the 17th day of the second month to the 17th day of the seventh month, c. 8, v. 4, and likewise of the tenth month, v. 5. and 40 days from the beginning of the 10th month, which extend to the twelfth month, whence that year must have been of 12 months: since indeed the Holy Spirit, having designated the months and days of the year of the flood, defined the same from the beginning of the flood to the end of it in such a way that it seems by no means obscure that 12 months of 30 days each constituted a full year. Add that the Gentiles also report that the life of those who followed the first men lasted for almost a thousand years. Berosus in the Chaldaica, Manetho in the Aegyptiaca, Hieronymus in the Phoenicia, Hestiaeus, Hecataeus, Hellanicus among the Greeks (all of whom Josephus cites as witnesses in Book I of his Antiquities, ch. IV, while their books still remained in his own time, and besides these Acusilaus, Ephorus, Nicolaus of Damascus) and among the poets Hesiod; not to mention that Servius noted in the 8th book of the Aeneid that the Arcadians were accustomed to live to 300 years.

QUESTION IV. What was the form of the year designated in the Holy Scriptures?

A judgment can be made about the ancient form of the year from the year of the flood. Before the Exodus, in the times of the Patriarchs in Chaldea and Egypt, the Hebrews had the equable Chaldean and ancient Egyptian year of 360 days, with a just intercalation of epagomenal days and superfluous hours, as B. D. Behmius establishes in Book I, tit. 2, ch. 3, and tit. 3, ch. 2 of his Manuductio Chronologica; he calls this year Egyptian, not because it is lunar, but because it is almost solar, since it came into Egypt through the Patriarchs. For since the flood began on the 17th day of the 2nd month, Gen. 7, 11, and the decrease began on the 17th day of the 7th month after 150 days, c. 7, 24, c. 8, 3, 4, it is indisputably certain that five months made 150 days: and from that it is further gathered that one month consisted of 30 days, and the same must be held regarding the remaining seven months. But because five days are thus lacking for the integrity of the year, there was need for their intercalation: which was done either by an intercalary month, or, as Kepler more correctly thinks in his Eclogae Chronicae p. 89, in such a way that the twelfth month was of 35 days. For there is no doubt that the years of the ancient Egyptians were of 365 days, and that they received that form from the Hebrews. Diodorus Siculus, concerning the Theban Egyptians, Book I of his Bibliotheca, says: They regulate their days not by the motion of the moon, but of the sun, and assign thirty days to their months, and after every twelfth month they add five days and a quarter, and in that way they complete the annual calculation. Herodotus in Euterpe, or Book II, concerning the Egyptians, says: They reported that the Egyptians were the first of all men to discover the year, dividing it into 12 months of the seasons, and they discovered this from the stars, and they do this more prudently, as it seems to me, than the Greeks, because the Greeks indeed introduce an intercalary month every third year on account of the seasons (or the opportune times of things), but the Egyptians, by the number of thirty days, to which they limit their 12 months, add five days every year, whence they have a consistent ratio of the cycle of the seasons returning to the same point. Strabo, Book 17, has this concerning the Egyptians: These count their years not by the moon, but by the course of the sun, with twelve months, each of which consists of 30 days, adding five days every year: to the completion of the whole year, since a certain particle of a day runs over, they compose a certain period. Quintus Curtius, Book 3, concerning the ancient Persians, says: The Magi, who were nearest, sang a national song, and 365 youths followed, veiled in purple cloaks, equal in number to the days of the whole year. Furthermore, Macrobius reports in Book I of his Saturnalia, ch. 14, that the Julian arrangement of the new year itself was made by the work of Sosigenes the mathematician, who was an Alexandrian, after the example of the Egyptians. (Caius Julius Caesar), having imitated the Egyptians, who alone were privy to all divine matters, strove to direct the year to the number of the sun, which completes its course in three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter. Polyaenus, Book 1 of his Strategemata, writes that Hercules gave his daughter 365 districts of India according to the days of the year. Censorinus, in De Die Natali, says: The civil year of the Egyptians has only 365 days, without any intercalary [day]. And Petavius, in Book 9 of De Doctrina Temporum, ch. 9, does not dissent from this opinion. Therefore, nothing prevents the individual months of the Patriarchs from the time of the flood from having been of thirty days: what remained of the solar year was either cast to the end of the year or admitted after certain intervals of years had elapsed.

Leonhard Marius, in his Commentary on Genesis, p. 69, observes that the Jews before the exodus from Egypt, and even the first Patriarchs, had the same reckoning of the year, inasmuch as it is found among all Oriental nations without any mention of its first institution; which he thinks the Patriarchs used because they were intermingled in Egypt, Canaan, Chaldea, and Mesopotamia with other nations among whom it was customary. But it is more correctly referred to the Patriarchs themselves as the authors, from whom it reached the Egyptians and other nations through their information or conversation, just as many other things did.

Nor is the calculation indeed detracted from by the more recent form of the Hebrew year, which is lunar but accommodated to the solar, consisting of 354 days distributed into 12 lunations, i.e., lunar months, of which some have 30 days, others 29; the former are called full, the latter hollow. Whence every year 11 days are lacking for the completion of the solar year, which are called epacts, from which is gathered a 13th month, ἐμβολιμαῖος, called Ve Adar, that is, another Adar, which is added at the end of the year and always has 30 days, so that an embolismic year is ordinarily of 384 days. This intercalation of a month ensures that nothing is lost in the total calculation of years, even if the form of individual years varies according to that triple reckoning already mentioned. See the treatise on the various forms of years published by Thomas Lydiat.

QUESTION V.

How are the months of the Hebrews designated?

In the Code of the Old Testament, the months are designated primarily by numbers; and thus mention is made of all the months: of the First Month Gen. VIII, 13, Exod. XL, 2 & 17. Of the Second Month Gen. VII, 11, Num. IX, 11. Of the Third 2 Chron. XV, 10. Of the Fourth Jerem. LII, 6. Of the Fifth Jer. LII, 12. Of the Sixth Haggai I, 1. Of the Seventh Gen. VIII, 4, II Chron. V, 3. Of the Eighth I Reg. XII, 32. Of the Ninth I Chron. XXVII, 12. Of the Tenth Gen. VIII, 5. Of the Eleventh Deut. I, 3. Of the Twelfth II Reg. XXV, 27. Finally, all twelve months are thus designated by numbers, 1 Chron. ch. XXVII. Yet the months are assigned other names in the Sacred Scriptures in the Hebrew text, as also in the Greek in the Maccabees. It is helpful to compare these names with the Roman ones, with the Egyptian names added on account of Ptolemy.

II, 1. Esth. III, 1. which is also Abib. Exod. XIII, 4. Phanemoth Ξανθικὸς. Josephus, Antiq. book I, ch. 5, calls Nisan Xanthicum. March. Second, Iiar, which is also Ziv. 1 Kings VI, 1. & 37. Pharmuthi Ἀρτεμίσιος. April. Third, Sivan, Esth. VIII, 9. Pachan Δαίσιος. May. Fourth, Tamuz Payni Πάνεμος. June. Fifth, Ab Epiphi Λῶος. Quintilis. Sixth, Elul, Neh. VI, 16. Mesori Γορπιαῖος. Sextilis. Seventh, Thisri, which is also Ethanim, 1 Kings VIII, 2. Thoth Ὑπερβερεταῖος. September. Eighth, Marchesvan, which is also Bul, 1 Kings VI, 38. Paophi Δίος. October. Ninth, Caslev, Nehem. I, 1. Zach. VII, 1. Athyr Ἀπελλαῖος. November. Tenth, Thebet, Esth. II, 16. Chojas Αὐδυναῖος. December. Eleventh, Sebeth. Tybi Περίτιος. January. Twelfth, Adar, Esth. III, 7. 13. Mochyr Δύςρος, which is Dioscorinthius, 2 Macc. XI, 21. February.

Some are accustomed to present the Hebrew months in a double order, of which they make one primeval, according to which the autumnal months come first, the winter ones follow, afterwards the vernal, and in the last place the summer ones; so that the year begins from the month Thisri and ends in the month Elul: but the other they call Exodic, which we have presented in the Table, from the vernal month Nisan to the month Adar, the last winter one. Therefore they are accustomed to establish a double year: a Political one beginning from the month Thisri, observed in markets and other Political affairs; and an Ecclesiastical one, which took its beginning from the month Nisan, according to which the festivals were celebrated.

However, this Jewish distinction is not approved by B. Luther in Comment. on Gen. c. 7. f. 130. But I do not approve of this reasoning of the Jews, who establish two beginnings of the year. For why do they make four beginnings, when there are four distinct seasons, according to the equinoxes and solstices? Therefore, the beginnings of these seasons will also be distinct; but it is safer to follow the divine ordinance. According to this, the first month is the month of April, or that lunation which is closer to the vernal equinox. For as to the fact that the Jews, because the autumnal equinox is called the exit of the year, also establish the autumnal beginning of the year, they do that out of ignorance; for they call it the exit of the year for no other reason than that at that time rustic labors ceased, and all the fruits had been collected and carried home. This is B. Luther. For in this passage, Exod. 23, 16, they seek the foundation of the civil year primarily from the exit of the year: but, in the judgment of our Luther, ignorantly, since the exit of the year is spoken of solely because of the cessation or end of rustic labors. Whence Edward Simson in Parasceve ad Chronicum Catholicum distinguishes between the civil year, which he does not make different from the ecclesiastical, and the rustic year. Leonh. Marius replies to the aforementioned passage thus: That the feast of tabernacles, which is celebrated in the 7th month, is said to be celebrated at the exit of the year, by the name of exit the latter half of the year is understood: as if he were to say, the two former feasts occur in the former part of the year, but the third, of tabernacles, in the latter. Others think that Moses spoke here of the term of the year according to the custom of the Egyptians, to which the Israelites were accustomed in Egypt. But he had warned that otherwise they had always begun the year from the spring, and that it was to be begun thus by the command of God himself, Exod. 12, 2. And thus תְּקוּבַת הַשָּׁנָה the revolution of the year is established in the spring near the vernal equinox, 2 Chron. 24, 33, at which time kings were accustomed to go out to war, 2 Sam. 11, 1, as also תְּשׁוּבַת הַשָּׁנָה the return or reversion of the year 2 Sam. 11, 1. 1 Kings 20, 22. & 26. 1 Chron. 20, 1.

Although indeed the Sabbatical and Jubilee years were to be begun from the autumnal equinox, Lev. 25, 9. 10, yet that was done because of rustic or rural labors, and had a peculiar reason (because if they had been begun from the spring, since one had to abstain from all sowing and reaping then, the Hebrews would have had to lack their harvest for two continuous years then, nay, for four whole years, if a Jubilee year had supervened in the following year; see Tirinus in Chron. sacro c. 5.) nor was that ordained from the foundation of the world, but only after the departure from Egypt, and from that time also in contracts of buying and selling the reason for this beginning of the year had to be taken into account: since in those one had to look to the Jubilee years, so that one's neighbor would not suffer loss, Lev. 15, 15. To which was added that the Israelites were accustomed to this revolution of the year in Egypt, whence Thekuphath Haschana, the revolution of the year, is commemorated at the feast of the gathering of fruits, which was in the autumn, Lev. XXIII, 39, Exod. XXXIV, 22, from the Egyptian custom, of which, however, an emendation was made in Exod. XII, 2, and it was commanded to the people that the month Abib,

Let them have Abib, or Nisan, for the beginning of the year, so that he might be recalled from that custom which he had contracted in Egypt to the pristine tenor of the Patriarchs and of the primeval world, at the beginning of the year. And therefore, what Josephus says in Book I of the History of the Jews, ch. 5, that Moses only established the month of Nisan as the first for festivals and divine matters, but in sales and purchases and other administration, he made no innovation regarding the pristine rite, is to be accepted only with a grain of salt: namely, in this sense: that he indeed left the pristine rite of the Egyptians to the Israelites thus far, as it served for contracts, because it could not be rashly changed, but he by no means sanctioned the month of Tishri by any decree as a peculiar beginning of the year. For ears should not be lent here so much to Josephus, who clings to the Egyptian rite, as to God, who establishes the law, which is certainly not alien to the custom of the prior world and Patriarchal observation, since Moses defined it simply, and without distinction of an Ecclesiastical and Political year, in Ex. 12:2: This month shall be the head of months for you, it shall be the first for you among the months of the year. For it is one thing to sanction a different beginning of the year, namely Ecclesiastical and Political, which Scaliger wants, but which is nowhere read to have been done by Moses: it is another thing to employ a different manner of speaking somewhere about the revolution and end of the year, which could have been done κατ’ ἄνθρωπον, or from a customary way of speaking, while only a single beginning of the year remained. For since months are designated in Scripture by numbers, it is certainly not consistent with the truth that that numerical designation was made by God Himself in one way and another, or used by the Holy Spirit with a different meaning, so that, for example, the month which is the seventh was, and was called, the first, and so on: especially because the Holy Spirit nowhere indicated that different method of enumeration by any sign, nor is He the author of confusion, but of order and distinction, since confusion easily arises from that different designation.

QUESTION VI.

Whether all the years that are referred to in Scripture without a diminishing particle are to be understood as complete?

There are those who deny that complete years are to be understood, because it is not likely that all of them begat sons in the very year in which they are referred to: whence Rollenhagen concludes that the precise enumeration of the whole sum is hidden from us. Dionysius Petavius also, in Book 9 of the Doctrine of Times, ch. 17, thinks that it cannot be gathered by any certain argument whether the years of the Patriarchs which are numbered in Scripture are complete and turning, or begun; and that it is credible that the years of not all the Patriarchs at least were whole when they begat children. And therefore, that the time of the epochs of the flood and the birth of Abraham cannot be established with certainty and without doubt. But Jacobus Capellus took the years of the first four generations, which end in round numbers (say, tens or fives), as begun or shortened.

But although it is not to be believed that the Patriarchs all begat on one and the same day or month, as some Hebrews, according to David Kimchi, supposed, that the Patriarchs were born in the first month, which for that reason was called Ethanim because of its excellence and strength: yet there should be no doubt for us concerning this, that those years which the Holy Spirit revealed for the sake of chronology, because no one could know from elsewhere about the time that had passed, are to be counted thus conjunctively and gathered into a sum, so that the sacred computation thence may be held as certain: for it is not to be thought that the Holy Spirit wished to leave us uncertain while He so solicitously calculates the years, if indeed He even goes before us, by gathering into a sum the years of begetting, and those which followed them to the end of life, Gen. 5. Rightly here Ussher, Sect. in Chron. sacra p. 57. That the last year of begetting of one Patriarch may fall short by a few months, while another's may have been extended within one or another month, makes no difference to the sum of the matter; since in both cases, with a compensation made in the aggregation of the years of the whole interval, an equalization is made, which is abundantly sufficient for revealing the age and series of the world.

There is therefore no reason for us to introduce Pyrrhonism into Biblical Chronology with Petavius, and render all things doubtful and uncertain, not without ignominy to the divinely inspired writers and the Holy Spirit Himself. For why would the Holy Spirit have so solicitously counted those years from the foundation of the world if He had wished us to remain uncertain? And unless He wished to hand down a Chronology by complete years, He would have added nothing certain, as Harvellæus rightly, Isagoge Chron. §. 14. col. 164. If it be permitted in the first age of the world (so argues Tirinus, Chron. sacræ c. 10.) to pluck away something at will from the whole years which Scripture expresses, the same will be permitted for all the following ages: and thus all the Chronology of all the Patriarchs, Judges, and Kings will be uncertain.

QUESTION VII.

What is to be thought of the computation of those who by many centuries exceed our calculation of the years of the world?

It is no longer a matter of a difference of a few years; because almost innumerable discrepancies are found among writers regarding the years of the world that have passed. But it is a matter of the opinions of those who exceed our computation of the years of the world by many centuries, and count five thousand years and more from the foundation of the world to the common Epoch of Christ: how the venerable Bede assigned 5199, Marianus Scotus 4192, Augustine and Philo 5195, Eusebius of Caesarea 5200, Isidore of Seville 5210, Sulpitius Severus 5469, Cedrenus 5493, Theophilus 5515, King Alfonso of Castile 6484 years from the foundation of the world: of which kind also is the computation of the Greeks, who count 5508 years, the Ethiopians, who count 5499, and the Romans in the Martyrology, who count 5198 years. From the Sicilian fasti 5608 years are gathered, not to mention the monstrous numbers of the Gentiles, since, as Diodorus testifies in book 2, the Chaldeans recount 43,000 years in their observations, and Plato claims that the Egyptians count ten thousand years, nay, he even hands down somewhere that ten thousand times ten thousand years of unknown years are counted.

That all these years of the world are multiplied too much, no one doubts today who looks up to and venerates the Hebrew truth of the sacred Code as is fitting. But Isaac Vossius, in the treatise on Chronology recently subjected to the Father, as also in his Dissertation on the true age of the world, and likewise Brian Walton in the prolegomena 9 to the English Polyglot Bible, at the end, contending sharply against the Hebrew truth, strive to enrich the years of the world by many centuries in the Calvinist Church. Vossius attempts to show in the said dissertation that at least 1440 years are missing from the creation of the world until the birth of the Patriarch Abraham: Nay, he brings forward the antiquities of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Seres as an argument: not much wiser than Isaac La Peyrère the Pre-Adamite, who in the first part of his System praises the Chinese, because in the year of Christ 1594 they counted the year 880,070. Who therefore, in the same religion otherwise with one voice, Robert Baillie gravely chastises, and laboriously refutes, in his Historical and Chronological work, book 1, chapter 2, question 4, and chapter 4, question 2, as also Greg. Horn, Professor of History at the University of Leiden, in his Diatribe against Vossius's dissertation.

Such absurdities scarcely deserve refutation. We shall, however, subjoin some things from Bail, by which he received his Vossius along with his antiquities. He ought not, he says on page 23, for a most learned man to attack the truth of the sacred texts with such arguments: those things which are told about the antiquities of the Chaldeans outside the Scriptures are pure fables and ravings. From the sacred books of the Chaldeans, the Magi brought forth deeds done, not only before the flood, but also before the creation by more than 400,000 years, as Cicero reports in De Divinatione, book 1, page 88, and from him Lactantius, book 7, chapter 14. Whichever books of the Chaldeans prove the δυναστίας of Africanus, the same testify to that enormous number of 47,000 years of Cicero: but Cicero wishes these to be mocked, despised, condemned for folly, vanity, and imprudence, nay, to be judged as lying, and as Lactantius has it, raving.

Concerning the fabulous Egyptian antiquities, he praises the testimony of Diodorus, who in book 1 says that he had indeed received from the Egyptian priests that heroes had reigned for eighteen thousand years, and after them mortal men before his own journey to Egypt, while Ptolemy Dionysius the younger was reigning, for fifteen thousand years; but he confesses that in Egyptian matters he finds no firmness worthy of belief before the Trojan times.

Concerning the chronology of the Seres or Chinese, Bail replies on page 24: Who will guarantee that the Augustinian monks (for the dynasties of the Chinese, described by Scaliger in book 2 of the Canones Isagogici, rely solely on their word) certainly knew that the writings kept in the archives of the Chinese were older than the days of Moses?

But as for the fact that the new disturbers of sacred chronology demand corruption of the Hebrew text and prefer the edition of the LXX Interpreters to it, in that they at least beg the question, and act as midwives to the Papists, and especially to the Parisian monk Morin.

This is the Πρῶτον ψεῦδος, and the primary sophism invented by Ludovicus Capellus, says Bail on page 9, consistent with no right reason, that the Hebrew texts used by the LXX Interpreters do not appear, do not exist, and are not now in the nature of things, distinct from those of today.

However, it is not the case that we should say with Ussher in his Syntagma on the LXX Interpreters that the version which is attributed to the LXX Interpreters was not composed by them, but rather by an obscure Hellenist who placed it in the library of Cleopatra, not of Ptolemy Euergetes: concerning which opinion of Ussher we have spoken in the prolegomena to the Commentary on Genesis. Walton himself acknowledges that the LXX Interpreters were not prophets so divinely inspired that their version was ever authentic. And the most learned Cardinal Bellarmine, among the Pontificians, confesses in book 2 of De Verbo Dei, chapter 6, that the version of the LXX which survives is so corrupted and vitiated that it seems to be something entirely different. And Vossius and Walton are rightly urged by Bail, because no discrepancy in the calculation is found here in the Hebrew codices: The passages of the Hebrew Bibles, he says, about which no one has ever moved a dispute of variant reading, ought not to be controverted. Capellus and Walton, through various readings, have called the sincerity of many passages into doubt more than is proper, very undeservedly; but where no various readings have ever been alleged, to wish to claim that the Hebrew source is corrupted is to overturn from the very foundations the authority, let alone the authenticity, of all the sacred Codices. Those with whom we are dealing confess that neither the version of the LXX Interpreters, nor the Latin, nor the Arabic, nor any other, whether ancient or new, is the authentic scripture: if, therefore, the authenticity and sincerity of the Hebrew sources be called into doubt even in those places where no various readings have ever appeared, nothing will remain certain in any Bibles. There was a great controversy between Protestants and Papists as to whether the Hebrew or the Latin texts were authentic, but this dispute ascends much higher: the certainty of faith is taken away from all Bibles; Protestants, with the agreement also of Walton and his associates, take away faith from the Greek, Latin, and all versions insofar as they differ from the Hebrew; if Walton and his own also impute error to the Hebrew Bibles, especially in those places where from the beginning to this day no difference of reading has been alleged, what divine scripture will finally remain, pure and without error? And what standard of truth will be left on earth to which it may be permitted to appeal securely in all things? This principle will lead many to the Roman Pontiff as the supreme judge of all controversies of religion, but more to the skepticism of Pyrrho and true atheism. Most people now laugh at the Papal authority long since exploded; they do not care about corrupted versions of the Bibles if, what was remaining, the authority of the original Bibles is enervated; there will be nothing upon which faith may certainly rest, and what Satan would uniquely desire, individuals in all sacred matters and in any truth whatsoever will be left to the guidance of their own minds. Furthermore, the truth of those passages in the Hebrew Bibles ought not to be called into question which all ancient versions, except for that of the LXX Interpreters, follow; for the authority of that version is not such that it should outweigh both the original text and all versions that exist. Now, indeed, in Walton's own Bibles, it appears to all readers that the Chaldean, Samaritan, Syriac, Arabic, and Latin versions contradict the Greek version in Gen. V, and follow the Hebrew truth, and the same consensus exists in all more recent versions, as appears in the French, English, Belgian, Spanish, Italian, and others. Furthermore, if the calculation of the Greek texts is preferred to the calculation of the Hebrew Bibles, then the entire sacred Chronology will be overturned from the foundations; for the addition of fifteen hundred years will disturb all the reasonings of all recent chronologers; their disagreement about days, months, or years will extend to fifteen whole centuries and more; whatever learned men have brought forward, either long ago or recently, from eclipses or the motions of the stars to fix the characters of the times, will all vanish with this addition of theirs of so many centuries. Thus did Baelius refute his Socinians. There is no reason for us to add anything to these. For frivolous comments are unworthy of a more extensive refutation.

SECTION II.

ON THE EPOCH OF THE ANTEDILUVIAN WORLD.

The lives of the Patriarchs recounted by Moses in Gen. V mainly constitute this: in which the doctrine of the Proto-Evangelium concerning the blessed seed of the woman was propagated through those holy Patriarchs, whose memory the ocean of historians has preserved. For the sake of propagating this more dexterously, a singular μακροβιότης, or longevity of life, was granted to the holy men of God, so that by that mutual συμβιώσει with the most ancient of mortals, and even with the protoplasts themselves, the faithful throughout the world could be informed and confirmed in the true recognition of the Messiah and the knowledge of salvation. Now the years of this epoch are as follows.

From the foundation of the world and the creation of the protoplasts, to whom the Gospel was first promulgated, to Seth flowed years - - - 130. From Seth to Enos, in whose time the public proclamation concerning the name of the LORD began. 105. From Enos to Kenan - - - 90. From Kenan to Mahalaleel - - - 70. From Mahalaleel to Jared - - 66. From Jared to Henoch - - - 162. From Henoch to Methusalah - - 65. From Methusalah to Lamech - - 187. From Lamech to Noah - - - 182. From Noah to the flood, Genes. VII, 11. - 600. The sum of the years of this Epoch 1656.

QUESTION I. At what time of the year was the world created?

This question does not regard so much the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, winter, as the certain part of the Zodiac, in which sign the Sun was placed at the beginning of creation, unless perhaps we wish to take into account Adam, or Palestine, in which the mysteries of redemption were to be performed. For by comparison with those who dwell across the equator, all things are in an inverted mode, and it is autumn for them when it is Spring for others. Nor is this question ἀπροσδιόνυσός, as it seemed to Hottinger in Histor. Creat. p. 12. for these seasons of the year do not look to nature beginning and imperfect, but to nature continuing and ordinary: because a beginning must be fixed as absolutely certain, and a time of the year, from which the rest may be deduced. Therefore, what he says: that this first beginning of creation is neither vernal nor autumnal, but οἰκονομικὸν, although it may be conceded concerning the first day of creation, it is not to be admitted concerning the day of the creation of the Sun: for some principle of the motion of the Sun must be posited, if a measure of time is to be taken, and years from its motion: whatever may be the case concerning the first three days of the world, extraordinarily constituted by the primordial light, which it is not so inconvenient to have been of divine dispensation. Furthermore, no one assigns the winter cardinal point to the Sun at the creation of the world; nor does anyone easily assign the summer one, if you except Gerhard Mercator. But for the vernal and autumnal time, chronologists, both ancient and modern, contend in rivalry.

The Egyptians favor autumn, and other Orientals, today beginning the year from autumn (see Hier. in Ez. c. 1.) along with the Etruscans, the most ancient of the Italians; likewise the Russians, and also the Jews for many centuries, who therefore in the lectionary of the ancient Synagogue assigned the first Parashah of chapter I of Genesis to the last Sabbath of the seventh month, because they believed the world was created at that same time, with the Chaldean Paraphrast in 1 Kings VIII, v. 2. and Josephus l. 1. Antiquit. l. 4. To which opinion is cited by Menasse Ben Israel in Conciliation in Exod. quest. XI, Rabbi Eliezer, and Gvemara Abodazara c. 1. But by Scaliger and others is urged the passage Exod. XXIII, 16. concerning the exit of the year, and c. XXXIV, 22. concerning the revolution of the year; as well as the constitution concerning the Sabbatical and Jubilee years to be begun in the month of Tishri, Lev. XXIII, 27. c. XXV, 9. as also the beginning of the flood, which began in the II month of the year, and which the Egyptians, concerning whom Josephus l. I. c. 4. and Firmicus Astronomus, l. VII. c. 3. may be seen to have had their own custom from Mizraim, the grandson of Noah, the founder of their nation, Genes. X, 6. or from Abraham, as Josephus lib. I. Antiq. c. IX. and lib. cont. Appionem from Alexander Polyhistor surmises. To which opinion, therefore, concerning the world created in autumn, they add their vote: Montan. lib. de secul. Mirandul. l. V. c. Astron. c. 6. Lyranus, Tostatus, Pererius, Petavius, Temporarius, Calvisius, Helvicius, Behmius, Mæstlinus, Bartholinus, Helwigius, Schillingius; Ubbo Emmius, Phil. Lansbergius, Jac. Usserius, Rob. Bailius, Drusius observ. l. I. c. 18. Wolphius, Maresius Syst. Theolog. p. 92. Whom most of these Scaliger preceded in the later edition of his work on the emendation of times, although in the former edition he had defined it for Spring.

For the vernal beginning of the world, moreover, along with the same perpetual enumeration of months in Scripture, which certainly would have mentioned the first month, which provided the beginning for the world, at least once, and would not have called the month Thisri by the name of the seventh month if that were the primordial one, other probable reasons also militate, which, however, do not properly pertain to Chronology; such as the analogy of the world, restored at the vernal time through the passion of Christ; and also the authority of great men, for which Torniellus alleges twenty, Ascanius Martinensis twenty-five, Molina and many others allege the Fathers, and which, by the consensus of all in the Palestinian Synod, gathered by Theophilus, Bishop of Caesarea, in the year 198, Beda testifies was approved in his book on the 6 ages and his Epistle on the celebration of Easter. Also addicted to this opinion concerning the vernal time are, among the Hebrews, R. Joshua, as well as the Arabs, Assyrians, and Chaldeans, as testified by Simplicius in book V of Aristotle's Physics. as well as the Persians, Armenians, Ethiopians, and other peoples of the Orient, and among the Fathers, among the Greeks, Basil in Hexaemeron, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem in Catechesis XIV, Eusebius, Nazianzen in his Oration on the New Sunday, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret in Question LXXII on Exodus, Cedrenus, Damascenus in book I of the Orthodox Faith, ch. 2. Among the Latins, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Leo the Great in Sermon IX on the Passion of the Lord, Isidore of Seville in book V of the Etymologies, Beda, Maximus the Monk, as well as Hermannus Contractus, Marianus Scotus, Strabus, Rabanus Maurus, the Author of the Sicilian Fasti, Paulus, Bishop of Forosempron, and also the Alphonsine Mathematicians. Of the more recent ones, B. Luther, Melanchthon, Mercerus, Polycarpus Lyserus, Krenzhemius, Buntingius, B. Gerhardus, Wilh. Langius, Vogelius, Joh. Wichmannus, Bucholcerus, likewise Codomannus, Edwardus Simsonius, Lud. Capellus, Thomas Lydiat, Joh. Henr. Alstedius: as well as Cajetanus, Delrio, Genebrardus, Baronius, Spondanus, Torniellus, Salianus, Bonfrerius, Tirinus, Henricus Philippi, Corn. à Lap., Joh. Baptista Ricciolus, Keplerus, and others. From the Arabs, Hottinger produces in the cited book, Elmacin, Ecclesiastical History, M.S. p. 4. At the time when God established night and day, the Sun was entering the head of Aries on the 13th day of the month Adar, which the Jews celebrate as a feast in Nisan, in which God said to Moses: This month shall be for you the first month, in which also, in the opinion of the learned, will be the end of the world. To which reasons we also, having weighed everything, accede, even if we were more favorable to the Autumn beforehand: since we see no reason why the Scaligerians, following the Egyptians and certain Jews, should have abandoned the natural beginning of the year; and should have departed from the clear letter concerning the head of the year, designated by God himself in Exodus XII, 2, which it is a matter of conscience for us to defer in favor of the novel inventions concerning Sabbatical and Jubilee years, to be started from the creation of the world.

QUESTION II.

Is the Epoch of the Antediluvian World correct according to the Hebrew Codices?

This first Epoch was made much older than is just by not a few, insisting on the version of the LXX Interpreters, especially among the Ancients. But these somewhat deserve excuse, because, being destitute of the knowledge of Hebrew letters, most of them could not consult the sources of truth. Eusebius in Book I of his Chronicle proposes a triple enumeration of years: according to the copies of the LXX Interpreters, according to the Hebrews, and according to the Samaritans; according to which this Epoch is completed in 1656 years by the Hebrew calculation; but by the Samaritan computation only 1307 years are counted, because they subtract 100 years from Jared before his begetting of children, 120 from Methuselah, and 129 from Lamech, and thus make the whole Epoch 349 years shorter; but according to the designation of the LXX Interpreters, 2242 years of this Epoch are found, exceeding the Hebrew truth by 586 years: because they add 100 years to six Patriarchs—Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Enoch—each before their begetting of children, and 6 years to Lamech, and on the other hand they deduct 20 years from Methuselah, whom they make to have not 187, but 167 years when he begat Lamech. Which 20 years indeed Africanus judged should be left to Methuselah before his begetting of children, as is reported in the Alexandrian Chronicle, although in other matters he agrees with the LXX Interpreters and Eusebius. Whence he counted 2262 years before the flood, which number is also assigned by Epiphanius and Augustine: but Josephus (if we believe Petavius, Book IX, ch. 2) counts 2656 years from the creation to the flood. And thus not only Eusebius followed the LXX Interpreters here, but also most of the Ancients, both Greek and Latin, as well as Georgius Syncellus, who the most ancient LXX edition of the Interpreters, as if it were once translated from an uncorrupted Hebrew source, he praises, as do Julian, Archbishop of Toledo, in Book III against the Jews, Onuphrius in his Ecclesiastical Chronicle, Antonius Contius in his notes to the Chronicle of Nicephorus of Constantinople, Hieronymus Vielmius in his fifth reading on the 6 days of the creation of the world, Christophorus Lauretus, and others, whom Scaliger noted in his notes to the Greek Chronicle of Eusebius, p. 252, with this censure: Nor are there lacking today Capitos who prefer the edition of the Alexandrian Hellenists to the Mosaic, and call those innovators who think otherwise. Thus indeed Jerome heard even from Augustine, a man above all exception, who nevertheless later thought otherwise.

But above all, these are hostile to the Hebrew text, and on the contrary, they extol the calculation of the LXX Interpreters; some modern followers of Calvin, Isaac Vossius and Brian Walton, and other more recent ones, for whose ἁμαρτήματα (errors) Baillie deplores the lot of the Reformed Churches: who, however, appear to have been seduced by Baronius and Morin.

But the calculation of the LXX Interpreters is refuted

(1.) From the highest consensus of the Hebrew Codices, which in this catalog and in the years of the Patriarchs before the flood do not differ by a single iota, but agree entirely. Turn and return all the various readings which either Walton in his sixth volume of the Bibles, or Capellus in his Critica (whom Walton plundered, as he did Hugo Grotius), or Morinus in his exercises were able to scrape together, no shadow of any variation will be detected in the Hebrew Codices in these numbers. (2.) From the agreement of the versions. For the Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Latin, French, English, Spanish, Italian, Danish, German, Belgian, and others agree perfectly with the Hebrew text.

LXX. indeed they entirely contradict. (3) From the variety of Greek copies. For the ancients, Josephus, Epiphanius, Clement of Alexandria, and Africanus did not read the edition which is believed to be that of the LXX. Interpreters by the same reckoning: for Josephus has a different calculation; Africanus a different one, and others a different one still. (4) From the variety of editions of the LXX. Interpreters. For this one, which we now use, indeed adds 100 years to the years of the Patriarchs before the procreation of children; but in turn subtracts them from those after procreation, so that the years of life do not increase; but it adds several centuries to the total sum which the Fathers used, whence the Chronology is greatly disturbed. (5) From the uncertainty or corruption of the version of the LXX. Interpreters, which therefore can in no way prejudice the sincere, incorrupt, and certain Hebrew Code. (6) From the evident error of the version of the LXX. Of the interpreters, one whose work can be felt by the hands even in the years of Methuselah; for he would have it that he begat Lamech in the 167th year of his age, and lived 802 years after his birth: and that Lamech begat Noah in his 188th year, in whose six-hundredth year the flood occurred: whence it remains that Methuselah still survived 14 years after the flood: for those 188 and 600 make only 788, whereas Methuselah lived 802 years after Lamech was born, according to that Greek calculation. From which arose inexplicable questions, where and how Methuselah lived during the flood? which, that he might escape, Africanus preferred to follow the Hebrew truth here, assigning to Methuselah 187 years before his παιδογονίαν and 782 years after the same. (7.) Let the authority of certain ancients be added; especially that of Jerome, who openly professes that the Greek edition erred here in his Hebrew Traditions on Genesis; and of Augustine, who, having been more correctly instructed later, acknowledged that the Hebrew truth is to be preferred, l. XV. de civ. Dei c. 14: That variety of numbers which is found between the Hebrew Codices and ours, if it has anything so diverse that both cannot be true, the credibility of the historical events must be sought from that language from which what we have was translated; as also the venerable Bede, who in the preface of his work on the reckoning of time: I, he says, confidently profess, who do not reproach the ancient chroniclers, who the translation of the LXX. Sometimes they followed the Interpreters, and sometimes (as they pleased) they are seen to have held them in contempt, but I prefer the entire purity of the Hebrew truth to all of these, which the learned Jerome in his books of Hebrew Questions, Augustine in his books on the City of God, and Eusebius the Chronographer himself in the third book of his Ecclesiastical History, from the words of Josephus the historian writing against Apion the Grammarian, prove to be a shorter series of times than is commonly said to be contained in the LXX edition. And the Papists themselves acknowledge that the LXX Interpreters, or the Fathers who followed them, are by no means to be followed here. Pererius the Jesuit in Genesis ch. VII, n. 130, says: It does not escape me that most of the ancients, both Greek and Latin, [followed] the chronology which is in the translation of the LXX. Interpretum, they preferred to follow, because they perceived that that translation had been reverently used and religiously cultivated in the Church of God for many centuries, and for that reason they considered it a matter of conscience to change it in any part, or not to follow it. But for my part (as far as concerns the Chronology, which is now being treated), the authority of the Hebrew Scripture and of the Latin Vulgate version, as well as the judgment and opinion of the two princes of the Doctors of the Church, Jerome and Augustine, carries more weight. Nor indeed can the Pontificians act otherwise, if they wish to defend the αὐθεντίαν of the Vulgate version, which here agrees with the Hebrew text. Therefore, the Jesuit Bonfrerius confidently says in his preface to Scripture, ch. XV, sect. 6: It is certain that the LXX version is faulty in these years in many places, and that in this calculation of years our Latin and the Hebrew text are to be followed.

But Walton in vain boasts here of the consensus of the universal Church, and of all the Greek and Latin Fathers except for two, Jerome and Augustine. For even these two, following the authentic text of Scripture, can be set against the whole world, and Walton acknowledges that the Latin Bibles here follow the Hebrew text. However, the mind of the Western Church is gathered more correctly from the Bibles read in it than from the opinions of individual Doctors. The same man acknowledges that Origen in his Hexapla proposed the Hebrew text to the Eastern Church: indeed, Bailius opposes Jerome as a witness to his Walton, that the LXX Interpreters placed in those Hexapla agreed here with the Hebrew text, even if the so-called κοινὴ differed. But that in the Martyrology, and thence in the Roman Breviary, the calculation of the Hebrew and Latin text is neglected, is a notable error, as one which Baronius indeed defends, but most of the most learned Papists desire to be corrected: and he gravely warns his otherwise companion in faith about it, as follows: Walton ought not to have confirmed the Papists in an error so manifestly obsolete. Certainly the complaint of the Reformed against the faction of innovators among themselves is not new, that they are a great scandal to the Papists, and place a great obstacle, by which very many thinking about departure from the Roman Church have been deterred, and impelled to remain where they were, with every plan of approaching the Reformed suffocated. And Malvenda the Papist had already replied concerning the Roman Martyrology in book I of On the Anti-Christ, chapter XVI. That the Roman Church in its public records seems to praise that reckoning of years which the LXX gave, it does not indeed do so because it thinks it late and uncorrupted; since it proposes that sum which is recorded in the Vulgate edition to be received by all, as being diametrically opposed to this one as true and genuine: but it only took care with a wholesome moderation that it might exhibit some old monument of venerable antiquity, even though torn, and deformed, and covered with rags and years; and might make it plain to all what method the ancient Fathers followed in enumerating the years from Sacred Scripture, from the world created to Christ born, since old monuments of antiquity, however corroded and worn, are accustomed to provide a pleasing view to those looking at them. Wherefore there is no need now to commend the common method of counting to the Greek Church, or to undertake the patronage of Greek copies against the Hebrew truth. Joh. Despieres illustrates this with an example in Disputation 2 on the version of the LXX Interpreters, doubt 5. Thus the Church and the entire Christian world uses the common Era, and the Dionysian calculation: although noble chronologists teach that it deviates not a little from the true and genuine calculation.

QUESTION III.

At what time of the year did the flood occur, and how does the diluvian year stand?

Most think that it occurred in the spring time, to whom Lansbergius and Gerhard also add the calculation of Joh. Vossius: since Moses acknowledges no other beginning of the year than the spring, and it would be absurd that Noah, having exited the ark, sustained himself and his own with the animals for almost an entire year until the time of the new fruits.

Others, however, prefer to follow the Jews along with Scaliger and Petavius, as also Josephus, who in Book I of the Antiquities, in the chapter on the flood, has it thus: This devastation happened in the second month, which is named Dius by the Macedonians; and the Targum of Jonathan, Gen. VIII, 4, [says] in the month Marcheshvan, on the 27th day of the month, the earth was dried. But this is the eighth from the spring.

But we have no solid reason why we should depart from the customary Mosaic enumeration, since the divine historian expressly and with care counts the months, the second, the seventh, the tenth, and likewise the first of the year; and since these months are expressed elsewhere in the Scriptures by their own names, as for example, the First

Abib, Exod. XIII, 4. The second, Iiar and Zius, 1 Kings VI, 1 and 37. The seventh, Thisri, and Ethanim, 1 Kings VIII, 6 and 37, having been called [by those names], why should we establish the first month in this place as Thisri, the second month as Marchesvan, and the seventh as Nisan? Whence B. Luther, Comment. on Genesis, ch. 7, fol. 131, page 1, establishes that the flood began in the vernal time. To which B. Polyc. Lyserus the Elder also assented in Hist. Noae, p. 136, and many others. These are favored by the most ancient historian Berosus, and those who follow him, Abydenus and Polyhistor. For he reports from the archives of the Chaldeans that the flood began in the spring, and not in the autumn. Nor is that reasoning of B. Luther lacking in probability, that it fell in that time when the year is most beautiful, and the world as it were grows green again, when birds sing, and cattle exult, and a new face of the world, as it were, opens itself after the horrid times of winter.

But as for the reasons favoring the autumn, B. Dn. D. Polyc. Lyserus refutes them vigorously in the place cited, whom it will be helpful to compare here: The authority of Josephus does not come into consideration here: he followed the Egyptians, to whom the flood happens as it were every year, so that the earth, with the waters dried up, might suffer sowing in the autumnal time, whence they believed the world was dried up and repaired again at the same time by the universal flood. B. Lyserus also arranged the form of the flood year, but he assumed the year M. 1657, which, however, we previously taught should rather be established as the leap year M. 1656.

Scaliger, in his book on the emendation of time, arranged the year of the flood thus: On the 1st day of the tenth month, that is, the 271st from the beginning of the year, the tops of the mountains were uncovered, Gen. VIII, 5. Forty days later, that is, on the three hundred and eleventh from the beginning of the year, the raven was sent forth, v. 6. Afterwards, the dove was sent forth after 40 days; whence 351 days result. Thus, after seven days, Noah sent forth the dove, and after another seven, he sent forth the dove a third time; and thus 365 days result, which constitute a full year. But that interval of 40 days between the sending forth of the raven and the first sending forth of the dove is assumed precariously, nay, contrary to the express words of Moses in Gen. VIII, 10. For Noah is said to have waited ANOTHER 7 days after the first sending forth of the dove. Therefore, not 40, but only 7 days intervened between the sending forth of the raven and the first sending forth of the dove.

Some Jews distinguish the 40 days of the rains from the 150 days of the increase, and thus count 190 days for the decrease of the waters: but because Moses counts five months and 150 days from the 17th day of the 2nd month up to the 17th day of the 7th month, when the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat, nothing is more certain than that only 150 days, and not 190, had elapsed from the beginning of the flood.

The Rabbis are foolish who maintain that three different principles must be considered in those passages in Rabbi Menasseh’s Conciliator, Gen. quest. 26, as do Rabbi Solomon, and Rabbi Nissim and others, to such an extent that they number the months according to the order of the year starting from Tishri, when the second month is mentioned: then they number the months from the time when the rains ceased, while the seventh month is commemorated: finally, a third from the time when the rains began, when the tenth month is designated. Which is mere confusion. But who does not understand that the second, seventh, and tenth months refer to one another, and that the second, seventh, as well as the tenth month are designated in the year by the same rationale? Whence R. Isaac Arama, R. Abarbanel, and R. Menasseh, along with R. Bahye, acknowledge that those Rabbis erred, including the 40 days of rain within those 150 days; and thus defining the year of the flood: that on the seventeenth day of the first month, Nisan, the ark came to rest, and from that time the waters were continuously diminished, so that on the first day of the tenth month, Tammuz, the tops of the mountains appeared: whence three months still remain to complete the year, or 90 days: namely those 40 days, towards the end of which the window of the ark was opened, and the three times seven days during which the ravens and doves were sent out. Which constitute two months. But in the third month the earth was dried; and thus Noah, who entered the ark on the 17th day of the month of Nisan, went out on the 27th day of the same month, in the following year. But those 11 days (for that is the difference) they say are those by which the Lunar year exceeds the Solar; so that Noah had a complete solar year in the ark.

600, he likewise asserts, but for another reason; namely that the world was founded around the autumnal equinox, but the flood began after the vernal, in the month of Iyar, or Ziv; but in such a way that the seventeenth month named by Moses would have already fallen into the 601st year of Noah (that is, with that imperfect year, or the other half-year of that year of Noah, completed), which contradicts the text, which refers the seventh and tenth month to the 600th year, and only after the twelfth month had elapsed begins the six hundred and first year.

The Latin interpreter adds ten whole days to the Hebrew number in Genesis VIII, 5. And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the 27th day of the month (in the Hebrew it is held to be the 17th day) as if the waters had indeed begun to decrease on the 17th day, but the ark had not rested until after a decrease of 10 days. But it was just as easy for the ark to rest on the 1st day of the decrease of the waters as on any later day: for the force of the winds applied to the summit of the highest mountain, when the waters were at their most prevalent, caused the weight of that great vessel to be such that so much of it was submerged by the waters as would easily exceed 16 cubits. For we see daily that loaded ships are submerged in water above their middle.

Nor is there any reason to insist that Noah was 600 years old when the flood began, which is Krenzheim's argument: for just as eight complete days are not to be understood when a son is said to be circumcised at eight days old, Genesis XVII, 12, so neither here are six hundred complete years necessarily understood when he is called a son of 600 years.

QUESTION IV.

Whether the flood began in the 599th year of Noah or indeed the 600th. And whether at the completion of this, or indeed at its beginning?

The primary difficulty is from the years of Methuselah: who was born in the year of the world 687 and lived for 969 years, which added together complete 1656 years: whence they conclude that the year of the world 1656 must be understood as the 600th year of Noah, so that Methuselah is not engulfed by the waters of the flood. But however undoubted it may be that Methuselah died before the flood began, in the 969th year of his life, in the same year in which the flood began, as Jerome reports in his Hebrew Traditions on Genesis, it is not however necessarily to be established that he lived exactly 969 complete years, nor is it likely that all the Patriarchs died precisely at the complete years which are attributed to them. For the reason for the years of procreation and the years of the entire life of the Fathers is not the same: the former are not to be mutilated, since the chronology of the world depends upon them: but the latter, even if they were sometimes incomplete, the calculation of the chronology suffers no detriment.

Petavius, in book IX de doctr. temp. c. 17, calls into doubt that the 600th year of Noah is to be taken precisely, as if Moses had used a round number and had not applied ἀκρίβειαν (precision). But in this way the calculation of Scripture is rendered entirely uncertain, which is indeed what Petavius intends, yet it is by no means to be conceded. For the rest, almost everyone has acknowledged that the flood began in the 600th year. Scaliger, however, rising up against everyone, states thus in Elenchus Orat. Parei p. 53, from Gen. IX, 28, 29: Noah lived 950 years, of which he lived 350 after the flood, therefore the flood began in the 599th year of Noah, and not the 600th, as ALL have thought hitherto. But this consequence is inconsequent; for with 350 deducted from 950, there remains the 600th year of Noah, not after the flood, but in which the flood covered the earth. And what is clearer than those words of Scripture, Gen. VII, 7. He (Noah) was 600 years old when the waters of the flood inundated the earth, or verse 11, in the six-hundredth year (not the five-hundred and ninety-ninth) of the life of Noah, in the second month, on the 17th day of the month, were all the fountains of the great deep broken up? Finally, how could the six-hundred and first year of Noah be commemorated, during the flood, if the flood began in the 599th year of Noah.

Vogelius's opinion is new, that the flood is to be defined by a space of 40 days, and that more truly in those 40 days Noah completed his 600th year, namely in the 3rd month, so that Noah had about 599 years and 11 months when the rains began: in the calculation of Germ. Chron. p. 11. But it deserves no assent: because thus after the flood Noah would have remained in the ark for a whole year still, and for almost the entire year after the flood Noah's ark would have floated on the waters; and the waters would have covered the surface of the whole earth; and the beginning of another world after the flood would have to be fixed while for several months the waters were still raised above the highest mountains, and the flood was inundating the whole earth.

But what Vogelius says, that the end of the 600th year of Noah fell at the end of the 40 days of rain, that cannot be deduced from Gen. VII, 16; even if it is stated in Gen. IX, 28, 29 that Noah lived 350 years after the flood, and his whole age was 950 years. For this calculation can be resolved without that new and unusual acceptance of the word flood. Nor is there any reason why the months of the 600th year of Noah should be distinguished from the months of that year of the world: because the calculation of the years and months of the world is derived chronologically from the years of the patriarchs' begetting and the age of Noah in the calculation up to the year of the flood, and thus the years are assumed as complete, or as if complete. For as for what Vogelius objects, that Adam was created not on the first, but on the sixth day of the world, that makes nothing for the discrepancy of the months, however much the days of the months may vary somewhat, since the difference of those few days does not bring about different whole months, nor was the birthday and the day of death precisely the same for those patriarchs through whom the chronology is woven. And here the argument of Ussher's Chronologia sacra, page 60, militates entirely. If the 600th year of the life of Noah were verging toward its end on the 17th day of the second month, on which the flood began, then in the next 7th month

Furthermore, concerning that six-hundredth year of Noah, some think that it began with the flood, others that it was completed at the beginning of the flood; which is the opinion of Funccius, Calvisius, Krenzhemius, Pererius, Behmis, and others. I do not know, however, whether it sufficiently agrees with the sacred text. For if the 600th year of Noah was completed at the beginning of the flood, how could the divine historiographer in Genesis 8:13 report that the flood ceased at the beginning of the 601st year of Noah's life? Furthermore, if the flood ended when the 601st year was finished, and Noah lived for 350 years after the flood, he must have lived not 950, but 951 years, which contradicts Moses. Therefore, Quintus Julius Hilarion rightly noted that the flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of Noah. Ussher defends this opinion at greater length in his Sacred Chronology, p. 60, against Krenzhemius and Funccius.

Lansbergius [holds] that the year of Noah's life was incomplete, and that the year 601 had begun to be counted. But the six hundred and first year was not noted by Moses on the 17th day of the 7th month, nor even on the 1st day of the 10th month, but the number of the Epoch was first changed on the first day of the first month: whence it may be gathered that the six hundredth year of Noah's life, if not in its entirety, at least in the greatest part of itself, to the year of the flooding deluge. Furthermore, as it is manifest from Gen. 11:10 that the Chronology of the renewed world is by no means deduced from the beginning of the deluge: so it seems altogether inconsistent that the year of the deluge itself should have been included by Moses in the times of the new world. For the year of the deluge belonged to the ancient world, as Peter calls it in 2 Epist. 2:5, not to the one which now is, 2. Petr. 3:6, 7; whose years Annianus himself and Berosus reckon from the salvation of the human race from the waters (as if the world were then newly reviving): just as Beda also calls the first day of the fruitful age; and Marianus calls that twenty-seventh day of the second month, on which day Noah went out of the ark, Gen. 8:14, 15.

Nor indeed would Scripture commemorate the 601st year of Noah from the first day of the first month in Gen. 8:13, if at that time a full month with some days had been lacking to Noah's 601st year; but rather in the following verse, 14, when it names the 27th day of the second month, it would make mention of the six hundredth year of Noah, as being the year then finally, or a little before, according to that hypothesis of Vogel, fully completed.

Meanwhile, Ussher rightly warns that whether we posit that the deluge began at the beginning of Noah's six hundredth year, and that two years elapsed from the end of the deluge until the birth of Arphaxad; or whether we say with Calvisius and Behm that the deluge began toward the end of the six hundredth year, and that two years elapsed from the beginning of the deluge until the birth of Arphaxad, no more than three years are found to be interposed between the beginning of Noah's six hundredth year and the birth of Arphaxad, and by no means, as Funccius posits, a four-year period: for thus the years of the world will be increased by the addition of one year, and from the beginning of Noah's 600th year until the beginning of the deluge one year, from the beginning of the deluge to the end of the same another year, and from the end of the deluge to the birth of Arphaxad again two years will be counted: which is repugnant to the passage in Gen. 9:29. For since Noah is said to have lived 350 years after the deluge, if 601 years had passed from the birth of Noah to the exit from the deluge, with 350 added, the total days of Noah would be not 950, as Moses has in the cited passage, but 951. Whence Vogel indeed speciously posits that Arphaxad was born two years after the 40 days of rain, and does not here increase the years of the world with Funccius: but because of the reasons already adduced, we withhold our assent from that new opinion.

Ques. 5. QUESTION 5. How Noah begat at five hundred years of age, and who his firstborn was.

The difficulty is not slight concerning the Mosaic words in Gen. 5:32, And Noah was a son of 500 years, and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth, by comparison made with Gen. 11:10, Shem was a son of 100 years, and begat Arphaxad two years after the deluge. If Shem was born when Noah was five hundred years old, how was he only a hundred-year-old son two years after the deluge? If you say that the phrase after the deluge must be taken inclusively, not exclusively, yet he must have been one hundred and one years old, two years after the deluge began, who was in his hundredth year when he entered the deluge. From which foundation of the right of primogeniture, the Rabbis in Bereshith Rabba, as also R. Aben Ezra, R. Levi Ben Gersom, Beroaldus, and other Chronologists, likewise Ussher and Tremellius, to this

&c. They adjudge it away from Shem. And when the sons of Noah, where they are listed as they were begotten, are placed in retrograde order, Japheth, Ham & Shem, R.
