Levi Ben Gerson, Lyranus, Tostatus, and others, think they were begotten in this order, and thus establish Japheth as the firstborn, and Ham as the middle one. Other Jews, however, especially Rabbi Moses Gerundensis, & some of the Reformed, Tremellius & Ussher, indeed grant the birthright to Japheth, but grant the middle place to Shem. Thomas Lidyatus, however, makes Shem the middle one in such a way that he says Ham was born in the first place, and Japheth in the third.

But there is no reason why we should dislodge Shem from that honor of primogeniture, which is assigned to him not only by those who make Japheth the last, with the author of the books of the Recognitions, book 1, Ambrose in his book on Noah and the Ark, Epiphanius, book 1, heresy 4, Augustine, book XVI, On the City of God, ch. 3, & R. Dav. Kimchi, such as Scaliger, Calvin, Behmius, Salianus & others; but also by those who, with Josephus, book 1, Antiquities, ch. 5, establish Japheth in the second place and Ham in the third, which was approved by Pererius.

We adhere to the order observed by the Holy Spirit when they are introduced as begotten. For this must be regarded as a general rule (ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ), when the question is asked, in what order were they begotten? unless, that is, Scripture shows otherwise elsewhere. Shem, however, is numbered in the first place, Ham in the second, and Japheth in the third: and this is so both in its proper seat, Gen. 5:32, and in other places of Scripture, ch. 6:10, ch. 9:18, ch. 10:1, 1 Chron. 1:4, where the genealogy of Noah is listed, from which order we are scrupulous about departing. Nor indeed is Scripture accustomed to list children born of legitimate marriage in any order other than that in which they were begotten, unless perhaps a peculiar reason underlies it: much less is that to be presumed where it is found to have observed the same order so frequently. If this is changed by us, no certainty will be left as to whom the first, whom the second, and whom the third place is owed, as is sufficiently apparent from the diversity of other opinions.

Nor indeed does any necessity compel us to change the order. For the fact that Shem is said to be a son of 100 years two years after the flood, it is not necessary that it be understood precisely as 100 years; just as it is not necessary, when Noah is said to have begotten at 500 years of age, that he begat the firstborn Shem precisely in the 500th year, because the structure of the years of the world does not depend on Shem's centennial, but on the two years after the flood, as Ussher admits in Chronol. sacr. p. 58, so that whether Arphaxad was born in Shem's precisely 100th year, or one or two years more or less, no increase or decrease to the age of the world results from it.

The same must be held regarding Noah begetting Shem in his 500th year. Although the sacred text does not even say that Noah begat Shem in his 500th year: it only reports this about Noah: And Noah was a son of 500 years, and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth, which report can maintain its truth, even if Noah had been one year or two beyond 500 when he begat the firstborn Shem. For that those words of Moses are to be taken in a broad sense (ὡς ἐν πλάτει) is evident from the fact that all three of them were not born to him in that one 500th year. For it is not to be thought, with Rabbi Eliezer, that they were born in one birth: not to mention that some explain those words thus, with B. D. Behmius: that Noah, in the 500th year completed and the 501st current, devoted effort to marital relations, and later, with the passage of time and nature, begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth. For Moses did not define in Gen. 5:32 in what year Noah begat each of his sons. Which explanation Ussher could not reject either, p. 68. Since he by no means received all these three in one and the same year, it is consistent that Moses meant nothing other than that Noah began to devote effort to children in his 500th year, and thus begat the firstborn. And when

Gen. XI, 10. A minute number may have been added, namely, that two years after the flood Shem was 100 years old, such as is not found in Gen. V, 32. Cornelius a Lapide rightly concludes that in chapter XI, rather than V, the years are precisely recorded: where, as Salianus warns, it is not asserted that the son was born in the 500th year of Noah, but it is only taught that these three sons were born after the 500th year of the Father, and not before. Cajetan explains this summarily, as does Pererius, who therefore responds to the argument drawn from the archives of the Jews: either that Noah did not begin to beget in the 500th year of his age precisely, but in the 502nd, and in that very year Shem was begotten, and for that reason two years after the flood he was 100 years old: or that Shem, in the second year after the flood, when he begat Arphaxad, was not 100 years old precisely, but was 102 years old: since it is the custom of the divine Scriptures, with small and minute numbers being silent and passed over, to commemorate only the maximum and whole number.

Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel and R. David Kimchi from among the Jews themselves support the view that Shem was the first son, Ham the second, and Japheth the third, in which order they are numbered in Scripture; and Abarbanel says it is not contradictory that Shem is said to have been 100 years old two years after the flood: for when Noah is said to have begotten Shem in the 500th year of his age, it does not follow from that that he was born at the beginning of the 500th year, but towards the end, so that the 500th year of Noah expired a few days after his birth. By similar reasoning, the flood did not begin when the 600th year of Noah had elapsed, but only after a few days of that year had passed, and thus Shem at that time was not more than 99 years old. And Arphaxad was born from Shem when he had exceeded his 100th year by a few months. But what is said about the two years after the flood is to be understood as the beginning of the year which is counted as the second from the start of the flood; as Rabbi Menasse Ben Israel reports in Concil. in Genes. qu. XX. p. 29. This explanation is favored if it is said that the son of 500 years is not understood so precisely, but according to the Hebrew mode of speaking, just as in Gen. XVII, 12, a son of eight days is said to be circumcised, not one who has completed eight days, but after the seventh day has been completed.

What of the fact that Menasse himself, in question 21, could not disagree with this opinion, stating thus: Either we shall say that Noah begat Shem when he was 500 years old, but that he was born in the first year after the 500th of his age, and thus at the beginning of the year which was the second after the flood began, Shem completed his 100th year; these are the words of Menasse.

What the Beroaldists, along with Lyranus, Tostatus, and the Jews, object from Gen. X, 21, that Japheth is called the elder brother of Shem, is from a misinterpretation of the words of Moses: the words of the authentic text hold the opposite and openly testify that not Japheth is the elder brother of Shem, but Shem is the elder brother of Japheth, and therefore older than both him and the other brother, Ham; for thus in the description of Shem, Moses says: And to Shem himself was born: (sons were born, or offspring was born,) Even he himself the father of all the sons of Heber, אֲחִי יֶפֶת הַגָּדוֹל the elder brother of Japheth. For it cannot be rendered: the brother of the elder Japheth. For if Japheth were said to be the elder, that [word] would undoubtedly have been added by which he is the elder. Nor did it matter here to describe whether Japheth is the elder or the younger. But that Shem is indicated as the elder brother served the characterization of that Patriarch, who is celebrated both as the Father of the Hebrews, or the stock of the Hebrew nation, and as the firstborn of Noah, the elder or greatest brother of Japheth. And not without reason did the blessed Gesnerus warn that the ה prefixed to the word גָּדוֹל indicates not a Genitive, but a Nominative. Finally, the Chaldean Paraphrasts interpreted it in this way, as did the common Latin Interpreter, Benedictus Arias Montanus, and others,

What is moved from Gen. IX, 24: And he knew what his little son had done to him, does not prejudice the firstborn status of Shem, yet it seems to render the order observed by Moses doubtful: according to which Japheth would be the little, or last, son of Noah, and not Ham. But neither is it necessary that we should judge the order accurately observed by Moses to be wavering here. Indeed, the Jews Aben Ezra and Rabbi Ben Gerson understand the little son not of Ham, but of Canaan, who committed something foul, which Scripture keeps silent about, whom Scaliger follows; but the text is clear about the sin of Ham, v. 22, and therefore that gloss is deservedly rejected, which Usserius refutes at length against the conjectures of Scaliger. The observation of R. Menasse from R. Solomon is slightly more correct, that Ham is called the younger son, not because he was younger in age, but because he was more contemptible than the others, and less esteemed, from a comparison with Jer. XLIX, 15, where the word קָטוֹן is used. Not to speak of others who say he is called little by reason of stature. It is most simply said that he is called little in respect to Shem, who is called the elder, or great, in Gen. X, 21, so that it is also clear from this comparison that not Ham, as some believe, but Shem is the firstborn; because Shem is called great, but Ham is called little in respect to him. But with Japheth, Ham has no contention, while the firstborn status of Shem is at least secure. For he is always listed in the middle place, never in another. To which contributes the fact that Augustine calls Ham younger than the firstborn (Shem) and older than the last (Japheth) in book XVI of The City of God, ch. 1. Noah cursed his middle son, i.e., younger than the firstborn and older than the last, who had sinned against his father, not in himself, but in his son Canaan, his grandson.

That Japheth, however, is mentioned first in the genealogy of the sons of Noah in Gen. 10:2, and Shem last, happens because Moses intended to continue the genealogy thereafter from Shem as the principal one. Whence he wished to place the genealogy of Japheth and Ham before his.

QUESTION VI.

Is the epoch of the former world 1656 completed years?

We call the epoch of the former world that whose terminus is the end of the flood: because the beginning of the renewed world must be taken not from the start of the flood, but from the end of the flood: for the flood pertains to the ancient world, of which it was the punishment: nor can the year of the flood be included in the times or the epoch of the new world. Thus St. Peter distinguishes the world that now is and the former world, 2 Epist. 3:6, 7, and ch. 2:5, and Bede calls the first day of the second age the 27th day of the second month, on which Noah went out from the ark, Gen. 8:14, 15; for from there began the new blessing of the renewed world, and the new covenant of grace, which the Lord entered into with Noah, as the parent of the new world, and his descendants.

If, therefore, it is asked how many years precisely are to be numbered to the end of the flood and the beginning of the renewed world? By no means are 1657 years to be computed, with Funccius and others, who added one year to the epoch of the first world; for if 601 years from the birth of Noah and 1657 years from the creation of the world are to be numbered until the exit from the flood, with the 350 years of Noah that elapsed after the flood added, all the years of Noah will become 951, which Scripture, however, makes 950.

Nor should one agree with those who, while they do not assign more than 950 years of Noah's life with Moses, nevertheless wish for Noah to have completed 600 full years before the flood, and thus number 1656 full years of the world until the beginning of the flood, and to the end of the flood 1657. But after the flood they do not assign to it 350, but only 349 years; nor do they wish 350 years to be indicated unless the year of the flood is included. Because the Holy Spirit accurately defined the years of the first world, that the flood began and was continued in the current 600th year of Noah, but was finished in the 601st year of Noah begun: so that it may be established with certainty and without doubt that the Epoch of the ancient world was precisely 1656 years.

Nor should that phrase of Gen. 9:28, after the flood, be vexed, so that it is not understood, as it sounds, concerning the years that followed the flood; but from the beginning of the flood: And Noah lived after the flood 300 years, and 50 years. For such an inclusive sense could not yet be taught, nor if the year of the flood were included, could it be conveniently said that so many years had flowed after the flood, but from the beginning of the flood.

SECTION III. The Epoch of the renewed World, and of the covenant of Grace in Noah, up to the illustrious Promise of the Messiah made to Abram, of 427 years.

The beginning of the renewed World is from the end of the flood, with the year of the world 1657. Its first biennium is that which is mentioned in Gen. 11:10, and (Shem) begat Arphaxad TWO YEARS AFTER THE FLOOD. Therefore, two years had elapsed after the finished flood in the renewed world when Arphaxad was brought to light: because there the divine historian accurately recounts the generations of Shem to that end, so that a certain Chronology of the post-diluvian world might be had. That beginning of the Epoch, therefore, which the Holy Spirit designed by design, must be religiously retained: and no more or fewer years than two after the flood are to be placed for the birth of Arphaxad: otherwise nothing certain will be had concerning the years of that Epoch, which, just as it is continued through the years of the procreation of the post-diluvian Patriarchs, so its beginning is accurately fixed in the birth of Arphaxad. Let those years now be added to those two years, which Moses designated in the generations of those Patriarchs, let the years be had to

Terah was born at the completion of 222. But Abram was born in the year of Terah not 70, but 130: because when Father Terah died, he was in his year not 135, but 75. Therefore, let 130 years be added up to the birth of Abram and from there to the promise made to Abraham, and his pilgrimage 75 years, which collected into a sum will make 427. What therefore Noah had received from his father Lamech, with whom he spent 595 years, and from his grandfather Methuselah, with whom he spent 600 years, concerning the seed of the woman promised to the Protoplast, which they had from the mouth of Adam, as being one with whom Lamech conversed for 56 years and Methuselah for 243 years: and which, having been confirmed to him after the covenant was initiated after the flood and the sign added to the covenant, could indeed flow down and propagate up to Terah, the parent of Abraham, through the same herald of righteousness, like a two-faced Janus, the Prophet of the ancient and modern world, through the former for almost six hundred years, but through the latter for 350, since he prolonged his life up to the 128th year of Terah; but because Terah had lapsed into the idolatry of the Chaldeans, it is to be attributed to singular divine grace that He deigned to manifest Himself by a special revelation to Abraham, the Father of believers, having made to him the promise concerning the blessed seed, which ought to arise from his own lineage, which promise (ἐπαγγελίαν) not only Abraham propagated to his descendants; but Noah's firstborn also, the Patriarch Shem, confirmed it by the proclamation of those things which he had received in both worlds, as one who had completed one hundred years in the ancient world with his parent and his great-grandfather Methuselah, and 95 with his grandfather Lamech: but in the renewed world he had been a contemporary (σύγχρονος) with most of the Patriarchs after the flood, even with Abraham for seventy-five years after the promise (ἐπαγγελίαν), and with Isaac for fifty years.

The epoch from the flood to the pilgrimage of Abraham from Haran into Canaan, Gen. 11 & 12.

From the flood to the begetting of Arphaxad by Shem, 2 years. From the birth of Arphaxad to the birth of Salah, 35. From Salah to Eber, 30 years. From Eber to Peleg, 34. From Peleg to Reu, 30. From Reu to Serug, 32. From Serug to Nahor, 30. From Nahor to Terah, 29. From the birth of Terah to the birth of Abraham, 130. The years of Abraham when he was called, having received the promise concerning the blessed seed, 75. Total 427. If to these are added the 1656 years of the prior world, there will have been completed from the creation of the world to the calling of Abraham 2083 years.

QUESTION I.

Does the Hebrew text hold correctly in the years of the Patriarchs after the flood?

A doubt has arisen from the text, both the Samaritan and especially the Greek of the LXX Interpreters. For according to the former, not 352 years, as in the Hebrew codex, but 942 are counted; according to the latter, however, 1072 years are counted from the flood to the παιδογονίαν (begetting of children) of Terah. For both the edition of the Samaritans and that of the LXX Interpreters added one hundred full years to the years of each of the first six Patriarchs: Arphaxad, Salah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, and Serug. They enriched the years of Nahor, when he begat Terah, by 50 years. The LXX version, moreover, has inserted a new patriarch, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Salah, to whom it assigns 130 years. Hence that different calculation arose. Most of the Ancients followed the LXX Interpreters; and even among the moderns, Isaac Vossius and Brian Walton strive to defend their enumeration against the Hebrew codices, but rashly and too imprudently. For an uncertain, impure translation, teeming with countless errors, is not to be preferred to the original and authentic text, which divine providence willed to be preserved as a perpetual canon for the Church; nor was cold comfort to be poured out for Papists who deny the sincerity of the original text. Although in this enumeration and chronology of the Patriarchs after the flood, not only the Hebrew and Chaldean Codices, but also the Latin Vulgate, which is authentic for the Papists, and other versions agree entirely: and only the Samaritan and what is commonly believed to be the LXX version differ, which nevertheless do not agree with each other, but in many ways disagree with themselves in the years before and after the παιδογονίαν (begetting of children), as well as in the years of life, no less than they disagree with the Hebrew truth, and thus leave no certainty.

But he is utterly absurd, says Vossius, and of unfortunate judgment, who thinks it happened—which the Hebrew calculation nevertheless posits—that Noah lived until the fifty-eighth year of Abraham and that Shem saw Jacob, his descendant in the thirteenth generation. Resp. But this is to set one's mouth against the heavens and openly speak against divine Scripture, and to accuse it of absurdity. And what is absurd in this? Did not Adam live 66 years with Lamech, even if he was the ninth from him? Yet according to the Hebrew text Noah did not reach the fifty-eighth year of Abraham, but died two years before Abraham was born

and Shem did not see Jacob, but died twelve years before Jacob was begotten. But various kingdoms had been established before Abraham, and several Egyptian dynasties are commemorated, yet none mention Noah, and not even Moses himself mentions that he still lived in the time of Abraham. Response: The ages of Noah, which the edition of the Seventy themselves assign in the same way as the Hebrew source, are within the bounds of the ἀδήλꙋ (obscure) time, about which Gentile writers are silent; the μυθικὸν (mythical) time began after the flood, about which they have nothing but fables, which are nevertheless full of accounts of Janus, who with his double face looked upon both worlds, etc. But Moses clearly taught that Noah still lived a little before Abraham, when he designated their years. And shall we deny that Methuselah was for several centuries σύγχρονον (contemporary) to Noah, for the reason that in the history of Noah, Moses made no further mention of him?

Vossius still urges against the Hebrew calculation that, according to it, the dispersion of the nations took place barely one century after the flood, when Noah was barely the third heir born. But in truth, Peleg was not the third, but the fifth from Noah; and the father of Vossius, Johann Gerhard, in Isag. Chronol. p. 53, proved that the division of languages and the dispersion of the nations did not take place at the birth of Peleg, but in the middle of his age, in the one hundred and twenty-eighth year after the flood. Ussher refuted that argument, along with others taken from the quiver of Morin, in Chronolog. Sacr. c. V. p. 78, et seqq.

Vossius also objects with the authority of the Samaritan Codex, as well as that of Josephus. But the former does not agree with the LXX Interpreters, and the latter is not consistent with himself: for in book 1, chapter 6, he establishes 292 years from the flood to the birth of Abraham; but if you add up the individual years of the Patriarchs, 933 result, which number agrees neither with the Hebrew, nor with the Samaritan, nor with the text of the LXX Interpreters. Whence it must be that the number in the calculation of the particular life of the Patriarchs in Josephus was corrupted by copyists, whose codices he acknowledges to differ greatly among themselves, and whom Vossius does not in the least doubt also erred by omitting Cainan. However, the true reading of the Hebrew text, in the time of Josephus, is found from the Chaldean Paraphrase, which arose at almost that very time, to be in complete agreement with our Hebrew text.

QUESTION II.

Are not the 130 years, which the LXX have, missing in the Hebrew text in the generation of Cainan?

There are not a few who defer to the Hebrew text in other respects, yet disapprove of the omission of the generation of Cainan; and for that reason they accuse it of corruption. These, therefore, deem that 130 years are missing from this epoch regarding the generation of Cainan: since in the edition of the LXX Interpreters, Genesis 11:12, it is held thus: Arphaxad at 135 years begat Cainan, Cainan at 130 years begat Salah, and not as Tirinus in his Chronicle: Arphaxad at 35 years begat Cainan: Cainan at 30 years begat Salah.

Many from the Papists contend for this Cainan: Lipomannus, Canus, Toletus, Bellarminus, Salmeron, Barradius, Ribera, Delrio, Huntlæus, Raderus, Mariana, Torniellus, Salianus, Spondanus, Bonfrerius, Tirinus: to whom also from the Reformed recently Vossius and Waltonus have joined themselves. But the Vulgate Version, which the Council of Trent declared authentic, validly refutes the Papists: for in it, neither in Genesis ch. 11 nor in the Chronicles, 1 Par. 1:18, 21, is there any mention of that Cainan. Nor must it be conceded in any way that the Hebrew text is corrupted here, as it is supported not only by the Latin Vulgate interpreter, but also by the Chaldean Paraphrasts, and not least by Josephus, and the chronology of the Hebrews, as also Berosus, book 1, ch. 7 of the Antiquities, cited by Josephus, and Eupolemus, brought forward by Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius, book 9 of the Evangelical Preparation, and Salianus also in the preface to Vol. 3. of the Annals, agree in the omission of Cainan, as do Beda, Ado, and others among the ancients. Whence the most learned Papists, Eugubinus, Cajetanus, Sixtus Senensis, Genebrardus, Driedo, acknowledge that Cainan to be supposititious: which also most of the Reformed, along with our own, establish with great consensus. And Usserius learnedly observed that even in the Martyrology of Beda itself, and likewise the Roman Martyrologies of Usuardus, Rabanus, Ado, and others, they preserved such a method of counting the years of the world at the 25th of December, which excludes that Cainan with his 130 years, as also Hieronymus in the Chronicles, Orosius book 1, ch. 1, Idacius, Victorinus in the Paschal computation, Prosper, Victor Tununensis, Marcellinus Comes, Cassiodorus, Isidorus, Gregor. Turonensis (book 1 of the History of the Franks, ch. 7, etc.), Nennius (in the history of the Britons), and others, who counted 942 years from the flood to Abraham, or 5199 years from Adam to Christ. These indeed, although in other matters they followed the calculation of the 70 Interpreters, yet in the addition of the years of Cainan they deserted them, and therefore one must wonder that, conversely, those with whom we are now dealing desert the 70 Interpreters in other matters and cling only to them in the years of Cainan, which the rest have abandoned as evidently false. Nor indeed do they only expunge or omit Cainan: the same has also been omitted, or not recognized as genuine, by the ancients in ecclesiastical antiquity: namely by Eusebius himself and Origen. For the former, in the first book of his Chronicle, exhibited the years of the Patriarchs from the triple text, Hebrew, Samaritan, and Greek, but in none of them did he report Cainan: and in the Greek, according to the 70 Interpreters, he recorded that Arphaxad begat not Cainan, but Sala, and he counted the years from the flood to the birth of Abraham not as 1072, but, omitting the 130 years of Cainan, as only 942. But this Origen marked those things which he found with an obelus, which we learn from Procopius of Gaza on Genesis 11: The Hebrew truth holds that Sala was begotten by Arphaxad: those things which are then placed in the middle are seen marked with an obelus. Add that Origen, in John, tract 20, acknowledges only ten generations from Noah to Abraham, excluding the generation of Cainan: Abraham was born the twentieth from the first man. For there are ten generations from Adam to Noah: and ten from Noah to Abraham. From which Usserius gathers that that edition, which was placed in the Hexapla by Origen, and held to be genuine, deposited in the Library of Cleopatra in Alexandria, and otherwise received at that time in Egypt, Palestine, and Syria, did not have Cainan, which he distinguishes from the common and vulgate, which was also called Lucian's: and he differentiates from both the primitive version of the Mosaic Pentateuch, which corresponded most exactly to the Hebrew text: since that which was once held to be genuine, the interpretation of the whole Old Testament, and the same being more copious, and composed after the fourth year of Ptolemy Philometor, in the course of time obtained the place and name of the 70 Elders: concerning which opinion of Usserius, what should be held was abundantly stated in the preliminaries of the Commentary on Genesis. Julius Africanus was of an age nearly equal to Origen, whom the computation of years to Phaleg also testifies to have neglected the years of Cainan: whom likewise Hesychius in

Christ's birth. Suidas in Φαλὲχ. John Malalas of Antioch, and George Cedrenus in their Chronicles, embrace it: Theophilus of Antioch was even older than these, who in book III to Autolycus, establishing a calculation of times according to the LXX, omitted Cainan and made Arphaxad the father of Sala. In the very times of the Apostles, Dositheus in the Hebrew text (which he gave to his Samaritans, having interpolated it) of the fathers after the flood, with the years before the begetting taken from the LXX edition, entirely omitted Cainan with his years, having counted 942 years from the flood to the seventieth year of Terah, ὁπόσα ἦν καὶ κατὰ τῶν ὁ, how many there were also according to the LXX, as George Syncellus reports from Eusebius, Chron. p. 88. To these also are added Josephus, an old Christian writer in his Greek Hypomnesticon, still unpublished, cited by Ussher, who, recounting the generations from Adam to Christ, after Arphaxad mentioned Sala, with Cainan omitted: as also Quintus Julianus Hilarion in his book on the duration of the world, written in the year of Christ 397, who likewise establishing a calculation of years according to the LXX, passed over the times of Cainan.

Finally, since that Cainan is acknowledged neither by the Hebrews, nor by their follower Berosus the Chaldean, nor by the Targums, he is not undeservedly exploded as illegitimate; just as the other Cainan, son of Shem, among the LXX in Genesis X, 22, is to be held as merely spurious or rather supposititious.

Nor indeed is there any certainty held concerning the number of years from the edition held for the seventy-two translators: for modern editions and the ancient LXX interpreters attribute 130 years to that Cainan when he begat Arphaxad, as does Marianus Scotus, who was the first of all in constructing a chronology of the world to admit the years of Cainan from the LXX interpreters. But the Papist writers, Pererius, Bellarmine, Tirinus, Huntlæus, Torniellus, Salianus, Harvillæus, and Henr. Philippi think that that addition of one hundred years is faulty, and assign to him only 30 years before Sala was begotten. Jornandes, however, in his book on the succession of kingdoms, page 6, and George the Syrian in his chronological tables ascribe 135 years to the same; some codices also, as George Syncellus testifies, Chronological page 186, claim 139 years for him, which latter number the Constantinopolitan authors of the computation received today by the Greeks and Muscovites, who referred Christ's birth to the year of the World 5509, were followed, Scaliger teaches in his Canon Isagogicus, book III, part 2, chapter 1.

We add to these the suffrages of the Jesuits of no low rank: the discourse of Benedict Pererius especially deserves to be mentioned. Book XVI on Genesis, Sect. 174. If I am accustomed to ponder with my mind: either this generation of Cainan was unknown to Moses, or it was known: who would dare to say that it was unknown to Moses, which had been perceived and known by the LXX interpreters? Since Moses was so much closer than they were to that age, and he alone wrote the history of those times with such diligence and care. But if that generation was known to Moses, why then did he omit it? especially, however, since the addition or subtraction of that generation varies not a little the chronology which is described by Moses between the flood and Abraham: that Moses wished to hand down this chronology whole, exact, and perfect, is the clearest indication, because he distinctly and accurately recounts the series of generations which were between the flood and Abraham, and properly assigns to each generation its own subtly computed years; how is it credible, therefore, that Moses, with the generation of Cainan omitted, either wished to hand down to us a faulty chronology, or, when he least wished to, handed it down unknowingly? Indeed, thinking long and much, I have not yet been able to find any reason (which would satisfy my mind) why Moses should or could have passed over the generation of Cainan, if indeed it intervened between Arphaxad and Sala. For, what some say, that Moses wished to reduce the generations which were before and after the flood to only two decades: that can neither be proved by them, and is light and futile, nor is it such that for its sake Moses should have had to disturb and confuse the chronology (the exact knowledge of which was of great moment). Add to these, that at least in the books of Chronicles, in which are supplied those things which had been left out elsewhere in the sacred scriptures, whence they even have their name, this generation of Cainan should have been mentioned: since in the beginning of the first book of Chronicles the series of generations which were before and after the flood are likewise recounted as here, yet no word is made about the generation of Cainan. And further, Sect. 178 seq. From these it is rightly concluded that the generation of Cainan was not in all the books of the LXX interpreters. Whence it is also probably conjectured that it was not handed down by the LXX interpreters: and that those books which lacked that generation, as those which agreed with the Hebrew codices, are to be judged true and whole: but those which had the generation of Cainan are to be judged and rejected as corrupt and faulty. Thus Pererius. Petrus Possinus, in his Genealogical Dialectics, ch. 2, praises more in that opinion: I assent, he says, to great men, Abulensis, Eugubinus, Cajetan, Cornelius, Jansenius Bishop of Ghent, Sixtus Senensis, Genebrardus, Benedict Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide, Dionysius Petavius, and many other older and more recent ones: That there was never any Cainan among men who was indeed the son of Arphaxad, but the father of Sala. I think I prove this by an invincible argument, by the express affirmation of Moses, who narrates that Sala was begotten by Arphaxad. That there can be no suitable reason brought forward why this testimony should not be accepted just as it sounds and just as it lies. If, therefore, when the same Moses in the same place says that Arphaxad was begotten by Shem, or Heber by Salah, he is believed to have revealed to us by the divine authority in which he excelled, and properly and ἀμέσως (directly), that Salah was the father of Heber, and Arphaxad the son of Shem. So that he who would dare to bring forward certain others, whose generation was intermediate between these, would seem to deserve to be repelled with reproach, as rash and rebellious against the light; a contumacious contemner, I say, of the divine Relation offered to us through Moses, the interpreter of the Holy Spirit, I do not see what place can remain for this opinion concerning the interpolated Cainan. These things the Jesuit Possinus, who observes that the exception of other Jesuits—that Moses followed the roundness of the number and wished to designate precisely two decades of generations to Abraham, and for that reason omitted Cainan—is the answer of Tornielli, Salianus, and Spondanus, touches upon with a just refutation and correction: It is sufficiently evident, he says, that Moses was eager to enter into the number of the times passed since the beginning of things: and with that mind and purpose he diligently noted what interval of years intervened between the births of the Patriarchs succeeding one another. But with this purpose, the voluntary suppression of any generation whatsoever clearly conflicts: from which, for whatever reasons it might finally be dispensed with, it was manifest that a wonderful perturbation of the calculations would necessarily arise.

What is to be held concerning the passage in Luke chapter III, we have said elsewhere expressly, namely in the Anti-Grotian Annotations to Luke III and in the Critici Sacri from page 750 to 761. Johannes Cordesius, among the Papists, certainly strives to confirm in his French booklet on the Genealogy of Christ that the name Cainan did not exist in the primitive codices of Luke, whose arguments, as if from an anonymous author, Spanheim reviewed against Cainan in part 1 of his Dubia Evangelica.

QUESTION III. How the two-year period after the flood up to Arphaxad is to be counted.

CONCERNING this two-year period, Genesis 11:10: Shem was 100 years old, and he begat Arphaxad two years after the flood; four opinions are found. For since the LXX render it δευτέρῳ ἔτει μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμὸν, in the second year after the flood, many, with Eusebius, Julian, the Toletan in book III against the Jews, and Augustine in book XVI of The City of God, chapter 10, understand the second year after the flood to be completed; others, with Jacob Capellus, understand it to be begun; some accept the second year as begun, but in such a way that they wish to include also the year of the flood, and thus they think that both the flood ended and Arphaxad was born at the beginning of the 601st year of Noah. According to these, therefore, only one year is established between the beginning of the 600th year of Noah and the birth of Arphaxad; according to Capellus, two; according to Eusebius, three years are left from the beginning of the 600th year of Noah to Arphaxad; finally, Funccius, with his followers, assigns a four-year period.

But just as Funccius makes the number larger by one just year, so Capellus has mutilated the calculation by the subtraction of one year. The others, however, with Theophilus of Antioch, Julius Africanus, and Sulpicius Severus, deduct the two-year period: to whom Scaliger accedes in his Elenchus of the oration of Pareus: In the beginning of the 601st year of Noah, Shem begat Arphaxad, being one hundred years old: the hundredth year having been completed after his father began to beget. But since by this arrangement it must be said that Shem devoted himself to the procreation of children in the ark, which is in no way plausible—nay, that there were not eight, but nine souls in the ark, which contradicts Peter in 1 Epistle 3:20—it must be admitted that Shem begat Arphaxad after the flood was completed, and since the text is clear, that he was born two years after the flood itself, this must be accepted no otherwise than as the text sounds, namely, that he was procreated when the two-year period after the flood was completed. For the phrase itself implies this: since Moses does not say בִּשְׁנַת הַשֵּׁנִית or בִּשְׁנַת שְׁתַּיִם, in the second year, as he is accustomed to speak when he denotes the current second year in the Holy Scriptures, as in Exodus 40:17, 1 Kings 15:25, Haggai 1:1, 15, chapter 4:10, Zechariah 1:1, 7, but simply uses the dual number word שְׁנָתַיִם, two years, as in Genesis 45:6: It is two years since the famine began: whence to Onkelos and Jonathan, Arphaxad is said to be born תַּרְתֵּין שְׁנִין, two years after the flood: and thus the Syriac and Jerome also render it, two years after the flood. Add that no reason can be given why, while in the rest of the entire chronology the years are taken as completed or as if completed through the genealogy of the Fathers, this second year should be understood as begun. Furthermore, because the sons of Shem are listed in Gen. 11:12, 1 Chronicles 1:17, Elam, Assur, and Arphaxad, if Arphaxad is the third according to that order, the second year after the flood ended, in which he was begotten, is necessarily understood as completed, unless we wish to say that the firstborn was conceived in the ark. Moreover, if it is established with Scaliger that Arphaxad was born at the beginning of the 601st year of Noah, the year of the Exodus will certainly not be the one which Scaliger established, namely 2453. Whence Dr. Behmius here deserted the footsteps of his Scaliger and asserted that Arphaxad was born after the two-year period after the flood had elapsed. Which he himself indeed wished to be understood as including the flood: but in such a way that nothing is detracted from the sacred calculation; for whether it is said, as we say, that the flood began toward the beginning of the 600th year of Noah and that two years elapsed from the end of the flood until Arphaxad was born: or whether it is asserted with the blessed Dr. Behmius that the flood began when the 600th year had finished and that two years ran from the beginning of the flood to the birth of Arphaxad, the chronology will be the same, and no more than three years will intervene between the beginning of the 600th year of Noah and the birth of Arphaxad. The former opinion, however, as being more consistent with the phraseology of Scripture, is deservedly preferred by us. For when it is said in Genesis 11 concerning Shem, Ham, and Japheth, sons were born to them after the flood, no one doubts that the end of the flood is understood: therefore, likewise here in Genesis 11:10, the phrase must be taken as two years after the flood was finished, of course, not begun. And since the divine historian is believed to be weaving the chronology of the renewed world here, he wished to deduce it from the birth of Arphaxad, which took place two years after the flood. But if he were to derive the epoch from the beginning of the flood, it would follow that the very year of the flood was included in the times of the new world, which however belongs to the ἀρχαῖον or ancient world, 2 Pet. 2:5. Wherefore we conclude that Arphaxad was born two years after the flood had ended: which Ussher says happened at the beginning of the year of the world 1659 and of the age of Noah 603.

QUESTION IV. Whether Abram was the firstborn of Terah, and in what year of his life was he born?

Two principal opinions are found here: The former is that of the Jews in Seder Olam, R. Isaac in Bereshith Rabba ch. XXXIX, Josephus b. I of Antiquities ch. 6, and of the Papists, Abulensis, Genebrardus, Pererius, Cornel. à Lapide, Sa, Petavius, Lorinus on Acts 7:7, as well as Scaliger and his followers, and Lansbergius, Alstedius, Brentius also, Osiander, Gesner, Helwigius, and others, to whose side not indeed all, as some rashly boast, but very many from ecclesiastical antiquity favor, that Abram was the firstborn, and born in the 70th year of Terah. Which from the words of Moses Gen. 11:26 might seem clear. And Terah lived seventy years and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran. For since all three were not born in that very year, Abram at least, through whose years the chronology is believed to be continued, is to be understood as born in that same seventieth year of Terah, since it seems to be admitted that in that chapter the chronological computation is woven through the years of the begetting of children of the Patriarchs after the flood. As therefore in the preceding Patriarchs, when the year of life is expressed in which each begat, the one who was begotten is added immediately: so they think it must be held here also. When in v. 24 it is said: Nahor lived twenty-nine years and begat Terah, everyone understands that Terah was born in the twenty-ninth year of Nahor. Why then likewise, when it is said here, Terah lived seventy years and begat Abram, should it not be understood that Abram was born in the seventieth year of Terah? Furthermore, when in the generation of sons, who are listed as begotten by a parent, with the year of generation added, Scripture does not change that order, but retains the order in which the sons were begotten, it does not seem to be doubted that Abraham, listed in the first place, was the firstborn of Terah, because he is listed in this way with the expression of the year of Terah's generation. Nor indeed could it be established beyond doubt in what year Abram was born, unless this order of generation were observed and the birth year expressed: but that Scripture should have expressly stated the birth year of the other Patriarchs in weaving the chronology according to the begetting of children, but should not have expressed the birth year of this eminent Patriarch, whom it commemorates in the same chronological series, or should have expressly mentioned the birth year of Nahor or Haran in that series, but not that of Abram the Father of believers, is by no means likely. Shall we believe, they say, that the Holy Spirit exactly defined the birth year of Arphaxad, but that of Abraham's birth, which in the series of those Patriarchs and ancestors of Christ should be considered among the most important, he has not expressly designated. Furthermore, it is impossible, says Dr. Behmius p. 15, that the best and greatest historian, scrupulously counting the various years of Abraham's age—the seventy-fifth in Gen. 12:4, the eighty-sixth in ch. 16:16, the ninety-ninth in ch. 17:24, the hundredth in ch. 21:5, the hundred and seventy-fifth in ch. 25:7, and indeed noting the years of the remaining Patriarchs after the flood for Abraham's sake—should have left the true year of Abraham's birth in doubt; upon which the rest of the Abrahamic life and the chronological fabric, all the years, depended. Dr. Behmius adds another reason: to Abraham, it seems unusual and like a miracle to beget a son in the 100th year of his age, Gen. 17:17. What need would there have been for this wonder if the parent had begotten him in his 130th year? Finally, he concludes from the absurdity thus: If Abraham in the 130th year of his age was finally begotten by Terah, and thus 60 years from the world were introduced into the chronological computation, lest there be a confusion of Sabbatical and Jubilee years, which nevertheless GOD, the author of order, began to arrange after the Exodus in such a way that they fell precisely into the years counted from the creation of the world, with Sabbatical years divided by 7 and Jubilee years by 49. And these are the stronger reasons for that opinion.

Nor is there any doubt that the term of this Epoch ought to consist of Moses himself, whom everyone easily acknowledges to have wished to hand down chronology entirely and perfectly. Since, however, in recounting the post-diluvian Patriarchs, the Holy Spirit looked most especially to Abraham as the term and goal, in order to pursue his history thereafter and especially the new Epoch from the calling of Abraham or rather from the peculiar ἐπαγγελίᾳ (promise) made to him, which was confirmed by certain signs and especially by the sacrament of the covenant, circumcision, and was repeated again to Abraham's son Isaac and his grandson Jacob, and thus was illustrated by new oracles, so that it might be a singular consolation to the Abrahamic race and the Israelite people throughout the whole time of their pilgrimage, up to the exodus from Egypt—as under this, with the laws promulgated and the hierarchy of the Lord's people established, the promise concerning the Messiah was to be sanctioned, established, and propagated—the time of Abraham's birth and his age when he was called and received that ἐπαγγελίᾳ (promise) divinely could by no means be passed over. And to that end, Moses, by commemorating the generation of Abraham, seems to have designated the year of Terah in which he begat him, namely the seventieth, but then after the digression about Terah and the year of his death, the year of Abraham's pilgrimage, Gen. 12:4. Nor, however, does he seem to have designated the year of Terah's death properly for the sake of chronology; but just as was done in the rest of the preceding Patriarchs, only so that it might be clear how long they lived and how they could communicate among themselves and συμβιβάσει (knit together), and by mutual conversation, devote effort to the doctrine concerning the Messiah and the propagation of the Church. For the divine Historian deduced the reasons for the sacred calculation not through the years of the death of the Patriarchs, as of any one of them; but through the years of παιδογονίας (child-begetting), as is admitted among chronologists, and he testified by no indication that this was not observed in the same way in Terah and Abraham, whom he commemorates in the same series with the others, nor could it be clear to anyone from Moses that a different method was adopted in these Patriarchs to weave together the chronology. For they do not think that it was indicated by Moses that, when Abraham was seventy-five years old and setting out from Haran, Terah his parent had already finished his life in Haran. For although Moses had previously commemorated the death of Terah in ch. 11:32, they judge that this was done for the reason that he might finish the history of Terah, and

thereafter pursue the history of Abraham, but it was not indicated by Moses by any jot that that departure from Haran was undertaken by Abraham after the death of Terah. Which no one could collect or presume from the history of Moses, whom everyone acknowledges and venerates as the sole steward and chronologist of those more ancient times of that Patriarchal antiquity. Which arguments, not of small moment, can easily draw us into agreement with the authority of great men, and have drawn us before; but where we now more accurately weigh the reasons of the other opinion, and especially the series of the Mosaic relation and the words of the Holy Spirit, which are very clear, we do not hesitate at all to yield to the truth and to retract our own views. For when Holy Scripture is clear, all preconceived opinions, however specious they may be, deservedly yield to it. Wherefore we judge that the other opinion is to be preferred, which maintains that Abraham was born not in the 70th year of Terah, but in the 130th, and cannot be considered Terah's firstborn. The reasons certainly brought forward for the 70th year do not sustain a more accurate examination. For although Moses says that Terah begat when he was 70 years old, he does not, however, testify that Abraham was begotten in that year; but he affirms that when Terah already had 70 years, he begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Which remains true, even if not Abraham, but Nahor or Haran was born in the seventieth year. For he does not indicate that all three were born in the same year; but that Terah began to beget in his seventieth year: which one of those three was the firstborn, however, is by no means clear from those words. For the reason here is not the same as that of the preceding generations, in which only one begotten person is named, and thus the year in which the generation took place is determined beyond doubt: therefore, although the chronological computation is undoubted and free from all controversy through the years of παιδογονίας (child-begetting) in the rest, because it is expressly defined in what year the Patriarchs begat each one; yet this computation is not free from doubt, because three sons are listed, and it is not explicitly stated which of the sons of Terah was begotten in that 70th year in which he began to beget, and is his firstborn. Nor does Moses maintain the same method in this generation as in the previous ones, tacitly indicating that the computation here must be entered into by another method. For it should have been said, after the manner of the former: Terah lived 70 years, and begat Abraham; and Terah lived, after he begat Abram, 135 years, and begat sons and daughters.

But the fact that it is sought from the order of the sons of Terah is only a topical argument: for Scripture does not always preserve the order of generation, as is evident in the example of the sons of Abraham 1 Chron. I, 28, and the sons of Jacob Gen. XLVI, and following (which example Scaliger and those who followed him wrongly allege for themselves, as inspection shows; for the children of Jacob are not enumerated in the order in which they were born) 1 Chron. II, 1, 2. And what need would there have been for Holy Scripture to openly designate who was first, who second, who third, which is sometimes done (as in 1 Chron. XXIII, 19, 20, etc.) if the natural order were observed everywhere. Wherefore, since it sometimes observes the order of dignity, and by reason of it places Isaac before Ishmael, Gen. XXV, 9, 1 Chron. I, 28, Jacob before Esau Josh. XXIV, 4, Ephraim before Manasseh Gen. XLVIII, 10, Moses before Aaron Exod. VII, 7, cannot it be said that Abram was mentioned in the first place here on account of dignity, even if he were not the πρωτότοκος? We learn that this opinion did not displease St. Augustine from Question XXV on Genesis. It is also possible to be solved in this way, since Scripture, which said that when Terah was 70 years old he begat Abraham and Nahor and Haran, did not certainly intend for this to be understood as if he begat all three in the same year of his life, but Scripture commemorated the year from which he began to beget. For it is possible that Abraham was begotten later, but Scriptures, he was named first, just as the Prophet named the younger one first (Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated) and in Chronicles, although Judas is the fourth in order of birth, he is named first, from whom the name was given to the Jewish people because of the royal tribe. Finally, even if we concede that one should not easily and without grave cause depart from the order in which sons are listed in genealogies, where there is a pregnant cause that compels one to depart, there is no reason why we should superstitiously adhere to the order, much less prefer that order to clear testimonies of Scripture.

3. Furthermore, what is urged, that unless primogeniture is attributed to Abraham, his birth date would be uncertain, is by no means to be admitted, since it can be established from elsewhere regarding the birth date, even if it is not expressed in Genesis 11:26.

4. Nor is it necessary that we establish that he was commemorated explicitly and in express words, just as it was done in the case of other Patriarchs: (no one would say that such an explicit commemoration, which occurs in others, is had here); it suffices if he was designated in meaning. Nor is the reason obscure why he did not express the birth of Abraham according to the generation of Terah in the same manner as he observed in the others, because this epoch had to be established in a new way, and one was not to proceed according to the years of child-begetting; but the beginning was to be fixed from the calling and pilgrimage of Abraham. Hence it pleased the Holy Spirit to break off that thread of child-begetting in Terah, by which the precise designation of the year of generation is made: so that although he noted the time when he began to beget, because something peculiar is apprehended in it, he did not, however, explicitly express the year in which Abraham was born; but left it to be elicited from a collation of history. But that which was peculiar in him was that, whereas the other Patriarchs after the flood begat much earlier, at the age of thirty or thereabouts, Terah began to beget first in the seventieth year of his life; just as in Noah, who was before the flood, he likewise expressed the year in which he began to beget, because he only begat children at the age of five hundred, because this was proper and peculiar to him, whereas no one of the others is found to have begat children at such a great age.

5. But that it seemed unusual and like a miracle to Abraham that he, being a centenarian, was still to beget a son, Gen. 13:12, this will seem strange to no one, even if he himself had been born in the 130th year of his father, because that too was already peculiar to his parent Terah at that time, as we have observed. Nor did Abraham look only at the years of his own age in that admiration, since he also begat Ishmael at the advanced age of 86, Gen. 16:6, and after the passing of Sarah and the marriage of Isaac, having taken Keturah, he still begat children when he had reached 140 years of life, Gen. 25:1, 2, but he looked primarily at the age and barrenness of his wife, the deadness of Sarah's womb, as the Apostle speaks in Rom. 4:19, as also his own body already dead, as the same Apostle warned.

6. Finally, what is objected, that Chronology would be disturbed if sixty years were added to the age of Terah when he begat Abraham, and that the deduction of Sabbatical and Jubilee years from the foundation of the world would not remain safe, can move nothing in those who prefer to insist strictly on the words of Scripture rather than to serve a precariously assumed hypothesis, or to rely on Topical arguments that are likewise merely arbitrary. For if the matter is certain from the Scriptures, that Abraham did not leave Haran until after the death of his parent, when he was seventy years old, those who hold the opposite view must disturb Chronology by the subtraction of 60 years, which Scripture added, and mutilate the system of the years of the world by as many years: which is inexcusable. For that must be kept entirely whole, without subtraction, whatever happens to the Sabbatical and Jubilee years; which Scripture nowhere even obscurely taught were to be deduced from the foundation of the world.

Therefore, it behooves us to be concerned primarily about this, whether Scripture has taught that those 60 years are to be added to the age of Terah when he begat Abraham, i.e., whether Terah begat him not when he was 70, but when he was 130? Which we judge to be established first from the series of the Mosaic narrative. For when Moses had reported that Terah began to beget in the seventieth year of his age, Gen. 11:26, having inserted a brief history of the children and life of Terah, he subjoined the year of his death, namely that he died in the 205th year, and furthermore the calling of Abraham. By which what else did he wish to teach than that the calling of Abraham from Haran happened only after the death of Terah? For why would Moses have inverted the order, and narrated the death of Terah before the calling of Abraham, if the latter had happened some years earlier? Why would he have immediately subjoined the calling of Abraham to his death, if this had happened long before the death of Terah? Nor is it permitted to invent a hysteron proteron at our own discretion, especially in a history so accurately recorded: but just as Moses indicated that Abraham's departure with Terah from Ur of the Chaldeans happened after his seventieth year, without explicitly mentioning the year, so he reports that the calling of Abraham from Haran, which comes into the chronological calculation, happened after the death of Terah, and he makes no mention of Terah afterwards. But as he openly testifies that the same happened in the seventy-fifth year of Abraham's age, so it is by no means obscure, since it happened immediately after the death of Terah, who was two hundred and five years old when he died, in what year of Terah Abraham was begotten; for if 75 years are subtracted from the two hundred and fifth year of his death, the one hundred and thirtieth year of Terah remains, in which he begat Abraham. Moses therefore did not pass over in silence the year of Abraham's birth, even though he did not designate it in express words; but left it to be gathered from that series of the narrative. For he who was called when 75 years old, when his parent was two hundred and five years old, and was meeting his own day, it is necessary that he was born in the 130th year of his parent. Furthermore, if Scripture had wished the chronological thread to be woven from the time of the first generation and the begetting of offspring, namely in the seventieth year of Terah, Moses would undoubtedly have indicated that Abraham was begotten in that year: but this was not done: he only signified that Terah began to beget children in his seventieth year, but he did not openly indicate which of the sons was begotten in that year: therefore he commemorated all three sons together, who certainly were not begotten in the same year, so that it might be understood that the series of the years of the world was to be continued not from the time of the first offspring begotten by him, but from his death and Abraham's departure into Canaan joined with it.

And thus, because the other argument for our opinion is entirely ἀδιάλυτον, Stephen the Protomartyr strictly adheres to this Mosaic account, and teaches with a resonant voice that the departure of Abraham into the land of Canaan (which took place in the 75th year of his age, as Moses testifies) happened finally after the death of Terah. For what could be clearer in support of this opinion than that narrative which the blessed Luke reports from the mouth of Stephen, Acts 7:2 ff.: Men, brethren, and fathers, hearken; the GOD of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt, πρὶν ἢ κατοικῆσαι αὐτὸν in Haran, and said unto him, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall show thee. Then came he out of the land of the Chaldeans, and dwelt κατῴκησεν in Haran. This calling of his was made in Ur of the Chaldeans, which Pliny, book 6, chapter 26, testifies belonged to Mesopotamia, placing Babylon itself within the borders of Mesopotamia, as also Orchoë, which Junius and Tremellius think is Ur: (compare also Josephus, book 1, chapter 8, who likewise counts the Chaldeans among the Mesopotamians) even though it is established that the tract to which Haran looked was called Mesopotamia by a special name. Moses described this calling in not dissimilar words in Genesis 12, verse 1: Get thee out of thy country, and from thy father's house, and come into the land that I will show thee; but because the protomartyr proceeds thus concerning the further removal and departure of Abram: And from thence (from Haran;) after his father was dead, he removed him (the GOD of glory μετῴκησεν αὐτὸν) into this land, wherein ye now dwell (that is, into the land of Canaan,) it must be placed beyond controversy, that is, unless we wish to contradict Stephen openly, that the removal from Haran was made μετὰ ἀποθανεῖν AFTER HIS FATHER WAS DEAD. Furthermore, St. Stephen adds significantly: And he gave him none INHERITANCE in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on: but he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, ἐν ὄντι αὐτῷ τέκνῳ when HE HAD NO CHILD: because that ἐπαγγελία or promise of the seed was added to this calling, which the protomartyr Stephen indicated more obscurely here, but Moses delivered openly in Gen. 12, verse 2: The Lord appeared unto Abraham, and said unto him, Unto thy seed will I give this land. From these characteristics, therefore, it is infallibly certain that Abraham, who was 75 years old when he was removed into the land of Canaan, could not have been 135 years old when his parent died, which the authors of the other opinion maintain. For thus the removal of Abraham into the land of Canaan would have had to take place 60 years before the death of Terah, which, however, happened only after the death of his parent. And since that removal not only took place after the death of Terah, as Stephen teaches, but also since, when Abraham was removed, as St. Stephen testifies along with the Mosaic history, the Patriarch did not yet have a son, how can it be believed that Abraham was 135 years old at the time of Terah's death? For he begat his son Ishmael when he was 86 years old, but Isaac when he was 100 years old. Furthermore, if Terah still survived for a full sixty years while Abraham was already dwelling in the land of Canaan, how did it happen that Moses, after the removal of Abraham, made not even the slightest mention of Terah? Or that Abraham never visited his parent of decrepit age, or betook himself to him in Haran when famine pressed upon the land of Canaan? But it is too manifest from the words of the protomartyr that the removal of Abraham and the promises made to him were after the death of Terah, and before Isaac was born, just as the Mosaic narrative also holds.

Whence Augustinus Torniellus urges in his Annals for the year of the world 2039, that if the contrary opinion concerning Abraham, born in the seventieth year of Terah's age, is admitted, the Scripture can scarcely be saved from many contradictions. For if it is so, then Abraham lived with his father for 135 years; for it is established that Terah himself died in the two hundred and fifth year of his life: therefore Abraham was at least one hundred and thirty-five years old when, his father being dead, he went out from Haran to come into the land of Canaan; therefore Isaac was already born in Haran before the death of his grandfather, namely, when Terah was in the one hundred and seventieth year of his life: for that was the hundredth year of Abraham, in which we shall say a little later that Isaac was born. Therefore Isaac was thirty-five years old when his father Abraham, at the Lord's command, went out from Haran, and he himself likewise came with his father into the land of Canaan. That these things, however, are not to be admitted is evident from those things which we read at the end of chapter 11 of Genesis and at the beginning of chapter 12 up to verse 6, namely, that Terah died in Haran, then Abraham went out from Haran and came into the land of Canaan, and it is expressly said that Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran; and it is subjoined: And he took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the substance that they had gathered, etc., with no mention at all made of his son Isaac, as if he were not yet born at that time. And there is no doubt that he would have said significantly: And he took Sarai his wife and Isaac his son, etc., if Isaac had been born at that time and had already become a man. But afterwards in the same chapter and following, many things are narrated which happened to Abraham himself in the land of Canaan and in Egypt: and finally at the beginning of chapter 21 the birth of Isaac himself is described, which is said in the same place, verse 5, to have happened in the hundredth year of the life of Abraham, who was then dwelling in the land of Abimelech, King of Gerar, as can be gathered from the same chapter and also from the preceding one. Likewise in chapter 7 of Acts, verse 4, it is openly said that GOD removed Abraham from Haran into the land of Canaan after his father was dead and when he did not have a son. But all these things, when compared with those which were said before, seem in no way able to agree. These are the words of Torniellus.

Jacobus Tirinus in Chron. S. p. 8. argues thus: If Abram (Tirinus omitted to say, he was 135 years old) at the death of his father, and GOD promising the land of Canaan to him, (for he must have had so many, if he was born in the 70th year of him who lived 205 years) therefore he had already begotten Ishmael and Isaac (for he begat the former in the 86th year, the latter in the 100th year of his life, according to Scripture) but St. Stephen in Acts VII, verse 4, says that he was moved into the land of Canaan, and the promise of that land was made to him, when he did not yet have a son. Tirinus adds other arguments also, which it is helpful to repeat: If Abram at the death of his father was 135 years old, when he received the commandment of circumcision in the 100th year of his life, why did he not also circumcise his parent, who survived for a full 35 years? Why is there no mention at least of him, why also is there no mention of a blessing bestowed by the grandfather upon his grandsons Ishmael and Isaac?

Again, if Abraham, already 135 years old, returned again to Haran, why did he not then take Rebecca or another of his kinswomen from there as a wife for his son Isaac, already a man of 35 years, rather than after 5 years sending his steward there at great expense for that reason, why does that steward speak of the affairs of Abraham, of his wealth, of the son born of Sarah, as if of unknown matters in Gen. XXIV. 35, if five years earlier Abraham had visited them and had divided the paternal inheritance with them?

Finally, how is it said at the end of chapter XXII that it was announced to Abraham concerning the sons: whom

Nahor had undertaken, if he himself had recently added them and had personally inspected everything.

B. Lyserus in his history of Adam, page 499, observes that this can be confirmed by the age of Lot, who was the son of Abraham's brother Aran and accompanied his uncle Abram, being of almost the same age as him; which can be gathered from the age of his daughters, who in Gen. XVI, verse 14, were already adult and marriageable, while Abraham was not yet a centenarian. But indeed, Lot could not have been both the son of his brother and of such an advanced age if Abraham had been the eldest among the brothers.

Some also draw an argument from the fact that Sarah, the wife of Abraham, was the daughter of Haran, his brother, or the wife of his cousin Abraham: but neither can be consistent with that opinion about Abraham, that he was begotten in the seventieth year of his father's age. For thus Sarah could not have been the daughter of Aran, being ten years younger than Abraham: and consequently it would be necessary that she was born in the eighth or ninth year of the life of her father Haran (being one or two years younger than Abraham), which the Rabbis indeed affirm in Sanhedrin Chapter XIX, as also in Seder Olam Rabba chapter II, and Genebrardus in his Chronology at the end of the second age; but most ineptly. Nor could she have been the cousin of Abraham: unless we say that she was the daughter of another unnamed brother of Abraham, who was begotten long before the seventieth year of Terah's age: about which matter we have nothing from the Holy Scriptures, nor from elsewhere: whence the common opinion is that Sarah was both the cousin of Abraham and the daughter of Aran. Hence Bellarmine, concerning the Sacrament of Matrimony, chapter 28, proves that Haran was the eldest son of Terah not only because he died before the others, and because another of the brothers, Nahor, took his daughter Milcah as a wife: but also because Abraham himself took another daughter of Haran, Iscah, as a wife, Gen. XI, verses 28 and 29. That by Iscah no one can be understood except Sarai, who, according to Josephus, had two names: because it is in no way credible that Scripture would have wanted to reveal the father of Milcah, and not the father of Sarai, a person of far greater dignity, nor is there any reason why mention should be made of Iscah if she is different from Sarai. Which is the common opinion not only of Josephus (book 1, Antiq. chapter VII, VIII) but also of all the ancient Hebrews, and accepted also by St. Augustine, book XVI, De Civit. DEI, chapters XII and XIX, and by the greater part of Christians. Whence B. Polyc. Lyserus, in the place cited, confirms that Abraham was not born in the 70th year of Terah, from the age of Sarah: She is believed to have been the daughter of Aran, brother of Abram, and sister of Lot; because Abraham himself said to King Abimelech, Gen. XX, verse 12, Truly she is my sister, the daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother; namely because Aran, her father, having died before Terah, her grandfather, Terah received Sarah into his house and raised her as a daughter. Abraham, however, was not more than ten years older than Sarah, Genesis XXIII, verse 1. Whence it follows that Abraham was born long after his brother, who was born in the seventieth year of Terah.

But if anyone wishes to say with Soto, Pererius, and Bellarmine that Nahor and Aran were born before the seventieth year of Terah's age, and thus born before Abraham, who was begotten in the 70th year, the words of Moses will by no means admit that meaning: And Terah lived 70 years, and begat Abraham, Nahor, and Aran, that is, he begat Abraham in the seventieth year, when he had already previously begotten the other two, Nahor and Aran. For who does not see how forced, and insolent, and unusual such an interpretation is? And therefore B. Lyserus more correctly concludes here: If anyone should contend at all that Abraham was born in the 70th and not the 130th year of Terah's age, then in the chronological calculation he will discover that Sarah survived Terah by at least two years and that Isaac was born 35 years while his grandfather Terah was still alive, which cannot be reconciled with the circumstances of the history. Since Abraham did not depart from his parent Terah while he was living. But whatever may be the case regarding Sarah's parent, that argument is primarily evident and invincible which is taken from the words of Stephen, which most clearly testify that Abraham was transferred into Canaan only after the death of Terah, who, it is established from Moses, was 75 years old when he was transferred: That this was the common opinion of the Jews at the time of Stephen, there is no doubt; just as Philo also testifies concerning it in the book περὶ ἀποικίας. It can escape no one who has applied study to the laws (or Mosaic books) that Abraham, indeed, first coming from the land of the Chaldeans, dwelt in Charan: but there, upon the death of his father, he also departed from it. The same is also the common opinion of all Samaritan chronologers to this very day, that Abraham's departure from Charan into the land of Canaan was joined with the death of his father, which the author of the Sicilian annals also followed, as noted by James Ussher in his Chronology. Sacr. p. 112. Nor did St. Chrysostom teach otherwise among the Greeks in Sermon XXXI on Genesis: GOD did not call him forth from there before Thara was dead. For then, he says, after he had died: And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy land. Likewise in Sermon XXXVI. Charan being occupied, after they had pitched their tent there, and Thara had died, it was again commanded him by GOD that he should go out from there: Go forth, he says, out of thy land, etc. The same was also the opinion of Procopius of Gaza on Genesis XII. It is asked, how Thara, born 70 years, begat Abraham, and then yielded to fate having been born 205 years? For Abraham was not 135 years old at that time; but he reached the year 70 (or rather 75) according to the testimony of Holy Scripture. But in truth it seems to me to shine forth that Thara begat Abraham (to some it seems it should be read Arran) not when the seventieth year was beginning, but perhaps when it was completed. Nor was Abraham born immediately when that year reached its end, but only in the 130th year of Thara. Nor does Moses record Abraham so as to commemorate him among the firstborn; but he mentions him as the first and chief, and the most famous of the sons, who becomes especially necessary for the relation of the present history. Hence one will understand that Arran preceded Abraham and Nahor in number of years: Although in the series of the narrative Abraham is placed in the first position, it does not happen that he is to be considered older than the others, but that is attributed to the honor of the Patriarch. Which Theodore also established in the Greek Catena of Aloysius Lipomanus, namely that Abraham was the youngest of the three sons born in the old age of the father. Which Augustine also indicated in Question XXV on Genesis. Which opinion has also been embraced by Cajetan, Lipomanus, Naclantus, Pontacus, Marzilla, Delrio, Leonh. Marius, Fromondus, Joh. Ferdinandus, Bonfrerius, likewise Calvin, Martyr, Musculus, Broughton, Tremellius, Junius, Pareus, Jacob and Louis Cappel, whose Chronology Brian Walton prefixed to the English Polyglot Biblical Work: the authors of the Belgian notes on the Holy Bible; from our own, the blessed Polycarp Lyser, the blessed Balduinus on Joshua Chapter XXIII, the blessed Walther, and others: as also not a few from the chronologists, Beroaldus, Temporarius, Ussher, Torniellus, Salianus, Tirinus, Henr. Philippi, Wilhelm Langius, Wichmannus, Vogelius,

Schillingius, Isaac Vossius, etc. Dr. Walther, having brought forward various other ways of reconciling the words of Moses and Stephen, finally judges that this opinion of Theodoret, Lyranus, Cajetan, and Torniellus is not to be rejected, and that it deserves credence for this very reason—a fact not denied by Pererius, even though he otherwise impugns it—because it exhausts every difficulty and leaves no dissonance, not even in appearance, in the Holy Scriptures; provided that Abraham was truly 75 years old when he came into the land of Canaan after his father's death, as Moses narrates. Whence Scaliger is entirely mistaken in Elenchus II of the Chronological Orations of Dr. Pareus, when he affirms that this opinion was first devised by Matthaeus Beraldus.

Nor was it observed rashly by the blessed Lyserus that the blessed Luther complains many times in his Commentaries on Genesis, especially in chapters XI, XII, and XIII, that 60 years had slipped away from him in the history of Abraham, which he could not find; and that those 60 years offer themselves to us most conveniently in the life of Terah, from the 70th year of Terah up to his 130th, if we investigate the year of Abraham's birth in retrograde order according to the guidance of Stephen and the number of years in which Abraham departed from Haran. We add, moreover, the express passages from the same Commentary of the blessed Luther on Genesis at chapter XXI, f. 162. We touched upon the disputation concerning the years of Abraham, whether he was the firstborn or not, above, and it is certain that the calculation of both the Jews and Lyra is false: for it removes sixty years. But more on these in another place. And in chapter XXII, f. 215. Lyra alone impugns this opinion of the Jews and concludes that Abraham was the last-born and 60 years younger than his brother, and he proves this with probable conjectures and arguments. But Stephen in the Acts moves me more, who says that Abraham departed after the death of his father; from there it follows that 60 years must be added to the age of Abraham at which he departs if you look at the history and count the years of Terah the father.

Those, however, who, with other dissenters, refer the birth of Abraham to the 70th year of Terah, when Stephen openly protests, do not find how they might extricate themselves from this knot. Jerome in Questions on Genesis calls this question insoluble. Joseph Scaliger in Elenchus II of the Chronological Orations says that Elias must be awaited to untie the knot. But Elias will be awaited in vain, unless perhaps he is to return with Enoch, so that, having untied the knot, he may be killed by the Anti-Christ. Melchior Canus does not fear to charge Stephen with a lapse of memory from the heat of his sermon. Bucholzer in his Chronological Isagoge says that the Acts are to be examined according to Genesis, not Genesis according to the Acts; that the wood is to be measured by the rule, not the rule by the wood; and that there are many things in Stephen's narrative which must be taken with a grain of salt (as they say) and softened by a convenient interpretation. But that the Holy Spirit spoke no less through Stephen than through Moses, and that the report of Stephen is to be held as no less a norm and rule of truth than that of Moses, ought to have been undoubted among all Christians; nor is it said with sufficient piety that the words of the Holy Spirit are to be taken with a grain of salt, which, however, Calvisius did not fear to repeat; indeed, he pronounced quite obscurely in his Chronological Isagoge, chapter XXXVI, that the words of Stephen conflict with the sources and the text. That it is affirmed from Stephen that Abraham went into the land of Canaan after Terah had died, that was borrowed from the version of the 70 Interpreters; but if the paraphrases of the 70 Interpreters conflict with the sources and the text, they are to be taken with a grain of salt. But here nothing else is found in the version of the LXX than what the sources of the Holy Scriptures contain. And will Stephen be pitted against Moses? Nor did Dr. Bohemus hesitate to impute an error to Stephen: But that error, he says, did not concern any head of religion, but only a circumstance of time; therefore he preferred to agree with the erring adversaries in a trivial matter than to be the cause of useless contentions, especially at that time. But that matter is not to be considered trivial, upon which the true method of chronology depends, nor is it to be presumed in any way concerning the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of Stephen, that He either erred Himself in any circumstance, or approved of an error, or made it His own.
