And what necessity would there have been for that addition of the circumstance that Abraham was moved only after the death of Terah: would it not have been better to pass that over than to adopt it along with the erring? But the fact that he says a similar example, and one sufficiently manifest, occurs in this very sermon of Stephen, v. 24, concerning the 75 souls, deserves no consideration; for it is equally a matter of religion for us to ascribe an error to the protomartyr as in the present question; and that knot can be untied without difficulty, as we have shown elsewhere, so that there is no need at all for that dangerous and pernicious opinion that the Holy Spirit approved of the error of the common people.

And therefore others have devised other methods of responding: But the words of Stephen are too clear to be obscured by any sophistries. Some seek an escape in the word μετῴκησεν, arguing that Stephen designated not so much the actual departure of Abram from Charran as the firm fixing of his residence there, such as Abulensis, Pererius, Emanuel Saa, Lorinus, Cornel. a Lapide, to which view Augustine also leans in book XVI of The City of God, ch. 15. But Stephen speaks of that translation which was joined with the first promise concerning the giving of the inheritance of that land to Abraham and his seed, and it happened when he did not yet have children. But if Abraham was already 135 years old after the death of Terah when he was thus moved, so that he received a fixed dwelling there, he had certainly already received the promise long before, and he already had children, not only Ishmael, but also Isaac, whom he had begotten when he was one hundred years old. Nor does Stephen speak of such a firm habitation, by which he might have acquired some possession for himself, such as a field and a cave, but he speaks simply of a translation; indeed, lest we think that any possession is being referred to, he adds that no κληρονομίαν was given there to Abraham, οὐδὲ βῆμα ποδὸς, and the word itself μετώκησε implies a translation without any regard for any possession; which he did not even obtain (unless that field and cave are to be taken into account), with his children not yet born; but only after the death of his wife Sarah.

Nor has history handed down anything concerning a double translation or departure of Abraham from Haran, which Abulensis devised and Pererius attempted to defend: nor is it in any way likely that Abraham was translated into Canaan twice, once when he was 75 years old, and again after 60 years, when he was 135 years old, after the death of his father. For who would believe that the most holy Patriarch, having disregarded the divine command about leaving his home and his kindred, would have wished to return to his ancestral hearths, so that there was need for a new divine translation into the land of Canaan? Especially because Holy Scripture expressly testifies, Heb. XI. verse 15, that the Patriarchs did not return to their homeland. If they had been mindful of that country from which they had gone out, they had the opportunity to return: which Moses observed most especially in Abraham: who, when famine pressed, preferred to set out for Egypt, not without present danger to his life, rather than to return to his own, Gen. XII, 10. 12. he took great care that his son Isaac should not return to that land from which he himself had departed by divine command, Gen. XXIV, verses 5. 6. 8.

More plausible is the newly devised exception of Ludovicus de Dieu in his Animadversions on Acts VII, etc., that the words εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην do not seem to imply the land of Canaan universally; but specifically determine that part which had fallen to the lot of Judah, in which the Jews, whom Stephen was addressing in Jerusalem, were then dwelling: and thus it refers to his habitation in Mamre, and indeed after he had fixed a firm seat there by buying a field (near Hebron in the middle of the tribe of Judah): But St. Stephen is not speaking of a translation from one place in Canaan to another; but of a translation into the land of Canaan itself, and indeed from Haran: κακεῖθεν, and from there (from Haran) God translated him εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην, into that land: therefore the discourse is about the land of Canaan, into which the holy Patriarch was translated from Mesopotamia by the solemn calling of the GOD of glory, not about the choice of some habitation in any peculiar place, for instance in Mamre: furthermore, concerning that translation which was joined with the ἐπαγγελίᾳ, by which that land was first promised: and therefore it concerns that land which was promised to him as an inheritance, i.e., the land of Canaan: not the Hebronite field, some small part. Finally, concerning a translation made when the Patriarch did not yet have children. Add that it is quite inconvenient to restrict the word 'this land' to some small part of a field: which name frequently occurs in this discourse, but concerning a region, not indeed a small part of a region: and that the discourse is about the land which they inhabited: but did they all inhabit that part of the Hebronite field? Finally, that it concerns that land in which GOD did not give Abraham an inheritance, not even a footprint, which must certainly be understood of the land of Canaan, not of the Hebronite field.

SECTION IV. The epoch of the years from the Promise of Abraham concerning the blessed Seed until the leading out from Egypt, or the promulgation of the Law, of 430 years?

The beginning of the third Epoch was provided by the divine promise made to Abraham, when, having been called from Haran, he set out for the land of Canaan after the death of his father. Which the Lord then repeatedly confirmed to him, and sealed with the Sacrament of circumcision. Because He knew that he would diligently instill this ἐπαγγελίᾳ, in which the hinge of the salvation of the human race turns, into his descendants with true piety, Gen. XVIII, 19. Nor yet did He deign to make the same only to him, but also to Isaac and Jacob, and through Jacob the Patriarch and his son, and especially Joseph the Viceroy, who held the principate for 80 years, He also propagated it in Egypt, Psalm CV, verse 22. Nor is there any doubt that after the death of Joseph it was propagated until the leading out performed by Moses: through whom the people of the Lord were informed about the Messiah, both in Midian by divine revelation in the burning bush in a singular and mystical Θεοφανείᾳ, and by instruction concerning the sacrifices to be offered to GOD, and then after the departure in the desert through the promulgation of divine ceremonial as well as moral laws: and thus the ἡ παρακαταθήκη entrusted to the holy Patriarchs and the people of the Lord concerning the blessed seed, the savior of the world, was preserved among the faithful

For Levi, the paternal great-grandfather of Moses, survived for 16 years after the death of Joseph, having died when he was 137 years old, Exod. VI, v. 16. Kohath, however, the grandfather of the same, lived for 130 years, and the life of his son, the father of Moses, Amram, was extended to the age of his grandfather, likewise to 137 years, so that he finished it finally a little before the leading out of the Israelites from Egypt, performed by his son Moses. Their piety does not permit us to doubt that the saving doctrine was propagated by them: which must likewise be judged concerning other faithful and religious people among the people of GOD. Moreover, this Epoch is distributed into the παροικίαν of the Patriarchs in Canaan, which was of 215 years until the descent into Egypt; and the παροικίαν of the Israelites in Egypt, which was likewise of as many years until the Exodus: whence the whole time of the παροικίας of the Hebrews from the calling of Abraham is 430. years until the leading out from Egypt, which space is defined in Exod. XII, verse 40, or as the Apostle loves to speak, from the ἐπαγγελίᾳ made to Abraham until the law was promulgated, Galat. III, 17, who likewise designated 430 years.

EPOCH FROM THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM TO THE LAW.

From the promise under Abraham's departure into the land of Canaan until the birth of Isaac 25 years. From the birth of Isaac until the birth of Jacob 60. From the birth of Jacob until his descent into Egypt 130. Thence until the death of Joseph 71. Thence until the birth of Moses 64. Thence until the exodus of the Israelites 80. Total, 430 years.

Others calculate the reckoning thus:

Abraham at 100 years of age begat Isaac after the calling (Gen. 21, 5.) 25 years. When Jacob was born, Isaac was 60 years old. Jacob, when Joseph was born to him, was 91 years old. Joseph lived 110 years. From the death of Joseph until the birth of Moses 64 years. Moses spoke to Pharaoh and led out the people (Exod. VII, 7.) in the 80th year of his age. Thus again the total of 430 is completed.

To which if you add the years elapsed from the flood to the promise of Abraham 427, you will have from the flood to the exodus 857; moreover, with the 1656 ante-diluvian years added, there will result from the creation of the world to the exodus of the Israelites 2513 years.

QUESTION I.

What is the terminus a quo of the 430 years of the sojourning of the Hebrews, Exod. XII. verse 40, Gal. III. verse 17.

The terminus à quo is the 75th year of Abraham, which, from what has been said in the preceding section, is manifest to have been the year of Terah’s death: for the calling and migration of Abraham are connected immediately with the death of Terah, both by Moses and by St. Stephen, so that unless one wishes to do violence to the Mosaic Scripture and to the most clear words of the Proto-Martyr, Acts VII, verse 4, it cannot be a matter of doubt that Abraham was translated into the land of Canaan after the death of Terah, in the seventy-fifth year of his age, and from that terminus that epocha of the migration must be begun: because from the time when, having left Haran, he set out into Canaan, he began to live as a foreigner in a land not his own, which GOD was promising to him and to his seed. For in those words of Exod. XII. v. 40, "Now the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years," the sojourning of the children of Israel is to be taken not exclusively, but inclusively, so that, namely, the years of the sojourning of the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are included, both because of that very close bond of relationship which exists between ancestors and descendants, and because of the divine promise, in which Abraham and his descendants are likewise joined: "To thee will I give this land, and to thy seed," Gen. XIII. verse 15, even though it was given not to Abraham, but only to his seed. As, therefore, the possession of the descendants is attributed to the Fathers, so also the sojourning of the fathers is attributed to the descendants: by which arrangement the Israelites also make the passage through the Red Sea common to themselves with their fathers, Psalm LXVI. verse 6; see similar passages Deut. XXVI. verse 9, Jud. XII. verse 12, 1 Sam. XII. verse 11, Hos. XII. verse 4, Amos V. verse 2, Acts VII. verse 42. It is to be observed, moreover, that in that Mosaic passage Exod. XII. verse 40, it is not said that the Israelites remained in Egypt for 430 years, but the time of the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt for a very long time in Egypt, is defined by the Epoch of 430 years. For the word מוֹשָׁב, when related to foreigners and strangers, denotes a sojourning, and the word תּוֹשָׁב denotes a foreigner, Gen. XXIII. verse 4; as also the Chaldean word תּותָב, Gen. XXI. verse 34, chap. XXIII. verse 4. But Egypt is mentioned specifically because the sojourning of the fathers in Canaan was of few men, and was interrupted several times, and caught the eyes of men less, and was less illustrious. Psalm CV, 12, 13.

Others say that the dwelling in Egypt is designated from the time of Abraham's first journey into Egypt: for they mean that Moses does not intend to signify a continuous dwelling, but to comprehend the whole time during which Egypt was inhabited, which from this point until the exodus contains 430 years. Thus Gerhardus Mercator in Chronol., but the matter comes back to the same thing: because he established that Abraham both departed from Haran and entered Egypt in the same year, compelled by famine: which is also the opinion of the Hebrews in Seder Olam Rabba c. 1.

That the sojourning of Abraham and other Patriarchs, dwelling in the land of Canaan, is certainly comprehended, those words of the Apostle in Heb. XI, 9 teach not obscurely: "By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise." Nor do the Hebrews doubt that the sojourning of the Patriarchs is comprehended by Moses at the same time: whom R. Menasse Ben-Israel praised in Concil. Gen. q. XLI. Nor is there any reason why we should be moved by the words, "The dwelling of the children of Israel": because, as R. Nathan in Bereshith Rabba and R. Mose Albelda in the book Resit Dan rightly understood these, the Patriarchs also had that name of Israel. Wherefore, in order to express the sense, the LXX Interpreters rendered it thus. ἡ δὲ παρώκησις (thus the most ancient Alexandrian codex of Armachanus reads: the Roman has ἡ κατοίκησις) τῶν ὑἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἧν παρώκησαν ἐν γῇ Ἀιγύπτω καὶ ἐν γῇ Χαναὰν ἀυτοὶ, κὴ οἱ πατέρες ἀυτῶν, ἔτη τετρακόσια τριάκοντα. The sojourning of the children of Israel, who sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, 430 years. The words ἀυτοὶ and οἱ πατέρες ἀυτῶν are indeed missing through the fault of a copyist in the Roman Codex, but they are found in the Alexandrian, Complutensian, Aldine, and all others not derived from the Roman, as in Eusebius in his Chronicon, Quintus Julius Hilarion in his booklet on the duration of the world, Augustine in quæst. XLVII in Exod., as also in the Samaritan Codex, translated by Dositheus from the Greek edition.

To this passage of Exod. XII. must be added the similar one in Gen. XV. verse 13, namely, the oracle revealed to Abraham: "Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years. And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance. And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age. But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again." For in this oracle there is mention both of four hundred years and of the fourth generation: and the terminus a quo of the beginning of the years of the sojourning of Abraham's seed is established. Where the Hebrews rightly observe three states described in the oracle: the first of sojourning; "thy seed shall be a stranger": the second of servitude; "and they shall make them serve": the third of affliction; "and they shall afflict them." But that epoch of 400 years does not apply to any one of those states separately and distinctly; but to those three states jointly, because those three events were to happen and be fulfilled within the space of 400 years, so that the sense is: Your seed, before it comes to possess the land of Canaan, promised to you and to it, will spend 400 years, in which space of time it will both sojourn in a foreign land, and for some time also be afflicted with harsh servitude. Concerning which R. Menasse Ben-Israel q. XLI. in Genes. says the state of sojourning begins from the Patriarchs, who always sojourned in foreign lands, according to that of the Psalmist: and they passed from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people, Psalm CV. verse 13. Jacob said he had sojourned in the land of the sojournings of his father Isaac. Genes. XXXVII, 1. and before Pharaoh chap. XLVII. verse 9. his days were spent among sojournings. The Israelites endured servitude in Egypt after the death of the XII Patriarchs, as the Holy Scripture says: And there arose a new King over Egypt, who knew not Joseph, Exod. I. verse 9. The state of harsh affliction takes its beginning from that time when Pharaoh ordered the newly born infants of the Hebrews to be drowned in the river. Therefore, as to the words בארץ לא להם in a land not theirs, the Vulgate and the Greeks correctly rendered them as to the sense ἐν γῆ οὐκ ἰδίᾳ, St. Stephen ἐν γῆ ἀλλοτρίᾳ in a foreign land, by which not only Egypt, but also the land of Canaan is to be understood, because the seed of Abraham was a sojourner in this also, as in a foreign land. Therefore Eusebius notably observes that he did not say, in Egypt, but in a foreign land shall the seed of Abraham be a sojourner. But the land of Canaan, which Isaac the seed of Abraham inhabited, had been foreign. Which the Apostle also clearly indicates Heb. XI. verse 9. πίςει παρῴκησεν εἰς τὴν γῆν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ὡς ἀλλοτρίαν, by faith he (Abraham) sojourned in the land of promise AS IN A FOREIGN LAND, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob.

But if it be objected that there not 430, as in Exodus, but only 400 years are defined for the sojourning, there is no reason why we should say with the Jews, and especially R. Moses and Isaac Abarbenel, as also R. Jehezquiel, that the decree of God was only for a sojourning of 400 years; but that it was extended by 30 years because of the sins of the Israelites: or why we should establish with R. Levi Ben Gersom that the time of sojourning was contracted by 30 years: A truer answer is at hand: this oracle is full and round that the number was employed, not strictly completed: as Augustine warned in book XVI of The City of God, ch. 24. Four hundred years are indeed spoken of because of the fullness of the number, although it was somewhat more. And therefore, even if regard were had to the whole time of the pilgrimage, which is designated in Exodus XII, it will be possible to say 30 years because of the roundness of the number, or because he wished to count only the centuries and generations of the Holy Scriptures, to be omitted. This is the response of Procopius of Gaza to Genesis XV. This passage does not conflict with that which we have in the book of Exodus, where it is said that after 430 years the Hebrew people had gone out of Egypt. For it is not said in this place that immediately, upon the 400 years having elapsed and been completed, the Jews were to go out of Egypt, by which words the remaining 30 years can also be included. But since it concerns the SEED of Abraham, 'your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own,' the calculation should rather be begun from the year of the birth of Isaac, from which 425 years are counted to the exodus from Egypt. By which arrangement only 5 years are missing in this rounding of the number: concerning which Augustine is again to be heard

Question XLVII on Exodus. Because it is written, 'in Isaac shall your seed be called,' from the year of the birth of Isaac until the year of the exodus from Egypt, 405 years are counted. When therefore you have subtracted from 430 the 25 which are from the promise (made to Abraham when he was coming into Canaan) until Isaac was born, it is not surprising if Scripture wished to call 405 years the solid sum of 400; which is accustomed to name times in such a way that what exceeds or falls short of the sum of the number of the journey is not counted.

Nor does the reasoning escape those who take the number as precise, as they begin it from the weaned Isaac and from the brother Ishmael mocked, when the son of the handmaid was cast out, and Isaac was declared the son of the free woman of the promise, which they say happened when Isaac was five years old. Concerning which Bede in chapter VII of Acts: It can also be understood thus, that from the fifth year of Isaac, in which he began to be afflicted by the son of the handmaid, the labor of four hundred years is confirmed. And long before him Jerome, from the very tradition of the Hebrews, in Hebrew Traditions on Genesis: Among the Hebrews there is a varied opinion: some asserting that the time of weaning was set at the fifth year, others claiming the twelfth year. We therefore, in order to choose the shorter age, have calculated after eighteen years that Ishmael was cast out with his mother. For then at last, as Ussher rightly says, when Ishmael was cast out and Isaac alone remained in the family of Abraham, and it had been announced to him by GOD, in

'In Isaac shall your seed be called,' Genesis XXI, 12, it was brought about that it was understood that the meaning of that oracle, 'Your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall subject them to servitude and afflict them for 400 years,' looked solely to Isaac and his progeny, and by no means at all to Ishmael and his descendants. The same was also observed by Menasseh ben Israel from the Rabbis, q. XLI on Genesis. It is to be noted that the seed of Abraham begins from Isaac. For the words of Holy Scripture are: 'because in Isaac shall your seed be called.' To which passage the wise men say, in Isaac, but not in all his lineage, for Esau is excluded. And a little later: That these years were fulfilled at the time when the Israelites departed from Egypt is thus proven: Isaac at sixty years of age begat Jacob, who at the age of 130 descended into Egypt. We have therefore 190; there remain two hundred and ten to complete the number of four hundred: these are the years they remained in Egypt. They apply to the same those words of Jacob, when, ordering his sons to procure provisions in Egypt, he says רדו שמה (descend there), because the word רדו in Hebrew number makes 210. So that the Patriarch seems to have predicted to them the space of time during which his descendants were to be in Egyptian servitude. Therefore, if we begin to count those four hundred years from the birth of Isaac, the number will agree. In this, however, the Rabbis are mistaken, that from the descent of Jacob to the exodus they count only 210 years, when 215 years should be counted. Ludovicus Capellus says that Abram received the call in Ur of the Chaldeans when he was 70 years old, but that he began his pilgrimage from Haran when his father was dead, when he was 75 years old, and thus he thinks those 400 years should be counted from the call. See his Chronology, Vol. I of the English Polyglot Works, p. 4.

Third, a notable passage for the beginning of this epoch is the Apostolic one, Gal. III, 17. "Now this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of GOD, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect": for there is no doubt concerning this, that those 430 years, which Moses designated in Exod. XII, 40, are to be held as the same epoch which the Apostle defines here. And the Pauline passage is clear, even apart from that parallelism, in favor of our opinion, that from the promise of Abraham made at his calling in Haran, Gen. XII, verse 3, "in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed," until the Exodus, 430 years flowed; from which calling of his, the comparison and parallelism of the Mosaic passage in Exodus with the Apostolic one clearly teaches that the years of sojourning are to be begun.

Therefore, the opinions of others cannot stand in any way, who begin those years either from the birth of Isaac, or from Abraham's hundredth year, because the promise had already been made 25 years earlier, or who start the same epoch from the selling of Joseph into Egypt, or who, with Thaddaeus, Tirinus, and Gilbert Genebrard, fix its beginning at the descent of Jacob into Egypt; because the Apostle Paul wishes them to be begun from the promise made to Abraham, which GOD confirmed by a covenant, inasmuch as it was by no means made void by the νομοθεσία (legislation) 430 years later. Nor does the opinion of those deserve support by any other reasoning, who initiate the epoch from the departure of Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans, unless insofar as it is assumed that in the same year the departure from Ur of the Chaldeans into Haran, and further from Haran into the land of Canaan, took place. For the fact that some, with the Rabbis, affirm that Abraham was called at seventy years of age from Ur of the Chaldeans and stayed in Haran for five years, rests on no foundation: nor are those things solid which Petavius in Doctrina Temporum, book IX, ch. 18, Harvillaeus and Bonfrerius on Gen. ch. XV, 13, or Thomas Pius produced for that opinion, that the beginning of the sojourning of Abraham and his descendants or of the 430-year epoch is to be taken from the departure from Ur of the Chaldeans, which preceded the removal from Haran by five years: which Ussher solidly discussed in Chronologia Sacra, p. 141 et seqq.

And finally, the new opinion of Pareus, proposed in his oration on the promotion of D. Klengler, is not to be admitted, which constitutes the term from which this epoch is the confirmation of the covenant divinely made to Abraham, which he judges to have occurred ten years after Abraham's exit from Haran: because the promise to Abraham was not first made then. But when Paul teaches that the law is later than the promise made to Abraham, he certainly does not look to later promises repeated to Abraham, but to that one which was the first of all: otherwise it would be doubtful which promise was being looked to: and the Apostle could have seemed to have detracted from the antiquity of the Abrahamic promise.

Nor is it necessary that by the διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τ῵ Θε῵ εἰς Χριστὸν (covenant confirmed before by God in Christ) anything else be understood than the ἐπαγγελίαν (promise), which by some are not inappropriately taken as synonyms, as if they were one and the same thing, so that the Apostle names the ἐπαγγελίαν (promise) by itself in respect of the promise, but the κύρωσιν (confirmation) of the διαθήκης (covenant) in respect of the thing, or of Christ included in the promise. Then, if it should please one to distinguish those things also, the Apostle does not fix the epoch in the κύρωσιν (confirmation), but in the ἐπαγγελίᾳ (promise); because, namely, the same, being 430 years prior to the law, has not been made void by it: because he says that the law does not make void τὴν διαθήκην (the covenant), εἰς τὸ καταργῆσαι τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν (so as to make the promise of none effect). He therefore looks primarily to the ἐπαγγελίαν (promise), and contends with the law concerning it, not the διαθήκην (covenant), which he only brings in for the sake of confirming the ἐπαγγελίας (promise), as is also evident from the following verses, where there is only a contention of the law and the promise, but not a contention of the law and the covenant. Moreover, the Apostle undoubtedly handed down its antiquity before the law, because he himself brought it here into contention with the law: Add that nothing is certain from Moses concerning a covenant ten years after the promise made to Abraham. A covenant sanctioned with Abraham is indeed reported in Gen. XV; but just as it is precariously assumed that the Apostle looked to that here, so it is rashly feigned that it was ten years after the promise. For Moses nowhere taught that; indeed, the contrary is gathered not obscurely from the fact that Abraham entered in to Hagar the handmaid ten years after his departure from Haran, Gen. XVI, 3. For it is not likely that in the very same year in which he had heard from the mouth of the Lord, 'He that shall come forth out of thy bowels, him shalt thou have as thine heir,' C. XV, 4, he had lain with Hagar, not having awaited the blessing and fulfillment of the divine promise through his wife Sarah: whom, even if he had already known her to be barren, he could nevertheless believe, by virtue of the promise made to him, that GOD could easily remove τὴν νέκρωσιν τῆς μήτρας (the deadness of the womb), as the Apostle speaks in Rom. IV, 19, and render the same fruitful. Piety certainly commanded to wait some time; whether the divine power would correct Sarah's barrenness or not. Nor could Pareus bring forward any patron for his opinion; for although he praises R. Solomon as a witness from Paul Fagius, it is the opinion not only of him, but of almost all the Hebrews, that the 430 years took their beginning from the time when God spoke to Abraham among the divided victims; but they do not wish that to have happened to him ten years after his entry into Canaan; but five years before his departure from Haran, when the Patriarch was seventy years old, which appears from the Chaldaic Paraphrase of Jonathan on Exod. XII, 40, Seder Olam Rabba c. 1, and the beginning of the history of the Cabala of R. Abraham Levita compared among themselves. Wherefore one must wonder at Pareus, that with no foundation, with no testimony of antiquity, he fixes the epoch at a time about which nothing can be determined from Holy Scripture: since he himself acknowledges that Chronologers, with ALMOST ONE CONSENT, place the beginning of the epoch at the departure of Abraham from Haran, when he was 75 years old. George Syncellus testified to this remarkable consensus in his Chronicle, p. 117. The calculation of the 430 years of the pilgrimage of Israel in the land of Canaan and in Egypt, according to the prediction of GOD made to Abraham, by the common suffrage of both interpreters and historians, takes its beginning from the 75th year of Abraham. Joseph Scaliger observes in Canon. Isagog. lib. III, p. 2, c. 2, that the most ancient Jews, both before and after Christ, likewise the Apostle Paul to the Galatians, Josephus, and ALL CHRISTIAN INTERPRETERS WITH ONE MOUTH begin those 430 years from the year of the promise (which is the seventy-fifth of Abraham), etc., and therefore to pronounce otherwise against so many opinions would be, as the lyric poet said, ὀμίσε χωρεῖν τ῵ χρόνῳ (to go against the time), to join battle with the reasons of time. Not to add that, by this compact, the divine word is exposed to insult, and is subjected to be vexed by the lust of furious, foolish, and most impotent interpreters.

QUESTION II.

How are the 430 years of the pilgrimage of Abraham and his descendants to be numbered?

This calculation is not difficult, as far as the former interval up to the descent of Jacob and his sons into Egypt. For from the departure of Abraham into the land of Canaan until the birth of Isaac, 25 years are counted. For he went there when he was 75 years old, but he was 100 years old when Isaac was born. Furthermore, from the birth of this one until Jacob was born, 60 years are designated, Gen. XXV, 26. But Jacob was 130 years old when he went down into Egypt,

Gen. 47:9. which years make two hundred and fifteen. Whence furthermore it remains that as many years remain until the exodus: provided that the whole time is of 430 years. Now these latter two hundred and fifteen years from the entry of Jacob into Egypt to the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt are to be computed thus: from the descent of Jacob into Egypt to the death of Joseph are 71 years: from thence until the birth of Moses 64, from thence until the exodus 80, which make 215. The former number is gathered thus: Joseph was 39 years old when Jacob descended into Egypt, but he died at 110 years of age. If you subtract those years from these, there will remain 71 years from the descent of Jacob to the death of Joseph. That Joseph was 39 years old at the arrival of his father is established thus: He was 30 years of age when he was appointed Viceroy in Egypt, Gen. 41:46. Now there had elapsed from that time not only seven years of plenty; but also two years of famine, when he summoned his father Jacob, Gen. 45:6, and thus nine years of Joseph's administration in Egypt. He was therefore 39 years of age at the arrival of his father. The third number of years from the birth of Moses until the exodus is designated in Exod. 7:7. If therefore those 71 years from the arrival of Jacob until the death of Joseph, and these 80 years are added, there result 151 years: if you subtract this sum from the total sum of years, namely from the arrival of Jacob into Egypt until the exodus, two hundred and fifteen years, there will remain 64 years from the death of Joseph until the birth of Moses.

And thus stands the demonstration of those years completed from the Scriptures: whereby the 430 years of the sojourn are distributed into two equal intervals of 215 years, as has been handed down by Eusebius and other Christian chronologists: Thus also Josephus proposed the same among the Jews; among foreigners before the times of Christ, Demetrius also handed it down, and from him Alexander Polyhistor. Josephus, book 1 of Antiquities, ch. 6, has it thus: They left Egypt in the month of Xanthicus, on the fifteenth day of the moon, 430 years after our forefather Abraham came into Canaan: but 215 years after the migration of Jacob into Egypt. Now Alexander Polyhistor from Demetrius in the book on the Jews in Eusebius, book 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, reports: From the time when Abraham was cast out from the nations, and came from Charan into Canaan, until the arrival of Jacob into Egypt, there were 215 years; then 17 years after the arrival of Jacob, Levi begat Caath, and this man, when he was 40 years old, begat Amram, and this man, when he was 78 years of age, begat Moses: in whose eightieth year the people were led out: Which years 17, 40, 78, and 80 joined together produce 215 years. Eusebius in his Chronicle has it thus: Joseph is leader in Egypt in the 30th year of his age, and of Jacob the Father 122, which principate he held for 80 years. After whose death the Hebrews served the Egyptians for 144 years. There were, therefore, 215 years which the Hebrews spent in Egypt, which are computed from the same time that Jacob with his sons descended into Egypt.

Those who contend that the stay of the Israelites in Egypt was not 215 years, but 225 with Pareus, 240 with Guilh. Langius, 430 with Genebrardus and Stapleton, or 431 with Tychonius, or who extend it beyond 400 years with Thaddaeus Danus and Nicolaus Abramus, rashly oppose themselves to this so evident truth. The common opinion of the Hebrews is closer to the truth of Scripture, by which they count 210 years: the closest is that of Joh. Benedictus and Laur. Codomannus, differing by only one year, who assign 216 years. But that so long a stay, as Genebrardus,

Stapleton, Tychonius, or even Thaddaeus Danus and Abramus have designated, can be attributed to the Israelites in Egypt, is openly shown not only by the divine testimony of the Apostle, who counted only 430 years from the promise made to Abraham up to the law, to which Josephus and other ancients agree entirely; but other chronological reasons, not a few, also confirm it: (1.) The years of the life of Caath, son of Levi, who descended into Egypt with his grandfather Jacob, Gen. 46:11, were 133; the years of his son Amram were 137, Exod. 6:18, 20. Whose son Moses's eightieth year was the year of the Exodus, which, collected into a sum, produce no more than 350 years; and from these must still be subtracted the years which Caath spent after Amram was born, and which Amram spent after Moses was born: as well as the years which Caath had when he descended into Egypt, so that the same years are not counted twice: (2.) The genealogy of Core, Dathan, and Abiram, who perished in the desert, Num. 16:1, 26:8, 9. For as far as concerns Core, he was the grandson of Caath through Jehezar, Num. 16:1, 1 Chron. 6:17, the brother of Amram, the parent of Moses, Exod. 6:18, 1 Chron. 6:2. But as for Dathan and Abiram, they were the sons of Eliah, whom Pallus, the son of Ruben, had already begotten in Egypt, Gen. 46:9, Num. 26:8. For this interposition of only one generation between those descending into Egypt and those seditious ones swallowed up in the desert clearly teaches that 430 years can by no means be attributed to the stay in Egypt. The minor objection of Thaddaeus, taken from the multiplication of the sons of Israel in Egypt, can make no one doubtful about the truth of that opinion, that the Israelites stayed in Egypt for only 215 years; if indeed only ten of Jacob's sons are assumed (omitting Levi and Joseph, and the grandsons who descended into Egypt with him) and their descendants in the following six thirty-year periods are placed as having begotten five males and as many females each, in the tenth year from the entry 50 males would have been begotten, in the 40th year 250, in the 70th year 1250 will have been born, in the 100th year 6250, in the 130th year 31250, in the 160th year 156250, in the 190th year 781250 males will be gathered as having been begotten, the youngest of whom would have been 25 and the oldest 34 years of age at the time of the exodus, namely in the 215th year. To whom if those older in age, not exceeding 64 years, are added, by joining the two final sums together, 937500 males will emerge, who according to those hypotheses could have been counted at the time of the exit, when nevertheless Moses counted only 603550 from the twentieth year of age, Exod. 12:37.

QUESTION III. Which year of the world is the year of the Exodus?

After we have examined the epochs separately, the year of the world at the time of the Exodus is not defined without difficulty, which is to say it was 2513. For thus the epochs are to be collected,

From the creation of the world to the flood 1656 years

From the flood to the beginning of the sojourn of the Hebrews begun by Abraham after the death of his father 427

Thence to the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt 430

Total 2513.

Joseph Scaliger, and those who follow him, establish the year of the Exodus as 2453. But because Scripture openly testifies that the sojourn of Abraham, who was 75 years old when he set out from Haran into the land of Canaan, happened only after the death of Terah, and not sixty years earlier, it is manifest that Scaliger is hallucinating, for he omitted those sixty years, concerning which the blessed Luther himself professed his ignorance, when he could reply nothing to the words of Stephen, Acts VII, 4: I, he says, do not yet have an answer to this question: and so with a due and humble confession of ignorance I conjecture thus, that GOD by His own certain counsel wished these years to be omitted in Abraham, so that from a certain calculation of the years of the world no one might presume to predict anything certain about the end of the world.

The reasons which they seek from certain characterisms and Jubilee and Sabbath years are more subtle than solid: and Petavius himself shows that those characterisms are of no moment in book IX of De doctrina temporum, chapters 23 and 25; nor does the most learned Ussher undeservedly pit Philip Lansberg against Scaliger here: for since he, likewise relying on his own characterisms, defined the year of the Exodus not as 2453, but as 2449 from the creation of the world: and from the fact that the day of the departure fell on the seventh day of the week, and the year of the departure itself was both Sabbath and Jubilee, he contends that this year of the world is to be recognized as the genuine and certain one, just as Scaliger, from the fact that the day of the departure from Egypt was the fifth day of the week, and that the year according to him was the forty-sixth Jubilee and likewise a Sabbath year, thinks this year of the world is the one completed. But concerning neither of those days of the week is there any account in the Scriptures: nor can it be demonstrated that there was any reckoning of Sabbatical years and the Jubilees arising from them before the entry of the Israelites into the promised land. For as to the proof which those who follow Scaliger seek from Exod. 16:1 et seqq., they assume precariously in the same that on the fifteenth day of the second month immediately both the murmuring occurred, and the promise of quails and manna was given, and thus at the beginning of the sixteenth day of the second month the quails were sent: since this is not clear from the text, the demonstration which they think can be established from it falls. Jac. Tirinus from Seder Olam c. 5 and Genebrard assigns the sixth day of the week to the Exodus. Ussher assigns the third day. What certainty is there, then, in this?

SECTION V. Concerning the Epoch of 480 years from the promulgated Law to the construction of Solomon's temple.

We proceed to the fourth Epoch, which the Holy Spirit has expressly defined as 480 years, 1 Kings 6:1, namely from the exodus to the beginning of Solomon's temple. The term from which is the leading out from Egypt, a figure of the redemption to come through Christ, and the promulgation of the law, of which Christ is the πλήρωμα, Rom. 10:4, as far as the moral law is concerned, which he had to fulfill for us: who is also the τὸ σῶμα of those things, of which the Ceremonial law exhibited the τύπον and εἰκόνα, Col. 2, Heb. 10.

The term to which is the Temple of Solomon, when it it was begun to be built: in which the ἐπαγγελία concerning Christ ought primarily to have been propagated, and which was a type of the temple of the body of Christ, John 2. But those years are to be collected from Moses, Joshua, also the book of Judges and the first of Samuel. By Moses the years of the wandering of the Israelites in the desert up to the leadership of Joshua and the entry into the land of Canaan are designated, Exod. 16, 35. Num. 14, 38. Add Josh. 5, 6. To which years are added seven for the κληροχίαν, or the division of the land, Josh. 14, 10. Num. 1, 1. ch. 9, 5. and from there to the death of Joshua ten years, which are to be collected by the subtraction of the other years, the designation of which from the sacred scriptures is by no means obscure, collected up to the fourth year of Solomon, thence from the exodus, from the total sum of 480 years designated by the Holy Spirit. From the death of Joshua to Eli 299 years are collected, although chronologists do not use the same method for collecting those years. For some count the times of the rule of the Judges; others, however, think that the times of the rest of the land designated by the Holy Spirit are to be counted. From Eli to Samuel 40 years are counted, and from there to David again 40, Acts 13, 21, and likewise from David to Solomon 40, 2 Sam. 5, 4, 1 Chron. last v. 27. For these, when reduced to a sum, with the addition of the 4 years of Solomon, make 480 years. Which sum, if it be added to the 2513 years from the creation of the world to the Exodus, we shall have the year of the world 2993. But if to these are added the 7 years of the construction of the Solomonic temple, 1 Kings 6, 38, there will be counted from the creation of the world to the built temple 3000 years.

would receive their iniquities, and that the same completion also implies this itself, Num. 32, 13. But those forty years of wandering were decreed not only as a punishment for the murmuring made after the return of the spies; but γενικῶς because of the fornications and iniquities of the people, which began immediately at the beginning of the leading into the desert through μοσχολατρείαν, and thus in the same place there is mention of iniquities generally, as also of fornications. Josephus also seems to have been of the same opinion, Antiquities book V, ch. 1, and thus also the Greek Roman and Aldine edition, Josh. 5, 6, reads 42 years. But with Augustine, question 6 on Joshua, these are to be corrected from the Hebrew text: therefore in the Complutensian edition those words were cut out, καὶ δύο: for it is too clear that the Israelites remained in the desert for only forty years.

EPOCH FROM THE EXODUS TO THE BEGUN CONSTRUCTION OF THE SOLOMONIC TEMPLE.

QUESTION II. How many years passed to the κληροχίαν from the exodus?

Caleb indicates this in Jos. XIV, 7. I was forty years old when Moses, the servant of the Lord, sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land. And Moses swore on that day, saying: The land which your foot has trodden shall be your possession: forty-five years are since the Lord spoke this word to Moses; when Israel was walking through the wilderness: today I am 85 years old, as strong as I was at the time when I was sent to explore. Since therefore he was 85 years old then, in the 45th year after the exploration of the land of Canaan, and he was 40 years old when he was sent from Kadesh-barnea for the exploration, which was done in the second year after the exodus from Egypt, or the 38th year before the distribution of the land, with 38 years subtracted from these 45 years, 7 years will remain, and thus in the seventh year from the entry into the land of Canaan, but in the forty-seventh year from the exodus from Egypt, the κληροχία, or distribution of the land, occurred. And thus in Seder Olam c. XI, the exploration of the land is said to have been done two years after the exodus from Egypt, and Caleb's 45 years are added to it, and thus 47 years are counted from the exodus to the partition of the land, and 7 years are attributed to the wars of Joshua up to the κληροχία: to which Josephus, book V, c. 1, attributes only 5; since he falsely, as was noted before, assigned 42 years of delay in the desert.

QUESTION I. How many years were spent in the desert?

That the Israelites wandered in the desert for 40 years is as clear from many places in Scripture as it is when it is clear at midday. Exod. 16, 35. Deut. 2, 7. c. 8, 2. c. 29, 5. Jos. 5, 6. Neh. 9, 21. Psal. 95, 10. Amos. 2, 10. c. 5, 26. Act. 7, 36. c. 13, 18. That only five days were lacking is manifest from a comparison of the exodus, which took place on the 15th day of the first month, and the crossing of the Jordan, which occurred on the tenth day of the same month, from Num. 33, 3. Joshua 4, 19. To these add the calculation of the years of the life of Moses and Aaron. For since at the time of the exodus Moses was 80 and Aaron 83 years old, Ex. 7, 7, and Aaron died in the fortieth year from the exodus, on the 1st day of the 5th month, being 123 years old, Num. 33, 38. 39. and Moses died in the same 40th year from the exodus on the 1st day of the 12th month, being 120 years old, Deut. 21, 2. c. 34, 7, what is more certain than that the delay in the desert must be concluded within a span of 40 years?

Mention of this distribution of the land made by lot is also held in Act. 13, 17. & 20. namely, that four hundred and fifty years after the election of the people of Israel from the birth of Isaac, in whom the election was made Gen. 21, 12., the partition of the land was made: He distributed their land to them by lot, as it were after 450 years: and after that he gave judges. Because from the birth of Isaac until the departure from Egypt 405 years flowed (inasmuch as he was born 25 years after the calling of Abraham from Charran, from which to the Exodus 430 years are numbered), but from the Exodus to the partition of the land 47 years flowed, or rather, if the calculation is entered more accurately, 46 years with 4 months, which if they are added to those 405, will produce 451 years and some months; which the Apostle said, ὡς, or as it were 450 years.

QUESTION III. How is the epoch from the κληροχία or partition of the land until the times of Eli to be defined?

However, Henry Wolphius, in book 1 of his Chronology, chapter 6, did not fear to oppose this so evident truth, adding to the two years after the exodus of the Israelites the 40 years in which they died in the desert, for the reason that in Num. 14, v. 33, 34, when they returned from Canaan after the 40th day of the scouts, it is decreed, according to the 40 days of exploration, that for forty years in the desert they... A twofold designation of this epoch is found: The one by the remaining years of Joshua and the Judges; the other, however, partly by the intervals of the rest of the land, and partly by the periods of the prefecture of the judges. As for the former method of calculation, no certainty is found among the authors following it, but they vary greatly: for some calculate the times of the servitude of the people separately, while others include the same in the times of the rule of the judges: and these in turn calculate differently, and differently, according to whether they include these or those years of servitude in the years of government, or judge them to be counted separately. Whence an almost infinite variety, so much so that not even that great number of 480 years, most explicitly expressed by the Holy Spirit in 1 Kings 6:1, is left beyond dispute and controversy, either among the ancients or among the moderns. For of those, Josephus in book 8 of the Antiquities, chapter 2, as D. Behmius reports his opinion, counted not 480 but 610 years from the exodus to the beginning of Solomon's Temple, although from the collection of individual numbers which Josephus reviewed, B. Behmius makes a sum of 595 years, and with the addition of the years of Thola and Abdon omitted by Josephus, he makes 627 years: Clement of Alexandria indeed in book 1 of the Stromata assigns 566, Nicephorus and other Eastern Greeks assign 633 years to that epoch up to the beginning of the Temple. Sabellicus and Melchior Canus attribute 592 years to the same, Laurentius Codomannus 598 years: Nicol. Raimarus 580, Woltherus 620. Concerning whom B. Behmius may be consulted in book 1 of the Chronological Manual, Title III, chapter 6. Nicol. Serarius assigns 680 years.

in 1 Kings 6. Proposition 2. The reason for such an excess of the number over that which the Holy Spirit designated, and for that variety, is the separation of the years of the government of Joshua and of the servitude, one way or another, from the years of the government of the Judges: since the years of servitude counted separately and added to the years of government (besides the years of Joshua) make 573. Nor indeed do those who retain that great number of 480 years agree among themselves; since Eusebius attributes 27 years to the leadership of Joshua and omits the decade of Eglon the Judge: Funccius, with the rule of Joshua passed, begins from the death of Moses the 40 years of which Judges 6:1 speaks, and then counts separately the 18 years of the Ammonite servitude: Tremellius, however, with those 18 years of Ammonite servitude excluded, assigns as many to the leadership of Joshua.

Finally, there is no solid consensus here even among the Scaligerians themselves; and B. Behmius acknowledges that it is difficult to choose the true opinion, and argues against the book of Judges, because all things seem to be counted intricately in it: therefore he does not dare to promise a certain calculation, but only one tolerable to a fair mind: which, however, he builds upon certain hypotheses, and in these he also assumes it is uncertain whether the judges who are counted in the book of Judges judged Israel successively, one after another, and that it could have happened that two reigned at the same time, and thus from that hypothesis he conjectures that the years of the judgeship of Samson and Eli are to be joined, which he also includes in the 40 years of Philistine servitude; just as he also wishes the six years of Jephthah to be included under the 18 years of Ammonite servitude. Which will be said by others to be assumed precariously: for most count the 20 years of Samson separately from the 40 years of Eli: nor do they concede that Samson presided at the same time as Eli. Whom Phil. Lansbergius also follows, placing the years of the Ammonite servitude, which Funccius and Behmius counted separately, before, or rather including them in the years of government.

We, having admitted this method of calculating, judge the calculation of Lansbergius to be the most convenient: Othniel (Judges 3:11) presided for 40 years, Ehud (chapter 3:30) for 80 years (a few months are to be attributed to Shamgar, if indeed he presided over the whole people, as no years are counted for him, see chapter 3:31), Barak or Deborah (chapter 5:31) presided for 40 years, Gideon (chapter 8:28) for 40 years, Abimelech (chapter 9:22) for 3 years.

Thola (chapter 10:2) for 23 years.

Jair (chapter 10:3) for 22 years.

Jephthah (ch. 12, 7.) - - 6

Ibzan (ch. 12, 9.) - - 7

Elon (ch. 12, 11.) - - 10

Abdon (ch. 12, 14.) - - 8

Samson (ch. 15, 20.) - - 20

Total, 299 years.

The rule of the Judges, therefore, from the death of Joshua according to this calculation was 299 years: to which if the 40 years of Eli and the 40 until the death of Saul are added, as well as likewise 40 until the death of David, and the three full years passed from the death of David until the beginning of Solomon's Temple, which was begun in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, the sum will come to 422; but with the 40 years added that passed from the exodus to the death of Moses, 462 years emerge. There are lacking, therefore, to the full sum of 479 completed years from the exodus until the fourth year of Solomon's reign and the beginning of the Temple, 17 years, which consequently must be attributed to the rule of Joshua.

And thus the prior method of calculation holds, having retained that hypothesis which Eusebius followed, and almost all Christian interpreters, Ussher not denying it, although he attributes it to Jewish authors, who, having judged that the people were never without a judge, attributed the years of the land's rest to the judge named therein: concerning which, however, Canus, Codomannus, Petavius, Possinus, and Nicol. note that inconvenience. Abramus, Ussher, that the years of the interregnums are reduced and contracted into those [years] during which the land is said to have rested from battles under the judges: since in those interregnums there was either perpetual war for the Jews against enemies, or miserable servitude without a judge, affairs were afflicted, everything was in turmoil, no rest: to extricate himself from which inconveniences Ussher judged that another method of calculation must be entered upon, which was not disapproved of by us in the Prolegomena to the book of Judges: noting a twofold method of calculation in the history of the Judges, which he elicited from a more accurate observation of the phrasing of the Holy Spirit: because, namely, the Holy Spirit counts the years differently in the first part until Gideon, and differently in the latter, since in the former it deals with the times of the land's rest, but here it expressly designates the years of the reign.

Therefore, as regards those intervals of the land's rest, the Holy Spirit seems to have designated that epoch not obscurely when in Josh. XI, v. 23 He says: And the land rested from war; and again ch. XIV, 15: And the land ceased from war, especially if the intervals of rest are compared, which, having raised up deliverers, they subsequently obtained now from these, now from other enemies, noted in the book of Judges: concerning which one may read generally in Jud. II, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, but specifically in the subsequent history.

For in chapter III, 11, after Israel was liberated from eight years of servitude under Cushan, King of Mesopotamia, by Othniel, the land is said to have rested for 40 years, but it is not expressed how many years Othniel presided: nor is it taught whether the liberation of Israel happened immediately from the beginning of his prefecture, or not? Since, therefore, this rest of the land is the next one from that which was obtained in the time of Joshua, Jos. 11, 23, cap. 14, 15, Ussher thinks it is designated here that 40 years elapsed from that time of Joshua's rest to the rest under Othniel: so that it is taught, not that the Israelites had peace for so many years after Cushan, King of Mesopotamia, was defeated by Othniel; but that the land began to rest in the fortieth year, after rest had been established in it by Joshua. He interprets the word ותשקט, and it rested, as began to rest, just as וילד in Gen. 5:32, ch. 11:26, according to him, is began to beget, and ויבן in 1 Kings 6:1, began to build; and furthermore, where in Scripture any King is said to have been of so many years במלכו, it is signified when he began to reign to rest in the fortieth year, that is, in the fortieth year from some preceding Epoch, because the Hebrews use cardinal numbers from ten onwards for ordinals. But he maintains that no more certain Epoch can be found from which the calculation of the first rest of the land (under Othniel) in the book of Judges may be derived than that most celebrated rest of the land which the Holy Spirit records that Joshua established (after the kings of Canaan, who had risen up against the Israelites with joined forces and all their troops, were defeated) and which was made prior to the partition of the land, Josh. 11:13 and 14:15. Therefore, the Mesopotamians having been overcome (who, after those foreigners, were the first to wage war against the whole Israelite land), rest began to be restored (forty years after the beginning of that former one): with Othniel subsequently victorious, administering the Republic until his death, and striving to keep the people in the worship of the true GOD, which is understood to have been the chief work of these Judges from ch. 2:17, 18, 19 (where we said the summary of this part of the History had been proposed). The blessed Behmius does not reject this ordinal sense in Manud. Chronol. p. 49. The Hebrew words שמנים and ארבעים are not always taken as adjectives, but sometimes as numerals of order, Num. 30:38, 1 Kings 6:1, and in this sense these words must be taken in the places alleged above: The land rested in the year ארבעים, that is, the fortieth, Jud. 3:11, ch. 5:31, ch. 8:28. The land rested in the year שמנים, ch. 3:30, that is, the eightieth, so that not the continuation of the whole time, but the term to which this formula of speaking points us, is indicated. Thus, therefore, within that space of 40 years, not only those eight years during which the Israelites served Chushan are to be included; but also the years during which Joshua survived after the partition of the land, and during which the Elders prolonged their days after Joshua, Josh. 23:31, that is, were survivors to him, as also the years of anarchy, concerning which in the first five chapters of Judges.

Therefore, a second Epoch is had in Jud. 3:3, where the words are similarly to be taken in an ordinal sense, not a cardinal one: and the land rested in the eightieth year; namely, from the previously designated rest of the land. For it is not taught that Ehud presided for so many years, nor is such a long reign probable in those times, but that it refers to Eglon, whom the Israelites served for 18 years, and that this happened in the eightieth year after the former peace restored to it by Othniel. For it is not probable that the land was quiet for 80 whole years and entirely free from battles: because they are said to have quickly forsaken the way in which their fathers had walked, and the Israelites were delivered into the hands of spoilers, in the general description of the history of the servitude and liberation of the people, Jud. 2:17.

The third special Epoch, Jud. 5:41, is of 40 years. And the land rested 40 years, namely, from the prior rest under Ehud, or in the fortieth year after the same was restored by Ehud: because, with the army of Jabin, king of Canaan, by whom the Israelites had been vexed for 20 years, having been routed, the land began to rest anew, with Deborah and Barak helping.

The fourth is likewise of 40 years, Jud. 8:28. And the land rested in the days of Gideon 40 years, or in the fortieth year after the rest of the land was restored by Deborah. For it is not said that Gideon reigned for 40 years: but that in the days of Gideon the rest of the land was restored; after the Israelites had served the Midianites for seven years, ch. 6:1.

These, therefore, are the epochs of the intervals of rest, which, if the years are added together from the rest under Joshua, make 200 years.

I. From the rest under Joshua to the rest begun under Othniel, years - - - - 40 (namely, 10 years to the death of Joshua, 8 under the government of the Elders, then some years under the ἀναρχίᾳ, so that in the thirty-third year from the rest under Joshua the oppression of Cushan began, and lasted for eight years, until the liberation and rest restored by Othniel.)

II. From the rest under Othniel until the rest restored by Ehud, there passed years - - 80 (namely, 62 years passed to the Moabite oppression, and the same had lasted for 18 years, until they were liberated by Ehud.)

III. From the rest of the land under Ehud until the liberation and rest restored by Deborah, years - - - - - 40 (Which are calculated thus: 20 years had passed from the restoration of peace under Ehud when the Israelites were infested and oppressed by King Jabin: which oppression likewise lasted for 20 years.)

IV. From the peace restored by Deborah until the liberation of Gideon, and the peace restored by him, years - - - - 40 (Namely, after the liberation of Deborah there was peace for 33 years: but then began the pressure of the Midianites, which lasted for seven years.)

Sum of the years from the rest under Joshua to the peace restored by Gideon, years - 200. But from the death of Joshua - - - 190

Furthermore, as to the remaining calculation in the book of Judges, since it is so expressly set forth according to the years of government that no one is permitted to doubt it, and to Abimelech were attributed (Jud. 9:22) 3 years, to Tola (Jud. 10:2) 23 years, to Jair (c. 10:3) 22 years (in which are included the 18 years of the oppression of the Philistines and Ammonites, Jud. 8:8), to Jephthah (c. 12:7) 6 years, to Ibzan (c. 12:10) 7 years, to Elon (c. 12:11) 10 years, to Abdon (c. 12:14) 8 years, to Samson (c. 15:20) 20 years. Who judged Israel in the days of the Philistines, or of their oppression (which lasted for 40 years, c. 13:1). Joined together they make 99 years; and I have added them to the 190 years from the death of Joshua to the peace or rest under Gideon, producing 289 years: to which if the 10 years of rest from the liberation by Gideon to the beginning of the government of Abimelech are added, they become 299 years, and the sum of the years from the death of Joshua to the passing of Samson agrees exactly.

From the death of Joshua to the peace restored by Gideon, years - - - - - 190. From the rest restored by Gideon to the beginning of the reign of Abimelech, son of Gideon, years - - 10. Abimelech's years - - - - 3. Tola's years - - - - - 23. Jair's years - - - - - 22. Jephthah's years - - - - - 6. Ibzan's years - - - - - 7. Elon's years - - - - - 10. Abdon's years - - - - - 8. Samson's years - - - - - 20. Sum, 299 years.

Concerning this method of calculating, we have spoken more fully in the preface to the book of Judges. It is clear, however, that by both methods from the death of Joshua until the times of Eli 299 years have elapsed.

QUESTION IV.

How many years elapsed from Eli until the beginning of Solomon's Temple, and how is the total sum from the Exodus to the beginning of the Temple to be collected?

Concerning these years there is no difficulty. For the years of the judgeship of Eli are designated in 1 Sam. IV, 18 as forty: and furthermore the years of the rule of Samuel and Saul are likewise expressly defined as 40, Acts XIII, 21. That the years of the Davidic reign were likewise 40 is beyond doubt, 1 Kings II, 11. Which joined together make 120 years, to which are finally added the 4 of Solomon, the sum will be 124 years. Therefore, from the death of Joshua until the beginning of the temple of Solomon, 423 years are counted. To which if 47 years are added from the departure of the people until the death of Joshua, 480 result.

From the departure of the people to the leadership of Joshua, 40 years

The leadership of Joshua, 17 years

From the death of Joshua until Eli, 299 years

From Eli until the beginning of the Temple, 124 years

Sum of the years 480.

QUESTION V.

For how many years did Joshua preside?

The time of Joshua's leadership is not expressly stated in the Holy Scriptures; but since the remaining numbers from the exodus to the leadership of 40 years, and from the death of Joshua to Eli 299, thence to the beginning of the temple 124, are established from the Scriptures, and the total sum of years from the exodus to the building of the Temple is expressly defined, and 480 years are counted from that point; the time of Joshua's leadership, or from the death of Moses to the passing of Joshua, cannot be hidden: namely, by adding those three partial numbers, which make 463, and subtracting that sum from the total number of 480 years. For the 17 years that remain are the years of Joshua's leadership.

The reason, however, that Josephus attributes 25 years to him seems to be that he counted the 8 years of the rule of the Elders who survived Joshua: which others count distinctly, or rather consider to be included in the 40 years of Othniel. Salianus, Torniellus, and others teach at length that Joshua served for seventeen years, neither more nor fewer, in his leadership: which is also the opinion of Bede, Adrichomius, Arias Montanus, Tirinus, Johannes Lucidus, Hugh Broughton, and most others. They err in excess who, with Massaeus, attribute 26 years to him, or 27 with Eusebius; but they err in defect who, with Cajetan, assign only a decade to his leadership.

QUESTION VI.

Should the 20 years of Samson be included in the 40 years of Eli's leadership, but the 20 years of Samuel be counted separately, so that 40 full years are left for the reign of Saul?

For the sum of the years of the great number from the exodus to the beginning of the temple, it truly makes no difference whether the years of Samson are included in the years of Eli, and the years of Samuel are counted separately, and are not considered to be included in those 40 years which seem to be assigned to the reign of Saul: Acts 13:21; or whether 20 years are left separately for the judgeship of Samson, or whether it is attributed that Eli presided for forty years after the death of Samson: but that the years of Samuel and Saul combined were only 40. For there are not lacking those who think that the 20 years of Samson should be included in the 40 years of Eli: thus assert Canus and Ussher; who maintain that Samson was raised up as a deliverer under the judgeship of Eli: and that he succeeded Abdon immediately, and that in his time the Israelites were delivered into the hands of the Philistines for 40 years, as is stated in the Annals of the Old Testament, p. 46. For he thinks these 40 years of oppression were terminated seven months after the death of Eli, and thus were begun as many months after the beginning of his leadership. But in order that the sum of the years may be consistent, he attributes 21 years to Samuel separately, and 40 to Saul. But because Samson is numbered among the other judges, and is said to have judged Israel, or the Israelite people, just as the other judges did, and that twice, Jud. XV, 20, c. XVI, 31, the common opinion prevails that Samson succeeded Abdon in that office, as the historical order has it, rather than that he was raised up only under the judgeship of Eli as a defender of the people. Masius, however, includes the 40 years of the servitude of the Philistines within the years of Samson and of certain preceding judges, as also of Eli himself.

Nor indeed is it fitting that 40 years be attributed to Saul: because David was anointed King by Samuel as soon as Saul was rejected, 1 Sam. 15:25, 28, c. 16:13, which happened according to the passive opinion in the second year of Saul's reign: if therefore David was anointed 38 years before the death of Saul, he would certainly have been anointed King a full 8 years before he was born: because at the death of Saul, when David took up the kingdom, he was only 30 years old. Add that Samuel was already old when he took his sons into a share of the government, and the Israelites sought a King: from which time 33 years flowed to David's first anointing, as Ussher counts, and some time from then until the death of Samuel. But there seems to have been no reason why he could not perform his duty on account of old age, he who still survived for nearly 40 years thereafter. And indeed Interpreters and Chronologists agree almost commonly that from the leadership of Samuel and the reign of Saul, no more than 40 years are made up together. For although among these Sanctius, Tirinus, and several others attribute 38 of these years to Samuel, and only two to Saul: others give 10 to Saul and 30 to Samuel with Funccius, others 25 to Samuel with Calvisius and 15 years to Saul: some even with Torniellus assign 18 to Saul and 22 to Samuel: yet they easily conspire on this, that 40 years cannot be attributed to his reign alone: and thus that the administration of Samuel and Saul taken together lasted for 40 years: so Eusebius, Augustine lib. XVII de Civ. Dei, Sulpitius, Bede, Lyranus, Abulensis, Freculphus, Bellarmine, Genebrardus, Mercator, Gordonus, Ribera, Pineda, Lorinus, Torniellus in Cornelius à Lapide on 1 Reg. XIII, 1. Who all take the words of Paul in Acts XIII, 20. Afterward God gave judges until Samuel the Prophet: and from then they asked for kings, and he gave them Saul, the son of Cis; a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years, they do not accept otherwise than that the government of these same Samuel and Saul, who are commemorated after the judges before David, is defined. For that 40 years cannot apply to the reign of Saul alone is shown both by the interval of 48 years, which would thus be rendered larger, and by the age of David, who aspired to the kingdom having thirty years, and by the time of his persecution, because thus the persecution of David would have lasted more than twenty years, which however was not even ten years long.

The opinion of the Hebrews, however, which is handed down in Seder Olam c. 53 and in the history of the Kabbalah by R. Abraham, and to Gerhard Mercator, Arias Montanus, Adrichomius, and Sanctius

The opinion that some attempt to support, that Saul reigned for only two years, does not deserve to be reckoned with; because it rests upon no solid argument, nor does such a tiny amount of time suffice for the history, deeds, and battles of Saul, nor is it likely that Saul was brought to the kingdom when nearly sixty, which that opinion posits, and must posit, because Ishbosheth, his son, was already forty years old when he succeeded his father, 2 Sam. 2:10; nor does it in any way suit the history that David, who was anointed king two years after Saul was made king, should have come to the government immediately upon Saul being killed, since the Davidic persecution involves many years.

Wherefore we persist in that opinion, as the most convenient, which attributes 30 years to the solitary principate of Samuel and 10 years to the reign of Saul: where this also must be diligently noted, that Samuel did not cease to judge until the end of his life: because this is expressly stated in 1 Sam. 7:15. Therefore, those years of the reign are to be arranged thus: that it be established that Samuel presided alone for 30 years, just as mention is made of 20 years having elapsed after the death of Eli in 1 Sam. 7:2, where Samuel is introduced not as one finally to be set over the principate, but as a Prince governing the people: nor is it likely that there was an interregnum during those 20 years, or that Eli lacked an immediate successor: nor does that great number, designated in 1 Kings 6:1, in any way support the establishment of an interregnum. Furthermore, after King Saul was created, as has been said, Samuel did not cease to judge the people; but under that king he still had his role in judging the people for eight years, because he is said to have instituted his visitations every year until the end of his life, 1 Sam. 7:16. Finally, after Samuel died, Saul seems to have reigned alone for two years: which years joined together make 40. And thus, with the calculation of this account begun, David, having been anointed two years after the creation of King Saul, would have been twenty-two years old: inasmuch as he was 30 years old when he succeeded Saul in the government, and was 24 years old according to the blessed Luther when he struck down Goliath.

If it be objected, regarding the history of Samson, that the passage Jud. 13:1 et seqq., from which it seems to be gathered that the Philistine persecution of 40 years began after the judgeship of Abdon, and that the birth of Samson was announced only after that had begun: and thus that he did not immediately succeed Abdon in the principate: the answer is not difficult, that the defection and the subsequent persecution of Israel are indeed referred to after the history of Abdon; but it cannot be firmly concluded from that, that this defection and persecution happened only after the times of Abdon. And those words of the past tense, Jud. 13:1, And the children of Israel added to do evil, and the Lord gave them into the hand of the Philistines, could conveniently be translated in the pluperfect, and they had added, and he had given: since that was done some years before, and as seems to most, about 20 years before the birth of Samson, when they were given into the hands of the Philistines, until deliverance was undertaken by the avenger himself, when he was about twenty years old, who is said to have presided over the people for 20 years likewise.

But as to the objection concerning the two-year reign of Saul from 1 Sam. 13:1, Tirinus indeed thinks that nothing can be clearer than those words for his opinion, that Saul reigned for only two years, with this added interpretation: Saul was a son of one year (as if the mark of similitude were omitted in the Hebrew manner, i.e., just as a son of one year, simple and upright) when he had begun to reign, and he reigned for two years over Israel: But although not a few, for instance Jerome (or whoever the author is) in his questions, Theodoret, Augustine in book VII of his Locutiones on Judges, Gregory, Procopius, Eusebius, Hugo, Rupert, Lyra, Abulensis, Dionysius the Carthusian: interpret the former words in this way, just as the Chaldean also translates them: Saul was like a son of one year, in whom there are no faults, when he reigned: yet that explanation is brought into the text, not elicited from the text. Others, therefore, do not take it as a similitude with infants, but as a mark of time: which the Hebrew phrase imports: and Joseph Scaliger, in his Elenchus Chronologicus, wishes it to refer to the year of his age; but he thinks that a number or a numeral mark has fallen out; he says, numbers were conceived in ancient times by numeral letters, not by words, whence that in 1 Sam. 13 arose, בֶּן־שָׁנָה שָׁאוּל for the numeral mark is missing. The Greek edition: υἱὸς ἦν ἐνιαυτοῦ. Other codices: υἱὸς τριάκοντα ἐτῶν, etc. He thinks, therefore, that the letter ל has fallen out as the mark of the 30th year, which Saul had when he began to reign. But it is assumed only precariously that numbers were expressed in the Hebrew codex by letters, not by words in ancient times; and it is rashly feigned that there was a loss of a numeral letter and a corruption of the authentic text: nor does the plural occur here, but the singular שָׁנָה year, whence there is no place for that suspicion concerning a lost number of years. Finally, no necessity compels us to admit a corruption in the Holy text here. 'Son of a year' is a customary formula of speaking: also 'son of a year' in reigning, or in the kingdom: meaning that he reigned for a year, or that he was in the first year of his reign. See Exod. 10:11, Isa. 65:20. Which periphrasis of time can be referred either to what follows or to what precedes. To what follows, so that it may be noted that this was done in the first year of his reign, which is then narrated in chapter 10:2, in which way the added words about the two years of Saul would have been inserted by parenthesis, and thus it was signified by them that Saul had legitimately administered the kingdom for only two years; concerning which see Junius at this place.

Nor do others inappropriately refer that periphrasis of time to the preceding matters, which, to wit, began to be commemorated in chapter 11, 1. and following, because they happened concerning that renewal of the reign of Saul, the protestation of Samuel, and the miracle that followed, when Saul was a son of a year in his reign, from the time namely that he was anointed king and accepted with public congratulation: so that the things which are subjoined, and he had reigned two years over Israel, are to be understood of those things which he now undertakes to narrate, when namely he chose for himself stationary soldiers. Which opinion, as being simpler and more convenient, is deservedly preferred, and pleased B. Luther in his version, Flacius in his Clavis, B. Glassius in his Gramm. S. book III. Tract. V. Can. 31. and among the Jews R. Levi Ben Gersom, as also Hugo Grotius on this passage, not to mention the Usserian explanation in his Annals, page 49. A more convenient sense cannot be rendered than this: That one year had passed after the Philistines were subdued by Samuel, when Saul began to reign: and that he reigned for two years thereafter free from the yoke of the Philistines. For in the times that followed, Saul was driven from his command by the Philistines: the Israelite people being oppressed by them with a heavy and long-lasting servitude. Which being at length removed, Saul is said to have received his kingdom over Israel, that is, to have recovered it anew, 1 Sam. 14, 47.

QUESTION VII.

How great is the interval from the departure out of Egypt to the beginning of the construction of the Temple, whether 480 years have elapsed since then, or more?

Others establish more. Josephus, Book VIII of Antiquities, ch. 3, in the Basel edition of Froben, year 1540, enumerates 502 years, nay 592, as is gathered from Book X, ch. 10, which also Sabellicus, Ennead I, Book XI, and Melchior Canus, Book XI of Theological Commonplaces, ch. 5, have assigned. Clement of Alexandria, Book I of Stromata, calculates 523 years from Joshua to the death of David. If to these are added the 40 years spent in the desert, and the 3 of Solomon, there result 566 years from the departure to the beginning of the temple. Nicolaus Raimarus defined 580 years for this epoch. Laurentius Codomannus 598. Not a few Eastern Greeks count 633 years. Nicolaus Serarius assigns 680 years; but both from a special calculation previously instituted, and indeed especially from the clear letter of the text in 1 Kings 6:1, it is liquidly evident that more than 480 are not to be counted. And it came to pass, says the Holy Spirit there, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the Israelites from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month Ziph, (that is the second month of the reign of Solomon over Israel,) that he began to build the house of Jehovah.
