Since this shines with its own light, therefore those who assign a different number, when they see themselves constrained, either invent that the text is corrupted, with Serarius and other Papists, as well as with Vossius, and Ludovicus Capellus, and Lansberg, or they attribute to it a different meaning: but since the Holy Spirit expresses numbers not by letters, but by whole words, there is clearly no room for suspicion of corruption, which the highest consensus of Hebrew, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin Codices, as well as Interpreters, also excludes.

And since from the death of Moses to the birth of David there intervene only four generations, Nahshon, Num. 1:7, 7:12, begat Salmon, Salmon Boaz, Boaz Obed, Obed Jesse, this one David, Ruth 4:22, 1 Chron. 11:12, Matt. 1:8, it must necessarily be established that those progenitors were 130 years old or more when they begat their sons, if an interval of 580 or more years is assigned. Who, therefore, could exhaust a far greater number of 580 or more years? For in order that those 4 generations, of Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse, might exhaust the number expressed in the text, it is assumed that Ruth married Salmon in the first year after the crossing of the Jordan, at the age of 28, that she bore Boaz in the 56th year of her age, i.e., 31 from the crossing, 71 from the departure, from which thus 336 years will remain until the birth of David. For if those 70 years are added to the 70 years of David's life and the 3 years of Solomon's reign, there result 144 years, which added to 336 years make the number 480 years. Those 336 years, therefore, will have to be distributed into the generation of Boaz, Obed, and Jesse, and thus if the distribution is made into equal parts, each of them would have begotten while having 112 years. Bailius assumes that Ruth married Salmon at the 17th year of her age, and bore Boaz to him in the 56th; hence he concludes that 327 years remained, to be distributed into the triple generation of Boaz, Obed, and Jesse, so that each of them (the distribution being made equally) begat at the one hundred and eighth year. That this, however, should not be considered a marvel, more recent examples teach, many of which may be seen produced by various authors in the Synopsis Criticorum and Interpreters of Matthew Poole, near the beginning of the book of Ruth, Vol. I, col. 1224 seq. Now if it seems hard to produce not only age, but also vigor for begetting, to the one hundred and eighth year in those more ancient centuries, how will those who still add a hundred years or more to the epoch from the Exodus to the construction of the temple be able to maintain their position? For thus it would have to be said that each of them begat in the one hundred and fortieth year.

A not insignificant difficulty, however, has arisen from Acts 13:20, where 450 years seem to be numbered from the distribution of the land by Joshua to Samuel. If to these are added the 40 years to David and 3 of Solomon, along with the 40 years of wandering in the desert, and the seven-year period from the death of Moses to the distribution of the land, 580 years result. Those who could not untie this knot thought it should be cut by accusing the Greek text of corruption, as if 350 years had been numbered by Paul, not 450, to which view B. Behmius also gave his assent, because the word τετρακοσίοις could easily have crept in for the word τριακοσίοις, in Chronol. Manud. l. c. Tit. III. L. VI. p. 50. Theodore Beza said that a single letter, Iota, had fallen out, thus amending the vulgate reading ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις to: ὡς ἔτεσι τε τριακοσίοις, which correction he claims to have read in one manuscript codex. But what B. Behmius warned a little earlier on page 47 must be piously believed concerning the most holy codex of the Old Testament—that God has holily preserved the same and has always defended it from every injury of corruption, otherwise a door would soon be opened wide to human wantonness for inventing any error whatsoever in the Old Testament under the pretext of corruption—the same must likewise be held concerning the most holy codex of the New Testament.

Hugo Grotius corrects the Greek text by the authority of some English manuscript codex in such a way that it should be read, not as it is held in all codices, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκοντα, but in this manner, that those words ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκοντα cohere with the preceding, and then those words are placed, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα: just as the Latin Vulgate reads: He distributed their borders by lot, as if after 450 years: and after that he gave unto them judges, until Samuel: and he understands the 450 years to be those which elapsed from the exodus from Egypt until that time when David cast the Jebusites out of Zion, because that much time had to be spent in settling the Hebrew nation in its seats. But since the Greek codices agree exactly, we ought not to value the authority of one manuscript so highly that we admit that corruption has crept into all the others. For if we prefer to follow the trustworthiness of one codex over another, neglecting the rest, what certainty will be left in the Holy Codex? Nevertheless, Bailius observes in Opere Histor. & Chron. lib. I. cap. VI. quæst. 2. pag. 48, that the Marquis Velesius also, in Walton's various Greek readings of the New Testament and Acts 13:20, p. 23, a collator of sixteen manuscripts, read with the Latin Vulgate μετὰ ταῦτα ἔδωκε κριτὰς after four hundred and fifty years, and Beza confesses that the Greek codex published at Paris agrees precisely with the Latin, with which the Greek Wichelian Bible, published at Frankfurt under the care of Franciscus Junius, also agrees.

Moreover, even if the common Greek reading is retained, the words can be conveniently explained so that they are not understood as referring to the times of the judges; but rather before the judges, and an epoch of about 450 years, from the birth of Isaac to the κληϱοχίαν [inheritance], which was 447 years, may be designated. Which opinion agrees excellently with the text. For that μετὰ ταῦτα [after these things] refers to the election of the Patriarchs; since it was said to Abraham: In Isaac shall your seed be called: concerning which election Paul was speaking most of all at present, just as he added the fulfillment of that promise later in verse 23. Therefore, having regard for this principal scope and intention, he rightly fixed the term from which at the birth of Isaac: but the term to which at the actual κληϱοδοσία [inheritance]; since indeed, along with the blessed seed, the land of Canaan had also been promised to Abraham, as a type of the heavenly country to be imparted to us in the blessed seed: and since Joshua was the first of the judges from the κληϱοχίᾳ [inheritance] onwards, and Samuel was the last, these epochs from Isaac to Joshua, and from Joshua to Samuel, cohere very well, and the words, so that the sense may become clearer, must be taken thus: καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετϱακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκον- τα (πϱαχθέντα) [and after these things, about 450 years having elapsed], he gave judges until Samuel the Prophet. Thus also the particle ὡς, 'about,' retains its emphasis: because not exactly 450 years flowed from the birth of Isaac to the κληϱοδοσία [inheritance]. For from the birth of Isaac to Jacob there are 60 years: in whose 130th year the entry into Egypt took place: add 210 years to the entry into the land of Canaan, and from there 47 years to the distribution of the land, and there emerge the 447 years which we mentioned, according to the calculation of Junius in his Sacred Parallels, book 1, parallel 95, of the old English Annotators in the Geneva notes, of Ludovicus de Dieu on Acts 13, of Robert Baillie, of B. Walther in his Harmony, and others. And to this interpretation, from among the Papists, come Arias Montanus, Adrichomius, Salianus, Torniellus, Tirinus, and also Cornel. a Lapide on Judges 3:14, who praises for this opinion the Ordinary Gloss, Bede, Hugo, Lyra, Dionysius, and counts the years from the birth of Isaac to the exodus from Egypt as 405, since indeed 215 years according to a more accurate computation intervened from the entry of Jacob into Egypt to the exodus, and furthermore 47 years from the exodus to the distribution of the land, which joined to those 405 years make 452 years, or if account is also taken of the months, 451 years and 4 months: in place of which the Apostle used the round number 450, with the addition of the little word ὡς.

Thus there will be no need, with Beroaldus and Langius, to say that Paul, following the received opinion of the Jews, which was also Josephus's, counted the years of the judgeships separately from the years of the servitudes, which in the books of Judges precisely make the sum of 450 years: for it is inconvenient, to say nothing harsher, to wish that Paul erred in his calculation with the Jews, or adhered to a common error. Nor furthermore do we have need to have recourse to that unusual rounding of the number, as if 450 years were placed in the stead of 436, which flowed from the exodus until the death of Samuel: which opinion is reported by the Belgian Interpreters. Nor indeed is it permitted to take the beginning of the numbering from the principate of Joshua with Grotius on 1 Kings 6; for if 17 years are given to his principate, since 299 years flowed from then until Eli, and Eli presided for 40 years, only 356 years will emerge from this. How then will those 94 years, which are missing for the sum of 450 years, be able to be supplied from the judgeship of Samuel? To whom no one has assigned more than 30 years. Finally, thus there will be no need to have recourse to other inventions because of the Pauline passage, or to render the text in the book of Kings perplexed by various opinions. For no certainty remains when one departs from the letter of the text: just as in that one place of the history of the Kings, Serarius and Vossius have brought forward seventeen different opinions. Which, indeed, are not yet all of them. So fertile are errors.

Wherefore one must persist entirely in that number of 480 years, defined so accurately and not without singular care by the Holy Spirit, and it must be held as indubitable that the foundations of Solomon's temple began in the four hundred and seventy-ninth year, after the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt was completed, but in the eightieth current year, just as the text most openly holds; that is, when the fourth year of Solomon was being conducted, which is connected with that eightieth year, whose second month and second day is defined, 2 Chron. 3:2. Since therefore the exodus took place on the 1st month, 15th day, from there 479 years and 17 days must have flowed to the laying of the temple's foundations.

SECTION VI.

The epoch from the construction of Solomon's Temple to the liberty of constructing the new Temple, after the destruction of the former, is 476 years.

This is the fifth epoch, the term to which we prefer to fix not at the destruction of the former temple, but at the promulgation of the indulgence for the return and rebuilding of the temple granted by Cyrus: because there a new light shone upon the people, of liberation from Babylonian servitude and the concession of a return to the land in which the MESSIAH was to be born and execute the redemption of the human race; as well as the construction of the temple, in which he was to perform his Prophetic office; and because the Holy Spirit loves to join with that liberation the liberation of the Messiah from spiritual servitude, of which that was a notable figure. Otherwise, 427 years are commonly counted from the construction of the temple to its destruction, if indeed 37 years elapsed from the third completed year of Solomon to the end of his reign (since the years of his reign itself were 40), and from there 390 years are usually counted to the destruction, which is how many days were given for the years of the sins of Israel from Jeroboam, who immediately at the beginning of his reign, through the erection of two golden calves, not only polluted himself with idolatry but also made Israel to sin (1 Kings 12:26), until the destruction of the temple, according to them, have elapsed. Others, however, more correctly end these years of the sins of Israel not at the destruction of the temple, but at the final desolation of the land, which occurred four years later, namely in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar, and thus they make the epoch from the construction to the conflagration of the Temple 424 years; and since that happened on the tenth day of the fifth month, just as the construction began on the second day of the second month, they assert that 424 full years, 3 months, and 8 days elapsed from the beginning of the construction to the destruction. Now, just as the temple was destroyed in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, which was the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar: so in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, which was the first of Nebuchadnezzar, the first servitude of the king and the Jewish people began, from which the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity are to be counted, Jeremiah 25:1, 29:10, that is, in the 406th year from its construction, 18 years before the destruction of the temple: whence it is necessary that there remain from the destruction of the temple to the end of the captivity, or Babylonian servitude, 52 years. But from the final desolation of the land to the liberation from captivity there are 48 years. If therefore there intervened from the structure of the temple to the destruction 424 years, 3 months, 8 days, which took place on the tenth day of the fifth month, with those 52 remaining years of captivity added, there will result 476 years to the end of the captivity. Which was resolved in the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, a solemn edict having been promulgated, granting liberty to the people both to return to their fatherland and to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem, 2 Chron. 36, 22. Ezr. 1, 1. 2. 7. chap. 5, 13. 14. c. 6, 2. 5. But how the same number of years is to be gathered from the Chronology of the kings of Judah, or how this is to be reconciled with the Chronology of the Kingdom and Kings of Israel, will be explained in the questions.

Israel is distinguished from the Jews, and it is not a matter of the personal sin of the King, but the common sin of the ten tribes; the term from which is not to be placed at the fall of Solomon, but at the μοσχοποιΐᾳ (calf-making) of Jeroboam, by which he himself sinned and caused Israel to sin, which is that sin of Israel which is most often exaggerated 1 Kings 12, 28. c. 13, 34. c. 14, 9. 15, 16. etc. Which is the almost common opinion of Interpreters and Chronologers. Nor indeed did 290, much less 390, years flow from the fall of Solomon to the deportation of Shalmaneser, since the kingdom of Israel, separated from the kingdom of Judah, stood for only 254 years, as the calculation is begun by Ussher and others.

The epoch from the building of Solomon's temple to the Liberty, after the destruction of the same, of building a new temple:

From the third year of Solomon to the end of his reign, 37 years

Thence to the final desolation of the land of Canaan, the years of the sins of Israel, - 390

Thence to the liberty of return and the building of the new temple, years - 49

Total, 476 years

It can also be arranged in this way:

From the building of the temple to the captivity which took place in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, years - 406

Thence to the liberty, years - 70

Total - 476

Item in this way:

From the structure of the temple to the destruction, 424 years

From there to the first [year] of Cyrus, & the liberty of the people 52

Total - 476

To which if the years of the World are added - 2993

which indeed flowed to the construction of the temple, there result - - 3469

Concerning the term to which, however, they vary: which some establish as the destruction of the City & temple; others indeed as the total devastation of the land, such as Funccius, Codoman, Book III of Chronology, ch. XVI, Ussher in the Annals of the O.T., Tremellius also, although he makes the beginning from the idolatry of Solomon, which he rejects to the 27th year of his reign. To whom we judge the calculation should be added: since Ezekiel, having received the news about the smitten Jerusalem, had predicted in ch. 33, 21. 29. that the land would be completely devastated: which happened when Nebuchadnezzar was besieging Tyre, situated at the border of the Israelite land, in the 23rd year of his reign, that is, the fourth after the destruction. For then Nebuzaradan deported the remnants of the Jews to the number of 745, Jer. 52, 30, and the land was left completely uncultivated.

This Epoch therefore began 37 years after the structure of the temple, which was begun in the fourth year of Solomon (inasmuch as he reigned for 40 years) under whose successor Rehoboam, when he was beginning his rule, the kingdom of Israel was divided from the kingdom of Judah, and the king of Israel Jeroboam set up the worship of the calves immediately at the beginning of his reign, 1 Kings 12, 27. Since therefore the beginning of the structure of the temple falls in the year of the world 2992, with the 37 remaining years of Solomon added, there result 3029 years from the creation of the World to the beginning of the rule of Rehoboam and the division of the kingdom of Israel from the kingdom of Judah or the rule of Jeroboam, and the institution of the worship of the calves, where the term from which of the sins of Israel is to be fixed, so that the end of that Epoch of 390 years of the sins of Israel falls in the 3420th year from the creation of the World.

QUESTION I.

How is the epoch of the years of the sins of Israel to be defined?

Ezekiel expressed this epoch in chapter 4, 5. For three hundred and ninety days make as many years, with the Lord himself as interpreter: 'For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days, 390 days,' verse 5. Add verse 6: 'I have appointed thee each day for a year.' Pareus wished to render this uncertain, because, forsooth, it is not clear from where these years are to be begun, or where they are to be ended; but he did so rashly, and against the opinion of all interpreters and chronologers, who hold this divinely expressed number in high regard, because this exactly defined number of 390 years contributes not a little to reconciling the ἐναντιοφανειαν in the connection of the Kings of Judah and Israel, where one would not infrequently be stuck as to whether they should be understood as complete or incomplete.

Tremellius and Grotius establish the term from which as the fall of Solomon himself: and the term to which as the deportation of the ten tribes by Shalmaneser: but since the years of the sins of Israel are designated, in what

Those who end the years of the sins of Israel at the destruction of the temple differ in their opinions. For Bucholzer and Crenzheim and others assign their beginning to the fourth year of Rehoboam and Jeroboam, because in 2 Chron. 11:17 the Israelites are said to have served the Lord for three years after the death of Solomon (which, however, is only asserted there of some, and Bucholzer rashly stuffed three years into the reign of Amaziah, in order to obtain his calculation, against the manifest letter of Scripture). But Scaliger, Bunting, Schubert, Temporarius, Calvisius, Behm, and other followers of Scaliger begin them immediately from the death of Solomon and the beginning of the apostasy of the ten tribes, or of the Israelite kingdom. But the fact that they urge that the intention of this vision of the prophecy of Ezekiel was to describe the siege of Jerusalem does not contradict us, because from that siege the beginning was made of the total devastation, which did not happen in the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar, ending throughout the whole land with the πανωλεθρίᾳ of the city and temple, but finally four years later, namely in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar. For there had still remained some remnants of the people, so that they might be vinedressers and husbandmen in the land of Judah, over whom Nebuchadnezzar had set Gedaliah the son of Ahikam of the same nation, Jerem. 39:10, ch. 40:5, 7, and 52:16, 2 Kings 25:11, 22, 23; and the leaders and soldiers who had fled by night from Jerusalem with Zedekiah returned to Gedaliah in their homeland, 2 Kings 25, 4. Jer. 52, 7. wandering here and there in the fields, and all the Jews who had betaken themselves to the Moabites, Ammonites, and neighboring nations Jer. 40, 7. 12. 2. Kings 25, 23. 24. who in the second year after the destruction of the temple, in the seventh month (Thisri), after Gedaliah and the Chaldeans and the military men had been nefariously killed by Ishmael, were indeed liberated from being led into Ammonite captivity by Johanan, son of Kareah, but with Jeremiah dissuading them in vain, they afterwards betook themselves into Egypt, having abandoned their native soil, Jer. 41, 16. seqq. from which Ezechiel predicted that extreme desolation would come to pass for their final remnants, c. 33, 21. 29. which finally followed in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer. 52, 30. To which some also refer the vision of Ezech. 5. chapter, concerning the remnants of the Jewish people, likewise about to be scattered in the most recent times.

If the followers of Grotius or Tremellius wish to urge that the years of the iniquity of the house of Israel were named by the Prophet, but the kingdom of Israel was led away long before the devastation of Jerusalem and the land of Judah: I respond that not a few from the remnants of the kingdom of Israel withdrew to the kingdom of Judah at the time of the devastation of Samaria, 2. Chron. 34, 29. who, persisting in idolatry and likewise seducing the house of Judah, were involved in destruction together with it.

QUESTION II.

How are the 40 years of Judah, Ezech. IV, 6, to be designated?

Pareus has attempted to introduce mere uncertainty here as well in those things which he opposed to Calvisius; but why would an epoch be expressed by the Holy Scriptures if nothing certain could be had concerning it? Pareus is mistaken, however, in that he thinks the years of the sins of Judah are to be numbered separately, and are to be begun after the 390 years of the sins of Israel are completed: from which, if the beginning is made from the death of Solomon, 340 years would emerge, a number which corresponds to no historical event. For although the Prophet had to lie down separately for the sins of the house of Israel and the house of Judah, these years are not therefore to be numbered separately in the application of the vision, since they meet at one term; namely, at the siege of Jerusalem, by which the beginning of the punishment was made, by which both the remnants of the Israelites still surviving in Judea after the Assyrian deportation and the house of Judah had to be affected, because the Jews had made themselves participants in the sins of Israel through the remnants remaining in Judea, and had been infected and seduced by them; whence a common destruction awaited both the Israelites and the Jews. But the years of the sin of Judah are numbered distinctly, and indeed as 40, because in the last 40 years sin had especially prevailed in the kingdom of Judah: whence chronologists agree on this, that the years of the sins of the house of Israel and the years of the sins of the house of Judah meet at the term to which they come, and have the same end. But because others, as we have said, constitute the end as the destruction of the city and the total devastation of the land, in the 23rd year of the same reign, ending in the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar, they therefore differ by five years in designating the beginning of this epoch: for others, with Scaliger, begin those 40 years from the 13th year of Josiah, in which Jeremiah began to prophesy, Jer. I, 2. c. XXV, 3. but others more correctly begin them from the 18th year of Josiah, in which the temple of Jerusalem began to be restored and the autograph of the law was found and publicly read; which beginning is far more illustrious and celebrated, because then not only was the temple repaired, and the book of the law read to the King, and the judgment of God impending over the people indicated through the Prophetess Huldah; but in a public congregation of the city before the whole multitude all the words of the law were read, and a solemn covenant was sanctioned before the Lord by the whole people, and with all idols renounced, the entire people received to serve the one God of Israel, and the Passover of the Lord was celebrated in Jerusalem with great solemnity, 2. Kings 22, 3. seqq. c. 23. 2. Par. 34, 8. seqq. & cap. 35, 19. Since, therefore, after the renewal of the covenant publicly made, the Jews fell away again, and left no room for the admonitions of either Jeremiah or Huldah, even though the devastation had already been proclaimed, and thus they contaminated themselves with a double sin, not only of the idolatry of Israel by participation, 2. Kings 22, 17. but also of their own defection from the new covenant, and disobedience against the Royal and Prophetic exhortations, therefore this special epoch of the sins of Judah is not undeservedly begun from the renewal of the covenant: which were all the more foul and detestable, and demanded a more severe punishment, the more studiously they had been recalled from them and bound to the observation of the divine covenant, both by a most pious King and by the Prophets of the Lord. Nor is there difficulty in the calculation of time. For these 40 years are gathered thus.

From the 18th year of Josiah to the end of his reign, which was of 31 years, 2 Kings 22:1, 2 Chronicles 34:1, there remain years - - - 13

Jehoahaz reigned for 3 months, 2 Kings 23:31. Jehoiakim (2 Kings 24:10) for 11 years

Jehoiachin for 3 months, 2 Kings 24:10.

Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:10) for 11 years, in whose last year the city with the temple was destroyed, in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, 2 Kings 25:8. - - 11

From then to the abduction of the remnant of the people, which took place in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar, Jeremiah 52:30. - 5

Total, 40 years

QUESTION III. How is the calculation of the years of the Kings of Judah to be understood, from the beginning of David down to the devastation of the temple?

It can be gathered in two ways: First, that to the 40 years of David, as also the 40 of Solomon, before the division of the Kingdom and the sin of Israel, that public and universal apostasy, the 390 years of the sins of Israel are to be added. Whence will emerge 470 years: But because the reign of Zedekiah ceased about 4 years before the abduction of the remnants of the people, those being subtracted, there remain 466 years of the Kings of Judah.

Then the calculation can be entered into according to the years of the reign of the Kings of Judah, in this manner:

David reigned for years, as is held 1 Kings II, 11. 1 Chron. XXIX, 27. - - - 40

Solomon, 1 Kings XI, 42. 2 Chron. IX, 30. for years 40

Rehoboam, 1 Kings XIV, 21. 2 Chron. XII, 13. for years - - - - - - - 17

Abijah, 1 Kings XV, 1. 2 Chron. XIII, 2. for years 3

Asa, 1 Kings XV, 10. 2 Chron. XVI, 13. for years 41

Jehoshaphat, 1 Kings XXII, 42. 2 Chron. XX, 31. for years - - - - - - - 25

Jehoram, 2 Kings VIII, 17. 2 Chron. XXI, 20. for years 8

Ahaziah, 2 Kings 8:26. 2 Chronicles 22:2. year 1

Athaliah, 2 Kings 11:3. 2 Chronicles 22:12. years 6

Joash, 2 Kings 12:1. 2 Chronicles 24:1. years 40

Amaziah, 2 Kings 14:1. 2 Chronicles 25:1. years 29

Azariah, or Uzziah, 2 Kings 15:1. 2 Chronicles 26:3. years 52

Jotham, 2 Kings 15:33. 2 Chronicles 27:1. years 16

Ahaz, 2 Kings 16:2. 2 Chronicles 28:1. years 16

Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:2. 2 Chronicles 29:1. years - - - - 29

Manasseh, 2 Kings 21:1. 2 Chronicles 33:1. years 55

Amon, 2 Kings 21:19. 2 Chronicles 33:21. years 2

Josiah, 2 Kings 22:1. 2 Chronicles 34:1. years 31

Jehoahaz, 2 Kings 23:31. 2 Chronicles 36:1. three months.

Jehoiakim, 2 Kings 23:36. 2 Chronicles 36:5. 11 years - - - - 11

Jehoiachin, 2 Chronicles 36:9. three months, 10 days.

Zedekiah, 2 Kings 24:18. 2 Chronicles 36:11. years - - - - 11

Jeroboam II. (2 Kings 14:23.) years - 41

Zechariah (2 Kings 15:8.) 6 months. - 0

Shallum (2 Kings 15:13) 1 month. - 0

Menahem (2 Kings 15:17) 10 years - 10

Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:23) 2 years - 2

Pekah (2 Kings 15:27) 20 years - 20

Hoshea (2 Kings 17:1) 9 years - 9

Sum of years 225, 7 months.

Sum of years 473, 6 months, 10 days.

The difference is 7 years and 6 months. But because that large number 390 is free from all doubt, that difference must lie in the specific years of the reign, in that incomplete years were counted as complete, current years as finished: just as 40 years are attributed to Joash, who was killed at the beginning of his fortieth year of reign: or that sons were admitted into a partnership of the kingdom while their parents were alive, whose years nevertheless are recorded as whole, just as, for example, 25 whole years are attributed to Jehoshaphat, who however after his 22nd year appointed his son Jehoram as partner in the kingdom, whence the first year of Jehoram coincides with the 23rd of Jehoshaphat, so that Jehoram alone, after his parent died, reigned for only 4 years, to whom however 8 years have been assigned. Thus Ahaz in the last year of his reign made Hezekiah a partner, so that the 16th of Ahaz and the 1st of Hezekiah coincide.

Thus, when the previous calculation is compared, 29 years are missing in the reigns of the Israelite Kings. Interpreters and chronologists seek the cause of the difference in interregnums and the different beginnings of the reigns; just as in the time of Josiah, King of Judah, after the death of Jeroboam II, King of Israel, some establish an interregnum of 23 years, others of eleven and a half years: likewise in the time of Ahaz, King of Judah, after the death of Pekah, King of Israel, they record an ἀναρχίαν (anarchy) in the kingdom of Israel for a space of 9 years: whence these must be examined specifically.

Two periods of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel can also be established; namely, that the first, begun from the first year of Rehoboam and Jeroboam, because they began to reign in the same year, ends at the death of Ahaziah, King of Judah, and Jehoram, King of Israel, because both were killed at the same time by Jehu, 2 Kings 8. The latter should begin with the reign of Athaliah, who invaded the kingdom of Judah, and Jehu, who invaded the kingdom of Israel, and be finished with the destruction of the Israelite kingdom, which falls in the 6th year of Hezekiah of Judah and the 9th of Hoshea, King of Israel. Thus the first period will comprise, according to the history of the books of Kings, 91 years of the Kings of Judah, namely Rehoboam 17, Abijah 3, Asa 41, Jehoshaphat 25, Jehoram 4, Ahaziah 1; but 98 years of the Kings of Israel, namely Jeroboam 22, Nadab 2, Baasha 24, Elah 2, Zimri 7 days, Omri 12 years, Ahab 22, Ahaziah 2, Jehoram 12. In the latter period, however, are included 165 years of the Kings of Judah, namely Athaliah 6, Joash 40, Amaziah 29, Uzziah 52, Jotham 16, Ahaz 16, and Hezekiah 6; then 127 years and 7 months of the Kings of Israel: namely 28 years of Jehu, 17 of Jehoahaz, 41 of Jeroboam II, 6 months of Zechariah, 1 month of Shallum, 10 years of Menahem, 2 years of Pekahiah, 20 of Pekah, and 9 of Hoshea. The chronology of the Kings of Israel is thus greater in the first period by 7 years: but in the latter, the chronology of the Kings of Judah is greater by 37 years and 5 months, so that in the whole epoch of the Kings of Judah and Israel, the former exceeded the latter by about 30 years, according to this enumeration, from the beginning to the end of the Israelite kingdom.

QUESTION IV. How does the calculation of the Kings of Israel stand?

The computation can be begun 1. according to the years of the Kings of Judah, because the kingdom of Israel began with Jeroboam at the same time as Rehoboam, and ceased again in the reign of Hezekiah, who began in the third year of Hoshea: whose ninth year brought an end to the Israelite kingdom: which therefore fell in the sixth year of Hezekiah. Now if the beginning of the counting is made from Rehoboam, up to the sixth year of Hezekiah, according to the former review, 260 years result: But since only 4 years are given to the sole reign of Joram, who presided for 8 years when the years of the joint reign are added, and only 39 whole years are left for Joash (not 40, because he was slaughtered at the beginning of the fortieth) and the first year of Hezekiah coincides with the last of Ahaz, so that both are deservedly held as one, 6 years will have to be subtracted by this agreement, and there will remain only 254 years of the reign of Israel, by which it was separated from the kingdom of Judah; as many as Ussher and others assign to it. And chronologists agree on this, that the kingdom of Israel lasted 250 years; although some add 4, others 6, others 8, others 10 years to this number. Nisbeth alone, a Reformed author, extends that kingdom to 306 years. But without any reason, indeed against the calculation of Scripture. And these things concerning the former method of computing.

QUESTION V. How Baasha, having died in the 26th year of Asa, 1 Kings 16:8, invaded Asa in the 36th year, 2 Chronicles 16:1.

The 36th year is to be understood not from the beginning of King Asa, but from the beginning of the State of his kingdom, of which he himself was King, which had lasted from Rehoboam over the Kingdom of Judah, divided from the Israelite one: from which time 17 years of Rehoboam, 3 of Abijah, and 15 of Asa himself had elapsed; for these make 35 years, and since the first of Baasha corresponds to the third of Asa, the twelfth of Baasha will be the fifteenth of Asa: and thus in the 13th of Baasha, that is, in the sixteenth of King Asa (but the thirty-sixth of the Kingdom, which Asa held after Rehoboam his grandfather), that war was begun by Baasha; so that there is no need, with Cajetan on 2 Chron. 15:6, J. Lucius book II of Chronology ch. IX, Cance book XI loc. 5, to complain here that all texts, as well Latin and Greek as Hebrew, are corrupt, and that for 36 years one ought to read 26, or with Grotius to read 26 against the faith of all the Codices, or with Paludanus to leave that knot as insoluble.

Then the calculation of the years can be begun, with the years of the Kings of Israel counted, which Scripture expressed in the books of Kings in this way:

Jeroboam reigned (1 Kings 14:20) for 22 years

Nadab (1 Kings 15:25) for years - - - 2

Baasha (1 Kings 15:33) for years - - 24

Elah (1 Kings 16:8) for years - - - 2

Zimri for 7 days (1 Kings 16:15) - - 0

Omri (1 Kings 16:23) for years - - 12

Ahab (1 Kings 16:29) for years - - 22

Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:last) for years - - 2

Joram (2 Kings 3:1) for years - - 12

Jehu (2 Kings 10:36) for years - - 28

Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:1) for years - - 17

QUESTION VI.

For how many years did Omri reign?

The reason for doubting is that, although 12 years are expressly ascribed to Omri, King of Israel, in 1 Kings 16:23, the beginning of his reign is nevertheless fixed in the 31st year of Asa, King of Judah, and it is implied that his son Ahab succeeded him in the 38th year of Asa. For from the 31st year to the 38th, not 12, but only 7 years are counted, or at most

8. But the doubt is easily resolved from verse 15; for there it is said that in the 27th year of Asa, Zimri reigned in Tirzah, and indeed only for 7 days, to whom Omri immediately succeeded, being elected King at the same time, verse 16, although a part of the people constituted Tibni as king; whence, because of that schism, Omri fully received the kingdom only four years later, after Tibni was extinguished, in the 31st year.

of Asa: so that two beginnings of his reign must be assigned, the first in the 27th year of Asa, when the other part of the people adhered to him, who had elected him, and he reigned with Tibni: the second in the 31st year of Asa, when he obtained the whole kingdom himself. Therefore, from the former beginning, which Scripture counts, ignoring the reign of Tibni as tumultuous, 12 years of Omri's reign elapsed until the 38th year of Asa. If the beginning of the number of 12 years of Omri were deduced from the 31st year of Asa, he would have outlived Asa, and Jehoshaphat would have begun his reign while Omri was still reigning, which contradicts history.

QUESTION VII,

How did Jehoram, the son of Jehoshaphat, begin to reign both in the seventeenth and twenty-second year of his father, and also after the death of his father, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign completed?

That he succeeded his deceased father, who reigned for 25 years, is held in 1 Kings 22:51, 2 Chronicles 20:51, chapter 21:1. But that Joram began to reign in the 17th year of his father Jehoshaphat is concluded thus: Joram the Israelite began to reign in the second year of Joram the Judean, 2 Kings 1:17. But he who is said to have been made king in Israel in the 18th year of Jehoshaphat: therefore the second year of Joram King of Judah was the 18th year of Jehoshaphat: and so it is necessary that Joram the Judean began the beginning of his reign in the 17th year of Jehoshaphat his parent. Again, 1 Kings 8:10. Joram the son of Jehoshaphat is said to have begun to reign in the 5th year of Joram the Israelite, and so in the 22nd year of Jehoshaphat, which such diverse beginnings make the history perplexed: but the difficulty is resolved if it be said that Joram was appointed deputy by his father Jehoshaphat in the 17th year, when the father had to undergo a very dangerous hazard of war against the Syrians: but that he was admitted into full partnership of the scepter in the 22nd year. of his father, now older, and as it were called Augustus from Caesar: from which the 8 years of his rule are counted: finally, that he undertook a solitary reign after the death of his parent, which did not last beyond 4 years. Thus falls here again the suspicion of Grotius concerning the corruption of the Hebrew text at 2 Kings 1:17.

QUESTION VIII.

How Ahaziah began to reign in his 22nd year, 2 Kings 8:26, who in 2 Chronicles 22:2 is said to have undertaken the kingdom at 42 years of age, during which he served for only a year.

Not only the Papists Cajetan, Torniellus, Salianus, Mariana, a Lapide, Petavius, Tirinus, Menochius, but also from the Reformed Capellus, Alstedius, Scaliger, as also Hugo Grotius at 2 Chronicles 22,

2. argue that the Hebrew text is corrupt. But this is not to solve the knot, but to cut it: by which artifice all difficulties could be resolved, namely by that one word, that the text is CORRUPT. And here they refute their own in the Papacy, and Serarius, Suarez, Sanctius, Mendoza, Genebrardus, Gordonus and others desert them. Nor can they do otherwise, if indeed they wish to defend their Vulgate, which agrees with the Hebrew Code. If anyone, however, because of the difficulties which that reading generates, should maintain here that the LXX interpreters read otherwise in their Hebrew, not only the Greek text of Nobilis and the manuscripts of Oxford, Cambridge, and the Polish will favor him, but also the Syriac Bible in Ussher, which he says the Church of Antioch used from the earliest times, translated not from the gaps of the LXX interpreters, but from the Hebrew source itself, Chron. S. p. 10, which answer, however, Ussher himself doubts is sufficiently safe. Deodatus, Gisb. Voetius and Henr. Philippi wish that Ahaziah reigned with Joram his parent; but they can neither prove this co-regency, nor do they resolve the difficulty concerning the 10 years: since Joram reigned only 8 years, and not, as Jerome wishes, 28. For thus 10 years would be added to the reigns of the Judean kings against historical and chronological truth, and the comparison with the Israelite kings would be more disturbed. Franciscus Junius therefore judged that in the latter case it was not the age of Ahaziah that was regarded, but the duration of the maternal family. That the age of Ahaziah certainly cannot be understood as 42 years, the previously designated age of his parent Joram, who lived only 40 years, clearly manifests. For thus it would have been necessary for Joram to have begotten Ahaziah, a son younger by two years, before his own birth, and older sons, by still more years, before he himself was born. Since therefore it is entirely certain that the age of Ahaziah itself can by no means be understood from those things which the Holy Spirit himself indicated, necessity compels that he be called a son of 42 years in another sense, either because many wish with Genebrardus, Serarius and Junius, because 42 years had elapsed to this age of his, when he became King, in the Samaritan era, which was founded in the 6th year of Omri, his maternal great-grandfather; from which 6th year there remained still years for the same grandfather, 22 for his son Ahab, and two are attributed to his son Ahaziah and 12 to his grandson Joram, which joined together make 42 years. For in the last year of Joram, Ahaziah reigned as King of Judah, 2 Kings 8:24 (which opinion seems to be confirmed from the fact that Athaliah is called the daughter of Omri here, even though her parent was Ahab, and Omri was the grandfather; which is to say, it is implied that the calculation is to be led from Omri) or because he is said to have been a son of 42 years in his kingdom, that is, a follower of that impiety which flourished for 42 years from his maternal great-grandfather, as in the Anti-Grotius at 2. 2 Chron. 21, 2. we have explained; or because 42 years have elapsed since the birth of Ahaziah, before his son Joash succeeded him, which interpretation of Lud. de Dieu we have also cited there: because the one year of Ahaziah, the 6 of Athaliah, who reigned unlawfully, and the 13 of Joash, during which he was still a minor, before he reached his 10th year, make 20 years, which added to the 22 years that he was old when Ahaziah began to reign, produce 42 years.

In the Junius-Tremellius Bibles, a transposition is imagined in the Hebrew text, as if it should be read thus: whose mother's name was Athaliah, daughter of Omri, being 42 years old, when Ahaziah was reigning. But that is a very harsh transposition: yet the most learned Ussher does not reject it in his Sacred Chronology, p. 11, but explains it otherwise, namely by changing the case, putting 'acting' (feminine) in place of 'acting' (masculine) and referring the designation of age to Athaliah herself, that she was then 42 years old: but that is repugnant to the Hebrew text; for thus it would have had to be said, not בֶּן but בַּת daughter of 42 years. See more on this passage in our Anti-Gr. Annotations to 2 Chron. 23, 2.

QUESTION IX.

How many are the chronological years of the reign of Jehoshaphat and Jehoram.

There are assigned to Jehoshaphat 25 years, 1 Kings 22:42, 2 Chronicles 20:31. To Jehoram his son 8 years, 2 Kings 8:17, 2 Chronicles 21:20. But since in the 5th year of Jehoram, King of Israel, Jehoshaphat, already elderly, admitted his son Jehoram into a partnership in the kingdom, as is clear from 2 Kings 8:16: in the 5th year of Jehoram, son of Ahab, King of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was then King of Judah, Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigned as King of Judah, so that the epoch of the years of the Kings of Judah is not extended more than is just, and increased by some years, either 22 years only are to be attributed to Jehoshaphat, and those not complete years, or rather 4 chronological years only to Jehoram, which we believe to be evident from the above, yet we have thought it necessary to give warning here for the sake of the calculation.

QUESTION X.

Whether an interregnum of some years is to be admitted in the kingdom of Judah?

Not a few chronologists, Bucholcer, Krenzheim, Temporarius, Calvisius, Behm, and Capellus, think that there was an interregnum of eleven years at Jerusalem from the death of Amaziah until the succession of Uzziah. Dr. Behm proves this in his Chronology of the World, p. 65, as follows: If the 15th year of Amaziah is the first of Jeroboam II, 2 Kings 14:2, 2 Chronicles 25:1. Therefore the last year of Amaziah falls in the 15th year of the reign of Jeroboam. For, as Scripture testifies, Uzziah or Azariah, the son of Amaziah, finally succeeded his parent in the kingdom in the 27th year of Jeroboam, 2 Kings 15:1. Therefore, from the death of Amaziah to the beginning of the reign of Uzziah or Azariah, there will be a gap of 11 full years. Bunting, in order not to admit a gap or interregnum, has recourse to a corruption of the number in the years of Jeroboam, 2 Kings 15:1, claiming that the 27th year was put for the 17th. But we are reluctant to posit that.

Junius and Tremellius think that Amaziah, King of Judah, reigned only 17 years, and that for the remaining 12, because of the conspiracy and flight about which 2 Kings 14:19 and 2 Chronicles 25:27 speak, he lived an exiled life, and that these 12 years should be attributed by common right not only to Amaziah but also to Uzziah, so that in this way the 18th year of Amaziah, which is the 4th of Jeroboam, is the first of Uzziah, and the 38th of Uzziah is the 41st or last of Jeroboam: to whom Dr. Behmius not undeservedly replies: that in this connection this is taken as granted which is in doubt. For it must be proven (1.) that in the 18th year of his reign a conspiracy was made against Amaziah and his flight to Lachish occurred, and that he lived there for 12 years a private and exiled life; the text of 2 Kings 14:19 and 2 Chronicles 25:27 seems to speak to the contrary, which inclines toward the fact that his death occurred immediately after the flight of Amaziah to Lachish. (2.) It must be proven that the last 12 years of Amaziah are to be included by enumeration in the 52 years during which Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, reigned. These are the words of the blessed Dr. Behmius. We object primarily to this: that by that reasoning 12 years of the epoch of the kings of Judah are lost, because Amaziah is imagined to have reigned only 17 years, whereas he actually reigned 29 years, and the last 12 years of his life are counted among the 52 years of Uzziah, and thus the great number of 390 years of the sins of Israel designated by the Holy Scriptures will not be fulfilled in that way. Add that the Junius-Tremellius exposition of the text of 2 Kings 16:2 ff., where it refers the 27th year of Jeroboam not to the beginning of the reign of Uzziah, but to the time when he was struck with leprosy, introduces a long parenthesis unusual in sacred history, c. 23

8. Rob. unties this knot by means of a synchronism

Bayly, in his Chronological Works, p. 79, 80, says: since the 15th of Amaziah coincides with the first of Jeroboam, it is not necessary that the 29th of Amaziah, and thus the first of Uzziah, should coincide with the 27th of Jeroboam, but rather the 16th; or if Uzziah did not enter upon his reign before the 27th of Jeroboam, the Judean throne must have been vacant for eleven years, and there must have been an interregnum of eleven years in Jerusalem from the death of Amaziah, for that many are counted from the death of Amaziah to the 27th of Jeroboam? I reply: that Jeroboam II had two beginnings of his reign, one in the sixth year of his father Joash and the fourth of Amaziah, which Junius notes in this place, when he was taken into partnership in the empire by his father, who was occupied against the Syrians; the other from the death of his father in the 15th year of Amaziah, from which his own 41 years are to be counted. The first eleven years of his reign, during which he administered the kingdom together with his father, are not chronological: even if that twenty-seventh year, which is compared with the first year in which Uzziah began to reign, is from the order of these non-chronological years. Therefore, that 27th year from the prior beginning of the Jeroboamite reign is only the 16th year from the posterior beginning of the same reign. But why Bayly prefers a synarchy here to an interregnum, he has eruditely given this reason, namely that it is harsh to admit any vacancy on the throne of Judah without express scripture, especially one that adds at least eleven years to the total sum of the epoch: from interregna in Israel or any other people, which do not vary the total sums of epochs, the principles of chronology are not disturbed. With this reconciliation accepted, there will be no need, with Scaliger, Funck, or Codomannus, to establish that Uzziah began to reign from the death of his parent Amaziah, when he was still a boy of 4 years, and to deduce the 52 years of his reign not from the 16th year of his age, but from the aforementioned 4th year, as if the kingdom had been administered by tutors for nearly 12 years, until the 27th of Jeroboam, the Israelite King, in the 16th year of his age he attained the kingdom, and for 36 years thereafter he administered the kingdom by his own authority, dying in the 56th year of his age. Since it is gathered from 2 Kings 15:2 that he died only in his 68th year, which Josephus also reported in Book 9 of the Antiquities, c. 11.

QUESTION XI. Whether there were interregna in Samaria?

Here, indeed, chronologists with great consensus establish an interregnum after the death of Jeroboam II. For in 2 Kings 14:23 it is said that the reign of Jeroboam II, King of Israel, who was of 41 years, began in the fifteenth year of Amaziah, King of Judah; and since Amaziah reigned for 29 years, and thus died in the 15th year of Jeroboam, and Azariah, or Uzziah, succeeded him, it is asserted in chapter 15 of the same book, verse 9, that Zechariah succeeded Jeroboam in the 38th year of Azariah. Now if the 37 years of Azariah that elapsed after the 15th year of Amaziah, during which Jeroboam was σύγχρονος (contemporary) in the kingdom, are added, there will result not 41 years, but 53 up to the reign of Zechariah, whence some posit an interregnum of Samaria of eleven years and a half between the death of Jeroboam and the beginning of the reign of Zechariah: to whom Ussher also accedes in Chron. S. p. 18. For since from the 15th year of Amaziah, King of Judah, Jeroboam II of Israel reigned for 41 years (2 Kings 14:23) and after him his son Zechariah is written to have reigned for 6 months in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah or Uzziah, then Shallum for 1 month in the thirty-ninth year of the same Uzziah (chapter 15:8, 13), in order for these things to be consistent, the interposition of an interregnum of years and 6 months will bring it about, if we admit that after the death of Jeroboam the Israelite republic was reduced to ἀναρχίαν (anarchy) for such a space of time by various disturbances and seditions. Therefore, what is said in 2 Kings 14:29, that upon the death of Jeroboam II his son Zechariah reigned in his stead, is not to be understood as an immediate succession without an interregnum, but that the kingdom was due to him both by hereditary right and from the promise of God in 2 Kings 10:30, 15:22, although due to intervening disturbances and seditions he could not possess it before the twelfth year. Others, however, and among them Calvisius, Behmius, and Capellus, extend that interregnum to 23 years, but there can be no necessity to posit an ἀναρχίαν (anarchy) of such an interval: and they are compelled, so as not to detract from the years of the Kings, to invent an interregnum of 11 years in the kingdom of Judah as well: in which they also contradict their own Scaliger, whom they otherwise follow from time to time. Franciscus Junius and Tremellius in their notes on this passage did not indeed overlook this difficulty, along with the English Annotators, whom Bailius therefore criticizes, nor did they wish to appear to commit a shameful anachronism, of which they are accused by him in Oper. hist. & Chronol. p. 80, when they called the first year of Zachariah the 38th of Uzziah and the last of Jeroboam: But they assumed this, albeit precariously, and with the sacred text not easily consenting 2 Kings 14:9, 2. Chronicles 25:7, that Amaziah the King of Judah reigned only 17 years, and spent the remaining 12 years living as an exile in Lachish on account of conspiracy and flight, and that these twelve years should be attributed by common right not only to Amaziah, but also to Azariah or Uzziah, so that by thus connecting the 18th year of Amaziah (which is the fourth of Jeroboam) with the first of Uzziah, and also the 38th of Uzziah with the 41st or last of Jeroboam, they admit no interregnum in Judah or in Israel: by which method they openly subtract 12 years from the chronology of the kings of Judah. Pareus certainly, however much he may argue against Calvisius that no interregnum should be admitted there, could nevertheless not deny that some hiatus of years intervenes between the reign of Jeroboam and Zachariah. See B. D. Behm. Chronol. Manud. p. 66 seq.

QUESTION XII. In what year did Ahaz beget Hezekiah?

It is said in 2 Kings 16:2 that Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and that he reigned 16 years, whence it remains that he lived only 36 years. But because his son Hezekiah was 25 years old when he succeeded his father 2 Kings 18:2, it must certainly be established that the father was only eleven years old when he begat his son Hezekiah: which most all chronologists also establish: Petavius, however, prefers with Tostatus of Avila to refer the year of Hezekiah's birth to the 13th or 14th year of his father: to which one should rather accede, so that the years are counted with the rounding of the number by past months, rather than giving assent to Calvisius, that Hezekiah was not the natural son of Ahaz, but either a brother, or a stepson, and only a legal son, and successor in the kingdom, and heir. Which opinion openly contradicts Scripture, which calls Hezekiah the son of Ahaz 2. Kings 16:20, ch. 18:2, where, lest it be ambiguous that a natural son is meant, the name of the mother is also added in v. 2, that she was Abi the daughter of Zechariah. Compare 2 Chronicles 28:27, 29:1. Junius and Tremellius in those passages 2 Kings 16 v. 2, 2 Chronicles 28:1, indeed admit that Ahaz's age is expressed, that he was 20 years old, but not when he himself began to reign, but rather when his father Jotham began to reign: But that explanation does not agree well with the words of the text and the customary manner of speaking of the Holy Scriptures. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and he did not do what was right in the sight of the Lord. It is plain that all these things—the time of age, the beginning of the reign, the time of the reign, and the impiety of the King—are attributed to one and the same subject, and nothing different can be introduced here.

QUESTION XIII. In what year did Hoshea, the last King of Israel, begin to reign?

In order that the connection of the years of the Kings of Judah and Israel may be consistent, a double beginning must be assigned to Hoshea; the first from the 20th year of the reign of Jotham, King of Judah, who is so called in 2 Kings 15:30. For although Jotham reigned only 16 years, 2 Kings 15:33, 2 Chronicles 27:8, the 20th year is nevertheless counted from the beginning of his reign, which was the fourth year of Ahaz, the son of Jotham, either because the Holy Scriptures had not yet made any mention of Ahaz, which reason is not improbably given by Junius and Tremellius, B. Behmius, and Ussher, or because out of indignation it did not wish to name King Ahaz as being most impious, and thus took the notation of time from the 20th year of Jotham, King of Judah, even though he had died four years earlier, which reason Funccius gave. The other beginning of Hoshea is designated from the 12th year of Ahaz. 2 Kings 17:1. The cause of this diverse numbering is sought by many in the diverse form of the kingdom; where Tremellius, Broughton, and others attribute to him a prior, pure, and free kingdom, which Dr. Behmius wishes him to have obtained for 8 full years, since in the ninth year of his reign (from the prior beginning), that is, the twelfth of Ahaz, 2 Kings 17:1, he became a tributary of Shalmaneser, v. 3, 4. But Matthieu Beroald thinks that Hoshea was a tributary of the Assyrian King Shalmaneser in his first years, and was not truly King: but having shaken off the yoke of the King of Assyria, because he was then his own master, he is said to have begun to reign in the 12th year of King Ahaz. But if the series of the sacred context is considered more attentively, in the judgment of Ussher, it will appear that Hoshea was made a tributary to Shalmaneser not only after the former, but even after this latter beginning. Wherefore, since Hoshea is read to have reigned for Pekah after he was killed, it is to be accepted in such a way that he attempted to occupy the kingdom then, although others were contending with him for the leadership (which did not pertain to him at all), and the state was led to anarchy, unless after nine years, with domestic disturbances settled, he finally possessed the kingdom peacefully, just as after Jeroboam II died, Zechariah is said to have reigned for him, 2 Kings 14:29, even though because of intervening disturbances he possessed it only in the 12th year, which was also the opinion of Peter of Troyes and L. Codomannus regarding the interregnum to be admitted here.

QUESTION XIV.

How are the years of the Kings of Judah and Israel to be connected?

We shall exhibit this from those things which have been explained thus far, ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (as in a sketch), adding, where there will still be need, the reasons for the connection from sacred history. Since, therefore, the 4th year of Solomon, in which the Temple began to be built, was the year of the World 2992, with the 37 remaining years of Solomon's life added, the year 3029 of the World will emerge, in which Rehoboam began his reign and Jeroboam his. From whence, furthermore, the chronological years of the Kings are to be connected in that manner, as can be seen in the Fourth Table, placed before the Chronicle, which is of the years of the Kings of Judah and Israel from the division until the end of the kingdom of Israel; from which it is clear that in the current year of the world 3283, around the 10th day of the 3rd month, the Israelite kingdom ceased, after it had stood for 253 years separated from the Kingdom of Judah: which was also the 253rd year of the sins of Israel, the 27th of the Era of Nabonassar, the first of Mardokempad.

QUESTION XV.

In what year was the breaking of Ephraim, Isaiah 7:8, foretold to happen?

This was the prophecy of Isaiah: Isaiah 7:8, within 65 years Ephraim shall be broken, that it be not a people. Which most refer to the end of the Israelite kingdom, when the Israelites were deported by Shalmaneser, and in Halah, Habor, and by the river of Gozan (where Tiglath-Pileser had previously carried the inhabitants of Persia, or the two tribes and a half beyond the Jordan, 1 Chron. 5, 26.) and they were placed in the cities of the Medes 2 Kings 17, 6. ch. 18, 10. 11. But because this prophecy was promulgated in the times of Ahaz, as is held in Is. 7, and from the first of Ahaz to the destruction of Ephraim and the captivity of Israel only 22 years intervened, Jerome noted from the Jews that it was not from the time when he prophesied these

Isaiah, but from the prophecy of Amos, which in ch. 7, 11. 17. predicted the same destruction of Samaria in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam II, that these 65 years are to be counted. Which interpretation is also approved by Cornelius a Lapide, Oecolampadius, Calvin, Pelican, the author of the notes to the Geneva Bible, Diodati, and Rob. Baillie: they follow therefore the chronology in Seder Olam ch. 19, Procopius, Thomas, Hugo, and Dionysius. But the words of the oracle hardly admit this opinion, as they fix the beginning at this very prophecy. It is added (from this time) 65 years. Wherefore others, such as Fr. Junius, the recent English annotators, James Ussher, etc., interpret it more correctly as concerning the final abduction, which was carried out by Esarhaddon (called Asaradinus by Ptolemy), which brought an end to the Israelite people 2 Kings 17, 31. Ezra 4, 2. 10. Where colonies from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim were brought into Samaria, so that they might henceforth possess Samaria by hereditary right and dwell in its cities. Therefore, although the greatest part of the people had been deported by Shalmaneser 44 years before, and the kingdom was entirely abolished, yet among the remnants that had remained in their own land, some appearance of a republic was retained. But then it ceased to be a people, when those meager remnants of the Ephraimites were almost overwhelmed by the multitude of arriving foreigners, with new colonies placed there. For that they were not entirely cast out from their ancestral seats is clear from the history of Josiah, cf. 2 Chron. 34, 6. 7. 33. ch. 35, 16. and 2 Kings 23, 19. 20. And from that time, when some of the Israelite priests deported from Samaria were granted by the King of Assyria to the new Samaritan colonists infested by lions, and they not only worshipped God in the calf according to the rite of Jeroboam, but also worshipped their own old idols 2 Kings 17, 25, there began from that time the hatred of the Jews and Samaritans, which was thereafter perpetual Ezra 4, 1. Neh. 4, 2. Sir. 50, 28. John 4, 29.

Hugo Grotius with his Capellus imagines that the corruption of the sources lies with Isaiah: namely, that the last letters ד were added to שש and that for ששם one should read שש and thus the Prophet designated only six years and five, i.e., eleven. But such evasions of his are scandalous in the judgment of the sounder Papists themselves, and render the entire Scripture suspect.

QUESTION XVI. In what year did Jehoiachin begin his reign?

A twofold beginning seems to be assigned to the reign of Jehoiachin, because in 2 Kings 24, 8 he is said to have entered upon his reign in his eighteenth year; but in 2 Chron. ch. 36, 9, in his eighth year: so that we do not have to say with Cajetan, Cano, and Mariana that the 8th year was put for the 18th by a slip, which insane audacity Abulensis, Torniellus, Henr. Philippi, and others from among the Papists themselves refute, and Abulensis rightly says this is too scandalous, because in the same way Scripture could be said to be corrupted in all places; nor will it be necessary with Junius to imagine a clearly insolent reference to the reign not of him whose reign is described, but of his father, in this way: Jehoiachin was eight years old when he (Jehoiakim, who was mentioned before, his father) began to reign, which interpretation Baillie rightly rejects as too subtle and forced. For the pronoun in the word בְּמָלְכוֹ, in his reigning, cannot refer to anything but the nearest person, as Junius also explained the same in the preceding and following Kings. The first beginning, therefore, according to Codomannus, Deodatus, Bailius, Abulensis, Torniellus, and Henr. Philippi, is the eighth year of his age, in which he was taken into partnership by his Father in the second year of his reign, so that the scepter might be more firmly established in the royal family during those turbulent times: The other, when, his Father being dead, he began to reign alone: from which he sat on the Jerusalem throne for only 3 months, soon carried off by Nebuchadnezzar with his wives, because he administered the kingdom poorly. Others prefer to understand the 8th year not of his age, but of the Babylonian servitude, to which he with his people was then subject, when he was 18 years old: which opinion is approved by Ussher. Since there is no doubt that from the taking of Jerusalem in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the eighth year was then counted, but the words: A son of eight years, imply age. But Matth. Beroaldus in Chronol. b. 3, ch. 5, as also Jac. Capellus in Chronic. at the year of the world 3392, deserve no calculation, who wish that Jeconiah began to reign in his eighth year and was abducted; for how could an eight-year-old boy have wives and at such a tender age be held guilty for a poorly administered kingdom!

QUESTION XVII. How is Zedekiah said to have gone to Babylon in his fourth year, Jer. 51, 59.

A voluntary journey seems to be understood there, different from that by which he was abducted into captivity, which happened only in the eleventh year of his reign. For Serajah is not said to have been sent to Babylon by Zedekiah, as Arias Montanus, Tremellius, the Italian and French versions, and also the English Annotators suggest, when they take the preposition אֶת for FROM or OUT OF: But with Zedekiah and others, which the use of that particle אֵת, which signifies with, and not from, as it is rendered in the old Latin Vulgate, Luther's German, and both the ancient and New English, can allow; whether Zedekiah, setting out for Babylon for the sake of private business, took Serajah with him, or whether he obtained there also a new confirmation in his kingdom from Nebuchadnezzar. Whence some perhaps not undeservedly think that in Jer. 28, 1, the fourth year is called the beginning of his reign, namely, as newly confirmed: And it came to pass in that year in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah King of Judah in the fourth year in the fifth month. For those who understand it either as the fourth from the Sabbatical year with Bailius and B. Behmius, or with Maldonatus, the Anglo-Douay scholars, and Jacobus Salianus, wish the fourth year to be called the beginning of the reign because it was before the middle of that reign, hardly deserve assent. There is no trace that the Sabbatical year is counted here: and it seems harsh that the fourth year of the reign is called the beginning of the same in the same respect. Let a different respect therefore prevail here, so that it was the fourth year from the first beginning: but the beginning of the reign more as now confirmed by Nebuchadnezzar.

QUESTION XVIII. How does the Beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, commemorated in Jer. 27, 1, stand?

Some say the passage is corrupt, and judge that the name of Zedekiah should be substituted for the name of Jehoiakim; Joseph Scaliger, on the contrary, in Par. Jac. Salianus at the year M. 3426, and also D. Joh. Behmius in Manud. Chronol. p. 746. Others, with Hippolytus of Portus, or whoever was the author of the Chronicle written in the 13th year of Alexander Severus, and Epiphanius in book 1 of the Panarion, think that Zedekiah was also called Jehoiakim. Since indeed v. 3, through the ambassadors, who were about to come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah King of Judah, the Prophet was commanded to signify the will of God to the nations of the neighboring regions, whence in the time of Zedekiah the word of the Lord seems to have been made to him: just as also in v. 12 Jeremiah asserts that he had spoken to Zedekiah according to all those words. But there is no need for a suspicion of an error, nor is a corruption of the Hebrew text to be admitted in any way, because to do so is, in the judgment of Baillie, not to untie the Gordian knot, but to cut it, and in order to avoid one inconvenience, to be precipitated into another far greater; nor does that δυσωνυμία of King Zedekiah rest on any foundation. But from an accurate inspection of the text and a collation of the times, the time of the revelation of Jeremiah made here under the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, which is referred to in the first 11 verses of chapter 27, must be distinguished from the time of the revelation proposed by Jeremiah to the King, the Priests, and the people: which is referred to in the latter 11 verses of the chapter. Thus, therefore, in the former part, the Prophet was commanded to prepare for himself bonds and yokes for that time in which Zedekiah would reign, but it is not indicated that at that time, when the revelation was made to the Prophet, Zedekiah was already reigning, nor does it follow that the Prophet walked in bonds for the whole 11 or 14 years from the first of Jehoiakim to the first or fourth of Zedekiah, as it seemed to Cornelius a Lapide: For although this prophecy was revealed to Jeremiah at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, it was not yet put into execution, nor was it to be put into execution, before the ambassadors had come to Jerusalem after the Kingdom had been entered upon by Zedekiah. And Codomannus judges in his annals for the year of the World 3512, that therefore eleven years before the reign of Zedekiah the word of the Lord was made to Jeremiah concerning sending a yoke to five kings by ambassadors sent to King Zedekiah, so that the Prophet might know that he was not to fear for his life from the impious King Jehoiakim: upon whose death he was to hand over the yoke to the ambassadors to be sent to the new successor in his kingdom who would have the name of Zedekiah.

QUESTION XIX.

How manifold is the deportation of the Jews that took place under Nebuchadnezzar?

It seems to be gathered from Jer. 52, 28 seqq. that there was only a triple deportation: the first in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, by which 3023 were led to Babylon: the second in the 18th year, by which 832 souls were led away from Jerusalem. The third, by which Nebuchadnezzar led away 745 souls from Judea through Nebuzaradan in the 23rd year of his reign. But if the passages 2 Chron. 36 and 2 Kings 24 & 25 are compared, it will be manifest that the Jews were transported on other occasions still under Nebuchadnezzar, and in a different number: For the opinion of Rabanus cannot have a place, that those same captivities are in those historical passages which Jeremiah designated there: so that the first of Jeremiah must be placed in the transportation of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah in 2 Chron. 36, the second in the transmigration of Jeconiah in 2 Kings 24. The third in the destruction of the city and Temple under Zedekiah: For thus it would have to be said that all the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syrian, Greek, and Latin codices were falsified regarding the years, and that for the seventh year one must read the first in the first captivity, in the second for the eighteenth one must read the eighth, in the third for the twenty-third one must read the nineteenth year, whence Melchior Cano, L. 9, Loc. Theol. c. 5, and Emmanuel Sa in his notes on Jer. 52, who warns that this deals with other translations than those of 4 Kings, reject that opinion of Rabanus. Add that the number of persons also demands that we understand different translations, since in the translation of Jehoiakim made in the 1st year of Nebuchadnezzar, 3023 Jews are nowhere read to have been transported in the historical accounts. But in the transmigration of Jeconiah, in the 8th year of Nebuchadnezzar, not 832 souls were led away, but 10,000, as is had in 2 Kings 24, 14. Finally, in the destruction of the city under Zedekiah in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, that number of captives which Jeremiah designated, 745, is not expressed in 2 Kings 25, nor is it likely that so few were led away then, with the city destroyed and the citizens evacuated, Jer. 39, 8, 9. What is more, that Judah is said to have migrated then from its land, with only vinedressers and diggers left in it, 2 Kings 25, 11, 21, whence no sane person would have dreamed of such a tiny number of those transported there.

Wherefore it must be admitted that those captivities described here in the books of Kings and Chronicles are entirely different from those which Jeremiah set forth. Nor without reason does Jac. Capellus in his Chronology, at the year of the World 3398 and 3414, make some deportations greater and others lesser. Three greater ones, which are described in the historical books, occurred in the 1st, 8th, and 19th years of Nebuchadnezzar: but three lesser ones noted by Jeremiah occurred in the 7th, 18th, and 23rd years: in which latter three the Prophet recorded that only 4600 souls were carried away, if they are gathered into a sum: whereas in the middle of the greater captivities alone, twice as many were transported.

Therefore, regarding these captivities, it must be held that first, indeed, in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, the fourth of Jehoiakim, the Lord delivered Jehoiakim into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, with part of the vessels of the House of God (Dan. 1, 2), which some gather was done in the 9th month, or Chislev, from the anniversary fast instituted on that month and day in memory, as it seems, of that calamity, Jer. 36, 9. Although indeed Jehoiakim was bound in chains by Nebuchadnezzar to be led away to Babylon (2 Chron. 36, 6), yet having agreed to conditions, he afterwards remained a servant in Jerusalem for three years.

The second abduction took place in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, but the tenth of Jehoiakim, after he had rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar following three years of servitude. For then, an army having been sent in, consisting of troops of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites, concerning which see 2 Kings 24, 1 seqq., those 3023 designated by Jeremiah in ch. 52, 28 were deported, which was also observed by the author of the Sicilian Fasti.

Accordingly, that occurred six years after Jehoiakim's servitude, and a full year before that great first deportation made under his successor Jeconiah, which was already the third captivity or deportation, made in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar, nearly completed, by which King Jeconiah was abducted with his mother and wives, and courtiers, and from all of Jerusalem both all the officials and all those strong in vigor, 10,000 captives, and all the woodworkers and blacksmiths, where none were left in Jerusalem except the poor people of the land; and from the rest of the region, moreover, 7,000 strong men and 1,000 woodworkers and blacksmiths, all robust and warriors, were abducted as captives to Babylon 2 Kings 24, 8 seqq., 2 Chron. 36, 10, Jer. 24, 1, ch. 29, 2, Ez. 17, 12 seqq.

The fourth occurred in the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar, who had surrounded Jerusalem with a siege, but when the forces of Pharaoh Hophra (or Vaphres) had gone out from Egypt to bring help to King Zedekiah of Judah, the Chaldeans departed from Jerusalem to meet them, and then Nebuchadnezzar caused 832 souls to be deported to Babylon from those who had defected to him before the siege of Jerusalem was lifted, Jer. 52, 29. For the deported Jerusalemites were of two kinds, as is gathered from 2 Kings 25, 11, Jer. 39, 9, and 52, 15. Some, induced partly by fear and partly by Jeremiah's persuasion (ch. 21, 9, ch. 38, 2), defected from the besieged city to the Babylonians: others remained in the city. Since therefore in the tenth year of Zedekiah, when the Egyptian army was approaching, the Chaldeans were forced to interrupt the siege, they sent those 832 Jerusalemites who had defected to them to Babylon in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, which we are taught by Jer. 32, 1 corresponds to the tenth of Zedekiah. The fifth [deportation] occurred in the following nineteenth year during the destruction of the city and temple, where, the walls of the city having been torn down, those who had been left in the city, and those who had defected to the King of Babylon along with the rest of the common people and the treasures of the King and the Princes, and the instruments of the house of God, were led away by Nebuzaradan into Babylonia Jer. 39, 8. ch. 52, 14. seqq. 2. Kings 25, 10. seqq. 2. Chron. 36, 18. seqq. Thus Judah migrated from its land Jer. 52, 17. 2. Kings 25, 21. in the 134th year from the destruction of the Israelite kingdom. Finally, the sixth and most recent deportation was of the remnants of the Jews and Israelites, who had still remained in the land of Judah after the destruction, and had not fled into Egypt Jer. 42. & 43. led away in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar, the heads are numbered at 745. Jer. 52, 20. Whence, since the land was left completely uncultivated in that extreme desolation, the 390 years of the sins of Israel and the 40 years of the sins of Judah had their end Ezech. 4, 5. 6. From these it is clear that those are mistaken who wish to describe in Jer. 52, 28. seqq. all the deportations that happened in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, and from there conclude that no captivity occurred in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (inasmuch as that is not commemorated by Jeremiah), against the most open letter of Dan. 1. v. 1. & 2. But if indeed this inference holds, then the spontaneous migration of Jeconiah will not be a captivity either, inasmuch as Jeremiah also omitted that one in that enumeration ch. 52, 28. from which nothing is more certain than that not all deportations are listed there.

may come: for which reason some distinguish, as noted by D. Behm, the time of the remission of the captivity in part, and the time of the plenary consummation of the captivity and liberty. Some begin the remission in part from the first year of Cyrus, others from the 10th, others from the 20th. They end the consummation in the second year of Darius Hystaspis, as can be seen in Clement of Alexandria, Augustine book 18 de civitate Dei ch. 26, and Eusebius in his Chronicle and book X of the Praeparatio Evangelica ch. 3, just as their opinion was reported in the Manud. Chronol. p. 112. And indeed there is no doubt that 70 years elapsed from the destruction of the temple to the second year of Darius Hystaspis, according to the Eusebian position: For from the conflagration of the temple to the first year of Cyrus in Persia 30 years are counted, and from there to his death likewise 30 years, by the common consent of chronologists, to which if one adds 8 of Cambyses with the 7 months of the Magi and two of Darius Hystaspis, there result 70 years. But since it is more certain than certain from Holy Scripture that the years of the Babylonian captivity had elapsed while Cyrus was alive, Is. 44, 28. 2. Chron. 36, 22, how can they be extended to the second year of Darius? Nor is there anywhere in the Holy Scriptures either a term from which fixed at the destruction, or a term to which in the second year of Darius. For the question here is not about the term of the desolation of the temple, but about the term of the captivity of the Jews. Then if the years of the captivity are to be begun only from the desolation of the temple, then those who were led away in the time of Jehoiakim, and those in the time of Jeconiah, would have been detained in captivity for 81, and some even for 89 years, which is repugnant to divine truth and promise. Finally, this opinion, as the blessed D. Behm observed, is today rejected by all chronologists: and rests on nothing but a false interpretation of the passage 1. Chron. 36, 21. Chron. 36, 21. in which it is not said that at that time, when the city is destroyed, the 70 years began, but until the 70 years were completed, the land rested in its Sabbaths with a penal rest and Sabbatization, which Moses threatened in Levit. 26, 33. seqq., and it concerns the 70 years not as beginning, but as running and being completed.

QUESTION XX.

Question 20. Which deportation gave the beginning to the 70 years of the Babylonian Captivity, and what is its term from which, as also the term to which?
