Since there were such diverse deportations, in those which we called the lesser ones, no one easily fixed the beginning of this Epoch, which is placed by these, those, and others in the remaining ones, which are called the greater ones, namely the first, third, and fifth, which are said to have happened in the first, eighth, and nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. For these are the more important opinions concerning the term from which of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity. First, that we may proceed in reverse order, it is the opinion of those who fix the beginning of the Epoch and the term from which at the destruction of the city and temple, and the deportation then made, namely in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar. Who constitute the term to which as the second year of Darius Hystaspis. Which Eusebius embraced as true in his Chronological Canon at the 4th year of the 54th Olympiad. In truth, those 70 years are to be begun from the desolation of the temple from the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar up to the second year of Darius Hystaspis. They agree as to the starting point, which not a few chronologers, both ancient and especially modern, and most of all the followers of Funccius, as well as the Jesuits Salianus and Torniellus and the Calvinist Dr. Nisbet, as also Bucholzerus, do not: Although as to the ending point not Another opinion fixes the starting point in the voluntary migration of Jeconiah, and establishes the ending point in the 28th year of the Persian reign of Cyrus, which is embraced by Scaliger, Tremellius, Calvisius, Dr. Behmius in his Manud. Chronol., and Grotius, following Clement of Alexandria: But that deserves no consideration. For (1.) in the Holy Scriptures neither the starting point nor the ending point of that famous 70 years' captivity is ever defined in such a way; nay, the ending point is openly designated in the first year of the monarchy of Cyrus, 2 Chron. 36, 22. Ezra 1, 1, which certainly was not the 28th year of his Persian reign: Whence it is clear that that ending point contradicts the definition made by the Holy Spirit Himself; constrained by the evidence of which passage, the Scaligerians sometimes invent a double beginning of the monarchy of Cyrus, one Biblical, the other exotic, which they claim is designated by profane writers: sometimes they pervert the sacred text with a new ψευδερμηνείᾳ, as if not the first year of Cyrus were definitely expressed (which hitherto all interpreters without exception have maintained) but indefinitely ONE, whosoever that may have been, YEAR; whereas nothing is better known than that a cardinal number is used for an ordinal among the Hebrews, ONE for FIRST, nor did the Holy Spirit intend for us to hesitate concerning the end of the captivity, or the beginning of the people's liberty, that the captivity was relaxed and liberty granted to the people in some ONE year of the monarchy of Cyrus, but that he has accurately defined the Epoch, and thus taught, that at the very beginning of the Monarchy of Cyrus, in the very first year, what had been predicted and promised was fulfilled, and he has designated the end of the 70 years which he had determined.

(2) That transmigration of Jeconiah under Nebuchadnezzar was not the first captivity or servitude, but he acknowledges others prior to it, especially that by which even the King of Judah himself was bound in chains and made a servant of Nebuchadnezzar, namely Jehoiakim; in the fourth year of his reign, the first of Nebuchadnezzar:

(3.) Nor indeed do Ezra and the author of the Chronicles place the end in the first year of Cyrus; but Jeremiah also prophesied in ch. XXV, 12 that those 70 years of captivity would end in the overthrow of the Monarchy of the Chaldeans. It is certain, however, that Babylon was captured and the Monarchy of the Chaldeans overthrown before the twenty-eighth year of Cyrus. And the fact that Scaliger and Calvisius, following the Rabbis, attribute only three years to the Monarchy of Cyrus is against the faith of almost all the ancients and moderns: But the fact that they do not refer the first year of Cyrus to the beginning of the Persian kingdom nor to that of his Monarchy in Ezra and the Chronicles; but make the first year in a new era, instituted by the Jews for their liberation, is not only merely precarious, but openly contradicts Ezra ch. VI, 2. Where even among the Persians, in the Royal edict, the captivity is said to have ended in the first year of Cyrus, and not in the first year of Jewish liberty. From the 8th year of Nebuchadnezzar, in which Jeconiah was carried away, to the Monarchy of Cyrus, 70 years did not elapse, but only 62, as the chronological calculation teaches. Hence the Scaligerians torment themselves vehemently here. Mr. Dr. Behmius, while he wishes to support this opinion, also inclines toward the shortening of those 70 years in his discussion of the term from which and to which of the Babylonian Captivity, in the year 1633, at Königsberg, in a public disputation proposed as thesis XXXVII. What if GOD, by the power of His mercy, in response to the ardent prayers of Daniel and the rest, to those deported with Jeconiah, had shortened that interval of 70 years to the space of one or two years, and Cyrus, according to this opinion, had survived for several years after the captivity was released? But while the opinion of Scaliger stands, the time of the Babylonian empire of Cyrus, during which he could say, 'The GOD of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth,' cannot be known, and thus neither can the true time of the released Babylonian captivity be known: as can be seen from Scaliger's notes to the fragments, pp. 16, 18.

(4) It is necessary to invent a third beginning for Cyrus: since the first is that of his Persian kingdom, used in exotic history: the second that of the Babylonian kingdom, accepted in the Holy Scriptures: but the third, according to Scaliger, arising in the 28th year of Cyrus the Persian, of Jewish liberty, which was subsequently not undeservedly rejected by Dr. Behmius himself, because it has no foundation in sacred or profane history.

(5.) As it is evident from Herodotus, Trogus, Justin, and other historians that Cyrus did not set foot into the Babylonian kingdom before his 20th year, so it appears from Ptolemy's Canon, which the Scaligerians revere as divine, and other documents, that nine years are to be attributed to the Monarchy of Cyrus, and that he aspired to the Monarchy after the 21st year of his Persian reign, and not finally in the 28th year.

(6.) Baillie urges in his Historical Chronological work, p. 146, that in Matth. I, 11. 12, the Babylonian captivity and transmigration is denominated from that Jeconiah who had brothers, i.e., according to many and the best interpreters, from Jehoiakim, the father of Jeconiah: and that those who take this passage concerning Jeconiah the son, must necessarily begin the captivity before Jeconiah had begotten any children: since Matthew says he begat Salathiel after the Babylonian captivity.

(7.) That opinion is repugnant to antiquity, for which the Scaligerians can bring forward no testimonies, except that of Clement of Alexandria alone, concerning the beginning to be taken from

Jechoniah's migration, although they do not deny that various and diverse opinions can be found concerning the same. In this disagreement of the ancients, says B. Behmius in Manuduction. Chronolog. p. 112. WE CANNOT wonder enough, for what reason they did not begin those years of captivity from the spontaneous transportation of Jechoniah: And in the previously praised discussion thes. X. WE CANNOT wonder enough, why he wrapped in deep silence that opinion, which terminates the term from which the LXX of those Babylonian subjugations ends in the spontaneous and most solemn deportation of Jechoniah from Judea to Babylon. But of this so solemn a term in the Ecclesiastical antiquity of the New Testament, THERE ARE SCARCELY ANY traces of remains, except for Clement of Alexandria ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ στρωμάτων, so they cannot but seize the minds of the learned with admiration, why the ancient Christians as it were completely set aside such a term of such a solemn abduction, and one made by divine counsel and command, in which the flower of the people was abducted, and which Ezekiel holds as sacred with a certain curious solicitude. However, he who, having set aside the Scaligerian hypothesis, has compared both sacred and exotic history with the Prophet Jeremiah and Daniel, will easily cease to wonder why the ancients did not adopt that deportation, as they discovered it to be in no way consistent. It would indeed be altogether wonderful if it were so consistent, as the Scaligerians maintain; since in all antiquity that consistency has been so little observed that one can scarcely find any traces of remains of that opinion in it.

But neither can they safely appeal to Clement of Alexandria. For he indeed designated the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, when Jechoniah reigned at the beginning of the captivity of the LXX years, yet he speaks inconsistently about it in the same place: for he also designated the eleventh year of Zedekiah. Nebuchadnezzar, he says, leads the blinded Zedekiah to Babylon, and makes the whole people migrate. Now this captivity was the captivity of the LXX years: And he established the end in the second year of Darius Hystaspes: but if we count back LXX years from this, it will not fall into the time of the deportation of Jechoniah, but of the destruction of the city and the temple. Furthermore, when he counted 482 years, 6 months, 10 days from the reign of David to the captivity which was made by the Chaldeans, a little later he designated 572 years, 6 months, 10 days from the reign of David to the restoration of the people. By what means are LXX years, and not XC, discovered to have flowed from the captivity μέχρι τῆς ἀποκαταστάσεως τοῦ λαοῦ until the restoration of the people proclaimed by the public decree of Darius?

How much support, therefore, Scaliger has in Clement, and whether this opinion of his is a completely new discovery, unknown to all antiquity, we now leave to be judged.

His protection is sought in vain from Ezekiel: for although Ezekiel institutes his calculation, and counts the years from the migration of Jechoniah, as he himself was also abducted by it and with which the years of Zedekiah began, yet by no indication, or even obscurely, does he demonstrate that those LXX years of captivity are counted by him: so that it is altogether wonderful that illustrious men have defined with such confidence from Ezekiel the beginning of those famous LXX years of Babylonian captivity, of which not a jot is found in Ezekiel. See what we have said to the annotations of Grotius on Jerem. XXIX, 10. and Ezech. XL, 1.

However, Mr. Dr. Behmius, when he was still occupied with the Scaligerian opinion, had arguments which he used to strengthen the same, Manud. Chron. p. 108. But they are easily dissolved. First of all, he thinks it is most clear that Ezekiel refers the 25th year of the captivity to the 14th of the destruction of the temple c. XLI, 1. by which reasoning he also refers the ninth year of the captivity to the time of the beginning of the siege chap. I, 2. c. XXIV, 1. and the twelfth year to that time, in which in the previous year the city had been struck c. XXXIII, 21. Answer. Ezekiel c. XL, 1. c. XXXIII, 21. has it thus; this happened in the XXV year. this in the XII year of our captivity, or rather migration. captivity and of those who were led away with him; he does not indeed designate that captivity, or that abduction, for which LXX years were divinely defined, which the Prophet Jeremiah had predicted: nay, which abduction he understands c. I, 2. he had already expressed: by which indeed Jeconiah had been led away captive, which he calls his own, because he had been led away at the same time, as Josephus relates l. X. Antiq. c. 8. he does not indeed point out the years of that solemn Epoch of captivity, nor does any character appear, from which it is certain that they are referred to.

Secondly, it is urged from Jer. c. XXIX. that the Prophet, intending to console the people, promised them liberation after the lapse of LXX years verse 2. 10. Answer. (1) There is expressed there in verse 2. the time of the written consolatory Epistle, after indeed Jeconiah with the Queen (mother) and court princes and others had been led away: but the beginning of the Epoch of the LXX years is not designated. (2) Even if in verse 10. liberation is promised when the LXX years are completed, yet there is not indicated there by any document the beginning of that solemn Epoch of these LXX years of captivity, nor is it hinted that they are to be begun first from the abduction of Jeconiah. For this beginning he had already indicated in c. XXV, 11. Nor indeed because in c. XXIX. the solution of the captivity is promised, when the LXX years are finished, is the beginning of the same indicated by that very fact to be taken from the time of this promise, unless also someone with some of the ancients wishes for that reason to begin them from the XIII year of Josiah, because in that year Jeremiah, promising the solution of the captivity, began to prophesy, so that they might end in the first year of Cyrus. Which could seem the more likely, because from the XIII year of Josiah to the first of Cyrus there are precisely LXX years, according to the standing allegation of the ancients; which opinion is however deservedly rejected by Scaliger. Nor finally when the Lord says v. 10. I will visit you, are those led away with Jeconiah precisely indicated, but ALL the migration is addressed v. 4. and so also that which had taken place in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and also that which had taken place in the seventh (Jeremiah c. LII, 28.): for the Lord was not leaving them without consolation: which would have to be said, if these things concerned only those led away in the third transportation, or voluntary surrender.

Thirdly, the blessed Dr. Behmius urges that the LXX years are to be counted from that captivity in which the flower of the Jewish people, and its greatest number, was led away, which he gathers from the captivity of Jeconiah from 2. Kings XXIV, 12. Jer. LII, 15. Ez. XVII, 12. 13. which also in Jer. XXIX, 4. 6. is called the deportation κατʼ ἐξοχὴν. Answer. The major proposition wavers: for why should we begin the years of captivity from that captivity in which the flower of the people and the greatest number was led away, rather than from the first, in which the captivity of the Jewish people took its beginning. Which certainly does not exclude the subsequent ones, nay it drew them after itself, and was the auspices of them, especially indeed of that which followed seven years later in the time of Jeconiah, because that abduction was made not so much on account of Jeconiah, who presided for only a three-month space, as on account of his father Jehoiakim, who reigned for 11 years, and had defected from Nebuchadnezzar; and it was as it were a continuation of the former deportation, just as the rest continued the preceding ones, until finally all had been led away, and no remnants remained in Judea. Nor is it to be admitted that Jer. XXVIII, 4. 6. treats only of the deportation made under Jeconiah: because liberation is promised by the Pseudo-Prophet Hananiah to ALL who had been deported up to that time: not only to those led away in that one deportation. Not to mention that Scaliger himself speaks of the abduction of Jehoiakim and Jeconiah as one and the same, if indeed although in l. IV. de emend. temp. he fixes the beginning of the LXX years in the I of Jeconiah, when Ezekiel was led away with the King and others, but not in the fourth of Jehoiakim, when Daniel migrated to Babylon with others. Yet in Book V. he says that Daniel and Ezekiel were led away to Babylon at the same time, not otherwise than if the captivity of Jeconiah and Jehoiakim were one and the same.

Wherefore, having now set aside the two more celebrated opinions concerning the Epoch of the 70 years, it remains that we adopt the third, which fixes the beginning at the abduction and captivity of Jehoiakim, in his fourth year, the first of Nebuchadnezzar, and the end at the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus: which is most consonant with Scripture, nay, is supported by most lucid characters, superior to every exception. For (1) since six deportations are commemorated in the Holy Scriptures, this was the first of all, of which the rest, as we have said, were certain quasi-continuations at different times, yet under the same King Nebuchadnezzar. Moreover, it is more convenient that the number of the years of the captivity be reckoned from the first beginning of the captivity than from any other term, since indeed Nebuchadnezzar, having made an expedition on account of the rebellion of the Satrap of Egypt and Coele-Syria and Phoenicia against the kingdom of Babylon, and having overcome the rebels, and having subdued the Syro-Egyptian region, proceeded to Jerusalem and made Jehoiakim, King of Judah—formerly a tributary to Pharaoh Necho, whom Nebuchadnezzar had defeated—a vassal and tributary to the Babylonian King, his father, while at the same time the Prophet Daniel with his companions, and others, were abducted into Babylon, as well as a good part of the vessels of the house of the Lord 2 Kings 24, 1. Jer. 46, 2. Dan. 1, 1. 2. For did not the abduction of the Jews into Babylon begin immediately from that very time (so asks D. Behmius in the Disputation on the year 1646 held at Königsberg, where, having dismissed the former, he chose our opinion)? Did not the last three Kings of the Jews, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, become vassals of the Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar from that time? Did not Judea become tributary to the Babylonian King from that time? Those who deny that the captivity occurred here openly resist the Holy Spirit Dan. 1, 1. 2. Although King Jehoiakim was indeed sent back, it was nevertheless necessary for him to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and when he shook off the yoke, Nebuchadnezzar, having sent an army, devastated Judea 2 Kings XXIV, 1. 2. and 302 Jews were abducted Jer. LII, 28. which was done before the voluntary surrender of the son of Jehoiakim. Nor, however, was Jehoiakim not a captive, or did the Babylonian captivity not yet begin, because the King himself is said to have remained and reigned for some years: because he had indeed been a captive and bound in chains: and some of the royal family were abducted into Babylon at that time, as were the sons of the nobles Dan. I, 3. And are the Scaligerians therefore going to say that the captivity did not begin in the time of Jeconiah, because afterwards his brother Zedekiah still reigned in Judea, even though he was a subject to Nebuchadnezzar? The artifice is therefore without consequence in their own argument, as D. Behmius likes to say elsewhere.

Secondly, Jer. XXV, 1 openly confirms our opinion. This is the word that came to Jeremiah concerning ALL the people of Judah, in the FOURTH year of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah, King of Judah, which is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babel. For in this very chapter v. 11, that Epoch was defined by Jeremiah, and those nations shall serve the King of Babel 70 years: but when those 70 years have been completed, I will visit the King in Babel etc. and so that we might not be ignorant of its beginning, Section VI. The fourth year of Jehoiakim was designated, and the same is linked with the first year of Nebuchadnezzar: in which he himself also first came into Judea, and subjugated it. (2) For that reason Jeremiah wished to repeat how, from the thirteenth year up to that fourth year of Jehoiakim, he had for 23 years recalled the people to repentance v. 3. & because he was unwilling to lend an ear, hence he threatens πανωλεθρίαν (total destruction) through Nebuchadnezzar to the whole region, and servitude of 70 years. From the thirteenth of Josiah UNTIL this day the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have preached to you now diligently for 23 years, i.e., now therefore is the time of divine judgment: until this day the long-suffering of God has invited you. (3) The Prophet added, moreover, that he had now (in this fourth year of Jehoiakim) received the cup from the hand of the Lord, to give to drink to all nations, but especially to Jerusalem, and to the other towns of Judea: and to the princes, that he might give them into desolation v. 15. 16. 17. from whom he was making a beginning, as he says in v. 21: Behold, in that city, which is called by my name, I AM MAKING A BEGINNING of the plagues. (4) Note must be taken in v. 17 of the ἔνδειξις (indication) of the Prophet: AS IS THIS DAY, indicating that at that time that desolation and devastation had already begun, so that in this place both the term from which and the term to which of the Babylonian captivity and servitude are designated.

Thirdly, the prophetic linking of the liberation of the people and the visitation of the King of Babylon contributes to this. For Jeremiah joins this visitation of the King of Babylon with the liberation of the people at the term to which of the captivity in c. XXV, 12, composing it thus: when the 70 years have been fulfilled, I will visit upon the King of Babylon. Therefore, what things are joined and linked by the Holy Spirit at the term of the captivity, those are not to be disjoined and separated in chronological calculation. But they would be disjoined and separated if the term to which were not the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus of the Persian reign, 22 or as others wish 24, but finally the 28th year of the same in the Persian kingdom. On the contrary, however, the end of the 70 years and the liberation of the people coincide with the end of the Babylonian kingdom in the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, as is evident from 2 Chron. last and Ezra I.

Fourthly, Daniel chapter I, 1 seqq. agrees with the Prophet Jeremiah. Namely, that in the third year completed (at the beginning of the fourth) of Jehoiakim, the surrender of King Jehoiakim took place, and the vessels were carried away from the house of the Lord with the chosen ones from the people of the Royal lineage and the nobles; among whom Daniel himself was with his companions. In which chapter, when it is noted near the end that Daniel lived until the first year of Cyrus, the term to which of the captivity is designated equally, just as by Jeremiah c. XXV. We have observed that both the term from which and the term to which were expressed.

Fifthly, the prediction of Isaiah chapter XXXIX, 7, made to Hezekiah, must also be compared, that with the treasures of the kingdom the royal seed is to be carried away into Babylon, and there it is to serve, and his descendants are to be eunuchs in the Palace of the King of Babylon. For that abduction is undoubtedly looked to, which Daniel designated in c. I, 1, and from it the beginning of the calamity and servitude of the Jews is deduced: from which, however, the same Prophet promised liberation through Cyrus in c. XLIV, 28, so that in this way both terms of the Babylonian servitude were insinuated by Isaiah also, both the term from which and the term to which.

Sixthly, the term to which or the end of the years of captivity is clearly expressed in 2 Chron. XXXVI, 13, Ezra I, 1, c. VI, 3, c. V, 13, that namely it was the first year of Cyrus, when the captivity was released, which cannot be understood otherwise than of the first year of Cyrus of his Monarchy, in which he could finally say, The Lord has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. From which if 70 years are counted backward, it will be manifest that the beginning cannot fall otherwise than as we assign it; nor can it be referred to the voluntary migration of Jeconiah, since 70 years did not intervene from that to the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus.

Seventhly, therefore, the completion must be observed above all. For from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, with which the first year of Nebuchadnezzar is linked, Jer. XXV, 1, which year was the 140th Nabonassarean, up to the first year of the Monarchy, or the 23rd year of the Persian reign of Cyrus, 70 years are counted. For that first year of Cyrus is the 210th Nabonassarean, if the calculation is entered according to the Babylonian Monarchy, with the canon of Ptolemy preceding; and since Nebuchadnezzar reigned for 43 years, Evil-Merodach 2, Neriglossar 4, Laborosoarchod 9 months, Nabonidus 17 years, 60 years emerge from there, and thus 4 years are missing according to this calculation: which, according to D. Behm in his later Chronological writings, is because Nebuchadnezzar reigned for a four-year period with his parent, and ruled alone for 43 years, as observed in the Annot. Anti-Grotian. on c. XXIX of Jeremiah. The Eusebian method of counting also agrees with this: For Eusebius, according to the opinion of Africanus, counts 30 years from the Jerusalemite πανωλεθρίᾳ (total destruction) to the beginning of the reign of Cyrus the Persian: connecting the year of the extermination with the 2nd year of the 47th Olympiad, or the 186th Olympic year, but making the first year of Cyrus the first of the 55th Olympiad, that is, the 216th Olympic year. If to these are added the 18 years from the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar to the year of the extermination of the temple, and the 22 years of the rule of Cyrus the Persian up to his Monarchy, 70 years will emerge; indeed, the same B. D. Behm observes that all chronologists, both Christian and profane, with a clearly unanimous consensus count only 30 years from the conflagration of the Solomonic temple to the beginning of the Persian reign, and 60 years to the death of Cyrus. Now since the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar, whose first year coincides with the fourth of Jehoiakim, was the year of the total destruction of the temple, 78 years will emerge from the first year of Nebuchadnezzar to the death of Cyrus, and thus 8 years before his death, with the 70 years of the captivity having elapsed, he granted liberty to the people. These things are thus according to the calculation of Dr. Behm. From whom Ussher does not depart much, in the term to which, and the assignment of the completion, differing only by a biennium, which he assigns to Darius the Mede, the father-in-law of Cyrus, after Babylon was taken: so that the Monarchy of Cyrus lasted seven years with one or two months. Concerning which determination, which deserves to be preferred, we shall see later. However, they agree on this (which suffices for us here), that the term to which of the captivity is none other than the beginning of the Monarchy of Cyrus, and that it is not to be begun from elsewhere than from the fourth year of Jehoiakim.

We therefore finally add to these documents the authority of great men, who, whether regarding the term from which, or regarding the term to which, or regarding both, are with us. For even if another beginning of the Epoch is assigned by some, while they are in agreement regarding the term to which or the end of the same, they are led in any case, whether they wish it or not, by counting back the 70 years to the same beginning which is assigned by us; nor can they assign it otherwise, without prejudice to chronological truth, since it is established from Herodotus, Trogus, Justin, and other historians that Cyrus did not set foot in the Babylonian kingdom before the twentieth year of his Persian reign, and concerning the time of the Babylonian Monarchy even the Scaligerians can be convinced from the Ptolemaic Canon. Thus Dr. Behm in Chronolog. Manud. (in which he still adhered to the footsteps of Scaliger) book II, title II, chapter III. The third year of Jehoiakim is the third year of the 43rd Olympiad, or the 167th Olympiadic year. & by the allegation of the ancients the twentieth year of Cyrus is the first of the 60th Olympiad, or the 237th Olympiadic year. if 167 are subtracted from this number, 70 remain. He acknowledges, however, that this was the opinion of the ancients there regarding the term from which and to which. That this already flourished before Eusebius is apparent from his Chronicle canon: The whole time of the captivity of the Jews is gathered to be 70 years, which according to SOME are computed from the third year of Eliakim (who is also Jojakim) until the 19th of Cyrus, King of the Persians. To these are added from the more recent ones the Beroaldists, Walton, James Ussher, Robert Baillie, Dionysius Petavius, Henry Philippi, and other most excellent chronologists; also from the followers of Scaliger, the blessed Lord Dr. Johann Behmius in his later writings. In the Theological-Historical-Chronological discussion of the term from which and to which of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, or servitude, accurately (as the title holds) extracted from Biblical and profane historical truth, as also from the celestial canon of Ptolemy, proposed at Königsberg in the year 1633 §. 32. it holds thus: According to this term of Babylonian servitude (since the 70 years of captivity begin from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria in the 3rd year of Jojakim completed, Daniel 1:1, the 4th current of Jeremiah 25:1, and are finished in the 21st of Cyrus, King of the Persians) every difficulty which is accustomed to be raised concerning these years is removed. Thus the relaxation of the captivity was made while Cyrus was living, nine full years before his death. And indeed, Scripture speaks almost everywhere that the Babylonian servitude of the Jews took its true beginning from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Palestine, and from there continued until the times of Cyrus. For from that time, when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho in a great battle at the Euphrates in the 4th year of Jojakim, Jer. 46:2, and occupied a good part of Egypt, Judea (which Pharaoh Necho had previously made tributary, 2 Kings 23:33, and following, 2 Chron. 36:2) came under the tribute of the Babylonian kingdom. For Nebuchadnezzar, returning from Egypt, besieged Jerusalem, occupied it, and made Jojakim tributary for three years, 2 Kings 24:1, and at the same time sent Daniel with his companions and many others to Babylon. Behold the beginning of the Babylonian servitude? In the passage of time, when Jojakim, King of Judah, rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar and defected, Nebuchadnezzar, almost at the end of the seventh year of his reign, came to Jerusalem again, and seized the rebellious king of Judah and cast him into chains, with the intention of taking him to Babylon, but in truth he was cast out unburied in chains, Jer. 22:19, ch. 36:30, 2 Chron. 36:6. Jojakim having died in chains, Jechoniah succeeded for only three months, after which he gave himself voluntarily to the Babylonian King, and was taken to Babylon with his mother, wife, princes, and the flower of the whole people, with Mathaniah or Zedekiah substituted as tributary, 2 Kings 24:17, for 11 years. He subjoins thesis 33. In our Chronological manual we were somewhat more unfavorable to this opinion regarding the term FROM WHICH of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria, from the fourth of Jojakim, King of Judah. But in the passage of time, having considered the matter and the circumstances of the matter more deeply, we became more favorable, and we established that from this term FROM WHICH to the last of Nabonidus, the Median Babylonian King, whom Cyrus conquered, precisely 70 years had elapsed. Which most sweet agreement leads me to easily add my calculation to those who make this the term FROM WHICH of the 70 years of servitude. Although indeed in thesis 39 he gave a free option to all and individual lovers of Historical-Chronological study, as to which opinion they might wish to choose, whether that which begins the years of servitude from the 4th of Jojakim and the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria, and finishes in the 21st of Cyrus of the Persian kingdom: or the other, which makes the term FROM WHICH of the years of captivity the voluntary deportation of Jechoniah to Babylon, and the term TO WHICH the 28th of Cyrus, King of the Persians, which both opinions he judged could subsist very well without confusion of the chronological system, and that he himself could not entirely set aside the one concerning the beginning from the voluntary migration of Jechoniah, as he still protested in the year 1633 in thesis 34; yet in the last years, having weighed everything more accurately, because of the evidence of Scripture, that opinion having been clearly set aside, without hesitation he embraced the one we have mentioned in the Biblical-Historical-Chronological Theme concerning the first year of Cyrus, the first King of the Persians, which is mentioned in the Sacred Scriptures and by Josephus the Historian, opposed to Benedict Pererius the Jesuit, publicly proposed at the Königsberg Academy in the year 1642: thesis 21. Wherefore, he says, do they depart from the Prophet Jeremiah, who begins the 70 years of Babylonian oppression from the fourth of Jojakim and the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Judea, ch. 25. Did not the abduction of the Jews into Babylonia begin immediately from that time? Were not the last three Kings of the Jews, Jojakim, Jechoniah, and Zedekiah, made vassals of King Nebuchadnezzar from that time? Was not Judea made tributary to the Babylonian King from that time?

Robert Baillie in his Historical and Chronological works, book 1, ch. 8, q. 34, p. 91, and ch. 10, q. 2, p. 144, also grants his assent to us at length, and refutes both those who place the beginning at the destruction of the city, and Scaliger and others who place it at the transmigration of Jechoniah; whence on p. 146 he holds thus: The Babylonian captivity of the Jews had various degrees; the first was in the fourth of Jojakim, the second in the eleventh of Jojakim, or the first of Jechoniah, the third in the eleventh of Zedekiah; the fourth five years after the temple was destroyed, when more than seven hundred of the remnants were led to Babylon by Nebuzaradan. Be it that the third degree was the most noble on account of many circumstances, yet the beginning of the captivity is to be taken not from the third degree, however noble, but from the first. And p. 147. We do indeed concede that the years of the captivity are to be begun with the Monarchy of Nebuchadnezzar, but that was established in his first year, for then he crushed both the Syrians and the Egyptians, just as his father Nabopolassar had subjugated those nations before, unless we wish to gratuitously strip all authority from ancient histories; the victories, however, which he later reported over the Jews or Egyptians were nothing other than the reductions of rebels and the bringing of those previously subjugated into a harsher servitude.

And these are the things concerning the three more celebrated opinions about the Epoch of the years of the captivity. Eusebius does indeed recount in his Chronological Canon at the 4th year of the 54th Olympiad yet another, which makes the beginning from the 13th year of Josiah, King of Judah, under whom Jeremiah began to prophesy; but the end, the first year of King Cyrus. For from that beginning designated in Jeremiah ch. 2 up to the 4th year of Jehoiakim, 23 years are counted, Jerem. 25, 3. Josiah reigned for 31 years, 2 Kings 22, 1; 2 Chron. 34, 1; with 12 full years subtracted, 19 remain; add the 4 years of Jehoiakim, and they become 23. From the 4th year of Jehoiakim to the 11th year of Zedekiah are 40 complete years: indicated in the 40 years of the sins of the house of Judah by Ezekiel ch. 4, 6. From the 11th year of Zedekiah or the destruction of the Solomonic temple to the beginning of the Persian reign of Cyrus, according to the constant and perpetual numbering of Eusebius, there are 30 complete years, which, added to the 40 years collected before, constitute 70 years. Therefore Eusebius opines that this opinion is probable; to the ancients it is not probable, but truly sandy and slippery: and since it rests on no foundation at all, and is now entirely deserted by chronologists, we have therefore studiously neglected to recount it with the others. For there is no indication, not even the slightest, in history, whether sacred or profane, that in the 13th year of Josiah the Babylonian King Nabopolassar, the parent of Nebuchadnezzar, led the Jews into slavery: the beginning of which was made by his own son Nebuchadnezzar from his first arrival in Syria. Nor does that terminus ad quem in any way correspond to historical truth. For Cyrus, at the beginning of his Persian reign, had no right to the Babylonian kingdom, and therefore could not then release the Jews from captivity. For first, as historical truth testifies, he stabilized the Persian kingdom, then he waged war with Croesus, King of the Lydians, for some years, having captured Croesus, captured Sardis, and destroyed the Lydian kingdom, in the 4th and 13th year of the Persian reign. Having defeated the King of the Lydians, he sent Harpagus to subdue the Ionians, who were also defeated. After the above, he subjected the upper parts of Asia to himself, as Herodotus testifies in book 1, in the 15th and 16th year of his Persian reign. Harpagus, having subdued Ionia, led the army into Caria, and subdued them without any trouble. The Lycians, however, resisted Harpagus fiercely, and for a long time, and could not be conquered except by slaughter in the 17th, 18th, and 19th year. Finally, having subdued Ionia, Caria, and Lycia, Cyrus moved against the Babylonians, and most recently attacked Babylon itself, and captured it. Ptolemy indeed in his Mathematical Canon assigns 9 years to Cyrus after Nabonidus, by that very fact implying that the Babylonian reign of Cyrus arises from the 22nd year of the Persian reign, for only when Babylon and the Babylonian kingdom were occupied could Cyrus finally release the Jews from captivity in Babylon.

QUESTION XXI.

How are the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity to be calculated from the 4th year of Jehoiakim to the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus?

The calculation according to Ptolemy's Canon is this: 43 years are assigned to Nebuchadnezzar, namely from the death of his parent Nabopolassar: two to Ilvarodamus (Evil-merodach): 4 to Niricassolassar: 17 to Nabonadius. Which make 66 years. And just as many are also counted in Berosus in Josephus's first book against Apion, and Eusebius, book IX of the Evangelical Preparation, chapter IV, from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Nabonadius. Therefore, 4 years are missing, and to supply them, the more outstanding chronologists enter upon a twofold reasoning. Some seek this only in a different beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar, if indeed one beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar is fixed in Scripture, and another in Ptolemy's canon and in Berosus: It is certain that the latter begin his years from the death of his parent Nabopolassar, while the former begins them from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria and Palestine, which took place while his father was still alive: For Berosus testifies in Josephus, book X of the Antiquities, chapter XI. and book I against Apion, and also in Eusebius, book IX of the Evangelical Preparation, chapter 4, that Nabopolassar, hearing that the Satrap of Egypt and Coele-Syria and Phoenicia had rebelled against the kingdom of Babylon, sent his son, who was still in the flower of his youth, with a good part of his military forces against the rebels, who, having engaged the rebels in several battles, emerged victorious and subdued the Syro-Egyptian region. With this, Scripture agrees, teaching that Nebuchadnezzar, having obtained a signal victory against Pharaoh Necho (who, after defeating Josiah, had despoiled all Judea and had also captured Gaza, a most fortified city, Jer. 47) at Carchemish near the Euphrates, in the 4th year of Jehoiakim (Jer. 46:2), pursued the same and came to Jerusalem, and defeated Jehoiakim, King of Judah, who was previously a tributary of Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:33): whence that first year of the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar is linked with the 4th year of Jehoiakim. And these things are placed beyond the hazard of doubt.

But in what year of his parent Nebuchadnezzar was taken into the partnership of the kingdom is not expressly held in the histories; therefore, from a comparison, some chronologists conclude that he was taken in the 17th year of his parent's reign and sent with an army into Syria and Palestine, and thus reigned for 4 years with his parent; which they think is evident both from the Eusebian calculation and also from the linking of the Nabonassar years: because the last year of Cyrus is the 218th Nabonassar year, and thus his first (since he reigned for 30 years) is the 188th Nabonassar year: and since 49 years are counted from the first of Cyrus to the first of Nebuchadnezzar, those being subtracted from the 188th Nabonassar year, 139 Nabonassar years remain to the first of Nebuchadnezzar. And Ptolemy in his Canon counts 143 years to the first of Nebuchadnezzar. The difference, therefore, is 4 years. Which is also concluded from the annals of the Phoenicians in Josephus's first book against Apion the Grammarian. For they count 49 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the first of the reign of Cyrus; with the 30 years of the reign of Cyrus added, there result 79 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar, according to the Phoenician annals, to the last of Cyrus: whereas the Ptolemaic Canon has only 75 from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Cyrus, namely 66 from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Nabonadius and 9 of Cyrus from the defeat of Babylon. Whence again a difference of 4 years is left. Which comparison, along with the Eusebian calculation and the annals of the Phoenicians, we leave to its own place. And this is the first method of supplying the missing years in the Ptolemaic years of reign, which the blessed Behmius has embraced.

We proceed thus from Biblical Chronology: Jer. 25:1 connects the first year of Nebuchadnezzar with the current fourth year of Jehoiakim: who reigned for eleven years, the last of which is the seventh ending, and the eighth of Nebuchadnezzar beginning, as Mr. Behmius admits from 2 Kings 25:12. Whence the abduction of Jeconiah, who succeeded Jehoiakim and reigned for only 3 months, occurred in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar: and the thirty-seventh year from that transportation will be the 44th year of Nebuchadnezzar, which is called the first of Evil-Merodach in Jer. 52:31. By this arrangement, it does not appear how there is such a difference in the calculation of Scripture regarding the years of Nebuchadnezzar from the Ptolemaic, since 43 years are also assigned to Nebuchadnezzar in Ptolemy's Canon, and the 44th year is the first of Evil-Merodach. Mr. Behmius himself likewise shows the agreement of Berosus with Holy Scripture in Manud. Chronolog. p. 219. They agree regarding the time of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. Scripture attributes to Nebuchadnezzar forty-three absolute years of reign. For the 37th year of the abducted Jeconiah is the first of Evil-Merodach, 2 Kings 25:27, Jer. 52:31. But Jeconiah was abducted to Babylon in the 7th absolute year of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer. 51:28, the 8th current, 2 Kings 24:12. These numbers added together make 43 years, which Scripture attributes to Nebuchadnezzar in his reign. The ancient Berosus, according to Josephus, does the same.

How, therefore, the number of 70 years is fulfilled up to the first year of Cyrus, when the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar does not seem to be calculated much differently, must be examined in Sacred history. Ussher's calculation is pleasing: who not inconveniently posits that Nebuchadnezzar was taken into partnership of the kingdom and sent into Egypt and Syria not four years before the death of his parent, but about twenty months before the same, at the end of the third and the beginning of the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and he thinks that from that time the prophecies of the things to be done by him were revealed to Jeremiah, by which he also warned the Jews about the approaching Nebuchadnezzar, and predicted that the servitude of 70 years would be undergone: which began a little later, with almost no delay interposed, when Jehoiakim was handed over into his hands. Furthermore, as regards the years of the government

of Cyrus, he assigns to him likewise 30 years in the Persian kingdom, and nine after Babylon was captured; he does not, however, hold that the Monarchy began immediately upon the capture of Babylon, but about two years later, so that he presided over it for seven years and a month or two until the end of his life. For once Babylon was occupied, he appointed Darius the Mede, the son of Ahasuerus or Cyaxares, as King of the Chaldeans, Dan. V, 31, and with matters settled in Babylon, he set out through the region of the Medes into Persia to his father Cambyses and his mother, who were still living: and having returned from there into Media, he took the only daughter and heiress of Cyaxares in marriage, having received the inheritance of all Media in the name of a dowry, and the wedding having been celebrated, he soon departed with her. And when he was in Babylon, he sent Satraps to the nations brought under his dominion: to Arabia, Megabytus; to Greater Phrygia, Artacamas; to Lydia and Ionia, Chrysantas; to Caria, Adusius; to Hellespontine Phrygia and Aeolis, Pharnuchus. But he sent no Persian Satraps to Cilicia and Cyprus and the Paphlagonians; because they had appeared of their own accord to have followed his standards against Babylon. But nevertheless, he imposed tributes to be brought by them as well. Xenophon, Institutes, book VIII. Finally, in the following year, which Ussher counts as the year of the World 3468, Cyrus, after his father Cambyses had died in Persia and his father-in-law Cyaxares in Media, took possession of the Monarchy of the East: from which, and from the beginning of his rule, Xenophon counts 7 years in the eighth of his education; and the Holy Scripture derives his first year from the very archives of the Medes and Persians. For it teaches that in this year that famous edict was promulgated, the beginning of which is: Thus says Cyrus King of Persia: Jehovah the GOD of heaven has delivered all the kingdoms of the earth to me. By which, with the 70 years of the Babylonian servitude now completed, as predicted by Jeremiah, according to the prophecy issued by Isaiah concerning him by name (chap. XLIV, 28. &c. XLV, 13.) he granted the Jews living in his entire kingdom the power to return to their homeland, and ordered those returning to rebuild the Temple for GOD in Jerusalem; with the measure of the structure also prescribed, or rather granted, (for if it had been observed by him, this house would have been far larger than that former one of Solomon, contrary to Hagg. II, 3.) with expenses supplied from the royal house, and the vessels of the house of GOD, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken away, restored (2 Chron. 36, 22. 23. Ezra 1, 1. 2. 7. 5, 13. 14. 6, 2.-5.) Cyrus appointed Sheshbazzar as the leader, or royal legate, of the returning Jews: to whom, by his order, Mithridates the treasurer handed over the sacred vessels, to be carried to Jerusalem and placed in the Temple (Ezra 1, 7.-11. & 5, 14. 15.) He is thought to have been called by the Chaldean or court name Sheshbazzar, who was Zerubbabel in Hebrew: from Ezra 3, 8. 10. compared with 5, 16. These are Ussher's words. To whose Chronological calculation, all things having been duly weighed, we not undeservedly add our own.

QUESTION XXII.

What is the thirtieth year of Ezek. I, 1.

The Chaldean Paraphrast, Osiander, Piscator, and Polanus understand the 30th year from the discovery of the book of the Law by Hilkiah, concerning which 2 Kings 22, 11. 12.; Laur. Codomannus thinks the 30th year of the sins of the house of Judah is indicated. But Franc. Junius more conveniently expresses that epoch from the solemn restoration of the public covenant made by Josiah: Others wish the 30th year from the birth of the Prophet to be noted, to which Wilhelm Langius, book II, on the years of Christ, chap. XIII, p. 314, subscribes. Some think the thirtieth is indicated from the Jubilee year. But neither does the reckoning of the Jubilees fit, nor are the Prophets accustomed to count the years of their own age in recording prophecies, of which matter no example can be produced. Theodoret understands the 30th year from the Divine oracle concerning the Babylonian captivity, 2 Kings 24, 16, to which Pererius and Maldonado add their calculation. Which opinion does not differ from the former ones in terms of the calculation. For the time of the discovered Law, and the restored covenant, and the divine oracle uttered through the Prophetess Huldah, as also the beginning of the years of the sins of the house of Judah, agree, since all those things fall into the 18th year of Josiah.

Moreover, the opinion of those who think the 30th year from the beginning of the reign of Nabopalassar is to be designated does not agree with chronology, nor with the custom of Scripture, so that the fifth year of the transmigration of Jechoniah is thus collected with the 30th from the reign of Nabopalassar, who presided for 21 years; whence here the 30th year will be the ninth of the solitary reign of the son of Nebuchadnezzar, and the year of the transmigration of Jechoniah will be the fourth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ceased to reign from the transmigration of Jechoniah in the 37th year, Jerem. 52, 31. For the last year of the reign and life of Nebuchadnezzar is connected there with the 37th year from the transportation: add the four years during which he presided under the transmigration of Jechoniah to those 37 years, and the 41 years of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar emerge. But to whom Ptolemy assigned 43 years in his solitary reign. From the time of the restoration of public worship, that is, the 18th year of Josiah, who reigned for 31 years, there still remain 14 years 2 Kings 22:1, to which if the 11 years of Jehoiakim are added, and the five of the transportation of Jechoniah, 20 years emerge from the restoration of worship and the solemn covenant of Josiah to the fifth of Jechoniah.

QUESTION XXIII. Who is the Balthasar of Daniel, and who is Darius the Mede, and whether this Nabonidus is to be considered the last monarch of the Chaldeans?

Scaliger, and those who follow him, and several others, Capellus, Rainoldus, Petavius, etc., make the Balthasar of Daniel either Niricassolassar, or Laboraffardochus, in whose place they say he presided under a tutelary name: but they wish Darius the Mede to be Nabonidus, the last monarch of the Chaldeans, concerning whom see D. Behmius in Chron. Manud. p. 215. But in truth, this new opinion is, having no calculation from antiquity, nor does it agree with prophecy or Biblical history. And therefore the common opinion pleases, that Balthasar is the son of Nebuchadnezzar by Evil-merodach, called Nabonadius by Ptolemy, Nabonidus by Berosus, Labynitus by Herodotus, and Nabarenidochus by Abydenus. But that Darius the Mede is Ahasuerus, the son of Cyaxares, the son of Astyages. For the Balthasar of Daniel was the last in the Babylonian kingdom: which the hand seen on the wall testified and indicated to him, Mene, Thekel, Upharsin, and the explanation delivered by Daniel, Dan. 5, 25. 26. 27. 28. Mene, God has numbered your kingdom and finished it: Thekel, you have been weighed in the balance and found wanting: Phares, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. For he says your kingdom, not that of your successor, is finished, not that it will be finished after many years, 17 for example, at last. God has numbered it and finished it in that king; and this he testifies openly here, that the number of days or years of that kingdom is now finished. He defined the time by this writing; namely, that its completion was now imminent, and that the number of days which He had defined for it in His secret counsel, with the measure of his impiety, was now finished: he did not indicate, however, only indefinitely that it would be finished at some time. He treated of his kingdom, and predicted that it was already being finished by the divine judgment, who, having been weighed in the balance of God's judgment, was found wanting. But that was Balthasar, and not his successor of him. Wherefore it cannot be doubted that the kingdom was finished in that Balthasar, as it is he for whose sins the judgment of GOD is here denounced. Furthermore, there is joined immediately with the rejection of Balthasar, who was found wanting in the balance, and the completion of the same kingdom, the division of the kingdom and the granting of it into the hands of the M those three things expressed in three words are joined together, and they strike that impious King, who saw the hand of the Lord, and heard His judgment, interpreted by Daniel. And the pronoun Your is repeated here again: The kingdom is divided not of your successor; but Yours; and it is given to the Medes and Persians, that is, it shall now be given. Finally, when it is subjoined immediately in verse 30, 31. In that same night Balthasar the King of the Chaldeans was slain, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being sixty-two years old: what is clearer than that the Holy Scripture wished to add the completion of this oracle immediately, not in one or another only, but in all those things which had been predicted here, i.e., not only that the kingdom of Balthasar was completed, and that the judgment of GOD was manifested, in that he himself was found wanting; but also, that his kingdom was given to the Medes and Persians, and that not anyone from the stock or kindred of the Chaldean Kings, but a stranger, namely Darius, and he a Mede, succeeded him in the kingdom. And this is the first foundation of our opinion, no less immovable than it is clear.

Furthermore, we also argue ἀνασκευαστικῶς (refutatively) for the continuity in Daniel: who testifies that immediately after Balthasar was slain, the Medes and Persians succeeded to the empire. Dan. V, 30. 31. For with this, the opinion of Scaliger cannot easily be reconciled: that they succeeded only after 17 years of Nabonidus. Since an immediate succession is denoted, and it coheres ἀμέσως (immediately) with the outcome of both Balthasar the Babylonian King and the Babylonian kingdom.

Thirdly, it is added that Darius the MEDE governed the kingdom according to the Laws of the Medes and Persians, and could not or should not change them, Dan. VI, 8. 12. 16. If that Nabonidus had also been an Assyrian, who could have bound the same to Medo-Persian laws? It is certainly by no means likely that the Chaldeans, before their empire was abolished by the Medes and Persians, either derogated from their own laws and the statutes of the kingdom, or added Medo-Persian laws, and voluntarily subjected themselves to the yoke of hostile statutes: since the capital enmities, which flourished until the end of the last Assyrian Monarch Nabonidus, would not have permitted it at all? Fourthly, it also militates for our and the common opinion against the new Scaligerian

discovery, that from Daniel chap. XI, 1. 2. the other Persian Monarchs are counted from Darius the Mede. YET (after Darius the Mede) three kings shall stand in Persia, and the fourth shall be enriched above all. Therefore the Monarchy already stood in Darius the Mede in Persia, and three more had to intervene, up to that richest of all, who is known to be Xerxes: namely Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius the first, son of Hystaspes.

Fifthly, the oracle concerning Nebuchadnezzar in Jer. XXVI, 7 is clear: and all nations shall serve him and his son, and his son's son. Whence it is certain that the Monarchy would obtain both his son Evil-merodach, and his son's son: and that this latter would be the last in that Monarchy: and thus it is necessary that Nabonidus, who was the last in the series of Chaldean Kings, is by no means Darius the Mede, but one sprung from the lineage of Nebuchadnezzar, and finally his son's son. But as for Niricassolassar, who intervened between Evil-merodach and Nabonidus, no account is to be taken of him, as he not only presided for a short time, but was also an unjust possessor of the kingdom. Nerigolassar, says D. Behmius Dec. 1. Observ. Chron. Observ. VII. p. 228. Manud. Chronolog., who reigned for four years after Evil-merodach, is not a natural and hereditary King, but occupied the kingdom tyrannically. Nor do the Scaligerians find anything here to say to such an evident place of Jeremiah, unless they invent that by son of a son, the son of a daughter is understood, that the word בן is general, and often comprehends both sexes, which however they cannot prove by even one example, and it is repugnant to Hebrew literature, which accurately distinguishes בן and בת, son and daughter. It certainly does not fit this place at all, where the Holy Scripture notably and with care expresses and describes the successor Monarchs, they shall serve Him, and HIS son, and the son of His son: nor can the name of Son be taken otherwise for the former, and otherwise for the latter, in that coherence and relation to Nebuchadnezzar the parent and grandfather, however else the name of son might perhaps be found to be taken, it is too manifest. For the third time the name of the son is repeated, without any indication of a different meaning: and the favor to be shown to Nebuchadnezzar is celebrated, because not only is he himself to be the supreme monarch, nor only his son, but also his son's son, and at the same time the period of that monarchy is defined, because it is to have its end in those so designated. Which, according to the common opinion, corresponded exactly in its fulfillment, but not so according to Scaliger's new commentary.

Sixthly, since they acknowledge that Laborosoardochus, the son of Nebuchadnezzar's daughter, reigned for only 9 months, how will he be the Belshazzar of Daniel, whose third year is commemorated by Daniel in chapter VIII, 1? But as for what they object, that even if Laborosoardochus alone presided for only 9 months, he nevertheless reigned under the guardianship of Neriglossar for 4 years, they can produce no trustworthy document for that matter, nor could D. Behmius confidently rely on this exception, therefore he added in the cited place: Let him who is not satisfied by these things show us better ones, if he can. But without doubt those things are better and more certain which rely on the truth of Scripture: which acknowledges no successor who is the son of Nebuchadnezzar's daughter, nor did it designate such a short reign of only 9 months, or of an underage King, but openly expressed the monarchs after the death of Nebuchadnezzar to be his son and his son's son, and testified that the Babylonian empire was to be preserved and ended in the family of Nebuchadnezzar, from which one must by no means depart; much less should it be established with Scaliger that the descendants of Nebuchadnezzar, the son and grandson, held that monarchy for scarcely three years; which, on the contrary, Darius the Mede, who did not belong to the family of Nebuchadnezzar and was joined to him by no affinity or kinship, held for seventeen whole years. Which can never be reconciled with the words of Jeremiah, or rather of Jehovah: And now I have therefore given all these lands into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylon, my servant: and furthermore I have given him the beasts of the field, that they may serve him, and all nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son, UNTIL the time of his land comes. Where by the word UNTIL the fatal end of the Babylonian monarchy is expressed, which was to come at the time of the reign of the son's son of Nebuchadnezzar, and with his reign was to bring the end of the land. For according to Scaliger, the fatal end of the Babylonian monarchy would not have to be fixed in the reign of his son's son; but in the reign of a certain foreigner, of Median seed or origin, as Daniel calls him Darius in chapter IX, 1, whom they assert, without a witness, to have been either born or raised in Babylon by a Median parent.

Seventhly, however, it is not likely that the Babylonians of their own accord wished to eradicate the entire family of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, and that for the sake of some stranger born of the Median race, with whom he was then fostering deadly enmities: or to have wished to kill the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, Laborosoardochus, by the cruel torment of tympanization, or βιαίῳ μόρῳ, in the ninth month of his reign, before they had experienced the character of the youth for one year.

Eighth, nor does it seem likely that that Belshazzar was a youth, and that he had presided for only 9 months, when he made that great banquet for a thousand nobles, as one to whom wives and concubines are attributed, Dan. V, 2, to whom God showed the hand writing on the wall, the judgment of the Babylonian Monarchy now imminent. Whose father, moreover, is said to be Nebuchadnezzar v. 2, 11, 13, and whom Daniel calls the son of Nebuchadnezzar v. 22. By which name a son's son, that is, a grandson by a son, is indicated more certainly by the phrase of Scripture, namely Nabonidus, than Laborosoardochus or Niricassolaffarus: for the οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας are uncertain whether they ought to make him or that other one Belshazzar, even though they establish Neriglossar or Niricassolaffarus alone as the son-in-law of Nebuchadnezzar and kinsman of Evil-merodach.

Ninth, if Darius the Mede was Nabonidus, since he is said to have entered the kingdom at 62 years of age, Dan. V, last, and Cyrus invaded Nabonidus in the 17th year of his reign, it will have to be established that he led that army and fought against Cyrus in the seventy-ninth year of his age: indeed, since, having been defeated by Cyrus, he is considered to have fortified cities and strongholds for a long time still, according to Scaliger's opinion, and to have defended himself bravely against the entire force of Cyrus, it would have to be asserted that this Senecio, after such labors of warfare, prolonged his life to the ninety-sixth year, and that in his own kingdom: where Bælius not undeservedly asks: Whom can Scaliger name, either of the ancients or even of the moderns among his greatest followers, in these dreams of his? Let us pass over the fact that here Scaliger himself departs from Berosus: for since 17 years of rule are assigned to Nabonidus by Berosus and Ptolemy, Scaliger in his Eusebius p. 28 and in his Notes to Berosus p. 15 asserts that the years of Nabonidus were 34. How then can he rely on the authority of Berosus in these matters?

Tenth, there are added the authorities not only of almost all the moderns, which the opposing party grants us, but also of very many of the ancients, both Doctors of the Church and Historians. The interpreters (on Dan. V, 22) agree, says D. Behmius in Chronolog. Manud. p. 227, almost ALL to a man, that this Belshazzar was the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Evil-merodach. The suffrage of Jerome does not detract from us, nor that of Josephus, who in book X of the Antiquities, ch. XII, makes Nabonidus Belshazzar, even if they diminish his credibility (whose authority, however, Scaliger himself in this place laboriously defends against detractors), but they say Jerome was deceived by Josephus, whom nevertheless they cannot deny to have examined the writings of the ancients most accurately, and to have weighed Berosus and Megasthenes no less than Josephus himself, and for no other reason, having left those, did he adhere to this one, than that he might not oppose the sacred scriptures. That Xenophon stands on our side here is granted with both hands by the followers of Scaliger: D. Behmius, dealing with Darius the Mede, Observat. IX, p. 231, says: Those who follow Xenophon's education, Josephus, Jerome, and others (which the greater part of chronologers do), wish this Darius to have been 1. Cyaxares the Younger, son of Astyages, brother of Mandane, the mother of Cyrus. 2. This Cyaxares to have been present with Cyrus at the taking of Babylon. 3. This Cyaxares to have given his daughter to Cyrus in marriage.

4. This Cyaxares to have succeeded his parent Astyages in the kingdom of Media; they drew all these things from books 7 and 8 of the education of Cyrus by Xenophon. Nor is there any doubt that that most serious writer agrees with the history of Daniel: inasmuch as in book VII of the Institutions of Cyrus, in describing the slaughter of Belshazzar by Gadatas, Gobryas, and the remaining Babylonian deserters, the Satraps of Cyrus, in the middle of a great banquet, he approaches closer to Daniel than any of the other ancients. For he testifies that the Babylonians, at the time of the siege made by Cyrus, indulged in carousing, in which Herodotus also agrees with him, book 1, ch. 191; which the Scaligerians indeed drag to the feast accustomed to be instituted for servants called the Sacaea, but against the will of Daniel: who testifies that this banquet was prepared for the nobles. And this opinion, that the history of the slain Belshazzar in Dan. V is the same as that by which Cyrus, as Xenophon testifies, took Babylon, is confirmed not only by Josephus, book X of the Antiquities, ch. XIII, that it was indeed done at the same time, and that that Belshazzar of Daniel is he whom the Greeks call Labynetus or Nabonidus, and that Darius the Mede is Cyaxares, the son of Astyages; but almost all chronologers today follow Josephus with Jerome, as D. Behmius admits, that this is the common and almost catholic opinion, which almost all chronologers embrace. Although he opposes that a common error prejudices nothing against the truth, it will now be shown that the things which are here set against the most well-founded truth in the Scriptures are empty and ridiculous.

The historical reliability of Xenophon's Cyropaedia is called into doubt in vain by that Ciceronian passage in Epistulae ad Quintum Fratrem, Book 1, Epistle 1, because they were written not for the sake of historical reliability, but as a portrait of a just empire. For these things concern only the end and intention of the writing, and do not teach that it is contrary to historical reliability. But the fact that Xenophon was a rival of Herodotus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies, does not prejudice his historical truth at all, for he teaches that he was a ζηλωτὴν (zealot/imitator) according to both characters, the τὸν τὲ πραγματικὸν, vel ἱστορικὸν (the pragmatic or historical) and the τὸν λεκτικὸν (the rhetorical), because he chose hypotheses of histories that were beautiful and magnificent and suitable for a philosopher (which certainly are not those that are repugnant to historical truth) and because they exhibit an image of a good and happy King, to which things that are alien to historical truth cannot contribute. Finally, that by the judgment of the same man, Xenophon was in many things ὀλίγωρ@ (negligent), does not prove that he was negligent or false in those matters in which Josephus, Jerome, and most others all follow him as being ὁμόψηφον (of the same vote/opinion) with sacred history. Bailius is right here: it is true that in that work Xenophon intends the name of a teacher more than the office of a historian: yet so that he does not wish to lie in those things which he asserts positively in history. Add that Herodotus also, whom Scaliger and his followers value most highly, asserts that Nabonidus, or Labinitus, was the son of Nebuchadnezzar, or of the great Labinitus and Nitocris, just as Daniel also called Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar.

Against this common and catholic consensus, to which among the more recent writers, having disregarded the authority of Scaliger, they adhere—among the Reformed, Franciscus Junius, James Ussher, Robert Bailius, and among the Papists, Torniellus, Salianus, Henricus Philippi, and Hovæus—the Scaligerians have almost nothing to object except certain fragments of Berosus and Megasthenes; for the things they are accustomed to add to them from the Scriptures are merely snatched up and accommodated to their hypothesis at will, so that while they rely solely on those fragments, and twist all other things to them, they still in some way [try to make] the Holy Code stand for them in order to persuade others, from whose open testimonies indeed we have already clearly shown that they go here into all other things. Whence not undeservedly candor is pleasing, and

the frankness of Rob. Baillie, who although he is of the same Reformed religion as Scaliger, and attributes much to the great man, as he deserves, in chronological matters, yet could not approve his dictatorship in these matters especially, where he sees him openly opposing Scripture, but detested it with just zeal: Scaliger commands, with a very high brow and a completely dictatorial authority, the whole nation of chronologers, that having deserted the former (common and catholic) opinion, they should run on foot to the second, which is his own. But in truth, they are too faint-hearted who, terrified by sesquipedalian words, do not dare to join battle and compare the weights of arguments on both sides with an equal scale of judgment.

But it is very manifest that too much is attributed by them to the fragments of Berosus, when they test what has been handed down in Scripture by him as if by some standard, nay, they twist the words of Scripture to their tenor, and for their sake they do not hesitate to strip of authority any other exotic writers, however serious and worthy of faith, and furthermore, what is most important, those who are consonant with sacred history, such as Xenophon and Herodotus, because in those fragments of Megasthenes indeed, in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book IX, chapter IV, they read that Nabonidochus the King was declared τῷ ὀὐδὲν προσήκοντα, having nothing to do with him, and that Cyrus, having captured Babylon, gave him the principality of Carmania as a gift; then indeed in Berosus also in the fragment produced by Eusebius, loc. cit., and by Josephus, book IX of the Antiquities, chapter II, and the former book against Appion, they find similar things, that by common opinion the kingdom was handed down to a certain Babylonian Nabonidus, a man of that faction, by whom Laborosodarchus was ἀποτυμπανίσθη, killed through torture, and that Cyrus, having captured Babylon, besieged Nabonidus at Borsippa, and that he, not bearing that siege, having made a surrender, was kindly received, and having been given Carmania to inhabit, was dismissed from Babylonia; which in no way agree with the Belshazzar of Daniel. But although those fragments deserve faith in the enumeration of the Assyrian Kings, and easily agree with Scripture, yet not even in that circumstance, by which against the open testimony of Scripture, Jer. XXVII, 7, they say the last King of the Babylonians was not the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, but some other man, having nothing to do with Nebuchadnezzar, a Babylonian man, or when, with Daniel contradicting, they deny that the Babylonian kingdom ended with Belshazzar killed at a solemn banquet, should one rather stick to those fragments than to other trustworthy historians, Herodotus and Xenophon, who are in agreement with Scripture. If anyone should say with Dr. Behm that greater faith should be had in this part in Berosus than in Herodotus, since he was a Chaldean, nay, a priest of Bel in Babylon, and thus had a more exact knowledge of the Babylonian Kings: Baillie denies that Berosus or Megasthenes are of as great authority as Herodotus or Xenophon: since these wrote after the times of Alexander the Great, but Xenophon much before, and Herodotus not many years after the times of Cyrus, and Scaliger himself is accustomed to prefer Herodotus on many counts to both Berosus and Megasthenes, nor does Eusebius hesitate to argue that Megasthenes erred in various things out of ignorance of the Holy Scriptures. Add that Berosus opposes the Canon of Ptolemy, confirmed by celestial characters, in which the years of Nabopalassar, which Ptolemy makes XXI, Berosus according to Scaliger makes XXIX, and that Scaliger himself contradicts Berosus in the years of Nabonidus, and that those fragments do not sufficiently agree among themselves: since Berosus makes Nabonidus a Babylonian by nation or lineage; but Megasthenes a Mede, if indeed those words in the prophecy of Nebuchadnezzar seized by madness, Mede the glory of the Assyrians, are to be understood of Nabonidus, Μήδης τὸ Ἀσσύριον ἄυχημα, as the Scaligerians wish: which Baillie understands of Nitocris, the Median wife of Nebuchadnezzar, in his Historical and Chronological works, page 153, or thinks it should be explained of the Medes, who were the glory of the Assyrians, on account of that marriage of Nebuchadnezzar, in a conspiracy with the Persians for the destruction of the family of Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian kingdom. Lest finally we say that the calculation of Berosus does not at all agree with the interval of the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity, whence Dr. Behm here greatly torments himself, now making it with Sulpitius Severus from the two years of Evil-Merodach 12, now conjecturing that GOD had shortened the term of the 70 years of captivity by the power of His mercy, and whatever his other exceptions are, Dec. 1, observ. VI, p. 226, in order to defend the faith of those fragments.

To these, so that they may attach one or another from the sacred writings, lest they collapse, they compare both the madness which Megasthenes attributes to Nebuchadnezzar with the madness divinely inflicted upon him in Daniel IV, 33, and they urge the absence of the Babylonian king from the city at the time when the city was captured, Jer. LI, 31, and they contend that the manner in which Darius the Mede arrived at the kingdom, Dan. VI, 1, chap. IX, 1, agrees with the fragments, but is repugnant to our opinion, that he was Cyaxares, the son of Astyages. But that madness of Nebuchadnezzar in Megasthenes has no connection with the history of Daniel: so that one might wonder why B. Behmius compares these, since they are most disparate. For the θεῖα ὁτέλεια, of which Megasthenes speaks, was joined with reason, and proper to those who prophesy: But the madness of which Daniel speaks exterminated reason from him, and cast him down to the beasts. The former, placed in the kingdom, shortly before his death, having been seized, having prophesied about future things θεσπίσας παραχρῆμα ἠφάνιστο, immediately disappeared: The latter, however, was punished, in such a way that he was driven from the kingdom, long before his death: and only afterwards, with the sanity of his mind restored, did he return to the former dignity of his empire.

The absence of the Babylonian King at the time of the city's capture is by no means indicated by Jeremiah c. LI, 31: it is only signified that a messenger had been brought to the King, who was secure and thinking of no such thing, that the city had been captured from the extremity; concerning which compare Junius's annotations on this passage. For such was the magnitude of the city that when those who inhabited the extreme parts of the city were already captured, those who inhabited the middle of the city did not notice it. See Herodotus l. 1. c. 191.

Finally, the fact that they attempt to deduce from Daniel that Darius the Mede arrived at the kingdom not by an armed hand, but by the kingdom being obtained through votes, has no strength: the Prophet uses the word קבל, he received the kingdom, chap. VI, 1. But one who obtains it by an armed hand can receive it just as much as one who receives something as if it were handed into his hands: nor is this repugnant to the formal meaning of the word, just as the Philistines are said by the same word to have taken the ark of GOD 1 Samuel V, 1, which was by no means handed to them: the soldiers πα- ρέλαβον Jesus, which was done by force John XIX, 26. Matth. XXVII, 17. and this verb is openly used regarding force 1 Sam. II, 16. Now you shall give, and if not, I will take by force: and Scaliger acknowledges on the fragments of Berosus p. 15 that πα- ραλαμβάνειν is said of one who received a kingdom by force. What if Cyaxares, the son-in-law and uncle of Cyrus the victor, received the kingdom handed to him by Cyrus, if anyone still wishes to quibble about that word, without cause? Nor indeed did the people spontaneously or voluntarily or through election or common votes [give] to Darius the Mede the kingdom handed over, as Daniel affirms; which is assumed in this argument precariously, and is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. These things being observed, the slipperiness of this principal thesis shines through, and the main argument, upon which they rely here, is discovered to be clearly frivolous. The Prophet also uses the word המלך which is passive in Hophal, Dan. IX, 1. and implies one constituted or made King: but not precisely made or constituted by right of succession or of votes, as Scaliger rashly affirms: This prop is likewise too weak, resting only on a small grammatical observation, and that one destitute of any foundation: that it ought not to be translated, Darius reigned, but he was constituted King, and that without force: Since by this word, according to Scaliger, whether we like it or not, all armed force is excluded. For even if he is said to be constituted, is it immediately noted by that word that he was constituted not by force, but by the vote of the people, or the counsel of the Princes, or by faction? Whence, I ask, will this force of the word be proven? When in Jud. VI Abimelech is constituted King of Israel, will no force intervene? When Rezin and Remaliah wish to constitute Tabeel King of Israel, when Pharaoh constitutes Jehoahaz, and Nebuchadnezzar constitutes Jeconiah King, was all force excluded and the matter effected by the faction of princes or the free vote of the people? Nothing, therefore, is more certain than that in general a constitution is designated by that word, whether it be GOD alone, or an army, or a prince, or the people, by whom someone is constituted on a royal throne. Finally, lest Darius the Mede be taken for Cyaxares, the son of Astyages, they appeal to Herodotus: who testifies both that the kingdom of the Medes devolved to the Persians after Astyages, and that Astyages begat no male offspring. But since Xenophon reports that Cyaxares the Younger was the son of Astyages, the brother of Mandane the mother of Cyrus, and that he gave his own daughter in marriage to Cyrus, and succeeded his parent Astyages in the kingdom of Media, and indeed was even present himself together with Cyrus at the storming of Babel, there is no reason why we should derogate from the credibility of Xenophon, who testifies about these things circumstantially and without hesitation, whom Scaliger, with his followers, is otherwise accustomed to value highly in historical matters. And how can it be presumed of a most serious writer that he fabricated these things out of hatred for Herodotus, which was not to be imputed to the same without most pregnant reasons?
