They reply that all historians testify that the kingdom of the Medes reached its end under Astyages and devolved to the Persians. Be it so: will the credibility of Xenophon therefore be endangered here? Was the kingdom of the Medes not devolved to the Persians in such a way that the Perso-Median Monarchy arose in Cyrus, for whose sake Darius the Mede, as his father-in-law, presided over it? Inasmuch as he had been an auxiliary to him in the Babylonian conquest, just as also in Daniel the kingdom of Darius and Cyrus is joined, Dan. V, 28. and Mr. Dr. Behmius himself observes the method of reconciling Herodotus with Xenophon, that Astyages indeed lacked a male heir according to Herodotus, yet he adopted Cyaxares as a son, and thus is called by Xenophon the son (that is, adoptive) of Astyages: although he says these are merely conjectures, Observ. 1. Poster. ad Decad. p. 237. But in histories we must not infrequently be content with conjectures when writers vary, which is certainly better than to oppose the Holy Scripture itself out of party zeal for the sake of one or another historian.

QUESTION XXIV. How are the Babylonian Kings to be numbered, and their years from the parent of Nebuchadnezzar according to the Canon of the Bible and Ptolemy?

IN the Canon of Ptolemy, twenty-one years are attributed to Nabopolassar, the parent of Nebuchadnezzar. Forty-three years to Nabocolassar, or Nebuchadnezzar, who is most celebrated in the Scriptures. Two years to Ilvarodamus, whom Scripture calls Evil-merodach, Jerem. LII. Four years to Niricassolassar, who is not found in the sacred writings as a king, even though his name seems to occur in Jerem. XXXIX, 3, where Neogalschar Ezer is the first of the Princes of the King of Babylon who stormed the city of Jerusalem. But it appears that the Holy Spirit did not deem him worthy of the name of King, or of the monarchical axiom in the designation of those to whom He was about to subject the peoples of the earth, Jer. XXVII, 7, inasmuch as he snatched that dignity for himself tyrannically and by an unjust title, having killed the King and his Lord Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God had subjected all nations. Nabonadius succeeds in the Canon of Ptolemy, who ruled for 17 years, whom we have just shown to be the grandson, or son of the son, of Nebuchadnezzar, the last in the Assyrian Monarchy: but before him Berosus and Megasthenes still name in their fragments the son of Neriglossar, who Berosus claims was indeed a boy, and ruled for no more than 9 months, for which reason he seems to have been neglected by Ptolemy.

For as for the rest, Berosus agrees with Ptolemy regarding the years of the monarchs. For his fragment holds as follows: Therefore Nebuchadnezzar, after he had begun the wall which we mentioned, fell into a weakness of mind and ended his life, having reigned 43 years. And his son Evil-Merodach succeeded him; when he ruled the empire wickedly and lasciviously, he was overcome by plots by his sister's husband Neriglossar, after he had reigned two years. He was succeeded by the same man who had overcome him, Neriglossar, and he reigned 4 years. His son Laborosoardochus, a boy, obtained the kingdom for nine months, and because he gave many signs of a depraved nature, he was overcome by plots by his friends and killed by torture. In the years of Nabopolassar, however, Berosus disagrees, counting 29. Megasthenes reviews the same kings, without mention of years: and with slightly changed names: Nebuchadnezzar, whom he calls ἡρακλέως ἀλκιμώτερον, stronger than Hercules; his son Evil-Merodach, whom his relative Neriglossar killed, with his son Labassoarassus left behind. By whose violent death he was killed, Nabonidus was declared King, having nothing to do with them.

Concerning which fragments we have already spoken: that the Kings easily agree with Ptolemy and the Holy Scriptures, even if they hallucinate in a few circumstances: with the exception, however, that the fragment of Berosus disagrees with the Canon of Ptolemy in the years of Nabopolassar, if that reading is true which Scaliger defends in Annot. ad fragment. Vet. p. 10, namely that he reigned not for 21 years, as Josephus has in Antiquities of the Jews X, but 29. Thus, however, the Nabonassar era, which is extracted from Ptolemy, is easily rendered doubtful and ambiguous, since the years of the reign differ, which the illustrious Scaliger holds as a kind of cynosure in chronological matters.

Of the other Babylonian Kings, many of whom Ptolemy designated as earlier, none is commemorated in the Scriptures, except Esarhaddon in Ezra IV, 2 and Merodach in Isaiah XXXIX, 1, called Mardokempad by Ptolemy, who did not succeed Nabonassar, as Alstedius in his Chronological index says, nor Esarhaddon, as others wish, but after Nabonassar, with Nadius, Chinzirus, and Porus intervening, he was the successor of Jugaeus or Dibalus, according to the Canon of Ptolemy, which, so that the innumerable variations and divergences of chronologers may be countered, and certainty may be had, confirmed by celestial characters, with the subsequent addition of a collation of those who are named in the Holy Code, we have exhibited in the seventh Table.

QUESTION XXV.

What is the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. II, 31, in which he saw the dream?

A difficulty arises here concerning that: because in the 3rd year of Jehoiakim (ending) Nebuchadnezzar was already King of Babylon, Dan. I, 1, from which time three years of private instruction elapsed before he was brought into the sight of the King, chap. I, 4, 5, 18, 19. How then was he brought to explain the dream in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar? Tremellius and Junius think the difficulty can be removed if the passage is translated 'in the second year,' namely not the second year of King Nebuchadnezzar, but while Nebuchadnezzar was reigning, and the year is understood as the second from when the four boys brought to the King stood before him, Dan. I, 18, 19; but that method of translation is harsher and unusual. Scaliger therefore rightly observes that that second year is counted from the death of his Father, from which time indeed the solitary reign of Nebuchadnezzar began: but that before this he had already been admitted into the partnership of the kingdom, while his Father was still living, and was called King of Babylon: just as also in Jeremiah and the Biblical history of the Kings, the years of Nebuchadnezzar are not counted from the death of his Father, but from his expedition into Syria and Judea, undertaken while his Father was living, by whom he was admitted into the partnership of the kingdom for his sake, as Berosus testifies in Josephus, book X of Antiquities, ch. II, and book 1 against Apion: which reconciliation is therefore to be preferred: namely, that it be said that Dan. I, 1 and in Jeremiah the year of the joint rule of Nebuchadnezzar is regarded, but that in Dan. II, 1, 31, the second year of the solitary reign of the same is designated.

QUESTION XXVI.

What was that first year in which Nebuchadnezzar was admitted into the partnership of the kingdom, and for how long a time was he a participant in his father's kingdom before, upon his father's death, he began to reign alone?

This question contributes to understanding the computation of Jeremiah and the Biblical history of the Kings, since they counted the years of Nebuchadnezzar from his first admission into the kingdom while his parent was still alive, or from the expedition undertaken into Syria and Judea, and his first arrival in Syria and Judea: and also to the just connection of the years of the Nabonassar era with the years of the Kings of Judah, according to the Ptolemaic Canon. For in the canon of the Babylonian kings, the years of Nebuchadnezzar are counted which are attributed to his rule from the death of his Father: but in the history of the Kings of Judah in Jeremiah, as we have already noted several times, the Epoch of his reign is deduced from his expedition into Syria and Judea, undertaken while his father was living.

The question therefore is the interval from the beginning of the joint reign to the beginning of the sole reign. Concerning which the opinions of chronologers and other writers vary greatly. Scaliger, taking for true a faulty reading of a passage of Berosus in Josephus, Against Apion, book 1, by which 29 years are attributed to Nabopolassar instead of 21, and abandoning the genuine reading which is held in Antiquities, book 10, believed that Nabopolassar died at the beginning of the 30th year of his reign, and he made that the thirteenth year of the reign shared with his son Nebuchadnezzar, Prolegomena to the book On the Emendation of Time, page 13, and notes on the fragments, page 10, following. Whence that second year of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 1, of which we spoke just now, of his sole reign in Babylon, is for Scaliger the 14th year of the expedition in Syria and of the joint reign, but the sixth of Zedekiah. But since the Canon of Ptolemy, which Scaliger and his followers take as a cynosure, and not undeservedly, assigns to Nabopolassar not 29 years but 21, and since in the Origins by Josephus also only 21 years are attributed to the same in the fragment of Berosus, Scaliger's calculation deserves no consideration. For who would prefer the conjectures of Scaliger to the Ptolemaic Canon, which is built upon celestial observations? Furthermore, from the calculation of Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book 1, nineteen years emerge during which Nebuchadnezzar reigned with his father. From Jerome on Daniel 2 and Josephus, Antiquities, book 10, chapter 11, 23 years are gathered; from Francis Junius, 34 years. B. D. Behmius, strictly following the footsteps of Scaliger in other matters, attributes only four years, no more, to the joint reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and that he was sent for the first time into Syria and Palestine in the 17th year of the reign of Nabopolassar, in Theological, Historical, and Chronological Discussions on the 70 years of the captivity. Babylon, cited several times, not unlearnedly gathers from a collation of the Phoenician annals in Josephus and the Eusebian enumeration, thesis 29, following. But if Biblical history, to which here and everywhere all others rightly yield, be diligently weighed, not even four years, let alone more, could be attributed to the joint reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and not even two full years, but only one year, seven months, and about 10 days, so that with the addition of 43 years of sole reign, he reigned in total only 44 years, 7 months, and about 10 days, as has been excellently observed by Ussher, a most accurate chronologer and most observant of Biblical calculation. For if in the third year of Jehoiakim, ending about the 15th day of the fifth month, the principate of Nebuchadnezzar began before the deportation of Jeconiah, which took place on the fifth day of the fourth month, and with the addition of those seven years, 10 months, and 20 days, thirty-six years, eight months, and 20 days, which elapsed from the deportation of Jeconiah to the beginning of the reign of Evil-Merodach, there emerge from that 44 years, 7 months, 10 days to be assigned to the whole reign of Nebuchadnezzar. Moreover, those hypotheses are confirmed from the Scriptures: And this latter one indeed from Jeremiah 52:31, 32.

where the beginning of the reign of the son and immediate successor of Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach, is gathered to be in the 37th year from the deportation of Jeconiah, in the 12th month, on the 25th day, which 25th day of his empire seems to have been his birthday, on which he initiated the plan for elevating Jeconiah, since the day of the elevation of Jeconiah to royal dignity is indicated to have been the 27th, 2 Kings 25:27. For the deportation having taken place on the 5th day of the 4th month, but the elevation on the 25th day of the 12th month of the 37th year, by the subtraction instituted, there are left from the beginning of the deportation 36 years, 8 months, and 20 days. Concerning the other hypotheses, we shall now look into them specifically.

QUESTION XXVII. At what time of the year did the deportation of Jeconiah take place?

Therefore, as to the remaining hypotheses, we must first look at the time of the deportation of Jeconiah, then at the day and month of the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture. Ussher, Chronology of the Sacred, page 28, gathers that the deportation of Jeconiah took place about the 5th day of the 4th month, about five days before the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah. In the fifth year from the deportation of King Jehoiakim, or Jeconiah, on the fifth day of the fourth month, the very first vision was shown to the prophet Ezekiel (chapter 1:1, 2). After he had sat for seven whole days among his deported countrymen, struck as it were by a kind of stupor (chapter 2:15, 16), he continued 390 days in public view of all, he was commanded by GOD to lie, (chap. IV, 4. 5.) One year and two months having then elapsed after the first, while he was sitting in his house with the elders of Judah, a new vision was shown; in the sixth year of the deportation of Jeconiah, on the fifth day of the sixth month (chap. VIII, 1.) A. 397 days having been deducted from the annual quantity of 365 days, 32 days are left, so that by completing the interval interposed between both visions, the space of a single month is lacking here only. Whence we conclude that the first vision was made about the very 5th year of the captivity of Jeconiah: and therefore that that captivity began about the fifth day of the fourth month. Whence since Jeconiah had presided for 3 months and 10 days after his parent Jehoiakim, 2. Chron. XXXVI, 9. as the end of the reign of Jehoiakim, so also the beginning of his son is left to be placed about the 25th day of the 12th month; for having subtracted from the 5th day of the 4th month, on which he was taken captive, they fall upon the 25th day of the 12th month.

QUESTION XXVIII.

At what time of the year did the first beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar commence?

We determine that it began towards the end of the third year of Jehoiakim, about the 15th day of the 5th month. That this undoubtedly fell in the ending third year of Jehoiakim is clear from a comparison of Jer. XXV, 1. and Daniel I, 1. Now Jehoiakim reigned in total for eleven years. 2 Kings XXIII, 36. 2 Chron. XXXVI, 5. and after him his son Jeconiah for 3 months and 10 days 2 Chron. XXXVI, 9. which having been completed, he was captured in the eighth year of the empire of Nebuchadnezzar 2 Kings XXIV, 12. whence it is gathered (1.) that the eleventh year of Jehoiakim was not complete: for since Nebuchadnezzar began to reign before the end of that third year, if he had presided for eight full years, Nebuchadnezzar would have already entered his ninth year when he gave Jeconiah as a successor to him, in whose fourth month, however, the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar was still counted. Furthermore, it is also gathered (2.) that the beginning of Jehoiakim cannot be placed between the 25th day of the 12th month, on which Jeconiah began to reign, and the 5th day of the 4th month, on which he ceased: for otherwise Nebuchadnezzar, whose first year began towards the end of the third year of Jehoiakim, would have spent the ninth year of his reign when Jeconiah was captured. It remains, therefore, that the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim must be sought between the 5th day of the 4th month and the 25th day of the 12th month.

And therefore before the feast of tabernacles, which is indicated in Jer. XXVI, 1. 2., celebrated in the middle of the seventh month, with some time interposed between the 5th day of the 4th month and that, and indeed approaching closer to the 7th than to the 4th month, the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim will have to be placed, and thus before the tenth day of the 7th month.

Further, that the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar and Jehoiakim must be sought after the tenth day of the 5th month, Ussher shows thus: The tenth year of Zedekiah, from the 10th day of the 4th month (which will be shown later), was the beginning of the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer. XXXII, 1. beginning at least one month after that tenth year of Zedekiah. For if Nebuchadnezzar had begun his reign on the very 10th day of the 4th month, when the temple was burned, on the 10th day of the 5th month (a full month after Zedekiah, ending in the eleventh year of his reign, was captured), he would have entered the twentieth year of his reign. But it is evident from Jer. LII, 12. that his nineteenth year was still running. Whence it follows that the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar, and then also of Jehoiakim, must be placed between the 5th and the 10th day of the 7th month. Which correctly agrees with that definition which determines that Jehoiakim succeeded Jehoahaz, who began his three-month reign on the 10th day of the 3rd month, on the 10th day of the 6th month. Then, to the beginning of Jeconiah, placed around the 25th day of the 12th month, 6 and a half months are counted, which are to be attributed to the ten years of Jehoiakim's entire reign only above those; from his eleventh year, five months and half of one are subtracted. Which indeed will be complete if we admit that Nebuchadnezzar began his first year 25 days before the end of the third year of Jehoiakim, and that he assumed, up to the completion of his eighth year, besides the 100 days of Jeconiah (for he reigned 3 months and 10 days) and 5 of the interregnum, also the first 35 days succeeding Zedekiah. By this reasoning, with the birthday of Nebuchadnezzar's empire established in the middle of the 5th month, his first year will also correspond to the fourth of Jehoiakim (being only 25 days prior to it) according to

Jerem. XXV, 1. and the eighteenth year in the tenth year of Zedekiah (40 days after the beginning of this one) according to Jerem. XXXII, 1. and there will be from its beginning to the deportation of Jeconiah (which occurred on the 5th day of the 4th month) 7 years, 10 months, 20 days; but to the destruction of the temple (on the 10th day of the 5th month) and the captivity of the people that followed it, 19 years less 5 days.

From these, therefore, it is manifest that Jehoiakim indeed began his reign around the 10th day of the 6th month. And that he did not hold it for eleven full years, but for about 10 years, 6 months, and 15 days: but towards the end of that third year, around the 15th day of the 5th month, Nebuchadnezzar began to reign 19 years less about five days before the burning of the temple; which was to be shown here.

QUESTION XXIX.

At what time of the year he began the reign of Zedekiah, and for how many years he reigned.

Its beginning must be deduced from the 10th day of the fourth month, exactly eleven years before the captivity of the same Zedekiah; and as many years and one month before the destruction of the Solomonic temple, which fell on the 10th day of the 5th month. For it is said that Jeremiah prophesied until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, and until the captivity of Jerusalem, which occurred in the fifth month, Jerem. I, 9. Moreover, in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, on the 9th day of the 4th month, the city having been breached and occupied by the Babylonians, the King fleeing by night was captured by the following forces of the Chaldeans in the plains of Jericho, Jerem. XXXIX, 2, 5, and LII, 4, 9; then on the 10th day of the following 5th month, the temple and city having been destroyed, the inhabitants of Jerusalem were led into captivity, ch. LII, 12, 15. Therefore, the abduction of the people falls in the twelfth year of Zedekiah, as Clem. Alexandr. notes in lib. 1 Strom., not in the eleventh, in which Josephus writes the temple was burned, lib. X Antiq. c. 11. Since before the month when Zedekiah was captured, his eleventh year had already been completed. Scaliger is especially mistaken when he asserts that Zedekiah reigned for only 10 full years, contrary to the express letter of Scripture, Animadv. Euseb. page 82, and Canon. Isag. page 327. In the 9th year of Zedekiah, on the 10th day of the 10th month, we understand from 2 Kings XXV, 1, Jerem. LII, 4, and Ezekiel XXIV, 1, 2, that Nebuchadnezzar began to besiege Jerusalem, and that he withdrew from there when Pharaoh's army arrived, from Jerem. XXXVII, 5, 11, and XXXIV, 21, 22. In the 20th year, on the 12th day of the 10th month, Ezekiel prophesied against Pharaoh and the Egyptians; that they had been a staff of reed to the house of Israel (Ezech.

XXIX, 1. 6.) For the army of Pharaoh having returned home with the matter unaccomplished, the Chaldeans returned again to the siege of the city, just as it had been predicted by Jeremiah (Jer. XXXVII, 7. 8.) in the same 10th year of Zedekiah, which was the 18th of Nebuchadrezzar or Nebuchadnezzar (c. XXXII, 1. 2.) so that when Jerusalem was occupied by the Babylonians at the end of the 11th year of Zedekiah, it appears that this later siege was continued beyond a year, yet not more than 25 days, as far as we can gather from Ezek. IV, 5. 8.; where in the type we find 390 days assigned to the Jerusalemite siege. Which, counted backwards from the 9th day of the 4th month of the 11th year of Zedekiah, on which the city was broken through (Jerem. XXXIX, 2.), lead us to the 15th day of the 3rd month in the 10th year of Zedekiah: which is to be established as the beginning of the renewed siege. As Ussher most correctly explained this in the place cited.

QUESTION XXX. How the times of the Kings of Judah are to be directed after the Israelite kingdom has ended.

Since Hezekiah had spent 6 years before the end of the Israelite kingdom, and reigned for 29 years, 23 years remain, from the time of which year, in which he began both the seventh and the remaining years of his reign, the beginnings of the four kings following him depend. For since their times are presented simply in Scripture, not (as had been done hitherto in the kingdom of Judah and Israel) compared with the beginnings of other kings: no argument is left, by the guidance of which it is permitted for us to subtract some months (without the mark of rashness) from the proposed years, and thence to shift the beginnings of the Kings into other and different parts of the year. Whence if, for example, we deduce the years of Hezekiah from the first day of the first month: it is necessary that we say Josiah also began to reign at the same time; unless it pleases us, by our own authority, either to increase or to diminish the 55 years of Manasseh and the two years of Amon that are interposed.

But with the times of the three last kings of Judah we have the years of Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian compared in Scripture; the collation of which teaches us that Jehoiakim did not spend eleven full years, but about 6 months and a half over 10 years in the kingdom; and thus that Jehoiakim began his reign about the 10th day of the 6th month, and Jehoahaz his brother about 3 months before, about the 10th day of the 3rd month. Whence it is also certain that both the beginning and the end of the 31 years of Josiah are to be placed about the 10th day of the 3rd month. Let Table VI be seen, or the Type of the years and times of the rule of the Kings of Judah in the Chronological Tables. From which it appears that the interval from the end of the Israelite kingdom to the end of the Jewish kingdom is 133 years and almost two months.

QUESTION XXXI. How the Epoch of the Solomonic temple is to be held exactly from the beginning to the end and destruction of the same.

The beginning is defined in 1 Kings 6, 1, the 480th year after the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, which was the Year of the World 2992, Month 2, day 2, but the end is the year of the World 3416, month 6, day 10, whence from the beginning of the construction of the temple to the destruction of the same, 424 years, 3 months, and 8 days have elapsed, which we judge to be manifest from those things which we have hitherto delivered. According to the years of the sins of Israel, the numbering is instituted thus: 37 years remained from the beginning of the temple to the death of Solomon: to which are to be added 387 years of the sins of Israel, from the beginning of Solomon, the successor of Jeroboam in the kingdom of Israel, to the destruction of the Jerusalemites, 424 years proceed. And since David ruled for 40 years, and Solomon for three, before he began to build the temple, with those 43 years added, 467 years proceed. There happened therefore the total destruction of the temple and city in the 468th year from the beginning of the Davidic reign, 388 years from the Schism and separation of the kingdom of Israel from the kingdom of Judah in religious worship, 134 years from the destruction of the Israelite kingdom, 19 years from the first Babylonian servitude; thus there are still wanting about four years of the sins of Israel, so that the whole number of 390 years may be completed. Since therefore the destruction of the temple happened in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, and in his 23rd year Nebuzaradan deported the remnants of the people of the Jews and the Israelites mixed with them, Jerem. c. LII, 30, and only then was the land left completely devastated and uncultivated, the limit of the Epoch of the sins of Israel is to be fixed in that year, namely in the 22nd year of Nebuchadnezzar completed, and the 23rd begun: for with four years added to the previous number of 386 completed years of the sins of Israel, 390 years proceed, and their end falls in the year of the world 3420. Which is also the end of the 40 years. Ezek. IV, 5, 6. The beginning of which, therefore, must be taken from the year of the world 3380, that is, the 18th year of the reign of Josiah, in which the covenant was solemnly renewed and a public reformation was made by that most pious King; but since the people did not keep the covenant, but most gravely violated it again, and the public worship was subsequently horribly deformed anew, there followed the servitude of King Jehoiakim 18 years later, namely in his fourth year, and indeed 36 years from that reformation of Josiah, the total destruction of the city and temple, and 40 years from the total desolation of Judea.

That was the 19th year of the Babylonian servitude, as it was also of the principate of Nebuchadnezzar and of his first arrival in Syria and Judea, from which we have shown above that he himself still reigned for about 26 years; if to those you add the two of Evil-Merodach, the four of Neriglissar with the 9 months of Labashi-Marduk, and also the 17 of Nabonidus and the two of Darius the Mede, from whose death Cyrus took up the full administration of the Monarchy, there result 51 years. If you join these to the 19 years of Nebuchadnezzar that had elapsed at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, the sum will be 70 years, as many as were defined for the Babylonian captivity.

QUESTION XXXII.

What those 70 years are, of which mention is made in Zech. I, verse 12.

Scaliger wishes the seventieth year to be designated from the edict of Xerxes against the Jews, although that does not harmonize with his own opinion; since he affirms that it does not fall into the second year of Darius Nothus, but into the fourth; and he is mistaken in that he makes Xerxes the Ahasuerus who was the husband of Esther, and that he refers these things to the times of Darius Nothus, in which part Willius, although he otherwise likes to follow him, acknowledges that he has erred as much as heaven is from earth, and confesses with L. Danaeus that these things pertain entirely to the times of Darius Hystaspes. Nor could Cocceius find anything in the Sacred or exotic writers concerning those 70 years that would be relevant here, when he still attempts to snatch these away to the times of Darius Nothus. But we think it is evident that they refer to Darius Hystaspes from those things which we said in the Annotations Anti-Grotianae on Jeremiah XXV, and which have been handed down here above. Baelius urges these things furthermore: The years of the fasts mentioned by Zechariah are wrongly called seventy, which were according to these men over two hundred; for besides the two seventieths conceded by Scaliger, there were other nearly seventy intermediate years: for from the first of Cyrus to the thirtieth of Darius Hystaspes there are at least sixty-seven, which joined Sect. VI. with the following [years] up to the second of Darius Nothus make two hundred and seven, in the beginning and middle of which the Jews fasted on account of the burned temple, the devastated Jerusalem, and the captivity of the people; it is therefore consistent that the people mourned for the seventy years immediately following those evils, but not for more than one hundred years after the return from captivity, and the temple founded, and Jerusalem built, even if not yet surrounded by a wall; And indeed, what reason can be imagined why the Jews, who having neglected the fast for all seventy years of the captivity, and also for sixty-seven years from the return, should have renewed those fasts only in the thirtieth of Darius? Likewise: Those seventy Scaligerian years beginning from the thirtieth of Darius ought to have had some significant event for the Jewish people, on account of which such an epoch might be established as a character. But let us turn and turn over again all the sacred and profane writings of the ancients, we shall find nothing significant in the last years of Darius Hystaspis that would conveniently establish the head of any new epoch. To decline this argument, Seth Calvisius invents that the head of this Scaligerian seventy is not placed in the thirtieth of Darius, but in the first of Xerxes, when Xerxes (Ahasuerus, husband of Esther) inhibited the building of the temple, from which calamity he wishes the Jews to have counted those seventy years of Zechariah. But this is an invention of Calvisius, in which he has neither predecessor nor follower. The times also do not square, for from the first of Xerxes to the second of Nothus, according to the calculation of Calvisius himself, there are only sixty-five years. Thirdly, who would believe that in the whole time of Ahasuerus, husband of Esther, and in the days of Artaxerxes his son, no benign decree towards the Jews was obtained by Esther and Mordecai.

This is Baillie. This same Robert Baillie in his Historical work, p. 190, excuses Luther and Philippus Melanchthon, those greatest of men, because, seduced by the impostures of Annius of Viterbo, not yet so clear in that age, they referred the 2nd year of Darius to Artaxerxes Longimanus, assigning by this reasoning new limits to the 70 years of Zechariah. But he himself follows Calvin, Gualther, Danaeus, the English Annotators, Pererius, and Salianus, who think that the 70 years of Zechariah are not to be distinguished from the 70 of Jeremiah, but that both end in the first of Cyrus, seventeen years before the second of Darius Hystaspis, in which the Angel spoke to Zechariah. He contends with them that the Hebrew text must be translated thus: in these seventy years, and not this seventieth year. But why would he have said in these 70 years, if 80 and almost 90 had already elapsed. But this is a vain refuge, joined with a corruption of the text, which implies that the seventy years had already long since elapsed. That ALREADY LONG SINCE is thrust into the text, which is a mark of rashness: by which method the times designated in the holy scriptures could easily be rendered doubtful, if, for instance, it were permitted to add anything of our own to the words of the Holy Spirit, nor would any certainty remain. And how would that little word be thrust into chap. VII. vers. 5. When you fasted and lamented in the fifth and seventh month, during these 70 years! Will it be necessary here to understand ALREADY LONG SINCE elapsed? That it indicates the time immediately preceding or elapsed, even D. Behmius could not deny in Chronol. Manuduct. lib. II. tit. II. cap. III. Luther, he says, in both places (Zachar. I. v. 12. & cap. VII. v. 5.) these 70. Year, which, to wit, immediately preceded, for thus the little word זה is customarily taken for the time immediately preceding, when it is constructed with numeral nouns and those denoting time: as is manifest from the following places. Gen. XXXI. vers. 38. & 41. likewise Num. XIV. v. 22. cap. XXXII, 2. likewise Deut. IIX, 2. & 1. Sam. XXIX, 3.

thence B. D. Behmius slipped into this, that he suspected that Zechariah understood other 70 years, of which no trace appears in the holy scriptures.

The matter, however, is most manifest if, with most interpreters and the better chronologists—Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, Cornelius a Lapide, Castro, Sanctius, Pererius, Henricus Philippi, Ussher, Capellus—the 70 years are understood not of the Babylonian captivity or servitude, but of the Jerusalemite ἐρημώσεως or devastation. For from the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, in which the devastation occurred, about 26 years of his reign remained; to the monarchy of Cyrus, 51 years and nine months flowed by, as was evident in the previous question, that is, to the 23rd year of his Persian reign, from which there still remain about seven years until his death, to which if eight of Cambyses and two of Darius Hystaspis are added, the sum of these will be about 18 years. To which, when added to the 51 years, 69 years result. We do not, therefore, see a reason why we should prefer the opinion of the moderns here, having abandoned the footsteps of the ancients.

For if they urge that in the second year of Darius 70 years had not yet elapsed since the destruction of the temple, which the angel established as the foundation of his prayers for removing the remnants of the desolations: because 70 years have already elapsed: I respond that the beginning of the calamity and desolation can be taken from the beginning of the siege which occurred in the tenth month, since 31 months intervened from the beginning of the siege to the devastation of the temple and city: that is, two years and seven months: to which, when added to the sum above, it will be established that 70 years have elapsed from the siege of the city, which brought total destruction to it and the temple, to those times of Zechariah and the vision, which occurred in the second year of Darius Hystaspis. Indeed, if the beginning is taken from the final siege, which occurred 390 days before the city was captured, as is gathered from the type in Ezekiel 4:5, 8, that is, one full year and two months before the destruction of the temple, those 70 years are gathered from the same siege of Jerusalem. from the beginning up to the second year of Darius: just as Ussher began the calculation in his annals. The time of the fasts, which Zechariah commemorated in chapter 7:3 and chapter 8:9, also favors this, inasmuch as they were celebrated in memory of the Jerusalemite devastation: as Cyril of Alexandria observed, namely, the fast of the tenth month on account of the siege of the city: of the fourth on account of the city being captured: of the fifth on account of the temple being burned: of the seventh on account of Gedaliah being killed, Jeremiah 52:4, 2 Kings 25:15.

QUESTION XXXIII.

In which year does the death of Nebuchadnezzar fall?

Jeremiah 52:31 counts the 37th year from the deportation of Jeconiah, in which Evil-Merodach began to reign. Since, therefore, the reign and deportation of Jeconiah fall in the year of the world 3405, and the eighth from the capture of Jehoiakim, or of the Babylonian servitude, which was also the eighth of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture 2 Kings 24:12, counted from his first arrival in Syria and Judea, the end of Nebuchadnezzar and the beginning of Evil-Merodach will fall in the year of the world 3442, and the forty-fifth of the Babylonian captivity, and from the beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, which is the Nabonassarean year, according to the canon of Ptolemy 186; whence an excellent concatenation is had of the years of Scripture with the notable Nabonassarean era, the beginning of which is referred to the year of the world 3257, the 12th of Jotham King of Judah, the 13th of Pekah King of Israel. Table VII, which pertains here, exhibits the type of the years of Nebuchadnezzar and other kings up to the end of the Babylonian servitude.

Of the Sixth Epoch from the obtained liberty of the people to the beginning of the weeks of Daniel, or the going forth of the word concerning the repairing of the Sacred things, and the rebuilding of the city, of 78 years.

After, by the favor of Cyrus who was raised to the Monarchy, God directing, the liberty of returning to the Fatherland and building the temple was granted, the Jews did indeed return, under the leader Zorobabel, called Sesbazzar (Ezra 1:8), and the high priest Joshua, a catalog of whom is woven in Ezra 2, and they began to lay the foundations of the temple (ch. 3:10) in the second year of the return; but the success of the work was hindered by antagonists, who bribed the counselors of Cyrus, in the times of Cyrus, as also of his successors Ahasuerus, that is, Cambyses, and Artaxerxes, or Smerdis the Magian, up to the second year of Darius Hystaspis, as is related in Ezra 4:15 seqq. and v. 24. But the Jews were at length aroused not only by Haggai and Zechariah the Prophets to the continuation of the work in the time of Darius; but when the matter was referred by the governor and the counselors of the province to the King, and an inquiry was made in the Archives of Achmetha, or Ecbatana in Media, the decree of Cyrus, by which power had already been given to rebuild the temple, was found, and a new, most gracious mandate was also promulgated by King Darius, concerning the structure of the temple not being hindered, and the means necessary for the sacrifices being supplied, with a most severe penalty ordained for transgressors, Ezra 5 and 6 chapters; and so the work was happily completed in the sixth year of Darius (Ezra 4:15), the second temple being built, the glory of which ought to have been greater, on account of the coming of the desire of nations, the Messiah, than was that of the former house, as Haggai prophesied (c. 2:8), inasmuch as He was to fill the temple with His majesty in the days of His flesh. Since, therefore, Cyrus is commemorated by Ezra, and his two nearest successors, under whom the structure of the temple was begun and hindered, and Darius is immediately added to them as the promoter of the work, we have here the first four Monarchs in the Persian empire: namely Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspis; of whom, however, Smerdis is an interloper or intruder, and is thus held unworthy of that diadem by St. Daniel.

11:2, where, introducing four Monarchs in Persia from Darius the Mede, after Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius Hystaspis, who are tacitly insinuated, he designated the fourth as the richest of all, whom History and the series of Monarchs in Persia declare to be Xerxes. The same history makes Artaxerxes Longimanus his successor, whom Ezra likewise proclaimed as the Patron of the Jews and of sacred or ecclesiastical affairs: by whom he himself, furnished with a royal decree, was sent to fully repair and restore the Sacred things (ch. 7), those who accompanied him being recounted at length, and the reformation instituted by him being described (ch. 8, 9, and 10), just as Nehemiah also in an entire book described the restoration of the Polity and the city of Jerusalem, done by him by the authority of the same King Artaxerxes, from chapter 1 to 13. In these Canonical Scriptures, therefore, we have those things which followed the liberating edict of Cyrus, up to the erection of the temple and the restoration of the city, as well as a historical description of the same, and thus also the term from which, and the beginning of the seventy weeks of Daniel, which commence from the going forth of the word concerning the repairing of the Sacred things and the restoration of the city. Which is the principal Epoch, and the same the last for defining the exhibition of the promised Messiah and the πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου.

But how great that is for investigating the truth of the oracle's fulfillment, since the years of the Persian Kings are not expressed in the Sacred writings, it remains to be learned from exotic history: and primarily from the Canon of Ptolemy, confirmed by celestial characters, from the collation of which, both the interval of cessation from the promulgation of the edict and the beginning of the structure of the temple, and the time of the structure itself, and the Epoch from the built temple to the edict of Artaxerxes concerning the Sacred things being fully repaired can be elicited: from which it will also be permitted to establish or define the beginning of the weeks of Daniel. And since Cyrus presided for seven years after undertaking the Monarchy, but Cambyses, including the empire of Smerdis the Magian, for eight years, to whom succeeded Darius Hystaspis, from the first promulgation of the edict of Cyrus to the new edict of Darius Hystaspis, granted in his second year, there result 17 years. Furthermore, since Darius Hystaspis reigned for 34 years from that time, and 21 years are assigned to Xerxes by Ptolemy, and the edict concerning the repairing of the Sacred things went forth in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, his son and successor, which we establish as the term from which of the weeks of Daniel, from entirely immovable foundations, 61 years emerge, which, added to the previous 17, make 78 years.

EPOCH FROM THE EDICT OF CYRUS TO THE GOING FORTH OF THE WORD CONCERNING THE RESTORING OF THE SACRED RITES AND THE CITY.

From the promulgation of Cyrus to the edict of Darius, 17 years. From the second year of Darius to the edict of Artaxerxes, 61. Total, 78 years. According to the Persian Monarchs, this Epoch is gathered thus: Cyrus presided over the Monarchy for 7 years. Cambyses, called Ahasuerus in Ezra 4, presided for 7 years and 5 months. Smerdis, called Artaxerxes in Ezra 4, presided for 7 months. Darius Hystaspis reigned for 36 years. Xerxes reigned for 21 years. Thence to the completed year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, 6. Total of years, 78. To which, if the years from the creation of the world to the Monarchy of Cyrus, 3467, are added, there result the years from the created World to the beginning of the weeks of Daniel, 3545. Understand the years as completed, so that in the 3546th year of the current world the edict went forth.

QUESTION I. Whether that Darius, up to whose reign in Ezra 4:5 the structure of the temple is said to have been hindered, is different from the Darius mentioned in the last verse?

Thus the Scaligerians invent; for in the former place they wish Darius Hystaspis to be indicated, by whom the structure of the temple was hindered: but in the latter, another Darius, under whom the structure of the temple succeeded, whom therefore they wish to be Darius Nothus. But just as they are greatly mistaken in designating this supporter and promoter of the sacred work, and deviate from all antiquity, so they do violence to the words of Ezra, when they establish that the Darius mentioned in chapter 4:5 hindered the structure of the temple, and distinguish him from the Darius in verse 24. For it is too manifest that by Ezra in verse 5 is designated the limit to which the sacred work was hindered, which words, written with the rays of the Sun, are in need of no interpretation. It came to pass, therefore, that the people of the land hindered the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building. And they hired counselors against them, to frustrate their purpose ALL THE DAYS OF CYRUS King of the Persians, AND UNTIL the reign of Darius King of the Persians. Where those are in error who contend that the particle עד is not to be understood in an exclusive sense, but an inclusive one. For, in the first place, the customary meaning of the word does not allow this, as it ordinarily introduces the limit of a thing or action: from which ordinary and proper meaning of the word one must not depart without necessity and most weighty causes. Although a doubt might be raised, whether in those places likewise, where a certain continuation has a place, that particle might not also introduce a limit in a certain way? But then the συνέχεια of Ezra's discourse does not allow it: who teaches that the success of the holy work was hindered AND ALL THE DAYS OF CYRUS AND UNTIL THE REIGN OF DARIUS, but not all the days of the reign of Darius. & under Artaxerxes, and he sets forth that whole matter and concludes his narrative v. 24. Then the work of the Lord in Jerusalem was interrupted, and was not done UNTIL THE SECOND YEAR of the reign of Darius King of the Persians. Which conclusion most openly explains that which he had previously indicated briefly v. 1. Until the reign of Darius King of the Persians: determining the end of the cessation in the second year of the same Darius: concerning which he further wove a fuller account in chapters V. and VI.: how the matter was done, and the structure succeeded, both through the prophecies and κελεύσματα of the Prophets c. V, 1. and through the indulgence and decree of King Darius, so that nothing is more manifest than that one and the same Darius is designated in v. 5. and 24. and subsequently in chapters V. and VI.: of which matter, however, more evident proofs will yet be revealed from the subsequent questions.

QUESTION II. Who is that Ahasuerus whom Ezra commemorates in chapter IV. verse 6.?

Scaliger with his followers wishes him to be Xerxes, but again against the suffrages of venerable antiquity, and from a mere conjecture of names, and that one fetched from very far away. For whom, I ask, will they persuade that these names Ahasuerus and Xerxes are the same? How many mutations are needed for Ahasuerus to be extracted from Xerxes? And what names could not thus be recalled to identity, if it were permitted to change squares into rounds in such a way? But then if this Ahasuerus is Xerxes, and the husband of Esther, which they themselves wish, how will it be consistent with the piety of Esther's husband that he himself and his son Artaxerxes Longimanus, whom Scaliger wishes to have been begotten by Esther, hindered the work of the restoration of the temple through all the days of their reign, and even obstructed it with decrees? For Esther's husband and his son were without doubt benefactors of the Jews, not enemies. Who therefore would believe that both gave place to the antagonists of the Jews throughout the whole time of their reign, and hindered the structure of the temple. Thirdly, since this Ahasuerus is immediately joined to Cyrus in the account of Ezra, namely that the holy work was hindered all the days of Cyrus until the reign of Darius, and thus under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, it is manifest that the immediate successor of Cyrus is designated by the name of Ahasuerus, who was Cambyses, his son. And indeed it would have been closer to a miracle if, while that monster was reigning, any holy matter had flourished: or if the holy work was hindered even in his days, how did Ezra pass that over in silence? For that Cambyses and the days of his reign are involved under the name and days of Cyrus is altogether ridiculous, even if Alstedius does not hesitate to assert it. Why do they not also say that the reign of Smerdis is involved under the same name, who without doubt likewise obstructed the work of the Lord? Or were Xerxes and Artaxerxes more cruel and harder against the Jews than Cambyses and Smerdis, so that their pressures were primarily to be commemorated by the Holy Spirit? Which the Scaligerians certainly would not say. Wherefore the opinion of the ancients is altogether to be preferred, that that Ahasuerus was Cambyses, who assumed this name for the sake of greater glory: since Ahasuerus according to Scaliger signifies a great Duke, from Ahasch great, Vav and Rosch head, and Cambyses, however much he was a worst King, was nevertheless a great Duke and warrior, who subdued all of Egypt with his arms. Whence Josephus, Lyranus, Lavaterus, Vatablus, Münsterus and most others commonly maintain that that Ahasuerus was Cambyses.

QUESTION III.

Who Artaxerxes is, who in Ezra 4:6 by mandate inhibited the construction of the temple.

Scaliger wishes that Artaxerxes to be Artaxerxes, called Longimanus, the son of Xerxes: whom not a few moderns follow: and that primarily to the end that they may maintain that Darius, of whom there is speech in v. 24, is τὸν Νόθον; but in such wondrous ways are the chronological limits disturbed, and violence done to Scripture, as will be evident in the following question: and it is falsely assumed that by Ahasuerus, whom Ezra mentioned before Artaxerxes, Xerxes is understood: which hypothesis collapsing, the idea that Artaxerxes is Artaxerxes Longimanus also collapses. And therefore more accurate chronologists and interpreters reject that opinion of Scaliger, even if they do not agree equally on who is to be understood by Artaxerxes.

Some think that Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes are the same subject: and thus the Latin Vulgate version holds, with this parenthesis inserted: (This Artaxerxes is Ahasuerus) which words, because they are not held in the original text, are deservedly rejected by Lyranus. Although meanwhile he himself, with the Hebrew and other interpreters, embraces the matter itself, that Artaxerxes was Ahasuerus, and that Cambyses was designated by both these names, since those names were common to the Kings of the Persians. But it is better to distinguish the persons, since Ezra treats of them distinctly: of Ahasuerus indeed, whom we have said is Cambyses, v. 6. in the reign of Ahasuerus in the beginning of his reign they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem; but of Artaxerxes v. 7. And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath etc. and therefore many from the Reformed alike, and from Ours and the Papists, prefer to understand by Artaxerxes, Tanyoxarces the Great, the successor of Cambyses, who was also called Smerdis: because he assumed such an august name for himself, for the sake of conciliating majesty, which they wish to signify a great warrior from Art, great, and Xerxes, warrior. And that the Kings of the Persians were almost all called Artaxerxes, as the Egyptians were called Pharaohs and Ptolemies, the Parthians Arsacids, the Philistines Abimelech etc., Alsted himself observed in Chronol. p. 182. so that it is ridiculous that Scaliger objects that two-bodied monsters are created when we affirm that Cambyses was called Ahasuerus and Smerdis was called Artaxerxes: who indeed likewise in book VI of the Emendation of times warned that it was accepted among the Kings of the Persians that they should assume other names when they were moved to the fasces: just as Darius Nothus was previously called Ochus, Artaxerxes Mnemon was previously called Arsicas and Oarses, and Codomannus, once named, obtained the name of Darius in the Monarchy. How futile, says Scaliger in his animadversions to Eusebius p. 85, is the objection about names, so that when all other things agree, the difference of names should make it so that Marius is not Marius.

However, it pleased the blessed Dr. Joh. Cluver in his Chronological calculation to have another view regarding these two named by Ezra, Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes: we append his opinion, as proposed by him, so that the learned may judge whether this one, which we have brought forward thus far, or indeed the Cluverian opinion is to be preferred: for as far as the Chronological calculation is concerned, it makes no difference which one a person follows. The first, he says, of those who hindered the building of the temple is Cyrus, who indeed dismissed the Jews, but moved by accusations afterwards, did not promote the continuation of the building of the temple. The second is Ahasuerus, to whom they sent the accusation of the Jews, who was (I believe) the brother of Cambyses, Tanyoxarses, whom Cyrus appointed King of the Bactrians, Parthians, Carmania, and Choramnia, as Ctesias of Cnidus writes in Photius in his Bibliotheca p. 54, and under whose name the Magus, the author of his murder, reigned afterwards. The third is Artaxerxes, by which name Cambyses was called, as Josephus rightly thinks. For by his private name he was Cambyses, namesake to his father Cyrus and his grandfather. But by his public and royal name he was Artaxerxes, just as Scaliger himself notes and proves that names were changed for Kings when they undertook the administration of the empire. They, therefore, became more hostile to the Jews. Since, therefore, it was publicly known that Cambyses had descended into Egypt after the death of his Father, and that the government of affairs was in the hands of his brother Tanyoxerxes or Oxerxes, he says that accusatory letters were written to him and soon also to Artaxerxes, or Cambyses, and thus the building of the temple was hindered until Darius the son of Hystaspes, just as has been said in a few words. This is Cluver.

QUESTION IV. Who is that Darius, in whose 2nd year the structure of the temple is said by Ezra c. IV, 24 to have been resumed?

By great consensus the Ancients teach that that Darius is Hystaspes, Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins. But Scaliger, who has everywhere moved the ancient boundaries in Chronology, contends that he is not Darius Hystaspes, but Darius Nothus. Induced by his authority, not a few are of the same opinion, especially among the Reformed, Lunius, Reinoldus, Deodatus, Ubbo, Emmius, the Anglican Annotators, Nisbeth, and others, and also from our own, Sethus Calvisius, Dr. Behmius, Dr. Helvicus, etc. However, there is no reason why we should depart here from the footsteps of antiquity. For the main argument, by which Scaliger and his followers triumph greatly, when rightly examined, is of no moment: namely, that Darius Nothus is to be understood because he is placed between two Artaxerxes by Ezra, that is, between Artaxerxes Longimanus and Memnon. Indeed, this is assumed gratuitously, as if it were admittedly certain, which is most of all a matter of dispute: that the Darius commemorated in Ezra IV, verse 24, is placed between those two Artaxerxes. Ezra indeed designates in c. IV, 5 an Artaxerxes who hindered the building of the temple, whom he makes prior to Darius: he also designates in c. IV, 14 and c. VII, 1 ff. an Artaxerxes, posterior to Darius, who promoted the restoration of divine worship. But that the former is Artaxerxes Longimanus and the latter is Artaxerxes Memnon is in question, nor can it be shown by any solid document. What they take from the names is not so firm that for its sake the boundaries of Chronology should be disturbed, since, as Scaliger himself admits, as we have just observed, the Kings of the Persians, when they aspired to the empire, were accustomed to assume other names, especially magnificent ones. And therefore nothing prevents the Magus Smerdis from having taken the name of Artaxerxes for himself out of pride, having cast off his viler name, when he ascended to the pinnacle of the kingdom: which the order and series of Persian Kings, whom Ezra introduces, confirms is indicated by Ezra in the former place. For teaching that the building of the temple was hindered from the time of Cyrus until the reign of Darius, he commemorates two Kings after Cyrus, under whose empire it ceased, namely Ahasuerus, c. IV, 6, and Artaxerxes v. 7, who intervened between the reign of Cyrus and Darius, as successors of Cyrus and predecessors of Darius. But because no other successors of Cyrus are found in the history of the Persian Kings than Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, and Smerdis the Magus, who preceded Darius, it is rightly concluded that by those two intermediaries of Ezra, as being the nearest successors of Cyrus and predecessors of Darius, the same are understood, and no others; that by the first, Ahasuerus, Cambyses is to be understood, who succeeded Cyrus immediately and took the name of Ahasuerus for himself, as being more magnificent than that which he had received from his grandfather, since according to Herodotus it denotes warlike, and according to Scaliger it signifies a great Duke, whom the Jews, Josephus, Lyranus, and most Christians understand; but by the other, Artaxerxes, namely in v. 7, Smerdis the Magus, the successor of Cambyses, is indicated, who in this glorious name of Artaxerxes sought the glory of the name. Whom Darius I, son of Hystaspes, follows in the series of Persian Kings in Ezra IV, 24, and afterwards, with Xerxes intervening, Artaxerxes the long-handed, or Longimanus, who therefore must be that Artaxerxes who is commemorated in Ezra IV, 14, c. VII, 1, 8, Neh. I, 1, c. II, 1, c. XIII, 6. By which arrangement sacred History agrees excellently with Exotic Writers, who recount the Persian Kings in this order: Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, Darius Hystaspes, Xerxes, Artaxerxes Longimanus. For these correspond in Ezra to Cyrus (Cyrus), Ahasuerus (Cambyses), Artaxerxes (Smerdis), Darius (Darius Hystaspes), Artaxerxes (Artaxerxes Longimanus), and only Xerxes is missing, whom, however, the Holy Scripture did not pass over in silence in Daniel, when it predicted that after Darius the Mede there would still be three Monarchs in Persia, and a fourth enriched exceedingly above all, c. XI, 2. For these three (disregarding the supposititious Smerdis, who did not seem worthy to be numbered among the others in the Prophetic oracle, even if in the historical account, where the matter demanded it, his mention was not neglected), Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius Hystaspes are they, and they do not allow the fourth, Xerxes, the richest of all, to be hidden.

Scaliger and his followers understand Xerxes by Ahasuerus, and make him the husband of Esther, but Artaxerxes Longimanus by Artaxerxes, his son. But it is by no means likely that the divine historian Ezra, accurately describing what happened regarding the structure of the temple, both hindered and promoted, would omit certain Kings under whom the work had been hindered; so far is it from the case that (as they are forced to say) he passed over several of them without a word, under whose rule the structure had to cease for many good years, namely Cambyses, Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspes, the three immediate successors of Cyrus; whence Baillie is forced to desert Scaliger here, whose authority he rightly calls great, lib. I. qu. VI. p. 157. Ahasuerus, he says, and Artaxerxes named by Ezra in the first place were the first of the Persian Kings who hindered the building of the temple against the command of Cyrus: But Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus were not the first hinderers of that work, for thus the Jews would have persevered in that work without any hindrance up to their reigns, and would have easily finished the temple before those kings were born, for after the interruption they undertook the work in the second year of Darius, and put the finishing touch to it in his sixth year, in the space of four years. How then did it happen that for the full seventeen years of Cyrus and Cambyses, and thirty-six of Darius Hystaspis, they, hindered by no one, did not complete that work before the reign of Xerxes and Artaxerxes.

Nor is there any reason to say that in v. 5 Darius Hystaspis and in v. 24 Darius Nothus are understood; for the text does not allow that different subjects be said to be designated: since Ezra affirms in v. 5 that the structure was hindered in the final times of Cyrus UNTIL the reign of King Darius, and in v. 6 and the following verses explains how immediately at the beginning of Ahasuerus, his next successor, who was none other than Cambyses, the work was obstructed by false ἐγκλήματα (accusations), and also how afterwards in the time of Artaxerxes, who succeeded Cambyses, i.e., Smerdis, through Bishlam, Mithridates, and others of the same ilk, the inhibition of the work was procured by accusatory letters, so that (as is subjoined by way of a συμπέρασμα (conclusion) at the end of the chapter, v. 24) the work in the house of the Lord ceased until the second year of Darius. Whence an invincible argument of this kind arises: That person is understood by King Darius in Ezra 4:5, until whose reign the structure was hindered, so that in the meantime it ceased, until that Darius reigned. But the structure was hindered until the reign of the Darius mentioned in v. 24, so that it ceased in the meantime: as is most clearly evident from the words of Ezra. Therefore, by King Darius in Ezra 4:5 is understood that Darius who is mentioned in v. 24, and not another.

To which proof against the Scaligerians it is favorable that Mithridates is introduced in the time of Artaxerxes in Ezra 4:7, then corrupted by money, as were other counselors of Cyrus, who previously, at the time of the liberating edict of Cyrus, had handed over the gold and silver vessels to Zerubbabel as treasurer in ch. 1:9; whom, if Artaxerxes Longimanus is to be understood by Artaxerxes, it would have been necessary to have held the highest dignities for over 72 years, even if he had attempted those things against the Jews in the first year of Longimanus.

Finally, if we suppose that after the Darius named in v. 5 those ἐγκλήματα (accusations) were at last brought to Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, how will that account now be consistent with itself: they hindered the counsel all the days of Cyrus UNTIL THE REIGN OF DARIUS Hystaspis: and afterwards in the time of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes (Xerxes and Artaxerxes) they wrote accusations? For once the final term of the inhibition has been indicated, namely the beginning of the reign of Darius, will the hindrance that occurred under his successors still be recounted? Furthermore, secondly, our opinion is confirmed by the series of the August promoters of the temple, who are celebrated by Ezra in ch. 6:14: Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes: And they built and finished it by the commandment of the GOD of Israel and according to the mandate of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, King of the Persians. For if Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes Mnemon are understood, it is necessary to say that the temple was built and divine worship restored nearly one hundred and forty years after the edict of Cyrus. Which is inconvenient. But if Darius Hystaspis is understood, in whose second year the structure of the temple succeeded, only about 20 years elapsed from the first edict to the completed work in the sixth year of Darius: and afterwards in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, i.e., fifty-eight years after the temple was built, a magnificent restoration of divine worship will have been made. Which, indicated here by prolepsis, is explained at length in the following seventh chapter and thereafter by design: how many ornaments and additions, both inside and outside, were added to the buildings adjacent and near to the temple for its sake.

Thirdly, Chronology does not permit that Darius Nothus be understood in Ezra 4:24. For from the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, if he held the same for only seven years, or as some from the opposing side wish, for only three years, to the second year of Darius Nothus 115 or 110 years are counted: according to that opinion, therefore, the Jews would have lacked the temple and the ordinary sacred rites to be performed in it for over a century after their return from Babylon (and for the temple building to have ceased for a whole century and more, and for the Jews to have lacked the ordinary performance of sacred rites in it, and to have languished most miserably in hope, would have been a heavier punishment than the seventy-year exile itself) and Joshua would have presided over the Priesthood and Zerubbabel over the Principate for more than 110 years, which is in no way likely, nor has anyone easily heard it said of anyone since the passing of the sons of Noah that any mortal has been engaged in a public office for such a long time.

Now if, fourthly, the 52 years elapsed from the destruction of the temple to the first of Cyrus are added, it will be necessary to say that some lived at least 162 or more truly 167 years from that very time to the continued structure in the second year of Darius, and if they were 12 or a little more at the time of the said πανολεθρία (total destruction), they would have reached 178 or 180 and more years by living: which is unheard of in that age, and inconvenient among the Jewish people. That such survivors existed in the second year of Darius, who had observed the glory of the former temple, is clear from Haggai 2:3 and Ezra 3:12; which, since Scaliger denies, he could with the same ease deny that the sun shines at midday.

Fifth, from Zechariah 1:12, it is clear that in the second year of Darius the seventieth year had elapsed since the destruction of the city, which in no way fits the second year of Darius Nothus. For indeed, from the destruction to that year, not 70 years are counted, but 164. But to the second year of Darius Hystaspis, precisely seventy years have elapsed. For since that destruction occurred in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, the 158th of the Nabonassar era, with 70 years added, the 228th year of the Nabonassar era is produced, which is the second year of Darius Hystaspis. And thus there is no need, with Dr. Behm, to accuse Zechariah of not having attended to an accurate calculation of those 70 years, or to invent that other years are indicated about which nothing certain is held, because that age suffered from a scarcity of prophets, or with Scaliger to likewise concoct another unnamed beginning for those years, since it is too manifest that the Prophet is speaking of the seventieth year from the destruction of the city, who also commemorates the fasts instituted in memory of the same, namely of the fifth and seventh month, Zechariah 7:5, because in the fifth the temple was burned, 2 Kings 25:8, and in the seventh Gedaliah was killed, v. 25, as also the fasts of the tenth month, in which the city began to be besieged, 2 Kings 25:1, and also of the fourth month, in which the city was taken, Jeremiah 39:2, Zechariah 8:19. Let those things be seen which are in the Compendium of Ecclesiastical History of the Most Serene Prince Ernest of Gotha, book 1, chapter 3, section 1, page 311 et seqq., among Dr. Florent. Schilling, Dr. Johann Cluver in his Chronology, and what we have said in the Annotations Anti-Grotian on Daniel chapter 9, and in the Diatribe on the seventy weeks of Daniel chapter 8, where still other reasons for this opinion concerning Darius Hystaspis and against Darius Nothus are adduced: and for this agreement in calculation, the following are cited: Josephus, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Theodoret, Cyril of Alexandria, Basil of Seleucia, Jerome, Augustine, Bede, Marianus Scotus, Bellarmine likewise, Genebrard, Salianus, Torniellus, Pererius, Sanctius, Petavius, Gordon, Huntley, Henry Philippi, and also Capellus, Ussher, Robert Baillie, Isaac Vossius, Johann Vorstius, and from our own side David Chytræus, Reusner, Christian Matthiæ, Wilhelm Lang, and Vogel. To these is added Edward Simson in his Chronology. Catholic, part 4, to the year 3485, who says: Josephus testifies that the building of the Jerusalem Temple, which had been interrupted, was resumed in the second year of Darius, and after him Clement of Alexandria.

Sect. VII. Eusebius, and indeed ALMOST ALL THE ANCIENTS. And to the year M. 3486. From the destruction of the temple to this vision (Zech. 1:12) seventy years, six months, and fourteen days have elapsed. For Jeremiah spoke of other years, and Zechariah of others. The former take their beginning from the first captivity, the latter from the third or that of Zedekiah, as the most learned father Theodoret rightly observes in his Commentaries on Dan. ch. 9 and on Zech. ch. 1. See, if you please, Fr. Ribera on this place of Zechariah. This is now the seventieth year, etc. Clemens speaks of these seventy years in book I of the Stromata: καὶ ἔμεινεν ἡ αἰχμαλωσία ἐπὶ ἔτη ἑβδομήκοντα, καταλήξασα εἰς τὸ δεύτερον ἔτος τοῦ δαρείου τοῦ ὑστάσπου, that is, the captivity lasted for seventy years, as it ceased in the second year of Darius Hystaspis. Josephus, Antiquities book XI, ch. 1, says: that the first year of Cyrus was the seventieth, that is, the seventieth of that Babylonian transmigration. Indeed, he spoke there of those LXX years of Jeremiah. But the same author, in Antiquities book X, ch. 2, writes thus: ἔρημος ἰουδαία πᾶσα καὶ ἱεροσόλυμα καὶ ὁ Ναὸς διέμεινεν ἔτεσιν ἑβδομήκοντα, all Judæa with Jerusalem and the temple remained desolate for seventy years. He speaks openly of these LXX years of desolation, which are mentioned in the Prophecy of Zechariah. The number of years is corrupt in the same Josephus, book I against Apion: Ναβουχοδονόσορος ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῳ τῆς αὐτοῦ βασιλείας ἔτει τὸν παρ' ἡμῖν ναὸν ἠρήμωσε, καὶ ἦν ἀφανὴς ἐπὶ ἔτη ἑπτά: (read seventy) Δευτέρῳ τε τῆς Κύρου βασιλείας ἔτει τῶν θεμελίων ὑποβληθέντων, δευτέρῳ πάλιν τῆς Δαρείου βασιλείας ἀπετελέσθη, that is, Nebuchadnezzar in the eighteenth year of his reign brought our temple to desolation, and it was destroyed for seven (nay, seventy) years, for the foundations having been laid in the second year of the reign of Cyrus, it was completed again in the second year of the reign of Darius. Thus Simson.

It is also helpful to add, for the sake of harmony and evidence, those things which the blessed Lord Dr. Cluverus, a historian and chronologist of no common rank, said here in the ear of the Scaligerians and opposed to their opinion, adhering as is proper to the traces of Scripture, and not abandoning them for the sake of the inventions of the Moderns. His Elenchus states it thus: Therefore, that they (the Scaligerians) may repent, I would wish them to consider, besides the sufficiently evident testimony of Zechariah adduced, first, that one should not depart from the consensus of the learned Fathers without the most urgent causes, whom they have in this question clearly against them. Next, how absurd it is to establish that in the time of that Darius the Jews were one hundred and ninety-six years old, such an age as we read of no mortal in any of those centuries. For they are forced to attribute so much to not a few who returned from captivity, unless they abandon that opinion about Darius Nothus. For the prophet Haggai, ch. 2:4, testifies that there were some in the second year of that Darius, who promoted the structure of the temple, who were survivors and had seen the house of the Lord in its former glory. If they were there in the second year of Darius Nothus, they had already lived to one hundred and ninety-six years. Let them have been only ten years old when they were carried off into servitude, they lived in servitude for LXX years up to the second year of Darius Hystaspis: add thirty-five years of Darius Hystaspis, 20 of Xerxes, 40 of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and one of Darius Nothus, and you will have their age of one hundred and ninety-six years. Absurd and truly strange that such sharp-sighted men have not noticed this at all.

Thirdly, let those chronologists see what they wish to do with the high priests, whom Nehemiah lists in order in ch. 12:10. For under Cyrus and Darius Nothus, Jesus the son of Josedech held the high priesthood for 112 years, as they indeed falsely opine. Let him therefore have died in the same year in which, according to them, the temple was finished, namely the sixth of Darius. Therefore there were five high priests in the one hundred and three years following up to Alexander the Great. Jesus alone therefore was long-lived beyond measure and standard, the rest were of very short life. On the contrary, however, how much more consistent is this calculation of ours, which we submit for the reader to briefly weigh. In it, Jesus holds the priesthood under Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius; his son Josabad (Ezra 8:33) or Jojakim (Neh. 12:10) under Xerxes and Artaxerxes, in his seventh year. Jesus' grandson Eliasib in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Neh. 3:1. The great-grandson Jojada towards the end of Artaxerxes, and under Darius Nothus. Johannes or Jonathas under Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes Mnemon, Neh. 12:10, 23. Joseph. book II of Antiquities, ch. 7. Jaddus under Ochus, Arses, and Darius Codomannus, Joseph. book II, ch. 8. Fourthly, let them see how true it is what Scaliger writes in book 3 of the Emendation of Time, that Nehemiah posits only two governors, Zerubbabel and himself. And therefore that Zerubbabel presided over the Jews up to the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Mnemon. For the contrary is evident from ch. VI of Nehemiah, v. 15, when he says: The former governors, who had been before me, burdened the people, and took from them in bread and wine and money daily forty shekels; but their ministers also oppressed the people. But I did not do so because of the fear of God.

Fifthly, let them see how little it agrees with the prophetic promises in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, if it is said that the returning Jews lacked a temple for 112 years. Thus D. Cluverus.

As for what the Scaligerians object from Ezra ch. 6, that a fairly long interval must have intervened from the edict of Cyrus up to the second year of this Darius. Indeed, it would have been necessary that the grant be sought in the archives of Cyrus at Ecbatana, or Achmetha, which had been buried in oblivion: But thus only 13 years would have intervened, if the second year of Darius Hystaspis were designated. I reply: Not 13, but 17 years flowed from then: namely 7 of Cyrus, 8 of Cambyses and Smerdis, and two of Darius: nor is it a wonder, in such a great confusion of the empire, and when meanwhile two other kings had disturbed the work of the temple with contrary edicts, which had been granted by Cyrus, that there was need for an accurate search of the autograph, so that the cause of the grant and likewise of the inhibition might be weighed in a just balance. And how many things in the courts of princes and kings are often consigned to oblivion within two or three lustra, which concern not the temple of a foreign and very poor nation, but the very reason of state of the Republic, especially in such turbulent times and changes of kingdoms? That is trivial, it is said in the Gotha Compendium p. 314, what they bring forward concerning the search for the edict of Cyrus. For how easy was it, in such a great kingdom consisting of so many provinces, for some edict, or its form and special contents, to fall into oblivion? And Darius the Fourth, if we do not exclude the tyrants, was king after Cyrus, raised to the summit from another family.

QUESTION V.

Who is the Artaxerxes of Ezra IV, 24, joined with Darius in promoting the restoration of the temple?

The followers of Scaliger wish Artaxerxes Mnemon to be understood here by their conjectures: whom they say reigned at the same time with his father Darius Nothus, and together established the edict concerning the completion of the temple. But they assume that Darius Nothus is indicated here by the name of Darius, which is repugnant to chronology, as is also history, according to which Mnemon was so far from reigning with his Father, that his mother Parysatis designated her second son Cyrus as Darius's successor, and rendered the right of succession ambiguous to Mnemon until the death of his Father. Finally, Mnemon was not born to his Father so early that he could have been introduced as a partner in the empire in the second year of the same reign.

Therefore James Ussher, in Annal. V. T. p. 160, thought that Artaxerxes here joined with Darius was a partner in the empire with Darius son of Hystaspes at that time, one of the seven Persians who suppressed the Magus, called Intaphernes by Herodotus: but he had no document from history to bring forward for this matter: nor did Monarchs give the august name of Artaxerxes to such men, but reserved it for themselves. Others take the particle Vau as explanatory, Darius and Artaxerxes, i.e., who is also Artaxerxes. But it is better to understand that Artaxerxes, whose munificence toward sacred matters is commemorated at length in the following. For although the edict of Artaxerxes did not properly contribute to the structure of the temple, which was completed in the second year of Darius, there is no doubt that it looked toward the ornaments and additions, which are celebrated here as having proceeded from him as the King most benevolent of all Persians toward the Jews after Cyrus and Darius.

QUESTION VI.

Who is that Artaxerxes, whose seventh year and the mandate granted by the same are commemorated in Ezra VII?

Josephus and a few others wish him to be Xerxes: Scaliger with the followers of Sulpitius Severus alone by authority make him Artaxerxes Mnemon; most of the ancients make him Artaxerxes Longimanus, Julius Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome, and other Greek and Latin Fathers, as well as Pontifical Chronologists, as also Capellus, Ussher, Lansbergius, Baillie, Samson, and others from the Reformed, as well as from our own Chytræus, Christian Matthiæ, Joh. Cluver, D. Godfr. Vogelius, Schilling, Lang, the author of the Compendium of Ecclesiastical History of Ernestini, and others.

Nor indeed is there need of new arguments, after it has already been proven that Darius, by whose edict the restoration of the temple followed, is not Nothus, but the son of Hystaspes. For the opinion concerning Xerxes has no place: who is distinguished from Artaxerxes not only by name, but also did not complete as many years in reigning as are attributed to Artaxerxes, inasmuch as his thirty-second year is commemorated by Nehemiah chapter 5, 14.

Only the doubt remains to be dissolved, which the Scaligerians raise from the age of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Sanballat: since it appears from Ezra and Nehemiah that they lived to reach the times of Alexander the Great. If, therefore, that Artaxerxes is ὁ μακρόχειρ (Longimanus), it would be necessary for them to have been very μακροβίως (long-lived) beyond the custom of that century. Which, however, can create no difficulty.

For concerning Ezra, nothing else is reported than that he lived in the time of Johanan, the father of Jaddua, Ezra 10:6, not that he lived to reach the age of Jaddua the High Priest, much less those times of his in which Alexander the Great is said to have met him, according to the author Josephus, Antiquities book XI, chapter VIII. Add that at the time when Ezra entered the chamber of Johanan, Johanan was still a youth, while his grandfather Eliashib was still performing the High Priesthood: although it may also seem doubtful whether Johanan was the father of Jaddua, since his father is said to be Jonathan, son of Jojada, grandson of Eliashib, Neh. 12:10.

But as far as Nehemiah is concerned, mention is made only in the book of Neh. ch. 12:22 of Jaddua the High Priest: but it is not indicated that at that time Jaddua the High Priest met Alexander the Great; concerning which there is nothing in Nehemiah. Therefore, there is no reason why we should call into doubt, even with Bailius, whether Nehemiah himself wrote the book bearing the name of Nehemiah?
