Concerning which there cannot easily be a doubt, since Nehemiah himself is introduced speaking of himself in the first person throughout: or why we should deny with Temporarius that the Jaddua named by Nehemiah as High Priest is that same one who met Alexander the Great. For could not Nehemiah have reported Jaddua as being begotten by Jonathan, as High Priest in ch. 12:22, even if Nehemiah departed in the first years of his priesthood, and did not reach the times of Alexander the Great? Here Bailius p. 159 is correct: Nehemiah as an old man could have looked upon Jaddua as a youth. The opponents maintain that Joshua entered the priesthood contrary to the law at barely his twentieth year of age, but that Jaddua was made High Priest according to the law at his thirtieth, and at the time of Alexander was ninety years old, which was not rare among High Priests. These things being posited, Nehemiah could have died sixty years before the times of Alexander, and indeed even before the death of Artaxerxes Mnemon, even if he lived for some time with Jaddua. But even if he had reached the times of Alexander the Great, if Nehemiah in the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, or even the 10th, was 25 years old, and from that time 31 years of Artaxerxes, 19 of Darius Nothus, 46 of Artaxerxes Mnemon, 21 of Ochus, 2 of Arses, and 4 of Codomannus have elapsed, when these are joined together, 148 years result, which cannot seem absurd to the Scaligerians for Nehemiah to have spent in living. Let us hear Dr. Behm discussing this with the Beroaldists in a similar dispute, book II, Man. Chron. p. 175. The absurdity which the Beroaldists derive from the longevity of Zerubbabel the Prince and Joshua the High Priest, we say is so constituted that an absurdity is feigned where there is nothing absurd. Is it absurd for a man to live 140 or 150 years? This argument proceeds from the βραχυβίᾳ (short-lived nature) of the Germans and other peoples.

Finally, as to Sanballat, Capellus, Petavius, Torniellus, and Henr. Philippi make this name double: one, who opposed Nehemiah in the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and whose son-in-law was expelled from the temple by Nehemiah in the days of Darius, not Codomannus, as Scaliger wants, but Nothus, Neh. 12:22. For in his days Jaddua could have entered the High Priesthood and easily persisted until Alexander the Great: for if he had been 30 years old under the 16th year of Darius Nothus, he would have reached the 106th year of his age at the end of Codomannus, which is by no means inconvenient or discordant. But they make another Sanballat, the son or grandson of the former, whose daughter Nicaso, Manasseh the brother of Jaddua the High Priest had taken as a wife; for which reason he was driven from the temple and city not by Nehemiah, but by his brother Jaddua, according to Josephus, and for his sake the second Sanballat, having obtained power from Alexander the Great, built the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim. But if he was also the same Sanballat who opposed Nehemiah in the 20th year of Longimanus, Bailius observes that he would not have been over 110 years old in the fifth year of Alexander, and if he died then, at the siege of Tyre, he would not have been older than 130 years: such longevity, as being sufficiently ordinary in that century, Scaliger and Calvisius defend in this place. Let those things be compared which the learned author of the Compendium of Ecclesiastical History answers here, which is a public writing, and composed with exceptional diligence, p. 313.

QUESTION VII. Who is Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther?

Here, indeed, there are as many opinions as there are heads of chronologers, so that the whole variety can scarcely be enumerated. First, there are those who wish this Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther, to be Astyages, the father of Darius the Mede and father-in-law of Cyrus, who is called Ahasuerus by Daniel, such as Gerhard, Mercator in his Chronology, Temporarius in book III of his Chronological Demonstrations, p. 185, Wanckelius, Professor of History at Wittenberg, in a formal academic dissertation, as well as Melchior Canus, Bishop of the Canary Islands, in book XI of his Places, ch. VI; others say that Darius the Mede himself was the second husband of Esther, as reported by Rob. Baillie: Others make Cambyses the third husband of Esther with the Hebrews in Seder Olam, R. Solomon, Lyranus, Vatablus, Genebrardus, Petavius, Tirinus, Wilhelmus Langius. Fourth, Darius the son of Hystaspes with R. Aben-Ezra,

Metasthenes, B. Luther, Philippus, Brentius, Joh. Carion, Funccius, Jac. Ussher, Schillingius, and also among the Papists Joh. Benedictus & Cornelius a Lapide &c. deem him worthy of this honor. Fifth, Scaliger, Tremellius, Junius, the Anglican Annotators, Diodati, Hervæus, Calvisius, D. Behmius, and others favor Xerxes. Sixth, for Artaxerxes Longimanus, they contend with Josephus, Book XI. of Antiquities, Ch. V., Sulpitius Severus, and Nicephorus, the Cardinals, Cajetan, and Bellarmine, as well as Salianus, and Sanctius, Petavius, Henricus Philippi, the Author of the Gothan Compendium

&c. Seventh, Eusebius, Bede on the six ages of the World at the year 3588, and Marianus Scotus in

Chronicles. Eighth, Serarius, Gordon, Huntlæus, Capellus, and Simson attribute this to Artaxerxes Ochus. Thus, there is almost no one left in the Persian empire to whom someone has not attributed this honor, that he was the husband of Esther.

But the first opinion is by no means true: Nor was Astyages the father-in-law of Cyrus, but Darius the Mede, or Cyaxares, the son of Astyages. And indeed before the captivity was ended, or rather before Cambyses, who obtained Egypt bordering on Ethiopia, no one ruled from India as far as Ethiopia, which is said of Esther's husband, Esth. 1, 1. Nor did the Persians rule over the Medes before the end of the captivity, nor is it credible that the Jews, during the Babylonian captivity, lived in Persia in such great numbers, or enjoyed such liberty that they could slaughter 75,000 of their enemies there in one day and kill 800 in the royal palace alone, which is reported in Esth. 9,

16. Concerning Darius the Mede also, no presumption holds place, since he is distinguished from Ahasuerus as from a father, nor did he possess many provinces before Babylon was occupied, and afterwards he ruled for a short time, scarcely two years, whereas the third year of Ahasuerus, Esther's husband, is commemorated, or rather the seventh and the twelfth.

Whence Cambyses is also excluded from this honor, who did not reign much longer than seven years, a man moreover who was impious, or rather a monster of men, and a most bitter enemy of the Jews.

Concerning the later kings Artaxerxes Mnemon and Ochus, there is likewise no difficulty, since nothing is found in their history akin to those things which are reported concerning Ahasuerus, Esther's husband, nor does the method of chronology permit referring that history to those times: for the reason that it is necessary, as Capellus himself confesses, that it be established by that agreement that Kish, taken away at two years old, did not beget the son of Shimei before his 80th year, nor did he beget Jair before the same 80th year, nor was Jair less than 80 years old when Mordecai was born to him, and finally that Abihail also at eighty years old begat Esther, all of which things to assume gratuitously without any authority is quite harsh, then especially because the Canonical Scripture was completed in the times of Ezra and Artaxerxes Longimanus, to which the book of Esther also belongs.

Nor does the history of Esther fit the time of Artaxerxes Longimanus: because at that age Mordecai, who is said to have been deported to Babylon with Jeconiah (Esth. 2, 5), would have been 150 years older, namely in the seventh year of Ahasuerus, even if he had been only ten years old at the time of the translation: and Esther, the cousin of Mordecai, if she had been even a hundred years younger than him in age, would have been at least 50 years old at that time of Ahasuerus. How then could she be celebrated as a virgin of flourishing age?

Scaliger proves that Xerxes was Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther, with arguments that are too slippery. Namely, that the name of Ahasuerus and Xerxes is one and the same, which how discordant it is, the very sound of the names teaches: and that the appellation of the wife of Xerxes, Amestris, corresponds to the name of Esther by casting off the first part of the composition, Am: which, however much they may agree in names, history nevertheless clearly resists: since Amestris was a Persian, the daughter of Otanes, a most noble Persian, not a Hebrew, and Xerxes married her before his reign: but Esther was married to the King: nor do those things which Herodotus reports about Amestris correspond to the piety of Esther: She was the worst and most cruel of women. But Esther is celebrated as most pious and most mild. Finally, how could Xerxes have married Esther in deep peace at Susa in the seventh year, if he is believed to be Ahasuerus, when histories testify that in the seventh and eighth years he was involved in a horrible war in Greece and Ionia.

Having therefore set aside all these opinions, with B. Luther we defer this honor to Darius Hystaspis, the chief restorer of the temple, that he was the husband of Esther and the savior of the Jewish people, called by the common name of Ahasuerus, which was accepted among the Persians, in the canonical history of Esther, whose wife, the daughter of Cyrus, Vasthi, called Atossa, Ussher established; but that name is more correctly said of Esther, who was certainly Hadassah to the Hebrews, called Artystone by Herodotus in book VI, ch. 8, and book VII, ch. 69, who seems to have been that virgin whom the same author reports that Darius loved most, and whose image he had made of solid gold. Moreover, this King's kindness toward the Jews, his residence in Susa, the length of his reign, the plurality of his wives, and other things not a little confirm our opinion, which deserves approval above all others. To which must be added what Funccius has for the same, and against the opinions of others, in Chron. at the year 3445, as also what Mr. Brentius annotated in the book of Esther, Vol. II of his Works, page 1115.

QUESTION VIII.

How does the Chronology of the Persian Monarchs stand?

In the designation of kings and years of reign in this Monarchy, we must have recourse to exotic history: in which there is no doubt about the kings themselves, but in the years of the Kings, Ussher varies from Ptolemy's canon in the Annals of the O.T. After Cyrus, who, including the two years of Darius the Mede, presided over affairs for 9 years from the conquest of Babylon, but alone held the Monarchy for seven years, as Ussher notes, Cambyses reigned, to whom he attributes 7 years and 5 months, and to Smerdis 7 months; Ptolemy, omitting Smerdis, assigned 8 years to Cambyses. Furthermore, both counted 36 years for the reign of Darius Hystaspis. But Ptolemy in his canon established 21 years for the reign of Xerxes, to which Ussher's annals leave scarcely 11 (for which reason I do not find). Again, Artaxerxes Longimanus has 41 years in Ptolemy's canon. But Ussher claims that he presided over the same for 48 years: and furthermore advises that two years should be attributed to Xerxes and Sogdianus as successors. The 19 years of Darius Nothus are established beyond doubt. But Ptolemy assigns 46 to Artaxerxes Mnemon and 21 to Ochus: Ussher ascribed only 43 to the former, but 23 to the latter, agreeing with Ptolemy on the two years of his successor Arses; but assigning a six-year period to Darius Codomannus, not 4 years as with Ptolemy. Since, however, he agrees exactly with Ptolemy in the universal computation of the years of the Persian Kings, and only varies in the particular years of their reign, it seems that little is lost from the chronological matter thereby: we prefer, however, to adhere to Ptolemy's Canon, approved by almost everyone, and built upon celestial characters: which, therefore, as far as the Persian Monarchy is concerned, we have exhibited in Table VIII, with a continued gathering of years from the Monarchy of the Assyrians.

& the beginning of the Medes or the Nabonassarean era, with the beginnings of Scripture added, which we consider should be compared here.

QUESTION IX.

How the years of the Epoch from the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus to the seventh of Artaxerxes, in which Ezra c. 7, 7, and the twentieth, in which Nehemiah was sent, are to be collected? Neh. 1, 1.

Since the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus brought the end of the Babylonian captivity and the beginning of the liberation of the people, but the seventh of Artaxerxes Longimanus is the term from which the 70 weeks of Daniel ought to be established, which will have to be demonstrated in the following chapter, it will not be difficult to collect the number of years of this Epoch by following the canon of Ptolemy like a cynosure, with this premised, that the beginning should not be taken from the 21st of the Persian reign of Cyrus, from which he reigned for nine years after Babylon was taken: or not immediately from the taking of Babylon, but only after the plenary administration of the Monarchy was undertaken after the death of Darius the Mede, who presided for two years from the time Babylon was taken, and thus the seven years which Cyrus spent in the Monarchy ought to be added to his rule for this Epoch: and that in the seventh current year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, Ezra was sent by this Monarch to repair the Sacred things.

However, concerning the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, in which Nehemiah is read to have been sent to restore the city, Neh. 2, 1, Chronologists raise a doubt, whether this is the 14th year from the mission of Ezra, or not? For some, with Gerhard, Mercator, and Dionysius Petavius, make a double beginning of the reign of Longimanus: one in which he was admitted by his parent Xerxes into a partnership of the reign: which they say Nehemiah followed: the other from which he himself began to reign alone after the death of his parent, which they establish to have been observed in the history of Ezra. For thus in sacred Chronology, in their judgment, the matter appears more straightforward: if indeed it is said that Artaxerxes reigned for a decade with his Father Xerxes, and that Nehemiah counts the years of Artaxerxes from the beginning of the partnership of the rule with his Father, as one who had been occupied in his court. But Ezra, who followed the Kings in order, according to the years of their own reign, designating the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus, the second of the reign of Darius, the seventh of Artaxerxes: as in those, so also in naming this one, he looked to the solitary reign: just as Philip Lansbergen in Chron. S. II. c. IX. p. 68, from historical observations and chronological characters, extracted by the calculation of eclipses that the seventh year of the solitary reign of the same was observed by Ezra, demonstrating that the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus was the two hundred and ninety-first from Nabonassar: which Tirinus in Chron. S. c. XXXIIX observes that Basil of Seleucia, Cedrenus, Corn. a Lapide, Bucholzer, Capellus, Funccius, and Angelocrator also look to the seventh year of the solitary reigning Artaxerxes.

Nor indeed is it unusual in Holy Scripture that they count now the years of the Solitary, now of the Partner in the reign, just as examples from the collation of the reigns of the Kings of Judah and Israel, and the comparison of the sacred computation in the history of the kings and the books of Chronicles have taught.

Dionysius Petavius gathers a double beginning of the reign of Artaxerxes from the fact that the flight of Themistocles from Greece and his arrival in Persia is conjectured by Diodorus Siculus to be in the second year of the 77th Olympiad, which preceded the slaughter of Xerxes by seven years: and that the same Themistocles, according to the account of Thucydides, had then given letters to Artaxerxes νεωστὶ βασιλεύοντα [newly reigning]. He was therefore νεωστὶ βασιλεύων [newly reigning] already seven years before the slaughter of his parent, and thus, he was admitted to the kingdom at least seven years before the death of his father: which also Wilh. Langius teaches in book II de annis Christi c. XV. p. 326, and Jac. Tiring executes more prolixly in the cited place p. 44. Furthermore, among the authors certain and of proven faith in Persian and Greek matters, no one, I believe, will deny Thucydides, Charon of Lampsacus, Phanias, Eratosthenes, Ephorus, Dio, Clitarchus, and Heraclides, who are contemporary to those of whom we now treat, whom Plutarch cites and praises: I pass over Athenaeus likewise, Cicero, Eusebius, Jerome, Aemilius Probus, Philostratus, Suidas, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, St. Antonius, Sigonius, Mercator, and other more recent ones. Yet all these say that Themistocles, the famous leader of the Athenians, when he had been condemned to death by his ungrateful citizens, fled into Asia to Artaxerxes Longimanus, the son of Xerxes, who was already then reigning in Persia, as if to an asylum, was introduced to Artaxerxes by Artabanus, the prefect of the militia, venerated the king in the manner of his father, and received Lampsacus from him as a gift: but a little later, having drunk poison, he brought death upon himself. But the same people ascribe this flight of Themistocles, some to the 13th, others to the 14th year of Xerxes, to the 1st year of the 77th Olympiad, and his death to the 2nd year. Twenty years, says Cicero, after the death of Coriolanus. Yet it is certain from Livy, Halicarnassaeus, Plutarch, and others, that Coriolanus died in about the 1st year of the 73rd Olympiad, in the consulship of Sp. Nautius Rutilus and Sex. Furius Medullinus. It is also certain that when Themistocles was fleeing from Athens, Pericles was substituted in his place in the 1st year of the 77th Olympiad, as can be gathered from Athenaeus. But that Xerxes survived then and administered the empire, no one can deny, since it is confessed by all among almost all the authors already cited, that Xerxes moved war against the Greeks in the 5th year of his empire, and crossed the Hellespont, when scarcely two months remained before the 75th Olympiad. But after that time he survived and reigned for a full 15 other years, until in the 1st year of the 79th Olympiad. he was killed by Artabanus, the prefect of the militia, with Artabanus also being killed immediately by Artaxerxes, who was avenging the slaughter of his father. From the arrival of Themistocles, therefore, Xerxes was still among the living and in the empire for a full 8 years at minimum; namely, as many as flowed from the beginning of the 77th until the beginning of the 79th Olympiad. The same, if it were necessary, I could prove from the similar flight of Timagoras to the same Artaxerxes: the same from the years of Hiero, Gelo, and Thrasybulus, kings of Sicily, at this very time of the flight of Themistocles and the empire of Xerxes, as Athenaeus, and from Stesimbrotus, Plutarch, Diodorus, Aristotle, and Pausanias write. But in a certain and manifest matter, I would not dare to be more prolix.

Thus Tirinus, with other chronologists of no small name: against which Robert Baelius indeed rises up, crying out against the wanton audacity of the Jesuits in book I of his Chronological work, p. 175, because that was the twenty-third year, and the thirty-second year, and the twenty-second year in Holy Scripture. But that this is not inconvenient, nor unusual, since in different books of Scripture different beginnings of reigning are numbered, we have already warned before, nor could Baelius himself deny it in other examples. Although indeed Tirinus and Nicolaus Abraham wish for the son to have been taken into partnership by Xerxes immediately in the fifth year (which indeed they could by no means prove from those histories which they brought forward), others however assert that he reigned with his father for only a decade, whence Sacred history can seem to be rendered uncertain, and what is the chief doubt, even the beginning of the weeks of Daniel falls; Yet from a comparison of histories and the computation of the angel, Dan. IX, they think that opinion has certainty which assigns to him a decade of joint rule: so that an interval of only three years, διάσημα, intervened between the two edicts of Artaxerxes Longimanus and the mission of Ezra and Nehemiah, and that the former occurred in the seventh year of the solitary rule of Artaxerxes, after the death of his parent, and the seventeenth year from his first admission to the partnership of the kingdom, but this latter one was made with the subsequent edict in the twentieth year from the admission to the partnership of the kingdom, which was the tenth of his solitary rule: for in no way does it seem to agree with those

as also the Priesthood and Sacrifice of the same, by which he had to offer himself to GOD the Father for us as a sweet-smelling savour, just as the typical sacrifices were once to be offered and performed at Jerusalem, in which his expiatory death was prefigured: partly by the very exhibition of Christ the leader, and the passion and death of the same to expiate iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, so that the ancient sacrifices might be fulfilled and abrogated: and also for the propagation of the Gospel concerning Christ to the nations, so that his kingdom might be diffused throughout the whole world. Which notable Epoch, the LXX annual weeks, that is, 490 years, containing, brought forth the most illustrious oracle, to Daniel, in the first year of Darius the Mede, King of the Chaldeans, when the LXX years of the Babylonian captivity were drawing to an end, at his most ardent prayers, revealed from heaven through the Angel Gabriel, Dan. 9, 24. seqq. by which it was simultaneously revealed that, shortly after the expiration of the term of these LXX annual weeks, the city and sanctuary would be laid waste, and that that devastation would be perpetual, and the desolation would have no end.

taneous Nehemiah for 13 years to have been unconcerned about the state of Jerusalem: or that in so long a time he had not had an opportunity of inquiring about it: just as it is reported in Neh. 1, 2, that, when Hanani, one of his brothers, came with his companions, he asked them in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (Longimanus) about the Jews who had survived the captivity, and about the city of Jerusalem, and learned that the Jews were still in great affliction and in reproach, and that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down, and the gates burned with fire. Who, they say, would presume of Nehemiah's piety, that he had so little care for his own people that for nearly three lustra he did not even wish to inquire about them, he who, being established in the Royal seat, in a chief office, as the King's Arch-Cupbearer, never lacked the opportunity of investigating their state? Which opinion, however, we leave to be discussed by others. But in our judgment it is better to say that this thirteenth year was from the mission of Ezra, for the reparation of sacred things, in which Nehemiah likewise obtained a mission for the restoration of the city: especially because by that reasoning all things hold well in the oracle and completion concerning the seventy weeks of Daniel. Of which in the following section. The sum of this Epoch is now gathered thus:

The beginning of this Epoch is fixed at the going forth of the word concerning the reparation of Jerusalem V, 15. and three parts, or smaller Epochs, are constituted of it: The first is of the seven prior weeks, that is, of 49 years from that going forth of the word, i.e., as we judge must altogether be accepted, the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus: The second is of the subsequent sixty-two weeks or 434 years, up to Christ the Leader solemnly declared from heaven in a notable theophany and the inauguration of the same through baptism: to whom therefore from that edict, the prior seven having been counted, sixty-nine weeks, 483 years, have elapsed. But because this inauguration was made in the year of Christ 30, as Luke c. 3, 23 testifies, it is not difficult to gather that to the birth of Christ from the edict of Artaxerxes, 30 years having been subtracted, 453 years have flowed. The third is of one week, namely the last or seventieth: which is again divided by the Angel into two halves. The prior half is specially designated for this reason, that the time of the passion and death of Christ, which was the primary intention of this revelation and the chief scope, might be determined, which is to be the half of the newest week; and since a half week consists of 3 and a half years, those being added to the number of the preceding Epoch, the years from the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus are defined as 486 and a half, for the passion and death of Christ, which brought an end to the sacrifices of the Old Testament. The posterior half of 3 and a half years elapsed from the passion and death of Christ to the taking in of the nations and the naming of the faithful, by which they were called Christians by Christ, when once the faithful had been designated by the name of Jews. That whole annual week of seven years was spent in the confirmation of the covenant: since through the passion, death, resurrection, the varied appearance of Christ and his ascension into heaven, as also the mission of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the Apostles, at the Feast of Pentecost, and upon the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius, Acts II and X, the covenant of grace had to be confirmed and established, Dan. 9, 29.

Years of the Persian Monarchy

Of the Monarchy of Cyrus 7

Of Cambyses and Smerdis 8

Of Darius Hystaspis 36

Of Xerxes 21

Of Artaxerxes Longimanus 6

Total, 78 years from the first year of Cyrus to the edict of Artaxerxes concerning the repairing of the Sacred things and the solemn mission of Ezra.

Now the first year of Cyrus falls in the year of the World 3468. For from the creation of the world to the destruction of the former temple there elapsed 3415 years, 20 months, 9 days: and from thence to the first year of Cyrus and of liberty there flowed 52 years, which joined together make 3467 complete years: if therefore to these are added the 78 years elapsed until the edict of Artaxerxes, there will be produced 3545 years, and the year of the World will be had, in which the edict of Artaxerxes falls, 3546.

SECTION VIII.

The epochs from the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus, or the going forth of the word concerning the restoration of the typical sacred rites of the Jews, which was the beginning of the seventy weeks of Daniel, to their end in the assumption of the Gentiles into the kingdom of Christ, are 490 years, from which is gathered the epoch to the advent of Christ of 453 years.

EPOCH FROM THE GOING FORTH OF THE WORD CONCERNING THE REPAIRING OF THE JERUSALEM POLITY TO THE SOLEMN ASSUMPTION OF THE GENTILES.

From the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, in which the edict went forth, the first seven weeks for the restoration of the sacred rites and the City, 49 years

Thence to the Leader Messiah solemnly declared from heaven again sixty-two weeks, 434 years

This is the final Epoch of the times of the O. Testament, connecting it with the fullness of time in the N. Testament: in which is contained both the latest revelation of the ancient computations concerning the advent, passion, and kingdom of the Messiah, made by the angel Gabriel to the Prophet Daniel, and the fulfillment of them exhibited partly by the restoration and preservation of the sacred rites and the city of Jerusalem, which were to remain in force until the Messiah, and which reflected their shadow and figure, of which we have the τὸ σῶμα in Christ Col. 2. Heb. 10. but this latter was destined for the proclamation of Christ, the Great Prophet, and the going forth of the Gospel into the whole world,

Thence to the consummation of the sacrifices through the death and sacrifice of Christ, half a week, 3 years, 6 months.

Thence to the solemn assumption of the Gentiles, again half a week, years 3. M. 6. Total 70 weeks, 490 years. The last week having been subtracted, the two prior partial Epochs of seven and sixty-two weeks make 483 years up to the Leader Messiah solemnly proclaimed, which was done at his Baptism: whence, having subtracted 30 years, which he had completed when he was baptized, there remain, as we have said, 453 years to the Nativity of Christ. And since the edict of Artaxerxes went forth in the year 3546 from the creation of the world, with the aforementioned 453 years added, there will result 3999 years. Which year of the World 3999 is 4709 of the Julian period. Since the world was created in the year 710 of the Julian period. And since we deduce the beginning of the common Christian era from the Kalends of January of the year 4714 of the Julian period, it is easily gathered that 4003 years and some months have elapsed to the common Christian era. But if the true era is considered, the Nativity of Christ falls in the current year of the world 4000, so that the common era of the nativity of Christ differs from the true one by four years, and the present year of the Dionysian era of Christ 1671 is, according to the truer era, 1675. Conf. Pref. of the Annals of the O. T. by James Ussher.

QUESTION I.

What kind of weeks are to be understood in the oracle of Gabriel, Dan. 9, 24. seqq.?

There is no need for us to prove here that the term of the advent of the Messiah was defined by Gabriel, since the letter of the text openly implies it, up to the LEADER MESSIAH, and all Christians acknowledge this with the highest consensus, if you except Grotius, who here acts as a midwife in part for the Jews, concerning whom see the Annotat. Anti-Grot. on this passage. However, the weeks are not to be understood as those of Jubilees, each of which is completed in 49 years, as some Jews wish, which kind of weeks are nowhere found in Holy Scripture, nor, as Origen, Hom. XXVIII. in Matth. X. invented, such as each contain decades of seven years, which he irrelevantly starts from the creation of the world, which are likewise unknown to the Holy Scriptures: (for which reason Origen defined them differently elsewhere) but weeks of years, each of which has 7 years. For in Scripture there are found only weeks of days, Exod. XXXIV, 22. Levit. XII, 1. or of years, Lev. XXV, 8. But weeks of days cannot be understood: for it is notoriously false that within 7 common weeks, or 49 days, the streets and walls of Jerusalem were built, and that within seventy weeks those things were fulfilled which are predicted here. Therefore, the sounder Jews acknowledge, R. Aben-Esra, R. Levi, R. Salomo, R. Joseph Jacchiades, R. Isaac Abarbanel, R. Menasse Ben Israel, that those 70 weeks are of years, which is also handed down in the Talmud in tract. Sanhedrin. c. Cheleck, and is beyond controversy among all Christians. Although they differ in the years, since Africanus understands Lunar ones in Vol. V. of his Chronography, and in Jerome on this passage, as well as Theodoret, and Bede, as also among the more recent ones Bened. Pererius and F. Matthias Chefneux in the Catholic Chronographic Mirror published at Liège in the year 1662, Proleg. 23. Jac. Gordonus, and Torniellus at the year of the world 3609, but others understand Usual and commonly received ones; to which, having entirely rejected the lunar ones, the calculation must be added; because it is established by no indication at all that Lunar ones were designated, nor are they accepted in the holy scriptures or Biblical Chronology: and therefore it is settled and certain that those 70 weeks make 490 customary years.

Are those 70 weeks both taken as a whole and continuous parts, or are they discontinuous?

That the weeks are to be understood as continuous is taught both by the letter of the divine oracle and required by the certainty of the oracle, so that, namely, a certain time may be determined which the heavenly revelation intended: and therefore, by the common consent of interpreters, they have hitherto been understood as continuous, until Constantinus L'Empereur began to think otherwise in his Commentary on R. Jachia on Daniel 9: who, although he acknowledges that the subsequent sixty-three weeks follow one another in a continuous series, nevertheless imagined that the first seven were discontinuous: and this so absurdly that, in seven weeks, that is, 49 years, he confesses that six weeks and four years, that is, the first 46 years, cohere in a continuous order, from the first of Cyrus to the first of Xerxes (of which, however, not 46 years are found, but 50), but that he tears apart the remaining three years by a very long interval: that the first interruption of the work happened in the first year of Xerxes, and he supposed it continued through the whole life of Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus up to the second year of Darius Nothus, from which time the work succeeded for three years, but not a complete one, and thus ceased again from the sixth year of Nothus to the seventh of Artaxerxes Memnon for 18 years, but then was completed in a few months by Ezra, who lacked the sixth year of Darius, by the addition of which the last or 49th year might emerge: by which method not 49, but 50, if the calculation of years in the Persian Monarchy of L'Empereur is correct, will emerge, because from the second year of Darius to the sixth, not three but four years are counted: and instead of 49 years, 139 will be counted, namely, how many flowed from the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus to the 7th of Artaxerxes Memnon. And yet there are still more absurdities. For L'Empereur makes these years not common or Solar, but Egyptian, which are completed in 360 days, so that he may complete 490 years up to the passion of Christ from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Memnon (with the previous 49 added), when he has counted at least 483 from that point. Since 483 common and accepted Solar years make 490 Egyptian years. By this invention, although very insipid, he still does not satisfy the angelic calculation: for from those 490 Egyptian years, with the reduction exactly established, they never turn out to be 483 common ones.

But Dr. Wasmuth assumed not indeed Egyptian years, but the former method of counting by intercalary years in the seven weeks, which, however, he established differently: namely, that the work was begun in three years under Cyrus, hindered in the following years up to Darius Hystaspes, but continued through the entire curriculum of that Darius for 36 years, likewise checked under Xerxes for the first 14 years and resumed in the last six years, and again ceased for over 40 years during the whole reign of Longimanus: but was brought to an end under Darius Nothus in about 4 years. Which he has from Alstedius: although he also departs from him in this, that Alstedius counts only 46 years for the construction of the temple, and not 49, and acknowledges that the foundations of the Temple were laid only in the second year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, and that the work on the structure of the temple was not carried on for three years.

But there is no need for us to refute at length here the new discovery, in which we have elsewhere detected many errors. Such an intercalary calculation is certainly insolent and unknown to the whole of Scripture, serving neither the intention of the Angel nor the Chronology or the calculation of times in any way, by which rather all things are rendered doubtful and uncertain. Whence Dr. Wasmuth himself noted Scaliger, who leaves only a single gap in the last week, joining years separated in time by number, because even if he correctly made the middle of the last week (by referring the death of Christ to it) without

HE HAS INTERPOSED EVERY METHOD (albeit quite imperiously) after that middle point with a GREAT GAP of 34 years, and has postponed the remaining half after the seventy weeks were completed, which is to say that merely to recount it is to refute it. How much less, therefore, are such diverse gaps to be admitted: first, from the third year of Cyrus to the first year of Darius Hystaspis, at least 12 years; then 14 years under Xerxes; thirdly, 40 years under Artaxerxes Longimanus, and two under Darius Nothus; not to mention the fourth gap from the 6th year of Darius Nothus to the 6th year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, over thirteen years.

Nor, finally, does the opinion of Hippolytus the Martyr deserve to be commemorated, who, finishing the LXIX weeks at the advent of Christ, snatched away the seventieth to the consummation of the age, leaving a very great gap, and distributed it into the preaching of Enoch and Elijah and the kingdom of the Anti-Christ. That these dreams in no way agree with the words of Gabriel is in the open.

QUESTION III.

What is the term from which and to which of the LXX Weeks of Daniel?

The opinions vary greatly, which we may reduce to three classes. In the first occur absurd opinions and ones hardly worthy of refutation, not a few: for example (1.) that of Origen, when he begins those weeks from the foundation of the world and ends them at the birth of Christ, which collapses by its own vanity. (2.) That of those who, according to Cornelius a Lapide, count them from the XIII year of Josiah, in which Jeremiah began to prophesy concerning the destruction, ch. 1, 2. But the going forth of the word is not designated concerning the destruction, but concerning the beginning of the rebuilding of Jerusalem. (3.) That of Lyranus, Burgensis, Vatablus, Raimundus in the Dagger of Faith part II. ch. 3, 11, 12, and Galatinus: who say that they began from the fourth year of King Zedekiah, Jerem. XXIX. In which place indeed it is a matter of the release from captivity, but there is no mention of the rebuilding of the city. Add that from that time not 490, but more than 600 years have elapsed to the term of the Epoch defined here. (4.) The Jews, beginning them from the first devastation of the city with R. Solomon, end them at the destruction of the later temple, and understand Cyrus by the Messiah. But here the going forth of the word concerning the restoration, not the destruction of Jerusalem, is constituted as the beginning of the Epoch: nor did only 70, but more than 90 weeks intervene between either destruction. Others (5.) much more ineptly begin the Epoch from the second devastation, which the Angel truly wishes to be computed not from the devastation, but from the going forth of the word concerning the rebuilding of the city. (6.) Hippolytus the Martyr places the beginning without any reason 50 years before the release from captivity. (7.) Tertullian in his book against the Jews refers it to the first of Darius the Mede, in which Daniel had this vision; but he errs openly in the Chronology of the Kings of the Persians, to whom he assigns only one hundred years: Cyril of Jerusalem likewise refers it to the first of Darius the Mede: but he confuses Darius the Mede with the Darius under whom the temple was built. (8.) Metasthenes and Philo begin this Epoch from the second of Darius Longimanus, whom they invent: but that masked Metasthenes, long since detected, is an insipid Monk, Johannes Annius of Viterbo, who created and introduced new Persian Kings at will. (9.) Some have referred the beginning to the second year of Cambyses, clearly ἀπροσδιονύσως. (10.) Isaac Vossius absurdly reduces it to the 25th year of Xerxes: whom he makes the Artaxerxes of Ezra and Nehemiah. Whereas Xerxes only reigned 21 years, but Artaxerxes is mentioned in Nehemiah ch. V, 14 as having reigned 32.

These opinions, therefore, having been rejected as absurd, those in the second class are to be noted, which have some appearance of probability, but are not entirely consistent with the divine oracle. First occur those who seek the beginning in the edict of Cyrus. Some of whom refer the end of the Epoch to the destruction that took place under Titus, with Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata; Eusebius, however (though disagreeing with himself), assigns the end of the weeks to the capture of Jerusalem by Pompey. But most terminate them at the Passion of Christ, with Matthaeus Beroaldus; such as Mornay, Broughton, Rainolds, David Pareus, and the English Annotations. Nisbet, Horn, and from our own side Stempelius and the blessed D. Ananias Weber, to whom, however, the interval of the Persian kingdom openly stands in opposition, which was already observed by Africanus in Jerome on this passage, which the Beroaldists, for the sake of their own opinion, contract against the faith of all historians, and thus disturb both chronology and history equally, as has been shown by Scaliger, Calvisius, D. Behm, Bailius, and others. For it is more certain than certain that far more than 70 weeks have elapsed since the edict of Cyrus. Nor indeed did the angel assign the beginning at the going forth of the word concerning the release from captivity, nor in a bare edict concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem, without effect, such as the edict of Cyrus was; but with the effect conjoined. Furthermore, II. some refer the beginning of this Epoch to the times of Darius Hystaspis, and the edict, concerning which Ezra 6:6 et seqq., with Johann Driedo and Cornelius Jansen, from which, however, likewise far more years have elapsed until the Messiah than 490. Whence Eusebius, having started these weeks from the sixth year of Darius Hystaspis, placed their end at the death of Hyrcanus.

III. Not a few today lead the beginning of the weeks of Daniel from the second year of Darius Nothus with Sulpicius Severus and Rupert, such as Scaliger, Junius, Polanus, Angelocrator, Molinaeus, Ubbo Emmius, Alsted, Cocceius, Calixtus, and from our own side Seth Calvisius, D. Joh. Behm, D. Helvicus, D. Joh. Tarnovius, Majerus, D. Georg König, the blessed Franckenberg, Schubert; as also Hugo Grotius: who, however, do not agree on the term of the Epoch to which: since Sulpicius Severus terminated the sixty-ninth week at the destruction of Jerusalem, but passed over the last one in silence: most others finish the seventieth and last at the destruction of the city: the illustrious Scaliger, the leader of the others, does not believe that seventy weeks were defined by Gabriel, but adds a half-week to them, and makes 493 1/2 years. let him count, although he may admit that this half-week extending beyond the sum of seventy has escaped the MOST SHARP-SIGHTED vigilance of ALL, as well the ancients as the moderns. Which is not surprising, since it nowhere appears in the oracle of Gabriel, nay rather it inflicts open violence upon the same; inasmuch as he precisely defines LXX. weeks. and taught that they were determined: but not 70 and a half. Which half-week Scaliger added ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων (from his own resources) in the later edition of his work on the emendation of times (for in the former he was not so sharp-sighted as to be able to see it) because he observed that from the second year of Darius Nothus to the destruction of Jerusalem, not 490, but 493 years are counted. Whom, therefore, we can commit along with his disciples and followers here, both regarding the explanation of the oracle and the calculation of the years: not to mention that Scaliger himself contradicts himself, because he inserted 34 years after the middle of the seventieth week, as we noted before, and thus made the final years discontinuous, and yet collected all the weeks into one sum, and made it 493 and a half years, disregarding the gap of 34 intermediate years, when everyone understands that discontinuous years cannot be collected into one sum. There is also one of the Scaligerians who begins both the seven weeks and also the 62 from the same starting point, namely the second year of Darius Nothus: indeed, he even makes that the beginning of the entire sum of 70 weeks, as Helvicus notes; which was also done by D. Georg. König, in vind. sacr. disput. XXXII. Hervartus, however, in the work inscribed Chronolog. adversus incredibiles errores, likewise begins the 62 weeks from the same term from which the first seven begin, but he places the term to which the 70 weeks reach at the extermination of the city, and by a monstrous fiction he posits that it is at the same time the middle of the last week: with whom Mr. D. Gerardus Gravius, by reason of the same beginning of both the first seven and the 62 following weeks, acted in his inaugural oration of the year 1657. Held at Jena, but he conjectured the term to which these reach to be the twelfth year of Christ, along with the aforementioned Anonymous in Helvicus and with D. König: but he does not refer that one week to the 70 weeks themselves, but begins it only from the last year of the seventieth week: which εὑρήματα (discoveries) with the comment of Isaac Vossius adding a half to the sixty-two weeks, hardly deserve to be refuted: however, those things which we said in our Diatribe on the 70 weeks of Daniel at chapter IX of the same may be seen regarding them; where the modern opinion of Scaliger is also discussed expressly.

In a few words, it diverges from that truth, both of Holy Scripture and of Chronology, because (1.) it takes its beginning from the structure of the temple, if indeed the angel makes the head of the Epoch not the going forth of the word to build the temple, but the building of the city, Dan. IX, 25, and no mention is made of the structure of the temple. (2.) Because it refers the rebuilding of the temple, of which Ezra IV, 24 and the following chapters speak, to the times of Darius Nothus: which we confirmed above to pertain to the reign of Darius Hystaspes. (3.) Because Joseph Scaliger, the chief author of that opinion, not content with the seventy weeks of Daniel, adds a half to them ἄτερ γραφῆς (without scripture) and against the angelic, nay, divine definition. (4.) Because he wishes the mystical distribution of the angel of 7 and 62 and one to be entirely devoid of any mystery. (5.) Because the intervals of the weeks are torn apart by Scaliger, and the continuity of the years is not assumed. (6.) Because the words of the Angel concerning the term of seven and sixty-two weeks v. 25 UNTIL MESSIAH THE PRINCE are perverted by the patrons of that opinion: by Grotius indeed, while it is denied against the intention of Gabriel that a certain term is defined for them: by others, while they understand by Messiah the Roman Emperor Vespasian: or where they are forced to admit Christ, they want him to be viewed here as the judge of the people, which is mere στρεβλότης (distortion). With the same ease, all things that treat of the coming of the Messiah could be perverted and snatched away to some divine judgment impending over this, that, or the other people. (7.) Since the time of the passion and death of Christ, by which our sins were expiated and eternal righteousness brought in, is accurately defined by the Angel, by joining seven and sixty-two weeks with a half, Scaliger takes the 62 weeks separately, and since he acknowledges that the event does not thus correspond to the calculation of the years, having made the beginning of the 62 weeks from the second year of Darius Nothus, he makes the time φανερώσιμον (manifest) not so much ambiguous in this oracle as entirely indefinite, as D. Georg. König says, the Angel pronounces ἀορίστως (indefinitely), that the cutting off of the Messiah is to be after and not before 62 weeks, although not immediately after the 62 weeks have elapsed, but with 22 solid years interposed. But in that way, without doubt, the angel would have said the Messiah will be cut off not after 62, but after 65 weeks, nor would he have neglected three whole weeks. Others despair of a solution in the partition of time made by the angel, with Calixtus in his dissertation on the 70 weeks. What is said by the Angel, he says, from the going forth of the word until Christ the Prince are seven and 62 weeks, that is 69. But soon, and after 62 weeks, Christ will be cut off, until Christ are 69 weeks, and Christ will be cut off after 62 weeks (where, however, the previously mentioned 7 weeks are not to be neglected, not to be separated, but to be joined, as a comparison teaches that this was said in an inclusive sense) if you wish to apply this to history, it is such an ἄπορον (impasse) that it can be explained by NO ONE, no matter how great his genius: namely, if he prefers to indulge a preconceived opinion about taking the beginning from Darius Nothus, rather than to yield to the truth. On the contrary, our blessed Franzius says in Schol. sacrif. disput. X. th. LVII. is that which Christ must be cut off at the end of the sixty-ninth week, and the beginning of the seventieth. For the text of Daniel expressly says, unto Christ the Prince seven weeks, sixty-two weeks. And these weeks together make sixty-nine weeks. Then it repeats, after sixty-two weeks shall Christ be cut off, namely, because the things which are expressed before this AFTER must happen in the former weeks, which are singularly separated from the sixty-two weeks, namely HE SHALL RETURN, the street and the wall shall be rebuilt in troublous times. This exposition must necessarily be admitted, otherwise the opinion which would emerge from comparing both would be most absurd, or self-contradictory, in this manner: (1.) Unto Christ the Prince seven weeks, sixty-two weeks. (2.) But after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be cut off. The hearer would be left uncertain whether he ought to embrace the former or the latter proposition. From the going forth of the word unto Christ the Prince, or the exalted one, there are intervals of sixty-nine weeks, and indeed seven weeks for rebuilding the streets and repairing the walls. But after sixty-two weeks have elapsed from the end of the preceding seven weeks, Christ shall be cut off (but also at the same time immediately exalted). This is our late blessed one. (8.) The Scaligerians do not find anything certain, regarding the epoch of the LXII. weeks, either the beginning or the end, on which they might fix their foot: For some of them begin them from the end of the 7 preceding weeks, others assign the same beginning to these 62 weeks, which is seven weeks, namely the second year of Darius: the former remain ambiguous about the end of the Epoch, nor do they agree among themselves, as ought to happen when one departs from the full meaning of the text: for truth is one and simple; but falsehood is manifold. Whence D.

Georg König preferred to assign the same beginning to both Epochs as Theobald Meuschius, and he established the end of these 62 weeks in the 12th year of Christ's age, because the word נגיד denotes not only a Leader, but also an Ecclesiastical Prelate, Neh. 11:11, Jer. 20:1. Which reasoning, however, confirms that the Epoch should be ended when Christ was proclaimed Doctor from heaven at His Baptism, rather than when He conferred with the Doctors in the temple as a twelve-year-old boy. For from that time he certainly did not conduct or exhibit himself as a Prelate of the Church, since he remained quiet for 18 years, nor is he read to have done anything publicly.

(9.) The Scaligerians are completely stuck as to which quota of the weeks they ought to understand by that ONE. Theobald Meuschius, following the first edition of Scaliger's De Emendat. tempor. p. 288, understands it partly by the three years of Christ's ministry on earth, and partly by the three years preceding the total destruction of the Jews, although he separates it from that former half-week by a few weeks, say four and a fraction, in Syst. Chronolog. p. 79. Which opinion, however, D. König refutes in Disputat. 32, Vind. sacr. thes. 40, but he invents nothing better, understanding by the covenant the divine threat made here concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, which was to be confirmed by word and deed during the last seven-year period. But that this threat neither pertains to these 70 weeks, will be taught from the scope or the words of the oracle, nor is it clear that it is called ברית. For who will call that threat federal, or will concede that a covenant and a threat are interchangeable, even if D. König has admitted that the word ברית is general, and signifies any agreement, whether it be accomplished by express or tacit consent? For what agreement, whether tacit or express, has a place regarding this threat concerning the destruction of Jerusalem?

(10.) Thus, therefore, the Scaligerians have nothing to say about the half-week, or even about the cessation of the sacrifice, or about the confirmation of the covenant: for they leave all these things as if unsaid, and as bringing forth nothing certain, since not a jot in the Scriptures, let alone in such great oracles, which designate everything so exactly and absolutely ὁριστικῶς (definitively), is in vain. But the things which some bring forward are so constituted that not even their inventors can be satisfied with them, let alone others. But we have spoken sufficiently about these and other matters in the cited place. We did not wish to τὸ πραχθὲν πράττειν (do what has been done), we only bring forward Baillie, who deservedly reproves his Scaliger here: that Scaliger may avoid this argument, he miserably entangles the weeks in both editions, discontinues their parts, and throws one, seven, and sixty-two weeks here and there, before, behind, with inexplicable confusion. But let him turn the parts of the weeks up, down, and every which way he wants, he will not escape the knot of the argument: for the Prophet affirms in the most explicit words that seven and sixty-two weeks flowed before Christ, whether born, or baptized, or having suffered, it is nothing to the present matter; provided that after Christ only one of the seventy weeks remains until the end of the period: given this (which is sufficiently manifest in the words of the Prophecy), the weeks cannot be concluded later than seven years after Christ.

They are concluded, however, by five seven-year periods and a fraction after Christ suffered, if we establish their end at the destruction of the city. These are his words, part 1, Oper. Histor. & Chronol. p. 174.

There remains, therefore, the opinion of those who indeed rightly refer the beginning of the Epoch to the times of Artaxerxes Longimanus: yet they still err from the truth in designating the years. Such (1.) is that which Suarez brought forward, not entirely disapproved by Tirinus in his Chronicon: that it should be begun from the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes mentioned in Neh. V, 12. Which, however, agrees neither with chronological calculation, nor with the present angelic oracle. For this wishes the beginning to be drawn from the going forth of the word. But no edict went forth then, nor could one be designated by anyone.

(II.) It is Tirinus's opinion that the beginning of the epoch should be referred to the 23rd year, in which the city was built and fully restored, and its dedication was performed. Neh. 12:4. But the angel did not begin it from the city being built, but from the going forth of the word to build the city: nor does anything appear from the Scriptures concerning that 23rd year designated by Tirinus. Nor does the definition of the term to which it is made in our oracle agree, unless (which Tirinus assumed precariously on p. 46) it is established that that 23rd year, from which Artaxerxes Longimanus began to reign together with Xerxes for the first time, was the eighth year from which he reigned alone, or the 28th from the beginning of the reign of Xerxes.

(III.) Chrysostom, Rupert, Gordian Huntlaeus, and Torniellus, as noted by Cornelius a Lapide, as well as Benedictus Pererius and also Matthias Chefneux, begin the epoch from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus and end it at the passion of Christ, with Julius Africanus, book 5 of the annals; but since 490 solar years have not elapsed from there, and they understand common lunar years, each of which contains 354 days, they say that 490 of such years elapsed from there, and made 475 solar years: But since Scripture nowhere uses such lunar years, nor are the Jews read to have used the same, such a computation cannot have a place, however fiercely the Jesuit Pererius may contend for it.

(IV.) Therefore, the blessed Osiander more correctly retains solar years, fixing the 20th year likewise as the beginning: but he makes the end seven years after the passion of Christ, gathering about 477 years from the 20th of Longimanus and the departure of Nehemiah into Judea until the passion of Christ; he saw well, however, that 6 years were still lacking in this way until the final week, which he attributes to the confirmation of the covenant after the passion and resurrection of the Lord, and he says those six years were neglected by historians through carelessness. But neither are the 69 weeks defined until the passion of the Lord, nor is the last week to be begun only after the passion, according to the oracle of Gabriel: and it is harsh to call the credibility of historians into doubt here on account of a preconceived opinion.

(V.) James Ussher begins the 70 weeks from the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, Nehemiah chapter 2, verses 1 and 6, and ends them 3½ years after the death of CHRIST, who approaches closer to the true determination than others: but since he attributes only 11 years to the reign of Xerxes, to which from the canon of Ptolemy most assign 21, hence the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus according to Ussher, which is 41 from the beginning of Xerxes according to others, is only 31 to him. Furthermore, Ussher enumerates the years of the reign of Artaxerxes and the rest differently than Ptolemy, and in such a way that 123 years still remain from the 20th of Artaxerxes, whereas only 113 years are left. 20th of Artaxerxes according to his calculation to the term designated by the angel, which Ussher acknowledges, could he find that number of years, and 70 complete weeks, unless he established that some years had intervened between the Baptism of Christ and his public ministry, which he admits ought not to extend beyond the middle of the week: which we judge to be new and unknown to Holy Scripture. And Baillie observes that all the supporters of that opinion acknowledge that the beginning is to be taken from the 20th of Longimanus, that not 490 years, but only 471, or 477 with the terms included, intervened until the passion of Christ: and thus 13 years are lacking.

(VI.) Dionysius Petavius and Wilhelmus Langius, having retained the beginning of the 20th year of Longimanus, and having counted not by lunar but by solar years, likewise end the Epoch in the fourth year after the cutting off of the Messiah, and refer this to the middle of the last week; but so that the calculation may be correct, they indicate the 20th year of the long-handed one [Artaxerxes] from Nehemiah, not from the death of Xerxes and the beginning of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes, but they compute from the first of his reign under the auspices of his parent: whence Petavius observes in book II, Ration. temp. c. X, that the tenth year of his solitary reign is that 20th designated by Nehemiah; here, however, he establishes in book II, de annis Christi, chapter 9, that Artaxerxes reigned for 7 years with his parent, so that that 20th year of his joint reign was for that reason the 13th of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes. Which opinions do not depart much from the genuine and truer explanation and computation.

(VII.) Funccius in his Chronology wishes the Epoch to have taken its beginning from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus (he wrongly calls him Darius Longimanus), but he makes the passion of Christ the end of the same, towards the beginning of book 1 of his Chronology; he is, however, mistaken in this, that he thinks the angel said Christ would suffer only when the 70 weeks were precisely finished; nor could he find how he might assign an entire week to the confirmation of the covenant made by Christ before his death, nor did he conveniently reduce the cessation of the sacrifice to the baptism.

Therefore, that we may finally arrive (VIII) at the true determination of the beginning and end of this Epoch, we judge that Philipp Lansbergen in his Sacred Chronology, book II, c. 12, has hit the mark in this most difficult question, who fixes the beginning in the first edict of Artaxerxes, but the end in the fourth year after the passion of Christ, with which also agrees

Eduardus Samsonius in his explanation of the 70 weeks of Daniel, part VII, Cathol. Chron. page 55. We begin, he says, these seven weeks in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, which is the third year of the 80th Olympiad: from there if you count seven weeks or 49 years, you will arrive at the first year of the 93rd Olympiad, which is the sixteenth year of Darius Nothus. And afterwards: if sixty-two weeks are counted from the first year of the 93rd Olympiad until the 4th year of the 201st Olympiad, they lead us to that year in which St. John was sent to baptize and to manifest to the Jews Christ the Savior of the World. Within the space of those 434 years, however, the city of Jerusalem felt many distresses. Our Liveleus, however, advised that this passage should be translated thus: And for sixty-two weeks the street and the wall were rebuilt, even in times of distress. So much for him. Robert Baillie agrees in his Oper. Chronol. p. 174. and also Cornelius a Lapide in his commentary on this passage, praising Cedrenus, Funccius, Bucholzer, Angelocrator, Helvicus, and Capellus for this opinion, though it is evident from the review already made that they do not all entirely agree. Bailius also cites Nicolaus Abramus the Jesuit, Sanctius, Henricus Philippi, and Tirinus: as well as Gualtherus, Bullinger, etc.

But so that we do not stray from the angelic definition, we note here the characters of the true determination, and at the same time apply them for the sake of confirming the truth: which are as follows: (1.) The beginning ought to be assigned to the going forth of a word, or of some Royal edict concerning the holy city of Jerusalem to be built: For this cannot be referred to the text of a Prophetic word: because it is not the custom of the Prophets to refer us to other Prophets in this way when they define some time. Nor can any beginning of the going forth of a Prophetic word be designated which would suit this matter, and the calculation, and the event, which would constitute the term from which the Epoch begins. There is no doubt, therefore, that a Royal edict is indicated. Since, however, various edicts went forth from this prophecy of Daniel, concerning the reparation of the temple, the sacred rites, and the city, in the time of Cyrus, in the first year of his monarchy, Ezra book 1, in the time of Darius, Ezra VI, v. 6, who is certainly Hystaspes, not Nothus, and also in the time of Artaxerxes Longimanus, who is commemorated by Ezra and Nehemiah, and since the first edict, namely that of Cyrus, does not apply here, for which only the foundations of the temple were laid, but the structure was not continued, nor the edict of Darius, which did not concern the city, but only the temple and the continuation of its structure so that it would not be hindered: it remains that we refer the going forth of the word concerning the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem to the times of Artaxerxes Longimanus. Furthermore, since Artaxerxes made the first edict not only concerning the expense and the provision of sacred vessels for the temple and the use of sacred rites, so that whatever still remained for the completing and adorning of the temple, and for the sacred rites to be performed in it, might be completed by Ezra and the others who were ascending with him, provided with a royal warrant and funds: Ezra VII, 16, 19, 20, 23. But also concerning judges and administrators to be set over the whole people, learned in the law of God, and for observing the law of the Lord v. 25, 26, by the power of which both the sacred rites could then be fully restored and the Republic also could be established, so that in this way the holy city of Jerusalem could be restored in its entirety as regards both the Polity and the Church and the Republic, there can be no doubt that this Epoch must be begun from this first and most solemn edict of Artaxerxes, joined with the mission of Ezra and its effect. For it is not fitting to pass over the earlier edict of this King, who was very clement and munificent toward the people of the Lord, and to make the beginning from his later letters, which concerned only the continuation of the edict and its enlargement or extension to external buildings; nor should one look only to the external structure of the city, but especially to the internal form, by which both sacred and political matters, although even regard should next be had to the external structure, and the same was also specifically designated by the angel, inasmuch as under the reign of the same King it was shortly after to be confirmed by a special mission and a royal letter-patent in the expedition of Nehemiah, so that the starting point might thus be fixed more expressly in the time of that King, who then had granted and sanctioned those things which made for the rebuilding of the city, for the perfection and adornment of the temple, for the use of the sacred vessels, for the ordering of any sacred things, for the sanctioning of laws, for the institution of judges, for the designation of administrators and prefects, and thus all things which were still remaining for the sacred and civil polity and for the εὐεξίᫀ of the Republic, and had even provided royal expenses for them: then also he had made an indulgence by a granted diploma concerning the external buildings to be built, the walls to be constructed, and the streets to be ordered. Who is none other than Artaxerxes Longimanus.

What the Holy Scripture wished to teach when it set forth with such great care no edicts, joined with the execution itself, which went forth after the completed captivity concerning the reparation of the temple and the city, than those which were made concerning the mission of Ezra and Nehemiah: to which indeed a great part of the book of Ezra and the whole book of Nehemiah is devoted לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת. For what else did it do with such laborious treatment, than that it might be certain to us concerning the beginning of the Epoch of Daniel, and the going forth of the word, predicted by Gabriel? for whose cause the hand of the Lord was upon Ezra in the presence of Artaxerxes, and thanks were conciliated to him before the King and his counselors, Ezra VII, 6, 28. I pass over the fact that it is prolixly proven by Nicolaus Abramus that the building of Jerusalem refers to the filling of the city with citizens, which it is established was excellently performed by Ezra, according to the edict of Artaxerxes and the prophecy of Daniel, but that the construction of the walls by Nehemiah looks not so much to the building of the city as to its fortification, which not only cities but most powerful states, Lacedaemon and Athens, lacked in their greatest glory: although it seems likely that Ezra also applied himself to the building of the walls of Jerusalem: for he had received much money and provisions not only for sacrifices, but for the uses which he also wished; moreover, he had brought with him a great multitude of men so that they might dwell in Jerusalem, and he had also obtained the power of appointing civil magistrates in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea, who might punish crimes either by death or by exile, or by fines according to the quality of the offense: and indeed in his prayers to God he acknowledges that a wall had been given to the people by God at Jerusalem, as Bailius has it on p. 174.

We add what Simsonius has in his Explanation of the LXX weeks. From the going forth of the word. The Angel Gabriel teaches from where the computation of the LXX weeks is to be begun, namely from the going forth of the word, that is, from the sending forth of the word or command concerning restoring and building: for so it is read in Hebrew לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת that is, concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Which the Greeks would call ἀνακτίζειν or ἀνοικοδομεῖν, the Hebrews express by two words joined together, because they cannot otherwise express the preposition ἀνὰ except by the verb שׁוּב. See Gen. 26, 18. Zach. 6, 1. Mal. 1, 4. By the word or command concerning the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem we understand the edict of the Great King, Artaxerxes, which exists in the book of Ezra ch. 7. concerning which edict, which was made in the VII year of Artaxerxes, we have said more in the Persica at A. M. 3547. Concerning the rebuilding of the Temple, King Cyrus and then Darius, son of Hystaspes, had made an edict, and under those Kings private individuals indeed restored their houses in Jerusalem. But Ezra and after him Nehemiah, sent into Judea by King Artaxerxes Longimanus, had rebuilt the walls of the city and restored the polity.

(II.) Such a beginning is to be assigned to the Epoch from the going forth of the word, and such an end, that from that to the term the whole Epoch may be adequately filled by LXX weeks, not by more nor by fewer. Which is manifest from the oracle, both because the LXX weeks are said to be defined and determined, or appointed by God, not abbreviated, as Pererius foolishly imagines, in order to hammer out shortened lunar years; and Bailius notes that weeks are said not to be defined in the plural, but defined in the singular, so that the deduction and distribution of that word or particular name through each of these parts may be signified: comparing Buxtorf in his Thesaurus p. 342 and 425. and also because the distribution of the parts is added, from which the LXX weeks are completed, with the mention of 7 and 62 and one of the weeks: so that it may not be permitted to doubt that just so many, neither more nor fewer, will have elapsed. Hence collapses the opinion of Rainoldus, who contends that no certain time is designated, so that he may sustain the Epoch from the first year of Cyrus to the σταυρώσιμον of Christ, which interval is not defined by 490 years, but comprises many more. Whom Rob. Bailius, of the same mind in the faith, refutes at length. The opinion of Pareus also collapses, who attempts to scrape away half of one week: as does that of Scaliger, who added half a week, and likewise that of the Jesuits, Pererius, Torniellius, Salianus, and others, who indeed do not extend the 71st week to the destruction of the city with Scaliger, yet in this they allowed themselves to be seduced by Scaliger, that beyond the seventieth week, he invented a new one, which they assign after the 70 complete ones are finished at the death of Christ. But the Prophet opposes these opinions about the middle of a new week, when he added He hajediah, and teaches that that same one week is indicated: in the middle of that week.

Where Scaliger is in vain, that the ה is not referred to the antecedent, but to something else entirely different: for the force of the same is not to be assigned according to our own will and rashly.

Furthermore, just as the named Jesuits make Daniel silent about the seventieth week, which he mentions individually above all the others, as the most wonderful of all, so Scaliger marks this seventieth week with no notable event, and closes the seventy weeks without any mystery: for at their end, he wishes neither for the Messiah to have died, nor for the city to have been destroyed, since he closes the seventy weeks thirty-six years after the death of Christ, and three and a half years before the city was destroyed, namely a year and a half before the final siege of Jerusalem, when nothing notable is brought forward by any author, as Bailius notes here on page 181. Finally, because God precisely defined the space of 70 weeks; neither the addition of some years, nor the subtraction, ought to be made by anyone to it.

Now if you look at the application, from the seventh year of Artaxerxes to the end of the Epoch, 70 weeks have precisely elapsed: which is the principal argument of Rob. Bailius: from the seventh year, he says on page 174, of Artaxerxes to Christ, seventy weeks of years, or four hundred and ninety years, have precisely flowed, as is admitted everywhere by all who place any trust in human writings, and who do not wish to accuse all the ancient Chaldean, Greek, and Latin historians and chronologers entirely of falsehood, even against the mind of all the Fathers of the Church. Although indeed Bailius calls these trifles (which does not quite suit a precise determination) whether the weeks are closed by death or three years after death, about which he does not wish to inquire, he nevertheless acknowledges later in the same place, p. 175, that after the public advent of Christ, one week still remained at the end of the weeks: which he proves from Dan. 9:25. From the going forth of the word unto Christ the Prince are seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks, where he observes that the sixty-nine weeks are to be counted from Christ being named and publicly initiated into his mediatorial office by baptism, after which only one remains. The calculation will then be subtracted.

(III.) The beginning of the Epoch is to be assigned thus: so that the seven and sixty-two weeks may reach unto Christ the Prince. For the oracle clearly indicates that those seven and sixty-two weeks are not to be torn apart as if discontinuous, but are to be taken as continuous, and jointly, not separately, with regard to this term to which, so that we may fix the end of all those sixty-nine weeks, or 483 years, in Christ the Prince: Know therefore and understand, from the going forth of the Word, that Jerusalem (thy holy city) be built again UNTO CHRIST THE PRINCE are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. What could be clearer than this definition? To which it is no objection that it is added, and after sixty-two weeks shall Christ be cut off: as if these two were to be understood as solitary: because these LXII are not begun except from the end of the seven preceding, concerning which the angel had said that within them the streets are to be built again, and the walls are to be erected. From these therefore having passed by, LXII weeks remain unto Christ the Prince: who, after those have elapsed, is to be killed, or cut off, according to the heavenly messenger's interpretation. And this is the common opinion of the ancients and the moderns, of the Papists and the Protestants, that these LXII weeks begin after the end of the seven weeks, and terminate at the advent of Christ the Prince, and before his death, so that the first of them is the eighth of the whole sum, and the last is the sixty-ninth. For the angel assigns the first place to the seven weeks, the last to the one, and the middle place to the sixty-two. And therefore they openly contradict the angelic oracle who place the seven weeks after the sixty-two, and openly disturb its method. Furthermore, the things done or facts follow one another in the oracle in the same order as those smaller numbers: for first the building of the streets and walls within seven weeks is hinted at, and among those things which were to happen, it is commemorated in the first place. The death and cutting off of Christ, mentioned in the third place, separates the third portion from the second, so that after the other part of time, likewise completed, sixty-two weeks, and in the third part of the angelic distribution, the cutting off of Christ is to happen: but to the second and middle part completed is attributed the advent of Christ the Prince. Whence it is now clear that they are mistaken (1.) who wish the beginning of both the seven weeks and the sixty-two to be the same, which we discussed above.

(2.) That Scaliger erred while he concluded in the later edition of the books on the emendation of times that the sixty-two weeks were seven years before Christ's death, when the Messiah ought to have come at the end of the sixty-two weeks, and that he erred even more while he finished them in the first edition seven years before the destruction of Jerusalem: because after the advent of Messiah the Prince only one week remained, which, however the advent of Messiah the Prince is taken, certainly cannot be begun seven years before the destruction of the city: whence also the beginning of these sixty-two weeks, both of the former edition in the 32nd year of Artaxerxes Memnon, and of the latter in the 5th of the same, cannot be correct, both of which are otherwise assumed merely precariously. Furthermore, it is repugnant to Chronology: for from the second year of Darius Nothus (whence Scaliger starts Daniel's weeks) to the fifth of Artaxerxes, which he chose in the later edition, only 23 years are counted, not seven weeks, or 49 years. Therefore Scaliger was forced to profess (which was observed by Bailius) that he did not know to which the seven weeks should be referred, whether they should precede, or whether they should follow the sixty-two, or finally consist within their limits, which is a wonderful confusion. He also involves the one and last week in the same confusion: for since that one clearly follows the sixty-two according to Daniel, and Scaliger truly closes the whole seventieth in the destruction of the city, he finds it necessary to mix that one week, in which the Messiah died, either with the seven, or with the sixty-two, or with both.

(3.) Junius and Deodatus are most grievously mistaken, while following the former opinion of Scaliger they place the excision of Christ before the sixty-two weeks are finished, and within their limits, which the angel predicted would happen after the sixty-two weeks in a sense clearly contrary. Therefore, they had need, serving the hypothesis, to deprave the text, as if it were written, after sixty-two weeks, Christ being excised, when there is יִכָּרֵת, the Niphal future, he shall be excised: that is, after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be excised.

(4.) Furthermore, he errs in the Theodoretian manner, making the first part of those seventy weeks 62 weeks, and the other part seven weeks, and counting 62 weeks, 434 years, from the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus to the last Hyrcanus of the Maccabees killed by Herod, and from there seven, or 49 years, to Christ, which calculation inverts the method of Daniel, and does not agree in any way with chronology or history.

(5.) Finally, they err who, with Chrysostom, place not only the sixty-two weeks but also that one week before the seven weeks, contrary to the method of the angel, and begin those 62 from the 32nd year of Artaxerxes Mnemon and finish them before the death of Christ: but they attribute the sixty-third to the passion and death of Christ, from which they enumerate the six following weeks, and thus they think the last or seventieth week is either vacant from the death of Christ, or touches the former ones through its beginning, as Bailius reported that opinion from Suarez: which collapses of its own futility.
