How, however, seven and sixty-two weeks, that is, 483 years, have elapsed exactly from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus until the advent of Christ the Leader, we shall teach subsequently: we only warn of this, that the advent is to be understood when he himself publicly, as Leader and our guide or the promised Messiah, was declared and came to undertake his public office, and was inaugurated from heaven, which was done at his Baptism, Matt. III, Luke III.

(IV.) The character holds thus: The beginning of the LXX weeks is to be assigned in such a way that the first seven weeks are numbered from the notable edict concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the holy city, and restoring it to its entirety, within the course of which both the walls were to be built and the streets established and ordained. I speak of the restoration of Jerusalem, which was the holy city, because seventy weeks are said to be determined upon the holy city and upon the people of the Lord. Wherefore, not only the external construction of walls and streets is looked at, even though express mention is also made of it, because Daniel had complained in his prayers, Jerusalem and thy people are a reproach to all that are round about us, and he had prayed, let thy anger, I beseech thee, and thy fury be turned away from the city Jerusalem and thy holy mountain: likewise, show thy face upon thy sanctuary, which is desolate, open thy eyes, and see our desolation, and the city, upon which thy name is invoked. And although he also makes mention of the sanctuary, only that which was to be dissipated by the latest destruction, from which Daniel could conclude with certainty that the building of the second temple would happen, inasmuch as it was to be destroyed again, not so long after the seventy weeks had elapsed, yet it is not the going forth of the word concerning the building of the sanctuary, or temple, but concerning the building of the holy city, and the restoring of the same to its entirety, that is pointed out, for which purpose Ezra was first sent by Artaxerxes Longimanus, so that that city, as far as the sacred things, without which the people of God could not be preserved, might be completed, and as far as the civil polity might be restored: to teach the law of God, and to rule the people: with whom it was granted to go to Jerusalem, to whomever it pleased, whether of the people of Israel, or of its Priests, and of the Levites: for which purpose also the King and his seven supreme counselors offered gold and silver of their own accord to the God of Israel, whose tabernacle was in Jerusalem: and whatever the people might wish to contribute, and how much besides was to be expended from the treasures and from the King's exchequer, so that besides the vessels, which were committed to Ezra for the ministry of the house of God, all other things, which were needed for the house of the Lord, might be procured, and consecrated for the use of the temple of the Lord. Finally, he also ordered that everything which pertains to the rite of the God of heaven be given diligently to the house of the Lord, and he granted the privilege of immunity from taxes, tributes, and provisions to all the Priests, and Levites, and Singers, Nethinim, and ministers of the house of God; and besides, he commanded Ezra to appoint judges and governors, so that they might judge and preside over all the people, with that grave threat added, that whoever does not do the law of God, and the law of the King diligently, judgment be pronounced upon him, whether to death, or to exile, or to the confiscation of his substance, or certainly to prison, Ezra 7. Which things certainly contributed not only to glorifying the house of the Lord, but also to restoring and establishing the civil polity, the soul of which is the observance of laws. Therefore Ezra and his companions are said to have lifted up both the people and the house of God, chap. 8, 36. And Ezra celebrates the Lord, chap. 9, 9, because he inclined mercy upon them before the King of the Persians, to exalt the house of the Lord, and to build its ruins, and to give them a hedge in Judah and Jerusalem. What of the fact that not only was the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy provided for by the authority of Artaxerxes Longimanus, by which the adornment of the temple and the ordination of all sacred things according to the law of the Lord, and the Political, as far as the institution of judges and governors versed in the law of the Lord; but also the economic, by which the dissolution of marriages contracted with Gentiles and the dismissal of foreign wives, by which all things in the holy city could be restored to their pristine form, by which all states and orders, and according to the law of the Lord, could be repaired. Which is truly to build the holy city of Jerusalem again.

But also, thirteen years after the more solemn and munificent, and truly royal, mission of Ezra, and the granting of immunities, Nehemiah was sent by the same king, instructed by Royal letters for the restoration of the walls and the construction and ordering of the streets, which were still desired for the repairing of the city: how these things were accomplished by him is taught in the entire book of Nehemiah as a matter of design; namely, how Jerusalem was built in walls, towers, and gates, with the neighboring adversaries, namely the Samaritans and other neighboring nations, offering no delay; likewise how he appointed and ordained guards in the city. To which, finally, so that both the Ecclesiastical and civil Polity might be preserved in the city, and the people might be governed according to the law of the Lord, and all things might be administered, there followed, after the separation from foreigners and the public repentance of the people, a renewal of the covenant with God, and a solemn sealing, concerning the observance of the precepts of God, especially also those which had been neglected, such as not mixing with foreigners and keeping the constitutions, concerning the Sabbaths, the seventh year, offerings, first fruits, and tithes; and also the designation by lot of the inhabitants of the holy city, together with those who offered themselves willingly to inhabit it. For the city, as is held in Nehemiah 7, 4, was too wide and great, and the people were small in the midst of it, and the houses were not built. Wherefore it is manifest how, by the mission, mandate, and authority of Artaxerxes Longimanus of both, namely Ezra and Nehemiah, the work succeeded in restoring the holy city, in building the walls and streets, and thus their buildings distributed among the future inhabitants, and in erecting and sanctioning its entire sacred and civil polity: for which not a few years were required. And in the book of Ezra and Nehemiah are counted the 7th year, the 20th year, and the 32nd year of the same Artaxerxes the Longimanus; nor is there any doubt that, after that distribution and designation of the inhabitants of the city, many more years were needed to fully restore it, before it was all restored to its entirety, and seven weeks, or 49 years, could easily have been spent on that work, and indeed were spent. However, therefore, as to where the sacred history of the first seven weeks ends here, since the Canon of Scripture does not extend that far: yet there is no reason to doubt this Epoch, since the angelic oracle is clear, and the terminus a quo of the same cannot now be ambiguous, namely the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, in which that edict went forth concerning the restoration of the city, than which no more solemn or more liberal one is recorded in that matter. Concerning which we again have the agreement of Edward Simson in his explanation of the LXX weeks, p. 55. Within this space of VII weeks the building of the city was completed, the wall restored, and the polity re-established. Ezra was sent into Judea in the VII year of King Artaxerxes, and was instructed with authority not only to order ecclesiastical matters, but also to appoint judges and governors who would rule the people. Indeed, it is likely that Ezra requested from the King the power to fortify the city, and attempted to build the walls before the arrival of Nehemiah. For Nehemiah himself, having been sent to Jerusalem by the same Artaxerxes 13 years later, and having successfully undertaken the restoration of the walls, completed that work with incomparable diligence and fortitude, prudently established the polity, and built for himself a palace or praetorian house. And when he had ruled Judea for twelve years, he did indeed return to Artaxerxes in the 32nd year of his reign, but not long after, having obtained leave again, having returned to Judea, he seems to have remained there until the 16th year of Darius Nothus, as we have noted in the Persian [chronology] according to the opinion of Jacques Cappel, who rightly observes that the Darius who is mentioned in Nehemiah ch. 12, 22 is Darius Nothus, who succeeded his father Artaxerxes.

(V.) This is the character: This epoch must be established in such a way that the expiatory death of Christ falls in the middle of the seventieth or last week, because the 70 weeks were established so that transgression might be finished and sin might receive an end; and iniquity might be blotted out, and everlasting righteousness might be brought in, which was done meritoriously through the death of Christ: likewise also, so that the vision and prophecy might be fulfilled, which in the same way looked primarily to the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ, and the sending forth of the Apostles into the world, and the ascension into heaven, with Christ as the interpreter, Luke 24, 26. 27. 46. 47. Finally, that the Holy of Holies might be anointed, who for the sake of executing the work of redemption, the expiation of sins, and the bringing in of eternal righteousness, was anointed with the immense gifts of the Spirit: which likewise was done during the last week, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him at his Baptism. Thus, therefore, those effects are hinted at, to be referred to the final times of the 70 weeks. But a clearer designation of the time of the συνεχωσίμς is had in v. 26, and after sixty-two weeks, following the first seven weeks, Christ shall be killed: For these things openly teach that Christ would suffer and be killed only after the 69th week, not sooner: nor even after the 70 weeks had completely elapsed, but within them, because only 70 are precisely defined here for those events: whence the death of Christ had to fall in the last week: finally, so that the time of death might be designated even more expressly and specifically, it is added in v. 27. & in the middle of the week (namely, the last one) the oblation and the sacrifice shall fail: because through the death of Christ, as the antitype, the types of sacrifices had to cease, and with the arrival of the body, the figures and shadows had an end. For the sacrifices were types and figures of the death of Christ. Whence Calvin, Rollock, Cornel. a Lapide, Petavius, Henr. Philippi, Lansbergius, Ussher, and not a few other more excellent chronologists acknowledge that Christ had to be cut off in the middle of the last week. Also Eduard Simson in Explic. LXX. hebdom. p. 55. For he finishes the 434 years, i.e., 62 weeks, at the Baptism of Christ; and concerning the words of Gabriel, 'in the middle of the week the oblation and sacrifice shall fail,' he holds thus: For since Christ himself had performed his ministry for three whole years and some months, in this middle of the seventieth week the oblation and sacrifice failed: by which words the death of the Messiah is signified, as Pererius notes: For Christ also died in the fourth year after his baptism, and after his death the sacrifices of the old law were abrogated, an illustrious argument for which was the fact that when Christ was dying, the veil of the temple was torn from the top even to the bottom: Thus, therefore, the half with a half of the ministry of Christ from his baptism, with Simson as author, is the middle of the week immediately following the end of the sixty-two weeks: and so the other half of the last week will be three years and a half after the death of Christ: although Simson is not sufficiently consistent with himself in this opinion, since in the same place he affirms that John the Baptist began his ministry in the autumn of the third year of the seventieth week, and that Christ himself was manifested in his Baptism around the beginning of the following [year], and began his office, and that the 30th year of Christ is the middle of the seventieth week.

Just as also the Chronicon of the same Simson does not agree with the previous explanation of the words of Gabriel, that the 62 weeks (after the first seven have elapsed: that is, 69) end at the baptism of Christ. For since he fixes the beginning of the seventy weeks in the year of the world 3547, of the city founded 296, his 69 weeks make 483 years; with those added, there emerge the years 4030 from the creation of the world, and 779 from the founding of the city, at which time the baptism of Christ would fall: which, however, Simson reports in his Chronicon as the year of the world 4033, U.C. 782.

However, the years of the Olympiad which he added easily convict the error in Simson's calculation. For since Simson linked the 319th Olympiad with that year of the world 3547 and of the city founded 296, with 493 years added, the year 802 emerges, which would be the first year of the baptism of Christ, but he himself referred the baptism of Christ to the year of the Olympiad 805. Since, however, that calculation is undoubtedly to be preferred which agrees with the genuine explanation of Daniel's oracle, and therefore as the 69 weeks end in the year of the world 4030 and U.C. 779, which according to Gabriel are to be ended at the Baptism of Christ, when the Leader was proclaimed; the birth of Christ, who was 30 years old when baptized, will bring the year 4000, U.C. 749, and the end of the 70 weeks the year M. 4037, U.C. 486, and so they will have to be ended not at the death of Christ, but three years and a half after the death of Christ.

For whatever may be the case regarding the calculation of Samson (we must return to that from which we digressed, that is, to the refutation of the Scaligerian opinion), ancient and modern interpreters and chronologists determine with great consensus that it must be referred to the final week of the passion and death of Christ, so that Scaliger is left almost alone with his followers in the new invention that it refers to the destruction of the city. But Scaliger himself also established in the earlier edition of the Emendation of Times that half of the final week was in those three and a half years in which Christ was baptized, preached the Gospel, and was crucified: although he very ineptly dragged the other half to the three and a half years in which Roman arms surrounded Jerusalem for its final devastation, by which arrangement the last week was torn apart, so that the one half was removed from the former by several whole weeks. Scaliger indeed corrected this error in the later edition, acknowledging with us one week, and that one continuous, and also that in the middle of which the death of Christ occurred. But he invented a new half of a week, which does not pertain to that one week, nor to the seventy weeks, but is far later than that, and reaches the destruction of Jerusalem: which is clearly repugnant to the angelic oracle. For in it not only are seventy weeks precisely defined; but it is taught that that half pertains to one, namely the last, and is not different from it. Wherefore those also hallucinate most gravely who indeed acknowledge that one last week, but drag it with Junius to the seven-year period before the destruction of the city; for how then is Christ said to be cut off after sixty-two weeks, and in the middle of the last week? Was Christ crucified within the middle of the seven-year period before the total destruction? How exactly the circumstances of the oracle agree in the application of this character to the time of the passion will be clear later.

(VI.) The character is that Christ is to confirm the Evangelical covenant with many in the last week, and this in such a way that in the middle of that week, through his own death, the Old Testament with its ceremonies, of which the principal ones were victims and sacrifices, is to be abolished v. 26. This confirmation of the covenant was made by Christ both in the days of his ministry, through the proclamation of the Gospel and the miracles performed by him, and through his death and resurrection, and after his ascension into heaven through the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles at the Feast of Pentecost, Acts 2, and upon the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius, Acts 10, as well as through the beginnings of the Apostolic preachings, initially among the Jews, then, having left them, among the Gentiles in the primitive Church of the New Testament. For here Christ is said to be cut off, through half a week, before his excision, after he was proclaimed Leader from heaven, to confirm the covenant: which he therefore did αὐτοπροσώπως, in the days of his flesh, for three and a half years: furthermore, he is said to be about to do the same in the other half of the week, after he was anointed as the Holy of Holies, Christ, and made Lord in the ascension into heaven, until the Gentiles were assumed. Thus, therefore, the beginning and end of the Epoch fit perfectly: the beginning was the restoration or repair of Jerusalem and the holy people of God to the legitimate form of polity: the end is, after the Evangelical covenant had been abundantly, but in vain, confirmed in Jerusalem and among the Jews, the assumption of the Gentiles into the peculiar people of God and the ecclesiastical polity of the remnants of Israel. The beginning was the repair of the sacred rites of the Jewish people according to the law of the Lord sanctified by the old covenant, so that the Levitical worship might flourish until Christ: the end was the abrogation of the Levitical sacred rites by the sanctioned New Testament, done both through the death of Christ and through the removal of the partition, or the middle wall dividing the Gentiles from the people of the Lord, after sufficient confirmation of the Evangelical covenant. Wherefore it is a depravation of the mind of the oracle when Grotius drags the confirmation of the covenant to a military confederation, when many were drawn into the league of the Jews, just as Josephus, Jewish War IV, 16, is the authority that 20,000 Idumeans came to their aid. Of which league no trace appears here. For the confirmation of the covenant is attributed to Christ, who is here the πρῶτον δεικτικὸν, whose advent, and likewise his killing, are the principal things which are relegated by the angel to the last of the weeks. But the fact that in v. 26 the destruction is mentioned, that is done only because it was spoken of the killing of Christ, the punishment for which was taken in the destruction: whence he immediately returns to Christ, and designates the confirmation of the covenant which he was about to perform: finally, however, when he said that the sacrifices were to cease in the middle of the week, lest anyone persuade himself of their temporary cessation only, and hope for a restoration, he adds the desolation of the temple and the total and final devastation of the city. Add that that military league had no place after the desolation of the city: all the Jews being killed and miserably perished, or led away into captivity. But the confirmation of the covenant after the cessation of the sacrifices (by which Grotius wishes the desolation of the city to be indicated) ought to have lasted for another half-week. Finally, since the angel counts only three years and a half after the excision of Christ to the completion of the calculation, it is most manifest that the end of the weeks cannot be set at the destruction of the city, which happened five weeks and more after the death of Christ.

And those who, in order that Scaliger's opinion may prevail, since they see that neither the confirmation of the Evangelical covenant fits his hypothesis, nor can they find the week of confirmation, or explain how the confirmation of the covenant falls into the last week, by a completely new invention understand the oracle about the destruction of the city through the covenant, and imagine that its confirmation ought to have been done by both words and deeds seven years before the destruction of the city; about which, however, they have nothing that they can bring forward from history, except that report of Hegesippus, concerning Joshua the son of Hanan, who for 7 years and 5 months cried out: A voice from the rising, a voice from the setting, a voice from the 4 winds, a voice over Jerusalem and the temple, etc. Which the first inventor of this gloss, D. Georg. König, Disp. XXXII. Vind., dragged here. Sacrar. th. 41, repeating his εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα here, behold the very seven years in which the covenant of God was corroborated with many in Judea. But God indeed predicted the destruction of the city and temple, but it is nowhere read that he made a pact or covenant about the destruction, nor are those predictions anywhere indicated by the word ברית, but that there is a discourse here about the covenant of grace or the Evangelical one, that illustrious federal promise of grace concerning the expiation of sins and the bringing in of eternal righteousness pertaining to the covenant of the New Testament sufficiently testifies: nor has there been any doubt among the Orthodox hitherto that the confirmation of the Evangelical covenant by the Messiah is designated here, from whose solid consensus one must by no means depart for the sake of the Scaligerian hypothesis. I pass over the fact that long before, predictions about the Jerusalem destruction had been confirmed by Christ himself both by words and signs in the days of his flesh, and that it was not finally predicted under the extreme times before the desolation of the city, from which, however, it cannot be shown that there was a peculiar week of such confirmation, which stood out above the rest, by which God made the imminent ruin attested by word and deed. That cry of Joshua alone is not of such weight, which Mr. D. König will not easily persuade anyone that Gabriel had in mind here.

But as for what Scaliger objects, that the weeks are not finished before the things commemorated in the oracle by the angel are completed, in which the destruction is also commemorated: I answer. If he understands generally those things which in any way are commemorated in that oracle, they will reach to the consummation of the age, because mention is made in his oracle that the desolation is to last until that time. Wherefore a distinction must be made between those things which pertain to the history of the weeks and are confined within their time, and those things whose mention is indeed made in the history of the weeks, and which are handed down together with the history of the times, but do not pertain to the history of the weeks itself. Add that the angel does not place the destruction before the end of the weeks, but after: for he ends the weeks at that one in which the covenant was to be confirmed, to the middle of which he had assigned the death of Christ: to say nothing of the fact that it was not the angel's purpose here to define the desolation of Jerusalem, but to lift up Daniel with the promise of the restoration of the city, the coming of the Messiah, and his propitiatory sacrifice: by which sins were to be blotted out, and eternal righteousness brought in, as well as the confirmation of the Evangelical covenant; whence, by a mention of the destruction injected as it were παραφυσιτικῶς (of which he had certainly not proposed to speak by design), it is taught how, on account of the cutting off of Christ, the Jews are to be cut off, and how, when they are cut off, the covenant made by God to Abraham shall nevertheless not fail, inasmuch as Christ himself is to confirm it, and that before the very excision of the people for seven whole years it is to be so confirmed, that concerning its duration until the consummation of the age, however long the desolation of Jerusalem may remain until that time, no doubt can remain for the faithful.

QUESTION IV. How are the 69 and a half weeks to be counted in the completion until the death of Christ?

Since the beginning must be taken from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus from the issuing of that solemn edict, which was made in that year, Ezra 7, the calculation can be begun either according to the years of the Monarchies and the Nabonassar era, or according to the Olympiads and the Iphitean years, until the solemn advent of Christ the Leader, at the time of the Baptism, or until his passion and death. Since, therefore, 41 years of Artaxerxes Longimanus are counted in the Canon of Ptolemy, from his seventh year to the 41st, 34 will remain, to which are added 19 of Darius Nothus, 46 of Artaxerxes Mnemon, 21 of Ochus, 2 of Arses, 2 of Darius Codomannus, and thus the remaining 125 years of the Persian Monarchy emerge. But 302 years of the Greek Monarchy are counted in the same canon, namely: of Alexander the Great 8, Philip Arrhidaeus 7, Alexander Aigos 12, of the Greek Kings in Egypt, Ptolemy Lagus 20, Ptolemy Philopator 35, Ptolemy Euergetes II 29, Ptolemy Soter 36, Dionysius 19, Cleopatra 22. These 302 years of the Greek Monarchy, joined to the previous remaining 125 of the Persian, make 427 years. Now there must be added to these from the Roman Monarchy 43 of Augustus after the death of Cleopatra, and 15 of Tiberius (in which 15th year of Tiberius Christ was baptized), that is, 58 years; 485 years emerge. Although, however, only 483 years complete the 69 weeks, that redundant biennium can easily be explained, by observing the distinction received by Chronologists of inclusive and exclusive numbering.

Lansbergius begins the calculation thus; he makes the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus the 291st of Nabonassar (just as it is also numbered thus in the Canon of Ptolemy), to these he adds 69 weeks or 483 years, 774 emerge for the principate of Christ from Nabonassar, and with the last seven-year period added, 780 years. James Ussher refers the beginning of the Nabonassar era to the year of the World 3257. Therefore, the 774th Nabonassar year will be the 4031st year from the creation of the World.

According to the Olympiads the calculation can be begun by counting backwards: for since Christ suffered in the fourth year of the 204th Olympiad, as is commonly established from the observation of Phlegon, that is, in the 808th Iphitean year, which observation is laid down here as a foundation, handed down with great consensus by Eusebius in his Chronicles, Tertullian, Africanus, Origen, book II against Celsus, Jerome, Paul the Deacon, and other Fathers concerning the extraordinary eclipse on the day of the great passion of Christ. If four hundred and eighty-six and a half years are subtracted from these (that is, sixty-nine and a half weeks), the seventh year of Longimanus will be the 320th Iphitean. But it is established from Diodorus Siculus, book XI of his Library, that the reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus began in the first year of the 79th Olympiad, or the 313th Iphitean: whence it remains likewise that the seventh year of Longimanus is the 320th year of Iphitus.

According to Francis Junius on Daniel 9:24, the death of Alexander the Great falls in the first year of the 114th Olympiad, that is, the 453rd Olympiadic year. From this year to the 808th Olympiadic or Iphitean year, which is the year of the crucifixion, there are 355 years; to which are added the remaining 125 years of the Persian Monarchy from the seventh year of Artaxerxes, along with the six years of Alexander the Great which Junius himself attributes to him, making 131, there will result 486 years, and thus 69 and a half weeks. From the death of Alexander until the death of Antony and Cleopatra, with whom the Macedonian empire clearly collapsed, 294 years are counted according to Ptolemy. Ussher designates 293 years and a quarter, Part II of the Annals of the Old Testament, page 489. From there, Ptolemy counts 43 years of Augustus: to which are added 15 of Tiberius, resulting in 58. These, therefore, with those 294, produce 352 from the death of Alexander to the 15th of Tiberius or to the year of the Baptism of Christ: half a week must be added, and there will result again the 355th year from the death of Alexander, or the 453rd Olympiadic year. Nor will any significant difference be discovered in the calculation of others, and it is a known chronological axiom that a difference of one year makes no difference in chronology: which, on account of the diverse beginnings of years in different eras, and complete and incomplete years, is not cared for at all.

With the blessed Lord John Pappus leading the way in his Commentary on Daniel, the method can be initiated thus: The death of Alexander the Great falls in the 1st year of the 114th Olympiad, that is, the 453rd of Iphitus. The interval, therefore, is 355 years up to the 808th of Iphitus or the year of Christ's crucifixion. To which you add the 34 of Artaxerxes Longimanus, 19 of Nothus, 43 of Mnemon, 23 of Ochus, 6 of Codomannus, and 6 of Alexander after Codomannus was defeated, which 131 years added to the previous 355 make a sum of 486 years, which is exactly how many flowed from the seventh year of Longimanus up to the passion of the Lord.

Simson, in his Explanation of the 70 weeks, initiates the calculation thus: The 7th year of Longimanus is the 3rd year of the 80th Olympiad (that is, the 319th Iphitean year); from there, with 7 weeks or 49 years counted, one arrives at the 1st year of the 93rd Olympiad (the 369th Iphitean year); from there, 62 weeks, or 434 years, to the baptism of Christ, we are led to the 4th year of the 201st Olympiad or the 204th Iphitean year; with the addition of the four-year ministry of Christ, the 208th Iphitean year of the crucifixion results.

The blessed Lord Doctor Behm, in his Chronological Manual, page 160, makes the second year of Darius Nothus the third year of the 59th Olympiad, that is, the 355th Iphitean year, from which to the 808th Olympiadic year, or to the passion of Christ, 453 years remain. From the 7th of Artaxerxes to the 2nd of Darius Nothus, 34 years intervened, to which, when those 453 are added, the 487th year from the seventh of Longimanus to the time of the passion of Christ will result. And Bailius observes, page 182 and following, that the calculations of other most learned chronologists, however much they differ otherwise, look toward this computation, and he promises that he will demonstrate this even from the tables of Ubbo Emmius, Petavius, and Henricus Philippus. Regarding the Olympiadic years alone, let the observation of Henricus Philippus in his Chronological Questions concerning the years of the birth and passion of the Savior be noted. Question 22, page 100, regarding Eusebius's report on the Olympiadic year of the passion of Christ according to the eclipse noted by Phlegon: Eusebius says, he could, according to ancestral custom, count the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad from October of the 76th Julian year. From which we gather (1) that Eusebius did not err while he marked the passion of Christ in the 3rd year of the 202nd Olympiad, calculated exactly, and in the same place he placed the fourth civil year of the same Olympiad, in which the eclipse of the Sun is noted by Phlegon. (2) That by this eclipse Baronius's opinion concerning the year of the Savior's passion is confirmed by the authority of Eusebius, while he rolls the 18th year of Tiberius, the third of the 202nd Olympiad by accurate calculation, but the eclipse of Phlegon and the fourth year of the same Olympiad by the usual reckoning, into one, as it were, ball. This is what he says: which things can contribute to the illustration and reconciliation of the diverse numbering observed regarding the year of this extraordinary eclipse.

QUESTION V. Since it is certain that the principate of Christ designated by Gabriel is to be connected with the 15th year of Tiberius?

Since the angel defined seventy-seven weeks, that is, 483 years, to the advent of Christ the Leader, when Christ was solemnly declared from heaven, or to the principate of Christ, to which he was anointed with the Holy Spirit in Baptism, which began when he undertook his public office, there is a dispute in the Scriptures concerning the designation of the term of this Epoch: which we believe is held in Luke 3. Not only the Jesuit Petavius attempted to render it doubtful with others, but also Friedrich Spanheim, a Calvinist Doctor, author of the Dubia Evangelica, was very industrious in this, acting with every effort so that we might have nothing certain from the Scriptures concerning the year of Christ, both his birth and his public office: For he finished a most troublesome labor, as he himself calls it, in digesting and explaining the diverse opinions on the birth of Christ and the year of his Baptism, at least to teach how perplexed and involved everything is, and how unsafe it is to establish anything here: and that those themes are similar to the squaring of the circle and Platonic numbers. He would have certainly placed his effort more rightly if, having dismissed the diverse opinions, he had investigated the truth from the Scriptures and other histories. Therefore, a just censure is noted in the same School by Rob. Baillie, l. II. Oper. Hist. & Chronic. c. II. qu. 1. pag. 29. Many complain much about the difficulty, and no one more than our most learned Spanheim at the beginning of the second part of his Dubia Evangelica. I confess that the things brought forward by many for the difficulty of this question are not light, yet I think that Petavius and other Jesuits exaggerate the difficulty here beyond merit, so that they may extenuate and excuse the manifest and rotten errors of their Church, as if in a matter so difficult that liquid truth cannot be found in it. Spanheim seems to sail too much into the wiles of those men, though thoughtlessly: certainly, although there are some knots in this question difficult enough to untie, yet many things are so liquid and certain that the errors of most, especially of the Roman Church, can be most easily and solidly demonstrated and exploded. This is Baillie. Yet Spanheim had as an adherent and follower Gisbertus Voetius, a compiler of various opinions and a questioner among the Reformed. Who, in part II, disput. select. disp. 1, renders all the characters indicated in the Scriptures doubtful, page 4. Since therefore we cannot SECURELY acquiesce in the text of Matt. 2, 1. and Luke 2, 1. 2. (why should we not be able to SECURELY acquiesce in the text of Scripture?) as Scultetus well observes in Exercit. Evangel. l. I. cap. 46. (Contrary to what Thomas Lyd. feels, as in the review of arguments for the emendation of Times, cap. 1. d. l. 1.) and the only sacred anchor remains, namely the text of Luke III, 1. 2. 3. which nevertheless does not perfectly or evidently ἐπεργάζεται (work out) this demonstration because of the difficulties already mentioned, it follows that we ought to be content if we find the year of the nativity approximately.

Spanheim gives these reasons for his Pyrrhonism, page 185, part II, Dub. Evangel. X. (1.) That chronologists suppose, but do not prove, the designation of the age of Christ according to the 15th year of Tiberius, Luke 3:1, which neither the words of Luke teach, nor can it be extracted from the context by any means: since Luke indeed connects the 15th year of Tiberius with the beginning of the preaching of John the Baptist, but not with the Baptism of Christ, nor with his age: nor is it certain how much time precisely intervened between the beginning of John and the Baptism of Christ, which is nowhere expressed: nor were the moments of time here observed anxiously by Luke. (2.) That it is not certain from where Luke draws the years of Tiberius, whether from that very month and day on which Augustus died, namely the 19th of August, Julian 59, or from Nisan according to the Jewish calculation, or from the Kalends of January of either that or the following year. (3.) That Luke does not precisely note the 30th year

But as to the first, for what other reason was the year of Tiberius designated by St. Luke, at the time of the arrival of the forerunner of Christ, unless it was that the age of Christ might be certain to us? For it was not of such great importance to know the year in which St. John began to baptize others, as that in which he baptized Christ, the Redeemer of the world, and inaugurated Him into His office, and in which Jesus was proclaimed Leader from heaven, for the designation of which there was certainly need, so that the fulfillment of the prediction of the Angel, and the calculation of the same, might be accurately established. Therefore it is not said simply that St. John came in that fifteenth year of Tiberius, or that the word was made to him, but because according to the prophecy of Isaiah he had to prepare the way for the Lord, Luc. 3, 4, and he testified to the people concerning the arrival of the Messiah, v. 16, and it is approached in such a way that it happened at that very time when the people were going out to be baptized, as in v. 7 and 21. Compared with one another, they clearly teach how Christ was also baptized, which therefore cannot be drawn to a time long following thereafter; but it must be accepted, by the force of the Evangelical narrative, concerning that time and year, defined with care by a certain character: otherwise, without doubt, Luke would have indicated and defined the time of Christ’s baptism with a new designation, so that we would not have need to hesitate as to at what time Christ finally approached John. Which indeed was not done, because the prior designation sufficed. Even if, therefore, the month and day are not here expressed so precisely, whether of the beginning of John’s ministry or even of the baptism of Christ, or the interval from the beginning of John’s ministry to the baptism of Christ is not ἀποτόμως defined, nevertheless the year itself of the baptism of Christ ought not for that reason remain entirely in uncertainty. Nor does it hinder anything that Luke does not seem to observe the moments of time anxiously, when he has interjected a mention of the imprisonment of John, since that is only introduced on the occasion of the τῆς παῤῥησίας used by St. John in his admonition and ἐπανορθώσει without distinction of persons, namely that he did not spare even King Herod in his time, even though he had to be consigned to prison for it; but these things, which are inserted so παραφραδικῶς & succinctly, do not prevent him from having an accurate account of time in the principal matter, about which St. Luke is primarily solicitous, which was the inauguration of Christ to his office, for the sake of which also the beginning of the proclamation & of the baptism of John was to be described. For that this is the chief argument of this place of the treatise, is taught both by the definition of the age of Christ immediately subjoined, v. 23, and by the prolix induction of his genealogy, and by the description of the temptation, which followed the baptism of Christ, added in ch. IV. It is added that the remaining Evangelists testify that the baptism of Christ happened at the same time when John began to baptize, and had the sermon described by Luke in this 3rd chapter, v. 16 seqq. For thus Matthew ch. 3, 13, τότε παραγίνεται ὁ Ἰησῦς, then or at that time Jesus comes: so that it is not permitted to imagine that one year, or perhaps even another, intervened; but Mark ch. I, 9, καὶ ἐγένετο, he says, ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις, and it happened IN THOSE DAYS. Finally, John the Evangelist, enumerating the days themselves, certainly does not permit one to think that those things happened in different years, ch. 1, 29. 32. Whence the designation of the year, which was made by St. Luke and has hitherto been assumed by interpreters and chronologists with great consensus without hesitation, as the indicator of the very year of the inauguration of Christ, is not called into doubt except very rashly.

2. As to the second, the beginning of the years of Tiberius of the Evangelist is solicited in vain, since it is by no means permitted to presume that the Holy Spirit wished to make a beginning other than that from which his reign truly began: for thus he would have rendered the calculations of chronology ambiguous on purpose. However, it is beyond controversy that the reign and the first year of Tiberius must be begun from the 19th day of the month of August, namely from that day on which Augustus Caesar died, as is evident from Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, as well as Onuphrius and Sigonius in their commentaries on the Fasti, and has been proven by Torniellus in his annals for the year of the World 4066. Namely, on the same day on which Augustus had once seized his first consulship, that is, the 19th of the month of August, he also met his fate.

Thirdly, although Luke uses the particle ὡσεὶ, which seems to render the year of the age of Christ ambiguous, whether it was precisely the thirtieth, concerning which such discrepant opinions are found among the ancients as well as the moderns, there remains nevertheless a certain concatenation of the 15th year of Tiberius with the beginning of the principate of Christ designated by Gabriel, concerning which we are inquiring here alone. The doubt concerning the word ἀρχόμενος discussed by Spanheim himself is sufficient: namely, that it is to be referred not to the year of age, but to the designation of the beginning of the office, which beginning (ministry) was as it were 30 years, Part II, dub. Evang. XI, p. 304, which he proves from the subject matter and parallel passages Luc. 23, 5, Act. 1, 22, ch. 10, 37; so that the sense is that Jesus was about 30 years old, ἀρχόμενος i.e., beginning his ministry. But Bailius, from a collation of the passages Luc. 23, 44, ὥρα ὡσεὶ ἕκτη, and Matth. 27, 45, where it is explained as ὥρα ἕκτη: likewise Act. 10, 3. ὥρα ὡσεὶ ἐννάτη, and v. 30, ὥρα ἐννάτη, as well as Marc. 8, 9, ὡς τετρακισχίλιοι, and Matth. 15, 38, τετρακισχίλιοι, teaches that in this place ἐτῶν τριάκοντα is correctly taken for truly thirty years, whether beginning or ending or completed: in Oper. Historic. Chronol. T. 2, p. 39. Concerning which there also exists a notable testimony of St. Ignatius, contemporary with the Evangelists, Epistol. ad Trallian. καὶ τρεῖς δεκάδας ἐτῶν πολιτευσάμενος ἐβαπτίσθη ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου, and when he had spent thirty years on earth, he was baptized by John.

4. Fourthly, the month of the baptism of Christ being doubtful does not immediately render the concatenation of the years of Tiberius and the principate of Christ doubtful: if there is a discrepancy in the months, must a discrepancy therefore be established in the years themselves? And could not the truth about the month be gathered from other documents, even if it is not had from the present relation of Luke? But he will not concede

Wilhelmus Langius or Walæus, who repeated the Langian view on Luc. 3, 21, that the month of the baptism of Christ is doubtful, concerning which see our Anti-Grotiana on Luc. 3.

Fifthly, it is by no means to be admitted that the baptism of Christ, or his age when baptized, is mentioned there only incidentally and ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ; since the subject is not John for the sake of Christ, but Christ for the sake of John; and the Holy Scriptures could have taught us here about Christ, or the genealogy recited so at length, from the design of the matter. Wherefore it is altogether better to adhere to this designation of the Holy Scriptures than, with Spanheim, to expose everything to Pyrrhonic and Sceptical doubt.

Whom Baillie here deservedly chastises, because, neglecting the consensus of the learned, he follows the Jesuit Petavius, Part II of his Historical Works, p. 38. Certainly, he says, before Petavius, as far as I understand, no one among the ancients or moderns, whether Protestant or Papist, called into doubt whether the first verse of the third chapter of Luke cohered with the 23rd, whether the 15th year of Tiberius corresponded with the thirtieth of Christ, or whether the preaching of John was joined with the baptism of Christ in at least the same year; for the primary purpose of Luke in that place is to arrange the times of Christ alone; chapter 2, verse 42, notes the twelfth year of Christ, chapter 3, verse 23, marks his thirtieth; to illustrate which, verse 1 notes very significant characters of many times, namely the year of the Roman Emperor, likewise his contemporaries, not only the Governor of Judea, but also the three Tetrarchs of the neighboring regions, and finally the two High Priests. The Evangelist joins these chronological characters with the Baptism of John, by no means for the sake of John, but of Christ, as not only the connection of those chapters demonstrates, but Luke himself also explains himself, Acts 1:20, where the time of the baptism and preaching of Christ, and his appearance in public office, is manifestly joined with the time of the baptism of John: so that to separate these, especially by a whole year's interval, seems to be a too manifest contradiction of Luke.

QUESTION VI. Can a certain method for the epoch of the 62 weeks that follow, just as for the 7 preceding ones, be initiated from a comparison of sacred and exotic history?

We have said that the beginning of the epoch established by the Angel is the going forth of the word concerning the restoration of Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus. Cyrus certainly did not order Jerusalem to be restored; but only the temple, and even if he had ordered it, the work did not succeed, as sacred history testifies. Darius Hystaspis, however, did not issue a new decree, but only confirmed the previous decree issued by Cyrus concerning the restoration of the temple. But Artaxerxes Longimanus issued a decree concerning the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem, the streets, and the entire Jewish polity to be reintegrated, from whom Ezra obtained all his petition according to the hand of the Lord upon him, Ezra 7:6, from whom also a diploma was given, that whoever wished in the Persian empire to return to their fatherland of Judea, might return freely, v. 13. Moreover, a huge quantity of gold and silver was donated by the King and the seven principal satraps of the kingdom for the use of the temple, the city, and the entire polity, v. 15, ch. 8:26, 27, and the prefects of the Royal treasuries were ordered to grant to Ezra whatever he requested; and immunity was granted to the Priests and all sacred ministers from every tribute and burden, as well as the power of appointing Judges and Magistrates, who would govern the people according to the divine law. Whence also immediately on the first day of the first month of the seventh year of this king Ezra strove to set out for Jerusalem, and came there on the first day of the fifth month with all his company, Ezra 7, 9. having brought 1728 men above the leaders designated in chapter 8, so that there can be no doubt that this was truly the word concerning returning to restore Jerusalem: since no King of Persia decreed more amply and liberally concerning the affairs of the Jews, and the dismissal of Ezra was further followed by the indulgence of the same King in the sending of Nehemiah to promote the repair of the walls and streets, Nehem. 1, 1. 2. by whom, with the same Monarch conceding, in the 32nd year of his reign the Jewish Polity and Republic was again reduced to order until the empire of Darius Nothus, Nehem. 12, 22. chap. 13, 6. Whence if from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus seven weeks, or 49 years of the repair of the city, are counted, because 34 years of his rule still remained, (for he presided for 41 years) the end of the seven weeks falls in the 15th year of Darius Nothus, his son. Xerxes indeed succeeded him, who alone was born to him from a legitimate bed, but he was killed by Sogdianus on the 45th day after the death of his parent, and Sogdianus was removed by Ochus in the seventh month of his reign; and thus Ochus obtained the Monarchy, who called himself Darius, and presided over it for 19 years.

From the 15th year of Darius Nothus, therefore, the beginning must be taken of another Epoch of 62 weeks until Christ the Leader; from whom to the death of Alexander the Great after Codomannus was defeated, 86 years are counted from Diodorus Siculus, Xenophon and others, namely 5 remaining years of Darius Nothus, 43 of Artaxerxes Memnon, 23 of Artaxerxes Ochus, 3 of Arses, 6 of Darius Codomannus, 6 of Alexander the Great. By which method of calculation, by which it differs in special years, the Canon of Ptolemy indeed differs in a few things: but the sum in the computation of years comes out the same, namely 86 years. Now from the death of Alexander the Great, the era of the Seleucids began in the 12th year, as is gathered from Eusebius, book VIII, Demonstratio Evangelica, whence according to Josephus, book XII, Antiquities, chapters VII and XIV, the years in the books of the Maccabees are to be computed. And when in the 150th year of the Seleucids Antiochus Eupator granted the principate to Judas Maccabeus, 1. Macc. 6, 20. 60. from which 126 flowed to the first year of Herod, when Jerusalem having been stormed, and Antigonus killed, he entered upon full government, as witnessed by Josephus, book XIV, last chapter, who reigned for 34 years after Antigonus was killed, if Christ is said to be born under the latest times of the same, and the 30 years of the age of Christ, when he was inaugurated in baptism, are added, 434 years will easily result, which make 62 weeks; namely 86 to the death of Alexander the Great, 11 completed to the beginning of the Seleucids, 149 whole to the Maccabees, 125 whole to Herod, about 33 of Herod to the birth of Christ, and 30 of the age of Christ. In which way the number of weeks can be confirmed from the years of the Persian kings and the addition of the era of the Seleucids.

Furthermore, if the years of the Kings of Egypt with the years of Augustus to the birth of Christ, and the age of Christ to his baptism, are added to the years of the Persian Kings, the same sum will emerge. For according to Clement of Alexandria, book I, Stromata, from Alexander the Great until the Actian victory of Augustus, when Antony and Cleopatra committed suicide, the years of the reign of the Greeks in Egypt are collected as 284, namely Ptolemy Lagus 40, Ptolemy Philadelphus 27, Ptolemy Euergetes 25, Ptolemy Philopator 17, Ptolemy Epiphanes 24, Ptolemy Philometor 35, Ptolemy Physcon 29, Ptolemy Lathyrus 36, Ptolemy Dionysius 29, Cleopatra 22. Which with the 86 years to the death of Alexander the Great make 370. Let the 28 years of Augustus Caesar after Antony was defeated be added (because Clement of Alexandria testifies that Christ was born in the 28th year of Augustus), 398 years result: and when the 30 years of the age of Christ baptized are added, 428. A six-year period is still missing, which intervenes between the death of Alexander and the years of the Ptolemies, under the principate of Alexander's brother Arrhidaeus: which being added, the sum of 434 years results until Christ the Leader. The years of the Greek Kings, which Clement constitutes as 302 with the years of Alexander the Great (brother Arrhidaeus included), Jerome in chapter 9 of Daniel and Hippolytus in the same place likewise assigned as 302, and the same number are collected from the Canon of Ptolemy. Julius Africanus, however, makes the kingdom of the Macedonians 300 years, which is a small difference, and can be easily resolved by the customary distinction of inclusive and exclusive numbering.

Johannes Cluverus, in his Chronological computation from the Olympiads, began his calculation in this way: that Darius Nothus died in the last year of the 93rd Olympiad according to Diodorus Siculus, book XIII, and therefore his fifteenth year was the fourth of the 92nd Olympiad. Moreover, he gathers from Josephus, book XIV, ch. 26, that Herod the Great obtained the kingdom of Judea from the Senate in the 2nd year of the 184th Olympiad, so that 367 years intervened; and since Herod, from the time he was designated King by the Roman Senate, reigned for 37 years, according to the same Josephus, book I of the War, ch. 21, because when added to the 367 years they make 404, and with the 30 years of Christ's age added, 434 years result: if he is posited to have been born in Herod's last year: so that in this way, from Diodorus Siculus and Josephus, most eminent historians, the same sum of 62 weeks is gathered which Daniel defined for this epoch.

Phil. Lansbergius, according to the Nabonassarean years, proceeds thus in Chron. S. book I, ch. X. The edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus was issued in the seventh year of his reign, around the vernal equinox, that is, in the 291st Julian year from Nabonassar (which he shows in ch. 9) with three months. But Christ was baptized in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and indeed one month after the winter solstice, that is, around January 25th, by his opinion: but the fifteenth year of Tiberius is the 775th Julian year from Nabonassar, which he concludes from an eclipse noted by Tacitus: whence an interval of 483 years and ten months remains. But we acquiesce in the former demonstrations.

To which is added that Julius Africanus, in Jerome on ch. 9 of Daniel, begins the 70 weeks from the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and ends them at the passion of Christ, but in such a way that he invents lunar years, entirely unused in Scripture, which calculation again favors our opinion: for the total sum of 490 lunar years exceeds the usual solar years by more or less 15, which are gathered thus, because we begin in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, whence a difference of 13 years arises at the beginning, and we end two and a half years after the passion of Christ, whence 16 years emerge, so that a very small difference intervenes, and with a reduction made, the computation of Julius is easily reconciled with our calculation.

QUESTION VII.

How do the characters of the Christian era indicated in the New Testament harmonize with the computation of Daniel?

IN the computation of Daniel we assumed that the Savior was 30 years of age when He was proclaimed CHRIST from heaven at His baptism, and that the 28th year of Augustus after the defeat of Antony was the year of the birth of our Savior. Now, in order that the characters of the birth year may be gathered from the Evangelical History and compared with one another, for the confirmation of the angelic computation, we observe that four characters occur in the Evangelical History contributing to this: The first is that Christ was born while Augustus was Emperor: the second, that he was born when the census of the whole world was taking place under Augustus, while Cyrenius was governor of Syria, Luke II, 1, 2. The third, that Christ was born while Herod the Great was still living, Matthew 2. The fourth, finally, that the fifteenth year of Tiberius is commemorated when Christ, being about 30 years of age, received baptism, Luke 3. Furthermore, if the fifteenth of Tiberius was the thirtieth of Christ, the first of Tiberius and the last of Augustus must have been the sixteenth of Christ, and thus Christ was born about 16 years before the death of Augustus; so that in the current 15th year of his successor Tiberius, he was 30, which St. Luke affirms of him. Now since 43 years are assigned to the reign of Augustus in the Canon of Ptolemy after the death of Cleopatra, it is gathered from that, that Christ was born in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus. Philo, in his book On the Embassy to Gaius, easily agrees with the Ptolemaic canon that he held Egypt for 43 years: because he finally attained full monarchy after the conquest of Alexandria and the death of Antony and Cleopatra, the last Queen of the blood of the Ptolemies: as does the observation of Dio, who (book 56) attributes 44 years to the reign of Augustus, minus 13 days, which are those that begin between the 19th of August, the day on which he died, and the 2nd of September, when the war was finished at Actium, Caesar and Messala Corvinus being consuls. (See Dio, book 51.) In which manner also Suetonius in Octavius, Aurelius Victor, as well as Eutropius, say that Augustus held the empire for 44 years. Those who count more years of his reign do not count from the victory at Actium or from the death of Cleopatra which followed a year later, but either from the slaughter of C. Julius Caesar on the 15th of March, when he was stabbed by Brutus and Cassius in the Senate in the second Julian year, they deduce the years of his reign: or they compute the years of his reign from his first consulship, from which, namely, after the consuls Hirtius and Pansa were killed in the 3rd Julian year, he was made consul on the 19th of August, and they say he reigned for precisely 56 years, or finally they begin his principate from the victory at Mutina itself, or rather three days after the same, in which battle Hirtius fell and Pansa received a lethal wound, from which he died after a few days: who therefore attribute to him 56 years, 4 months, and one day, as is evident from Theophilus of Antioch, Book 3 to Autolycus, and Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata, if the error of the scribe in his text is corrected, who placed the number of years as 46 instead of 56 for him, as James Ussher observes in his Chronological Annotations on the sixth age of the world, page 386. But it is not for us to reconcile the varying designations of years, much less the diverse characters which are observed among authors, in which chronological minutiae discrepancies are found which cannot easily be resolved.

As it is certain from the Evangelical History that Christ was born while Augustus was reigning, and it is gathered quite clearly from Luke 3 that Christ was fifteen years old when Augustus expired, or that Augustus died in the sixteenth year of Christ: if indeed in the 15th year of his successor Tiberius he was 30 years old. Thus the observation of Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the Stromata will not differ much, who says: Our Lord was born in the 28th year, when they first ordered a census to be made in the time of Augustus, if indeed you count the years of Augustus from the capture of Alexandria and the death of Cleopatra: and the account of Irenaeus in book 3 against heresies, ch. 25, will also easily agree. Our Lord was born ABOUT the forty-first year of the reign of Augustus, the calculation being begun, namely, from his first consulship: And also Tertullian in his book against the Jews: we see, since in the forty-first year of the reign of Augustus, who (this is how it must be read entirely with Rigaltius, and not 'Quo', as it is commonly read erroneously) reigned after the death of Cleopatra, Christ is born. Eusebius also agrees, who in book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6, has it thus: ἦν δὴ ἦν τῦτο δεύτερον καὶ τεσσαρακοστὸν ἔτος τῆς Αὐγύστυ βασιλείας. Αἰγύπτου δ' ὑποταγῆς καὶ τῆς τελευτῆς Ἀν- τονίου, καὶ Κλεοπάτρας ὄγδοον ἔτος καὶ εἰκοσὸν. It was the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus (namely from the slaughter of Julius Caesar), but from the subjugation of Egypt and the death of Antony and Cleopatra, the twenty-eighth year; (similar things are read in the Chronicle of Eusebius in the 13th year of Augustus) as also in Epiphanius, heresy LI. For the Savior is born in the fortieth year of Augustus, King of the Romans, which was the twenty-ninth year of the union of the Romans with the Jews. For Augustus reigns thirteen years before Judea was perfectly joined to the Romans. For the Savior is born in the forty-second year of Augustus, King of the Romans, which indeed was the twenty-ninth year of the union of the Romans with the Jews. For Augustus reigned thirteen years before the Jews were perfectly joined with the Romans. The most illustrious Langius, in book 2, chapter 3, page 369, on the years of Christ, seems to seek the beginning of Epiphanius from the death of Julius Augustus. He adds that Clement of Alexandria also designates the 28th year, namely the Actian or from the death of Antony, which began on the 29th day of August of the 43rd Julian year and ended in the 44th, so that Christ was born either at the end of the 43rd or the beginning of the 44th Julian year, just as his birthday is conjectured to be either on the 8th of the Kalends or the 8th of the Ides of February.

As regards the years of Herod (about which chronologists argue in various ways), since he was first declared King by the Senate in the fifth year of Augustus from the death of Julius, or the sixth of the Julian era, in the consulship of C. Domitius Calvinus II and Asinius Pollio, and from that time ruled for 37 years according to Josephus, with Christ born in the 42nd year of Augustus, he would have survived for almost an entire year after the birth of Christ, if Herod died around the 25th day of our November, namely in the seventh month of Cislev, which the Jews therefore celebrate solemnly because in it Herod, who hated the wise men, met his death, as Edward Lively noted from the volume of Fasting in his Chronology, and from him James Ussher. But Josephus teaches that he died a little before the Passover: in which way he would have lived a three-month space after the birth of Christ. Concerning the years of his reign, Josephus speaks thus in Antiquities, book 17, chapter 10. He dies having reigned 34 years after he killed Antigonus, but 37 years after he was declared King by the Romans, that is, he dies (Herod) having reigned 34 years after the removal of Antigonus, but 37 years after he was declared King by the Romans. And in the Jewish War, book 1, last chapter: he dies having reigned 34 years from the time he killed Antigonus and took control of affairs, but 37 years from the time he was declared King by the Romans, that is, he died having held the kingdom for 34 years after he killed Antigonus, but 37 after he was declared King by the Romans. Epiphanius, in heresy 51, joins the 42nd year of Augustus with the 33rd year of Herod, which connection is not inconvenient if the years of Herod's reign are understood and counted from the killing of Antigonus: and he refers the birth of Christ to the 13th consulship of Octavius Augustus and the consulship of Silvanus: and counts from there 30 years. of Christ, which he had when he was baptized, designating Silvanus and Nerva as consuls in the thirtieth year, to whom the two Gemini consuls succeeded.

If the calculation is established according to the Olympiads, it is evident from Josephus, book XIV, chapter 26, that in the 184th Olympiad, that is, in the 736th year of the Iphitean era (others make the first year of the 185th Olympiad the 737th year of the Iphitean era, thus correcting Josephus, which one may also observe in the Strasbourg edition), Herod was raised to the height of his kingdom: therefore, adding 37 years, the 773rd or 774th Olympiadic year, or the 1st or 2nd year of the 194th Olympiad, emerges as the year of Herod's death. Since, however, Christ suffered and died in the 808th year of the Iphitean era, it is manifest that 31 or 35 years thus intervened between the death of Herod and the passion of Christ: and since the year of Christ's passion was the fourth year of his public ministry, which he began at thirty years of age, it is gathered from this that between the death of Herod and the birth of Christ there intervened either a year and three months, or only three months.

The Scaligerians, lest they be forced to make Herod's death earlier than the birth of Christ according to their own opinion concerning the year of Christ's birth, argue that the testimonies of Josephus are not correctly handled, whether by the fault of the author or the scribes; whom Edward Simson also supports in part VII of his Catholic Chronicle, p. 2, contending that Herod truly reigned 37 years after he had driven Antigonus from the kingdom, and 39 years after he had been declared King of the Jews by the Romans. But since Josephus recounts the years of Herod's reign in the same way in different places, and there is no proof of any corruption of the numbers in them, such a suspicion is not to be rashly admitted, for once it prevails, almost nothing certain remains in historical matters. Therefore, Robert Baillie, in his Historical Works, book II, p. 40, rightly corrects Spanheim here for pretending the same corruption in Josephus. This correction of the text of Josephus by Spanheim is rash, against the faith of all manuscripts, not only those printed. Secondly, since Scaliger himself suspects this emendation of his, and does not assert it strongly, and Calvisius himself never embraced it (for he never extends Herod's reign here beyond 38 years), Spanheim ought not to have brought it forward. Thus Baillie.

Then, as for Quirinius and the census made by him, it is not the case that we should imagine, even with Beza, that Luke's text is corrupt and that the word Cyrenius was put in place of Quintilius, which seems to be gathered from Josephus, that Quintilius Varus was Governor of Syria (which suspicion, however, Beza himself corrected in the second edition of his notes); or that we should set Luke against Tertullian, who in book IV against Marcion, chapter XIX, reported the census taken in Judea under Augustus by Sentius Saturninus. For although Sentius Saturninus then still held the Proconsulship of Syria, to whom Quintilius Varus was later given as a successor; yet Cyrenius or P. Sulpitius Quirinius, either as a censor with extraordinary power in neighboring Syria, when he himself held the Proconsulship of Cilicia at that time, or certainly was waging war in Cilicia, which is adjacent to Syria, and had a clear understanding of Eastern affairs, could easily have been sent, or even as Caesar's Procurator with ordinary power; of whom St. Luke wished to make mention rather than of Saturninus, both because he was instituting the census in Judea himself, and because he judged that the present registration should be compared with the other one, made ten years later by the same Quirinius when Archelaus had been relegated into exile. For which reason he also called this the first: although this also deserved to be called the first: because, although the Jews had been paying some tribute to the Romans for many years, we do not read that anyone was sent by the Romans into Judea before this arrival of Quirinius who would describe the fortunes of the Jews and compile census records. Certainly, the word hegemoneuein, which St. Luke uses, teaches that it is used of any power, especially a greater one, as Casaubon teaches: just as the word epitropos, by which Justin in Apology II designates Quirinius, is more general, and can apply to any command, even one mandated extra-ordinarily, so that there was no need for him to have been the prefect for governing the province, but only to have had the power to make a description of goods. Moreover, that census was not made so that a poll tax might be indicated to the Jews, or a tribute imposed, as it seemed to Eusebius, Suidas, Bede, Baronius, Barradius, Piscator, and others, which the Romans do not seem to have done at all before the confiscation of Archelaus's property, provided that tributes were paid to King Herod, who was bound to give the prescribed taxes to the Roman empire: but so that Augustus might investigate the resources, forces, and strength of the empire throughout the whole world: whence Tertullian appeals to the census records in Book IV against Marcion, chapter VII. Concerning the census of Augustus, finally, which the Roman archives keep as the most faithful witness of the Lord's birth.

QUESTION VIII.

At what time of the year was CHRIST born?

Concerning the time of the year, month, and day in which Christ was born, diverse opinions occur. There are those who judge that the time of the year, let alone the month or day, can in no way be defined, not even probably, and they act with great care to add that the time of the birth is entirely doubtful; because they merely call the opinions of others, who define something certain, under censure, but they themselves determine nothing, nor do they think it can be determined. This effort was occupied primarily by Frideric Spanheim in Dubiis Evangel. part II. and Gisbertus Voetius Tom. II. disp. select. page 15. seqq. and also Robert Baillie in Oper. Histor. & Chronol. Tom. II. page 4.

Others, however, define the birthday with certainty, although not all from the same principles: some strive to elicit the same from the Holy Scriptures: most rely on the tradition of the ancient Doctors of the Church, or even on the definition of the Church. That was done by Scaliger, Philipp Lansbergen, and others, who attempted to collect the time from the priestly calendars and the hieratic cycle according to the designation of Luke 1:5.

This is done primarily by Roman Catholics. Finally, those who walk a middle path, even if they deny that the time of birth can be defined apodictically or indubitably, nevertheless maintain that the designation of the ancients is probable.

Most, however, refer the birthday of Christ to the winter season, and indeed either to the 25th day of the month of December or to the 6th day of January. The former opinion is more common, and not only received in the Western Church from antiquity, but also approved by the Greeks for many centuries: thus Chrysostom in fragments on Luke, sermon on the nativity of the Baptist: The Lord is born in the month of December, in the time of winter, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the ripe olives are pressed, so that the anointing, that is, the charisma, may be born. And in the sermon on the nativity of the Lord: Up to this day the darkness grows, from this day the darkness decreases: the light grows, the darkness decreases: the day grows, the night decreases: truth succeeds error, today the Sun of righteousness is born for us.

Where among other things he has it thus: The things which we speak are not our own, it is the opinion of our ancestors: And in another homily on the birthday of Christ: It is clear from the Evangelist Luke that Christ was born at the time of the first census: And to whomsoever it might please to read the ancient historical codices, which are publicly kept at Rome, one will be able to learn the time of this description quite easily and accurately. But what is this to us, someone might say, who are not there, nor ever were? Listen, do not distrust, if from those who have an EXACT knowledge of this matter, who inhabit that city, we have RECEIVED THIS DAY. For those very people who dwell there, celebrating the day itself BEFORE, and from ANCIENT tradition, have now transmitted the notice even to us. Although indeed Bailius objects that Tertullian, Justin Martyr, and others, who affirm that the year of the description of Cyrenius, and thus the birth year, was kept in the Roman archives, have said no word about the birthday, yet the credibility of Chrysostom is not to be called into doubt on that account. For one witness affirming is worth more than ten who are silent. To Chrysostom is added a witness approved in the Latin Church, St. Augustine, Enarrat. in Psal. CXXXII. The dispensation of man was becoming lesser, which was signified in John: the dispensation of GOD in our Lord JESUS CHRIST was increasing, which is also shown by their birthdays. For he was born, AS THE CHURCH TRADITIONS, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the days of the world are already beginning: but the Lord was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the days are already beginning to increase. Hear John himself confessing: he must increase, but I must decrease. Bailius is therefore mistaken when he says that Augustine does not base his opinion on the tradition of the Church, but bases the practice of the Church on that reasoning from John 3:31: For he expressly appeals to the tradition of the Church; and from the Johannine passage he does not prove the opinion or the practice of the Church, but what he had said about the dispensation of man and the dispensation of God: which he teaches had been shown also by the decrease and increase of the days around the birthday of John and of Christ, but he does not seek the argument for the birthday from those words of John; much less does he teach that the Church drew its opinion about the birthday of Christ from there, whatever may be the case with writers of later centuries, who perhaps even used those words of St. John to illustrate the opinion and practice of the Church. St. Augustine also appeals to the tradition and authority of the Church in Book IV de Trin. § 5. Which number of 276 days completes nine months and six days, which are imputed to women giving birth as ten months: not because all reach the sixth day after the ninth month, but because the very perfection of the Lord's body is found to have been brought to birth in so many days, just as the authority of the Church, receiving what HAS BEEN HANDED DOWN BY THE ANCESTORS, maintains. For He is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April: But He IS TRADITIONALLY SAID TO HAVE BEEN BORN on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Which Augustine likewise handed down in the book of 83 questions, quest. LVI. That nine months and six days are to be computed, as from the EIGHTH day before the Kalends of April, on which day the Lord IS BELIEVED to have been conceived, up to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on which day He was born.

Nor are those things to be accepted in any other way which are here compared from the said passage of John III by St. Ambrose, who is entirely of one mind with St. Augustine, Serm. XII de Natal. Domini, Tom. III. p. 290. It is true what St. John the Baptist says, speaking of the Lord Savior: he must increase, but I must decrease. Indeed, this is first approved by the times themselves. For behold, at the birth of Christ the day increases, and at the birth of John it decreases. With the former rising, the light progresses; with the latter being born, it diminishes. For the very times, in a way, serving their parts, when the servant is born, they suffer a loss, but when the Lord is born, they obtain an increase. The day clearly makes progress when the Savior of the world arises; it suffers a defect when the last Prophet is generated. For it is written, The Law and the Prophets were until John. Doubtless those things are to be understood, as I have said, homiletically, not to be examined acroamatically. They exhibit some allusion and convenience, not a demonstration or proof: yet they teach the opinion of St. Ambrose, which was common and accepted at the time. For he does not undertake to show first that Christ was born at that part of the time, but St. Ambrose assumes that as undoubted, and in it, according to his custom, seeks some mystery: Whence it is no wonder, he says later, if the day increases, which the most splendid light of truth illuminates. A similar allusion is in Peter Chrysologus, serm. CLIX. Before these days, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of this month, when the day began to increase, because the true day shone forth, Christ Jesus the Lord born in the flesh, etc. And he who was much older than him, Gregory of Nyssa, Orat. in diem Natal. Dom. col. m. 684. On this (day) the darkness begins to diminish, and with the increasing splendor, the boundaries of the night are contracted. For these things do not happen by chance or of their own accord, brothers, on this solemn day, on which the divine life shines upon human life: but through those things which are seen by those who strain the edge of their mind, nature shows a certain secret, and, as it were, uttering a voice, teaches those who can hear what it means that at the coming of the Lord the day is increased and the night is diminished. For I seem to hear it speaking thus: Consider, O man, who beholdest these things, that from those things which are seen, those things which were founded are opened to you. Do you see that the night has reached its maximum length, and when it can proceed no further, it stops and retreats? Think that the night of destructive sin, which had grown to the highest heap of malice by all evil arts, has been cut back today, lest it creep further, and is henceforth driven to such a point that it may clearly fail and be destroyed. Do you see the richer rays of light, and the sun higher than usual? Consider the presence of the true light illuminating the whole world with the rays of the Gospel.

There is, therefore, no reason for Voetius to attack the Fathers here, as if they used such inept arguments in establishing the birthday of the Lord, as those who rely not on reason, but on tradition: for the time of the birth cannot be concluded by arguments, which depended solely on the divine will. This is also clear from the author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament in the works of Augustine, vol. IV, page 736, question LIII; when he investigates the reason why the Savior was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January: Therefore Christ, descending from the sacred seats to grant salvation to the world, so that he might also teach the world itself and the times instituted by him, willed to be born as a man, to increase the diminution of the human race toward God, when from the great diminution the light, which is the day, begins to receive an increase: so that the time of his nativity might correspond in reason to the divine doctrine, which began to multiply men from the shadow of death unto life. In vain, therefore, does Voetius argue in his 2nd Select Disputation. 22. that the testimony itself worthy of faith is not [so] because of vain, uncertain, and fallacious arguments or conjectures of testimony. For the testimony is not supported by the Fathers with arguments, but the arguments with testimony: which, even if some are vain, uncertain, and fallacious, nevertheless detract nothing from the authority of the testimony and tradition. Rightly does Mr. Wichmann, Chronology, page 231, say: This opinion of the ancients relies not on uncertain arguments, as the others do, or on conjectures, but on the tradition of testimony.

To these authors many others can be added. Syflyga cites the Constitutions of Clement, the tradition of Evodius, and the Acts of the Martyrs. Petavius praises in support of that opinion Paulinus in S. Felic. and the ancient Martyrologies. Suarez [cites] Maximus the Monk, Bede, Theophylact; Azorius [cites] Anastasius of Nicaea in his book of questions, qu. XCII. and the Menologium of the Greeks: Voetius, l. c. p. 35, also brings forward Jerome, and also Prudentius, p. 37 and 40, with no mention of the place made.
