Likewise Paul the Silentiary in the Panegyric of St. Sophia, as also Orosius, Bernard, Nicephorus: and concerning Orosius he says that he followed the COMMON tradition in the Church. Spanheim says that Sulpitius Severus, Cassiodorus, and countless others are of the same mind as Augustine. Stephanus Gobarus in Photius in Myriobibl. 232. §. 3. p. 291. [says] Christ on the eighth of the Kalends of January was born, indicating that it rests on the testimonies of other Fathers, even if he does not approve of that opinion or consider it Ecclesiastical: which Voetius, l. c., falsely attributes to him: so that he may defame the common opinion by the name of the heretic Tritheitae: why he is so hostile to this, he does not conceal: because, namely, the Feasts of Christians please him less, and the remembrance of benefits to be celebrated annually on a certain day, as the work of the day is done on its day, seems to him mere Judaizing and will-worship, p. 48.

But it is a vain conjecture, to note this in passing, which he has from his Hospinian, that the ancients first instituted this feast to be celebrated in the month of December, not because they believed that the Lord was born then (which the testimonies brought forward showed was entirely believed by them) but so that they might change the solemnity of the Saturnalia, which was celebrated at Rome at this very time, into this feast. But for this cause neither Hospinian nor his follower Voetius brings forward any document from antiquity.

Meanwhile, the same Voetius acknowledges that that opinion about Christ being born on December 25th has been common and accepted for some centuries, which was defined Ecclesiastically in the Council of Basel, Sess. XXXVI, and consigned as if in eternal tablets in Calendars, Martyrologies, Breviaries, Diurnals, offices of Mary, Missals, the Rationale of Durandus, l. VI, and Bilethic. LXVIII. Finally, defended hitherto by common doctrine according to Thomas, p. III, q. 35, and observed by use or ecclesiastical practice in the celebration of feasts: For which there is no reason why he should call it common and accepted in the Papacy: since it was accepted and common before the Papacy, in the time of Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, and Chrysostom, and has nothing in common with the Papacy, and after the reformation of the Papacy it has been approved and defended no less by many Protestants than by Pontificians.

We do not deny, however, that another opinion, which refers the birth of the Lord to the 6th day of January, was also approved by many in the ancient Church. Scaliger in the Eusebian Canons, Isagog. l. III, says that the whole Church in the parts of the East, in the century of Eusebius, and the preceding and following, believed that Christ was born on the 8th of the Ides of January, in which, however, Voetius acknowledges that he said a little too much; indeed, he admits that in the Oriental Churches opinions were uncertain and varying. Clement of Alexandria certainly already in his time noted that some set the day of the birth on the 25th of Pachon, or May, but others on the 24th or 25th of Pharmuthi, or April. Therefore, however SOME in the age of Chrysostom may have thought that the Lord was born on the Epiphany, that is, the 6th of January: which he himself

Chrysostom noted in the loc. cit., in his homily on the birthday of the Lord in the Tome on diverse New Testament homilies, XXXI, edited by Fronton du Duc, and the feast of the nativity was not then observed at Constantinople on December 25th, but that knowledge came to them recently, whence some accused them, that that day is new and recently invented, which Chrysostom does not deny; it is not yet the tenth year, he says, since this very day became known to us, yet it was not unknown elsewhere, and it was transmitted and received by the Westerners, as Chrysostom observes, and thus the custom was corrected, which had crept in there, without doubt, from the confusion of the Epiphanies, the nativity, and the Baptism, because that name was attributed to both, and it was recalled to the norm of the Roman custom, which rested on the Census tablets of Quirinius. Thus within the region of Egypt in the fourth century, as Cassian testifies, collation X, cap. 2, because it was contemporary with Chrysostom, that custom was also observed, that the nativity of Christ was celebrated on the day of the Epiphany (January 6th): because, namely, the priests of that province defined the day to be EITHER of the Lord's Baptism, OR according to the canon of the nativity (they were therefore stuck, whether Christ was born on that day, or indeed only baptized) and therefore (because of that doubt) they celebrated the solemnity of BOTH sacraments, not in two ways, as in the western provinces, namely, but under one day the festival of this. Whence also Epiphanius, book II, Tom. I, haeres. LI, says that Christ was born around the month of January, that is, before the eighth of the Ides of January, which is the fifth of the month of January according to the Romans, according to the Egyptians the eleventh of Tybi. From which it appears: that the Tradition which was kept in the Churches of the West, and among the Romans, to whom the census tablets of Quirinius were open, concerning the day of December 25th, was older and more certain, since the Constantinopolitan Church itself amended its custom for its sake: and Chrysostom, or whoever is the ancient author under his name in the homily on the birthday of the Lord, derived it from the Apostles themselves. These are not our own, he says, which we speak: it is the opinion of the elders. The WHOLE World speaks against the opinion of this province (concerning January 6th). He adds: That the Churches learned this from Peter and Paul and the other Apostles of Christ. So that the boasting of the Oriental Armenians is vain, who, until the year 1170, celebrating the feast of the nativity and Baptism of Christ together, boasted that all Churches had celebrated it thus ever since the Apostles, as the General, or Catholic, Epistle of the Armenians to the Emperor Manuel testifies. Comnenus in the Legation of the Emperor Manuel Comnenus or the disputation of Theosianus with the Catholic, page 131, Leunclavius edition, Basel, 1578. Therefore that opinion concerning the 6th of January today hardly has supporters, if you except Philipp Lansberg: who too confidently thinks he has demonstrated so clearly that Christ was born on the sixth day of January, that no one hereafter will have cause to doubt concerning the birthday of Christ: but the demonstration which he boasts of is very weak, nay, futile: derived from the Hieratic sphere and Ephemerides, and resting upon various precariously assumed, twisted, and fallacious hypotheses. Namely, because Zacharias the Priest is designated as having been of the course of Abia, Luke 1:5, he gathers, through various windings, that Elizabeth conceived on the 6th day of November, but that CHRIST was conceived about the sixth day of April, and born about the sixth day of January. But from the same Ephemerides Scaliger trusts that he has demonstrated that Christ was born not in the month of January, but at the end of September or the beginning of October, in the appendix to the book on the emendation of times, as also in the Isagogic Canons, book III.

Samuel Petit, in Book I of his Eclogae Chronologicae, ch. 13, likewise thinks he has demonstrated from the same sources that Christ was born around the 6th of the Ides of November. Thus boast most of those who depart from the common tradition, [offering] demonstrations from the Hieratic cycle, and yet they vary greatly in their opinions concerning the birthday: what certainty is there, then, in this? For as the hypotheses they assume are not the same, so there is no mathematical certainty; all are highly doubtful and uncertain. Lansbergius, in Book 3 of his Chronologia, ch. 4, assumes that the epoch of the Ephemerides, which he claims to have unearthed not without sweat and labor, began in the last or penultimate year of David, on the 22nd of Tishri or the 6th of October: he assumes that David died in the year 2925, but his calculation of this is faulty, as is clear from the above: he assumes in Book 3, ch. 17, that Christ was born in the year of the World 3960, in which hypothesis it is certain that he again deviates from the truth: whence the calculation of the Hieratic cycles, resting upon these precarious, nay, false hypotheses, falls to the ground: not to mention that he assumes without foundation that Elizabeth conceived when nine days had passed since Zechariah's departure from the temple; that John was carried in the womb for precisely 9 Julian months, as was Christ the Savior: therefore Voetius rightly acknowledges, in the work cited, p. 41, that there is no demonstration here, and he also rejects the hypotheses of the demonstration of Scaliger and Petit as uncertain, pp. 42, 43. Just as the Scaligerian ἀπόδειξις [demonstration] was likewise refuted by Fr. Spanheim, to which Bailius indeed attempted to respond, yet was forced to admit that Scaliger's subtle demonstration rests upon so many hypotheses that, if one should fail, the whole edifice would collapse, so that it seems quite doubtful even to him.

The authorities also which Lansbergius brings forward have little certainty. For Epiphanius designated the eleventh of the month Tybi: but the 6th day of January falls not on the eleventh, but on the 17th of Tybi according to Lansbergius. Therefore the passage from Epiphanius does not favor him, whence he suspects there is an error, but in vain, since Epiphanius repeatedly and frequently names the same 11th of Tybi. But as regards Paulus Orosius, although he writes in Book III, T. III, that Christ was born on the day of the Epiphany, he explains himself elsewhere, saying that Christ was born on the 8th of the Kalends of January, when all the increments of the turning year first begin, as Lansbergius himself observes; nor is there any doubt that he, as a disciple of Augustine and a Spanish presbyter, was with Augustine and others in the Western Church. Therefore, he spoke there of the Epiphany not of the Baptism, but of the birth of Christ. Stephanus Gobarus could have been added, who, according to Photius, makes this the opinion of the Church, that Christ was born at midnight on the fifth of January, which is the eighth of the Ides of January; but he was a Tritheite, and he understood his own church, not the catholic one: and he simultaneously brought forward the contrary opinion of other ancients (in the Catholic Church, namely) that the Savior was born not on the 5th of January, but on the 8th of the Kalends of January.

Finally, for reconciling or explaining the diverse opinions of the ancients, Montacutius observes that this variety arose partly from the confusion of two feasts, the Epiphany (which is so called today) and the Nativity, from the ambiguity of the word ἐπιφανίας [epiphany]: because that former feast falls on the 6th of January: and partly from the fact that all the ancients, at least from the times of Constantine, ascribed the winter solstice to the birth of Christ: but not all fixed that solstice on the same day, and thus, while they indeed celebrated the feast of the Nativity at the time of the winter solstice, they varied in assigning the days of the solstice. For the Jews (witness Scaliger, Book 1, de emendat., ch. 16) refer this solstice to the 6th or 7th of January. Although these observations are considered by Voetius—who reciprocates a long-winded saw of controversy with Montacutius—to be mere trifles, what we have said about these opinions will show that they are not devoid of their own probability. Johannes Kepler, the Imperial Mathematician, as noted and not disapproved by Spanheim, p. II, Dub. XII, page 210, thinks that the difference which arose among the ancients concerning the birthday was due to a slip of the scribes, who substituted the 8th of the Ides of January, i.e., Jan. 6, for the 8th of the Kalends of January, i.e., Dec. 25, or the Kalends for the Ides. Johannes Herwart, as the same Spanheim says in the work cited, also has here a conjecture sufficiently subtle and ingenious for reconciling the opinions about which Clement of Alexandria speaks, with the opinion and practice of the Western Church. The Egyptians therefore celebrated the τὰ ἐπιφάνια [epiphany] in the months of Paschon and Payni, because those were the ninth and tenth from the beginning of their year, namely the month of Thoth, which corresponds to our September, because they had heard that Christ was manifested in the ninth and tenth month of the year, which is December, by a calculation made from the beginning of the Sacred year. Not attending to the beginning of the year, therefore, the Egyptians stuck to the number of the months, and thus departed from the common opinion. Hence it also happened that they fixed the ἐπιφάνια [epiphany] on the 25th day, with the change left only in the month because of the different beginning of their year. Jerome certainly refutes those who made the 5th of January the birthday, which was the day of the Epiphany, in Ezech. ch. 1. He adds the fifth day of the month, however, to signify the baptism, in which the heavens were opened to Christ; and the day of the Epiphany is HITHERTO venerable, not as SOME think, the birthday in the flesh, for then he was hidden and did not appear. He says that some had thought so, but he implies that this is alien to the common opinion of the Church, inasmuch as for it, the fifth day of January had been VENERABLE until then, not as the feast of the birthday, but of the Epiphany.

Besides these more celebrated and older opinions concerning the birthday of the Lord, others have still been newly devised: but to have recited them is to have refuted them. For they rely on no support, except either fictitious analogies or ephemerides arranged at will: Of the former class is the very recent discovery of Nisbet, who dreamed that Christ was born on the very day of the Passover, and at the very same hour in which the Passover was sacrificed; and thus he referred the birth of the Lord to the vernal season: which the same Reformed Church holds as a paradox, and Bailius refutes: who nevertheless does not seem to depart much from those whom Clement of Alexandria reviewed, lib. 1. Stromat., as having designated the birthday of Christ on the 24th or 25th of Pharmuthi: for this corresponds to the month of April: to whom has also been added Johannes Temporarius, defining the birthday as the 25th of Pharmuthi or the middle of April, page 166. To this pertains the opinion of Paul of Middelburg, Bishop of Fossombrone, who, in a special volume published concerning the birthday of Christ in the year 1523, attempted to demonstrate that Christ was born on the same vernal equinox on which the world was created, that is, March 26th. To these must finally be added Thomas Lydiat, likewise assigning the vernal season, but May 20th for the birthday.

Finally, Matthæus Beroaldus first began to cast the birth of Christ back into the autumn, whom Henricus Wolfius followed in his Chronicles, and Jos. Scaliger, lib. IV. de emendat. Tempor., as also lib. III. Canon. Isagog. annot. 102, defining from ephemerides that Christ was born at the end of September or the beginning of October: and he who for the most part adheres to him, Sextus Calvisius, as well as Constantinus L'Empereur in his Scholia to Jarchi on Daniel IX. He also referred

That the Alexandrian Church assigned the birth of Christ to October, but rather to the 23rd day than to the beginning of the month, is gathered from Cyril of Alexandria, homily on the birth of the Baptist, because it was accustomed to celebrate the birthday of John on the 28th day of Pharmuthi, that is, the 23rd of April: which opinion, however, little aids Scaliger's definition from the Hieratic orbs: otherwise than Casaubon thought in Exercit. ad Appar. Baron. Sect. XXV. Finally, Samuel Petitus also favors autumn from the same reasoning of the Hieratic orbs, but he does not relegate the birth of Christ to October, but rather to November: defining him as born about the 6th of the Ides of November. Spanheim notes that Epiphanius also mentions this opinion in the Panarion, which, however, I do not find in him. But Petitus's proof does not deserve any refutation, indeed not even a review.

Wherefore, all things having been weighed, the more accepted opinion concerning the 25th day of December, fortified by the authority of the ancients and the tradition of the Church, is altogether to be preferred, which our Bunting also acknowledged. The demonstration of Beroaldus, he says, does not satisfy us. For more weight must be given to the traditions of so many Holy Fathers, received and approved by the universal Church of GOD, than to the conjecture of Beroaldus alone, which cannot be sufficiently proven from the Holy Scriptures. Especially since the traditions of the Holy Fathers agree with the Holy Biblical and Mathematical observations, from which Beroaldus sometimes deviates sufficiently. Frederick Spanheim, l. c., acknowledges that the opinion of Beroaldus, Scaliger, Calvisius, and those of the same mind is not only new, but supported by no solid foundation, while ours is ancient, resting on the foundation of practice and ancient custom. This, therefore, without a doubt, is deservedly to be preferred. To say nothing of the fact that Kepler and Petavius observe that, even with the calculation standing by the Hieratic orbs, the ministry of Zechariah fell on the nineteenth of September, and thus the birth of Christ on the twenty-fifth of December. Let there now also be compared William Langius on the years of Christ, and those who from him transferred to their commentary those things which pertain to this matter, Bald. Walaeus on Luke II, 7.

QUESTION IX.

How may the former half of the seventieth week of Daniel be gathered from the Evangelical history?

Half a week makes three years and a half. But that former half, because it begins from the Baptism of Christ up to the death of Christ, comprises the years of Christ's ministry, which are gathered from the observation of the Passovers in the Evangelical history, or from the description of the ministry of Christ designated therein. As therefore in Daniel three years and a half are defined up to the death of Christ, so it is necessary that Christ spent four, no more, nor fewer Passovers in his public ministry, which if they are gathered from the Evangelical history in that place, it will be the more certainly established that the event corresponds to the angelic prediction.

However, there are found diverse opinions concerning the number of Passovers and the years of Christ. Some have sinned in excess, primarily Irenaeus, who in book 2, ch. XXXIX and XL, asserted that Christ was indeed baptized in his 30th year, but only began to teach in his fortieth year, and, when he had taught for some years, had reached an older age, which was not far from fifty: as also those whom Augustine mentioned in book 2 of De doctrina Christiana, ch. 28, who determined that Christ suffered in the 46th year of his age, as well as Paul, Bishop of Sempronium, who reported that he was taught in a dream by the Apostle Paul that Christ was 36 years old, and that all chronologists err by three years: then also Jacob Hainlin, who attributes to Christ's ministry five full years and about a half after his baptism: Finally, Temporarius and Scaliger with their followers, who wish that Christ celebrated five Passovers in the days of his ministry, such as Calvisius, Helvicus, Casaubon, Moulin, Calixtus, Wilhelmus Langius, and others; who therefore judge that Christ administered his ministry for four years and some months. But the oracle of Daniel as well as the Evangelical History convinces that they err entirely in excess, since by the power of Gabriel's oracle he ought to have preached, and, as the Evangelical History testifies, he did preach, for only half a week.

Whence furthermore not a few others have erred in deficiency: such as those who first established that Christ spent only one single year in public ministry, along with Tatian; who in his Evangelical Harmony included everything done from the Baptism of Christ to his passion in a period of one year: Thus Tertullian, book against the Jews, ch. VIII, though differing from himself in book 1 against Marcion, ch. XV, and Julius Africanus in Jerome on ch. IX of Daniel, who said that Christ suffered in the 15th year of Tiberius, and also Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata, who confirmed that Christ preached for only one year from Isa. 61:2, Luke 4:9, 'The Lord sent me to preach the acceptable year': furthermore Lactantius, book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 10, as also Augustine himself, Epistle LXXX, defining only thirty years from the birth of Christ until his resurrection. But it is again manifest that this opinion agrees neither with the oracle of Daniel nor with the Evangelical History: therefore it is refuted by Irenaeus, book 2 against heresies, ch. 39, from St. John, who commemorates more Passovers of Christ: for which reason the Alogi, as Epiphanius testifies, heresy LI, defending the opinion of a single year of Christ's ministry, did not fear to reject the Gospel of St. John. So that you might wonder entirely that Gerhard Johann Vossius, a most learned man and most versed in antiquity, still patronizes the same, and thus maintains that Christ suffered under the Emperor Tiberius, with two Passovers having been completed since his Baptism. Let us hear Irenaeus refuting the ancient Gnostic heretics, from whom that opinion took its origin: 'But it is greatly to be wondered at how they, saying that they have discovered the deep things of God, have not searched in the Gospels how many times the Lord, according to the time of the Passover, went up to Jerusalem after his baptism, according to what was the custom for the Jews to assemble in Jerusalem from every region every year and celebrate the feast day of the Passover there. And first indeed, as he made wine from water in Cana of Galilee, he went up to the feast day of the Passover. Since it is also written that many believed in him, seeing the signs which he was doing, as John the disciple of the Lord mentions. Then again, withdrawing himself, he is found in Samaria, when he also disputes with the Samaritan woman; and he cured the son of the Centurion while absent by a word, saying: Go, your son lives.' And after this he went up a second time to the feast day of the Passover in Jerusalem, when he cured the paralytic who was lying by the pool for 38 years, ordering him to rise and take up his bed and go, and departing from there across the sea of Tiberias: where, when a great crowd had followed him, he satisfied all that multitude with five loaves, and twelve baskets of fragments remained over. Then when he had raised Lazarus from the dead, and plots were being made by the Pharisees, he withdrew to the city of Ephraim, and from there six days before the Passover he is written coming into Bethany, and ascending from Bethany into Jerusalem and eating the Passover, and on the following day he suffered. But that these three times of the Passover are not one year, everyone will confess. These are the words of St. Irenaeus. By this argument Epiphanius also refutes the heretical Alogi: The error of all these is refuted, while the doctrine according to the truth is clearly found. Wherefore not only the circuit of two Passovers is found in the Gospel, but also of three. And afterwards p. m. 202. For also from the consulships, and from the years, and from the confirmation of the Prophet Isaiah, and from the Gospel of Luke and John and Matthew, Mark, and simply from everywhere those erroneous ones are refuted. Since he did not only complete one Passover after the beginning of his preaching according to the circuit of the year of time, but fulfilled the Passover according to the circuits of three consulships, after the baptism of John. And their entire understanding of the aforementioned reasoning collapses, utterly erroneous, delirious, and filled with madness and ignorance, which not only does not know its own life, but also falsely and in vain fights against the truth.

Wherefore others assigned a biennium to the ministry of Christ; such as Apollinaris of Laodicea: In the thirtieth year of his age, he says, the Lord began to preach the Gospel in the flesh, and according to the Evangelist John, through three Passovers he completed two years afterwards: Which words of his Jerome reports in ch. 9 of Daniel. Cyril of Alexandria in ch. 29 of Isaiah. Through a biennium only, he says, Christ, traversing all of Judea, delivered the Evangelical preaching to the Jews. Jerome agrees in the loc. cit. Cassiodorus in the Chronicles. Orosius b. VII. ch. 4. and Epiphanius is not much different in b. 1. Panar. Vol. II. near the end: as also in the Anacephalaeosis of heresies: who explains his own opinion in heresy 51, refuting Valentinus, who [stated] that 30 years Christ lived only, and from there he fabricated his 30 aeons: Ignorant, he says, that he not only completed thirty years, but was baptized in his thirtieth, when he had completed twenty-nine years and ten months, as I have said, on the twelfth of the month of Athyr, before the sixth of the Ides of November, and afterwards he preached the acceptable year of the Lord, and afterwards another year, during which he was contradicted, and seventy-four days, during which he was contradicted, from the day on which he was baptized, so that all the years of his presence in the flesh, from his birth until his passion, are thirty-two years and one hundred and thirty-four days.

Although indeed, as the blessed Chemnitius notes, there are some who have gathered a triennium from the calculation of three Passovers, yet the praised Theologian observed that they are mistaken: Epiphanius rightly gathers from that only two years and some days, which are those that remain from the Baptism until the first Passover: for Christ began his ministry not long before the Passover and was crucified at the third feast of the Passover, according to Epiphanius. And this calculation does not make a triennium, but a biennium. Among the more recent, Tostatus, Pererius b. 11 on Daniel, Melchior Canus, Maldonatus, Petavius, Lansbergius, Helwigius, and others assign a biennium to the ministry of Christ. But just as this opinion likewise disagrees with the prediction of Gabriel, since a biennium cannot constitute half an angelic week: so the Evangelical History also does not at all agree, which testifies that not only three, but four Passovers were completed by Christ in the days of his ministry; whence, as our blessed Gerhard notes in Harm. Evangel. Chap. CLXVI, the common opinion of the Church is that Christ suffered in the 34th year of his age, current, at the fourth Passover after his Baptism: which Cornelius à Lapide also says is the common opinion of the Doctors in his notes to ch. V of John v. 1. which not only the Pontificals, Cardinals Fr. Toletus and Baronius, Jansenius, Eman. Saa, Joh. Ferus, Torniellus, Henricus Philippi, and others; among the Reformed, Beza, Junius, Rollocus, the Batavian Annotators on John 6, 4, as also Hugo Grotius, but also among our own, after the blessed Luther and Chemnitius, most maintain, both chronologists and interpreters of the Holy Scriptures, if you except the followers of Scaliger. However, no solid reason is brought forward why one should adhere to the innovator Scaliger rather than to the ancient Doctors and the common opinion of the Church, nor does that 'he himself said it' suffice for us in such matters. Although the invention of a fifth Passover is to be attributed not to Scaliger, but rather to Gerhard Mercator, [a Passover] entirely unknown to the ancients.

Then we have an infallible celestial Chronologist, St. Gabriel, who by divine decree defined the years of the ministry of Christ by the space of half a week, which was determined from the time Christ openly declared [it] until his passion, which ought to have brought completion and an end to the sacrifices of the Old Testament. Concerning which the blessed Chemnitius in the prolegomena of the Harmony, ch. 3, p. 9. The thoughts of Luther and others are learned, who gather such a calculation from Daniel. For the Prophet says: (he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease) namely, by the offered victim of his own body. But half a week makes three years and a half. Hence the common and received opinion has been taken, which also exists in the fragments of Theophilus, that Christ in his ministry was occupied in saying and doing for three years, and as many months, or days, as intervened from his Baptism to the first Passover.

Thirdly, one must insist entirely upon the Evangelical History in such a way that neither more nor fewer Passovers are assigned to the Ministry of Christ than have been commemorated by the Evangelists. For if anyone says with the author of the Scholastic history that the Evangelists could have passed over some Passover, he will call into question the accurate diligence of the Evangelists in a matter so arduous and necessary, and with the same ease he will be able to add not only a fifth Passover, but even a sixth, and more, if it is free for anyone to indulge in their own speculations. Nor does our blessed Chemnitius rashly appeal to the design of St. John, as St. Irenaeus designated it: First, he says, Irenaeus observed this, that John therefore, after the narratives of the others, noted down some feasts of the Passover, to which Christ ascended during the time of his ministry, so that the calculation and distribution of the years, which he saw neglected by the others, could be gathered from certain foundations. Moreover, four Passovers are gathered from St. John. The first is named most openly in John 2:13, nor can any earlier one be imagined: since St. John would not have passed it over, and it was fitting that the reformation of the temple should be undertaken by Christ immediately in the first year; nor does the Evangelical and historical harmony, which St. John wove, permit another. Furthermore, in John 5:1, a feast of the Jews is mentioned again, which Christ attended, by which name the Passover is understood, not only as the absolute mention of τῆς ἑορτῆς implies, since by the name of the feast κατʼ ἐξοχὴν the primary festival of the Jews, and the beginning of the other feasts, namely the Passover, is accustomed to be designated. See Matt. 26:17, 27:15, Luke 2:42, John 4:45, 12:12, 13:29. But the circumstances also clearly convince one of this. For after the first Passover, when Christ had returned into Galilee, John 4:3, before he set out for Jerusalem for that feast designated in John 5:1, there were still four months until the harvest, John 4:35, which immediately after the Passover was begun, Exod. 13, 4. chap. 34, 12. Levit. 23, 10. Numb. 28, 26. Deut. 16, 9. whence it is manifest that the time of this discourse of Christ fell in December: from which it further follows that by τὴν ἑορτὴν [the feast] cannot be understood either the feast of tabernacles or the feast of dedication of the first year of the ministry; for the former had already been celebrated in September, the latter in November, and the former was seven months distant from the harvest, the latter five, not four: nor can the feast of Pentecost be understood, which followed immediately after the Passover described in John 2, 13, in the first year of Christ's ministry. For how could the four months remaining until the harvest be said to have intervened between those feasts, which were only 50 days apart? Add that the barley harvest was begun immediately after the feast of the Passover, but the wheat harvest began in Judea before the feast of Pentecost Exod. 34, 22. chap. 23, 16. 20. Numb. 28, 26. Furthermore, since between the month of December and the following Passover no legal feast intervened for the celebration of which one had to go up to Jerusalem, and no other occurred before the Passover, it is certainly manifest that the feast in John 5 is the feast of the Passover. Finally, whatever feast it is posited to be in John 5, as the blessed Chemnitius rightly and accurately [states], it is certain that it is not of that year whose beginning is the Passover in John 2, v. 13. Nor can it be referred to that year whose beginning the Passover in John 6, 4 makes. For the order of the text manifestly refutes that. Whatever feast of the second year, therefore, you may have posited it to have been, you cannot escape that in John 5 without being forced to concede that there was another intermediate Passover between that which is described in John 2, v. 13 and that which follows in John 6, 4. For the Passover is the beginning of the remaining feasts of each year.

The third Passover, therefore, is that which is expressly referred to in John 6, 4. 'And the Passover, a feast of the Jews, was nigh.' The fourth is that which is commemorated in John 11, 55. 'And the Jews' Passover was nigh at hand': which was the σταυρώσιμον [crucifixion-time] John 12, v. 1. chap. 13, 1. Irenaeus confuses these two later ones in book 4, chap. 39, and therefore lists only three Passovers; but when they are distinguished, as they are entirely distinct and are acknowledged as such by all, four emerge. The fifth, however, nowhere appears in the Evangelical History.

For the traces of the same which Scaliger and his followers seek are too meager and obscure. We grant that that second-first Sabbath, on which the disciples plucked the ears of corn, Matt. 12, 1. Mark 2, 23. Luke 6, 1, can indeed be referred to the Passover, provided that the time agrees with the ripe crops, and Epiphanius perhaps not inappropriately explains the second-first Sabbath as that which followed immediately after the solemnity of the Passover ἀπὸ δευτέρας τοῦ πάσχατος [from the second day of the Passover], or from the 26th day of the month Nisan, from which the seven following weeks were to be counted, Levit. 23, 15. Deut. 16, 9, and they obtained their name, so that the first was called second-first, the second second-second, and so on. But that had to be proven, that it is a different Passover from that which is indicated by the general name of ἑορτῆς [a feast] in John 5, 1, and that it was omitted by John; for the proof of which they indeed bring this forward, which Bailius deems entirely firm, that Christ could not have left the city before the seventh day of unleavened bread at the Passover, the feast not yet being finished, and therefore it is likely that that Sabbath, when he walked through the cornfields, was spent in Galilee, since he did not go up to Jerusalem for fear of the Jews: But that proof is devoid of strength: because the days of unleavened bread began from the evening of the 14th day of the month Nisan: Therefore, on the second-first Sabbath the seven days of unleavened bread had already finished: And it is ambiguous to Bailius himself whether the second-first Sabbath to Epiphanius, whom he follows, is the natural Sabbath after the first day of the Passover, or the seventh from the first day of the Passover, p. 77. Add that the learned differ greatly concerning the second-first Sabbath, and that it is no more inconvenient for Christ to have walked with his disciples through the cornfields before the seventh day of unleavened bread than to have plucked ears of corn on the Sabbath. Finally, it must be carefully observed that the series of histories proves that that Passover is the same as the feast in John 5, 1, not different, which is gathered from the history of the feeding of the five thousand, which preceded the third Passover in John 6. Nor do those who otherwise adhere more closely to Scaliger deny this, Calvisius and Helvicus, who betake themselves here indeed to Luke 9, 51, chap. 10, 2, but there not even a faint indication of the feast of the Passover appears; not to mention that it is evident from the very series of histories that that sending out of the disciples happened after the feast of Pentecost, and as it seems to some, around the feast of trumpets at the time of the second harvest, and before the fourth Passover of Christ's ministry, as was observed by our blessed Gerhard, in Harmon. chap. 166.

The fourth point favoring the opinion concerning the three years of Christ's Ministry is the parable in Luke 13:7. 'Behold, these three years I come, seeking fruit on this fig tree.' For that three-year period which Christ had spent almost entirely in his Ministry is indicated. Nor is it an objection that he asks for a fourth year to be granted still, because it is not unusual in Scripture for parts of years to be called years, and the third year was then still being spent, it had not yet been completed. Therefore, four years with some months of Christ's Ministry cannot be concluded from that.

Finally, the authorities of the Ancients are added; since our opinion both enjoys the hoariness of antiquity and is commonly approved, whereas the Scaligerian view, first introduced by Gerhard Mercator, has no testimony from antiquity.

In the fragments of Theophilus these things are read which are entirely in agreement with our opinion: that Christ was occupied in his ministry by teaching and doing for three years, and as many months as intervened from his Baptism to the first Passover.

St. Ignatius in his Epistle to the Trallians testifies that Christ, when he had completed three decades of years and preached the Gospel for three years, and performed signs and wonders, was judged by the Jews and Pilate.

Irenaeus, in book 2, chapter 39, indeed gathers three Passovers from John, and he most correctly advised that they should be gathered; but since a fourth, the τὸ ἅπαξιδάϊμον, must be distinguished from those three, with him leading the way, four Passovers are easily concluded.

And thus also from Epiphanius, although he assigns only three, the blessed Chemnitz concluded four: 'It is pleasant to consider by what reasoning that fourth Passover has been investigated in the Evangelical History. For Irenaeus and Epiphanius showed certain traces of it, for although both count only three Passovers: the former by taking the feast in John 5:1 as a Passover feast, and the latter by explaining the "second-first Sabbath" in Luke 6:1 as a Passover, they pointed out certain traces of a fourth Passover. Rupert, however, from the words of Christ in John 4:35 concerning the four months before the harvest, began to gather what kind of feast is to be understood in John 5:1. The Historia Scholastica, because it posits that Christ was baptized on the sixth of January, and on the same day after a year had revolved performed his first sign: since therefore it will be necessary that a Passover intervened in that year, it says that one Passover not expressed in the Gospel is to be understood in this way.' But Andreas Osiander was the first, so far as I know, who learnedly, certainly, and clearly demonstrated that fourth Passover in the narrative of John. These are the words of Chemnitz.

Sect. VIII.

Venerable Bede and Marianus Scotus also agree with us, the latter of whom teaches in his Chronicle that Christ suffered while in the thirty-fourth year of his age, having begun it by three months: the former, indeed, not only fosters the same opinion, but also testifies that this is the faith of the Church, in de ration. tempor. cap. XLV. He holds, if I am not mistaken, that the faith of the Church is that the Lord lived in the flesh a little more than thirty-three years up to the time of his passion. Which opinion has therefore commonly prevailed in the Church, the traces of which some also seek in the Midras Tehillim in the words of R. Jonathan: For three years and a half the presence stood on the Mount of Olives, giving voice and saying: seek the Lord while he can be found.

Whence the blessed Chemnitz in his Harmony, which can never be praised enough, arranges the years of Christ's ministry thus: From the first Passover, John 2:13, up to the feast in John 5:1, is the first year. From that feast up to the Passover, mention of which is made in John 6:4, is the second year. And further up to the Passover in John 13:1, in which Christ was crucified, the third year is reckoned. The account of the time, however, which intervened from the Baptism up to the first Passover, extends the calculation into a fourth year, which is not complete, as will be said later concerning that time. And Nicephorus says: He did not complete the whole four-year period. And in chapter 4, Prolegom. page 15, he arranges the Evangelical History both according to Passovers and according to years; We shall distribute the time of Christ's ministry, he says, in two ways. First, by that method which the fragments of Ammonius follow, so that, namely, the order of the histories is distributed according to the Passovers 1. from the Baptism of Christ up to the first Passover, which is described in John 2:13, 2. from that first Passover up to the second, the description of which exists in John 5 and Luke 6:1, 3. from that second Passover up to the third, of which mention is made in John 5:4. 4. from the third feast of the Passover up to the last, in which the Son of God was crucified. This will be one method of distribution. Then we shall also distribute that time into certain years at the same time, having shown the beginning and end of each year, so that it may be observed to which year individual histories belong. The beginning of the first year is, however, when Christ was baptized in the Jordan, anointed with the Holy Spirit, and sent to preach, and it includes the histories up to the imprisonment of the Baptist. The beginning of the second year is when, after John was handed over, Christ returns through Samaria into Galilee. And to that year belong the histories up until Christ contemplates the sending out of the Apostles. Those histories provide the beginning for the third year when, in Matthew 9:35 and Mark 6:34, Christ, as a visitor, travels through the cities and villages: and because he finds the sheep miserably scattered, without true pastoral care, he therefore sends out the Apostles afterwards. That third year, however, includes the histories up to the feast of the Dedication, John 10:22. The fourth year is begun around that feast of the Dedication, and is not completed. For at the Passover of that year Christ is crucified. Peter, however, said that the 40 days after the resurrection, up to the ascension, also pertained to the time of Christ's ministry. Acts 1:22. In this way, therefore, we shall distribute the order of the histories, with an added explanation of the circumstances and words, and thus we shall show the sources of the doctrine at the same time. Thus far the blessed Chemnitz concerning the order of the acts of Christ from the series of the Evangelical Harmony. And by this method also, according to the four Passovers, the chronologist and historian, no less than the most excellent theologian, Dr. Johann Cluver, arranged his Evangelical Harmony: as also, from the Reformed, James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, with John Richardson, Bishop of Ardagh, whose entire Evangelical Harmony he inserted into his annals, to say nothing of others now.

QUESTION X.

Whether a whole year or more had elapsed after the baptism of Christ before the first Passover of Christ's ministry approached?

It is necessary to decide thus for those who wish that the Baptism of Christ and the miracle performed at the wedding in Cana occurred on the same day, that is, the 6th of January; just as the Roman Catholic Church has designated in its liturgies. This opinion is that of Rupert, Alcuin, Bernard, Thomas, Durand, Cajetan, Suarez, Barradius, Salianus, Mariana, and many others. See Henricus Philippi in his questions on the birth and suffering of Christ, p. 66. James Ussher in Annalib. Vet. T. part II, page 567, acknowledging that Christ was baptized in the first year of the ministry of St. John the Baptist, in the year of the world 4030, nevertheless determines that the Lord began to execute his first Prophetic office in the fourth year of the ministry of John, namely in the year of the world 4033: in which way it is necessary that not one, but several Passovers intervened between the baptism of Christ and his public ministry. But since the Archangel Gabriel, from the coming of Christ the Leader, manifested at his Baptism, left only one week to fulfill the 70 weeks, and the middle of that week is finished by the death of Christ, which Ussher admits with Richardson: namely, that from the first Passover of the ministry of Christ, John 2:13, the first year of the 70 and the last week of Daniel begins, in which the covenant was confirmed with many, by comparing therefore Dan. 9:27 with Matt. 26:28, it is clear that those two years from the baptism of Christ to his public ministry are excluded; otherwise, from the baptism of Christ to his death, not half a week, but six years with some months would have elapsed.

Nor can the opinion of the Papists stand: that a year elapsed from the baptism of Christ to the wedding at Cana: for thus not only four Passovers, but five would have intervened, nor would the half-week defined by Gabriel be correctly held, which argument Bailius acknowledges is difficult to solve, even though the opinion concerning five Passovers seems very probable to him. He indeed brings forward Nisbeth's distinction between the private and public ministry of Christ: who began the former from the baptism, the latter from the Passover in John 2, attributing half a year to the former and three years to the latter: but he rightly warns that no private ministry of Christ should be acknowledged: since the teaching and miracles of Christ in Galilee were no less public than those in Jerusalem, nor does he dare to tackle that difficult controversy concerning the period of John's proclamation after the baptism of Christ, nor does he wish to contend against so many and such great authors who assign only four Passovers.

But to us, the definition of the Archangel concerning only half a week from the baptism of Christ to his death is more sacred and certain than that we should think we ought to depart from it even by a fingernail's breadth because of any difficulty raised by chronologists or the custom and liturgies of the Roman Church.

That argument from Daniel was indeed also proposed by Bayle, nor could he find what to reply to it: Daniel, he says, chap. 9, v. 27, the preaching of the Gospel by the Messiah before his death is asserted to be about to happen through half a week, that is, for three years and a half; unless, however, you count four Passovers until the passion, so much time will not be given to the ministry of the Messiah; for three Passovers make only two years; but four make three and as many months as flowed from the baptism to the next Passover, which were at least three according to the common calculation, by which the Baptism is referred to January 6th, and the following Passover to March 25th, or April 3rd. Those three years with three months fill the half of the Prophetic week of years, even if not mathematically and precisely to the month, day, hour, and moment, yet civilly and politically, where according to the common mode of speaking the calculation is looser. These things Bayle, loc. cit., p. 92. Who, since he does not easily pass over other difficulties with a dry foot, left this argument without a solution, because he held it to be ἀδιάλυτον [indissoluble].

QUESTION XI. Did Christ celebrate the last Passover with the Jews?

Alcuin, Thomas Aquinas, Gerson, Tostatus of Avila, Franc. Toledo, Bellarmine, Baronius, Barradius, Cornelius à Lapide, Guilhelmus Estius, and also Beza, Brugthomus, the latest English Annotators, Cloppenburg, and among our own D. Caspar Brochmand, p. m., maintain the affirmative, and that both the Jews and Christ celebrated the Passover on the ordinary day, the fourteenth of the moon, on Thursday, the fifth day of the week; but it is more correctly denied that the Passover was celebrated by Christ on the same day as the Jews.

And indeed the more recent Greeks wish that Christ anticipated the legal term of the Passover, the fourteenth of Nisan, and thus celebrated his last Passover on the thirteenth: which can also be seen in the censure of the Augsburg Confession by Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, ch. 13, whose opinion, however, has been deservedly rejected by the Westerners: since in that way Christ would have acted against the law, and would have been made subject to the divine threat, Num. VIII, 13: but he who fulfilled all the righteousness of the law, Matt. III, 15. Add that Christ celebrated his last Passover on the first day of Unleavened Bread, which in a different respect was the fourteenth and the fifteenth, by no means the thirteenth: as B. Gerhard, Harm. ch. 166, p. 1067, observed: that the fourteenth day was the beginning of the eating of unleavened bread, Exod. 12, 18. according to the civil computation, by which that evening of the slaughter and eating of the lamb was referred to the preceding day as a clause of the same, as having begun at midnight: but according to the disposition of the law it was referred to the following day, the fifteenth, by virtue of which feast days began from the evening, Levit. 23, verse 32.

Others note that the beginning of the unleavened bread was on the 14th ending, and the 15th beginning, but the slaughter of the paschal lamb was done between the two evenings, at our 3rd hour post meridiem, Exod. XII, 6. Compare Joh. Wichmann, Chronol. Sacr. book 1, p. 12, 14, who observes that the 14th day was called by the Evangelists Matt. 26, verse 17, Mark 14, 12, Luke 22, 7, the first of unleavened bread, because on it immediately after lunch all leaven was removed from the houses and unleavened breads were prepared, which on the following evening, which [was] the 15th day.

was beginning, they began to be eaten. Finally, what is clearer than the words of Luke c. 22, v. 7: 'Then came the day of unleavened bread, when the Passover must be killed'? It was necessary, indeed, according to the law, which the Savior did not wish to be violated, but observed.

Others, therefore, after Paul of Burgos, solidly teach that Christ observed the legal deadline, but that the Jews ate the Passover not on the same day, but on the following fifteenth; which is the opinion of most of our people, as well as of the Reformers, Calvin, Diodati, Piscator, Scaliger, Casaubon, Baflius, the Anglican Annotators, and also among the Catholics, Jansenius, Maldonatus, and Petavius: that the Jews celebrated their Passover at the end of the fifteenth day and the beginning of the sixteenth, as Friday was ending and the week was beginning. Which is proven first from John 18, v. 28, that the Jews did not want to enter the praetorium, when Jesus was led in the morning by Caiaphas into the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover. They had not, therefore, yet eaten the Passover: which Christ had already eaten the previous night: which most evident passage the trio of most learned Cardinals, Toletus, Bellarmine, and Baronius, could not refute otherwise than by such a fiction, which is clearly contrary to the text, that John is not to be understood as speaking of the Paschal lamb, but of the sacrifices which were offered during the seven days of unleavened bread. But John says expressly, 'that they might eat the PASSOVER,' not 'that they might offer sacrifices': likewise, 'that they might not be defiled,' which the solemnity and holiness of the Passover itself especially required.

But the fact that Marcus Antonius de Dominis in lib. V. de Rep. c. 6. §. 272, following, as Casaubon shows in Exercitat. 16. §. 12, Cedrenus, Peter of Alexandria, Metrodorus, and some other anonymous author, denies that Christ ate the Paschal lamb at the Last Supper, is openly contrary to the Evangelists, Matt. 26, 17 seqq. and Luke 22, 15; and that those following them, Hugo Grotius at Matt. 28, 18, and his associate Hammond at Mark 14, 12, pretend that Christ ate only a μνημονευτικὸν (commemorative) Passover, not a θύσιμον (sacrificial one), and therefore, even if he ate it on the thirteenth day, he did not violate the law, because that commemorative Passover was not commanded by the law, but was a voluntary rite, by which unleavened bread with bitter herbs was eaten in memory of the Passover, is not free from blasphemy, namely that Christ, having neglected the divine law, followed a voluntary superstition, and that his Passover was not a Passover, except equivocally; as Grotius expressly says, this commemorative supper of the Passover, although ἄθυτος (un-sacrificed), is called Passover equivocally.

Then, John 13, 1, Christ is said to have celebrated the Last Supper before the feast day of the Passover, which cannot be taken otherwise than, as our opinion holds, that he celebrated his supper, and in it the Passover, before the day of the Jews' Passover feast.

It is added thirdly, that Christ in John XIX, 14 is said to have been condemned on the Preparation of the Passover, and therefore before the Passover of the Jews, who had already celebrated their Passover with his disciples the previous night.

Fourthly, with John 19:31. The Sabbath after the death of Christ is called great; it is from no other cause than that the first day of unleavened bread, according to the celebration which was performed by the Jews, fell upon a Sabbath; whence the solemnity of that day was greater for them, because it was the first feast of unleavened bread, and thus the Sabbath, augmented by this festivity, was held to be great. Whether, however, from the ignorance of the Priests and the uncertain calation of the New Moons, which seemed so to Petavius after Ludov. Dievius, or from the translation of the first day of unleavened bread to the Sabbath, lest two great solemnities should follow one another continuously, the first day of Unleavened Bread fell on the Sabbath, which Paul of Burgos, Scaliger, and Casaubon prove from the testimonies of the Rabbis, and refer to the decree of the Sanhedrin, matters little: although this opinion is more similar to the truth, nor does that transfer of the holidays seem to be rashly denied with Gerhard Johann Vossius, Dievius, and Cochius, and the clear testimonies of the Jews, and the consensus of the principal Chronologists and Philologists, from whom the blessed Gerhard praised Johann Lucidius, Onuphrius, Stöfler, Bunting, Liveley, Calvisius, Hentenius, Gagney, Jansenius, Salmeron, Maldonatus, Münster, Osiander, Flacius, Bucer, Chemnitz, Hunnius, and those who preceded these, Paul of St. Mary of Burgos, as well as Paul of Middelburg and the bishops of Fano, as also the one prior to them, Rupert on chapter 26 of Matthew.

5. Fifth, if the Jews had celebrated the Passover on the same day as Christ, namely the fourteenth day of the moon, then on the following day, as the first of the Unleavened Bread, and thus a feast day, servile works would have been illicit, from which they would have abstained by the religion of the Sabbath. But on the fifteenth day, or the sixth day of the week, they were conducting capital cases, and were crucifying Christ, and were performing other works alien to a feast day, even those who were most superstitious in the observation of the ceremonial law, and therefore also, lest a riot should arise, they were afraid to attempt such things on a solemn feast day, as Matthew testifies in chapter 26, verse 5; for they said: Not on the feast day, lest a riot occur among the people.

6. Sixth, Nicodemus and Joseph on the day on which Christ had celebrated the Passover bought spices and a linen cloth, and took the body of the crucified Christ down from the cross, and having anointed it, buried it, Mark 15, verse 46, Luke 23, 53, which the Jews would not have permitted them to do if they had celebrated the Passover on that day. And Mark openly testifies that it was then still προσάϐϐατον. John chapter 19, 42 adds that this was done, because they placed Christ in the tomb, on account of the preparation of the Jews: so that they might finish this duty before their Paschal feast.

7. Seventh, what can be clearer than that account of John in chapter 19, 31: The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation (they had not yet therefore celebrated the Passover), so that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (the feast of the Passover), for that was a great Sabbath day. From which it is most evidently established that the feast of the Passover of the Jews was still impending when Christ had already expired, and that the Passover had not yet been celebrated by them with Christ.

What is objected from Matthew 26, 2, 'you know that after two days the Passover will come to pass,' is to be understood that the Passover according to the law was about to be, and ought to have been celebrated. Concerning which also the words of Mark in chapter 14, 12 are to be taken, 'when they sacrificed the Passover,' that is, when it was necessary for the Passover to be sacrificed, as Luke explains in chapter 22, 17, and thus they also sacrificed who, dismissing traditions, were observers of the law, of which sort it is likely there were still some among the Jews. Certainly, his disciples were of the information of Christ, to whom those words, 'when they sacrificed the Passover,' can also not badly be referred, as Bailius observes. See more on this question in the Harmony of the blessed Gerhard, chapter 166, page 1077, and in the discourse of Paul of Burgos on the Paschal celebration instituted by Christ and the Jews, illustrated with the notes of Dr. Johann Behm, as well as in our Anti-Grotian Annotations on the cited passages of the Evangelists.

Did Christ suffer on the fifth day of the week, or on the sixth?

The latter is affirmed by the unanimous consent of the Doctors of the Church, and the interpreters of Holy Scripture, and the chronologists: from whom, however, it pleased Wilhelm Langius to depart, who in book II of the years of Christ, page 379, did not hesitate to assert that the infallible and ἀναντίλεϰ[τος] (indisputable) character of the passion is that it falls on the fifth day of the week, or Thursday; not the sixth day of the week, or Friday, as has hitherto, as he says, been wrongly believed. And on page 422, he says, that Christ suffered on the Preparation of the Passover, the fifth day of the week, is so demonstrated from the Scriptures that it is not permitted for any Christian to speak against it. This rashness was deservedly chastised by the Lord Dr. Wandalinus, now the principal Bishop in the kingdom of Denmark, our singular friend, in his Historical-Theological Diatribe on the day of the passion, published at Leipzig in 1651. The new opinion certainly contradicts the most express testimonies of Scripture: which names the day of Christ's passion the Preparation: and indeed not only παρασκευὴν τõ πάσχα (the preparation of the Passover), John 19:31, lest by chance it be denied that the Passover of the Jews fell on a Sabbath, but absolutely the preparation, by which name, when placed absolutely, the sixth day of the week is always designated, namely that day which precedes the Sabbath, just as on the contrary, where the preparation of some annual feast is implied, the mention of that feast is always added; indeed, so that it might be more clearly established that it was the preparation of the weekly Sabbath, Luke, describing the day thus, ἡμέρα ἦν παρασκευῆς (it was the day of preparation) ch. 23:54, adds: καὶ σάββατον ἐπέφωσκε (and the Sabbath was dawning): which means that it was the sixth day, which the σάββατον ἐπιφῶσκον (dawning Sabbath), the weekly Sabbath dawning, immediately followed: where Blessed Luther rightly: And it was the Preparation-day and the Sabbath began. For the word παρασκευῆς (of preparation) is taken sometimes ὁλικῶς (wholly) for the day of Friday, John 19:14, and sometimes μερικῶς (partially) for the last vigil of the day, which begins from the ninth hour, according to the computation of the Jews, as is evident from Josephus in the edict of Augustus Caesar and John ch. 19:42. Add that Mark, so that nothing may be lacking for the evidence of the matter, ch. 15:42, defines what the Preparation was by a very clear periphrasis: ὅ ἐςι προσάββατον (which is the day before the Sabbath), by which name προσάββατον (day before the Sabbath) nothing else is ever noted than the sixth day of the week immediately preceding the weekly Sabbath, which the interpreter rendered: ante-Sabbatum (before-Sabbath). For it was the day before the Sabbath, the day immediately preceding the Sabbath, to which the Jews refer the feast of the Passover. Among us it is the sixth day of the week, namely that day on which God created man, the epitome of the whole universe, Gen. 1:31. Theod. q. 72 in Exod. Therefore, that Christ willed to be adjudged to the punishment of death on the same day, by that very fact it is shown that Christ by his death perfected the work of redemption, which is an ἀνάκτησις (recovery), and a certain ἀνάπλασις (re-formation), as Justin speaks, as Blessed Gerhard has in Harm. Pass. ch. 11. Whence the Arab interpreted the day of the congregation, that is, the sixth day of the week, which is so called by the Mahometans because they have their congregations on that day, which Christians institute on the first day of the week, and Nonnus in his Paraphrase calls it the Sixth day.

(2.) That the Passover of the Jews, in whose Preparation Christ suffered, fell on a Sabbath, Luke teaches not only in chapter 23:54, but also in verse 56, when he testifies that the women, after Christ was buried, returned and observed the rest of the Sabbath: καὶ τὸ μὲν σάββατον ἡσύχησαν κατὰ τὴν ἐντολήν (and on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment). And St. John calls that feast the day of the Passover the day of the Sabbath, and also the great day, according to the observance of the Jews, ἧν γὰρ μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη τῦ Σαββάτη, for that day of that Sabbath was a great day: chap. 19, 31. Whence it is not permitted to doubt that it was the day of the Sabbath: which was therefore considered great by the Jews, because according to their own decrees and observance of the Passover and the weekly Sabbath occurred on the same day.

(3.) That day, which immediately followed the passion and death of Christ, on which the chief priests and Pharisees gathered to deliberate about guarding the sepulcher of the Lord, was the weekly Sabbath itself, which immediately follows the Preparation, as the description of Matthew indicates, chap. 27, 62. ἡ ἐπαύριον ἥτις ἐςὶ μετὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν, the next day, which is after the Preparation, the chief priests gathered: Since therefore this was the seventh day, having immediately followed the Preparation, or the sixth, it must be that Christ suffered on the Preparation, that is, on the sixth day.

(4) The day of rest in the sepulcher is designated as only one single whole day, namely that day on which the pious women rested because of the religion of the Sabbath and the great feast (which fell on the Sabbath) Luke 23, 56. καὶ τὸ μὲν Σάββατον ἡσύχησαν. He did not say that they rested for two Sabbaths, or for two days; but only for the Sabbath; and thus a single whole day with the preceding and following nights, and also a portion of the light of the previous day. Therefore, the women spent one Sabbath in rest, and Christ spent one in the sepulcher.

(5.) There are expressly numbered by Luke chap. 23. (1.) the day of the passion and burial, the Preparation, ver. 54. (2.) the day of rest after the day of burial, the day of the Sabbath, in the same verse and 56. and also (3.) the day of the resurrection chap. 24, 1. as immediately following one another, which last Mark expresses thus chap. 16, 1. διαγενομένε τῦ Σαββάτε when the Sabbath had passed, as Grotius and Casaubon rightly explain: or the Sabbath having intervened and passed, as Beza interpreted. Compare Acts 25, 13. chap. 27, 9. Therefore only the day of the Sabbath, or the seventh day, intervened between the passion and the resurrection, and thus Christ suffered on the sixth day, and the seventh day having intervened and passed, he rose on the first day.

(6.) The disciples confirm this in the appearance of Christ, who were heading to the village of Emmaus, Luke 24, 21. ἀλλάγε σὺν πᾶσι τύτοις τρίτην ταύτην ἡμέραν ἄγει σήμερον ἀφ’ ὗ ταῦτα ἐγένετο, which words Blessed Luther rendered very well: And besides all that, today is the third day since these things happened. For Grotius rightly observed that the active is taken here impersonally for the passive, as often, and that the sense is: the third day is now being spent, as the Syrian and Arab also expressed: Now if Christ had suffered on the fifth day, that would have been the fourth day, not the third. For the fifth, sixth, and seventh days are counted with that first day which was being spent, and it will be clear that this is the fourth. That this appearance happened on the very day of Christ's resurrection, the comparison of ver. 1 and 13 clearly teaches.

(7.) What of the fact that it is held in the Scriptures not once, but more often, that Christ would rise and had risen on the third day: which Hosea had predicted chap. 6, 2. and Christ himself, on different occasions. Matt. 16, 21. chap. 18, 33. chap. 20, 19. Mark 10, 34. Luke 9, 22. John 2, 18. 19. and the Angels testified Luke 24, 7. and the Apostles Acts 10, 39. 40. 1 Cor. 15, 4. But if it were asserted that Christ suffered on Thursday, he would have risen not on the third, but on the fourth day, not ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις in three days, or within three days, as he predicted, John 2, 18. 19. but after three days had passed, he would have raised the temple of his body.

As all these things are set forth as if in the sun's disk, so no one has ever doubted them, all with one voice have professed the same opinion, namely that Christ on the third day raised up the temple, which had been dissolved by the Jews. Ignatius, Epist. ad Smyrn., rose again within three days, which he explains in Epist. ad Trallian. thus: on the Preparation day before sunset he was buried, on the Sabbath he remained under the earth in the monument in which Joseph of Arimathea placed him, at the dawning of the Lord's day he rose from the dead, according to that which he had said. The preparation day therefore embraces the passion, the Sabbath the burial, the Lord's day the resurrection. Irenaeus, lib. 5. adv. haeres. cap. 23. It is manifest, he says, that the Lord suffered death on that day on which Adam, disobedient to God, died, being obedient to the Father. Recapitulating this day therefore in himself, the Lord came to the passion on the day before the Sabbath, which is the sixth day of creation, on which man was formed; granting a second formation, that which is from death, through his passion. Which opinion Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, Tractat. 1. in Exod., similarly handed down: on the sixth day of the week, on which God had made man, he suffered for the same, and on the Lord's day, which is called in the Scriptures the first of the Sabbath, on which the world had taken its beginning, he rose again. And to embrace many things in few words, the Fathers and the whole Church have with great consensus affixed the Lord's Passion to the sixth day of the week, as they have the pact of the Jews' betrayal to the fourth, which for that reason instituted fasts on those two days in memory of the sale and Passion of Christ.

Concerning which Peter, Bishop and Martyr of Alexandria, in the Synodicon brought forward by Fr. Sylburgius in Not. ad Clem. Alexandr. Strom. 7. Let no one blame us, who observe the fourth and sixth days of the week, on which it has been conveniently established that we should fast according to tradition: the fourth day indeed on account of the counsel initiated by the Jews concerning the betrayal of the Savior; the sixth truly on account of his passion undertaken for us. Concerning which days Clem. Alexandr. loc. cit. and Tertull. de jejun. adversus Psych. cap. 14. Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. 10. in Levit. Leo M. Serm. IV. in Quadrag. may be seen, as well as Epiphanius haeres. LXXI. who appeals to universal consensus: Who is there anywhere in the world who does not agree in this, that the fourth or sixth day of the week is consecrated by a solemn fast in the Church? Augustine also appealed to universal consensus concerning the day of the Passion, Epist. LXXXVI. ad Casulanum: This day therefore being passed over, the Lord suffered, WHICH NO ONE DOUBTS, on the sixth of the Sabbath (or Week), for which reason the sixth (day of the week) itself is rightly deputed to fasting; as also Bede, who lib. de tempor. rat. l. XL. reckons this opinion among those of which it is permitted to no CATHOLIC to doubt. Whence Broughton in the English, and Jacobus Genius in the Latin harmony of Holy Scripture, page 136. Christ died on the same day on which Satan was made a murderer in the beginning of things, Genes. 3. and through death he abolished him who has the power of death. Concerning the day of Adam, the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Arabs, Greeks, and Latins agree.

Although indeed the same Bede seems in lib. de aequinoct. vern. to allege to the contrary the opinion of Theophilus of Caesarea, on whose testimony Langius relies, that the Lord suffered from the 11th of the Kalends of April, on which night he was betrayed by the Jews, and rose again on the 7th of the Kalends of April, these things are nevertheless to be accepted in such a way that the passage already brought forward, which no Catholic may doubt concerning the sixth day of the crucifixion, and his books on the reckoning of time, chapters 11 and 45, permit; where these things are read: That the Lord suffered from the 11th of the Kalends of April and rose again from the 7th of the Kalends of April. Therefore, it seems to be understood concerning the beginning of the passion, which began following the evening of the 11th of the Kalends of April, when it indicates the night in which he was betrayed by Judas, if indeed he asserted that Christ was crucified not on the 11th of the Kalends of April, but on the 10th, as Bede testifies in his book on the reckoning of time, chapter 65; whence it is deservedly believed, if a truer opinion does not prevail, that the blessed Theophilus, disputing about Easter with the rest of the bishops, not only of Palestine but also of very many other regions, wrote that the Lord was crucified on that same 10th day of the Kalends of April. For it was fitting that on one and the same day, not only of the week but also of the month, according to the second Adam, who was lulled to sleep by a life-giving death for the salvation of the human race, he should sanctify for himself the Church as a bride with the heavenly sacraments produced from his side, on which day, namely, he himself had created the first Adam, the father of the human race, and taking a rib from his side, built the woman, by whose help he propagated the human race.

In the same way, Chrysostom is cited in vain by Langius, who says that he wished Christ to have been dead for three days in Homily 44 on Matthew. For Chrysostom speaks of civil days or νυχθημέροις [days and nights], and in Sermon 82 he calls the day on which they sought Christ for the celebration of the Passover the fifth of the Sabbath (or week), which immediately preceded the day of the Passion. Therefore, he acknowledged that Christ suffered on the sixth day.

Whence, to the primary objection from Matt. 12:40 concerning the three days and nights, the answer is at hand: not indeed that the beginning should be taken from the start of the captivity (not from the burial), which seemed to be the case to Erasmus, annot. on Mark 8:31, nor that he rose again sooner to declare his power, as Chrysostom, Isidore, and Leo the Great judged, nor that the Jews, in the manner of the Romans, began the day from the 12th hour of the night, as Torniellus, Spondanus, Cornel. à Lapide, and others thought, but that three natural days of 24 hours, distinctly computed, are not to be understood: but civil ones, or three νυχθήμερα [days and nights], by an accepted Hebraism, for the sake of which compare 1 Sam. 30:12, Esth. 4:16, by which Christ was to rise again not when three days were completed, but ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις [in three days], and τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ [on the third day], John 2:17, 18, Matt. 17:23. Luke 9:22, and that not entire, but taken synecdochically; if indeed Christ suffered on the Preparation of the Passover and the Sabbath, and gave up the Spirit at the ninth hour (which is our third in the afternoon), and was buried at the tenth hour, or our fourth, from which there were still two hours remaining of that νυχθήμερον [day and night], from which that civil day could be denominated synecdochically, as the whole from the parts, to which the entire day of the Sabbath spent in the sepulcher succeeded, as a second νυχθήμερον: and the third began around the evening of the Sabbath, from which until the hour of the resurrection on the third day about ten hours elapsed. In which way Jerome explains in the Latin Church on Matt. 12, that the whole is understood synecdochically from a part, not that the Lord remained in hell (in the sepulcher) for all three days, but that in a part of the Preparation and of the Lord's day and the whole day of the Sabbath, three days and as many nights are understood: And St. Augustine, Book III, on the Consensus of the Evangelists, chapter 4. It remains, therefore, that by that most common mode of speaking of the Scriptures, by which the whole is understood from a part, we find the last day, the time of the Preparation, in which the Lord was crucified and buried, and from that very last part we take the whole day, with its night, which had already been completed: but the middle one, that is, the day of the Sabbath, not from a part, but entirely the whole. The third again from its first part, that is, from the night, the whole with its daytime: and thus it will be a triduum, just as those eight days, after which he ascended the mountain, whose middle ones Matthew and Mark, attending to the whole, said were after six days, which Luke said were after eight days. And book 4 on the Trinity, chapter 6. That the triduum itself was not whole and full, Scripture is witness, but the first day was counted as a whole from the last part: the third day, however, from the first part, and it too as a whole: the middle one between them, that is, the second day, absolutely whole, with its twenty-four hours, its twelve nocturnal and twelve diurnal. For he was crucified first by the voices of the Jews at the third hour, when it was the sixth day of the Sabbath. Then he was suspended on the cross itself at the sixth hour, and gave up the spirit at the ninth hour. From the hour of death, therefore, until the dawn of the resurrection, there are forty hours, as even the ninth hour itself is commemorated. But from the evening of the burial until the dawn of the resurrection there are thirty-six hours, which is a squared six. And Isidore of Pelusium establishes the same thing also concerning the delay of Jonah in the belly of the whale, as a type of Christ, that he did not remain in it for three whole days and nights, but in that space of time also he agreed with the antitype, and spent as many hours in the belly of the whale as Christ spent in the heart of the earth. Book 1, Epistle 114. He who had undertaken to express the type of Jonah, since he knew him exactly (inasmuch as he was also present with Jonah when he was driven headlong into the deep, and was cast out from the deep), he also undoubtedly fulfilled it, remaining in the sepulcher for as much time, namely, as Jonah did in the belly of the whale.

QUESTION XIII. At what hour was Christ crucified, and at what hour did he expire?

Gottfried Vogelius, in his German Chronological computation on page 194, beginning the seventy weeks of Daniel from the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus and finishing them precisely at the death of Christ, opines that not only the 490 whole years, but the months, the days, and even the very hours themselves correspond exactly to the death of Christ: for he maintains that the edict went forth on April 7th of the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, which he makes the year of the world 3548, as indicated by Gabriel in Daniel 9, and from there up to April 3rd of the year of the world 4037, in which he places the crucifixion of Christ, he counts 489 years and 11 months, and with the addition from April 7th of the year of the world 3547 up to April 3rd of the year of the world 4037, not yet counting the 26 days and the four-day period which he judges must be added on account of the equinox according to the Julian calendar, he produces 490 whole years: Finally, he judges it not improbable that Ezra received the edict, or the royal concession concerning the edict, from Artaxerxes at the same hour that Christ cried out, 'It is finished,' and expired, so that not even that day, nor indeed any hour at all, could be missing from Gabriel's computation: but since Dr. Vogelius assumes many things in that computation without proof, and openly errs in the term of Gabriel's epoch, finishing it at the death of Christ, no place is left for that conjecture.

We are here concerned only with the reconciliation of the Evangelists, so that the hour of the crucifixion and likewise of the death of Christ may be correctly defined from history. For Mark says in chapter 15:25 that it was the third hour when Christ was crucified, whereas John, in chapter 19:14, testifies that it was ὡσεὶ, about the sixth hour: where there is no need for us to conclude, either with Peter of Alexandria, Theophylact, and Camerarius, that the text of John is corrupted and that the third hour should be read instead of the sixth, or with Peter Comestor to attribute a corruption to the text of Mark which is not to untie, but to cut the knot: nor is it free from danger, when the authentic Scripture is established as corrupted at least somewhere; for what happens to one text could happen to any. Yet not only Papists are inclined to this opinion concerning the corruption of the modern sacred text, such as Thomas Aquinas, Cajetan on Mark 15:25, Sixtus Senensis Bibl. lib. VI. ann. 131, Melchior Canus, and Petavius, who wish it to be read in Mark as the sixth hour, which reading the Ethiopic Bibles have, but also among our own, Wilhelmus Langius, thinking that in Mark, because of two lower lines struck out, an r had crept in for an E, and therefore it should be read there ὥρᾳ πέμπτῃ instead of τρίτῃ: and likewise among the Reformed, James Ussher, who agrees that John's text rather is corrupted; and Casaubon cites this opinion in Exercit. XVI. num. CX. He cites the very ancient Paraphrast, who either read in John, or judged should be read, ὥρα ὡσεὶ τρίτη, since he rendered it thus: ἦν δὲ τιταινομένη τριτάτη θανατη- φόρῳ ἠώς.
