And Peter of Alexandria in his disputation on the Passover, who appealed to the autograph of John: ἦν δὲ παρασκευὴ, ὥρα ἦν ὡσεὶ τρίτη· καθὼς τὰ ἀκρι- βῆ βιβλία περιέχει, ἀυτότε τὸ ἰδιόχειρον τῦ Εὐαγγε- λιςῦ· ὅπερ μέχρι τῦ νῦν πεφύλακται χάριτι Θεῦ ἐν τῇ Ἐφεσίων ἁγιωτάτῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ· καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν πι ςῶν ἐκεῖσε προσκυνεῖται. It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the third hour: as the accurately described books have; and thus the autograph itself written by the own hand of the Evangelist John: which, preserved by the grace of God to this day, exists in the most holy Church of the Ephesians, and is visited with great reverence by the faithful approaching there. Joachim Camerarius also reports this in his annotations. on Mark 15, that he had a certain old manuscript codex, in which it was read in John ὥρα δὲ ὡς τρίτη. Robert Estienne and Theodore Beza also appeal here to old Greek copies: nor does Ussher doubt in his dissertation on Polycarp and Ignatius, ch. 11, p. 75, that at least in John it was read by the interpolator of both the Clementine Constitutions and the Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians as ὥρα ὡσεὶ τρίτη, if indeed the autograph of the Evangelist John had it so; which the author of the Constantinopolitan Chronicle, edited by Matthæus Raderus under the name of the Alexandrian, p. 518, 520, asserts was preserved to these times in the Church of the Ephesians.

But the Jesuit Maldonatus rightly says in his Commentary on Matthew 27:45: 'That conjecture, that the number in Mark was vitiated by the fault of the scribes, has always seemed too bold to me, and because it relies on no other argument than that those who use it cannot explain the difficulty of this passage: And we ought not, in order to interpret Scripture, to corrupt it.' Nor did Hugo Grotius, who otherwise easily inclines toward the corruption of the sacred text, see a cause for changing the reading here, and in his annotations on Mark 15:25 he professes: 'Nothing in the Scripture of Mark or John is to be changed against the authority of the most ancient Codices and translators.' And those commentaries on the Psalms of Jerome are not Jerome's, but supposititious, to which Jerome has nothing similar in his commentaries on Matthew and Mark. Furthermore, what is cited in the name of Peter of Alexandria concerning the autograph of John seems to Robert Baillie, not undeservedly, a mere fable: for who would believe that the autograph of John existed in his days? And therefore Baillie disapproves of this opinion, as rejected by Papists and all other Protestants, as it opens too wide a door for rash minds to correct the Holy Scriptures. Nor, if we say with Ussher that at least John's text is corrupted, will there be harmony with the other Evangelists or Ignatius. For if Christ began to be condemned about the third hour, he cannot be said to have been crucified at the third hour, according to Casaubon (which is asserted by Mark), since it is certain to Casaubon that between this voice of Pilate, 'Behold your King,' and the rising of the darkness, there was need of no small time for the Lord to be condemned, handed over, led away to the place of punishment outside the city, mocked, and crucified, which is the opinion of almost all Doctors. How then, according to Mark, was he crucified at the third hour, if he was crucified only at the sixth hour? Must it not also be said that the passage of Mark is corrupted, so that then in John it should be read as the third hour, when Christ began to be condemned, and in Mark as the sixth hour, which opinion B. Gerhard reports to be that of Peter Comestor in his Harm. Pass. ch. 11? By what means, finally, will the testimony of Ignatius be consistent with itself in his Epistle to the Trallians, as also that of Clement in the Constitutions? book 5, chapter 13, of which the former has it thus: τῇ ἴν παρασκευῇ τρίτῃ ὥρᾳ ἀπόφασιν ἐνδέξατο παρὰ τῶ Πιλάτῳ, συγ- χωρήσαντος τῷ πατρὸς, ἕκτῃ ὥρᾳ ἐσαυρώθη, ἐννά- τῃ ἀπέπνευσε, πρὸ ἡλίγ δύσειον ἐτάφη. 'On the Preparation, therefore, at the third hour he received the sentence from Pilate, the Father permitting it. At the sixth hour he was crucified, at the ninth he breathed his last, before sunset he was buried.' This, however, is reported thus by Ussher, l. c.: Δήμιοι δὲ παραλα- βόντες τὸν τῆς δόξης κύριον, ἕκτῃ μὲν ὥρᾳ ςαυρώσαν- τες ἀυτὸν, τρίτῃ δὲ ὥρᾳ τὴν ἀπόφασιν δεξάμενοι τὴν περὶ ἀυτῶ υςι. ὅς καὶ περὶ τὴν ἐννάτην ὥραν ἀναβο- ήσας, ἀπέπνευσε καὶ θάπτεται πρὸ ἡλίγ δύσεως ἐν μνημείῳ καινῷ. 'The executioners, when they had taken the Lord of glory, affixed him to the wood of the cross at the sixth hour, but at the third hour they received the sentence pronounced against him, etc. Who, about the ninth hour, having uttered a cry, expired, and was buried before the setting of the Sun in a new sepulcher.' But Ussher himself does not recognize those Ignatian writings, nor those ascribed to Clement, as genuine, but judges them to have proceeded from some interpolator, and he confesses that the reading of the sixth hour is attributed to Mark against the faith of all copies, and Theodore Beza does not hesitate to call that solution violent.

Nor does the second, more subtle than solid, response of Augustine satisfy, which he treats in both places: in John ch. 17 and in Psalm 64, 3. The former, that Christ was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the blaspheming Jews, but at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers, which does not agree with the text. For it speaks openly of a crucifixion not metaphorical, but literal: the latter, that it was the sixth hour not of the day, but of the παρασκευῆς, which began from the ninth hour of the night: which Thomas does not disapprove of in part III, sum. quest. XLVI, second to the second, and in the Catena on Matthew 27, 25. And yet the preparation, spoken of generally as the first hour of the day, but understood specifically or partially, began at the ninth hour before evening, in which the Passover was eaten, but not the ninth hour of the night!

Nor can we give our assent to Johannes Piscator, even if Erasmus on Matthew 27, 45, Ludovicus de Dieu on Mark 15, 45, the Belgian Annotators on John 19, 14, and the English on Luke 23, 44, also lean toward this, as does the blessed D. Anselm, that John speaks according to the custom of the Romans, who begin the hours of the day from the rising of the sun, and Mark according to the custom of the Jews, who begin from midnight, and that the sixth hour from midnight fell into the third hour from the rising of the sun, which in Judea would have risen then at the fourth hour of the morning: since not even at the equinox, which coincides in Judea with the Passover, does the sun ever rise before the sixth hour of the morning, and Christ according to the opinion of those men [would have been crucified] for nine, or at least six had hung on the cross for hours, from the sixth after midnight (from the third after the rising of the sun) until the third in the afternoon, or as others interpolate the opinion of Piscator, from the ninth hour of the morning to the third, when nevertheless only three hours are to be assigned to Christ on the cross, John 19:14, concerning which see Bailius, Oper. Histor. Chron. II, p. 87.

Therefore, Baronius, Maldonatus, Barradius, Ferus, Valentia, Suarez, Jansenius bring forward another method of reconciliation: and from the Reformed, Calvin, Gualterus, Rollocus, Deodatus, Alstedius, Bailius, as also from our own B. Gerhardus, B. Waltherus, and others, with the authors of the Centur. Magdeburg. cent. I, lib. I, cap. X, p. 140, leading the way. That the day was divided into four quadrants or greater hours, just as the night was divided into four watches: in the way that mention is made of the first watch in Lamentations 2:19, so that three hours were assigned to each quadrant and watch: and Mark called the second quadrant from its beginning the third hour, but John from its end the sixth: within which the crucifixion occurred, i.e., in the time intermediate between the third and sixth hour: namely, that quadrant which begins from the third hour and ends at the sixth. Which Bailius explains thus on page 89. That Christ is said by Mark to have been crucified at the third hour, because he was crucified within the space of that quadrant which is denominated from the third: then that he is said by John and the rest to have been crucified at the sixth hour, or about the sixth hour, because the sixth was the other extreme of that second quadrant, so that actions performed between the third and sixth were said to be performed either at the third or the sixth, denominated namely from either extreme, at the discretion of the speakers. Which method of reconciliation would be quite expeditious, as B. Affelmann says in Tetrad. verborum Testam. thes. 9, if only it were certain. Concerning which, however, he modestly doubts: since this method of counting rests on no testimony of antiquity, and not even on Censorinus, whom he says is alleged in bad faith for this matter. He grants that the Jews divided the night into four watches, which watches, φυλακὰς, Augustine handed down were held to be an observation of three hours each, and with him Arnobius. But concerning the opinions on the division of the day into four hours, and this enumeration, whence, he says, will you finally convince me? I add that it is supported by no document that the quadrants of the day were accustomed to be denominated both from the beginning and from the end, so that, namely, another quadrant of the day was denominated from the sixth hour no less than from the third: and that those synonyms must be held to be: the second quadrant of the day, the third hour, the sixth hour. For although the second quadrant of the day, given that distinction, comprises the three-hour period from the third to the sixth, and things that happen from the third to the sixth happen in the second quadrant, they are not therefore said to happen at the third hour and at the sixth hour; since they could also have happened at the fourth or fifth.

Furthermore, is the hour of the crucifixion of Christ not rendered so uncertain, which the holy Evangelists nevertheless studiously wished to define? For concerning what was done between the third and sixth hour, or in the second quadrant of the day, I cannot pronounce with certainty whether it was done at the fourth, or the fifth, or finally at the sixth hour itself. Which the explanation of others renders even more doubtful, who reconcile it thus: at the sixth hour Christ was judged, namely of the day, when those things which John narrates had not yet been heard about it: but he was crucified at the third, i.e., in the third quadrant of the day, which began from the sixth hour of the day and ended at the ninth, but he was crucified within this limit. For if the Evangelists are explained thus differently concerning different quadrants by others, not even certainty will remain concerning the quadrant of the day in which Christ was crucified, let alone the hour of the crucifixion.

And hence the judgment will now also be the same concerning a similar reconciliation, sought from the distinction between the hours of prayer and of the day; that those were comprised by a quaternary, these by a duodenary, and therefore the Evangelists, as they were describing a sacred matter, followed the hours of the temple and of prayer. Which Grotius made his own here in his annotations to Matthew 27:45, p. 489. A manner of speaking born from the custom of the Temple, where sacrifices and prayers were accustomed to be made at the third, sixth, and ninth hour: as we are taught in Numbers 10:10, whereby it happened that these hours were celebrated as being more commonly known; nor will you find other names of hours where there is mention of fixed prayers. See Acts 3:1, 10:3, 9, and Tertullian on fasts, where he says these are the more notable hours in human affairs, which distribute the day, which distinguish business, which resound in public. With which agree what Cyprian writes on the Lord's Prayer, and Jerome both to Laetus and to Demetrias. And to this pertains what is above, 20:3, 5, where between the third, sixth, and ninth no hour is named, when after the ninth the eleventh is mentioned. But whatever had happened between those fixed times of prayer is said to have been done at the third or sixth hour, as things that are placed in the middle are accustomed to be referred now to this, now to that limit. For this is the same as if it were said that something was done in the second three-hour period, as the astrologers speak. Hesychius teaches us that parts of the day were also signified by the sound of a trumpet among certain Greeks, in which place he says that the time of the night is called by Sophocles the time without a trumpet. These are the words of Grotius: which testify that it is left uncertain from the Evangelical history at what hour Christ was affixed to the cross. For it happened at the third or sixth hour of the day, which had occurred between those fixed times of prayer; but at what hour it happened, is by no means defined.

It will therefore be more suitable if that distinction by three-hour periods, or quadrants of the day, is admitted in Mark, so that in John we may understand the sixth hour not as the second quadrant of the day, named from the sixth hour, but as the hour itself, which is counted from the beginning of the day: although Mark perhaps designated the second quadrant of the day, so that in this way the time of the indicated crucifixion is defined by John: which was at about the sixth hour, when Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross, and handed him over to the Jews: so that the sixth hour had not yet been heard, yet with that hour imminent Christ was handed over, and shortly after, at that very hour, he was crucified, just as Matthew and Luke indicated, when they testify that from the sixth hour, that time and moment at which he himself, having been affixed to the cross, began to hang suspended among the thieves, darkness arose and lasted until the moment of death, namely the ninth hour: which is also noted by Mark in chapter XV, 33. Wherefore in the same Mark, with verse 25, ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη καὶ ἐςαύρωσαν αὐτὸν, the hour of the crucifixion cannot possibly be designated as the third hour of the day: because he was condemned to the cross and handed over to the Jews only when the sixth hour of the day was imminent; how therefore can he be said to have been crucified at the third hour of the day? Therefore, having posited the aforementioned distribution of the day into quadrants, and the naming of each quadrant from its first hour, so that the first quadrant is named from the first, the second from the third, the third from the sixth, the fourth from the ninth, and thus the second quadrant is understood by the great third hour, Mark is to be considered to have indicated not the third hour of the day, ἀποτόμως

and specifically, but a three-hour period, and the quarter generally and commonly, to which the third hour provides both the beginning and the denomination. But since that denomination is doubtful and uncertain, as we have said, and does not sufficiently fit, because from the beginning the second quarter should be marked not with the name of the third, but of the fourth hour, in which it begins, just as the third should be marked not with the name of the sixth, but of the seventh, and the fourth not with the name of the ninth, but of the tenth; perhaps the explanation of Daniel Heinsius on Mark 15:26 is rather to be approved, which Bailius thinks he received from the most learned Roman monk Marcellus, although he conceals it, which Ludovicus de Dieu also hints at (even if he does not follow it), as well as Balduinus Walaeus, namely that the division of Christ's garments was made at the third hour from the crucifixion: so that the words of Mark are to be rendered thus: and it was the third hour, and they crucified him, and it was the third hour, or the hour was already passing, from which he had been driven onto the cross, as if you were to say and it was the third hour after he was crucified, or it was the third hour of his crucifixion, the third hour after his crucifixion, or the hour of his crucifixion: so that the Hebraism in the copula does not divide; but joins. Similar is the passage

Jos. 7:25. and they burned them with fire, and they stoned them with stones, which are not to be rendered: and they burned with fire, and they stoned with stones, which interpretation tortured Augustine wonderfully out of ignorance of the Hebraism, but as the Targumist rendered it, they burned with fire, AFTER they had stoned them with stones: so here and they crucified him is the same to Heinsius as from which they crucified, from which, or after they had crucified him. And so also

The Persian. For after he translated the Greek literally, not through tautology, as Bailius argues against him, but for the sake of explanation and unfolding the Hebraism, he seems to have added these things: after they had suspended him on the cross. Although one may also presume that the time was designated in this way by this interpreter for the inscription placed on the cross, namely that at the third hour from the crucifixion they placed the title, which Matthew seems to hint was placed only after the division of the garments: for thus the Persian translation has it in its entirety: And when they had driven him onto the cross, at the third hour. From which they had suspended him on the cross. The pretext of his death was written in the book. Which sense, if it was that of the Persian interpreter, this will be a new method of reconciliation, but the particle and, which Mark inserted in verse 26, will be omitted: and the inscription was, which prevents us from taking the third hour as the time of the imposition of the title. And Bailius concedes that the Persian interpreter (which is more likely) understood the third hour as the time of the division of the garments, although he later confuses the Ethiopic version with the Persian. For the same reason Dievius also interprets the Arabic version: And he joins that about the third hour when he was crucified with the preceding verse, where the division of Christ's garments was treated. That was done, he says, at the third hour from the crucifixion. He does not understand, therefore, that it was the third hour when Christ was being crucified: but when the soldiers were dividing his garments, then it was the third hour from when he had been affixed to the cross. In that sense, crucified should be translated by the pluperfect, in this way, and it was the third hour, when they had crucified him. These things he says concerning the sense of the Arabic version, which Bailius did not understand, rashly refuting Dievius: in which opinion he also interprets the Syriac: whose version Dievius teaches is better rendered thus when they had crucified him, than as Tremellius, when they were crucifying him: and that the Greek language easily admits the pluperfect here.

Suarez and Bailius do indeed reject that explanation, but with less than firm arguments. Bailius first urges that Mark would thus have passed over the time of the crucifixion and would have designated the time of a less noble action. But Mark did not pass it over; rather, he indicated the time of the crucifixion in verse 53 by the same reasoning as Matthew and Luke: namely, designated by the character of the darkness that arose. And if he is to be blamed for having passed it over, Matthew and Luke would likewise have to be blamed; but since it is expressed by John and noted by the others with a striking character, how can it be said to have been passed over by the Holy Spirit? Nor is that circumstance of the division of the garments so ignoble that it would have been worth no effort to note its time, since it was expressly predicted in the Old Testament in Psalm XXII, the fulfillment of which all the Evangelists described, an act which St. John also commemorated with particular diligence. Not to mention that that third hour, from which he began to be crucified, the hour of the division and plundering of Christ's garments, seems to look back to that hour when the first-created, feeling their nakedness, tried to cover and clothe themselves with fig leaves; for man could not be reclothed, as Bernard says in sermon 1 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary, or receive back the garments (of original justice) taken from him, unless Christ lost his own; for just as he could not be brought to life in the soul without the intervening bodily death of Christ, so neither could he be reclothed without his despoiling.

Bailius urges secondly that the Evangelists, and Mark himself, immediately subjoin the division of the garments to the crucifixion: therefore he could not have deferred this for three whole hours after the crucifixion; but these things are not opposites: for cannot a narrative be immediately subjoined to a thing which followed three hours later?

Bailius argues thirdly thus: the garments were divided according to the accounts of Matthew, Mark, and Luke before the darkness arose. But if the darkness (let alone the actions before the darkness) did not arise until three hours after the crucifixion, then Christ would have hung on the cross for more than six hours. But although the darkness is commemorated after the division of the garments, it did not, however, arise only after the same, but with the crucifixion itself: for it is said to have arisen at the sixth hour itself. But it was the third hour (ὡσεὶ ἕκτη) when Pilate ascended the tribunal to condemn Christ, John XIX, 14.

He inculcates fourthly that no text can be brought forward where in one verse enclosed by its own punctuation a determined time is assigned to a certain action by a copulative conjunction, in which that same time is to be separated from that same action and referred to another: which we concede first regarding the copulative conjunction taken COPULATIVELY; that this sense must necessarily be retained here cannot be proven, since it is well known that the copulative particle is very often taken in many other ways and is not always understood copulatively. Secondly, it cannot be referred to another action unless the text itself suggests another: which happens here: verse 24, 'and having crucified him they divided his garments, and it was the third hour.' Thirdly, it is indeed referred to the crucifixion, not so that the time of the beginning of the crucifixion is indicated, but the third hour after he had been crucified, and not that the hour of the crucifixion itself is designated as having been the third hour, which would contradict John.

We add, however, another solution for the learned to weigh: ought not the third hour in Mark to be understood from the handing over to Pilate? So that the Evangelist thus insinuated all the principal acts defined by a three-hour period, and indeed in the first three-hour period of the day the meeting of the Sanhedrin was celebrated, and at the first hour of the day of the Preparation Mark XIV, 1. consultation instituted, a new examination undertaken by the whole Sanhedrin Luke XXII, 67. seqq. a decree made, how he is to be handed over to Pilate. From that handing over, therefore, which took place around the third hour of the day, that is to say three hours before the crucifixion, for it was the third hour (from that handing over) when he was crucified, there occurred those things which were done before Pilate and by Pilate, until he condemned Christ and handed him over to be crucified; which therefore was done around the sixth hour of the day or at the meridian time, as the Ethiopic version added for the sake of ἐξηγήσεως John XIX, 14. And it was the Preparation of the Passover at the meridian time, the sixth hour. Which sixth hour of the day Mark himself also expressed in verse 33. Third, that which as the principal thing on this day of the great passion, namely after the consultation and decree of the Sanhedrin, after the accusation in the Praetorium, and the condemnation of Christ to death, after the very crucifixion of the Savior, is commemorated by Mark at the end of the ninth hour, or the third three-hour period and quarter of the day, and the beginning of the last, is the death of Christ, who therefore he commemorates as having expired his soul toward the end of the darkness, at the ninth hour.

And this is the common opinion of the Doctors, that the crucifixion took place at the sixth hour, when the darkness arose, and that Christ hung on the cross for three hours: Nor does the comparison of John XIX, 14 with Luke XXIII, 44 create a difficulty here, such that there is a need, with Casaubon Exercit. XVI. n. LX, to say here that one must wait for Elijah, who might solve the insoluble parts of the Scriptures. For what stands in the way of that knot being solved in such a way that, according to John, it was ὥρα ὡσεὶ ἕκτη when Christ began to be condemned, because the sixth was shortly impending: but according to Luke, it is understood in the sense that it was about the sixth hour, because the sixth had not passed by so long: or even that that hour about the sixth is understood to be completed, which was completed half an hour before or after the sixth: but that could easily have been accomplished within an hour, especially by the enemies of Christ, who, out of the fury of malice, were also hastening and precipitating the end of Christ with all force and zeal: such as the condemnation, the handing over, the leading away to the place of punishment, and the crucifixion. Nor are the words of the Evangelists to be understood with mathematical rigor, but broadly and morally, or according to common usage, therefore the particle 'about' is added.

Moreover, however much the moment of the crucifixion may not be so determinately expressed, nor is there entirely the same opinion of all concerning the same, yet there is not easily found a disagreement concerning the hour of the death of Christ: provided that all agree that Christ expired his soul at the ninth hour of the day, or the third as we speak in the afternoon, and most also agree that the crucifixion took place around midday, namely at the sixth hour of the day, at which hour Adam is also considered to have fallen, so that the hour, no less than the day of the transgression, corresponds to the hour and day of redemption: just as Theophylact observes: On the sixth day man was created, who also at the sixth hour ate from the tree: therefore at the same hour that the Lord created man, he also cured the fall, being affixed to the cross on the sixth day and at the sixth hour. Thus the hour of the death of Christ can also be compared with the time of the judgment of the first-created and the promulgation of the Proto-Evangelium. For the Lord came to the rest of the day, as the Targum Onkelos rendered the words of Moses in Genesis III, 8, 'at the breeze of the day', that is, around the evening, at about the ninth hour of the day: to which time the Hebrews, with Lyranus as witness, refer this, so that he might cite and condemn, and at the same time by the voice of the Gospel might raise up and vivify the first-created, who, as Irenaeus lib. V. advers. haeres. warned, in the last days, at the evening of the world, likewise had to undergo death around the evening of the day of the great passion, and by his death liberate us from condemnation and death and vivify us. The paschal lamb was to be slaughtered between the two evenings, Exodus XII, 6, that is, at the third hour in the afternoon, before the fifth, or sunset, Deuteronomy XVI, 6, or as the sun was declining toward sunset, therefore, as Josephus reports in lib. XVI. Antiq. cap. X, from the ninth hour until the eleventh of the day according to the Hebrews, the paschal victims were slaughtered. Christ, the true paschal Lamb, willed to be slaughtered for us around the evening of the day, at the ninth hour, which is our third.

QUESTION XIV.

How does the other half of the last week of Daniel stand?

That the other half must be commenced from the passion and death of Christ by reason of the term from which, is indubitably certain from the words of Daniel. The term to which, therefore, must be sought in the fourth year after the death of Christ. However, it is not necessary that we investigate the half of the fourth year after the death of Christ precisely and mathematically, just as the passion of Christ did not fall so precisely into the middle of the fourth year of his ministry: it will be sufficient for the completion of the angelic prophecy if the character of the completed epoch of Daniel manifests itself about four years after Christ suffered. Such as we consider to be both the reception of the Gentiles into the communion of the Church, and the new denomination of the faithful, which they received from Christ at Antioch. For about four years after the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, Peter entered unto the Gentiles (Acts 10) and conferred with Paul (Galatians 1:17), and the nomenclature of Christians began (Acts 11), as Leonhard Crenzheim at the year 4008, Bucholzer in his Chronological Index, and Alsted in his Chronology observe after the blessed Luther. In the fourth year after the death of Christ, Peter learned by the vision of the sheet full of serpents that the Gospel was to be preached also to the Gentiles, and he baptized the Centurion with his family, as Tirinus notes in his Sacred Chronicle, chapter 50, and in the autumn of that year the 70 weeks of Daniel end. Johannes Temporarius, in his Chronological Demonstrations, book 3, page 198, agrees that the 69 weeks of Daniel, that is, 483 years, definitely fall into the 15th year of Tiberius, in which Christ was washed by John in the Jordan: For then, he says, the Messiah appeared, proclaimed in heaven: This is my beloved Son: Proclaimed on earth: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. From that time Christ began to perform his office, to which he had been destined before the ages. He takes on disciples, he exerts signs of divine power at the wedding. He casts the merchants out of his Father's house, he publishes the Gospel, teaching that the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand (Matthew 4, Mark 1, Luke 3, and John 1). Furthermore, Temporarius teaches that Christ was to be cut off, and that the last week, though not completed, yet the half of the 70th week was to put an end to the sacrifices and victims, which were a shadow of the Lamb once immolated. The Chronicle of Carion also, book 3, page 125, ends the 69 weeks at the Baptism of Christ, and places the passion of Christ in the middle of the last year

Christ 34. Furthermore 35. He observes that Christ, in the 19th year of Tiberius, Paul was converted, and stayed in the city of Damascus, and because of plots was let down from the wall and departed into Arabia, and taught there for three years, afterwards came to Jerusalem and stayed there fifteen days with Peter, and that this meeting of Peter and Paul fell either at the end of Tiberius or the beginning of Caligula, namely in the year of Christ 38. Thus the Belgian annotators, as well as Vorstius, and also Wilhelmus Langius and Philippus Lansbergius, begin the last week with the Ministry of Christ, and finish it in the fourth year after the death of Christ; the latter, in book II of Sacred Chronology, chapter 11, teaches that the LXX weeks began in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, from there LXIX flowed to the baptism of Christ, in the middle of the last week sacrifices were abolished by the death of Christ, and by the rending of the veil of the temple the cessation of legal sacrifices and worships was signified. Four years after the death of Christ, Paul met with Peter in Jerusalem, and from there set out into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, preached the Gospel to the Gentiles, and the LXX weeks were completed. Johannes Wichmann also agrees concerning the end of the weeks in book I of Sacred Chronology, page 171, that Christ himself performed the public duty of teaching for the latter half of the last week, that is, for 3 1/2 years, but after his death, the remaining part of that week was fulfilled by the Apostles. I pass over the fact that some observe that the Council of Jerusalem was celebrated almost four years after the ascension of Christ: in which it was concluded that Jews and Gentiles belong to the Church without discrimination, to which the authors of the Weimar Annotations also subscribe. Blessed Luther judges, in the Chronology exhibited in Tom. IV of the Jena edition, page 600, that almost in the third year after the resurrection of Christ, the law was abrogated by a public decree in the council of the Apostles, and liberty from the law was promulgated. And the same great man determines, in his explanation of the LXX weeks of Daniel, that this was done almost in the 3rd or 4th year after the resurrection, that is, in the middle of the last week, page 617. If anyone should call this last point into doubt from the Chronotaxis, the former characters are nevertheless easily sufficient for designating the end of the other half of the LXX weeks. And here let this be the end of our Biblical Chronicle: for which granted favor may the Triune God be blessed without end, for ever and ever Amen.

Latin:

I. N. J. CHRONICON BIBLICUM DE EPOCHIS ET ANNIS VET. TEST. A MUNDI CONDITU AD FINEM LXX. HEBDOMADUM DANIELIS. PRÆMITTUNTUR TABULÆ CHRONOLOGICÆ Cum QUÆSTIONUM INDICE. Subjuncta est DISCUSSIO INFALLIBILITATIS NOVÆ CHRONOLOGIÆ BIBLICÆ CHRISTIANI RAVII. Et Præfatio de SCALIGERI, & aliorum in Chronologia Sacra a Canone Scripturæ divaricationibus & Chronici S. emenda- tioris necessitate, & utilitate. AVTORE D. ABRAHAM CALOVIO, P.P. PRIMARIO ET ELECT. SAX. SUPERINT. GENER.

illustrem Abramo factam, annorum CCCCXXVII.

David natus est.

Saul Constitutus est Rex Israelis: ac regimini per 10. annos præfuit.

D. ABRAHAM ET SUPERI GENE CHRONICO

SECTIO I. DE EPOCHIS VET. TESTAM. PRÆ- CIPUIS IN GENERE.

Epochas, quæ annos complectuntur mutuo se excipientes, usque ad finem hebdoma- dum Danielis, quibus tempora Vet. Test. terminantur, quantum ad complemen- tum vaticiniorum de Christo Propheticorum, im- primis utile est, ac necessarium, sedulo observare. Nam uti scopus sacrarum literarum præcipuus est Christus, cujus adventui definitum fuit in arcano SS. Trinitatis τὸ πλήρωμα τẽ χρόνẽ, Gal. 4, 4. de quo quæsiverunt, & scrutati sunt Prophetæ, εἰς τίνα ἢ ποῖον καιρὸν ἐδήλꙋ τὸ ἐν ἀυτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστẽ, in quod & quale tempus significavit in eis Spiritus Christi, prænuncians eas, quæ in Christo sunt, passiones, & po- steriores glorias, 1. Pet. 1, 11. ita de illis maxime tem- poribus in ἐρευνήσει Scripturæ Propheticæ nos oportet esse solicitos. Cætera enim tempora ob il- lud πλήρωμα τẽ χρόνꙋ indicata sunt, aut ad regnum Christi, ad gloriam divinam in throno Majestatis exaltati pertinent, ac statum ejusdem sub N. T. concernunt. Quæ vero minus luculenta sunt, quoad usque nondum luce complementi illustran- tur; utpote quæ in Daniele designata, quæ aliquam sane lucem ex Apocalypsi, a Filio Dei, discipulo cha- rissimo tradita accipiunt, clausi tamen sunt, signa- tique sermones illi, usque ad præfinitum comple- menti tempus, Dan. 12, 9. quoad plenam, solidam, ac certam intelligentiam.

EPOCHARUM autem illarum, quæ inter se cohærent ad semen benedictum Verum MES- SIAM, CHRISTUM JESUM, ejusque passionem, resurrectionem, ascensionem, ac sceptri ejus ad gentes emissionem Septem deprehenduntur per- quam illustres.

Prima est a Prot-Evangelio, de semine mulie- ris, caput infernalis serpentis contrituro, CHRI- STO nempe JESU, τῷ Θεανθρώπῳ, Mundi Redem- tore, mox a mundi conditu & Protoplastorum la- psu, a Filio Dei promulgato, usque ad diluvium, quo primus mundus, Præconi justitiæ Christi Noa- cho incredulus, exceptis paucis, octo nempe ani- mabus, periit, servato illo fideli Dei servo cum suis in arca, propter Semen illud benedictum, ob quod etiam instaurandus per illas primi mundi reliquias erat novus orbis. Quæ complectitur annos 1656.

Secunda Annorum periodus, vel Epocha in- de a repetitione, & confirmatione Prot-Evangelii, in novo orbe, post diluvium facta, de gratia homi- ni, etsi tantum prono ad malum ab infantia, ob sa- crificium odoris suavitatis, per quod solum propi- tii reddimur Deo, exhibenda, incipit, quod nempe Deus ultra maledicere terræ haud velit, idque pro- pter Adamum, vel hominem illum unum, in quo ob- tingit omnibus gratia, Gen. 8, 21. Rom. 5, 15. quodque propter eundem dignatus fuerit de novo benedi- cere mortalibus Noæ, & filiis ejus, statuto gratiæ pacto cum humano genere, atque illustri signo Iridis confirmato, Gen. 9, 1. 11. seqq. Terminus Epochæ est promissio Abrahæ, Patri credentium, de semine be- nedicto facta, cum in Ure Chaldæorum vocaretur, & e Charane in Canaan peregrinaretur, Gen. 11, 31. c. 12, 1. 2. 3. 4. Tota periodus est 427. annorum, nempe 222. a diluvio usque ad Tharam, 130. usq; ad Abrahamum, & 75. ad Ἐπαγγελίαν, Abrahæ factam Gen. 12, 4. quæ postea eidem Patriarchæ Sacramen- to Circumcisionis obsignata fuit, Gen. 17.

Tertia Epocha initium cœpit a dicta promis- sione, Abrahæ facta, ejusdemque peregrinatione; & terminata est in Exodo, scil. eductione ex Ægypto, cum Sacramentum agni Paschalis institutum, ac porro Lex tradita, non ut evacuaretur promissio, sed ut pædagogus ad Christum esset. Quæ comple- ctitur 430. annos, teste Apostolo Gal. 3, 17. ipsoque Mose, Exod. 12, 40.

Quarta ab Exodo fluxit ad exstructionem Tem- pli Salomonei, quod typus erat templi corporis Chri- sti, & in quo doctrina de Messia propagata, cum Verbi præconio, tum figurarum, qua Sacerdotium, sa- crificia, altaria, arcam fœderis, & ejusmodi alia, ad- umbratione. Hæc annorum fuit 480. 1. Reg. 6, 1.

Quinta est ab exstructione Templi Salom. ad indulgentiam libertatis populi, novique templi ædifi- candi a Cyro, post servitutem LXX. annorum Baby- lonicam, & πανολεθρίαν prioris templi, divino munere concessam: siquidem in terra promissa, temploque posteriori Messias officium suum pera- gere debuerit. Atque hæc fuit annorum 424. usque ad prioris Templi destructionem, quibus acce- dunt porro anni 52. usque ad libertatis indulgentiam sub Cyri Monarchia, ut hæc Periodus tota annorum 476. sit.

Sexta Epocha a soluta captivitate Babylonica porrigitur usque ad initium LXX. hebdomadum Danielis, vel exitum sermonis de reparandis sacris, & rædificanda urbe, in certitudinem adventus Messiæ, h. e. usque ad annum septimum Artaxerxis Longimani. Quæ complectitur annos 78.

Septima est hebdomadum LXX. Danielis. In quarum sexagesimam quintam currentem incidit nativitas Christi, in initium vero ultimæ auspicium muneris Christi, in medium passio, mors, resurrectio & ascensio ejusdem, in finem vocatio Gentium, & no- vum fidelium nomen, quod a Christo acceperunt, Christiani nuncupati: ubi Vetus Testamentum pro- prie desiit, Novum plene incepit. Hæc tota est 490. annorum. Sed 483. usque ad Christi mini- sterium, 453. ad nativitatem ejusdem.

Ita ergo se habebunt Epochæ ad Christum a condito mundo, vel promulgatione Prot-Evange- lii:

I. A mundi conditu (quem brevi post sequuta est promissio seminis mulieris Paradisiaca) usque ad diluvium anni 1656

II. A renovatione promissionis gratiæ Noacho fa- ctæ, usque ad vocationem Abrahæ 427

III. Ab ἐπαγγελίᾳ Abrahæ de semine benedicto, usque ad eductionem ex Ægypto 430

IV. Inde ad exstructionem Templi Salomonici 480

V. Inde ad libertatem exstruendi novi Templi 476

VI. Inde ad initium septimanarum Danielis 78

VII. Inde ad Adventum Christi 453

Ad Baptismum ergo Christi anni fluxere ab orbe condito 4030. qui cum cadat in annum ætatis Christi 30. annus nativitatis Christi erit annus Mundi 4000. & additis ad annum baptismi Christi a mundi conditu 7. annis postrema septimana Danielis, prodituri sunt anni 4037. a mundi nempe conditu, usque ad finem LXX. hebdomadum.

QUÆSTIO I. An Nox prior Die fuerit in Creatione?

Philoponus, Marius Victorinus, ut & Procopius Gazæus diem priorem faciunt; at historia Creationis contrarium docet, quia tenebras primum super faciem abyssi, condita massa primigenia, quam Chaos vulgo dicimus, fuisse testatur, quæ primordiales tenebræ per horas duodecim ante lucem conditam durarunt, & noctem primam constituerunt; ubi vero lux a Deo crearetur, mane primum exortum est, & per reliquas νυχθημερινꙋ horas diffusa lux, motuque ejus peracto, donec tenebræ redirent, prima constituta est dies. Negat quidem Petavius tenebras primordiales noctem primam fuisse, sed quia nullæ aliæ lucem primigeniam anteverterunt, illæ utique noctem primam constituerunt, etsi non privatio tantum lucis fuerit, ut in sequentibus diebus, sed mera negatio, atque ideo Moses vesperam priorem facit diluculo in Hexaëmeri descriptione: Et fuit vespera, & fuit mane, Gen. 1, 5.

Unde Judæi etiam a vespera initium diei faciunt, qui non aliunde id acceperunt, quam a Patriarchis & Adamo. Conf. Exod. 12, 18. qui mos aliis etiam gentibus & populis a priscis temporibus receptus fuit. Idem etiam de Atheniensibus, Phœnicum in multis discipulis, tradit Gellius l. III. c. 2. De Numadibus Nic. Damascenus, Numidæ, inquit, in Lybia non ex diebus, sed ex noctibus tempora sua computant. De Druidibus Plinius l. XVI. Hist. Natural. c. ult. Luna quæ principia mensium annorumque hic facit. Etiam Gallos olim id in usu habuisse Cæsar docet l. VI. Belli Gallici: Spatia omnis temporis, non numero dierum, sed noctium finiunt; quod de Germanis quoque antiquis Tacitus notavit: Nec dierum numerum ut nos, sed noctium computant: sic constituunt, sic condicunt, nox ducere diem videtur. Servare hunc morem etiam nunc Bohemos, & Polonos, Grotius alicubi observavit.

QUÆSTIO II. An Dies septima inde a divino Creationis Sabbato cultui divino consecrata fuerit?

NOn a creatione statim, sed demum circa legis promulgationem Sabbati sanctificationem institutam esse, cum Joh. Prideaux, Rob. Loco, Franciscus Gomarus post Tostatum Abulensem contendit, sed a prima creatione eam deducendam esse, primum ex ipsa Creationis historia Gen. 2, 2. 3. liquet: Deus benedixit diei septimo, & sanctificavit eum, ubi nec ὑσέρωσις, nec παρένθεσις locum habet: Mosen enim ea in simplici & luculenta historia conjunxisse, quæ maximo temporum intervallo disjuncta fuerint, perabsurdum foret. Quod de- inde ex loco Apostolico Ebr. 4, 9. etiam confirmatur, qui quietem diei Sabbati, a perfectione operum Dei intra hexaëmeron, deducit. Adhæc ex ipsa lege de Mannæ collectione, Exod. 16, 27. idem haud obscure comprobatur, quia Sabbati sanctificatio ibi exigebatur, lege nondum promulgata, non ut res nova, sed quæ olim jam instituta. Porro inconveniens est, Patriarchas vel nullum statum diem cultus divini habuisse, vel ex mera ἐθελοθρησκεία sibi aliquem diem definiisse. Deniq́; non penes Ebræos tantum extra dubium fuit, Sabbatum in- stitutum fuisse, cum Deus septimo mundi die quievit, uti Philo l. III. de Vita Mosis, diem Sabbati a na- tura ait habere privilegium, ex quo mundo natalis fa-ctus est. (Adde & Joseph. l. I. Antiq. c. 2.) Sed & nationes aliæ ab omni ævo septem dierum revolutio-nem observarunt, cujus originem nullam aliam esse potuisse Andreas Rivetus in Append. ad Explic. De-calogi colligit, quam inveteratam opinionem, quod sex diebus mundus creatus fuerit, & septimo cessatum ab opere sit, & ita ab hac prima hebdomade reliquæ nu-meratæ sint. Antiquissimas gentes, priusquam apud eas obtineret ratio computandi per annos & menses, temporum spatia per septimanas distinxif-se e Chronologicis Georg. Syncelli observat Salmasius. Josephus adversus Appionem nullam, ait, esse ur-bem Græcam, nullam barbaram, quam non pervaserit mos septimæ diei, qua Judæi feriantur. Philo de die septimo, Est, inquit, dies festus, non uni urbi, aut re-gioni, sed universo. Quibus adde, quod ex Aristo-bulo adfert Euseb. lib. XIII. Præpar. Evang. c. 12. ex Hesiodo, Homero, & Callimacho Clemens Alex. l. V. Strom. & quod Dion. Cassius l. 33. morem per septe-nos dies tempora computandi, ab Ægyptiis ad omne humanum genus manasse docet; quem vetustissi-mum fuisse, ex Herodoto l. II. constat.

Neque de eo, quod ab initio mundi institutum fuerit Sabbatum, vel inter Patres dubium fuit, vid. Chrysost. Homil. IX. in c. II. Genes. Tertull. l. IV. ad-versus Jud. & contra Marcion. l. IV. c. 12. Theodoret. ad Gen. 2. Augustinus ad Casalanum; vel inter Pontificios, (si Abulensem excipias;) Videatur Ca-tharinus, Genebrardus, Salianus, Emanuel Saá, Cor-nel. a Lap. Tirinus; vel inter Reformatos, qui præter Triumviros illos Neotericos omnes communi vo-ce id affirmant: Zwinglius, Calvinus, Beza, Mar-tyr, Pelicanus, Bullinger, Gualtherus, Zanchius, A-retius, Ursinus, Bucanus, Junius, Bertramus, Pa-ræus, Zepperus, Martinius, Alstedius, &c. vel inter Nostros, qui ὁμοθυμαδὸν hic consentiunt. Videan-tur ea, quæ Rivetus & Walæus Gomaro opposue-re. Denique Judæos etiam modernos nonnullos, Sabbatum ante Abrahamum aliosque Patriarchas cultum esse, fateri, e Menasse Ben-Israel problema-te 8. de creatione constat, qui eam sententiam in-ter alia confirmat e Schemoth Rabba, quod Moses a Pharaone in Ægypto petierit, ut afflicto populo per-mitteret unum diem in hebdomade cessare a labori-bus, eoque impetrato ex traditione Sabbatum elegerit.

Quod vero Abulensis, & Gomarus ad Justinum, Irenæum, Tertullianum, Eusebium & Damascenum provocant, qui Sabbatum e lege Mosaica deducere videntur, observandum, illos vel de rigore in lege sancito loqui, vel certe non novitatem sanctificatio-nis Sabbati, sed innovationem ejus sub Mose tantum respicere.

QUÆSTIO III. Utrum anni a Spiritu S. designati tum ante, tum post diluvium ejusdem quantitatis sint?

NOn defuerunt, qui annos a Mose in Vitis Pa-triarcharum ante diluvium designatos, reli-quis haud pares, sed multo minores esse putarint, ne insolitam Patriarcharum illorum μακροβιότητα admitterent. Sed annos Mosaicos menses XII. ha-buisse e plurimis Scripturæ locis constat, nec ullo modo credendum est Spiritum S. alios atœ, alios an-nos in diversis Scripturæ locis constituisse; sic enim omnia incerta redderentur in calculo sacro, omnes-que Chronologiæ rationes facile everterentur. Porro cum posteriorum Patriarcharum anni de mensibus aut trimestribus intelligi nequeant, ut-pote quod Abrahamus 100. Jacobus 130. annos nati, ceu decrepiti seneciones introducuntur, & plerique Jacobi filii ante 20. annum liberos pro- creasse dicuntur; in prioribus vero nullum distin- ctionis vel diversitatis vestigium appareat, summa temeritas fuerit, aliter priores annos intelligere, ac distinctionem aliquam annorum præter Scri- pturam comminisci. Et quam absurda sit illa menstruorum, bimestrium, ac trimestrium annorum computatio, ab exemplis facile patet: v. c. cum le- gimus Mahaleelem & Enochum genuisse anno æta- tis 65. si menstrui anni intelligantur, sexto anno so- lari eos generasse dicendum erit; si bimestres, de- cimo; si trimestres, decimo quinto. Denique ne dubium supersit, quales anni a Mose intelligantur, Moses ipse in descriptione diluvii annum definivit cum Mensibus suis, cum mentionem fecit 150. die- rum anni diluviani, Gen. 7, 24. qui quinque absolve- rint menses, a secundi mensis die 17. ad septimi mensis diem 17. c. 8, v. 4. decimi item mensis, v. 5. & 40. dierum ab initio mensis X. qui ad duodecimum mensem porriguntur, unde annum illum 12. men- sium fuisse oportet: siquidem Spiritus S. designa- tis mensibus, & diebus anni diluviani, eundem ita definiverit ab ineunte diluvio ad finem ejusdem, ut 12. menses τριακονθημέρους integrum annum con- stituisse, minime obscurum videatur. Adde quod gentiles etiam illorum, qui primos homines secuti sunt, vitam ad mille fere annos durasse perhibeant. Berosus in Chaldaicis, Manetho in Ægyptiacis, Hieronymus in Phœnicis, Hestiæus, Hecatæus, Hella- nicus in Græcis, (quos omnes Scriptores suo adhuc tempore manentibus libris testes citat Josephus li- bro I. Hist. antiquæ c. IV. ac præter hos Acusilaum, Ephorum, Nicolaum Damascenum) & inter Poetas Hesiodus; ne dicam quod Arcadas ad 300. annos vivere solitos, ad VIII. Æneidos notarit Servius.

QUÆSTIO IV. Quænam forma Anni fuerit, in sacris Literis designati?

DE antiqua anni forma ex anno diluviano judi- cium fieri potest. Ante Exodum, Patriar- charum temporibus in Chaldæa, & Ægypto Ebræos annum æquabilem Chaldaicum & veterem Ægyptia- cum dierum 360, cum justa dierum ἐπαγομένων & superfluarum horarum intercalatione, habuisse, B. D. Behmius lib. I. tit. 2, c. 3. & tit. 3, c. 2. Manuduct. Chronol. statuit, quem annum non Lunarem, sed fere solarem, quia per Patriarchas in Ægyptum ve- nit, Ægyptium nominant. Nam cum diluvium inierit die 17. mensis II. Gen. 7, 11. decrementum vero die 17. mensis VII. ceperit post 150. dies c. 7, 24. c. 8, 3. 4. quinque menses fecisse 150. dies ἀναν- τιῤῥήτως certum est: atque inde porro colligitur, mensem unum diebus 30. constitisse, idemque de reliquis septem mensibus habendum esse. Quia vero ad anni integritatem ita desunt quinque dies, eorum intercalatione opus fuit: quæ vel per men- sem Embolimeum, vel ut rectius Keplerus in Eclo- gis Chronicis p. 89. putat, ita facta est, ut duodeci- mus mensis 35. dierum fuerit. Nam 365. dierum fuisse annos Veteres Ægyptiorum; & hos illam for- mam ab Ebreis accepisse, dubitandum non est. Diod. Siculus de Thebais Ægyptiis l. I. Biblioth. Dies, inquit, non ad Lunæ, sed Solis motum exigentes, tricenos mensibus dies tribuunt, & post duodecimum quemvis mensem quinque dies cum quadrante adji- ciunt, eoque pacto calculum annuum absolvunt. Hero- dotus in Euterpe, seu lib. II. de Ægyptiis, Refere- bant, inquit, omnium hominum primos Ægyptios annum reperisse, distinguentes eum in 12. temporum menses, & hæc comperisse ex astris, qui eo prudentius hæc agunt, ut mihi videtur, quam Græci, quod Græ- ci quidem tertio quoque anno intercalarem mensem in- troducunt ob tempestates (seu opportuna rerum tem- pora) Aegyptii vero numero triginta dierum, qui- bus 12. menses taxant, adjiciunt quotannis quinos dies, unde eis ratio circuli temporum constat eodem redeuntis. Strabo l. 17. de Aegyptiis ita habet: Hi non Lunae, sed Solis cursu annos numerant duodecim mensibus, quorum quisque 30. constet diebus, quinq́; dies quotannis adjicientes: Ad totius anni comple- mentum, cum quaedam diei particula excurrat, pe- riodum quandam componunt. Quintus Curtius l. 3. de priscis Persis, Magi, inquit, proximi Patrium carmen canebant, Magos 365. Juvenes sequebantur, puniceis amiculis velati, diebus totius anni numero pares. Porro ipsam Julianam anni novi dispositio- nem opera Sosigenis Mathematici, qui Alexandri- nus erat, ad exemplum Aegyptiorum factam Macro- bius perhibet l. I. Saturnal. c. 14. Imitatus (Cajus Julius Caesar) Aegyptios, solos divinarum rerum omnium conscios, ad numerum Solis, qui diebus sin- gulis tricenis sexaginta quinque & quadrante cursum conficit, annum dirigere contendit. Polyaenus l. 1. Stra- tegemat. scribit, Herculem filiae donasse 365. pagos Indiae secundum anni dies. Censorinus de die natali, Annus civilis Aegyptiorum, ait, solos habet dies 365. sine ullo intercalari. Neque abnuit huic sententiae Pe- tavius l. 9. de Doctr. Temp. cap. 9. Itaq́; Patriarcha- rum a diluvii tempore nihil prohibet menses singulos tricenarios extitisse: quod reliquum erat ex anno so- lari, id est in calcem anni rejectum, aut certis anno- rum evolutis spatiis admissum.

Leonhard. Marius Comment. ad Gen. p. 69. observat, quod Judaei ante egressum ex Aegypto, ac primi etiam Patriarchae anni eandem rationem habuerint, utpote quae apud omnes gentes Orientales inveniatur, sine ulla prima illius institutionis mentione, quam Patriarchas ideo adhibuisse censet, quod in Aegypto, Cananaea, Chal- dea, Mesopotamia admixti aliis gentibus fuerint, penes quos illa usitata. Sed rectius refertur ad Patriarchas ipsos auctores, a quibus ad Aegyptios, aliasque gentes per eorundem informationem vel conversationem, ut alia multa, pervenit.

Nec vero computo derogatur per formam recentiorem anni Ebraei, qui Lunaris est, sed ad sola- rem accommodatus, diebus constans 354. in 12. lu- nationes, s. menses lunares distributus, quorum alii 30. alii 29. dies habent; illi pleni, hi cavi appel- lantur. Unde quotannis ad complementum An- ni Solaris dies 11. desiderantur, qui Epactae dicuntur, ex quibus colligitur mensis 13. ἐμβολιμαῖος, dictus Ve Adar, id est, alter Adar, qui in fine anni adjicitur, & semper 30. dies habet, ut Annus Embolimaeus ordinarie sit 384. dierum. Quae mensis intercala- tio facit, ut universo annorum calculo nihil decedat, etiamsi forma annorum singulorum juxta triplicem illam jam commemoratam rationem variet. Vi- deatur de variis annorum formis tractatus a Thoma Lydiat editus.

QUAESTIO V.

Quomodo designentur Ebraeorum Menses?

IN Codice Veteris Testamenti designantur Men- ses imprimis numeris; atque ita omnium Men- sium fit mentio: Primi Mensis Gen. VIII, 13. Exod. XL, 2. & 17. Secundi Mensis Gen. VII, 11. Num. IX, 11. Tertii 2. Chron. XV, 10. Quarti Jerem. LII, 6. Quinti Jer. LII, 12. Sexti Aggaei I, 1. Se- ptimi Gen. VIII, 4. II. Chron. V, 3. Octavi I. Reg. XII, 32. Noni I. Chron. XXVII, 12. Decimi Gen. VIII, 5. Undecimi Deut. I, 3. Duodecimi II. Reg. XXV, 27. Denique omnes duodecim men- ses ita numeris designati sunt, I. Chron. XXVII. cap. Sortiuntur tamen menses alias quoque appel- lationes in Sacris in textu Ebræo, ut & in Græco in Maccabaicis. Quæ nomina juvat cum Romanis conferre, adjectis ob Ptolemæum Ægyptiacis ap- pellationibus.

TABULA NOMINUM MENSIUM EBRÆORUM & ALIORUM, juxta ordinem BIBLICUM.

Apud Ebræos ante & post captivitatem Babylo- nicam. |Apud Chaldæos & Ægyptios. | Apud Macedonas & alios Græcos in li- bris Maccab. | Apud Roma- nos. Primus, Nisan, Neh. II, 1. Esth. III, 1. qui & Abib. Exod. XIII, 4. Phanemoth Ξανθικὸς. Nisan Xanthi- cum dicit Joseph.l.I. antiquit. c. 5. Martius. Secundus, Iiar, qui & Ziv. I. Reg. VI, 1. & 37. Pharmuthi Ἀρτεμίσιος. Aprilis. Tertius, Sivan, Esth. VIII, 9. Pachan Δαίσιος. Majus. Quartus, Tamuz Payni Πάνεμος. Junius. Quintus, Ab Epiphi Λῶος. Quintilis. Sextus, Elul, Neh. VI, 16. Mesori Γορπιαῖος. Sextilis. Septimus, Thisri, qui & Ethanim, I. Reg. VIII, 2. Thoth Ὑπερβερεταῖος. September. Octavus, Marchesvan, qui & Bul, 1. Reg. VI, 38. Paophi Δίος. October. Nonus, Caslev, Nehem. I, 1. Zach. VII, 1. Athyr Ἀπελλαῖος. November. Decimus, Thebet, Esth. II, 16. Chojas Αὐδυναῖος. December. Undecimus, Sebeth. Tybi Περίτιος. Januarius. Duodecimus, Adar, Esth. III, 7. 13. Mochyr Δύςρος, qui διοσκορίνθιος, 2. Macc. XI, 21. Februarius.

Solent quidam gemino ordine Menses Ebræo- rum exhibere, quorum alterum primævum fa- ciunt, juxta quem autumnales menses præcedunt, sequuntur hyemales, postea vernales, ultimo loco æstivales; ut annus inchoetur a Mense Thisri, finia- tur in mense Elul: alterum verò dicunt Exodicum, quem in Tabella exhibuimus, a Mense Nisan ver- nali ad Mensem Adar, ultimum hyemalem. Ideo geminum annum constituere solent: Politicum a mense Thisri incipientem, in nundinationibus, aliisque Politicis rebus observatum; & Ecclesiasti- cum, qui mense Nisan exordium sumserit, juxta quem festivitates celebratæ sint.

Non autem probatur B. Luthero hæc Judaica distinctio Comment. in Gen. c. 7. f. 130. Sed ego hanc Judæorum rationem non probo, qui statuunt duo anni principia. Cur enim quatuor principia fa- ciunt, cum quatuor distincta tempora sint, secundum æquinoctia & solstitia? igitur horum temporum initia etiam erunt distincta; sed tutius est sequi ordinatio- nem divinam. Secundum hanc primus Mensis est Mensis Aprilis, seu illa Lunatio, quæ æquinoctio ver- no est proximior. Nam quod Judæi, quia æquino- ctium autumnale exitus anni dicitur, etiam initium anni autumnale statuunt, id ex imperitia faciunt; non enim alia ratione exitum anni vocant, quam quod tum cessabant opera rustica, & omnes fructus collecti erant, ac deportati domum. Hæc B. Lutherus. In hoc enim loco Exod. 23, 16. de anni exitu præcipue fundamentum quærunt anni civilis: sed, Luthero nostro judice, imperite, cum solum exitus anni ob cessationem, vel finem operarum rusticarum dica- tur. Unde Edwardus Simsonius in Parasceve ad Chronicum Catholicum, inter annum civilem, quem ab Ecclesiastico non facit diversum, & annum rusticum distinguit. Leonh. Marius ad locum prædict. ita respondet: Quod festum tabernaculo- rum, quod 7. mense celebratur, in exitu anni celebran- dum dicitur, nomine exitus posterior anni medietas comprehenditur: quasi dicat, duo priora festa in prio- ri anni parte occurrunt, tertium vero, tabernaculo- rum, in posteriore. Alii Mosen ex Ægyptiorum consuetudine hic de anni termino locutum esse censent, cui assueti in Ægypto Israelitæ erant. A- lias autem semper a vere inchoasse annum, ac Dei ipsius mandato ita inchoandum esse, monuisse, Exod. 12, 2. Atque ita תְּקוּבַת הַשָּׁנָה revolutio anni in vere sub æquinoctium vernale constituitur, 2. Chron. 24, 33. quo tempore reges in bellum prodire solebant, 2. Sam. 11, 1. ut & תְּשׁוּבַת הַשָּׁנָה reditus vel reversio anni 2. Sam. 11, 1. Reg. 20, 22. & 26. 1. Chron. 20, 1.

Quanquam vero Sabbatici & Jobelæi anni ab auctumnali æquinoctio incipiendi fuerint, Lev. 25, 9. 10. id tamen ob rusticas, vel rurales operas factum est, & peculiarem rationem habuit, (quia si a vere in- choati fuissent, cum ab omni satione & messe tum abstinendum fuerit, debuissent semper Ebræi con- tinuis duobus annis tum messe sua carere, imo qua- driennio integro, si tum sequenti anno Jobelæus supervenisset annus; vid. Tirinus in Chron. sacro c. 5.) nec inde ab orbe condito, sed post egressum ex Ægypto demum ordinatum id fuit, atque ex eo etiam in contractibus emtionis & venditionis hujus initii anni ratio habenda fuit: siquidem in illis re- spiciendum fuerit ad annos Jobelæos, ne proximus damnum pateretur, Lev. 15, 15. Quibus accede- bat, quod in Ægypto huic revolutioni anni assueti fuerint Israelitæ, unde Thekuphath Haschana, re- volutio anni, in festo collectionis frugum, quod in auctumno erat, Lev. XXIII, 39. commemo- ratur Exod. XXXIV, 22. ex consuetudine scil. Ægyptiaca, cujus vero epanorthosis facta est Exod. XII, 2. populoque mandatum, ut mensem Abib,

Abib, vel Nisan habeant pro anni principio, ut ab illa consuetudine, quam in Ægypto contraxerat, revocaretur ad pristinum Patriarcharum, & pri- mævi mundi tenorem, in anni initio. Ideoque non nisi cum grano salis accipiendum, quod Josephus lib. I. Hist. Jud. c. 5. Mosen tantum in festivitatibus & rebus divinis mensem Nisan primum constituisse, in venditionibus autem & emtionibus, & alia guber- natione, nihil de pristino ritu innovasse ait: nimirum eo sensu: quod pristinum quidem Ægyptiorum ritum hactenus Israelitis reliquerit, qua inservie- bat contractibus, quia temere immutari non pote- rat, nequaquam autem pro peculiari anni principio mensem Thisri decreto aliquo sanciverit. Non enim tam Josepho Ægyptiaco ritui adhærescenti, quam Deo, legem, non utique alienam a prioris orbis & Patriarchalis observationis consuetudine, figenti, aures hic præbendæ sunt, cum simpliciter Moses, & sine distinctione anni Ecclesiastici & Politici definiverit Ex. 12, 2. Mensis iste vobis caput mensium erit, primus ipse vobis in mensibus anni. Aliud enim est, sancire diversum anni principium, Ecclesiasti- cum nempe & Politicum, quod Scaliger vult, in Mose autem nuspiam factum legitur: aliud diver- sam alicubi de revolutione & exitu anni adhibere locutionem, quod κατ’ ἄνθρωπον, vel ex consueto mo- re loquendi fieri potuit, manente unico tantum anni principio. Cum enim menses in scriptura numeris consignentur, sane haud consentaneum vero est, illam numericam designationem alio atque alio modo a Deo ipso factam, vel diversa significatione a Spiritu S. adhibitam esse, ut v. g. primus fuerit, ac dictus sit mensis, qui septimus est, & ita porro: ma- xime quia Spiritus S. nuspiam diversam illam enu- merationis rationem indicio aliquo designavit, neque confusionis, sed ordinis & distinctionis autor est, cum ex illa diversa designatione facile oriatur confusio.

QUÆSTIO VI.

Utrum Anni omnes completi intelligendi sint, qui referuntur citra particulam imminuen- tem in Scriptura?

SUnt, qui negant, completos intelligendos esse, quod verisimile non sit, omnes, plane exacto anno illo, quo referuntur, filios genuisse: unde concludit Rollenhagen, nos latere præcisam totius summæ numerationem. Dionysius etiam Petavius l. 9. de doctr. temp. c. 17. Nullo argumento certo col- ligi posse censet, utrum, qui anni Patriarcharum in Scriptura numerantur, completi sint, ac vertentes, an inchoati? ac credibile esse, non omnium saltem Patriarcharum annos integros fuisse, cum genue- runt. Ideoque tempus Epocharum diluvii & natalis Abrahæ certo, ac sine dubitatione minime constitui posse. Jacobus vero Capellus quatuor primarum ge- nerationum annos in numeros rotundos definen- tes (denarios puta, vel quinarios) pro inchoatis vel decurtatis accepit.

At quamvis non credendum, uno eodemque die, vel mense, Patriarchas omnes genuisse, uti Ebræi nonnulli, referente Davide Kimchio, existimarunt, Mense primo Patriarchas natos esse, qui ideo Etha- nim a præstantia & fortitudine dictus fuerit: de eo tamen dubium nobis esse non debet, annos illos, quos Chronologiæ causa, quia de tempore præter- lapso aliunde constare nemini poterat, revelavit Spiritus S. ita conjunctim numerandos esse, & in summam colligendos, ut computus inde sacer certo habeatur: non enim existimandum, incertos re- linquere nos voluisse Spiritum S. dum tam solicite annos putat, siquidem etiam ipse nos præeat, in summam colligendo annos παιδογονίας, & qui eos ad vitæ finem fequuti sunt Gen. 5. Recte hic Ufferius Sect. in Chron. sacra p. 57. Ut postremus annus παιδογονίας unius Patriarchæ mensibus aliquot deficiat, alterius vero intra unum, aut alterum mensem protensus fuerit, ad summam rei nihil interest; quum utrobique compensatione facta in annorum totius intervalli aggregatione fiat exæquatio, quæ ad mundi ætatem, & seriem patefaciendam abunde sufficiat.

Non ergo est, ut cum Petavio hinc Pyrrhonismum in Chronologiam Biblicam invehamus, omniaque dubia & incerta, non absque ignominia Scriptorum θεοπνεύστων, atque ipsiusmet Spiritus S. reddamus. Quorsum enim tam solicite annos illos a mundi conditu numerasset Spiritus S. si nos incertos hærere voluisset? Ac nisi voluerit tradere Chronologiam per annos completos, nihil certi addiderit, ut recte Harvellæus Isagoge Chron. §. 14. col. 164. Si liceat prima mundi ætate (ita arguit Tirinus Chron. sacræ c. 10.) ab integris, quos scriptura exprimit, annis aliquid pro lybitu decerpere, idem sequentibus omnibus ætatibus licebit: atque ita erunt incerta omnes omnium Patriarcharum, Judicum & Regum Chronologia.

QUÆSTIO VII.

Quid de Computo habendum eorum, qui multis seculis calculum nostrum de annis mundi excedunt?

NOn jam de differentia aliquot annorum res est; quia innumeræ propemodum discrepantiæ in annis mundi præterlapsis penes scriptores reperiuntur. Sed de opinionibus eorum, qui pluribus seculis computum nostrum annorum mundi excedunt, & quinque millia annorum & ultra numerant a mundi conditu ad Epocham Christi vulgarem: quomodo venerabilis Beda 5199. Marianus Scotus 4192. Augustinus, & Philo 5195. Eusebius Cæsariensis 5200. Isidorus Hispalensis 5210. Sulpitius Severus 5469. Cedrenus 5493. Theophilus 5515. Alphonsus Rex Castiliæ 6484. annos a conditu mundi assignarunt: cujusmodi etiam computus est Græcorum, qui annos 5508. Æthiopum, qui 5499. Romanorum in Martyrologio, qui 5198. annos numerant. E fastis Siculis colliguntur anni 5608. ut taceamus gentilium portentosos numeros, quum, Diodoro libro 2. teste, Chaldæi 43000. annorum in suis observationibus recenseant, & Plato perhibeat, Ægyptios decem annorum millia numerare, imo tradat alicubi μυρίαν & μυρία ἔτη decies millies dena annorum millia ignotorum annorum numerari.

Quos omnes annos mundi nimium multiplicare, nemo dubitat hodie, qui veritatem Ebraicam Codicis sacri, prout par est, suspicit, ac veneratur. Isaacus vero Vossius tractatu Chronologiæ Patris nuper subjecto, ut & in Dissert. de vera ætate mundi, nec non Brianus Waltonus prolegom. 9. in Biblia πολύγλωττα Anglicana, in fine, acriter adversus Ebraicam veritatem decertantes, multis seculis annos mundi locupletare in Calviniana Ecclesia satagunt. A mundi creatione usque ad Abrahami Patriarchæ natalem annos minimum 1440. desiderari dissertatione dicta ostendere conatur Vossius: Imo Ægyptiorum, Chaldæorum, Serum antiquitates in argumentum adducit: non multum prudentior Isaaco Peirerio Præ-Adamita, qui parte prima System. Chinenses laudat, quod anno Christi 1594. numerarint annum octingenties octuagesies millesimum septuagesimum. Qui proinde, in eadem religione alias ὁμοψήφως, Robertus Bailius graviter, caftigat, atque operose refellit, opere Historico & Chronologico l. 1. c. 2. quæst. 4. & c. 4. quæst. 2. ut & Greg. Horn. Prof. Hist. in Acad. Leydensi in Diatribe contr. Vossii dissertationem.

Vix merentur confutationem tales ineptiæ. Subjiciemus tamen nonnulla ex Bailio, quibus Vos- sium suum cum antiquitatibus suis excepit. Non debuit, inquit pag. 23. doctissimus vir talibus argu- mentis sacrorum textuum veritatem oppugnare: quæ de Chaldæorum antiquitatibus extra Scripturas nar- rantur, pure puta sunt fabulæ, & deliria. Ex libris sacris Chaldæorum Magi proferebant res gestas, non modo ante diluvium; sed & ante creationem plus- quam 400000. annorum, ut refert Cicero de di- vinat. libro 1. pag. 88. & ex eo Lactantius l. 7. c. 14. Quicunq; Chaldæorum libri δυναστίας Africani pro- bant, iidem enormem illum Ciceronis numerum anno- rum 47000. testantur: hos autem Cicero vult deri- dendos, contemnendos, condemnandos stultitiæ, vani- tatis & imprudentiæ, imo judicandos mentiri, & ut habet Lactantius, delirare.

De Ægyptiacis antiquitatibus fabulosis Dio- dori laudat testimonium, qui l. 1. accepisse quidem se dicit a Sacerdotibus Ægyptiacis, Heroas a Sole regnasse annos octies decies mille, & post eos homines mortales ante suum in Ægyptum iter, regnante Pto- lomæo Dionysio juniore annos quindecies mille; sed fatetur in rebus Ægyptiacis nullam se firmitatem fide dignam, ante Trojana tempora, reperire.

De Chronologia Serum seu Chinensium re- spondet Bailius p. 24. Quis præstabit Augustinianos Monachos (nam ipsorum sola fide nituntur Chinarum Dynastiæ lib. 2. Can. Isag. a Scaligero descriptæ) certo cognovisse, in Archivis Chinensium custodita scripta diebus Mosis antiquiora?

Quod vero textum Ebræum corruptionis po- stulant, eique editionem LXX. Interpretum præ- ferunt novelli Chronologiæ sacræ turbatores, in eo principium saltim petunt, ac Papistis, & impri- mis Monacho Parisiensi Morino obstetricantur.

Πρῶτον ψεῦδος hoc est, & primarium a Ludovico Capello inventum Sophisma, inquit Bailius pag. 9. nulli rectæ rationi consonum, textus Ebraicos a LXX. Interpretibus usurpatos, ab hodiernis distinctos, non apparere, non extare, non nunc esse in rerum natura.

Non autem est, ut cum Usserio in Syntagmate de LXX. Interpretibus dicamus, versionem, quæ LXX. Interpretibus tribuitur, non ab iis esse compo- sitam; sed ab Hellenista potius obscuro, qui eam in Cleopatræ, non Ptolomæi Evergetæ Bibliotheca collo- carit: de qua Usserii opinione diximus in prolego- men. Commentar. in Genes. Agnoscit ipse Wal- tonus LXX. Interpretes non fuisse Prophetas divini- tus ita inspiratos, ut eorum versio unquam fuerit Authentica. Et fatetur e Pontificiis doctissimus Cardinalis Bellarminus l. 2. de verbo Dei c. 6. adeo corruptam esse & vitiatam, quæ superat, versionem LXX. ut omnino alia esse videatur. Recteque ur- gentur Vossius & Waltonus a Bailio, quod nulla hic discrepantia in calculo reperiatur in Ebræis Codi- cibus: Loci, inquit, Bibliorum Ebræorum, quibus nullus unquam variæ lectionis litem movit, non debent controverti. Capellus & Waltonus per varias lectio- nes sinceritatem locorum nimis quam multorum vo- carunt in dubium, valde immerito, sed ubi nullæ un- quam variæ lectiones allegatæ sunt, velle depravatum fontem Hebræum, est ab imis fundamentis autorita- tem, nedum authentiam omnium sacrorum Codicum evertere. Confitentur quibuscum agimus, neque LXX. Interpretum versionem, neque Latinam, neq Arabicam, nec ullam aliam seu antiquam, seu no- vam esse authenticam scripturam: si ergo Authen- tia & sinceritas fontium Ebræorum etiam in iis lo- cis, ubi nullæ unquam variæ lectiones apparue- runt, vocetur in dubium, nihil in ullis Bibliis mane- bit certum. Protestantibus cum Pontificiis magna fuit controversia, utrum textus Hebræi, an Latini essent authentici, sed hic multo altius ascendit lis: demitur certitudo fidei Bibliis omnibus; Græcis, Latinis & omnibus versionibus, quatenus ab He- bræo discrepant, Protestantes omnes, consentiente etiam Waltono, & sociis, fidem adimunt, si Walto- nus, & sui Bibliis etiam Hebræis errorem impin- gant, imprimis in illis locis, ubi a principio ad hunc diem nulla lectionis differentia allegata est, quæ tandem supererit scriptura divina, pura absque errore? & quæ in terris relinquetur veritatis norma, ad quam secure in omnibus liceat provocare? Hoc principium multos deducet ad Romanum Pontificem, ut con- troversiarum omnium Religionis summum judi- cem, sed plures ad Pyrrhonis Scepticam, & verum atheismum. Pontificiam autoritatem dudum explo- sam pleriq; jam rident, corruptas Bibliorum versiones non morantur, si, quod reliquum erat, Bibliorum ori- ginalium auctoritas enervetur, nihil erit cui fides certo innitatur, & quod unice vellet Satan, singuli in rebus omnibus sacris, & veritate quacunque suarum men- tium ductui relinquentur. Porro veritas illorum lo- corum in Bibliis Hebraicis non debet solicitari, quos versiones omnes antiquæ, præter unam LXX. In- terpretum sequuntur; non enim ea est auctoritas istius versionis, quæ cum textui originali, tum omni- bus, quæ extant, versionibus præponderet. Jam vero in ipsis Waltoni Bibliis, omnibus legentibus appa- ret versionem Chaldaicam, Samaritanam, Syria- cam, Arabicam, Latinam versioni Græcæ Gen. V. contradicere, & Hebraicam veritatem sequi, idem- que est in recentioribus omnibus versionibus con- sensus, ut in Gallica, Anglica, Belgica, Hispanica, Italica, & aliis apparet. Adhæc si calculus Græcorum textuum præferatur calculo Bibliorum Hebræorum, tum Chronologia tota sacra funditus evertetur; additio enim annorum mille quingentorum, omnes ra- tiones omnium recentium Chronologorum conturba- bit, eorum dissensus de diebus, mensibus, aut annis, ex- tendetur ad integra quindecim & plura secula, quic- quid ex eclipsibus, aut motibus astrorum lucis ad tem- porum characteres figendos viri docti vel olim, vel nu- per attulerunt, totum evanescet hac eorum additione tot seculorum. Sic Bælius suos sociennos confuta- vit. Non est, quod addamus his quicquam. Indigna enim uberiori confutatione sunt commenta fri- vola.

SECTIO II.

DE EPOCHA MUNDI ANTE- DILUVIANI.

HAnc vitæ Patriarcharum a Mose Gen. V. recensitorum præcipue constituunt: in qua propagata fuit doctrina Prot-Evangelii de se- mine mulieris benedicto, per sanctos illos Pa- triarchas, quorum memoriam Oceanus histori- corum conservavit. Ob quam eo dexterius pro- pagandam singularis μακροβιότης, vel longævitas vitæ sanctis Dei hominibus concessa, ut mutua illa συμβιώσει cum vetustissimis mortalium, ipsis- que adeo protoplastis fideles per orbem informari, & confirmari in vera Messiæ agnitione, & scien- tia salutis possent. Sic autem habent Epochæ hujus anni.

A conditu mundi & creatis protoplastis, quibus Ev- angelium est primitus promulgatam, ad Se- thum fluxere anni - - - 130. A Setho ad Enosum, cujus tempore cœptum est pu- blicum de nomine DOMINI præconium. 105. Ab Enos ad Kenan - - - 90. A Kenan ad Mahalaleel - - - 70. A Mahalaleel ad Jared - - 66. A Jared ad Henoch - - - 162. Ab Henoch ad Methusalah - - 65. A Methusalah ad Lamech - - 187. A Lamech ad Noah - - - 182. A Noah ad diluvium, Genes. VII, 11. - 600. Summa annorum hujus Epochæ 1656.

QUÆSTIO I. Quo anni tempore mundus conditus sit?

QUæstio hæc non respicit tam tempestates ve- ris, æstatis, autumni, hyemis, quam certam par- tem Zodiaci, in quonam signo Sol positus fuerit, sub initium creationis, nisi forte Adami, aut Palæ- stinæ rationem habere velimus, in qua mysteria re- demtionis peragenda erant. Nam comparatione eorum, qui trans æquatorem habitant, omnia inver- so modo se habent, & autumnus illis est, quando aliis Ver. Neque quæstio hæc ἀπροσδιόνυσός est, ut Hottingero visum fuit in Histor. Creat. p. 12. q. hæc anni tempora non spectent ad naturam inchoan- tem, & imperfectam, sed ad continuantem & ordina- riam: quia omnino certum oportet figi initium, annique tempus, unde deducantur cætera. Quod ergo dicit: hoc primum creationis initium nec vernum, nec autumnale esse, sed οἰκονομικὸν, etsi de primo cre- ationis die concedi possit, non tamen de die condi- ti Solis admittendum est: Poni enim debet motus Solis aliquod principium, si mensura temporis ca- pienda est, & anni ab ejus motu: quicquid de pri- mo mundi triduo sit, extraordinarie à luce primoge- nia constituto, quod dispensationis divinæ fuisse adeo inconveniens non est. Cæterum Hyemalem cardi- nem Soli sub creatione mundi nemo assignat; nec æstivum facile quisquam, si Gerhardum Mercato- rem excipias. Pro Verno vero & autumnali tem- pore certatim dimicant Chronologi tam veteres, quam recentiores.

Autumno favent Ægyptii, & alii Orientales, hodie annum ab auctumno inchoantes (vid. Hier. in Ez. c. 1.) cum Hetruscis Italorum antiquissimis; Russi item, nec non Judæi à multis seculis, qui ideo in lectionario priscæ Synagogæ primam Pa- rascham capitis I. Genes. tribuere ultimo Sabbato mensis septimi, quod eodem mundum conditum crederent, cum Chaldeo Paraphrasta in 1. Reg. VIII. v. 2. & Josepho l. 1. Antiquit. l. 4. In quam senten- tiam laudatur à Menasse Ben Israel in Conciliatio- ne in Exod. quæst. XI. Rabbi Eliezer, & Gvemara Abodazara c. 1. A Scaligero vero & aliis urgetur locus Exod. XXIII, 16. de anni exitu, & c. XXXIV, 22. de revolutione anni; nec non constitutio de annis Sabbaticis & Jobelæis mense Thisri inchoandis, Lev. XXIII, 27. c. XXV, 9. ut & initium diluvii, quod men- se II. anni cœpit, quodque Ægyptii, de quibus Jose- phus l. I. c. 4. & Firmicus Astronomus, l. VII. c. 3. videantur à Nepote Noæ Mizraim Gentis suæ conditore Genes. X, 6. aut ab Abrahamo, ut Josephus lib. I. Antiq. c. IX. & lib. cont. Appionem ex Ale- xandro Polyhistore autumat, suam consvetudinem habuisse. Cui proinde sententiæ de mundo in au- tumno condito calculum addunt Montan. lib. de secul. Mirandul. l. V. c. Astron. c. 6. Lyranus, Tostatus, Pererius, Petavius, Temporarius, Calvi- sius, Helvicius, Behmius, Mæstlinus, Bartholinus, Helwigius, Schillingius; Ubbo Emmius, Phil. Lans- bergius, Jac. Usserius, Rob. Bailius, Drusius observ. l. I. c. 18. Wolphius, Maresius Syst. Theolog. p. 92. Quibus plerisque præivit Scaliger posteriori operis de emendatione temporum editione, etsi priori editione pro Vere definiverit.

Pro Vernali autem mundi initio, cum eadem perpetua Mensium in Scriptura dinumeratione, quæ utique vel semel tantum mensem primum dixisset, qui mundo initium præbuit, nec septimi mensis no- mine mensem Thisri vocasset, si ille primordialis foret, aliæ etiam probabiles rationes militant, quæ vero ad Chronologiam proprie non spectant; ut & analogia mundi, per Christi passionem vernali tempore reparati; nec non autoritas magnorum virorum, pro qua Torniellus viginti, Ascanius Martinensis viginti quinque, Molina & alii plures allegant Patres, quamque omnium consensu in Synodo Palæstina, à Theophilo Episcopo Cæsariensi Ann. 198. congregata, probatam esse, Beda lib. de 6. ætat. & Epist. de Paschatos celebratione testa- tur. Addicti etiam huic sententiæ de vernali tem- pore sunt ex Ebræis R. Josua, ut & Arabes, Assyrii, & Chaldæi, teste Symplicio l. V. Phys. Aristot. nec non Persæ, Armenii, Æthiopes, aliique Orientis populi, & è Patribus inter Græcos Basilius in Hé- xaëm. Athanasius; Cyrillus Hierosol. Cathech. XIV. Eusebius, Nazianzenus Orat. in Novam Domin. Cyrillus Alexandrinus, Theodoretius Quæst. LXXII. in Exod. Cedrenus, Damascenus I. de fid. Orth. c. 2. Inter Latinos Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Leo M. Sermon. IX. de Passion. Dom. Isidor. Hispa- lens. l. V. Etym. Beda, Maximus Monachus, ut & Hermannus Contractus, Marianus Scotus, Strabus, Rabanus Maurus, Autor Fastorum Siculorum, Paulus Episcop. Forosempron. nec non Alphonsini Mathematici. E recentioribus B. Lutherus, Me- lanchthon, Mercerus, Polycarpus Lyserus, Krenzhe- mius, Buntingius, B. Gerhardus, Wilh. Langius, Vo- gelius, Joh. Wichmannus, Bucholcerus, item Codo- mannus, Edwardus Simsonius, Lud. Capellus, Tho- mas Lydiat, Joh. Henr. Alstedius: nec non Cajeta- nus, Delrio, Genebrardus, Baronius, Spondanus, Tor- niellus, Salianus, Bonfrerius, Tirinus, Henricus Phi- lippi, Corn. à Lap. Joh. Baptista Ricciolus; Keplerus, & alii. Ex Arabibus producit Hotting. l. c. Elmacin. Histor. Eccles. M. S. p. 4. Tempore, quo constituit Deus noctem & diem, ingrediebatur Sol caput arietis die 13. Mensis Adar, quo festum Judæi celebrant in Nisan, in quo Deus Mosi dixit: Hic mensis vobis erit in primum mensem, in quo etiam eruditorum senten- tia erit finis mundi. Quibus etiam nos rationibus omnibus expensis accedimus, etsi faventiores an- teà Auctumno fuerimus: cum nullam rationem videamus, cur naturale anni principium, Ægyptios, & Judæos quosdam secuti Scaligeriani, relinquerint; & à litera diserta de anni capite, à Deo ipso designa- to Exod. XII, 2. discesserint, quam in adinventio- num novellarum de annis Sabbaticis & Jobelæis, in- de à mundi conditu inchoandis, gratiam deferere, nobis religio est.

QUÆSTIO II.

An rectè se habeat Epocha Mundi Antediluvia- ni juxta Ebræos Codices?

PRimam hanc Epocham multo annosiorem ju- sto fecerunt non pauci, LXX. Interpretum versioni insistentes, imprimis è Veteribus. Qui verò excusationem quodammodo merentur, quod Ebraicarum literarum cognitione destituti pleri- que fontes veritatis consulere nequiverint. Eusebius libro I. Chron. triplicem proponit annorum dinumerationem : secundum LXX. Interpretum, secundum Ebræorum, & secundum Samaritanorum exemplaria ; juxta quam Ebræorum calculo quidem 1656. annis absolvitur hæc Epocha ; at Samaritano- rum computo tantum anni numerantur 1307. quia Jaredo ante Pædogoniam 100. Mathusalæ 120. Lamecho 129. annos detrahunt, adeoque 349. annis Epocham totam breviorem faciunt; secundum de- signationem vero LXX. Interpretum reperiuntur anni Epochæ hujus 2242. Ebræam veritatem 586. annis excedentes : quia sex Patriarchis, Adamo, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Enocho, singulis ante παιδογονίαν 100. Lamecho autem 6. adjiciunt annos, & ex adverso 20. annos derogant Mathusalæ, quem non annos 187. sed 167. habentem faciunt, cum Lamechum genuit. Quos vero annos 20. Mathusalæ ante pædogoniam relinquendos censuit Africanus, uti refertur in Chronico Alexandrino, etsi in cæteris cum LXX. Interpretibus & Eusebio faciat. Unde annos ante diluvium 2262. numeravit, quot assignati quoque ab Epiphanio & Augustino sunt : Josephus vero (si Petavio credimus l. IX. c. 2.) à creatione annos numerat ad diluvium 2656. Adeoque non Eusebius tantum sequutus hic est LXX. Interpretes, sed plerique etiam Veteres tam Græci quam Latini, Georgius item Syncellus, qui antiquissimam LXX. Interpretum editionem, ceu ex incorrupto Hebraico fonte quondam traductam laudat, ut & Julianus Archi-Episcopus Toletanus l. III. contra Judæos, Onuphrius in Chronico Ecclesiastico, Antonius Contius in notis ad Nicephori Constantinopolitani num Chronicon, Hieronymus Vielmius de 6. diebus conditi orbis lectione V.
