S. allocutus seu instinxerit, ubi confero cum me- is diebus, semper video eos incidere in ♀ ♄ ♂, non ☉ ☽ ☿ ♃ E. gratia Gen. 7. dicitur 17. die m. 2. cœpere Imbres futuræ admonuit, nam Nono die m. 2. Deus ejus rei 1. 2. 3 4 5. 6. 7. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16.

septimana erat lapsa: ubi video meos dies in Syfte- mate, video eum esse ♄ diem revelationis. Sic Gen. IIX. die 27. jubet Deus Noam exire cum suis ex arca. Video meos dies, incidit is in ♀ & sequens dies sacri- ficialis in ♄. Sicque habeo 60. exempla, neque datur contrarium exemplum. Hæc cum ita sint, PATRO- NE MAXIME, rogo, si Tua Magnifica Excellentia habet, quod eam dubiam teneat, ut me exerceat, non dubito ad singula respondere Chronologica revelata etiam gravissima.

Quod si, uti spero, ACERRIMUM TUUM JU- DICIUM videt nullum deesse diem, nullum super- esse, tum, si liceat rogare, devote & humiliter rogi- tem tuum sincerum Judicium, Patrone Optime, ut mihi perscribas. Ego illam Tuam Censuram cum summorum Virorum Censuris, quas accepi, impri- mendam tradam, & ero gratus publice pro tanta Tua Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ honori asserta gloria. Sic & conjunctissimus in Christo Frater Dn. D. Wasmu- thius, qui T. Excell. devote salutat, in Accentuatio- ne incredibile protraxit arcanum, & quale T. Excel- lentia dudum suis scriptis desideravit. Tentabi- mus paulo post adire Judæos Hamburgi, & Altena- vii, & tentare lucrum spirituale. Ergo quæsumus de- votissime, ut supra Collegio Orientali de Propagan- da Fide Nostra Vestrum Fac. Theol. Judicium Magni momenti futurum, quia a tanto loco profe- ctum, accelerare ne dedignemini. B. V. Deo Opt. Max. Diu Sacer & Salvus. Kilii 20. Mart. 1670.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Of the Discussion of the Ravian Chronology
In the Name of Jesus. OF THE DISCUSSION OF THE RAVIAN CHRONOLOGY.

SUMMARY.

General Treatise. The occasion and cause of this discussion. The diligence and skill in Oriental languages of Mr. Ravius is commended. He rashly adds 140 years to the System of the years of the World, and 190 years to the Biblical Epochs. Nor does he begin the Babylonian captivity with Scripture. He followed Codomannus. Who hitherto has easily had no followers. Nor indeed did he boast of infallibility. Mr. Ravius renders the Exotic Epochs uncertain and suspect. He calls the Ptolemaic Canon into doubt without cause. He suspects its Kings were invented by Berosus. Whom, however, he praises in the Sum of the years. How is Biblical Chronology alone infallible? He deduces the entire Chronology from Scripture alone. And he thinks that Jews and Atheists can be convinced by it. The confession of Pareus, that three things here are greater than human genius. Which Ravius boasts that he has performed. I. Concerning the first beginning of the created world. The first Ravian proof is examined from chapter 12 of Exodus. As also the other, concerning the departure of the Abrahamids from Egypt, Exod. XII, 40, 41, 51. Regarding which Abraham speaks of the entry into Egypt. From one epoch in Ex. XII and Gal. III, Ravius made two. II. Concerning tables of perpetual motions. III. Concerning the linking of epochs and singular events. Whether political months are used everywhere in the Scriptures? Concerning certain other problems, concerning the new moon, the time of the Passover, and Pentecost. Ravian paradoxes. Ravian examples, brought forward for confirming his tables, are weighed. 1. Concerning the character of the entry of Abraham into Egypt. His postulate concerning the complete years of the epochs. 2. Concerning the beginning of the construction of the temple. 3. Concerning the character of the third year of Cyrus, Dan. X, v. 4. The Ravian postulate concerning the days of divine revelations. A special treatise ON THE XII EPOCHS of Ravius. In which he criticizes all chronologists. From the FIRST Epoch up to the flood. From the SECOND up to the entry of Abraham into Egypt. Which is not expressed in Scripture. From the THIRD to the weaning of Isaac, which has no proof from Scripture. From the FOURTH, the exodus of Israel. The starting point of which is not thus defined by the Holy Scriptures. Nor is the Epoch itself so determined. A new version and interpretation of the passage Ex. XII, 40 is discussed. It is somewhat contrary to Gal. III, 17. And to the Sacred text. From the FIFTH Epoch to the first Mosaic Jubilee. Which requires many hypotheses concerning Sabbaths and Jubilees. It has no foundation. A false interpretation of the passage Lev. XXV, 2. 9. He rashly contradicts other chronologists: and that with arguments which should not even be considered as topics. Indeed, even the Holy Scriptures. The SIXTH Epoch is clearly intercalary, from the first real Jubilee to the end of the occupation of Canaan. First introduced by Codomannus, from whom, however, Ravius differs in various ways. It is clearly contrary to the Scripture of 1 Kings VI, 1. To which the History of the Judges and the passage Acts XIII are not opposed with sufficient religious care. Not without distortion of the words of 1 Kings VI, 1. Which passage Ravius attempts to batter. Concerning the meaning of the passage Acts XIII, 20. The precarious postulates of Ravius concerning the history of the Judges. It is destitute of authorities. Concerning the words of Jephthah, Jud. XI, 26. The rash divination of Ravius. A truer calculation. The SEVENTH Epoch to the fourth year of Solomon's beginning is not correctly assumed. Concerning the EIGHTH, Ravius's errors regarding the years of the sins of Judah. And a voluntary divorce from the common opinion concerning the NINTH, regarding the years of the sins of the house of Israel. Concerning the passage Ezek. IV, 4. Ravian inconstancy. His partition of the 390 years. The first part of 91 years is 95 years. The difficulty concerning one year of Ahaziah from 2 Kings VIII, 25 and 2 Chron. XXII, 2. The triumph over the same, revealed to himself, is vain. The second part of 164 years, which in the History of the Kings of Israel are 143. He absurdly makes King Hoshea the same as the Prophet Hosea. The third part, a period of 135 years. He does not correctly finish the years of the sins of Israel. He badly confuses Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and Nabonassar. The Funccian error. Ravius, with Funccius, confuses Nabonassar and Nebuchadnezzar. He attributes 30 years to Evil-Merodach, without authority. He eliminates Niricassolassar, Nabonadius, and Nabopallassar from Ptolemy's Canon. He assigns only 14 years to Belshazzar. He enriches the years of the kings in the Ptolemaic Canon by 14 years. His connection of the years of Hezekiah and the Nabonassarean era is merely arbitrary. The TENTH Epoch of Mr. Ravius. He badly begins the Babylonian captivity from the burning of the temple. He is in conflict with Codomannus. And with himself. Whether Dan. X, 1 concerns the third year of the Persian reign of Cyrus: The ELEVENTH Epoch. The beginning of the LXX weeks of the Beroaldists is badly seized upon. A slippery foundation for a demonstration. A paralogism. The reasons for that beginning are discussed. A small argument from parity. The benevolent edicts of Xerxes and Darius Nothus are rashly invented. Which Persian monarchs were the patrons of the Jews? 72 years are rashly and falsely inserted into the cycle of the 70 weeks. Concerning the passages Zech. I, 12, c. VII, 5. The calculation of 121 years is not correct. Ravius boasts of a special revelation (outside of Scripture). Which does not agree with Ezra and Nehemiah. Concerning the Darius of Ezra VI, 14, 15. The new iron-wood mystery of Ravius. Ravius increases the 70 weeks of Daniel by 10 weeks and 2 years. A wonderful and merely arbitrary intercalation of the Ravian structural disturbance: As is the definition of the years of the success of the work. From one Darius, Ravius makes two. Contrary to the open passage of Ezra IV, 5, VI, 14, 15. He makes Gabriel the Holy Spirit, contrary to Scripture. He perverts the text of Dan. IX, 24, 25. The Ravian paraphrase. What is to be desired in it? He wrongly explains the word Nechtach, which refutes the discontinuation of the weeks. He confuses the end with the objection. And the term of the guilt with the expiation of the same. He restricts the sins of the world to the idolatry of the people. He injects the baptism of Christ into the text. And draws the guilt of the people to that end. He added the edict of Cyrus by a private interpretation. He substitutes the restitution of the people for the rebuilding of the city. He perverts the meaning of the little word 'ad'. He inverts the term to which the Epochs belong. He invents a parenthesis without necessity. Which is also inconsistent. He concocts an intercalary distress for the sake of his own intercalation of years. Which he made of 72 years without foundation. Concerning the XII Epoch of the seven-year periods, 63. The first part of 62 seven-year periods. He carries it to the times of Artaxerxes Mnemon, which belong to the reign of Longimanus. He inconveniently leaves the city without walls for more than a century and a half. He is forced to call the Canon of Ptolemy to his aid, which he either approves or disapproves when it pleases him. The other part of the Epoch, the last week. The beginning of the latter half. Is it Es. LX, 21? or Es. LXI, 1 defined? Is a temporal Jubilee year designated there, or indeed a spiritual one? Concerning the month and day of the passion and conception of Christ, which Ravius proves with weak arguments. His hypotheses do not agree. The Ravian paraphrase of the passage Luke III, 23. A new Ravian self-contradiction concerning the day of the passion of Christ. In which he rashly ends the Epoch of Gabriel. He gathers the day of the conception of Christ from Zech. I, 7 in vain. A weak inference concerning the day of the week of the apparition of Gabriel. A false attachment of the apparition of Zech. I to the times of Darius Nothus. A more than Kabbalistic invention concerning the prediction of the year of the flood in Gen. IV, 24. And concerning the coincidence with the birth year of Christ. And the day and month of the conception. A paraphrase of the latter verses of the Angelic Prophecy by Ravius. In which those things concerning the final end, and concerning the CRUCIFIXION of Christ, are rashly added. As also concerning the ascension into heaven. In the place of Gen. IV, 24, brought in here to no purpose. What does the phrase NON SIBI introduce here? Ravius confuses the constitution and the confirmation of the New Testament. Nor is it to be attributed to the end of the last seven years; but to the whole mystical week. The abolition of sacrifices is not correctly referred to the latter half of the same. The time of the death of Christ is not the end of the mystical weeks, but the middle of the last week. The error of Ravius concerning the term to which of the weeks of Daniel. Conclusion. The author's protestation. Concerning other tables to be adorned with a similar tenor, with the truth of Scripture and the Canon of Ptolemy preserved. Why this discussion seemed fit to be published? Why an appendix was added from the Biblical work? Why the NEW Chronology cannot be approved? The cause of the added letters of Mr. Ravius. The author's final vow.

DISCUSSION OF THE INFALLIBILITY OF THE NEW RAVIAN CHRONOLOGY.

Mr. Christian Ravius, Royal Professor of Hebrew and Oriental Languages at Uppsala, very recently published a Biblical Chronology, which he inscribed as the only true and infallible one: but because he anxiously asked for my judgment concerning the same on two occasions, and has now publicly exposed it to the light, it seems necessary to warn in a few words what is to be thought of it, in place of a conclusion, lest anyone be made doubtful concerning the certainty of the epochs handed down in this our Chronicle by that new Biblical Chronology, hitherto for the most part unheard of, nor let the divine truth concerning their designation in the sacred writings be endangered.

The diligence which the author devotes to a most useful study is truly worthy of favor, whom I have loved for many years, since he enjoyed my company at the Regiomontana Academy, for his distinguished erudition in Oriental letters; and therefore I dedicate this work, whatever it may be, not to disparage his reputation, but solely to vindicate the authority of Scripture. For this Chronology adds to the System of the years of the world several, namely 140 years, nay it inserts 190 years which are redundant in Biblical Chronology, and nowhere else appear; such as 118 from the first real Jubilee year celebrated by Moses to the end of the journey of the Israelites, i.e., the occupation of Canaan, and 72 intercalary years inserted here and there, at will, into the 7 prior weeks of Daniel; which not only do not occur in Scripture, but also stand in opposition to the Epochs designated by the Holy Spirit καδδιάμετρον; nor does it begin the Babylonian captivity with Scripture from the first of Nebuchadnezzar, or the fourth of Jehoiakim, but from the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, or from the burning of the temple; most of which, not so much invented by him as by Laurentius Codomannus already 90 years ago, along with several other things handed down in this Chronology so highly praised, will never be able to be reconciled with the sacred writings and historical truth. The Chronology of Codomannus had no followers for almost an entire century, even though he himself praised it highly, because, forsooth, it does not allow others to remain any longer in Chronological Labyrinths, but extricates them through a certainty which God, having pity on us, has granted to him through most laborious means, and criteria that will have weight even among adversaries. What followers this same work, now encrusted by Mr. Ravius after about 100 years, will have, time will tell; yet the modesty of Codomannus seems more praiseworthy, who is so far from boasting of the infallibility of his Chronology that he protests rather, since it is human to err, and many observing accurately see more than one, that he does not despise the judgments of others, nor wish to be wise only to himself.

Although Mr. Ravius indeed attempts to render even most Exotic Epochs (which was not done by Codomannus) uncertain and suspect, because he understands very well that they in no way serve the hypothesis which he has preconceived in his mind, we shall not, however, be much concerned about them now; but this must not be passed over in silence, that the celestial Canon of Ptolemy is called into doubt without cause, which better chronologists have hitherto held in great esteem, as being entirely consistent with historical truth and celestial observations. For at the very threshold, in the general introduction, for example, §. 4, Mr. Ravius thinks too contemptuously of it. Ravius, as an example of the uncertainty of exotic matters, than which a more uncertain one can hardly be given, alleging the Kings of the Assyrians designated in the Canon of Ptolemy, because it is ambiguous whether they were fabricated by Berosus, whom he himself, but against the faith of antiquity, suspects to be the author of the Ptolemaic Canon, and judges that he merely played with the names of the Kings and the number of years of their reign assigned to them, but without any demonstration, and thus quite rashly; in which manner everything in antiquity could easily be rendered suspect; nay, he disperses the years in the Canon at will, and changes and corrects it, even though he is forced to acknowledge that in the sum of the 122 years of the Assyrian Kings up to the years of Nebuchadnezzar inclusive, the Ptolemaic Canon does not err, but retains the true sum.

Furthermore, we must have the greatest regard for Biblical Chronology, which Mr. Ravius rightly makes the only infallible one, provided he does not for that reason call it the only true one in such a way as to render the praise of truth entirely doubtful or derogate from Exotic ones, which was certainly done in §. 5 and 6: nor should he believe that the entire Chronology is to be deduced from Scripture alone, which he establishes with Beroaldus, Broughton, and David Pareus in §. 8, even though he acknowledges that while it was indeed attempted by them to be demonstrated from the authority of Holy Scripture alone, it was not brought to an end, but he considers that this was first done by himself. Which μεγαλίαν f. I would wish the postulate, or problem, to be so demonstrated that it would be right to congratulate the world (as the author requests), I would certainly join those congratulating with more willingness, especially if from that, Jews and Atheists, just as he himself sells it, could be infallibly convinced of the time of the birth of the Messiah, so that it could be demonstrated to them to the eye from the O.T. for their conversion. But unless other demonstrations than by a precise calculation of the years up to the coming of Christ, and of all of them to be deduced from Scripture alone, have been applied, it is much to be feared that the work of the conversion of Jews and Atheists, which Mr. Ravius seems to piously meditate, may be vain and fruitless.

Pareus himself certainly acknowledges that those who promise that they can give us the Astronomical time from the first point of creation to the beginning of the Christian era, exact, are attempting something greater than human ingenuity, and that from the fact that neither the first point of motions can be given as certain a priori, nor can true and certain tables of perpetual motions be exhibited from the first point to the birth of Christ; and finally, that the attachment of Epochs and individual or principal events to the tables of motions cannot be designated as true and certain. Pareus frankly confessed these three things to be greater than human ingenuity, but Mr. Ravius affirms with great confidence that he can perform them, nay, that he has performed them.

And first indeed, as regards the vernal equinox, he is persuaded that it can be apodictically proved from Holy Scripture that it was not the autumnal beginning of the created world. Although we acknowledge that opinion to be more probable, that the world began in the spring time, which we confirmed with many authorities in Sect. II, q. I, yet perhaps no one except Mr. Ravius has hitherto dared to boast of a demonstration, and a manifold one at that, here. And it is truly a great presumption, from chapter XII of Exodus for that opinion; but to construct an infallible demonstration from it in this way: because there the year began from the spring, i.e., the month of Nisan, therefore also the first year of the world began from the spring, hardly anyone else would say. Furthermore, how is our man going to return to favor with Codomannus, or others, who do not cast the beginning of spring, and the vernal equinox, on the first day of creation, but on the fourth day, when the luminaries were created? For so Bede, book on the nature of things, ch. VI. The first day of the century was three days before the vernal equinox, which corresponds to the fourth day on account of the luminaries created then. Which many others follow. But if not even the beginning of the world, as regards the day, is infallibly certain, how does the Author presume that he can have all the days of the world in a numbered sequence, and demonstrate them apodictically and infallibly? And this is the first Apodixis of our Chronologist.

The second relies on the principle that Abraham entered Egypt on the same day of the week, namely Thursday, as that on which the Abrahamites departed from Egypt, and that both years of the world, both the entry of Abraham and the departure of the Abrahamites, namely the year 2085 and the year 2514, began on the same day of the week. But from where will that principle be taught? Here Mr. Ravius confidently asserts in Exegesis 12, 40, 41, 51, that this conjunction and concentricity is observed twice: But I could not see it there even once, nor have other interpreters and chronologists, sufficiently sharp-sighted indeed, been able to do so thus far. For there is no word in the text about the day or day of the week of Abraham's entry into Egypt, but there is mention only of the time of the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt, under which name, although Let us admit that Abraham is included as the stock, yet the day of his entry into Egypt is not expressed, much less is that συγκυρία & concentricity defined, that on the same day of the week on which the Israelites went out of Egypt, Abraham entered Egypt. Furthermore, the year of Abraham's calling, which he makes the same year as his entry into Egypt (which, however, is not found expressly defined in Scripture), is not the year 2085 from the creation of the world, but 2083, and thus the year of the Exodus is 2513. But assuming that hypothesis, that Abraham entered Egypt in the year 2085, and that 430 years defined by the Holy Spirit in Exodus XII ought to be counted from there, there result not the year 2514, but 2515. Whence the author of the new Chronology, of whom later, was forced to twist the text of Exodus so that it might agree with his hypothesis. Finally, in support of his opinion, he forms two different Epochs, whereas Scripture has handed down only one, namely of 430 years from the promise made to Abraham to the departure from Egypt, Ex. XII, 40, Gal. III, 17; for from that, Ravius distinguishes an Epoch from the entry of Abraham into Egypt up to the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, which he wishes to be completed precisely in 429 full years; of which distinction of Epochs neither a trace nor a vestige appears in the Scriptures.

Now therefore it easily appears that the second Parean postulate has by no means been fulfilled by Mr. Ravius: for if not even that first point of the world is apodictically certain, how could tables that are undoubtedly true be deduced from it? But what Mr. Ravius assumes, that the series of years from the world up to the destruction of Jerusalem is 4212, and that it is read as being denounced twice in the O.T., was not to be brought forward nakedly, but to be solidly proven. For no one has been found thus far who has found that series of years even once. And even if it be admitted that the months in Scripture are not Solar, but Lunar, which indeed many of the Chronologists will by no means concede, yet tables of perpetual motions cannot be held as certain regarding months, weeks, and days of the week, where not even regarding years does infallible certainty exist, which will be evident later concerning the Ravian Chronology. Finally, no Astronomical tables of perpetual motions are seen in this Chronology; it is therefore a wonder that the author boasts so much that they are exhibited here.

The third postulate of Pareus was that the binding of Epochs and individual or principal events to the tables of motions be made true and certain, which Mr. Ravius is most persuaded has been done by him, so much so that he does not hesitate to make the Holy Spirit Himself the author of this binding of his. But since no tables of perpetual motions constructed from Astronomical principles appear in the Ravian Chronology, how can the binding of the Epochs be said to have been made to them? If he says that the months in Scripture are not solar, nor lunar, whether we look to the φάσιν or the σύνοδον, but Political, each of 30 days, all full, none hollow, and therefore there is no need for other tables than those which are adorned from the observation of the weekly days of the week, we leave it to be discussed by others who devote effort to general and abstract Chronology; for this opinion, perhaps asserted or heard by no one until now, seems to be of deeper inquiry. Thus indeed there will be a great compendium in Biblical Chronology, and we shall easily be able to do without many other Astronomical characters. And that opinion might seem not a little probable, especially from the year of the flood, and also from the fact that it does not seem consistent that a different form was observed in other years by divine law, or that a rude people were restricted to Solar or Lunar years, and the observation of the New Moon or the full moon: whence to that opinion, if it is proposed σοχασικῶς as probable, and not sold as infallible, a place might perhaps be left. Similarly, therefore, we permit inquiry into those problems which occur here, such as 1. whether the νεωμενία is drawn and called from the new political month rather than from the new Moon? 2. whether the observation of the first and fourteenth Moon, i.e., of the new moon and full moon, is commanded anywhere in Scripture? 3. whether the Abrahamids went out of Egypt at the full moon of the Passover. 4. whether the Passover was ever ordered to the Moon, or whether it was always restricted to the fifteenth day of the year or of the first political month? Since Mr. Ravius affirms the latter, he boldly pronounces that the whole question of the East and West concerning the Passovers, and the ordination of the Nicene Fathers, is of hardly any moment, and he judges that we Christians can always celebrate the fifteenth, 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st of Nisan, on whichever day of the Sun the resurrection of Christ might fall. 5. whether the Hebrews always celebrated their Pentecost in the time of the Old Testament as we Christians do in the New Testament on the day of the Sun, and that according to the law of Levit. XXIII, 15, 16, which he renders, Mimmachorath hassabath, i.e., that Pentecost is to be counted from the day after the Sabbath falling into the Paschal week, and not from the day after the Passover. If this explanation of his is to be admitted, where the Passover fell on a Monday, the counting of the seven weeks to Pentecost would have had to begin only from the day of the Sun, or the Sunday following the weekly Sabbath, and not 50 days having intervened between the Passover and the feast of Pentecost, but 57, which how it is consistent with the Law and Jewish practice under the Old Testament, I do not see. Thus far, certainly, all those ἀνίσoματα were held as paradoxes, and such an interpretation of the divine Law was not easily heard before Codomannus, who in book I, Chron. c. 9, tried in vain to reconcile it with the Passover celebrated in Jos. V, 14. In great errors, indeed, the whole learned world would have stuck perpetually for so many centuries until now, especially the Chronologists and Interpreters of Scripture, not only the Jews, but also the Christians, if these Ravian hypotheses were to be admitted. But whatever may be the case regarding those things, as far as the authority of Holy Scripture permits, they might perhaps be able to be discussed τοπικῶς, but they can hardly be defined ἀποδεικτικῶς.

But Mr. Ravius brings forward some examples to confirm his tables, yet because those are joined with a begging of the question, it is not worth the effort to dwell upon them. From the discussion of the epochs themselves, it will sufficiently appear whether Ravius's persuasion concerning the certainty of the connection is true or vain. Let us, however, see the examples in a few words. In the first, without proof and gratuitously, it is assumed that Abraham entered Egypt on the fifteenth day of the month Nisan, on a Thursday. For where is this written, either in the book of Scripture or of nature, to both of which he appeals? That, indeed, is also contrary to Scripture, which in the same example says that only 429 years had intervened. It is also manifest from Gal. III, 17, that the term from which this epoch is to be fixed should not be set at Abraham's entry into Egypt, but at the promise made to him. That this epoch of the Apostle is not different from the Mosaic one in Ex. XII, 40, but is exactly the same, both the comparison of the passages teaches, and it has been believed by all hitherto. Nor is it solid, what he here and throughout assumes as a postulate or axiom, as if the years of the epochs, by reason of the term from which and to which, were so ἀποτόμως (abruptly/precisely) integral, and to be taken integrally, that the days also might exactly correspond, and with 430 years named, as many days as those make up were defined by the Holy Spirit, which will be demonstrated precisely neither for this nor for other epochs. Nor indeed, because the day of the exodus is designated here as the 15th of Nisan, and the years of the sojourn of the Abrahamites are numbered, is it a consequence that from the first day of the sojourn to the first day of the exodus those years, as regards months, weeks, and days, were entirely completed, so that not one day is missing: for the letter of the text teaches that years were only numbered by the Holy Spirit regarding the time of sojourn or habitation, but that a limit of the begun and finished habitation was not fixed regarding the very days themselves, (let alone that the same day of the week was defined at the term from which and to which those years belong). And indeed that precise determination is not fitting, because Moses sets the term to which of this epoch as the exodus that happened after 430 years, but Paul makes the term to which of the same the promulgation of the law: even though the Exodus and νομοθεσία were separated by 50 days; which is a clear indication that days are not precisely attended to, but only the years of this epoch are defined.

Similarly, there is an ἀντίγραφον in the second example, that the Temple of Solomon fell in the 481st year, 2nd month, 2nd day regarding the beginning of the structure, since the 480th year and its second month is openly defined in 1 Kings 6:1, in which its beginning was made.

In the third example concerning the third year of Cyrus, Dan. 10:4, it is rashly asserted that the Holy Spirit added the calendar character of the year, Thursday, and likewise in Haggai ch. 1 and 6, as also for Zechariah the character of Tuesday: for in no place among these Prophets is mention made of Tuesday, or the third day of the week, either κατὰ γράμμα or κατὰ πρᾶγμα. And so it is with the others. But let these things be said concerning the general introduction; how far it is from an infallible ἀπόδειξις, can now be clear. It will, however, be clearer in the special introduction and the demonstration, which he calls, of infallibility from the book of Nature and Scripture.

But this must still be premised concerning the foundations of that Chronology, that although the author asserts it is deduced from the book of Nature and Scripture, yet concerning those things which pertain to the collation of the book of Nature, he assumes this as a διδόμενον, (for other things do not look to this, nor are they of our profession: let Mathematicians see to it, and those who treat Chronology in the abstract, how he himself attempts to render almost all characters uncertain, and the Julian period useless) that divine revelations were always made either on the seventh day, the feast day of the Sabbath, or on the day before the feast, the sixth day, which is of Venus, or on the day between feasts, Tuesday, the third day of the week; but that this should be granted and admitted to him, there is no necessity. And since he everywhere sells demonstrations, what, I ask, could be brought forward as a demonstration of this hypothesis, either a priori or a posteriori?

Furthermore, concerning the Epochs which he has distinctly produced from the Holy Scriptures in his breviary of times in this Chronology, we must first look into them here, concerning which he warned generally thus: All Chronologists hitherto omit some here and there, or insert others invented by themselves, they change squares into rounds, and rounds into squares. A grave ἔγκλημα against not perhaps some, but ALL Chronologists. He himself, however, made XII Epochs, which he later reduced to nine. Concerning the FIRST from the beginning of the world to the year of the flood, there is no reason for us to warn; for Section II of the Chronicle will teach our ὁμοψηφίαν.

The SECOND from the year of the flood inclusive to the entry of Abraham into Egypt exclusively of 429 years is not expressly held in the Scriptures; for nowhere is either that number of 429 years or the beginning of the Epoch tied to a certain day found, or its term so designated. But the Epoch from the flood to the Ἐπαγγελία made to Abraham of 427 years is defined in Section III of the Chronicle.

The THIRD, to the years of the weaning of Isaac exclusively, 29 years, although it may perhaps be admitted as probable, will never be demonstrated apodictically from the Holy Scriptures.

The FOURTH, to the year of the exodus, is expressed as 400 years as far as the number of years in the Sacred writings is concerned, but that it takes its beginning from the weaning of Isaac is not defined. Nor indeed is the number of years expressed in such a way as Ravius wishes: for the 400 years are counted by the Holy Spirit to the time of the exodus in such a way that 430 are said to have elapsed from the promise to Abraham to the Exodus, nor is the exodus assigned to the beginning of the 430th year, much less is it tied to the same day of the month or day of the week on which Abraham entered Egypt, Exod. 12, 40. Whence Mr. Ravius could not save his hypothesis without devising a new version and interpretation of the Sacred text, which little artifice is very characteristic of him, as the specimens of a new version and interpretation of the earlier chapters of Genesis which he published some years ago have abundantly shown, which consequently have been suppressed by public authority in the renowned kingdom of Sweden. For he contends in letters given to me from Kiel on March 20 of this year 1670 that the passage of the exodus should be rendered and understood thus: 'Toward the beginning of the 430th year, it happened that the military hosts of Jehovah went out from the kingdom on the same day of the week, namely, on which Abraham entered Egypt.' Which version and interpretation is hitherto truly unheard of, and is not brought forth from the authentic text, but is brought to it. For nothing is expressed there concerning Abraham's entry into Egypt, nothing at all is even obscurely indicated concerning the day of the week, much less concerning the same day on which Abraham entered Egypt. Furthermore, it is not the beginning of the 430th year, but the end that is commemorated there by the word קֵץ, which is not 'toward the beginning,' but 'from the end of the 430th year,' or 'after the 430th year': just as St. Paul also has in Gal. 3, 17, μετὰ ἔτη τετρακόσια κὶ τριάκοντα, 'after 430 years'. Add that it is explicitly held in the text of Moses that the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt was not only of 429 years, but of 430 years, lest anyone, if by chance קֵץ should occur anywhere for 'beginning' (which, however, has not been shown hitherto, nor does it suit the meaning of the word, which denotes an end, not a beginning), should understand here the initial limit of the year. Those words בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, which Pagninus and Arias Montanus render 'in the body of this day,' and Junius and Tremellius 'on this very day,' are not taken by any interpreter or Doctor, so far as I know, with reference to that day of the week on which Abraham entered Egypt, but are considered to look to that day of which Moses treated there, on which, namely, the Passover was celebrated. Nor can that reference to the day of entry be gathered from the text; indeed, mention is made of the night in which, namely, and the Passover was celebrated, and the exodus is said to have taken place, and it is not on that account observable, and it is not commanded that it be observed by the Israelites, so that it may be established that regard is had for the entry of Abraham into Egypt, but so that the memory of the time of the exodus may be preserved. What kind of Ravian demonstrations these are, therefore, is again evident from this example.

The FIFTH Epoch to the first real year of the Jubilee celebrated by Moses and the κληρυχίας, exclusive of 39 years from the exodus, requires many hypotheses, so that here no one except Mr. Ravius would rashly admit a demonstration. 1. I will not speak of the proleptic Sabbatic and Jubilee years celebrated before the law was given, which are truly imaginary, yet which are often thrust forward by the author, if not in this place, then elsewhere. 2. The real Jubilee year of Moses has no foundation in fact; for it is clear from Lev. XXV that Moses indeed commanded the celebration of Jubilee years, but we nowhere read that he himself celebrated them. 3. That Moses predicted this real Jubilee, or even a Sabbatic year, 38 years before, is from ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει. That prediction exists nowhere in the Holy Scriptures. In Lev. 25, 2, it is not a prophecy that is held, but a command; which passage is therefore [treated] with a new version, and of his version The most distinguished man attempted to adapt [it] to his hypothesis by interpolation, but not without perversion. Who the authors of that version and exposition are, let him see to it himself. The Lord indeed commanded that after the entry into the land of Canaan and thereafter the land should keep a Sabbath to the Lord, v. 2. which Moses explains further in the following verses, how it is to be observed, namely, that for six years from the entry into the land of Canaan the land should be sown, but in the seventh year it should rest. Mr. Ravius, however, tears verse 2 away from the following ones as far as the sense is concerned, and makes verse 2 a prophecy concerning the rest of the land and the first Sabbath, forced in the first 6 months in the Cis-Jordanic kingdoms, and in the 6 later months to be celebrated in the land of Canaan, but he wishes the institution of the spontaneous Sabbath of the Hebrews to be exhibited in the remaining verses: which is a mere misinterpretation. That there is no prophecy here, but that only precepts are proposed by Moses, both the antecedents and the consequents sufficiently teach. 4. It had to be proven apodictically that the last year of Moses' life was the first real Sabbatical and Jubilee year of the world, 2553. For others, by great consensus, from the autumn of the year 2554 after the death of Moses, in which it first happened to the Israelites to sow the land after the cessation of the Manna, just as they count the first year of agriculture, so they also fix the root of the Sabbatical years there, by the force of this passage Lev. 25, 2 and 9, as also Deut. 15, 1 and 9, 31, 10. But the arguments which are brought forward for the new opinion are not even probable, let alone apodictic. He says that it had been predicted 38 years before that the 10th day of September, on which the battle was fought with King Sihon, would be favorable, and that from that day that forced Sabbatical year was begun, which was at the same time a Jubilee, because mere jubilees prevailed among the victorious Israelites everywhere. But that prediction is feigned in vain, nor can any testimony concerning that beginning of the forced Sabbatical year, or the year itself, be brought forward from all the Mosaic writings: nor is the Jubilee year ever called so because of mere jubilees of victories, but because of other causes and ends, for the sake of which the Jubilee years were sanctioned. Finally, those 39 years which are assigned to this Epoch by the author are already included in the years of another Epoch, as being the one which he then recounts from the exodus of the Israelites to the fourth year of Solomon, which Mr. Ravius makes the seventh in order from 1 Kings 6, 1, which must be said entirely, unless one is to contradict the Holy Spirit who assigns that Epoch there in that way. And let it suffice to have said these things regarding the fifth Ravian Epoch.

THE SIXTH likewise is clearly intercalary, designated from the first real Jubilee year celebrated by Moses to the end of the journey of the Israelites or the occupied Canaan by the twelve tribes exclusively, of 79 years. Concerning which no trace is found either in Holy Scriptures or in antiquity. But Mr. Ravius owes this Epoch (although he conceals this) to Laurentius Codomannus, who first introduced it into a Chronological System, but has not yet found applauders; from whom Mr. Ravius himself has also departed in several points; as, for instance, making the year of the world 2514 exotic (which Codomannus made 2515) and assigning the first of the Jubilee years to Moses, celebrated in the year 2553 when Sihon was defeated (when Codomannus maintains that Sihon was defeated only in the year of the world 2554, and the first Jubilee was celebrated under Joshua in the year 2561); and feigning the end of the journey or the occupied Canaan in the year of the world 2631, which Codomannus places in the year of the world 2633, and what other discrepancies could be noted. And indeed this Epoch is not only feigned without art, but it is also openly anti-scriptural, if indeed in 1 Kings 6, 1, from the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt until the temple began to be built by Solomon, no more than 480 years are counted by the Holy Spirit, which number it is a matter of religious scruple for all pious minds to change: from which definition, however, Codomannus and Ravius depart, counting not 480, but 599 years from the exodus of the Israelites to the beginning of the temple: whence Codomannus torments himself around this passage in book 1. Chron. ch. 17, preferring the consensus of the history of the Judges and the Pauline narrative in Acts 13 to the present testimony of the Holy Spirit (which, however, can well consist with that consensus, and ought not to be opposed to it, but should be received holily alongside the History of the Judges and the Pauline account), and thus he distorts that Epoch of the book of Kings: [claiming] that the term from which, which is expressly established there as the exodus of the Israelites, is not their exodus from Egypt, but the end of the occupation of the land of Canaan, namely the 25th year after Othniel's victory, when the tribe of Dan first possessed its lot: which things are certainly as far apart as heaven and earth: since the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt is one thing, and the end of the occupation of the land of Canaan is another, which will be taught to be equivalent in Scripture to the Greek Calends: and yet Mr. Ravius seems to acquiesce in this not so much explanation as depravation of Codomannus, Ravius, nor could he find another solution suitable to his preconceived opinion. But Codomannus does not speak with sufficient reverence toward the Spirit of God, the author of Scripture, in the aforementioned book of Chron. p. 113. God Himself, he says, does not wish the assertion of one witness to be preferred to the testimony of two trustworthy ones (which is true concerning human witnesses, but is applied less piously to the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which, whether it is brought forward only once or more often, is always trustworthy and unquestionable), whom it is necessary to say admit either false things or a hidden interpretation, not obvious to everyone (and yet the words are not obscure, but most clear, and most obvious to everyone in the passage 1 Kings 6, 1), etc. Who will admit that the Holy Spirit speaks false things anywhere, unless he is clearly impious?

But let us return to Ravius: who does not fear to batter this great number in the book of Kings with several arguments, and to establish his own opinion against the insertion of 118 years for the journey from Egypt to the finished occupation of the promised land. 1. That otherwise there would not be 450 years to the beginning of Samuel the public minister, which he says Luke assigns in Acts 13:20. But Luke does not assign so many years from the distribution of the land by Joshua to Samuel, but says that those things which he had related were accomplished within about 450 years, since from the birth of Isaac to the distribution of the land, of which he had treated, 447 years had elapsed, and he asserts that after those things were accomplished, Judges were given up to Samuel the Prophet: as we warned above toward the end of the fifth section. 2. That the book of Judges recounts 430 continuous years from the first servitude, to which if the 20 years of the Elders who presided after Joshua are added, 450. Ravius says that these will produce the years of Luke. But we warned in its proper place, that is, in the third question of Section V, that the years in the book of Judges are to be counted far differently, and we showed in the same place that 450 years are not found from the death of Joshua to the passing of Eli, but only 339 years. Mr. Ravius assumes many things precariously in the special computation of those 450 years, concerning the years of the rule of the Judges, of which it is not relevant to speak specifically here, since a judgment can be made about them from the aforementioned place. 3. He thinks the book of Joshua demonstrates these 118 years in a disputed manner, but he brings forward no proof: First, he says the 40 years of Moses are tacitly supposed in the book of Joshua: But those are included in that illustrious Epoch of 480 years. Therefore they cannot be snatched away to the years that preceded it, or to any antecedent Epoch: Now those 70 years, which are attributed to the ten tribes for occupying the seats assigned to them, so that each occupied theirs in seven years, are invented rashly and out of human ingenuity: that 20 and more years of these were spent while Joshua was alive, rests on a similar, that is, no foundation: since that Joshua presided for 20 years (excluding the rule of the Elders after the death of Joshua) can be established by no document. Finally, the eight years of Cushan, which are added to those 40 of Moses and 70 of the occupation of the ten tribes, fall, according to the author's mind, into the times of Issachar: but it is necessary that they also extend to the times of Asher, because to each tribe 7, to none 8, years are assigned by him (although that assignment is merely voluntary); nor, if they are referred to the times of Issachar, can they be counted separately beyond those ten seven-year periods, as was done by Ravius, since they are contained within the complex of those seven-year periods. 4. The argument is taken from the character of the day of the week, but since it is not permitted to determine the day of the week, with a whole year, nay, with several years conflicting with the sacred computation, there is no reason why we should dwell on that.

The fifth point does not assist the learned Author by authorities: because of those 21 authors, there is no one who supports him in the computation or in assigning those 118 years of wandering: nor will he easily produce for himself a fellow-voter from antiquity, perhaps not even from the moderns, besides Codomannus. In particular, therefore, it is superfluous to examine those individual authorities. Some exceed the number of 480 years from the exodus to the temple; some even transcend the number of years assigned by Ravius. There is little comfort thence for the definition of the 118 years precisely. This variety teaches nothing else than that those who desert the Epoch most expressly designated by the Holy Spirit in 1 Kings 6:1 proceed unhappily. For a lie is nowhere consistent with itself; truth alone is immovable. 6. The words

Jephthah, Judges 11:26, concerning the 300 years from the time of the habitation of Israel, do nothing for these supernumerary 118 years without scriptural authority; but in order that they may be forced to agree, he now orders the 71 years of the five servitudes, which Ravius had previously counted distinctly, to rest or be omitted, so that they do not come into the computation and are useless to him, namely 8 of Cushan, 18 of Eglon, 20 of Jabin, 18 of Ammon, 7 of the Midianites; and to fill out the number, he says that Jephthah, speaking prophetically, added the six years of his own rule that were still to come, even though he speaks of years that had elapsed, not future ones, and he assigns 25 years of the rule of Joshua and 20 to the government of the Elders at his own pleasure (certainly outside of Scripture). Behold a splendid demonstration! Is this not changing squares into rounds? But when 248 years are counted, which are established from Scripture, from the death of Joshua until Jephthah, to which the last of Moses and the 17 of the leadership of Joshua are added, they become 266 years: therefore, by rounding the number, 300 years could easily be said, because the Israelites possessed those lands for almost three centuries; so that there is no need to resort to such a violent and tumultuous calculation. And these are those infallible demonstrations, about which the author does not fear to pronounce concerning this fictitious Epoch; to whom these do not suffice to demonstrate the 118 years of the Israelite journey, nothing suffices. I would rather say that he who does not see that these are not apodictic sees nothing. He adds, however, as an afterthought, a demonstration of the years of the leadership of Joshua from the Jubilee and Sabbatical years, but what, of what kind, and how great that is, can already be clear from those things which we said before about the Jubilee and Sabbatical years. These things, therefore, also concerning the Sixth Epoch.

THE SEVENTH is to the fourth year of Solomon when the temple began to be built, excluding 480, which indeed is correct in itself, but because its beginning is not assumed according to the guidance of the Holy Spirit from the exodus of the Israelites, therefore an error is committed in the calculation, while 3111 years are counted from the creation of the world to the temple of Solomon, with Codomannus counting 3112. We have provided a truer calculation in our Chronicle. He assigns the EIGHTH to the end of the idolatry of the house of Judah, or to the Schism of Israel, excluding 40 years. But that the idolatry of the house of Judah both began with the fourth year of Solomon and had its end in the fourth year of Rehoboam is said rashly and without Scripture; nay, it is contrary to Scripture, which sufficiently teaches that Solomon, when he was building the temple of the Lord, to which he devoted seven years, was by no means immediately given to idolatry, but was only seduced into it afterwards by his foreign wives, 1 Kings chapters 8 and 11. and that the Schism of Israel began immediately with the beginning of the reign of Jeroboam, it testifies, 1 Kings 12, not to mention that it cannot be explained how the years of the sins of Judah reached their end in the fourth year of Rehoboam.

The NINTH Epoch, therefore, comprising the years of the idolatry of the house of Israel up to the burning of the temple, diverges in this point from the common opinion regarding the years of the sins of the house of Judah and the house of Israel, because it computes and finishes the years of both separately; whereas they attain their end at the same term. The contrary argument, that that Epoch in Ezek. 4, 4, concerning the sins of Judah and Israel, has two sides, the right and the left, and therefore cannot be conceived simultaneously under the years of Josiah and those following, is of no moment, because Ezekiel ought to lie upon two sides, not because the punishment for idolatry had to be endured by the house of Judah and the house of Israel in discontinuous years, but because the house of Judah, in the end, also, because it could not be recalled to continued repentance through the admonitions and example of the most pious King Josiah, but returned to its vomit, was to be swept away to punishments, and to be cut off with the Israelite remnants on account of sins and idolatry. Pareus, certainly, who counts those years separately, despaired of investigating that sum from the history of the Kings of Judah and Israel, and thus professed it to be uncertain from where these years are to be begun and where they are to be finished. Ravius, however, assigns 40 years from the 4th of King Solomon to the first of Rehoboam (although only 37 years have elapsed up to that point, nor can or should the fourth year of Rehoboam be confused with the first), and divides the remaining 390 years into three parts; the first is of 91 years up to the single year of Ahaziah. The second of 164 years up to the sixth of Hezekiah inclusive. The third of 135 up to the destruction of Jerusalem. In the former part, however, he does not find 91 years, but 95, namely: Rehoboam 17, Abijah 3, Asa 41, Jehoshaphat 25, Jehoram 8, Ahaziah 1, in the years of the Kings of Judah: but in the years of the Kings of Israel 98, namely Jeroboam 22, Nadab 2, Baasha 24, Elah 2, Zimri 7 days, Omri 12, Ahab 22, Ahaziah 2. Jehoram 12, which, how he strives to reconcile, it is not worth inquiring. Our reconciliation from the Table of the Kings of Judah and Israel may be compared. That difficulty, however, of the one year of Ahaziah, 2 Kings 8:25, 2 Chron. 22:2, how it is said that Ahaziah reigned with his father Jehoram there as a son of 22 years, but here as a son of 42 years, when after his father died at 40 years of age, his successor was a son 42 years old, 2 Chron. 21:20, and thus it must be established that he was two years older than his father, he attempts to resolve by saying that Ahaziah was 22 years of age, and had his single year falling into the 42nd of his century: in which reconciliation, revealed to him, Ravius triumphs greatly, because no one hitherto has observed this reconciliation of Holy Scripture. But Scripture is nowhere accustomed to define the years of a century, so as to say that this person reigned in this or that year of the century current from the creation of the world, or did this or that: therefore that exposition is without example, which he devised for the protection of his Chronology, as if the 42nd year of the thirty-third century of the world, or the year of the world 3242, were indicated by the 42 of Ahaziah. But that year is more correctly counted from the beginning of the Samaritan era, which began in the 6th year of Omri, the maternal great-grandfather, as we noted in the Chronicle. See our Anti-Grot. on 2 Chron. 23:2.

Regarding the second order of the parallel Kings of Judah and Israel, 164 years are enumerated 165 years of the Kings of Judah in the same, namely Athaliah 6, Joash 40, Amaziah 29, Josiah 52, Jotham 16, Ahaz 16, and Hezekiah 6; but 143 years of the Kings of Israel from Jehu up to the 9th of Hosea, the equalization of which by Ravius should be compared with ours delivered in the table of Kings: But I confess that I do not grasp this, who says that Hosea is King and Prophet at the same time, since the Israelite King Hosea is greatly distinguished from the Prophet of this name; if indeed it is established that he invaded the kingdom after killing Pekah and reigned impiously, 2 Kings 15:30, ch. 17:1.

The third member of the 390 years of Israelite idolatry according to Ravius is completed by a period of 135 years, namely from the end of the Israelite Kingdom to the end of the Judean kingdom: but the years of the sins of Israel are more correctly finished in the 23rd year than the 19th of Nebuchadnezzar, when all the remnants of the Jews were led away from Judea by Nebuzaradan, in the fifth year of the destruction of Jerusalem, Jer. 52:30. Which term Codomannus also assigns, l. III. Chron. ch. XVI. Ravius, when he sees that he cannot complete that number of 135 years from the years of the kings of Judah after the end of the Israelite kingdom, makes the three months of Jehoahaz a full year, and likewise the year from Jehoiachin 3 months and 10 days, not to mention other things that might be desired in his computation. Where, to touch upon exotic matters in passing, Ravius confuses Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and Nabonassar, and considers them the same King. But Scripture distinguishes Sennacherib from Shalmaneser, 2 Kings.

XVI and XVIII, and makes Esarhaddon the son of Sennacherib, 2 Kings XIX, 37. Whence Codomannus also distinguished them, and made Shalmaneser the father of Sennacherib: although with Funccius he wishes Shalmaneser himself to be Nabonassar; which error the blessed D. Behmus, l. II. Chronol. Manud. Tit. III. c. IV., has refuted at length from sacred letters and exotic writers, to whom we wish Mr. Ravius to be referred. Shalmaneser was King of Assyria or Nineveh, 2 Kings 17:31. Nabonassar was King of Babylon; that these two kingdoms were then diverse is established from the history of Hezekiah: because after the destruction of Sennacherib, King of the Assyrians, Merodach, King of Babylon, sent ambassadors to Hezekiah, for the sake of giving thanks, 2 Kings XIX. Add also Jer. L, 17, 18, Ezek. XXXI, 11, where these kingdoms are openly distinguished. Similarly, Ravius with Funccius confuses the Nabopolassar of Ptolemy with the Nebuchadnezzar of Scripture, whom Josephus, from a fragment of Berosus, lib. III. Antiquit. c. 11, taught to be the son of the former: and whom Ptolemy distinguished by the name of Nabopolassar. Furthermore, Ravius attributes 30 years to Evil-Merodach, the son of this most famous King Nebuchadnezzar, and says that Holy Scripture has them, but where Scripture has them, he neither indicates, nor do I find. Ptolemy assigned no more than two years to Ilvarodamus, the son of Nabopolassar. Ravius, by his own authority, exterminates Niricassolassar and Nabonadius just as much as Nabopolassar in the Canon of Ptolemy, even though the fragment of Berosus, priest of Bel, agrees with it, and he substitutes Belshazzar immediately after Evil-Merodach, with 14 years of rule, which he confidently asserts that Scripture requires: when on the contrary, Nabonidus, the last of the Assyrian Monarchs, who is established to be the Belshazzar of Daniel, reigned for 17 years, according to the celestial Canon of Ptolemy. Therefore, Mr. Ravius adds those 14 years of his own, which he attributes to Belshazzar, enriching his years in the Canon of Ptolemy (the sum of which he nevertheless assumes), so that he may conclude that the first year of Nabonassar began from the first year of Hezekiah, from which to Cyrus 209. Ptolemy counts, let him conclude, and thus connect the first of Nabonassar with the first of Hezekiah: which computation and connection is indeed purely arbitrary, and contrary to the calculation of all chronologists, as is established even from this, that according to Ravius to the birth of Christ 740.

years of Nabonassar are to be calculated: since, as Usserius observes in Annal. V. T. p. 88, at the year of the world 3257, from the noon of the first day of the Egyptian month Thoth, in the year 747 (not 740) before our common Christian era, ALL astronomers with UNANIMOUS CONSENT deduce the Epoch of Nabonassar. By our calculation, the Nabonassarean era is to be commenced not from the first, nor from the seventh of Hezekiah, but from the 12th of Jotham, 20 years before Hezekiah. But more of this elsewhere.

We must now proceed to the TENTH Epoch, which Ravius makes the 71 years of the Babylonian captivity with the first of Cyrus, starting the same from the burning of the temple: but we have shown in our Chronicle that it did not begin from there, but from the fourth of Jehoiakim, nor is there any reason for us to add anything further here: we only compare Codomannus with Ravius. For the former makes the year of the burning of the temple 3534 from the creation of the world, which the latter establishes as 3541; and both rely not only on Sabbatical years but also on Jubilees, and both calculate days with months. Nor can we reconcile those Ravian points, that in the year of the world 3541 the temple was burned, and from it the years of the Babylonian captivity are to be counted, which end at the beginning of Cyrus: and that the third of Cyrus was the year of the world 3586; for by adding to those 3541 the 70 years up to Cyrus, and the two of Cyrus, it will not be the year 3586, but 3614. If he should perhaps say that the third year of the Persian reign is the year of the world 3586, and not the third of the Monarchy of Cyrus: it is rashly assumed that Daniel ch. 10, v. 1 speaks of the third year of the Persian reign of Cyrus, not of the third of his same Monarchy, which is repugnant to the text: because toward the end of the chapter there is mention of the first year of Darius the Mede, as already passed, who certainly had not yet aspired to the empire in the third year of the Persian reign of Cyrus. Cf. Dan. 5:30, 31.

He makes the ELEVENTH Epoch of 121 years and starts it from the first of Cyrus, which is composed of the 7 first weeks of Daniel, of the beginning and completion, as he says, of the second temple, and the 72 years of Zechariah ch. 1, v. 12, ch. 7, v. 5. Here, however, Mr. Ravius is first mistaken, while he makes the first year of Cyrus, or rather the second, the beginning of the LXX weeks of Daniel. Which opinion has long since been defeated among the Beroaldists, and could not even prove itself to Codomannus himself, in whose footsteps Ravius gladly clings. See what we have said against it in Chron. S. Sect. VIII, quest. 3. Nevertheless, the foundation of Ravius must be weighed here, which he seeks especially from the character of the third year of Cyrus, the sixth of the beginning of the second temple, namely the year of the world 3614, from Dan. 10:4; which he hawks as apodictic. But we do not even acknowledge it as topical. He says that that day, the 24th of the first month, was a Sabbath day, and from there concludes: Therefore the year began on a Thursday: Therefore it was the year of the world 3586. But what does this have to do with the year of the world 3614, which he was going to prove: And whence is it certain that that day, the 24th, was a Sabbath day, and not a Sunday, or even a Tuesday, or Friday, which he also thinks were dedicated to revelations? Finally, who does not see that one proceeds from the undistributed to the distributed, when it is inferred thus: That year began on a Thursday, or the fifth day of the week. Therefore it was the year of the world 3586; or, therefore it was 3614. If it be reduced to form, the flaw will immediately appear: The year of the world 3614 begins on the fifth day of the week: The 3rd year of Cyrus began on the fifth day of the week, therefore the third year of Cyrus is the year of the world 3614. For did not many other years of the world begin on the fifth day of the week? But this paralogism and vicious method of arguing is almost customary for Mr. Ravius: whence it is easy to gather what should be thought of his demonstrations.

Then he adds arguments for his beginning of the weeks of Daniel: but which contribute little to the matter. For what has this to do with the beginning of the 70 weeks, which Isaiah predicted Cyrus would release the Jewish people c. 43, 10. 44, 28. c. 45, 1. and which Jer. 29, 10. he prophesied that the years of the Babylonian captivity would be seventy only, no more, no fewer, and that the promises of Isaiah and Jeremiah were fulfilled, about all of which no one doubts; but that is ὀδὲν πρὸς δυόνυσον. Furthermore, that the edict of Cyrus was primary and the first, and that many Jews returned to it, and that the foundations of the temple were laid under Cyrus, to which the Jews also appealed before Tattenai, and that Darius ordered an inquiry, all these things contribute nothing to the edict concerning the construction of the city and the walls of Jerusalem, when joined with the effect. But that the Holy Spirit said it was imminent, and that very closely, this edict, does not appear from the words of Gabriel. Did Cyrus restore to the Jews the dignity of a free Republic, and of a Church not subject to any, but dependent on God alone? it would have to be investigated, yet that would not contribute much to the beginning of the weeks of Daniel, because the question is not about a restoration intended, but one brought to effect, which was not done under Cyrus, nor even under his immediate successors. That the Holy Spirit in the address of Daniel alludes to the LXX years of the Babylonian captivity is neither proven, nor if it were done, does it contribute to defining the beginning of the LXX weeks of Daniel; but that the LXX heptads are connected by the intervening of a single year only is asserted by a mere αἴτησιν τῶ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Nor does it follow that the beginning of the LXX years of the Babylonian captivity is left in doubt, unless, that is, the LXX weeks of Daniel begin from the end of the same: for we have shown in the Chronicon that both beginnings are sufficiently clear, and defined in such a way that no just cause for doubting remains. And although the scope of the Prophets is to instruct the people concerning the certainty of things, it is by no means a consequence, with that Beroaldian opinion excluded, that the people were not instructed by Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel concerning the certainty of things: because another mode of information remained, besides that Beroaldian one. Furthermore, it is stated nakedly that Jerusalem with the temple was completely overturned at the beginning of the seventieth year of the Babylonian captivity: because it cannot be proven that the beginning of that captivity is to be fixed there: nor does that contribute to this point, where the beginning of the LXX weeks is being investigated.

Mr. Ravius adds this as a sort of reason, that it is thus easy to calculate 76 years from the 11th of Zedekiah, namely with 26 years of Nebuchadnezzar, 14 of Belshazzar, and 30 of Evil-merodach intervening; but the matter now is not about the calculation of the years of the Babylonian captivity, but about the beginning of the LXX weeks of Daniel: nor is there any foundation found in the Scriptures for that Ravian calculation, by which 30 years of Evil-merodach and 14 of Belshazzar are used. Moreover, he urges in vain the absurdity that otherwise the land of the Jews could not have rested for 70 years: for why could they not have rested for so many years, even if the LXX weeks of Daniel do not begin from the beginning of Cyrus? Finally, he also brings this forward, that no evident passage from the Scriptures can be brought forward for the beginning of the Babylonian captivity from the deported Jeconiah. Which we can easily concede, we who take the beginning from the first of Nebuchadnezzar and the fourth of Jehoiakim with Jeremiah and Daniel; but we do not see what that can contribute to taking the beginning of the LXX weeks from the beginning of Cyrus. And these are those 14 reasons of Mr. Ravius, succinctly exhibited, which any sensible person, without my saying so, will be able to judge how much strength they have for that beginning of the LXX weeks of Daniel.

Now, besides the characteristic foundation and those reasons just weighed, he thinks he can teach the same thing from a parallel: that among the four promises made to Abraham in Gen. 12, 15, 17, 22, the first was the principal one, and therefore the edict of Cyrus should also be considered the main one, upon which the benevolent edicts of Darius Hystaspes, Xerxes, and Darius Nothus relied. But not only is this comparison not similar, but all things in this comparison limp. For more promises made to Abraham can be counted than four; especially that which was made to him in Gen. 18 in a solemn manner in a truly singular appearance of the Son of GOD: nor are those four benevolent edicts, as Ravius lists them, correct, because the third was not of Xerxes, but of Artaxerxes Longimanus, nor was the fourth in Nehemiah of Darius Nothus, but of the same Artaxerxes: nor if that designation were most correct, would it contribute anything to the present matter, where the question is not which edict was principal or first, but which edict Gabriel looked to, which is to be learned from the periphrasis and circumstances of the text, and other things, not from extraneous places: although even that which is described in Gen. 12 is not to be held as the principal one among the promises made to Abraham, but rather that which was last in order: as being confirmed by an oath, which the Apostle values most highly above others in Heb. 6:13. But here one must wonder and ask, whence does Mr. Ravius have those two last benevolent edicts proceeding from Xerxes and Darius Nothus? For if one wishes to understand Xerxes himself by the Artaxerxes of Ezra 7 (which, however, does not please Ravius himself, for he understands Artaxerxes Mnemon), where is the edict of Darius Nothus to be sought, which he makes the last? Among the Patrons of the Jews, certainly, only three are listed who favored the rebuilding: Cyrus, Darius (Mr. Ravius makes that one Hystaspes with us, who is celebrated in Ezra 4), and Artaxerxes in Ezra 6:14. Nor is there any reading anywhere in the sacred writings about a patron Darius Nothus. If he distinguishes that Darius in Ezra 4:24 from the Darius in Ezra 6:14, and wishes this one to be Darius Nothus, Ezra would have wrongly counted only three Patrons of the rebuilding of the temple, because he should have counted four, namely Cyrus, Darius Hystaspes, Xerxes, and Darius Nothus, since according to Mr. Ravius he lists only three, and indeed Cyrus, Darius Nothus, and Artaxerxes Mnemon, whom, however, Ravius, contradicting himself, grants contributed nothing to the structure of the temple, as it had been completed under his predecessor Darius Nothus. But let these things suffice concerning the term from which the weeks of Daniel begin, in which it is evident how greatly Mr. Ravius has erred.

It is a more serious ἁμάρτημα [error], that it stuffs 72 whole years into the cycle of 70 weeks. For it does this firstly without any authority: for the 70 years of Zech. 1:12, ch. 7:5, had already elapsed before the beginning of Daniel's weeks in the time of Darius Hystaspis from the beginning of the calamity and desolation of Jerusalem: For from the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, in which the devastation occurred, to the Monarchy of Cyrus, or the 23rd year of the Persian reign, are counted 51 years and 9 months: let there be added to them the 7 remaining years of Cyrus, 8. of Cambyses (including the 7 months of Smerdis) and two of Darius Hystaspis, there result about 69 years: if the number is begun from the beginning of the final siege, which occurred 390 days before the city was captured, Ezek. 4:5, 8, and thus a full year and two months before the destruction of the temple, the 70 years of the Jerusalem calamity had almost elapsed in the second year of Darius Hystaspis: which sum of 70 years will be exceeded if we take the beginning from the first siege of Nebuchadnezzar, as it occurred two years and seven months before the destruction of the temple. For from the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, or the time of the destruction of the temple, to Darius are counted 66 years, 9 months; let the 2 years of the siege with seven months be added, there result 69 years and 4 months: to which are added the 1st year of Darius and 10 months from Zech. 1:7, and thus there result 71 years with two months, so that the angel of the Lord could truly say that God had already been angry for 70 years with this city. Compare what we said almost at the end of Section VI. But where, I ask, is it taught that those 70 years took their beginning from the third year of Cyrus according to Zechariah? And how will it be established that seven weeks of years, that is, 49, as well as 72 or 121 years, have already elapsed by the second year of Darius, even if we assume that Darius Nothus is understood by Zechariah, although that is by no means to be conceded. From the first year of Cyrus (the 7th of the Monarchy) or including the two years of Darius the Mede, nine of his years are counted; add to these 8 of Cambyses and Smerdis, 36 of Darius Hystaspis, 21 of Xerxes, 41 of Artaxerxes Μακρόχειρος, and two of Darius Nothus, and there result at most 117 years, but from the fifth of Cyrus 112. But let us admit even here that that number of 121 years is correct; whence will it be proven that 72 years are to be intercalated into the first seven weeks? Mr. Ravius indeed gives thanks to the Holy Trinity for this discovery; but how is he going to convince us that it was divinely revealed? He says that 72 years of disturbance of the work intervened; but by whom was the construction of the temple disturbed for so many years? Or how will that epoch of feigned disturbance be reconciled with the History of Ezra and Nehemiah? For both testify that after the reign of Darius I or Hystaspis, under whom the temple was also built, Artaxerxes, who reigned before Darius Nothus, in the 7th year of his reign, as also again in the 20th year, gave edicts and a concession for the repair of the Sacred things and the city: which were also carried into execution by Ezra and Nehemiah. How then can the desolation of the temple be extended after Artaxerxes Longimanus up to the times of Darius Nothus, so that there was still cause for complaint about it in the 2nd or even the 4th year of Darius Nothus? For Ravius extends it up to that point from Zechariah 7:5.

Furthermore, how is Ravius going to reconcile those 49 years of liberty with Ezra? If indeed Ezra clearly teaches (ch. 4:5 seqq.) that after the indulgence of Cyrus, that liberty was immediately disturbed for all the remaining days of Cyrus, up to the reign of Darius Hystaspis. What liberty was there then, and how could the work have proceeded in those times, which Ezra expressly testifies ceased and was hindered in those times?

But if Darius Nothus is to be understood in Ezra, whom Ravius understands in chapter 6:14, 15, then it must certainly be said that the temple was built only 121 years after the concession of Cyrus, and so the Jews must have lacked a temple not only for the years of their liberty, which he calls 49, but also for more than 70 others, which is extremely absurd. Furthermore, a new difficulty reveals itself, when Ravius says that the complaint about the desolation arose in the second year of Darius Nothus, according to Zechariah 1, and extends it even to the fourth year of Darius Nothus: by what arrangement, namely, is it said that the structure of the house of the Lord was finished in the sixth year of Darius Nothus in Ezra 6:15?

Was it built within two years? But Mr. Ravius promises that some secret concerning this biennium will reveal itself in his Chronological Dissertation. Is that, therefore, perhaps still to be awaited? μέγα λίαν μυστήριον: since he wishes the fourth year of Darius Nothus to be the very same as his sixth, which mystery certainly involves a contradiction. Besides, how will only 70 weeks remain until the passion of Christ, which Ravius makes the term of this epoch, if 72 whole years are to be intercalated, that is, 10 whole annual weeks plus two years? For thus there will not be 70 weeks anymore, but 80, with two years: which is openly contrary to the words of the angel. But that Ravian intercalation is also altogether wonderful, and purely arbitrary, and I add, clearly unheard of: For as can be seen from his Table V, from the fifth year of Cyrus he intercalates 14 years of disturbance of the structure, but from that he counts 36 years of the structure and the success of the work from the first year of Darius Hystaspis: and furthermore, under the reign of Xerxes, he continues the years of disturbance through the first 15 years of his same Empire, which calculation is again purely arbitrary and feigned. For where is it taught in the Scriptures that the work of the structure of the temple succeeded for three years under the empire of Cyrus, and indeed up to his fifth year, and furthermore for the whole 36 years of Darius Hystaspis? Where is it taught that it was disturbed again for 15 years of Xerxes? Where, finally, is it even hinted by a word that the work was continued again in the last 6 years of Xerxes? All these things are said without Scripture, nay, they are clearly invented. But he proceeds further with his inventions, and wishes that the structure of the temple rested and was disturbed during the entire reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus, about which likewise he could not produce a jot from Scripture: and finally he contends that the fabric of the temple was completed in the four years of Darius Nothus, namely from the second to the sixth. Thus, therefore, he discontinues and separates the years of the 7 weeks of Daniel and the 72 years which he snatches here from Zechariah through various intercalation at will: whereas it is necessary to understand them as continuous, as in the remaining 63 weeks, so also in these first 7 weeks of years: concerning which matter we have warned both in the Anti-Grotian notes on Daniel chapter 9, and in the Sacred Chronology, and we have refuted that new discovery before the Ravian Chronology was seen in the double opinion of Mr. Wasmuth. Finally, Ravius makes two out of one Darius of Ezra. For in Ezra chapter 4, 5, and 24. It is certain and a point agreed upon by Ravius's own opinion that Darius Hystaspis is understood. But in the time of this very man (as Ezra immediately adds in chapter 5:1), with Haggai and Zechariah inciting the people with their prophecies, the work of the structure succeeded; which certainly cannot by any reason be snatched away to times long later under Darius Nothus: since the continuity of chapter 4 and 5 is clearer than the midday sun, that the work succeeded at that same time under those Prophets, which Ezra had defined in chapter 5:24 by the mention of the second year (which second year Zechariah chapter 1 and Haggai chapter 1 and 2 also commemorate), and the comparison of Ezra 6:14, 15 sufficiently teaches that the same Darius is understood, in whose 6th year the work is said there to have been finished: so that no doubt about it remains, the clause of the mandate v. 12. I Darius have commanded this, and its transmission made by the same Darius v. 13, as well as the mention of that very Darius, and the conjunction with Haggai and Zechariah v. 14, infallibly show that it is not another, but the same Darius, in whose second year the work was resumed, but in the 6th year was completed: and thus it is most clear that it was perfected within 4 years, and not, as Ravius wishes, in 121 years. Furthermore, lest this novel opinion and intercalation should seem to be destitute of a foundation, Ravius has twisted to that end the prophecy of Gabriel, whom he himself says was the uncreated Angel, the Holy Spirit, who namely and brought this prophecy to Daniel, and announced to Mary the conception of the Son of God, nay, he even affirms that Christ was comforted by that uncreated Angel in Luke 22:43 in his agony at the Mount of Olives, so that nothing should be lacking to his novelties; which, however, is openly repugnant to both more famous Theology, which acknowledges only one uncreated Angel, the Son of God, and to historical narration, and to the sacred texts Dan. 8:16, Luke 1:19 and 35, chap. 22:43, since from them it is most manifest that Gabriel is a created Angel.
