Deniq; quis non videt procedi a non distri- buto ad distributum, cum ita colligitur: Annus ille cœ- pit a die Jovis, vel feria quinta. E. fuit annus M. 3586. vel, ergo fuit 3614. Si in formam redigatur, transpa- rebit statim vitium: Annus M. 3614. incipit a feria quinta: Annus 3. Cyri a feria quinta incepit, E. annus tertius Cyri est annus M. 3614. Annon enim plures a- lii anni Mundi a feria quinta incepere? Sed hic pa- ralogismus, & vitiosa argumentandi ratio fere so- lemnis est Dn. Ravio: unde quid de demonstrationi- bus ejus habendum sit, facile colligere licet.

Deinde addit rationes pro suo initio hebdo- madum Danielis: sed quæ parum ad rem faciunt. Nam quid hoc ad initium LXX. hebdomadum, quod Esaias prædixit Cyrum relaxaturum populum Judaicum c. 43, 10. 44, 28. c. 45, 1. quodq; Jer. 29, 10. septuaginta tantum fore annos captivitatis Babylo- nicæ, non plures, non pauciores vaticinatus est, & quod promissa Esaiæ & Jeremiæ impleta sint, de qui- bus omnibus nemo dubitat; sed illa ὀδὲν πρὸς δυό- νυσον. Porro quod edictum Cyri primarium fuit, & primum,quodque ad illud multi Judæi redierint,& sub Cyro primajacta sint templi fundamenta, ad quod provocarint etiam Judæi apud Tabnei, quodq; inqui- ri jusserit Darius, hæc omnia ad edictum de extru- ctione urbis,& mœniorum Hierosolymæ, cum effe- ctu conjunctum nihil faciunt. Quod autem Spiri- tus S. instare dixerit,idq; proxime, hoc edictum, e ver- bis Gabrielis non apparet. An restituerit Cyrus Judæis dignitatem liberæ Reipublicæ,& Ecclesiæ non subjectæ, sed a Deo solo dependentis? disquirendum foret, nec tamen id ad initium hebdomadum Danielis multum faceret, quia non de restitutione intenta, sed ad effe- ctum deducta, quæritur, quod sub Cyro factum non est, ac ne quidem sub proximis ejus successoribus. Spi- ritum S. vero in alloquio Danielis alludere ad LXX. annos captivitatis Babylonicæ, nec probatum est, nec si id fiat, ad initium LXX. hebdomadum Danielis definiendum facit; illis autem unico solum anno inter- eedente septennia LXX. connecti per meram αἴτησιν τῶ ἐν ἀρχῇ asseritur. Neq; ideo dubium prorsus relin- qui LXX. captivitatis etiam Babylonicæ annorum ini- tium sequitur, nisi sc. inde a finita eadem ineant LXX. hebdomades Danielis: nam utrumque initium satis clarum,& ita, ut justa causa dubitandi non supersit, definitum esse a Spir. S. in Chronico ostendimus. Et quanquam Prophetarum scopus sit de rerum certitudi- ne instruere populum, minime tamen, exclusa senten- tia illa Beroaldica, consequens est populum ab Esaia, Jeremia & Daniele de rerum certitudine instructu non fuisse: quia alius supererat informationis mod9,præ- ter illuBeroaldicum. Ulterius initio septuagesimi anni Babylonicæ captivitatis Jerusalem cum templo plane e- versam fuisse, nude dicitur : quia ibi initium figen- dum illius captivitatis esse probari non potest: nec id huc facit, ubi de initio LXX. hebdomadum disqui- ritur.

Addit & hoc rationis instar Dn. Ravius, quod sic facile sit computare 76. annos ab XI. Sedekiæ elapso, sc. 26. Nebucadnezaris, 14. Belfazaris, & 30. Evilmero- dachi annis interjectis; At non de calculo jam res est annorum captivitatis Babylonicæ, sed de initio LXX. hebdomadum Danielis: neq; de illo Raviano calculo, qua annos 30. Evilmerodachi,& 14. Belfazaris in Scri- pturis ullum reperitur fundamentum. Absurdum insuper nequicquam urget, quod alias per 70. annos fundi Judæi requiescere non potuerint:quidni enim per tot annos potuerint requiescere, etsi non a Cyri ini- tio LXX. Hebdomades Danielis ineant? Denique & hoc adfert, quod nullus evidens locus e Scripturis pro initio Babylonicæ captivitatis a deportato Jechonia adferri possit. Quod facile nos concedere possumus, qui a primo Nebucadnezaris & quarto Jajakimi cum Jeremia & Daniele initium capimus; sed quid illud facere queat pro initio LXX. Hebdomadum a Cyri i- nitio capiendo, non videmus. Atque hæ sunt illæ 14. rationes Dn. Ravii, succincte exhibitæ, quæ quantum roboris pro illo initio LXX. hebdomadum Danielis habeant, quivis cordatus, me tacente, arbi- trari poterit.

Jam præter fundamentum characteristicum, & rationes istas nunc expensas, a pari se id docere posse arbitratur: quod inter quatuor Abrahamo facta promissa Gen. XII. XV. XVII. XXII, primum fuerit præcipuum, adeoque etiam principale edictum Cyri habendum sit, cui innitebantur Darii Hystaspi- dis, Xerxis, & Darii Nothi edicta benevola. Ast non hoc simile solum, sed omnia in hoc simili clau- dicant. Numerari enim plura possunt Abrahamo facta promissa quam quatuor; imprimis illud, quod Gen. XVIII. solemni modo in apparitione prorsus singulari Filii DEI factum eidem est: neque quatuor illa edicta benevola, prout ea Ravius recenset, recte se habent, quia tertium non Xerxis, sed Artaxerxis Longimani fuit, neque quartum apud Nehemiam Da- rii Nothi, sed ejusdem Artaxerxis: nec si rectissime se haberet illa designatio, ad rem præsentem quic- quam faceret, ubi non quodnam præcipuum, aut primum fuerit edictum, quæritur, sed quodnam edi- ctum respexerit Gabriel, quod e περιφράσει & cir- cumstantiis textus, aliisque discendum est, non e lo- cis alienis: quanquam etiam id pro præcipuo haben- dum non sit inter promissa Abrahamo facta, quod Gen. XII. descriptum est, sed potius illud, quod ordi- ne postremum fuit: utpote jurejurando confirma- tum, quod præ aliis maximi facit Apostolus Ebr. 6, 13. Mirari autem hic, & quærere oportet, undenam habeat Dn. Ravius illa duo postrema edicta benevola a Xerxe & Dario Notho profecta? Nam si maxime per Artaxerxem Esdr. VII. Xerxem ipsum intelligere quis velit, (quod vero nec ipsi Ravio placet, intel- ligit enim Artaxerxem Memoriosum) ubinam quære- tur Darii Nothi edictum, quod postremum facit? In- ter Patronos certe Judæorum non nisi tres recensen- tur, qui reædificationi faverint, Cores, Darius, (Hy- staspidem illum nobiscum facit Dn. Ravius, qui Es- dr. IV. celebratur) & Artachsashta Esdr. 6, 14. Nec de patrono Dario Notho ullibi in sacris literis legere est. Si distinguat Darium illum Esdr. 4, 24. a Dario Esdr. 6, 14. atque hunc esse velit Darium Nothum, Esdras male tantum tres numerasset Patronos reædifica- tionis templi, quia quatuor numerare debuisset, ni- mirum Cyrum, Darium Hystaspida, Xerxem & Darium Nothum, quum juxta Dn. Ravium recenseat tantum tres, & quidem Cyrum, Darium Nothum & Artaxer- xem Memoriosum, quem vero postremum ad templi structuram nihil contulisse Ravius sibi ipsi contradi- cens, largitur, utpote quod sub Dario Notho ante- cessore completum fuerit. Sed ista de termino a quo hebdomadum Danielis sufficiant, in quo quan- topere lapsus sit Dn. Ravius, ita constat.

Gravius est ἁμάρτημα, quod integros 72. annos inferciat cyclo LXX. hebdomadum. Nam id fa- cit primo sine ulla autoritate: LXX. enim anni Zach. 1, 12. cap. 7, 5. ante septimanarum Danielis initium elapsi jam erant tempore Darii Hystaspis inde ab i- nitio calamitatis & desolationis Hierosolymæ: Nam a 19. anno Nebucadnezaris, quo facta est devastatio, ad Monarchiam Cyri, vel annum 23. regni Persici nu- merantur 51. anni 9. menses: addantur illis 7. reliqui Cyri, 8. Cambysis (inclusis 7. mensibus Smerdis) duo Darii Hystaspidis, prodeunt 69. circiter anni: si ab obsidionis extremæ initio numerus ineatur, quæ 390. diebus ante captam urbem facta Ez. 4, 5. 8. adeoq; an- no integro & duobus mensib9 ante excidium templi, elapsi propemodum fuere Darii Hystaspis secundo anno LXX. anni calamitatis Hierosolymitanæ: quæ summa 70. annorum excedetur, si initium capiamus a prima Nebucadnezaris obsessione, utpote duobus annis, & mensibus septem facta ante excidium tem- pli. A Nebucadnezaris erim 19. vel tempore excidii templi ad Darium numerantur 66. anni, 9. Menses; addantur anni obsidionis 2. cum septem mensibus, prodeunt 69. anni 4. menses: quibus accedunt I. annus Darii & 10. Menses e Zach. 1, 7. ac prodeunt ita 71. anni cum duobus mensibus, ut vere angelus Domini dicere potuerit, jam 70. annis Deum iratum fuisse huic urbi. Confer quæ fere sub finem Sect. VI. diximus. Ubi vero, obsecro, docetur, quod anni illi 70, Zachariæ a Cyri tertio initium sumserint? Et quomodo Darii secundo jam elapsa statuentur se- ptem septennia, hoc est, 49. ut & 72. vel 121. anni, etiamsi ponamus Darium Nothum a Zacharia intel- ligi, quanquam id minime concedendum sit. A Cyri primo (Monarchiæ 7.) vel inclusis Darii Medi duobus, novem ejus numerantur anni, his adde 8. Cambysis & Smerdis, 36. Darii Hystaspidis, 21. Xerxis, 41. Artaxerxis Μακρόχειρος, & duos Darii Nothi, prodeunt ad summum 117. anni, a quinto vero Cyri 112. Sed admittamus & hic numerum illum 121. an- norum recte se habere, unde evincetur, intercalan- dos esse 72. annos septem hebdomadibus prioribus? Gratias agit quidem Dn. Ravius S. S. Trinitati, pro hac inventione; sed quomodo fidem facturus est eandem divinitus revelatam esse? Dicit 72. annos di- sturbationis operæ intervenisse; sed a quonam distur- bata per tot annos fuit exstructio templi? aut quo- modo cum Historia Esdræ & Nehemiæ conciliabi- tur illa disturbationis commentitiæ Epocha? Te- statur enim uterque post Darii I. vel Hystaspis re- gnum, sub quo etiam templum exstructum est, Ar- taxerxem, qui ante Darium Nothum regnavit, 7. an- no imperii sui, ut & anno iterum 20. edicta, & con- cessionem dedisse ad reparationem Sacrorum & ur- bis: quæ etiam exequutioni data per Esdram & Ne- hemiam sunt. Quomodo ergo desolatio templi post Artaxerxem Longimanum usque ad Darii Nothi tempora extendi potest, ut conquerendum adhuc de eadem anno 2. vel etiam quarto Darii Nothi fue- rit? nam eo usq; e Zach. 7, 5. extendit eandem Ra- vius.

Porro libertatis illos annos 49. quomodo conci- liaturus cum Esdra est Ravius? siquidem post Cyri indultum statim libertatem illam turbatam esse o- mnibus diebus Cyri reliquis, usque ad Darii Hysta- spis regnum, palam doceat Esdras c. 4, 5. seqq. Quæ- nam tum libertas fuit, & quomodo succedere opus potuit istis temporibus, quod diserte testatur Es- dras istis temporibus cessasse, & impeditum fuisse?

Si vero intelligendus apud Esdram Darius No- thus sit, quem cap. 6, 14. 15. intelligit Ravius, utique dicendum erit, annis 121. demum post concessionem Cyri templum exstructum fuisse, adeoq; caruisse o- portet Judæos templo non tantum annis libertatis suæ, quos vocat 49, sed etiam plus quam 70. aliis, quod perquam absurdum est. Ulterius nova se pro- dit difficultas, cum Darii Nothi anno secundo Zach. 1. querelam de desolatione ortam dicit Ravius, eam- que extendit ad quartum etiam annum Darii Nothi: quo pacto, nempe sexto Darii Nothi anno dicatur structura domus Domini consummata Esdr. 6, 15.

Num intra biennium exstructa illa fuit? Sed de bien- nio isto arcanum aliquod se proditurum in Diss. Chro- nol. promittit D. Ravius. Id ergo forsan adhuc expe- ctandum erit? μέγα λίαν μυστήριον: quandoquidem quartum Darii Nothi velit esse ipsummet ejusdem sextum, quod mysterium sane contradictionem in- volvit. Adhæc quomodo manebunt tantum 70. hebdomadæ usque ad passionem Christi, quam Epcchæ hujus terminum facit Ravius, si anni 72. integri in- tercalandi sunt, hoc est, 10. integræ hebdomades annuæ cum biennio? Ita enim non 70. hebdomadæ amplius, sed 80. erunt, cum duobus annis: quod verbis ange- li aperte contrariatur. Sed & mirabilis omnino, ac mere arbitraria addo & inaudita plane est illa inter- calatio Raviana: Nam ut ex Tabula ejus V. videre est. a quinto Cyri intercalat 14. annos disturbationis stru- cturæ, ex eo vero numerat a primo Darii Hystaspis 36. annos structuræ, & successus operis: ac porro sub Xerxis regimine disturbationis annos continuat per 15. annos priores Imperii ejusdem, qui calculus iterum mere arbitrarius est, & commentitius. Ubi enim in Scripturis docetur, quod per triennium sub imperio Cyri, & quidem usque ad quintum ejus annum, & porro per integros 36. annos Darii Hy- staspida opus structuræ templi succefferit? ubi doce- tur, quod per 15. Xerxis annos disturbatum iterum id fuerit? ubi denique vel verbo innuitur, quod po- stremis 6. annis Xerxis denuo continuatum sit opus? hæc omnia ἄτεργραφῆς dicuntur, imo plane fin- guntur. Procedit autem ulterius commentis suis, & sub Artaxerxis Longimani toto regimine vult quie- visse, & turbatam fuisse structuram templi, de quo itidem, ne apicem e Scriptura producere potuit: ac denique quatuor Darii Nothi annis, a secundo nem- pe ad sextum absolutam esse fabricam templi con- tendit. Sic ergo annos hebdomadum 7. Danielis, & annos 72. quos e Zacharia huc abripit discontinuat, & sejungit per variam intercalationem pro lubitu: quos vero continuos, ut in reliquis 63. hebdomadis, ita etiam in his 7. primis septenniis intelligere opor- tet: qua de re tum in Anti-Grotianis ad Dan. 9. ca- put, tum in Chron. sacro monuimus, & novum illud inventum ante visam Ravianam Chronologiam in Dn. Wasmuthi gemina sententia confutavimus. De- nique ex uno Dario Esdræ duos facit Ravius. Nam apud Esdram cap. 4, 5. & 24. Darium Hystaspida intelligi certum est, & ὁμολογέμενον ipsius Ravii sententia. At hujus ipsius tempore (ut immediate subjungit cap. 5, 1. Esdra) Haggai & Zacharia vati- ciniis suis instigantibus populum opus structuræ succeffit; quod utique nulla ratione abripi potest ad tempora longe posteriora sub Dario Notho: si- quidem συνέχεια cap. 4. & 5. sole meridiano clarior sit, eodem illo tempore succeffisse opus sub istis Pro- phetis, quod cap. 5, 24. Esdras anni secundi Darii mentione definiverat, (quem annum secundum et- iam commemorant Zacharias cap. 1. & Haggæus c. 1. & II.) & collatio Esdræ 6, 14. 15. eundem Darium, cujus anno 6. absolutum opus illic dicitur, intelligi satis docet: quod ne dubium de eo ullum supersit, mandati clausula v.12. Ego Darius hoc mandavi, ejus- que transmissio ab eodem Dario facta v. 13. nec non commemoratio ipsius illius Darii, & conjunctio cum Haggæo & Zacharia v. 14. infallibiliter ostendunt, non alium, sed eundem esse Darium, cujus anno se- cundo opus reassumtum, anno vero 6. absolutum fuit: adeoque intra 4. annos id perfectum esse luculen- tissimum est, non vero, ut Ravius vult annis 121. Cæ- terum ne fundamento novella hæc sententia & in- tercalatio videatur destitui, detorsit eo Ravius va- ticinium Gabrielis, quem ipse dicit Angelum increa- tum Spiritum S. fuisse, qui sc. & Danieli hoc vatici- nium attulerit, & Mariæ conceptionem Filii Dei annunciarit, imo etiam ab Angelo illo increato Chri- stum Luc. 22, 43. confortatum esse in agone ad montem oliveti, ne quid novitatibus defit, affirmat; quod vero & Theologiæ famiori, quæ non nisi unum an- gelum increatum Filium DEI agnoscit, & Histori- cæ narrationi, & textibus sacris aperte repugnat Dan. 8, 16. Luc. 1, 19. & 35. cap. 22, 43. quum inde Angelum creatum esse Gabrielem manifestissi- mum sit. Pervertit autem textum Danielis non una ratione, & ut hic primum de prioribus addamus 7. hebdomadibus, cum cæteræ ad postremam Ravii Epocham pertineant, versum 24. cap. IX. Danielis ita reddidit: Septennia 70. in partes, intervalla, & spatia sunt concisa, interstincta, & distincta in bonum populorum tuorum & politiæ, urbisque sanctæ Tuæ, ut tum incipiat finiri culpa transgressionis, & obliterari reatus, & expiari idololatria, & procurari salus æterna, & obsignari visio & Prophetia, cum bapti- zatus fuerit sanctissimus. Versum vero sequentem 25. ita interpretatus est: Attende igitur, ut discas, & Chronologus evadas, inde a promulgatione edicti Cy- ri proximi de restituendis popularibus, & de reædi- ficanda Hierosolyma perstitura ultra Christum me- diatorem prima sunt septennia septem (posteaq́; septen- niis 62. reædificabuntur amplæ portæ & muri) quan- quam intercalari angustia eorum temporum. Ha- ctenus paraphrasis Raviana priorum commatum duorum vaticinii Angelici. In qua hæc deside- ramus (1.) Nihil in textu habetur de hebdo- madis in partes, intervalla, & spatia concisis. Verbum Ebræum נֶחְתַּךְ a liquando est, liquido determina- tæ, vel eliquatæ sunt hebdomades, vel unaquæque earum. Singulare enim adhibetur verbum, con- structum cum nomine plurali, idque Avenario in Lexico notante, ut intelligatur, illas septima- nas tam certo implendas esse, ac si esset una. Un- de continuitas septimanarum harum colligitur, non vero discontinuatas easdem esse: quia hæc discontinuatio Raviana penitus repugnat unitati, neque ad liquidam determinationem ullatenus fa- cit, sed definitionem divinam dubiam, incertam, maximeque illiquidam, quantum in ipso est, red- dit. (2.) Super populum Danielis, & super civi- tatem sanctitatis ejus decisæ vel determinatæ dicun- tur septuaginta septimanæ, non in spatia, & in- tervalla; concisæ perhibentur in bonum populi, & politiæ: adeoque objectum, populus nempe Do- mini & civitas designatur, non vero finis, seu bo- num ejus. (3.) Consummatio prævaricationum non de fine vel termino culpæ populi Israelitici, sed de ablatione iniquitatum totius generis humani me- ritoria intelligenda; Conf. Zach. 3, 9. Ebr. 9, 26. 28. ubi per ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας & τὸ πολλῶν ἀνε- νεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας describitur. Neque vero obsigna- tio peccatorum, vel expiatio iniquitatum, ad pec- cata aut idololatriam populi restringenda est, siqui- dem Christus portare peccata mundi Joh. 1, 29. & propitiatio pro totius mundi peccatis fieri debuerit 1. Joh. 2. 2. utpote cui toti etiam salus æterna ab ipso meritorie procuranda, vel adducenda erat. (4.) De Baptismo Christi nihil διαῤῥήδην tradit Gabriel: sed de ungendo sanctissimo: neque tum populi Judaici culpam finem habituram docet, cum baptizatus fuerit Christus: sed hæc conjungit eadem ratione, & constructione: nimirum determinatas esse 70. septi- manas ad consumendam transgressionem & ad ungen- dum Sanctissimum. Finem, id est, causam finalem esse consumtionem vel ἀθέτησιν transgressionum & expia- tionem iniquitatum admittimus: non autem con- sumtionem transgressionum ad tempus unctionis, vel etiam baptismi, adstringendum esse, concedi- mus. (5.) Paraphrasi textus temere ingeritur edi- ctum Cyri: quia angelus nihil aliud exprimit, quam exitum sermonis, qui vel de sermone Prophetico, vel de edicto Regio explicatur; neq; Cyri edictum, quod erat de reædificando templo & magnam partem irri- tum factum est: sed tale, quod cum successu conjun- ctum futurum sit, & quidem qua reædificationem mu- rorum & platearum, adeoq; reparandam ipsam ur- bem ac politiam Hierosolymitanam hic spectatur. Proinde non agitur hoc loco de restituendis popula- ribus, sed de reædificanda urbe: nam id phrasis im- portat Ebræa, ad revertendum & ad ædificandum, id est, ad reædificandum, vel ad revertendum ad ædifica- tionem Hierosolymæ: Nec (7.) de Hierosolyma ULTRA Christum Mediatorem perstitura vers. 25.

quicquam τὸ ῥητὸν vaticinii habet. Nimirum per- vertitur sensus voculæ עד quæ est USQUE, non vero ULTRA: & durationis Hierosolymæ tempus, quod hisce verbis definitum minime est, temere iisdem ingeritur. Nihil enim habetur, hoc quidem loco, de Hierosolyma PERSTITURA, vel quo- usque ea conservanda. Tempus definitur, vel Epocha inde ab exitu sermonis de reædificandis Hierosolymis usque ad Messiam ducem: cujus Epochæ terminus a quo est exitus verbi, terminus ad quem est Christus Dux, declaratus publice, quod factum esse in Ba- ptismo admittimus. Paraphrasi vero Raviana ter- minus ad quem prorsus intervertitur, ut constare non possit, quousque illa Epocha a sermonis exitu definita sese hic porrigat: adeoq; plane pervertitur sensus oraculi de tempore adventus Christi Ducis, ut nulla supersit certitudo, nedum convictio Judæorum inde desumi queat. (8.) Parenthesis illa præter ne- cessitatem fingitur de septenniis 62. Cohærent n. LXII. illæ hebdomadæ cum præcedentibus septem, imo connectendæ necessario sunt, ut ita LXIX. se- ptimanæ usque ad Christum Ducem determinatæ indi- centur; quas in duas partes dístribuere libuit Sp. S. idque,ut apparet,ideo,ut septem integra septennia, non interrupta aut intercalata (hæc enim ignorat Scriptura, nec admittit præsens computus) sed con- tinua impendenda esse structuræ urbis denotaret. (9.) Non constat sibi Parenthesis Raviana. Quid enim? num 62. septennia requirebantur, ut portæ & muri reædificarentur? (10.) Quod de interca- lari angustia temporum hic intercalatur (quod pri- marium est in hac Chronologia Raviana) a verbis Gabrielis prorsus alienum est, nullum enim Jota in illis de intercalatione habetur, nec si maxime iis- dem congrueret, ad illum tam multiplicem ἐμβο- λισμὸν, quem supra ex Raviana sententia recensui- mus, probandum ullo modo sufficeret. Certe nemo eundem e verbis illis exsculpere posset: ne- mo etiam hactenus eundem exsculpere aut adse- rere præsumsit. Coarctationis & angustiæ tempo- rum mentio fit, uti etiam reddidit ipse Dn. D. Wasmuth Ebraicæ literaturæ scientissimus: non vero intercalaris angustia, nec intercalationis AN- NORUM, nedum tam variæ intercalationis, mi- nime omnium adeo discontinuæ, per temporum in- tervalla concisa & definita. Quicquid ergo hic de illa distincta intercalatione adferunt, ἐξ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως est: neque ex historia sive sacra sive pro- phana ullo pacto probari potest, ideoque eadem fa- cilitate rejicitur, qua adseritur. (11.) Provocat hic Dn. Ravius ad Dn. D. Wasmuthi vindicias tex- tus Hebraici a parte II. p. 241. Sed ad illas abun- de responsum jam est in Anti-Grotianis nostris ad Dan. IX. (12.) Intercalares annos esse 72. eosque sub diversis Imperatoribus Cyro & successoribus ejus quibusdam usque ad Darium Nothum inclu- sive ingerendos, hypotheses mere sunt precariæ; quia de intercalandis totidem annis altum in Scri- pturis est silentium. Atque hæc etiam de XI. Epocha.

DUODECIMA, & postrema est septen- niorum LXIII. reliquorum Danielis, quam ab anno septimo Darii Nothi orditur, & finit in pas- sione Christi, annorum 441. Quam in duas par- tes distribuit: Prior est LXII. septenniorum, ut- pote 13. annorum Darii Nothi & 20. Artaxerxis Memoris, cujus anno septimo Esdram, vigesimo Nehemiam Hierosolymam profectum esse, putat, ut adeo per 153. annos urbs mœnibus destituta fue- rit; reliquos ex Canone Ptolemaico depromens.

Ubi hæc notamus, 1. Quod perperam Artaxerxis Memoriosi tempore facta esse dicat, quæ sub Longimani imperio gesta esse in Chronico ostendimus. 2. Quod inconvenienter per integros 153. annos, adeoque ultra sesquiseculum urbem mœnibus destitutam adferat. 3. In subsidium Chronologiæ suæ assumit Ptolemei Canonem, & quidem quoad annos bene multos, quam tamen se unice e Scripturis petere cum Pareo jactitat. 4. Ptolemei Canonem antea non uno modo in dubium vocavit: jam vero vice mutata vehementer commendat, quod præsumtione certitudinis nitatur ex Medorum, Græcorum, Ægyptiorum & Romanorum Regum & Imperatorum Catalogo, quodque in eo omnia se recte habeant,

Altera pars hujus Epochæ est ultima hebdomas Danielis, in qua primo posterioris dimidii initium venatur Ravius, tum in cap. LX. Esaia v. 21. quasi loquatur illic DEUS Pater ad Filium de tempore descensus Spiritus S. super ipsum, cum potius sermo ibi sit de Ecclesiæ perpetuo informanda & gubernanda per Spiritum S. nullo autem verbo ipsummet officium Christi propheticum attingatur: tum in Esa. 61, 1. quasi illic itidem de visibili descensu Spiritus S. super Christum in Baptismo agatur, quod pro certo assumit Ravius. Hunc locum, inquit, agere de die baptismi temporali omnes facile concedent. Nec tamen ullum invenire hactenus potuit, qui hic diem Baptismi definitum esse asseruerit ex universa interpretum caterva. Arguit etiam inde ἀνακολύθως de temporali anno Jobeleo hunc locum agere omnes consequenter concessuros esse: quem vero communiter de spirituali anno Jobeleo explicant interpretes. Interim probare id conatur e locorum aliorum collatione, utpote Lev. 25, 20. Jer. 34, 8. 15. & 16. Ezech. 46, 17. sed argumento plane infirmo & ficulneo. Quæ enim, obsecro, hæc est consequentia: In istis locis annus Jobeleus temporalis intelligitur: Ergo etiam Es. LXI. temporalis, non vero spiritualis intelligendus est? nulla: quia illic de Jobeleo Vet. Test. sermo erat, qui typicus fuit: hic autem de anno Jobeleo, quem annunciaturus erat Christus in Novo Testamento vaticinatur Propheta, qui illo adumbratus & præfiguratus fuit. Neque tempus hoc loco definitur præconii Evangelici Christi, quod nempe anno Jobeleo id incepturus sit, sed objectum hujus Evangelicæ prædicationis designatur, quod annunciaturus sit annum placationis, sive gratiæ, & libertatis spiritualis. Denique admisso etiam hoc αἰτήματι de anno temporali Jobeleo ab Esaia indicato, multis adhuc parasangis & circuitionibus, iisque parasyllogisticis opus erit, ut scopo Raviano id velificetur.

Porro, ut ad mensem & diem passionis Christi imo & conceptionis hinc descendat, anno Vet. Test. in duo diviso, in XV. sc. Septembr. quo festum Tabernaculorum incipiebat, & 15. Nisan, quo Pascha celebratum, cum Christus XV. Nisan passus sit, concludit, eundem die XXII. Octobr. qui Sabbati fuerit, natum fuisse. Cujus vero illationis firmitudo nulla apparet, cum eo imprimis nitatur fundamento, quod tabernaculorum festum Patribus primum adventum Christi notet: quod ipse ad diem etiam natalem in festi illius diem incidentem, privata autoritate extendit, & autoritatem tamen, quod mireris, divinam Scripturæ prætendit.

Denique, ut non excutiam, quomodo reductio illa mensium & dierum a 15. Septembris ad 22. Octobris sese habeat, & quam firma nitatur destina, non consonant certe secum hypotheses Ravia- ne. Nam a Die 22. Octobris, quem natalem Christi facit, ad diem 15. Nisan, quem diem constituit passionis Christi, non intercedit annus dimidius, sed desiderantur adhuc 38. dies ad semestre spatium: contendit autem Ravius, præcise dimidium annum cum triennio requiri a tempore Baptismi Christi (quod cum natali Christi ratione mensis & diei coincidere ait) uti Christum etiam præcise 30. annorum fuisse, cum baptizaretur decernit, nec aliter locum Luc. 3, 23. accipiendum esse contendit: disputans vocem ὡσεὶ esse præcise, atque ita verba textus reddens: Cæterum ipsus ille Jesus præcise (eo die) incipiebat esse 30. annorum: ubi vero communiter hactenus interpretes particulam ὡσεὶ exposuere CIRCITER vel QUASI, non vero præcise. Et quomodo consonant sibi illa, quod semel Ravius dicit 15. Nisan Christum passum esse, iterum vero disertis verbis asserit, quia 14. Nisan Adam lapsus fuit, ut Synodus Cæsariensis & alii Patres definierunt, etiam 14. Nisan mori Christum debuisse; additque 14. Nisan feria 6. post 3 1/2. annum a suscepto baptismo Christum mortuum esse? Hæc certe ἀσύστατα sunt. Nec adhuc quicquam circa hanc scripturæ autoritatem, quam vocat, de eo monuimus, quod temere assumat Ravius Epocham Gabrielis finiri in die passionis Christi, quam vero terminari triennio & semestri post passionem Christi suo loco demonstravimus.

Addit autem aliam adhuc Scripturæ Sacræ autoritatem, nimirum e Zach. 1, 7. quia die 24. XI. mensis Sebath anno II. Darii vidit Propheta virum inter myrteta, qui Jehovah dicitur: adeoque Θεάνθρωπον. Unde colligit, illo die 24. XI. mensis vel Januarii conceptum esse Christum. Sed quænam hic ratio consequentiæ? Largimur sane, Virum illum esse DEI Filium: ast probandum est, hic imaginem haberi conceptionis Filii DEI temporalis. Imago est præsentiæ Filii DEI in medio Ecclesiæ, & inter suos: non autem conceptionis: imo ne quidem ἐνσαρκώσεως; licet enim dualitatis naturarum in Christo & ἐνανθρωπήσεως aliquod præludium loca illa exhibeant, in quibus Filius DEI in forma humana κατ' οἰκονομίαν ad tempus assumpta apparuit, non tamen in omnibus istis locis figenda est sedes τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως, quasi illic id ex instituto agatur, ut adumbretur incarnatio, seu finis & causa apparitionis in omnibus istis locis sit ipsa ἐνσάρκωσις, multo minus definitur illic tempus conceptionis Filii DEI. Ita Jos. 5, 13. Filius DEI in forma viri apparuit Josuæ, ceu princeps exercitus Domini circa Pascha: num vero inde colligendum apparitionis istius causam fuisse adumbrationem ἐνσαρκώσεως & conceptionis Christi, aut inferendum Christum ideo circa festum Paschatos concipi debuisse? Ea utique ratione multa, & multum diversa tempora conceptionis Christi e Scriptura colligentur. Et cur non nativitatis Christi tempus, sed conceptionis ex illa apparitione Zachariæ facta concluditur? cur non passionis aut resurrectionis, quam hic figuratam dicit Rupertus Dn. Ravio laudatus?

Nec firmior est illatio de feria septimanali, die nempe Sabbati Gabrielem ad Mariam venisse Luc. 1. siquidem ut Prophetas alloquitur DEUS die Sabbati, sic & Mariam ea feria allocutus sit Gabriel. Nam nec allocutionem Prophetarum ordinarie Sabbato factam esse, certa demonstratione nititur, nec alligatus ideo ad illum diem fuit magis DEUS ad alloquia & revelationes Mariæ, aut aliis faciendas, quam Christus ad apparitiones & alloquia discipulorum post resurrectionem; quæ utique facta die Solis constat, tum ante ascensionem, tum Johanni etiam post ascen- sionem ejusdem Apoc. 1, 10. Denique assumitur temere, imo falso in hac Zachariæ apparitione, factam eam esse anno secundo Darii Nothi: quam vero non Darii Nothi, sed Hystaspis tempore con- tigisse, suo loco evicimus.

His duabus autoritatibus Scripturæ tertio typicam συγκυρίαν adjungit Dn. Ravius ex anno di- luviano: quem a Lamecho, Tubalcaini parente sibi & suis exitialem, & futurum Mundi 1656. prædi- ctum fingit: e Gen. 4, 24. id Cabbala nova, ni fal- lor, deducturus. Qualis vero illa συγκυρία sit, vel ex his patet: quia annum diluvialem 1656. bis & dimidio sumi vult, ut inde producatur annus Nativatis Christi 4140. conceptionis vero Christi Mensem & diem colligit undecimi Mensis diem 24. quia eo columba viride folium attulit. Qui vero mensis non illius 4140. quem antea Cabbalistice collegerat, sed præcedentis 4139. anni esse debuit: quum conceptus sit anno natalem præcedente; nec in feriam 7. aut 24. Januar. sed in seriam I. & 24. Febr. docente B. Polycarpo Lysero, incidit ille columbæ cum viridi folio reditus. Sed hæc di- scussione digna non sunt: cætera ne quidem attin- gi merentur.

Id unum restat, ut paraphrasin reliquæ partis vaticinii angelici, commatum nempe duorum po- stremorum Ravianam adhuc expendamus: quam talem subministrat: v. 26. Pro ultimo finali, elapsis illis 62. septennis, CRUCIFIGETUR Messias, & in cælum ascendendo non apparebit. (Postea ipsam urbem & sanctum templum destruet exercitus Ducis Occidentalis, ut utriusque finis sit cum inundatione diluvialis, sic ut ad finem belli sint meræ vastitates) v. 27. Tum constituet Novum Testamentum pro omni- bus, septennii unici ultimi fine. Nam a posteriori di- midio ejus septennii præsens abolebit typica sacrificia & seria sacra; cumque per alas abominabiles hostiles desolatio sit facta, tum ad finem usque mundi decretum premet locum desolate jacendi. Huc usque illa pa- raphrasis; in qua notamus sequentia;

1. Illud pro ultimo finali non deprehenditur in textu, nec CRUCIFIXIONIS ulla sit mentio, sed simplici- ter dicitur: Et post septimanas sexaginta & duas ex- cindetur Messias. Vox יִכָּרֵת excisionem passim no- tat, crucifixioniem vero nuspiam.

2. De ascensione in Cælum nihil hic habet Gabriel. Nec enim e collatione phraseos Gen. 5, 24. de Enocho adhi- bitæ וְאֵינֶנּוּ ascensio Christi colligi potest, quia nec illic quidem e sola ista voce assumptio Enochi proba- tur, sed potius sequentibus verbis, totaque sen- tentia: Et non erat ipse amplius, quia tulit eum DEUS. Hoc vero loco de Christo exciso διαρρή- δην agitur, non de Christo DEO assumto; nec is ideo dicitur non fuisse amplius in terra, quod DEUS eum in cælum assumserit, sed exscindendus prædicitur, וְאֵין לוֹ & id non sibi: non pro se, sed nostri causa, ut in Anti-Grot. ad hunc locum diximus.

3. Ducis venturi exercitum denominat Gabriel, non vero ducis occidentalis. Etsi enim vox Ebræa etiam de Solis occasu occurrat, nuspiam ta- men absolute posita, sine mentione Solis, eum si- gnificat, vel Occidentem notat.

4. Non de con- stitutione, sed corroboratione Novi Testamenti lo- quitur Angelus, nec eam refert ad septennii uni- ci ultimi finem, sed per unam eandemque inte- gram septimanam fœdus a Christo roboratum iri docet: quod ab ipso partim immediate per tres & dimidium circiter annum factum in diebus mi- nisterii ejus: partim mediate per Apostolos post mortem ejus expeditum.

5. Non in posteriori

medietate hebdomadæ ultimæ aboliturus dicitur Christus typica sacrificia : sed in media septimana ultima, ut specjalius exprimatur tempus passionis & mortis Christi, per quam abolita illa sunt. Quum enim post 62. septimanas excindendum esse Christum antea dixerit Angelus, jam expressius definit tem- pus mortis, quod nempe non sub initium, nec sub finem hebdomadæ ultimæ, sed in ejus medietatem, adeoque post expletos ministerii annos, qui tres erunt cum dimidio fere, ipse passione & morte sua finem impositurus sit typis. Unde non levi- ter errat in computo angeli Dn. Ravius, cum in septuagesimæ hebdomadæ finem conjicit Sacrifi- ciorum abolitionem, & mortem Christi, ceu ve- rum sacrificium propitiatorium : quod in medie- tatem septimanæ septuagesimæ retulit Gabriel; quemadmodum ostendimus in Anti-Grot. & in Chronico Biblico.

Atque hæc de Chronologia Raviana, quæ il- lo ipso tempore a Dn. autore mihi transmissa, quo finem imponebam Chronico Sacro; unde avide per- lustratam, quum tanta παῤῥησίᾳ infallibilitatem ejusdem jactaret Autor, omnino expendendam duxi, Vestris etiam hac parte non defuturus, Au- ditores Clariffimi, desideriis, adeoque mantissæ lo- co infallibilitatis istius discussionem subjeci. Nec tamen animus est cum Dn. Autore vel quoquam alio ferram contentionis reciprocare, aut conten- dere, de quo sancte hic protestor: non enim va- cat aut opportunum est gravissimis muneribus, operisque aliis magis necessariis districto, inani- bus & vitreis argutiis operosius discutiendis tem- pus impendere, nec ætas provectior id permit- tit; Et solius veritatis cœlestis amore ad vindi- candam Scripturam Sacram, ac Chronologiam Biblicam, cui omnino vim inferri per novam il- lam Chronologiam animadvertebam, hoc quic- quid est operæ unice suscepi. Optassem autem, communicasset illa meletemata sua Dn. Ravius ante divulgationem publicam, vel etiam prius- quam tam laboriosam operam Tabulis conficien- dis impenderet. Neque enim dubito, simili te- nore, admissis etiam illis de Cyclis Solis, annis, men- sibus & feriis hebdomadalibus postulatis, & hypo- thesibus generalibus Ravianis juxta Epochas, quæ in Scripturis S. expresse definita sunt, neque salva pietate in dubium vocari possunt, nec insuper ha- bito cœlesti Ptolemei Canone, aut spreta autorita- te exoticorum Scriptorum optimorum, quorum fides temere solicitanda non est, si quis parilem impendere velit operam, gemellas Tabulas confi- ci, & adornari posse Chronologicas, in quibus omnia se recte habeant, ut opus non sit novellas, nuspiam neque in Sacris, neque apud prophanos Scriptores probatas sententias, ac divinationes in- vehere Scripturæ, quæ sacratiori tractanda est ma- nu, verba, & textus ad præceptas opiniones ab- ripere, aut mere voluntariis & inauditis glossis, vel Cabalifticis, Judæorum næniis haud absimilibus, adinventionibus, in iisdem ludere, denique fre- quenti ἑαυτομαχίᾳ se, & sua conficere.

Quum vero emissa in publicum Raviana illa sint (quæ non edita fuisse in incluta Upsaliensi Aca- demia, ubi publico munere Dn. Autor fungi- tur, forte mirari quis posset) privatam ἐπίκρισιν inutilem jam & intempostivam fore, haud im- merito censebam: unde discussionem præsen- tem, quam mereri videbatur novella Chronolo- gia, quamque initio vobis, o Mei, solis destina- ram, publici itidem juris facere propemodum de- crevi: ea potissimum de causa, quod eidem orbi insinuandæ undiquaque suffragia corrogari, intel- ligam; ut ita, quibus volupe est hanc nostram considerationem simul conferre, rationes, quæ meum sufflaminant, imo prohibent suffragium, æqua judicii lance expendant.

sto Elencho Theologico pridem conceperam, una cum hac discussione novellæ Chronologiæ in lu- cem prodeant: quam Chronologiam ut parili cum ipso loco, hoc est, pro unice vera & infalli- bili habeam, non permittunt LUCULENTÆ a Scriptura, sola infallibili, DIVARICATIO- NES, & VIOLENTÆ ejusdem INTERPRE- TATIONES, neque persuadere nova εὑρήματα aptæ natæ sunt MAGIS SPECIOSÆ quam SO- LIDÆ TABELLÆ, utpote vix Topicis, nedum Apodicticis argumentis innixæ, imo ex hypothesi- bus precariis, & paralogismis propemodum per- petuis enatæ; ideoque ne Dn. Autor quidem, con- fido, ægre feret JUDICIUM, quod a me perami- ce, literis iteratis expetiit, quarum (posteriorum faltim) exemplum ideo his præmittendum videba- tur: imprimis quia etiam in nonnullis menti ejus explicandæ inserviunt: quod proinde judicium citra verborum lenocinia, & anfractus, & prout res omnino postulabat, fide Theologica, ac parili prorsus, qua redditum fuit Dn. D. Wasmuthio responsum in causa Conringiana, nomine publico, ferendum censui: id exoptans unice, ut agnita Æ- ræ Codomanniæ (ad nullam enim aliam accedit proxime hæc Raviana) justo amplius sesquiseculo propemodum adaugentis Systema annorum Mun- di, nec non Epocharum quarundam a Scripturæ expressa determinatione aberrantium luculenta falsitate, tum vero hypothesium specialium in desi- gnandis Mensibus, septimanis, & feriis, e characte- ribus τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει collectis, mera Lubricita- te, nec motis, citra causam, antiquis terminis, quod infeliciter Scaligero, & aliis cessit, aut de pon- te, quod ajunt præcipitata cana antiquitate, per generales, si lubeat, hypotheses periculum Dn. Au- tor ὁ Φιλόπονος, vel quisquam alius facere non gravetur. Res ipsa, opinor, docebit, parili specie, & probabilitate emersura, contra vero Scripturæ, nativo suo sensu acceptæ, divinam infallibilitatem, longe magis commendatura, Ecclesiæ denique utilitatem multo luculentiorem allatura singula.

Quo vero ea, quæ primaria fere sunt in hac CHRONOLOGIA Raviana, jam pridem ex- pensa diligentius, & discussa abs me esse, (ante- quam forte manus admoveret huic operæ Dn. Autor) palam constet, conferri hic poterunt, quæ ante aliquot annos, cum Diatriben meam de LXX. Septimanis, inaugurali Dn. L. Georgii Meieri, templi Lambertini, quod LUNÆBURGI est, Pastoris disputatione publicitus Anno cIɔIɔCLXIII. die 28. Octobris hic propositam, forte recense- rem, & in Vindiciis S. Hebreæ Scripturæ Dn. Mat- thie Wasmuthii Professoris tum in Acad. Rostochiensi Anno cIɔ Iɔc LXIV. Rostochii editis, parte II. Lo- cum Danielis c. 9, 24. seqq. cætera erudite pertra- ctatum perlegerem, in chartam, veritatis studio, eaque fini conjeci, ut nempe Beroaldica senten- tia, ad quam præ aliis accedere Alstediana ista LXX. hebdomadum computatio videbatur, di- scussa, de eadem, prouti speciose a Dn. Wasmu- thio novissime tum ornata erat, me, ac lectorem meum plenius informarem, judicium ferrem: si- quidem a veritate, ista Diatriba prolixe asserta, in plusculis ea discederet. Uberiori enim di- scussioni Ravianæ sententiæ illa non parum, cre- do, inservient, utpote quæ affinis maxime est, in hac Epocha Danielitica, Alstedio-Wasmuthianæ: etsi in nonnullis in diversum abeat, & terminum ad quem imprimis aliter assignet. Amicus uter- que mihi est, & a multis annis fuit, ob rariores ingenii dotes, & excellentem in Orientalibus literis eruditionem; sed quia monente Apostolo, ὀυδυνά- μεθά τι κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας, 2. Cor. 13, 8. AMICUS sit RAVIUS, AMICUS WASMUTHIUS, AMICA tamen magis esto VERITAS. Placuit Dn. D. Wasmuth in gratiam CHRONOLOGIÆ, etiam τὰ ἴδια ἀνασχεῖν, circa ultimam hebdomadam, quam rectissime nobiscum antehac in professione nominis Christia- ni Antiochena finiendam docuerat: jam autem oculos præstringentibus Tabulis Ravianis, in mor- te Christi terminat. Non displicebit ergo, quod in gratiam VERITATIS CHRONOLO- GICÆ, hæc, quæ citra ullam insectationem, ju- γένοιτο, γένοιτο!

## 1:1 Introduction: I. In the Name of God. Abraham on Hebrew Coins. Where Also Concerning the Weights Cited, a
I. In the name of God. Abraham on Hebrew coins. Where also concerning the weights cited, and the law according to the sacred

CHAPTER I. Names of coins.

Nummus is derived by some from Numa, the second King of the Romans: whom Suidas reports to have been the first to give the Romans coins made of iron and bronze, and to have called them nommia (assaria) from his own name. For Numus is also written with a single m: as Hesychius has nomia. Simon of Cassia, book XI, ch. 52, says: Numisma is named from the marked and inscribed metal from the time of Numa Pompilius, the second King of the Romans, who ordered metals of different kinds to be made for the use of the people for spending and for making the exchange of things. Others, however, derive the word more correctly from the Greek νόμῳ: concerning which it is observed by Suidas himself under the word νόμῳ, that the Dorians use the word νόμος for a coin; which the Romans pronounce Numus with the letters slightly changed, as it always occurs with a single m in the books of the Pandects. Therefore Pollux, book IX, says: Nummus indeed seems to be a Roman name: but it is a Greek word in Italy and Sicily among the Dorians. And Aristotle in the Republic of the Tarentines says that a coin is called nummus among them, on which was engraved Taras, son of Neptune, riding a dolphin.

The Greek νόμισμα is related, which is called numisma among the Jurisconsults and Horace: from the verb νομίζειν, to establish, to sanction, to estimate, because it obtains its value and price by the decree and statute of a prince, or a nation, or a state: concerning which Aristotle, book V of the Ethics to Nicomachus, says: τ᾽ ὄνομα δ᾽ ἔχει νόμισμα, ὅτι ὐ φύσει, ἀλλὰ νόμῳ ἐσί: It has the name nummus, because it exists not by nature, but by law. This word νόμισμα occurs in this sense in 1 Maccabees 15:6, where power is granted by Antiochus to Simon the High Priest to coin money, as also in the New Testament, Matthew 22:19, τὸ νόμισμα τῦ κένσε, the coin of the census: and specifically for דַּרְכְּמוֹן (daric) in Nehemiah 7:71, they gave gold drachmas, as the Vulgate translates. The LXX have: χρυσῦ νομίσματα.

It is also called Moneta, from its purpose and function, because a coin warns us by the impression of a sign and the inscription of a certain author, time, weight, and value, and other things, as Martial derives the word from monendo (warning): whence also the German Münze, and the Greek μονητάριον in Hesychius, τὸ κέρμα ἐργαζόμενος, he who makes or mints small change.

Pecunia is named from form and image, not from the hide of cattle, as Isidore wishes, book XVI, ch. 17, but because cattle (pecus), as Festus testifies, were accustomed to be stamped on coins, and Servius Tullius, the sixth King of the Romans, was the first among the Romans to stamp bronze with the image of sheep and oxen, when they had previously used raw bronze at Rome. See Pliny, book XVIII, ch. 3, and book XXXIII, ch. 3, from which word some derive the German Pfennig. Ulpian called it coined money in the book 'cum aurum' in the Digest, title 'de auro legato'.

A more common material among the Latins is the term aes (bronze/copper), because money first began to be minted from bronze, whence all money is called by the name of bronze by synecdoche: We even call gold coins bronze, says Ulpian, L. 159. ff. de Verbor. signific. Which nevertheless

J. J. M CALOVIUS, ON THE HEBREWS AND GREEKS, bronze, and Measures of capacities and lengths. THE CODE.

the word specifically denotes a bronze coin. Among the Hebrews נחשת (nechosheth), bronze, is used generally for money, Ez. 16, 36. Because your bronze was poured out: as the Vulgate rendered it: ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἐξέχεας τὸν χαλκόν σε, the LXX have.

The name of silver is also accustomed to be used for money, because money consisted of silver: the name of silver retains coined money, says Cicero in the Topics. Pollux, book III, says: τὸ δὲ ἀργύριον, is called wealth and coins, silver is called money and coins; and Varinus says: ἀργύριον, is any coin whether in bronze or in gold, silver is any coin whether in bronze, or in silver, or in gold. Thus the Hebrew כסף (keseph), silver, from כסף (kasaph), to desire, because men are held by desire for it, is used everywhere generally for money, Gen. 23, 9. ch. 42, 25. Ex. 21, 11. etc., where the LXX rendered it ἀργύριον: although the name of silver also occurs in a special sense regarding a certain silver coin, a drachma or denarius, about which later. Once the LXX translated it by χρήματα, Job 27, 17, which name designates money among the Greeks from its use, because it contributes to the acquisition of necessary things, although sometimes it is used in general for any possession which is of use in household affairs. Thus, what the LXX called χρήματα, the blessed Luther rendered as money, the Vulgate as riches, Prov. 17, 16, where in Hebrew it is מחיר (mechir), price: but in Jos. 22, 8, 2 Chron. 1, 11, 12, χρήματα in Hebrew undoubtedly denotes נכסים (nechasim), riches and wealth in general, and thus they are rendered by the Vulgate and the blessed Luther: The Hebrew word denotes collections, or things acquired and gathered from elsewhere.

Similarly, the word for gold is used generally for any coin, not only among the Latins, as in Horace it is to be sold for gold, but also χρυσὸς and τὸ χρύσιον among the Greeks, as Pollux witnesses in the aforementioned book, just as those who are destitute of money are called ἄχρυσοι by Plato in book III of the Laws. By special usage, however, a certain gold coin is not infrequently denoted. Which is also observed in certain Hebrew words denoting gold, which, when they are used regarding money, almost specifically denote certain gold coins when the words are placed absolutely, though in general they also denote gold, whether ἐπίσημον (stamped) or ἄσημον (unstamped). Such are 1. זהב (zahav), gold, so called from its tawny color. Neh. 7, 70. 71. 72. 2. רהב (rahab), Is. 14, 4. 3. בצר (betzer), denoting a gem of gold: He will place Bezer for dust, that is, gold; and v. 23, the Almighty will be to you בצריך (betzarecha), much gold (in the plural), as the blessed Luther rendered it. The word בצר (betzer) otherwise denotes a fortification and is used regarding gold, because it can be like a defense: because he who abounds in gold can easily protect himself against all evils, and fortify himself as if with a strong wall. For the mention of Ophir and silver teaches that it is used here regarding gold. 4. אוֹפִיר (Ophir), which name most wish to be taken for gold, from this very passage Job 22, 24 and Ps. 45, 11, Isa. 13, 12: but it is the name of a place, 1 Kings 22, 49, 1 Chron. 29, 4, 2 Chron. 8, 18, which the LXX also called Σωφὶρ, 2 Chron. 9, 10, from which the most excellent gold was brought; and thus it can be taken in Ps. 45, 11, Isa. 13, 11, כתם אופיר (kethem Ophir), a mass of gold from Ophir. In the place however, in Job, Ophir is taken for gold from Ophir. Whence some wish obryzum to be said as if Ophirisum: which nevertheless others, with Suidas, prefer to interpret πολλάκις ἑψηθὲς, more often refined, and most pure. For the more often it has burned, the more it has advanced to goodness, as Pliny has it, book XXXIII, ch. 3. 5, כֶּתֶם of best or purest gold, such as is either Indian or Arabian, denotes a mass, Jer. 31, 24. If I have made gold my hope, where however the LXX take it for λίθω πολυτελεῖ, a precious stone: B. Luther more correctly rendered it Goldklumpen, because in the present hemistich the word זָהָב indicates gold: for one is exegetical of the other. Conf. Job.

28, 16. In which place the word 6. סָגוּר is also taken for gold in verse 15, and indeed, as appears from the other member, for coined gold: Gold is not given for it, and silver is not weighed out as its price. For among the ancients, money was accustomed to be weighed, not counted. The LXX render it συγκλεισμὸν, a conclusion, inconveniently, even though money has its name from inclusion, because it is accustomed to be included and kept with care. 7. פָּז is gold in that same place of Job, most solid and best, or pure, ch. 28, 17, from פָּזַז, he consolidated: which can be judged to have been named from the place where it is dug: from Uphaz, Jer. X, Dan. X. The LXX sometimes render it χρυσίον ἄπυρον, obryzum gold, Is. 13, 12, sometimes τοπάζιον, Topaz, Ps. 119, 126. 8. They also interpret the word חָרוּץ as gold, Job 41, 22, LXX, Vulg., and R. Solomon. But others more correctly take it as a sharp thing: yet that meaning of gold occurs in Ps. 68, 14. Prov. 3, 14. c. 8, 10. 19. c. 16, 16. from חָרַץ, he exerted his power and virtue, because gold is of the greatest virtue and efficacy.

These things concerning the names taken from the material, which are exhibited together as gold, silver, and bronze coins in general, Matt. 10, 9, μὴ κτήσασθε χρυσὸν, μηδὲ ἀργύριον, μηδὲ χαλκὸν εἰς τὰς ζώνας ὑμῶν, do not acquire gold, nor silver, nor bronze for your belts.

Finally, from quantity, a coin is called κέρμα, which Seneca explains as a small piece of bronze, from the verb κείρω, which is to cut, whence also κερματίζειν, which among other things signifies to exchange larger coins for smaller ones. It is taken, however, in general also for any coins whatsoever, just as Eustathius in the IXth Iliad understood denarii by κέρματα, and among Pollux, book VI, κερμάτια are specifically called by diminution, and ἀκερμία among the same is generally a lack of coins. And in that sense τὸ κέρμα is also taken in John 2, 14, when Christ is said to have poured out the bronze of the money-changers (B. Luther rendered it with the common word Geld): not only smaller coins, but all the bronze. Species of coins are also accustomed to be taken generally for money, in which way the word denarii is used in Prov. 12, 15, Luke 20, 24, for νομίσματι, as is clear from the parallel passage Matt. 22, 19. For by the words, show me a denarius, Christ was designating nothing other than the very kind of money, or νόμισμα τῦ κήνσυ, whatever that might be, by which the tribute was then accustomed to be paid to the Romans.

CHAPTER II. Definition.

A coin is defined by Suidas: νόμισμα τὸ κόμμα τῦ τετυπωμένυ χαλκῦ: a coin is an expressed mark of stamped bronze. In which definition, however, it is desired first that the material cause be inadequately exhibited, because money is not made from bronze, nor indeed from metal only, but sometimes also from other material, as leather, bark, paper, earthenware, etc., coins are proof, although more commonly and ordinarily coins are made from metal, and indeed from that triple [kind of] gold, silver, and bronze, nor do coins of another kind occur in the Scriptures. Then that the efficient cause is passed over: namely, that a coin is stamped by the authority of the Magistrate, which is necessary both because of adulterated, false, and useless coins: and because of public estimation and value: and because of the certainty of just weight, and a convenient price, which depends on the fair judgment of superiors: in which way, besides matter and form, the Philosopher, as also Isidore, book XVI. Etym. c. 17. it requires size and weight. Thirdly, the end was not to be neglected, which is easier exchange. For money was established by institution as a certain substitute, an ὑπάλλαγμα, for poverty and need, as Aristotle says in book V of the Ethics, and likewise Plato in book V of the Laws: Money is almost necessary for the sake of daily exchange, by which also craftsmen exchange. I add that money is not κόμμα, as Ludovicus Cælius thinks in book X, c. 2, but refers to the type and image, χάραγμα, χαρακτῆρα, and τύμμα; whence, with these joined, a fuller definition of this kind emerges: Money is that which is sanctioned and marked by the authority of the Magistrate with an expressed character, a certain size, and a just weight, so that the difficulty of exchanges may be relieved. But in what way Aristotle roundly says in book IV of the Nicomachean Ethics, νόμισμα ᾧ χρήματα πάντα, ὅσων ἡ ἀξία μετρεῖται: Money is that by which all things, of which there is a price, are estimated.

But there is need of an image and type, partly so that from it good money may be distinguished from counterfeit, partly so that the price established by the Prince, or the people, or some community may have its value by the authority of the same; partly so that, by avoiding laborious testing and weighing, the goodness and just value of the money may be immediately evident from the image itself: partly so that we may sometimes also be reminded of other things from the inscription or type of the money: just as Christ, from the ἐπιγραφῇ and inscription of the coin, reminded the Jews of the Roman jurisdiction under which they were established, and thus ordered that the things which are Caesar's be given to Caesar, Matt. 22, 20. Regarding the figures of Hebrew coins, one may consult Antonius Augustinus, Joh. Baptista Vilalpandus, Cass. Waserus, Joh. Morinus, Selden, and others. And therefore money bearing a genuine type is called νόμισμα γνήσιον, ἄδολον, ἀκέραιον, ἀκίβδηλον, ἀδιάφθορον in Pollux, book IX. In the Scriptures, a νόμιμος or legitimate coin is described as that which passes to merchants, Gen. 23, 17, which is current and accepted: in which way also money is called passing in 2 Kings 12, 4, which is current and accepted: where, however, others prefer that that didrachma be designated, which those counted in the population were compelled to pay annually for the use of the temple by passing it. Full silver in 1 Chron. 21, 22, 24 is money of just weight.

CHAPTER III. Origin and Antiquity.

You would rashly seek the origin of coins from foreign sources. For among them, just as the first antiquity and the true origin of things is among the unknown, so it is undoubted that coins are far older than all profane history. Pliny ascribes this to Servius Tullius, the sixth King of Rome, that he first coined bronze at Rome: others say that King Numa, the second of Rome, first took care that coins be made from iron and bronze: but Pollux in book IX, Strabo in book VIII, and Aelian in book XII of Varia Historia attribute this to Phidon of Argos, who was about two centuries older than Numa, that he began to coin money. But the use of coins is still far older in Sacred History. For whatever may be the case regarding the antediluvian time, in which some think that Tubal-Cain, designated by Moses as the author of the art of metallurgy and a smith and hammerer in Gen. 4, 22, had already coined money and bronze, indeed from Josephus some also presume the same thing about Cain, whom he reported to have increased his house with a multitude of riches, rapine, and violence, and to have changed the tranquility in which men previously lived among themselves by the invention of weights and measures: the origin of coins is perhaps not rashly traced from the times of Noah after the flood, when he came second into Italy, which they think happened in the twentieth century of the World under Ninus. To which opinion ancient coins seem to favor, bearing on one side indeed the two-faced Janus, who is believed to be Noah, and on the other the prow of a ship, concerning which Ovid in book I of the Fasti and Pliny in book XXXIII, ch. 3. Although some wish them to have been minted only in memory of Janus, not by Janus. But concerning the Patriarch Abraham, than whom Phido was eleven centuries later, it is not only reported in Gen. XIII, v. 2 that he was very opulent in the possession of gold and silver: which could perhaps be understood of silver and gold unrefined and not stamped; but it is also reported that Abimelech gave him a thousand silver pieces, ch. XX, 12, which is the first mention of coins in the Scriptures, and how he himself established a contract of purchase with Ephron for a certain sum of money, ch. XXIII, whence it is manifest that coins were already in use in his time. Now Abraham was at Gerar with Abimelech, King of the Philistines, in the year of the world 2107, from which the antiquity of coins can be estimated, even if nothing certain can be defined about their first origin.

CHAPTER IV. The species of Hebrew coins, and first indeed the Shekel.

Since, however, there are various species of coins, we are especially concerned with those that occur in the sacred code: of which some are found in the Old Testament, others in the New. In the Old Testament only silver or gold ones are read of. Bronze ones nowhere appear in the Hebrew Code. The silver ones are the Shekel and its parts. As the Shekel is the most ancient of coins, and most used among the ancient Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Syrians, so it is the measure and cynosure of the others, to which the rest ought to be compared. Which the ancient Rabbis in the book Misnajoth teach to have been the most celebrated currency of the first house, and proper to the Israelites: Arias Montanus calls it the first index of all coins and weights, and as it were the sower in his Ephron.

Now only the silver shekel is found, not a gold, nor a bronze, or iron one in the Hebrew Code. And it is commemorated first of all among coins in the Scriptures: tacitly indeed under the name of silver, i.e., the shekel: as the Chaldean added, Gen. XX, 15, but expressly ch. XVIII, 16. It is pleasing, however, to compare Biblical coins to our Misnian ones, which was also done by Georg Agricola and Matthaeus Host as Germans and Misnians: just as Bilibaldus Pirckheimer, a patrician of Nuremberg, compared them with Noric coins, the Frenchman Guillaume Budé with French ones, the Spaniard Diego Covarruvias y Leyva, Bishop of St. Dominic, with Spanish ones, and the Englishman Edward Brerewood, Professor of Astronomy in London, in his treatise on the weights and prices of ancient coins, compared them with English coins. And since the imperial or Joachim thaler, so called because it began to be minted first in the Joachim valley, contains twenty-four groschen, but a groschen twelve small coins, which are called thirds, Metsnische Pfennig, just as a sixth is a Heller, a half-groschen three Hellers, an ounce a half Heller, or Scherf, in the Faber-Buchnerian Thesaurus: it is helpful to institute a comparison with them.

The shekel is named from שׁקל, he weighed, he hung, because coins were once accustomed to be weighed and hung, not counted, Gen. 23:16, Exod. 22:27, 1 Kings 20:39, Ezra 8:25, Job 28:15, Zech. 11:12, Matt. 26:15. The Chaldeans said תּקלא or מתקלא, the Greeks σίκλον. Moreover, it is easily accepted and undoubted among all that a shekel makes half an Imperial, or 12 groschen, and weighs half an ounce of silver, or four Attic drachmas, as will be said later. But because the invention of the Rabbis concerning a double shekel in terms of price and value—namely, one sacred and ecclesiastical, and another profane and common, of which the former is twice as large as the latter, so that when the former is worth half a Joachimsthaler, or twelve groschen, or four Attic drachmas, the latter is worth only a quarter of an Imperial thaler, or six Misnian groschen, and thus two drachmas—has caused no small confusion, it will have to be examined whether there is only one shekel of the same value and kind in the Holy Scriptures, or indeed different ones? We are concerned, I say, with the Holy Scriptures according to the authentic text, not with other writings or writers, or with interpreters of Scripture, Rabbis, or Christians.

Moreover, the name שׁקל occurs in the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament both for a weight and for a coin. For a weight, משקל is commonly used for balancing, a balance, which word the LXX interpret as σταθμὸν (a balance), Gen. 43:21, ch. 27:3, 35, Job 28:26, 1 Sam. 17:5, 2 Sam. 12:30, ch. 21:16, 1 Kings 7:47, ch. 10:14, 2 Kings 24:36, 1 Chron. 20:2, ch. 22:3, 14, ch. 28:14, 15, 16, 17, 2 Chron. 9:13, Ezra 8:19, 33, Jer. 52:17, in which places it occurs regarding a balance and the weight of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and those not stamped, and thus they do not pertain to the present matter concerning coins; much less those places in which it is used for the balance of bread, such as Lev. 26:26, Ezek. 4:10, 16. Nor do those places pertain here in which the Seventy Elders interpreted משקל as σταθμὸν (weight), where it concerns weight in general, such as Lev. 19:35, 2 Kings 21:13, Ezek. 5:1, Amos 8:5.

The word משקל is also rendered by the LXX interpreters as ὁλκὴν (weight), and it undoubtedly denotes a weight, not a coin: 2 Chron. 3:9, ch. 4:18, and it is also explained in this way by Blessed Luther in 1 Chron. 21:25, as also in Gen. 24:22. In other places, Num. 7:1, 3, 19, 25, 31, 37, 43, 49, 55, 61, 67, 73, 79, Josh. 7:21, it is explained as price, but it can also most conveniently be understood as weight, from which, however, the price may be estimated. Similarly, משקל is also explained by Blessed Luther in Gen. 24:22, when the golden earrings given to Rebekah are described: where the LXX have δραχμὴν (drachma), although the same people, in the verse immediately following, when it concerns necklaces, interpret the same word as ὁλκὴν (weight).

From which induction of places it is evident that the word משקל is never used for a coin, but always for a weight. But as for the word שׁקל, it is also taken for weight, and is sometimes rendered by the word σίκλο (shekel) in Num. 7:13, 19, 25, 31, 37, 43, 49, 55, 61, 67, 73, 79, 85, 86, ch. 31:52, 1 Sam. 17:5, 7, 2 Sam. 14:26, ch. 21:16, 2 Chron. 3:9, Ezek. 4:10, and doubt cannot easily arise concerning that meaning in those places; sometimes it also occurs with that meaning when the LXX interpreters explained the word as δίδραχμον (didrachma), as in Josh. 7:21. But it is taken for a coin both where the LXX likewise interpret it with the word σίκλος (shekel), Lev. 5:15, Num. 3:47, 50, ch. 18:16, 2 Sam. 24:24, 2 Kings 7:1, 16, 18, ch. 15:20, 1 Chron. 21:25, Ezek. 45:12, Jer. 32:9, and also where the LXX explain the same as δίδραχμον (didrachma): which is observed in Gen. 23:15, 16, Ex. 21:32, ch. 30:13, 15.

Lev. 27, 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 25. Num. 3, 47. Neh. 5, 15. chap. 10, 32. And these are all the places in which the name שקל occurs.

From which, when accurately weighed, I do not see by what reason that distinction can be carved out, although it is most common and accepted between the shekel of the sanctuary and the profane, which is therefore deservedly rejected: 1. Because it is ἄγραφός, inasmuch as it is not taken from the Holy Scriptures, but must be attributed solely to Rabbinic commentaries: which, however, as in other things, so also in monetary matters vary greatly, some indeed bringing in a diversity of shekels, but by reason of material, not by reason of weight; others, however, by reason of weight and use in ecclesiastical and common affairs; others establishing a double shekel, others a triple, namely, ecclesiastical, common, and royal. Thus others believed the shekel of the sanctuary to have been smaller than the common one, such as R. Solomon and Lyranus: who give 24 obols to the common shekel, only 20 to the sacred; others, on the contrary, made it larger than the common one, and that again in various ways: for Pagninus gives 20 obols to the common shekel, but 40 to the sacred; but Vatablus, Fagius, Lipomanus, and Covaruvius in his book on coins, ch. II, n. 9, make the common one of 10 obols, but the sacred one of twenty, so that finally you have nothing certain from it: and whatever may be the case regarding their opinion, since it does not rest upon Holy Scripture, it will not be permitted to gather any undoubted certainty from it concerning the value and price of shekels received in the Holy Scriptures. 2. The measure and standard of the shekel, when there is talk of coins, is established in the Scriptures as unique, namely the shekel of the sanctuary, but nowhere is there mention of a dual measure or δοκιμασίας of the shekel, Ex. 30, 13. chap. 38, 24. 25. Num. 14, 47. Num. 18, 16. 3. Nor is there any other weight than the weight of the shekel of the sanctuary, and by no means is a common weight of the shekel designated anywhere. See Ex. 30, 24. chap. 33, 24. 25. 29. Num. 7, 13. 19. 25. 31. 49. 55. 61. 67. 73. 79. 85. etc. 4. The shekel is accurately defined as a coin, namely that it consists of 20 Geras or obols: as in Exod. 30, 13. Jer. 27, 35. Num. 5, 47. Ezek. 45, 12. But nowhere is there any mention of a shekel that was only ten Geras or obols, nor does any trace of one appear. 5. Mere uncertainty would arise, and Scripture would be rendered ambiguous, if the silver shekel signified twenty Geras or obols at one time, and only half that value at another. For whence would we be made more certain whether this or that signification obtains, or why it is taken in one sense in this place rather than that? If it be said that where mention is made of the shekel of the sanctuary, it is to be understood as a shekel of 20 Geras, there are places where mention of the shekel of the sanctuary is not added, and yet a shekel of 20 Geras is to be understood, such as Ezek. 45, 12. Jos. 7, 21. Neh. 10, 32. Lev. 27, 3. 4. 5. 7. 25. or certainly in those places where mention of the shekel of the sanctuary is not added, the matter will be doubtful as to how they are to be explained. 6. The divine definition in Lev. 27, 25 is most explicit: every valuation shall be weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary. The shekel has twenty obols. Since EVERY valuation had to be made in this way by divine constitution, how will the Rabbis deserve to be believed, who teach that not every valuation, but only that in sacred matters, is to be instituted in this way? Where the law does not distinguish, it is not for us to distinguish: where the law speaks universally, it is not for us to understand it particularly, or to restrict the law. Furthermore it is said: every valuation shall be weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary (not computed, which is how it would have to be said if this sacred shekel were worth more), where the Septuagint translate, and every price shall be by holy measures, i.e., every shekel, and every weight and price shall be weighed by the shekel, and the most just measure, which is kept for this purpose in the sanctuary, as Cornel. observes on Ex. 30, 13. It deals there also with profane matters, such as not only the field which has been sanctified to GOD, but also that which he must in turn yield to its owner in the year of Jubilee, from whom, namely, it had been bought, v. 24. Which Bonfrerius on Exod. 30, verse 24, also observed: It is commanded, he says, Ex. 30, 24, that all contracts, sales, and purchases should be made according to the weight of the shekel of the Sanctuary; for it had immediately preceded concerning such public contracts, therefore there were no other public weights than those of the Sanctuary.

7. And what places will finally remain in which the shekel is named, when there is talk of coins, and the name of the sanctuary is not added, or that description of 20 Geras or obols? Scarcely three or four will be found, in which, however, there appears no reason why a shekel of the same value and price as that by which shekels always pass in the Scriptures should not be understood; such as Gen. 23, 15. 16. 2 Kings 7, 1. chap. 15, 20. Num. 5, 15. For in the remaining places there is no doubt that the talk is of shekels of 20 Geras.

But why should one think otherwise of those? For the field which Abraham bought from Ephron for a hereditary monument, which is said to have cost 400 shekels in Gen. 23, 15. 16., what is absurd about it being worth 200 Imperials? But the small amount of wheat, which, how rare and expensive it was before Samaria was freed from the siege, is evident from 2 Kings 6, suddenly reduced to such a vile price that it could suddenly be bought for one shekel, that is 20 Geras, or 12 Meissen groschen, chap. 7, 1, is that not to be considered a miracle? But no one will wonder at the poll tax of 50 shekels established in Israel by Menahem, which would have amounted to 25 of our Imperial coins, who has weighed how much had to be paid to Phul, King of the Assyrians, in order to confirm the kingdom for Menahem.

And since in Nehemiah 5:15 the heavy burden imposed upon the people by the former governors is discussed, namely a tribute of 40 shekels, would it be anything foreign to the truth if we were to say that 20 imperials were to be contributed? Indeed, it would be rather inconsistent if the word shekel were said to be used by the same Nehemiah in one sense here and in another in chapter 10:32. For why would he have used that homonymy and left us uncertain about the true meaning? The same must be said of Moses and the author of the books of Kings. For why would Moses have always taken the word and value of the shekel in the same way elsewhere, but in that one single passage, Gen. 23, understood a different coin of half the value, and likewise the author of the books of Kings in only one single passage, namely 2 Kings 7?

8. If the public and common weight had been different from the weight of the Sanctuary, its use would have been in contracts and civil matters: but the matter was otherwise: because in such matters and contracts it occurs with שקל, as in 2 Kings 7:1, 16, 18, Jer. 32:9, Ez. 4:10, where no other shekel appears, and it is rendered by the Vulgate as a stater, which is known to have been a tetradrachm. Indeed, in Exod. 21:32, where it is certain that civil matters are being dealt with, Arias Montanus in his Ephron, as he calls it, understands by the 20 shekels, which were paid for a manservant or maidservant, 15 ounces, and thus half-ounce shekels.

What of the fact that in Ezekiel 45:12 the common shekel, or that which ought to be used in common usage and civil matters, is openly established as 20 gerahs, or grains, which is exactly how many the shekel of the sanctuary had in Exod. 30:17? Which passage evidently refutes that common distinction.

10. Nor indeed was the shekel called of the Sanctuary so that it might be distinguished from a profane shekel, of which distinction neither trace nor vestige is found in the Scriptures, but because the measure of it was kept in the sanctuary, which reason Scripture itself gives, as often as it names the shekel, ACCORDING TO THE SHEKEL of the sanctuary: for by this formula of speaking the standard is designated: whence Bonfrerius rightly has this to say regarding the words weight of the sanctuary in Ex. 30:24: Not that the weights were different, some of the Sanctuary, others public, namely these being by half smaller, as it seemed to some; but that all weights should be reduced to the standard of that first one, which was kept in the Sanctuary, so that although the weights of private individuals might be easily changed by the slightest addition or subtraction, whether ignorantly or by industry, there would nevertheless be one certain, sacrosanct standard in the Sanctuary, to which all weights and measures of private individuals should be conformed. Arias Montanus thinks the holy shekel is so named by the people, in his Ephron concerning the shekel: it was called, he says, the holy Shekel, or the shekel of the sanctuary, that same one which is called the Shekel of Israel in coinage: for Israel was made the sanctification of the Lord.

11. When Scripture makes mention of the Royal weight in 2 Sam. 14, 16, it does not teach that there was one weight of shekels and another Priestly one, because a just weight was prescribed to the Kings, which was to be observed holily. Therefore, the mention of the Royal does not denote different weights, but this appellation indicates that the Rule of Lev. 27, v. 25 and the just measure of weight were observed also by the Kings; indeed, as it seems to some, that the measure of weights was kept by the King after he was established in the Republic of the Jews; or because, just as Kings ought to be studious of justice, so also their weights ought to be considered just, so that they could be the rule of just weights. 12. Josephus lib. III. Antiqu. c. 9, testifies that shekels were worth four Attic drachmas, or half an ounce of silver; nor does he designate anywhere other shekels of half the value, and he makes the shekel the same as the Attic stater, with which Jerome in c. IV agrees, as does Hesychius at the word Shekel. 13. Arias Montanus, a diligent investigator of shekels, acknowledges no distinction between a profane and a sacred shekel: he observes, however, that if any different shekels are found in profane uses, they were of greater weight, and that from the greed of certain Princes and rich men, who in hard and more difficult times, in order to despoil the poorer more quickly, increased the shekel, of which Amos 8, 5. But concerning that distinction, Arias Mont. says thus: There are those who distinguish between the shekels of the sanctuary, and the profane, and the royal, I know not whether as certainly as they do curiously. 14. Some even of the more recent writers reject that distinction: especially Villalpandus part. II. de appar. templ. l. II. c. 28. Ribera in Amos 8, n. 15. seq. Bonfrer. l. c. as also Corn. a Lap. in Ex. 30, 13. This distinction, he says, of the sacred and common shekel was unknown to the Ancients, such as Josephus, St. Jerome, and others; indeed, that these shekels were equal is evident from Ex. 45, 12, for there it is said that the common shekel has 20 obols, as many as it is said here (Ex. 30, 13) the sacred one has. For that Ezekiel speaks of the common shekel of laymen, rich and poor, is evident from the preceding. Finally, there is added to these that they commonly hold the shekel and the stater to be the same: which Brerewood also acknowledges l. c. p. 3. The shekel of the Israelites, he says, was altogether equal to the stater of the Athenians, and for that reason it is sometimes rendered in Greek by Symmachus, and mostly by Aquila, as σατὴρ. B. Gerhard also acknowledges this in Harm. c. 168, praising Jerome p. 1184. The stater or shekel has four drachmas; and c. CLIV. p. 1142. Making the stater of the Hebrews a νόμισμα: The stater, he says, in Matt. 17, v. 27, is properly the name of Jewish currency, just as the drachma, which is mentioned in Luke 15, v. 7, was an Attic coin. For the stater was called by the name of the nation אסתירי, and doubled the didrachm: that is, it contained four drachmas, as is gathered from Matt. 17, v. 27. But nowhere is it possible to find another common stater of only two drachmas.

It remains that we should still explain what are brought forward for that common distinction: But first Brerewood appeals to the LXX Interpreters, 2 Sam. 14, 26, where mention is made of the Royal Shekel (the Vulgate said public), because for two hundred shekels of Royal weight the LXX rendered one hundred shekels, understanding the shekels of the sanctuary to be twice as large. But there (1.) the discourse is about the shekel as a weight of Absalom's hair, not about the shekel as a coin. (2.) The twin supporters of the coins do not agree on what they understand by the Royal shekel, which some make the same as the public, as those who do not wish to desert the Vulgate ought to do, while others distinguish it from the public; just as Hostus l. IV. de re numm. c. 1 says the profane, public, and common shekel weighs a didrachm, but makes the Sacred one twice as large as the profane: and thinks the Royal one was struck during the time of the Kings as three drachmas. Concerning which, therefore, let them settle it among themselves. (3.) The LXX Interpreters did not look at Brerewood, for they do not have one hundred, but διακοσίας σίκλες, two hundred shekels there, and agree entirely with the Hebrew text.

But as for what Hostus brings from Josephus l. VII. archaeol. that two hundred shekels made five minas, and thus forty shekels were to be reckoned as tridrachms (which make thirty sacred tetradrachm shekels) to the mina, so that a mina is 120 Attic drachmas, we think there is an error in that in Josephus. Certainly, tridrachm shekels, or those of three Attic drachmas, or nine Misnian groschen, which Hostus thinks, are never found. That the ancient Hebrew mina contained one hundred Hebrew drachmas, that is 50 shekels, is gathered from a comparison of 2 Chr. 9, v. 15 and 1 Kings 10, v. 17: therefore two hundred shekels would have been only four minas, not five. That passage of Josephus is indeed suspect to others also in this, that he says the depth of Absalom's hair was such that they could scarcely cut it in EIGHT DAYS. For it is incredible that eight days were needed for Absalom's haircut. What of the fact that Hostus himself later enters into a different calculation l. V. c. 2. p. 668. This Royal Maneh, he says, if you look at the crowned COINS, makes 12 silver ones, 15 ounces, that is 30 shekels. Therefore, five minas would thus have made 150 shekels, not 200, as the sacred text has. Thus, because of the suspect passage of Josephus, that author makes the Mina now 30 shekels, now 40.

Next, for the common sacred shekel, Brerewood cites the passage 1 Macc. 10:42, where Demetrius is said to have remitted to the Jews 5000 shekels, but Josephus, in Antiquities book XIII, ch. 5, has 10000 drachmas: whence he concludes that this shekel weighed two drachmas. Hostus also uses this argument in book IV, ch. 3, p. 633. But the Maccabean text teaches that those sacred shekels are to be understood: because those shekels were accepted for sacred uses, as IN THE FIRST YEARS OF THE SANCTUARY, and pertained to the priests. However, Josephus is to be understood there not as speaking of Attic drachmas, but of Hebrew or Alexandrian ones, concerning which Brerewood wrote above: The Hebrew and also the Alexandrian drachma was double the Attic.

Thirdly, they urge the authority of the Rabbis: from whom Buxtorf, in his Rabbinical Lexicon under the word סלע, alleges Maimonides, part 1, concerning staters. But just as we readily grant that shekels of only two drachmas could have been given in the time of the Rabbis, or even found in the writings of the Rabbis, so here the question is not about the shekels of the Rabbis, but about the shekels of Scripture; and we have already warned that not much is to be attributed to the Rabbis in such matters: and in a similar case concerning the price of the pieces of silver for which Christ was sold by Judas, Isaac Casaubon warned Caesar Baronius in Exercitation XVI, no. 8, p. 802, that no faith at all should be placed in them, unless we wish to be deceived and to deceive. However, it will appear later that the Rabbis do not agree here.

Furthermore, according to Epiphanius in his book on weights, the shekel, which is also called a quadrans, is the fourth part of an ounce, having half of a stater which contains two drachmas. To which passage Corn. a Lap. responds that Epiphanius's memory lapsed, or that an error crept into his manuscript: for Epiphanius openly contradicts the LXX, who call the didrachma (the Hebrew, which was the Attic tetradrachma) a stater or shekel: he also contradicts Jerome, who in book XIV on Ezekiel, at ch. XLV, 12, says: The shekel, which is called in Greek stater, contains twenty obols. Now that the Greek stater was four Attic drachmas, Brerewood acknowledges: A stater, he says in ch. 1 on weights, p. 6, Matt. 17, verse 27, denotes by its Greek name the shekel of the Hebrews, entirely equal in weight to the Attic stater. For it contained two didrachmas, when it was paid as tribute for Christ and Peter. So also Hostius, book III, ch. 7, p. 482, on the passage in Matt. 17. Here I understand the stater to be a silver coin, the tetradrachma, which contains two didrachmas, which he could give for two, for himself and Peter, to those who were collecting and demanding the didrachmas. Although Joach. Camerarius preferred to understand a gold didrachma there, because Christ, as the author of that benefit, wished something to remain over, and to give more than was asked.
