And Epiphanius himself, in the same place, says: A pound, he says, has twelve ounces, but an ounce has two staters: but a stater is indeed half an ounce, yet it has didrachmas: that is, two Attic drachmas. And Cleopatra testifies that a stater is four drachmas, when she says: A stater is worth four drachmas: they call it a tetradrachma: and a dispondium is likewise worth four drachmas. In which manner also Hesychius, when he had said Palladis effigies stater, added stater is a tetradrachma, that is, half an ounce. And further: γλαῦξ νόμισμα Ἀθηνήσι τετράδραχμον, An owl is a tetradrachma coin at Athens: γλαῦξ δὲ τὸ ἐπιχάραγμα τῦ ςατῆρος. But the owl is the engraved mark of the stater: Isidore has the same in book XV, ch. 24 of the Etymologies. A stater is half an ounce.

And from this equality of value and the equivalence of the terms stater and shekel, the value of the shekel is not difficult to gather: for the stater among the Greeks is said to be derived from the verb ἱσάναι, which is to weigh, just as שקל among the Hebrews is derived from שקל, he weighed, he balanced, as can be seen from Zech. 11: They weighed my wages, thirty pieces of silver. The LXX: καὶ ἔστησαν τῦ μισθέμενός τριάκοντα ἀργύρυς. Doubtless the shekel is likewise four Attic drachmas for the Hebrews, as the stater is for the Greeks, called סלע by the Chaldeans: for thus in the Targum, for the word שקל is סלעא. Concerning which Buxtorf warns in his Talmudic Lexicon under the word סלע from the Baal-Aruch under זוז. The shekel of the law is סלע in silver, says Buxtorf; it contained four drachmas, which are called in Chaldean זוזין, denarii, whence it was called a tetradrachma. Although the same Buxtorf notes regarding the Talmudists, in Bechor f. 11, that there seems to be a distinction between סלע and שקל. Whom he also observes often making mention of the סלע נרוניר, the shekel of Nero. Benedict Arias Montanus notes that סלע in the book of the Mishnah on vows 51. 43, and in the tract on Shebuot ch. 6, is a double shekel, and is worth four denarii, that is, as he himself explains, four didrachmas, which he shows in various places: but he warns that this ratio was of the most common סלע, that is, the Tyrian, which had the weight of a whole ounce of silver, but that this ratio of the ZZELAGH was neither perpetual nor everywhere constant, we are taught also by the various reading. For primarily the Chaldean paraphrasts, whom we call a shekel in Hebrew, rendered it ZZELAGH, as in Gen. 23, Exod. 31, and 38 in the Targum. And in the Aruch the same is handed down. And Elias Levites writes in the Tishbi that ZZELAGH is a silver shekel, and is worth four ZZUZIM. These are the words of Montanus. Whence it is not surprising that the Rabbis speak differently about the value of the shekel, according to the diversity of the shekels. Nor if different shekels are found among the Talmudists does it follow that shekels of unequal value must be admitted in the Scriptures as well. Meanwhile, the value which we said is that of a stater, of four drachmas, is attributed to the shekels by the Rabbis from R. David Kimchi on 1 Sam. 9, 8: it is established that השקל ארבעה זוזים, the shekel contained four Susas. A Zusa, however, is a coin, as Buxtorf says in his Lexicon, an ancient Jewish coin worth a fourth part, that is, a drachma of the sacred shekel, just as in 1 Sam. 9, 8, for a quarter of a silver shekel (as it is in the Hebrew) the Targum has one silver Susa. R. Solomon Jarchi in Exod. 39 teaches that a shekel is half an ounce of silver. Bened. Arias Montanus cites R. Moses Nachmanides Gerundensis, who flourished 500 years ago in Catalonia, who in his commentary on Ex. 39 wrote that he did not easily agree with the opinion of R. Solomon, but when he had finished the whole commentary, having finished the work, with a chapter added specifically for that matter, he approved the estimation of the shekel made by R. Solomon (having changed his own mind), for the reason that he himself had seen in Palestine a very ancient silver coin, yet conspicuous with clear signs and letters, the inscription of which was Sekel Israel on one side, and Jerusolaim Kedescha on the other, which, when weighed on a balance, yielded the weight of half an ounce of silver: and that there was shown there another coin of half the weight, with exactly the same figures, which however was not called SEKEL, but HAASZI SEKEL, that is, half a shekel. The same Arias Montanus reports that a similar shekel was given to him, which, when examined on a balance, yielded four whole silver drachmas, that is, half an ounce, not of the common ounce, but of that which pharmacists use in weighing medicinal material, which the ancients called the Attic semi-ounce. To which designation the testimony of Josephus in book III agrees perfectly. Αρχαιολ. ὁ δὲ σίκλος νόμισμα ἑβραίων ὢν ἀττικὰς δέχεται δραχμὰς τεσσάρας, that is, The shekel, being a coin of the Hebrews, takes four Attic drachmas. And the suffrage of Hesychius: σίκλος τετράδραχμον ἀττικὸν scil. νόμισμα, that is, A shekel is a coin, to wit, of four Attic drachmas.

There is no reason for us to treat the figure of the Shekel here: let it suffice to have indicated only this, that a remarkable shekel of antiquity has come into my possession, which I keep as a κειμήλιον, on which in the usual Hebrew letters on one side is inscribed שקל ישראל, where a smoking censer is displayed, but on the other side ירושלים הקודשה with the flowering rod of Aaron in prominent figures, the value of which is half an ounce or half a Joachim.

And these things concerning the Shekel, the likeness of which currency was also found among the Tyrians, since the Τύριον νόμισμα according to Suidas was of the same weight and value as the Hebrew Shekel, and according to the testimony of Josephus in book II of the Jewish War, chapter 43, the Tyrian coin was worth four Attic drachmas.

Furthermore, although the shekel, as we warned above, was only silver among the Hebrews, not gold nor bronze, which was also observed by Arias Montanus and others: yet when money was paid out, whether in gold, or silver, or even bronze, every calculation was referred to the value of the shekel, so that, for example, twenty shekels in gold was as much as twenty silver shekels were worth. Therefore, when mention of a shekel of gold or bronze occurs in the Scriptures, a certain coin or value is not understood, but weight, as in Num. 7, v. 87, the weight of the golden spoons (the Vulgate calls them mortars) is said to have been ten shekels. For the shekel cannot be understood by reason of value (which some contend), but it is indicated that the material of the spoon weighed ten shekels, that is, five ounces; ounces, I say, not of gold, but of silver. For when it is a matter of weight, the weight of the shekel, that is, half an ounce, is designated: and thus the material of gold of ten shekels, by reason of weight, denotes the weight of five silver ounces.

For the ratio of ounces of gold is one thing, and that of silver is another, not only regarding value, but also regarding weight. Since it has been observed from ancient drachmas and didrachmas that the weight of gold is almost double that of silver, so that silver coins of the value of a denarius weighed a single drachma, while gold ones of the same size obtained the weight of two drachmas.

Regarding the weights of bronze, steel, and iron, which are read of in the Sacred Scriptures, where they are signified by the name of shekels, Benedict Arias Montanus likewise notes that these are to be referred to this same ratio: Although there are not wanting those who maintain that individual metals had their own certain shekels by which they were weighed, he himself, however, observed no example by whose argument he might concede to that opinion. Thus, therefore, the spear of Goliath, which is said in 1 Sam. 17:7 to have had six hundred shekels, was not of six hundred minae, as R. Sal. Jarchi wishes, but of three hundred ounces, or 25 pounds, and the coat of mail, which had 5000 shekels: not of as many minae, but of 2500 ounces, or 208 1/3 pounds; which, how great a weight of breastplate that is, there is no one who does not sufficiently understand.

CHAPTER V. Keseph, Silver pieces.

The word כסף when it is used for coin in the Sacred Scriptures, is rendered by the LXX Interpreters sometimes by σίκλον (shekel) Deut. 22:19, Isa. 7:23, sometimes by δίδραχμον (didrachm) Gen. 20:15, sometimes by ἀργύριον (silver piece) Judg. 17:2, Jer. 32:9. And all these occur with the same sense, so that the shekel is designated: whence the Chaldean also rendered it סלעא. Twice, however, the LXX Interpreters explained it as χρυσᾶς (gold pieces) Gen. 37:28, in the sale of Joseph, and ch. 45:22, in the gift made to Benjamin, perhaps because the price of Joseph seemed too light, and the gift to Joseph, so great a viceroy, less worthy, if silver shekels were retained. But one must not depart from the letter of the history. Arias also observes that gold shekels, when there is talk of coin (not weight), are nowhere found in the Sacred Scriptures. A silver piece, therefore, in the Scriptures is the same as a shekel: in which authors easily agree. Therefore

2 Sam. 18:11, also the Vulgate Latin Interpreter, as also the Chaldean Paraphrast, explained silver pieces as shekels. Yet some Rabbis have produced a difficulty here also; forasmuch as Elias in Thisbi compiled a Rule from the books of the earlier Rabbis: כסף, silver or a silver coin, as often as it is placed absolutely, is taken in the Law for a Shekel, in the Prophets for a mina, in the Hagiographa for a קנטרין (centenarium), or talent. Although we readily concede that changes occurred in monetary matters among the Jews, as among all peoples, just as Epiphanius says, ἀργυρίων δὲ πολλοὶ τύποι κατὰ καιρὸς γεγόνασι, various forms of silver coins existed at various times, those times, however, which followed the Prophets have nothing to do with the matter, nor in the books of Sacred Scripture (whatever may be the case with the books of the Rabbis) is one ratio of silver found in the Law, another in the Prophet, and another in the Hagiographa; so far is it from being the case that that Canon can be demonstrated from the Holy Scriptures; but a comparison of the passages Gen. 22:16, Deut. 22:19, Jer. 32:9, 1 Chron. 21:25 teaches that כסף is taken in the same way when it is used regarding coins. Nor indeed do the Rabbis agree: For R. David Kimchi in 2 Kings

ch. 12:4, 5, interpreted the name of silver in such a way that he made three silver pieces equal to half a shekel. Which one may also observe in his Commentary on Jer. 32:9. But the ancient Rabbis in the book of the Mishnah, tractate Becheroth ch. 8, report that a silver piece in the time of Moses had the weight of 320 grains of barley. But in the time of the second temple it had been increased up to the weight of 384 grains, and had the same ratio as the shekel.

Benedict Arias-Montanus also adds his vote to this opinion. John Buxtorf, however, in his Talmudic Lexicon, cites a Talmudic text that all silver in the Law is Tyrian silver, but that the silver of the Rabbis is common and provincial, and is taken for an eight-part coin, the silver coin of Tyre. Thus, nothing certain can be had from the Rabbis.

But that valuation of the silver coin which we mentioned also has a place in the New Testament: for in Matt. 26:15, the silver coin, just like כסף, denotes a shekel according to the usage of the Jews, because a Jewish coin is designated there. Whence Origen, tract. 35 on Matthew, and Eusebius, book X of the Evangelical Demonstration, ch. 4, translated it as thirty staters, which Matthew had called thirty pieces of silver. And therefore the 30 pieces of silver for which Christ was sold amount to 15 imperials. They are not a little mistaken, however, who understand denarii by the pieces of silver, since the denarius is a Roman coin, not a Jewish one, and makes only a fourth part of a shekel, in which case 30 pieces of silver will only amount to 3¾ Joachimics, which would have been too small a price for the avarice of Judas's betrayal. 2. Those who wish the common shekels, as they call them, to be designated with Marloratus, who produce 7½. Joachimics, such as Budé in his book on the As claims to have seen regarding the shekels given to Judas, weighing a didrachm: but let those who wish, the Papist relic-worshippers, believe that. 3. Those who, with Heinrich Uranius in his booklet on coinage, think the silver coin was worth a third of a French gold coin, whence the sum of 30 pieces of silver comes to 10 crowns, 12½ Joachimics. Which calculation rests on no foundation at all. 4. Those who, with Baronius, Torniellus, Luca Burgensis, and Victor Strigelius, in Jer. 32, say that the thirty pieces of silver equaled a sum of 300 gold coins, just as Camerarius in his book on Greek and Latin coins says that each piece of silver is the same as an Attic mina of one hundred, that is, one hundred Attic drachmas: by which notion 30 pieces of silver will amount to 375 Joachimics, or 300 French crowns, since Budé valued the Attic mina at ten French crowns. But such a valuation suits neither the avarice of the Pontiffs nor the usage of the word silver coin. For as to the passage of Epiphanius in his book on Weights and Measures, it by no means favors this opinion if it is correctly understood. Cornarius translated it: They say that Abraham brought the form of it (the silver coin) into Canaan, τὸ δὲ ταλέντε τὸ ἐκ λίτραι μία. Furthermore, one pound is from one hundred and twenty-five parts of a talent. Which words do not pertain to the silver coin, but to the talent. Zechariah certainly says the price was not great, and uses the term כסף, by which not a mina, but a shekel is designated, ch. 11:12. Cast it to the potter, the handsome price at which I was valued by them. Cf. B. Gerhard in Harmony, ch. 168, and Hostus, book IV, ch. 5.

And these things regarding the Jewish silver coins. But a silver coin also occurs when there is talk of Greek coins, Acts 19:19, where it has been correctly observed by most writers that an Attic drachma (a fourth part of a Jewish silver coin) is denoted by the term argenteus, whence the pieces of silver are correctly rendered by the Vulgate as denarii. For the Greeks counted sums of money in drachmas, as the Jews did in shekels, and the Romans in sesterces. Ephesus, however (to which those silver coins belonged), was a Greek city, a colony of the Athenians, as Strabo, book XIV, and Pausanias in his Achaica teach. Therefore, those magic books burned at Ephesus were worth 50,000 denarii, or 6,250 Joachimics.

Brerewood indeed cites in ch. III, for a gold shekel, the passage 1 Chron. 21:25. And David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. But there, six hundred shekels counted in gold can be understood. And thus with Villalpando, Vol. III, p. 414, Alcazar on weights & measures, prop. XXI, p. 60, and Andreas Masius on Josh. ch. VII, v. 24, understand silver shekels. The LXX have σίκλες χρυσίε ὀλκῆς ἑξακοσίες: six hundred shekels of gold or in gold (counted or paid out) by weight. For if gold shekels were meant, that threshing floor would have cost 3600 Joachimics, which is not likely. Although the aforementioned authors in the parallel passage 2 Sam. 24, v. 24 think that gold shekels are designated: David therefore bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty silver shekels, as the Vulgate has it, and thus they reconcile the passage of Chronicles, because fifty gold shekels make six hundred silver shekels: yet this explanation neither fits the letter, because not gold but silver is commemorated, he is said to have bought בְּכֶסֶף for silver for fifty shekels, not indeed for gold: it cannot be applied to the certain explanation of the Vulgate, which expressly has fifty silver shekels: nor does it sufficiently fit the text, because only the threshing floor was bought, as much as was needed for that sacrifice with the oxen, which can certainly be bought for 50 silver shekels, and was not worth the price of six hundred shekels; nor does it respond to the usage of the word, because a shekel, when there is talk of money, is nowhere else in the Scriptures taken otherwise than for a silver shekel. And the reconciliation is easier, handed down by Jerome, the Glossa Ordinaria, Lyranus, Hugo, Dionysius the Carthusian, Benedictus Arias Montanus, Salianus, Serarius, Cornelius a Lapide, and others, consonant with the words of both texts, that David gave 50 silver shekels for the partial threshing floor of the altar and the oxen, just as Josephus likewise clearly teaches in book VII, c. 13, that they were paid for the threshing floor of the Altar; but for the whole threshing floor of Araunah later, when the temple was built upon it, he paid six hundred shekels; where however some understand gold shekels, others indeed, in the manner of Scripture, silver shekels, even if paid in gold, which is especially the explanation of Arias Montanus.

Some also bring forward the passage Job 42, 11, where the LXX interpreters have τετράδραχμον χρυσέν ἄσημον, but Hostus acknowledges in book V, c. 8, that that version is repugnant to the Hebrew truth: and that what is added ἄσημον renders the passage suspect, because how is a gold coin a tetradrachm, which lacks a stamp? Finally, it has nothing to do with the present, where the question is about a Jewish gold coin, not an Arabian one. In the Hebrew it is held: and each one gave one gold earring. But whether gold shekels were minted among the Jews in later times, we do not care, of which mention might be made by others outside the canon, as Hostus gathers from Josephus in the cited book, p. 776, if indeed he narrates in book V of the Captivity, c. 36, that the Jews besieged in Jerusalem swallowed gold coins, which the deserters soon collected after they were excreted from the dung, whence also the deserters were cut open by the enemies, so that they might obtain the gold: which they redeemed for twelve Attic drachmas, because previously they were worth 25: whence he concludes that there were gold didrachms among the Jewish people then. But those would have been only half-shekels, or such a coin as the Beka is called in silver, not indeed whole shekels. We are not concerned here with silver or shekels outside the Canon, but those which are commemorated in the Scriptures.

CHAPTER VI. Half-shekel: third, and quarter.

There are however in the Scriptures also parts of a shekel as peculiar coins, which have obtained their name from its division: namely, the half-shekel is then expressed by the word בֶּקַע from בָּקַע to cleave, to divide, Gen. 21, v. 22, Ex. 38, v. 25, where in both places the LXX explain it as δραχμὴν, understanding the Hebrew coin as a drachma, which made two Attic ones, because in the latter place the sacred shekel is expressly named in the authentic Hebrew text, as also in the Chaldean and the LXX interpreters, even if the Vulgate (wrongly indeed) has omitted the mention of the half-shekel for each head equally as a measure according to the weight of the Sanctuary: then by the word חצה from חצה to descend, to divide, Ex. 30, 15, as a tribute or offering is imposed upon every head from twenty years and above in the Sanctuary מַחֲצִית הַשֶּׁקֶל half a shekel according to the shekel of holiness. The LXX render it τὸ ἥμισυ τῶ διδράχμ&, and chapter 38, v. 25, where בֶּקַע is explained by מַחֲצִית הַשֶּׁקֶל the LXX have δραχμὴ μία τῇ κεφαλῇ τὸ ἥμισυ τῶ σίκλυ κατὰ τὸν σίκλον τὸν ἅγιον. They understand however in these places also the didrachm of the Hebrews (which is the tetradrachm of the Attics) or the shekel: using this word in another sense than was done by Matthew, c. 17, 24, where it is manifest that by δίδραχμον (taken in Attic value) not a whole shekel, but a half-stater, or shekel is understood. A half-didrachm therefore according to the LXX or the Hebrew shekel is a fourth part of an ounce or a Joachimic, 6 Misnic groschen. And such a half-shekel was a peculiar coin among the Hebrews, as Arias observed. The third of a shekel שְׁלִישִׁית הַשֶׁקֶל occurs in Neh. 10, v. 33, the third part of a shekel, which Nehemiah imposed for the restoration and preservation of the temple and external divine worship, to be paid annually by everyone; it was a silver coin of 4 Misnic groschen. The quarter of a shekel רֶבַע הַשֶׁקֶל is commemorated in 1 Sam. 9, v. 8. as the price to be offered to the man of God, namely the fourth part of a shekel (one Attic drachma), which was a silver coin of three Misnian groschen. From which Arias rightly gathers that the stater of the Greeks, which is of equal weight with the shekel, and the didrachm with the half-shekel, and the drachma with the fourth part, were accepted in imitation of the Hebrew coins and weights.

CHAPTER VII. Gera, Agora, Keschitah.

To the parts of the Hebrew shekel belongs the Gera. It is called גֵרָה from גָּרַר to draw, to gather, either because men willingly gather and draw coins to themselves, or because many Geras must be gathered so that one may possess some notable sum of wealth. From this some derive the word γερὺ. The shekel has twenty Geras, as the Holy Spirit has defined several times, not only in Moses, but also in the Prophets, Ex. 30. v. 13. Lev. 27. v. 25. Num. 3. v. 47. c. 18. v. 16. Ez. 45. v. 12. It is therefore the twentieth part of the Hebrew shekel: And since a shekel is 12 Misnian groschen, which make 144 small coins (Pfennige), by the division made by 20, there result 7 Misnian small coins (Pfennige) with one fifth part of a small coin. The LXX Interpreters render it with the word ὀβόλων, which is rendered by trientes, small coins, obols. Concerning which Cleopatra in her Cosmetics: τὸ Ἰταλικὸν δηνάριον ἔχει δραχμὴν ἁ, ἡ δραχμὴ ὀβολὲς ς' χαλκᾶς μή: The Italic denarius has one drachma, but a drachma has six obols, forty-eight chalci. With which, as regards the number of obols in a drachma, those things agree which are held in the book of commandments c. XXI, as noted by Drusius: A shekel has four denarii; a denarius six obols: an obol according to tradition weighs sixteen barleycorns. A shekel therefore will have 384 barleycorns: and since the Gera is the twentieth part of a shekel, the Gera will have by that reasoning 19 1/5 barleycorns, or grains, since an obol has only 16 barleycorns. But if 320 barleycorns are attributed to a shekel, the twentieth part of the shekel will be 16 barleycorns, which the Jewish tradition assigned to an obol. Whence it appears that 320 barleycorns are more rightly attributed to a shekel than 384: and by that agreement either a denarius will have only five obols, or if 6 obols are attributed to it, that tradition will be false: and no more than 13 1/3 barleycorns will have to be assigned to an obol. Brerewood has it thus in chap. I. p. 4. A Gerah is the twentieth A part of the shekel, that is, the fifth part of a drachma, as the (LXX.) Interpreters not accurately enough render an obol for a Gerah, since an obol is the sixth part of a drachma. The Chaldean always explains it as מָעָה. See the Targum on Exod. 30, v. 13, and Isa. 45, verse 12. So also Rambam, chap. IV, Maaphor Scheni: A Sela contains four דִינָרִים or denarii, a denarius six מָעִין Maja. Regarding the weight of the shekel, R. Levi of Barcelona in the law of the Hebrews explained by Hottinger, book IV, p. 132. The weight of half a shekel is 80 barleycorns. For a whole shekel in the time of Solomon was 160 grains. He understands the common shekel, which the Rabbis found. Therefore, a genuine shekel is twice as large, 320 grains, so that 16 grains of the Gerah are left over.

But a Gera is also called אֲגוֹרָה Agora from אגר 'he gathered', 'he hired for wages', or as some prefer from גָרַר 'to cut', because it is a cut and diminished small portion of silver, 1 Sam. 2, v. 38, where the LXX likewise have ὀβολὸν and the Chaldean מָעִית regarding the wages which were contributed for the ministry of the word. Forsterus explained it as a scruple of silver. From this they derive the Greek ἀγορὰ, about which John Tzetzes the Grammarian writes in Hesiod. Agora is also a coin with which one buys. And the Hebrews have those as synonyms, Gera and Agora.

They believe the same small coin is designated by the word קְשִׂיטָה Kesitha, Gen. 33, verse 19, Jos. 24, verse 32, Job 42, 11, which may have its name from a lamb, because it was marked with the image of a lamb, just as 'pecunia' (money) is said to be from 'pecus' (cattle). Some infer from the circumstances of the places in which it is mentioned that it was peculiar to the Chaldeans or Arabs. R. Akiva reports from his Arabian journey that the same thing is Kesitha to the Arabs as Megha or Gerah is to the Jews, in the Talmudic tractate רֹאשׁ הַשָׁנָה ch. 3. 'When I was traveling through Africa, I heard it called מָעָה there as קְשִׂיטָה.' See also R. David Kimchi in his Roots and R. Solomon Jarchi on Genesis 33, as well as R. Levi Ben Gerson in the Pentateuch. Therefore, the hundred Kesith, for which Jacob bought the portion of the field in which the bones of Joseph were buried, Genesis 33, verse 19, Jos. 24, verse 32, constitute five shekels, or two and a half Joachim thalers. If one were to imagine profane shekels, only one Joachim thaler and a quarter would have been the price, which is certainly too cheap. Others understand by Kesitha a lamb or a ewe, as the Targum explained it as מֵאָה חוּרְפָן 'a hundred lambs', because in ancient times they were accustomed to trade by the exchange of goods. Just as also in Job 22, verse 11, the Vulgate, LXX, and Chaldean interpreted this word as a lamb, as did R. Aben Esra, although R. Solomon preferred to understand it as a coin: with whom B. Luther and Dr. Seb. Schmid and others agree.

CHAPTER VIII. Ἀσσάριον, κοδράντης, λεπτὸν.

CONCERNING the coins in the New Testament, Matt. XVII, verse 27, we have spoken about most of them on the occasion of the coins of the Old Testament: namely, about the larger ones. Because the στατὴρ and ἀργύριον in chap. XXVI, 15, are equivalent to a shekel: the didrachmon to a Beka, or half a shekel: the δηνάριον (denarius) corresponds to the fourth part of a shekel or a drachma: and thus the δραχμὴ in Luke 15, verse 8, and the δηνάριον in Matt. 18, verse 28, chap. 20, verse 2, and 22, verse 19, are equivalent. In the same sense, the word ἀργύριος, as it is used in Acts 19, verse 19, is explained. It remains that we should still speak about the smaller coins which are read in the New Testament. Such are the ἀσσάριον, κοδράντης, and λεπτὸν. Now the ἀσσάριον is the Assarius, to the later Hebrews אִסָר, if it is estimated according to the ancient writers as half an As, as from Varro, Agricola, book II, on foreign weights, and from Cleopatra in Cosmer. Brerewood on Coins, ch. II. teaches, to which the Assarius weighs two drachmas, if indeed in the time of Cleopatra, and long before, they were semuncial Asses by the law of Papyrius. Cf. Plin. book 33, ch. 3. But according to the Hebrews in the Mishnah, tractate Gittin ch. 1, § 1, and tractate Mezikim ch. VIII, § 5, it is the ninety-sixth part of a shekel, as far as price and value are concerned: but it is more correctly set as the 80th part of a shekel according to value: because it is the twentieth part of a denarius, if you look at the price, which constitutes the fourth part of a shekel. Whence, according to some of ours, the Assarius is 1 Pfennig, as we call it, with 4/5. The As was worth the tenth part of a Roman denarius, as Brerewood says, loc. cit. ch. XII. Mention of it is made in Matt. X, verse 29: 'Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion?' In the Syriac text, it is likewise אִסָר. The Belgian annotators say it is worth a half-sestertius: others increase its value up to a sestertius.

Kodrantes, a quadrans, denotes a fourth part of a follis according to Hesychius, or rather a fourth part of an as according to others, if indeed it is not permitted to find other quadrantes among the Romans in monetary matters. It is therefore half of an assarius, and weighs a drachma, but is worth two lepta, or a dupondium, Mark 12:42, according to some minor Mishnaic scholars 1/16 of one of those we call Pfennig, and 13/16 of those we call Heller: but not, as Hesychius, and Scaliger following him on monetary matters, wishes, that it is an assarion and one lepton. The Syriac interpreter in Mark 12:42 and Luke 12:59 and 21:2 rendered the lepton, two of which make a kodrantes, as שְׁמוֹנָא, that is, an eighth part, which Beza explains at the passage in Mark from Pollux, book IX, regarding the eighth part of an Italian obol, 'the obol indeed had eight chalci,' and likewise: the two chalci, which is also called a dichalcon, were called a quadrans, because they were the fourth part of an obol.

The lepton, therefore, or 'minutum,' is not correctly explained in Luke 21:21 by Chrysostom as an obol; for it is half of a quadrans and the eightieth part of a denarius or drachma: just as the quadrans is the fortieth part of a denarius: and it weighed indeed a half-drachma, but was worth, according to our small coins, 7/160 of one of those coins of the type called Heller: and thus 1/5, in those coins which are called Scherf. The Italian obol, however, is the sixth part of a drachma and a denarius, worth 6 of the coins we call Pfennige.

But because the name of the drachma is understood differently in the Hebrew Code than in the New Testament, and the LXX interpreters also vary here, although something has been said about the drachma and denarius regarding the Hebrew shekel, some things must still be noted here specifically about the drachma.

CHAPTER IX. Drachma, denarius, Zuz, didrachmon, tetradrachmon, bus, geaus.

For there is also among the Hebrews in use דַרְכְּמוֹן as a type of coin; which some think is composed of דרך (way) and מנה (distributes, deputes), as if to say 'viaticum' (travel money), which is spent by a traveler, from which is derived, according to some, the drachma of the Greeks and the drachma of the Latins, Ezra 2:69, Nehemiah 7:70, 71, where the LXX employ the more general word νόμισμα: and the Chaldean אדרכנים [Adarkonim], the drachma of Ezra 8:27, 1 Chronicles 29:7, in which latter place the LXX nevertheless have χρυσῦς [gold coins], the Vulgate solidos [solidi], and B. Luther rendered it Gülden [gold coins] everywhere: but in the New Testament, Luke 15:8-9, he translated δραχμὴν [drachma] as Groschen. But the LXX interpreters otherwise use the word δραχμὴ for a half-shekel in Exodus 30:24-25, as also for משׁקל [weight] in Genesis 24:22. One may read of silver drachmas in 2 Maccabees 4:9, chapter 10, verse 20, and chapter 12, verse 43. Whence it is clear (since these passages all occur in the Sacred Scriptures) that gold drachmas are designated in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, and silver ones in the LXX interpreters and in the Maccabees, as also in Luke. Brerewood makes the word Adarcon Persian (Chapter III, p. 10), from Darius, King of the Persians, by whose image the Adarcon was marked, as Plutarch testifies in his Artaxerxes, just as Herodotus reports that the best gold coins were minted by Darius, which he calls the Daric. Adarcon, therefore, he says is the name of a gold coin, but Drachma is the name of a weight; and by the Greek interpreters both are translated as δραχμὴν [drachma] with respect to the Alexandrian and Hebrew weights, which are double the Attic weights of the same name. Moreover, the word drachma, to which both of those are related, seems as to its first origin to be derived from Greece rather than Persia: because it is said to be as if δραγμὴ [dragme], i.e., a handful, from δράττομαι [drattomai], which is to apprehend, to seize with the hand, and thus Eustathius in the 2nd Iliad observes that it is a collection of obols, namely, as many as a hand can grasp: and Suidas says, ἡ δὲ δραχμοὶ Ὀβολῶν ἕξ, a drachma, he says, is of six obols, namely Attic, which is also noted by Cleopatra and Plutarch; and the Attic drachma is the most common, which is agreed to be equal to the Roman denarius: just as the Attic drachma was the daily wage among the Attics, the denarius was the daily wage among the Latins. And according to Hesychius it is τὸ ὀγδόον τῆς ἐγγίας, the eighth part of an ounce, in which manner Jerome also in Ezekiel 4 reports that eight drachmas make one Latin ounce: which, since the silver Joachimic coin of one ounce equals it, the eighth part of a Joachimic, or three Misnian groschen, will constitute an Attic drachma and a Roman denarius. For although according to an accurate calculation made by Agricola the drachma is a seventh part lighter than the denarius, nevertheless the Latins, interpreting Greek, compare the drachma with the denarius ὡς ἔγγιςα [as closely as possible]. Which name δηναρίε [denarius] (so that I may speak of it here at the same time) is more frequent in the New Testament: because it was then already under the Roman Monarchy. See Matthew 18:28, chapter 20:2, 9, 10, 13, chapter 22:19, Mark 6:37, chapter 12:15, chapter 14:5, Luke 7:41, chapter 10:35, chapter 20:24, John 6:7, chapter 12:5, Revelation 6:6, since neither in the LXX interpreters nor in the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament does that name occur anywhere: but it was used by the Rabbis as דינרין [dinarin], and also by the Chaldean Paraphrasts, who however are found to speak only of gold denarii, as Elias notes in his Thisbi: A Dinar is a coin worth almost the same as a zuz, except that the zuz is silver, but the dinar is gold; although דינרא [dinara], a denarius in the Syrian or Talmudic language, may not only denote a certain species of coin, but sometimes also be used for any kind of money or currency whatsoever, as observed by Selden. Indeed, the Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity, under the Monarchy of the Persians and the Greeks ruling in Asia, began to use drachmas for the most part, with the name itself even inflected with a Hebrew ending and adapted also to gold coins, as is evident from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. But the Greeks themselves, while dominating the East, used drachmas to such an extent that the name of shekels seemed almost to have vanished: but after the Romans later took power, they began to deal in denarii and other Roman coins, yet in such a way that the word drachma and the distribution of its subdivisions were adapted to the Roman denarius itself, albeit with an unequal calculation, since the Roman denarius, as has been said, is a seventh part heavier than the Attic drachma. Whence furthermore a double drachma is observed in Cleopatra: namely, the Italian and the Attic, each of which is valued at six obols, but again at different ones—some Italian, some Attic—and indeed the Italian obols were exchanged for eight chalcis or small copper coins (48 of which constitute a Roman denarius), and the Attic for seven chalcis. But as for what was said about the זוז [zuz], as per the Targum on 1 Samuel 9:8 and in the New Testament Syriac version, let us add that in them, for the word drachma, that word is substituted which is read in both the Mishna and Gemara; Selden makes that coin equal to a Roman denarius, or to the fourth part of a silver shekel, when it is mixed, having namely seven parts of copper and an eighth of silver, according to the old mixture of copper and silver; but when it consists of pure silver, it is equated to two shekels, as Selden observed from Maimonides and other Masters.

Furthermore, the gold denarius, according to Hesychius, is δραχμὴ χρυσί́α [gold drachma] or a gold coin δραχμιαῖος [drachm-weight], struck at the weight of a drachma, according to the proportion of Pollux brought from the poet Menander, is worth 10 silver drachmas or denarii, i.e., 30 Misnian groschen, which proportion Hesychius also reports from Polemarchus, namely that a drachma of gold is worth ten drachmas of silver coin. For others, according to Plato in the Hipparchus, the proportion of gold to silver is twelvefold: for this makes the δωδεκασάδιον [dodekasadion] to gold, which proportion is more accepted, which Stanislaus Grsepsius, a Pole, argues from 1 Kings 10, 2 Chronicles 1, and Book 8 of Josephus's Antiquities was once customary among the Jews. See Hostus, Book V, Chapter 4, p. 715, and the proportion which comes very close to that which Cornelius Tacitus, Book XVII, is the author was in force in the time of the Emperor Galba, as it was twelve and a half fold. And according to that, a drachma of gold makes 12 denarii, 36 Misnian groschen, one silver sesquiuncia [ounce and a half]: if the Attic drachma is considered. But since the Hebrew, as also the Alexandrian, as Brerewood rightly observed, is twice as large, a drachma of gold, such as only occurs in the Old Testament in the Hebrew Code, will be of three ounces or Imperial [weights]. In the New Testament, however, in Luke 15:8, in the common meaning at that time, the Attic drachma is to be understood.

Furthermore, a didrachma is a double drachma in its proper meaning: and in that sense τὰ δίδραχμα occur in the New Testament, Matt. 17, v. 24, concerning two drachmas. It is used, however, by the Septuagint interpreters for שקל, Gen. 23, 15, 16; Exod. 21, 32, & 30, 13, 15, 27, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 25; Lev. 27, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 15; Num. 3, 47; Josh. 7, 21; Neh. 5, 15, chap. 10, 32. Since it is established that a shekel contains not two but four Attic drachmas, and a didrachma is only half a part of a shekel. Such a didrachma, for the use of the temple and divine worship, each person among the people of God was bound to contribute, Exod. 30 & 38; but afterwards, when Judea was made tributary, they were compelled to pay it annually into the public treasury, as witnessed by Dio in Vespasian and Josephus, book VII, of the Jewish War, ch. 27. Therefore, the Septuagint interpreters ought to have rendered it not as didrachmas, but as tetradrachmas. For these made up a shekel. Nor indeed can they be reconciled, if it be said that they understood the common shekel, not the sacred one. For besides the fact that that distinction has no foundation, the Septuagint interpreters rendered it as didrachmas where it is expressly added, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, as in Exod. 30, 13. Therefore, nothing else remains to be said, except that either the translation of the LXX elders is not correct in those places, which I would by no means say, or they themselves understood another kind of drachma, of double value in comparison with the Attic ones, just as it is established that the Aeginetan drachma was heavier than the Attic, and contained not only six, but ten Attic obols, that is, five Meissen groschen, which the Athenians therefore called παχεῖαν, that is, a thick drachma: thus, therefore, according to the LXX interpreters, the drachma would be even thicker, namely of twelve Attic obols, or 6 Meissen groschen, so that the didrachma would be 12 groschen. Which meaning must be considered proper to them. In Egypt, at any rate, the drachma was of even smaller value, as Cleopatra noted, that the Egyptian drachma was the sixth part of an Attic drachma, weighing one obol, and the Egyptian shekel once had a weight of only sixteen Attic obols, which, however, was later diminished, so that the silver Egyptian shekel was only eight obols, as Stan. Grsepsius observes, concerning the shekel and talent. The LXX therefore said didrachmon, not as the Greeks commonly did, as for example βῦς νόμισμα δίδραχμον, a bull, a didrachm coin, today called an uncial quadrans, or the fourth part of an ounce, as Hesychius warned, but for a tetradrachm, such as the tetradrachm coin among the Athenians was the glaux, the owl, a coin on which was inscribed the owl, a bird sacred to Pallas among them: as it is in the interpreter of Aristophanes on the Birds. The owl, he says, in Scripture was of a tetradrachm, as Philochorus says. The tetradrachm coin was then called an owl. For the owl was the emblem or mark, and the face of Pallas: whereas the earlier ones were didrachms, and had an OX as an emblem. Therefore, the LXX are found to have used the word drachma in a different meaning than that accepted among the Greeks, since they translate the word דרכמון in Ezra 8:46 and אדרכון in 1 Chron. 29:7 and 2:69 with drachma, who also use the same word drachma for משקל, a weighing or weight, in Gen. 24:22, where other Greek interpreters have didrachmen, from which it is likewise permitted to conclude that the drachma of the LXX elders is what others called a didrachmon or didrachmen, and thus for them a didrachmon is what others called a tetradrachmon: which appears more clearly from chapter Ex. 38:25. For there the LXX interpreters call a drachma half a shekel of the sanctuary, which by everyone's consent is 12 groschen, or half an ounce of silver, from which is left the didrachmon according to the LXX interpreters. or that two drachmas are equivalent to a shekel of the sanctuary, and thus are said in the same sense as they are called a tetradrachmon by others. For thus they have in the same place: 'One drachma per head, half of the shekel according to the holy shekel.' Which is also without doubt the reason that they translate the word שקל sometimes as didrachmon, sometimes as shekel, even where the discussion is beyond controversy about the shekel of the sanctuary, interchanging these words among themselves. Bonfrerius does not poorly resolve the matter in Gen. 20:16. A didrachmon (among the LXX) is the same as a shekel, and so they translate shekel or silver piece throughout, which might seem strange to someone, since we have said those shekels were tetradrachms. But it must be noted that not all talents or drachmas were equal, and what the proportion of talent to talent is, the same is that of drachma to drachma: furthermore, every talent contains six thousand of its own drachmas: furthermore, the Hebrew talent, or that of the sanctuary (which alone seems to have been in use in those most ancient times, and afterwards, while the Jewish Republic stood, was called the talent absolutely and by excellence) was double the Attic talent, or one hundred and twenty minae, since the Attic weighed only sixty minae of silver, and thus the drachma of the Hebrew talent was also double the Attic drachma:

A shekel of this kind therefore contained two double drachmas, and thus four Attic drachmas; therefore, the shekel is rightly called a didrachmon by the LXX throughout, and the half-shekel a drachma. What Bonfrerius says about the talent, we leave in its place: here we are concerned only with the drachma and didrachma. Cornel. à Lapide on Exod. 30:13 distinguishes between the didrachmon of the Hebrews and the Attic. The Septuagint, he says, take the didrachmon in the Hebrew manner, not the Attic. But the Hebrew didrachmon was an Attic tetradrachmon: for one Hebrew drachma made two Attic ones. The Septuagint therefore call two Hebrew silver pieces a didrachmon, five of which weighed two Attic drachmas, as Budaeus testifies in book 5 of De Asse. Similarly, almost, Edward Brerewood on the weights of the ancients. Although the LXX interpreters often translate שקל as didrachmon, as in Gen. 23:15, Exod. 21:32, Levit. 27:3, 4, 5, 6, 7, etc., Jos. 7:21, etc. They are not, however, to be understood with respect to the Attic drachma, but the Hebrew or Alexandrian: For since the interpreters themselves were Hebrews, and were translating the sacred books into Greek at Alexandria, it is entirely credible that they looked either to the weights of their own region or to those of Alexandria. But the Hebrew and also the Alexandrian drachma was double the Attic: For the Alexandrian talent contained 12,000 Attic drachmas, according to VARRO, which is also how much the Hebrew was: But that every talent contains 6,000 drachmas proper to the place whose talent it is said to be, POLLUX and SUIDA have reported: Therefore, the didrachmon by Hebrew or Alexandrian weight was a tetradrachmon by Attic weight.

CHAPTER X. מנה μνᾶ, mina.

It is not poorly distinguished, when dealing with the coins occurring in Holy Scripture, between the kinds of coins and the sums of coins. And as regards Hebrew coins and their kinds, some are silver, such as the שקל shekel, which is also כסף silver, the בקע half-shekel, or מצית, and further the שלישית השקל third of a shekel, and the רבע השקל fourth part of a shekel, then the גרה, and the אגורת twentieth part of a shekel, to which they wish the קשיטה to be equivalent: Others, however, are gold, such as the דרכמון and אדרכנן Adarcon and Drakmon, about which we have spoken thus far, with the kinds of Greek coins occurring in Holy Scripture likewise explained. It remains, therefore, that we should still examine the sums of coins, two of which are celebrated among the Hebrews, namely the מנה and the ככר.

As for מנה or מני (from מנה to number, to compute) a pound, a weight, the Greeks call it μνᾶν, the Latins a Mina; it, if one asks about a gold one, weighs 200 Attic drachmas, 50 silver shekels, the proportion of which to gold, because it is twelvefold, hence as 50 shekels in silver make 25 Joachim thalers, so in gold they will be worth 300 Joachim thalers. Camerarius on Luke 19:18, where μνᾶ occurs, makes the price of a mina one hundred denarii, but 12 ½ thalers. But Brerewood more correctly observes that the mina contains one hundred drachmas as a Hebrew weight, but 200 Attic ones, which weigh 50 shekels, and thus 25 thalers, when the discourse is about gold minas: but that silver minas among the Hebrews comprise 60 shekels, and thus 240 Attic drachmas, or as he notes that Josephus in book 14 of the Antiquities, chapter 12, expresses it in the same sense, two and a half pounds of silver: which therefore is worth 30 Joachim thalers. But as for what is said by the Hebrews in the book Misnajoth tractate on the Corner chapter 8, § 5, that a mina is said to contain 100 denarii or drachmas (namely Attic ones), that is to be understood to be of a more recent institution of that name, and to have prevailed among the Hebrews from the commerce of the Greeks and other nations. Some, and among them Johannes de Leusden in Philologo-Ebræo mixto p. 197, go about to prove that the profane minas, as they call them, contain one hundred shekels, from 2 Chron. 9 verse 16 compared with 1 Kings 10 verse 17, because three minas of gold are explained there as three hundred shekels of gold: But in the Hebrew text no mention of shekels is made, nor do golden shekels occur anywhere as coins in the Holy Scripture. If the weight is understood as three hundred shekels of gold, since the weight of gold is double that of silver, the weight of 150 shekels of silver will be implied in place of three minas, and thus 50 shekels will still have to be assigned in place of one mina. It is better, however, to say that three hundred drachmas of gold are understood, as being equivalent to three minas, since a mina of gold contains one hundred drachmas of gold by Hebrew weight, that is, two hundred Attic ones.

But concerning the mina of silver, it is certain from Isa. 45 v. 12 that it comprises 60 shekels among the Hebrews. Which some call the new mina or that of Ezekiel. Regarding its distribution in the said place, that it contains twenty, twenty-five, and fifteen shekels, Arias Montanus observes in his Ephron that a fourth part of 15 shekels, and a third of twenty, and a third with a twelfth portion of 25 shekels are distinctly named, because from the comparison and opposition of these parts, various proportions could be formed in adding and subtracting weight or price. For if twenty-five are opposed to fifteen on the other side of the balance, there will be produced on the other side a sixth part of a mina, that is, ten shekels. If twenty are opposed, a twelfth part of a mina will be produced, namely five: If we oppose twenty to fifteen, the same will happen. Again, it also happens in this way in comparisons: With twenty-five and fifteen added, forty emerge, that is, two thirds of a mina: but with twenty and twenty-five joined, two thirds and a twelfth are made. Then twenty and fifteen make a half with a twelfth: but fifteen repeated make half a mina: twenty-five repeated make a half with a sixth.

The Papists, for the sake of supporting the Vulgate version, which in 1 Kings 10 verse 17 has 300 minas, such as Cornelius à Lapide, Jacobus Tirinus, and others, say that shekels are sometimes understood by minas, but without example. The Vulgate is entirely erroneous there, as we have shown at that place. For in the Hebrew text three minas are read. And so have the LXX, Pagnini, Arias Montanus, Münster, Tigurinus, and others. Three weights of gold, Junius, Tremellius, and Piscator. The ellipsis of the word מאות which Malvenda imagines must be supplied from 2 Chron. 9 verse 16 is inept. For who would concede this, or can concede it without prejudice to the authority of the divine word, that in place of three minas, three hundred should be substituted, under the pretext of an ellipsis and the omitted word מאת, a hundred? And who could carry 300 minas, whether a mina weighs 60 shekels, as in Ezek. 45 verse 12, or one hundred drachmas (or 50 shekels) as Mariana seeks here?

This would be the just burden of an ass, not the shield of a man, as Sanctius admits: Who indeed, for the sake of the Vulgate version, objects that these were prepared not so much for military use as for the ornament of the royal house: But such ornaments also must have a just proportion, otherwise they will be not so much decorative as disgraceful.

CHAPTER XI. ככר A talent.

There remains the Talent, in Hebrew ככר, in Chaldean ככרא, and thence called κίγχαρ by Josephus and others, which the Greeks otherwise call τάλαντον, ἀπὸ τῶ τλῆναι τὸ βάρ[?] Whence do they call it Ki- kar? They explain the Hebrew word by reason of its etymology as the greatest roundness, either in quantity, in plane, or in weight, as כור is a most capacious measure of dry things. The Kickar or talent of the Hebrews contains in weight 3000 shekels, or 1500 Imperials, just as is clearly taught in Exod. 38. v. 25. 26. for 300,000 men offering as many half-shekels make 600,000 shekels: these indeed are said in the same place to make up one hundred talents: whence it remains that one talent contains 3000 shekels, that is 12,000 Attic drachmas. From which it is also evident that the Hebrew talent is double the Attic talent: for this contained 6000 Attic drachmas. This agrees with Epiphanius: because he says the talent weighs 125 pounds, that is, 1500 ounces, which make 3000 shekels. Although Kickar was a name of weight, nevertheless it was paid out in counted silver shekels, as Arias Montanus advises: because shekels were of a certain weight, and from them a certain Kickar could be forged: whence a Kickar of silver is said to be counted in the Sacred Scriptures.

There are certainly not lacking those who have judged that the talent after the times of David was of lesser weight and value than before the times of David, to which opinion Joh. Mariana also accedes: but they are easily refuted by Biblical examples: For 2. Chron. 25. v. 6. King Amaziah of Judah is read to have hired 100,000 robust men from Israel for the sum of 100 talents of silver, that is, retaining the ancient value, at the wage of a shekel or 1 1/2 Joachim per head for both common soldiers and leaders. We leave it to be considered whether they could have been hired for a smaller wage. Thus with two talents of silver, that is, 3000 Joachimites, King Omri of Israel bought the entire mountain of Samaria 1. Kings 16. v. 24. namely as much space as could suffice for founding a most vast royal city, and for surrounding it on all sides with suburbs, boundary lines, and citadels. Could it have been bought for a cheaper price? Conf. Villalpando, Vol. II, on Ezekiel.

We add here a table of the coins occurring in the Holy Code, reduced to our Misnian ones, with the weights contained in the Sacred Code added at the same time, according to the explanation already handed down, so that they may be had in one view.

CHAPTER XII. Concerning cubic measures in the Holy Code, and first of dry ones, such as Cab, Gomer, Seah, Ephah, Semichomer, Chomer, Cor. choinix, koros, saton.

Cubic or capacity measures are some for dry things, others for wet. The former [occur] both in the Old Testament and in the New. In the Old [Testament] these occur, and since they are estimated among the Jews according to the number or capacity of eggs, they are as follows: I. קַב Cab, the smallest measure of dry things, 2 Kings 6:25. It is the sixth part of סְאָה or Seah according to R. D. Kimchi, Tirinus, and others, and according to R. Nathan it holds 24 eggs: and it is according to some like the choinix of the Greeks, a measure of daily food, but according to others it more correctly contains double the Choenix. It occurs only in the cited passage: namely, that a fourth part of a Cab of dove's dung was sold for five pieces of silver, that is 2 1/2 Joachimic [coins], where Franciscus Junius wrongly explained it as the hollow of the belly, since קֵבָה is one thing, which denotes the stomach or crop, and קַב is another, which Tremellius in the Thesaurus M.S., as noted by Leusden and other interpreters, interprets as a type of measure. LXX. Jonathan, the Syrians, the Arabs, Münster, Pagninus, Montanus, Castalio, Strigelius. Thus the head of an ass, because it was otherwise an unclean animal and was sold for food and for sacrifices (Exod. 13:13) for 80 pieces of silver, that is 40 Joachimic [coins], a fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver, or two and a half Thalers: since the whole cab was hardly a measure of daily food.

II. GOMER עֹמֶר is the tenth part of an Ephah, as is held in Exod. 16:36, and since likewise in v. 16 a Gomer is designated for each head, for Aben-Ezra a Gomer is the food of one man for one day, although Fagius reads it thus, Gomer for the sum of the number of your souls. It contained according to the Jews, and Casp. Waserus on measures, a cab and a half, or as much as 43 eggshells hold. Waserus attributes nine Roman pounds to it, others eight; from which they gather how liberally God acted with the Israelites, since it is established that the Choenix, which was only two pounds, was formerly the daily ration measured out to Roman shepherds. Manna was lighter than wheat, containing more empty space in itself than wheat: therefore a larger measure of Manna than of grain had to be assigned. Some translate the word עֹמֶר as usual from עָמַר as the service of someone.

III. SATUM סְאָה Gen. 18. vers. 6. 2. Reg. 7. v. 1. 18. is a measure more than three times larger than a Gomer, namely 144 eggs: and thus it contained six cabs, and was the third part of an Ephah. So R. Solomon in Levit. c. 14. says a Satum contains six Cadi: R. David Kimchi: A Sea is the third part of the measure which they call an Epha. And therefore a satum of fine flour 2. Kings 7. v. 1. at the time of the siege of Samaria sold for a single Shekel or 12 Mishnaic grossi contained as much as 144 eggs.

IV. EPHA איפה is three times larger than a Satum or containing three Sata, it is 18 Cabs, 432 eggs. David brought an Epha of parched corn to his brothers 1. Sam. 17. v. 17. A Gomer is the tenth part of an Epha, as we have said. It is said in Ruth 2. verse 17 that an Epha contained three Sata. It was the tenth part of a Cor. Tirinus makes an Epha equal to a Roman amphora of 80 pounds.

V. CHOMER חומר has its name from an ass חמור, because it is the heaviest burden of an ass or a mule, and it contains 30 Sata, or ten Ephas, as is held in Ezekiel 45, 11. An Epha contains a tenth of a Chomer. It will therefore have 4320 eggs. Efa. 5. v. 10. He who sows a Chomer, shall reap an Epha, i.e., the tenth part. See Lev. 27. v. 16. Num. 11, 32. There is also לתך Hos. III. v. 2. (that is, an elevation, as it were a burden, which a vigorous youth can lift and place upon an ass) which is half a Chomer, R. Sal. Jarchi, containing fifteen Sata, or five Ephas, 2160 eggs. But the same thing as a Chomer is a CORUS כור which word, however, is more recent than the former, and seems to have come to the Hebrews from foreigners, and it is also read twice concerning liquids, it is properly for dry things. Ezekiel 45. v. 14 expresses that it is of the same quantity as a Chomer. Whence R. Kimchi says, a Gomer, he says, is the same as a Corus, and it holds ten Ephas, and 30 Seas. Tirinus, a Homer, he says, in Hebrew, a Corus of the Greeks contains ten Ephi or Roman amphorae, 30 modii, and it was the largest measure of the Hebrews, of 800 pounds.

Furthermore, in the New Testament occurs I. χοῖνιξ Choenix, Apoc. 6. v. 6. which denotes such a measure as a man needed to sustain life, by which food was distributed to servants; therefore it is called ἡμεροτροφὶς. The Choenix varied, however, just as the daily ration could also be different according to the variety of places and persons, whence Jacobus Capellus in his book on the measures of the cubit, Sect. 22, assigns six different measures of the Choenix, and in Ap. VI. he understands the smallest, which was two pounds, and barely sufficed for a man living sparingly and meagerly for his daily food: since only half a part of a Cab, a fourth of a Gomer assigned to the Israelites for daily food, was contained, and it held only 12 eggs.

II. Σάτον, Satum, Matt. 13:33, which is equivalent to the Hebrew סאה and likewise 144 eggs, although the Greeks were not accustomed to count according to eggs, as the Hebrews were.

III. Κόρος, Corus, Luke 16:7, that this measure is the same as the Hebrew כור is beyond doubt.

CHAPTER XIII. Measures of liquids, Log, Hin, Bath, Cor, ξέστης, μετρητὴς, βάτος.

Measures of liquids in the Old Testament are read as follows: I. LOG, לוג Leviticus 14:10, according to R. David Kimchi in the Book of Roots, is the smallest measure of liquids, the twenty-fourth part of a Sea or Satum, containing six eggs. Malvenda says it contains the 12th part of a Hin and six eggs. II. Hin, הין, according to Kimchi, holds 12 logs and therefore 72 eggs. Exodus 30:24, Take of olive oil a Hin, that is, as much as is contained by 72 eggshells. Leviticus 19:36, mention is made of half a Hin; Numbers 28:14, as also of the third and fourth part; the half is 36, the third part 24, the fourth 18 eggs. Compare Exodus 29:40.

III. BATH, בת, is of the same measure as the Ephah, according to Ezekiel 45:11, and therefore contains six Hins, 72 logs, or 432 eggs. There are those who distinguish between a common or vulgar Bath and a sacred one, and make the former smaller than the latter by a third part, such as Mariana, Tirinus, and Cornel. à Lapide from Villalpando and Alcafara, because 2 Chronicles 4:5 says the bronze sea could hold three thousand baths, but according to 1 Kings 7:26 it held two thousand baths. But because an ambiguity or diversity in sacred measures is not to be rashly admitted, it is better with Junius, Piscator, the Belgian Interpreters, Ribera, and Grotius to reconcile these in such a way that it could indeed hold three thousand at the maximum, but was not accustomed to be filled except to two thousand. For the upper circumference, because it was very wide, easily held a thousand baths.

IV. COR, כור, concerning liquids, occurs in 1 Kings 5:11 and Ezekiel 45:14, of the same capacity in them as the Cor is in dry measures.

In the N. T. these liquid measures occur: I. ξέστης Sextarius, Mark 7:4. It corresponds with the Hebrew Log.

II. Μετρητὴς Metreta, John 2:6. Some understand it as a Cados, along with Erasmus, Beza, Camerarius, and Drusius, who in his Præterita says: The quadrans is the same measure as the amphora, which is a Cadus, and it comes to the same thing as the metreta. But if we take the Attic amphorae, which exceeded the Roman by half, that is, by an urn, those individual water-pots held, as Beza notes, two hundred or three hundred pounds of wine each, of twelve ounces each: because Georgius Agricola estimates the weight of a metreta at one hundred pounds. According to Budaeus, the metreta is to be estimated at a weight of 120 pounds. For he relates in his book De Asse that the metreta and the cadus are the same measure, containing ten Congii, and that a Congius contains six sextarii, and a sextarius contains two heminae or cotylae, and that a hemina weighs one pound, that is, six cyathi. That cyathi contain two ounces of liquid. Robertus Senalis teaches that the metreta and the cadus hold the same amount as the Bath or Epha: which measures he shows from Josephus to contain 72 Attic Sextarii, that is, 108 measure-pounds. For an Attic sextarius holds half a pound, and is the same as the Hebrew Log, which measure is capable of holding 6 eggs. And thus βάτος in Luke 16:6 will be the same as μετρητὴς, and as בת. To the Hebrews, one metreta, just like the βάτος, contained 36 Hinnas, each of which is of one measure, which we here specifically call thus, eines Masses minus 1/5. For those 36 Hinnas make 30 of our accepted measures. It is to be noted, however, in this designation of eggs, that eggs among the Jews were somewhat larger than ours, as Menochius and others have observed.

We set forth all these things for view in this way: TABLE OF MEASURES.

CHAPTER XIV.

Measures of lines, or of intervals, Digit, palm, Span, feet, pace, Cubit, measuring reed. στάδιον, ὁδὸς σαββάτε, μίλιον.

Cubic measures are followed by measures of lines, or of intervals, by which we measure the distances of places, which occur in the Old Testament as follows: I. Digit אצבע δάκτυλος is four grains, and the sixteenth part of a foot, Jerem. 52, 21. II. טפח παλαιςὴ vel δοχμὴ Palm is four digits and the fourth part of a foot, Exod. 25, 15. 1 Kings 7, 26. Ps. 39, 6. III. זרת Span consists of three palms, and digits, as Kimchi notes in the Book of Roots, Exod. 28, 16. c. 39, 9. 1 Sam. 17, 4. Isa. 40, 12. Ez. 43, 13. Some distinguish between the lesser palm of 4 digits, and the greater, such as Martyr understands in 1 Sam. 17, 4: but Matth. Hostus rightly warns in Histor. Monomach. David. c. IV. that a double palm is invented in vain: because the lesser palm of 4 digits, a quadrant of a foot, is the one and only true palm: nor do approved authors acknowledge another. IV. פעם foot contains 16 digits, four palms, Ezek. 41, 6. according to Kimchi. V. אמת cubit, which some make another, a common one, such a space as is from the middle of the arm to the tips of the fingers, of the length of a foot and a half; another sacred one, accustomed to be used in sacred buildings, for the sake of reconciling the passages 2 Chron. 3, 15. 1 Kings 7, 15. as Piscator from Junius and Leusden: but because in both places the discourse is about the same sacred building, that distinction has no place, nor is a different cubit to be invented without cause. The reconciliation of those passages is clear from the words themselves; for there it is a matter of the measure of both columns: he made two columns of thirty-five cubits in length: here of one column: He formed two bronze columns, eighteen cubits was the height of one column, as Sanctius from Vatablus, and Ribera, and Mariana from Villalpando, and Salian. Menochius and Tirinus observe: that 18 is to be understood as more or less; not so much because Scripture does not care about a precise quantity, or that the reason for small numbers is not held, as some wish, but because by a collation of both passages the precise measure is clear, namely that it was exactly 17 and a half cubits. Some also assign a third kind of cubit, namely the King's cubit, as they call it, from Targum Onkelos, and the Arabic version Deut. 3, 11. and they make it three digits longer than the common cubit. But there the King's cubit is not named in the source, but the cubit of a man: The Syrian rendered it as the cubit of giants: Fagius explains the Targumic King's cubit as the public cubit, whose measure is certain by the decree of the Magistrate. Meanwhile, it is not without reason noted by Martyr, that the Hebrew cubits were larger than ours by a third, or rather a fourth part, which is not improbable to Bonfrerius and Tirinus, since the measure of the cubit was established at that time when the stature of men was greater, and could not subsequently be changed. And from that it seems to be that in Ez. 43, 13. the true or legal cubit is defined, that it had a common cubit (such as is commonly a foot and a half among the Romans, Greeks, and Hebrews; and a palm (contracted) of which legal cubit Tirinus notes from Villalpando that Scripture and Josephus speak everywhere, so that there is no need to invent another cubit in the Scriptures than that which is clearly defined here, larger than the common one by four digits placed transversely. Indeed, the cubit was the fourth part of the stature of a man of that age, since everyone has four of his own cubits in his own stature: and he also makes as many cubits of his own body when he extends his arms to the side, as St. Jerome, Vitruvius, and others have handed down everywhere. Compare Sanctius on 1 Kings 2, 2.

Leusden also adds a fourth kind of cubit, namely the Geometrical, which contains six common cubits, citing the Dutch Interpreters in Gen. 6, 15. But Buteo in his booklet on Noah's ark, and Matth. Hostus, have already taught that common cubits, not Geometrical ones, are to be understood in the passage of Genesis, even though that opinion once handed down by Lyranus regarding the Geometrical cubit prevailed generally. For such a building could neither have been joined with beams, nor would it have been capable of navigation or of carrying burdens, and it would have to be said that the ark was one hundred and thirty times larger than it ought to be, or, since others assert that the Geometrical cubit contained 9 common cubits, more than two hundred times larger. Wherefore Lyranus, Estius, Menochius, and Ainsworth, along with Josephus, Buteo, and Hostus, determine that common cubits are to be understood there: since Moses does not distinguish the cubits, and Buteo has taught that common ones suffice abundantly for containing everything in the ark geometrically, as also primarily Wilkins does in Matth. Polus in the Synopsis on this passage.

VI. צעד a pace, or step, commonly contains two feet and a half, and thus ten palms, 40 digits, and it is explained in this way by some in 2. Sam. 6, 13, where, however, others understand a stadium.

VII. There occurs קנה a measuring reed in Ezech. 42, 16, which Jonathan in Ez. 40, 1 says was of six cubits in the cubit defined by Ezechiel, and thus Jacobus Capellus in his book on the Measures of Intervals, s. 14, says it consisted of six median Hebrew cubits, or nine feet.

In the New Testament there is I. σάδιον, a stadium, Luke 24, 13; John 11, 18, which word they derive ἀπὸ τῆς σάσεως, from standing, because Hercules had covered such a distance by running before he had need to stop: it is called a measure of 625 feet, 125 paces, of which each contains the space of five feet, and 4000 make a German mile, which are called greater paces. And II. μίλιον, a mile, Matthew 5, 41, which is considered to have contained a thousand greater paces: the Hebrew mile was also called a Sabbath day's journey, whence the Syriac in Acts 1, 12 explained a Sabbath day's journey as being about seven stadia. The Hebrews defined it by two spaces of land: of which one (כברת ארץ Gen. 35, 16. 2. Kings 5, 19.) 4 stadia, it will have to be said for that reason: Where, however, the Syriac translates as a journey of about a stadium of land, Münster likewise explained it as a stadium: Mercerus as a jugerum, that is to say, as much as could be plowed in one day, just as Fuller also in book II of his Miscellanies, chapter 15, interprets the Chaldean word in the Targum of Onkelos in the same sense as a plowing. Others, with Rabbi Solomon on Gen. 48, 7, speak of the Sabbath journey itself, or of a mile with the Arab, in which way also Rabbi David Kimchi on 2 Kings 5, 19 says it is the measure of a mile, and thus Buxtorf in his Chaldean Lexicon also explained the Chaldean word כרוב as a mile. But some, following the aforementioned Rabbi David Kimchi in his Book of Roots, say that in the Hebrew word the כ is servile, and the theme is ברך, and that it signifies a space of a journey, as much as a man covers from morning until a meal. In which way Drusius translates it as about a day's journey of land, i.e., as much space as a man covers between refreshments, e.g. from morning to breakfast, or from breakfast to lunch. But it is especially to be observed that Rambam, as Mercerus reports, testifies that he visited those places, and that there is not a mile between the burial of Rachel and Bethlehem. It is certain that a small space of land is designated, as Burgensis observes on Gen. 48, that the Hebrew expression does not signify spring nor time, but a small measure of land, and Christoph. Cartwright in his Electa Targumico-Rabbinica, having compared the various interpretations, finally concludes on p. 289: All things weighed, nothing occurs as more probable than what Mercerus thinks, namely that Chibrath of land is a measure of a journey, but a small one, and unknown to us. And therefore wrongly and inappropriately by The Vulgate is rendered in Gen. 35:16 as 'in the spring time', and in 2 Kings 5:19 as 'a chosen time', even though כברת means 'he chose', or even 'he fed', as some say, according to the time when the earth brings forth food and crops: Malvenda invokes כרא here, with the meaning that it is when the earth begins to produce fruits; nor is Fuller's view more convenient, that it is a patent, public, and royal way, so that כרחה is of the same meaning as ברת and ברא, namely ἐκκαθαίρειν, to render pure and clean, or a cleared way, through which there exists a free opportunity of running to and fro, since from the words of Gen. 35:16 and 48:7 it is clear that a certain space of land is denoted. Nor does the exposition of a certain Hebrew in Fagius in Collat. and Munster and Oleaster deserve credit regarding a large or ample space of land (from כביר, 'great', 'much') because the place in Gen. 35:16 was near a city. Cf. Gen. 48:7, 1 Kings 10:2, Matt. 2:18, and what Adrichomius has. The version, as far as the sense is concerned, not the word, which they rendered as 'hippodrome' according to Jerome, as if they had taken כברת for רכבת (by metathesis), which is the space of an equestrian course; for the Alexandrian Hippodrome, as Bonfrerius noted, was a thousand cubits, namely from goal to goal; then the exposition of Lud. de Dieu, who says, 'My conjecture is this, that כברת is in the construct form, from ברה which the Rabbis say is בר, the Targum is ברא, and it is the same as שרך, but this signifies not only fields, the country in general, but also arable land, or as much length of land as a plowman makes by drawing furrows, as in 1 Sam. 14:14. Thus Onkelos and Targ. Jeros. כרוב ארעא, literally 'a plowing of the land', that is, a jugerum. In the Hebrew concordances, חבל, 'a rope', sometimes denotes כברת הארץ, a tract of land, as much as the dimension of one rope would complete, that is, a jugerum. And Benjamin says it is near Bethlehem at about half a mile: for מיל is two thousand cubits. These are Dievius's words. Related to this is the one mentioned above by Mercer and approved by the Tigurine, as well as the exposition of those who explain the word ברת from the Syriac ברא, which means the country or field around a city, so that the sense is that Naaman, who in 2 Kings 5:19 departed not far from the city, signifies by 'cultivated land' that which was adjacent, and also R. Levi's interpretation, that between that place and the city there were only cultivated fields adjacent to the city, and vineyards and gardens pertaining to it. In general, Meir Nethib took it for a portion and segment of land, which is indeed too vague, as are the 'tract of land' of the Samaritans and Montanus, and the 'plain' of Junius and Piscator, and 'field of land'.

Since, therefore, this periphrasis is uncertain or indefinite, one must rather acquiesce in that opinion which holds it for a small space of land or interval, than that a peculiar and definite measure of length should be fixed here.

And so much also for measures. Let there be compared from the apparatus to the Royal work of Bened. Arias Montanus: Tubalcain, or On Sacred Measures; Sara, or On the Satum; and Ezechiel, or On the Batum, which treatises are included together with his Ephron, or On the Shekel, in Vol. VI of the Royal work, in which are also exhibited those two notable Tables of the Land of Canaan, the former according to the time of Abraham and before the arrival of the sons of Israel: the latter according to the distribution among the tribes of the sons of Israel. We shall only add below the measure of lengths in summary:

TABLE OF MEASURES OF LENGTHS.

A palm - - - - - - - - - - 4 digits.

A span - - - - - - - - 3 palms, 12 digits.

A foot - - - - - - - - - 4 palms, 16 digits.

A cubit - - - - - - - - 7 palms, 28 digits.

A pace - - - - - - - - 10 palms, 40 digits.

Measuring rod - - - - - - 42. palms. 168. digits.

Stadion - - - - 125. paces. 625. feet. 2500. palms.

Μίλιον (Italian) mile, Sabbath day's journey } - - 8. stadia. 1000. paces. 5000. feet. 20000. palms.

The German mile has 32. stadia, 4000. paces. 20000. feet. 80000. palms.

THE END. To God alone be glory.

The Vulgate is rendered in Gen. 35:16 as 'in the spring time,' and 2 Kings 5:19 as 'a chosen time,' although ברה means 'he chose,' or even 'he fed,' as some say, according to the time when the earth brings forth food and crops: Malvenda invokes ברא here, i.e., when the earth begins to produce fruits; nor is Fuller's view of a patent, public, and royal road more convenient, so that ברה might be of the same meaning as ברא and ברר, namely ἐκκαθαίρειν, to render pure and clean, or a cleared road through which there exists a free ability to run to and fro, provided that from the words of Gen. 35:16 and 48:7 it is clear that a certain space of land is denoted. Nor does the interpretation of a certain Hebrew in Fagius in Collat. and Munster and Oleaster regarding a great or ample space of land (from כביר 'great, much') deserve credit, because the place in Gen. 35:16 was near a city. Cf. Gen. 48:7, 1 Kings 10:2, Matt. 2:18, and what Adrichomius has. The LXX interpreters approach closer. The version, as far as the sense is concerned, not the word, who rendered it ἱππόδρομον (hippodrome) according to Jerome, as if they had taken כברת for רכבת (by metathesis), which is the space of an equestrian course. For the Alexandrian Hippodrome, as Bonfrerius noted, was a thousand cubits, namely from goal to goal; then the exposition of Lud. de Dieu, who says, 'My conjecture is this, that כברת is of the construct form, from ברה which the Rabbis call בר, the Targum ברא, and it is the same as שדה, but this signifies not only fields, the countryside in general, but also arable land, or as much length of land as a plowman makes by leading furrows, as in 1 Sam. 14:14. Thus Onkelos and Targ. Jeros. כרוב ארעא, literally the plowing of the land, that is, a jugerum.' In the Hebrew concordances, חבל (a rope) sometimes denotes כברת הארץ, a tract of land, as much as the dimension of one rope would complete, that is, a jugerum. And Benjamin says it is near Bethlehem at about half a mile: for מיל is two thousand cubits. These are the words of Dievius. Similar is the one handed down above by Mercer and approved by the Tigurina, as well as the exposition of those who derive ברת from the Syriac ברא, which signifies the countryside or field surrounding a city, as well as the interpretation of R. Levi, who in 2 Kings 5:19 explains the word as cultivated land which was around the city, so that the sense is that Naaman had not departed far from the city, for between that place and the city there were only cultivated fields adjacent to the city, and vineyards and gardens pertaining to it. In general, Meir Nethib took it for a portion and segment of land, which is indeed too vague, as are the 'tract of land' of the Samaritans and Montanus, and the 'plain' of Junius and Piscator, and 'field of land'.

Since, therefore, this periphrasis is uncertain or indefinite, one must rather acquiesce in that opinion which holds it for a small space of land or interval, rather than that a peculiar and definite measure of length should be fixed here.

And so much also concerning measures. Let there be compared from the apparatus to the Royal work of Benedictus Arias Montanus: Tubalcain, or On Sacred Measures; Sara, or On the Sato; and Ezechiel, or On the Bato, which treatises, together with his Ephron, or On the Shekel, are comprised in Vol. VI of the Royal work, in which are also exhibited those two notable Tables of the Land of Canaan, the former according to the time of Abraham and before the arrival of the sons of Israel: the latter according to the distribution among the tribes of the sons of Israel.
