CAPUT XII. De Mensuris cubicis in Sacro Codice, & primo Aridorum, ut sunt Cabus, Gomer, Sea, Epha, Semichomer, Chomer, Corus. χοῖνιξ, κόρυ, σάτον.

MEnsuræ cubicæ seu capacitatis aliæ sunt arido- rum, aliæ siccorum. Ille tum in Vet. Testam. tum in Novo. In Veteri hæ occurrunt, & quum apud Judæos secundum numerum vel capacitatem ovorum æstimentur, ita sese habent: I. קַב Kabus mensura aridorum minima, 2. Reg. 6. v. 25. Sexta pars est סְאָה sive Sati juxta R. D. Kimchium, Tiri- num & alios, & juxta R. Nathan capit 24. ova: estque juxta nonnullos uti χοῖνιξ Græcorum men- sura victus diurni, at juxta alios rectius duplum Chænicis continet. Occurrit tantum in loco citato: quod nempe quarta pars Cabi stercoris Columba- rum quinque argenteis divendita sit, hoc est 2 1/2. Joachimic. ubi Francisc. Junius cavum ventris per- peram exposuit, quum aliud sit קֵבָה quod ventri- culum vel ingluviem notat, aliud sit קַב quod Tre- mellius in Thesauro M. S. notante Leusdenio, cæ- terisque Interpp. pro mensuræ genere interpretatur. LXX. Jonathan, Syri, Arabs, Münsterus, Pagninus, Montanus, Castalio, Strigelius. Ita caput asini, quia alias immundum animal erat & ad cibum & ad sacrificia Exod. 13. v. 13. vendebatur 80. argenteis, id est 40. Joachimicis, quarta pars cabi stercoris columbarum quinque argenteis, vel duobus Thale- ris cum dimidio: quum totus cabus vix mensura diurni victus fuerit.

II. GOMER עֹמֶר decima pars Ephæ est, ut habetur Exod. 16. v. 36. & quum itidem v. 16. Go- mer ad singula capita designetur, Aben-Ezræ Go- mer est cibus viri unius die uno, licet Fagius ita le- gat, Gomer pro summa numeri animarum vestra- rum. Continebat juxta Judæos, & Casp. Waserum de mensur. supra cabum & semis, sive quantum capiunt testæ ovorum 43. Novem libras Romanas Waserus, alii octo ei tribuunt; unde colligunt, quam liberaliter Deus egerit cum Israëlitis, quum con- stet Chænicem, quæ bilibris tantum fuerit, olim opilionibus Romanis dimensum diurnum fuisse. Fuit Manna tritico levius, plus vacui in se con- tinens, quam triticum: ideo amplius demensum Mannæ, quam frumenti assignandum erat. Usua- lem vertunt nonnulli vocem עֹמֶר ab עָמַר uti ali- cujus ministerio.

III. SATUM סְאָה Gen. 18. vers. 6. 2. Reg. 7. v. 1. 18. mensura est plus quam triplo major, quam Gomer, nimirum 144. ovorum: adeoque sex cabos continuit, & tertia Ephæ pars fuit. Ita R. Salomo in Levit. c. 14. Satum habet sex Cados: R. David Kimchi: Sea est tertia pars mensuræ, quam Epha vo- cant. Ideoque satum similæ 2. Reg. 7. v. 1. tempo- re obsidionis Samariæ unico Siclo vel 12. grossis Misnicis divenditum tantum continuit quantum 144. ova.

IV. EPHA איפה triplo major Sato vel tria Sata continens est 18. Caborum, 432. ovorum. Epham aristarum tostarum tulit David ad fratres suos 1. Sam. 17. v. 17. Gomer est decima pars Ephæ, ut diximus. Tria Sata continuisse Epham Ruth 2. vers. 17. dicitur. Decima pars fuit Cori. Tirinus Epham æqualem facit amphoræ Romanæ 80. li- brarum.

V. CHOMER חומר ab asino חמור nomen habet, quia onus est asini, vel muli gravissimum, con- tinetque 30. Sata, vel decem Ephas, ut habetur Ezech. 45, 11. Epha contineat decimam Chomeris. Ha- bebit ergo 4320. Ova. Efa. 5. v. 10. Qui seminat Chomerum, metet Epham, h. e. decimam partem. Vid. Lev. 27. v. 16. Num. 11, 32. Est & לתך Hos. III. v. 2. (id est, elevatio, utpote onus, quod vegetus adolescens elevare & asino imponere potest) quod dimidium Chomer est R. Sal. Jarchi, quindecim Sa- ta, vel quinque Ephas, ova 2160. continens. Idem autem quod Chomer est CORUS כור quæ vox ta- men priori recentior, & ab Exteris ad Ebræos ve- nisse videtur, ac de liquidis etiam bis legitur, pro- prie est aridorum. Ejusdem quantitatis esse cum Chomere exprimit Ezech. 45. v. 14. Unde R. Kim- chi, Gomer, inquit, est idem, quod Corus, capitq; de- cem Ephas, & 30. Seas. Tirinus, Homer, inquit, Hæbræum, Corus Græcorum continet decem Ephi vel amphoras Romanas, 30. modios, erat que maxima men- sura Ebræorum, librarum 800.

Porro in Nov. Test. occurrit I. χοῖνιξ Chœnix, Apoc. 6. v. 6. quæ denotat talem mensuram, qua homo ad sustentandam vitam indigebat, qua cibus servis distribuebatur; ideo vocatur ἡμεροτροφὶς. Va- riavit tamen Chœnix, uti etiam dimensum diurnum pro varietate locorum & personarum diversum esse potuit, unde Jacobus Capellus lib. de mensur. cubit. Sect. 22. sex diversas Chœnicis mensuras assignat, & Ap. VI. minimam intelligit, quæ bilibris fuerit, & ho- mini parce ac tenuiter victitanti vix sufficiebat pro diurno victu: quum media tantum pars Cabi quar- ta Gomeris Israëlitis in diurnum cibum assignati fuerit, ac 12. ova solum continuerit.

II. Σάτον, Satum, Matth. 13. v. 33. quod æqui valet Ebræorum סאה atque itidem 144. ovorum, etsi Græci secundum ova numerare non consueve- rint, ut Ebræi.

III. Κόρος, Corus, Luc. 16. v. 7. quam mensuram eandem esse cum Ebræa כור dubio vacat.

CAPUT XIII. Mensuræ liquidorum, Log, Hin, Bathus, Corus, ξέστης, μετρητὴς, βάτος.

MEnsuræ liquidorum in Vet. Test. hæ legun- tur I. LOGUS, לוג Levit. 14. vers. 10. juxta R. David Kimchi in libr. Radic. Sextarius est men- sura liquidorum minima, vigesima quarta pars Sea, five Sati, sex ova continens. Malvenda, continet, inquit, 12. partem Hin & sex ova. II. Hin הין juxta Kimchium capit 12. logos adeoque 72. ova. Exod. 30. vers. 24. Accipe olei olivæ Hinem, h. e. tantum, quantum 72. testis ovorum continetur. Levit. 19. vers. 36. dimidii Hinis mentio fit Num. 28. vers. 14. ut & tertiæ & quartæ partis; dimidium est 36. tertia pars 24. quarta 18. ovorum. Conf. Exod. 29, 40.

III. BATHUS בת ejusdem cum Epha men- suræ est, teste Ezech. 45, 11. adeoque sex Hinnos con- tinet, 72. logos, vel 432. ova. Sunt qui distinguant inter Bathum communem seu vulgarem, & sacrum, & illum tertia parte hoc minorem faciant, ut Ma- riana, Tirinus & Cornel. à Lapide ex Vilalpando, & Alcafaræ, quia 2. Paral. 4. v. 5. mare æneum dici- tur capere potuisse tria millia batorum, at juxta 1. Reg. 7. v. 26. duo millia batos capiebat. Sed quia non est temere admittenda æquivocatio, vel diver- sitas in mensuris sacris; præstat cum Junio, Piscato- re, Belgic. Interpp. Riebera, Grotio hæc ita concilia- re, quod nempe ad summum potuerit continere ter mille, sed non consueverit impleri nisi ad bis mille. Peripheria enim superior, quia erat amplissi- ma, facile capiebat mille batos.

IV. CORUS כור de liquidis occurrit 1. Reg. 5, 11. Ezech. 45, 14. ejusdem in illis capacitatis, cujus Corus est in aridis.

In N. T. liquidæ mensuræ hæ occurrunt I. ξέ- στης Sextarius, Marc. 7, 4. convenit cum Log Ebræo- rum.

II. Μετρητὴς Metreta, Joh. 2, 6. Nonnulli Ca- dos intelligunt cum Erasmo, Beza, Camerario, Dru- sio, qui in Præterit. Quadrantiæ, inquit, eadem men- sura est cum amphora, quæ est Cadus, & eodem redit cum metreta. Quod si amphoras Atticas accipiamus, quæ Romanas dimidio, id est, urna superabant, ca- piebant Beza notante istæ singulæ hydriæ ducenas aut trecenas libras vini pondo singulas unciarum duo- decim: quia pondus metretæ vim æstimat centum libris Georg. Agricola. Juxta Budæum metretæ æsti- manda erit 120. librarum pondere. Tradit enim V. de Asse, metretam & cadum eandem esse mensuram, continentem decem Congios, Congium vero sex conti- nere sextarios, sextarium duas continere heminas vel cotylas, Heminam appendere libram unam, h. e. sex cyathos. Cyathos continere duas uncias liquoris. Ro- bertus Senalis docet, metretam & cadum idem ca- pere, quod Bathum seu Epha: quas mensuras ex Jo- sepho ostendit continere 72. Sextarios Atticos, h. e. libras mensurales 108. Atticum enim sextarium ca- pere selibram, & idem esse cum Log Ebræorum, quæ mensura capax est 6. ovorum. Atque ita βάτος Luc. 16, 6. idem erit, quod μετρητὴς, & quod בת. Ebræis una metreta æque ut βάτος continebat 36. Hin- nas, quarum quæque est unius mensuræ, quas nos hìc speciatim ita vocamus, eines Masses minus ⅕. nam 36. illæ Hinnæ faciunt 30. nostras mensuras receptas. Notandum autem in hac ovorum desi- gnatione, quod ova apud Judæos aliquanto majora nostris fuerint, ut Menochius, & alii observarunt.

Hæc omnia ita conspectui exponimus: TABULA MENSURARUM.

LIQUIDORUM. Log & ξέστης continet ova - - 6 Hin - - - - - - 72 Bathus, μετρητὴς & βάτος - - 432 Corus - - - - - - 4320.

CAPUT XIV.

Mensuræ linearum, seu intervallorum, Digi- tus, palmus, Spithama, pedes, passus, Cu- bitus, Calamus mensorius. ςάδιον, ὁδὸς σαϐ- ϐάτε, μίλιον.

MEnsuras cubicas excipiunt mensuræ linea- rum, seu intervallorum, quibus distantias lo- corum metimur, quæ in Vet. Test. occurrunt se- quentes: I. Digitus אצבע δάκτυλος est quatuor granorum, & decima sexta pars pedis, Jerem. 52, 21. II. טפח παλαιςὴ vel δοχμὴ Palmus quatuor digito- rum & quarta pars pedis est Exod. 25, 15. 1. Reg. 7, 26. Pf. 39, 6. III. זרת Spithama constat tribus palmis, & digitis, notante Kimchio in libro Radic. Exod. 28, 16. c. 39, 9. 1. Sam. 17, 4. Esa. 40, 12. Ez. 43, 13. Non- nulli distinguunt inter palmum minorem 4. digito- rum, & majorem, qualem Martyr 1. Sam. 17, 4. intel- ligit: sed Matth. Hostus recte in Histor. Mono- mach. David. c. IV. monet frustra fingi duplicem pal- mum: quia palmus minor 4. digitorum pedis quadrans unicus solus & verus palmus est: nec alium agnoscunt autores probati. IV. פעם pes continet 16. digitos palmis quatuor Ezech. 41, 6. secundum Kimchium. V. אמת cubitus, quem nonnulli alium communem faciunt, quale spacium est à medio brachii usque ad extremos digitos, longitudinis sesquipedis; alium sacrum in ædificiis sacris adhiberi solitum, ob con- ciliationem locorum 2. Chron. 3, 15. 1. Reg. 7, 15. ut Piscator ex Junio & Leusdenus: sed quia utrobiq; de eodem ædificio sacro sermo est, nullum locum habet illa distinctio, neque præter causam diversus fingendus est cubitus. Locorum istorum concilia- tio ex verbis ipsis patet; ibi enim de mensura utrius- que columnæ agitur: fecit duas columnas cubitorum tricenum quinum longitudinis: hîc de unius columnæ: Formavit duas columnas æneas, octodecim cubitorum erat altitudo columnæ unius, ut Sanctius ex Vatablo, & Riebera, ac Mariana ex Vilalpando, & Salian. Meno- chius ac Tirinus observant: ut 18. plus minus intelli- gendj; non tam quod Scriptura haud curet de quan- titate præcisa, aut quod exigui numeri ratio non ha- beatur, ut nonnulli volunt, quam quod collatione utriusque loci pateat præcisa Mensura, quod nempe exacte fuerit 17. cubitorum cum medio. Assignant etiam nonnulli adhuc tertium cubitorum genus, ni- mirum cubitum Regis, quem vocant, ex Targ. Onke- los, & versione Arabica Deut. 3, 11. & tribus digitis longiorem faciunt communi cubito. Sed ibi non cubitus Regis nominatur in fonte, sed cubitus viri: Syrus reddidit in cubito gigantum: Fagius Targumi- cum Regis cubitum exponit de publico cubito, cujus mensura ex decreto Magistratus certa est. Interim non abs re Martyri notatum, quod cubiti Ebraici majores nostris fuerint parte tertia, vel potius quarta, quod non improbabile est Bonfrerio & Tirino, cum cubiti mensura eo tempore constituta fuerit, quo hominum major erat statura, nec deinceps imutari potuerit. Atque inde esse videtur, quod Ez. 43, 13. cubitus verus seu legalis definitur, quod habuerit cu- bitum communem (qualis apud Romanos, Græcos & Ebræos vulgo est sesquipes; & palmum (contractum) de quo legali cubito passim Scripturam & Josephum loqui è Vilalpando notat Tirinus, ut opus non sit sin- gere cubitum alium in Scripturis, quam qui hîc aperte definitus est, communi quatuor digitis trans- versim positis major. Nimirum quarta pars staturæ hominis istius ætatis cubitus erat, quum quisque in sua statura quatuor sui cubitos habeat: ac totidem etiam faciat sui corporis cubitos, quando brachia in latum expandit, ut S. Hieronymus, Vitruvius & alii passim tradidere. Cons. Sanctius in 1. Reg. 2, 2.

Addit Leusdenus & quarti generis cubitum, Geo- metricum nempe, qui sex communes cubitos conti- neat, Gen. 6, 15. provocans ad Interpp. Belgicos. Sed in loco Geneseos intelligendos esse communes cubi- tos, non Geometricos Buteo in libello de arca Noæ, & Matth. Hostus jam docuere, etsi quondam illa apud Lyranum tradita opinio de Geometrico cubi- to in universum obtinuerit. Nam tantum ædificium nec contignari potuisset, nec navigationis, one- rumve patiens fuisset, & arcam centies trigesies ma- jorem fuisse dicendum erit, quam oporteat, aut quum alii Geometricum cubitum 9. communes habuisse cubitos asserant, supra ducenties. Quapro- pter communes ibi intelligendos esse cubitos Lyra- nus, Estius, Menochius, Ainsworth cum Josepho, Bu- teone, Hosto statuunt: siquidem Moses cubitos non distinguit, & communes abunde sufficere omnibus in arca continendis Geometrice Buteo docuerit, ut & imprimis Wilkinsius apud Matth. Polum in Synops. ad h. l.

VI. צעד passus, vel gressus communiter continet binos pedes, & semissem, adeoque palmas decem, digitos 40. & ita explicatur à nonnullis, 2. Sam. 6, 13. ubi tamen alii stadium intelligunt.

VII. Occurrit קנה Calamus mensorius Ezech. 42, 16. quem Jonathan in Ez. 40, 1. sex cubitorum in cu- bito ab Ezechiele definito fuisse, ait, atque ita Jaco- bus Capellus l. de Mens. intervall. s. 14. constitisse dicit sex medianis Hebræorum cubitis, vel pedibus novem.

In N. T. habetur I. σάδιον stadium, Luc. 24, 13. Job. 11, 18. quam vocem ἀπὸ τῆς σάσεως à stando de- ducunt, quod Hercules tantum spatium currendo confecerit, antequam consistere necessum habue- rit: dicitur mensura 625. pedum, 125. passuum, quo- rum singuli contineant spatium quinque pedum, & 4000. faciant milliare Germanicum, qui passus ma- jores dicuntur. Et II. μίλιον milliare Matth. 5, 41. quod passus majores mille continuisse censetur: Milliare Ebraicum dictum & fuit iter Sabbati, unde Syrus Act. 1, 12. iter Sabbati exposuit, quod circiter septem stadiorum fuerit. Definiebant id Ebræi duo- bus spatiis terræ: quorum unum (כברת ארץ Gen. 35, 16. 2. Reg. 5, 19.) 4. stadiorum fuisse ea ratione dicen- dum erit: Ubi tamen Syrus vertit itinere quasi Stadii terræ, Münsterus itidem de stadio exposuit: Merce- rus jugerum, quantum scil. uno die arari potuit, uti etiam vocem Chaldaicam in Targum Onkelos Fülle- rus l. II. Miscell. c. 15. eodem sensu arationem inter- pretatur. Alii cum R. Salomone ad Gen. 48, 7. de ipso Sabbati itinere, aut de milliari cum Arabe, quomodo etiam R. David Kimchi ad 2. Reg. 5, 19. est mensura, inquit, milliaris, atque ita vocem Chaldaicam כרוב etiam per milliare exposuit Buxtorf. in Lex. Chald. Nonnulli vero præeunte prædicto R. David Kim- chio in libr. Rad. in voce Ebræa כ servile esse ajunt, & thema ברך, ac significari spatium viæ, quantum homo conficit à mane usq; ad pastum. Quo pacto Dru- sius vertit circiter diætam terræ, h. e. tantum spatium quantum homo conficit inter refectionem, v. c. à mane ad jentaculum, vel à jentaculo ad prandium. Sed im- primis observandum, quod Rambam, Mercero re- ferente, testatur, se loca ista invisisse, ac inter sepultu- ram Rachelis, & Bethlehem non interesse milliare. Id certum est, spatium terræ exiguum designari, uti Bur- gensis ad Gen. 48. observat, dictionem Ebræam non significare vernum nec tempus, sed mensuram par- vam terræ, & Christoph. Cartwright. in Elect. Tar- gum. Rabb. diversis interpretationibus collatis, concludit tandem p. 289. Omnibus pensitatis nihil oc- currit probabilius, quam quod putat Mercerus, Chi- brath sc. terræ esse mensuram itineris, sed exiguam, & nobis ignotam. Ideoq; perperam & inconvenienter à Vulgata redditur Gen. 35, 16. verno tempore, & 2. Reg. 5, 19. electo tempore, etsi כברת fit elegit, vel etiam ciba- vit, ut nonnulli juxta tempus, quo terra cibum & sege- tem effert: Malvenda כרא huc advocat h. m. cum terra incipit procreare fructus; nec convenientius Fullerus viam patentem publicam ac regiam, ut כרחה ejusdem significationis cum ברת & ברא fit, nem- pe ἐκκαθαίρειν purum ac mundum reddere, vel viam patefactam, per quam libera ultro citroque curren- di facultas existit, siquidem e verbis Gen. 35. v. 16. c. 48, 7. luculentum sit spatium quoddam terræ de- notari. Nec calculum meretur cujusdam Ebræi apud Fagium in Collat. & Munster. ac Oleastri ex- positio de magno vel amplo terræ spatio (à כביר magnum, multum) quia prope urbem erat locus Gen. 35, 16. Conf. Gen. 48, 7. 1. Reg. 10, 2. Matth. 2, 18. & quæ habet Adrichomius. Propius accedit tum LXX. Interpp. versio, quantum ad sensum, non vocem, qui reddidere ἱππόδρομον teste Hierony- mo, ac si כברת accepissent pro רכבת (per meta- thesin) quod est spatium decursionis equestris, Hippo- dromus enim Alexandrinus, quod Bonfrerius no- tavit, erat mille cubitorum, nempe à meta ad me- tam, tum Lud. de Dieu expositio, qui, Mea conje- ctura, inquit, hæc est, כברת esse constructæ formæ, à ברה quod Rabbini dicunt בר, Targum ברא estque idem, quod שרך, hoc autem significat non tantum agros, rus in genere, sed etiam arvum, sive tantam agri longitudinem, quantam ducendis fulcis arator efficit, ut 1. Sam. 14, 14. Sic Onkelos & Targ. Jeros. כרוב ארעא ad verbum arationem terræ, id est, ju- gerum. In concordantiis Hebraicis חבל funis inter- dum denotat כברת הארץ tractum terræ, quantum unius funis dimensio absolvebat, id est, jugerum. Et Benjamin dicit esse prope Bethlehem ad dimi- dium circiter miliare: nam מיל est bis mille cubito- rum. Hæc Dievius. Affinis est Merceri supra tra- dita & Tigurina probata, ut & eorum ἔκθεσις, qui ברת à Syriaco ברא quod rus aut agrum urbi cir- circa urbem, vocem exponit, ut sensus sit, Naama- tio, qui 2. Reg. 5, 19. per terram cultam, quæ fuit cumjacentem significat, nec non R. Levi interpreta- nem non longe ab urbe discessisse, inter illum enim lo- cum & urbem non fuisse nisi agros cultos urbi adjacen- tes, vineasque ac hortos ad eam pertinentes. In genere pro portione & segmento terræ accepit Meir Nethib, quod vero nimis vagum est, ut & tractus terræ Samaritani & Montani, nec non Junii & Pi- scatoris planum, & campus terræ.

Quum ergo incerta aut indefinita sit hæc περί- φρασις, acquiescendu potius illi sententiæ, quæ pro exiguo terræ spatio, aut intervallo habet, quam pecu- liaris, & definita mensura longitudinis hic figenda.

Et tantum quoque de mensuris. Conferatur ex apparatu ad opus Regium Bened. Ariæmonta- ni Tubalcain, sive de Mensuris Sacris, Sara, sive de Sato, & Ezechiel, sive de Bato, qui tractatus una cum Ephrone ejusdem, sive de Siclo Tom. VI. operis Regii comprehenduntur, in quo etiam ex- hibentur duæ illæ insignes Tabulæ Terræ Canaan, prior juxta tempus Abrahæ, & ante adventum fi- liorum Israël: posterior juxta distributionem in tribus filiorum Israël. Subjiciemus solum adhuc mensuram longitudinum ἐν συνόψει:

## 1:1 Introduction: I. N. J. D. Abraham Calovius’s Illustrated Bible of the Old Testament, Volume I. Part One
I. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS’S ILLUSTRATED BIBLE OF THE OLD TESTAMENT, VOLUME I. PART ONE EXHIBITING ANNOTATIONS ON THE MOSAIC OR LEGAL BOOKS, Which they commonly call the PENTATEUCH, GENESIS, EXODUS, LEVITICUS, NUMBERS, DEUTERONOMY.

Latin:

I. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVII BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA VETERIS TESTAMENTI, TOMUS I. PARS PRIMA EXHIBENS ANNOTATA AD LIBROS MOSIS VEL LEGALES, Quos vulgo PENTATEUCHUM vocant, GENESIN, EXODUM, LEVITICUM, NUMERORUM, DEUTERONOMIUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Dedicatory Preface of the Anti-grotian Annotations on the Pentateuch. To the Generous, Mos
DEDICATORY PREFACE OF THE ANTI-GROTIAN ANNOTATIONS ON THE PENTATEUCH. TO THE GENEROUS, MOST NOBLE, MOST STRENUOUS LORD HAUBOLD VON MILTITZ, Councilor and most eminent Chamberlain of the Most Serene Elector of Saxony, most praised President of the renowned High Council and Ecclesiastical Senate which is in Dresden, formerly Marshal of the Most Serene Court, then Councilor of the Chamber to the same Most Serene Elector, today Privy Councilor and Supreme Director of Provincial Revenues, hereditary Lord of Schenckenberg, Oberau, and Scharffenberg, etc.: AND ALSO TO THE MOST REVEREND, MAGNIFICENT, NOBLE, AND EXCELLENT LORD JACOB WELLER, hereditary Lord of Molsdorff, Karsdorff, etc., most celebrated Theologian, and one who has served and still serves the Church of Christ most illustriously, primary Ecclesiastical Councilor, Sacred Confessor, and Court Preacher to the Most Serene Elector of Saxony: To the LORDS and PATRONS to be honored above all, health and prosperity of every kind!

How much the apparatus of philology contributes to the illustration of the Holy Scriptures, if one does not neglect the most proper hermeneutical means, the biblical context, the parallelism of passages, and the analogy of faith, no one will judge or explain more correctly than YOU, MOST EXCELLENT WELLER. For you have hitherto clearly proven this to the Church by your own illustrious example. This, as your very recent and most learned Commentary on the golden Epistle of the holy Apostle to the Romans, among other various studies, will especially testify. But when a philologist occupied by heterodox opinion approaches, or has furthermore held the remaining means of sacred ἑρμηνείας (interpretation) in low regard, I would not say in vain that the Church will have to fear from no one more detriment, or a more violent and harmful distortion of Scripture. And the more instructed he is by an exotic apparatus of every kind, the more gravely the danger will arise if he has set his critical claws into the Scriptures. There is no reason why I should now present as an example Origen Adamantius, Desiderius Erasmus, or any other Great Man: let Hugo suffice, GREAT in deed as well as in name. For after he had once conceived in his mind a new form of theology and indeed of all religion, he finally brought it forth and published it, truly monstrous and bearing ὐδὲν ὑγιὲς (nothing sound), however much the MAN of great reading strove to clothe it with the grace and charm of antiquity by means of some scheme: concerning which his various henotic [writings], very profitable to the Roman Anti-Christ and to Socinian impiety, can publicly testify. He by no means rested there; he even dared to attack the very Sacrosanct volumes, and this with this end primarily in mind, that he might attribute the mind which he had formed for himself to the most holy Spirit of God Himself, and drag Him into his own parties, even most unwillingly. I have observed this throughout with pain, horror, and detestation of soul. Yet I groaned especially at this, that the great man brought an apparatus of such erudition, both foreign and ecclesiastical, primarily to pervert the chief oracles of Scripture: for from this it happened that, under a great appearance, even absurd and impious meanings were sometimes brought into the Holy Scripture, which no one but GROTIUS, or someone like him, could have adorned with such colors. Who can doubt that this is not free from danger? For can one not refer to the precious stone, which Irenaeus has in Book I against heresies not far from the beginning, an emerald of great price, to which a glass vessel is sometimes assimilated in its disparagement, as long as there is no one present who can test it and expose the artifice, that it was done deceitfully? And when brass has been mixed with silver, who, being unskilled, will easily be able to test this?

For I do not deny that many things have been observed by Grotius that are very learned, and not a few that are highly relevant to the matter; those Annotations also have their silver, they have their gold. But otherwise, they are now so mixed with brass and dross by that art—not chemical, but philological—that the precious cannot easily be distinguished from the vile by the unskilled; and I would almost dare to assert that those papers bring more harm than benefit to the Church. For I believe that heavenly truth would have suffered no loss, the Holy Codex none, if, having taken care of his own affairs, the Ambassador of the Swedish Kingdom had left sacred things untouched. But when he flew beyond the boundaries of his vocation and applied critical hands to the Scriptures themselves according to the whim of his mind, one must be blinder than Tiresias not to see how much divine truth and the authority of the sacred Codex are brought into jeopardy. For it can be taught by countless examples that both the meaning of the divine oracles and the authentic text itself have been obscured or rendered ambiguous, not illustrated, by the Grotian shadows cast upon them. Nor are there few or obscure proofs in these Anti-Grotian Annotations on the PENTATEUCH: yet I have found that far more and more illustrious ones exist in the PROPHETIC and APOSTOLIC books.

Although I doubted at the beginning whether that Camarina should be moved, or whether at least in these places, where sumptuous volumes are in the hands of a few, so that the danger does not seem so much to be feared, these corruptions should be brought onto the stage? Yet the nature of heresies and errors always hovered in my mind, that they creep like gangrene, and that it is far more useful to the Church of God to manifest the pernicious corruptions of Scripture, wherever they cling, than to pass over in silence those that creep in secretly. Nor is it new for such things, adorned with such distinguished colors (which I could testify to with examples regarding the Grotian ones), to be insinuated to men who are even Theologians, or to be transferred not cautiously enough from winding volumes into others; which spread themselves more quickly without harm than they are detected as erroneous. For the tares grow, which the enemy sows for those who were sleeping, who ought to have been watching, and they easily propagate themselves in the Lord's field. A more ready precaution is that which St. Cyprian advises in his third treatise, *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, where there is manifest dread. And the mind is prepared beforehand for the struggle when the adversary reveals himself. An enemy is more to be feared and guarded against when he creeps in secretly, when, through the image of peace, he deceives and crawls with hidden approaches. Whence he also received the name of serpent. Such is his craftiness always, such is the blind and dark deceit of circumventing man. Which seem to graphically adumbrate the character of the Grotian Commentaries. For there you may see the image of peace, but a deceitful and treacherous one, and hidden and occult approaches. For the Annotations show nothing less than a zeal for disseminating Φορτικὰ ἀκόσματα: they are occupied in the illustration of the sacred texts, while they contend with no adversary: so that by doing something else they may inject and insinuate heterodox opinions. This entire method is composed for the purpose of deceiving. Even if these Annotations were worn out by only a few, account must still be taken of them. If they are a scandal or a harm to even one or two, is it not right to remove it, as far as one may? But then, shall we not value the glory of the divine name, or the truth of the heavenly word, so highly that we judge it alien to our duty to defend the same against any machinations whatsoever? Chas veschalom! Therefore, by how much more significant the apparatus with which the word of God is attacked, by so much more accurate an effort must it be brought to bear. And since it is not right to treat even a single letter in Scripture lightly, but one must believe that not only great mountains of doctrines, as the Rabbis say, hang from every single point, but that any point is more powerful than heaven and earth, nay, that heaven and earth must perish before even one iota or one point perishes from Scripture, as Truth itself testifies: Who will be of such a foolish mind as to wish to judge the work that is placed in vindicating the chief oracles to be in any way superfluous? To me, certainly, it has always seemed that no more useful labor is undertaken than that by which the purity and integrity of Scripture is championed and defended, the so-called classical passages are explained and asserted, and finally, the obscure and difficult ones are illustrated. However much effort we may place in Positive and Didactic, or in Polemic and Elenctic Theology, we must finally return to the sources and to the very principles themselves, when Philistine enemies or false brethren attempt to obstruct the sources for us and render the principles doubtful: nor can the conscience rest in anything else, unless it be solidified, constituted, and strengthened by the one and only indubitable principle and foundation of faith, the Word of God. Therefore, those who cultivate the sacred letters must be recalled to the classical sayings of Scripture, upon which the structure of all Theology rests as upon a most solid base, in correct information: and these are not to be recited nakedly, which we have perceived with pleasure is done by third-class boys in school; but they must be drawn from the sources of Hebrew and Greek truth, defended against the κυβείας of those who contradict, and freed from the στρεβλότητι of anyone whatsoever, and defended as is fitting. This was the reason that I decided to lead the Youth entrusted to our faith to the authentic Codex itself by means of these Biblical Dissertations, and those public ones, and at the same time to note with just censure the corruptions of a great man. It was indeed my intention only to designate, as if in a heap, the passages that have been depraved by this Critic: but because the corruptions could not be placed in the open light so that they might be seen or recognized by all; nor could the doubts or adversarial arguments be resolved, or the genuine senses of the sayings of Scripture be brought forward, I judged it to be for the public use, and therefore I undertook, these somewhat longer labors, though moderated and tempered by a welcome brevity regarding great matters. All of which I now expose to your judgment, BEST PATRONS, to whom the care and inspection of the Churches and Schools in these provinces has been entrusted. I took up this web, as is no doubt still fresh in your memory, with your knowledge and counsel, and with your support. Nor do I doubt that it was more useful to have it woven through public Disputations than if, as was easy to do, such things or similar ones were dictated to Students for their pens over a long passage of time. For in this way, not only were those things completed more quickly and easily, but I believed they could also be read and weighed more accurately by more people, then also examined and elucidated through a public collation of opinions, and finally propagated even to foreigners, and

could be translated for the uses of the whole Church. Therefore, let these be the terminal points here by your authority: or, if it shall seem so, I must proceed henceforth, and having briefly dispatched the remaining Historical books—for in these not so many things are found which demand an Elenchus—I must approach the so-called Poetical and Prophetical books: in which it is entirely possible to see here how much the craftiness of one man, or rather of the Devil himself (for he is the father of every lie) has been able to do! So that it may seem a great reward for the labor, if the significant oracles, with Rabbinical and heretical glosses wiped away, are restored to their pristine luster. For almost no Prophetic prediction dealing literally with Christ is left; so are all things twisted and perverted into an alien sense: Nor do the oracles remain intact, upon which our faith in most articles relies: for our Author believed that a great part of these were devoid of the Old Scriptures. But the foundations of errors and heresies have been laid everywhere, or traps have been prepared: nay, you may see here a certain bilge, into which both the Remonstrant ἀποχὴ, and the Socinian impiety, and the Papistic abomination, and finally the Jewish incredulity and perfidy itself have emptied themselves.

Receive, however, at the same time, GREAT PATRONS, a new document of gratitude; which, although it may not correspond to your illustrious honors nor to the dignity of your merits, I trust it will nevertheless have splendor from its divine subject matter, and value also in your eyes. For how much, to YOU indeed, ILLUSTRIOUS PRESIDENT, the Davidic Counselors and divine testimonies are of value, with how much care and solicitude the deposit of the uniquely true and salvific doctrine, the custody of which has been divinely entrusted to your faith, is cultivated and propagated by YOU, and finally with how much love its faithful defenders are cherished, I have no need to testify with words, since the testimonies of the things themselves are present. I cannot, however, refrain from congratulating the illustrious Saxony again and again on such a president of the Churches and Schools and of the supreme sacred senate, and from requesting with daily prayers the long-lived possession of such a deposit. To you, however, GLORY OF THEOLOGIANS, INCOMPARABLE WELLER, this is your own and perpetual praise: the more accurate scrutiny of the sacred fountains, which those preparations of multivarious erudition render the more wholesome, the more exquisitely you investigate Jesus Christ, the most suitable σκόπον, the kernel, the marrow, and the treasure of Scripture in the ancient oracles. And the Church would indeed not undeservedly grieve that he was much abstracted from these most illustrious studies, her greatest delights, from whom, above countless others, she promised herself the most abundant fruit; were it not that she ought rather to rejoice that a huge bulwark of the Orthodox was reserved for greater things, and raised to the very helm of Ecclesiastical government, for a more brilliant benefit, after, with an altogether happy omen, this light having risen again in this hemisphere of Upper Saxony, it has seemed to shine not only for these lands, but for the whole Lutheran world for now nearly fifteen years.

That you both may shine, and for a very long time, and for the greatest good of the universal Church, and that you may not be inserted into the higher firmament except very late, so that you may coruscate with eternal splendor, like stars of the first magnitude, I do not cease to pray to God the Best and Greatest. But I humbly contend that you may shine upon me and mine henceforth, especially my son-in-law Mr. DEUTSCHMANN, as also my only son of the same name, with the rays of your favorable kindness.

Wittenberg, the day before Jubilate Sunday, in the year of Christ 1659.

The perpetual cultivator of your Illustrious and Most Eminent Name, Abraham Calovius, D.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO DEDICATORIA ANNOTATORUM ANTIGROTIANORUM AD PENTATEUCHUM. GENEROSO, PRÆNOBILISSIMO, MAXIME STRENUO DOMINO HAUBOLDO A MILTITZ, Serenissimi Electoris Saxonici Consiliario, & Camerario eminentissimo, incluti Proto-Synedrii, & Sena- tus Ecclesiastici, qui Dresdæ est, Præsidi laudatissimo, post aulæ Serenissimæ Marschallo, tum Eidem Sereniss. Electori à Consiliis Cameræ, hodie Consiliario intimo, & Redituum provincialium Directori supremo, Toparchæ in Schenckenberg/ Oberau & Scharffenberg/ &c. hæreditario: NEC NON MAXIME REVERENDO, MAGNIFICO, NOBILISSIMO, EXCELLENTISSIMO DOMINO JACOBO WELLERO, a Molsdorff/ hæreditario in Karsdorff &c. Theologo celeberrimo, deque Ecclesia Christi præclarissime merito, & adhuc merenti, Serenissimo Ele- ctori Saxoniæ à Consiliis Ecclesiasticis, Confessionibus sacris, & Concionibus aulicis primariis : DOMINIS, & PATRONIS summopere honorandis salutem & prosperitatem omnigenam!

QUantum ad illustrandas Scripturas Sacras Phi- lologiæ apparatus conferat, si media quis her- meneutica maxime propria, contextus Biblici, pa- rallelismi locorum, & analogiæ fidei haud negligat, nemo TE rectius, WELLER E SUMME, arbitrabitur, aut exponet. Id enim proprio & illustri exemplo præclare hactenus comprobasti Ecclesiæ. Quod cum variis meletemasi aliis nuperrimus Commentarius in Auream S. Apostoli ad Romanos Epistolam lon- ge eruditissimus imprimis testabitur. Sed ubi opi- nione heterodoxa occupatus accesserit Philologus, aut reliqua sacræ ἑρμηνείας media insuper habuerit, non frustra dixerim, à nemine plus detrimenti Ec- clesia, aut magis violentam atque noxiam detorsio- nem Scriptura metuere habebit. Et quo instructior ille ab omnigeno apparatu Exotico fuerit, eo gra- vius orietur periculum, si ungues Criticos in Scri- pturas immiserit. Non est, quod in Exemplum nunc sistam Origenem Adamantium, Desiderium Era- smum, aut quemquã alium Magnum Virum: suffici- at Hugo, re pariter, atq; nomine MAGNUS. Postquam enim ille semel animo concepisset novam Theolo- giæ atque adeo universæ religionis formam, partu- riit deniq; illam ac in lucem edidit monstrosam pro- fecto,ac ὐδὲν ὑγιὲς referentem,quantocunque sche- mate antiquitatis gratiam & venustatem VIR magnæ lectionis induere ipsi sategerit: de quo henotica ejus varia & Anti-Christo Romano,& impietati Socinia- næ perquam proficua, publice testari possunt: Neu- tiquam acquievit illis, aggredi etiam ausus fuit ipsa Sacrosancta volumina, idque hac imprimis fini, ut mentem,quam sibi formaræt, ipsimet sanctissimoDei Spiritui affingeret, Eumq; in partes suas, etiam ma- xime invitu, pertraheret.Observavi hoc passim cum dolore, horrore, animiq; detestatione: Id tamen in- gemui præprimis, quod tantæ Eruditionis, cum ex- teræ,tumEcclesiasticæ apparatum Vir sumus ad per- vertenda Scripturæ præcipua oracula potissimum attulerit: inde enim factum,ut magna specie absurdi etiam quandoq;, ac impii sensus Sacrosanctæ Scri- pturæ illati fuerint,quos nemo nisi GROTIUS, aut ipsi similis talibus coloribus exornare quiverit, Quod periculo haud vacare, ecquis ambigere potest? An- non enim lapidem pretiosum, quod Irenæus habet lib. I. adversus hæreses non longe ab initio, Sma- ragdum magni precii, apud quosdam vitreum etiam vas, in ejus contumeliam assimilatum referre potest, quoad usque non adest, qui potest probare, & artifi- cium arguere, quod subdole sit factum? Et quum com- mixtum fuerit æramentum argento, quis facile pote- rit, rudis cum sit, hoc probare?

Non enim diffiteor, multa perquam erudite, nec pauca apprime ad rem facientia passim observata esse Grotio, habere etiãAnnotata illa argentum, ha- bere auru suum : Cæterum ita ista arte non Chimica, sed Philologica, æramentis, scoriisq; permixta jam sunt, ut neq; discerni facile ab imperitis preciosum à vili queat;& asseverare propemodum ausim,Sche- diasmata illa plus damni Ecclesiæ adferre, quam commodi. Nullam enim,credo, jacturam passa fuis- set cælestis veritas, nullam Codex Sacrosanctus, si, rebus suis curatis, Regni Suedici Legatus sacra intacta reliquisset. At ubi extra metas vocationis ista involavit, Scripturisque ipsis, pro animi libidi- ne, manus Criticas adhibuit, quantopere in discri- men adducatur divina veritas, sacrique Codicis au- toritas, Tiresia cæciorem esse oportet, qui non vi- deat. Utrumque enim & sensum oraculorum di- vinorum, & textum ipsum authenticum, affusis Grotianis tenebris, obscuratum, aut ambiguum redditum esse, non illustratum, innumeris exemplis doceri queat. Neq; pauca,vel obscura compareht in his Annotatis in PENTATEUCHUM GROTI- ANORUM Elencticis documenta: Quibus vero longe plura atque illustriora in libris PROPHETICIS, & APOSTOLICIS prostare compertum habeo.

Quanquam vero dubitarim initio, num Camari- na illa movenda, aut num saltim his in locis, ubi in paucorũ manibus sumtuosa versantur volumina, ut tantũ haud metuendũ videatur periculi,corruptelæ istæ in scenam producendæ sint? Semper tamen ani- mo obversabatur hæresium atque errorum natura, quod gangrænæ instar serpant,& quod longø utilius Ecclesiæ Dei sit, corruptelas Scripturæ perniciosas, ubicunq; hærent,manifestare, quam latenter obre- pentes silentio transmittere. Neq; vero novum est, insinuari Viris etiam Theologis talia, insignibus ejusmodi coloribus exornata, (quod de Grotianis testari, exemplis possem) aut è sinuosis Volumini- bus in alia non fatis caute traduci; quæ se diffundant citius non absq; noxa, quam deprehendantur erro- nea. Crescunt enim & zizania, quæ inimicus dormi- entibus jiis, qui vigilare debebant, serit, ac facile se propagant in agro Dominico. Facilior cautio est, quod S. Cyprianus tractatu tertio de Prælatorum simplicitate monet, ubi manifesta formido est. Et ad certamen animus ante præstruitur, quando se adversa- rius confitetur. Plus metuendus & cavendus est inimi- cus, cum latenter obrepit, cum per pacis imaginem fal- lens occultis accessibus serpit. Unde & nomen ser- pentis accepit. Ea est ejus semper astutia, ea est cir- cumveniendi hominis cæca & latebrosa fallacia. Quæ graphice videntur indolem Grotianarum Com- mentationum adumbrare. Nam & pacis ima- ginem ibi videas, sed fallacis & infidiosæ, & la- tentes, atque occultos accessus. Nihil enim mi- nus præ se ferunt Annotata, quam studium dis- seminandi Φορτικὰ ἀκόσματα: In textuum sacro- rum occupantur illustratione, cum nullo adversario contendunt: ut aliud agendo ingerant, atque insinuent sententias heterodoxas. Quæ ratio tota ad fallendum composita est. Etiamsi vero à paucis solum Annotata ista tererentur, illorum tamen habenda etiam est ratio. Si uni aut alteri tantum scandalo sint, aut damno, annon æquum est, id, quantum licet, amoliri? Tum vero gloriam divini nominis, aut verbi cælestis veritatem num tanti haud æstimabimus, ut tueri eandem adversus quascunq; molitiones à nostro munere alienum judicemus? Chas veschalom! Quanto ergo insigniori apparatu impugnatur verbum Dei, tanto accuratiori opera id adferendum est. Et quum ne unicam in Scriptura literam fusq; deque habere fas sit, quin credere oporteat, non magnos modo, quod Rabbini ajunt, doctrinarum montes ab unoquoq; pendere apice, sed cælo etiam terraq; potentiorem esse apicem quemlibet, imo cælum & terram oportere prius interire, quam vel unum jota aut apex unus de Scriptura pereat, teste ipsa veritate: Ecquis tam infrunitæ mentis erit, ut quæ oraculis palmaribus vindicandis locatur opera, eam ullo modo supervacaneam judicare velit? Mihi certe ita visum semper fuit, nullum utiliorem laborem suscipi, quam eum Scripturæ puritas, atq; integritas propugnatur ac defenditur, loca classica, quæ vocantur, explicantur, atq; asseruntur, obscura demum & difficilia illustrantur. Quantumcunq; operæ locemus in Positiva & Didactica, quantum in Polemica & Elenctica Theologia, redeundum deniq; nobis ad fontes, & ad ipsa principia est, cum Philistini hostes, aut falsi fratres obstruere nobis fontes, & principia dubia reddere conantur: neq; acquiescere conscientia cæteris potest, nisi unico atque solo indubitato fidei principio, ac stabilimento, Verbo Dei solidetur, constituatur, ac firmetur. Ad classica ergo Scripturæ dicta, quibus structura universæ Theologiæ ceu basi solidissima inititur, revocandi sacrarum literarum cultores, in dextra informatione: nec illa nude recitanda, quod à tertiæ classis pueris in Schola fieri, cum voluptate percepimus; Sed ex fontibus Ebraicæ, Græcæque veritatis eruenda, adversus κυβείας contradicentium propugnanda, & à στρεβλότητι quorumvis liberanda, ac prout par est, defendenda sunt. Quæ causa mihi fuit, ut Juventutem fidei nostræ creditam Dissertationibus hisce Biblicis, iisq; publicis, ad Codicem ipsum authenticũ deducere, ac eadem simul opera insignes Viri magni corruptelas justa censura notare constituerim. Propositum quidem erat, solum velut per saturam loca designare, quæ ab hoc Critico depravata sunt: Sed quia nec corruptelæ poterant in aperta luce collocari, ut ab omnibus viderentur aut agnoscerentur; nec dubia aut argumenta adversaria expediri, aut genuini dictorum Scripturæ sensus adferi, hasce etiam paulo prolixiores operas, moderatas tamen & grata rerum magnarum brevitate temperatas occupandas, ex usu publico duxi, adeoque occupavi. Quæ omnia vestro nunc judicio, PATRONI OPTIMI, expono, quibus cura & inspectio Ecclesiarum ac Scholarum in his provinciis demandata est. Cepi, ut sine dubio in recenti hæret memoria, telam istam, vobis consciis & consultis, addo & suffragantibus. Neque ambigo, utilius per Disputationes publicas eandem pertextam, quam si forte, quod in proclivi erat, Studiosis ad calamum talia, aut similia longo temporis tractu dictarentur. Ita enim non absolvi modo ista citius, ac facilius, sed legi etiam à pluribus atque expendi accuratius, tum examinari quoque, ac dilucidari per publicam sententiarum collationem, deniq; ad exteros etiam propagari, &

ad usus Ecclesiae totius traduci posse, credebam. Vestra ergo authoritate vel terminalia hic sunto: vel, si ita videbitur, progrediendum erit deinceps mihi, & expeditis breviter reliquis Historicis, in his enim non ita multa reperiuntur, quae Elenchum postulent, ad Poëticos, quos vocant, & Propheticos libros accedendum: in quibus omnino videre hic licet, quantum potuerit unius hominis, vel Diaboli potius ipsius (hic enim omnis mendacii pater est) versutia! Ut magnum adeo videri queat operae pre- tium, si oracula insignia, detersis Rabbinicis, atque haereticis glossis, pristino restituantur nitori. Nul- lum enim fere Propheticum vaticinium ad literam de Christo agens relinquitur; ita torquentur & per- vertuntur in alienum sensum omnia: Neq; sarta te- cta remanent oracula, quibus fides nostra in pleris- que articulis innititur: horum enim magnam par- tem Veteres Scripturas expertes credidit Noster. Errorum autem atque haeresium etiam fundamenta passim jacta sunt, aut paratae destinae: imo videas hic sentinam quandam, in quam exonerarit se & ἀποχὴ Remonstrantica, & impietas Sociniana, & abomi- natio Papistica, & incredulitas denique ac perfidia ipsa Judaica.

Suscipite autem simul, PATRONI MAGNI, no- vum grati animi documentum; quod etsi nec illu- stribus honoribus vestris, nec dignitati meritorum respondeat, ab argumento tamen divino splendo- rem, ac penes Vos pretium quoq;, confido, habitu- rum est. Quanto enim, TIBI quidem, PRAESES IL- LUSTRIS, in pretio sint Davidici Consiliarii, divina testimonia, quanta cura ac solicitudine depositum unice verae, ac salvificae doctrinae, cujus custodia fi- dei tuae divinitus credita est, abs TE colatur, ac pro- pagetur, quanto deniq; amore propugnatores ejus- dem fideles foveantur, verbis testari opus non ha- beo, quum adsint ipsa rerum testimonia. Non pos- sum tamen, quin iterum iterumq; inclutae Saxoniae de tanto Ecclesiarum & Scholarum, summique sena- tus sacri praeside gratuler, ac depositi tanti longaevam possessionem quotidianis precibus exposcam. Tibi vero, THEOLOGORUM DECUS, WELLERI INCOM- PARABILIS, propria & perpetua haec laus est scruti- nium accuratius sacrorum fontium, quod apparatus illae multivariae eruditionis tanto reddit salubrius, quanto exquisitius in Antiquis oraculis Jesum Chri- stum σκόπον σκοπιμώτατον, nucleum, medullam, ac thesaurum Scripturae indagas. Et doleret profecto non immerito Ecclesia, ab hisce praeclarissimis stu- diis, summis suis deliciis, multum abstractum illum, abs quo, prae innumeris aliis uberrimum sibi polli- cebatur fructum; nisi gaudere potius deberet, Ma- joribus reservatum ingens Orthodoxorum Praesi- dium, & ad ipsum regiminis Ecclesiastici clavum, luculentiori emolumento, subvectum, postquam, felici omnino omine, lumen istud iterum in hoc Sa- xoniae superioris hemisphaerio exortum, per tria propemodum lustra jam non his terris tantum, sed toti orbi Lutherano fulsisse visum est.

Utrique ut fulgeatis, & diutissime, & maximo Ec- clesiae universae bono, nec nisi sero admodum subli- miori firmamento inseramini, quo aeterno splendo- re, stellarum instar primae magnitudinis, coruscetis, Deum Opt. Max. precari non desisto. A Vobis au- tem, ut mihi, ac meis porro, imprimis Genero meo D. DEUTSCHMANNO, ut & filio unico cognomi- ni, radiis favoris benefici affulgeatis, submisse con- tendo.

Witebergae, pridie Domin. Jubi- late A. C. MDCLIX.

Illustris, & Eminentissimi Nominis Vestri Cultor perpetuus Abraham Calovius, D.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius's Preface to the Annotations on the Old Testament. To the Reader
GROTIUS'S PREFACE TO THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE OLD TESTAMENT. TO THE READER.

My intention at the beginning had been to make public only those things which I had noted down for my own use in the margins of the books of the Old Testament. But while I was re-reading the text, the desire to help those who come after me carried me further, so that whatever seemed to have some obscurity, I might bring to it as much light as I could. I have annotated, however, what I thought should be annotated, according to the Latin version, long since accepted, which I have always valued highly, not only because it contains no unhealthy dogmas, but also because it has much erudition in itself, although in a rather rough style of speaking, for the explanation of which I have sometimes used more polished words: sometimes also I have endeavored to render the sense clearer from the Hebrew books, whether such as we now have them by the work of the Masoretes, or such as the LXX once had. Interpreters, having also taken the help of the same and other Greek interpreters, and not rarely of the Chaldeans, having also inspected the versions of a more recent age, the chief of which are the Tigurine and the Tremellian. Of the ancients who wrote commentaries, I found Jerome most useful, on account of his knowledge of the Hebrew language and of places and histories. And yet in some things Chrysostom saw more than he did, by the help of the Jews whom he knew at Antioch. There are also the not-to-be-despised labors of our age by Vatablus, Francis Junius, and those whom Johannes Stephanus Menochius read, and having contracted them for us, with his own excellent thoughts added, placed before our eyes. From these I have followed now this one, now that one, and sometimes those things which seemed right to me, with reasons added. In the Law, I have added the sense and the causes of the precepts and the customs pertaining to them, taken mostly from the ancient Jewish Masters. In the Prophets, I have put forth much effort so that I might refer individual passages to the histories corresponding to them: in which matter, it will be for the fair reader to judge what I have accomplished. In this part, I have referred some passages, which the ancients referred to Christ and the times of the Gospel, to histories closer to the age of the Prophets, but which nevertheless have the figure of Christ and the Evangelical times wrapped within them. I have done this because, unless it were done, I saw that the series of words and things among the Prophets, which is otherwise most beautiful, would cohere poorly. And such passages indeed reveal to us Christians the counsel of God, who shadowed forth the Messiah to us, and the benefits to be exhibited through him, not only through words but also through things. But for convincing the Jews, even a few passages, directly describing Christ and the time when he was to come, are sufficient. To the moral or civil maxims of the Hebrews, I have added similar ones from the most excellent Greek and Latin writers. I have also brought from external histories whatever pertains to the confirmation or explanation of Sacred history. But if any shall feel nausea at things known to them, or at the same things repeated too often, I pray them not to be angry with me, if I have endeavored to help the progress of as many as possible, but to lessen their labors. If anyone truly wishes to read these things of ours usefully, it is necessary that he procure for himself what we have written on the truth of the Christian Religion with annotations, likewise on the Law of War and Peace with annotations, and what we have annotated on the Gospels: for we often refer the reader to those things. On the Calends of March, in the year 1644.

I. OBSERVATIONS OF MR. ABRAHAM

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTIANA AD ANNOTATA VET. TEST. LECTORI.

COnsilium initio fuerat, ea tantum, quæ ad oram librorum veteris instrumen- ti meos ad usus notaveram, facere publici juris. Sed dum contextum relego, studium juvandi posteros provexit me longius, ut quæcunque obscu- ritatis aliquid habere viderentur, iis quantum possem lucis adferrem. Annotavi autem quæ annotanda duxi ad Latinam versionem, pridem re- ceptam, quam semper feci plurimi, non modo quod nulla dogmata insalu- bria contineat, verum etiam quod multum in se habeat eruditionis, quan- quam in dicendi genere satis horrido, ad cujus explicationem verbis interdum usus sum nitidio- ribus: interdum etiam sensum studui reddere clariorem ex Hebraicis libris, sive quales nunc ha- bemus opera Masoreticonum, sive quales olim habuere LXX. Interpretes, assumpto etiam auxi- lio eorundem & aliorum Græcorum interpretum, non raro & Chaldæorum, inspectis & recen- tioris ævi versionibus, quarum præcipuæ sunt Tigurina ac Tremelliana. Veterum qui Commen- tarios scripsere utilissimum reperi Hieronymum, ob linguæ Hebreæ locorumque ac historiarum notitiam. Et tamen in quibusdam plus ipso vidit Chrysostomus, Judæorum ope, quos Antiochiæ noberat. Sunt & nostræ ætatis non spernendi labores Vatabli, Francisci Junii, atque eorum, quos multos legit, contractosque nobis, additis & suis præclaris cogitatis, ob oculos posuit Jo- hannes Stephan. Menochius. Ex his nunc hunc, nunc illum secutus sum aliquando, aliquando ea, quæ mihi videbantur, additis rationibus. In Lege sensum & causas præceptorum & mores eo perti- nentes, ab antiquis Judæorum Magistris maxime sumpta, addidi. In Prophetis plurimum posui operæ, ut singulas ad respondentes ipsis historias referrem: in quo quid præstiterim, æqui lectoris erit æstimatio. In hac parte locos nonnullos, quos veteres ad Christum & Evangelii tem- pora retulere, retuli ad historias ævo Prophetarum propiores, sed quæ tamen involutam habent Christi & Evangelicorum temporum figuram. Feci autem hoc, quod, ni id fieret, viderem male co- hærere verborum rerumque apud Prophetas seriem, quæ cæteroqui pulcherrima est. Et talia quidem loca nobis Christianis Dei consilium patefaciunt, qui non per verba tantum, sed & per res nobis Messiam, & beneficia per ipsum exhibenda, adumbraverit. Judæis autem convincen- dis vel pauca, Christum & tempus quo is venturus erat directe describentia, sufficiunt. Sen- tentiis Hebræorum moralibus aut civilibus similes addidi ex præstantissimis Scriptoribus Græcis & Latinis. Attuli etiam ex historiis externis quicquid ad Sacræ historiæ confirmationem aut explicationem pertinet. Si qui autem ad sibi nota, aut eadem repetita sæpius nauseabunt, eos oro ne mihi succenseant, si quamplurimorum profectus adjuvare, labores autem minuere stu- dui. Si quis vero hæc nostra utiliter legere volet, is necesse est sibi comparet, quæ de veritate Religionis Christianæ scripsimus, cum annotatis, item de jure Belli ac Pacis cum anno- tatis, & quæ ad Evangelia annotavimus: sæpe enim lectorem ad ista rejicimus. Calendis Martiis anni cIɔ Iɔc XLIV.

I. OBSERV. D. ABRAHA

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
PREFACE

§. I. HUGO GROTIUS, a youth of monstrous genius, once called by Jacobus Gillotus, councilor to the King of the Gauls in the Parisian Senate, as Johannes Meursius, in his 'Athenae Batavae' under the entry for Scaliger, testifies, was an old man of monstrous religion. Daniel Heinsius, an unwitting prophet, predicted in an epigram in Meursius's 'Athenae Batavae' under the entry for Grotius that his mother, Batavia, would rightly shudder and not believe that she had given birth to him. Enrolled in the Order of Advocates at The Hague very early, namely when he was in his seventeenth year, he demonstrated how much he achieved in the defense of cases, not only in the Treasury in his advocacy before the States of Holland, or in the Syndicship of the city of Rotterdam, or in bringing forward the Dutch right of Indian commerce before the King of Britain, or in the causes of the Swedish kingdom before the King of the Gauls. Having slipped away from the forum, the Republic, and the business of the kingdom to the causes of the Church, and having suddenly become a theologian from a jurist and politician, by his own will alone, what? A conciliator and arbiter of religious controversies, which could not be decided for a century and more, also an interpreter of the entire Scripture, and a discussor of any doubts whatsoever in the same, even those infinite and insoluble, he believed that he could easily defend any religion whatsoever with his patronage, and maintain whatever doctrines he chose: having followed the parties of diverse men, truly a multiform monster, as Epiphanius said of a heretic of similar bran.

§. 2. He was born and educated in the Calvinist religion; whose Catechism he once defended against Arminius himself; as Andreas Rivetus testifies in the 'Dissolutio' of the Grotian discussion, page 595. When, however, the Remonstrants departed from the rest of the disciples of Calvin in a different direction, in some chapters, he devoted himself to their parties, which at the beginning were certainly not a little better, and therefore he also undertook the defense of the 'Pietas' of the States of Holland against Sibrandus Lubertus. Although he was vehemently hostile to the Reformed and their doctrine, especially after he was consigned to perpetual imprisonment as a disturber of the State of Religion and Politics, and was liberated from there by a wondrous stratagem, he was nevertheless moved to the embassy of the Swedish kingdom and agitated for plans to unite the Reformed with the Lutherans for the sake, as it appears, of the English; indeed, he testified to the English syncretist John Dury that he had always vowed this concord, which one must marvel at. I have ALWAYS wished, he writes from Paris to the same on September 11, in the year 1637, in Rivetus's 'Apologeticus pro vera pace Ecclesiae' p. 304, and I shall never cease to wish, that those who made a secession from the Roman Pontiff for most grave causes, may coalesce among themselves more closely in spirit and by conspicuous testimonies of their spirits. But what the plan of Grotius was, is manifest from other letters written to the same Dury, on November 21 of the same year from Paris. It seems to both the English Ambassador and to me, that a meeting should be instituted of all those who are Protestants everywhere; these times do not bear that even that common peace of human society stands among them. It would therefore be best that, just as the kingdoms of Sweden and Britain are joined together in friendship, and perhaps shortly will be joined by a treaty; so also the Churches of those kingdoms should issue a public profession of their concord, and first give an example to the Danes and Norwegians, neighbors of Sweden, and then to others, which they may imitate. Once such a body of Churches is constituted, there is hope that others will subsequently aggregate themselves. Grotius was therefore entirely devoted then to the syncretism of the Protestants against the Papists: he showed that he was urging them to a CONSPIRACY to come together into one body: and he vehemently and at length in the same letters disapproved of the effort of someone who encrusts all the Reformed as subject to the Roman Pontiff, and [encrusts] almost all superstitions and dogmas in which the most grave causes of secession from him are contained.

§. III. But two years had scarcely passed, when Grotius departed entirely from his former self, and began to pursue very different, nay, entirely contrary designs, and undertook that negotiation which he had previously defined as being not far removed from collusion. Therefore, so that the Roman Pope might no longer be believed to be the Anti-Christ, which he saw was the greatest obstacle to his negotiation, he wished to persuade the world, by a commentary on the more illustrious prophecies concerning this matter, of something that had not hitherto entered the mind of anyone, not even in a dream to the worst parasites of the Roman whore: that those passages refer partly to Caligula and Simon Magus, partly to Bar Kokhba and Domitian, and partly to Apollonius and Trajan, to whom he himself, by a wondrous and portentous invention, twisted them. Then indeed, having progressed further, he attempted to excuse, gloss over, or defend most of the Papal abominations, and, as ambassador of the Swedish crown, the most valiant defender of the Augsburg Confession, he took upon himself the advocacy of the Roman Curia, having published an Appendix on the Anti-Christ, in which Papal superstitions and dogmas are in large part defended or adorned with new colors. He seems, however, to have believed it safer for the person he was sustaining if he were to take on the role of moderator above all else; wherefore, since he thought that through the felicity of his genius he could do all things, even those which had hitherto been impossible, he meditated on a reconciliation of the Papal religion with the Augsburg Confession, and labored to couple the Arctic pole with the Antarctic, in his Annotations on the consultation of Cassander concerning the articles of the Augsburg Confession, and other works published to that end. He was not unaware that Cassander the Belgian had labored in vain in such a work; that Vicelius the German had done so in vain, both having been employed by Emperors in a certainly better time; and that the most learned Archbishop Spalatin had rolled this stone with no result but an unhappy outcome; yet he himself, a Jurisconsult by profession and an ambassador of a Lutheran Kingdom by function, instructed by no calling to that end and having no authority to act, thought he must labor at it, promising himself from a grateful posterity the reward which he despaired of in our own age. That the great man was wasting his effort, Andreas Rivetus, a septuagenarian theologian of the Reformed party, clearly demonstrated in his learned Animadversions on the Grotian annotations, and in other writings by which he defended the same against Grotius a second and third time, namely in his Examination and his Apologetic. gus; but he achieved nothing else by so many writings than that he finally made the superstitions of the Papacy entirely his own, having long been tossed by the heat of the fawning parties, and when previously an inept moderator, in the midst of Ecclesiastical peace, he had placed the Bull of Pius IV, Roman Pontiff, concerning the form of the oath of the profession of faith, in the first place, he would finally offer the Jesuits, in his most recent writing, the discussion of the Apologetic, an argument for composing the Grotian Testament, by which they might persuade the world that the author had not only inclined toward the side of the Papists, but would have openly crossed over, had not God, while he was thinking of such things, removed him from the midst after he had been brought to those provinces from which the Roman Religion is exiled. That this omen is not vain, or sprung from the futile boasting of Papists, the letters which he sent to Dionysius Petavius the Jesuit, along with many others, openly testify. They close the procession in the second edition of the letters to the French, which, because they are brief and entirely relevant here, I shall append in full. TO THE REVEREND DIONYSIUS PETAVIUS, distinguished Theologian. Reverend Lord, I AM OFTEN COMPELLED to be troublesome to you, & TO TAKE REFUGE IN THE HELP HITHERTO HAPPILY KNOWN TO ME. Against my last booklet written for peace, Rivetus has opposed an Examination, which I send, but it is mutilated in the last pages, which I handed over to Mr. Milleterius, because they pertain to him. I have taken this last effort to defend my previously stated words, and also my reputation, which has been barked at by MINISTERS. In that writing (he speaks of the Examination of Rivetus) if there is anything either DISCORDANT WITH CATHOLIC SENTIMENTS, or otherwise alien to the TRUTH, or less suitable for Peace, I am very eager to BE WARNED about it by you, a most learned man, and whose judgment I value highly. I ask that you permit me to light A LIGHT FROM LIGHT. Paris, 16 Aug. 1642. It is not obscure that Grotius at that time fostered implicit faith: for whatever is congruent or discordant with Catholic sentiments in the writings of Rivetus, he found it necessary to learn finally from a Jesuit, and for that reason TO TAKE REFUGE in his help, so that a light of the Catholic faith might be lit for him from the Jesuit light: nor is it ambiguous with whom he conspired in his latest age: namely with the Jesuits, with Milleterius who was condemned by the Sorbonne itself, and those like them; or whose heifer he plowed with in refuting the writings of Rivetus: for he was compelled to be troublesome to Petavius the Jesuit, and to take refuge in his help, and to ask him to allow a light to be lit from light: whose help he also does not hide that he used in his earlier writings, as in this one, which he was then deciding was his last, even if it was not the last, when he praises the help, happily known to him before, whence we are easily persuaded, even if perhaps those writings did not appear under the Grotian name, as they are accustomed to be issued under the names of apostates and scoundrels by Jesuit work, that nevertheless a great deal of the Roman-Catholic Theological erudition, which those Grotian works display, is to be credited to Petavius and similar Papistic lights. So that you would hardly find Grotius in Grotius, or certainly distinguish him from the Jesuit. What kind of peace that is, which Grotius sought with the Protestants in his final age, is manifest from the fact that he hung the same, and whatever should be considered suitable for it, upon the judgment of the Jesuits, from whom Protestants can no more promise themselves peace than sheep from wolves or a hyena. Yet that this Pacifier and Advocate received little thanks from that party, whose cause he uniquely pleaded, was shown by the example of P. Franc. Maria de Monaco of the Theatine Clerics Regular in his book on the unity of the Faith; and by Henricus Dormalius of Liège, who praises him, in his Explanation of the Poems of Maffeo Barberini: the former of whom, according to the judgment of the latter, approved by the Vicar and the Master of the Palace, dissected and refuted the writings of Grotius while he was still alive and serving as ambassador to the King of the French.

§. IV. Nor indeed did he hope that only the desperate cause of the Papacy could be made better by his advocacy, but since his talent was so ample that it could be constrained by no boundaries of religion, he did not hesitate to excuse publicly, nay to varnish, the impious dogmas of the ill-fated Socinus (against whom he had once defended the Catholic faith concerning the satisfaction of Christ, and whose heresy he had called such that at its mention all the pious would shudder, and whose furies, along with those of the Servetians and Samosatenes, he had openly detested), which were diametrically opposed to the Catholic faith, and thus heresies and furies. Thus, therefore, he deemed neither the Papistic Tyranny nor the unbridled license of the Socinians, both of which he had once accused, unworthy of his patronage. But to defend the faith of the universal Church concerning the satisfaction of Christ against the adversary whom he had encountered, who was sufficiently sharp, Joh. Crellius, was a matter of religious scruple for him, or at least he judged it unworthy of his person. How he excused Servetus from the difficulty of the dogma concerning the Trinity, because it pertains nothing to the amendment of morals; how he extenuated his heresy, because he only did not well distinguish the divine persons, his Annotations on Cassander and the Votum of Grotius have shown. When Samuel Maresius, in a dissertation against Grotius concerning the Roman Anti-Christ, had said that Grotius, even if he seems to agree with the Socinians in most things, would perhaps concede that the Photinians and Socinians are Anti-Christs, denying the eternal divinity of Christ, he replied only these things, which follow, in the Appendix; that I do not agree with Socinus in ALL things, I think it is sufficiently evident. If he drew that doctrine, which is most necessary for piety, either from the Scriptures or from antiquity, or in whatever way he fell into it, that doctrine has not become any worse for that reason. I have expressed what I think about the necessity of works no less than of faith, not in the words of Socinus, but in the words of the Apostles and of those who imitated the Apostles as closely as possible. Nor do I fear any contradictor in this matter; the cause of GOD is much more at stake in this than in those things which many often treat ἀυθαδῶς boldly and dangerously, ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύοντες. He said that the defenders of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity ἀυθαδῶς, ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύοντες, are occupied in those things in which the cause of GOD is not so much at stake as when Socinus's doctrine concerning faith and good works is defended, and that the Socinians numbered Grotius among their chief supporters and friends, I know, not only Rivetus testifies, but a copy of the letters also, at Königsberg in Prussia, in the year, if I remember correctly, 1640, when I was still engaged in the Theological Profession there, was shown to me by Andr. Canowsky, a Polish nobleman, the most serene Elector of Brandenburg's Minister, in which Grotius gave thanks to Johannes Crellius, just as Paracelsus did to the Devil, according to Riolanus, because he opened his eyes. I could hardly give credence then to the copy and to the Socinian man who presented it, but when the man's latest writings appeared, they seemed easily to win belief for them. For in these, Hugo so gratified the Socinians that, especially in perverting the testimonies of Scripture and insinuating the dogmas of that impious sect, he seems to be considered as by no means the least of its advocates. Which one may especially perceive in his Annotations on the Old and New Testament.

§. V. That he himself is not far from Arius and Socinus concerning the divinity of Christ, Samuel Maresius judged from his Annotations on the Gospels, which appeared in the year 1641. And that this judgment ought not to be considered vain, the unfolding of the same will teach. For although he does not deny the προϋπαρξιν before the temporal birth, he seems, however, to depart further from the Catholics regarding the ὁμοουσίαν of the Son of God than from Arius and Socinus, in so far as the latter agrees with the former. I will bring forward only one thing from the confession of Thomas on John XX, 18, to which he noted these things: Here for the first time is that word found in the Evangelical narrative attributed to JESUS by the Apostles, after, to wit, he had proved by his resurrection that he was the one from whom life, and indeed eternal life, ought to be expected. See above XI, 25. That custom then remained in the Church, as it appears, not only in the Apostolic writings, as Rom. IX, 5, and those of the ancient Christians, as is to be seen in Justin Martyr against Trypho, but also in the Epistle of Pliny to Trajan, where he says that the Christians sang songs to Christ as to GOD. Grotius denies in these places that the name of GOD is attributed to Christ anywhere in the Evangelical books, outside of this passage. Thus, therefore, he believed that the name of GOD was not assigned to the Word, the Son of GOD, in the prologue of John either. Furthermore, he thinks that Christ is called GOD merely according to a certain custom prevailing in the Church, and that he is called GOD in no other sense than that which Pliny conceived regarding the songs of the Christians; so far is he from admitting that the name of GOD implies a divine nature and essence, and that Christ is GOD by nature (τῇ φύσει). For if he is GOD by nature, he was certainly not called so merely by custom, but the name of GOD belongs to him most truly and most properly, equally as to GOD the Father, with whom he is of one essence. He therefore imitates the Socinians, who say that Christ is GOD because he confers eternal life, not because he is true GOD by nature. Now if the Annotations on the Old Testament are joined, as well as the Posthumous works on the remaining books of the New Testament, far more and clearer testimonies of the Grotian approximation in this article to the borders of Socinianism will be had.

§. VI. But how can the article concerning the satisfaction of Christ be sincerely believed, if his eternal Deity is not believed without doubt? Therefore, when he had to speak about that in his most recent writing, his discussion at least, he says, Christ is our righteousness, just as he is our sanctification, that is, the cause in us of both righteousness and holiness. Which no Socinian denies. And although he says that the doctrine that Christ satisfied for the sins of men is true and catholic, but strangely depraved by Calvin and those following him, so that their error is in this matter more dangerous than the error of Socinus, he does not, however, explain who and how great this error of Socinus is. Crellius, the refuter of Grotius, also protests in his preface that he believes that Christ satisfied the divine will for our sins, and so, in the judgment of Grotius, however much he may still be implicated in some error here, he does not, however, depart from the Catholic faith. Nor does Grotius explain either the satisfaction or the merit of Christ by any other reasoning than that which could be pleasing to the Socinians. Christ satisfied for us generally, because by his passion he acquired a right for those who are about to convert themselves through Christ. In like manner, Christ merited a right to glory for those who are about to live holily. Which the school of Socinus admits willingly, even if the things which he adds, 'for those who are about to convert themselves,' that is, for those who are about to satisfy God for their crimes; and, 'the saints themselves merit that right to glory,' seem to be added for the sake of the Syncretism of the Socinians with the Papists; which, however, will be able to be approved by no one, either of the Socinians, who reject all satisfactions and merits, or of the Papists, who utterly abhor the Socinians (to whom even the Grotian dogma, that that satisfaction is made to GOD through baptism and prayers, is entirely new and unheard of).

will be able to be approved. And for whose sake, if not for the sake of Socinus and his followers, does he deny that the satisfaction and righteousness of Christ are imputed, and assert that that faith, which is so highly preached, is this, by which we believe that Christ suffered, died, and was raised from the dead, and THEREFORE that those things which he brought to us in the name of God, whether by commanding or by promising, are true? Do not these things smell of the lamp of Socinus; that it was imputed to Abraham for righteousness, that is, it was held as a magnificent deed, not because he believed that the Messiah was about to endure death for his sins, which whether he knew, I will not dispute here, but because he trusted in God calling and commanding? More things of this kind, which demonstrate that the Spirit of Socinus was very familiar to Grotius, we produced already a decade ago from the notes on the golden Epistle to the Romans, in the preface to the Apostolic Roman Theology.

§. VII. But it is necessary to wonder how the spirit of Arminius and the Pope dwelt together in one Grotius without discord. Since neither does the Pope bear the heresy of Socinus or Arminius, but strikes it with anathema, and Socinus, as also Arminius, admit anyone rather than the Pope and the Papists into their communion? Although Grotius allowed himself to be ruled by the spirit not only of sects which have been whitewashed with the Christian name, but also of the Jews, the enemies of the Christian name, when almost everywhere in the testimonies of faith and the Prophetic oracles, the glosses of the Rabbis prevail and triumph in his Annotations with Socinus, so that Rivetus not without reason judged that the Jews and Socinians owe most to his interpretations.

§. VIII. But it is altogether difficult to pronounce of what religion Hugo finally was in his latest age? That he was a man of no party, but wished to erect a new one from different sects, I judged in the preface to the Roman Theology, and I cannot yet judge otherwise; if indeed he did not cast off Arminianism, and the Socinianism into which it degenerated, but contracted Papism from his conversation with the Jesuits, whose counsels he confesses he used, just as he was ensnared by the reading of the Rabbis and their opinions and glosses, and finally exhibited a Socinian-Judaizing Papist, that is, a new monster hitherto unknown to the world, perhaps brought into Europe by the right of the Indian trade. He seemed so to Maresius in the year 1640. To have the name of Evangelicals, the Pelagianism of the Remonstrants, the Photinianism of the Socinians, the Anti-Christianism of the Papists, (I add, the Judaism of the new Rabbis, which subsequently revealed itself) as a new sphinx, fashioned out of all these, he is seen to fashion a different kind of Panther mixed with a camel. This was without doubt the reason that he asserted in a public writing that it was not necessary to communicate with others through Creeds, and for a long time did not communicate with others, because, to wit, he could nowhere find others who were ὁμοψήφες with him in religion.

§. IX. I shall explain what his end was, in the words written to me by Mr. Dr. Johann Quistorp, Senior of the Theological Faculty of Rostock, on the 18th of October in the year 1645: Hugo Grotius, sick, was brought to us from Sweden, after he had suffered shipwreck on the borders of Cassubia. He had me called to him. I approached, and found him almost in his death throes. I advised him to prepare himself for a blessed departure. He confessed that he was a sinner, and declared that all his hope was placed in Christ alone, and thus he said his final farewell to the world. It is to be wished that, having acknowledged his most grave errors and seriously deplored the scandals given to the Church, [he had] by faith apprehended the sole merit of the God-man, (which, from such a general profession of this kind, under which it is certain that an Arminian, a Papist, a Socinian, or any Arian can hide, is truly not clear) lest he who suffered shipwreck of his honors in Sweden, and of his goods and life in Cassubia, should have had the necessity of suffering the shipwreck of his salvation in the shadow of death. To Rivetus it certainly seems (Dial. p. 596.) breathing out threatenings & lying wholly in ferment; nay, that he had departed to the majority in the gall of bitterness, with no sign of repentance exhibited, as far as is known, much less of satisfaction, which he himself judged necessary, after calumnies and detractions, malice and hatred toward his neighbors: and that it happened by the just judgment of God, that he who mocked the voices of the Ministers of Christ promising to sinners lying in their extremities, if they would seriously repent and were contrite for the sins committed, that God was ready to remit and forgive them, could not hear him who had approached to suggest the Evangelical message to him. He adds, however, that he does not judge another man's servant, who has stood or fallen to his own Lord. We also commit the judgment to the Lord: although that warning of the Apostle in Rom. XIV concerns not those who are strangers to the true faith, but brothers in the faith of one mind, serving the same Lord.

§. X.
