It is indeed greatly to be lamented that he applied that apparatus of all-embracing erudition, which the illustrious man brought to the Annotations on the Old and New Testament, in the principal places of faith and the clearest prophecies, not so much to the asserting of the Christian and Catholic faith, as to the encrusting of the manifold corruptions of the Rabbis and heretics. For although in many things the unusual learning of the man served the Church excellently, for explaining the emphasis of words, for eliciting the sense of the text, for illustrating history, and for discussing various doubts, yet in those things which are of greater moment and concern the faith, nay, the very foundation of faith and religion, the man wished to gratify the enemies of the faith—in the judgment of St. Peter, unlearned and unstable—so that, having called into use the instruments and racks of manifold literature, he distorted and depraved the most holy Scriptures in a miserable manner, as if agitated by a Jewish and heretical spirit. Specimens of which matter, neither few nor obscure, we have produced elsewhere from the annotations on the principal Epistle of the Apostle, which was written to the Romans. It would be for the use of the Church that all the depraved passages from the Grotian Annotations, which are worn by the incautious hands of many, should either be marked only by a syllable, or be restored to the true sense by elenctic annotations. That this might be accomplished by others equipped with greater apparatus, and not by such distracted labors, I have wished more than once. I see even now that the veteran Reformed Theologian, whom I have praised several times, has sought similar things. Dialys. pag. 504. That audacity, he says, others perhaps will refute, by which Grotius deformed the Prophetic books in their principal oracles concerning Christ, as if he had been hired for that purpose by the enemies of the Christian name. And a little later again: Someone will arise, if he has not already arisen, and girded for that holy war, who will call to examination all those corruptions by which that man perverted the Holy Scripture in many ways, and will repel that poison with necessary antidotes. But there has arisen, as far as I know, no one yet, either from the Reformed or from our own Theologians, who has taken this upon himself: therefore, lest there be lacking at least to those who delight in the pleasures of Philology, or even to those who are occupied with the Exegetical works of the Holy Scriptures, an opportunity for investigating these such things more abundantly, I have decided to submit most of the things in which the Grotian private interpretation has been observed by me, as much as other duties and other things which are under my hands allow, to the disputations of the Auditors and to the collation of Sentences, for the good of our Academy and of the Church, especially regarding the places of faith, in which he tried to aid the adversaries with his inventions, or to enervate the interpretation of the Church and the orthodox, or to render it merely suspected and uncertain; and also regarding the prophetic oracles, which he attempted to deprive of their principal core, the Messiah, and his spiritual and heavenly goods, or to make doubtful by introducing a double sense. May the Father of lights be present for this purpose, and may He reveal to us through His Spirit the genuine sense of His most holy word, which He willed to be the testimony of Jesus, but to us the sole foundation of faith, a sense in every way consistent with His own mind, which none of the princes of this world have known, so that we may know first of all what things God has graciously given to us, and may bring them forth not in speech which human wisdom, but which the most holy Spirit of Christ has taught, explaining those things which the Spirit of Christ foretold in the Prophets, through those things which Christ Himself opened to us by His Spirit, to the glory of His Name and our salvation!

Latin:

PRÆFATIONEM

§. I. HUGO GROTIUS, portentosi ingenii juvenis, quondam Jacobo Gilloto Regis Galliarum in Senatu Parisiensi consiliario dictus, Johanne Meursio, Athenis Batavis in Scaligero, teste, portentose religionis Senex fuit. Quem jure matrem Bataviam horrere, & haud credere, se sibi peperisse, vates inscius prædixit Daniel Heinsius Epigrammate apud Meursium Athenis Batavis in Grotio. Ordini Advocatorum perquam mature Hagæ Comitis adscriptus, cum nempe ætatis annum decimum & septimum ageret, quantum in causarum patrocinio profecerit non in Fisco solum advocatione penes Ordines Hollandiæ, aut in Syndicatu civitatis Roterodamensis, aut in adferendo Batavorum jure Indicani commercii apud Regem Britanniæ, aut in regni Svedici causis apud Regem Galliarum demonstravit. A foro, Republica, Regni negotiis ad Ecclesiæ dilapsus causas, subitoque è Jcto ac Politico Theologus, sola voluntate, factus, quid? Controversiarum Religionis, quæ per seculum & ultra decidi non potuere, Conciliator & arbiter, Scripturæ quoque universæ interpres, & dubiorum quorumvis in eadem etiam ἀπείρων, καὶ ἀλύτων discussor, Patrocinio suo facile sequamcunque religionem defendere posse credidit, & quæcunque elegerit placita, tueri: diversorum partes sequutus, vere πολύμορφον τεράστιον, ut Epiphanius de similis furfuris hæretico.

§. 2. In religione natus atque educatus fuit Calviniana; cujus Catechesin quondam contra ipsum Arminium defendit; Andrea Riveto teste, in discussionis Grotianæ διαλύσει pag, 595. Quum v. Remonstrantes à reliquis Calvini discipulis in diversum abirent, in nonnullis capitibus, eorum partibus, quæ initio sane haud paulo meliores erant, se addixit, ideoque Pietatem etiam Ordinum Hollandiæ adversus Sibrandum Lubertum defendendam suscepit. Quanquam vero Reformatis, & doctrinæ eorum vehementer infensus esset, imprimis, ex quo carceri perpetuo ceu Status Religionis & Politiæ perturbator mancipatus, miroque strategemate inde liberatus fuit, admotus tamen Regni Svedici legationi consilia de uniendis Reformatis cum Lutheranis in gratiam, uti apparet, Anglorum agitavit, imo hanc sese concordiam semper vovisse, quod mirari oportet, Anglorum Syncretistæ Johanni Duræo testatus est. Optavi SEMPER, scribit Lutetiæ ad eundem XI. Septembr. Anno cIɔ Iɔc XXXVII. apud Rivetum Apologetico pro vera pace Ecclesiæ p. 304. & optare nunquam desinam, ut, quæ à Pontifice Romano gravissimis de causis discessionem fecere, Ecclesiæ, inter se propius animis & animorum conspicuis testimoniis coalescant. Quale autem Grotii fuerit consilium, è literis ad eundem Duræum aliis, XXI. Nov. ejusdem anni Lutetiæ perscriptis, manifestum est. Utrique Angliæ Legato videtur, ut & mihi, ut conventus instituatur omnium, qui ubique sunt, Protestantium, non ferre hæc tempora, per quæ illis ne pax quidem illa communis humanæ societatis constat inter se. Optimum igitur fore, ut, sicut amicitia inter se junguntur, brevi etiam forte jungen- tur fœdere Suediæ Britanniæque Regna; ita & eorum regnorum Ecclesiæ suæ concordiæ edant professionem publicam, primumque vicinis Svediæ Danis & Norwe- gis, deinde & aliis dent exemplum, quod imitentur. Constituto semel tali Ecclesiarum corpore, spes est, sub- inde alios se aggregaturos. Totus ergo tum Syn- cretismo Protestantium adversus Pontificios dedi- tus fuit Grotius: quorum CONSPIRATIONEM illos urgere, ut in unum corpus coëant, ostendit: operamque non neminis, qui omnes Reformatos Pontifici Romano subjectos, & superstitiones pleras- que omnes ac dogmata, in quibus continentur gravis- simæ causæ discessionis ab eo incrustet, vehementer & prolixe iisdem literis improbavit.

§. III. Sed vix elapsum biennium, cum totus à se migravit Grotius, ac longe alia, imo prorsus contraria agitare consilia, eamque negotiationem cepit, quam non procul abesse à prævaricatione antea definiverat. Ne itaque deinceps Papa Ro- manus Anti-Christus credatur, quod negotia- tioni suæ maximè obstare videbat, commentatio- ne ad illustriora hac de re vaticinia Orbi persuasum voluit, quod nemini hactenus, ne pessimis qui- dem Romanæ Thaidos parasitis per somnium in mentem venit, loca illa, partim ad Caligulam & Simonem Magum, partim ad Barcochebam, & Domitianum, partim ad Apollonium & Traja- num spectare, ad quos ipse, miro & portentoso commento, ea detorsit. Tum vero progressus ul- terius, pleraque Papalia βδελύγματα excusare, in- crustare, aut defendere tentavit, curiæque Ro- manæ advocationem coronæ Svedicæ, Augustanæ Confessionis propugnatricis fortissimæ, legatus, in se suscepit, edita Appendice de Anti-Christo, qua superstitiones & dogmata Papalia magnam partem propugnantur, aut novis ornantur colo- ribus. Tutius tamen suæ personæ, quam sustine- bat, credidisse videtur, si ante omnia moderato- ris partes susciperet, quapropter quum omnia se posse per ingenii felicitatem, etiam, quæ hacte- nus impossibilia fuere, putaret, conciliationem religionis Pontificiæ cum Augustana Confessione meditatus, polum Arcticum cum Antarctico copu- lare laboravit, Annotatis ad consultationem Cas- sandri de articulis Augustanæ Confessionis, aliisque eam in rem editis. Non ignorabat, frustra in ejusmodi opera Cassandrum Belgam fuisse; frustra Vicelium Germanum, utrumque ab Imperatori- bus, meliore sane tempore, adhibitum; nec nisi infelici exitu eruditissimum Spalatinum Archi- Episcopum hoc saxum volvisse; in eo tamen ipse, professione Juris-Consultus, functione Regni Luthe- rani legatus, nulla ad id vocatione, nulla agendi facultate instructus, laborandum duxit, pretium, quod de nostro desperabat ævo, à grata posterita- te sibi pollicitus. Operam Virum Magnum lude- re, Animadversionibus eruditis ad annotata Grotia- na, aliisque scriptis, quibus easdem adversus Gro- tium secundo & tertio defendit, Examine nempe, & Apologetico, luculenter demonstravit Andreas Ri- vetus, septuagenarius Reformatæ partis Theolo- gus; sed nihil aliud tot scriptis profecit, quam ut a- perte denique superstitiones Papatus universas, diu partium abblandientium æstu jactatus, suas faceret, ac quum antea ineptus moderator, inter media pa- cis Ecclesiasticæ, Bullam Pii IV. Rom. Pontificis, su- per forma juramenti professionis fidei, primo loco constituerit, scripto novissimo Apologetici discussio- ne Jesuitis tandem argumentum præberet, Grotia- num Testamentum concinnandi, quo auctorem non tantum ad partes Pontificiorum inclinasse, sed aper- te tansiturum fuisse, orbi persuaderent, nisi Deus eum talia cogitantem delatum ad eas provincias, è quibus Romana Religio exulat, è medio sustulisset. Quod au- gurium ne vanum, aut à futili Papistarum jactantia profectum credamus, cum aliis multis, literæ, quas ad Dionysium Petavium Jesuitam dedit, palam te- stantur. Agmen illæ claudunt in secunda Epistola- rum ad Gallos editione, quas, quia breves sunt, & totæ huc faciunt, adscribam integras. V. R. DIO- NYSIO PETAVIO, insigni Theologo. Reverende Do- mine, SÆPE tibi molestus esse COGOR, & ad OPEM ANTEHAC FELICITER MIHI COGNITAM REFUGERE. Postremo libello meo pro pace scripto opposuit Rivetus Examen, quod mitto, sed postremis paginis mutilum, quas tradidi D. Milleterio, quia ad eum pertinent. Sumsi hanc ultimam operam, mea an- tehac dicta, & famam quoque à MINISTRIS alla- tratam tuendi. In eo scripto (de Examine Riveti lo- quitur) si quid est, aut CATHOLICIS SENTEN- TIIS DISCONGRUENS, aut cæteroqui à VERI- TATE alienum, aut minus idoneum ad Pacem, de eo abs te viro eruditissimo, & cujus judicium plurimi facio, MONERI percupio. Rogo permittas mihi LUMEN DE LUMINE accendere. Lutet. XVI. Aug. cIɔ Iɔc- XLII. Haud obscurum est, Grotium fidem impli- citam tum fovisse: quicquid enim Catholicis sen- tentiis congruum aut discongruens sit in Riveti scri- ptis, à Jesuita demum cognoscere, eoque nomine ad opem ipsius REFUGERE necessum habuit, ut sibi lumen fidei Catholicæ de lumine Jesuitico ac- cenderetur: neque id ambiguum est, cum quibus conspiravit novissima ætate: cum Jesuitis nempe, cum Milleterio ab ipsa Sorbona damnato, horum- que similibus; aut quorum vitula araverit in refu- tandis Riveti scriptis: coactus enim fuit molestus esse Petavio Jesuitæ, & ad opem ejus refugere, eum- que rogare, ut lumen de lumine accendi patere- tur: cujus etiam opera in prioribus scriptis, uti in hoc, quod ultimum tum decernebat, etsi ultimum non fuerit, sese usum haud dissimulat, cum opem, fe- liciter sibi antehac cognitam, deprædicat, unde facile persuademur, etsi forte scripta illa non ita sub Gro- tiano nomine prodierint, uti sub apostatarum, fæ- perudium, nominibus Jesuiticæ operæ emitti so- lent, magnam tamen eruditionis Theologicæ Ro- mano-Catholicæ, quam præ se ferunt Grotiana ista, Petavio, & similibus luminibus Papisticis, accepto ferendam esse. Ut Grotium vix in Grotio reperi- as, aut certo à Jesuita dignoscas. Qualis etiam illa pax, quam cum Protestantibus postrema ætate sua ambiit Grotius, censenda sit, ex eo manifestum est, quod eandem, & quicquid ad illam idoneum ha- beri debeat, à judicio Jesuitarum, ceu paxillo su- spenderit, à quibus Protestantes non magis pacem sibi, quam oves à lupis, vel ab Hyæna, promittere possunt. Exiguam tamen gratiam reportasse hunc Pacificatorem & Advocatum penes illam partem, cujus causam unice egit, exemplo suo P. Franc. Ma- ria de Monaco Congreg. Cler. Reg. Theatinorum li- bro de unitate Fidei; &, qui illum laudat, Henricus Dormalius Leodius Explicat. in Poëmata Maphæi Barbarini docuere: quorum ille, juxta hujus ini- κρισιν, à vices gerente, & Magistro Palatii approba- tam, scripta Grotii, dum adhuc vivebat, & apud Regem Galliarum legatione fungebatur, veritatis stylo diduxit & induxit.

§. IV. Nec vero Papatus solum causam despe- ratam meliorem advocatione sua fieri posse spera- vit, sed quum ingenium ipsi tam amplum fuerit, quod nullis religionis terminis coarctari posset, infausti etiam Socini, (adversus quem fidem Catho- licam de satisfactione Christi quondam defenderat, cujusque hæresin talem dixerat, ad cujus mentionem pii omnes exhorrerent, cujus furores, cum Servetianis & Samosatenis, palam detestatus erat,) impia dogmata, fidei Catholicæ è diametro adversa, adeoque hæreses, & furores publice excusare, imo incrustare haud dubitaret. Ita ergo neque Tyran- nidem Papisticam, neque effrenem licentiam Socini- starum, quam utramque olim accusarat, patroci- nio suo indignam censuit. Fidem autem Ecclesiæ universæ de satisfactione Christi contra adversa- rium, quem nactus erat satis acrem, Joh. Crellium tueri religio ipsi fuit, aut certe sua id indignum ju- dicavit persona. Quomodo Servetum excusarit à difficultate dogmatis de Trinitate, quod ad emen- dationem morum nihil pertineat; quomodo hæresin ejus extenuarit, quod divinas personas solum non bene distinxerit, Annotata in Cassandrum, & Vo- tum Grotii docuere. Cum Samuel Maresius dis- sertatione de Anti-Christo Romano Grotio op- posita dixisset, Grotium, etsi in plurimis videa- tur cum Socinianis sentire, forte concessurum, Pho- tinianos & Socinianos Anti-Christos esse, æternam Christi divinitatem negantes, hæc solum, quæ se- quuntur, reposuit in Appendice; Socino me non in OMNIBUS consentire, satis patere existimo. Si idem eam doctrinam, quæ ad pietatem vel maxime necessa- ria est, vel ex Scripturis vel ex antiquitate hausit, vel quocunque modo in eam incidit, nihil ea doctrina ob id deterior facta est. Ego quid de operum non minus, quam Fidei necessitate sentiam, non Socini verbis, sed Apostolorum, & eorum, qui Apostolos quam proxime imitati sunt, verbis expressi. Nec in hac re quempiam contradictorem reformido, DEI causa multo magis in hoc agitur, quam in illis, quæ multi ἀυθαδῶς audacter & periculose sæpe tractant, ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύοντες. Defensores mysterii de Sacrosancta Trinitate ἀυθαδῶς dixit, ἃ μὴ ἑώ- ρακεν ἐμβατεύοντες, in iis occupatos, in quibus non ita DEI causa agatur, quam cum Socini do- ctrina de fide & bonis operibus propugnatur, So- cinianos vero Grotium inter præcipuos fautores & amicos numerasse, se scire, non Rivetus solum testatur, sed apographum etiam literarum, Re- giomonti Borussorum, Anno, si recte recordor, CIɔ IɔC XL. cum adhuc in Professione Theologica ibi agerem, mihi monstravit Andr. Canowsky, nobilis Polonus, Serenissimi Electoris Brandenburg. Minister, quibus Johanni Crellio Grotius, non secus, atque Paracelsus, apud Riolanum, Diabolo, gratias egit, quod oculos sibi aperuerit. Fidem tum apographo, & qui id exhibebat, homini So- ciniano adhibere vix poteram, sed cum postrema viri scripta prodirent, facile illis fidem conciliare videbantur. In his enim ita gratificatus est Hugo Socinianis, ut imprimis in pervertendis Scriptu- ræ testimoniis, insinuandisque sectæ impiæ dog- matibus pro advocato ejusdem minime postremo habendus videatur. Quod in Annotatis ad Ve- tus & Novum Testamentum maxime deprehendere licet.

§. V. De divinitate Christi non procul abesse ipsium Ario & Socino, Samuel Maresius ex Anno- tatis ad Evangelia, quæ Anno cIɔ Iɔc XLI. prodie- re, judicavit. Neque vanum hoc judicium censeri debere, evolutio eorundem docebit. Quamvis enim προϋπαρξιν ante temporalem nativitatem non neget, qua ὁμοουσίαν tamen Filii Dei longius à Catholicis, quam ab Ario & Socino, in quantum hic illi conspirat, abire videtur. Unum tantum addu- cam è confessione Thomæ Job. XX, 18. ad quam ista notavit: Hic primum ea vox in narratione Ev- angelica reperitur ab Apostolis JESU tributa, post- quam scil. sua resurrectione probaverat, se esse, à quo vita, & quidem æterna exspectari deberet. Vide supra XI, 25. mansit deinde ille mos in Ecclesia, ut ap- paret, non tantum in scriptis Apostolicis, ut Rom. IX, 5. & veterum Christianorum, ut videre est apud Ju- stinum Martyrem contra Tryphonem, sed & in Plinii ad Trajanum Epistola, ubi ait Christianos Christo, ut DEO, carmina cecinisse. Negat hisce Grotius, us- piam in libris Evangelicis Christo nomen DEI tri- bui, extra hunc locum. Sic ergo nec in procœ- mio Johannis nomen DEI λόγῳ Filio DEI assigna- tum fuisse, credidit. Porro Christum DEum vo- cari, pro more quodam saltim habet, in Ecclesia ob- tento, nec alio sensu, quam quem Plinius de carmi- nibus Christianorum concipiebat, DEUM appel- lari censet, tantum abest, ut nomen DEI naturam & essentiam divinam inferre, ac Christum τῇ φύσει natura DEUM esse, admittat. Nam si natura DE- US est, utique non ex more tantum ita vocatus est, sed nomen DEI verissime ei convenit, & pro- priissime, æque ut DEO Patri, quocum unius est essentiæ. Socinianos ergo imitatur, qui Chri- stum DEUM dicunt, quod vitam æternam confe- rat, non quod natura verus DEUS sit. Jam si Annotata ad Vetus Testamentum jungantur, nec non Posthuma ad reliquos Novi Testamenti libros, longe plura & luculentiora habebuntur testimo- nia approximationis Grotianæ in hoc articulo ad confinia Socinianismi.

§. VI. Quomodo vero articulus de satisfa- ctione Christi sincere credi potest, si æterna ejus Deitas non creditur indubitato? Ideo cum de illa dicere debuit, in novissimo scripto, discussione sua saltem, Christus, inquit, est justitia nostra, quomodo idem est nostra sanctificatio, id est, causa in nobis tum justitiæ, tum sanctitatis. Quod nemo Socinianus negat. Et quamvis, satisfecisse Christum pro homi- num peccatis, doctrina, inquiat, est vera & catholi- ca, sed mire à Calvino & eum sequentibus depravata, ita ut error eorum errore Socini hac in re sit periculo- sior, non tamen quis & quantus hic sit error Socini explicat. Satisfecisse Christum divinæ voluntati pro peccatis nostris, se credere protestatur etiam Crellius confutator Grotii, in præfatione, itaque judicio Grotii, utut errore aliquo hîc adhuc impli- cetur, non abit tamen à fide Catholica. Nec alia ra- tione vel satisfactionem vel meritum Christi ex- plicat Grotius, quam quæ Socinianis grata esse possit. Satisfecit pro nobis Christus generatim, quia passione sua jus acquisivit, se per Christum conversu- ris. Pari modo meritus est Christus jus ad gloriam sancte victuris. Quæ ultro admittit Socini schola, etsi ea, quæ addit, se conversuris, id est, Deo satis- facturis pro criminibus suis; Et, sancti ipsi merentur id jus ad gloriam, Syncretismi Socinianorum cum Papistis gratia addita videantur; qui vero nemini vel Socinistarum, satisfactiones & merita omnia reprobantium, vel Pontificiorum à Socinianis prorsus abhorrentium, (quibus etiam Grotianum dogma, per baptismum & preces illam satisfactionem DEO fieri, novum prorsus atque inauditum est,)

probari poterit. Et in quorum, nisi Socini, & se- quacium gratiam, negat satisfactionem & justiti- am Christi imputari, asseritque fidem illam, quæ tan- topere prædicatur, hanc esse, qua credimus Christum passum, mortuum, & excitatum à mortuis, ac PROPTEREA veræ esse, quæ is Dei nomine sive præ- cipiendo, sive promittendo nobis attulit. Annon hæc Socini lucernam olent; credere Abrahamo im- putatum est ad justitiam, id est, pro magnifico facto id habitum est, non quod Messiam credidit pro peccatis ipsius mortem toleraturum, quod an noverit, hic non disputabo, sed quod Deo vocanti & jubenti confisus est? Plura ejusmodi, quæ Socini Spiritum Grotio perquam familiarem fuisse, demonstrent, ex no- tis in auream ad Romanos Epistolam, Theologia A- postolica Romana in præfatione, jam ante decenni- um, produximus.

§. VII. Mirari autem necesse est, quomodo Ar- minii, & Papæ spiritus uno in Grotio simul habita- rit, sine discordia. Quum neque Papa Socini, aut Arminii hæresin ferat, sed anathemate feriat, & Socinus, ut & Arminius quosvis potius, quam Papam & Papistas in communionem suam admit- tant? Quanquam non sectarum tantum, quæ Chri- stiano dealbatæ sunt nomine, sed Judæorum quo- que Christiani nominis hostium, spiritu regi sese passus fuerit Grotius, quum undiquaque ferme in fidei testimoniis & oraculis Propheticis, cum Socino, Rabbinorum glossæ in Annotatis ejus obtineant, ac triumphent, ut plurimum interpretationibus illius debere Judæos & Socinianos, non abs re judicarit Rivetus.

§. VIII. Difficile autem omnino pronuncia- re, cujus denique Religionis Hugo fuerit ætate novissima? Nullarum partium hominem fuisse, sed è diversis sectis novam erigere voluisse, præfatione in Theologiam Romanam censui, neque adhuc aliter censere possum; siquidem Arminianismum, &, in quem illo degeneravit, Socinianismum non exue- rit, Papismum autem è conversatione cum Jesuitis, quorum consiliis se usum fatetur, contraxerit, uti è lectione Rabbinorum opinionibus & glossis eorum inescatus fuit, Sociniano - Judaizantem Papistam denique exhibuerit, hoc est, novum monstrum orbi hactenus incognitum, jure Indicorum com- merciorum forte in Europam traductum. Ma- resio visus est Anno cIɔ Iɔc XL. Evangelicorum no- men habere, Remonstrantium Pelagianismum, Pho- tinianismum Socinianorum, Anti-Christianismum Papistarum, (addo, Judaismum novorum Rabbi- norum, qui deinceps sese prodidit) ut sphyngem novam, ex his omnibus confectam fingere conspiciatur diversum Panthera genus confusa camelo. Quæ cau- sa sine dubio fuit, quod cum aliis communicare per Symbola necessum haud esse, scripto publico asseru- erit, diuque cum aliis haud communicarit, quia scil. alios sibi in religione ὁμοψήφες nuspiam re- perire potuit.

§. IX. Quis ei fuerit exitus, verbis Dn. D. Jo- hann. Quistorpii Facultatis Theologicæ Rostoch. Senio- ris p. m. XIIX. Octobris Anno cIɔ Iɔc XLV. ad me perscriptis, exponam: Hugo Grotius æger ad nos ex Suecia, postquam in Cassubiæ finibus naufragium pas- sus esset, delatus est. Me ad se vocari curavit. Accessi, in agone ferme constitutum offendi. Ut ad beatam emigrationem se componeret, monui. Peccatorem se confitebatur, & in solo Christo omnem suam spem repo- sitam esse adferebat, atque ita supremum vale mundo dicebat. Optandum, ut agnitis gravissimis erroribus ac serio deploratis scandalis, Ecclesiæ datis, vera fide unicum θεανθρώπω meritum apprehenderit, (quod ex generali ejusmodi profeffione, sub qua Arminianum, Papistam, Socinianum, Arianum quemque latere posse certum est, profecto non liquet) ne qui naufragium honorum in Suedia, bonorum & vitæ in Cassubia passus, salutis nau- fragium in mortis umbra pati necessum habue- rit. Riveto fane videtur (Dial. p. 596.) ἐμπνεῶν ἀπειλῆς & totus in fermento jacens; imo in felle ama- ritudinis ad plures abiisse, nullo, quod constet, pœni- tentiæ signo exhibito, multo minus satisfactionis, quam necessariam judicavit ipse, post calumnias & obtre- ctationes, livorem & odium in proximos: justo que Dei judicio accidisse, ut qui irridebat voces Ministro- rum Christi peccatoribus in extremis jacentibus pro- mittentibus, si serio resipiscerent & contriti essent ob peccata commissa, DEum paratum esse eis remitte- re & condonare, non potuerit audire eum, qui ac- cesserat, ut Evangelicum nuncium ei suggereret. Ad- dit vero, se tamen non judicare alienum servum, qui Domino suo stetit & cecidit. Nos judicium Domi- no quoque committimus: etsi monitum illud Apo- stoli Rom. XIV. non à vera fide alienos, sed fra- tres in fide ὁμοψήφες, eidem Domino servientes, concernat.

§. X. Id vero fummopere dolendum est, quod apparatu illud eruditionis omnigenæ, quem ad Annotata in Vetus & Novum Testamentum vir illustris attulit, in locis fidei præcipuis, ac vaticiniis clarissimis, non tam ad fidem Christianam & Ca- tholicam adserendam, quam ad corruptelas Rabbi- norum & hæreticorum multivarias incrustandas ad- hibuerit. Quum enim in multis præclare, ad ver- borum emphasin explicandam, ad sensum textus eruendum, ad historiam illustrandam, dubiaque varia discutienda, Ecclesiæ inservierit inusitata Vi- ri doctrina, in iis tamen, quæ potioris sunt κόμ- ματ&, & fidem concernunt, imo fundamentum ipsum fidei & religionis, gratificari fidei hostibus ita voluit homo, judicio S. Petri ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀσή- ρικτ&, ut in usum vocatis multivariæ literaturæ fidiculis, atque equuleis Scripturas sanctissimas miserum in modum, veluti Judaico atque hæreti- co spiritu agitatus, detorserit ac depravarit. Cujus rei specimina nec pauca nec obscura, ex annotatis in præcipuam Apostoli, quæ ad Romanos exarata est, Epistolam, alias produximus. Ex usu autem Ecclesiæ fuerit, ut loca universa depravata, ex An- notatis Grotianis, quæ multorum teruntur incau- tis manibus, vel per fyllabum designentur tantum, vel annotatis elencticis vero restituantur sensui. Quod ab aliis majori apparatu instructis, nec tan- tis districtis laboribus expediri, non semel optavi. Video etiam nunc, Veteranum Theologum Re- formatum, quem aliquoties laudavi, similia expe- tiisse. Dialys. pag. 504. Audaciam illam, inquit, alii fortasse redarguent, qua Grotius Propheticos li- bros in præcipuis eorum de Christo oraculis ita defor- mavit, quasi ab hostibus Christiani nominis ad id fu- isset conductus. Et paulo post iterum: Exorietur ali- quis, si jam non ortus fuerit, & ad sacrum illud bel- lem accinctus, qui corruptelas omnes illas, quibus S. Scripturam multis modis pervertit vir ille, ad exa- men revocabit, & necessariis antidotis venenum istud propellet. Exortus autem, quantum mihi quidem constat, nullus adhuc est, qui hoc sive è Reforma- tis, sive nostris Theologis in se susceperit: ideo ne deesfet saltem Philologiæ delitiis sese oblectantibus, aut illis etiam, qui Exegeticis S. literarum operis va- cant, hæc talia uberius indagandi occasio, plera- que, in quibus ἴδια ἐπίλυσις Grotiana mihi obser- vata, quantum per officia cætera, & alia, quæ sub manibus sunt, disputationibus Auditorum, ac Sententiarum collationi, Academiæ Nostræ, atque Ecclesiæ Bono, subjicere placet, imprimis quoad fidei loca, in quibus juvare adversarios commentis suis, aut Ecclesiæ & orthodoxorum interpretationem enervare, vel suspectam solum atque incertam reddere; nec non quoad vaticinia etiam prophetica, quæ Nucleo suo præcipuo, Messia, bonisque ejusdem spiritualibus & cælestibus privare, aut gemino inducto sensu dubia facere conatus est. Adsit proposito Pater luminum, ac verbi sui sanctissimi, quod μαρτύριον JEsu, nobis autem ϑεμέλιον fidei unicum esse voluit, sensum genuinum, menti suæ per omnia consentaneum, quemque nemo principum hujus mundi cognovit, revelet nobis per Spiritum suum, ut sciamus imprimis, quæ DEus gratificatus est nobis, & adferamus ea non sermone, quem humana sapientia, sed quem sanctissimus Christi docuit Spiritus, exponentes ea, quæ Spiritus Christi in Prophetis prædixit, per ea, quæ Christus ipse Spiritu suo nobis aperuit, ad Nominis sui gloriam nostramque salutem!

## 1:1 Introduction: Preparatory Dissertation on the Grotian Preface
PREPARATORY DISSERTATION ON THE GROTIAN PREFACE.

§. I.

Grotius forewarned the reader concerning the Latin version, the Hebrew text, certain other versions and commentaries, and also concerning this work of his annotations on the Law and the Prophets. He added his notes to the Latin version long since received, because he always valued it highly, not only because it contains no unhealthy dogmas, but also because it has much erudition in itself. We shall not now reproach the Vulgate with what Erasmus has somewhere regarding its author, whom our man values highly, if anyone should inquire whether he was a Gaul or a Sarmatian, a Jew or a Christian, a man or a woman, that its patrons would have nothing to answer readily: not because the Jesuit conspicuous for his Cardinal's mitre, easily the foremost of all his order, Bellarmine, says the Vulgate edition is not of one author, but has some things from Jerome, some from Lucian, some from some other unnamed interpreter; but it seems foolish to say that Theodotion the heretic could not have erred and also that Jerome nowhere erred: book II de V. D. ch. XI. which certainly do little to adorn or commend the authority of the Vulgate version. Let the Old (we do not deny) deserve its praise; but which one is that long-received one, whether the edition of Sixtus V or indeed that of Clement VIII, Grotius has not defined. But those fight among themselves with an irreconcilable war. Which dispute of the preceding Pontiffs, because each fortified his own edition with a Bull (although Clement, having removed the Bull of Sixtus, substituted his own, and sold it under the name of Sixtus through the crime of forgery), those following will never be able to decide. Therefore, Papists will never have any version, those who are subject to the judgment of the Pope have none, with Grotius, which they can acknowledge as long-received; indeed, while they have discrepant authentic versions, in reality they have none: since more than one thing cannot be true. Nor indeed do they differ among themselves in few or trivial matters; indeed, the errors of the Sixtine edition were judged to be of such moment, that Gregory XIV, as witnessed by Jacobus Fuligattus in the life of Bellarmine, book I, chapter 9, by the counsel of Cardinal Bellarmine, decided that the Sixtine Bible should be thoroughly purged, that individual parts should be compared to ancient editions, to manuscript copies, and to the Commentaries of the Fathers, and that he entrusted this task to Bellarmine, M. Antonio Columna, and Alanus, Cardinals, and four others, by whose work, through the authority of Clement VIII, a new edition was produced, refashioning and conforming the Sixtine [edition] in more than two thousand places to the Hebrew and Greek sources. So that it is only deceitfully pretended in the preface prefixed to the Clementine [edition], whose author was Bellarmine, that only the faults of the press had crept into the edition of Sixtus, and that it had needed repeated diligence; even though the Pope's own Bull protests against this, inasmuch as he declares by his own hand that he had corrected any faults that had crept in from the presses (how much diligence Sixtus applied to this is taught by Angelus Rocha, prefect of the Vatican Library, an eyewitness in the Vatican Library, page 219.) and thus commands that all receive his edition as true, legitimate, authentic, and indubitable. But more on these matters elsewhere,

§. II. But whichever edition is chosen, it will not attain the praise of Grotius, whether you look at the dogmas, which in an authentic Scripture ought not only to have nothing unwholesome, but also nothing alien to the truth; or at that grace of erudition, for which this [version] ought especially to be preferred to other versions, and indeed even to the Hebrew text itself, which Grotius even places after it. That dogmas alien to the truth, and indeed unwholesome, along with countless and enormous faults not befitting the dignity of such great erudition, are in the Vulgate version has been demonstrated by very many theologians, both of our own and of the Reformed party. Which we have also pursued at length in the Critico Sacro from page 502 to 667. Of errors impinging upon faith and morals, and thus unwholesome, we produced nine classes there, and among them, fables and inventions thrust into the Vulgate under the name of divine truth to be believed, false opinions encrusted, divine constitutions undermined, passages of faith enervated, and heresies confirmed. We do not wish to do what has already been done.

§. III. Nor does Grotius detract little from this encomium of his, by which, without doubt, he sacrificed the same [version] for the sake of the authority assigned to it by the Council of Trent—that is, that it is authentic—when he acknowledges a style of speaking that is sufficiently harsh and a sense that is less clear, which is rendered clearer from the Hebrew books, such as we now have them, and other versions, and when he subsequently corrects the same in his annotations and prefers the Hebrew text. These things do not agree with the decree of the Council, which wills that the old and Vulgate version be held as authentic in public readings, disputations, preachings, or EXPOSITIONS, which no one should dare or presume to reject FOR ANY PRETEXT. It should have been said FOR ANY pretext; thus such great contentions about the meaning of the decree would not have arisen. Moreover, whether that [decree] is taken absolutely, as Menochius, primarily commended by Grotius, along with Pineda, Gregorio de Valentia, and Ludovico de Tena, accepted and the congregation of Cardinals in the year 1576 defined that it must be accepted; or only restrictedly and comparatively, so that this is recognized as authentic with respect to other versions and at least never deviating in the rules of faith and morals, which is the interpretation of Bellarmine, Mariana, Lindanus, and others, which Grotius also seems to intend when he affirms that that version alone contains no unwholesome dogmas, i.e., those impinging upon faith and morals—concerning which different explanation of the Decree, most bitter contentions and battles flourished in Spain, about which the Spanish Jesuit Mariana complains at length in his tract on the Vulgate,

edition, chapter I, and no decision could yet be made by the Pope, so that it is not yet established in the Papacy whether they have Bibles that are authentic in all respects, or rather only less corrupted than others? Such as they can be held to be, even if they are most corrupt in countless places. However, in whatever way they interpret that decree, the text of other versions and the Hebrew text, as it is now held, is constituted as the norm. To which the Grotian project does not at all conform. For how can that version be held as the norm for other versions, or be preferred to the Hebrew text, when it must be corrected now from the Hebrew text, now from other versions, and must needs borrow light from them? But because Grotius sometimes also corrects the Hebrew text from the Vulgate version, we add the judgment of Johannes Drusius on this matter: Not badly, he says, in my judgment, did the Fathers of the Council of Trent receive the Vulgate interpreter in the schools. For although it may have some errors, others have theirs too, and perhaps more than it. But to correct the Hebrew truth from it, if it is permitted to call a spade a spade, is to be insane with reason. For where there is truth, there is no error; where there is no error, what need is there for correction? Either, therefore, there is no Hebrew Truth (thus the Fathers and Scholastics call it) or it ought to be amended from that which was poorly translated. There are not a few sounder men among the Papists themselves who, even after the Council of Trent, prefer the Hebrew truth, and, so that they may be allowed to be safe from the thunderbolt of that [decree], they defend themselves with this shield (this is not the place to say how secure this makes them, or could make them): that the Vulgate is not compared with the Hebrew text, much less preferred to it, but is only compared with other Latin translations and judged better than them: which Alphonsus Salmero, one of the first ten theologians of the Society of Jesus and one of the assessors of the Council of Trent himself, in his prolegomena to the Holy Gospel, Nicolaus Serarius, Julius Rugerius on the canonical books, Philippus Grammacheus, Valerianus Flavignius, theologians of the Sorbonne, Johannes de Espieres, Simeon de Muis, and others have asserted. A decision from the shrine of the Papal breast is still awaited in this cause.

§. IV. Grotius distinguishes the Hebrew text, such as it is now held by the work of the Masoretes, and such as the LXX Interpreters once had; with the Papists, he accuses the modern text of corruption, which is to be seen here and there in his annotations. But that the original and authentic text of Scripture, which God willed to be the perpetual norm of the Church and the foundation of faith, is corrupted—with a universal corruption that has penetrated all codices—conflicts with divine providence, with the end and intention of God, and with the protestation of Christ in Matthew 5:18, that heaven and earth must sooner pass away than even one iota or the smallest apex of the Word of God perish. Then, if the Hebrew text was corrupted before the times of Jerome, how could an uncorrupted version have been transcribed from a corrupted text? If the corruption happened after the times of Jerome, which seems to be the case for most Papists, will Grotius say that it came about through the malice of the Jews, or indeed through the mere carelessness of the scribes? If he chooses the former, others from among the Papists will oppose him with the religion of the Jews toward the sacred books, their dispersion throughout the world, and the multitude of Christian codices, so that the Jews neither would have wanted to, nor could have, depraved the text, and he will have business with Johannes Isaac, Marcus Marinus, Francisco Ribera, Driedo, and Bellarmine himself. But I do not believe Grotius accuses the Jews of perfidy, to whom he himself attributes a great deal. If, however, the corruption happened through the carelessness of the scribes, how could the same have penetrated all the codices so that no uncorrupted copy survives? And since Grotius ascribes the text which we now have to the work of the Masoretes, how will he render that same text suspect of corruption? For it was the study of the Masoretes to vindicate it from every corruption, and to propagate it sincere and uncorrupted to posterity; hence the Masora is called סיג לתורה, the hedge of the law. If by chance he imagines with Gordon Huntley that the Masoretes were Jews of Tiberias of the fifth century after Christ was born (by which opinion Ludovicus Capellus is also carried away in his Criticus), that fabrication is refuted by the common opinion of the Hebrews, since, as Elias Levita testifies, they assert with unanimous suffrage that Ezra and other men of the Great Synagogue began the Masora. Concerning which, Johann Buxtorf the Elder can be read at length in his Tiberias. We have discussed the absurdities of Huntley in the Criticus Sacer, as also those of other Papists who accuse the Hebrew Codices of having suffered depravation after the age of Jerome, page 401 et seqq. Johann Buxtorf the Younger refuted Ludovicus Capellus in his Anti-Criticus. If, therefore, the text which we have proceeded from the Masoretes, that is, from Ezra, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, and other contemporaries, it ought to be for us entirely sacrosanct and above all exception. In which place also the Tikkum Sopherim (if by chance Grotius objects to them with Galatinus) are held by Cardinal Bellarmine, not as being a corruption (if they are not a fable), but a true emendation, not made by just any scribes, but by Ezra and other holy Prophets who repaired the sacred books after the return from captivity. Whence in the Masora parva on Numbers 12:12 they are expressly called תקון עצרים. Must it be said that Ezra and other holy men of God corrupted the text? Let our Criticus be seen regarding these matters on page 387, as also D. Glassius, Philolog. Sacr. lib. 1, p. 39, and Joh. Buxtorf in the same, in the addenda at the foot of lib. 1, p. 493, where, being asked, he explained his mind concerning the Tikkum Sopherim. Coccejus on Job 7:20 notes that no mutation of Scripture is indicated by them: but that it is a kind of interpretation, when the Ancients judged that Scripture speaks otherwise for the sake of euphemism than the instituted discourse demanded: nor do all Hebrews agree that this which the Ancients judge should be read, should be replaced in the text. Which he shows by an induction of passages, concluding that it appears from thence that the Hebrews call that תִקּוּן, a correction of the Scribes, which is now also written, or a deflection of the style from its order to that which is less atrocious: so that it is a kind of interpretation to indicate this correction. Sixtinus ab Amama indeed in his Anti-Barb. Bibl. laboriously argues on p. 470 that diverse readings are introduced through the Keri and Kethib, not because both are of divine authority, which Amand. Polanus rashly defended, but because the marginal reading or the Keri is solely from God, but that he was imprudently seduced by the author of the secret of the points, that is, by Capellus, whom others also applauded without having sufficiently examined the matter: just as he allowed himself to be seduced by Jews and Papists, whence he also pleads the cause of the Papists, not denying that corruptions have crept into the sources through the length of time, the multitude of exiles, and the duration and severity of various calamities, even if he adds that, because of one or two blemishes (which nevertheless ought not to have been placed in the sacred text), the palm cannot be taken away from the most beautiful virgin (the original text of Scripture), much less given to another which is deformed in its whole body (namely, the Vulgate version); indeed, he protests that he submits that opinion of his to the judgment of the Reformed Churches, and would by no means hesitate to retract it if anyone should show something more certain and true. Without doubt, however, Buxtorf and Coccejus have shown more certain and true things in these matters which pertain equally to the Holy Language and to Holy Scripture, and are to be preferred by far to that tyro of theology who has not arrived at just maturity and was almost only a pure grammarian. We have asserted the purity of the Hebrew source at length in the cited book from page 366 to page 438. There is no reason for us to do what has already been done. Against the newest machinations in the Papacy against the Hebrew truth, which were those of Johann Morin, Simeon de Muis, Royal Professor at Paris, pleaded the cause of the Hebrew Truth with a triple assertion, which the Doctors in the Theological Faculty of Paris, the Sorbonnists, Du Fresne de Minse, and A. de Breda approved, H. Bachelier, Sorbonnist Doctor of Theology, vehemently praised, and Valerius de Flavigni of the Faculty of Theology Paris, likewise a Sorbonnist Doctor, judged it so adorned that he pronounced that no one could henceforth doubt, even against the will of its detractors, the authentic truth of the sacrosanct Hebrew edition. Which judgments Claudius de Avergne, Royal Professor of Sacred and Hebrew letters at Paris, exhibited with the works of Muis in the year 1650.

§. V. Grotius seems to make the version of the LXX Interpreters purer than the Hebrew text, when he asserts that we do not now have the Hebrew books such as they had them of old, and he not rarely prefers the version of the Interpreters. I do not know whether he has lent his ears to Johann Morin, a Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, who extols the Greek of the Seventy exceedingly, and thinks that it can not improbably be equated to the Vulgate through the authority of Sixtus V, by which he provided by decree that it should be received by all, and that no one should change anything in it by adding or subtracting, Diatr. Elenctic. de autorit. Ebraici Græcique textus page 233. But whence will Grotius teach that such a Greek version is now held as was once translated from the Hebrew; or that the Hebrew text has been corrupted by him rather than that Greek translation? Although indeed Sixtus V greatly praised the edition of the LXX Interpreters procured by Cardinal Antonius Caraffa, Cardinal Baronius did not hesitate to proclaim it even as a divine work and divinely inspired in Appar. annalium number 119, with Johannes Morinus applauding in Exerc. IX. cap. 4. pag. 441; however, the Morinian arguments are of no moment, nor is he consistent with himself, nay, from the preface prefixed to that Roman edition, Nicolaus Serarius proved with more than ten arguments that that edition is not the very version of the LXX Interpreters, pure and uncorrupted everywhere, much less to be held as a divine work; concerning which our Sacred Critic can be read at length from page 830 to 840. Let the collection of vindications of Mr. D. Dorscheus in Exod. cap. 2. pag. 35 also be compared on this matter. Grotius's inference would have to be entirely inverted if an argument is to be sought here from the diversity of the reading. Because the Greek text not rarely reads otherwise than the Hebrew, the Greek text has undergone change, adorned by human industry, not the Hebrew codex, which we all acknowledge to be divinely inspired: Although that diversity can sometimes be said to have proceeded from the fact that they did not attain the sense, or did not sufficiently express the original text. Jerome already complained in his own age that the genuine and ancient translation of the LXX Elders had been corrupted and violated in his preface to Paralipomenon, nay, that it was too corrupted, in his Preface to the Pentateuch, and who does not know that it was often amended by Origen, and accused by Justin, who was older than them, of corruption having been committed by the Jews? We have here the most learned of the Papists confessing; Andreas Masius in his preface to the book of Joshua, confesses that he did not fail to make a mistake in any part of it. Bellarmine says that it survives so corrupted and violated that it seems to be something entirely different, so that it is no longer safe to correct Hebrew or Latin texts from Greek codices. Grotius ought to have consulted those rather than Morinus have crept into the Greek LXX version and still remain. What of the fact that to some of the Jews, as R. Gedalia notes, it seems that the LXX did not translate from the holy language, but from a Syriac exemplar into Greek? Johannes Buxtorf the Younger in his treatise on points, part 1, chapter 9, had proposed the opinion of R. Azariah, that that translation was made from a certain Chaldean version: but in his Vindication of the Hebrew Truth part II, chapter II, page 552, he adds: If that opinion seems less consistent with the truth, it could nevertheless be the case that the Seventy Interpreters sometimes consulted, and perhaps followed, such Chaldean interpretations as were then held among the Jews: but some other very learned recent critics, such as Ludovicus de Dieu on Matthew 19:5, John Selden in De mari clauso, page 37, and Johannes Henricus Hottinger in Thesaurus Philologicus, page 262, judge that the Greek version was adorned from a Samaritan codex: which is also the opinion of Guillaume Postel in Tabulae linguarum, Table II. Our Hugo is pleased with the contrary at Leviticus 17:14. Two versions, he says, are confused: one which had applied a convenient interpretation to those general words; another which followed the Hebrew κατὰ πόδας: whence followed a vain repetition, which also flowed from the Greek LXX into the Samaritan: For the Samaritan codices which we now have were made according to Greek exemplars, from the time when the Samaritans were forced by Justinian to accept Christianity. These

Grotius; by which the authority of the modern Samaritan codex, celebrated too much by Morinus and more than once preferred to the Hebrew reading even by Grotius himself, is not a little shaken, and the reliability of the Greek LXX version, which we now have, is rendered highly suspect. For if it is confused from two versions at times, it cannot undoubtedly make us certain about the true reading. What happened to any one place could have happened to any other. More probable, however, is Hottinger's opinion: that the version of the LXX Interpreters arose from Samaritan or other poorly corrected codices. Namely, that the Alexandrian Jews, by whose work that version was adorned, did not have the Hebrew codices which the Jerusalem Jews kept in a more corrected state and, because of rivalries and hatreds, did not share with the Alexandrians, but rather the more faulty Samaritan ones, or others. Let those things be compared which we have spoken of more fully concerning the version of the LXX Interpreters in the Critica Sacra. For there, if we are not mistaken, we have struck at the root of the Grotian hypotheses, which he seems to have cherished concerning the authority of the version of the Seventy, since he not rarely prefers it to the Hebrew text: and we have treated at length concerning its authors—whether it was procured by the authority of Philadelphus through Demetrius and adorned by the LXXII Elders, which the illustrious Scaliger denies, or whether an archetypal exemplar was used, or whether it was a translation approved by the Jews, in what estimation it was held by the Christian Church and the ancient Doctors, and above all, what is to be thought of the Apostolic citation? We have brought into the middle the places where the Apostles do not follow the LXX Interpreters, even though they agree with the Hebrew, as well as those where they do not differ from the Hebrew text, and also those where they followed the Hebrew text rather than the LXX Interpreters when they deflect from it, and various errors of the LXX Interpreters and discrepancies from the Vulgate version, demonstrated with a most vain examination and discussion of Morinus's reconciliation, who strives to compose even things that are contradictorily opposed: finally, a dissertation is subjoined concerning the existence and sincerity of the version of the LXX Interpreters. Which, having been completed thirty years ago, we leave to be weighed by Pseudo-Critics, so that they may cease to hawk that version as a different reading of the Hebrew text and to ascribe to it the authority of an ancient codex. If the Greeks had adorned their version entirely from the Hebrew text, if the LXXII Elders had been employed for the translation, as is believed—both of which are highly doubtful and uncertain—even if their genuine translation still survived, just as it came from their own hands, which those will not concede who judge it to be corrupted by the loss of the authentic exemplar in the fire of Pompey's army along with the library of Ptolemy, and by the fault of both Jews and heretics, but especially by the inexperience, rashness, audacity, oversight, and lack of judgment of the scribes, with the addition primarily of the variety of other Greek versions, and the confusion of Origen's Hexapla and the interpretations of Theodotion, Symmachus, and others (which Grotius does not deny): (for which you would expect no sufficient remedy from the work of Caraffa;) if no different readings were available in the LXX Interpreters' own translation, as there are indeed various ones surviving; yet it would still be doubtful whether the LXX used a pointed codex or not, which those who make the points a recent invention of the Jews—which Capellus contends entirely, with Grotius not denying it—cannot affirm; nor is it plausible to others; because it is too manifest everywhere that the authors of that translation added points according to their own judgment; it would also be doubtful whether the exemplar they used was sincere in all things and immune from all errors that easily creep in through the carelessness of copyists; it would also be doubtful whether those varieties that are found between the Hebrew text which we have and the translation often proceeded from the mind and judgment of the translators themselves rather than from a different reading of the codices of that time; indeed, various causes can be given here among the Interpreters themselves, some of which, since he did not do so without reason, Johannes has assigned along with other critics. Buxtorf the Son, in Vindication of Hebrew Truth, Part II, Chapter VIII, page 55, it is helpful to transcribe them here: Thirdly, therefore, he says, the (Critics) place the principal cause in the Interpreters themselves, who 1. deceived by the similarity of letters and elements, which is very easy in manuscripts, have interpreted certain things otherwise. 2. not correctly grasping certain things, they read them otherwise in their own mind, not in their codex: 3. not sufficiently skilled in grammar, which perhaps was not yet held to exist at that time, nor attending to its laws, they attributed the same meanings to related words and terms, and took things that are different for the same and signifying the same: 4. they attributed peculiar meanings to certain words, whence it happens that, since those are unknown today, they are thought to have read something else. 5. they resolved things that were said metaphorically into proper expressions, which they seemed to themselves to have. 6. in many things they often guessed, so that no judgment appears in them, and the reason they had for translating in this way is completely unknown. 7. they used such liberty, or rather license, that at their own discretion they sometimes added certain things to the Text in place of an exposition, and also at their own discretion subtracted and omitted certain things. 8. very often they rendered the sense, not the words and the letter. 9. they also committed many things out of ignorance, of which thing innumerable traces have been detected and noted in that version by learned men. This is what he says. Jerome certainly not rarely passed a similar judgment about them, where he observed now that they had translated badly, now that they had been deceived by the similarity of letters, now that they had looked more to the sense than to the words.

§. VI. We do not disapprove of the fact that Grotius made use of the versions of other Greeks and Chaldeans, and also of the more recent Tigurine and Tremellian versions. Provided that he had followed the ancient Chaldeans and the Christian versions of a more recent age, rather than the recent Jews, enemies of the Christian name. The Belgian himself gave no place to the Belgian translation, from which he could have been more correctly informed in most Prophetic oracles, had he not preferred to ἰουδαΐζειν.

§. VII. This, indeed, must not be neglected here at the outset, that Grotius, when he compares the versions of the LXX Interpreters, of other Greeks, of Chaldeans, of Arabs, or others, or even the Samaritan Pentateuch, does not hesitate to prefer a reading which is found in them sometimes to the Hebrew text, without the authority or suffrage of any Hebrew Codex, or to invent a new reading from his own ingenuity: whence it is gathered not obscurely that he was seduced by that recent Pseudo-Critic Ludovicus Capellus, Professor at Saumur, or at least otherwise cherished common hypotheses with him: For he praises Capellus's Critic vehemently in a letter given to him, which is in volume CLXXXI of the Letters to the French, together with the secret of punctuation: Just as, however, in that labor (he speaks of the Arcanum revelatum) you surpassed others who preceded you, so in sacred Criticism, you have surpassed even this labor of yours. In which I know not whether I ought to admire more the indefatigable diligence, or the most abundant erudition, or the most refined judgment; which three praises in this work contend among themselves in such a way that it remains in doubt to which of the three the first prize is owed. There are indeed some things, as you have rightly noted, εὐδιάβλητα, but it is given to no one to please everyone, least of all those who are wise above the common herd. Therefore, be content with great rather than many praisers. Nor, however, should one despair that what often happens in other things may happen in this one too, that the few who are eminent are followed by those who only count for their number. I profess that I owe much both to you and to those through whom your work reached my hands. And in these notes he appeals to Capellus's Critic, which Grotius had read in manuscript thirteen years before it was issued, at Gen. ch. V, v. 18. Concerning the many discrepancies which appear in this and the following Chapters regarding the numbers of years in the Hebrew, Samaritan, and Greek Codices, I have nothing better to say than what the most learned Capellus said in his Sacred Critic. J. Buxtorf set forth the sum of the hypotheses, which are not so well known here, from that Critic in these very words in the dedication of his Anti-Critic.

It is, of course, imagined that the ancient Mosaic letters were changed, and that those we have today are Assyrian, handed down to the Jews by Ezra only after the Babylonian captivity, the former genuine ones being left to the Samaritans: That the vowel points, which are ascribed to Hebrew codices today, are neither from the sacred Authors themselves, nor from other Prophetic Men, nor do they represent the true, first, and genuine Reading, but were devised only about 500 years after Christ by certain Tiberian Masoretes, and added and ascribed according to their own judgment and discretion: Hence the sacred Hebrew Codex is called, through contempt and mockery, Jewish and Masoretic from time to time: That the Hebrew Codices experienced the same fate as all other ancient authors, so that through the sloth, sleepiness, ignorance, or even the rashness and audacity of the correctors of the librarians or scribes, very many various Readings, that is, changes and errors, have crept into them: indeed, that there is no other condition of these books, nor could there be, than that of all other books in general: That Divine providence did not watch over the preservation of the sacred codices intact any more than for all other kinds of books and authors: and that it is sufficient that it did not allow them to be either abolished or so corrupted by any fraud, force, malice, or tricks of men that the sincere, pure, and uncorrupted doctrine of salvation could not be drawn from them: For there are many things in Scripture that are not momentous, in which it is all the same, however you read. That there is no certain Codex to which one can have recourse in the discrepancies of Interpreters and in places controversial regarding the true reading, nor is the Hebrew codex such a thing: indeed, that it is not even necessary that such an authentic Codex exist and be held: That parallel places of Scripture, discrepant or conflicting among themselves, argue for the change and corruption of one of them: That the Versions of ancient Interpreters discrepant from the Hebrew Codex very often and indeed in infinite places have arisen from the discrepancy and variety of the Hebrew codex which they used in translating, and therefore they are to be called various Readings, to be compared with the reading of our books, and very often even to be preferred: That as many Hebrew codices are to be said to exist from this as there are ancient Interpreters departing from the current reading: That the whole body of authentic Scriptures is diffused and mixed, both in the Hebrew fountains and in any streams of Translations whatsoever: That all Translations, together with the Original Text, are equally authentic, sacred, divine, θεοπνεύσας: That all Interpreters are to be compared to perceive the true reading, and from them finally it is to be elicited, divined, and collected: That discrepant Interpretations are not to be measured and compared to the current Hebrew Text, but in those discrepancies one must judge concerning the true reading from our own reason, and whatever reading this dictates to us, that is to be preferred, in whatever Codex it may finally be found: That it is not only permitted sometimes to make new conjectures about the true reading, but also useful, and so much so that it is sometimes necessary, on account of many ἄπορα, ἀδιάλ- λακτα, that is, insoluble and irreconcilable passages, which cannot be reconciled by any other method than by admitting a slight error, and correcting it by such a conjecture; nay, in certain places, one must even acknowledge an error of the Sacred Writers themselves, insofar as they were weak men: Nor should it be fixed and settled among us that all things, even the smallest words, expressions, and letters in the original text of Scripture, are from the internal ἐνθεσιασμῷ of the Holy Spirit. Thus far Buxtorf. Let us hear the Critic himself: It must be established, he says, and conceded (which cannot be denied) that the modern Jewish codex and the Samaritan codex and the rest of the codices, from which all the ancient translations were made, are just as many different codices of the sacred books, differing among themselves by various readings: Likewise: However, the true, good, and convenient reading is not to be sought in one codex only, for instance the modern Jewish one, but now in this one, now in that one, now in another; that is, in one place a more convenient reading will be found in the modern Jewish one, in another place it will be found in the Samaritan Codex, in another place in the translation of the LXX, in another place in the Chaldean Paraphrases, and so on regarding the other ancient interpreters; Nay, he contends that the modern Hebrew text is not to be preferred to the Samaritan or any other for any other reason, nor for any other cause, except insofar as it can be shown that the sense which arises from its reading is ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ better and more convenient than that which is born from the reading of other Codices. Therefore, wherever it can be demonstrated that the reading which is in the Samaritan Codex, or which the LXX interpreters followed, or the Chaldean Paraphrast, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, or Jerome, yields a more congruent sense, and one more coherent with the preceding, the following, and the whole analogy of Scripture, no one ought to be so unfair as not to embrace that one rather, and at the same time the reading which yields that sense from itself. All these things Capellus says. To whom it is not even so absurd, if someone should say that the Codex of the LXX and that of Jerome are two Hebrew sources; and should further pronounce that the whole body of (authentic) Scriptures is diffused and intermingled, both in the Hebrew sources and in whatever rivulets of translations there may be (for which hypothesis of the Critics, the most learned Buxtorf rightly requires a most subtle and rarely granted sacred chemical art, by which this fifth essence might be distilled and extracted through some most ingenious alembic) and should contend that there is not held today such a Codex to which one could return in the discrepancies of Interpreters and in places debated concerning the true reading, nor that such a modern Hebrew Codex exists, nor that it is necessary that such a Codex be held, which might be an infallible and immovable norm of translations; because in very many and indeed countless places, a manifold variation and alteration has slipped into the Hebrew codex, God permitting, from human and blameless infirmity, and from the carelessness and rashness of the Scribes; Whence with great effort Capellus collected a huge number of various, as he calls them, readings through ten distinct classes, from the collation of various books of the O.T. among themselves, from parallel places of the O. and N.T., from the Keri and Ketib of the Jews, from the various readings of the Orientals and Occidentals, likewise of Ben Asher and Ben Napthali, from the Samaritan Codex of the Pentateuch, from various editions of the Hebrew text collated among themselves, from the Greek translations of the LXX Interpreters, of Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus; from the Targumim, or Chaldean paraphrases, from the Latin Vulgate translation, from the fragments of the ancient Latins, from the Jewish writings of the Talmud, Rabboth, Masora, and the commentaries of the Rabbis, and even from new and personal conjectures, from all of which, having also collated the Syriac and Arabic translations and those of more recent Interpreters, if any Critic, having applied his own judgment, should seek out the true reading piece by piece, and as it were beg for it, or elicit it by a more liberal inquiry, as he himself calls it, there would then at last emerge a genuine codex, or one closest to the genuine, or certainly much nearer, in his own judgment, in countless places, than the Jewish and that modern Masoretic one is now, which he is accustomed to call by such contempt.

§. VIII. An egg is not so like an egg as the Grotian requests or principal doctrines, which reveal themselves here and there in his work of Annotations, are to most of these Capellian ones, so that one must believe he either plowed with his heifer, or through a perverse ambition emulated the same, or certainly, having applied his own judgment, and having also collated the Syriac and Arabic translations which he did not apply, or perhaps could not apply, he wished to institute a gleaning after the harvest. But those hypotheses are either already refuted by us elsewhere, or they collapse of their own accord by their own vanity. Why the Hebrew letters should be established as foreign, of the Assyrians or Phoenicians, as Grotius wishes in his annotations to book I of the truth of the Christian religion, §. XV, p. 18, or why the Samaritan ones should be held for the ancient Hebrew ones, although great names incline toward that, I do not see sufficient causes. I asserted in the Sacred Critic, p. 325, that they are the proper ones of the Hebrews, nor have I observed hitherto that it could be drawn into another mind: Buxtorf taught in his dissertation on the true Hebrew letters that this is the common and received opinion among the Hebrews. Although that hypothesis, indeed, concerning the changed Hebrew character, does little harm to the truth of the Hebrew source, provided that the authority of the Samaritan Pentateuch is not built upon it; the other one is more serious, concerning the Hebrew vowel points and accents by the Masoretes

(fictitious) Tiberians: which, however, we have already refuted in Capellus, Sacred Critic, p. 331 ff., with historical and chronological arguments, likewise with the testimonies of the Rabbis and the Talmud, and not least with the words

of Christ, Matt. 5:18, from the nature of the vowel points, the certainty of divine revelation, the perspicuity and perfection of Holy Scripture, which were vindicated there from the exceptions of Capellus and his contrary arguments were overthrown. Meanwhile, Mr. Buxtorf published a treatise on the origin and antiquity of the Hebrew vowel points and accents, in which he says he has shown that all Hebrews, both ancient and recent, stand and fight for the antiquity of the points, and refer their origin either to Moses and the authors of the sacred books themselves, or at least their invention and addition to the sacred books to Ezra, with the exception of one, Elias, a recent grammarian of the Hebrews, who flourished in the previous century. For although others refer the origin of the vowel points to Adam according to R. Azaria in Meor Enajim, to which Anton. Rudolphus and Petrus Cavallerius, Matth. Flacius and Gvilhelm. Postellus subscribe: others to the times of Moses, whom they establish by the authority of the Zohar, Cosri, Bechai, and Kimchi to have been taught the points by God together with the law itself: others to Ezra and other men of the Great Synagogue, such as Ephodeus, Abarbenel, etc., yet all defend the antiquity of the points; Elias alone, in no way to be compared with the others, attributes them to the post-Talmudic Tiberians: all the Rabbis of all nations who flourished both before him and after him differ from that Elias, Germans, Gauls, Poles, Bohemians, Spaniards, Italians, Cretans, Arabs, Palestinians, Babylonians, Africans, etc. Buxtorf, in the cited treatise, part II, ch. IV, asserts; and perhaps those opinions of the ancient Jews can be reconciled if it is said that the origin of the vowel points is indeed to be referred to the times of Adam, but that which vowel points suit the divine law, and according to which it ought to be read, that was handed down to Moses by God, and preserved and propagated by Moses and his successors through the tradition of the living voice until Ezra, while the Prophets and men inspired by God were still living and flourishing, so that the tradition might not be unfaithful; but from Ezra, before the Prophets failed, the same were added to the Sacred Codex by the divine Spirit, and thus transmitted to our times by divine providence. Let others see to that.

§. IX. Much more dangerous still is the hypothesis concerning Hebrew Codices, not only regarding the points, but also the letters and consonants, to be emended according to various versions, the Samaritan Pentateuch, parallel passages, and our own judgment without the authority of Codices or Interpreters, and concerning novel readings to be found from the easy commutation of points or letters. By which method the θεόπνευστος Hebrew Codex will be accused of corruption in infinite places. But that which is said to have been done before the Masoretes cannot be, since in the Talmud, in the ancient Midrashim, and in the Kabbalists, neither a trace nor a vestige of such a mutation is detected, nor could it have been done subsequently, since the Masora, as a kind of hedge, has kept the sacred text protected from corruption. Worthy of note is the observation of Aben Ezra concerning the stupendous diligence of the Masoretes, which should be observed here also; when he treats of the word תיעשה at Exodus 25:31: I inspected, he says, the books which the Sages of Tiberias examined. And fifteen of their elders affirmed under oath that they carefully considered three times every single word and every single point, every full and every defective spelling, and behold, the Yod was written in the word תעשה even though I did not find it so written in the Spanish, French, and overseas books. On which passage of Aben Ezra, Schickard in Bechina, page 12, exclaims: O incredible diligence even in the most minute details! O singular benefit of the divine! O admirable agreement of so many copies dispersed through all the corners of Europe, Africa, and Asia, for so many centuries down to us, and the salutary harmony. Schickardus deals with this more fully there concerning the Masora, and observing this in particular, that the varieties of readings in the Hebrew Bibles are older than the Masora, and are all accurately noted by it. Furthermore, since there are found among the Jews, among the Christians in the East, and in the West, not a few very old copies written six, seven, or more centuries ago, who will believe that in none of these were at least some of those various readings left, which are imagined from the discrepancy of the Versions, if the Hebrew Codices themselves had it otherwise; and how were these Codices so removed that, although they were held to be authentic in the age of the translators, none of them survives any longer? If, whether by the persecution of Antiochus, or by the envy of the Pharisees and Scribes as enemies of the version of the LXX, which Capellus also maintains, the copies of the Hebrews and those similar to them, which they used, were brought into contempt and finally completely perished, where then did those Hebrew Codices go, which the Chaldean Interpreters, Jonathan, Onkelos, the Author of the Jerusalem Targum, or the other Greeks, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, or Jerome used, so that Capellus says those diverse readings, which he here imagines from their versions, can nowhere be found? Nor is it in any way likely that such a great variety could have crept in by chance by the scribes, without any notice of the Rabbis, as is imagined here. But Capellus himself does not admit that it was done with the intent of corrupting; indeed, he professes that the Jews strongly clear themselves of this crime; although soon, forgetful of himself, he affirms that out of rashness and audacity they sometimes compose different words, sometimes divide composed ones, which are truly inconsistent. For the scribes were not so unskilled and ignorant, but, as Buxtorffius notes, they occupied no low seat among the Jewish Doctors, who were employed to transcribe the law; nor could it happen that errors born of inexperience or oversight would not have been detected and corrected, since there were so many copies of the law among the Jews, not only in the synagogues of individual places, but also in almost every house, and from the age of Ezra the law was read and explained publicly every Sabbath in a continuous verse. But that the beginning and study of the Masoretes is to be referred to the times of Ezra, and to the 120 men of the Great Synagogue of that age, Joh. Buxtorfius the Elder demonstrates in his Tiberias; to which not even Morinus himself, otherwise a less than fair judge of those he calls non-Catholics, and a supreme enemy of Hebrew truth, could deny his praise, but that he confessed, in his Animadversiones in Censuram Exercitationis Samaritanae, p. 397, 367, that Buxtorfius was the first and only one of the Christians hitherto to have understood this Criticism (of the Masoretes): But the men of the Great Synagogue lasted until Simeon the Just, from which time until the LXX Interpreters version, hardly an entire century elapsed; during which there can be no doubt that the disciples left by the men of the Great Synagogue propagated the Hebrew codex with faithful custody; if indeed no significant calamity befell the Jews in the meantime, by which it could be presumed that all the corrected copies perished, nor could such great varieties have crept in, without any record, before the times of Antiochus, when the study of the Critics still flourished, and thus a remedy against corruptions was not lacking. Since hardly 80 years intervened from the time of the version of the LXX Interpreters until the times of Antiochus. Or if such variations had indeed insinuated themselves at that time, shall we believe that they would not have been corrected either by the Critics of subsequent times, whose diligence and fidelity Capellus praises greatly, or if the envy and malevolence of the Jews here against the version of the LXX version had discharged itself upon the Hebrew Codices themselves, as is imagined against all credibility, would not Christ have rebuked the Jews in his own time, and given warning about the Canon, as was fitting? To whom, however, he himself referred without any caution or warning.

§. X. But then, are we to believe that divine providence would have allowed the Original text of the Holy Scripture, which He willed to be the perpetual norm for the Church, to be so greatly corrupted and disturbed, namely, by countless diverse readings introduced in such a way that it is finally permitted to no one in the Church, even if all the Doctors of the whole world were gathered into one, to say with certainty which is the true and genuine reading in almost infinite places? By which method all certainty of the sacred Codex is utterly shaken, the foundation of faith is undermined and leveled to the ground, nor can any assurance of faith remain any longer, and nothing further remains but that mere Pyrrhonism be admitted in those things which consist of divine revelation, and thus atheism itself finally raises its head and triumphs. For with the same ease that universal corruption could creep into those countless places, of the Old as well as the New Testament, which the Critic mixes together, the human mind, being very prone to Pyrrhonism, will presume that it could have rushed or crept into others, and indeed into those which contain the axioms of faith, in such a way that it will by no means be able to extricate itself here by that distinction between fundamental dogmas and others not concerning the foundation.

Both these and those are the words of the living GOD, say the Hebrews. Therefore, the reason for all things that are held in the Scriptures is the same until now. All Scripture is God-breathed. 2 Tim. III, 16. And where at last is that license of correcting going to end, if such a great gate is opened to it, that it is lawful to amend the Hebrew text not only from versions, but also from one's own conjectures? If it must be done so and it is lawful for one to do so, will it not be lawful for many to do the same? If for Reuben, why not likewise for Simeon, and for anyone else? Indeed, why not, says Capellus, for this one and that one, and also for another, indeed for anyone, provided he can do it and does it with judgment? But who will suffer the judgment to be taken away from himself? Who, especially among the Critics, who are often wont to be a bit bold, will not exalt himself by his own judgment? What norm of contentions will then remain, if the Hebrew Codex has been cast down from this pinnacle? And how will he then be able to maintain the authority of the fountain, how the authority of the Hebrew truth, which all attribute to it, when such great license is permitted to anyone against it, so that it is now amended from the Chaldean versions, now from the Greek, now from the Latin, now from others, now from the Samaritan Pentateuch, now from the collation of passages and one's own conjectures, and new readings are fashioned and refashioned, without measure, without number; so that versions are thrust forward instead of the fountain, or as different readings of the fountain, and the Original text must at last be forged from various versions, reasonings, and conjectures, and, until that happens, the Church must be entirely without an authentic text.

§. XI. One must therefore wonder at those most illustrious men, Matthaeus Cotterius, Guilhelmus Eyre, Arnoldus Bootius, Isaacus Vossius, and even Fridericus Spanhemius, that they have subscribed to this most dangerous Criticism. Concerning Grotius, it is not a wonder, who was a Vertumnus in those things which pertain to religion, almost always, especially towards the end of his life.
