But that Vossius, in his little commentary on the true age of the world, pronounces that Ludovicus Capellus has deserved well, if anyone has, by that famous work of his on the divine Scriptures, and bids others to accustom themselves to this light, so that, having dispersed the mist of their intellect, they may recognize that they have been blind in the light, in that very thing he is deceived by a vain and blind persuasion concerning that light of his, [while] of the true light we think they have deprived themselves. For concerning the Jews, to whom the Apostle testifies that the oracles of God (τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ) were entrusted, he boldly affirms that whatever they hand down concerning the perpetual and constant preservation of the Sacred books are mere impostures. Although he cannot entirely disapprove of the labor of the Masoretes, he gravely criticizes them because they did not correct the errors of the Codex from versions, and especially from the LXX; he asserts that there are very many flaws and lacunae in the Hebrew text; he decrees that the version of the LXX Interpreters is not only the best of all translations, but that it ought to be preferred even to modern Hebrew Codices. Who could read these things with a calm mind and without detestation? But Spanheim was led to second thoughts, and having read Buxtorf’s treatise on the points, he rejected that Criticism, which was also done by Boëtius in his letter written to Armathanus concerning the certainty of the Hebrew text against the Criticism of Lud. Capellus. Andreas Rivetus indicated that it had also imposed upon learned and grave men, but those not exercised in such matters: he himself judges it to be truly most base and profane; he pronounces that if it should prevail, it would be almost all over for the entire Scripture of the O.T., and that it would be nothing other than the buskin of Theramenes, to be fitted to all feet: Johannes Deodatus calls it a most dangerous section of the first foundation of divine doctrine. Another certain person from the middle of France proclaimed the Capellian Criticism to be a support for the Alcoran, a trumpet of impiety, a propagator of all errors, to be held as such by the judgment of all wise men. Christian Schotanus, a Franeker Theologian, in his Tohu, or Library of Sacred History, examining a new invention of Vossius concerning the first age of the world, who contends in two ages (p. 174) that the birth time of the world anticipates the common era by at least 1440 years, Ludov. Capellus, who distributes canonical authority between the Hebrew and Samaritan Codices, and into all ancient Versions, is judged by the illustrious Buxtorf, among others, to have so ground down and discussed the new dogma, that those who are blind in broad daylight must be owls. And indeed, the Criticism of Capellus has received these eulogies unanimously among the Reformed in the faith:

It was not received much more kindly in the Papacy itself, in which it is very well known that the Hebrew text is otherwise held in low esteem, and the Vulgate version, or even the translation of the LXX Interpreters, is far preferred. For a certain man of great name among the Roman Catholics signified that the Parisian Hebraists opposed that Criticism, for the reason that it follows from it that the Hebrew text is corrupt and erroneous in many places, and that from there we can establish nothing certain in the Christian religion: For what kind of streams are they, if the fountains are corrupt? Another most famous Doctor of that Church judged that it would bring the greatest detriment to the Christian Republic: Another judged that this whole work of Capellus offers malignant and lethal poison in that golden cup, and unless those subtleties are refuted, the time will come when the authority of the Sacred Bibles will seem to be endangered and wavering; who did not hesitate to compare it with the Alcoran of the most treacherous Mahometan impostor, and, which is worthy of mention, reported; when some, offended by the French edition of the Alcoran, had complained about the privilege granted, a similar complaint was instituted by a certain distinguished Doctor against the Sacred, or rather execrable, Criticism of Ludovicus Capellus, by which any Biblical text, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Arabic, Syriac, etc., is rendered and proposed as changeable, doubtful, and uncertain, by which consequently the dogmas of faith and piety are torn down and a broad path is paved to Atheism. If that Critical canon is valid, wrote Marinus Mersennus in a similar case, we have nothing certain anymore in the Hebrew books. If there is room for any conjectures in restoring the Hebrew text, I greatly fear that human Scripture will finally be foisted upon us instead of divine Scripture, writes Simeon de Muys, Royal Professor at Paris, somewhere. But these and many other things are proposed in the most learned Anti-Criticus of D. Buxtorf; who tore the mask off that most perverse and truly Diabolical Criticism, so that it can no longer easily terrify or disturb anyone. We have thought it necessary to repeat some things from there, so that the admirers not only of him, but also of Grotius, in whose judgment he greatly triumphs, may understand in what place and estimation those arts ought to be held, which in the work of Grotius make up almost every page, and have been held, even by those among whom he himself lived, and to whose stage he accommodated himself. For there are never lacking talents who willingly thrust such a Critical sickle into that Sacred harvest, or who easily, but less cautiously and prudently, applaud others who are thrusting it. But Isaac Vossius shows by his own example to what lengths it goes, concerning whom Schotanus in book 5: I wish he had first exercised his hands in his bosom, and had lifted them up to GOD the Best and Greatest, and prayed for help and light, before he pronounced on such a great matter, about to insolently insult the judgment and common consent of the entire Church: 1. That we believe that the oracles of GOD were entrusted to the Jews, and that the Canon has reached us sound and entire, he declares that this rests on the fables of the Jews. But he himself argues against the Christian faith from the fables of the Jews. 2. He says that the Rabbis admit that there was once such discrepancy and confusion of the Sacred Codices that hardly anything certain could be elicited from such a variety of expressions. But where, and who said so? Perhaps he had in mind the passage from Juchasin, which the most learned Cunæus praises in book 1 of his Republic of the Hebrews, chapter 18. But that author testifies that in the kingdom of Leon the book ארבעה ועשרים was erroneous, which Rabbi Hillel had transcribed, and that all copies were amended on his authority. I do not read that they were so confused and corrupt that nothing certain could be elicited from them. 3. He thinks that that uniformity which has since been found in the copies of the Hebrew Code is owed to the Masoretes. That is, he judges that they themselves, out of their own ingenuity, restored or rather formed a certain work, which by those who follow the Hebrew Code is variously and ineptly held to be the authentic work of Moses. Namely, that it has become a human farrago out of an inextricable confusion, which good men take for a divine canon. 4. He reproves the Masoretes because, trusting in their own judgment in unraveling the confusion, they did not employ versions, and especially that of the LXX, the best and most ancient. Must it be said that it follows from this that they undertook such a great work relying only on their own judgment, because they did not take versions into counsel? All those versions either interpreted the Hebrew reading or were an emendation of their own ingenuity. The copies themselves, which the Masoretes had collected, had encompassed the entire variety of the Hebrew reading. This suffices, that they safely left behind emendation from ingenuity. Unless you think that the interpreters could have followed another reading of the Hebrew Code than that which the Masoretes did not find in their own copies. That is not likely, or if it is so, it was some obscure copy of no name. For the Masoretes could have had whatever there was of approved copies throughout all the schools and synagogues of the Jews, and if they were as diligent as is proclaimed, and as Vossius does not deny, they collected them. For if they had not done so, that school and synagogue which had seen its own copy and accustomed reading disregarded would not have received the copies amended by the Masoretes. It is also certain that whatever was amended and received in the reading of the Sacred Code was publicly amended and received. Nor was an emendation made, but only the variety of readings was noted, some of which were placed by punctuation, that is, קרי, others by letters, that is, כתיב. Thus far Schotanus.

§. XII. Capellus and Grotius ought rather to have listened here to the Jews, from whom R. Joseph Albo at length proves that the law, which is in our hands today, is the same, according to the continuous tradition from the Fathers to the sons, as that which was given to Moses on Mount Sinai, without any change; if a diversity is found among other nations, the change is on the part of the translators, who were not sufficiently exercised in the law. The author of the book Cosri and his commentator R. Jehuda Muscatus deny that anything should be changed if anything seems to be beyond or against the reading, proportion, or collation, even if one or another Codex favors it; because if that reasoning, choice, and judgment dominates in these and similar things, whole books will be changed, first in letters, soon in words, then in sentences, points, and accents, and thus the sense will be changed everywhere. R. Aben Ezra, far be this, far be it, he exclaims: for this is not right in the words of profane authors, how much less in the words of the living GOD. And for that reason the Rabbis of the Jews, the Author of Cosri, Muscatus, and Aben Ezra condemn the Karaites, because they change the reading of the Law at their own discretion, (although Andreas Legerus, a Genevan Theologian, and Hottinger from his letters at the end of his Philological Thesaurus asserts that the Karaites acknowledge that even the vowel points of the sacred text are from Moses and the Prophets) indeed R. Moses Nachmannides in his Novellae on the Talmudic chapter ישניחרין fol. 91, says that the correction of books from opinion or conjecture is an absolute transgression, and on account of it one deserves to be excommunicated: in the Talmud itself there are very grave warnings about this matter in Sota c. 3. My son, be cautious in your work, if your work is the work of heaven; (divine, occupied with Scripture.) For if you happen to subtract or add even a single letter, you will be held as if you were destroying the whole world. In the Talmud Sanhedrim, last chapter. Whoever also says of a single letter of the law that it is not from heaven, is of those of whom it is written, He has despised the word of the Lord. (Num. 15, 31.) But in other things, where they err, Capellus did not disdain to follow the Jews, but here, where they were deservedly to be followed, he preferred to go in all other directions. We must return to our Grotius.

§. XIII. Grotius praises the work of the Ancients, Jerome and Chrysostom, especially: but that he celebrates the former for his knowledge of the Hebrew language, places, and histories, and the latter for those things which he observed with the help of the Antiochene Jews; yet that he follows the work of neither in the scrutiny of contexts, nor in eliciting the proper scope and core of the Prophetic writings, is by no means to be approved. For he could not see Christ, who is the scope and most scope-like of the sacred letters, in them, because of an excessive study of histories and a blind affection toward the Jews. Since he was of this mind, the labors and commentaries of our age, of which not a few very learned ones exist, were little to his taste. He says that only Vatablus and Franc. Junius are not to be despised, yet he seems to prefer the Jesuit Johan. Stephanus Menochius and those whom he presented in abridged form to all others, if you except those things which he devised by his own genius or drew from the Jews. What wonder, because this one is a Catholic with his own, but those are non-Catholics to Grotius? He did not hesitate to entrust the work of his annotations to the Jesuit Dionysius Petavius, whom he calls an eminent Theologian, to be judged, enriched, and corrected, as witnessed by the letters sent to Petavius, which are read among the Epistles to the French at the end: I ask, he writes to the same, that, as soon as it can be done at your convenience, that is, publicly, I may have what you have observed; and may it be permitted to me with your help to add, remove, and correct what will be necessary for promoting truth and peace. Item: Note if anything seems to need changing in the matters themselves: I will take this as a great favor. Item: If you have leisure to read, I ask that, when you have done so, you advise me what should be omitted

& what you think should be changed: What may have come to your mind, or to another to whom you have given them to be read, regarding the former part (of the annotations on the O.T.), I will await. For which reason he also gave thanks to the Jesuit, and sought that light might be further kindled from his light: I owe many thanks to your courtesy, because you did not wish the inspection of those things which we noted on the O.T. to be burdensome to yourself, because you entrusted a more exact reading to those who had more leisure, and because you wished to advance this work by your recommendation. Now when I see some way of publishing that work, I ask you that, as soon as possible, it may return to me with your advice. When the second part, on which I am now working, is described, I will dare to intervene again with your labors, although they are both most grave and most useful, and to use such ready kindness. Paris, Kalends of November, year 1641. In other letters he extols the help of the Jesuit happily provided to him on August 16, 1642. Given at Paris; which we produced earlier. How much, therefore, he permitted the Jesuits in his annotations, how much he valued the judgments of the Papists in the interpretation of Scripture, and with how much eagerness he composed himself to their advice, which who would doubt was accommodated to Roman Catholic doctrine, is no longer obscure.

§. XIV. He confesses, however, that he took the sense of the law and the reason for the precepts, and the customs pertaining to them, mostly from the ancient Masters of the Jews, which he ought to have professed equally regarding the Prophetic prophecies, in which the thing itself teaches that the Masters of the Jews pleased him more than the Christians. But he also ought not to have forgotten the warning of Christ, that if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit. He boasts, however, that he devoted much effort to the Prophecies; but in such a way (for he does not hide this) that he referred the passages which the Ancients referred to Christ and the times of the Gospel to histories closer to the age of the Prophets, left under the veil of the figure of Christ and the Evangelical times. Thus, therefore, he deserted the footsteps of the Ancients, and went into all other things. That he adhered closely to the Jews, and to the more recent ones rather than the ancient ones, the collation testifies. It was therefore necessary for him to have put off the Papist: nor were the Catholic Papists to him any longer, nor did he care much for the Catholics, drunk with the Rabbinic spirit.

§. XV. He had prescribed rules in his vow on p. 139 concerning the observance of tradition, and that there is a just presumption that what is found everywhere in the Church was handed down by the Apostles; but he removed from sight the tradition of the ancient Doctors in explaining prophecies. We hear, he says, those witnesses whom the Church has always approved. But what witnesses approved by the Church will he produce for his glosses? He commends the necessity of traditions in the interpretation of the Scriptures, but he will never teach that his glosses agree with the tradition of Christians. He praises the Rule of the Council of Trent, about not interpreting Scripture against the unanimous consent of the Fathers; but he himself held the same in most Prophecies.

§. XVI. He says that the sequence of words and things in the Prophets coheres poorly unless the prophecies are referred to nearer histories, which otherwise is most beautiful. But not to mention that there is no need for the sequence to cohere regarding times closer to the Prophets, since not rarely, with the Spirit suggesting, they turned themselves to the better times of the New Testament, both to lead the faithful to the chief goal which they have fixed for themselves, and to raise minds from type to antitype, from punishments and torments to the source and apex of all consolations, from the sense of imminent or present things to the hope and expectation of future ones, and nowhere unmindful of their primary duty, which was to lead men to the Messiah and faith in him, would accomplish that very thing intentionally: Grotius certainly ought not to have seemed wiser to himself than all Christians, ancient and modern, who certainly showed a comparison, even if they explained the prophecies concerning Christ and the times of the New Testament. What? Was he wiser than the Apostles themselves, wiser than Christ himself, the eternal wisdom of the Father? But they teach

The Apostles [teach that] the Spirit of Christ, who was in the Prophets, was testifying beforehand of the sufferings of Christ, and the glory after them, 1 Pet. 1:11. They teach that ALL the Prophets bear witness to Christ, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins, Acts 10:43. They protest that they teach nothing outside of those things which Moses and the Prophets said would come to pass, Acts 26:22. But if Grotius's glosses are to be admitted, we will easily have no Prophet testifying to the sufferings and glory of Christ, who did not want to interpret even those clearest testimonies of Ps. 16 and Is. 53 concerning Christ, twisting the former to David, the latter to Jeremiah. Which are explained by the older Jews themselves concerning the Messiah. The former by R. Moses Hadarsch. in Ps. 49:11. This verse is said concerning King Messiah, who will die, so that he may redeem the Fathers, and afterwards live forever. The latter in the Thargum Jonath. itself in the book Sanhedrim c. Heleck, in l. Siphre in Midrasch Ruth, c. 2:14, by R. Moses Hadarschā in Gen. 1:3, c. 24:67, and Ps. 49; therefore R. Aben Ezra in Is. 52:13 seq., as also R. Abarbaneel, teach that the ancient Masters of the Hebrews, as also R. Moses Nachmanides, a man of great name among the moderns, explain it: from the reading of which one prophecy alone J. Isaacus testifies that he himself was converted to the Christian faith, adv. Lind. But it is so far from the case that Grotius leaves this to ALL the Prophets, that they have testified concerning the remission of sins through faith in the name of Christ, that he is likely to assign this to hardly any of the Prophets, who believes Socinus asserting that the remission of sins was rather first announced by Christ: nor did he hand down anything in his annotations on the Prophets concerning faith in the name of Christ and the remission of sins through faith; that is to be obtained. But how could he, who was persuaded with the Papists that the Apostles not only taught many other things orally which are clearly not written, but leaves almost nothing of those things which the Apostles taught concerning Christ in Moses and the Prophets through his annotations, believe that the Apostles taught nothing outside of those things which Moses and the Prophets teach in their writings, in which they are proposed by Christ to be heard, Luke 16:29?

§. XVII. But Christ, whom the heavenly voice proclaimed must be heard alone, commanded us to search the ancient Scriptures in such a way that we might investigate that eternal life which is held in them and the testimony which they bear concerning Christ, in order to obtain life through faith in him, that ἐρευνήσεις, John 5:39; not so that we might pass over the testimonies concerning eternal life, and concerning Christ the author of eternal life, or faith in Christ, or twist them to any other things whatsoever. Grotius certainly did not believe that testimonies concerning eternal life are held in the Scripture of the O.T., because he was fascinated by the dark opinions of Socinus: but concerning Christ, so that I may have eternal life in him through faith, one can find neither will nor trace in the Grotian annotations. Christ also explained the Scriptures of the O.T., but in such a way that he demonstrated his passion and resurrection from Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets. These are, he says, the words which I spoke to you, when I was still with you, that it is necessary that all things be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me. Then he opened, adds St. Luke, their understanding, that they might UNDERSTAND the Scriptures, and said, that thus it is written, and thus it behooved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. c. 24:44 seqq. But if the glosses of Grotius prevail, not even in the Psalms and the Prophets, let alone in Moses, will anything be shown concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ from the dead, and the proclamation to be made in his name, and the beginning of the same at Jerusalem, because, forsooth, the series of words and things looks to nearer times.

§. XVIII. The whole Old Testament, therefore, is to be left solely to the Jews; nothing of it will pertain to us, if a few prophecies, perhaps three or four, concerning the time of the coming of the Messiah are excepted. What, therefore, will become of the disputations of Christ and the Apostles, or the passages brought by them from the O.T. which they themselves interpret concerning the Messiah? They will go into a sponge, nor will the Jews be able to be convinced by them, or have they been able to in the past, if you listen to Grotius, inasmuch as they deal with things far different. Let not the Angel now, Matt. 1:23, say that what was said by the Lord through Isaiah is fulfilled, Behold a virgin shall have in the womb: It was not said concerning Christ the son of the virgin, but concerning the son of Isaiah. Let him not say that what was said by the Prophet Isaiah concerning the land of Zabulon and Naphthalim and Galilee of the Gentiles is fulfilled, when Christ arrived at those borders, and began to preach there. The prophet did not look to those, but to the times of Hezekiah, and the liberation from Sennacherib: Not Christ, but Hezekiah is that child born, counselor, (Grotius perverts it to consultant) mighty God, (to be read according to Grotius's σφεέλστη[α Consultant of the mighty God) eternal Father.

§. XIX. Let not Matthew testify, c. 8, 17, that Isaiah spoke of Christ when he sang that he bore our sorrows, c. 53, 4; or Peter, that Christ is he by whose stripes we are healed, in whose mouth no guile was found, 1 Ep. 2, 22, 24; or Mark, that Jesus is he whom he predicted would be reckoned among the wicked, c. 15, 28; nor let Philip explain these of Christ, Acts 8, 32, because Isaiah prophesied there of Jeremiah. Nor is there any reason why Matthew should say so prolixly that the prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled by Christ, c. 12, 18, concerning the servant who would not contend, who would manifest the judgment of God to the nations, in whose name the nations would hope, c. 42, 1. For the Prophet prophesied concerning himself: or that he should bring forward the prophecy of Zechariah, c. 9, 9, concerning the entry of Christ upon a donkey, with Matthew c. 21, 5, John c. 12, 15, for these things must be accepted concerning Zerubbabel; or that both, Matthew c. 27, 35. & John c. 19, 21, when the garments of Christ were divided, should teach that the prophecy of David, Ps. 22, 19, was fulfilled, for this must be understood of David himself μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), that they divided his confiscated fortunes among themselves, just as the Latins speak of spoil concerning any thing whatsoever, when properly spoils are garments. Or that St. John c. 19, 37, should affirm the transfixing of Christ to have been predicted by Zechariah c. 12, 10. Our sense, says Grotius, is the best; they are said to pierce God who provoke him with reproaches.

§. XX. Nor could Peter, Acts 2, demonstrate either that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles was predicted by Joel c. 2, 28; or the resurrection of Christ from the prophecy of David, Ps. 16, 8, that the holy one of God should not see corruption; or testify, Acts 3, that Moses predicted that the Messiah would be raised up as a great Prophet from the brethren of the Jews, Deut. 18, 5. For Joel speaks of Isaiah and other Prophets. David acts for himself, Moses of any prophet whatsoever to be raised up, where great necessity or evident utility demanded it. Nor could the Apostle of the Gentiles urge his demonstration with Peter, Acts 2, 29, c. 13, 36, that David saw corruption entirely, and therefore spoke of the Messiah, not of himself. For this sense is only that there would not be power for Saul to kill David. Paul and Barnabas will not be able to appeal, c. 13, 47. that the Lord had commanded them to turn to the Gentiles, when he predicted through Isaiah c. 49, 6, that Christ would be a light to the Gentiles. For Isaiah testified concerning himself that he also would convert many of the Gentiles. Nor could the Apostles in the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15, 16, confirm the calling of the Gentiles from Amos c. 9, 11. For the Tabernacle of David, of which he treats, was already raised up in Zerubbabel.

Nor is there any reason why they should appeal to Mark ch. 1, 3 or Luke ch. 3, 4 regarding Isaiah ch. 40, which he sang about John who was to preach in the desert. The Prophet at least warned that those who were to live during the time of the exile should cry out, and that they should prepare the way for the Lord in the desert.

§. XXI. But it will also be necessary for Christ himself to be silent, lest he say that he is the stone which David predicted the architects, Pharisees, and priests would reject (Ps. 118, 22) when he spoke of himself being rejected by Saul and his court; or (Luke 21, 37) that he is the one who, as Isaiah (ch. 53, 12) prophesied, would be reckoned among the wicked, because the words of the Prophet must be taken as referring to Jeremiah; or (Matt. 26, 21) the Shepherd whom Zechariah (ch. 13, 7) predicted would be struck, for this is Judas Maccabeus, who died in battle against Bacchides. Let him not exclaim (Luke 4, 18), having read the prophecy of Isaiah (ch. 4, 1), 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, today this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears.' For Isaiah spoke of himself. And what then will remain in the Prophetic Scriptures that deals with Christ and the times of the Old Testament, if those things which Christ and the Evangelists most clearly explained, and which the Apostles of Christ explained, are distorted by such inventions into a completely different meaning? Let the fair reader judge; for Grotius permits judgment to him: is this not to prefer the glosses of the infidel Jews to the opinion of Christ and the Apostles, that is, darkness to light, Belial to Christ?

§. XXII. Grotius therefore flattered himself too much with the beauty of the συνεχείας (continuity) he devised, so that he placed it under his glosses like a foundation, when it is easy, where we are certain of the subject and the matter, as they call it, from the mouth of Christ and the Apostles, and indeed even from the emphasis of the oracles of the Holy Spirit, to demonstrate the συνέχειαν (continuity) of the text. Nor indeed is it sufficient for sustaining the explanation of Christ and the Apostles that Grotius posits that those prophecies have an involved figure of Christ and the evangelical times, and that God exhibits the Messiah and his benefits to us not only through words, but also through things. Because an invincible demonstration cannot be sought from figures alone; therefore the force of the proofs of Christ and the Apostles will perish: nor are these things brought forward as types, as when the paschal lamb and other things are presented as types, but as prophecies which deal with Christ and are fulfilled in him: Christ teaches that the figure is not only in the things themselves, as when he himself unfolds a figure involved in a sound, or the Apostles do, provided they urge the proper sense of the words and prophecies: if that sense concerns others, not Christ, their interpretation could be rejected as false. Will the enemies of the Christian name, therefore, triumph—Julian, Porphyry, Lipomannus, and the like? If he says that those things were applied to Christ in a mystical sense, but speak literally of someone else, the Jews and other enemies of the Christians will laugh that a mystical sense and typical accommodation are always used in place of a solid proof and demonstration, that the proper sense of the Prophets is never urged, that the Prophets never prophesied about Christ or his benefits, and that the matter is always only involved in types and figures and the life of the saints is shadowed forth, which shadowing forth, however, neither existed for the people at that time, nor could it be had from words or deeds, nor can it exist today. Which, perhaps, Grotius asserts was not even known to the Prophets themselves who uttered those prophecies, along with the Jews, whose opinions he willingly follows. To what use, therefore, had that shadowing forth been? Then indeed it is certain that a single statement has only one sense, and that the literal and genuine one; that multiple senses are brought into the same statement, if Grotius thought as the Papists do, is protested by the nature of words, which, once placed in the same sentence, must obtain one and the same certain meaning, because meaning is the form of a word, and it is undoubted that there is one form of one thing: it is protested by the divine intention, which was to indicate something certain in its oracles, and not to propose an ambiguous speech or opinion which you could understand one way or another as the occasion arises, or rather ought to interpret in a diverse manner, at one time about others who lived long ago, and at another time about the Messiah; it is protested by the genuine method of ἑρμηνείας (interpretation): by the force of which no more than a single opinion consistent with the mind of the speaker is to be elicited from the context; unless perhaps the absurdities of Cardinal Bellarmine, book III de verb. Dei ch. 3, pleased Grotius, so that he believed it to be proper to Scripture, because it has God as its author, that it contains multiple senses, literal and mystical, or the Papist-leaning hypothesis of his Capellus in his Critic. I do not see why it should be denied that the spirit of God in various places (not everywhere) intended not only one, but a double, or truly even a triple literal sense; for this pertains to declaring his πολυποίκιλον (manifold) wisdom: or the invention of the Rabbis: 'Scripture is never without a simple sense, but it has it just as it has a mystical one, so it has a simple one; it is not the case that it lacks these two.' Namely, according to that saying of Solomon, Prov. 25, 11: 'apples of gold in settings of silver, a word spoken according to both its faces.' Which are utterly repugnant to the clarity and purpose of Holy Scripture, which is to make us certain of the divine mind. For where there is equivocation, or ἀμφιβολία (ambiguity), there we are carried away into diverse senses, and we can have no βεβαιότητα (certainty) about the opinion of the one speaking. And will not the proofs of Christ and the Apostles be rendered completely ineffective in this way, if they are instituted from a figurative sense alone, and never drawn from the literal and proper opinion of the oracles? The opinion of Irenaeus is well known, book II, ch. 46: 'That parables can receive many interpretations, and that those who abandon the search for God to affirm from them what is certain and undoubted and true are very much precipitating themselves into danger and are irrational, who among those who love the truth will not confess?' The observation of Jerome on Matt. 13 is well known: 'A parable and the doubtful understanding of enigmas can never contribute to the authority of dogmas.' The judgment of St. Augustine, Ep. XLVIII to Vincentius the Donatist, is well known. Who would not most impudently strive to interpret something placed in an allegory in his own favor, unless he has elsewhere most manifest testimonies by which obscure things are illustrated. If he had been unwilling to hear these, he ought at least not to have forgotten the rule of Thomas, part 1, q. 1, art. 10: only the literal sense is argumentative, which holds the status of an axiom among the Papists, so that Bellarmine himself assumes this as indubitable. IT IS ESTABLISHED, he says, l. III. de V. D. c. 3, between us and our adversaries, that effective arguments must be sought from the literal sense alone. Unless, therefore, the arguments of Christ and the Apostles are to be called ineffective, one must confess that it was that literal and proper sense which they are read to have pressed and employed both in the confirmations of their sayings and deeds, and in their disputes with adversaries. What the whole Church has believed until now, Grotius alone, even though he makes tradition the interpreter of Scripture, here feeds upon the inventions of the Jews. Whose chief study it seems to have been to sell the interpretations of the Rabbis to Christians—whether because he wished to show off that he was well-versed in their writings, or rather because he was fascinated by their glosses—and to take into counsel the Rabbinical traditions themselves, and sometimes even Talmudic trifles, rather than Scripture as its own unaccountable interpreter. So that the sounder ones among the Jews themselves seem to be those whom the others call by contempt קראים, textual scripturists, because, having dismissed traditions and the Talmud, they admit only Scripture as the foundation of faith, and judge that the exposition of the law should be drawn from the very words of the law. But Grotius did not wish to be a scripturist: which is what the Papists cast upon us as a crime. And he seems to have been little removed from the opinion of the Rabbis, who say that the article concerning the Messiah is believed only through tradition, and that there is NO prophecy, neither in the law, nor in the Prophets, because it necessarily predicts his advent, to such an extent that from the circumstances of the passages it cannot be taken otherwise; that this is the mind of most Interpreters (Jews), R. Joseph Ben Albo testifies, who finally went so far as to assert in Orat. IV. c. 42 in the book Ikkarim, that the faith by which one believes in the advent of the Messiah is not such a foundation that the law would collapse entirely if someone did not have that faith. See Abrah. Hülfig in Theol. Judaic. part. I. qu. II. For that Rabbi disapproves of the opinion of Maimonides, that faith in a future Messiah constitutes a foundation, because, namely, he would thus have to be numbered among the Apostates and those falling away from Religion, to whom there is no part in the future world, R. Hillel. Whom, however, he excuses thus in Orat. I. c. I. R. Hillel did not believe that there would be a future Messiah, but yet for that reason he is not to be reckoned among the Apostates, as Maimonides wrote, inasmuch as it [the religion] consists without him. In this certainly our author yields nothing to R. Joseph Albo, nay, he carries off the palm, because while he [Albo] proposed various reasons for doubting regarding some most noble prophecies about the Messiah, whether they might not be said to have been fulfilled partly under the first temple, partly under the second in this or that instance, and admits the opinion of R. Hillel, that the prophecies of Isaiah regarded King Hezekiah, Grotius interprets almost everything not skeptically, but categorically about another than the Messiah, and twists the prophecies of Isaiah to King Hezekiah with a most perverse reasoning; it is a wonder that he did not also grant to Hillel that the Israelites in the times of Hezekiah possessed their Messiah, since in Isaiah, the most brilliant of all the prophets concerning the Messiah, the prophet and herald, Hezekiah is substituted from time to time in the place of the Messiah, and as far as the literal sense is concerned, he does not find or leave the Messiah in the whole book of Isaiah. Grotius certainly could not convince the Jews concerning the Messiah from Isaiah and most other prophets, since he twisted almost all the prophecies into a sense that is clearly alien, and interprets none of them skillfully with the Christians.

§. XXII. But for convincing the Jews, even a few things directly describing Christ and the time when he was to come are sufficient. Grotius leaves absolutely few; scarcely three or four. One from Genesis, the prophecy of Jacob, one from Daniel, concerning the LXX weeks, one from Haggai concerning the second temple, as also from Malachi concerning the forerunner of Christ: But what will become of the other Prophets? Were they mute concerning Christ? Did David, confirmed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, say nothing, did Isaiah say nothing, he who is held by the Evangelists to be more a true prophet than a prophet, did Hosea, Zechariah, and the rest of the Prophets say nothing? Who therefore ALL bore witness concerning Christ, which Peter says in Acts 10:43? Who Moses and ALL THE PROPHETS from Samuel, and thereafter, who have spoken, have indicated these days, which the same Peter affirmed before the Jews, with them not contradicting, because it was undoubted among all, Acts 3:23? And indeed not only are the Jews to be convinced concerning the time of the advent of the Messiah, but concerning his miracles, benefits, parts of his office, and other marks and characters of the same.

§. XXIII. If the scripture of the New Testament fails or is ineffective in applying these, the Jews will be confirmed in their errors, or they will be convinced that the Messiah has indeed come, but they will by no means be able to be convinced that Jesus of Nazareth is that promised Messiah; nay, if all those prophecies are believed to treat of another than the Messiah according to the letter, they would convince Christ and the Apostles of falsehood, because they snatched them into another sense, and Christ could bring forward no saying for himself, the Apostles none for Christ. And indeed those things brought forward concerning the time in Gen. 49, Dan. 9, Hag. 2 are nowhere brought forward in the New Testament. The prophecies of Malachi c. 3 & 4 are indeed brought forward, but likewise, as the prophecy of Isaiah is brought forward, as is clear from Mark c. 1, 2, 3. Since therefore these do not treat of the Messiah and his forerunner in the literal sense according to Grotius, that also can be taken thus, as if not brought forward, as far as the proper sense is concerned. And will the Jews not be able with equal ease to feign another literal sense in those remaining prophecies of Grotius, and interpret the words especially of Malachi or Haggai concerning someone else? Just as the prophecy from Moses concerning Jacob provided no small handle for evasion, when he contended that the word שילח looked especially to the pool of Siloah. Although Grotius also perverts those from the Jewish Prophets with inventions: while in the passage of Daniel he wishes Christ to be indicated as a leader, who ought to have freed the people from impending evils, if he had been obeyed, and in Malachi he explains the ruler thus: That promised Shiloh, who will bring you the greatest goods even in the public state, if you obey him. Which, just as they openly favor the dreams of the Jews concerning an earthly kingdom of the Messiah, so it is very manifest that the Judaizing Grotius is undermining the foundation of Christianity most of all, as if an earthly kingdom and earthly goods were promised to the Jews through the Messiah, and the promises concerning the Messiah were only hypothetical and conditional. The Jews therefore have that which they may pretext for their unbelief, even concerning the time of the advent of the Messiah; that the promised political ruler has not yet arrived, and that those promises were only conditional, which condition, since it has not been fulfilled by the Jews, it is no wonder that the promised ruler Shiloh has not arrived, or is not going to arrive at all, as the desperate ones among them say today. Their argument is certainly indissoluble. The Messiah is promised as a political ruler, about to restore the public state of the Jews, under the condition, if they are to obey. Which is the Grotian proposition. Jesus of Nazareth is not a political ruler, who protests whether the Jews themselves are to obey or not, that his kingdom is not of this world. Therefore Jesus of Nazareth is not the promised Messiah. Well done, triumph, Jews, you have found a great defender!

§. XXIV. But what is the wonder, that Grotius should thus undermine the foundation of Christianity by his hypotheses, when he directly overturns the Canonical Scriptures, which are the foundation of our faith. For if, as we observe here at the threshold regarding the books which he has undertaken to explain in the last place, one asks what Grotius holds concerning the authority of the same, he certainly does not believe that all those proceeded from the Holy Spirit which the universal Church has believed to be such. He denies that the Gospel of Luke, in the vow on p. 136, was written by divine inspiration, with this argument, that he made mention of witnesses, which is utterly futile: because unless he had been governed by the inspiration of the Spirit, he could easily have erred in the selection of witnesses and their testimonies, and therefore he had need of the same entirely. But Epiphanius, in heresy LI, [says] that he was compelled and excited to write by the secret promptings of the Holy Spirit. And Titus of Bostra affirms that he wrote by the inspiration of the heavenly Spirit; whose books also the whole Church has always held without doubt to be canonical. Nor does Grotius call into doubt Luke alone; he denies that all the books which are in the Hebrew canon were dictated by the Holy Spirit, or that there was a need for histories to be dictated by Him. He distinguishes between divine inspiration and pious impulse. But many write by pious impulse who, in writing, are not ἀνυπεύθυνοι (unaccountable) and infallible. It is necessary, therefore, that a great part of the sacred books should fall out of the canon of the Old Testament. Thus, the historical books in Holy Scripture, and indeed the histories which are sometimes inserted into other writings, such as those of Isaiah and the remaining Prophets, will be attributed to pious impulse indeed, but not to divine inspiration, nor will they have a place in the Canon. Whence it is no wonder that Grotius applies his critical hand to them, and his censorious rod, as if he were dealing with human writings. So that he does not seem to have been altogether alien to the opinion of his Capellus, that it is not impossible, nay perhaps in reality there are some lighter σφάλματα (errors) of this kind in the Scriptures, which are to be attributed even to the sacred writers themselves (insofar as they were weak men): which, however, does not sufficiently agree with the other pronouncement of the same Critic: Not only the things, but also the words and phrases were, as it were, dictated or inspired to the Prophets and sacred writers by the secret motion and inspiration of the Spirit of God. I would be insane if I thought otherwise. Nor indeed, when warned of his most grave error, does Grotius [yield], either to reasons or even to the [testimonies] of the Hebrews themselves

He could be moved by the authority of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, who acknowledges all the hagiographic books as written through the Holy Spirit, or of Jachias, who confessed that Ezra wrote his own book and the Chronicles through the Holy Spirit—an authority which he is otherwise accustomed to value highly—without still calling into doubt the canonical authority of the historians of the Holy Code in his Discussio, his most recent writing. He even added the moral sentences of the Hebrews (it is a dispute about the Canon of the Hebrews) as if they were not such that it would be a sin to doubt them. To these must be compared those things which he has concerning the book of Proverbs near its beginning; this seems to be an ἐκλογὴ (selection) of the best sentences from very many writers who were before Solomon, such ἐκλογὰς (selections) as many of the Emperors of Constantinople caused to be written down for their own uses. Such judgments, or ones not much different, he is also read to have passed concerning the recording of most other books in the sacred Code. And to this point also contributes the fact that in Explicat. Decal. p. 26, he wrote that Moses refers to the words described in Exodus from MEMORY in Deuteronomy; as if those things which are contained in Deuteronomy were proposed and written down by human study, and not indeed by the afflatus of the Holy Spirit and divine inspiration. Scarcely, therefore, will half remain in the Canon written by divine afflatus, which he truly treats with such an unfaithful hand, by adding, subtracting, correcting, and perverting, that one must judge he has believed without doubt that almost nothing divine remains in it. Nor does he merely call the vowel points into doubt, change the letters and the words themselves, or render them suspect, and thus he leaves little certainty to the sacred scriptures; which, finally, a man ought not to have valued highly, since in his most recent writing, the Discussio, p. 147, he professed that Scripture was by no means necessary for recognizing the will of God, nor did the Apostles write by the command of Christ, and that there were also many barbarian nations who believed in Christ without PAPER and INK, and other such Popish emblems of his. Not to mention that when he disputes about the Canon of the New Testament, he says that the question about mere histories is not of great moment, whether those things which are narrated are true or whether they are not true: from which Rivetus collects (dialys. p. 493) that it is all the same to him whether the histories which are recounted in the books of the New Testament are true or false, by which method the authenticity of the sacred Gospels is plainly overturned.

MANTISSA.

Grotius undoubtedly gratifies the Papists also in this, when he affirms in the Appendix de Anti-Christ that many of Paul's Epistles have perished. Although a distinction must be made between sacred writings that proceeded from men inspired by God (θεοπνεύσοις) and Canonical writings, divinely consecrated to the perpetual Canon of the Church, and it does not follow that if certain sacred writings of the Apostles have perished, some Canonical Scriptures are immediately missing—indeed, even among the Papists, Salmero (proleg. IX. can. 4) and Stapleton (de princ. doctr. fidei Contr. V. l. IX. c. 5) acknowledge that no Canonical books have perished, lest the Church be accused of negligence in the deposit entrusted to it—yet most Pontificians are accustomed, both to derogate from the perfection of the Scripture Canon (which is to be estimated not from the number of books, but from the divine will and the sufficiency of information and dogmas) and to contend in disparagement of the Holy Scriptures

Latin:

DISSERTATIO ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΙΚΗ DE PRÆFATIONE GROTIANA.

§. I.

PRæmonuit Grotius Lectorem de versione Latina, textu Ebræo, versionibus aliis quibus- dam & commentariis, nec non de hac an- notationum suarum opera in Lege & Prophetis. Ad versionem Latinam pridem receptam adjecit notas suas, quod semper eam fecerit plurimi, non modo, quod nulla contineat dogmata insalubria, verum eti- am, quod multum in se habeat eruditionis. Non ex- probrabimus nunc Vulgatæ, quod Erasmus alicubi de autore ejus habet, quem magni facit noster, si quis percontetur, Gallus fuerit, an Sarmata, Ju- dæus, an Christianus, Vir, an mulier, nil habituros ejus Patronos, quod expedite respondeant: non quod Cardinalitia conspicuus mitra Jesuita, omnium fui ordinis facile præcipuus, Bellarminus, vulgata editio non est unius autoris, sed quædam habet ex Hie- ronymo, quædam ex Luciano, quædam ex alio quo- dam interprete innominato; Stultum autem videtur dicere, Theodotionem hæreticum non potuisse errare & etiam Hieronymum nuspiam errasse: lib. II. de V. D. c. XI. quæ sane versionis vulgatæ auctoritatem parum ornant, aut commendant. Mereatur Vetus (non diffitemur) laudem suam; sed quænam illa sit pridem recepta, an Sixti V. num vero Clementis IIX. editio, non definivit Grotius. Pugnant autem illæ inter se bello irreconciliabili. Quam litem præ- cedentium Pontificum, quia uterque suam editio- nem Bulla muniit, (etsi Clemens sublata Sixti bulla, suam surrogavit, eamque per crimen falsi, Sixti venditarit nomine) nunquam poterunt sequentes decidere. Nullam ergo habebunt unquam versio- nem Papistæ, nullam habent, qui Papæ judicio obnoxii sunt, cum Grotio, quam pro pridem rece- pta agnoscere queant, imo dum discrepantes versiones authenticas habent, reaple nullam ha- bent: quum plus uno verum esse non possit. Nec vero in paucis, aut leviculis illæ inter se discrepant; imo judicata sunt errata Sixtinæ editionis tanti momenti, ut Gregorius XIV. teste Jacobo Fuligatto in vita Bellarm. l. I. c. 9. ex consilio Cardinalis Bel- larm. Sixtina Biblia de integro repurganda duxerit, conferenda singula ad antiquas editiones, ad M. S. exemplaria, & ad Commentarios Patrum, idque ne- gotium cum Bellarmino, M. Antonio Columna, & Alano, Cardinalibus, aliisque quatuor commise- rit, quorum opera, Clementis VIII. autoritate, prodiit nova editio, in Sixtina ultra bis mille textus ad fontes Ebræos & Græcos refingens & confor- mans. Ut non nisi dolose in præfatione, Clemen- tinæ præmissa, cujus auctor Bellarminus fuit, præli tantum vitia in editionem Sixti irrepsisse, ac iterata diligentia indiguisse, prætexatur; reclamante eti- am ipsa Pontificis Bulla, utpote qua sua ipsius ma- nu, si qua præla obrepserunt vitia, se correxisse, (quan- tam in eo adhibuerit Sixtus diligentiam docet An- gelus Rocha Bibliothecæ Vaticanæ præfectus, testis αὐτόπτης in Bibl. Vatican. pag. 219.) profitetur, adeoque mandat, ut omnes editionem suam, pro ve- ra, legitima, authentica, & indubitata recipiant. Sed de his alias,

§. II. Utra autem eligatur editio, laudem Gro- tii non assequetur, sive dogmata spectes, quæ in Scriptura authentica non modo nulla insalubria esse debent, sed nulla etiam à vero aliena; sive illam eruditionis gratiam, ob quam aliis versionibus præ- ferri hæc maxime debeat, imo ipsi textui Ebræo, quem etiam postponit Grotius. Dogmata à ve- ro aliena, imo insalubria, cum vitiis innumeris & enormibus eruditionis tantæ decori non conveni- entibus, in versione vulgari demonstrarunt pluri- mi, cum nostræ, tum Reformatæ partis Theolo- gi. Quæ persequuti etiam prolixe sumus in Critico sacro à pag. 502. ad 667. Errorum in fidem & mo- res impingentium, adeoque insalubrium, Novem ibi classes produximus, & inter eas, cum sub nomi- ne veritatis divinæ fabulæ & commenta obtrusa in Vulgata, credenda, cum falsæ opiniones incrustatæ, cum divinæ constitutiones labefactatæ, cum loca fidei enervata, cum hæreses confirmatæ. Nolumus actum agere.

§. III. Neque parum derogat huic encomio suo Grotius, quo dubio procul eandem, in gratiam authoritatis à Tridentino Concilio ipsi assignatæ, hoc est, authenticæ, mactavit, cum dicendi genus sa- tis horridum, & sensum minus clarum, qui ex Ebrai- cis libris, quales nunc habemus, aliisque versionibus cla- rior reddatur, agnoscit, & cum subinde eandem in annotatis corrigit, ac Ebræum textum præfert. Non conveniunt ista Concilii decreto, quod vult, ut vetus & vulgata versio in publicis lectionibus, dispu- tationibus, prædicationibus, aut EXPOSITIONI- BUS pro authentica habeatur, quam nemo QUOVIS PRÆTEXTU rejicere audeat vel præsumat. UL- LO prætextu dici debebat, ita de sensu decreti contentiones tantæ non fuissent exortæ. Cæte- rum sive illud absolute accipiatur, uti Menochius, à Grotio imprimis commendatus, cum Pineda, Gregorio de Valentia, Ludovico de Tena, accepit & accipiendum Cardinalium congregatio Anno CIƆ IƆ LXXVI. definivit; seu tantum restricte & comparate, ut respectu aliarum versionum hæc au- thentica & saltem in regulis fidei ac morum nunquam devia agnoscatur, quæ Bellarmini, Marianæ, Lin- dani & aliorum est interpretatio, quam etiam in- tendere videtur Grotius, cum versionem illam so- lum nulla insalubria, h. e. in fidem & mores impin- gentia dogmata continere affirmat, de qua diffe- renti Decreti explicatione acerrimæ concertatio- nes & pugnæ in Hispania, de quibus prolixe con- queritur Mariana Jesuita Hispanus tract. de vulg.

edit. cap. I. viguere, neque ulla à Papa fieri adhuc potuit decisio, ut nondum adeo in Papatu con- stet, anne habeant Biblia per omnia authentica, an vero minus solum, quam alii, corrupta? qualia ha- beri possunt, etiam in innumeris locis corruptis- sima sint. Quacunque tamen istud decretum inter- pretentur ratione, norma constituitur aliarum Ver- sionum textusq; Ebræi, qualis nunc habetur. Cui institutum Grotianum minime convenit. Quo- modo enim versio illa haberi potest pro aliarum versionum norma, aut Ebræo textui præferri, quæ modo ex Ebræo textu, modo ex aliis versionibus corrigenda est, indeque lucem mutuari necessum habet? Quia vero nonnunquam etiam corrigit Grotius Ebræum textum è Vulgata versione, addi- mus Joh. Drusii hac de re judicium: Non male, inquit, meo judicio, Patres Concilii Tridentini rece- perunt in scholis interpretem vulgatum. Nam ut er- rores aliquos habeat, habent & alii suos & fortasse plures, quam ille. Verum ex eo corrigere veritatem Hebraicam, si licet scapham scapham dicere, est cum ratione insanire. Nam ubi veritas, ibi nullus error, ubi nullus error, quid opus correctione? Aut igitur nulla est Veritas Hebraica (sic eam appellant Patres & Scholastici) aut ex eo emendari debet, quod male trans- latum. Saniores sunt ex ipsis Papistis non pau- ci, qui etiam post Concilium Tridentinum Ebrai- cam veritatem præferunt, &, ut ab istius fulmine tutis sibi esse liceat, hoc se tuentur scuto (quod quam securos ipsos præstet, aut præstare posset, hîc non est dicendi locus) non conferri cum textu Ebræo Vulgatam, nedum præferri eidem, compa- rari solum cum aliis Latinis translationibus, iisque meliorem censeri: Quod Alphonsus Salmero, unus è decem primis societatis JEsu Theologis & ex ipsis assessoribus concilii Tridentini, prolegom. in S. Evangel. Nicolaus Serarius, Julius Rugerius de libr. canon. Philippus Grammacheus, Valerianus Flavignius, Theologi Sorbonici, Johannes de Espie- res, Simeon de Muis, & alii asseruere. Expecta- tur & in hac causa adhuc è scrinio Papalis pecto- ris decisio.

§. IV. Ebræum textum distinguit Grotius, qualis nunc habetur opera Masoretarum, & qualem olim ha- buere LXX. Interpretes; cum Papistis modernum textum corruptionis postulans, quod passim in annotatis ejus videre est. At textum originalem & authenticum Scripturæ, quam Deus voluit perpe- tuam normam esse Ecclesiæ & fundamentum fidei, corruptum esse, corruptione universali, quæ omnes codices penetrarit, pugnat cum providentia di- vina, cum fine atque intentione Dei, & cum pro- testatione Christi Matth. V, 18. quod prius cœlum ac terram interire oporteat, quam vel unum jota aut minimus apex de Verbo Dei pereat. Tum si ante Hieronymi tempora corruptus textus Ebræus fuit, quomodo è corrupto textu versio incorrupta tran- sumi potuit? Si post Hieronymi tempora accidit corruptio, quod plerisque Papistis videtur, num malitia Judæorum, an vero sola incuria Librariorum eandem evenisse dicturus est Grotius? Illud si eli- gat, opponent alii è Pontificiis, Judæorum adver- sus libros sacros religionem, eorundemque per or- bem terrarum dispersionem, codicumque Christi- anorum multitudinem, ut neque voluerint, neque potuerint Judæi textum depravare, ac negotium erit ei cum Joh. Isaaco, Marco Marino, Francisco Rie- bera, Driedone, ipsoque Bellarmino. Sed non ar- guet, credo, Grotius Judæos perfidiæ, quibus plu- rimum ipse tribuit. Si autem incuria librariorum accidit corruptio, quî eadem in omnes codices ita penetrare potuit, ut nullum incorruptum exem- plar superet? Et quum textum, quem nunc habe- mus, operæ Masoretarum adscribat Grotius, quo- modo suspectum eundem reddet corruptionis? Masoretarum enim studium fuit, eundem ab omni corruptela vindicare, atque sincerum, & incorru- ptum ad posteritatem propagare, inde Masora סיג לתורה Sepes legis dicitur. Si forte cum Gordono Huntlæo fingat, Masoretas Judæos esse Tiberiades, quinti è nato Christo seculi, (quo etiam Ludovicus Capellus in Critico suo abripitur) refragatur com- mentum illud communi Ebræorum sententiæ, quum Elia Levita teste, Esdram, aliosque viros Synagogæ magnæ Masoram cepisse, unanimi suf- fragio asserant. Quo de prolixe Johann. Buxtorfius Senior in Tiberiade legi poterit. Huntlæi ineptias discussimus in Critico Sacro, ut & aliorum Papista- rum, qui Codices Ebræos post Hieronymi æta- tem depravationem passos criminantur, pag. 401. seqq. Ludovicum Capellum confutavit Johann. Buxtorfius Junior in Anti-Critico suo. Si ergo à Masoretis, hoc est ab Esdra, Haggæo, Zacharia, Malachia aliisque ὁμοχρόνοις profectus est textus, quem habemus, sacrosanctus & omni exceptione major nobis omnino esse debet. Quo loco etiam Cardinali Bellarmino Tikkum Sopherim, (si forte cum Galatino illas obvertat Grotius) habentur, quod non corruptio sint, (si fabula non sint) sed vera emendatio, non facta à quibuscunque scribis, sed ab Esdra & aliis sanctis Prophetis, qui post reditum à captivitate libros sacros reparaverunt. Unde in Ma- sora parva Numer. XII, 12. expresse תקון עצרים vocantur. Num Esdram aliosque sanctos Dei vi- ros textum corrupisse dicendum? Videatur de his Criticus noster pag. 387. ut & D. Glassius Philolog. Sacr. lib. 1. p. 39. & Joh. Buxtorfius apud eundem in addendis sub calcem lib. 1. p. 493. ubi mentem suam de Tikkum Sopherim rogatus explicavit. Coccejus ad Job. VII, 20. notat, nullam iisdem indigitari Scripturæ mutationem: Sed esse genus interpre- tationis, quum judicaverunt Veteres, Scripturam aliter loqui εὐφημίας ergo, quam instituta oratio po- stulabat: nec Ebræos omnes consentire, ut hoc quod censent legendum Veteres, in textu repona- tur. Quod per inductionem locorum ostendit, con- cludens, apparere inde Hebræos id vocare תִקּוּן διόρ- θωσιν Scribarum, quod nunc etiam scribitur, sive defle- xionem styli à suo ordine ad id, quod minus atrox: ita ut sit genus interpretationis, indicare hanc correctio- nem. Sixtinus ab Amama sane in Anti-Barb. Bibl. operose disputat p. 470. diversas lectiones per τὸ Keri & Kethib inferri, non quod utraque divinæ autoritatis sit, quod Amand. Polanus temere pro- pugnavit, sed quod marginalis lectio vel τὸ Keri uni- ce à Deo sit, sed seductus ille imprudenter ab auto- re arcani punctorum fuit, hoc est à Capello, cui alii etiam re non satis examinata applausere: quemad- modum ille à Judæis & Papistis se passus est seduci, unde etiam Papistarum causam agit, temporis lon- gitudine, exiliorum multitudine, & duratione, cala- mitatum variarum diritate, librorum varietate cor- ruptelas in fontes irrepsisse non abnuens, etsi addat, propter unum alterumve nævum (qui tamen ponen- dus in textu sacro minime erat) palmam pulcherri- mæ virgini (Scripturæ originali textui) auferri non posse, nedum alteri dari, quæ toto corpore defor- mis est (vulgatæ nempe versioni) imo protestetur se illam sententiam suam Reformatarum Ecclesia- rum judicio subjicere, neutiquam tergiversaturum eam retractare, si quid certius, & verius aliquis ostenderit. Sine dubio autem certiora & veriora ostenderunt Buxtorfius & Coccejus in hisce, quæ ad S. Linguam pariter & Scripturam Sacram per- tinent, tyroni illi Theologiæ, qui ad justam ma- turitatem non pervenit, ac fere tantum purus Grammaticus fuit, longe præferendi. Fontis Ebræi puritatem prolixe asferuimus libro citato à pag. 366. ad pag. 438. Non est, quod actum aga- mus. Adversus novissimas in Papatu molitiones contra Ebræam veritatem, quæ Johann. Morini fuere, Simeon de Muis, Professor Regius Parisien- sis, triplici assertione Veritatis Ebraicæ causam egit, quam Doctores in Facultat. Theologica Pa- ris. Sorbonici, Du Fresne de Minse, A. de Breda approbarunt, H. Bachelier Theologiæ Doctor Sor- bonicus vehementer laudavit, Valerius de Flavigni Facult. Theol. Paris. itidem Sorbonicus Doctor ita adornatam judicavit, ut de Sacro-sanctæ editio- nis Ebraicæ authentica veritate nullum posse imposte- rum, invitis etiam ejus obtrectatoribus, amplius du- bitare, pronunciarit. Quæ judicia cum operibus Muisii exhibuit Claudius de Avergne, Sacr. & Ebraic. literarum Parisiensis Professor Regius An- no cIɔ Iɔc. L.

§. V. Versionem LXX. Interpp. puriorem E- braico textu facere videtur Grotius, cum libros Ebraicos nos nunc ita non habere, quales olim habue- re illi, asserit, nec raro versionem Interpp. præ- fert. Nescio, an Johanni Morino Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero aures præbuerit, qui Græcam τῶν ἑδομήκοντα summopere extollit, eamque per Sixti V. autoritatem, qua, ut ab omnibus recipe- retur, neve quis addendo vel demendo aliquid in ea mutaret, diplomate cavit, Vulgatæ non improbali- liter æquari posse, existimat, Diatr. Elenctic. de au- torit. Ebraici Græcique textus pag. 233. At unde do- cebit Grotius, talem nunc haberi versionem illam Græcam, qualis olim ex Ebraico transumpta est; aut Ebræum textum ab eo corruptum esse potius, quam Græcam illam translationem? Quanquam vero editionem LXX. Interpp. ab Anton. Caraffa Cardinali procuratam, Sixtus V. magnopere lau- darit, Cardinal. Baronius etiam ceu opus divinum ac divinitus inspiratum in Appar. annalium numer. 119. applaudente Johann. Morino Exerc. IX. cap. 4. pag. 441. deprædicare non dubitarit, rationes ta- men Morinianæ nullius sunt momenti, nec sibi satis ipse constat, imo è præfatione Romanæ illi editioni præfixa Nicolaus Serarius plus, quam de- cem argumentis probavit, editionem illam non esse ipsam LXX. Interpp. versionem ubique pu- ram & incorruptam, nedum pro opere divino habendam; de quibus legi prolixe poterit Criticus noster Sacer à pag. 830. ad 840. Conferatur etiam hanc in rem Sylloge vindiciar. Dn. D. Dorschei in Exod. cap. 2. pag. 35. Invertenda omnino illatio Grotii fuerit, si à diversitate lectionis argumen- tum hîc petendum. Quia aliter non raro legit Græcus, quam Ebraicus textus, mutationem pas- sum Græcum esse, humana industria adornatum, non Ebræum codicem, quem divinitus inspiratum agnoscimus omnes: Quanquam diversitas illa quandoque inde profecta dicit possit, quod sen- sum assequuti non sint, aut non expresserint satis originalis textus. Conquestus est jam sua ætate Hieronymus, germanam & antiquam LXX. Senio- rum translationem corruptam atque violatam esse in præfat. Paral. imo nimis corruptam esse, Præfat. in Pentat. & quis nescit, eam sæpe ab Origene emendatam, à Justino illis antiquiore corruptionis, à Judæis factæ, accusatam? Habemus hîc confi- tentes Papistarum doctissimos; Andreas Masius præfat. in libr. Jos. in nulla sui parte vitium non fe- cisse fatetur. Bellarminus adeo corruptam & viola- tam superesse dicit, ut omnino alia esse videatur, ita ut jam tutum non sit, Ebraicos vel Latinos textus ex Græ- cis codicibus emendare. Illos potius consuluisse de- bebat Grotius, quam Morinum audaculum, qui tandem profitetur ipse, multas mendas in Græcam LXX. versionem irrepsisse, atque etiamnum inhærere. Quid, quod nonnullis è Judæis, notante R. Geda- lia, videatur, LXX. non ex lingua sancta, sed ex Sy- riaco exemplari in Græcum transtulisse. Joh. Buxtor- fius Filius in tractat. de punctis part. 1. c. 9. R. Asa- riæ sententiam, quod translatio illa è Chaldaica quadam versione facta sit, proposuerat: in Vindic. vero Veritatis Hebraic. part. II. c. II. p. 552. addit: Si ea sententia minus videatur veritati consentanea, fieri tamen posse, ut quandoque hujusmodi interpreta- tiones Chaldæas, quæ tum inter Judæos habebantur, consulerent, & forte sequerentur Septuaginta Inter- pretes: alii vero nonnulli recentiores Critici do- ctissimi, utpote Ludovicus de Dieu, in Matth. XIX, 5. Joh. Seldenus de mari claus. pag. 37. Joh. Heinricus Hottingerus in Thesaur. Philol. p. 262. ex Samarita- no codice Versionem Græcam adornatam esse cen- sent: quæ etiam Ghilhelmi Postelli in Tabul. lin- guar. Tab. II. est sententia. Hugoni nostro contra- rium placet ad c. XVII. Levit. v. 14. Confusæ, inquit, sunt duæ versiones: altera, quæ interpretamentum com- modum generalibus illis verbis adhibuerat; altera, quæ Hebræum κατὰ πόδας sequebatur: unde secuta repe- titio inanis, quæ & ex Græco LXX. in Samaritanum fluxit: Nam Samaritani, quos nunc habemus, Codices, facti sunt ad Græca exemplaria, ex quo Samaritani ab Justiniano coacti sunt suscipere Christianismum. Hæc

Grotius; quibus & Samaritani moderni codicis, à Morino nimium quantum celebrati, ab ipso etiam Grotio non semel lectioni Ebrææ præpositi, auto- ritatem non parum labefactat, & Græcæ LXX. In- terpp. versionis, quam nunc habemus, fidem admo- dum suspectam reddit. Nam si illa confusa est ex versionibus duabus quandoque, non potest indu- bie de vera lectione nos certos reddere. Quod cui- quam loco accidit, cuivis accidere potuit. Proba- bilior tamen Hottingeri opinio: è Samaritanis, aut aliis parum emendatis Codicibus versionem LXX. In- terpp. enatam. Alexandrinos nempe Judæos, quo- rum opera ornata illa versio, non habuisse Ebræos codices, quos Judæi Hierosolymitani emenda- tiores asservarint, & ob simultates & odia Alexan- drinis non communicarint, sed mendosiores Sama- ritanos, aut alios. Conferantur, quæ de versione LXX. Interpp. uberius diximus in Critico sacro. Ibi enim hypothesibus Grotianis, quas de versionis τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα autoritate, quum eam Ebræo tex- tui non raro præferat, fovisse videtur, nervum, nisi fallimur, incidimus: ac prolixe de autoribus ejus- dem, an nempe autoritate Philadelphi per Demetrium ea procurata, à LXXII, Senioribus adornata, quod illustris Scaliger inficiatur, an exemplar archetypum adhibitum, an approbata à Judæis translatio, quo in censu habita sit penes Ecclesiam Christianam, & veteres Dd. & cumprimis, quid de Apostolica alle- gatione habendum? tractavimus, locis, quibus non sequuntur Apostoli LXX. Interpp. etsi cum Ebræo consentientes, tum quibus eosdem à textu He- bræo haud discrepantes, nec non quibus Ebræum potius textum, quam LXX. Interpp. ab eodem de- flectentes sequuti sunt, in medium adductis, variis- que erroribus LXX. Interpp. & discrepantiis à vul- gata versione, cum vanissima conciliationis Morini qui contradictorie opposita etiam componere sat- agit, examine, ac discussione, demonstratis: Sub- juncta denique dissertatione de existentia & fince- ritate Versionis LXX. Interpp. Quæ ante XXX. an- nos jam expedita, Pseudo - Criticis adhuc expen- denda relinquimus, ut desinant versionem illam pro diversa Ebræi textus lectione venditare, Co- dicisque antiqui autoritatem eidem adscribere. Si omnino è textu Ebræo versionem suam adornas- sent Græci, si LXXII. Seniores translationi, uti creditur, adhibiti fuissent, quod utrumque admo- dum dubium & incertum, si etiam translatio eo- rum genuina adhuc superaret, prout à manibus ipsorum prodiit, quod haud concedent, qui au- thenticum exemplar cum Bibliotheca Ptolomei exercitus Pompeji incendio absumptum, apogra- pha tum Judæorum, tum hæreticorum culpa, ma- xime vero scribarum imperitia, temeritate, auda- cia, ἀβλεψίᾳ & ἀκρισίᾳ, accedente imprimis etiam aliarum Græcarum versionum varietate, & Hexa- plorum Origenis, ac interpretationum Theodo- tionis, Symmachi, aliorum confusione, (quam non diffitetur Grotius) corrupta censent: (qui- bus medelam sufficientem nequicquam à Caraffæ opera expectes; ) si nullæ suppeterent diversæ in ipsa LXX. Interpp. translatione lectiones, uti omni- no variæ supersunt; Dubium tamen adhuc esset, an codice punctato usi fuerint LXX. nec ne, quod qui puncta recens inventum Judæorum faciunt, quod omnino contendit Capellus, non abnuente Grotio, affirmare non possunt; neque aliis sit verisi- mile; quod nimis manifestum passim sit, pro judi- cio proprio puncta addidisse autores istius transla- tionis; Dubium etiam esset, an exemplar, quo usi sunt, per omnia sincerum, & ab omnibus prorsus erroribus, qui per incuriam librariorum facile sub- repunt, immune fuerit; Dubium, anne varietates illæ, quæ inter Ebræum textum, quem habemus, & translationem reperiuntur, sæpe ex ipsorummet translatorum mente, & judicio potius, quam è di- versa Codicum istius temporis lectione profectæ sint, imo in ipsis Interpretibus causæ variæ hîc dari possunt, quarum nonnullas quum non abs re cum aliis Criticis assignarit Joh. Buxtorfius Filius vindic. veritat. Ebraic. part. II. cap. VIII. pag. 55. eas hîc adscribere juvat: Tertio ergo, inquit, causam præci- puam (Critici) ponunt in ipsis Interpretibus, qui 1. si- militudine literarum & Elementorum, quod in MM. SS. facillimum, decepti aliter quædam interpretati sint. 2. quædam non recte assequentes, in mente sua aliter legerunt, non in suo codice: 3. Grammaticæ, quæ tum nulla forte adhuc habebatur, non satis periti, nec ad ejus leges attendentes, affinibus vocibus & ver- bis easdem significationes attribuerunt, & quæ diversa sunt, pro iisdem & idem significantibus acceperunt: 4. quibusdam vocibus peculiares significationes attri- buerunt, unde sit, ut, cum illæ hodie ignotæ sint, ali- ud legisse existimentur. 5. quæ metaphorice dictæ sunt, in proprias, quas sibi videbantur habere, locutiones re- solverunt. 6. in multis sæpe divinabant, ut nullum in ipsis judicium appareat, &, quam causam hîc verten- di habuerint, prorsus ignoretur. 7. ea libertate aut licentia potius usi sunt, ut pro suo arbitrio quædam nonnunquam Textui, ceu expositionis loco adderent, quædam etiam pro suo arbitrio detraherent, & omit- terent. 8. sæpissime sensum, non verba & literam red- diderunt. 9. etiam ex imperitia multa commiserunt, cujus rei innumera vestigia in illa versione deprehensa & animadversa sunt à Viris doctis. Hæc ille. Hiero- nymus certe non raro simile de ipsis judicium tulit, ubi modo male eos transtulisse, modo similitudine literarum eos deceptos fuisse, modo sensum magis, quam verba spectasse, observavit.

§. VI. Versiones aliorum Græcorum & Chal- dæorum, nec non è recentioribus Tigurinam & Tremellianam quod adhibuerit Grotius, non im- probamus. Modo Chaldæas Veteres & versio- nes recentioris ævi Christianas potius, quam Judæos nuperos, Christiani nominis hostes, sequu- tus fuisset. Belgicæ translationi Belga ipse locum nullum dedit, abs qua in plerisque oraculis Pro- pheticis rectius informari poterat, nisi ἰουδαΐζειν maluisset.

§. VII. Id vero hic in limine etiam haud ne- gligendum, quod Grotius, cum versiones confert LXX. Interpp. aliorum Græcorum, Chaldæorum, Arabicas aut alias, vel etiam Pentateuchum Samari- tanum, non dubitet lectionem, quæ in illis reperi- tur, præferre quandoque textui Ebræo, sine auto- ritate vel suffragio ullius Ebræi Codicis, aut ex proprio ingenio lectionem novam comminisci: unde haud obscure colligitur, eundem à Pseudo- Critico illo nupero Ludovico Capello Salmuriensi Professore seductum esse, aut certe alioquin com- munes cum ipso fovisse hypotheses: Laudat enim vehementer Capellæ Criticum in Epistola ad ipsum data, quæ in volum. Epistolar. ad Gallos CLXXXI. est, una cum arcano punctuationis: Sicut autem in eo labore (de Arcano revelato loquitur) alios qui te præcesserant, ita in sacra Critice, etiam istum laborem tuum superasti. In quo nescio magisne indefessam se- dulitatem mirari debeam, an uberrimam eruditio- nem, an judicium limatissimum; quæ tres laudes in hoc opere ita inter se certant, ut in ambiguo maneat, cui de tribus prima palma debeatur. Sunt quidem nonnulla, ut recte notasti, εὐδιάβλητα, sed omnibus placere, nemini datum est, minime vero iis, qui supra vulgus sapiunt. Contentus ergo esto magnis potius, quam multis laudatoribus. Neq; desperandum tamen, quin, quod in aliis rebus sæpe, in hac quoque eveniat, ut paucos eminentes sequantur & illi, qui tantum ad nu- merum valent. Ego & tibi & iis, per quos opus tuum ad meas pervenit manus, plurimum me debere profiteor. Et in notis hisce provocat ad Capelli Criticum, quem tredecim annis, antequam emitteretur, ma- nuscriptum legerat Grotius ad c. V. Gen. v. 18. De multis discrepantiis, quæ in hoc & sequentibus Capiti- bus circa numeros annorum apparent in Codicibus He- bræis, Samaritanis, Græcis, nihil melius, quod dicam, habeo, quam quæ dixit in Critico sacro eruditissimus Capellus. Sumam hypothesium, quæ non usque ad- eo hic notæ sunt, ex Critico isto his omnino verbis proposuit J. Buxtorf. in dedicat. Anti-Critici.

Ni- mirum fingitur, literas veteres Mosaicas esse mutatas, & quas hodie habemus, esse Assyriacas, ab Esdra de- mum post captivitatem Babylonicam Judæis traditas, prioribus illis genuinis Samaritis relictis: Puncta voca- lia, quæ codicibus Hebraicis hodie sunt adscripta, neque esse ab Autoribus sacris ipsis, vel aliis Viris Propheticis, neque etiam veram, primam & genuinam Lectionem repræsentare, sed esse demum 500. circiter post Chri- stum annis, à quibusdam Masoretis Tiberiensibus ex- cogitata, & pro suo judicio & arbitratu addita & ad- scripta: Hinc Codex sacer Hebraicus per contemtum & ludibrium vocatur subinde Judaicus & Masoreti- cus: Codices Hebraicos idem, quod reliqui autores ve- teres omnes, fatum expertos, ut per librariorum sive scribarum desidiam, somnolentiam, ignorantiam, aut vero etiam temeritatem & audaciam correctorum, plurima in illos variæ Lectiones, hoc est, mutationes & errores irrepserint: imo nullam aliam nec esse, nec po- tuisse esse librorum horum conditionem, quam omni- um in universum librorum cæterorum: Divinam providentiam non magis pro conservandis intemeratis codicibus sacris invigilasse, quam pro cæteris omne ge nus libris & autoribus: & sufficere; quod illos non passus sit ulla hominum vel fraude vel vi, aut malitia technisve vel aboleri, vel ita corrumpi, ut ex iis since- ra, pura atque incorrupta salutis doctrina hauriri non possit: Multa quippe esse in Scriptura non momentosa, in quibus perinde sit, quomodocunque legas. Nul- lum haberi certum Codicem, ad quem in discrepantiis Interpretum, & locis de vera lectione controversis, possit recurri, neque talem esse codicem Hebraicum: imo nec necesse esse, ut talis aliquis Codex authenticus extet & habeatur: Loca Scripturæ Parallela, inter se discrepantia, vel secumpugnantia, arguere alterius ex illis mutationem & corruptionem: Veterum Interpre- tum ab Hebræo Codice discrepantes Versiones sæpissime atq; adeo infinitis in locis provenisse ex discrepantia & varietate codicis Hebraici, quo in vertendo sunt usi, ac proinde varias Lectiones dicendas, cum nostrorum li- brorum lectione conferendas, sæpissime etiam præfe- rendas esse: Totidem hinc dicendos esse codices Hebrai- cos, quot sunt Veteres Interpretes ab hodierna lectione recedentes: Totum Scripturarum authenticarum corpus diffusum & permixtum esse, tum in Hebrai- cis fontibus, tum in quibuslibet Translationum rivu- lis: Translationes omnes, una cum Textu Originali, pariter esse authenticas, sacras, divinas, θεοπνεύσας: Ad veram lectionem percipiendam conferendos esse omnes Interpretes, & ex illis demum eam eruendam, divinandam & colligendam: Discrepantes Interpre- tationes non esse ad Textum Ebraicum hodiernum exigendas & conferendas, sed in illis discrepantiis de vera lectione esse judicandum ex nostra ratione & quam hæc nobis dictat lectionem, eam esse præferen- dam, in quocunque demum Codice reperiatur: Non solum licitum esse aliquando conjecturas novas facere de vera lectione, sed & utile, atq; adeo etiam aliquan- do necessarium id esse, propter multa ἄπορα, ἀδιάλ- λακτα, id est, insolubilia & irreconciliabilia loca, quæ alia ratione conciliari nequeant, quam levem admit- tendo errorem, eumque tali conjectura corrigendo; imo in quibusdam locis agnoscendum etiam esse errorem Scriptorum Sacrorum ipsorum, quatenus illi homi- nes infirmi fuerunt: Nec debere apud nos fixum ra- tumq; esse, omnia, etiam minimas voces, dictiones & literas in Scripturæ textu Originali esse ab in- terno ἐνθεσιασμῷ Spiritus Sancti. Hactenus Bux- torfius. Audiamus Criticum ipsum: Statuendum, inquit, & concedendum est, (quod negari non potest) codicem hodiernum Judaicum & codicem Samariii- cum cæterosq; codices, ex quibus factæ sunt Transla- tiones omnes veteres esse sacrorum librorum totidem diversos codices, variis lectionibus inter se discrepan- tes: Item: Non est autem vera, bona & commoda le- ctio in uno tantum codice quærenda, puta hodierno Ju- daico, sed modo in hoc, modo in illo, modo in alio, hoc est, uno in loco commodior lectio invenietur in hodierno Ja- daico, alio in loco invenietur in Codice Samaritico, alio in loco in translatione τῶν LXX. alio in loco in Para- phrasiis Chaldæis, & sic de cæteris antiquis interpreti- bus; Imo contendit; hodiernum textum Ebræum non esse alia ratione, neque alia de causa præferendum vel Samaritico vel alii cuilibet, nisi qua & quatenus ostendi potest, sensum, qui oritur ejus lectione, esse ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ meliorem & convenientiorem eo, qui na- scitur ex lectione aliorum Codicum. Itaque sicubi de- monstrari potest, lectionem, quæ est in Codice Samariii- co, vel quam sequuti sunt LXX. Interpp. aut Chaldæus Paraphrastes, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, vel Hieronymus, congruenttiorem fundere sensum, & an- tecedentibus, consequentibus, totiq; Scripturæ analogiæ magis cohærentem, neminem tam iniquum esse debere, ut istum non potius amplectatur, atq; una lectionem, quæ sensum illum ex se fundat. Hæc omnia Capel- lus.
