IX, 17, expresses emphatically; from which passage the blessed Luther collects in his Commentary on Genesis, p. 56: Therefore it was necessary for the Son of God to become a victim, so that he might accomplish these things for us, that he might take away sin, devour death, and restore the lost obedience. these treasures in Christ, but in hope. Thus Adam, thus Eve, thus all believers up to the last day, live and conquer by that hope. Nor do Orthodox theologians, B. Gerhard and others, interpret the bruising of our Ophiomachus, the Messiah, in the heel, without reason as referring to the crucifixion, in which the feet of Christ were fixed to the cross with nails. Nor indeed does the blessed Polycarp Lyserus teach that the genuine meaning concerning the σωτηρίῳ passion of Christ was hidden from the Patriarchs, as he excellently shows in his Commentary, p. 284. Concerning the office of this Mediator, we know that he is about to deliver us through his passion and death: for thus we understand that saying: you shall bruise his heel: But did Adam also understand this? Entirely. For that reason he taught his sons to sacrifice: And Noah also opposes a sacrifice to the wrath of God. But that sacrifices were types and figures of the passion of Christ, Paul teaches clearly in various places, and most especially in the Epistle to the Hebrews. That the Fathers therefore understood the bruising of the heel in the same way as we do, they demonstrated by their sacrifices. And what else do those mystical prophecies of Jacob concerning Shiloh, Gen. 49, 11, mean: he shall wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the Grape, than that he was about to shed his blood copiously, and with it to dye his body, which is as it were the garment of the Deity, which commentary of the Orthodox is confirmed not obscurely by Isa. 63, 1 and Rev. 19, 13; therefore Justin Martyr, Apol. II for the Christians: The Word, washing his stole in the blood of the grape, foretold the passion of Christ, which he was about to undergo, cleansing and purifying for himself those who believe in him through his blood, etc. What is Calixtus going to say about Job's profession of faith concerning the Goël, which without doubt, before the Psalms of David, and if faith is to be placed in the Hebrews and Origen, was committed to writing or translated by Moses himself? which St. Jerome celebrates with his own merit in Epist. LI to Pammachius. Christ the Lord was not yet dead, and the Athlete of the Church saw his Redeemer rising from the dead. What about the manifold types of sacrifices, the ram offered in place of Isaac, the paschal lamb, the scapegoat, the red heifer, the bronze serpent, as also of the Patriarchs, Adam falling asleep, Isaac being sacrificed, Joseph sold by his brothers, Moses cast into the river, Gideon likewise, Samson, and other Judges of the Jews, concerning whom Jerome writes learnedly in Ep. CIII to Paul. In the book of Judges, there are as many figures as there are princes of the people. But these and many more of this kind we cannot now pursue, as is proper: however, it pleases me to append an excellent passage of Irenaeus concerning the writings of Moses, for the sake of Calixtus, from book IV, ch. XXIII. The Son of God is sown everywhere in the Scriptures of Moses, sometimes indeed speaking with Abraham, sometimes about to eat with the same, sometimes however bringing judgment upon the Sodomites, and again when he is seen, and directs Jacob on his way, and speaks with Moses from the bush. And it is impossible to count the number of places in which the Son of God is shown by Moses, whose day of passion he also did not ignore, but foretold him in a figure, naming him the Passover, and the Lord suffered on that very same day which had been predicted by Moses so long before, fulfilling the Passover. But he not only described the day, but also the place from the extremity of the times, and the sign of the setting of the sun, saying, you shall not be able to sacrifice the Passover in any other of your cities, which the Lord your God gives you, except in that place which the Lord your God shall choose for his name to be invoked there. You shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening at the setting of the sun. And what need is there of more? Does not Christ himself clearly say in Ps. 40, 8, Behold I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me, ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίῳ, as the Holy Spirit explains in Heb. 10, 7 (which, whether you take it as the book of Genesis with Jerome in his Hebrew Traditions on Genesis, or as Holy Scripture in general with others, without doubt includes the books prior to the Psalms of David), I do your will willingly; Which is that very will by which, having been performed, we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ once made, figured by the offerings of the Old Testament, as interpreted by the Holy Spirit in Heb. 10, 10, etc.

Concerning the Interpreters of Moses, there is still more to be said. But besides those who have commented on the whole of Scripture, or at least on the Old Testament, others have devoted some effort to the Pentateuch, among the Jews Agathobulus, and also Aristobulus the Elder 350 years before Christ, Aristobulus the Younger 215 years before Christ, who wrote in the Greek language on the Pentateuch of Moses: whose aim was to show that the entire Peripatetic Philosophy had been drawn from the law of Moses. See Clem. Alexandr. book V, Stromata; Eusebius, book VIII, on the Preparation for the Gospel. Among the Rabbis, R. Abraham Hispanus, R. Bechai, R. Mose Hadarschan, R. Ezechias (under the title Candelabrum of Light), R. Isaac Ben Arama (he entitles it The Binding of Isaac). Another, whose Cabbalistic Commentary is the Zohar; Another whose vague commentary is called Tanchuma; R. Menasse Ben Israel published reconciliations through questions on the five books of Moses.

Among Christian Doctors, after Cyril of Alexandria, who around the year of Christ 430 composed an allegorical work on the Pentateuch, are celebrated Erhard the Benedictine Monk around the year of the Lord 1050 for his commentary on the Pentateuch, as also Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne, and likewise Alan of Lille, who, having obtained the surname of Universal Doctor for his all-encompassing erudition in all things, wrote commentaries on the Pentateuch in the year of the Lord 1300, and his contemporary Albert of Padua, who commented on the five books of Moses in the Scholastic manner; John Zacharias wrote on the Pentateuch in the year 1460. Benedict Stendal of Halle published five books of Scholastic Explanations on the Pentateuch in the year 1470: Paul Ricius, a converted Jew, composed one book concerning the six hundred and thirteen edicts of the Mosaic sanction or Pentateuch in the year 1500. Augustinus Steuchus, Eugubinus, in the year 1540, adorned his annotations on the Pentateuch, diligently explaining Hebrew locutions, as well as the Cosmopoeia in the first three chapters of Genesis. Hieronymus ab Oleastro in the year 1556 likewise carefully expounded the Hebrew text: Jac. de Lusanna wrote scholastically on the Pentateuch, as did Matthaeus Ebroicensis. In the Twelve-Volume Bibles, these authors are presented on the Pentateuch according to alphabetical order: Ambrose, Augustine, Cyril, Alexander, Gregory the Great, Isidore, Origen, Procopius, Rabanus, Rupert, and Theodoret, who, along with Strabo’s ordinary gloss and the interlinear postil of Anselm of Laon, were employed in that work alongside the editions of Burgensis and the replies of Doring on the Pentateuch, although most of these contributed at least some particles or sentences. But as to which of our own are to be added, or rather preferred, if you depart from the Fathers: B. Luther, Brentius, Osiander, the Weimar commentators, and other universal commentators and paraphrasts, as well as Erasmus Marbachius, and also Christophorus Pelargus, who particularly illustrated the Pentateuch. Among the Reformed are celebrated John Calvin, and Francis Junius, Ainsworth the Englishman (who adorned his annotations in the English language), Drusius,

Sixtinus ab Amama, who wrote on the Pentateuch, and Willet the Englishman, who wrote on Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. Some more recent Roman Catholic scholars also deserve praise for their diligence, erudition, and excellent judgment, especially Jacob Bonfrerius and Leonhardus Marius, following Cornelius a Lapide, who was praised above. And so much for the Interpreters.

The distribution of the Mosaic writings into five books is rightly attributed to Moses himself by Philo; in these, first in GENESIS is the planting and propagation of the Church. Then in EXODUS, its protection and governance in Egypt and the desert: Furthermore, in LEVITICUS, the ecclesiastical constitution: then in the book of NUMBERS, the political administration: Finally, in DEUTERONOMY, the further confirmation of the ecclesiastical and political hierarchy is exhibited. Lyranus proceeds thus: It must be known that the law was not given to one person, but to a community of gathered people: therefore, first, the gathering of the faithful people under the worship of one God is described, which is done in the book of Genesis. Second, the legislation is described, and this is done in Exodus and the two following books; Third, the repetition and explanation of the aforementioned law is set forth, and this is done in Deuteronomy.

Mosaic history can be distributed by dichotomy in this way: that it describes both the Patriarchal Church before Moses, in the first book, or Genesis: and the Israelite Church under Moses, in the remaining four books: and that partly as the first promulgation of the law, and partly as the repetition of the law. Exodus exhibits the first promulgation of the law in general, and the state of the Israelites up to the erection of the Tabernacle: In particular, however, Leviticus sets forth the τάξιν ἱερατικὴν (priestly order) and ecclesiastical matters or sacred law after the Tabernacle was erected, up to the numbering of the people: But the book of NUMBERS orders and sanctions the political governance by certain specific degrees, functions, and classes, so that a fixed seat for the Church might be established, with the enumeration of the people and the stations in the desert, and thus in this book the itinerary of the Israelites is exhibited through the space of almost 39 years of nomadic pilgrimage. Finally, the repetition and confirmation of the law is had in Deuteronomy, which is a certain commentary on the law, or a book of digests of Israelite Law, with the deeds of a few days from the beginning of the eleventh month up to the seventh day of the twelfth month, of the fortieth year from the exodus.

The entire Pentateuch comprises a history of 2252 years, from the beginning of the world up to the end of the public mourning for the death of Moses. And so much in general about the Pentateuch. Now some things must also be prefaced in particular regarding GENESIS: but very briefly, concerning the names of the book, its object, scope, time of writing, chronology, distribution, and its interpreters.

ON GENESIS.

Latin:

N. J. [---]AM CALOVII [---]A AD PENTATEU- [---]M MOSIS.

aquis extrahere 2. Sam. 22, 16. Non autem opus est, ut dicamus filiam Regis ei nomen dedisse in sua lingua, quod Ebræi postea in suam verterint, uti ex Aben Ez- ra refert Münsterus, quod lingua Ægyptiaca voca- tum statuat מניוס Monjos, quod Ebraice sonet משוי. Non enim ignara erat ilia linguæ Ebrææ, unde Ebræo puero non Ægyptium, sed Ebræum no- men potius imposuit.

Libri Mosis quinq; Ebræis dicuntur חֲמִשָּׁה חֻוּמָשִׁים quinque quintæ : quia quilibet liber Mosis חֹומֶשׁ vocatur, notante Hottingero in Thes. Phil. p. 460: una quinta legis pars. Græcis πεντάτευχον, vel ġ πεν- τάτευχος (sc. βίβλιος) a τεύχω struo vocantur, q. d. Quinstructuram seu scriptum in quinq; volumina distributum. In Sacris Pentateuchus vocatur תּוֹרָה lex, & liber legis, liber legis Mosis, 2. Par. 25, 4. 34, 14. Esdr. 6, 18. Neh. 11, 1. Luc. 24, 44. ut & liber fœderis Ex. 24, 7. 2. Reg. 23, 21. 2. Par. 24, 30.

De autoritate divina & Canonica librorum Mosis, de antiquitate, & quod Moses non quidem primus Scriptor ἁπλῶς fuerit: sed initium tamen Scripturæ Canonicæ inter viros θεοπνεύsτες fecerit, nec non de Monumentis Mosaicis, quod hæc ipsa Scriptura, quam Mosaicam dicimus, Pentateuchus nempe a Mose profecta, deniq; de Scopo Mosis præ- cipuo diximus in Prolegom. Comment. ad Genesin. Ex- cellentiam Mosi singularem conciliarunt (1) miracu- losa ex aquis extractio, (2) Regia a Filia Pharaonis in aula Regia Educatio Ex. II. & (3) in omni sapientia Egyptiaca informatio Actor. 7, 22, (4) Illustris e ru- bo ardenti ab ipso DEI Filio αὐτοπρωσόπως facta vocatio. (5) Donorum necessariorum cum virtute θαυματυργικῇ plane inusitata ad legationem sole- mnissimam, nec minus eminentissimam concessio, ut esset δυνατὸς ἐν λόγοις καὶ ἐν ἔργοις, Ex. 3. & 4. capp. Act. 7, 22. (6) Populi Israelitici ex Ægypto li- beratio & eductio. (7) Ejusdem miraculosa per ma- re rubrum deductio. (8) Imperatoria potestas in po- pulum Domini universum, ejusdemq; Theocratica gubernatio. (9) Singularissima Dei revelatio, qua non ut cum aliis servis suis Deus, sed eminentiori ratio- ne, ac longe familiarius cum Mose servo suo in tota domo sua, universa Israelis Ecclesia, fideli, Ebr. 2, 2. egit, seq; eidem פֶּה אֶל פֶּה ab ore ad os cum ipso colloquendo manifestavit, Num. 12, 7. seq. (10) Diuturna, & iterata cum Deo in monte conver- satio, qua per 40. dies & noctes binis vicibus DEO adfuit, Ex. 24, 18. c. 34, 28. unde facies ejus adeo co- ruscavit, ut splendorem ejus Israelitæ ferre nequi- verint. (11) Tabularum legis, quibus Decalogus a DEO inscriptus fuit, a Deo acceptio. (12) Legum di- vinarum authentica consignatio. (13.) Summi Sacer- dotis investitura, & ordinatio Lev. 8. (14.) Taberna- culi fœderis erectio. (15.) Serpentis ænei in deserto ex- altatio Num. 21. (16.) Regis Amorrhæorum, & Regis Basan devictio. (17.) Legis divinæ repetitio, Deut. 1. (18.) Divina Mosis sepelitio, Deut. 34. (19.) Mosis re- suscitati in cœlum evectio, quæ facta videtur brevi post sepulturam, cum Diabolus corpus ejus ad idolola- triam prostituere vellet, unde increpatus non tan- tum a Michaele Archangelo fuit, sed subductum etiam corpus Mosis in cœlum, utpote in quo con- spectus ipse est in gloria in transfiguratione Christi

Matth. 17, 3. cum Elia Propheta. Cæterum ad divinissimum & sanctissimum o- pus PENTATEUCHI non voluntate propria ac- cessit, sed mandato divino instructus Ex. 34, 27. & motu Spiritus Sancti interno agitatus 2. Petr. 1, 21. 2. Tim. 3, 16. Cujus θεοπνευστίας & autoritatis divinæ non tantum in ipsis Mosaicis Scriptis testis DEUS ipse frequenter introducitur, sed etiam in aliis Scri- pturis S. per totum Codicem Vet. & Novi Testam. & evincit eandem tum rerum ipsarum, quas exhi- bet, conditio, utpote Historia creationis, lapsus, Prot-Evangelii, gestorum ante diluvium, in dilu- vio, & post diluvium, qua propagationem genti- um, confusionem linguarum, vitas Patriarcharum, legum divinarum promulgationem, oracula, & vaticinia divina, & alia, quæ aliunde habere non potuit, nisi e divina revelatione, tum sermonis di- divini character indubitans, ut alia interna κριτήρια taceamus. Exotica de Mose testimonia in proleg. ci- tat. adduximus ex Eupolemo, quod Moses Propheta fuerit, & primus sapiens; ex Artapano, quod permul- ta humano generi utilissima tradiderit, & Mercurius ob S. literarum interpretationem appellatus parem superis honorem retulerit; e Numenio, quod preces e- jus apud DEUM potentissimæ fuerint, quibus gravissi- mas quasque calamitates in Ægyptum invexerit; e Ma- hummedanis, utpote Beidavi, quod solus ille cum DEO loquutus sit, ut & Kessæo, quod lex filiis Israel de- missa sit liber DEI ejusque verbum; ex Alcorano ipso, quod Moses cum DEO loquutus sit, & lex Mosis liber sit, qui facem præfert in religione &c. Orpheus apud Euseb. l. XIII. Præpar. Evangel. cap. 12. juxta emen- dationem Scaligeri, & approbationem Grotii in an- not. ad libr. I. de verit. Relig. Christ. ita de Mose cecinit: Ὡς λόγος ἀρχαίων, ὡς ὑδογενὴς διέταξεν, Ἐκ θεόθεν γνώμαισι λαβὼν κατὰ δίπλακα θεσμὸν, Ut veterum fama est, ut jussit flumine natus, Dona DEI tabulas geminas qui sensibus hausit.

Polemonem Africanus, & ex Africano Eusebius in Chronicis adducit, de exitu ex Ægypto ita testan- tem: Ἐπί Ἄπιδος τοῦ Φωρωνέως μοῖρα τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων στρατοῦ ἐξέπεσον Αἰγύπτου, οἱ ἐν τῇ Παλαιστίνῃ λεγο- μένῃ Συρίᾳ οὐ πόῤῥω Ἀραβίας ᾤκησαν. Regnante Apide Phoronei filio pars exercitus Ægyptiaci Ægypto exiit, habitaruntque illi in ea Syria, quæ Palæstina dici- tur, ab Arabia non longe. Josephus vero contra Ap- pionem de eodem exitu laudat ex Ægyptiis ipsis Manethonem, Lysimachum, Chæremonem, etsi falsa veris miscentes, e quibus constat, Ebræos ab Assyriis ortos parte Ægypti potitos: ibi pastoralem egisse vitam: sed operis postea servilibus pressos, exiisse ex Ægypto, Ægyptiis etiam quibusdam ipsos comitantibus Mose duce, perque Arabum terras postremo pervenisse in Sy- riam Palæstinam, ibique instituta eos sequutos Ægyptio- rum institutis contraria. Diodorus Siculus inter eos, qui DEOS autores legibus suis inscripserint Mosen hisce verbis refert l. 1. παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δὲ Μωσῆν τὸν Ἰάω ἐπικαλούμενον Θεὸν, Mosen apud Judæos DEUM, qui Jao vocatur. Nomen tetragrammatum יהוה respicit. Justinus Parænesi ad Græcos præter Dio- dorum Siculum, & Polemonem nominat & Appio- nem, Ptolemeum, Mendesium, Hellanicum, Philocho- rum, Castorem, Thallium, Alexandrum Polyhistorem. Conf. & Cyrillus l. I. contra Julian. Strabo l. XVI. do- cet a Mose sacra instituta, & ritus nec impensis gravia, nec limfatico furore odiosa. Præcepta ei haud obscu- ra divina tribuens. Juvenalis, Judaicum, inquit, ediscunt & servant, & metuunt jus.

Tradidit arcano quodcunque volumine Moses.

Dionysius Longinus, qui tempore Aureliani Impera- toris vixit, in libro de sublimi dicendi genere Mosen hoc modo in exemplum sistit, qua ratione de DEO lo- quentes id operam dare debeant, ut eum nobis magnum sincerumque & impermixtum exhibeant. Sic egit, in- quit, & is, qui Judæis leges condidit, vir minime vul- garis ingenii, ut qui potestatem DEI digne & concepe- rit, & elocutus fuerit, statim in principio legum hæc scri- bens, Dixit, ait, DEUS. Quid? Fiat lux, & facta est, Fiat terra, & facta est. Chalcidius de Mose, Sapien- tissimus, inquit, Moses, non humana facundia, sed di- vina, ut ferunt, inspiratione vegetatus.

De Objecto & Scopo præcipuo Mosis egimus in programmate quodam Academico, quod hîc subjicere placet: Quemadmodum universæ Scripturæ Sacræ tam Propheticæ, quam Apostolicæ σκοπὸς σκοπιμώτα- τος, principium & finis, Α & Ω est Christus θεάν- θρωπος: ita præcipue de Christo passio ejus saluti- fera in Scriptura utriusque fœderis a sanctis DEI vi- rit tradita est, & proposita; ut pie dixerit Theolo- gus quidam Scripturam ita legendam esse, ac si sangui- ne Christi scripta foret. Ut enim in Novo Testamen- to Apostolorum Coryphæus nihil aliud se scire pro- fessus est, nisi Jesum Christum, eumque crucifixum 1. Cor. 2, 2. Ita in Veteri Spiritus Christi, qui in Pro- phetis fuit, prænunciavit eas, quæ in Christo sunt, pas- siones & posteriores glorias, S. Petro teste 1. Ep. 1, 11. Nec vero par erat de illo tacere, in quo unice salus sita omnium, cujus cognitione atque fide non mi- nus Veteres justificati sunt, quam nos hodie Novi fœderis tempore. Cognitione sui justificabit ipse justus Servus meus multos, ait, Es. c. 53, 11. Quænam illa cognitio justi servi alia est, quam de qua ibi ex instituto Propheta, & tam clare vaticinatus est, ut Evangelista Hieronymo atque Augustino dici merue- rit, passionis scil. atque mortis ipsius, quemadmodum ilico addita docet ratio; Et iniquitates ipsorum ipse portabit. Quia ideo factus est ipse peccatum pro no- bis, ut reddamur in ipso justitia 2. Cor. 5, 21. Quæ unica justificationis & fidei justificantis ratio pro- posita est in Scriptura, ut præter illam excogitari alia non possit, nisi universa Scriptura evertatur. Ut mirari satis nequeant pie docti, quo Spiritu agi- tatus (non certe Spiritu CHRISTI, qui in Prophetis fuit) inter alia φορτικὰ ἀκούσματα CHRISTI glo- riam miris modis obfuscatia Calixtus effutierit in der Widerlegung th. 19. nihil de passione Christi legi in libris prioribus Psalmis Davidis; Von Esaia ist auch das Leiden und Sterben Messiæ deutlicher pro- phezeyet, als vorhero geschehen, davon ehe David sei- ne Psalmen geschrieben, in vorigen Büchern nichts zu lesen. Quid enim hoc aliud est, quam in os con- tradicere Spiritui S. qui luculentissime de passione Christi a MOSE æque ut a cæteris Prophetis prædi- cta testificatus est. Act. 10, 38. & imprimis Act. 26, 22. ubi Paulus λευκάδι φωνῇ profitetur, sese nihil ex- tra ea dixisse, quæ locuti sint Prophetæ futura & Mo- ses, quod sc. passurus sit Christus, & primus futurus ex resurrectione mortuorum lumen annunciaturus po- pulo & gentibus. Quid hoc aliud est, quam ipsi- met Christi in os contradicere, qui non tantum e Psalmis & Prophetis, sed etiam e Mose cum disci- pulis Emaunticis, tum Apostolis demonstravit passionem & resurrectionem suam, Luc. 24, 25. Ipse dixit ad eos: O stulti & tardi corde ad creden- dum omnibus, quæ locuti sunt Prophetæ; (dictum hoc sibi quoq; putet Calixtus) Nonne hæc oportuit pati Christum, & ita intrare in gloriam suam? Et incipiens a MOSE & OMNIBUS PROPHETIS, interpreta- batur illis omnem Scripturam, quæ de ipso erat. Si e Mose pariter & Prophetis illud, nonne oportuit pati Christum, & ita intrare gloriam suam, demonstravit, qua fronte negabitur in Mose pariter & Prophetis passionem Christi prædictam esse? Et vers. 44. ac seqq. Dixit ad eos, hæc sunt verba, quæ locutus sum ad vos, cum adhuc essem vobiscum, quoniam ne- cesse est impleri omnia, quæ scripta sunt in lege Mo- sis, in Prophetis, & Psalmis. Tunc aperuit illis sensum, ut intelligerent Scripturas. Quas vero? Mosis, Prophetarum & Psalmorum, ut ipsiusmet verba habent. Et dixit eis: Quoniam sic scri- ptum est: quid vero scriptum est? Sic oportebat Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis tertia die & prædicari in nomine ejus pœnitentiam, & remis- sionem peccatorum in omnes gentes. Hæc Chri- stus, cui κατδιάμετρον sese opponit Calixtus, in Mo- se nihil tale, sive de passione, sive de resurrectione Chri- sti a mortuis, scriptum haberi. Vtri fidem habe- bimus? Christo, qui est ipsa veritas? an vero Calixto? Quod si viam & rationem pie scrutemur, qua per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi salutem nobiscum adepti sunt fideles, ante Davidem, non sane cum per- fidis & damnatis hæreticis Photinianis alia est adape- rienda via, quam quæ sola atque unica in Scripturis monstratur per sanguinem Jesu Christi: quia prote- statur Os Apostolorum S. Petrus, non esse in ullo alio salutem, neœ alíud nomen datum esse sub cælo homini- bus, in quo oporteat salvari, quam nomen Jesu Cruciji- xi, & a mortuis resuscitati, Lapidis illius angularis in passione reprobati, Act. 4, 10. seqq. extra & præter quem alius non est positus in fundamentum salutis, sive per Prophetas Veteris, sive per Apostolos Novi Testamenti, Eph. 2, 20. Ideo justitiam Dei, quæ per fidem habetur in sanguinem Christi, absœ lege, seu o- peribus legis, manifestatam esse, docet S. S. & com- probatam testimonio LEGIS & Prophetarum, quod scil. justificemur gratis per gratiam DEI, per redemtio- nem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, quem proposuit Deus pro- pitiationemper fidem in sanguine ipsius Rom. 3, 21. 24. Non dicit, data est, inquit Chrysost. in h. l. sed mani- festata est, ut novitatis objectionem præscindat: Quod enim manifestatur, velut vetus, & quod aliquamdiu absconditum fuerat, manifestatur. Neqœ hoc tantum, sed etiam quæ sequuntur, satis ostendunt, non novam & recens natam esse justitiam, de qua loquitur. Cum enim dixit, manifestata est, subjungit testimonio comprobatam a lege & Prophetis. Ne absterrea- ris, inquit, ab ea, quod jam primum data est, nec tur- beris, ac sires esset temporaria, peregrinaque. Jam vero inde ab initio illam lex & Prophetæ prædixerunt. Et ne dubium ullum supersit, Abraham Pater o- mnium credentium introducitur Rom. IV. & ceu exemplar sistitur justificationis per imputationem fidei. Quænam vero illa fides? qua credimus in eum, qui Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum a mortuis resuscitavit, utpote in mortem traditum proprer pec- cata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram v. 23. 24. Sed & Ebr. XI. nubes testium V. Testamen- ti exhibetur, qui fide in Jesum ejusque crucem respe- xerint, inde a primordio Ecclesiæ, ut demonstretur fide in Christi passionem, qui scopus est universæ i- stius tractationis, salutem nos adipisci, quo de B. A- thanasius hom. in S. Patr. & Prophet. Fides, quæ in viam cognitionis Dei, & probam atque irreprehensihi- lem conversationem pedes nostros dirigit, non recens habet principium, ut impii & perditi Judæi affirmant: sed inde a sanctis piisque patribus, Abel dico & Enoch, & Noe, atque Abraham, cæterisque omnibus justis de- ducitur. Quod ibidem exequitur Athanas. proli- xius. Magnificum certe illud fidei Mosaicæ elogi- um, quod probra Christi majores æstimavit divitias, quam thesauros quoscunque Ægypti v. 28. dubitare non sinit, Mosen veram fidem de passione salutifera Christi, quam omnibus mundi divitiis præferendam duxit, sedulo in populo DEI propagasse. Jam si ad scripta θεόπνευσα descendatur, Passionem Chri- sti & oraculis præclaris, & typis egregiis in S. literis ante Davidis tempora propositam fuisse, qua veri specie negari poterit? In ipso statim πρωτευαγγελίῳ Gen. 3, 15. quod Calixtus, utut alias non raro Judai- zet, de Messia caput serpentis contrituro, id est, Diabo- li opera destructuro, & peccato, morti & conde- mnationi, quæ a Diabolo introducta sunt, vires ad- empturo, explicat l. c. Bb 3. prædictum est, Diabolum contriturum ipsi calcaneum, ad designandam seminis mulieris passionem, eamque gravissimam, quam ver- bum תשופנו de gravissimis vulneribus & afflictionibus Jobi adhibitum c. IX, 17. emphatice exprimit; e quo loco colligit B. Lutherus Comm. in Genesin p. m. 56. Itaq; Filium Dei oportuit victimam fieri, ut hec nobis conficeret, ut tolleret peccatum, devoraret mortem, & amissam obedientiam restitueret. Hos thesauros in Christo possidemus, sed in spe. Sic Adam, sic Heva, sic omnes credentes usque ad novissimum diem, Spe ista vivunt & vincunt. Nec abs re conculcationem Ophiomachi nostri Messiae in calcaneo de crucifixione interpretantur Orthodoxi Theologi B. Gerhardus, & alii, in qua pedes Christi clavis cruci affixi sunt. Neque vero genuinam de passione Christi σωτηρίῳ sententiam latuisse Patriarchas, B. Polycarp. Lyserus eximie docet in Comm. p. 284. De officio hujus Mediatoris nos scimus, quod nos liberaturus sit per suam passionem & mortem: Sic enim nos intelligimus illud: mordebis calcaneum ejus: Num vero Adamus quoq; hoc intellexit? Omnino. Nam propterea docuit filios suos sacrificare: Et Noachus quoq; irae Dei opponit sacrificium. Sacrificia autem fuisse typos & figuras passionis Christi, Paulus diversis in locis, maxime autem in Epistola ad Ebraeos perspicue docet. Quod igitur Patres morsum calcanei eode modo, quo nos, intellexerint, id sacrificiis demonstrarunt. Et quid aliud sibi volunt illa Jacobi mystica vaticinia de Schilo Gen. 49, 11. lavabit in vino vestimentum suum, & in sanguine Uvae pallium suum, quam quod sanguinem suum copiose sit effusurus, eoque corpus suum, quod veluti vestimentum est Deitatis, tincturus, qui commentarius Orthodoxorum Esa. 63, 1. Apoc. 19, 13. haud obscure confirmatur; Ideoq; Justin. Martyr. Apol. II pro Christian. Verbum lavans in sanguine uvae stolam suam passionem Christi, quam subiturus erat prenunciavit, per sanguinem lustrans atque purificans sibi credentes &c. Quid de Jobea fidei professione de Goële, quae dubio procul ante Davidis Psalmos, & si Ebraeis atque Origeni habenda fides, ab ipso Mose literis consignata, vel translata, dicturus est Calixtus? quam merito suo celebrat S. Hieronymus Epist. LI. ad Pammach. Nec dum mortuus erat Christus Dominus, & Athleta Ecclesiae Redemtorem suum videbat ab inferis resurgentem. Quid de typis multifariis sacrificiorum, arietis loco Isaaci oblati, agni paschalis, hirci emissarii, vaccae rufae, serpentis aenei, ut & Patriarcharum, Adami obdormientis, Isaaci immolandi, Josephi a fratribus venditi, Mosis in profluentem projecti, Gideonis item Samsonis & aliorum Judicum Judaeorum, de quibus scite Hieronymus Ep. CIII. ad Paul. In Judicum libro quot principes populi, tot figurae sunt. Sed haec & alia hujus generis plura nunc quidem, prout par est, persequi non possumus: Irenaei tamen locum egregium de Mofis scriptis, in gratiam Calixti subjungere placet e libro IV. c. XXIII. Inseminatus est ubique in Scripturis Mofis Filius DEI, aliquando quidem cum Abraham loquens, aliquando cum eodem comesturus, aliquando autem Sodomitis inducens judicium, & rursus cum videtur, & in viam dirigit Jacob, & de rubo loquitur cum Mose. Et non est numerum dicere, in quibus a Moyse ostenditur Filius Dei, cujus & diem passionis non ignoravit, sed figuratum prenunciavit eum, Pascha nominans, & in eadem ipsa, quae ante tantum temporis a Moyse praedicata est, passus Dominus adimplens pascha. Non solum autem diem descripsit, sed & locum ex extremitate temporum, & signum occasum solis dicens, non poteritis immolare Pascha in ulla alia civitatum tuarum, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, nisi in eo loco, quem delegerit Dominus Deus tuus invocari nomen suum ibi. Immolabis pascha ve- spere ad occasum solis. Et quid pluribus opus? An- non luculenter Christus ipse Psal. XL, 8. Ecce venio, in volumine libri scriptum est de me, ἐν κεφαλίδι βι- βλίγ, ut exponit S. S. Ebr. 10, 7. (quod sive de Gene- seos libro cum Hieronymo in tradit. Hebraic. in Genes. sive de Scriptura S. in genere cum aliis accipias, sine dubio complectitur libros Davidis Psalmis priores,) voluntatem tuam facio libenter; Quæ illa ipsa volun- tas est, qua præstita sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Christi semel factam, oblationibus Vet. Test. figuratam, interprete S.S. Ebr. 10,10. &c.

De Interpp. Mosis adhuc dicendum. In Pen- tatevchum autem præter illos, qui in totam Scriptu- ram,vel in Vetus Testamentum saltim commentati sunt, operam aliquam contulerunt, e Judæis Agatho- bulus, nec non Aristobulus Senior ante Christum 350. annis, Aristobulus Junior annis ante Christum 215. qui Græco sermone in Pentateuchum Mosis scri- psere: quorum Is id egit, ut ostenderet universam Philosophiam Peripateticam ex lege Mosis haustam fu- isse. Vid. Clem. Alexandr. l. V. Stromat. Euseb. IIX. de præparat. Evangel. e Rabbinis R. Abraham Hispanus, R. Bechai, R. Mose Hadarschan, R. Ezechias (sub titulo Candelabrum lucis) R. Isaac Ben Arama (ligationem Isaaci inscribit.) Alius, cujus Com- mentarius Cabbalisticus Zohar; Alius cujus Com- mentarius vagus Tanchuma dicitur, R. Menasse Ben Israel conciliationes per quæstiones in quinque li- bros Mosis edidit.

E Christianis Doctoribus celebrantur post Cy- rillum Alexandrinum, qui circa ann. Christi 430.in Pentat. opus allegoricum concinnavit, Erhardus Monachus Benedictinus circa ann. Domini 1050.ob commentar. in Pentatevch. ut & Bruno Archiepisc. Colonionsis, Alanus item Insulensis, qui ob omnige- nam rerum omnium eruditionem Doctoris univer- salis cognomen consecutus commentaria in Penta- tevchum scripsit Anno Domini 1300. eiq; σύγχρο- νƧ Albertus Patavinus, qui Scholastico more com- mentatus in quinq; libros Mosis Johan. Zacharias Anno 1460. in Pentatevch. scripsit. Benedictus Sten- dal, Hallensis Anno 1470. Explanationum Scholasti- carum libros quinque in Pentatevchum edidit : Paulus Ricius Judæus conversus de sexcentis & tre- decim Mosaicæ sanctionis seu Pentatevchi edictis, librum unum composuit An. 1500. Augustinus Steu- chus, Eugubinus Anno 1540. annotationes in Penta- tevchum locutiones Ebraicas diligenter explican- tes, ut & in capita tria Genes. Cosmopœiam adornavit. Hieronymus ab Oleastro Anno 1556.Ebraicum textum itidem sedulo exposuit: Jac. de Lusanna Scholastice in Pentatevchum scripsit, ut & Matthæus Ebroicen- sis. In Bibliis Duadecensibns in Pentatevchum jux- ta ordinem Alphabeticum hi sistuntur Autores, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Cyrillus, Alex. Greg. M. Isido- rus, Origenes, Procopius, Rabanus, Rupertus, & Theo- doretus, qui cum Strabi glossa ordinaria, & Anshelmi Laudunensis interlineari Postilla Lyrani, Editionibus Burgensis, & Replicis Doringi in Pentatevchum ad- hibiti sunt in illo opere, licet plerique istorum sal- tim aliquas particulas aut sententias contulerint. Quibus vero e Nostris addendi, imo præferendi, si a Patribus abeas, B. Lutherus, Brentius, Osiander, Vina- rienses, aliiq; universales C̄õmentatores, & Paraphra- stæ, ut & Erasmus Marbachius, nec non Christophorus Pelargus, qui Pentatevchũ peculiariter illustrarunt. Inter Reformatos celebrantur Joh. Calvinus, & Franc. Junius Ainsworthus, Anglus (qui Anglica- uo sermone Annotata sua adornavit (Drusius,

Sixtinus ab Amama, qui in Pentateuchum, Willetus Anglus, qui in Genesin, Exodum & Leviticum scri- psere. Laudem etiam recentiores nonnulli Pontifi- cii merentur ob diligentiam, eruditionem, & judi- cium eximium imprimis Jacob Bonfrerius, & Leon- hardus Marius post Cornelium a Lapide supra lauda- tum. Atque hæc de Interpretibus.

Distributio Scriptorum Mosaïcorum in quin- que Libros Mosi ipsi auctori a Philone recte tribui- tur; in quibus primo in GENESI Ecclesiæ plantatio, & propagatio. Deinde in EXODO protectio & gu- bernatio in Ægypto & deserto: Porro in LEVITICO Ecclesiastica constitutio: tum in Libro NUMERO- RUM Politica administratio: Deniq; in DEVTE- RONOM. ulterior Ecclesiasticæ & Politicæ Hierar- chiæ confirmatio exhibetur. Lyranus ita procedit: Sciendum,quod lex non data uni personæ, sed commu- nitati populi adunati: ideo primo describitur adunatio fidelis populi sub cultu unius Dei, quod fit in libro Ge- nefeos. Secundo describitur legislatio, & hoc fit in Exodo, & duobus libris sequentibus; Tertio ponitur prædictæ legis repetitio & explicatio, & hoc fit in Dev- teronomio.

Distribui potest Historia Mosaïca per διχοτο- μίαν hoc modo: quod tum Ecclesiam Patriarchalem describat ante Mosen, primo Libro, vel Genesi: tum Ecclesiam Israëlitiçam sub Mose, reliquis quatuor li- bris: eamq; partim qua primam legis promulgationem, partim qua legis repetitionem. Primam legis pro- mulgationem in Genere, & statum Israëlitarum usq; ad Tabernaculi erectionem Exodus exhibet: In fpecie autem τάξιν ἱερατικὴν & Agenda Ecclesiastica seu jus sacrum sistit Leviticus post erectum Tabernaculum usque ad numerationem populi: Gubernationem ve- ro Politicam certis quibusdam gradibus, functioni- bus & classibus ordinat & sancit liber NUMERO- RUM, ut sedes certa constituatur Ecclesiæ, cum enu- meratione populi & stationum in deserto, adeoque in hoc libro itinerarium exhibetur Israëlitarum per spatium fere 39. annorum peregrinationis Eremiticæ. Deniq; repetitio & confirmatio legis habetur in Dev- teronomio, quod est Commentarius quidam ad legem, vel liber digestorum Juris Israëlïtici, cum rebus gestis paucorum dierum ab initio undecimi Mensis usque ad diem septimum duodecimi Mensis, anni quadra- gesimi ab exitu.

Tota Pentateuchus historiam complectitur an- norum 2252. ab initio mundi, usque ad finem luctus publici ob obitum Mofis. Atque hæc in genere de Pen- tateucho. Jam prælibanda etiam nonnulla in Specie ad GENESIN erint: sed paucissimis, de Nominibus libri, objecto, scopo, tempore scriptionis, Chronologia, Distributione, & Interpretibus ejusdem.

AD GENESIN.

## 1:1 Introduction: Τὰ Προλεγόμενα
ΤᾺ ΠΡΟΛΕΓΌΜΕΝΑ.

GENESIS to the Latins, from the Greek custom, by which the first book of Moses is called γένεσις, to which is analogous the appellation of the Hebrews ספר יצירה (Book of Formation), of the Christian Arabs the book of creation, of the Muhammadans the book of the beginning; Ahmed Ibn Edris, as Hottinger praises in Histor. creat. p. 1, called it the book of life from its object, because it exhibits the generation of heaven and earth, as the creation is indicated in Gen. 2:4, and of all things that are in them, as well as the generations of men, and especially of the Patriarchs before and after the flood, who occur in the genealogy of the Messiah. Otherwise, it is called by the Hebrews, as also by the Arab Jews, from the initial word בראשית, as are the remaining Mosaic books and the book of Lamentations. Although Schickard, Bechin. Happ. p. 18, would have it that this is done rashly, as he would have the names attributed to the remaining Mosaic books be those of the Parashot rather than of the entire books. For the commentary on the whole of Genesis written by Rabba Bar Nachmoni already in the year of Christ 300 is inscribed בראשית רבא (Bereshit Rabbah). By Eusebius it is called the Prooemium of the Sacred Laws, in which Moses, a truly great theologian, consecrated the lives of the Hebrew Fathers to indelible memory; l. VII. de Praepar. Evang.

Its primary scope is CHRIST, who is the end of the whole Scripture Joh. 5, 39. 46. Psal. 40, 8. Act. 10, 43. 2. Tim. 3, 15. whom indeed Grotius in his Annotations has regarded little, and seems to neglect almost entirely. For his sake the creation of man in the image of God, which was lost through the fall and restored in us by Christ, is set forth first, and the history of the fall is subjoined with the Prot-Evangelium concerning Christ, through whom the human race, handed down to Adam the first parent of all mortals, is to be liberated from sin, the power of Satan, and death Gen. 3, 15. Certain ἐξηγήσεις of this are the promises made to Noah the progenitor of another world, to Abraham the father of believers, and likewise to Isaac and Jacob, just as the histories of these Patriarchs exhibit notable βεβαιώσεις of the Prot-Evangelium, and present the origins of the Church, in which the doctrine concerning Christ was propagated.

The present book was written by Moses, not in the land of Midian, or before the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, because he had not yet been appointed a Prophet then, but after his calling, indeed after the leading out of the people, when the Law was promulgated by God, and Moses was recognized as a notable and truly θεοδίδακτος Prophet from his conversation with God on the mountain, so that the people of the Lord might be bound to observe more religiously the law now divinely promulgated, following the example of their ancestors, who did not have the law so solemnly promulgated, but received it by παλαιοπαράδοσιν ever since Adam. That was done, as is probably believed, around the year of the World 2514. GENESIS, however, comprises the history of nearly twenty-four centuries, namely from the creation of the world up to the death of the Patriarch Joseph, which falls in the year of the World 2369, being 1656 before the flood, and 713 years from the flood: which are counted thus: to the calling of Abraham there are 427 years, from then indeed 25 years flowed to the birth of Isaac, from the birth of Isaac up to the birth of Jacob 60 years are counted, from then indeed up to the descent of Jacob into Egypt 130, from which 71 years have elapsed to the death of Joseph, which numbers joined together make 713 years. Concerning which [see] in the Sacred Chronicle.

GENESIS is therefore best distributed according to the Patriarchs: ADAM from c. I. up to VI. NOAH from c. VI. to XII. ABRAHAM from c. XII. to XXV, 10. ISAAC from c. XXV. v. 11. to XXIIX, 9. JACOB from c. XXIIX. v. 10. to c. XXXVII. and JOSEPH from c. XXXVII. up to c. L. or the last. Which, along with other things necessary to be observed in advance regarding GENESIS, such as the Sum and Causes of the written Genesis, of which we have brought forward eleven, and the utilities, which we have executed more prolixly and accurately in the Prolegomena prefixed to the Commentary on Genesis, regarding the Didactic, Elenctic, Parenetic, Epanorthotic, and Paracletic use, as well as the General and Special Chronology of Genesis.

Those who have contributed their ἐπιβάλλον μέρος to the illustration of the Book of GENESIS, besides the Commentators on the whole Bible, as also on the Old Testament, and also on the Pentateuch of Moses, are from the Jews the Author of Bereschith Ketanna, R. Bar Nachmani, the author, as is believed, and Bereschith Rabba, and R. Obadias, as also Moses Barcepha the Syrian, among the Christians, Origen among the Fathers, indulging too much in allegories, and Chrysostom, who wrote Homilies on Genesis from the Greeks, from the Latins not only did St. Augustine set forth Questions on Genesis, but he also wrote on Genesis according to the letter. The books of Explanations on Genesis are also attributed to Eucherius, but because the author often cites Gregory the Great, they are without doubt by someone else, and as it seems to Bellarmine in De Script. Eccles., by some Englishman shortly after the times of Gregory; Albinus Alcuin resolved questions on Genesis. Aloysius Lippomannus edited a chain from the Fathers on Genesis. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, wrote on the Hexaemeron, and on Paradise: on Cain and Abel; on Noah and the Ark; on Abraham: on Isaac and the soul; on Jacob and the blessed life: on Joseph the Patriarch: on the blessings of the Patriarchs. Gregory of Nyssa and Basil the Great on the Hexaemeron; Anastasius Sinaita, Bishop of Antioch, produced Anagogical contemplations in 11 books on the Hexaemeron. Cardinal Bonaventure [wrote] 23 sermons on various places of Genesis: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola adorned Book VII on chapter 1 of Genesis and on the work of the six days. In the Douay Bibles, there are cited besides, from the Greeks, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Cyril of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Epiphanius, Acacius, Theodorus, Damascenus, with the Greek Gloss, and Philo the Hebrew: From the Latins, Cyprian, Hilary, Prosper, Cassian, Gennadius, Junilius, Bernard, and others, but the opinions of these are only sometimes cited: for they did not edit complete Commentaries on Genesis.

Of our own, B. Luther, B. Polycarp Lyser, B. Gesner, B. David Rungius, the Wittenberg Theologians, B. Gerhard of Jena, B. Chytreus, and Mr. August Varenius of Rostock have commented on this book. Those who wish may also consult our Commentary on Genesis, as well as what we have compiled concerning the works of the Hexaemeron in Vol. III of the System of Theology. B. Aegidius Hunnius illustrated chapter 21 of Genesis with questions. Johannes Draconites and Paulus von Eizen also wrote succinctly on Genesis: Paul Fagius instituted a Collation of Paraphrases, and after him Otto Gualtperius. To say nothing of the Homiletics of Sim. Musaeus, Gediccus, and others. From the Reformed, Johannes Mercerus, D. David Pareus, Andr. Willet, and Andr. Rivetus have commented on this book: Joh. Henr. Hottinger explained the history of creation. P. Picherellus edited annotations on the first three chapters. Christopher Cartwright edited Electa Thargumico-Rabbinica from the triple Targum and R. Solomon and Aben Ezra, etc., on Genesis. From the Papists, Martin Del-Rio, Benedictus Pererius, Marinus, Mersenne, and Ascanius Martinengus wrote on Genesis. Gabriel a Costa of Coimbra, a Doctor, wrote on chapter 49. Sixtus Senensis lists more in Bibliotheca S. Book IV, p. 394. But most either illustrated only a few chapters, or are even lost and no longer exist.

Latin:

ΤᾺ ΠΡΟΛΕΓΌΜΕΝΑ.

GENESIS Latinis, e Græca consuetudine, qua Liber primus Mosis γένεσις vocatur, cui analoga est appellatio Ebræorum ספר יצירה Liber formationis, Arabum Christianorum liber creationis, Muhamedanorum liber initii; Ahmed Ibn Edris, laudante Hottingero in Histor. creat. p. 1. liber vitæ nuncupata est ab objecto, quia generationem cœli & terræ, uti indigitatur creatio Gen. 2, 4. omnium- que quæ in illis sunt, nec non generationes hominum, imprimis autem Patriarcharum ante, & post diluviñ, qui in genealogia Messiæ occurrunt, exhibet. A- lias Ebræis, ut & Arabibus Judæis, a voce initiali בראשית uti reliqui libri Mosaici, & Threnorum liber nuncupatur. Etsi Schickardus, Bechin. Happ. p. 18. sed temere hoc, ut & reliquis libris Mosaicis tributa nomina Parascharum potius, quam integro- rum librorum esse velit. Nam Commentarius in Ge- nesin totam a Rabba Bar Nachmoni jam Anno Christi 300. conscriptus בראשית רבא inscriptus est. Eusebio dicitur Prooemium Sacrarum Legum, in quo vitas Patrum Ebræorum memoriæ indelebili consecra- vit Moses, θεόλογος ἀληθῶς μέγας: l. VII. de Præ- par. Evang.

Scopus ejus præcipuus est CHRISTUS, qui to- tius Scripturæ finis Joh. 5, 39. 46. Psal. 40, 8. Act. 10, 43. 2. Tim. 3, 15. quem vero in Annotatis suis Grotius parum respexit, & tantum non omnino negligere videtur. Hujus gratia creatio hominis ad imaginem Dei, quæ per lapsum amissa, a Christo reparata in no- bis, præmittitur, & historia lapsus Prot-Evangelium subjungitur de Christo, per quem a peccato, Satanæ potestate, ac morte liberandum sit genus huma- num, Adamo primo omnium mortalium parenti Gen. 3, 15. traditum. Cujus ἐξηγήσεις quædam sunt promissiones cæteræ Noacho alterius mundi proge- nitori, Abrahamo patri credentium, Isaaco item, & Jacobo factæ, quemadmodum historiæ horum Patri- archarum βεβαιώσεις exhibent Prot-Evangelii in- signes, & Ecclesiæ, in qua doctrina de Christo propa- gata est, origines sistunt.

Scriptus liber præsens a Mose est, non in terra Midian, aut ante egressum Ebræorum ex Ægypto, quia tum nondum Propheta constitutus erat, sed post vo- cationem ejusdem, imo post eductionem populi, ubi Lex a Deo promulgata, & Moses ceu insignis, ac vere θεοδίδακτος Propheta, e conversatione cum Deo in monte agnitus fuit, ut ad legem divinitus jam pro- mulgatam exemplo majorum suorum, qui non ha- buere legem ita solemniter promulgatam, sed per παλαιοπαράδοσιν inde ab Adamo acceptam, religio- sius observandam adstringeretur populus Domini. Factum id, ut probabiliter creditur, circa annum Mundi 2514. Complectitur autem GENESIS histo- riam viginti quatuor propemodum seculorum, nimi- rum inde a creatione mundi usq́; ad mortem Josephi Patriarchæ, quæ in annum M. 2369. incidit, utpote 1656. ante diluvium, & 713. annorum a diluvio: qui sic numerantur: ad Abrahami vocationem anni sunt 427. inde vero ad natum Isaacum 25. anni fluxere, a nativitate Isaaci usque ad nativitatem Jacobi nume- rantur anni 60. inde vero usque ad descensum Jacobi in Ægyptum 130. ex quo lapsi sunt 71. anni ad mortem Josephi, qui numeri juncti efficiunt 713. annos. De quibus in Chronico Sacro.

Distribuitur itaque optime GENESIS secun- dum Patriarchas: ADAMUM a c. I. usque ad VI. NOACHUM a c. VI. ad XII. ABRAHAMUM a c. XII. ad XXV, 10. ISAACUM a c. XXV. v. 11. ad XXIIX, 9. JACOBUM a c. XXIIX. v. 10. ad c. XXXVII. & JOSEPHUM a c. XXXVII. usque ad c. L. vel ul- timum. Quæ cum aliis ad GENESIN in antecessum observatu necessariis, utpote de Summa, & Causis conscriptæ Geneseos, quarum undecim adduximus, & utilitatibus, qua usum Didacticum, Elencticum, Paræneticum, Epanorthoticum, & Paracleticum, nec non Chronologiam Generalem, & Specialem Geneseos prolixius & accuratius exequuti sumus in Prolego- menis Commentario in Genesin præmissis.

Qui ad illustrationem Libri GENESEOS suum ἐπιβάλλον μέρος contulerunt, præter Com- mentatores in universa Biblia, ut & in Vetus Testa- mentum, nec non in Pentateuchum Mosis, sunt e Ju- dæis Autor Bereschith Ketanna, R. Bar Nach- mani, Autor, ut creditur, & Bereschith Rabba, & R. Obadias, ut & Moses Barcepha Syrus, e Christianis, inter Patres Origenes, nimium allegoriis indulgens, & Chrysostomus, qui e Græcis Homilias in Genesin scripserunt, e Latinis non tantum Quæstiones in Ge- nesin S. Augustinus expediit, sed & de Genesi ad lite- ram scripsit. Tribuuntur & Eucherio libri Explana- tionum in Genesin, sed quia auctor sæpe Gregorium M. citat, sine dubio alterius cujusdam sunt, & ut Bellarmino de Script. Eccles. videtur Angli cujus- pam paulo post tempora Gregorii; Albinus Alcui- nus quæstiones in Genesin resolvit. Catenam e Pa- tribus in Genesin edidit Aloysius Lippomannus. Am- brosius Episcop. Mediol. in Hexaemeron scripsit, & de Paradiso: de Cain, & Abel; de Noa & Arca; de Abraham: de Isaac & anima; de Jacobo, & beata vi- ta: de Joseph Patriarcha: de benedictionibus Patri- archarum. Gregorius Nyssenus, & Basilius M. in He- xaemeron; Anagogicas contemplationes libris XI. in Hexaëmeron prodidit Anastasius Synaita Episc. Antiochenus. Bonaventura Cardin. sermones XXIII. in diversa loca Geneseos: Joh. Picus Mirandul. L. VII. in cap. I. Gen. & de opere sex dierum adornavit. In Bibliis Duacenis allegantur insuper e Græcis Ire- næus, Clemens Alex. Cyrillus Alex. Euseb. Cæsar. Epi- phanius, Acacius, Theodorus, Damascenus, cum Glossa Græca, & Philone Ebræo: E Latinis Cyprianus, Hila- rius, Prosper, Cassianus, Gennadius, Junilius, Bernhar- dus & alii, sed horum tantum sententiæ nonnun- quam citantur: neque enim integra Commentaria ediderunt in Genesin.

E nostris in hunc librum commentati sunt B. Lutherus, B. Polyc. Lyserus, B. Gesnerus, B. David Rungius, Wittebergenses Theologi, B. Gerhardus Jenensis, B. Chytreus, & Dn. August. Varenius Ro- stochienses. Conferre etiam poterunt, quibus lu- buerit, Commentarium nostrum in Genesin, nec non quæ de operibus Hexaemeri T. III. Syst. Theol. con- cinnavimus. B. Ægid. Hunnius cap. XXI. Geneseos quæstionibus illustravit. Scripsere & succincte in Genesin Joh. Draconites, & Paulus ab Eizen: Col- lationem Paraphrasium instituit Paul. Fagius & post eum Otto Gualtperius. Ut Sim. Musæi, Gedicci, & a- liorum Homiletica taceamus. E Reformatis com- mentati in hunc librum sunt Joh. Mercerus, D. Da- vid Pareus, Andr. Willetus, Andr. Rivetus: Joh. Henr. Hottingerus Historiam creationis exposuit. P. Pi- cherellus annotata ad priora tria capita edidit. Chri- stophorus Cartwrightus Electa Thargumico-Rabbi- nica e triplici Thargum & R. Salomon & AbenEz- ra &c. in Genesin edidit. E Pontificiis in Genesin scripsit Martinus Del-Rio, Benedictus Pererius, Ma- rinus, Mersennus, & Ascanius Martinengus. In c. XLIX. scripsit Gabriel a Costa Conimbric. Diactor. Plures recenset Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. S. l. IV. p. 394. Sed plerique vel pauca tantum capita illustra- runt, vel etiam deperditi sunt, nec amplius extant.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. OF GENESIS. THE HISTORY OF ADAM. from chapter 1 up to 6.

CHAPTER I. The creation of heaven and earth according to the works of the Hexaemeron.

Vers. 1. IN THE BEGINNING GOD CREATED) Better: in the beginning to create God, that is, before God created or formed. Moses rightly placed the history from the founding of the World before the laws. For the World harmonizes with the law, and the law with the World, as Philo says.

Grotius thinks it is better rendered, in the beginning to create God, that is, before God created or formed heaven and earth: that is, this universe, such as it is now, then the earth was void and empty. A version suitable and pleasing to the mind of philosophers and heretics, concerning an unmade world and eternal matter. For thus Moses would have signified nothing else than that, before God formed this universe, AS IT IS NOW, the earth was empty and void. Whence Thomas Gataker of London acknowledges in his Cinnus, or Miscellaneous Adversaria, Book II, ch. 1, converting the initial words of Genesis into various forms, or weighing those converted, [notes that] this translation of Grotius provides an opportunity for suspecting what Hermogenes once dreamed, that matter existed before creation began, which itself always was, neither born nor made, nor having any beginning or end at all, from which God afterwards made all things: or also what Valentinus raved, of an unbegotten, immense, invisible, eternal Bythos, who was before all these things, or what the Theosophia Teutonica of the New Luminaries, as the initiates of this secret point out, recently produced: that before all creation of things, two immense and infinite [realities] existed from eternity, God and the abyss: that this abyss is neither absolutely nothing, nor God himself, although after the Deity it is a supreme participant in the reality of being, but as it were the body or dwelling-place of the Deity: and that almost all things which philosophers ascribe to their prime matter can be attributed to this abyss. Which in truth is Gehenna, although before the defection of Lucifer it did not break forth into its Gehennal act (which portent we shall observe Episcopius later formed even from the Abyss, but created long before the visible world), from the property of which abyss, with rays emanating from the center of the Deity in a single struggle, the majestic light was created from eternity, and that it is the very wisdom of which Solomon [spoke], born of the Father GOD and the abyss as mother, the author of that impious nonsense invented. All of which things were devised for this end, that it might be believed that creation is not out of nothing.

Petrus Picherellus, in his Paraphrase of the Mosaic Cosmopoeia, although he rendered this clause thus: 'By that which existed at the beginning, heaven and earth, by that God created them': nevertheless, in his annotation he added this: 'In the Hebrew it is, In the beginning God created heaven and earth, that is: in the beginning of heaven and earth God created them.' Which explanation, however, leaves it in doubt whether that beginning was the first commencement of all things that exist besides GOD or not?

What of the fact that Grotius himself explained those words more correctly in his Annotations on the Gospel of John: 'When the Universe first began to be created,' understanding the word 'to create' as production out of nothing, and 'beginning' as the commencement of the Universe. Regarding the first beginning of time, Basil accepted it with Ambrose and Chrysostom, in Hexaem. Orat. I. ἐν ἀρχῇ, that is, in this beginning which is according to time. But Tertullian explained them most explicitly of all in Against Hermogenes, ch. XIX: 'We claim for each word its own property; that beginning is a commencement, and it was fitting that it be placed thus for things beginning to be made. For nothing that is to be made can exist without a beginning, since the beginning is that very thing, while it begins to be made.' Thus, beginning or commencement is a word of inception, not the name of any substance.

Now Grotius followed here from the Jews R. Solomon Jarchi, or rather Robert Stephanus, who observed that some Hebrews translate it thus: 'Others say that בְּרֵאשִׁית is joined (which they otherwise call being in regimen) with the following verb בָּרָא, and they translate, In the beginning of God's creating. i.e. In the beginning when God created, that is, when God first created, etc. then the earth, etc. so that it refers to the following verse.' Then, however, בָּרָא will be as if it were written בְּרוֹא. and at the beginning of the second verse it will be taken for Then, or it will be redundant. But more rightly with the LXX Interpreters the Vulgate Version, which Grotius ought not to have set aside as authentic for the Tridentines: In the beginning, namely of all things, God created heaven and earth. And the earth was void and empty. Which relies on the propriety of the words; in the beginning, says Moses: designating a true and proper creation. For it is not right for us to depart from the native meaning. The following [words] also cohere through the copulative particle, AND the earth was empty. Then Moses explains in order the works of the first Hexaemeron, so that he may teach that he has indicated the first beginning of all things. Which he further confirms in the recapitulation in chapter II, 1, just as also in verse 4 the beginning of creation is indicated by the word Bereschith, Job 41, verse 2, Jer. 28, v. 29. David also explains concerning the beginning of all things in Psalm 102, 26, In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth. And Solomon concerning the beginning of the ways of the Lord, Prov. 8, v. 23. And also John chapter 1, v. 1, In the beginning was the Word. All things were made through him. It is too manifest that the Holy Spirit in these places looks to the Mosaic beginning, so that the first words of Genesis must necessarily be rendered thus, in the beginning God created heaven and earth. In which sense the Fathers commonly accept them, not only those whom we have already cited, Tertullian, Basil, Ambrose, Chrysostom, but also the Lateran Council, C. firmiter de Summ. Trinit. & fid. Cathol. Some among Augustine [say] IN THE BEGINNING, that is, before all things, so that God created nothing before, at the beginning of the divine work. Which sense agrees with ours. Among the Jews also Philo, and also R. Saadia in the Arabic paraphrase. Fagius in his collation of translations also cites Kimchi, explaining it thus: In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and then those things which proceeded from them. R. Moses Maimonides. in More Nebuch. part II, chapter XXX. The inseparable preposition Beth is the Beth of a vessel or instrument, and the true exposition of that place is this: in the beginning God created the superior and inferior [things]. Stephani also notes that some of the Hebrews understand הכל, so that you may translate, First of all he created. For it is frequent for the Hebrews, in things not ambiguous, to suppress something, as Job 3, 10, Is. 8, 4. But there is no need for that ellipsis. For the Hebrew Doctors acknowledge that the sense is clear without a supplement, as Stephani himself observes, rendering it, in the beginning God created. The Chaldean Paraphrase of Jerusalem translates in Wisdom, therefore perhaps it is held here in the Hebrew IN THE SON, [as] Tertullian in the book against Praxeas and Hilary in the exposition of the Psalm noted (as Jerome observes), who could easily confuse the Hebrew text with the Chaldean, taking Wisdom for the Son of God; just as Origen also accepted this first word of Genesis concerning the Son of God, and in the interlinear gloss these two or three expositions are joined, in the beginning of time, or before other things, or in his Son. Stephani explains the Targum as in Wisdoms, that is, most wisely. But the Targum Onkelos has, as it is in the Hebrew בְּקַדְמִין In the beginnings, i.e., of all things, before all created things. Jonathan בְּאוֹלָא in the beginning. Thus also the Greek Interpreters, not only the LXX Elders, but also Symmachus and Theodotion ἐν ἀρχῇ: only Aquila ἐν κεφαλαίῳ in the chapter.

Therefore from these words Maimonides refutes the Philosophers, l. c. The exposition (that which he had said was true, in the beginning God created the superior and inferior things) is consistent with the novelty of the world. For the foundation of our law is that God created this world from nothing and without a temporal beginning, etc. Ambrose likewise opposes these to the opinions of the Philosophers, saying, St. Moses, foreseeing by the Divine Spirit that these errors of men would be and perhaps had already begun, says thus in the beginning of his discourse: in the beginning God made heaven and earth.

Comprehending the beginning of things, the author of the world, the creation of matter - - - and that He Himself gave a beginning to things being generated, and that He Himself is the creator of the world, not as an imitator of matter, led by some idea, from which He would form His works not according to His own will, but according to a proposed pattern. St. Chrysostom opposes these things equally to heretics and to the Gentiles: For whether the Manichaean comes forward, saying that matter existed beforehand, or Marcion, or Valentinus, or the Gentiles, say to them: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Therefore, Episcopius's commentary is to be rejected, because these things do not treat of the beginning of the Hexaemeron, nor of the beginning of the creation of the world, but of some earlier beginning, by which God created the heaven and the angels, and also the rude earth, which lay desolate for a long time, lib. IV. Instit. Sect. III, 17. For Scripture knows no other beginning of creation except the beginning of the Hexaemeron. Nay, he expressly testifies that all creatures were perfected within the Hexaemeron, and that every work of God was completed on the seventh day, Gen. II, 1. And he mingles the angels with the works of the Hexaemeral, or if I may so speak, six-day creation, Psalm 104, 4. Nay, he asserts that God created the mountains and the earth, and the world, the abysses and the fountains of waters, the lights and the foundations of the earth, and the heavens at the same time; but he does not assert that the earth was created long before with the heavens, before the rest were formed, Psalm 91, 5. Prov. 8. 22. And thus he acknowledges no other beginning of creation than that which began with the first day of the Mosaic Hexaemeron.

Of a similar bran is the opinion of Petavius, l. 1. of the work of the six days, c. X. that perhaps a day or two, or even longer before the first day of the Hexaemeron, the earth and water were created: which two make up, as it were, the matter from which the rest, and the heaven itself, and the remaining elements were produced. This is openly false, and too absurd. For Moses clearly testifies that in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, not first the earth, and then finally produced the heaven from the earth. Nor can any time or some antecedent creation be imagined before the Hexaemeron, since the entire creation was completed within the six days. Furthermore, will it not have to be said in this way, that all creation properly so called was done only before the Hexaemeron; but that within the Hexaemeron nothing was created from nothing, but only this visible world was then formed from pre-existing matter? But on the contrary, the History of creation testifies, and the words of the Decalogue also testify, Exod. 20, 11. and the entire Holy Scripture [testifies] that within six days the heaven and the earth, and all things that are in them, were created. And Moses teaches that the earth and water under their form, in which they now exist, were not created before that six-day period, but on the third day of the same, even though at the beginning of creation the earth was created immersed in water under a rude and ἀκατασκεύαςος form. Nor does Moses teach that the Heaven was produced from water, which Petavius wishes, or even the air and fire, even though Becanus also thinks this, in Theol. Schol., but he hints that bodies were produced from that entire confused mass: which consisted primarily of earth and water; of which Mass we shall treat later.

Since, however, the origin and novelty of the world is asserted here by Moses, by the common suffrage of the Christian Church, that בראשית is to be opposed to the opinion of some Gentiles concerning the eternity of the world. For if in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth from nothing, it must be that before that beginning of creation all these things were nothing besides God. Therefore, eternal wisdom says that it was when the abysses were NOTHING, Prov. 8, 24. and 2. Maccab. 7, 28. The faith of the Church of the Jews concerning this article is set forth thus: Look to the heaven and to the earth, and all that is in them, and know that He made them FROM NOTHING, ἐκ ἐξ ὄντων.

GOD. In which manner also Paul says Rom. 4, 17. that God calls the things that are not, as things that are. And Heb. 11, 3. he says the worlds were framed by the word, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων [τ]ὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι.

And indeed not a few among the Gentiles themselves acknowledged the origin of the world, which, since they could not have it from the light of nature, they undoubtedly received through tradition from the doctrine of the Jews and the Mosaic writings. Zoroaster, the most ancient of the gentiles, whom they believe to have flourished around the final times of Noah, and to have been the son or grandson of Ham (if he was not Ham himself) and King of the Bactrians, is said to have instructed the Chaldean and Persian Magi thus: The Father perfected all things and delivered them to the second mind, which the whole human race worships as the first. Mercury Trismegistus, who is thought to have flourished around the times of Moses and to have drawn all of Greece from his fountains, has it thus in the Pæmander c. III. There was in the abyss an infinite shadow, and water from above. And a thin intellectual Spirit was moved by the power of GOD in that indigested mass. Thence blossomed a holy splendor, which commanded the elements to emerge from the sand and the humid nature. It is not unknown that Casaubon in Diatr. X. Exerc. I. to the Appar. Annal. of Baronius argues that the writings of Mercury are spurious. But, as regards this chapter, Cyril of Alexandria in book II, along with other ancient Doctors, produced similar things from the same: E. g. That God by his holy, intellectual, and creative Word pronounced: Let the Sun exist, and the Sun was immediately made; likewise, that by the power and force of the same Word the elements were separated, and the stars and herbs were produced with seed. Many things could be brought forward from the ancient Poets, Linus, Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and others, and likewise many from the Philosophers Thales, Pythagoras, Anaximander, Anaximenes, and others (for Plutarch is a witness that the more ancient ones almost all agree here), but especially from Plato and his followers Plotinus, Iamblichus, Crantor, Epictetus, Arrian, then Cicero, Seneca, and Macrobius, if there were need. But Plutarch treats of this in his work on the dogmas of the Philosophers and in his work on Pythagoras, and Augustinus Steuchus Eugubinus in his work on the perennial Philosophy, and also Mornay in his work on the truth of the Christian Religion c. IX. and we have here Grotius agreeing, who also produced not a few things from the Gentiles in his annotations to the book on the truth of the Christian Religion. He excepted Aristotle, however, and attributed to him the opinion that the world never had a beginning. Although he observes, with Moses Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed part III. p. 13, that he speaks hesitantly about that matter in several places, as for instance that in book II of On the Heavens c. 1. he says this is a matter of belief, not a demonstration; in book XII of On the Generation of Animals he ascribes a beginning of existence to animals; and in Topics book CIX he adds this to the questions which can be disputed on both sides: whether the world is from eternity, or not? Whence Grotius concludes: Take from Plato that the world had some origin, from Aristotle that it was not generated, and you will have the very opinion of the Jews and Christians.

And indeed not only concerning the opinion of Aristotle, but also of Plato himself, even his own disciples disputed. Thus Proclus contends that Plato taught the world was eternal, against the Christians. Yet Aristotle, who had heard him for XXII years, undoubtedly knew Plato's mind more correctly, and testifies that he always taught that the world was made. Philo teaches that Plato received this opinion from Hesiod. But Plutarch in the aforementioned book refutes those who think otherwise about Plato thus: Some, he says, who are otherwise students of Plato, twist his words in every way, so that he may appear to deny the creation of the world and the soul, and to assert the eternity of time. But let them see that they do not by this reasoning take away from him that excellent speech of the Gods against the impious, than which nothing is more worthy of Plato, nothing more Platonic. But what need is there for one or two passages to be brought forward, when the Timaeus explains the creation of the world clearly and of set purpose. One will be able to read about these in Mornay c. 8. on the Truth of the Christian Religion.

As far as Aristotle is concerned, although various judgments are found about him, it seems it could nevertheless be obtained that he acknowledged creation in some way, not only from the book On the World, but also from his other undoubted writings, as we showed in Natural and Revealed Theology p. 142 seqq. Whence most weighty authors judge that Aristotle did not entirely ignore God the creator and the creation of the world; Ibn Rushd, who is commonly called Averroes, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Thomas Aquinas, Scotus, Thomas of Argentina, Hervaeus, and among the moderns Francis Suarez, Scaliger, and not a few others. Therefore, the contrary passages of Aristotle should be understood as meaning that he disputed at least against the novelty of the Platonists or the origin of the world through generation: but he did not simply deny the novelty, origin, or creation of the world.

These words of Moses are also to be opposed by R. Abhu, as Maimonides expressly testifies, because God built worlds before this orb and destroyed them again, and by other Rabbis who asserted that time existed before the creation of the world. Furthermore, the Bays of the Japanese, and the Gymnosophists of the Indians, who posited the eternity of the world, from whom, however, most of the rest of the nations thought differently.

The assertion of the Jews concerning the seven things created before the world, as R. Eliezer has it, the Law, Gehenna, Paradise, the throne of glory, the Sanctuary, Repentance, and the Name of the Messiah, is perhaps more symbolic, brought forth in their figurative manner, and respects divine destination rather than contradicting this Mosaic Bereshith.

On R. Menasseh Ben Israel. The corruption of these initial words in Conciliat. p. 3, that בְּרֵאשִׁית means with the beginning, that is, when time was being created, is not something we need to discuss; yet he leaves it that the world was created in time, and that here the first beginning of time is designated. Gadaker in the cited place will suggest other corruptions of these words, if anyone desires them. They are unworthy of being referred to here. From a varied and wonderful, and more than Cabbalistic, combination of the letters of the first word, Pico della Mirandola constructed an entire sentence, which Gualtper brings forward in Collat. translation. page 4.

In the same verse: GOD CREATED.

In Hebrew it is בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים. The cause of creation is thus expressed, the glorious GOD, so that with the unity of essence a plurality of divine persons is simultaneously hinted at. Because the creator of heaven and earth is God blessed, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; therefore, under the very beginning of Genesis and of the entire Scripture, that mystery is insinuated by a peculiar kind of speech, while by a singular verb indeed the one most singular divine creative essence is [signified], but by a plural noun in that one most singular essence, that is, in God μονότατως μόνῳ, a plurality of hypostases and persons is designated, namely that there are several Elohim, who, as they are of the same glorious and majestic divinity to be adored by all, so they exist as the one cause of the creation of all things, the one Creator of heaven and earth, and of all things that are in them, who by one undivided, omnipotent, and infinite power, by one and undivided act, and not by associated work, created the entire machine of the world. Moses surely wished to designate the true God, creator of heaven and earth, immediately at the beginning, lest the Israelites, to whom he was proposing this history of creation, should defer this honor to the demigods and idols of the Egyptians.

Although indeed many do not acknowledge that the mystery is insinuated by the word Elohim, such as the Jews, Arians, and Photinians, who [reject] the mystery

Those who most fiercely attack the Most Holy Trinity, and also Christians who with us venerate and adore the Holy Trinity, include from the Papists Tostatus the Bishop, and the Cardinals, Cajetan in this place and Bellarmine, Book II on Christ, ch. 6 (whose ἑαυτομαχίαν [self-contradiction] in this matter we shall note later), Pagninus in his Lexicon, Sixtus Senensis in his Library, Book 5, annotation 1. Pererius likewise the Jesuit in this place, Vasquez and others: from the Reformed, Calvin and Mercerus in this place, Martyr, Danaeus, Pareus in this place and in his Orthodox Calvin, Book II, ch. 9, Chassanion in his Commonplaces, Book I, ch. 4, Buxtorf in his Thesaurus, Book II, ch. 2, Drusius in his tract on Elohim, Rivet in his First Exercise on Genesis, Fuller, Book I of Miscellanies, ch. 3, Book III, ch. 8, Sixtinus Amama in his Antibarbarus Biblicus, Hottinger in his preface to the Thesaurus Philologicus. and also from the Innovators, Calixtus, having followed Tostatus primarily, and his followers: to whom Hugo Grotius also adds his vote: yet this was solidly proven by our theologians primarily: and against the Socinians primarily, and the Calixtines, it was established in the Assertion of the plurality of divine persons in the O.T., ch. 1, which entirely pertains to this. Concerning the origin and meaning of the name Elohim, it has been treated abundantly in Natural and Revealed Theology, p. 408 et seqq. Its etymon and proper force from the Arabic, because the root of the name אֱלָהּ is no longer used in Hebrew, are rightly deduced by Erpenius, Amama, Dievius, B. D. Glassius, Edvardus, Pocockius in his Miscellaneous Notes to the Port of Moses, ch. III, p. 34, Hottinger in his preface to the Thesaurus Philologicus, and others: to whom Baidavius seems to assent at Surah II, v. 159, cited by Hottinger in his History of Creation, p. 20. It denotes properly a Numen to be honored, σεβασὸν, or σέβασμα, ἄξιον δυλείας [worthy of service]. Compare Deut. 6, v. 10, but not, as Bisterfeld foolishly claims against Crellius, p. 104, 'most united' or those who are one in the most orderly way, as if אֱלָהּ were properly 'to unite in an orderly fashion'.

As for Grotius's exception concerning the Ellipsis, which he suggests at Deut. 10, v. 17, it is new, if I am not mistaken, and first devised by him. Certainly, as far as is known, it never entered the mind of any of the Jews or Socinians, who are the implacable enemies of the Most Holy Trinity. Furthermore, an Ellipsis should not be invented without just cause. But whence will Grotius teach that the word אֱלֹהֵי is to be understood here, so that the sense is, 'In the beginning created אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים [God of Gods] the heaven and the earth'? In the beginning of creation, at any rate, there were no gods in respect to whom Jehovah could be called God of Gods. Who, therefore, would be said to have created in the beginning, when nothing existed besides the one God? Nor is the singular name אֱלֹהֵי found in Deut. 10, 17, but the double plural אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים. If, therefore, the supreme God is denoted by the former word, and this is a full expression, as Grotius wishes, such an exposition will emerge: 'The supreme Gods of the gods'. An Ellipsis certainly cannot be invented here, since the former is placed in the construct state and demonstrates a full expression. It must therefore be admitted that the name placed in the construct state, אֱלֹהֵי, is no less plural in meaning than in determination, and thus it is insinuated that that God, who is three in persons, is the God and Lord of the so-called gods. What is more, those passages in which another plural name joined to the name אֱלֹהִים is found most openly explode that ellipsis. For example, Deut. 5, 26: 'What is all flesh that hears the voice of אלהים חיים [living Gods] speaking from the midst of the fire?' Apply here Grotius's observation about supplying the singular name God, and you will have the name אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים חיים [God of the living Gods]. Who, therefore, are those living gods of whom Jehovah is GOD? Is not that epithet חיים used here as proper to the true God and as a periphrasis? Thus Josh. 24, 19: 'You will not be able to serve Jehovah, because he is אלהים קרשים [holy Gods].' Is it said that an ellipsis has a place here, and that the sense is full, because אלה אלהים קרשים [God of holy Gods], and by 'Saints' he understands the so-called gods? I pass over the fact that this plural name, Elohim, is sometimes used of the true GOD, even when constructed with a plural verb. Which construction certainly admits no ellipsis. E.g., Gen. 20, v. 13: 'They caused me to wander' התעו Elohim from my father's house. Here certainly it cannot be denied that several Elohim are indicated, who called and ordered Abraham to wander: nor does that Ellipsis have a place. Similar examples also occur in Gen. 35, v. 7; 2 Sam. 7, 23. Nor is there any reason for you to say that the Hebrews observed no mystery here; for if even the Hebrews had not noticed or marked the plural meaning, must it therefore be denied? (2.) Nor is it new that sometimes one to whom the language is not vernacular, but acquired by art, observes something that a native speaker has not noticed, since he often judges more accurately from the precepts of art and notices idioms more diligently. (3.) What wonder is it that Christians, illuminated by the light of the N.T., see more in the O.T. concerning the mysteries of the faith than the blinded and obstinate Jews? (4.) How, moreover, will it be taught that no Jew noticed it? Are the writings of all of them extant? How little is it that is known to us about the ancient Hebrews? (5.) That this did not escape the Jews entirely is evident from Bereshith Ketanna, which is not obscure to them and is held in great esteem among them, where this expression is observed as μυςηριώδης [mysterious]; it would not have been permitted for anyone to say thus: ברא אלהים [God created] unless it had been written so. And Rabbi Semlai taught that the reason for that mystery is to be learned from the ancient Masters, being asked how many Elohim created the world, answering: 'I and you, let us ask from the days of old.' Furthermore, the Talmudists on Josh. 22, to the question, 'Why is the name of GOD repeated three times by the sons of Gad and Reuben?', answer: 'They said first GOD, GOD, GOD, because by THESE THREE the world was created, and then they said: God, God, God, because by these three also the light was given.' Ainsworth observes this in the Talmud in this place, citing the statement of R. Simeon Ben Jochai in the Zohar on the 6th Section of Leviticus: 'Come and see the mystery of the word Elohim: there are three degrees, and each degree by itself alone, that is, distinct, yet they are one, and are joined into one, nor is one divided from the other.'

And he brought many such things to light already four hundred years ago in a distinguished work, whose name is THE DAGGER OF FAITH against the Moors and Jews, by Friar Raymond Martini of Subirats, of Catalonia, of the Order of Preachers, who by the wonderful providence of God came upon the more recondite books of the Jews. For when in the year of Christ 1263 his brother Paul the Christian had engaged in a public debate before King James with the most learned Rabbi Moses of Gerona, and had carried off the victory by the reckoning of all, and for that reason was employed to instruct the Jews, and was investigating all the secret volumes of the Jews, and having further convicted another Rabbi equally skilled but very crafty, called Bonastruc, who was publishing false commentaries upon the completed disputation, Pope Clement IV commanded that the perfidious Rabbis should be treated more harshly.
