The Rabbis, however, alleged that nothing blasphemous or contrary to the Holy Scriptures was contained in their books; it came to pass, therefore, that the King decreed by public edict that the Jews should hand over their books and prove that they were such; and that among others Raymond of Peñafort and Raymond Martini should be appointed as judges, from which source the latter obtained the books of the Hebrews, and thus from this iron the honest craftsman forged the DAGGER OF FAITH against the Moors and Jews. From then on, all the secrets of Jewish impiety were uncovered, the weapons of the enemies served the triumph of the Church, palms were plucked from the field of the infidels, Hebrew writings were read by public authority, and schools of Oriental languages were [established] in Christian academies

& masters of the Council of Vienne were established by decree. Francis Bosquet, Bishop of Lodève, explains these and other things concerning this Raymond at length in a letter to Joseph de Voisin, by whose help and effort he first brought the Pugio Fidei to light in Paris in the year 1651, and adorned it with various observations. This work Joseph Scaliger falsely ascribed to Raymond Sebon, a writer on natural theology who lived about two hundred years later, in his 3rd response to Casaubon, A.D. 1603. Others have suspected that Raymond of Penyafort, Master General of the Order of Preachers, was its author, whom Philip James Mausacus makes out to be a helper in this work in his Prolegomena to the Pugio Fidei, whereas the true author, Raymond Martin, brought it to completion three years after his death, namely in the year 1278. But from this source, Peter Galatinus, two hundred and thirty years later, took his Arcana of the Catholic truth, as far as it contains good and useful things, having added many things from the book Zohar of doubtful faith, and from the Gale Razia, which is even more suspect; and likewise Porchetus de Salvaticis, a Genoese Carthusian, in his Victory against the impious Jews, published five years after Galatinus’s Arcana, namely in the year 1520, but in good and sincere faith, and not without praise for the author Martin, that he was an excellent man in Hebrew and Arabic Scriptures as well as in Latin, derived many things. Whence John Morinus is entirely mistaken when, in Exerc. Biblic. part 1, c. 2, p. 16, he argues that Peter Galatinus copied his material from Porchetus, since Porchetus was later than Galatinus, and both drew their material from the source of Raymond. Furthermore, Raymond pursues this argument in the Pugio Fidei, part 3, dist. 1, c. 3, proposing authorities speaking of GOD in the plural, and the observations of the Rabbis concerning the phrase 'He created Elohim,' which have been brought forward in part from Galatinus before. In Bereschith Ketana or the lesser [commentary] on this passage: 'In the beginning created Gods.' R. Hunna said in the name of Bar Cappara: 'If this kind of speech had not been written, it would not have been lawful to say, Gods created the heaven.' In Bereschith Rabba, R. Moses Hadarschan: 'In the beginning created Elohim.' Heretics asked R. Samlai, saying, 'How many Gods created the world?' 'I and you,' he said, 'let us seek this from the Law.' They said to him: 'Behold it is written in Deut. 4:7, For what great nation is there that has אלהים קרובים עליו Gods near to it (I would prefer the word Elohim be retained)?' They said to him: 'Behold two principles שתי ראשיות.' He said to him: 'Read the end of the verse.' Just as 'The Lord our God' in all our calling upon him, it is not written 'TO THEM,' but 'TO HIM.' They said to him: 'Behold it is still written in Josh. 24:19, You will not be able to serve the Lord, because he is אלהים קדשים Holy Gods.' He said to them, 'Read the end of the verse; it did not say, because they are holy Gods, but HE HIMSELF.' They said to him again, 'Behold it is written in 2 Kings 7:23, And who is like thy people, like Israel, a nation one in the earth, for which הלכו אלהים went the Gods to redeem?' He said to them, 'Read the end of the verse, or what is written consequently, to redeem FOR THEMSELVES, it is not written in the plural, but FOR HIMSELF in the singular: and to set for HIMSELF a name.' Again they also said to him, 'Behold it is written in Jer. 23:26, And you have inverted the words of the אלהים חיים Living Gods, or of the living.' He said to them, 'Read the end of the verse; it is not written thus, Lord of hosts, but Lord of Hosts of our GOD.' A passage is also brought forward there from the same book, Bereschith Rabba, by R. Moses Hadarschan on Gen. 1:23. 'I ask you, let us seek from the Law. Gods created, it is not written here, but Gods created Adam, Gen. 1:26.' Again they asked him, what is it that is written in Gen. 1:1, 'In the beginning created Gods the Heaven and the earth?' He said to them, 'In the beginning created Gods, it is not written thus: but in the beginning CREATED Gods.' R. Samlai also said: 'In every place where you find an objection for the heretics, you will also find its remedy at its side.' Again they also asked him, what is it that is written in Gen. 1:26, 'And said Gods: let us make Adam in OUR image according to OUR likeness:' he said to them, 'Read what is written immediately after v. 27, And created Gods, it is not written thus, but, And created Gods.' Something similar to those things said above is also found in Midrash Koheleth, or Gloss on Ecclesiastes c. 2, on that verse 12: 'And I looked to see wisdom and folly and madness. For what is man that he should come after the King את אשר כבר עשיהו because they have already made him?' After the King, that is, after the King, namely the holy and blessed God of other kings, you will be able to stand, etc. He teaches, however, that it should be said through this, that it is not written, 'who made him,' but 'who made him' (plural), which, since it is written in the Law, it is possible to say, i.e., it can be said, the holy and blessed God, and the house of judgment made him, etc. If, however, you say, therefore there are two principles because of this: it does not follow: for was it not already said in Deut. 32:6, 'He himself made and fitted you, or prepared and adorned you?' Raymond adds to these testimonies: 'Understand that neither this Rabbi nor the aforementioned, nor any of the ancients whose sayings I have seen on this matter, deny the mystery of the Trinity, but only multiple principles, or multiple Gods, which certainly the whole Christian religion detests no less than they do, nay, even more.' For in the detestation of two or more principles of the world, or Gods, he entirely rejects the aforementioned way of speaking about GOD, whenever it is a matter of GOD. Which observation of Raymond is to be well noted, that no ancient Rabbi denied the mystery of the Trinity: and that they only denied multiple principles, or multiple Gods, yet they observed the plurality in the word Elohim, and acknowledged it to be plural not only in termination, but also in signification. For from thence those doubts arose, and that comparison of plural expressions with singular ones tends to this, namely, that they might teach that, while the singularity of the essence is preserved, there is a certain plurality in God. Which they also designate by the house of judgment, as Raimundus further shows there: because in the next gloss to Eccles. 2, that GOD holy & blessed & the house of judgment made Adam: by the house of judgment the Son & the Holy Spirit, who with the Father are one principle of visible & invisible creatures, are to be understood: & that בית דין house of judgment was called among the Jews, when three judges at the least gave some sentence. Whence also it seems that God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit is called the house of judgment, to which opinion he also brings Midrash Shir HaShirim on Cant. 1, 9. where these things are read: What is that which is written Jer. 10, 10. And the Lord God is truth? Because he himself is namely אלהים חיים living Gods & eternal King. R. Eleasar said: Wherever in Holy Scripture it is said ויהוה And the Lord, it is understood of himself & of the house of his judgment. Truly, sometimes the Son & the Spirit come under the name of the house of judgment with the Father, from whom they have their origin, sometimes on account of the ὁμοοσίαν, & the unity of the power of judging, & of the judgment itself, those three, Father, Son, & Holy Spirit, are called the house of judgment, & that name was perhaps attributed by the ancients to the most holy Council or Consistory of the Trinity, because they believed אלהים to be said from judging.

Raimundus brings forward besides other places also of plural expressions, in which this mystery of the plurality of persons may be detected, inasmuch as they were expounded concerning God by the Jews: A similar, he says, manner of speaking about GOD is Eccl. 12. verse 1. זכור את בוראיך Remember THY CREATORS, where the gloss, or Midrash, says: This is the King of Kings, the holy and blessed God: this saying is spoken

Hos. 12, 12. But Judah still [is] Lord with GOD and with the HOLY ones faithful. The gloss, however, of R. Solomon Jarchi, [says] Lord with God, that is, ruling with the terror of the Lord. רד ruling is spoken here. Thus Num.

24, 19. And with the HOLY ones faithful still, i.e., their King is still faithful with God. This is R. Solomon (understanding God by קדושים). Likewise in the great exposition on Gen. 54, 20. What is it that Prov. 30, 3 said? And I know the knowledge of the HOLY ones. He called the holy blessed God קדושים HOLY ONES: BECAUSE WHATEVER PERTAINS TO HIM IS IN HOLINESS (שכל עניינו בקדושה הם) as it is said in Josh. 24, 19. You cannot serve the Lord, because HE is a Holy God. כי אלהים קדושים

HE. Likewise in Midrash Koheleth on that c. 5. v. 7. For the high one above the high one watches. וגבהים עליהם And there are HIGH ONES above them. The high one above the high one watches. These are the Angels. And the high ones above them. This is the holy and blessed God. This is Raimundus from the Hebrews. Whence it is evident that it was not entirely hidden from the Jews that by these plural locutions some plurality in God was designated, without prejudice, however, to the unity of the divine essence: which the Christian Church calls a plurality of hypostases or divine persons.

In the same verse: THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.

Jacob Gaffarel contends that the little word את should be read as אות, a sign, so that he may carve out, with the Astrologers and certain Kabbalists, a heaven glittering with letters and distinguished by Alphabetic figures, a Schema of which Kircher exhibits in Oedip. Aegypt. Vol. I. page 215. But these absurdities do not deserve a refutation. See the Heaven of the East by B. D. Thomas Bang, our former friend, Exerc. 2. Moment. 7. And why do they not also imagine the earth to be distinguished by letters, to which Moses here also prefixes the same particle ואת הארץ. Is the word אות to be substituted there as well?

R. Aben-Ezra thinks the word את denotes the substance of a thing, whence Hottinger in Histor. creat. p. 23 observes that the text of this passage is explained in the Syro-Arabic Lexicon of Isa-bar Ali MS. as the substance of heaven and earth: nor does he altogether reject this meaning, so that only the bare substance of the earth, as regards the rude and undigested mass, and of the heaven, as regards its essential perfection reserved for the following days of decoration, might be indicated. But that meaning of the word is unusual.

R. Maimonides, More Nev. book 2, ch. 30, wishes the particle את to signify the preposition with, as if to say that God created with the heavens whatever is in the heavens, and with the earth whatever is in the earth; to which Hottinger, p. 23, partly agrees. But in that way God would have created not only the angels in the heavens, but also living creatures and men on the earth in the very beginning. This the Rabbis indeed affirm, but it is contrary to the Mosaic history, nor does Maimonides prove it except ineptly from Is. 48, v. 13. It is well known to beginners in the Holy language that the particle את is the sign of the Accusative if it is constructed with an active verb, or of the Nominative if with a Passive. Grotius says this regarding these words:

HEAVENS AND EARTH) that is, this universe, such as it now is. For the Hebrews express this with those two words. Whence also the world to come is called by this name, 2 Pet. 3, 13. But in the following verse the earth is called the abyss itself, or the first mass, ἰλὺς to the Phoenicians, concerning which matter and the whole creation see what we have collected in the first book on the Truth of the Christian religion.

Others also think that the summary of the whole universe and its creation described afterwards is comprised: whom Grotius supports here, and Pareus defends this opinion above all. But if the following description is exhibited by these in summary, and this whole universe, such as it now is, is comprised by those two words, then neither the creation of the heavens nor of the earth would have been described by Moses. For in the special account of the works of the Hexaemeron, it is not commemorated how the heaven was created, or how the earth was created; only how the firmament or רקיע, as some wish, was interposed between the waters above and below, or certainly how the dark firmament was produced from that mass of heaven, earth, and water, and interposed for the separating of the waters, which had been immersed or confused with the waters: and similarly how on the third day the Lord ordered only the earth to emerge from the waters and appear, Moses explains, but the creation of the heaven, or even of the earth from nothing, on what day it was done, according to this explanation, Moses would not describe; indeed, thus according to the Grotian interpretation of the prior words, before God created this universe, such as it now is, the earth was void and empty, the earth such as it was will have been described, before the historiographer inspired by God had taught that the same was founded, or when it was founded: and in that way room would be left for suspicion, whether that void and empty earth had already existed many centuries before? which Episcopius dreams, likewise distorting the words of Moses, or whether it had been altogether coeval with God? which Hermogenes and other Materialists invented, as Tertullian testifies, and before them the Stoics, while they kept saying that matter and confused Chaos had existed for eternal times, no less than the Mind as two principles, and that at a certain time at last matter was elaborated by the mind: against which profane opinion Lactantius in book 2 of the Institutes, ch. 8, and Eusebius in book 7 of the Evangelical Preparation, ch. 8, acted. What Grotius nourished in reserve here, whether he sided with Episcopius or not, is not sufficiently clear. Whose ravings, however, we discussed in Vol. 3 of the System of Common Theological Places, p. 1014.

Furthermore, what earth Moses indicated in the first clause of verse 1, he explains immediately in the second clause: But the earth was empty and void. Therefore he does not speak of the earth, such as it now is, or in summary embrace the whole universe, but teaches that that earth was created in the beginning of all things, which was Tohu Vabohu. Besides, Moses himself indicated that he was occupied with the work of the first day of the six-day creation; and it was evening and morning, one day, v. 5. And that earth, which had been empty and void, must have been founded first, or in the first creation on the first day, or it must be asserted that it was founded before the Mosaic beginning of creation or not founded at all: from which the Christian faith shrinks. Then indeed it is open that Moses here begins the first day from the evening, because he had said that God had founded the dark earth at the beginning of that day, and had previously designated the darkness, which was over the face of the abyss, before the first-created light. Moses presented the summary of the six-day work not at the beginning of the book of Genesis, but after the completed treatment of the six days in Genesis 2, verse 1. Therefore the heavens and the earth (namely, by that Hexaemeron) and all their host were created. However, there is no reason for us to think that he wished to include the summary itself in such a concise description both at the beginning and at the end of the Hexaemeron by way of tautology.

Although, therefore, among the other opinions of others, that one not undeservedly seemed probable to Augustine in book 1. against the adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, ch. 10, that spiritual and corporeal nature was generally indicated here, or even, as others among Augustine (l. 1 de Gen. ad lit. c. 3), Ambrose (l. 2 Hexaem. c. 3), Basil (Hom. 3), and with them Cyril of Alexandria (l. 2 contr. Julian.), and most Calvinists, Bucanus, Pareus, Keckermann, Timpler, wish: that corporeal creatures alone are comprehended here: The opinion of those, however, who deny that the sum of creatures is comprehended by those initial words is more probable, nay, certain, because of the reasons adduced. Otherwise, we have noted and refuted the various opinions of others, such as that of Menasse Ben-Israel, that by the first Mosaic words a triple world—Angelic, Celestial, Elemental—is indicated; of R. Moses the Egyptian, that the elements as if separately created first, before they were mixed, such as earth, water, and spirit, or air, and also fire through darkness, are indicated, which Menasse wished to be understood through the primordial light; of the Fanatics, Physicists, and Chemists, who strive to extract their own principles from this, just as each has invented them for himself; then of the Papists, who call the empyrean heaven, which they call barbarously (since it is not ὁ ἐμπύρεος, but ἐμπύριος, meaning fiery); likewise of the Calvinists, who contend that their local Heaven above the firmament, which they call angelic, and the first celestial beings are designated; as Hottinger wishes the empyrean heaven to be indicated with the Papists Lombard, Lyranus, Abulensis, Catharinus, and with his Alting, Wollebius, and Maresius, and at the same time the inhabitants of the Empyrean heaven, as he says, the Angels, created: or even, as interpreted by Cloppenburg, they believe that the Heaven of God, the Heaven of Angels, the Angels themselves, and the starry Heaven are designated, attributing so many and such diverse significations to one and the same word at the same time; and also those peculiar opinions of Lud. Crocius, who in his Alphabetum Mosaicum (Syntagm. Theol. p. 770) feigns that by Heaven are described the Angels and their domicile, but by earth the triune body and the created monotriad, consisting of the slime of the earth, the abyss, and water; and of Episcopius, who hints that heaven and earth were made much earlier than the earth itself was fashioned, and makes that abyss the tartarus into which the Demons were cast: finally, of Petavius, who likewise feigns that earth and water were created before the first day of the Hexaemeron as a kind of matter from which Heaven itself and the elements were produced; and other such inventions of this kind, we have noted and refuted in Syst. Theol. l. c. p. 929 seqq.

All these things having been discussed, no explanation is more convenient than that by these words a rude and undigested mass, as the first work of GOD from nothing but at the very beginning of the hexaemeron, is designated as having been produced, which we are accustomed to call Chaos, which was named by anticipation by the name of heaven and earth, because the matter of heaven and earth, which were afterwards formed from it, existed. For thus the Mosaic principle is rightly understood first, by which he expressed the beginning of all things, or of the universe, before which there was nothing except GOD the creator, which is called by Basil τὸ πρῶτον τẽ χρόνε νῦν. Thus, secondly, the word בָּרָא will retain its proper and primary meaning, by which it denotes production from nothing. Provided that that matter was produced immediately from nothing. To which it contributes that

Gen. 2, v. 3, it is held that God rested from his work, which he had created to be done, with the word בָּרָא designating that creation by which matter was produced from nothing as a kind of first instance, but with the word עָשׂה expressing the subsequent fabrication of things, by which he prepared and fashioned various kinds of things from the same; just as the Rabbis also distinguish בָּרָא and יָצַר, in that the former designates the production of a thing from nothing, the latter the induction of form into matter; concerning which distinction see Hotting. Hist. creat. p. 17.

Thus, thirdly, the words of heaven and earth will not need to be interpreted as referring to I know not what fictitious heavens or what earth, but they will denote, as is commonly the custom, this heaven and this earth, as the He Hajediah expresses, although proleptically and materially only, not under the form and disposition which it would subsequently assume. For there was in truth a heaven, there was an earth in that primeval mass, even if not distinguished and formed from one another, which was the work of the following days. For here Moses is still occupied with the theogenemata of the first day. Thus שמים, Heaven, which is above, will denote in respect to the earth: which is so called not from שם there, or אש fire, or שא sustain, or מים waters, as if it were waters there, or fire and waters, or a support for the waters, not from שום placed, as R. Mardochai Nathan wishes: not from שם or שמה, an adverb of a remote place, as B. Walther in Spongia Mosaica p. 54 wishes, not from an unusual root which might designate a certain circular height, or Sphere, as ען a center, and through that שמים the sphere of sublunary fire might be noted, which Marcus Marinus wishes in arc. Noæ f. 23, not from שמד admired, which according to the Portuguese is understood by that name as all wonderful bodies; but from a root now indeed no longer used in Hebraism: whose meaning, however, can be sought from Arabism, a related language, in which שמר becomes, to be sublime, elevated, high, as Aben-Ezra, Fagius, Erpenius, Hottinger, Pocock, and other philologists have noted. Aben-Ezra on this passage has it thus: The meaning of שמים is height and eminence, as also in the Israelitic language, which in most respects conforms to the holy language; which meaning suits the thing itself, Job 11 v. 8. Its singular is שמי which occurs among the Ethiopians, from which the plural שמים is formed after the pattern of מצרים. For it is not of the dual number, as is commonly thought, but plural, as also among the Syrians and Chaldeans, who lack a proper dual, the word שמיא, so that there is no need to seek reasons why it is of the dual number: See Hotting. Smegm. Or. p. 82 and Hist. creat. p. 26. Similarly, ארץ here will designate the earth, which is below, just as it was still in that crude mass. Which has its name not from רוץ running, nor from רצץ crushing, but from ארץ, whose meaning must likewise be sought from the Arabic language, in which Aradza is to be humble, depressed, just as also to the Chaldeans the earth is called ארעא as if it were the lowest, because according to Aben-Ezra it is inferior to all things. Nor yet are the higher and lower things to be understood by heaven and earth with Maimonides, whom Hottinger joins. For this meaning is entirely unused in Scripture.

Thus, fourthly, that earth, which is described immediately, will be said to have been created in the beginning: which, namely, was תהו ובהו, by which words its horrible vastness is expressed. For since that rude, indigested, and empty Chaos is designated, which Paræus also, as well as Grotius and others admit, it certainly cannot be doubted that by the former word, by which that earth is said to have been created, the same Chaos is designated. For thus Grotius: In the following verse the earth is called the abyss itself, or the first mass, ἰλὺς to the Phoenicians. And it is certain to Paræus: That Moses in the second verse deals with Chaos. A vast mass, he says, Moses calls that earth, not by any catachresis or synecdoche, by which a thing is called by its material, iron, sword, wood, ark, but by anticipation, i.e., The earth on the first day was a rude and vast mass.

Thus, fifthly, the appellation of abyss will be most appropriate, by which a deep whirlpool is noted by the word תהום and ἄβυσσος is ἄβυθος, over which there was mere darkness. Whence that tenebricose Chaos is not undeservedly designated in this way.

Thus, sixthly, the Davidic description agrees, by which the work of the first day in Psalm 104 v. 6 is said to be that God founded the earth upon its stability, the abyss being as his garment, and that the waters stood above the mountains: which afterwards fled from the rebuke of GOD (on the third day).

Thus the opinion of the seventh book of Wisdom and of the Jewish Church will be consistent with itself: according to which the omnipotent hand of God created the world ἐξ ἀμόρφου ὕλης from formless matter, as is held in Wisd. 11:18. Which R. Moses Maimonides also seems to have hinted at in More Nebuch. p. 2, c. 30, when he says that on the first day all things were created at once; on the remaining days they were only separated. Cf. Men. Ben-Israel Probl. 4, de creat.

Thus in the eighth [section] will be revealed the origin of the opinion concerning primeval Chaos, which flowed out to the Gentiles and undoubtedly proceeded from the Mosaic narrative. Which Grotius also connects here, explaining the first mass described by Moses from the most ancient histories of the Phoenicians, which Philo of Byblos translated as collected by Sanchuniathon, and which Eusebius brought forward in Praepar. Evang. l. 1, c. 10: there also, according to Phoenician theology, Eusebius establishes the first principle of this universe as a turbid Chaos, enclosed by darkness. Which the Greeks seem to have received from the Phoenicians. Whence Linus, who came from Phoenicia, asserted that in the primeval time all things were mixed together, and Orpheus asserted that there was Chaos and dark night, concealing all things that are under the ether. See Scaliger, Chron. Euseb. l. 1; Grotius on de verit. Relig. Christian. l. 1. Epicharmus, the most ancient of the Greek comic poets, says that Chaos existed before all things; and so also did Hesiod, Apollonius, Aristophanes, and the Platonists; the Latins received these from the Greeks, especially Ovid in his Metamorphoses. And the Egyptians handed down similar things, as Diodorus Siculus testifies, that the beginning is a confused mass. Grotius brought forward more such things in his annotations to de verit. Relig. l. 1. But concerning these, it must be observed that they are similar to ours, not the same, and they ought not to be confused with ours, as seems to have been done by Grotius, who wishes that that first mass, which Moses described, was the ἰλὺς of the Phoenicians. The Phoenicians and Egyptians indeed received such things from the Hebrews, and the Greeks from them, and the Latins from these, but they involved them in their own fables and inventions, and were ignorant of the true beginning. Whence they also invented an eternal Chaos, being destitute of revelation, which alone teaches that it was founded IN THE BEGINNING. And for that reason Justin shows that Plato received from the Church what he said, that God created the world from formless matter, Apol. 2 pro Christ. p. 72.

Thus, therefore, the opinion of the ancient Doctors of the Church will agree with the Ninth [point]: those who acknowledged that Mosaic Chaos, for instance Justin, l. c., Basil the Great, Hom. 2 in Hexaem., who teaches that heaven and earth were made before the primordial light, but were unformed; and especially Augustine, l. de Genes. contra Manichaeos c. 5, 6, 7, lib. 12 Confess. c. 3, 29, as also Eucherius, who says on Gen. 1: Matter was made from nothing: but the form of the world [was made] from unformed matter, which was called by the name of heaven and earth, not because it was this, but because it could be this. To these, after our blessed Luther, most of our theologians add their vote: Gesner, Rungius, Lyserus, Pelargus, Hutterus, Gerhardus, Waltherus, who can be consulted at length on these matters in his Spongia Mosaica, and others; as well as, from the Pontifical side, Lombardus, lib. 3, sent. dist. 12. and those who follow the Master, the Sententiaries, along with Bonaventura, Albertus, Alensis, the author of the Glossa, Tostatus, Catharinus, and among the Calvinists, Zanchius, lib. 1 de oper. creat. c. 23, Martyr and Junius in h. l., Polanus, lib. 5 Syntag. c. 4, Alstedius in Phys. Harm. c. 1, Altingius, part. 1 Probl. Theol. 19, who explain the words of Moses with us.

Latin:

PARS I. GENESEOS. HISTORIA ADAMI. a cap. I. usque ad VI.

CAPUT I. Creatio cœli & terræ juxta Hexaemeri opera.

Vers. 1. IN PRINCIPIO CREAVIT DEUS) Melius in principio creare Deum, id est priusquam crearet si- ve formaret Deus. Bene autem legibus præposuit Moses histo- riam a Mundo condito. Mundus enim legi, lex Mundo con- cinit, ut ait Philo.

MElius reddi censet Grotius, in principio creare Deum, id est, priusquam crearet, sive formaret Deus cœlum & terram : id est, universum hoc, quale nunc est, tunc terra erat inanis & vacua. Versio apta, & grata Philosophorum, atque hæreticorum menti, de mundo infecto, & materia æterna. Sic enim nihil aliud annuisset Moses, quam, priusquam hoc universum, QVAlE NVNC est, formaret Deus, terram fuisse vacuam & inanem. Unde agnoscit Thomas Gatakerus Londinensis in Cinno, sive Adversariis Miscellan. L. II. c. 1. varias in formas initialia verba Geneseos convertens, vel conversa expendens, hanc Grotii translationem ansam præbere suspicandi, quod Hermogenes olim somniavit, ante creationem inchoatam materiam extitisse, quæ ipsa semper fuerit, neq́; nata, neque facta, nec initium habens omnino, nec finem, ex qua Deus omnia postea fecerit: vel etiam quod Valentinus deliravit, Bython innatum, immensum, invisibilem, æternum, qui ante hæc omnia fuerit, vel quod Luminarium Novorum, ut arcani hujus mystæ indigitant, Theosophia Teutonica nuper prodidit: ante omnem rerum creationem ab æterno extitisse immensa & infinita duo, Deum & abyssum: Abyssum hanc nec penitus nihil, nec Deum ipsummet esse, licet post Deitatem de realitate entis summe participem, sed Deitatis veluti corpus, vel habitaculum: & abysso huic attribui posse fere omnia, quæ Philosophi materiæ suæ primæ adscribunt. Quam revera Gehennam esse, licet ante Luciferi defectionem in æctum Gehennalem suum non proruperit, (quale portentum etiam ex Abysso, sed longe ante mundum visibilem condita, formasse Episcopium deinde observabimus) ex cujus abyssi proprietate cum radiis e centro Deitatis emanantibus unica colluctatione, conditam esse ab æterno lucem majestaticam, eamque esse ipsam sapientiam, de qua Salomo, Patre DEO, abysso matre progenitam, impie matæologiæ illius autor commentus est. Quæ omnia eo fine excogitata, ut credatur, creationem non esse ex nihilo.

Petrus Picherellus in Cosmopœias Mosaicæ Paraphrasi, etsi hoc comma ita reddiderit: Quo extiterunt initio cœlum & terra, eo Deus illa creavit : In annotatione tamen sua hæc subjunxit: In Hebræo est, In principio creavit Deus cœlum & terram, id est: in principio cœli & terræ Deus creavit illa. Quæ vero explicatio dubium etiam relinquit, anne principium illud fuerit primum initium omnium rerum, quæ præter DEUM existunt nec ne?

Quid quod ipse Grotius rectius illa Annot. in Evangel. Joh. exposuerit: Cum primum Universitas cæpit creari, verbum creandi de productione ex nihilo, & principium de initio Universitatis intelligens. De primo temporis initio, ea cum Ambrosio & Chrysostomo, Basilius accepit, in Hexaem. Orat. I. ἐν ἀρχῇ, τουτέστιν, ἐν ἀρχῇ ταύτῃ τῇ κατὰ χρόνον. Sed disertissime omnium exposuit ea Tertull. adversus Hermogenem c. XIX. Nos unicuique vocabulo proprietatem suam vindicamus; principium initium esse, & competisse ita poni rebus incipientibus fieri. Nihil enim, quod fieri habet, sine initio esse, quum initium sit illud ipsum, dum incipit fieri. Ita principium sive initium, inceptionis esse verbum, non alicujus substantiæ nomen.

Sequutus autem hic Grotius est e Judæis R. Salomon Jarchi, vel potius Rob. Stephan. qui nonnullos Ebræos ita vertere observavit: Alii dicunt בְּרֵאשִׁית conjunctum esse (quod alias vocant esse in regimine) cum sequente verbo בָּרָא, & vertunt, In principio creandi Deum. i. e. In principio quo creavit Deus, hoc est, quum primum creavit Deus, &c. tum terra, &c. ut referatur ad sequentem versum. Tunc autem בָּרָא erit ac si esset scriptum בְּרוֹא. & in prin- cipio secundi versus accipietur pro Tum, aut redunda- bit. At rectius cum LXX. Interpp. Vulgata Ver- sio, quam ceu authenticam Tridentinis, posthabere non debuit Grotius: In principio, rerum sc. omnium, creavit Deus cœlum & terram. Terra autem erat inanis & vacua. Quæ verborum proprietate niti- tur; in principio creavit, inquit Moses: veram ac propriam creationem designans. Neque enim fas est nobis a fignificatu nativo discedere. Cohærent etiam sequentia per particulam copulativam, ET terra erat vacua. Tum exponit Moses ordine ope- ra primi Hexaemeri, ut primum rerum omnium principium sese indicasse doceat. Quod in ἀνακε- φαλαιώσει cap. II, 1. porro confirmat, ut & vers. 4. creationis initium voce Bereschith indicatur Job. 41. vers. 2. Jer. 28. v. 29. De principio rerum omnium explicat quoque David Psal. 102, 26. Initio tu Do- mine terram fundasti. Et Salomo de principio via- rum Domini Prov. 8. v. 23. Nec non Johannes cap. 1. v. 1. In principio erat verbum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Nimis manifestum est, Spiritum S. his in lo- cis ad Mosaicum initium respicere, ut prima Ge- neseos verba necessario ita reddenda sint, in princi- pio creavit Deus cœlum & terram. Quo sensu acce- perunt ea communiter Patres, non modo quos jam adduximus, Tertull. Basilius, Ambrosius, Chryso- stomus, sed & Concilium Lateranense C. firmiter de Summ. Trinit. & fid. Cathol. Nonnulli apud Au- gust. IN PRINCIPIO, id est ante omnia, ita, ut nihil Deus creavit prius, initio operis divini. Qui sensus nostro convenit. E Judæis etiam Philo, nec non R. Saaida in paraphrasi Arabica. Fagius in col- latione translationum adducit etiam Kimchium, ita exponentem: In principio creavit Deus cœlum & ter- ram, ac deinde ea, quæ ex istis prodierunt. R. Moses Maimonid. in More Nebuch. part. II. cap. XXX. Præpositio inseparabilis Beth est Beth vasis seu instru- menti, Et vera illius loci expositio est hæc: in prin- cipio Deus creavit superiora & inferiora. Notat & Stephani nonnullos ex Ebræis subaudire הכל, ut vertas, Primum omnium creavit. Frequens enim est Hebræis, in rebus non ambiguis aliquid subti- cere, ut Job. 3, 10. Es. 8, 4. Sed ea ellipsi opus non est. Sensum enim sine supplemento perspicuum esse, Doctores Ebræi agnoscunt, observante ipso- met Stephani, reddentes, initio creavit Deus. Chal- dæus Paraphr. Hierosol. vertit in Sapientia, ideo for- te in Ebræo hic haberi IN FILIO Tertul. in libr. contr. Prax. & Hilar. in expos. Psalm. annotarunt (observante Hieronymo) qui facile confundere po- tuere Ebræum textum cum Chaldæo, Sapientiam de Filio Dei accipientes; uti etiam Origenes de Fi- lio Dei hoc primum Geneseos verbum accepit, & in glossa interlineari conjunguntur hæ duæ, vel tres expositiones, in principio temporis, vel ante cætera, vel in Filio suo. Stephani exponit Targum in Sapi- entiis, id est, sapientissime. At Targum Onkelos ha- bet, ut in Ebr. est בְּקַדְמִין In principiis scil. omnium rerum, ante res omnes creatas. Jonathan בְּאוֹלָא in principio. Sic & Græci Interpp. non tantum LXX. Seniores, sed etiam Symmachus & Theodotio ἐν ἀρχῇ: solus Aquila ἐν κεφαλαίῳ in capitulo.

Proinde ex his verbis Philosophos refellit Mai- monides l. c. Expositio (illa, quam veram dixerat in principio Deus creavit superiora & inferiora) conve- niens novitati mundi. Fundamentum enim legis no- stræ est, quod Deus mundum hunc creavit ex nihilo & absq; principio temporali &c. Ambrosius opponit pariter hæc Philosophorum opinionibus, Divino, inquit, Spiritu prævidens S. Moses hos hominum er- rores fore & jam forte cepisse, in exordio sermonis sui, sic ait: in principio fecit Deus cœlum & terram.

Initium rerum, autorem mundi, creationem mate- riæ comprehendens - - - & ipsum dedisse gignendis re- bus initium, & ipsum esse creatorem mundi, non ideà quadam duce, imitatorem materiæ, ex qua non ad arbitrium suum, sed ad speciem propositam sua opera formaret. S. Chrysostomus hæreticis æquè, & genti- bus hæc opponit: Nam sive Manichæus prodeat, materiam prius extitisse dicens, sive Marcio, sive Va- lentinus, sive gentiles, dicito ipsis: In principio fecit Deus cælum & terram. Reprobandum ergò Epi- scopii commentum, quòd hæc non de principio Hexaëmeri, neque de principio creationis mundi, sed de anteriori quodam principio agant, quo Deus cæ- lum creavit, & Angelos, nec non terram rudem, quæ diu jacuerit desolata, lib. IV. Instit. Sect. III, 17. Nul- lum enim aliud creationis principium novit Scri- ptura, nisi principium Hexaëmeri. Imò diserte te- statur, intra Hexaëmeron esse perfectas omnes creaturas, completumque fuisse die septimo omne opus Dei Gen. II, 1. & Angelos operibus creationis Hexaëmericæ, ut ita loquar, vel sextiduanæ im- miscet Psalm. 104, 4. imò montes & terram, & or- bem, abyssos & fontes aquarum, lumina & cardi- nes terræ, & cælos simul condidisse Deum; non verò longe ante à terram conditam fuisse cum cæ- lis, antequam cætera efformarentur, asserit Psalm. 91, 5. Prov. 8. 22. adeoque aliud nullum principium creationis agnoscit, quam quod cum primo die Hexaëmeri Mosaici cœpit.

Similis furfuris est opinio Petavii l. 1. operis sex dier. c. X. ante primum Hexaëmeri diem fortassis uno alterove die, vel etiam longius creatam esse terram & aquam: quæ duo quasi materiam faciunt, ex quâ cætera & cælum ipsum & elementa reliqua producta sint. Falsum hoc aperte, nimisque ineptum. Te- statur enim clarè Moses, in principio Deum cælum & terram creasse, non primum terram, tum demum e terra cælum produxisse. Neque fingi potest an- te Hexaëmeron tempus aliquod aut creatio quædam antecedanea, quum intra sextiduum absoluta sit universa creatio. Porro, annon dicendum ita erit, creationem proprie dictam omnem non nisi ante Hexaëmeron factam; intra Hexaëmeron autem ni- hil creatum esse e nihilo, sed mundum tantum hunc visibilem tum e materia præexistente formatum es- se? At ex adverso testatur Historia creationis, te- stantur etiam verba Decalogi Exod. 20, 11. & univer- sa Scriptura S. intra sex dies cælum & terram, & o- mnia, quæ in eis sunt, creata esse. Nec terra & aqua sub forma sua, qua nunc existunt, ante sextiduum il- lud, sed tertio ejusdem die condita esse, Moses do- cet, etsi sub initium creationis terra aquæ immersa sub rudi forma & ἀκατασκεύαςος creata fuerit. Neque Cælum ex aqua productum Moses docet, quod Petavius vult, aut etiam aerem atque ignem, etsi hoc Becanus etiam putet, in Theol. Schol. sed ex uni- versa illa confusa mole: quæ imprimis terra & aqua constabat, producta esse corpora innuit; de qua Massa deinde acturi sumus.

Quum autem asseratur hic a Mose, communi Ecclesiæ Christianæ suffragio, mundi ortus & novi- tas, illud בראשית opinioni de æternitate mundi gentilium nonnullorum opponendum. Si enim in principio e nihilo creavit Deus cælum & ter- ram, ante principium illud creationis omnia hæc præter Deum nihil fuisse oportet. Ideo sapientia æterna se fuisse dicit, quum abyssi essent NIHIL Prov. 8, 24. & 2. Maccab. 7, 28. Ecclesiæ Judæorum de hoc articulo fides ita exponitur: Respice ad cæ- lum & ad terram, & omnia, quæ in eis sunt, & co- gnosce, quod EX NIHILO, ἐκ ἐξ ὄντων illa fecit

DEUS. Quo pacto etiam Paulus ait Rom. 4, 17. Deum vocare τὰ μὴ ὄν[τ]α, ὡς ὄν[τ]α. Et Ebr. 11, 3. secula dicit a- ptata verbo, ut ex invisibilibus fierent visibilia, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων [τ]ὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι.

Et sane agnovere non pauci inter ipsos Genti- les ortum mundi, quem quum e naturæ lumine ha- bere nequiverint, sine dubio, per traditionem e Ju- dæorum doctrina, scriptisq; Mosaicis accepere. Zo- roaster antiquissimus gentilium, quem circa extre- ma Noëh tempora floruisse, ac Chami filium, aut ne- potem (si non fuerit ipse Cham) & Regem Bactria- norum fuisse, credunt, Chaldæos & Persas Magos ita instituisse dicitur: Pater perfecit omnia & tradidit secundæ menti, quam universum genus humanum tan- quam primum colit. Mercurius Trismegistus, qui cir- ca Mosis tempora floruisse, & ex ejus fontibus uni- versa Græcia hausisse putatur, in Pæmandro ita ha- bet c. III. Erat in abysso umbra infinita, aqua vero de- super. Et tenuis Spiritus intellectualis per DEI virtu- tem in illa indigesta mole versabatur. Inde effloruit san- ctus splendor, qui ex arena & natura humida elementa emergere jussit. Non ignotum est, Casaubonum in Diatr. X. Exerc. I. ad Appar. Annal. Baronii νοθείας scripta Mercurii arguere. Sed, quod ad hoc caput, similia produxit Cyrillus Alexand. l. II. cum aliis an- tiquis Dd. ex eodem: E. g. Deum suo sancto, intelle- ctuali & opifice λόγῳ pronunciasse: Existat Sol, & continuo factum Solem, item, ejusdem λόγου virtute & vi elementa discreta condita, astra, herbas cum semine productas. Possent multa e Poetis antiquis, Lino, Or- pheo, Homero, Hesiodo & aliis, multa item e Philoso- phis Thalete, Pythagora, Anaximandro, Anaximene, aliisq; (antiquiores enim ad unum fere omnes hîc consentire Plutarchus testis est) cumprimis vero e Platone, ejusq; sectatoribus Plotino, Jamblichio, Crantore, Epicteto, Ariano, tum Cicerone, Seneca, Macrobio adduci, si opus esset. Sed agit id Plutar- chus de dogmat. Philosophior. & in Pythagor. & Augustinus Steuchus, Eugubinus de perenn. Philof. nec non Mornaeus de verit. Relig. Christ. c. IX. & habemus hic Grotium assentientem, qui etiam non pauca annot. ad libr. de verit. Relig. Christ. e Gen- tilibus produxit. Aristotelem tamen excepit, eiq; opinionem de mundo nunquam cæpto tribuit. Quanquam hæsitanter eum compluribus in locis ea de re loqui cum Mose Maimonide Ductor. dubitant. part. III. observet p. 13. utpote quod l. II. de Cæl. c. 1. πίςον hoc dicat, non ἀπόδειξον l. XII. de gener. anim. initium existendi animalibus adscribat, & To- pic. l. CIX. quæstionibus, quæ in utramq; partem disputari possint, hanc accenseat, an ab æterno sit mundus, an non? Unde concludit Grotius: Sume de Platone, mundi originem fuisse aliquam, ab Aristo- tele, non esse genitum, & habebis ipsam Judæorum & Christianorum sententiam.

Et sane non tantum de Aristotelis, sed etiam de Platonis ipsius sententia disputarunt ipsimet etiam discipuli nonnulli. Sic Proclus Platonem mundum æternum docuisse adversus Christianos contendit. Quo tamen sine dubio rectius Platonis mentem no- vit Aristoteles, qui cum XXII. annos eum audiverat, perpetuo mundum factum ipsum docuisse testa- tur. Quam opinionem ab Hesiodo Platonem ac- cepisse Philo docet. Plutarchus vero l. c. ita re- fellit aliter opinantes de Platone: Quidam, inquit, Platonis alioqui studiosi torquent omnibus modis ejus verba, ut creationem mundi & animæ negare, tempo- risque æternitatem asseverare videatur. At videant, ne egregiam illam Deorum adversus impios orationem ei hac ratione tollant, qua nihil Platone est dignius, nil Platonicum magis. Quid autem uno aut altero lo- co prolato opus est, cum Timæus creationem mun- di diferte, & de industria exponat. Legi de his po- terit Morneus c. 8. de Verit. Relig. Christ.

Aristotelem quod attinet, etsi reperiantur va- ria de eodem judicia, eum tamen creationem aliquo modo agnovisse non tantum e libro de mundo, sed ex aliis quoq; indubiis ejus scriptis videtur obtineri potuisse, uti ostendimus Theol. nat. & revel. p. 142. seqq. Unde gravissimi autores censent, Aristotelem Deum creatorem, & creationem mundi non omni- no ignorasse; Ibno Raschid, qui vulgo Averrhoës di- citur, Alex. Aphrodiseus, Thomas de Aquin. Scotus, Thomas de Argent. Hervæus, & e modernis Franc. Suarez, Scaliger, aliiq; non pauci. Loca ergo con- traria Aristotelis eo accipienda fuerint, quod saltem contra Platonicorum novitatem vel ortum mundi per generationem disputarit: non vero simpliciter mun- di novitatem, ortum vel creationem negarit.

Opponenda hæc Mosis verba etiam R. Abhu, Maimonide teste professo, quod Deus ante hunc or- bem ædificarit mundos, eosq; iterum destruxerit, & aliis Rabbinis, qui tempus ante mundi creationem extitisse asseruerunt. Bays insuper Japonensium, & Gymno- sophistis Indorum, qui æternitatem mundi statue- runt, a quibus cæteri tamen pleriq; e gentibus di- versum sensere.

Judæorum assertum de rebus septem ante mun- dum conditis, ut R. Eliezer habet, Lege, Gehenna, Pa- radiso, throno gloriæ, Sanctuario, Resipiscentia, & No- mine Messiæ, forte magis Symbolicum est, figurato ipsorum more prolatum, ac destinationem divinam potius respicit; quam huic Bereschith Mosaico repu- gnat.

De R. Menass. Ben Israel. corruptela horum ini- tialiũ verborum in conciliat. p. 3. quod בְּרֵאשִׁית sit cum principio, id est, cum tempus crearetur, non est, quod dicamus, relinquit tamen illa, mundum in tempore creatum esse, & hic primum temporis ini- tium designari. Alias vocum harum corruptelas Gadakerus l. c. suggeret, si quis eas desideret. Indi- gnæ sunt, quæ huc referantur. E varia & mirabili, ac plus quam Cabbalistica literarum primæ vocis com- binatione Picus Mirandul. integram sententiam ex- truxit, quam adfert Gualtper. in collat. translation. pag. 4.

Versu eodem: CREAVIT DEUS.

In Ebræo est בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים Exprimitur ita causa creationis, DEUS gloriosus, ut cum essentiæ u- nitate personarum divinarum pluralitas simul innua- tur. Quia creator cœli & terræ est Deus benedictus, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S. sub ipsum ergo Geneseos & Scripturæ universæ initium mysterium illud insi- nuatum est peculiari loquutionis genere, dum verbo quidem singulari unica singularissima essentia divina creatrix, nomine autem plurali in unica illa singula- rissima essentia, hoc est, in Deo μονότατως μόνῳ hy- postassium & personarum pluralitas designata, quod nempe plures Elohim sint, qui ut ejusdem gloriosæ & majestaticæ, ab omnibus adorandæ, divinitatis sunt, ita unica creationis rerum omnium causa, unus Creator cœli & terræ, ac omnium, quæ in illis sunt, existant, qui una indivisa, omnipotenti atq; infinita virtute, uno & indiviso actu, non vero opera socia, creaverint universam mundi machinam. Nimirum verum Deum creatorem cœli & terræ initio statim designare voluit Moses, ne Ægyptiorum Deastris, & Idolis Israëlitæ, quibus hanc creationis historiam proponebat, hunc honorem deferrent.

Quanquam vero multi non agnoscunt, voce Elohim mysterium illud insinuatum esse, utpote tum Judæi, Ariani, ac Photiniani, qui mysterium

S. S. Trinitatis acerrime impugnant, tum etiam Christiani, qui Sacram Trinitatem nobiscum venerantur, & adorant, e Pontificiis Tostatus Episcopus, & Cardinales, Cajetanus in h. l. ac Bellarm. l. II. de Christo c. 6. (cujus ἑαυτομαχίαν in hac causa deinde notabimus) Pagninus in Lexico, Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. S. l. 5. annot. I. Pererius item Jesuita in h. l. Vasquetz & alii : e Reformatis Calvinus & Mercerus, in h. l. Martyr, Danæus, Pareus in h. l. & in Calvino Orthod. l. II. c. 9. Chassan. in Loc. Com. l. I. c. 4. Buxtorf. in Thef. l. II. c. 2. Drus. tract. de Elohim, Rivet. Exerc. I. in Genes. Fullerus l. I. Miscell. c. 3. l. III. c. 8. Sixtinus Amama in Antibarb. Bibl. Hotting. præfat. in Thes. Philolog. nec non e Novatoribus Calixtus, Tostatum imprimis secutus, ejusq; asseclæ: quibus calculum quoque adjicit Hugo Grotius: probatum tamen id a nostris imprimis Theologis solide fuit: & adversus Socinianos imprimis, & Calixtinos evictum Assertione pluralitatis personarum divinarum in V. T. cap. I. quod totum huc pertinet. De nominis etiam Elohim origine, ac significatione actum abunde Theol. natur. & revel. p. 408. seqq. Cujus etymon & vim propriam ex Arabismo, quia radix nominis אֱלָהּ non amplius in Ebraismo usitata est, recte deducunt Erpenius, Amama, Dievius, B. D. Glassius, Edvardus, Pocockius in Notis Miscell. ad Port. Mosis c. III. p. 34. Hottinger. præfat. Thesaur. Philol. & alii: quibus annuere videtur Baidavius ad Sur II. v. 159. Hottingero laudatus Hist. creat. p. 20. Notat proprie Numen honorandum, σεβασὸν, vel σέβασμα, ἄξιον δυλείας. Conf. Deut. 6. v. 10. non vero, ut ineptit Bisterfeld. contr. Crellium p. 104. unitissimos seu eos, qui ordinatissime unum sunt, ac si אֱלָהּ proprie sit ordinate unire.

Quantum ad exceptionem Grotii de Ellipsi, quam ad Deut. 10. v. 17. suggerit, nova ea, nisi fallor, & ab ipso primum excogitata est. Nemini certe, quod constet, Judæorum, aut Socinianorum, qui ἄσπονδοι SS. Trinitatis hostes sunt, in mentem venit. Porro fingenda non est Ellipsis citra justam causam. Unde vero docebit Grotius, hic subaudiendam esse vocem אֱלֹהֵי, ut sensus sit, in principio creavit אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים Deus Deorum Cœlum & terram. In principio utiq; creationis Dii nulli erant, quorum respectu Jehovah Deus Deorum potuerit vocari. Qui ergo Deus Deorum in principio creasse diceretur, quum præter unum Deum extiterit nihil? Neq; vero singulare nomen אֱלֹהֵי reperitur Deut 10, 17. sed plurale geminum אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים. Si ergo priori voce Deus summus notetur, & plena sit hæc locutio, uti vult Grotius, expositio talis emerget, Dii summi Deorum. Ellipsis certe fingi hic non potest, quum prius in statu regiminis positum sit, plenamque locutionem demonstret. Fateri ergo oportet, nomen in regimine positum אֱלֹהֵי non minus significatione, quam determinatione plurale esse, adeoq; Deum illum, qui personis trinus est Deum & Dominum Deorum λεγομένων esse, insinuari. Quid quod apertissime ellipsin istam ea loca explodant, in quibus nomen aliud plurale nomini אֱלֹהִים junctum reperitur. Exempli gratia Deut. 5, 29. Quæ caro omnis, quæ audiat vocem אלהים חיים loquentis in medio ignis? Applica hic observationē Grotii de supplendo nomine singulari Deus, habebis nomen אֱלֹהֵי אֱלֹהִים חיים Deę Deorum viventium. Quinam ergo sunt illi Dii viventes, quorū Jehovah DEUS est? Annon Epitheton illud חיים ut veri Dei proprium, & περιφρασικὸν hic adhibetur? Sic Jos. 24, 19. non poteris servire Jehovæ, quia אלהים קרשים ipse. Num dicitur9 es, ellipsin hic locum habere, sensumque plenum esse, quia אלה אלהים קרשים Deus Deorum sanctorum ipse, ac per Sanctos intelligit τοὺς θεοὺς λεγομένους? Taceo, quod nomen hoc plurale, Elohim, nonnunquam etiam cum verbo plurali constructum, de vero DEO usurpatur. Quæ constructio utique nullam ἔλ- λειψιν admittit. E. g. Gen. 20. v. 13. Errare me fece- runt התעו Elohim de domo Patris mei. Hic certe negari nequit, plures Elohim indigitari, qui vocarint & peregrinari jusserint Abraham: nec locum habet illa Ellipsis. Qualia etiam exempla occurrunt Gen. 35, v. 7. 2. Sam. 7, 23. Nec est, quod dicas, Ebræos hic nullum observasse mysterium; Nam si maxime (1) Ebræi non advertif- sent vel notassent pluralem significationem, num ea idcirco neganda? (2.) Nec novum est, ut quando- que is, cui lingua non est vernacula, sed arte acquisi- ta, aliquid observet, quod vernaculus non animad- verterit, quum ille sæpe accuratius ex præceptis artis judicet, diligentiusque idiotismos advertat. (3.) Quid mirum Christianos luce N. T. collustratos plus videre in V. T. de mysteriis fidei, quam excæcatos & obstinatos Judæos? (4.) Quomodo adhæc docebitur neminem Judæorum advertisie? Num omnium pro- stant scripta? Quantulum id est, quod de veteribus Ebræis nobis cognitum? (5.) Non fugisse autem hoc omnino Judæos e Bereschith Ketanna, quod non obscurum est iis, & in magno pretio apud eos habetur, constat, ubi observatur hæc locutio, ut μυςηριώδης; Non licuisset cuiquam ita dicere: ברא אלהים nisi ita scriptum fuisset. Et Rabbi Semlai ejus mysterii rationem a Magistris antiquis di- scendam docuit, quæsitus quot Elohim crearint mun- dum, respondens: Ego & vos quæramus a diebus an- tiquis. Talmudistæ insuper sup. Jos. 22. ad quæstio- nem, Cur bis nomen DEI a filiis Gad & Ruben repe- tatur ternum? respondent: Dixerunt primo DEUS, DEUS, DEUS, quia per HOS TRES creatus est mun- dus, & deinde dixerunt: Deus, Deus, Deus, quia per hos tres etiam data est lux. Hoc in Talmude Ains- worthus in h. l. observat, citante Matth. Polo dictum R. Simeon Ben Jochai in Zoar ad 6. Levitici Sectio- nem: Veni & vide mysterium verbi Elohim: sunt tres gradus, & quilibet gradus per se solus, id est, distin- ctus, veruntamen sunt unus, & in unum conjunguntur, nec unus ab altero dividitur.

Et produxit talia plura jam ante quadringen- tos annos in apricum opere insigni, cui nomen PUGIO FIDEI contra Mauros & Judæos F. Rai- mundus Martinus de Soubirath, Catiloniæ, Ordinis Prædicatorum, qui mirabili Dei providentia in reconditiores Judæorum Codd. incidit. Quum enim Anno Christi 1263. Frater ejus Paulus Christiani cum Rabbino doctissimo Mose Gerundensi publi- ce coram Rege Jacobo congressus, victoriam, omnium calculo, reportasset, eaque de causa ad Judæos edocendos adhibitus, arcana quæque Ju- dæorum volumina indagaret, & convicto porro alio Rabbino æque perito, sed valde vafro, Bona- struc nuncupato, eoque disputationis peractæ falsos Commentarios edente, præcepit Clemens IV. R. P. ut perfidi Rabbini durius tractarentur. Rabbini autem obtendebant nihil in suis libris blasphemum aut S. Scripturis adversum contineri; factum adeo est, ut Rex decerneret edicto publico, ut extrade- rent Judæi libros suos, eosque tales esse proba- rent: judicesque inter alios constituerentur Rai- mundus a Penna forti & Raimundus Martinus, unde nactus hic fuit Ebræorum libros, adeoque ex hoc ferro probus artifex PUGIONEM FIDEI ad- versus Mauros & Judæos confecit. Exinde arcana quæque Judaicæ impietatis detegi, Ecclesiæ triumpho hostium arma deservire, palmas ex infidelium agro de- cerpi, scripta Ebraica publica autoritate legi, ac in A- cademiis Christianis linguarum Orientalium Scholas

& Magistros Concilii Viennensis decreto institui. Quæ & alia de hoc Raimundo prolixe exponit Franciscus Bosquet Episcopus Ledoviensis Epist. ad Josephum de Voisin: cujus ope & opera hic Pugio- nem Fidei Parisiis Anno 1651. primum in lucem produxit, variisque observationibus exornavit. Quod opus Josephus Scaliger falso Raimundo Sebon Theologiæ naturalis Scriptori ducentis circiter annis recentiori adscripsit, respons. 3. ad Casaubon. An. 1603. Alii Raimundum a Penna forti ordinis Prædicatorum Magistrum Generalem auctorem ejus esse suspicati sunt: quem quasi adjutorem ope- ris hujus facit Philippus Jacobus Mausacus in il- lius Prolegom. in Pugion. Fid. quod verus auctor Raimundus Martinus triennio post illius obitum, Anno nempe 1278. ad finem perduxerit. Ex quo vero tum Petrus Galatinus Arcana sua Catholicæ ve- ritatis, quantum ad ea, quæ bona & utilia habet, post ducentos & triginta annos desumpserit, multis e libro Zohar dubiæ fidei, & e Gale Razia, qui ma- gis adhuc suspectus, adjectis; tum Porchetus de Salvaticis Genuensis Carthusianus in victoria adver- sus impios Judæos quinquennio post Galatini Ar- cana edita Anno nempe 1520. sed bona & sincera fide, nec absque autoris Martini elogio, quod fuerit Vir eximius tam in Scripturis Hebræis & Arabicis, quam in Latinis, plurima derivavit. Un- de fallitur omnino Joh. Morinus, cum in Exerc. Biblic. part. 1. c. 2. p. 16. Petrum Galatinum ex Por- cheto sua descripsisse arguit: quum Porchetus Gala- tino posterior fuerit, & uterque sua e fonte Rai- mundi hauserit. Cæterum pe sequitur Raimundus hoc argumentum in Pugione Fidei part. 3. dist. 1. c. 3. proponens auctoritates pluraliter de DEO lo- quentes, & Rabbinorum observationes de phrasi Creavit Elohim, quæ ex parte e Galatino antea ad- ductæ sunt. E Bereschith Ketana vel minori super h. l. In principio creavit Dii. Dixit R. Hunna in no- mine Bar Cappara השמים nisi hujusmodi sermo scri- ptus esset, non fuisset licitum dicere, Dii creavit cœ- lum. In Bereschith Rabba R. Moses Hadarschan: In principio creavit Elohim. Interrogaverunt hære- tici R. Samlai dicentes, כמה quot Dii creaverunt se- culum? Ego & vos, inquit, quæramus hoc a lege. Di- xerunt ei: Ecce scriptum est Deut. 4. v. 7. Quæ est enim Gens magna habens אלהים קרובים עליו Deos ma- gnos (malim retineri vocem Elohim) propinquos sibi? Dixerunt ei: Ecce duo principia שתי ראשיות Dixit ei: legite finem versus. Sicut יהוה אלהינו Dominus Deus noster in omni invocatione nostra ad eum, non scriptum est AD EOS, sed AD EUM. Dixerunt ei: Ecce adhuc scriptum est Jos. 24. 19. Non poteritis servi- re Domino, quia אלהים קדשים Dii sancti. Dixit eis, legite finem versus, non dixit; quia Dii sancti ipsi, sed IPSE. Dixerunt iterum ei, Ecce scriptum est 2. Reg. 7, 23. Et quis ut populus tuus, ut Israel gens una in terra, propter quam הלכו אלהים iverunt Dii ad redimendum? Ait eis, legite finem versus, vel quod scri- ptum est consequenter, ad redimendum SIBI IPSIS, pluraliter non est scriptum, sed SIBI IPSI singulari- ter: & ponendum SIBI nomen. Rursum quoq; dixerunt ei, Ecce scriptum est Jer. 23, 26. Et invertistis verba אלהים חיים Deorum viventium, sive vivorum. Dixit eis, legite finem versus, Dominorum exercituum non est scriptum sic, sed Domini Exercituum DEI no- stri. Adducitur etiam illic locus e libro eodem Be- reschith Rabba R. Mose Hadarschan ad Gen. 1, v. 23. Rogo & vos, quæramus a lege. Creaverunt Dii, non hic scriptum est, sed creavit Dii Adam Gen. 1. v. 26. Iterum interrogaverunt eum, quid est, quod scri- ptum est Gen. 1, 1. In principio creavit Dii Cœlum & terram? Dixit eis, in principio creaverunt Dii, non scriptum est sic: sed in principio CREAVIT Dii. Dixit quoq́; R. Samlai: in omni loco, in quo tu invenies objectionem pro hæreticis, tu quoque invenies medicamentum ejus in latere ipsius. Rursus etiam in- terrogaverunt ipsum, quid est, quod scriptum est Gen. 1. v. 26. Et dixit Dii: faciamus Adam in ima- ginem NOSTRAM tanquam similitudinem NOSTRAM: dixit eis, legite, quod scriptum est statim post v. 27. Et creaverunt Dii, non scriptum est ita, sed, & creavit Dii. Simile istis supra dictis ha- betur adhuc in Midrasch Kobeletb, sive Glossa su- per Ecclesiast. c. 2. super illud v. 12. Et respexi ad videndum sapientiam & stultitiam atque insaniam. Quid enim est homo ut veniat post Regem את אשר כבר עשיהו quia jam fecerunt eum? Post Regem, id est, post Regem, videlicet Regum aliorum Deum sanctum & benedictum tu valebis stare &c. Docet autem dicendum per hoc, quod non est scriptum, qui fecit eum, sed qui fecerunt eum, quod ex quo in lege scriptum est, possibile est dicere, f. dici potest Deus san- ctus & benedictus, & domus judicii fecerunt eum &c. Si vero dicis, propter hoc duo igitur princi- pia sunt: non sequitur: nonne enim jam dictum erat Deut. 32, 6. ipse fecit & aptavit te, vel paravit & or- navit te? Addit his testimoniis Raimundus: Inten- de, quod neque iste Rabbi neque prædicti, nec aliquis de antiquis, cujus dicta de ista materia viderim, infici- antur mysterium Trinitatis, sed tantum plura prin- cipia, vel plures Deos, quod certe omnis Christiana re- ligio non minus ipsis, imo amplius detestatur. In duo- rum quippe vel plurium mundi principiorum, sive Deorum detestationem prædictum de DEO loquendi modum, quandocunque de DEO agitur, omnino recusat. Quæ observatio Raimundi probe no- tanda est, quod nemo Rabbinorum antiquorum mysterium Trinitatis negarit: quodque tantum plu- ra principia, vel plures Deos inficiati sint, plurali- tatem tamen in voce Elohim observarunt, eamque non terminatione tantum, sed significatione etiam pluralem esse agnoverint. Inde enim illa dubia enata, eoque tendit illa pluralium locutionum cum singularibus collatio, ut nempe salva essentiæ singularitate in Deo quandam pluralitatem esse do- cerent. Quam etiam per domum judicii designant, uti porro Raimundus illic ostendit: quod in pro- xima glossa ad Eccles. 2. quod DEUS sanctus & benedictus & domus judicii fecerunt Adam: per do- mum judicii Filius & Spir. S. qui cum Patre unum principium sint creaturarum visibilium & invisi- bilium, intelligantur: & quod בית דין domus judicii apud Judæos dicta sit, quando tres judices ad mini- mum dabant aliquam sententiam. Unde etiam vi- detur, domum judicii dici Deum Patrem, Filium & Spirit. sanctum, in quam sententiam adducit etiam Midrasch Schir Haschirim in Cant. I, 9. ubi hæc le- guntur: Quid est, quod scriptum est Jer. 10, 10. Et Dominus Dii veritas? Quod ipse videlicet אלהים חיים Dii vivi & Rex æternus. Dixit R. Eleasar: Ubicunq́; in Sacra Scriptura dicitur ויהוה Et Do- minus, intelligitur de ipso & de domo judicii sui. Ni- mirum modo Filius & Spiritus domus judicii nomi- ne cum Patre, a quo originem habent, veniunt, modo propter ὁμοοσίαν, & potestatis judicandi, ipsiusque judicii unitatem tres illi Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus domus judicii appellantur, no- menque illud sanctissimo τῆς τριάδος Consilio vel Consistorio fortassis ab antiquis tributum, quod אלהים a judicando dici crediderint.

Adfert præterea Raimundus alia etiam loca pluralium locutionum, in quibus mysterium hoc pluralitatis personarum deprehendatur, utpote quæ de Deo exposita fuerint a Judæis: Similis, in- quit, modus loquendi de DEO est Eccl. 12. versu 1. זכור את בוראיך Memento CREATORUM TUO- RUM, ubi glossa, sive Medrasch, Hic est Rex Re- gum Deus sanctus & benedictus: h. m. dictum est

Os. 12, 12. Juda vero adhuc Dominus cum DEO & cum SANCTIS fideli. Glossa autem R. Salomo Jarchi, Dominus cum Deo, id est, Dominans cum ter- rore Domini. רד dominans dictum est hic. Sic Num.

24, 19. Et cum SANCTIS fidelis adhuc sc. Rex eo- rum adhuc fidelis est cum Deo. Hæc R. Salomo (per קדושים intelligens Deum.) Item in magna expositio- ne super Gen. 54, 20. Quid est, quod dixit Prov. 30, 3. Et notitiam SANCTORUM nosco. Deum sanctum benedictum vocavit קדושים SANCTOS: QUIA QUÆCUNQUE AD IPSUM PERTINENT, IN SAN- CTITATE SUNT (שכל עניינו בקדושה הם ) ut dictum est Jos. 24, 19. Non potestis Domino servire, quia Dii Sancti IPSE. כי אלהים קדושים

הוא. Item in Midrasch Koheleth super illud c. 5. v. 7. Nam excelsus super excelsum custodiens. וגבהים עליהם Et EXCELSI sunt super eos. Excelsius desuper excelsum custodiens. Isti sunt Angeli. Et excelsi super eis. Iste est Deus sanctus & benedictus. Hæc Rai- mundus ex Ebræis. Unde constat, non omnino latuisse Judæos, quod pluralibus istis locutionibus aliqua in Deo pluralitas designata fuerit, salva ta- men essentiæ divinæ unitate: quam Ecclesia Chri- stiana dicit pluralitatem hypostaseon vel personarum divinarum.

Versu eodem: COELOS ET TERRAM.

Voculam את Jacob Gaffarellus legendam esse אות signum contendit, ut exsculpat cum A- strologis & Cabbalistis quibusdam cælum literis coru- scum figuris Alphabeticis distinctum, cujus Schema exhibet Kircher. Oedip. Ægypt. T. I. pag. 215. Sed hæ ineptiæ refutationem non merentur. Vid. B. D. Thomæ Bangi amici quondam nostri Cælum Orien- tis, Exerc. 2. Moment. Sept. Et cur non terram fin- gunt quoque literis distinctam, cui præmittit hic etiam Moses eandem particulam ואת הארץ. Num ibi etiam vox אות substituenda?

R. Aben-Ezra vocem את notare substantiam rei censet, unde Hottinger. in Histor. creat. pag. 23. textum hujus loci Syriace in Lexico Syro-Arabico Isa-bar Æli MS. ita exponi, substantiam cæli & ter- ræ, observat: neque omnino huic significationi abnuit, ut nuda tantum substantia terræ, quoad ru- dem & indigestam molem, cæli, quoad perfectio- nem essentialem διακοσμήσει sequentibus diebus reservata, indicata sit. Sed ea vocis significatio in- usitata est.

R. Maimonid. More Nev. l. 2. c. 30. particu- lam את vult significare præpositionem cum, q. d. Deum creasse cum cælis, quæcunque sunt in cælis, & cum terra, quæcunque sunt in terra; cui ex parte ac- cedit Hotting. p. 23. Sed ita non Angelos solum in cœlis, verum etiam animantia & homines in terris condidisset in primo initio Deus. Quod affirmant quidem Rabbini, sed contra Historiam Mosaicam, nec nisi inepte probat Maimonides ex Es. 48. v. 13. Notissimum est tyronibus S. linguæ particulam את Accusativi notam esse, si cum verbo activo, vel Nominativi, si cum Passivo construatur. Ad verba hæc ita Grotius:

COELOS ET TERRAM) id est, universum hoc, quale nunc est. Id enim Hebræi duabus illis vocibus exprimunt. Unde & mundus futurus hoc nomine appellatur 2. Pet. 3, 13. At sequente versu terra dicitur ipsa abyssus, sive prima moles, ἰλὺς Phœnicibus, qua de re totaque creatione vide quæ a no- bis congesta ad librum primum de Veritate religionis Chri- stianæ.

Summam comprehendi totius universi & creationis ejusdem postea descriptæ, alii etiam existimant: quibus hic suffragatur Grotius, & propugnat cumprimis eam sententiam Pareus. Sed si hisce συλλήβδην sequens descriptio exhibeatur, totumque hoc universum, quale nunc est, comprehendatur duabus illis vocibus, neque cæli neque terræ creatio a Mose descripta fuerit. Nam in speciali διεξόδῳ operum Hexaëmeri ut cælum creatum fuerit, vel ut creata terra, non commemoratur; solum quomodo aquis superantibus & inferioribus interpositum sit ςερέωμα vel רקיע ut nonnulli volunt, aut certe quomodo ex illa massa cæli, terræ & aquæ, tenebricosum ςερέωμα productum, & aquis separandis interjectum fuerit, quod aquis immersum vel confusum fuerat: ac similiter quomodo tertio die solum terram ex aquis emergere, atque apparere jusserit Dominus, exponit Moses, creationem vero cæli, aut etiam terræ ex nihilo, quoto die facta sit, juxta hanc explicationem, Moses non describeret, imo sic juxta priorum verborum interpretationem Grotianam, Priusquam crearet Deus hoc universum, quale nunc est, terra erat vacua & inanis, terra qualis fuerit, descripta erit, antequam eandem conditam esse, aut quando condita fuerit, docuisset Historiographus Θεόπνευ- ςος: eoque pacto relinqueretur locus suspicioni, anne terra illa vacua & inanis jam multa ante secula extiterit? quod somniat Episcopius, pariter verba Mosis detorquens, aut plane Deo coæva fuerit? quod Hermogenes, & alii Materiarii commenti sunt, Tertulliano teste, & ante illos Stoici, dum ὕλην & Chaos confusum æternis temporibus, non minus quam νοῦν Mentem ceu duo principia extitisse ac certo tempore tandem a mente materiam elaboratam fuisse dictitarunt: adversus quam profanam opinionem Lactantius libr. 2. Instit. c. 8. & Eusebius lib. 7. Præp. Evang. c. 8. egere. Quid hic in recessu aluerit Grotius, an cum Episcopio fecerit necne, haud satis liquet. Cujus vero deliria discussimus Tom. 3. System. Theol. Locor. Commun. p. 1014.

Porro quamnam terram priori Commate versus 1. indigitarit Moses, actutum commate altero explicat: Terra autem erat inanis & vacua. Non ergo de terra, qualis nunc est, loquitur, aut ἐπιτομικῶς totum universum complectitur, sed terram illam creatam fuisse docet in principio rerum omnium, quæ erat Tohu Vabohu. Adhæc indigitavit Moses ipse, se versari in primæ diei τῦ ἑξαημέρꙋ opificii; factumque est vesperi & mane dies unus, v. 5. Et terram illam, quæ vacua & inanis fuerat, primum, vel in prima creatione conditam fuisse primo die oportet, aut ante principium creationis Mosaicam conditam aut plane non conditam esse asserendum erit: a quibus fides Christiana abhorret. Tum vero apertum est, Mosen hic a vespera ordiri primum diem, quia in principio diei illius Deum terram tenebricosam conditam dixerat, tenebrasque, quæ super faciem abyssi erant, ante lucem πρωτόκτιστον erant, antea designarat. Summarium vero opificii sextiduani exhibuit Moses non in principio libri Γενέσεως, sed post absolutam ἑξαημέρꙋ tractationem Genes. 2. vers. 1. Igitur procreati sunt cæli & terræ (scil. illo Hexaëmero) & omnes ornatus eorum. Non autem est, quod putemus, & in principio & in fine Hexaëmeri κατὰ ταυτολογίαν in tam compendiosa descriptione summarium ipsum complecti voluisse.

Quamvis ergo inter cæteras opiniones aliorum probabilis non immerito visa illa fuerit Augustino l. 1. contra advers. legis & Prophet. c. 10. quod spiritua- lis corporalisque natura generaliter hic indigitata fue- rit, vel etiam, uti alii apud Augustin:um l. 1. de Gen. ad lit. c. 3. Ambrosius l. 2. Hexaem. c. 3. Basilius Hom. 3. & cum illis Cyrillus Alex. l. 2. contr. Julian. & Calviniani plerique, Bucanus, Pareus, Keckerman- nus, Timplerus volunt, creaturas corporeas solas comprehensas hic esse: Probabilior tamen, imo certa est, ob adductas rationes, eorum sententia, qui negant, verbis illis initialibus summam creatu- rarum comprehendi. Cæteroquin varias opinio- nes aliorum, utpote Menasse Ben-Israel, quod ver- bis Mosaicis prioribus mundus triplex, Angelorum, Cœlestis, Elementaris, R. Mosis Ægyptii, quod elementa ceu seorsim primum condita, antequam miscerentur, utpote terra, aqua, & spiritus, vel aer, nec non per tenebras ignis, indicentur, quem per lumen primigenium intelligi voluit Menasse; Fa- naticorum, Physicorum, Chymicorum, qui sua prin- cipia hinc eruere satagunt, prout quisque eadem sibi commentus est; tum Papistarum, qui cœlum empyreum, quod barbare vocant (quum non ὁ ἐμ- πύρεος, sed ἐμπύριος sit igneus) Calvinianorum item, qui Cœlum suum locale supra firmamentum, angelicum, quod vocant, & primos Cœlites desi- gnari contendunt; uti Hottingerus cœlum empyreum cum Papistis Lombardo, Lyrano, Abulensi, Catha- rino, & cum Altingio suo, ac Wollebio, & Maresio indicari vult, ac simul cœli, ut ait, Empyræi incolas creatos, Angelos: vel etiam Cloppenburgio interpre- te, Cœlum Dei, Cœlum Angelorum, ipsosque Ange- los, & Cœlum stelliferum designari credunt, uni ei- demque voci tot, ac tam diversas significationes si- mul affingentes; nec non peculiares illas opiniones Lud. Crocii, qui per Cœlum quidem Angelos, eorumque domicilium, per terram autem corpus triunum, & monotriada creatam, constantem terræ limo, abysso & aqua describi fingit in Alphabeto suo Mosaico, Syntagm. Theol. p. 770. & Episcopii, qui cœlum & terram multo ante tempore facta innuit, quam terra ipsa elaborata fuerit, & abyssum illam tartarum, in quem præcipitati sint Dæmones, facit: Petavii de- nique, qui itidem terram & aquam ante primum Hexaëmeri diem quasi materiam, ex qua Cœlum ipsum & elementa producta sint, creata fingit; & quæ hujusmodi commenta sunt alia, notavimus & confutavimus Syst. Theol. l. c. p. 929. seqq.

Quibus omnibus discussis nulla convenientior superefl explicatio, quam quod his verbis rudis & indigesta moles, ceu primum DEI opificium ex nihilo sed in ipso hexaëmeri principio designetur produ- cta, quam Chaos appellare consuevimus, quæ κατὰ πρόληψιν cœli & terræ nomine nuncupata fuerit, quia materia cœli ac terræ, quæ inde efformata de- inde sunt, extitit. Sic enim primo recte intelligitur principium Mosaicum, quo rerum omnium, seu uni- versitatis initium, ante quod nihil, præter DEUM creatorem fuit, expressit, quod τὸ πρῶτον τẽ χρόνε νῦν Basilio dicitur. Sic secundo verbum בָּרָא signifi- catum proprium retinebit, ac primarium, quo pro- ductionem e nihilo notat. Siquidem materia illa e ni- hilo immediate producta fuerit. Quo facit, quod

Gen. 2, v. 3. habeatur, requievisse Deum ab opere suo, quod creaverat ad faciendum, voce בָּרָא designata creatione illa, qua e nihilo materiæ primæ quasi in- star quoddam productum, voce vero עָשׂה ex- pressa subsecuta postea rerum fabrica, qua ex eadem varia rerum genera paravit, & efformavit; quem- admodum etiam Rabbini בָּרָא & יָצַר distinguunt, quod illo rei e nihilo productio, hoc formæ in mate- riam inductio designetur; de quo discrimine vid. Hotting. Hist. creat. p. 17.

Sic tertio voces cæli & terræ non erit necessum de nescio quibus fictitiis cælis, aut qua terra inter- pretari, sed notabunt, quod communiter solent, hoc cælum & hanc terram, ut He Hajediah expri- mit, quamvis προληπτικῶς & materialiter solum, non sub ea, quam deinceps induere, forma, & disposi- tione. Fuit enim revera cælum, fuit terra in illa massa primæva, etsi non a se invicem discreta & efformata, quod sequentium dierum opus erat. Hic enim adhuc in primæ diei θεογενήμασι versatur Moses. Sic שמים Cœlum, quod supra est, respectu terræ notabit: quod ita vocatur non a שם ibi, vel אש ignis, vel שא sustine, aut מים aquis, quasi ibi aquæ, vel ignis & aquæ, vel sustentaculum aquarum, non a שום posuit, uti R. Mardochai Nathan vult: non a שם vel שמה adverbio loci remoti, ut B. Walther in Spongia Mosaica p. 54. vult, non a ra- dice inusitata, quæ altitudinem quandam circularem, aut Spheram, ut ען centrum designet, ac per illud שמים Sphæra ignis sublumaris notetur, quod vult Marcus Marinus in arc. Noæ f. 23. non a שמד ad- miratus est, quod juxta Lusitanum eo nomine omnia corpora θαυμαστὰ intelligantur; sed a radice nunc in Ebraismo quidem non amplius usitata: cujus vero significatio ex Arabismo, cognata lingua peti possit, in quo שמר fit, sublimis, elatus, altus fuit, ut Aben-Ezra, Fagius, Erpenius, Hottingerus, Pocockius & alii Philologi notarunt. Aben-Ezra ad h. l. ita habet: Significatus שמים est altitudo, & eminen- tia, ut etiam in lingua Israelitica, quæ in plerisque linguæ sanctæ conformis est; quæ significatio rei ipsi convenit Job. 11. v. 8. Singulare ejus est שמי quod apud Æthiopes occurrit, ex quo formatur pluralis שמים ad formam מצרים. Non enim dualis est nu- meri, ut vulgo putatur, sed pluralis, uti etiam apud Syros & Chaldæos, qui duali proprio carent, vox שמיא, ut adeo opus non sit causas quærere, cur dualis numeri sit: Vid. Hotting. Smegm. Or. p. 82. & Hist. creat. p. 26. Similiter ארץ hic terram, quæ infra est, designabit, prout ea in rudi illa massa ad- huc erat. Quæ nomen habet non a רוץ currendo, nec a רצץ conterendo, sed ab ארץ cujus fignificatio itidem e lingua Arabica petenda, in qua Aradza est humilis, depressus fuit, uti etiam Chaldæis terra ארעא quasi ima dicitur, quia juxta Aben-Ezram omnibus rebus inferior est. Nec tamen ideo per cœlum & terram superiora & inferiora cum Mai- monide, cui accedit Hottinger. intelligenda. Hæc enim fignificatio in Scriptura prorsus inusitata est.

Sic quarto terra illa, quæ statim describitur, initio creata dicetur: quæ nempe fuerit תהו ובהו quibus vocibus horribilis ejus vastitas exprimitur. Nam cum Chaos illud rude, indigestum & inane de- signetur, quod Paræus etiam, nec non Grotius, alii- que fatentur, dubitari certe non potest, priori vo- ce, qua terra illa creata dicitur, idem Chaos desi- gnatum esse. Ita enim Grotius: Sequenti versu ter- ra dicitur ipsa abyssus, sive prima moles, ἰλὺς Phœni- cibus. Et certum est Paræo: Mosen versu secundo de Chao agere. Vastam, inquit, molem Moses vocat illam terram, non Catachresi, aut Synecdoche aliqua, qua materia dicitur, res, ferrum, gladius, lignum, arca, sed anticipatione, q. d. Terra primo die fuit rudis & vasta moles.

Sic quinto abyssi appellatio apprime conve- niet, qua profunda vorago notetur voce תהום & ἄβυσσος sit ἄβυθος, super quam meræ erant tenebræ. Unde Chaos illud tenebricosum non immerito ita designatum.

Sic sexto congruit descriptio Davidica, qua primæ diei opus Psalm. 104. v. 6. dicitur, quod ter- ram fundarit Deus super stabilitatem suam, abyssus sicut vestimentum ejus fuerit, quodque aquae supra montes steterint: quae postea ab increpatione DEI (die tertia) fugere.

Sic septimo libri Sapientiae, & Ecclesiae Judai- cae sententia sibi constabit: juxta quam omnipotens Dei manus orbem terrarum creavit ἐξ ἀμόρφι ὕλης ex informi materia, uti habetur Sap. 11, 18. Quod innuisse videtur etiam R. Moses Maimonides in More Nebuch. p. 2. c. 30. cum ait, primo die omnia simul creata; reliquis diebus tantum separata. Conf. Men. Ben-Israel Probl. 4. de creat.

Sic octavo patebit origo opinionis de Chao primaevo, quae ad gentiles dimanavit, & e Mosaica narratione profecta sine dubio est. Quam hic etiam Grotius consert, primam molem a Mose descri- ptam, e Phoenicum historiis antiquissimis, quas a Sanchuniathone collectas Philo Biblius vertit, & Eusebius l. 1. Praepar. c. 10. adduxit, explicans: ibi etiam juxta Phoenicum Theologiam Eusebius pri- mum hujus universi principium Chaos turbidum, a caligine interclusum constituit. Quod a Phoenicibus accepisse videntur Graeci. Unde Linus, qui a Phoe- nice venit, primaevo tempore simul omnia mixta fuisse, Orpheus Chaos fuisse & noctem tenebrosam, omnia occultantem, quae sub aethere sunt, asseruit. Vi- deatur Scaliger l. 1. Chron. Euseb. Grotius ad lib. 1. de verit. Relig. Christian. Epicharmus Comico- rum Graecorum antiquissimus, ante omnia Chaos extitisse ait; Atque ita etiam Hesiodus, Apollonius, Aristophanes, Platonici; A Graecis haec Latini ac- cepere, Ovidius imprimis lib. Metamorph. Et tradidere similia Aegyptii, teste Diodoro Siculo, principium esse molem confusam. Qualia plura ad- duxit Grotius annotat. ad lib. 1. de verit. Relig. De quibus vero id observandum, similia esse ea nostris, non eadem, neque cum nostris confundi debere, uti factum videtur a Grotio, qui vult, quod prima illa moles, quam Moses descripsit, Phoenicum ἰλὺς fue- rit. Ab Ebraeis accepere quidem talia Phoenices, Aegyptii, & ab istis Graeci, atque ab his Latini, sed fa- bulis & commentis suis involvere, verumque ini- tium ignorarunt. Unde etiam commenti sunt Chaos aeternum revelatione destituti, quae IN PRINCI- PIO id conditum esse sola docet. Atque ea ratione Justinus Platonem ab Ecclesia accepisse ostendit, quod dixit, Deum materia informi versa mundum creasse Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 72.

Sic ergo Nono consonabit veterum Dd. Ec- clesiae sententia: Qui Chaos illud Mosaïcum agno- vere, Justini puta l. c. Basilii M. Hom. 2. in Hexaem. qui ante lucem primigeniam Coelum & terram facta esse docet, sed incomposita; & cumprimis Augustini l. de Genes. contra Manichaeos c. 5. 6. 7. lib. 12. Con- fess. c. 3. 29. ut & Eucherii, qui in Gen. 1. Materia, inquit, facta est de nihilo: mundi autem species de in- formi materia, quae caeli & terrae nomine appellata est, non quia hoc erat, sed quia hoc esse poterat. Quibus calculum adjiciunt post B. Lutherum nostrum ple- rique omnes nostrates Theologi, Gesnerus, Run- gius, Lyserus, Pelargus, Hutterus, Gerhardus, Wal- therus, qui in Spongia Mosaica prolixe de his con- ferri poterit, aliique; nec non e Pontif. Lombardus lib. 3. sent. dist. 12. & qui Magistrum sequuntur sententiarii, cum Bonaventura, Alberto, Alensi, autore Glossae, Tostato, Catharino, & Calvinianis Zan- chius lib. 1. de opor. creat. c. 23. Martyr & Junius in h. l. Polanus lib. 5. Syntag. c. 4. Alstedius in Phys. Harm. c. 1. Altingius part. 1. Probl. Theol. 19. qui nobiscum verba Mosis explicant.

## 1:2
Verse 2. BUT THE EARTH WAS VOID AND EMPTY) then the earth was, etc. He calls the whole mass by the part more known to us, which he will immediately call ἄβυσσον (abyss).

Grotius rightly understands [this] as the whole unformed mass and bulk, which is called both earth and ἄβυσσος (abyss): as the Mosaic description testifies. But if it must be translated, THEN THE EARTH WAS, it is necessary that that mass be said to have been created first, before it is explained what it was like when it was created. For Moses wished to explain the very beginnings of things, and he started from the BEGINNING of all things, and therefore it is necessary that we admit that by the preceding words that same mass was signified, namely that it was created IN THE BEGINNING of all things, whether it is said to be signified by the name of earth alone or by both the names of heaven and earth, which is more certain, because in that whole mass heaven also existed: indeed, everything existed, just as that Chaos is described by Grotius himself.

But Episcopius, lib. 4 Instit. Sect. 3, c. 5, corrupts this very badly: But the earth was for a long time, that is, it lay desolate and void.
