He imagines, namely, that GOD IN THE BEGINNING, not of the world or of the creation of the Hexaemeron, but of some ANTERIOR [time] I know not what, created heaven and the raw earth: he imagines that the creation of heaven and earth took place a long time before the elaboration of the earth itself: he imagines that the Spirit of the Lord, or a great wind raised from the waters constituting one globe with the earth, brooded over the waters, so that in the meantime the earth would not, as it were, rot, so that he might ventilate the waters, cherish them, and keep them immune from rot and corruption: he imagines that GOD, when he founded this heaven (a long time before the Mosaic Hexaemeron), also created the angels, not so that they would be angels or ministers, but as inhabitants of Heaven, and his own household and, as it were, companions, and that they were not in that dwelling for a short time, but lived in it for a very long time: he imagines that the angels fell away from God in a long and protracted rebellion, and finally were afterwards precipitated into that EARTH, which at that time, when the Republic of the angels or the world lasted, had lain desolate, as if into Tartarus and the abyss. These trifles, more vain than Sicilian nonsense, are not worthy of refutation. Scripture describes the eternity of GOD in such a way that he was before the mountains and the earth, or before the world was founded, Psalm 90, verse 1; that he was before the abysses existed, the mountains and the hills, before the earth existed: in the beginning of his ways, Prov. 8, verse 23. It was therefore produced in the beginning of the ways of the Lord, but it was not a beginning a long time before, before the earth was elaborated and disposed. Nor is it taught anywhere that the earth was void for a long time. Only in the beginning of creation, on the first day of the Hexaemeron, when GOD produced heaven and earth, does Moses teach that the earth was void. A double beginning of creation, one which Moses designates here, another far earlier than that, is a mere fabrication. And how could there have been a danger of rot in that first mass created by GOD? How could a violent wind arise from that crude mass? Nor indeed did Moses speak here of wind, but of the Holy Spirit Himself, which Episcopius himself admits in lib. 4. Instit. Sect. 2. cap. 32. Whence furthermore is it evident to Episcopius that the Angels were created first, so that they might be only the household of GOD, not that they might be Angels? Is GOD enclosed in heaven, and does He have His own messmates? Were not the Angels created so that they might minister to GOD and be πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ? Whence does Episcopius have the insight that the rebellion of the angels was long and lasting? And who would believe that GOD did not immediately cast the apostate Angels into Tartarus, but allowed Himself to be insulted by them through a long and lasting rebellion? Who would admit that that primeval mass, the Mosaic Chaos, is the Tartarus into which were cast the rebel Angels? Episcopius himself admits that the earth was fashioned from that. But if that desolate earth became the Tartarus of the Devils, how was it fashioned into a dwelling for men and other living creatures? But enough and more than enough of these trifles.

V. 2. AND THE EARTH WAS WITHOUT FORM AND VOID) That the words תהו ובהו are rightly explained thus appears from Jer. 4, verse 23. Thus Sophocles on the destruction of the world: 'Earth bereft of trees.'

Sophocles is wrongly brought in here. Who will learn the force and emphasis of a Hebrew word from a Greek poet ignorant of these matters? It is certain, however, that those words signify a horrible desolation, both from a comparison with Is. 34:11 and Jer. 4:23, and from the etymology of the words and most translations. Edward Pocock, in his Miscellany Notes, ch. 3, p. 35, notes the meaning of these words from the Arabic: in which 'Taha' is the same as 'he neglected,' 'he held in neglect,' 'he deserted,' and 'Tavah' with transposed letters is 'he perished'; 'Baha,' however, is 'to be empty and void,' whence 'Al Bahi' is an empty and deserted house: so that 'Tohu' and 'Bohu' are neglected deserts. In which manner they are rendered by Onkelos as 'desolate and empty,' as Pagninus and Vatablus also interpreted. The Jerusalem and Jonathan Targums, as well as the Syriac Paraphrase, retain these Greek words. Nicolaus Füller, book 3. Miscel. sacr. ch. 3, draws the meaning from the Chaldean and Syriac language: because in Chaldean 'teheh' signifies 'to be astonished,' and 'beheh' in Chaldean or Syriac is 'to blush' and 'to be ashamed,' so that it is explained literally as a thing to be wondered at and to be ashamed of: because confusion and deformity, which were still present in the raw and undigested mass of corruptible things, are wont to bring astonishment and shame: and he wishes it to be said thus relatively with respect to the admirable order and beauty that follows, not absolutely. That interpretation is also approved by Hottinger. Whence he says that such a deserted and undigested mass is designated, on account of which one might be astonished. The LXX rendered it 'invisible and unformed,' the former of which the same Füller thinks can be understood through a Hebraism according to the mind of the LXX Interpreters, as if it had been written 'there was no vision,' that is, 'no appearance to it,' i.e., it had no aspect, that is, nothing worthy of sight, or by appearance or form: which would have been 'formless' or 'without shape,' unformed, or even deformed. The latter, 'unformed,' is rendered by others as 'incomposite and incondite': he himself, however, prefers 'not yet instructed with any things,' so that it lacks its equipment. Hottinger, in his preface to the Thesaurus Philologicus, observes that Ibn-Sina, as well as the Mauritanian Arabic edition, also translated it according to the mind of the LXX Interpreters. Symmachus explained it as 'inert and indistinct,' a thing sluggish, idle, destitute of every faculty of acting or performing its manifold work, indistinct, not separated, digested in no order; so that that ancient and primary Chaos is hinted at, in which the whole nature of things lay hidden. Grotius also admits that this is signified here. Aquila and Theodotion explained it as 'emptiness' or 'void and nothing': which is likewise to be understood relatively, with respect to the subsequent formation. Otherwise, this primary Chaos was produced from nothing. But because that matter was clearly undisposed, and from it all things were subsequently produced and created, therefore it is also called 'nothing,' not negatively, but privatively, as they say. The Paris Arabic version of Saad. rendered it: 'The earth was covered by abysses, and overwhelmed by the sea.' Hottinger, in his History of Creation, p. 33, explains the word 'bohu' itself from the Arabic, because it is noted by the Arabs as an uncultivated house, empty of furniture, such as the earth was then.

Which likewise agree with that ancient Chaos, as the ancient Egyptians, according to Diodorus Siculus in his Historical Library, book 1, handed down, that at the beginning of all things, 'according to the constitution of all things from the beginning, they had one form, heaven and earth being mixed, their nature being one.' Laertius, in his Proem, agrees with Diodorus in reporting the opinion of the ancient Egyptians. That the beginning is a confused mass, from which the elements were separated. Concerning which also among the Greeks, Linus: 'There was once a time, in which all things were grown together,' in primeval time all things were mixed together. And Orpheus, according to Timotheus the Chronographer: 'There was dark Chaos and night, and it covered all things which were under the ether.' There was Chaos and dark night concealing all things which were under the ether. 'The earth was invisible under the darkness.' These things, however, those Greeks [received] from the Phoenicians: who had their own from the Hebrews. Similar things are read in Anaxagoras: 'All things were together, but the mind separated them and ordered them, and brought what was confused into order.' These are the words of Anaxagoras; whom Aristotle prefers to the ancient Greek physicists in Metaphysics 1, ch. 3, as a sober man among drunkards, because they had looked only at matter: but this man had added that cause which acts by purpose, which Aristotle calls nature; Anaxagoras more happily [calls it] mind, and before him the first, Thales of Miletus, and Moses [calls it] God, as does Plato, concerning whom Laertius [writes], where he deals with the principles according to the opinion of Plato: whom the ancients testify to have penetrated even to Egypt for the sake of knowing sacred things. Numenius of Apamea, a Syrian, a Pythagorean philosopher, accuses Plato of having stolen his opinion about God and the origin of the world from the Mosaic Scriptures, and for that reason he described him thus: 'What is Plato, but Moses speaking Attic?' Nor are those things dissimilar which are read in Hesiod in his Theogony, and elsewhere concerning Chaos, and in Aristophanes in the Birds, brought forward by Lucian in the Philopatris; and which Epicharmus, the most ancient of the comic poets, reported from ancient tradition. Which, having been received by the Greeks, Ovid has excellently encompassed in book 1 of the Metamorphoses.

Before the sea and the lands, and that which covers all things, the Heaven, etc.

It is not surprising that these and other things could have penetrated to the Egyptians. For Abraham lived in Egypt, who saw and spoke with that second Noah, that other Adam (as he is called by Theodoret), who was still alive, whose grandfather Methuselah (with whom Noah associated for six hundred years) saw and heard the first Adam, the parent of the whole human race: and the Israelites dwelt in that kingdom for over two hundred years. To say nothing of the fact that Hermes Trismegistus, who taught in Egypt, and from whom doctrine flowed to the Greeks, is believed to have lived in the time of Moses; while Zoroaster, by whom the Chaldeans and Persians were instructed, is believed to have been a contemporary of Noah himself.

Whether the opinion of R. Nachman, who says that the whole universe was created on the first day, but brought into the open on the following days, should also be recalled to this sense regarding Chaos being created first, might seem ambiguous. Certainly the wise men among R. Moses Maimonides, in Guide for the Perplexed, book II, chapter 30, who likened creation to a farmer sowing different kinds of seeds in the ground at the same time: of which one part springs up after one day; another, however, after two: even though all the seeds were cast in one hour: seem to have believed that all things were created in one instant, which opinion Nicolaus Abramus, a Jesuit of Pont-à-Mousson, recently made his own in Pharos of the Old Testament, book 1, page 38, [stating that] the substance of all things, if you exclude the soul of man, was produced simultaneously at the first moment of time: but that in the six days of creation following, the substances themselves, with the qualities and perfections owed to their nature, sooner or later according to the nature of each, by natural emanation were produced, by which, instructed by the inclination of nature, they might strive toward their natural place. But that portent of Abram’s opinion, which, having been begotten by the Rabbis and Philo the Jew, and reared by Cardinal Cajetan and Melchior Cano, that Jesuit enriched with new paradoxes and absurdities, and wished to foist upon the Church, System. Theol. Vol. III. de Creat. c. 11. quæst. IV., we have refuted. Moses certainly testifies that within the six days, not in one moment, were all things created, and that God rested only on the seventh day from creation; not that He finished creation in the first instant and left nature to its own operation. Although all things were then produced from Chaos, yet the perfect substances in it did not produce their own qualities during the six days, but within that six-day period the substances themselves were produced by God in order, and attained their essential perfection through the operation of the omnipotent word, but they did not emerge of themselves in that primordial mass by natural emanation.

Verse of the same. AND DARKNESS WAS UPON THE FACE OF THE DEEP.

Hottinger takes the particle ו here in a causal sense, that the earth was therefore waste and void because darkness covered everything, not only the surface of the earth, but whatever space remained up to the heavens: As Chrysost. hom. III. Whatever was seen was an abyss of waters veiled in darkness. Darkness here, however, is the absence of light: not privatively, because no light had preceded: but negatively, just as the negation of sound is silence: the absence of clothing is nakedness. Philo’s interpretation concerning the idea of air, that of the Manichaeans and Marcionites concerning an evil God, and that of others concerning an angelic nature not yet turned to God, deserves no refutation.

Verse of the same. SPIRIT OF GOD) ἡ δύναμις ἡ διαπλαστικὴ, or as Chrysostom speaks, ἐνέργεια ζωτικὴ. See what is said to the book on the Truth of the Christian religion, and add Job 26. v. 13.

WAS MOVING) מרחפת that is, was hovering over, as this interpreter translates this word in Deut. 32. v. 11. ἐμφέρεσθαι, Numenius said this very thing, Tertullian, was being carried over.

Hugo wrote these things for the sake of the Socinians. It is not a bare power or ἐνέργεια that is designated; but the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Godhead. The name Spirit of God absolutely nowhere easily denotes a bare ἐνέργεια; it is commonly used for the Holy Spirit. And the predicate מרחפת implies an act proper to a hypostasis or person, a truly divine work. It is not merely that it hovered over; the Hebrew word is more emphatic, which, like a bird warming its chicks, and like a dove, moved itself over the waters, and sustained them by its life-giving power and as it were impregnated them. Whence afterwards various divine things were produced by its power. Which is rendered by Augustine as being carried over by a certain craftsman-like power.

Grotius himself admits this interpretation in the first book on the truth of the Christian religion §. XVI. in the annotations. But because the word מרחפת properly signifies the brooding of a dove over an egg, it follows in Sanchuniathon that living creatures, that is, the stars, were in that slime as in an egg, and hence that Spirit is called by the name of a dove, by the likeness of which dove Rabbi Solomon also explains that word מרחפת. Nigidius in the German Scholiast: That he found there an egg of wondrous size, which they rolling cast upon the earth, and thus a dove sat upon it, and after some days hatched it, which is called Venus in Syria. Lucius Ampelius in his book to Macrinus. It is said also that a dove sat for many days upon a fish’s egg in the river Euphrates, and hatched the Goddess, kind and merciful to men for a good life. The egg as a likeness of the world in Macrobius, Saturnalia book VII. cap. 16. &c. Wherefore it follows, that in the Baptism of Christ the same Spirit was seen to have brooded over the waters in the form of a dove. All of which prove the person of the Holy Spirit: which Spirit is called Elohim, either by apposition Spirit God, or by regimen Spirit of the Elohim, namely of the Father and of the Son, who are those Elohim from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, or whose Spirit it is, as in the parallel passage Ps. 33 v. 6 he is called the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord. That a divine person is hinted at is so manifest that the Muhammadans, rejecting the mystery of the Holy Trinity, because of this locution, the Spirit of Elohim was borne over the waters, have accused Scripture of corruption here, as Hottinger testifies in Thesaur. p. 276. The Talmudists themselves also explain the force of the word in this way: Just as a dove broods over its young. And thus the Arabic verb רף, which is the very Hebrew רחף, is explained in the Lexicon called Kamus, a dove fluttered over its eggs, and spread its wings, as observed by Ludovicus de Dieu on Acts 7, 43. Which sense Basil the Great drew from the Syrian, as he testifies in Hexaëm.: he said that in the word ἐπεφέρετο, they explain it instead of he warmed, and gave life to the nature of the waters, according to the image of a bird brooding, and infusing a certain vital power into those things being warmed. In the same way Theodore of Tarsus explained the emphasis of the word in the manuscript chain of the Fathers: the Hebrew word, that of ἐπεφέρετο, wishes to signify that just as a bird warms eggs with its wings—gently spreading them out to give life, so also the Spirit was borne over the waters, warming them into life. That the Arabic version uses that word which, according to Kamus, is of a hen that broods over eggs and spreads its wings, was also noted by Hottinger, Hist. Creat. p. 43, and he defends that interpretation against Joh. Morinus in the same place. And that the Holy Spirit is designated here as the author of creation, parallel passages teach, Ps. 33 v. 6, Job 26 v. 33, ch. 33 v. 4. Let Acts 1 v. 16 and ch. 4, 25 also be compared with one another. Hugo ought to have heard his Rabbis here. For the Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum render: And the Spirit of mercies from the face of Jehovah was resting over the waters. In Bereshith Rabba it is asked, what is it that is said, the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters? And it is answered, that it is nothing else but the Spirit of the Messiah, of whom Isaiah 11 says, and the Spirit of Jehovah shall rest upon him. It is observed by Mercer that the Hebrews call the Spirit כסה הכבוד the Throne of the glory of the Lord, which they make here to be in the air above, as it were brooding over the waters, in the manner of a bird brooding over waters. Nor was it right to reject the Holy Fathers, interpreting it of the Holy Spirit, since the Greeks, Origen, Basil, Theodoret, Cyril book 1 against Julian, as well as the Latins, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine book 13 Confess. ch. 1 and 8, de C. D. ch. 11.

Chrysostom's vital energy does not exclude the Holy Spirit, just as for Gregory Neo-Caesariensis the Word is called the Son of God, the creative power of the whole creation. For the ancient Greeks use the word ἐνεργείας of substance: Ignatius in his Epistle to the Magnesians called the Word the substance of divine energy, who was born from the substance of the Father.

Some of the ancients indeed understand the Spirit of God here as a person, but judge that the Son of God is designated through the same: as Prudentius singing of Christ: — — — who as the Spirit of old hovered with Fatherly mouth poured out upon the waves, not yet distinguished nor enclosed by a certain shore. And thus Grotius, observing on Mark 2, 8, notes that the ancient writer Poimander, whom he believes to be a Christian, called the Spirit of God brooding over the waters the Word of God. But it is not the second Person of the Trinity, but the third, who is designated in the Scriptures by the name Spirit of God, although the Word is not excluded here, just as the Father is not in works ad extra, since works ad extra are undivided. We have satisfied the exceptions of the Socinians elsewhere.

That waters are taken for air in v. 12 is false. For reptiles were not produced from the air, but as the words of Moses expressly state that they were produced from the waters, so in this simple account one must not depart from the letter. But what it ought to contain regarding the birds, we shall examine at the said verse. But from where will it be taught that the air already existed at this beginning? For not a few interpreters maintain that it emerged only when the waters were separated from the dry land on the third day. Therefore, the waters are to be understood as being in the chaos, not yet separated, nor enclosed by a certain shore, as Prudentius sang. The word מים is not of the dual number, as if twin waters were noted below and above the firmament, for such a separation and distinction had not yet been made here: but it is plural, and that entire abundance of waters, which was later separated, is comprehended by one word, from which it is clear that the מים which are above the firmament are not of a different kind from those which are below it. That word in Hebrew has no singular; by some it is derived from the Chaldean מוי, by others it is derived from the Arabic מה, but more correctly by Gataker in Cinnus p. 166 from the Ethiopic מי, from which it cannot be anything but plural, unless it is מים.

Latin:

Vers. 2. TERRA AUTEM ERAT INANIS ET VA- CUA) tunc terra erat, &c. Terram vocat totam molem ex parte nobis notiore, quam statim dicet ἄβυσσον.

De tota mole ac massa indisposita, quæ & terra & ἄβυσσος vocata, recte Grotius intelligit: uti descriptio Mosaica testatur. Sed si vertendum, TUNC TERRA ERAT, oportet prius creatam illam molem dici, antequam qualis fuerit, quando creata est, exponatur. Voluit enim Moses ipsa rerum primordia exponere, & a PRINCIPIO rerum omnium exorsus est, ideoque necessum est, fateamur verbis præcedentibus significatam esse eandem illam molem, quod nempe illa IN PRINCIPIO rerum omnium creata fuerit, seu solius terræ nomine dicatur significata seu utroque cæli & terræ nomine, quod certius, quia in illa tota mole etiam cælum erat: imo erant omnia, uti Chaos istud ab ipso Grotio describitur.

Pessime autem Episcopius lib. 4. Instit. Sect. 3. c. 5. hoc ita corrumpit: Terra autem diu erat, id est, jacebat desolata & inanis. Fingit nempe, DEUM IN PRINCIPIO, non mundi, aut Hexaëmeri creationis, sed nescio, quo ANTERIORI, Cælum & terram rudem creasse: fingit, creationem cæli & terræ multo ante tempore factam, quam terræ ipsius elaborationem: fingit, Spiritum Domini, vel ventum magnum ex aquis unum globum cum terra constituentibus elevatum aquis incubuisse, ne interea terra veluti computresceret, ut nempe aquas ventilaret, foveret, & a putredine ac corruptione præstaret immunes: fingit DEUM, cum cælum hoc condidit (multo ante Hexaëmeron Mosaicum tempore) Angelos etiam condidisse, non ut angeli seu ministri essent, sed tanquam Cæli incolas, & domesticos suos ac quasi contubernales, nec brevi tempore in isto domicilio fuisse, sed diu admodum in eo versatos esse: fingit, Angelos a Deo defecisse longa ac diuturna rebellione, ac tandem postmodum in TERRAM illam, quæ tempore isto, quo Angelorum Respubl. vel mundus duravit, desolata jacuerat, ceu in Tartara, & abyssum præcipitatos esse. Quæ nugæ gerris Siculis vaniores, refutatione dignæ haud sunt. Scriptura æternitatem DEI ita describit, quod fuerit antequam montes & terra, vel antequam mundus conderetur, Psalm. 90. vers. 1. quod fuerit ante, quam abyssi essent, montes & colles, antequam terra existeret: in principio viarum Prov. 8. vers. 23. Ea ergo in principio viarum Domini producta, non vero principium multo ante tempore fuit, priusquam terra elaborata & disposita fuerit. Nec diu fuisse terram inanem, uspiam docetur. Solum in principio creationis, in primo Hexaëmeri die, cum produceret DEUS cælum & terram, terram fuisse inanem Moses docet. Geminum principium creationis, aliud quod hic Moses designat, aliud eo longe anterius, merum est commentum. Et quomodo in prima illa massa a DEO condita tum periculum esse poterat putredinis? quomodo e rudi illa mole ventus vehemens oriri poterat? Nec vero de vento, sed de ipso Spiritu Sancto hic Moses loquutus, quod Episcopius ipse fatetur lib. 4. Instit. Sect. 2. cap. 32. Unde porro constat Episcopio Angelos conditos primum fuisse, ut DEI solum domestici essent, non ut Angeli essent? Num cælo inclusus est DEUS, suosque habet Contubernales? annon Angeli conditi sunt, ut DEO ministrarent & πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ essent? Unde perspectum habet Episcopius longam ac diuturnam fuisse angelorum rebellionem? Et quis credat, DEUM non statim Angelos Apostatas præcipitasse in Tartarum, sed passum esse insultari sibi ab iisdem longa ac diuturna rebellione? Quis admittetet, molem illam primævam Chaos Mosaicum tartarum esse, quo præcipitati fue- rint Angeli rebelles? Fatetur ipse Episcopius, terram inde fuisse elaboratam. Si vero terra illa desolata Tartarus evasit Diabolorum, quomodo elaborata fuit in domicilium hominum & aliorum animantium? Sed de his nugis plus satis.

V. 2. TERRA AUTEM ERAT INANIS ET VACUA) Ita recte explicari voces תהו ובהו apparet ex Jer. 4. vers. 23. Sic de mundi interitu Sophocles: Γῆ δενδρέων ἔρημος.

Perperam huc Sophocles trahitur. Qui ex Poëta Græco harum rerum ignaro vis & emphasis Ebrææ vocis discetur? Certum autem est, significari vocibus illis horribilem vastitatem, tum e collatione Es. 34, 11. Jer. 4, 23. tum e vocum Etymo & plerisque translationibus. Eduardus Pocock. not. miscell. c. 3. p. 35. notat ex Arabismo vocum harum significationem: in quo Taha idem ac neglexit, neglectui habuit, deseruit, & Tavah transpositis literis periit; Baha autem est inane & vacuum esse; unde Al Bahi domus vacua & deserta: ut sint Tohu & Bohu neglecta deserta. Quo pacto redduntur ab Onkelo צדיא ורקניא desolata & vacua, uti etiam interpretatus est Pagninus, ac Vatablus. Targum Hierosolym. & Jonath. ut & Syr. Paraphr. voces has Græcas retinent. Nicolaus Füllerus lib. 3. Miscel. sacr. c. 3. ex Chaldæa & Syra lingua depromit significationem: quia Chaldæis תהה significat stupere, בהה Chaldaice vel Syriace erubescere est, & pudere, ut ad verbum exponatur res stupenda & pudenda: quia confusio & deformitas, quæ adhuc rudi indigestæque rerum corruptibilium massæ inerat, stuporem & pudorem afferre solent: atque ita dictum vult comparate respectu admirabilis ordinis & pulcritudinis sequentis, non autem absolute. Ea interpretatio probatur etiam Hottingero. Unde tam desertam & indigestam molem designari ait, ob quam quis obstupescat. LXX. reddidere ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος, quorum prius per Hebraismum ita intelligi posse censet idem Füllerus ex mente LXX. Interpp. quasi scriptum fuisset οὐκ ἦν ὅρασις, ἤτοι εἶδος αὐτῇ, i. e. non erat ei aspectus, hoc est, quicquam aspectu dignum, vel specie aut forma: quod fuerit ἄμορφος vel ἀνειδής, informis, aut etiam deformis. Posterius ἀκατασκεύαστος redditur ab aliis incomposita & incondita: ipse autem mavult nondum instructa rebus ullis, ut apparatu suo careat. Ad mentem LXX. Interpretum etiam transtulisse Ibn-Sina, ut & Maur. Edit. Arab. observat. Hottinger. præfat. ad Thesaur. Philol. Symmachus exposuit ἀργὸν κὶ ἀδιάκριτον res iners, ignava, otiosa, omni facultate agendi vel præstandi opus suum multiplex, destituta, indiscreta, non distincta, nullo ordine digesta; ut innuatur Chaos illud antiquum & primum, in quo latuerit universa rerum natura. Quod hic significari fatetur etiam Grotius. Aquila & Theodot. exposuere κένωμα vel κενὸν, καὶ οὐδὲν rem inanem, & nihilum: quod itidem comparate, respectu sequentis efformationis, intelligendum. Alias e nihilo productum fuit Chaos hoc primævum. Sed quia materia illa indisposita plane fuit, & ex ea producta ac creata deinde omnia sunt, ideo etiam nihilum dicitur non negativum, sed privativum, uti loquuntur. Versio Arabica Paris. Saad. reddidit: Terra erat abyssis cooperta, & obruta mari. Vocem ipsam בהו ex Arabismo explicat Hottinger. in Histor. creat. p. 33. quod ea Arabibus notetur domus inculta, suppellectile vacua, qualis tum erat terra.

Quæ itidem Chao illi antiquo congruunt, uti Veteres Ægyptii, referente Diodoro Siculo lib. Hist. Bibl. tradiderunt, rerum omnium principio κατὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς τῶν ὅλων σύστασιν μίαν ἔχειν ἰδέαν οὐρανόν τε καὶ γῆν μεμεγμένην αὐτῶν τῆς φύσεως. Diodoro consonat in referenda Ægyptiorum antiquorum sententia Laertius in Proœm. Principium esse mo- lem confusam, ex hac discreta elementa. Quo de etiam apud Græcos Linus, ἦν ποτέ τοι χρόνῶ ἔτος, ἐν ᾧ ἄρα παντ' ἐπεφύκει, Tempore primævo simul omnia mixta fuerunt. Et Orpheus apud Timotheum Chronographum, ἦν χάθω νὺξ τοφερὰ, πάντα δὲ ἐκάλυπτε τὰ ὑπὸ τὸν αἰθέρα. Erat Chaos & nox tene- brosa omnia occultans, quæ sub æthere. ἡ γῆ ὑπὸ τῶ σκότος ἦν ἀόρατος. Terra præ tenebris erat incon- spicua. Hæc autem Græci illi a Phœnicibus: qui ab Ebræis sua habuere. Similia apud Anaxagoram le- guntur: πάντα χρήματα ἦν ὁμῦ πεφυμένα, ὁ νῦς δὲ αὐτὰ διῆρε, καὶ διεκόσμησε, κὰ ἐκ τῆς ἀταξίας ἐν τάξιν ἤγαγε. Cuncta simul erant: at mens ea discrevit or- dinavitque, & quæ confusa erant, ordinavit. Hæc Anaxagoras; quem veteribus Græcorum Physicis Aristoteles præfert Metaph. 1. cap. 3. tanquam so- brium ebriis, quod illi solam materiam spectassent: Hic vero addidisset eam causam, quæ ex proposito agit, quam Aristoteles naturam vocat; Anaxagoras feli- cius mentem, & ante eum primus Thales Milesius, Deum Moses, ut & Plato, de quo Laërtius, ubi de principiis ex sententia Platonis agit: quem ad Æ- gyptum usque penetrasse sacrorum cognoscendo- rum causa testantur Veteres. Numenius Apomen- sis Syrus, Pythagoræus Philosophus Platoni impu- tat, quod ex Mosaicis Scriptis suam de Deo & ortu mundi sententiam surripuerit, atque ob id eum sic descripsit, τί ἐσι πλάτων, ἢ Μωυσῆς Ἀττικίζων; Quid est Plato, nisi Moses Attice loquens? Nec absimilia sunt, quæ apud Hesiodum in Theogo- nia, & alibi de Chao leguntur, & apud Aristo- phan. in Avibus producta a Luciano in Philopa- tride; quæque Epicharmus Comicorum antiquissi- mus e veteri traditione retulit. Quæ a Græcis ac- cepta, eximie complexus est Ovidius lib. 1. Me- tamorph.

Ante mare & terras, & quod tegit omnia Cælum, &c.

Hæc & alia ad Ægyptios penetrare potuisse mirum non est. In Ægypto enim vixit Abraham, qui Noam alterum illum Adamum (uti Theodoreto vocatur) in vivis adhuc conspexit, & compellavit, cujus avus Mathusalem (cum quo sexcentis annis Noah conversatus est) vidit & audivit primum A- damum, totius humani generis parentem: & com- morati sunt in regno illo Israelitæ ultra ducentos annos. Ut taceam, quod Mercurius Trismegistus, qui in Ægypto docuit, & a quo ad Græcos doctri- na dimanavit, tempore Mosis vixisse; Zoroaster, vero, a quo Chaldæi & Persæ instituti, Noæh ipsi σύγχρονος fuisse creditur.

An ad hunc sensum de Chao primum con- dito revocari etiam debeat R. Nachmanni opinio, qui primo die totum universum conditum dicit; se- quentibus vero diebus ductum in apertum, ambi- guum videri possit. Sapientes certe apud R. Mosen Ægypt. l. II. Doct. perplex. c. 30. qui creationem assi- milarunt agricolæ seminanti diversa genera seminum simul in terra: quorum pars una oritur post unum diem; alia vero post duos: etsi omnia semina pro- jecta sint in una hora: omnia uno instanti condita credidisse videntur, quam sententiam nuper suam fecit Nicolaus Abramus Jesuita Muslipont. in Phar. V. T. l. 1. pag. 38. omnium rerum substan- tiam, si ab anima hominis discesseris, primo mo- mento temporis simul productam: sex diebus vero creationem rerum sequentibus, ipsas substantias, qualitates, perfectionesque naturæ suæ debitas, se- rius, ocyus secundum cujusque naturam, emanatione naturali, productas esse, quibus instructæ ad naturalem locum inclinatione naturæ contenderent. Sed porten- tum illud opinionis Abrami, quod a Rabbinis, & Philone Judæo procreatum, a Cajetano Cardina- li & Melchiore Cano educatum, Jesuita ille novis paradoxis atque absurditatibus locupletavit, & Ec- clesiæ obtrudere voluit, System. Theol. Tom. III. de Creat. c. 11. quæst. IV. profligavimus. Moses certe intra Sextiduum, non uno momento omnia creata & septimo demum die a creatione Deum quievisse testatur; non primo instanti absolvisse creationem ac naturæ suam reliquisse operationem. Quamvis e Chao deinde producta omnia, non tamen substan- tiæ perfectæ in illo per sextiduum qualitates suas ipsæ produxerunt, sed intra illud sextiduum ordine ipsæmet substantiæ productæ a Deo sunt, & effen- tialem suam perfectionem verbi omnipotentis operationem consequutæ, non vero naturali ema- natione ipsæmet in illa primæva mole emerserunt.

Vers. eod. ET TENEBRÆ ERANT SU- PER FACIEM ABYSSI.

Particulam ו hic sensu causali accipit Hottin- gerus, terram propterea fuisse vastam, & horridam, quod tenebræ totam operirent, non modo superficiem terræ, sed quicquid supererat interstitii usq; ad cælum: Ut Chrysost. hom. III. Quicquid videbatur, erat abyssus aquarum tenebris obvelata. Tenebræ autem hic luminis absentia sunt: non privative, quia nulla præcesserat lux: sed negative, prout negatio soni est silentium: absentia vestitus est nuditas. Philonis interpretatio de idea aeris, Manichæorum, & Marcionitarum de Deo malo, aliorum de angelica natura ad Deum nondum conversa, nullam meretur refutationem.

Vers. eod. SPIRITUS DEI) ἡ δύναμις ἡ διαπλαστικὴ, sive ut Chrysostomus loquitur, ἐνέργεια ζωτικὴ. Vide quæ ad dictum librum de Veritate religionis Christianæ, & adde Jobum 26. v. 13.

FEREBATUR) מרחפת id est supervolitabat, ut hic interpres hanc vocem vertit Deut. 32. v. 11. ἐμφέρεσθαι hoc ipsum dixit Numenius, Tertullianus supervectari.

Hæc in Socinianorum gratiam Hugo. Non nuda potentia, aut ἐνέργεια designatur; Sed Spiritus San- ctus, tertia Divinitatis persona. Nomen Spiritus Dei absolute nuspiam facile nudam ἐνέργειαν notat, communiter de Spiritu S. adhibetur. Et prædicatum מרחפת actum hypostasi vel personæ proprium infert, opus vere divinum. Non id tantum est super- volitavit; ἐμφατικώτερον verbum Ebræum est, quod instar avis pullos foventis, & instar columbæ se super aquas motitarit, easque virtute sua vivifica sustenta- rit ac velut imprægnarit. Unde postmodum varia divina ejusdem virtute producta. Quod Augustino viquadam fabrefactoria superferri redditur.

Admittit hanc interpretationem Grotius ipse pri- mo de veritate religionis Christianæ §. XVI. in annot. Quia vero vox מרחפת proprie incubitum columbæ su- per ovo significat, ideo in isto limo animantia, id est, sidera ut in ovo fuisse, sequitur apud Sanchuniathonem & hinc Spi- ritus ille columbæ dictus nomine, cujus columbæ similitudine etiam vocem illam מרחפת explicat Rabbi Salomo. Nigidius apud Scholiastem Germanicum: Ibi ovum inve- nisse miræ magnitudinis, quod volventes ejecerint in terram, atque ita columbam insedisse, & post aliquot dies exclusisse eam Syriæ, quæ vocatur Venus. Lucius Ampelius libro ad Macrinum. Dicitur & in Euphratis fluvio ovum piscis co- lumba adsidisse dies plurimos, & exclusisse Deam benignam & misericordem hominibus ad bonam vitam. Ovum mun- di simulacrum Macrobio Saturnalium lib. VII. cap. 16. &c. Quo facit, quod in Baptismo Christi in forma co- lumbæ idem Spiritus aquis incubasse visus est. Quæ omnia personam Spiritus S. probant: qui Spiritus dicitur Elohim, vel per appositionem Spiritus Deus, vel per regimen Spiritus τῶν Elohim, Dei nempe Patris, & Filii, qui sunt Elohim illi, a quibus Spi- ritus S. procedit, vel quorum est Spiritus, uti in loco parallelo Pf. 33. v. 6. vocatur Spiritus oris Do- mini. Personam divinam innui adeo manifestum, ut Muhammedani, mysterium S. S. Trinitatis respu- entes, ob hanc locutionem, Spiritus Elohim fere- batur super aquas, Scripturam corruptionis hic in- simularint, teste Hottingero in Thesaur. p. 276. Vim vocis ita etiam exponunt ipsi Talmudici: Quem- admodum columba incumbit pullis suis. Atque ita Arabicum verbum רף, quod est ipsum Ebræum רחף, in Lexico Kamus dicto explicari, agitavit co- lumba super ova sua, & extendit alas, Ludovico de Dieu observatum ad Act. 7, 43. Quem sensum a Syro hausit Basilius M. uti in Hexaëm. testatur: τὸ ἐν ἐπεφέρεῤο ἔφη, ἐξηγῦνται ἀντὶ τῦ συνέθαλπε, κ, ἐζωογόνει τὴν τῶν ὑδάτων φύσιν, κατὰ τὸν εἰκόνα τῆς ἐπωαζούσης ὄρνιθος, καὶ ζωτικήν τινα δύναμιν ἐνιεί- σης τοῖς θαλπουμένοις. Eodem modo emphasin ver- bi explicavit Theodorus Tarsensis in catena Patrum MScr. βύλεται ἡ ἑβραικὴ λέξις, ἡ τῦ ἐπεφέρετο, ση- μαίνειν, ὅτι καθάπερ ὄρνις ὠὰ θάλπει ταῖς πλέρυξιν - ἁπαλῶς ἐφαπλομένει εἰς τὸ ζωογονεῖν, ὅτω καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα ἐπεφέρετο τοῖς ὕδασι ζωοθαλπῶν. Arabicam versionem vocem eam adhibere, quæ teste Kamu- sio Gallinæ sit, quæ incubat ovis, & alas suas extendit, notavit etiam Hottinger. Hist. Creat. p. 43. eamque interpretationem adversus Joh. Morin. ibidem defendit. Nec obscure Spiritum S. creationis au- torem hic designari, parallela loca docent, Pfal. 33. v. 6. Job. 26. v. 33. c. 33. v. 4. Conferantur etiam in- ter se Act. 1. v. 16. c. 4, 25. Audire hic debuisset Hu- go Rabbinos suos. Targum enim Jonathanis & Hierosolymitanum reddunt: Et Spiritus misericor- diarum a facie Jehova requiescebat super aquis. In Bereschith Rabba quæritur, quid est, quod dicitur, Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas? Et respon- detur, nihil aliud esse, nisi Spiritum Messiæ, de quo Esai. 11. & requiescet super eum Spiritus Jehova. Mercero observatum, Ebræos appellare Spiritum כסה הכבוד Thronum gloriæ Domini, quem in aere desuper velut incubantem aquis, hic faciunt, more avis aquis incubantis. Nec respuere par erat S. Patres, de Spiritu S. interpretantes, cum Græcos, Origenem, Basilium, Theodoretum, Cyrillum l. I. contr. Jul. tum Latinos, Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Augustinum l. 13. Confess. c. 1. & 8. de C. D. c. 11.

Chrysostomi ἐνέργεια ζωτικὴ non excludit Spiri- tum S. uti Gregorio Neo-Cæsariensi λόγος Filius Dei dictus δύναμις τῆς ὅλης κτίσεως ποιητική. Utuntur enim veteres Græci voce ἐνεργείας de substantia: Ignatius Epistol. ad Magnes. λόγον ἐνεργείας θεϊκῆς ὐσίαν dixit, qui e substantia Patris prognatus est.

Nonnulli Veterum Spiritum Dei hic quidem de persona intelligunt, sed per eundem Filium Dei de- signatum censet: uti Prudentius de Christo canens: - - - qui Spiritus olim Ore superfuso Patrio volitabat in undis, Nondum discretis nec certo littore clausis. Atque ita scriptorem antiquum Pæmandrum, quem Christianum credit, observat ad Marc. 2, 8. Grotius, Spiritum Dei aquis incubantem λόγον Θεῦ vocasse. Sed non secunda Persona Trinitatis, verum tertia nomine Spiritus Dei in Scripturis designatur, ta- metsi λόγος non excludatur hic, uti nec Pater in opere ad extra, quum opera ad extra sint indivisa. Socinianorum exceptionibus satisfecimus alibi.

Aquas pro aere v. 12. accipi, falsum. Neque enim ex aere producta sunt reptilia, sed ut expresse habent verba Mosis, ex aquis ea producta esse, ita in hac simplici relatione a littera disceden- dum non est. Quid autem de avibus habere debeat, ad dictum versum dispiciemus. Aerem autem jam in hoc initio extitisse unde docebitur? Nam emersisse demum eundem cum aquæ ab arida discretæ fue- runt die tertio, non pauci interpretes statuunt. A- quæ ergo in chao intelligendæ, nondum discretæ, nec certo littore clausæ, ut Prudentius cecinit. Vox מים non dualis est numeri, quasi geminæ notentur aquæ sub & supra firmamentum, talis enim separa- tio & discretio nondum hic facta erat: sed pluralis, & tota illa aquarum copia, quæ postea discreta est, una voce comprehensa, unde patet, non esse alterius generis מים quæ supra firmamentum, ab iis, quæ infra illud sunt. Vox illa in Ebraismo singularem non habet, a nonnullis a Chald. מוי, ab aliis ab Ara- bico מה deducitur, at rectius a Gatakero in Cinno p. 166. ex Æthiopico מי unde plurale nisi מים esse nequit.

## 1:3
verse 3. AND GOD SAID: LET THERE BE LIGHT, AND THERE WAS LIGHT) Concerning these words, see the passage of Dionysius Longinus, which we have produced in the said Annotations.

He refers to the annotations on book 1 of the Truth of the Christian Religion, from Dionysius Longinus. Who, in his book on the sublime style of speaking, when he had said that those speaking about GOD ought to take care that they present Him to us as great, sincere, and unmixed, adds these things: So also acted he who founded laws for the Jews, a man of no common genius, as one who had worthily conceived and expressed the power of GOD, writing these things immediately at the beginning of his laws, he said, GOD said. What? Let there be light and But by this mode of speaking, not only the δύναμις and power of GOD is designated, because He created all things by a word and a nod, said and done. The mystery of the hypostatic λόγος, through whom all things were founded, is simultaneously insinuated. Because GOD did not say it without that Word, without whom nothing was made. Thus David explains in Psalm 33:6, and Solomon in Proverbs 8:23 seqq., whose creative wisdom, which was with GOD the Father, composing all things, as he speaks in verse 30, is the hypostatic word itself. And most clearly of all St. John ch. 1, 1. 2. 3. whom Grotius acknowledges that these words of Moses regard, in the annotations to John 1:1. He also confesses that this λόγος is indicated by the word דבר by David in Ps. 33:5, and that this appellation has its origin from the Mosaic passage. The Chaldean interpreter took from here his מימרא word, which he uses everywhere; soon in the 3rd chapter of Genesis v. 8. And they heard the voice of the Lord GOD, the Chaldean has: And they heard the voice of the word מימרא of the Lord GOD: For although the Chaldean uses that word in some places where the notion of the hypostatic word does not sufficiently fit, yet from those it does not seem that that signification should be denied, at least in those places which befit the Son of GOD: for the Interpreter is not always equally accurate, nor is the primary signification taken away by a secondary usage: in which primary notion it is used also in this matter in Isa. 45:12, where it is read in Hebrew: I made the earth and created man upon it; in the Chaldean it is: I in my word made the earth, and created men upon it; c. 48:13, in the Hebrew it is read: My hand founded the earth; in the Chaldean, By my Word I founded the earth. Hottinger also agrees with these along with Fagius, abandoning Hackspan, who went into all other things, certainly not to the glory of our religion concerning the use of Rabbinical Scripture p. 365. For he openly professes in Hist. creat. p. 56 that there are some places which can scarcely be understood in the Targum in any other way than of the Messiah, such as Ps. 110:1, Gen. 3:8, praising Buxtorf, Capellus, and Cameron to that effect, as also Guadagnolus, regarding the passage Jer. 17:15, Tremellius Hag. 2:5, 6, others from Ps. 54:2, 107:20, Isa. 40:8. Mr. Varen has brought forward more in Gen. p. 130. Blessed Selneccer collected all the passages of the Targum in which he understands the Son by the word in a special booklet. Grotius acknowledges that this naming arose from the present Mosaic text, and judges that the Apostle Peter also followed the Chaldean interpreter in 2 Ep. 3:5, ὀυρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι καὶ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα, τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγῳ. Finally, from this they observe that the Greeks had from the ancients, namely from the books of the Chaldeans, what they hand down concerning the λόγος, the writer of the Orphics, Heraclitus, and Zeno. Which Tertullian had also noted against the Gentiles: Among your wise men also the λόγος, that is, speech and reason, is agreed to seem the artificer of the universe. For Zeno defines this as the maker, who formed all things in their arrangement. The passage of Zeno was in the book περὶ ὀυσίας, where he called the efficient cause τὸ ποιοῦν the λόγος, whom Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archidamus, and Posidonius followed, as Laertius teaches in Zeno. But especially Amelius the Platonist introduced the λόγος as the efficient cause of all things, who nevertheless learned this from John the Evangelist, whom he calls the Barbarian. Καὶ ὗτος ἄρα ἦν ὁ λόγος, καθ' ὃν ἀεὶ ὄντα τὰ γενόμενα, ὡς ἂν καὶ ἡράκλειτος ἀξιώσειε καὶ νῆ δῒ ἂν ὁ βάρβαρος ἀξιοῖ ἐν τῇ τῆς ἀρχῆς τάξει τε κὶ ἀταξίᾳ καθεστηκότα πρὸς Θεὸν εἶναι δι' ὗ πανθ' ἁπλῶς γεγενῆσθαι, ἐν ᾧ τὸ γενναόμενον ζῶον κὶ ὂν πεφυκέναι. This, therefore, is that reason through which those things that are made always are, just as Heraclitus also judged. Truly the same things which THAT BARBARIAN indicates, that in the first founding of things, nay even in the unformed state, it stood by GOD, through whom all things were absolutely made, in whom that which becomes a living being would have its existence. The words are read in Eusebius l. XI. Præparation. c. XIX. and Cyril of Alexandria l. VIII. against Julian. Philo, a Jew indeed, but leaning toward Platonic dogmas, likewise says that the world was founded through the λόγος, whom he also calls the image and son of GOD. It is known that Plato himself called the λόγος the exemplar of the world. Although he understood a different λόγος than the divine writers. It is clear, however, how something concerning the highest mystery became known to outsiders, which they, however, obscured with their own commentaries.

Thus therefore Moses expressed the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity soon at the beginning of Genesis, when he introduced not only GOD, but also the Spirit of GOD, and his λόγος, as the supreme architect, which was likewise done by David in Ps. 33, 6. Concerning which our blessed Luther speaks gravely in Comment. on Genesis fol. 4. The distinction of persons is manifest here. For he says that GOD is, so to speak, the Speaker, who creates, and yet does not use matter, but by the Word alone, which he brings forth, makes heaven and earth out of nothing. Now apply here the Gospel of John: In the beginning was the Word (For he agrees well with Moses). He says that before the world was founded there was nothing of created things. Yet God had the Word. What is this Word, or what does it do? Hear Moses, he says, Light was not yet. But darkness is turned from its nothingness into that most excellent creature, which is light. By what? By the word. Therefore in the beginning and before every creature is the Word, and it is so powerful a Word, that it makes all things out of nothing. Hence it follows irrefragably, what John adds: That this Word is GOD, and yet is a distinct person from GOD the Father, just as the word and he who brings forth the word are distinct things. And yet this distinction is of such a kind, that a most unified, if I may so say, unity of essence remains. And fol. 2. There is a great consensus of the Church concerning the mystery of the Trinity revealed here. The Father through the Son, whom Moses calls the Word, creates heaven and earth out of nothing. Upon these the Holy Spirit broods. For just as a hen broods over eggs, so that she may hatch chicks, warming the eggs and by heat as if animating them: thus Scripture says the Holy Spirit as it were brooded over the waters, so that He might vivify those bodies which were to be animated and adorned. For it is the office of the Holy Spirit to vivify. These are the words of B. Luther.

Although Hugo (I mean Grotius) saw these things, he preferred to wrap them in the opinions of the Rabbis rather than to unfold them skillfully according to the mystery of the faith, confusing the hypostatic λόγον with the power of GOD, which we call an attribute of GOD. Whether he did this in favor of Servetus, whose cause he pleaded against Calvin and Rivet, or because he was ensnared by the dogmas of the Platonists and Jews, I will not say. Let his words in the annotations to John 1:1 bear witness. Because Moses had written, GOD said, let there be light, and there was light, and so on regarding the rest; hence it came about that the Hebrews called that power or προβολὴν or ἀπόᄤοιαν (for ancient Christians use these words in this matter) of GOD, which created things from nothing and brought about various and excellent things, דבר, as can be seen in Ps. 33:6, Ps. 148:8. See Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, book 1, ch. 23, 45, and 66. Grotius not infrequently follows this blind guide. A little later, Hugo speaks of this mystery as if Christians had it from the Platonists, not the Platonists from the divine writers. When he had explained that, ὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, almost according to the mind of Servetus, that the λόγον is to be understood as GOD in such a way that it also remains that He was with GOD, that is, that the ὁ λόγος was not all that which is GOD; he adds what it is helpful to add here: Origen and others after him called it a distinction of hypostases, but it is to be noted that this word ὑποστάσεων, as also τριάδος, ὁμουσίε, and certain others, were not used by the first Christians, since Athanasius, the Nicene and Sardican Synods, and some Roman ones spoke against μίαν ὑπόστασιν, but were taken from Platonic writers, with the sense somewhat changed. This is false. The Apostle said ὑπόστασιν in Heb. 1:3; the word τριάδος is taken from 1 John 5:7; the Fathers likewise derive τὸ ὁμούσιον from the Scriptures; no one says it proceeded from the Platonists. Let Athanasius on the Nicene Synod be read, and what was done concerning it in the Synod. That three hypostases should be said was defined in the Alexandrian Synod, with Athanasius himself, Bishop of Alexandria, as the author: nor was μία ὑπόστασις said in any other sense before, than that ὑπόστασις was accepted for ὀσία. All of which we have explained elsewhere, namely in the Commonplaces, Vol. III of the Systematics, as also in the Apodixis on the Holy Trinity. But now let Grotius continue: Among the Platonists there are three hypostases: τὸ ἀυτὸ ὀν, and νῦς the creator, and the soul of the world. And because νῦς has a meaning which does not seem to differ from the λόγυ, and the same νῦς is also called a birth by them, therefore many Christians transferred what is said about νῦς by the Platonists to the λόγον or Son. Among the Platonists you may find: ὑποστάντες τρεῖς ἐξ ἑνὸς: likewise: ἐξαίρειν δεῖ τὴν μονάδα τῆς τριάδος, ἐξάπτειν δὲ τὴν τριάδα τῆς μονάδος. Similarly, Christians began to speak, as in Lucian, or whoever that author of the dialogue Philopatris is: the high-throned God, the immortal God, heavenly, son of the father, spirit proceeding from the father, one from three and from one three: The Hebrew Cabbalists followed both, more Christian in words, more Platonic in sense. For they say: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקרש אלהים שלש באחד אחר בשלשה: Christians did not follow the Platonists, but the Platonists wrapped in the coverings of their inventions what Moses and other divine writers had handed down from the truth. But Grotius could have learned from his own Petavius that those inventions are very different from our faith. And from where will it be taught that the sense of the Hebrews was more Platonic? One could more easily prove Hugo to be more Platonic. He praises there that passage of Chalcidius on the Timaeus: And the reason of GOD is GOD consulting human affairs, who is the cause for men of living well and happily. Which favor Sabellius more than the Catholic faith, which distinguishes the divine persons. Such confusion can be seen here and there in the annotations of Grotius. The most convenient and least intricate explanation seemed to Grotius to be that which the Greek Church, which was at Constantinople at the time when that city was captured, exhibited to the Sultan of the Turks, in which the λόγος and the Spirit are called actions of GOD arising from the nature of GOD, ch. IV. See his annotations to art. I of the Augsburg Confession. He could never have preferred this explanation to other Symbolical and Synodic ones sanctioned in Ecumenical Councils, unless he had wished to gratify Sabellius, Servetus, and the like, rather than the Catholic faith in this dogma.

Moreover, by the primordial light, Origen, Augustine, Eucherius, Bede, Rupert, and others understand angels, abandoning the evident letter in the narration of the history without cause. For Moses does not speak of spiritual light, but of corporeal and sensible light, which he opposes to the darkness of the abyss: nor can the element of fire be understood, as Danaeus and Polanus think: which opinion Füller exposed in Miscell. book 1, ch. 12, because it is not the office of fire to distinguish day from night: nor the day itself, as Hottinger thinks in Histor. creat. p. 95, because the light πρωτόκτις ⅅ and the day are distinguished as cause and effect: nor the splendor of the Empyrean heaven, which they imagine, as Bruno, Halensis, and Guilh. Parisiensis do, according to Mersenne. they wish; nor the Sun, as R. Menasse Ben-Israel wishes, or the light of the Sun; because this was not yet created then, nor the light which is reserved by GOD, much less all lights, namely the superior ones, nor angels, souls, and the light of the fabric, as Menasse again thinks in de Creat. Probl. XVI. nor some extraordinary light, the subject of which is passed over in silence, which seemed so to Scharpius; much less an accident without a subject, as the Papists, Bellarmine and Becanus wish: which accident ἰδιοσύσατον is iron-wood: but a certain luminous substance mobile around the primordial mass, which seems to have then ceased into the matter of the stars, which, what kind it was, we freely profess with Augustine, book XI de Civit. DEI ch. VI, cannot be sufficiently explained by us. See concerning these things what we have said in Vol. III of the System. Theol. Article on Creation, chapter II, question V. Regarding the luminous body, Bede, Hugh, Lombard, and Maresius provide explanations: regarding the luminous cloud, some Hebrews and certain Scholastics, Zanchius, and Füllerus. Grotius, in book I of On the Truth of the Christian Religion, chapter XVI, says: The sun, he says, is not the primordial light, but a receptacle of light, δόχημα καὶ ὄχημα τῶ πυρὸς, as a certain one of the ancient Christians speaks, and Empedocles acknowledged. Concerning whom (as he has in his Annotations) Laërtius says, τὸν ἥλιόν φησι πυρὸς ἄθροισμα μέγα, he said (Empedocles) that the sun is a great heap of fire. He who wrote the opinions of the Philosophers, which are in the works of Plutarch, book II, chapter 6, says: Empedocles, he says, first of all cast off the ether; then fire, after that earth, from which, constricted by the very force of agitation, water bubbled forth, and from this air exhaled. The heaven, however, was born from the ether, the sun from fire. Philolaus said that the sun is of a glassy nature, which receives into itself the reflection of the fire that is in the world; but that it distills light to us. Anaxagoras, Democritus, and Metrodorus said that the sun is a certain ignited mass. And Democritus shows that these opinions are most ancient, as Laërtius narrates. These are the words of Grotius.

However, those things were not to be rashly mixed with the Mosaic history of creation. For although it might perhaps be conceded that something concerning the primordial light flowed down to the Gentiles; whence Empedocles seems to have spoken of two suns, one archetypal and original, the other which appears; yet the Gentiles wrapped the truth in their own inventions: nor are those things which appear in any way analogous to be immediately seized upon as the same. And since Grotius accepts these things concerning the primordial light, what else is one permitted to gather here, than that he judged it to be the same fire which, having been collected into the sun as a receptacle, was afterwards made? But this is by no means to be admitted: for it is neither the nature of fire to produce the day, which the primordial light produced, or to rotate around Chaos, which is attributed to it: nor is the Sun ignited, or does it consist of fire, or can it be considered a receptacle of it, which indeed produces heat, but is itself subjectively or formally hot, like fire, not in the least.

Moreover, the Hebrews teach from Bereschith Rabba that that primordial light, after the luminaries were created on the fourth day, was hidden by GOD and preserved for the use of the righteous: likewise, that GOD wrapped Himself in it as a garment, Ps. 104. In the book Ialkut from the ancient book Pefikta on Isa. 60, 1, it is said that that Light is the Light of the Messiah, and those words, GOD saw that the light was good, teach this, that GOD foresaw the age of the Messiah and his works before the world was created, and therefore hid it for the Messiah from his generation in his throne of glory. See our annotations on the passage Isa. 60, 1.

Latin:

vers. 3. DIXITQVE DEUS : FIAT LUX, ET FACTA EST LUX) De his verbis vide Dionysii Longini locum, quem in dictis Annotatis protulimus.

Remittit ad annotata ad librum 1. de veritate Religionis Christianæ, e Dionysio Longino. Qui libro de sublimi dicendi genere, cum dixisset, de DEO loquentes curare debere, ut eum nobis magnum sincerumque & impermixtum exhibeant, hæc subjicit: Sic egit & is, qui Judæis leges condidit, vir minime vulgaris ingenii, ut qui DEI potestatem digne & con- ceperit & elocutus fuerit, statim in principio legum hæc scribens, dixit, ait DEUS. Quid? Fiat lux & Sed modo hoc loquendi non solum δύναμις & potentia DEI de- signatur, quod verbo & nutu creavit omnia, dictum factum. Mysterium λόγου ὑποστατικοῦ, per quem omnia condita sunt, simul insinuatum. Quia non dixit DEUS absque Verbo illo, sine quo nihil factum est. Ita explicat David Psal. 33, 6. & Salomo Prov. 8, 23. seqq. cujus sapientia opifex, quæ cum DEO Patre erat, cuncta componens, uti versu 30. loquitur, est ipsum verbum hypostaticum. Et luculentissi- me omnium S. Johannes c. 1, 1. 2. 3. quem hæc verba Mosis respicere agnoscit Grotius, annotatis ad Joh. 1, 1. Hunc etiam λόγον indigitari voce דבר a Davide Ps. 33, 5. eamq; appellationem e Mosaico loco originem habere, fatetur. Desumpsit hinc Chaldæus inter- pres suum מימרא verbum, quod passim adhibet; mox in 3. capite Geneseos v. 8. Et audierunt vocem Domini DEI, Chaldæus habet: Et audierunt vocem verbi מימרא Domini DEI: Quamvis enim in ali- quibus locis ea voce utatur Chaldæus, quibus non satis convenit notio verbi hypostatici, ex iis tamen neganda non videtur illa significatio, saltem in iis locis, quæ Filio DEI conveniunt: non enim sem- per æque accuratus est Interpres, nec principalis si- gnificatio per secundariam usurpationem tollitur: in qua primaria notione in hac etiam materia adhi- betur Esa. 45, 12. ubi in Ebræo legitur: Ego feci terram & hominem super eam creavi; in Chaldæo est: Ego in verbo meo feci terram, & homines super eam creavi; c. 48, 13. in Ebræo legitur: Manus mea fundavit terram; in Chaldæo, Verbo meo funda- vi terram. Annuit etiam hisce cum Fagio Hottinge- rus, deserens Hackspanium, qui in alia omnia ivit, non sane cum gloria religionis nostræ de usu Script, Rabb. p. 365. Profitetur enim palam Hist. creat. p. 56. aliqua esse loca, quæ de Messia, vixque alio com- mode in Targum intelligantur, utpote Psal. 110, 1. Gen. 3, 8. laudans in eam sententiam Buxtorf. Capell. & Cameronem, ut & Guadagnolum, quoad locum Jerem. 17, 15. Tremellium Hag. 2, 5. 6. alios e Pfal. 54, 2. 107, 20. Efa. 40, 8. Plura adduxit Dn. Varen. in Gen. p. 130. Loca omnia Targum, quibus per verbum intelligit Filium, peculiari libello collegit B. Selneccerus. Quam nuncupationem e Mosaico præsente textu ortam agnoscit Grotius, ac Chaldæum interpretem sequutum etiam esse Petrum Apostolum censet 2. Ep. 3, 5. ὀυρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι καὶ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα, τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγῳ. Denique hinc observant, Græcos e veteribus, nempe Chaldæorum libris habuisse, quæ de λόγῳ tradunt, Orphicorum Scriptorem, Heraclitum & Zenonem. Quod notarat quoque Tertullianus adversus gentes: Apud vestros quoque sapientes λόγον, id est sermonem atq́; orationem constat artificem videri universitatis. Hunc enim Zeno determinat factitatorem, qui cuncta in dispositione formaverit. Locus Zenonis fuit libro περὶ ὀυσίας, ubi τὸ ποιοῦν causam effectricem vocabat λόγον, quem sequuti Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archidamus, Posidonius, docente Laertio in Zenone. Sed imprimis Amelius Platonicus λόγον ceu effectricem rerum omnium causam introduxit, qui tamen a Johanne Evangelista, quem Barbarum vocat, id didicit. Καὶ ὗτος ἄρα ἦν ὁ λόγος, καθ' ὃν ἀεὶ ὄντα τὰ γενόμενα, ὡς ἂν καὶ ἡράκλειτος ἀξιώσειε καὶ νῆ δῒ ἂν ὁ βάρβαρος ἀξιοῖ ἐν τῇ τῆς ἀρχῆς τάξει τε κὶ ἀταξίᾳ καθεστηκότα πρὸς Θεὸν εἶναι δι' ὗ πανθ' ἁπλῶς γεγενῆσθαι, ἐν ᾧ τὸ γενναόμενον ζῶον κὶ ὂν πεφυκέναι. Hæc itaque illa ratio, per quam semper sunt, quæ sunt facta, quomodo etiam Heraclitus censuit. Eadem profecto, quæ BARBARUS ILLE indicat, in primo rerum conditu, imo & in incondito statu DEO adstitisse, per quem omnia omnino facta, in quo id, quod fit animal, esse suum haberet. Verba leguntur apud Eusebium l. XI. Præparation. c. XIX. & Cyrillum Alexandr. l. VIII. contra Julianum. Philo, Judæus quidem, sed ad Platonica tamen dogmata deflectens, pariter per λόγον mundum conditum dicit, quem etiam εἰκόνα & υἱὸν Θεῦ vocat. Platonem ipsum mundi exemplar λόγον dixisse, notum est. Quamvis alium ille λόγον intellexerit, quam divini Scriptores. Patet tamen, quomodo aliquid de summo mysterio innotuerit exteris, quod vero suis illi commentis obfuscarint.

Ita ergo Moses SS. Trinitatis mysterium mox initio Geneseos expressit, cum non DEUM modo, sed Spiritum DEI quoque, ac λόγον ejus, ceu supremum architectum introduxit, quod pariter a Davide factum Ps. 33, 6. Quo de graviter B. Lutherus noster Comment. in Genes. fol. 4. Manifesta hic est distinctio personarum. Dicit enim DEUM esse, ut sic loquar, Dictorem, qui creat, & tamen non utitur materia, sed solo Verbo, quod profert, ex nihilo facit cœlum & terram. Jam huc adhibe Evangelium Johannis: In principio erat Verbum (Nam probe facit cum Mose) Dicit ante mundum conditum nihil erat creaturarum. Deus tamen habebat Verbum. Hoc Verbum quid est, aut quid facit? Audi Mosen, Lux inquit, nondum erat. Sed tenebræ ex suo nihilo esse vertuntur in illam præstantissimam creaturam, quæ est lux. Per quid? per verbum. Ergo in principio & ante omnem creaturam est verbum, & est tam potens Verbum, quod ex nihilo facit omnia. Hinc sequitur irrefragabiliter, quod Johannes addit: Hoc Verbum esse DEUM, & tamen esse distinctam personam a DEO Patre, sicut distinctæ res sunt verbum, & is, qui verbum profert. Et tamen hæc distinctio ejusmodi est, ut unissima, ut sic dicam, unitas essentiæ maneat. Et fol. 2. Magnus Ecclesiæ consensus est de mysterio Trinitatis hic prodito. Pater per filium, quem Verbum Mose vocat, creat cælum & terram ex nihilo. His Spiritus S. incubat. Sicut enim gallina incubat ovis, ut pullos excludat, ova calefaciens & ca- lore quasi animans : ita Scriptura dicit Spiritum S. quasi incubasse aquis, ut ista corpora, quæ animanda & ornanda erant, vivificaret. Nam Spiritus S. officium est vivificare. Hæc B. Lutherus.

Quæ etsi viderit Hugo, (Grotium intelligo) involvere tamen ea maluit Rabbinorum placitis, quam juxta mysterium fidei dextre evolvere, con- fundens λόγον hypostaticum cum potentia DEI, quam attributum DEI vocamus. Num Serveti in favorem, cujus causam adversus Calvinum & Rivetum egit, an quod Platonicorum & Judæorum dogmatibus inescatus fuerit, non dixero. Verba ejus testentur annot. ad Joh. 1, 1. Quia Moses scripserat, dixit DEUS, fiat lux, & facta est lux, & ita de cæteris; hinc factum est, ut vim sive προβολὴν aut ἀπόῤῥοιαν (has enim voces hac in re Christiani veteres usurpant) DEI illam, quæ res ex nihilo condidit, atque varia & eximia effecit, Hebræi appellarent דבר, ut videre est Ps. 33, 6. Ps. 148, 8. Vide Maimonidem Duce dubitantium l. 1. c. 23. & 45. & 66. Hunc cæcum ductorem non raro sequitur Grotius. Paulo post de hoc mysterio ita loquitur Hugo, ac si a Platonicis id Christiani, non a divinis Scriptoribus Platonici habeant. Cum explicasset illud, ὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν fere ad Serveti mentem, λόγον ita DEUM esse intelligendum, ut & illud maneat, fuisse apud DEUM, id est, ut non fuerit ὁ λόγος omne id, quod est DEUS; addit quæ hic addere juvat : Hypostaseon distinctionem Origenes & post eum alii vocavere, sed notandum est, hanc vocem ὑποστάσεων, ut & τριάδος, ὁμουσίε & alias quasdam non a primis Christianis usurpatas, cum contra μίαν ὑπόστασιν dixerit Athanasius, Synodi, Nicena & Sardicensis, & Romanæ aliquot, sed defumtas ex Platonicis scriptoribus, sensu nonnihil immutato. Falsum hoc. ὑπόστασιν dixit Apostolus Ebr. 1, 3. vox τριάδος 1. Joh. 5, 7. desumpta; τὸ ὁμούσιον e Scripturis itidem deducunt Patres; nemo a Platonicis profectum dicit. Legatur Athanasius de Synodo Nicena : & quæ de ea in Synodo acta sunt. Τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ut dicerentur, in Synodo Alexandrina, autore ipso Athanasio Alexandriæ Episcopo definitum: neque μία ὑπόστασις alio sensu dicta antea, quam uti ὑπόστασις pro ὀσία accipiebatur. Quæ omnia alias expedivimus, in locis scil. communibus Tom. III. Systemat. ut & Apodixi de SS. Trinitate. Sed nunc pergat Grotius : Apud Platonicos tres ὑποστάσεις sunt τὸ ἀυτὸ ὀν, & νῦς ὁ δημιυργὸς, ἡ τῶ κόσμυ ψυχὴ. Et quia νῦς significationem habet, quæ ἀπὸ τῶ λόγυ non videtur abludeve, & idem νῦς etiam γέννημα ipsis dicitur, ideo quæ περὶ νῦ dicuntur Platonicis, multi Christianorum ad τὸν λόγον sive Filium transtulerunt. Apud Platonicos reperias : ὑποστάντες τρεῖς ἐξ ἑνὸς: item : ἐξαίρειν δεῖ τὴν μονάδα τῆς τριάδος, ἐξάπτειν δὲ τὴν τριάδα τῆς μονάδος. Similiter Christiani loqui cæperunt, ut apud Lucianum sive quisquis ille est autor dialogi Philopatridis: ὑψιμέδοντα θεὸν, θεὸν ἄφθιτον ἐρανίωνα, υἱὸν πατρὸς, πνεῦμα ἐκ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον, ἕν ἐκ τριῶν καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς τρία : Utrosque sequuti Cabbalistæ Hebræi, verbis magis Christianos, sensu magis Platonicos. Ajunt enim: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקרש אלהים שלש באחד אחר בשלשה: Non Platonicos sequuti Christiani, sed commentorum involucris complexi sunt Platonici, quæ ex vero Moses, aliique divini Scriptores tradiderant. Commenta autem illa multum diversa esse a fide nostra, vel a Petavio suo didicisse poterat Grotius. Ebræorum autem sensum magis Platonicum fuisse, unde docebitur ? Hugonem Platonicum magis, facilius quis evicerit. Laudat ibi illud Chalcidii ad Timæum : Et ratio DEI DEus est humanis rebus consulens, qui causa est hominibus bene beateque vivendi. Quæ Sabellio magis favent, quam Catholicæ fidei, personas divinas distinguenti. Qualem confusionem passim videri licet in annotatis Grotianis. Commodissima ac minime intricata visa est Grotio explicatio, quam Ecclesia Græca, quæ Constantinopoli erat, tunc cum urbs ea caperetur, Turcarum Sultano exhibuit, in qua λόγος & Spiritus vocantur actiones DEI ex natura DEI ortæ cap. IV. Vid. annotata ejus ad artic. I. Aug. Confess. Quam explicationem nunquam aliis Symbolicis, & Synodicis in Oecumenicis conci- liis sancitis præferre potuisset, nisi Sabellio, Serve- to, & similibus potius, quam Catholicæ fidei in hoc dogmate gratificari voluisset.

Cæterum per lucem primigeniam Origenes, Augustinus, Eucherius, Beda, Rupertus, Ange- los intelligunt, citra causam literam evidentem in historiæ narratione deserentes. Moses enim non de luce Spirituali, sed corporali & sensibili, quam tenebris abyssi opponit, loquitur: neque ignis Ele- mentum intelligi potest, uti Danæus & Polanus pu- tant: quam sententiam exposuit Füller. Miscell. l. 1. c. 12. quia ignis officium non est, diem a nocte disterminare: neque dies ipse, ut censet Hottinger. Histor. creat. p. 95. quia lux πρωτόκτις ⅅ & dies distinguuntur tanquam causa & effectus: neque Cœli Empyræi, quod fingunt, splendor, ut Bruno, Halenfis, Guilh. Parisienf. apud Mersenn. volunt; neque Sol, ut R. Menasse Ben - Israel vult aut lux So- lis; quia hic conditus tum nondum erat, neque lux, quæ a DEO reservatur, nedum omnes luces, su- periores nempe, neque angeli, animæ & lux fabri- cæ, ut iterum Menasse censet de Creat. Probl. XVI. neque lux aliqua extraordinaria, cujus subje- ctum taceatur, quod Scharpio visum est; nedum accidens sine subjecto, uti Papistæ, Bellarminus & Becanus volunt: quod Accidens ἰδιοσύσατον est σιδηρόξυλον: sed substantia quædam luminosa mobilis circa massam primævam, quæ in stellarum materiam deinde cessisse videtur, quæ qualis fuerit, satis a no- bis explicari non posse cum Augustino lib. XI. de Civit. DEI cap. VI. ultro profitemur. Vide de his, quæ diximus Tom. III. System. Theol. Artic. de Creat. cap. II. qv. V. De corpore lucido explicant Be- da, Hugo, Lombardus, Maresius: de nubecula luci- da Ebræi nonnulli, & Scholastici quidam, Zanchius, Füllerus. Grotius lib. I. de Verit. Relig. Christ. cap. XVI. Solem, inquit, non esse lucem primigeniam, sed lucis receptaculum, δόχημα καὶ ὄχημα τῶ πυρὸς, ut veterum Christianorum quidam loquitur & agno- vit Empedocles. De quo (ut in Annotationibus habet) Laërtius, τὸν ἥλιόν φησι πυρὸς ἄθροισμα μέγα, solem dicebat (Empedocles) magnum esse acer- vum ignis. Is qui placita scripsit Philosopho- rum, quæ sunt in operibus Plutarchi l. II. c. 6. Em- pedocles, inquit, primum omnium secretum abjebat æthera; deinde ignem, post terram, quæ constricta impetu ipso agitationis ebulliisse inde aquam, ex hac exhalasse aërem. Cœlum autem ex æthere natum, Solem ex igne. Philolaus dixit, Solem vitrea natu- ra, qui ignis ejus, quem in mundo est, repercussum in se splendorem recipiat; Lumen autem ad nos destillet. Anaxagoras, Democritus, Metrodotus solem massam quandam ignitam dicebant. Et has sententias esse antiquissimas ostendit Democritus, narrante Laertio. Hæc Grotius.

Non erant autem illa temere commiscenda cum historia creationis Mosaica. Nam utut ali- quid ad Gentiles dimanasse de luce primigenia concedi fortassis possit; unde Empedocles videtur duos soles dixisse; alterum ἀρχέτυπον originalem, alterum, qui appareat, commentis tamen suis in- volverunt veritatem gentiles: nec ea quæ utcunque apparent analoga, pro iisdem actutum arri- pienda semper sunt. Et quum hæc de luce primi- genia accipiat Grotius, quid aliud hic colligere li- ceat, quam quod eundem ignem esse censuerit, qui in solem ceu receptaculum collectus postea fue- rit? Quod vero neutiquam admittendum: nam neque ignis est efficere diem, quem lux primige- nia effecit, aut rotari circa Chaos, quod illi tri- buitur: neque Sol ignitus est, aut igne constat, ejus- ve receptaculum censeri potest, qui calorem qui- dem efficit, sed ipse subjective vel formaliter cali- dus, ignis instar, minime est.

Cæterum Ebræi lucem illam primigeniam e Bereschith Rabba docent, posteaquam luminaria quarto die condita sint, a DEO fuisse absconditam & in usum justorum asservatam: item, DEUM se in ea ceu vestimento involvisse Psal. 104. In libro Ial- kut ex antiquo libro Pefikta ad Efa. 60, 1. dicitur Lux illa esse Lux Messiæ, & verba illa, vidit DEUS, quod lux esset bona, hoc docere, quod præviderit DEUS seculum Messiæ & opera ejus, antequam crearetur mundus, ac proinde absconderit eam pro Messia ex ejus generatione suo solio gloriæ suæ. Vide annotata nostra ad Locum Efa. 60, 1.

## 1:4
verf. 4. THAT IT WAS GOOD) That is, consistent with His purpose. Pherecydes: ζᾶς ποιεῖ φάρος μέγα τε καὶ καλὸν κὰι ἐν αὐτῷ ποικίλλῃ γῆν κὰι ὠγενον κὰι τὰ τῶ ὠγένο δώματα. Where understand the houses of Ocean as islands. To Plato, the world is beautiful. Seneca, epistle LXV, concerning GOD: He is good, He made good things.

Latin:

verf. 4. QUOD ESSET BONA) Id est proposito suo congruens. Pherecydes: ζᾶς ποιεῖ φάρος μέγα τε καὶ καλὸν κὰι ἐν αὐτῷ ποικίλλῃ γῆν κὰι ὠγενον κὰι τὰ τῶ ὠγένο δώματα. Ubi Oceani domos insulas intellige. Platoni καλὸς ὁ κόσμος. Seneca epistola LXV. de DEO. bonus est, bona fecit.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. EVENING AND MORNING) See the stated Annotations. Those three first and extraordinary days, made before the Sun was created, were not made by the emission and contraction of rays, which seems to be the opinion of Basil and Damascenus, but by the motion of a luminous body, the primordial light, which was moved around the rude mass in such a way that by its approach it signaled day, and by its withdrawal night, and in the space of 24 hours returned to the same point; whence the first natural day was made, with darkness lasting for twelve hours before the light was created, which was the first night; but when light was created by GOD, the first morning arose, and with the light and motion diffused through the remaining hours of the nychthemeron, until the course was completed and darkness returned, the first day was established.

However, the opinion of Philoponus, Marius Victorinus, and Procopius, who translate the Mosaic nychthemeron as a hemeronyction and make the evening later than the dawn, is not to be approved. Because Moses does not make the beginning from the light, but from the evening: and in the morning time he places the end of the first day, whence also the Jews begin the day from the evening, which they received from the Patriarchs and from Adam himself. That this was also passed on to the Gentiles, Grotius rightly observed, that Thales, as Laertius testifies, taught from ancient discipline that darkness was prior to light, which is also among the Orphics and Hesiod, and from there the nations most tenacious of ancient custom counted time by nights. The Numidians in Libya do not compute their time by days, but by nights, says Nicolaus Damascenus. Tacitus testifies this of the Germans, and the Bohemians, Poles, and formerly the Gauls, still observe this custom, which Caesar observed in book VI of the Gallic War. This was noted regarding the Druids by Pliny in book XVI. Hist. natural. last chapter, regarding the Athenians in Gellius book III, chapter 2. Who in this matter also seem to be disciples of the Phoenicians. יוֹם day according to Ainsworth is said from tumult and its works, Laila night from the howling of wild beasts. עֶרֶב Evening from עָרַב to bind, because it binds the day with the night, בֹּקֶר morning from בָּקַר to discern, because then things are discerned from one another, notes Hier. ab Oleastr.

But when Moses says ONE DAY, he uses the cardinal for the ordinal according to customary usage, see Gen. 3, 1; Hag. 1, 1; so that the sense is, from evening and morning the first day is completed. The part for the whole: evening signifies night, morning signifies day. We do not, however, reject the observation of Ambrose, that the first day was also called one day for this reason, because this was as it were the general measure of all days, as if one were to say the time of one day.

Latin:

Vers. 5. VESPERE ET MANE) Vide dicta Annotata. Tres illi dies primi & extraordinarii ante crea- tum Solem facti non sunt per emissionem & con- tractionem radiorum, quæ Basilii & Damasceni videtur sententia, sed per motum luminosi corpo- ris, lucis primigeniæ, quod ita circa rudem mo- lem motum fuit, ut accessu suo diem, recessu vero noctem indixerit, & 24. horarum spatio ad eun- dem terminum redierit; unde primus dies natura- lis factus, tenebris per horas duodecim durantibus ante lucem conditam, quæ prima nox fuit; ubi ve- ro lux a DEO crearetur mane primum exortum, & per reliquas spatii νυχθημερίνε horas diffusa luce ac motu, usque dum absoluto cursu tenebræ redi- rent, dies prima constituta est.

Probanda autem non est Philoponi, Marii Vi- ctorini, & Procopii opinio, qui νυχθημέρινον Mosai- cum vertunt in ἡμερονύχθιον, & vesperam posterio- rem faciunt diluculo. Quia Moses non a luce, sed a vespera initium facit: in matutino autem tempore finem ponit primæ diei, unde etiam Judæi a vespera diem inchoant, qui a Patriarchis, & ab Adamo ipso id accepere. Quod ad Gentiles etiam traductum re- cte observavit Grotius, quod tenebras luce priores ex veteri disciplina Thales, teste Laërtio, docuerit, quod etiam apud Orphicos, & Hesiodum est, atque inde antiqui moris retinentissimæ Gentes tempora per noctes numerabant. Numidæ in Lybia non ex diebus, sed ex noctibus tempora sua computant, ait Nicolaus Damascenus. De Germanis Tacitus id testatur, & servant hunc morem etiam Bohemi, Po- loni, olim & Galli, quod Cæsar lib. VI. Belli Gallici observavit. De Druidibus id notatum Plinio lib. XVI. Hist. natural. cap. ult. de Atheniensibus Gel- lio lib. III. cap. 2. Qui hac in re quoque Phœnicum videntur discipuli. יוֹם dies juxta Ainsworth. dicitur a tumultu & operibus ejus, Laila nox ex ululatu ferarum. עֶרֶב Vespera ab עָרַב ligavit, quod liget diem cum nocte, בֹּקֶר mane a בָּקַר discer- nere, quod tunc res ab invicem discernantur, dici notat Hier. ab Oleastr.

Cum autem Moses dicit DIES UNUS, mo- re consveto Cardinalem pro ordinali ponit, Vid. Genef. 3, 1. Hag. 1, 1. ut sensus sit, ex vespera, & mane completus est primus dies. Pars pro toto: vespera noctem, mane diem significat. Non re- re- probamus tamen Ambrosii observationem, quod etiam ideo dies unus dictus primus dies, quia hic mensura quasi generalis fuit omnium dierum, velu- ti diceretur unius diei tempus.

## 1:6
vers. 6. GOD ALSO SAID.

The word 'said' is repeated nine times in this chapter; the Hebrews say the tenth is included in the first words, 'In the beginning GOD created heaven and earth.' From this arose the saying, 'The world was founded by GOD with ten words,' as Lud. Dievius notes.

verse. The same. LET THERE BE A FIRMAMENT) The word רקיע is properly rendered τάσις, which word Plato uses in the Timaeus regarding this very matter. The likeness seems to be taken from a tent, which is supported by certain ropes so that it does not fall. See Psalm 104:2. It is said, however, not only of the starry heaven, but also of the heaven which is called the air, to use the words of Lucretius. The former meaning appears below in 14, the latter below in 21, in the Chaldean Paraphrase of Psalm 19, and in Kimchi on Psalm 77.

The name רקיע is not badly rendered τάσις, by others 'expanded,' because it was then expanded and unfolded, not otherwise than as a rolled-up thing is accustomed to be expanded and unfolded: which is gathered not only from Psalm 104:2, but also from other places, Isaiah 40:22, chapter 42:1, chapter 44:24, chapter 51:19, Jeremiah 50:15, Job 26:7. And it seems to be indicated here that Heaven previously lay as if rolled up in that primordial mass, but now by that omnipotent word, LET THERE BE A רקיע EXPANSION, it was evolved and expanded into this form in which it is even now seen, which at the consummation of the age will in turn not only be rolled up and folded like a book, Isaiah 34:4, but will also fail like smoke, be dissipated and consumed, Isaiah 51:6, and thus will clearly perish, Luke 21:33. Concerning which see Justin in Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, question XCIV. Just as the Holy Scriptures have compared the making of the firmament by comparison sometimes to the stretching of a skin, sometimes to smoking smoke, sometimes to the roundness of a vaulted dome; so also they have compared its dissolution by comparison sometimes to a book that is rolled up, sometimes to an element that is dissolved by fire, sometimes to a garment growing old. Blessed Luther explains the manner thus: 'This is now the work of the second day, how from that rude nebula, which he called Heaven, he produced a beautiful and elegant Heaven. That rude mass of nebula created from nothing on the first day, GOD apprehends by his word and commands that it be extended in the manner of spheres, just as a bladder is extended in a circular form when it is inflated.' For I will use a rustic comparison, so that the matter may become clearer: 'Just as a tent (he explains later from Psalm 104) is unfolded and fixed in a field when it is folded up, so you expand and as it were evolve your rude Heaven with your word.'

Moreover, the LXX rendered it ςερέωμα, whom the Vulgate followed as 'Firmament,' and Blessed Luther explained as 'Expanse': by which word, although the emphasis of the Hebrew does not seem to be so well expressed, Heaven is nevertheless not badly described, if it is understood not by reason of hard or firm matter, but by reason of form and end, so that Heaven may be considered so called on account of its perfection, distinction, and firmness or perpetuity; so that Sixtinus Amama and others here agitate against Blessed Luther's version in vain. What? That Nicol.
