Fuller, book I, Miscellanies, chapter VI, [says] the chief meaning of the word רקיע is from the Syriac רקע, to press, compress, constipate, compact, that which is pressed, or most properly that which is felted and felt, which is pressed on all sides, and collected or gathered into itself or impacted, and therefore firm. and solid, may excellently explain how that word applies indeed also to the earth, or to the terrestrial globe, which GOD רָקַע Psalm 135, 56. Isaiah 42, 5. chap. 44, 24. when he gathered together all things that are παχυμερῆ or thick and somewhat thick, πεπιεσμένα καὶ τὰ πιλήματα, compressed, forced, and compacted: yet by a special reason that upper and celestial globe claims this name רָקִיעַ for itself everywhere in the Holy Scriptures: because the celestial רָקִיעַ is the totality τῶν λεπτομερῶν, namely of those things which are of a thin and subtle nature, gathered and strengthened into the upper region, which GOD in the beginning of created things רָקַע, that is, compressed, forced, and compacted by himself, gathered into its place, and thus ἐστερέωσε, strengthened. Because that globe is of a magnitude clearly admirable and almost immense, so that when compared with it, this lower and terrestrial one, having lost all magnitude, reduced to a point, as it were vanishes. But Füller is worthy to be read more fully concerning these things. Hottinger in Histor. creat. page 20 praises Schindler, because רָקַע signifies to extend a contracted thing into breadth, as metals are extended into plates, or as gold leaf is drawn out by thinning, comparing Ex. 39, 9. Isa. 40, 19. Jer. 10, 9.

By רָקִיעַ, however, Grotius understands both the starry heaven and also the air: indeed, if what he has in Book I de Verit. Rel. Christ. is compared, he includes in this word also the seat of GOD, for when in chapter XVI he compares the opinions of the Gentiles with the history of Moses, he says that Aratus and Catullus acknowledge a divine dwelling place above the locations of the stars. Which explanation is an exposition of Episcopius's imagination concerning the vaulting of three Heavens, by which the first Heaven is called air, the second heaven the azure vault, the receptacle of the stars, the third the palace of GOD and the Angels, which is also that of certain Calvinists, of Piscator, who thinks the angels were created with this heaven, and of others, but increased by Episcopius with new absurdities, when he made the air the receptacle of the Planets as well as of meteors, and the starry heaven water, and made the stars in it watery, and constituted that as a sort of curtain and tapestry of the divine and celestial palace: he imagines one produced from the lower waters, the others from the upper, which to have recited is to have refuted.

But how can the Heaven of the blessed be understood by רָקִיעַ, when the use of this is to distinguish the lower waters from the upper? Will that be done by the heaven of the blessed? Or how can such diverse significations have a place at the same time in the one word רָקִיעַ? Not to mention that it has not yet been shown that רָקִיעַ is ever taken for the Heaven of the blessed. That thing, however, which this explanation presupposes as certain, concerning a divine dwelling place constituted τοπικῶς or by reason of place and site above the starry Heaven, we judge to be in agreement with the inventions of the Gentiles indeed, but not with the Mosaic and other divine Scriptures; and since we consider that local heaven, the dwelling place of the blessed, of the Angels, or even of GOD himself, which the Papists and Calvinists imagine for themselves, to have been already eliminated in Tom. III. Syst. Theol. de creat. c. II, there is no reason why we should labor here.

Although indeed the opinion of those is more probable who understand the air by רָקִיעַ, as for instance from the Jews Aben-Ezra, and also from the Papists Rupert, Cajetan, Pererius, Valentianus, Petavius, from the Reformed Calvin, Borrhaus, Zanchius, Martyr, Junius, Mercerus, Danaeus, Bucanus, Gomarus, Voetius, Grossius, Willet, the Authors of the annotations to the English and Belgian Bibles, and finally approved also by our own Dr. Joh. Musaeus: yet we are forbidden to add our vote to it, since verse 14

Let it be noted that in that Heaven, which He Haje-diab points out (which is indeed designated here), the stars were placed, which certainly were not placed in the air. Others, therefore, believe that that word embraces the ethereal Heaven together with the air, such as Cornelius a Lapide, Tossanus, Pareus, Keckermannus, as also Schindlerinus, Hottingerus, and the Blessed Jacob Martini, Coll. II. contr. Becan. Disp. VII. thes. 10. But the opinion of most of the Fathers and of the Blessed Luther seems to be preferred, that only the ethereal Heaven is designated here by that word: because it is not sufficiently fitting that both heaven itself and the air be designated together by one and the same word in the History of creation, and verse 14 says: Let there be Luminaries in the EXPANSE OF THOSE HEAVENS. Whence in verse 20 they also understand the ethereal Heaven: but they explain על־פני רקיע as 'over against' or 'opposite to' the expanse, as Helvicus in Vindic. p. 57, or 'before the expanse,' and 'before the sight of the expanse of heaven,' or 'under heaven,' as others interpret. P. Fagius says the preposition על is not rarely taken for 'beside' or 'near': And the sense is, under Heaven in the air, or beside, that is, near Heaven. For the face of Heaven is called that which turns itself toward us and is visible to us. Here, therefore, they understand not the air, but only the ethereal Heaven by the word רקיע, both because this word is nowhere taken for the air alone, or for the air included, and because the air did not yet exist on the second day, but emerged only when the waters were separated from the dry land on the third day. For where the thick mass of waters was condensed and gathered into one place and separated from the dry land, there also the air emerged, namely that purer, perfect, and full one, to which the air of the first day stood in relation, just as the primordial light stood in relation to the splendor of the stars, that is, somewhat thickly and somewhat imperfectly, as the Blessed Walther explains from the Blessed Gesner, Disp. I. in Gen. quæst. XVIII, in Spong. Mosaic. on Gen. I, 6. 7. 8. page 61, who treats of these things more fully and, for this opinion that the ethereal heaven is designated here, cites Tertullian, Caesarius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Theodoret, Acacius, Severianus, Gennadius, Chrysostom, Olympiodorus, Anastasius, Augustine, Jerome, Bede, Procopius, cited by Salianus in Annal. Eccles. Tom. II. fol. 28, as also Polanus among the Reformed, lib. V. Syntagm. c. IX.

verse same. WATERS FROM THE WATERS) Pliny, book XXXI. What can be more wonderful than waters standing in the heaven?

Latin:

vers. 6. DIXIT QUOQUE DEUS.

Verbum dixit Novies in hoc capite repeti- tur, decimum Ebræi includi ajunt in primis ver- bis in principio creavit DEUS cœlum & terram. Ex eo ortum dicterium Decem verbis mundum à DEO conditum, notante Lud. Dievio.

vers. Eodem. FIAT FIRMAMENTUM) Vox רקיע proprie redditur τάσις, qua voce Plato in Timæo hac ipsa de re utitur. Videtur autem similitudo sumpta a tentorio, quod funibus quibusdam sustinetur ne decidat. Vide Psal. 104, 2. dicitur autem non tantum de cœlo astrifero, sed & de cœlo qui dicitur aer, ut Lucretii verbis utar. Prior signi- catio apparet infra 14. altera infra 21. apud Chaldæum Para- phrasten Psal. 19. Kimchi ad Psal. 77.

Nomen רקיע non male τάσις redditur, ab aliis expansum, quod tum expansum & explicatum fue- rit, non secus atque res convoluta expandi atque explicari solet: quod non ex Psalmo tantum 104. vers. 2. sed etiam aliis locis colligitur Esai. 40, 22. cap. 42, 1. cap. 44, 24. cap. 51, 19. Jerem. 50, 15. Job. 26, 7. Et videtur hic indicari Cœlum antea ve- luti convolutum in illa massa primigenia latuisse, nunc autem verbo illo omnipotenti, FIAT רקיע EXPANSUM, id evolutum & expansum fuisse, in hanc, qua etiam nunc conspicitur, formam, quod in consummatione seculi vicissim non tantum li- bri instar convolvetur & complicabitur Esa. 34, 4. sed etiam sicut fumus deficiet, dissipabitur & consu- metur Esa. 51, 6. adeoque plane interiturum est Luc. 21, 33. Quo de Justinus in qq. & resp. ad orth. qv. XCIV. Quemadmodum firmamenti fa- cturam S. literæ per collationem assimularunt quan- doque pellis extensioni, aliquando fumo fumanti, ali- quando rotunditati testudinis cameratæ; Sic & ejus solutionem per comparationem assimularunt aliquan- do libro, qui convolvitur, quandoque elemento, quod igne solvitur, nonnunquam vestimento veterascenti. Modum ita explicat B. Lutherus: Hoc nunc se- cundi diei opus est, quomodo ex ista rudi nebula, quam Cœlum appellavit, produxerit Cœlum formo- sum & elegans. Istam rudem massam nebulæ pri- mo die ex nihilo conditæ apprehendit DEUS per verbum & jubet, ut extendatur in modum Sphæ- rarum, sicut vesica Sais circulari forma extenditur, cum inflatur. Utar enim rustica similitudine, ut res flat clarior: Sicut castrum (ita explicat postea e Psalm. 104.) complicatum explicatur & figitur in agro, ita tu expandis & quasi evolvis verbo tuo rude Cœlum.

Cæterum LXX. reddiderunt ςερέωμα, quos sequuti Vulgatus Firmamentum, & B. Lutherus Veste exposuit: qua voce etsi emphasis Ebrææ non adeo exprimi videatur, Cœlum tamen non male describitur, si ea intelligatur non ratione materiæ duræ vel firmæ, sed ratione formæ & finis, ut ob perfectionem, distinctionem & firmita- tem sive perpetuitatem ita dictum Cœlum cen- seatur; ut hic frustra Sixtinus Amama & alii B. Lutheri versionem exagitent. Quid? quod Nicol. Fuller. l. I. Miscell. c. VI. vocis רקיע significa- tum præcipuum e Syriaco רקע πιέζειν premere; comprimere, constipare, compingere, τὸ πεπιεσμέ- νον aut maxime proprie τὸ πεπιλημένον & τὸ πί- λημα, quod pressum est undique, & in se collectum vel confertum aut impactum, atque idcirco firmum & solidum, eximie explicet, quomodo vox ea terræ quidem etiam conveniat, vel globo terre- no, quem רָקַע DEUS Psalm. 135,56. Esai. 42, 5. cap. 44, 24. quum παχυμερῆ seu crassa omnia & crassiuncula πεπιεσμένα καὶ τὰ πιλήματα compres- sa, coacta & constipata conglobaret : præcipua ta- men ratione globus ille superus & cælestis hoc no- men רָקִיעַ ubique in S. Literis sibi vendicet: quia cælestis רָקִיעַ est universitas τῶν λεπ]ομερῶν, videl. eorum, quæ sunt tenuis subtilisque naturæ in regionem supernam conglobata & firmata, quæ DEUS prin- cipio rerum conditarum רָקַע hoc est, compressa, coa- cta & constipata per se in locum suum conglobavit, adeoque ἐστερέωσε firmavit. Quia globus ille est magnitudinis plane admirandæ ac prope immen- sæ, adeo ut collatus cum eo inferus hic & ter- restris omni magnitudine amissa in punctum re- dactus velut evanescat. Sed dignus est Fülle- rus, qui de his plenius legatur. Hottinger. in Histor. creat. pag. 20. Schindlemum laudat, quod τὸ רָקַע fit rem contractam in latitudinem exten- dit, ut metalla in laminas extenduntur, vel ut auri bractea extenuando deducitur, conferens Ex. 39, 9. Esa. 40, 19. Jer. 10, 9.

Per רָקִיעַ autem intelligit Grotius tum cælum stelliferum, tum etiam aerem : imo si conferan- tur, quæ lib. I. de Verit. Rel. Christ. habet, com- plectitur etiam hac voce DEI sedem, ubi enim XVI. gentilium sententias cum Mofis historia conferens, supra astrorum loca divinum esse domi- cilium Aratum & Catullum agnoscere ait. Quæ explicatio imaginationi Episcopii de trium Cælo- rum concameratione, qua primum Cælum aër di- citur, cælum alterum fornix cæruleus stellarum receptaculum, tertium palatium DEI & Angelo- rum, quæ etiam Calvinianorum quorundam, Pi- scatoris, qui cum hoc cælo angelos creatos putat, & aliorum est ἔκθεσις, sed ab Episcopio absurdita- tibus novis aucta, cum aerem Planetarum æque ac meteororum receptaculum, & cælum stellatum aquam, ac ftellas in eo aqueas fecit, idque velut si- parium & aulæum palatii divini constituit cæli- tumque : unum ex aquis inferioribus, cætera e supe- rioribus producta fingit, quæ commenta recitasse est refutasse.

Sed quomodo Cælum beatorum intelligi per רָקִיעַ potest, quum usus hujus sit discriminare aquas inferiores a superioribus ? num id fiet per cælum beatorum ? aut quomodo tam diversæ significa- tiones in voce una רָקִיעַ simul locum habere pos- sunt? ut taceam, ostensum nondum esse, רָקִיעַ uspiam de Cælo beatorum accipi. Id vero quod hæc explicatio præsupponit, tanquam certum, de domicilio divino supra Cælum stelliferum τοπι- κῶς seu loei ac situs ratione constituto, genti- lium quidem commentis, non vero Mofaicis, aliisque divinis Scripturis consentaneum esse ju- dicamus; & quum Cælum illud locale domici- lium beatorum, Angelorum aut ipsius etiam DEI, quod Papistæ & Calviniani sibi fingunt, eliminatum jam censeamus Tom. III. Syst. Theol. de creat. c. II. non est, quod hic laboremus.

Quanquam vero probabilior illorum sit sen- tentia, qui per רָקִיעַ aerem intelligunt, utpote e Judæis Aben-Ezræ, nec non e Papistis Ruper- to, Cajetano, Pererio, Valentiano, Petavio, e Reformatis Calvino, Borrhai, Zanchio, Mar- tyri, Junio, Mercero, Danæo, Bucano, Go- maro, Voetio, Grossio, Willeto, Autoribus an- not. ad Bibl. Angl. & Belgic. denique e nostris etiam Dn. D. Joh. Musæo probata : calculum tamen ei adjicere vetamur, siquidem vers. 14.

notanter dicatur in illo Cælo, quod He Haje-diab demonstrat (quod nempe hic designatur) sidera collocata fuisse, quæ utique non in aëre collocata sunt. Alii ergo Cælum æthereum simul cum aëre vocem illam complecti credunt, utpote Cornelius a Lapid. Tossanus, Pareus, Keckermannus, ut & Schindlerinus, Hottingerus, ac B. Jacob. Martini Coll. II. contr. Becan. Disp. VII. thes. 10. Sed præferenda videtur Patrum plerorumque & B. Lutheri sententia, quod solum æthereum Cælum hic designetur voce illa: quia in Historia creationis & cælum ipsum & aërem una eademque voce simul designari non satis conveniens, & vers. 14. dicitur: Fiant Luminaria in EXPANSO ILLORUM COELORUM. Unde vers. 20. etiam Cælum æthereum intelligunt: sed eum ita exponunt על־פני רקיע e regione vel ex adverso expansi, uti Helvicus in Vindic. p. 57. vel coram expanso, & ante conspectum expansi cæli, vel sub cælo, uti alii interpretantur. P. Fagius, præpositio על inquit, pro juxta, prope non raro etiam accipitur: Estque sensus, sub Cælo in aëre, vel juxta, id est proxime Cælum. Facies enim Cæli dicitur, quæ se ad nos vertit, nobisque conspicua est. Hic ergo non aërem, sed solum æthereum Cælum intelligunt voce רקיע tum quod hæc vox nuspiam de aëre vel solo, vel incluso aëre accipiatur; tum quod aër secundo die nondum fuerit, sed emerserit demum, quum aquæ ab arida secretæ sunt tertio die. Ubi enim crassa aquarum congeries condensata inque unum locum congregata & ab arida discreta fuit, ibi simul & aër emersit, nempe purior, perfectus & plenus ille, ad quem sese primi diei aër habuit, perinde ut lux se habuit primigenia ad astrorum splendorem, id est, crassiuscule & imperfectiuscule, ut e B. Gesnero Disp. I. in Gen. quæst. XVIII. Dn. D. Waltherus explicat Spong: Mosaic. ad Gen. I, 6. 7. 8. pag. 61. qui de his fusius agit & pro hac quod cælum æthereum hic designetur, sententia, laudat Tertullianum, Cæsarium, Cyrill. Hieros. Theodoretum, Acacium, Severianum, Gennadium, Chrysostomum, Olympio-dorum, Anastasium, Augustinum, Hieronymum, Bedam, Procopium, allegatos a Saliano in Annal. Eccles. Tom. II. fol. 28. ut & Polanum e Reformatis lib. V. Syntagm. c. IX.

vers. eod. AQUAS AB AQUIS) Plinius libro XXXI. Quid esse mirabilius potest aquis in cælo stantibus?

## 1:7
verse 7. ABOVE THE FIRMAMENT) Which he called above the Heavens, Psalm CXLVIII, 4. Hence the cataracts of heaven, below VII, 12.

Not of the clouds, whence waters, rains, and showers descend; but this discourse is about the waters established above the celestial expanse. For clouds are not properly waters, nor were they placed above the CELESTIAL EXPANSE, which is said to have been founded here. Therefore we have here the supracelestial waters asserted ῥητῶς (expressly), which Pliny and universal nature are ignorant of, but which Scripture reveals here. However much, therefore, the Calvinists may attack them, following the lead of some Jews, but more recent ones, R. Dav. Kimchi and others, one must adhere to the ῥητῷ (literal) sense of the θεοπνεύστῳ (God-breathed) words of Moses, who places these waters מעל לרקיע ABOVE THE FIRMAMENT, as the Vulgate rendered it; which sense of the word מעל occurs in Gen. 22, 9, and is necessary here by the force of the opposite מתחת (below). Clouds are nowhere called waters in the Scriptures, so far is it from being the case that they were so called in this description and history of the primordial creation, where Moses loved to speak properly; nor can one gather from Gen. 2, 5 that they were within the Hexaemeron may it be permitted. To say nothing of the fact that it does not appear how a division is made through the air between the waters of the clouds and the lower waters. And there is added the testimony of David celebrating the waters above the firmament, Psalm 104:2, Psalm 148:4, as also Job ch. 38:8, 9, 10, 11, where the subject is distinctly the supercelestial and lower waters, as we shall see in that place: as well as the three children, Dan. 3:60, which, although it is ἀπόκρυφον, can nevertheless testify to the faith of the ancient Jews. Which is also confirmed by the suffrage of Philo, Josephus, R. Onkelos, and other ancients; and among the ancient Christians, Justin, Basil, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Procopius the Greeks, as well as the Latins Ambrose, Augustine, Bede, and others, it was undoubted, so much so that Augustine professes that the authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of our intellect. Conf. our System, l. c. Qv. II. p. 1032, where he also scatters the structure of the Papists who fabricate a Crystalline Heaven from those waters, and at the same time the crystalline [heavens] of Baranzanus that refresh the sight of the blessed. We have, concerning the supercelestial waters, our own people agreeing after the blessed Luther, almost all of them, as well as from the Papists Oleaster, Lipmannus, Molina, Cornel. a Lapide, Becanus, Salianus, Menochius, Tirinus, Bonfrerius, and from the Calvinists Georg Sohnius Tom. I. oper. p. 114, and Joh. Scarpius. P. Fagius notes that the Hebrews gather from the words in the midst of the waters that the distance of the supercelestial waters from the firmament is as great as that of the terrestrial waters to the firmament, and they consider it a great miracle that they are thus suspended by divine power.

Hottinger, in a lengthy discussion instituted concerning these waters, finally teaches against Calvin that clouds are not to be understood by them, and he praises Danaeus, who asserts that it is absolutely necessary (lest the command of GOD be vain) that some waters exist above this expansion, and that they be perpetual, consisting and remaining always in that place, just as they are below it. See Histor. creat. p. 85. Polus, according to his custom, brings forward arguments on both sides, but defines nothing. Piscator's argument, that clouds are also called waters, Ps. 104:3, when Moses acknowledges only two kinds of waters, begs the question (τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ): because nothing prevents the supercelestial waters from being understood in the passage of the Psalm, and it has not been proven that clouds are designated.

Latin:

vers. 7. SUPER FIRMAMENTUM) Quod supra Cælos dixit, Psalm. CXLVIII, 4. Hinc cataractæ cæli, infra VII, 12.

Non de nubibus, unde aquæ, pluviæ & imbres descendunt; sed de aquis supra cœleste expansum constitutis hic sermo est. Nam nubes proprie non sunt aquæ, nec illæ supra EXPAN-SUM COELESTE, quod hic conditum dicitur, positæ sunt. Ideo habemus hic ῥητῶς assertas aquas supracælestes, quas Plinius & universa natura ignorat, sed Scriptura hic detegit. Quomodocunque ergo illas impugnent Calviniani, præeuntibus Judæis nonnullis, sed recentioribus, R. Dav. Kimchio & aliis, inhærendum est τῷ ῥητῷ verborum Mosis θεοπνεύστῳ, qui מעל לרקיע SUPRA FIRMAMENTUM ponit has aquas, ut reddidit Vulgatus; qui sensus vocis מעל Gen. 22, 9. occurrit, & vi oppositi מתחת infra hic necessarius est. Nubes nuspiam in Scripturis aquæ vocantur, tantum abest ut hac in descriptione & historia primævæ creationis, ubi proprie loqui amavit Moses, ita vocatæ sint; neque intra Hexaëmeron eas fuisse e Gen. 2, 5. colligere liceat. Ut taceam, quod non appareat, quomodo per aerem inter aquas nubium & aquas inferiores divisio fiat. Et accedit Davidis testimonium aquas supra firmamentum celebrantis Psalm. 104, 2. Psalm. 148, 4. ut & Jobi cap. 38, 8. 9. 10. 11. ubi distincte de aquis supraccœlestibus, & inferioribus agitur, ut illo loco visuri sumus: nec non trium puerorum Dan. 3, 60. quod etsi ἀπόκρυφον, de fide tamen Veterum Judæorum testari potest. Quæ etiam Philonis, Josephi, R. Onkelos & aliorum veterum suffragio comprobatur: ac penes Christianos antiquos, Justīnum, Basilium, Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Procopium Græcos, tum Latinos quoque Ambrosium, Augustinum, Bedam aliosque indubia fuit, adeo ut Augustinus profiteatur, majorem esse Scripturæ hujus autoritatem, quam ingenii nostri capacitatem. Conf. System. nostri l. c. Qv. II. p. 1032. ubi etiam Papistarum Cœlum Crystallinum ex aquis illis fabricantium structura disjecta, simulque Baranzani crystallinæ beatorum visum recreantes dissipatæ. Habemus de aquis supraccœlestibus consentientes nostrates post B. Lutherum plerosque omnes, tum e Pontificiis Oleastrum, Lipmannum, Molinam, Cornel. a Lapide, Becanum, Salianum, Menoch. Tirinum, Bonfrerium, & e Calvinianis Georg. Soh nium Tom. I. oper. p. 114. & Joh. Scarpium. P. Fagius notat Ebræos e verbis in medio aquarum colligere tantam esse distantiam aquarum supraccœlestium a firmamento, quanta est terrestrium aquarum ad firmamentum, idque pro magno miraculo ducere, quod ita divina virtute pendulæ sint.

Hottingerus prolixa instituta de his aquis disputatione tandem contra Calvinum docet, per eas non intelligi nubes, & Danæum laudat afferentem, omnino oportere, (ne vanum sit DEI præceptum) ut supra hanc expansionem existant aliquæ aquæ, eæque perpetuæ, in eo loco consistentes, & permanentes semper, quemadmodum sunt infra eum. Vid. Histor. creat. p. 85. Polus pro more suo argumenta in utramque partem adducit, nihil autem definit, Piscatoris argumentum, quod nubes etiam aquæ dicuntur, Pf. 104, 3. quum Moses duplices tantum agnoscat aquas, τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ petit: quia in loco Psalmi aquas supraccœlestes intelligi nil vetat, nubes designari probatum non est.

## 1:9
verf. 9. AND GOD SAID) The Hebrews explain: When God had said, as an ἐπάνοδος. For they think this was done on the second day. To the Hebrews, the same past tense has the meaning now of the perfect, now of the imperfect, now of the pluperfect. Thus shortly 2:2, he finished, that is, he had finished.

These refer, with Mercerus and Cocceius not denying it, to Job 38:3, and Petavius l. de opif. c. XXII, the gathering of the waters under the heaven and the production of the earth to the second day, lest, forsooth, that clause be lacking which was added to the others: And GOD saw that it was good. But it is not likely that Moses, after he had already subjected that formula, And there was evening and morning the second day, verf. 8, to the construction of the firmament, would have still wished to refer some ὕστερον belonging to the second day: not to mention the distinctive mark פ by which the preceding verses are accustomed to be distinguished from the following ones. Conf. Hottinger. l. c. p. 89.

But why he did not add that encomiastic clause to the second day (concerning which some inquire laboriously) is no reason for us to be troubled, since a general eulogy was added looking to all the works of the Six Days, by which the works of the second day were certainly also celebrated, because they were very good in the judgment of GOD the Creator himself. This cause, however, seems to be the reason, namely, that the discourse concerning the ordering of the separated waters might be continued, and that the whole work of the separation of the waters—the upper ones by the firmament, the lower ones by the collection of the waters and the uncovering of the earth—might be adorned with the same eulogy, even though it was done on two distinct days. Which reason R. Solomon rendered. Thus, there is no need to impute a transposition here to the carelessness of the Scribes, nor to suspect a corruption of the text. And it thus becomes plain why that eulogy is repeated twice on the third day: because, namely, the first pertains to the separation of the waters, clearly perfected only on the third day: but the second to the procreation of plants. However, it is by no means fitting, as with Aben-Ezra and Grotius, that those words וַיֹּאמֶר should be rendered here otherwise than throughout the whole chapter, namely, in the pluperfect: since it is too manifest that they are always repeated by Moses in the same sense. Moses therefore begins here the works of the third day, which are both the gathering of the waters into one place and the uncovering of the earth, and the procreation of plants. Concerning these and the remaining works of the Hexaemeron, let our Systema Theol. T. III. p. 947 seqq. be consulted. And we see by the example of Petrus Picherellus, whose paraphrase on the Cosmopoeia described by Moses, along with certain others, Thomas Gadakerus praises in Cinnus Lib. II. c. 1. p. 137, how far that itch for pouring words into a new meaning goes, who likewise wishes that what is narrated as done in verses 9 and 10 was accomplished within the second day, and not the third. And so he paraphrases the ninth verse thus: But yet after GOD had said, let the waters which were under the expanse gather themselves into one place, and let the dry land appear, and so it had come to pass: and GOD had called that dry land earth, and the gathering of the waters the sea. He had foreseen that it would be good. For Picherellus, having used this license, also pulls back the production of terrestrial living creatures, torn from the sixth day, to the fifth day: rendering the words of Moses in verse 24 with this paraphrase: but after yet also GOD had said, let the earth produce living creatures according to their species, namely, cattle, creeping things, and wild beasts, and so it had come to pass. For GOD had made the wild beasts according to their species, the cattle according to their species, and all things creeping upon the earth according to their species also, when he had foreseen that this too would be good. He brings forward two reasons for this new opinion of his: first, that since GOD created from the earth on one and the same day, namely the third, herbs and trees endowed with a vegetative soul, it is fitting that he should also have made from the earth on one and the same day, namely the fifth, birds and all terrestrial living creatures endowed with a sentient soul. Then that Adam, a creature so noble, and with him Eve, were worthy; that for them and for the things that concerned them, a day of their own should be given for their creation: so that just as there was one day for those which had a vegetative soul, and likewise one for those which had a sensitive soul: so, because it was more important, a day should likewise be devoted to those which had a rational soul. But if the series of creation is to be assigned according to human ingenuity, what finally will be held as certain? For there are as many opinions as there are heads. If it is permitted to interpret the same word אָמַר, repeated frequently by Moses in this chapter without any indication of diversity, in different ways, now in the pluperfect, then in the perfect, it would not be difficult, by a similar artifice, to tear apart the remaining works of the hexaemeron as well, and to confuse the θεσεγνήματα of different days, so that you could not certainly define what was created on which day, even though Moses set everything forth in a simple, plain, and clear style and order. The word יִקָּו Aquil. and Symm. translate συςήτω, let it be established; it properly means to strive with a straight course and impetus, because קָו is a plumb line, a straight line, whence Fuller, lib. III. Miscell. c. 4, observes that the force of straight motion, as being the shortest, was here imparted to the elements, especially to the water. But how this could have happened, since the waters covered the whole earth, Poole explains thus from Cornelius and Bonfrère: 1. That the water, previously sweet, having now become saltier and thicker, occupies less space; 2. that there is a huge abyss and chasm of waters in the bowels of the earth. 3. That GOD on this day made the earth rise into mountains, and subside into valleys, and huge channels. But he omits the principal reason. Namely, that a great part of the water collected is preserved above the firmament of heaven. Which we have executed in Syst. Theol. T. III.

Latin:

verf. 9. DIXIT VERO DEUS) Hebræi exponunt: Cum dixisset Deus, ut sit ἐπάνοδος. Putant enim hoc factum die secundo. Hebræis idem præteritum modo perfecti, modo imperfecti, modo plusquamperfecti habet significationem. Sic mox 2, 2. complevit, id est, compleverat.

Referunt hi, non abnuente Mercero, Coccejo ad Job. 38, 3. & Petavio l. de opif. c. XXII. congregationem aquarum sub cœlo & productionem terræ ad secundum diem, ne sc. illa destituatur clausula, quæ cæteris adjecta: Et vidit DEUS, quod esset bonum. Sed non est verisimile Mosen postquam illam formulam, Et factum est vesperi & mane dies secundus verf. 8. jam subjecerat firmamenti fabricæ, adhuc referre voluisse ὕστερον aliquod ad secundum diem pertinens: ut taceamus notam distinctivam פ qua superiores versiculi ab inferioribus discriminari solent. Conf. Hottinger. l. c. p. 89.

Cur vero non adjecerit ad secundum diem illam clausulam encomiasticam, (quo de operose nonnulli disquirunt) non est, quod angamur, quum generale elogium additum sit ad omnia opera Sextidui spectans, quo celebrata utique etiam opera sunt diei secundæ, quod fuerint ea valde bona ipsiusmet DEI conditoris judicio. Causa tamen hæc videtur, ut nempe continuaretur oratio de separatarum aquarum ordinatione, totumque illud separa- tum tionis aquarum opus fuperiorum per firmamentum, inferiorum per collectionem aquarum & reţectionem terræ eodem elogio, etsi duobus distinctis diebus factum, exornaretur. Quam rationem reddidit R. Salomo. Ita neque trajectionem incuriæ Scribarum hic impingere opus est, neq; corruptionem textus suspicari. Et planum ita evadit, cur tertio die elogium illud bis repetatur: quia scil. primum pertinet ad aquarum separationem, plane tertio die demum perfectam: alterum vero ad plantarum procreationem. Nequaquam autem convenit, ut cum Aben-Ezra & Grotio verba illa וַיֹּאמֶר hic aliter, quam per totum caput, nimirum in plusquamperfecto, reddantur: quum eodem sensu semper ea repeti a Mose nimis manifestum sit. Orditur ergo hic Moses tertiæ diei opera, quæ sunt tum aquarum in unum locum congregatio, terræq; detectio, tum plantarum procreatio. De quibus & reliquis operibus Hexaëmeri videatur Systema nostrum Theol. T. III. p. 947. seqq. Et videmus exemplo Petri Picherelli, cujus paraphrasin in Cosmopoïam a Mose descriptam cum aliis quibusdam, mirum quantum laudat Thomas Gadakerus in Cinño Lib. II. c. 1. p. 137. quo abeat istud verborum in novam significationem transfundendorum Cacoëthes, qui itidem intra diem secundum, non autem tertio peractum vult, quod versu 9. ac 10. factum narratur. Itaque versum nonum ita παραφράζει: Sed tamen postquam DEUS dixisset, in unum congregarent se locum, quæ sub extento erant aquæ, & siccum appareret, sicque extitisset: & siccum illud appellasset DEUS terram, aquarum vero congregationem mare. Præviderat autem illud fore bonum. Usus enim hac licentia Picherellus, animantium etiam terrestrium productionem ad diem quintum a sexto revulsam retrahit: Mosis verba versu 24. hac paraphrasi reddens: sed postquam tamen etiam dixisset DEUS, terra animantia juxta eorum species produceret, nimirum jumenta, reptilia & feras, sicq; extitisset. Feras enim secundum species suas, jumenta juxta suas species, & omnia super terram reptantia juxta etiam suas species fecerat DEUS, cum hoc quoque bonum fore prævidisset. Cujus suæ novæ opinionis rationes duas profert, primo quod cum uno eodemque, tertio nempe die, herbas & arbores quasque vegetativa præditas anima DEUS e terra creaverit, par sit, ut anima prædita sentiente volatilia & animantia terrestria quæque uno eodemque die, quinto nimirum, ex terra quoque fecerit. Deinde Adamum plasma tam nobile, & cum ea Evam dignos fuisse; quibus & eis quæ eos contingebant, creandi suus daretur seorsim dies: ut sicut quibus vegetans erat anima, unus; quibus anima sentiens, item unus: sic quia potius, quibus anima rationalis suus itidem impenderetur dies. Sed si ex ingenio humano assignanda creationis series, quid denique certi habebitur? Quot enim capita, tot sensus. Si verbum idem אָמַר crebro a Mose sine diversitatis indicio in hoc capite repetitum, diversimode exponere licitum, modo in plusquamperfecto, unde in perfecto, haud difficile fuerit, parili artificio reliqua etiam opera hexaëmeri divellere, ac θεσεγνήματα diversorum dierum confundere, ut quid tandem, quo die conditum sit, certo definire haud possis, utut Moses simplici, plano & perspicuo stylo, & ordine, omnia exposuerit. Verbum יִקָּו Aquil. & Symm. vertunt συςήτω constituatur, proprie est recto cursu impetuque contendant, quia קָו est perpendiculum, linea recta, unde hic vim recti motus, utpote brevissimi, elementis, aquæ imprimis inditam observat Fuller. lib. III. Miscell. c. 4. Quomodo autem hoc fieri potuerit, quia aquæ totam ter- ram tegebant, Polus ex Cornel. & Bonfrer. ita ex- plicat: 1. Quod aqua antea dulcis, salfior jam facta & crassior minorem locum occupet; 2. quod ingens abyssus & vorago aquarum in visceribus terræ sit. 3. Quod DEUS hoc die terram as- surgere fecerit in montes, & subsidere in valles, & ingentes alveos. Sed præcipuam rationem omittit. Quod nempe aqua magnam partem col- lecta supra firmamentum cœli asservetur. Quod in Syst. Theol. T. III. exequuti sumus.

## 1:10
ver. 10. AND GOD CALLED THE DRY LAND. Thus the earth is called dry Jon. 1, 9. c. 2, 10. ξυρὰ Matth. 23, 15.

ver. Same. AND THE GATHERINGS OF THE WATERS HE CALLED SEAS. The Chaldean translates it house of the gathering of waters. Fagius prefers to render it channel. Malvenda less conveniently interprets it as expectations of waters. They are called SEAS, because not one sea surrounds the earth.

Latin:

vers. 10. VOCAVITQUE DEUS ARIDAM TERRAM. Sic terra vocatur arida Jon. 1, 9. c. 2, 10. ξυρὰ Matth. 23, 15.

vers. Eod. CONGREGATIONESQUE AQUARUM APPELLAVIT MARIA. Chald. vertit domum congregationis aquarum. Fagius mavult alveum reddere. Malvenda mi- nus commode exspectationes aquarum interpreta- tur. MARIA dicuntur, quod non unum mare terram ambit.

## 1:12
ver. 12. GREEN HERB) In Hebrew it is דשׁא עשׂב of which the former signifies tender herb, the latter more robust.

So also Kimchi and Mersennus. Mercerus, however, and Abarbenel wish the former word to indicate all things born spontaneously from the earth, and the latter herb, and sown sprouts, such as wheat and barley. Hottinger more conveniently judges that דשׁא denotes generally any things born of the earth, of which the species are עשׂב herb, or plant, and עץ tree, and shrub, just as the Syrian and Arab also accepted it.

Augustine, lib. V. de Gen. ad liter. c. 4. & 5., seems to establish that the earth produced these by power alone, but most Hebrews and Ambrose more rightly feel that they were actually brought forth immediately: because the remaining creatures were also actually produced within the Hexaemeron, and not merely by power, to which, however, through the blessing, a plastic force and the faculty of propagating their species was simultaneously implanted.

Moreover, by the word 'let it sprout' no activity of the earth arising in the primordial creation is ascribed to it: because it behaved only passively then; and therefore the opinion of Digb. in App. Theol. de Orig. mundi cap. 20 is to be disapproved, that the generation of plants proceeded from the very active fecundity of the earth with such heat acting, and by the extraordinary and miraculous concurrence of GOD. For this would not have been creation, but generation. By the word of GOD they were produced, as were the remaining creatures, so also the herbs: not by the active fecundity of the earth.

ver. same. YIELDING SEED) מזריע seeding, as Pliny speaks. All species of herbs and trees were certainly founded in the beginning, but because all things were created very good, poison and malice are rightly deduced not from the first creation, but from sin. Concerning these and others, see what we have said in System. Theol. Tom. III. on the works of the Hexaemeron and in the Commentary on Genesis. We do not wish to do what is already done.

Latin:

vers. 12. HERBAM VIRENTEM) In Hebræo est דשׁא עשׂב quorum hoc tenellam herbam, illud robu- stiorem significat.

Ita & Kimchius & Mersennus. Mercerus tamen & Abarbenel priori voce omnia sponte ter- ra nascentia, posteriori herbam indicari vult, & germina sativa, ut sunt tritici, hordei. Hottin- gerus commodius דשׁא generaliter quælibet terræ nascentia notare censet, cujus species sunt עשׂב herba, sive planta, & עץ arbor, ac frutex, quemadmodum etiam Syrus & Arabs accepere.

Produxisse autem terram hæc potentia solum Au- gustin. lib. V. de Gen. ad liter. c. 4. & 5. statuere vi- detur, actu vero statim ea prolata fuisse Ebræi ple- rique & Ambrosius rectius sentiunt: quia & reliquæ creaturæ actu productæ sunt intra Hexaëmeron, non vero tantum potentiâ, quibus tamen per be- nedictionem vis πλασικὴ & facultas speciem pro- pagandi simul indita.

Cœterum verbo germinet non adscribitur terræ activitas aliqua in primæva creatione exor- ta: quia se passive solum tum habuit; adeoque improbanda Digb. in App. Theol. de Orig. mundi cap. 20. sententia, plantarum generationem ex ipsa activa fœcunditate terræ tanto calore agente, atque extraordinario, & miraculoso concursu DEI pro- fectam esse. Hæc enim non fuisset creatio, sed generatio. Verbo DEI productæ sunt ut crea- turæ reliquæ, ita & herbæ: non activa terræ fœ- cunditate.

vers. eod. FACIENTEM SEMEN) מזריע sementan- tem, ut Plinius loquitur. Omnes sane species herbarum & arborum initio conditæ, sed quia omnia valde bona creata, venenum & malitia non prima crea- tione, sed a peccato merito deducitur. De his, & aliis vid. quæ in System. Theol. Tom. III. de ope- rib. Hexaem. & in Commentar. in Genes. diximus. Nolumus actum agere.

## 1:14
ver. 14. AND GOD SAID, LET THERE BE LIGHTS. Because the lights were created by the word and nod of GOD, they cannot be worshipped as Gods and divinities:

and therefore Astrolatry is here immediately overthrown by Moses, such as was that of the Egyptians, who worshipped the Sun under the name of Moloch, of the Persians, who under that of Adad, of the Phoenicians, who worshipped the Moon under the word Astarte, and of other gentiles: Wisdom 13:3. See Hottinger's Idolographia of the Old Testament in his Primitiæ

Heidelberg, and Vossius on idolatry, and Selden on the Gods of the Syrians. In the Hebrew, "let there be lights" is an idiom familiar to Orientals, yet a distribution is not to be denied: that is to say, let there be each of the lights. But why the lights were created on the fourth day, Augustine and Thomas explain thus: namely, that just as mention was made of the three from the beginning, heaven, water, and earth, so first the heaven was distinguished, then the waters, thirdly the dry land: and in that order they were further adorned, the heaven first with stars on the fourth day, then the waters with birds and fish, and finally the earth with living creatures.

verse same. LET THEM BE FOR SIGNS) Homer: "He fashioned the earth, and the heaven, and the sea. And all the constellations with which the heaven is crowned." Aratus on God: "He himself fixed those signs in the heaven." Although signs may be demonstrative, as Hottinger calls them, of the creatures of GOD, yet that is not looked at here as common to all visible creatures (Rom. 1:19), but that the signs are prognostic of natural events, especially of storms (Matt. 16:2). However, the magic of the Chaldeans, regarding special prognosis, as also that of the Egyptians, whom the history of Joseph shows to have been dream-interpreters, has no foundation here, and is prohibited by divine law (Deut. 18:10, 14; Isa. 8:8).

AND SEASONS) Proclus calls the stars the instruments of time in Theology VI.

Time is not understood simply, because there is peculiar mention of years and days, nor are festivals, for these depend not on a natural cause, but on the will of GOD, and therefore neither the explanation of Heinrich Wolf, book I, on time, chapter 6, who presents the seasons as sacred testimonies and pledges of divine promises, nor that of Hottinger, who wishes both sacred and profane, and this both civil and natural, to be understood, has a place here: but the four seasons of the year are looked at, which the Sun brings about by its motion.

Latin:

vers. 14. DIXIT AUTEM DEUS, FIANT LUMINARIA. Quia verbo & nutu DEI creata luminaria sunt, pro Diis & numinibus coli non possunt:

ideoque Astrolatria hic statim a Mose profliga- tur, qualis fuit Ægyptiorum, qui Solem sub Molochi nomine, Persarum, qui sub Adadi, Phœnicum, qui Lunam sub Astarte voce colue- runt, & aliorum gentilium: Sapient. 13, 3. Vid. Idolographiam Vet. Test. Hottingeri in primitiis

Heidelb. & Vossium de idololatr. ac Selden. de Diis Syror. In Ebræo sit luminaria idiotismus est Orientalibus familiaris, non tamen negan- da distributio: q. d. sit unumquodque luminarium. Cur autem quarto die luminaria condita sint, Au- gustin. & Thomas ita exponunt: quod nempe uti trium mentio facta ab initio cæli, aquæ &, ter- ræ, ita primum cælum distinctum fuerit, deinde aquæ, tertio arida: & eo ordine porro exornata illa, primum cælum stellis quarto die, deinde avi- bus & piscibus aquas, tertium denique animantibus terram.

vers. eod. SINT IN SIGNA) Homerus: Ἐν μὲν γαῖαν ἔτευξ᾽, ἐν δ᾽ ὠρανὸν, ἐν δὲ θάλασσαν. Ἐν δὲ τὰ τείρεα πάντα τάτ᾽ ὠρανὸς ἐςεφάνωται. Aratus de Deo: Αὐτὸς γὰρ τάγε σήματ᾽ ἐν ὠρανῶ ἐςήριξε. Etsi signa sint ἀποδεικτικα, ut Hottinger. vo- cat, creaturis DEI, id tamen ceu commune omni- bus creaturis visibilibus Rom. 1, 19. hic non re- spicitur, sed quod signa sint προγνωςικὰ even- tuum naturalium, imprimis tempestatum Matth. 16, 2. Magia tamen Chaldæorum, quoad πρόγνωσιν specialem, ut & Ægyptiorum quos Onirocriticos fuisse Historia Josephi docet, hic fundamentum non habet, & lege divina prohibita est Deut. 18, 10. 14. Esa. 8, 8.

ET TEMPORA) Sidera ὄργανα τῶ χρόνε vocat Proclus Theologiæ VI.

Non tempus simpliciter intelligitur, quia an- norum & dierum peculiariter sit mentio, nec fe- stivitates, hæ enim non a causa naturali, sed ar- bitrio DEI dependent, ideoque nec Henric. Wol- fii lib. I, de temp. cap. 6. explicatio, qui tempora Sacra testimonia & sponsiones exhibentia divinarum promissionum, nec Hottingeri, qui tam sacrorum, quam prophanorum, & hoc tam civile quam naturale intelligi vult, hic locum habet: sed qua- tuor anni tempora respiciuntur, quæ Sol motu suo efficit.

## 1:17
verse 17. TWO GREAT LIGHTS.

But the Moon and the Sun are called great lights from their use and office, both because they shine most upon us, and preside over day and night, and because they are of the greatest virtue and efficacy upon these sublunary things. Moses refutes the fiction of the Jews, that the Sun and Moon had the same splendor in the beginning, when he says that the Moon was created at the very beginning as a lesser light. The gloss of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff, on the chapter "Solitae" concerning Major and Obedience: GOD made two great lights, that is, he instituted two dignities, which are the Pontifical authority and the Royal power. But that which presides over days, that is, spiritual things, is greater, but that which presides over carnal things is lesser, so that as great as is the difference between the Sun and the Moon, so great may be known to be the difference between Pontiffs and Kings; this can be an argument of how the Pontiffs handle Holy Scripture: it is utterly sacrilegious and profane.

Latin:

vers. 17. DUO LUMINARIA MAGNA.

Luna autem cum Sole luminaria magna di- cuntur ab usu & officio, tum quia nobis maxime lucent, & diei ac nocti præsunt, tum quia ma- ximæ sunt virtutis & efficaciæ in hæc sublunaria. Commentum Judæorum, quod Sol & Luna ini- tio eundem splendorem habuerint, redarguit Mo- ses, cum initio statim Lunam ceu luminare minus conditam dicit. Innocentii III. R. P. de Major. & Obedient. C. solitæ glossa, fecit DEUS duo lu- minaria magna, id est, instituit duas dignitates, quæ sunt Pontificalis autoritas, & Regalis potestas. Sed illa quæ præest diebus, id est spiritualibus, major est, quæ vero carnalibus, minor, ut quanta est inter So- lem & Lunam, tanta inter Pontifices & Reges dif- ferentia cognoscatur, argumento esse potest, qua manu Pontifices S. Scripturam tractent: Sacrilega prorsus & prophana.

## 1:18
verse 18. That it might RULE OVER THE DAY) ἥλιον ἄςρον ἡμεροφαὲς Aristot. Top. 6, 3.

The Sun is called the fountain of light, and אור light is indicated in opposition to the Moon, Job 31:26. Nor yet is the Moon to be established as opaque in itself with Anaxagoras, Anaximander, and certain more recent thinkers, because it is also called a luminary here, and has its own light, 1 Corinthians 15:41, and is called κόσμῳ φωτίζον by Sirach, chapter 43:10, and by the Gentiles Urania, named from אור light, and עשתרת Astarte, that is, זהרת ונעש shining: whence Herodian on the Moon: The Africans call this Urania, the Phoenicians Astroarche, he meant to say Astarte. See Fuller, Misc. book I, chapter 13; Hottinger, Hist. creat. p. 102. They are called stars commonly כוכבים, not from כבה, extinguished, as the Jews wish, but from the quadriliteral root כוכב, which is still used by the Arabs, and denotes to twinkle and to shine. Therefore, the name אור is attributed to the Sun alone ἐξοχικῶς, and by the Egyptians Orus or Horus, who is otherwise Apollo.

But that the Sun and Moon might preside over the day and night, they have motion, and that from within, or by a nature implanted in them: not from an external principle, or intelligences, as the Rabbis, Stoics, Platonists, Peripatetics, Scholastics, and some Calvinists fable, nor yet, because they are moved by themselves, do they obtain a soul: which was the opinion of the Sabeans concerning the planets, and of the Arabs in the Mirror of the World in Hottinger, l. c. page 123. Likewise of Plato and Simplicius and Philoponus, and even of Origen, Homily XXIII in Numbers, as also of Abelard and the Priscillianists. For a soul has need of an organic body, such as the body of the planets is not.

Latin:

vers. 18. Ut PRÆESSET DIEI) ἥλιον ἄςρον ἡμεροφαὲς Aristot. Top. 6, 3.

Fons luminis Sol dicitur, & אור lumen indi- gitatur in oppositione ad Lunam Job. 31, 26. Nec tamen Luna per se opaca statuenda cum Anaxa- gora Anaximandro, & recentioribus quibusdam, quia hic luminare etiam dicitur, & lumen suum habet 1. Corinth. 15, 41. ac κόσμῳ φωτίζον Sy- racidi vocatur cap. 43, 10. & gentilibus urania ab אור luce nuncupata, & עשתרת Astarte, id est, זהרת ונעש lucida: unde Herodianus de Lu- na: Hanc Afri Uraniam vocant, Phœnices Astroar- chen, dicere voluit Astarten. Vid. Fuller. Misc. lib. I. cap. 13. Hotting. Hist. creat. p. 102. Dicun- tur tur & stellæ communiter כוכבים non à כבה extinxit, ut Judæi volunt, sed à Radice quadrilitera כוכב, quæ adhuc Arabibus usitata est, & notat micare, ac fulgere. Ideo solum ἐξοχικῶς Soli tribuitur no- men אור & Ægyptiis Orus vel Horus, qui alias Apollo.

Ut autem diei & nocti præesse possent Sol, & Luna, motum habent, idque ab intrinseco, vel natura ipsis indita : non ab extrinseco principio, vel intel- ligentiis, ut Rabbini, Stoici, Platonici, Peripatetici, Scholastici, & Calviniani nonnulli fabulantur, nec tamen ideo, quia per se moventur, animam ob- tinent: quæ Sabeorum de Planetis fuit opinio, & Arabum in speculo Mundi apud Hottinger. l. c. pag. 123. Platonis item, & Simplicii ac Philoponi, imo & Origenis Hier. XXIIIX. in Num. ut & Abailardi, & Priscillianistarum. Anima enim opus habet corpore organico, quale non est Planetarum corpus.

## 1:20
Verse 20. REPTILE.) רמשׂון. Νηυτὸν, says Grotius. Furthermore, שרץ among the Hebrews signifies everything that crawls, in whatever element it may be, and they use the rowing of feet, or wings, or even fins. Therefore, the water also has its שרצים, fishes; the earth has its own, lizards, mice, and other living things, or those without feet, or with small feet; and the air has its own; birds, four-footed or many-footed, as are flies, wasps, beetles, as Hottinger reminds us on page 208, who nevertheless observes that the word for reptiles, even if it is more specific, must be retained because a better one does not occur among the Latins, and that primarily שרץ is said of reptiles on the earth, and secondarily of flying and swimming creatures.

Verse same. AND A FLYING THING UPON THE EARTH. Some here correct the Vulgate: because it ought to have rendered, and let a flying thing fly upon the earth: but it rendered the sense correctly: word for word it would sound thus, and a bird, which may fly upon the earth, as Onkelos and Uziel rendered it: for however the Athnach may intervene, the verb can nevertheless be repeated from the former ἀπὸ κοινῦ, and let them produce a flying thing, which may fly upon the earth. For it is not a question here of the place where birds are found produced, but of the origin from whence they were produced. See what we have said about these in our Commentary. Hottinger, page 212, acknowledges that Jerome, Augustine, Cyril, Damascene, and Rupert favor our opinion.

Latin:

Vers. 20. REPTILE.) רמשׂון. Νηυτὸν, ait Grotius. Cæterum שרץ apud Ebræos omnia, quæ se trahunt, in quocunque versentur elemento, significat, & vel pedum, vel pennarum, vel pinnarum etiam utuntur remigio. Ideo & aqua suos habet שרצים pisces, suos habet terra, la- certos, mures, cæteræque animantia, vel ἄποδα, vel μικρόποδα suas habet & aër; aves τετράποδες sive πολύποδες, ut sunt muscæ, vespæ, scarabæi, mo- nente Hottingero p. 208. qui tamen observat repti- lium vocem etsi specialiorem retinendam esse, quia melior non occurrit apud Latinos, & primario שרץ de reptilibus in terra dici, secundario de vola- tilibus & natalibus.

Vers. eod. ET VOLATILE SUPER TERRAM. Corrigunt hîc nonnulli Vulgatam: quod red- dere debuerit, & volitet volatile super terram: sed qua sensum recte reddidit: verbotenus ita sonaret, & volucrem, quæ volitet super terram, ut Onkelos & Uziel reddidere: utut enim Athnach interce- dat, repeti tamen verbum potest è priori ἀπὸ κοινῦ, & producant volatile, quod volitet super terram. Non enim hîc de loco, ubi productæ inveniuntur, aves, sed de origine, unde productæ sint, agitur. Vid. quæ de his in Comment. diximus. Favere nostræ sententiæ Hieronym. August. Cyrill. Damascen. Ru- pertum agnoscit Hottingerus p. 212.

## 1:26
Verse 26. AND GOD SAID. Whether the Father said to the Son and Holy Spirit, let us make man, or whether the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are noted here by the name Elohim, and thus said it, Mr. Varenius disputes in his Decades on Genesis, page 139, and the opinion stands for the latter, warning however that neither opinion was condemned in the Council of Sirmium, but only the heresy of the Anti-Trinitarians, by which only one person is imagined here, who said these things to himself, or of himself alone.

LET US MAKE.) It is the custom for the Hebrews to speak of God as of a King. Kings do great things by the counsel of their chief men, 1 Kings 12:6, 2 Chronicles 10:9. So also God, 1 Kings 22:20.

Jewish & Socinian gloss. One must attend not to what is the custom of the Hebrews, but to what is the custom of the Holy Spirit. Although Grotius did not approve of that [gloss] regarding the Hebrews either. God does not love that grandiloquence, nor does His majesty, which is in itself supreme and greatest, need it to express itself in words. That is also foreign to the genuine simplicity of sacred discourse, which is solemn to God. If kings perform great matters by the counsel of their leading men, whom does God acknowledge as leading men, whom He might have called into counsel, when He wished to create man? The Prophet’s sentiment is clear, that God used no counselor: Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been His counselor, and has shown Him? With whom did He take counsel, and who instructed Him? Isa. 40, verses 13, 14. Therefore, he who here adds leading men to God, called into counsel, contradicts the Holy Spirit. Kings 22, 20. The whole heavenly host stands before God on the right and on the left, not so that counsel may be taken with Him, but so that it may minister to Him and execute His will. Furthermore, those who here consult among themselves about creating man, to whose image—as the words of the text have it, let us make man to our image and likeness—man was created. But was he created to the image of anyone other than God? And God created man to His own image, to the image of God He created him, says Moses, Gen. I, 17. The Apostle, however, makes this periphrasis proper to God, Coloss. 3, 9: He who created man to His own image. Rightly, therefore, have Christians here acknowledged the mystery of the plurality of the divine persons. Because several Elohim are introduced; several consult among themselves, and a plural verb is used, Let us make, and a double plural pronoun, to our image and likeness, and those several, to whose image man was created, are later called Jehovah, that one God, Gen. II, 4, so that it may be manifest that several persons are designated in one divine essence. By this great consensus, the ancient Doctors of the Church have taught, and even entire Councils. Which unanimous explanation cannot be rejected by one who affirms that tradition interprets Scripture without doubt, along with the Papists. Epiphanius speaks gravely in the Ancoratus: These very words ought to refute you, whoever you are that have a hardened heart. Learn from there that the Son has always existed with the Father. For this word Let us make does not signify one only, but expresses the Father speaking with the Son. And St. Ambrose, book 6, Hexaemeron, ch. 7. To whom does He speak? Not to Himself, certainly, because He does not say I will make, but Let us make. Not to the Angels, because they are ministers. But servants cannot have work or partnership with the Lord and with the Creator. But He speaks to the Son, even if the Jews are unwilling, even if the Arians object. And older than these is Irenaeus, book IV, against heresies, ch. XXXVII. The Word and Wisdom, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are always present with Him, through whom and in whom He made all things freely and holily, to whom He also speaks, saying, Let us make man to our image and likeness. Barnabas in the Catholic Epistle, which Grotius is accustomed to praise, asserts that the Father said these things about the Son: He says to the Son, let us make man to our image and likeness. Justin agrees with them in the Dialogue with Trypho, Theophilus in book II to Autolycus, Origen against Celsus, Eusebius of Caesarea, book 1, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 11, Athanasius, Oration 1 against the Arians, Nyssenus in his Oration on these words: Basil the Great, book 11, on the Hexaemeron. Basil of Seleucia, Oration I on the beginning of Genesis: Cyril of Alexandria, book I against Julian, Augustine, book XII on the Trinity, ch. 6, Fulgentius on the faith to Peter the Deacon, ch. 1, and others: And thus it was decreed in the Council of Antioch, Tom. I of the councils of Binius, page 209, in the Synod of Sirmium according to Socrates, book II, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 25, in the Nicene Synod a special [disputation] is held, as Gelasius of Cyzicus reports, book II of the Acts of the Nicene Council, ch. 15 and following, a disputation was held with a certain Arian philosopher concerning this saying, Let us make man: this Catholic explanation being asserted by Eustathius of Antioch, Hosius of Corduba, Leontius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and Eupsychius of Tyana, bishops; which can be read in Gelasius. Nor do most Papists think otherwise: Cardinal Cajetan, Dominicus à Soto, Santes Pagninus, Benedictus Arias Montanus, Marcus Marinus, Cardinal Bellarmine, Genebrardus, Pererius, Delrio, Cornelius à Lapide, Mersennus, Estius, Aloysius Novarinus, Tirinus. And he whom our author values most highly, Menochius. Some Jews were even more sharp-sighted than Grotius, who saw that some mystery lay beneath it. R. Solomon, Bar Nachman, with R. Jonathan, in Bereshith

Rabba, asserting that Moses, when he was writing these words, said, 'Lord, why do you provide an occasion for erring in your most simple divinity?' And R. Semlai, inquiring in Galatinus, book 11, on the secrets of Catholic truth, chapter 9: 'How many Elohim created the world?' Others have fled to that desperate asylum, that the word נעשה is a verbal noun from the Niphal conjugation, and בצלמנו are the words of Moses, to wit: 'And God said, let man be made: and thus he made him according to his image.' Aben Ezra acknowledges this to be the explanation of a foolish man. See Hottinger, History of Creation, p. 243. Nor were they so foolish as to invite angels into the society of creation here; indeed, in Bereshith Rabba they proved from Isaiah 44 that no one was with God in the creation, and that He alone created. From the Socinians also, Valentinus Smalcius protests that he does not at all approve of that opinion of the Jews, that God here addressed the angels, against Schopper, p. 8. Socinus himself in a fragment, page 84: 'We do not assert that God spoke with the angels.' The Mahometans themselves reject this exception of the Jews as inept: Ahmed Ibn-Edris says, 'The Jews posit that the Almighty God had partners in creation, when nevertheless He has no partner.' Yet those corruptions of the Jews R. Aben Ezra, R. Jehuda Levita, and Abraham Ben-David pleased Hugo, as well as the Enjedini Photinian, which Socinus also judged not absurd. Grotius therefore deserves that we address him here with Athanasius, book III, on the Trinity: 'Receive in this saying, O you also similar to the Synagogue of Satan, a false name, O Hypostatic Jew, who assert that the Father spoke to the angels: Let us make man in our image and likeness.' Our invincible assertion of the plurality of divine persons from the Old Testament, chapter 11, has expressly vindicated that very significant Mosaic passage.

Verse same. TO OUR IMAGE AND LIKENESS.) It is frequent for the Hebrews to join words signifying the same thing exegetically, as Homer does 'to wage war and to fight.' You may read both joined together also concerning human generation, which produces children similar to their parents, below V, 3. But separately, 'to the likeness of God' Gen. V, 1, 'to the image of God' IX, 6; Ovid said 'to the effigy': 'For we are also his offspring,' Aratus. Thus also the new creation, 'according to the image of him who created him,' Coloss. 3, 10, that is, 'according to God,' Eph. 4, 24. In what, however, man was created to the likeness of God, the following words explain, as also in Ovid: 'And that he might rule over the rest.' Namely, on account of the intellectual faculty, concerning which see Galen in his exhortation to the arts, and Basil in this place: Antiphon: 'By art we master those things in which we are overcome by nature.' Euripides: 'Short indeed,' etc. Whoever wishes to read this explained more broadly, let him approach Plutarch on Fortune, and Oppian in the fifth book of his Fishing. Man is also an image of God to Plato. See Lucian on Images.

Hugo rightly accepts these exegetically, otherwise than Bellarmine and some others among the Papists, Gregory of Valentia, Stapleton, Conzen, etc., as also among the Reformed, Zanchius, Martyr, Ursinus, Junius, who refer the image to the natural intellect and will, and the likeness to wisdom and justice. But that they are placed by epexegesis, or by hendiadys as an image of likeness, or by Hebraism as an image most similar, we have proved from the consistency of the decree and the execution, Gen. I, 26, 27, and the collation of Gen. 5, 3, chapter 9, 6, James 3, 9, Vol. I, System, p. 618: and Cornelius and Tirinus acknowledge the hendiadys: and Pererius and Petavius acknowledge the same force of the words. But he explains the image of God badly with the Socinians: 'In what, however, man was created to the likeness of God, the following words explain, as also in Ovid: And that he might rule over the rest: Namely, on account of the intellectual faculty, concerning which see Galen in his exhortation to the arts.' Not Ovid, not Galen, nor Plutarch and the like are to be heard here, who understood that likeness of God on a par with the most ignorant: But Paul, Col. 3, 10, in the knowledge of him who created man, Ephes. 4, 24, placing the image of GOD in righteousness and true holiness: indeed Moses, who openly distinguishes the image of God from dominion, when in verse 27 he says: 'And God created man to his own image, to the image of God he created him.' Then indeed in the following verse he finally adds: 'God blessed them, and said, increase and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all living creatures.' Whence it is manifest that this dominion is something different from the co-created image, or at least that this is not properly and principally situated in that. Which without doubt must be placed in that which was most excellent in man. But wisdom and justice are certainly superior to dominion. And the image of God is restored to us in renewal, dominion is not restored; or if he prefers to side with Socinus here, the image of God is not even lost through sin; but dominion was lost through sin. Therefore, the image of God understood properly is one thing, dominion is another: the image of GOD, says Ambrose, Hexaemeron, book VI, chapter 6, is virtue, not infirmity. The image of GOD is wisdom, and the image of God is justice. That soul is painted by God which has in itself virtue, the grace shining back, and the splendor of piety. In Irenaeus, Adam is said, book III, c. 37, to have lost through disobedience the robe which he had from the Spirit of holiness. But Grotius, following Socinus, did not acknowledge the wisdom and justice of the first men as co-created, as we shall say at chapter 2, 9. Therefore he preferred to place the image of God in dominion with him.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET DIXIT DEUS. An Pater ad Filium & Sp. S. dixerit faciamus ho- minem, an vero Pater, Filius & Spir. S. nomine Elo- him hîc notentur, atque ita dixerint, disputat Dn. Va- renius Dec. in Gen. pag. 139. & pro posteriori stat sententia, monens tamen neutram sententiam in Concilio Syrmiensi damnatam, sed solum hæresin Anti-Trinitariorum, qua una solum persona hîc fingitur, quæ sibi ipsi, vel de seipsa sola hæc dixerit.

FACIAMUS.) Mos est Hebræis de Deo, ut de Rege loqui Reges res magnas agunt de consilio primorum, 1. Reg. 12, 6. 2. Par. 10, 9. Sic & Deus 1. Reg. 22, 20.

Glossa Judaica & Sociniana. Non quis E- bræis, sed quis Spiritui S. mos sit, attendendum. Quanquam nec illum de Ebræis probarit Grotius. Non amat Deus illum magnatismum, nec indiget eo majestas ejus per se summa, & maxima, ut verbis se efferat. Alienum id quoque à simplicitate germana sacri, Deoque solemnis sermonis. Si reges de consilio primorum magnas res agunt, quosnam Deus agnoscit primores, quos in consilium voca- rit, cum hominem condere vellet? Diserta est Prophetæ sententia, nemine Deum usum fuisse consiliario: Quis adjuvit Spiritum Domini, aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit, & ostendit illi? Cum quo iniit consilium, & instruxit eum? Esa. 40. vers. 13. 14. Contradicit ergo Spiritui S. qui hîc Deo primores adjungit in consilium vocatos, 1. Reg. 22, 20. assi- stit Deo omnis cælestis exercitus à dextris & sini- stris, non ut cum eo consilium agitetur, sed ut mi- nistret ei, & voluntatem ejus exequatur. Porro, qui hîc inter se consultant de homine condendo, ad eorum imaginem, ut habent verba textus, fa- ciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem no- stram, creatus est homo. Num vero ad ullius imaginem, quam Dei conditus est? Et creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit illum, inquit Moses Gen. I, 17. Aposto- lus vero hanc περίφρασιν facit Dei propriam, Coloss. 3, 9. Ille, qui creavit hominem ad imaginem suam. Merito itaque agnoverunt hîc Christiani mysterium pluralitatis personarum divinarum. Quia plures introducuntur Elohim; plures consultant inter se invicem, & verbum plurale adhibetur, Faciamus, & pronomen geminum plurale ad imaginem & simi- litudinem nostram, illique plures, ad quorum imagi- nem homo conditus est, dicuntur postea Jehovah, unus ille Deus, Gen. II, 4. ut manifestum sit plures personas in una divina essentia designari. Magno hoc consensu docuerunt veteres Ecclesiæ Docto- res, integra etiam Concilia. Quam explicatio- nem unanimem reprobare non potest, qui tradi- tionem indubitato interpretari Scripturam cum Pontificiis affirmat. Graviter Epiphanius in An- corato: Vel hæc ipsa verba te redarguere debent, qui- cunque obduratum cor habes. Disce illinc Filium apud Patrem semper extitisse. Nam hoc verbum Faciamus non unum duntaxat significat, sed Patrem cum Filio colloquentem exprimit. Et S. Ambrosius l. 6. Hexaëm. c. 7. Cui dicit? Non sibi utique, quia non dicit Faciam, sed Faciamus. Non Angelis, quia Ministri sunt. Servi autem cum Domino & cum Autore non possunt habere operam aut consortium. Sed dicit Filio, etsi Judæi nolint, etsi Ariani repu- gnent. Et antiquior hisce Irenæus lib. IV. contr. hæref. c. XXXVII. Adest ei semper Verbum & Sa- pientia, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus, per quos & in quibus omnia libere & sancte fecit, ad quos etiam lo- quitur dicens, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Barnabas in Epist. Ca- thol. quam laudare solet Grotius, Patrem hæc de filio dixisse asserit: Λέγει τῷ υἱῷ, ποιήσομεν κατ᾿ εἰ- κόνα καὶ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμῶν τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Consonat illis Justinus in Dial. cum Tryph. Theophilus lib. II. ad Antolyc. Origenes contr. Celsum. Eusebius Cæsariens. l. 1. Histor. Eccl. c. 11. Athanas. Orat. 1. contr. Arian. Nyssenus Orat. in hæc verba: Basi- lius M. lib. 11. in Hexaëm. Basilius Seleucens. Orat. I. in Genes. initium: Cyrillus Alexandr. libr. I. contra Julian. August. lib. XII. de Trinit. cap. 6. Fulgentius de fide ad Petr. Diacon. cap. 1. & alii: Atque ita decretum fuit in Concilio Antiocheno, Tom. I. concil. Binii pag. 209. Synodo Syrmiensi apud Socratem l. 11. Hist. Eccles. c. 25. in Synodo Ny- cæna peculiaris, referente Gelasio Cyziceno lib. II. Actor. Concil. Nic. c. 15. & seqq. habita est disputa- tio cum Philosopho quodam Ariano de hoc dicto, Faciamus hominem: asserente hanc Catholicam ex- plicationem Eustathio Antiocheno, Hosio Cordu- bensi, Leontio Cæsariensi in Cappadocia, & Eupsi- chio Thyanensi Episcopis; quæ penes Gelasium le- gi poterunt. Neque aliter Papistæ plerique: Car- din. Cajetanus, Dominicus à Soto, Santes Pagni- nus, Benedictus Arias Montanus, Marcus Marinus, Cardinalis Bellarminus, Genebrardus, Pererius, Del- rio, Cornelius à Lapide, Mersennus, Estius, Aloysius Novarinus, Tirinus. Et quem maximi facit noster, Menochius. Oculatiores etiam Grotio fuere Judæi nonnulli, qui viderunt subesse aliquid mysterii. R. Salomo, Bar Nachman, cum R. Jonathan, in Bereschith

Rabba, asserente, Mosen, cum in scribendis his ver- bis esset, dixisse, Domine, quare occasionem præbes errandi in simplicissima tua divinitate? & R. Sem- lai quærens apud Galat. l. 11. de arcan. Cathol. veri- tat. c. 9. Quot Elohim crearint mundum? Alii ad desperatum illud asylum confugerunt, verbum נעשה esse nomen verbale, ex conjugatione Niphal, & בצלמנו esse verba Mosis h. m. Et dixit Deus, fit factus homo: & sic fecit eum secundum imaginem suam. Quam vero esse explicationem hominis fa- tui agnoscit AbenEsra. Vid. Hotting. Hist. creat. p. 243. Neque adeo suffeni fuere, ut Angelos in socie- tatem creationis hîc advocaverint : imo in Bere- schith Rabba probarunt ex Esa. 44. nullum in crea- tione cum Deo fuisse, eumque solum creasse. E Socinia- nis etiam Valentinus Smalcius protestatur, sese non approbare prorsus illam Judæorum sententiam, quod Deus hîc alloquutus sit Angelos, contra Schopper. p. 8. Socinus ipse in fragm. pag. 84. Non asserimus, Deum cum Angelis locutum esse. Reprobant ipsi- met Mahumedani hanc exceptionem Judæo- rum ceu ineptam: Ahmed Ibn-Edris, Ponunt, in- quit, Judæi Deo O. M. socios in creatione, cum ta- men socium nullum habeat. Hugoni tamen placuere corruptelæ illæ Judæorum R. Aben-Ezræ, R. Je- huda Levitæ, & Abrahami Ben-David, nec non En- jedini Photiniani, quas Socinus etiam non abfur- das judicavit. Meretur itaque Grotius, ut cum Atha- nasio l. III. de Trinit. ipsum hîc alloquamur: Acci- pe in hoc dicto & Tu consimilis Synagogæ Satanæ, nomen falsum, Hypostatice Judæe, qui asseris, Pa- trem ad Angelos locutum fuisse: Faciamus homi- nem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Lo- cum illum Mosaïcum perquam insignem ex profes- so vindicavit invicta assertio nostra pluralitatis perso- narum divinarum è V. T. c. 11.

Vers. eod. AD IMAGINEM ET SIMILITUDINEM NOSTRAM.) Frequens Hebræis jungere voces idem si- gnificantes ἐξηγητικῶς, ut Homerus πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μά- χεσθαι. Utrumque conjunctum etiam de humana generatio- ne, quæ liberos producit parentibus congeneres, legas infra V, 3. Seorsim autem ad similitudinem Dei Gen. V, 1. ad ima- ginem Dei IX, 6. ad effigiem dixit Ovidius : τὲ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμὲν, Aratus. Sic & nova creatio, καθ' εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος. Coloss. 3, 10. id est, κατὰ θεὸν, Eph. 4, 24. In quo autem ho- mo creatus sit ad Dei instar, explicant sequentia, ut & apud Ovidium: Et quod dominari in cætera posset. Nimirum διὰ τὸ ἐπιστημονικὸν, de quo vide Galenum in ex- hortatione ad artes, & Basilium hoc loco : Antiphon: Τέχνη κρατῦμεν ὧν φύσει νικώμεθα. Euripides: Βραχύ τοι &c. Latius id explicatum legere qui volet, adeat Plutarchum de Fortuna, & Oppianum de Piscatu quinto. Homo Dei simulacrum etiam Platoni. Vide Lucianum de Imaginibus.

Recte hæc ἐξηγητικῶς accipit Hugo, secus atque Bellarminus, & alii nonnulli è Pontificiis, Grego- rius de Valentia, Stapletonus, Conzen &c. ut & è Re- formatis Zanchius, Martyr, Ursinus, Junius, qui imaginem ad naturalem intellectus & voluntatis, si- militudinem ad sapientiam & justitiam referunt. Quas vero per ἐπεξήγησιν poni, vel per Hendyaden imaginem similitudinis, aut per Ebraismum ima- ginem quam simillimam designari, è consonantia decreti & executionis, Gen. I, 26. 27. & collatione Gen. 5, 3. cap. 9, 6. Jac. 3, 9. Tom. I. Syst. p. 618. probavimus: & agnoscit Cornelius & Tirinus Hen- dyaden: ac eandem vocum vim Pererius & Petavius. At male cum Socinianis imaginem Dei explicat: in quo autem homo creatus sit ad Dei instar, explicant sequentia, ut & apud Ovidium. Et quod dominari in cætera posset: Nimirum διὰ τὸ ἐπιστημονικὸν, de quo vide Galenum in exhortatione ad artes. Non Ovidius, non Galenus hîc audiendus, aut Plutar- chus, & similes, qui juxta cum ignarissimis illud in- star Dei intellexere: Sed Paulus Col. 3, 10. in agni- tione ejus, qui creavit hominem, Ephes. 4, 24. in ju- stitia & sanctitate vera collocans imaginem DEI: imo Moses qui aperte distinguit imaginem Dei a dominio, quum versu quidem 27. dicat: Et creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit illum. Tum vero sequenti demum ver- su subjungat: Benedixit illis Deus, & ait, crescite & dominamini piscibus maris, & volatilibus cœli, & animantibus universis. Unde manifestum est, Domi- nium hoc aliquid diversi esse ab imagine concrea- ta, vel certe hanc in isto proprie & principaliter si- tam non esse. Quæ sine dubio in eo locanda, quod præstantissimum fuit in homine. Præstat au- tem utique sapientia & justitia dominio. Et imago Dei restituitur nobis in renovatione, dominium non restituitur; aut si hic etiam cum Socino facere malit, imago Dei ne deperdita quidem per peccatum; dominium autem per peccatum amissum. Aliud ergo imago Dei κυρίως intellecta, aliud dominium: ima- go DEI, inquit Ambros. Hexaëm. lib. VI. cap. 6. virtus est, non infirmitas. Imago DEI sa- pientia est, & imago Dei justitia est. Illa anima a Deo pingitur, quæ habet in se virtutem, gratiam re- nitentem, splendoremque pietatis. Apud Irenæum Adam dicitur lib. III. c. 37. quam habuit a Spiritu sanctitatis stolam amisisse per inobedientiam. Sed non agnovit Grotius, Socinum sequutus, sapientiam & justitiam primorum hominum concreatam, uti ad c. 2, 9. dicemus. Ideo cum ipso in dominio imaginem Dei locare maluit.

## 1:27
Verse 27. MALE AND FEMALE HE CREATED THEM.) It is wonderful how the explanations of the Rabbis on this matter agree with those which Plato has in the Symposium: which, however, from wherever they proceeded, I do not doubt are vain. For it is a prolepsis of that which is said below II, 21, which figure is frequent in these books, as in others.

The Jews trifle that Adam and Eve were created not with two bodies, but with one body, and side-by-side, to such an extent that Adam was placed in front, Eve at the back, and she was glued to the man's shoulders, and thus they wish for the words, 'male and female he created them,' to denote an ἀνδρόγυνα, and they dream that this two-person being was then divided into male and female, as Menasseh recounts from R. Samuel Baruachman in Conc. p. 4, and R. Solomon, Aben Ezra, R. Babye, Eliezer the German, and Isaac Karo praise the patrons of that opinion; which portent also seems probable to Menasseh, inasmuch as he adduces for it both a similar Platonic fable and the passage Ps. 139:5, 'You have fashioned me behind and before'; nor is Francesco Giorgio Veneto, or Agostino Steuco, or a certain person in Franconia mentioned by Cornelius a Lapide on this passage, averse to this monster. But Moses does not say, 'he created him,' but rather 'he created them'; and thus he indicates that they were two separate individuals, male and female, who are designated by the common name Adam for man, which is of nature when it is an appellative, so that he might teach that a woman is a human being just as much as a man, and that both are of the same nature, which a certain anonymous scoffer, a γυναικομαστὶξ, denied. Therefore R. Solomon confesses that Scripture simply means that God created male and female on the sixth day, but in what manner he did it, he would explain more accurately afterwards; which opinion Menasseh acknowledges leaves no difficulty.

Isaac Peyrère, an atheist and scoffer, has recently invented the idea that the humans described here are clearly others, distinct from Adam and Eve, and far older than them, whom he makes into pagans created by God in a large number at the same time, so that they might immediately fill the earth, while establishing Adam only as the [father] of the Jewish race, but not indeed as the first parent of the whole human race. A parallel passage, however, Gen. V, 1, most openly convinces that that Adam, whose age and generation is described there, who is said to have lived 930 years, when he begat [a son] in his own image, is comprehended here in ch. I, 27, by the name Adam, whom God created in His own image, and with his wife Eve is called male and female: and it is absurd that the Gentiles should be said to have been created in the image of God, and not Adam, that the Gentiles received the blessing, and not Adam, Gen. I, 28. Indeed, it is manifest from Gen. 2, 19, that not the fictitious Pre-Adamites, but Adam obtained dominion over the living creatures. Therefore, it was not to them, but to him that this was to be assigned in this place, nor is it openly taught in ch. II, 5, that there was any man before Adam who cultivated the earth: for he was alone, nor were any men found on the earth from whom help could be taken for him when Eve was being created, as God Himself testifies in Gen. 2, 18. Finally, since God rested on the seventh day from all the work of creation, with what rashness is it imagined that a new creation began some centuries later, namely that of Adam and Eve. B. Micrælius and Dn. D. Danhauerus from our side, and D. Samuel Maresius from the Reformed, have refuted this monstrosity: we have summarized the sum of the Elenchus in Tom. III. Syst. p. 149. seqq.

Not unlike this is the fiction of the Gentiles Empedocles and Parmenides, as well as the Chinese, concerning men born from the earth, which you may see, if you wish, in Voëtius, Disput. Select. T. I. p. 783, and of the Sabians who imagined other Protoplasts besides Adam and Eve, in Hottinger, Hist. creat. p. 7. Andr. Cæsalpinus babbles that the most ancient of mortals were made like mice or frogs in the most temperate places, which he places under the Torrid Zone, but inaccessible and unknown to other men, by putrefaction, and that others are still being made. On the contrary, Hottinger, l. c., teaches that not only the Hebrews, but also the Arabs, Turks, and Persians, as well as the Samaritans and Copts, along with most of the remaining Orientals, acknowledge Adam as the first man.

Moreover, the male is called זָכָר because in him is the memory (זֵכֶר) of the family, just as, on the contrary, the Hebrews say that women are called נָשִׁים from נָשָׁה (he forgot), because according to the Hebrew jurists, the family of the mothers is not a family. Here the woman is called נְקֵבָה from נָקַב (he engraved, he perforated).

Latin:

Vers. 27. MASCULUM ET FOEMINAM CREAVIT EOS.) Mirum quam conveniant Rabbinorum super hac re explicationes, & ea, quæ Plato habet in Convivio: quæ tamen undecunque profecta sunt, vana esse non dubito. Est enim πρόληψις ejus, quod dicitur infra II, 21. quæ figura, ut aliis, ita his libris frequens.

Nugantur Judæi Adamum & Evam creatos fuisse non bicorpores, sed concorpores, & collate- rales, adeo, ut Adam in fronte, Eva a tergo con- stitueretur, & viri scapulis agglutinata esset, adeoque his verbis, masculum & fœminam creavit eos, ἀν- δρόγυνα designari volunt, illumque bihominem divi- sum dein somniant in marem & fœminam, ut e R. Samuel Baruachman recenset Menasses Conc. p. 4. ac sententiæ illius Patronos laudat R. Salo- mo, AbenEzra, R. Babye, Eliezerum Germanum, & Isaacum Karum; quod etiam portentum Me- nassi probabile videtur, utpote qui pro eodem ad- ducit tum Platonicam fabulam consimilem, tum lo- cum Pf. 139, 5. retro & ante formasti me; neq; alienus est ab hoc monstro Franc. Georg. Venetus, aut Augu- stin. Steuchus, cum quodam in Franconia apud Cor- nel. a Lapide in h. l. Sed Moses non inquit, creavit eum, verum creavit eos; adeoque duo separata indi- vidua, masculum & fœminam fuisse indigitat, qui communi Adam hominis nomine, quod naturæ est, cum appellativum est, designantur, ut mulierem æque ac marem hominem esse, & utrosque ejusdem esse naturæ, quod Empæcta quidam anonymus γυναικο- μαστὶξ negavit, doceret. Ideo R. Salomo fatetur, simpliciter id velle Scripturam, Deum sexto die marem & fœminam creasse, qua ratione autem id fecerit, post- ea accuratius exponere; quam sententiam nihil diffi- cultatis relinquere agnoscit Menasse.
