Isaacius Peyrerius homo atheus & empæcta nuper commentus est homines hic describi plane alios ab Adamo & Eva diversos, iisque longe antiquiores, quos paganos facit magno numero simul a Deo conditos, ut statim terram implerent, Adamum progenitorem tantum Judaicæ gentis constituens, non vero pri- mum totius generis humani parentem. Locus au- tem parallelus Gen. V, 1. apertissime convincit, A- damum illum, cujus ætas & generatio ibi describi- tur, qui 930. annos vixisse dicitur, cum ad imagi- nem suam genuit, hic c. I, 27. nomine Adam, quem Deus ad imaginem suam condidit, comprehendi, & cum uxore sua Eva marem & fœminam dici: & ineptum est gentiles dici ad imaginem Dei conditos, non Adamum, gentiles accepisse benedictionem, non Adamum, Gen. I, 28. imo non Præ-Adamitas com- mentitios, sed Adamum dominium in animantia obtinuisse e Genes. 2, 19. manifestum est. Non er- go illis, sed huic id assignandum hoc loco fuit, neq; ante Adamum fuisse ullum hominem, qui terram coleret, aperte c. II, 5. docetur: solus enim ille erat, nec ulli reperiebantur in terra homines, e quibus adjutorium ei adsumi posset, cum Eva conderetur, teste ipsomet Deo Gen. 2, 18. Denique cum quieve- rit Deus septima die ab omni opere creationis, qua temeritate fingitur aliquot post seculis novam cœ- pisse creationem, Adami nempe & Evæ. Porten- tum hoc profligante e nostris B. Micrælius, & Dn. D. Danhauerus, e Reformatis D. Samuel Maresius: Summam Elenchi complexi sumus Tom. III. Syst. p. 149. seqq.

Non absimile est Gentilium Empedoclis & Parmenidis, nec non Sinensium commentum de hominibus e terra natis, quod vide sis apud Voëtium Disput. Select. T. I. p. 783. & Zabæorum alios præ- ter Adamum & Evam Protoplastos fingentium, apud Hottinger. Hist. creat. p. 7. Andr. Cæsalpinus mortalium vetustissimus instar murium aut rana- rum in locis temperatissimis, quæ sub Zona torrida collocat, sed cæteris hominibus inaccessa, & inco- gnita putredine factos, & etiamnum alios fieri nu- gatur. Contra non Ebræos tantum, sed & Arabes, Turcas & Persas, ut & Samaritanos, ac Cophtas, cum reliquis plerisque Orientalibus Adamum primum ho- minem agnoscere Hottinger. l. c. docet.

Cæterum masculus dicitur זָכָר quod in eo fa- miliæ זֵכֶר memoria, uti contra mulieres נָשִׁים à נָשָׁה oblitus fuit, Ebræi dictas ajunt, quia juxta JCtos Ebr. familia matrum non est familia. Hic vocatur mulier נְקֵבָה e נָקַב exaravit, perforavit.

## 1:29
Vers. 29. THAT THEY MAY BE FOR YOU FOR FOOD.) The other nourishment is common to man with other living creatures. But what is born from trees is proper to man.

Latin:

Vers. 29. UT SINT VOBIS IN ESCAM.) Cætera ali- menta homini cum animantibus aliis communia. Sed quæ de arboribus nascuntur, homini propria.

## 1:30
Vers. 30. THAT THEY MAY HAVE FOR EATING.) Namely herbs, which is added here in the Hebrew. Therefore, living creatures did not feed on living creatures from the beginning, but that only began to happen then, when not only men, but also other living creatures corrupted their way, Gen. 6, 7. 12.

Most of the Fathers and the Papists, as well as Petr. Martyr, also maintain this with the Jews: yet Cajetan, Victoria, and Dominicus à Soto, according to Pererius, say that the eating of flesh was granted and lawful even before the flood. Because God nowhere forbade it: and there were flocks of sheep then, of which Abel was the shepherd. Nor do Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Pererius deny this, even if they think that more religious men, as the descendants of Seth, abstained from it, because God expressed only herbs here, not flesh. But this is asserted rashly concerning the more religious men: it may be conceded that men abstained from the eating of flesh for some time, on account of the nature of the place, and out of liberty, but not indeed on account of any religion or prohibition. Conf. Hotting. Histor. creat. p. 307. and what we have said at ch. 9, 3. But concerning the living creatures which are said to have corrupted their way, Gen. 6, 7. 12, one must be careful not to imagine that they were subject to the same sin. For sin does not fall upon brute nature.

Latin:

Vers. 30. UT HABEANT AD VESCENDUM.) Herbas nempe, quod hic in Hebr. additur. Non ergo ab initio animan- tia animantibus vescebantur, sed tum demum id cœptum fieri, cum non homines tantum, sed & alia animantia viam suam corruperunt, Gen. 6, 7. 12.

Id etiam cum Judæis Patres plerique ac Ponti- ficii, ut & Petr. Martyr statuunt: Cajetanus tamen, Victoria, Dominicus à Soto apud Pererium esum car- nium etiam ante diluvium concessum & licitum fuisse dicunt. Quia Deus nusquam vetuit: & gre- ges tunc fuere ovium, quarum pastor Abel. Neque id negant Chrysostomus, Theodorethus, Pererius, etsi viros religiosiores, utpote Sethi posteros ab eo abstinuisse putent, quia Deus hic olera tantum expressit, non carnes. Sed hoc de viris religiosio- ribus temere asseritur: abstinuisse aliquo usque homines ab esu carnium, ob naturam loci, & ex libertate, non vero ob religionem aliquam, aut in- terdictum, concedi potest. Conf. Hotting. Histor. creat. p. 307. & quæ diximus ad cap. 9, 3. De ani- mantibus autem, quæ viam suam corrupisse dicun- tur, Gen. 6, 7. 12. cavendum, ne fingatur eadem pec- cato obnoxia fuisse. Peccatum enim non cadit in naturam brutam.

## 1:31
Verf. 31. THE SIXTH DAY.) Which number is φύσεως νόμοις γεννητικώτατος (most generative by the laws of nature), as Philo says: attributed to Venus for that reason, as Capella says. Add τὰ θεολογύμενα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς (The Theological Principles of Arithmetic), where it is said in this number ἐνεψυχῶσθαι καὶ καθηγεῖσθαι τὸν κόσμον τυχόν τε ὁλότητος καὶ διαμονῆς (the world is ensouled and guided, and has attained wholeness and permanence). The same book adds that this number is called the world (κόσμον).

Catharinus errs here by asserting that Eve was created only on the seventh day, to which Thomas also seems to incline in Part 1, Question 23, Article 1; and Salmasius, in his work on the Climacteric years, attributes that opinion to the Hellenistic Jews. For it pertains to the sixth day that Moses says: Male and female He created them.

Latin:

Verf. 31. DIES SEXTUS.) Qui numerus φύσεως νόμοις γεννητικώτατος, ut ait Philo: Veneri ob id attributus, ut ait Capella. Adde τὰ θεολογύμενα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς, ubi in hoc numero dicitur ἐνεψυχῶσθαι καὶ καθηγεῖσθαι τὸν κόσμον τυχόν τε ὁλότητος καὶ διαμονῆς. Addit idem liber hunc numero- rum vocari κόσμον.

Errat hîc Catharinus septimo die demum E- vam conditam esse asserens, quo etiam inclinare Thomas videtur prim. quæst. 23. art. 1. tribuitque eam sententiam Judæis Hellenistis Salmasius de an- nis Climacteriis. Ad sextum enim diem pertinet quod Moses ait: Masculum & fœminam creavit eos.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. The Sabbath blessed. The production of man, who was placed in Paradise. The law given to him. Eve formed. Holy matrimony.

Verse 1. THEREFORE THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH WERE FINISHED.

The word כלה denotes being finished entirely, and brings with it at once the end of the action and the perfection of the thing produced. The whole universe is distributed into heaven and earth, and what is contained in them: which are designated by the name of host, so that the boundary of creation is described by the completion, end, and complement of the divine operation, and the perfection of the created work, situated in the abundance of all things and their ordered arrangement, destined for certain uses: and let there be noted at the same time the obedience of the creature, complying with a certain law and order divinely prescribed for itself, to the Creator as the author and leader of the host, without whose nod they do nothing. Compare Ps. 148, 2 ff., Ps. 104, 2 ff.

Verse of the same. AND ALL THE ORNAMENT OF THEM.) צבא שמים are sometimes the stars, Deut. 4, 19; Isa. 7, 26; sometimes the Angels, 1 Kings 22, 19. Here the former meaning is to be preferred, because it is a more probable opinion that Moses is dealing only with the creation of the things which we see.

He thinks the stars are indicated, not the Angels, because it is a more probable opinion that Moses is dealing only with the creation of the things which we see. But could he not have been dealing only with visible things, by describing their creation in order, even though he might here insinuate that the angels also and the creatures created in the hexaemeron were included, lest anyone should either entirely exclude them from the census of creatures, or believe they were created long before, and not within that hexaemeron? Nor indeed are the angels called צבא שמים only in 1 Kings 22, 19. A clearer passage is found for this opinion: that the angels are included; namely, Nehemiah 9, 6: Thou thyself, O Lord, alone, thou hast made heaven, and the heaven of heavens, and all their host, the earth and all things that are in it; the seas and all things that are in them; and thou givest life to all these, and the host of heaven worships Thee. What is the host of heaven here, if not the angelic? These seem to point with the finger to the present passage, Gen. 2, 2. Compare 1. Kings 22, v. 19. Psalm 33, 6. Zeph. 1, 5. But when the angels were created, we explained in Vol. III of the System of Theology, p. 988 ff. Piscator wrongly concludes from there that the angels were created with the firmament or Rakia, and not on the first day, because the heaven was created ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου or after the foundation of the world: but neither is the domicile of the angels, as they call it, denoted by the word רקיע, nor is there any room left for that figment about the third heaven being produced before the Angels, concerning which see the same place, page 996; nor does ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου denote time after the foundation of the world, but rather eternity itself, Rev. 13, 8; ch. 17, 8, even if it sometimes designates time elsewhere. Compare Eph. 1, v. 4 with Matt. 25, 34.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Sabbatum benedictum. Productio hominis, qui in Paradiso locatus. Lex ei data. Eva formata. Matrimonium sanctum.

Verf. 1. IGITUR PERFECTI SUNT COELI ET TERRA.

Verbum כלה notat ex toto consummari, in- fertque simul actionis finem & rei productæ perfe- ctionem. Totum universum in cælum & terram, & quæ iis continentur, distribuitur: quæ exercitus nomine designantur, ut ita describatur terminus creationis absolutione, fine, & complemento opera- tionis divinæ, & perfectione operis conditi, sita in rerum universarum copia, & ordinata collocatio- ne, destinata certis usibus: noteturque simul obe- dientia creaturæ, certa lege atque ordine, sibi divi- nitus præscripto, obtemperans creatori tanquam exercitus autori & duci, sine cujus nutu nihil agunt. Conf. Pf. 148, 2. feqq. Pf. 104, 2. feqq.

Verf. eod. ET OMNIS ORNATUS EORUM.) צבא שמים modo sunt stellæ, Deut. 4, 19. Efa. 7, 26. modo An- geli 1. Reg. 22, 19. Hic prior significatio præferenda, quia Mo- sem non nisi de rerum quas conspicimus conditu agere proba- bilior sententia est.

Stellas indicari, non Angelos putat, quia Mo- sen non nisi de rerum, quas conspicimus conditu agere probabilior sit sententia. Sed annon poterat agere solum de rebus visibilibus, earum creationem ordi- ne describendo, utut insinuaret hîc angelos etiam & creaturas, hexaëmero conditas, comprehensos es- se, ne quis eos aut plane creaturarum censu exime- ret, aut longe antè, nec intra illud hexaëmeron con- ditas crederet. Nec vero tantum 1. Reg. 22, 19. An- geli צבא שמים dicuntur. Reperitur luculentior locus pro hac sententia: quod angeli comprehen- dantur; utpote Nehem. 9, 6. Tu ipse, Domine solus, tu fecisti cælum, & cælum cælorum, & omnem exer- citum eorum, terram & universa, quæ in ea sunt; ma- ria & omnia, quæ in eis sunt; & tu vivificas omnia hæc, & exercitus cæli Te adorat. Quis hîc cæli exer- citus, nisi angelicus? Digito monstrare videntur il- la præsentem locum Gen. 2, 2. Conf. 1. Reg. 22. v. 19. Psalm. 33, 6. Soph. 1, 5. Quando autem angeli con- diti sint, exposuimus T. III. Syst. Theol. p. 988. feqq. Piscator cum firmamento vel Rakia angelos con- ditos, non vero primo die, perperam inde colligit, quia cælum ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου seu post fundatio- nem mundi creatum: sed neq; voce רקיע domicilium quod vocant Calvin. angelorum notatur, aut figmen- to illi de cælo tertio ante Angelos producto locus re- linquendus, de quo l. c. pag. 996. nec ἀπὸ καταβο- λῆς κόσμου tempus post mundi fundationem, sed æter- nitatem potius ipsam notat Apoc. 13, 8. c. 17, 8. etsi alias nonnunquam tempus designet. Conf. Eph. I. v. 4. cum Matth. XXV, 34.

## 2:2
Verse 2. AND GOD FINISHED ON THE SEVENTH DAY HIS WORK WHICH HE HAD MADE: AND HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY FROM ALL THE WORK WHICH HE HAD DONE. The Hebrew words are to be rendered HAD COMPLETED, as Vatablus, Mercer, and others note. For on the sixth day he had already completed all his work: thus there is no need for the empty distinctions of Cajetan, between positive action and cessation or negation from further operation, and of Lyranus between the perfection by which something attains its due form and that by which something goes forth into its due operation: or for the trifles of the Hebrews, as Jerome reports in Quaest. Hebr. in Gen., as if the Sabbath had been dissolved by God himself even then, while God worked on the Sabbath completing his works in it, or as it is rendered with Targ. Hier. for completed and וחמיד desired, so that R. Levi Ben-Gerson might remove every such scruple, R. Menass. Ben Israel in Concil. p. 21, thinks in this sense, God desired his work, i.e., by the preservation of all things which he had made; or as it may be said with this Menasse that something else is noted, than that it was then discovered that the work had been perfect, because for six days new creatures were produced daily, but on the seventh nothing new was created, or with R. Gveruba, that the world was distributed with a great good, namely rest, which it finally attained on the Sabbath, or finally with R. Isaac Arama and R. Abarben., however much God gave all things their being, which they had in the space of six days, they nevertheless did not have their natural motion and operation before the seventh day, on which the Lord blessed them: which opinion seems most probable to Menasse. There is no need, I say, for such trifles, if it is rendered in the pluperfect. And thus, as regards the sense, the LXX correctly expressed it: καὶ συνετέλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ. For these are easily equivalent: God had completed his work on the seventh day, and God completed his work on the sixth day.

Latin:

Verf. 2. COMPLEVITQUE DEUS DIE SEPTIMO OPUS SUUM, QUOD FECERAT: ET REQUIEVIT DIE SEPTIMO AB UNIVERSO OPERE QUOD PA- TRARAT. Ebræa reddenda sunt COMPLEVERAT, ut Vatabl. Mercer. & alii notant. Nam sexto die jam opus omne compleverat: ita non opus inanibus distinctionibus Cajetani, inter actionem positivam, & cessationem vel negationem ab ulteriore opera- tione, ac Lyrani inter perfectionem, qua aliquid for- mam debitam assequitur, & eam qua exit aliquid in operationem sibi debitam: aut tricis Ebræorum re- ferente Hieronymo, Quæst. Ebr. in Gen. quasi jam tum Sabbatum ab ipso Deo dissolutum, dum in Sab- bato Deus operatus complens in eo opera sua, vel ut cum Targ. Hier. reddatur pro complevit & וחמיד desideravit, ut R. Levi Ben-Gersonem omnem ita scru- pulum adimere R. Menass. Ben Israel in Concil. p. 21. censet hoc sensu, Deus desideravit opus suum, h. e. con- servatione omnium rerum quas fecerat; aut ut dicatur cum hoc Menasse aliud notari, quam tunc comper- tum esse, opus perfectum fuisse, quia sex diebus novæ quotidie creaturæ productæ sunt, septimo autem ni- hil novi creabatur, aut cum R. Gveruba, mundum fuisse distributum ingenti bono, nimirum quiete, quam demum adeptus sit Sabbato, aut denique cum R. Isaac Arama, & R. Abarben. utcunque Deus rebus omnibus suum esse dederit, quod sex dierum spatio habuerint, naturalem tamen motum & operationem eadem non habuisse ante diem septimum, quo Domi- nus benedixerit: quæ opinio Menassi maxime pro- babilis videtur. Talibus tricis opus, inquam, non est, si in plusquamperfecto reddatur. Atque ita quoad sensum recte expressere LXX. καὶ συνετέλε- σεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ. Hæc enim æquipol- lent facile: compleverat Deus die septimo opus suum, & complevit Deus die sexto opus suum.

## 2:3
Ver. 3. AND HE BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY, AND SANCTIFIED IT, BECAUSE IN IT HE HAD CEASED FROM ALL HIS WORK, WHICH GOD CREATED.

These things are not said by prolepsis, as R. Solomon and others wish: there is no cause for it. He blessed it immediately when he ceased from his work. But he blessed this day, not because the six preceding ones were cursed, but because he granted a peculiar blessing to the seventh day above the others, and therefore consecrated it separated for holy worship from profane uses, so that man might enjoy that blessing. From that time, therefore, the Sabbath was consecrated, not instituted only after the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt: and therefore in the state of innocence the seventh day would also have been sacred. Which, contrary to Tostatus, Gomarus, and a few others, almost all interpreters, ancient and modern, Jews and Christians, maintain, namely that from the beginning of the world God sanctified and instituted the seventh day for his worship.

Ver. eod. TO MAKE.) that is, by making, exegetically. For often עשה is put for ברא. Thus ὁ ποιήσας, Acts 4:24. Yet others distinguish לעשות here from ברא, lest a tautology be made: To create is to produce from nothing: to make also looks to the end, that all things were desired for their own uses.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET BENEDIXIT DIEI SEPTIMO, & SANCTIFICA- VIT ILLUM, QUIA IN IPSO CESSAVERAT AB OMNI OPERE SUO, QUOD CREAVIT DEUS.

Non per prolepsin hæc dicuntur, ut R. Salo- mo aliique volunt: nulla ejus causa est. Benedixit statim, cum cessavit ab opere. Benedixit autem huic diei, non quod sex præcedentes maledicti fue- rint, sed quod peculiarem benedictionem diei septi- mo concesserit præ aliis, eumque ideo consecrarit sancto cultui separatum ab usibus prophanis, ut benedictione illa homo fruatur. Ab illo ergo tem- pore Sabbatum consecratum fuit, non institutum demum post Israëlitarum eductionem ex Ægypto: ideoq; in statu innocentiæ etiam septimus dies fuis- set sacer. Quod contra Tostatum, Gomarum, & paucos alios plerique omnes Interpp. veteres & recentio- res, Judæi & Christiani sustinent, nimirum à primor- dio mundi Deum septimum diem ad cultum suum sanctificasse, & instituisse.

Vers. eod. UT FACERET.) id est, faciendo ἐξηγητικῶς. Sæpe enim עשה ponitur pro ברא. Sic ὁ ποιήσας, Act. 4, 24. לעשות tamen alii à ברא hic distinguunt, ne ταυτολογία fit: Creare est è nihilo producere: fa- cere finem etiam respicit quod ad usus suos optata sint omnia.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. THESE ARE THE GENERATIONS OF THE HEAVENS AND OF THE EARTH, WHEN THEY WERE CREATED.

The word תולדות denotes generations: here, however, it is taken metaphorically for creation, as in Job 38:28, 29; therefore it is added for the sake of declaration, in their being created, or when they were being created. The LXX have: ἄυτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως, this is the book of generation, that is, a catalog, or description and enumeration. Compare Matt. 1:1. The Rabbis in Schemoth Rabbi on Ex. 21:1 observe that the word Tholedoth is written fully here and in Ruth 4:18, here because all things were founded upright and without defect or sin in the beginning: in the other place, because the Messiah is to arise from the family of Phares, through whom sin is to be destroyed. In the remaining places it is written defectively without a vav.

Ver. eod. IN THE DAY, IN WHICH THE LORD GOD MADE HEAVEN AND EARTH.) This day signifies time. Thus בְּיוֹם Num. 8:17, concerning night time.

God is one in essence, whom the essential name tetragrammaton designates, and three in persons, which plurality of persons the name אֱלֹהִים implies. Concerning that name יְהוָה we have treated expressly, as to its origin, signification, application, etc., in Theol. natur. & revelatæ, from p. 218 up to p. 395. Also concerning the reading of this name, that it ought to be pronounced entirely as it is written יְהוָה Jehovah, and that those points are proper to it. Concerning which one may also compare Joh. Coccejus in the admonition prefixed to the last things of Moses, who thinks that the genuine points of this name are manifest even from the name Eliehoenai alone, Ezra 8:4, which he says is abbreviated from El Jehovah enni, to Jehovah are my eyes. He adds Deut. 32:6 הַלְ יְהוָה to the form הַלְיַעֲקֹב, where it cannot be read Haladonai, since the patach point does not exist under the letter ה. Concerning the name Elohim we have treated in a special solemn disputation concerning the plurality of the divine persons demonstrated from the O. Test., held here at Wittenberg in the year 1651. Furthermore, in Hebrew, earth and heaven are placed in a different order than the Vulgate has, with earth placed first, otherwise than it is held in Gen. 1:1, because heaven, which began to be first, was perfected and adorned after the earth: as Isaac Abarbanel and R. Tanhuma explain, as well as R. Aben-Ezra, and Rab. Solomon, with R. Johanan: as far as creation is concerned, heaven preceded, if you look at the adornment, the earth: because the latter was adorned with plants before the former was with stars. Whence there is no need, as with the Academy of Hillel, to posit that heaven is named first only on account of dignity, Gen. 1:1, or as others do, that all things were created at the same time. The Academy of Samai acknowledged, as Menasseh notes, that Gen. 1:1 is the proper place of creation. That Scripture there speaks according to the order of time in which individual things began to be, even if here the earth is placed first, which he thinks was done so that heaven might be equated to earth, and earth to heaven. But the former reason is truer.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ISTÆ SUNT GENERATIONES COELI ET TERRÆ, QUANDO CREATA SUNT.

Vox תולדות generationes notat: hîc vero pro creatione accipitur metaphorice, ut Job. 38, 28. 29 ideo additur declarationis causa in creari ea, vel cum crearentur ea. LXX. habent: ἄυτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως hic est liber generationis, id est, Catalogus, vel de- scriptio & enumeratio. Conf. Matth. 1, 1. vocem Tholedoth hic & Ruth. 4, 88. plene scribi obser- vant Rabbini in Schemoth Rabbi ad Ex. 21, 1. hic quod omnia recta, & sine defectu vel peccato ini- tio condita: in altero loco, quod ex familia Phares Messias oriturus sit, per quem peccatum destruen- dum. In reliquis locis defective sine vav scribi- tur,

Verf. feod. IN DIE, QUO FECIT DOMINUS DEUS COELUM & TERRAM.) Dies hic tempus fignificat. Sic בְּיוֹם Num. 8, 17. de tempore nocturno.

Deus in effentia unus, quem nomen effentiale tetra- grammaton defignat, in perfonis trinus, quam perfo- narum pluralitatem nomen אֱלֹהִים infinuat. De illo nomine יְהוָה ex profeffo, qua originem, fignificatio- nem, applicationem &c. egimus in Theol. natur. & re- velatæ, a p. 218. usq; ad p. 395. Etiam de lectione hu- jus nominis, quod omnino ita, ut fcribitur, pronun- ciari debeat יְהוָה Jehovah, & puncta illa ei fint pro- pria. De quo conferri etiam poterit Joh. Coccejus in admonit. præmiffa ultimis Mofis, qui manifefta effe genuina nominis hujus puncta vel ex folo nomine Eliehoenai Efdr. 8, 4. putat, quod abbreviatum di- cit ex El Jehovah enni, ad Jehovam funt oculi mei. Addit Deut. 32, 6. הַלְ יְהוָה ad formam הַלְיַעֲקֹב, ubi legi non poffit Haladonai, quum punctum patach fub litera ה non extet. De nomine Elohim peculiari difputatione folemni egimus e V. Teft. perfonarum divinarum pluralitate demonftrata, Anno cIɔIɔcLI. hic Wittebergæ habita. Cæterum in Ebræo alio or- dine quam Vulg. habet ponuntur terra & cœlum præmiffa terra, fecus atque habetur Gen. I, 1. quia cœlum, quod primo effe cœpit poft terram perfe- fectum & exornatum : ut Ifaac Abarb. & R. Tanhu- ma exponunt, nec non R. Aben-Ezra, & Rab. Salo- mo, cum R. Johanan : quantum ad creationem cœlum præceffit, fi exornationem refpicias terra: quia hæc prius plantis, quam cœlum ftellis ornabatur. Unde opus non eft, ut cum Academia Hillelis ftatuatur cœlum tantum ob dignitatem prius nominari, Gen. I, 1. aut cum aliis fimul omnia condita effe. Agnovit Aca- demia Samai notante Menaffe, quia Gen. I, 1. proprius creationis locus eft. Scripturam ibi loqui fecundum ordinem temporis, quo fingula effe cœperunt, etfi h. l. terra præmittatur, quod factum putat, ut cœ- lum terræ, & terra cœlo æquiparetur. Sed prior ratio verior eft.

## 2:5
Verse 5. AND EVERY SHRUB OF THE FIELD BEFORE IT GREW IN THE EARTH.) שִׂיחַ also includes trees. And thus this interpreter translates Gen. 21:15, where the Greeks have ὑποκάτω ἐλάτης.

AND EVERY HERB OF THE REGION BEFORE IT GERMINATED.

The word שִׂיחַ has its origin from conversation, because shrubs agitated by the winds emit a certain sound of noises. But God is said to have created every shrub and tree before they were (through natural causes) in the earth. These things pertain to the explanation of the work of the third day: which he explains specifically, lest anyone presume that they sprang up spontaneously from the earth. This, therefore, is taught, that just as heaven and earth, so also shrubs and trees, and herbs, were created by the sole nod and word of God in the primordial creation without the intervention of natural causes.

Verse same. FOR THE LORD GOD HAD NOT RAINED UPON THE EARTH, AND THERE WAS NO MAN TO TILL THE EARTH.

Natural causes are removed here and thus it is taught at the same time how, according to the order of nature, herbs and shrubs arise after the first creation, which, namely, He subsequently sanctioned through blessing: on which occasion, Moses explains that they come forth through the irrigation of rain and the cultivation of men, then the origin of rains from vapors ascending from the earth, then the formation of man from the clay of the earth, and thus he also treats of Paradise planted by the creation of the Lord with trees without the work of man, so that, namely, the natural origin of generation may be more clearly distinguished from the rise of the primordial creation in these matters. While, however, he says, THERE WAS NO MAN, he effectively excludes PRE-ADAMITES.

Latin:

Verf. 5. ET OMNE VIRGULTUM AGRI ANTEQUAM ORIRETUR IN TERRA.) שִׂיחַ etia arbores comprehendit. Et fic interpres hic vertit Gen. 21, 15. ubi Græci ὑποκάτω ἐλάτης.

OMNEMQUE HERBAM REGIONIS PRI- USQUAM GERMINARET.

Vox שִׂיחַ a confabulatione ortum habet, quia fru- tices ventis agitati ftrepitum quendam fonorum e- dunt. Omne autem virgultum & arbores creaffe di- citur Deus antequam (per caufas naturales) effent in terra. Pertinent hæc ad explicationem operis tertiæ diei : quod fpecialiter exponit, ne quis fponte e terra illa prognata effe præfumat, Id ergo docetur, ut cœ- lum & terram, ita etiam frutices & arbores, atque herbas, folo Dei nutu & verbo procreatas effe in primæva creatione fine caufarum naturalium inter- ventu.

Verf. eod. NON ENIM PLUERAT DOMINUS DEUS SUPER TERRAM, ET HOMO NON ERAT, QUI OPE- RARETUR TERRAM.

Removentur hic caufæ naturales atque ita fimul docetur, quomodo fecundum naturæ ordinem her- bæ & frutices oriantur poft primam creationem, quem fc. deinceps per benedictionem fancivit: qua occafione, quod nempe per pluviæ irrigationem, ho- minumq; culturam proveniant, explicat Mofes, tum pluviarum originem e vaporibus e terra afcenden- dentibus, tum hominis formationem e luto terræ, adeoque agit etiam de Paradifo arboribus fine ope- ra hominis creatione Domini confito, ut nempe origo naturalis generationis ab ortu primævæ crea- tionis in hifce apertius diftinguatur. Dum autem ait, NON ERAT HOMO, efficaciter PRÆADA- MITAS excludit.

## 2:6
Verse 6. BUT A FOUNTAIN WAS ASCENDING FROM THE EARTH, IRRIGATING THE WHOLE SURFACE OF THE EARTH.)

In the most ancient Codex, which Saadias used, a negative particle was placed here, which I would not disapprove of, if there were a consensus of many codices, so that Moses might provide a reason why God established that garden, of which he is now about to speak, among great rivers, namely because, since the sky was still retaining its purity, rains were not falling, and with the recent departure of waters from the lands into their own channels, no new springs were bubbling up from the earth. For what is here in Hebrew as אד is πηγὴ for the LXX Interpreters, and fons for the Latins: ἐπίφλυγμὸς, as Aquila placed here, or ἐπίβλυσμὸς, as Symmachus, Job 30:12 and Prov. 1:26. It is, however, frequent for those LXX, as also for the writers of the New Testament, to put πηγὴν for any eruption of moisture whatsoever. See what we have said at Mark 5:29.

Our author observes that R. Saadias read a negative particle added in the most ancient Codex: nor does he disapprove of this, if there is a consensus of many codices. But we ought not to be so easy in admitting diverse readings, let alone in designating errors. Saadias could have added the negative, even if he did not find it in his codex, for the sake of a clearer sense, to be repeated ἀπὸ κοινοῦ from the two preceding clauses, just as was done by R. David Kimchi, and observed by Fagius, that a negative placed at the beginning of a sentence in Hebraism is not rarely referred to several things; which is manifest in Ps. 9:19, 'The needy shall not always be forgotten, the expectation of the poor shall not perish forever.' Junius in this place renders the conjunction AND disjunctively; when Jehovah GOD had not sent rain upon the earth, and there had been no man to cultivate the earth, or vapor ascending from the earth, which might irrigate the whole surface of the earth: that is, which is now accustomed to ascend by the law of nature. He says that it is very common for the conjunction to be taken disjunctively, as in Exod. 21:15. Nor does the French edition deny it: Others, however, prefer to take it adversatively, but a vapor was ascending: as it is in the Belgian translation and the version of B. Luther: or to render with Mercer: furthermore, then, a vapor was ascending from the earth. Since the sense is also consistent without the negative particle. The Hebrew אד the LXX render as πηγὴν; Aquila as ἐπίβλυγμὸν, an eruption of waters. The Chaldean renders it as a cloud, because a misty vapor like a cloud had settled upon the earth; Petavius says, lib. 1 de opif. sex dier. c. 14, that a cloud like a fountain had irrigated the dry earth by settling and fostering it. B. Luther [renders it] as a mist: 'But a mist went up from the earth.' The Vulgate interpretation is most inconvenient, which Grotius should have corrected here rather than the Hebrew fountain. For that was the cause why, in the investigation of this fountain ascending from the earth, those who consulted the Hebrew fountain here labored much with vain effort. An example is Augustine, lib. 5 de Gen. ad liter. c. 19, whom Bened. Pererius refutes, and teaches that the Hebrew word ought to be rendered by VAPOR: which Martin Delrio and Mariana also acknowledge. Likewise, Cornelius à Lapide does not want the word אד to be understood as a fountain, but as the abyss, which covered the whole earth, c. 1:2. Petavius also poorly assists the Vulgate. For a CLOUD, even if it is like a fountain, is one thing, and a FOUNTAIN ascending from the earth is another. Nor does Marin. help it any better. Marsennus: that the fountain is nothing other than some vapor enclosed in the caverns of the earth, resolved into fountain waters: for those vapors do not ascend from the earth, but are enclosed in the caverns of the earth. As for the meaning itself, others want all natural causes to be removed here from the production of plants, namely that God created the shrub of the field, and every herb of the earth, before it SPRANG UP from the earth, in the way it is accustomed to spring up in a natural manner: For there was not yet a man to cultivate the earth, nor had rain yet descended upon the earth, nor vapor from the earth. Others [think] that human cultivation and irrigation by rain are indeed removed, but that the fertilization is ascribed to a vapor or rather to a cloud settling upon or a mist irrigating the earth: others judge more correctly that the common principle of herbs and shrubs, which He subsequently established in nature for producing herbs and plants, is subjoined to the first creation made by the power of God, and when Moses said that there was no rain, no man as a cultivator of the earth, when the herbs were first produced, he now takes the opportunity to speak both of the origin of rains, and of vapors ascending from the earth, and of the formation of man from the earth, whose dust was also to be moistened by a gentle vapor, when man was to be formed from it. See Rivetus on these matters, Exerc. 15 in Genes. That Adam prayed to GOD for the first rain, which he saw was necessary for the maturity of the plants, is a fiction of R. Solomon. Other Rabbis, asserting that the vapor had already ascended on the third day so that the earth might become green, contradict [the text]. Our wise men, says R. Moses Maimonides in Moreh Nevukhim part 2, c. 30, observed that God produced herbs and trees from the earth only after the rain irrigated it, and that what is said: 'And a vapor ascended from the earth,' contains a narration of the thing prior to and preceding that, 'let the earth bring forth grass': Hence Onkelos translated: 'And a cloud had ascended from the earth.' But that observation is contrary to the text: which openly testifies that rain had not yet descended when God created every shrub and every herb of the field. Ludov. de Dieu in his animadversions on this place is clearly singular; to bring forward his interpretation in this place does not seem worth the effort. For it has nothing to do with the matter.

Latin:

Verf. 6. SED FONS ASCENDEBAT E TERRA, IRRIGANS UNIVERSAM SUPERFICIEM TERRÆ.)

In antiquissimo Codice, quo usus est Saadias, apposita hic erat negans particula, quod non improbem, si adsit plurimum codicum consensus, ut rationem reddat Moses, cur hortum illum, de quo jam aget, Deus inter magna flumina constituerit, nempe quia de cœlo adhuc suam puritatem retinente, non cadebant imbres, & recens facta aquarum à terris in suos alveos discessione, nullæ novæ scatebræ è terra ebulliebant. Nam quod hîc in Hebræo est אד πηγὴ est LXX. Interpretibus, & fons Latinis: ἐπίφλυγμὸς, ut hic posuit Aquila, aut ἐπίβλυσμὸς, ut Symmachus, Job. 30, 12. & Prov. I, 26. Frequens autem est illis LXX. ut & Novi Testamenti Scriptoribus, πηγὴν ponere pro qualicunque humoris eruptione. Vide quæ dicta nobis ad Marc. V, 29.

Observat Noster, R. Saadiam in antiquissimo Codice legisse additam negativam particulam: nec id improbat, si adsit plurium codicum consensus. Sed non tam faciles esse debemus in admittendis diversis lectionibus, nedum in mendis designandis. Potuit Saadias addidisse negativam, etsi in codice suo non repererit, evidentioris sensus causa eandem ἀπὸ κοινοῦ è præcedentibus duobus commatibus repetendam, uti factum à R. David Kimchio, & Fagio observatum, negativam in principio sententiæ positam in Ebraismo non raro ad plura referri; quod Ps. 9, 9. manifestum, non in æternum oblivioni erit egenus, expectatio pauperum peribit in perpetuum. Junius in h. l. reddit conjunctionem ET disjunctive; quum non dimisisset Jehova DEUS pluviam supra terram, & nullus homo fuisset ad colendam terram, aut vapor ascendens è terra, qui irrigaret superficiem universam terræ: id est, qui nunc solet ascendere ex naturæ lege. Conjunctionem autem disjunctive accipi, usitatissimum esse ait, uti Exod. XXI, 15. Nec abnuit editio Gallica: Alii tamen adversative malunt accipere, sed vapor adscendebat: uti sit in Belgica translatione, & versione B. Lutheri: vel cum Mercero reddere: porro dein- ceps ascendebat è terra vapor. Quum sensus etiam constet, sine negante particula. Ebræum אד LXX. πηγὴν reddunt; Aquila ἐπίβλυγμὸν, aquarum eruptionem. Chaldæus reddit nubem, quod vapor nebulosus instar nubis terræ incubuerit; Petavius nubem instar fontis solo incubitu atq́; fotu siccam tellurem irrigasse, ait l. I. de opif. sex dier. c. 14. B. Lutherus nebulam: Aber ein Nebel gieng auf von der Erden. Vulgata interpretatio maxime inconveniens, quam potius hîc castigare debuisset Grotius, quam fontem Ebræum. Illa enim causa fuit, ut in hujus fontis è terra ascendentis investigatione, qui fontem Ebræum hîc consuluere, multum laborarint Interpp. irrito conatu. Exemplo est Augustinus l. V. de Gen. ad liter. c. 19. quem refellit Bened. Pererius, docetque, Ebræam vocem per VAPOREM reddi debere: quod agnoscit quoque Martinus Delrio & Mariana. Cornel. item à Lapide non de fonte intelligi vult vocem אד, sed de abysso, quæ totam terram tegebat c. 1. 2. Petavius quoque male succurrit Vulgatæ. Nam aliud est NUBES, etsi instar fontis sit, aliud FONS, è terra ascendens. Neque melius ei opitulatur Marin. Marsennus: fontem nihil aliud esse, quam vaporem aliquem in cavernis terræ inclusum, resolutum in aquas fontanas: vapores enim illi non ascendunt de terra, sed in terræ cavernis includuntur. Quod ad sententiam ipsam, alii removeri hîc volunt omnes causas naturales à plantarum productione, Deum nempe creasse virgultum agri, & omnem herbam terræ, antequam ORIRETUR è terra, quemadmodum hunc oriri solet naturali modo: Nondum enim erat homo, qui terram coleret, neque pluvia descenderat adhuc supra terram, neque vapor è terra. Alii, removeri quidem hominis culturam & pluviæ irrigationem, sed vapori aut potius nubi incumbenti vel nebulæ irriganti terram adscribi fœcundationem: alii rectius subjungi censent primae creationi virtute Dei factae herbarum & virgulti communem ratio- nem, quam deinceps constituerit in natura ad her- bas & plantas producendas, ac quum dixerit Mo- ses, non fuisse pluviam, non hominem terrae culto- rem, cum primum herbae producerentur, occasio- nem nunc sumere agendi cum de origine pluvia- rum, e vaporibus ascendentibus e terra, tum de for- matione hominis e terra, cujus pulvis blando va- pore etiam fuit perfundendus, cum inde forman- dus erat homo. Videatur de his Rivetus Exerc. XV. in Genes. Pluviam primam, quam ad ἀκμὴν plan- tarum necessariam videret, exorasse precibus a DEO Adamum, R. Salom. commentum est. Alii Rabbini jam tertio die vaporem ascendisse, ut her- besceret terra, asserentes, contradicunt. Sapientes nostri, ait R. Moses Maimonides in more Nabu- chim part. II. c. 30. observarunt, quod Deus herbas & arbores e terra demum produxerit, posteaquam pluvia illum irrigavit, & quod id, quod dicitur: Et vapor adscendit e terra, contineat narrationem rei prioris ac praecedentis illud, herbescat terra herbam: Hinc transtulit Onkelos: Et nubes ascenderat e ter- ra. Sed observatio illa textui contrariatur: qui non- dum pluviam descendisse, cum crearet Deus omne virgultum, omnemque herbam regionis, aperte testa- tur. Ludov. de Dieu in animadvers. ad h. l. plane sin- gularis est; cujus interpretationem ut hoc loco ad- ducamus, operae pretium non videtur. Nihil enim illa πρὸς Διόνυσον.

## 2:7
Verse 7. AND THE LORD GOD FORMED MAN OF THE DUST OF THE GROUND.) Martial said clay: Callimachus twice [used] πηλὸν: Hesiod [used] γαῖαν ὕδει φύρειν.

In Hebrew it is dust of the earth, which God, with the best liquid added, coagulated into mud and as it were clay, according to Tertullian, because dry dust is unsuitable for molding. אדמה sometimes signifies red earth, whence Jerome, Lyra, Hugo, Abulensis, Adrichomius, and others observe, from the tradition of the Hebrews, that Adam was created from red earth, which is in the field of Damascus—not the city of Damascus, but a certain field so called, which is Hebron—which tradition, however, Corn. a Lapide wishes had other authors besides the fabulous Hebrews. And it is certain that earth in general is sometimes signified by that word אדמה; and beasts were also formed from the ground, Gen. 2, 19, so that the origin is common to man and beasts, for whom the dwelling place of the earth is common. Moreover, the word אדמה denotes

also the dust of the earth 1. Sam. 4, 12. 2. Sam. 15, 32. and man is said to be formed of dust from the earth, so that it may be signified that he is not only from the dust of the earth, but is nothing but the dust of the earth, if his nature is estimated from the principle of his origin, apart from the soul and the co-created image of God. Whence, this having been lost, he heard in Gen. 3, 12, you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

The form and manner of production is expressed by the words עשה and יצר, and it can indeed be illustrated by the force of the former word, by the likeness of a potter forming some vessel from clay or mud; yet a successive production is not to be thought of, as if first a statue were produced from mud, then some form of human flesh were induced upon it, and finally the heterogeneous forms of the individual parts were reconciled to it, as Corn. a Lapide wishes with the Scholastics, because neither is the dust of the earth apt for molding, nor did God use that process, but He produced man in a moment. The Talmudists trifle in the Gemara Sanhedrim c. 4. Sect. 10, that on the sixth day at the first hour the dust was collected; at the second, the unformed mass was compacted; at the third, the limbs were figured from it; at the fourth, the soul was infused; at the fifth, the man was raised to his feet from the ground in which he lay.

Sixth, names imposed upon the living creatures; Seventh, that she received the woman; Eighth, they say, two went up to bed and four came down: Ninth, they received a commandment; Tenth, they transgressed; Eleventh, they underwent judgment; Twelfth, they were cast out of the garden. But these are frivolous, or even openly false. Who will believe that God needed five hours for the creation of man, and that man could impose names on all living creatures in one hour? And at what hour, pray, were the animals created, which Moses testifies were created on the sixth day, not on the fifth, as some Jews dream.

The efficient cause of creation is established as God alone, both here and elsewhere throughout. And therefore Thomas errs, and those who follow him, Cornel. à Lapide, and others, that God with the angels produced the statue from clay, thus patronizing the Jews R. Jehuda Levita and R. Aben Ezra, who trifle that God spoke to the angels in Gen. 1:27, to which error it is evident that Grotius also leans from chapter 1:26.

Verse same. AND HE BREATHED INTO HIS FACE THE BREATH OF LIFE.) Although the spirit of other living creatures can also be said in some sense to be from God, yet not without cause did Moses say this specifically of the spirit of man, as being more divine, and Job 33:4. Nor indeed is this spirit said to be put into the nostrils, but into the whole face, the index of the mind and capable of speech, for which reason the Chaldean paraphrast placed the speaking Spirit here. But he who compares and considers the passages of Job 34:14, Ps. 104:29, Acts 17:25, Eccl. 12:7 will see that this does not treat of immortality. Truly, this is not of the first, but of a new creation.

It does not sufficiently appear what Grotius means, whether that God breathed from his own substance, as the Stoics, Epictetus, Seneca, and Cicero called the soul a particle of divine aura, and as the Manichaeans and Priscillianists taught that human souls existed from the substance of GOD, whom the Council of Braga c. V therefore condemned, because the substance of God cannot be shared and is indivisible, Isa. 42:6. Or whether with the Socinian Crellius he desires the spirit of man to be recalled to the same genus as the spiritual essence of God, or how he establishes the spirit of man as more divine by reason of the inspiration made by God, if this is not to be referred to the origin of the soul from GOD? But it is certain that God is said to have breathed in the soul through anthropopathy, not as if the created soul existed before it was put into the body, but that it began to be through that inspiration. Nor indeed is the breath of life the Holy Spirit, as Philastrius wishes in Catal. hæret. c. 99, but the rational soul itself, because in man it is simultaneously vegetative and sensitive, from which arises respiration and expiration, whence ψυχὴ, from ψυχάζω I catch cold, נפש from נפש he breathed, is so called.

However, it must not be denied that through the inspiration of the soul the image of God was communicated to man at the same time, provided that the soul was not put into the body naked or in pure naturals, as the Scholastics call them, but shining and coruscating in the image of God, since man was created to the image and likeness of GOD, concerning which see Cyril of Alexandria, book 1, de Spiritu & Verit., and Nazianzen, Orat. 38. It is unworthy of refutation what Augustinus Eugubinus and Oleastrius invent, as if God here took on a human form and breathed the soul from his own lungs. Lombard rightly, Lib. II. Dist. 17, from Augustine, says: the breath by which he animated man was made by God, not from God, not from any matter, but from nothing. Therefore, one must observe here the distinction handed down by the Apostle, 1. Cor. 15:26, that the first man was made into a living soul, the second into a life-giving spirit, which Theophylact interprets thus: that the former became a participant in animal life and a living animal through creation, the latter became a participant in the spiritual essence of the life-giving divine, the true and life-giving God through the hypostatic union.

But it is absurd, as Grotius observes, that the Spirit is said to have been breathed not into the nostrils, but into the whole face, the index of the mind and capable of speech: understanding by face only the external countenance, and believing that the Spirit or breath of life was breathed into the external countenance alone, and explaining the Spirit by the speaking spirit. But neither was the Spirit breathed into the face only, nor was it only a speaking Spirit, as he observes from the Chaldean Paraphrase, but a living soul, whence man is said to have been made into a living soul. For that Spirit, breathed in by divine inspiration, rendered the whole body vivifying with a life proper to man, so that man might emerge from it living, sensing, and understanding. The inspiration of God into the face of man is the transmission of the rational soul, says Alcuin in Genesis. By inspiring, however, He transfused His image into it, or rather He inspired a soul, instructed by His image. It is called the breath of LIVES, so that the twofold life of man, temporal and eternal, may be signified; just as the image of the immortal God also brings with it immortality. The incorruptible, says Basil the Great in Hexaemeron X, is not figured by the incorruptible, and the corruptible is not the image of that which is incorruptible. Man was created ישׁר ἐυθὺς, upright, perfect, whole, namely in soul and body, Eccl. 7, last verse. But did it not pertain to the perfection of the soul, insofar as it is the ἐντελέχεια of man, that it should actuate and inform its own body, toward which it has a natural propensity, so much so that dissolution is not natural to it, but arose from a principle contrary to nature and from hostile sin? Did it not require for the integrity and uprightness of the body that it should labor under no δυσκρασίᾳ, which therefore before sin was not miserable and subject to death, but these were finally inflicted as a punishment for sin, Gen. III, 17 seqq. To Grotius it does not seem that immortality is treated here, from the consideration of Job 34:14, Psalm 104:29, Acts 17:25, Eccl. 12:7, and because this is not of the first, but of the second creation. But those passages do not at all stand in the way of concreated immortality, nor does it appear by what rack an argument can be extracted against it. Moreover, the reason adduced savors of Pelagius and Socinus. But the Church believed far otherwise; that man indeed received immortality at the first creation, but that having been lost through the fall, there was need of restoration, which is by the second creation; He who was immortal before sin, became mortal through sin, and thus succession has mortality, says Didymus of Alexandria against the Manichaeans, Tom. I, Biblioth. Patr. page 367. After the devil despoiled the first parents of immortality, incorruptibility, and blessedness, that enemy of God and murderer truly revives, and immediately accuses the man who had transgressed before God, says Caesarius, Dialog. III, Biblioth. Patr. T. IV, page 669. Let Augustine be seen especially, Epist. 106 and 63, de Civ. Dei c. 15, as also ad Quod vult Deum haer. 28, etc. In the Council of Milevis also, an anathema was pronounced against the Grotian opinion: Whoever says that Adam, the first man, was made mortal, so that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body, i.e., would depart with the body, not by the merit of sin, but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema. Nor did the Jewish Church believe otherwise. God did not make death, says the author of Wisdom 1:23, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living. For God created εἰς τὸ ἗ναι, that all things might be, and that the nations of the world might be salutary, σωτήριοι, and there is not in them Φάρμακον ὀλέθρε, which is to be rendered poison of destruction, or deadly. For the word Φάρμακον is of middle meaning; here, however, it is taken in a worse sense, as both the added word ὀλέθρε and what precedes clearly teach. And Wisd. 2, 23.24. God created man for incorruption, and made him in the image of his own nature: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world: What? that the Rabbis acknowledge this also in the book Shemoth, Exod. 21. When they give this as the reason why the word תּוֹלְדוֹת is written in the Code only twice with a full vav, because, to wit, death did not exist before sin. For that is the reason they wish it to be written fully still in Gen. II, 4, and defectively in the others after the commemoration of the fall, except in the Genealogy of the Messiah in Ruth II. v. 4, where it is written fully again, because in the time of the Messiah death is to be abolished, Isa. 25, 8. These are their words. Joh. Buxtorf, in an addendum to his dissertation on the confusion of the Hebrew language, proves from many Hebrew monuments, from the book Zohar, R. Bechai, and R. Moses Gerundensis, that man would not have died if he had not sinned: Which was also done by Joh. Hornbeck in Disp. V. against the Jews concerning the state of sin and Socinianism, refuted in book III, ch. IV. Indeed, it is said by R. Menasse Ben-Israel himself in book III, de Resurrect. ch. 11, in the Chaldean Paraphrase of Ruth IV, v. last, that through the counsel which the serpent gave to Eve, all the inhabitants of the earth are guilty of death. Nor should that in the book Zohar be passed over in silence. The first man rebelled against his Lord, and was the cause of death to the world. And why the Jews, after the fall, call Sammael, whom they make the Prince of Demons and the seducer of our first parents, the Angel of death מלאך דמותא, because, as they themselves explain, he was the cause of death to the whole world. Thus the Jews, the Apellae, are wiser than the Christian Grotius, and add to them the Mahometans, who here agree with the Jews.

Verse same. AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.

Not by transmutation, but by communication: because the breath of life, infused into the body formed from the slime of the earth for union and communication, was such that the body and soul constituted one suppositum, one person, and the soul communicated life, motion, and sense to the body, and because it was a rational soul, it made him live an intellectual life. Man, therefore, was made by that inspiration, and indeed made a person or suppositum living with an intellectual life; Conf. 1 Cor. 15, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 7. FORMAVIT IGITUR DOMINUS DEUS HO- MINEM DE LIMO TERRAE.) Lutum dixit Martialis: πηλὸν Callimachus bis: Hesiodus γαῖαν ὕδει φύρειν.

In Ebraeo est pulvis de terra, quem Deus opti- mo liquore addito in limum & quasi argillam coa- gulavit, secundum Tertullianum, quia pulvis ari- dus inidoneus est ad plasmandum. אדמה nonnun- quam terram rubram significat, unde ex terra rubra, quae est in agro Damasceno, non urbis Damasci, sed agri cujusdam ita dicti, qui est Hebron, creatum A- damum esse, ex traditione Hebraeorum, Hieronymus, Lyranus, Hugo, Abulensis, Adrichomius & alii obser- vant, quam tamen traditionem Corn. a Lapide alios optat habere auctores praeter Hebraeos fabulosos. Et certum est terram in genere quamvis per eam vo- cem אדמה quandoque significari; ac formatae et- iam sunt bestiae de humo, Gen. 2, 19. ut commune sit ortus homini & bestiis principium, quibus commu- ne est terrae habitaculum. Notat autem vox אדמה

etiam pulverem terrae 1. Sam. 4, 12. 2. Sam. 15, 32. & formatus homo dicitur pulvis de terra, ut significetur eum non solum de pulvere terrae, sed nil nisi terrae pulverem esse, si absque anima & concreata imagi- ne Dei, ex ortus sui principio natura ejus aestimetur. Unde hac amissa audiebat Gen. 3, 12. pulvis es, & in pulverem reverteris.

Forma & modus productionis verbo עשה & יצר exprimitur, ac illustrari quidem potest vi supe- rioris verbi, similitudine figuli, ex argilla, vel luto vas aliquod formantis; non tamen cogitanda est successiva productio, quasi primum statua e luto producta, tum forma aliqua eidem inducta carnis humanae, denique formae heterogeneae singularum partium eidem conciliatae, prout cum Scholasticis Corn. a Lapide vult, quia nec pulvis terrae aptus est ad plasmationem, nec Deus eo usus est processu, sed in momento hominem produxit. Thalmudici nugantur in Gemara Sanhedrim c. 4. Sect. 10. die fexto hora prima collectum fuisse pulverem; secun- da, massam informem compactam; Tertia, ex ea membra figurata; Quarta, animam infusam; Quin- ta, hominem humo in qua jacebat, in pedes erectum.

Sexta nomina animantibus imposita; Septima mu- lierem accepisse; Octava lectum, inquiunt, ascende- runt duo & descenderunt quatuor: Nona præceptum accepere; Decima transgressi sunt; Undecima ju- dicium subiere; Duodecima de horto expulsi sunt. Sed hæc frivola, vel etiam aperte falsa sunt. Deum quinque horis opus habuisse ad hominis creatio- nem, & hominem una hora omnibus animantibus nomina imponere potuisse ecquis credet? Et qua tandem hora condita erunt animalia, quæ etiam sexto die, non uti Judæi nonnulli somniant, quinta creata Moses testatur.

Causa efficiens creationis solus Deus constituitur, tum hîc, tum alibi passim. Ideoque errat Thomas & qui eum sequuntur Cornel. à Lapide, aliique, Deum cum Angelis statuam è luto produxisse, patroci- nantes ita Judæis R. Jehuda Levitæ, & R. Aben Ezræ, qui Deum allocutum esse Angelos Gen. 1, 27. nu- gantur, in quem errorem propendere etiam Gro- tium è cap. I, 26. constat.

Vers. eod. ET INSPIRAVIT IN FACIEM EJUS SPI- RACULUM VITÆ.) Quanquam & aliorum animantium spiritus à Deo esse aliquo sensu dici potest, non tamen sine causa speciatim hoc de hominis spiritu, ut diviniore, dixit Moses, & Job. 33, 4. Neque vero hic spiritus in nares indi- tus dicitur, sed in faciem totam, mentis indicem, & loquendi capacem, qua de causa Spiritum loquentem hic posuit para- phrastes Chaldæus. De immortalitate vero hic non agi vide- bit qui contulerit inter se, & consideraverit loca Jobi 34, 14. Pf. 104, 29. Act. 17, 25. Eccl. 12, 7. Nimirum hoc non primæ, sed novæ est creationis.

Non apparet satis, quidnam velit Grotius, anne quod inspirarit Deus de sua substantia, uti Stoici, Epictetus, Seneca, Cicero, animam divinæ particulam auræ dixerunt, & ut Manichæi, ac Pri- scillianistæ animas humanas ex DEI substantia ex- stitisse docuerunt, quos ideo Bracarense Conci- lium c. V. damnavit, quia Dei substantia communi- cari nequit, & indivisibilis est Esa. 42, 6. An vero cum Crellio Sociniano spiritum hominis cum spi- rituali Dei essentia, ad idem genus revocatum cu- piat, aut quomodo hominis spiritum diviniorem ratione inspirationis à Deo factæ statuat, si non hoc referendum sit ad originem animæ à DEO? Cer- tum autem est, insufflasse dici Deum animam per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν, non quasi anima creata prius ex- stiterit antequam corpori indita fuerit, sed quod per illam inspirationem esse ceperit. Neque vero spiraculum vitæ est Spiritus S. uti vult Philastrius in Catal. hæret. c. 99. sed ipsa anima rationalis, quia in homine simul est vegetativa & sensitiva, ex qua oritur respiratio & exspiratio, unde ψυχὴ, à ψυχά- ζω frigus capto, נפש à נפש respiravit dicta.

Cæterum non negandum tamen per inspira- tionem animæ communicatam simul fuisse homini imaginem Dei, siquidem anima non nuda aut in puris naturalibus, quæ vocant Scholastici, sed in imagine Dei fulgens & coruscans indita corpori fuerit, cum homo creatus sit ad imaginem & simi- litudinem DEI, quo de vid. Cyrillus Alex. lib. 1. de Spiritu & Verit. & Nazianzenus Orat. 38. In- dignum refutatione est, quod Augustinus Eugubi- nus, & Oleastrius fingunt, quasi formam humanam hîc induerit Deus, animamque ex pulmonibus suis in- spirarit. Recte Lombardus Lib. II. Dist. 17. ex Augustino, flatus, inquit, quo hominem animavit, factus est à Deo non de Deo, non de aliqua materia, sed de nihilo. Ideo distinctionem hîc observare oportet ab Apostolo traditam, 1. Cor. 15, 26. quod primus homo in animam viventem, secundus in spiritum vivificantem factus sit, quam ita interpre- tatur Theophylactus, quod ille animalis vitæ par- ticeps & animal vivum evaserit per creationem hic particeps spiritualis essentia divinæ vivificatricis verus & vivificus Deus factus sit per hypostaticam unio- nem.

Ineptum autem est, quod observat Grotius, inditum dici Spiritum non in nares, sed in faciem to- tam mentis indicem & loquendi capacem : per fa- ciem vultum tantum externum intelligens, & in externum vultum solum Spiritum vel spiraculum vitæ inditum credens, ac Spiritum de loquente spi- ritu explicans. At neque in faciem tantum Spiritus inditus neque solum loquens Spiritus, uti e Para- phrasi Chaldæa observat, sed anima vivens, unde homo factus dicitur in animam viventem. Spiritus enim ille per inspirationem divinam inditus totum corpus vivificum reddebat vita homini propria, ut vivus, sentiens, atque intelligens inde prodiret ho- mo. Inspiratio Dei in faciem hominis est traditio animæ rationalis, inquit Alcuinus in Genes. Inspi- rando autem transfudit in eam imaginem suam, vel potius inspiravit animam, imagine sua instructam. Dicitur Spiraculum VITARUM, ut significe- tur gemina hominis vita, temporalis, & æterna; quemadmodum etiam imago Dei immortalis im- mortalitatem infert. Incorruptibile, inquit Basi- lius M. in Hexaëm. X. non figuratur incorruptibili, & corruptibile non est imago ejus, quod est incor- ruptibile. Conditus fuit homo ישׁר ἐυθὺς, rectus, perfectus, integer, anima nempe & corpore, Eccl. 7. vers. ult. Annon autem ad animæ, quatenus est ἐντελέχεια hominis, perfectionem pertinebat, ut actuaret, & informaret ipsa corpus suum, ad quod natura habet propensionem, adeo, ut dissolutio ei naturalis non sit, sed à principio naturæ contrario & inimico peccato orta sit. Annon ad integrita- tem & rectitudinem corporis requirebatur, ut nul- la δυσκρασίᾳ laboraret, quod proinde ante pecca- tum miserum, mortique obnoxium non erat, sed ea demum in pœnam peccati inflicta sunt, Gen. III, 17. seqq. Grotio non videtur de immortalitate hîc agi, è consideratione Job. 34, 14. Psalm. 104, 29. Act. 17, 25. Eccl. 12, 7. & quod hoc non primæ, sed secun- dæ sit creationis. Sed loca illa nihil obstant con- creatæ immortalitati, nec apparet, quibus fidiculis extrahi argumentum adversus eandem possit. Ra- tio autem adducta Pelagium & Socinum sapit. Lon- ge aliter vero credidit Ecclesia; creatione prima immortalitatem accepisse quidem hominem, sed ea per lapsum deperdita, opus fuisse restauratione, quæ secunda sit creatione; Qui erat ante peccatum im- mortalis, factus est per peccatum mortalis, atque ita successio mortalitatem habet, inquit Dydimus Alex. contra Manich. Tom. I. Biblioth. Patr. pag. 367. Postquam spoliavit diabolus primos parentes ita- mortalitate, incorruptibilitate & beatitudine, reipsa reviviscit hostis ille Dei & homicida, moxque homi- nem, qui transgressus erat, apud Deum accusat, ait Cæsarius Dialog. III. Biblioth. Part. T. IV. pag. 669. Videatur imprimis Augustinus Epist. 106. & 63. de Civ. Dei c. 15. ut & ad Quod vult Deum hæref. 28. &c. In Concilio etiam Milevitano anathema dictum fuit Grotianæ sententiæ : Quicunque dicit Adam primum hominem mortalem factum, ita ut, sive peccaret, sive non peccaret, moreretur in corpo- re, h. e. cum corpore exiret, non peccati merito, sed ne- cessitate naturæ, anathema sit. Nec aliter credidit Ecclesia Judaica. Deus mortem non fecit, inquit au- tor Sapient. I, 23. nec lætatur in perditione vivorum. Creavit enim Deus εἰς τὸ ἗ναι, ut essent omnia, & ut salutares, σωτήριοι sint nationes mundi, & non est in illis Φάρμακον ὀλέθρε, quod reddendum venenum perditionis, vel mortiferum. Vox enim Φαρμάκε mediæ est significationis; hîc vero accipitur in se- quiorem partem, uti cum addita vox ὀλέθρε, tum quæ antecedunt, luculenter edocent. Et Sap. 2, 23.24. Ὁ Θεὸς ἔκτισε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ, καῤ εἰκόνα τῆς ἰδίας ἰδιότητος ἐποίησεν αὐτον: Φθόνῳ δὲ διαβόλε θάνατος εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον: Quid? quod agnoscant hoc quoque Rabbini in libro Sche- moth, Exod. 21. Cum causam, cur dictio תּוֹלְדוֹת bis tantum cum pleno vav in Codice scribatur, hanc red- dunt, quia scil. mors non fuerit ante peccatum. Ea enim de causa Gen. II, 4. plene adhuc scribi volunt, & in cæteris defective post lapsus commemorationem, præterquam in Genealogia Messiæ Ruth. II. v. 4. ubi rursus plene scribitur, quia tempore Messiæ mors ab- olenda sit, Esa. 25, 8. Hæc illi. Joh. Buxtorfius in additamento ad dissertationem de linguæ Ebraicæ confusione, multis probat ex Ebræorum monu- mentis, è libro Zoar, R. Bechai, R. Mose Gerund. hominem non moriturum fuisse, si non peccasset: Quod etiam à Joh. Hornbeck factum Disp. V. ad- vers. Judæos de statu peccati & Socinism. confu- tat. l. III. c. IV. imo ab ipso R. Menasse Ben-Israël lib. III. de Resurrect. cap. 11. in Paraphrasi Cal- daica Ruth. IV. v. ult. dicitur per consilium, quod serpens Evæ dedit, reos mortis esse omnes incolas ter- ræ. Nec tacendum illud in lib. Zohar. Primus ho- mo rebellavit Domino suo, & causa extitit mortis mundo. Et cur Sammaëlem, quem Principem Dæ- monum & seductorem primorum parentum fa- ciunt Judæi, post lapsum vocitant Angelum mortis מלאך דמותא, quam quia, ut ipsi explicant, causa extitit mortis universo orbi. Ita rectius sapiunt Apellæ Judæi Grotio Christiano, adde & Mahume- tanis, qui hîc Judæis consentiunt.

Vers. eod. ET FACTUS EST HOMO IN ANIMAM VIVENTEM.

Non per transmutationem, sed communica- tionem: quia Spiraculum vitæ corpori è limo terræ formato inditum ad unionem & communicatio- nem, ita, ut corpus & anima unum constituerent suppositum, unam personam, & corpori anima vi- tam, motum & sensum communicarit, eumque quia anima rationalis fuit, vitam intellectualem vivere fecit. Homo itaque per illam inspirationem factus est, & quidem factus persona vel suppositum vivens vita intellectuali; Conf. 1. Cor. 15, 26.

## 2:7 Addition
On Gen. 2. v. 7. HE FORMED &c. at p. 234. a.

IN Hebrew the word, וייצר in this place at least, and nowhere else, is written fully with two Jods. But at Gen. 2. v. 9. concerning the beasts, and elsewhere, it is written defectively. R. Solomon observes that the two Jods denote the two ages for which man was created, the present age and the future. But that the beasts were created for one age only.

Latin:

Ad Gen. 2. v. 7. FORMAVIT &c. ad p. 234. a.

IN Ebræo verbum, וייצר in hoc faltim loco, nec uspiam alibi scribitur plene cum duobus Jodim. At Gen. 2. v. 9. de bestiis, & alias de- fective scribitur. R. Salomo observat, duo Jod duo secula denotare, ad quæ creatus sit homo, seculum præsens & futurum. Bestias autem uni se- culo tantum creatas esse.

## 2:8
Verse 8. AND THE LORD GOD HAD PLANTED A PARADISE OF PLEASURE FROM THE BEGINNING: IN WHICH HE PLACED THE MAN, WHOM HE HAD FORMED.

The Vulgate had to be corrected here by Grotius. For it did not render 'from the beginning' conveniently: because it denotes not time, but place and situation, as also in ch. 3, v. 24, the Cherubim are said to be placed מקדם on the eastern side of the garden. The LXX also rendered it more correctly as παράδεισον ἐν Ἐδὲν, than the Vulgate did as a Paradise of pleasure: because Eden is to be taken as the proper name of the place. See Gen. 4, 16. 2 Kings 19, 12. Ezek. 27, 23. And the letter ב designates the place, so that it is expressed as a garden in Eden.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PLANTAVERAT AUTEM DOMINUS DEUS PARADISUM VOLUPTATIS A PRINCIPIO: IN QUO POSUIT HOMINEM, QUEM FORMAVERAT.

Corrigenda hîc erat Vulgata à Grotio. Non enim commode reddidit à principio: quia non tempus, sed locus & situs denotatur, uti etiam cap. 3, v. 24. Cherubim collocati dicuntur מקדם à parte horti Orientali. Rectius etiam LXX. reddidere παράδεισον ἐν Ἐδὲν, quam Vulgata Paradisum vo- luptatis: quia Eden ut proprium loci nomen acci- piendum. Vid. Gen. 4, 16. 2. Reg. 19, 12. Ezech. 27, 23. & litera ב locum designat, ut hortus in Eden expri- matur.

## 2:9
Verse 9. AND THE LORD GOD BROUGHT FORTH FROM THE GROUND EVERY TREE BEAUTIFUL TO BEHOLD, AND PLEASANT TO EAT.

Although these were already brought forth on the third day with Paradise, yet because for the sake of religion and the state of primeval happiness in Paradise these had to be explained specially with the very creation of man, even though these were also already accomplished in the hexaemeron designated in chapter 1, namely on the sixth day of the world, so that it could be referred to concerning the tree of both life and the knowledge of good and evil, as they were entirely unique and extraordinary, and therefore to be distinguished with care from the rest.

Verse of the same. THE TREE ALSO OF LIFE IN THE MIDST OF THE GARDEN.

The tree of life was a natural and true tree, but, as we have said, a singular and extraordinary one, having a power divinely infused for preserving the life of man, lest it should fall into decay through infirmity or age, because immortality was indeed granted to man, but not absolutely, such as it will be in the future life, but rather with the use of means ordained for prolonging life, such as was also the eating of the fruit of the tree of life. Nor was it merely a symbol or a sign that was significant, but an effective and active medium for producing a long-lived, healthy, and robust, cheerful and joyful, and constant and perpetual life, until it pleased God to transfer man into the other life, without the failure of strength and the intervention of death, and to make him from a natural being into a spiritual one.

Verse of the same. AND THE TREE OF THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOOD AND EVIL.) See what we have noted on this matter in chapter 2, book 2, of the Law of War and Peace. Josephus calls it a plant of the knowledge of the mind. Man does not bring knowledge with him, nor is he miserable for that reason, since Euripides dared to say: For in learning there is nothing sweeter in life, until you learn both to rejoice and to grieve. Who also says elsewhere: He who knows nothing, does nothing wrong. Cicero, in the third book of the Nature of the Gods, says that prudence consists of the knowledge of good and evil things; and of things that are neither good nor evil: but to him who has no evil, there is no need for a choice of good and evil. And he says later that very few use cunning well, who nevertheless are often oppressed by those who use it badly: but countless numbers use it badly, so that this gift seems to have been bestowed upon men for fraud, not for goodness. But naturally, just as man is not knowing, so he is also desirous of all knowledge, even that which is not necessary, and often not useful. See Aristotle at the beginning of the Metaphysics. At that time, therefore, with all other things abounding, no more effective temptation could be brought to man.

Knowledge, says our author, man does not bring with him, nor is he miserable for that reason. But naturally man, just as he is not knowing, so he is desirous of all knowledge, even that which is not necessary, and often not useful. See Aristotle at the beginning of the Metaphysics. At that time, therefore, with all other things abounding, no more effective temptation could be brought to man. So far he: he also refers to book II, chapter II, of the Law of War and Peace, and what he noted there. Proving from the words of Seneca, Epistle XX, that there was simplicity in the first men and ignorance of vices rather than knowledge of virtue; by ignorance of things they were innocent. And a rude life had certain things similar to all these virtues (justice, prudence, temperance, fortitude). But these things the Church has long since condemned in the Pelagianizing Socinus. The state of innocence is to be learned not from Seneca or Aristotle, who had knowledge of it along with the most ignorant, but from Holy Scripture. Which bestowed upon man, created in the image of God, not ignorance, but the knowledge and recognition of Him who created him, Colossians 3:10, and not a rude life devoid of knowledge, but one conspicuous in true justice and holiness, Ephesians 4:24. For wisdom shining in the mind, and justice and holiness in the will, reflected the image of the most wise, most just, and most holy God. He was created upright and perfect in mind and will, Ecclesiastes 7:30. Which uprightness Grotius, in the cited passage of the Law of War and Peace, perversely interprets as simplicity joined with ignorance. Solomon opposes to that uprightness not knowledge, but perverse pursuits. God, he says, created man upright, but they have sought out for themselves evil thoughts. Which designate a depravation of both the intellect and the will, opposed to the original wisdom and holiness. The perversion of the passage in Wisdom 1:23 is no lighter, when incorruptibility is taken as simplicity. For that it signifies what that word properly denotes, incorruptibility, is clear from the opposite regarding death and corruption brought in through the envy of the devil. Nor is incorruptibility ever used for simplicity in the Scriptures to denote. Some interpret it regarding sincerity, Eph. VI. v. last, but it can best be explained regarding incorruptibility, for the sake of which the grace of God is desired, and which is the end of the love of Jesus Christ. Although indeed man does not now bring knowledge with him, there still remain some ruins and certain sparks, which are inherent in nature and are brought when man is begotten; And was he therefore crude and ignorant of all things when he was created in the image of God, if he is such now? Whence then that knowledge of his, by which he was able to impose upon living creatures names appropriate to the nature of each, which God himself approved and judged suitable? Whence the prudence by which he had need for dominion over the other creatures? Nor indeed does that ignorance accord with the happiness of man in his primordial state. It is a paradox of Grotius that he who labors under ignorance is not miserable, which he himself refutes at ch. 3, 5, annotating thus: It is divine to know as much as possible. Knowledge of the gods is life to Cicero in the Hortensius: Now after the fall, indeed, man is not naturally knowing, but he is miserable for that reason: Formerly, however, he was created in knowledge, to which we ought to be RENEWED, as the Apostle warns in Coloss. 3. 10. RENEWAL to knowledge certainly presupposes the loss of knowledge, to which we are to be renewed. The wiser Rabbis themselves acknowledge that Adam was endowed with excellent knowledge. There is no doubt, it is said in Schalschelot, that the first man, who was the formation of the hands of the blessed God, was thoroughly imbued with all natural and divine wisdoms. That we are desirous of knowledge that is often not useful, that is from the first disordered appetite for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Such disorder in a man who was whole and upright, while he was such as he was created by God, had no place. It is false, therefore, that no more effective temptation could be brought; because man was sufficiently instructed by nature against temptation, nor could greater knowledge of good and evil be expected from the tree: nor was it God's way to propose to him an effective temptation to sin:

For God is untempted by evils, and he himself tempts no one, Jac. 1, 13. And that Judaic-Socinian delirium, which has its origin from the persuasion of the lying serpent, that that tree could produce the knowledge of good and evil, is refuted; which tree had that name rather because it was as it were a certain altar, at which man ought to learn how great a good it is to persist in concreated justice; how great an evil to fall away from the same. Here Adam was learning the kindness of God the author and legislator, and the good of his own integrity, in which he was created, so that he might acknowledge God and be able to worship him reverently, and finally that there is nothing better and more acceptable to God than to obey the divine will. Therefore God proposed a most beautiful contest and struggle to man at that tree, as Theodoret warns, in which he might prove himself not so much a theoretical as a practical theologian. But just as he acknowledged the good, so, having heard the command of God, he could not be ignorant of what was evil, since he had learned from God's warning what disobedience was, and what death was; after the fall, however, the same tree retains the name of the knowledge of good and evil from the most sad outcome. See our B. Gesner, disp. II. on Genesis ch. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PRODUXITQUE DOMINUS DEUS DE HU- MO OMNE LIGNUM PULCHRUM VISU, ET AD VE- SCENDUM SUAVE.

Hæc etsi tertio die jam producta cum Para- diso, tamen quia religionis & status felicitatis pri- mævæ in Paradiso gratia hæc specialiter explicanda erant cum ipsa hominis creatione, utut hæc etiam jam in hexaëmero cap. 1. designato peracta, Sexto nempe mundi die, ut ita de arbore cum vitæ tum scientiæ boni & mali referri posset, utpote quæ prorsus singulares erant, & extraordinariæ, adeoque à reliquis cum cura distinguendæ.

Vers. eod. LIGNUM ETIAM VITÆ IN MEDIO PARA- DISI.

Arbor vitæ naturalis & vera arbor, sed, ut di- ximus, singularis & extraordinaria erat, vim divi- nitus inditam habens vitam hominis conservandi, ne infirmitate, vel ætate in deterius rueret, quia concessa fuit quidem homini immortalitas, sed non absolute, qualis in altera vita futura, verum cum usu mediorum ad prorogandam vitam ordina- torum, quale etiam erat esus de fructu arboris vi- tæ. Nec vero tantum Symbolum vel signum fuit σημαντικὸν, sed medium efficax & ἐνεργητικὸν vitæ efficiendæ longævæ, valentis & robustæ, hilaris & lætæ, ac constantis, & perpetuæ, donec Deo pla- cuisset hominem transferre in alteram vitam, sine virium defectu, mortisque interventu, & ἐ ψυχικῷ efficere πνευματικὸν.

Vers. eod. LIGNUMQUE SCIENTIÆ BONI ET MA- LI.) Vide quæ hac de re annotavimus ad cap. 2. lib. 2. de Jure Belli ac pacis. Φυτὸν ὀξήτητο διανοίας vocat Josephus. Scien- tiam homo secum non adfert, nec ideo miser est, quin dicere ausus Euripides: Ἐν τῷ μαθεῖν γὰρ κδὲν ἥδιστο βίο, Ἕως τὸ χαίρειν καὶ τὸ λυπεῖσθαι μάθης. qui & alibi: Ὁ μηδὲν εἰδὼς ὐδὲν ἐξαμαρτάνει. Cicero tertio de natura Deorum prudentiam constare ait ex scientia rerum bonarum & malarum; & nec bonarum nec ma- larum: cui autem mali nihil est, ei nihil opus delectu bonorum & malorum. Et postea dicit, calliditate perpaucos bene uti, qui tamen ipsi sæpe à male utentibus opprimantur: innumera- biles autem male uti, ut donum hoc ad fraudem hominibus, non ad bonitatem impertitum esse videatur. At naturaliter ho- mo sicut sciens non est, ita omnis etiam non necessaria, sæpe nec utilis, scientiæ est appetens. Vide Aristotelem initio τῶν μετὰ τὰ φυσικά. Illo igitur tempore, rebus cæteris affluenti- bus, nulla potuit homini adferri tentatio efficacior.

Scientiam, ait Noster, homo secum non ad- fert, nec ideo miser est. At naturaliter homo, sicut sci- ens non est, ita omnis, etiam non necessariæ, sæpe nec utilis scientiæ est appetens. Vide Aristotelem initio τῶν μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ. Illo igitur tempore; rebus cæteris affluentibus, nulla potuit homini adferri tentatio effi- cacior. Hactenus ille: remittit etiam ad l. II. c. II. de jure pacis & belli, & quæ ibi annotavit. Simpli- citatem in primis hominibus fuisse & ignorationem magis vitiorum, quam cognitionem virtutis, è Sene- cæ verbis Epist. XX. probans; ignorantia rerum in- nocentes erant. Et omnibus his virtutibus (justitia, prudentia, temperantia, fortitudine) habebat similia quædam rudis vita. Sed hæc in Pelagianizante Socino jam pridem reprobavit Ecclesia. De Statu inno- centiæ non è Seneca aut Aristotele, qui ejus noti- tiam cum ignarissimis habuere, sed è Scriptura S. discendum. Quæ homini ad imaginem Dei con- dito non ignorantiam, sed notitiam & ἐπίγνωσιν ejus, qui condidit illum Col. III, 10. & non vitam rudem & expertem notitiæ, sed justitia & sanctita- te vera conspicuam tribuit Eph. IV, 24. Sapientia enim in mente, justitia & sanctitas in voluntate lu- cens, imaginem Dei sapientissimi, justissimi & san- ctissimi referebat. Rectus creatus fuit & integer mente ac voluntate. Eccl. VII, 30. Quam rectitu- dinem perverse Grotius loco citato de jure pacis & belli, de simplicitate cum ignorantia conjuncta inter- pretatur. Opponit Salomo rectitudini illi non scientiam, sed studia perversa. Deus, inquit, creavit hominem rectum, sed ipsi quæsiverunt sibi cogitatio- nes malas. Quæ depravationem cùm intellectus tum voluntatis oppositam primigeniæ sapientiæ & sanctitati designant. Perversio non levior est loci Sap. I, 23. cum ἀφθαρσία de simplicitate accipitur. Significari enim id, quod proprie vox illa notat, incorruptibilitatem, ex opposito de morte & corruptio- ne per invidiam diaboli invecta, luculentum est. Neque uspiam ἀφθαρσία simplicitatem in Scripturis denotat. De sinceritate nonnulli Eph. VI. v. ult. ac- cipiunt, sed optime de incorruptibilitate, cujus cau- sa gratia Dei optatur, & quæ finis est dilectio- nis JEsu Christi, locus explicari potest. Quamvis vero nunc homo non adferat secum scientiam, su- perant tamen adhuc nonnulla ἐρείπια & scintillæ quædam, quæ natura insunt & adferuntur, cum procreatur homo; Et num ideo cum ad imaginem Dei conderetur, rudis erat, rerumque omnium igna- rus, si nunc talis? Unde ergo illi scientia ista, qua animantibus nomina naturæ quorumvis congrua, quæ Deus ipse approbavit, & idonea judicavit, im- ponere potuit? Unde prudentia, qua ad dominium in creaturas cæteras opus habuit? Nec vero cum fe- licitate hominis in statu primævo convenit illa in- scitia. Paradoxon Grotii est, miserum non esse, qui laborat ignorantia, quod refellit ipse ad c. 3, 5. ita annotans: Divinum est scire quam plurima. Scientia Deorum vita Ciceroni in Hortensio: Nunc post lapsum quidem naturaliter homo sciens non est, sed miser ideo est: Olim autem conditus fuit in cognitione, ad quam RENOVARI nos debe- mus, monente Apostolo Coloss. 3. 10. RENOVA- TIO ad cognitionem præsupponit certe cogni- tionis amissionem, ad quam renovandi sumus. A- gnoscunt sapientiores Rabbini ipsi Adamum ex- cellenti notitia præditum fuisse. Non est dubium, dicitur in Schalschelot, hominem primum, qui fuit plasma manuum Dei benedicti, penitus fuisse imbutum omnibus sapientiis naturalibus & divinis.
