Quod appetentes simus cognitionis sæpe non utilis, id à pri- mo inordinato appetitu ligni scientiæ boni & ma- li est. Qualis ἀταξία in homine integro & recto, dum talis erat, qualis à Deo creatus, locum non habebat. Falsum itaque nullam tentationem effica- ciorem adferri potuisse; quia satis instructus erat ho- mo natura adversus tentationem, nec major à ligno scientia boni & mali expectari poterat: neque Dei erat efficacem ei tentationem proponere ad peccatum:

ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐσι κακῶν, πειράζει δὲ αὐτὸς οὐδένα, Jac. 1, 13. Et resipit id Judaico-Socinianorum delirium, quod à serpentis mendacis persuasione ori- ginem habet, scientiam boni & mali arborem illam parere potuisse; quæ arbor istud nominis inde po- tius habuit, quod velut ara quædam fuerit, ad quam homo discere deberet, quantum bonum sit, in concreata justitia persistere; quantum malum ab eadem deficere. Discebat hic Adam benignita- tem Dei autoris, & legislatoris, & integritatis suæ bonum, in qua erat conditus, ut Deum agnosceret & reverenter colere posset, ac denique nihil esse me- lius Deoque acceptius, quam voluntati divinæ ob- temperare. Ideo pulcherrimum ἀγῶνα & certamen Deus ad arborem istam homini, monente Theodo- reto, proposuit, in quo se non tam Theoreticum, quam Practicum Theologum probaret. Quem- admodum autem bonum agnoscebat, ita concione Dei audita, quid esset malum, ignorare non pote- rat, quandoquidem quid esset inobedientia, & quid mors, Deo monente, didicerat; post lapsum autem eadem arbor nomen scientiæ boni & mali ab even- tu retinet tristissimo. Vid. B. Gesnerus noster disp. II. in Genes. c. 13.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

AND A RIVER WAS GOING FORTH.) This river is put for a great abundance of waters. For there are otherwise four rivers, as now follows. This appears evidently in verse 14.

IT IS DIVIDED INTO FOUR HEADS.) In the Hebrew it is more properly divided, and is into four heads. Where 'in' abounds, as in Matthew 19, 6. It appears, however, from two undoubted rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, that these gardens were in those places of which Dionysius Periegetes speaks.

The land that lies contained by the Euphrates and the Tigris, the ancient settlers called this the land between the rivers. Let not the shepherd of that land despise its pastures, nor let him who, singing to Pan and happy with the rustic reed, guards his nocturnal sheep, nor the planter of the garden, despise the huge heaps of all kinds of fruits. So great is the harvest there, happy pastures bloom, and the grasses are green and in form surpass all, that race of men is beautiful and equal to the immortal gods.

Curtius, Book V. The lands lying between the Tigris and the Euphrates are of such rich and fertile soil that cattle are said to be driven away from grazing, lest satiety destroy them. The cause of the fertility is the moisture which flows from both rivers, seeping through the whole soil almost everywhere by veins of water. Pliny also proclaims the richness of this soil in Book V, chapter 26, and in Book 18, 17. Yet in Babylon they cut the crops twice and graze them a third time, otherwise they would only become leaves. Thus also the thinness of the soil returns harvests with fifty-fold increase: but for the more diligent, with a hundred-fold. Nor is the care difficult. They are glad to water them for as long as possible, so that the very fat and dense richness may be diluted. However, the Euphrates and the Tigris do not bring in silt, as the Nile does in Egypt, nor does the earth itself produce herbs. Yet they are of such great richness that in the following year the crop becomes self-sown with the seeds pressed into the tracks. Jerome notes that in Mesopotamia sheep give birth twice. Thence the name Heden for that whole region, that is, ἡδονῆς, 2 Kings 19:12, Ezekiel 27:23.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET FLUVIUS EGREDIEBATUR.) Fluvius hic ponitur pro magna aquarum copia. Sunt enim alioqui amnes quatuor, ut jam sequitur. Apparet id evidenter commate 14.

DIVIDITUR IN QUATUOR CAPITA.) In Hebræo magis proprie dividitur, & est in quatuor capita. Ubi in abun- dat, ut Matth. 19, 6. Apparet autem ex duobus non dubiis amnibus Euphrate & Tigride hos hortos illis in locis fuisse, de quibus Dionysius Periegetes.

Ὅσση δ' Εὐφρήτου καὶ Τίγριδος εἴδοθι γαῖα Τήνδε περικτίονες μέσσην ποταμῶν ἐνέπουσι. Οὐ μέν τοι κείνης γε νομεὺς ὀνόσαιτο βοώτης, Οὐδ' ὅσις σύριγγι κεραύυχα πῶα γεραίρων Μήλοις ἀγραύλοισιν ἐφέσπεται, ἐδὲ μὲν ὕλην Παντοίην φυτοεργὸς ἀνὴρ ἀθερίσσατο καρπῶν Τοίη ἐπὶ κείνης ἄροσις πέλει· εἰ μὲν ἀέξειν Ποίην, εἰ δὲ νοκεὺς εὐανθέας· ἐν δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν Φύτλην καλλίςην τε καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοίην. Quæ jacet Euphrate contenta & Tigride Tellus Hanc inter fluvios prisci dixere coloni. Subsequa non ejus contemnat pascua terræ, Nec qui Pana canens & arundine lætus agresti, Nocturnas custodit oves non consitor horti Omnigenum ingentes pomorum spernat acervos. Tanta illic Messis, felicia pascua florent, Et frondent herbæ & forma supereminet omnes, Gens ea pulchra virum Dîs immortalibus æqua.

Curtius libro V. Inter Tigrim & Euphratem jacentia tam ube- ri & pingui solo sunt, ut à pastu repelli pecora dicantur, ne satie- tas perimat. Causa fertilitatis est humor, qui ex utroque amne manat, toto fere solo per venas aquarum resudante. Ubertatem ejus soli & Plinius prædicat libro V. cap. 26. libro autem 18, 17. Babylone tamen bis secant, tertio depascunt, alioquin folia tan- tum fierent. Sic quoque cum quinquagesimo fœnore messes reddit exilitas soli: verum diligentioribus cum centesimo. Neque est cu- ra difficilis. Quam diutissime aquari gaudent, ut prapinguis & densa ubertas diluatur. Limum autem non invehunt Euphrates & Tigris, sicut in Ægypto Nilus, nec terra ipsa herbas gignit. Ubertatis autem tantæ sunt, ut sequente anno restibilis fiat seges impressis vestigio seminibus. Hieronymus notat in Mesopota- mia oves bis parere. Inde toti illi tractui nomen Heden, id est, ἡδονῆς, 2. Reg. 19, 12. Ezech. 27, 23,

## 2:11
Verse 11. PHISON.) Because this is joined to the Tigris, they call it the Pasitigris, preserving the antiquity of the name. See Pliny, Book VI, 29; Curtius, in the aforementioned Book V; Strabo, Book XV.

ALL THE LAND OF HEVILATH.) In Hebrew it is החויליה, but the Syrians put ח for ה as becomes חוילת, and often with the addition of א they say חויליתא: whence the Chaulotaioi to Eratosthenes in Strabo. Haitho mentions the river Phison between Nisibis and Aspa.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PHISON.) Hunc quia Tigridi jungitur, servata nominis antiquitate Pasitigrin vocant. Vide Plinium libro VI, 29. Curtium dicto libro V. Strabonem libro XV.

OMNEM TERRAM HEVILATH.) In Hebræo est החויליה, sed Syri pro ה ponunt ח ut fit חוילת, & sæpe ad- dito א dicunt חויליתא : unde χαυλοταῖοι Eratostheni apud Strabonem. Phisonis fluminis inter Nisibim & Aspam memi- nit Haitho.

## 2:12
Verse 12. BDELLIUM.) More correctly pearl, as Kimchi and Benjamin intended, where he describes Catipha.

Latin:

Vers. 12. BDELLIUM.) Rectius margarita, ut voluit Kim- chi & Benjamin, ubi Catipham describit.

## 2:13
Verse 13. GEHON.) גיחון, it is a name which is not found in only one place. See 1 Kings 1:33, 2 Chronicles 32:30, ch. 33:14. For it signifies ἐκβολή, that is, a diversion of a river. It is either the Armalca, named by Pliny, though corruptly, in Book V, ch. 26, more correctly by Ammianus Marcellinus as Naarmalcha נהר מלכא in two places in books 23 and 24; to Strabo, from the name translated from Syriac into Greek, the royal river, and thus to that same Marcellinus in the aforementioned book 23, but in another place, the royal river: or if that is less pleasing, because it is believed that this channel was made by some king, and from that it has its name, the Chaboras: which Ptolemy testifies is joined with the Euphrates. See also Strabo. The Persian history names the river by the name Gichon with the Tigris. See Teixeira.

OF ETHIOPIA.) To the Hebrews כוש, whence the Kissioi to Aeschylus in Strabo.

Latin:

Vers. 13. GEHON.) גיחון, Nomen est, quod non uno in loco reperitur. Vide 1. Reg. 1, 33. 2. Paral. 32, 30. c. 33, 14. Signi- ficat enim ἐκβολὴν, id est, divertigium fluminis. Est autem aut Armalca Plinio, sed corrupte, nominatus libro V. c. 26. rectius Ammiano Marcellino Naarmalcha נהר מלכא duobus locis libris 23. & 24. Straboni ex Syriaco in Græcum translato no- mine βασιλικός ποταμὸς, & sic eidem illi Marcellino dicto lib. 23. sed alio loco, flumen regium: aut si id minus placet, quod à regum aliquo factus is credatur alveus, & inde nomen habere, Chaboras: quem cum Euphrate conjungi Ptolemæus testatur. Vide & Strabonem. Flumen Gichon nomine cum Tigride no- minat Persica historia. Vide Teixeram.

ÆTHIOPIÆ.) Hebræis כוש, unde κίσσιοι Æschylo apud Strabonem.

## 2:14
Verse 14. TIGRIS.) In Hebrew חדקל, whence with the Syriac addition, about which we have already said something, it became חדקלתא, and with the first guttural, which easily perishes, extracted, Diglito, which is the name in Pliny, Book V, 27. Thence the Greeks, by a corrupt pronunciation, made it Tigris. See what we shall say at 2 Kings 15:29.

IT GOES TOWARD THE ASSYRIANS.) In Hebrew קדמת אשור, that is, in the sight of Assyria, in which sense κατέναντι, which the LXX Interpreters have here, is often taken: therefore in other places they translate it ἐνώπιον.

EUPHRATES.) In Hebrew הוא פרת, that excellent river called by the name Pherath or Phrahatis. For there are also elsewhere rivers called by that name from their fruitfulness. From that article designating excellence, and from that more common name, the Greek name Euphrates was made.

It is not said that the river was divided into four heads in Paradise, but after Paradise had been irrigated, which some make to be the Euphrates, inasmuch as, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, and Pliny, it diffuses itself into different channels and obtains different names. It is certain that by פרת the Euphrates is denoted, Gen. 15, Deut. 1, 7, ch. 11, 24, Josh. 1, 24, 2 Kings 29, 21. But חדקל is the Tigris, see Dan. 10, 4. But what is to be understood by פישון Phison, and what by גיחון Gihon, is highly doubtful. Which [is discussed] by Cornelius à Lapide, Pererius, Zeamannus concerning the image of God, and our Tom.

IV. Syst. Theol. p. 432. Let them be seen. Josephus wishes גִיחוֹן to be the Nile, פּישׁוֹן to be the Ganges. But the Ganges is a river of furthest India, the Nile of Africa, while the Tigris and Euphrates are of Asia, which is 70 degrees distant from the Ganges: how then could those rivers be considered neighbors, or to have arisen from one river? Therefore, Paradise is not to be placed in India with Philostorgius, or in Taprobana or America with others, or around the Jordan in Palestine with Circellus and Alphonso à Vera Cruce, or in the vicinity of Damascus with Eugubinus and Oleaster, or in Arabia Felix with Isaac Peyrerius, who makes that a region of the Holy Land, much less is all Armenia, Syria, Media, Persia, or almost all of Asia and Africa to be assigned to it, for thus it would not have been a garden, but the world. Most feel it was situated in Mesopotamia around Babylon, because Eden is a part of Babylonia, such as Pererius, Corn. à Lapide, Petavius, Zanchius, Rivetus, Willetus, Voetius, to whom Grotius rises here, as does B. Gerhardus. Some make its seat that highest part of Babylonia which is called Auranitis by Ptolemy. Tremellius, Junius, and Pareus describe Paradise by its rivers and boundaries as if they had surveyed everything close at hand: yet Pareus admits in Gen. 2 that no geography can now show us the topography of Paradise: for nowhere, he says, is that one river flowing out of Eden now found, which is divided into four rivers so called, and flowing as Moses writes. Hence the location of Paradise remains doubtful and uncertain. But Mr. Varenius thinks otherwise, Decad. Genes. p. 115, teaching from the more accurate maps of our century that the Mosaic topography agrees in every part with modern geography as well. Compare what is argued against Bellarmine concerning the seat of Paradise in Zæmannus, On the Image of God, page 297, and Mr. Varenius, l. c.

Latin:

Vers. 14. TIGRIS.) In Hebræo חדקל, unde cum addi- tamento Syriaco, de quo jam aliquid diximus, factum חדקלתא, & prima gutturali, quæ facile perit, extrita, Digli- to, quod nomen est apud Plinium lib. V, 27. Inde Græci cor- rupta pronunciatione Tigridem fecere. Vide quæ dicemus ad 2. Reg. 15, 29.

IPSE VADIT CONTRA ASSTRIOS.) In Hebr. קדמת אשור id est, in conspectu Assyriæ, quo sensu κατέναντι, quod hic LXX. Interpretes habent, sæpe sumitur: ideo aliis in locis vertunt ἐνώπιον.

EUPHRATES.) In Hebræo הוא פרת, ille eximius amnis nomine Pherath aut Phrahatis dictus. Nam sunt & alibi amnes eo nomine à fœcunditate appellati. Ex illo articulo excellen- tiam designante, & ex nomine illo communiore, factum Græ- cum nomen, Euphrates.

Non dicitur fluvium in Paradiso, sed post ir- rigatum Paradisum divisum fuisse in quatuor ca- pita, quem nonnulli Euphraten faciunt, utpote qui juxta Ptolemæum, Strabonem & Plinium in diver- sos canales se diffundit, & diversa nomina sortitur. Per פרת Euphratem notari certum est, Genes. 15. Deut. 1, 7. cap. 11, 24. Jos. 1, 24. 2. Reg. 29, 21. חדקל vero Tigris est, Vid. Dan. 10, 4. Quid vero per פישון Phison, quid per גיחון Gihon intelligatur, ma- xime dubium est. Quod de Cornel. à Lapide, Pe- rerius, Zeamannus de imagine Dei, & Tom. noster

IV. Syst. Theol. p. 432. videantur. Josephus גִיחוֹן Nilum, פּישׁוֹן Gangem esse vult. At Ganges Indiæ extremæ, Nilus Africæ fluvius est, Tigris vero & Euphrates Asiæ, qui à Gange 70. gradibus distat: quomodo ergo illa flumina vicina, aut ex uno flu- mine orta censeri potuere? Non itaq; in India cum Philostorgio vel in Taprobana aut America cum aliis, vel circa Jordanem in Palæstina cum Circelo & Alphonso à vera cruce, vel in vicinia Damasci cum Eugubino & Oleastrio, vel in Arabia felici, cum Isaaco Peyrerio, qui illam terræ sanctæ regionem facit, collocandus Paradisus, multo minus omnis Armenia, Syria, Media, Persia, aut tota fere Asia, & Africa eidem assignanda, sic enim non hortus, sed orbis fuisset. Plerique in Mesopotamia circa Ba- bylonem situm fuisse sentiunt, quia Eden pars est Babyloniæ, utpote Pererius, Corn. à Lapide, Peta- vius, Zanchius, Rivetus, Willetus, Voetius, quibus hîc assurgit Grotius, ut & B. Gerhardus. Nonnulli sedem ejus faciunt partem illam Babyloniæ sum- mam, quæ Ptolomæo Auranitis dicitur. Tremel- lius, Junius & Pareus Paradisum fluviis & limiti- bus suis ita describunt, ac si cominus perlustrassent omnia: fatetur tamen Pareus in Gen. 2. nunc nul- lam Geographiam Paradisi Topographiam nobis exhibere posse: nusquam enim, inquit, fluvius ille unus ex Eden egrediens jam reperitur, qui in quatuor fluvios sic dictos, & sic currentes, ut Moses scribit, di- vidatur. Hinc locus Paradisi manet dubius atque in- certus. Secus vero censet Dn. Varenius Decad. Ge- nes. p. 115. ex accuratioribus nostri seculi tabulis docens, ab omni parte cum hodierna quoque Geo- graphia convenire Topographiam Mosaicam. Conf. quæ adversus Bellarminum de sede Paradisi disputantur apud Zæmannum de imagine Dei, pag. 297. & Dn. Varen. l. c.

## 2:15
Verse 15. HE TOOK.) By persuasion. Rabbi Solomon here. Thus ἀνήχθη Matthew 4, 1.

Whether it was done by persuasion, or by angels, or by immediate translation, matters little. But it is manifest from this that Adam was created outside of Paradise, as he was the one who was then translated into it. Yet Paradise was not intended to be the perpetual seat of man, so that he would dwell only in that garden, which certainly would not have been capable of holding all contemporary men. And for what purpose would things have been created outside of Paradise, or how would they have served the use of man, if man had remained enclosed within Paradise? Paradise was therefore like a certain citadel, and a seat and dwelling, or as it were the metropolis of Adam, from which he could go forth into the rest of the earth and survey it, Gen. 1, 26, 28, 29. Therefore the purpose of why man was translated into Paradise was 1. The inhabitation of this royal palace. 2. The custody of the garden, which consisted both in the preservation of the dignity of Paradise and in warding off wild beasts, which he could nevertheless command by a mere nod and voice. 3. The cultivation of the garden, so that man might work in it, not laboriously, but delightfully, and reminding the mind of a prudent man of great and useful things, as Augustine says, book 8, On Genesis literally, ch. 80. 4. The exercise of piety through the tree of knowledge. 5. The preservation of life and health through the tree of life. 4. A symbolic foreshadowing of the heavenly Paradise, in which, free from sin and death and every danger, we shall speak familiarly with God, be refreshed by living rivers, and enjoy the tree of life, Apoc. 22, 1. Paradise was therefore a school and gymnasium of piety, the seat of the Church, the palace of the monarch of the world, and a type of eternal life.

Verse same. AND HE PLACED HIM IN THE PARADISE OF PLEASURE, TO WORK AND KEEP IT.

There is therefore no doubt that Adam was created outside of Paradise, because after his creation God is said to have translated him into Paradise: whom, because he had to cultivate it, labor was also enjoined upon him in the state of integrity. But He translated not only Adam, but also Eve into Paradise: for neither was she created in Paradise, as the Scholastics on book 2, Sentences, dist. 18, with Basil the Great, maintain, but outside of Paradise; and after the divine union with Adam, the blessing, and the concession of dominion over living creatures, ch. 1, 28, 29, and the ordering of the food of man and animals, v. 29, 30, she was translated with Adam into Paradise, and the fruits of Paradise were granted to both, except however for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Gen. 3, 5. Which things being done thus on the sixth day, the sanctification of the Sabbath was instituted on the following seventh day, and the Sabbath was celebrated by the first-formed pair. Compare Commentary on Genesis, p. 285, seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 15. TULIT.) Suasione. Rabbi Salomo hîc. Sic ἀνήχθη Matth. 4, 1.

Sive suasione, sive per Angelos, aut immediata translatione id factum fuerit, parum refert. Mani- festum autem inde est, quod Adamus extra Para- disum conditus fuerit, utpote in quem deinde translatus est. Neque tamen Paradisus sedes hominis perpetua esse debuit, ut tantum in horto illo habi- taret, qui utique omnium hominum συγχρόνων ca- pax non fuisset. Et ad quid condita forent extra Paradisum, aut quomodo in usum hominis cessis- sent, si homo conclusus intra Paradisum mansisset? Fuit ergo Paradisus instar arcis cujusdam, ac sedes & habitatio, vel quasi metropolis Adami, ex qua in reliquam terram prodire, eamque lustrare potuit, Gen. I, 26. 28. 29. Finis itaque cur translatus homo in Paradisum, fuit 1. Regiæ hujus inhabitatio. 2. Horti custodia, quæ tum in conservatione dignita- tis Paradisi, tum in arcendis feris sita erat, quibus tamen solo nutu & voce imperare poterat. 3. Cul- tura horti, ut in eodem operaretur homo, non la- boriosa, sed deliciosa, & mentem prudentis ma- gna atque utilia commonens, ut ait Augustinus lib. IIX. de Gen. ad lit. c. 80. 4. Exercitium pietatis per arborem cognitionis. 5. Conservatio vitæ & sanitatis per arborem vitæ. 4. Symbolica adumbra- tio Paradisi cælestis, in quo liberi à peccato & mor- te & omni periculo, familiariter cum Deo collo- quemur, fluminibus vivis recreabimur, & arbore vitæ fruemur, Apoc. 22, 1. Erat ergo Paradisus Scho- la & Gymnasium pietatis, sedes Ecclesiæ, Regia Monarchæ orbis, ac typus vitæ æternæ.

Vers. eod. ET POSUIT EUM IN PARADISO VOLU- PTATIS, UT OPERARETUR & CUSTODIRET ILLUM.

Non ergo dubium est, conditum fuisse Ada- mum extra Paradisum, quia post creationem ejus dem Deus dicitur ipsum in Paradisum transtulisse: Quem quia colere debuit, labor in statu integrita- tis eidem etiam injunctus fuit. Non autem so- lum Adam, sed etiam Evam in Paradisum transtu- lit: nam nec illa in Paradiso condita, uti cum Basi- lio M. Scholastici ad lib. II. Sent. dist. XIIX. sta- tunt, sed extra Paradisum; & post divinam cum A- damo copulationem, benedictionem, & dominii in animantia concessionem, c. I, 28. 29. victusque hominis & animantium ordinationem v. 29. 30. cum Adamo in Paradisum translata, fructusque Paradisi utrique concessi, excepta tamen arbore scientiæ boni & ma- li, Gen. 3, 5. Quibus ita sexta die factis sequente se- ptima Sabbati sanctificatio instituta, & à protoplastis Sabbatum celebratum est. Conf. Commentar. in Genes. p. 285. seqq.

## 2:16
Ver. 16. OF EVERY TREE OF THE PARADISE YOU SHALL EAT.

Homer: – – – – – and all good things were theirs, and the life-giving earth bore fruit of its own accord, much and abundant.

Let us leave to Grotius his own style of commenting, from Homer and other writers of that kind. Which is frequent in these annotations. God gives man the most free power of eating the fruits of all trees, that one excepted, which He specifically forbids. By which this prohibition could seem less burdensome, because the use of the other trees was free. Whence Rupertus, book II on the Works of the Trinity, chapter 50: 'The abstinence from one tree would have been light in such great abundance, if benevolence, the leader of abstinence, had not been lacking.' However, this expression, 'by eating you shall eat of every tree,' is not preceptive, as Thomas wishes in part I, question 97, article 3, but permissive: because man, by the guidance of nature, with no one commanding, was going to do that, nor did he need a mandate more for using food than for using drink. Nor indeed was it necessary to eat from every fruit, but it was free. Gen. 3, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 16. EX OMNI LIGNO PARADISI COMEDE.)

Homerus: – – – – – ἐσθλὰ δὲ πάντα Τοῖσιν ἔην, καρπὸν δ᾽ ἔφερε ζείδωρος ἄρουρα Αὐτομάτη, πολλόν τε καὶ ἄφθονον.

Relinquamus Grotio suum commentandi genus, ex Homero, & id genus aliis Scriptoribus. Quod frequens est in his annotatis. Dat Deus ho- mini liberrimam potestatem vescendi omnium ar- borum fructibus, ea excepta, quam peculiariter vetat. Quo minus gravis videri poterat hæc prohi- bitio, quia cæterarum arborum usus erat liber. Un- de Rupertus lib. II. de Operib. Trinit. cap. L. Levis fuiffet in tanta copia unius arboris continentia, si non defuisset continentia dux benevolentia. Non est au- tem hæc loquutio, comedendo comedes ex omni ar- bore, præceptiva, uti Thomas vult part. I. quæst. XCVII. art. 3. sed permissiva: quia homo naturæ ductu, nullo jubente, id erat facturus, nec magis de cibo, quam de potu usurpando mandato indige- bat. Neque vero necessarium erat ex omni fructu comedere, sed liberum Gen. 3, 2.

## 2:17
Ver. 17. BUT OF THE TREE OF THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOOD AND EVIL YOU SHALL NOT EAT.

In the Hebrew is added תאכל 'you shall not eat' from it, which, as Abenezra observes, is not added pleonastically, but either to declare the sense more clearly, or for the sake of emphasis, so that the sense may be that not even the least bit is to be eaten from that tree. Severianus in the Greek Catena says: Three differences of trees occur in Paradise, one given to man that he might live, another that he might live well, the third that he might live forever.

Ver. same. FOR IN WHATEVER DAY YOU SHALL EAT.) that is: as soon as you shall eat. A similar form of speaking, Dan. 3, v. 5, 15.

YOU SHALL DIE THE DEATH.) Your powers, sustained before by the tree of life, will fail: which is the way to death. The Syrian interpreters here had, 'you will be mortal': which Ambrose and Jerome note.

The gloss is too jejune. For God does not threaten only a failure of powers, nor only mortality. If that gloss held ground, God would threaten nothing but the deprivation of the tree of life, which He would no longer wish to grant for the sustaining of powers, so that not only a deficiency of powers, but death itself would follow naturally and of its own accord. Which was the error of the Pelagians: 'They say that Adam himself also, if he had not sinned, would have died in body, and not died by the merit of guilt, but by the condition of nature,' says Augustine on heresies, chapter 88. Now it is the error of the Socinians, with their UNLUCKY Master leading the way, whose opinion this was: 'Adam, before he sinned, as far as his nature pertains, was mortal, as he was after sin. But after sin, he was not only mortal by nature, but also thoroughly liable to death.' Then also of some Anabaptists and Arminians; Stephanus Curcellæus, book on the Law of God, ch. 11, p. 130. Even if Adam were mortal, it did not necessarily follow that he had to die: for God, out of special grace, could have preserved him from death; indeed, as we believe, He would have actually preserved him, if he had persisted in his original integrity. To this matter the tree of life would have first contributed. -- But since by sin he had rendered himself unworthy of that favor, God left him to his own fragile nature, and no longer granted him the use of the tree of life, which could have strengthened it, so that he necessarily had to die, just as God had threatened. Moreover, that other explanation of the Syrians, which Grotius praises and does not disapprove, refutes that fiction: the Syrian interpreters held here, 'you will be mortal,' which Ambrose and Jerome note. We add the fuller paraphrase of Theodoret, who interprets it from Symmachus thus: 'you will be mortal, and every day you will expect death.' But most fully Augustine, book 13, On the City of God, ch. 15. That threat has encompassed whatever there is of death up to the last, which is called the second, and after which there is none later. Which he explains at greater length in the same place: and as regards the spiritual death of the soul, which consists in the privation of the grace of God, or separation from the spiritual life which is in God, Eph. 4:18, thus St. Augustine paraphrases this threat: 'On the day that you desert me through disobedience, I will desert you through justice,' and there can be no doubt concerning the death of grace; because through the turning away from God, the first-formed humans deprived themselves of the grace and life of GOD. Moreover, it seems to be explained also concerning bodily death in Wisdom 2:24, when 'he was created for incorruption,' but 'by the envy of the devil death entered into the world,' man contracted the guilt and debt of death through transgression, so that he was not only made mortal from immortal, but became subject to death itself, which he also began to feel, deprived of the good of immortality. Concerning which Gregory the Great, homily 37 on the Gospels: 'that daily decay of corruption, what else is it but a certain prolixity of death?' Regarding these things, however, as far as temporal death is concerned, whether it was designated here or not? See, if you please, our 'second thoughts' in our Commentary on Genesis, p. 265 ff. and p. 481 ff. But eternal and infernal death, as it was brought in by sin, so it was entirely included in the divine threat: which follows the death of grace or spiritual death without doubt, and cannot but follow, unless man is received back into grace. 'The wages of sin is death,' Rom. 6:23. 'Through sin death entered,' Rom. 5:12. Which are asserted more fully elsewhere against the Socinians. It was the duty of Grotius, who constitutes tradition as the interpreter of Scripture, not to neglect the tradition of the ancients, which he has in this case as entirely opposed to himself. For antiquity did not only condemn this error of Grotius in Pelagius, as Augustine testifies everywhere: which was also done in the plenary African Council of Milevis: by pronouncing anathema on him who taught that Adam was made mortal: But even before Pelagius was born, the most ancient Doctors of the Church denied that man was mortal by nature: Cyprian, Sermon on the Good of Patience, says in that, 'in the first transgression of the commandment, the firmness of the body departed with IMMORTALITY, and with death came infirmity.' Tertullian, book on the Soul, ch. 52: 'We who know the origins of man, boldly determine that death followed man NOT FROM NATURE, but from fault, and not even from NATURAL fault.' Finally, 'if he had not sinned, he would by no means have died': Thus it was not NATURE, which happened from the power of choice through WILL, not from the authority of the institution through necessity. And before these, Tatian, Oration against the Greeks: Then Irenæus also, book 3, ch. 20. We have brought forward other Doctors of the Church from antiquity in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony, Sect. 11, ch. 11, subsection 4, p. 251 ff.

Latin:

Vers. 17. DE LIGNO AUTEM SCIENTIÆ BONI ET MALI NE COMEDAS.

In Ebræo additur תאכל non comedes ex ea, quod observante Abenezra non pleonastice adjectum, sed vel ad sensum magis perspicue declarandum, vel em- phaseos causa, ut sensus sit, ne minimum quidem ex ea arbore esse comedendum. Severianus in Cat. Græc. Tres arborum, inquit, differentiæ in Paradiso occur- runt, una homini data ut viveret, altera ut bene viveret, tertia ut semper viveret.

Vers. eod. IN QUOCUNQUE ENIM DIE COMEDE- RIS.) id est: cum primum comedes. Simile loquendi Genus Dan. 3. v. 5. 15.

MORTE MORIERIS.) Vires tuæ sustentatæ ante per arborem vitæ, deficient: quæ via est ad mortem. Syri inter- pretes hic habebant, mortalis eris: quod notant Ambrosius & Hieronymus.

Glossa nimis jejuna. Nec enim tantum vi- rium defectum minatur Deus, neque solum mortali- tatem. Si glossa illa locum haberet, nil nisi privatio- nem arboris vitæ Deus minaretur, quam ad virium sustentationem concedere nollet amplius, ut na- tura & sponte sequutura sit non tantum deficien- tia virium, sed ipsa mors. Qui Pelagianorum fuit error: Ipsum quoque Adam dicant, si non peccasset, fuisse corpore moriturum, neq; mortuum merito cul- pæ, sed conditione naturæ, ait Augustinus de hæresi c. LXXXIIX. Nunc est Socinianorum, præeunte INFAUSTO Magistro, cujus hæc fuit sententia. Adamus, antequam peccaret, quod ad ipsius naturam attinet, erat mortalis, ut post peccatum. Sed post pec- catum non modo natura mortalis, sed etiam morti penitus obnoxius fuit. Tum Anabaptistarum quoque nonnullorum & Arminianorum; Stephanus Cur- cellæus lib. de jure Dei c. 11. pag. 130. Etsi Adamus esset mortalis, non ideo necessario moriendum ipsi erat: Deus enim ex speciali gratia eum à morte servare poterat, imo ut credimus, reapse servasset, si in pri- ma integritate perstitisset. Cui rei primum inser- viisset arbor vitæ. -- Sed cum per peccatum se isto favore indignum reddidisset, Deus eum naturæ suæ fragili permisit, nec amplius arboris vitæ usum, quæ illam corroborare poterat, indulsit, ita, ut necessario ipsi, prout Deus comminatus erat, moriendum esset. Cæterum commento illi refragatur altera Syro- rum, quam laudat, non improbat Grotius, explica- tio: Syri interpretes hîc habebant, mortalis eris, quod notant Ambrosius & Hieronymus. Addimus ple- niorem Theodoreti paraphrasin; qui è Symmacho ita interpretatur: mortalis eris, & singulis diebus ex- pectabis mortem. Sed plenissime Augustinus lib. 13. de Civ. Dei c. 15. Quicquid est mortis usque ad novis- simam, quæ secunda dicitur, & qua est nulla posterior, comminatio illa complexa est. Quod ibidem plu- ribus exponit: & quod ad mortem spiritualem & animæ, quæ in privatione gratiæ Dei, vel separatione à spirituali vita, quæ in Deo est, consistit, Ephes. IV, 18. ita παραφράζει hanc comminationem S. Augu- stinus: Qua die me deserueritis per inobedientiam, deseram vos per justitiam, neque de morte gratiæ ul- lum esse potest dubium; quia per aversionem à Deo privarunt se Protoplasti gratia & vita DEI. Cæterum etiam de morte corporali explicari vide- tur Sap. II, 24. cum ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ conditus fuerit, invidia vero diaboli mors in mundum venerit, reatum atque debitum mortis contraxit homo per transgressionem, ut non tantum mortalis ex immor- tali factus sit, sed ipsi morti obnoxius, quam etiam sentire cœpit, bono immortalitatis privatus. Quo de Gregorius M. hom. XXXVII. in Evang. ipse quo- tidianus corruptionis defectus, quid aliud est, quam quædam prolixitas mortis? De hisce tamen quan- tum ad mortem temporalem, num ea designata hîc fuerit, nec ne? Φροντίδας δευτέρας vide sis in Com- ment. nostro in Genes. p. 265. seqq. & pag. 481. seqq. Mors autem æterna & infernalis uti per peccatum invecta, ita omnino comminatione divina com- prehensa fuit: quæ mortem gratiæ vel spiritualem indubitato sequitur, & non potest non sequi, nisi homo recipiatur vicissim in gratiam. Stipendium peccati mors est, Rom. 6, 23. Per peccatum mors in- travit, Rom. 5, 12. Quæ alias adversus Socinianos fusius adseruntur. Grotii traditionem Scripturæ interpretem constituentis hîc erat, traditionem vete- rum non negligere, quam habet in hac causa sibi prorsus adversam. Non enim damnavit solum antiquitas in Pelagio errorem istum Grotii, ut pas- sim testatur Augustinus: Quod in plenario etiam Africano Concilio Milevitano factum: Anathema- te dicto illi, qui Adamum mortalem factum docue- rit: Sed ante enatum etiam Pelagium hominem na- tura mortalem fuisse inficiati sunt vetustissimi Ec- clesiæ Doctores: Cyprianus Serm. de bona patient. in illa, inquit, prima transgressione præcepti firmi- tas corporis cum IMMORTALITATE discessit, & cum morte infirmitas venit. Tertullianus lib. de anima cap. LII. Qui primordia hominis novimus, au- denter determinamus, mortem NON EX NATU- RA secutam hominem, sed ex culpa, ne ipsa qui- dem NATURALI. Denique si non deliquisset, ne- quaquam obiisset: Ita non erat NATURA, quod ex oblationis potestate accidit per VOLUNTA- TEM, non ex instituti auctoritate per necessita- tem. Et ante hos Tatianus Orat. contra Græ- cos: Tum Irenæus quoque l. III. c. 20. Alios exam- tiquitate Doctores Ecclesiæ adduximus Harm. Ca- lixtino-Hæret. Sect. 11. c. 11. subsect. 4. p. 251. seqq.

## 2:18
Verse 18. IT IS NOT GOOD, THAT MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.

It is indicated in this way not only the goodness and necessity of marriage for preserving the human species, because God did not wish to create humans all at once like the Angels, but to derive the human race from one blood through propagation, Acts 17:26. But also with respect to the individual, because a companion of life made for the well-being of Adam, on account of the society of life, sweet conversation, and mutual help, as will now be indicated.

Verse same. A HELP LIKE TO HIMSELF.) In Hebrew 'kenegdo', before him, that is, that she may minister to him. Thus it is placed 1 Sam. 29:8, 1 Kings 10:8. Paul expressed the sense 1 Cor. 11:9, see also below 3:12. Cicero from Xenophon's Economics: 'Martial marriage is so arranged by nature, that not only the most pleasant, but also the most useful society of life might be entered into, and so that the human race might not perish through the length of time. For this reason the male is joined with the female: then so that from this same mortality, helps for old age, and no less bulwarks, might be prepared.' Where you see the very word 'help'.

Lud. de Dieu explains the word 'kenegdo' otherwise: 'According to his anterior parts,' from 2 Kings 1:13, Psalm 38:12, that is, that it corresponds to his anterior parts, so that the use of matrimony is regarded; and he wishes that Onkelos translated it thus; 'according to his anterior,' and Jonathan, 'it is not right that man should sleep alone; I will make for him a wife, who will be leaning against his anterior'; and in that way he interprets also the Arabic translation. Neither explanation satisfies. There is a greater emphasis in the Hebrew word, which denotes such a help, which is always before him, and around him, and is not at all torn away from him, and thus we accept Onkelos' 'kekablah' (near, before him), indeed that word is explained even by Moses v. 24 through the verb 'dabaq', which implies individual association and conversation, Ruth 2:7, 2 Sam. 20:2, as also the closest bond of love, Psalm 63:9, Jerem. 13:11, which is [used] by the LXX Interpreters as also by Matt. ch. 19:5, Mark 10:7. In Paul to the Ephesians 5:31, προσκολληθήσεται is rendered as 'shall be glued to'. The little word נגד comes from נגד, 'he indicated'. Therefore, the sweetness of conversation and of living together is indicated at the same time, and that he can use her services as a messenger, as some explain. It signifies 'in the presence of', 'before', 'near', and is a noun of presence, so that an inseparable and most sweet 'before-ness', if I may say so, or presence is designated, by which they may always provide mutual services to one another and offer helping hands, and that most intimate, most sacred, most honorable, and most pleasant companionship, an inviolable bond of friendship, and the most solid foundation of most certain love may be expressed.

Latin:

Vers. 18. NON EST BONUM, HOMINEM ESSE SOLUM.

Indicatur ita non solum bonitas & necessitas conjugii ad speciem humanam conservandam, quia noluit Deus homines ut Angelos simul universos creare, sed ex uno sanguine genus humanum per propagationem deducere, Act. 17, 26. Sed etiam respectu individui, quia ad bene esse Adami faciebat vitæ consors, ob vitæ societatem, suavem conver- sationem, & mutuum adjutorium, uti jam indica- bitur.

Vers. eod. ADJUTORIUM SIMILE SIBI.) Hebraice כנגדו coram ipso, id est, ut ministret ipsi. Sic ponitur 1. Sam. 29, 8. 1. Reg. 10, 8. Sensum expressit Paulus 1. Cor. 11, 9. vide & infra 3, 12. Cicero ex Oeconomicis Xenophon- tis: Martiale conjugium sic comparatum est natura, ut non so- lum jucundissima, verum etiam utilissima vitæ societas iniretur, & ne genus humanum temporis longinquitate occideret. Pro- pter hoc mas cum fœmina est conjunctus: deinde ut ex eadem hac mortalitate adjutoria senectutis, nec minus propugnacula præparentur. Ubi vides ipsam adjutorii vocem.

Aliter explicat vocem כנגדו Lud. de Dieu: Secundum anteriora ejus è 2. Reg. 1, 13. Psalm. 38, 12. id est, quod anterioribus ejus respondeat, ut usus matrimonii respiciatur; Atque ita Onkelosum trans- tulisse vult; secundum anterius ipsius, & Jonatha- nem, non est rectum, ut homo dormiat solus; faciam ei uxorem, quæ erit incumbens in anteriori ejus; eoque modo interpretatur etiam Arabicam translatio- nem. Neutra explicatio satisfacit. Major empha- sis est in voce Ebræa, quæ tale adjutorium notat, quod semper coram eo, & circa eum sit, & ab eo minime avulsum sit, atque ita accipimus Onkelosi כקבלה juxta, coram eo, imo ita exponitur etiam ea vox à Mose v. 24. per verbum דבק quod indivi- duam associationem & conversationem infert Ruth. 2, 7. 2. Sam. 20, 2. ut & arctissimum amoris vinculum Psalm. 63, 9. Jerem. 13, 11. quod à LXX. Interpp. ut & à Matth. c. 19, 5. Marc. 10, 7. Paulo ad Ephes. 5, 31. redditur προσκολληθήσεται agglutinabitur. Vo- cula נגד est à נגד indicavit. Ideo suavitas con- versationis & collocationis simul indicatur, & quod ejus opera tanquam nuntii maritus uti possit, ut nonnulli explicant. Significat coram, ante, prope, & nomen est præsentiæ, ut indivulsa & sua- vissima anteitas, ut ita dicam, vel præsentia de- signetur, qua semper mutuas sibi operas præstare, ac manus auxiliatrices præbere possint, & arctissi- mum, sacratissimum, honestissimum & jucundissi- mum illud contubernium, inviolabile amicitiæ vin- culum, solidissimum amoris certissimi firmamentum exprimatur.

## 2:18 Addition
Ver. 18. HE SAID ALSO &c. IT IS NOT GOOD. at p. 238. b.

Stapleton wishes this to be personal, said of Adam alone. at 1 Cor. 7, 1. from the demonstrative ה: But just as God founded all in the first man, so in the first marriage He sanctified the marriage of posterity. And if this concerned Adam alone, where would the human race have remained? How would the institution of marriage pertain to posterity? God did not say: It is not good for this man to be alone: but: It is not good, namely for the whole species to be procreated, for this man to be alone. Therefore afterwards it is said without the article: על־כן man shall leave Father and mother: Perer. Comm. in Gen. p. 463. says that this holds only for the O. T., where the human race was not yet propagated, but that in the N. T. that 1 Cor. 7, 1 obtains: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. In which error Tertullian, Jerome, and Augustine also were. But in that way the Hieracites would not have been justly condemned: Since, however, Christ by His coming neither abolished nor contracted the blessing of marriage, but willed it to be increased and sanctified it, by being born in marriage, though not from marriage: whence He was also present at weddings, and vindicated marriage from blemishes, Matt. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DIXIT QUOQUE &c. NON EST BONUM. ad p. 238. b.

Personale hoc esse de solo Adamo dictum vult Stapleton. ad 1. Cor. 7, 1. ex ה demonftrativo: Sed ut Deus in primo homine omnes condidit, ita in primo conjugio conjugium posterorum sanctifi- cavit. Et si Adamum solum hoc concerneret, ubi mansisset genus humanum? Quomodo institutio conjugii ad posteros pertineret? Non dixit Deus: Non est bonum huic homini esse solum: sed :- Non est bonum, nempe toti speciei procreandæ hunc ho- minem esse solum. Ideo postea absque articulo dicitur: על־כן homo relinquet Patrem ac matrem: Perer. Comm. in Gen. p. 463. hoc valere tantum de V. T. ubi genus humanum nondum propagatum, de N. vero T. obtinere ait illud 1. Cor. 7, 1. Bonum est homini, non attingere uxorem. Quo in errore et- iam Tertul. Hieron. Aug. fuerunt. Sed ita non essent juste damnati Hieracitæ: Quum tamen Christus adventu suo benedictionem conjugii neque sustu- lerit neque contraxerit, sed auctam voluerit atque sanctificarit, nascendo in conjugio, licet non ex conjugio: unde & nuptiis interfuit, & a nævis conjugium vindicavit Matth. 19.

## 2:19
Verse 19. THEREFORE, THE LORD GOD HAVING FORMED FROM THE GROUND ALL THE LIVING CREATURES OF THE EARTH, AND ALL THE BIRDS OF THE HEAVEN, BROUGHT THEM TO ADAM.

All the living creatures of the earth are indeed said to be formed from the ground, and all the birds of the heaven are also said to be formed, but it is not necessary for that 'from the ground' to be extended to the birds, as Corn. à Lap. and Menoch. observe. Therefore, Bochart in his Hierozoicon denies in vain from this passage that birds were produced from the water. Compare Gen. 1:19.

These were the first, as it were, assemblies of the world, to which all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the heaven were gathered by the edict of the supreme Monarch, God, so that they might be subjected to the power and dominion of man: they were brought, however, not only by an ideal representation made before the mind, as Cajetan thinks, but by a real gathering, though not through a daily and laborious collection, but solely by the nod and command of God, to whom all things obey, and in a moment they stand ready.

Verse same. THAT HE MIGHT SEE WHAT HE WOULD CALL THEM.) It is a sign of Dominion, as Chrysostom rightly noted. This is manifest from Psalm 147:4.

Not only is Dominion designated here, but the primeval wisdom of Adam is also indicated, who from the mere inspection of the living creatures was able to impose suitable names upon each one. Nor is there any need for us to conclude with Peyrère that he consumed many days in a prolix examination and reasoning of the animals, much less to admit the insipid fiction about Adam's Preceptor, by whom he himself as a youth was taught natural history, as the Sabaeans or Nabataeans, Arabs, Idolaters, and Heaven-worshippers dreamed, that Adam was a man born of a man and a woman, an Apostle of the Moon, who called men to the worship of the Moon, and that his Preceptor was one named Jambuscha, as witnessed by R. Judah in the book Cosri ch. 3, to which the Pre-Adamite does not entirely disagree. Since Adam was created most wise by GOD, and either had the notions of created things impressed upon his mind, or certainly from the light of nature perceived the natures of living creatures far more profoundly than all Anatomists with their countless dissections: there is no doubt that that inspection could have been done in a short time and without prior instruction.

Verse same. FOR EVERY LIVING SOUL THAT ADAM CALLED, THAT IS THE NAME THEREOF.

In Hebrew it is: WHAT HE SHALL CALL. Thus the Adamic naming is confirmed by the most wise Judgment and sentence of God, from which it appears that names highly suitable to the nature of the animals and birds were imposed by Adam; through wisdom God-given and divinely implanted. Truly blessed Luther here: There exist various books which describe the natures of plants and beasts, but how much time, how long an observation was needed, while these were being collected thus through experience. There was a different light in Adam, who as soon as he inspected an animal, had its entire nature and powers known, and far better than we, even when we devote our whole life to the investigation of these things. This knowledge in Adam, just as it was an excellent gift of God, so also it wondrously pleased God and was acceptable to Him. St. Chrysostom, he says, GOD did this, not only to demonstrate to us the great Wisdom of Adam, but also so that the Symbol of Dominion might be known through the imposition of names. For it is the custom for men to do this as a sign of Dominion, as when they buy slaves, they change their names. Whence also he instructs Adam to impose names upon all brutes as their Lord. Cf. also Lyranus in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 19. FORMATIS IGITUR, DOMINUS DEUS, DE HUMO CUNCTIS ANIMANTIBUS TERRÆ, ET UNIVERSIS VOLATILIBUS COELI, ADDUXIT EA AD ADAM.

Formata de Humo quidem dicuntur cuncta animantia terræ, formata etiam universa volatilia cœli, sed non necessum est illud de humo ad volati- lia pertrahi. Ut Corn. à Lap. & Menoch. obser- vant. Ideo frustra ex hoc loco negat Bochardus in Hierozoic. aves ex aqua productas esse. Conf. Gen. I, 19.

Erant hæc prima q. mundi comitia, ad quæ congregabantur edicto Dei supremi Monarchæ omnia terræ animantia, & omnia cœli volatilia, ut subderentur potestati & imperio hominis: ad- ducta autem non solum repræsentatione ideali co- ram mente facta, ut Cajetanus putat, sed reali con- gregatione, non tamen per diurnam & operosam collectionem, sed solo nutu & mandato Dei, cui omnia parent, & in momento se sistunt.

Vers. eod. UT VIDERET QUID VOCARET EA.) Est id Dominii fignum, ut recte notavit Chrysostomus. Mani- festum id ex Psalmo CXLVII, 4.

Non tantum Dominium hîc designatur, sed in- dicatur etiam primæva Adami sapientia, qui ex so- la inspectione animantium cuivis nomina conve- nientia imponere potuit. Neque vero opus est, ut cum Peyrerio prolixa animantium διασκέψει ac ratiocinatione dies multos ipsum consumsisse sta- tuamus, nedum ut insulsum commentum de Præ- ceptore Adami, à quo ipse Ephebus naturalem historiam edoctus fuerit, admittamus, uti somnia- runt Sabæi vel Nabothei, Arabes, Idololatræ ac Cæ- licolæ, Adamum virum fuisse, ex viro & fœmina progenitum, Apostolum Lunæ, qui homines vo- carit ad cultum Lunæ, & Præceptorem ejus fuisse Jambuscha nomine dictum, teste R. Juda in libr. Cosri c. 3. quibus non omnino abnuit Præ-Ada- mita. Cum Adam sapientissimus à DEO conditus fuerit, & vel impressas habuerit menti suæ rerum creatarum notiones, vel certe ex lumine naturæ ani- mantium naturas longe profundius aspexerit, quam Anatomici omnes sectionibus innumeris: illam lu- strationem brevi tempore, ac sine prævia institutio- ne fieri potuisse, dubitandum non est.

Vers. eod. OMNE ENIM QUOD VOCAVIT ADAM ANIMÆ VIVENTIS, IPSUM EST NOMEN E- JUS.

In Ebræo est: QUOD VOCABIT. Con- firmatur ita ὀνομαθεσία Adamica, Sapientissimo Dei Judicio, & sententia, unde apparet nomina ap- prime naturæ animantium & volatilium convenien- tia ab Adamo imposita fuisse; per Sapientiam θεόσδοτον, ac divinitus implantatam. Vere B. Luthe- rus hîc: Extant varii libri, qui Plantarum & be- stiarum naturas describunt, sed quanto tempore, quam longe observatione opus fuit; dum hæc per ex- perientiam ita colligerentur. Aliud in Adamo lumen fuit, qui statim ut inspexit animal, totam ejus naturam, & vires habuit cognitas, ac longe melius quam nos, etiam cum totam vitam ad inquisitionem harum rerum conferimus. Hæc cognitio in Ada- mo, sicut fuit donum Dei excellens, ita etiam Deo mi- re placuit & grata fuit. S. Chrysostomus, fecit, inquit, hoc DEUS, non solum demonstraturus nobis magnam Adami Sapientiam, sed ut & Symbolum Dominii per nominum impositionem cognoscatur. Nam hominibus mos est, hoc facere in signum Domi- nii, ut cum servos emerint, ipsorum nomina mutent. Unde & Adam instruit, ut omnibus brutis tanquam Dominus nomina indat. Conf. & Lyran. in h. l.

## 2:20
Verse 20. AND ADAM CALLED BY THEIR NAMES ALL LIVING CREATURES; AND ALL THE BIRDS OF THE HEAVEN, AND ALL THE BEASTS OF THE EARTH.

Adam did not record those names in a codicil, as the Pre-Adamite feigns, nor did he lose them through the fall, as some wish, for thus a new naming would have been necessary; and God testifies here: every living soul that Adam called, that IS its name. The names remained, even if the reason for the imposed names, along with that very primeval wisdom and knowledge of the nature of animals, has been much obliterated.

Verse same. BUT FOR ADAM THERE WAS NOT FOUND A HELPER LIKE UNTO HIM.

That is to say, with Chrysostom as interpreter: these all (the animals) were indeed produced, and received their names from Adam, yet nothing from all these was found worthy of being his helper. For however much service these brutes exhibit to us, yet another helper is more excellent, LIKE UNTO HIMSELF, that is, of the same substance, and in dignity nothing inferior to him.

Latin:

Vers. 20. APPELLAVITQUE ADAM NOMINI- BUS SUIS CUNCTA ANIMANTIA; ET UNIVER- SA VOLATILIA COELI, ET OMNES BESTIAS TERRÆ.

Ea nomina neque Codicillo, ut fingit Præ- Adamita, consignavit Adam, neque ut nonnulli volunt deperdidit per lapsum, sic enim nova ὀνό- μαθεσία opus fuisset; & testatur hic Deus: omne, quod vocaverit Adam animam viventem, ipsum EST nomen ejus. Nomina manserunt, etsi ratio impositorum nominum cum ipsa primigenia sapien- tia, & cognitione naturæ animantium multum ob- literata sit.

Vers. eod. ADÆ VERO NON INVENIEBATUR AD- JUTOR SIMILIS EJUS.

Q. d. interprete Chrysostomo: hæc omnia qui- dem (animalia) producta sunt, & ab Adam sua no- mina acceperunt, nihil tamen ex his omnibus dignum fuit inventum illius adjutorio. Quantumcunque enim ministerium exhibent nobis hæc bruta, aliud tamen adjutorium est excellentius, SIMILE SIBI, id est, ejusdem substantiæ, dignitateque illo nihil in- ferius.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. THEREFORE GOD SENT A DEEP SLEEP UPON ADAM.

Aquila interpreted the word תרדמה as κατάφορὰν [a heavy sleep], Symmachus as κᾰρον, i.e., a heavy and profound sleep. Procopius says that it is called a sleep or ecstasy because Adam was deprived of his usual faculty of sensing, as God sometimes is accustomed to do, so that He may fittingly bring His own purposes to an end. Therefore, Lyranus concludes that this sleep was not naturally caused, but sent by God, so that Adam would not see the removal of his rib. Rupertus, however, thinks that while the senses of the body were closed, the sense of the mind was left free through the sleep, so that he might know what the artificer of all things, the wisdom of God, was doing regarding him. But it was a true sleep, not an ἔκςασις, which God sent, so that Adam would not be a spectator of that divine formation, but an admirer of the formed work, just as he found the remaining works of GOD created in the world, but saw the creation of none himself.

Vers. eod. OF HIS RIBS.) The Chaldean explained the word צלע as a part: as Maimonides observed: thus also the Greeks translated it μέρος in Exod. 26, 26. 35. c. 36, 27. The Egyptians, according to Achmetes, referred ribs in dreams to wives.

The name of a part is general: but here the discourse is specifically about a rib. It is not necessary to translate these as 'two-bodied' according to R. Menasse in Conciliat. quest. 8, page 14, regarding the Rabbis who babble that Adam and Eve were created joined together at the beginning, but rather 'ONE OF HIS SIDES,' because the word צלע also denotes a side, Exod. XXVI, 20. So that the sense is that God split and dissected that androgynous body, and divided one from the other when the woman was glued to the man's shoulders as if with pitch, so that Adam was in front and Eve was behind. Menasse brings forward clear proofs of this commentary of his, worthy of the Rabbinical genius, from Ps. CXXXIX, 5, 'You have fashioned me behind and before,' and from the fable of Plato in the Symposium from Aristophanes about the androgynous beginning of the human race: and so that nothing is missing, he even removes the scruple for those who ask, which of them walked forward when the male and female were joined? deciding from the Gemara in favor of Adam's body as being more robust.

But we dismiss the Rabbinical dreams, which even our Hugo held to be vain. We also dismiss the commentaries of the Egyptians; but it is helpful to hear Augustine, who declares this first and extraordinary sleep spiritually in quest. XLV to Orosius, for he thinks a mystery is signified there. God could have done it otherwise, but He judged it more congruent to do it in such a way that something might be signified. For just as a rib is drawn from the sleeping Adam so that a spouse may be made; so also blood is poured out from the side of the dying Christ so that the Church may be constructed. For the Church of Christ is made a communicant to the body and blood of Christ, becoming His spouse. The same in the Sentences n. CCCXXIIX. Adam sleeps, so that Eve may be made; Christ dies, so that the Church may be made: While Adam sleeps, Eve is made from his side; when Christ is dead, His side is pierced by a lance, so that the Sacraments may flow forth, by which the Church is formed. Hence therefore, some are accustomed to fix the type of the death and resurrection of Christ in the sleeping Adam, when Eve was fashioned from the rib taken from his opened side, and that was closed again with flesh, whence the newly formed woman was given in marriage to Adam as he awoke from a deep sleep. But one must distinguish here between allegory and type. For allegory, these things can be admitted, so that a certain comparison is established between the first Adam and the second, regarding the sleep, the opening of the side, the taking of the rib, the formation of the spouse, and her matrimonial union after he had awakened; but to establish a type in these things, as if God had wished by that means to foreshadow the future death and resurrection of Christ, is by no means permitted. For in the state of integrity there was no need for the passion or death of Christ, nor for the foreshadowing of the same: for this is done to that end, namely, that what is signified by the type may be embraced by faith. For faith in the Messiah had no place before the fall.

Verse same. AND HE FILLED UP THE FLESH IN ITS STEAD.

What Hugo of St. Victor in the Douai Bible says was done, he says, lest there be an unsightly pit, if it were entirely empty, or if bone were regenerated for bone, no sign would remain of the removed rib, by which it is evident that there is only one beginning of the human race, and therefore the sign was retained, just as the scars of Christ also for a triumph.

Latin:

Vers. 21. IMMISIT ERGO DEUS SOPOREM IN ADAM.

Vocem תרדמה Aquila κατάφορὰν, Symma- chus κᾰρον, i. e. gravem & profundum soporem inter- pretati sunt. Procopius, Sopor, inquit, vel ecstasis di- citur ideo, quod Adamus fuerit solitæ sentiendi fa- cultate privatus, ut assolet interdum Deus, quo sua decenter ad finem deducat, facere. Ideo Lyranus colligit, quod iste sopor non fuerit naturaliter cau- satus, sed à Deo immissus, ne Adam videret amotio- nem costæ suæ. Rupertus tamen obturatis sensibus corporis sensum mentis liberum relictum per soporem, putat, ut scire posset, quid erga se ageret omnium ar- tifex sapientia Dei. Cæterum somnus verus fuit, non ἔκςασις, quem immisit Deus, ut Adam divinæ istius formationis non spectator, sed formati operis admirator esset, uti etiam reliqua DEI opera in mundo creata invenit, nullius creationem ipse vidit.

Vers. eod. DE COSTIS EJUS.) Chaldæus vocem צלע exposuit partem: ut observavit Maimonides: sic & Græci μέ- ρος verterunt Exod. 26, 26. 35. c. 36, 27. Ægyptii costas in so- mniis ad uxores referebant, teste Achmete.

Partis nomen generale est: hic vero speciali- ter sermo est de costa. Rabbinos, qui concorpo- res conditos initio Adamum & Evam nugantur, non bicorpores vertere hæc secundum R. Menasse in Conciliat. quæst. 8. pag. 14. oportet, UNUM EX LATERIBUS EJUS, quia vocabulum צלע etiam latus notat, Exod. XXVI, 20. ut sensus sit discidisse & dissecasse Deum corpus illud ἀνδρόγυνον, & alterum ab altero divisisse cum mulier viri scapu- lis quasi pice agglutinata esset, ita ut à fronte Ada- mus, à tergo Eva esset. Cujus commenti sui præ- claras & Rabbinico genio dignas probationes ad- fert Menasses è Ps. CXXXIX, 5. retro & ante forma- sti me, & è fabula Platonis in Symposio ex Aristo- phane de principio humani generis androgyno: ac ne quid desit, scrupulum etiam eximit illis, qui quærunt, uter ex illis, cum juncti erant mas & fæmi- na, antrorsum incesserit? decidens è Gemara pro Adami corpore ceu robustiore.

Sed mittimus somnia Rabbinica, quæ Hu- go etiam noster pro vanis habuit. Mittimus etiam commenta Ægyptiorum; Augustinum vero juvat audire, spiritualiter somnum hunc primum, & ex- traordinarium declarantem quæst. XLV. ad Oro- sium, significatum enim ibi mysterium putat. Poterat id Deus etiam aliter facere, sed ideo con- gruentius judicavit, ut sic faceret, unde aliquid si- gnificaretur. Sicut enim dormienti Adæ costa de- trahitur, ut conjux efficiatur; ita & Christo morienti de latere sanguis effunditur, ut Ecclesia construatur. Communicans nempe corpori & sanguini Christi efficitur Ecclesia Christi conjux. Idem in sententiis n. CCCXXIIX. Dormit A- dam, ut fiat Eva, moritur Christus, ut fiat Eccle- sia: Dormiente Adam fit Eva de latere; mortuo Christo lancea perforatur latus, ut supereffluant Sacramenta, quibus formatur Ecclesia. Hinc er- go solent nonnulli typum mortis & resurrectionis Christi in Adamo dormiente figere, cum è latere ejus aperto costa exemta Eva fabricata est, idque carne vicissim clausum fuit, unde Adamo è somno profundo evigilanti in matrimonium data noviter formata mulier. Sed distinguere hîc oportet inter Allegoriam & typum. Pro allegoria ista admitti possunt, ut instituatur comparatio quædam inter Adamum primum, & secundum, quoad dormitionem, lateris apertionem, costæ exemtionem, sponsæ efformationem, ejusdemque postquam evigilasset, matrimonialem copulationem; Typum vero in istis constituere, quasi voluerit Deus Adamo ea ratione futuram Christi mortem & resurrectionem adumbrare, neutiquam licet. In statu enim integritatis neque passione aut morte Christi opus erat, nec ejusdem adumbratione: Hæc enim eo fine fit, ut nempe fide suspiciatur, quod per typum significatur. Fides enim in Messiam ante lapsum locum non habuit.

Vers. eod. ET REPLEVIT CARNEM PRO EA.

Quod Hugo de S. Victore in Bibl. Duacens. factum, ait, ne aut turpis esset fossa, si vacua omnino, aut si os pro osse regeneraretur, nullum signum remanere ablatæ costæ, per quod constat unum tantum principium generis humani, & ideo retentum est signum, sicut etiam cicatrices Christi in triumphum.

## 2:22
Verse 22. AND THE LORD GOD BUILT THE RIB, WHICH HE HAD TAKEN FROM ADAM, INTO A WOMAN: AND BROUGHT HER TO ADAM.

St. Ambrose says that it is not idle that the woman was made not from the same earth from which Adam was fashioned, but from his own rib, so that we might know that there is one nature of body in man and woman, one fountain of the human race; therefore not two were made from the beginning, man and woman, nor two men, nor two women, but first man, then from him woman. Theodoret: God fashioned the female from the side of Adam, so that He might join two species together, and reconcile loves, and they might be coupled together by a certain natural friendship: which, so that it might be done more tightly and tenaciously, He also joined with the bond of marriage. It was done, therefore, both because of the ὁμουσίαν or unity of substance, and because of the unity of the beginning and origin of all men from one man, because Eve was from him, just as all others were from the same joined rib: and also because of the natural friendship and love with the spouse. Hugo Victor further observes: it was not taken from the head, nor from the feet, that from which the woman was to be made: lest she be thought either a mistress, if from the head, or a handmaid, if from the feet: therefore, he says, it was fitting to be taken from the middle, that is, the rib, so that she might be understood as a companion. The word 'built' implies both an accurate structure, and the likeness of a building, and use, because a woman is to a man as a house; but that the rib was built not into the body of the woman, but into the woman, is an argument for traducianism, as Augustine notes in book 1 de orig. anim. c. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET ÆDIFICAVIT DOMINUS DEUS COSTAM, QUAM TULERAT DE ADAM, IN MULIEREM: ET ADDUXIT EAM AD ADAM.

S. Ambrosius, illud non otiosum, inquit, quod non de eadem terra, de qua plasmatus est Adam, sed de ipsius costa facta est mulier, ut sciremus unam in viro & muliere esse corporis naturam, unum fontem generis humani; ideo non duo à principio facti vir & mulier, neque duo viri, neque duæ mulieres, sed primum vir, deinde ex eo mulier. Theodor. Deus è latere Adam fœminam finxit, ut duas species inter se conjungeret, & amores conciliaret & naturali quadam amicitia inter se copularentur: quod ut arctius, atque tenacius fieret, nuptiarum vinculo etiam conjugavit. Factum ergo id tum ob ὁμουσίαν seu unitatem substantiæ, tum ob unitatem principii & originis omnium hominum ex uno homine, quia ex illo Eva, uti & ex eodem costæ suæ juncto cæteri omnes: tum ob naturalem cum conjuge amicitiam & amorem. Observat porro Hugo Victor: non de capite, nec de pedibus sumptum esse id, unde fieret mulier: ne aut Domina, si de capite, aut ancilla, si de pedibus, putaretur: ideo, inquit, de medio, id est, costa sumi decuit, ut socia intelligeretur. Vox ædificavit & accuratam structuram, & ædificii similitudinem, & usum, quia mulier viro pro domo est, innuit; quod autem costa non in corpus mulieris, sed in mulierem ædificata, argumentum est pro traduce, notante Augustino libr. 1. de orig. anim. c. 17.

## 2:23
Verse 23. BONE OF MY BONES.) As if born from me. Servius on that line of the fourth Aeneid: 'Arise, some avenger, from our bones.' Indeed, the Punics say that descendants arise from bones: whom we call from blood. The Punic language is very close to Hebrew, as noted by others and by us elsewhere. Add 1 Cor. 11:8.

VIRAGO.) The Romans once called women 'V'. Noted by Festus. Thus in old Germanic from 'Man', which signifies man, comes 'minne', that is, woman, in the way that nurses are now called. Thence 'Meerminne', woman of the sea, Siren or Nereid: thence the verb 'minnen' γυναικοφιλεῖν, which was later used more loosely. Symmachus, when he could find nothing similar in the Greek language, coined the word ἀνδρίδα. This is more correct than that Theodotion derives נשה from נשא, which sometimes signifies to take up.

Adam speaks not of generation, but of divine creation, and that mediated, made from his flesh and his bones, or from his own substance, by the divine omnipotent hand. That the whole woman was produced from Adam was rightly observed by Grotius; which we have already warned that the Reformed wrongly deny. Furthermore, Jerome observes that Theodotion implies another etymology in this way: This shall be called 'taking', because she was taken from man. Because he thought that אשה could be deduced from נשא, to take. But from the Hebrew text it is too manifest that the appellation of woman is deduced from איש.

Latin:

Vers. 23. OS EX OSSIBUS MEIS.) Velut de me genita. Servius ad illud IV. Æneidos. Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor. Sane Punici ex ossibus dicunt oriri posteros: quos nos ex sanguine. Punicà lingua Hebrææ proxima, ut notatum & aliis, & nobis alibi. Adde 1. Cor. 11, 8.

VIRAGO.) V Romani olim feminas vocabant. Notatum Festo. Sic veteribus Germanicis à Man, quod virum fignificat minne, id est, foemina, quomodo nunc nutrices vo- cantur. Inde Meerminne, foemina maris, Siren sive Nereis: inde verbum minnen γυναικοφιλεῖν, quod postea laxius usurpatum. Symmachus cum in Græca lingua nihil re- periret simile, finxit vocem ἀνδρίδα. Hoc rectius, quam quod Theodotion נשה derivat à נשא, quod interdum si- gnificat affumere.

Non de generatione, sed creatione divina eaque mediata facta ex carne sua, & ossibus suis, vel ex sui substantia, divina omnipotente manu, lo- quitur Adam. Recte autem totam mulierem ex Adamo productam observatum Grotio; quod perperam negare Reformatos jam monuimus. Cæterum Hieronymus observat Theodotionem aliam Etymologiam innuere hoc modo: Hæc vocabitur affumtio, quia ex viro sumta est. Quod אשה à נשא affumere deduci posse censuerit. At è textu Ebræo nimis manifestum est deductam ab איש esse mulieris appellationem.

## 2:24
Verse 24. THEREFORE SHALL A MAN LEAVE HIS FATHER AND MOTHER.

Not by reason of filial love, but by reason of cohabitation, which the Targum expresses here: because a son, as Lyranus holds, when he is married, is immediately emancipated, and has to provide for himself and his wife, and his family. In vain, therefore, do the Papists infer from this passage that marriages can be entered into without the consent of parents, because the son is not commanded to pass over his parents by reason of contracting a marriage, which is repugnant to the commandment concerning obedience toward parents, but to leave the same after a marriage contracted with their consent.

Verse of the same. SHALL CLEAVE.) The Greeks more properly προσκολληθήσεται, as also the interpreter of Matthew XIX, 5. Mark X, 7. Paul Eph. V, 31.

That the Greek text of Matthew proceeded not from an interpreter, but from Matthew himself, the Apostle, has been shown before. That Matthew wrote in Hebrew cannot be demonstrated by solid documents. Tertullian rendered it 'shall be glued together.' Noted is both the undivided bond of love, Psalm LXIII, verse 9, and a perpetual and individual association and adhesion, not otherwise than if they were glued together, 2 Sam. II, v. 22. Micah II, v. 7.

Verse of the same. AND THEY SHALL BE TWO IN ONE FLESH.) That 'two,' which the Latin has here, both the Greeks, and the Samaritan, and the interpreter of Matthew XIX, 5, judged should be added to express the sense more fully. Aristotle in II Politics IV reports the opinion of Socrates thus: 'that those who are in love wish that, being two, they both become one.' Plutarch in his Symposiacs: 'so that being two they have become one.' Ovid in Tristia IV, 4.

Who were two in bodies, one in minds.

That explanatory particle can be elicited from the following verse: BOTH were naked. Moreover, there is a Hebraism in 'one flesh,' that is, one flesh, as Deut. XXVIII, v. 44, 'for a head, for a tail,' 1 Sam. IV, v. 9, 'for men.' Which Christ explains as 'one flesh,' Matt. XIX, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 24. QUAPROPTER RELINQUET HOMO PA- TREM SUUM ET MATREM.

Non ratione amoris filialis, sed ratione co- habitationis, quam hîc exprimit Targum : quia filius, ut Lyranus habet, cum est uxoratus, statim est emancipatus, & habet providere sibi & uxori, & familiæ. Nequicquam ergo ex hoc loco Pon- tificii colligunt sine consensu parentum iniri posse matrimonia, quia non præterire Parentes jube- tur filius ratione conjugii contrahendi, quod repu- gnat præcepto de obedientia erga parentes, sed re- linquere eosdem post conjugium, cum consensu eo- rum contractum.

Vers. eod. ADHÆREBIT.) Græci magis proprie προσκολ- ληθήσεται, ut & Matthæi interpres XIX, 5. Marcus X, 7. Pau- lus Eph. V, 31.

Græcum Matthæi textum non ab interprete, sed à Matthæo ipso, Apostolo profectum esse, antea ostensum. Ebraice Matthæum scripsisse, solidis documentis demonstrari nequit. Tertul- lianus reddidit conglutinabitur. Notatur tum indivisum amoris vinculum, Psalm. LXIII. vers. 9. tum perpetua & individua associatio, & adhæsio, non secus ac si conglutinati essent, 2. Sam. II. v. 22. Mich. II. v. 7.

Vers. eod. ET ERUNT DUO IN CARNE UNA.) Il- lud duo, quod hîc habet Latinus, ad sensum plenius expri- mendum addendum censuere & Græci, & Samaritanus, & Matthæi interpres XIX, 5. Socratis sententiam sic refert A- ristoteles II. Polit. IV. ἐρῶντας γενέσθαι ἐκ δύο ὄντων ἀμφοτέ- ρους ἕνα. Plutarchus Symposiacis: ὥσε δύο ὄντας ἕνα γεγονέναι. Ovidius Tristium IV, 4.

Qui duo corporibus, mentibus unus erant.

Erui potest particula illa ἐξηγητικὴ è versu sequente: AMBO erant nudi. Est autem E- braismus in carne una, id est, caro una, ut Deut. XXIIX. v. 44. in caput, in caudam, 1. Sam. IV. v. 9. in viros. Quem explicat Christus una caro, Matth. XIX, 6.

## 2:24 Addition
On ver. 24. towards the end note p. 240. b.

From that therefore it is evident that simultaneous polygamy is repugnant to the matrimonial law. For since these two are one flesh, namely the man with his spouse, if he were to join himself with another, he would certainly separate those whom God has joined, i.e., himself from his spouse, and would join himself with another against the divine ordination, as Christ most openly taught in the place cited. From which it is decided that he does not violate marriage who separates himself from his spouse by divorce, since the matrimonial bond is not immediately dissolved for that reason, but he who marries another woman, or whoever joins to himself such a one separated without legitimate cause, Matt. 19, 9. Nor is there any reason for the patrons of polygamy to say that a polygamist man can be one flesh with any of his wives, so that between them, even if he is joined to different ones, a relation is given, just as a Father has a relation to several Sons. Because here such a relation is not bare, as it is between Father and Son, but as two are one flesh, which relation if it be spread to many, the man will no longer be one flesh with one spouse, but with many, when nevertheless the man no longer has power over his own body, because of that relation to his own spouse, because he is already one flesh with her 1 Cor. 7, 4. and has entered into a covenant with her, which is not to be violated Mal. 2, 14. concerning which Aben-Ezra: women enter into the covenant of God with men, so that the man may not become perfidious against the woman, and vice versa. Conf. Ez. 16, 60. And Chrysost. Homil. 19. in Ep. ad Corinth. When a harlot has approached to tempt you, say that it is not your body but your wife's. Likewise also let the wife say against those who wish to assault her chastity: My body is not my own, but my husband's.

Latin:

Ad vers. 24. sub finem notar. p. 240. b.

Ex eo ergo constat, Polygamiam simultaneam legi matrimoniali repugnare. Quum enim hi duo una sint caro, vir nempe cum conjuge sua, si cum alia se jungeret, separaret utique, quos Deus conjunxit, h. e. semetipsum a conjuge sua, & cum altera contra divinam ordinationem se con- jungeret, uti l. c. Christus apertissime docuit. Ex quo decidit, conjugium violare, non qui a con- juge per divortium sese separat, quum ideo non statim vinculum matrimoniale dissolvatur, sed qui aliam mulierem ducit, aut quisquis talem ci- tra legitimam causam separatam sibi jungit, Matth. 19, 9. Nec est quod Polygamiæ patroni dicant, posse virum πολύγαμον cum quavis sua uxore esse in carnem unam, ut inter illos, etsi diversis jungatur, de- tur relatio, quemadmodum Pater ad Filios plures σχέσιν & relationem habet. Quia hic non nuda talis est relatio, qualis inter Patrem & Filium, sed qua duo in carnem unam sint, quæ σχέσις si ad plures spar- gatur, non amplius vir cum una conjuge, sed cum pluribus caro una erit, quum tamen vir non habeat amplius potestatem in corpus suum, ob istam rela- tionem ad propriam conjugem, quia cum ea jam est una caro 1. Cor. 7, 4. & fœdus cum ea iniit, quod violandum non est Mal. 2, 14. de quo Aben-Ezra: mulieres cum viris intrare fœdus Dei, ne vir fiat per- fidus contra mulierem, & vice versa. Conf. Ez. 16, 60. Et Chrysost. Homil. 19. in Ep. ad Corinth. Cum ad tentandum meretrix accesserit, dicas, non esse tuum corpus sed uxoris. Itidem & uxor dicat adversus eos, qui volunt expugnare pudicitiam: Corpus meum non est meum, sed viri.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

The fall of our first parents. The seed of the woman promised. The denunciation of the cross, and the ejection from Paradise.

Verse 1.

SERPENT.) Hence, I think, that serpent the guardian of the golden apples among the poets.

In the Hebrew, because of the He, it may be seen that the serpent is understood not as a species, but as a specific individual, the nature of which the subjoined history teaches, namely not a mere serpent, but one possessed by the Devil: for it is added concerning him, who said to the woman. Conf. 2. Corinth. XI, 3. But Eve was ignorant of this, who seems to have known nothing yet of the fall of the Angels. Which ignorance of pure negation could have had a place in the state of innocence. It did not escape Eve, says Tirinus, that these voices were formed by supernatural power, but she did not attend sufficiently, as she ought, to the fact that they were composed to tempt her. If you understand it of the species, the words must be taken in this way: And the serpent was more crafty than all the living creatures of the earth. And he said (repeating the word serpent ἀπὸ κοινοῦ) to the woman, so that it is now understood that he said this in the serpent, and through the serpent, which the context compels one to understand; or some serpent, but one possessed by Satan.

MORE CRAFTY.) Thus also Aquila, πανῦργος ἀπὸ παντὸς ζώυ: Thus Paul attributes craftiness to the serpent in 2. Corinth. XI, 3. and the Greeks everywhere in Job and Proverbs translate the Hebrew ערום as πανῦργον. But the LXX here [translate it as] φρονιμώτερος. For the word φρονιμος is accustomed to be taken in both a good and a bad sense, as appears in Luke XVI, 8. it is placed in a neutral sense in Matthew XVI, 16. where Christians are commanded to be φρόνιμοι as serpents. See concerning the asp in Psalm LVIII, 5. 6. It is to be noted, however, what Servius notes on the second Georgic, that some serpents crawl with their whole body, others are raised by a part of their body, where he also cites this verse of Lucan: And content to furrow the ground with its tail. Pliny, book 8, ch. 23, relates that the javelin, a kind of serpent, is vibrated from the branches of trees. Here it is called the flying serpent of the Arabs by Lucan in book 6, and in the same book 9, flying javelins. In the same book: Behold from afar the savage, barren serpent, under the trunk of a tree, twisted and launched (he calls it a javelin in Africa) &c. The image corresponds to its reality. For the Devil also, Samael to the Jews, נחש, ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος in Revelation XII, 9. ch. XX, 2. is most crafty in 2. Corinth. II, 11. XI, 14. Ephesians VI, 11. 12. Revelation XII, 9. and proud in 1. Timothy III, 8. and swift in 1. Peter V, 8. To Pherecydes of Syros, the prince of evil is ὀφιονεὺς.

Concerning the craftiness of the serpent, let Estius be compared in book 2 of the Sentences. But it is not for us to conclude with the Hebrews that the first serpent was endowed with human affections, and therefore more crafty. It is noted that the wily Devil used a crafty instrument, and one suited to himself.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Lapsus primorum parentum. Semen mulie- ris promissum. Crucis denunciatio, & è Paradiso ejectio.

Vers. 1.

SERPENS.) Hinc, puto, ille serpens malorum aureorum cu- stos apud Poëtas.

In Ebræo ob He Hajediah videatur ferpens intel- ligi non qua speciem, sed certum individuum, quod quale fuerit historia subjuncta docet, nimirum non merus serpens, sed obsessus à Diabolo : de eo enim additur, qui dixit ad mulierem. Conf. 2. Co- rinth. XI, 3. Id autem ignoravit Eva, quæ videtur de lapsu Angelorum adhuc nihil scivisse. Quæ ignorantia puræ negationis in statu innocentiæ lo- cum habere potuit. Non latebat, inquit Tirinus, Evam, has voces supernaturali virtute formari, sed non attendit satis, ut debebat, ad se tentandum con- sictas esse. Si de specie intelligas, hoc modo acci- pienda erunt verba: Et serpens erat callidior cunctis animantibus terræ. Et dixit (repetendo ἀπὸ κοι- νῦ vocem serpens) ad mulierem, ut jam intelligatur id dixisse ille, in serpente, & per serpentem, quem subintelligere contextus cogit; vel aliquis serpens, sed obsessus à Satana.

CALLIDIOR.) Sic & Aquila, πανῦργος ἀπὸ παντὸς ζώυ : Sic πανυργίαν serpenti tribuit Paulus 2. Corinth. XI, 3. & He- bræum ערום per πανῦργον vertunt Græci ubique in Jobo & Proverbiis. At LXX. hic φρονιμώτερος. Solet enim vox φρονιμος & in bonam & in malam partem sumi, ut apparet Luc. XVI, 8. in sensu medio ponitur Matth. XVI, 16. ubi Christiani jubentur esse φρόνιμοι ut serpentes, Vide de aspi- de Psalm. LVIII, 5. 6. Notandum vero quod Servius notat ad II. Georgicon, serpentium alios repere toto corpore, ali- os erigi corporis parte, ubi & Lucani hunc versum citat : Et contentus humum cauda sulcare pareas. Jaculum serpentis genus, ex arborum ramis vibrari tradit Pli- nius lib. 8. c. 23. Hic Arabum volucer serpens dicitur Lucano lib. 6. eidem lib. 9. Jaculique volucres. Eodem libro : Ecce procul sævus sterilis sub robore trunci Torsit & immisit (Jaculum vocat Africa) serpens &c. Respondet imago rei suæ. Nam & Diabolus, Samael Judæis, נחש, ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος Apocal. XII, 9. cap. XX, 2. callidis- simus 2. Corinth. II, 11. XI, 14. Ephes. VI, 11. 12. Apocal. XII, 9. & superbus 1. Timoth. III, 8. & celer 1. Petr. V, 8. Phere- cydæ Syro ὀφιονεὺς mali princeps.

De calliditate serpentis conferatur Estius in libr. 2. sentent. Non autem est, ut cum Ebræis statua- mus serpentem primum humanis affectibus præditum fuisse, indeque callidiorem. Id notatur, quod va- fer Diabolus usus sit instrumento callido, sibique accommodo.

## 3:3
Verse 3. AND THAT WE MIGHT NOT TOUCH IT.) He recites the law poorly, for GOD had said nothing about touching: having soon experienced that touching was harmless, she hoped the same concerning the tasting.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET NE TANGEREMUS ILLUD.) Male re- citat legem, nam de tactu nihil DEUS dixerat : mox tactum experta innoxium, idem de gustu speravit.

## 3:4
Verse 4. YOU SHALL NOT DIE BY DEATH.) As if he were to say, there is nothing deadly in that fruit.

An inept gloss. If the ancient serpent had indicated nothing else, he would not have deceived. For there was certainly nothing deadly in the fruit. But he opposes his YOU SHALL NOT DIE BY DEATH directly against the divine threat, YOU SHALL DIE BY DEATH, showing himself to be the enemy and adversary of God. For what God affirms, the Devil, the father of lies, openly denies, most mendaciously accusing God, who is truth itself, of a lie.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NEQUAQUAM MORTE MORIEMINI.) quasi dicat, nihil in eo pomo est mortiferum.

Glossa inepta. Si nihil aliud indicasset serpens antiquus, non fefellisset. Nam in pomo certe nihil erat mortiferum. At opponit suum NEQUA- QUAM MORTE MORIERIS καθδιάμετρον di- vinæ comminationi, MORTE MORIERIS, ho- stem & adversarium Dei se ostendens. Quod enim Deus affirmat, Diabolus mendacii parens palam negat, Deum, qui veritas ipsa est, mendacissime arguens mendacii.

## 3:5
