Verse 5. FOR GOD KNOWS.) There is כי in the Hebrew, but the meaning of that particle is often adversative, so that you may rightly translate it by 'but'.

YOU SHALL BE LIKE GODS KNOWING GOOD AND EVIL.) It is divine to know as many things as possible. Homer says of Jove that he knew more. And elsewhere: The gods know all things. Epicharmus: but the divine reason follows all the arts. Knowledge is the life of the Gods to Cicero in the Hortensius. This gift, as much as was necessary, they ought to have obtained from God by prayers for the use of the dominion divinely given to them, but not to take it for themselves. For this tree, the Poets substituted fire; the instrument, indeed, of almost all arts and of more delicate living. Claudius Neapolitanus joined both together in Porphyry's first book on Abstinence. Add the poem of Moschion in Stobaeus under the title concerning time.

Onkelos, like Magnates, Princes, who ought to discern between good and evil. Others like Angels, with certain Hebrews (Fagius, Vatablus, and Drusius observing this). Ainsworth warns that the seducing Devil could have understood the evil angels, who had experienced both good and evil. Furthermore, the Protoplasts were not lacking the gift of knowledge, having been created in the image of God. But it is absurd that God should have granted them dominion over all living creatures, yet not have imparted the gift necessary for the use of the dominion granted, and that He should have established infants (for such he makes the protoplasts) ignorant of things, and crude masters of all things. Which is a figment of the Socinians. The serpent promised one thing, although falsely; the protoplasts also aspired to another, namely a knowledge far more sublime, by which they would become like GOD; not content with that original and concreated wisdom of Colossians III, 10. by which knowledge, because they did not use it purely, those who were from the beginning (the Protoplasts) were stripped by the imposture of the serpent, as Justin speaks toward the end of his Epistle to Diognetus.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SCIT ENIM DEUS.) Est in Ebræo כי, sed ejus particulæ sæpe adversativa est fignificatio, ut recte per sed vertas.

ERITIS SICUT DII SCIENTES BONUM ET MA- LUM.) Divinum est scire quam plurima. Homerus de Jo- ve πλείονα ᾔδεε. Et alibi : Θεοὶ δέ τε παντ᾽ ἴασιν. Epichar- mus : ὁ δὲ γε τὰς τέχνας ἅπασι συνέπεται θεὸς λόγος. Sci- entia, Deorum vita Ciceroni in Hortensio. Hoc donum, quantum opus erat, à Deo precibus impetrare debuerant ad usum imperii sibi divinitus dati, non autem id per se sumere. Pro hac arbore ignem substituerunt Poetæ ; instrumentum quippe artium prope omnium & victus delicatioris. Conjun- xit utrumque Claudius Neapolitanus apud Porphyrium libro de Abstinentia primo. Adde Moschionis carmen apud Sto- bæum titulo de tempore.

Onkelos, sicut Magnates, Principes, qui de- bent discernere inter bonum & malum. Alii sic- ut Angeli, cum Ebr. quibusdam (Fagio, Vatablo, & Drusio observantibus.) Ainsworthus monet po- tuisse Diabolum seductorem Angelos malos intelli- gere, qui & bonum & malum experti essent. Cæ- terum Protoplasti non carebant dono scientiæ con- diti ad imaginem Dei. Absurdum vero est, Deum ipsis imperium concessisse super omnia animantia, donum ad usum imperii concessi necessarium non impertiisse, infantes (tales enim protoplastos facit) ignaros rerum, & rudes Dominos rerum omnium constituisse. Quod Socinianorum est commen- tum. Aliud promittebat, quanquam falso, ser- pens; aliud etiam affectabant protoplasti, scientiam nempe longe sublimiorem, qua DEO similes evade- rent; non contenti primigenia illa & concreata sa- pientia Coloss. III, 10. qua vero cognitione, quia pure usi non sunt, qui ab initio erant (Protoplasti) impostu- ra serpentis nudati etiam sunt, uti loquitur Justinus sub finem Epistol. ad Diognet.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. AND PLEASANT TO THE SIGHT.) In Hebrew נחמד להשכיל and in Greek ὡραῖόν ἐσι τὸ κατανοῆσαι, that is, wholesome, as far as could be conjectured from the appearance.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ASPECTUQUE DELECTABILE.) In Hebræo נחמד להשכיל in Græco ὡραῖόν ἐσι τὸ κατανοῆσαι, id est salubre, quantum ex adspectu conjectari poterat.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. AND WHEN THEY KNEW, THAT THEY WERE NAKED.) That is, had they learned what is the use of a male, what of a female? Nakedness to the Hebrews is τὰ γεννητικά. See 1 Corinthians XII, 23, and the cited passage in the Law of War and Peace. Aristotle says at the end of the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics that shame does not belong to a perfectly good man.

The Rabbis dream that before the fall men were blind and lived a brutal life. But Grotius casts them down below the beasts, which know this use by nature. But whom will he persuade that Adam was ignorant of that use, who had taught so extensively about marriage and its purpose in the preceding chapter? Whence all the instruction that is held concerning marriage flowed as from its source. Therefore they did not learn it through sin, as Grotius foolishly claims with Socinus: the punishment of this fall is described here, not a benefit: But they knew, as the words of the Holy Spirit have it, that they were naked, which are clear enough by themselves and need no gloss. It should only be observed that words of knowledge among the Hebrews are accustomed to imply an affection, sometimes of approval, sometimes also of displeasure. Here they saw themselves naked now with displeasure and shame, whereas before they were devoid of shame on account of their holy innocence. But the observation of external nakedness alone is not designated. The eyes were opened at the same time, through the sense of sin and the sting of conscience. They saw therefore that they were naked and despoiled of original righteousness. Augustine should rather have been heard here from book 13 of The City of God, chapter 13. After the transgression of the commandment was committed, immediately, with divine grace deserting them, they were confused about the nakedness of their bodies. They felt a new movement of their disobedient flesh, as a reciprocal punishment for their disobedience. Before the fall, nakedness testified both to nature and integrity of morals, and to the perfect symmetry and harmony of the members, as well as to continence and most holy justice. Nothing deformed was in them which they needed to cover with garments, nor was there anything to be feared from any injury of the air. And since they had a conscience polluted by no stain of sin, and the members of the body did nothing immodestly beyond the dictate of reason, there was no cause for shame. Why should they be ashamed, says Bede, when they had felt no law in their members warring against the law of their mind? There was no movement in the body to which shame was owed. They thought nothing needed to be veiled, because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained. That nakedness, therefore, was not for disgrace, but for an ornament. But when they see themselves despoiled of the glory of God, which had shone in body and soul, Rom. III, 23, they feel their nature depraved by sin and their flesh seething with the stings of lust, their conscience is miserably tortured and tormented. The eyes of the mind are therefore opened to man, so that he may see how shameful that nakedness itself is now, and how much he himself is changed from that former state. Eve's were not opened before she had seduced Adam:

For she was entirely occupied with the delights of the forbidden tree, and so fascinated by it, that she had not yet recognized her own nakedness. By the OPENING of the EYES, therefore, is understood indeed an external noticing of nakedness, but only insofar as it was shameful: and therefore the sense of prevarication is inserted.

Verse same. THEY SEWED FIG LEAVES.) Much like the Homeric Ulysses of the Odyssey, book 6. 'So saying, the noble Odysseus crept out from the bushes, and with his stout hand broke off a leafy branch from the thicket, so that he might cover the nakedness of a man about his body.' Gataker, in Cinn. page 200, translates it, 'and with folded or woven fronds they made loincloths,' because תפר signifies to apply, to fold, Job 16:15, Ezekiel 13:18. And עלה also denotes a branch and a sprout, Genesis 8:11, Proverbs 11:28, Nehemiah 8:15. The Syriac renders it 'they fitted together' instead of 'they sewed.' Fig leaves were used because of their breadth.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CUMQUE COGNOVISSENT, SE ESSE NU- DOS.) Id est, didicissent, quis maris, quis fœminæ usus? Nuditas Hebræis τὰ γεννητικά. Vide 1. Corinth. XII, 23. & dictum locum de jure Belli ac Pacis. Pudorem non esse viri perfecte boni dicit Aristoteles fine quarti Nicomacheorum.

Rabbini ante lapsum cæcos fuisse homines & vi- tam brutalem vixisse somniant. Sed infra bruta, quæ hunc usum natura norunt, eos abjicit Gro- tius. Cui autem persuadebit, usum illum Adamum ignorasse, qui tam prolixe de conjugio, ejusque fine, capite præcedenti, docuerat. Unde omnis, quæ de conjugio habetur, institutio tanquam è fonte suo scaturiit. Non ergo id didicere per peccatum, uti cum Socino ineptit Grotius: pœna hic lapsus, non beneficium describitur: Cognoverunt autem, quem- admodum verba Spiritus S. habent, se nudos esse, quæ per se clara satis sunt, glossa nulla indigent. Modo observetur, quod verba notitiæ apud Ebræos affectum inferre soleant, quandoque approbationis, nonnunquam etiam displicentiæ. Hic nudos se nunc cum displicentia & pudore viderunt, quum antea pudoris, ob sanctam innocentiam, expertes essent. Non autem nuditatis solum externæ animadversio designatur. Oculi aperti simul sunt, per peccati sen- sum, & conscientiæ stimulum. Viderunt itaque se nudos, & originali justitia spoliatos. Augustinus hic potius audiendus erat è l. 13. de Civ. Dei c. 13. Post- quam præcepti facta transgressio, confestim gratia dese- rente divina de corporum suorum nuditate confusi sunt. Senserunt novum motum inobedientis carnis suæ, tanquam reciprocam pœnam inobedientiæ suæ. Ante lapsum nuditas cum naturam & morum inte- gritatem, membrorumque συμμετρίαν & ἁρμονίαν perfectam, tum continentiam & justitiam sanctissi- mam testabatur. Nihil deforme illis inerat, quod vestibus operirent, neque ab ulla aëris injuria me- tuendum fuit. Et cum conscientiam haberent nul- la peccati labe pollutam, nihilque præter rationis dictamen membra corporis inverecunde agerent, nulla pudoris causa erat. Quid eos puderet, inquit Beda, quando nullam legem senserant in membris suis repugnantem legi mentis suæ? Nullus erat motus in corpore, cui verecundia deberetur. Nihil putabant velandum, quia nihil senserant refrenandum. Nu- ditas ergo illa non dedecori, sed ornamento erat. At ubi gloria Dei, quæ in corpore & anima fulse- rat, se spoliatos vident Rom. III, 23. naturam suam peccato depravatam & carnem libidinum stimu- lis æstuantem sentiunt, conscientia ipsorum mise- re torquetur & angitur. Aperiuntur ergo homi- ni oculi mentis, ut videat, quam turpis sit jam ipsa nuditas, & quantum ipse mutatus ab illo. Evæ aperti non sunt antequam Adamum seduxisset:

tota enim occupata fuit in vetitæ arboris deliciis, adeoque illa fascinata, ut nuditatem suam nondum agnoverit. Per OCULORUM ergo APERTIO- NEM intelligitur quidem externa nuditatis anim- adversio, sed quatenus ignominiosa illa erat: ideo- que insertur sensus prævaricationis.

Vers. eod. CONSUERUNT FOLIA FICUS.) Ferme ut Ulysses Homericus Odysseæ ζ'. Ὣς εἰπὼν θάμνων ὑπεδύσατο δῖος ὀδυσσεύς Ἐκ πυκινῆς δ' ὕλης πτόρθον κλάσε χειρὶ παχείῃ Φύλλων, ὡς ῥύσαιτο περὶ χροῒ μήδεα φωτός. Gataker. in Cinn. pag. 200. vertit, & frondibus complicatis, vel contextis fecerunt subligacula, quia תפר significat applicare, complicare, Job. 16, 15. E- zech. 13, 18. & עלה etiam ramum & termitem notat Genes. 8, 11. Prov. 11, 28. Nehem. 8, 15. Syrus reddit coaptarunt pro consuerunt. Folia ficus propter latitudinem adhibita.

## 3:8
Verse 8. AT THE BREEZE.) With a certain unusual movement of the air, which is a sign of the divine presence, 1 Kings 19:12, Acts 2:2.

AFTER MIDDAY.) Or at midday itself: for the most important part is accustomed to take the name of the whole. At that time, the Greeks also expected visions. Theocritus, Idyll 1: 'It is not right, O shepherd, it is not right for us to pipe at midday; we fear Pan.' Ovid, Tristia 4.4: 'May we not see the Dryads, nor the baths of Diana, nor Faunus, when he presses the fields at midday.'

Latin:

Vers. 8. AD AURAM.) Cum motu quodam aëris infoli- to, qui signum divinæ præsentiæ 1. Reg. 19, 12. Actor. 2, 2.

POST MERIDIEM.) Aut ipso meridie לרוח: solet enim pars potissima totius nomen induere. Eo tempore visa & Græci exspectabant. Theocritus Idyllio I. Οὐ θέμις, ὦ ποιμὰν, τὸ μεσαμβρινὸν, ὐ θέμις ἄμμιν Συρίσδεν· Τὸν πᾶνα δεδοίκαμες. Ovidius Tristium IV, 4. Nec Dryadas, nec nos videamus labra Dianæ. Nec Faunnm, medio, cum premit arva die.

## 3:11
Verse 11. FOR WHO TOLD THEE.) That is, had told thee. See above 1:9.

Latin:

Vers. 11. QUIS ENIM INDICAVIT TIBI.) Id est, in- dicaverat. Vide supra I, 9.

## 3:14
Verse 14. UPON THY BREAST SHALT THOU GO.) That agility having been repressed.

AND DUST SHALT THOU EAT.) That is, thou shalt feed on the very dust, Isaiah 65:25. Cast out of Paradise, thou shalt no longer enjoy the fruits of the trees. For the allegorical sense, see Micah 7:17, Psalm 72:9, Isaiah 49:23.

Metaphorically, the phrase 'to lick the dust' is used in Psalm 72:9, Isaiah 49:23, or rather metonymically, so that reverence and subjection are noted, by which they prostrate themselves so low upon the ground that they seem to lick the dust of the earth. An allusion is also made in Micah 7:17 to the curse of the serpent made to it here; but a new sense of this curse, which Grotius calls allegorical, is not handed down, whether in Micah or in the other cited passages, which certainly cannot be asserted without absurdity. For what connection has either the reverence of the faithful, or the fear and dread of the unfaithful, with this punishment inflicted upon the serpent, such that one might say that the allegorical sense of this divine edict is explained there?

That only the repression of serpentine agility is designated here is not likely, since it is commanded to crawl upon its breast. The Greeks, Basil the Great and Didymus in the Catena of Lipomanus, more correctly observe that the serpent previously walked erect. Joseph Mede, in the Anglican Dissertations praised here by Matthew Poole, dissertation 37, understands it of one kind of serpent, and that by far the most noble, which surpassed not only other serpents but also the rest of the animals in both beauty and sagacity (yet not a Basilisk, which still walks erect in the middle, as Pliny testifies, book 8, Natural History, ch. 21), which, with respect to inherent perfections, was made viler than all, and most destitute of external aids for preserving life. That Mede prefers the words to be rendered 'upon thy breast' rather than 'upon thy belly.' The breast, he says, is the upper part of the body from the navel to the head. Therefore, that it walked upright before, because serpents still often raise themselves up, and the basilisk walks in this way today, which God perhaps may have willed that one to walk in such a way, so that it might be a monument of the truth of this curse? And Mede thinks that this would be more credible if we affirm, with Basil, Ephrem the Syrian, Moses Bar-Cepha, and others, that the serpent once had feet, etc.

It is not certain whence Grotius has it that the serpent was accustomed to enjoy the fruits of the trees in Paradise, even if it is now commanded to feed only on the dust of the earth. I would not deny, however, that it could have fed on herbs, grass, or even certain fruits of trees along with other living creatures before. Some here, with Pareus, also invent a mystical and allegorical sense concerning the Devil, that he feeds on the earthly excrements of crimes and wickedness, just like a pig; Mede also handed down such a double sense: but although GOD institutes a judgment against that ἐνδιαβολισμένον serpent, and addresses that σύνθετον subject, it must nevertheless be observed entirely that in this curse and denunciation of punishment, some things concern the instrument of seduction, the natural serpent, and others concern the Devil, the author of the seduction. And that this edict in verse 14 is indeed promulgated against the natural serpent alone, the thing itself teaches: to which a curse is denounced above all the animals of the earth, a movement upon the breast, and a pasturage of the dust of the earth; but in the following verse the speech is directed to the Devil lurking under the serpent. For although the discourse is made to the same subject, the denounced punishment testifies that in that subject another nature, namely the invisible one, which had put on the serpent, is being addressed. For such are the subjects as they are permitted to be by the predicates.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SUPER PECTUS TUUM GRADIERIS.) Re- pressa illa agilitate.

ET TERRAM COMEDES.) Id est, solo pulvere pa- sceris, Esa, 65, 25. Ejectus è Paradiso non ultro arborum po- mis frueris. Allegoricum sensum vid. Michææ 7, 17. Psalm. 72, 9. Esa. 49, 23.

Metaphorice phrasis, pulverem lingere, usur- patur Psalm. 72, 9. Esa. 49, 23. vel potius Metonymi- ce, ut notetur reverentia & subjectio, qua ita pro- nos se in terram prosternunt, ut videantur pulve- rem terræ lingere. Allusio etiam fit Mich. 7, 17. ad serpentis maledictionem hîc ei factam; non autem novus sensus hujus maledictionis, quem Grotius allegoricum vocat, traditur, sive apud Micheam, seu in aliis adductis locis, quod certe absque absur- ditate asseri non potest. Nam quid commercii ha- bet vel reverentia fidelium, vel timor & metus infi- delium cum hoc supplicio serpenti inflicto, ut di- cere liceat, ibi allegoricum sensum hujus edicti di- vini expositum esse?

Solam agilitatis serpentinæ repressionem hîc de- signari, non est verisimile, cum jubetur super pe- ctus repere. Rectius observant Græci Basilius M. & Didymus in Catena Lipomani, serpentem antea erectum incessisse. Josephus Medus in Anglican. Dissertationib. Matthæo Polo hîc laudatus dissert. 37. de uno serpentum genere eoque longe nobilissimo, quod & pulchritudine & sagacitate non serpentes solum alios, sed etiam reliqua animantia superarit, intelligit (non tamen Basilisco; qui adhuc erectus in medio teste Plinio lib. 8. Nat. Hist. c. 21. incedit) quod & inhærentium perfectionum respectu vili- us omnibus factum sit, & externis vitæ conservan- dæ subsidiis maxime destitutum. Mavult Medus ille verba reddi super pectus tuus, quam super ventrem tuum. Pectus, inquit, est superior corporis pars ab um- bilico ad caput. Hoc igitur erecto antea incedebant, quia serpentes se adhuc sæpe erigunt & basiliscus hodie ita incedit, quem unum Deus forte ita ince- dere voluerit, ut monumentum esset veritatis hu- jus maledictionis? idque credibilius fore putat Me- dus, si affirmemus, cum Basilio, Ephrem Syro, Mose Bar-Cepha & aliis serpenti olim fuisse pedes &c.

Pomis arborum in Paradiso frui consuevisse serpentem, unde Grotius habeat, non constat, etiamsi solo pulvere terræ pasci nunc jubeatur. Non negarim tamen, quod cum aliis animantibus antea herbis, gramine vel etiam fructibus quibus- dam arborum vesci potuerit. Fingunt & hic non- nulli cum Pareo mysticum & Allegoricum sensum de Diabolo, quod terrenis pascatur scelerum & ne- quitiarum, sicut porcus, excrementis; qualem ge- minum sensum etiam Medus tradidit: sed quam- vis judicium DEUS instituat adversus serpentem illum ἐνδιαβολισμένον, & suppositum illud σύν- θετον alloquatur, observandum tamen omnino, alia in hac maledictione, ac pœnæ denunciatione concernere organum seductionis, serpentem natu- ralem, alia Diabolum seductionis auctorem. Et hoc quidem vers. 14. edictum promulgari adversus ser- pentem solum naturalem, res ipsa docet: cui de- nunciatur maledictio præ omnibus animantibus ter- ræ, ingressus super pectus, & pastura pulveris terræ; In sequenti autem versu oratio dirigitur ad Dia- bolum sub serpente latentem. Etsi enim ad idem subjectum sermo fiat, in illo tamen subjecto alte- ram naturam, invisibilem nempe, quæ serpentem induerat, compellari, pœna denunciata testatur. Talia enim sunt subjecta, qualia permittuntur esse à prædicatis.

## 3:15
Verse 15. BETWEEN THEE AND THE WOMAN.) For the woman is more fearful of such things than the man. See the allegorical sense in Revelation 12.

AND THY SEED.) Every kind of serpent. Allegorically, the wicked. John 8, verse 44; Acts 13, verse 10; 1 John 3, verse 8. Thus the Canaanites are the seed of the serpent, according to Abarbanel on this passage.

AND HER SEED.) The seed of the woman or born [from a woman are all men outside of Adam. Job 14, verse 1; chapter 15, verse 14; chapter 25, verse 4; Matthew 11, verse 11; Luke 7, verse 28; Sirach 10, verse 17. The same is σπέρμα as γέννημα, and it is also said of women, as below IV, 25. Just as allegorically the woman is the Church, so the seed of the woman are the individuals who belong to the Church. Galatians 4, verse 26.

Although only the woman is mentioned, the man is not excluded; nor is the woman named because she is more fearful, but because it is more shameful to the ancient serpent, the infernal Dragon, to be opposed by the same miserable and seduced woman whom he himself had first dragged into his snare and precipitated into extreme misery. For here that King of the proud, that strong armed man of Job 41, verse 25 and Luke 11, verse 21, is committed to battle with the ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει (weaker vessel) of 1 Peter 3, verse 7, and is overcome by it. For in that, as blessed Luther says, the sun of consolation rises, that Eve not only does not hear that she is being cursed like the serpent, but that she hears that she is set as if in battle array against a condemned enemy, and that with the hope of the help which the Son of GOD was to bring.

These things were not said to the natural serpent, or about a natural hatred between the serpent and men, as R. Aben-Ezra and R. Solomon do with the Jews, the Photinians Smalcius in his book on the divinity of the Son of GOD, chapter 2, Sommer in his refutation of Petr. Carol. book 2, chapter 3, and among the Reformed, Calvin, Musculus, Beza, and most others: as also some Papists, Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide, Bonfrer, etc., wish. Because GOD, says Cornelius, deprived man of dominion over the beasts on account of sin, the serpent began to be harmful and lethal to man, and in turn man began to be a serpent-killer, whereas before sin there had been neither antipathy, nor horror, nor hatred, nor a desire to harm between man and the serpent. Pareus again refers this kind of punishment both to the serpent and to the Devil, and imagines a double sense. Which, however, is absurd. Yet Antonius Cregutus involves himself in a greater absurdity in his recent Arcanor. revelat., where he contends that there is a triple sense of this oracle: first, literally concerning the animal serpent, and the woman, and her descendants; second, mystically, but yet literally concerning Christ, who is understood antonomastically as the seed of the woman, and concerning the serpent Devil; third, that by the seed of the woman are understood also all the faithful, who are inserted into Christ the primordial Seed, and conversely by the seed of the serpent all the reprobate, who are the progeny of Satan p. 107. These words, therefore, and he himself shall crush thy head, he explains with respect to the brute serpent, whereby its head is crushed by man, and with respect to the ancient serpent, whereby its head is crushed by the Seed of the woman, Christ, and its horn is broken, and finally with respect to the Devil also and the infidel serpents and serpent-born, whose head is crushed by the faithful p. 119. Thus, therefore, the pronoun He himself, according to Cregutus, denotes first all men, then the faithful, and finally Christ alone: the other pronoun Thy denotes first the animal serpent, then the Devil and the infidels, and finally the Devil alone: the noun head denotes first the physical head of the animal serpent, then the power of demons and infidels, and finally the empire of the Devil. The verb To crush is taken according to him both properly for the trampling which is done by the feet; and improperly both of the victory which the faithful gain over the Devil and infidels, and of the victory which Christ alone gained in death over the Devil: there, says Cregutus page 121, the serpent bites the heel, but the seed of the woman crushes the head of the serpent: because Christ died, but revived as victor, but the Devil, both bound and conquered, is never to be released and to rise again from eternal death. Where note both the grammatical barbarism of the Calvinist Professor and Pastor in the Academy and Church of Die, in the word RESURGENDUS, and the theology concerning the eternal death of the Devil, from which he is not to be raised up; and he reconciles that triple sense (which Cregutus defends as if intended by the Holy Spirit, and most excellently and most theologically extracted, so that consequently that multiform wisdom of the Scriptures may become more illustrious, and those tongues of divided fire may appear more miraculously, so that he inveighs sharply against other Calvinist Doctors, who coldly embrace only one sense here, and calls those cavils, about nothing, and περὶ τῶν Φλυαρίων page 108.) with the arguments and reasons by which he himself proves that the seed of the woman is to be understood here in a most singular way concerning Christ p. 100, whom he says is called antonomastically elsewhere the son of man, because he was not made ἐκ σαρκὸς (which phrase smacks of the heresy of the Anabaptists) but κατὰ σάρκα: here, however, the seed of the woman, because it is the seed of the woman only, and not of a man, with respect to temporal generation, just as with respect to eternal it is the seed of the Father, eternally ὁμοόσιον (which phrase of Cregutus is again ἄγραφος καὶ ἀθεόλογος, nay, it is horrible) and he judges that by the seed of this woman is designated individually the seed of this virgin Mary, and that such fortitude belongs to none except Christ, that he should crush the head of the serpent: nay, that only an antithesis is instituted in this oracle between the first and second Adam: How therefore can this oracle be interpreted of any other than Christ? For these things are openly ἀντιφατικὰ, The woman here is Mary, and The woman here is not Mary, but Eve, The seed of the woman here is Christ alone, and The seed of the woman is not Christ alone, but all the descendants of Eve, likewise not all the descendants of Eve, but only the faithful. And furthermore, Christ alone crushes the head of the serpent: and not Christ alone, but also the faithful crush the head of the serpent, etc. But let us leave these arcana to their author, who does not hesitate to hawk other rather many paradoxes as revealed arcana: of which it is helpful to have observed here one or two that are not entirely ἀλλότριον: Inasmuch as this crushing of the serpentine head imports meritorious satisfaction, he objects against the same page 64 that it seems unjust for a single person to suffer for others: and he answers, by no means; for that person is considered either εἰδικῶς, or as it is τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον: If in the former way, that which he taught on page 64, that with Christ suffering the whole human nature suffers, because it is one and the same in all men; likewise since the whole human race was subject to death, Christ also as contained under the species was subject to death: likewise Christ is not corrupt in himself, but for what reason? unless because he was sanctified by grace to this end, that he might satisfy for others: Likewise Christ was sanctified in the womb of the virgin by the Holy Spirit: Likewise Christ was innocent not by nature, but by grace, so that he might satisfy for us to divine justice. From these it will be easy to judge of other arcana, as the lion from the claw. But the whole Prot-Evangelium, the foundation of all promises, is overturned by the Grotian Ψευδερμηνεία, that by the seed of the serpent the whole genus of serpents, and by the seed of the woman all her descendants are understood according to the literal sense. Which is easily refuted from those things which have already been said. Indeed, in this whole process, as has been shown, as a judicial act,

GOD’s business was not only with the serpent, but primarily with him who used the serpent as an instrument. And to him indeed the penalty had already been denounced. And therefore GOD deals no longer with him. Here, therefore, the speech is directed to Satan, the occupant of the serpent, and judgment is denounced to him: and therefore, while God himself establishes enmities, and opposes the woman to the serpent as an enemy, and the seed of the woman to the seed of the serpent, it is not a matter of hostility between the race of serpents and the children of Eve, or the human race, for whose sake surely it was not necessary that judgment be celebrated before the divine tribunal, nor that a remedy be promised or prepared for the human race, with such great apparatus. But the woman is set in battle array against the enemy, the seducer, the ancient serpent, Satan, lurking under that snake, and his whole race: Nor is the sense here finally allegorical or mystical, but native and literal, intended first by GOD. There is no need, therefore, for a double sense of the same statement here: which Grotius seems to assign, one literal concerning the natural serpent; the other mystical or allegorical, concerning the Devil. For which reason the same man, in the following words, 'and you shall lie in wait for his heel,' likewise handed down a double sense. The former, which might suit serpents lying in wait for the heel, Genesis 49, verse 17. The latter, which might suit the Devil, acting from ambush. Of a single statement there can be only one sense, unless you make divine oracles ambiguous, such as those of Apollo, that is, of the Deceiving Demon, which is impious even to think. We shall have nothing certain concerning the divine mind, once an ἀμφιβολογία (ambiguity) of this kind has been admitted. The natural serpent had already been dealt with in the preceding verse, to whom a triple curse was made. By what reason, therefore, would it be dealt with again in a primary and literal sense concerning the serpent, and only secondarily and allegorically concerning the Devil, the proper author of the seduction, who used the serpent only as his instrument? Nor indeed does man hate and kill only serpents, but other harmful and venomous animals as well. Nor is that antipathy with serpents so natural to men that they are not sometimes found with whom they might agree well, which experience testifies regarding Tiberius by Suetonius, regarding the Troglodytes eating the flesh of serpents by Pliny in book V, chapter 8, and regarding the jugglers and Magi soothing serpents through incantation. But will any art be able to remove the hostility placed by God?

I would say that Grotius is seduced here by Calvin, who in his Commentary on Genesis says, "I interpret SIMPLY, that there will always be hostile discord for the human race with serpents, such as is seen today," unless he were also greatly hostile to Calvin, and both seemed to be seduced rather by those recent and sworn enemies of the Messiah, the Jews, whose commentaries Grotius loves too much, so that he even forgets his own Papists in comparison to them. They, with an almost unanimous opinion, make a literal sense of this passage, which Grotius wants to be only allegorical. Which is also observed in the more ancient Jews: the Targum of Onkelos is a witness, and especially the Jerusalem Targum, which is clearer here: It holds thus: "I will put enmity between you and between the woman and between your son and her son: He will watch you, for what you did to him from the beginning, and you will watch him in the end." This, with Fagius as interpreter, explained the oracle thus: "And it will be, when the sons of the woman devote effort to the law and perform the precepts, then they will strive to crush your head and they will kill you. But when the sons of the woman have abandoned the precepts of the law, and will not keep the commandments, you will devote effort to bite them in their heels, and thus harm them. Nevertheless, there will be a remedy for the sons of the woman, but for you, serpent, there will be no remedy: since it will come to pass that they will remove the bite which was made in the heel, in the end of days, namely in the days of the Messiah." Which are also held in almost the same words in the Targum Jonathan. The interpretations of the ancient Jews are also witnesses, concerning which Maimonides warns in Moreh Nevuchim, book 2, chapter 30. Nebuch. book 2, chapter 30. You must know how they explain that in the Midrash: Namely, that the serpent was ridden, which in size approached a camel: But that the rider was he who deceived Eve: Sammael indeed, which nomenclature they attribute absolutely to Satan. R. Bechai is also a witness in this place, writing thus: "We do not have enmities more with the serpent than with other reptiles. Wherefore this Scripture mystically hints at him who was hidden in the serpent. For the body of the cunning serpent was an instrument, apt for receiving the power joined with him. And he is the one who caused the earth to sin, whence death entered into all his progeny. And this is the enmity between the serpent and between the seed of the woman. And this is the mystery of the holy tongue, that the serpent is elsewhere called Saraph, according to the name by which an Angel is also called Saraph."

The serpent, therefore, whom God addresses here in verse 15, is that ancient serpent, the standard-bearer of the Devils, Apoc. 12:9, and the supreme one among them, who had attacked the first-formed in the serpent. But his seed is to be understood not by generation, but by imitation and ὁμοψηφίᾳ or consensus regarding the rest of the troop of Devils, just as ranks are established elsewhere among the Devils: Beelzebub as ἄρχων, some prince among them, Luke 11:15; others are called ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι, Col. 2:15, and δυνάμεις, Rom. 8:38; others are indicated as worse than others, Luke 11:26; indeed, an open distinction is established between the Devil or the ancient dragon the serpent, and his angels, Matt. 25:41, Apoc. 12:6. The Jews make the prince of Demons the seducer of the first-formed, and attribute to him the name Sammael, as we noted a little before from Maimonides in Moreh Nevuchim, book 2, chapter 30.

By a not dissimilar trope, the Pharisees and other impious men are called a brood of vipers and to be from the Father the Devil, Matt. 23:33, John 8:44, on account of consensus, namely, and imitation: because he who commits sin is of the Devil. For the Devil sins from the beginning, 1 John 3:8. Our Lord Dr. Walther exhibited a full exegesis of this proto-evangelium for us in his *Officina Biblica*: but the blessed Lord Aegidius Hunnius exhibited a more abundant refutation of the Jewish gloss; who defeated it in the Judaizing Calvin and his champion David Pareus. Therefore, it is not to be admitted what Grotius asserts; that the impious are understood here allegorically, like the Canaanites being the seed of the serpent according to Abarbanel. But as the seed of the woman is of the same nature with the woman, so here the seed of the ancient serpent is indicated as ὁμοούσιον, the remaining troop of Devils. For the comfort to be provided to the first-formed was for the whole human race, against the entire troop of Devils, and enmities were not to be established of some men against the Diabolical power, but a remedy was to be prepared for all men, who in the first-formed sustained the person of their whole race, having been cast down (for in one we all sinned, Rom. 5:12). Therefore, that partition of men into pious and impious has no place here, where in the person of the mother of the living, the restoration of salvation is promised to all. For which reason, neither those who belong to the Church are to be understood by the seed of the woman, nor the impious by the seed of the serpent, with Grotius; whatever sense you may finally call it, whether mystical or literal: But as one Christ is designated by the seed of the woman; so the entire troop of Devils by the seed of the ancient serpent: against which whole troop to be overcome, one Christ is opposed in this counsel and decree of God, who alone abundantly suffices, nor could anyone else be designated here outside of him. In this one is salvation, nor is any other name given under heaven, in which it is necessary to be saved, Acts 4:12. Human power is indeed not of such a kind that it can be opposed to the serpent and his seed. But whatever the human race avails against the ancient serpent and his seed, that we avail solely in Christ, in whom alone is our strength and righteousness, Isa. 45:25. Whence, as a corollary and consequently, the fruit of that established hostility redounds to us, which we acknowledge yields to our good even against the impious and their machinations; but the meaning of this oracle is not to be fixed there, as we shall now say. And therefore Joseph Mede wrongly understands by the seed of the woman in this place the mystical Christ, as he calls him, the head with the members.

IT SHALL CRUSH THY HEAD.) As if it were a matter of the woman, in a sense not bad. But the Hebrew text, which we now have, prefers the masculine both in the pronoun and in the verb, so that it may appear to refer to the seed זרע, which for the Hebrews is of the masculine gender. And thus Irenaeus explains this passage in III, 38. The LXX placed ἀυτὸς from the Hebrew, although among the Greeks σπέρμα is of the neuter gender. And so they made the construction as if there had preceded not σπέρμα, but what signifies the same thing, σπορά. Irenaeus follows them in IV, 78. And Cyprian in Testimony 11, book 2, against the Jews. Such are everywhere many constructions πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. It shall crush thy head ישופך ראש Rom. 16, 20. To trample the head is a mark of contempt. Ezech. 34, 18. Hence those who trust in divine protection are said to trample the asp, Psalm 91, 12. πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων Luke 10, 19. Tertullian, against Marcion 4, spoke of the power of trampling upon serpents and scorpions. The same author urges trampling the beast with the heel in Scorpiace. For in the head of the serpent is the greatest force of evil. Ecclesiasticus 25, v. 21. Thus, with Christ as leader, Christians easily resist the devil and overcome him. James 4, 7. 1 Peter 5, 9. 1 John 2, 13. 14.

But that the Hebrew text now has it differently than it had it formerly must be proven. Which, however, that glutton could not show by even one piece of evidence from antiquity. Why, therefore, does he defend the Vulgate, unless for the sake of the Council of Trent, and the Roman Pontiff? Indeed, it is easily proven that the Hebrew text did not have היא or she herself, but הוא he himself or it itself: since all Hebrew Codices read הוא. For what is noted in the margin of the interlinear edition as קרי, was added by an unfaithful hand for the sake of the Latin Vulgate, without the authority of any Hebrew Codex, with Arias Montanus furthermore protesting that this was done without his knowledge, concerning which Franciscus Lucas Brugensis. It is also refuted not only from the Masorah observing at Gen. 3:15 [36, 27] that there are eleven places having הוא in which this text is not found: but also from the words themselves, namely both from the affixed pronoun and from the verb, which Grotius is forced to acknowledge must be of the masculine gender in Hebrew in both cases, not the feminine, and was never read otherwise there. And thus, he says, Irenaeus explains this passage in ch. 3, v. 38, concerning the seed of the woman. Therefore, in the time of Irenaeus, the Church did not read IPSA in the feminine gender. Nor did the Interpreters LXX. read it so. The LXX, says our author, placed αὐτὸς from the Hebrew: although among the Greeks σπέρμα is of the neuter gender. And so they made the construction as if not σπέρμα had preceded, but, which signifies the same thing, σπόρος. Irenaeus follows them in v. 78, and Cyprian in Testimony 11 of the book against the Jews: Such constructions πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον are found everywhere. So much for Grotius. Therefore, he cannot retreat to his κρησφύγετον, that the Hebrew text had it one way formerly and has it another way now, unless the conscience of a truer man resists. What therefore remains, but that he confess that the feminine IPSA is read wrongly and against the original text in the Latin. And not only did the LXX render it so, the Targum of Onkelos also reads הוא in the masculine, He himself will be watching you; as also R. Aben-Ezra, his seed will strike you on the head. Indeed, Jerome himself reads it so, and translated it in the masculine IPSE, in his questions on Genesis, where he produced the LXX Interpreters translation, He himself will preserve your head, he adds; It is better in the Hebrew: He himself will crush your head. Thus the Samaritan Codex, the Samaritan-Chaldean, likewise the Arab, just as the Greek and Chaldean editions read he himself. But who will believe that it is read wrongly in all other Codices, for the reason that the Latin Vulgate alone reads IPSA. What of the fact that the Lovanists themselves observe in the Catalogue of Various Readings, that not only do all Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek codices have the masculine pronoun, but also two Latin MS. Codices; such Latin copies were also observed by Franciscus Lucas and Robertus Stephanus. Nor did Leo the Great explain it otherwise in Sermon 2 on the Nativity of the Lord. God here denounced to the serpent the future seed of the woman, which by its own power will crush the elevation of the harmful head, namely Christ who is to come in the flesh. Which Roman Pontiff Grotius ought to have reconciled with Sixtus V and Clement VIII, if he could. But how could he, if he seriously believed the authority of the Pontiffs to be infallible? Unless perhaps someone says that these pronounced the Vulgate authentic from the Chair, and thus did not err, and that Leo the Great erred entirely from the true reading outside the chair: even though Leo the Great has on his side Hebrew, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin codices, nor did Irenaeus, or Cyprian, or Jerome read it otherwise. Yet Johannes Benedictus, Franc. Lucas, Augustinus Steuchus, Johannes Isaacus, Sacrobosco, Franc. Georgius Venetus, Andradius, Felisius (Elucid. Decal. praec. 1. cap. 48.), Hect. Pintus (in cap. 12. Es.), Lindanus (de optim. gener. interpr. lib. 3. p. 126.), Hartus (colloqu. cum Rainold. c. 6.), and Cardinal Cajetan, Melch. Canus, Canar. preferred to follow the older Leo rather than the recent Pontiffs pronouncing from the chair. Bishop, as well as the leaders from the Jesuit School, Pererius and Ribera, who all refer the pronoun not to the woman, but to the seed of the woman. Thomas Malvenda the Spaniard. I prefer, he says, the masculine or neuter to the feminine reading, so that the glory of redemption may be preserved entirely for Christ. The slip from Ipse to Ipsa was easy, says P. Picherellus. Finally, Ludovicus Capellus also acknowledges the depravation here in the Vulgate translation in the work so highly praised by Grotius, Crit. Sacr. lib. 5. c. 11. p. 370. It is easy, he says, to see that that reading, although ancient, IPSA, is depraved from the ignorance of a scribe, who when he saw that the pronoun IPSE did not agree in gender with the preceding noun, thought it should be read IPSA, and that it should be referred to the name of the woman; and so he changed the masculine pronoun into the feminine IPSA.

And what is that NOT BAD sense concerning the woman? Certainly the worst and idolatrous sense of the Papists. Who from this make Mary a co-redemptrix, who crushed the head of the serpent. Therefore they adore her in the Antidotarium animae fol. 118. I adore and bless your most holy feet, with which you crushed the head of the ancient serpent. Similar things may be seen in the Mariale of Bernardinus de Busto, approved by Sixtus IV, part 11, Sermon 2, and p. 12, Sermon 2. And in Bellarmine himself, l. 1. de septem verbis Christi in cruce c. 12. p. 102. Will Grotius excuse that sense? But he made the woman the Church, and the seed of the woman individuals who belong to the Church. And thus, with Christ as leader, to crush the head of the serpent, that is, to easily resist the Devil and overcome him, he says is for Christians, Jac. 4. v. 7. 1. Petr. 5. v. 9. 1. Joh. 2. v. 13. 14. But if by the pronoun IPSA the Church is understood allegorically, what woman then is understood here in the proper sense? And is not Christ thus clearly excluded here, to whom Gordon Huntlaeus admits that this sentence especially applies, as by his power all others crush the Devil, even if he understands the Church by the feminine pronoun literally, and consequently Mary, as a member of the Church; nor do I think anyone will deny it. Grotius acknowledges that the head of the serpent is crushed with Christ as leader. But while that not bad sense of his stands, no place is left here for Christ, since in the proper sense Eve is understood by the pronoun, and in the allegorical sense the Church, just as the faithful are understood by the seed of the woman. Therefore no promise was made here concerning Christ, about whom, however, the same thing was subsequently explained by God himself to the Patriarchs in Gen. 22:18, ch. 26:4, ch. 28:14, as concerning the blessed seed of the woman: and also by the Apostle in Gal. 3:18. He does not say 'in seeds', as if of many, but 'in seed', as if of one, which is Christ. The Apostle observes that the promise was made concerning the Patriarchs, but he teaches by this example of his that it ought to be observed in the same way in this πρωτευαγγελίῳ. For it is one and the same seed which crushes the head of the serpent, and in which one the curse is removed, and the blessing befalls all the nations of the earth, as the Apostle interprets. Nor is it doubtful even to the Papists themselves that the word 'seed' is more properly taken of one individual, namely singularly, than collectively. See Gen. 4, 25. c. 15, 3. c. 21, 13. Ruth 4, 12. 13. 2 Sam. 7, 22. 1 Chron. 17, 13. Here, however, it cannot be taken otherwise. Because the predicate of the crushing of the serpent's head designates the destruction of the power and kingdom of the Devil, which consists in the violence of sin and death 1 Cor. 15, 16. Heb. 2, 14, which is of infinite power and proper to Christ alone 1. John 3, 8. although the fruit of that crushing and destruction is communicated to the faithful, who through faith in Christ trample upon the Dragon Ps. 91, 13, overcome the Devil 1 John 2, 13, and through the blood of the Lamb Rev. 12, 11. For victory is given to them by God through our Lord Jesus Christ 1 Cor. 15, 57. Cf. Mark 16, 17. 18. Luke 10, 19. Rom. 16, 20. Therefore Grotius is indeed true, but far too insufficient: 'The trampling of the head is a mark of contempt' Ez. 34, 18. We have said more about these things in Crit. Sacr. p. 669. sqq. I add here the most ancient of the Fathers, Irenaeus' explication of book 4, chapter 78. Wherefore God indeed separated from his conversion him who secretly sowed the tares by himself, that is, the transgression which he himself brought in; but he had mercy on the man who accepted the disobedience, albeit negligently, but wickedly, and he turned back the enmity, through which he wished to make the man an enemy to GOD, upon the very author of the enmities, taking away indeed his own enmity which was against the man, but turning it back and sending it upon the serpent: Just as also the Scripture says that the Lord said to the serpent, and I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and the seed of the woman; he shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt watch his heel: And the Lord recapitulated this enmity in himself, having been made man from the woman, and bruising his head. And in book V. Therefore, recapitulating all things, he has also recapitulated the war against our enemy, and crushing him who in the beginning had led us captive in Adam, and bruising his head, just as it has in Genesis that God said to the Serpent: And I will put enmity between thee and between the woman and between thy seed and her seed, he shall watch thy head and thou shalt watch his heel. For from him who was to be born of the woman, a virgin, according to the likeness of Adam, it was proclaimed that he would watch the head of the serpent, i.e., the seed, of which the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians, The law of works was placed, until the seed should come, to whom it was promised. But he shows him manifest in the same Epistle, saying: But when the fullness of the time was come, God sent his Son, made of a woman. For the enemy would not have been justly conquered, unless it were a man from a woman who conquered him. For through the woman he dominated man from the beginning, setting himself up as contrary to man. On account of this also the Lord confesses himself the son of man, recapitulating in himself that primary man from whom the formation which is according to the woman was made, so that just as through a conquered man our race descended into death, so again through a conquering man we might ascend into life. And just as death received the palm through a man against us, so again we might receive the palm against death through a man. But the Lord would not have recapitulated in himself that ancient and first enmity against the serpent, fulfilling the promise of the Demiurge and perfecting his precept, if he had come from another Father, but since it is one and the same who from the beginning formed us, and in the end sent his Son, the Lord perfected his precept, having been made of a woman and destroying our adversary, and perfecting man according to our image and likeness. These things all, which Irenaeus [writes], demonstrate clearly the faith of the ancient Church concerning the Proto-Evangelium, as entirely consonant with the doctrine of the modern Orthodox Church, and solidly refute the Grotian glosses.

AND THOU SHALT WATCH HIS HEEL.) Thus snakes are accustomed to do, Gen. 18, 17. Nicander on the water-snake: Or he strikes in the ankle or in the footprint of the foot. Ovid, Metamorphoses 10: He dies with the serpent's tooth received in the heel. Hence the name solpuga. Claudius Neapolitanus: Snakes when stepped upon bite. Thus the Devil, after he fell from empires and compelling force, acts mostly from ambushes, 2 Cor. 2, 11; ch. 11, 3, 14; Eph. 6, 11. That word 'thou shalt watch' seems to be from the Greek reading τηρήσεις, for which other codices have τειρήσεις, that is, thou shalt bite, which approaches closer to the Hebrew תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ.

He unfolds a double sense; the literal concerning the natural serpent, the allegorical concerning the Devil. But we have previously warned that there is only one single sense of one saying. Nor is it a matter here of a serpent, but only of the Devil in this verse indeed: much less primarily of a serpent. But then he whose heel is to be bruised is none other than the 'serpent-fighter,' who will bruise the head of the serpent. Which we have taught is Christ alone. Therefore, it is not directly a matter of the ambushes of the Devil against the faithful or the Church: but against Christ, the seed of the woman. Not of those things which he does after he fell from empires: But which he plots at that very moment, while his head is being bruised. Namely, that while the seed of the woman is in the act of bruising the head of the ancient serpent, which was done primarily in the work of redemption, he is to receive a wound in the heel from the ancient serpent, in his passion and death, just as Irenaeus has already explained. Which interpretation is entirely consistent both with the words themselves, and with the scope and intention of this Proto-Evangelium, and with the explanation handed down in the Scriptures. The words do not imply only the ambushes of a solpuga: But death and the bruising of the heel. Whence Grotius himself corrects the Vulgate version from the Hebrew, but silently, so as not to offend the Papists. That 'thou shalt watch,' he says, seems to be from the Greek reading τηρήσεις, for which other codices have τειρήσεις, that is, thou shalt bite, which approaches closer to the Hebrew: תשופנו. The Hebrew word is more emphatic, however: because it brings not only death, but bruising, which is more apt for designating a more grievous passion. Therefore, the same word is used concerning the bruising of the serpentine head, by which it is most grievous to the ancient Dragon, and his power is utterly bruised and destroyed, as the Johannine explanation has it, 1 Epistle 3, 8. But this difference is to be observed here: that for the ancient serpent the HEAD was to be bruised, for the seed of the woman only the HEEL. His power and empire had to be destroyed, which indeed will not happen without the injury and passion of the latter, and that most grievous, so that he may seem to be utterly bruised, but because the head is safe, only the heel will be bruised, he will prevail in this fight, he will emerge from passion and death and will carry off the victory. שׁוּף is he bruised, struck, shattered, crushed: as it is used concerning Job, ch. 6, 17, in a whirlwind he will bruise me; the Chaldean expounds, he will crush; R. Levi, he will crush. Therefore R. Solomon rendered it in this place by to crush and R. Aben-Ezra by to strike; the Targum of Jonathan expounded it as to wound, the Jerusalem [Targum] as to kill in the former clause, although in this latter one it interprets it as נשך, he bit. Contrition is attributed to both, albeit with a different outcome, in that by the one the head is crushed, by the other only the heel, but with the same effort, because in both cases the same word is applied. The scope of this sermon was certainly to propose to the protoplasts, crushed by the sentence of the law, a remedy against sin and Satan; by grasping which through faith they might raise themselves up, which the older Jews themselves saw. But what other remedy is there than that which the passion and death of Christ provides for our sins? Blessed Luther says this excellently. The first parents and their descendants learned this first consolation, and as it were the fountain of all mercy and the source of all promises, with the greatest diligence. For they saw that, if they were without this promise, a generation would indeed remain among men, as among the rest of living creatures. But one which is nothing other than a generation unto death. That gift therefore, divinely added to nature, is here increased, nay consecrated, since there is hope of such a generation, through which the head of Satan is to be crushed, so that not only is his tyranny broken, but also nature, condemned to death on account of sin, may attain eternal life. For Moses is no longer speaking here of a natural serpent, he is speaking of the Devil, whose head are death and sin. As Christ says in John 8, that he is a murderer and the father of lies. His power therefore being crushed, that is, sin and death being removed through Christ, what remains but that we, the sons of God, should be saved? In this way Adam and Eve then understood the text, and comforted themselves against sin and despair, by the hope of this crushing to be performed by Christ, and by the hope of this promise they will also rise again on the last day into eternal life.

And a little later: Included therefore in this sentence is redemption from law, sin, and death, and there is shown a manifest and certain hope of resurrection and renewal in another life, after this life. For if the serpent's head must be crushed, it is surely necessary that Death be abolished. If death is abolished, the merit of death is also abolished, that is, sin. If sin, then the law also is abolished: And not only that, but at the same time the obedience which was lost is restored. But all these things, because they are promised through this Seed, it is sufficiently clear that human nature after the fall could not by its own powers either take away sin, or escape the punishments of sin and death, or recover the lost obedience; For these things require greater force and greater strength than that of men. Therefore it was necessary for the Son of GOD to become a victim, that he might accomplish these things for us, that he might take away sin, devour death, and restore the lost obedience. These treasures we possess in Christ, but in hope. Thus Adam, thus Eve, thus all believers until the last day live and conquer by this hope. So far the blessed Luther. But how the antediluvian Patriarchs raised themselves up by this πρωτευαγγελίῳ [protoevangelium], how it was explained more fully after the flood through the Spirit of Christ to the Patriarchs and Prophets, until it was irradiated by the far clearest light of fulfillment, our own people have explained after the great man Luther in various places; the blessed Polycarp Lyserus in the Patriarchs; the blessed Cramerus in the Prophetic writings: Waltherus in Officin. Bibl. Glassius in Mosaic Christology. We note here at least three parallel passages from the scriptures: One from the Psalms, one from the Prophets, one from the New Testament. From the Psalms, Psalm 110:6 pertains here. He shall strike through the head over much land. Concerning which the blessed Gesner beautifully says: In particular David looked to the promise made to the first parents in Paradise, the seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. Therefore he also names in the singular number one head of much or great land, from which the rest are inflated, which is that of the ancient Dragon, which rules in the children of disobedience and is the prince of this world: What is added, he shall drink of the brook in the way, corresponds in our oracle to the final words: You shall crush his heel: because by the drinking from the brook in the way the Lord's passion and death is expressed, which is here designated by the wounding and crushing of the heel. From the Prophets we bring forward the words

Isaiah 27:1. In that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great and strong sword upon Leviathan the straight serpent, and upon Leviathan the crooked serpent, and he will kill the whale that is in the sea. For the Prophet looked without doubt to our oracle, and the battle established in it between Leviathan the ancient, truly crooked serpent, and the Lord, who visited him with a hard, great, and strong sword especially then, when he crushed his head in the passion. To which battle David, full of thanks, rouses this serpent-killer

Psalm 45:4. Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O Hero, with your glory and your majesty. But the most illustrious passage is Hebrews 2:14. Since the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise became a partaker. We have the subject, the seed of the woman, ὁμούσιον [consubstantial] to us: Therefore he adds that he assumed the seed of Abraham, so that indeed the Son of GOD might become the seed of the woman through the ἐπίληψιν [taking hold of] and assumption of human nature. For what end, however, was that done? That through death he might abolish him who has the empire of death, that is, the Devil. By which the predicate is explained: the head of the serpent through κράτος θανάτε [the power of death], the infernal serpent through Him who has the empire or power of death, which he obtained through the fall or the sin of men: the crushing of the serpentine head through the destruction or abolition of that power and empire, and of the Devil himself, by which he has that power. And hence that enmity is άσπονδος [implacable]: because, namely, he did not assume Angels, but the seed of Abraham, that he might liberate not the Angelic nature, but the human; but might destroy the power of the evil angels. By what reason, however, was that to be done? THROUGH DEATH, which is the very crushing of the heel in our oracle.

Thus therefore, that we may embrace its summary in a few words, the ancient serpent, the prince of the Devils, who had come forth from the infernal troop as if destined for this act of seduction of the Protoplasts, ὁ διάβολος [the devil], who with his Angels held the κράτος θανάτε [power of death] and had the human race under his feet, obtains as an antagonist the miserable and defeated woman, (with the Man, who had been seduced by the same, and the offspring about to arise from these miserable slaves of the Devil not excluded, but included) with hostility denounced by GOD himself to the Devil, as they say today, a MANIFEST hostility, which he must henceforth expect from the human race; since the seed of the woman, as the defender of the human race and most powerful Hero, is about to trample under his feet the Dragon with his entire seed, the infernal troop, and is about to crush his head, his strength and his power, and indeed then, when he himself will be most crushed by the infernal Dragon, namely by the most grievous passions and a truculent death, so prostrated that it might seem to be all over for him. That one seed will prevail against the entire Diabolical troop, whose heel, although the Devil lying beneath him will inflict a not light wound, yet through the same his head will be crushed, and all Diabolical power will be destroyed. His feet, pierced with nails on the cross and stained with blood, which will be the crushing of the heel, will gloriously triumph over the Dragon: because through this very crushing of the heel the head will be crushed for him. Whence his feet seem like burnished bronze, as if refined in a furnace, Rev. 1:15, because they are adorned with the light of heavenly glory and equipped with the power to crush enemies and to torment them with eternal fire. See Glassius, diss. IV, Christol. Mosaicæ, thes. XXXVI.

Latin:

Vers. 15. INTER TE ET MULIER.) Mulier enim ad talia viro magis meticulosa. Sensum allegoricum vide Apocal. 12.

ET SEMEN TUUM.) Omne serpentum genus. Alle- gorice impii. Johann. 8. vers. 44. Actor. 13. vers. 10. 1. Joh. 3. vers. 8. Sic Chananæi semen serpentis, Abarbaneli ad hunc locum.

ET SEMEN ILLIUS.) Semen mulieris sive nati [ex muliere sunt homines extra Adamum omnes. Job. 14. vers. 1. cap. 15. vers. 14. cap. 25. vers. 4. Matth. 11. vers. 11. Luc. 7. vers. 28. Sirac. 10. vers. 17. Idem est σπέρμα quod γέννημα, dicitur- que etiam de mulieribus, ut infra IV, 25. sicut allegorice mu- lier Ecclesia, ita semen mulieris, singuli qui ad Ecclesiam per- tinent. Galat. 4. vers. 26.

Etsi mulieris solum mentio fiat, non tamen ex- cluditur vir; neque mulier nominatur, quod il- la magis meticulosa, sed quod magis probrosum serpenti sit antiquo, Draconi infernali, opponi eidem miseram & seductam mulierem, quam ipse primum in nassam suam pertraxerat, & in extre- mam miseriam præcipitarat. Committitur enim hîc Rex ille superborum, fortis ille armatus Jobi 41. vers. 25. Luc. 11. vers. 21. cum ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει 1. Petr. 3. vers. 7. & ab eo superatur. In eo enim sol consolationis, dicente B. Luthero, oritur, quod Eva non modo non audiat, sibi maledici sicut serpenti, sed quod audiat, se tanquam in acie constitui contra ho- stem damnatum, idque spe auxilii, quod Filius DEI laturus erat.

Non dicta hæc ad serpentem naturalem, aut de odio naturali serpentis, & hominum, ut cum Judæis R. Aben-Esra, R. Salomone, Photiniani Smalcius de divin. Filii DEI c. 2. Sommerus refut. Petr. Carol. lib. 2. cap. 3. & è Reformatis Calvinus, Musculus, Beza, plerique alii: ut & Pontificii non- nulli, Bellarmin. Cornel. à Lapide, Bonfrer. &c. vo- lunt. Quia DEUS, inquit Cornelius, hominem ob pec- catum Dominio in bestias privavit, serpens cœpit ho- mini esse noxius, & lethalis, & vicissim homo cœpit esse serpenticida, quum ante peccatum nec ἀντιπάθεια, nec horror, nec odium, nec nocendi studium fuisset inter hominem & serpentem. Pareus iterum hoc genus supplicii & ad serpentem, & ad Diabolum refert, ac sensum duplicem fingit. Qui vero ab- surdus est. Majori tamen absurdidati se involvit Antonius Cregutus in arcanor. revelat. nupero qui triplicem hujus oraculi sensum esse contendit, ut primo literaliter de serpente animali, & de muliere, illiusque posteris; secundo mystice, sed tamen lite- raliter de Christo, qui antonomastice semen mulieris intelligatur, & de Diabolo serpente: tertio, ut per semen mulieris intelligantur etiam omnes fideles, qui in Christo Semine primigenio inseruntur, & contra per semen serpentis omnes reprobi, qui Sa- tanæ sunt progenies p. 107. Hæc itaque verba, & ipsum conteret tibi caput, explicat respectu serpentis bruti, qua caput ei ab homine conteritur, & respe- ctu serpentis antiqui, qua a Semine mulieris Chri- sto conteritur ei caput, ejusque cornu infringitur, & denique respectu Diaboli etiam & infidelium ser- pentum & serpentigenarum, quorum caput a fideli- bus conteritur p. 119. Ita ergo Pronomen Ipsum, Creguto autore, notat primum omnes homines, tum fideles, denique unum Christum: pronomen alterum Tibi notat primum serpentem animal, tum Diabo- lum & infideles, denique solum Diabolum: Nomen capitis notat primum caput Physicum serpentis ani- malis, tum potentiam Dæmonum & infidelium, de- nique imperium Diaboli. Verbum Conterere acci- pitur secundum ipsum & proprie pro conculcatione quæ pedibus fit; & improprie tum de victoria, quam reportant fideles a Diabolo & infidelibus, tum de victoria, quam Christus solus in morte reportavit a Diabolo: ibi, inquit Cregutus pag. 121. serpens mordet calcaneum, at semen mulieris conterit caput serpentis: quia Christus mortuus, sed revixit victor, at Diabolus & vinctus & victus nunquam solvendus atque resurgendus a morte æterna. Ubi tum barbari- em Grammaticam Professoris & Pastoris Calvinia- ni in Academia & Ecclesia Dienfi nota, in voce RE- SURGENDUS, tum Theologiam de morte Dia- boli æterna, ex qua resuscitandus non sit; & conci- lia triplicem illum sensum (quem ceu a Spiritu S. intentum, & optime ac θεολογοτάτως erutum, ut per consequens illustrior evadat multiformis illa Scriptu- rarum sapientia, & magis miraculose appareant illæ linguæ dispertitæ ignis, ita tuetur Cregutus, ut acriter in Doctores alios Calvin. invehatur, qui frigide unum tantum sensum hic amplectuntur, easque vitilitigationes dicat, de hilo, & περὶ τῶν Φλυαρίων pag. 108.) cum argumentis & rationibus, quibus ipse probat semen mulieris hic modo singularissi- mo intelligendum esse de Christo p. 100. quem di- cit antonomastice vocari alias filium hominis, quia non est factus ἐκ σαρκὸς (quæ phrasis Anabaptista- rum hæresin resipit) sed κατὰ σάρκα: hic vero se- men mulieris, quia est semen duntaxat mulieris, non autem viri, respectu temporalis generationis, uti respectu æternæ est semen Patris æternæ ὁμοόσιον (quæ phrasis Creguti iterum ἄγραφος καὶ ἀθεό- λογος, imo horrida est) & individualiter per se- men mulieris hujus designari censet semen hujus virginis Mariæ, nec ulli præter Christum tantam for- titudinem competere, ut caput serpentis conterat: imo tantum institui antithesin in hoc oraculo in- ter primum & secundum Adamum: Quomodo er- go hoc oraculum de alio quam Christo interpreta- ri potest? Hæc enim aperte ἀντιφατικὰ sunt, Mu- lier hic est Maria, & Mulier hic non est Maria, sed Eva, Semen Mulieris hic est solus Christus, & se- men mulieris non est solus Christus, sed omnes posteri Evæ, item non omnes posteri Evæ, sed soli fideles. Et porro, solus Christus conterit caput ser- pentis: & non solus Christus, sed etiam fideles con- terunt caput serpentis &c. Sed relinquamus hæc arcana autori suo, qui alia pluscula paradoxa pro arcanis revelatis venditare non dubitat: è quibus unum atque alterum solum hic non plane ἀλλό- τριον observasse juvat: Siquidem contritio hæc capitis serpentini satisfactionem meritoriam im- portet, objicit adversus eandem pag. 64. injustum videri unicam personam pati pro aliis: & respon- det, nequaquam; nam illa persona vel consideratur εἰδικῶς, vel ut est τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον : Si priori modo il- lo, quod pag. 64. docuit, Christo patiente totam naturam humanam pati, quia ea una & eadem in omnibus hominibus sit; item cum totum hu- manum genus morti esset obnoxium, etiam Chri- stum ceu sub specie contentum obnoxium fuisse morti: item Christus non est corruptus per se, at quamob- rem? nisi quia per gratiam sanctificatus in hunc fi- nem, ut pro aliis satisfaceret: Item Christus in virgi- nis utero à Spiritu Sancto fuit sanctificatus: Item Christus fuit innocens non ex natura, sed ex gratia, ut pro nobis justitiæ divinæ satisfaceret. Ex istis ju- dicare de aliis arcanis in proclivi erit, uti ex ungue de leone. Totum vero Prot-Evangelium, funda- mentum promissionum omnium, evertit Grotiana Ψευδερμηνεία, per semen serpentis omne serpentum genus, per semen mulieris omnes ejus posteros secun- dum literalem sensum intelligi. Quæ ex iis, quæ jam dicta sunt, facile profligatur. Nimirum in toto hoc processu, uti ostensum, tanquam actu judiciali,

DEO res erat non cum serpente tantum, sed im- primis cum eo, qui serpente ceu organo uteba- tur. Et illi quidem jam ante pœna denunciata erat. Ideoque cum illo non amplius agit DEUS. Hîc ergo ad Satanam insessorem serpentis oratio dirigitur, eique judicium denunciatur: ideoque dum inimicitias Deus ipse ponit, hostemque ser- penti opponit mulierem, ac semini serpentis se- men mulieris, non de hostilitate inter genus ser- pentum, & liberos Evæ, vel humanum genus agi- tur, cujus gratia sane tanto cum apparatu, neque judicium coram tribunali divino celebrari, neque remedium humano generi promitti aut parari ne- cessum erat. Sed constituitur in acie mulier ad- versus hostem seductorem, serpentem antiquum, Satanam, sub angue isto latentem, ejusque genus universum: Neque hîc demum allegoricus aut mysticus est sensus, sed nativus & literalis, primo à DEO intentus. Non opus itaque gemino dicti ejusdem sensu hîc est: quem assignare Grotius videtur, alterum literalem de serpente naturali; alterum mysticum vel allegoricum, de Diabolo. Ob quam causam idem verbis sequentibus, & tu in- sidiaberis calcaneo ejus, geminum pariter sensum tradidit. Priorem, qui serpentibus conveniat cal- caneo insidiantibus Genes. XLIX. vers. 17. Posteri- orem, qui Diabolo, ex insidiis agenti. Unius di- cti non potest nisi unicus tantum sensus esse, nisi divina oracula ambigua facias, qualia erant Apol- linis, hoc est Dæmonis Deceptoris, quod vel cogitatu impium est. Nihil certi de mente di- vina habebimus, ubi semel admissa fuerit ejus- modi ἀμφιβολογία. De serpente naturali versu præcedenti jam actum erat, cui triplex maledictio facta. Qua ergo ratione iterum sensu primario & literali de serpente ageretur, nec nisi secunda- rio & allegorico de Diabolo, proprio seductionis autore, qui serpente tantum ceu organo suo usus fuit? Nec vero serpentes tantum odit ho- mo, atque enecat, sed alia quoque noxia & ve- nenata animantia. Neque ita hominibus naturalis est illa ἀντιπάθεια cum serpentibus, ut non re- periantur quandoque, quibus bene cum illis conveniat, quod de Tiberio Svetonius, de Tro- glodytis serpentum carne vescentibus Plinius lib. V. cap. 8. de agyrtis & Magis per incantationem demulcentibus serpentes, experientia testatur. Num vero hostilitatem à Deo positam ars ulla tol- lere poterit?

A Calvino hîc seductum dicerem Grotium, qui in Commentar. super Genes. SIMPLICITER, in- quit, interpretor, hostile semper fore dissidium huma- no generi cum serpentibus, quale hodie cernitur, ni- si & Calvino maximopere infensus esset, & à Judæis potius nuperis illis ac juratis Messiæ hostibus, uter- que seductus videretur, quorum commenta nimi- um deperit Grotius, ut Papistarum etiam suorum præ illis obliviscatur. Qui unanimi ferme senten- tia literarem sensum hujus loci faciunt, quem alle- goricum tantum vult Grotius. Quod in Judæis quo- que antiquioribus observatur: Testis est Paraphra- sis Onkelos, ac imprimis Hierosolymitana, quæ hîc clarior: Illa ita habet: Inimicitiam ponam inter te & inter mulierem & inter filium tuum & filium ejus: Ipse observabit tibi, quod fecisti ei ab initio, & tu ob- servabis ei in fine. Hæc, interprete Fagio, sic expli- cuit oraculum: Et erit, quando Filii mulieris ope- ram dabunt legi & fecerint præcepta, tunc studebunt tibi conterere caput & occident te. Cum vero deserue- rint filii mulieris præcepta legis, nec servabunt man- data, tu operam dabis, ut mordeas eos in calcaneis eo- rum, & ita noceas eis. Veruntamen remedium erit fi- liis mulieris, tibi vero serpenti nullum erit remedium: quandoquidem futurum est, ut amoveant morsum, qui factus est in calcaneo, in fine dierum, in diebus scil. Messiæ. Quæ iisdem pene verbis habentur quoque in Thargum Jonathan. Testes etiam interpretatio- nes Judæorum veterum, de quibus monet Maimo- nid. in Mor. Nebuch. l. 2. c. 30. oportet te scire, quo- modo illud explicent in Midrasch: Videlicet serpentem fuisse equitatum, qui magnitudine ad Camelum acce- deret: Sessorem autem eum fuisse, qui decepit Evam: Sammaëlem nempe, quam nomenclaturam Satanæ absolute tribuunt. Testis etiam R. Bechai in h. l. ita scribens: Non sunt nobis inimicitiæ magis cum serpen- te, quam cum ceteris reptilibus. Quamobrem Scri- ptura hæc mystice innuit eum, qui in serpente occulta- batur. Corpus enim serpentis callidi erat instrumen- tum, aptum ad recipiendum virtutem conjunctam cum eo. Et ille est is, qui terram peccare fecit, unde mors intravit in omnem progeniem ejus. Et hæc est inimicitia inter serpentem & inter semen mulieris. Et hoc est mysterium linguæ sanctæ, quod serpens alibi appellatur Saraph juxta nomen, quo Angelus etiam appellatur Saraph.

Serpens itaque, quem hic quidem v. 15. alloqui- tur Deus, est antiquus ille serpens, Diabolorum an- tesignanus, Apoc. 12, 9. & supremus inter ipsos, qui aggresfus erat protoplastos in serpente. Semen vero ejus intelligendum non generatione, sed imitatione & ὁμοψηφίᾳ seu consensione de reliqua Diabolorum caterva, quemadmodum ordines alibi inter Dia- bolos constituuntur Beelzebub ἄρχων princeps ali- quis inter ipsos Luc. 11, 15. alii ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξσσίαι Co- loff. 2, 15. καὶ δυνάμεις Rom. 8, 38. vocantur; alii aliis deteriores indigitantur Luc. 11, 26. imo discri- men apertum inter Diabolum vel Draconem anti. quum serpentem, ejusque angelos. Matth. 25, 41. Apo- cal. 12, 6. constituitur. Judæi principem Dæmo- num seductorem Protoplastorum faciunt, eique nomen Sammaël tribuunt, uti è Maimonide in Mor. Nebuch. lib. 2. c. 30. paulo ante notavimus.

Non absimili tropo progenies viperarum, & ex Patre Diabolo esse dicuntur Pharisæi, aliiqve impii Matth. 23, 33. Johann. 8, 44. ob consensum scil. atqve imita- tionem: quia qui perpetrat peccatum, ex Diabolo est. Diabolus enim peccat ab initio 1. Joh. 3, 8. Plenam ἐξήγησιν hujus πρωτευαγγελίε nobis exhibuit Dn. D. Waltherus noster in Officina Biblica: Refutatio- nem autem uberiorem glossæ Judaicæ B. Dn. Ægi- dius Hunnius; qui eam in Calvino Judaizante ejus- que hyperaspista Davide Pareo profligavit. Non er- go admittendum, quod asserit Grotius; allegorice impios hîc intelligi, uti Cananæi semen serpentis Abar- beneli dicti. Sed ut mulieris semen ejusdem naturæ est cum muliere, ita hîc semen antiqui serpentis ὁμοό- σιον indigitatur, caterva reliqua Diabolorum. Nam solatium protoplastis subministrandum erat pro toto humano genere, adversus universam Diabolo- rum catervam, nec inimicitiæ constituendæ aliquo- rum hominum contra Diabolicam potestatem, sed omnibus hominibus in protoplastis totius generis sui personam sustinentibus, præcipitatis, (in uno enim peccavimus omnes Rom. 5, 12.) remedium pa- randum erat. Non ergo locum hîc habet partitio illa hominum in pios atque impios, ubi in persona matris viventium omnibus salutis restauratio pro- mittitur. Qua proper nec per semen mulieris, qui ad Ecclesiam pertinent, nec per semen serpentis impii cum Grotio intelligendi; quemcunque eum tan- dem dicas sensum, sive mysticum sive literalem: Sed uti per mulieris semen unus Christus designatur; ita per semen antiqui serpentis universa Diabolorum ca- terva: cui toti superandæ unus Christus opponitur in hoc Dei consilio ac decreto, qui unus abunde sufficit, nec extra eum quisquam alius hîc desi- gnari poterat. In hoc uno salus est, nec datur aliud nomen sub cælo, in quo salvari oporteat Actor. 4, 12. Humana potestas tanti quidem non est, ut opponi possit serpenti ejusque semini. Quicquid autem adversus antiquum serpentem, ejusque semen va- let humanum genus, id unice in Christo valemus, in quo solo est fortitudo & justitia nostra Esa. 45, 25. Unde πορισματικῶς & consequenter ad nos redun- dat fructus constitutæ illius hostilitatis, quam etiam adversus impios, eorumque machinationes nostro cedere bono agnoscimus; sed in eo non est figen- dus sensus hujus oraculi, ut jam dicemus. Ideoque perperam Josephus Medus per semen mulieris Christum mysticum, ut vocat, caput cum membris in- telligit hoc loco.

IPSA CONTERET CAPUT TUUM.) Quasi de mu- liere ageretur, sensu non malo. Sed Hebræus textus, quem nunc habemus, masculinum præfert tum in pronomine, tum in verbo, ut appareat, referri ad semen זרע, quod He- bræis est generis masculini. Et sic hunc locum explicat Irenæus III, 38. LXX. ἀυτὸς posuere ex Hebræo, quanquant apud Græcos σπέρμα neutrius est generis. Itaque sic con- structionem fecere, quasi præcessisset non σπέρμα, sed quod idem significat σπορά. Eos sequitur Irenæus IV, 78. Et Cyprianus Testimonio 11. libr. 2. adversus Judæos. Tales ubi- que multæ sunt constructiones πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. Conte- ret caput tuum ישופך ראש συντρίψει Rom. 16, 20. Caput calcare est contemtus nota. Ezech. 34, 18. inde qui præsidio divino confidunt, dicuntur aspidem calcare Psalm. 91, 12. πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων Luc. 10, 19. Potestatem calcandi super colubros & scorpios dixit Tertullianus adversus Marcionem 4. Idem urgere bestiam calce in scorpiaco. In capite enim serpentis vis maxima mali. Ecclesiastici 25. v. 21. Sic Christo duce, diabolo facile resistunt, eumque superant Christiani. Jac. 4, 7. 1. Petr. 5, 9. 1. Joh. 2, 13. 14.

At Ebræum textum nunc aliter habere, quam habuerit olim, probandum. Quod vero ne uno in- dicio antiquitatis heluo docere potuit. Cur ergo Vulgatam defendit, nisi in gratiam Conciliabuli Tri- dentini, & Pontificis Romani? Imo textum Ebræum non היא seu ipsa, sed הוא ipse vel ipsum habuisse convincitur facile: siquidem omnes Codices Ebræi legant הוא. Nam quod in editione interlineari ad marginem notatum est קרי, à manu infida adjectum est in gratiam Vulgatæ Latinæ, sine ullius Ebræi Codicis autoritate, protestante insuper Aria Mon- tano, se inscio hoc factum, de quo Franc. Luc. Brugens. Refellitur etiam id non solum è Masora observante ad Genes. 36, 27. undecim loca habere הוא in quibus hic textus non habetur: nec non è verbis ipsis, puta tum è pronomine affixo, tum è ver- bo, quod utrobique generis Masculini esse, non fœ- minini in Ebræo, nec aliter unquam ibi lectum es- se, agnoscere cogitur Grotius. Et sic, inquit, hunc locum explicat Irenæus cap. 3. v. 38. de semine mulieris. Tempore ergo Irenei Ecclesia non legit in fœmini- no genere IPSA. Neque etiam Interpp. LXX. ita le- gere. LXX. inquit Noster, αὐτὸς posuere ex Hebræo: quanquam apud Græcos σπέρμα est neutrius generis. Itaque sic constructionem fecere, quasi præcessisset non σπέρμα, sed, quod idem significat, σπόρος.
