Eos se- quitur Ireneus v. 78. et Cyprianus Testimonio 11. libri adversus Judæos: Tales ubique multæ sunt constructio- nes πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. Hæc Grotius. Non er- go ad κρησφύγετον suum se recipere potest, aliter olim habuisse textum Hebræum, aliter nunc habere, nisi refragante verioris conscientia. Quid itaque restat, quam ut fateatur, male & contra textum ori- ginalem in Latina legi fœmininum IPSA. Nec tan- tum LXX. ita reddidere, Targum etiam Onkelos in masculino legit הוא, Ipse erit obversans tibi; ut & R. Aben-Ezra, semen ejus percutiet te in capite. Imo Hieronymus ipse ita legit, & transtulit in masculino IPSE, in quæst. in Genes. ubi producta LXX. In- terpp. translatione, Ipse servabit caput tuum, sub- jungit; Melius habet in Ebræo: Ipse conteret caput tuum. Ita Samaritanus Codex, Samaritano-Chal- dæus, item Arabs, perinde uti Græcæ & Chaldaicæ editiones legunt ipse. Quis vero credet male in omnibus aliis Codicibus legi, propterea, quod sola Latina Vulgata legat IPSA. Quid quod ipsi- met Lovanienses observent in Catalogo Variarum lectionum, non tantum omnes Hebræos, Chaldæos, Græcosq; codices pronomen masculinum habere, sed & duos MMS. Latinos Codices; qualia Latina exem- plaria observata etiam Francisco Lucæ & Roberto Stephani. Nec aliter Leo M. explicavit Serm. 2. de Nativ. Dn. DEus hîc denunciavit serpenti futurum semen mulieris, quod noxii capitis elevationem sua virtute conteret, Christum in carne scil. venturum. Quem Pontificem Romanum conciliaffe cum Six- to V. & Clemente VIII. si poterat, debebat Groti- us. At quomodo potuit, si serio Pontificum au- toritatem infallibilem credidit? Nisi forte quis dicat, hos è Cathedra pronunciasse authenticam Vulgatam, adeoque non errasse, Leonem M. extra cathedram omnino aberrasse à vera lectione: etsi Leo M. pro se habeat Ebræos, Chaldæos, Græcos, La- tinos codices, nec Ireneus, aut Cyprianus, aut Hiero- nymus aliter legerint. Maluere tamen antiquiorem Leonem, quam de cathedra pronunciantes nuperos Pontifices sequi Joh. Benedictus, Franc. Lucas, Au- gustinus Steuchus, Johannes Isaacus, Sacrobosco, Franc. Georgius Venetus, Andradius, Felisius (Elucid. De- cal. præc. 1. cap. 48.) Hect. Pintus (in cap. 12. Es.) Lindanus (de optim. gener. interpr. lib. 3. p. 126.) Hartus (colloqu. cum Rainold. c. 6.) & Cardinalis Cajetanus, Melch. Canus, Canar. Episc. nec non præ- cipui è Schola Jesuitica Pererius & Ribera, qui omnes non ad mulierem, sed ad semen mulieris pro- nomen referunt. Thomas Malvenda Hispan. Fœ- minæ lectioni, inquit, præfero masculinam vel neu- tram, ut gloria redemtionis in solidum Christo ser- vetur. Facilis fuit lapsus, inquit P. Picherellus ab Ipse ad Ipsa. Agnoscit denique etiam depravatio- nem hîc in vulgata translatione Ludovicus Capel- lus in opere tantopere laudato Grotio Crit. Sacr. lib. 5. c. 11. p. 370. Facile, inquit, est videre lectionem illam, licet antiquam, IPSA, esse depravatam ex librarii inscitia, qui cum videret pronomen IPSE non convenire genere cum antecedente nomine, puta- vit legendum esse IPSA, illudque referri ad nomen mu- lieris; itaque commutavit pronomen masculinum in fœmininum IPSA.

Et quis ille sensus NON MALUS de muliere est? Papistarum certe sensus pessimus & idololatricus. Qui hinc Mariam corredemtricem faciunt, quæ caput serpentis calcavit. Idcirco adorant eandem in Antidotario animæ fol. 118. Adoro & benedico sanctissimos pedes tuos, quibus antiqui serpentis ca- put calcasti. Similia videantur in Mariali Bernardini de Busto, approbato à Sixto IV. part. 11. Serm. 2. & p. 12. Serm. 2. Et apud ipsum Bellarm. l. 1. de septem verbis Christi in cruce c. 12. p. 102. Num excusa- bit sensum illum Grotius? Sed mulierem is fecit Ec- clesiam, semen mulieris singulos, qui ad Ecclesiam per- tinent. Atque ita Christo duce caput serpentis con- terere id est Diabolo facile resistere eumque superare Christianos ait, Jac. 4. v. 7. 1. Petr. 5. v. 9. 1. Joh. 2. v. 13. 14. Verum si per pronomen IPSA intelligitur Ecclesia allegorice, quænam ergo mulier sensu pro- prio hîc intelligitur? Et annon ita hîc excluditur plane Christus, cui præcipue convenire sententiam istam, utpote cujus virtute cæteri omnes calcant Dia- bolum, fatetur Gordonus Huntlæus, etsi ad literam intelligat per pronomen fœmininum Ecclesiam, & per consequens Mariam, ceu membrum Ecclesiæ; ne- que arbitror diffitebitur quisquam. Christo duce ca- put conteri serpentis agnoscit Grotius. At stante illo ejus sensu non malo, nullus hîc Christo relinquitur locus, quum sensu proprio per pronomen Eva, alle- gorico Ecclesia intelligatur, ut per semen mulieris fi- deles. Nulla ergo de Christo facta hîc promissio, de quo tamen eadem explicata deinceps fuit penes Patriarchas ab ipso Deo Genes. 22, 18. cap. 26, 4. cap. 28, 14. ceu de semine mulieris benedicto: nec non ab Apostolo Galat. 3, 18. Non dicit in seminibus, quasi in multis, sed semine, quasi in uno, qui est Christus. Quod de Patriarchis facta promissione observat A- postolus, sed pariter observari debere in πρωτευ- αγγελίῳ hoc suo exemplo docet. Unum enim idemque semen est, quod conterit caput serpentis, & in quo uno tollitur moledictio, & benedictio ob- tingit omnibus nationibus terræ, uti interpretatur Apostolus. Neque dubium est ipsismet Papistis, vocem seminis magis proprie de uno individuo, nem- pe singulariter, quam collective accipi. V. Gen. 4, 25. c. 15, 3. c. 21, 13. Ruth. 4, 12. 13. 2. Sam. 7, 22. 1. Par. 17, 13. hîc autem ne aliter quidem accipi potest. Quia prædicatum capitis serpentini contritio destructio- nem potestatis, & regni Diaboli, quod in violentia peccati & mortis consistit 1. Cor. 15, 16. Ebr. 2, 14. de- signat, quæ infinitæ virtutis est & uni Christo pro- pria 1. Joh. 3, 8. etsi fructus contritionis & destructi- onis istius fidelibus communicetur, qui per fidem in Christum conculcant Draconem Ps. 91, 13. vin- cunt Diabolum 1. Joh. 2, 13. & per sanguinem Agni Apoc. 12, 11. Datur enim ipsis victoria à Deo per Do- minum Jesum Christum 1. Cor. 15, 57. Conf. Marc. 16, 17. 18. Luc. 10, 19. Rom. 16, 20. ideo vere quidem, at insufficienter nimium Grotius: Capitis calcatio est contemtus nota Ez. 34, 18. Plura de his diximus Crit. Sacr. p. 669. sqq. Addo hîc antiquissimi Patrum Irenæi explicationem l. 4. c. 78. Quapropter & Deus eum quidem, qui à semetipso Zizaniam absconse seminavit, id est, transgressionem, quam ipse intulit, separavit à sua conversione, Eum autem, qui negligenter quidem, sed male accepit inobedientiam, hominem miseratus est, & retorsit inimicitiam, per quam inimicum DEO facere voluit, in ipsum inimicitiarum autorem, auferens quidem suam, quæ erat adversus hominem, inimicitiam, retorquens autem illam & mittens illam in serpentem: Quemadmodum & Scriptura ait, dixisse serpenti Dominum, & inimicitiam ponam inter te & mulierem, & inter semen tuum, & inter semen mulieris; Ipse tuum calcabit caput, & observabis calcaneum ejus: Et inimicitiam hanc Dominus in semetipsum recapitulavit, de muliere factus homo, & calcans ejus caput. Et l. V. Omnia ergo recapitulans recapitulatus est & adversum inimicum nostrum bellum provocans, & elidens eum, qui initio in Adam captivos duxerat nos, & calcans ejus caput, quemadmodum habet in Genesi dixisse Serpenti DEum: Et inimicitiam ponam inter te & inter mulierem & inter semen tuum & semen ejus, ipse tuum observabit caput & tu observabis ejus calcaneum. Ex eo enim, qui ex muliere virgine habebat nasci secundum similitudinem Adam, præconiabatur observans caput serpentis, i. e. semen, de quo ait Apostolus in Epist. ad Galatas, Legem factorum positam, donec veniret semen, cui promissum est. Manifestus autem in eadem ostendit Epistola, dicens: Cum autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit DEus Filium suum, factum de muliere. Neque enim juste victus fuisset inimicus, nisi ex muliere homo esset, qui vicit eum. Per mulierem enim homini dominatus est ab initio, semetipsum contrarium statuens homini. Propter hoc & Dominus semetipsum filium hominis confitetur, principalem hominem illum, ex quo ea, quæ secundum mulierem est, plasmatio facta, in semetipso recapitulans, uti quemadmodum per hominem victum descendit in mortem genus nostrum, sic iterum per hominem victorem adscendamus in vitam. Et quemadmodum accepit palmam mors per hominem adversus nos, sic iterum nos adversus mortem per hominem accipiamus palmam. Non autem Dominus antiquam illam & primam adversus serpentem inimicitiam in semetipso recapitulatus fuisset, adimplens promissionem Demiurgi & perficiens præceptum ejus, si ab alio venisset Patre, sed quoniam unus & idem est, qui ab initio plasmavit nos, & in fine Filium suum misit, præceptum ejus perfecit Dominus, factus ex muliere & destruens adversarium nostrum, & perficiens hominem secundum imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Hæc omnia Ireneus, quæ præclare veteris Ecclesiæ fidem de Prot-Evangelio, cum doctrina Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ modernæ ex asse consonantem demonstrant, solideque glossas Grotianas refellunt.

ET TU INSIDIABERIS CALCANEO EJUS.) Ita solent serpentes Genes. 18, 17. Nicander de Chelydro: Ἤτοι ὅγ’ ἐν κώληπ@ ἠὲ ἐν ποδὸς ἴχνεϊ τύψῃ. Ovid. Metam. 10. Occidit in talum serpentis dente recepto. Inde nomen solpugæ. Claudius Neapolitanus οἱ ὄφεις πατηθέντες δάκνουσι. Sic Diabolus postquam de imperiis & vi cogente decidit, ex insidiis maxime agit 2.Cor. 2, 11. cap. 11, 3. 14. Ephes. 6, 11. Illud vero insidiaberis videtur esse ex lectione Græca τηρήσεις, pro quo alii Codices habent τειρήσεις, id est, mordebis, quod propius accedit ad Hebræum תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ.

Geminum sensum pandit; literalem de serpente naturali, Allegoricum de Diabolo. Sed unicum tantum esse unius dicti sensum antea monuimus. Neque hîc agi de serpente, sed tantum de Diabolo in hoc quidem versu: multò minus primario de serpente. Tum vero is cujus calcaneus conterendus, non est alius, quam ὁ ὀφιομάχ@, qui caput serpentis conteret. Quem unum Christum esse docuimus. Non ergo de insidiis Diaboli adversus fide- les vel Ecclesiam directe agitur: sed adversus Chri- stum, semen mulieris. Non de iis quæ agit, post- quam de imperiis decidit: Sed quæ eo ipso, dum caput ei conteritur, machinatur. Quod nempe dum semen mulieris in eo est, ut caput conterat serpenti antiquo, quod in opere redemtionis im- primis factum, ab antiquo serpente in calcaneo plagam accepturum sit, in passione & morte, uti jam Ireneus explicavit. Quæ interpretatio tum ver- bis ipsis, tum scopo & intentioni hujus πρωτευαγγε- λίꙋ, tum explicationi in Scripturis traditæ ex asse consentanea. Verba non inferunt tantum insidias solpuga: Sed mortem & contritionem calcanei. Unde Grotius ipse versionem Vulgatam, sed tacite, ne ægre Papistis faciat, ex Ebræo corrigit. Illud insi- diaberis, inquit, videtur esse ex lectione Græca τηρή- σεις, pro quo alii codices habent τειρήσεις, id est, mor- debis, quod propius accedit ad Hebræum: תשופנו. Ἐμφατικώτερον tamen est verbu Hebræum: quia non tantum mortem, sed contritionem infert, quæ pas- sioni graviori designandæ aptior est. Ideo de con- tritione capitis serpentini verbum idem adhibetur, qua ægerrime sit antiquo Draconi, ejusq; potestas pror- sus conteritur ac destruitur, ut Johannea habet ex- plicatio 1. Epist. 3, 8. Sed hæc differentia hîc obser- vanda: quod antiquo serpenti quidem CAPUT conterendum fuerit, femini mulieris solum CAL- CANEUS. Illius potestas & imperium destrui de- buit, quod non quidem absque hujus læsione ac passione fiet eaque gravissima, ut conteri plane vi- deatur, sed quia caput salvum est, calcaneus tantum conteretur, prævalebit in hac pugna, è passione & morte emerget & victoriam reportabit. שׁוּף est contrivit, percussit, conquassavit, contudit: uti de Jobo adhibetur c. 6, 17. in turbine conteret me, Chaldæus exponit, comminuet, R. Levi contundet. Ideo R. Salomo reddidit hoc loco per comminuere & R. A- ben-Ezra percutere; Targum Jonath. vulnerare, Hie- rosolymitanum occidere in priore commate exposuit, quamvis in hoc posteriori נשך momordit interprete- tur. Contritio utrique tribuitur, dispari quidem eventu, qua ab altero caput, ab altero calcaneus tan- tum conteritur, sed eodem conatu, quia utrobique idem adhibetur verbum. Scopus certe hujus con- cionis erat remedium adversus peccatum & Satanam protoplastis sententia legis contritis proponere; quo fide apprehenso sese erigere possint, quod Ju- dæi ipsi antiquiores viderunt. Quodnam autem ali- ud remedium est, quam quod passio & mors Chri- sti pro peccatis nostris suppeditat? Præclare hic B. Luther. Hanc primam consolationem & tanquam fontem omnis misericordiæ & omnium promissionum scaturiginem, primi Parentes & eorum posteri summa diligentia didicerunt. Viderunt enim, si absq; hac promissione essent, mansuram quidem inter homines, sicut inter reliqua animantia, generationem. Sed quæ nihil aliud sit, quam generatio ad mortem. Illud igitur donum divinitus naturæ additum hic augetur, imo consecratur, cum spes sit talis generationis, per quam Satanæ conterendum sit caput, ut non solum ejus tyran- nis infringatur, sed etiam natura propter peccatum morti addicta consequatur vitam æternam. Non enim agit hic Moses amplius de serpente naturali, de Dia- bolo loquitur, cujus caput sunt mors & peccatum. Sicut Christus Joh. 8. quod sit homicida & pater mendacii. Contrita igitur potestate ejus, h. e. subla- to per Christum peccato & morte, quid restat, quam ut Filii Dei salvemur? Ad hunc modum Adam & Heva tunc textum intellexerunt, & consolati sunt se contra peccatum & desperationem, spe hujus con- tritionis per Christum futuræ, ac spe hujus promissionis in novissimo die etiam resurgent in æternam vitam.

Et paulo post: Includitur igitur in hanc sententiam redemptio à lege, peccato & morte, & ostenditur ma- nifesta spes & certa resurrectionis & innovationis in altera vita, post hanc vitam. Si enim serpentis caput conteri debet, profecto oportet aboleri Mortem. Si mors aboletur, etiam mortis meritum aboletur, hoc est, peccatum. Si peccatum, ergo lex quoque aboletur: Nec id tantum, sed restituitur simul obedientia, quæ amissa est. Hæc autem omnia, quia promittuntur per Semen hoc, satis clarum est, naturam humanam post lapsum suis viribus nec peccatum tollere, nec pœnas peccati & mortem effugere, nec obedientiam amissam recuperare potuisse; Majorem enim vim & robur majus, quam hominum est, requirunt ista. Itaque Filium DEI opor- tuit victimam fieri, ut hæc nobis conficeret, ut tolleret peccatum, devoraret mortem & amissam obedientiam restitueret. Hos thesauros in Christo possidemus, sed in spe. Sic Adam, sic Heva, sic omnes credentes usque ad novissimum diem spe ista vivunt & vincunt. Hactenus B. Lutherus. Quomodo autem hoc πρωτευαγγελίῳ se erexerint Patriarchæ antedilu- viani, quomodo id explicatum uberius post diluvi- um fuerit per Spiritum Christi, Patriarchis & Pro- phetis, donec luce complementi longe clarissima irradiaretur, exposuere post Megalandrum Luthe- rum passim nostrates; B. Polycarpus Lyserus in Patri- archis; B. Cramerus in scriptis Propheticis: Wal- therus in Officin. Bibl. Glassius in Christologia Mo- saica. Tria saltim hic è scripturis notamus paralle- la loca: Unum è Psalmis, unum è Prophetis, unum è Nov. Test. E Psalmis huc facit CX, 6. Transfi- get caput super terram multam. Quo de B. Gesne- rus pulchre: Imprimis David respexit ad promissio- nem primis parentibus in Paradiso factam, semen mu- lieris conteret caput serpentis. Ideo etiam in singulari numero nominat unum caput multæ seu magnæ ter- ræ, à quo cætera inflantur, quod est antiqui Draconis, quod dominatur in filiis incredulitatis & princeps est hujus mundi: Quæ adduntur, de torrente in via bi- bet, respondent in nostro oraculo postremis ver- bis: Tu ipsi conteres calcaneum: quia per bibitionem de torrente in via passio & mors Dominica exprimi- tur, quæ hîc per vulnerationem & contritionem cal- canei designatur. E Prophetis adducimus verba

Esa. 27. 1. In die illa visitabit Dominus in gladio suo duro & grandi & forti super Leviathan serpentem re- ctum, & super Leviathan serpentem tortuosum, & occidet cetum, qui in mari. Respexit enim sine du- bio Propheta ad oraculum nostrum, & pugnam in eo constitutam inter Leviathan serpentem anti- quum vere tortuosum, & Dominum, qui eum gla- dio duro, grandi & forti imprimis tum visitavit, cum caput ei in passione contrivit. Ad quam pugnam hunc serpenticidam gratulabundus excitat David

Psalm. 45, 4. Accingere gladio tuo super semen tuum Heros, gloria tua, & decore tuo. Sed maxime illustris locus est Ebr. 2, 14. Quoniam pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est. Habemus subjectum semen mulieris no- bis ὁμούσιον: Ideo addit semen Abrahæ eum assum- psisse, ut nempe Filius DEI semen mulieris fieret per humanæ naturæ ἐπίληψιν & assumtionem. Quo fine autem illa facta? Ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, Diabolum. Qui- bus predicatum explicatur: caput serpentis per κρά- τος θανάτε, serpens infernalis per Eum, qui impe- rium mortis vel potestatem habet, quam per lapsum vel peccatum hominum consequutus est: contritio capitis serpentini per destructionem vel abolitionem potestatis & imperii istius, & Diaboli ipsius, qua pote- statem illam habet. Atque hinc άσπονδος est illa inimicitia: quia scil. non Angelos, sed semen Abrahæ assumsit, ut liberaret non naturam Angelicam, sed humanam; potestatem autem angelorum malo- rum destrueret. Qua autem id fieri ratione de- buit? PER MORTEM, quæ est ipsa calcanei con- tritio in nostro oraculo.

Ita ergo, ut summam ejus paucis complecta- mur, serpens antiquus Diabolorum princeps, qui ad hunc seductionis Protoplastorum actum veluti de- stinatus à caterva infernali prodierat ὁ διάβολος, qui cum suis Angelis κράτος θανάτε obtinebat & sub pedibus genus humanum habebat, antagoni- stam consequitur miseram & debellatam mulierem, (Viro, qui ab eadem seductus erat, atque propagi- ne à miseris hisce Diaboli mancipiis oritura non ex- clusis, sed comprehensis) denunciata ab ipso DEO per MANIFESTUM, uti hodie loquuntur, hosti- litate Diabolo, quam deinceps expectare habeat ab humano genere; quandoquidem semen mulie- ris ceu generis humani hyperaspistes & Heros poten- tissimus, Draconem cum universo semine suo, caterva infernali sub pedes suos prostratum conculcaturum, contriturum caput, robur & potestatem ejus de- structurum sit, & quidem tum, ubi maxime ipsum à Dracone infernali conteretur, passionibus nem- pe gravissimis ac morte truculenta ita prostra- tum, ut actum de ipso videatur. Unum illud semen adversus totam catervam Diabolicam prævalebit, cujus calcaneo etsi plagam sub eo jacens Diabolus inferet non levem, per eandem tamen caput ipsi conteretur, omnisque Diabolica potestas destrue- tur. Ipsi pedes in cruce clavis transfixi & sanguine madefacti, quæ calcanei erit contritio, gloriose triumphabunt de Dracone: quia per ipsam hanc contritionem calcanei caput conteretur eidem. Unde similes aurichalco videntur pedes, ut in camino igniti Apoc. 1, 15. quia lumine gloriæ cœlestis con- decorati, & virtute conterendi hostes ac igne æter- no excruciandi eosdem instructi. Vid. Glassius diss. IV. Christol. Mosaicæ thes. XXXVI.

## 3:16
Verse 16. I WILL GREATLY MULTIPLY THY SORROW AND THY CONCEPTION.) That is, sorrows from conception, namely the evils of pregnant women. A figure of speech frequent in Holy Scripture, hendiadys. See what we noted at John 3:5.

It is correctly used here as a hendiadys: but incorrectly at John 3:5. For it is not a watery Spirit that is noted there, but we are said to be regenerated in baptism from Spirit and water. Because the Holy Spirit and His power and efficacy are joined to the waters of baptism.

IN SORROW THOU SHALT BRING FORTH CHILDREN.) For if she had obeyed the divine law, the tree of life would have made her childbirths easier than any birthwort. Now, among all living creatures of the female sex, the woman is most vexed in childbirth: which was noted by Aristotle in the History of Animals 7, 9.

Not only is greater ease implied, but the absence of all pain, and the fall and sin of Eve are established as the cause of the pains of childbirth. It seemed altogether credible to Socinus, concerning the state of the first man, ch. X, p. 278, that the woman, even if she had not sinned, would have brought forth children with pain. But Grotius Socinianizes not obscurely. The tree of life was not an antidote against the difficulty of childbirth, but a remedy for preserving life. Oleastrius is also mistaken, as if the time of gestation were prolonged for the woman here, who imagines that she would have given birth immediately upon the fetus being formed in the state of integrity, and would not have waited laboriously for birth for nine months.

Verse same. THY DESIRE SHALL BE TO THY HUSBAND, AND HE SHALL RULE OVER THEE.) That Hebrew phrase אֶל־אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ, literally: to thy husband thy desire, the interpreter has expressed very well here, as has Aben-Ezra: for that expression signifies the diminution of that liberty which a person naturally desires, as below concerning the right of the firstborn 4:7. The sense is: husbands will not always deal with women in a friendly manner and with condescension. Often they will command things that displease their wives: nevertheless, they must be obeyed according to the general law of the human race.

Liberty is the power of doing what one pleases, as the Romans define it. Zeno defines liberty as ἐξουσίαν αὐτοπραγίας (the power of self-action). Persius: Is anyone else free, except the one who can lead his life as he has wished? Dio of Prusa in Oration XIV: the free, that which is subject to no one, but simply does what seems right to itself. And shortly after: having himself the power of acting as he wishes or not, is free. Arrian in the Epictetean discourses: he is free who lives as he wishes, whom no one can compel, nor hinder, nor force. Aristotle, Politics 6, 2: to live as one wishes; for they say this is the work of liberty, since it is the lot of the slave not to live as he wishes. There is indeed some servitude, not being able to do what you wish because another does not want it: but this servitude, after the loss of that primal simplicity and innocence, is very necessary to the human race, and for that reason is to be borne patiently. See Paul concerning women, 1 Corinthians. 11, 3. 8. 9. Ephesians 5, 22. 23. 24. Colossians 3, 18. 1 Peter 3, 1. Concerning civil obedience, Romans 13, 1. 1 Peter 2, 13. 17. Concerning domestic, Ephesians 6, 12. Colossians 3, 20. Concerning ecclesiastical, Hebrews 13, 17.

Since the punishment is here decreed for the woman, these things are not to be taken as concerning obedience under the general law of the human race. For this general law would have had a place even in the state of integrity, namely, reverence and the woman's obedience. But there would have been no enmities then, no dissensions, or unjust actions, or sinister affections of the man against the woman. Therefore, servitude is not only necessary for the woman because of the lost simplicity and innocence, but by the force of divine justice it is imposed upon her because of the transgression, as a burdensome thing and a punishment for the violation of divine law: and therefore it is designated not as simple obedience and servitude, but joined with trouble, and not without struggle and resistance; by which the woman, whether she wants to or not, is bound to bear the dominion of the man and to submit herself to his power, even if he should be crooked. Which was not to be feared in the state of integrity.

Latin:

Vers. 16. MULTIPLICABO ÆRUMNAS ET CONCE- PTUS TUOS.) Id est, ærumnas ex conceptu, prægnanti- um scil. mala. Frequens S. Literis figura ἕν διὰ δυοῖν. Vide quæ notavimus ad Joh. 3, 5.

Recte hîc Hendyade ponitur: sed male Joh. 3, 5. Non enim ibi Spiritus aqueus notatur, sed ex Spiritu & aqua in baptismo regnerari dicimur. Quia aquæ baptismi junctus est Spiritus S. ejusque vis & efficacia.

IN DOLORE PARIES FILIOS.) Nam si legi divinæ obsecuta esset, arbor vitæ faciliores ei fecisset partus, quam ulla aristolochia. Nunc inter omnia fœminini sexus ani- mantia maxime in partu vexatur mulier: quod notatum Ari- stoteli de Historia animantium 7, 9.

Non tantum facilitas major, sed absentia doloris omnis innuitur, dolorumque partus causa lapsus & peccatum Evæ constituitur. Mulierem, etiamsi non peccasset, cum dolore filios parituram credendum omnino visum fuit Socino de statu primi hominis c. X, p. 278. Socinizat vero non obscure Grotius. Arbor vitæ non adversus difficultatem partus an- tidotum, sed ad conservandam vitam remedium erat. Fallitur etiam Oleastrius, quasi hîc gesta- tionis tempus protelatum mulieri sit, quam fingit formato fœtu statim parituram fuisse in statu inte- gritatis, non vero per novem menses moleste par- tum præstolaturam.

Vers. eod. SUB VIRI POTESTATE ERIS, ET IPSE DOMINABITUR TIBI.) Hebræum illud אֶל־אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ ad verbum: ad virum appetitus tuus, optime expressit hîc interpres, ut & Aben-Esdra: significat enim ea locutio libertatis ejus, quam homo naturaliter appetit, im- minutionem, ut infra de jure primogenitorum 4, 7. Sensus est: non semper cum mulieribus mariti agent amice, & κατὰ συγκατάβασιν. Sæpe imperabunt quæ uxoribus displicent: tamen parendum erit ex lege generali humani generis:

Libertas est facultas ejus quod cuique facere libet, ut Roma- ni definiunt. Zeno libertatem definit ἐξουσίαν αὐτοπραγίας. Persius: An quisquam est alius liber, nisi ducere vitam Cui libet ut voluit? Dion Pruseensis oratione XIV. τὸ ἐλεύθερον, τὸ μηδενὸς ὑπή- κοον, ἀλλὰ πράττειν ἁπλῶς τὰ δοκοῦντα ἑαυτῷ. Et mox: ἔχων αὐτὸς τὴν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ πράττειν ὡς βούλεται ἢ μὴ ἐλεύθερος. Arrianus in Epicteteis: ἐλεύθερός ἐστιν ὁ ζῶν ὡς βούλεται, ὃν οὐκ ἀναγκάσαι ἔστιν, οὔτε κωλῦσαι, οὔτε βιάσασθαι. Aristoteles Politicorum 6, 2. τὸ ζῆν ὡς βούλεταί τις· τοῦτο γὰρ τῆς ἐλευ- θερίας ἔργον εἶναί φασιν, εἴπερ τοῦ δούλου ὄντος, τὸ ζῆν μὴ ὡς βούλεται. Est sane aliqua servitus, non posse facere quod ve- lis, quia nolit id alius: sed hæc servitus post amissam illam primævam simplicitatem atque innocentiam, humano gene- ri perquam necessaria est, & ob id placide ferenda. Vide de mulieribus Paulum 1. Corinth. 11, 3. 8. 9. Ephes. 5, 22. 23. 24. Coloss. 3, 18. 1. Petr. 3, 1. de civili obedientia Rom. 13, 1. 1. Petr. 2, 13. 17. de domestica Ephes. 6, 12. Coloss. 3, 20. de Ecclesia- stica Hebr. 13, 17.

Quum pœna hîc mulieri dictetur, non de pari- tione ex lege generali humani generis hæc accipi- enda erunt. Hæc enim generalis lex etiam in statu integritatis locum habuisset, reverentia nempe, ac paritionis mulieris. Sed nullæ tum inimicitiæ, nul- læ simultates, aut iniquæ actiones, aut sinistræ affe- ctiones fuissent viri adversus mulierem. Non ergo tantum servitus, ob amissam simplicitatem atque in- nocentiam, mulieri necessaria est, sed vi justitiæ divi- næ ob prævaricationem imponitur eidem, tanquam res onerosa, & pœna transgressionis legis divinæ: ideoque non simplex paritio & servitus, sed cum molestia conjuncta, nec sine lucta & repugnantia de- signatur; qua mulier velit, nolit, dominium viri ferre teneatur, seque potestati ejus submittere, etsi σκολιὸς fuerit. Quod in statu integritatis metuen- dum non erat.

## 3:17
Verse 17. CURSED IS THE GROUND.) It will not be like Paradise, which nourished you with things born spontaneously and provided you with vigor, but, subdued with much labor, it will not even then bring forth pure fruits, as the following verses explain: and Hebrews 6, 8. For the curse of the earth, as of other things, has its own degrees. See below 3, 17. Leviticus 27, 24. 38. 39. 40. 42.

This comparative explanation of the divine curse does not exhaust the punishment; by force of which the earth not only yields in fertility to Paradise, which even in the primal state was more pleasant, more fruitful, and happier than the rest of the earth, but, being deprived of its pristine and primal fertility because of sin, it germinates thorns and thistles, that is, by synecdoche, herbs of every kind that are useless and harmful.

Verse of the same. IN YOUR WORK.) From the Greek ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σ8. In Hebrew בעבורך, that is, as far as it concerns you, it will be troublesome to you. Hesiod: Never by day will they cease from toil and woe, nor by night; and the gods will give grievous cares. Jerome is of a different opinion, according to whom the Hebrew 'because of you' is to be explained as 'because of your sin,' and thus the Greek is also to be understood: Works, he says, here do not signify the tilling of the field, as most think, but sins, as is held in the Hebrew: and Aquila does not disagree, saying, cursed is the ground because of you. And Theodotion, in your transgression. Compare Sixtinus Amama in Censura Versionis Vulgatae. It is strange that he does not argue for the corruption of the Hebrew text with his Capellus: who contends that the LXX interpreters read כעבודך with a dalet. But 'abod' among the Hebrews is not in use for 'work': which the Hebrews call 'abodah'. And the Chaldean and Aquila agree with the Hebrew text. Compare the Anti-Criticus of Buxtorf, p. 784. Whence Bellarmine does not ascribe the Vulgate version to a variant reading, but strives to reconcile it thus with the Hebrew, 'in your work,' that is, in the past, meaning 'because of your sin.'

Latin:

Vers. 17. MALEDICTA TERRA.) Non erit qualis Paradisus, qui te sponte natis alebat vegetumque præstabat, sed subacta multo labore ne sic quidem puras fruges proferet, ut sequentia exponunt: & Hebr. 6, 8. Habet enim κατάρα terræ, ut & rerum aliarum, suos gradus. Vide infra 3, 17. Lev. 27, 24. 38. 39. 40. 42.

Comparata hæc maledictionis divinæ explica- tio non exhaurit pœnam; vi cujus terra non mo- do Paradiso fertilitate cedit, qui etiam in statu pri- mævo reliqua terra amœnior, fœcundior, ac feli- cior erat, sed fertilitate sua pristina ac primæva ob peccatum privata spinas, & tribulos germinat, hoc est, per Synecdochen, omnis generis herbas inuti- les, atque noxias.

Vers. eod. IN OPERE TUO.) Ex Græco ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σ8. Hebraice בעבורך, id est, quod ad te attinet, molesta tibi erit. Hesiodus: Οὐδέποτ᾽ ἦμαρ Παύσονται καμάτου καὶ ὀϊζύος, ὐδέ τι νυκτὸς. Γινομένης· χαλεπὰς δὲ θεοὶ δώσεσι μερίμνας. Aliter Hieronymus, juxta quem Ebræa propter te, exponenda, propter peccatum tuum, atque ita Græca etiam intelligenda: Opera, inquit, hîc non ruris colendi, ut plerique putant, sed peccata significant, ut in Hebræo habetur: & Aquila non discordat, di- cens, maledicta humus propter te. Et Theodotio, in transgressione tua. Conf. Sixtin. Amam. in Cen- sur. Version. Vulg. Mirum, quod non cum Ca- pello suo textum Hebræum corruptionis arguat: qui LXX. Interpp. legisse כעבודך contendit cum ד. Sed עבוד apud Ebræos pro opere non est in usu: quod Ebræi vocant עבודה. Et consonat Ebræo textui Chaldæus, & Aquila. Conf. Anti-Criticus Buxtorf. p. 784. Unde Bellarm. non variæ lectioni adscribit versionem vulg. sed eam ita cum Ebr. conciliare nititur, in opere tuo, præterito scil. id est, propter peccatum tuum.

## 3:18
Verse 18. YOU SHALL EAT THE HERB OF THE FIELD.) 'eseb', which the Greeks translate as 'chorton' and the Latins as 'herbam' (herb), also includes grain in itself, and is opposed to those fruits of the trees of the field.

Latin:

Vers. 18. COMEDES HERBAM TERRÆ.) עשב quod χόρτον vertunt Græci, Latini herbam, etiam frumen- tum in se comprehendit, opponiturque illis beararum arbo- rum fructibus.

## 3:19
Verse 19. IN THE SWEAT OF YOUR FACE YOU SHALL EAT BREAD.) Usually the punishment corresponds to the sin. He who had sinned in food is punished in food. That was noted by Maimonides.

FOR YOU ARE DUST.) Below 17, 27. Psalm 103, 12. Ecclesiastes 12, 7.

AND TO DUST YOU SHALL RETURN,) Psalm 104, 28. 146, 4. 22, 16. Thus Homer: But may you all become water and earth. Euripides, Hypsipyle: — — — — Carrying earth to earth. The same in The Suppliants: Spirit indeed to the ether, but the body to the earth. Which are almost the same words as those of Ecclesiastes. Cicero, De Re Publica, Book III: For nature would not suffer that which was of the earth not to remain in the earth. Therefore GOD then, having removed the heavenly power, permitted nature to do its own things.

Is Cicero a distinguished interpreter of Scripture? He ought rather to praise Socinus. For with him, nature makes a mortal man before the fall: Or the Scholastics and Papists, from whom he has a supernatural power added to nature, which being removed, and nature left to itself, in the state, as they say, of pure naturals, man would finally have had to die. But here GOD decrees a punishment on account of sin, therefore He does not describe the condition of nature. Because you have eaten from the forbidden tree, in the sweat of your face you shall eat bread עד שוב until you return and until you return to the earth. Whatever, therefore, by the force of the divine threat on account of the transgression of the law was adjudged to man as a penalty and punishment, he was in no way subject to it by nature before and outside of sin. If GOD had made man mortal from the beginning, He would by no means have condemned him to death for sinning: for no one condemns a mortal with mortality. Thus Gregory of Nyssa, even before the rise of Pelagius, in De Creat. homin. chap. II. Therefore blessed Augustine, book XII of The City of God, chap. IV, says: it is agreed among Christians who truly hold the Catholic faith, that even this death of the body was inflicted upon us not by the law of nature, by which GOD made no death for man, but by the merit of sin, since GOD, avenging sin, said to man, in whom we all then were, you are earth and to earth you shall go. Therefore, by the judgment of Augustine, Grotius should not be reckoned among Christians who truly hold the Catholic faith.

Nor is this the only Pelagian hypothesis of his in this matter. Many others are read in the Annotations to Cassander, art. II. That man, when he was first created, had no promises of heavenly life, but of earthly. And therefore also that powers were given to him corresponding to such a reward. That the image of GOD to which Adam was created is one thing, and that to which we are reborn through Christ is another. That the sin of Eve and Adam was a proof of human weakness, destitute of the promise of a heavenly reward. That for heavenly life to be given to us, an extraordinary holiness of mind is required, and one which far exceeds that state of Adam when he was first created. That it is required to be such as makes us equal to the Angels, while the difference remains which human bodies, being distant from angelic ones, carry with them. That the sin of Eve and Adam brought a certain stain, and that in men, when they are born, there is something not suitable for attaining heavenly life. That to attain it, there is need to be reborn, that is, to be raised above the powers of human nature through the precepts and heavenly promises of GOD: That to abstain from every sin at all and always is above the human condition, and that it is therefore innate in man to sin, Sopater, Hierocles, and Seneca among the philosophers, Philo among the Jews, Thucydides among the historians, and very many among the Christians have declared. However, it can be doubted whether these are rightly and properly called sins, since they do not have the freedom, which they seem to have in species, when considered in their generality. Pelagius has revived, not now only in Socinus, but also in Grotius: whose those dogmas once were, if by chance you except for the paradox concerning angelic bodies. Which we have transcribed from Grotius's annotations on Cassander in his own words. Having added, however, at the end from book III of De jure pacis & belli, ch. XXI, Sect. 19, to which place he referred us there. By which, when compared with those things which he adduced from Philo, Sopater, Hierocles, Celsus, Pythagoras, and Aristotle they might teach what Grotius believed concerning the יצר הרע with the Hebrews; not original sin, as the Catholic Church holds, of which the philosophers knew nothing, but the τὶ πεφυκὸς ἀντιβαίνον τω̣̃ λόγω̣ of Aristotle, which he himself does not consider to be sin. For it is known that Aristotle denies that we are either evil or good τη̃ φύσει, Ethic. ad Nicom. l. II, c. 5, but let it suffice to have pointed this out once, lest the Grotian books on the law of war and peace, indeed very learned, should perhaps carry away the unwary into the Φορτικὰ ἀκόσματα with which they abound.

Now to return to the present matter: That conversion into dust is not deduced here from the condition of nature or human matter, but is judicially decreed for man on account of guilt. And so that statement, 'you are dust, and to dust you shall return,' is to be understood thus: just as you were first formed from corruptible dust, although I created you to my image ἐπ̓ ἀφθαρσία̣ in incorruptibility, and, if you had observed my law, I would have clearly wished to lead you to eternal life, so now, since you have transgressed the law and eaten from the tree, the use of which I had forbidden under penalty of death, you will altogether return to dust, and will be subject not only to death but also to corruption. Thus St. Augustine above with the Catholic Church: whose words these also are, l. 1, de peccat. merit. & remiss., c. II & III. If Adam had not sinned, he was not to be stripped of his body, but was always to be clothed with immortality and incorruption, so that the mortal might be absorbed by life, that is, that he might pass from the animal to the spiritual. Add the opinion of Leo the Great, Bishop of Rome, Serm. IV, on the birth of the Lord. 'Which most beautiful dignity of his nature, if he (Adam) perseveringly cultivated it through the observance of the given law, he would lead that very quality of the earthly body to heavenly glory.'

That the first-formed were not destitute of the promise of a heavenly reward if they obeyed, is manifest from the threat of eternal death if they did not obey, and also from the tree of life, which was a sacrament of eternal life. Which primordial wisdom, in which they were created, did not permit them to be ignorant of either. Nor does the fact that they lacked the strength to aspire to it, which true justice and holiness, which pertained to the image of God shining in them, convince us of. For two images of God are absurdly imagined: we are said to be RENEWED to the same image to which we were created in the first-formed, Coloss. 3:10, Ephes. 4:24. Nor was the faith of the ancient Jewish Church any different, to observe this again. God created, it is said in Wisdom 1:14, that all things might be, that is, all men, as Grotius interprets from Ephes. 1:10, Mark 16:15. And he created that they might be, that is, that they might live eternally, as again on this passage. Grotius, who wishes to gather from this the διαμονὴν τω̃ν ψυχω̃ν, which is to the Hebrews השאר הנפש, 'He made all the nations of the earth curable,' that is: The nature of men is such by the goodness of God that it can be rendered fit for eternal life. 'And there is no medicine of destruction in them': i.e., there is nothing in the nature of the human soul such that it must necessarily perish, just as a man perishes when poison is taken. All these interpretations are owed to Grotius on this passage. How then does he assert that man was created mortal by nature? Why does he deny that he was created for eternal life in the beginning? Why does he, with Socinus, assign the first proclamation of eternal life to the New Testament? Which he later removes here in the preface to the book of Wisdom by his own confession, that after Ezra the universal judgment, eternal life, and the punishments of Gehenna began to be proposed more explicitly: if eternal life was then proposed more explicitly, then its proposal or preaching was not reserved finally for the New Testament. But it is in vain, when he observes that God is said to create as often as men are conceived, Job 10:10, because here the discourse is about the primordial creation, and what the nature of men was through it. Which the preceding words confirm: 'For God did not make death.' For Grotius admits that these speak of the primordial creation. Which again cry out against his fiction about Adam being created mortal: for thus God would have made death, and death would have been in the nature of man, so that he would necessarily have to perish eventually if he were left to himself, because he is therefore called mortal. But that the second death is understood here, in an exclusive sense, that is, that alone, is false, because it is simply denied that God made death. That other living creatures were consigned to death by God is irrelevant, where the subject is man, not other living creatures: but we say that man was created in such a way that he could die, this is the point in question; we say he was created in such a way that he could not die: but not created mortal, who, if left to his own nature, could not only die, according to the Grotian opinion, but could not not die. The mind of the author of the book of Wisdom is far different, and that of the ancient Jewish Church. Wisdom 2:23: 'For God created man to be inextinguishable,' in the Greek ἐπ' ἀφθαρσία̣. Which we have noted before that Grotius in book II of De jure pacis & belli tries to corrupt, as if it should be rendered 'in simplicity': now it is possible to observe him departing from himself in his annotations on this passage: while he explains it, 'he created him in the hope of immortality.' More correctly indeed, but not fully enough, because hope is not designated here, but the thing itself, just as he says he made him to his own image and likeness, certainly not just to the hope of his image and likeness: nor consistently enough; because he immediately distorts that 'he created,' that is, he made everyone to be born. Although it is plain that the subject is man first created, and created to the image of God, not how or with what hope each person is born, although it is false that everyone is born into the hope of immortality: because after the fall we are all born in sin and are by nature children of wrath, not of blessed hope, Eph. 2:5. But there is the clearest light of the antithesis subjoined, by which the darkness of the Grotian gloss, together with his hypothesis which we are now examining, is thoroughly put to flight. 'But by the envy of the Devil death entered into the world.' Which Grotius therefore could not obscure. For he explains it thus: By the envy of the Devil, whom Moses intended to be understood under the figure of the serpent, death entered into the world, the first death through the fault of Adam; but the second death through the impiety, injustice, and deceits of individuals. He confesses, therefore, that the first death entered through the fault of Adam. Whence it is left that there was no place for it before and outside of the fault, that GOD did not make it, nor did He create man mortal. But he wrongly separates the second from the first death. For did not the fault of Adam merit the second death? Is it not to be imputed to the fall of man?

Latin:

Verf. 19. IN SVDORE VVLTVS TUI VESCERIS PANE.) Plerumque poena peccato respondet. Qui in ci- bo peccaverat, in cibo punitur. Notatum id Maimonidæ.

QUIA PULVIS ES.) Infra 17, 27. Psalm. 103, 12. Eccle- siast. 12, 7.

ET IN PULVEREM REVERTERIS,) Psalm. 104, 28. 146, 4. 22, 16. Sic Homerus: Ἀλλ᾽ ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε. Euripides Hypsipyle: — — — — Εἰς γῆν φέροντες γῆν. Idem supplicibus: Πνεῦμα μὲν πρὸς αἰθέρα. Τὸ σῶμα δ᾽ εἰς γῆν. Quæ eadem prope verba cum illis Ecclesiastæ. Cicero de Rep. lib. III. Neque enim natura pateretur, ut id quod esset de terra, nisi in terra maneret. Ergo DEUS tunc amota vi su- perna naturæ res suas agere permisit.

Præclarus interpres Scripturæ Cicero? Socinum potius laudare debebat. Cum eo enim natura mor- talem hominem ante lapsum facit: Aut Scholasticos & Papistas, à quibus habet vim supernam naturæ additam, qua amota, naturaque sibi relicta, in statu, ut illi ajunt, purorum naturalium moriendum denique homini fuerit. At hîc pœnam decernit DEUS ob peccatum, non ergo conditionem natu- ræ describit. Quia comedisti ex arbore vetita, in su- dore vultus tui vesceris pane עד שוב ad revertendum & usque dum revertaris in terram. Quicquid ergo vi comminationis divinæ propter legis transgressio- nem in pœnam & supplicium adjudicatum fuit ho- mini, ei ante & extra peccatum nullatenus obno- xius fuit per naturam. Si DEUS hominem à prin- cipio mortalem fecisset, nequaquam peccantem morte condemnasset: nam mortalem mortalitate nullus con- demnat. Ita Gregor. Nyssenus jàm ante exortum Pelagium de Creat. homin. cap. II. Ideo B. Augu- stinus lib. XII. de Civit. DEI cap. IV. constat, inquit, inter Christianos veraciter Catholicam tenentes fidem, etiam ipsam nobis corporis mortem non lege naturæ, qua nullam mortem homini DEUS fecit, sed merito inflictam esse peccati, quoniam peccatum vindicans DEUS dixit homini, in quo tunc omnes eramus, ter- ra es & in terram ibis. Non ergo Christianis Catho- licam fidem veraciter tenentibus accensendus fuerit Grotius, judicio Augustini.

Nec una hæc ipsius hypothesis Pelagiana in hac causa. Plures aliæ in Annotatis ad Cassandri art. II. leguntur. Hominem, cum primum est con- ditus, promissa nulla habuisse vitæ cœlestis, sed terre- stris. Itaque & vires ei datas tali præmio respondentes. Aliam imaginem DEI esse, ad quam Adamus est condi- tus, aliam, ad quam per Christum renascimur. Evæ & Adami peccatum documentum fuisse imbecillitatis humanæ, pollicitatione præmii cœlestis destitutæ. Ad vitam cœlestem nobis dandam sanctitatem animi re- quiri eximiam, & quæ illum Adami, cum primum conditus est, statum longe excedat. Requiri eam, quæ nos Angelis æquet, manente tamen eo discrimine, quod corpora humana ab angelicis distantia secum ferunt. Evæ & Adami peccatum labem quandam attulisse, & in hominibus, cum nascuntur, aliquid esse non idone- um ad vitam cœlestem adipiscendam. Ad eam adipi- scendam renasci opus esse, id est, per DEI præcepta & promissa cœlestia attolli supra vires humanæ naturæ: Ab omni quidem omnino peccato & semper abstinere supra humanam conditionem est, inde connatum ho- mini esse peccare, inter Philosophos Sopater, Hierocles, Seneca, inter Judæos Philo, inter historicos Thucidi- des, inter Christianos plurimi prodiderunt. Dubitari autem potest, an hæc recte & proprie peccata dicantur, cum libertatem, quam in specie habere videntur, in sua generalitate considerata non habeant. Revixit Pelagius non jam tantum in Socino, sed etiam in Grotio: cujus quondam illa fuere dogmata, si forte paradoxon excipias de angelicis corporibus. Quæ è Grotii annotatis in Cassandrum verbis propriis transcripsimus. Additis tamen postremo è libro III. de jure pacis & belli cap. XXI. Sect. 19. ad quem locum nos ibi remisit. Quo illis, quæ ex Philone, Sopatre, Hierocle, Celso, Pythagora, & Aristotele ad Luc. 3, 22. adduxit, collata, docerent, quid de יצר הרע cum Ebræis crediderit Grotius; non pec- catum originale, cum Ecclesia Catholica, de quo nihil Philosophi novere, sed τὶ πεφυκὸς ἀντιβαίνον τω̣̃ λόγω̣ Aristotelis, quod pro peccato ipse non ha- bet. Notum enim est, quod neget Aristoteles nos aut malos aut bonos esse τη̃ φύσει Ethic. ad Nicom. l. II. c. 5. sed hæc semel monuisse sufficiat, ne Grotiani libri de jure pacis & belli, sane perquam eruditi, in- cautos in Φορτικὰ ἀκόσματα, quibus abundant, forte abripiant.

Jam ut ad rem præsentem redeamus: Illa in pul- verem conversio non è conditione naturæ vel ma- teriæ humanæ hìc deducitur, sed ob culpam homi- ni judicialiter decernitur. Adeoque illa, pulvis es, & in pulverem converteris, ita accipienda; uti è pul- vere corruptibili formatus primum, quamvis ad ima- ginem meam ἐπ̓ ἀφθαρσία̣ in incorruptibilitate con- diderim, ac, legem meam si observasses, ad vitam æter- nam te perducere plane voluissem, ita nunc, quum legem transgressus sis, & de arbore comederis, cujus usui sub mortis pœna interdixeram, omnino in pulve- rem converteris, non morti tantum, sed & corruptio- ni obnoxius eris. Ita supra S. Augustinus cum Ec- clesia Catholica: cujus hæc etiam sunt l. 1. de pec- cat. merit. & remiss. c. II. & III. Si non peccasset A- dam, non erat exspoliandus corpore, sed semper vesti- endus immortalitate & incorruptione, ut absorberetur mortale à vita, id est, ab animali in spirituale transi- ret. Adde Leonis Magni Romani Episcopi sen- tentiam, Serm. IV. in natal. Domini. Quam na- turæ suæ speciosissimam dignitatem, si per observanti- am legis datæ perseveranter excoleret (Adam) ipsam illam terreni corporis qualitatem ad cælestem gloriam perduceret.

Pollicitatione præmii cælestis non destitutos fu- isse Protoplastos, si obedirent, è comminatione æter- næ mortis, si non obedirent, manifestum est, nec non ex arbore vitæ, quæ Sacramentum æternæ vitæ fuit. Quam etiam ignorare non permittebat pri- migenia sapientia, in qua conditi. Neque vires eis defuisse, eo adspirandi, justitia & sanctitas vera, quæ ad imaginem DEI in iis effulgentem pertine- bat, convincit. Duæ enim imagines DEI absurde finguntur: Ad eandem RENOVARI dicimur, ad quam in Protoplastis conditi eramus Coloss. 3, 10. Ephes. 4, 24. Neque alia fides fuit veteris Judai- cæ Ecclesiæ, ut iterum hoc observemus. Creavit DEUS, dicitur Sap. 1, 14. ut essent omnia, id est, omnes homines, ut interpretatur Grotius ex Ephes. 1, 10. Marc. 16, 15. Et creavit ut essent, id est, ut æter- num vivant, ut iterum ad h. l. Grotius, qui hinc colli- gi vult διαμονὴν τω̃ν ψυχω̃ν, quod Hebræis השאר הנפש, Sanabiles fecit nationes omnes terrarum, id est: Natura hominum DEI bonitate talis est, ut apta reddi possit ad salutem æternam. Et non est in illis medicamen- tum exterminii: i. e. Nihil est tale in animi humani natu- ra, cur necessario interire debeat, sicut homo interit sumto veneno. Omnes hæ interpretationes Grotio de- bentur ad h. l. Quomodo ergo natura hominem mortalem conditum asserit? Cur advitam æternam initio creatum negat? Cur cum Socino primum æternæ vitæ præconium Novo Testamento adsignat? quod posterius hìc in præfat. in libr. Sapientiæ pro- pria confessione, quod post Esdram explicatius pro- poni cœperint judicium universale, vita æterna, suppli- cia gehennæ, tollit: si explicatius tum proposita vi- ta æterna, non ergo demum Novo Testam. ejus reservata propositio, vel prædicatio. Frustra autem est, cum creare DEUM dici observat, quoties conci- piuntur homines Job. 10, 10. quia hîc de creatione primæva sermo est, qualis hominum natura per eandem fuerit. Quod verba præcedentia confir- mant: Quoniam DEUS mortem non fecit. Hæc enim de primæva creatione loqui fatetur Grotius. Quæ iterum ejus commento de Adamo mortali condito reclamant: Sic enim mortem fecisset De- us, & in natura hominis mors fuisset, ut necessario tandem ei intereundum, si illa sibi relinqueretur, quia ideo mortalis dicitur. Mortem autem secun- dam hîc intelligi, exclusivo sensu, id est, eam solam, falsum est, quia simpliciter negatur, Deum mor- tem fecisse. Quod animantia cætera à DEO morti addicta sunt, ἀπροσδιόνυσον est, ubi de homine, non de aliis animantibus agitur: hominem vero ita creatum, ut mori posset, hoc est τὸ κρινόμενον; crea- tum dicimus ita, ut posset non mori: non autem creatum mortalem, qui natura sibi relicta, non tan- tum mori poterat, Grotiana sententia, sed non po- terat non mori. Longe alia mens autori libri Sapi- entiæ est, & veteri Ecclesiæ Judaicæ. Sap. 2, 23. Quo- niam DEUS creavit hominem inexterminabilem, in Græco ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ. Quod frustra Grotius lib. II. de jure pacis & belli corrumpere, quasi ita reddi debeat, in simplicitate, antea notavimus: nunc à seipso abire eum, in annot. ad h. l. observare licet: dum exponit, in spem immortalitatis creavit. Re- ctius quidem, sed non plene satis, quia non hic spes designatur, sed res ipsa, perinde, uti ad imaginem & similitudinem suam fecisse ipsum dicit, non certe ad spem solum imaginis & similitudinis suæ: neque con- stanter satis; quia actutum illud creavit detorquet, id est, nasci quemque fecit. Quum tamen palam sit, agi de homine primum creato, & ad imaginem DEI condito, non quomodo aut qua spe quisque nascatur, quamvis falsum sit, quemque in spem immortalitatis nasci: quia post lapsum nascimur omnes in pecca- to & τῇ φύσει filii iræ sumus, non beatæ spei Eph. 2, 5. Sed clarissima lux est ἀντιθέσεως subjunctæ, qua tenebræ Grotianæ glossæ, una cum hypothesi ejus, quam nunc examinamamus, penitus profligantur. Invidia autem Diaboli mors intravit in orbem terra- rum. Quam proinde obfuscare non potuit Gro- tius. Ita enim exponit: Invidia autem Diaboli, quem sub serpentis figura intelligi Moses voluit, mors intravit in orbem terrarum, mors prima per Adami culpam; mors autem secunda per singulorum impieta- tem, injustitiam & falsimonias. Fatetur ergo mortem primam per Adami culpam introiisse. Unde relinqui- tur, eidem ante & extra culpam locum non fuisse, ean- dem DEUM non fecisse, neque hominem mortalem condidisse. Male autem separat à morte prima se- cundam. Annon enim Adami culpa mortem se- cundam meruit? Annon ea lapsui hominis impu- tanda?

## 3:20
Verse 20. HEVA.) The Greeks well [translate it] ζωὴ, which is a woman's name among the Greeks. But Philo of Byblos translates it αἰῶνα, where in Sanchoniathon it was חוה.

But Adam did not then look to natural life, for that would have been nothing singular, that this woman would be the mother of all living, because there was no other woman in the world: but to heavenly life: because Adam made application to himself through faith with the woman of the promise of the seed of the woman, as if he were to say, although on account of sin you my wife are to bear children with pains, yet that promised seed of the woman which will crush the head of the infernal serpent consoles and raises us up, that not as we deserved by sin, are they to be condemned to death who are to arise from us, but that they can attain eternal life through faith in that promised Redeemer. It is not to be thought, says Brentius, that the woman is called Eve for this reason only, because she is the mother of other living men: but since Adam had heard a little before the Gospel concerning the seed of the woman, or concerning the son of the virgin, and had received together with his wife from it the greatest consolation, and even life itself, in those supreme terrors and death, in which he was dwelling before the tribunal of GOD, for that reason he imposes upon his wife the name Eve, that is, of life, or life-bearing, as a monument of that Gospel, concerning that seed, which was about to be born from the woman only, and was about to bring true life to all who believe in him. But above all, the blessed Luther deserves to be heard here: It appears from this passage that Adam, having received the Holy Spirit, had been wonderfully enlightened, and had believed and understood the word concerning the Seed of the woman who would crush the head of the Serpent, and had also wished to distinguish and adorn this faith of his with the name of his Wife, which for that reason he bestowed upon no other creature, so that by this appellation of his spouse he might nourish the hope of the future Seed, and confirm his own faith, and console himself, because he believed in life even then, when all nature was already subject to death. For unless he had sensed future life, his spirit could not have been raised up, nor would he himself have imposed such a joyful name upon his Wife. But because he imposes this name upon his Wife, he sufficiently shows his spirit raised up through the Holy Spirit by the confidence of the remission of sins through the Seed of Eve, whom he therefore calls Eve, so that this name might be as a memorial of the promise, from which he himself also revived, and might leave the hope of eternal life to his posterity. He paints this hope and faith with this name as if with colors on the forehead of his wife, just as those liberated from enemies set up trophies and other signs of joy. Both the preceding and the following confirm this sense. For when the first-created had heard that Evangelical sermon, it had to be explained how they received it, lest anyone believe that they had held it in contempt, or that no ἐνεργείας (energy/effect) of the same had been with them: therefore, by this profession of his, and the name imposed upon his spouse, which was like a perpetual μνημοσύνης (memorial) of their faith, he wished to testify: whence, in order that GOD might also testify to the righteousness of the Redeemer imputed to them through that faith by some likewise perpetual memorial, He made tunics for both from the skins of a sacrificed lamb, signs of the lamb of GOD to be sacrificed for men, with whose righteousness believers are to be clothed. For these things follow one another: the preaching of the Gospel, the reception of the same through faith, and the justification of the faithful, when the righteousness of the Redeemer is imputed to them, and their sins are veiled and covered by it.

Latin:

Vers. 20. HEVA.) Græci bene ζωὴ, quod nomen mulie- bre apud Græcos. At Philo Byblius vertit αἰῶνα, ubi in San- choniathone fuit חוה.

Non autem Adam tum ad vitam naturalem re- spexit, id enim nihil singulare fuisset, mulierem hanc fore matrem omnium viventium, quia alia nulla in mundo erat mulier: quam ad vitam cœ- lestem: quia applicationem fecit sibi per fidem Adam cum muliere promissionis seminis mulieris, quasi dicat, quamvis ob peccatum cum doloribus tu mea uxor liberos paritura sis, promissum tamen illud semen mulieris contriturum caput serpentis infernalis nos solatur, atque erigit, quod non uti peccato merui- mus, ad mortem condemnandi sint, qui ex nobis orituri sint, sed quod æternam vitam consequi possint per fi- dem in promissum illum Redemtorem. Non est sentiendum, inquit Brentius, quod mulier hac tantum causa dicatur Eva, quia sit mater aliorum hominum viventium: sed cum Adam paulo ante audierat Ev- angelium de semine mulieris, seu de filio virginis, & acceperat una cum uxore sua ex eo maximam consola- tionem, adeoque vitam ipsam, in summis illis terrori- bus ac morte, in quibus ante tribunal DEI versaba- tur, idcirco imponit uxori nomen Evæ, hoc est, vitæ, seu viviparæ, tanquam monumentum illius Evange- lii, de semine illo, quod nasciturum erat è mulie- re tantum, & allaturum veram vitam omnibus, qui in ipsum credúnt. Sed imprimis audiri hìc mere- tur B. Lutherus: Apparet ex hoc loco Adamum, recepto Spiritu S. mirabiliter fuisse illustratum, & credidisse ac intellexisse verbum, de Semine mulieris contrituro caput Serpentis, ac voluisse quoque hanc su- am fidem insignire & ornare vocabulo Uxoris suæ, quod ideo nulli alii creaturæ indidit, ut aleret hac appellatione conjugis suæ spem futuri Seminis, & confirmaret fidem suam, seque consolaretur, quod crederet vitam etiam tum, cum jam morti tota na- tura esset subjecta. Nisi enim sensisset vitam futu- ram, non potuisset erigi animus ejus, nec ipse tam lætum vocabulum imposuisset Uxori. Quia autem hoc nomen imponit Uxori suæ, satis ostendit animum erectum per spiritum Sanctum fiducia remissionis pec- catorum per Semen Hevæ, quam ideo Hevam appel- lat, ut hoc nomen esset ceu memoriale promissionis, ex qua ipse quoque revixit, & spem vitæ æternæ relinque- ret posteris. Hanc spem & fidem nomine hoc ceu colo- ribus in fronte uxoris pingit, sicut liberati ab hostibus trophæa & alia signa lætitiæ statuunt. Quem sen- sum & antecedentia confirmant & consequentia. Nam cum audivissent Protoplasti concionem illam Evangelicam, exponendum erat, quomodo eam exceperint, ne eam insuper habuisse ipsos, aut nul- lius eandem ἐνεργείας penes ipsos fuisse quis cre- dat: id ergo hac professione sua, & nomine conjugi imposito, quod instar perpetui μνημοσύνης erat fidei ipsorum, testari voluit: unde per fidem illam im- putatam ipsis justitiam Redemtoris DEUS aliquo itidem, eoque perpetuo memoriali testaturus tuni- cas utrique fecit è pellibus mactati agni sacrificialis, indices mactandi pro hominibus agni DEI, cujus justitia credentes vestiendi sint. Hæc enim sese consequuntur, prædicatio Evangelii, ejusdem per fidem receptio, & fidelium justificatio, cum impu- tatur ipsis Redemtoris justitia, eaque velantur & te- guntur peccata ipsorum.

## 3:22
Vers. 22. HE SAID.] To the angels. See Gen. 1:26. AS ONE OF US.] For to know many things, as we have said, is divine and angelic: but this mostly distracts men from better things. Eccles. 12:12, 13.

Petulant depravation. He said to the angels. Where is it held that GOD spoke these things to the angels? If it is permitted to infer into the text whatever one pleases in this way, what will not be fashioned out of Scripture? But he wished to gratify his Socinus and the Jews, lest more persons in the Deity be proven here. But it is too manifest that a plurality of divine persons is designated. For who is speaking? Jehovah Elohim. We have, therefore, who those are who speak of themselves πληθυντικῶς (in the plural): Behold Adam has become as ONE of US. Not those who are called Elohim for any reason whatsoever, but those called Elohim in the most eminent way, or rather κυριολεκτικῶς (properly speaking) in the proper use of the word, who are Jehovah, that one GOD. Nor can it be similarly gathered from the following words that these things were said to the angels, even if those former things were admitted to be directed to the angels. Could not GOD have turned himself to the angels only afterwards?

CHAP. III. v. 20. 21.

Nor, if these things were even said to them, are they included under the word US. Because only those are included in this word who are speaking here, not those before whom these things are uttered. This, therefore, is invincible: he who speaks here says that Adam has been made like himself: He has been made, he says, as ONE OF US, not as ONE OF YOU. But where there is a μερισμὸς (division) of speech as between one and another, there is truly a plurality. He who speaks of one of the Elohim indicates more Elohim. One of many cannot be said where there is only a single person. But for GOD to include the angels with Himself, and to number them with Himself in this way, is extremely absurd. For here parity and equality are designated, when one of the Elohim is mentioned, to whose likeness Adam aspired. The speaking person implies that Adam was made similar to himself, but he calls himself one out of many who are not unequal, but who are of the same dignity. Certainly incongruous and alien to the majesty of GOD, which Rivetus also admits in Exercit. XL. on Genesis, p. 201, that GOD said such things to the angels, who are His ministers and servants, as if to his companions and of equal condition, and of the same dignity and authority. Nor indeed was there need to say that he was made similar to the angels then, who was created in the beginning in the image of GOD, and thus was similar to the angels regarding the knowledge of good and evil. Truly, from the serpent, a likeness not with the angels, but with GOD Himself was promised, by far, namely, greater and more eminent than the angelic, which man, led by a vain persuasion, was also affecting. Therefore GOD says, Behold, Adam has become as one not of the angels or heavenly beings, but as ONE of US, looking back to His divine college, if I may so speak, into which certainly no angel or archangel is admitted. Since not even that has been said to any of the Angels, 'sit at my right hand,' it is so far from the case that any one is admitted into the fellowship of Jehovah Elohim, the most high and all-holy creator of all things, which this speech would imply if it included the Angels as well. This is so clear that the version of Jonathan here, which Grotius followed along with the blind Jews, is corrected by the Jerusalem Chaldean interpretation itself, which much more rightly refers the partitive speech to Jehovah himself: 'And the word of Jehovah said: Behold the man, whom I have created, is unique or only-begotten in the world, just as I am unique in the high heavens.' Nor could that invention please Calvin, who otherwise willingly Judaizes: 'Some,' he says, 'refer the plural number to the angels, as if GOD were distinguishing man, a terrestrial and despised animal, from the celestial creatures. But it seems a far-fetched exposition.' Rightly, therefore, Augustine, book II de Genes. ad litteram cap. XXX. 'It is not to be understood otherwise, what he says, ONE of US, except that the plural number is to be accepted on account of the Trinity, just as it was said: Let us make man; just as he says of himself and the Father, we will come to him and make our abode with him.' And long before Augustine, Justin Martyr, Dial. with Trypho, p. m. 222, says that from those words it is indisputably recognized that God spoke those things to someone who is both numerically ANOTHER and rational: and so when he said, 'as one of us,' he indicated both the number of those who were together, and at the very least two; and that the offspring truly brought forth by the Father, who was with the Father before all creatures, brought forth the things spoken with the Father. He has similar things on p. 281, and adds: 'Nor do those words admit a figurative locution, just as the Sophists, who can neither speak nor conceive the truth in their minds, strive to explain them.' We vindicate this notable passage by a formal assertion of the plurality of persons, c. XII.

AND NOW THEREFORE LEST PERCHANCE.) An aposiopesis of one in haste. It is understood: we must look to ourselves. Once generation was discovered, if remedies against death had been present at the same time, the human race would have been too pleased with itself and would have clung to earthly things.

GOD had no need to hasten. No remedies against death remained now, except those which were drawn from the storehouse of divine mercy. Generation was not discovered only after the fall, but was instituted by GOD in the state of integrity. Nor is the human race cast out of paradise and deprived of its delights so that it may not henceforth be too pleased with itself regarding earthly things, but as a punishment for the sin committed. Mercerus observes that this reticence is customary in other languages as well, and he gives the reason why the Lord broke off his speech: namely, so as not to cast down man, who was already sufficiently sad and sorrowful. Elliptical expressions are not unusual in sharper rebukes.

Latin:

Vers. 22. AIT.] Angelis. Vid. Genes. I, 26. QUASI UNUS EX NOBIS.] Est enim scire multa, ut diximus, divinum & Angelicum: sed homines id plerum- que à potioribus distrahit. Eccles. XII, 12. 13.

Petulans depravatio. Ait Angelis. Ubi hoc habetur, quod Angelis locutus hæc sit DEUS? si sic licet inferere textui, quicquid lubet, quid non è Scriptura efformabitur? Voluit autem Socino suo ac Judæis gratificari, ne hîc plures in Deitate personæ evincantur. Sed manifestum nimis, plu- ralitatem personarum divinarum designari. Ecquis enim loquitur? Jehovah Elohim. Habemus ergo quinam illi sint, qui de se πληθυντικῶς loquantur: Ecce Adam factus, quasi UNUS ex NOBIS. Non qui quacunque ratione Elohim dicantur, sed Elo- him eminentissimo modo dicti, vel potius κυριο- λέκτως proprio vocis usu, qui Jehovah sunt, unus ille DEUS. Neque è verbis consequentibus similiter colligi potest, hæc ad Angelos dicta, etiamsi priora illa ad Angelos directa admitterentur. Anon potuit DEUS deinde demum ad angelos se convertere?

CAP. III. v. 20. 21.

Neque si hæc etiam ad illos dicta, sub voce NOBIS illi comprehenduntur. Quia illi demum hac voce comprehenduntur, qui hîc loquuntur, non coram quibus hæc proferuntur. Invictum ergo hoc est: ille qui hîc loquitur, ait sibi similem factum esse Ada- mum: Factus, inquit, quasi UNUS EX NOBIS, non quasi UNUS EX VOBIS. Ubi autem μερισμὸς est orationis tanquam inter alium atq; alium, ibi ve- re est pluralitas. Qui loquitur de uno ex Elohim, ille plures indicat Elohim. Non potest unus ex multis dici, ubi unica tantum persona est. DEUM autem angelos secum comprehendere, eosque sibi ita aunumerare, perquam absurdum. Hîc enim pari- tas & æqualitas designatur, cum unus ex Elohim commemoratur, ad cujus similitudinem adspira- vit Adam. Similem sibi persona loquens factum innuit Adamum, se autem unum dicit è pluribus non inæqualibus, sed qui ejusdem sint dignitatis. Incongruum certe & à DEI majestate alienum, quod Rivetus etiam fatetur Exercit. XL. in Genesin. p. 201. DEUM Angelis, qui ejus ministri sunt, & servi, quasi sodalibus suis & æqualis conditionis, ejus- demque dignitatis & autoritatis talia dixisse. Neque vero sententia angelis tum demum similem factum di- cere opus erat, qui conditus initio erat ad imagi- nem DEI, adeoque angelis quoad cognitionem boni & mali similis fuit. Profecto à serpente non simi- litudo cum angelis, sed cum DEO ipso promissa erat, longe scil. major atque eminentior, quam est Angelica, quam etiam vana persuasione inductus affectabat homo. Ideo DEUS, ecce, inquit, Adam factus quasi unus non ex Angelis aut cœlitibus, sed quasi UNUS ex NOBIS, suum respiciens divinum collegium, ut ita loquar, in quod utique nullus an- gelorum aut archangelorum admittitur. Quum ne illud quidem ulli Angelorum dictum sit, sede à dextris meis, tantum abest, ut intra consortium Je- hovæ Elohim τοῦ ὑπερυψήλου καὶ παναγίου rerum omnium creatoris admittatur ullus, quod fane hæc oratio inferret, si ea Angelos simul complectere- tur. Quæ adeo clara, ut hic versio Jonathanis, quam sequutus cum cæcis Judæis Grotius, corrigatur ab ipsa interpretatione Chaldaica Hierosolymitana, quæ longe rectius partitivam orationem ad ipsum Jehovam refert: Et dixit verbum Jehove: Ecce homo, quem creavi, unicus seu unigenitus est in mundo, sicut ego unigenitus sum in cælis excelsis. Neque placere potuit id commentum Calvino, qui alias libenter Judaizat: Quidam, inquit, plu- ralem numerum ad angelos referunt, ac si homi- nem DEUS terrestre & despectum animal à cœlestibus creaturis discerneret. Sed videtur longe petita ex- positio. Recte itaque August. lib. II. de Genes. ad litteram cap. XXX. Non aliter intelligendum est, quod ait, UNUM ex NOBIS, nisi ut propter Trini- tatem numerus pluralis accipiatur, sicut dictum est: Faciamus hominem; sicut de se & Patre dicit, ve- niemus ad eum & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Et longe ante Augustinum Justinus Martyr Dial. cum Tryphon. p. m. 222. ex illis verbis ἀναμφιλέ- κτως cognosci ait, ad aliquem, qui & numero ALIUS & λογικὸς sit, DEum illa loquutum esse: adeoque cum dixit, quasi unus ex nobis, tum numerum eorum, qui una essent, tum minimum duos indicasse; eaque ipsa à Patre revera editam progeniem, quæ ante crea- turas omnes cum Patre fuit, cum Patre colloquutam protulisse. Similia habet p. 281. additque: Neque ea verba figuratam loquutionem admittunt, quemadmo- dum ea exponere moliuntur Sophistæ, qui neque dice- re neque mente concipere veritatem possunt. Lo- cum insignem ex professo vindicamus invicta as- sertione pluralit. personar. c. XII.

NUNC ERGO NE FORTE.) Aposiopesis properantis. I- ntelligitur, prospiciendum nobis erit. Generatione reperta, si simul adfuissent contra mortem remedia, nimis sibi placitu- rum, hæsurumque rebus terrestribus fuerat humanum genus.

Non opus habebat properare DEUS. Nulla nunc supererant contra mortem remedia, nisi quæ è penu divinæ misericordiæ depromebantur. Ge- neratio non post lapsum demum reperta, sed in sta- tu integritatis à DEO instituta erat. Neque ne sibi deinceps placeat nimis humanum genus terre- stribus rebus, sed in pœnam peccati commissi para- diso ejicitur, ejusque deliciis privatur. Mercerus observat, reticentiam eam usitatam esse in aliis etiam linguis, & causam reddit, cur abruperit orationem Dominus, ne scil. hominem satis mæstum & contrista- tum dejiceret. Non inusitatæ sunt ellipticæ oratio- nes in acrioribus reprehensionibus.

## 3:23
Ver. 23. AND HE CAST OUT ADAM AND PLACED.) That is, having cast him out, he indeed placed.

Latin:

Vers. 23. EJECITQUE ADAM ET COLLOCAVIT.) Id est, ejecto vero eo collocavit.

## 3:24
Ver. same. CHERUBIM AND THE FLAMING SWORD.) It is the custom for the Hebrews to call all the works of GOD, which GOD uses outside of the ordinary, Angels, such as winds and fire, Psalm 104:4. Thus, what in Psalm 18:11 is said of GOD sitting upon a Cherub, Psalm 104 explains as being about the winds. Therefore, this is also a hendiadys. A Cherub and a flaming sword, for a Cherub, that is, a flaming sword. For a flaming sword the Hebrew text has להט החרב, that is, the flame of a sword. But a sword here signifies division, as in Matthew 10:34, comparing the passage of the same saying in Luke 12:51. For what is μάχαιραν there, is διαμερισμόν here. Now the Greeks are accustomed to use μάχαιραν or ῥομφαίαν indiscriminately for חרב. The sense, therefore, is that Paradise was blocked off by an impassable fire. There is a field in Babylonia that burns by day, mentioned by Pliny in book II, ch. 109, and in the same Babylonia a tract full of naphtha, which has a great affinity for fire, as the same Pliny had said in the preceding chapter. Curtius mentions in the same places caverns pouring out a huge amount of bitumen. The Babylonians called this type of bitumen Naphtha, a most rapid fire: concerning which see Strabo in book XV; Plutarch has much on it in his Life of Alexander: these things among others: 'It is so sensitive to fire that, before touching the flame, it often ignites the air between them by the very light radiating from it.' He adds: 'For Babylonia is very fiery, so that the barley often leaps and is shaken from the ground, as if by a throbbing of the places due to inflammation.' In those places, therefore, was paradise, and there is bitumen there, no less than at Sodom, the remains of fire sent down divinely.

Who would have elicited this sense from those words, except Grotius, who can make anything out of everything? Finally, from there he constructs out of the Cherubim some kind of most rapid fire, called Naphtha in the Babylonian field, so that he may fix paradise in those places, and the bitumen as the remains of fire sent down divinely, as at Sodom. We have, therefore, the Cherubim of Grotius: the fire sent down and its remains, naphtha. So great an artificer of fire or creator of bitumen, before him, as far as I know, there was no one who could have produced naphtha from this in the Babylonian field. It is a wonder that he did not construct a purgatorial fire from it in favor of the Papists, along with some others: but perhaps he saw that that fire is posited by the Papists, not to exclude men from paradise, but to help and promote those excluded for a time. Moreover, he invents the custom of the Hebrews from his own ingenuity; he does not prove it from the Biblical Codex, whose phraseology is the subject here. Psalm 104:4 concerns the creation of angels, but the name of angels is not attributed to the winds. The interpretation of the Holy Scriptures in Hebrews 1:7 is without doubt more certain than the gloss of Grotius, in which he is not consistent with himself. For in the annotations to this passage of the Psalm, he does not think the winds are marked with the name of angels, but he invents certain angels of an aerial nature, just as he does others of a fiery nature, following the fables of the Jews and the commentaries of Pythagoras and Plato. For he appeals to these things there, so that he may claim matter and bodies for the angels. Nor are the Cherubim, whose mention in Psalm 18:11 is explained in Psalm 104, about the winds. If those passages are compared, they teach rather that by Cherubim are designated the Angels, who are compared to the winds for their speed and agility, just as the word כרוב is believed by some to be derived from רכב, to fly or to ride, signifying a winged human face. Our blessed Gesner very well: David, in this picture, by which he introduces GOD sitting upon the Cherubim, looks to the mercy seat or the ark of the covenant. For on Mount Sinai GOD himself manifested himself to Moses in this way, and commanded the tabernacle and the mercy seat to be fashioned according to the image of the form shown on the mountain, Exodus 25. A similar revelation of the divine Majesty is described in Isaiah 6. For which reason this epithet is attributed to GOD everywhere in the Scriptures, as Psalm 21:2, Psalm 29:1, that he sits above the Cherubim. For that fiery chariot is the army of angels, אש רכב, by which Elijah is carried into heaven, 2 Kings 2, and by whose protection Elisha is freed from the Syrian siege of Dothan, chapter 5. Now this name was given to the angels partly because of their speed, whence the Chaldean Paraphrast here (Psalm 18:11) adds an epithet, and calls the Cherubim most swift; partly because they manifested themselves to men in such a form, and in the mercy seat, and afterwards in Solomon's temple, by the command of GOD himself, they were depicted and formed in that way. According to Josephus, Antiquities book III, ch. 6, the Cherubim were winged living creatures, of a new species, never seen by any man, which Moses had seen figured on the Throne of GOD; whence GOD is said to sit upon the Cherubim, of whose presence the ark was a symbol, 1 Samuel 4:4, 2 Samuel 6:2, 2 Kings 19:19, 1 Chronicles 13:1, Isaiah 37:16, and that this is alluded to in 2 Samuel 22:11, Psalm 19:11, as Petrus Ravanellus of Utica, from Orcitania, observed after others in his Bibliotheca under the word Cherub. Moses therefore adapts himself here to the grasp of the Jews, to whom the Cherubim in the tabernacle were known, by which name also the Angels have been called in the Scriptures ever since this divine command concerning placing the Cherubim on the lid of the ark of the covenant, so that it might be indicated that they are both ministers of GOD and guardians of the Church.

Regarding the origin of the word, see B. Gerhard on this passage, Rivetus, Exercitation XLI. What if the meaning of the word, because the root is no longer used in Hebrew, is sought from Arabic, a neighboring language, in which כרב means to press, to distress, to afflict; for the Cherubim placed before the garden of Eden did truly distress and afflict men, whom R. Solomon interprets as exterminating or scourging angels; just as Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Fagius, and Drusius also betake themselves here to the related Chaldean and Syriac language, in which the word רביא denotes a boy from רבא, to grow, because they appeared in the form of a charming youth, and sometimes those images also exhibited the appearance of boys or youths; which etymology they handed down in Talmud Chagigah, fol. 13. Because it is כרוב, R. Assu said, כרביא, as if an adolescent (the appearance of a boy), for thus in Babylonia they call a boy רביא, which tradition Buxtorf observes that almost all modern Jews also accept—R. Solomon, R. Levi Ben Gerson, Maimonides, and others—in his Exercitation on the History of the Ark of the Covenant, chap. IX, p. 100. But Lud. de Dieu called this conjecture inept in his animadversions on this passage, and that it does not square with grammatical analogy, likewise taking refuge in the neighboring Arabic language, in which, according to Schindler, כרוב is a skiff, a transport ship, and asserting that כרוב is the same as, with the letters transposed, רכוב, a vehicle, a chariot, because the angels are called the vehicle of GOD, Ps. 68:18, Zech. 6:1, etc. Mercer in Pagninus' Lexicon: This name, he says, has an affinity with רכב, which is to be carried. For it seems that by this name is signified either a spiritual thing or a bodily image fashioned by the hand of an artisan, which was carried as if it were a bird with wings expanded, or because of the speed of its motion it seemed to be carried and to fly.
