Whence Psalm 18 and 2 Samuel 22 calls a cloud a Cherub, because clouds are as it were the wings of GOD. Ezekiel

C. X. sufficiently shows that he understands by מַרְכָּבָה (chariot) the very כְּרוּבִים (cherubim) themselves or the four winged living creatures themselves, which appeared to be carried and to fly, whence the affinity of these two roots appears. And thus also other philologists derive the meaning of the root כרב, now unused in Hebrew, partly from Arabic and partly from the related word רכב, just as Avenarius in his Lexicon and Kircher in his Concordances demonstrate with examples that such related roots often illustrate each other in the Hebrew language: to which our own B. Gesner, Andr. Rivetus among the Reformed in Exod. XXV, 18, and Cornel. à Lapide among the Catholics on Ezech. XXVIII, 14, do not dissent; by metathesis Cherub is said to be as it were רכוב (riding). But he seems not to be consistent with himself, for in the same place he also wants Cherub to be as it were כְּרַב, that is, like Rabbi, like a wise man, or even like a great one, which explanation the Commentary on Gen. III, 22 also hints at. But on Exod. XXV, 18, when he deals expressly with the origin of the word, he wants Cherubim to be said, with Pagninus, from כָּבַר (he knew) and רַב (much), and proves that they are named from a multitude of wisdom and knowledge by the authority of Dionysius, Philo, Origen, Jerome, Anastasius, Theodoret, Philastrius, Sophronius, Isidore, Bede, and the common consent of the Scholastics: but he makes other allusive derivations, namely that this name alludes to the root כביר as if it were manifold in knowledge, strength, form, and figure, and to רכב (chariot), and to כפר (mercy seat), etc. Let those things also be compared which we said in Diatribe X. §. XXXVIII. However, whatever may be the case regarding the etymology, there is no doubt that this name is attributed to the Angels, upon whom GOD is said to sit, because He commands the Angels, even if this phrase also alludes to the images joined to the throne of the Lord in Exod. XXV, 18, inasmuch as the celestial majesty of GOD is shadowed forth, so that there is no need for the conjecture of Ribera, why He is said to sit upon the Cherubim, not the Seraphim, lib. II. de templo cap. 6.

Most of the more learned interpreters certainly acknowledge that the Angels were placed here before Paradise, if perhaps you except Musculus, who, with equal success to Grotius, extracted from Ps. XVIII, 11, large and terrible birds, whom he nevertheless distinguishes from fiery flames, so that they were not placed in one spot, but in different places prohibited all access to Paradise: and Theodoret, and Procopius of Gaza, who posit a certain species as if of fearsome animals placed before the gates of Paradise, along with לַהַט הַחֶרֶב. By which words, since the word לַהַט denotes partly a flame, partly a polished blade shining like a flame, others understand it more correctly as a flame having the form of a sword, others with Aben-Ezra as a sword glowing with fire, flashing, and as it were vomiting flames, because the sword is said to be turning itself every way, or versatile, with which the armed Cherubim terrified men, just as the Angel was seen with a drawn sword by Balaam in Num. XXII, 12, 23, and by Joshua in chapter VI, 1. Blessed Luther says, a certain splendor as if of an unsheathed sword, which appeared in the hand of the angels and was agitated by continuous motion, and struck the eyes with horror like lightning, kept those who were about to approach away. But perhaps no one besides Grotius understood חרב as διαμερισμὸν (division): nor does that Hebrew word ever signify division, even if the Greek word machaira, which is used in Matt. X, 34, and diamerismos, by metonymy, because division is made by the sword, seem to be interchanged in Luke chapter XII, 51.

Latin:

Vers. eod. CHERUBIM ET FLAMMEUM GLADI- UM.) Mos Hebræis omnia DEI opera, quibus extra ordi- nem DEUS utitur, appellare Angelos, ut ventos & ignem Psalm. 104, 4. Sic quod in Psalm. 18, 11. DEUS insidere Che- rubino dicitur, Psalm. 104. de ventis exponit. Est ergo & hic ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Cherub & flammeus gladius, pro Cherub, id est, flammeus gladius. Pro flammeo gladio Hebræus textus habet להט החרב, id est, flammam machæræ. Ma- chæra autem hic significat divisionem, ut Matth. 10, 34. col- lato loco ejusdem dicti Lucæ 12, 51. Nam quod ibi est μάχαι- ραν, hîc est διαμερισμόν. Solent autem Græci promiscue pro חרב ponere μάχαιραν, aut ῥομφαίαν. Sensus ergo est, igne impervio obseptum Paradisum. Est in Babylonia cam- pus interdiu flagrans, Plinio memoratus lib. II. c. CIX. & in eadem Babylonia tractus naphthæ plenus, cui magna ignium cognatio, ut præcedente capite dixerat idem Plinius. Cur- tius iisdem in locis cavernæ meminit, ingentem vim bitumi- nis effundentis. Id bituminis genus ignis rapidissimum Naph- tha vocabant Babylonii: de quo vide Strabonem libro XV. multa de eo Plutarchus in vita Alexandri: hæc inter alia: Οὕτω δὲ εὐπαθὴς πρὸς τὸ πῦρ ἐστι, ὥστε πρὶν ἢ θίγειν τὴν φλό- γα, δι' αὐτῆς τῆς περὶ τὸ φῶς ἐξαπτομένης ἀυγῆς τὸν μεταξὺ πολλάκις ἀέρα συνεκκαίειν. Addit καὶ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ Βαβυλωνία σφό- δρα πυρώδης, ὥστε τὰς μὲν κριθὰς χαμόθεν ἐκπηδᾶν καὶ ἀποπάλ- λεσθαι πολλάκις, οἷον ὑπὸ φλεγμονῆς τῶν τόπων σφυγμὸς ἐχόν- των. In illis igitur locis paradisus fuerit, estq; bitumen ibi, non minus, quam apud Sodoma, ignis divinitus immissi reliquiæ.

Quis hunc sensum è verbis illis elicuisset, præ- ter Grotium, qui ex omnibus facere potest omnia. Inde denique extruit è Cherubim aliquid bitu- minis genus ignis rapidissimum, Naphtha dictum in campo Babylonico, ut in illis locis paradisum figat, & bitumen, ignis divinitus immissi, ut apud Sodo- ma, reliquias. Habemus ergo Cherubim Grotii: ignem immissum ejusque reliquias, naphtham. Tan- tus ignis artifex aut conditor bituminis ante ipsum, quod sciam, nemo fuit, qui hinc naphtham in campo Babylonico procreare potuerit. Mirum, quod non in favorem Papistarum purgatorium ignem inde extruxerit cum nonnullis: Sed vidit fortassis, ignem illum à Papicolis poni, non ut excludat homines paradiso, sed ut juvet ac pro- moveat ad tempus exclusos. Morem autem E- bræorum primum ex ingenio suo fingit: è Co- dice Biblico, de cujus phraseologia hîc agitur, non probat. Psalm. 104, 4. de angelorum creatione agitur, non autem ventis nomen angelorum tribui- tur. Interpretatio S. S. Ebr. 1, 7. certior sine du- bio est glossa Grotii, in qua sibi ipse non constat. Annotatis enim ad hunc Psalmi locum, non an- gelorum nomine insignitos ventos censet, sed an- gelos aëreæ naturæ quosdam comminiscitur, uti alios igneæ, Judæorum fabellas & Pythagoræ ac Pla- tonis sequutus commenta. Ad hæc enim ibi pro- vocat, ut angelis materiam & corpora vindicet. Nec Cherubim, quorum mentio Psalm. 18, 11. expli- cantur Psalm. 104. de ventis. Quæ loca si confe- rantur, id potius docent, per Cherubim Ange- los, qui ventis ob celeritatem & agilitatem com- parantur, designari, uti etiam vox כרוב quibus- dam à רכב volavit, vel equitavit deducta, faciem humanam alatam significare creditur. Optime B. Gesnerus noster: Respicit David hac pictura, qua inducit DEUM insidentem Cherubinis, ad pro- pitiatorium seu arcam fœderis. Nam in monte Si- nai DEUS ipse ita sese Mosi manifestavit, jussitque ad formæ in monte ostensæ imaginem tabernaculum & propitiatorium efformari, Exod. 25. Similis reve- latio divinæ Majestatis describitur Esa. 6. Quam ob causam DEO passim in Scripturis, ut Psalm. 21, 2. Psalm. 29, 1. hoc Epitheton tribuitur, quod super Cherubim sedeat. Angelorum enim exercitus est il- le igneus currus אש רכב, quo Elias in cælum vehi- tur, 2. Reg. 2. & cujus præsidio Elisa à Syrorum ob- sidione Dothan liberatur cap. 5. Angelis autem id no- minis datum est partim ob celeritatem, unde Chaldæus Paraphrastes hic (Psalm. 18, 11.) addit Epitheton, & vocat Cherubim levisssimos; partim quod tali forma sese hominibus manifestarunt & in propitiatorio, po- steaque Salomonis in templo, ipsius DEI jussu, ita de- picti & formati sunt. Josepho autore Antiquit. l. III. c. 6. Cherubim erant animantia volucria, nova spe- cie, nec unquam hominum cuiquam visa, quæ Moses in DEI Solio viderat figurata; Unde Cherubinis insi- dere dictus DEUS, cujus præsentiæ arca erat Sym- bolum 1. Sam. 4, 4. 2. Sam. 6, 2. 2. Reg. 19, 19. 1. Chron. 13, 1. Es. 37, 16. eoque alludi 2. Sam. 22, 11. Ps. 19, 11. post alios observavit Petrus Ravanellus Uticensis Orcitanus in Biblioth. in voce Cherub. Accommo- dat itaque se Moses hic captui Judæorum, cui noti erant Cherubim, in tabernaculo, quo nomine eti- am Angeli inde ab hoc mandato divino de impo- nendis Cherubim operculo arcæ fœderis, ut indi- caretur eos & DEI ministros, & Ecclesiæ custodes esse, in Scripturis nuncupati sunt.

De vocis origine videantur B. Gerhardus in h. l. Rivetus Exercitat. XLI. Quid si vocis signifi- catio, quia radix in Ebræo non usitata est am- plius, ex Arabismo, lingua vicina, petatur, cui כרב est pressit, anxit, afflixit; vere enim anxere & afflixere homines Cherubim ante hortum Eden positi, quos R. Salomo interpretatur Angelos exter- minatores vel vapulationis; quemadmodum etiam ad cognatam Chaldaicam & Syriacam linguam hîc se recipiunt Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Fagius & Drusius, in qua vox רביא puerum à רבא crescere, notat, quod in forma blandi adolescentis apparuerint, quando- que & imagines istæ puerorum, vel adolescentum speciem exhibuerint; quam Etymologiam tradide- re in Talmud Chagigah f. 13. Quia est כרוב R. Assu dixit, כרביא quasi adolescens (species pueri) sic enim in Babylonia puerum vocant רביא quam tra- ditionem etiam omnes fere neotericos Judæos re- cipere R. Salomon, R. Levi Ben Gerson, Maimonidem, aliosque observat Buxtorfius in exercit. ad histor. Arc. Fœd. cap. IX. p. 100. Sed ineptam dixit hanc conjecturam Lud. de Dieu animadv. ad h. l. neque quadrare Grammaticæ analogiæ, pariter confugiens ad vicinam Arabicam linguam, in qua, Schindlero teste כרוב sit cymba, navis vectoria, ac כרוב idem es- se, quod transpositis literis רכוב vehiculum, currus, asserens, quia Angeli dicuntur vehiculum DEI Ps. 68, 18. Zach. 6, 1. &c. Mercerus in Lexico Pagnin. Hoc nomen, inquit, cum רכב quod est vehi, affinitatem habet. Videtur enim hoc nomine significari vel res spiritualis, vel corporalis imago artificis manu fabre- facta, quæ tanquam volucris alis expansis vehebatur, vel ob motus celeritatem vehi, ac volare videbatur Unde Psalm. 18. & 2. Samuel. 22. nubem appellat Cherub, quod nubes sint velut alæ DEI. Ezechiel

C. X. satis ostendit se per מַרְכָּבָה quadrigas ipsos כְּרוּבִים seu ipsa quatuor animantia alata, quæ alata vehi & volare apparebant, intelligere, unde apparet duarum harum radicum affinitas. Atque ita etiam alii Philologi Radicis nunc in Ebraïsmo inusitatæ כרב significationem partim ex Arabismo partim ex cognata voce רכב, uti sæpe affines ejusmodi ra- dices se mutuo in Ebraïca lingua illustrare Avena- rius in Lexico, & Kircherus in Concordantiis ex- emplis demonstrant, eruunt: quibus non abnu- unt è nostris B. Gesnerus, è Reformatis Andr. Rive- tus in Exod. XXV, 18. è Pontificiis Cornel. à Lapid. ad Ezech. XXVIII, 14. per Metathesin Cherub dici- tur quasi רכוב equitans. Qui vero sibi non constare videtur, nam & Cherub ibidem vult esse quasi כְּרַב id est, sicut Rabbi, sicut sapiens, vel etiam sicut ma- gnus, quam explicationem innuit quoque Coment. ad Gen. III, 22. Sed ad Exod. XXV, 18. cum ex pro- fesso de origine vocis agit, Cherubim dici vult, cum Pagnino, à כָּבַר cognovit, & רַב multum, eosque à multitudine sapientiæ & scientiæ denominari è Dio- nysii, Philonis, Origenis, Hieronymi, Anastasii, Theo- doreti, Philastrii, Sophronii, Isidori, Bedæ autoritate & consensu Scholasticorum communi probat: alias vero derivationes allusivas facit, quod nempe no- men hoc alludat ad radicem כביר quasi multiplex scientia, robore, forma & figura, & ad רכב currus, & ad כפר propitiatorium &c. Conferantur etiam, quæ diximus Diatribe X. §. XXXVIII. Quicquid autem de Etymo sit, nullum dubium est, Angelis hoc nomen tribui, quibus insidere DEUS dicitur, quia imperat Angelis, etsi hac phrasi etiam ad ima- gines alludatur, throno Domini junctas Exod. XXV, 18. utpote quoma jestas cœlestis DEI adum- brata est, ut non opus sit conjectura Riberæ, cur Che- rubinis insidere dicatur, non Seraphinis lib. II. de tem- plo cap. 6.

Angelos certe hic collocatos fuisse ante Para- disum agnoscunt plerique omnes doctiores inter- pretes, si forte Musculum excipias, qui è Ps. XVIII, 11. volucres grandes & terribiles, parili cum Grotio felicitate exsculpsit, quos tamen à flammis igneis di- stínguit, ut non uno loco positæ, sed diversis locis omnem Paradisi aditum prohibuerint: & Theodo- retum, ac Procopium Gazæum, qui speciem quandam velut animalium formidolosorum præ foribus Para- disi locatam statuunt, cum לַהַט הַחֶרֶב. Quibus verbis, quum vox לַהַט partim flammam, partim laminam politam instar flammæ fulgentem notet, alii flammam habentem formam gladii, alii cum Aben- Ezra gladium igne candentem, fulgurantem, & flam- mas quasi vomentem rectius intelligunt, quia gla- dius vertens se undiquaque, seu versatilis dicitur, quo armati Cherubim homines terruerunt, quem- admodum gladio stricto visus est Angelus Bileamo Num. XXII, 12. 23. & Josuæ cap. VI, 1. Absterrebat, inquit B. Lutherus, accessuros splendor quidam qua- si gladii evaginati, qui apparebat in manu angelo- rum & continuo motu agitabatur, atque oculos ceu fulgur cum horrore perstringebat. Per חרב vero διαμερισμὸν divisionem præter Grotium forte nemo intellexit: neque vox illa Ebræa unquam divisio- nem significat, etsi machæra Græca vox, quæ Matth. X, 34. adhibetur, & διαμερισμὸς, per metonymi- am, quia per gladium fit divisio, apud Lucam cap. XII, 51. commutari videantur.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

The procreation and sacrifices of Cain and Abel. Abel is killed. The exile and generations of Cain, the birth of Seth and Enos.

Verse 1. BY GOD.) Thus also the Greeks in this place translate אֶת־יְהוָה by διὰ. For fruitfulness is a singular benefit of GOD. Below 30, 2.

Of this there is no doubt, that fruitfulness is a benefit of GOD: But that the word אֶת־יְהוָה ought to be rendered thus, or that this was Eve's intention, that had to be proven. The custom of the Hebrews opposes this, who, when they wish to explain that σὺν θεῷ, with GOD, or by GOD, or by the help of GOD, never say אֶת־יְהוָה but בַּיהוָה or בֵּאלֹהִים Ps. 60, last, Ps. 108, last, Jerem. 3, 23, Hos. 1, 7, Isa. 45, 17, Deut. 23, v. penultimate. Grotius could not teach anything else from the idiom of the Hebrews. On the contrary, the little word אֶת is ordinarily the sign of the accusative case, which, since it is repeated nine times in this, and the preceding and following verse, is never used otherwise; and in the verse immediately following it is read in exactly the same manner of apposition; which custom of the Hebrews is most well-known, and therefore was not obscure to Grotius, Gen. 4, 1. And Adam himself knew אֶת־חַוָּה Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore אֶת־קַיִן Cain and said, I have obtained אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה the Lord Jehovah. And v. 3. And she added to bear אֶת־אָחִיו his brother אֶת־הֶבֶל Abel cap. 26, 34. And he took אִשָּׁה אֶת־יְהוּדִית a wife Jehudith, see more cap. 12, 3. and elsewhere passim. Jerem. 17, 13. עֹזְבֵי מְקוֹר מַיִם חַיִּים אֶת־יְהוָה they have forsaken the fountain of living waters. Eth-Jehovah the Lord. Which example is entirely similar to ours. Add also Ezech. 4, 1. Engrave upon it עִיר a city אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלַם Jerusalem. Whence it is most manifest that the Hebrew words ought to be rendered thus: I have acquired a man, or I have possessed the Lord: Because the ordinary and perpetual Hebrew manner of speaking demands this, from which it is not right to depart; but they are by no means to be rendered as Grotius wishes: because the idiom of the holy language resists it, from which not one similar example can be brought forward. Let this rule only be observed: Wherever the article אֶת is found before any noun which an active and transitive verb governs, there it is ordinarily the sign of the accusative case.

Add now the observation of the blessed Luther concerning the word אִישׁ T. VIII. Jen. Germ. f. 157. that, where it is read alone without mention of a wife, it denotes not simply a man, but with eminence a distinguished man; which therefore cannot be applied to a newborn boy, it occurs only of that hero who, born a boy, is at once predicted as God the mighty and the everlasting father, Is. 9, 6. See Genes. 32, 21. Exod. 15, 4. Jos. 5, 23. Esa. 53, 3. Zach. 6, 12. But especially add the desire of the mother of all, intent solely on the promised seed of the woman. Whence she exclaims for joy: I have acquired the man the Lord. Add also that to the husband, who wished to give a profession of faith by the name imposed on his wife, cap. 3, 20. the same being called EVA or LIFE-GIVER, Eve wished here to agree, being about to give a similar profession of faith by the name imposed on her firstborn son, namely that in the God-man apprehended by faith she has her only hope and consolation, and the very possession of heavenly riches. The blessed Luther also urges the emphasis of the name in his Commentary p. 70. The text shows that the word Cain is from the verb Kanah, which signifies to possess or to acquire, so that by this name she might console herself against the evils received, and oppose the acquisition of life and salvation through the seed of Cain to the loss of life and salvation through sin and Satan, as if to say: I remember what we have lost through sin, but now let us hope for and speak of nothing but recovery and acquisition. For I have acquired the man of GOD, who will acquire that lost glory for us again.

Which interpretation Johannes Reuchlin in book 1 of the Cabbala, as also Conradus Pelicanus, confirmed from the Rabbis themselves and the Cabbalists; which is supported by R. Jonathan in the Chaldean Paraphrase rendering it thus: And Adam knew Eve his wife, who was desiring THAT ANGEL, and she conceived, and bore Cain, and said: I have acquired a man, or as Manahem's reading has it, that very Angel of Jehovah. Nor can the Greek and Latin Vulgate versions be opposed to the text and likewise the interpretation of Isidorus Clarius, Fagius, Forster, Schindler, Osiander, Lud. de Dieu, and B. Luther from Tom. VIII. Jen. Germ. have deservedly followed. There follow also, with Petrus Canus, Toffanus, and Constantinus L'Empereur, notes added to the Belgian version, and these distinguished theologians solidly support this explanation: Joh. Brentius, Urb. Rhegius, Dav. Chytraeus, Nic. Selneccerus, Osiander, and likewise Polycarp. Lyserus, Sal. Gesnerus, Dav. Rungius, Chr. Pelargus, and especially Aegid. Hunnius in Calvino Judaizante, and Anti-Pareo, B. Gerhard on this passage, as well as B. Helvicus on the desire of the mother Eve, B. Glassius in Christol. Mosaïc. Disput. V. Dn. D. Waltherus, in offic. Bibl. observ. in Gen. XXI. One may also compare our disputation on the faith of the ancients in Christ §. 38. seqq. But Grotius preferred to applaud the blind Jews, and Socinus, and to prefer the Latin Vulgate and the Greek version to the evidence of the text and the sources themselves.

Others meet the objection concerning the error, or rather the idolatry of Eve, if she believed Cain to be the God-man, by saying that she did not err except in the application to this individual; but Dn. D. Seb. Schmidius, in the disputation on the faith of the mother Eve held at Strasbourg in the year 1667, taught that not even this error should be conceded, eruditely showing how Eve here professed her faith, not indeed persuaded that this firstborn of hers was that promised seed, but by the name imposed on this son of hers, she testified that she had possessed through faith that man who is Jehovah, not that she thought her firstborn son was that very Messiah, whom she would thus already possess outwardly present in the flesh, but that she possessed him in faith and inwardly, not yet born, but to be born and manifested in his own time, whose promise, apprehended by true faith, could save men even before his advent in the flesh: that she rejoiced more in this promise made to her, that she exulted more in this man Jehovah, than in the male recently born to her, although she ought also to rejoice not a little in him as the firstborn of the human race, so that she might wish a monument of her faith and joy to exist in his name for all human posterity. I have acquired, or rather possessed, a certain Man, who is Jehovah himself, in whose honor and eternal memory I wish my son and the firstborn of the human race to be called Kain, that is, Jehovah is my possession. Which is illustrated by the name of the son of Moses, Eliezer, that is, GOD is my help, by which it is not noted as if the son himself is GOD, his help, but that he wished this to be a monument of his faith in GOD.

This elegant explanation can be more fully illustrated in that Eve wished to testify by this mnemonic name of her firstborn son that she possessed a certain man, who is Jehovah himself, spiritually through faith, and through spiritual conception made by the word of the Gospel: just as she possessed this son of hers corporally, through natural conception, and held him as her possession, more excellent than all the treasures and goods of the world, as one in whom she uniquely has the possession of all spiritual and heavenly goods, and eternal life, and the possession and eternal enjoyment of God himself. And they confirm this interpretation 1. The propriety of the word: because קניתי properly signifies possession: even if it is transferred to acquisition, as far as the possession of a thing is reached: and קניתי is a verb of the past tense, not that she was beginning to possess the man only now when she conceived the firstborn, but that she had possessed him long before, namely from the announced Proto-Evangelium, from which she conceived him spiritually by the power of the Holy Spirit, and thus the mother of all always possessed him with a faithful mind and heart. And without doubt the faithful Eve had the spiritually conceived Messiah as her POSSESSION more than the corporally conceived firstborn: because that possession was everlasting, this one temporary: that was of itself saving, but this one was not of itself saving, even if that firstborn had been believed to be the Messiah himself. Then, however much some mother might be able to speak of her son, just as the personal wisdom of God says somewhere, The Lord possessed me; yet in human style we are not accustomed to speak so properly, because human possessions are placed in others rather than in sons: but spiritual and mystical possession is that by which we have the Messiah for ourselves by faith, so that he is ours, and we are his, and we are saved through him, as Dn. D. Schmidius rightly says here. 2. The emphasis and use of the name איש, which denotes a MAN, and is not used anywhere of Christ as an infant, or from conception and birth: who is indeed called אִישׁ גִּבּוֹר, but is not called by the name איש in corporal conception. But that Christ the Redeemer is possessed by the faithful in spiritual conception as a man, who is Jehovah, there is no doubt. Dominus D. Schmied urges here also that this name is placed without an article, and denotes a vague subject: I have possessed a certain man, Jehovah; which vague locution does not fit the firstborn already present and placed before the eyes: which he says all who know the genius of the language will admit: But it fits very well the profession of faith issued concerning the naming of Cain: I have possessed a certain excellent man, namely that man who is Jehovah. 3. Comparison of other names. For as often as the reason for the naming is given, in which a name proper to God is included, which it is manifest is done here, that divine name is not claimed as incommunicable for Him to whom the name is imposed, but only some profession concerning the true God is made, succinctly comprised or insinuated by a new name, as if by a certain memorial: but the style is formed otherwise when the reason of the name concerns the one born himself, and explains what is proper to him: as for instance when it is said in Matt. 1:21: you shall call his name Jesus; for he himself shall save his people from their sins. 4. Comparison of the preceding history. The pains of childbirth had been denounced to Eve, which without doubt she experienced when she brought forth Cain: she had been cast out of Paradise, excluded from the tree of life with all her posterity, and yet she attributed this most illustrious name to her firstborn, and to the whole human race: the reason for which is given thus: And, either because she said: she professed: I have possessed a man, who is Jehovah, whom, although she could not think that this very one, conceived by the ordinary law of procreation known to her from Adam, and brought forth with pains, was the firstborn, she nevertheless wished to be named after Him whom she had embraced by faith, and firmly possessed, so that the memory of that man of promise, who is Jehovah, the crusher of the serpent's head, might always be before her eyes, as if she were to say, I have indeed brought forth my son with pain, an exile from Paradise, and excluded from the tree of life, but because I have conceived by faith from the word of the Proto-Evangelium, I have embraced, and have possessed until now that seed of the woman, which is to crush the head of the serpent, which is to arise from my progeny, I am full of spiritual joy, as a life-giving mother, happy and blessed in this deliverer, not unhappy and cursed, whose children can be heirs of eternal life through faith in this Redeemer. Him therefore I have long since possessed by faith, the man who is Jehovah, and I still possess him, and have him, as my own property and proper good, and with him I have all treasures, all good things: in Him I rejoice, and I delight uniquely, who alone is my true possession: therefore let my son's name be Cain, as a symbol and memorial, that this man Jehovah is my true and eternal, and only possession, whom while I have, I expect neither heaven, nor earth, nor whatever is in heaven or earth, besides Him. Ps. 73, 25. The text shows, says our blessed Luther, that Cain's name is from the verb Kanah, which means to possess, or to acquire, so that by this name he might console himself against the evils received, and oppose the acquisition of life and salvation through the seed to the loss of life and salvation through sin and Satan. But enough of this interpretation, concerning which the praised disputation of Dr. Schmid deserves to be read entirely.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Caini & Abelis procreatio, & sacrificia. Occi- ditur Abel. Caini exilium, & generatio- nes, Sethi & Enos nativitas.

Vers. 1. PER DEUM.) Sic & Græci hoc loco אֶת־יְהוָה per διὰ vertunt. DEI enim beneficium singulare est fœcun- ditas. Infra 30, 2.

DE hoc nullum est dubium, quod fœcunditas DEI sit beneficium : Sed quod vox אֶת־יְהוָה ita reddi debeat, aut hæc fuerit Evæ intentio, id pro- bandum erat. Repugnat Ebræorum consuetudo, qui cum exponere illud σὺν θεῷ, cum DEO, vel per DEUM, aut DEI ope volunt, nunquam ajunt אֶת־יְהוָה sed בַּיהוָה vel בֵּאלֹהִים Ps. 60, ult. Ps. 108, ult. Jerem. 3, 23. Hos. 1, 7. Esa. 45, 17. Deut. 23, v. penult. Aliud ex Ebræorum Idiotismo docere non potuit Grotius. Ex adverso vero vocula אֶת ordi- narie est nota quarti casus, quæ quum novies in hoc, & antecedente ac consequente versiculo repe- tatur, nunquam aliter adhibetur; Et in versu sta- tim sequente eadem plane appositionis ratione legi- tur; Quæ consuetudo Ebræorum est notissima, ideoque Grotio obscura non fuit, Gen. 4, 1. Et ipse Adam cognovit אֶת־חַוָּה τὴν Evam uxorem suam, & concepit & peperit אֶת־קַיִן τὸν Kainum & dixit, adepta sum אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה τὸν κύριον Jehovam. Et v. 3. Et addidit parere אֶת־אָחִיו τὸν fratrem ejus אֶת־הֶבֶל τὸν Habelem cap. 26, 34. Et accepit אִשָּׁה אֶת־יְהוּדִית uxorem τὴν Jehuditham, vid. plura cap. 12, 3. & alibi passim. Jerem. 17, 13. עֹזְבֵי מְקוֹר מַיִם חַיִּים אֶת־יְהוָה dereliquerunt fontem aquarum vi- varum. Eth-Jehovah τὸν κύριον. Quod exemplum nostro prorsus simile est. Adde & Ezech. 4, 1. Scul- pe super eo עִיר urbem אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלַם Jerusalem. Un- de manifestissimum, verba Ebræa ita reddi debe- re: Acquisivi virum, vel possedi Dominum : Quia po- stulat hoc ordinaria & perpetua loquendi ratio E- braica, à qua recedere fas non est; neutiquam au- tem ita reddenda esse, uti vult Grotius: quia refra- gatur idiotismus linguæ sanctæ, è qua ne unum ex- emplum simile adferri potest. Observetur modo hæc regula: Ubicunque reperitur articulus אֶת ante aliquod nomen, quod verbum activum regit & transi- tivum, ibi ordinarie accusativi casus nota est.

Adde jam observationem B. Lutheri de voce אִישׁ T. VIII. Jen. Germ. f. 157. quod, ubi ea solum legitur sine mentione uxoris, non simpliciter virum, sed cum eminentia insignem virum denotet; quæ pro- inde de puero recens nato adhiberi nequit ψιλῷ ἀν- θρώπῳ solum de heroë illo occurrit, qui puer na- tus & Deus fortis, & pater æternus simul prædicatur Es. 9, 6. Videatur Genes. 32, 21. Exod. 15, 4. Jos. 5, 23. Esa. 53, 3. Zach. 6, 12. Sed imprimis adde desideri- um παμμήτερος, semini mulieris promisso uni- ce intentæ. Unde præ gaudio exclamat: Acquisivi virum Dominum. Adde etiam quod Marito, qui professionem fidei nomine uxori imposito edere voluit, cap. 3, 20. vocata eadem EVA seu VIVI- PARA, concinere hîc voluerit Eva, similiter fidei professionem nomine primogenito filio imposito editura, quod nempe in θεανθρώπῳ fide apprehen- so unicam habeat spem, & consolationem, ipsam- que cœlestium divitiarum possessionem. B. Luthe- rus urget quoque emphasin nominis in Comentar. p. 70. Textus ostendit dictum Cain à verbo Kanah, quod significat possidere, seu acquirere, ut hoc nomi- ne se consoletur contra accepta mala, & opponat acqui- sitionem vitæ & salutis per Cain semen, amissioni vi- tæ & salutis per peccatum & Satanam, q. d. Memini, quid amiserimus per peccatum, sed nunc nihil nisi re- cuperationem & acquisitionem speremus & loquamur. Acquisivi enim virum DEI, qui amissam istam glori- am iterum acquiret nobis.

Quam interpretationem è Rabbinis ipsis & Cabbalistis Johannes Reuchlinus lib. 1. Cabbalæ, ut & Conradus Pelicanus confirmarunt; Cui suffragatur etiam R. Jonathan in Paraphrasi Chaldaica sic red- dens: Et Adam cognovit Evam uxorem suam, quæ erat desiderans ILLIUS ANGELI, & concepit, & peperit Cainum, & dixit: Adepta sum viro, vel ut Manahemi lectio habet, verum illum Angelum Jeho- væ. Neque opponi possunt versiones Græca & Latina Vulgata textui authentico, utpote qui solus θεό- πνευστος. Quem proinde merito sequuta manuscri- pta quædam versio Syra, interpretatio item Isidori Cla- rii, Fagii, Forsteri, Schindleri, Osiandri, Lud. de Dieu, & B. Lutheri e Tom. VIII. Jen. Germ. emendata. Sequuntur etiam cum Petro Cano, Toffano & Constan- tino L'Empereur, Belgicæ versioni additæ notæ, solide- que adstruunt hanc explicationem Theologi insi- gnes Joh. Brentius, Urb. Rhegius, Dav. Chųtræus, Nic. Selneccerus, Osiander, itemq; Polycarp. Lyserus, Sal. Gesnerus, Dav. Rungius, Chr. Pelargus, imprimis vero Ægid. Hunnius in Calvino Judaizante, & Anti-Pareo, B. Gerhard. in hunc locum, nec non B. Helvicus in desiderio Matris Evæ, B. Glassius in Christol. Mosaïc. Disput. V. Dn. D. Waltherus, in offic. Bibl. observ. in Gen. XXI. Conferri etiam potest disput. nostra de fide Veterum in Christum §. 38. seqq. Sed Grotius applaudere maluit cœcis Judæis, & Socino, ac Vul- gatam Latinam, Græcamque versionem evidentiæ textus fontibusque ipsis anteponere.

Objectioni de errore, imo idololatria Evæ, si Cai- num credidit θεάνθρωπον alii occurrunt, quod non nisi in applicatione ad individuum hoc errarit; sed Dn. D. Seb. Schmidius disp. de Fid. matris Evæ A. 1667. Argentorati habita, ne hunc quidem errorem con- cedendum esse docuit, erudite ostendens, quomo- do fidem suam professa hîC Eva sit, non persuasa qui- dem, hunc primogenitum suum esse semen illud promis- sum, sed nomine filio huic suo imposito testata, se posse- disse per fidem virum istum, qui Jehovah sit, non quod filium suum primogenitum esse ipsum illum Messiam, quem adeo jam in carne præsentem foris possideret, ex- istimaret, sed quod eum in fide & intus possideret non- dum natum, suo autem tempore nascendum & manife- standum, cujus nihilo minus promissio vera fide ap- prehensa etiam ante adventum in carnem salvare homines posset: hac promissione sibi facta se magis gaudere, hoc viro Jehovah se magis exultare, quam masculo sibi recens nato, quanquam hoc quoque tanquam humani generis primogenito, non parum etiam lætari debeat, ut in hujus nomine monumen- tum fidei & gaudii sui extare in omnem posteritatē humanam velit. Acquisivi vel possedi potius Virum aliquem, qui Jehovah ipse est, in cujus honorem & æter- nam memoriam filium meum & humani generis primo- genitum Kain, hoc est, Jehovah est possessio mea, appel- latum volo. Quod illustrat nomine filii Mosis Eliezer, hoc est, DEUS est auxilium meum, quo non notatũ, quasi filius ipse DEUS sit auxilium suum, sed quod hoc monumentum fidei suæ in DEUM esse voluerit.

Elegans hæc explicatio ita uberius illustrari po- test, quod hoc nomine mnemonevtico filii primo- geniti testari voluerit Eva, se virum aliquem, qui Jehovah ipse est, ita possidere spiritualiter per fidem, & per spiritualem conceptionẽ per verbum Evangelii fa- ctā: quemadmodum hunc filium suum possedit corpora- liter, per conceptionem naturalem, eundemq́ habere pro possessione sua, omnibus thesauris & bonis mundi præ- stantyore, utpote in quo unice habeat possessionem omni- um bonorum spiritualium & cœlestium, & vitæ æternæ, ipsiusq́ Dei possessionem, & fruitionem æternam. Et confirmant hanc interpretationem 1. Verbi proprie- tas: quia קניתי proprie possessionem significat: etsi ad acquisitionem, quoad rei possessionem pervenitur, transferatur: & קניתי verbum præteriti temporis, non nunc demum, cum primogenitum concepit, se in- cipere possidere virum, sed jam pridem possedisse, inde sc. ab annunciato Prot-Evangelio, e quo eun- dem spiritualiter concepit Spiritus S. virtute, atque ita semper fideli animo, & corde possedit παμμή- της. Et magis sine dubio Messiam spiritualiter conceptum POSSESSIONEM suam habuit fide- lis Eva, quam primogenitum conceptum corpora- liter: quia illa possessio sempiterna erat, hæc tempo- raria: illa per se salutifera, hæc vero per se non erat salutifera, etiamsi primogenitus ille creditus fuisset ipse Messias. Tum utut mater aliqua de filio suo ita loqui possit, sicut sapientia Dei personalis alicubi ait, Dominus possedit me; in humano tamen stylo non ita vulgo proprie loqui solemus, quod humanæ possessiones in aliis potius, quam in filiis positæ sunt: possessio autem spiritualis & mystica est, qua fide habemus nobis Mes- siam, ita ut noster sit, & nos ipsius, atq; per ipsum sal- vemur, ut recte hic Dn. D. Schmidius. 2. No- minis איש emphasis & usus, quod VIRUM notat, nec de Christo infante, vel inde a conce- ptione, ac nativitate adhibetur uspiam: qui אִישׁ גִּבּוֹר quidem dicitur, non autem nomine איש vo- catur in corporali conceptione. At spirituali conce- ptione possideri a fidelibus Christum Redemto- rem ceu virum, qui Jehovah est, nullum est dubium. Urget Dominus D. Schmied, hic etiam, quod nomen hoc positum sine articulo sit, ac subjectum vagum no- tet: Possedi virum aliquem Jehovam; quæ locutio vaga non quadrat in primogenitum jam præsentem, & ob oculos positum: quod fassuros esse omnes, ait, qui genium linguæ norunt: Convenit autem optime professioni fidei circa ὀνομαθεσίαν Caini editæ: possedi virum aliquem excellentem, virum illum nem- pe qui est Jehovah. 3. Aliorum nominum compa- ratio. Nam quoties ratio τῆς ὀνομαθεσίας redditur, in qua nomen Deo proprium includitur, quod hîc fieri manifestum est, non illi, cui nomen imponitur, divinum istud nomen ἀκοινώνητον vindicatur, sed a- liqua de vero Deo professio solum fit, novello nomi- ne, ceu memoriali quodam succincte comprehensa, vel insinuata: aliter autem stylus formatur, cum ratio nominis ipsum natum concernit, & quod ejus est proprium, explicat: utpote cum Matth. 1, 21. dicitur: vocabis nomen ejus Jesum; ipse enim salvum faciet popu- lum suum a peccatis suis. 4. Præcedentis historiæ colla- tio. Denunciati erant Evæ dolores partus, quos sine dubio experta est, cum Cainum peperit: ejecta erat e Paradiso, exclusa ab arbore vitæ cum tota posteritate, & primogenito tamen suo, & totius humani generis hoc tam præclarum nomen tribuit: cujus ratio hæc redditur: Et, vel quia dixit: pro- fessa est: Possedi virum, qui est Jehovah, quem hunc ipsum ordinaria procreationis lege a se ab Ada- mo cognita conceptum, & cum doloribus edi- tum, primogenitum opinari non poterat, ab il- lo tamen, quem fide complexa erat, ac firmiter possidebat, denominatum volebat, ut semper memoria viri illius promissi, qui Jehovah est, contritoris capitis serpentini ob oculos versare- tur, quasi dicat, Genui quidem cum dolore filium meum, extorris e Paradiso, & exclusa ab arbore vitæ, sed quia e verbo Prot-Evangelii fide concepi, complexus sum, & possedi hactenus semen illud mulie- ris, quod contriturum est caput serpentis, ex progenie mea oriturum, plena sum gaudio spirituali, ceu ma- ter vivipara, felix & beata in hoc liberatore, non in- felix & maledicta, cujus liberi esse possunt per fidem in hunc Redemtorem vitæ æternæ hæredes. Illum ergo fide possedi jam pridem virum, qui Jehovah est, & adhuc eum possideo, atque habeo, tanquam meum peculium & bonum proprium, & cum illo omnes ha- beo thesauros, omnia bona: in eo lætor, & gaudeo unice, qui solus vera est mea possessio: ideo filii mei nomen esto Kain, in symbolum & memoriale, quod hic vir Jehova mea vera & æterna, atque unica sit possessio, quem dum habeo, nec cœlum, nec ter- ram, aut quicquid in cœlo vel terra est, præter ipsum expecto. Ps. 73, 25. Textus ostendit, inquit B. Lutherus noster, dictum Cain a verbo Kanah, quod significat pos- sidere, seu acquirere, ut hoc nomine se consoletur contra accepta mala, & opponat acquisitionem vitæ & salutis per semen amissioni vitæ & salutis per peccatum & Sa- tanam. Sed hæc de ista interpretatione, de qua o- mnino meretur legi laudata Dn. D. Schmidii dispu- tatio.

## 4:2
verf. 2. ABEL A SHEPHERD OF SHEEP AND CAIN A TILLER OF THE GROUND) Two most ancient kinds of life, as Dicaearchus notes in Porphyry's On Abstinence IV, and Servius at the beginning of Virgil.

Latin:

verf. 2. ABEL PASTOR OVIVM ET CAIN AGRI- COLA) Antiquissima duo vitæ genera, ut notat Dicæarchus apud Porphyrium de Abstinentia IV. & Servius initio ad Vir- gilium.

## 4:3
verf. 3. THAT CAIN MIGHT OFFER.) Not by any command of God, but by the dictate of reason that honor should also be rendered to God in a visible way, and that this could be done best by giving to God those things which are most dear to man. See the response to the Orthodox among the works of Justin CXIX, and what we have written in book V of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

These things are said according to the mind of certain Jews, to whom the Annotations on book V of the Truth of the Christian Religion appeal, and especially in favor of the Papists: who require an external sacrifice for religion, and therefore make it necessary while religion flourishes, and say that it is of the law of nature that God should be worshipped by some external sacrifice. See Bellarmine, lib. II. de Sacr. c. 31. Salmero, disput. IIX in 1. Tim. 2. Pererius in h. l. Their scope is to lay down the moral and perpetual observation of the Mass as a foundation. This opinion also gratifies the Socinians, who subscribe to the same, while they deny that the sacrifices looked toward Christ. But how would Abel's sacrifice have been pleasing to God, if it were offered without God's command, from a private intention, for which no will-worship is approved in Deut. 4, 2; Num. 15, 39; Isa. 29, 13? How can it be said to have been offered through faith, Heb. 11, 4, if he offered it without a divine mandate? For faith and the word of God are related. Faith is born not from the dictate of reason, but from the word, Rom. 10, 17. Nothing is certain to reason concerning sacrifices: we know by the light of reason that God must be worshipped, but reason is entirely ignorant that God must be worshipped through sacrifices. Sacrifices were instituted to foreshadow the one expiatory sacrifice, concerning which nothing is known outside of revelation. They depend, therefore, solely on the will of God, just as the true sacrifice of Christ, as an antitype, so also the typical and representative sacrifices. How, therefore, could they consist without divine revelation? If God can be served best by giving those things which are best to man, then the soul must be consecrated and offered to God. But how God is served by the offering of cattle or fruits, reason does not perceive; indeed, it considers it foolishness, because it finds no analogy between an immaterial God and corporeal things, nor is it able to grasp how the slaughter of victims can be pleasing to God. If God is a spirit, says Cato, as the songs tell us, He should be worshipped by you especially with a pure mind. Although it is certain by the natural knowledge of God that God must also be served by an external rite, yet the cult of sacrifices cannot be determined by nature: since nature rather dictates that God does not need such things: God is worshipped, says Seneca, not by the slaughter of the rich bodies of bulls, not by gold, not by silver, not by money poured into treasuries; but by a pious and upright will. Which Suarez acknowledged, part 3, sum. Thom. q. 83, art. 1, distinct. 71, sect. 8. There is no natural precept from which the determination of that mode of worship, namely, through sacrifice, can be sufficiently gathered for the honesty of morals. There is, therefore, no doubt that, just as the distinction between clean and unclean animals was made manifest by divine revelation before the flood, Gen. 7, 2, so also the doctrine of sacrifices was handed down to the Patriarchs. The Papists require for a sacrifice the destruction of the thing which is offered: but that is not accepted by God except as a sign and symbol; and consequently not without the intervention of the institution of positive law: since it is not a natural sign, but one by institution, when not even the thing signified depends on anything other than divine ordination and economy. Sacrifices were not always, nor do they have a place now, even though religion has always existed and will endure until the end of the age. The state of innocence had no sacrifices; they began only after the fall, and from the promulgation of the protoevangelium, concerning which the first parents undoubtedly instructed Cain and Abel. They ceased, however, after all things were consummated by the sacrifice of Christ, and the body being exhibited, the shadows and figures vanished; because sacrifices had to cease, according to Daniel's prophecy, chapter 9, 23, but religion must never cease. It is gathered to be of natural law, as Grotius teaches, l. I. de Jure Belli & Pacis c. 1. §. 10, that which is believed to be such among all more civilized nations. But did all more civilized nations sacrifice in the past, or do they still sacrifice? Natural law, according to the same, is so indubitable that it cannot be changed even by God. Therefore, sacrifices could not have been abrogated if they had been of natural law. Although it is not expressly mentioned when or how the rule of sacrifices was first handed down, there is no doubt that it was received from God, since it could not have been devised by human ingenuity, nor could it have pleased God if it had been devised. For it is impossible to please God without faith, Heb. 11, 6. Whence Nauclerus: It is believed, however, that Adam, who also flourished with the gift of prophecy, taught them to offer tithes and firstfruits to God, or sacrifices. It is the pious conjecture of some that God, when He prepared garments from skins for the first parents, taught them to sacrifice. Since it should not be thought that He was concerned only with the covering of the body, while neglecting the remedy of the soul, as blessed Gerhard speaks: and those slaughtered animals were a type of the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. For He was slain from the foundation of the world. Apoc. 13, 8. Compare Isa. 61, 10; Gal. 3, 27. What is usually brought forward from the writings of the Gentiles only proves among them some knowledge concerning sacrifices, it does not teach that it arose from the light of nature. However, it could have penetrated to them through tradition, or have proceeded from the suggestions of Satan, who is the ape of God's works, and a hinderer. Lyra confesses that Adam taught his sons to worship God through offerings.

Latin:

verf. 3. VT OFFERRET CAIN.) Non ullo Dei jussu, sed dictante ratione honorem Deo etiam conspicuum habendum, idque optime fieri posse, datis Deo iis, quæ homini sunt chariffi- ma. Vide responsum ad Orthodoxos inter Justini opera CXIX. & quæ nos ad lib. V. de Veritate Relig. Christianæ.

Hæc ad Judæorum quorundam mentem, ad quos provocat Annotat. ad lib. V. de Verit Relig. Christ. & imprimis in favorem Papistarum dicta: qui externum sacrificium ad religionem requirunt, ideòque id necessarium faciunt, dum religio viget, & de jure naturæ id esse dicunt, ut colatur DEUS externo aliquo sacrificio. Vid. Bellarmin. lib. II. de Sarc. c. 31. Salmero disput. IIX in 1. Tim. 2. Pereri- us in h. l. Scopus eorum est, ut moralem & perpe- tuam observationem Missæ pro fundamento sub- sternant. Gratificatur etiam hac opinione Soci- nianis eidem subscribentibus, dum Sacrificia Chri- stum respexisse, inficiantur. At quomodo DEO gratum fuisset Abelis sacrificium, si absque jussu DEI, ex privata intentione oblatum, cui nulla ἐθελοθρησκεία probatur Deut. 4, 2. Num. 15, 39. Esa. 29, 13.? Quomodo per fidem obtulisse dici po- test, Ebr. 11. 4. si absque DEI mandato obtulit? Fides enim & verbum DEI sunt relata. Non è dictamine rationis, sed e verbo fides nascitur Rom. 10, 17. Rationi nihil constat de sacrificiis : colen- dum esse DEUM, rationis luce novimus, sed per sacrificia DEUM colendum esse, ignorat prorsùs ratio. Instituta sunt sacrificia ob unicum sacrifici- um expiatorium adumbrandum, de quo extra re- velationem nihil constat. Dependent ergo unice a DEI voluntate, uti sacrificium Christi verum, ceu ἀντίτυπον, ita etiam sacrificia typica & repræsentati- va. Qui itaque absque revelatione divina consta- rent? Si DEO optime serviri potest, datis etiam il- lis, quæ homini sunt optima, DEO ergo consecran- dus & offerendus est animus. Quomodo autem DEO serviatur oblatione pecudum aut frugum, id ratio non percipit, imo pro stultitia habet; quia nullam analogiam invenit inter Deum immateria- lem & res corporeas, neq; quomodo victimarum ma- ctatio DEO grata esse possit, assequi valet. Si DEUS est animus, inquit Cato, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic tibi præcipue pura sit mente colendus. Etsi autem co- gnitione DEI naturali constet, externo etiam ritu DEO serviendum esse, non tamen determinate cultus sacrificiorum per naturam constare potest: quum natura potius dictet, DEUM talibus non in- digere: Colitur Deus, inquit Seneca, non taurorum opimis corporibus contrucidatis, non auro, non argento, non in thesauros stipe infusa; sed pia & recta voluntate. Quod agnovit Schvarez part. 3. sum. Thom. q. 83. artie. 1. distinct. 71. sect. 8. Nullum est naturale præ- ceptum, ex quo sufficienter colligi possit determinatio il- lius ad talem modum cultus sc. per sacrificationem ad morum honestatem. Nullum itaque dubium, uti discrimen mundo- rum & immundorum animalium e revelatione divi- na patefactum fuit ante diluvium Gen. 7, 2. sic etiam sacrificiorum doctrinam Patriarchis traditam fuis- se. Requirunt ad sacrificium Papistae destructionem ejus rei, quae offertur: at ea non est accepta DEO, nisi tanquam signum atque Symbolum; ac proinde non nisi interveniente institutione legis positivae: siqui- dem non sit signumaliquod naturale, sed ex instituto, quum ne quidem res signata aliunde, quam ab or- dinatione dependeat & οἰκονομίᾳ divina. Non fue- runt semper sacrificia, nec amplius nunc locum ha- bent, etsi semper fuerit religio, atq; duratura sit usque ad consummationem seculi. Status inno- centiae nulla habuit sacrificia; cepere demum post lapsum, & a promulgatione πρωτευαγγελίε, de quo instituere sine dubio Protoplasti Cainum & A- belem. Desiere autem postquam omnia Christi sacrificio consummata, & corpore exhibito umbrae ac figurae evanuere; quia sacrificia cessare debuere, juxta Danielis vaticinium cap. 9, 23. religio autem cessare nunquam debet. Juris naturalis, docente Grot. l. I. de JureBelli & Pacis c. 1. §. 10. esse colligitur id, quod omnes apud gentes moratiores tale esse creditur. Num autem gentes moratiores omnes sacrificarunt olim, aut etiamnum sacrificant? Jus naturale, juxta eundem, adeo est indubitat o, ut ne a Deo quidem mu- tari queat. Non ergo abrogari potuissent sacrifi- cia, si juris naturalis fuissent. Quamvis vero non commemoretur expresse, quando, aut quomodo tradita primum fuerit sacrificiorum regula, non ta- men dubium est, a Deo eandem acceptam esse, quu humano ingenio excogitari nequiverit, neque ex- cogitata Deo placere potuerit. Impossibile enim est, DEO sine fide placere Ebr. 11, 6. Unde Nauclerus: Creditur autem Adam, qui & Prophetiae dono florebat, docuisse decimas & primitias offerre Deo, vel sacrificia. Pia quorundam est conjectura, DEUM, quando ex pellibus primis Parentibus vestes paravit, sacri- ficare eos docuisse. Siquidem cogitandum non sit, quod de corporis duntaxat tegumento solicitus fue- rit, neglecto animae remedio, uti B. Gerhardus loqui- tur: ac mactata illa animantia typus fuerint agni Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Hic enim occisus est inde ab origine mundi. Apoc. 13, 8. Conferatur Es. 61, 10. Gal. 3, 27. Quae adduci solent e gentilium scriptis, apud eos solum aliquam de sacrificiis notitiam e- vincunt, ex lumine naturae eam enatam non docent. Potuit autem ea per traditionem ad ipsos penetras- se, aut e Satanae, qui operum Dei simia est, & empe- cta, suggestionibus profecta esse. Fatetur Lyra, Ada- mum docuisse filios, colere Deum per oblationes.

## 4:4
verse same. HE OFFERED OF THE FIRSTLINGS OF HIS FLOCK, AND OF THE FAT THEREOF.) Since nothing is accustomed to be consecrated to GOD, except what is in use by men, but to eat of living creatures before the flood, as the more probable opinion holds, was not permitted, it could be said that wool and the richest milk were offered, which is called חלב here. For the LXX translated חלב by γάλα. Gen. 18, 8. 49, 12. Exod. 3, 8. 17. 23, 19. Lev. 20, 24. Num. 13, 28. 14, 8. Deut. 6, 3. 14, 21. 26, 9. 15. 27. 31, 20. 32, 14. & often in other books. Porphyry teaches from many histories that it was a very ancient custom to offer wool and milk. You have [evidence] about milk in Virgil: about wool there is a passage of Sophocles in Polyidus: Ἡι μὲν γὰρ διὸς μαλλὸς, ἦν δὲ κ᾿ ἀμπέλων Σπονδή τε καὶ ῥὰξ εὖ τεθησαυρισμένη. Pausanias concerning the Phygalian Ceres: Ἔθυσαν τῷ Θεῷ κᾀμ κατ᾿ οἱ ἐπι- χώριοι νομίζωσιν ὀδὲν. Plato has something similar in Book VI of the Laws, θύματα δὲ ἐκ ἦν τῆς θεοῖσι ζῶα, πέλανοι δὲ καὶ μέλιτι καρποὶ δε- δευμένοι, καὶ τοιαῦτα ἄλλα ἁγνὰ θύματα. Empedocles concerning the most ancient times: Ταύρων δὲ ἀκρίτοισι φόνοις ἐ δεύεθο βωμός; But let it be permitted to interpret the firstborn, which are spoken of here from the Hebrew בכור, as those things which were of extraordinary magnitude and form. Thus בכור מות is a most lethal disease, בכורים a most fruitful fig tree, בכרה a most swift camel. These things indeed can be said not implausibly: But the Talmudists think that in those very first times, before men ate flesh, burnt offerings were in use, from which nothing came to men, and through which GOD, the Lord of all things and of life and death, was acknowledged: Therefore, even after the law, they accepted victims from uncircumcised foreigners only for burnt offerings, not for other sacred rites instituted by the law.

Nothing could be brought forward here by which it might be taught that it was customary among the people of GOD to offer milk and wool. He only adopts Gentiles as a support, but who does not know that their customs were often most alien to divine institutions? And shall we elicit the meaning of Moses, who describes the first worship of the world, from Porphyry, Virgil, Sophocles, Pausanias, or Empedocles? This method of interpreting is as new as the interpretation and Gloss is peculiar to Grotius. Certainly, it never came into the mind of any of the Christian Doctors that Abel did not offer animals, but milk and wool. But, what is most important, the words of Moses do not bear that gloss. For he says that Abel offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. Moreover, to offer from the firstborn of the flock is to offer the firstborn of the flock. Furthermore, חלבהן denotes their fat, from חלב, which Grotius wrongly confuses with חלב, milk. For this lacks a plural. And it should have been said חלבן for their milk. Nor do those passages from the LXX Interpreters, which he brought forward, in which, to wit, γάλα is found, make to the point: for in those occurs חלב, which no one denies signifies milk, not חלב, for which no example could be brought forward where it occurs with the meaning of milk. But what Grotius adds, that the firstborn, which are spoken of here, can be explained from the Hebrew בכור as those things which were of extraordinary magnitude and form: such as בכור מות, a most lethal disease, בכורים, a most fruitful fig tree, בכרה, a most swift camel, this, not to mention anything about the examples, is plainly inappropriate in this place. For Moses describes in a simple historical style what he offered from the firstborn of the flock. If, therefore, he had spoken of the most excellent wool of sheep of extraordinary magnitude and form, he ought to have expressed it more clearly. And what does their extraordinary magnitude have to do with the offering of wool and milk, about which Grotius dreams there is a discussion? But because he finally concedes to the opinion of the Talmudists concerning burnt offerings in the first world, he cuts his own vines at the same time. For before that, nothing was consecrated to GOD except what had been in the use of men. Therefore, those things which were consecrated and offered to GOD by the first men from cattle and clean animals must also have been in the use of men before the flood. Which was denied by him himself.

Grotius therefore wrongly takes these things to be about wool and very rich milk. The text explicitly says that he offered from the FIRSTBORN of the flock and from their fat. Therefore, the fat is not to be separated from the firstborn of the cattle, as if he offered only the fat, but, as Mercerus warned, the name of the fats is to be referred to the animals, so that the fattest and best are understood to have been offered: since it is probable that this sacrifice of Abel, who by faith offered πλείονα θυσίαν, a more abundant sacrifice (the Greek word has its name from slaughtering, and is used of the sacrifice of Christ, Eph. 5:2, Heb. 9:26, 10:12), Heb. 11:4, was a propitiatory sacrifice, which primarily looked to the sacrifice of Christ. The argument of Grotius, that nothing is accustomed to be consecrated to God unless it is in the use of men, and that it was not permitted to eat animals before the flood, totters on both legs. For whence will he prove this or that? Neither fat nor blood was in the use of sacred rites among the Jews

Lev. 7:17, which nevertheless had to be offered to GOD in sacrifices. But then, indeed, the distinction between clean and unclean animals existed before the flood, as can be seen from Gen. 7. And Grotius himself also observes that the Talmudists think that in those very first times burnt offerings were in use, from which nothing came to men, and through which GOD, the Lord of all things and of life and death, is acknowledged.

vers. 4. THE LORD HAD REGARD) Theodotion ἐνεπύρισεν, that is, he consumed the offerings with fire sent from heaven, and thus proved them to be pleasing to himself. A certainly probable interpretation, which also pleased Julian. Compare the history in Lev. 9:24, Jud. 6:21, 1 Kings 18:38, 2 Chron. 7:1. Servius on the 12th Aeneid: Among the ancients, altars were not kindled, but they elicited divine fire with prayers, which kindled the altars. The writer to the Hebrews 11:4, μαρτυρῦντος ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις ἀυτῦ τῦ Θεῦ.

This is also observed in the sacrifice of Abraham, Gen. 15:16, where a lamp of fire passed between the divisions: and 1 Chron. 21:26, when GOD is said to have heard David from heaven through fire: and it is likely that Nehemiah, when sacrificing at the dedication of the second temple, similarly had fire descend from heaven, which the author of 2 Maccabees 1 invented was produced from water. Which is the reason why they had to preserve the fire sent down from heaven for the uses of sacrifices, lest it be offered with strange fire, Lev. 10:1, which Buxtorf in his history of sacred fire, ch. 1, Exercit. p. 228, proves had to be fostered perpetually by the care of the priests by adding natural fire. Whence I might not undeservedly say that the fire which descended upon Abel's sacrifice was preserved to kindle the primeval sacrifices thereafter. Moreover, the sacrifices were not to be kindled by any other than heavenly fire, so that they might foreshadow the sacrifice of Christ, which was to be kindled by the heavenly fire of divine wrath and justice. Not only Christian interpreters, Jerome, Procopius, Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, but also the Hebrews agree in this sign of inflammation, as noted by Buxtorf in the place cited.

Latin:

vers. eod. OBTULIT DE PRIMOGENITIS GREGIS SUI, ET DE ADIPIBUS EORUM.) Cum DEO nihil sacra- ri soleat, nisi quod in usu sit hominum, animantibus autem vesci ante diluvium, ut probabilior fert sententia, permissum non fuerit, dici posset, oblatam lanam & lac pinguissimum, quod hic חלב vocetur Namחלב per γάλα transtulereLXX. Gen. 18, 8. 49, 12. Exod. 3, 8. 17. 23, 19. Lev. 20, 24. Num. 13,28. 14,8. Deut. 6,3. 14,21. 26, 9.15. 27. 31, 20. 32, 14. & in aliis libris saepe. Vetustissimum autem morem fuisse lanam & lac offe- rendi, ex multis historiis docet Porphyrius. De lacte habes a- pud Virgilium: de lana locus est Sophoclis Polyido: Ἡι μὲν γὰρ διὸς μαλλὸς, ἦν δὲ κ᾿ ἀμπέλων Σπονδή τε καὶ ῥὰξ εὖ τεθησαυρισμένη. Pausanias de Cerere Phygaliensi: Ἔθυσαν τῷ Θεῷ κᾀμ κατ᾿ οἱ ἐπι- χώριοι νομίζωσιν ὀδὲν. Simile quid habet Plato VI. de legibus, θύματα δὲ ἐκ ἦν τῆς θεοῖσι ζῶα, πέλανοι δὲ καὶ μέλιτι καρποὶ δε- δευμένοι, καὶ τοιαῦτα ἄλλα ἁγνὰ θύματα. Empedocles de tempo- ribus antiquissimis: Ταύρων δὲ ἀκρίτοισι φόνοις ἐ δεύεθο βωμός; Primogenita autem quæ hic dicuntur ex Hebræo בכור liceat interpretari ea, quæ eximiæ erant magnitudinis ac formæ. Sic בכור מות morbus maxime lethalis, בכורים fi- cus maxime fructifera, בכרה camelus velociffimus. Hæc quidem sic non improbabiliter dici possunt: At Thalmudistæ omnino illis primis temporibus, antequam carnibus homines vescerentur, holocaufta in usu fuisse putant, unde nihil ad ho- mines pervenerit, & per quæ DEVS rerum omnium vitæque ac necis Dominus agnosceretur: Itaque & post legem ab alieni- genis incircumcisis victimas ad holocausta tantum accipie- bant, non ad sacra alia per legem instituta.

Nihil hic proferri potuit, quo doceretur apud populum DEI lac & lanam offerri consvevisse. Gen- tiles solum in subsidium adsciscit, sed quis nescit ho- rum consuetudines sæpe alienissimas ab institutis divinis fuisse? Et num Mosis primos cultus mundi describentis sensum e Porphyrio, Virgilio, Sophocle, Pausania, Empedocle eruemus? Nova hæc ut inter- pretandi ratio, ita interpretatio & Glossa est Grotio propria. Nemini certe Dd. Christianorum un- quam in mentem venit, Abel non animalia obtulis- se, sed lac & lanam. Sed, quod præcipuum est, non ferunt verba Mosis istam glossam. Obtulisse enim dicit Abelem de primogenitis gregis sui & de adipibus eorum. Offerre autem de primogenitis gregis est primogenita gregis offerre. Porro חלבהן adipes eo- rum notat, a חלב quod perperam confundit Gro- tius cum חלב lac. Hoc enim plurali caret. Et lac earum dicendum fuisset חלבן. Neq; loca illa ad rem faciunt, quæ e LXX. Interpretibus adduxit, qui- bus scil. γάλα habetur: nam in istis occurrit חלב quod lac significare nemo negat, non חלב, de quo nullum exemplum adduci potuit, quod lactis signi- ficatione occurrat. Quod autem addit Grotius, pri- mogenita, quæ hic dicuntur, ex Hebræo בכור posse explicari ea, quæ eximiæ magnitudinis ac formæ fue- rint: ut בכור מות, morbo maxime lethalis, בכורים ficus maxime fructifera, בכרה Camelus velocissimq, id, ne de exemplis quicquam dicam, hoc loco plane inconveniens est. Nam describit Moses simplici historico stylo, quod de primogenitis gregis obtule- rit. Si ergo de præstantissima lana ovium eximiæ magnitudinis ac formæ loquutus esset, clarius ex- primere id debuisset. Et quid eximia magnitudo earum ad lanæ & lactis oblationem, de qua sermo- nem esse somniat Grotius? Sed quia concedit tan- dem in Thalmudistarum sententiam de oblatis in pri- mo mundo holocaustis, propria simul vineta cædit. Nam antea DEO nihil sacratum fuit, nisi quod in usu hominum fuerit. Illa ergo quæ de pecoribus, & mundis animantibus ab hominibus primis DEO sa- crata & oblata sunt, ante diluvium oportet etiam in usu hominum tum fuisse. Quod ab ipso negatum fuit.

Perperam ergo hæc accipit Grotius de lana & lacte pinguissimo. Textus diserte de PRIMOGENITIS gregis & de a- dipibus eum obtulisse dicit. Non ergo separandus adeps a pecudum primogenitis, quasi solum adipem obtulerit, sed, uti Mercerus monuit, adipum nomen ad animalia referendum, ut pinguissima & optima oblata intelligantur: quum probabile sit, sacrifici- um hoc Abelis, qui fide πλείονα θυσίαν plurimam hostiam (vox Græca a mactatione nomen habet, & de sacrificio Christi adhibetur Eph. 5, 2. Ebr. 9, 26. 10, 12.) obtulit Ebr. 11, 4. fuisse sacrificium propitiatori- um, quæ imprimis respexerunt sacrificium Christi. Argumentum Grotii, quod nihil Deo sacrari soleat, nisi quod in usu sit hominum, quodq́; animantibus vesci an- te diluvium permissum non fuerit, utroq; crure vacil- lat. Unde enim hoc vel illud probabit? Neq; adeps, neque sanguis in usu sacrorum fuit apud Judæos os

Lev. 7,17. quæ tamen offerri DEO debebant in sa- crificiis. Tum vero viguisse ante diluvium discri- men animalium mundorum &immundorum eGen. VII, videre est. Et observat quoque ipse Grotius, Thalmudistas omnino primis illis temporibus holocau- sta in usu fuisse putare, unde nihil ad homines pervenit, & per quæ DEUS,rerum omnium vitæque ac necis Do- minus, agnoscatur.

vers. 4. RESPEXIT DOMINVS) Theodotion ἐνεπύρισεν, id est, igne de cœlo immisso oblata consumpsit, ac sic grata si- bi esse probavit. Probabilis sane interpretatio, quæ & Julia- no placuit. Confer historiam Lev. 9,24. Jud. 6,21. 1. Reg. 18,38. 2. Paral. 7,1. Servius ad XII. Æneidos: Apud majores aræ non incendebantur,sed ignem divinum precibus eliciebant, qui incen- debat altaria. Scriptor ad Hebræos 11, 4. μαρτυρῦντος ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις ἀυτῦ τῦ Θεῦ.

Observatur id etiam in sacrificio Abrahæ Gen. 15, 16. Ubi lampas ignis transiit inter divisiones : & 1. Chron. 21, 26. cum DEUS de cœlo per ignem Davi- dem exaudiisse dicitur : ac verisimile est, Nehemia in secundi templi dedicatione sacrificante similiter ignem de cœlo dalapsum esse , quem ex aqua productum auctor 2. Maccab. 1. commentus est. Quæcausa est, cur ignem cœlitus demissum as- servare debuerint ad usus sacrificiorum, ne alieno i- gne offerretur Lev. 10,1. quem perpetuo cura sacer- dotum suffecto igne naturali fovendum fuisse Bux- torf. in histor. ignis sacri cap. 1. Exercit. p. 228. pro- bat. Unde non immerito dixerim, ignem super A- belis sacrificium delapsum asservatum fuisse ad pri- mæva sacrificia deinceps accendenda. Non erant autem alio, quam cœlesti igne accendenda sacrifi- cia, ut adumbrarent sacrificium Christi, quod igne cœlesti iræ ac justitiæ divinæ incendendum fuit. Consentiunt in hoc signo inflammationis non tan- tum Christiani Interpp. Hieronymus, Procopius, Cy- rillus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, sed etiam Ebræi, ut notatum Buxtorfio loc. cit.

## 4:5
vers. 5. HIS COUNTENANCE FELL) A sign of shame, to which is opposed below in verse 7, שְׂאֵת, a countenance lifted up, a sign of a good conscience. vers. 7. THOU SHALT RECEIVE) In the Hebrew שְׂאֵת, but that can signify erection no less than reception, and it easily admits the meaning which we have already stated.

Others prefer the meaning of acceptance, in this way: There will be acceptance for you, that is, you will be received into favor. We approve, however, of that meaning of lifting up, but so that the whole sentence may be skillfully explained, the sense of which is this: If you do well, that is, if having done penance you have believed in the seed of the woman, for this is the work which is required of us, John 6:29. Therefore others from Heb. 11:4 so explain it, if by faith you have offered a sacrifice, because no one can do well unless he who believes in the Messiah, Heb. 11:6. There will be שְׂאֵת to lift, or the lifting of the face, that is, you will be able to lift up your face, about to have a cheerful and good conscience, there will be no need for your face to fall. Whence the word face is to be repeated here ἀπὸ κοινῦ; and thus the opposition will be consistent, for the promise and the threat, being opposed, mutually illustrate each other. Which sense a similar passage confirms, Job 11:15.

Latin:

vers. 5. CONCIDIT VVLTVs EJVS ) Signum pudoris, cui opponitur infra 7. שְׂאֵת vultus erectus bonæ consci- entiæ signum. vers. 7. RECIPIES ) In Hebræo שְׂאֵת id autem non minus erectionem, quam acceptionem significare potest, & sensum, quem jam diximus, facile admittit.

Alii malunt acceptionis significatum, hoc mo- do : Erit tibi acceptio, id est, recipieris in gratiam. Probamus tamen illam erectionis significationem, sed ut dextre tota sententia explicetur, cujus hic est sensus; Si bene feceris, id est, si pœnitentia acta in semen mulieris credideris, hoc enim est opus, quod a nobis requiritur, Joh. 6, 29. ideo alii ex Ebr. 2, 4. ita expli- cant, si fide obtuleris sacrificium, quia nemo potest bene agere, nisi qui in Messiam credat Ebr. 2, 6. E- rit שְׂאֵת levare, vel levatio faciei, id est, elevare fa- ciem poteris, hilarem bonamque conscientiam ha- biturus, non opus erit, ut concidat facies tua. Unde ἀπὸ κοινῦ faciei vox hic repetenda; atque ita con- gruet oppositio, promissio enim & comminatio op- posita mutuo se illustrant. Quem sensum confirmat locus similis Job. 2, 15.

## 4:7
verse of the same. SIN WILL BE PRESENT IMMEDIATELY AT THE DOOR.) Punishment presses upon guilt as a companion, says Horace. For it is frequent for the Hebrews to signify punishment by the name of sin metonymically. The Greeks read these Hebrew words far differently: if you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? be quiet; which interpretation Julian also follows, except that for you have sinned he recites sin in the same sense. They seem, however, to have perceived that things were indeed offered by Cain which it was right to offer, but not the best of their kind, or at least less than a tenth, which was God's portion from the most ancient centuries, below 14:20, 28:22. Traces remain also in Greek and Latin histories everywhere.

Grotius understands it metonymically concerning punishment. So also Cornelius a Lapide and, among the Calvinists, Toussain, Piscator, Rivetus, and others. Both Targums, the Onkelos and the Jerusalem, interpret it concerning the day of the final judgment. But it is not necessary to depart from the literal meaning of the word, since it can be understood of sin itself, which may lie quiet for some time, but with a wakeful conscience, it stirs up incredible barking and anguish, like a dog that sleeps before flowers and is easily awakened by the noise of a door. Just as in the other member, 'If you do well, will there not be an elevation for you,' or 'you will lift up your face,' a cheerful conscience is designated: Job 11:14-15. 'If you put away the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent, then you will be able to lift up your face without spot, and you will be stable, and you will not fear.' That fits the text best. For the opposite preceded it before: 'Why has your countenance fallen?' Therefore the word פנים must be repeated from there. Grotius notes here that the version of the LXX Interpreters was approved by Julian, but he does not disapprove of it, as was proper, and as was done ingenuously by Sixtus of Siena, Bibl. Annot. l. VI, 15. The LXX Interpreters confused everything and deviated vehemently from the truth of the Hebrew text. Grotius says they read the Hebrew far otherwise, but by what sign, or at least by what obscure indication, can this be taught? For they wander as far as heaven from the Hebrew text: ὀυκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἤμαρτες; ἡσύχα- ζον. 'If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be quiet.' What agreement does this have with the Hebrew letter? Therefore Steuchus preferred to acknowledge that it is detected from this place that the LXX were not so exquisitely skilled in Hebrew grammar. Louis Cappel, although he values the interpretation of the Seventy very highly, and all but prefers it to our Hebrew codex, nevertheless confesses that it is seen everywhere in that translation that those men very often changed the gender, number, state, tense, mood, conjugation, and person of words, almost at will, so that they might carve out some convenient sense (as it seemed to them) in those places in which otherwise a suitable and appropriate sense did not seem to them to be able to be elicited. It is clearly evident how great a loss the ignorance of the sacred language is, by the example of the Ancients, to whom this perverse version fixed a cross, as Augustine notes, De C. D. l. XV. The LXX Interpreters seem to some, and to Grotius, to have sensed that things were indeed offered by Cain which it was lawful to offer, but not the best of their kind, or certainly less than a tenth: But the Apostle teaches that Abel offered a greater (literally: more) sacrifice, because he offered by faith. The excellence, therefore, is to be understood not so much by reason of the material or by reason of the quantity, as by reason of the mind of the offerer and of faith: although it pleases our blessed Gerhard not improbably that, by divine institution, sacrifices of the firstlings of the cattle ought to have been offered, which most especially looked to the expiatory sacrifice of the Messiah, but that Cain offered fruits from his own will-worship, which also could not be done from faith, as it is that which relies solely on the word of God. How Abel was a type of Christ, Walther teaches in Officin. p. 685, and Irenaeus led the way, lib. 4, c. 67. 'The passion of the just one from the beginning prefigured in Abel, etc.' Add also Cyprian, sermon 6, on the Lord's Prayer. But the sacrifice of Abel was primarily typical. (1) Because sacrifices were generally figures of Christ. (2) Because through this sacrifice Abel was declared righteous, Heb. 11:4. Whence, however, was his sacrifice expiatory if not by the virtue of the Antitype, 1 John 2:2. (3) Because Abel offered by faith, Heb. 11:4. But the faith of Abel, as also of the other martyrs recounted by the Apostle, looked to Christ and his cross and death, Heb. 12:1. (4) Add that the word θυσίας implies slaughter and the shedding of blood, and is applied to the sacrifice of Christ slain for us, Apoc.

13:8, Eph. 5:2, Heb. 9:25, as also the word προσήνεγκε, 1 Pet. 2:24, Heb. 7:27, ch. 9:25, 28. By which words, therefore, the Apostle described the Levitical sacrifices as types of Christ, and so also wished to describe this sacrifice of Abel, Heb. 11:4. (5) And what else does that continuous act of the speech of Abel's blood teach, than that it testifies to the sacrifice of Christ, as a certain illustrious figure, since Abel is placed in the first position in the cloud of witnesses, and is indicated to have testified through faith when he offered a sacrifice to GOD. It is also said to speak to us, dead through the faith which is required of us in Christ, that it may still speak, so that we may imitate it, and by its example not hesitate to shed our blood for it as well. Conf. B. Glassius, Thes. 27, Disput. V, Christol. Mos. vers. 7.

same verse. BUT ITS APPETITE WILL BE UNDER YOU, AND YOU WILL RULE OVER IT.] It must be repeated from what preceded, 'if you do well,' so that the sense is: if you do well, Abel's will will be subject to your authority, as that of a younger brother. Thus those words: 'But if not, sin will immediately be present at the door': the words will be parenthetical, such as also occur often in these books. See Exod. 39:29 and Num. 4:7, Ps. 99:6-7. For firstborns, through the death of the father or the father's absence, had in a certain way authority over their brothers: But this right could be lost by sin, as appears below 49:3-4, 1 Chron. 5:1. Add 1 Kings 1:25 and following.

Grotius wished here to follow the Rabbis and the LXX Interpreters. It is not surprising that Chrysostom, Hom. XVIII in Gen. lib. XI against the Jews, follows them; because he had only the Greek text at hand, which explicitly refers these things to the brother. To which, however, Calvin, Toussain, Chamier, and Rivetus also rise here; and also from our own, Mr. Johann Tarnovius in Exercit. Bibl. p. 106. But Grotius saw well that that sense does not fit, unless a parenthesis is posited. But parentheses are not to be invented at will in the sacred text. Nor is the opposite member accustomed to be read in a parenthesis, when the other member is constituted outside the same, which is the case here. And how can these pronouns be referred to the brother Abel, of whom no mention had been made in this whole speech of GOD? What is this to the purpose of GOD, who is dissuading from fratricide, that the primogeniture of Cain should be extolled, by which his pride would have been increased rather than depressed? But if the pronouns are referred to the preceding noun, as is proper, just as the former ones in the speech of GOD contained both rebuke and instruction, so that from the former contrition might be excited in Cain, and through the latter faith; so these present an exhortation, that it may leave no place for appetite or depraved concupiscence, but that he may master it. The appetite of sin is toward Thee, that is, sin clings to your members, and will continually tempt you with its concupiscences, but Thou shalt master it, that is, you shall curb its untamed impulses, as our blessed Rungius interprets: Toward you, says Augustine, book XV de C. D. ch. 7, is the turning. Is it of the brother? Far be it. Of whom then, if not of sin? For GOD forbids that sin should reign in our mortal body, that we should obey it in its concupiscences. Rom. VI. But then, as Augustine further holds, everyone will master sin, if he has not proposed to himself to defend it, but has subjected it by repenting; otherwise he will also serve it as master, if he has applied patronage to it as it approaches.

The Papists will find nothing here for the freedom of the will in spiritual matters, to add this ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ. For if we can abstain from external crimes, shall we immediately have internal concupiscences in our power? For the noun תשוקה denotes an internal affection, but one which boils up like boiling water and erupts into an external act. Although in the Hebrew text it is not read SUB TE: or as Romeus corrupts it, SUBTER TE, but AD TE, and it is not the subjection of appetite that is designated here, but its boiling up: the appetite is AD TE, before Thee, or over Thee. That it may desire to prevail, but Cain ought to dominate it: so that when the vehemence of sin seething in Cain is insinuated, then dominion over those perverse concupiscences is commanded to him. Grotius therefore wrongly follows the Vulgate version here, its appetite shall be under thee, that is, Abel's will shall be SUBJECT to thy command. Therefore it is better, with the Jerusalem Targum, Augustine, Author of the book on the calling of the Gentiles, ch. 4, Gregory the Great, Morals IV, ch. 12, Eucherius, Bede, Ambrose, bk. 2 on Cain, ch. 6, Jerome in Hebrew Questions, Bede, Rupert, Ordinary Gloss. and the interlinear, Mercer, Gesner, Rungius, B. Gerhard, and others to understand these things of sin, even though the affixes are not of the feminine gender; because an enallage of genders is not infrequent among the Hebrews; as in Ruth 1:7, Esther 1:20, Ecclesiastes 12:5, and in this place, in the verse immediately preceding; although some think that the noun חטאת is common in meaning, because it is found in the plural with a masculine termination just as well as a feminine; Ecclesiastes 10:4, Psalm 103:10, Jeremiah 5:15. But Chamier, Vol. III, Panstrat. bk. III, ch. XIII, and Rivetus in this place oppose this interpretation in vain, whose arguments can easily be resolved from those things which we have now observed.

Latin:

vers. eod. STATIM IN FORIBVS PECCATVM ADE- RIT.) Culpam pœna premit comes, ait Horatius. Nam peccati nomine μετωνυμικῶς pœnam significare frequens Hebræis. Longe aliter Hebræa hæc legere Græci : ὐκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγ- κῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες ; ἡσύχασον ; quam interpreta- tionem sequitur & Julianus, nisi quod pro ἥμαρτες recitat ἁμάρτημα sensu eodem. Sensisse autem videntur illi, oblata quidem a Caino, quæ fas erat offerri, sed non sui generis opti- ma, aut certe minus decima, quæ ab antiquissimis seculis DEI portio, infra 14, 20, 28, 22. Vestigia manent etiam in Græcis, La- tinisque historiis passim.

De pœna intelligit μετωνυμικῶς Grotius. Ita etiam Cornelius a Lapide & e Calvinianis Toffanus, Piscator, Rivetus, alii. Targum utrumque, Onckel. & Hierosolymit. de die judicii extremi interpretantur. Sed non est necessum a proprietate difcedere vo- cis, quum de peccato ipso, quod aliquandiu qui- escat, sed conscientia vigilante, latratus & ango- res incredibiles excitat, instar canis, qui ante flo- res dormit, ac strepitu januæ facile excitatur, ac- cipi possit. Quemadmodum in altero membro, Nonne si bene feceris, elevatio erit tibi, vel elevabis faciem tuam, hilaris conscientia designatur: Job. 11, 14. 15. Si iniquitatem, quæ est in manu tua, abstu- leris a te, & non manserit in tabernaculo tuo injustitia, tunc levare poteris faciem tuam absque macula, & eris stabilis, & non timebis. Id optime convenit textui. Præcedebat enim antea oppositum: Cur concidit vultus tuus? Itaque inde repeti debet vox פנים. Notat Grotius hic LXX. Interpp. versionem Juliano approbatam, non autem improbat eam, uti par erat, & a Sixto Senensi factum est ingenue l. VI. Biblic. annot. 15. LXX. Interpretes omnia perturbarunt, de- viaruntque vehementer a veritate textus Ebraici. Lon- ge aliter eos legisse Hebræa, ait Grotius, sed quo vel obscuro saltem indicio doceri hoc potest? Toto enim cœlo exerrant ab Ebræo rextu: ὀυκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἤμαρτες; ἡσύχα- ζον. Nonne si recte obtuleris, non autem recte diviseris, peccasti? quiesce.
