Quæ hic cum Ebræa litera conve- nientia. Ideo agnoscere maluit Steuchus, ex hoc loco deprehendi, non adeo exquisite LXX. Grammaticam Hebraicam calluisse. Ludovicus Capellus etsi maxi- mi faciat interpretationem τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα, eamque tantum non præferat nostro Ebræo codici, fatetur tamen passim in illa translatione conspici, quod nimi- rum illi homines vocum genus, numerum, statum, tem- pus, modum, conjugationem & personam sæpissime immutarint, pene pro arbitrio, ut sensum aliquem (uti ipsis videbatur) commodum exsculperent iis in locis, in quibus alioqui sensus non videbatur ipsis elici posse aptus & accommodatus. Patet sane, quanto damno sit ignorantia linguæ sacræ, exemplo Ve- terum, quibus hic versio perversa crucem fixit, notante August. l. XV. de C. D. Sensisse nonnullis & Grotio videntur LXX. Interpp. Oblata quidem a Caino, quæ fas erat offerri, sed non sui generis optima, aut certe minus decima: Sed Apostolus Abelem πλείονα θυσίαν plurimam (ad verbum) hostiam ob- tulisse docet, quia fide obtulit. Præstantia itaque non tam ratione materiæ, aut ratione quantitatis in- telligenda, quam ratione animi offerentis & fidei: quamvis B. Gerhardonoftro haud improbabiliter placeat, ex institutione divina offerri debuisse sacrificia de primogenitis pecudum, quæ ἱλαστικὸν sacrificium Messiæ maxime respiciebant, Cainum autem e propria ᾽θελοθρησκεία obtulisse fruges, quod etiam fieri non potuit ex fide, utpote, quæ solo Dei verbo nititur. Quomodo Abel typus Christi fuerit, docet Walther. in officin. p. 685. ac præivit Irenæus lib. 4. c. 67. Pas- sio justi ab initio præfigurata in Abel &c. Adde & Cy- prianum serm. 6. de orat. Domin. Sacrificium autem Abelis imprimis typicum fuit. (1.) Quia Sacrificia communiter fuere figuræ Christi. (2. Quia per sacrificium hoc Abel justus declaratus est, Ebr. 11, 4. Unde autem sacrificium ejus expiatorium fuit nisi virtute Antitypi, 1. Joh. 2, 2. (3.) Quia fide obtulit Abel Ebr. 11, 4. Fides autem Abelis, ut & cæterorum Martyrum ab Apostolo recensitorum respexit Christum, ejusque crucem & mortem Ebr. 12, 1. (4.) Adde, quod vox θυσίας macta- tionem & effusionem sanguinis inferat, & de sacrifi- cio Christi pro nobis occisi adhibeatur, Apoc.

13, 8. Ephes. 5, 2. Ebr. 9, 25. ut & verbum προσήνεγκε 1. Petr. 2, 24. Ebr. 7, 27. cap. 9, 25. 28. Quibus verbis proinde Apostolus Levitica sacrificia ceu typos Christi descripsit, adeoq; etiam hoc Abelis sacrifi- cium describere voluit Ebr. 11, 4. (5.) Et quid aliud docet continuus ille loquela sanguinis Abelis actus, quam quod testatur de sacrificio Christi, ceu figura quædam illustris, siquidem Abel primo loco in nu- be testium constituatur, & per fidem testatus innua- tur, cum obtulit DEO sacrificium. Dicitur etiam nobis mortuus loqui per fidem, quæ a nobis in Chri- stum requiritur, etiamnum loquatur, ut eam imite- mur, ejusq; exemplo etiam sanguinem pro ea fun- dere non dubitemus. Conf. B. Glassius Thes. 27. Disput. V. Christol. Mos. vers. 7.

vers. eod. SED SUB TE ERIT APPETITUS EJUS, ET TV DOMINABERIS EI.] Repetendum ex eo, quod præ- cessit, si bene egeris, ut sensus sit, si bene egeris, Abelis voluntas tuo imperio subjecta erit, ut fratris minoris. Ita illa: Sin autem male statim præ foribus peccatum aderit: erunt dicta παρενθε- τικῶς, qualia & in his libris multa occurrunt. Vid. Exod. 39, 29. & Num. 4, 7. Ps. 99, 6. 7. Primogeniti enim per Patris aut mortem aut absentiam paternam, quodammodo auctoritatem in fratres habebant: Sed hoc jus peccato amitti poterat, ut apparet in- fra 49, 3. 4. 1. Par. 5, 1. Adde 1. Reg. 1, 25. & sequentia.

Sequi hîc voluit Grotius Rabbinos & LXX. Interpp. Quos Chrysostomum Hom. XVIII. in Gen. lib. XI. contra Judæos sequi mirum non est; quia Græcum tantum textum præ manibus habebat, qui deserte hæc ad fratrem refert. Quibus tamen etiam Calvinus, Tossanus, Chamier, & Rivetus hic assurgunt; nec non e nostris Dn. Johan. Tarnovius in Exercit. Bibl. p. 106. Vidit autem probe Grotius, non congruere illum sensum, nisi statuatur paren- thesis. At non fingendæ sunt pro arbitrio paren- theses in textu sacro. Neque membrum opposi- tum in parenthesi legi solet, cum alterum membrum extra eandem constituitur, quod hic sit. Et quo- modo ad fratrem Abelem pronomina referri hæc possunt, cujus in tota hac DEI oratione nulla facta erat mentio? Quid hoc ad scopum DEI dehortan- tis a fratricidio, quod extollatur primogenitura Caini, quo auctus potius, quam depressus fuisset e- jusdem fastus? At si ad nomen præcedens referan- tur, uti par est, pronomina, uti priora in oratione DEI tum objurgationem, tum instructionem habuere, ut ex illa quidem in Caino contritio, per hanc vero fides excitaretur; ita hæc cohortationem exhibent, ut appetitui vel concupiscentiæ pravæ locum non relinquat, sed eidem dominetur. Peccati appeti- tus est ad Te, id est, hæret peccatum in membris tuis, & subinde concupiscentiis suis te tentabit, sed Tu dominaberis ei, hoc est, frenabis indomitos ejus impetus, ut interpretatur B. Rungius noster: Ad te, inquit Augustin. l. XV. de C. D. c. 7. conver- sio est. Numquid fratris? Absit. Cujus igitur, nisi peccati? Prohibet enim DEUS, ne peccatum regnet in mortali nostro corpore, ut obtempere- mus ei in concupiscentiis ejus. Rom. VI. Tunc autem, ut porro Augustinus habet, dominabitur quisq; peccato, si id non sibi defendendo proposue- rit, sed pœnitendo subjecerit; Alioquin & illi serviet dominanti, si patrocinium adhibuerit acce- denti.

Nihil hic pro arbitrii libertate in spiritua- libus, ut hoc ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ addam, inveni- ent Papistæ. Nam si ab externis sceleribus nos abstinere possimus, num actutum internas concupiscentias in potestate habebimus? No- men enim תשוקה internum affectum notat, sed qui instar ferventis aquæ ebullit, & in externum a- ctum erumpit. Quanquam in Ebræo textu non legatur SUB TE : vel uti Romæus corrumpit, SUBTER TE, sed AD TE, nec appetitus sub- jectio hic, sed ejusdem ebullitio designetur: Appeti- tus est AD TE, coram Te, vel super Te. Quod prævalere cupiat, sed dominari ei debeat Cain: ut cum peccati in Caino æstuantis vehementia insinuie- tur, tum Dominatus in concupiscentias illas perver- sas eidem imperetur. Male ergo versionem vul- gatam hîc sequitur Grotius, sub te erit appetitus ejus, id est, voluntas Abelis tuo imperio SUBJECTA erit. Ideo præstat, cum Targum Hierosolymit. Augustino, Autore libr. de vocatione gent. c. 4. Gregor. M. Mo- ral. IV. cap. 12. Eucherio, Beda, Ambrosio, l. 2. de Cain c. 6. Hieronym. in qq. Ebr. Beda, Ruperto, Glossa Ordinar. & interlineari, Mercero, Gefnero, Rungio, B. Gerhardo, aliis de peccato hæc intellige- re, utut affixa generis fæminei non sint; quia non in- frequens apud Ebræos est generum enallage; uti Ruth 1, 7. Esth. 1, 20. Eccles. 12, 5. & hoc in loco, versu proxime præcedenti; quanquam nomen חטאת si- gnificatione commune esse, nonnulli censeant, quod in plurali mascula terminatione æque ac fœ- minea reperiatur; Eccles. 10, 4. Psal. 103, 10. Jer. 5, 15. Nequicquam autem se opponit huic interpretatio- ni Chamier T. III. Panstrat. l. III. c. XIII. & Rivetus in h. l. quorum argumenta ex his, quæ nunc obser- vavimus, facile expediri poterunt.

## 4:8
v. 8. LET US GO OUT.] In Greek, διέλθωμεν εἰς τὸ πεδίον, which the Samaritan also added, as noted by both Jerome and Cyril. The Syriac, and the Jerusalem, and Jonathan also added it. In the Hebrew it is omitted by abbreviation, because from those things which follow, what Cain said can be sufficiently understood. Interpreters often take for themselves the not useless liberty of supplying such reticences. That saying of Ovid fits this history: The affection of brothers is also rare.

Since that is not contained in the Hebrew, lest the Vulgate be accused of error, Grotius defends it by the consensus of the Greek Version and the Samaritan Codex: likewise by the translation of the Syriac and the Jerusalem and Jonathan. But the Hebrew Codices consistently omit those words: which perhaps were first added by someone taking the preceding words, 'and Cain said to Abel,' in that way, and earned applause from the rest, as is wont to happen; otherwise the Hebrew can be rendered: And Cain spoke with Abel his brother; that he spoke familiarly with him, with hatred concealed, see Psalm 4:5, Ps. 139:20, so that there is no need for that supplement. Grotius thinks that from those things which follow, it can be sufficiently understood what Cain said; namely, that he exhorted him, 'Let us go out.' But Jerome and Aben Ezra hold that he related to him the speech of GOD held toward himself. It is likely, says our Gesner, that Cain said something about the discourse of God, and feigned great piety and singular love toward his brother: for the word Vejomer looks back to the preceding: as if Moses had said, 'And Cain indicated this very thing to his brother Abel.' But that there is nothing missing in the Hebrew text, which not even Grotius dared to say, is confirmed by the Masoretic note, which Buxtorf in the Key to the Masorah, ch. II, teaches should be rendered thus: there are twenty-eight verses which end in the middle of a verse, or at the Athnach accent. If Grotius wished to listen to the Targum here, he ought to have admitted the prolix conversation which the Jerusalem paraphrast inserted; let the Jew Apella believe that this ought to be referred to the liberty of supplying reticences.

Latin:

vers. 8. EGREDIAMVR FORAS.] Græce, διέλθωμεν εἰς τὸ πεδίον, quod addidit & Samaritanicus, ut notatum & Hierony- mo & Cyrillo. Addidere & Syrus, & Hierosolymitanus & Jo- nathan. In Hebræo per compendium id omittitur, quia ex his, quæ sequuntur, quid Cain dixerit, satis intelligi potest Reticen- tias tales supplendi libertatem non inutilem sæpe sibi sumunt Interpretes. Convenit huic Historiæ illud Ovidii: Fratrum quoq; gratia rara est.

Quum in Ebræo id non habeatur, ne erroris arguatur Vulgatus, Græcæ Versionis & Samaritici Codicis consensu eundem tuetur Grotius : Syri item & Hierosolymitana ac Jonathanis translatione. Sed Ebræi Codices constanter omittunt illa : quæ forte ab aliquo, verba præcedentia ita accipiente, & dixit Cain ad Abel, primum addita a reliquis ap- plausum, ut fieri amat, meruere; Cæterum Ebræa reddi possunt : Et locutus est Cain cum Abele fratre suo; quod familiariter cum ipso loquutus fuerit, dissimulato odio, vid. Psal. 4, 5. Pf. 139, 20. ut sup- plemento illo opus non sit. Grotius ex his, quæ se- quuntur, satis intelligi posse, quid Cain dixerit, autu- mat; quod nempe hortatus fuerit eundem, Egredia- mur foras. Sed Hieronymus & Aben Ezra volunt, quod illi retulerit orationem DEI ad se habitam. Verisimile est, inquit Gefnerus noster, Cainum de Con- cione Dei aliquid dixisse, & magnam pietatem, singu- laremq; erga fratrem amorem simulasse: Verbum enim Vejomer præcedentia respicit: quasi Moses dixisset, & indicavit hoc ipsum Cain Abeli fratri suo. Non autem deesse aliquid in Ebræo textu, quod nec Gro- tius fuit ausus dicere, nota Masoretica confirmat, quam Buxtorf. in clave Masoræ c. II. ita reddendam esse docet: viginti octo versus sunt, qui desinunt in me- dio versu, vel accentu Athnach. Si Targum audire hîc voluit Grotius, prolixum Colloquium, quod para- phrastes Hierosolymitan. inseruit, admittere debu- it; quod ad libertatem reticentias supplendi refer- ri debere, credat Judæus Apella.

## 4:9
v. 9. AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?] That is, παιδαγωγός, in which sense it is used in Horace, 'The beardless youth at last with guardian removed.'

Latin:

vers. 9. NVM CVSTOS FRATRIS MEI SVM EGO] Id est παιδαγωγός, quo sensu apud Horatium est, Imberbis juvenis tandem custode remoto.

## 4:12
v. 12. A VAGABOND AND A FUGITIVE SHALT THOU BE UPON THE EARTH.] Orestes in Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris, '...driven by the successions of the Furies, fugitives, outcasts from the land,' etc.

Latin:

vers. 12. VAGVS ET PROFVGVS ERIS SVPER TER-RAM.] Orestes in Iphigenea Taurica apud Euripidem, - - - διαδοχαῖς δ' ἐρινύων Ἠλαυνόμεσθα, φυγάδες, ἔξεδροι χθονὸς, &c.

## 4:14
v. 14. AND FROM THY FACE I SHALL BE HIDDEN. He complains that he is excluded from his parents, and thus from the Church, in which GOD manifests His face. Mercer prefers, from thy favor and protection. The Chaldean took it interrogatively, as it appears, because he rendered it negatively: 'And from thy sight it cannot be that I should be hidden.' But Aben Ezra himself acknowledges that the place is understood in which GOD peculiarly manifests Himself.

v. same. EVERY ONE THEREFORE THAT FINDS ME, SHALL KILL ME) By the dictate of nature: 'If he should suffer what he inflicted, just judgment would be done.' See what has been said by us on this place, and on those things which follow, in the first book on the Law of War and Peace, ch. II, § 5, and in the Annotations.

Grotius errs in bk. I of the Law of War and Peace, ch. II, § 5, that he is innocent by the dictate of nature who has killed a homicide, and that God himself admitted this: until, with the institution of courts, he restricted it for supreme reasons to judges alone. Nature indeed dictates that force can be repelled by force. But it does not suggest that a homicide can be killed by anyone. It confirms the former, the law of Rhadamanthus in Apollodorus, bk. II: 'If anyone has avenged himself on him who first offered violence, let him bear it with impunity'; but not this latter. 'If everyone should bear what he has done, let it become law, and just.' But let him bear it from him who has the right to inflict it. For this right was not restricted to judges only through Moses. At all times there have been powers, which the Apostle calls ministers of God constituted by God, and not bearing the sword in vain, but being ministers of God, avengers for wrath to him who does evil, Rom. 13:4. Therefore, it was not from a sense of natural equity that Cain, conscious of his parricide, said: 'Whoever finds me will kill me,' but from the fear of retaliation, which murderers, by whomever it may be inflicted, are accustomed to fear even today—not because nature dictates that it is permitted for anyone to inflict it, but because conscience, which usually follows even by the command or permission of GOD, convinces them that it is deserved. That right, which the one most closely related by blood to the slain person possessed under the Law of Moses in the Jewish polity, was proper to it, and does not flow from the dictate of nature, nor can it be considered a vestige of ancient custom.

Latin:

v. 14. ET A FACIE TUA ABSCONDAR. Queritur, quod a parentibus excludatur, adeoque ab Ecclesia, in qua DEUS faciem suam manifestat. Mercerus mavult, a favore, & præsidio tuo. Chald. interrogative, ut apparet, accepit, quia negative red- didit: Et a conspectu tuo fieri non potest, ut abscondar. Sed agnoscit Aben Ezra ipse locum intelligi, in quo DEUS peculiariter se manifestat.

Vers. eod. OMNIS IGITUR, QVI INVENERIT ME, OCCIDET ME) Ex naturæ dictato: Ἔι κε πάθοι[τακ'] ὄρεξε, δίκη κ' ἰθεῖα γένοιτο. Vide quæ de hoc loco, & iis quæ sequuntur dicta a nobis libro primo de Jure belli ac pacis c. II. §. 5. & in Annotatis.

Errat Grotius l. I. de jure Pacis & belli cap. II. §. 5. naturæ dictato insontem esse, qui homicidam occi- disset, Deumq́; id admisisse ipsum: donec institutis ju- diciis summas ob causas ad solos judices id restrinxe- ret. Dictat sane natura, vim vi repelli posse. Sed a quovis homicidam occidi posse, non suggerit. Prius illud Rhadamanti jus apud Apollod. l. II. Si quis se ultus sit de eo, qui prior vim intulerit, impune id ferat, confirmat: non autem hoc posterius. Quæ fecit, si quisq́; ferat, jus fiat, & æquum. Sed ferat ab eo, qui jus inferendi habet. Non enim per Mosen tantum restrictum hoc jus ad judices fuit. Omni tempore fuere potestates, quas a Deo constitutas di- cit Apostolus ministros Dei, nec frustra gladium ge- rere, sed ministros Dei esse, vindices ad iram ei, qui ma- lum agit Rom. 13, 4. Non ergo ex naturalis æqui- tatis sensu Cain, parricidii sibi conscius, dixit: Qui in- veniet me, interficiet me: Sed ex metu talionis, quam homicidæ, a quocunq; eadem fiat, etiam hodie me- tuere solent, non quod natura dictet, cuivis eam in- ferre licere, sed quod promeritam convincat con- scientia, quæ DEI jussu aut permissu plerumque etiam sequitur. Jus illud, quod occisum sanguine proxime attingens per legem Moysis habuit in poli- tia Judaica, huic proprium erat, non vero e naturæ dictato redundat, aut moris pristini vestigium censeri potest.

## 4:16
verse 16. IN THE LAND) The name of the land, Nod, is omitted here, which the Greeks call Naid. This happened after GOD changed the punishment of perpetual flight into the milder one of sedentary exile, but with harsher locations assigned to it, such as the Arabian desert: where, according to Josephus, he is said to have been the first of all to begin to practice brigandage.

Latin:

vers. 16. IN TERRA) Omissum hic nomen terræ נוד Græcis ναΐδ. Factum autem hoc, postquam DEVS pœnam perpetuæ fugæ in mitiorem exilii sedentarii mutavit, sed ad- scriptis illi locis durioribus, qualis erat Arabia deserta: ubi la- trocinari cœpisse primus omnium dicitur Josepho.

## 4:17
verse 17. HIS WIFE.) The same one who was his sister, called Save or Azaa by Epiphanius, but Ripha by Chrysostom.

Latin:

vers. 17. VXOREM SVAM.) Eandemque sororem, quæ Save seu Azaa Epiphanio, at Chrysostomo Ripha.

## 4:19
verse 19. ADA) A feminine name, which remained among the Caras.

Latin:

vers. 19. ADA) Nomen muliebre, quod apud Caras man- sit.

## 4:21
verse 21. AND THE ORGAN) In Hebrew עוגב, the Greeks call it a cithara. But the Chaldean calls it אבוביא. The scholiast of Horace says: 'Ambubiae' are called female flute-players in the language of the Syrians. For among the Syrians, a flute or symphony is called an ambubaja.

Latin:

vers. 21. ET ORGANO) Hebraice עוגב Græci κιθάραν. At Chaldæus אבוביא. Scholiastes Horatii: Ambubaiæ di- cuntur mulieres tibicinæ lingua Syrorum. Etenim Syris tibia sive symphonia, ambubaja dicitur.

## 4:25
verse 25. AND SHE CALLED HIS NAME) The mother, that is. For it is a verb that is joined to feminine subjects.

Latin:

vers. 25. VOCAVITQVE NOMEN EJVS) Mater scili- cet. Est enim verbum, quod fœmininis jungitur.

## 4:26
verse 26. THIS ONE BEGAN TO CALL UPON THE NAME OF THE LORD.) Or he began to be called by the name of GOD. Cyril approves this sense, so that as if he were an ambassador of GOD to men, he therefore received the name of GOD, as Angels are accustomed to do. And therefore, below in 6, 2 and 4, the same Cyril interprets the 'sons of God' as the descendants of Enoch. Aquila seems to have intended this when he translated it, τότε ἤρχθη τῶ καλεῖσθαι ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίε. Irenaeus 4, 30 favors this sense.

This interpretation cannot be proven. And the hypothesis is false, that ambassadors of God to men receive the name of GOD, nor can this be taught by any example. Not even regarding the Angels: since GOD does not give His glory to another, Isaiah 42, 6. Concerning which we have treated at length against the Socinians, especially in Tom. II of the Augustan Confession, in the chapter on Natural and Revealed Theology, chapter 4. It is another matter that, below in chapter 6, 24, most interpret 'sons of God' as the descendants of Enoch, by which name all the faithful are also designated. For do you conclude that Enoch was therefore called by the name of GOD, as if he were an ambassador of GOD to men? Is GOD, whose sons are indicated there, Enoch, so that he was designated there absolutely by the name אלהים? It is absurd. Others prefer to hold that the distinction was made then, which is noted in ch. 6, 2. 4. of the sons of GOD, and the sons of men. Which sense pleased Eusebius, Emissenus, and Cornelius Bertram in his Polit. Judaic. ch. II, and is not entirely disapproved of by Rivet in Exerc. XLVII. Some, with the Targum of Onkelos, Jonathan, and the Hebrews R. Solomon and Maimonides, explain that the profanation of the name of the Lord began then, as Lambert Daneau, Tremellius, and Junius did in the first edition of their version. Thus the Arabic interpreter of Erpenius: Then men began to fail in their obedience to GOD. However, Junius later amended his version in this place as follows: then it was begun to call upon the name of Jehovah: which most take to refer to the beginning of public preaching: To which opinion, as being most suitable, our theologians, along with Mercer, Drusius, Torniellus, and Pererius, subscribe ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one mind): so that by the invocation of the name of the Lord, as a part of divine worship, the whole of divine worship is designated. Moses therefore indicates that Enoch was the first to begin the public ministry of teaching by divine command, the human race having by then become more numerous, so that in his age the form of the Church began to be seen, and the public invocation of the divine name flourished. For having described the pursuits and profane customs of Cain and his descendants, who were little concerned with the worship of GOD, Moses commemorates who were the authors who devoted effort to restoring true religion, and who defended the same by public exercise against the Cainite profanation. It is not credible that Moses should have narrated the pursuits of an ungodly generation so prolixly, yet have wished to commemorate nothing of the pursuits of the pious in the Church of GOD. Let what is said concerning the faith of the Ancients in Christ in §. XLIII be compared. The Arab historian Elmacinus agrees: p. 7. Enosch governed his people and insisted with them on the way of justice and fear. — And when the departure of Enosch approached, the fathers of his grandsons and great-grandsons were gathered to him, that they might obtain a blessing from him, and having called them to himself, he commanded by testament that they should devote effort to holiness; and he exhorted them not to mingle with the offspring of Cain the murderer. And after he had appointed Kenan as his successor, he died. Henriquetz in l. XII. c. 5 shamefully gave himself away when he says that Enoch, who began to call upon the name of the Lord, was translated to Paradise as a virgin, ignorantly confusing Enoch with Enosch, and imagining a virgin who has children. Are such virgins, and such celibacy, which the Papists boast of so greatly?

Latin:

vers. 26. ISTE CŒPIT INVOCARE NOMEN DO- MINI.) Aut cæpit appellari nomine DEI. Quem sensum Cy- rillus probat, ut velut DEI ad homines legatus, propterea DEI nomen acceperit, ut Angeli solent. Et ideo infra 6, 2. & 4. Filios DEI idem Cyrillus interpretatur Enochiposferos. A- quila videtur hoc voluisse, cum transtulit, τότε ἤρχθη τῶ κα- λεῖσθαι ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίε. Favet huic sensui Irenæus 4, 30.

Non probari potest hæc interpretatio. Et hy- pothesis falsa est, Dei ad homines legatos nomen DEI accipere, neque id ullo exemplo doceri potest. Ne de Angelis quidem: quum gloriam suam DEUS alteri non det Esai 42, 6. Quo de prolixe contra Socinianos imprimis Tom. II. in August. Conf. Theol. natural. & revelat. cap. 4. egimus. Ali- ud est, quod infra cap. 6, 24. Filios Dei de E- nochi posteris interpretantur plerique, quo nomine etiam omnes fideles designantur. Num enim ideo Enochum nomine DEI appellatum esse, ceu DEI le- gatum ad homines, concludes? Num DEUS, cujus filii ibi indigitantur, est Enoch, ut nomine אלהים ibi designatus fuerit absolute? Absonum. Alii rectius cepisse tunc distinctionem volunt, quæ nota- ta est c. 6, 2. 4. filiorum DEI, & filiorum hominum. Qui sensus Eusebio, Emisseno, & Cornelio Bertramo de Polit. Judaic. c. II. placuit, nec omnino impro- batur Riveto Exerc. XLVII. Nonnulli cum Targ. On- kelos, Jonath. & Ebræis R. Salom. & Maimonide, ex- ponunt, cæpisse tunc prophanationem nominis Domi- ni, ut Lambert. Danæus, Tremellius & Junius in pri- ma versionis editione. Sic Arabs interpres Erpenii: Tunc cæperunt homines deficere ab obedientia DEI. Versionem tamen suam Junius deinde hoc in loco ita emendavit: tunc ceptum est invocari nomen Jeho- vah: quod de initio præconii publici pleriq; accipiunt: Cui sententiæ, utpote convenientissimæ, nostrates Theologi cum Mercero, Drusio, Torniello, Pererio ὁμοθυμαδὸν subscribunt: ut ita per invocationem no- minis Domini, ceu partem cultus divini, totus cultus divinus designetur. Indicat ergo Moses, Enochum primum divino mandato publicum minister ium docen- di cepisse, auctiori tum reddito jam humano genere, ut ejus ætate forma conspici ceperit Ecclesiæ, & pu- blica invocatio nominis divini viguerit. Descri- ptis enim Caini & posterorum studiis, & moribus prophanis, qui parum de cultu DEI solliciti fuere, commemorat Moses, quinam autores veræ religio- ni restaurandæ operam dederint, eandemq; publi- co exercitio adversus prophanationem Cainianam propugnarint. Non credibile est, Mosen tam pro- lixe studia generationis improbæ enarrasse; nihil autem de studiis piorum in Ecclesiam DEI comme- morare voluisse. Conferantur, quæ de fide Vete- rum in Christum §. XLIII. Consentit Elmacinus A- rabs Historicus: pag. 7. Enosch gubernavit popu- lum suum & cum iis institit viæ justitiæ & timoris. — Cumq; appropinquasset discessus Enoschi, congregati sunt ad ipsum Patres nepotum ejus, & pronepotes, ut benedictionem ab ipso consequerentur, iisque ad se vo- catis testamento mandavit, ut Sanctimoniæ darent ope- ram; & hortatus est eos, ne miscerentur cum prole Kai- ni homicidæ. Et postquam successorem constituisset Kenanem, mortuus est. Turpiter hic se dedit Hen- riquetz. l. XII. c. 5. cum Enochum, qui invocare nomen Domini cepit, virginem translatum in Paradisum di- cit, Enochum cum Enoscho imperite confundens, virginemque fingens, quæ liberos habeat. Num tales virgines, talisque cælibatus, quem tantopere Papi- stæ jactitant?

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

The genealogy of Adam, and the chronology up to Noah.

Ver. 1. THIS IS THE BOOK OF THE GENERATION OF ADAM. By the word ספר, a catalog, from ספר, to enumerate, is understood, just as by βίβλον in Matt. 1, 1. And so also in Num. 21, 14, it is observed by some that not a book, but a catalog of the wars of the Lord is designated: it is said, or is accustomed to be said, in the review of the wars of the Lord. That catalog, however, is called not of a generation, but of generations, and thus the genealogy of the Patriarchs is exhibited here, which is woven for the sake of the knowledge of that Church of the time, for the chronology of the years of the World, and for the lineage of the Messiah.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

Genealogia Adæ, & Chronologia usque ad Noam.

Vers. 1. HIC EST LIBER GENERATIONIS ADAM. Per vocem ספר Catalogus a ספר enumerare, uti per βίβλον Matth. 1, 1. intelligitur. Atq; ita etiam Num. 21, 14. non librum, sed Catalogum bellorum Domini designari, nonnullis observatum: dicitur, vel dici solet in recensionem bellorum Domini. Ca- talogus autem ille non generationis, sed generatio- num dicitur, adeoq; Genealogia Patriarcharum hic exhibetur, quæ ob notitiam veræ temporis istius Ecclesiæ, ob Chronologiam annorum Mundi, & ob Prosapiam Messiæ texitur.

## 5:18
ver. 18. ONE HUNDRED SIXTY-TWO YEARS. Concerning the many discrepancies which appear in this and the following chapters regarding the numbers of the years in the Hebrew, Samaritan, and Greek Codices, I have nothing better to say than what the most learned Capellus said in his Critica Sacra.

We could likewise have referred the reader to our Critica Sacra in this matter. For Capellus praised Morinus here, whose nonsense we discussed there on p. 791; indeed, he professed in l. III. c. XX of the Critica Sacra that he did not have a copy of the Samaritan Codex, and therefore that he only culled a few things from those which the most learned Morinus had gleaned and annotated concerning that diversity, both in the preface which he prefixed to the edition of the LXX Interpreters newly instituted by himself, and in his Ecclesiastical Exercitations—examples of various readings, as he calls them, among which he placed the numbers of the years of the lives of the Patriarchs in the first place: both before the flood and after the flood, in which they are said to have begun to beget, or to have lived after they began to beget, according to the Jews and Samaritans: to which he then also compares the same years according to the LXX Interpreters. Moreover, Capellus testified that it was not his intention either to settle such disputes among them, as he says, or to inquire into and assign the causes of this difference. What good, therefore, will the reader gain from that reference to the Critica of Capellus, unless perhaps Grotius considers it a good thing if it is left doubtful what one should finally conclude about the years of the Patriarchs, and judges all chronology henceforth to be doubtful and uncertain, where no certainty can be had concerning the years of the Patriarchs before or after the flood, with the Jewish, Samaritan, and Greek Codices varying so greatly. When, according to the Jews, he had counted only 292 years from the flood to the birth of Abraham, according to the Samaritans 942, and finally according to the LXX Interpreters 1072, the Pseudo-Critic dismissed the reader with this character of certainty: Which calculation is truer, that of the Jews, or that of the LXX, or that of the Samaritans, I do not now dispute.

What if that comparison of diversity tends to this, that it may teach that the Hebrew codex was otherwise, which the Samaritans received from the priest sent by the order of Shalmaneser for the sake of teaching the law: concerning which, however, no authentic or trustworthy document can be produced, and therefore Capellus attributes little to it, or at least what the Samaritans had from that time, from which Samaria was destroyed by Hyrcanus, that nation was subject to the Jews: it may also prove that it was read otherwise in the Hebrew Codex, and thus render the modern reading of the Hebrew source doubtful and suspect. Whence he says that that diversity seems to have arisen (at least in part) from the lapse of scribes or copyists in transcribing the sacred books, which is easy and prone to happen especially in numbers (perhaps from the similarity and affinity of numerical signs). Nor is it obscure, since Capellus is sufficiently hostile to modern Hebrew Codices, and for that end turns everything that seemed to him able to induce some ambiguity about them, but that he can be considered more inclined here either to the Samaritan or to the Greek Codices than to the modern Hebrew ones themselves. But by what arguments will the authority, antiquity, and sincerity of the Samaritan Codex, which Morin praises, be asserted, so that it can in any way come into contention with the Hebrew ones? Will that dregs of so many most superstitious nations render the palm in any way doubtful against the people of GOD, to whom the oracles of GOD were entrusted, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 3:4, concerning whose supreme religion against the Hebrew Codices it is sufficiently evident? Christ and the Apostles do not refer us to the Scripture of the Samaritans, but to that of the Jews. The ancient Fathers do not appeal to the Samaritan, but to the Hebrew truth. And who will make us certain of the purity of the Samaritan Codex, whose most ancient copies have an age of scarcely four centuries, as Morin admits, and which some most learned critics [consider to be] from a bold and by unlearned men interpolated from the Hebrew and Greek Codex of the LXX Interpreters, with many things added which agree with neither, they judge, in which Hottinger has already detected many errors clearly enough in his Exercit. Anti-Morianis; as also John Selden on the succession to the goods of the deceased, ch. 27. Schotanus in Tohu p. 64. Which Codex, he says, do the Samaritans have, and whence did they receive it? From an Israelite priest. When? In the time of King Hezekiah, when those people, having been instructed in the worship of God, were translated there by the King of the Assyrians. But they, having been instructed by the priest Jeroboam, mixed the worship of the true GOD with their ancestral idolatry. From that time, therefore, there was hatred between the Jews and the Samaritans, and no commerce. From the death of King Hezekiah to Christ being taken up into heaven, more than 730 years have elapsed. In all that intervening time, the Church of the Jews was the depository of the oracles of GOD, not the Synagogue of the Samaritans. Will you say that the Samaritans were the keepers of the Jews' books, as was once truly said of the Jews for the Church of Christ? If the Jews afterwards so diligently guarded the sacred letters of the O.T., which were also delivered to them, what is there to prevent us from saying that they performed this in preceding times, when they had not yet been broken off from the olive tree? I grant that the Samaritans, after they had mixed the worship of GOD with their own stench, did not wish to amend their own codex (received from that priest) from any Hebrew one, or to transfer anything into it. For the hatred and stubbornness were too great. Therefore, whatever of right and good is in their codex, that is owed to that most ancient Hebrew one, when they were first imbued with the law of Moses under Hezekiah: but whatever deviates and is crooked must be examined by the standard of the right deposited among the Jews and original. Thus Schotanus. Although it must not be conceded that modern Samaritan Codices agree with that ancient one: since in that treacherous people, over such a long time, the care of the sacred Codex was not always held to be accurate. It is certain that among the Jews, a more accurate method was certainly held by the Levites for the Pentateuch, of which there was greater use, nor could the books, which were always read in the Synagogues, be easily corrupted, without even the smallest discrepancy having been observed by the memory of the people. And who would doubt that divine providence kept watch more for the Codex, which it had destined for the Canon of the Church and entrusted to the Jews, than for the Scripture of the Samaritans, which was exhibited for the sake of a profane mixture of divine worship. Not to mention that Eulogius, Patriarch of Alexandria, as observed by James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, in his letter to Arnold Boot, taught that the corruptions of the Mosaic volume among the Samaritans were made, and proceeded from the heresiarch Dositheus, a contemporary of Simon Magus. Nor is it consistent or probable that lapses and errors crept in from known numerical signs, if indeed the numbers of the years were described in express words, as is the case today in Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac books; indeed, that this was done long ago is most well-known from Jewish manuscripts, concerning which see Hackspan on the use of Jewish writers in Theology, ch. 11, p. 335; nor is it established that the numbers were designated by bare signs alone; and those changes are so constituted that even a mere inspection of them can teach that those errors did not arise from the carelessness or inadvertence of numerical signs.

But whatever the cause or origin of that diversity may be, there is no reason why we should suffer the faith of the Hebrew truth, which God willed to obtain the place of a rule and canon in the Church, and which has been religiously held and preserved by the Jews, to whose standard other editions have always been recalled, to be called into question because of the diversity of either a suspect, obscure, and in many ways corrupted Codex of some profane and abominable people, such as the Samaritan, or of a Greek translation, which the LXX.

Interpreters is said, and in countless places it is found to be of doubtful faith and depraved. Jerome indeed, the steward of better antiquity, already thirteen centuries ago did not attribute much to the Samaritan Codex, which he could have had much purer and more emended than those modern ones, unless he found it consonant with the Hebrew: for then, because of the agreement with it, he opposed it to the erring translations: and for that reason he also refuted the LXX Interpreters from the consonance of both the Hebrew and Samaritan Codices in these patriarchal anachronisms. Thus Jerome observes, e.g., in the years of Methuselah in his Hebrew Traditions on Genesis, when the Greek version has in Gen. 5:25-26: And Methuselah lived 167 years and begat Lamech; And Methuselah lived, after he begat Lamech, 802 years. and begat sons and daughters, he found it written thus not only in the Hebrew, but also in the books of the Samaritans, just as the Hebrew Codex still has it, and Methuselah lived 187 years and begat Lamech: and Methuselah lived, after he begat Lamech, 782 years, and begat sons and daughters. Now if the modern Samaritan Codices and the LXX Interpreters are compared, both are found to be changed here: since in the Samaritan of Morinus, Methuselah is said to have begotten Lamech in his 67th year, and thereafter to have lived only 653 years, so that according to the Samaritans the entire age of Methuselah was only 720 years, whose age, however, the LXX Interpreters, both according to the Hieronymian reading and as they now have it, extend with the Hebrew sources to 969 years, and whom all acknowledge as the most long-lived of all mortals. Concerning whom it is held in the Schalscheb thus: His years were 969, nor did any man live so long. To this point tends the observation of the Talmudists in בוחלין: Seven doubled the world; Methuselah saw Adam, whom he served for 243 years. Shem saw Methuselah, whom he served for 48 years; Jacob saw Shem, whom he served for 20 years. Amram saw Jacob. Ahijah the Shilonite saw Amram for 7 years, and was 61 years old when he went out of Egypt; Elijah saw Ahijah; but Elijah is still alive. Among the Arabs, Patricides reports that Methuselah died in the year 600 of Noah, on Friday about midday, the 21st of Elul. As the Orientals agree ὁμοθυμαδὸν that he died before the flood, so they also agree in this, that he surpassed all in the longevity of his life. And here one may detect a triple Samaritan reading in the years of the generation of Methuselah: for he begat Lamech, according to the Samaritan reading of Jerome, in the 187th year; according to the reading of Morin, in the 67th year; according to Scaliger in his notes to the Greek fragments of Eusebius, in the 77th year. Whence it is manifest with what truth Capellus wrote, in book 5, page 710, that Eusebius, one thousand and three hundred years ago, observed the SAME discrepancy in those numbers between the codex of the Jews and that of the Samaritans.

Nor can the calculation of either the Samaritans or the Greeks be reconciled in any way with the sacred Chronology. For according to the sacred Chronology, 1656 years are counted to the flood. But according to the Samaritan codex of Morin, only 1307 years are reckoned to the flood, and according to the same, not only Methuselah, but also Jared and Lamech would have died in the very year of the flood, and Mahalaleel 17 years before the flood. But since to Methuselah, as the most long-lived among the Patriarchs according to the consensus of all Hebrew codices, and of the edition of the LXX Interpreters themselves, and also according to the Samaritan codices of Jerome, there are 969 years of age, if Methuselah begat Lamech in the 67th year of his age, Lamech begat Noah in the 53rd year, as Morin's Samaritan has it, and the flood broke upon the 600th year of Noah, it must be said that in the seven hundred and twentieth year of the age of Methuselah, the flood inundated the earth. Where then did Methuselah remain during the flood, for the completion of whose age 249 years are still required? According to the Hebrews, however, says Jerome, and the Samaritans (of his time) the codices from the day of the birth of Methuselah until the day of the birth of Noah are 369 years. (Morinus's Samaritan Codex has only 120 years.) To these add the 600 years of Noah, because in the 600th year of his life the flood occurred, and thus it happens that in the 969th year of his life Methuselah died, in the year in which the flood began. Thus the modern Samaritan Codex is clearly convicted of error: which, even if it otherwise agrees with the Hebrew Codices regarding the years of the lives of the Patriarchs after the flood, up to Terah, nevertheless assigns the years in which they began to beget in a far different way; it also takes away 60 years from the age of Eber, and reports that he lived in total only 404 years: and likewise it subtracts just as many years from the age of Terah, and says that he lived only 145 years, when according to the Hebrew truth he lived 205 years: Whence the sacred Chronology is again confounded.

How much more the edition of the LXX Interpreters disturbs this, if indeed from the creation of the world until the flood they count not 1656, but 2242 years, having added 586 years to the age of the ante-diluvian Patriarchs, and furthermore add 780 years to the years of the post-diluvian Patriarchs up to Abraham, whence a notable anachronism of the Greeks arose in calculating the years of the world. But here again there is a manifest corruption in the years of Methuselah, which Jerome thus proves in the cited passage; For when Methuselah was 167 years old (according to the LXX) he begat Lamech, again Lamech when he was 188 years old (according to the same) begat Noah. And there are up to the day of the birth of Noah 355 years of the life of Methuselah. But in the six-hundredth year of the life of Noah the flood occurred. And by this, having made the calculation by parts, it is proven that the flood was in the 955th year of Methuselah. Since, however, he is said above to have lived 969 years (according to the LXX Interpreters) it is doubtful to no one that he lived (according to the LXX Interpreters) 14 years after the flood. Hence therefore Jerome invincibly concludes that, as in MOST (according to the LXX Interpreters), so also in this there is an error in the number. In vain, therefore, as Jerome notes, have the wits of interpreters and Doctors, who could read no version but that of the LXX Interpreters, been fatigued by that question ventilated in the disputation of all the Churches, how Methuselah is reported to have lived 14 years after the flood, and yet it is true, as is said in 1 Peter 3, that only eight souls were saved in the ark; when according to the Hebrew and Samaritan Codices it is in the open that Methuselah died in the 969th year of his life, and finally the flood began. Some, adhering to the version of the LXX Interpreters, when they were ignorant of the Hebrew truth, as Augustine testifies in book 15 of The City of God, ch. 11, were driven to the point of inventing that Methuselah lived through those years with his father Enoch, until the flood passed. Augustine, however, although otherwise intensely addicted to the Greek Codices, was not at all afraid to claim that their entire computation was an error, introduced partly by the carelessness of scribes, partly by the fraud of some, in the cited book, ch. 13, with this general maxim added, which should be observed especially by untimely Critics: I would not doubt that it is by no means done rightly, that when something different is found in both Codices, since both cannot be true for the sake of the faith of historical events, that language should rather be believed from which the translation was made into another by the Interpreters. But truly ridiculous, nay, a fool is this Morinus, when because of the Roman Church, which both the calculation of the LXX Interpreters in the Martyrology on the 25th of December and the Hebrew calculation retained in the vulgate version has canonized, he leaves both computations, even if they are completely contradictory to each other, nevertheless in the middle with Cano and Mariana (for how can he leave them, when the Church has approved both?) but he sells both as true in Exercit. 7, ch. 1, with Antoninus T. I. Chron. ch. 1, that the Holy Spirit did not dispose it so without a mystery, for the greater merit of faith; as if the Holy Spirit disposes contradictorily opposed things for the merit of faith, which is to impiously and blasphemously impute a lie to the Spirit of truth, and from there to build up merit, if such impiety is believed or admitted.

Latin:

vers. 18. CENTUM SEXAGINTA DUOBUS ANNIS. De multis discrepantiis, quæ in hoc & sequentibus capitibus circa numeros annorum apparent in Codicibus Hebræis, Sama- ritanis, Græcis, nihil melius quod dicam habeo, quam quæ dixi in Critico sacro eruditissimus Capellus.

Remittere pariter lectorem poteramus ad Criticum nostrum sacrum in hac causa. Capellus enim laudavit hic Morinum, cujus affanias ibi dis- cuffimus p. 791. imo professus est l. III. c. XX. Cri- tic. sacr. Codicis Samaritani copiam se non habuisse, adeoque tantum ex illis, quæ Morinus vir doctissimus delibavit, atque de illa diversitate annotavit tam in præfatione, quam præfixit edit. LXX. Interpp. a se de- nuo institutæ, quam in Ecclesiasticis suis Exercitationi- bus pauca se decerpere, variæ lectionis, uti vocat, exem- pla, inter quæ numeros annorum vitæ Patriarcharum primo collocavit loco:tum ante diluvium,tum post diluvium,quibus dicuntur cepisse gignere, aut vi- xisse, postquam gignere cœperunt, secundum Judæ- os & Samaritanos: quibus deinde etiam comparat annos eosdem secundum LXX. Interpp. Cæterum testatus est Capellus, animum sibi non esse, vel tantas inter ipsos componere, ut ait, lites, vel causas hujus dis- criminis inquirere & assignare. Quid ergo ex ista ad Criticum Capelli remissione boni lucrabiur Le- ctor, nisi forte hoc pro bono habeat Grotius, si du- bius relinquatur, quid tandem de annis Patriarcha- rum statuere debeat, omnemque Chronologiam porro dubiam & incertam judicet, ubi nulla de Pa- triarcharum ante, aut post diluvium annis certitu- do,variantibus tantopere Judæis, Samaritanis, Græ- cis Codicibus, haberi potest. Quum secundum Ju- dæos a diluvio ad natum Abrahamum annos dun- taxat 292. secundum Samaritanos v. 942. secundum LXX. denique Interpp. 1072. numerasset, cum hoc certitudinis charactere, dimisit Lectorem Pseudo- Criticus: Uter a. epilogismus sit verior, Judæorum, an LXX. vel Samaritanorum, jam non disputo.

Quid quod eo tendat illa diversitatis collatio, ut aliter Ebræum habuisse codicem, doceat, quem e Sacerdote, Salmanassaris jussu, legem docendi causa misso, acceperint Samaritani: quo de tamen nullum documentum authenticum aut fide dignum proferri potest, ideoque parum illi tribuit Capel- lus, aut quem saltem ab eo tempore habuerint Sa- maritæ,ex quo deleta per Hyrcanum Samaria,gens illa Judæis subjecta fuit: aliter etiam lectum fuisse in Hebræo Codice, evincat, adeoque dubiam & suspectam reddat modernam fontis Ebræi lectio- nem. Unde diversitatem illam ortam videri ait, (ex parte saltem) ex Scribarum seu librariorum in descri- bendis sacris libris lapsu, qui præsertim in numeris (ex notarum forte numericarum similitudine atœ affinita- te) facilis sit atque proclivis. Neque obscurum est, quum satis infestus sit Capellus modernis Ebræis Codicibus, & eo fine omnia convertat, quæ visa ipsi sunt ambiguitatem aliquam de iisdem induce- re posse, quin propensior hic censeri possit sive in Samaritanos, sive in Græcos Codices, quam in ipsos Ebræos modernos. At quibus argumen- tis Samaritani Codicis, quem Morinus laudat, au- toritas, antiquitas, sinceritas adseretur, ut ullate- nus in contentionem cum Ebræis venire queat? Num fex illa tot superstitiosissimarum gentium populo DEI, cui credita sunt eloquia DEI, teste Apostolo Rom. 3, 4. de cujus summa adversus Codices Ebræos religione affatim constat, pal- mam ullatenus dubiam reddet? Non ad Samari- tanorum, sed ad Judæorum Scripturam Christus & Apostoli nos remittunt. Non ad Samaritcam, sed ad Ebræam veritatem provocant Patres anti- qui. Et quis de puritate Samaritani Codicis certos nos reddet, cujus antiquissima exemplaria vix qua- tuor seculorum ætatem habent, Morino fatente, quemq; Critici nonnulli eruditissimi ab audaculo & rudi homines interpolatum ex Ebræo & Græco Co- dice LXX. Interpp. multis, quæ cum neutro conveni- unt, adjectis, judicant, in quo multos etiam errores satis clare Hottingerus in Exercit. Anti-Morianis jam detexit; nec non Joh. Seldenus de successione in bona defunctor. c. 27. Schotanus in Tohu p. 64. Quem Samaritani,inquit, Codicem habent, unde ac- ceperunt? ab Israëlitico sacerdote. Quando? Tem- pore Ezechia Regis,cum instituti ad cultum Dei populi isti ab Assyriorum Rege illuc translati. Illi autem in- stituti a Sacerdote Jeroboamo λαϊκῶ DEI veri cultum miscuere cum patria idololatria. Exinde igitur odium inter Judæos & Samaritas, nec ullum commercium. Ab Ezechia Regis obitu ad Christum in cœlos evectum plures quam 730.anni elapsi sunt. Intermedio isto omni tempore Judæorum Ecclesia fuit depositaria elo- quiorum DEI non Samaritanum Synagoga. Anne di- ces, Samaritas Judæorum fuisse capsarios,ut de Judæis pro Ecclesia Christi olim vere dictum est? Si postea Ju- dæi tam diligenter custodire sacras literas V. T. quæ ipsis quoque traditæ fuerunt, quid est, quo minus an- teeuntibus temporibus, cum nondum ab olea defracti essent, id præstitisse eos dicamus. Id largior Samari- tas suum codicem(acceptum ab illo Sacerdote)postquam DEI cultum miscuerant cum suo fœtore, e nullo Hebræo voluisse emendare, aut in eum aliquid transsumere. Nam odium & pervicacia nimia erat. Itaq̃ quicquid recti bonique in eorum codice inest, id antiquissimo illi Hebræo,cum sub Ezechia primum imbuti sunt lege Mo- sis,deberi: at quicquid deviat & obliquatur, ad nor- mam recti apud Judæos depositam & originariam de- bet examinari. Hæc Schotanus. Quanquam nec id concedendum quod moderni Codices Samarita- ni antiquo illi congruant: quum in perfida ista gen- te tam diuturno tempore non habita accurata sem- per fuerit Codicis sacri cura. A Levitis certe Pen- tatevchi,cujus major erat usus, accuratiorem ratio- nem apud Judæos habitam esse, certum est, neque facile corrumpi libri potuere, qui in Synagogis le- gebantur semper, quin vel minima discrepantia per memoriam populi observata fuisset. Et quis am- biget excubasse potius divinam providentiam pro Codice, quem Canoni Ecclesiæ destinarat & Judæis crediderat,quam pro Samaritanum Scriptura, pro- fanæ commixtionis cultus divini gratia exhibita. Ut taceam,quod Eulogius, Patriarcha Alexandrinus, observante Jacobo Usserio, Archi-Episcopo Armacha- no in Epist ad Arnoldum Bootium docuerit, Mosai- ci voluminis apud Samaritas corruptelas factas, & a Dositheo hæresiarcha, Simoni Mago æquali, profectas esse. Neque vero consentaneum aut probabile est, e notis numerabilibus lapsus & errores irrepsisse, siquidem expressis verbis numeri annorum descri- pti sint, uti hodie in Ebraicis, Chaldaicis, Syriacis li bris sit,imo olim ita etiam factum esse e M. SS. Ju- daicis notissimum est, quo de vid. Hackspan. de scri- ptor. Judaic. in Theol. usu c. 11. p. 335. neque nudis solum notis numeros designatos fuisse constat; ac mutationes istæ ita comparatæ sint,ut vel sola inspe- ctio earum docere possit,ex incuria vel inadverten- tia numericarum notarum errores istos haud esse profectos.

Quæcunque vero diversitatis illius causa vel origo sit, nulla causa est, cur Ebraicæ veritatis, quam Deus voluit regulæ & canonis vicem obtine- re in Ecclesia,quæque religiose a Judæis habita & asservata est, ad cujus normam revocatæ semper sunt aliæ editiones, fidem sollicitari patiamur ob diversitatem sive Neoterici suspecti, obscuri, maxi meque dubii, imo multis modis corrupti Codicis alicujus prophanæ & abominabilis gentis, qualis est Samaritica, sive translationis Græcæ, quæ LXX.

Interpp. dicitur, ac in innumeris locis sublestæ fi- dei ac depravata deprehenditur. Hieronymus sa- ne, melioris antiquitatis promus condus, jam ante tredecim secula Samaritano Codici, quem longe pu- riorem ac emendatiorem Neotericis istis habere potuit, non multum tribuit, nisi cum eundem Ebræo consonantem invenit: Tum enim ob consensum cum eodem translationibus aberrantibus ipsum opposuit: atque ea ratione etiam LXX. Interpp. red- arguit ex utriusq; Codicis Ebræi & Samaritici con- sonantia in his anachronismis Patriarchalibus. Ita observat Hieronymus e. g. in annis Mathusalæ in tra- dition. Ebraic. in Genes. cum Gen. V, 25. 26. Græca versio habet: Et vixit Mathusale annis 167. & genuit Lamech; Et vixit Mathusalah, postquam genuit Lamech, annis 802. & genuit filios & filias, non in E- bræis tantum, sed & in Samaritanorum libris ita scri- ptum sefe reperisse, uti adhuc Codex Ebræus habet, & vixit Mathusala 187. annis & genuit Lamech: & vi- xit Mathusala, postquam genuit Lamech, 782. annos, & genuit filios & filias. Jam si conferantur moder- ni Codices Samaritani & LXX. Interpp. uterq; hic mutatus deprehenditur: quum in Samaritano Mo- rini Mathusalah anno jam 67. genuisse Lamechum dicatur, & deinceps vixisse tantum 653. annos, ut juxta Samaritas universa ætas Mathusalæ tantum fuerit 720. annorum, cujus tamen ætatem LXX. In- terpp. & juxta lectionem Hieronymianam, & pro- uti nunc habent, cum Ebræis fontibus ad annos 969. porrigunt, quemque μακροβιώτατον omnium mor- talium agnoscunt omnes. De quo in Schalscheb ita habetur: Anni ejus erant 969. neque quisquam homi- num tam diu vixit. Huc Thalmudicorum facit ob- servatio in בוחלין: Septem duplicarunt mundum, Mathusalah vidit Adamum, cui serviit annos 243. Schem Methuschalahum, cui serviit 48. annos; Ja- cob vidit Schemum, cui ministravit 20. annos. Am- ram vidit Jacobum. Achias Schilonites vidit Amra- mum 7. annos, habuitque annos 61. cum Ægypto exi- ret; Elias vidit Achiam; Elias autem adhuc est super- stes. Ex Arabibus Patricides Anno 600. Noachi mortuum Methusalah die Veneris circa meridiem die 21. Elud, tradit. Ut ante diluvium eum mortuum Orientales ὁμοθυμαδὸν consentiunt, ita etiam in eo conveniunt, quod vitæ longævitate omnes supera- rit. Et deprehendere hic licet triplicem lectionem Samaritanam in annis generationis Mathusalæ: ge- nuit enim Lamech, juxta lectionem Samaritanam Hieronymi, anno 187. juxta Morini lectionem anno 67. juxta Scaligeri in notis ad Græca Eusebii fra- gmenta, anno 77. Unde manifestum est, qua verita- te Capellus l. 5. p. 710. scripserit, Eusebium ante mil- le & trecentos annos EANDEM in numeris illis inter Judæorum & Samaritanorum Codicem discrepantiam observasse.

Nec conciliari ullatenus potest calculus sive Samaritanorum, sive Græcorum cum Chronologia sacra. Ad diluvium enim juxta Chronologiam sacram numerantur 1656. anni. At juxta Samarita- num Morini Codicem, 1307. solum anni recensen- tur ad diluvium, mortuusque fuerit juxta eundem non Mathusalah solum, sed & Jared & Lamech ipso diluvii anno, Mahaleel 17. annis ante diluvi- um. Quum vero Mathusalæ ceu maxime lon- gævo inter Patriarchas secundum consensum o- mnium Codicum Ebræorum, ipsiusque LXX. In- terpp. editionis, nec non juxta Samaritanos Hiero- nymi Codices 969. ætatis anni, si Mathusalah 67. ætatis anno genuit Lamechum, Lamech 53. anno Noa- chum, uti habet Morini Samariticus, & 600. an- no Noæh irruit diluvium, dicendum erit, septin- gentesimo vicesimo ætatis Mathusalæ anno, diluvium terram inundasse. Ubi ergo in diluvio mansit Mathusala, ad cujus ætatem complendam ita adhuc 249. anni desiderantur? Juxta Hebræos autem, inquit Hieronymus, & Samaritanos (sui temporis) Codices a die nativitatis Mathusalah usŕ; ad diem nativitatis Noæb sunt anni 369. (Morini Samariticus Codex habet tantum annos 120.) Eis adde 600. annos Noæb, quia in 600. anno vitæ ejus factum est diluvium, atŕ, ita fit, ut 969. anno vitæ suæ Mathusalah mortuus sit, eo anno, quo cœpit esse diluvium. Ita manifeste erroris convincitur modernus Codex Samariticus: qui etsi in annis vitæ Patriarcharum post diluvium Ebræis Codicibus de cætero consentiat, usque ad Thare, longe tamen aliter annos, quibus gignere cœperunt, assignat; Heberi etiam ætati 60. annos adimit, eumq; in universum tantum 404. annis vixisse refert: ac pariter totidem annos derogat quoque ætati Thare, & eum vixisse tantum 145. annos dicit, quum secundum Ebraicam veritatem 205. annis vixerit: Unde Chronologia sacra iterum confunditur.

Quam magis adhuc perturbat LXX. Interpp. editio, siquidem a condito mundo usque ad diluvium non 1656. sed 2242. annos, additis nempe 586. annis ad Patriarcharum ante-diluvianorum ætatem, numerent, ac porro adjiciant annis Patriarcharum post-diluvianorum usque ad Abrahamum 780. annos, unde insignis anachronismus Græcorum in supputandis mundi annis exortus. Manifestaria autem iterum hic est corruptela in Mathusalæ annis, quam sic evincit Hieronymus loco laudato; Etenim cum esset Mathusalah annorum 167. (secundum LXX.) genuit Lamech, rursum Lamech cum esset annorum 188. (secundum eosdem) genuit Noe. Et fiunt usŕ, ad diem nativitatis Noæ anni vitæ Mathusalæ 355. Sexcentesimo autem anno vitæ Noæ diluvium factũ est. Ac per hoc habita supputatione per partes, 955. anno Mathusalæ diluvium fuisse convincitur. Cum autem supra 969. annis vixisse sit dictus (apud LXX. Interpp.) nulli dubium est, 14. annos eum (secundum LXX. Interpp.) vixisse post diluvium. Hinc ergo invicte concludit Hieronymus, quod ut in PLERISQUE (apud LXX. Interpp.) ita & in hoc sit error in numero. Nequicquam igitur, notante Hieronymo, quæstione illa omnium Ecclesiarum disputatione ventilata interpretum & Doctorum, qui non nisi LXX. Interpp. versionem legere potuere, fatigata sunt ingenia, quomodo Mathusala 14. annos post diluvium vixisse referatur, & verum tamen sit, quod 1. Petr. 3, dicitur, octo tantum animas in arca salvas factas esse; quum juxta Ebræos & Samaritanos Codices in aprico sit, anno 969. vitæ suæ Mathusalam mortuum esse, tandemque cepisse diluvium. Nonnulli LXX. Interpp. versioni adhærescentes, quum veritatem Ebraicam ignorarent, Augustino lib. 15. de Civ. Dei c. 11. teste, eo adacti sunt, ut fingerent, Mathusalam per istos annos cum Patre suo Enocho vixisse, donec diluvium præteriret. Augustinus tamen, utut impense alias addictus Græcis Codicibus, universum computum eorum erroris postulare minime veritus est, partim librariorum incuria, partim fraude quorundam invecti, libro laudato, c. 13. addita hac generali maxima, intempestivis Criticis imprimis observanda: Nullo modo recte fieri dubitaverim, ut cum diversum aliquid in utrisque Codicibus invenitur, quandoquidem ad fidem rerum gestarum utrumque esse non potest verum, ei linguæ potius credatur, unde est in aliam per Interpretes facta translatio. Ridiculus vero, imo μωρὸς hic est Morinus, cum ob Ecclesiam Romanam, quæ & calculum LXX. Interpp. i- Martyrolog. IIX. Kal. Jan. & supputationem Hebræ- am in vulgata versione retentam canonizavit, utrū- que computum, etsi prorsus sibi contrari9 sit, tamen cum Cano, & Mariana in medio relinquit, (quo- modo enim potest relinquere, quum utrumque probarit Ecclesia?) sed pro vero venditat utrumq; Exercit. 7. cap. 1. cum Antonino T. I. Chron. c. 1. Spiritum S. non sine mysterio sic disposuisse, ad majus meritum fidei; quasi Spiritus S. contradictorie oppo- sita disponat, ad fidei meritum, quod est Spiritui ve- ritatis mendacium impie ac blaspheme impingere, atque inde adhuc meritum extruere, si talis impie- tas credatur, aut admittatur.

## 5:22
Verse 22. AND ENOCH WALKED WITH GOD) That is, as the Greeks translate here and in v. 24, Enoch pleased God. The same sense is found in the Syriac. The writer to the Hebrews 11, 5, has been testified to have pleased God.

It is certain that Enoch pleased God from Heb. 11, 5. But that to walk with God is the same thing for him, whence, I pray, is it evident? That those are different things, no one fails to see. The one expresses those things which were pleasing to God in Enoch, faith and piety: the other indicates that Enoch was pleasing to God. But the emphasis of the word walked with God, as it sounds in the Hebrew, was explained by Blessed Luther, who can be consulted here.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET AMBVLAVIT ENOCH CVM DEO) Id est, ut Græci & hic & v. 24. vertunt εὐηρέστησεν Ἐνὼχ τῷ Θεῷ. Idem sensus apud Syrum. Scriptor ad Hebræos 11, 5. μεμαρτύρη- ται εὐηρεστηκέναι τῷ Θεῷ.

Certum est, placuisse Deo Enochum ex Ebr. 11, 5. Sed quod ambulare cum Deo idem illi sit, unde obsecro, constat? Diversa illa esse, nemo non videt. Alterum ea, quæ Deo grata erant in Enocho, fidem & pietatem exprimit: alterum quod Enoch gratus Deo fuerit, indicat. Emphasin autem vocis ambulavit Deum, uti in Ebræo sonat, exposuit B. Lu- therus, qui hic consuli poterit.

## 5:24
Verse 24. AND HE DID NOT APPEAR, BECAUSE GOD TOOK HIM] The Samaritan: His Angel took him. Onkelos: God did not kill him: that is, he did not suffer him to die. Jonathan: He was taken away, and ascended into heaven by the command before the Lord. The writer to the Hebrews: By faith Enoch was translated so as not to see death and was not found, because God had translated him. Josephus: He departed to the divinity. The same about Enoch and Elijah, that they became invisible. He was translated into Paradise, says the Arab in the cited passage to the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET NON APPARVIT, QVIA TVLIT EVM DEVS] Samaritanus: accepit eum Angelus ejus. Onckelos: Non occidit eum Deus: id est, non passus est mori Jonathan: Sublatus fuit, & ascendit in cælum ex mandato coram Domino. Scriptor ad Hebræos: πίστει Ἐνὼχ μετετέθη τοῦ μὴ ἰδεῖν θάνατον καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκετο, διότι μετατέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεός. Josephus, ἀνεχώρησε πρὸς τὸ θεῖον. Idem de Enocho & Elia, ὅτι γεγό- νασιν ἀφανεῖς. Translatus est in Paradisum, ait Arabs dicto ad Hebræos loco.

## 5:27
Verse 27. NINE HUNDRED SIXTY NINE YEARS] Besides the testimonies of this longevity which exist in Josephus, Varro also noted from histories that the ancients lived up to a thousand years, but he himself wrongly took months for years; in which there would be nothing to wonder at. See Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book II, ch. 13.

On this matter, in book 1 of On the Truth of the Christian Religion, p. 20, Grotius has it thus: Berosus in his Chaldaica, Manetho in his Aegyptiaca, Hiromus in his Phoenicia, Hestiaeus, Hecataeus, and Hellanicus in their Greek works have recorded that the life of those who followed the first men lasted for nearly a thousand years. And specifically Pausanias and Philostratus among the Greeks, and Pliny among the Romans. In the Annotations to this passage, page 39, he added these things concerning μακροβιότητι [longevity]: Josephus cites all these writers as witnesses, while their books were still extant in his own time, in Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 4, and besides these, Acusilaus, Ephorus, and Nicolaus of Damascus. Servius, in his note on Aeneid VIII, notes that the Arcadians were accustomed to live for 300 years. Regarding the huge stature of men, Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book V, chapter 2. There remained even then a race of giants, who, because of the size and shape of their bodies, which were very different from other men, were a stupendous spectacle and terrible in their reputation: their bones, which exceed all belief of the common people, are shown to this day. Gabinius, in his description of Mauretania, said that the bones of Antaeus were found by Sertorius, the structure of which was sixty cubits. Phlegon of Tralles, in chapter 9 of his Mirabilia, mentions the skull of Ida that was dug up, which was triple the usual size. The same author adds that many bodies were found in Dalmatia, the ulnae of which exceeded 16 ulnae. The same author narrates, from Theopompus, that a structure of human bones 24 cubits long was found in the Cimmerian Bosporus. There exists a booklet by the same Phlegon on long-lived people, truly worthy of reading. Pausanias in his Laconica mentions human bones, but of unusual size, which were shown in the Temple of Asclepius near the city of Asopus: And in the first book of his Eliaca, he mentions a bone brought up from the sea, which had once been kept at Pisa and was believed to be that of Pelops. Philostratus, at the beginning of his Heroicus, says that many giant bodies are uncovered in Pallene by rains or earthquakes. Pliny, book 7, chapter 16. In Crete, a mountain having been broken by an earthquake, a standing body was found, which some report to have been Orion's, others Ection's. The body of Orestes, dug up by the command of an oracle, is reported by records to have been seven cubits long. Now, indeed, nearly a thousand years ago, that poet Homer did not cease to complain that the bodies of mortals were smaller than those of the ancients. Solinus, chapter 1. For who is not born smaller than his parents in this age? Moreover, the remains of Orestes himself attest to the size of the ancients, whose bones, found at Tegea in the fifty-eighth Olympiad by the Spartans, who were warned by an oracle, we learn filled a length of seven cubits. Writings also, which summon memories from antiquity to the assurance of truth, have even received this, that in the Cretan war, when swollen rivers had broken through the lands with more than riverine force, after the departure of the floods, among many fissures in the ground, a human body was found of thirty-three cubits, at the sight of which L. Flaccus the Legate, and Metellus himself, were so greatly captivated by the miracle that they enjoyed with their own eyes what they had refuted by hearsay. Concerning a molar tooth of a man seen by him, see Augustine, book 15, On the City of God, chapter 11. These are the words of Grotius.

It is not permitted to infer from an unusual stature that long-lived life. For the reason for each is different. Nor were those who were long-lived so polluted by such a monstrous stature; nor was the portentous stature of giants common to the age of the Patriarchs, in which that longevity flourished remarkably. Furthermore, this deviation is like a monster; it cannot be referred to the common order. But that long life was natural then, and almost ordinary: certainly to be acknowledged as an eminent benefit: by which God rewarded the piety of the ancients, and which served the propagation of the heavenly doctrine, which took place through tradition handed down from fathers, and the cultivation of astronomy and other arts. And the Patriarchs were closer to the first origin, the temperament was better, and the nourishment of the ancients was simpler; Adam with the other Patriarchs used a more moderate diet of herbs and fruits; the earth not yet devastated by the flood, the plants were more wholesome and the animals of a stronger nature, the air purer; the infection and corruption of the elements from sin, now increased, is even greater now, and contagions are more frequent; finally, they were chaster in the past, and perhaps in their 80th year first contracted marriages: and other causes similar to these are brought forward by others. Moreover, that men before the flood were not of greater stature is evident even from this, that the cubits of the ark did not differ from the cubits by which they measured in the time of Moses. The increase and decrease of age is from sin, not so of stature. The age of men before the flood exceeded ours tenfold or ninefold: if you think that difference existed in stature, what monsters would you have produced?

Latin:

Vers. 27. NONGENTI SEXAGINTA NOVEM ANNI] Præter testimonia hujus longævitatis, quæ apud Josephum ex- stant, etiam Varro ex historiis notavit antiquos ad mille annos victitasse, sed male ipse pro annis accepit menses; in quo nihil esset mirandum. Vide Lactantium institutionum lib. II. c. 13.

Hac de re lib. 1. de Verit. Relig. Christ. p. 20. ita habet Grotius: Eorum, qui primos homines secuti sunt, vitam ad mille ferme annos durasse Berosus in Chaldaicis, Manethos in Ægyptiacis, Hiromus in Phœnicis, Hestiæus, Hecatæus, Hellanicus in Græ- cis prodiderunt. Ac nominatim Græcorum Pausa- nias & Philostratus, Romanorum Plinius. In An- notatis ad h. l. pag. 39. de μακροβιότητι hæc adjecit: Omnes hos Scriptores suo adhuc tempore manentibus libris, testes citat Josephus Antiquæ historiæ lib. 1. c. 4. ac præter hos Acusilaum Ephorum, Nicolaum Damascenum. Arcadas ad CCC. annos vivere soli- tos notat ad VIII. Æneidos Servius. De statura ve- ro hominum ingenti Josephus Antiquæ Histor. lib. V. c. 2. Restabat etiam tum gigantum genus, qui ob cor- poris magnitudinem ac figuras multum aliis hominum dispares stupendum erant spectaculum, & fama terri- biles: monstrantur in hunc diem eorum ossa fidem o- mnem vulgi excedentia. Gabinius in Mauritaniæ descriptione dicebat a Sertorio reperta Antæi ossa, quo- rum compagem fuisse cubitorum sexaginta. Phle- gon Trallianus Mirabilium cap. 9. meminit effossi ca- pitis Idæ, quod triplo esset ad solitum modum quanti- tatis. Addit idem in Dalmatia reperta corpora multa, quorum ulnæ XVI. ulnas excederent. Nar- rat idem ex Theopompo in Bosphoro Cimmerio repertam ossium humanorum compagem longam 24. cubitos. Ejusdem Phlegontis exstat libellus de lon- gævis, dignus sane lectu. Pausanias in Laconicis meminit ossium humanorum sed insolitæ magnitudi- nis, quæ in Templo Æsculapii ad Asopum urbem osten- debantur: Et in Eliacorum priore ossis e mari educti, quod olim Pisæ custoditum, Pelopisque creditum fuerat. Philostratus in Heroicorum initio multa ait gigantea corpora in Pallene detegi per imbres aut terræmotus. Plinius lib. 7. c. 16. In Creta terræ motu rupto monte inventus est corpus stans, quod alii Orionis, alii Ectionis fuisse tradunt. Orestis corpus Oraculi jussu refossum septem cubitorum fuisse monumentis traditur. Jam vero ante annos prope mil- le vates ille Homerus non cessavit minora corpora mor- talium, quam prisca conqueri. Solinus cap. 1. Quis enim non ævo isto minor parentibus suis nascitur? Priscorum autem testantur molem etiam Orestis supre- ma, cujus ossa Olympiade quinquagesima octava Tegeæ inventa a Spartanis Oraculo monitis discimus implesse longitudinem cubitorum septem. Scripta quoque, quæ ex antiquitate memorias accersunt in fidem veri, hoc etiam receperunt, quod bello Cretico, cum elata flumi- na plusquam vi amnica terras rupissent, post discessum fluctuum inter plurima humi discidia humanum cor- pus repertum sit cubituum trium atque triginta, cujus inspectandi cupidine L. Flaccum Legatum, Metellum etiam ipsum impendio captos miraculo, quod auditu re- futaverant oculis potitos. De molari hominis dente a se conspecto vid. Augustinum lib. 15. de Civit. Dei c. 11. Hæc Grotius.

Non colligere licet e statura inusitata ad vitam illam longævam. Nam dispar est utriusque ratio. Nec qui μακρόβιοι adeo fuere, monstrosa ejusmodi statura polluerunt; aut Pattiarcharum ætati, qua μακροβιότης ista insignis vigebat, portentosa gigan- tum statura communis fuit. Tum deviatio hæc naturæ & monstri instar est; non ad ordinem com- munem referri potest. At illa longæva vita natu- ralis tum fuit, ac pene ordinaria : Pro beneficio certe eminenti agnoscenda : qua Deus pietatem majorum remunerabatur, ac propagationi doctri- næ cœlestis, quæ per traditionem πατροπαράδοξον fiebat, & culturæ Astronomiæ, ac aliarum artium velificabatur. Et propinquiores erant Patriarchæ primæ origini, temperamentum erat melius, & nu- trimentum antiquorum simplicius, Adamus cum aliis Patriarchis moderatiori victu herbarum & fru- ctuum utebatur, terra nondum vastata diluvio erant plantæ salubriores & animalia fortioris naturæ, aër purior, infectio & corruptio Elementorum ex pec- cato jam auctiori major etiam nunc est, & frequen- tiora contagia; castiores denique olim fuere, ac 80. forte anno primum contraxere matrimonia: & quæ his similes aliæ causæ ab aliis adducuntur. Homi- nes autem ante diluvium majoris staturæ non fuisse, vel ex eo patet, quod cubiti arcæ non discreparint a cubitis, quibus Mosis tempore metiebantur. Æ- tatis incrementum & decrementum a peccato est, non ita staturæ. Ætas hominum ante diluvium nostram decies, aut novies excessit: quod si diffe- rentiam eam in statura fuisse putes, quanta monstra dederis?

## 5:29
Verse 29. HE SHALL COMFORT US) The sense is the same, but the etymology does not correspond to the name. Therefore, the Greeks more correctly read יניחנו instead of ינחמנו. For they translated it as 'he shall give rest,' which exactly shows the origin of the name. Thus also Philo cites in his book, 'The worse lies in wait for the better.' In the Hieronymian index of names: Noah, cessation, rest. The Samaritan Paraphrast: 'He shall sustain our works, and the oppression of our hands,' that is, he shall be our substitute for the works of the field.

Verse of the same. AND FROM THE LABORS OF OUR HANDS] The Chaldean [translates it] from weariness. Thus it appears that the word עצב is correctly taken in Proverbs 10:22 and 14:23.

Thus, therefore, Grotius corrects not only the Hebrew text but also the Vulgate version, which is authentic among the Papists. He prefers the Greek text, and thinks that the Hebrew Codices of the Seventy Interpreters once had it otherwise. But there is no need for this invention. For it can be said that either the name Noah had its origin from 'he comforted,' or if it is derived from 'he rested,' Lamech wished to interchange related words, so that he might express more effectively what he had conceived in his mind concerning this son of his; namely, that he would be both a tranquilizer, as he designated him by his proper name, and a comforter: which he testified by the reason of the appellation added: as he would bring rest by that very fact, because he would comfort from labor and from pain. Nor does the Chaldean Interpreter read it here otherwise than it is now held in the Hebrew Codex, or the author of the Vulgate version. The former rendered יְנַחֲמֵנִי 'He shall comfort us.' The Seventy, however, rendered it 'he shall give rest,' because, as it appears, they looked to the name Noah, or did not distinguish related words, as is often done.

Moreover, the explanation of this birthday congratulation, which Grotius subjoins, 'he shall be our substitute for the works of the field,' is too rustic, and is twin to the delirium of the Jews, that Noah discovered an easier method of agriculture through the labor of beasts of burden. The most holy Patriarchs were not so carnal and earthly that they would rejoice that they had obtained relief or help in the works of the field at the birth of their sons, and from that even impose names upon their sons. Nor does this gloss in any way correspond to the sweetness of the name or to the congratulation of Lamech. Is that famous rest, is that remarkable comfort in the labors and sorrows of the earth, which the Lord cursed, truly worthy of such a great Patriarch, that he believed he had begotten a rustic and a certain son of the earth?

But it is no wonder that Grotius feels such abject things about the Patriarchs, who, with Socinus, thought the ancients were fattened only by the hope of earthly goods and destitute of spiritual promises. But since those for whose sake the first gospel concerning the crushing of the serpent's head was first promulgated undoubtedly understood its power most correctly, and by the faithful memory of it always sustained themselves in the labors and sorrows of earthly life, there is no doubt that the pious ancients preferred to give evidence of their trust and hope, and everything in those ancient centuries of profound wisdom and true piety, in the naming of their children, rather than to have a taste only for earthly things.

The emphatic words of this speech certainly breathe the remarkable faith of Lamech, so that we cannot but agree here with our blessed Luther. His explanation is entirely worthy of being read here. The simplest, he says, and true meaning is that after Lamech the grandson sees his grandfather Enoch taken away from those miseries, afflictions, and labors of original sin with a certain indication of a future life, and a son is born to him, he calls him Noah, i.e., rest, because he hopes it will come to pass that through him deliverance from the curses of sin and from sin itself will occur. This interpretation is analogous to faith, and confirms the hope of the resurrection and eternal life. Those Patriarchs were most holy men and adorned with the highest gifts, as Heroes of the whole world. In them we see the highest desire for the future seed. That is of the highest value among them; they so thirst, hunger, burn, and gape for Christ who is to come. For Lamech expressly urges that the curse must be removed. But the curse or punishment of sin cannot be removed unless the sin of origin itself is first removed. This is blessed Luther.

This interpretation agrees not only with the faith and desire of the Patriarch, and other patriarchal congratulations, and the omens of the names which they imposed upon their sons, such as Cain, Gen. 4:1, and Seth, v. 3, concerning which B. Glassius writes in his Mosaic Christology, and with the narrative of Moses, the leader of the Prophets, who is commended as a remarkable witness of the Messiah, and whom Christ himself particularly celebrates because he wrote of him, John 5:46, but it especially agrees also with the name which is imposed here, and the congratulation of Lamech, and the individual words of the same, which proclaim with a clear voice that he had the same Messiah in mind.

The name נוּחַ denotes a tranquillizer, who brings rest. But who was to bring true rest, except him who exclaims in Matthew 11:28-29: Come to me ALL, WHO LABOR AND ARE HEAVY LADEN, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς: I will refresh you. You will find ἀνάπαυσιν REST for your souls. It cannot be doubted that Lamech was more concerned for the rest of the soul than of the body. That is obtained solely in the Messiah, was expected solely from him, and happened solely in him and through him to ALL believers. Christ here uses the same word ἀναπαύσω, which the LXX interpreters used in rendering the reason for the name Noah. And he promises rest from burdens and labors: which words οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι respond to the Hebrews in the prayer of Lamech in such a way that Christ can be considered to have pointed his finger at that, namely, that he is that tranquillizer whom Lamech was panting for so greatly. And indeed the Patriarch expected not just any rest, but true and solid rest: which that true Noah brings solely, so that in this life, amidst various labors and burdens or anxieties, believers find true rest in him alone, and in the other life hope for ἀνάπαυσιν through him, immune from all labor and pain: just as the blessed who die in this LORD ἀναπαύσωνται ἐκ τῶν κόπων αὐτῶν, REST from their LABORS. But the WORKS or the fruits of those works will follow them, Revelation 14:13. Compare Hebrews 4:11.

Furthermore, that pointing out by Lamech זֶה יְנַחֲמֵנוּ HE SHALL COMFORT US, demonstrates a Comforter not common, but most distinguished, whom believers have vehemently desired until now: as if to say זֶה HE is the one whom we have expected, he now shall comfort us: He will not only be the author of true rest, but also our comforter. God had designated him with a similar pronoun הוּא in Genesis 3:15. Moreover, the Ancients hoped for solid consolation in the Messiah in such a way that, because of the expectation of him, the announcing prophet thought he should exclaim nothing other than this very word נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ Comfort, comfort my people, Isaiah 40:1. For they sought this consolation with perpetual sighs, Psalm 80:8; with this they raised themselves up, by the example of David, Psalm 23:4. By this they were raised up by the Prophets of the Lord, Isaiah 49:13. Compare verses 6 and 8. Because this office is proper to the Messiah, for whose sake he was to be sent לְנַחֵם to comfort all who mourn, Isaiah 61:2, therefore the παράκλησις consolation of Israel was expected by the faithful, Luke 2:25.
