And this is also the reason why he called himself by this name of Paraclete, John 14:16, and wished to be called so, 1 John 2:1.

Now if those words are weighed by which Lamech expresses the miseries in need of consolation, מִמַּעֲשֵׂנוּ work, which the Chaldean rendered עִיבָדָנָא servile work, and B. Luther rendered Mühe (toil), and עִצְבוֹן from עָצַב (to grieve, to be sad and anxious). The LXX render it ἀπὸ τῶν λυπῶν from sorrows; some explain them not badly in this way, that by the former they wish to designate temporal punishments and evils of the body and fortune, which they call external; but by the latter, the internal anxiety and sadness of the heart and soul. But those things are best declared by κόποις (labors) and φόρτοις (burdens) which produce anxiety in the golden words of Christ in Matthew 11. But who is he through whom the Patriarchs believed they would be freed from these evils and anxieties, if not הַגֹּאֵל that redeemer whom the Patriarch Jacob celebrates with this eulogy: WHO has delivered me from ALL EVIL, Genesis 48:16. And lest it be ambiguous that the punishments denounced to Adam and Eve after the fall are being referred to here, Lamech wished to use here that very word which GOD had used twice—once regarding the sorrows of women, then regarding the sorrows of man to be endured thereafter, indicated immediately after the Paradisiacal promise—so that he might signify that for the whole human race, in both sexes, refreshment and consolation were now to be expected in whatever sorrows and punishments of sin. Nor does it seem to be without reason that he added the word יָדֵינוּ of our hands, since the origin of evils is indicated in this way. For by the extension of hands to the forbidden tree, Genesis 3:6, those labors and sorrows were brought upon the human race, in which they desired refreshment. Finally, the description of the earth must not be passed over here, because the same words הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר אֲרְרָהּ the earth, which he cursed, are used in this place, which are read in the first threatening of punishments, Genesis 3:17. אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה let the earth be cursed. For against that curse, which was inflicted upon the whole earth through the first sin, only the one Messiah could bring consolation. It is most evident that he speaks of the whole earth, and of the curse of the earth, which was from sin.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ISTE CONSOLABITUR NOS) Sensus idem, sed Etymologia nomini non respondet. Itaque rectius Græci pro ינחמנו legunt יניחנו. Verterunt enim διαναπαύσει, quod originem nominis exacte ostendit. Sic & Philo citat li- bro, pejorem insidiari meliori. In Hieronymiano nominum in- dice: Noe, cessatio, requies. Samaritanus Paraphrastes: sustentabit opera nostra, & oppressionem manuum nostrarum, id est, erit ad ruris opera vicarius noster.

Vers. eod. ET LABORIBUS MANUUM NOSTRARUM] Chaldæus a lassitudine. Sic vocem עצב recte sumi apparet Prov. 10, 22. & 14, 23.

Ita ergo corrigit Grotius non modo Ebræum textum, sed & Vulgatam versionem Pontificiis au- thenticam. Præfert vero textum Græcum, & Ebræ- os Codices LXX. Interpretum aliter quondam ha- buisse censet. Sed non opus hoc commento. Dici enim potest, vel נוח nomen suum habuisse a נחם consolatus est; aut si a נוח quievit, deduca- tur, voluisse Lamechum permutare cognata verba, ut eo efficacius exprimeret, quod animo concepe- rat de hoc filio suo; Eundem nempe fore & tran- quillatorem, uti nomine proprio ipsum designabat; & consolatorem: quod per rationem appellationis adjunctam testabatur: utpote eo ipso quietem alla- turum, quod consolaturus sit a labore & a dolore. Nec aliter legit hîc Chaldæus Interpres, quam nunc habe- tur in Ebræo Codice, vel autor Vulgatæ versionis. Ille reddidit יְנַחֲמֵנִי Hic consolabitur nos. LXX. vero reddiderunt διαναπαύσει, quod, ut apparet, respexerint nomen Noah, aut cognata verba, uti fæ- pe factum, non distinxerint.

Explicatio autem gratulationis hujus γενεθλια- κῆς, quam subjungit Grotius, hic erit ad opera ruris noster vicarius, nimis rustica, & Judæorum delirio, Noam faciliorem agriculturæ ratione per jumentorum operam invenisse, gemina est. Non fuerunt ita σαρ- κικοὶ καὶ χοϊκοὶ sanctissimi Patriarchæ, ut in filiorum nativitate levamen vel adjutorium in operibus ru- ris se consequi tripudiarint, inde etiam nomina filiis imposuerint. Neque vel nominis suavitas, vel gratulationi Lamechi hæc glossa ullatenus respon- det. Annon præclara illa quies, annon insignis il- la in laboribus & doloribus terræ, cui maledixit Dominus, consolatio tanto Patriarcha omnino di- gna, quod rusticum & terræ filium quendam pro- creasse se crediderit?

Sed non mirum, tam abjecta de Patriarchis Grotium sentire, qui cum Socino terrenorum tan- tum bonorum spe saginatos Veteres promissionibus spiritualibus destitutos existimavit. Quum vero πρωτευαγγελίε de contritione capitis serpentini vim illi, quorum causa primo id promulgatum fuit, sine dubio rectissime intellexerint, ejusdem fideli memoria se nunquam non in laboribus & doloribus terrenæ vitæ sustentarint, dubium non est, pios Ve- teres fiduciæ, speique suæ documenta & omnia in priscis illis profundæ sapientiæ veræque pietatis se- culis in ὀνομαθεσίᾳ liberorum suorum edere potius voluisse, quam terrena tantum sapuisse.

Verba certe emphatica hujus orationis spi- rant insignem Lamechi fidem, ut non possimus non cum B. Luthero nostro hîc facere. Cujus expli- catio digna omnino est, quæ hic legatur. Simpli- cissima, inquit, & vera sententia est, quod postquam Lamech nepos videt avum Henoch sublatum ex istis miseriis, afflictionibus & laboribus peccati originalis cum certa significatione futuræ vitæ, eique nascitur Fi- lius, appellat eum Noah, h. e. quietem, quia sperat futurum, ut per eum liberatio a maledictionibus peccati & ipso peccato contingat. Hæc interpretatio est analoga fidei, & confirmat spem resurrectionis & vitæ æternæ. Fuerunt illi Patriarchæ homines sanctissimi & summis donis ornati, tanquam Heroes totius mun- di. In his videmus summum desiderium futuri seminis. Id apud eos in summo pretio est, ita sitiunt, esuriunt, ar- dent, inhiant in Christum venturum. Diserte enim ur- get Lamech, maledictionem tollendam esse. Atqui ma- ledictio seu pœna peccati non potest tolli, nisi prius tol- latur ipsum peccatum originis. Hæc B. Lutherus.

Congruit hæc interpretatio non tantum fidei & desiderio Patriarchæ, aliisque gratulationibus Patriarchalibus, & nominum, quæ filiis suis im- posuerunt, ominibus, utpote Caini, Gen. 4, 1. & Sethi v. 3. de quibus in Christol. Mosaic. B. Glassius, ac narrationi Mosis Antefignani Prophetarum, qui ceu insignis Messiæ testis commendatur, quemque Christus ipse peculiariter celebrat, quod de se scri- pserit Joh. 5, 49. sed imprimis convenit ea etiam nomini, quod hic imponitur, & gratulationi La- mechi, ac singulis verbis ejusdem, quæ λευκάδι φω- νῇ Messiam eundem in mente habuisse, proclamant.

Nomen נוּחַ tranquillatorem, qui quietem afferat, notat. Quis autem veram quietem afferre debuit, præter eum, qui Matth. 11, 28. 29. exclamat: Venite ad me OMNES, QVI LABORATIS ET ONERATI ESTIS, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς: ego recreabo vos. Invenietis ἀνάπαυσιν REQUIEM animabus vestris. De animæ requie sollicitum magis fuisse Lamechum, quam corporis, dubitari nequit. Ea vero unice in Messia obtinetur, unice ab eodem expectabatur, OMNIBVSQVE fidelibus unice in ipso & per ipsum contigit. Idem hic verbum adhibet Christus ἀναπαύσω, quo in reddenda nominis Noæh ratione usi sunt LXX. Interpp. & quietem ab oneribus & laboribus promittit: quæ voces οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι ita respondent Ebræis in oratione Lamechi, ut eo digitum intendisse Christus censeri possit, se nempe illum esse tranquillatorem, quem tantopere anhelabat Lamechus. Nec vero requiem qualemcunq́;, sed veram atque solidam expectavit Patriarcha: quam unice affert verus ille Noachus, ut hac quidem vita inter labores atque onera vel anxietates varias in ipso solo veram quietem inveniant fideles, in altera vero vita ἀνάπαυσιν per ipsum sperent, ab omni labore & dolore immunem: uti beati in hoc DOMINO mortui ἀναπαύσωνται ἐκ τῶν κόπων αὐτῶν, REQUIESCANT a LABORIBUS suis. OPERA vero vel fructus operum illorum sequentur ipsos Apoc. 14, 13. Confer Ebr. 4, 11.

Porro δεῖξις illa Lamechi זֶה יְנַחֲמֵנוּ ILLE CONSOLABITUR NOS, Consolatorem non vulgarem, sed maxime insignem, quem vehementer desiderarunt hactenus fideles, demonstrat: q. d. זֶה ILLE est, quem expectavimus, ille nunc consolabitur nos: Non tantum quietis veræ autor erit, sed etiam consolator noster. Quem simili pronomine הוּא designarat Deus Genes. 3, 15. Consolationem autem solidam ita Veteres in Messia sperarunt, ut ob expectationem ejus non aliter exclamandum censuerit prænuncius vates, quam hoc ipso verbo נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ Consolamini, consolamini populum meum Es. 40, 1. Hanc enim consolationem suspiriis expetierunt perpetuis Ps. 80, 8. hac erexerunt sese, Davidis exemplo Ps. 23, 4. Hac erecti sunt a Prophetis Domini Es. 49, 13. Confer v. 6. 8. Quod munus Messiæ proprium est, cujus gratia mitti debuit לְנַחֵם ad consolandum omnes lugentes Esa. 61. v. 2, ideo expectata fuit a fidelibus παράκλησις consolatio Israelis Luc. 2, 25. Atque hæc etiam causa est, quod hoc παρακλήτου nomine sese tum appellarit ipse Joh. 14, 16. tum appellari voluerit 1. Joh. 2, 1.

Jam si verba illa expendantur, quibus exprimit Lamechus miserias consolationis indigas מִמַּעֲשֵׂנוּ opus, quod Chaldæus עִיבָדָנָא opus servile B. Lutherus Mühe reddidit, & עִצְבוֹן ab עָצַב doluit, tristis & anxius fuit. LXX. reddunt ἀπὸ τῶν λυπῶν a tristitiis; explicant nonnulli ea non male hoc pacto, ut priori pœnas temporales & mala corporis & fortunæ, quæ vocant externa; posteriori vero interiorem cordis & animæ anxietatem & tristitiam designari velint. Sed optime illa κόποις laboribus, & φόρτοις oneribus anxietatem parientibus in aureolo Christi Matth. 11. declarata sunt. Quis vero est, per quem crediderint Patriarchæ ab hisce malis & anxietatib9 se liberatum iri, nisi הַגֹּאֵל redemtor ille, quem Jacob Patriarcha hoc elogio celebrat; QUI me liberavit ab OMNI MALO. Genes. 48, 16. Et ne ambiguum sit, respici hic pœnas Adamo & Evæ post lapsum denunciatas, ipsam illam vocem quam duabus vicibus semel de mulierum doloribus, tum de doloribus viri deinceps exantlandis, immediate post Paradisicam promissionem indicatis adhibuerat DEUS, hic quoque adhibere voluit La- mechus, ut toti humano generi, in utroque sexu refo- cillationem & consolationem in quibuscunque dolo- ribus, pœnisque peccati jam expectandam esse, significaret. Nec abs re addidisse videtur vocem יָדֵינוּ manuum nostrarum, quum indicetur ita origo malorum. Manuum enim extensione ad arborem veti- tam Gen. 3, 6. labores & dolores illi generi humano accersiti erant, in quibus refocillationem desidera- bant. Tandem non prætermittenda hic terræ de- scriptio, quod eædem voces הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר אֲרְרָהּ terra, cui maledixit, hoc loco adhibeantur, quæ in prima pœnarum comminatione leguntur Gen. 3, 17. אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה maledicta sit terra. Adversus eam enim maledictionem, quæ per primum pecca- tum universæ terræ inflicta est, consolationem adfer- re non nisi unus Messias poterat. De terra univer- sa, & de maledictione terræ, quæ a peccato erat, ipsum loqui evidentissimum est.

## 5:31 Addition
On Gen. 5:31. NOAH WHEN HE WAS FIVE HUNDRED YEARS OLD BEGAT.

It is asked why he did not beget until then, before his five-hundredth year? And the answer: God seems to have disposed it thus, because He had determined to save him with his posterity: for if they had begun to beget in the hundredth year like the others, there would have been so many children born from him who could not have been competently kept in the ark with the necessities, and many of them would have been evil, whom it would not be worthy to save. Thus Lyranus. The ἐπίκρισις (critique) which Matthew Polus delivered in this place in his Synopsis Crit. p. 73, concerning the opinion of Walton in his Proleg. in Bibl. n. 58 and Morin in his Exerc. Bibl. 7, 2, that the calculation of years of the LXX edition is to be preferred to the Hebrew text, and the contrary opinion of Ussher in his Chron. Sacr. c. 5, deserves censure altogether. Whichever opinion the reader follows, he will easily perceive that the truth and ἀυτοπιστία (self-credibility) of Holy Scripture are kept intact and that every handle for caviling is taken away from atheists. For if he follows the Hebrew calculation, the faith and truth of Scripture will be sufficiently established from the things said and the deeds done (which historians report): If he prefers the Greek, and accuses the Hebrew codices of corruption, our faith or the certainty of Scripture will not for that reason waver in matters of greater moment (in the protection of which divine providence has watched more carefully, as is sufficiently evident from the supreme consensus among all kinds of codices regarding them), because in matters of lesser weight, e.g., chronological and historical, God has allowed some σφάλματα (errors) to creep in for the exercise of our faith, which to our blinded minds, and those ignorant of the unspeakable things of the first age of the world, still seem insoluble. For in this way it will be permissible to bring the sincerity of the original text into jeopardy even in other parts of greater moment, and chronological truth, which cannot be had outside of Holy Scripture concerning these most ancient things, will be endangered and will waver completely; when, however, one departs from the Hebrew codices without cause, and corruption is attributed to them, it is entirely contrary to Divine Providence, which watches over the sincerity of its word to the very last apex. Matt. 5:18; Luke 17:17. Similar is this skepticism of Polus concerning the equally impious opinion of Vossius in his diss. de ætat. mund. c. 9. 'If, however, we subtract the times according to the received Scripture of the Hebrew Codex, we will bring mere night not only upon the histories of the nations, but upon the Holy Scriptures themselves.' For thus Polus writes of it on p. 76. What exactly Vossius establishes here, it is not for me to pass judgment. Let whoever wishes see what Hulsius, Hornius, and others respond to these arguments, and what Vossius retorts, among whom this saw is reciprocated quite prolixly. It seemed to me only to exhibit briefly and ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (as in a sketch) the opinion of that learned man here, leaning upon its own supports. But upon what supports, I pray, can an opinion openly adverse to authentic Scripture lean?

Latin:

Ad Gen. 5, 31. NOE CUM QUINGENTORUM ESSET ANNORUM GENUIT.

Quæritur quare eousque non generarit, ante quingentesimum annum? & Resp. Sic Deus disposuisse videtur, quia statuerat eum cum sua posteritate servare: quod si centesimo anno ut reliquis generare cepissent, orti ex eo tot liberi fuissent, qui non potuissent cum necessariis competenter in arca servari, & multi ex iis mali, quos non esset dignum salvari. Sic Lyranus. Censuram omnino meretur ἐπίκρισις, quam hoc loco Matthæus Polus in Synopsi Crit. p. 73. tradidit, de sententia Waltoni Proleg. in Bibl. n. 58. & Morini Exerc. Bibl. 7, 2. quod præferendus sit calculus annorum editionis LXX. Ebræo textui eique contraria Usserii in Chron. Sacr. c. 5. Vtramvis sententiam sequatur lector, veritatem & ἀυτοπιστίαν S. Scripturæ sartam tectam esse & ademptam Atheis omnem cavillandi ansam, facile perspiciet. Nam si Hebraicum calculum sequatur, ex dictis satis constabit & rebus gestis (quæ referunt historici) fides & Scripturæ veritas: Si Græcum præferat, & corruptionis arguat Hebraicos codices, non idcirco vacillabit fides nostra aut certitudo Scripturæ in rebus majoris momenti, (quibus tutandis curatius invigilavit divina providentia, ut ex summo inter omnigenos codices in illis consensu satis patet,) quod in rebus minoris ponderis, Chronologicis v.g. & historiis ad exercitium fidei nostræ passus sit Deus nonnulla σφάλματα irrepere, quæ cæcutientibus nostris animis, rerumque primæ mundi ætatis infandum ignaris, adhuc insolubilia videntur. Nam hoc pacto sinceritatem textus originalis in aliis etiam majoris momenti partibus in discrimen adducere licebit, & veritas Chronologica, quæ extra S. literas de antiquissimis hisce haberi nequit, periclitabitur, & penitus vacillabit: Quum tamen citra causam a Codicibus Ebræis discedatur, iisque affricetur corruptio, advigilanti pro sinceritate verbi sui ad extremum usque apicem Providentiæ divinæ prorsus contraria. Matth. 5, 18. Luc. 17, 17. Similis est Poli hujus Scepticismus de Vossiana æque impia sententia diss. de ætat. mund. c. 9. Si autem tempora subducamus juxta receptam Hebraici Codicis Scripturam, non gentium tantum historiis, sed ipsis Sacris literis meram noctem inferemus. Ita enim de ea Polus p. 76. Quam certe hæc statuat Vossius, non meum est judicium ferre. Videat cui lubet, quid his argumentis respondent Hulsius, Hornius, aliique, & quid regerit Vossius, inter quos hæc serra prolixe satis reciprocatur. Mihi tantum visum fuit breviter & ὡς ἐν τύπῳ sententiam istius viri docti suis nixam fulcris hic exhibere. Quibusnam vero, obsecro, fulcris niti potest opinio Scripturæ authenticæ aperte adversa?

## 6:1 Argument
PART II. THE HISTORY OF NOAH IN GENESIS. CHAPTER VI.

The cause of the flood: from which Noah is exempted by the construction of the ark enjoined upon him.

Latin:

PARS II. GENESEOS HISTO- RIA NOÆ. CAPUT VI.

Diluvii causa: a quo Noa injuncta arcæ fabri- ca eximitur.

## 6:2
Verse 2. THAT THEY WERE BEAUTIFUL] Judging by the eyes more than by the ears regarding a wife. Xenophon: that the race of men always becomes worse by mixing the worse with the better.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUOD ESSENT PULCHRÆ] Oculis magis quam auribus de uxore judicantes. Xenophon: κατὰ γίγνεσθαι τὸ γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων κάκιον ἀεὶ μιγνύμενον τὸ χεῖρον τῷ βελ- τίονι.

## 6:3
Verse 3. SHALL NOT REMAIN] That is, I do not wish it to remain for long. The Greeks: ὀυ μὴ καταμείνῃ, or ὀυ καταμενεῖ. The Spirit given by me to man shall not remain in man long enclosed as if in a sheath, since it is of no good use, no more than a sword covered. For נָדָן is a sheath, 1 Chronicles 21:27, and the body is called so in Chaldean, Daniel 1:15, namely because it contains the Spirit within itself. Hence it may be permitted to interpret that passage 1 Peter 3:19, τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι, those human spirits which God complained were being detained as if in a sheath, useless: so that you may understand with πορευθεὶς, Psalm 109:31. Philargyrus on the second Georgic, Syllepsis from the assumption of a case, for a nominative is to be assumed from the ablative. The Spirit of Christ was in Noah in such a way as it was in the Prophets, 1 Peter 1:11.

IN MAN (The Greeks: ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τόυτοις, in the men of this age.

FOR EVER (לְעוֹלָם), that is, for many times.

He explains the Spirit of GOD as the human soul, following the LXX and the Chaldean, who understood it as the Spirit of man. Thus formerly Origen in Ps. 38, whose opinion was this: that God does not wish the soul to be defiled any longer by the dwelling and, as it were, the contagion of an impure body; which is akin to the ravings of the Manichaeans and Pythagoreans. Cornel. a Lap. and Tirinus, thus: the soul of man will not remain for a long time, because after 120 years I will destroy all men. Others, they will not live as long as the ancients lived, with Menochius. But God is speaking of His Spirit. Moreover, He is not accustomed to call the soul His Spirit. Nor does the word 'will remain' fit the Hebrew word יָדוֹן. Although Santes Pagninus had rendered it 'will contend', Arias Montanus indeed explained in the margin, 'it will be as in a sheath', as Grotius did, deriving this word from נָדַן: but that root is unused in Hebraism, and therefore he judged that the word ought to be derived from the root דִּוּן or דִין, 'to judge', 'to dispute', 'to contend'. Grotius ought therefore to have acknowledged the error of the Vulgate Interpreter, not excused it with an inconvenient gloss. For the sake of defending him, it is a wonder that he did not, with Leo Castro, Lindanus, Cornelius, Marius, and some others, accuse the Hebrew reading here, that it was once read יָלוּן from לִין, 'to lodge', 'to remain'. For he is facile in finding fault with Hebrew Codices.

The plain sense, however, is that God is unwilling to litigate and contend with men any longer through the Patriarchs ( for thus the world interprets the reproving office of the Holy Spirit, which considers the heralds of the Word as authors of quarrels, and sermons as contentions) that it is time for Him to exercise His judgment against the wickedness of the age: Which is wont to be the beginning of divine vengeance, when He takes away His Word Is. 3, 1. Am. 8. v. 11. Thus contention is called the e̔́λεγχο̂ς of the Holy Spirit, either κατὰ μίμησιν, as has already been noted, or because of the disputation which He undertakes with impious men, in order to overcome and convince them: R. Solomon similarly explains: My Spirit shall not dispute, shall not contend in judgment. The interpretation concerning the Spirit of GOD disputing with Himself is foreign: I will not continue to dispute with myself with an ever-anxious mind, I will finally decide what I am about to do. For it is a matter of a disputation with men, who are flesh. Nor does that of Fuller please, My Spirit shall not exercise judgment (immediately, suddenly, as they have deserved) forever, although they are flesh itself. Because that word 'suddenly' is thus inserted. And the explanation which we provided earlier, as it is more accepted, so it is more expeditious. Nor is an adversative found in the Hebrew; but a copulative, even he is flesh, where Piscator and Ainsworth posit a tacit Antithesis: as if he were saying, not only the Cainites, but also the Sons of GOD are flesh.

But in vain does Grotius wish to borrow light from a false interpretation of this more difficult passage 1 Pet. 3, 19, concerning those τοι̃ς ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ πνεύμασι, those human Spirits, which God complained were useless, as if detained in a sheath, so that you might understand 'Noah' from the following for the word πορευθεὶς. Which is an open perversion of the Petrine passage. For it is not said there that Noah went and preached, but Christ in the Spirit ζωοποιηθεὶς τω̃͂ πνεύματι, ἐν ω̷̃ καὶ τοι̃ς ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν. Who would not see that these things pertain to Christ? that in His Spirit He ALSO went and preached to the Spirits. By whom are understood not Spirits contained in human bodies as in a sheath, but Spirits ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ in prison, who indeed were in prison at the time when Peter wrote this. Therefore he adds ἀπειθήσασί ποτε, that they were once incredulous. The name Noah follows long after, and in the oblique case, ἐν ἡμέραις Νω̃ε, and therefore Noah cannot be understood there through that herald. Which Grotius acknowledges in his Annotations on this text of Peter; and therefore he explained the same as Christ having gone in the Spirit after the ascension, πορευθεὶς after He ascended into Heaven, as soon after v. 22. John 14, 2. 3. 12. 28. chap. 15, 17. 28. Christ is said to have preached to the Gentiles, because the Apostles did so in His name and by His power. Nor could he deny that Φυλακὴ is called a prison. For which matter he himself brought forward the following passages: Gen. 40, 3. 4. 7. 41, 11. 42, 17, 19. Lev. 24, 12. Jud. 16, 22. 26. 2 Sam. 22, 27. 1 Kings 22, 27. 2 Kings 17, 4. 24, 47. 48. 2 Chron. 18, 26. Is. 42, 7. Jer. 32, 28-1. chap. 33, 1. 37, 4. 17. 21. 25. 27. Ez. 19, 9. Although he adds that a sheath is as it were a prison for a sword, and that the Chaldeans call the body of a man נרכא a sheath in the same way Dan. 7, 15. Thus also that Tertullian calls the flesh a sheath of the breath of GOD in his book on the resurrection of the flesh. Be it so, let the body be called the sheath of the soul: is it therefore also called Φυλακὴ here by Peter? And how did Christ after the ascension preach to those souls which were detained in the sheath of the body in the time of Noah, unless it be said that this was done through a descent into hell, whether by a real or verbal proclamation, with our Theologians, who understand this ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ to have been done in the infernal prison. But after the ζωοποίησις, as the Petrine words have it, not only after the ascension. But Grotius does not intend that: and therefore he invents that Christ did not preach to the same Spirits, but to similar ones: twisting the words ἀπειθήσασί ποτε thus, such minds as once in the times of Noah did not obey. He speaks as if they had been the same, and they had been the same Spirits or minds not ἀριθμῷ, as Aristotle speaks, but in kind, that is, in mind, equally useless to GOD. These things Grotius: But what is more evident than that the souls ἐν φυλακῇ, to whom Christ preached after the ζωοποίησις, are those same ones whom Peter further describes there, that they were once incredulous. Here Grotius directly contradicts Peter: Peter says Christ preached to those who were once incredulous, τοῖς ἀπειθησασί ποτε; Grotius to those who believed: Peter makes them the same Spirits who are ἐν φυλακῇ, and who were once incredulous. Grotius not the same, but different, yet similar; which similarity, however, he cannot find, because those were clearly useless in the time of Noah, and did not believe his preaching: but he confesses that these to whom Christ preached had believed Him. Nothing of the sort in Jerome, and therefore this is truly a new interpretation, nay, clearly a perverse one.

But to the Mosaic passage again: the sense of which he now renders differently in his annotations on the Epistle of Peter: it will not be that this Spirit of mine in man is detained in a sheath, i.e., the mind which I gave him Wis. 12, 1 (This passage does not concern the soul of man, but the eternal Spirit of God, preserving and directing all things) will not be useless, like a sword in a sheath, which accomplishes nothing of that for which it was made. How does this interpretation agree with the divine intention? For Grotius confesses that God is complaining about men in Moses. According to this sense, however, He is not complaining, but predicting that minds will no longer be useless; which prediction is certainly not confirmed by the event, nor does it agree with this Petrine sentence, concerning souls useless to God, and incredulous.

Verse of the same. BECAUSE HE IS FLESH.) He strives to feed and delight the flesh without the fear of God. This is said of the human race of that age, with very few accepted: See Matt. 24. verse 38.

An overly weak interpretation. Flesh is not spoken of merely on account of the ἀταξίαν (disorder) of the sensitive appetite, just as the Papists locate sin only in the lower part of the soul, namely the sensitive appetite, but on account of the corruption of all the faculties of man; even the higher ones: therefore idolatry and heresies are reckoned among the desires of the flesh. That which is born of the flesh is flesh, John 3:6. On which words the Jesuit Maldonatus: The whole man is said to be born of the flesh and to be entirely flesh, and the mind itself, although a spiritual substance, is defiled by sin. It cannot be denied, says Bellarmine, book V on the state of sin, chapter 15, that a vice is found also in the higher part of the soul. For that part of the soul also is prone to desire honors, empty show, and other vanities. Thus Moses himself explains these words: because he is flesh, v. 5, that every thought of the heart is intent upon evil at all times.

Verse of the same. AND HIS DAYS SHALL BE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS] Commonly they interpret this concerning the shortened span of human life. And hence a report was spread even among the nations, that it was revealed by GOD to Moses that no one would live beyond that span of time. See Josephus in chapter VII of the first book of Antiquities, and the life of the Emperor Claudius, he who ruled after Gallienus. But the Greeks here: ἔσονται δὲ αἱ ἡμέραι αὐτῶν ἑκατὸν εἴκοσιν ἔτη (and their days shall be one hundred and twenty years). Which makes the best sense, that God would not delay the πανωλεθρίαν (total destruction) of that age of men, which was so corrupt, beyond so many years.

The exposition of Josephus, Philo, Lactantius, Procopius, Rupert, and Tostatus, as also that of Castalio, does not agree in any way: for many after the flood far exceeded this limit, which is observed even today in certain places. Rightly, therefore, with the Chaldean, the LXX, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 24, Luther, Cornelius, Menochius, Bonfrer, Piscator, Ainsworth, Rivet, and our own countrymen, it is acknowledged as a space of repentance given to the men of that age: whence these things were said in the 480th year of Noah's life, twenty years before the birth of Shem. From this some deduce the age of the Hebrews, which was 120 years, after the expiration of which the Egyptians and Chaldeans intercalated a month. Which was also a century for the Romans. See Scaliger, III. de Emend. Temp. and Gataker.

Latin:

vers. 3. NON PERMANEBIT] Id est, nolo diu perma- neat. Græci ὀυ μὴ καταμείνῃ, vel ὀυ καταμενεῖ. Spiritus a me da- tus homini non manebit in homine diu inclusus velut in vagi- na, quippe nulli bono usui non magis quam ensis tectus. Nam נָדָן est vagina 1. Paral. 21, 27. & corpus Chaldaice sic dicitur Dan. I. 15. nempe quod Spiritum intra se contineat. Hinc in- terpretari liceat illud 1. Petr. 3, 19. τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι illis spiritibus humanis, quos velut in vagina detineri inutiles Deus querebatur: ut ad πορευθεὶς subintelligas Psal. 109, 31.. Phi- largyrus ad II. Georgicon, Syllepsis ex assumtione casus, nam ex ablativo assumendus nominativus. Spiritus Christi ita in Noe fuit, ut in Prophetis, 1. Petr. 1, 11.

IN HOMINE (Græci ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τόυτοις, in hu- jus ævi hominibus.

IN ÆTERNUM( לְעוֹלָם , id est, per multa tempora.

Spiritum DEI de anima humana explicat, LXX. & Chald. sequutus, qui de Spiritu hominis accepe- re. Ita quondam Origenes in Ps. 38. cujus hæc fuit sententia: Deum non velle animam impuri corporis habitaculo & quasi contagio diutius coinquinari; quod Manichæorum & Pythagoreorum deliriis affine. Cor- nel. a Lap. & Tirinus, ita: non permanebit anima ho- minis in longum tempus, quia post 120. annos omnes homines abolebo. Alii, non vivent, quamdiu Ma- jores vixere, cum Menochio. Sed Deus de Spiritu suo loquitur. Animam autem non solet Spiritum suum nominare. Neque verbum manebit congruit Ebrææ voci יָדוֹן. Quod cum Santes Pagninus reddidisset, contendet: Ariasmontanus quidem explicavit in margine, erit, ut in vagina, uti Grotius, a נָדַן verbum hoc deducens: sed Radix illa in Ebraïsmo est inusi- tata, ideoque a Radice דִּוּן vel דִין judicavit, discepta- vit, contendit, verbum derivari oportet. Agnoscere itaque vulgati Interpretis errorem, non glossa in- convenienti excusare debebat Grotius. Cujus de- fendendi causa, mirum, quod non cum Leone Ca- strio, Lindano, Cornelio, Mario, aliisque nonnullis le- ctionem Ebræam hic accusarit, quod olim יָלוּן le- ctum fuerit a לִין pernoctavit, permansit. Facilis enim est in arguendis Ebræis Codicibus.

Sensus autem planus est, nolle Deum amplius litigare, ac contendere cum hominibus per Patriar- chas) ita enim elencticum S. S. munus interpreta- tur mundus, qui praecones verbi pro rixarum auto- ribus, conciones pro contentionibus habet) tempus esse, ut judicium exerceat suum adversus improbitatem seculi: Quod initium vindictae divinae esse solet, cum verbum suum aufert Es. 3, 1. Am. 8. v. 11. Ita contentio dicitur e̔́λεγχο̂ς Spiritus S. vel κατὰ μίμησιν, uti jam monitum, vel ob disceptationem, quam cum ho- minibus impiis suscipit, ut eosdem expugnet atque convincat: R. Salomo similiter exponit: Non disce- ptabit, non judicio contendet Spiritus meus. Aliena est interpretatio de Spiritu DEI secum disceptante: non anxio semper animo disceptare pergam mecum, tandem decernam, quid facturus sim. Nam de disceptatione cum hominibus, qui caro sunt, agitur. Nec placet il- la Fülleri, Spiritus meus non exercebit judicium (illi- co repente, ut meriti sunt) in sempiternum, quamvis ipsa caro sint. Quia sic ingeritur illud repente. Et ex- plicatio, quam antea tradidimus, uti receptior, ita expeditior est. Nec adversativa in Ebraeo reperitur; sed copulativa, etiam ipse caro, ubi tacitam Antithe- sin Piscator & Ainsworth ponunt: quasi dicat, non Cainitae tantum, sed etiam Filii DEI caro sunt.

Frustra autem e falsa loci hujus interpretatio- ne difficiliori 1. Petr. 3, 19. lucem foenerari vult Gro- tius, de τοι̃ς ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ πνεύμασι illis Spiritibus hu- manis, quos velut in vagina detineri inutiles Deus que- stus fuerit, ut ad πορευθεὶς subintelligas ex sequentibus Νω̃ε. Quae aperta est loci Petrini perversio. Non enim ibi profectus Noë praedicasse dicitur, sed Christus in Spiritu ζωοποιηθεὶς τω̃͂ πνεύματι, ἐν ω̷̃ καὶ τοι̃ς ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν. quis non videat ad Christum haec pertinere? quod in spiritu suo ETIAM profectus fuerit ac praedicaverit Spiriti- bus. Per quos non Spiritus in humanis corporibus ceu vagina contentos, sed Spiritus ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ in carcere intelliguntur, qui nempe tum, cum haec scriberet Petrus, in carcere erant. Ideo addit ἀπειθήσασί ποτε, quod quondam increduli fuerint. Nomen Noë lon- ge post demum sequitur, & in obliquo casu, ἐν ἡμέραις Νω̃ε, ideoque Noah per illum praeconem ibi intelli- gi non potest. Quod agnoscit Grotius Annotatis ad hunc Petri textum; ideoque de Christo in Spiritu pro- fecto post adscensionem explicavit eundem, πορευθεὶς postquam in Caelum adscendit, ut mox v. 22. Joh. 14, 2. 3. 12. 28. cap. 15, 17. 28. Christus dicitur praedicasse gen- tibus, quia Apostoli id ejus nomine ac virtute fecerunt. Neque diffiteri potuit, Φυλακὴν carcerem dici. In quam rem loca adduxit ipse sequentia: Gen. 40, 3. 4. 7. 41, 11. 42, 17, 19. Lev. 24, 12. Jud, 16, 22. 26. 2. Sam. 22, 27. 1. Reg. 22, 27. 2. Reg. 17, 4. 24, 47. 48. 2. Par. 18, 26. Es. 42, 7. Jer. 32, 28-1. cap. 33, 1. 37, 4. 17. 21. 25. 27. Ez. 19, 9. Quamvis addat, vaginam esse veluti carcerem gladio, Chaldaeosque נרכא vaginam eodem mo- do corpus hominis vocare Dan. 7, 15. Sic & Tertullia- num carnem vaginam dicere adflatus DEI lib. de re- surr. carn. Sit ita, vagina dicatur corpus animae: num ergo etiam dicitur hîc Petro Φυλακὴ? Et quomodo Christus post adscensionem animabus illis, quae in vagina corporis detentae fuere, tempore Noæh praedicavit, nisi per descensum ad inferos id factum, seu reali seu verbali praeconio cum Theolo- gis nostris dicatur, qui hoc ἐν Φυλακη̃͂ in carcere infernali factum intelligunt. Sed post ζωοποίησιν, uti verba habent Petrina, non post adscensionem de- mum. At id Grotius non intendit: ideoque com- miniscitur, non iisdem Spiritibus praedicasse Christum, sed similibus: verba ἀπειθήσασί ποτε sic torquens, quales animi olim Noæh temporibus non obtempera- runt. Loquitur, quasi iidem fuissent, & fuerant ne- iidem Spiritus sive animi non ἀριθμῷ, ut Aristoteles lo- quitur, sed genere, id est, animo, pariter DEO inutiles. Hæc Grotius: Sed quid evidentius, quam quod ani- mæ ἐν φυλακῇ, quibus Christus prædicavit post ζωο- ποίησιν, sint iidem illi, quos ibi describit porro Pe- trus, quod fuerint quondam increduli. Directe hic Grotius Petro contradicit: Petrus Christum prædi- caffe illis dicit, qui quondam fuere increduli, τοῖς ἀπει- θήσασί ποτε; Grotius illis, qui crediderunt: Petrus eosdem Spiritus facit, qui ἐν φυλακῇ sunt, & qui quon- dam increduli fuere. Grotius non eosdem, sed diver- sos, similes tamen; quam vero similitudinem inveni- re non potest, quia illi plane inutiles erant, tempore Noæh, ejusq́; prædicationi non crediderunt: hos autem quibus Christus prædicarit, ei credidisse fatetur. Ni- hil tale apud Hieronym. ideoque vere nova hæc est interpretatio, imo plane perversa.

Sed ad locum Mosaïcum denuo: cujus sensum in annotat. ad Epist. Petri nunc alium ita reddit: non erit ut in vagina detentus hic Spiritus meus in ho- mine, i. e. non erit inutilis animus, quem ei dedi Sap. 12, 1. (Locus hic non de anima hominis, sed æterno Dei Spiritu, conservante & dirigente omnia; agit) sicut ensis in vagina, qui nihil efficit ejus, ad quod factus est. Quomodo congruit hæc interpretatio divinæ intentioni? Queri enim Deum de hominibus apud Mosen fatetur Grotius. Juxta hunc autem sensum non queritur, sed prædicit non amplius fore inutiles animos; quæ prædictio sane ab eventu non compro- bata est, neq; Petrinæ huic sententiæ convenit, de animabus inutilibus Deo, & incredulis.

Vers. eod. QUIA CARO EST.) Carni pascendæ & oble- ctandæ studet sine Dei timore. Hoc de humano genere illius æ- tatis, paucis valde acceptis, dicitur: Vide Matth. 24. vers. 38.

Diluta nimis interpretatio. Non dicitur caro tantum ob ἀταξίαν appetitus sensitivi, quemadmo- dum Pontificii peccatum in inferiore tantum animæ parte, appetitu nimirum sensitivo, collocant, sed ob corruptionem omnium facultatum hominis; etiam su- periorum: ideo inter concupiscentias carnis recen- sentur idololatria & hæreses. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est Joh. 3, 6. In quæ verba Maldonatus Jesuita: Totus homo dicitur ex carne nasci & caro esse totus, & animus ipse, licet substantia spiritualis pecca- to inquinata est. Non negandum est, inquit Bellarmin. l. V. de statu peccati c. 15. in parte superiori animæ et- iam vitium reperiri. Nam ea quoq́; animæ pars prona est ad concupiscendos honores, inanem fucum, & alias vanitates. Ita explicat Moses ipse verba hæc: quia caro est, v. 5. quod cuncta cogitatio cordis intenta sit ad malum omni tempore.

Vers. eod. ERUNTQVE DIES ILLIUS CENTUM VIGINTI ANNORUM] Vulgo interpretantur de curtato vitæ humanæ spatio. Et hinc fama etiam inter gentes prodita, Mosi a DEO id patefactum neminem ultra id temporis spati- um provicturum. Vide Josephum capite VII. libri primi anti- quæ Historiæ, & vitam Cæsaris Claudii ejus, qui post Galliénum imperavit. At Græci hic: ἔσονται δὲ αἱ ἡμέραι αὐτῶν ἑκατὸν εἴκο- σιν ἔτη. Quod sensum facit optimum, non ultra tot annos Deum dilaturum τὴν πανωλεθρίαν ejus ætatis adeo corruptæ hominum.

Nullatenus congruit Josephi, Philonis, Lactan- tii, Procopii, Ruperti, ac Tostati, ut & Castalionis ex- positio: nam multi post diluvium longe supergressi sunt hunc terminum, quod hodie etiam in qui- busdam locis observatur. Recte ergo cum Chal- dæo, LXX. Hieronymo, Chrysostomo, Augustino l. 15. de Civ. Dei c. 24. Luthero, Cornelio, Menochio, Bonfrer. Piscat. Ainsvvorth, Riveto & nostratibus spatium pœnitentiæ hominibus istius ætatis da- tum agnoscitur: unde hæc anno ætatis Noæ CCCCXXC. dicta sunt, viginti annis ante nativi- tatem Sem. Deducunt hinc nonnulli seculum Ebræorum, quod 120. annorum fuerit, post quorum decursum Ægyptii & Chaldæi mensem intercala- bant. Quod & Romanis seculum fuit. Vid. Scalig. III. de Emend. Temp. & Gadaker.

## 6:3 Addition
On Gen. 6, verse 3, page 264, column a, towards the end of the notes.

But as to the scruple which some raise here, that GOD said this about 120 years after the account of Noah's procreation at age 500, Augustine indeed answers that 500 years were stated instead of 480 by the rounding of the number, book 15 of The City of God, chapter 24. Jerome, however, in his Traditions on Genesis, thinks that GOD anticipated the flood by twenty years, but the former is less consistent with the simplicity of Scripture, the latter with divine kindness and truthfulness. Therefore, an anticipation should rather be posited here, because Moses wished to weave together the generations from Adam up to the flood before inserting that divine threat, even though it was made active before the generation of Noah. Compare Blessed D. Georg König in Vindic. Sacr. Disp. 29, section 97.

Latin:

Ad Gen. 6. verf. 3. pag. 264. a. sub finem notarum.

Quod vero ad scrupulum, quem nonnulli hic movent, quod hæc de 120. annis DEUS dixe- rit, postquam de Noæ 500. annos nato παιδογονίᾳ actum, respondet quidem August. 500. annos pro 480. per rotundationem numeri dictos, lib. 15. de Civ. Dei cap. 24. Hieronym. vero in Tradit. in Gen. DEUM viginti annis diluvium anticipasse putat, sed prius Scripturæ simplicitati, posterius di- vinæ benignitati & veracitati minus convenit. Id- eo statuenda potius hic anticipatio, quia voluerit Moses prius generationes ab Adamo usque ad di- luvium pertexere, quam divinam illam commina- tionem inferere: etsi ea ante generationem Noæ activam facta sit. Conf. B. D. Georg. König in vin- dic. Sacr. Disp. 29. loco 97.

## 6:4
Verse 4. BUT THE GIANTS WERE) Such men as the Greeks describe under the name of Giants or Titans. Symmachus not badly οἱ βίαιοι (the violent). Aquila, who follows the origins strictly, οἱ ἐπιπίπτοντες (the falling upon). Lucian in Dea Syria concerning these same men: 'Being very insolent, they performed lawless deeds. For they neither kept oaths, nor welcomed strangers, nor listened to suppliants, for which the great calamity came upon them.'

Verse the same. THESE ARE THE MIGHTY) הַגִּבֹּרִים which by a slight change of a related letter can be called הַכֹּבִירִים, the Kabeiroi, the great gods to Virgil, as Servius notes, to the Greeks Θεοὶ δυνατοὶ (mighty gods), in the books of the augurs, as Varro notes in book 4, divine powers: discoverers of navigation, and for that reason worshipped in Samothrace, as if they were lords of the winds and the sea: pirates without doubt, such as in later centuries, the Cretan Jupiter and his son Minos.

Concerning the Giants, the Hebrew word נְפִלִים occurs in Num. 13, v. 37, whom R. David Kimchi wishes to be so called because men fall from fear of them: Others, because by their tyranny and oppression they make others fall, with Munster and Estius: Others wish them to be called as if deserters, because נפל is so taken in Jer. 37, 13, chap. 38, 19. Cf. 2 Kings 25, 11. Thus Ainsworth and Piscator. Cf. Drusius in h. l. To whom, however, this reason for the name seems deservedly too general. But Josephus more correctly understands here not giants, but any insolent men; despising all law and right through confidence in their strength; Cyril, book 9 against Julian, understands rustic, ferocious, and robust men: and B. Luther, Polyc. Lyser, and Gerhard best interpret it as the violent oppressions of others, who, having abused the strength of their powers, rushed upon others by force, and made them fall before them, and subjected them to their power: just as Philo also understands them as most wicked men. For the cause of the sent punishment of the flood is rendered here. Whence the Burgensis with the Rabbis wrongly understands demons clothed in human form. Moses himself sufficiently indicates that he is speaking of powerful men, who could have had their origin from nowhere else than from one blood, Acts 17, 26. Nor does Grotius deny it, yet he wrongly inclines toward a change of the word, although a slight one, which is clear in itself and fits perfectly. For not a point or an iota ought to be changed in Scripture.

Latin:

Vers. 4. GIGANTES AUTEM ERANT) Tales homines, quales Græci sub Gigantum aut Titanum nomine describunt. Symmachus non male οἱ βίαιοι. Aquila, qui origines addictē sequitur, οἱ ἐπιπίπτοντες. Lucianus in Dea Syria de iisdem ho- minibus : ὑβρισαὶ κάρτα ἐόντες ἀθέμισα ἔργα ἔπρασσον. οὔτε γὰρ ὅρκια ἐφύλασσον, ὔτε ξένους ἐδίκοντο, ὔτε ἱκετίων ἀνέίχοντο, ἀνθ᾽ ὧν σφίσιν ἡ μεγάλη συμφορὴ ἀπίκετο.

Vers. eod. ISTI SUNT POTENTES) הַגִּבֹּרִים quod mutatione levi literæ affinis potest dici הַכֹּבִירִים'οἱ κάβειροι, dii magni Virgilio, ut Servius notat, Græcis Θεοὶ δυνατοὶ, in au- gurum libris, ut Varro notat libro 4. divi potes : repertores na- vigationis, & ob id in Samothrace culti, tanquam ventorum marisque Domini : piratæ haud dubie, quales posterioribus se- culis, Jupiter Cretenfis & filius ejus Minos.

De Gigantibus vox Ebræa נְפִלִים occurrit Num. 13. v. 37. quos ita dictos R. David Kimchi vult, quod illorum pavore homines cadant : Alii, quod ty- rannide & oppressīone sua alios cadere faciant, cum Munstero & Eftio : Alii dictos volunt quasi defecto- res, quod ita נפל accipiatur Jer. 37, 13. cap. 38, 19. Conf. 2. Reg. 25, 11. Ita Ainsworth & Piscator. Conf. Drusius in h. l. Cui vero hæc ratio nominis merito nimis generalis videtur. Rectius autem hic non gi- gantes, sed quosvis insolentes intelligit Josephus ; fi- ducia roboris omne jus & fas contemnentes ; Cyril- lus l. 9. adv. Julian. agrestes, feroces, ac robustos : opti- meque B. Luther. Polyc. Lyser. & Gerhardus de vio- lentis aliorum oppressionibus interpretantur, qui ro- bore virium abusi per vim in alios irruerunt, eosque coram se cadere fecerunt, ac suæ potestati subjecerunt : quemadmodum & Philo sceleratissimos in- telligit. Nam causa hic redditur immissi supplicii diluvii. Unde perperam Burgenfis cum Rabb. dæmo- nes humana specie indutos intelligit. Moses ipse sa- tis indicat, se loqui de potentibus viris, qui non a- liunde originem habere potuere, quam ex uno san- guine Act. 17, 26. Nec abnuit Grotius, male tamen in vocis immutationem etsi levem propendet, quæ per se clara est, & optime congruit. Non enim apex aut iota immutari debet in Scriptura.

## 6:6
Verse 6. AND HE REPENTED) Onkelos and Jonathan וְתַב כִּמֵימְרֵיהּ, he returned to his word: that is, into himself. For so the Chaldeans speak: Symmachus ἀνέστρεψεν (he turned back). But Aquila μετεμελήθη (he repented).

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET POENITVIT EVM ) Onkelos & Jonathan וְתַב כִּמֵימְרֵיהּ reversus est ad verbum suum : id est, in se. Ita enim loquuntur Chaldæi : Symmachus ἀνέστρεψεν. At A- quila μετεμελήθη.

## 6:11
Verse 11. WAS FILLED WITH INIQUITY) With rapines, the Chaldean.

You would more correctly render those Targumim, he turned (GOD the Father) to his Word, λόγον ὑποστατικὸν (the hypostatic Word), whom they are accustomed to designate in that way. Which was also observed by Grotius on John 1, 1. However, the translation of Aquila and the Vulgate is to be retained; but repentance is said of God anthropopathically, since God repents of nothing, Num. 23, 19, 1 Sam. 15, 29. See Augustine, book 17 de civ. Dei, ch. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 11. REPLETA EST INIQVITATE ) Rapinis, Chaldæus.

Illa Targumim rectius reddas, conversus est (DEUS Pater) ad Verbum suum, λόγον ὑποστατικὸν, quem ita solent indigitare. Quod observatum etiam Grotio ad Joh. 1, 1. Retinenda autem Aquilæ & Vul- gati translatio ; sed pœnitentia dicta de Deo ἀνθρω- ποπαθῶς, siquidem Deum nullius rei pœniteat, Num. 23, 19. 1. Sam. 15, 29. Vide August. l. 17. de civ. Dei c. 7.

## 6:12
Verse 12. FOR ALL FLESH HAD CORRUPTED ITS WAY] With foul lusts. Not only that: But also with other sins, especially idolatry. Cf. B. Lyser and B. Gerhard in h. l.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OMNIS QUIPPE CARO CORRUPERAT VIAM SUAM ] Fœdis libidinibus. Non tantum : Sed aliis etiam peccatis, impri- mis idololatria. Conf. B. Lyferum & B. Gerhard. in h. l.

## 6:14
Verse 14. MAKE THEE AN ARK] That most ancient name of constructed ships, from the likeness to which they were made, the LXX called it κιβωτὸν (chest) here, and the interpreter of Matthew 24, 38, and Luke 17, 27, and Peter 1, 3, 20. But λάρνακα (chest/coffin) in the same sense exactly, Apollodorus in the Bibliotheca, Lucian in Dea Syria, Alexander Polyhistor produced by Cyril, and Josephus. Thus Simonides on those sailing with Danae: 'in a cunningly wrought chest.' Concerning these, and concerning the whole history of the flood, see what I have gathered from the monuments of all nations in book 1 de Verit. Relig. Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14. FAC TIBI ARCAM ] ld antiquissimum naviun constructarum nomen ex similitudine ad quam factæ erant κιβωτὸν hic dixere LXX. & Matthæi interpres 24, 38. & Lucas 17 27. & Petrus 1. 3, 20. At λάρνακα eodem plane sensu Apollodo rus in Bibliotheca, Lucianus in Dea Syria, Alexander polyhi stor productus a Cyrillo & Josephus. Sic de Danae navigant Simonides : λάρνακι ἐν δαιδαλέᾳ. De his, deque omni histori diluvii, vide quæ ex omnium Gentium monumentis congesfi mus ad lib. 1. de Verit. Relig. Christ.

## 6:16
Verse 16. LOWER, SECOND, AND THIRD STORIES SHALT THOU MAKE IN IT] The name 'coenaculum' is of a genus. The interpreter here put it for a flooring under the deck of the ship, 'tristegon' for the lowest. For he begins from the top. In Acts 20, 9, τρίστεγον; that is, the third flooring from the bottom is called the third coenaculum by the interpreter. Symmachus in this place κατὰ δίστεγα καὶ τρίστεγα (by second and third stories). In the Hebrew word for word, lower, second, and third.

Latin:

Vers. 16. COENACULA ET TRISTEGA FACIES IN EA ] Cœnaculum nomen est generis. Id hic Interpres posu it pro contignatione sub tabulato navis, tristegon pro infi mo. Incipit enim a summo. In Actis 20, 9. τρίστεγον; id est ab imo tertia contignatio, tertium cœnaculum interpreti dici- tur. Symmachus hoc loco κατὰ δίστεγα καὶ τρίστεγα. In He- bræo ad verbum, inferiora secunda & tertia.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. The entry of Noah into the ark, and the sending of the flood.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. Ingressus Noæ in arcam, & emissio diluvii.

## 7:2
Vers. 2. CONCERNING THE UNCLEAN ANIMALS.] Not from the law of Moses, which was not yet given, but from those which had begun to feed on flesh. Thus Tacitus, in the 4th book of his Histories, called foul animals profane.

Grotius seems to ascribe sin even to brute animals. Which was done by Socinus concerning the state of the first man, ch. 6, p. 158. Just as in book 1 of De Veritate Religionis Christianae, § 10, he asserted that there is something in animals, as it were in place of intellect. He calls those unclean which had begun to feed on flesh. But that was neither prohibited by law, nor, if it were prohibited, does it concern beasts, for whom no law can be prescribed. See B. Nicol. Hunnius, Exam. Error. Photin. de stat. homin. prim. & sec. Sect. 2, cap. 3, th. 2. Nor indeed are animals ever considered unclean from the eating of flesh. Although, therefore, the law concerning the distinction of clean and unclean animals had not yet been solemnly given by Moses, it appears nevertheless from this passage that such a distinction had been handed down by God before the flood; where the doctrine of sacrifices also could not have been drawn from elsewhere than from divine institution at the first.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DE ANIMANTIBUS VERO IMMVNDIS.] Non ex lege Mosis, quæ nondum data, sed ex iis, quæ carne pasci cœperant. Sic animalia fœda, profana dixit Tacitus Hi- storiarum 4.

Videtur Grotius animantibus etiam brutis peccatum adscribere. Quod a Socino factum de statu prim. hom. c. 6. pap. 158. Quemadmodum l. 1. de Ver. Rel. Chr. §. 10. animantibus aliquid esse, quasi vice intellectus asseruit. Immunda dicit, quæ carne pa- sci cœperant. At id neque lege prohibitum fuit, neq; si prohibitum, bestias concernit, quibus lex præscri- bi nulla potest. Vid. B. Nicol. Hunnius Exam. Error. Photin. de stat. homin. prim. & sec. Sect. 2. cap. 3. th. 2. Neque vero uspiam immunda æstimantur ani- malia e pastu carnis. Licet ergo lex a Mose nondum solenniter lata de discrimine animantium mundorū & immundorum, apparet tamen ex hoc loco, ante diluvium a Deo tale discrimen traditum fuisse; ubi sacrificiorum quoque doctrina aliunde, quam e di- vino instituto primum hauri non potuit.

## 7:4
Vers. 4. AND I WILL DESTROY EVERY SUBSTANCE] יקום, which is here in the Hebrew, according to the interpreters Abenesdra and Kimchi, signifies whatever lives: if you look to the origin, it is that which raises itself: whence the Greeks here translate it ἀνάστημα. But elsewhere ὑπόστασιν.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET DELEBO OMNEM SUBSTANTIAM ] יקום quod hic in Hebræo est, interpretibus Abenesdra & Kimchi, significat quicquid vivit: ad originem si spectes est quod se erigit: unde ἀνάστημα hic vertere Græci. At alibi ὑπόστασιν.

## 7:11
Vers. 11. AND THE WINDOWS OF HEAVEN WERE OPENED] There is a not dissimilar description in Seneca, Natural Questions, book 3, ch. 27. But the passage moves me to ask, when the fatal day of the flood has come, in what way a great part of the lands is overwhelmed by the waves, whether it happens by the forces of the Ocean, and the external sea rises against us: or whether frequent, incessant rains, and winter, having banished summer, cast down an immense force of waters from broken clouds: or whether the earth pours forth rivers more abundantly, and opens new fountains: or whether there is not one cause for so great an evil, but every reason concurs, and at the same time rains fall, rivers increase, the seas, stirred from their foundations, overflow, and all things in one column press down for the destruction of the human race. I will speak of this passage of Seneca in his own words: You have conceived as great an image as you ought; with all lands overwhelmed, with the very sky falling upon the earth.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET CATARACTÆ COELI APERTÆ SUNT] Non dissimilis apud Senecam διατύπωσις Naturalium quæstio- num libro 3. c. 27. Sed movet me locus, ut quæram, cum fata- lis Dies diluvii venerit, quemadmodum magna pars terrarum undis obruatur, utrum Oceani viribus fiat, & externum in nos pelagus exfurgat: an crebri sine intermissione imbres, & elisa æstate hyems pertinax immensam vim aquarum ruptis nubibus dejiciat: an flumina tellus largius fundat, aperiatq; fontes novos: aut nō situna tanto malo causa,sed omnis ratio consentiat, & simul imbres cadant, flumina increscant,maria sedibus suis excita per- currant, & omnia uno agmine ad exitium humani generis incum- bant. Dicam de hoc Senecæ loco ipsius verbis,Concepisti ima- ginem quantam debebas; obrutis omnibus terris, cælo ipso in ter- ram ruente.

## 7:11 Addition
On Gen. 7, 11. THE WINDOWS OF HEAVEN. After Grotius's notes on p. 264, column b.

Pole observes that Gregory of Oxford understands this as the supernal heavens, as if waters had fallen from there onto the earth, which are retained above the heaven by the word of God, because if they descended according to their nature, they would extinguish everything in a moment, as Mercer says. Others among the Calvinists for the most part hiss at those supercelestial waters. Let this testimony therefore be noted in favor of them.

Latin:

Ad Genes. 7, 11. CATARACTÆ COELI. post notas Grotii ad p. 264. b.

De cælis supernis accipere Gregorium Oxo- niensem, quasi aquæ inde in terras delapsæ sint, ob- servat Polus, quæ supra cælum verbo Dei retinean- tur, quia si pro natura sua descenderent in momento extinguerent omnia, Mercero dicente. Alii è Calvi- nianis plerique aquas illas supracælestes exibilant. Notetur ergo hoc testimonium pro iisdem.

## 7:22 Addition
On verse 22, ibid. AND ALL IN WHOSE NOSTRILS WAS THE BREATH OF LIFE ON THE EARTH DIED.

I confess that I cannot see how Isaac Vossius's novel opinion, that not even the hundredth part of the globe was covered by the waters, can be reconciled with this Catholic assertion of Moses: For if everything that has the living spirit in itself was extinguished on the whole earth, and the flood was not particular but universal, how was scarcely the hundredth part of the globe covered by waters?

Latin:

Ad vers. 22. ibid. ET CUNCTA IN QUIBUS SPIRACULUM VITÆ EST IN TERRA MORTUA SUNT.

Cum hac Catholica assertione Mosis quomo- do Isaaci Vossii novella sententia, ne centesimam qui- dem partem orbis aquis fuisse obrutam, conciliari possit, me videre non posse fateor: Nam si omne, quod spiritum viventem in sese habet, extinctum est, in terra universa, & diluvium non particulare, sed universale fuit, quomodo vix centesima orbis pars aquis obruta?

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. The diminution of the waters, and the new promise after the exit and offering of Noah.

Latin:

CAPUT IIX. Imminutio aquarum, & post egressum & obla- tionem Noæ nova promissio.

## 8:4
Vers. 4. UPON THE MOUNTAINS OF ARMENIA) This interpreter was content with a general name. But those are the mountains which had the old name Ararat, which is here in the Hebrew, called afterwards the Gordyæi, which name Josephus has here, the two Chaldean interpreters, and the Arab, but with one letter corrupted. Mention of them is in Strabo, Curtius, Pliny, as we noted in book 1 of De Veritate Christiana. Philostorgus says the name Ararat itself remained among the Armenians until his own times.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SUPER MONTES ARMENIÆ) Generali no- mine contentus fuit hic interpres. Sunt autem ii montes, qui vetus nomen habuere Ararat, quod hic est in Hebræo, dicti postea Gordyæi, quod nomen hic habet Josephus, duo Chal- dæi interpretes, & Arabs, sed litera una corrupta. Mentio eo- rum apud Strabonem, Curtium, Plinium, ut ad librum 1. pro Veritate Christiana notavimus. Nomen ipsum Ararat ad sua tempora apud Armenios mansisse ait Philostorgus.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. WHICH WENT FORTH, AND DID NOT RETURN.) So also all the Greeks: καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἐκ ἀνέστρεψε; Whence it appears that there were formerly various codices here.

He does not dare to say that the Hebrew Codex is now corrupted, which the Bishop of the Canary Islands, Melchior Canus, contends; but he explains the Hebrew text so that it may harmonize with the Vulgate and the Greeks: the Hebrew reading can be explained thus, that the raven is said to have flown now further from the ark, now to have flown closer to it, yet so that it did not enter the ark. The raven was finding corpses in the mountains, although they were damp, on which it might feed. The olive loves dry and low ground. Cardinal Bellarmine had preceded him in book 2, de V. D. c. 2. In the Hebrew, however, it is not held AND RETURNED, but ויצא יצוא ושוב, and it went out going and returning, until the waters were dried up. Which does not signify that the raven returned inside the ark, but that it flew around the ark going and returning, as birds are accustomed to do, and perhaps even returning to the roof of the ark, and departing from there, and that quite often, until the waters were dried up. With which well coheres that saying: it went out and did not return, that is to say, into the ark. There is no need, therefore, for us to imagine here a variety of Hebrew reading. The Greeks, and with them the Vulgate, expressed the sense; they did not interpret the words word for word. Bellarmine therefore observes more correctly that it cannot be gathered from this that the Hebrew Codex once varied. He adds that there are also not lacking Latin Codices which have, it went out and did not return, as can be known from the various readings annotated to the Louvain Bibles. Many things of this kind are found in which either the LXX or the Vulgate or both rendered otherwise than the Hebrew text has. It does not follow that it was once otherwise here. Errors or falsifications are rather to be placed in the Interpreters than that a corruption of the original text should be admitted. Which we have demonstrated with many examples, both from the Greek and the Latin version, in the Critici Sacri. But if the Vulgate had rendered word for word here, there would have been no place for the most fabulous questions about the place of the raven sent out by Noah, where it rested outside the ark, which Steuchus says were stirred up here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVI EGREDIEBATUR, ET NON REVER- TEBATUR.) Sic & Græci omnes: καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἐκ ἀνέστρεψε; Unde apparet, olim hic variasfe codices.

Non audet dicere, corruptum nunc esse Ebræ- um Codicem, quod contendit Canariensis Episco- pus, Melchior Canus; sed exponit Ebræum textum, ut Vulgatæ & Græcis consonet: Hebræa lectio sic exponi potest,ut corvus dicatur modo longius avo- lasse ab arca, modo eam propius advolasse, sic tamen, ut in arcam non intraret. Corvus in montibus quanquam hu- mentibus cadavera reperiebat, quibus pasceretur. Olea sic- cum amat & humile. Præiverat Cardinalis Bellarmi- nus l. 2. de V. D. c. 2. In Hebræo autem non ha- betur ET REVERTEBATUR, sed ויצא יצוא ושוב & exiit exeundo & redeundo, donec sicca- rentur aquæ. Quod non significat, corvum rediisse intra arcam, sed volitasse circa arcam eundo & red- eundo, ut aves solent, & fortasse etiam redeundo ad tectum arcæ, & inde abeundo, idque sæpius, do- nec siccarentur aquæ. Cum quo bene cohæret il- lud egrediebatur & non revertebatur, nimirum, intra arcam. Non ergo opus est, ut fingamus hîc varieta- tem lectionis Ebraicæ. Græci & cum iis Vulgatus sen- sum expresserunt, non κατὰ πόδα verba interpreta- ti sunt. Rectius ergo Bellarminus observat, non col- ligi hinc posse, variasse olim Hebræum Codicem. Addit, quod etiam non desint Latini Codices, qui habeant, egrediebatur & non revertebatur, ut ex variis lectio- nibus ad Biblia Lovaniensia annotatis cognosci potest. Multa reperiuntur hujusmodi, in quibus vel LXX. vel Vulgatus vel utrique aliter reddidere, quam habet Ebræus textus. Non ideo hîc olim secus ha- buit. παροράματα potius aut falsationes in Inter- pretibus ponendæ, quam corruptio textus origi- nalis admittenda. Quod pluribus exemplis, cum è Græca tum Latina versione in Critico Sacro de- monstravimus. Si autem verbum verbo hîc reddi- disset Vulgatus, nullus fabulosissimis quæstionibus locus fuisset de loco corvi à Noah emissi, ubi extra ar- cam resederit, quas Steuchus hic motas dicit.

## 8:9
Verse 9. AND WHEN IT HAD NOT FOUND, WHERE ITS FOOT MIGHT REST.) No dry plain in the fields.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QUÆ CUM NON INVENISSET, UBI RE- QUIESCERET PES EJUS.) Nullam in campis siccam plani- tiem.

## 8:13
Verse 13. AND HE SAW THAT THE SURFACE OF THE EARTH WAS DRIED.) So that the shrubs could be seen: not yet fully, as in the second month. Therefore the Greeks here placed the water failed: but in the following, it was dried up. In the Hebrew also the words differ, ויבשׁה and חרבו.

It is a discourse about the earth, which had been covered by waters. He teaches, therefore, that the same earth was dried and restored, not that a new one was uncovered. This is the fiction that Josephus Antonius Gonzages de Sala devised. For he himself thinks that the continent earth, which was before the flood, remained destroyed and submerged in the depths by the waters, but that another earth, which God had brought forth from the waves, was granted to Noah and his descendants after the Cataclysm for cultivation. Which unheard-of discovery, as he himself confesses, ought to be rejected if only because it is such, and betrays itself sufficiently by its stupendous novelty. For although the Syrian Fathers made the earth double, namely that one in which Paradise was, and the first men around it until the Cataclysm, and another, our own, into which the family of Noah was carried with the Ark when all things were covered by the waves, in order to cultivate it: (which opinion is indeed repugnant to history, since the whole earth was covered by the waters of the flood) yet no one hitherto has dreamed that another earth emerged from the waves; rather, Moses openly testifies that the same earth was dried which GOD had covered with waves on account of the sins of men. But He had not covered any other than that which was inhabited by men before the flood: For how could that which was covered by waters from the foundation of the world be inhabited? He adorns this unheard-of invention of his with other equally unheard-of discoveries (as one absurd thing being granted, others are wont to be born immediately), namely that the heaven was rendered desolate, the place and seat of the delinquents having been removed and expunged from it, as if that part of heaven were snatched away in which the evil angels had remained, and the heaven is no longer whole, such as it was created by God: likewise, that men sinned not only on the earth, but also with the earth, which therefore also had to be punished, but that the sea and the fish in the sea were not liable to punishment, because men before the flood did not use the sea. For how can sin be attributed to the earth? And how would the fish in the sea have been more innocent than the wild beasts hidden in the mountains and woods, with which men had no commerce, which nevertheless had to perish? Finally, Gonzages imagines that the olive tree was born in the sea, nay, that groves and forests remained safe under the waters for one thousand and six hundred years. But we dismiss those fictions, which to recount is to refute, and we return to Grotius.

But the former word in the source means to be dried in such a way that the earth still remains muddy, just as the Red Sea was dried. Ps. 106, 9. By the latter word, however, it is implied that the earth was so dried that, with the swampy moisture being plainly consumed by the heat of the Sun and the wind, it returned to its pristine aridity, and was equal in the solidity of its surface to bearing the bodies of animals.

Latin:

Vers. 13. VIDITQUE QUOD EXSICCATA ESSET SU- PERFICIES TERRÆ.) Ita, ut virgulta conspici possint: non- dum plene, ut mense altero. Ideo Græci hic posuere ἐξέλιπε τὸ ὕδωρ: in sequenti vero ἐξηράνθη. In Hebræo quoque verba differunt ויבשׁה & חרבו.

De terra, quæ aquis obruta erat, sermo est. Eandem ergo exsiccatam & restitutam, non novam retectam esse docet. Quod commentum Josephus Antonius Gonzages de Sala excogitavit. Putat enim ipse terram continentem, quæ ante diluvium fuit, aquis deletam, mersam profundis mansisse, aliam au- tem Noë posteris à Cataclysmo, quam ex undis extule- rat Deus, cultui concessam esse. Quod ἔυρημα in- auditum, ut ipse fatetur, vel ideo, quia tale est, ac stupenda novitate se prodit satis, reprobari debet. Quamvis enim Patres Syri terram duplicem fece- rint, illam nempe, in qua Paradisus, & primi circa eum homines usque ad Cataclysmum, alteram nostram, in quam undis omnia tegentibus cum Arca Noë delata sit familia, ut eam excoleret: (quæ vero sententia historiæ repugnat, quum tota terra diluvii aquis obruta fuerit) nemo tamen hactenus somniavit, terram aliam ex undis emersisse, imo Mo- ses eandem terram exsiccatam esse, quam DEUS propter peccata hominum undis obruerat, aperte testatur. Non autem obruerat aliam quam eam, quæ ab hominibus ante diluvium incolebatur: Ea enim quæ à conditu mundi aquis tecta fuit, quomodo incoli potuit? Hoc inauditum inventum suum, aliis æque inauditis ἐυρήμασι (uti uno absurdo dato alia subinde solent enasci) exornat, quod nempe cœ- lum desolatum redditum sit, inde amoto & expuncto loco ac sede delinquentium, quasi pars illa cœli abre- pta sit, in qua angeli mali hæserint, nec amplius cœlum integrum sit, quale à Deo conditum: item, quod homines non tantum in terra, sed & cum ter- ra peccarint, quæ puniri proinde etiam debuerit, mare autem & pisces in mari pœnæ obnoxia non fuerint, quia homines ante diluvium mare non usurparint. Quomodo enim peccatum terræ tribui potest? Et quomodo pisces in mari magis innoxii ita fuissent, quam feræ in montibus & sylvis abdi- tæ, cum quibus nullum hominibus fuerat commer- cium, quas tamen perire oportebat? Denique fin- git Gonzages olivam in mari natam, imo nemora, & sylvas sub aquis per mille & sexcentos annos salva mansisse. Sed mittimus illa commenta, quæ recital- se est refutasse, & ad Grotium revertimur.

Verbum autem prius in fonte est exsiccari eo modo, ut adhuc terra maneat limosa, uti mare ru- brum exsiccatum fuit. Pf. 106, 9. Posteriori vero verbo innuitur, terram ita exsiccatam fuisse, ut hu- more uliginoso, Solis calore, & vento plane absumto, ad pristinam ariditatem redierit, & soliditate dorsi sui ferendis animalium corporibus par esset.

## 8:20
Verse 20. AND NOAH BUILT AN ALTAR TO THE LORD.) In mountainous places, in which was the first habitation after the flood. Plato, Laws 3.

This is the first altar of which there is mention in Scripture. On it were offered burnt offerings from that seventh of the clean animals, but a solitary one, a male: concerning which, verse 2, as Diodorus of Tarsus observes in the Catena.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ÆDIFICAVIT AUTEM NOE ALTARE DO- MINO.) In locis montanis, in quibus prima post diluvium habitatio. Plato de Legibus 3.

Primum hoc altare est, cujus in Scriptura mentio sit. In illo oblata fuere holocausta ex septi- mo isto mundorum animalium, sed solitario, ma- sculo: de quo vers. 2. observante Diodoro Tarsensi, in Catena.

## 8:21
Ver. 21. AND THE LORD SMELLED A SAVOUR OF SWEETNESS.

He is said to have smelled not only by way of ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (anthropopathy), but also metaleptically, so that it may be described a posteriori, that the Lord burned the sacrifice, because there is a smell from a burned sacrifice, just as He burned the sacrifice of Abel, Gen. 4, 4. and of David 1 Chron. 21, 26. as also of Elijah 1 Kings 18, 38. by which manner He testified that it was pleasing to Him, and in it He smelled at the same time ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας a savour of sweetness, Eph. 5, 2. which the Messiah, the promised seed of the woman, was one day to exhibit in His own sacrifice. For then God was said to smell sacrifices, when they were burned by divine power, as Victor Strigelius rightly notes on the passage 1 Kings 18.

Ver. same. AND HE SAID.) in the Hebrew here is added to his heart: πρὸς τὴν καρδίαν ἑαυτῦ, word for word Theodotion: for which Symmachus [has] πρὸς ἑαυτὸν. Maimonides explains: he did not reveal this purpose of his to anyone at that time.

We add the explanation of the Chaldean: He said in his word: that is, in the Son, the promised Messiah, whom the Chaldean is accustomed to express by the word מימרא. The explanation of Maimonides cannot be approved. For God did not keep this gracious decree of his hidden, but revealed it to Noah. It is spoken Ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (anthropopathically): He said in His heart, that is, He decreed within Himself. But that it was revealed to Noah, there is no doubt, because Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord, and GOD smelled the savour of his sacrifice; and therefore He manifests to this servant of His the grace to be shown to the human race, of which Noah was as it were the second parent and restorer. Some wish this decree to be hinted at here BECAUSE OF THE SEED OF THE WOMAN, and that the Evangelical promise is contained in the following words: I WILL NOT AGAIN CURSE THE EARTH FOR MAN'S SAKE, namely that one whom He promised to the human race in Paradise, the second Adam; because for the sake of this one God does not curse, but blesses the earth, for the sake of this one's merit alone He has mercy on us, without regarding the demerit and sin of the first Adam, which passed into the whole human race. Which sense Forsterus suggested in the collation of the Biblical revision, instituted with the blessed Luther.

Ver. same. FOR THE IMAGINATION AND THOUGHT OF THE HUMAN HEART ARE EVIL FROM HIS YOUTH.) that is, not for the reason that men are corrupt will I hereafter punish all, but the more wicked ones. The Hebrew construction bears this sense well.

As for the Hebrew construction, that the particle כי can be explained as 'Although', our own blessed Johann Tarnovius in Exercit. Bibl. and blessed Glassius in Grammat. Sacr., as also Junius and Rivetus, have already observed. But Grotius does not rightly understand the corruption of men. Orthodox theologians, along with the ancient Fathers, believe and demonstrate that original sin is indicated. Especially from the Hebrew text, which the Vulgate here rendered poorly. For there it is not 'sense' or 'thought' that is held, but the 'figment' of the heart, which is more general. Every figment of the thoughts of the heart is said in the parallel passage Gen. 6. nor is this said to be prone to evil, but the evil יצר absolutely; so that the discussion is not so much about the propensity as about the habitual and natural malice. Such evil is mentioned in Gen. 6:5. Nor is it held in the Hebrew as 'from youth,' but מנעריו, from earliest infancy or childhood. For the word נער is used of a newborn boy in Exod. 2:6. And they certainly include ALL DAYS, which are held in the parallel passage Gen. 6:5, even the days of infancy. As soon as the days of man begin, the imagination of his heart is already evil. Therefore Onkelos rendered מנעורוה as 'from childhood.' Rabbi Solomon explained it as 'from the time he is taken from his mother's womb,' clearly designating original sin. So also Menasse Ben Israel, De fragil. hum. p. 129, 'from infancy,' that is, from the time he comes forth from his mother's womb. In the Talmud, Sanhedrin ch. 11, the Emperor Antoninus asks Rabbi Jehuda Hakkadosh from what time concupiscence dominates man, whether from the moment of complete formation or from birth? and it is answered to him: from formation. R. David Kimchi in Isa. 43:26: 'Behold, your first father sinned; and he is the first Adam': For sin is fixed in the nature of man, because the imagination of his heart is evil from infancy. Similar things are also held in Midrash Tillim, Psalm 34:23: 'The evil imagination was born with man, and grew with him all his days, as it is said: for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his childhood.'

Since Grotius does not at all believe this with Pelagius and Socinus, he invents a hyperbole in the words of R. Solomon, and indeed even in the words of David in Psalm 51:7, with the same Socinus leading the way. But neither do these words bear that, as we shall teach there in v. 9, nor does the opinion of R. Solomon admit it; for the Jews here are sounder than Grotius, and they did not deny original sin entirely. Thus R. Solomon on Psalm 51: 'How not sins? My origin is corrupt.' And R. Esra on the same Psalm: 'Because of the concupiscence innate to the human heart, it is said, I was born in iniquity: and the sense is that from birth an evil imagination has been implanted in the human heart.'

FROM HIS YOUTH.) ἐκ νεότητος αὐτᾶ, as the LXX generally translate this word. Onkelos, מנעורוה, 'from childhood.' Rabbi Solomon, 'from the time he is taken from his mother's womb,' a hyperbole such as is in Psalm 58:4, 71:6, Isa. 48:8, Job 31:18.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ODORATUSQUE EST DOMINUS ODOREM SUAVITATIS.

Odoratus dicitur non tantum per ἀνθρωποπά- θειαν, sed etiam metaleptice, ut nempe à posteriori describatur, quod Dominus sacrificium incenderit, quia ex incenso sacrificio odor est, quemadmodum Abelis sacrificium incendit, Gen. 4, 4. & Davidis 1. Par. 21, 26. ut & Eliæ 1. Reg. 18, 38. quo pacto gra- tum id sibi testatus est, & in eo odoratus simul est ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας odorem suavitatis, Eph. 5, 2. quem ex- hibiturus olim in sacrificio suo erat Messias pro- missum semen mulieris. Tunc enim sacrificia diceba- tur Deus odorari, cum divinitus incendebantur, ut ad locum 1. Reg. 18. recte Victor. Strigelius.

Vers. eod. ET AIT.) in Hebræo hic additur ad cor suum: πρὸς τὴν καρδίαν ἑαυτῦ, ad verbum Theodotion: pro quo Symmachus πρὸς ἑαυτὸν. Maimonides explicat: nemini hoc suum propositum eo tempore patefecit.

Addimus Chaldæi explicationem: Dixit in verbo suo: id est, in Filio, promisso Messia, quem voce מימרא exprimere solet Chaldæus. Maimo- nidis explicatio probari non potest. Non enim hoc gratiosum suum decretum clam habuit Deus, sed Noæ manifestavit. Ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dictum est: Dixit in Corde suo, id est, apud se decrevit. Id autem patefactum fuisse Noæ, dubium non est, quia Noa invenit gratiam in oculis Domini, & odo- ratus est DEUS odorem sacrificii ejus; ideoque gratiam generi humano exhibendam, cujus velut alter parens, & instaurator erat Noa, huic servo suo manifestat. Nonnulli factum hoc decretum PROPTER SEMEN MULIERIS hîc innui, & promissionem Evangelicam haberi in verbis seqq. volunt: NEQUAQUAM ULTRA MALEDI- CAM TERRÆ PROPTER HOMINEM, illum scil. quem in Paradiso humano generi promisit, Ada- mum secundum; quia propter hunc Deus non ma- ledicit, sed benedicit terræ, propter hujus meritum unice miseretur nostri, non attento demerito & peccato Adami primi, quod in totum humanum genus transiit. Quem sensum Forsterus suggessit in collatione revisionis Biblicæ, cum B. Luthero in- stituta.

Vers. eod. SENSUS ENIM ET COGITATIO CORDIS HUMANI IN MALUM PRONA SUNT AB ADOLE- SCENTIA SUA.) id est, non ob id, quod corrupti sunt ho- mines, posthac puniam universos, sed sceleratiores. Bene fert hunc sensum Hebræa constructio.

Quod ad Ebræam constructionem, particu- lam כי exponi posse Quamvis, observarunt jam è nostris B. Johann. Tarnov. in Exercit. Bibl. & B. Glassius in Grammat. Sacr. ut & Junius, & Rivetus. Sed corruptionem hominum non recte intelligit Grotius. Peccatum originale indigitari cum priscis Patribus Orthodoxi Theologi credunt, & de- monstrant. E textu imprimis Ebræo, quem hîc male reddidit Vulgatus. Non enim ibi sensus, nec cogitatio habetur, sed figmentum cordis, quod gene- ralius est. Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis, dicitur in parallelo loco Gen. 6. nec pronum dici- tur hoc ad malum, sed יצר malum absolute; ut non tam de propensione, quam habituali & naturali ma- litia sermo sit. Tantum malum dicitur Gen. VI, 5. Nec in Ebræo habetur ab adolescentia, sed מנעריו à prima infantia vel pueritia. Vox enim נער de puero recens nato adhibetur Exod. 2. v. 6. Et com- prehendunt certe OMNES DIES, qui in loco gemino habentur Gen. 6. verf. 5. dies etiam infan- tiæ. Quamprimum incipiunt dies hominis, ma- lum jam est figmentum cordis ejus. Ideo Onke- los reddidit מנעורוה à parvitate R. Salomon expo- suit, ex quo exceptus est è visceribus matris suæ, aperte peccatum originale designans. Sic etiam Menasse Ben Israël de fragil. hum. p. 129. ab in- fantia, hoc est, ab eo tempore, quo prodit è ventre suæ matris. In Talmude Sanhedrin cap. 11. quærit An- tonius Imper. ex R. Jehuda Hakkadosch, concu- piscentia ex quo tempore dominatur homini, utrum à momento absolutæ formationis, an à nativitate? & respondetur ipsi: à formatione. R. David Kimchi in Esa. 43. verf. 26. Ecce Pater tuus primus pecca- vit; & is est primus Adam : Nam hominis naturæ infixum est peccatum, eo, quod figmentum cordis ejus malum est ab infantia. Qualia etiam habentur in Midrasch Tillim Psalm. 34, 23. Figmentum ma- lum natum est cum homine, ac crevit cum eo omni- bus diebus ejus, sicut dictum est: quoniam figmen- tum cordis hominis malum est, à pueritia ejus.

Quod quum Grotius minime credat cum Pelagio ac Socino, hyperbolen in verbis R. Salomonis, imo etiam in Davidis verbis Psalm. 51. verf. 7. eodem Socino præeunte, comminiscitur. Sed eam neque hæc ferunt, ut v. 9. ibi docebimus, neque R. Salo- monis admittit sententia; Saniores enim hîc Judæi Grotio sunt, neque omnino negarunt originale peccatum. Ita R. Salomo in Psalm. 51. Quomodo non peccata? Origo mea corrupta est. Et R. Esra in eund. Psalm. Propter concupiscentiam innatam cordi hu- mano dicitur, in iniquitate genitus sum: atque sen- sus est, quod à nativitate implantatum sit cordi huma- no figmentum malum.

AB ADOLESCENTIA SUA.) ἐκ νεότητος αὐτᾶ, quomo- do plerumque vertunt hanc vocem LXX. Onkelos מנעורוה à parvitate. Rabbi Salomo, ex quo exceptus est è visceribus ma- tris suæ, hyperbole tali qualis est Psalm. 58, 4. 71, 6. Esa. 48, 8. Job. 31, 18.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. The blessing of Noah given, and the covenant confirmed by the rainbow. Ham the mocker of his father is cursed. Shem and Japheth are blessed.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Benedictio Noæh facta, & fœdus iride firma- tum. Cham irrisor Patris maledictus. Sem & Japhed benedicuntur.

## 9:2
Verse 2. AND YOUR ERROR AND TREMOR SHALL BE UPON ALL ANIMALS.
