Although dominion over irrational creatures, which was a consequence of the divine image, was lost through the fall, yet since God did not wish to destroy human nature, He also did not wish to strip it of all dominion whatsoever and expose it to the ferocity of beasts; rather, just as the earth, cursed because of the fall, is blessed once God is appeased through the appointed Mediator, so also that dominion is in a way restored, and thus it is here solemnly intimated after the flood; which otherwise naturally belongs to men because of a certain prudence and order of nature, by which the imperfect is ordered to the perfect, although not without resistance? Cf. Tostatus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET ERROR VESTER AC TREMOR SIT SU- PER CUNCTA ANIMALIA.

ETsi dominium in Creaturas irrationales; qua Consequens fuit imaginis divinæ per lapsum amissum fuit tamen; quum noluerit Deus naturam humanam destruere, noluit etiam eam omni pror- sus dominio exuere, & ferociæ bestiarum expone- re, quin sicut terra ob lapsum maledicta placato per Mediatorem destinatum DEO, benedicitur, ita & dominium illud quodammodo redditur, adeoque hîc folemniter post diluvium intimatur; quod cæteroquin hominibus naturaliter propter quandam prudentiam & ordinem naturæ, quo im- perfecta ordinatur ad perfecta, convenit, licet non sine repugnantia? Conf. Tostat. in h. l.

## 9:3
Verse 3. EVERYTHING THAT MOVES AND LIVES SHALL BE FOR YOU AS FOOD, LIKE THE GREEN HERBS I HAVE GIVEN YOU ALL.) This passage, and the exception concerning blood which follows, seems clearly to indicate what we said before, that before the flood man indeed had a right over living things, so that he might use their milk, wool, and the remains of those that died by their own fate, but not that he might turn them into food: concerning which most ancient right, kept by some nations even after the flood, see what Jerome collected from all histories in Book II against Jovinian, to which add Porphyry in his book on this subject, and what we said in our book De Jure Belli ac Pacis, book 2, ch. 20, § 9, and in the annotations to that place. GOD shows here that individual men are cared for by Him, and that the genera of other living things, and the more imperfect ones, are ordered by Him for the use of the more perfect.

To Grotius, this passage clearly seems to indicate that it was not granted to man before the flood to turn living things into food. But it could be said that the original right, which he had over them from dominion, is here expressly repeated. We easily allow, however, that anyone may abound in his own sense here. Agreeing with Grotius are Chrysostom, Theodoret, Thomas, Hugo, the authors of the Glossa Ordinaria, Lyranus, Abulensis, Brentius, Gerhard, Martyr, etc., especially from a comparison with Gen. 1:29, and because it is added here, 'as the green herbs I have given you,' as if he were saying, 'hitherto I have granted you only herbs, now I likewise grant you the flesh of animals for food.' They add that fruits alone do not suffice for men after the flood, when they have increased immensely, in sterile places, and that they, as weaker, now need stronger supports, the produce of the earth having been miserably corrupted by the flood, which reasons they bring forward for this concession. Theodoret also says it was done because God foresaw that men, prone to idolatry, would worship living things, whence He allowed their flesh for food, so that they might gather how absurd it is to worship religiously those things which they were permitted to kill and eat. But Tertullian, Montanizing, wrongly refers that eating to the incontinence of men, nor does Jerome, in Book 1 against Jovinian, more correctly judge that the concession was made because of hardness of heart. Furthermore, it does not seem probable to others that, since God gave the skins of animals to man for clothing after the fall, their flesh was cast away as useless; and since there is hardly any use for fish other than eating, that God would have wished to make the waters fruitful with such a multitude and not have granted the eating of them, or that more power was given to man over animals after the flood than at the beginning of the world. These and other reasons are urged by Cajetan, Dominicus à Soto, and Cornel. à Lapide, Piscator, and Rivetus, from whom they conclude that the eating of meat was permitted.

On Gen. 1:29 they say that the eating of meat is not denied there, even if mention is made only of herbs and the fruits of trees: nay, that the use and also the eating of living creatures is included under the dominion; and that the present passage is not to be opposed to that one, but to illustrate it; since here there is a confirmation of the prior right and power, which is expressly defined in this place for the reason that God wished here to sanction the law concerning not eating blood and things strangled, and to add that exception here for the first time. And certainly, unless lambs had been given to men for food at that time, there would have been no praise for Abel in the fact that he chose the fat firstlings for sacrifice: for it would have been all the same to him to sacrifice fat ones as lean ones, if he were not pasturing the flock for the sake of the eating of meat, but only for the use of the skins. These are their words. Grotius, however, argues otherwise elsewhere, namely in book 2 of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter 20. Psalm 9. that it was not even permitted for man to kill beasts before this law, or before God had made known His will concerning the turning of other living creatures into food for men. Thus Democritus, interpreting it according to natural law. Regarding the killing or not killing of living creatures, the matter stands thus: whoever kills those that wish to do injury, or do so, is pure, to such an extent that it is more right to have done this than not to have done it. And further: It is right to kill entirely and all those things which unjustly harm us. Grotius adds, it is not improbable that upright men lived in this manner before the flood. But whence will this be proved? The dominion of man over all living creatures certainly teaches enough that even those which did not do harm could be killed.

But it is worthy of more serious consideration what Grotius adds here to Genesis, namely that GOD shows here that individual men are cared for by Him, while only the species of other living creatures and their imperfections are ordered by Him for the use of more perfect ones, if, as it appears, he understood this from the mind of the Jews, which R. Moses in Moreh Nevukhim ch. 136 explained thus: That no corruptible individuals are subject to divine providence, except men, on account of the intellect, which is incorruptible. Has Grotius therefore perhaps changed his opinion, as in other matters, so also in this chapter? Whatever may be the case regarding him, those things are entirely solid which he argued against that profane error in book 1 of De Veritate Religionis Christianae §. 11. argued, and are worthy to be opposed to the same here: Nor are they less mistaken who wish universals to be cared for by Him, but not individuals (than those who include this providence in the spheres of heaven, which he had said err greatly.) For if they wish individuals to be unknown to GOD, which some profess, the knowledge of GOD will not be infinite. But if GOD knows those things, why should He not also care for them, especially since both individuals, as they are individuals, are ordered to a certain end, both peculiar and universal: and the very species of things, which those same authors acknowledge to be preserved by GOD, do not subsist except in individuals, so that if individuals can perish, the species themselves can be abandoned by divine providence. Add to these the sayings of Scripture, which openly establish a universal providence of God extending to all things and individuals, Job 38:41, Psalm 104:21, Matthew 6:26, 10:6, Acts 17:25, Colossians 1:17, Hebrews 1:3, Wisdom 13:13.

Latin:

Vers. 3. OMNE, QUOD MOVETUR ET VIVIT, ERIT VOBIS IN ESCAM, QUASI OLERA VIRENTIA TRA- DIDI VOBIS OMNIA.) Videtur plane hic locus, & quæ se- quitur exceptio de sanguine, indicare quod ante diximus, ante diluvium jus quidem homini fuisse in animantia, ut scilicet la- cte, lana & mortuorum suo fato exuviis uteretur, non ut in cibum ea verteret: de quo jure antiquissimo, à quibusdam et- iam gentibus post diluvium servato, vide, quæ ex omnibus hi- storiis congessit Hieronymus II. adversus Jovinianum, cui adde Porphyrium hujus argumenti libro, & quæ nobis dicta de jure belli ac pacis libro 2. cap. 20. §. 9. & in annotatis ad eum locum. Ostendit hîc DEUS homines à se curari singulos, aliorum animantium sola tantum genera, & imperfectiora à se ordinari in usum perfectiorum.

Grotio plane videtur hic locus indicare homini ante diluvium concessum non fuisse, ut in cibum verteret animantia. Sed dici posset, jus pristinum, quod è dominio habuit in eadem, hîc expresse repetitum. Permittimus tamen facile quemvis hîc abundare sensu suo. Cum Grotio consentiunt Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Thomas, Hugo, Autores glossæ ordinariæ, Lyranus, Abulensis, Brentius, Gerhardus, Martyr, &c. è collatione imprimis Gen. 1. versu 29. & quod hîc loci addatur, quasi olera virentia dedi vobis, ac si dicat, hactenus vobis solum olera concessi, nunc perinde etiam animalium carnes vobis in cibum concedo. Addunt, solas fruges hominibus post diluvium in immensum auctis non sufficere in locis sterilibus, eosque ceu infirmiores jam validioribus fulturis opus habere, terræ nascentibus misere per diluvium corruptis, quas rationes hujus concessionis adferunt. Theodoretus etiam eam factam ait, quod præviderit Deus homines ad idololatriam pronos, animantia adoraturos, unde pro cibo carnem eorum indulsit, ut colligerent, quam absurdum sit, eas res religiose colere, quas ipsis occidere & comedere permissum esset. Perperam vero Tertull. Montanizans esum illum refert ad incontinentiam hominum, neque rectius Hieronymus libr. 1. contra Jovianum concessionem factam censet, ob σκληροκαρδίαν. Cæterum aliis non videtur probabile, cum post peccatum ad vestitum pelles animantium dederit Deus homini, carnes earum abjectas fuisse, ceu inutiles; & cum vix usus alius sit piscium quam esus, Deum tanta multitudine aquas fœcundare voluisse, nec esum concessisse, aut plus datum fuisse homini potestatis in animalia post diluvium, quam in mundi initio. Quæ & aliæ rationes urgentur à Cajetano, Dominico à Soto, Cornel. à Lapide, Piscatore, & Riveto, unde licitum fuisse esum carnium concludunt.

Ad Gen. 1, 29. dicunt, non negari illic esum carnium, etsi herbarum & fructuum arborum mentio solum fiat: imo comprehendi sub dominio in animantia usum & esum quoque eorum; neque locum præsentem illi opponendum esse; sed eundem illustrare; siquidem hîc prioris juris & potestatis confirmatio habeatur, quæ expresse hoc in loco definitur ea de causa, quia voluit Deus hic legem de sanguine & suffocato non comedendo sancire, & exceptionem illam primo hîc addere. Et certe nisi tunc agni dati fuissent hominibus ad esum, nulla Abeli ex eo laus fuisset, quod primogenitos pingues elegerit ad sacrificium: perinde enim ipsi fuisset pingues atque macilentos sacrificare, si non propter esum carnium, sed propter solum pellium usum gregem pascebat. Hæc illi. Disputat autem alias Grotius, libro nempe 2. de jure Pacis & Belli c. 20. Psalm. 9. ne interficere quidem licuisse homini bestias ante hanc legem, seu antequam Deus suam voluntatem de vertendis in hominum alimenta cæteris animantibus prodidisset. Ita Democritus de naturali jure accipiens. De occidendis, aut non occidendis animantibus ita se res habet: quæ injuriam facere volunt, aut faciunt, quisquis occiderit, purus est, adeo quidem, ut hoc fecisse, quam non fecisse sit rectius. Et porro: Ea, quæ injuste nobis nocent, omnino & omnia fas occidere. Addit Grotius, non improbabile est, hoc more vixisse viros probos ante diluvium. Sed unde hoc probabi- tur? Dominium certe hominis in animantia omnia satis docet, ea etiam occidi potuisse, quæ non nocuere.

Sed graviori animadversione dignum, quod his in Genesin addit Grotius, quod nempe ostendat hîc DEUS, homines à se curari singulos, aliorum ani- mantium sola tantum genera, & imperfectiona à se ordinari in usum perfectiorum, si, quod apparet, ex Judæorum mente id intellexit, quam R. Moses direct. perplex. c. 136. ita exposuit: Nulla indivi- dua corruptibilia subjacere divinæ providentiæ, nisi homines, propter intellectum, qui est incorruptibilis. Num ergo mutavit forte sententiam Grotius, ut in aliis, ita etiam in hoc capite? Quicquid de eo sit, solida omnino sunt, quæ adversus prophanum illum errorem lib. 1. de V. R. C. §. 11. disputavit, & digna, quæ hîc eidem opponantur: Neque minus falluntur, qui universalia ab eo curari volunt, non & singula- ria (quam qui providentiam hanc cœli orbibus inclu- dunt, quos multum errare dixerat.) Nam si ignorari à DEO singularia volunt, quod quidam profitentur, non infinita erit scientia DEI. Quod si illa cognoscit DEUS, quidni & curet, præsertim cum & singula, qua singula sunt, ordinentur ad finem certum tum peculiarem, tum universalem: & ipsa rerum genera, quæ à DEO conservari illi ipsi auctores agnoscunt, non subsistant, nisi in singulis, ita, ut si singula perire pos- sunt, abdicari à divina providentia possint & ipsa gene- ra. Adde his dicta Scripturæ, quæ universalem Dei providentiam ad omnia & singula se porrigen- tem, palam adstruunt, Job. 38. v. 41. Psalm. 104, 21. Matth. 6, 26. c. 10, 6. Act. 17, 25. Coloss. 1, 17. Ebr. 1, 3. Sap. 13. v. 13.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. EXCEPT THAT YOU SHALL NOT EAT FLESH WITH THE BLOOD.) In the Hebrew it is, only flesh in its soul with its blood you shall not eat. The Greeks, πλὴν κρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς ὐ φάγεσθε. Aquila, ἐν ψυχῇ ἀυτῶ αἷμα αὐτῶ. Symmachus, ἐσὺν ψυχῇ ἅμα ἀυτῶ. More recent Hebrews, and, as I believe, out of hatred for Christians, feel that the eating of a limb torn from a living animal is forbidden here, such delicacies as I see once pleased the Americans. Both Arnobius and others make mention of it as having been customary long ago. But certainly Josephus teaches sufficiently that the older Hebrews did not interpret it so, who says χωρὶς αἵματος ἐν τουτῳ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή: which sense Rabbi Saadias expressed here in almost the same words, and certain not ignoble masters of the Hebrews follow: namely that Moses first said that flesh with the soul was not to be eaten, then explaining himself he added, that is, with the blood. The name of soul is given to blood, because, as Empedocles felt, ψυχὴ ἐν τῇ αἵματος συσάσει. Blood is to the vital soul what oil is to a lamp. Plutarch on Homeric Poetry, τὸ αἷμα νομὴ καὶ τροφή ἐστι τῷ πνεύματι. Servius on that line 'Purpureus flores': Blood is either the soul, or the seat of the soul. To eat flesh with blood is to eat sausages distended with gore, as Tertullian speaks in the Apologeticus, section 9, and if there are any things similar to these. An open passage in Deuteronomy 23 does not allow us to doubt the meaning, where to eat blood is explained as eating the soul with the flesh. Thus the Apostles of Acts 15:29 understood the passage of Moses. Indeed, as Tertullian speaks in his book De Monogamia: In Christ all things are recalled to the beginning, so that faith has returned from circumcision to the integrity of that flesh, as it was from the beginning: and the freedom of foods and abstinence from blood alone, as it was from the beginning: and the indissolubility of marriage as it was from the beginning: and the restraint of divorce, which was not from the beginning. The same author, dealing with this law in his book on fasting: Likewise after the flood in the reformation of the human race, one law sufficed for the time being to abstain from blood, with the use of other things permitted. Sulpitius Severus in this history: He received the commandment of God, not to feed on blood. Concerning those sausages, that is, blood stuffed into intestines as if into tunics, see also Leo, Novella 58. The Apostles equate these with τὰ πνικτὰ, as do the Hebrews. See the book Chulin. Rightly so, because in strangled things all the blood was studiously preserved, and it was boiled in the flesh. See Athenaeus. The Troglodytes, a savage race, used blood together with milk, as Strabo teaches us. The same is reported of the Scythians, Concani, and other barbarians. Among milder nations this was disapproved: Pliny in book 28, at the beginning, dealing with blood: Since it is not right for human blood to be brought to the mouth even from the wounds of wild beasts. The cause of the precept is partly physical, as we shall say below, and partly moral, signifying that the desire for vengeance, which feeds itself on blood, is to be avoided.

Latin:

Vers. 4. EXCEPTO QUOD CARNEM CUM SANGUI- NE NON COMEDETIS.) In Hebræo est, tantum carnem in anima ejus cum sanguine ipsius non comedetis. Græci, πλὴν κρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς ὐ φάγεσθε. Aquila, ἐν ψυχῇ ἀυτῶ αἷμα αὐτῶ. Symmachus, ἐσὺν ψυχῇ ἅμα ἀυτῶ. Hebræi recen- tiores, &, ut credo, Christianorum odio, sentiunt vetari hic esum membri rapti de animali vivo, quales delicias & Ameri- canis quondam placuisse video. Faciunt ejus jam olim usita- ti mentionem & Arnobius & alii. At certe vetustiores He- bræorum non ita interpretatos satis docet Josephus, qui ait χωρὶς αἵματος ἐν τουτῳ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή: quem sensum iis- dem prope verbis hic expressit Rabbi Saadias, & quidam se- quuntur non ignobiles Hebræorum magistri: nimirum ut Mo- ses primum dixerit, carnem cum anima non comedendam, de- inde semet exponens addiderit, id est, cum sanguine. Sangui- ni datur nomen animæ, quia, ut Empedocles sentiebat, ψυχὴ ἐν τῇ αἵματος συσάσει. Est id animæ vitali sanguis, quod ole- um Lychno. Plutarchus de Homerica Poësi, τὸ αἷμα νομὴ καὶ τροφή ἐστι τῷ πνεύματι. Servius ad illud Purpureus flores: San- guis aut anima, aut animæ sedes. Carnem cum sanguine come- dere, est comedere botulos cruore distentos, ut Tertullianus loquitur in Apologetico, sectione 9. & si qua his sunt similia. Non sinit nos de sensu dubitare locus apertus Deut. 23. ubi san- guinem comedere, explicatur, animam comedere cum carni- bus. Sic intellexere Mosis locum Apostoli Actorum 15, 29. Nimirum ut Tertullianus loquitur libro de Monogamia: In Christo omnia revocantur ad initium, ut & fides reversa sit à circumcisione ad integritatem carnis illius, sicut ab initio fuit: & libertas ciborum & sanguinis solius abstinentia, sicut ab ini- tio fuit: & matrimonii individuïtas sicut ab initio fuit: & repudii cohibitio, quod ab initio non fuit. Idem de jejunio de hac lege agens: Æque post diluvium in reformatione generis humani, suffecisse unam interim legem à sanguine abstinendi, permisso usu cæterorum. Sulpitius Severus in hac historia: Dei præceptum accepit, ne sanguine vesceretur. De botulis illis, id est, de sanguine intestinis, tanquam tunicis, infarcto, vide & Leonem Novella 58. His æquant Apostoli τὰ πνικτὰ, ut & Hebræi. Vide librum Chulin. merito, quia ἐν πνικτοῖς san- guis omnis studiosé asservabatur, & in carne elixabatur. Vi- de Athenæum. Sanguine simul cum lacte usi Troglodytæ, gens effera, ut Strabo nos docet. Idem de Scythis, Concanis, aliis- que barbaris proditum. Mitioribus gentibus id improbatum: Plinius libro 28. in principio de sanguine agens: Cum è plagis hunc ne ferarum quidem admoveri ori fas sit humano. Causa præcepti partim physica est, ut infra dicemus, partim moralis, fignificans vitandam ultionis cupidinem, quæ fanguine fe pascit.

## 9:5
Vers. 5. FOR I WILL REQUIRE THE BLOOD OF YOUR SOULS FROM THE HAND OF ALL BEASTS.) That is, the Hebrews say, I will punish those who exposed men to beasts.

The Hebrew phrase demands another sense: and therefore our people more correctly observe here an argument from the lesser to the greater. If even brutes lacking reason do not kill a man with impunity, how much less will murderers among men be free from punishment, Exodus 21:9.

HIS BROTHER.) For nature established a certain kinship among us, says Florentinus, l. Ut vim, ff. de justitia et jure.

Latin:

Verf. 5. SANGUINEM ENIM ANIMARUM VESTRA- RUM REQUIRAM DE MANU CUNCTARUM BESTIA- RUM.) Id est, ajunt Hebræi, puniam eos, qui homines bestiis objecere.

Alium sensum postulat phrasis Ebræa: ideoque rectius nostri hîc observant argumentum à minori ad majus. Si nec bruta ratione carentia impune occidunt hominem, quanto minus homicidæ inter homines à pœna erunt liberi, Exod. 21, 9.

FRATRIS EJUS.) Cognationem enim quandam inter nos natura constituit, ait Florentinus l. Ut vim ff. de justitia & jure.

## 9:6
Vers. 6. WHOEVER SHEDS HUMAN BLOOD, HIS BLOOD SHALL BE SHED.) In the Hebrew, shedding the blood of man, in man his blood shall be shed. Where the Hebrews interpret 'in man' as 'by man', and draw it to what follows, so that the sense is that the death of the murderer is to be inflicted by the judgment of judges pronounced from the testimony of witnesses. But when this law was given, judgments had not yet been established. Therefore, it is more true that the natural law of retaliation is indicated here, which, when the human race had increased and was distributed into nations, was deservedly permitted only to judges, except for certain excepted cases, in which that primordial right remained. See what we wrote in De Jure Belli ac Pacis book 1, ch. 2, § 5, and book 2, ch. 20, § 8. Not badly, therefore, do you interpret that 'by man' in such a way that he who is devoted to death is understood, not only he who committed the homicide with his own hand, but also he who ordered it.

Grotius, serving his own peculiar hypothesis, tears the text apart, while he accuses others of that crime. For both the system of accents and the words themselves teach that that באדם belongs to what follows, and it was accordingly observed by the Hebrews. What sense is there, if they are snatched away to what precedes, 'shedding the blood of man in man'? Two are not expressed here, as Grotius wishes, he who commits homicide and he who commands, but the discourse is about one. Otherwise, only this would be hinted at, that he who sheds blood through another is to be devoted to death in turn: but not he who does it by the command of another; and indeed it is not even said of him who himself, not through another, commits homicide, only of him who commits it through another. Therefore, τὸ באדם belongs entirely to what follows, and must be rendered 'by man,' as Grotius renders it. That this is badly omitted in the Vulgate, our author ought to have noted. But he sees σφάλματα in the Hebrew only where they are not, and where they are in the Vulgate, he cannot see them. That these words 'by man' are to be understood of the Magistrate is evident to him from the paraphrase of Onkelos and Jonathan.

But the hypothesis which Grotius supposes is most false: that by the natural law of retaliation it was permitted to anyone to kill a homicide in turn. Which we have refuted before. The reason is also false, that when this law was enacted, courts had not yet been established. Even if the Jewish ones according to the Mosaic forensic law were not established: other nations had their own Magistrates, their own judges; those also had them who constituted the Church of God. For it could not have subsisted without a Magistrate or superior power. Although indeed GOD armed the superior power with the sword for punishment against criminals, as the Apostle testifies in Romans 13, verse 4. It is necessary that he form in his mind a wonderful polity for himself throughout the whole world up to the judgments instituted by Moses, if there were no judgments for so many centuries. Which paradox we leave to be further chastised by Politicians and Jurists. Since in the former [work] concerning the law of retaliation, Arminius, whom Grotius willingly follows, Disp. Theol. 25, teaches in thesis 8, page 246, that the use of political power would have had a place even in the primeval integrity of men, it was much more necessary after the fall. Without rule, says Cicero in book 3 of the Laws, no house, nor city, nor nation, nor the whole race of men can stand, nor can the whole nature of things, nor the world itself endure.

But there seems to be hidden something ὑπηλόν: since it is known that the Anabaptists and Socinians, desiring to abolish capital punishment in the New Testament, restrict it only to the Jewish polity. To whom perhaps, since he could not be constrained by the arguments which he adduced in book 1, de jure pacis & belli c. 2. §. 7, he wished to gratify them only in part. But if he does not intend this, he at least wished to introduce that natural right concerning lawful revenge, which he pursues especially in book 2, de jure Pacis & belli c. 20. §. 9, which, however, ought by no means to be approved.

What he brings forward there from Justin and others ought to have been ascribed to the abuse of the law of nature and the blindness of the Pagans, rather than to liberty. Such as that of Mithridates: against a robber, if they cannot for safety, yet for their own REVENGE all draw the sword. Such things as these are not approved even by the saner Gentiles, so far are they from being referred to the law of nature, as those things teach which he himself adduced from Demosthenes: it was resolved to exercise judgment concerning all these injuries according to the laws; but not from the impulse and whim of each person. And that of Quintilian: the compensation of injury is not only hostile to law, but to peace. For there is law, a forum, a judge, unless one is ashamed to vindicate by law. If it is hostile to law, how is it consistent with natural law? Then that of Seneca: We would not afflict even vipers and water-snakes, and if any others harm by bite or sting, if we could tame them like the rest, or ensure that they were not a danger to us. Therefore we will not harm even a man because he has sinned, but so that he may not sin. If it is not right to harm a man because he has sinned, how is private revenge consistent with natural law?

But when Grotius objects to those things, that the power of vindicating the injured was given to constituted judges to these alone, with the liberty which nature had indulged being taken away from the rest: he is mistaken in more than one way. If by this the liberty of nature is taken away, this constitution will be contrary to the law of nature, which no one will admit. Therefore, divine precepts, which severely prohibit private revenge, are more contrary; which it is by no means to be believed are in conflict with the law of nature. Nor were judges constituted only by human whim, as Grotius implies: There is no power but from God; and the powers that be are ordained of God, Romans 13:1. And did many families only then come together into one place when judgments were constituted among the Jews? For Grotius admits that, because we are corrupted in our own affairs and by the affection for our own, many families came together into one place, judges were constituted, and to these alone was given the power of vindicating the injured.

Latin:

Verf. 6. QUICUNQUE EFFUDERIT HUMANUM SAN- GUINEM, FUNDETUR SANGUIS ILLIUS.) In Hebraico, effundens sanguinem hominis, in homine sanguis ejus effundetur. Ubi in homine per hominem interpretantur Hebræi, trahunt- que ad sequentia, ut sensus sit, ex testium testimonio judicum pronunciato mortem homicidæ inferendam. At cum hæc lex lata est, nondum constituta erant judicia. Itaque naturale jus talionis hîc indicari verius, quod aucto humano genere, & in gentes distributo, merito solis judicibus permissum fuit, ex- tra cafus quosdam exceptos, in quibus mansit jus illud pri- mævum. Vide, quæ nos de Jure belli ac pacis lib. 1. c. 2. §. 5. & lib. 2. c. 20. §. 8. Non male igitur illud per hominem sic in- terpreteris, ut morti devotus intelligatur, non is tantum, qui manu sua perpetravit homicidium, sed & is, qui mandavit.

Grotius peculiari suæ hypothesi δελεύων discerpit textum, dum alios ejus criminis arguit. Nam & accentuum ratio, & verba ipsa docent, illud באדם ad sequentia pertinere, idque proinde observatum fuit Ebræis. Quis sensus, si ad præce- dentia abripiantur, effundens sanguinem hominis in homine? Non duo hîc exprimuntur, uti vult Gro- tius, is, qui perpetrat homicidia, & qui mandat, sed de uno sermo est. Alias solum id innueretur, eum, qui per alium effundit sanguinem, iterum morti devovendum: Non autem hunc, qui alte- rius mandato id facit: ac ne de eo quidem id dici, qui ipse, non per alium, homicidium patrat, solum de eo, qui per alium id committit. Omnino ergo ad sequentia τὸ באדם pertinet, & per hominem reddendum est, uti reddit Grotius. Quod in Vul- gata male omitti, annotasse debebat Noster. Sed is in Ebræo solum videt σφάλματα, ubi non sunt, in Vulgata, ubi sunt, videre ea non potest. Quæ verba per hominem de Magistratu intelligenda, ipsi è pa- raphrasi Onkelos, & Jonathan constat.

Falsissima autem est hypothesis, quam sup- ponit Grotius: quod naturali jure talionis homici- dam vicissim occidere cuivis licuerit. Quam antea confutavimus. Falsa etiam ratio, cum hæc lex lata est, nondum constituta fuisse judicia. Etiamsi Judai- ca secundum legem forensem Mosaicam, non consti- tuta: habuerunt aliæ gentes suos Magistratus, suos judices; habuerunt & illi, qui Ecclesiam Dei con- stituebant. Non enim sine Magistratu vel potesta- te superiori consistere potuisset. Quamvis enim potestatem superiorem DEUS armavit gladio in pœnam, adversus facinorosos, teste Apostolo Roman. 13. verf. 4. Mirabilem necessum est animo suo formet sibi politiam per universum orbem usq; ad instituta per Mosen judicia, si nulla judicia per tot secula fuere. Quod paradoxon ulterius casti- gandum Politicis atque JCtis relinquimus. Quum in priori de jure talionis Arminius, quem liben- ter sequitur Grotius, Disp. Theol. 25. politicæ po- testatis usum etiam in primæva hominum integrita- te locum habiturum fuisse, doceat thef. 8. pag. 246. multo magis post lapsum necessaria fuit. Sine im- perio, inquit Cicero lib. 3. de legibus, non domus ul- la, nec civitas, nec gens, nec hominum universum genus stare, nec rerum natura omnis, nec ipse mundus durare potest.

Sed latere videtur ὑπηλόν τι: quum notum sit, Anabaptistas & Socinianos capitalem pœnam in No- vo Testamento tollere cupientes, non nisi ad poli- tiam Judaicam eam restringere. Quibus fortassis, quum ex asse argumentis, quæ l. 1. de jure pacis & belli c. 2. §. 7. adduxit, constrictus, non possit, ex parte solum gratificari voluit. Si vero hoc non in- tendit, jus saltem illud naturale de ultione licita inge- rere voluit, quod imprimis l. 2. de jure Pacis & bel- li c. 20. §. 9. persequitur, quod vero probari nulla- tenus debet.

Quæ ibi è Justino, & aliis profert, abusui juris naturæ & cæcitati Paganorum potius adscribenda erant, quam libertati. Quale illud est Mithridatis: adversus latronem, si nequeunt pro Salute, pro UL- TIONE tamen sua omnes ferrum stringere. Hæc ta- lia ne gentilibus sanioribus quidem probata sunt, tantum abest, ut ad jus naturæ referri debeant, uti ea docent, quæ ipse è Demosthene adduxit: placuit de omnibus his injuriis ex legibus judicium exercere; non autem ex cujusque impetu atque arbitrio. Et illud Quintiliani: injuriæ compensatio non solum juri ini- mica, sed paci. Est enim lex, forum, judex, nisi quem jure vindicare pudet. Si inimica juri, quomodo consentanea juri naturali? Tum Senecæ istud: Ne viperas quidem & natrices, & si quæ morsu aut ictu nocent, affligeremus, si ut reliqua mansuefacere posse- mus, aut efficere, ne nobis alicui periculo essent. Ergo ne homini quidem nocebimus, quia peccavit, sed ne peccet. Si nocere homini fas non est, quia pecca- vit, quî juri naturali convenit privata ultio?

Cum vero ad illa excipit Grotius, judicibus constitutis potestatem vindicandi læsum his solis da- tam, ademta cæteris, quam natura indulserat, liber- tate: non uno modo fallitur. Si ademta per hoc naturæ libertas, contraria erit juri naturæ hæc con- stitutio, quod nemo admittet. Magis ergo contra- ria præcepta divina, ultionem privatam severe pro- hibentia; quæ pugnare cum naturæ lege haudqua- quam credendum. Neque constituti solum judices humano arbitrio, uti Grotius innuit: Non est po- testas, nisi à Deo; quæ autem potestates sunt, à Deo ordinatæ sunt Roman. 13, 1. Et num familiæ multæ tum demum in unum locum convenere, cum Ju- dæis constitutæ sunt judicia? Fatetur enim Gro- tius, quia in rebus nostris & nostrorum affectu cor- rumpimur, simul multas familias in unum locum con- venisse, judices constitutos, & his solis datam potesta- tem vindicandi læsos.

## 9:13
Verse 13. I WILL SET MY BOW IN THE CLOUDS, AND IT SHALL BE A SIGN OF THE COVENANT BETWEEN ME AND THE EARTH.) Even among the Poets, Iris is the messenger of the Gods. The three colors in the Rainbow signify God's severity, clemency, and beneficence.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ARCUM MEUM PONAM IN NUBIBUS, ET ERIT SIGNUM FOEDERIS INTER ME ET TER- RAM.) Etiam apud Poëtas Iris Deorum nuncia. Tres in Iride colores significant Dei severitatem, clementiam & be- neficentiam.

## 9:25
Verse 25. A SERVANT OF SERVANTS SHALL HE BE UNTO HIS BRETHREN.) By the law of nature, servitude is the punishment of a graver sin. It is expedient for the imprudent to be under another. Philo in his book, that every good man is free.

Latin:

Vers. 25. SERVUS SERVORUM ERIT FRATRIBUS SUIS.) Jure naturæ servitus pœna peccati gravioris. Im- prudenti expedit esse sub alio. Philo in libro, omnem virum bonum esse liberum.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. The genealogy of the sons of Noah, and the distribution of the peoples of the earth according to them.

Verse 1. HAM AND JAPHETH.) Concerning the ancient traces of all the names in this chapter, see what we have noted on book 1, de Veritate Relig. Christianæ.

Latin:

CAPUT X. Genealogia filiorum Noëh, & distributio popu lorum terræ secundum eosdem.

Vers. 1. CHAM ET JAPHET.) De omnium in hoc ca pite nominum vestigiis veteribus, vide, quæ notavimus ad li brum 1. de Veritate Relig. Christianæ.

## 10:9
Verse 9. A MIGHTY HUNTER BEFORE THE LORD.) Happy in hunting, because he gave a part of the prey to God. Aben Ezra. Things are said to be done before God, either which are very pleasing to God, or which displease him.

Most people take this in the worse sense. Things that are said to be done before God, as Grotius observes, are those which are very pleasing to God, or which displease him: this latter sense fits better with the description that he was a mighty hunter, which is wont to be attributed to oppressors and persecutors, Jer. 16:16, Lam. 3:11, Ezek. 33:30. Cf. also Psalm 91:3, and also with the lineage which he drew from the impious family of Ham, and his pursuits in building towers and fortifications, among which the tower of Babylon seems to have been, and it is approved by the Hebrews generally, if you depart from Aben Ezra: and it is confirmed by the calculation of the paraphrases themselves, which are of great authority among them. For thus Jonathan: This was a hero rebellious before Jehovah; therefore it was said: from the days of the creation of the world there has not existed one like Nimrod, powerful in hunting, and rebellious before the Lord. And the Jerusalem Targum: This was powerful in hunting, in sin before Jehovah, because he hunted the sons of men with his tongues, and said to them: Depart from the instituted rites of God, and adhere to the institutes of Nimrod, therefore it was said: Nimrod was a hero powerful in hunting and in sin before Jehovah. It is absurd for this to be understood only of happiness in hunting wild beasts. For Moses is occupied here in describing far graver things. Among Christian interpreters, it is undoubted that the tyranny of Nimrod is designated, which was so great that from the first and notable tyrant a proverb began to be used of others: This is like another Nimrod.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ROBUSTUS VENATOR CORAM DOMI NO.) Felix in venatu, quia prædæ partem Deo dabat. Aben Ezra. Coram Deo fieri dicuntur, aut quæ Deo pergrata sunt, aut quæ ei displicent.

IN sequiorem partem plerique hoc accipiunt. Qui coram Deo fieri dicuntur, uti observat Grotius quæ Deo pergrata sunt, aut quæ ei displicent : hic poste- rior sensus descriptioni, quod robustus venator fue- rit, quæ oppressoribus & persequutoribus tribui solet, Jer. 16, 16. Thren. 3, 11. Ezech. 33, 30. Conf. & Psalm. 91, 3. nec non prosapiæ, quam traxit ex impia Cha- mi familia, ac studiis in turribus ac munitionibus exstruendis, inter quas turris Babylon fuisse vide- tur, magis congruit, & Ebræis fere, si ab Aben- Ezra discesseris, probatur: ipsarumque paraphra- sium, quæ magnæ penes ipsos sunt autoritatis, cal- culo confirmatur. Ita enim Jonathan: Hic fuit he- ros coram Jehovah rebellis; propterea dictum est: à diebus creati mundi non extitit velut Nimrod potens in venatione, & rebellis coram Domino. Et Hie- rosolymitanorum Targum: Hic fuit potens in vena- tione, in peccato coram Jehovah, quia fuit venatus filios hominum linguis suis, & dixit eis: Discedite ab institutis ritibus Dei, & adhærete institutis Nimro- di, propterea dictum fuit: Fuit Nimrod Heros potens in venatione & peccato coram Jehovah. Ineptum est, de felicitate in venatu solum ferarum id intelli- gi. Moses enim in longe gravioribus describendis hic occupatur. Inter Christianos interpretes in- dubitatum hoc est, Tyrannidem Nimrodi designa- ri, quæ tanta fuit, ut à primo atque insigni tyranno proverbium usurpari ceperit de aliis: Hic est velut alter Nimrod.

## 10:22
Verse 22. THE SONS OF SHEM. In the Hebrew five are recounted; in the Greek text of the LXX Interpreters a sixth is added, Kanan, against the faith of all the Codices, which is without any ambiguity alien and interpolated: no less than Cainan for Arphaxad v. 24 and chapter 11:12, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 22. FILII SEM. In Ebræo quinque re- censentur; in Græco LXX. Interpretum textu sex- tus additus est Kanan, contra omnium Codicum fidem, qui citra omnem ambiguitatem alienus & irreptitius est: non minus quam Arphaxadi Cai- nan v. 24. & cap. 11, 12. 13.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

The Tower of Babel, and the confusion of languages: as also the Genealogy of Shem down to Abram.

Vers. 1. AND THE EARTH WAS OF ONE LIP.) The Hebrews call that language their own: the Syrians theirs. But the Hebrew language is the language of עברים, of those who came from Chaldea. For this is the origin of the name of the Hebrews, not from Heber. See Josh. 24, 2. 3. That Hebrew language of Abraham, therefore, by the dwelling of his descendants in Canaan, approached ever closer and closer to the Canaanite, nor does it differ from the Punic, except in certain properties of dialect, as has been shown by most learned men. Wherefore it is more true that the primeval language exists nowhere in its pure state, but that there are remnants of it in all languages: but the proper names of Adam, Eve, and the rest, expressed in the Hebrew tongue by Moses, are for the sake of the Hebrews of the same meaning that they had in the primeval language. Thus Curtius says that certain soldiers were called immortals by the Persians, that the entrance to Cilicia was called Pylae by the inhabitants: that those who were in command of each thousand soldiers were called Chiliarchs by the Persians: that other narrow passes were called Susian Pylae by the Persians: and many things of that kind occur everywhere among historians. Eusebius says that certain serpents were called ἀγαθὲς δαίμονας by the Phoenicians. Herodian says Venus was called ὀρανίαν by the Africans. In Africa the names Pithecusae and Ampelusiae are translated from Punic into Greek, as Diodorus testifies in book 20. Mela in book 1. Thus what is Aspis to the Greeks, is Clupea to the Latins. Athenaeus in book 6 says: Κελτοὶ περιάγονται καὶ μεθ' ἑαυτῶν καὶ πολεμῦντες συμβιωτὰς ὃὺς καλὲσι παρασίτες: that is, they call them by a Gallic word, which signifies parasites. A hump is for Marcellinus what Procopius calls κυρτὸν. The same Procopius for the Venetian Charioteers said κυανίες. And we, writing in Latin, call the city of Brabant the Duke's Wood, and the Greek interpreters of the sacred books set down not a few names of places in Greek, such as δρῦν ὑψηλὴν, βάλανοι πένθες, πόλιν γραμμάτων, σιαγόνα.

Three things are touched upon here in our author rather than treated. The first is the origin of the name of the Hebrews. The second is the kinship of the Hebrew language with the Punic. The third is the distinction of the primeval language from the Hebrew. The origin of the name from Heber does not please Grotius: he prefers it to be called כפרים, those who came from Chaldea. Josh. XXIV. By a similar reasoning, Theodoret in Genesis 4, verse 6, and Jerome in [commentary] derive the Hebrews from עבר, to cross over, as if they were crossers.

Isa. 19:18, and in Ezek. ch. 7. Origen in Num. hom. 19, Chrysostom in Gen. hom. 35, and Augustine, Questions on Gen. 39, observe that it is derived from עָבַר, because Abraham, passing from Mesopotamia into Canaan, was called עִבְרִי, as if to say 'transfluvial,' Hottinger in Thesaur. Phil. p. 48; but even if we concede this regarding Jerome, who says that עִבְרִי sounds like περάτην, a 'transitor': it is certainly not clear regarding Augustine. We shall teach something else from the same person later. Whether Origen alluded to the name or actually rendered an etymology does not appear. The Hebrews, he says, interpret it as 'those who cross over': therefore, the Hebrew people are also called by this very name, who crossed from Egypt to the land of promise, from darkness to light, from death to life. Chrysostom wishes Abraham to be called περάτην in Gen. 14:10, or 'transitor,' because he went out from Chaldea and had his dwelling across the Euphrates, but he does not express the reason for the name of the Hebrews; indeed, he thinks out of ignorance of the holy tongue that he was called by the name Abram because he was about to migrate across the Euphrates. Theodoret derives it from Hebrew, which he falsely asserts is the same as Euphrates in the language of the Syrians. Therefore, that opinion does not have anything by which it might exalt itself through those authors. However, that the reason for the name of the Hebrews is explained in Josh. ch. 24 is a matter of dispute.

Buxtorf in Dissert. de linguæ Ebr. conserv., Rivet in Exercit. in Gen. 66, Nicholas Fuller in Miscell. Sacr. b. 4, ch. 4, and Balthasar Meisner in part 1, Phil. Sob. p. 19, show that it should rather be derived from Eber. Rivet also refutes the arguments of his colleague Erpenius for the former opinion, which is Grotius's. Moses seems to indicate the origin of the appellation in Gen. 10:21: 'This is the father of all the sons of Eber,' deriving the origin of the Hebrews from the Patriarch Shem, just as when he says that Ham was the father of Canaan, he signifies that the Canaanites descended from him. And Balaam in Num. 24:24: 'so that ships coming from the shore of the Chittim will afflict Asshur, and will afflict Eber,' so that by Asshur the Assyrians named after him are designated, and by Eber the Hebrews named after the same. Josephus clearly expresses this origin in b. 1, Antiqu. ch. 6: 'and Eber, from whom the Jews were called Hebrews from the beginning.' And St. Augustine in b. 16, de Civ. Dei ch. 3. Therefore, it is not in vain that he (Eber) himself is named first in the lineage coming from Shem and is preferred even to his sons, although he is the fifth grandson, unless it is true, as is handed down, that the Hebrews were surnamed from him, as Hebrews, although there could be another opinion, so that they seem to be called from Abraham as Abrahami. The Holy tongue opposes this opinion, nor does Augustine approve of it, and he retracts it where it was approved elsewhere in b. 3, Retract. ch. 16. However, Augustine defends the fact that they were called Hebrews from Eber, and says it is a tradition that this was the common opinion; which he also repeats in ch. 11 and b. 18, ch. 39. R. D. Kimchi in his Lexicon, Suidas in his Lexicon, our B. Luther in Gen. XI, and most of our people also defend it; indeed, Buxtorf and Hottinger observe that the same is most accepted among Jews and Christians. Selden, in de Diis Syr., is almost in doubt as to which opinion should be subscribed to, although he is more inclined toward the Grotian one. But if Abraham was called a Hebrew because he crossed the Euphrates, all his sons should likewise be called by the same name. However, the Ishmaelites and other nations descending from Abraham were never called so, but only the Israelites. I pass over the fact that the names of peoples are taken in the Holy tongue, if not from the regions they inhabited, certainly from the authors themselves. More can be seen about these in our Critico sacro p. 307 ff.

Now, as to the kinship with the Punic language, that Hebrew does not differ from it except in certain properties of dialect—which is a new invention of some—has not yet been shown, and it is much less likely that the Hebrew language approached closer and closer to the Canaanite language through the dwelling of Abraham and his descendants in Canaan. Jerome, most skilled in languages, in ch. 19 of Isaiah, says that the Canaanite language is between Egyptian and Hebrew, and is in large part akin to the latter, but does not differ only in certain properties of dialect. Similarly, Augustine, T. 10, Tract. in Evang. Joh. ch. 15, acknowledges that Hebrew, Punic, and Syriac are at least related and akin. However, it is by no means probable that Abraham abandoned his own language and approached the dialect of Canaan so that he might worship God in it; since the Patriarchs and other holy men always strove to be most alien from the idolatrous nation; and Nehemiah was inflamed with great zeal, even in later times, when he found Jews speaking Ashdodite, not Judaic, Nehem. 13:24.

Thus, indeed, it would necessarily have to be concluded (as the most learned Fuller speaks in b. 4, Miscell. Sacr. ch. 4, in his examination of this new opinion) that those whom God had once shut off as if by a most firm wall by the benefit of the confusion of languages (for thus divine kindness is accustomed to elicit its own goods from our evils), and had rendered easily avoidable, Abraham had joined more closely to himself by the common use of the same language (which is the primary degree of all commerce), and, having broken through, indeed demolished, that wall, had made them more difficult to avoid for himself, and almost inevitable for his descendants. For who does not see how great an obstacle, how ruinous a precipice into idolatry, the natural community of the same language with the Canaanites would have been for the Israelites? How great a window—I do not say window, but door, indeed how immense a gate—would have been opened by this reason to the contagion of the cursed nation, which was constantly about to persuade the chosen people? whom, however, the divine counsel wished to be removed as far as possible from that by all means: to which no pious or sensible person, I think, would ever deny that Abraham served most vigilantly in all things. Wherefore, he who even refused entirely the fellowship of his own burial with idolatrous nations would undoubtedly have rejected all the more the entire commerce of speech, by as much as the latter could have harmed piety more than the former. Nor does Fullerus observe beside the point that the Hebrew language, the mother of the others, was divinely preserved in the θεοπνεύστοις monuments, so that it might be held as a rule let down from heaven, to which all judgments of all languages might be directed, so that from a greater or lesser agreement or discrepancy, the integrity or corruption of each language might be discerned: and as the sight of the rainbow brought to memory the flood, so the hearing of the Hebrew language might bring to memory the most just punishment of the Babylonian confusion which spread through all nations. For this greatly conduces to the glory of the supreme judge (which is the main point) being amplified, and extended and promulgated to the perpetual ages of the centuries. Therefore, that a treasure of such great value should have been committed and handed over to the faith and care of the cursed Cham, and specifically of Canaan and his descendants, seems in no way probable. Indeed, it is entirely credible that it remained hidden among the members of the household of the Church of God, Noah, Shem, and Eber, who were not participants in the nefarious and impious conspiracy forged in the plain of Shinar.

Fullerus also learnedly discussed the supports of the new opinion. That the Hebrew names of persons or places, Abimelech, Melchisedech, Adonibezek, Bethlehem, Kiriatharba, Gen. 14. verse 20. Ch. 35. v. 19. Jos. 15, 15, are Canaanite, or imposed by the Canaanites, cannot be proven: since ancient names given by the indigenous Canaanites could have been pronounced by the Hebrews in the Hebrew manner, especially if it is established that the Syriac language is Canaanite, whence because of their affinity only a slight change of names is needed: and thus the nerve of the opposing party's main argument is cut. We add, however, those things with which Füller concludes his dissertation on p. 482. In sum, it pleases the proponents of that new opinion, especially some of the more keen ones, to grant now a little more than we had granted at the beginning. We therefore grant that the language which is called Hebrew in the New Testament is Canaanite, or Tyrian, or Punic, yet on this condition: that they do not disdain to leave to those whose proper study that language is—I mean theologians and candidates of theology, all of whose secrets are stored in the sacrosanct depths of the Hebrew language—the one that is preserved pure in the Old Testament as absolutely Hebrew.

There is therefore no reason why Grotius should deny that the Hebrew language is the first of all and the most ancient. But what, in the end, does he make the first? None. For he says that the first exists nowhere, but that its remnants are in all languages. Cluverius preceded him in Germ. antiqv. book 1, ch. 8, establishing that at the construction of the tower GOD dissipated that one first language into many idioms, which thenceforth prevailed in the world with the mother extinct, but that the mother is to be recalled from those dissipations then when there shall emerge one shepherd and one flock. If you seek the argument for the new opinion, you will scarcely receive any other than that many words of the same meaning are found in different languages, which cannot be referred to anything else but the remnants of the first speech. But Cluverius did not teach which those many, or thousand, words are: he was scarcely able to bring forward one or two. And why could those not be referred to the Hebrew speech, of which few remain today, namely only those which are read in the Holy Hebrew Code. Nor is it permitted to conclude from the agreement of some languages in certain words to all of them, much less to their matrix and its remnants dispersed throughout all.

Furthermore, that the Hebrew language is the first is the common opinion of Jews and Christians, from which it is not right to depart without grave arguments. Perhaps only Theodoret, in q. 8 of his Genesis, claims this glory for his own, that is, the Syriac language, from the ancients. Whom, among the more recent, Georgius Amira, Bishop of Antioch and primate of Mount Lebanon, and Joh. Caspar Myricæus follow, but with weak reasons, refuted in the preface to the Syro-Chaldaic Grammar by M. Majerus in Phil. Sacr. Kircher, in Oedip. Tom. II, cl. 2, p. 51, commemorates a version of the Maronites which has it thus: And the languages were confused, and a division was made of their Syriac language. Patricides, the Arab historian, also reports that opinion: But there was then one language of men and one speech. Some wish it to have been Syriac. Which is also observed by Elmacinus: There are, however, he says, historians who establish that Adam and his descendants spoke Syriac until the confusion of languages. Nor does Athanasius Kircher deny it, yet he distinguishes between the doctrinal language, which he wishes to have been Hebrew, not known to all, used in teaching the disciplines, and the idiomatic or usual one, which he makes Syriac. But with no arguments that have any strength. For the boasting of the Syrians proves nothing. And the Hebrew language is without doubt prior and simpler than the Syrian. Patricides also commemorates that some made the Greek language the first, and he says that opinion seems truer to him; but with no, or only a plausible, pretext. The invention of Goropius Becanus, that the Cimbrian or Brabantine language is the most ancient, is rejected by all as a paradox. And truly the trifles of that Becanus, as the inscription has it, Bekkeselēnoi, are by his own merit marked by the author himself with the title of folly, which he laboriously produced for this opinion. Just like the dream of Philastrius concerning the nations of various languages before the confusion of tongues in the Catalogue of Heretics. ch. 6, which openly protests against this text of Gen. 11:1.

Most, therefore, with a unanimous voice defer this glory to the Hebrew language. Of the Hebrews, perhaps it is not surprising: from whom R. Solomon explains this passage concerning the holy language, just as Josephus in book 1, ch. 4, asserts its antiquity. But the Chaldean interpreters also explained our text concerning the Hebrew language. Jonathan and the author of the Jerusalem Targum, who adds: That all spoke the holy language, in which the world was founded, from the beginning. The rest of the interpreters and almost all commentators also take our text, that the whole earth was of one lip and the same words, as concerning the Eberine language. Elmacinus, the Arabic historian, praises Phriton for this opinion: The wise Phriton says that Seth is the inventor of letters, or elements of writing, and that he showed them in the Hebrew language. Nor is the reason obscure, from the proper names imposed before the confusion of languages. For it is futile what is said, that all those things were expressed by Moses with the same meaning that existed in the primeval language. For proper names remain immutable in all languages: just as those very Hebrew names Adam, Eve, Cain, Seth, and the rest have remained. For they are called by no other name in any language. Then if Moses invented those names, who asserts that those same names were imposed by the Patriarchs, as, for instance, that Adam called his spouse Chavvah because she is the mother of the living, Gen. 3:20; that Eve called her firstborn Cain, from possession, ch. 4:2, and another Seth, because GOD placed another seed, verse 26; that Lamech named his son Noah from rest and consolation, ch. 4:29; that Eber called his son Peleg in his own language (still before the confusion of languages), because he foresaw the division of peoples by a prophetic spirit, Gen. 10:25. Moses did not call them so, but those names were composed by Adam, by Eve, by Lamech, by Eber, as Moses testifies. If the names of the Hebrew language imposed after the γλωττοσύγχυσιν are compared with these, that agreement and similarity of names before the confusion and after the same sufficiently teaches that the primeval language was none other than Eberine or Hebrew. They agree so neatly that it is certain that no other language flourished in the family of Abraham and among the Israelites than the primeval one, used before the confusion, nay, before the flood and from the creation. Add the etymologies of all proper names, which is Mercer's observation, that before the flood and after, up to the division of languages, they cannot be attributed to any other language, just as neither can those others after that time which Moses uses, than the Hebrew: as אדם from אדמה, חוה because she was the mother of all living, Kain, Abel, Seth, Mahalaël, Kenaan, Noë, etc., the source of all of which and of the rest can be none other than Hebrew. But if you say that Moses could have transferred the names of those earlier fathers from the first language into his own, I ask how he could have been able to do that in all cases, to find everywhere as certain and constant an etymology of names as in that primeval language, whereas in few languages—as אדם from אדמה, man from earth—is it found in others; the Chaldean איש or גברא does not admit it, nor does ἀνὴρ or ἄνθρωπος among the Greeks, or in any other language. This is Mercer. And not only personal proper names, but also gentilic ones testify to this, for example, the Medes from Madai, the Ionians from Javan, and others, which smack of a Hebrew origin and signify nothing in other languages. See Jerome, Questions on Genesis; Arias Montanus, page 3, Biblical Apparatus; B. Luther, Commentary on Genesis. not only proper nouns, but also appellative ones, which in no language correspond so much to the nature and property of things as in Hebrew, so that there is no doubt that Adam, the Monarch of the world, imposed names upon living creatures, Gen. 2, 19. For everything that Adam called a living soul, that is its name. But this would not be its name if those primordial names had utterly perished. In the same language those etymologies also fit perfectly which are observed to have been rendered before the confusion, for example Gen. 2, 23. This shall be called אִשָּׁה woman, because she was taken מֵאִישׁ from man &c. Nor is it in any way likely that the proper name of GOD יְהוָה, which no one doubts is Hebrew, had any other form in the primordial language, which GOD willed to be his perpetual memorial; which not only Moses used, but also the most ancient Patriarchs; as is evident from the example of Eve Gen. 4, 1. I have acquired a man JEHOVAH: not to mention the name אֱלוֹהִים, which GOD used before the confusion of languages, Gen. 9, 6. and the serpent in Paradise Gen. 3, 5. whose plural force GOD himself expressed in primordial times Gen. 1, 26. chap. 3, 22. so that it appears that this mystical name is most ancient, not arising only from the confusion of languages.

Furthermore, an argument is also usually drawn from the names of the letters. For the very words for letters and characters are Hebrew. But that must be the first language in which the prior use of letters exists. And you would say that the most ancient use and invention of letters is there, where the letters found their own names. These figures also had names from their inventors, which were not accepted except through assimilation with other things, from which they were named. You will not find the complete and uncorrupted names of letters except in the Hebrew language.

Other nations deviated or rejected them. Scaliger thought that the names of the vowels were not correctly assigned except from their sound, since he did not notice that they were the appellations not of the elements themselves, but of the figures. It is certain that the names which are among the Greeks, Arabs, and Assyrians, the most ancient of peoples, came from Hebrew names. Which the Greeks themselves were not entirely ignorant of regarding their own letters, for they attributed the names of their gods and the invention of letters to the Phoenicians, since it is certain from etymology that those whom they praise as the first inventors, Cadmus and Palamedes, had Hebrew names.

Nor is that reason obscure which is taken from the simplicity of the Hebrew language:

For it is agreed among the learned that Hebrew is the simplest of all languages, to which the rest also owe their birth, as is clearly taught by the fact that none of the others departs so far from Hebrew that it does not retain certain traces and a resemblance to its matrix. Franc. Junius in the preface to his Grammar—whom Grotius esteems as almost the only one among the Calvinists—writes that not only the Indian, Persian, Babylonian, Armenian, Syrian, and Arabic, but also the Gothic language are most closely joined to Hebrew, and that many proofs of this matter exist in Procopius, Agathias, and Jornandes. See also his Academ. chap. II. and the Oration on the antiquity of the Hebrew language. The same was taught regarding the Greek, Latin, and other languages by the most illustrious men, Schickard and Helvicus; also Cruciger, Professor at Marburg, in his collation of the four principal languages, Becmann in his book on the origin of the Latin language, Daniel Heinsius in Aristarch. chap. 1, Glassius in Grammat. c. 1. 18. Vol. III. p. 770. Compare. Flacius in Clav. Script. part 1, under the word terrible &c. Forster in the Preface to his Lexicon says that the great glory and happiness of this language above others is that it claims or borrows nothing from other languages; but other languages borrow many words from it. Therefore Jerome on chapter III of Zephaniah calls the Hebrew language the matrix of all languages. Christian Schotanus pursues this argument in Tohu p. 85, from Nicolaus Fuller and Rivet, in this way: That is primary to which others can be reduced. Among languages, one must also consider that one primary, to which the words of others can be brought and reduced. Which is done in two ways. First, insofar as many words remained whole in that confusion and division (for confusion begat division) which we recognize in Hebrew: according to itself and its own primary forms. Secondly, since some one of the oriental languages, which settled not far from Babylon, must be that matrix language, because GOD did not destroy the first, but added others. Thus are found related among themselves the Syrian and Arabic with the Hebrew, but the Hebrew is the simplest, which the Syrian and Arabic acknowledge as their mother, and since the Hebrew is simpler than them, they concede the palm to it. And yet the Syrian and Arabic have greater simplicity than all other languages of the world, which will be manifest to one examining them. They have triliteral roots, and do not join many consonants in a simple and primary word. For the primary word among the Hebrews is always triliteral, a trigrammaton. Nor is there any Hebrew word which cannot be reduced to such a root; in other languages the root is found to be a polygrammaton: but that which is of more owes its origin to that which is of fewer letters. That, which no language gives, except the Hebrew. There are also found little words in which those three do not consist, as far as the form of their speech is concerned, yet they will consist in Hebrew analogically. GOD therefore changed the simple language of the Hebrews into those degenerate from the mother, by the ejection of vowels, and the transposition and addition of consonants. Therefore, it will be possible to reduce and recognize the obliquity and impurity in that most simple and first one.

Nor should the argument be omitted which is sought from the name: since the Hebrew language is named from Eber. St. Augustine deals with it at length in book XVI of The City of God, chap. XI. Since the language common to all before remained in the family of Eber, while the other nations were divided into other languages, it was thereafter called Hebrew. For then there was a need to distinguish it from other languages by a proper name, just as other languages also were called by proper names. But when it was the one language of all, it seemed to be nothing other than human language or human speech, because the whole human race spoke it alone. Worthy also are those things which Augustine adds shortly after there, which may be read here: Nor in vain did he not transmit that language, that is, the one which Abraham held, to all his sons, but only to those who, propagated through Jacob, and coalescing more notably and eminently into the people of GOD, were able to have the testaments of GOD and the lineage of Christ. Nor did Heber himself pour the same language into his entire progeny: but only into that which has its generations led down to Abraham. Wherefore, even if it is not evidently expressed that there was some pious race of men when Babylon was being founded by the impious: this obscurity did not avail to this end, that the seeker should be defrauded, but rather that his intention should be exercised. For when it is read that there was originally one language for all, and before all the sons of Shem, Heber is commended, although he is the fifth in descent from him: and that language is called Hebrew, which the authority of the Patriarchs and Prophets preserved not only in their speech, but even in the sacred letters: truly, when it is asked in the division of languages where that language could have remained which was previously common: because without any doubt, where it remained, that punishment which was brought about by the change of languages did not exist: what else occurs, except that it remained in the family of this man, from whose name it received its name, and that this trace of the justice of this family appeared not small, that when other nations were punished by the change of languages, such a punishment did not reach this one? Similarly Suidas in this word: Hebrews are called from Eber the son of Salah, who among the peoples of the earth distributed called his own Hebrews. Because he was not among the founders (of that tower of that nation), his speech was not changed. The Hebrew language is also called לשון הקדש not only because the sacred mysteries unknown to all nations were handed down in it, but also for the reason that it has the most holy GOD as its immediate author, who implanted it in the Protoplasts created in holiness, when he sent other languages as a punishment. Therefore Jarchi on those words אחד :דברים שפה says it is לשון הקדש. Add that the word of God had to be preserved in the first and most excellent language: and since the architects of Babylon were punished by the confusion of languages, for those who were not partners in the insane work, their ancient language had to be left.

And the Gentiles themselves concede that the Hebrew language is the first, whose testimonies may be seen in Josephus, Eusebius, and Cyril. Whence also R. Gedalia presents the consensus of the nations here: The wise men of the Gentiles investigated which was the language of the ancients, and finally with unanimous opinion they established that from Adam until the division their speech was Hebrew, which was left to Abraham our Father, and to his seed. And this you will find in the Commentary on the Law of R. Jacob, Baal Hatturim, and the Preface to the Commentary of Rambam. So far he. In Schalschel. Hakkod. p. 807, these things are held: They say that from him (Eber) the Jews received the name of Hebrews, in whom also and in his seed the holy language was left. In the beginning, however, this language was called אומנה Umanah. But these things concerning the Hebrew language, which name Grotius always utters with an aspiration, we [utter] without it, not against the original word, as Hornbeck thinks at the beginning of his book against the Jews, but according to it: because Grammarians do not utter ע with the aspiration H, whence he would be judged absurd who would want to write the name Immanuel with an H, Himmanuel. But the reason for this name is the same. It is no wonder that Grotius calls the antiquity and purity of the Hebrew language into doubt, who has not feared to carp at the antiquity and purity of the Hebrew text in many places.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Turris Babel, & confusio linguarum: ut & Ge- nealogia Semi usque ad Abramum.

Vers. 1. ERAT AUTEM TERRA LABII UNIUS.) Eam linguam Hebræi suam dicunt: Syri suam. At Hebræa lingua, lingua est עברים advenarum è Chaldæa. Hæc enim origo nominis Hebræorum, non ab Hebero. Vid. Jos. 24, 2. 3. Lin- gua igitur illa Hebræa Abrahami, & ejus posterorum incolatu in Chananæa, ad Cananæam propius semper propiusque acces- sit, nec differt à Punica, nisi dialecti quibusdam proprietati- bus, ut à viris eruditissimis ostensum est. Quare verius primæ- vam linguam nullibi puram exstare, sed reliquias ejus esse in linguis omnibus: nomina autem propria Adami, Evæ, & cæ- tera Hebraico sermone à Mose expressa Hebræorum causa eo- dem significatu, qui in primæva lingua fuerat. Sic Curtius milites quosdam ait à Persis vocatos immortales, aditum Cili- ciæ ab incolis Pylas dici: qui singulis militum millibus præe- rant, eos vocatos à Persis Chiliarchos: angustias alias à Persis Susidas Pylas vocari: multaque ejus generis passim apud hi- storiços occurrunt. Eusebius serpentes quosdam à Phœnici- bus ait vocari ἀγαθὲς δαίμονας. Venerem ab Afris ὀρανίαν Herodianus. In Africa Pithecusæ & Ampelusiæ nomina sunt in Græcum ex Punico translata, teste Diodoro lib. 20. Mela libro 1. Sic quæ Aspis Græcis, Clupea Latinis. Athenæus li- bro 6. Κελτοὶ περιάγονται καὶ μεθ' ἑαυτῶν καὶ πολεμῦντες συμ- βιωτὰς ὃὺς καλὲσι παρασίτες: id est, appellant eos Gallica voce, quæ parasitos significat. Gibbus Marcellino est, quem Procopius κυρτὸν vocat. Idem Procopius pro Aurigis Vene- tis dixit κυανίες. Et nos Latine scribentes urbem Brabantiæ vocamus Silvam ducis, & Græci interpretes sacrorum librorum, locorum nomina haud pauca Græce ponunt, ut δρῦν ὑψηλὴν, βάλανοι πένθες, πόλιν γραμμάτων, σιαγόνα.

Tria hîc tanguntur verius apud nostrum, quam tractantur. Primum est nominis Ebræorũ origo. Alterum Linguæ Ebrææ cum Punica cognatio. Ter- tium primævæ linguæ ab Ebræa distinctio. Non pla- cet Grotio origo nominis ab Ebero: mavult כפרים dici advenas è Chaldea. Jos. XXIV. Simili ratione Ebræos ab עבר transire q. transitores deducere Theodoretum in Genes. 4. vers. 6. Hieronymum in

Esa. 19, 18. & in Ezech. c. 7. Origenem in Num. hom. 19. Chrysostom. in Gen. hom. 35. & Augustinum Quaest. in Gen. 39. ab עָבַר trans, quod ex Mesopo- tamia in Cananeam transiens Abraham עִבְרִי quasi transfluvialis, dictus sit, Hottingerus in Thesaur. Phil. p. 48. observat; sed ut de Hieronymo id con- cedamus, qui עִבְרִי περάτην transitorem sonare ait: de Augustino certe id non liquet. Aliud ex eodem deinde docebimus. Origenes an alluserit ad nomen, an vero Etymologiam reddiderit, non apparet. He- bræi, inquit, transeuntes interpretantur: Isto ergo ipso populus etiam Hebræus dicitur, qui transiit de Ægy- pto ad terram repromissionis, de tenebris ad lucem, de morte ad vitam. Chrysostomus Abrahamum περάτην dictum Gen. 14, 10. vult, seu transitorem, quod ex Chaldæa exierit, & trans Euphratem domicilium ha- buerit, sed nominis Ebræorum rationem non ex- primit, imo nomine Abram vocatum, quia trans Euphratem migraturus erat, ex ignorantia linguæ sanctæ censet. Theodoretus ab Hebræa deducit, quod Syrorum lingua idem, quod Euphratem esse, falso asserit. Non ergo habet ista sententia, quod illis au- toribus sese efferat. Jos. autem cap. 24. rationem nominis Ebræorum exponi, κρινόμενον est.

Ab Ebero potius id deducendum esse Buxtor- fius Dissert. de linguæ Ebr. conserv. & Rivetus Ex- ercit. in Gen. 66. Nicol. Fullerus in Miscell. Sacr. l. 4. c. 4. Balth. Meisner. part. 1. Phil. Sob. pag. 19. ostendunt. Rationes etiam Collegæ sui Erpenii pro superiori, quæ Grotii est, sententia refellit Rive- tus. Indicare originem appellationis videtur Mo- ses Gen. 10, 21. Hic Pater omnium filiorum Eber: à Semo Patriarcha originem Ebræorum deducens, uti cum Chamum Patrem Canaan fuisse dicit, Ca nanæos ab eo descendisse significat. Et Bileam Num. 24, 24. ut naves è littore Chittæorum solventes affli- gent Assur, & affligent Eber: ut per Assur Assyrii ab eo dicti, per Eber Ebræi ab eodem nuncupati desi- gnentur. Clare autem hanc originem exprimit Josephus l. 1. Antiqu. cap. 6. τὸν δὲ Ἔβερον, ἀφ᾽ ὗ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἑβραίους ἀρχῆθεν ἐκάλευν. Et S. Augustinus l. 16. de Civ. Dei c. 3. Non itaque frustra ipse (Hebe- rus) primus nominatus est in progenie veniente de Sem & prælatus est etiam filiis, cum sit quintus nepos, nisi quia verum est, quod traditur, ex illo Hebræos esse cognominatos, tanquam Hebræos, cum & alia possit esse opinio, ut ex Abraham tanquam Abrahami dicti esse videantur. Cui vero opinioni lingua Sancta adversatur, nec approbat eam Augustinus, alibique approbatam retractat l. 3. Retract. c. 16. Illam au- tem quod ab Ebero appellati sint Ebræi, tuetur Augustinus, ac traditionem dicit, quod communis ea fuerit sententia; quam etiam cap. 11. & lib. 18. cap. 39. repetit. Tuetur quoque illam R. D. Kim- chi in Lex. Suidas in Lex. B. Lutherus noster in Gen. XI. & plerique nostrates, imo receptissimam eandem esse penes Judæos & Christianos Buxtorfius, & Hottingerus observant. Joh. Seldenus de Diis Syr. ambigit fere, utri sententiæ subscribendum sit, quamvis in Grotianam sit propensior. At si Abra- ham ideo Ebræus dictus, quod Euphratem transie- rit, omnes ejus filii pariter eodem dicendi nomine. Nunquam autem Ismaëlita, nec aliæ gentes ab Ab- rahamo descendentes ita dictæ, sed soli Israëlitæ. Taceo quod nomina populorum desumuntur in S. lingua, si non à regionibus, quas inhabitabant, certe ab ipsis autoribus. Videri autem de his pote- runt plura in Critico nostro sacro p. 307. seqq.

Jam quod ad cognationem cum lingua Punica, non differre Ebræam ab eadem, nisi Dialecti quibus- dam proprietatibus, quod novum quorundam com- mentum est, nondum ostensum, multo minus ve- risimile est, linguam Ebream Abrahami & postero- rum ejus incolatu in Cananæa ad Cananæam propius semper propiusq́; accessisse. Hieronymus linguarum peritissimus in cap. 19. Esaix linguam Cananæam in- ter Ægyptiam & Ebræam mediam esse, & huic ma- gna ex parte confinem dicit, non autem solum Diale- cti quibusdam proprietatibus differre. Similiter Augustinus T. 10. Tract. in Evang. Joh. c. 15. Ebrai- cam, Punicam & Syram cognatas saltim agnoscit & confines esse. Abrahamum autem linguam suam abdicasse, & Cananææ dialecto accessisse, ut ea Deum coleret, neutiquam probabile est: quum semper alienissimi esse studuerint ab idololatra gente Pa- triarchæ, aliique sancti; & Nehemias magno Zelo accensus fuerit, etiam sequioribus temporibus, cum Judæos Azotice loquentes inveniret, non Judaice, Nehem. 13, 24.

Ita profecto necessario statuendum foret, (ut doctissimus Füllerus l. 4. Miscell. Sacr. c. 4. in exa- mine novæ hujus opinionis loquitur) quos Deus olim linguarum confessionis beneficio (sic namque solet divina benignitas ex malis nostris sua elicere bona) quasi firmissimo muro discluserat, facileque evitandos reddiderat, Abrahamum, communi ejusdem linguæ usu (qui primarius est omnis commercii gradus) pro- pius sibi conjunxisse, & perfosso, imo diruto muro illo, sibi quidem difficilius evitandos, posteris autem inevitabiles propemodum effecisse. Quis enim non vi- det, naturalis ejusdem linguæ communitas cum Cha- nanæis quantum offendiculum, quam exitiosum in idololatriam præcipitium fuisset Israëlitis? Quanta, non dico, fenestra, sed janua, imo quam immanis por- ta hac ratione patuisset contagioni gentis maledictæ, populum electum jugiter persuasuræ? quem tamen ab illa modis omnibus quam longissime semotum esse voluit consilium divinum: cui Abrahamum per omnia vigi- lantissime subservisse nemo sane pius, aut cordatus, unquam opinor negaverit. Quamobrem qui vel ipsius sepulturæ cum gentibus idololatris consortium penitus abnuit, eo magis universum sermonis commer- cium haud dubie respuisset, quo plus hoc, quam illud, pietati nocere potuisset. Neque præter rem obser- vat Füllerus, linguam Ebræam cæterarum matri- cem divinitus servatam esse, in θεοπνεύστοις monu- mentis, ut quasi regula haberetur de cælo dela- psa, ad quam omnia omnium linguarum judicia dirigerentur, ut ex majore minoreve convenien- tia vel discrepantia, quæ & quanta esset cujusque linguæ integritas, aut pravitas, dignosceretur: & ut Iridis aspectus diluvium, sic Hebraicæ linguæ auditus confusionis Babylonicæ pœnam justissi- mam gentes omnes pervagatam in memoriam re- digeret. Hoc enim supremi judicis gloriæ (quod caput est) amplificandæ, & in perpetuas seculo- rum ætates prorogandæ & promulgandæ magno- pere conducit. Tanti igitur pretii thesaurum ma- ledicti Chami, ac nominatim Chanaani, posterorumq́; ejus fidei, curæque commendatum & traditum fuisse, nullo sane pacto probabile videtur. Imo penes do- mesticos Ecclesiæ Dei, Noachum, Semum, Heberum, nefariæ impiæque conspirationis in campo Sennaar con- flatæ non participes reconditum mansisse omnino cre- dibile est.

Fulcra etiam novæ opinionis erudite dis- cussit Füllerus. Nomina personarum vel locorum Ebræa Abimelech, Melchisedech, Adonibezek, Bethlehem, Kiriatharba, Gen. 14. vers. 20. C. 35. v. 19. Jos. 15, 15. Cananæa esse, vel à Cananæis imposita, probari non potest: siquidem vetusta ab indige- nis Cananæis indita nomina ab Ebreis Ebraico more proferri potuerint, imprimis si statuatur, Syriacam linguam Cananæam esse, unde ob cogna- tionem levi mutatione nominum solum opus: atqu ita de argumento præcipuo adversæ partis nervu inciditur. Addimus autem ea, quibus dissertatio nem suam concludit Füllerus p. 482. Ad summam novæ istius opinionis propugnatoribus, præsertim acrioribus quibusdam libet plusculum, quam initi concesserimus, jam largiri. Damus igitur sermo nem illam, qui in Novo Testamento Hebræus nomi natur, Chananaum, sive Tyrium, sive Punicum esse hac tamen lege, ut eum, qui in Vetere purus asserva tur, pro absolute Hebræo relinquere ne dedignentur eis, quorum proprium est illius linguæ studium; Theo- logos dico, & Candidatos Theologiæ: cujus arcana universa in sacrosanctis Hebrææ linguæ penetralibu sunt reposita.

Nihil ergo causæ est, quod Grotius linguam Ebræam primam omnium & antiquissimam neget. Quam vero tandem primam facit? Nullam. Pri- mam enim nullibi extare dicit, sed reliquias ejus esse in linguis omnibus. Præivit ei Cluverius l. 1. Germ. antiqv. c. 8. statuens, in turris constructione DEUM unam illam primam linguam dissipasse per multa idio- mata, quæ inde in orbe obtinuerint matre extincta, matrem autem revocandam ex illis dissipationibus tum cum evadet εἷς ποιμὴν καὶ μία ποίμνη. Argu- mentum novæ sententiæ si requiras, aliud vix acci- pies, quam quod multæ voces in diversis linguis ejus- dem significationis reperiantur, quæ alio referri non possint, nisi ad reliquias primi sermonis. Sed quænam illæ multæ, aut millenæ voces sint, non docuit Cluverius: vix unam atque alteram proferre po- tuit. Et quidni referri illæ possint ad Ebræum ser- monem, cujus hodie pauca supersunt, ea scilicet tantum, quæ in Ebræo Codice S. leguntur. Neque ex nonnullarum linguarum convenientia in vocu- lis quibusdam concludere licet ad universas, ne- dum ad earum matricem, ejusque reliquias per universas dispersas.

Porro Ebræam linguam primam esse, commu- nis est Judæorum & Christianorum sententia, à qua sine gravibus argumentis discedere fas non est. Unus forte Theodoretus q. 8. in Gen. suæ, hoc est, Syriacæ linguæ ex antiquis hanc gloriam vindicat. Quem è recentioribus Georgius Amira Episcopus Antiochenus primas montis Libani, & Joh. Caspar Myricæus sequitur, at infirmis rationibus, in præ- fat. Gramm. Syro-Chald. refutatus à M. Majero in Phil. Sacr. Kircherus Oedip. Tom. II. cl. 2. p. 51. commemorat versionem Maronitarum: quæ ita habeat: Et confusæ sunt linguæ, & divisio facta est linguæ eorum Syriacæ. Patricides Arabs Historicus refert etiam illam sententiam: Fuit autem hominum tum lingua una & sermo unus. Quidam volunt Sy- riacum fuisse. Quod observatum quoque Elmaci- no: Sunt tamen, inquit, Historici, qui statuunt, A- damum, ejusq́; posteros ad confusionem usq́; linguarum Syriace loquutos.
