Neque abnuit Athanasius Kirche- rus, distinguit tamen inter linguam doctrinalem, quam Ebræam fuisse vult, non omnibus notam, in Disciplinis tradendis adhibitam: & idiomaticam sive usualem: quam Syriacam facit. Sed argumentis nullis, quæ robur habeant. Jactantia enim Syrorum nihil probat. Et prior ac simplicior sine dubio est Ebræa lingua, quam Syra. Commemorat etiam Pa- tricides, quosdam Græcam linguam primam fecisse, eamque sententiam sibi veriorem videri, ait; sed nullo vel probabili solum prætextu. Goropii Beca- ni commentum, quod Cimbrica vel Brabantica lin- gua antiquissima sit, ceu paradoxum ab omnibus re- jicitur. Vereque Becani istius, ut inscriptio habet, Βεκκεσέλnνοι, nugamenta sunt, merito suo ab autore ipso fatuitatis titulo insignita, quæ in hanc senten- tam operose prodidit. Perinde uti Philastrii de variarum linguarum gentibus ante γλωσσοσύγχυσιν in Catal. hæret. c. 6. somnium, quod huic textui Gen. 11, 1. aperte reclamat.

Plerique ergo unanimi voce Ebrææ linguæ hanc gloriam deferunt. De Ebræis forte non mirum: è quibus R. Salomo hunc locum de lingua sancta exponit, uti Josephus l. 1. c. 4. antiquitatem ejus astruit. Sed & Chaldæi Interpretes de Ebræa lingua textum nostrum exposuere. Jonathan & autor Hierosolymitani Targum, qui addit: Omnes loquutos esse lingua sancta, in qua conditus est mundus, ab initio. Cæteri quoque Interpretes & commentatores plerique omnes textum nostrum, quod universa terra labii unius & verborum eorundem fuerit, de lingua Eberina accipiunt. Elmacinus Arabicus historicus Phritonem in hanc sententiam laudat: Dicit Sapiens Phriton, Sethum inventorem esse literarum, sive elementorum scribendi, easdemque in lingua Hebraica monstrasse. Neque obscura est ratio, à nominibus propriis ante confusionem linguarum impositis. Futile enim est, quod dicitur, ea omnia à Mose expressa esse eodem significatu, qui fuerit in primæva lingua. Nomina enim propria in linguis omnibus manent immutabilia: quemadmodum illa ipsa Ebræa nomina Adam, Eva, Cain, Seth & reliqua manserunt. Nulla enim lingua aliter nuncupantur. Tum si Moses nomina illa excogitavit, qui asserit, eadem illa nomina imposita esse à Patriarchis, utpote, quod Adam vocarit conjugem חוה quia sit mater viventium, Gen. 3, 20. quod Eva primogenitum nuncuparit Kain, à possessione c. 4, 2. & alium Seth, quia aliud posuit semen DEUS vers. 26. quod Lamech filium nominavit Noah à requie & consolatione c. 4, 29. quod Eber filium suum lingua sua (adhuc ante confusionem linguarum) vocavit Peleg, quia divisionem populorum prævidit Spiritu Prophetico, Gen. 10, 25. Non Moses ita illos vocavit, sed ab Adamo, ab Eva, à Lamecho, ab Ebero nomina illa composita sunt, teste Mose. Quibus si comparantur nomina linguæ Ebrææ post γλωττοσύγχυσιν imposita, convenientia ista & similitudo nominum ante confusionem & post eandem satis docet, non aliam fuisse linguam primævam, quam Eberinam vel Ebræam. Ita concinne eadem conveniunt, ut non aliam linguam in familia Abrahæ & apud Israëletas, quam primævam ante confusionem, imo ante diluvium & à creatione usitatam, viguisse certum sit. Adde etyma omnium nominum propriorum, quæ est Merceri observatio, ante diluvium & post usque ad divisionem linguarum non posse ulli alii linguæ tribui, sicut nec aliorum post illud tempus, quibus Moses utitur, quam Ebraicæ: ut אדם ab אדמה, חוה quod mater omnium viventium fuerit, Kain, Abel, Seth, Mahalaël, Kenaan, Noë &c. quorum omnium & cæterorum fons non nisi Ebraicus esse potest. Quod si dixeris, potuisse Mosen nomina priorum illorum patrum ex lingua prima transfundere in suam, qui quæso id in omnibus potuisset, ita ubique certam & constantem etymologiam nominum, ut in lingua illa primigenia invenire, quam in paucis linguis, ut אדם ab אדמה homo ab humo, sic in aliis id non invenitur איש Chaldæum aut גברא id non admittit, nec ἀνὴρ aut ἄνθρωπος apud Græcos, aut in alia lingua. Hæc Mercerus. Neque solum nomina propria personalia, sed etiam gentilia hoc testantur, exempli gràtia Medorum à Madai, Jonum à Jovan, & alia, quæ originem Ebræam resipiunt, in linguis aliis nihil significant. Vid. Hieronymus quæst. in Genes. Ariasmontanus pag. 3. Apparat. Bibl. B. Lutherus Commentar. in Gen. mina solum propria, sed etiam appellativa, quæ in nulla lingua adeo respondent naturæ & proprieta- ti rerum, uti in Ebræa, ut dubium non sit, hac lin- gua animantibus nomina imposuisse Adamum, or- bis Monarcham Gen. 2, 19. Omne enim quod voca- vit Adam animæ viventis, ipsum est nomen ejus. Non esset autem hoc nomen ejus, si nomina illa primæva penitus interiissent. In eadem lingua etymologiæ illæ etiam apprime congruunt, quæ ante confusionem redditæ observantur, verb. grat. Gen. 2, 23. Hæc vocabitur אִשָּׁה vira, quoniam מֵאִישׁ de viro sumta est &c. Neque ullatenus verisimi- le est, nomen proprium DEI יְהוָה, quod Ebræ- um esse nemo dubitat, aliter in lingua primæva habuisse, quod DEUS memoriale suum perpetuum esse voluit; quo non tantum Moses usus, sed etiam Patriarchæ antiquissimi; uti exemplo Evæ con- stat Gen. 4, 1. possedi virum JEHOVAH: ne de nomine אֱלוֹהִים dicam, quo usus est ante confu- sionem linguarum DEUS, Gen. 9, 6. & serpens in Paradiso Gen. 3, 5. cujus vim πληθυντικὴν DEUS ipse expressit primævis temporibus Gen. 1, 26. cap. 3, 22. ut appareat, mysticum hoc nomen antiquis- simum esse, non à confusione demum Linguarum oriundum.

Porro argumentum etiam desumi solet à nomini- bus literarum. Ipsa enim literarum & characterum vocabula sunt Ebraica. Illam autem linguam pri- mam esse oportebit, in qua prior usus literarum est. Illic autem esse antiquissimum literarum usum & in- ventionem dixeris, ubi literæ vocabula sua inve- nerunt. Figuræ etiam istæ ab inventoribus suis no- mina habuerunt, quæ recepta non fuerunt nisi per adsimulationem cum rebus aliis, à quibus denomi- natæ sunt. Non invenies integra & incorrupta lite- rarum nomina, nisi in Ebræo sermone.

Aliæ gentes deflexerunt aut rejecerunt. Scaliger nomina vocalium non recte assignari, nisi à sono, putavit, quum non animadverteret, non ipsorum elementorum, sed figurarum appellationes esse. Constat ab Ebræis nominibus venisse nomina, quæ apud Græcos, Arabes, Assyrios sunt, antiquis- simos populorum. Quod de suis literis ne ipsi qui- dem Græci plane ignorarunt, qui ad Phœnices Deorum suorum nomina & literarum inventio- nem retulerunt, quoniam quos primos inventores laudant, Cadmus & Palamedes Ebraica nomina habuisse certum est ex Etymo.

Neque obscura ista ratio, quæ à linguæ Ebrææ simplicitate desumitur:

Simplicissimam enim omnium linguarum esse Ebræam inter Eruditos constat, cui etiam reliquas natales suos debere haud obscure id docet, quod nulla cæterarum ab Ebræa tam longe recedat, quin vestigia quædam & similitudinem matricis suæ retineat. Franc. Junius in præfat. Grammati- cæ; quem fere unum inter Calvinianos æstimat Grotius, scribit, non tantum Indicam, Persicam, Babylonicam, Armeniam, Syram, Arabicam, sed & Gothicam linguam Ebrææ esse conjunctissimas, ac hujus rei multa extare apud Procopium, Agathium, & Jornandum documenta. vid. etiam ejusdem Aca- dem. cap. II. & Oratio de linguæ Ebr. antiquit. Idem de Græca, Latina & aliis linguis docuerunt viri Clarissimi, Schickardus & Helvicus; Cruciger etiam Marpurg. Profess. in collatione linguarum quatuor principalium, Becmannus l. de orig. lingu. Latin. Daniel Heinsius Aristarch. cap. 1. Glassius Grammat. c. 1. 18. T. III. p. 770. Confer. Flacius in Clav. Script. part. 1. voce terribilis &c. Forsterus in Præfat. Lex. ingentem dicit & gloriam & felicita- tem hujus linguæ præ cæteris, quod ab aliis linguis ni- bil vendicet aut mutuetur; aliæ vero ab hac multas voces mutuentur. Ideo Hieronymus super c. III. So- phon. vocat Ebræam linguam omnium linguarum matricem. Exsequitur hoc argumentum Christia- nus Schotanus in Tohu p. 85. e Nicol. Fullero & Ri- veto hoc pacto: Id primum est, ad quod reduci possunt alia. Inter linguas etiam illam primam censere opor- tet, ad quam aliarum voces possunt exigi & reduci. Quod fit dupliciter. Primo, quatenus multæ voces integræ manserunt in illa confusione & divisione (con- fusio enim divisionem genuit) quas recognoscimus in Ebræa: secundum se & suas primas. Secundo, qua orientalium linguarum aliquam, quæ haud procul Babylone confederunt, oportet esse illam matricem linguam, quoniam non sustulit DEUS primam, sed addidit alias. Sic reperiuntur affines inter se, Syra, Arabica, cum Ebræa, simplicissima autem est Hebræa quam pro matre agnoscunt Syra & Arabica, cum Ebræa simplicior sit illis, palmam illa concedunt. At- qui Syra & Arabica habent simplicitatem majorem omnibus mundi linguis cæteris, quod examinanti erit manifestum. Radices habere triliteras, plu- res consonas non conjungere in simplici & prima vo- ce. Nam prima vox apud Hebræos semper est trilite- ra τριγράμματος. Nec est ulla vox Ebræa, quæ ad talem radicem non queat reduci; In aliis sermonibus radix invenitur πολυγράμματος: quod autem plu- rium est, originem debet illi, quod est pauciorum lite- rarum. Id, quod nulla dat lingua, nisi Hebræa. In- veniuntur etiam voculæ, in quibus non constant illæ tres, quoad formam sermonis sui, constabunt tamen in Hebræa ἀναλογικῶς. DEUS igitur simplicem Hebæorum linguam mutavit in illas à matre degene- res, ejectione vocalium, trajectione & adjectione conso- narum. Obliquitatem igitur & impuritatem reducere & agnoscere licebit in illa simplicissima & prima.

Neque prætermittendum est argumentum, quod à nomine petitur: siquidem Ebræa lingua ab Ebero dicitur. Prolixe vero de ea agit S. Au- gustinus lib. XVI. de C. D. cap. XI. Quoniam in familia Eber communis antea omnium lingua reman- sit, divisis per alias linguas cæteris gentibus, ideo de- inceps Ebræa est nuncupata. Tunc enim opus erat distingui eam ab aliis linguis nomine proprio, sicut aliæ quoque linguæ vocatæ sunt nominibus propriis. Quando autem erat una omnium, nihil aliud, quam humana lingua vel humana locutio videbatur, quod ea sola universum genus humanum loquebatur. Di- gna sunt & ea, quæ paulo post ibi subjungit Au- gustinus, quæ hîc legantur: Nec frustra linguam istam, hoc est, quam tenuit Abraham, nec in omnes filios suos transmittere potuit, sed in eos tantum, qui propagati per Jacob, & insignius atque eminentius in DEI populum coalescentes DEI testamenta & stir- pem Christi habere potuerunt. Nec Heber ipse eandem linguam in universam progeniem suam re- fudit: sed in eam tantum, cujus generationes per- ducuntur ad Abraham. Quapropter etiamsi non evidenter expressum est, fuisse aliquod pium genus hominum, quando ab impiis Babylonia condebatur: non ad hoc valuit hæc obscuritas, ut quærentis frau- daretur, sed potius ut exerceretur intentio. Cum enim legitur, unam fuisse linguam primitus omni- um, & ante omnes filios Sem commendatur Heber, quamvis ab illo quintus oriatur: & Hebræa voca- tur lingua, quam Patriarcharum & Prophetarum, non solum in sermonibus suis, verum etiam in literis sacris custodivit autoritas: profecto cum quæritur in divisione linguarum, ubi lingua illa remanere potue- rit, quæ fuit ante communis: quia sine ulla dubita- tione ubi remansit, non ibi fuisse illa pœna, quæ fa- cta est mutatione linguarum: quid aliud occurrit, nisi quod in hujus gente remanserit, à cujus nomine nomen accepit, & hoc justitiae gentis hujus non parvum apparuisse vestigium, quod cum aliae gentes plecteren- tur mutatione linguarum, ad istam non pervenit tale supplicium? Similiter Suidas in voce hac: Ebrai dicuntur ab Eber filio Salah, qui inter populos terra distributa suos appellavit Ebræos. Hic quia non inter conditores (turris illius gentis) fuit, ejus ser- mo non est mutatus. Vocatur Ebræa lingua etiam לשון הקדש non tantum, quod sacra mysteria omnibus gentibus incognita eadem tradita sint, sed etiam eo nomine, quod DEUM sanctissimum immediate autorem habeat, qui Protoplastis in sanctitate conditis eandem indidit, quum alias linguas in pœnam immiserit. Ideo Jarchius ad il- la verba אחד :דברים שפה dicit esse לשון הקדש. Adde quod verbum Dei conservari oportuerit in pri- ma & præstantissima lingua: & cum Babylonis ar- chitecti confusione linguarum puniti sint, illis, qui non erant insani operis socii, prisca sua lingua relin- quenda fuerit.

Et concedunt ipsimet gentiles, Ebræam lin- guam primam esse, quorum testimonia videantur apud Josephum, Eusebium & Cyrillum. Unde etiam R. Gedalia gentium consensum hic sistit: Sapien- tes gentilium investigarunt, quænam esset lingua an- tiquorum, unanimi tandem omnes sententia statue- runt, ab Adamo ad divisionem usque sermonem eorum fuisse Hebræum, qui esset relictus Abrahamo Patri nostro, ejusque semini. Atque hoc invenies in Com- ment. super legem R. Jacob, Baal Hatturim, & Præ- fat. Comment. Rambam. Hactenus ille. In Schal- schel. Hakkod. p. 807. hæc habentur: Dicunt ab eo (Eber) Judæos nomen accepisse Ebræorum, in quo etiam & semine ejus relicta est lingua sancta. Initio autem hanc linguam appellatam fuisse אומנה Uma- nah. Sed hæc de Ebræa lingua, quod nomen cum aspiratione semper effert Grotius, nos sine eadem, non contra λέξιν primogeniam, uti Hornbeck censet sub initium libr. contr. Jud. sed juxta eandem: quia ע non efferunt Grammatici cum aspiratione H, unde absurdus judicaretur, qui nomen Immanuel per H. scribere vellet Himmanuel. Eadem autem hujus nominis ratio. Non mirum, Grotium an- tiquitatem & puritatem Ebrææ linguæ in dubium vocare, qui antiquitatem & puritatem Ebræi tex- tus passim vellicare veritus non est.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. WHEN THEY JOURNEYED. After the descendants of Ham had journeyed from Armenia toward Babylon, to which that is eastern. It should be rendered in the pluperfect: because the construction of the tower followed some years later.

Latin:

Vers. 2. CUM PROFICISCATUR. Postquam Posteri Cham ex Armenia versus Babyloniam, cui illa orientalis est, profecti fuerant. Reddendum in plusquamperfecto: quia aliquot annis post sequuta est exstructio turris.

## 11:3
Vers. 3. AND ONE SAID TO HIS NEIGHBOR.) The greater part took that counsel. BRICKS FOR STONES.) The baked walls of Babylon, in Ovid: walls surrounded by a fragile roof, in Lucan: a city fortified by potters, in Juvenal.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DIXITQUE ALTER AD PROXIMUM SUUM.) Pars major id cepit consilium. LATERES PRO SAXIS.) Coctiles muri Babylonis, Ovi- dio: fragili circumdata tecto mœnia, Lucano: figulis munita urbs, Juvenali.

## 11:4
Vers. 4. WHOSE TOP MAY REACH TO HEAVEN.) Thus lofty trees are ὠρανομήκεις in Homer. Cicero called such substructures insane. BEFORE WE ARE DIVIDED OVER ALL THE LANDS.) Whether because GOD had ordered them to depart, as Josephus wishes, or because they foresaw that the multitude would eventually overflow, and from there poverty would come, if all were crowded into one place.

Latin:

Vers. 4. CUJUS CULMEN PERTINGAT AD CŒ- LUM.) Sic celsæ arbores ὠρανομήκεις Homero. Tales substru- ctiones infanas dixit Cicero. ANTEQUAM DIVIDAMUR IN UNIVERSAS TER- RAS.) An quod DEUS discedere illos jusserat, ut vult Jose- phus, an quod prospiciebant exundaturam multitudinem ali- quando, & inde inopiam venturam, si omnes uno in loco co- arctarentur.

## 11:9
Vers. 9. THEREFORE ITS NAME WAS CALLED BABEL; BECAUSE THERE THE LIP OF THE WHOLE EARTH WAS CONFUSED.) This word seems to have been preserved from the primeval language, whence those remain in various languages: βαβάζειν, balbus, babil. But Josephus well refutes the fables of the Greeks, who ascribe the construction of Babylon to Semiramis, from Berosus against Apion I, from Philo of Byblos, and from Dorotheus of Sidon, Julius Firmicus. But because the lip was confused, for this reason men are called μέροπες by the Greek Poets.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ICCIRCO VOCATUM EST NOMEN EJUS BABEL; QUIA IBI CONFUSUM EST LABIUM UNI- VERSÆ TERRÆ.) Videtur hæc vox servata è lingua primæ- va, unde maneant istæ in linguis variis, βαβάζειν, balbus, ba- bil. Græcorum autem fabulas, qui Babylonis fabricam Semi- ramidi adscribunt, bene refutat ex Beroso Josephus contra A- pionem I. ex Philone Byblio; & ex Dorotheo Sidonio Julius Firmicus. Quia vero confusum est labium, ex hac causa homi- nes Græcis Poëtis μέροπες.

## 11:12
Vers. 12. AND HE BEGAT SALE.) Concerning Cainan inserted here, see what we have noted on Luke III.

He wishes it to be an interpolation there: which he proves with some arguments. I do not disapprove. For I confirmed that much more fully before the seen Grotius in the Critici Sacri p. 754 seqq., where it is also explained how Cainan seems to have crept in here. Only here I warn again that the corruption of the original text cannot be taught from that, which the Papists contend: since that has not pervaded all the Greek Codices of Luke, when Scaliger in his prolegomena to the Chronicle of Eusebius makes mention of some who do not have Cainan here, and Beza did not find the same in a certain very ancient Codex: and it betrays itself from the collation of the Old Testament. But especially the place 1 Chron. I, 24, where Kainan is excluded by the note of the Masoretes, which is as follows: There are two verses, in each of whose words the letter ש stands. For this has no place in the name קינן. Whence neither the Chaldean, nor the Arabic, nor the Latin, or any other translation in the Old Testament has Kainan, except only the LXX Interpreters. Nor do the Samaritan Codices know him, or even the ancient Jews, Josephus, Philo, and others. For the most ancient Hebrews count only ten generations from Noah to Abraham. Add that Kainan is seen no less in the Vulgate version in Luke, which the adversaries nevertheless believe to be sincere and authentic. If, however, anyone does not wish to admit that Kainan crept in, on account of the consensus of almost all the Greek Codices, and also the Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate versions, he will be able to say that Sala is binominal, so that it is τῷ Καιναν, who was also called Kainan, with Nauclerus, Hermannus Contractus, Joh. Lucid., Franc. Gomarus, Ludovic. de Dieu, or that Arphaxad also had the name Kainan, which is the opinion of Hottinger, with whom, however, there is no need to have recourse to traditions, as if Luke had to draw from them whether Arphaxad or Sala was also called Kainan: since the Historian could have had that from divine inspiration, being carried by the Holy Spirit.

It must not be concealed, however, that these opinions, although more probable than the others, are pressed by various difficulties, whence we have already long since deemed that opinion to be preferred which establishes Kainan as παρείσακτον [an interpolation]; but in order that a more correct judgment may be formed concerning this intricate doubt, it will be worth the effort to repeat those things which we have elsewhere handed down concerning him, since those works are in the hands of few, with the addition of some things which we have meanwhile observed regarding this matter. The venerable Bede, in his Preface to the Acts of the Apostles, states it thus: that the Evangelist added this generation from the LXX edition, although it is not held in the Hebrew truth. He has the same also in his exposition of Luke, chapter 3. The same is the opinion of Ado, Bishop of Vienne, in his Chronicon abbreviatum, age II, as also of Augustinus Steuchus, and Cornelius Jansenius in his Concordia Evangelica, chapter 14. Bede judges that it is better to admire the reason for this matter reverently than to inquire into it anxiously. That this was done, however, not from the Evangelist's own opinion, but from the hypothesis and sense of others, is stated among others by the Papist Guilhelmus Genebrardus in book I of his Chronicon, at the year of the world 1659: namely, that Luke placed Kainan there according to the opinion of the LXX, and indeed for the sake of the Greeks to whom he was writing, and to whom only the copies of the LXX were known; since, as Augustine testifies in book 2 against the Epistle of Parmenianus, it is not new for Scripture to speak according to the sense and opinion of others, not the truth of the matter. Genebrardus adds, however, another method of reconciliation also: that Arphaxad can be said to have begotten Sala through the intermediary Kainan, so that there is no need to make him ὑποβολιμαῖον [a supposititious child]. Jacobus Naclantus treads almost the same path in his Medulla Scripturae Sacrae, or Arcana Christi; that Luke placed the generation of Kainan not from his own [opinion], but from the opinion of the Septuagint translators, although he brings it forward hesitantly: since he also inclines toward the opinion of Lyranus, that Salah himself could have been the son both of Kainan and of Arphaxad, the former according to the law, the latter according to nature, namely, that Kainan having died childless, his brother Arphaxad begat Salah from the widow left behind. Sixtus of Siena also favors this opinion, but with a doubtful mind, book 5, B. S., ann. 88, and book 6, ann. 143, and book 7, heresy 4. Cardinal Cajetan, however, proposes it more confidently in Comment. on ch. 3 of Luke, that this generation is superfluous, yet Luke is excused: because he reviewed the genealogy as he found it written by the LXX, among whom this genealogy is read written as superfluous, and is deservedly excused, because at that time the interpretation of the LXX was of great authority among the Greeks and other nations.

Among the Calvinists, Joseph Scaliger favors that opinion in Eusebius, as does James Ussher, Diss. on Kainam, regarding that hypothetical proposition: if blessed Luke, the amanuensis of the Holy Spirit, judged in the genealogy of Christ that Kainam must be interposed between Sala and Arphaxad, no place is left any longer for doubting about that matter: he answers by distinguishing: If this passage was the Evangelist's own opinion, it is true; if it was from others, it is not. Certainly no more than it must be believed that Melchizedek in reality had no father, no mother, no genealogy, and had neither beginning of days nor end of life; because the Apostle pronounced that according to the commonly received opinion (Heb. 7:3); for it is the custom of the Scriptures that a historian narrates the opinion of many in the way it was believed by all at that time. Just as Joseph by Mary herself also (Luke 2:48). was called the father of Jesus; so also Herod is said to have been saddened, because those reclining at table thought this: says Jerome, Comment. on Matthew ch. 14:6, and in Jeremiah ch. 28:10, the Seventy did not call the prophet Ananias: lest, namely, they should seem to call him a prophet who was not a prophet. As if many things are not said in the Holy Scriptures according to the opinion of that time in which the deeds are related, and not according to what the truth of the matter contained. And in book 2 against Helvidius: The Evangelists, expressing the opinion of the crowd, which is the true law of history, called Joseph the father of the Savior. Thus therefore the Evangelist Luke, proposing to himself that all the fathers of the Savior should be reviewed, as well those commonly held as such as the true ones, began his genealogy thus, ὤν, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, υἱὸς Ἰωσήφ, τοῦ Ἠλὶ, τοῦ Μάτθαν, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, the son of Eli (the father of Mary the Mother of God), the son of Matthan (with that nominative, υἱὸς, repeated in all the following from the common): in the progress also of the same he could name Kainam among the fathers of Christ; not that he was such in reality, but because he was numbered among the ancestors of Abraham by the Hellenistic Jews and Christians who used no other than the Greek interpretation of the Old Testament (of whom the number was greatest).

But Francis Junius follows out that opinion most diligently in Anal. Genes. ch. II. Vol. I. of his Works, Col. 167, where he asserts that Luke followed the faith of the LXX, and explains his purpose in this matter thus: When he saw that the salvation of the pious was not placed in this matter, but that an error had long ago been rashly introduced by ancestors and was received among all nations in that age, and could not be torn out of the minds and books of men so suddenly without grave offense, Luke gave to charity and piety toward the Church of God what rashness had previously introduced, and therefore allowed the name of Kenan to be inserted in the same order in his narrative, lest while the truth of history was being pursued (in which he saw little was placed), the piety of the weak should be shaken, and charity should be dissolved; which in those first times of the nascent Church had to be supported by all means. And in parallel. Sacr. part 60. Col. 14. 43. This is not, he says, a mnemonic error, but a sinless concession, that is, a modest concession free from sin, a kind of speech which Scripture not rarely uses.

But Catharinus, Pererius, and Spanheim recognize that opinion concerning the errors of the LXX version admitted into the New Testament to be full of danger and altogether false, concerning which see what we have said in Critic. Sacr. p. 730 seqq.; where this Kainam also was expressly dealt with. That he is indeed an interpolation to be removed from the tribe is evident from Moses, who omits him not in one, but in two distinct places, ch. 10 and 11 of Genesis, and indeed in an accurate genealogical review and chronological computation. Where, against the exception of Cajetan, that Kainam fell out, we observe: that a bare name could not have fallen out in different places, much less his generation and the years of his life reviewed separately at the same time: but also that many things refute this suspicion and clearly convict it of vanity, such as the perpetual and constant consensus of all Hebrew Codices in omitting and excluding Kainam, with which the Samaritan Codex also conforms; furthermore, the uniform repetition by which, with Kainam omitted, that genealogy is related four times in all Hebrew Codices: moreover, the votes of the Chaldean Paraphrases, in which there is no trace of Kainam, neither in Onkelos nor in Jonathan; the chronology and history of the ancient Hebrews, which is utterly ignorant of that Kainam; the observation of the Masoretes, which excludes Kainam; finally, the Vulgate version, authentic to the Papists, which likewise knows nothing of that generation. Which arguments most of them are urged by Corn. à Lapide, adding the most certain Rule of Augustine, book XV. de C. D. ch. 3: If a translation disagrees with the original, that language is rather to be believed from which the translation was made into another through interpretation. Add that Kainam is not found to be inserted for the same reason in the Greek edition, for Gen. 10:22 he is one son of Sem: but the other, Gen. 11:12, is the son of Arphaxad. Neither is acknowledged by Moses. That both are interpolations is revealed by that different method of inserting.

The Author of the Chronicles, inspired by God, provides a second argument, who likewise hands down the series of generations in two instances, with Cainan omitted, nor does he anywhere hint that he is to be supplied; first he says that Arphaxad begat (not Cainan, but) Shelah 1 Chron. 1:18; then in the recapitulation of the generations, verse 24, he repeats Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah: in which verse, since three ש occur, the Masoretes added this note, כפסו דאירן בכל מליהון שׁין, that is, there are two verses in each of whose words the letter ש stands, which could not have been added here if the name קֵינָן had been inserted.

Thirdly, the Chaldean Paraphrases, whose authority is great among the Hebrews, eliminate this Cainan. For Cainan is omitted by them both in Moses Gen. 10:24, chap. 11:12, by Onkelos and Jonathan, and in the Chronicles book 1, 18 and 24. Fourthly, Jacob Capellus, as also the Anonymous Writer in Spanheim, p. 1, dub. Evang. p. 174 (whom James Ussher in his dissertation on Cainan teaches was Jean Cordesius from the Papist camp, who wrote in the French language concerning the genealogy of Christ), appeals to the testimony of Berosus the Chaldean, who is older than the LXX Interpreters, who placed Abraham in the tenth generation after the flood, as Josephus and Eusebius testify in book 9 of the Praeparatio Evangelica. Abraham, however, would not be the tenth, unless Cainan were excluded. To these, fifthly, Ussher adds Eupolemus, in his work concerning the Jews, produced by Alexander Polyhistor in the same Eusebius, loc. cit. Salianus, in the Preface to Vol. III of his Annals, concedes that Berosus and Eupolemus undoubtedly learned this decimal number of generations, with Cainan excluded, from the Hebrews, who were scattered over the whole world after the destruction of the ten tribes. Sixthly, the edition of the LXX Interpreters itself, published by the authority of Sixtus V and the care of Cardinal Carafa, expunges Kainan in the place of 1 Par. 1, whence Pererius concludes that the generation of Kainan did not exist in all the books of the LXX Interpreters, especially the more ancient and corrected ones: Cornelius a Lapide does not hesitate to infer that it must also be expunged from Gen. 11, since the same series is described in both places. Seventh, Pererius and Cornelius urge that Josephus, who is accustomed to follow the LXX Interpreters almost always, in book 1 of the Antiquities, when recounting the generations that were from the flood up to Abraham, did not mention this generation of Kainan at all. The latter adds Philo, who likewise follows the edition of the Hellenists, since he was little skilled in the Hebrew language.

Eighth, let Irenaeus be added, whose agreement Grotius here grants to us, though he otherwise willingly gratifies the Papists, and indeed even the rest of the fathers in the three prior centuries; the number of Irenaeus also, he says, shows that the name of Kainan was not read at that time; nor could you certainly find indications of that reading, which now appears, before the fourth century. Ninth, Origen can be brought forward, whose words these are in Tract. XX on John: Ἀβραάμ εἰκοστὸς γεγέννηται ἀπὸ τῦ πρωτοπλάσε, δέκα γὰρ γενεαὶ ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ ἐπὶ Νῶε, κὴ δέκα ἀπὸ Νῶε ἐπὶ Ἀβραάμ. Abraham was born the twentieth from the first man, for there are ten generations from Adam to Noah, and ten from Noah to Abraham. These are the words of Origen. For as Noah, with the genuine Kainan mentioned, is the tenth from Adam, so Abraham, unless the controversial Kainan is excluded, will by no means be able to be counted the twentieth. Tenth, Jerome in tradit. in Gen. Pererius teaches that he [Jerome] had curiously investigated and diligently annotated every dissonance of reading that is in the book of Genesis between the Hebrew Codices and the LXX, but that he did not even touch with a word this dissonance which is about the generation of Kainan, which is so significant and notable. From this, Pererius gathers that it is permitted to understand that that generation did not exist in the books of the LXX Interpreters which Jerome had at that time. Moreover, Jerome testifies that he followed the pure edition of the LXX existing in the Hexapla of Origen. This argument is also urged by Corn. a Lap. Eleventh, Epiphanius makes no mention of it in heresy LV, Melchised. Sect. 6, although according to the translation of the LXX Interpreters he explains the years of the individual generations that intervened between the flood and Abraham. Pererius and Cornelius use this argument likewise. For Epiphanius counts ten generations between Shem and Abraham: if Kainan is added, there will be eleven. To these he adds the time assigned to Kainan from Shem to Melchisedech, which, if it were added, would add over eleven hundred and 70 years. But if Epiphanius had found the generation and years of Kainan in the purer Codices of the LXX version, he certainly would have counted them here, because he could have thus urged the Samaritans more strongly that Shem was not Melchisedech, because more generations and years had intervened between Shem and Abraham. Add that Epiph. l. de pond. & mens. Sect. 23 & 24 makes Jacob the twenty-second from Adam, who nevertheless would be the twenty-third, if indeed Kainan had intervened. These things are so clear that what he has elsewhere in many places about Kainan, where he does not dispute expressly nor make exact calculations, such as in the beginning of the Panarion Sect. 4 and her. LXX Sect. 84 and in the Ancor. Sect. 116, can deservedly be seen as added from corrupted copies of the LXX version, which fraud could not have happened in the places cited above: or they may even have been taken by Epiphanius himself from different copies of the edition of the LXX. Twelfth, Eusebius in Chron. p. 9, having passed over Kainan, recounts the generations four times, Ἀρφαξὰδ γενόμενῶ ἐτῶν (ρλε) γεννᾷ τὸν Σαλᾶ, and that not only according to the Hebrew calculation, and according to the Samaritan calculation, but also according to the LXX Interpreters and according to Africanus. Therefore, that Arphaxad is said afterwards to have begotten Kainan is not undeservedly judged to be from a depravation. Thirteenth, therefore, Julius Africanus opposes Kainan, who around the year 220 wrote a dissertation to Aristides concerning the genealogy of Christ described by Matthew and Luke. For Eusebius in the cited place proposed his calculation and series, which is in this part conformable to the Hebrew text. However, it seems that the genuine copy of the LXX was not unknown to Julius Africanus, to which he had continuous access at the Alexandrian Library, in which it was preserved.

Fourteenth, that Cainan is to be expunged, is gathered from Theophilus, the seventh Bishop of Antioch after Peter the Apostle, who was even older than Julius, and compiled the Harmony of the Evangelists (witness Jerome to Algasia, Epistle 142, question 6) by Jacobus Capellus and the Anonymous Author recently praised, as also by Ussher, since he also eliminates the same, and in Book III to Autolycus, establishing a summary of times according to the LXX, with Cainan omitted, makes Arphaxad the father of Sala. What of the fact that in the fifteenth, in the times of the Apostles themselves, Dositheus, as Ussher observes, in the Hebrew text which he gave to his Samaritans, which was interpolated, having taken the years of the fathers after the flood before the birth of children from the LXX edition, had altogether omitted Cainan with his years: having counted in this way from the flood up to the first of Abraham (or rather the 70th of Terah) 942 years, ὁπόσα ἦν κ̓ κατὰ τῶν ό how many there were also according to the LXX, as George Syncellus reports from Eusebius, Chron. 1, 88.

Sixteenth, Cornelius à Lapide brings forward Procopius of Gaza from the fifth century, who observes that the Hebrew truth holds that Sala was begotten by Arphaxad: and that the generation of Cainan was marked with an obelus, as he teaches it to be superfluous. To whom the Anonymous author adds Paul Orosius, Gregory of Tours, Isidore of Seville, the Venerable Bede, and Bishop Freculphus, from all of whom, he says, the generation of Cainan is omitted as spurious and of bad quality. Ussher adds, besides the followers of Eusebius, also Josephus in his Hypomnesticon, which is still unpublished, and Quintus Julius Hilarion in his little book on the duration of the world, written in the year of the Christian Era 397: who, having established a calculation of years according to the LXX, passed over the times of Cainan.

Seventeenth, the collation of the Hebrew text and the LXX version does not allow for Cainan: Because Moses asserts expressly that Arphaxad in the 35th year of his age begat Sala. But Cornelius à Lapide judges this to be absolutely false if we interject Cainan from the LXX, for the reason that according to them Cainan was begotten by Arphaxad in this very year, but Sala after thirty years from Cainan, not from Arphaxad. But as for what Pererius objects, when Arphaxad is said to have begotten his son Sala at 36 years of age, that this is not to be understood as if he then begat him in act, but only in virtue and power, because in that year he begat Cainan, the father of that Sala, in whom he himself, Sala, was contained as a son in a father in virtue and power; Cornelius says that this solution seems harsh and violent, nay, a lie in Chronology.

Eighteenth, it is added that in the edition of the LXX, not only are other errors found here and there, and the chief of the adversaries are bound to acknowledge corruption in various places, especially in chronological and genealogical matters, but also in this review of generations, and specifically in enumerating the years of the life of Cainan, one hundred years have been added, as even those who favor Cainan admit, Torniellus, Salianus, and Pererius, whom Bellarmine, Huntlaeus, and Samerius also support. It is not surprising, therefore, if this error of the inserted Cainan has also crept in.

Nineteenth, reasons not to be despised from Chronology fight against Cainan, and the 130 years assigned to him by the LXX, which chronologists bring into the battle line; whence the leaders among them, Ado of Vienne, Beroaldus, Funccius, Scaliger, Calvisius, Helvicus, Capellus, Philippus Lansbergius, and others, [reject] Cainan with his years from their tribe, and to them also join themselves those who acknowledge here the error of the LXX in the interpolated Cainan, although they believe that Cainan was retained by Luke on purpose. To these is added finally the twentieth point, that in the Greek editions the numbers vary considerably; for some copies attribute to Cainan after the birth of Sala 330 years, but some which George Syncellus followed, in his Chronicle p. 115, as also a certain Syrian Chronographer of Ussher, who also had the name of George, 430 years. But the Arabic interpreter of Genesis of Ussher counts 363 years. Again, the Roman Greek edition counts 400 years for Arphaxad after the birth of Cainan. The Latin version of Flaminius Nobilius 330. The Aldine and German editions with the most ancient Cottonian copy of all, the Syrian Chronographer of Ussher, and the Sicilian fasti 330. George Syncellus 355. The Arabic interpreter of Genesis of Ussher 363. The Complutensian with the Alexandrian, which is preserved in England, [counts] 420. Which inconstancy of the Greek reading argues a depravation of the text.

Moreover, from these reasons well weighed, it must be concluded entirely that this error did not come from the LXX interpreters themselves, but long after the Greek translation was made, it crept into its copies, which in the time of Berosus, Eupolemus, Josephus, Philo, Theophilus, Julius Africanus, Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Eusebius, Jerome, and Quintus Julius Hilarion, still existed pure, knowing nothing of the generation of this interpolated Cainan, although in the age of those later ones it had already appeared stuffed into certain copies of the version of the LXX, whence Augustine l. XVI. de C. D. c. 3. and Nazianzen in his genealogical meter recount Cainan in the series of generations, namely from corrupted copies: but Epiphanius, as also Eusebius, if only fraud was not committed against them, according to the purity or impurity of the copies which they used, institute a diverse enumeration of generations, now including Cainan, now omitting him. Although such a diversity cannot be shown of Eusebius from his genuine writings. But in subsequent centuries it occupied almost all the copies of the LXX, although in some, signs of fraud and corruption remained, while 1 Par. 1, the ancient and emended copies omit this fictitious generation; but in Genesis ch. 11, they render the same suspect by the added years, because, namely, in the version of the LXX, the very same years of both generation and life lived after generation are attributed to Cainan and Sala.

But the observation of the most learned Ussher seems not unsuccessfully at all to resolve this difficulty concerning the Greek editions; who distinguishes between the primitive version of the Mosaic Pentateuch, which corresponded most exactly to the Hebrew text, and this interpolated Cainan, which could not have been acknowledged in those times either by the Hebrews or by their follower Berosus the Chaldean; and a freer interpretation of the whole Old Testament, which, prepared after the 4th year of Ptolemy Philometor, in the course of time obtained the place and name of the LXX elders: and here furthermore he wishes it to be distinguished, with Jerome Ep. 135 to Sunia and Fretela, that there is one edition, which Origen and Eusebius and all Greek commentators call the common and Vulgate, which by most was called Lucian's, and another is the LXX interpreters, which was found in the Hexaplar copies. For although the LXX edition itself is also common, Jerome observes that this difference exists between both, that the common is an edition corrupted for places and times and for the will of the ancient writers: but that which was held in the Hexapla is the very one which was believed to be reserved in the books of the learned as the incorrupt and immaculate translation of the LXX. In that common one, both the old, which was in use before the times of Origen, and the new interpolated by Lucian the Martyr, Ussher acknowledges that Cainan had been inserted, but in the other, which is held by the learned as the incorrupt and immaculate LXX edition, and which Origen took care to have inserted into his Hexapla, having been deposited in the Alexandrian library of Cleopatra and then received in Egypt, Palestine, and Syria, he denies that Cainan had a place: in the common edition of the LXX. Origen mixed the edition of Theodotion, marking with asterisks what had been lacking, and with little lines what seemed to have been added as superfluous, as Jerome has in Ep. 107 to Chron., where he also signifies that those copies elaborated by Origen were handed over by Eusebius and his companion Pamphilus to his Palestinians. Here therefore Origen left those things which pertain to Cainan just as he found them, but marked with a little line or obelus: which we understand from those of Procopius of Gaza in Gen. XI. The Hebrew truth holds that Sala was begotten by Arphaxad. Which are then placed in the middle, seen marked with an obelus. But Eusebius himself, when in the first book of his Chronicle he recounts the years of the fathers from a triple text, Hebrew, Greek, and Samaritan, placed Cainan in none of them, but in that also which is according to the interpretation of the seventy, he commemorates that Arphaxad, born at 135 years, begat Sala. Which also Julius Africanus, Origen's contemporary, did before Eusebius, and the even more ancient Theophilus of Antioch, and also Dositheus in the time of the Apostles themselves, as we noted before. We have decided to set forth here this Usserian observation just as it was explained by him: to which, however, we do not wish to agree in everything and add our vote. For we doubt not without reason whether those things which he hands down concerning that former distinction of the genuine version of the seventy and that which succeeded into its place, the Cleopatrine, and which Ussher explained rather prolixly in a special treatise, can sustain the accurate examination of the learned; indeed, we have shown in the Prolegomena to Genesis prefixed to our commentary that they cannot sustain it. They are certainly new, and not easily handed down by anyone before him or, as far as I know, approved by anyone after him. But that distinction between the LXX interpreters' version proposed in the Hexapla, which Jerome acknowledges as the incorrupt and immaculate version of the seventy, and the common or Vulgate, we judge not useless for resolving this matter. But these things concerning Cainan according to the Greek Mosaic text.

As for the review of Luke ch. 3, 36, where not only in the Greek text, but also in the older versions, the Syriac, Arabic, and Latin Vulgate, that Cainan is inserted into the catalogue of the fathers, this likewise ought not to be imputed to Luke himself, but deservedly judged to have proceeded from a corrector or rather a corrupter of his work, for these reasons: (1.) Because it is not likely that Luke would have wished to depart from the Hebrew truth. (2.) Because it has been sufficiently shown, and is no longer called into doubt by the principal interpreters or writers, that that Cainan is fictitious; whom it is by no means to be believed was interspersed by Luke among the genuine generations. (3.) Because it is not to be presumed in any way that the Holy Spirit wished to disturb the series of generations and the sacred chronology, and deliberately to fix a cross for all Christians, which would necessarily have to be said if Cainan were inserted by the Holy Spirit. (4.) Because in the purer edition of the LXX Interpreters that Cainan is not found, even after the times of the Apostles, nor did he proceed from the LXX Interpreters. Therefore the Evangelist followed neither the authority of the LXX Interpreters nor depraved codices: nor did he insert Cainan into the catalogue of the fathers, whom he found neither in the Hebrew codex nor in the Greek edition. (5.) Because in certain manuscript Greek codices of Luke those words τοῦ Καϊνὰν v. 36. c. 3. are omitted. Beza's most ancient codex, found in the year 1562 in the monastery of St. Irenaeus at Lyons, which is still preserved today in the University of Cambridge, and is believed to have been written over 1200 years ago, passes over those words, by whose authority, and relying on the Mosaic review in Gen. 11, 12, Beza did not hesitate to expunge the same. An anonymous author also reviews a Codex, in which there is absolutely no mention of Kainan, who Spanheim doubts whether he is that same one whom Beza mentions, or indeed another ὁμόψηφος [of the same number], but the description of the same teaches that he was that very one. There is, however, no doubt that he had several ὁμοψήφες [of the same number] Codices in this part, although perhaps they did not survive the age, or did not reach our shores. (6.) Finally, Irenaeus himself, a most ancient writer among Christians, in book 3, chapter 33, counts seventy-two generations in Luke from the generation of the Lord to Adam, which number, if Kainan is absent, is consistent with itself, but if he is present, it fails: Whence again a not light conjecture can be drawn, that the name Kainan appeared neither in the edition of the LXX nor in the text of Luke in the time of Irenaeus. To all these things is added, that it is far more probable that Cainan was inserted into Luke by others through error, than that Luke either studiously followed the error of the LXX. Int. or even that Kainan was deliberately omitted by Moses and the writer of Chronicles, neither of whom can be said to be such that the Holy Spirit himself, who directed their pen, is accused of error, whether of commission or omission.

But how the error could have crept into almost all modern Codices, both of the LXX Int. and of the N.T., there is no reason for us to wonder, especially if that corruption had already occurred in the time of Jerome and Augustine: the reasons for which Spanheim investigates at greater length in the aforementioned book.

Grotius thinks that the error first crept into the Codex of Luke, which also seemed more likely to us in the Critico Sacro, because the genuine Kainan, son of Enos from verse 37, simultaneously brought in a supposititious Kainan into the immediately preceding verse 36. But having read Ussher's most learned dissertation on Cainan, I confess that by his observation from the Chronology of Demetrius I am easily induced to believe rather that that spurious Kainan was first brought into the edition of the LXX. Whence not undeservedly the Archbishop of Armagh noted Grotius here. For although in the edition which was deposited at Alexandria in the Cleopatra Library, it was shown that there was no mention of that Cainan, which was later held for the genuine LXX. of the Elders: yet in the κοινῇ [common] or Vulgate, which had been in more common use, Demetrius in his book on the Chronology of those who reigned in Judea, proposed by Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius (in book 9 of the Evangelical Preparation), demonstrates that Cainan held a place even before the times of Christ. For that [chronology], counting up to the descent of Jacob and his sons into Egypt, from Adam 3624 years, from the Flood 1360 (or rather 1362), from the arrival of Abraham from Haran into Canaan 215, necessarily requires the interposition of 130 years of Cainan. If this had been noticed by Grotius, he would never have conceded to the opinion that in Luke 3:36 the name of Cainan was first replaced by some error, and then, when that reading had begun to be widely scattered through the copies of Luke, Greek Christians also interposed the name of Cainan between Arphaxad and Sala in the version of Genesis according to the Seventy, with years also added, so that the authority of Luke, whom they thought had written thus, might be more established. Far more probable, therefore, is the other opinion, that the name of Cainan was transferred from the κοινῇ [common] or Vulgate edition of Genesis, just as into the first chapter of the first book of Chronicles (where it is not yet found inserted, neither in the Greek Vatican Codex, nor in the Arabic version of the Javanic Bibles, nor in the old Ruthenian or Illyrian translation), so into the genealogy of Christ in Luke. Concerning him in 2. of his Chronicles, Christian Massaeus: First, it may seem doubtful whether blessed Luke wrote thus. For who would dare to assert what he cannot prove? But who does not see that it could have happened that it was inserted not by him, but by other Greeks after his death, if they saw that the Gospel disagreed with their Bibles (which it was agreed should not have happened), especially in that place where the series of generations was written; where it could most easily have been thought that not will, but inadvertence of the writer was present? And in the Commentaries on chapter 2 of Genesis, Benedictus Pererius: From these it is rightly concluded that the generation of Cainan was not in all books of the Seventy Int. Whence it is also probably conjectured that it was not handed down by the Seventy Int. And those books which lacked that generation, as those which agreed with the Hebrew Codices, were to be judged true and entire; but those which had the generation of Cainan were to be judged as corrupt and faulty and to be rejected. It was easy, however, for someone who had obtained books of the Seventy Int. in which there was the generation of Cainan, to have transferred it from there into the Gospel of Luke: which, not being noticed from the beginning, not only stuck in that one book, but was later derived into those which have been copied up to this day. But indeed, if what has been sufficiently well proven concerning the truth of the books of the Seventy Interpreters regarding the generation of Cainan were also proven concerning the Evangelical book of B. Luke, I would embrace this same opinion with full assent. But there is no book of B. Luke at this age which does not have the generation of Cainan in the genealogy of the Savior, nor has it ever been read that anyone said that either by himself or by others was any Codex of B. Luke seen which lacked such a generation. So he. And yet we ourselves saw the Greco-Latin book of B. Luke described in the most ancient parchments, in capital letters, without breathings and accents: where in Greek τῷ Φαλεκ, τῷ Ἔβερ, τῷ Σαλα, τῷ Ἀρφαξάδ, τῷ Σήμ, in Latin: qui fuit Phalec, qui fuit Eber, qui fuit Sala, qui fuit Arphaxad, qui fuit Sem, was clearly read; with the mention of this Cainan entirely omitted. That Codex, comprising the histories of the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, once brought from Greece into Gaul, is deposited in the monastery of S. Irenaeus, in the suburb of Lyon, and was found there when the civil war arose in the year 1562, and was finally donated by Theodore Beza in the year 1581 to the public library of the Cambridge Academy. Nor is there any other Greek MS of this kind, either mentioned by Beza, or recently sent to England from Greece: whatever Hugo Grotius may say in his annotations to this place of Luke. This is from the Archbishop of Armagh.

Johannes Cordesius, one of the Papists, in his book on the Genealogy of Christ in French, also praised by Grotius, agrees, confirming that the name Cainan did not exist in the primitive Codices of Luke. Then Corn. a Lap. in his Commentary on Gen. 11, 12, who teaches that Cainan crept into Luke by the error of copyists or some sciolist who, being ignorant of Hebrew, when he found Cainan added in the LXX version, which was once the vulgate, in Genesis, transferred the same from the LXX into Luke and thought it should be inserted into it. Furthermore, Dionysius Petavius, who in book IX of De Doctrina Temporum, chapter 17, says that it should not seem strange or incredible if we suspect that the name of Cainan overflowed from the corrupted books of the LXX into the Gospel of Luke. Finally, Petrus Possinus in his Diallacticus on the Genealogy of Christ, chapter 9, who confidently concludes that the name of Cainan was inserted into the books of Luke by sciolist scribes long after the fact, from an edition of the LXX that was already corrupted. For who does not know, he says, that the New Testament was the most frequently copied of all books? Therefore, semi-learned Greeks, accustomed to the edition of the LXX which was already faulty, when they approached the copying of the Gospels, did not hesitate to restore, as it seemed to them, the name omitted in Luke; which hallucination had the authority of a learned emendation, so that it was spread into all the Codices in a short time, if indeed into all. To these we also add Grotius himself, who is of the same opinion in that Cainan is an interpolation in both the Old and New Testaments, whose words have been cited in his Annotations on Luke 3, 36. τꝵ Σαλὰ, τꝵ Ἀρφαξὰδ. Thus do some Greek Manuscripts have it, which Beza mentions, and what is most important, one written in a most ancient script, which belonged to the Church of Lyons, was later brought to Cambridge, and another recently sent to England from Greece (what should be held regarding this, Ussher warned beforehand, to whom we here add Walton, T. 1. Oper. Bibl. Angl. Proleg. IX. Regarding the other M we print with the Roman in this edition, I say that D. Grotius was poorly informed. For in this copy, which as I write these things is before my eyes, the name of Cainan is expressed. This is Walton.) The number of Irenaeus also shows that the name of Cainan was not read at that time: nor indeed could you find indications of the reading that now appears before the fourth century, etc.

But one must wonder why recently Brian Walton, author of the English Biblical work polyglot, in the apparatus of Vol. I, prefixed to Prolegomena IX, page 68, although he was not ignorant of the documents of Ussher's dissertation, still preferred to accede to the opinion of Bonfrère rather than leave room for those, unless perhaps this is to be attributed to Walton's fervor against Beza: whose annotations and observations he seems to have taken pains to discredit not only here, but also in other places, whence he also praises the studies of Boys: As Beza defended the Vulgate against Erasmus, so the learned man John Boys, at the urging of the Bishop of Winchester, D. Lancelot Andrewes, defends the same against the often unjust censures of Beza. Thus, however, he holds for this reason: If it be granted that the Hebrew Codices never had this name, it could be said that Moses deliberately omitted this generation (which the LXX, from certain tradition or the suggestion of the Holy Scriptures, and Luke supplied) just as Matthew omitted certain ones in the same Genealogy, and as he here distributed his genealogy into 14 generations, omitting the rest: so Moses, in weaving his own to Abraham, divided it into two decades, with this single generation omitted, for a reason unknown to us: and in this way it could be said by Moses: Arphaxad begat Sala, who nevertheless was begotten by Cainan, just as it is said in the Gospel that Joram begat Ozias, who nevertheless was begotten by another, both of which are true, not by immediate generation, but by mediate. For thus Arphaxad begat Sala, because he begat Cainan, in whom as a parent Sala existed. Thus Bonfrère and others, whose opinion is much more probable than those who accuse the text of error. But that many things render that opinion less probable, those things which we discussed above sufficiently teach.

Walton says that the most ancient Greek copies, even before the times of Christ, had the name of Cainan, as Ussher proves from the Chronology of Demetrius, who wrote before Christ. But Ussher proves this regarding the vulgar version, which is called the common; regarding the genuine interpretation of the 70, those things which both he and others have noted teach the contrary, and since those have already been brought forward, we do not wish to do here what has already been done. Furthermore, it is certain to Walton that Eusebius and Epiphanius, although they omit the name of Cainan in some places, nevertheless express it in others, and never deny it. But that is by no means certain: and regarding Eusebius, it had already been refuted in the Henry Philippean by Ussher, who had said that Eusebius indeed sometimes conceals Cainan: but since he expresses him elsewhere, he is not to be judged to have denied him. Here his associate James Salianus deceived him: who in the Proem of the third Annal confirms this from the Latin version of Eusebius' Chronicle, in the preface, whose beginning is, 'the times begin,' and from several places making for Cainan described from that rotten little book of Barbaro-Latin Excerpts, edited by Scaliger, he concludes that from them we can see for which opinion Eusebius should be judged to stand:

as if one who sees anything at all could be ignorant that those Excerpts were taken not from Eusebius alone, but also from others who differ greatly from Eusebius' Chronography: and that Scaliger himself did not warn that that other preface (as it pleased Salianus to call it) is either of another author or has a few Eusebian things intermingled, and did not sufficiently prove that it pertains to the present case, that in it 1072 years are counted from the year of the flood until the birth of Abraham. Whereas Eusebius calculated 942 years from the flood until the first year of Abraham, both according to the Septuagint interpretation and according to the Samaritan text. And since Eusebius consistently retains this method of counting in all his Epilogisms, and through it completely excludes the years of Cainan from his Chronology, and for this very reason it is established that he was criticized not only by George Syncellus, but also by the Alexandrian Chronographers far more ancient than him, Anianus and Panodorus: certainly those cannot escape the mark of rashness who have either affirmed that Eusebius acknowledged Cainan, or have denied that the generation of Cainan was absent from the edition of the LXX which he had proposed should be followed. Thus far Ussher. Regarding what should be held about Epiphanius, we have explained above. Although therefore it is probable that the Codices of the Greek translation varied somewhat in the time of Eusebius and Epiphanius, and that in some the name of Cainan was inserted, which Walton brings forward, nevertheless in those Codices which exhibited the more sincere translation of the LXX Interpreters, as it had been in the Hexapla, he will never show that the name of Cainan was found; indeed Eusebius testifies in the first book of his Chronicle, when he reviews the years of the Patriarchs not only from the Hebrew and Samaritan, but also from the Greek text, that Cainan was in none of them, and that the text of the LXX had it thus, that Arphaxad at 135 years old begat Sala. There is no doubt, however, that Eusebius thought that that series of years of the world should be selected from the Hexapla themselves, deposited in the Caesarean Library by his Pamphilus, and inserted it primarily into his Chronicle, which he judged to be more congruent with the genuine opinion of the LXX Interpreters; nor is it otherwise abundantly evident that Origen himself was persuaded about this passage, from the fact that he himself counted only ten generations from Noah until Abraham.

Wherefore it is not to be doubted that a corruption was made by the addition of Cainan, both in the common Greek editions of the O.T. and in the text of St. Luke, which the observation of Scaliger himself also confirms, testifying in the prolegomena to the Chronicon of Eusebius that in the most ancient copies of the Gospel according to Luke that Cainan does not exist: and Pererius the Jesuit also admits that this opinion is less improbable than the others, and less liable to censure, in Disp. XI. l. 16. on Genesis. Nor does Petavius deny it. Moreover, Cornelius a Lapide in his commentary on Genesis, Job Corderius, and Petrus Possinus expressly defend the same. Finally, Beroaldus in his Chronicon, Beza on Luke ch. 3, Pareus and Rivetus on Genesis, Jacobus Capellus in his Sacred and Exotic History, Sixtinus Amama in his Antibarbarus go into this opinion, and Fridericus Spanhemius treats of the same most extensively of all in Dub. Evangel. p. 1. Dub. 33, as does also Jacobus Ussher of Armagh in his recently published dissertation on Cainan with the Syntagma on the LXX version. But of our own, Mr. Dr. David Rungius, Mr. Dr. Salomon Gesnerus, Mr. Dr. Johann Gerhardus in his commentary on Genesis, as also Mr. Dr. Waltherus in his Harmonia Scripturae, and others, embrace the same. Nor indeed can the Papists obtain anything from that against the integrity of the sources, since that corruption not only does not touch the foundation of the faith at all, but is also so constituted that it has not invaded all the Greek Codices, some being left uncorrupted, and it betrays itself from a collation of the Old Testament, whence the authentic text can be restored in its entirety. What of the fact that this Cainan is seen no less in the Vulgate Latin version than in most Greek Codices? Yet the Papists believe that version to be sincere nonetheless.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET GENUIT SALE.) De Kainane hic inferto vide, quæ notavimus ad Luc. III.

Vult ibi ἐμβολιμαῖον esse: quod argumentis nonnullis probat. Non improbo. Longe enim id uberius ante visum Grotium confirmavi Criti- co Sacro p. 754. seqq. ubi etiam quomodo Cainan hic irrepsisse videatur, expositum. Solum hic iterum moneo, non posse inde corruptionem textus originalis doceri, quod Papistæ contendunt: siqui- dem non omnes Codices Græcos Lucæ illa pervaserit, quum Scaliger prol. in Chron. Euseb. quorundam mentionem faciat, qui Kainanem hic non habe- ant, ac Beza in vetustissimo quodam Codice eun- dem non invenerit: & è collatione V. T. seipsum prodat. Maxime vero loci 1. Par. I, 24. ubi Maso- retharum nota excluditur Kainan, quæ ita habet: Luo sunt versus, in quorum singulis dictionibus extat litera ש. Hæc enim in nomine קינן locum non ha- bet. Unde neque Chaldaica, neq; Arabica, neque La- tina, aut alia translatio in V. T. Kainanem habet, præter solam LXX. Interpp. Nec Samaritani Co- dices illum norunt, aut Judæi etiam veteres, Jose- phus, Philo, alii. Numerant enim vetustissimi E- bræi à Noah ad Abrahamum tantum decem genera- tiones. Adde quod non minus in Vulgata versione Kainan apud Lucam conspiciatur, quam sinceram & authenticam nihilo secius credunt adversarii. Si tamen quis Kainanem irrepsisse, ob consensum Co- dicum, Græcorum pene omnium, Syriacæ etiam, Arabicæ ac Vulgatæ versionis admittere nolit vel Salam binominem dicere poterit, ut τῷ Καιναν sit, qui & Kainan dictus, cum Nauclero, Hermanno Contracto, Job. Lucid. Franc. Gomaro, Ludovic. de Dieu, vel Arphaxado nomen etiam fuisse Kainan, quæ sententia est Hottingeri, cum quo tamen opus non est recurrere ad traditiones, quasi ex illis hau- rire necessum habuerit Lucas sive Arphaxadum, sive Schalam etiam Kainanem dictum fuisse: quum id ex inspiratione divina habere potuerit ὑπὸ πνεύ- ματος ἁγίε φερόμενος Historicus.

Non dissimulandum tamen, variis difficultati- bus hasce sententias, etsi cæteris probabiliores, ur- geri, unde jam olim eam præferendam duximus sententiam, quæ Kainanump statuit παρείσακτον, ut autem de dubio intricato rectius formetur judici- um, operæ pretium erit, ea quæ alias de illo tradidi- mus, quum ista in paucorum manibus versentur, repetere, additis nonnullis, quæ eam in rem interea observavimus. Venerabilis Beda Præfat. Act. Apo- stol. ita statuit: Evangelistam ex LXX. editione hanc generationem adjecisse, quamvis in Ebraica veritate non habeatur. Quæ habet etiam in expos. Luc. c. 3. Eadem est mens Adon. Vienens. Episc. Chronic. ab- breviat. ætat. II. ut & August. Steuchi, & Cornel. Jan- senii Concord. Evang. c. 14. Rationem ejus rei satius esse reverenter admirari, quam anxie disquirere, cen- set Beda. Id vero factum esse, non ex propria Evan- gelistæ sententia, sed ex hypothesi, & sensu alio- rum, statuit inter alios è Pontificiis Guilh. Genebrar- dus l. I. Chronic. ad A. M. 1659. quod nempe ex opi- nione LXX. non sua Kainanump posuerit Lucas & qui- dem Græcorum, ad quos scribebat, & quibus sola ex- emplaria LXX. notæ erant, causa; quum August. te- ste l. 2. contr. Epistol. Parmen. novum non sit, Scri- pturam loqui ex aliorum sensu & opinione, non rei ve- ritate. Addit tamen Genebrardus aliam quoque conciliationis rationem; quod nempe Arphachsad Selam dici possit genuisse per intermedium Kainan, ne opus sit hunc facere ὑποβολιμαῖον. Eadem fere cal- cat vestigia Jac. Naclant. in Medull. Script. S. seu Arcan. Christi; Lucam posuisse generationem Kai- nan, non ex propria, sed ex LXX. Int. sententia, quanquam id suspense adferat: cum inclinet quo- que in Lyrani sententiam, ipsum Sale tum Kaina- nis, tum Arphaxadi filium esse potuisse, illius secundum legem, hujus secundum naturam, ut sc. Kainano sine liberis defuncto frater ipsius Arphaxad ex relicta vidua genuerit Sale. Favet isti sententiae quoque Six- tus Senensis, at mente dubia l. 5. B. S. ann. 88. & l. 6. ann. 143. & lib. 7. haer. 4. Confidentius vero eam proponit Cardinal. Cajetanus Comment. in cap. 3. Luc. superfluam esse hanc generationem, excusari ta- men Lucam: quia recensuerit genealogiam, ut in- venit eam scriptam a LXX. apud quos scripta legi- tur haec genealogia superflua, & merito excusari, quia tunc temporis interpretatio LXX. magnae erat authoritatis apud Graecos & nationes alias.

E Calvinianis fovet eam sententiam Josephus Scaliger in Eusebium, ut & Jac. Usserius, Diss. de Kainane ad hypotheticam illam propositionem, si B. Lucas Spiritus S. amanuensis in Christi genea- logia Kainanen inter Salam & Arphaxadum inter- ponendum esse censuit, ea de re dubitandi nullus am- plius relinquitur locus: distinguendo respondet: Siquidem ex propria sententia hic locus Evan- gelista fuerit, veram eam esse; sin ex aliorum, non item. Non magis certe, quam Melchisede- cum reipsa sine patre, sine matre, sine genealogia, neque initium dierum, neque finem vitae habuisse, oportere credi; quia ex vulgo recepta sententia id Apostolus pro- nunciaverit (Hebr. 7, 3.) consuetudinis enim Scri- pturarum est, ut opinionem multorum sic narret histo- ricus, quomodo illo tempore ab omnibus credebatur. Sicut Joseph ab ipsa quoque Luc. 2, 48. Maria appel- labatur Pater Jesu; ita & Herodes dicitur contrista- tus, quia hoc discumbentes putabant: inquit Hiero- nymus, Comment. in Matthaei cap. 14, 6. & in Jere- miae cap. 28, 10. Septuaginta Prophetam non dixere Ananiam: ne scil. Prophetam viderentur dicere, qui Propheta non erat. Quasi non multa in Scripturis Sanctis dicantur juxta opinionem illius temporis, quo gesta referuntur, & non juxta quod rei veritas con- tinebat. Atque in libro 2. adversus Helvidium: Ev- angelistae opinionem vulgi exprimentes, quae vera hi- storiae lex est, patrem dixerunt Joseph Salvatoris. Ita igitur Evangelista Lucas, Patres Salvatoris omnes, tam vulgo ita habitos, quam veros, recensendos sibi propo- nens, genealogiam ipsius ita exorsus, ὤν, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, υἱὸς Ἰωσήφ, τοῦ Ἠλὶ, τοῦ Μάτθαν, existens, ut putabatur, fi- lius Joseph, filius Eli (Patris Mariae Deiparae) filius Matthan (nominativo illo, υἱὸς in sequentibus omnibus ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repetito:) in progressu quoq́; ejusdem inter Christi Patres & Kainanē nominare poterat; non quod talis revera ipse esset, sed quod a Judaeis Hellenistis & Christianis non alia, quam Graeca Testamenti Veteris interpretatione usus (quorum maximus erat numerus) inter Abrahami majores numeraretur.

Sed sententiam illam exsequitur imprimis dili- genter Franc. Junius Anal. Genes. c. II. Tom. I. Oper. Col. 167. ubi Lucam sequutum esse LXX. fidem asserit, ejusq; consilium hac in re ita exponit; Cum videret, non esse positam in hac re piorum salutem, sed errorem jam olim temere majoribus invectum & apud omnes gentes aetate illa receptum, non posse sine gravi offensione tam repente convelli ex mentibus & libris hominum, de- dit Lucas charitati & pietati in Ecclesiam Dei, quod te- meritas ante invexerat, ac proinde Kenanis appellationē eodem ordine in sua narratione inferi passus est, ne dum historiae veritas ageretur (in qua parum positum videbat esse) labefactaretur pietas infirmorum, & dissueretur charitas; quae primis illis temporibus nascentis Ecclesiae omnibus modis fuit suffulcienda. Et in parallel. Sacr. par. 60. Col. 14. 43. Non est hoc, inquit, μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα, sed συγχώρησις ἀναμάρτητος, id est, modesta concessio peccato vacans, quo genere sermo- num Scriptura non raro utitur.

At sententiam illam de admissis in N. T. erroribus versionis LXX. Interpp. plenam periculi, & omnino falsam esse, agnoscunt Catharinus, Pererius, Spanhemius, quo de vid. quæ Critic. Sacr. p. 730. seqq. diximus; ubi de hoc etiam Kainane ex professo actum. Quem utique ἐμβολιμαῖον ex tribu movendum esse 1. E Mose constat, eum non uno, sed duobus distinctis locis omittente, cap. 10. & 11. Genes. & quidem in accurata recensione genealogica, & computatione Chronologica. Ubi adversus Cajetani exceptionem, q. exciderit Kainan, observamus : quod in diversis locis excidere haud potuerit nudum nomen, nedum simul generatio ejus, annique vitæ seorsim recensiti: sed & multa hanc suspicionem refellere, ac vanitatis luculenter convincere, utpote omnium Ebræorum Codicum perpetuum, & constantem in prætermittendo & excludendo Kainane consensum, quibus etiam conformis est Samaritanus Codex; adhæc repetitionem uniformem, qua, omisso Kainan, quater in Ebræis Codd. omnibus refertur illa genealogia : Suffragia insuper Paphrasium Chaldaicarum, in quibus nullum vestigium Kainani, nec apud Onkelosium, nec apud Jonathanem; Ebræorum veterum Chronologiam & historiam, quæ Kainanem illum penitus ignorat; Masoretharum observationem, quæ excludit Kainam; Vulgatam denique versionem, Pontificiis authenticam, quæ pariter nescit istam generationem. Quæ argumenta pleraque urget Corn. à Lapide, adjiciens Regulam Augustini certissimam lib. XV. de C. D. c. 3. Si translatio ab originali dissentit, ei linguæ potius credendum esse, unde in aliam per interpretationem facta est translatio. Adde, quod non eadem ratione insertus reperiatur Kainan in editione Græca, Nam Gen. 10, 22. est unus Semi filius : alter vero Gen. 11, 12. est filius Arphaxadi. Neuter à Mose agnoscitur. Utrumque ἐμβολιμαῖον esse prodit diversa illa ratio inserendi.

Alterum argumentum subministrat Autor Chronicorum θεόπνευστος, qui pariter binis vicibus generationum seriem tradit, prætermisso Kainane, nec uspiam eum explendum innuit; primo Arphachsad genuisse (non Kainan, sed) Sela dicit 1. Par. I, 18. deinde in generationum ἀνακεφαλαίωσις vers. 24. repetit Sem, Arphachsad, Sela: in quo versu cum tria ש occurrant, Masorethæ hanc notam adjecerunt, כפסו דאירן בכל מליהון שׁין, hoc est, duo sunt versus, in quorum singulis dictionibus extat litera ש, quæ hic adjici non potuisset, si consertum fuisset nomen רֵינָן.

Tertio eliminant Kainanuin istum Paraphrases Chaldaicæ, quarum magna est apud Ebræos autoritas. Prætermittitur enim ab iisdem Kainan tum in Mose Gen. 10, 24. cap. 11, 12. ab Onkelo & Jonathane, tum in Chronicis l. 1, 18. & 24. Quarto provocat Jacob. Capellus, ut & Scriptor Anonymus apud Spanhem, p. 1. dub. Evang. p. 174. (quem Jacobus Usserius dissertat. de Kainane docet è Pontificiis castris fuisse Johannem Cordesium, qui Gallica lingua de genealogia Christi scripsit :) ad Berosi Chaldæi, LXX. Interpretibus antiquioris testimonium, qui Abrahamum in decima post diluvium generatione collocavit, teste Josepho & Eusebio l. 9. de præp. Evang. Abraham autem non esset decimus, nisi Kainan excluderetur. Quibus quinto Usserius addit Eupolemum, ἐν τῷ περὶ ἰκδαίων ab Alexandro Polyhistore apud eundem Eusebium l. c. productum. Denarium autem hunc generationum numerum, secluso Kainane, Berosum & Eupolemum ab Ebræis, qui à clade decem tribuum toto terrarum orbe sparsi fuerunt, haud dubie didicisse Salianus Præfat. in T. III. Annal. concedit. Sexto expungit Kainan ipsorum LXX. Interpp. editio, Sixti V. autoritate, Cardin. Carafae cura, publicata in loco 1. Par. 1. unde concludit Pererius, generatio- nem Kainan non extitisse in omnibus libris LXX. Interpp. praesertim antiquioribus, & emendatiori- bus: Cornelius a Lapide inferre non dubitat, expun- gendum etiam esse Gen. 11. cum eadem utrobique series describatur. Septimo Josephum, qui fere sequi solet LXX. Interpretes l. 1. Antiqu. percensente ge- nerationes, quae fuerunt a diluvio usq; ad Abraham, in iis hanc generationem Kainan minime comme- morasse, urget Pererius & Cornelius. Addit hic Philo- nem, qui pariter sequitur Hellenistarum editionem, cum Ebraicae linguae parum gnarus fuerit.

Octavo Irenaeus accedat, cujus consensum hic no- bis largitur Grotius, alias libenter Papistis gratifi- cans, imo etiam patrum reliquorum in tribus secu- lis prioribus; Irenaei quoq; numerus, inquit, ostendit Cainani nomen non lectum eo tempore; nec certe ejus, quae nunc apparet, lectionis indicia reperias ante quar- tum seculum. Nono Origenes adduci potest, cujus haec sunt Tract. XX. in Joh. Ἀβραάμ εἰκοστὸς γεγέννηται ἀ- πὸ τῦ πρωτοπλάσε, δέκα γὰρ γενεαὶ ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ ἐπὶ Νῶε, κὴ δέκα ἀπὸ Νῶε ἐπὶ Ἀβραάμ. Abraham a primo homine vigesimus natg est, decem enim sunt generationes ab Adamo ad Noe, & decem a Noe ad Abraham. Haec Origenes. Ut Noe enim genuino Kainano commemo- rato ab Adamo decimus, ita Abrahamus ab eodem, nisi se- cluso Kainane controverso, numerari nullo modo poterit vicesimus. Decimo Hieronymum in tradit. in Gen. do- cet Pererius, omnem dissonantiam lectionis, quae est in libro Γενέσεως inter Codices Ebraeos, & LXX. curiose per- vestigasse & diligenter annotasse, dissonantia vero hanc, quae est circa generationem Kainan, adeo insignem & no- tabilem, ne verbo quidem attigisse. Ex eo licere intelli- gere, colligit Pererius, non extitisse generationem il- lam in libris LXX. Interpp. quos tunc habuit Hiero- nymus. Testatur autem Hieronymus, se puram edi- tionem LXX. in Hexaplis Origenis extantem sequutum esse. Quod argumentum etiam urget Corn. a Lap. Un- decimo nullam ejus mentione facit Epiphanius haere- si LV. Melchised. Sect. 6. quamvis secundum trans- lationem LXX. Interpp. exponat annos singularum generationum, quae inter diluvium, & Abraham in- tercesserunt. Utuntur hoc argumento itidem Pere- rius & Cornelius. Numerat quippe Epiphanius inter Sem & Abrah. decem generationes: Si aure addatur Kainan, erunt undecim. Ad haec sumam reducit a Se- mo ad Melchised. tempus assignatu Kainano, quod si adjungeretur, supra mille centum & 70. adderet. Quod si Kainani generationem & annos in puriori- bus LXX. versionis Codicibus invenisset Epiphani- us, hic certe annumerasset, quia ita fortius urgere potuisset Samaritas, Sem non esse Melchisedechum, quod plures generationes annique inter Sem & Ab- raham intercessissent. Adde quod Epiph. l. de pond. & mens. Sect. 23. & 24. Jacobum vigesimum secundum constituit ab Adamo, qui tamen vigesimus tertius esset, siquidem intercessisset Kainan. Haec adeo per- spicua sunt, ut quae alibi pluribus locis habet de Kai- nan, ubi ex professo non disputat, nec exacte ratio- nes init, utpote in principio παναρία Sect. 4. & haer. LXX. Sect. 84. & in Ancor. Sect. 116. merito videri possint addita e corruptis exemplaribus LXX. ver- sionis, quae fraus ita fieri non potuit locis supra ad- ductis: vel etiam ab ipso Epiphanio desumta sint e diversis exemplaribus editionis LXX. Duodecimo Eusebius in Chron. p. 9. praeterito Kainane quater recenset generationes, Ἀρφαξὰδ γενόμενῶ ἐτῶν (ρλε) γεννᾷ τὸν Σαλᾶ, idq; non modo secundum cal- culum Ebraeum, & secundum calculu Samaritanum, sed & secundum LXX. Interpp. & secundum Africa- num. Quod ergo postmodum Arphachsad dicatur genuisse Kainan, à depravatione esse non immerito judicatur. Decimo tertio itaque Kainano refragatur Julius Africanus, qui circa ann. 220. de genealogia Christi à Matth. & Luca descripta dissertationem ad Aristidem perscripsit. Hujus enim calculum, & seriem Ebræo textui hac in parte conformem l. c. proposuit Eusebius. Non ignotum autem Julio Africano videtur fuisse genuinum exemplar τῶν ό, cui ad Bibliothecam Alexandrinam, in qua id asservabatur, continuus patebat aditus.

Decimo quarto Kainan expungendum esse, è Theophilo, septimo post Petrum Apostolum Antiocheno Episcopo, qui adhuc antiquior Julio fuit, & Harmoniam Evangelistarũ concinnavit, (teste Hieronymo ad Algas. Epist. 142. qu. 6.) colligit Jacobus Capellus & Autor Anonymus proxime laudatus, ut & Usserius, cum is eundem etiam eliminat, & libro III. ad Avtolycum, temporum Epilogifmum juxta LXX. instituens, omisso Kainane, Arphachsadum Salæ patrem faciat. Quid quod decimo quinto ipsorum Apostolorum temporibus Dositheus, observante Usserio, in textu, quem interpolatum Samaritanis suis dedit, Hebraico, patrum post diluvium añis ante παιδογονίαν ex lxx. editione desumtis Kainanem cum suis annis prorsus prætermiserit: numeratis hoc modo à diluvio usq; ad primum Abrahami (vel 70. Thare potius) annis 942. ὁπόσα ἦν κ̓ κατὰ τῶν ό quot erant & juxta LXX. ut ex Eusebio refert Georgius Syncellus Chron. 1, 88.

Decimo sexto adducit Corn. à Lap. Procopium Gazæum è seculo quinto, qui observet Ebraicam veritatem habere; Salam genitum esse ab Arphachsad: & generationem Kainan obelo fuisse notatam, ut superfluam docet. Cui addit Anonymus Paulum Orosium, Gregorium Turonensem, Isidorum Hispalensem, Vener. Bedam, & Freculph. Episc. Lex. à quibus omnibus prætermitti, ait, generationem Kainan, ut notham, & mali commatis. Usserius addit præter Eusebii sequaces etiam Josephum in hipomnestico suo adhuc inedito, & Quintũ Julium Hilarionẽ in libello de mundi duratione, An. Ær. Christ. 397. conscripto: qui annorũ calculo juxta lxx. instituto, Kainanistempora præterierunt.

Decimo septimo non patitur Kainanun collatio Ebræi textus & LXX. versionis: Quia Moses asserit diserte, Arphachsad anno ætatis 35. genuisse Sala. Họ c autem absolute falsum esse Cornel. à Lap. censet, si ex LXX. interjiciamus Kainan, eo quod secundum illos Kainan genitus fuerit ab Arphachsad hoc ipso anno, Sale vero post triginta annos à Kainan, non ab Arphachsad.
