Quod vero excipit Pererius, cum Arphachsad annos 36. natus genuisse dicitur filium Sale, non id esse intelligendum, quasi tunc actu genuerit, sed tantum virtute ac potentia, quia eo anno genuit Kainam Patrem ipsius Sale, in quo ipse Sale, ut in Patre filius virtute ac potestate continebatur; solutionem dicit Cornelius duram & violentam videri, imo mendacium in Chronologia.

Decimo octavo accedit, quod in editione LXX. non modo alii errores passim deprehendantur, variisque in locis præsertim in Chronologicis & genealogicis corruptionem agnoscere teneantur præcipui ex adversariis, sed & in hac recensione generationum, & nominatim in enumerandis annis vitæ Kainan centum anni superadditi sint, fatentibus etiam illis, qui Kainano favent, Torniello, Saliano & Pererio, quibus suffragantur etiam Bellarminus, Huntlæus, Samerius. Non ergo mirum, si error hic insarti Kainanis quoque irrepserit.

Decimo nono rationes non contemnendæ è Chronologia militant adversus Kainanurn, annosque 130. ei assignatos à LXX. quas in aciem producunt Chronologi; unde Primipili ex ipsis, Ado Vienensis, Beroaldus, Funccius, Scaliger, Calvisius, Helvicus, Capellus, Philipp. Lansbergius, aliique Kainanem cum annis suis tribu movent, & ejiciunt, quibus etiam sese jun- gunt, qui errorem LXX. hic agnoscunt in Kainane ad- jectitio, tametsi consulto à Luca Kainanem retentum censeant. Quibus accedit denique vicesimo, quod in Græcis editionibus numeri admodum varient; nonnulla enim exemplaria tribuunt Kainani post genitum Salam annos 330. nonnulla vero quæ Geor- gius Syncellus sequutus est, in Chronico p. 115. ut & Syrus quidam Chronographus, Usserii, cui etiam Ge- orgii nomen fuit, annos 430. Arabicus vero Gene- seos interpres Usserii annos numerat 363. Rursus annos Arphaxadi post genitum Cainanum Græca editio Romana numerat 400. Latina Flamminii Nobilii versio 330. Aldina & Germanica editiones cum omnium antiquissimo exemplari Cottoniano, Syro Chronographo Usserii, & fastis Siculis 330. Georgius Syncellus 355. Arabicus Usserii Interpres Geneseos 363. Complutensis cum Alexandrino, qui in Anglia asservatur Codice 420. Quæ lectionis Græ- cæ inconstantia textus depravationem arguit.

Cæterum è rationibus istis probe pensitatis con- cludendum omnino, non esse hunc errorem ab ipsis LXX. Interpp. sed longe post factam Græcam transla- tionem irrepsisse in ejusdē exemplaria, quæ tempo- re Berosi, Eupolemi, Josephi, Philonis, Theophili, Julii Africani, Irenæi, Epiphanii, Eusebii, Hieronymi, Quinti Julii Hilarionis, pura adhuc exstititerint, gene- rationem Kainanis istius irreptitii nescientia, quan- quam posteriorū illorum ætate jam infarta eadem comparuerit in exemplaribus quibusdam versionis LXX. unde Augustinus l. XVI. de C. D. c. 3. & Nazi- anzenus in metro genealogico Kainanē in serie ge- nerationum recensent, nempe è corruptis exem- plaribus: Epiphanius vero ut & Eusebius, si modo il- lis fraus facta non sit, pro puritate vel impuritate ex- emplarium, quibus usi fuerunt, diversam generatio- num enumerationem instituunt, Kainanum jam ac- censentes, jam prætermittentes. Quanquam de Eu- sebio ex genuinis ejꝫ scriptis talis diversitas monstra- ri non possit. Subsequentibꝫ vero seculis omnes pe- ne occupavit Codices LXX. Int. quanquam in non- nullis fraudis & corruptelæ remanserint indicia, dum 1. Par. 1. antiqui & emendati Codices præter- mittunt hanc generationem fictitiam; in Genesi ve- ro cap. 11. suspectam reddunt eandem anni adjecti, quod nempe in versione LXX. iidem prorsus anni & generationis, & vitæ post generationem actæ tribuantur Kainano & Sale.

Videtur autem non infeliciter omnino hanc de Græcis editionibus difficultatē expedire observatio Eruditissimi Usserii; qui distinguit inter primitivam Mosaicæ Pentatevchi versionem, quæ Hebraico tex- tui exactissime responderit, & Kainanū istum infiti- tium neq; ab Ebræis neq; ex eorum sequace Beroso Chaldæo illis temporibus agnitū habere non potue- rit; & liberiorem totius V. T. interpretationem, quæ post 4. Ptolemei Philometoris annum concinnata, procedente tempore LXX. seniorum locum & nomen obtinuit: atq; hic porro distinguendum esse vult, cum Hieronymo Ep. 135. ad Suniā & Fret. quod nempe alia sit editio, quam Origenes & Eusebius, omnesq; Græci tractato- res κοινὴν communem appellant atq; Vulgatam, quæ plerisq; λουκιανὸς dicebatur, alia vero sit LXX. Int. quæ in Hexaplis Codd. reperiebatur. Etsi enim com- munis etiā sit ipsa LXX. editio, hoc tamen interesse inter utramque, observat Hieronymus, quod κοινὴ pro locis, & temporibus, & pro voluntate scriptorum veterum corrupta editio sit: ea autem, quæ habeba- tur in Hexaplis, ipsa sit, quæ in Eruditorū libris in- corrupta & immaculata LXX. Int. translatio reserva- ri credita fuerit. In communi illa, tum vetere, quæ ante Origenis tempora in usu erat, tum nova à Lu- ciano Martyre interpolata Cainanem interjectum fuisse agnoscit Usserius, in altera vero, quæ incorru- pta & immaculata LXX. editio à Doctis habita est, quamque in Alexandrina Cleopatræ Bibliotheca repo- sitam, & in Ægypto, Palæstina & Syria tum receptam Hexaplis suis inserendam curavit Origenes, Cainanũ locum habuisse negat: in communi editione τῶν LXX. Origenes, Theodotionis editionem miscuit, asteriscis designans, quæ minus fuerant, & virgulis, quæ ex su- perfluo videbantur apposita, ut in Ep. 107. ad Chron. habet Hieronymus, ubi & Codices istos ab Origene elaboratos Palæstinis suis Eusebium & sodalem ejus Pamphilum tradidisse significat. Hic ergo Origenes ea, quæ ad Cainanum spectant uti invenit, ita & reli- quit, sed virgula, sive obelisco prænotata: quod ex illis Procopii Gazæi in Gen. XI. intelligimus. Hebraica veritas habet, Salam genitum esse ab Arphaxad. Quæ deinde inmedio ponuntur obelisco signata visuntur. Ipse vero Eusebius cum priore Chronici sui libro annos patrum ex triplici textu, Ebræo, Græco, & Samari- tano recenset, in nullo eorum Cainanem posuit, sed in eo etiam, quæ est κατὰ τῶν ὁ ἑρμηνείαν, Arphachsa- dum, annos 135. natum genuisse Salam commemorat. Quod & ante Eusebium Origenis æqualis Julius Afri- canus fecit, & eo adhuc antiquior Theophilus Antio- chenus, nec non ipsorum Apostolorum tempore Do- sitheus, ut antea notavimus. Observationem hanc Usserianam ita prout ab ipso exposita est, sistere hîc placuit integram: cui tamen per omnia suffragari calculumque adjicere non lubet. Quæ enim de di- stinctione illa priori versionis τῶν ὁ genuinæ, & ejus, quæ in locum istius successit Cleopatrinæ, tradit, ac pe- culiari syntagmate exposuit prolixiuscule Usserius, dubitamus non immerito, an examen accuratum Eruditorum sustinere queant, imo sustinere non posse in Prolegomen. ad Genesin Comentario nostro præmissis ostendimus. Nova certe sunt, nec facile ab ullo ante ipsum tradita aut cuiquam post ipsum quod sciam probata. Distinctionem autem illam inter LXX. Interpp. versionem in Hexaplis proposi- tam, quam Hieronymus incorruptam & immacula- tam τῶν ὁ versionem agnoscit, & κοινὴν vel Vulgatam huic rei expediendæ non inutilem judicamus. Sed hæc de Cainane juxta Græcum textum Mosaicum.

Quod deniq; ad recensionem Lucæ c. 3, 36. ubi non solum in Græco textu, sed & antiquioribus versioni- bus, Syra, Arabica & Vulgata Latina Kainan ille pa- trum Catalogo inseritur, id pariter non ipsi Lucæ imputandum, sed à correctore vel potius corruptore ejus profectum merito censeri debet, his de causis. (1.) quod verisimile non sit Lucã discedere voluisse à veritate Ebraica. (2.) quod satis ostensum, nec ab interpretibus aut scriptoribus præcipui conatis am- plius revocetur in dubium, Kainanem illum fictiti- um esse; quem γνησίοις generationibus à Luca inter- mistum minime credendum est. (3.) Quod turbare voluisse Sp. S. seriem generationum & Chronologia sacram, omnibusq; Christianis de industria crucem figere nullatenus præsumendum, id quod inserto à S. S. Kainane necessario dicendũ foret. (4.) Quod in puriori editione LXX. Int. Kaina ille non repertus, etiam post Apostolorum tempora, nec à LXX. Int. profectus sit. Non ergo vel authoritatem LXX. Int. vel Codices depravatos sequutus est Evangelista: nec inseruit Kainanem Patrum Catalogo, quem nec in Ebræo Codice, nec in editione Græca invenit. (5.) Quod in quibusdam manuscriptis Lucæ Codici- bus Græcis verba illa τῦ Καϊνὰν v. 36. c. 3. omissa sint. Bezæ Codex vetustissimus, An. 1562. in S. Irenæi Mo- nasterio Lugd. repertus, qui hodieq; in Academia Cantabrigiensi asservatur, & ante 1200. annos exa- ratus creditur, præterit illa verba, cujus autorita- te, & Mosaica recensione Gen. 11, 12. fretus, non dubitavit Beza eadem expungere. Autor Anony- mus recenset quoq; Codicem, in quo nulla prorsus extet mentio Kainan, qui utrum sit ille ipse, cujus Beza meminit, an vero alius ὁμόψηφος, ambigit Spanhemius, sed descriptio ejusdem docet eundem illum fuisse. Nullum autem dubium est, quin plures habuerit is hac in parte ὁμοψήφες Codices, licet forte ætatem non tulerint, aut nostras in oras non pervenerint. (6.) Irenæus denique ipse, scriptor in- ter Christianos antiquissimus l. 3. c. 33. à generatione Domini ad Adamum usque septuaginta duas gene- rationes in Luca numerat, qui numerus Kainan ab- sit, sibi constat, præsente autem eo fallit : Unde iterum non levis conjectura duci potest, nomen Kainan nec in editione LXX. nec in textu Lucæ tempore Irenæi comparuisse. Quibus omnibus accedit, quod longè probabilius sit, Cainan per errorem infartum esse ab aliis in Lucam, quam vel Lucam studiofe sequutum esse errorem LXX. Int. vel etiam Kainanem à Mose & scriptore Paralipomenon consulto prætermissum fuisse, quorum neutrum dici potest, quin erroris sive commiffionis, sive omissionis postuletur ipse S. S. qui calamum eorum direxit.

Quomodo autem in modernos Codices pleros- que omnes tum LXX. Int. tum N. T. irrepere po- tuerit error, non est, quod miremur, præsertim si jam Hieronymi & Augustini tempore facta fuerit ea corruptio: cujus rationes prolixius indagat Spanhemius l. c.

Primum errorem irrepsisse in Lucæ Codicem censet Grotius, quod nobis etiam magis vero simile visum fuit in Critico sacro, quod γνήσιος Καϊνὰν, Fi- lius Enos è v. 37. simul invexerit ὑποβολιμαῖον Kai- nanem in versum immediate præcedentem 36. Sed le- cta Usserii doctissima de Cainane dissertatione fa- teor, observatione ejusdem è Demetrii Chronologia facile me induci, ut potius credam primum in LXX. editionem Kainanem illum spurium invectum esse. Unde non immerito hic Grotium notavit Armachanus Episcopus. Etsi enim in editione, quæ Alexandriæ in Cleopatrina Bibliotheca reposita, pro genuina LXX. Seniorum postea est habita, Cainanis istius nullam extitisse mentionem ostensum fuerit: In κοινῇ tamen sive Vulgata, quæ in communiori usu fuerat, Cainanem locum etiam ante Christi tempora obti- nuisse, Demetrii in libro de his, qui in Judæa regna- verunt Chronologia, apud Eusebium (in Evange- licæ præparationis l. 9.) ab Alexandro Polyhistore proposita, demonstrat. Ea enim, usque ad Jacobi & filiorum descensum in Ægyptum, ab Adamo a. 3624. à Diluvio 1360. (vel potius 1362.) ab Abrahami ex Charane in Chananæam adventu 215. denumerans 130. annorum Cainanis interpositionem neceffario requirit. Quod si à Grotio fuisset animadversum, in eam opinionem nunquam concessisset in Luc. 3, 36. primum Cainanis nomen errore quodam fuisse repositum, deinde cum late spargi ea lectio per Lucæ exemplaria cœpisset, Græcos Christianos etiam in versione Geneseos secundum Septuaginta inter Arphaxadum & Salam interposuisse nomen Cainanis, annis etiam additis, quo magis Lucæ, quem sic scripsisse arbitrabantur, sua auctoritas constaret. Longe igitur probabilior altera est sententia, Cainanis nomen ex κοινῇ sive vulgata Geneseos editione, ut in primum libri prioris Para- lipomenon capitulum (ubi neque in Græco Codice Vaticano, neque in Bibliorum Javanorum versione Arabica, neq; in Ruthenica sive Illyriaca translatio- ne vetere, adhuc insertum illud reperitur) ita in Christi apud Lucam genealogiam fuisse transfusum. De eo in 2. Chronicorum suorum libro, Christia- nus Massæus: Imprimis dubium videri potest, utrum beatus Lucas ita scripserit. Quis enim audeat assevera- re, quod probare non potest? Quis autem non videat po- tuisse contingere, ut non ab ipso, sed ab aliis Græcis pos mortem ejus insertum sit, si viderint Evangelium à suis Bibliis discrepare (quod fieri non debuisse constabat :) in eo maxime loco, ubi generationum series scribeba- tur; ubi facillime putari potuisset, non voluntatem sed inadvertentiam affuisse Scriptoris ? Et in Com̃enta- riis ad 2. c. Gen. Benedictus Pererius: Ex his recte concluditur generationem Cainan non fuisse in omni- bus libris Septuaginta Int. Unde probabiliter etiam conjicitur, eam non fuisse traditam à Septuaginta Int. Atq́; eos libros, qui ea generatione carebant, ut qui cum Hebraeis Codicibus congruerent, veros & integros esse judicandos; eos autem qui generationem Cainan habe- bant, ut corruptos atque mendosos esse abjudicandos ac rejiciendos. Facile autem fuit, aliquem nactum libros Septuaginta Int. in quibus erat generatio Cainan, inde eam transtulisse in Evangelium Lucae: quod à principio non animadversum, non solum inhaesisse in uno eo libro, sed in eos postea, qui usq́; ad hanc diem exscripti sunt, esse derivatum. At enim vero, si quod de veritate libro- rum Septuaginta Interpp. circa generationem Cainan satis bene probatum est, idem quoq́; de libro Evangelico B. Lucae probaretur; eandem sententiam hanc toto as- sensu complecterer. Verum neq́; hac ætate ullus est liber B. Lucæ, qui in genealogia Salvatoris non habeat gene- rationem Cainan, nec legi fuisse unquam aliquem, qui diceret vel à se, vel ab aliis visum esse Codicem ullum B. Lucæ, qui tali generatione careret. Ita ille. Atqui li- brum B. Lucæ Græcolatinum in antiquissimis membranis, literis majusculis, sine spiritibus & accentibus, descriptum ipsi vidimus: ubi in Græco τꝵ Φαλεκ, τꝵ Εϐερ, τꝵ Σαλα, τꝵ Αρφαξαδ, τꝵ Σημ, in Latino: qui fuit Phalec, qui fuit Eber, qui fuit Sala, qui fuit Arphaxad, qui fuit Sem, exerte legebatur; Caina- nis hujus mentione prorsus prætermissa. Codex ille quatuor Evangeliorum & Actorum Apostolicorum historias complectens, ex Græcia olim in Galliam perductus, in monasterio S. Irenæi, in suburbio Lugdunensi est repositus, ibique oriente civili bello Anno 1562. repertus, à Theodoro Beza anno de- mum 1581. publicæ Cantabrigiensis Academiæ Bi- bliothecæ est donatus. Neque hujus generis Græcus ullus MS. est alius, vel à Beza commemoratus, vel in Angliam è Græcia nuper missus: quicquid in nota- tionibus suis ad hunc Lucæ locum dicat Hugo Gro- tius. Hæc Armachanus.

Astipulatur è Pontificiis Johannes Cordesius l. de Gen. Christ. Gallico à Grotio quoque laudatus, qui Cainanis nomen in primitivis Lucæ Codicibus non extitisse confirmat. Tum Corn. à Lap. in Comm. ad Gen. 11, 12. qui docet Cainan in Lucam irrepsisse erro- re librariorum vel Scioli alicujus, qui Ebraice ne- sciens cum in versione LXX. quæ olim vulgata fuit, in Genesi inveniret additum Cainan, eundem ex LXX. in Lucam transtulit, illumque ei inserendum putavit. Adhæc Dionysius Petavius, qui l. IX. Doctr. temp. c. 17. non debere mirum, aut credibile videri, ait, si Cainani nomen ex LXX. corruptis libris in Evange- lium Lucæ redundasse suspicemur. Deniq; Petrus Possi- nus in Diallactico Gen. Christi c. 9. qui confidenter concludit, ex corruptà jam editione LXX. longo demũ intervallo libris Lucæ inditum à Sciolis exscriptoribus fuisse nomen Cainani. Nam quis nescit, inquit ille, Test. Nov. librorum omnium frequentissime fuisse descriptũ? Quod ergo assueti editioni LXX. jam mendosæ semido- cti Græculi, cum ad descriptionem Evangeliorum acce- derent, restituere, ut ipsis quidem videbatur, omissum apud Lucam nomen non dubitaverunt, quæ hallucinatio emendationis eruditæ authoritatem habuit, ut in omnes brevi Codices vulgaretur, si tamen in omnes. Quibus et- iam subjungimus Grotium ipsumet, in eo quod Cai- nan & in Vet. & in N. T. instititius sit, ὀμόψηφον, cujus verba adducta sunt Annot. ad Luc. 3, 36. τꝵ Σαλὰ, τꝵ Ἀρφαξὰδ. Sic habent Manuscripti Græci aliquot, quorum meminit Beza, & quod potissimum est, antiquissima litera scriptus unus, qui Lugdunensis Ecclesiæ fuit, Cantabrigiam posteà delatus, & alter in Angliam e Grecia nuper missus (quid de hoc habendum monuit antea Usserius, cui Waltonum hic adjungimus T. 1. Oper. Bibl. Angl. Proleg. IX. De altero MS. exemplari, quod nos Alexandrinum dicimus, & cum Romano in hac editione imprimimus, dico D. Grotium male informatum fuisse. Nam in hoc exemplari, quod dum hæc scribo, oculis objicitur, exprimitur Cainanis nomen. Hæc Walthonus.) Irenæi quoque numerus ostendit Cainani nomen non lectum eo tempore: nec certe ejus quæ nunc apparet lectionis indicia reperias ante quartum sæculum &c.

Mirari autem oportet, cùr nuper Brianus Waltonus operis Biblici Anglicani πολυγλώτᆸ auctor in apparatu Tom. I. præmisso Prolegom. IX. pag. 68. etsi Usserianæ dissertationis documenta non ignorarit, adhuc Bonfrerii potius opinioni accedere maluerit, quam illis locum relinquere, nisi forte tribuendum id fervori Waltoni adversus Bezam: cujus annotatis & observationibus non hic tantum, sed in aliis etiam fidem ut derogaret, operam navasse videtur, unde laudat etiam studia Boysii: Ut Vulgatam contra Erasmum defendit Beza, ita eandem contra Bezæ censuras sæpe injustas justo volumine tuetur vir doctus Johan. Boys, hortatu Episcopi Wintoniensis D. Lanceloti Andrewes. Sic autem hac de causa habet: Si concedatur Hebræos Codices hoc nomen nunquam habuisse, dici posset, Mosen consultò hanc generationem omisisse (quam ex certâ traditione, vel S. S. suggerente LXX. & Lucas suppleverunt) sicut Matthæus in eadem Genealogia quasdam omisit, & ut hic in 14. generationes genealogiam suam distribuit, omissis reliquis: ita Moses suam contexendo ad Abrahamum in duas decades eam divisit, hac unica generatione omissa, ob causam nobis ignotam: & hoc modo dici potuisse à Mose: Arphaxad genuisse Sale, qui tamen genitus est a Cainane, ut in Evangelio dicitur Joram genuisse Oziam, qui tamen ab alio genitus est, quorum utrumque verum est, non generatione immediata, sed mediata. Sic enim genuit Arphaxad Sale, quia genuit Cainanem, in quo ut Parente extitit Sala. Sic Bonfrerius & alii, quorum opinio multo probabilior est, quam eorum, qui textum erroris accusant. Sed opinionem illam multa reddere minus probabilem, ea, quæ supra disputavimus, satis docent.

Dicit Walthonus, antiquissima exemplaria Græca, etiam ante Christi tempora habuisse nomen Cainanis, ut probat Usserius ex Demetrii Chronologia, qui ante Christum scripsit. Sed id de vulgata versione, quæ κοινὴ dicta, probat Usserius; de germana τῶν ὀ interpretatione, contrarium docent ea, quæ & ipse, & alii notarunt, quæ quum adducta jam sint, nolumus hic actum agere. Porro certum est Walthono Eusebium & Epiphanium licet Cainanis nomen alicubi omittant, tamen alibi exprimere, nunquam negare. Id vero certum minime est: & de Eusebio in Henrico Philippeo jam refutatum fuit ab Usserio, qui pariter Eusebium quidem aliquando dissimulare Cainan: sed quum eum alibi exprimat, negasse non esse censendum, dixerat. Fefellit hic eum socius ipsius Jacobus Salianus: qui in tertii Annalis Proëmio hoc ex Latina Eusebii Chronici versione, in præfatione, cujus est initium, incipiunt tempora, confirmat; atque locis aliquot pro Cainane facientibus ex putido illo Excerptorum Barbarolatinorum libello, a Scaligero edito, descriptis, ex illis videre nos posse concludit, pro qua sententia Eusebius stare censendus sit:

quasi qui aliquid omnino videt, Excerpta illa non ex Eusebio solo, sed ex aliis etiam ab Eusebii Chronographia summe dissentientibus, desumta fuisse ignorare potuerit: & alteram illam præfa- tionem (ut eam Saliano appellare libuit) aut alius auctoris esse aut pauca Eusebiana intermixta ha- bere, ipse Scaliger non monuerit, & illud ad præ- sentem causam attinere satis non evicerit, quod in ea ab anno diluvii usque ad nativitatem Abrahæ anni 1072. numerentur. Quum Eusebius tam juxta Septuaginta interpretationem (κατὰ τῶν ὀ ́ ερ- μηνεῖαν) quam juxta textum Samaritanum, a di- luvio usque ad primum annum Abrahæ annos 942. supputaverit. Cumque in omnibus suis Epilo- gismis hunc numerandi modum Eusebius constan- ter retineat, & per eum Cainanis annos a sua Chro- nologia penitus excludat, atque ob hoc ipsum non a Georgio Syncello, sed etiam ab illo longe anti- quioribus Chronographis Alexandrinis, Aniano & Panodoro, reprehensum eum fuisse constet: te- meritatis certe notam illi effugere non possunt, qui vel Eusebium Cainanem agnovisse affirmave- rint, vel ab editione τῶν LXX. quam ille sequen- dam proposuerat, Cainanis generationem abfuisse negaverint. Hucusque Usserius. De Epiphanio quid habendum sit, supra exposuimus. Etsi ergo probabile sit, Codices Græcæ translationis Eu- sebio & Epiphanii tempore nonnihil variasse, & in aliquibus nomen Cainanis insertum fuisse, quod Waltonus adfert, in illis tamen Codicibus, qui sinceriorem exhibebant LXX. Interpp. trans- lationem, prout ea in Hexaplis fuerat, nomen Cai- nanis repertum fuisse nunquam ostendet; imo Eu- sebius testatur in priori Chronici sui libro, cum an- nos Patrum non tantum ex Hebræo & Samarita- no, sed etiam ex Græco textu recenset, in nullo eo- rum Cainanem fuisse, textumque LXX. ita habuis- se, quod Arphaxad annos 135. natus Salam genue- rit. Nullum autem dubium est, Eusebium ex ipsis Hexaplis, in Cæsariensi Bibliotheca a Pam- philo suo repositis illam annorum mundi seriem se- ligendam putasse, Chronicoque imprimis suo inse- ruisse, quam germanam LXX. Interpp. sententiæ magis congruentem esse judicavit; nec aliter Ori- genem ipsum de hoc loco persuasum fuisse, ex eo abunde constat, quod ipse decem tantum gene- rationes a Noah usque ad Abrahamum numerarit.

Quapropter dubitandum non est, factam es- se corruptelam additione Cainanis, tum in editio- nibus Græcis V. T. vulgatis, tum in textu S. Lucæ, quod etiam ipsius Scaligeri observatio confirmat, testantis in proleg. ad Chron. Euseb. in vetustis- simis exemplaribus Evangelii secundum Lucam il- lum Kainan non extare: eamque sententiam cæ- teris minus improbabilem, & minus reprehensio- ni obnoxiam fatetur quoque Pererius Jesuita Disp. XI. l. 16. in Genes. Neque abnuit Petavius. Propugnat autem eandem ex professo Cornel. a Lapid. comment. in Genesin, Job. Corderius ac Petrus Possinus. Eunt denique in hanc senten- tiam Beroaldus in Chronic. Beza in Luc. cap. 3. Pareus & Rivetus in Genes. Jacob. Capell. in Hi- stor. Sacr. & Exot. Sixtinus Amam. in Anti- bar. & fusissime omnium exsequitur eandem Fri- der. Spanhem. in Dub. Evangel. p. 1. Dub. 33. ut & Jacob. Usserius Armachanus novissime edita cum Syntagmate de LXX. versione dissert. de Cainane. E nostris autem amplectuntur eandem Dn. D. David Rungius, Dn. D. Salomon Gesnerus, Dn. D. Johann Gerhardus comment. in Genes. ut & Dn. D. Waltherus in Harmon. Script. aliique. Nec vero inde Pontificii quidquam obtinere po- terunt adversus sinceritatem fontium, quandoqui- dem corruptela illa non modo fidei fundamentum nihil attingat, sed & ita comparata sit, ut nec omnes Codices Græcos invaserit, quibusdam incorruptis relictis, & e collatione Vet. Test. seipsam prodat, unde in integrum restituti potest textus authenticus. Quid quod non minus in vulgata versione Latina conspiciatur hic Cainan, quam in plerisque Græcis Codd. Illam autem nihilominus sinceram credunt Pontificii.

## 11:13
v. 13. THREE HUNDRED THREE YEARS. Thus falsely the Vulgate with the LXX Interpreters from the edition of Caraffa. For the Hebrew and Chaldean constantly have 403 years for the life of Arphaxad after the begetting of Salah; indeed, even the LXX Interpreters according to the Complutensian and Royal editions, as well as many old Latin copies, as Cornelius a Lapide admits: which is more consistent with the age of that era. Grotius therefore ought to have corrected the Vulgate.

Latin:

v. 13. TRECENTIS TRIBUS ANNIS. Ita falso Vulg. cum LXX. Interpp. ex editione Caraffæ. Ebræa enim & Chald. constanter habent 403. annos de vita Arphaxadi post generatum Sale; imo etiam LXX. Interpp. juxta editionem Complut. & Regiam, nec non multa vetera Latina exemplaria, fatente Cornel. a Lapide: quod magis ætati istius ævi consentit. Corrigere ergo Grotius debuisset Vulgatam.

## 11:26
Vers. 26. BEGAT ABRAM) He is placed first here, not by privilege of age, but of dignity, as also Shem above.

Latin:

Vers. 26. GENUIT ABRAM) Hic primus ponitur, non ætatis, sed dignitatis privilegio, ut & supra Sem.

## 11:31
Vers. 31. UR OF THE CHALDEANS) The name remained in the place until the times of Ammianus Marcellinus, whom see in book XXV.

AS FAR AS HARAN) חרן Carræ to the Romans, which place the Saracens even now honor, because it was inhabited by Abraham. See Benjamin.

Shem is wrongly cast down from the axiom of primogeniture. It is certainly agreed that some Jews and Beroaldists, as well as Paraeus, derogate that dignity from him and ascribe it to Japheth; but the opinion of the Chaldean, of Augustine in book XVI of The City of God, ch. 1, 2, 3, of Scaliger, Calvisius, D. Behm, and others is to be preferred. For Shem is recounted in sacred History as the first, Ham the second, Japheth the third: but in the middle place Shem is not commemorated even once in the divine records. And the Holy Spirit observes that order where He describes their birth in Gen. 5:32, ch. 6:10, as also ch. 10:1, where He weaves together their generations. Furthermore, Scripture is accustomed commonly and ordinarily to recount children born from legitimate marriage in the order in which they were generated; see Gen. 22:21, 25:13, 35:33, 36:10, 14, etc. Add that this order has always been precisely observed among the children of Noah, not only in Genesis, but also in the first book of Chronicles, ch. 1:4. But that in Gen. 10 one proceeds in inverted order, so that 1. the descendants of Japheth, 2. of Ham, 3. of Shem are recounted, it is clear that this was done because Moses wished to continue the genealogy of Shem thereafter, whence he judged that the generations of Japheth and Ham should be set forth first.

We readily admit that Abraham was not the firstborn. And the Jews themselves, who otherwise boast much in Abraham, acknowledge that he was not the firstborn: (in Gemara Sanhedrin ch. 8, R. Azaria, Menasse Ben-Israel,) to whom are added Lyranus, Temporarius, Codomannus, the Beroaldists, Cajetan, Torniellus, Tremellius, Junius, Paraeus, even though the Scaligerians defer the right of primogeniture to Abraham. But concerning these in the Sacred Chronicle.

Latin:

Vers. 31. UR CHALDÆORUM) Mansit loco nomen ad Ammiani Marcellini usque tempora, quem vide libro XXV.

USQVE HARAN) חרן Carræ Romanis, quem locum nunc etiam honorant Saraceni, quod ab Abrahamo fuerit habitatus. Vide Benjaminem.

Perperam Semus dejicitur a primogenituræ axiomate. Constat sane, quod Judæi nonnulli & Beroaldistæ, ac Paræus illam dignitatem eidem derogent, eamque Japheto transcribant; sed præferenda Chaldæi, Augustini lib. XVI. de Civit. Dei c. 1. 2. 3. Scaligeri, Calvisii, D. Behmii, aliorumque sententia. Sem enim ut primus, Cham secundus, tertius Japheth in sacra Historia recensetur: medio vero loco Sem ne semel quidem commemoratur in fastis divinis. Et observat illum ordinem Spiritus Sanctus, ubi ortum eorum describit Gen. 5. 32. cap. 6, 10. ut & c. 10, 1. ubi generationes eorum pertexit. Adhæc consuevit Scriptura communiter & ordinarie eo, quo sunt generati ordine, liberos ex legitimo natos matrimonio recensere; Vid. Gen. 22, 21. 25, 13. 35, 33. 36, 10. 14. &c. Adde, quod semper ordo iste inter liberos Noæ præcise observatus sit, non in Genesi tantum, sed etiam in Chronicis lib. I. cap. 1, 4. Quod vero Gen. 10. inverso ordine procedatur ut 1. Japheti, 2. Chami 3. Semi posteri recenseantur, id ideo factum esse in aprico est, quod Moses Genealogiam Semi deinceps continuare voluerit, unde Japheti, & Chami generationes præmittendas censuit.

Abrahamum vero primogenitum haud fuisse, facile admittimus. Et agnoscunt ipsimet Judæi, qui alias multum gloriantur in Abrahamo, eundem non fuisse primogenitum: (in Gemara Sanhedrim cap. 8. R. Azaria, Menasse Ben-Israel,) quibus accedunt Lyranus, Temporarius, Codomannus, Beroaldistæ, Cajetanus, Torniellus, Tremellius, Junius, Paræus, utut Scaligeriani Abrahamo jus primogenituræ deferant. Sed de his in Chronico S.

## 12:1 Argument
PART III. OF GENESIS, THE HISTORY OF ABRAHAM. CHAPTER XII.

Abraham, having been called, journeys into Canaan with the promise of the Seed and sacrifices there. Because of famine he withdrew into Egypt. He receives back his wife, who had been taken into the King's house, untouched.

V. 1. GO INTO THE LAND WHICH I WILL SHOW THEE) A Pythagorean saying ἕπε Θεῷ, mention of which is found in Seneca, De Vita Beata, ch. 15, in Hippodamus, Epictetus, Arrian, Book II, M. Antoninus, and Boethius; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II, and Ambrose on this passage praise and explain it from this place.

BUT it is not a following of that kind which consisted in Pythagorean principles, but one which had to proceed from faith: because, as was noted before, faith is proclaimed by the Holy Spirit under this name for Abraham, because he followed God and went out, not knowing whither he went. The Gentiles were far otherwise, both in that they warned that God must be followed, and in that they followed Him in their own way according to the leading of the light of nature. Because they possessed neither the true light, which shows the one way, nor the Spirit as a guide, nor the strength to follow God, which faith provides. Concerning which, elsewhere against the Pelagians and their remnants, the Socinians.

Latin:

PARS III. GENESEOS, HISTORIA ABRAHAMI. CAPUT XII.

Abraham vocatus, cum promissione Seminis in Canaan profectus sacrificat ibidem. Ob famem secessit in Ægyptum. Uxorem in domum Regis sublatam intactam recipit.

V. 1. VENI IN TERRAM QVAM MONSTRABO TIBI) Dictum Pythagoricum ἕπε Θεῷ, cujus mentio apud Senecam de vita beata c. 15. apud Hippodemum, Epictetum, Arrianum libro II. M. Antoninum, Boëthium, laudant & ex hoc loco explicant Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. II. & Ambrosius ad hunc locum.

AT non est ejusmodi sequela, quæ Pythago- ricis constiterit, sed quæ e fide prodire de- buit: quia, ut antè monitum, a Spir. S. prædicatur hoc nomine fides Abrahæ, quod sequutus Deum sit, & exierit, nesciens quo iret. Longe aliter gentiles & monuerunt Deum sequendum esse, & juxta ductum luminis naturæ suo modo sequuti sunt. Quia nec veram lucem habuere, quæ unam viam monstrat, nec Spiritum ductorem, nec vires sequendi Deum, quas fides sufficit. De quo alias contra Pelagianos, eorumque reliquias Socinistas.

## 12:3
Vers. 3. IN THEE SHALL ALL THE FAMILIES OF THE EARTH BE BLESSED.) In thee, i.e., through thee they shall be blessed, that is, they shall receive the highest goods. This, however, is because from the descendants of Abraham was to come He who was to provide those goods to all the nations. See below 18, 18; 26, 4.

This is a too perfunctory explanation of the Gospel promise, if you depart from the one in Paradise, the principal and most ancient one: For Grotius does not hand down anything more concerning it in the places to which he referred. But in Gen. 18, 18, where the same promise is repeated to Abraham, he handed down a far colder gloss: All the nations of the earth are to be blessed in him. From him and his descendants they will learn that there is one God, the author of all things. By this method the mind of God is perverted, both regarding the author of the blessing, whom God here made not the person of Abraham, not his descendants, but the SEED of Abraham, which is Christ, as the Apostle interprets in Gal. 3, 16, from whom and in whom alone every blessing is obtained; and regarding the effect or the blessing itself, which is placed in mere information; so that it can be seen that this information of the nations concerning one God, the author of all things, is that highest good according to the opinion of Grotius, which they are to receive: and regarding the object to whom the blessing is promised; for the blessing is promised here not only to the nations alien to the posterity of Abraham, but primarily also to the posterity of Abraham, and thus to all the nations of the Earth. Four promises occur in this place; the first is the constitution of Abraham into a blessing: And be thou a blessing: by which justification and all heavenly goods, with which God blesses us in every spiritual blessing, are comprehended, Eph. 1, 3; Matt. 25, 34. Cf. Zech. 8, 13. The second is the defense and preservation of the Church to be propagated from Abraham; And I will bless them that bless thee: which means not only that Abraham will be in the highest honor, but also that those who will provide friendly hospitality to the Church will themselves be blessed in turn by God. The third is the overthrow of enemies. And I will curse them that curse thee. The fourth and last, but first in dignity and in the order of nature, the cause and fountainhead of the rest, is the blessing of the whole earth in the Messiah. Which the sacred Psalmist explains in Ps. 72, 17, Peter in Acts 3, 25, and especially St. Paul in Gal. 3, 8, 16. Grotius seems to have understood it in a proper and immediate sense concerning Abraham, as appears primarily from the Annotations on Gen. 18, 18: although he wishes it to be said of Abraham that from him is to be procreated He through whom the blessing is. And therefore by the pronoun THEE he understands Abraham. But the divine interpretation is above all exception, both in the designated places and in Genesis itself, partly made to Abraham himself in Gen. 22, 18, IN THY SEED; partly repeated to Isaac in Gen. 26, 4, and to Jacob in Gen. 28, 14. In which last place the prefixed Vav is to be taken exegetically: In THEE shall all the families of the earth be blessed, &, that is, in THY SEED. The holy Apostle in Gal. 3, 8 ff. took such care, lest by that pronoun THEE in the protoevangelium promulgated to Abraham in Gen. 12, 18, anyone other than Christ be understood, that he held those promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, even though made at different times, to be entirely the same, and to that Jacobite promise it appears that he pointed his finger specifically; for from there the words καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σε, because of the copulative particle καὶ, seem to be repeated. He does not say AND IN SEEDS, as in many, but as in one. And in thy Seed, which is Christ. Wherefore the customary sense of the preposition ב, IN THEE, can be retained. Truly, so that the blessing may be obtained in Abraham not immediately, or in the person of Abraham, but mediately, or in the seed of Abraham. There is no need, therefore, to explain the preposition IN as BY, since it is said that the blessing is obtained in Christ, so that we may know that he is not only an instrumental or meritorious cause, but also an efficient and formal cause, so that our righteousness is not in us, but outside us in Christ: See Is. 45, 17. 24. Jer. 23, 16. whence Abraham could recognize that righteousness and blessing were not in himself or others, but in his seed: as the blessed Polycarp Lyserus advised in ch. 22, Gen. Thus, as to the words, the Targum of Jerusalem rendered it. In thy righteousness shall all nations be blessed. The effect, blessing, is expressed both in the Niphal, they shall be blessed; and in the Hithpael, they shall account themselves blessed: and our blessed Cramer in Class. I. Schol. Proph. p. 42 expressed the sense here excellently. The whole human race is dying completely in the extreme curse, under which it is miserably cast down because of sins through the rigor of the law: Therefore I have had mercy on it, and have promised the seed of the woman, which is about to crush the head of the serpent: which promise I now repeat again, and I certainly designate thy nation, from which that seed will come forth: Whence will emanate the blessing, which will pertain equally to all nations. Whosoever shall have received this blessing by faith, they will no longer remain under the curse, but in this blessed seed they themselves also will be both blessed and blessing themselves. But you may see this sense of the divine oracle more fully confirmed in the aforementioned Theologians, and also in Dr. D. Walth. in Spongia Mosaïc. p. 408. seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 3. IN TE BENEDICENTUR UNIVERSÆ CO- GNATIONES TERRÆ.) In te, i. e. per te benedicentur, id est, summa bona accipient. Hoc autem ideo, quia ex Abra- hami posteris erat futurus is, qui gentibus omnibus ea bona erat præstiturus. Vid. infra 18, 18. 26, 4.

Promissionis Evangelicæ, si a Paradisica disces- seris, principis & antiquissimæ nimis perfuncto- ria hæc explicatio est: Nec enim quicquam am- plius de illa tradit Grotius locis, ad quæ remisit. At Gen. 18, 18. ubi eadem promissio Abrahamo re- petita, longe frigidiorem tradidit glossam: Bene- dicendæ sunt in illo omnes nationes terræ. Ab ipso, posterisque ejus discent unum esse Deum, rerum omnium auctorem. Quo pacto mens Dei & quoad auto- rem benedictionis pervertitur, quem Deus hic fecit non Abrahami personam, non posteros ejus, sed SE- MEN Abrahæ, quod est Christus, interprete Apo- stolo Gal. 3, 16. a quo & in quo solo omnis benedi- ctio obtingit; & quoad effectum seu benedictionem ipsam, quæ in sola informatione collocatur; ut vi- deri possit, hanc informationem gentium de uno Deo, rerum omnium autore, esse summum illud bonum ex sententia Grotii, quod accepturæ sint: & quoad objectum, cui promissa est benedictio; non enim tantum gentibus alienis a posteri- tate Abrahæ, sed imprimis etiam Abrahæ posteris, omnibusque adeo nationibus Terræ benedictio hic promissa. Quatuor occurrunt hoc loco promif- siones; prima est Abrahami in benedictionem con- stitutio: Et esto benedictio: qua justificatio, omniaque bona cœlestia, quibus Deus nos benedicit in omni benedictione spirituali comprehenduntur Eph. 1, 3. Matth. 25, 34. Conf. Zach. 8, 13. Altera est, Ecclesiæ ex Abrahamo propagandæ defensio & conservatio; Et benedicam benedicentibus te: quod non solum in semmo honore futurus sit Abraham, sed & futuri sumper, qui Ecclesiæ amicum hospitium præbitu- ri sint, vicissim a Deo benedicendi. Tertia Hostium eversio. Et maledicam maledicentibus Quarta & postrema, sed dignitate & naturæ ordine prima reli- quarum causa & scaturigo est universæ terræ in Messia benedictio. Quam explicat Hieropsaltes Ps. 72, 17. Petrus Act. 3, 25. & imprimis S. Paulus Gal. 3, 8. 16. Grotius sensu proprio & immediato videtur de Abra- hamo intellexisse, uti imprimis ex Annot. ad Gen. 18, 18. apparet: tametsi velit, de Abrahamo illa dici, quod ex ipso procreandus sit is, per quem benedictio sit. Ideoque per pronomen TE Abrahamum intelligit. Sed interpretatio divina omni exceptione superior est cum locis designatis, tum in ipsa Genesi, partim ad Abrahamum ipsummet facta Gen. 22, 18. IN SE- MINE TUO; partim ad Isaacum Gen. 26, 4. & ad Jacobum repetita Gen. 28, 14. Quo postremo loco præfixum Vav ἐξηγητικῶς accipiendum: Benedicen- tur in TE omnes familiæ terræ, &, id est, in SEMINE TUO. S. Apost. Gal. 3, 8. seqq. adeo cavit, ne per il- lud pronomen TE in προτευαγγελίῳ Abrahamo promulgato Gen. 12, 18. alius, quam Christus in- telligatur, ut promissiones illas Abrahæ, Isaaco & Jacobo, etsi diversimodis temporibus factas, pro iisdem omnino habuerit, & ad illam Jocobeam pe- culiariter digitum intendisse appareat; inde enim verba καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σε, ob particulam copulativam καὶ, repeti videntur. Non dicit ET IN SEMINIBUS, ut in multis, sed ut in uno. Et in Semine tuo, qui est Christus. Quapropter retineri potest usitatus præpositionis ב sensus, IN TE. Verum ut in Abrahamo non immediate, vel in persona Abrahami, sed mediate, vel in semine Abrahami benedictio obtingat. Non ergo opus est, præpositionem IN explicare PER, quum in Christo dicatur benedictio obtingere, ut sciamus, eum non esse tantum instrumentalem vel meritoriam, sed etiam efficientem & formalem causam, ita ut justitia nostra non sit in nobis, sed extra nos in Christo: Vid. Es. 45, 17. 24. Jer. 23, 16. unde Abraham agnoscere potuit, justitiam & benedictionem non esse in se aut aliis, sed in semine suo: uti monuit B. Polyc. Lyserus in c. 22, Gen. Ita, quod ad verba, reddidit Targum Hierosolymit. Benedicentur in justitia tua omnes gentes. Effectus, benedictio exprimitur & in Niphal benedicentur; & in Hithpael benedictas ducent se: sensumque eximie hic expressit B. Cramerus noster Class. I. Schol. Proph. p. 42. Totum genus humanum commoritur plane in extrema maledictione, sub qua misere abjectum est propter peccata per legis rigorem: Itaque ego illius misertus sum, & sum pollicitus semen mulieris, quod conculcaturum est caput serpentis: quam promissionem nunc iterum repeto, & certo designo tuam gentem, ex qua semen illud prodibit: Unde emanabit benedictio, quæ pertinebit ex æquo ad omnes gentes. Quam benedictionem quicunque acceperint fide, non manebunt amplius sub maledictione, sed in benedicto hoc semine erunt ipsi quoque & benedicti & sibi benedicentes. Sed confirmatum plenius hunc oraculi divini sensum vide sis apud dictos Theologos, nec non apud Dn. D. Walth. in Spongia Mosaïc. p. 408. seqq.

## 12:5
v. 5. THE SOULS WHICH THEY HAD GOTTEN IN HARAN) The slaves which they had acquired for themselves. Thus Apoc. 18, 13. ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων, servants, whom later Greek called ψυχάρια. V. 8. BETHEL) A prolepsis, such as are many in these books. See below 28. v. 19. HAVING BETHEL ON THE WEST) And he prayed to God toward that place, so that he might depart as far as possible from the custom of the Chaldeans, who superstitiously worshipped the rising Sun. Conversely, Christians prayed turned toward the East to express certain passages of Scripture dealing with Christ, and also to distinguish themselves from the Jews. V. 11. I KNOW THAT THOU ART FAIR) Thus also the Greeks, omitting that הנה נא, which is for the sake of gaining an audience for oneself. Therefore the Hebrews wrongly infer from these words that Sarah was untouched by Abraham before that time. You may more correctly note the burdensome baggage for a traveler, a beautiful woman. AND THE PRINCES TOLD PHARAOH) As courtiers are wont to seek favor for themselves with Kings even by pimping. Moreover, the name of Pharaoh remained for the Kings of Egypt until the times of Ezekiel, whom see 32, 2. Perhaps hence the island of Pharos: A common name among Herodotus is given to one, φέρω. This name is written also Φαραώθης and Φερεθώνης. Grotius should have corrected the Vulgate here. For the fountains of Hebrew truth, with which the LXX agree, have it thus: The Egyptians saw that she was very fair, and the Princes of Pharaoh also saw her, and praised her before Pharaoh. Nor is there any room for that interpretation: And the Princes told Pharaoh, because these names are placed in construction, and therefore they ought to be rendered the Princes of Pharaoh.

Latin:

v. 5. ANIMAS QVAS FECERANT IN HARAN) Mancipia quæ sibi comparaverant. Sic Apoc. 18, 13. ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων, servi, quos posterior Græcia ψυχάρια vocavit. V. 8. BETHEL) Πρόληψις, quales multæ in his libris. Vide infra 28. v. 19. AB OCCIDENTE HABENS BETHEL) Et ad eum locum versus Deum orabat, ut quam longissime discederet a more Chaldæorum, qui Solem orientem superstitiose venerabantur. Contra Christiani ad Orientem versi orabant ad exprimenda loca quædam Scripturæ de Christo agentia, tum & ut a Judæis se discernerent. V. 11. NOVI QVOD PULCHRA SIS) Sic & Græci omisso illo הנה נא, quod audientiam sibi conciliantis est. Male ergo ex his verbis Hebræi colligunt Saram ante id tempus intactam Abrahamo. Rectius notes molestam peregrinanti sarcinam formosam mulierem. ET NUNCIAVERUNT PRINCIPES PHARAONI) Ut solent aulici etiam lenocinio gratiam sibi Regum quærere. Pharaonis autem nomen Ægypti Regibus mansit ad tempora Ezechielis, quem vide 32, 2. Forte hinc insula Pharos: Commune nomen apud Herodotum uni datur φέρω. Scribitur hoc nomen & Φαραώθης & Φερεθώνης. Corrigere hic Vulgatam debuisset Grotius. Fontes enim Ebraicæ veritatis, quibus congruunt LXX. ita habent: Viderunt Ægyptii, quod pulchra esset valde, & viderunt eam etiam Principes Pharaonis, & laudaverunt eam coram Pharaone. Nec vero locus est illi interpretationi: Et nunciaverunt Principes Pharaoni, quia in constructione posita sunt hæc nomina, ideoque reddi debent Principes Pharaonis.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. Returning from Egypt he separates himself from Lot, and dwells in Canaan. The divine promises are repeated to him.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. Ex Ægypto redux a Loto se separat, & in Canaan habitat. Iterantur ei promissiones divinæ.

## 13:7
Vers. 7. HENCE THERE WAS STRIFE BETWEEN THE HERDSMEN) Dicaearchus in Porphyry IV. on Abstinence, where he describes the most ancient life of herdsmen: for there were already notable possessions existing. Some made it a point of honor to be drawn out, gathering together, and encouraging one another, others to preserve them. Musonius says that the pastoral life is most suitable for a Philosopher.

Strifes arose from there, because each party claimed the better and richer pastures for their own flocks. But at the same time, the envy of the Canaanites and Perizzites, the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, was added. But that the land of Canaan could not support the family of Lot and Abram, which the Israelites bore in a huge number 1 Chron. 21, 5, is to be understood of that part of that land which they themselves inhabited, since the remaining parts had been occupied by the Canaanites themselves.

V. the same. CANAANITE, AND PERIZZITE.

That is, the Canaanites, and Perizzites, of whom mention is made, even though more peoples lived there, because Abraham lived among the former, and Lot among the latter.

Latin:

Vers. 7. UNDE FACTA EST RIXA INTER PA- STORES) Dicæarchus apud Porphyrium IV. de Absti- nentia, ubi vetustissimam pastorum vitam describit: ἤδη γὰρ ἀξιόλογα κτήματα ἧν ὑπάρχοντα. οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ τὸ παρελκεσθαι φιλοτιμίαν ἐποιοῦντο, ἀθροιζόμενοί τε, κὰὶ παρακαλοῦντες ἀλλήλους, οἱ δ᾽ ἐπὶ τὸ διαφυλάξαι. Musonius maxime ait convenire Phi- losopho vitam pastoralem.

RIxæ oriebantur inde, quia utraque pars melio- ra, & uberiora pascua gregibus suis vindica- bat. Accedebat autem simul invidia Cananæorum & Perizzæorum, incolarum terræ Canaan. Quod vero terra Canaan ferre non potuerit Lothi & Abræ familiam, quæ Israelites ingenti numero tulit 1. Par. 21, 5. intelligendum est de illa parte illius terræ, quam ipsi inhabitabant, quum reliquæ par- tes ab ipsis Cananæis occupatæ fuerint.

V. eod. CANANÆUS, ET PERIZÆUS.

Id est, Cananæi, & Perisæi, quorum solum men- tio sit, etsi plures ibi populi habitarint, quia inter illos Abraham, inter hos Loth habitabat.

## 13:9
Vers. 9. BEHOLD THE WHOLE LAND IS BEFORE THEE) Let the greater divide: let the lesser choose: an old law.

IF TO THE LEFT) That is, to the North.

TO THE RIGHT) That is, towards the south. Thus the Chaldean, following a mode of speech familiar to the Hebrews and their neighbors. For they were not Aristotelians, for whom the sunrise is the right, the sunset the left, the South Pole above, and the North Pole below. But Plutarch in his Isis teaches us that for the Egyptians the northern regions were the right, the southern the left: the eastern the front: the western the back.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ECCE UNIVERSA TERRA CORAM TE EST) Major dividat: minor eligat: lex vetus.

SI AD SINISTRAM) Id est, ad Septentrionem.

AD DEXTRAM) Id est meridiem versus. Ita Chal- dæus, ex familiari Hebræis & eorum vicinis locutioni. Non enim illi erant Aristotelici, quibus ortus est dextrum, occasus sinistrum, Polus australis sursum, septentrionalis deorsum. At Ægyptiis Septentrionalia fuisse dextra docet nos in Iside Plutarchus, Australis læva: Orientalia ante- riora: Occidentalia posteriora.

## 13:10
Ver. 10. AS THE GARDEN OF THE LORD) As Mesopotamia. For this and Egypt are lands of exceptional fertility.

In the Hebrew, as the garden of the Lord, i.e., which the Lord had prepared for Adam: that is, as Paradise, Gen. 2:8. For just as that was irrigated by rivers, and was most fertile and most pleasant, so too was this whole Pentapolitan region of the Jordan, especially from that place in which Abram was, going towards Zoar, irrigated, fertile, and pleasant.

Latin:

Vers. 10. SICUT PARADISUS DOMINI) Sicut Meso- potamia. Hæc enim & Ægyptus terræ sunt fœcunditatis eximiæ.

In Ebræo sicut hortus Domini, sc. quem Do- minus Adamo instruxerat: h. e. sicut Paradisus, Gen. 2, 8. Ut enim ille a fluminibus irrigabatur, & fœcundissimus, ac amœnissimus erat, ita & tota ista Regio Jordanis Pentapolitana, maxime a loco illo, in quo erat Abram, eundo versus Seghor irri- gua fuit, fœcunda, & amœna.

## 13:11
Ver. 11. FROM THE EAST) So also the Greeks ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν. But it should be noted that the particle מן is often used by the Hebrews for the preposition towards: as above 11:8, 1 Sam. 14:5, 2 Sam. 2:2, when compared with this other passage 1 Chron. 13:6.

Therefore translate that מקדם as: into the region situated to the east with respect to the land of Canaan, in which Abram dwelt. But because the plain, into which Lot was withdrawing, also belonged to the land of Canaan, one must understand specifically that part of Canaan which the Canaanites, specifically so called among the seven peoples, inhabited.

Latin:

Vers. 11. AB ORIENTE) Sic & Græci ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν. Sed notandum, particulam מן Hebræis sæpe poni pro præ- positione versus: ut supra 11, 8. 1. Sam. 14, 5. 2. Sam. 2, 2. collato huic loco altero 1. Par. 13, 6.

Illud מקדם ergo redde: in regionem sitam ab oriente respectu terræ Canaan, in qua habitavit Abram. Quia vero etiam planities, in quam Loth concedebat, ad terram Canaan pertinebat, intelli- genda est speciatim illa Cananææ pars, quam Ca- nanæi ἐιδικῶς sic inter septem populos dicti inha- bitarunt.

## 13:16
Ver. 16. AS THE DUST OF THE EARTH) So the Greeks ὅση κόνις & ψαμμακόσια.

It is not precisely indicated by this that the seed of Abraham will be multiplied according to the number of the dust of the earth: lest anyone imagine a hyperbole: but just as the dust of the earth can be counted by no man, even if it is not absolutely innumerable, so the multitude of Abraham's posterity will be such that it can be comprehended or explained by no mortal in a certain number.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SICUT PULVEREM TERRÆ) Sic Græci ὅση κόνις & ψαμμακόσια.

Non id præcise indigitatur, semen Abrahæ secundum numerum pulveris terræ multiplicatum iri: ne quis hyperbolen fingat: sed sicuti a nullo ho- minum terræ pulvis numerari potest, etiamsi abso- lute innumerabilis non sit, ita eam fore posterita- tis Abrahæ multitudinem, quæ a nemine morta- lium certo numero comprehendi, vel explicari queat.

## 13:17
Ver. 17. ARISE AND WALK THROUGH THE LAND) Take possession by way of declaration. Possession is signified by walking, l. possideri, §. 1. de acq. poss.

It had to be proven that it is accepted in this way not in law, but in Scripture. It was not possession, but rather a survey of the land that was to be made by walking through it. Nor should one imagine here, with Pererius, that God or an angel presented an image of the whole land to his eyes. He could both walk through a great part of it, and look around at it from some mountain, so that by both means he might recognize the goodness of that land.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SURGE ET PERAMBULA TERRAM) Dicis causa possessionem sume. Possessio ambulando significatur l. possideri, §. 1. de acq. poss.

Probandum erat, non in jure, sed in Scriptu- ra ita accipi. Non possessio, sed lustratio potius terræ fieri debebat perambulando. Neque hic fingendum cum Pererio est, Deum vel angelum imaginem totius terræ oculis ejus objecisse. Potuit & magnam partem perambulare, & e monte ali- quo eandem circumspicere, ut utraque ratione ter- ræ istius bonitatem præcognosceret.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

Abram succors the Sodomites after they are defeated and Lot is taken captive. Having been brought back from the victory, he gives tithes to Melchizedek, and having received a blessing from him, he returns everything to the King of Sodom.

v. 1. ARIOCH KING OF PONTUS) Thus Aquila. In Hebrew אלסר, which seem to be the Elisar in Arabia named by Ptolemy.

Elisar is a city of Coele-Syria. Amraphel is King of Sennaar, that is, of Babylon, Gen. 9, 2, whom Jonathan calls Nimrod, others call him Ninias, the fourth from him, from whom Justin begins the history of Trogus Pompeius. Therefore Josephus called this the war of the Assyrians. Kedarlaomer is King of the Elamites, that is, of the Persians, Gen. 10, 24. Thideal is called King of the nations. B. Luther understands the inhabitants of the Mediterranean Sea: others understand Upper Galilee, which was called of the Nations. Epiphanius, in Heresy LV, wishes this war against the kings of the pentapolis to have been waged in the 88th year of Abraham's age. Others refer it to about the 82nd year, and that more correctly.

v. same. KING OF THE ELAMITES) See above XI, 22, and the notes by us on the book concerning the truth of the Christian Religion.

KING OF THE NATIONS) That is, of the gathered people, to which the Greek word placed here by Symmachus, παμφυλίας, corresponds. I should think, however, that these gathered people were in Syria Palestine, where Galilee was later, and that by the argument of the passage in Joshua 12, 23. Add what is at Matthew 5, 14. See how old it is for greater kings to make trouble for lesser ones, as whales do to fish.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV.

Sodomitis devictis & Loto captivo fuccurrit Abram. Latus de victoria decimas Melchi-sedeco dat, & ab eo benedictione accepta cun-cta Regi Sodomorum reddit.

v.1. ARIOCH REX PONTI) Ita Aquila. In Hebr. אלסר, qui videntur esse Elifari in Arabia Ptolemæo nominati.

ELisar urbs Cælo Syriæ est. Amraphel Rex Se-near, id est, Babylonis Gen. 9, 2. est, quem Jo-nathan Nimrodum, alii quartum ab ipso Niniam, a quo Justinus Historiam Trogi Pompeji orditur, dicunt. Ideo bellum hoc Assyriorum vocavit Jo-sephus. Kedarlaomor Rex Elamitarum, id est, Per-sarum est Gen. 10, 24. Thideal Rex gentium dici-tur. B. Lutherus maris mediterranei accolas intelli-git: alii Galilææ superioris, quæ dicta est Gentium. Bellum hoc adversus Reges πενταπόλεως anno 88. ætatis Abrahæ Epiphanius gestum vult Hæref. LV. Alii id referunt ad annum 82. circiter, idque rectius.

vers. eod. REX ELAMITARUM) Vide supra XI, 22. & annotata a nobis ad librum de veritate Religionis Christianæ.

REX GENTIVM) Id est convenarum, cui respondet vox Græca hic a Symmacho posita, παμφυλίας. Putem autem hos convenas fuisse in Syria Palæstina, ubi Galilæa postea, idque argumento loci Josuæ 12, 23. Adde quæ ad Matth. 5, 14. Vide quam vetus sit reges majores minoribus negotium facere, ut balænæ faciunt piscibus.

## 14:3
v. 3. SALT SEA) Thus Plutarch concerning another land in his book on the virtues of men and women: "the whole plain blossomed with salt and was utterly destroyed, the earth having become bitter." Compare Deut. 29, 23.

Latin:

v. 3. MARE SALIS) Sic Plutarchus de alia terra in li-bro de virtutibus virorum & mulierum. πᾶν τὸ πεδίον ἐξήν-θησεν ἁλμυρίδα καὶ διέφθαρτο παντάπασι τῆς γῆς πικρᾶς γενο-μένης. Confer Deut. 29, 23.

## 14:4
v. 4. THEY DEPARTED FROM HIM) Weary of servitude.

Latin:

v. 4. RECESSERVNT AB EO) Pertæsi servitutis.

## 14:5
v. 5. REPHAIM) The Greeks [translate] "the giants": the Chaldean [translates] "the mighty ones." See above VI, 4. These were men who practiced robbery, such as those Arabs and Chaldeans in Job 1.

ZUZIM) From the Hebrew, as we now read it זוזים. But the LXX read עזוזים "strong nations."

WITH THEM) בהם. Thus also the Greeks [translate] "together with them." The Chaldean, however, took it as the name of a place, and brought it out in the Syrian manner with a prolonged ending, בהמתא.

Latin:

vers. 5. RAPHAJM) Græci τές γίγαντας : Chaldæus גבריא. Vide supra VI, 4. Erant hi homines latrocinantes, quales illi Arabes & Chaldæi Job. 1.

ZUZIM) Ex Hebræo, ut nos nunc legimus זוזים At LXX. legerunt עזוזים ἔθνη ἰσχυρά.

CUM EIS) בהם. Sic & Græci ἅμα ἀυτοῖς. Chaldæus autem ut nomen loci accepit, & Syriacum in morem pro-ducta terminatione extulit בהמתא.

## 14:6
v. 6. TO THE PLAINS OF PHARAN) Which is believed to have been the later seat of Job.

Latin:

vers. 6. AD CAMPESTRIA PHARAN) Quæ sedes postea Jobi fuisse creditur.

## 14:7
v. 7. TO THE SPRING OF MISPHAT) At which judgments were exercised among neighbors: the Hebrew word sounds like this, and thus the Chaldean and Rabbi Solomon interpret it.

Latin:

v. 7. AD FONTEM MISPATH) Apud quem judicia inter vicinos exercebantur: id sonat vox Hebræa, & sic in-terpretantur Chaldæus & Rabbi Salomo.

## 14:13
vers. 13. AND BEHOLD ONE WHO HAD ESCAPED,) From the battle, of course, as in Job 1:15 and 17. The LXX: one of those who had been saved; Symmachus: one of those who had fled. But the Rabbis, men too often ridiculous, say that this was Og the giant, saved from the flood by the benefit of his size, from whose descendants was that Og mentioned in Num. 21:33 and elsewhere.

vers. eod. ABRAM THE HEBREW) The Greeks well [translate it] as the passer-by, Aquila as the passer-through. For the name is not from Eber, as many think, since so many other ancestors had intervened, but Abraham was so called by the Canaanites and their neighbors because he had come from the regions across the Euphrates.

Grotius notes here again, Not from Eber, since other ancestors had intervened; but that he was so called by the Canaanites because he had come from the regions across the Euphrates. What is to be thought of this, we have observed at Chapter 11, 1. He was called [Hebrew] from Eber, even though others intervene, because the language of Eber was preserved in his family, from which they named the Hebrew himself. Therefore, one should not look here to the Greek translation, which has 'passer-by', any more than to the premonition of Moses in Gen. 10:2, that Shem was the father of all the sons of Eber, who consequently received both their denomination and their language from him.

THEY HAD STRUCK A COVENANT WITH ABRAHAM) Many heads of families were then autonomous.

Latin:

vers. 13. ET ECCE UNUS QUI EVASERAT,) Ex prælio scilicet, ut Job. 1, 15. & 17. LXX. τῶν ἀνασωθέντων τις: Symmachus τῶν διαφυγόντων. At Rabbini, homines nimis sæpe ridiculi, hunc ajunt fuisse Ogum gigantem bene-ficio magnitudinis suæ servatum e diluvio, e cujus posteris fuerit ille Ogus memoratus Num. 21, 33. & alibi.

vers. eod. ABRAM EBRÆO) Bene Græci τῷ περάτῃ Aquila περαΐτῃ. Non enim, ut multi existimant, ab Hebero id nomen, cum tot alii Parentes intercessissent, sed ita dictus Cananæis, eorumque vicinis Abraham, quod ex locis Trans-euphratensibus venisset.

Notat hic iterum Grotius, Non ab Ebero, quum alii parentes intercesserint; sed quod ex locis trans - Euphratensibus venisset, Cenanæis ita dictum esse. Quid de eo habendum, ad Cap. 11, 1. observa-vimus. Dictus est ab Ebero, etsi alii intercedunt, quia Eberi lingua in familia ejus conservabatur, a qua Ebræum ipsum nuncupabant. Non ergo ad Græcam hic translationem, quæ περάτη habet, ma-gis, quam ad Mofis præmonitionem Gen. 10, 2. quod Sem Pater omnium filiorum Eber fuerit, qui ab ipso proinde & denominationem & linguam acceperunt, respiciendum.

PEPIGERANT FOEDVS CVM ABRAHAM) Multi tum Patresfamilias erant ἀυτόνομοι.

## 14:17
v. 17. IN THE VALLEY OF SHAVEH) Where the King and the Princes exercised themselves. For 'Shaveh' is also translated as 'to be made fit'. This meeting is a sign of honor.

Those three men, Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner, were confederates of Abraham, from which some conclude that it was lawful to enter into covenants with men of a different religion, which, if necessity urges, and the covenants are for just defense against common enemies, or for non-aggression between the confederates, or for protecting borders, but not for harming neighbors, for preserving public peace, for mutual commerce, and apart from the communion of infidelity for purely political reasons, from which no danger to religion is to be feared, is not to be disapproved. Nor is it certain, however, that those three men, even if they were Amorite idolaters, could not have been converted to the true God, which seems likely, because otherwise they would have either joined themselves to Abraham, who was opposing powerful enemies with a small band, or would have offered themselves to be led.

Latin:

v. 17. IN VALLE SAVE) Ubi Rex & Principes se exer-cebant. שוה enim etiam καταρτίζεσθαι vertitur. Hic occur-sus honoris signum.

Tres illi viri Mamre, Escol & Haner fœdera-ti erant Abrahami, unde colligunt nonnulli, lici-tum fuisse cum diversæ religionis hominibus fœ-dera inire, quod si urgeat necessitas, & fœdera sint justæ defensionis adversus hostes communes, vel non offensionis inter fœderatos, aut de finibus tuen- dis, sed non lædendis proximis, de pace publica conservanda, de mutuis commerciis, & citra com- munionem infidelitatis ob rationes solum politicas, e quibus religioni nullum metuendum periculum, improbandum non est. Neque tamen certum est, tres istos viros, etsi Amoreos idololatras fuisse, cum potuerint ad verum Deum conversi es- se, quod verisimile videtur, quia alioquin Abraha- mo exigua manu potentibus hostibus sese oppo- nenti, se aut conjunxissent, aut ducendos præ- buissent.

## 14:18
vers. 18. BRINGING FORTH BREAD AND WINE) He brought forth bread and wine. To Abraham, of course: he gave food to Abraham and his army, as Josephus and Rabbi Solomon interpret here: and Rabbi Samuel cited in Bereshith Rabba. For it is the custom of neighbors to do this. Deut. 23:4, Jud. 8:5, 6, 15. Thus Epiphanius and Ambrose explain it; and they refer that [passage] about the Priesthood of Melchizedek to what follows, not to what precedes. Nor is the opinion improbable that this act preceded the sacrifice: Philo says he offered a victory sacrifice. For even an offering of fine flour is called 'Mincha' by the Hebrews and 'thusia' by the Greeks, Levit. 2, as explained at length by us at Mark 9:49, and it is the custom of all nations to pour out wine before a meal to God. See what [is written] below at chapter 44.

Grotius admits that these things were brought forth to Abraham, not offered to God; for the refreshment of the Patriarch, not for the sake of a sacrifice. And he confirms this. He gave food to Abraham and his army, as Josephus and Rabbi Solomon interpret here; and R. Samuel cited in Bereshith Rabba. For it is the custom of neighbors to do this, Deut. 23:4, Jud. 8:5, 6, 15. Thus Epiphanius and Ambrose: and they refer that [passage] about the Priesthood of Melchizedek to what follows, not to what precedes. Although these things are manifest, Grotius nevertheless wished to help the Papists with some 'wise medicine'. Yet he says, the opinion is not improbable that this act preceded the sacrifice: Philo says he offered a victory sacrifice. For even an offering of fine flour is called 'Mincha' by the Hebrews and 'thusia' by the Greeks, Lev. 2, and it is the custom of all nations to pour out wine before a meal to God. Moses does not hint by a single word that a sacrifice preceded. This is therefore purely precarious, nay, fictitious. Nor is fine flour or anything used in a Mincha signified here by bread, but whatever contributes to sustenance and the quenching of hunger, as the Hebrews are accustomed to designate these things by bread, Gen. 18:5, 6, c. 33:31, c. 49:20, Is. 58:7. For it is not likely that Melchizedek brought forth only bread, from which this act [was done] not only for the refreshment of the soldiers, but also for the sake of congratulation and to testify to his joy; just as gifts were accustomed to be presented to victors. But as for the fact that pouring out wine before a meal to God was accepted among the nations, what has this to do with Melchizedek? Who was neither accustomed to the rites of idolatrous nations, nor did he meet Abraham for the purpose of offering wine to God, but to honor and bless him with such a gift. That act was one of Royal munificence; not, however, of priestly offering. And therefore Josephus calls these 'xenia' (gifts of hospitality) brought by Melchizedek to the army of Abraham, book Antiquities, chapter 2, and he has nothing about an offering in the Vulgate, but uses the verb 'to bring forth', which is not sacrificial. Most believe that Melchizedek was Shem, Cajetan, Tostatus, Torniellus, and others. But Shem would not have offered in the manner of the nations, but of other Patriarchs, who are nowhere read to have offered bread and wine. Nor indeed would the Epistle to the Hebrews have omitted the sacrificial act in its long comparison of Melchizedek with Christ in chapter VII, if one had preceded: since it brings forward other acts of the Priesthood, and is primarily occupied in explaining that. Grotius seems to have drawn this fiction from Corn. Lap. the Jesuit, who likewise it is conjectured that Melchizedek sacrificed, by burning part of the bread and pouring out part of the wine. But even if this were admitted to the greatest extent (although it ought not to be admitted), it would contribute nothing at all to transubstantiation or the Papal sacrifice, since it would rather, together with the use of one kind, utterly overturn it; for in that way not the transubstantiated body of Christ, but bread according to the type of Melchizedek ought to be offered, and not only bread, but the use of wine also ought to be granted in the holy Supper. If victims were slaughtered by Melchizedek, as Philo hints, what will the Papists gain from the type of bread and wine?

verse same. FOR HE WAS A PRIEST OF THE MOST HIGH GOD.) Virg. III. Aen. King Anius, king also of men and priest of Phoebus. Where Servius: Indeed this was the custom of the ancients, that a king should also be a priest or pontiff. Hence the house in which the pontiff lived was called the royal house, as the same Servius teaches on the eighth book of the Aeneid, who also often notes that all priestly rights are attributed to Aeneas by Virgil.

Latin:

vers. 18. PROFERENS PANEM ET VINVM) Ἐξή- νεγκεν ἄρτυς καὶ οἶνον. Abrahamo scilicet : alimenta dedit Abrahamo exercituique ejus, ut hic interpretatur Josephus & Rabbi Salomo: & Rabbi Samuel citatus in Bereschith Rab- ba. Id enim facere mos finitimis. Deut. 23, 4. Jud. 8, 5. 6. 15. Sic explicant Epiphanius & Ambrosius ; referuntque illud de Sacerdotio Melchisedeci ad sequentia, non ad præcedentia. Neque tamen improbabilis sententia, factum hoc sacrificio præcedente : ἐπινίκια ἔθυε ait Philo. Nam & e simila obla- tio Hebræis מנחה, Græcis ϑυσία dicitur Levit. 2. ut late explicatum a nobis ad Marc. 9, 49. & vinum ante mensam Deo libare mos omnium gentium. Vide quæ infra ad cap. 44.

Fatetur Grotius hæc Abrahamo prolata, non Deo oblata esse; in refectionem Patriarchæ, non sa- crificii causa. Idque confirmat. Alimenta dedit Abrahamo exercituique ejus, ut hic interpretatur Jo- sephus, & Rabbi Salomoh; & R. Samuel citatus in Bereschith Rabba. Id enim facere mos finitimis Deut. 23, 4. Jud. 8, 5. 6. 15. Sic Epiphanius & Am- brosius : referuntque illud de Sacerdotio Melchisedeci ad sequentia, non ad præcedentia. Quanquam ve- ro hæc manifesta sunt, juvare tamen voluit Grotius Papistas aliquo σοφῷ Φαρμάκῳ. Neque tamen, in- quit, improbabilis sententia, factum hoc sacrificio præcedenti : ἐπινίκιον ἔθυε ait Philo. Nam & e simila oblatio Hebreis מנחה Græcis ϑυσία dicitur Lev. 2. & vinum ante mensam Deo libare mos omnium gen- tium. Præcessisse sacrificium nullo verbulo Moses innuit. Mere ergo precarium hoc, imo com- mentitium. Neque per panem hic simila aut quic- quid in Mincha adhibetur, sed quicquid ad vi- ctum, famemque sedandam facit, significatur, uti so- lent Ebræi ea per panem designare, Gen. 18, 5. 6. c. 33, 31. c. 49, 20. Es. 58, 7. Non enim verisimile est, Melchisedechum solum tantum panem protu- lisse, a quo factum hoc non ad refectionem solum militum, sed & ad gratulationem & lætitiæ suæ con- testandæ gratia; quemadmodum victoribus mu- nera exhiberi consuevere. Quod autem vinum ante mensam Deo libare penes gentes receptum, quid hoc ad Melchisedechum? qui neque gentium idololatricarum ritibus assuetus, neque Deo vi- num offerendi causa Abrahamo obviam factus, sed ipsum munere tali mactandi & benedicendi. Actus ille erat Regalis munificentiæ; non autem sacerdotalis oblationis. Ideoque Josephus hæc ξένια dicit exercitui Abrahami a Melchisedecho de- lata, lib. Antiqu. cap. 2. neque de oblatione Vul- gata quicquam habet, sed verbo proferendi utitur, quod sacrificiale non est. Credunt plerique, Melchisedechum Semum fuisse, Cajetanus, Tosta- tus, Torniellus, alii. Sem autem non more gen- tium, sed aliorum Patriarcharum obtulisset, qui nuspiam leguntur panem & vinum obtulisse. Nec sane prætermisisset Epistola ad Ebræos in prolixa comparatione Melchisedeci cum Christo c. VII. actum sacrificialem, si aliquis antecessisset: quum alios actus Sacerdotii adducat, & in eodem explican- do imprimis occupetur. Hausisse hoc commentum videtur Grotius a Corn. Lap. Jesuita, qui pariter su- spicatur sacrificasse Melchisedecum, partem panis cremando & partem vini libando. Quod vero si ma- xime admitteretur, (quanquam admittendum non fit) nihil omnino ad transsubstantiationem vel sa- crificium Papale faceret, quum id potius una cum unius speciei usu prorsus evertat; siquidem ita non corpus Christi transsubstantiatum, sed panis juxta typum Melchisedeci offerri deberet, neque panis solum, sed & vini usus in sacra Cœna concedendus esset. Si victimæ mactatæ a Melchisedecho, quod Philo innuit, quid e panis & vini typo lucrabuntur Papistæ?

vers. eod. SACERDOS ENIM ERAT DEI ALTISSI- MI.) Virg. III. Æn. Rex Anius, rex idem hominum Phœbique sacerdos. Ubi Servius: Sane majorum hæc erat consuetudo, ut rex esset etiam sacerdos vel pontifex. Hinc domus in qua ponti- fex habitabat, regia dicebatur, docente eodem Servio ad VIII. Æneidos, qui & sæpe notat a Virgilio omnia jura sa- cerdotalia tribui Æneæ.

## 14:20
BY WHOSE PROTECTION YOUR ENEMIES ARE IN YOUR HANDS) Melchizedek therefore believed no less than Abraham in one God, as powerful over arms and war as He is over heaven and earth.

Grotius ought to have corrected the Vulgate here: because it added a causal particle of its own. But from it the Papists deduce the sacrifice of Melchizedek: whom he favors in this, as I have already warned. Moreover, the causal is not found in the original text: it is said; And he was a priest of the most high. Nor did the preceding act pertain to his priesthood, but to the royal munificence which a friend was showing to a victorious friend. The blessing, however, which is mentioned next, is an act of the priestly office. Therefore Cajetan ingenuously warns that the Vulgate edition in this place departs from the Hebrew text, which reads thus: And he was a Priest of the Most High, and he blessed him. For he adds (these are the words of the Cardinal) the priestly dignity to the royal dignity and liberality, etc. The same was also observed by Jerome ab Oleastro, and also by Vatablus, whose words deserve to be written down here from the annotations on this passage. Melchizedek brought out bread and wine, i.e., he refreshed the weary and hungry army with royal liberality. For it is not to be explained, as is commonly done, that he himself brought out bread and wine in order to offer them to God in thanksgiving, because he was a Priest. For he says two things, which must necessarily be distinguished, that Melchizedek himself was King and Priest. Because he was King, he received Abraham and his companions with hospitality, and fed them with bread and wine; by the name of bread understand every kind of food. But because he was Priest, he blessed by right of a Priest and received tithes from him. Now this was an ancient custom, that those who were kings should at the same time perform the priesthood. Compare on this passage B. Helvicus, Vindication of the most important passages of the Old Testament, and B. Hutter on the sacrifice of the Mass.

It is too meager, what he says about Melchizedek, that he believed no less than Abraham in one God of heaven and earth. For even the Gentiles, destitute of divine revelation, know that. But that Melchizedek was endowed with true faith is not to be doubted at all, since he is celebrated as a Priest of the Most High, and stood as a notable figure and type of Christ, as the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies.

Latin:

QVO PROTEGENTE HOSTES IN MANIBVS TVIS SVNT) Credidit ergo Melchisedecus non minus quam Ab- rahamus unum Deum, ut cœli & terræ, ita & armorum ac belli potentem.

Castigare hic Vulgatam debuisset Grotius: quod particulam causalem de suo addiderit. Sed ex ea Papistæ sacrificium Melchisedeci deducunt: quibus in eo favet, uti jam monui. Cæterum non habetur in originali textu causalis: dicitur; Et erat sacerdos altissimi. Nec ad sacerdotium ejus actus præcedens pertinebat, sed ad regiam munificentiam, quam amicus amico victori exhibebat. Benedictio autem, quæ deinceps commemoratur, actus est Sa- cerdotalis muneris. Ideo ingenue monet Cajeta- nus, vulgatam editionem hoc loco discedere a textu Hebræo, qui sic habet: Et ipse erat Sacerdos Altissi- mi, & benedixit ei. Adjungit siquidem regiæ digni- tati (verba sunt Cardinalis) ac liberalitati Sacer- dotalem dignitatem &c. Idem etiam observatum Hieronymo ab Oleastro, nec non Vatablo, cujus ver- ba hic adscribi merentur ex annot. ad h. l. Melchi- sedecus protulit panem & vinum, i. e. lassum & fa- melicum exercitum Regia liberalitate refecit. Neque enim exponendum est, ut vulgo, ipsum protulisse pa- nem & vinum, ut offerret Deo in gratiarum actio- nem, quod Sacerdos esset. Nam duo dicit, quæ ne- cessario distingui debent, ipsum Melchisedech fuisse Regem, & Sacerdotem. Quod esset Rex, Abra- ham ac comites ejus hospitio excepit, atque aluit pane & vino; panis nomine intellige omne cibi genus. Quod autem Sacerdos, benedixit jure Sacerdotis & decimas ab eo recepit. Vetus autem hic mos fuit, ut, qui reges erant, simul sacerdotio fungerentur. Confer. de hoc loco B. Helvic. vindic. locor. potissim. V. T. & B. Hutterus de Miss. sacrific.

Nimis exile est, quod de Melchisedecho ait, credidisse ipsum non minus quam Abrahamum unum Deum cœli & terræ. Nam id norunt etiam gentiles revelatione divina destituti. Vera autem fide præditum fuisse Melchisedecum, minime dubitan- dum est, cum ut Sacerdos Altissimi celebretur, & insignis figura ac typus Christi extiterit, teste Epi- stola ad Ebræos.

## 14:22
verse 22. I LIFT UP MY HAND) The gesture of those swearing.

Latin:

vers. 22. LEVO MANUM MEAM) Gestus jurantium.

## 14:23
verse 23. I WILL NOT TAKE FROM ALL THAT IS THINE, LEST THOU SAY: I HAVE MADE ABRAHAM RICH.) Similar is the spirit of Cato the Elder, in whose life Plutarch says: he says that nothing of the captured goods came to him, except what he drank or ate; and I do not blame, he says, those who seek to profit from these things, but I wish rather to vie with the best in virtue than with the wealthiest in money. Such also before Cato was Timoleon, who, as the same Plutarch narrates, judged: it is not shameful to take from such things, but it is better not to take, and the abundance of virtue is shown in those things which one is permitted to have, by needing nothing. And before him Pittacus of Mitylene, of whom Valerius Maximus VI. 1 says: when half of the recovered land was offered to him by the consent of all, he turned his mind away from that gift, judging it shameful to diminish the glory of virtue by the magnitude of the booty. Regarding Paulus Aemilius the same Plutarch says: the people praised his liberality and magnanimity no less than anything else, since he did not even wish to see much silver and much gold gathered from the royal treasures, but handed the public property over to the treasurers. Regarding Mummius, the Latin writer of lives says: Mummius despoiled Corinth of statues and paintings, with which when he had filled all of Italy, he brought nothing into his own house. Pliny in book XV says: Manius Curius swore that he had touched nothing from the booty except a beech-wood vessel, with which he might sacrifice.

Latin:

vers. 23. NON ACCIPIAM EX OMNIBUS QVÆ TUA SUNT, NE DICAS: EGO DITAVI ABRAHAM.) Similis majori Catoni animus, in cujus vita Plutarchus: εἰς δ' ἀυτὸν τῶν ἁλισκομένων ἐδὲν ἐλθεῖν λέγει, πλὴν ὅσα πέ- πωκεν ἢ βέβρωκε; καὶ ἐκ αἰτιῶμαί, φησι, τὲς ὠφελεισθαι ζη- τῶντας ἐκ τέτων, ἀλλὰ βέλομαι μᾶλλον περὶ ἀρετῆς τοῖς ἀ- ρίσοις ἢ περὶ χρημάτων τοῖς πλυσιωτάτοις ἀμιλλᾶσθαι. Ta- lis & ante Catonem Timoleon, qui eodem Plutarcho nar- rante censuit: ὀυ τὸ λαβεῖν ἐκ τοιούτων ἀισχρὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ λαβεῖν κρεῖττον καὶ περιουσία τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐν οἷς ἔξεστιν, ἐπιδει- κνυμένης τὸ δεόμενον. Et ante eum Pittacus Mitylenæus, de quo Valer. Max. VI. 1. cum recuperati agri dimidia pars con- sensu omnium offerretur, avertit animum ab eo munere, de- forme judicans virtutis gloriam magnitudine prædæ minue- re. De Paulo Æmilio idem Plutarchus: ὀδενὸς δὲ ἧττον αὐτό τὴν ἐλευθερότητα καί τὴν μεγαλοψυχίαν ἐπήνουν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, πολὺ μὲν ἀργύριον, πολὺ δὲ χρυσίον ἐκ τῶν βασιλικῶν ἠθροισ- μένον οὐδ᾽ ἰδεῖν ἐθελήσαντος, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταμίαις τὸ δημόσιον παραδόντος. De Mummio Latinus vitarum Scriptor: Mum- mius Corinthum fignis tabulisque spoliavit, quibus cum totam repleffet Italiam, in domum suam nihil contulit. Plinius libro XV. Manius Curius juravit se e præda nihil attigisse præter gut- tum faginum, quo sacrificaret.

## 14:24
verse 24. EXCEPT THOSE THINGS WHICH THE YOUNG MEN HAVE EATEN, AND THE PORTIONS OF THE MEN) There was no right of postliminy in such matters. Whether that right existed then in the case of men, can be doubted because of verse 21 above.

Latin:

vers. 24. EXCEPTIS HIS QVÆ COMEDERVNT JV- VENES, ET PARTIBVS VIRORVM) Non erat in re- bus talibus jus postliminii. An in hominibus id jus tum fuerit, dubitari potest ob comma 21. supra.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV.

Abram, believing the promise of God, is justified: and offering the sacrifice prescribed by God, he is informed about the future pilgrimage of his posterity.

Vers. 1. BY A VISION) which is more than by inspiration. AND THY REWARD EXCEEDING GREAT.) You shall have from me the reward of the noble deed, which you refused to accept from the spoil.

A too diluted interpretation of a magnificent promise. How, I ask, will it be persuaded that God here looked back, either solely or primarily, to the reward and spoil not accepted, but refused, from the King of Sodom? For there is neither a trace nor a footprint of that deed here! A clearly peculiar vision, occurring at a different time, is described. However, it pleased our author here again to Judaize. R. Solomon, when God warns, Fear not Abram: imagines that the Patriarch feared that, having obtained that signal victory, he had received all the reward of his righteousness from God. Perhaps he also wished to gratify the Papists, who, as appears from Leonhard Marius on this passage, extract the merits of their works from this. Therefore he interprets it as the reward of a noble deed. But there is no mention here of the deed, no mention of the works of Abraham. And Pererius admits that the words can be taken not only causally, I will remunerate your labors; but also substantially, I myself will be your reward. But who will establish a proportion between our works and the infinite God, such as that between merit and reward? Therefore, reward does not always have a relation to merit. A reward is given which is of debt, and a reward is also given which is of grace. As children are called the free gift of God, Ps. 127:4. And the holy Apostle clearly distinguishes that twofold reward: To him that worketh, the reward is not reckoned of grace, but of debt. Rom. 4:4.
