Therefore the Orthodox, with Ambrose in Epistle 1 and Augustine on Ps. 31, make one reward due, another undue; one of justice, another of liberality and grace; one legal, another Evangelical. But more on these against the Papists elsewhere.

If we weigh the text correctly here, God does not promise a reward for deeds, but promises an Evangelical promise out of mere grace, and that a most august one. For God offers Himself both as a shield to Abraham, in the warding off of all evils: especially spiritual ones. Deut. 31:29; 2 Sam. 22:3, 31; Ps. 18:31; Ps. 11:4; and as a reward in the abundance of all good things, especially heavenly ones. As God makes Himself a shield here, so also a reward; and therefore the word ἔσται should not be inserted with the LXX interpreters; thy reward SHALL BE exceeding great, but with the Vulgate both are to be understood of GOD, so that there is one subject, I, and a double predicate: A shield to you, your reward.

For just as in the former, God presents Himself for defense with a metaphorical military word; so in the latter, He offers Himself for a gracious reward or prize with an economic metaphor. Therefore He adds, your reward הרבה מאד very great, too great, as the Vulgate has it. What greater reward can be conceived, what more excellent prize, than God Himself? Who gives His whole self to the faithful, and in the other life is to be all in all to them 1 Cor. 15, 28. Nor are the proofs obscure that the Son of God was seen here by Abraham: The Word of the Lord is said to have been to Abraham in a vision, saying v. 1 and 4. Therefore the address of Abraham is attributed to the Word of the Lord. Which word is ὑποςατικὸν. And this word testifies: I am your shield: which the Chaldean rendered: my word is your strength, and your reward too great. And therefore where Moses has v. 6, He believed the Lord, Onkelos renders: He believed in the word of the Lord. It is said of the word of the Lord v. 5. And he led him outside, and said: which are the characters of the ὑποςατικὸν word. Furthermore, he who acts here with Abraham is that Lord who led him out of Ur of the Chaldeans v. 7. Who was seen by him in Bethel, to whom he also built an altar Gen. 12, 8. But the Lord in Bethel is the angel Goel, as appears from a comparison of Gen. 35, 1 and c. 48, 16, and thus the Son of God, the Lord of the Church by right, and its head, which Bethel is the House of this Lord, and by that Bethel was not only figured, but exhibited. For truly Bethel, the House of God, was there, because God was worshipped there. He who was seen here by Abraham as Lord is that Lord who appeared to him at the oak of Mamre Gen. 18, 1. Which a comparison of the places confirms, and the circumstances of the text teach. Add that these things which are held here pertain peculiarly to the Son of God. He Himself is a shield to the faithful against the fiery darts of Satan, for which reason faith itself, apprehending the same, is called a shield Eph. 6, 16. He Himself is our reward and prize, who gives His whole self to us, so that we may have all things with Him; which sweetest consequence the Apostle connects Rom. 8, 32. Therefore He is celebrated by the Hieropsalmist; My shield, and the horn of my salvation 2 Sam. 22, 3. Ps. 18, 3. The Lord God is a Sun and a shield, the Lord will give grace and glory: He will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence Ps. 84, 12. Nor was it under any other name that Abram was either seeking, because seed was denied to him, or that God was promising to him an heir descending from his womb, than that the Patriarch desired the fulfillment of the promise Gen. 12, 3 made to him concerning the blessed seed, but God now confirms him concerning the same. And this is what is added, Abram believed, and this was imputed to him for righteousness. For the faith by which the Patriarch was justified was not borne toward the promise concerning carnal seed: who will admit this, when the Father of believers was justified by the same faith by which we ought to be justified, as the Apostle demonstrates in Rom. 4, but it had for its object the blessed seed about to come forth from Abram's womb, nay, the Lord Himself, the Redeemer or Savior, and Benefactor, the Shield and prize of Abram and of all the faithful. Which eulogy is proper and perpetual to Christ. Therefore the reward is said to be coming with Him and salvation, nay, He Himself is ישועה salvation itself, both in the first advent Is. 62, 11. Behold your salvation comes, Behold his reward is with him. Let c. 40, 10 be compared. And in the last advent. Apoc. 22, 12. Nor is there any other name under heaven, which is the shield and prize, defense and blessedness of the faithful, than this one name, in which alone is strength and righteousness and thus our salvation Is. 45, 21. 22. 24. Therefore we are forbidden to glory in any other than this one Lord Jer. 9, 24. 1 Cor. 1, 31. In whom alone is our trust and blessedness, as David testifies Ps. 2, 12. Which seems to be indicated here also: Do not fear Abram; I am your protection, and your very great reward. For that, do not fear, can be taken thus, be confident Abram, or place your trust in me, and apprehend and embrace me as your protection and reward with true confidence of heart. A similar mode of speaking is Rom. 4, 10. μὴ ἀσθενήσας he was not weak in faith, i.e., he was very strong in faith, nay, most strong. Is. 42, 3. he will not break the bruised reed, i.e., he will consolidate and comfort it; he will not extinguish the smoking flax, i.e., he will kindle it more; on which words the Blessed Luther: That figure is very sweet and powerful for consolation; so that if someone is pusillanimous and fears to approach the Sacrament because of reverence etc., he may persuade himself otherwise, why do you fear? approach; For Christ will not give you poison. Therefore these negatives are very uplifting, because they exclude most powerfully that which is feared, the evil, and at the same time include most opulently that which is sought, the good. It is a meiosis, by which negating words are accustomed to be put for the contrary affirming ones. Do not fear, be of a strong and confident mind. Trust in me. I am your shield and reward. A reward, I say, in this and in the future age you will receive from me the most ample retribution: nay, I will give myself to you as a reward and prize through a salutary enjoyment, both gracious in this life, and glorious in the other. To which evangelical imperative responds the effect excited by the virtue of the word itself: Abraham believed. Not weakened by faith did he fear, but in hope against hope he believed.

Latin:

CAPUT XV.

Abram Dei promiffioni credens justificatur: & offerens præscriptum a Deo sacrificium de peregrinatione posteritatis futura in- formatur.

Vers. 1. PER VISIONEM) quod plus, quam per afflatum. ET MERCES TVA MAGNA NIMIS.) Mercedem fa- cti egregii, quam ex præda accipere noluisti, a me habebis.

Promiffionis magnificæ nimis diluta interpre- tatio. Quî persuadebitur, obsecro, Deum vel unice, vel potissimum mercedem ac prædam a Rege Sodomæ non acceptam, sed recusatam, hic respexisse? Neque enim de facto illo vel vola hic vel vestigium! Plane peculiaris & diverso tempo- re facta describitur visio. Placuit autem iterum hic Nostro ἰυδαἺζειν. R. Salomo n. quum moneat Deus, Ne timeas Abram: fingit, timuisse Patriar- cham, ne insignem illam adeptus victoriam omnem justitiæ mercedem a Deo retulerit. Forte etiam gratificari Papistis voluit, qui, ut e Leonh. Mario in h. l. apparet, hinc merita operum suorum excul- punt. Ideo mercedem facti egregii interpretatur. Sed nulla hic facti mentio, nulla operum Abraha- mi. Et fatetur Pererius, verba accipi posse non modo causaliter, Ego labores tuos remunerabor; sed etiam substantialiter, Ego ipsemet ero merces tua. Quis autem proportionem inter opera no- stra & infinitum Deum, talem, qualis inter meri- tum & mercedem, constituet? Non ergo semper merces respectum habet ad meritum. Datur mer- ces, quæ est ex debito, datur & quædam ex gratia. Uti liberi gratuitum Dei donum merces dicuntur Ps. 127, 4. Et distinguit geminam illam merce- dem aperte S. Apostolus: Ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Rom. 4, 4. Ideo Orthodoxi cum Ambrosio Epist. 1. & August. in Ps. 31. mercedem aliam faciunt debitam, aliam indebitam; aliam justitiæ, aliam liberalitatis & gra- tiæ: aliam legalem, aliam Evangelicam. Sed de his contra Pontificios alias.

Hic si textum recte expendamus, non pro factis mercedem Deus pollicetur, sed promiffionem Evangelicam promit ex mera gratia, eamque lon- ge augustissimam. Offert enim seipsum Deus & in scutum Abrahamo, in depulsione omnium ma- lorum: imprimis vero spiritualium. Deut. 31, 29. 2. Sam. 22, 3. 31. Ps. 18, 31. 3. Ps. 11, 4. & in mercedem in affluentia omnium bonorum, maxime cœlestium. Uti scutum semetipsum Deus hic facit, ita & merce- dem; ideoque non inferendum cum LXX. in- terpp. verbum ἔσται; merces tua ERIT valde ma- gna, sed cum vulgata utrumque de DEO in- telligendum, ut subjectum unum fit אָנֹכִי Ego, prædicatum geminum: Scutum tibi, merces tua.

Ut enim priori Deus in defensionem se verbo me- taphorico militari sistit; ita posteriori in mercedem gratiiosam vel præmium sese offert metaphora œco- nomica. Ideo addit, merces tua הרבה מאד valde multa, magna nimis, ut vulgata habet. Quæ ma- jor merces cogitari potest, quod præstantius præ- mium, quam Deus ipse? Qui se totum fidelibus do- nat, & in altera vita ipsis futurus est omnia in omni- bus 1. Cor. 15, 28. Neque obscura sunt documenta, visum hic Abrahamo esse Filium Dei: Verbum Domini di- citur fuisse ad Abrahamum in visione, dicendo v. 1. & 4. Verbo ergo Domini tribuitur alloquium Abrahami. Quod verbum est ὑποςατικὸν. Et testa- tur verbum hoc: Ego sum scutum tuum: quod Chal- dæus reddidit: verbum meum fortitudo tua, & mer- ces tua multa nimis. Ideoque ubi Moses habet v. 6. Credidit Domino, Onkelos reddit: Credidit in ver- bum Domini. Dicitur de verbo Domini v. 5. Et eduxit eum foras, & dixit: qui characteres verbi ὑποςατικᾶ. Porro is, qui hic agit cum Abrahamo, est Dominus ille, qui eduxit eum de Ur Chaldæorum v. 7. Qui in Bethel visus ipsi, cui etiam ædificavit altare Gen. 12, 8. Dominus autem in Bethel est angelus Goel, uti e collatione Gen. 35, 1. c. 48, 16. apparet, adeoque Filius Dei, Dominus Ecclesiæ Jure, ejusdemque caput, quæ Bethel Domus Do- mini hujus est, illoque Bethel figurabatur non tan- tum, sed exhibebatur. Vere enim ibi erat Bethel, Domus Dei, quia colebatur ibi Deus. Is qui hic vi- sus est Abrahamo Dominus, est Dominus ille, qui ei in quercu Mamre apparuit Gen. 18, 1. Quod collatio locorum confirmat, περιςάσεις textus do- cent. Adde, quod peculiariter hæc Filio Dei con- veniant, quæ hic habentur. Ipse est scutum fidelibus adversus ignita Satanæ tela, ob quem fides etiam ipsa, eundem apprehendens, scutum dicitur Eph. 6, 16. Ipse est merces præmiumque nostrum, qui se to- tum nobis donat, ut cum ipso habeamus omnia; quam dulcissimam consequentiam nectit Aposto- lus Rom. 8, 32. Ideo celebratur ab Hieropsalte; Scutum meum, & cornu salutis meæ 2. Sam. 22, 3. Ps. 18, 3. Dominus Deus est Sol & scutum, gratiam & gloriam dabit Dominus: Non privabit bonis eos, qui ambulant in innocentia Ps. 84, 12. Neque alio hic nomine vel querebatur Abram, denegatum sibi semen, vel promittebat Deus eidem hæredem de utero ejus descendentem, quam quod desidera- ret Patriarcha complementum promissionis Gen. 12, 3. de semine benedicto sibi factæ, Deus vero de eodem ipsum nunc confirmatit. Atque hoc est, quod additur, credidit Abram, & hoc imputatum est ei in justitiam. Fides enim qua justificatus Patriar- cha est, non ferebatur in promissionem de carnali semine: quis hoc admittet, quum eadem fide justifi- catus fuerit Pater credentium, qua nos justificari oportet, demonstrante Rom. 4. Apostolo, sed pro objecto habebat semen benedictum ex Abrami ute- ro proditurum, imo Dominum ipsum Redemto- rem vel Salvatorem, & Evergetam, Scutum & præ- mium Abrami, & omnium fidelium. Quod elo- gium Christo proprium est, & perpetuum. Ideo merces cum ipso ventura dicitur & salus, imo ipse ישועה salus ipsa est, tum in adventu primo Es. 62, 11. Ecce salus tua venit, Ecce merces ejus cum ipso. Conferatur c. 40, 10. tum in adventu novissimo. Apoc. 22, 12. Neque aliud nomen est sub cælo, quod scutum atque præmium, defensio ac beatitudo fi- delium sit, quam hoc unum nomen, in quo uno est fortitudo & justitia adeoque salus nostra Es. 45, 21. 22. 24. Ideo prohibemur gloriari in alio quam in hoc uno Domino Jer. 9, 24. 1. Cor. 1, 31. In quo uno nostra est fiducia & beatitudo, teste Davide Ps. 2, 12. Quod indicatum etiam hic videtur: Ne timeas Abram; Ego sum protectio tua, & merces tua copiosa valde. Illud enim, ne timeas, ita accipi potest, confidas Abram, vel fiduciam in me colloces, meque protectionem & mercedem tuam vera cordis fiducia apprehendas, atque amplectaris. Similis loquendi modus est Rom. 4, 10. μὴ ἀσθενήσας non imbecillis fide fuit, h. e. fuit fide perquam fortis, imo fortissi- mus. Es. 42, 3. arundinem quassatam non franget, h. e. consolidabit & confortabit; linum fumigans non extinguet, i. e. magis accendet; in quæ verba B. Lu- therus: Est illa figura valde dulcis & potens ad con- solationem; ut si non pusillanimis aliquis sit & metuat accedere Sacramentum propter reverentiam &c. persuadeat aliter, cur metuis? accede; Non enim Chri- stus venenum tibi dabit. Valde ergo erigunt ista ne- gativæ, quia excludunt hoc, quod metuitur, malum, potentissime, & simul includunt affirmative, quod pe- titur bonum, opulentissime. Est μείωσις, qua verba negantia pro contrariis affirmantibus poni solent. Ne metuas, forti & confidenti esto animo. In me confidas. Ego sum scutum & merces tua. Merces, inquam, in hoc, & in futuro seculo a me accipies re- tributionem amplissimam : imo ego meipsum do- nabo tibi in mercedem & præmium per salutarem fruitionem tum gratiosam in hac vita, tum glorio- sam in altera. Cui imperativo Evangelico respon- det effectus verbi ipsius virtute excitatus: Credidit Abraham. Non infirmatus fide metuit, sed in spem contra spem credidit.

## 15:2
vers. 2. SON OF THE STEWARD) The LXX took משק here for the proper name of him who was the father or progenitor of Eliezer. Nor did Julian say otherwise in Cyril. The Latin preferred to follow Aquila and Theodotion.

Latin:

vers. 2. FILIVS PROCVRATORIS) LXX. משק hic pro nomine proprio ejus, qui Pater aut progenitor Eliezeris fuerit, accepere. Nec aliter Julianus apud Cyrillum. Lati- nus Aquilam & Theodotionem sequi maluit.

## 15:3
vers. 3. HE SHALL BE MY HEIR) By testament, since I have no one dearer. Thus we showed also among the Greeks that the custom of making a will was most ancient from Sophocles, Euripides, Homer at the end of chapter VI, book II, of the Law of War and Peace. It is an evil of childlessness, to have an heir not one's own.

Latin:

vers. 3. HÆRES MEVS ERIT) Ex Testamento, cum alium cariorem non habeam. Sic & apud Græcos vetu- stissimum fuisse testandi morem ostendimus ex Sophocle, Euripide, Homero ad finem cap. VI. lib. II. de Jure belli ac pacis. Malum est orbitatis, hæredem habere non suum.

## 15:5
vers. 5. AND HE LED HIM OUTSIDE) By the Spirit acting, as Matt. 4, 1. Luke 4, 1. COUNT THE STARS IF YOU CAN) Catullus: Or as many stars as when the night is silent: Ovid: how many stars the heaven.

Latin:

vers. 5. EDVXITQVE EVM FORAS) Spiritu agente, ut Matth. 4, 1. Luc. 4, 1. NVMERA STELLAS SI POTES) Catullus: Aut quam sidera multa cum tacet nox: Ovidius: quot cœlum stellas.

## 15:9
vers. 9. A THREE-YEAR-OLD COW) Not otherwise the Greeks. But the Chaldean interprets three cows, and in a like manner the word משלש in the following. Rabbi Solomon follows. And certainly that word is not found elsewhere in the meaning of three-year-old, but in the meaning of a triple thing, as Ezek. 4, 26. Ecclesiastes 46, 6.

Latin:

vers. 9. VACCAM TRIENNEM) Non aliter Græci. At Chaldæus tres vaccas, parique modo vocem משלש in sequentibus interpretatur. Sequitur Rabbi Salomo. Et cer- te vox illa in fignificatione trimi non reperitur alibi, sed in significatione rei triplicis, ut Ezech. 4, 26. Ecclesiastæ 46, 6.

## 15:10
ver. 10. HE DIVIDED THEM) Here is signified the dispersion of the descendants of Abraham into diverse settlements: Canaan, Arabia, Idumea, Gerar, Egypt, Ethiopia.

Latin:

vers. 10. DIVISIT EA) Significatur hic disparatio poste- rum Abrahami in sedes diversas Cananæam, Arabiam, Idu- mæam, Gerarem, Ægyptum, Æthiopiam.

## 15:11
ver. 11. AND THE BIRDS DESCENDED) Rapacious Egyptians. ABRAHAM DROVE THEM AWAY) By blowing. Thus the Hebrew text which we use. So also Aquila, ἀπεσόβησεν. But the LXX, συνεκάθισεν ἀυτοῖς Ἀβράμ, having made a derivation from ישב, not from נשב. Which is not to be disapproved, so that the long delay of the descendants of Abraham in Egypt might be indicated. For the authors of a race are taken for their race.

Latin:

vers. 11. DESCENDERVNTQVE VOLVCRES) Ægy- ptii rapaces. ABIGEBAT EOS ABRAHAM) Sufflando. Ita textus Hebræus quo utimur. Sic & Aquila ἀπεσόβησεν. At LXX. συνεκάθισεν ἀυτοῖς Ἀβράμ, facta derivatione a ישב, non a נשב. quod non improbandum, ut indicetur mora diutina Abrahami posterum in Ægypto. Auctores enim generis pro suo genere sumuntur.

## 15:12
ver. 12. A DEEP SLEEP) That is the original meaning of this word, from which Aquila, who translates it καταφορὰν, and Symmachus, who translates it κάρον, do not depart. But the LXX, having deduced it to a similar meaning, placed ἔκσασιν, with whom Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed II, 41, II, 45 also agrees. Conf. Acts X, 10, XI, 5, XXII, 17. AND A GREAT AND DARK HORROR INVADED HIM) Signifying that final and most grievous vexation of his descendants in Egypt.

Latin:

vers. 12. SOPOR) Ea est originaria hujus vocis significa- tio, a qua non abeunt Aquila, qui καταφορὰν, Symmachus qui κάρον vertunt. At LXX. ad simile deducto significatu ἔκσασιν posuere, quibus consentit & Maimonides ductore du- bitantium II, 41. II, 45. Conf. Act. X, 10. XI, 5. XXII, 17. ET HORROR MAGNVS ET TENEBROSVS IN- VASIT EVM) Significans postremam illam ac gravissi- mam posterum ipsius in Ægypto vexationem.

## 15:13
v. 13. FOUR HUNDRED YEARS) That is, until almost the four-hundredth year from this time.

Latin:

v. 13. ANNIS QVADRINGENTIS) Id est, usque annum ferme quadringentesimum ab hoc tempore.

## 15:16
ver. 16. BUT IN THE FOURTH GENERATION) Namely, of the Amorites, which is to be understood from what follows. FOR NOT YET ARE THE INIQUITIES OF THE AMORITES) The measure of judgment, as the Hebrews speak. When that is completed, Kingdoms are changed.

Latin:

vers. 16. GENERATIONE AVTEM QVARTA) Nem- pe Amorrhæorum, quod ex sequentibus subintelligendum. NEC DVM ENIM COMPLETÆ SVNT INIQVI- TATES AMORRHÆORVM) Mensura judicii, ut He- bræi loquuntur. Ea ubi consummata est, mutantur Regna.

## 15:17
ver. 17. A SMOKING FURNACE AND A LAMP OF FIRE PASSING BETWEEN THOSE DIVISIONS) This signifies the burning vengeance of God against the Egyptians, already indicated above in 14. God accommodated Himself to the custom of those times, the traces of which remained even later. For Peleus, having killed the wife of Acastus, διελὼν τὰ μέλη διήγαγε τὸν στρατὸν, as Apollodorus teaches from ancient history. And Cyril notes in his tenth book against Julian that this custom existed among the Chaldeans. See such a dismemberment of cattle in 1 Sam. 11 and Jer. 34, 19. Zenobius: οἱ Μόλοττοι ἐν τοῖς ὁρκωμοσίοις κατακόπτοντες εἰς μι- κρὰ τὺς βῦς τὰς συνθήκας ἐποιῦντο. Livy book 29. The head of a dog is cut in the middle and the front part is placed to the right, the rear to the left of the road. Armed troops are led between this divided victim. Plutarch in his Roman Questions: Βοιωτοῖς δημοσία καθαρμός ἐστι κυνὸς διχοτομηθέντος τῶν μερῶν διεξελθεῖν· clearly the Boeotians, born from them, had drawn this from the Phoenicians.

But the traces which Grotius has, show that this custom migrated from the Church to the Gentiles through κακοζηλία (misguided zeal), rather than vice versa. For God did not accommodate Himself in such matters to the sacred rites of the Gentiles or their customs. Which I see observed also by our blessed Gerhard in this place, p. 335. The rite of ratifying a covenant through the dissection of animals seems to have been derived from this covenant of God and Abraham. However, the covenant was not merely confirmed by these dissected animals, nor was something only foreshadowed by their burning, but a sacrifice was made here at the same time; so that there is a triple use of them: federal, symbolic, and sacrificial. Moreover, by the smoking furnace was signified not so much the vengeance against the Egyptians as the harsh servitude of the Israelites in Egypt, Deut. 4, 20. Moreover, the lamp of fire was a symbol of the divine presence: although some wish for both the smoke and the burning lamp to designate it, and apply them to the pillar of cloud and fire, Exod. 13, 21. But that the animals themselves, which were chosen here, were sacrificial, not by Abraham's private choice but by divine instinct, is manifest from the law of sacrifices, Lev. 1, 2: which it is certain were ignited here by no other fire than divine. For no man applied the fire.

Latin:

vers. 17. CLIBANVS FVMANS ET LAMPAS IGNIS TRANSIENS INTER DIVISIONES ILLAS) Significan ardentem Dei vindictam in Ægyptios jam indicatam su- pra 14. Accommodavit autem se Deus mori illorum tem- porum, cujus vestigia & serius mansere. Peleus enim, oc- cisa uxore Acasti, διελὼν τὰ μέλη διήγαγε τὸν στρατὸν, ut ex veteri historia docet Apollodorus. Eumque morem Chal- dæis fuisse notat Cyrillus decimo contra Julianum. Vide ta- lem pecudum dispartitionem 1. Sam. 11. & Jerem. 34, 19. Zenobius: οἱ Μόλοττοι ἐν τοῖς ὁρκωμοσίοις κατακόπτοντες εἰς μι- κρὰ τὺς βῦς τὰς συνθήκας ἐποιῦντο. Livius lib. 29. Caput mediæ canis præcisa & prior pars ad dextram, posterior ad lævam viæ ponitur. Inter hanc divisam hostiam copiæ armatæ traducun- tur. Plutarchus quæstionibus Romanis: Βοιωτοῖς δημοσία καθαρμός ἐστι κυνὸς διχοτομηθέντος τῶν μερῶν διεξελθεῖν· ni- mirum a Phœnicibus hoc hauserant nati ab ipsis Bœoti.

At quæ habet Grotius vestigia, morem po- tius hunc ab Ecclesia per κακοζηλίαν ad gentiles mi- grasse ostendunt, quam vice versa. Non enim Deus in talibus se sacris gentilium aut ritibus eo- rum accommodavit. Quod video observatum etiam B. Gerhardo nostro in h. l. p. 335. Ritus san- ciendi fœderis per animalium dissectionem videtur ex hoc Dei & Abrahæ fœdere traductus. Non au- tem confirmabatur tantum per hæc animantia dis- secta fœdus, neque per eorum incensionem adum- bratum aliquid solum, sed fiebat hic simul sacrifi- cium; ut triplex usus illorum sit: fœderalis, symbo- licus, sacrificialis. Significabatur autem per ar- dentem Clibanum non tam vindicta in Ægyptios, quam dura Israelitarum in Ægypto servitus Deut. 4, 20. Lampas autem ignis divinæ præsentiæ sym- bolum erat: quanquam nonnulli per utrumque fumum & lampadem ardentem eam designatam ve- lint, illaque ad columnam nubis & ignis applicent Exod. 13, 21. Animantia autem ipsa, quæ hic de- lecta, non privato Abrahæ arbitrio, sed instinctu divino, sacrificialia fuisse, ex sacrificiorum lege Lev. 1, 2. manifestum est: quæ non alio igne, quam di- vino hic accensa fuisse, constat. Nullus enim ho- minem ignem applicuit.

## 15:18
ver. 18 I WILL GIVE THIS LAND) The best title for acquiring is a gift from the Lord of all things.

FROM THE RIVER OF EGYPT EVEN UNTO THE GREAT RIVER EUPHRATES.

The river of Egypt here is not the Nile, as R. Solomon and R. David Kimchi with Jonathan wish, because the Kings of Israel did not rule in Egypt, nor did they occupy Arabia, Midian, and other regions which the Nile washes: but it is a small river which divides Palestine from Egypt, which is everywhere called the torrent of Egypt, and in Amos 6, the last verse, the torrent of the desert, because it flows through the wilderness into the Mediterranean Sea between Pelusium and Gaza: it is called by the LXX in Is. 27, 12, Rhinocorura from the neighboring city, which was so named from the cut-off noses, a punishment which a certain King of Egypt had established to curb thefts and robberies. See Strabo book XVI, Diodorus Siculus book II, c. 1. It separates Judea from Egypt, and closes it on the southern side. EUPHRATES, however, antonomastically called the river, and here the great river, rises in Paradise, Gen. 2, in Greater Armenia, from the northern side of Taurus, where it first flows towards the west, then turned to the south it separates Cappadocia and Lesser Armenia from Greater Armenia, and having emerged from the straits of Taurus, it divides Commagene Syria from Mesopotamia: then turned towards the winter sunrise it flows past Babylon, under which, having received the Tigris at Apamea, it separates Susiana and Babylonia: and finally pours into the Persian Gulf. But how was it fulfilled that the Israelites possessed the borders of the promised land from the torrent of Egypt even unto the Euphrates? Resp. In the time of David and Solomon the dominion was extended as far as the Euphrates, and all the intervening peoples were made tributary, and thus far in some way such an ample dominion began to be fulfilled, as is clear from 2 Sam. 8, 3, 1 Par. 8, 3, 1 Kings 4, 21, 9, 20, Josephus book VI of Antiquities, c. 2, Augustine. Q. in Jos. 21, who distinguishes between hereditary and tributary lands, Cajetan and Oleastri teach: which, however, as we have said, is to be understood in a qualified sense, that it only began to be fulfilled in some way, as Bonfrerius rightly warns: and that it ought to have been fulfilled more fully, so that the hereditary possessions of the Israelites might also extend as far as the Euphrates, if indeed in Deut. 19, 9 the Israelites are commanded to add three other cities of refuge to the dilated borders, which dilation is to be understood regarding habitation: because in land which they did not inhabit, there is no place for cities of refuge, and the Empire of the Israelites was dilated that far in the time of David and Solomon, as is clear from the cited place: not indeed that they possessed all the places properly, but that they rendered the peoples tributary to themselves. Therefore that promise concerning the dilation of borders in Deut. 19 is to be understood with the condition of obedience, which not being fulfilled, they did not even possess the narrower borders of Canaan quietly and fully, if indeed they could not exterminate the Philistines. See Jerome, Ep. 129 to Dardanus, and in Ezech. 22, 8. Andr. Masius and Serar. in Jos. 1.

Latin:

vers. 18 DABO TERRAM HANC) Optimus acquiren- di titulus donum a Domino rerum omnium.

A FLUVIO ÆGYPTI VSQVE AD FLVVIVM MA- GNVM EVPHRATEM.

Fluvius Ægypti hic non est Nilus, ut R. Salo- mo, & R. David Kimchi cum Jonathane volunt, quia Reges Israel non imperarunt in Ægypto, nec Arabiam, Medianitim & alias regiones, quas Ni- lus alluit, occuparunt: sed est fluvius exiguus, qui Palæstinam ab Ægypto dividit, qui passim vocatur torrens Ægypti, & Am. VI. ult. torrens deserti, quia influit per solitudinem in mare mediterraneum in- ter Pelusium & Gazam: a LXX. dicitur Es. 27, 12. Rhinocoura a vicina urbe, quæ ita a præcisis nari- bus, quam pœnam Rex quidam Ægypti, ut furta ac latrocinia compesceret, statuerat, appellata. V. Strab. l. XVI. Diodor. Sicul. l. II. c. 1. Disterminat Judæam ab Ægypto, illamque claudit a parte Au- strali. EUPHRATES vero antonomastice flu- vius nonnunquam, hic fluvius magnus dictus ori- tur in Paradiso, Gen. 2. in Armenia majore, ex Tauri latere Boreali, ubi primum occidentem ver- sus fluit, inde ad meridiem flexus Cappadociam & Armeniam minorem ab Armenia majori, & ex Tauri angustiis egressus Syriam Comagonem a Mesopotamia dirimit: inde ad ortum brumalem conversus Babylonem perfluit, sub qua Tygride ad Apamæam excepto, Susianam & Babyloniam dis- terminat: ac in sinum Persicum tandem effunditur. Sed quomodo id impletum, ut fines terræ promissæ a torrente Ægypti usἱ ad Euphratem possederint Israe- lœ litæ? Resp. Davidis & Salomonis tempore domi- nium prolatum fuit usque ad Euphraten, & omnes interjecti populi redditi vectigales, atque hactenus aliqua ratione impleri cœptum tam amplum domi- nium, ut e 2. Sam. 8, 3. 1. Par. 8, 3. 1. Reg. 4, 21. 9, 20. Josepho l. VI. Antiqv. c. 2. Augustin. Q. in Jos. 21. qui inter terras hæreditarias, & tributarias distinguit, Cajetanus & Oleastrius docent: quod tamen, ut diximus, secundum quid intelligendum, quod id aliquo modo solum impleri cœperit, ut recte monet Bonfrerius: ac plenius debuerit impleri, ut hæreditariæ etiam possessiones Israelitarum se usq; ad Euphraten porrigerent, siquidem Deut. 19, 9. Israelitæ jubeantur dilatatis terminis addere tres alias civitates refugii, quæ dilatatio intelligenda est quoad habitationem: quia in terra, quam non inha- bitarint, locus non est civitatibus refugii, & eo usque dilatatum fuerit Israelitarum Imperium Da- vidis & Salomonis tempore, ut e l. c. constat: non quidem quod possederint proprie loca omnia, sed quod sibi tributarios reddiderint populos. Pro- missio itaque illa de terminorum dilatatione Deut. 19. intelligenda cum conditione obedientiæ, qua non impleta ne angustiores quidem Cananææ termi- nos quiete possederunt & plene, siquidem Phili- stæos exterminare non potuerint. Vid. Hieron. Ep. 129. ad Dardan. & in Ezech. 22, 8. Andr. Ma- sius & Serar. in Jos. 1.

## 15:19
vers. 19. KENITES) Who are otherwise called Salmaei, according to the Chaldean here. Ptolemy places three Salmas in Arabia. The Salmani and Measaei are Arabs according to Pliny, book V, ch. 26. Those three peoples, the Kenites, Kenizzites, and Kadmonites, who are named here with the other seven, are nowhere else mentioned among the Canaanite nations in the Scriptures. Augustine, Questions on Joshua 21, thinks these are from the nations that lived outside the borders of the Canaanites and later became tributary to the Israelites. Jerome, in ch. 1 of Joshua, thinks that because of the violation of the covenant, God gave only seven nations to the Israelites. Deut. 7, 1. Josh. 24, 11. Acts 13, 19. Perhaps some of these peoples dwelt with others, or are indicated elsewhere by other names.

Latin:

vers. 19. CINÆOS) Qui aliter dicti Salmæi, teste hic Chaldæo. Salmas in Arabia tres ponit Ptolomæus. Salmani, & Measæi Arabes apud Plinium libr. V. c. 26. Tres illi populi Cinæi, Cenezæi, Cedmonæi, qui hic cum cæteris septem nominantur, nusquam ali- bi inter gentes Cananæas in Scripturis memoran- tur. August. quæst. in Jos. 21. putat, hos esse e gen- tibus, quæ extra terminos Cananæorum habitabant, & postea factæ sunt Israelitis vectigales. Hieronym. in c. 1. Jos. existimat, ob violationem fœderis Deum tantum septem gentes Israelitis dedisse. Deut. 7, 1. Jos. 24, 11. Act. 13, 19. Forte quidam populi ex istis cum aliis coluerunt, aut aliis nomi- nibus alibi indigitantur.

## 15:20
v. 20. REPHAIM. Of these also there is no mention elsewhere among the Canaanite nations. They are named, however, in Gen. 14, 5, and seem to have lived across the Jordan in Bashan or Batanea. Josh. 12, 4; ch. 13, 2. Whom the LXX translate as giants, because they were of gigantic stature, descended from Rapha the giant, 1 Chron. 20, 6.

Latin:

v. 20. RAPHAIM. Horum quoque nulla alibi inter Cananæas gentes sit mentio. Nominantur autem Gen. 14, 5. & videntur trans Jordanem in Basan seu Batanæa habitasse. Jos. 12, 4. c. 13, 2. Quos LXX. vertunt gigantes, quod gigantea essent magnitudine, oriundi a Rapha gigante 1. Paral. 20, 6.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI.

Hagar, given as a wife to Abram, when she had become pregnant and had despised her mistress, being afflicted by her, took to flight, and being called back by an Angel, gave birth to Ishmael.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI.

Hagar Abræ uxor tradita, cum gravida facta Dominam contemsisset, ab illa afflicta fu- gam iniit, ab Angelo revocata Ismaelem peperit.

## 16:1 Addition
On Gen. ch. 16, towards the end of page 284, column a.

That the angel seen by Hagar is the Son of God, even among the Reformed, Piscator, Ainsworth, and the Belgic Annotations acknowledge. Compare what is in the Commentary on Genesis at this place and System. Theol. Vol. 4, p. 216.

Latin:

Ad Gen. c. 16. sub finem pag. 284. a.

Angelum Hagari visum Filium Dei esse, etiam è Reformatis Piscator, Ainsworthus, & Belgic. Annot. agnoscunt. Conf. quæ in Comment. in Ge- nes. ad h. l. & System. Theol. Tom. 4. p. 216.

## 16:2
vers. 2. HAGAR) Whence the city of Agra, which Pliny places in Arabia. Agraioi and Agabioi according to Strabo and Stephanus.

Latin:

vers. 2. AGAR) Unde Agra urbs, quam in Arabia ponit Plinius. Ἀγραῖοι ἑδρ&gt; Ἀγάβιοι Straboni & Stephano.

## 16:3
v. 3. GAVE HER TO HER HUSBAND AS A WIFE) Rather, as a wife: for thus the Hebrew le-ishah is often taken: that is, in the place of a spouse, as ancient inscriptions have it. A concubine imitates a wife, says Julian the predecessor.

Latin:

v. 3. DEDIT EAM VIRO SVO UXOREM) Potius pro uxore: ita enim לאשה Hebræum sæpe sumitur: id est, vice- conjugem, ut habent inscriptiones veteres. Uxorem imita- tur concubina, ait Julianus antecessor.

## 16:5
v. 5. YOU DEAL UNJUSTLY AGAINST ME) Chamsi, which is here in the Hebrew, the Chaldean translates as a complaint, and the Greeks sometimes as reproach. I have that of which I may complain about you, which I may object to you. Childbearing is accustomed to make women proud.

Latin:

v. 5. INIQVE AGIS CONTRA ME) חמסי quod hic in Hebræo est, Chaldæus querelam vertit, & Græci interdum ὄνειδος. Habeo quod de te conquerar, quod tibi objiciam. Partus superbas solet facere feminas.

## 16:6
v. 6. USE HER AS IT PLEASES YOU) For at that time masters and mistresses had the right of life and death over their menservants and maidservants.

Latin:

v. 6. UTERE EA UT LVBET) Jus enim vitæ ac necis eo tempore Domini ac Dominæ in servos & ancillas habebant.

## 16:9
vers. 9. SUBMIT YOURSELF UNDER HER HAND) Indeed, and one must bear the ignorance of those in power.

Latin:

vers. 9. HVMILIARE SVB MANV ILLIVS) Quippe & Τὰς τῶν κρατούντων ἀμαθίας χρεὼν φέρειν.

## 16:12
vers. 12. HIS HAND AGAINST ALL, AND THE HANDS OF ALL AGAINST HIM) In Hebrew, against all and against him. He will cause trouble for everyone, and others for him. Such is the posterity of Hagar, the Saracens and other Arabs.

IN THE PRESENCE OF ALL HIS BRETHREN HE SHALL PITCH HIS TENTS) In Hebrew, before all his brethren, that is, with the children of Keturah looking on, and not being able to hinder him, he shall extend his borders.

Latin:

vers. 12. MANVS EJVS CONTRA OMNES, ET MA- NVS OMNIVM CONTRA EVM) In Hebræo in omnes & in eum. Negotium omnibus facesset, & alii ipsi. Talis posteritas Agaris Saraceni Arabesque alii.

E REGIONE OMNIVM FRATRVM SVORVM FI- GET TABERNACVLA) In Hebræo coram omnibus fratri- bus suis, id est, aspectantibus Cethuræ liberis, neque impedire valentibus extendet fines suos.

## 16:13
vers. 13. AND SHE CALLED THE NAME OF THE LORD, WHO WAS SPEAKING TO HER) The Chaldean: she prayed in the name of the Lord speaking to her, i.e., she invoked God himself, as if present in the Angel: You see me, O God. The Jerusalem Targum: God also revealed himself to me, and indeed in the desert through Angels.

Therefore, he thinks that a created Angel appeared, along with the Jews, Papists, and Socinians. Which is also the opinion of certain Calvinists: and also of Calixtus and his accomplices, as we have warned before. But these words openly testify that it was JEHOVAH who spoke to Hagar and appeared to her. She called the name of the LORD, who spoke with her. Therefore, it was not a created angel, a minister of the Lord, but the angel Lord himself who was seen here. Whom Hagar also addressed thus: You are the God who has seen me. Certainly, angels are never read to have been addressed in such a way. She also gave a name to the well from the Lord, when she called it the Well of the LIVING ONE and of the ONE SEEING me. Therefore, she testifies that she saw no other than Jehovah God, the LIVING ONE, graciously looking upon her.

Some interpret these words in such a way that she marvels that she still sees, or beholds the light, and lives after seeing God, Gen. 32:30, Jud. 13:23. For she recognized God himself from that authoritative speech, by which this angel claimed for himself a work that is truly new: Multiplying, he says, I will multiply your seed. Thus, therefore, from the proper name of God, Jehovah and God, and likewise from the attribute and divine idiom of the LIVING ONE, and also from the divine work of gracious providence and omnipotence, and from the divine worship of religious adoration and invocation, it is clearer than light that the Angel was uncreated, the Son of God, who did not judge the work of the restoration and conversion of the wandering Hagar unworthy of his care, since for that reason he also willed to become man in the fullness of time, that he might seek that which was lost, Luke 19:10. And hence it is that this appearing Lord speaks of the Lord, who heard the misery of Hagar, v. 11. For our Advocate is Jehovah the Son of God before Jehovah God the Father, and the same is the redeemer and Savior: and he has always shown himself to be such. Hebrews ch. 13, v. 8.

Latin:

vers. 13. VOCAVIT AVTEM NOMEN DOMINI, QVI LOQVEBATVR AD EAM) Chaldæus, oravit in nomine Domini loquentem ad se, i. e. Deum ipsum invocavit, velut in Angelo præsentem: Tu me vides o Deus. Hiero- solymitanus: Deus se etiam mihi, & quidem in deserto per An- gelos patefecit.

Cum Judæis itaque, Papistis ac Socinianis Angelum creatum apparuisse, existimat. Quæ Cal- vinianorum etiam quorundam sententia est: nec non Calixti & Complicum ut antea monuimus. At verba hæc aperte testantur, JEHOVAM fuis- se, qui loquutus est ad Hagarem eique apparuit. Vocavit nomen DOMINI, qui locutus est cum ipsa. Non ergo Angelus creatus, minister Domini, sed angelus Dominus ipse hic visus est. Quem Ha- gar ita etiam alloquuta est: Tu Deus, qui vidisti me. Nunquam profecto ita compellati leguntur Angeli. A Domino etiam nomen puteo dedit, cum appellavit eum Puteum VIVENTIS & VI- DENTIS me. Non ergo alium apparuisse testatur, seque vidisse, quam Jehovam Deum VIVENTEM, gratiose se respicientem.

Quæ verba ita accipiunt nonnulli, quod mi- retur, se adhuc post visum Deum videre, vel lucem aspicere, atque vivere Gen. 32, 30. Jud. 13, 23. De- um enim ipsum agnovit ex illa authoritativa lo- quutione, qua opus vere novum sibi vindicavit hic angelus: Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo se- men tuum. Ita ergo e nomine Dei proprio Jeho- vah & Deus, ex attributo item, & idiomate divino VIVENTIS, nec non ex opere divino gratiosæ providentiæ & omnipotentiæ, & ex cultu divino ad- orationis atque invocationis religiosæ luce clarius constat, Angelum fuisse increatum, Filium Dei, qui indignum cura sua non judicavit opus reductio- nis & conversionis Hagaræ errantis, quum ideo etiam homo fieri voluerit in plenitudine temporis, ut quæreret, quod perierat Luc. 19, 10. Atque hinc est, quod loquatur hic Dominus apparens de Do- mino, qui exaudierit miseriam Hagar, v. 11. Advo- catus enim noster est Jehovah Filius Dei apud Je- hovam Deum Patrem, idemque redemtor & Sal- vator: ac talem nunquam non se præbuit. Ebræor. c. 13. v. 8.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII.

Circumcision commanded, and the promise of the Son from Sarah accepted, expedited.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII.

Circumcisio præcepta, & promissione Filii e Sara accepta, expedita.

## 17:2
Vers. 2. AND I WILL ESTABLISH MY COVENANT.) Circumcision, as below v. 10, namely, external literally: internal mystically.

ALTHOUGH in v. 10 it is said, this is my covenant, you shall circumcise every male among you: yet it is not handed down here that circumcision is the covenant, which the Calvinists elicit from this, so that they may obtain that 'is' is taken for 'signifies': But this is the proposition of the Lord: This is my covenant, that every male among you be circumcised, where it is manifest that the copula 'is' is not placed for 'signifies', or 'significantly': for thus the covenant of the Lord would become the sign, and circumcision the thing signified. See D. D. Seb. Schmid. Disp. on those propositions, circumcision is the covenant of the Lord, and is a sign of the covenant of the Lord. Furthermore, as far as appears from the annotations to this chapter, Grotius does not acknowledge circumcision as a Sacrament, or a means of the remission of sins, of grace and of salvation. He seems to have believed it to be only a sign of the divine covenant with the Papists. Therefore, it is no wonder that he also noted at v. 12 that circumcision could have been performed by private persons and by women even outside the case of supreme necessity. 12. But that better men among the Rabbis thought more sublimely about this institution of God, even the very formula of the blessing which was used confirms: The living God our portion and our protector commanded that our soul be rescued from the netherworld because of his covenant, which he placed in our flesh. For God instituted circumcision not only so that grace might be signified, but so that through this medium infants might be received into grace: just as both the promise of grace added, I will be your God, and the opposing threat made to neglected circumcision in v. 14 testify. By Paul it is called a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11, by which it was sealed in the hearts of the faithful. Therefore, it was not a merely significant sign, but an effective one.

Latin:

Vers. 2. PONAMQVE FOEDVS.) Circumcisionem, ut infra v. 10. nempe externam κατὰ πόδας: internam μυσικῶς.

ETsi v. 10. dicatur, hoc est fœdus meum, cir- cumcidi vobis omnem masculum: non tamen hic traditur circumcisionem esse fœdus, quod Cal- viniani hinc eliciunt, ut τὸ est pro significat accipi obtineant: Sed hæc est propositio Domini: Fœ- dus meum est hoc, ut circumcidatur vobis omne masculum, ubi manifestum est, copulam est non poni pro significat, vel σημαντικῶς: sic enim fœdus Domini fieret signum, & circumcisio signatum. Vid. Dn. D. Seb. Schmid. Disp. de illis proposi- tionibus, circumcisio est fœdus Domini, & est si- gnum fœderis Domini. Cæterum quantum appa- ret ex annotatis ad hoc caput, non agnoscit Gro- tius circumcisionem Sacramentum, seu medium remissionis peccatorum, gratiæ & salutis. Signum solum fœderis divini cum Papistis credidisse vide- tur. Ideo non mirum, quod etiam per privatos ac per mulieres extra casum quoque supremæ necessi- tatis fieri circumcisionem potuisse ad v. 12. anno- tavit. At sublimius sensisse meliores e Rabbinis de hoc instituto Dei, vel ipsa formula benedictio- nis, quæ adhibita fuit, confirmat: Deus vivus pars nostra & protector noster præcepit, erui animam no- stram ab inferis propter fœdus suum, quod posuit in carne nostra. Non enim tantum ut significaretur gratia, sed ut per hoc medium in gratiam recipe- rentur infantes, instituit Deus circumcisionem: quemadmodum tum promissio gratiæ addita, Ero Deus tuus, tum opposita comminatio intermissæ cir- cumcisioni facta v. 14. testatur. Paulo dicitur σφραγίς sigillum justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4, 11. quo ea obsignata fuit in cordibus fidelium. Non ergo fuit signum mere σημαντικὸν, sed ἐνεργητικὸν.

## 17:6
v. 6. AND KINGS SHALL COME OUT OF THEE) From all time there is no one who can be compared with Abraham in the manifold progeny of Kings. From him were the Hebrew Kings of the twelve tribes, of the two tribes, of the ten tribes. From him the ancient Idumean Kings, and after a long interval, Kings born from Herod. From him in Africa the Kings of the race of Keturah. From him the Saracen Kings in Arabia, Babylon, Egypt, so many in Africa, so many in Spain, kings of the same race. From him finally the Messiah, King of all Christian kings.

Indeed, King of all Kings simply, (not of Christians only,) and Lord of Lords: Ap. 17 and 19, which title is proper to God. For the dominion of the Father and the Son is one, there is one Lord of lords, 1 Tim. 6:16. The Lord through whom are all things, 1 Cor. 8:6.

Latin:

v. 6. REGESQVE EX TE EGREDIENTVR) Ab omni ævo nullus est qui cum Abrahamo comparari possit multipli- ce Regum progenie. Ab illo fuere Reges Hebræi duodecim tribuum, duarum tribuum, decem tribuum. Ab illo Reges Idumæi veteres, & longo intervallo ab Herode geniti Reges. Ab illo in Africa Reges Cethuræ genus. Ab illo Reges Sa- raceni in Arabia, Babylone, Ægypto, tot in Africa, tot in Hi- spania gentis ejusdem Reges. Ab illo denique Messias Rex omnium regum Christianorum.

Imo Rex omnium Regum simpliciter, (non Christianorum tantum,) & Dominus Dominan- tium: Ap. 17. & 19. qui titulus est Deo proprius. Unum enim est Patris & Filii Dominium, unus est Dominus dominantium, 1. Tim. 6, 16. Dominus per quem omnia 1. Cor. 8, 6.

## 17:7
v. 7. AND BETWEEN THY SEED) For there are certain personal covenants: others, like this one, passing to successors.

Latin:

v. 7. ET INTER SEMEN TUUM) Sunt enim fœdera quædam personalia: alia, ut hoc, ad successores transeuntia.

## 17:12
v. 12. OF EIGHT DAYS) Because before that day the infant is too weak to be equal to the pain, as Maimonides notes. Aristotle, book VII, chapter VII of the History of Animals, dealing with infants: τὰ πλεῖστα δὲ ἀναιρεῖται πρὸ τῆς ἑβδομῆς· διὸ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τότε τίθενται, ὡς πιστεύοντες ἤδη μᾶλλον τῇ σωτηρίᾳ. This is the reason why the offspring of cattle are not consecrated to God before the eighth day, Exodus 22:20. Moreover, circumcision was performed by day, so that the matter might be better known. The foreskin was thrown into the dust. Circumcision could be performed by Priests, by Levites, by private individuals, even by women, though not by outlaws.

AS WELL THE HOMEBORN AS THE PURCHASED) An uncircumcised person could indeed live in the land given to the Hebrews under good laws: but not in the house of any Hebrew, lest customs be confounded by a different example.

Latin:

v. 12. OCTO DIERVM) Quia ante eum diem infir- mior infans quam ut par sit dolori, ut notat Maimonides. Aristoteles l. VII. cap. VII. de Historia animalium, agens de infantibus: τὰ πλεῖστα δὲ ἀναιρεῖται πρὸ τῆς ἑβδομῆς· διὸ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τότε τίθενται, ὡς πιστεύοντες ἤδη μᾶλλον τῇ σωτηρίᾳ. Hæc causa, cur pecudum partus ante octavum diem Deo non consecrentur Exodi 22, 20. Fiebat autem circumcisio de die, ut res esset notior. Præputium in pulverem projicieba- tur. Poterat fieri circumcisio per Sacerdotes, per Levitas, per privatos, etiam per mulieres, non tamen per exleges.

TAM VERNACVLVS QVAM EMTITIVS) Incircum- cisus in terra quidem Ebræis data vivere poterat sub bonis legibus: non item in domo Hebræi alicujus, ne mores exem- plo diverso confunderentur.

## 17:14
vers. 14. THE MALE WHOSE FLESH OF THE FORESKIN SHALL NOT BE CIRCUMCISED, THAT SOUL SHALL BE CUT OFF FROM HIS PEOPLE) The Chaldean: he who shall not have cut off the flesh of his foreskin: that is, he who shall not have taken care to be circumcised when he has reached the proper age, say the 13th year, as the Hebrew Interpreters wish: for from that time, if parents and public parents, that is, Magistrates, have neglected it, he himself begins to be obligated. I do not know by whom the words τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ὀγδόῃ were badly added here in the Greek, as Augustine often cites it. Concerning circumcised peoples, see what was said in book I of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

There are those who think that the covenant of circumcision did not pertain to the Ishmaelites or the Keturahites: and they understand v. 10, THY SEED AFTER THEE, in such a way that it does not pertain to the Seed which was then Abraham's, or which was raised up to him while he was living, but to the seed raised up after Abraham in his family. But in that way, that covenant would not concern Isaac either, who was born while Abraham was living. Therefore, the words Thy seed after thee include all who were born of him, whether while he was living or after his death. For all those, as they were begotten by him, so also are they subsequent to him. The whole Seed of Abraham is therefore included, and therefore Ishmael also had to be circumcised. That the commandment of circumcision was given to Abraham first of all was also taught by Theodorus in a poem about the Jews, whose verses Eusebius, book 9 of the Evangelical Preparation, chapter 22, reports.

That the Ishmaelites have been circumcised from antiquity, although in that year of his age in which Ishmael was, Josephus is the author, book I, ch. 12, 13, and Origen in the dissertation against Fabius, which is also found in Eusebius, book VI, ch. 11. Whom Epiphanius calls Saracens against the Ebionites: and the Turks received this from the Saracens. Grotius teaches that the Keturæans observed the same rite of circumcision, book I, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, noting that Afer, a son from Keturah, whence the Africans, from the passage of Alexander Polyhistor brought forward by Josephus, book I, ch. 16, and Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book IX, ch. 10, is he who is 'Afer' to Moses, and thus teaching that the Ethiopians, who are a great part of the Africans, received circumcision from Abraham, which they also had in the time of Herodotus, and even now those of them who are Christians retain, not from the necessity of religion, but from reverence for a most ancient custom.

Latin:

vers. 14. MASCVLVS CVJVS PRÆPVTII CARO CIR- CVMCISA NON FVERIT, DELEBITVR ANIMA IL- LA DE POPVLO SVO) Chaldæus: qui non præciderit carnem præputii sui: id est, qui non curaverit se circumcidi, ubi ad justam ætatem pervenerit, annum puta 13. ut volunt Hebræi Interpretes: ex eo enim tempore, si parentes & publi- ci parentes, id est, Magistratus, neglexerint, ipse obligari in- cipit. Male hic nescio a quo additum in Græco τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ὀγδόῃ, quomodo sæpe citat Augustinus. De circumcisis popu- lis vide quæ ad lib. I. de Veritate Religionis Christianæ dicta.

Sunt qui circumcisionis fœdus non spectasse ad Ismaelitas, aut Cethuræos arbitrentur: & v. 10. SEMEN TUUM POST TE ita intelligant, ut non pertineat ad Semen, quod tum Abrahamo erat, aut quod eidem viventi excitatum fuit, sed ad semen post Abrahamum in familia ejus excitatum. Verum ita nec Isaacum, qui natus est Abrahamo vivente, fœdus illud concerneret. Verba itaque Se- men tuum post te complectuntur omnes, qui ab ipso nati sunt, vel vivente ipso, vel post fata ipsius. Illi enim omnes ut ab ipso procreati sunt, ita etiam ipso posteriores sunt. Totum ergo Semen Abrahæ com- prehenditur, & ideo etiam Ismael circumcidendus erat. Abrahamo primo omnium datum circum- cisionis præceptum etiam Theodorus docuit in car- mine de Judæis, cujus versus Euseb. lib. 9. præpar. Evang. c. 22. refert.

Ismaelitas ab antiquo circumcisos esse, etsi eo æta- tis anno, quo Ismael, Josephus autor est l. I. c. 12. 13. & Origenes in dissert. contra Fabum, quæ etiam apud Euseb. habetur l. VI. c. 11. Quos Sarracenos vocat Epiphanius contra Ebionæos : & a Sarrace- nis hoc acceperunt Turcæ. Eundem circumcisio- nis ritum Cethuræos observasse docet Grotius lib. I. de Ver. Religion. Christianæ, filium e Cethura Afer, unde Afri, ex Alexandri Polyhistoris loco a Josepho lib. I. c. 16. & Eusebio præparat. Evang. lib. IX. c. 10. adducto, illum esse notans, qui Mosi עפר, adeoque docens, Æthiopes, qui magna pars Afro- rum, circumcisionem ab Abrahamo accepisse, quam & Herodoti tempore habuerint, & nunc etiam qui eorum Christiani sunt, non ex religionis necessitate, sed ex vetustissimi moris reverentia, re- tineant.

## 17:20
ver. 20. HE SHALL BEGET TWELVE PRINCES) From these are the twelve phylarchs of the Arabs according to Strabo. The same are the phylarchs of the Saracens according to Menander Protector.

Latin:

vers. 20. DVODECIM DVCES GENERABIT) Ab his sunt duodecim Arabum φυλάρχοι apud Strabonem. Iidem Sarracenorum Phylarchi apud Menandrum Protectorem.

## 17:21
v. 21. BUT MY COVENANT I WILL ESTABLISH WITH ISAAC) Namely, of the nations: not merely personal, or of short duration.

These things are to be understood not of a covenant of the nations, but of the promise of the Messiah. For that was the principal covenant which God had entered into with Abraham: In Isaac shall thy seed be called. Which federal promise is now confirmed. For the lineage of the Messiah was restricted to Isaac: although Ishmael was excluded neither from the benefits of the Messiah, nor from the Sacrament of circumcision.

Latin:

v. 21. PACTVM VERO MEVM STATVAM AD ISAAC) Nempe gentilium : non mere personale, aut exigui temporis.

Non de pacto gentilitio, sed de promissione Messiæ hæc intelligenda. Nam illud erat fœdus præcipuum, quod cum Abrahamo inierat Deus: In Isaaco vocabitur tibi semen. Quæ promissio fœderalis nunc confirmatur. Prosapia enim Mes- siæ ad Isaacum restringebatur : etsi Ismael nec a Messiæ beneficiis, nec a Sacramento circumcisio- nis exclusus fuerit.

## 17:22
v. 22. GOD WENT UP FROM ABRAHAM.) The radiance of God. The Chaldean.

Truly the radiance of God, the brightness of the glory of God; the Son of God, Heb. 1, 3, whose day Abraham also saw here, John 8, 56, whose delights were to be with the sons of men, Prov. 8, 31. If, however, you wish that God the Father appeared here, since there is no certain character that proves a theophany of the Word, we do not object. Which the Chaldean translation hints at in v. 2: I will give my covenant between MY WORD and between thee. For it is accustomed for the most part to designate the hypostatic Son in this way: in whom, as the mediator of God and men, God gave his covenant.

Latin:

v. 22. ASCENDIT DEVS AB ABRAHAM.) Fulgor Dei. Chaldæus.

Vere Dei fulgor ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ; Filius Dei Ebr. 1, 3. cujus diem etiam hic vidit Abraham Joh. 8, 56. cujus deliciæ esse cum Filius ho- minum Prov. 8, 31. Si tamen velis, Deum Pa- trem hic apparuisse, quum nullus certus character sit, qui λογοφανείαν evincat, non refragamur. Quod translatio Chaldæa v. 2. innuit: Dabo fœdus meum inter VERBUM MEUM & inter te. Solet enim ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ita designare Filium ὑποστατικὸν: in quo ceu mediatore Dei & hominum Deus pa- ctum suum dedit.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

A theophany made to Abraham with the promise of a son from Sarah. The destruction of the Sodomites foretold with the intercession of Abraham.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

Θεοφανεία Abrahæ facta cum promissione filii ex Sara. Sodomorum eversio prædicta cum deprecatione Abrahæ.

## 18:2
ver. 2. THREE MEN APPEARED STANDING BY HIM) Homer, Odyssey P. 'And the gods, looking like strangers from other lands, taking all sorts of shapes, visit the cities, observing the insolence and the good order of men;' which compare with Heb. 13, 2.

Latin:

vers. 2. APPARVERVNT TRES VIRI STANTES JVXTA EVM) Homerus Odyss. P. Καί τε θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι, Παντοῖοι τελέθοντες ; ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας, Ἀνθρώπων ὕβριν τε καὶ εὐνομίην ἐφορῶντες. quæ confer cum Hebr. 13, 2.

## 18:3
V. 3. LORD) So also the Greeks, 'kyrie'. He addresses one eminent person, to whom the others were present as if companions and ministers. Yet this is plural, but for the sake of honor; as 'adonim' in Isa. 19, 4; therefore a verb of the singular number follows.

There was altogether one more honorable, whom Theodoret calls. To whom two attendant angels were present, as observed by Grotius at v. 31. That man, therefore, was not a minister, but the Lord of angels: he did not represent the person of God, which Grotius, along with the Jews, Socinians, and some Papists, wished to maintain at v. 22: But he was God himself: for Abraham is said there to have stood before the Lord, JEHOVAH. Not before an Angel, who represented the person of God; that is never denoted by לפני יהוה in the Scriptures, but before the Lord. He, therefore, who was present with Abraham, is expressly called Jehovah; whom Moses also calls by this name more frequently here, And Jehovah appeared to Abraham v. 1. And JEHOVAH was saying to Abraham v. 13. 14.

26. And v. 33. JEHOVAH was departing. Therefore Jehovah came to Abraham, Jehovah spoke with him, Jehovah stood by him, Jehovah departed from him, as Moses testifies. He never says that he was an Angel of the Lord, and he does not hint at it by any indication. Nor does he who appears here speak otherwise than as the true God. He testifies and proves himself to be a knower of hearts v. 13. 16. and omniscient v. 17. 19. and the avenger of all crimes, to whom sins cry out v. 20. who has the power of remitting sins, and of pardoning the supreme punishment impending over the whole Sodomite province: v. 26. 28. 29. 30. 31. 32. In which manner an Angel bearing the person of God never spoke. Thus, indeed, that more eminent guest manifested himself here with the marks of divinity and divine proofs, so that unless he is God Jehovah himself, it must never be believed that God Jehovah was seen or manifested himself. For he could not have manifested himself more clearly. Nor did Abraham doubt concerning him, but acknowledged the same as that supreme God, who alone has the power of destroying and saving, the judge of the whole earth v. 23. 24. 25. he acknowledged him as Jehovah, just as he called the same v. 27. 31. 32. Therefore he invoked the same, and prayed for indulgence toward the Sodomites, although he judged himself unworthy to speak with the Lord and to entreat the same v. 29. Which things cannot be understood of a created Angel: nor would any created angel have endured them. Rev. 19, 7. Ch. 22, 19. Wherefore that אֲדֹנָי with Kametz is not undeservedly recognized as plural, but used in the singular, which form indeed is never used for the sake of honor concerning some creature (that אֲדֹנָי in Is. 19, 4 is different, nor should it be confused with the Adonai with Kametz, a name, by the confession of all Rabbis, proper to God alone), but is always used of the supreme God, in whom there is some plurality of persons, or of some divine person, as one who is not without the other divine persons, since one is in the other, according to the essential περιχώρησιν. For this mystery is indicated by the use of the plural number, which appears even more clearly in the name Elohim.

Moreover, that this divine person was the Son of God is manifest from that character in particular, that he is called the judge of the whole earth. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son Joh. V, 21. Who is also the messenger and interpreter of the divine promise. Thus the Fathers with great consensus: Irenaeus l. IV. against Heresies c. 23. The Son of God is sown everywhere in the Scriptures, sometimes indeed speaking with Abraham, sometimes about to eat with the same, sometimes bringing judgment upon the Sodomites. Tertull. l. III. against Marc. He appeared with the Angels of the Lord to Abraham in the truth of flesh indeed, but not yet born, because not yet about to die, but already beginning to converse among men. See similar things concerning the flesh of Christ c. 17. Hilar. lib. IV. on the Trinity. Then, the three men having been seen, two depart, but he who remains is both Lord and God, and he is not only Lord and God, but is also judge. Chrysost. hom. XLII. in Gen. three indeed were seen in the tent of Abraham, both the Angels and their Lord at the same time; but afterwards they indeed were sent as ministers for the subversion of those cities. But the Lord himself remained and, as a friend with a friend, communicated with the just man what he was about to do. Most all the Fathers teach that the Son of God appeared here. In the second century with Irenaeus, Justin Martyr dial. with Trypho. Athenagoras Apol. Theophilus of Antioch l. II. to Autolycus. Tatian orat. II. against the Gentiles. In the third with Tertullian, Novatian on the Trinity c. 26. Clement of Alexandria V. Strom. Origen hom. IV. in Gen. lib. VI. against Celsus, Cyprian the Martyr lib. II.

against the Jews, ch. 8. and also the Fathers of the Council of Antioch in their Synodal Epistle to Samosatenus. This one, (the Son of God) Scripture says, descended, and appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, one of the three, with whom the Patriarch was conversing as with the Lord and judge, and who had received all judgment from the Father, of whom it is written, The Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord. In the fourth century with Hilary, and Chrysostom, Athanasius in orations II and IV against the Arians, Basil the Great in book II against Eunomius, Gregory of Nyssa in Euthymius, Nazianzen in oration II on Theology, Caesarius in Dialogue I to Constantius, Eusebius of Neo-Caesarea in book V of the Evangelical Demonstration, ch. 8, Epiphanius in the Ancoratus and heresy LXXI, Phoebadius against the Arians, ch. 54, Ambrose in the book on the faith against the Arians, ch. 8, Philastrius, Heresy 37, Jerome in Vol. I of his works in the Epitaph of Paula the mother, ch. V to Eustochium, and in his Commentary on Isaiah, ch. 7, on Daniel, ch. 8, Prudentius in the Apotheosis against Noetian. Finally, the Fathers of the Council of Sirmium; who decreed this under anathema as follows: if anyone should assert that Abraham did not see the Son, but the unbegotten God or His Father, let him be anathema, Canon XIV. Add also the Council of Ancyra. For that Sirmium Council praised this one in Epiphanius, heresy LXXIII. In the fifth century Sulpitius Severus, Paulinus of Nola in Epistle IV to Severus, Cyril of Alexandria in book III of the Thesaurus, ch. 2, book IX, ch. 3, Theodoret on Genesis, Q. 78, Cassian on the Incarnation, book IV, ch. 9, Isidore of Pelusium, book III, Epistle 188, Leo the Great, Epistle 13, Salvian, book I on the government of God, Vigilius, book V against Eutyches, etc., as also Gregory the Great, Homily 18 on the Gospels. Eusebius, book I of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 2, teaches that this was a common tradition, as does Constantine the Great in Eusebius, book III on the life of Constantine, ch. 51, which subsequently also prevailed, as witnessed by Nicephorus, book VIII of his History, ch. 30, Procopius of Gaza observes in his Commentary on this passage, that those were considered Judaizers who did not believe that one of those three was God, and that the remaining two were to be referred to the number of angels. Nor does Philo the Jew altogether deny this in his book on Abraham. The third, as far as I understand, was He who truly is. John Calvin also, who otherwise willingly Judaizes, confesses here with Vatablus that the Son of God appeared with two angels. Which those among the Papists, Masius and Fernandus, also acknowledge, and as many as ascribe the books of the Constitutions to Clement of Rome are bound to acknowledge, in which book V, ch. 21, it is held: Abraham received this one (the true Son of God) as a guest and confessed Him to be judge and his own Lord. Grotius, however, departs here from his own norm of interpretation, the consensus of the Fathers, and preferred to side with the Jews, and the Papists, and the Photinians, the enemies of the Deity of the Son of God. Blessed Augustine that it is not at all foreign to the opinion of the other Fathers here, neither Gregory the Great, nor Fulgentius or Bede, we have shown in our disputation on the pre-Abrahamic pre-existence of the Son of God, thesis XII and following. See also what we have said on this matter in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony, book 3, ch. 5. Compare also Mr. D. Dorscheus, collation on the Council of Sirmium, p. 140, and Mr. D. Clotz, Angelolatry, disp. V, p. 155, Andr. Rivetus, Commentary on Hosea, ch. 12.

Latin:

V. 3. DOMINE) Sic & Græci κύριε. Unum alloquitur eminentem, cui alteri velut comites ac ministri aderant. Est tamen hoc plurale, sed honoris causa ; ut אדנים Es. 19, 4. ideo sequitur verbum numeri unitatis.

ERat omnino unus τιμιώτερος, quem vocat Theodoretus. Cui duo aderant angeli stipatores, ut ad v. 31. observatum Grotio. Non ergo vir il- le erat minister, sed angelorum Dominus: non re- ferebat personam Dei, quod ad v. 22. cum Judæis, Socinestis & Pontificiis nonnullis voluit Grotius: Sed erat Deus ipse: Abraham enim ibi dicitur ste- tisse coram Domino, JEHOVAH. Non apud Angelum, qui Dei personam referebat; nunquam id לפני יהוה in Scripturis notat, sed apud Domi- num. Qui ergo aderat Abrahamo, diserte vocatur Jehovah; Quem etiam crebrius hoc nomine hic ap- pellat Moses, Et apparuit Jehovah Abrahamo v. 1. Et dicebat JEHOVAH ad Abrahamum v. 13. 14.

26. Et v. 33. discedebat JEHOVAH. Venit ergo ad Abraham Jehovah, loquutus est cum eo Jeho- vah, stetit apud eum Jehovah, discessit ab eo Jeho- vah, teste Mose. Nunquam Angelum fuisse Domini ait, ac ne ullo indicio id innuit. Neque aliter lo- quitur, qui hic apparet, quam verus Deus. Testa- tur & probat se καρδιογνώστην v. 13. 16. & omni- scium v. 17. 19. & vindicem omnium scelerum, ad quem peccata clamant v 20. qui potestatem habet re- mittendi peccata, & supplicium supremum univer- sæ provinciæ Sodomiticæ imminens condonandi: v. 26. 28. 29. 30. 31. 32. Quo pacto nunquam lo- quutus est Angelus Dei personam gerens. Ita profecto eminentior ille hospes divinitatis notis, & τεκμηρίοις divinis sese hic manifestavit, ut nisi ipse Deus Jehovah sit, nunquam Deum Jehovam vi- sum esse vel sese manifestasse credendum sit. Non enim poterat se manifestare luculentius. Neque dubitavit de eo Abraham, sed agnovit eundem summum illum Deum, qui unus potestatem habet perdendi & salvandi, judicem universæ terræ v. 23. 24. 25. agnovit ipsum Jehovam, uti vocavit eun- dem v. 27. 31. 32. Ideo invocavit eundem, ac indul- gentiam adversus Sodomitas oravit, quamvis indi- gnum sese judicarit, qui cum Domino loqueretur, & eundem deprecaretur v. 29. Quæ de Angelo creato intelligi nequeunt: neque ea etiam crea- tus quispiam angelus tulisset. Apoc. 19, 7. C. 22, 19. Quapropter illud אֲדֹנָי cum Kametz non immerito agnoscitur plurale, sed in singulari adhibitum, qua vero forma nunquam honoris causa de creatura quadam (illud אֲדֹנָי Es. 19, 4. diversum est, neq; cum Adonai Kamezato, nomine, confessione omnium Rabbinorum soli Deo proprio, confundi debet) semper de Deo summo adhibetur, in quo aliqua est personarum pluralitas, vel de persona aliqua divina, utpote quæ non est sine reliquis divi- nis personis, quum una sit in alia, secundum περι- χώρησιν essentialem. Hoc enim mysterium usus pluralis numeri indicat, quod in nomine Elohim adhuc luculentius apparet.

Personam autem hanc divinam Filium Dei fuisse ex illo imprimis charactere, quod vocetur judex universæ terræ, manifestum est. Non enim Pater judicat quenquam, sed Filio dedit omne judi- cium Joh. V, 21. Qui etiam nuncius est & interpres divinæ promissionis. Ita Patres magno consensu: Irenæus l. IV. contra Hæres. c. 23. Inseminatus ubique est in Scripturis Filius Dei, aliquando quidem cum Abrahamo loquens, aliquando cum eodem come- surus, aliquando Sodomitis inducens judicium. Ter- tull. l. III. advers. Marc. Ipse cum Angelis Domini apud Abraham in veritate quidem carnis apparuit, sed nondum natæ, quia nondum morituræ, sed edifcen- tis jam inter homines conversari. Videantur simi- lia de carn. Christi c. 17. Hilar. lib. IV. de Trinit. Viris deinde conspectis tribus, duo abeunt, sed qui resi- det & Dominus & Deus est, neque solum Dominus & Deus est, sed & judex est. Chrysost. hom. XLII. in Gen. tres quidem in tabernaculo Abrahæ & Angeli & eorum Dominus per idem tempus visi sunt; postea vero illi quidem ut ministri missi sunt ad subversio- nem illarum civitatum. Ipse autem Dominus man- sit & quasi amicus cum amico justo communicabat, quænam facturus esset. Plerique omnes Patres Fi- lium Dei hic apparuisse docent. Seculo secundo cum Irenēo, Justinus Martyr. dial. cum Triph. Athenagoras Apol. Theophil. Antiochen. l. II. ad Autolyc. Tatian. orat. II. contr. Gent. Tertio cum Tertulliano Novatianus de Trinit. c. 26. Clemens Alexandr. V. Strom. Origenes hom. IV. in Gen. lib. VI. contra Celsum, Cyprianus Martyr. lib. II.

advers. Jud. c. 8. nec non Patres Concilii Antioche- ni Epist. Synod. ad Samosat. Hunc, (Filium Dei) dicit Scriptura, descendisse, & Abrahae apparuisse ad quercum Mamre, unum ex tribus, cum quo Pa- triarcha, tanquam cum Domino & judice colloque- batur, & qui omne judicium accepisset a Patre, de quo scriptum est, Dominus pluit ignem & sulphur a Domino. Seculo quarto cum Hilario, & Chry- sostomo, Athanasius orat. II. & IV. contra Arian. Basilius M. l. II. contr. Eunom. Gregorius Nysse- nus apud Euthymium, Nazianzen. orat. II. de Theol. Cæsarius Dial. I. ad Constant. Eusebius Neo-Cæsariens. lib. V. demonstr. Evangel. c. 8. Epiphanius in Ancorat. & hæres. LXXI. Phœba- dius contr. Arian. c. 54. Ambrosius l. de fid. contr. Arian. c. 8. Philastr. Hæres. 37. Hieronymus T. I. oper. in Epitaph. Paulæ matris c. V. ad Eustoch. & Comment. in Es. c. 7. in Dan. c. 8. Prudentius in Apotheos. contr. Noetian. Denique Patres Concilii Syrmiensis; qui id sub anathemate ita san- rivere: si quis Abraham non Filium, sed ingenitum Deum aut Patrem ejus vidisse assereret, anathema est Can. XIV. adde & Synodum Ancyranam. Hanc enim laudavit Syrmiense illud Concilium apud Epiphanium hær. LXXIII. Seculo quinto Sulpitius Severus, Paulinus Nolanus Epist. IV. ad Sever. Cy- rillus Alexandr. lib. III. Thes. c. 2. lib. IX. cap. 3. Theodoretus in Gen. Q. 78. Cassianus de incarnat. lib. IV. c. 9. Isidorus Pelusiota l. III. Epist. 188. Leo M. Epist. 13. Salvianus l. I. de gubernat. Dei. Vi- gilius l. V. contr. Eutych. &c. ut & Gregor. M. Homil. 18. in Evangel. Eusebius l. I. Hist. Eccl. c. 2. communem hanc traditionem fuisse docet, ut & Constantinus M. apud Eusebium l. III. de vit. Constantini c. 51. quæ deinceps quoque obtinuit, teste Nicephoro l. IIX. Histor. c. 30. Procopius Gazæus observat in Comment. ad h. l. illos Judai- zantes habitos, qui non credidere ex tribus illis unum esse Deum, reliquos duos in Angelorum numerum esse referendos. Nec abnuit omnino hic Philo Ju- dæus l. de Abrah. Tertius, quantum ego quidem in- telligo, erat ille, qui vere est. Johannes Calvinus etiam, qui libenter alias judaizat, Filium Dei cum Angelis duobus apparuisse hic cum Vatablo fatetur. Quod agnoscunt quoque e Pontificiis Masius & Fernandus, & agnoscere tenentur, quotquot Cle- menti Rom. libros Constitut. adscribunt, in qui- bus lib. V. c. 21. habetur: Hunc (verum Dei Fi- lium) Abraham hospitio exceptum judicem, suum- que Dominum confessus est. Grotius vero hic a sua interpretationis norma, consensu Patrum, discedit, Judæisque accedere maluit, ac Papistis, & Deitatis Filii Dei hostibus Photinianis. B. Augustin. non alienum omnino esse hic a cæterorum Patrum sen- tentia, neque Gregorium M. neque Fulgentium aut Bedam, disput. de προϋπάρξει Filii Dei Ante-Abra- hamica th. XII. seqq. ostendimus. Vide etiam, quæ hac de re diximus in Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica l. 3. c. 5. Conf. item Dn. D. Dorscheus, collat. ad Concil. Syrm. p. 140. ac Dn. D. Clotz Angelolatr. disp. V. p. 155. Andr. Rivetus Comment. in Hos. c. 12.

## 18:5
Verse 5. AND I WILL SET A MORSEL OF BREAD.) Abraham, as a good man, promises a little, gives much: see below 8.

It seems that the custom of the Hebrew language has escaped the Great Man, by which all kinds of food are denoted by bread, Isaiah 58, 7, and elsewhere.

FOR THEREFORE HAVE YOU TURNED ASIDE TO YOUR SERVANT) כִּי־עַל־כֵּן here is 'since'. Since you have turned aside here, it is fair that you should take food with me.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PONAMQVE BVCCELLAM PANIS.) Abra- ham, ut vir bonus, paullum pollicetur, dat multa: vid. in- fra 8.

Excidisse videtur Viro Magno consuetudo linguæ Ebrææ, qua per panem notantur omnis generis esculenta, Es. 58, 7. & alibi.

IDCIRCO ENIM DECLINASTIS AD SERVUM VESTRVM) כִּי־עַל־כֵּן hic est quandoquidem. Quando hic divertisstis, æquum est ut cibum sumatis mecum.

## 18:6
V. 6. TO SARAH, AND HE SAID TO HER) Leaving to the mother of the family her duties in the house.

Latin:

V. 6. AD SARAM, DIXITQVE EI) Relinquens matri familias suas in domo partes.

## 18:10
V. 10. I WILL CERTAINLY RETURN TO YOU AT THIS TIME, LIFE BEING COMPANION) I will find you alive.

So indeed the Chaldean: according to the time in which you (will be) alive or safe. And the Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum: In the coming year, and you (will be) safe. Which sense R. Solomon and Abenezra also render. Fagius, see from the collation of 2 Kings 4, as also Gualtperius: according to the time of life, that is, according to the manner in which an infant is accustomed to be quickened in the womb and born, so Isaac also will be quickened and born. Which opinion does not seem inappropriate.

Latin:

V. 10. REVERTENS VENIAM AD TE TEMPORE ISTO, VITA COMITE) Vivos vos reperiam.

Ita quidem Chaldæus: secundum tempus, quo vos (eritis) vivi seu incolumes. Et Targum Jonath. & Hierosolym. Anno futuro, & vos (eritis) incolu- mes. Quem sensum etiam reddit R. Salomo & Abenezra. Fagius v. e collatione 2. Reg. 4. ut & Gualtperius juxta tempus vitæ, id est, secundum mo- rem, quo solet infans vivificari in utero & nasci, ita vivificabitur & nascetur Isaac quoque. Quæ sen- tentia non videtur inconcinna.

## 18:18
Verse 18. IN HIM SHALL ALL THE NATIONS OF THE EARTH BE BLESSED.) From him and his descendants they will learn that there is one God, the author of all things.

See what we have said about this gloss on ch. 12, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 18. BENEDICENDÆ SUNT IN ILLO OMNES NATIONES TERRÆ.) Ab ipso posterisque ejus discent, unum esse Deum rerum omnium auctorem.

Vide, quæ de hac glossa diximus ad c. 12, 3.

## 18:19
THAT THEY MAY KEEP THE WAY OF THE LORD AND DO JUDGMENT AND JUSTICE.) When justice is distinguished from judgment, it signifies beneficence. By these words that law before the law of Moses is comprehended.

V. 19. FOR I KNOW THAT HE WILL COMMAND HIS CHILDREN) Or rather: I know that he is a teacher of his children, that is, I know this is his custom, that what he himself has learned, he teaches his own. Therefore I will make him a participant in my counsel.

The law before Moses was not exhausted by judgment and beneficence. There were many other chapters of it. The entire Decalogue was inscribed upon the human mind in the primeval creation. Although these notions were for the most part obliterated by the fall, the pagans, destitute of all revelation of the word, are witnesses that many precepts flowed from the remaining sparks. For those things only concern the second table, concerning which, however, many things were also known through the light of nature. Furthermore, to exercise justice and judgment was required even after the law was given, Ps. 106, 3. 119, 21. Is. 56, 1. ch. 58, 2. Ez. 18, 3. 27. ch. 33, 14. 16. 19. and without doubt something more than what the law before Moses, according to Grotius, comprehends. According to some, this phrase generally implies good works and equity; others say justice is when to each his own is attributed; judgment, however, when moderation is applied, in the reverse manner to what Grotius wishes. Flacius does not badly distinguish between the common, forensic, spiritual, and ecclesiastical use: the former admits the explanation already stated; by the latter, he wishes judgment to designate the condemnation of the guilty, and justice the absolution of the innocent, or even by the former the adjudication, and by the latter the execution of the judged matter: but in this ecclesiastical sense, he refers judgment to the Law, and justice to the Gospel, which are the two parts of the way of the Lord.

Latin:

UT CUSTODIANT VIAM DOMINI ET FACIANT JUDICIUM ET JUSTITIAM.) Justitia cum a judicio di- stinguitur, beneficentiam significat. His verbis compre- henditur lex illa ante legem Mosis.

V. 19. SCIO ENIM QVOD PRÆCEPTURUS SIT FILIIS SUIS) Aut potius: Scio eum præceptorem esse filio- rum suorum, id est, scio hunc morem esse illi, ut quæ didi- cit ipse, ea doceat suos. Ideo participem eum consilii mei faciam.

Lex ante Mosen non absolvebatur judicio & beneficentia. Erant multa alia ejus capita. Decalo- gus universus humanæ menti inscriptus est in primæva creatione. Quæ notitiæ etsi per lapsum obliteratæ sint maximam partem, e residuis tamen scintillis præcepta plura redundasse, pagani omni revelatione verbi destituti testimonio sunt. Ista enim tantum concernunt tabulam secundam, de qua tamen etiam plura per naturæ lumen cognita sunt. Cæterum justitiam & judicium exercere etiam post legem latam requisitum fuit Ps. 106, 3. 119, 21. Es. 56, 1. c. 58, 2. Ez. 18, 3. 27. c. 33, 14. 16. 19. ac fine dubio aliquid amplius, quam quod lex ante Mosen juxta Grotium, comprehendit. Juxta quosdam phrasis hæc γενικῶς bona opera & æquita- tem infert; alii justitiam dicunt, cum suum cuique tribuitur; judicium vero cum moderatio adhibe- tur, inversa, quam vult Grotius, ratione. Flacius non male distinguit inter usum vulgarem, forensem & spiritualem, atque Ecclesiasticum: Isto jam dictam explicationem admittit; illo per judicium conde- mnationem nocentum, per justitiam innocentium absolutionem, vel etiam priori dijudicationem, po- steriori rei judicatæ exequutionem designari vult: Hoc autem Ecclesiastico sensu judicium ad legem, justitiam ad Evangelium refert, quæ duæ partes sunt viæ Domini.

## 18:21
v. 21. I WILL GO DOWN) By the Angels. All these kinds of speaking are tempered to the form of human judgments.

A bold addition. For where does the Lord say He will go down by the angels? He speaks of Himself, not of the Angels. However, the customary figure occurs. For God is said to descend when He manifests Himself on earth, as an inspector, judge, or for another reason.

THE CRY WHICH HAS COME TO ME) Homer: Τῶν ὕβρις τε βίηλε σιδήρεον ὐρανὸν ἧκει.

HAVE COMPLETED THE WORK) The Chaldean: have caused to cease, that is, have shown repentance. Not badly, for often כלה signifies to abstain, to pause, to rest. There are many places: it will suffice to see Num. 17, 10.

IS IT NOT SO THAT I MAY KNOW) In the Hebrew: If not, I will know, that is, according to the Chaldean interpreter: if they have not yet repented, I may know what I must do. In the tenth generation the flood was sent upon the world: in the tenth generation after that, Sodom was punished: signs of long-suffering.

Latin:

v. 21. DESCENDAM) Per Angelos. Omnia hæc loquen- di genera ad formam judiciorum humanorum temperantur.

Audax additio. Ubi enim per angelos de- scensurum se ait Dominus? De se, non de Angelis loquitur. Occurrit autem usitata figura. Descen- dere enim Deus dicitur, cum se in terra manifestat, ut inspectorem, judicem aut alia ratione.

CLAMOREM QVI VENIT AD ME) Homerus: Τῶν ὕβρις τε βίηλε σιδήρεον ὐρανὸν ἧκει.

OPERE COMPLEVERINT) Chaldæus: cessare fecerint, id est pœnitentiam ostenderint. Non male, sæpe enim כלה significat ἀπέχειν, παύειν, ἀναπαύειν. Multa sunt loca: suffi- ciet videre Num. 17, 10.

AN NON EST ITA UT SCIAM) In Hebræo: Sinon, sciam, id est, Chaldæo interprete: si nondum resipuerint, norim quid mihi agendum sit. Decima generatione im- missum orbi diluvium: decima post id generatione punita Sodoma: signa longanimitatis.

## 18:22
v. 22. AND THEY TURNED FROM THENCE) Namely, those two attendant Angels.

BUT ABRAHAM WAS STANDING BEFORE THE LORD) That is, he was praying, as the Chaldean interprets here. For עמד is prayer, says Maimonides. See what is noted on Matt. 6, 5.

before the Lord, לפני יהוה in the presence of the Angel, who was representing the person of God: Whence below 32, 30. The Angel is called פניאל πρόσωπον θεũ by Josephus. Thus shortly in verse 26. & 33. Jud. VI, 19. & elsewhere the Angel is called יהוה.

To stand before the Lord, although otherwise it might perhaps signify the same thing as prayer, here however it denotes that which the letter implies and the proper meaning of the word.
