The Lord appeared to Abraham, having entered into the tent, and when the three men are seen turning themselves toward Sodom, Abraham is said to have accompanied them, and the Lord continued to speak to Abraham: but when the attendant Angels also turned themselves toward Sodom, Abraham still stood before the Lord, and he approached him and said: Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? The conversation finally finished, the Lord went away, after he ceased speaking to Abraham. Although therefore the end, why he stood before the Lord and approached him, was properly prayer, and intercession for the Sodomites; yet that standing here is not praying. Nor is standing before the Lord standing before an Angel representing the person of the Lord. Nowhere is this phrase so accepted. Nor does the context allow these things to be understood of a created Angel. That the Lord himself appeared in person, in the form of a man, however, which he assumed, is too manifest. Below XXXII, 30. not the Angel is called פניאל the face of the Lord, but the place in which the Angel appeared. If you say that he received the name of Angel, the Angel who appeared certainly was not created, but the Son of God himself, the uncreated Angel, the face of the Lord. The express image of his person and the Angel of the face of the Lord, as he is called Heb. 1, 3. Isa. 63, 9. Neither in Jud. 6, 19. nor elsewhere are created Angels called by the name of Jehovah, which is called incommunicable and the explicit name. It is read of no one except the one Angel, who is the same Jehovah, an angel, as he was sent by the Father, Jehovah, as he is one with the Father, John 10, 30; of another it occurs nowhere throughout the whole Scripture.

Latin:

v. 22. CONVERTERVNTQVE INDE) Nempe duo illi stipatores Angeli.

ABRAHAM VERO STABAT CORAM DOMINO) Id est, orabat, ut hic interpretatur Chaldæus. עמד enim est oratio, ait Maimonides. Vide, quæ notata ad Matth. 6, 5.

coram Domino, לפני יהוה apud Angelum, qui Dei per- sonam referebat: Unde infra 32, 30. Angelus appellatur פניאל πρόσωπον θεũ Josepho. Sic mox commate 26. & 33. Jud. VI, 19. & alibi Angelus dicitur יהוה.

Stare coram Domino, etsi alias forte idem si- gnificare possit, quod oratio, hic tamen id notat, quod litera infert ac propria vocis significatio. Ap- paruit Dominus Abrahamo, ingressus in taberna- culum, & cum tres viri videantur versus Sodomam sese convertere, Abraham comitatus illos dicitur, ac Dominus loqui ad Abrahamum perrexit: cum vero Angeli stipatores se etiam adversus Sodo- mam converterent, adhuc coram Domino stetit Abraham, & accessit ad eum & dixit: Num justum perdes cum iniquo? Finito tandem colloquio abiit Dominus, postquam cessavit loqui ad Abraham. Licet ergo finis, cur staret coram Domino & acce- deret ad ipsum, proprius fuerit oratio, & interpella- tio pro Sodomitis; non tamen illud stare hic est orare. Nec coram Domino stare est coram Angelo personam Domini repræsentante. Nuspiam hæc phrasis ita accipitur. Nec contextus patitur, de Angelo creato hæc intelligi. Dominum ipsum αὐ- τοπροσώπως apparuisse, in forma tamen viri, quam assumsit, nimis est manifestum. Infra XXXII, 30. non Angelus vocatur פניאל facies Domini, sed lo- cus, in quo apparuit Angelus. Quem si nomen Angeli accepisse dicas, Angelus, qui apparuit, cer- te non fuit creatus, sed ipse Filius Dei, increatus Angelus, facies Domini. χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτũ & Angelus faciei Domini, uti vocatur Ebr. 1, 3. Esa. 63, 9. Neque Jud. 6, 19. neque alibi creati Angeli Jehovæ nomine, quod ἀκοινώνητον & שם המפורש appellantur. Non nisi de uno Angelo, qui idem Jehovah est, angelus, qua missus a Patre, Jehovah, qua unum cum Patre, Joh. 10, 30. legi- tur; de alio nuspiam occurrit per totam Scri- pturam.

## 18:30
Ver. 30. I WILL NOT DO) That is, I will not strike, from that which preceded.

Latin:

Vers. 30. NON FACIAM) Id est, non percutiam, ex eo quod præcessit.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. The destruction of Sodom, and the incest of Lot.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. Excidium Sodomæ, & Lothi incestus.

## 19:3
Ver. 3. AND HE BAKED UNLEAVENED BREAD) As in great haste, those who were prepared for the family not being sufficient.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET COXIT AZTMA) Ut in magna festinatio- ne non sufficientibus, qui familiæ parati erant, panibus.

## 19:8
Ver. 8. ABUSE THEM) From the Greek χρᾶσθε ἀυταῖς the Hebrews עשׂו. Thus also it is taken by the Latins to do. There was in Lot a praiseworthy goodness, but a weak faith. Therefore he is called by Philo unjust, ambiguous.

By the Holy Spirit, whose judgment was rather to be feared, he is celebrated, 2 Pet. 2, 7. 8. 9. as righteous, a righteous soul, godly, whom God, on account of faith, without which there is no righteousness, nor can anyone please God, delivered from those who tormented him from day to day.

Furthermore, that Lot here wishes to prostitute his daughters cannot be excused from sin with Chrysostom, Thomas, Cajetan, because evils are not to be done so that evils may be avoided, Rom. 3, 8. yet it proceeded from perturbation of mind and lack of counsel, not with an evil mind, since he wished to spare his guests, and that was without doubt amended through repentance.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ABUTIMINI EIS) Ex Græco χρᾶσθε ἀυταῖς Hebræi עשׂו. Sic & Latinis sumitur facere. Erat in Lotho bonitas laudabilis, sed fides tenuis. Ideo Philoni dicitur ἀδίϰαιῶ, ὑπαμφίβολος.

ASpiritu Sancto, cujus judicium potius offen- dendum erat, celebratur, 2. Petr. 2, 7. 8. 9. ceu δίκαιος, ψυχὴ δικαία, ἐυσεβὴς, quem Deus, ob fi- dem, sine qua nulla est justitia, nec Deo placere quis potest, eripuerit ab iis, qui ipsum de die in diem torferint.

Cæterum quod hic prostituere vult Loth fi- lias suas, excusari a peccato non potest cum Chry- sost. Thoma, Cajetano, quia non sunt facienda mala, ut evitentur mala, Rom. 3, 8. profectum tamen id ex perturbatione animi & inopia consilii, animo non malo, cum hospitibus suis parci vellet, idque per pœnitentiam sine dubio emendatum fuit.

## 19:9
Ver. 9. YOU HAVE ENTERED, AS A STRANGER) Thus enemies called Cicero the Arpinate Romulus.

Latin:

Vers. 9. INGRESSUS ES, UT ADVENA) Sic Cicero- nem inimici vocabant Romulum Arpinatem.

## 19:11
Vers. 11. THEY STRUCK WITH BLINDNESS) With a scotoma, such as you have in 2 Kings 6:18.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PERCUSSERUNT CÆCITATE) Scotomate, quale habes 2. Reg. 6, 18.

## 19:14
Vers. 14. AND HE APPEARED TO THEM AS IF JOKING) They did not think that God would take vengeance so severely and suddenly. They also sin who extend the mercy of God further than is right.

Indeed, they utterly despised such threats and held them for play and a joke. In Lot, an example of faith is proposed; in Lot's sons-in-law, an example of carnal security: the former is followed by deliverance, the latter by destruction and ruin. But why did he give his daughters to such impious men? Since Abraham had no sons or grandsons, and the neighboring Canaanites were no better than the Sodomites, he judged that he would act more rightly if he gave his daughters to the Sodomites, whom he could enlighten with pious instruction and holy example, and whom he could keep in line by his presence.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ET VISUS EST EIS QVASI LUDENS LO- QVI) Non putabant Deum tam severe ac subito vindictam sumturum. Peccant & qui Dei misericordiam ultra quam rectum est extendunt.

Imo contemnebant prorsus tales commina- tiones & pro ludo ac joco habebant. In Lotho exemplum fidei; in generis Lothi exemplum car- nalis securitatis proponitur: illam sequitur libera- tio, hanc exitium & interitus. Cur vero tam im- piis hominibus filias suas elocavit? Cum Abraham non haberet filios, vel nepotes, ac vicini Cananæi Sodomitis nihilo meliores essent, judicavit se re- ctius facturum, si filias suas elocaret Sodomitis, quibus pia informatione, sanctoque exemplo præ- lucere, quosque præsentia sua in officio continere posset.

## 19:15
Vers. 15. THE TWO DAUGHTERS WHOM YOU HAVE) Not given in marriage, but who are virgins in your household.

Grotius thinks that Lot had more daughters, namely others given in marriage who remained in Sodom, and others who were virgins. But that does not appear from the history; indeed, it is rather hinted here that he had only two daughters, whom he snatched from the fire with his wife.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DUAS FILIAS QVAS HABES) Non eloca- tas, sed quæ virgines in tuo sunt lare.

Putat Grotius, plures habuisse Lothum fi- lias, alias nempe elocatas, quæ remanserint in So- doma, alias virgines. Sed id ex historia non appa- ret: imo hic potius innuitur, eum solum duas ha- buisse filias, quas ex incendio eripuerit cum con- juge.

## 19:16
V. 16. WHILE HE HESITATED. The LXX: ἐταράχθησαν, and they were troubled. But the Hebrew text has, he lingered, as Aquila: ἐμέλλησε. Lot was delaying, either because he wanted to induce his sons-in-law to join them, as Ambrose says, or because he was packing up his household goods, as the Greek Scholiast and Rupert think.

Latin:

V. 16. DISSIMULANTE ILLO. LXX. ἐταράχθησαν, & turbati sunt. Sed Ebraicus textus habet, cunctabatur, uti Aquila, ἐμέλλησε. Moras autem nectebat Loth, sive quod generos ad societatem inducere vellet, ut Ambro- sius, sive quod supellectilem componeret, ut Græ- cus Scholiastes ac Rupertus putant.

## 19:17
Vers. 17. DO NOT LOOK BEHIND YOU) In the Pythagorean sayings: when departing from the house, do not look back. The fable about Orpheus points to the same thing. Hannibal also was forbidden by a specter to look back. Cicero is a witness in the first book of On Divination.

BUT SAVE YOURSELF IN THE MOUNTAIN) Similar to that in Metamorphoses 8: The neighborhood shall pay the deserved penalty for its impiety, they said: to you it shall be granted to be immune from this evil: only leave your roofs, and accompany our steps, and go together into the heights of the mountain.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NOLI RESPICERE POST TERGUM) In dictis Pythagoricis: ἀποδημῶν τῆς οἰκίας μὴ ἀποσρέφῦ. Eo- dem spectat de Orpheo fabula. Annibal quoque a spectro vetitus respicere. Cicero testis de divinatione primo.

SED IN MONTE SALVUM TE FAC) Simile illud Metamorphos. 8. - - meritasq; luet vicinia pœnas Impia, dixerunt: vobis immunibus hujus Esse mali dabitur: modo vestra relinquite tecta, Ac nostros comitate gradus & in ardua montis Ite simul.

## 19:19
Vers. 19. THAT YOU MIGHT SAVE) In Hebrew להחיות, to make alive. The Greeks: τῦ ζῆν τὴν ψυχήν με. Because the Greeks do not have a Hiphil, the Greek translators use a Greek active for it. Thus they say βασιλέυειν for to make to reign. Symmachus is more expressive: ζωῶσαι.

Latin:

Vers. 19. UT SALVARES) Hebraice להחיות ad vivificandum. Græci τῦ ζῆν τὴν ψυχήν με. Quia enim Græci Hiphil non habent, Græci interpretes activo Græco pro eo utuntur. Sic dicunt βασιλέυειν pro facere regnare. Symmachus expressius ζωῶσαι.

## 19:21
Vers. 21. I HAVE ACCEPTED YOUR PRAYERS) In Hebrew, I have accepted your face, that is, I have had regard for you.

Latin:

Vers. 21. SUSCEPI PRECES TUAS) Hebraice suscepi faciem tuam, id est, respectum tui habui.

## 19:22
Vers. 22. SEGOR) From the Greek Σηγώρ. In Hebrew צוער. Perhaps Zoara in Arabia according to Ptolemy.

Theodoret, Procopius, Suidas, and Lyranus think that it also perished after Lot betook himself to the mountain, but that is contradicted by the divine promise in v. 20, and travelers testify that Zoar still survives, which is commemorated in Isaiah 15:5. Therefore Jerome, in On Hebrew Places, says: Bela, which is Segor, is now called Zoara, the only one of the 5 cities reserved by the prayers of Lot. It overlooks the Dead Sea, and a garrison of Roman soldiers is stationed in it. But as to the fact that in Wisdom 10:6 fire is said to have descended upon the Pentapolis, it is to be understood that the whole region was exposed to danger, even if one city was saved from it by a special grace. Compare Deuteronomy 29:23, Hosea 11:8, Amos 4:11.

Latin:

Vers. 22. SEGOR) Ex Græco Σηγώρ. Hebraice צוער. Zoara forte Ptolemæo in Arabia.

Theodor. Procop. Suidas, & Lyran. putant, eam etiam periisse, postquam Loth in montem se contulit, sed id refragatur divinæ promissioni v. 20. & testantur peregrinationes etiamnum Zoar superesse, quæ commemoratur in Es. 15, 5. ideo Hieron. in de loc. Ebr. Bela, inquit, quæ est Segor, nunc Zoara nuncupatur, sola de 5. urbibus Loth pre- cibus reservata. Imminet autem mari mortuo, & præsidium in ea est positum militum Romanorum. Quod vero Sap. 10, 6. ignis in Pentapolim descen- disse dicitur, ita intelligendum est, quod regio tota periculo exposita fuerit, etsi ex eadem civitas una peculiari gratia servata sit. Conf. Deuter. 29, 23. Hos. 11, 8. Amos. 4, 11.

## 19:24
Vers. 24. THE LORD RAINED.) יהוה that is, that Angel, who, as we have said, sustained the person of God. RAINED) In the Hebrew, he caused to rain. FROM THE LORD) By power divinely granted to him.

That an Angel thus sustains the person of God is a Rabbinical-Socinian fiction. Which we expressly refute in Natural and Revealed Theology, chap. 2, page 326. We have already shown that it was not a created Angel who appeared to Abraham, but Jehovah himself. Therefore, the same is said here to have rained, or to have caused to rain, from Jehovah God the Father. Because whatsoever the Father does, the same also the Son does likewise, John 5:19, who as he is from the Father, so he also works from the Father, to whom the Father has also given all judgment. The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing. That, therefore, from the Lord denotes not dependency or a ministerial power granted by God, but the origin of the Son from the Father. In Hebrew the emphasis is greater: The Lord rained מֵאֵת A with the Lord, because the Son works both from the Father and with the Father. The former on account of the origin of the hypostasis: the latter on account of the identity of essence; therefore mention is made of the plural אֱלֹהִים, who are said to have overthrown Sodom and Gomorrah, certainly not of Angels, but of those who are that one God. Am. 4, 11. Jer. 50, 40. Nor does an Angel representing the person of God rain or cause to rain. No such thing is read, namely that in these and similar matters pertaining to the work of preservation, another bears the person of God, and sends down rain, for example, fire and brimstone from Heaven, which are the works of God himself, who effects them either mediately or immediately, and not indeed a creature bearing the person of God. Nor is the overthrow of Sodom ever ascribed to an Angel in Scripture, but always to GOD. Therefore the Council of Sirmium in Canon XVI struck with anathema those who do not understand this of the Father and of the Son. For the Lord the Son rained from the Lord the Father. Which orthodox Sirmian formula is different from the formula forged by the Arians in the Council of Sirmium, and thus approved not only by Socrates, Book II, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 34, and Sozomen, Book IV, ch. 5, 6, but also by Hilary, On the Synods against the Arians, Epiphanius, Heresy LXXIII, Vigilius against Eutyches, Book V, Philastrius, Heresy XXXVII, and also praised by the Synod of Ancyra, as Epiphanius testifies. The same was the opinion of all the Fathers commonly. Ignatius, Epistle to the Antiochians; Justin, Dialogue with Trypho; Irenaeus, Book III, ch. 3; Tertullian, Against Praxeas, ch. 13 and 16, Book IV, Against Marcion, ch. 39; Cyprian, Against the Jews, Book II, ch. 33; Athanasius, Oration against the Gregal-Sabellians; Eusebius, Book VII, On the Preparation for the Gospel. ch. 5, Book XI, ch. 9, and Book V, Demonstration of the Gospel, ch. 8. Hilary, Book V, On the Trinity; Epiphanius in the Ancoratus and in the Samaritan heresy, no. V; Gregory of Nyssa, On the Knowledge of God and On the Trinity; Basil the Great, Against Eunomius; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration III, On Theology; Chrysostom, Homily on the Trinity, Vol. III; Philastrius, Heresy VIII; Jerome on Hosea 1, 7; Augustine, Vol. IV, on Genesis, q. 59, and Vol. VI, On Heresies, ch. 33; Theodoret, Book II, On the Cure of Greek Affections; Cyril, Book I, Against Julian, and Book IX, Thesaurus, ch. 3; Prudentius in the Apotheosis; Idacius Clarus, Heresiology; Euthymius Zigabenus, Panoplia, p. 1; Marius Victorinus the African, Book I, Against the Arians; Isidore of Pelusium, Book II, Epistle 143; Isidore of Seville, Vol. I, On the Nativity. of the Lord, ch. 3, to which, along with the great Luther, our own people, all of them to a man, including from the Calvinists Bullinger, Franciscus Junius, Bucanus, Sohnius, Polanus, Hornbeck, and others; and from the Papists Delrio, Bonfrerius, Serarius, Cornelius a Lapide, Ruizius, Menochius, and others, subscribe. What is more, even the Chaldean paraphrases favor it. Targum Jonathan: the word of Jehovah sent down benign rains upon Sodom and Gomorrah so that they might repent: Who said: evil works are not revealed before Jehovah. Therefore, brimstone and fire were sent down upon them from the word of Jehovah from the heavens. Similar things are also read in the Jerusalem Targum. We have defended the passage more fully with an invincible assertion of the plurality of the divine persons from the O.T., ch. XVI.

Verse of the same. FROM HEAVEN) So also Luke 17, 29. Naturally, that sulfurous fire came from nowhere else but from heaven. Tacitus, Histories V, says that these cities burned with heavenly fire; he had said before, by the casting of lightning bolts. For lightning also has the power of sulfur, and thence in Greek sulfur is called θεῖον. Strabo said, asphaltic and sulfurous waters.

INTO A STATUE OF SALT) That is, a pillar. For thus this interpreter often uses the word statue here. But salt had fallen with the fire from heaven. See above 14, 3. Deut. 29, 23. Josephus says that this pillar existed in his own time. The Jerusalem Paraphrase says it will always remain. See also Burchard and others who have been there.

Latin:

Vers. 24. DOMINUS PLUIT.) יהוה id est, Angelus is, qui Dei personam, ut diximus, sustinebat. PLUIT) In Hebræo fecit pluere. A DOMINO) Potestate sibi divinitus concessa.

Angelum ita personam Dei sustinere commen- tum est Rabbinico-Socinianum. Quod Theologia naturali & revelata cap. 2. pag. 326. ex professo pro- fligamus. Non Angelum fuisse creatum, qui Abra- hamo apparuit, sed Jehovam ipsum, jam osten- dimus. Idem ergo hic a Jehova Deo Patre pluisse dicitur, vel fecisse pluere. Quia quæcunque facit Pater, eadem similiter facit Filius Joh. 5, 19. qui uti a Patre est, ita operatur etiam a Patre, cui Pater etiam dedit omne judicium. Non potest Filius a- se quicquam facere, nisi quod videt Patrem facien- tem. Illud ergo a Domino non dependentiam aut potestatem ministerialem divinitus concessam, sed originem Filii a Patre notat. In Ebræo emphasis major est: Pluit Dominus מֵאֵת a cum Domino, quia Filius & a Patre & cum Patre operatur. Illud ob hypostaseos originem: hoc ob essentiæ identi- tatem, ideo plurium אֱלֹהִים fit mentio, qui sub- vertisse dicuntur Sodomam & Gomorrham, non certe Angelorum, sed qui sunt unus ille Deus. Am, 4, 11. Jer. 50, 40. Neque Angelus personam Dei re- ferens pluit aut pluere fecit. Non tale quid legi- tur, quod nempe in his & similibus ad opus conser- vationis pertinentibus alius Dei personam gerat, & pluviam v. g. ignem & sulphur immittat de Cœ- lo, quæ Dei ipsius opera sunt, ea sive mediate, sive immediate efficientis, non vero creaturæ personam Dei gerentis. Nec uspiam in Scriptura Angelo, semper DEO adscribitur Sodomæ eversio. Ideo Concilium Syrmiense Canone XVI. anathemate fe- riit eos, qui non intelligunt hoc de Patre & de Filio. Pluit enim Dominus Filius de Domino Patre. Quæ orthodoxa Syrm. formula diversa est a formula ab Arianis in Concil. Syrm. cusa, & ita non Socrati tan- tum l. II. Hist. Eccl. cap. 34. & Sozomeno l. IV. c. 5. 6. sed Hilario quoque de Synod. contr. Arian. Epi- phanio hæres. LXXIII. Vigilio contra Eutych. l. V. Philastrio hær. XXXVII. probata & ab Ancyrana Synodo quoque laudata, teste Epiphanio. Eadem sententia fuit Patrum communiter omnium. Igna- tii Epistola ad Antioch. Justin. dial. cum Tryphon. Irenei lib. III, c. 3. Tertul. advers. Prax. c. 13. & 16. lib. IV. contr. Marcion. c. 39. Cypriani advers. Jud. l. II. c. 33. Athanasii orat. contr. Gregal. Sa- bell. Eusebii lib. VII. de præpar. Evangel. c. 5. lib. XI. c. 9. & lib. V. demonstr. Evangel. c. 8. Hilarii l. V. de Trin. Epiphanii in Ancorat. & in hæresi Samarit. num. V. Gregorii Nysseni de cognit. Dei & de Trinit. Basilii M. contr. Evnom. Gregorii Nazianzeni Orat. III. de Theol. Chrysost. hom. de Trinitat. T. III. Philastrii hæres. VIII. Hieronymi in Os. 1, 7. Augustini T. IV. in Gen. q. 59. & T. VI. de hæresibus cap. 33. Theodoreti lib. II. de cu- rand. Græcor. affect. Cyrilli lib. I. contr. Jul. & l. IX. thesaur. c. 3. Prudentii in Apotheos. Idacii Cla- ri Hæresiolog. Euthymii Zigabeni Panopl. p. 1. Marii Victorini Afri lib. 1. contr. Arian. Isidori Pe- lusiotæ l. II. Epist. 143. Isidori Hispalensis T. I. de Nativ. Dom. c. 3. cui cum Megalandro Luthero nostrates ad unum omnes e Calvinianis etiam Bul- lingerus, Franciscus Junius, Bucanus, Sohnius, Po- lanus, Hornbeck, alii: e Papistis Delrio, Bonfrerius, Serarius, Cornelius a Lapide, Ruizius, Menochius, alii adstipulantur. Quid quod paraphrases etiam Chaldaicæ faveant. Targum Jonathan: verbum Jehovah dimisit pluvias benignas super Sodomam & Gomorrham propterea, ut agant pœnitentiam: Qui dixerunt: non revelata sunt coram Jehovah opera mala. Demissa igitur sunt super illos sulphur & ignis a verbo Jehovah de cælis. Qualia etiam legun- tur in Targum Hierosolymit. Vindicavimus lo- cum uberius assertione invicta pluralitatis persona- rum divinarum e V. T. cap. XVI.

Vers. eod. DE CŒLO) Sic & Lucæ 17, 29. Nimirum ignis ille sulphureus non aliunde quam ex cœlo veniebat Urbes has igne cœlesti flagrasse ait Tacitus Historiarum V ante dixerat fulminum jactu. Nam & fulmen vim habet ful- phuris, & inde Græcis sulphur, θεῖον dicitur. ὕδατα ἀσφαλ- τώδη καὶ θειώδη, dixit Strabo.

IN STATURAM SALIS) Id est, columnam. Ita enim statuæ vocem sæpe hic interpres usurpat. Sal autem cum igne de cœlo deciderat. Vide supra 14, 3. Deut. 29, 23. Han- columnam suo tempore extitisse ait Josephus. Semper man- suram ait Paraphrasis Hierosolymitana. Vide & Burchar- dum, & alios qui ibi fuere.

## 19:28
verse 28. AS THE SMOKE OF A FURNACE) A sign of divine wrath. See above 15, 17.

Latin:

vers. 28. QVASI FORNACIS FVMUM) Signum irae divinae. Vide supra 15, 17.

## 19:30
verse 30. AND HE REMAINED IN A CAVE) Strabo teaches us that there are many such in that region.

Latin:

vers. 30. ET MANSIT IN SPELUNCA) Quales multas esse in ea regione docet nos Strabo.

## 19:33
v. 33. TO DRINK WINE THAT NIGHT) Night and wine suggest nothing moderate.

AND SHE SLEPT WITH HER FATHER) Thinking it lawful. Which she understood to be done daily by the neighboring Arabs. For we learn from Strabo that this was a custom not only among the Persians, but also among the Arabs. Clement and Bardesanes mention this custom among the Persians and neighboring peoples.

Latin:

v. 33. BIBERE VINUM NOCTE ILLA) Nox & vinum nihil suadent moderabile.

DORMIVITQVE CUM PATRE) Licitum id arbitra- ta. Quod ab Arabibus vicinis fieri quotidie intelligebat. Non enim Persis tantum, sed & Arabibus hunc fuisse morem ex Strabone discimus. Moris ejus apud Persas vicinasque gentes meminere Clemens & Bardesanes.

## 19:37
verse 37. Moab) Hence Characmoba in Arabia has its name in Stephanus, from which the reading of Ptolemy is to be corrected. حسرت صواب the laceration of Moab, because the Moabites were slaughtered there.

Latin:

vers. 37. Moab) Hinc nomen habet Characmoba in Ara- bia apud Stephanum, ex quo corrigenda Ptolemaei lectio. حسرت صواب laceratio Moab, quod ibi caesi Moabitae.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

While Abraham is sojourning in Gerar, his wife is taken by the King, but is returned untouched along with gifts.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

Abrahae in Gerar peregrinanti uxor a Rege tolli- tur, sed intacta cum donis redditur.

## 20:3
ver. 3. FOR SHE HAS A HUSBAND) Certain Hebrews interpret this as, she has lain with a husband. For thus, before the law, marriages were completed by the law of nations.

Latin:

vers. 3. HABET ENIM VIRUM) Hebraei quidam in- terpretantur, concubuit cum marito. Ita enim ante legem gen- tium jure nuptiae perficiebantur.

## 20:9
ver. 9. YOU HAVE BROUGHT UPON ME AND UPON MY KINGDOM A GREAT SIN) That is, you have caused me to sin to the detriment of myself and my kingdom. Thus Alexander, when a girl was brought to him, and she had said that she had waited until her husband was asleep, ἐπετίμησε παισίν, ὡς μικρῦ δι’ αὐτὺς μοιχὸς γενόμενος. The Gentiles, of course, who had received no law from God beyond the dictates of nature, knew indeed that adultery was base, but did not think fornication to be a crime, no more than Micio did in Terence, or Cato in Horace. Therefore, they had need to be seriously admonished about that matter by the Apostles, Acts 15:29 and elsewhere.

Cornelius understands this of the fault of Abraham not having been sufficiently examined as to whether Sarah was married, and of the desire and license to take Sarah, and of material adultery. But because the sin is said to have been brought not only upon the king, but upon the kingdom, it is more correctly understood metonymically of the punishment of sin, as Tostatus explains, which Abraham could easily have brought upon Abimelech for that reason, and in part had already brought, v. 17.

The same verse.

WHICH YOU OUGHT NOT TO HAVE DONE.

In the Hebrew: Works which are not done, that is, which ought not to be done, because the Hebrews often express law and duty with active verbs. See Leviticus 4:2, 1 Kings 3:5, 2 Kings 3:37.

Latin:

vers. 9. INDUXISTI SUPER ME ET SUPER RE- GNUM MEUM PECCATUM GRANDE) Id est, prope me peccare fecisti meo & regni malo. Sic Alexander adducta ad se puella, cum ea dixisset expectasse se donec maritus dor- miret, ἐπετίμησε παισίν, ὡς μικρῦ δι’ αὐτὺς μοιχὸς γενόμενος. Gentes scilicet, quae praeter naturae dictata legem a Deo nul- lam acceperant, adulterium quidem turpe esse norant, scor- tari non putabant esse flagitium, non magis quam apud Te- rentium Mitio, aut apud Horatium Cato. Ideo ea de re se- rio admoneri ab Apostolis opus habuere, Act. 15, 29. & alibi.

DE culpa non examinati satis Abrahami, num Sara conjugata sit, & cupiditatis ac licentiae assumendi Saram, & adulterii materialis intelligit Cornelius. Sed quia peccatum non tantum super regem, sed super regnum inductum dicitur, re- ctius metonymice de poena peccati intelligitur, uti Tostatus explicat, quam facile ea ratione in- duxisset Abraham in Abimelechum, & ex parte jam induxerat v. 17.

Vers. eod.

QVAE NON DEBUISTI TACERE.

In Ebraeo: Opera quae non fiunt, id est, fieri non debent, quia Ebraei saepe jus & debitum ver- bis activis explicant. Vid. Levit. 4, 2. 1. Reg. III, 5. 2. Reg. 3, 37.

## 20:11
Ver. 11.

PERHAPS THERE IS NO FEAR OF GOD IN THIS PLACE) Where there is no fear of God, there all vices reign. Moreover, this thought of Abraham is not unlike that of Ulysses in Homer’s Odyssey, Book 6: “Alas, to what land of mortals have I come? Are they violent and wild, and not just, or are they hospitable, and is their mind god-fearing?”

Latin:

Vers. 11.

FORSITAN NON EST TIMOR DEI IN LOCO ISTO) Ubi timor Dei non est, ibi omnia vitia regnant. Est autem haec cogitatio Abrahami non dissimilis isti Ulyssis apud Homerum Odysseae Z. Ὢ μοι ἐγώ, τέων αὖτε βροτῶν εἰς γαῖαν ἱκάνω; Ἦρ’ οἵγ’ ὑβρισαί τε καὶ ἄγριοι, οὐδὲ δίκαιοι, Ἠὲ φιλόξεινοι, καί σφι νόος ἐσὶ θευδής;

## 20:12
Ver. 12.

NOT THE DAUGHTER OF MY MOTHER) For among certain nations, in avoiding marriages, the maternal line, as being more certain, was more regarded. Philo on the special laws, dealing with the marrying of sisters: “Solon among the Athenians, while permitting the marriage of those who shared a father, forbade those who shared a mother.” The scholiast on that passage in the Clouds of Aristophanes, “How that brother, O you wretch, [married] his sister who shared the same mother,” says: 'Since among the Athenians it was permitted to marry sisters from one's father.' The Latin writer of the life of Cimon: 'He had, however, in marriage his own full sister named Elpinice, led not more by love than by ancestral custom. For it is permitted to the Athenians to marry wives born of the same father.' See Deut. 13, 6, where a sister by the same mother is posited as being more closely related. Achilles Tatius, book 1, attributes this death to the Phoenicians. But many things came to the Athenians from the Phoenicians, as we have shown elsewhere. And by the customs of Noah, the Hebrews allow marriages prohibited with sisters related by the mother, but not with those who are from the father only. Sarah, if we follow most Hebrews, was the daughter of Terah by another wife. But as others judge, Sarah is called Abraham's sister in the Hebrew manner, since she was not ἀδελφὴ but ἀδελφιδῆ. Concerning the custom of the Egyptians in this matter, see Diodorus Siculus.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

NON FILIA MATRIS MEAE) Nam apud gentes quasdam in vitandis nuptiis genus maternum, ut certius, magis attendebatur. Philo de specialibus legibus, agens de sororibus ducendis: ὁ μὲν ἕν Ἀθηναίοις Σόλων ὁμοπατρίους ἐφιεὶς ἄγεσθαι, τὰς ὁμομητρίους ἐκώλυσεν. Scholiastes ad illud in nubibus Aristophanis, ὡς ἐκεῖνος Ἀδελφὸς, ὦ λεξίκακε, τὴν ὁμομητρίαν ἀδελφήν, ait: ἐπειδὴ παῤ Ἀθηναίοις ἐξῆν γαμεῖν τὰς ἐκ πατέρων ἀδελφάς. Scriptor Latinus vitæ Cimonis: Habebat autem in matrimonio sororem germanam suam nomine Elipnicen, non magis amore quam patrio more ductus. Nam Atheniensibus licet eodem Patre natas uxores ducere. Vid. Deut. 13, 6. ubi frater ex ma- tre ponitur ut conjunctior. Hunc mortem Phœnicibus tri- buit Achilles Tatius lib. 1. Multa autem a Phœnicibus ad Athe- nienses venere, ut ostendimus alibi. Et moribus Noæ liberùm volunt Hebræi interdicta matrimonia cum sororibus ex matre conjunctis, non cum iis quæ ex solo patre. Sara, si Hebræos plerosque sequimur, Tharæ fuit filia ex altera uxore. Ut vero alii censent, Saræ soror Abrahami dicitur more Hebræo, cum non esset ἀδελφὴ sed ἀδελφιδῆ. De more Ægyptiorum in hac re vide Diodorum Siculum.

## 20:13
Verse 13. GOD BROUGHT ME OUT.) The verb is plural, whence it is permitted to translate אלהים as 'angels,' as the Greeks did in Gen. 31, 24; Job 38, verse 7; Psalm 8, v. 6; 96, 8; 137, v. 1, whom the writer to the Hebrews follows, verse 7; see below 48, v. 16. Properly: 'They made me wander.'

Grotius is diligent in this, to cut the nerve of testimonies bringing forward a plurality of divine persons: certainly not for the sake of the Catholic faith. He has no reason, however, to defer here to the Vulgate, which he otherwise holds as authentic. Nor is it sound to substitute 'angels' for the word אלהים in the version: for although that word is sometimes used of angels, which is manifest in Psalm 8, v. 6 and 96, v. 8; whence Paul followed the Greeks in this in Heb. 1, v. 6 and chapter 2, 7; yet it is not to be explained here by 'angels': nor was that done by the Greeks. Abraham was not called by angels, nor through angels, but by God himself immediately, Gen. 12, v. 1. And the word אלהים is without doubt used here in the same sense in which it was accepted in verse 11, that is, of the true God. The Socinians themselves, whom Grotius has here acted as midwife for, acknowledge that these words must be accepted as referring to the true God: therefore they use other exceptions, which we have discussed in the book cited in chapter 8. It is sufficiently manifest that not only the noun אלהים is plural, but also the plural verb, which Grotius renders 'they made me wander,' is used to initiate the mystery of the plurality of the persons of Elohim, who are that one GOD. For he who called Abraham, and made him wander from his father's house, is no other than that one GOD. But several Elohim called him. Therefore, several Elohim are that one God. Which argument we have confirmed more fully, and defended against Socinian exceptions in 'Affert. invict. plural. person. divin.' §. 55 et seqq.

Latin:

Verf. 13. EDUXIT ME DEVS.) Verbum est plurale, unde אלהים liceat angelos vertere, ut fecere Græci Gen. 31, 24. Job. 38. verf. 7. Pfal. 8. v. 6. 96, 8. 137. v. 1. quos sequitur scri- ptor ad Hebræos, verf. 7. vide infra 48. v. 16. Proprie palabun- dum me fecerunt.

Sedulus in eo est Grotius, ut testimoniis plura- litatem personarum divinarum afferentibus ner- vum incidat: non certe in gratiam fidei Catholicæ. Nullam autem causam habet deferendi hic Vulga- tam, quam pro authentica alias habet. Neque in- tegrum est, loco vocis אלהים substituere angelos in versione: Etsi enim de angelis aliquando ea vox adhibeatur, quod Psalm. 8. v. 6. & 96. v. 8. manife- stum est; unde Græcos sequutus est in eo Paulus Ebr. 1. v. 6. cap. 2, 7. non tamen hic per angelos ex- plicanda: neque a Græcis id factum. Non ab Ange- lis, non per Angelos vocatus est Abraham, sed a Deo ipso immediate Gen. 12. v. 1. Et vox אלהים sine du- bio eodem sensu hic adhibetur, quo verf. 11. acce- pta fuit, hoc est, de vero Deo. Agnoscunt ipsimet So- ciniani, quibus hic obstetricatus est Grotius, verba hæc de vero Deo accipienda esse: Ideo aliis utuntur exceptionibus, quas discussimus lib. citato c. 8. Ma- nifestum satis, non tantum nomen אלהים plurale, sed etiam verbum plurale, quod reddit Grotius pa- labundum me fecerunt, adhiberi ad ineundum my- sterium plurium personarum Elohim, quæ sint unus ille DEUS. Qui enim Abraham vocavit, eumq; de domo Patris peregrinari fecit, nullus alius est, quam unus ille DEUS. At plures Elohim vocarunt. Er- go plures Elohim sunt unus ille Deus. Quod argu- mentum uberius confirmavimus, & ab exceptioni- bus Socinianis vindicavimus Affert. invict. plural. person. divin. §. 55. feqq.

## 20:16
Verse 16. THIS SHALL BE TO THEE A COVERING OF THE EYES.

Aben-Ezra and Christoph. Cartwright refer the pronoun to Abraham. That Abraham was a covering of the eyes for Sarah, that she would be safe under his protection, and as it were covered by a veil, so that no one inflamed by her beauty would dare anything against her: But Abimelech did not provide that Abraham should be this; it was Abraham by himself: nor does this suit the following words, 'to all who are with thee': The Chaldean more correctly understood it of the gifts given to Abraham, ולו. Compare what we have said in the commentary on this place.

Verse same. AND REMEMBER THAT THOU ART CONVICTED) נכחת, that is, 'upright.' Which the Chaldean supplies as having been. The LXX, however, 'be' πάντα ἀλήθευσον. I would prefer this.

Latin:

Verf. 16. HOC ERIT TIBI IN VELAMEN OCULORUM.

Pronomen ad Abrahamum refert Aben-Ezra & Christoph. Cartwright. Abrahamum Saræ prove- lamine oculorum esse, eam ejus præsidio tutam, ac q.ve- lamine tectam fore, ne quis pulchritudine ejus inflam- matus in eam quicquam auderet: Sed hoc ut Abra- ham esset, non præstabat Abimelech, per se id erat Abraham: nec id convenit verbis sequentibus, ad omnes, qui tecum sunt: Chaldæus rectius de donis Ab- rahamo datis accepit illud ולו. Conf. quæ in comm. ad b. l. diximus.

Verf. eod. MEMENTOQVE TE DEPREHENSAM) נכחת, id est, recta. Quod Chaldæus supplet fuisse. LXX. vero esto. πάντα ἀλήθευσον. Hoc malim.

## 20:17
v. 17. AND THEY BORE) ילדו, in this place you would more correctly translate 'they conceived,' or 'they were made pregnant,' as the Chaldean.

Latin:

v. 17. ET PEPERERVNT) ילדו hoc quidem loco rectius vertas conceperunt, aut gravida facta sunt, ut Chaldæus.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI.

The birth and circumcision of Isaac. The casting out of Ishmael. The covenant of Abraham with Abimelech.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI.

Isaaci nativitas & circumcisio. Ismaelis eje- ctio. Fœdus Abrahæ cum Abimelecho.

## 21:3
Verse 3. ISAAC] Eupolemus said 'Laughter.' Add this to those things which are above 11, 1.

Latin:

Verf. 3. ISAAC] Γέλωτα dixit Eupolemus. Quod adde his, quæ supra 11, 1.

## 21:9
PLAYING) More correctly 'exposing to mockery': for it is an allusion to the name. See the same word below 39, 7. 14. But he seems to have mocked the piety of Isaac. Thus the Hebrews.

Latin:

LVDENTEM) Rectius irrisui exponentem: est enim no- minis allusio. Vide verbum idem infra 39, 7. 14. Videtur au- tem irrisisse pietatem Isaaci. Sic Hebræi.

## 21:13
Verf. 13. INTO A GREAT NATION) From the Greek. But Jonathan לעם לססט into a predatory people. Not badly, for גוי is said more of barbarian nations, and עם of those with good morals. Thus λαὸς is a holy people, the others ἔθνη, whence ἔθνικὸς. Thus what precedes וגם will be adversative, and that 'Isaac to you a seed' will signify also a son of morals.

NAY, very badly is it rendered 'predatory people.' For a promise is held here. What indeed would that promise be: 'He shall be into a predatory people'? And the reason for this promise is added, why indeed Ishmael also is to turn into a great nation: because, to wit, he himself also is the seed of Abraham. Whence the particle וגם is to be understood not in an adversative, but in a copulative sense, which is proper to it. But how that 'Isaac to you a seed' can be explained as 'also a son of morals,' and what the sense of these may be, I confess I am unable to grasp. Grotius perhaps dreamed when he wrote these things.

Latin:

Verf. 13. IN GENTEM MAGNAM) Ex Græco. At Jo- nathan לעם לססט in populum prædatorem. Non male, nam גוי de nationibus barbaris magis dicitur, de bene mora- tis גוי .עם Sic λαὸς populus sanctus, cæteri ἔθνη, unde ἔθνι- κὸς. Ita quod præcedit וגם erit adversativa, & illud Isaac tibi semen, significabit morum quoq; filius.

IMO pessime populus prædator redditur. Habe- tur enim hic promissio. Quænam vero illa pro- missio foret: Erit in populum prædatorem? & ad- ditur ratio hujus promissionis, cur nempe etiam I- smael in gentem magnam evasurus sit: quia sc. ipse etiam semen Abrahæ est. Unde particula וגם non adversativo, sed copulativo intelligenda sensu, qui ei proprius est. Quomodo vero illud Isaac tibi semen explicari possit morum quoque filius, & quis horum sensus sit, fateor me capere non posse. So- mniavit forte cum hæc scripsit Grotius.

## 21:16
Verf. 16. FROM A DISTANCE) From the Greek. But the Hebrew מנגד you would rightly translate 'from afar,' as appears in Ps. 38:12, when the fulfillment of the Psalm is compared. Matt. 26:58, 27:35, Mark 14:54, 15:40, Luke 22:54, 23:49. Thus also 2 Kings 2:7 and 4:25.

Latin:

Verf. 16. E REGIONE) Ex Græco. At Hebræum מנגד recte vertas eminus, ut apparet Pf. 38 12. collato Psalmi imple- mento. Matth. 26,58. 27, 35. Marci 14,54. 15,40. Luc. 22,54.23, 49. Sic & 2. Reg. 2,7. & 4,25.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII.

Abraham's faith proved by the immolation of Isaac, and the promise confirmed to him by an oath. The sons of Nahor.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII.

Abrahæ fides per Immolationem Isaaci proba- ta, & promissio juramento eidem firma- ta. Filii Nachor.

## 22:2
Verf. 2. TAKE YOUR SON] In the Hebrew is added נא, which is of one exhorting, as often νῦν among the Greeks.

ONLY) Μονογενῆ, that is, ἀγαπητὸν, as Aquila interprets. For these two meanings are wont to be mixed among the Hebrews and among the Greeks. Thus Solomon is called David's only one, that is, most beloved, 1 Chron. 29:1. See what is said at John 1, verse 14.

These things smell of the lamp of Socinus: who in John 1:14 and elsewhere wishes the Son of GOD to be called μονογενῆ, not because he alone was begotten from the substance of the Father, which the Catholic Church believes; but because he is ἀγαπητὸς, beloved by God above others. And they appeal likewise to the passage Gen. 22:2 and 1 Chron. 29:1. But that those two meanings are mixed in the Hebrew or Greek text of the Holy Scriptures has not yet been demonstrated. And why he prefers the interpretation of Aquila here to others, when Isaac was truly μονογενὴς from Sarah, who had been his principal wife, and by that much more God moved the paternal bowels in this prayer to the Patriarch, and recalled to memory the promises which He had made concerning this only-begotten one. For Isaac was the only one, because Ishmael by divine command had already been disinherited from the family as a mocker. Gen. 21:12. Solomon is called David's only one from Bathsheba in comm. 22. In 1 Chron. 3:3 it is read that four sons were born to David in Jerusalem; but that all were born from Bathsheba herself, whence, I pray, is it certain? Could not mention of Bathsheba have been made on account of Solomon, since the mother of the preceding ones is not expressly named? But Lyra and Vatablus think those were Uriah's sons merely adopted by David; which, however, we do not prove, since Nathan was undoubtedly David's son.

Verf. eod. INTO THE LAND OF VISION.] From Aquila, who rightly translated מריה as ὀπτασίας. The allusion to that name below in verse 14 shows this. This was later the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, on which David sacrificed in 2 Sam. 24 at the end: and after that the temple of Solomon. Thus with great consensus the Hebrews, who also say that Abel sacrificed in the same place.

Latin:

Verf. 2. TOLLE FILIUM TUUM] In Hebræo appositum est נא, quod est adhortantis, ut sæpe νῦν apud Græcos.

UNICUM) Μονογενῆ, id est, ἀγαπητὸν, ut Aquila inter- pretatur. Solent enim hi duo significatus misceri apud Hebræ- os & apud Græcos. Sic Salomon Davidi unicus, id est dilectis- simus dicitur 1. Par. 29,1. Vide quæ dicta ad Joh. 1. verfu 14.

REdolent hæc Socini lucernam: qui Joh. 1, 14. alibi Filium DEI μονογενῆ dici vult, non quod solus genitus sit e substantia Patris, quod Catholica Ecclesia credit; sed quod ἀγαπητὸς dilectus præ cæteris Deo sit. Et ad locum Gen. 22, 2. 1. Paral. 29, 1. pariter provocant. Sed misceri illos duos signifi- catus in Ebræo aut Græco S. S. Textu, nondum de- monstratum est. Et cur Aquilæ interpretationem hic cæteris præfert, quum vere Isaac fuerit μονογε- νὴς e Sara, quæ conjux principalis fuerat, eoq; ma- gis Deus τὰ σπλάγχνα paterna in hac oratione commoverit Patriarchæ, ac in memoriam revoca- rit promissiones, quas de unigenito hoc fecerat. E- rat enim unicus Isaac, quia Ismael ex mandato divi- no tanquam illusor ex familia jam erat abdicatus. Gen. 21. v. 12. Salomon unicus Davidi e Bathseba di- citur comm. 22. 1. Par. 3, 3. legitur Hierosolymis Da- vidi quatuor natos esse filios; omnes vero e Bathseba ipsa natos esse, unde obsecro constat? Nonne Bath- sebæ mentio fieri potuit propter Salomonem, cum præcedentium mater expresse non nominetur? Ly- ra vero & Vatablus putant, illos Uriæ filios fuisse a Davide solum adoptatos; quod tamen non proba- mus, quum Nathan indubie fuerit Davidis filius.

Verf. eod. IN TERRAM VISIONIS.] Ex Aquila, qui מריה recte transtulit ὀπτασίας. Ostendit id allusio ad id nomen infra 14. Hic postea fuit area Araunæ Sebusæi, in qua sacrificavit David 2. Sam. 24. in fine: ac post id templum Sa- lomonis. Ita magno consensu Hebræi, qui & Abelem ibidem sacrificasse ajunt.

## 22:4 Addition
On ch. 22, v. 4. THE THIRD DAY, p. 289, column b.

Ainsworth notes here a passage from Bresith Rabba worthy of note: There are three days in Scripture, among which is the day of the Resurrection of the Messiah. Isaac was a type, who was dead for three days in the heart of Abraham.

Latin:

Ad cap. 22. v. 4. DIE TERTIO p. 289. b.

Notat hic locum è Bresith Rabba notatu di- gnum Ainsworth: Multi sunt tres dies in Scri- ptura, inter quos dies Resurrectionis Messiæ. Ty- pus erat Isaac, qui per triduum mortuus erat in corde Abrahami.

## 22:9
Verf. 9. AND WHEN HE HAD BOUND ISAAC HIS SON) For it is a most ancient custom that victims be bound. Servius notes this on that line of the Aeneid, 'and the bonds to the rock.' Ovid, 3 de Ponto, Elegy 2, concerning Orestes and Pylades in Tauris:

Forthwith they are said to be at the pitiless altar of Trivia, their hands bound behind their backs.

We have spoken of this offering of Isaac in the festive Program: which therefore it will not be useless to insert here. But it runs thus:

Truly stupendous is the history of Abraham's temptation, a twin to which you would hardly find in any age, and for the worthy explanation of which not even the eloquence of the most fluent orator would suffice. Blessed Luther judged no one other than St. Paul to be suitable for illustrating it. But what was not done by such a great Apostle, that Megalander, full of the Spirit of God, executed in his golden and gem-like Commentary on Genesis, in such a way that, although he is not to be compared with that disciple of the heavenly school, he nevertheless left the most eloquent of the Fathers—Ambrose in the Latin Church, who, in the judgment of Erasmus, flows with truly heavenly ambrosia, and Chrysostom, the golden mouth of eloquence, in the Greek—far behind him in the explanation of this history. Although the bare account of the divine historian would easily have turned into astonishment anyone who had not weighed it perfunctorily. Let one only consider that command, not entirely ἄστοργος and full of horror, given to the holy Patriarch: TAKE THY SON, THINE ONLY SON, WHOM THOU LOVEST, ISAAC, AND GO INTO THE LAND OF MORIAH, AND OFFER HIM THERE FOR A BURNT OFFERING, in which there is no word that was not a sharp sword in the heart of Abraham. The great weight of the precept, says Chrysostom, hom. 47. See how through those words he kindles a greater fire, and more violently excites the furnace of love with which the righteous man was affected toward Isaac. Take thy beloved son, whom thou hast loved, Isaac. Each word by itself would suffice to wound the soul of the righteous man. For he did not simply say Isaac, but added: Thy son: whom beyond all expectation, and in old age itself, you have begotten, your beloved and desirable one, whom you love so immoderately; Isaac, whom you expect to succeed you, from whom also your seed is to be multiplied, so that it may be equal to the multitude of the stars and the sand which is by the seashore; take that very one, and go into the high land, and offer him there for a burnt offering, upon one of the mountains which I shall tell thee. I admire how the righteous man could bear these things with his ears? Chrysostom rightly admired these things, but one must admire even more with what spirit he could sustain the commanded offering of his ONLY son, whom he had received from Sarah his wife alone. For when the whole force of natural love which a father has toward his offspring is expressed by the word son, it is much increased by the word only: for love divided among many is less, and the loss of one of many is more easily borne than that of one which is unique, and has nothing equal or similar, by whose substitution the loss of the former might be compensated. Therefore, there can be no greater grief than in the death of an only son, as the Holy Spirit Himself testifies: They shall mourn for him as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn, Zech. 12, 10. Here, indeed, upon hearing that word of an only son, not only that which is of nature occupied the Patriarch's mind, but especially that which was above nature—the singular and admirable kindness of God in the gift of this son, which He had shown to him and his wife. But when the Lord further added the name of Isaac, no one could easily express in words with what a wound the heart of holy Abraham was struck. For he had received concerning him from the Lord: I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him. Gen. 17, v. 19. The marrow and soul of which covenant was this: in HIM shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, Gen. 18, 18. For what else could Abraham think, led by the dictates of reason, than that all that promise would be void? By what means can it happen that branches sprout when the root is cut out, or fruits come forth when the tree is felled, or rivers return when the fountain is dried up? According to human reason, such things are not possible, as Chrysostom says here again. How, therefore, could the Patriarch's heart be more grievously wounded than when he understood that he was to be killed in whom he had received the promised seed, the Savior of the World, the magnitude of which temptation no one can attain. Now Isaac was not only to be killed, but the Parent himself was commanded to kill him, not through others, whether enemies or friends; the paternal hands themselves were to be defiled with the blood of the son. And not only was the slaughter of the only son commanded to him, but he had to offer him as a burnt offering, that is, to bind him, to pile up the wood, to cut his throat, to kindle the fire beneath, and to keep turning him until he was resolved into ashes and embers, and thus all his hope and consolation, even concerning the Seed, might vanish into smoke. Nor was he to do this immediately, but in the land of Moriah, upon one of the mountains, to which a journey of three days had to be completed: if that struggle had been of one or two hours, he would have overcome it more easily. Therefore, this delay amplifies his obedience. Meanwhile he thought: Behold, I am walking with my son, a youth of the highest hope; he must die. He endured such maceration of the flesh for these three days together with the arrows of Satan, yet he had to mutter and be silent because of the command, by which he is supported, confirmed, and preserved. Nor did Blessed Luther think those words, which could seem of small moment, should be passed over lightly: HE SADDLED HIS ASS. These, he says, are all described so diligently in order to signify that the delay also exercised his faith somewhat. The Parent himself must seek the wood, cut it, and place it on the ass to burn his son. Meanwhile, he undoubtedly felt the greatest trembling of the flesh. For he was not of an iron heart, but of a most tender nature, and the thought of the burnt offering was perpetually present in his mind, for which the promised only-begotten son, the hope of future seed and posterity, was to be slaughtered, and was to be burned with those very logs which the Father collected. Was there not more to be deliberated in a matter so sad and stupendous? Were not counsels to be conferred with mother Sarah? These things are signified in those, as it appears, useless words; otherwise these could have been said most briefly. But Moses wishes to indicate what motions he felt at individual moments, to which undoubtedly ineffable groans, sighs, sobs, and paternal tears were added. But regarding those words of the Sacred text: AND THOSE TWO WENT TOGETHER, this from the Man of GOD: Such a transition, as this is, is nowhere described in Sacred Scripture. Two. Who? The dearest Father, and the most beloved Son. With what mind? With this mind: Isaac ignorant of the matter, and yet prepared to obey: Abraham most certain to sacrifice the son, and to reduce him to ashes. But above all, most stupendous is the dialogism of the son with the Father, which the Divine Historian describes with these: But Isaac said to his Father: My father; but he answers: Behold I, my son. He says: Behold the fire and the wood, where is the animal for the burnt offering? Abraham answers: GOD will provide for Himself an animal for a burnt offering, my son. Concerning which our Luther: A huge movement indeed is this, and a vehement πάθος, which Moses did not wish to pass over. Isaac the victim addresses the Father, and irritates that στοργὴν φυσικὴν, as if to say: You are a Father to me: and the parent in turn: you are a son to me: these things undoubtedly penetrated and struck the paternal soul. Let us hear here also Chrysostom of Constantinople: Isaac said to Abraham his Father: Father: This word was sufficient to rend the vitals of this righteous man. But he said: What is it, my son? You call me father, who will shortly be bereaved: and I call you son, who not long after will ascend the altar, to be slain by my hands. O fortitude of soul, o solidity of the Spirit! With what eyes did he behold the boy bringing the wood, upon which he was not long after to place him? How could his hands bear the fire and the sword? And indeed his hands bore the fire, which was sensible, but within it burned his mind, and consumed his reason, and persuaded him that love for GOD should prevail. But we must hasten to the very history of the offering; concerning which blessed Luther says gravely: The altar now having been built, when the climax itself is reached, Moses is silent, and either despairs of expressing these things: because the matter is greater than can be uttered by any eloquence; or he could not write for tears. And thus he leaves stupor and admiration in the minds of the hearers, and wishes that they themselves should weigh the matter, which he is unable to attain with words. For now, the altar having been built, the knife prepared, and the fire kindled, it was necessary that some words should pass between the Father and the son, by which Isaac was instructed concerning the will and command of God. The Father said: You, my most beloved son, whom God has given to me, are destined for a burnt offering. There the son undoubtedly was stunned, and in turn reminded the Father of the promise. Think, my Father, that I am the seed to whom posterity, Kings, peoples, etc., have been promised. God gave me to my mother Sarah through a great miracle. How, therefore, can the promise be fulfilled, if I am slain? Let us, however, first confer and converse about that matter. All those things should have been written here; why Moses omitted them, I do not know. But I do not doubt that the Father's speech to the son was very remarkable, and I believe that its principal state was the command of God and the resurrection of the dead. GOD has commanded, therefore it behooves us to obey Him, and since He is omnipotent, He can keep the promise, even with you dead and reduced to ashes. Let us hear what blessed Luther adds concerning the climax: In a brief sentence Moses encompasses that wonderful and stupendous history: The Father is about to slaughter his son. The son offers his throat, with eyes lifted to heaven, and expects to be reduced to ashes; thus both are brought by GOD to the extreme crisis of life. If faith had not been there, or if GOD had slumbered for one moment, it would have been all over with the son's life. Because the knife is ready, the son is bound, he is placed upon the pile of wood, the throat is sought. I could not have been a spectator, let alone an actor and slayer. It is a stupendous thing that the dearest Father should have moved the knife to the throat of his dearest son, and I acknowledge indeed that I can attain these thoughts and affections neither by words nor by meditating.

But what has this so sad spectacle to do with Paschal joys? It carried us away, we confess, a little further than the intention of both Chrysostoms allowed, concerning the stupendous narration with stupendous eloquence. Yet Christ, having risen again, did not abhor conversations about his passion and death while he was celebrating Paschal joys; nay, he repeatedly instituted long sermons on these solemn occasions, from Moses and the Prophets, concerning the same. Nor is there any doubt that this remarkable figure of Isaac, which stands out especially in Moses, was explained by the Doctor of the triumphant death to the disciples at Emmaus and Jerusalem. The sum of which explanation we consider to be comprehended by the holy Apostle in Hebrews 11:17, in few words indeed, but with divine wisdom. By faith Abraham offered up Isaac, when he was tested, and he who had received the promises was offering up his only begotten son, to whom it was said: In Isaac shall your seed be called, accounting that GOD is able to raise him up even from the dead, from whence he also received him in a parable. Which things teach with what eyes we ought to behold that spectacle in Mary, not that we should linger in the obedience of Abraham, but that we should look primarily to the faith of the Father of believers in the author and finisher of faith, JESUS, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross: which, as the same Apostle explained in Romans 4:25, was fixed solely upon him who was about to raise Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, as one who was to be delivered for our offenses, and to be raised again for our justification. Which things were figured in this spectacle. For Abraham received Isaac ἐν παραβολῇ IN A FIGURE. Isaac, therefore, was a figure of Christ, that only son of Abraham, foreshadowing the only begotten Son of GOD; born not according to the power of nature, but according to the promise of God, born according to the promises made to the Fathers, by the power of the Holy Spirit: ready for the offering, most ready for the immolation of his body. Chrysostom certainly does not know whether he should more justly admire the strong Spirit of Abraham or the obedience of Isaac, because he neither resisted nor took the deed ill, but yielded and complied with those things which were done by the Father, and like a lamb lay down upon the altar in silence, awaiting the Father's right hand. The paternal affection of Abraham, submitting itself to the stupor of the counsel of God, is a shadow and a certain image of the affection of God the Father toward his Son, and of that admirable συγκατάβασις to the eternal counsel concerning our salvation. But if we wished to pursue all those things, we would have to return again to the week of the passion, and to Mount Moriah, on which the Lord was immolated. For all these things, to speak here again in the words of Chrysostom, were a figure of the cross, for which reason Christ also said to the Jews: Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it, and was glad. How did he see it? He who preceded in time? Through a figure, through a shadow. For just as a sheep was offered for Isaac, so also the rational lamb was offered for the world. See, I beseech you, how all things were prefigured through shadows: the only begotten there and the only begotten here, the beloved there and the brother, the beloved and here also the brother. He is offered by the Father as a burnt offering, and this one the Father delivered up. Thus far the shadow; afterwards the truth of the things is shown with great excellence. For this rational Lamb was offered for the whole world, purified the whole orb of the earth, freed men from error, and led them to the truth: He made earth heaven, not by the changed nature of the elements, but by heavenly conversation brought to men living upon the earth: One must see concerning the figure of the resurrection. Abraham beheld it in his revived son, who for three days had been dead in the heart of the Father, but afterwards was restored alive to the Father. No creature could restore the same; for by the voice of no creature would the Patriarch have allowed himself to be drawn back from the slaughter of his son. By the right hand of GOD Himself, therefore, he was to be freed, by whom Isaac had been commanded to be immolated in Sacrifice. An angel, therefore, descended from heaven, and as it seemed to B. Luther, a new light shone, and a multitude of angels was present, by which majesty terrified, Abraham cast away both the knife and the thought of the slaughter at the same time. As Christ was delivered into death by God, so by divine power He was raised from the dead, in which glory of resurrection it is to be believed that a multitude of attendant angels was not lacking. But that we may not remain in the shadow, that uncreated angel, who appeared to Abraham, is the very antitype of Isaac: who not in figure, but truly underwent death, not in figure, but truly rose from the dead, not raised by another's power, but revived by His own virtue. But also Isaac, if Macarius on the exaltation of the Holy Cross is to be heard, insinuated divine impassibility, being prohibited from dying by divine command; but by the ram humanity was signified, and the death which Christ undergoes according to His human nature.

What therefore the Patriarch hears there: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed Gen. 22. this is, as B. Luther interprets, they shall boast of the victory of death, of the abolition of sin, of the donation of eternal life, not because of their own merits, but in thy seed, of which on this day especially, the multitude of the faithful throughout the world exults. For by the resurrection of Christ this blessing is produced for us. The Pasch of Christ, as S. Augustine says, is the Kingdom of heaven, the salvation of the world, the life of believers, the setting of hell, the glory of the heavenly, the resurrection of the dead, the testimony of the divine resurrection, the price of human redemption, the knowledge of abolished death. This therefore is the day which the Lord has made, higher than all, brighter than all, in which he acquired for himself a new people by the Spirit of regeneration, in which he filled the minds of individuals with joy and exultation. This day of the resurrection of Christ is therefore life to the dead, pardon to sinners, glory to the saints. Blessed therefore be God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us, into a living hope, by the resurrection of Christ from the dead. Let us strengthen our faith also by the example of Abraham and Isaac. For the victory of Abraham and Isaac (as our Hero in faith says again) and of all the Saints is faith: He who has this, overcomes the fear of death, and conquers and triumphs forever. That is to be admired and is impossible to reason to believe, that God can and will abolish death, and change it into life. But this is much more wonderful, that Abraham and Isaac had the persuasion that this whole action (concerning the occasion and offering commanded by God) was a game and not death. And that death is a game to GOD, anyone easily believes, but that the same must be established for me and in my body, that death is not death, this neither a Physician, nor a Philosopher, nor a Jurisconsult will ever persuade. For who will join and reconcile those things, death is not death, but life. Moses himself affirms the contrary. For if you hear the law, it will say: In the midst of life we are in death, according to that old and pious song in the Church, but it is only legal. The Gospel however and faith invert this song, and sing thus: In the midst of death we are in life; we praise thee Redeemer, thou hast raised us from death, and saved us. Hence Paul triumphs Col. 2. Despoiling Principalities and Powers, he showed them openly. Likewise 2. Cor. 6. As dying, and behold we live. This is the power of faith, which so mediates between death and life, and transmutes death into life and immortality, which it knows is given through Christ. Whence the divine man establishes a wonderful and excellent description of death; Death has a soul and a body. The body is the extinction of the death of the soul. The soul of death is the very fear and horror of death. But if the soul of death is dead, the death of the body is sleep. We believe this, therefore we insult death joyfully: O death where is thy sting, where is thy victory? In the midst of death we are in life. I shall not die &c. He who knows this art, let him give thanks to GOD. But effort must be given, that we hold it not only speculatively in the mouth, but virtually and with the whole heart. This is the wisdom of God, the knowledge of the Saints, a sublime cognition above the grasp of the world. And it did not leave us empty, nor without fruit &c.

Latin:

Verf. 9. CUMQVE ALLIGASSET ISAAC FILIUM SUUM) Mos enim antiquissimus ligari victimas. Notat Ser- vius ad illud Æneidos, & vincula rupi. Ovidius 3. de Ponto Elegia 2. de Oreste & Pylade in Tauris:

Protinus immitem Triviæ dicuntur ad aram, Evincti geminas ad sua terga manus.

De hac Isaaci oblatione diximus in Program- mate festivo: quod proinde hic inferere non inutile erit. Sic autem illud habet:

Vere stupenda est tentationis Abrahami Histo- ria, cui geminam in ulla ætate temere haud inve- nias, & ad quam pro merito explicandam nec diser- tissimi Oratoris eloquentia sufficiat. B. Lutherus neminem alium, quam S. Paulum ad eandem illu- strandam, idoneum judicavit. Sed quod a tanto Apostolo non factum, Megalander ille, Spiritu Dei plenus, ita exequutus est in aureo gemmeoq; ad Genesin Commentario, ut non cum illo quidem cœlestis Scholæ discipulo componendus sit, Patrum tamen eloquentissimos, Ambrosium in Latina Ec- clesia, qui, Erasmo judice, vere cœlesti manat Am- brosia, & Chrysostomum aureum eloquentiæ os, in Græca, in historiæ hujus explicatione longo post se reliquerit intervallo. Quanquam nuda Historici di- vini relatio in stuporem facile illum converterit, qui eandem non perfunctorie expenderit. Cogi- tet solum non plane ἄστοργος illud horroris ple- num mandatum, Sancto Patriarchæ datum: TOL- LE FILIUM TUUM UNIGENITUM, QUEM DILIGIS, ISAAC, ET VADE AD TERRAM MORIA, ET OFFERES EUM IN HOLO- CAUSTUM, in quo verbum nullum est, quod non acutus fuerit gladius in corde Abrahami. Ma- gnum præcepti pondus, ait Chrysostomus hom. 47. Vide, quomodo per verba ista majus incendium suc- cendit, & fornacem amoris, quo Justus in Isaacum affectus erat, violentius excitat. Accipe filium tuum dilectum, quem dilexisti, Isaac. Unumquodque verbum per se sufficeret ad sauciandam animam justi. Non enim simpliciter dixit Isaac, sed addidit: Filium tuum: quem præter omnem expectationem, & in ipsa seneclute genuisti, dilectum desiderabilem tuum, quem tam immodice diligis; Isaacum, quem successurum tibi expectas, ex quo & semen tuum multiplicandum, ut stellarum multitidini & arenæ, quæ est juxta littus maris, adæquetur; illum ipsum accipe, & vade in terram excelsam, & offer eum ibi in holocaustum, super unum montium, quem tibi dicam. Admiror ego, quomodo hæc justus auribus ferre potuerit? Ad- miratus ista merito est Chrysostomus, sed magis ad- mirari oportet, quo animo sustinere potuerit præ- ceptam oblationem filii UNICI, quem solum e Sa- ra Conjuge susceperat. Nam quum voce filii ex- primatur tota vis naturalis amoris, quem Pater ha- bet erga prolem, eadem multum augetur voce uni- ci: minor enim est amor divisus in plures, & facilius fertur jactura unius ex multis, quam ejus, quod u- nicum est, neq; æquale aut simile habet, cujus sub- stitutione prioris jactura compensetur. Ideo gra- vior dolor esse non potest, quam in obitu filii unici, teste ipso Spiritu S. Plangent eum planctu quasi super unigenitum, & dolebunt super eum, ut doleri solet in morte primogeniti Zach. 12, 10. Hic vero ea filii unici voce audita, non id tantum animo Patriarchæ ob- versatum fuit, quod naturæ est, sed illud imprimis, quod supra naturam singularis & admiranda Dei benignitas in filii hujus donatione, ipsi, ac conjugi ejus exhibuerat. Ubi autem porro adderet Dominus Isaaci nomen, quo vulnere sancti Abrahami cor percussum fuerit, nemo facile verbis expresserit. Nam de eo acceperat a Domino: illi constituam pa- ctum meum in fœdus sempiternum, & semini ejus post eum. Gen. 17. v. 19. Cujus pacti medulla & anima hæc erat; in IPSO benedicentur omnes nationes ter- ræ Gen. 18, 18. Quid enim aliud secundum ratio- ne nis ductum cogitare poterat Abraham, quam irri- tam fore omnem illam promissionem? Quo pacto fieri potest, ut radice execta rami pullulent, vel succisa arbore fructus proveniant, vel fonte arefacto fluvii reddantur? Juxta hominis rationem talia fieri non est possibile, ut hic iterum Chrysostomus. Quo- modo ergo gravius vulnerari potuit cor Patriar- chæ, quam ubi illum occidendum esse intelligebat, in quo semen benedictum, Salvatorem Mundi sibi promissum acceperat, cujus tentationis magnitu- dinem nemo assequi potest. Jam non occidendus tantum erat Isaac, sed Parens ipse jussus est eum oc- cidere, non per alios, sive hostes, sive amicos; fœ- dandæ erant ipsæ manus paternæ sanguine filii. Nec solum cædes filii unici eidem præcipiebatur, sed offerre eum in holocaustum debuit, hoc est, ligare, strui lignorum imponere, jugulare, ignem subtus accendere, & tamdiu versare, usque dum in cineres & favillas resolvatur, atq; sic omnis simul ipsius spes & consolatio etiam de Semine in fumum abeat. Ne- que hoc statim facere debebat, sed in terra Moria, super unum montium, ad quem iter tridui conficiendum erat: si unius aut alterius horæ ἀγὼν ille fuisset, facilius superasset. Ideo hæc mora obedientiam ejus amplificat. Interea cogitavit: Ecce incedo cum filio summæ spei juvene, ei moriendum est. Ejusmodi carnis mace- rationem hosce tres dies simul cum Satanæ sagittis su- stinuit, mussitandum tamen & silendum fuit propter mandatum, quo nixus confirmatur & servatur. Neq; etiam verba illa temere transmittenda duxit B. Lu- therus, quæ exigui videri poterant momenti: CIN- XIT ASINUM SUUM. Hæc, inquit, omnia ideo tam diligenter describuntur, ut significetur, etiam mo- ram fidem ejus nonnihil exercuisse. Ipsi Parenti quæ- renda sunt ligna, secanda & imponenda asino ad cre- mandum filium. Interim haud dubie maximam car- nis trepidationem sensit. Neque enim ferreo pectore fuit, sed tenerrima natura, & animo ejus perpetuo ob- versata est cogitatio de sacrificio holocausti, ad quod filius unigenitus promissus, spes futuri seminis & posteri- tatis mactandus, & illis ipsis lignis, quæ collegit Pater, cremandus erat. Annon in re tam tristi & stupen- da deliberandum amplius erat? annon conferenda consilia cum matre Sara? Hæc in istis, ut apparet, inu- tilibus verbis, significantur, alioqui potuissent hæc bre- vissime dici. Sed vult indicare Moses, quos motus sen- serit singulis momentis, quibus haud dubie gemitus inenarrabiles, suspiria, singultus & lachrymæ pa- ternæ accesserunt. Ad verba vero ista textus Sacri: ET PERGERANT ILLI DUO SIMUL, hæc Vir DEI: Talis transitus, qualis hic est, nus- quam in Scriptura Sacra descriptus est. Duo. Qui? Pater charissimus, & dilectissimus Filius. Quo ani- mo? Eo animo: Isaaci rei ignarus, & tamen obedire paratus: Abraham certissimus mactare filium, & in cineres redigere. Sed præ omnibus maxime stu- pendus est Dialogismus filii cum Patre, quem hisce describit Divinus Historicus: Dixit autem Isaac ad Patrem suum: Pater mi; at ille respon- det: Ecce ego, fili mi. Ait ille: Ecce ignis & ligna, ubi est pecus ad holocaustum? Respondet Abraham: DEUS providebit sibi pecus in holocaustum, fili mi. De quo Lutherus noster: Ingens vero hic motus, & vehemens πάθος est, quod Moses noluit præterire. Isaac victima alloquitur Patrem, & irritat illam στοργὴν φυσικὴν, q. d. Tu mihi es Pater: & parens vicissim: tu mihi filius: hæc penetrarunt & percule- runt haud dubie animum paternum. Audiamus hic & Chrysostomum Constantinopolitanum: Dixit Isaac ad Abrahamum Patrem suum: Pater: Sufficiebat hoc verbum ad lancinanda Justi hujus visce- ra. Ille autem dixit: Quid est fili? Patrem vocas paulo post futurum orbum: & ego filium appello, qui non multo post altare ascensurus est, meis occidendus manibus. O animæ fortitudinem, o Spiritus solidi- tatem! Qualibus oculis spectabat puerum ligna affe- rentem, super quæ non multo post eum impositurus e- rat? Quomodo manus ferre potuit ignem & gladium? Et manus quidem ferebat ignem, qui sensibilis erat, in- tus autem incendebat ipsius mentem, & rationem absu- mebat, & persuadebat, ut vinceret amor in DEUM. Sed ad ipsam oblationis historiam properandum; de qua graviter B. Lutherus: Constructo jam altari cum ad ipsam Epitasin perventum est, tacet Moses, & vel desperat ista eloqui: quia res major est, quam ut ulla eloquentia efferri possit; vel præ lachrymis non po- tuit scribere. Atque ita stuporem & admirationem in animis auditorum relinquit, & vult, ut ipsi rem ex- pendant, quam verbis assequi non valet. Jam enim constructo altari, parato cultro & igne accenso, necesse fuit aliquos sermones inter Patrem & filium intercede- re, quibus Isaac edoctus est de voluntate & mandato Dei. Pater dixit: Tu mi dilectissime fili, quem Deus mihi dedit, destinatus es ad holocaustum. Ibi filius haud dubie obstupuit, & Patrem de promissione vicissim admonuit. Cogita, mi Pater, me esse se- men, cui promissa est posteritas, Reges, populi &c. Dedit me Deus matri meæ Sara per magnum mira- culum. Quomodo igitur poterit impleri promis- sio, me occiso? Sine tamen nos antea de ea re con- ferre & colloqui. Illa omnia hic scribenda fuissent, cur omiserit Moses, nescio. Non autem dubito, quin insignis admodum oratio fuerit Patris ad filium, & principalem ejus statum fuisse existimo mandatum Dei & resurrectionem mortuorum. DEUS præcepit, ideo nos oportet ei obedire, & cum sit omnipotens, potest servare promissionem, etiam te mortuo & in cinerem redacto. Audiamus, quæ de Epitasi B. Lutherus addit: Brevi sententia complectitur Moses illam mira- bilem & stupendam historiam: Pater filium jamjam jugulaturus est. Filius jugulum præbet, sublatis oculis in cœlum, & expectat, ut in cineres redigatur, ita in ex- tremum discrimen vitæ uterq; a DEO adducitur. Si ibi non fuisset fides, aut DEUS dormitasset unum mo- mentum, actum fuisset de filii vita. Quia culter pa- ratus, filius vinctus, in struem lignorum positus est, ju- gulum petitur. Ego non potuissem esse spectator, nedum actor & mactator. Stupenda res est, quod Pater ca- rissimus filii carissimi jugulo cultrum admoverit, & a- gnosco sane, me hasce cogitationes, & affectus nec verbis, nec meditando assequi posse.

Sed quid hoc tam triste spectaculum ad gau- dia Paschalia? Abripuit nos, fatemur, paulo longi- us, quam intentio ferebat, utriusq; Chrysostomi, de stupenda narratione stupenda Eloquentia. Ne- que tamen abhorruit Christus redivivus colloquia de passione, & morte sua lugubria, cum Paschalia ageret gaudia, imo prolixas conciones iterato hisce solemnibus, è Mose & Prophetis, de eadem insti- tuit. Nec dubium est, insignem hanc Isaaci figu- ram, quæ in Mose imprimis eminet, a Doctore de morte triumphante, discipulis Emaunticis & Hiero- solymitanis expositam fuisse. Cujus explicationis summam a S. Apostolo Ebr. 11, 17. paucis sane verbis, sed divina sapientia comprehensam arbitramur. Fide obtulit Abraham Isaac, cum tentaretur, & unigenitum offerebat, qui susceperat repromissio- nes, ad quem dictum est: Quia in Isaac voca- bitur tibi semen, arbitrans, quia & a mortuis suscita- re potens est DEUS, unde & eum in parabola accepit. Quæ docent, quibus oculis spectaculum illud in Maria intueri debeamus, non ut hæreamus in Abrahami obedientia, sed fidem imprimis Patris credentium in auctorem fidei, consummatorem JE- SUM, qui proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, respiciamus: quæ ut idem Apostolus Rom. 4, 25. exposuit, unice in eum defixa fuit, qui suscitaturus erat Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum a mortuis, utpote qui tradendus erat propter delicta nostra, & resuscitandus propter Iustificationem nostram. Quæ in hoc spectaculo ipsi figurabantur. Nam recepit Abraham Isaacum ἐν παραβολῇ IN FIGURA. Erat ergo Isaacus figura Christi, Filius ille Abrahami unicus, adumbrans unigenitum DEI Filium; natus non secundum virtutem naturæ, sed secundum promissionem Dei, natum secundum promissio- nes Patribus factas, virtute Spiritus Sancti: prom- tus ad oblationem promtissimum ad immolatio- nem corporis sui. Nescit utique Chrysostomus, utrum justius miretur fortem Abrahæ Spiritum, an Isaaci obedientiam, quod neque reluctatus est, neque factum ægre tulit, sed cessit & obtemperavit his, quæ a Patre facta sunt, & sicut agnus cum silentio super al- tare accubuit, expectans Patris dextram. Affectus paternus Abrahami ad stuporem se submittens consilio Dei, umbra & imago quædam est affectus Dei Patris erga filium, & admirandæ illius συγκα- ταϐάσεως ad æternum consilium de salute nostra. Sed si omnia illa persequi vellemus, regrediendum denuo nobis esset in Septimanam passionis, & ad montem Moria, in quo immolatus est Dominus. Hæc enim omnia, ut hîc iterum loquamur verbis Chrysostomi, figura fuerunt crucis, propterea & Chri- stus Judæis dicebat: Abraham Pater vester exulta- bat, ut videret diem meum, & vidit, & gavisus est. Quomodo vidit? qui temporibus præcessit? per figu- ram, per umbram. Sicut enim ovis oblata est pro Isaac, ita & rationalis agnus oblatus est pro mun- do. Vide obsecro, quomodo omnia per umbras præ- figurata sunt, unigenitus illic & unigenitus hic, dilectus illic & germanus, dilectus & hic atq; germanus. A Patre ille in holocaustum offertur, & hunc Pater tra- didit. Hucusq; umbra, postea rerum veritas magna excellentia monstratur. Agnus enim hic rationalis pro toto mundo oblatus est, totum orbem terrarum pu- rificavit, homines ab errore liberavit, & ad veritatem adduxit: terram cœlum fecit, non elementorum immu- tata natura, sed conversatione cælesti hominibus super terram degentibus allata: De resurrectionis figura videndum. Eam in redivivo filio suo conspica- batur Abraham, qui per triduum in corde Patris mortuus erat, sed postea vivus Patri redditus est. Nulla eundem creatura reddere poterat; nullius e- nim creaturæ voce a jugulatione filii retrahi se pas- sus fuisset Patriarcha. Ipsius ergo DEI dextra li- berandus erat, a quo in Sacrificium immolari jussus erat Isaacus. Angelus itaq; delapsus est cælo, & ut B. Luthero visum, adfulsit nova lux, adfuit una mul- titudo angelorum, qua majestate perterritus Abraham, cultrum & cogitationem simul de mactatione abjecit. Ut a Deo in mortem traditus Christus, ita divina virtute a mortuis resuscitatus est, in qua resuscita- tionis gloria non defuisse angelorum stipatorum multitudinem, credendum. Sed ut ne in umbra hæreamus, angelus ille increatus, qui Abrahæ ap- paruit, est ipse Isaaci antitypus: qui non in figura, sed vere mortem subiit, non in figura, sed vere a mortuis resurrexit, non aliena suscitatus potentia, sed propria redivivus virtute. Sed & Isaac, si Macarius de exalt. S. cruc. audiendus, divinam im- patibilitatem insinuavit, divino mandato mori prohi- bitus; ariete autem humanitas significabatur, & mors, quam Christus secundum humanam naturam subjicit.

Quod ergo ibi audit Patriarcha : Benedicentur in se- mine tuo omnes gentes Gen. 22. hoc est, ut B. Luthe- rus interpretatur, gloriabuntur de victoria mortis, de abolito peccato, de donatione vitæ æternæ, non propter sua merita, sed in semine tuo, de eo hodierno impri- mis die exultat gentium, per orbem fidelium, multi- tudo. Nam resurrectione Christi parta nobis hæc benedictio. Pascha Christi, dicente S. Augustino, Regnum est cæli, salus mundi, vita credentium, occasus inferni, gloria supernorum, resurrectio mortuorum, te- stimonium resurrectionis divinæ, pretium redemtionis humanæ, cognitio mortis abolitæ. Hic igitur est dies, quem fecit Dominus, celsior cunctis, lucidior universis, in quo sibi novam plebem regenerationis Spiritu acquisi- vit, in quo singulorum mentes gaudio & exultatione perfudit. Hic ergo dies resurrectionis Christi defun- ctis vita, peccatoribus venia, sanctis est gloria. Benedi- ctus itaq; Deus Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui secundum misericordiam suam magnam regeneravit nos, in spem vivam, per resurrectionem Christi ex mor- tuis. Fidem nostram exemplo etiam Abrahæ & Isaa- ci firmemus. Victoria enim Abrahæ & Isaac (ut ite- rum noster in fide Heros) & omnium Sanctorum est fides: Hanc qui habet, superat pavorem mortis, & vin- cit & triumphat in æternum. Admirandum illud & rationi impossibile creditu, quod Deus possit & velit mor- tem abolere, & mutare in vitam. Sed hoc multo mirabi- lius, quod Abraham & Isaac persuasum habuerint, i- stam totam actionem (de occasione & oblatione a Deo præcepta) esse ludum & non mortem.
