## 30:3
verse 3. HANDMAID] The Greeks [use] παιδίσκην. Josephus relates that both this woman and Zilpah were free-born servants. And the Hebrew word is taken in this way in Exodus 2:5.

AND I MAY HAVE CHILDREN BY HER] That is, I may care for them as my own.

He therefore hints at the adoption of children, but not, as the foolish Hebrews imagine, that she wished to be incited in this way to give birth and to be warmed for conception.

Latin:

vers. 3. FAMVLAM] παιδίσκην Græci. Ministram fuisse in- genuam, & hanc & Zelpham tradit Josephus. Et sic sumitur vox Hebræa Exod. 2,5.

ET HABEAM EX ILLA LIBEROS] Id est, eos tanquam meos curem.

ADoptionem ergo innuit liberorum, non vero ut Ebræi ineptiunt, quod incitari ita ad parien- dum & ad concipiendum calefieri voluerit.

## 30:11
ver. 11. HAPPILY AND THEREFORE SHE CALLED HIS NAME GAD] Some Greeks say ἐν τύχῃ, others ἐντύχηκα. Gad signifies prosperity, by which name the Arabs of Cedrenus called a star, which is Tzedek to the Hebrew astrologers, and Jupiter to the Greeks, because it was believed by astrologers to be most fortunate. Abarbaniel notes this: and add Isaiah 65:11.

Jonathan and Jarchi take Gad to mean the goddess of fortune; but this meaning is clearly unwritten, even if it is customary among the Chaldeans and Rabbis: and therefore Gad ba is more correctly explained as A TROOP HAS COME of children, because this is now the fifth son of Leah. See Mr. Varenius, Decad. Genes. p. 518. Hottinger, Histor. Creation. p. 20, explains it as GOD, noting that the Hebrew and Arabic Gur is called a good God, just as in German Gott is said as if it were Gut; i.e., Gad ba, God has come. But he himself is doubtful about this explanation of his. If the Chetib is to be preferred, I do not see why the explanation of Blessed Luther should be postponed; concerning which he says thus in his Commentary on this passage: We have remained in the root of the verb, which signifies to be girded; and Moses confirms this interpretation of ours below in chapter XLIX, in the blessing of the sons of Gad, where it is said, a troop shall gird him, he shall fight. This authority is sufficient for us against the wrangling of the Rabbis, Gad soll fürher gehen; therefore we translate it, Rüstig, es will angehen [Sturdily, it is beginning]. Whoever wishes to follow others, let him do so by all means. Rachel had said when Naphtali was born, I have prevailed, I have conquered: Leah says here, I shall prevail, I have now a victor, es gehet rüstig an, daß ich noch ein Knecht habe [it is beginning sturdily, that I have yet another servant], who may conquer and propagate my family.

Latin:

vers. 11. FELICITER ET IDCIRCO VOCAVIT NO- MEN EJVS GAD] Græci alii ἐν τύχῃ, alii ἐντύχηκα. גד pro- speritatem significat, quo nomine Cedreni Arabes stellam no- minabant, quæ צדק Hebræis Astrologis, Græcis Jovis, quod ea felicissima ab Astrologis crederetur. Notat Abarbaniel: & ad- de Esaiam 65,11.

Jonathan, & Jarchius גד de fortuna Dea acci- piunt; Sed hæc significatio plane ἄγραφος est: etsi apud Chald. & Rabbin. usitata sit: Ideoque בא גד rectius exponitur VENIT TURMA fi- liorum, quia quintus hic jam Leæ filius. Vid. Dn. Varenius, Decad. Genes. p. 518. Hottingerus Histor. Creation. p. 20. exponit DEUS, Hebr. & Arabib. גור bonum Gut DEUM dici notans, uti Germani- cis Gott dicitur quasi Gut; h. m. בא גד Venit DEUS. Sed ipse dubius est de hac sua expositione. Si τὸ כתיב Chetib præferendum sit, non video, cur B. Luther. explicatio posthaberi debeat: de qua ita habet in Comment. ad h. l. Mansimus in radice verbi, quæ significat accinctum esse; & con- firmat hanc interpretationem nostram Moses infra cap. XLIX. in benedictione filiorum Gad, ubi dicitur, accinctus præliabitur. Hæc autoritas nobis sufficit ad versus Rabbinorum rixas, Gad soll fürher gehen; Ideo nos vertimus Rüstig, es will angehen. Qui alios vult sequi, faciat sane. Rahel dixerat nato Naph- tali, prævalui, vici: Lea hic dicit, prævalebo, habeo jam victorem, es gehet rüstig an, daß ich noch ein Knecht habe, qui vincat, & familiam meam pro- paget.

## 30:14
Vers. 14. MANDRAKES) The seed of the mandrake when drunk cleanses the womb. Pliny 25, 15.

It is believed to have the power of a love potion, as noted by Dioscorides and Theophrastus, and to promote fertility according to Aristotle, book II, On the Generation of Animals. And therefore these fruits are thought to be called dudaim from love. The LXX also render them mandrake apples: and this meaning is usually derived from the Arabic language: and it is evident from Canticles 7:14 that they are fragrant and beautiful fruits. Concerning the flowers, however, Mercerus gives thanks for their odor and color: some Hebrews interpret them as jasmine, Franciscus Georgius Venetus as lilies, others as violets. Concerning the blackberries of the bramble, T. XI. Witteb. p. 187, Blessed Luther explains: but in the marginal gloss he leaves it in the middle, whether they are blackberries, or lilies, or what in the end they are?

Latin:

Vers. 14. MANDRAGORAS) Semen mandragoræ potum vulvam purgat. Plinius 25, 15.

Vim Philtri habere creditur, notante Diosco- ride & Theophrasto, & promovere fœcunditatem juxta Aristotelem lib. II. de gen. animal. Ideoque hæc po- ma דודאים ab amore dici putant. μῆλα μαν- δραγορῶν etiam LXX. reddunt: & ex Arabica lin- gua educi solet hæc fignificatio: constatque e Cant. 7, 14. esse odoratos & pulchros fructus. De floribus ta- men odore & colore gratis Mercerus: de herba Jasmen Ebræi nonnulli, de liliis Franc. Georg. Venetus, de violis alii interpretantur. De moris Rubi T. XI. Wit- teb. p. 187. B. Lutherus explicat: at in glossa margi- nali in medio relinquit, an mora sint, an lilia, aut quid denique sint?

## 31:19
vers. 19. IDOLS] Teraphim. So also the Greeks. Below they are called the gods of Laban 30. τύποι τῶν Θεῶν [types of the gods] according to Josephus. Images made for a certain position of the stars with the figures of the stars, from the ancient superstition of the Syrians and Arabs. Rachel took these away, so that Laban might not learn the plan of their flight from them. Thus Aben Ezra. But Josephus [says it was] so that she might have a refuge against her father's anger, if by chance they were caught in flight.

Grotius believes they were images made for a certain position of the stars with the figures of the stars from the ancient superstition of the Syrians and Arabs. Let Selden be consulted concerning them in De Dis Syris, book I. And what we have observed at Judg. 17, 5. He gives a twofold reason why Rachel took them away: the one from Aben Ezra, that Laban might not learn the plan of their flight from them: the other from Josephus, that she might have a refuge against her father's anger. But whence is it certain that Rachel, instructed in the true worship of GOD, attributed so much to her father's idols that she could either learn the plan of their flight from them, or that they could provide a refuge? Basil and Nazianzen, Orat. 2 on Easter, more correctly suppose that she wished to recall her father from idolatry by this means. But if one thinks with Chrysostom that something of her father's superstition still clung to her, it must nevertheless be believed that she placed no confidence in those idols.

Latin:

vers. 19. IDOLA] Teraphim. Sic & Græci. Infra dicun- tur dii Labanis 30. τύποι τῶν Θεῶν Josepho. Imagines ad cer- tum stellarum positum factæ cum stellarum figuris, ex veteri Syrorum & Arabum superstitione. Abstulit hæc Rachel, ne ex iis Laban consilium fugæ disceret. Sic Aben Esdra. At Josephus, ut perfugium haberet contra patris iram, si forte in fuga deprehenderentur.

Imagines ad certum stellarum positum factas cum stellarum figuris ex veteri Syrorum & Arabum su- perstitione credit Grotius. De illis Seldenus videa- tur de DisSyr. l. I. Et quæ nos observavimus ad Jud. 17, 5. Causam cur Rachel abstulerit, geminam reddit: Alteram ex Aben Esra, ne ex iis consilium fugæ disceret Laban: Alteram ex Josepho, ut perfugium haberet contra Patris iram. Sed unde constat, quod Patris idolis tantum Rachel in vero DEI cultu informata tribuerit, quod vel consilium fugæ inde cognoscere queat, vel perfugium illa præstare possint? Rectius Basilius & Nazianz. Orat. 2. de Pasch. autumant, voluisse eam Patrem ab idololatria hoc pacto revocare. Si vero hæsisse adhuc aliquid ipsi de superstitione paterna cum Chrysostomo putet, nullam tamen con- fidentiam in idola illa ipsam locasse, credendum.

## 31:42
Verf. 42. THE GOD OF MY FATHER ABRAHAM, AND THE FEAR OF ISAAC] He does not say the God of Isaac, because Isaac was still living. But God is not surnamed after anyone who is still leading a mortal life.

Why not? Did not God himself testify to Abraham while he was living, I am thy GOD Gen. 17, 7. Was he not called the GOD of Abraham, while he himself was still living Gen. 24, 27, and the GOD of Isaac Gen. 28, 13, while he himself was still acting among mortals? That observation is therefore false. But that the fear of Isaac is to be understood objectively concerning him whom Isaac fears and reveres, is evident from verse 53. Compare Isa. 8, 13. For one must swear only by God, Isa. 65, 16.

Latin:

Verf. 42. DEUS PATRIS MEI ABRAHAM, ET TIMOR ISAAC ] Non dicit Deus Isaaci, quia vivebat adhuc Isaac. Non cognominatur autem Deus a quoquam mortalem adhuc agente vitam.

Quidni? annon Deus ipse Abraham testatus est viventi, Ego DEVS tuus sum Gen. 17, 7. Annon vocatus DEUS Abrahami, cum adhuc ipse viveret Gen. 24, 27. & DEUS Isaaci Gen. 28, 13. ipso adhuc inter mortales agente? Falsa ergo est illa observatio. Pavorem autem Isaaci objective intelligi de eo, quem pavet ac timet Isaac, e versu 53. constat. Conf. Esa. 8, 13. In solo enim Deo jurandum, Esa 65, 16.

vers. 46. A MOUND) βουνὸν here for the Greeks. Xenophon in the fourth book of the Anabasis calls such a monument Κολωνὸν.

Verf. 53. THE GOD OF NAHOR] בעל שמין The Sun, in the greatest honor among the Syrians, as the most beautiful and most useful of those things which are beheld.

That certainly seems sure, that Laban, by the Gods of Abraham, the Gods of Nahor, and the Gods of their father Terah, understands the false gods which they worshipped in Ur of the Chaldeans, Jos. 24, 2.

Latin:

Verf. 53. DEUS NACHOR] בעל שמין Sol maximo apud Syros in honore, ut pulcherrimum & utilissimum eorum, quæ spectantur.

Id utique certum videtur, Labanum per Deos Abrahæ, Deos Nachor, & Deos Patris eorum Tha- ræ, intelligere falsos Deos, quos illi in Ur Chaldæo- rum coluere, Jos. 24. 2.

## 32:2
verf. 2. MAHANAIM. Others take this to mean two angelic camps. Mr. D. Varenius interprets it as one camp of Jacob's and another of the angels. We adhere to the common explanation, which the words of the text confirm; the angels of God met him, and when he saw them, he said, These are the camps of God, and he called the name of that place Mahanaim.

Latin:

verf. 2. MAHANAIM. Accipiunt id de duo- bus castris angelicis alii. Dn. D. Varenius de uno Jacobeo, altero angelico interpretatur. Adhære- mus communi explicationi: quam verba textus fir- mant; fuerunt ei obviam angeli Dei, quos cum vidisset, ait, Castra Dei sunt hæc, & appellavit nomen loci illius Mahanaim.

## 32:3 Addition
To Gen. 32. verse 3. page 298. a. INTO THE LAND OF SEIR THE REGION OF EDOM.

Junius, Piscator, and the Dutch understand it as the Southern Idumea. But a different view appeared to Bonfrerius. For if Esau had lived so far away, there was no reason why Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia and now descending from Mount Gilead, should fear him; nor could Esau come so quickly, nor could Jacob send messengers to him so quickly. It is necessary, therefore, to distinguish a double Idumea and a double Mount Seir. Thus distinguish Borchardus and

Adrichomius and Dominicus Marius Niger in their Geographies and Torniellus in his Annals. There is one Eastern Idumea (which is treated in this place), another Southern. The Idumeans inhabited these regions not simultaneously, but alternately: first indeed the Eastern, where Mount Seir is, which is a part of Mount Gilead more to the north and verging toward Lebanon; here Esau and his descendants lived for a long time. Finally, they abandoned the Eastern and occupied the Southern, having driven out the Horites, before the exit of the Israelites from Egypt: as is evident both from Deut. 2. verses 12, 22 and Num. 20. v. 14 and Jos. 15. v. 21, and from the fact that when the Israelites entered the promised land, the Idumeans were not there, but Sihon and Og, etc. Add to these that Job was an Idumean, and of the stock of Esau, and lived in the land of Uz, which was across the Jordan, not far from Mount Gilead, as witnessed by Borchardus, Adrichomius, and Jerome. Therefore the Idumeans lived there at that time, and from there they migrated later, as has now been proven; the only difficulty can be from Lam. 4. v. 21. O Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz. But it is likely that the Idumeans, having changed their habitation, gave the names of their former places to many locations; as Bonfrerius and Matthew Poole hold here.

Latin:

Ad Genes. 32. vers. 3. pag. 298. a. IN TERRAM SEIR IN REGIONEM EDOM.

De Idumæa Australi Junius, Piscator, Belgæ intelligunt. Aliud autem visum Bonfrerio. Si enim tam remotus habitasset Esau, non erat cur Jacob, rediens ex Mesopotamia, & jam descendens à monte Galaad, ab eo timeret; nec aut Esau poterat tam cito venire, aut Jacob ad eum tam cito nuncios mittere. Necesse ergo est distinguere duplicem Idumæam, & du- plicem montem Seir. Sic distinguunt Borchardus &

Adrichomius & Dominicus Marius Niger in suis Geographicis & Torniellus in Annalibus. Est Idu- mæa una Orientalis, (de qua hoc loco agitur) alia au- stralis. Has regiones non simul, sed vicissim, Idumæi habitarunt: primo quidem Orientalem, ubi est mons Seir, qui pars est montis Galaad septentrionalior, & ad Libanum vergens; hic Esau & posteri diu habita- runt. Tandem orientalem deseruerunt, & australem occuparunt, Horræis pulsis, ante exitum Israëlitarum ex Ægypto: ut constat tum ex Deut. 2. vers. 12. 22. & Num. 20. v. 14. & Jos. 15. v. 21. tum ex eo, quod in- gressis Israëlitis in terram promissam, non ibi erant Idumæi, sed Sehon & Og &c. His adde quod Job fuit Idumæus, & de stirpe Esau, habitavitque in terra Hus, quæ erat trans Jordanem, non procul a monte Galaad, testibus Borch. Adrich. & Hieron. Ergo tum ibi habitarunt Idumæi, indeque postea migrarunt, ut jam probatum; Tantum difficultas esse potest ex Thren. 4. v. 21. Edom, quæ habitas in terra Hus. Sed ve- risimile est Idumæos, mutato habitatione, nomina priorum locorum multis locis indidisse; ut hic habent Bonfrerius & Matthæus Polus.

## 32:11
Vers. 11. THE MOTHER WITH THE CHILDREN) A proverbial expression, that is, let him cause slaughter.

Latin:

Vers. 11. MATREM CUM FILIIS) Proverbialis locutio, id est, internecionem faciat.

## 32:23
Verf. 23. AND HAVING BROUGHT ALL OVER) That word 'all' seems to have been in certain Hebrew codices, because of the great consensus of the Samaritan, the Syriac, the Greek, and the Latin.

If the Latin is said to have followed the Greek LXX, these the Syriac, and the Syriac indeed the Samaritan, what will that consensus avail against the original text? Or if the Alexandrian Codices, which the LXX Interpreters had, are judged to have been such as the Syriac and Samaritan had, will they prejudice the sincere Codices kept by the Jerusalemites? Finally, could that little word not have been added by the interpreters for the sake of evidence, even if it were not in the πρωτοτύπῳ? Since the sense is the same in the Hebrew: having brought over what belonged to him, he remained alone. For it is manifest that all things were brought over by him: because he is said to have remained alone, and to have brought over indefinitely those things which belonged to him.

Latin:

Verf. 23. TRADUCTISQVE OMNIBVS ) Illud omnibus videtur fuisse in codicibus Hebraicis quibusdam, ob tantum consensum Samaritani, Syri, Græci, Latini.

Si Latinus Græcos LXX. hi Syrum, Syrus vero Samaritanum sequutus dicatur, quid ille consensus juvabit adversus textum originalem? aut si Alexan- drini Codices, quos habuere LXX. Interpp. tales fuisse censeantur, quales habuerit Syrus & Samari- tanus, num præjudicabunt illi sinceris Codicibus, penes Hierosolymitanos asservatis? Denique, annon adjici evidentiæ causa vocula illa potuit ab inter- pretibus, etsi in πρωτοτύπῳ non haberetur? Quum sensus idem in Ebræo sit: traductis, quæ ad se perti- nebant, mansit solus. Manifestum enim est, omnia traducta esse ab ipso: quia solus mansisse, & indefinite ea, quæ ad se pertinebant, traduxisse dicitur.

## 32:25
vers. 25. AND IMMEDIATELY HE WITHERED) This mystically signifies συστολὴν οἰήσεως [the contraction of pride]. Philo, περὶ ἄθλων [On Rewards].

Concerning the Wrestler of Jacob.

of one undivided essence, which belongs to no creature,) is read to have been applied: yet the name אל, from which Jacob is called Israel, can by no means belong to an Angel, because we have demonstrated in our treatise on divine names in Natural and Revealed Theology that it is proper to the one GOD. But he was called Israel for this reason, that he prevailed with Elohim. He, therefore, who is called Elohim, with whom Jacob wrestled, is El, that is, that strong GOD. Just as he also gave the name פני אל to the place, the face of GOD, because he saw אלהים there. Therefore, this Elohim, or one of the Elohim, must have been אל, that strong God. Nor would Jacob have sought a blessing from an Angel, even if he were imagined to have represented the person of GOD. Otherwise, it would be lawful to invoke angels representing the person of GOD, which, even if Grotius might perhaps willingly wish it with the Papists, is repugnant to the first table of the law. Nor is it granted by the Angels themselves, Apoc. 19 & 22. But this man did not only grant that, but also heard Jacob's petition and blessed him, which belongs to no angel; whence Jacob rejoiced greatly that he had seen GOD and his soul was saved. Hosea says both angel and GOD, with whom Jacob wrestled, c. 12, 3. 4. He was therefore indeed an angel, but an angel GOD, an angel of Elohim and El, that is, an uncreated angel, to be adored by all, which the name Elohim implies in its proper meaning. And thus no other than the Son of GOD, whose name is אל, Isa. 9, 6, whom Jacob acknowledges, celebrates, and invokes as the angel גאל, the redeemer, who delivered him from all evil, and thus prays for a blessing from him for his grandsons. Gen. 48, 16. Therefore, Grotius ought to have acknowledged with venerable antiquity the wrestler of Jacob here, the Son of GOD; but he preferred to ἰδέαιζειν καὶ σοφικίζειν [to play with ideas and be a sophist]. With Jacob, says Clement of Alexandria, lib. 1. Pædag. cap. 7. The Holy Lord Jesus is also said to wrestle. Cyril of Alexandria, lib. IX. against Julian. That the man wrestling against Jacob is the only-begotten λόγος of GOD, showing beforehand to the Holy Fathers from those things which Moses wrote how he was to be in our form in his own time, one might consider quite easily. Cyril therefore judges that the Son of GOD showed the Fathers that form of ours which he was about to assume. Justin Martyr agrees with these, Dial. with Trypho. Tertullian, II. & III. against Marcion & cap. XVI. against Praxeas. Novatian on the Trinity, c. xxvii. Athanasius, orat. IV. against the Arians & in the Epistle on the Synods of Ariminum & Seleucia. Hilary, l. IV. on the Trinity. Eusebius, l. I. Eccl. Hist. c. 2, Demonstr. Evang. l. V. c. II. Basil against Eunomius, l. II. Nazianzen, orat. II. on Theology. Epiphanius, l. I. against Heresies, LVIII. Ambrose on the faith against the Arians, T. VIII. Jerome on Hosea, c. 12, 3. Phæbadius against the Arians, c. XXXIV. following. Chrysostom, homily LVIII. on Genesis. Euthymius Zigabenus in the Panoplia, part I. T. II. Paulinus of Nola, l. I. Epist. II. to Severus. Sulpitius Severus, l. I. Sacred History, c. 13. Theodoret on Gen. Q. XII. John Maxentius, dial. l. II. Procopius of Gaza, Commentary on this passage. Nor did the Roman Pontiffs deny their consent. Clement of Rome, l. V. Constit. cap. 21. (which we cite κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον [humanly speaking]) Jacob saw this Son of God as a man, and said: I have seen GOD face to face and my soul is saved. Leo the Great, Epist. XIII. to Pulcheria. How (the Son of GOD) appeared to the Patriarchs and Prophets in the form of flesh, when he either entered into a contest or held a conversation. Nor did the entire Councils: the Council of Antioch, celebrated in the year 226 against Paul of Samosata, whose Synodal Epistle, unearthed from antiquity by Franc. Turrianus, Baronius reviews in the Annals for the year 267, n. 4. Severinus Binius, T. I. of the councils. And after the struggle and that of the man prefigured, it is subjoined: And Jacob called the name of that place, Face of GOD. For I have seen GOD face to face and my soul has been saved. But we say that the man prefigured is the Son of GOD, whom Scripture itself has declared to be GOD. The Council of Sirmium pronounced anathema on those who deny this: If anyone says that it was not the Son who wrestled with Jacob, but the unbegotten adhered to the rules of his interpretation of Scripture and the consensus of the Fathers. Whom the Catholics Vatablus in this place and Fernandus de vision. p. 180 have followed more correctly.

Latin:

vers. 25. ET STATIM EMARCVIT ) Id mystice signifi- cat συστολὴν οἰήσεως. Philo, περὶ ἄθλων.

De Collu- ctatore Ja- cobi.

unius indivisæ essentiæ, quod nulli creaturæ conve- nit,) adhibitum legitur: nequaquam tamen nomen אל, unde Jacob Israel vocatur, Angelo conveni- re potest, quod uni DEO proprium esse, tractatu de nominibus divinis in Theol. natur. & revel. demon- stravimus. Ideo autem dictus est Israel, quod præ- valuerit Elohim. Is ergo, qui Elohim dicitur, quocum pugnavit Jacob, El, hoc est, fortis ille DEUS est. Quemadmodum etiam inde loco nomen dedit פני אל faciei DEI, quod ibi viderit אלהים. Hunc ergo Elohim vel unum ex Elohim oportet fu- isse אל Deum illum fortem. Nec ab Angelo, etsi fingatur personam DEI repræsentasse, Jacob bene- dictionem petiisset. Alias angelos personam DEI referentes integrum esset invocare, quod, etsi liben- ter cum Papistis vellet fortassis Grotius, primæ tabu- læ legis repugnat. Nec ab Angelis ipsis concedi- tur Apoc. 19. & 22. Hic vero vir non concessit id mo- do, sed exaudivit quoque petitionem Jacobi, eidem- que benedixit, quod nullius angeli est; unde oppido lætatus est Jacob, quod viderit DEUM & salva sit a- nima sua. Hoseas & angelum & DEUM dicit, quo- cum luctatus Jacob, c. 12, 3. 4. Fuit ergo quidem angelus, sed angelus DEVS, angelus Elohim & El, hoc est, increatus angelus, adorandus ab omnibus, quod nomen Elohim infert significatu proprio. Ad- eoque nullus alius, quam Filius DEI, cujus nomen אל est Ef. 9, 6. quem angelum גאל redemtorem agnoscit, celebrat atque invocat Jacob, qui se ab o- mni malo liberarit, adeoque ab eo benedictionem nepotibus suis precatur. Gen. 48, 16. Agnoscere er- go cum antiquitate veneranda hîc debuit Grotius colluctatorem Jacobi, Filium DEI; sed maluit ille ἰδέαιζειν καὶ σοφικίζειν. Cum Jacobo, inquit Cle- mens Alex. lib. 1. Pædag. cap. 7. Sanctus Dominus Jesus colluctari quoq, dicitur. Cyrillus Alex. lib. IX. contra Julian. Quod autem homo luctans contra Ja- cob sit unigenitus DEI λόγος, quomodo futurus esset suo tempore in specie nostra, præmonstrans Sanctis Pa- tribus ex his, quæ Moses scripsit, admodum facile quis confideraverit. Censet itaque Cyrillus præmonstras- se Filium DEI Patribg speciem illam nostram, quam assumturus erat. Consonant his Justinus Martyr Dial. cum Tryph. Tertul. II. & III. contr. Marc. & cap. XVI. contr. Prax. Novatianus de Trin. c. xxvii. Athanas. orat. IV. contra Arian. & in Epist. de Sy- nod. Arimin. & Seleuc. Hilarius l. IV. de Trin. Eu- seb. l. I. Hist. Eccles. c. 2. demonstrat. Evangel. l. V. c. II. Basilius contr. Eunom. l. II. Nazianz. orat. II. de Theol. Epiphanius l. I. advers. Hæref. LVIII. Am- bros. de fide contra Arian. T. VIII. Hieronymus in Hof. c. 12, 3. Phæbadius contra Arian. c. XXXIV. seq. Chrysost. homil. LVIII. in Genes. Euthymius Ziga- benus in Panoplia part. I. T. II. Paulinus Nolanus l. I. Epist. II. ad Sever. Sulpitius Severus l. I. Histor. Sacr. c. 13. Theodoretius in Gen. Q. XII. Job. Ma- xentius dial. l. II. Procopius Gazæus Comment. ad h. l. Neque denegarunt consensum Pontifices Ro- mani. Clemens Rom. l. V. Constit. cap. 21. (quem κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον adducimus) Hunc Dei Filium vi- dit Jacob ut hominem, & dixit: vidi DEUM facie ad faciem & salvata est anima mea. Leo M. Epist. XIII. ad Pulcher. Quomodo Patriarchis & Pro- phetis in specie carnis (Filius DEI) apparuit, cum aut certamen iniit, aut sermonem contulit. Neque Con- cilia integra: Antiochenum Anno CCXXVI. cele- bratum contra Paulum Samosat. cujus Epistolam Synodicam a Franc. Turriano ex antiquitate eru- tam recenset Baronius Annal. ad ann. 267. n. 4. Se- verinus Binius T. I. concil. Et post luctam eamq, ho- minis præfigurati subjungitur : Et appellavit Jacob nomen loci illius, Facies DEI. Vidi enim DEUM facie ad faciem & salva facta est anima mea. Ho- minem autem præfiguratum dicimus esse Filium DEI, quem ipsa Scriptura DEUM esse declaravit. Syrmiense Concil.anathema dixit hoc negantibus: Si quis cum Jacob non Filium colluctatum esse dicat, sed ingenitum DEUM, aut patrem ejus, anathema esto. Ita regulæ suæ interpretationis Scripturæ, Patrum consensui inhæsit Grotius. Quam rectius e Pontificiis se- quuti sunt Vatablus in h. l. & Fernandus de vision. p. 180.

## 32:31
verse 31. AND THE SUN ROSE UPON HIM IMMEDIATELY] See above 26. The Plautine Jupiter: I wish to leave the city before it dawns. The Virgilian Anchises in the fifth book of the Aeneid: And now farewell: the humid night turns its middle course, and the savage dawn has breathed upon me with panting horses. Thus Achilles departs at the cock's crow in Philostratus' Life of Apollonius: which is also noted by Eusebius against Hierocles: Chrysis in Lucian. And Aeneas of Gaza observes this as a general rule in nocturnal visions in his Theophrastus.

Latin:

vers. 31. ORTUSQVE EST EI STATIM SOL] Vide su- pra 26. Juppiter Plautinus: Exire ex urbe priusquam lucescat, volo. Anchises Virgilianus Æneidos quinto: Jamque vale: torquet medios nox humida cursus, Et me sævus equis oriens afflavit anhelis. Sic Achilles ad Galli cantum abit apud Philostratum vita A- pollonii: quod & Eusebio notatum contra Hieroclem: Chrysis apud Lucianum. Et generale hoc in nocturnis visis observat Æneas Gazæus Theophrasto.

## 33:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIII. Esau meeting him.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIII. Esavus obvius.

## 33:10
verse 10. AS IF I HAD SEEN THE FACE OF GOD) That is, an Angel. Compare above 32, 30. and 2 Sam. 14, 17.

Others prefer to understand the face of Princes with Onkelos, compare Exod. 21, 6. chap. 22, 27. 1 Sam. 2, 25.

Latin:

vers. 10. QVASI VIDISSEM VVLVTM DEI) Id est, Angelum. Confer supra 32,30. & 2. Sam. 14, 17.

ALii malunt vultum Principum intelligere cum Onkeloso, conf. Exod. 21, 6. cap. 22, 27. 1. Sam. 2, 25.

## 33:14
verse 14. AND I WILL FOLLOW GENTLY THE STEPS OF HIM, AS I SHALL SEE THE LITTLE ONES ABLE) In Hebrew, at the foot of the flock before me, and at the foot of the children. Where 'foot' is used for 'foot-pace', as the ancient Latins used to say. But מלאכה signifies both work, and those things which are possessed, among which at that time cattle were the chief.

Münster says, it calls the whole family 'work', especially the flocks and herds. Piscator observes that 'work' is put for the thing about which someone works or is occupied, by metonymy of the adjunct; thus Exod. 22, 8. and 36, 6. Thus everything that Jacob had is included. Malvenda says: but because Jacob distinguishes the children from the WORK, they certainly cannot be included under this name. Pagninus therefore more correctly understands the flock by that word, as does the Syriac, rendering it 'as the cattle bear'.

verse of the same. UNTIL I COME TO MY LORD IN SEIR.

It is not reported in Scripture that he went to his brother: just as it is not recorded that he went to his parent, except ten years later: yet it is not credible that he delayed the visitation of his parent for so long. Therefore it must not be denied that he visited his brother, as he received him, even if Scripture does not record it; indeed, it should rather be said that Scripture records it by this very fact, that Jacob promised it here: and it is not to be believed that he did not keep this promise. For it is rashly asserted by Lyra, Cornelius, and Mendoza that he proposed to go, but afterwards, fearing the disposition of Esau, changed his mind: because he already knew the disposition of Esau before, and here he acknowledged him as already reconciled to him by divine intervention. There was therefore no reason for him to distrust his brother.

Latin:

vers. 14. ET EGO SEQVAR PAVLATM VESTIGIA EJVS, SICVT VIDERO PARVVLOS POSSE) Hebraice, ad pedem gregis ante me, & ad pedem natorum. Vbi pes pro pedatu, ut Latini veteres dicebant. מלאכה aute.n & opus significat, & ea quæ possidentur, in quibus tunc præci- puum erant pecora.

Münsterus, opus, inquit, vocat universam fami- liam, præsertim greges & armenta. Piscator ob- servat opus poni pro re circa quam aliquis operatur, vel occupatur Meton. adjuncti; sic Exod. 22,8. & 36, 6. Ita includi omnia, quæ erant Jacobi Malvenda ait: at quia distinguit Jacobus natos ab OPERE, illi utique sub hoc nomine comprehendi nequeunt. Re- ctius ergo Pagninus gregem per istam vocem intel- ligit, ut & Syrus reddens quatenus ferunt pecora.

vers. eod. DONEC VENIAM AD DOMI- NUM MEUM IN SEIR.

Non refertur in Script. quod ad fratrem ive- rit: Sicut nec ad parentem ivisse traditur, nisi decen- nio post: neque tamen credibile est, eum tamdiu distulisse parentis visitationem. Ideo non negan- dum, quod fratrem, ut recepit, visitarit, etsi Scriptu- ra id non tradat; imo hoc ipso tradere id Scriptu- ram potius dicendum, quod hic promiserit id Ja- cob: quem promissum nõ servasse minime creden- dum. Nam temere asseritur a Lyr. Cornel. Men. quod ire proposuerit, at postea ingenium Esavi veritus mentem mutarit: quia jam ante ingenium Esavi no- verat, & hic eum sibi jam divinitus reconciliatum agnoscebat. Non ergo erat quod fratri diffide- rer.

## 33:19
verse 19. LAMBS] Nay, it was money, Acts 7, 16. Learn therefore from the Hebrews that 'lambs' was the name of money worth a lamb, and for that reason having the figure of a lamb. Thus 'bos' (ox) among the Greeks, and 'pecunia' (money) from 'pecus' (cattle): and 'opes' (wealth) was once 'oves' (sheep), just as 'opilio' (shepherd) for 'ovilio'.

Luther, Schindler, Eugubinus, and Arias also explain [the passage] concerning coins marked with the image of a lamb: however, Onkelos, the LXX, Aben Ezra, Jerome, Lyranus, and the Vulgate take it as lambs: But because קשיטה in Job 42:11 is taken for coins, as also among the Arabs; and the first bronze [money] was marked with the sign of a beast, as witnessed by Plutarch in Publicola and Pliny in book XXXIII, 3, the former account is certainly to be preferred. However, in Acts 7:16, it is not a question of a purchase made by Jacob, but by Abraham in Gen. 23:8.

Latin:

vers. 19. AGNIS] Imo pecunia erat, Act. 7,16. Disce igitur ex Hebræis agnos nomen fuisse pecuniæ agnum valentis, & ob id agni habentis figuram. Sic bos apud Græcos, & pecunia a pecu: & opes olim oves, ut opilio pro ovilio.

De nummis imagine agni notatis etiam expli- cant Lutherus, Schindlerus, Eugubinus, Arias: De agnis tamen accipiunt Onkelos, LXX, AbenEzra, Hieronym. Lyranus & Vulgata: Sed quia pro num- mis accipitur קשיטה Job. 42, 11. ut & apud Ara- bes; primumq; æs nota pecudis signatum, teste Plu- tarcho in Publicola, & Plinio l. XXXIII, 3. præferen- da prior utique relatio. Actor. tamen VII, 16. non de emtione a Jacobo, sed ab Abrahamo facta Gen. 23, 8. agitur.

## 34:2
ver. 2. PRINCE OF THAT LAND. More correctly (the son of Hamor the Hivite) prince of that land.

Latin:

verf. 2. PRINCEPS TERRÆ ILLIUS. REctius (filius Hemor Hevæi) principis terræ illius.

## 34:7
ver. 7. THAT HE HAD WROUGHT A FOUL THING IN ISRAEL. Ainsworth thinks that Moses is speaking in the language accepted in his time IN ISRAEL. But it is better to understand by Israel the family and house of Israel, which also pleased Piscator. 'A THING NOT TO BE DONE' is added. In Hebrew, 'and so it shall not be done' is an idiom in this sense, since it was not permitted to be done thus.

Latin:

verf. 7. QVOD FAEDAM REM OPERA- TUS ESSET IN ISRAEL. Loqui Mosen sermone suo tempore recepto IN ISRAEL, Ainsvworth putat. Sed præstat per Israel fa- miliam & domum Israel intelligere, quod etiam Pi- scatori placuit. Additur REM ILLICITAM. In Ebr. & sic non fiet, Idiotismus est hoc sensu, quum non liceret sic fieri.

## 34:21
Ver. 21. PEACEABLE) The origin of the word שלמים bears this. But Aquila, otherwise accustomed to anxiously express origins, preferred κατηρτισμένοι [fitted/perfected], because that word often signifies that which is perfect in its own kind; and therefore it is usually translated as whole, full, perfect, and also just: which seems to be the sense of this place.

Hamor and Shechem scarcely acknowledged Jacob and his people as righteous: therefore it is better with others to take it in the sense that they had lived peaceably and quietly among them until now. For these things happened about nine years after the arrival in Canaan. Cf. Gen. 30:21, 24; Ch. 37:2.

Latin:

Verf. 21. PACIFICI) Sic fert origo vocis שלמים. At Aquila, solitus alioqui origines anxie exprimere, maluit κατ- ηρτισμένοι, quia sæpe ea vox id quod in suo genere perfectum est, significat; ideoque verti solet ὁλόκληρος, πλήρης, τέλειος, etiam δίκαιος: qui hujus loci videtur esse sensus.

Vix agnovere Hemor & Sichem Jacobum cum suis pro justis: ideo præstat cum aliis eo acci- pere sensu, quod pacifice & quiete hactenus apud eos vixerint. Contigere enim hæc circiter novem annis post adventum in Canaan. Conf. Gen. 30, 21. 24. C. 37, 2.

## 34:22
Ver. 22. IMITATING THE RITE OF THE NATION] Peoples coalesce better through the parity of rites.

Latin:

Verf. 22. RITUM GENTIS IMITANTES] Melius coa- lescunt populi rituum paritate.

## 34:25
Ver. 25. WHEN THE PAIN OF THE WOUNDS IS MOST SEVERE) In Hebrew, when they were in pain. So also the Greeks: ὅτε ἦσαν ἐν τῷ πόνῳ [when they were in pain], naturally because on that day fevers often arise from inflammation.

It is a critical day. The Targum rightly: when the pains were growing stronger. Whence they believed the Shechemites could not resist on account of the pains. Cf. Hippocrates, book on fractures, comm. 3; Franciscus Valesius, book on the Sacred Philosophy, 12. Calvin rashly denies that the pain grows stronger on the third day.

ver. same. AND HAVING KILLED ALL THE MALES.

But at ver. 29, they took captive טפם [their little ones]. The Syriac and LXX respond: they translate it as 'goods': Others as 'little ones.' It can also be said that not all the males were circumcised and killed, but only those who were going out through the gate.

Latin:

Verf. 25. QVANDO GRAVISSIMUS VVLNERVM DOLOR EST) Hebraice, cum essent dolentes. Sic & Græci: ὅτε ἦσαν ἐν τῷ πόνῳ, nimirum quia eo die sæpe febres nascun- tur ex inflammatione.

Dies est Criticus. Recte Targum: cum in- valescerent dolores. Unde credebant Sichemitas ob dolores non posse resistere. Conf. Hippoc. l. de fractur. com. 3. Francisc. Vales. l. de S. Phil. 12. Teme- re negat Calvinus die tertia dolorem invalescere.

verf. eod. INTERFECTISQVE OMNIBUS MASCULIS.

At vers. 29. captivos duxerunt טפם Resp. Sy- rus & LXX. vertunt supellectilem: Alii parvulas. Di- ci etiam potest non omnes masculos & jam parvu- los, sed eos tantum, qui per portam egrediebantur circumcisos & occisos fuisse.

## 34:27
Ver. 27. THEY PLUNDERED THE CITY) One by deed, others by help or reception.

Latin:

Vers. 27. DEPOPVLATI SVNT VRBEM) Unus facto, alii auxilio aut receptu.

## 34:30
Ver. 30. YOU HAVE MADE ME ODIOUS) Pisistratus to his sons, who were meditating most savage things against those who had abducted their sister: What, he says, shall we do to our enemies, if we do these things to our lovers.

In the text, it is added 'to make me stink'. Odor is used for reputation. Therefore, that which is done by Simeon and Levi is praised in Judith 9:2, sufficiently teaches that that book is not canonical.

Latin:

Verf. 30. ODIOSVM FECISTIS ME) Pisistratus filiis suis sævissima meditantibus in raptores sororis: Quid, ait, fa- ciemus hostibus, si haec amatoribus facimus.

In textu additur ad fætere faciendum me. Odor pro fama ponitur. Quod ergo factum Simeonis & Levi laudatur Judith 9, 2. satis docet, librum illum Canonicum non esse.

## 35:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXV. Jacob's journeys. The death of Rachel and Isaac. The incest of Reuben.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXV. Jacobi itinera. Mors Rabelis, & Isaaci. Incestus Rubeni.

## 35:2
Verse 2. STRANGE GODS] Those Teraphim. Of which one, Gedalia says, was unearthed and worshipped by the Samaritans a long time later.

Whether it still clung to the wives, just as Rachel had stolen the idols of Laban; or whether some idolatry clung to the menservants or maidservants, or whether any of the idols remained from the spoil of the Shechemites, or even had been carried off by the captive Shechemites. The cleansing of garments is also commanded, so that by external worship the necessary purity of the soul might be signified.

Latin:

Verf. 2. DEOS ALIENOS] Teraphim ista. Quorum u- num Gedalia ait multo post tempore erutum cultumque a Sa- maritis.

SIve adhuc uxoribus, uti Rahel idola Labani fu- rata erat; sive servis aut ancillis hæserit aliquid idolometriæ, sive idolorum quid e præda Sichemita- rum reliquum fuerit, vel etiam a captivis Sichemitis abductum. Mundatio etiam vestimentorum præci- pitur, ut externo cultu mundities animi necessaria innuatur.

## 35:4
Verse 4. EARRINGS WHICH WERE IN THEIR EARS) Dedicated, clearly, to some fictitious deity: a custom of the Syrians of old which came into Africa through the Syrian Phoenicians. Therefore, Augustine, in 'On Christian Doctrine', book 2, counts earrings at the top of each ear among superstitious things. The same author [speaks] more extensively in Epistle LXXIII. 'But the execrable superstition of amulets, among which the earrings of men suspended at the tops of their ears on one side are also reckoned, is employed not to please men, but to serve demons.' But who could find the specific prohibitions of wicked superstitions in the Scriptures, Since the Apostle says generally: I do not want you to become partners with demons: and again: For what agreement has Christ with Belial? unless perhaps because he named Belial, and prohibited general association with demons, it is permitted for Christians to sacrifice to Neptune: because we read nothing properly decreed about Neptune. Let the miserable be warned in the meantime, that if they are unwilling to obey salutary precepts, at least they should not defend their sacrileges, lest they implicate themselves in a greater crime. But what is to be done with them, if they fear to loosen their earrings, and do not fear to receive the body of Christ with the sign of the devil? There were, however, in those earrings certain sidereal marks, whence such things were called σφραγῖδες. Lactantius on Statius: although they have colder ones: it should be read although they have magic seals. Such were also rings, partly for performing miracles, like that of Gyges in Plato's Republic II, in Cicero's De Officiis II, and in Pliny's book XXXIII. mentioned, partly believed to be effective for driving away demons, as witnessed by Lucian in the Philopatris, partly against diseases, as witnessed by Alexander of Tralles, Marcellus Empiricus, and others. Thus also we learn from the poets about hair dedicated to the gods, and about curls in the hair, from Ammianus book XXII.

Some understand the earrings, which hung from the ears of the servants, on which images of idols had been engraved, with Cornelius a Lapide; others understand them as those with which idols, in the manner of men (after the fashion of the modern Papacy), were adorned in the ears, with Bonfrerius. So that no trace of idolatry might remain, and for the execration of the same. She therefore BURIED them, the whole family being ignorant of the place: perhaps first broken or melted down, as in Exodus 32:20, 2 Kings 18:4. UNDER THE TEREBINTH, as the LXX, or oak, as others. Oaks long persisted, nor were they cut down, Gen. 21:33, Deut. 12:2. Which was observed by Ainsworth.

Latin:

verf. 4. INAURES QVÆ ERANT IN AURIBVS EO- RVM) Dicatas scilicet alicui fictitio numini: qui mos olim Syrorum per Syros phœnicas in Africam venit. Ideo Augusti- nus de doctrina Christiana l. 2. inter superstitiosa numerat in- aures in summo aurium singularum. Idem latius epistola LXXIII. Exsecranda autem superstitio ligaturarum, in qui- bus etiam inaures virorum in summis ex una parte auriculis suspensæ deputantur, non ad placendum hominibus, sed ad ser- viendum dæmonibus adhibetur. Quis autem posset speciales nefariarum superstitionum prohibitiones in Scripturis invenire, cum generaliter Apostolus dicat: Nolo vos socios fieri dæmonio- rum: & iterum: Quæ enim congruentia Christi ad Belial? nisi forte quia Belial nominavit, & generalem societatem dæmonio- rum prohibuit, licet Christianis sacrificare Neptuno: quia nihil proprie de Neptuno seitum legimus. Moneantur interim mise- ri, ut si obtemperare nolint præceptis salutaribus, saltem sacrile- gia sua non defendant, ne majori se scelere implicent. Quid autem cum eis agendum sit, si solvere inaures timent, & corpus Christi cum signo diaboli accipere non timent? Erant autem in illis inauribus notæ quædam siderales, unde talia σφραγῖδες di- cebantur. Lactatius ad Statium: licet magis frigidas habent: legendum licet magi sphragidas habent. Tales & annuli partim ad mira perpetranda, ut ille Gygis Platoni de Republica II. Ci- ceroni de officiis secundo, Plinio libro XXXIII. memoratus, partim valere crediti dæmonibus pellendis, teste Luciano in Philopatride, partim contra morbos, teste Alexandro Trallia- no, Marcello Empirico & aliis. Sic & comas diis dicatas ex Poetis discimus, & cirros in comis, ex Ammiano libro XXII.

Alii de inauribus, quæ pendebant ex auribus famulorum, quibus insculptæ fuerint imagines ido- lorum, cum Cornelio a Lapide intelligunt, alii de iis, quibus idola, instar hominum (ad hodierni Papatus morem) in auribus ornabantur, cum Bonfrerio. Ne quod superesset vestigium idololatriæ, & ad execra- tionem ejusdem. Illa ergo INFODIT tota fami- lia locum ignorante: forte prius confracta aut lique- facta, ut Exod. 32, 10. 2. Reg. 18, 4. SUBTER TERE- BINTHUM ut LXX. vel quercum, ut alii. Quer- cus diu perstiterunt, nec cædebantur Gen. 21, 33. Deut. 12, 2. Quod Ainswortho observatum.

## 35:7
verse 7. FOR THERE GOD APPEARED TO HIM] Angels appeared to him. For the verb is plural in Hebrew. But it is customary for the company of other Angels to appear with one prince Angel, as we have also noted above, and as can be seen in Luke 2:9, 13.

אלהים cannot be explained as referring to Angels. Because the אלהים, who appeared, are called אל, which name is proper to the one GOD. Therefore it is undoubted that GOD is indicated, so that the plural number may introduce the mystery of the plurality of the divine persons: just as is manifest from the altar built in honor of him who appeared, and from the history of the apparition in Gen. 28:14, 19, where he professes himself to be Jehovah the GOD of Abraham, the GOD of Isaac. Socinus (who dared everything) did not dare to define that Angels were designated here: he says it could be taken of Angels, and perhaps ought to be, see defens. animadv. 131. and fragm. duor. scriptor. p. 47. Enjedinus, however, no less bold in corrupting passages of Scripture, openly professes that it cannot be taken of angels, in explic. loc. Script. p. 34. Although in Gen. 35:7 a plural verb is added to the word Elohim, nevertheless it signifies one GOD alone. For Moses refers to those things which are contained in Gen. 28:13. Jacob saw Jehovah leaning on the ladder, saying to him: I am Jehovah the GOD of Abraham your Father, and the GOD of Isaac. Although the same Interpreter, whom we just mentioned (Calvin), interprets this passage also as referring to Angels, yet both REASON and the CONSENT OF ALL DOCTORS stand against him. See the invincible assertion of the plurality of divine Persons from the O.T. chapter 9. Piscator and Ainsworth acknowledge the plurality of divine Persons here.

Latin:

vers. 7. IBI ENIM APPARUIT EI DEUS] Apparuerunt ei Angeli. Est enim verbum plurale in Hebræo. Solet au- tem cum uno Angelo principe apparere Angelorum aliorum comitatus, ut & supra notavimus, & videri potest Lucæ 2, 9. 13.

Non potest אלהים exponi de Angelis. Quia אלהים, qui apparuerunt, dicuntur אל, quod nomen uni DEO proprium est. Proinde indubium est, DEUM indigitari, ut pluralis numerus myste- rium pluralitatis personarum divinarum inferat: quemadmodum & ex altari in ejus, qui apparuit, honorem ædificato, & ex historia apparitionis Gen. 28, 14. 19. manifestum est, qua se Jehovam DEUM Abraham, DEUM Isaac profitetur. Non ausus fuit Socinus (qui nihil non ausus) definire, hîc Ange- los designari: Posse de Angelis accipi, ac fortassis debe- re, ait, vid. defens. animadv. 131. & fragm. duor. scri- ptor. p. 47. Enjedinus vero non minus audax in depravandis Scripturæ locis palam profitetur, non posse de angelis accipi, in explic. loc. Script. p. 34. Etsi Gen. 35, 7. voci Elohim verbum plurale est additum, tamen significat unum solum DEUM. Respicit enim Moses ad ea, quæ habentur Gen. 28, 13. vidit Jacob Je- hovam nixum scalæ, dicentem sibi: Ego sum Jehovah DEUS Abraham Patris tui, & DEUS Isaac. Quan- quam etiam hunc locum idem Interpres, cujus nunc me- minimus (Calvinus) de Angelis interpretatur, sed & RATIO & CONSENSUS OMNIUM DOCTO- RUM contra eum stat. Videatur invicta assertio pluralitat. Personar. divin. e V. T. cap. 9. Agnoscit hic pluralitatem Personarum divinarum Piscator, & Ainsworthus.

## 35:16
verse 16. IN THE SPRINGTIME. Fuller teaches that it was rather the autumn season, l. II. Miscell. c. 15. and says that a notation of place, not of time, underlies it. Understanding a small part of the land, or a small distance of the journey to be completed. Poole has laboriously collected many opinions here.

Latin:

vers. 16. VERNO TEMPORE. Autumnale tempus potius fuisse docet Fuller. l. II. Miscell. c. 15. & loci, non temporis notationem subesse ait. Modicum intelligens terræ, vel exiguum spatium itineris conficiendum. Multas sententias hic operose collegit Polus.

## 35:19
verse 19. BENJAMIN, THAT IS, SON OF THE RIGHT HAND.] Or rather in the Syriac language, of which Jacob still retained much, son of days, that is, of old age. This agrees very well with that which is below in 44:20. Nowhere is it read that Jacob used any Syriac word. Much less is it likely that the Patriarch would have imposed a name in a foreign Syriac language upon a son, whom he desired to be as far removed as possible from the established customs and habits of that nation. And to the mother's name Benoni, son of sorrow, son of the right hand is rightly opposed, not likewise son of old age. Therefore there is no cause for departing from the Vulgate: which the Tridentines decreed should not be abandoned under any pretext. In Gen. 44:20, the name Benjamin is not explained (the explanation would be too obscure), only that Benjamin was born to the Father in his old age is commemorated, so that compassion toward the aged Patriarch might be excited.

Latin:

vers. 19. BENJAMIN, ID EST, FILIUS DEXTRÆ.] Aut potius Syriaco sermone, cujus multum adhuc retinebat Jacobus, filius dierum, id est, senectutis. Convenit id optime cum eo, quod infra est 44, 20. Nusquam legitur verbum Syriacum ullum, quod Jacobus adhibuerit. Multo minus verisi- mile est, peregrina Syriaca lingua nomen imposi- turum Patriarcham fuisse filio, quem ab institutis moribusque gentis illius cupiebat quam semotissi- mum. Et nomini matris Benoni filius doloris recte filius dextræ, non item filius senectutis opponitur. Non habet ergo causam a Vulgata discedendi: quam nullo prætextu deferendam Tridentini sancivere. Gen. 44, 20. non nomen Benjamin explicatur, (ni- mis obscura foret explicatio) solum Benjaminum in senectute Patri natum commemoratur, ut com- miseratio erga Patriarcham grandævum excite- tur.

## 35:20
verse 20. AND JACOB ERECTED A PILLAR) That is, a small column, as Cicero calls it in 1 De Legibus, and in the fifth of the Tusculans. στήλην, Homer and the Greek epigrammatists, whom the LXX also followed here.

Bochart teaches that it was a very elegant pyramid. Which would be a memorial of Rachel's death, or rather would testify to the faith of a second life and a blessed resurrection.

Latin:

vers. 20. EREXITQVE JACOB TITVLVM) Id est, co- lumellam, ut Cicero vocat 1. de Legibus, & quinto Tusculana- rum. στήλην Homerus & Epigrammatarii Græci, quos & hic se- cuti LXX.

Pyramidem perelegantem fuisse docet Bo- chartus. Quæ memoriale foret mortis Rachel, vel potius secundæ vitæ, & beatæ resurrectionis fidem te- staretur.

## 35:21
ver. 21. BEYOND THE TOWER OF THE FLOCK. It was distant only a thousand paces from Bethlehem: in which place the Angels appeared to the Shepherds, Luke II, because it was very rich in pastures. The Samaritan, Syriac, and Arias Montanus have Tower of Eder; Pagninus and Malvenda have Migdal-Eder.

Latin:

vers. 21. TRANS TURREM GREGIS. Mille passibus tantum distabat a Bethlehem: in quo loco Angeli Pastoribus apparuere Luc. II. quia erat pascuis uberrimus. Turrem Eder habet Samar. Syr. Ariasm. Migdal - Eder Pagn. & Mal- vend.

## 35:22
ver. 22. NOW THE SONS OF JACOB WERE TWELVE) Justin, in book xxxvi: 'The birth of ten sons made Israel more famous than his ancestors.'

Latin:

vers. 22. ERANT AVTEM FILII JACOB DVODECIM) Justinus libro xxxvi. Israelem felix decem filiorum proventus majoribus suis clariorem fecit.

## 36:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVI. The posterity of Esau.

ver. 1. NOW THESE ARE THE GENERATIONS OF ESAU) Moses wished to attach this incidentally to the affairs of Jacob, so that the posterity of Jacob might know the borders of the Idumeans and abstain from them, except for those that were of the Amalekites. See below 17, 14, and Deut. 23, 7.

It was not done only for that reason, but primarily so that the truth of the oracle in Gen. 27, 40 might be shown.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVI. Posteritas Esavi.

vers. 1. HÆ SVNT AVTEM GENERATIONES ESAV) Obiter hoc attexere Moses rebus Jacobi voluit, ut Jacobi po- steritas Idumæorum fines nosset, eisque abstineret, exceptis eis, quiera nt Amalecitarum. Vide infra 17, 14. & Deut. 23, 7.

Non ideo tantum id factum, sed imprimis, ut ostenderetur veritas oraculi Gen. 27, 40.

## 36:21
ver. 21. ANAH) The name is masculine and feminine, as is Thanna.

Latin:

vers. 21. ANÆ) Nomen est masculinum & fœmininum, ut & Thanna.

## 36:24
ver. 24. HE FOUND HOT SPRINGS.) He reads מַיִם, but we read יֵמִם, that is, mules. The Greeks retained the Hebrew word ἰαμείν.

Grotius therefore acknowledges that it existed in the Hebrew at the time of the Greek LXX Interpreters, just as it is held now. Why then does he not correct the Latin Vulgate, because it read poorly and did not apply judgment: because מַיִם denotes waters, not hot waters. Therefore Cornelius a Lapide imagines that חַימִים was read formerly, which he says is composed of חַם hot and יָמִים waters. But this is a stony observation. For it is necessary to depart to those who are settled in the opinion that the original text should be corrected from the sources. Nor are hot waters owed to human invention; but they are a work of divine power, or of nature, as it was founded by God, without human work. Anah is said to have found יֵמִם when he was pasturing donkeys, therefore B. Luther rightly understood it as wild asses in his version, because he was the first to mix herds of horses with donkeys; whence he produced new animals παρὰ φύσιν; as R. David Kimchi in the Book of Roots interprets יֵמִים concerning mules. Bochart in Hierozoicon. He understands the Emim as giants in Deut. 2, 10, 11, who are written as אֵימִים and יֵמִים; that he found them, that is, that he stumbled upon them unexpectedly. Which we leave in its own place. It is strange that Grotius does not derive his hot waters from the proximity of the Punic language, which he thinks is the same as Hebrew. For Jerome observed that concerning certain things, while he collected various opinions here: 'Some think that hot waters are signified by this word, according to the proximity of the Punic language, which is adjacent to the Hebrew.' Which Jerome says is the opinion of most.

Latin:

vers. 24. INVENIT AQVAS CALIDAS.) Legit מַיִם, at nos יֵמִם, id est, mulos. Græci Hebræam vocem retinuere ἰαμείν.

Agnoscit ergo Grotius in Ebræo extitisse, tem- pore Græcorum LXX. Interpp. uti nunc habetur. Cur ergo non emendat Vulgatam Latinam, quod male legerit, neque judicium adhibuerit: quia מַיִם aquas notat, non aquas calidas. Ideo Cornelius a Lap. comminiscitur, lectum olim fuisse חַימִים quod compositum ex חַם calidus & יָמִים aquæ, dicit. Sed hæc lapidea est observatio. Huc enim abire o- portet, quibus sedet, textum originalem e fontibus emendare. Neque calidæ aquæ inventioni huma- næ debentur; sed opus sunt divinæ virtutis, vel na- turæ, prout a Deo condita est, sine humana opera. Invenisse dicitur Anah יֵמִם, cum asinos pasceret, ideo onagros recte B. Lutherus in versione intellexit, quod primus equorum greges cum asinis commise- rit; unde nova animantia παρὰ φύσιν produxerit; Uti R. David Kimchi in lib. Rad. יֵמִים de mulis in- terpretatur. Bochartus in Hierozoic. Emæos gigantes intelligit Deut. 2, 10, 11. qui & אֵימִים & יֵמִים scribantur; quod eos invenerit, hoc est, in eos incide- rit ex improviso. Quod suo loco relinquimus. Mi- rum, quod Grotius non e linguæ Punicæ vicinia, quam eandem cum Ebræa putat, derivet aquas suas calidas. Id enim de quibusdam observavit Hiero- nymus, dum varias hic sententias collegit: Nonnulli putant aquas calidas, juxta Punicæ linguæ viciniam, quæ Ebrææ contermina est, hoc vocabulo significari. Quam plerorumque sententiam dicit Hieronymus.

## 36:31
ver. 31. NOW THE KINGS WHO REIGNED IN THE LAND OF EDOM) These kings who follow are not from Esau, but of another nation. Thus Maimonides. Kings but they differed from the leaders in this, that they had a crown. Moreover, the grave memory of these kings was a lesson to the Israelites, not to impose a foreigner upon themselves.

BEFORE THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL HAD A KING.) Before the descendants of Israel obtained the land of Canaan and the neighboring regions, before which time it was not permitted for them to make a king for themselves. Deuter. 17, 14.

This favored those who think such things were added after Moses by him who arranged the diaries of Moses: unless you say they were added by a prophetic Spirit, or through a King, which pleases others, such as Junius, Malvenda, and Ainsworth, so that you understand Moses himself, who is called King in Deuter. 33, 5.

Latin:

vers. 31. REGES AVTEM QVI REGNAVERVNT IN TERRA EDOM) Hi qui sequuntur reges non ab E- savo sunt, sed gentis alterius. Ita Maimonides. Reges- autem à ducibus eo differebant, quod coronam habebant. Horum autem regum gravis memoria documentum erat If- raelitis, ne sibi alienigenam imponerent.

ANTEQUAM HABERENT REGEM FILII ISRAEL.) Priusquam Israelis posteri terram Canaanæ ac vicinas sunt adepti, ante quod tempus regem ipfis facere non licuit. Deu- ter. 17, 14.

Id favebat eis, qui talia addita putant post Mosen ab eo, qui Mofis diaria digeffit: nifi dicas prophe- tico Spiritu ea adjecta, aut per Regem, quod aliis placet, utpote Junio, Malvendæ, Ainswortho, Mosen ipfum, qui Rex dicitur Deuter. 33, 5. in- telligas.

## 36:33
Verse 33. JOBAB. Augustine and Ambrose on Romans understand JOB, to whom we agree in our Commentary on this passage, however much it may seem otherwise to some Hebrews and to Malvenda, who derive him from the stock of Nahor, Genesis 22, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 33. JOBAB. Augustin. & Ambros. ad Rom. JOBUM intelli- gunt, quibus annuimus in Comment. ad h. l. utut Ebræis nonnullis & Malvendæ aliud videatur, qui eum ex stirpe Nachor deducunt Genef. 22, 21.

## 36:35
Verse 35. BALANAN.) בעל חנן clearly the same name as Hannibal, but inverted.

Latin:

Vers. 35. BALANAN.) בעל חנן plane idem nomen quod Hannibal, sed inversum.

## 36:41
Verse 41. THEMAN.) Whence the Temanite people [mentioned] by Herodotus.

PART VI. AND THE LAST OF GENESIS, THE HISTORY OF JOSEPH.

Latin:

Vers. 41. THEMAN.) Unde populus Themanæi He- rodoto.

PARS VI. ET ULTIMA GENESEOS, HISTO- RIA JOSEPHI.

## 37:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVII. The selling of Joseph.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVII. Venditio Josephi.

## 37:2
Verse 2. AND THESE ARE HIS GENERATIONS.) The things done by him and his children. See above 6, 9. and Num. 3, 1. where the same word תלדות [is used]. Aben-Ezra also noted it.

Ta and Fagius, Vatablus, Menochius. In which sense the word for begetting is taken in Proverbs 27, 1. Thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.

JOSEPH WHEN HE WAS SIXTEEN YEARS OLD.) In the Hebrew it is XVII, which the Greeks follow. But a person is said to be a son of this or that year who is in that year, as appears in Exodus 12, 5. Therefore the Latin [translator] correctly expressed the sense.

But it was more correctly observed by Steuchus at the end of his revision after the index, that it should not be believed that this proceeded in this way from Jerome (or the interpreter). Rather, that the codices were corrupted in the passage of time. For the Vulgate is accustomed to follow the LXX Interpreters for the most part, who here have δέκα καὶ ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν ἦν. Which certainly is not, 'he was in his seventeenth year,' but 'he was seventeen years old.' Therefore the Pontiffs ought not to have canonized this error; nor should Grotius excuse it, who acknowledges that the Greeks followed the Hebrew text. Not to mention that flowing years are accustomed to be counted in sacred [texts] as if they were completed.

Vers. eod. HE WAS FEEDING THE FLOCK.) A prelude to the governing of peoples. From this rank he was led to governing a household, then to the care of a kingdom, GOD disposing these things by degrees.

ACCUSAVIT FRATRES SUOS.) That they might be warned by their Father and repent. For in Hebrew there is ובא דבה, which is said in a good sense, as ולא in a bad one.

CRIMINE PESSIMO.) Like κτηνοβάτας. In Hebrew, nothing is held regarding a 'most wicked crime.' Therefore, Grotius defined it in vain. Nor is this, which he assumes following some Hebrews regarding the consent of beasts, approved by Lyranus. Steuchus acknowledges that in the Vulgate this passage is too exaggerated. Grotius's observation on the use of the word דבה is to be entirely preferred to Amama's observation brought from the Hebrews; because that word, signifying an evil rumor and infamy, is taken for a false rumor when it is constructed with the verb הוציא, as in Num. 13:33, concerning the lying report of the spies; but for a true rumor when it is constructed with the verb הביא, as in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET HÆ SUNT GENERATIONES EJUS.) Res ab eo ejusque liberis gestæ. Vide supra 6, 9. & Num. 3, 1. ubi eadem vox תלדות. Notavit & Aben-Esdra.

Ta & Fagius, Vatabl. Menochius. Quo sensu gignendi vox sumitur Proverb. 27, 1. Nefcis quid pariat dies.

JOSEPH CUM SEDECIM ESSET ANNORUM.) In Ebræo est XVII. quod sequuntur Græci. Sed filius anni hu- jus vel illius efse dicitur, qui eum annum agit, ut apparet Exod. 12, 5. Sensum ergo recte expressit Latinus.

At rectius observatum Steucho in calce recogni- tionis fuæ post indicem, credendum non efse, hoc ita ab Hieronymo (vel interprete) profectum efse. De- pravatos potius Codices progressu temporis. Solet enim Vulgatus LXX. Interpp. plerumque sequi, qui hîc habent δέκα καὶ ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν ἦν. Quod certe non est, agebat annum decimum septimum, sed erat septendecimum annorum. Non debebant ergo Pon- tifices canonizasse hoc mendum; Nec id excusare Grotius, qui agnoscit, Græcos sequutos esse Ebræ- um textum. Ut taceam, quod anni fluentes soleant in sacris numerari, quasi completi.

Vers. eod. PASCEBAT GREGEM.) Regimini popu- lorum præludens. Ab hoc gradu ad familiam gubernan- dam perductus est, inde ad regni curam, DEO per gradus hæc difponente.

ACCUSAVIT FRATRES SUOS.) Ut à Patre moniti refipiscerent. Est enim in Hebræo ובא דבה, quod in bo- nam partem dicitur, ut ולא in malam.

CRIMINE PESSIMO.) Ut κτηνοβάτας. In Ebræo nihil habetur de crimine pessimo. Id- eo frustra id definivit Grotius. Neque hoc, quod Ebræos sequutus nonnullos assumit de jumento- rum consensu, Lyrano probatum. Steuchus agnoscit in vulgato locum hunc nimis exaggeratum. Obser- vationi Grotianæ de usu vocis דבה præferenda omnino est Amamæ observatio ex Ebræis adducta; quod vox ea rumorem malum & infamiam signifi- cans pro rumore falso fumatur, cum construitur cum verbo הוציא, ut Num. 13, 33. de exploratorum men- daci relatione; pro vero autem rumore, cum con- struitur cum verbo הביא, ut hoc loco.

## 37:9
Vers. 9. AS IF THE SUN AND THE MOON AND THE ELEVEN STARS WERE WORSHIPPING ME.) Achmes, Onirocriticon, chap. CLXVIII, from the discipline of the Persians and Egyptians: 'If anyone sees that he was teaching all the other stars, he will rule over all peoples.'

It is credible that the Sun, Moon, etc., were seen descending to his feet, and soon returning to their own places, and not, as pleases Tirinus from Philo, that he himself saw the sun and stars coming to him in human form: for whence would he have known these to be images of the Sun, Moon, etc., if they had appeared in human bodies? Furthermore, in the former vision, no mention of Father and mother was made, because at first only the brothers, and finally also the Father with Bilhah, worshipped Joseph, sent him gifts, and sought his favor, Gen. 47:29. Which act Fagius in Collat. and Drusius also think occurred with Gen. 47:31, 'he worshipped on the bed!' for they judge that this adoration was done in honor of Joseph as a prince.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QUASI SOLEM ET LUNAM ET STEL- LAS UNDECIM ADORARE ME.) Achmes Onirocri- ticon cap. CLXVIII. ex Persarum & Ægyptiorum disciplina: ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐδίδασκε τῶν ἄλλων ἀσέρων πάντων, δεσπόσει πάντων λαῶν.

Credibile est visum Solem, Lunam, &c. ad ejus pedes descendere, & mox ad sua se loca recipere, non vero, quod Tirin. placet è Philone, ipsum vidisse ve- nientem solem & stellas ad se humano corpore venire: unde enim has esse imagines Solis, Lunæ &c. co- gnovisset, si humanis corporibus comparuissent. Cæterum in priori visione nulla Patris & matris mentio facta, quia primo soli fratres, tandem etiam Pater cum Bilha adoravit Josephum, ei misit mu- nera, ejusque gratiam expetiit Genef. 47, 29. Quod factum etiam Fagius in Collat. & Drusius putant cum Gen. 47, 31. in lecto adoravit! in honorem enim Josephi utpote principis, eam adorationem fa- ctam censent.

## 37:10
ET MATER TUA.) Bilhah, the nurse of Rachel's children. Thus in Plautus, the mother who gave the breast.

Latin:

ET MATER TUA.) Bala Rachelis liberūm educatrix. Sic Plauto, mater quæ mammam dedit.

## 37:25
Vers. 25. ISMAELITAS.) Onkelos put 'Saracens,' rightly. It was a συνοδία, or, as they say now, a Caravan, from various Arab peoples, whence they are soon called Midianites.

Augustinus, quæst. CXXIV. in Genef., thinks the Ishmaelites are later called Midianites in c. 37:36, because the descendants of Ishmael lived in part in Midian. The Junian notes hold thus: Midianites are also called Ishmaelites here and in Jud. 8:24 because of their confused habitation with the Ishmaelites, although they were descendants of Abraham from Keturah, not from Hagar, Gen. 25:2. These were therefore Midianites by race, Ishmaelites by habitation: just as they are called Cherethites 2 Samuel 9:4, Uriah the Hittite 2 Sam. 11, Ittai the Gittite 2 Sam. 15:19. Justin, from Trogus Pompeius, book XXXVI, chap. 2, reports thus concerning this deed: 'Joseph, the youngest in age among his brothers: fearing his excellent talent, the brothers intercepted him secretly and sold him to foreign merchants, by whom he was carried off into Egypt.'

Latin:

Vers. 25. ISMAELITAS.) Onkelos Saracenas pofuit, re- cte. Erat συνοδία, sive, ut nunc loquuntur, Caravana, ex va- riis Arabum populis, unde mox Madianitæ vocantur.

Augustinus quæst. CXXIV. in Genef. Ismaelitas postea Madianitas c. 37, 36. dici putat, quod Ismaelis posteri in Midian ex parte habitarent. Junian. notæ ita habent: Midianitæ propter confusam cum Ismaelitis habitationem etiam Ismaelitæ appellantur hîc & Jud. 8, 24. quamvis Abrahæ posteri ex Kethu- ra, non ex Hagara essent. Genef. 25, 2. Midianitæ er- go hi fuerunt genere, Ismaelitæ habitatione: quomo- do dicti sunt Cerethei 2. Samuel. 9, 4. Uria Chitteus 2. Sam. 11. Ittai Gitthæus 2. Sam. 15, 19. Justinus ex Trogo Pompejo lib. XXXVI. cap. 2. de hoc facto ita refert: Jofeph minimus ætate inter fratres : cujus excellens ingenium veriti fratres, clam interceptum peregrinis mercatoribus vendiderunt, à quibus depor- tatus in Ægyptum.

## 37:35
Vers. 35. AD FILIUM MEUM.) On account of my son. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi and Hisceuni. For that the particle אל is so taken appears elsewhere, and 2 Sam. 21:2.

IN INFERNUM) εἰς ἄδη. See what is said at Luke 16:23.

Lyranus and other Papists take this concerning the infernal limbo of the Fathers; upon whom an Anonymous author pours cold water, so to speak, in a 'Serious Disquisition' on the place, state, and life of souls after this life, although he has devised from it a completely novel opinion concerning the Sheol of souls, adorned with various and profane rather than Biblical circumstances. However, nothing prevents us from explaining the word שאול in this place as the grave, with Jonathan, R. Solomon Jarchi, and Aben-Ezra. Which interpretation also finds supporters among the Papists, Augustinus Steuchus, Arias Montanus, as well as Pagninus, and also Christ. a Castro. For Jacob does not say that he will descend into his son's grave, which he did not know if or where he had received, but that he would descend mourning to Sheol, which some take as future, περίλυπον ἕως τῦ θανάτε, 'sorrowful even unto death,' or the grave, or that he would descend mourning אל 'on account of' his son, or if you take it in the common interpretation, that he would descend to his son mourning to Sheol, that he would come into the same state: so that it is noted that the grave hangs over him, which would hasten death on account of grief, just as it was necessary for the son to perish through an unexpected and sad fall, and to be converted into the earth or the dust of the earth. Indeed, the common state of death is designated, as in Job 5:28, all the dead are said to be about to come forth from monuments, even if most of them were never buried in monuments: the Patriarch says he will come into the census of those who are accustomed to be buried, and are converted into the earth from whence they were taken. How also can the Father, mourning vehemently for his son submerged in the waters, and even unto death, say that he will descend to his mourning son into Scheolah, even though he does not in the least think, or intend, that he will perish in the waters.

Latin:

Vers. 35. AD FILIUM MEUM.) Propter filium meum. Rabbi Salomon Jarchi & Hisceuni. Sic enim sumi particu- lam אל & alibi apparet, & 2. Sam. 21, 2.

IN INFERNUM) εἰς ἄδη. Vide quæ ad Lucam XVI, 23.

Lyran. & Papistæ alii de infernali Patrum limbo accipiunt; quibus frigidam quodammodo suf- fundit Anonymus Seria disquifitione, de loco, statu, & vita animarum post hanc vitam, licet novellam prorsus sententiam inde commentus sit de Scheol animarum, variis, & prophanis potius quam Bi- blicis circumstantiis ornato. Nihil autem ob- stat, quo minus de sepulcro h. l. vocem שאול cum Jonathane R. Salom. Jarchi, & Aben-Ezra expo- namus. Quæ interpretatio etiam inter Papistas fautores invenit Augustinum Steuchum, Ariæmont. æque ac Pagn. ut & Christ. a Castro. Nec enim Ja- cob dicit se in filii sepulcrum, quod an & ubi acce- perit, ignorabat, descensurum, sed descensurum lugentem Scheolah, quod accipiunt nonnulli fu- turum περίλυπον ἕως τῦ θανάτε triftem usque ad mortem vel fepulcrum, vel descensurum lugentem אל propter filium, vel si communi interpretatione ac- cipias, descensurum ad filium lugentem Scheolab, in eundem venturum statum: ut notetur imminere sibi sepulcrum ob luctum mortem acceleraturum, quemadmodum filium per inopinatum & tristem casum perire, & in terram vel pulverem terræ con- verti oportuit. Nimirum communis mortis sta- tus designatur, uti Job. 5, 28. è monumentis pro- dituri dicuntur omnes mortui, etsi plurimi eo- rum nunquam monumentis conditi sint: in cen- sum nempe eorum se venturum ait Patriarcha, qui sepeliri solent, & in terram, unde sumti sunt, con- vertuntur: quomodo etiam Pater ob filium aquis mersum vehementer, & ad mortem usque lugens dicere potest, se descensurum ad filium lugen- tem Scheolah, etsi aquis se periturum minime co- gitet, aut intendat.

## 37:35 Addition
To chap. 37. 35. toward the end. p. 301. b.

As for the word על in 1 Sam. 1:27, when Anna says she prayed על הנער, this is not 'to' but 'on account of' that boy. Compare our commentary on this passage of Genesis.

Latin:

Ad cap. 37. 35. sub finem. p. 301. b.

Quod ad vocabulum על 1. Sam. 1, 27. cum Anna orasse sese dicit על הנער non est hoc ad sed propter puerum istum. Conf. Comment. noster ad hunc Genes. locum.

## 38:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVIII. Onan the Sodomite, and the incest of Judah.

Verse 1. AT THE SAME TIME. We solve the chronological doubt in the Commentary on this passage.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVIII. Onan Sodomita, & incestus Judæ.

Vers. 1. EODEM TEMPORE. Dubium Chronologicum solvimus in Comment. ad h. l.

## 38:5
Verse 5. AND WHEN HE WAS BORN SHE CEASED TO BEAR.) In Hebrew: He was in Chezib, when she bore him. In Greek: αὕτη δὲ ἦν ἐν Χασβὶ, ἡνίκα ἔτεκεν αὐτός. It appears that the place is Jos. 15, 44; Mich. 1, 14, where the preposition א is written, which is frequent in proper names. But here that place is called so by prolepsis. For it seems to be called so because Sue ceased to bear there, as the Latin says here. For כזב among other things also signifies to cease, as in Isaiah 58, where in the Greek it is ἐξέλιπε.

Grotius acknowledges that the LXX Interpreters here agree with the Hebrew: yet he wishes to assist the Latin, because the place seems to be called so by prolepsis, because Sue ceased to bear there. But it was the duty of the interpreter to express the place where the name of the place is found in the text. Which was not done by the Vulgate. Therefore, this error should not have been canonized by the Popes. Nor excused by Grotius. Nor does any reason for that prolepsis appear; or that it received its name from the cessation of birth. Nor are those supports sufficiently reliable that the word כזב signifies to cease. For that only holds when it is used in Piel. As in Isa. 58, 11. But the Latin was seduced by Aquila, which the great man ought not to have been ignorant of, as noted by Jerome in the Hebrew Questions. Besides the LXX, Onkelos, Aben-Ezra, R. Solomon, Levi, Hiscan, and others explain that as the name of a place. But these things are to be understood not of the mother, but of the Father: And HE was in Chesib, because the absence of the Father is brought forward as the cause why names were imposed on the sons by the mother.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QUO NATO PARERE ULTRA CESSA- VIT.) Hebraice : Erat in Chezib, cum ipsa eum pareret. Græce : αὕτη δὲ ἦν ἐν Χασβὶ, ἡνίκα ἔτεκεν αὐτός. Locum esse apparet Jos. 15, 44. Mich. 1, 14. ubi scribitur præpositio א quod in nominibus propriis frequens. Hîc autem sic ap- pellatur is locus per πρόληψιν. Dictus enim sic videtur, quod ibi Sue parere cessaverit, ut hîc dicit Latinus. Nam כזב inter alia & cessare significat, ut Esaiæ 58. ubi in Græco ἐξέλιπε.

Agnoscit Grotius LXX. Interpp. hîc Ebræo con- sonare : Juvare tamen vult Latinum, quod locus ita per πρόληψιν dictus videatur, quod Sue ibi pare- re cessaverit. Sed interpretis erat locum exprime- re, ubi in textu reperitur nomen loci. Quod à Vulgato non factum. Non ergo error hic cano- nizari debuit à Pontificibus. Non excusari à Gro- tio. Neque προλήψεως istius ulla ratio apparet; aut quod à cessatione partus nomen acceperit. Neque suppetiæ illæ satis fidæ sunt, quod ver- bum כזב cessare significet. Id enim tantum ob- tinet, cum in Piel adhibetur. Uti Esa. 58, 11. Se- ductus autem est Latinus ab Aquila, quod nota- tum Hieronymo in quæst. Ebraic. non ignorafse de- bebat vir Magnus. Id nomen loci exponunt præ- ter LXX. Onkelos, Aben-Ezra, R. Salomo, Levi, Hiscan, alii. Non autem de matre, sed Patre hæc accipienda: Et IPSE erat in Chesib, quia Patris ab- sentia ceu causa adducitur, cur à matre imposita sint filiis nomina.

## 38:6
Verse 6. ER.) ער in Hebrew. And an Armenian name in Plato, Republic X.

Latin:

Vers. 6. HER.) ער in Hebræo. Et Armenium nomen apud Platonem de Republica X.

## 38:7
Verse 7. WICKED IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.

Wicked רַע is a metathesis of the name עֵר, he who was watchful through sin was turned into a wicked one, as Cornelius notes, in the sight of the Lord, that is, notably evil. The same, as it is believed that Onan did not design the sin out of envy, but out of lust. Compare 1 Chron. 2, 3; he was killed just like his brother by an unusual plague, and one manifest to men, perhaps by an evil angel, says Menochius.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NEQUAM IN CONSPECTU DO- MINI.

Nequam רַע metathesis nominis עֵר, vigil per peccatum conversus est in nequam, ut notat Cornel. in conspectu Domini, id est, insigniter malus. Idem, quod Onanem peccatum non ex invidia, sed libi- dine ipsum designafse creditur. Conf. 1. Paral. 2, 3. occisum æque ut fratrem plaga insolita, & homini- bus manifesta forte ab angelo malo, ait Menochius.

## 38:14
Verse 14. AT THE CROSSROADS.) That they were accustomed to have victims of public lust outside the city, both the Hebrews note, and Chrysippus in the Isagoge of goods and evils. 'First, outside the city, the harlots, wearing masks, would hire themselves out to those who wished. Later, having cast off the masks, and not being permitted by the laws to enter the cities, they were outside of them.' Hence, among the Chaldeans, a harlot is called a wanderer: a stray whore to Horace.

Fagius in the Collation does not think it absurd that עינים is a Mercurial statue showing the way, as in Num. 10, 'you shall be for us instead of eyes,' that is, like a guide of the way. The LXX, however, the Samaritan, Pagninus, Oleaster, and others take it as a proper name: in the opening or entrance of Enajim.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IN BIVIO ITINERIS.) Extra urbem solitas se habere victimas publicæ libidinis, & Hebræi notant, & Chrysippus in Isagoge bonorum & malorum. Πρῶτον μὲν ἔξω πόλεως καὶ προσωπεῖα περικείμεναι αἱ ἑταῖραι ἐξεμίσθει ἑαυ- τὰς τοῖς βυλομένοις. Εἶθ' ὕστερον καταφρονήσασαι ἀπέθεντο τὰ προσωπεῖα, κὰι ὑπὸ τῶν νόμων μὴ ἐπιτρεπόμεναι εἰσιέναι εἰς τὰς πόλεις, ἔξω ἦσαν αὐτῶν. Hinc Chaldæis meretrix, vagatrix dicitur: devium scortum Horatio.

Fagio in Collat. non absurdum עינים esse sta- tuam mercurialem viam monstrantem, ut Num. 10. tu nobis pro oculis, id est instar ducis viæ. LXX. ta- men, Samarit. Pagn. Oleast. & alii accipiunt ceu no- men proprium: in apertura vel ostio Enajim.

## 38:18
Verse 18. THY RING.) Namely, a signet ring, which the word חתמת signifies, for which Aquila said σφραγῖδα. Just as the LXX also translate in other places.

AND THE BRACELET.) ὁρμίσκον in the LXX, σρεπτὸν in Aquila. It seems to have been something made of gold in the manner of a twisted thread. For that is what פתיל properly signifies, as appears in Exod. 39, 3; Jud. 15, 9; Ezech. 40, 3. The Greek interpreters seem to have believed that it was suspended from the neck.

The Syriac rendered it 'headband'. Chald. Jun. Ainswort. 'Sudarium' (napkin), Oleastr. 'pannum' (cloth) with which the head is wrapped, or a binding made of twisted threads, because it denotes something twisted; R. Solomon, 'a garment with which she covered herself'; Pagn. 'mantle'. These pledges do not seem to have been of great value, because they were given as security for a kid.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ANNULUM TUUM.) Nempe signatorium, quod significat vox חתמת pro quo σφραγῖδα dixit Aquila. Quomodo & LXX. vertunt aliis in locis.

ET ARMILLAM.) ὁρμίσκον LXX. σρεπτὸν Aquila. Videtur fuisse aliquid ex auro ad modum fili contorti. Id enim proprie significat פתיל, ut apparet Exod. 39, 3. Jud. 15, 9. Ezech. 40, 3. id de collo fuisse suspensum Græci interpre- tes credidisse videntur.

Syrus reddidit fasciam. Chald. Jun. Ainswort. Sudarium, Oleastr. pannum quo caput involvitur, vel ligamen ex tortis filis conflatum, quia notet tor- tum quid, R. Salomo vestem, qua se tegebat, Pagn. pallium. Non magni prætii hæc pignora fuisse vi- dentur, quia pro hædo oppignorata sunt.

## 38:21
Verse 21. WHERE IS THE WOMAN WHO SAT AT THE CROSSROADS?) In the Hebrew, קדשׁה, which is translated as πόρνη (harlot) by the LXX both here and in Deut. 23:17. Thus also a male prostitute, קדשׁ, Deut.

23:17. The reason for the name is from a similarity: for just as sacred things are not proper to anyone, but common in use, so are those women. In Plautus there is a similar translation: 'I am not a polluta pago' (an offering to the district): for 'pollucere' is to consecrate. See Festus and Macrobius.

Others think a harlot is so called from there, because they were accustomed to be perpetrated under the guise of religion, see 2 Kings 23:7, Hosea 4:14; but it is more correctly said to be from קדש, to prepare, because she was prepared for prostitution, as the most learned Münster notes.

Latin:

Vers. 21. UBI EST MULIER QUÆ SEDEBAT IN BI- VIO.) In Hebræo קדשׁה quod πόρνη vertitur à LXX & hîc & Deut. 23, 17. Sic & scortum masculum קדשׁ Deut.

23, 17. Causa nominis ex simili: nam ut sacra nemini sunt pro- pria, usu communia, sic illæ fœminæ. Apud Plautum simi- lis translatio: Non ego sum pollucta pago: pollucere enim est sacrare. Vide Festum & Macrobium.

Alii inde ita scortum dici putant, quod perpe- trari consueverint sub specie religionis, V. 2. Reg. 23, 7. Os. 4, 14. sed rectius à קדש præparare dicitur, quod præparatum sit ad prostitutionem, notante Doctiss. Münstero.

## 38:23
Verse 23. LET HER TAKE IT: CERTAINLY SHE CANNOT ARGUE US OF LYING.) In the Hebrew: 'Let her take it, lest we be a laughingstock.' The Greeks: μήποτε καταγελασθῶμεν (lest we be laughed at). Not badly: for 'ἐπονείδιστος καὶ αἰσχρὰ ἡ πρὸς ταύτας ὁμιλία' (the association with these women is disgraceful and shameful), says Porphyry, dealing with harlots, in Book IV of 'On Abstinence'. For the sake of avoiding contempt and mockery, he left her what he had handed over, lest he be exposed to mockery on account of levity, petulance, and shamefulness, as Münster, Vatablus, Fagius, and Cornelius say. He speaks in the plural, 'Let us be', because the contempt would redound upon himself and his family. However, they favor Luther's version, which follows, because he excuses himself for having kept faith, because he had sent the kid, but that harlot had not been found, being unknown.

Latin:

Vers. 23. HABEAT SIBI: CERTE MENDACII NOS ARGUERE NON POTEST.) In Hebræo: Habeat sibi, ne simus ludibrio. Græci: μήποτε καταγελασθῶμεν. Non ma- le: nam ἐπονείδιστος καὶ αἰσχρὰ ἡ πρὸς ταύτας ὁμιλία, ait de meretricibus agens Porphyrius IV. de Abstinentiâ.
