Contemtus & ludibrii declinandi causa reliquit illi quæ tradiderat, ne exponeretur ludibrio ob levi- tatem, petulantiam, & turpitudinem, ut Münster. Vatablus, Fagius, Cornelius. In plurali loquitur, Simus, quia contemtus in se & familiam suam re- dundaret. Favent tamen Lutheri versioni, quæ sequuntur, quod excuset se præstitisse fidem, quia miserit hædum, sed inventa non fuerit meretrix illa incognita.

## 38:24
Verse 24. THAT SHE MAY BE BURNED.) For she was the daughter of a priest of those places, as the Hebrews say. Many of Moses' laws are from ancient customs. Thus also that one in Lev. 21:9. Others think the law was peculiar to that family. That crime was judged to be punishable by death, Deut. 22:23, 24, even among the heathens, Jer. 29:22, 23, and long before the law, which the Belgians have noted. Concerning the law of this sentence, see what we have said in the Commentaries.

Latin:

Vers. 24. UT COMBURATUR.) Erat enim filia Sacer- dotis illorum locorum, ut ajunt Hebræi. Multæ Mosis leges ex antiquis moribus. Sic & illa Lev. 21, 9. Alii putant legem fuisse peculiarem istius familiæ. Illud crimen morte plectendum judicabatur, Deut. 22, 23. 24. etiam apud Ethnicos Jer. 29, 22. 23. & diu ante legem, quod Belgæ notarunt. De ju- re hujus sententiæ vid. quæ in Commentar. dixi- mus.

## 38:26
Verse 26. SHE IS MORE RIGHTEOUS THAN I. Because Judah had not stood by his promises, and had unjustly prevented her from receiving offspring from Shelah. 'More righteous,' he says, not 'more chaste': because Tamar sinned by adultery and incest, and gave Judah the occasion for sinning. Therefore Dievius renders the additions thus: 'For because I did not give her to my son, she did this'; in his commentary on the Gospel of John 7:22.

Latin:

Vers. 26. JUSTIOR ME EST. Quia Judas promissis non steterat, & injuste impedivit, ne prolem ex Sela susciperet. Justior, inquit, non castior: quia Thamar adulterio & in- cesto peccavit, & occasionem peccandi Judæ dedit. Ideo sic reddit Dievius, quæ adduntur: Nam pro- pterea quod non dedi eam filio meo, supple fecit hoc; in Evangel. ad Joh. 7, 22.

## 38:29
Verse 29. WHY HAVE YOU BROKEN THE WALL OVER YOURSELF?) A proverb, that is, why, by anticipating your brother who had begun to be born, do you bring a dispute about birthright into the house? The interpretation of others is simpler—Vatablus, Malvenda, and the Tigurines—who render it thus: 'Why have you broken a breach over yourself?' or by breaking the partition, or the membrane with which you were covered, or by passing by your brother, who was placed like an intermediate wall: or, so that it may be an exclamation and wonder: 'How you have broken through! Over you (is) the breaking!' There was no need to think about a dispute, or at least he was not easily thinking about it then. Nor is it certain that this proverbial formula was used then. Those things were done by divine dispensation, by which the right of the firstborn was destined for Perez, from whom the Messiah was to be born. Which is also the reason for this history being recounted, namely, so that it might be established concerning the genealogy of the Messiah, who willed to be born from sinners, because He came for the sake of sinners. Matt. 1:3.

Latin:

Vers. 29. QUARE DIVISA EST PROPTER TE MA- CERIA?) Proverbiale, id est, quare prævertendo fratrem, qui nasci cœperat, litem de primogenitura infers in domum? Simplicior est aliorum interpretatio, Vatabli, Malvendæ, Tigurin. qui ita reddunt: Quare ru- pisti super te rupturam? vel interstitium, seu mem- branam, qua operiebaris, rumpendo, vel fra- trem prætergrediendo, qui instar muri interme- dii oppositus erat: vel, ut exclamatio & admira- tio sit: Quam perrupisti? super te (est) perruptio! De lite cogitare opus non habebat, aut certe tum non facile cogitabat. Nec de proverbiali ista for- mula tum usitata constat. Divina illa facta sunt dispensatione, qua primogeniti jus Pherezio desti- natum erat, ex quo procreandus Messias. Quæ causa etiam est recensitæ hujus historiæ, ut nem- pe de Messiæ genealogia constaret, qui è pecca- toribus nasci voluit, quia ob peccatores venit. Matth. 1, 3.

## 38:30
Verse 30. ZARAH. Some explain it as 'rising', because he ought to have risen first. Bochart, in 'Hierozoicon', explains it as 'Resplendence', on account of the brightness of the scarlet.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ZARAH. Nonnulli exponunt oriens, quod prius oriri de- buit. Bochart. in Hieroz. explicat Refulgentia, ob coccini fulgentiam.

## 39:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIX. The chastity and imprisonment of Joseph.

Verse 1. EUNUCH.) Thus also above 37:36, where the Greek version has 'τῷ σπάδοντι' (the castrated one), which prevents us from understanding 'eunuch' here, from its origin rather than its usage, as a chamberlain. He may therefore have been one of the Egyptian king's court officials, such as were later accustomed to be promoted to various dignities. See 2 Kings 8:6, 1 Sam. 8:15, where the customs of neighboring kings are described: and Jerem. 34:19, with the customs of the Hebrews now corrupted. The Chaldean translates it 'רברבא', as if you would say 'magnate'.

It is likely that an honored minister in the court is meant, who is called the chief of the guards in Gen. 37:36, whom they call a Marshal today, as that word is taken not only in other books, 1 Sam. 8:15, 1 Reg. 22:9, 2 Reg. 8:6, but also in Genesis chapter 40:2. Grotius below at chapter 41:34 observes that the word פקידים, rendered by the Vulgate as 'prefects' and by the Greek word ἐπιτρόπους, and explained by that Greek word by Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum, which the LXX interpreted as 'toparchs', is rendered by Onkelos as מהימני, and that the Syriac is accustomed to interpret it as 'eunuchs'.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIX. Castitas & carcer Josephi.

Vers. 1. EUNUCHUS.) Sic & supra 37, 36. ubi Græca versio τῷ σπάδοντι, quod obstat, quo minus εὐνοῦχος hic, ex origine magis quam ex usu, cubiculi præpositum intelli- gamus. Fuerit ergo aliquis ex exoletiis Ægyptii regis, qua- les deinde ad diversas dignitates promoveri solebant. Vide 2. Reg. 8, 6. 1. Sam. 8, 15. ubi mores vicinorum regum descri- buntur: & Jerem. 34, 19. moribus Hebræorum jam corruptis. Chaldæus vertit רברבא quasi dicas megistana.

Mimistrum honoratum in aula intelligi, qui princeps satellitum Genes. 37, 36. dicitur, quem Marschallum hodie vocant, verisimile est, uti vox ea non tantum in aliis libris, 1. Sam. 8, 15. 1. Reg. 22, 9. 2. Reg. 8, 6. Sed etiam in Genesi cap. 40, 2. accipitur. Grotius infra ad cap. 41, 34. vocem פקידים a vulgata per præpositos, ἐπιτρόπως redditam, eaque Græca voce a Jonathane & Hierosolymitana expositam, quam LXX. interpretati sunt τοπάρχας, ab Onkeloso reddi מהימני, atque ita Syrum solere interpretari εὐνέχες observat.

## 39:2
Verse 2. DOING PROSPEROUSLY IN ALL THINGS.) The LXX: a man succeeding; Aquila: being directed; Symmachus: being prosperous; all not badly. The sense is in that Homeric verse: 'Who labors much for him, and God increases the work.' Which is the interpretation of the name Joseph itself.

Latin:

Vers. 2. IN CUNCTIS PROSPERE AGENS.) LXX. ἀνὴρ ἐπιτυγχάνων: Aquila κατευθυνόμενος. Symmachus εὐοδόμενος, non male omnes. Sensus in illo Homerico versu: Ὅς οἱ πολλὰ κάμησι, Θεὸς δ’ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἀέξῃ. quæ interpretatio ipsius nominis Josephi.

## 39:6
Verse 6. AND HE KNEW NOTHING ELSE EXCEPT THE BREAD WHICH HE ATE.) Secure in all matters, he indulged only in feasts.

We do not disapprove of this explanation of Münster, Vatablus, Fagius, Estius, Tirinus, Menochius, and Rivetus, although others, following Aben-Ezra, prefer it to be indicated that he had everything in common with Joseph except bread, because the Egyptians did not take food with the Hebrews (chapter 43:32), or that Joseph had provided for everything most accurately except for the bread.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NEC QUICQUAM ALIUD NOVERAT NISI PANEM QUO VESCEBATUR.) Securus rerum omnium epulis tantum indulgebat.

Non improbamus hanc Münsteri, Vatabli, Fagii, Estii, Tirini, Menochii, Riveti explicationem, etsi alii ex Aben-Ezr. malint indicari, omnia habuisse eum cum Josepho communia præter panem, quia Ægyptii non capiebant cibum cum Ebræis cap. 43, 32. aut omnia accuratissime providisse Josephum excepto pane.

## 39:11
Verse 11. THAT JOSEPH MIGHT ENTER THE HOUSE.) The name Joseph was judged necessary to be added here for a clearer sense by the LXX, and also by the Samaritan and the Syriac.

It is said that this happened ON A CERTAIN DAY, which Münster and Fagius understand as an opportune day, when no one from the household was at home.

Latin:

Vers. 11. UT INTRARET JOSEPH DOMUM.) Nomen Joseph ad sensum clariorem addendum hîc censuere & LXX. Samarites quoque & Syrus.

Dicitur QUODAM DIE id factum, quod Münster. & Fag. de die oportuno intelligunt, cum nemo ex familia esset domi.

## 39:12
Verse 12. HE WENT OUTSIDE. He could have snatched the cloak from his mistress: but he did not want to, partly out of reverence, so as not to offer violence to his mistress, partly because the most immediate remedy against the temptations of lust is not struggling, but flight, and partly so that he would neither touch the woman nor be touched by her, as Cornelius notes here.

Latin:

Vers. 12. EGRESSUS EST FORAS. Potuisset heræ extorquere pallium: sed noluit, partim ex reverentia, ne vim heræ inferret, partim quia præsentissimum remedium contra tentationes libidinis est non colluctatio, sed fuga, partim ne vel mulierem tangeret, vel ab ea tangeretur, ut hîc Cornelius.

## 39:15
Verse 15. AND WHEN I HAD CRIED OUT AND HE HAD HEARD MY VOICE, HE LEFT HIS CLOAK.) Similar is that in Seneca's Hippolytus: '...lo, he departs headlong, and astonished, he left his sword in trembling flight.' It follows in the same place: 'We hold the pledge of the crime.' Indeed, to use the words of Juvenal from Satire X: 'She blushed, indeed, as if at a scorned rejection,' etc. For Stheneboea brought a similar calumny against Bellerophon, as did Astydameia against Peleus.

But he must have been blinded by jealousy, because he did not notice that this evidence had rather proceeded from violence by the woman, as noted by Philo.

Latin:

Vers. 15. CUMQUE EGO SUCCLAMASSEM ET AUDISSET VOCEM MEAM, RELIQUIT PALLIUM.) Simile illud in Hippolyto Senecæ: ————— en præceps abit Ensemq; trepida liquit attonitus fuga. Sequitur ibidem: Pignus tenemus sceleris. Nimirum, ut Juvenalis utar verbis ex Satyra X. Erubuit nempe hæc ceu fastidita repulsa &c. Similem enim calumniam Bellephoronti intentavit Sthenebœa, ut & Astidamæa Peleo.

Excæcatum autem oportet fuisse præ Zelotypia, quod non adverterit hoc indicium potius fuisse violentiæ a muliere profectæ, ut Philoni notatum.

## 39:21
Verse 21, HE GAVE HIM THANKS. Junius and Piscator place a hypallage in the Hebrew ויתן חסדו, without it Oleaster [translates] h. m. and he gave (the Lord) his grace.

IN THE SIGHT OF THE CHIEF OF THE PRISON.

Malvenda seems to have been here the administrator and trustee of Potiphar, the keeper: but Potiphar was the Royal Provost.

Latin:

Vers. 21, DEDIT EI GRATIAM. Hypallagen Jun. & Piscat. ponunt in Ebr. ויתן חסדו, sine ea Oleaster h. m. & dedit (Dominus) gratiam suam.

IN CONSPECTU PRINCIPIS CARCERIS.

Malvenda videtur hic fuisse Potipharis administer, & fidei commissarius, custos: Potiphar autem Commentariensis Regius.

## 39:23
Vers. 23. AND HE KNEW NOT ANYTHING OF ALL THAT WAS ENTRUSTED TO HIM. The Vulgate rendered the sense. You may render it word for word thus: not seeing (or caring for) anything at all in his hand.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NEC NOVERAT ALIQUID CUNCTIS EI CREDITIS. Sensum reddidit vulgatus. Κατὰ πόδα ita reddas: non videns (vel curans) omne quicquam in manu ejus.

## 39:23 Addition
To chap. 39. verse 34. AND HAVING TORN HIS GARMENTS HE WAS CLOTHED IN SACKCLOTH.

It was the custom of those mourning, as also of those repenting. Thus David ordered mourning with torn garments and girded with sackcloth because of the death of Abner, 2 Sam. 3, 31, and these were signs of those repenting. Neh. 9, 1, 2; 1 Kings 21, 27; Dan. 9, 3; Joel 2, 13. Which was done with sackcloth either assumed immediately upon the flesh, 1 Kings 21, 27; 2 Kings 6, 30, or with parts of the body first bared, or even with other garments covered by sackcloth worn, Is. 37, 1, 2. Schindler in his Lexicon, p. 1930, takes sackcloth for a woolen or hempen garment, which one puts on over his flesh. For having taken off or torn their more splendid garments, in place of an undergarment they covered their body with sackcloth, a most vile, dense, and hard garment, or they girded their loins, they put on sackcloth or girded themselves. So also Philippus Aquinas in his Lexicon says sackcloth was a woolen, dense, and hard garment, which one was accustomed to put on in time of affliction and repentance. Conf. Mr. Dr. Geier on the mourning of the Hebrews, ch. 22, and Mr. Dr. Joh. Adam Scherzer in his solemn exercises on Matthew 11, verse 25, thesis 41.

Latin:

Ad cap. 39. vers. 34. SCISSISQUE VESTIBUS IN- DUTUS EST CILICIO.

Mos erat lugentium, ut & pœnitentium. Ita lu- gere jubebat David scissis vestimentis & ciliciis ac- cincti ob Abneri mortem 2. Sam. 3, 31. & signa hæc erant pœnitentium. Nehem. 9, 1. 2. 1. Reg. 21, 27. Dan. 9, 3. Joel. 2, 13. Quod fiebat sacco vel imme- diate super carnem assumpto 1. Reg. 21, 27. 2. Reg. 6. 30. vel partibus corporis prius nudatis, aut etiam vestimentis aliis opertis sacco indutis Es. 37, 1. 2. Schindler. in Lex. p. 1930. saccum habet pro veste lanea, aut cannabidea, quam quis induit super car- nem suam. Exutis enim aut laceratis vestibus splen- didioribus loco interulæ sacco veste vilissima, densa, & dura corpus operiebant, aut lumbos constringebant, induebant saccum aut accingebant. Sic etiam Phi- lippus Aquinas in Lexic. Saccum dicit fuisse vesti- mentum laneum, densum & durum, quod indui con- sueverat tempore afflictionis, & pœnitentiæ. Conf. Dn. D. Geierum de luctu Ebræor. c. 22. & Dn. D. Joh. Adam Scherzerum exercit. solemn. ad Matth. 11. versu 25. thes. 41.

## 40:1 Argument
CHAPTER XL. The dreams of the cupbearer and the baker.

Latin:

CAPUT XL. Somnia Pincernæ, & Pistoris.

## 40:17
Vers. 17. AND IN ONE BASKET WHICH WAS HIGHER, TO CARRY ALL FOOD FOR ME, AND THE BIRDS TO EAT FROM IT.) An omen similar to this dream is in Homer's Odyssey, book 2: ————— τῷ δ’ αἰετὼ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς, &c. soon the augur explaining:

Μνήσησιν δὲ μάλισα πιφύσκομεν, τάδε εἴπω. Τεῖσιν γὰρ μέγα πῆμα κυλίνδεται. Vers. 13. PHARAOH WILL REMEMBER YOUR SERVICE.) The very same expression is below in 19, wherefore you will rightly translate it in the same way in both places: Pharaoh will reckon your accounts. Thus the word ראש is taken in Numbers 1:49, Exodus 30:11. Thus also the Greeks generally use κεφάλαιον.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected: For there is nothing in the source about the remembrance of service. Furthermore, Grotius has his explanation from Aben-Ezra and from Mercer. Junius provides another, approved by B. Gerhard: but that of Aben-Ezra seems simpler. The interpretation concerning the lifting up of the head is not inelegant, if the head of each is understood to be lifted up, the one exalted into his former dignity, the other onto a cross; just as the word of exaltation is used concerning the cross of Christ in John 12:32.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET IN UNO CANISTRO QUOD ERAT EXCELSIUS, PORTARE ME OMNES CIBOS, AVESQUE COMEDERE EX EO.) Simile huic somnio augurium in Homeri Odysseæ B'. ————— τῷ δ’ αἰετὼ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς, &c. mox augur explicans:

Μνήσησιν δὲ μάλισα πιφύσκομεν, τάδε εἴπω. Τεῖσιν γὰρ μέγα πῆμα κυλίνδεται. Verf. 13. RECORDABITUR PHARAO MINISTERII TUI.) Eadem plane locutio infra 19. quare eodem modo utrobique recte verreris: Exputabit Pharao rationes tuas. Sic fumitur vox ראש Numer. 1, 49. Exod. 30, 11. Sic ferme & Graeci κεφάλαιον ufurpant.

REcte corrigitur Vulgata: Nihil enim in fonte de recordatione ministerii. Caeterum expli- cationem suam Grotius ab Aben-Esdra habet & à Mercero. Aliam Junius tradit, probatam B. Gerhardo: sed ista Aben-Esdtæ simplicior vide- tur. Interpretatio de levatione capitis non incon- cinna, si utriusque caput levatum intelligatur, al- tero in dignitatem pristinam, altero in crucem exal- tato; uti & de Christi cruce vox exaltationis adhibe- tur Joh. 12, 32.

## 40:19
Vers. 19. AND THE BIRDS SHALL TEAR YOUR FLESH.) What Horace said: You shall feed the crows on the cross.

Latin:

Verf. 19. ET LACERABUNT VOLUCRES CARNES TUAS.) Quod Horatius dixit: Pasces in cruce corvos.

## 40:20
Vers. 20. BIRTHDAY.) Herodotus, Calliope, in the affairs of the Persians: τῦτο τὸ δεῖπνον κατασκευάζεται ἅπαξ τῦ ἐνιαυτῦ, ἡμέρῃ τῇ ἐγένετο βασιλεύς. Add Matthew 14:6.

Latin:

Verf. 20. DIES NATALITIUS.) Herodotus Calliope in Persarum rebus: τῦτο τὸ δεῖπνον κατασκευάζεται ἅπαξ τῦ ἐνιαυτῦ, ἡμέρῃ τῇ ἐγένετο βασιλεύς. Adde Matth. XIV, 6.

## 41:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLI. The interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams.

Latin:

CAPUT XLI. Interpretatio somniorum Pharaonis.

## 41:2
Vers. 2. IN MARSHY PLACES.) The LXX: ἐν τῷ Ἄχεί: a word undoubtedly used in Egypt, where the LXX were writing. I judge that it signifies green fields, with the Nile stagnating in them. For also to the Arabs أجام are marshes. The son of Sirach (40:16) preserved the Egyptian word in Greek, where in the Latin it is 'greenness'. That word also exists in the Hebrew of Job 8:11, rendered there by the Greeks as πάπυρος, and in Latin as 'bulrush'. For the papyrus was born on the banks wet from the river. Thus Josephus translates אחו in his History, which is Exodus 2:4.

The cows are rightly said to ascend from the Nile, because fertility or sterility comes to Egypt from it, as Bonfrerius notes.

Latin:

Verf. 2. IN LOCIS PALUSTRIBUS.) LXX. ἐν τῷ Ἄχεί: voce haud dubie usitata in Ægypto, ubi scribebant LXX. Ar- bitror significari campos virentes, stagnante in illis Nilo. Nam & Arabibus أجام stagna. Vocem Ægyptiam serva- vit in Graeco Sirachides 40, 16. ubi in Latino viriditas. Ex- stat illa vox & in Hebræo Jobi 8, 11. reddita ibi à Graecis πά- πυρος, Latino scirpus. In ripis nimirum ab amne madenti- bus papyrus nascebatur. Ita אחו transfert Josephus in Hi- storia, quæ est Exod. 2, 4.

REcte ex Nilo afcendere dicuntur boves, quia ab eo provenit Ægypto fertilitas, aut sterili- tas, notante Bonfrerio.

## 41:3
Vers. 3. FROM THE RIVER.) That is, when it has subsided into its channel and is not irrigating the fields, which is a sign of famine. Pliny, book 18, 18. On the contrary: ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐπλήμμυρεν ὁ ποταμὸς, εὑρήσει ὁ κατοι- κῶν χαρὰν καὶ εὐφορίαν. Achmes, chapter 176. Oneirocriticon from the discipline of the Egyptians.

ON THE VERY BANK OF THE RIVER.) That is, not flooded. What is added here, 'in green places', is neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek. The error arose from the fact that where in the Greek it is παρὰ τὰς βόας, the Latin reads παρὰ τὰς πόας. That years are signified by cows is in the Oneirocriticon of Asaph Setha. Likewise in Achmet, whose words are in chapter 239, from the discipline of the Egyptians: τὰ βοίδια θήλεα εἰς χρόνυς˙ καὶ εἰ μέν εἰσι πιόνα, χρόνυς εὐφό- ρυς δηλῦσιν˙ εἰ δὲ πτωχὰ καὶ λεπτὰ, χρόνυς δυσφόρυς. He has similar things from the Persians.

Latin:

Verf. 3. DE FLUMINE.) Depresso scil. intra alveum & non irrigante agros, quod famis signum. Plinius lib. 18, 18. Contra ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐπλήμμυρεν ὁ ποταμὸς, εὑρήσει ὁ κατοι- κῶν χαρὰν καὶ εὐφορίαν. Achmes cap. CLXXVI. Onirocriti- con ex Ægyptiorum disciplina.

IN IPSA AMNIS RIPA.) Non inundata scilicet. Quod additur hic in locis virentibus, neque in Hebræo est, neque in Græco. Error inde ortus, quod ubi in Græco est παρὰ τὰς βόας, Latinus παρὰ τὰς πόας legit. Per vaccas annos signi- ficari est in Onirocritico Asaph Setha. Item in Achmete, cu- jus verba sunt cap. CCXXXIX. ex Ægyptiorum disciplina: τὰ βοίδια θήλεα εἰς χρόνυς˙ καὶ εἰ μέν εἰσι πιόνα, χρόνυς εὐφό- ρυς δηλῦσιν˙ εἰ δὲ πτωχὰ καὶ λεπτὰ, χρόνυς δυσφόρυς. Si- milia ex Persis habet.

## 41:4
Verf. 4. HE SLEPT AGAIN.) Dreams sent by God are accustomed to express the same thing twice, as below 32. Thus in Daniel the same tree and image. Thus concerning the dream of Ptolemy, Tacitus, Histories V. The same appearance, now more terrible and more pressing.

Latin:

Verf. 4. RURSUM DORMIVIT.) Somnia divinitus immissa solent rem eandem bis exprimere, ut infra 32. Sic apud Danielem idem arbor & imago. Sic de somnio Pto- lemæi Tacitus Histor. V. Eadem species terribilior jam & in- stantior.

## 41:5
SEVEN EARS OF CORN.) See another dream in Josephus, book XVII, 15 of the Antiquities, and concerning the Jewish War II, chapter XI, where he says that years are similarly signified by ears of corn. In Tacitus, Annals XI, ears of corn seen in a dream, likewise turned backward, were believed to predict a shortage of grain.

Latin:

SEPTEM SPICÆ.) Vide aliud somnium apud Josephum lib. XVII, 15. antiquæ historiæ, & de bello Judaico II. cap. XI. ubi similiter per spicas ait annos significari. Apud Tacitum Annalium XI. in somno itidem visæ spicæ retro conversæ gra- vitatem annonæ prædicere creditæ.

## 41:8
Verf. 8. INTERPRETERS.) The word חרטמי is not Hebrew, but Egyptian. The LXX translate it as ἐξηγητάς (interpreters). Aquila as κρυφια- στάς (those who interpret hidden things), Symmachus as μάγυς (magi). But in Exodus and Daniel they are called ἐπαοιδοὶ (enchanters), elsewhere in Exodus φαρμακοὶ (sorcerers): with which names the institutions of the Magi, mentioned by Pliny and others, agree well.

Fuller, in book V of his Miscellanies, chapter XI, denies that it is an Ethiopic word because of the great discrepancy between this and the Hebrew language, and with others derives it from חרט, a writing stylus, because they used characters for magical arts: thus Aucharius says it is composed from חרט, a stylus, and אטם, he compressed or closed, because tricksters are accustomed to draw characters and circles, whence they are called circulators. Rabbi Saadia composes it from חר, a hole, and אטום, closed: because divinations were accustomed to be drawn from a stopped-up hole: Hottinger, in Thesaurus page 57, makes it a Persian word from the Persian verb חרד, with the ד changed into ש, meaning he knew or recognized. Compare also Svaningius, Commentary on Daniel 1, 20.

Verse of the same. AND HAVING SUMMONED HE TOLD THE DREAM.) A custom long retained in Egypt. Tacitus, Histories IV, concerning Ptolemy: Ptolemy, stirred by an omen and a miracle, reveals his nocturnal visions to the priests of the Egyptians, whose custom it is to understand such things.

Latin:

Verf. 8. CONJECTORES.) Vox חרטמי non Hebrai- ca est, sed Ægyptiaca. LXX. vertunt ἐξηγητάς. Aquila κρυφια- στάς, Symmachus μάγυς. At in Exodo & Daniele dicuntur ἐπαοιδοὶ, alibi in Exodo φαρμακοὶ: cum quibus nominibus be- ne conveniunt Magorum instituta Plinio, & aliis memorata.

Negat Æthiopicam esse vocem ob magnam dis- crepantiam hujus & Hebraicæ linguæ Fuller. lib. V. Misc. cap. XI. & cum aliis à חרט stylo scriptorio de- rivat, quod characteres adhibuerit ad artes Magi- cas: ita Aucharius à חרט stylo, & אטם compressit, occludit, compositam ait, quia præstigiatores cha- racteres, & circulos ducere solent, unde circula- tores dicti. R. Saadia è חר foramen & אטום clau- sus componit: quia ex foramine obdurato deduci solitæ divinationes: Hottingerus in Thef. pag. 57. Persicam vocem facit à חרד verbo Persico, mutato ד in ש scivit, cognovit. Conf. & Svaningius Com- ment. in Dan. 1, 20.

Vers. eod. ET ACCERSITIS NARRAVIT SOMNI- UM.) Mos diu in Ægypto retentus. Tacitus Historiarum IV. de Ptolemæo: Ptolemæus omine & miraculo excitus, sa- cerdotibus Ægyptiorum, quibus mos talia intelligere, nocturnos visus aperit.

## 41:14
Verse 14. HAVING CHANGED HIS GARMENT.) For those mourning or in squalid attire could not approach the king. See below L, 4, and Esther 4, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 14. VESTE MUTATA.) Lugentes enim aut sor- didati regem adire non poterant. Vide infra L, 4. & Esther. 4, 4.

## 41:16
Verse 16. WITHOUT ME GOD WILL ANSWER PROSPEROUS THINGS TO PHARAOH.) Symmachus had, not I, but GOD: which expression is to be interpreted like that similar one in Matthew 10, 20.

Justin, book XXXVI, ch. 2, also handed down these things about Joseph from Trogus Pompeius: And he was most sagacious in prodigies and was the first to establish the understanding of dreams: and nothing of divine or human law seemed unknown to him: so much so that he even foresaw the sterility of the fields many years before: and all Egypt would have perished from famine, had he not, by his warning, ordered the King by edict to store up grain for many years: and his experiments were so great that the answers seemed to be given not by a man, but by GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ABSQUE ME DEUS RESPONDEBIT PRO- SPERA PHARAONI.) Symmachus habuit, non ego, sed DEUS: quæ locutio interpretanda, ut illa similis Matth. 10, 20.

De Josepho hæc etiam ex Trogo Pompejo tra- didit Justinus lib. XXXVI, c. 2. Et prodigiorum sa- gacissimus erat & somniorum primus intelligentiam condidit : nihilque divini juris, humanique ei incogni- tum videbatur: adeo, ut etiam sterilitatem agrorum ante multos annos providerit: periissetque omnis Æ- gyptus fame, nisi monitu ejus Rex edicto servari per multos annos fruges jussisset : tantaque ejus experimen- ta fuerunt, ut non ab homine, sed à DEO responsa da- ri viderentur.

## 41:17
Verse 17. I THOUGHT I WAS STANDING UPON THE BANK OF THE RIVER.) The very words which were above are repeated: which is frequent in both the Holy Scriptures and Homer: Macrobius, book V, Saturnalia, ch. 16. I know not how that repetition uniquely becomes Homer: and it is worthy of the genius of the ancient Poet. See a similar instance above 24, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 17. PUTABAM ME STARE SUPER RIPAM FLUMINIS.) Repetuntur verba ipsa quæ supra fuere: quod frequens & sacris literis & Homero: Macrobius lib. V. Saturn. cap. 16. Nescio quomodo Homerum repetitio illa unice decet: & est genio antiqui Poetæ digna. Simile vide supra 24, 37.

## 41:25
Verse 25. THE DREAM OF THE KING IS ONE.) The signification of both is the same. It is a metonymy. To make good use of dreams, not only of those sleeping but also of those watching, is the mark of a statesman. Philo.

WHAT GOD IS ABOUT TO DO, HE SHOWS TO PHARAOH.) More openly and plainly than the magi think, who thought that Pharaoh's daughters were to be understood by the cows. Thus the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 25. SOMNIUM REGIS UNUM EST.) Utriusque eadem fignificatio. Est metonymia. Somniis bene uti, non dormientium tantum, sed & vigilantium, politici est. Philo.

QUÆ FACTURUS EST DEUS, OSTENDIT PHA- RAONI.) Aperteius & planius quam magi putant, qui per vaccas putabant intelligendas Pharaonis filias. Sic Hebræi.

## 41:34
Verse 34. OVERSEERS.) Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum here usurp the Greek word Ἐπιτρόπους. The LXX, τοπάρχας. Onkelos, מחימנין, in the way the Syrian is accustomed to interpret eunuchs. Just as in peace one must think of war, so in fruitful years one must think of sterility.

Latin:

Vers. 34. PRÆPOSITOS.) Ἐπιτρόπους Græcam vocem hic usurpant Jonathan & Hierosolymitanus. LXX. τοπάρ- χας. Onkelos מחימנין, quomodo Syrus solet interpretari εὐνούχυς. Sicut in pace de bello, sic in fœcundis annis de sterilitate cogitandum.

## 41:35
Verse 35. LET ALL THE CORN BE GATHERED UNDER PHARAOH'S POWER, AND BE KEPT IN THE CITIES. AND LET IT BE PREPARED FOR THE FUTURE SEVEN YEARS OF FAMINE.) A similar passage is in Cassiodorus, book 12, 12. Let your prudence overcome future want with old grain: because the happy abundance of the past year was so great that it suffices even for the future months. See, if you please, also what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 35. OMNE FRUMENTUM SUB PHARAONIS POTESTATE CONDATUR, SERVETURQUE IN UR- BIBUS. ET PRÆPARETUR FUTURÆ SEPTEM AN- NORUM FAMI.) Simile apud Cassiodorum lib. 12, 12. De veteribus frugibus prudentia tua futuram vincat inopiam: quia tanta fuit anni præteriti felix ubertas, ut etiam futuris mensi- bus provisa sufficiant. Vide si placet, & quæ sequuntur.

## 41:40
AT THE COMMAND OF YOUR MOUTH ALL THE PEOPLE WILL OBEY.) In the Hebrew: upon your mouth shall all the people kiss: that is a sign of subjection.

The Hebrew word נשק does not only signify to kiss; but also to arm, to feed, to govern. Therefore Kimchi, Aben-Ezra, Münster, Pagninus, and Oleaster render it: At your word or mouth shall they be armed, i.e., you shall be Master of the soldiers: But Joseph was appointed to the duties of peace, not of war. Therefore R. Solomon, with Onkelos, the Samaritan Version, the Tigurine, and Fagius, explain it as: at your mouth or according to your command shall the people be fed. But the dignity of Joseph must be extended entirely: the Chaldean and Samaritan have the people shall be governed. Thus the Vulgate expressed the sense, with the LXX and the Syrian, which Oleaster also renders in this way: At your mouth or word shall they gather themselves for those things which are of peace or of war. Nor does the interpretation of Dievius deviate much, who makes ישק the future Niphal from שקק, to run about for the sake of business, i.e., according to your mouth shall the people be provided for. The same sense remains, as far as the matter is concerned, when the kiss of subjection is understood: even if because of the preposition על Grotius renders otherwise than others, namely Piscator, Ainsworth, and the Belgian, who explain it as: at your mouth or command shall the people kiss, namely, the hand, as a sign of subjection. For they observe that 'at the mouth' is the same as 'at the command' in Exodus 38, 21, Numbers 3, 16, Joshua 19, 50, and they compare Job 31, 27, Hosea 13, 2. Which opinion, because of the passage in Job, is to be preferred, unless perhaps with the learned Hebrew you take it metaphorically, i.e., Whatever you say, I wish it to be understood that all the people, by a single consensus, would as it were offer a kiss; amicably and obediently, etc., as also Menochius: the precept of your mouth shall be kissed, shall be venerated, and they shall willingly obey it, because, as Dieu has in his Collations with Cloppenburg, it seems to be doubted whether princes in the East were accustomed to admit commoners to a kiss of the mouth, since they do not do so today.

Latin:

AD TUI ORIS IMPERIUM CUNCTUS POPULUS OBEDIET.) In Hebræo: supra os tuum osculabitur omnis populus: id signum subjectionis.

Vox Ebræa נשק non osculari tantum significat; Sed & armare, cibare, gubernare. Ideo Kim- chi, Aben-Ezr. Münster. Pagn. Oleast. reddunt: Ad sermonem vel os tuum armabitur, q. d. tu eris Magister militum: Sed Joseph ad pacis non belli munia præfectus fuit. Proinde R. Sal. cum On- kel. Vers. Samar. Tig. & Fag. exponunt ad os tuum sive secundum jussionem tuam cibabitur populus. Verum ampliandum omnino est ἀξίωμα Josephi: Chald. Samar. habent gubernabitur populus. Ita Vulg. sensum expresserit, cum LXX. & Syr. quem etiam hoc modo reddit Oleast. Ad os sive sermo- nem tuum congregabit se ad ea, quæ pacis sunt vel belli. Neque multum deviat Dievii interpretatio, qui ישק facit futurum Niphal à שקק discursitare ne- gotiorum causa h. m. secundum os tuum procu- rabitur populus. Idem fere sensus manet, quantum ad rem, cum osculum subjectionis intelligitur: etsi ob præposit. על Grotius aliter quam alii reddat, Piscator nempe, Ainswort. Belg. qui exponunt ad os vel imperium tuum osculabitur populus, scil. ma- num, in signum subjectionis. Observant enim juxta os idem esse, quod juxta mandatum Exod. 38, 21. Num. 3, 16. Jos. 19, 50. & conferunt Job. 31, 27. Hos. 13, 2. Quæ sententia ob locum Jobi συγχρόνυ præ- ferenda, nisi forte cum Docto Ebræo Metaphorice accipias, q. d. Quicquid dixeris, uno populi con- sensu quasi osculum omnes porrigerent excipi vo- lo; amice & obedienter &c. uti & Menoch. oris tui præceptum exosculabitur, venerabitur, eique libenter parebit, quia ut Dieu in Collat. cum Cloppenb. habet, dubitandum videtur, an principes in oriente con- sueverint ad osculum oris plebejos admittere, quum id hodie non faciant.

## 41:43
THAT ALL MIGHT KNEEL BEFORE HIM.) The word אַבְרֵךְ which is here in the text is itself Egyptian; I believe it is a certain παιχνισμός (play on words), and therefore omitted by the LXX. Onkelos interprets it from the Syriac as Father of the King. For רֶךְ stands for King in Syriac, but the Egyptian language is one thing, the Syriac another. There are those who translate it as tender father: as if there were two Hebrew words. There are those who form it from the Hebrew word בָּרַךְ, as the Latin does here, with little probability.

Latin:

Verf. 43. UT OMNES CORAM EO GENU FLE- CTERENT.) Quæ hic in textu est vox אַבְרֵךְ & ipsa Æ- gyptia est, credo παιχνισμός quidam, ideoque omissus à LXX. Onkelos ex Syriaco interpretatur Pater Regis. Nam רֶךְ pro Rege Syriacum, sed alia lingua Ægyptia, alia Syriaca. Sunt qui Pater tener transferunt: quasi duæ voces essent Hebrææ. Sunt qui ab Hebræa voce בָּרַךְ formant, ut hîc Latinus, pa- rum probabiliter.

## 41:44
WITHOUT YOUR COMMAND NO ONE SHALL MOVE.) That is, weapons.

OR FOOT.) No one shall undertake an expedition.

Therefore, the Latin version does not please the Papist-leaning Grotius. Whom he ought rather to have left in other errors, and those not rarely more serious, than to excuse. Although here the translation of the Latin may not seem so improbable, if it be believed that אַבְרֵךְ is said for הַבְרֵךְ, bend the knees, in accordance with R. Jonathan and R. David Kimchi; thus the Hebrews are accustomed sometimes to use a characteristic א: or if it be taken in the first person with Aben-Ezra, as if everyone from the crowd cried out: אַבְרֵךְ I will bend the knees. Certainly Buxtorf in the root בָּרַךְ establishes an infinitive Hiphil having an א in place of a ה after the Chaldean form, so that it was proclaimed by the Royal heralds that knees were to be bent. The Latin version is also approved by Mercerus, Franc. Junius lib. II. Gram. cap. 8, Piscator quæst. 48 in Genes., and B. Johann. Gerhardus. Add that Aquila also interpreted it as γονατισμόν, kneeling, which word is found in Genesis 24:11. That other etymology through the division of the word, so that it might be tender father, Jerome brought forward from the tradition of the Hebrews, quæst. in Genes. Tom. III. pag. 223, whom B. Luther seems to have followed in his version: and R. Judas, who notes that Joseph was a father or elder in wisdom, but tender in years. Which Beda hints at in Tom. III. of his Works in the book of Hebrew Interpretations of names, if indeed רַךְ is tender from רָכַךְ to soften, to be tender or delicate. Although the interpretation of B. Luther might rather have taken רַךְ for king, just as רַךְ and רֵכָא or רֵיכָא denotes King and Kingdom among the Talmudists, as witnessed by Buxtorf in his Talmudic Lexicon, because Joseph himself was truly the father of the Kingdom, and testified that he was placed as a father to the king in Genesis 45:8, because Pharaoh wished to depend upon his counsel and complied with him in the affairs of the kingdom. And thus Onkelos also rendered it: and they cried before him דֵּין אַבָּא לְמַלְכָּא This is the father of the King, or of the Kingdom. Jonathan seems to join both, while he adds these things to them: בְּשְׁנַיָּא רַב בְּחָכְמְתָא וְרַכִּיךְ, great or learned in wisdom, and tender in years. With which the Targum Hierosolymitanum agrees. Dn. Fesselius prefers this interpretation in Advers. lib. IX. pag. 377, and says that it is similar to the common surname of the Philistine Kings אֲבִימֶלֶךְ that is, father of the King, but it does not seem likely that an Egyptian herald used the Chaldean or Syrian language before the Egyptian people in a public proclamation, as R. Salomo wishes רֶךְ to denote King in the Aramaic language: nor does Mercerus note without reason that violence is done to the expression when one word is torn apart. And therefore the seventy elders, not understanding the foreign word or not knowing how to render it in the Greek language, preferred to omit that little word rather than to use an unsuitable or false one: Symmachus, however, retained the word Ἀβρέχ, which was also done by Arias Montanus and the Genevans. We easily agree, therefore, that it should rather be considered an Egyptian word, which there is no doubt Pharaoh used in a public proclamation; which Moses, therefore, being instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, as is declared in Acts 7:52, wished to retain, as he did some other things, which the Egyptian appellation given to Joseph in verse 46 also testifies. However, that little Egyptian word was well enough known then we observed in the Critico Sacro, page 321. Some think it means MY LORD, but it is more correctly taken as a congratulation. So also Rivet: who wishes it to be the same as LONG LIVE. Drusius renders it BLESS, or LET HIM BE BLESSED. Cf. B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhard's dissertation on this word held at Jena.

Latin:

Verf. 44. ABSQUE TUO IMPERIO NON MOVE- BIT QUISQUAM MANUM.) Id est arma.

AUT PEDEM.) Nemo expeditionem suscipit.

Non ergo placet Grotio Papizanti Latinus. Quem pariter in aliis erratis, iisque non raro gravi- oribus relinquere potius debuisset, quam excusa- re. Quanquam hic non ita improbabilis videri possit translatio Latini, si cum R. Jonathan & R. David. Kimchi אַבְרֵךְ pro הַבְרֵךְ flecte genua dictum credatur, ita solent Ebræi nonnunquam א Cha- racteristicum adhibere: aut cum Aben-Ezra in prima persona accipiatur, quasi quisque è tur- ba clamavit: אַבְרֵךְ genua flectam. Sane Buxtor- fius in radice בָּרַךְ infinitivum Hiphil statuit א ha- bens loco ה ad formam Chaldaicam, ut procla- matum sit per præcones Regios flectenda esse ge- nua. Latinam versionem probant etiam Mer- cerus, Franc. Junius lib. II. Gram. cap. 8. Piscator quæst. 48. in Genes. & B. Johann. Gerhardus. Ad- de quod & Aquila γονατισμόν adgeniculationem interpretatus sit, quod verbum reperitur Genes. 24, 11. Alteram illam ἐτυμολογίαν per divisionem vocis, ut sit Pater tener, Hieronymus ex tradi- tione Ebræorum adduxit, quæst. in Genes. Tom. III. pag. 223. quem sequutus videtur B. Lutherus in versione: & R. Judas qui Josephum Patrem vel senem sapientia, tenerum autem annis fuisse no- tat. Quam innuit Beda Tom. III. Operum in libr. Interpr. Ebr. nomin. siquidem רַךְ sit tener à רָכַךְ mollescere, tenerum vel delicatum esse. Quam- vis B. Lutheri interpretatio potius רַךְ pro rege acceperit, sicut רַךְ & רֵכָא vel רֵיכָא Regem & Regnum apud Talmudistas notat, teste Bux- torfio in Lexic. Talmud. quia vere pater fuit Re- gni, seque in regis patrem positum esse testaba- tur Josephus ipse Genes. 45, 8. quod Pharao ab ipsius consilio pendere voluerit, eique morem gesserit in regni negotiis. Atque ita reddidit eti- am Onkelos: & clamarunt ante eum דֵּין אַבָּא לְמַלְכָּא Hic est pater Regis, sive Regni. Jonathan utrumque conjungere videtur, dum istis hæc ad- dit: בְּשְׁנַיָּא רַב בְּחָכְמְתָא וְרַכִּיךְ, magnus vel doctus quoad sapientiam, & tener quoad annos. Cui consonat Targum Hierosolymitanum. Præ- fert hanc interpretationem Dn. Fesselius in Ad- vers. lib. IX. pag. 377. ac simile dicit esse commu- ne Philistinorum Regum cognomen אֲבִימֶלֶךְ id est, pater Regis, sed Chaldaica aut Syra Lingua præconem Ægyptium coram populo Ægyptio in publica proclamatione usum esse non fit veri- simile, uti R. Salomo lingua Aramæa vult רֶךְ Regem notare: nec abs re monet Mercerus vim dictioni fieri, cum una vox divellitur. Ideoque peregrinam vocem non intelligentes LXX. senio- res aut lingua Græca reddere nescientes, ma- luere illam voculam omittere, quam inconve- nientem aut falsam adhibere: Symmachus vero retinuit vocem Ἀβρέχ, quod etiam ab Aria Montano & Genevensibus factum. Facile er- go assentimur, Ægyptiam potius habendam esse vocem, qua in publica proclamatione Pharao- nem usum fuisse nullum dubium est; quam proin- de Moses in omni Ægyptiorum sapientia instructus, uti Actor. 7, 52. prædicatur, retinere voluit, uti alia nonnulla, quod etiam appellatio Ægyptiaca vers. 46. Josepho data testatur. Satis autem tum nota fuit, etsi hodie nobis ignota sit vocula illa Ægypti- aca. Quod in Critico Sacro observavimus pag. 321. Nonnulli putant significare DOMINUS MEUS, sed rectius pro gratulatione habetur. Ita etiam Ri- vetus: qui vult idem esse quod VIVAT. Drusius reddit BENEDIC, vel BENEDICTUS SIT. Conf. B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhardi Dissert. de hac voce Jenæ habita.

## 41:46
Verse 46. SAVIOR OF THE WORLD.) An Egyptian word here, which is written in Hebrew צפנת פענח, the LXX and Josephus write Ψονθομφανήχ. Now Josephus himself, and Philo, Onkelos, Jonathan, R. Solomon, and R. Levi all interpret it as a discoverer of hidden things. Wherefore one must not depart from this opinion.

The Syrian could be added, who, as noted in the Scholium to the Roman Bible, rendered it as one knowing hidden things: and the three Arabs Ibn-Sina, R. Saadia, as well as the Mauritanian Codex of Erpenius, the Chaldeo-Samaritan translation, and among the Hebrews Baal Thurim, R. Bechai, R. Kimchi, R. Aben-Ezra, and the rest, who unanimously explain it as a revealer of secrets. Diodorus explains it similarly in the Catena Patrum, as does Theodotion as an interpreter of mysteries, Chrysostom, Procopius of Gaza, Vatablus, Montanus, Oleastrius, and others. It is helpful here to hear Athanasius Kircher, an expert in the Egyptian language: In his Coptic Prodromus, he says, They are mistaken who assert that that צפנת פענח is anything other than Egyptian. Which all the Rabbis also concede. We say, therefore, that the word צפנת פענח is the same as the Egyptian or Coptic ΨΟΝΤΟΜ ΠΑΝΗΚ, or ΨΟΝΤΟΜ ΦΑΝΗΚ, of which the former, ΨΟΝΤΟΜ, in the Egyptian language signifies future, and ΠΑΝΗΚ or ΦΑΝΗΚ signifies a prophet or augur, or one who reveals future or hidden things. Now the Coptic or Egyptian Pentateuch, which has been saved from the injury of time and is today preserved in the Vatican Library for the greatest benefit of the Republic of Letters, teaches that this is so, where ΨΟΝΤΟΜ ΠΑΝΗΚ is read for the Hebrew צפנת פענח. Thus also the LXX translated it Ψοντομφανὴχ. For they called all those who predicted the future by this Egyptian word. But the Chronicon Alexandrinum especially asserts that Moses was honored by the Egyptians with these words: 'The Egyptians called Moses, after he had brought the plagues upon them, ψοντουφαχθῆ, which is interpreted as he to whom the future was revealed.' So far Kircher. And thus in this place Philo the Jew also interpreted this word as 'he to whom the future was revealed.' The opinion of the blessed Luther is nearly similar, rendering it 'the secret counselor.' But Grotius departs again from the Vulgate. For whom some support might perhaps have been prepared from Jerome's observation in the Hebrew Traditions on Genesis. Because this name is placed by an Egyptian, it ought to have regard for that language. He interprets it, therefore, in the Egyptian tongue as Savior of the world, because he delivered the world from the imminent destruction of famine. Although it does not appear, in the judgment of men versed in oriental languages, how those words sound as 'Savior of the world.' John Gregory, ch. 16, in Notes and Observations on some Scriptural places: 'Whoever,' he says, 'revealed this gloss to St. Jerome, imposed upon him sufficiently. For R. Moses the Egyptian diligently inquired of the Egyptians themselves, and had this notation of this name, namely, Revealer of Secrets.' The Arabic Pentateuch affirms the same. Thus also the Greek interpreters Theodoret, Zonaras, Philo, etc. Item: it is thought to be an Egyptian word, says Buxtorf. Nay, it is certain from the authority of Philo, Rambam, and others

and the Coptic Pentateuch. The name, says Bonfrerius, ought not to have been imposed by an Egyptian King as anything other than Egyptian. A certain Jew, as the same Gregory notes, inscribed his commentaries on the Pentateuch 'Tsophnath Paaneah'; another calls his book 'Paaneach Razah,' that is, interpreter of secrets. Let someone tell me, says Sixtinus ab Amama in his Censura of the Vulgate translation at this place: 'Which word, the former or the latter, signifies world or Savior? Let him show any trace of these meanings from the Egyptian language: let him bring forward even one conjecture that adds strength to that version, and we will gladly admit it, as it would be more fitting to the mystery of Christ, of whom antiquity has piously handed down that Joseph was in most things a type.' However, Jerome himself confesses that it sounds in Hebrew as 'discoverer of hidden things.' The former word צפנת certainly coincides by reason of its origin with the Hebrew צפן 'he hid'; and it is certain beyond doubt to Sixtinus that the Egyptian, Punic, Arabic, and those other oriental dialects are of the Hebrew mother, and very closely related. But this is not approved by Hottinger in his Exercitationes Anti-Morinianae on the Samaritan Pentateuch: because, as he himself says, there are hardly two or three words that are purely Egyptian which agree in any way with Hebrew, as the Coptic-Arabic Lexicon testifies. But Mr. Augustus Pfeiffer, Professor here of the Holy and Oriental languages, our beloved friend, opposes Hottinger again in a philological dissertation on this name held in the year 1669, having adduced 30 other Egyptian words that agree with Hebrew in both sound and sense. We therefore subscribe here to Kircher, who teaches that this is an Egyptian word: to whom, as he explains it from that language, Sam. Bochart in Phaleg p. 62 and Viccars in Decapla on Psalm 105 rise up. Hottinger, Exerc. Anti-Mor. p. 47. Walton, dissertation on Oriental Languages § 88. Cartwright on Genesis, and others. Yet Mr. Pfeiffer raises not light scruples against the same, especially that the word ψόντομ is corrupt, and that the Hebrew צפנת is wrongly accused of corruption by Kircher p. 130: as also by Henningius of Henningius in his Muhammedan prayer p. 192, and that the letter ψ is not found in any Coptic word, much less explained in lexicons as 'future.' He brings forward another explanation from the Egyptian language: observing that צפנת is the Coptic ψοωνστ, or ψοτωστ, i.e., desired, sought but not found, and פענח is πανηχ, i.e., Doctor, or index, so that Joseph was called the index of desired things, which all were anxiously seeking, but no one could find. Which onomatology he illustrates from Hebrew words, because not a few Coptic words agree with Hebrew, Mr. Pfeiffer, since ψοτωστ & צפנת, as well as פענח & πά- νηχα have a great correspondence. Moreover, the Samaritan Codex wrongly writes the second word with ת as פענת, of which kind of errors in the same Codex Hottinger has noted many.

Latin:

Vers. 46. SALVATOREM MUNDI.) Vocem hic Æ- gyptiam, quæ Hebraice scribitur צפנת פענח LXX. & Jo- sephus scribunt Ψονθομφανήχ. Interpretantur autem Jose- phus idem, & Philo, Onkelos, Jonathan, R. Salomo, R. Levi omnes κρυπτῶν εὑρετὴν. Quare ab hac sententia disceden- dum non est.

Addi poterant Syrus, qui notante Scholio ad Bibl. Rom. reddidit εἰδὼς τὰ κρυπτὰ: & Arabes tres Ibn-Sina, R. Saadiæ, nec-non Codex Erpenii Mauritanus, translatio Chaldæo-Samaritica, & ex Ebræis Baal Thurim, R. Bechai, R. Kimchi, R. Aben-Esra, ac reliqui, qui unanimiter arcanorum revelatorem explicant. Similiter exponit Diodo- rus in Catena Patrum ut & Theodotio τῶν ἀποῤῥή- των ἑρμήνευτὴν, Chrysostomus, Procopius Gazæus, Vatablus, Montanus, Oleastrius, alii. Juvat hîc au- dire Athanasium Kircherum Ægyptiacæ linguæ pe- ritum: Is in Prodromo Coptico, Falluntur, inquit, qui illud צפנת פענח aliud, quam Ægyptiacam esse asse- runt. Quod & Rabbini omnes concedunt. Dicimus itaque vocabulum צפנת פענח idem esse, quod Ægy- ptiacum seu Copticum ΨΟΝΤΟΝ ΠΑΝΗΚ, vel ΨΟΝ- ΤΟΜ ΦΑΝΗΚ, quorum prius ΨΟΝΤΟΜ in Ægy- tica lingua, futura, ΠΑΝΗΚ vel ΦΑΝΗΚ vatem vel Augurem significat, aut EUM, qui futura vel abscondita aperit. Hoc autem ita esse docet Pen- tateuchus Copticus seu Ægyptiacus, qui ab injuria temporum vindicatus, summo literariæ Reipublicæ bono, hodie in Bibliotheca Vaticana asservatur, ubi ΨΟΝΤΟΜ ΠΑΝΗΚ pro Hebræo צפנת פענח legitur. Sic etiam verterunt LXX. Ψοντομφανὴχ. Nam omnes eos, qui futura prædixerunt, Ægyptiaca voce hac ap- pellarunt. Maximè vero Mosen ab Ægyptiis coho- nestatum fuisse asserit Chronicon Alexandrinum his verbis, τὸν Μωῦσιν μετὰ τὸ ἐπαγαγεῖν ἀυτὸν τὰς πληγὰς, οἱ Αἰγύπτιοι ψοντουφαχθῆ προσηγόρευ- σαν, ὃ ἑρμηνέυεται, ᾧ ἀπεκαλύφθη τὸ μέλλον. Ha- ctenus Kircherus. Atque ita hoc loco etiam Philo Judæus interpretatus est hanc vocem, ᾧ ἀνεκαλύ- φθη τὸ μέλλον. Affinis fere est sententia B. Lutheri, reddentis den geheimen Rath. Discedit autem ita Grotius iterum à Vulgata. Cui ab Hieronymi observatione patrocinium forte aliquod paratum erat è tradit. Ebr. in Genes. Quia hoc nomen ab Æ- gyptio ponitur, ipsius linguæ debet habere rationem. Interpretatur ergo sermone Ægyptio Salvator mundi, eo quod orbem terræ ab imminenti famis excidio libe- raverit. Quanquam non appareat, judicio viro- rum in orientalibus linguis versatorum, quomodo voces illæ Salvatorem mundi sonent. Joh. Gregorii c. 16. in Notis & Obs. in aliquot Script. loca: Quicun- que, inquit, hanc glossam S. Hieronymo revelavit, satis illi imposuit. Nam ab Ægyptiis ipsis diligenter quæsi- vit R. Mos. Ægyptius, & hanc hujus nominis notatio- nem habuit, nempe Revelator Secretorum. Idem af- firmat Arabicum Pentateuchum. Sic & Græci Interpp. Theodoretus, Zonarus, Philo &c. Item: putatur esse vocabulum Ægyptiacum, inquit Buxtorff. imo cer- tum est ex autoritate Philonis, Rambam, & aliorum

& Pentateuchi Coptici. Debuit nomen ab Ægyptio Rege, inquit Bonfr. non aliud imponi quam Ægy- ptiacum. Judæus quidam notante eodem Gregor. Commentaria sua in Pentateuchum inscripsit Tsoph- nath Paaneah; alius librum suum vocat Paaneach Razah, id est, interpretem secretorum. Dicat mihi aliquis, ait Sixtinus ab Amama Censur. vulg. vers. ad h. l. Utra vox, prior an posterior mundum vel Salvatorem significet, monstret ullum vestigium harum significationum ex lingua Ægyptiaca: afferat vel unam conjecturam, quæ versioni isti robur addat, & lubenter admittemus, utpote quæ magis factura essent ad mysterium Christi, cujus Josephum in pleris- que fuisse typum, pia tradidit antiquitas. Fatetur autem Hieronymus ipse Ebraice sonare repertorem absconditorum. Prior sane vox צפנת ratione originis coincidit Ebræo צפן occultavit; & certo certius est Sixtino, Ægyptiacam, Punicam, Ara- bicam cæterasque illas orientales Ebrææ matris Dialectos, admodumque affines. Quod vero Hot- tingero in Exercit. Anti-Morin. de Pentateuch. Samarit. non probatur: eo, quod, ut ipse ait, vix duo, triave verba extent pure Ægyptiaca, quæ vel aliqua ratione cum Ebræis conveniant, teste Lexi- co Copto-Arabico. Sed Hottingero rursus ob- viat Dn. Augustus Pfeifferus Lingv. Sanct. & Orien- tal. hîc Professor, amicus noster dilectus in disserta- tione Philologica de hoc nomine An. cIɔ Iɔc LXIX. habita adductis XXX. aliis vocabulis Ægyptiacis cum Ebraicis & sono, & sensu convenientibus. Sub- scribimus itaque hîc Kirchero, vocem Ægyptiacam hanc esse docenti: cui eam ex lingua illa explican- ti assurgunt Sam. Bochartus in Phaleg p. 62. Viccar- sus in Decapl. in Psalm. 105. Hottinger. Exerc. An- ti-Mor. p. 47. Waltonus dissert. de Lingv. Orient. §. 88. Cartwrightus in Genes. & alii. Scrupulos tamen adversus eandem movet Dn. Pfeiffer. non leves, imprimis, quod vox ψόντομ' corrupta sit, & Ebræa צפנת perperam à Kirchero p. 130. corru- ptionis arguatur: ut & ab Henningio Henningii in Muhammed. precante p. 192. quodque litera ψ in nulla dictione Coptica reperiatur, nedum in Lexi- cis per futura exponatur. Qui aliam profert ex- plicationem è lingua Ægyptiaca: observans צפנת esse Copticum ψοωνστ, vel ψοτωστ, i. e. desidera- ta, quæsita nec inventa, & פענח πανηχ, i. e. Doctor, vel index, ut adeo Josephus dictus sit index rerum desideratarum, quas omnes anxie quærebant, sed nemo invenire poterat. Quam ὀνοματολογίαν ex Ebræis vocibus, quia non pauca Coptica cum E- bræis conveniunt, illustrat Dn. Pfeifferus, quando- quidem ψοτωστ & צפנת, nec non פענח & πά- νηχα magnam convenientiam habeant. Cæterum Samaritanus Codex perperam vocem alteram cum ת scribit פענת, cujusmodi plura ejusdem Codicis errata Hottingerus notavit.

## 41:51
Verse 51. MANASSEH.) Which name also came into Africa through the Carthaginians. Appian in the fourth book of the Civil Wars is the witness.

Latin:

Vers. 51. MANASSES.) Quod nomen & in Africam per Pœnos venit. Testis Appianus Civilium quarto.

## 41:54
Verse 54. IN ALL THE WORLD. Egypt lying round about, Syria, Canaan, as in verse 57. ALL THE EARTH, that is, all the inhabitants of the whole earth neighboring them. The Hebrews understand the land of Canaan, Palestine, Arabia, according to Mercer.

Latin:

Vers. 54. IN UNIVERSO ORBE. Ægypto circumjacente, Syria, Cananæa, ut v. 57. UNIVERSA TERRA, id est, omnes incolæ totius terræ illis vicinæ. Terram Canaan, Palæstinam A- rabiam Ebræi intelligunt apud Mercerum.

## 42:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLII. The journey of Joseph's brothers into Egypt, and their for- (tune. Verse 1. HEARING.

IN the Hebrew it is He saw: To see for to hear is frequent among the Hebrews, as also for to touch, for to smell Ex. 5, 21, for to taste Ps. 34, 9. There is therefore no reason why we should say with Lyra that he saw it through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, as the Hebrews wish. THAT CORN WAS SOLD: In

In Hebrew, that which (was) שבר, a breaking, that is, a distribution of bread or grain, Isa. 58:7, Lam. 4:4. The Syriac, Merc[erus], Pagnin[us], and Oleast[er] rendered it 'grain'.

Latin:

CAPUT XLII. Fratrum Josephi in Ægyptum profectio, & for- (tuna. Vers. 1. AUDIENS.

IN Ebræo Vidit: Videre pro audire frequens est Ebræis, ut & pro tangere, pro odorari Ex. 5, 21. pro gustare Ps. 34, 9. Non ergo est, quod cum Lyrano di- camus eum per revelationem S. S. id vidisse, uti E- bræi volunt. QUOD ALIMENTA VENDERENTUR: In

Ebræo quod (esset) שבר fractio, id est, distributio panis vel frumenti Esa. 58, 7. Thren. 4, 4. Syrus, Merc. Pagnin. Oleast. frumentum reddidere.

## 42:8 Addition
On chapter 42:8. HE WAS NOT KNOWN BY THEM. p. 306. a.

And yet Egypt was not far distant from Canaan, and there was frequent commerce between these nations; why then did he not send for 23 years to his parent? This must be attributed to divine providence and an extraordinary instinct, since God willed that the virtue of Jacob and Joseph should thus be rendered more manifest, and that the God-sent dreams should be fulfilled.

Latin:

Ad cap. 42, 8. NON EST COGNITUS AB EIS. p. 306. a.

Atqui Ægyptus non procul distabat a Canaan, & crebra inter hasce gentes erant commercia, cur ergo non misit 23. annis ad parentem? Imputandum id divinæ providentiæ, & instinctui extraordina- rio, quum id voluerit Deus, ut virtus Jacobi & Josephi ita patefactior redderetur sibi, & somnia Θεόπεμπτα implerentur.

## 42:9
Verse 9. YOU ARE SPIES. Thus the word מרגלים is rendered by almost everyone, as if to say, those who migrate from place to place. It is not a lie. For he does not call them so assertively, but tentatively, as Thomas, Bonavent[ura], Cornel[ius], and Tirin[us] note. THE NAKEDNESS OF THE LAND in Hebrew, the nakedness of the land, that is, in what part we are naked and less fortified.

Latin:

Vers. 9. EXPLORATORES ESTIS. Sic vox מרגלים redditur fere ab omnibus, q. d. qui migrant de loco in locum. Non est mendaci- um. Non enim assertive ita eos vocat, sed tentative, ut notat Thomas, Bonavent. Cornel. Tirin. INFIRMI- ORA TERRÆ in Ebr. nuditatem terræ, id est, qua parte nudi, ac minus muniti simus.

## 42:11
Verse 11. WE ARE PEACEABLE.) כנים. The LXX [render it] ἐἰρηνικοὶ, Aquila ὄρθοὶ, Symmachus ἁπλοῖ. The sense is, men of good faith, as appears below 19:31, 34. How untrue this claim of theirs about themselves was, Josephus notes: they knew Emor and Sichem.

In this matter, however, they were upright: for they had not come as spies, as they were accused.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PACIFICI VENIMIS.) כנים LXX. ἐἰρηνικοὶ, Aquila ὄρθοὶ, Symmachus ἁπλοῖ. Sensus est, viri bonæ fidei, ut apparet infra 19, 31. 34. Quam non vera esset hæc ipsorum de se prædicatio, notat Josephus: norant Emor & Sichem.

In hac tamen causa recti erant: non enim vene- rant ceu exploratores, uti arguebantur.

## 42:14
Verse 14. THIS IS. From the fact that you pretend to have another brother, I gather that the rest are also false: because, namely, they had previously said they were only ten, now twelve. Joseph feared, says Lyranus, lest they had plotted evil against him (Benjamin).

Latin:

Vers. 14. HOC EST. Ex eo, quod fingitis vos alium fratrem habere, colligo cætera quoque falsa: quia scil. prius se de- cem tantum fuisse dixerant, jam duodecim. Timebat Joseph, inquit Lyranus, ne machinati fuissent contra eum (Benjaminum) malum.

## 42:15
Verse 15. BY THE LIFE OF PHARAOH.) A most grave oath among the Egyptians, which, if anyone violated, brought with it the penalty of death. Aben-Ezra from Egyptian writers. Thus the Romans swore by the genius of the Prince.

One must not presume such an impious formula of oath regarding the piety of Joseph, as was done by Calvin and Piscator: and therefore it must be said that it is only a serious affirmation, by which we are accustomed to interpose dear pledges to create trust. See Deut. 30:19, 2 Kings 2:6, Isa. 1:2, 2 Cor. 1:23, as if to say, how dear to me is the life of Pharaoh.

Latin:

Vers. 15. PER SALUTEM PHARAONIS.) Gravissimum apud Ægyptios juramentum, si quis violaret pœnam capitis secum trahens. Aben-Esdra ex scriptoribus Ægyptiis. Sic Romani per genium Principis jurabant.

Non præsumere licet de pietate Josephi tam im- pia juramenti formula, ut à Calvino & Piscatore fa- ctum: ideoque dicendum, quod tantum sit seria af- feveratio, qua solemus ad fidem faciendam chara pignora interponere. Vid. Deut. 30, 19. 2. Reg. 2, 6. Esa. 1, 2. 2. Corinth. 1, 23. q. d. quam chara mihi est Pharaonis vita.

## 42:20
Verse 20. THEY DID. That is, they promised to do.

Latin:

Vers. 20. FECERUNT. Id est, facere promiserunt.

## 42:21
Verse 21. WE ARE GUILTY OF THIS. In Hebrew, Truly guilty, Arias-Mont[anus], Oleast[er]; debtors, Syr[iac], Jun[ius], Tremell[ius]. The eyes which guilt closes, punishment opens, says Gregory the Great.

Latin:

Vers. 21. MERITO HÆC PATIMUR. In Ebr. Vere rei Arias - Mont. Oleast. debito- res Syr. Jun. Tremell. Oculos quos culpa claudit, pœ- na aperit, ait Gregor. M.

## 42:22
Verse 22. AND YOU DID NOT HEAR ME.) Thus we also say in Latin: If you would hear me.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET NON AUDISTIS ME.) Sic & Latine di- cimus: Si me audias.

## 42:28
Verse 28. ASTONISHED. In Hebrew, Their heart went out. Cf. Cant. 5:6.

Latin:

Vers. 28. OBSTUPEFACTI. In Ebr. Egressum est cor eorum. Conf. Cant. 5, 6.

## 43:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLIII.

The return, and the departure of Benjamin.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIII.

Reditus, & abdicatio Benjaminis.

## 43:2
Verse 2. RETURN AND BUY. That is, returning, buy. Vatablus notes that two imperatives are used without a conjunction for the sake of greater acceleration.

Latin:

Vers. 2. REVERTIMINI ET EMITE. ID est, revertentes emite. Vatablus duos impe- rativos sine copula ob majorem accelerationem adhiberi notat.

## 43:5
Verse 5. WE WILL NOT GO. That is, we cannot go without the violation of our promise and danger.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NON IBIMUS. Id est, non possumus sine promissi violatione & periculo ire.

## 43:8
Verse 8. THE BOY. That is, the youngest by birth. For he was already 24 years old according to Menochius and Cornelius, indeed 30, being only seven years younger than Joseph according to Piscator, and he already had sons, chapter 46, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PUERUM. Id est, natu minimum. Erat enim jam 24. anno- rum juxta Menoch. & Cornel. imo 30. utpote septen- nio tantum Josepho minor juxta Piscat. & habebat jam filios cap. 46, 10.

## 43:11
Verse 11. OF THE BEST FRUITS OF THE LAND. In Hebrew, of the singing, song, or praise of the land, of those things which are accustomed to be praised.

AND TEREBINTH. Thus with the LXX, Samaritan, and Arabic. The word is ἅπαξ λεγομένη, in Hebrew בטנים. The Chaldean, Münster, and Oleaster explain them as nuts, namely hazelnuts, as Aben-Ezra, R. Nathan, Mordechai, Mercerus, and Pomarius render it. The Tigurine has walnuts, Junius and Tremellius have terebinth nuts. Others from the Hebrew have pistachios. Which interpretation Bochart prefers in Canaan 1, 10. 419.

Latin:

Vers. 11. DE OPTIMIS TERRÆ FRUCTI- BUS. In Ebr. de cantatione, carmine vel laude terræ, de iis, quæ laudari solent.

ET TEREBINTHI. Ita cum LXX. Samar. & Arab. Vox est ἅπαξ λεγομένη, in Ebr. בטנים Nuces exponunt Chald. Münster. Oleast. nimirum avellanas, ut reddunt Aben-Ezr. R. Nathan Mardo- chai, Merc. Pomar. Juglandes habet Tigur. nuces terebinthinas Jun. Tremell. Alii ex Ebr. pistacia. Quam interpretationem præfert Bocart. in Cha- naan 1, 10. 419.

## 43:18
Verse 18. THAT HE MAY CAST UPON US CALUMNY. Thus the LXX and Samaritan. The Chaldean and Samaritan version: that he may lord it over us. Syriac: that he may insult us. Oleaster: that he may roll himself upon us, as if it were like a millstone. Tigurine: that he may cast this upon us.

Latin:

Vers. 18. UT DEVOLVAT IN NOS CA- LUMNIAM. Ita LXX. & Samar. Chald. & vers. Samar. ut do- minetur nobis. Syr. ut insultet nobis. Oleastr. ut de- volvat se super nos q. d. instar molaris lapidis. Ti- gur. ut devolvat hoc in nos.

## 43:29
Verse 29. HE SAW BENJAMIN. Before, incidentally; now, a little more diligently.

Latin:

Vers. 29. VIDIT BENJAMIN. Antea obiter, jam paulo diligentius.

## 43:32
Verse 32. FOR IT IS UNLAWFUL FOR THE EGYPTIANS TO EAT WITH THE HEBREWS, AND THEY CONSIDER SUCH A BANQUET PROFANE.) That which Aben-Ezra thinks, that the Egyptians abstained from the eating of all animals, has no ancient witness. Many teach that they abstained from sheep, except, as Strabo adds, in the Nitriote Nome. But this cause was not grave enough why the Egyptians should shun all sharing of a table with the Hebrews. Therefore, certain special institutions of the Egyptians in the preparation of food stood in the way: on account of which the Egyptians did not use the knife or pot of the Greeks, as Herodotus teaches us. Moreover, those institutions were so proper to the Egyptians that they did not impose the same upon foreigners living among them, such as Joseph was.

Others attribute this to the pride of the Egyptians, because they openly despised the Hebrews on account of circumcision and the pastoral life, Genesis 46, 34. The Targum of Onkelos, however, brought forward the reason that the cattle which the Egyptians worship, the Hebrews eat, Exodus 8, 26. Thus also Lyranus, Tirinus, Menochius. Sheep, goats, and bulls were their deities. Not indeed that these were set before the Hebrews now, but they knew that the Hebrews were accustomed to eat them.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ILLICITUM ENIM EST ÆGYPTIIS CO- MEDERE CUM HEBRÆIS, ET PROFANUM PU- TANT HUJUSCEMODI CONVIVIUM.) Quod Aben- Esdra putat omni animalium esu abstinuisse Ægyptios nul- lum testem habet antiquum. Ab ovillo pecore eos abstinuis- se multi docent: excepto, quod Strabo addit, Nomo Ni- triote. Hæc vero causa non erat satis gravis, cur Ægyptii omnem mensæ communicationem cum Hebræis defugerent. Obstitere ergo specialia quædam Ægyptiorum in cibis paran- dis instituta: ob quæ Ægyptii Græcorum nec cultro nec olla utebantur, ut nos docet Herodotus. Erant autem illa in- stituta ita Ægyptiis propria, ut eadem extraneis apud se ha- bitantibus, qualis erat Josephus, non imponerent.

Alii id tribuunt fastui Ægyptiorum, quod præ se contempserint Ebræos, ob circumcisionem & vitam pastoritiam Genes. 46, 34. Targum tamen Onkelos eam attulit rationem, quod pecus, quod Ægyptii colunt, Ebræi comedant Exod. 8, 26. Sic & Lyr. Ti- rin. Menoch. Oves, hirci, tauri erant eorum numi- na. Non quidem ista nunc Ebræis erant apposita, sed sciebant iis vesci solitos Ebræos.

## 44:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLIV. The dismissal with the cup.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIV. Dimissio cum Scypho.

## 44:2
Verse 2. BUT MY SILVER CUP.) LXX: τὸ κόνδυ, which Athenaeus says is a type of Attalic cup. Aquila: σκύφον. Symmachus: φιάλην. The Scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps narrates something similar done to Aesop: οἱ Δελφοὶ χαλεπήναντες φιάλην ἱερὰν τοῖς Αἰσώπω σκέ- υεσιν ὑπέβαλον. Ὁ μὲν ἔν ἐκ εἰδὼς τὴν εἰς Φωκίδα φέρουσαν ὥρ- μησεν ὁδόν. Οἱ δ᾽ ἐπιδραμόντες καὶ φωράσαντες ἱεροσυλίας αὐ- τῶ κατηγόρει. Just as Joseph tests his brothers here, so does Ulysses with Eumaeus in Homer.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SCYPHUM AUTEM MEUM ARGENTE- UM.) LXX. τὸ κόνδυ, quod poculi Attalici genus esse ait Athenæus. Aquila σκύφον. Symmachus φιάλην. Simile quid Æsopo factum narrat Scholiastes ad Aristophanis Ve- spas : οἱ Δελφοὶ χαλεπήναντες φιάλην ἱερὰν τοῖς Αἰσώπω σκέ- υεσιν ὑπέβαλον. Ὁ μὲν ἔν ἐκ εἰδὼς τὴν εἰς Φωκίδα φέρουσαν ὥρ- μησεν ὁδόν. Οἱ δ᾽ ἐπιδραμόντες καὶ φωράσαντες ἱεροσυλίας αὐ- τῶ κατηγόρει. Sicut hîc Josephus fratres tentat, ita ferme Eumæum Ulyffes apud Homerum.

## 44:5
Ver. 5. HE IS THAT IN WHICH MY LORD DRINKETH, AND IN WHICH HE IS WONT TO DIVINE.) Although the word נחש is taken in the Law concerning superstitious divinations, I would nevertheless believe that it was once a neutral word, and is taken here and below in verse 15 for divinely sent omens, for which Joseph prepared himself by sacrifice: in sacrifices, however, there was the use of a phial, as we have already heard from the Scholiast. The same Scholiast on that passage of Aristophanes' Peace: πρῶτον δέ σοι δῶρον δίδωμι τὴν δ᾽ ἵνα σπέν- δειν ἔχῃς. This is a stage direction. For having said this, he gives him a golden phial. In this sense also are the σπονδεῖα in Ecclesiasticus 50:15, which the writer of 1 Maccabees 1:23 joins with phials, and Philo in his embassy. Josephus often mentions σπονδεῖα, as do Athenaeus, Pollux, and Plutarch in his Cato. Such was the beechwood guttus with which Manius Curius used to sacrifice: Pliny, book XVI. Statius, Thebaid 1: The son of Iasus demanded a bowl from his servants according to custom, with which Danaus and the elder Phoroneus were accustomed to make libations to the gods. You have the use of a mixing bowl in auspices in Homer, and in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VI. See Numbers 15:5 and 10, Judges 9:13, Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 12:2.

This explanation is fetched from too far away: and from where will Grotius make the matter credible, that Joseph used a cup in sacrifices? Truly, it is a very different thing to divine with a cup, and to use a cup in sacrifices, by which preparation is made for omens. The simplest interpretation is that of those who render the text thus: Is not that the cup in which my Lord is wont to drink? And (does he not) himself explore by experiment through it (stolen away, or from the fact that you stole it) what kind of men you are? Which is the explanation of Aben-Ezra, Junius, and Piscator: how this is to be proven, we teach in our Commentary on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IPSE EST IN QUO BIBIT DOMINUS ME- US, ET IN QUO AUGURARI SOLET.) Quanquam vox נחש in lege de superstitiosis augurationibus sumitur, credam tamen olim fuisse vocem mediam, & sumi hîc & infra 15. pro immissis divinitus præsagiis, ad quæ Josephus se sacrificio præparabat: in sacrificiis autem usus phialæ, ut jam ex Scholiaste audivimus. Idem Scholiastes ad illud Pa- cis Aristophanicæ : πρῶτον δέ σοι δῶρον δίδωμι τὴν δ᾽ ἵνα σπέν- δειν ἔχῃς. Τοῦτο παρεπιγραφή. Τοῦτο γὰρ εἰπὼν δίδωσιν ἀυτῷ φιάλην χρυσῆν. In hunc sensum & σπονδεῖα Ecclesiast. 50, 15. quæ cum phialis conjungit scriptor 1. Maccab. 1, 23. & Philo in legatione. Meminere σπονδείs Josephus sæpe, Athenæus quoque, Pollux, & Plutarchus Catone. Tale fuit Manio Cu- rio guttum faginum quo sacrificaret: Plinius libro XVI. Sta- tius 1. Thebaidos: Jasides pateram famulos ex more poposcit, Qua Danaus libare deis seniorque Phoroneus Assueti. Crateris usum in auspiciis apud Homerum habes, & apud Cle- mentem Alexandrinum Strom. VI. Vide Num. 15, 5. & 10. Jud. 9, 13. Josephum Antiquæ historiæ 12, 2.

NImis longe petita hæc declaratio: & unde fi- dem rei faciet Grotius, scypho in sacrificiis usum Josephum? Multum sane diversa sunt scypho augu- rari, & scypho uti in sacrificiis, quibus præparatio fit ad præsagia. Simplicissima est eorum interpre- tatio, qui sic textum reddunt: Nonne ille est Scy- phus, in quo bibere solet Dominus meus? & (annon) ipse experimento explorat per illum (furto ablatum, vel inde quod furto eum abstuleritis) quales nempe vos sitis? Quæ explicatio Aben-Ezra, Junii & Pisca- toris est: quæ quo pacto probanda sit, in Commen- tario ad h. l. docemus.

## 44:16
Ver. 16. WHAT SHALL WE ANSWER?) Sudden calamities take away speech even from the eloquent.

Latin:

Vers. 16. QUID RESPONDEBIMUS?) Subitæ calami- tates etiam disertis sermonem adimunt.

## 44:17
Ver. 17. HE WHO HAS STOLEN THE CUP, HE SHALL BE MY SERVANT.) Servitude is the penalty for theft.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QUI FURATUS EST SCYPHUM, IPSE SIT SERVUS MEUS.) Servitus pœna furti.

## 44:21
Ver. 21. AND I WILL SET MY EYES UPON HIM.) I will favor him.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET PONAM OCULOS MEOS SUPER IL- LUM.) Favebo illi.

## 44:31
Ver. 31. THAT HE IS NOT WITH US.] From the Greek, which added μεθ' ἡμῶν to complete the sense. The Samaritan and the Syriac have 'with me'.

Latin:

Vers. 31. EUM NON ESSE NOBISCUM.] Ex Græco, qui ad sensum explendum μεθ' ἡμῶν addidit. Mecum Sama- ritanus & Syrus.

## 45:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLV. The recognition of Joseph.

Latin:

CAPUT XLV. Agnitio Josephi.

## 45:5
Verse 5. FOR YOUR SALVATION INDEED.) In Hebrew, strictly, for vivification. Which Aquila translates εἰς ζώωσιν. Moreover, to vivify, for the Hebrews, is also to preserve in life.

Others explain it as for the sake of sustenance: because מחיה, as βίος for the Greeks, denotes not only life, but also the sustenance necessary to support life: whence the Targum rendered it for sustenance: See Jud. 6, 4. chap. 17, 10. Ezra 9, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PRO SALUTE ENIM VESTRA.) In Hebræo proprie ad vivificationem. Quod Aquila vertit εἰς ζώωσιν. Vi-vificare autem Hebræis etiam in vita servare est.

Alii exponunt victus causa: quia מחיה ut Græcis βίος non tantum vitem, sed & victum ad vitam sustentandam necessarium notat: unde Targum reddidit ad sustentationem: Vid. Jud. 6,4. cap. 17, 10. Esdr. 9, 8.

## 45:6
Verse 6. NEITHER TO BE PLOWED NOR TO BE REAPED. Except in very few places by the bank of the Nile. In other regions there was sterility on account of the lack of rain.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NEC ARARI NEC METI. Nisi paucissimis locis ad Nili ripam. In aliis re-gionibus sterilitas erat propter pluviæ defectum.

## 45:7
Verse 7. YOU MAY HAVE FOOD TO LIVE. In Hebrew, that I may vivify you with a great escape. By Hebraism. Escape for those who escape. Compare 2 Chronicles 30, 6. Isaiah 10, 20.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ESCAS AD VIVENDUM HABE-RE POSSITIS. In Ebr. ut vivificem vos evasione magna. Per E-braism. Evasio pro iis qui evadunt. Conf. 2. Chronic. 30, 6. Es. 10, 20.

## 45:8
Verse 8. NOT BY YOUR COUNSEL. He does not refer the sin of the brothers to GOD, but his own passage into Egypt, as Estius notes. Compare the commentary on this place.

Latin:

Vers. 8. NON VESTRO CONSILIO. Non refert in DEUM peccatum fratrum, sed transitum suum in Ægyptum, notante Estio. Conf. Comment. in h. l.

## 45:12
Verse 12. MY MOUTH SPEAKS TO YOU.) In the Hebrew language, which the Egyptians did not understand. And so it was explained to the Egyptians that the brothers of Joseph had come. But they were ignorant of what had been committed by the brothers long ago.

Previously Joseph spoke with his brothers through an interpreter, Genesis 42, 13, in the Canaanite language, of which they were knowledgeable: but now he speaks to them in the Hebrew language, which was familiar to them.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OS MEUM LOQUATUR AD VOS.) He-bræo sermone quem Ægyptii non intelligebant. Itaque ex-plicatum Ægyptiis, venisse fratres Josephi. At illi à fratribus olim admissa ignorarunt.

Antea per interpretem loquebatur Josephus cum fratribus Genes. 42, 13. lingua Cananæa, cujus gnari erant illi: jam vero loquitur ipsis Ebræa lin-gua, quæ illis familiaris fuit.

## 46:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVI. The departure of Jacob into Egypt, and his reception.

Verse 1. TO THE GOD OF HIS FATHER ISAAC.) Now dead. See above 35, 29.

Latin:

CAPUT XLVI. Jacobi in Ægyptum profectio, & exceptio.

Vers. 1. DEO PATRIS SUI ISAAC.) Jam mortui. Vi-de supra 35, 29.

## 46:2
Verse 2. HAVING SLAIN VICTIMS THERE TO THE GOD OF HIS FATHER ISAAC, HE HEARD HIM THROUGH A VISION OF THE NIGHT CALLING HIM.) Namely, through the ministry of an Angel.

The text does not teach that the ministry of an angel was employed; nor is there any trace of it, or any sign of it in the whole narrative. Therefore, it should not have been added rashly. But that God spoke immediately, the following clearly teaches:

Latin:

Vers. 2. MACTATIS IBI VICTIMIS DEO PATRIS SUI ISAAC, AUDIVIT EUM PER VISIONEM NO-CTIS VOCANTEM SE.) Nempe per Angeli ministerium.

Adhibitum fuisse ministerium angeli, textus non docet; nec ullum ejus vestigium est, aut vola ulla in tota narratione. Non ergo temere adjici-endum erat. Deum vero immediate loquutum esse, sequentia clare docent:

## 46:3
Ver. 3. GOD SAID TO HIM: I AM THE MOST MIGHTY GOD OF THY FATHER.] In the Hebrew, and he said (the Angel, to wit) I am GOD, the God of thy father. Where Maimonides acknowledges ἕλκυσιν [a drawing/attraction], as if the Angel were saying: God has commanded these things to be said to thee: I am the God of thy father, etc.

But as I have said, Moses made no mention of an Angel: he testified that these things were spoken by God himself, who appeared to Jacob through a vision of the night. Therefore, there is no need at all for that Rabbinical ἑλκύσεως [drawing/stretching], which, if one were allowed to force it upon the text at will, all Theophanies would be snatched away from us, nor would it ever be certainly established whether God spoke, or another sent by God, to whom God had commanded these things to be said? He who appeared here most explicitly testified that he was God, the God of Isaac, and added a promise which no angel could fulfill: Go down into Egypt, for I will make thee a great nation. I will go down with thee thither, and I will bring thee up again. Therefore, God himself appeared, not an angel.

Latin:

Vers. 3. AIT ILLI DEUS: EGO SUM FORTISSIMUS DEUS PATRIS TUI.] In Hebræo, & dixit (Angelus nem-pe) Ego DEUS, Deus Patris tui. Ubi ἕλκυσιν agnoscit Mai-monides, quasi diceret Angelus: Hæc Deus mandavit dicen-da tibi: Ego sum DEus Patris tui &c.

Verum uti dixi, nullam Angeli mentionem fecit Moses: à Deo ipso, qui per visionem noctis ap-paruit Jacobo hæc dicta testatus est. Illa ergo ἑλ-κύσεως Rabbinica nullatenus opus, quam si inge-rere pro lubitu liceat textui, omnes Θεοφανείας eri-pientur nobis, neque unquam certo constabit, lo-quutusne Deus sit, an alius à Deo missus, cui ea dicenda mandavit Deus? Ille qui apparuit hîc, di-sertissime testatus est, se esse DEum, DEum Isaaci, addiditque promissionem, quam præstare angelorum nemo poterat: Descende in Ægyptum, quia in gen-tem magnam faciam te. Ego descendam tecum illuc, & ego inde adducam te revertentem. Deus ergo ipse apparuit, non angelus.

## 46:4
Ver. 4. AND I WILL BRING THEE UP AGAIN.) In thy descendants, who are reckoned as the same with their progenitor.

JOSEPH ALSO SHALL PUT HIS HANDS UPON THINE EYES.) Which the Latins call to close the eyes. Children performed this duty for their dying parents.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET EGO INDE ADDUCAM TE REVER-TENTEM.) In posteris tuis, qui cum progenitore eidem censentur.

JOSEPH QUOQUE PONET MANUS SUAS SUPER OCULOS TUOS.) Quod sugillare oculos dicunt Latini. Id officium parentibus morituris exhibebant liberi.

## 46:8
Ver. 8. WHO ENTERED INTO EGYPT.) So both the Hebrew Codex and the Greeks. But those whom Jacob found in Egypt must also be counted, Joseph and his two sons, and then indeed Jacob himself, the head of the family. It is therefore a συνεκδοχή [synecdoche].

The LXX, which number is expressed in verse 27. But both the version of the LXX and also Luke, or Stephen the proto-martyr in Acts 7:14, create no small difficulty. Who count seventy-five souls. Grotius, on Acts 7, since he could not untie the knot, wished to cut it, and judged that an error had crept not only into the LXX interpreters but also into Luke. It is helpful to cite his words: ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε [in seventy-five souls]. This reading is old enough, as appears from the Syriac, Arabic, and Latin. And hence it happened that, just as in the case of the name Cainan being repeated, the Greek books received a change here also from Christian copyists. For in Genesis 46:27, where seventy souls are named in the Hebrew, as Josephus and the Chaldean interpreters also have it, the Greek texts now have ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε [seventy-five], with certain words added which are missing in the Hebrew and pertain to completing this number; indeed, even in Deuteronomy 10:22. where the same history is related, the same change was made in the Greek books after the times of Jerome. For he clearly signifies in his Questions on Genesis that the number LXX existed in that place. But just as in the name of Cainan, from one poorly written copy of Luke, the error flowed into all that we have, so I believe it happened here also: and that the origin of the error was that after ó, that is, seventy, there was a note ε to signify the fifth part of the section pertaining to Stephen. Thus far Grotius. But we have defended the authenticity of the text of St. Luke expressly in the Critico Sacro, p. 736 et seqq. The opinion of those who do not count the grandsons or great-grandsons in the catalogue of those who entered into Egypt is entirely preferable, and who, with Epiphanius, lib. 1, haer. 8, wish Jacob and his sons, and the wives, to wit, of his sons, and those born from them to be enumerated, just as Matth. proposed it, although doubtfully. Flacius in the gloss of the N.T. on Acts 7, verse 14. Perhaps, however, Stephen counted the wives of the sons of Jacob, whom Moses expressly excludes in Genesis 46, counting only those who were born of Jacob. But here it is said, his whole kindred, not only those born of Jacob, therefore more are counted. We have explained this enumeration at greater length in the l.c. See also Ludov. de Dieu in his animadversions on the Acts of the Apostles, c. 7, 14, who concludes from there that the text of the LXX interpreters is corrupted in Genesis 46, verse 27, and indeed by Christians, who amended the Greek text of Moses so that it could be demonstrated whence Stephen drew these things. In which part we prefer the conjecture of Ludov. Capellus, if this number is not to be ascribed to the LXX interpreters themselves, but crept in from elsewhere, namely that ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε [seventy-five] are enumerated in Genesis 46:27, because an entire little verse was added, which makes the whole catalogue richer by five grandsons of Joseph: But the inserted little verse crept into the text from the margin (when the descendants of Joseph had been added to the margin by someone, and thus it was spread into all the codices of the translation of the LXX). The signs of that corruption are that not only do all the Hebrew copies consistently read 70, and Josephus also read it so in lib. 2, Antiq. c. 4.
