And therefore without doubt it was read so in the LXX codices as well, but also that that interpolated verse varied and was corrupted in the age of Augustine and Jerome, the one counting only four grandsons of Joseph, the other five, according to the faith of the edition of the LXX interpreters, the one making Barath, the other Edam the son of Sutula, as can be seen in the Tradit. Ebr. in Genes. of Jerome and lib. 16 de C. D. of Augustine. Where also a new method of reconciliation of the enumeration of the LXX interpreters, attempted by Augustine, deserves observation, in order to sustain those inserted grandsons of Joseph: namely that the entry of Jacob into Egypt, when Scripture commemorates him among 75 people, was not one day, or one year, but that whole time during which Joseph lived, through whom it was brought about that they entered. However, it is by no means necessary, or even right, with Jerome and Beza (even if some of our own incline that way) to either accuse or excuse St. Luke, or the Protomartyr, because he wished to follow the seventy-man edition, as if it were already published among the Gentiles, even if it is erroneous here. The Holy Spirit does not need our excuse, nor is it an act of piety to impute to the Holy Spirit things that need an excuse, much less to accuse the same of an approved or admitted error, or to say with the English Annotations, 'Stephen was not the amanuensis of the Holy Spirit': but neither were the Apostles themselves always equally illuminated. Indeed, the matter is straightforward in St. Stephen's calculation, provided we pay attention. Naturally, with the children of Judah, Er and Onan, having died, and Joseph with his two sons, and his father Jacob, who is commemorated separately from Stephen, there will remain from the seventy-man number of Moses sixty-four souls, namely eleven brothers, one sister Dinah, and fifty-one sons of the brothers, along with one granddaughter Serah, to whom if we add the surviving wives of the eleven brothers and of the parent, whom Joseph necessarily summoned along with the husbands, and who altogether belonged to τὴν συγγένειαν (the kindred), we will have πᾶσαν τὴν συγγένειαν ἀυτᾶ ἐν ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς (all his kindred in seventy-five souls). See what we have observed in the Commentary on Genesis at this place.

Latin:

Vers. 8. QUI INGRESSI SUNT IN ÆGTPTUM.) Sic & Hebræus Codex & Græci. Sed annumerandi & illi, quos in Ægypto reperit Jacob, Josephus & filii ejus duo, tum vero & ipse Jacobus familiæ caput. Est ergo συνεκδοχή.

LXX. qui numerus verf. 27. expressus est. Sed dif- ficultatem parit non levem tum LXX. viralıs ver- fio, tum etiam Lucas, vel Stephanus proto-mar- tyr Act. 7, 14. Qui animas numerant LXXV. Gro- tius ad Act. VII. cum nodum solvere non posset, se- care voluit, & errorem non modo in LXX. Interpp. sed etiam in Lucam irrepsisse censuit. Verba ejus adducere juvat: ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε. Vetus satis est hæc lectio, ut ex Syro, Arabe, Latino apparet. Et hinc factum, ut sicut in Cainanis nomine repetito, libri Græci etiam hic mutationem reciperent à Christianis exscriptoribus. Nam Genes. 46, 27. ubi in Hebræo septuaginta animæ nominantur, quomodo habet & Josephus & Chaldæi interpretes, Græca nunc habent ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε, additis & vocibus quibus- dam, quæ in Hebræo desunt, & ad explendum hunc nu- merum pertinent; quin & in Deuteronomio 10, 22. ubi eadem refertur historia, eadem mutatio in Græcis li- bris facta post tempora Hieronymi. Nam is eo in lo- co extitisse numerum LXX. aperte significat quæstioni- bus ad Genesin. Sicut autem in nomine Cainani ex uno exemplari Lucæ male scripto, error in omnia fluxit, quæ habemus, ita & hîc factum arbitror: originemque erroris fuisse, quod post ó, id est, septuaginta annota- tum fuit ε ad significandam quintam particulam se- ctionis ad Stephanum pertinentis. Hactenus Gro- tius. Sed vindicavimus τὴν γνησιότητα textus S. Lucæ ex professo in Critico sacro p. 736. seqq. Præ- stat omnino eorum sententia, qui Judæ seu nepo- tes, seu pronepotes Catalogo non annumerant eo- rum, qui in Ægyptum ingressi sunt, & cum Epipha- nio lib. 1. hæref. 8. Jacobum & filios ejus, & uxo- res, scil. filiorum ejus, & prognatos ex illis recen- seri volunt, prout eam, quanquam dubitative pro- posuit Matth. Flacius in glossa N. T. sup. Actor. 7. vers. 14. Forte autem Stephanus annumeravit uxores filiorum Jacob, quas Moses expresse excipit Genes. 46. numerans tantum eos, qui erant ex Jacobo nati. Sed hîc dicitur, totam cognationem suam, non solos ex Jacobo genitos, ideo plures numerantur. Pluribus vero hanc enumerationem exposuimus l. c. Vid. etiam Ludov. de Dieu in animad. ad Actor. Apostol. c. 7, 14. qui inde colligit textum LXX. Interpp. cor- ruptum esse Genes. 46. vers. 27. & quidem à Christia- nis, qui textum Græcum Mosis emendarunt, ut de- monstrari possit, unde hæc Stephanus hauserit. Qua in parte magis placet nobis Ludov. Capelli conje- ctura, si numerus hic adscribendus non sit ipsis LXX. Interpp. sed aliunde irrepserit, quod nempe ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε recenseantur Genes. 46, 27. eo quod additus sit integer versiculus, qui Catalogum totum quinque nepotibus Josephi reddit auctio- rem: Insititius autem versiculus è margine irrepserit in textum (cum à quopiam adscripti fuissent posteri Jose- phi ad marginem, atque ita diffusus sit in omnes trans- lationis τῶν LXX. Codices. Indicia istius corru- ptionis sunt, quod non tantum omnia exemplaria Ebræa constanter legant 70. & sic legerit quoque Josephus l. 2. Antiq. c. 4. Ideoque sine dubio etiam in Codd. LXX. ita lectum fuerit, sed & quod ver- sus ille ἐμβολιμαῖος ætate Augustini & Hieronymi varıarit & corruptus fuerit, isto quatuor tantum nepotes Josephi, hoc quinque recensente è fide editionis LXX Interpp. isto Barath, hoc vero E- dam Sutulæ filium constituente, ut videre est in tradit. Ebr. in Genes. Hieron. & l. 16. de C. D. Augu- stin. Ubi quoque observationem meretur nova conciliationis ratio enumerationis LXX. Interpp. ab August. tentata, ut nepotes istos institios Jose- phi sustinerer: quod nempe introitus Jacob in Æ- gyptum, quando eum in 75. hominibus Scriptu- ra commemorat, non unus dies, vel unus annus, sed totum illud tempus sit, quamdiu vixit Joseph, per quem factum est, ut intrarent. Nullatenus au- tem opus, vel etiam fas est, cum Hieronymo & Beza (etsi illuc etiam nostratium nonnulli propendeant) S. Lucam, vel Protomartyrem seu accusare, seu ex- cusare, quod LXX. viralem editionem, ceu in gen- tibus jam divulgatam, utut hic erroneam, sequi voluerit. Non eget nostra excusatione Spir. S. ne- que pietatis est ea Spir. S. imputare, quæ excusatio- ne egeant, nedum eundem approbati, vel admissi erroris accusare, aut cum Angl. Annotat. dicere, Stephanus non erat amanuensis Spirit. Sancti: Sed nec ipsi Apostoli æqualiter semper illuminati erant. Imo res expedita est in S. Stephani calculo, modo ani- mum advertamus. Nimirum separatis liberis Ju- dæ defunctis Ger & Onan, & Josepho, cum duobus filiis, ac Patre Jacobo, qui seorsim à Stephano com- memoratus est, supererunt ex Septuagenario Mosis numero sexaginta quatuor animæ, nempe undecim fratres, una soror Dina, & quinquaginta, & unus fratrum filii, cum nepte una Serah, quibus si ad- jungantur undecim fratrum & Parentis superstites uxores, quas necessario Josephus una cum maritis accersivit, quæque omnino ad τὴν συγγένειαν perti- nebant, habebimus πᾶσαν τὴν συγγένειαν ἀυτᾶ ἐν ἑϐδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς. Vid. quæ in Commen- tario in Genesin ad h. l. observavimus.

## 46:21
Verse 21. AND ECHI, AND ROS, AND MOPHIM.) In Hebrew אחי וראש מפים. An old error in the books, as appears from the Greek. But if anyone compares the passage Num. 26:38 and 39, he will see that it was written thus long ago אחירם ושפופם. Such slips are easy in proper names.

He very badly attributes an error here to the Hebrew, and to the Latin Vulgate text canonized by the Roman Church, which agrees with it. Nor does it appear from the Greek translation, whether I consult the Basel edition published in the year 1545, or that which was published in London according to the Vatican exemplar. For those three Hebrew names have equally ἠ ἀγχὶς, ἠ ῥὼς ἠ μαμφὶμ. Even if the passage Num. 26:38 and 39 omits the middle one, it is not therefore to be expunged in Genesis. It also omits other sons of Benjamin, and indeed of other children of Jacob: because it lists only the surviving families. Two other names are pronounced a little differently. But that happens, without error of Scripture, both in other sons of Benjamin (Levit. 9:1 seqq.) and in other names: since proper names are often slightly changed by the transposition or variation of letters, through departures or translations, or for other causes, and not a few are read as πολυώνυμοι (having many names). Some think there are two other sons of Benjamin who are mentioned in Num. 26; but it is better to say that Acher is the same who is called Echi, and in 1 Chron. 8:1 is called Achram. And that Schephupham is the one who is called Muppim in this place. Moreover, that three names must be retained here entirely according to the Hebrew reading, Grotius could have learned from the number of Rachel's children. Of whom 14 are counted. But if those three are contracted into two, there will be only 13. Add that R. Solomon Jarchi in his Commentary on Gen. 43:30 lists and explains all those names which are had in this place from Maschechet Socha. Joseph asked Benjamin, 'Do you have a brother by the same mother?' He answered himself: 'I did have a brother, but I do not know where he is now.' 'Do you have sons?' He answered him, 'I have ten.' He said to him, 'And what are their names?' He answered him, 'Bela and Becher etc.' He said to him, 'What is the condition of these names?' He answered him, 'All refer to the name of my brother and to the evils that happened to him. Bela, because he was swallowed up among the peoples. Becher, because he is the firstborn of my mother. Asbel, because God holds him captive; Gera, because he dwells among strangers. Naaman, because he was excellently beautiful. Echi and Rosch, because he was my brother and my head. Muppim, because he learned from the mouth of my Father. And Chuppim, because he did not see my bridal chamber, nor I his. And Ard, because he descended among the peoples or nations quickly.' Having heard these things, the compassions of Joseph grew warm. Nor do those two names in 1 Chron. 9 disagree badly. For to the name Achi is added רם (high): so that it is 'my brother is high': and because Muppim learned from the mouth of my Father, Schophupham is explained from this as 'highly excellent,' from שפף, which in Niphal is to be eminent, it resulted.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET ECHI, ET ROS, ET MOPHIM.) In He- bræo אחי וראש מפים. Vetus in libris error, ut ex Græco apparet. At si quis conferat locum Num. 26, 38. & 39. videbit sic scriptum olim fuisse אחירם ושפופם. Faciles tales la- psus in nominibus propriis.

Pessime hic Errorem Ebræo, & qui illi conso- nat, Vulgato Latino ab Ecclesia Romana canoni- zato textui affricat. Nec è Græca translatione is apparet, sive Basiliensem editionem de anno clɔ lɔ XLV. editam, seu quæ juxta exemplar Vati- canum Romæ editum prodiit Londini, consulam. Ha- bent enim pariter ista tria Ebræa nomina ἠ ἀγχὶς, ἠ ῥὼς ἠ μαμφὶμ. Etsi locus Num. 26, 38. & 39. me- dium omittat, non tamen ideo in Genesi id expun- gendum. Omittit & alios Benjaminis filios, nec non aliorum liberorum Jacobi: quia recenset tantum familias superstites. Duo alia nomina paulo aliter efferuntur. Sed id, sine Scripturæ errore, cum in filiis aliis Benjamin Levit. 9, 1. seqq. tum in nomi- nibus aliis contingit: quum sæpe nomina propria parum immutentur literarum transpositione aut va- riatione, per profectiones aut translationes, aut ob alias causas, nec pauci leguntur πολυώνυμοι. Non- nulli duos alios filios Benjaminis esse, qui Num. 26. memorantur, censent; Sed præstat dicere, Ache- ram esse eundem, qui Echi dicitur, & Paral. 8. v. 1. Achram nuncupatur. Schephupham vero eum es- se, qui Muppim hoc loco vocatur. Quod autem hic omnino juxta lectionem Ebræam tria nomina retinenda sint, è numero liberorum Rachel, didi- cisse poterat Grotius. Quorum 14. numerantur. Si vero illa tria in duo contrahantur, erunt tan- tum 13. Adde, quod R. Salomo Jarchi in Commen- tar. ad Genes. 43, 30. omnia illa nomina recenseat & explicet, quæ hoc loco habentur ex Maschechet Socha. Interrogavit Josephus Benjaminum, estne ti- bi frater ex matre? Respondit ipse: Fratrem quidem habui, sed nescio, ubi nunc sit. Suntne tibi filii? Re- spondit ei, sunt mihi decem. Dixit ei, & quænam sunt eorum nomina? Respondit ei, Bela & Becher &c. dixit ei, quæ conditio horum nominum? Respon- dit ei, omnia referuntur ad nomen fratris mei & ad mala, quæ ipsi evenerunt. Bela, quia absorptus is est inter populos. Becher, quia ipse est primogenitus ma- tris meæ. Acbeel, quia captivum ipsum detinet De- us; Gera, quia commoratur inter peregrinos. Naa- man, quia pulcher erat excellenter. Echi & Rosch, quia frater meus & caput meum erat. Muppim, quia ex ore Patris mei discebat. Et Chuppim, quia nec vi- dit ipse thalamum meum, nec ego ipsius. Et Ard, quia descendit inter populos seu gentes confestim. His auditis incaluerunt miserationes ejus Josephi. Nec male conveniunt illa duo nomina 1. Par. 9. Ad no- men Achi enim additur רם excelsus: ut sit frater meus excelsus: & quia Muppim ex ore Patris mei di- scebat, explicatur hinc Schophupham excellens maxi- mè, à שפף, quod in Niphal est eminere, evasit.

## 46:34
Verse 34. FOR THE EGYPTIANS DETEST ALL SHEPHERDS OF SHEEP.) Naturally because shepherds took the life of the flock and ate the meat. See what we have below concerning sacrifices at Exod. 8:26. From this diversity of life between the Shepherds, who were called Hycsos, and other Egyptians, you may learn from Manetho in Josephus that very serious wars once existed between them. This, therefore, is the cause of the hatred, such as that in Juvenal's time between Coptos and Tentyra. Concerning the Jews, Tacitus, where he opposes their institutions to the Egyptians. A ram having been slaughtered as if in insult to Ammon. An ox is also sacrificed, which the Egyptians worship as Apis. Manetho concerning Moses, whom he also calls Osarsiph: 'ὁ δὲ πρῶτον μὲν αὐτοῖς νόμον ἔθετο μήτε τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ θεμιτευομένων ζῴων ἀπέχεσθαι μηδενός' (but he first set a law for them neither to abstain from any of the animals worshipped in Egypt). I am not surprised that abstinence from eating the animals of the field was ancient. Yet I find no certain traces of idolatry as yet in Joseph's century, in Egypt at least. That disease began from the Syrians, and gradually propagated itself. But the Egyptians also had those cattle as more superstitious, but for the sake of wool and milk, see below 47:6.

Latin:

Vers. 34. QUIA DETESTANTUR ÆGYPTII OMNES PASTORES OVIUM.) Nimirum quia pastores pecori vi- tam adimebant, & carne vescebantur. Vide quæ de sacrifi- ciis infra Exod. 8, 26. Ex hac diversitate vitæ inter Pastores, qui Hycsos dicebantur, & Ægyptios alios, gravissima olim bella inter eos extitisse ex Manethone apud Josephum discas. Hæc ergo odii causa, qualis Juvenalis tempore inter Copton & Tentyram. De Judæis Tacitus, ubi ipsorum instituta Ægy- ptiis opponit. Cæso ariete velut in contumeliam Ammonis. Bos quoque immolatur, quem Ægyptii Apim colunt. Mane- thon de Mose, quem & Osarsiphum vocat: ὁ δὲ πρῶτον μὲν αὐτοῖς νόμον ἔθετο μήτε τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ θεμιτευομένων ζῴων ἀπέχεσθαι μηδενός. Abstinentiam ab esu animalium ruris veterem fuisse non miror. Idololatriæ tamen nulla adhuc Josephi seculo, in Ægypto quidem, certa vestigia reperio. A Syris cœpit is morbus, paulatimque propagatus est. Pecora autem & Ægyptii illi superstitiosiores habebant, sed lanæ & la- ctis causa infra 47, 6.

## 47:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVII. The grant of the land of Goshen. The famine worsening. Joseph adjured concerning the burial of Jacob in Canaan.

Latin:

CAPUT XLVII. Terræ Gosen concessio. Fames ingravescens. Jo- sephus de sepultura Jacobi in Canaan adju- ratus.

## 47:2
Verse 2. ALSO THE EXTREME OF HIS BROTHERS.) The Greeks are better here: ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἀδελφῶν αὐτῦ παρέλαβε (and from his brothers he took). For the Hebrew מקצה is often translated as 'part'.

This observation does not displease. Compare our Commentary on this place.

Latin:

Vers. 2. EXTREMOS QUOQUE FRATRUM SUO- RUM.) Melius Græci hîc: ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἀδελφῶν αὐτῦ πα- ρέλαβε. Nam מקצה Hebræum sæpe μέρος vertitur.

Non displicet hæc observatio. Conf. Commen- tarius Noster ad h. l.

## 47:6
Verse 6. GIVE THEM THE LAND OF GOSHEN.) Does that in Manetho's history pertain here: 'τὴν τότε τῶν ποιμένων ἐρημωθεῖσαν Ἄβαριν συνεχώρησεν' (he granted Avaris, which had been deserted by the shepherds at that time)?

INDUSTRIOUS MEN.

In Hebrew, men of virtue or strength, both of body and of mind, skilled in the tending of cattle.

MASTERS OF CATTLE.

In Hebrew, princes of the cattle, or of the livestock business, over that which is mine, or over those who are mine.

Latin:

Vers. 6. TRADE EIS TERRAM GESSEN.) An huc pertinet illud in Manethonis historia: τὴν τότε τῶν ποιμένων ἐρημωθεῖσαν Ἄβαριν συνεχώρησεν.

VIROS INDUSTRIOS.

In Ebr. viros virtutis vel roboris tum corporis tum animi, peritos pecoris alendi.

MAGISTROS PECORUM.

In Ebr. principes pecoris, vel rei pecuariæ, super quod mihi, vel super illos, qui mihi sunt.

## 47:12
Verse 12. PROVIDING FOOD TO EACH.) The Greeks [say] σῖτον κατὰ σῶμα. In the Hebrew, to the mouth of the little one, that is, he gave them food according to the number of children they had.

We do not disapprove of this explanation. Let those things, however, which we said in the Commentary on this passage be compared here.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PRÆBENS CIBARIA SINGULIS.) Græci σῖτον κατὰ σῶμα. In Hebræo, ad os parvuli, id est, alimen- ta illis dedit pro numero liberûm quos habebant.

Non improbamus hanc explicationem. Con- ferantur tamen hîc, quæ diximus in Commentar. ad h. l.

## 47:21
Verse 21. AND HE SUBJECTED IT TO PHARAOH, AND ALL HIS PEOPLES FROM THE FARTHEST BORDERS OF EGYPT EVEN TO ITS EXTREME ENDS.) There is more in the Hebrew: he moved them into the cities, namely, he transferred them far from their native soil, and separated them from their kin and acquaintances, so that he might remove the material for seditions, which had been most grave; and might abolish the memory of their old dominion, and the pain from that memory. In Africa, the Vandal women stirred up a most atrocious sedition because they had been permitted to remain on the lands whose right they had lost in war.

This transfer was also a public testimony of the sale of the fields: for the exchange of the tenant farmers is a sign of a lease, and excludes the opinion of proprietary possession.

Latin:

Vers. 21. SUBJECITQUE EAM PHARAONI, ET CUNCTOS POPULOS EJUS A NOVISSIMIS TER- MINIS ÆGYPTI USQUE AD EXTREMOS FINES E- JUS.) Plus est in Hebræo: transmovit eos in urbes, nem- pe longe à natali solo eos transtulit, ac inter se cognatos no- tosque segregavit, ut seditionibus, quæ gravissimæ fuerant, materiam subtraheret: veterisque dominii memoriam, & ex memoria dolorem aboleret. In Africa Vandalorum feminas atrocissimam seditionem commoverunt, quod hærere permis- sæ essent in fundis, quorum jus bello amiserant.

Erat etiam hæc translatio publicum testimoni- um venditionis agrorum: nam permutatio colo- norum signum est locationis, & excludit proprie- tariæ possessionis opinionem.

## 47:26
Verse 26. THE FIFTH PART IS PAID.) This custom remained for a very long time. See Josephus.

EXCEPT FOR THE PRIESTLY LAND, WHICH WAS FREE FROM THIS CONDITION.) From the condition of tribute, or emphyteutic [rent]. Diodorus Siculus mentions this immunity. Under the name of priests, however, were included all who devoted themselves to astrology, medicine, the knowledge of natural things, surveying, arithmetic, and history. See the same Diodorus and Clement of Alexandria.

Others understand political prefects and court ministers. There is, however, no reason why the common interpretation should not be retained: with which the Chaldean agrees, understanding hierophants. For although the priests were idolatrous in Egypt, immunity was nevertheless given to them by Pharaoh: which Joseph granted in his name; who, however, was doing this so that he might lead them to the true religion, and thus he provided for them with the hope of conversion Pf. 105, 12.

among all evils there are also spiritual ones, which are the most significant. Then an equal conjunction with GOD, as also divine blessing, attributed to both God and an angel in one and the same word: Never, says Athanasius, orat. 4. contr. Arian., would anyone pray to receive something from God and from angels, or from other created things: nor did anyone conceive this form of words: May God and the Angel give to you. Cyril, lib. 3. thesaur. c. 1. If, he says, the HERETICS confess that Jacob was adorned with a prophetic spirit and do not deny that Jacob was a holy man, by what grace do they contend that he erred so much that he joined an angel with God, and thought that he could bless together with God? Do not, I pray, so disparage a holy man, etc. Cyril therefore makes the Grotian explanation heretical. Nor is there any doubt that by הַמַּלְאָךְ Hajediah that Angel is pointedly demonstrated, who was often mentioned before in that history, and appeared to Jacob. But that he was not a created angel, but uncreated, we have pointed out several times, and it is manifest from Gen. 31, 11. chap. 32, 14. seqq. c. 35, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 26. QUINTA PARS SOLVITUR.) Mansit hic mos diutissime. Vide Josephum.

ABSQUE TERRA SACERDOTALI, QUÆ LIBERA AB HAC CONDITIONE FUIT.) A conditione vecti- gali, sive emphyteutica. Meminit ejus immunitatis Dio- dorus Siculus. Sacerdotum autem nomine comprehende- bantur omnes qui Astrologiæ, Medicinæ, rerum naturali- um cognitioni, mensoriæ, numerariæ, historiis operam dabant. Vide eundem Diodorum & Clementem Alexan- drinum.

Alii præfectos politicos, & ministros aulicos intel- ligunt. Non autem causa est, cur non retineatur vulgata interpretatio: cui consonat Chald. hiero- phantas intelligens. Etsi enim Sacerdotes idolo- latræ erant in Ægypto, immunitas tamen ipsis data à Pharaone: quam ejus nomine Josephus concessit: qui vero id agebat, ut eos ad veram religionem per- duceret, adeoque conversionis spe illis prospexit Pf. 105, 12.

inter mala cuncta etiam spiritualia sunt, quæ potis- sima. Tum æqualis conjunctio cum DEO, ut & be- nedictio divina, uno eodemque verbo & Deo & an- gelo tributa: Nunquam, inquit Athanas. orat. 4. contr. Arian. quispiam precaretur accipere aliquid à Deo & ab angelis, aut ab aliis rebus creatis: nec quisquam hanc verborum formam concepit: Det tibi Deus & Angelus. Cyrillus lib. 3. thesaur. c. 1. Si Pro- phetico, inquit, spiritu decoratum Jacobum HÆRE- TICI fatentur & sanctum Jacob fuisse virum non ne- gant, cujus gratia ita ipsum errasse contendunt, ut Angelum cum Deo conjunxerit, & una cum Deo be- nedicere posse putaverit? Nolite, quæso, sanctum vi- rum ita vituperare, &c. Hæreticam ergo explicatio- nem Grotianam facit Cyrillus. Neque dubium est, per הַמַּלְאָךְ Hajediah Angelum illum signanter demon- strari, qui sæpe in historia illa ante commemora- tus fuit, Jacoboque apparuit. Quem vero non fu- isse creatum angelum, sed increatum, aliquoties monuimus, & è Genes. 31, 11. cap. 32, 14. seqq. c. 35, 1. manifestum est.

## 47:31
Vers. 31. ISRAEL WORSHIPPED GOD TURNING TO THE HEAD OF THE BED.] That is, prostrate upon the bed, he leaned upon his pillow to give thanks to GOD for the burial promised to him. Thus also David is read to have worshipped in his bed 1 Kings 1, 47, where God is similarly understood, which the interpreter added here to the Hebrew.

Some understand a civil adoration made in honor of Joseph, as being a prince: by which Joseph's dream was completed. Fagius in Collat. Paraphras. & Drusius.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ADORAVIT ISRAEL DEUM CONVERSUS AD LECTULI CAPUT.] Id est, super lectum prostratus cervicali suo incubuit ad agendas DEO gratias pro sepultu- ra sibi promissa. Sic & David legitur adorasse in lecto suo 1. Reg. 1, 47. ubi similiter subauditur Deum, quod hic inter- pres ad Hebræum addidit.

Nonnulli adorationem civilem intelligunt in honorem Josephi, utpote principis factam: qua completum Josephi somnium. Fagius in Collat. Paraphras. & Drusius.

## 48:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVIII. The blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIIX. Benedictio Ephraim & Manassis.

## 48:2
Vers. 2. WHO STRENGTHENED HIMSELF AND SAT UPON THE BED.] The Hebrew word הַמִּטָּה, because of the diversity of vowel points, which formerly were not written and were often and variously accustomed to be pronounced, can signify a bed just as well as a staff, with which sick people are accustomed to support themselves when they begin to grow weary of lying down: and thus the writer to the Hebrews 11, 21 took it.

Although it may be conceded that the LXX used a copy destitute of points, it is not to be concluded from that, however, that there were as yet no vowels, concerning which we have dealt in the Critico sacro p. 329. Here, however, the LXX read no differently than as the Hebrew points now have it: καὶ ἐνισχύσας Ἰσραὴλ ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τὴν κλίνην. Nor did the Apostle look to this place in Heb. 11, 21, to which nothing twin is held in the words: But to the preceding chapter, where in the last verse the very words brought by the Apostle are read, καὶ προσεκύνησεν Ἰσραὴλ ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ, the Vulgate has, Israel worshipped God turning to the head of the bed. For the Apostle brought the version of the LXX Interpreters; because it was then in use, not because he judged that reading to be preferred. Which even Grotius does not prefer, however not sufficiently fair to the original Code, when he sees the Vulgate agree there. But the matter as far as the Apostle's purpose is concerned comes to the same thing: therefore he did not wish to depart from the received interpretation. By faith Jacob dying blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshipped (at, which preposition the Vulgate badly omits, whence the occasion for iconolaters to err) the top of his rod. He commemorates two acts of faith, the blessing of the sons of Joseph described in chap. 48: and the adoration of GOD, by which, bowed over the top of the staff with which he supported himself, he gave thanks to God for the obtained promise of burial in the land of Canaan, and prayed to God that the promise might be brought into effect.

Wherefore it is necessary to confess with Athanasius, Cyril, Chrysost. Hom. 66. in Genes., Novatian. l. de Trin. cap. 26. 27., Procopius of Gaza in h. l., and others, that the angel of the new covenant, the Son of God, is indicated here, who alone is joined with the Father and the Holy Spirit in that manner in blessings, and is our only redeemer, who redeemed us from ALL EVILS, גֹּאֵל, who by right of consanguinity claimed us into his power, and vindicated us for himself. Which name is peculiarly proper to him. As Grotius acknowledges here. That the Messiah is called גֹּאֵל in Isa. 59, 19, although he rescinds this explanation in the annotations to that place, and contends that the discourse there is about Cyrus. The Angel of the face of the Lord, who is called Israel גָּאַל, is the Son of GOD Isa. 64, v. 9. We teach in Tom. 3 of the System of Theology that the Holy Trinity is invoked in this Patriarchal blessing. Let the Commentary of our blessed Luther on this place be compared. And those of ours who have disputed more prolixly against the Socinian-Papistic gloss: Dn. D. Walther in the sponge, Dn. D. Klos de Angelolat. and against Calixtus, (who blows the same pipes here,) Dn. D. Dorscheus, in Judic. Argentor. de disput. Laterm. and his Apology. What Grotius observes about the word גֹּאֵל being said in this way in Hebrew laws, that he who by right of kinship marries someone and thus frees her from the reproaches and inconveniences of celibacy, is a particular case, from Deut. 25. For it is known that he is also called גֹּאֵל according to the law who by right of kinship redeems an heir, Lev. 25, and also he who by the same right of a kinsman avenges a death, Num. 35. All of which agree excellently with the Son of GOD, who, having become our brother, redeemed us for himself as a Bride and spouse, asserted the heavenly inheritance for us, and vindicated us against the infernal murderer, and freed us from his power by right of kinship Heb. 2, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUI CONFORTATUS SEDIT IN LECTU- LO.] Hebræa vox הַמִּטָּה pro diversitate punctorum vo- calium, quæ olim nulla scribi, sæpe & varie pronunciari so- lebant, tam lectum potest significare, quam baculum, quali se sustentare solent ægroti, ubi eos cubandi cœpit tædium: & sic sumsit Scriptor ad Hebr. 11, 21.

Quamvis concedi possit, exemplari usos LXX. punctis destituto, non tamen inde colligen- dum, tum nullas adhuc vocales fuisse, quo de in Critico sacro egimus p. 329. Hic vero non aliter le- gere LXX. quam prouti nunc Ebræa puncta ha- bent: καὶ ἐνισχύσας Ἰσραὴλ ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τὴν κλί- νην. Neque ad hunc locum respexit Apostolus Ebr. 11, 21. cui nihil geminum in verbis habetur: Sed ad caput præcedens, quo vers. ult. ipsa verba Aposto- lo adducta leguntur, καὶ προσεκύνησεν Ἰσραὴλ ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆ ῥαβδῒ αὐτᾶ, Vulgatus habet, adoravit Israel DEum conversus ad lectuli caput. Adduxit enim LXX. Interpp. versionem Apostolus; quod ea tum usitata esset, non quod lectionem illam præ- ferendam judicaret. Quam nec Grotius præfert, utut non satis æquus Codici originali, quum con- sonare videat ibi Vulgatam. Res autem quantum ad institutum Apostoli eodem redit: ideo noluit dis- cedere à recepta interpretatione. Fide Jacob mo- riens singulos filiorum Joseph benedixit, & adoravit (ad, quam præpositionem male omittit Vulgatus, unde iconolatris errandi occasio) fastigium virgæ ejus. Commemorat duos fidei actus, benedictio- nem filiorum Josephi cap. 48. descriptam: & adora- tionem DEI, qua super fastigium baculi, quo se su- stentabat, incurvatus Deo gratias egit, pro obtenta promissione sepulturæ in terra Canaan, oravitque Deum, ut promissio in effectum deducatur.

Quapropter necessum est, fateri cum Athana- sio, Cyrillo, Chrysost. Hom. 66. in Genes. Nova- tian. l. de Trin. cap. 26. 27. Procopio Gazæo in h. l. & aliis, angelum fœderis novi Filium Dei hic indigi- tari, qui solus cum Patre & S. S. ea ratione conjun- gitur in benedictionibus, & unicus est redemtor noster, qui nos ab OMNIBUS MALIS redemit, גֹּאֵל qui jure consanguinitatis nos in potestatem suam asseruit, sibiq; vindicavit. Quod nomen ipsi pecu- liariter proprium est. Uti Grotius hic agnoscit. Messiam גֹאֵל dici Efa. 59, 19. quamvis annot. ad lo- cum istum hanc explicationem rescindat, & de Cyro ibi sermonem esse contendat. Angelus faciei Domini, qui Israel גָּאַל vocatur Filius DEI Ef. 64. v. 9. Benedictione hac Patriarchali S. S. Trinitatem invocatam esse, Tom. 3. Systematis Theol. doce- mus. Conferatur B. Lutheri nostri Comment. in h. l. Et qui prolixius adversus glossam Sociniano-Pa- pisticam disputarunt è nostris Dn. D. Waltherus in spongia, Dn. D. Klos de Angelolat. & adversus Ca- lixtum, (qui easdem tibias hic inflat,) Dn. D. Dor- scheus, in Judic. Argentor. de disput. Laterm. & A- pologia ejusdem. Quod observat Grotius de voce גֹאֵל ita in Ebræis legibus dici, qui jure propinquitatis aliquam ducit in uxorem & sic eam ab opprobriis, in- commodisque cælibatus liberat, particulare est, è Deu- ter. 25. Notum enim, quod גֹּאֵל etiam dicatur jux- ta legem, qui jure propinquitatis hæredem redimit, Lev. 25. nec non qui eodem jure cognati mortem vin- dicat Num. 35. Quæ omnia Filio DEI egregie con- veniunt, qui frater noster factus, nos sibi redemit in Sponsam & conjugem, hæreditatem cœlestem nobis asseruit, & adversus infernalem homicidam nos vindicavit, eque potestate ejus jure propin- quitatis nos liberavit Ebr. 2, 14.

## 48:16
Vers. 16. THE ANGEL, WHO DELIVERED ME FROM ALL EVILS.] LXX. ὁ ῥυόμενός με ἐκ πάντων τῶν κακῶν. Thus the Messiah is called גֹּאֵל in Isaiah 59, 19. Some have translated here ὁ ἀγχιστεύς, because in Hebrew laws he is called גֹּאֵל who by right of kinship marries someone, and thus frees her from the reproaches and inconveniences of celibacy. After GOD he names the Angel, as a minister of GOD.

Vers. eod. LET MY NAME BE INVOKED UPON THEM.] That is, although they are grandsons, they shall be called my sons by right of adoption, and just as sons they shall bear individual portions: they shall succeed by heads, not by the name of the stock.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ANGELUS, QUI ERUIT ME DE CUNCTIS MALIS.] LXX. ὁ ῥυόμενός με ἐκ πάντων τῶν κακῶν. Sic Messias גֹּאֵל dicitur Esaia 59, 19. Quidam verterunt hic ὁ ἀγχιςεύς, quia גֹּאֵל in legibus Hebræis is dicitur, qui jure propinquitatis aliquam ducit in uxorem, & sic eam ab opprobriis incommodisque cælibatus liberat. Post DEUM Angelum nominat, ut DEI ministrum.

Vers. eod. INVOCETUR SUPER EOS NOMEN ME- UM.] Id est, quanquam nepotes sunt, vocabuntur filii mei adoptionis jure,ac perinde ut filii singulas partes ferent: in ca- pita succedent, non stirpis nomine.

## 48:19
Vers. 19. HIS YOUNGER BROTHER SHALL BE GREATER THAN HE.] Because of the kingdom of the ten tribes, which began in the posterity of Ephraim and remained for a long time. See 1 Kings 11:26. Therefore the Prophets call that kingdom by the name of Ephraim.

This gloss is clearly Socinian, Arian, and Papistic. For Socinians understand a ministering Angel, because they deny the προϋπαρξιν of the Son of God before his temporal birth. Arians, because they deny the Deity of the same. Papists, because they assert the invocation of Angels, as has been done by Tostatus, Lorinus, Becanus, Bailius, Gretserus, and others. But that a ministering angel cannot be understood, many things teach; First, the description, 'who delivers me from all evils.' Which suits no single Angel, nor indeed all of them together; because

Latin:

Vers. 19. FRATER EJUS MINOR MAJOR ERIT EO.] Propter regnum decem tribuum, quod in Ephraimi posteritate cœptum, diuque consedit. Vide 1. Reg. 11, 26. Ita- que Prophetæ illud regnum Ephraimi nomine appellant.

Glossa hæc plane Sociniana est, Ariana, atque Papistica. Socinistæ enim Angelum ministrum in- telligunt, quia προϋπαρξιν Filii Dei ante nativita- tem temporalem inficiantur. Ariani, quia ne- gant Deitatem ejusdem. Papistæ, quia Angelorum invocationem adstruunt, ut à Toftato, Lorino, Beca- no, Bailio, Gretsero, aliis factum. At angelum mi- nistrum intelligi non posse, multa docent; Primum descriptio, qui eruit me de cunctis malis. Quod nulli uni Angelo, ac ne universis quidem convenit; quia

## 48:20
Vers. 20. MAY GOD MAKE THEE AS EPHRAIM AND MANASSEH.) That is said solidly to Hebrew boys: but to girls: May GOD place thee as Sarah and Rebecca.

Latin:

Vers. 20. FACIAT TIBI DEUS SICUT EPHRAIM ET MANASSE.) Solidum id dici pueris Hebræis: puellis vero: Ponat te DEUS sicut Saram & Rebeccam.

## 48:22
Vers. 22. I GIVE THEE ONE PORTION BEYOND THY BRETHREN.) That is, in Latin, I give thee this prerogative. The word portion in Hebrew שְׁכֶם at the same time enigmatically signifies the place itself, namely Shechem, which name the LXX have placed here as a proper noun.

I HAVE TAKEN.] I shall take through my descendants. It is the custom of the Prophets to announce future things with words of the past or present tense, as being no less certain. Servius on that passage of the 12th Aeneid,

I see them coming together: for 'that they are about to come together': although she used the present tense as if she were a Goddess, who also perceived future things. Moreover, fathers are said to do what their children do because of the communion of blood and name. Above 46, 4. This is more correct than referring this to the treacherous deed of Simeon & Levi, which Jacob also detested above 34, 30, and will soon detest 49, 5.

See what we have said about this passage in the Commentary.

Latin:

Vers. 22. DO TIBI PARTEM UNAM EXTRA FRA- TRES TUOS.) Id est, Latine, do tibi hoc præcipuum. Vox partem in Hebræo שְׁכֶם simul ipsum locum ænigma- tice significat, Sicima scilicet, quod nomen proprium hic po- fuere LXX.

CEPI.] Capiam per posteros meos. Mos Propheta- rum verbis præteriti vel præsentis temporis futura, tanquam non minus certa enunciare. Servius ad illud 12. Æneidos,

Video concurrere : pro concursurum esse : licet quasi Dea bene praesenti usa sit tempore, quae etiam futura cernebat. Dicuntur autem patres facere quod liberi faciunt ob sanguinis nominis- que communionem. Supra 46, 4. Id rectius quam referre hoc ad perfidum factum Simeonis & Levi, quod & supra detesta- tus est Jacobus 34, 30. & mox detestabitur 49, 5.

Vide quae de hoc loco diximus in Comment.

## 49:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLIX. Prophecies concerning the 12 tribes, & the death of Jacob.

Ver. 1. IN THE LAST DAYS.) That is, in times to follow, far removed from my age. Thus אחרית is translated not only by ἔσχατον, but also by ὕστερον. And in Exodus 4, 9, some translate that Hebrew word into Greek as δευτέρῳ, others as ἐσχάτῳ, others as ἑπομένῳ.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIX. Vaticinia de 12. tribubus, & mors Jacobi.

Vers. 1. IN DIEBUS NOVISSIMIS. ) Id est, secuturis temporibus multum remotis è mea aetate. Ita אחרית, non per ἔσχατον tantùm, sed & per ὕστερον vertitur. Et Exodi 4, 9. vocem illam Hebraeam alii Graece vertunt δευτέρῳ, alii ἐσχάτῳ, alii ἑπομένῳ.

## 49:3
Ver. 3. FIRST IN GIFTS, GREATER IN POWER.) You would have been, that is, had you not deprived yourself of that right by sinning. The greater part of the inheritance and the leadership belonged to the firstborn. This is given to Judah: the former to Joseph: but the Priesthood, which is the third right, was given to Levi.

Latin:

Vers. 3. PRIOR IN DONIS, MAJOR IN IMPERIO. ) Fuisset scilicet, nisi te eo jure privasses delinquendo. Pri- mogenitorum erat pars major in hereditate & principatus. Hic datur Judae : illa Josepho : Sacerdotium autem, quod jus tertium, datum Levi.

## 49:5
Ver. 5. VESSELS OF INIQUITY WARRING.) מכרתיהם is explained in various ways; some by understanding a ב as 'in their habitations', others as 'from covenants', so that מ is a preposition. It is most probable that the word is Persian, which came from the Persians into Greece as μάχαιρα. For Xenophon calls Persian swords machaeras. Their machaera is an instrument of iniquity, namely because of those things which were narrated above in chapter 34.

These things are said for the sake of defending the Vulgate version. And they are taken from the Rabbis, Leo Juda, & R. Eleazar. Our Doctors, or R. Levi, said that it is a Greek word, so that it is rendered thus: vessels of their huge sword. But that a habitation is designated, not only R. Levi & R. David (as R. Aben-Ezra designates a dwelling) but also the Targum Onkelos judged. See Sixtinus ab Amama in his censure of the Vulgate version on this passage. Nor is it likely that in the time of Moses, Persian words originating from Greece had already penetrated into Hebraism: although we do not deny that this happened in later centuries, concerning which it is spoken in the Critico Sacro p. 323.

Latin:

Vers. 5. VASA INIQUITATIS BELLANTIA. ) Varie exponitur מכרתיהם, alii subaudito ב in habitationi- bus, alii ex pactis, ut מ sit praepositio. Maxime probabile est vocem esse Persicam, quae à Persis in Graeciam venerit μάχαι- ρα. Gladios enim Persicos Xenophon machaeras vocat. Ma- chaera eorum instrumenta iniquitatis, nimirum ob ea, quae nar- rata sunt supra cap. 34.

Dicuntur haec liberandae vulgatae versioni. Et à Rabbinis, Leone Juda, & R. Eleazar petita sunt. Di- xerunt Doctores nostri, aut R. Levi, vocem Graecam esse, ut sic reddatur, vasa ingentis machaerae ipso- rum. Sed inhabitationem designari, non R. Levi modo & R. David (uti commorationem R. Aben- Ezra) sed etiam Targum Onkelos censuit. Vid. Sixtinus ab Amama in cens. Vulg. vers. ad h. l. Ne- que verisimile, Mosis tempore jam voces Persicas è Graecia oriundas in Ebraismum penetrasse : tametsi sequioribus seculis id factum non negemus, quo de in Critico Sacro p. 323. dictum.

## 49:6
Ver. 6. IN THEIR ASSEMBLY LET NOT MY GLORY BE.) The Chaldean is better: when they assembled among themselves, my glory did not descend. He reads תֵּרַד, not תֵּחַד, and took both this and the preceding תָּבֹא in the past sense. The sense is: I did not contaminate my reputation by consenting to their assembly.

THEY DUG THROUGH A WALL.) The Greeks & the Hierosolymitan [Targum] say, they cut down a bull, that is, they wanted to kill Joseph 37, 20. The ox was on the standard of Ephraim, because Joseph had restored agriculture. Furthermore, ταῦρος τὸν τυχόντα σημαίνει, says Artemidorus: namely because the bull holds the primacy among tame animals, as Macarius says. Furthermore, in the Hieroglyphics of the Egyptians, Horapollon notes that a man who is both strong and temperate, such as Joseph was in an exceptional way, is designated by the image of a bull. And some think that the veneration of Apis among the Egyptians arose from this. See Theophilus of Antioch, and book 1 of the Miracles of Scripture, chapter 15, in the works of Augustine.

Latin:

Vers. 6. IN COETU ILLORUM NON SIT GLO- RIA MEA. ) Melius Chaldaeus, cum illi inter se coirent, non descendit gloria mea. Legit תֵּרַד, non תֵּחַד, & sumsit tum hoc, tum quod praecesfit תָּבֹא in sensu praeterito. Sen- sus est : Non contaminavi famam meam, consentiendo ipso- rum coitioni.

SUFFODERUNT MURUM. ) Graeci & Hierosolymi- tanus, exciderunt taurum, id est, occidere voluerunt Jo- sephum 37, 20. Bos erat in vexillo Ephraimi, ideo quod Jo- sephus agriculturam restituerat. Praeterea ταῦρος τὸν τυ- χόντα σημαίνει, ait Artemidorus : nimirum quia taurus in- ter mansueta animantia principatum habet, ut ait Macarius. Praeterea in Hieroglyphicis Aegyptiorum virum simul fortem & temperantem, qualis eximie fuit Josephus, tauri imagine designari notat Horapollon. Et quidam Apidis veneratio- nem apud Aegyptios hinc ortam putant. Vide Theophilum Antiochenum, & lib. 1. de mirabilibus Scripturae cap. 15. in operibus Augustini.

## 49:7
Ver. 7. I WILL DIVIDE THEM.) An evil assembly is punished by division.

Latin:

Vers. 7. DIVIDAM EOS. ) Mala coitio divisione pu- nitur.

## 49:8
Ver. 8. JUDAH, YOUR BRETHREN SHALL PRAISE YOU.

Coccejus, on the last of Moses §. 775, says that the brethren will adore Judah, either with civil adoration, which is owed to Kings, and thus the Kingdom of David & Solomon is predicted: or with religious [adoration]; and in that way the Son of Judah, Christ, is understood. But these things are with difficulty extracted from those words. He observes more correctly that, when it is said that the Scepter shall not be taken from Judah, another scepter is foreseen as having arisen and been removed among the ten tribes.

Latin:

Vers. 8. JUDA TE LAUDABUNT FRA- TRES TUI.

Coccejus ult. Mos. §. 775. Judam adoraturos fra- tres ait, vel civili adoratione, quae Regibus debetur, & ita Regnum Davidis & Salomonis praedictum : vel religiosa; atque ea ratione intelligi Filium Ju- dae, Christum. Sed haec è verbis illis aegre exscul- pentur. Rectius observat, cum dicitur, Sceptrum de Juda non auferendum, praevisum aliud sceptrum in tribubus decem ortum, & amotum.

## 49:9
Verse 9. A LION'S WHELP, JUDAH. ) Refer this to his generous spirit, which appeared in Gen. 37:26 and in the whole history of events in Egypt. This is the beginning of his excellence.

TO THE PREY, MY SON, YOU HAVE ASCENDED, RESTING YOU HAVE COUCHED AS A LION. ) Refer this to the growth of the tribe of Judah. Especially in the times of David, when most of his neighbors were subdued. See Num. 24:17, Psalm 2 and 59, 2 Sam. 8, 10, 12. For the chapters on the mighty men who were of that time, see 2 Sam. 23.

AND AS A LIONESS. ) In Hebrew: as a greater Lion: by which the third degree of excellence is signified as fulfilled.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CATULUS LEONIS JUDA. ) Refer ad gene- rosum ejus animum, qui apparuit Genes. 37, 26. & in omni hi- storia rerum in Aegypto. Hoc initium est excellentiae ipsius.

AD PRAEDAM FILI MI ASCENDISTI, REQUI- ESCENS ACCUBUISTI UT LEO. ) Hoc refer ad incre- mentum tribus Judae. Jud. 1. Davidis maxime temporibus cum vicinorum plerique subacti. Vide Num. 24, 17. Psalm. 2. & 59. 2. Sam. 8. 10. 12. capp. de viris fortibus qui fuere eo tem- pore vid. 2. Sam. 23.

ET QUASI LEAENA. ) Hebraice : quasi Leo major : quo tertius gradus excellentiae significatur impletus.

## 49:10
Verse 10. THE SCEPTRE SHALL NOT DEPART FROM JUDAH.) οὐκ ἐκλείψει. The word is יסור, and in Zechariah, indeed joined with the word שבט, that is, of the sceptre, where the Greeks say καὶ σκῆπτρον Αἰγύπτο περιαιρεθήσεται, which passage illustrates this remarkably and refutes the cavils of more recent Jews. The Chaldean well expressed יסור by עבר. Among the Jews, who have their name from Judah, the empire remained, which is indicated by the name of the sceptre, until the times of Christ. This is attributed to Judah rather than to other tribes, because the ten tribes carried away by the Chaldeans did not return. Judah returned with Benjamin, which tribe of Benjamin was an accession to Judah, whence the land was called Judaea, and the people Jews. The power of the empire was first in military leadership, Judg. 1, at which place Josephus says Ἰουδαία φυλὴ ἡ ἡγεμονία παρέρχεται: Then in the royal name, afterwards of the Ethnarchs, and again royal, until the kingdom was taken away from Archelaus and Judaea was made a province of the Romans; it never recovered the sceptre afterwards. Under the Hasmoneans and Herod, the empire was in the hands of Judah, no less than it was in the hands of Rome when Gauls or Thracians were elected to the empire. The interruptions were brief, if compared to the space of nearly fifteen hundred years, under foreign tyrants mentioned in the history of the Judges, under Saul, and the seventy years of exile, which are hardly to be counted, because the Prophets had given a certain hope of the restoration of the empire of Judah. During that space which we have mentioned, the Jews indeed sometimes revered the Persian, Macedonian, Egyptian, and Roman magnitude, but the empire remained safe for them, which Chrysostom shows not badly in his oration, that Christ is GOD. Let the Jews therefore depart with their new inventions, by which they wish to understand either a tribe or punishments through שבט, against all the ancient interpreters: of whom Aquila, retaining the words, said σκῆπτρον, where the LXX said ἄρχων, Symmachus ἐξουσία, the Chaldeans שלטן, with the meaning exactly the same.

AND A LEADER FROM HIS THIGH.) From the Greek: καὶ ἡγούμενος ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ. For leader, the Hebrew text has מחקק, which the Chaldean explains very well with the word for Scribe, that is, teacher. Such men are also rightly called leaders of the people, namely, in regard to knowledge. The word חקק, from which that noun or participle flows, is translated by the Greeks as ἀφορίζειν, γράφειν, διαγράφειν, ἐξερευνᾷν, διατάττειν. Whence Aquila translates מחקק as ἀκριβασὴν, not inappropriately. For that phrase 'from his thigh' in the Hebrew, it is 'from between his feet'; where that 'between his feet' is a decent circumlocution for the genitals, as in Deut. 28:57. Thus the Latins call the same part the interfeminium, and the act itself 'to lift the feet,' not only in Martial, but also in Cicero. The meaning, therefore, is that teachers from the posterity of Judah will lead the people until the times of the Messiah, who is to be the supreme Emperor and Teacher, and will be not only of the Jews, but also of all nations. The Schools of Sameas and Hillel flourished until the times of Christ.

Verse same. UNTIL HE COMES WHO IS TO BE SENT.) The words which are Hebrew here, the Jews of later times strangely distort, some interpreting it as the place Silo, others as Saul, others as Nebuchadnezzar. The consensus of the ancients who have great authority among them also contradicts them here. Onkelos, Jonathan, the Jerusalemite, the Paraphrasts, the Talmudic writers, Beresith Rabba, Rabbi Solomon, Echa Rabthi: all agree that the Messiah is indicated here: But others interpret the word itself differently. For some explain Silo as בנו, his son, derived from the afterbirth, others as the peaceful one from the word שלה, others think it is a compound of the relative and the dative case of the demonstrative pronoun, so that ש is put for אשר, which is not without examples: from which particles, in order to elicit the meaning, the Greeks added the participle τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ: which, since it is harsher and savors more of the Hebrew phrase, other Greek interpreters likewise placed more clearly ὧ ἀπόκειται, namely, 'all things,' to whom all things are reserved: whose is the right of the kingdom, says Rabbi Solomon after the Jerusalemite Paraphrast. The meaning of both expositions is the same, except that the latter savors more of a Hebraism. Whence it appears that Christians are undeservedly accused by Julian of having changed the version here, since it is of no interest to them. And so Justin against Trypho uses now these words, now those, and affirms that the Codices of the LXX of his time had ὧ ἀπόκειται, which I easily believe regarding certain Codices. Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian, Origen, Eusebius, and Cyril bring forward this passage for themselves in the former way. To me, the Latin version proves itself most, so that שילה is for שילוח. For what is easier than that, either by a varying dialect or by a straying script, letters so close in both sound and shape should be changed among themselves? Siloh is therefore the name most proper to the Messiah, the ἀπεσαλμένος, who was sent by God with supreme power and authority. See Matt. 10:40, 9:34, 10:16, John 3:17, 34, verse 36, 6:57, 7:29, 10:36, 11:41, 17:3, 8, 18, 18:21, 23, 25, Acts 9:17, 1 John 4:9, 10, 14, Heb. 3:1, in which places everywhere is the verb ἀποστέλλειν, or words derived from it. The same is expressed elsewhere by the verb πέμπειν, John 4, verse 34, verse 23, 24, 30, 37, 6:37, 40, 44, 7:16, 19, 28, 33, 8:16, 18, 26, 29, 9:4, 12:44, 45, 49.

13, 20. 14, 24. 15, 21. 16, 5. Rom. 8, 3. all of which passages, but especially that concerning Siloam, which is John 9, 17, as we said there, seem to look toward this prophecy.

Grotius has left this almost as the only oracle concerning the Messiah in Genesis. And perhaps in the whole Pentateuch. For I have observed no other thus far. He seems to be constrained here by the very consensus of the Jews. For Onkelos, as he himself observes, Jonathan, the Jerusalemite, the Paraphrasts, the Talmudists, Bereschith Rabba, R. Solomon, Echa Rabthi all agree that the Messiah is indicated here. One could add R. Bechai, R. Moses Bar Nachman, R. Arama, R. Isaac Abarbenel, R. Moses Alsich, the Author of the Arba Turim, Aben-Meleck, whom Morinus praises and cites in the appendix to his Diatribe Elenctica, p. 278. R. Menasse Ben Israel, the Cabbalists, etc. The family of R. Sila in the tractate Sanhedrim c. 11. The author of the book Halcuth, etc.

Nor is there any reason for us to be anxious here about many things regarding its interpretation, namely that the empire indicated by the name of the scepter ought to have remained among the Jews, who have their name from Judah, with the illustrious Doctors of the people, from his posterity, up to the times of the Messiah, who is to be the supreme Emperor and Doctor, not only of the Jews, but also of all nations. It is known that some of the Ancients, Justin, Eusebius, Chrysostom, Augustine, explain the oracle concerning the Jews named from this tribe, to whom, however, others especially oppose the fact that the Patriarch is not prophesying here about the whole people, but specifically about the tribe of Judah, bestowing proper blessings upon individual tribes, just as the other things here are also proper to the tribe of Judah. Then, that the kingdom of the Jews remained in Herod until the destruction of Jerusalem.

But that by מחקק a scribe or Doctor alone is understood, and that the Schools of Samea and Hillel flourished until the times of Christ, is designated here, has not been proven. For were all such Doctors from the posterity of Judah? And do the Jews not still have their own Schools and Doctors? It is more correctly explained as Legislator; the LXX render it ἡγύμενos, Leader. In the book Sanhedrin, according to R. Solomon, it is explained as the Sanhedrin; which, although it was not collected from the tribe of Judah alone, nevertheless always had a President from the family of David, as the histories of the Jews testify. Which some also gather to have proceeded from the Davidic constitution, from Psalm 112, 4. 5. And thus R. Menasse Ben Israel also interprets this word in Concil. p. 88, along with R. Aben-Ezra, R. Moses Gerundensis, R. Joel Ben Sueb, as Legislators in the Sanhedrin.

Concerning the fulfillment of the prophecy, as it corresponds to its proper sense, our B. Luther should by all means be consulted, Tom. 8. Jen. Germ. von den Jüden, und ihren Lügen; our Dn. D. Waltherus treats it at length in his Exercit. Biblic. It is helpful now only to hear Justin Martyr here, Dial. cum Tryphon. p. 211. Furthermore, that there has never before ceased to be in your nation either a Prophet or a Prince, from the time it received the empire, you do not even dare to say imprudently, nor can you prove. For alleging Herod the Ascalonite, under whom Christ suffered, you nevertheless say that there was a high priest of sacred things in your nation; so that even then it was permitted to you, according to the law of Moses, to offer sacrifices and observe other lawful things: but then also that Prophets existed in their succession up to John: just as then also, when your people were led away to Babylon, the land laid waste, and the sacred vessels taken away, there did not cease to be a Prophet among you, who was the Lord and leader and prince of your people: But after the manifestation and death of our Jesus Christ in your nation, there has by no means existed, nor does there exist, a Prophet. But you also ceased to be under your own king. Furthermore, your land is also desolate, and left behind like a watchman's hut in a cucumber field. Which the Arabs also acknowledge, who are alien to the Christian faith, among whom is Ahmed Ibn-Idris, as Hottinger observes in his Thesaurus, p. 163. The text, he says, of the law confirms the prophecy of (Jesus) upon whom be peace, when it says: The scepter shall not depart from Judah nor the legislator from between his feet, until the Messiah shall come. That which happened: for there were not lacking kings (to the Jews) and an empire until the time of the Messiah, upon whom be peace. For then they became a vile reproach and a captive people, which is indeed so true that they cannot deny it. And this argument is evident for the prophecy of (Jesus) upon whom be peace. For Moses, p. m., predicted that they would be addicted to vanity at that time, but that the Messiah would bring the truth, which would strike down vanity or falsehood.

But these things being set aside, since Grotius agrees in the application of the prophecy, it must now only be seen how he attempts to free the version of the LXX and the Vulgate from the interpretation of the name שִׁילֹה. He observes that the Jews interpret this word in different ways. Others, he says, explain Silo as בְּנוֹ his son, from the word derived from the afterbirth: others as peaceful from the word שָׁלָה, others think it is composed of a relative and the Dative case of a demonstrative pronoun, so that לוֹ is placed for לוֹ, which is not without examples: from which particles, in order to elicit a sense, the Greeks added the participle τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ: which, because it is harsher, and savors more of Hebrew phrasing, other Greek Interpreters likewise rendered more clearly, ᾧ ἀπόκειται, namely all things, to whom all things are reserved, whose is the right of the kingdom, says R. Solomon after the Jerusalemite Paraphrast. The sense of both expositions is the same, except that the former savors more of Hebrew. And afterwards: The Latin version pleases me most, so that שִׁילֹו is for שִׁילֹה. For what is easier than that, either by a varying dialect, or by a wandering script, letters so close in both sound and figure should be changed among themselves. Therefore Siloh is the name ἀποσταλμένos, most proper to the Messiah. With the passages subjoined, in which Christ is said to be sent in the New Testament, he judges that especially that concerning Siloam, John 9, v. 17, seems to look toward this prophecy. Thus Grotius generally chooses the worst, prepared to defend anything. Why does the explanation of R. David Kimchi not please, that שִׁילְיוֹ is the sacculus, in which the infant remains in the mother's womb, which is sometimes used in Scripture for an embryo in the matrix, which also R. Bechai in h. l. and Morinus in the appendix to his Diatribe. In the Elenctic, page 269, as R. Ben Gerson, Arama, Aben-Meleck, and others observe, it was pleasing and was approved by Galatinus in book 4 of De Arcanis, chapter 4, that it was indicated in this way, that the Messiah would be born of a mother without a father. R. Bechai interprets it as 'His son, who will be born from the afterbirth of a woman.' To which Jonathan's interpretation in the Targum also seems to return: 'The Messiah, the little one of his sons.' And analogous to that is the etymology of Aben-Ezra, that שִׁילְיָה properly signifies a son from שָׁלָה, to bring forth, as some say that ה is placed for the suffix ו, 'His,' while others take it for a feminine suffix, so that the mother is indicated. Grotius himself, in book 5 of De Veritate Religionis Christianae, chapter 1, brought forward into this opinion that שִׁילֹו becomes בְּנוֹ, 'his son,' the Chaldean, R. Silo, R. Bechai, R. Salomo, Aben-Ezra, and Kimchi: But he was mistaken concerning R. Salomo and Aben-Ezra, though not in naming the Chaldean: for he could not have been pointing to Onkelos, but to Jonathan. And therefore, since Gisbertus Voetius, with Cartwright leading the way in his Notes on Genesis 49, verse 10, reproved Grotius in part 2 of his Disputationes Selectae, page 61, because of the falsely cited explanation of the name for that passage, along with R. Salomo and Aben-Ezra, and Onkelos, because he saw through the eyes of others here, or reported these things on the authority of others (perhaps because those authors were either not understood or, on account of his occupations, not inspected), he himself incurs this reproof. Why does that derivation from שׁלה, to be peaceful, quiet, or fortunate, displease, since nouns of the same form are not lacking, such as קיטור smoke and קימוש nettle? Whence Blessed Luther and most of our theologians, and also among the Pontificians Vatablus and Johann Ferus, as well as Mercerus and others, both Papists and some Reformed, hold this etymology to be the simplest, and wish for the Savior to be signified as happy, fortunate, august, and the author of peace and happiness.

Certainly all those interpretations enjoy greater probability than the Greek or Latin ones. For if it is a pronoun with a vocative, it is שׁלוֹ or, if substituted, שׁלה; whence then the long Hirek? And what is the sense, WHAT TO HIM? By what right is that participle ἀποκείμενα added here, when with equal ease any other could have been added? Under what pretext, under what appearance is ᾧ ἀπόκειται substituted by others? Those interpretations are purely arbitrary: that the ancients, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian, Eusebius, Cyril, used them is no wonder, because they had no other text; for they were ignorant of Hebrew, if you except Origen. Therefore they retained the reading of the LXX Interpreters, which Grotius acknowledges to be harsher, although he observes from Justin that in some codices it was read ᾧ ἀπόκειται. If we listen to him, the version of the LXX Interpreters will be rendered doubtful at the very least. namely, whether they rendered τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ in the way it is usually alleged by the Fathers. I could, says Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, p. 273, O men, contend against you concerning the expression which you bring forward in interpreting, asserting it to be said, ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ, until those things which are laid up for him shall come, etc. For those Seventy did not translate it so: But ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ᾧ ἀπόκειται, until he comes to whom it is laid up. In which manner also St. Ambrose, Jerome, Athanasius on the Cross, Leo the Great, or Morinus, u. s., read it.

It is strange that Grotius, in order to defend the interpretation of the Greeks, does not, according to his custom, pretend that it was read differently in the past, and accuse the Hebrew text of corruption. In which Morinus is quite occupied, who brings forward, or rather invents, a fivefold reading of the word. But he considers the LXX Interpreters, Onkelos, the Jerusalem Paraphrasts, R. Solomon Jarchi, R. Saadia Gaon in the Arabic translation of the Pentateuch, and the Syriac interpreter, R. Aben-Meleck in the book Mislal Jophi, to be the most ancient; who neither read nor could have read it otherwise than שׁלוֹ, which is either 'whose' or 'to whom': now, however, he contends that this has been transformed into שׁילה by the perfidy of the Jews. But Grotius preferred here to defend the Vulgate, and to invent another corruption, or to approve one fabricated by the Jesuit Gordon Huntlaeus: That in the Hebrew it was once written שׁילוח. But by what argument? Is it because the Vulgate rendered it 'He who is to be sent'? But he assumes it as a conceded fact, which is entirely a matter of judgment, that the Hebrew text should be corrected from the Vulgate version. Why does he not correct it from the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters, or from so many interpretations that agree with Morinus? Or by dividing the word into two from the ancient Midrash and R. Solomon Jarchi: שׁי לוֹ, i.e., a gift or present to him, which explanation Morinus judges to contain a wonderful and truly Christian sense. Just as Leo Castrius, l. 3. Apol., wishes the LXX Interpreters to have read שׁילה as a gift or promise to him. However, it is easily evident that no corruption has a place in the Hebrew text. For whatever may be the case regarding the LXX, whose countless slips or misinterpretations one may observe, and whatever may be the case regarding others, who, as is wont to happen, either followed the LXX Interpreters, or had a non-pointed or faulty codex, or might seem to have used divination in a difficult matter: the Masora certainly added that word to those which are written elsewhere as either שׁלה or שׁלו, not because the Masoretes indicated that the place should be understood of the city of Silo, as Morinus perverts it, but because they wished the true reading to be guarded by this note of theirs (for the Masora is consecrated not to interpreting, but to reading and defending against corruptions of writing and reading), whence it is indubitable that in their time it was written and read as שילה and not as שלו or שלוח. And so also the Talmudists read it. Therefore in the codex Sanhedrim ch. 11 it is so written; R. Jonathan said, What is the name of the Messiah? Those from the School of R. Schela answered שילו, according to that, until Schilo comes. Similarly it is written in the ancient book Tanchuma, as Morinus himself observes on page 275. Thus also the Commentators read it: The author of the book Jalcuth, which is a commentary on the entire Bible woven together from the Talmud and from ancient commentators; R. Moses Bar Nachman in his commentary on this passage, as well as R. Arama in the famous and diffuse commentary on the law, which is inscribed עקידת יצחק, the Binding of Isaac, and also R. Moses Alsich on this passage. Nor does the author of the most ancient commentary Bereschith Rabba read it otherwise, or R. Bechai, or R. Aben-Meleck in the book Mislol Jophi, or Ben-Gersom and others, who interpret it as His Son. R. Abarbenel or R. Abraham Seba in his commentary on the law read it no differently, even if they seek other etymologies elsewhere. Nor do the Kabbalists read it otherwise, for whom שילה is by Gematria the same as משיח, as is evident from Arba Turen. Indeed, Jonathan in the Targum reads it no differently, explaining it as the least of his sons. Perhaps, says Morinus, that Paraphrast read שילה as the Hebrew text now has it, and interpreted it as an embryo, as some Jews now do. Indeed, the converted Jewish Professor of the Hebrew language, Philippus de Aquino, acknowledges that the word should be read as it is in the original text, and he explains the word שילה not with the Vulgate or Morinus, but with the Hebrews as בנו, his son, in the most absolute dictionary, as he calls it, published in Paris in the year 1629. Therefore there is no suspicion of any corruption or mutation of the text. Nor does that שילם agree with grammar, since it should have been שלום; it does not agree with the Samaritan text, which retains the He in this name, expressing it as שלה, and it departs as far as possible from the reading of all the Paraphrasts, Onkelos, Jonathan, Hierosolymit, and the LXX. and of the remaining Greek interpreters, likewise the Syriac, the Arabic of R. Saadia Gaon, and of all the Talmudist and Cabbalist commentators, to all of whom to prefer the one Vulgate interpreter is foolish. But that Christ is said to be sent, that is from other places of Scripture, nor is the name more proper to him in the O.T. than that ἐρχόμενος, the one who is to come, although it is appropriated to him by a certain reason, and you may regard the promise of the advent and mission of the Messiah made in the O.T. even in this very prophecy. Moreover, I do not see how the name of the pool of Siloam, which is had in John 9:7, can be relevant here. The Hebrews wish it to be called Siloah, because water was sent forth from there, therefore it is explained as ἀπεσταλμένος; but what does this κολύμβηθρα τοῦ Σηλωάμ or τοῦ ἀπεσταλμένος have to do with the prophecy of Jacob concerning the advent of Shiloh? But these things regarding Grotius.

The new distortion of the Jacobean Oracle by Wilhelm Lange in his book on the years of Christ must not be passed over here through a new interpretation and version: the scepter shall not be taken away from Judah and the lawgiver from between his feet forever; because Shiloh shall come. Which is truly new to Christian ears, even if it is not new among the Jews, from whom he received it. Since indeed Menasseh Ben Israel produces one clearly similar in Concil. qv. LXV, nor the lawgiver from his feet forever, when the Messiah shall come, which he attributes to Anqueli of Ger; but Onkelos, whom they call הגר the proselyte, leaves the little words עד־כי undivided, and translates them just as the others.

The Rabbis [say] עד דייתי until he comes; but he inserts the word עד עלמא from his own [mind], rendering it thus: 'and a scribe from the sons of his sons, for an age, until the Messiah comes.' Helvicus, however, notes (T. IV. Diss. Giess. Diss. 12. p. 304) that this corruption is found in R. Bechai and is common among modern Jews, inasmuch as they deny that a limit for the coming of the Messiah is set here, and wish to teach only what will happen after his coming. But he solidly refutes them, both from the pausing accent Athnach, which precedes the word עד and teaches that it is to be referred not to the preceding, but to the following [words], and from the perpetual usage of this little word when it is joined to the particle כי, because עד־כי is always and everywhere UNTIL, until the time that, and nowhere in this conjunction does it denote perpetuity, and also from the universal consensus of the remaining Jews and Christians, who interpret it as UNTIL. Thus, therefore, Langius, in the Jews whom he favors, was already refuted by Helvicus before he even arose. His compatriot, Mr. Joh. Wandalin the Dane, refutes him more copiously in his Historico-Theological Diatribe on the feast of the passion and the Triduum of the death of Christ, opposed to his new and paradoxical opinions, ch. 9, p. 131.

Verse same. AND HE SHALL BE THE EXPECTATION OF THE NATIONS) יקהת, because of its diverse meaning in Hebrew and neighboring languages, is translated in various ways, for example προσδοκία expectation, obedience, gathering. The sense is what we have already touched upon, that the Messiah would be in an eminent way both King and Teacher, not only of the Jews, but also of all nations. The Jerusalem [Targum] here: 'To him shall the kingdoms of the earth be subservient.' See Dan. 7, 14. Is. 11, 10. 49, 6. 55, 4. 60, 3. and other prophecies. Bereschith Rabba at this place: 'It shall come to pass that the nations of the age shall bring gifts to the Messiah, the son of David.'

Latin:

Vers. 10. NON AUFERETUR SCEPTUM DE JU-DA.) ἐκ ἐκλείψει. יסור vox est & in Zacharia, & quidem conjuncta cum voce שבט, id est, sceptri, ubi Graeci καὶ σκῆπτρον Αἰγύπτο περιαιρεθήσεται, qui locus hunc egregie illustrat, & Judaeorum recentiorum cavillationes refellit. Chaldaeus יסור per עבר bene expressit. Inter Judaeos, qui a Juda nomen habent, mansit imperium, quod sceptri nomine indicatur, ad Christi tempora. Judae hoc potius tribuitur quam tribubus aliis, quia decem tribus abductae a Chaldaeis non rediere. Rediit Judas cum Benjamine, quae tribus Benjamin Judae fuit accessio, unde terra Judaea dicta, gens Judaei. Imperii vis primum in ductu militari Judic. 1. quo loco Josephus Ἰουδαία φυλὴ ἡ ἡγεμονία παρέρχεται: Deinde in nomine regio, post Ethnarcharum, iterumque regio, donec Archelao ereptum regnum ac Judaea, provincia Romanorum facta, nunquam postea sceptrum recuperavit. Sub Asmonaeis & Herode imperium penes Judam fuit, non minus quam penes Romam Gallis aut Thracibus in imperium electis. Intercisiones fuere breves, si ad spatium annorum prope mille & quingentorum comparentur, sub tyrannis externis in Judicum historia memoratis, sub Saule, LXX. annis exsilii vix computandis, quia Prophetae restituendi imperii Judae spem certam fecerant. Illo autem quod diximus spatio reveriti quidem Judaei interdum magnitudinem Persicam, Macedoniam, Aegyptiam, Romanam, sed salvo ipsis manente imperio, quod non male ostendit Chrysostomus oratione, Christum esse DEUM. Abeant ergo Judaei cum suis commentis novis, quae per שבט aut tribum aut castigationes volunt intelligi contra interpretes veteres omnes: quorum Aquila verborum retinens σκῆπτρον dixit, ubi LXX. ἄρχων, Symmachus ἐξουσία, Chaldaei שלטן, sensu plane eodem.

ET DUX DE FEMORE EJUS.) Ex Graeco: καὶ ἡγούμενος ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ. Pro duce Hebraeus textus habet מחקק. quod optime explicat Chaldaeus Scribae, id est, doctoris vocabulo. Tales autem & duces populi recte dicuntur, ad scientiam scilicet. Verbum חקק unde id nomen aut participium fluit, Graecis vertitur ἀφορίζειν, γράφειν, διαγράφειν, ἐξερευνᾷν, διατάττειν. Unde Aquila מחקק ἀκριβασὴν vertit non incommode. Pro illo de femore ejus in Hebraeo est de inter pedes ejus; ubi illud inter pedes est honesta circumlocutio genitalium, ut Deut. 28, 57. Sic Latini eandem partem interfeminium vocant, & operam ipsam pedes tollere non apud Martialem tantum, sed & apud Ciceronem. Sensus ergo est, doctores ex Judae posteritate praeturos populo ad tempora usque Messiae, qui summus & Imperator & Doctor futurus sit, nec Judaeorum tantum sit, sed & omnium gentium. Florebant ad Christi tempora Sameae & Hillelis Scholae.

Vers eod. DONEC VENIET QUI MITTENDUS EST.) Verba quae hic sunt Hebraea, Judaei posteriorum temporum mire distorquent, alii Silo locum interpretantes, alii Saulem, alii Nabuchodonosorum. Repugnat & hic illis veterum consensus eorum qui magnam apud ipsos auctoritatem habent. Onkelos, Jonathan, Hierosolymitanus, Paraphrastae, Thalmudici, Beresith Rabba, Rabbi Salomo, Echa Rabthi: omnes Messiam hic indicari consentiunt: Sed horum vocem ipsam alii interpretantur aliter. Alii enim Silo exponunt בנו filium ejus a secundinis deducto vocabulo, alii pacificum a שלה verbo, alii compositum censent ex relativo & dativo casu pronominis demonstrativi, ut ש sit pro אשר positum, quod non caret exemplis: ex quibus particulis, ut sensum elicerent Graeci, addidere participium τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ: quod cum durius sit, & Hebraeam phrasin magis sapiar, alii itidem Graeci interpretes clarius posuere ὧ ἀπόκειται, nempe πάντα, cui omnia servantur: cujus est regni jus, ait Rabbi Salomo post Hierosolymitanum Paraphrasten. Utriusque expositionis sensus idem, nisi quod illud magis Hebraismum sapit. Unde apparet immerito a Juliano Christianos accusari mutatae hic versionis, cum ipsorum nihil id intersit. Itaque Justinus adversus Tryphonem modo his, modo illis verbis utitur, affirmatque Codices LXX sui temporis habuisse ὧ ἀπόκειται, quod de quibusdam Codicibus facile credo. Priori autem modo hunc locum pro se adducunt Clemens Alexandrinus, Cyprianus, Origenes, Eusebius, Cyrillus. Mihi maxime se probat versio Latina, ut sit שילה pro שילוח. Quid enim facilius, quam aut variante dialecto, aut scriptura aberrante, mutari inter se literas tam vicinas & foni & figurae? Est ergo Siloh ἀπεσαλμένος nomen maxime Messiae proprium, qui summa cum potestate atque auctoritate a Deo missus est. Vide Matth. 10,40. 9,34. 10,16. Joh.3,17. 34. commate 36. 6, 57. 7,29. 10, 36. 11,41. 17,3. 8. 18. 18, 21. 23. 25. Act. 9, 17. 1. Joh. 4, 9. 10. 14. Hebr. 3, 1. in quibus locis ubique est verbum ἀποστέλλειν, aut inde derivata. Idem alibi exprimitur verbo πέμπειν, Joh. 4. vers. 34. commate 23. 24. 30. 37. 6, 37. 40. 44. 7, 16. 19. 28. 33. 8, 16. 18. 26. 29. 9, 4. 12, 44. 45. 49.

13, 20. 14, 24. 15, 21. 16, 5. Rom. 8, 3. quæ omnia loca, sed ma- xime illud de Siloa, quod est Joh. 9, 17. ut ibi diximus, hoc vaticinium respicere videntur.

Hoc unum fere in Genesi oraculum de Messia reliquit Grotius. Et fortassis in toto Pentateucho. Nullum enim aliud hactenus observavi. Vide- tur ipso Judæorum consensu hic constrictus. On- kelos enim, ut ipse observat, Jonathan, Hierosoly- mitanus, Paraphrastæ, Talmudici, Bereschith Rab- ba, R. Salomo, Echa Rabthi omnes Messiam hîc in- dicari consentiunt. Addi poterat R. Bechai, R. Mo- ses Bar Nachman, R. Arama, R. Isaac Abarbenel, R. Moses Alsich, Autor Arba Turim, Aben-Meleck, quos laudat & adducit Morinus append. Diatr. E- lenct. p. 278. R. Menasse Ben Israel, Cabbalistæ &c. Familia R. Sila in tractat. Sanhedrim c. 11. Autor libri Halcuth, &c.

Neque de interpretatione ejus est quod hic multis soliciti simus, quod nempe inter Judæos, qui à Juda nomen habent, manere debuerit imperium sceptri nomine indicatum, cum Doctoribus populi præclaris, ex posteritate ejus, ad tempora usque Mes- siæ, qui summus & Imperator & Doctor futurus sit, nec Judæorum tantum, sed & omnium gentium. No- tum est, quod Veteres nonnulli, Justinus, Eusebius, Chrysostomus, Augustinus de Judæis ab hac tribu denominatis oraculum explicent, quibus vero id imprimis alii opponunt, quod non de toto popu- lo, sed de tribu Juda hîc peculiariter vaticinetur Patriarcha, singulis tribubus proprias benedictio- nes tribuens, uti reliqua etiam hîc tribui Judæ propria sunt. Tum quod in Herode regnum Ju- dæorum usque ad Hierosolymitanum excidium man- serit.

Per מחקק vero scribam vel Doctorem solum in- telligi, & quod floruerint ad Christi tempora Sa- mea & Hillelis Scholæ, hîc designatum esse, haud pro- batum. Num enim tales Doctores erant omnes è posteritate Judæ? Et annon adhuc Scholas ac Doctores suos habent Judæi? Rectius id de Le- gislatore exponitur; LXX. ἡγύμενⓄ Dux red- dunt. In libro Sanhedrin juxta R. Salomonem de Synedrio explicatur; quod quamvis non fuerit è sola tribu Judæ collectum, semper tamen Præsidem è familia Davidis, testibus Judæorum historiis, ha- buit. Quod nonnulli etiam è constitutione Davi- dica profectum esse, è Psalm. 112, 4. 5. colligunt. At- que ita interpretatur quoque hanc vocem R. Me- nasse Ben Israel in Concil. p. 88. cum R. Aben-Ezra, R. Mose Gerundensi, R. Joel Ben Sueb, per Legisla- tores in Sanhedrim.

De complemento vaticinii, prouti sensui ejus proprio respondet, videatur omnino B. Lutherus noster Tom. 8. Jen. Germ. von den Jüden, und ih- ren Lügen; Prolixe illud expendit Dn. D. Walthe- rus noster, in Exercit. Biblic. Juvat nunc solum Justinum Martyrem hîc audire Dial. cum Try- phon. p. 211. Porro nunquam prius in gente vestra esse desiisse neque Prophetam, neque Principem, ex quo imperium accepit, ne imprudenter quidem vel dicere audetis, vel probare potestis. Nam Herodem Ascalo- niten, sub quo passus est Christus, allegantes, nihilomi- nus dicitis in genere vestro fuisse sacrorum antistitem; adeo ut etiam tum vobis licuerit, juxta legem Mose, offerre oblationes & legitima alia custodire: tum au- tem Prophetas successione sua usque ad Johannem ex- stitisse: quemadmodum tum quog, cum Babylonem ab- ductus est populus vester, terra vastata, & sacris va- sis sublatis, non desiit esse ex vobis Propheta, qui Do- minus & dux & princeps populi vestri fuerit: At post Jesu Christi nostri in genere vestro manifestationem & mortem, haudquaquam Propheta extitit, nec exstat. Sed & sub rege proprio esse desiistis. Adhæc & terra vestra desolata est, & tanquam custodia pomorum de- relicta. Quod agnoscunt quoque Arabes, a fide Christiana alieni, è quibus Ahmed Ibn-Idris obser- vante Hottingero in thesauro p. 163. Textus, inquit, legis confirmat Prophetiam (Jesu) super quo pax, quan- do dicit: Non recedet sceptrum à Juda neque legis- lator à pedibus ejus, usque quo venerit Messias. Id quod evenit: nec enim deerant reges (Judæis) & im- perium ad Messiæ usque tempus, super quo pax. Tunc enim facti sunt opprobrium vile & populus captivus, quod quidem tam verum est, ut negare non possint. Atque hoc argumentum evidens est pro prophetia (Je- su) super quo pax. Prædixit enim Moses, p. m. su- turos illos tunc temporis vanitati addictos, veritatem autem, quæ pulsura esset vanitatem seu mendacium, allaturum Messiam.

Sed hisce missis, quum in applicatione vatici- nii consentiat Grotius, videndum nunc solum, quomodo versionem LXX. & Vulgatam interpre- tationem nominis שִׁילֹה liberare conetur. Judæos vocem hanc alios aliter interpretari observat. Alii, inquit, Silo exponunt בְּנוֹ filium ejus à secundinis deducto vocabulo: alii pacificum à שָׁלָה verbo, alii compositum censent ex relativo & Dativo casu prono- minis demonstrativi, ut לוֹ fit pro לוֹ positum, quod non caret exemplis: ex quibus particulis ut sensum elicerent Græci, addidere participium τὰ ἀποκείμε- να ἀυτῷ: quod cum durius sit, & Hebræam phrasin magis sapiat, alii itidem Græci Interpp. clarius posue- re, ᾧ ἀπόκειται, nempe πάντα, cui omnia servantur, cujus est regni jus, ait R. Salomo post Hierosolymita- num Paraphrasten. Utriusque expositionis sensus idem, nisi quod illud magis Hebraicum sapit. Et postea: Mihi maxime se probat versio Latina, ut sit שִׁילֹו pro שִׁילֹה. Quid enim facilius, quam aut variante dialecto, aut Scriptura abbærrante, mu- tari inter se literas tam vicinas & soni & figuræ. Est ergo Siloh ἀποσταλμένos nomen maxime Messiæ pro- prium. Subjunctis locis, quibus in Novo Testa- ment. missus dicitur Christus, maxime illud de Si- loah Joh. 9. v. 17. hoc vaticinium respicere videri, ju- dicat. Ita plerumque pessimum eligit Grotius, ad quævis defendenda paratus. Cur non placet R. Da- vid Kimchi explicatio, שִׁילְיוֹ est sacculus, in quo manet infans in utero matris, qui aliquando in Scri- ptura pro embryone in matrice usurpatur, quæ etiam R. Bechai in h. l. & Morino in append. ad Dia- trib. Elencticam pag. 269. observante R.
