Ben Ger- son, Arama, Aben-Meleck & aliis placuit, & pro- bata fuit Galatino lib. 4. de Arcan. c. 4. quod indi- catum fuerit ita, Messiam à Matre absque Patre nasciturum. R. Bechai interpretatur Filius ejus, qui nascetur ex secundinis mulieris. Quo redire etiam videtur Jonathanis interpretatio in Thargum: Messias parvulus filiorum ejus. Et analoga illi ἐτυ- μολογία Aben-Ezræ, quod שִׁילְיָה proprie signi- ficet filium à שָׁלָה parere, uti nonnulli ה pro af- fixo ו Ejus positum dicunt, alii pro fœmineo affixo habent, ut mater innuatur. Adduxit lib. 5. de Verit. Relig. Christ. cap. 1. Grotius ipse in hanc sententi- am, quod שִׁילֹו fit בְּנוֹ filius ejus, Chaldæum, R. Silo, R. Bechai, R. Salomo, Aben-Ezra & Kimchi: Sed de R. Salomone, & Aben-Ezra falsus fuit, non item in nominando Chaldæo: non enim Onkelo- sum, sed Jonathanem indigitare potuit. Ideoque cum ob falso laudatum pro ista nominis explicatio- ne, cum R. Salomone & Aben-Esdra, Onkelo- sum, Gisbertus Voetius Grotium, præeunte Carth- wrigtho in Notis ad Genes. 49. v. 10. reprehen- dit parte 2. disput. select. p. 61. quod alienis oculis hic viderit, aut aliena fide hæc retulerit, (sorte au- toribus illis aut non intellectis aut propter occupatio- nes non inspectis) ipse hanc reprehensionem incur- rit. Cur displicet illa à שׁלה pacificus, quietus, item fortunatus fuit, quum non desint nomina ejusdem formæ, uti est קיטור fumus & קימוש urtica. Unde B. Lutherus & plerique nostrates, nec non è Ponti- ficiis Vatablus, & Johann. Ferus, ut & Mercerus alii- que cum Papistæ, tum Reformati nonnulli Etymo- logiam istam pro simpliciffima habent, ac Salvato- rem felicem, fortunatum, augustum, pacis & felicita- tis autorem significari volunt.

Certe omnes illæ interpretationes majori gau- dent probabilitate, quam Græci vel Latini. Si enim pronomen cum vocativo sit שׁלוֹ vel substi- tuto שׁלה unde ergo Hirek longum? Et, quis sen- sus, QUÆ ILLI? Quonam jure illud participi- um ἀποκείμενα hîc additur, quum parili facili- tate quævis alia addi potuerint? Quo prætextu, qua specie substituitur ab aliis ᾧ ἀπόκειται? Me- re arbitrariæ illæ interpretationes: quibus usos veteres esse Justinum, Clementem Alexandrinum, Cyprianum, Eusebium, Cyrillum, non mirum, quia alium textum non habebant; Ebræa enim, si Ori- genem excipias, ignorabant. Lectionem itaque LXX. Interpp. retinebant, quam duriorem agno- scit Grotius, tametsi è Justino observet, in non- nullis Codicibus lectum esse ᾧ ἀπόκειται. Quem si audiamus, dubia ad minimum reddetur versio LXX. Interpp. utrum nempe ita, quemadmodum allegari solet à Patribus, reddiderint τὰ ἀποκείμε- να ἀυτῷ. Poteram, inquit Just. Dial. cum Tryph. p. 273. ὀ viri adversus vos decertare de loquutione, quam vos interpretando profertis, dictum esse asseve- rantis, ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀυτῷ, donec ve- niant ea, quæ reposita sunt &c. Nam Septuaginta illi non ita verterunt: Sed ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ᾧ ἀπόκειται, do- nec veniat, cui repositum est. Quo pacto etiam legis- se S. Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Athanasium de Cruce, Leonem M. aut Morinus. u. s.

Mirum, quod Grotius, ut Græcorum inter- pretationem tueretur, non pro more suo aliter olim lectum esse, fingat, textumque Ebræum cor- ruptionis arguat. In quo Morinus admodum oc- cupatus est, qui quintuplicem lectionem dictionis af- fert, vel comminiscitur potius. Sed antiquissimam censet LXX. Interpp. Onkelos, Paraphrastæ Hiero- solymitani, R. Salomo Jarchi, R. Saadia Gaon, in Pentateuchi Arabica translatione, & interpretis Syri, R. Aben-Meleck in libro Mislal Jophi; qui aliter nec legerint nec legere potuerint, quam שׁלוֹ quod, vel quam ipsi, vel cujus, aut cui est: nunc autem id Judæorum perfidia in שׁילה transformatum esse, contendit. Sed maluit hîc Grotius vulgatam tueri, aliamque corruptelam fingere, aut à Gordo- no Huntlæo Jesuita confictam approbare: Quod in Ebræo olim שׁילוח scriptum fuerit. Quo vero argu- mento? Num quia vulgatus reddidit Mittendus? At ita assumit ceu ὁμολογύμενον, quod omnino κρι- νόμενον, Ebræum textum è vulgata versione cor- rigendum esse. Cur non è Græca versione LXX. Interpp. aut tot consentientibus interpretationi- bus cum Morino eandem emendat? Aut ex anti- quo Midrasch & R. Salomone Jarchi vocem in duas dirimeme. שׁי לוֹ h. e. munus, seu donum ipsi, quam explicationem mirabilem & vere Christianum sen- sum complecti Morinus judicat. Uti & Leo Castrius l. 3. Apol. שׁילה donum seu promissum ei LXX. In- terpp. legisse vult. Nullam autem corruptionem in Ebræo textu locum habere facile patet. Quic- quid enim sit de LXX. quorum παροράματα aut παρερμηνείας innumeras observare licet, quicquid de aliis, qui, uti fieri amat, aut LXX. Interpp. se- quuti sunt, aut Codicem non punctatum vel men- dosum habuere, aut divinationem in re difficili usi videri possint: Masora certe vocem illam adjunxit iis, quæ vel שׁלה vel שׁלו alibi scribuntur, non quod de urbe Silo intelligendum locum Masorethæ indigitarint, uti pervertit Morinus, sed quod hac nota sua veram lectionem custoditam voluerint (le- gi enim non interpretandæ, sed à corruptelis scri- ptionis & lectionis vindicandæ consecrata est Ma- sora) unde indubium, ipsorum tempore שילה non vero שלו vel שלוח scriptum lectumque esse. Atque ita etiam Talmudici legere. Ideo in Codice Sanhedrim cap. 11. ita scriptum; R. Jonathan dixit, Messiæ quod est nomen? Qui de Schola R. Schela re- sponderunt שילו juxta illud, donec veniat Schilo. Similiter in libro antiquo Tanchuma scriptum, ob- servante ipso Morino pag. 275. Ita legerunt quo- que Commentatores: Autor libri Jalcuth, qui Commentarius est in universa Biblia è Talmude & ex antiquis Commentatoribus contextus; R. Moyfes Bar Nachman Commentar. in h. l. nec non R. Arama Commentario celebri & diffuso in legem, qui inscribitur עקידת יצחק legatio Isaaci, itemque R. Moses Alsich in hoc loco. Nec aliter le- git Autor Antiquissimi Commentarii Bereschith Rabba, aut R. Bechai, aut R. Aben-Meleck in li- bro Mislol Jophi, aut Ben-Gersom aliique, qui Fi- lium ejus interpretantur. Non aliter R. Abarbenel aut R. Abraham Seba in comment. in legem, etsi alias hi Etymologias quærant. Nec Cabbalistæ ali- ter, quibus שילה Gematrice idem est, quod משיח ut ex Arba Turen constat. Imo nec aliter legit Jonathan in Targum, exponens parvulum filiorum ejus. Forsan, inquit Morinus, legit iste Paraphra- stes שילה ut nunc habet textus Ebræus, & embryo- nem interpretatus est, ut nunc nonnulli Judæi. Imo ita legendam esse vocem, ut est in originario textu, agnoscit Professor Ebrææ linguæ Judæus conver- sus Philippus de Aquino, qui exponit vocem שילה non cum Vulgato aut Morino, sed cum Ebræis בנו filium ejus in dictionario absolutissimo, ut vocat, An- no 1629. Parisiis edito. Non ergo ulla corrupte- læ aut mutationis textus suspicio. Neque conve- nit illud שילם Grammaticæ, quum dicendum fue- rit שלום, non convenit Samaritano textui, qui He in hoc nomine retinet, id exprimens שלה & quam longissime abit à lectione Paraphrastarum omnium, Onkelos, Jonathan, Hierosolymit. LXX. & reliquo- rum Græcorum Interpretum, Syri item, Arabici R. Saadiæ Gaon, & commentatorum Thalmudistarum & Cabbalistarum omnium, quibus omnibus unum vulgatum interpretem præferre insulsum. Quod vero Christus missus dicitur, id ex aliis est Scripturæ locis, neque magis nomen est illi proprium in V. T. quam illud ἐρχόμενος venturus, quamvis certa ra- tione ipsi approprietur, ac promissionem adventus & missionis Messiæ in V. T. etiam in hoc ipso vati- cinio factam respicias. Nomen autem piscinæ Siloë, quod Joh. 9, 7. habetur non video, quî huc facere possit? Siloah Ebræi dictum volunt, quod inde aqua emitteretur, ideo explicatur ἀπεσταλμένος; quid vero hæc κολύμβηθρα τοῦ Σηλωάμ vel τοῦ ἀπεσταλ- μένος ad vaticinium Jacobi de adventu Schilo? Sed hæc de Grotio.

Non prætereunda hîc Oraculi Jacobæi nova στρεβλότης Wilhelmi Langii libr. de annis Christi per novam interpretationem & versionem: non auferetur sceptrum de Juda & legislator ab inter pedes ipsius sempèr; quia veniet Siloh. Quæ vere nova est Christianis auribus, etsi inter Judæos nova non sit, à quibus eam accepit. Siquidem Menasse Ben Israel similem plane producat in concil. qv. LXV. neque legislator à pedibus ejus in æternum, quando veniet Messias, quam Anqueli à Ger tribuit; sed Onkelos, quem הגר proselytum vocant, relinquit voculas עד־כי indistractas, & transfert easdem uti cæteri

Rabbini עד דייתי usque dum veniat ; illud vero עד עלמא de suo inferit, sic reddens : & scriba de filiis filiorum ejus, in seculum, donec veniat Messias. Notat autem Helvic. T. IV. Diss. Giess. Diss. 12. p. 304. depravationem illam apud R. Bechai reperiri & frequentem esse hodiernis Judæis, utpote qui negent statui hic terminum adventus Messiæ, & id solum doceri velint, quid post adventum ejus futurum sit. Quos vero solide refutat tum ex accentu pausante Athnach, qui antecedit vocem עד eamque referendum esse non ad antecedentia, sed consequentia docet, tum e perpetuo voculæ hujus, cum jungitur particulæ כי usu, quod עד־כי semper & ubique sit DONEC, usq́; dum, nuspiam autem in hac conjunctione perpetuitatem notet, tum e consensu Judæorum reliquorum & Christianorum universali, qui per DONEC interpretantur. Sic ergo Langius in Judæis, quibus velificatur, refutatus jam ab Helvico fuit, antequam oriretur. Quem copiosius refellit Sympatriota ipsius Dn. Joh. Wandalin. Danus in Diatribe Historico-Theologica de feria passionis & Triduo mortis Christi novis ac paradoxis ejus opinionibus opposita c. 9. p. 131.

Vers. eod. ET IPSE ERIT EXPECTATIO GENTIUM) יקהת pro diverso significatu in Hebræa vicinisque linguis diversis modis vertitur, puta προσδοκία exspectatio, obedientia, aggregatio. Sensus est quem jam attigimus, Messiam eximio modo & regem fore & Doctorem, non Judæorum modo, sed & omnium gentium. Hierosolymitanus hic : Ei servitura sunt regna terræ. Vid. Dan. 7, 14. Es. 11, 10. 49, 6. 55, 4. 60, 3. & vaticinia alia. Bereschith Rabba h. l. Futurum est, ut Gentes sæculi deferant munera Messiæ filio David.

## 49:11
v. 11. HE SHALL WASH HIS GARMENT IN WINE) So great will be the abundance of wine in his portion.

Latin:

v. 11. LAVABIT IN VINO STOLAM SVAM) Tanta erit in forte ejus vitium abundantia.

## 49:12
HIS EYES ARE MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN WINE) You would translate it better: 'His eyes shall be red from wine,' and thus what follows, 'and his teeth shall be white from milk,' namely because that portion of the land abounds as much in pastures as it does in vineyards.

Grotius the Christian sees less here than the older Jews, who understand these things of the Messiah and of his spiritual benefits. But he himself, with the more recent blinded Jews, preferred to be wise here in mere earthly and carnal things. But he is easily refuted from the context. For the subject here is not the tribe of Judah, but Shiloh, to whom shall be the obedience of the peoples: whom the Patriarch predicts will bind his foal to the vine and his ass's colt to the choice vine, who further adds, 'He shall wash his garment in wine.' Since these things all cohere, therefore, and treat of the same subject, they cannot, without corruption of the text, be explained of another subject, namely the descendants of Judah. Nor does the bodily sense fit. Asses are not bound to a vine, much less to an excellent vine, to carry grapes or to feed on grapes, which would have been more correctly said of a goat or a deer, which delight in vines. But for an ass, not a vineyard or clusters, but thistles and straw are suitable. Moreover, that one vine should bear so much wine that an ass could be loaded with it happens even in our regions; therefore, it would not be promised as something peculiar to the Holy Land or the tribe of Judah: although it is entirely different things to bind an ass to a vine and to load it with wine. Then what is more inept than to wash clothes in red wine? By which method you will soil them more than you will clean them, and Scripture praises white garments; how, therefore, can it be understood of that literal washing? As B. Luth. rightly [notes] here, who works these things out more laboriously. Furthermore, however much eyes may be red from wine (Prov. 23, 29), teeth do not become white from milk. Therefore, the Holy Fathers understood these things spiritually. Justin Martyr teaches that the things said about the ass and the colt look to the calling of the Gentiles just as much as the Jews to the kingdom of Christ, and that the bringing of the colt with the ass at the entry of Christ into the city of Jerusalem was signified by the same: Dial. with Trypho, p. 211, and Apol. II for the Christians. p. 57. But by the words 'washing his garment in the blood of the grape,' he says, he foretold his passion, which he was about to undergo, cleansing and purifying for himself those who believe through his blood. Therefore, he received the garment from the faithful. Concerning which in the Dial. with Trypho: 'The Holy Spirit called those who received remission of sins through him his garment: in whom he is continually present by his power, but he will be manifestly present at his second coming.' But that he says the word 'blood of the grape,' he explained very elegantly, that Christ indeed has blood, but not from the seed of man, but from the power of God. For just as man did not create the blood of the vine, but God: so he predicted that the blood of Christ himself would be not from the human race, but from the power of God. Thus also Origen interprets [it] in Homily XVII on Genesis, and Ambrose on the Gentiles in the book on the blessing of the Patriarchs, ch. IV: 'He shall wash the nations in his blood.' Most others understand by the garment the human nature of Christ, which is as it were the clothing of the Deity (Eph. 93, 1 [sic]; Apoc. 19, 13). These explanations are subordinate; if it be said that in the immediate sense the passion of Christ is designated, in which his flesh was properly washed in blood, but so that regard is had at the same time to the fruit, that by the power of the same we are washed from sins by the blood of Christ. Concerning these and the following words, St. Augustine [says] thus in book XVI of the City of God, ch. 41: 'His garment, moreover, which he washes in wine, i.e., cleanses from sins in his blood, the sacrament of which blood the baptized know; whence he also adds: "And in the blood of the grape his clothing," what is this but the Church? And his eyes are tawny from wine, his spiritual [eyes] inebriated by his cup. Concerning which the Psalm sings: "And thy cup inebriating, how excellent is it?" And his teeth whiter than milk: which little ones drink at the Apostle's, namely, nourishing words, not yet fit for solid food.' Some wish for red eyes to be attributed to Christ on account of his passion, during which he shed bloody tears for our sake; and white teeth, on account of his innocence, in which sense it is said in Cant. 5:10 that he is white and ruddy. But since the passion has been described earlier, the application of the same, which is done through the heralds of the word, seems to be more correctly designated here. This is excellently explained by the Blessed Luther in this passage, who departs from Justin and Augustine in that he does not interpret the washing of the garment as referring to the passion of Christ, as the Ordinary Gloss does with them; but he interprets it as the mortification of our flesh in this life, because this miserable life is like a garment and a tabernacle, about which the saints complain in 2 Cor. 5 and 1 Cor. 15. Such, he says, is the Christian life, to be bound daily to the vine, i.e., to the word, and to be inebriated either by the goods of the Spirit or by the word. Secondly, not only to be thus inebriated with the Spirit and filled with confidence, which is a most wholesome drunkenness for the new man, but also to be washed according to the old man in wine—the old rogue must still be washed, not with soap-water, but through the word, through the blood of the Son of God, which is sprinkled among us through the ministry of the word. For when we teach, we do nothing other than sprinkle and distribute the virtue of the blood of Christ among the people. Furthermore, he explained the redness of the eyes and the whiteness of the teeth in almost the same way that had been indicated by Augustine. To this also pertains, he says, the redness of the eyes, the dim, full, drunken eyes of Christ in his people and believers, which is not only to be understood when we ourselves are drunk, but when we have the Holy Spirit and are purged daily from the old leaven, and then we ought also to care for and govern others. For in the sacred scriptures the eye signifies a governor or teacher, and by the teeth are also denoted teachers, who ought to bite and rebuke vices. This is a true and good allegory, or rather, it is a spiritual and more proper understanding. And a little later: Thus the ministers of Christ are despised and rejected on account of this drunkenness of the Holy Spirit, because they do not speak gracious, pleasing, beautiful, mild, and acceptable things to men; they do not have charming eyes like girls, but sad and shamefully red ones. For it is not a pleasure for carnal men to hear the word, according to that passage in 1 Cor. 2: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him. People soon say: He is a complete fool, a hostile man, a heretic.

Such is the ministry, in the judgment of the whole world, which is most pure and most beautiful before God. For there are not red eyes there, but the eyes of Angels. But because the doctrine is hateful and contemptible, not pleasant and mild, but rather it refutes and offends the hearers, and speaks of things alien to reason, and altogether vile and foolish, therefore they clamor that the Apostles and the rest of the ministers are full of new wine, and yet they are eyes most pleasing to God, who govern, teach, and raise up afflicted minds with the word. Furthermore, the teeth are also whiter than milk, because they are full of consolation, and although they bite, yet they propose the best and sweetest things. The correction of the ministry does not kill, but rather heals and cures consciences; although we rebuke strongly and fix our teeth by refuting, correcting, and excommunicating, yet they are milky, that is, the rebuke of the ministers is wholesome and sweet. In this way I said that I understand this passage concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of the word, through which gifts the Holy Spirit is distributed among the people, and thus the kingdom of Christ is established. The Church hears the drunken and red eyes, and the white teeth, and is daily purged by the Spirit of judgment and of burning, Is. 4, unto eternal life. For thus the Patriarch described the Church with absurd words, in which a spiritual sense, not an allegorical one, is to be sought. For they are proper words, not allegorical. Thus the Blessed Luther. Conf. Exerc. D. VValth. on this passage. To Grotius here we still oppose only the Jews, who interpreted these things not of Judah or his tribe, but of the Messiah, and in part observed the mysteries in this oracle; both the commentators and the paraphrasts. Of these, Targ. Onkel. explained it thus: There shall be just men in his (the Messiah's) circuit, and doers of the law according to his doctrine. Fine purple shall be his garment, his covering silk dyed with scarlet and various colors. But the Targ. Hieros. rendered it in this way: How beautiful is King Messiah, who is about to rise from the house of Judah. He will bind his loins and go out into battle against his enemies. Kings will be killed with Princes. He will redden the rivers with blood and whiten his hills with the fat of their mighty ones. His garments will be imbued with blood. He himself, however, will be like the appearance of clusters. In the Rabbinical commentaries these things are observed: In Beresch. Rabba it is asked: What is it that Jacob says: binding his foal to the vine, etc.? And it is answered: He shows us that when the Messiah comes to save Israel, he himself will saddle his ass and ride upon it, and will come to Israel with poverty. R. Cabanna in his commentary on Phil. has it thus: Those words 'and to the branch, my son,' signify his ass, because the divinity and the Son of God will be united to the ass, i.e., to his matter, since חמר i.e., the material ass is interpreted. Just as an ass also carries burdens and the clothes of travelers: So King Messiah will carry the sins of the whole world upon himself. But when he says, he will wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape, the meaning is the same in different things, since garment signifies matter. See Galat. lib. 8 de Arc. Cath. ver. c. 9 and lib. 10 c. 7. P. Veidn. convers. Jud. in loc. fid. Christ. præcip. tr. 11. p. 234. We have dealt expressly with the Jacobite Oracle concerning Shiloh in our commentary on Genesis. We have also treated it in an academic program, which we append here.

Like a most shining gem in the Mosaic Genesis, the latest prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob shines through, by which he wished to rouse himself to endure the impending struggle of death with fortitude, and to lead his sons and grandsons, nay, what? his whole posterity, indeed not only his own posterity, but the very nations themselves to a like faith, I add, and to bind them as if by a testamentary sanction. And it is illustrious, and deservedly holds a chief place, not only because of its primeval antiquity, but because of the most eminent comprehension of the highest mysteries of the faith, and the most effective consolation, not of one or another nation, but in the common stock, the protoplasts, representing the place of all, for the whole human race, that Gospel which was promulgated in Paradise itself, so that he might be conscious of the reparation just as he was of the integrity and the fall: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. For in it, as the Blessed Luther has in his golden commentary, the Sun of consolation, previously as if wrapped in certain shadows of dark clouds, is lifted above the clouds, and looks upon terrified hearts with most pleasant light; because Adam and Eve not only do not hear themselves cursed, as the serpent is, but because they hear that they are established as if in a fortress against the condemned enemy, and that by the hope of the help which the Son of God, the Seed of the woman, is to bring to them. Here, therefore, the remission of sins and plenary reception into grace is shown to Adam and Eve, as if absolved from guilt, and redeemed from death, as if already liberated from hell and those terrors by which they were all but killed in the sight of God. Therefore Megalander deservedly calls this first consolation the fountain of all mercy and the source of all promises, which the first parents and their descendants learned with the greatest diligence; since they saw that if they were without this promise, a generation would indeed remain among men, as among other living creatures, but one which would be nothing other than a generation unto death: when, on the contrary, here there is hope of such a generation, through which the head of Satan is to be crushed, so that not only is his tyranny broken, but also nature, addicted to death on account of sin, may attain eternal life. Nor is the promise made to Abraham regarding his blessed seed ignoble, in which not only those who were to come from the loins of Abraham, but all the nations of the earth could obtain a blessing, nay indeed, if you look at the counsel and most gracious intention of God, they even ought to have obtained it; which therefore the Lord made not only to Abraham, but by which He also made the same Abraham, i.e., the Father of many nations, namely of all believers, who embrace the same promise with true faith and involve themselves in it, and insist upon the footsteps of the Abrahamic faith. Which also was judged by Jehovah to be worthy to be repeated many times, both to that prince of the Patriarchs, and to his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob, likewise most eminent Patriarchs, whose God the Lord deigned to call Himself by a peculiar formula. But if you weigh somewhat more accurately the power and ἐνέργειαν of this so significant promise, which the Apostle also called διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ εἰς χρισὸν Gal. 3, 7. for grave reasons, you will easily agree with the blessed Luther that it should be written in golden letters and celebrated by the tongues of all, since it offers eternal treasures, and from this promise have flowed all the sermons of the Prophets concerning Christ and His kingdom, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the gift of the Holy Spirit, concerning the preservation and government of the Church, concerning the punishments of the incredulous, etc. For they saw that these consequences were certainly connected to it: if the seed of Abraham will do this, it is necessary that He be a natural and true man; conversely, if He will also bless others, and indeed all the families of the earth, it is necessary that He also be something greater than the seed of Abraham. Because the seed of Abraham needs this blessing on account of sin. This is the day of Christ, in the judgment of Luther, of which He preaches in John, which Abraham did not see with bodily eyes, but saw in spirit and rejoiced. This promise also, as the blessed Luther again has it, entirely agrees with the sentiment of Christ: Go, preach the Gospel to every creature: Whoever shall have believed and been baptized, shall be saved. For what He says, all the families of the earth, is not to be understood only in breadth, concerning the families of one time, but in length, as long as the world shall stand. And we rightly oppose the blessing in this place to the curse, under which all men are on account of sin, which has been removed through Christ, and the blessing transferred to all who embrace Him and believe in His name. This therefore is that memorable benefit, that, freed from sin, from death, from the tyranny of the Devil, we are associated with the Angels of God and are made partakers of eternal life. These things concerning the earlier and most ancient promises [were said by] that mellifluous eloquence of a truly incomparable Theologian; than whom no one was better able either to unearth more accurately the hidden riches of Scripture, or, once unearthed, to bring them into the light and expose them more effectively to the eyes and minds of men. But the Jacobite prophecy also, which we have indicated, has its own significant prerogatives, which, if you look at the author, were brought forth by him through the Spirit of God, whom God had already ennobled in his mother's womb, whom He had never ceased to surround with His heavenly Mahanajim, to whom He had appeared more frequently and in more illustrious visions than to others, whom God the Father had sustained by a wonderful covenant, whom God the Son, the Angel Goel, had delivered from all evil in a peculiar way, God the Spirit S. in His sight, as the God of his fathers, Abraham and Isaac, had caused to walk, to whom the Lord had opened heaven on earth, and had shown the ladder by which he might ascend, and Himself also at the top of the ladder, with whom He had undergone a struggle—which was the most stupendous of all other stupendous things, the divine ὄραμα—and by whom the omnipotent and immense God Himself had allowed Himself to be overcome: Jacob, I say, from whom Christ the Messiah was called the God of Jacob, truly Jacob, and a supplanter, by whom the Son of God Himself was as it were supplanted in that wonderful struggle, so that from thence

May Israel be called the victor of God. If you weigh the prophecy itself, we have here the symbol of Jacob’s confession of faith, the foundation of the old Jewish polity and Church, the bulwark of Christianity, the compendium of Christology, the summary of the entire Christian religion, and the kernel of all Prophetic and Apostolic scripture. Here is presented, as the blessed Luther says, a balsam and a rose refreshing the heart; a rich fountain is exhibited, from which the Prophetic streams have overflowed most abundantly. The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall the gathering of the nations be. What forbids us to hear again the man of God, who in this place above all, which he animated with an inspired voice, ought to be heard more frequently, as to how he here opens the living fountain of doctrine and consolation by the divine spirit. In this manner, he says, Jacob speaks: That Leonine kingdom, and the Lion ordained divinely, shall stand and be governed by Doctors, Elders, and counselors, until the Son of the virgin comes, that is, the secondary one, if I may so say, or the son of the womb. This kingdom (he has it in Tom. IIX. Jen. against the Jews p. 64) in the tribe of Judah, says the Holy Spirit, is mine; no one shall take it from me, however evil and powerful he may be, even if they were the gates of hell; it shall therefore mean: It shall not be taken away. You devils and heathens may well say: It shall be taken away, we will devour it, we will silence it, as the 74th Psalm complains; but it shall remain for me undevoured and undevastated; neither the scepter nor the sultan shall depart from the house of Judah, nor the scribe from his children’s children, even if you all become mad and foolish, until Shiloh or the Messiah comes. And when he comes, it shall be much different and more glorious. For since you would not suffer the tribe of Judah in a narrow little corner, I will first make a truly great lion out of him, who shall become sultan and scribe in all the world. And I will make it so that he shall not draw a sword, nor shed a single drop of blood, but the nations shall, unforced, willingly make themselves subject and obedient to him. That shall be his kingdom, for it is after all the kingdom and everything is his. And these things concerning the person and the time of the advent of King Messiah, which he excellently executes in the same place against the blinded Jews. But what his kingdom is like, what the worship of this King is like, and what benefits are to be expected under his rule, our Doctor discourses thus from the present prophecy: Not by sword, not by flame, not by force, but by hearing or by the report and doctrine of faith shall Shiloh reign, and not only the Jews, but all the peoples of the whole world shall obey him: And then: In the time of the Messiah there shall be such glory, opulence, and fertility that even donkeys and the foals of donkeys shall eat grapes and clusters. The donkey shall for once have good days and drink wine. According to nature, the binding of a donkey to a vine is indeed most alien, and Jacob would have said it more correctly of a goat or a stag, which delight in vines; but for a donkey, not vineyards or clusters, but thistles and straw are suitable. I understand, therefore, that Jacob speaks in the Holy Spirit of the admirable kingdom of Christ and its opulence, in which even donkeys and the foals of a donkey shall eat grapes and drink wine and be inebriated, namely with a spiritual inebriation: for this ought to reign in the time of the Messiah, when the hearing of the peoples shall begin, but let us see how the washing of garments corresponds to this. There was a great use in those regions of white and fine linen garments, especially at festivals. How, therefore, will a white stole be washed in red wine? It is a most absurd thing, like the binding of a donkey to a vine; therefore, this particle also must be taken concerning the opulence of the Holy Spirit, who, when he is given, all things shall flow with milk and honey and the best wine, in which they shall even wash their garments, nor will there be need of water, because all things shall abound with wine. First we are inebriated like the donkey and the foal of a donkey with wine in those vineyards; that is, with the divine promise in the Holy Spirit, who is the vine, the grape, and the wine, which lifts us up and makes us proud and contemners of the Devil and death. But what remains washes and purges in the old man, until we rise again in incorruptibility, then we shall be entirely clean. Let everyone, therefore, with this Doctor of ours leading, say: I, compelled and urged by the salvation of souls, wish to be bound to the vine, like a foal, and to the choice vine. I am a poor donkey, but I like to eat good grapes and also like to drink good wine. I wish to be washed by the blood of this Shiloh and the blood of grapes, or the gifts of the Holy Spirit. I will also hear my Hachilim, who have red and despised eyes and white teeth in the world, because they rebuke me and teach Christ; they bite me with their teeth, but they seek not my destruction, but my salvation. Thus the man of God searched into these Jacobite veins for the treasures of heavenly wisdom, which divine eloquence explains more fully, etc.

Latin:

PVLCHRIORES SVNT OCVLI EJVS VINO) Melius vertas : Rubebunt oculi ejus ex vino, & sic quod sequitur, & candidi erunt dentes ejus ex lacte, nimirum quod illa terræ portio ut vinetis ita & pascuis abundet.

Minus hic videt Grotius Christianus, quam antiquiores Judæi, qui hæc de Messia intelligunt ac de spiritualibus ejus beneficiis. Sed maluit ipse cum recentior. excæcatis Judæis mera terrena & carnalia hic sapere. Refellitur autem facile e contextu. Non enim subjectum h. l. est tribus Juda, sed Schilo, cui erit obedientia populorum : quem ligaturum ad vitem pullum suum & ad generosam vitem asinam suam prædicit Patriarcha, qui porro subjungit, Lavabit in vino stolam suam. Hæc ergo cum cohæreant omnia, & de eodem subjecto agant, non possunt absque depravatione textus de alio subjecto, nimirum de posteris Judæ explicari. Neque convenit sensus corporalis. Non ligantur ad vitem asini, nedum ad vitem optimam, ut uvas portent aut ut uvis pascantur, quod de capro aut cervo rectius dictum foret, qui delectantur vitibus. Asino vero non vinea aut botri, sed tribuli & paleæ conveniunt. Unam autem vitem tantum vini ferre, ut eo possit asinus onerari, etiam in nostris contingit regionibus, non ergo aliquod proprium terræ S. aut tribui Judæ ita promitteretur : quamvis diversa omnino sint, ligare asinum ad vitem, & onerare eum vino. Tum quid ineptius est, quam lavare vestes in rubro vino? qua ratione magis eas pollues, quam elues, & Scriptura laudat vestimenta candida; quomodo igitur intelligi potest de lotione illa literali? ut recte hic B. Luth. qui operosius ista exequitur. Porro utut oculi e vino rubeant Prov. 23, 29. a lacte tamen dentes candidi non fiunt. Ideo spiritualiter hæc intellexere S. Patres. Justinus Martyr, quæ de asino & pullo dicuntur, vocationem gentium æque uti Judæorum ad regnum Christi, & qua eadem significata, adductionem pulli cum asina sub ingressum Christi in urbem Hierosolym. respicere docet : Dial. cum Tryph. p. 211. & Apol. II. pro Christian. p. 57. Verbis autem lavans in sanguine uvæ stolam suam, passionem, inquit, ejus, quam subiturus erat, prænuntiavit, per sanguinem lustrans atque purificans sibi credentes. Stolam itaque accepit de fidelibus. Quo de Dial. cum Tryph. Stolam ejus vocavit Sp. S. eos, qui per illum remissionem pecca- torum acceperunt: in quibus continenter virtute adest, manifeste autem aderit in secundo adventu suo. Quod vero verbum sanguinem uvæ dicit, pereleganter decla- ravit, sanguinem quidem habere Christum, verum non ex hominis semine, sed ex Dei virtute. Quemadmodum enim vitis sanguinem non homo creavit, sed Deus: sic & ipsius Christi sanguinem non ex humano genere, verum ex Dei virtute fore prædixit. Ita etiam interpretatur Orig. de Ecclesia Hom. XVII. in Genes. & Ambrof. de gentibus l. de benedict. Patriarch. c. IV. Lavabit gentes sanguine suo. Alii pleriq; per stolam humanam Christi naturam intelligunt, quæ veluti vestimentum Deitatis est Ef. 93, 1. Apoc. 19, 13. Quæ explicationes subordinatæ sunt; Si dicatur, immediato quidem sensu designari passionem Christi in qua lota probe sanguine fuit caro ejus, sed ut respectus habeatur si- mul ad fructum, quod vi ejusdem nos abluamur san- guine Christi a peccatis. De his & sequentibus verbis ita S. Aug. l. XVI. de Civ. Dei c. 41. Stolam porro ejus, quam lavat in vino, i. e. mundat a peccatis in sangui- ne suo, cujus sanguinis sacramentum baptizati sciunt; unde & adjungit: Et in sanguine uvæ amictum suum, quid est nisi Ecclesia? Et fulvi oculi ejus a vino spiri- tuales ejus inebriati poculo ejus. De quo canit Ps. Et calix tuus inebrians, quam præclarus est? Et dentes ejus candidiores lacte: quod potant apud Apostolum parvuli, verba sc. nutrientia, nondum idonei solido ci- bo. Nonnulli Christo oculos volunt tribui rubicundos propter passionem; qua sanguineas lacrumas propter nos effudit; dentes vero albos, propter innocentiam, quo fere sensu Cant. 5, 10. dicatur candidus & rubicun- dus. Sed quum passio prius descripta fuerit: hic ejus- dem applicatio, quæ fit per verbi præcones, rectius designari videtur. Quod præclare explicat B. Luth. in h. l. qui in eo a Justino & Augustino abit, quod non de passione Christi, uti Glossa ordinaria cum illis ex- ponit, vestimenti lotionem accipiat; sed de mortifica- tione carnis nostræ in hac vita, quia miserabilis hæc vita velut indumentum & tabernaculum est, de quo Sancti queruntur 2. Cor. 5. 1. Cor. 15. interpretetur. Talis, inquit, est vita Christiana, ligari quotidie ad vi- tem, i. e. ad verbum, & inebriari vel bonis Spiritus vel verbo. Secundo non solum sic inebriari spiritu & im- pleri fiducia, quæ novo homini saluberrima ebrietas est, sed etiam lavari secundum veterem hominem in vi- no, der alte Schalck muß noch gewaschen werden, nicht mit Seiffen-Wasser, sed per verbum, per san- guinem Filii Dei, qui spargitur inter nos per ministerium verbi. Quando enim docemus, nihil aliud agimus, quam quod spargimus & dividimus virtutem sanguinis Christi in populum. Cæterum rubedinem oculorum & dentium candorem eadem ferme ratione, quæ ab August. indigitata erat, exposuit. Huc pertinet etiam, inquit, rubedo oculorum, die blöden, vollen, vertrun- cken Augen Christi in suis populis & credentibus, quæ non tantum intelligenda est, cum nos ipsi sumus ebrii, sed cum habemus Sp. S. & purgamur quotidie a fer- mento veteri, deinde alios quoque curare debemus & gubernare. Oculus enim significat in sacris literis guber- natorem, doctorem, & per dentes etiam notantur do- ctores, qui debent mordere & reprehendere vitia. Hæc vera & bona allegoria, imo potius spiritualis & pro- prius intellectus est. Et paulo post: Ita ministri Christi spreti & abjecti sunt, propter hanc ebrietatem Sp. S. quia non loquuntur gratiosa, non placentia, non pulcra, non blanda & grata hominibus, non habent oculos venustos, ut puellæ, sed tristes & turpiter ru- bentes. Non enim voluptas est hominibus carna- libus audire verbum, juxta illud 1. Cor. 2. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Stul- titia enim est illi. Man spricht bald: Es ist ein voller Narr, ein feindseliger Mensch, ein Ketzer.

Tale est ministerium, totius mundi judicio, quod coram Deo est purissimum & pulcherrimum. Ibi enim non sunt rubentes oculi, sed oculi Angelorum. Quia vero est doctrina odiosa & contem- ptibilis, non jucunda & blanda, quin potius arguit & offendit Auditores, ac loquitur de rebus alienis a ratione, & omnino vili- bus & stultis, ideo clamitant esse plenos musto Apostolos, & reli- quos ministros, & tamen sunt oculi Deo gratissimi, qui gubernant, docent & erigunt verbo afflictas mentes. Deinde dentes quoque lacte candidiores sunt, quia sunt pleni consolatione, & quan- quam mordent, tamen proponunt optima, & suavissima. Corre- ptio ministerii non occidit, sed sanat potius, & medetur conscien- tiis, tametsi fortiter increpamus & infigimus dentes arguendo, corripiendo, & excommunicando, tamen lactei sunt, h.e. salutaris & suavis increpatio est ministrorum. Ad hunc modum dixi me in- telligere hunc locum de donis Sp. S. & ministerio verbi, per quæ dona Sp. S. distribuitur in populum, & sic constituitur regnum Christi. Ecclesia audit temulentos & rubentes oculos, & albos dentes, & quotidie purgatur per Sp. judicii & ardoris Es. 4. ad vitam æternam. Ita enim verbis absurdis descripsit Patriarcha Ecclesiam, in quibus sensus spiritualis, non allegoricus quærendus est. Sunt enim verba propria, non allegorica. Hæct. B. Luth. Conf. Exerc. D. VValth. in h. l. Grotio hic tantum adhuc opponimus Judæos, qui hæc non de Juda aut tribu ejus, sed de Messia inter- pretati sunt, & ex parte gemina observarunt mysteria in hoc oraculo; eosq; cum Commentatores, tum Paraphrastas. Ex his Targ. Onkel. ita exposuit: Erunt justi in circuitu ejus (Messia)& factores legis juxta doctrinam ejus. Purpura bona erit vestimen- tum ejus, operimentum ejus sericum tinctum Coccino variisq; co- loribus. Targ. vero Hieros. hoc modo reddidit: Quam pulcher est Rex Messias, qui surrecturus est de domo Juda. Ligabit lum- bos suos & exibit in prælium adversus hostes suos. Occidentur Re- ges cum Principibus. Rubefaciet fluvios sanguine & dealbabit col- les suos pinguedine fortium illorum. Vestimenta ejus imbuentur sanguine. Ipse autem similis erit formæ botrorum. In Comm. Rabb. hæc observata sunt: In Beresch. Rabba quæritur: Quid est, quod dicit Jacob: ligans ad vitem pullum &c. & respondetur: O- stendit nobis, quod cum venerit Messias ad salvandum Israel, ipse sternet asinum suum & equitabit super illum, & veniet in Israel cum paupertate. R. Cabanna in Com. ad Phil. ita habet: Verba il- la & ad Palmitem, o Fili mi, asinum suum significant, quod divi- nitas & Dei Filius unietur asino, i. e. materiæ suæ, quoniam חמר i. e. asinus materialis interpretatur. Quemadmodum etiam asinus fert onera & vestes viatorum: Ita Rex Messias delicta totius orbis super se portabit. Cum autem dicit, lavabit in vino vestem suam, & in sanguine uvæ pallium suum, eadem est sen- tentia diversis rebus, quoniam vestis dicit materiam. Vid. Galat. l. 8. de Arc. Cath. ver. c. 9. & l. 10. c. 7. P.VVeidn. convers. Jud. in loc. fid. Christ. præcip. tr. 11. p. 234. Ex professo autem de Oraculo Jacobæo deSchilo egimus in Com. nostro in Gen. Tractavimus etiam in programmate aliquo Academico, quod hic subjicimus.

Instar gemmulæ nitidissimæ in Genesi Mosaica, pellucet Prophetia Patriarchæ Jacob novissima, qua fese ad agonem mortis imminentem fortiter su- stinendum excitare, filios vero, nepotesque suos, quid ? totam posteritatem, imo non suam modo posteritatem, gentes ipsas universas ad parilem fi- dem deducere, addo & testamentaria veluti san- ctione obstringere voluit. Et illustre est, & prin- cipem merito locum obtinet, non ob antiquitatem modo primævam, sed ob eminentissimam summo- rum fidei mysteriorum complexionem, & efficacis- simam, non unius aut alterius gentis, sed in commu- ni stipite, protoplastis, vicem omnium referenti- bus, totius generis humani consolationem, Evan- gelium illud, quod in ipso adhuc Paradiso, ne non uti integritatis ac prævaricationis, ita etiam re- parationis idem conscius esset, promulgatum fuit: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. In eo enim, ut B. Luth. aureus habet comment. Sol consolationis, antea quasi tenebris quibusdam caliginosarum nubium involutis, supra nubes attolli- tur, & jucundissimo lumine territa corda aspicit; Quod Adam & Heva non solum non audiunt, sibi maledici, sicut serpenti, sed quod audiunt, se constitui tanquam in arce contra damnatum hostem, idque spe auxilii, quod eis laturus sit filius Dei, Semen mu- lieris. Hic igitur remissio peccatorum, & plenaria receptio in gra- tiam Adæ & Hevæ ostenditur, tanquam absolutis a culpa, & re- demtis a morte, tanquam liberatis jam ex inferno & illis pavori- bus, quibus in conspectu Dei tantum non occisi sunt. Hanc ergo primam consolationem merito fontem omnis misericordiæ, & omnium promissionum scaturiginem appellat Megalander, quam primi parentes, & eorum posteri summa diligentia didicerint; Si- quidem viderint, si absque hac promissione essent, mansuram qui- dem inter homines, sicut inter reliqua animantia, generationem, sed qua nihil aliud sit, quam generatio ad mortem: quum e contra hic spes fiat talis generationis, per quam Satanæ sit conterendum caput, ut non solum ejus tyrannis infringatur, sed etiam natu- ra, propter peccatum morti addicta, consequatur vitam æternam. Nec ignobilis est promissio, Abrahæ facta, de be- nedicto ipsius semine, in quo non tantum, qui ex lum- bis Abrahæ prodituri erant, sed gentes terræ omnes benedictionem consequi poterant, imo vero, si Dei spe- ctes consilium, atque gratiosissimam intentionem, consequi etiam debebant; Quam proinde non Abra- hamo tantum fecit Dominus, sed qua eundem etiam Abrahamum fecit, h. e. Patrem multarum gentium, omnium nempe credentium, qui eandem promissio- nem vera fide amplectuntur eique sese involvunt, & vestigiis fidei Abrahamicæ insistunt. Quæ etiam di- gna a Jehovah judicata est, ut multoties repeteretur, cum ad illum Patriarcharum principem, tum ad fil. Isaacum, & nepot. Jacobum, Patriarchas itidem eminentissimos, quorum Deum peculiari formula Deus sese nuncupare dignatus est. Quod si vim & ἐνέργειαν hujusce tam insignis promissionis, quam etiam διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ εἰς χρισὸν Gal. 3, 7. ob graves causas dixit Apost. paulo accu- ratius expendas, aureis literis eam scribendam & omnium linguis celebrandam esse B. Luth. facile adsti- pulaberis, quandoquidem æternos thesauros offerat, & ex hac promissione fluxerint omnes Prophetarum con- ciones de Christo & regno ejus, de remissione peccato- rum, de donatione Sp. S. de Ecclesiæ conservatione & gubernatione, de pœnis incredulorum &c. Nam has vi- derunt consequcntias inde certo connecti, si semen Abra- hæ hoc faciet, necesse est, ut sit naturalis & verus homo, contra si etiam alios, & quidem omnes familias terræ benedicet, necesse est, ut etiam majus aliquid sit, quam semen Abrahæ. Quia semen Abrahæ propter peccatum hac benedictione indiget. Hic est dies Christi judice Luthero, de quo concionatur in Johanne, quem Abra- ham oculis corporeis non vidit, sed vidit spiritu & gavi- sus est. Hæc etiam promissio, ut rursus habet. B. Luth. prorsus convenit cum Christi sententia: Ite, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ: Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Quod enim dicit, omnes familiæ terræ, non in latitudinem tantum intelligen- dum est, de familiis unius temporis, sed in longitudinem, donec mundus steterit. Et recte opponimus benedictio- nem hoc in loco maledictioni, sub qua omnes homines sunt propter peccatum, quod per Christum sublatum est, & benedictio translata in omnes, qui eum amplectun- tur & credunt in nomine ejus. Hoc ergo memorabile il- lud beneficium est, quod liberati a peccato, a morte, a ty- rannide Diaboli, associamur Angelis Dei & participes efficimur æternæ vitæ. Hæc de prioribus & antiquissi- mis promissionibus melliflua illa Svada Theologi vere incomparabilis; quo divitias Scripturæ recon- ditas vel eruere accuratius, vel erutas in apricum producere, hominumque & oculis, & mentibus ex- ponere efficacius valuit nemo. Habet autem Jaco- bæa quoque, quam indigitavimus, Prophetia insi- gnes suas prærogativas, quæ, si autorem spectes, ab eo per Sp. Dei prolata est, quem in utero matris jam nobilitarat Deus, quem cœlestibus suis Mahanajim nunquam non stipaverat, cui præ reliquis frequen- ter & illustrioribus visionibus apparuerat, quem Deus Pater mirabili pacto sustentarat, Deus Filius, Angelus Goel, ab omni malo peculiari ratione li- berarat, Deus Spir. S. in conspectu suo, ceu Dei Pa- trum suorum, Abrahami, & Isaaci, ambulare fecerat, cui cœlum in terris aperuerat Dominus, & scalam, qua conscenderet, ac seipsum quoque in cacumine scalæ ostentarat, quicum, quod præ omnibus aliis stupendis maxime stupendum erat divinum ὄραμα, conflictum subierat, & quo ipse omnipotens & im- mensus Deus sese superari passus fuerat: Jacob, in- quam, a quo Christus Messias Dei Jacob dictus, vere Jacob, & supplantator, a quo ipse Filius Dei in mi- rabili illo agone veluti supplantatus fuit, ut inde

Israel victor Dei nuncupatus sit. Si vaticinium ipsum expendas, habemus hic confessionis fidei Jacobae symbolum, veteris Judaicae politiae & Ecclesiae funda- mentum, Christianismi firmamentum, Christologiae compendium, universae Christianae religionis summa- rium, totiusq́; scripturae Propheticae & Apostolicae nu- cleum. Sistitur hic, ut B. Luth. loquitur, Balsamum & ros corda refrigerans; exhibetur dives scaturigo, e qua Prophetica fluenta largissime redundarunt. Non aufe- retur sceptrum de Juda, & legislator de pedibus ejus, donec veniat Schilo, & ad illum gentes congregabun- tur. Quid vetat iterum audire virum Dei, qui hoc imprimis loco, quem enthea animavit voce, fre- quentius audiri debet, quomodo divino spiritu fon- tem vivum doctrinae & consolationis hic aperiat. In hunc, inquit, modum loquitur Jacob: Regnum illud Leoninum, & Leo ordinatus divinitus stabit, & guber- nabitur a Doctoribus, Senioribus, & consiliariis, do- nec veniat virginis Filius, hoc est, secundinarius, ut sic dicam, seu uteratis filius. Diß Königreich (habet Tom. IIX. Jen. contra Judaeos p. 64.) im Stamm Juda, spricht der H. Geist, ist mein, das soll mir niemand weg- nehmen, wie böse und mächtig er sey, wenns gleich der Höllen Pforten wären, es soll also heissen: Non aufe- retur, ihr Teuffel und Heyden sprecht wohl: Aufere- tur, wir wollens fressen, wir wollens stille machen, wie der 74. Psalm klaget; Aber es soll mir ungefressen, un- verwüstet bleiben, es soll der Schevet, noch der Sultan nicht vom Hause Juda wegkommen, noch der Saphra von seinen Kindes-Kindern, wenn ihr gleich alle toll und thöricht würdet, biß der Silo oder Messia komme. Und wenn derselbe komt, so solls noch viel anders und herrlicher werden. Denn da ihr den Stamm Juda nicht habet wollen leiden in einem engen kleinen Win- ckel, will ich allererst einen rechten grossen Löwen aus ihm machen, der in aller Welt Sultan und Sapyra werden soll. Und wills also machen, daß er kein Schwerdt zücken soll, noch einigen Tropffen Bluts vergiessen, sondern die Völcker sollen ungezwungen sich selbst und gern ihm unterthänig und gehorsam machen. Das soll sein Königreich seyn, denn es ist doch das Reich und alles sein. Atque haec de persona & tempore adventus Regis Messiae, quae adversus ex- coecatos Judaeos praeclare ibidem exequitur. Quale vero ejus regnum, qualis Regis hujus cultus, qualia sub regimine ejusdem beneficia expectanda sint, ita e vaticinio praesenti edisserit Doctor noster: Non gladio, non flamma, non vi, sed audientia sive auditu & doctrina fidei regnabit Schilo, & obedient ei non solum Judaei, sed omnes populi totius orbis terrarum: Et dein- ceps: Tempore Messiae erit tanta gloria, opulentia & fertilitas, ut etiam asini & pulli asinarum voraturi sint uvas & botros. Der Esel soll einmahl gute Tage haben und Wein sauffen. Secundum naturam quidem alie- nissima ligatio est asini ad vitem, ac rectius de capro, aut cervo id dixisset Jacob, qui delectantur vitibus, Asino ve- ro non vineae, aut botri, sed tribuli & paleae conveniunt. Intelligo igitur, Jacob loqui in Spiritu S. de admirabili regno Christi, & opulentia ejus, in qua etiam asini & pulli asinae comedent uvas, & bibent vinum, ac inebria- buntur, spirituali nempe ebrietate: Haec enim regna- re debet tempore Messiae, quando incipiet audientia po- pulorum, sed videamus, quomodo lotio vestimentorum ad haec congruat. Magnus usus fuit in istis regionibus candidarum vestium, & byssinarum, praesertim in festi- vitatibus. Quomodo igitur lavabitur stola alba in vino rubro? Absurdissima res est, sicut ligatio asini ad vitem, ideo accipienda est & haec particula de opulentia S. S. qui cum dabitur, fluent omnia lacte & melle, & vino oprimo, in quo etiam vestimenta lavabunt, nec opus erit aqua, quia abundabunt omnia vino. Primum inebria- mur sicut asinus, & filius asinae vino in vineis illis; hoc est, promissione divina in S. S. qui est vitis, uva, & vi- num, quod nos erigit, & facit superbos, & contemtores Diaboli & mortis. Quod vero reliquum est, in veteri ho- mine lavat & purgat, donec resurgamus in incorrupti- bilitate, da werden wir gar rein seyn. Dicat ergo quis- que præeunte hoc Doctore nostro: Ego, salute ani- marum cogente & urgente, volo ligari ad vitem, ut pul- lus, & ad Sorek. Bin ein armer Esel, ich eß aber gerne gute Trauben, trinck auch gern guten Wein. Volo la- vari sanguine hujus Schilo & sanguine uvarum, seu donis Sp. S. Audiam etiam meos Hachilim, qui habent oculos rubentes, & contemtos, & dentes albos in mun- do, quia corripiunt me, & docent Christum, dentibus suis me mordent, verum non perditionem, sed salutem meam quærunt. Ita scrutatus est in his venis Jaco- bæis thesauros cœlestis sapientiæ Vir Dei, quos di- vina eloquentia explicat uberius &c.

ver. 22. AND COMELY IN APPEARANCE) For עלי עין he seems to have read עליון as also the LXX, who translate it ζηλωτός.

v. 23. THEY HAVE STRIFE) Both this Interpreter and Rabbi Solomon read as if it were from רוב, not from רבב, as we now read. But that which the Hebrew codex has agrees better with what follows. And thus the Greeks read, ἐνεῖχον.

## 49:24
v. 24. BY THE HANDS OF THE MIGHTY ONE OF JACOB: THENCE THE SHEPHERD WENT FORTH, THE STONE OF ISRAEL.

Coccejus in the last of Moses §. 832. renders it from the hands of the Hero of Jacob thence where he is (a common brevity in Hebrew for מאשר שם) the Shepherd the Stone of Israel, that is to say, from heaven, where the Son of God is, who feeds Joseph and Israel, or thus: Thence (understand from the hands of the Hero Joseph) is the Shepherd the Stone of Israel. He who will give the Shepherd his Son as a sustainer and the hope of Israel, he also will grant that your bow may be placed in a high and fortified place. But these things are distorted. Nor does the accentuation permit that construction, feeding Israel. The interpretation of others is simpler, that it is from God (from the mighty one of Jacob) that Joseph was the Shepherd of the Egyptians, and the stone or Rock of refuge for the Israelites.

Latin:

v. 24. PER MANVS POTENTIS JACOB: INDE PA- STOR EGRESSVS EST, LAPIS ISRAEL.

Coccejus in ult. Mos. §. 832. reddit a manibus Herois Jacobi inde ubi est (breviloquium usitatum in E- bræo pro מאשר שם( Pastor Lapis Israelis, q. d. e cœlo, ubi est Filius Dei, qui pascit Josephum & Israe- lem, vel sic: Inde (intellige a manibus Herois Jose- phi) est Pastor Lapis Israelis. Qui dabit Pastorem Fi- lium suum sustentatorem, & spem Israelis, is quoque dabit, ut arcus tuus sit in edito & munito loco posi- tus. Sed distorta hæc sunt. Neque accentuatio per- mittit illam constructionem, pascens Israelem. Sim- plicior est aliorum interpretatio, quod a Deo sit (a forti Jacobi) quod Josephus Pastor fuerit Ægyptio- rum, & lapis sive Petra refugii Israelitarum.

## 50:3 Addition
On chapter 50:3. AND WEPT FOR HIM SEVENTY DAYS. on page 385. b.

To the 40 days of embalming they added another 30 days of mourning. Among the Jews, both embalming and mourning together were otherwise only 30 days. See Num. 20:29, Deut. last chapter. Therefore, great honor was shown to Jacob, and almost royal. For the mourning of kings in Egypt was 72 days, according to Diodorus Siculus, book 1. It was decided to subtract only two days, either so that there might be some distinction between him and the King, as seemed right to the blessed Quistorpius the Elder, or because the number of seventy days was considered religious; see verse 10.

Latin:

Ad c. 50, 3. FLEVITQUE EUM SEPTUAGIN- TA DIEBUS. ad pag. 385. b.

Ad dies 40. condituræ adhuc alios 30. dies addidere luctus. Fuerunt Judæis alias & condi- turæ & luctus simul tantum 30. dies. Vid. Num. 20, 29. Deut. ult. Magnus ergo honor exhibitus Jacobo est: & pene Regius. Luctus enim Regum in Ægypto fuit 72. dierum: teste Diodor. Sic l. 1. duos ergo tantum dies demere placuit, sive ut in- ter hunc & Regem discrimen aliquod esset, uti vi- sum Beat. Quistorpio Seniori, sive quod decies se- ptenarius dierum numerus religiosus haberetur; vid. vers. 10.

But it seems that bought should be taken for acquired by purchase. For Abraham had bought it from Hamor. Acts 7, 10. The title of the author is the title of the heir.

Latin:

## 50:19
Ver. 19. CAN WE RESIST THE WILL OF GOD?) in the Hebrew it is now: Am I instead of God? Which Symmachus, retaining the interrogation, translates: μή γὰρ ἀντὶ θεῦ ἐγώ; Aquila, with the interrogation explained by a negation, ὅτι μὴ θεῦ ἐγώ. But formerly for המחת it was in Samaritan codices older than those which we now have דחלתי, whence it is that the Greek Scholiasts translate, 'for I am a God-fearing man,' which there is no reason to dislike. For so also the Chaldean.

Quite confidently, nay, too boldly, Hugo alters the original text from mere conjecture regarding the reading of the Greek Scholiasts and the interpretation of the Chaldean, against the consensus of all Hebrew Codices, the reading of Symmachus, Aquila, the Samaritan Interpreter, I add also the LXX Elders, as well as the Syrian Interpreter. Although he could also have brought forward the Arabic version of the Pentateuch, edited by Erpenius for the Moorish Jews, as also R. Saadia Gaon, and that which is contained in the Parisian Heptapla, which also has: 'I fear the Lord': in which manner Nobilius observes that the Samaritans also read. But it would have had to be read דחלתי which indeed ought to be explained transitively, 'I terrified': from דחל 'he was terrified, struck with fear,' as Hottinger observes in the Thesaurus Philologicus, p. 272. Nor can those interpretations prejudice the older Greeks and the consensus of the Hebrew Codices: with which the ancient Syriac translation is in conformity; because 'I am under God.' From which it appears that the Chaldean and those Arabs did not indeed read otherwise, but acted here as Paraphrasts rather than Metaphrasts: For what else is that, 'Am I in the place of God?' And, 'Am I not under God?' or affirmatively, 'because I am under God just as you are': which they further explained thus: 'because I fear God': for he who is under God, it is his duty to fear God: it is also his duty not to resist the will of God, so that even in this way the Vulgate may be brought into harmony.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NVM DEI POSSVMVS RESISTERE VO- LVNTATI?) in Hebræo nunc est: Numquid pro Deo ego? Quod Symmachus interrogatione retenta vertit: μή γὰρ ἀντὶ θεῦ ἐγώ; Aquila, interrogatione per negationem explica- ta, ὅτι μὴ θεῦ ἐγώ. At olim pro המחת fuit in Codicibus Sa- maritanis vetustioribus, quam quæ nunc habemus דחלתי, unde est, quod Scholiastæ Græci vertunt, καὶ γὰρ φοβούμενος θεόν εἰμι ἐγώ, quod non est, cur displiceat. Nam sic & Chaldæus.

Satis confidenter, imo audacter nimis ex mera conjectura de Scholiastarum Græcorum lectione, & interpretatione Chaldæi, contra consensum omnium Codicum Ebræorum, lectionem Symmachi, Aquilæ, Samaritani Interpretis, addo & LXX. Seniorum, ut & Syri Interpretis, textum originalem immutat Hugo. Quamvis etiam adducere potuisset versio- nem Arabicam Pentateuchi, Judæorum Maurorum ab Erpenio editam, ut & R. Saadia Gaon, & quæ in Parisienfibus Heptaplis habetur, quæ etiam habet: Ego timeo Dominum: quo pacto Nobilius in Bibliis Samaritanos quoque legisse observat. Sed ita legen- dum fuisset דחלתי quod vero transitive explicari deberet, terrui: a דחל territus, timore perculsus fuit, ut observat Hottingerus in thesauro Philolog. p. 272. Nec præjudicare possunt illæ interpretationes antiquioribus Græcis, & consensui Ebræorum Codi- cum: quibus conformis antiqua Syriaca translatio; quia sub Deo ego sum. E qua apparet, Chaldæum & Arabes illos non aliter quidem legisse, sed Para- phrastas potius, quam Metaphrastas hic egisse: Nam quid aliud illa, Num ego loco Dei? Et, Annon ego sub Deo? vel affirmative, quia ego sub Deo pariter atque vos: quod illi ulterius ita exposuerunt: quia ego ti- meo Deum: qui enim sub Deo est, ejus est timere Deum: ejus etiam est non resistere voluntati Dei, ut vel sic etiam ad consonantiam redigatur Vulgatus.

Vers. 24. WITH YOU) The Samaritan, the Syrian, and the LXX, whom the Latin follows, append this either to complete the sense or from other Codices.

Latin:

Vers. 24. VOBISCVM) Hoc aut ad sensum explendum, aut ex Codicibus aliis apponunt Samaritanus, Syrus, LXX. quos Latinus sequitur.

## 50:25
Vers. 25. HE DIED HAVING COMPLETED ONE HUNDRED AND TEN YEARS OF HIS LIFE. He saw his grandsons to the third generation, namely Sutelah and Tahan, the sons of Ephraim, and Hadan (or Haran, Num. 26:36), the son of Sutelah: and likewise Machir the son of Manasseh, and Gilead, his grandson, whence the LXX Interpreters, adding these five born after the arrival of Jacob in Egypt, made the number of 75 souls, the families of Jacob and Joseph, which was said to consist of 70 heads, Gen. 46:27 and Deut. 10:22, 1 Chron. 7. Joseph therefore held the prefecture in Egypt for a full 80 years, and that under different Kings. Eusebius in his Chronicle arranged the series of years thus: Joseph becomes Leader of Egypt in the 30th year of his age, the 122nd of his father Jacob, which leadership he held for 80 years. After whose death the Hebrews served the Egyptians for 144 years. The total number of years which the Hebrews spent in Egypt is 215, which are computed from the same time that Jacob went down into Egypt with his sons.

Latin:

Vers. 25. MORTUUS EST EXPLETIS CENTUM DECEM VITÆ SUÆ ANNIS. Vidit Nepotes suos ad tertiam generationem, Sutelacho nimirum, & Tachane Ephraimi filiis & Hadane, (sive Harane Num. 26, 36.) Sutelachi filio : itemque Machir Manassis filio, & Gilead, nepote, unde LXX. Interpp. familiæ Jacobi & Josephi, quæ 70. capitibus constare dicebatur Gen. 46, 27. & Deut. 10, 22. hos quinque post adventum Jacobi in Ægypto natos 1. Chron. 7. adjicientes, 75. animarum numerum effecerunt. Gessit itaque Josephus præfecturam in Ægypto integris XXC. annis idque sub diversis Regibus. Annorum seriem ita digessit in Chronic. Eusebius : Joseph Dux Ægypti fit anno ætatis 30. Jacobi patris 122. quem principatum tenuit annis 80. Post cujus interitum Hebræi Ægyptiis servierunt annis 144. Fiunt autem omnes anni, quos Hebræi in Ægypto fecerunt 215. qui ab eodem tempore computantur, quo Jacob cum filiis suis descendit in Ægyptum.

# Exodus

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. D. ANNOTATIONS ON EXODUS.

Latin:

I. N. D. ANNOTATA AD EXODUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
PREFACE.

That most of the things which Grotius inserted into his annotations on GENESIS are of such a nature that, if you depart from those things by which it seemed good to that Great Man to either display his Philological erudition and polymathy to the world or to apply it at times to Sacred matters, he could be judged to have wished to act not only as an advocate for various heterodox persons and heretics, but also as a patron of Jewish opinions, our Elenctic Dissertations and the annotations opposed to Grotius have, I think, quite clearly shown. Nor indeed did he himself dissimulate that he studied to please all who today bear the name of Christ. But for me, he wrote in the preface to the annotations on the books of the Gospels, when I was annotating these things I was a captive: when I was finishing them I was a private citizen, when I was publishing them I was established in some honor, it was ALWAYS my purpose not to serve any of those parties into which we Christians have been divided by the great evil of our age, but TO ALL CHRISTIANS PLAINLY, and to direct my own [efforts] to the knowledge of Evangelical truth and the increase of piety. While he wished to serve all, he dedicated his efforts even to those who adhere to the Roman Pontiff, and thought the abominations of the Roman Synagogue should either be excused or adorned, which truly Christians abhor most of all. What? He even wished to gratify the Photinian and Arian impiety, which, covering itself with a Christian guise, creeps openly in Socinian assemblies and covertly among the followers of Arminius; so that he might not fail to serve all Christians plainly. But in truth, he did not bestow his patronage only on those who are whitewashed with the Christian name: he often thought the cause of the Jews also should be pleaded, whether because he believed that through confidence in his erudition he could sustain whatever he wished, or because by the various winds of opinions

The former must be assumed: For Paraphrasts often use that liberty. But if the corruption of Codices is to be posited as often as one or more of them interprets otherwise, or adds some things for the sake of completing the sense, what finally will remain certain and uncorrupted?

And let these suffice in this place. For those who may perhaps desire what is needed for the explanation of this book, let them seek it from our Commentary, if they please. Which it will be useful to compare with the present Annotations.

We conclude Genesis for the present with the thanksgiving of the 24 Elders, Rev. 4:11: THOU ART WORTHY, O LORD OUR GOD, to receive glory and honor and power, for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they were, and were created. To Thee be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM.

QUæ annotatis suis in GENESIN illevit Grotius, pleraque ita comparata esse, ut si ab illis abeas, quibus eruditionem Philologicam, & πολυϊστορίαν vel orbi ostentare, vel applicare quandoque ad Sacra viro Magno visum fuit, advocatum non tantum vario- rum heterodoxorum, & hæreticorum, sed Patro- num quoque opinionum Judaicarum agere voluis- se censeri possit, Dissertationes nostræ Elencticæ, & annotationes Grot. oppositæ, haud obscure, opi- nor, docuere. Neque vero id dissimulavit ipse, quod placere omnibus studuerit, qui Christi nomen hodie præ se ferunt. Mihi autem, scripsit præfatione annotationum ad libros Evangeliorum, cum ista annotarem captivus: cum perficerem privatus, cum ederem in aliquo jam honore constitutus, propositum SEMPER fuit, non alicui earum servire partium, in quas ingenti seculi nostri malo divisi sumus Christiani, sed CHRISTIANIS PLANE OMNIBUS, meaque dirigere ad notitiam Evangelicæ veritatis & incremen- tum pietatis. Dum servire omnibus voluit, illis etiam, qui Pontifici Romano adhærent, operam suam dicavit, & βδελύγματα Romanæ Synagogæ aut excusanda aut ornanda duxit, quæ vere Chri- stiani horrent maxime. Quid? Photinianæ etiam, atque Arianæ impietati, quæ se Christiano schemate tegens, in Socinianis cœtibus aperte, in Arminii se- quacibus operte serpit, gratificari voluit; ne non omnibus plane Christianis inserviret. Verumenim- vero non illis tantum, qui Christiano dealbati sunt nomine, patrocinium suum impendit: Judæorum etiam causam non raro perorandam censuit, sive quod eruditionis fiducia, quicquid vellet, sustinere posse crediderit, sive quod variis opinionum ventis

Prius assumendum : Sæpe enim ea libertate utuntur Paraphrastæ. Quod si Codicum corruptio toties statuenda, quoties unus vel plures eorum aliter interpretatur, aut sensus explendi causa nonnulla addit, quid denique certi & incorrupti superabit?

Atque hæc hoc loco sufficiant. Quæ enim desiderari forte possint ad explicationem hujus libri, e Commentario nostro petant, quibus libuerit. Quem cum præsentibus Annotatis utiliter conferre licebit.

Concludimus impræsentiarum Genesin εὐχαρισίᾳ 24. Seniorum Apoc. 4, 11. DIGNUS ES DOMINE DEUS NOSTER accipere gloriam, & honorem & virtutem, quia tu creasti omnia & propter voluntatem tuam erant, & creata sunt, Tibi gloria sit in seculorum secula. Amen.

## 1:1 Introduction: N. J. Otata Odum
N. J. OTATA ODUM.

like a reed: he was tossed about, in faith altogether ἀσή[ρως?], secure with no πληροφορίᾳ (full assurance). Thus, he who wished to be everywhere was finally nowhere. So that I cannot but approve the judgment of a certain Swedish Nobleman: GROTIUS WOULD TRULY BE GREAT, if he had let theology alone. A certain Dutch theologian, in an epistle written to Grotius himself, did not hide that learned men greatly admired three things in him: namely, that being a lawyer by profession he meddled in theological matters; that he acted as a dictator everywhere; and that, concealing the matter itself here and there, he behaved in the manner of heretics or the misled in devious ways; but a fourth could be added: namely, that he was persuaded that all the worst opinions could be rendered just by his advocacy, as an advocate for all parties. Whence the judgment of the same Dutchman, praised by the blessed Mr. Dr. Joh. Schmid, Theologian of Strasbourg, in his Disputation on the first part of the priestly office of Christ, namely satisfaction for the sins of the world, instituted from Isaiah ch. 53, he finally became a GREAT TRIFLER, if one might use the word 'Nugo' for a trifler. All of which the Annotations of the same man on Exodus, if the explanation of the Decalogue is added in particular, joined to the annotations on the Gospels, will not a little confirm.

But because it seemed good at the same time to unravel the remaining difficulties that occur in this book, so that these Annotations might be like a proper commentary, it is helpful to prefix those things which may serve in place of a prolegomenon; nor will it be useless to bring forward the Grotian Annotations at the same time.

Prolegomena to Exodus.

The name Exodus was received among the Greeks and Latins from the principal and most οἰκείῳ (appropriate) subject matter of the book, the Departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. For although those things which happened concerning the giving of the law are described in it, these are nevertheless explained in part in Deuteronomy as well. But the history of the departure is described nowhere else, which is, as it were, the foundation of the remaining things that are handed down in this book. By the Hebrews it is called from the first words of the book ואלה שמות, These are the names, or simply שמות names, because at the beginning of the history of the exodus the names of the heads of the families are designated, which went down into Egypt; which manner of naming from the initial words some of the Hebrews ascribe to superstition, others more correctly to modesty, because they did not wish to take so much upon themselves as to assign names to anonymous books. The Hebrews also call this book in the Masora at Gen. 24, 8. נזיקין damages, or the book of damages, because in it there is treatment of damage and its restitution, see Buxtorff in Lex. Talmud. p. 1325. But that appellation is too synecdochical.

The order and coherence of Exodus with the preceding history of Genesis is clear. For after the foundation of the Israelite Church was laid in the 12 Patriarchs, the sons of Jacob, which, oppressed in Egypt, increased by a numerous multitude, had need of liberation, a certain seat, and a polity, which the Lord had also promised to Abraham in Gen. 15, 14, having premised the servitude and oppression of the Israelites after the death of Joseph, in which Genesis ends, and of the remaining Patriarchs in Egypt, which had likewise been signified to Abraham by an oracle, their liberation divinely accomplished through Moses is described; namely, how Moses was called and sent to it, how they were led out with a high hand, so that they might possess that promised seat, and by what laws they were bound and governed in the desert, regarding the worship of God and the polity of the people, as those by whom they were to be governed thereafter in the promised land. Indeed, Joseph lived for eighty years in the government of Egypt, and looked after the Church and his paternal family, which flourished happily until that time. But after his death, when the Israelites were growing and increasing greatly, and the memory of Joseph's merits had been obliterated among the new Kings, plans were agitated as to how such a great multitude of foreigners could be oppressed with craft. When these were being put into effect, and the sighs of the Israelites penetrated to heaven, God, hearing the groans of His people, liberated them from tyrannical oppression and led all the Israelites out of the most miserable Egyptian servitude with a high arm. Therefore, when Moses has explained this, he recounts the laws, both moral, ecclesiastical, and judicial, handed down by God, in order to strengthen and instruct the Church and Polity among them; and he narrates how God erected His tabernacle among the Israelites, so that He might dwell among them as their King. Whence the next two Mosaic books, namely Leviticus and Numbers, continue that history concerning the sojourn of the Israelites in the desert for 40 years, to which they had been condemned on account of their murmuring against God.

The book of Exodus therefore comprises the history of 145 years, namely from the death of Joseph until the erection of the tabernacle, which took place in the second year, in the 1st month, on the first day of the month, after the departure from Egypt, Ex. 40, 1. The years are collected thus: we have shown at Gen. 15, 14 that 64 years intervened from the death of Joseph until the birth of Moses. But the exodus took place in the eightieth year of Mosaic age; thus 144 years result, to which a year must still be added, because the tabernacle was erected in the first month of the year following the exodus; whence those 145 years result which we mentioned. But if to the aforesaid 144 years the 71 years which flowed from the descent of Jacob until the death of Joseph are added, 215 years will result, which the Israelites spent in Egypt. Just as many flowed likewise from the calling of Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans, which joined together make 430 years, a number expressly defined by the Holy Spirit, Exod. 12, 40, Gal. 3, 17. Because Abraham then began to sojourn from his Fatherland, and then also received the promises and blessings which the Apostle designates, as is clear from Gen. 12, 4. For the Apostle does not count the 430 years from the calling of Jacob, or from the passage into Egypt, but from the calling and sojourning of Abraham. This opinion is favored by Augustine, quest. 47 in Exodus, Athanasius (others make Anastasius the author) in the Synopsis of Holy Scripture on Exodus, Eusebius in the Chronicle, Rupertus, Tostatus, Corn. a Lap., Salianus, Tirinus in the Chronicle, and of our own, B. Luther, D. Behm, and others. In which manner also Athanasius in the Catena of Franciscus Zephyrus at the beginning of Exodus counted 215 years, from the entry of Jacob to the exit from Egypt. Which years, as they are strictly collected from those things which are expressed in Scripture, so the Hebrews must be mistaken, as are Lyranus and Cajetan, when they count only two hundred and ten years. But since the history of GENESIS is terminated in the year of the world 2369 at the death of Joseph, with the addition of the 145 years of the history of Exodus, it will end with the year of the world 2514.

Moreover, the purpose of this history is observed to be fivefold in particular: The first is the confirmation of divine truth. For since God promised Abraham a most abundant multiplication of his race, and a most gracious liberation from a land not his own, where his posterity was to serve, he now executes those promises, and the present history narrates in what manner he executed them. The second is the manifestation of divine glory, which God wished to show openly and in the sight of the nations by this embassy to Pharaoh, and by the powerful liberation of his people from his hand, accomplished in the public light, as well as by the miraculous sustenance of his people in the desert and the most solemn promulgation of the law, so that he might assert his power and glory not only among his own people, but also among the infidels. The third is the gathering and propagation of the Church, so that God might redeem for himself a people in whom he would have his fire and hearth, to whom he would manifest his judgments, by whom he was to be acknowledged and celebrated, in whom the benefits of the blessed seed were to be described, and whom he wished to lead to eternal salvation; then indeed so that his Church, glorified by so many prodigies among the nations, might summon others by that fame of his name and his people, and call them together as if by the blast of a trumpet. The fourth is the sustenance of faith, so that by these illustrious testimonies, which are exhibited especially in this book, he might confirm the faith of his own in adversity, and teach them that he exercises his gracious and often miraculous care when they are oppressed by others or seem to be consumed by poverty and want. The fifth, finally, is the typical adumbration of the state of the Church, so that it might be taught here ὡς ἐν τύπῳ what the state of the Church is on this earth, when, liberated from the servitude of the infernal Pharaoh, we are led through the desert of this world, to be directed by divine laws, so that we may aspire to the heavenly inheritance. For the Apostle teaches that these were our types, 1 Cor. 10, 3, and the spiritual exodus of the children of God from the world is most aptly compared with the bodily exodus of the Israelites from Egypt; the washing of the faithful in the baptism reddened by the blood of Christ, and the drowning of vices and the liberation of the souls of the faithful from the power of Satan, is compared with the liberation of the people through the crossing of the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh. The battle of the Israelites under Joshua with Amalek is σημαντικῶς the battle and victory of the faithful under Christ and the confusion of the Devil. To the law given on Mount Sinai corresponds the instruction of the Christian man, by which, lifted from earthly things, he learns to subject himself to heavenly discipline: to the pilgrimage in the desert, the pilgrimage in this world: to the feeding by manna and the drinking from the rock, the refreshment of the heavenly bread and the spiritual rock:

To the construction of the tabernacle, the Church of God and the various functions of the faithful, twin to the various vessels of the house of God: to bodily sacrifices, spiritual sacrifices; to the anointing and external θυμιάμασι (incense), the interior sanctification of the Spirit, and the sweet odors of prayers and praises. For just as in Genesis the creation of the world and the human race is described, so in Exodus the type of redemption is recorded; whence Rabanus said that almost all the Sacraments of the present Church are shadowed forth and expressed in Exodus, which St. Augustine explained especially in Homily 20, Volume 10. The past time suffices to have served the clay works of sins, as if to the domination of the Egyptians. Now the Red Sea, namely baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ, has carried us across, has destroyed the Egyptians; we fear nothing concerning past sins, as if they were enemies following at our backs. For the rest, let us consider that we are traversing the wilderness of this life, and arriving at the land of promise, the heavenly Jerusalem, the land of the living. Add what Augustine has in his work to Honoratus on the usefulness of believing, chapter 3: if we diligently retrace those stations and encampments and the conditions of the places which are contained in Exodus, we shall see great wonders in the heavenly journey itself.
