Nor should what occurs in the same Doctor, St. Augustine, in Psalm 72 be passed over: Whatever that people suffered in the wilderness, and whatever God bestowed upon them, whatever those scourges were, and whatever those gifts, they are significations of things which we, walking in this solitude of this life and seeking our fatherland in Christ, both receive for consolation and suffer for probation.

The principal scope of this book is the same as that of the whole Scripture: Christ. For this is He of whom Moses testifies, John chapter 5, verse 39; He is the τέλος νό- μ8 (end of the law), Romans 10:4. On account of Him, God placed His people, led out of Egypt by wondrous portents, into the certain seat of the promised land, and rendered it illustrious by many revelations, so that, namely, it might be clear to the whole human race from what region and lineage the Messiah was to be expected, and so that all might be called to His kingdom. Moses, therefore, himself bore the type of the Messiah in leading the people out of the servitude of Pharaoh, of whom Tertullian says, book 4 against Marcion: Christ, he says, was prefigured in the person of Moses as the intercessor and offerer of the human soul for the salvation of the people. And Augustine, sermon 86 on the season: just as blessed Isaac and Jacob and Joseph, so also Moses bore the type of Christ, and great mysteries were prefigured in him. Furthermore, the Paschal Lamb also shadowed forth Christ, 1. Corinthians 5:7; manna given from heaven, John 6:33; the Rock pouring forth waters, 1 Corinthians 10:4; the mercy-seat, which was upon the ark of the covenant, Romans 3:24; sacrifices, Ephesians 5:2 and Hebrews chapters 9 and 10; anointings, Hebrews 1:6; and thus the high Priest with all his adornment and the administration of his office, Hebrews 9. The moral law itself, too, by taking away from men all hope of salvation, drives them to seek a Savior, Galatians 3:24. Commentators, besides those who have written on the whole Bible, or the Old Testament, or the Pentateuch, have devoted some effort to this book of Exodus from among the Ancients, and those employed in the Douay Bibles are Philo Judaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil the Great, Epiphanius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Cyril of Alexandria, Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, Bede, Bernard. Of the more recent: B. Rungius, Jos. Simler, Andr. Rivet (who also wrote specifically on chapter XX of Exodus), Andr. Willet, Joh. Hesselius. On Genesis and Exodus, Hippolytus is also mentioned among the ancients, circa the year 220. And various authors in the Catena of Aloysius Lippomannus, both Greek and Latin

compiled in the year 1559. Compare Sixtus of Siena in his Bibliotheca Sancta. Jerome, in his Epistle to Paulinus, has embraced the argument and parts of the book thus: Exodus is manifest with the 10 plagues, with the decalogue, with mystical and divine precepts. Whence, by a dichotomy, it is conveniently distributed into the history of the departure and the Law given by God. In the first part is the commemoration of the memorable things which happened to the people of Israel in Egypt and in their exit. The second is the constitution of the Republic in that nation. The former part exhibits the birth of the Israelite Church, subject to many difficulties in Egypt. The latter describes its education, how God appointed Moses as a tutor to this firstborn of His, and accustomed him to the duties of piety and human society by various precepts and chastisements. If a trichotomy does not displease, let the first part be called historical, concerning the reduction up to Mount Sinai, to chapter 19. The second part is dogmatic, concerning the νομοθε- σίᾳ (legislation) or the tradition of laws, up to chapter 25. The third part is poetic, concerning the σκηνοποιίᾳ (tabernacle construction) or the construction of the tabernacle, up to the end of the book. As for the leading out, its ἀφορμὴ (occasion) and cause pertain to the antecedents, the oppression of the Israelites, chapter 1; as well as the παρασκευὴ (preparation), to which must be referred the birth, education, and calling of Moses the liberator, chapters 2, 3, 4; as also the succession of the liberation, and the expedition of the embassy to Pharaoh, chapters 5, 6, and with the 10 plagues of Egypt up to chapter 12, namely the water turned into blood, chapter 7; of frogs, lice, flies, chapter 8; of pestilence, ulcers, hail, chapter 9; of locusts and darkness, chapter 10; and of the firstborn, chapter 11. Regarding the concomitants, the preparation for the exit is delivered through the celebration of the Passover, chapter 12, and the departure and crossing through the Red Sea, chapters 13, 14, with the Eucharistic song, chapter 15. Regarding the consequences, those things are commemorated which befell the people until they had arrived at Mount Horeb, such as the proofs of sustenance through Manna ch. 16, water from the Rock ch. 17, the defeat of enemies through the slaughter of the Amalekites ch. 17, and political governance through the first ordination of Judges ch. 18. As for the second part concerning the νομοθεσίᾳ, there is described in ch. 19 the preparation, in ch. 20 the promulgation of the Decalogue or moral law with certain political laws in ch. 21 & 22, and Ecclesiastical laws concerning feasts and first fruits in ch. 23, and the confirmation of the legal covenant in ch. 24. In the third part, first the plan is set forth for constructing the tabernacle in which divine worship was to be exercised, concerning the material of which, and especially the ark of the covenant, the table and the lampstands ch. 25, concerning the curtains and boards ch. 26, concerning the altar and the court ch. 27, concerning the adornment and initiation of the Priests ch. 28, 29, concerning the altar of incense ch. 30, and the craftsmen ch. 31, it was treated. Afterwards the impediment is set forth by which the structure of the tabernacle was interrupted, the calf-worship ch. 32, with the repentance of the people ch. 33, and the repair of the tablets ch. 34. Finally, it is commemorated how the work proceeded, through the contribution of the people ch. 35, the construction of the tabernacle ch. 36, the ark ch. 37, and the altar of burnt offering ch. 38, as well as the priestly attire ch. 39, and also the actual erection of the tabernacle ch. 40.

Latin:

N. J. OTATA ODUM.

arundinis instar: agitatus fuerit, in fide prorsus ἀσή[ρως?], nulla πληροφορίᾳ securus. Ita qui ubique esse voluit, nusquam denique fuit. Ut judicium Sueci cujusdam Nobilis non possim non approbare : Vere MAGNUS ESSET GROTIUS, si missam fecisset Theologiam. Tria in ipso maximopere viros eruditos mirari Batavus quidam Theologus Epist. ad ipsum Grotium perscripta haud dissimulavit: utpote quod professione JCtus Theologicis sese immiscuerit : Quod ubique dictatorem egerit, & quod passim rem ipsam dissimulans, in deviis hæreticorum vel seductorum more versatus sit; Sed addi quartum poterit: Quod nempe pessimas quasque sententias, partium omnium advocatus patrocinio suo justas reddi posse, persuasus fuerit. Unde quod ejusdem Batavi judicium fuit, a B. Dn. D. Joh. Schmidio, Theol. Argent. Disput. de officii Christi sacerdotalis parte priori, satisfactione nempe pro mundi peccatis ex Esai. c. 53. instituta, laudatum, factus tandem ille est NUGO MAGNUS, si Nugonem dicere liceret pro nugatore. Quæ omnia Annotata ejusdem in Exodum, si accedat cumprimis explicatio Decalogi, annotationibus ad Evangelia subjuncta, non parum confirmabunt.

Quia vero eadem opera visum est reliquas difficultates quæ in hoc libro occurrunt, enodare, ut justi commentarii instar sint hæc Annotata, præmittere juvat ea, quæ προλεγομένων loco esse queant; neque Annotata Grotiana simul adducere, inutile erit.

Προλεγόμενα in Exodum.

Exodus nomen apud Græcos & Latinos accepit a præcipuo & maxime οἰκείῳ argumento libri, Exitu filiorum Israel ex Ægypto. Quamvis enim describantur in eo quæ circa legis traditionem accidere, hæc tamen ex parte in Deuteronomio quoque exponuntur. At egressus historia nuspiam alias descripta est, quæ reliquarum, quæ in hoc libro tra- duntur, velut fundamentum est. Ebræis a primis libri vocibus appellatur ואלה שמות, Hæc sunt no- mina, vel simpliciter שמות nomina, quia sub in- gressum historiæ eductionis nomina capitum fa- miliarum designantur, quæ in Ægyptum descen- derunt, qualem denominandi rationem a verbis initialibus nonnulli Ebræorum superstitioni, alii rectius modestiæ adscribunt, quod noluerint tan- tum sibi sumere, ut libris anonymis nomina tri- buerent. Vocant & Ebræi hunc librum in Ma- sora ad Gen. 24, 8. נזיקין damna, vel librum de da- mnis, quia in illo de damno, ejusque restitutione agitur, vid. Buxtorff. in Lex. Talmud. p. 1325. Sed illa appellatio nimis Synecdochica est.

Ordo & cohærentia Exodi cum præcedenti Ge- nefeos historia in aprico est. Postquam enim fun- damentum Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ jactum fuit in 12. Patriarchis Jacobi filiis, quæ pressa in Ægypto, au- cta numerosa multitudine, liberatione, certa sede & politia opus habebat, quam etiam Abrahamo pro- miserat Dominus Gen. 15, 14. præmissa Israelita- rum post mortem Josephi, in qua desinit Genesis, & reliquorum Patriarcharum, servitute, ac pressura in Ægypto, quæ per oraculum itidem Abrahamo significata erat, liberatio eorum divinitus per Mo- sen facta describitur; quomodo nempe ad eam Moses vocatus & missus, quomodo ipsi elata manu educti fuerint, ut sede illa promissa potirentur, & quibus in deserto adstricti & gubernati fuerint le- gibus, qua cultum Dei, ac politiam populi, utpote quibus in terra promissa etiam gubernandi dein- ceps erant. Nimirum vixit Joseph per XXC. annos in regimine Ægypti, ac prospexit Eccle- siæ & familiæ paternæ, quæ eo usque feliciter floruit. Post ejus vero fata, quum cresce- rent, & augerentur valde Israelitæ, ac meritorum Josephi memoria penes novos Reges obliterata esset, consilia agitata sunt, quomodo cum astu op- primi tanta peregrinorum multitudo possit. Quæ ubi in effectum deducerentur, & suspiria Israëlit- rum in cælum penetrarent, Deus exaudiens po- puli sui gemitus a Tyrannica oppressione eundem liberavit, & e servitute Ægyptiaca miserrima excel- so brachio universos Israelitas eduxit. Id ergo ubi exposuit Moses, leges & morales, & Ecclesiasticas, & Judiciales a Deo traditas, ut Ecclesiam & Poli- tiam inter illos sibi firmaret, & instrueret, recen- set: & quomodo tabernaculum suum inter Israeli- tas erexerit Deus, ut ceu Rex eorum inter ipsos ha- bitaret, enarrat. Unde proximi duo Mosaici libri, Leviticus nempe & Numerorum, historiam illam per- texunt de commoratione Israelitarum in deserto per XL. annos, ad quam ob murmurationem contra Deum condemnati erant.

Complectitur itaque liber Exodi historiam CXLV. annorum, a morte nempe Josephi usque ad erectionem tabernaculi, quæ facta est anno secun- do, mense 1. prima die mensis, post exitum ex Ægy- pto, Ex. XL, 1. Anni sic colliguntur: a morte Jose- phi usque ad nativitatem Mosis LXIV. annos inter- cessisse, ad Gen. 15, 14. ostendimus. Anno autem æ- tatis Mosaicæ octuagesimo facta est eductio; prode- unt itaque anni CXLIV. quibus jungendus adhuc annus est, quia mense primo anni eductionem se- quentis erectum est tabernaculum; unde prode- unt anni illi CXLV. quos diximus. Si vero annis prædictis CXLIV. anni LXXI. qui fluxere a de- scensu Jacobi usque ad obitum Josephi, addantur, prodituri sunt anni CCXV. quos transegerunt Israelitæ in Ægypto. Totidem effluxere pariter a vocatione Abraham'ex Ur Chaldæorum, qui jun- cti efficiunt CCCCXXX. annos, numerum expref- se definitum a Spiritu S. Exod. 12, 40. Gal. 3, 17. Quia tum peregrinari e Patria sua cœpit Abraham, tum accepit etiam promissiones ac benedictiones, quas Apostolus designat, uti e Gen. 12, 4. liquet. Non enim numerat Apostolus annos 430. a vocatione Jacobi, aut a transitu in Ægyptum, sed a vocatione ac peregrinatione Abrahami. Cui sententiæ favet Augustinus quæst. 47. in Exodum, Athanas. (alii Anastasium autorem faciunt) in Synopsi S. Scripturæ in Exodum, Eusebius in Chronic. Rupertus, Tostatus, Corn. a Lap. Salianus, Tirinus in Chronic. & e nostris B. Lutherus, D. Behm. & alii. Quo pacto etiam Athanas. in Catena Francisci Zephyri sub Exodi initium 215. annos numeravit, ab ingressu Jacobi ad exitum ex Ægypto. Qui anni uti ἀποτόμως ex iis colliguntur, quæ in Scriptura expressa sunt, ita falli oportet Ebræos, ut & Lyranum & Cajetanum, cum ducentos tantum & decem annos numerant. Quum autem GENESEOS historiam in Josephi morte anno M. 2369. terminetur, additis Historiæ Exodi annis 145. desinet illa cum anno M. 2514.

Cæterum finis hujus Historiæ quintuplex potissimum observatur: Primus est Veritatis divinæ confirmatio. Quum enim Abrahamo promiserit Deus multiplicationem generis copiosissimam, & liberationem e terra non sua, ubi posteritas ejus servire debebat, gratiosissimam, exequitur nunc illa promissa, & quo pacto ea executus sit, narrat præsens historia. Alter est, gloriæ divinæ manifestatio, quam Deus hac legatione ad Pharaonem, ac potenti suorum e manu ejus liberatione in luce publica facta, nec non miraculosa suorum in deserto sustentatione ac solemnissima legis promulgatione palam & in conspectu gentium ostendere voluit, ut non tantum penes populum suum, sed etiam penes infideles suam virtutem atque gloriam assereret. Tertius est Ecclesiæ collectio & propagatio, ut redimeret sibi Deus populum, in quo ignem & focum suum haberet, cui judicia sua manifestaret, a quo agnoscendus & celebrandus erat, in quo beneficia seminis benedicti describenda erant, quemque ad æternam salutem perducere volebat, tum vero ut Ecclesia sua tot prodigiis per nationes glorificata, alios fama ista nominis & populi sui accerseret, ac veluti tubæ clangore convocaret. Quartus est fidei sustentatio, ut illustribus hisce testimoniis, quæ in hoc cumprimis libro exhibentur, fidem suorum in adversis confirmaret, eorumque curam se gratiosam sæpe & miraculosam gerere doceret, cum premuntur ab aliis aut egestate ac penuria consumendi videntur. Quintus denique est typica status Ecclesiæ adumbratio, ut hic ὡς ἐν τύπῳ doceretur, qualis sit Ecclesiæ status in his terris, cum liberati a servitute infernalis Pharaonis per desertum hujus mundi deducimur, legibus divinis dirigendi, ut adspiremus ad cœlestem hæreditatem. Hæc enim typos nostros fuisse docet Apost. 1. Cor. 10, 3. & aptissime comparatur cum corporali exitu Israelitarum ex Ægypto spiritualis filiorum Dei e mundo egressus, cum liberatione populi per transitum maris rubri & submersionem Pharaonis, salutaris in Baptismo Sanguine Chr. rubicantis ablutio, nec non submersio vitiorum, & animarum fidelium a potestate Satanæ liberatio. Pugna Israelitarum sub Josua cum Amalek, σημαντικῶς est pugna & victoria fidelium sub Christo ac Diaboli confusio. Legi datæ in monte Sina respondet hominis Christiani instructio, quo a terrenis sublatus subjicere se discat cœlesti disciplinæ: peregrinationi in deserto peregrinatio in hoc mundo: cibationi per manna ac potationi e petra panis cœlestis, & petræ spiritualis refectio:

Exstructioni tabernaculi Ecclesia Dei & diversæ fidelium functiones, vasis domus Dei diversis ge- minæ : sacrificiis corporalibus spiritualia sacrificia, unctioni & θυμιάμασι externis, sanctificatio inte- rior Spiritus, & orationum ac laudum odoramenta. Quemadmodum enim in Genesi mundi & generis humani creatio describitur, ita in Exodo redemtio- nis typus consignatur ; unde Rabbanus dixit, omnia pene Sacramenta præsentis Ecclesiæ in Exodo adum- brata & expressa esse, quod exposuit cumprimis S. Augustinus Hom. 20. Tom. 10. Sufficit præteri- tum tempus luteis operibus peccatorum tanquam Ægy- ptiorum dominationi servivisse. Jam mare rubrum, baptisma sc. Christi sanguine consecratum nos traje- cit, Ægyptios interemit, nihil de peccatis præteritis, tanquam de insequentibus a tergo hostibus formide- mus. De cætero cogitemus vitæ hujus eremum per- meare, & ad terram promissionis, supernam Hieru- salem, terram viventium pervenire. Adde quæ habet Augustinus ad Honoratum de utilitate cre- dendi cap. 3. si diligenter stationes eas, mansionesque castrorum & conditiones locorum, quæ Exodo con- tinentur, retractemus, magna in ipsis cælestis itine- ris mirabilia cernemus. Nec prætermittenda quæ occurrunt apud eundem Doctorem S. Augustin. in Ps. 72. Quicquid in eremo passus est populus ille, & quicquid eis Deus largitus est, quæcunque illa fla- gella fuerunt, & quæcunque dona, significationes sunt rerum, quas in hac solitudine hujus vitæ ambulantes & in Christo quærentes patriam, & accipimus ad consolationem, & patimur ad probationem.

Scopus præcipuus libri hujus idem est, qui totius Scripturæ, Christus: Hic enim est, de quo testatur Moses Joh. cap. 5. v. 39. hic τέλος νό- μ8 est Rom. 10, 4. propter hunc Deus po- pulum suum mirandis portentis ex Ægypto edu- ctum in certam sedem terræ promissæ colloca- vit, & multis patefactionibus illustrem reddidit, ut sc. toti humano generi constaret, ex qua regio- ne & genere Messias esset expectandus, utq; omnes ad regnum ejus convocarentur. Moses igitur ipse typum gessit Messiæ educendo populum ex servi- tute Pharaonis, de quo Tertull. lib. 4. contra Mar- cion. Christus, inquit, in persona Mosi præfigura- tus est deprecator & oblator animæ humanæ pro po- puli salute. Et August. serm. 86. de tempore: sicut B. Isaac & Jacobus & Joseph, ita & Moses Christi typum prætulit, & magna in ipso præfigurata sunt my- steria. Porro Christum adumbravit quoque Agnus Paschalis, 1. Cor. 5, 7. manna de cœlo datum Joh. 6, 33. Petra aquas fundens 1. Cor. 10, 4. propitia- torium, quod erat super arcam fœderis Rom. 3, 24. Sacrificia Eph. 5, 2. & Ebr. 9. ac 10. capp. Unctio- nes Ebr. 1, 6. adeoque summus Sacerdos cum omni ornatu suo & officii administratione Ebr. 9. Ipsa quoque lex moralis, adimendo hominibus omnem spem salutis, adigit eosdem ad quærendum Salva- torem Gal. 3., 24. Commentatores præter il- los, qui in Biblia universa, vel V. T. vel in Penta- teuchum scripsere, ad hunc Exodi librum e Veteri- bus operam aliquam contulerunt & in Bibliis Dua- censibus adhibiti sunt Philo Judæus, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Clemens Alex. Origenes, Eusebius, Gre- gor. Nyssen. Basilius M. Epiphanius, Gregor. Na- zianz. Cyrill. Alexandr. Hilarius, Hieronym. Am- brosius, Augustin. Isidorus, Beda, Bernhardus. E recentior. B. Rungius, Jos. Simlerus, Andr. Ri- vetus (qui etiam peculiariter in c. XX. Exodi scripsit) Andr. Willetus, Joh. Hesselius. In Ge- nesin & Exodum etiam ex antiquis commemora- tur Hippolytus circa Ann. 220. Et autores varii in Caten. Aloysii Lippomanni cum Græci tum Latini

Ann. 1559. concinnata. Conf. Sixt. Senenf. in Bibl. S. Argumentum & partes libri sic complexus est Hieron. Epistola ad Paulin. Patet Exodus cum 10. plagis, cum decalogo, cum mysticis divinisque præ- ceptis. Unde per διχοτομίαν commode distribui- tur in historiam egressus, & Legis a Deo traditæ. Parte prima habetur commemoratio rerum memo- rabilium, quæ in Ægypto & exitu in Israelis popu- lo contigere. Altera Reipubl. in illa gente consti- tutio. Pars prior exhibet Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ multis difficultatibus obnoxiæ in Ægypto nativitatem. Altera ejusdem describit educationem, quomodo Deus huic primogenito suo Mosen pædagogum præfecerit, & variis præceptis & castigationibus eundem ad officia pietatis & humanæ societatis assuefecerit. Si τριχοτομία non displiceat, Pars prima dicatur ἱστορικὴ de reductione usque ad montem Sinai, ad c. 19. Pars altera δογματικὴ de νομοθε- σίᾳ vel legum traditione, usque ad c. 25 Pars tertia ποιητικὴ de σκηνοποιίᾳ vel tabernaculi constructione usque ad finem libri. Quod ad eductionem, ad an- tecedentia pertinent ejusdem ἀφορμὴ & occasio, pressura Israelitarum c. 1. nec non παρασκευὴ & præparatio, ad quam referenda Mosis liberatoris nativitas, educatio & vocatio c. 2. 3. 4. ut & libera- tionis διαδοχὴ, & legationis ad Pharaonem expe- ditio c. 5. 6. & cum 10. plagis Ægypti usque ad c. 12. verpote aquæ in sanguinem conversæ c. 7. ranarum, pediculorum, muscarum cap. 8. pestis, ulcerum, grandinis c. 9. locustarum, & tenebrarum c. 10. & primogenitorum c. 11. Quoad concomitantia tra- ditur præparatio exitus per celebrationem Paschatis c. 12. & profectio actransitus per mare rubrum c. 13. 14. cum carmine Eucharistico c. 15. Quoad conse- quentia commemorantur ea, quæ populo obtige- runt, donec ad montem Horeb pervenissent, ceu sunt documenta sustentationis per Manna c. 16. Aquam de Petra c. 17. devictionis hostium per cladem Ama- lekiatarum c. 17. & gubernationis politicæ, per pri- mam Judicum ordinationem c. 18. Quantum ad alteram partem de νομοθεσίᾳ, describitur c. 19. præ- paratio, c. 20. Decalogi vel legis moralis promul- gatio cum legibus quibusdam politicis c. 21. & 22. & Ecclesiasticis de festis & primitiis cap. 23. ac fœ- deris legalis confirmatio cap. 24. Parte tertia pri- mo ratio exponitur construendi tabernaculi, in quo cultus divinus exercendus erat, de cujus materia ac cumprimis arca fœderis, mensa & candelabris c. 25. de cortinis, & asseribus cap. 26. de altari & atrio c. 27. de ornatu & initiatione Sacerdotum c. 28. 29. de ara thymiamatis c. 30. ac artificibus c. 31. actum est. Postea impedimentum exponitur, quo tabernaculi structura interrupta fuit, Moschola- tria c. 32. cum resipiscentia populi c. 33. ac tabu- larum reparatione c. 30. Denique commemora- tur, quomodo opus processerit, qua contributionem populi c. 35. constructionem tabernaculi c. 36. arcæ, c. 37. atque altaris holocausti c. 38. nec non habitus Sacerdotalis c. 39. ut & erectionem ipsam taberna- culi c. 40.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. The historical [part] of Exodus CONCERNING THE LEADING OUT OF THE PEOPLE AS FAR AS MOUNT SINAI CH. XIX. CHAPTER I. The Egyptian oppression of the children of Israel.

Verse 1. THESE ARE THE NAMES.

In Hebrew, the initial Vav is either redundant, as in Ez. 1:1, or indicates that the Pentateuch was one continuous book. Moreover, the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt are listed because they individually constituted tribes with their descendants, of which tribes mention is often made thereafter. The souls of those who entered are numbered at 70 (concerning which we spoke at Gen. 47), so that from a comparison of that small number with the huge multitude of those who left, the fulfillment of the divine promise concerning multiplication might be made more illustrious, Gen. 13:16, ch. 15:5, because within 215 years the number had increased so much that at the departure there lived, besides little ones and wives, six hundred thousand, Exod. 12:37.

Latin:

PARS I. Exodi ἱστορικὴ DE POPULI EDU- CTIONE USQVE AD MONTEM SINAI C. XIX. CAPUT I. Filiorum Israel pressura Ægyptiaca.

Vers. 1. Hæc SUNT NOMINA.

IN Ebræo Vav initiale vel redundat, ut Ez. 1, 1. vel indicat Pentateuchum unum fuisse librum conti- nuum. Recensentur autem nomina filiorum Israel, qui Ægyptum ingressi sunt, quia singuli tribus con- stituere cum posteris suis, quarum tribuum deinde sæpe mentio fit. Numerantur animæ ingresso- rum LXX. (de quo ad Gen. 47. diximus) ut e comparatione exigui istius numeri cum ingenti egressorum multitudine divinæ promissionis de multiplicatione feminis complementum illustrius fiat Gen. 13, 16. c. 15, 5. quod intra annos 215. ita auctus fuerit numerus, ut in egressu simul vixerint præter parvulos & uxores sexies centena millia Exod. 12, 37.

## 1:5
Verse 5. BUT JOSEPH WAS IN EGYPT.

The meaning is that Joseph was not numbered in the first verses with the rest of his brothers because he did not enter Egypt with them, but was already in Egypt. He is therefore excluded not from the immediate number of 70 souls, but from the catalog of those who are said in verse 1 to have descended into Egypt with Jacob.

Latin:

Vers. 5. JOSEPH AUTEM IN ÆGYPTO ERAT.

Sensus est, numeratum ideo versibus pri- mis non fuisse Josephum, cum cæteris fratribus, quia is ingressus Ægyptum non est cum iisdem, sed in Ægypto jam erat. Excipitur ergo ipse non a numero proximo 70. animarum, sed a Catalogo eorum, qui vers. 1. dicuntur cum Jacobo in Ægy- ptum descendisse.

## 1:6
Verse 6. AND WHEN HE WAS DEAD, AND ALL HIS BRETHREN, AND ALL THAT GENERATION.

Understand it as that which had entered with Jacob, or which was included under that number of 70 souls. For that reason, the word הדור ההוא with the he (i.e., the demonstrative) notably designates that kindred, namely, the one previously defined, or rather generation, as the LXX more correctly render it by γενεὰν. Nor are these things to be taken as if that wonderful multiplication began only after their decease, which the Vulgate implies and Cornel. a Lapide contends, because the multiplication began while the Patriarchs themselves and their sons were living. Moses therefore indicates here that after all these had died and the Israelites had been vehemently increased, their pressure began, so that two markers of the time of servitude are designated. For it is not necessary that these things be understood successively, as if first all were said to have died, and only then did the multiplication begin. Eusebius in his Chronicle, and those who follow him, Marianus Scotus and Ado, hallucinate openly when they start this oppression from the death of Joseph, as if it lasted for 144 full years, because Moses begins the same not after the death of Joseph, but after the death of all his brothers and of all the generation that entered with Jacob. The Hebrews in Seder Olam think Joseph was the first of all the brothers to depart from the living, and from Exod. 6:16 it is evident that Levi, who was only four years older than Joseph, prolonged his life to 137 years, and thus survived Joseph by 23 years. To these must be added those years in which the rest of the kindred died, and the memory of Joseph perished from the minds of the Egyptians, and the Israelites grew into such a multitude that they were believed to be about to become stronger than the Egyptians, Exod. 1:9. Whence at least 50 years from the death of Joseph must be counted before the servitude began, so that it began about a decade before the birth of Moses, when his sister Miriam was born, who the Hebrews note received her name from bitterness. Thus, therefore, the servitude seems to have lasted for about 90 years, as is also observed by Salianus, Bonfrerius, Corn. a Lapide, Tirinus, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 6. QUO MORTUO ET UNIVERSIS FRATRIBUS EJUS, OMNIQVE COGNA- TIONE ILLA.

Eam intellige, quæ ingressa erat cum Jacobo, vel quæ comprehensa sub isto 70. animarum nu- mero. Nam ideo notanter הדור ההוא cum bajediab, (s. demonstrativo) cognatio illa sc. antea definita designatur vel potius generatio, uti rectius LXX. per γενεὰν reddunt. Neque hæc ita accipienda, quasi post illorum decessum demum mira illa mul- tiplicatio cœperit, quod Vulgata innuit, & Cornel. a Lapid. contendit, quia multiplicatio cœpit viven- tibus ipsis Patriarchis, eorumque filiis. Hic ergo indicat Moses mortuis istis omnibus & vehementer adauctis Israëlitis cœpisse pressuram ipsorum, ut duo characteres designentur temporis servitutis. Non enim necessum est, ut ista successive intelli- gantur, quasi primum omnes mortui dicerentur, ac tum demum cœperit multiplicatio. Halluci- natur autem aperte Eusebius in Chronico, & qui eum sequuntur Marianus Scotus, Ado, cum hanc oppressionem a morte Josephi ordiuntur, quasi du- rarit per 144. integros annos, quia Moses non post Josephi, sed post omnium fratrum ejus, omnisque generationis, quæ cum Jacobo ingressa est, de- cessum eandem inchoat. Ebræi in Seder Olam Josephum putant primum omnium fratrum e vi- vis excessisse, & e cap. 6. Exod. v. 16. constat Levi, qui Josepho quadriennio solum major erat, vitam protraxisse ad 137. annos, adeoque 23. annis Jose- pho supervivisse. Quibus addendi illi anni erunt, quibus reliqua cognatio decessit, ac memoria Jose- phi e mentibus Ægyptiorum periit, atque Israelitæ in tantam multitudinem excrevere, ut fortiores evasuri crederentur Ægyptiis Exod. 1, 9. Unde ad minimum 50. anni a morte Josephi numerandi erunt ante cœptam servitutem, ut ea decennio cir- citer ante nativitatem Mosis cœperit, cum Miriam Soror ejus nasceretur, quam adeo ab amaritudine nomen accepisse notant Ebræi. Ita ergo per an- nos 90. circiter durasse videtur servitus, ut etiam a Saliano, Bonfrerio, Corn. a Lapid. Tirino & aliis observatur.

## 1:7
Verse 7. AS IF SPROUTING.

The increase of the Israelites is described by three very emphatic verbs: 1. פרו, he fructified; it is very general, applied to the promise of multiplication made in the first creation, Gen. 1:28, and denotes the act of fructification or bearing fruit of the Israelites and the propagation of the species according to the generation of one from another. The second, שרץ, he crept, which denotes that they were multiplied after the manner of reptiles or frogs and fish, whose breeding is wonderful, as Pliny testifies, book 9, ch. 2, and Aristotle, book 6, de animalibus, ch. 7, noting the wonderful degree of that propagation through one birth of twins, or even three, four, or more children. The third, רבה, to be multiplied, is repeated from the first blessing. The Septuagint render it χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο, they became poured out, because their abundance was so great as if they had been poured out upon the earth. Thus is noted the state and effect of multiplication through the propagation of many from one, both at one birth and at repeated births. It came about from this that, in the exodus, there were numbered of warriors only from the 20th year of age 600,000, not counting the Levites, the old men, the boys, and the women, Num. I. If all these are added, the number could be tripled without error of calculation. Whence it can be seen that the Israelites had spread from the land of Goshen, which was too narrow, into the neighboring places of Egypt as well. Although Egypt was indeed very fertile, since a certain woman in Egypt gave birth to twenty at four deliveries, according to Aristotle, and Pliny lib. 7. c. 3. reports from Trogus that seven are carried at once in one womb in Egypt, yet this was neither common nor ordinary, and this multiplication of the Israelites is to be attributed not to the land of Egypt, but to the divine blessing promised to Abraham. Therefore, however much a remarkable multitude could be propagated from 70 men within 215 years, even while the order of nature was preserved, there is nevertheless no doubt that a special divine blessing was added here, and that the Hebrews grew by their multiplication being divinely fecundated, as Augustine speaks, lib. 18. de Civ. Dei cap. 17. Such a blessing there was also after the flood, because in 250 years the human race had been so multiplied from the three sons of Noah that Ninus alone, according to Diodorus Siculus lib. 3. c. 2., led out against the Bactrians one million seven hundred thousand infantry and two hundred thousand cavalry.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVASI GERMINANTES.

Describitur incrementum Israelitarum tribus verbis valde emphaticis 1. פרו fructificavit, valde generale est, promissioni multiplicationis in prima creatione factæ adhibitum Gen. 1, 28. notatque fructificationis seu fœtificationis Israelitarum & pro- pagationis speciei secundum generationem unius ex alio actum: Alterum שרץ serpsit, quod reptilium aut ranarum ac piscium more, quorum mira est fœ- tura, teste Plinio lib. 9. c. 2. Aristotele lib. 6. de animalibus c. 7. multiplicati fuerint, notans propa- gationis istius per unum partum gemellorum, vel etiam trium, quatuor aut plurium liberorum mirabilem gradum. Tertium רבה multiplicari repetitur e prima benedictione. Septuaginta red- dunt χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο, effusi facti sunt, quod tan- ta eorum fuerit copia, ac si in terram effusi essent. Notatur ita multiplicationis per propagationem multorum ex uno, tum uno tum iterato partu sta- tus & effectus. Factum inde est, ut in egressu nume- rentur bellatorum solum a 20. ætatis anno 600000. non accensitis Levitis, Senibus, pueris ac mulieri- bus Num. I. qui omnes si addantur, triplicari sine errore calculi numerus poterit. Unde videri pos- sunt diffusi fuisse Israelitæ e terra Gosen, quæ nimis angusta erat, in vicina etiam Ægypti loca. Quan- quam vero Ægyptus valde fertilis fuerit, cum mu- lier quædam in Ægypto 4. partubus viginti ediderit, teste Aristotele, & ex Trogo referat Plinius lib. 7. c. 3. in Ægypto septenos uno utero simul geri, ta- men nec hoc commune aut ordinarium fuit, & vin- dicatur hic Israelitarum multiplicatio, non terræ Ægypti, sed benedictioni divinæ Abrahamo pro- missæ. Utut ergo naturæ etiam ordine servato e 70. viris intra annos 215. insignis multitudo pro- pagari possit, nullum tamen dubium est, accessisse hic peculiarem divinam benedictionem, & crevis- se Ebræos divinitus fœcundata eorum multiplicatio- ne, ut loquitur Augustin. l. 18. de Civ. Dei cap. 17. qualis benedictio etiam fuit a diluvio, quod annis 250. e tribus Noachi filiis genus humanum ita mul- tiplicatum fuerit, ut solus Ninus teste Diodoro Si- culo lib. 3. c. 2. contra Bactrianos eduxerit peditum decies septies centena millia, & equitum ducenta millia.

## 1:7 Addition
On Exodus 1:7, towards the end, at page 319, column b.

It can also be shown how, by the ordinary natural way, such a number, indeed a much larger one, could have come forth. Let us assume the Israelites spent only 200 years in Egypt, and only 40 years of age for those who begat, and that each had only three males, and they did not beget them before the twentieth year; thus, through ten twenty-year periods, a much larger number will result: For in the first twenty-year period 120 will come forth. In the second 360. In the third 1080. In the fourth 3240. In the fifth 9720. In the sixth 29160. In the seventh 87480. In the eighth 262440. In the ninth 787320. In the tenth 2361960.

Latin:

Ad Exod. 1, 7. sub finem ad pag. 319. b.

Potest etiam ostendi, quomodo ordinaria via naturali tantus numerus, imo longe major prodire potuerit. Assumamus annos tantum 200. Israeli- tas exegisse in Ægypto, & 40. tantum qui genera- rint, & cuilibet tantum tres masculos fuisse, nec ante vigesimum annum eos generasse, ita per de- cem vicenarios multo major numerus proditurus est: Nam primo annorum vicenario prodibunt 120. Secundo 360. Tertio 1080. Quarto 3240. Quinto 9720. Sexto 29160. Septimo 87480. Octavo 262440. Nono 787320. Decimo 2361960.

## 1:8
Verse 8. THERE AROSE MEANWHILE A NEW KING.

Cajetan wrongly thinks that he was an Assyrian by origin, drawing to this Is. 52. v. 4., where nothing else is noted than that the same people suffered from the King of Babylon what they once did in Egypt. Others, with Pererius and Torniel, more correctly say that he was the Egyptian Amenophis. He is called new, however, not because he was from another dynasty, but because he was from a different family, unless you prefer that he is called new on account of a new manner of reigning, and because he was of a different disposition from his predecessors.

Verse the same. WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH. He was unmindful of those things which Joseph had performed and advised for Egypt, and of those things which had been promised to him. Truly it is said: φεῦ τῶν θανόντων ὡς τάχ' ὄλλυται χάρις. What wonder is it that human benefits easily slip from minds when the same happens with divine benefits? See Jud. II, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SURREXIT INTEREA REX NOVUS.

Assyrium illum origine fuisse perperam pu- tat Cajetanus, eo trahens Es. 52. v. 4. ubi nihil aliud notatur, quam quod idem populus passus sit a Rege Babyloniæ, quod olim in Ægypto. Rectius alii Ægyptium Amenophim fuisse dicunt, cum Pererio & Torniello. Dicitur autem novus, non quod ex alia Dynastia, sed quod e familia diversa esset, nisi malis novum dictum, ob novam regnandi rationem, & quod diverso ingenio a prioribus fuerit.

Vers. eod. QVI IGNORABAT JOSEPH ) Immemor erat eorum, quæ Ægypto præstiterat, & consuluerat Jose- phus, & eorum, quæ ipsi promissa fuerant, Vere dicitur: φεῦ τῶν θανόντων ὡς τάχ' ὄλλυται χάρις. Quid mirum beneficia humana facile excidere animis cum & divinis beneficiis idem eveniat? Vid. Jud. II, 10.

## 1:10
10. LEST PERCHANCE HE MULTIPLY) There is a threefold fear from foreigners where their multitude increases greatly: lest they oppress the natives by conspiracy, lest they join themselves to enemies, lest they seek an exit by force.

Latin:

10. NE FORTE MVLTIPLICETVR) Triplex est me- tus a peregrinis, ubi multum increscit eorum multitudo, ne conspiratione indigenas opprimant, ne hostibus se adjun- gant, ne vi exitum quærant.

## 1:11
Verse 11. TASKMASTERS.

The LXX [render it] taskmasters. But the Hebrew מסים denotes tributes, not works; therefore the first degree of the oppression of the Israelites is expressed here, namely the exaction of tributes, which exhausted their wealth; from that word מס, Leonhard Marius ineptly derives his Missa. The second degree was of services, when they had oppressed them with personal forced labor and burdens, namely in building the cities מסכנות: The Vulgate renders it, tabernacles. But that word is used for treasuries, 2 Chron. 16, 4. c. 17, 12. c. 32, 28. And therefore some translate it cities of treasuries, B. Luth. Schatz-Häuser, render, which however most explain concerning the repositories and granaries of grain with Jerome, because Egypt was as it were a common storehouse of neighboring nations, and therefore grain was stored in border cities, which for that reason had to be fortified. For these were the riches of Egypt. See Amama in Cens. Vulg. Vers. on this passage. But those opinions easily agree: because those treasure cities could be built for the preservation of both riches and provisions, and indeed even of arms, since the word treasure has a very wide meaning. Compare Deut. 28, 12. Joel 1, 17. Prov. 3, 10. Moreover, hard labor in clay and brick is attributed to the Hebrews in v. 14, which is to be understood either through a hendiadys, in clayey bricks, or in that manner, so that labor is designated both in digging up clay and in making bricks; to which was added the cultivation of the land, because they had to be occupied in works of the earth, whether in cultivating fields, or as Josephus observes, in dividing the Nile into many ditches for the irrigation of individual fields. Josephus adds the insane substructures of the pyramids imposed upon the Hebrews. Nor indeed is it to be believed that they were occupied only with bricks: that labor is named hard and troublesome by way of example, so that from this one burden others might be learned. For it is not likely that such a great multitude of men was used for many years solely for bricks for the said buildings. To which also are added from the comparison of chapter V, 14, blows and scourgings, as those who were forced to work in a servile manner. God, however, permitted these things because of the sins of the people, who had defiled themselves with the idolatry of the Egyptians, which is clearly gathered from Jos. 24, 24. and Ezech. 20, 7. 8., with Pererius in vain denying it: And so that under dire servitude they might strive all the more earnestly with vows and sighs toward the promised liberation. Nor, however, must it be said with the Calvinists that God impelled the Egyptians to evil or turned their hearts to hatred and deceit, for what Rivetus objects, that God is thus not made the author of evil, even if He turns the hearts of men to evil, provided He does not make good hearts evil by instilling malice, that is by no means sufficient to excuse the Calvinists. For not only must one beware that God is not established as the physical cause of evil, by effecting or instilling malice, but also that He is not held as the moral cause, which certainly follows from the opinion of the Calvinists, with Rivetus himself not denying it, provided he imputes to God that He moves and bends evil wills in themselves, just as a rider impelling a horse that is lame by itself, which indeed He does not command evils, or impel toward them insofar as they are evils, but as they are the hidden judgments of God: but what is this other than God being the moral cause of sin? As regards Ps. 105, 25, those words: He turned their heart, so that they might pursue His people with hatred, are explained neutrally by the Chaldean, their heart was perverse, which sense agrees very well with the Hebrew text, if it is rendered thus: each one, namely of them, turned his own heart. Meanwhile, if it were referred especially to God, and rendered actively, it would have to be understood according to the analogy of faith and so that it does not conflict with this history, in which all blame is transferred to the Egyptians; wherefore it can be taken in three ways, (1.) ἀφορμητικῶς, by occasion given not for that end, but seized by the Egyptians: concerning which August. on this passage, not by making their heart evil, but by doing good to His own people, He turned their heart, evil of its own accord, to hatred. (2.) παραχωρητικῶς or permissively, as Theodor. explains: He did not Himself change the mind of the Egyptians, but gave place to free will, and did not at all prohibit their snares, so that He might show those who were suffering the snares to be superior to those laying them. (3.) ἀφαιρετικῶς or privatively, because God deprived the Egyptians of His grace, whence their heart became malignant and malice grew more and more. (4.) διατακτικῶς by governing, namely, that malignant affection so that He might turn the calamity brought upon the Israelites to their own good and to the glory of His name; for that the Egyptians conceived hatred by their own nature and entered into plans for oppressing the Israelites, Moses expressly testifies, and since their ingratitude against the merits of Joseph, as well as envy and hatred, is reproved by the Holy Spirit, how can it be attributed to God as the author?

Vers. on the same. SO THAT THEY MIGHT AFFLICT THEM WITH BURDENS) Manethos in the Egyptian History concerning this matter: of those who had suffered enough time in the quarries. The cause of making pyramids for the Kings of Egypt, so that the common people would not be idle. Pliny book 36, ch. 12. Aristotle Polit. V. ch. 11. and it is tyrannical to make the subjects poor, so that neither a guard is maintained, and being occupied with daily tasks they are unable to plot. For a similar reason Tarquinius plunged the Roman common people into draining ditches and sewers. Tacitus concerning Germany: An idle hand of armed men easily becomes wanton. The same, Annal. I. He had interrupted the usual duties. From that beginning the soldier became wanton. Life of Agricola: There was labor from discord, when the soldier accustomed to expeditions became wanton in idleness. Remedies for this evil were sought by the Princes. Thus ramparts, ditches, and other things, not always out of necessity, often sought against the idleness of camps, that same Tacitus in Annals 1 records: elsewhere he adds bridges to an amphitheater.

Remedies against lasciviousness or idleness were not being sought here. Pharaoh was rather acting with his counsels here, as to how the Israelites might be oppressed by craft, whom he scarcely dared to attack in open warfare. Therefore, through public burdens, through most foul services, through the infanticide of midwives, he was attempting it.

Verse same. PHITOM) Which is Pathomus near Bubastis according to Herodotus. Whence the Pathmetic mouth in Ptolemy in his description of Egypt. Those were (Phithon, & Raemses) fortresses at the entrance of Egypt: already indeed built before, but here to be fortified more and more.

Latin:

Vers. 11. MAGISTROS OPERUM.

LXX. ἐπιστάτας ἔργων. Sed Ebræum מסים tri- buta, non opera notat, ideo primus gradus pressuræ Israelitarum hic expressus est, tributorum nempe exactio, quæ eorum opes exhauriebat; e voce illa מס inepte deducit Leonhard. Marius suam Missam. Alter gradus erat servitiorum, cum personalibus angariis, & oneribus eosdem oppressissent, utpote in extruendis urbibus מסכנות : Vulgatus reddit, ta- bernacula. Sed vox illa pro thesauris usurpatur 2. Chron. 16, 4. c. 17, 12. c. 32, 28. Ideoque urbes the- saurorum nonnulli, B. Luth. Schatz-Häuser, red- dunt, quod tamen plerique de thecis & granariis frumentorum explicant cum Hieronymo, quia Ægy- ptus erat horreum quasi commune nationum vici- narum, ideoque in Civitatibus limitaneis repone- bantur frumenta, quæ ea de causa muniendæ erant. Hæc enim opes erant Ægypti. Vid. Amama in Cens. Vulg. Vers. ad h.l. Facile a. conveniunt illæ sententiæ: quia urbes illæ Thesaurariæ & ad opum, & ad annonæ, imo etiam ad armorum as- servationem condi potuere, quum latissime vox thesauri pateat. Conf. Deut. 28, 12. Joel 1, 17. Prov. 3, 10. Tribuuntur autem Ebræis v. 14. opera dura in luto & latere, quod vel per Hendyaden intelli- gendum, in lutosis lateribus, vel ea ratione, ut tum labor in effodiendo luto designetur, tum in confi- ciendis lateribus; quibus accedebat terræ cultura, quia in operibus terræ occupari debebant, sive in agris excolendis, sive ut Josephus observat, in Nilo in multas fossas diducendo ad irrigandum agros sin- gulorum. Addit Josephus Pyramidum insanas substructiones Ebræis impositas. Neque enim cre- dendum, quod solis lateribus vacarint: nominatur is labor durus, & molestus exempli causa, ut ex hoc uno onere discantur alia. Nam tantam hominum multitudinem per complures annos solum ad late- res pro ædificiis dictis adhibitam esse, non sit vero simile. Quibus etiam accedunt e collatione ca- pitis V, 14. verbera & flagellationes, utpote qui- bus servilem in modum ad opera cogebantur. Per- misit autem hæc Deus ob peccata populi, qui se ido- lolatria Ægyptiorum polluerat, quod luculenter e Jos. 24, 24. & Ezech. 20, 7. 8. nequiequam id inficiante Pererlo, colligitur: Et ut sub dira ser- vitute votis ac suspiriis ad promissam liberationem tanto enixius contenderet. Neque tamen cum Calvinianis dicendum, Deum Ægyptios impulisse ad malum aut corda eorum ad odium & dolum con- vertisse, nam quod Rivetus excipit, Deum ita non fieri autorem mali, etsi corda hominum ad malum convertat, modo non corda bona efficiat mala, instil- lando malitiam, id ad exculpandos Calvinianos minime sufficit. Nam non tantum cavendum est, ne causa mali Physica Deus statuatur, efficiendo vel instillando malitiam, sed etiam ne habeatur pro causa morali, quod certe ex Calvinianorum sen- tentia sequitur, non diffitente ipso Riveto, siqui- dem Deo imputet, quod voluntates malas in se mo- veat & flectat, perinde ut eques impellens equum per se claudum, quod non imperet quidem mala, aut ad ea impellat, quatenus mala sunt, sed qua sunt occulta judicia Dei: quid vero hoc aliud est, quam Deum esse causam moralem peccati? Quod ad Ps. 105, 25. attinet, verba illa: convertit cor eorum, ut odio pro- sequerentur populum suum, neutraliter exponuntur a Chaldæo, perversum fuit cor eorum, qui sensus cum Ebræo textu optime congruit, si ita reddatur: con- vertit unusquisque sc. eorum, cor suum. Interim si ad Deum maxime referretur, & active reddere- tur, intelligendum id esset juxta analogiam fidei & ne huic historiæ refragetur, in qua culpa omnis in Ægyptios transfertur; quapropter id tribus modis accipi potest, (1.) ἀφορμητικῶς, occasione non eo fine data, sed ab Ægyptiis arrepta: de quo August. ad h. l. non cor illorum malum faciendo, sed po- pulo suo benefaciendo, cor illorum sponte malum con- vertit ad odium. (2.) παραχωρητικῶς vel permissive, ut Theodor. explicat: non ipse Ægyptiorum men- tem mutavit, sed libero arbitrio locum dedit, eorumque insidias minime prohibuit, ut eos, qui insidias patie- bantur, superiores insidiantibus ostenderet. (3.) ἀφαι- ρετικῶς vel privative, quod Deus gratia sua Ægy- ptios destituerit, unde cor ipsorum malignum ac malitiam magis magisque profecit. (4.) διατακτι- κῶς gubernando sc. malignum illum affectum ut ca- lamitatem Israelitis illatam ipsis in bonum & in glo- riam nominis sui verteret; quod enim odium Ægy- ptii suopte ingenio conceperint & de opprimen- dis Israelitis consilia inierint, diserte testatur Mo- ses, & cum ingratitudo eorum adversus merita Josephi, nec non invidia, atque odium a Spiritu S. reprehendatur, quomodo Deo ceu auctori tribui poterit?

Vers. eodem. UT AFFLIGERENT EOS ONERIBUS) Manethos in Historia Ægyptiaca de hac re: τῶν δὲ ταῖς λα- τομίαις ὡς χρόνου ἱκανὸς ταλαιπωρησάντων. Pyramidum fa- ciendarum causa Regibus Ægypti, ne plebs esset otiosa. Pli- nius l. 36. c. 12. Aristoteles Polit. V. c. 11. καὶ τὸ πένητας ποιεῖν τὸς ἀρχομένες τυραννικὸν, ὅπως μήτε φυλακὴ τρέφηται, κὰι πρὸς τῷ καθ’ ἡμέραν ὄντες ἄσχολοι ὦσιν ἐπιβυλεύειν. Pari de causa Tarquinius plebem Romanam in fossas cloacasque ex- hauriendas demersit. Tacitus de Germania: Otiosa arma- torum manus facile lasciviunt. Idem, Annal. I. Intermiserat solita munia. Eo principio lascivire miles. Vita Agricolæ: Discordia laboratum, cum assuetus expeditionibus miles otio la- sciviret. Huic malo remedia quæsita a Principibus. Ita val- lum, fossas, aliaque, non ex necessitate semper, sæpe adversus otium castrorum quæsita, idem ille Tacitus Annalium 1. me- morat: alibi amphitheatro pontes adjicit.

Non adeo remedia adversus lasciviam vel otium hic quærebantur. Id agebat potius hic con- siliis suis Pharao, quomodo astu opprimi possent Israelitæ, quos aperto Marte aggredi vix audebat. Per onera ergo publica, per fœdissima servitia, per obstetricum infanticidium tentabat.

Vers. eod. PHITOM) Quæ Pathomus ad Bubastim Herodoto. Unde Pathmeticum ostium Ptolemeo in descriptione Ægypti. Fuerunt illa (Phithon, & Raemses) fortalitia in aditu Ægypti: jam ante quidem extructa, sed hic magis magisque munienda.

## 1:15
Verse 15. BUT THE KING SAID TO THE MIDWIVES OF THE HEBREWS.

This is the third degree of Israelite oppression, tending toward the extirpation of the male offspring. Furthermore, those two midwives must have been either the chiefs of the midwives or prefects over the rest, as Vatablus notes, since two could by no means have sufficed for all the Hebrew women. The Hebrews trifle that they were Jochabeth and her daughter Miriam. But whether they were Hebrews or Egyptians is debated: most modern Pontificians, Tostatus, Pererius, Salianus, and Cornel. a Lap. urge the latter opinion with Hugo, Lyranus, and Oleastrius, as does Bellarmine, in order to prove that gentiles without faith or special help can perform a moral good work uncontaminated by any sin, which Bellarmine strives to prove especially from the example of the Egyptian midwives in book V de gratia & lib. arbit. cap. 9. But it is uncertain that these women were Egyptians. They make them Hebrews with the Targum Hierosolym. & most Rabbis, Aug. lib. contra mendacium cap. 15, Eman. Saa, Joh. Lorinus, Richardus, and other Pontificians, to which Trem. & Jun. also incline, as well as Rivetus and others. Nor indeed has it been proven thus far by argument or solid testimony that they were Egyptians. Josephus, book 2, chapter 5, has nothing concerning the command given to the midwives. However, the reasons which those who posit they were Egyptians bring forward—namely, that they themselves in verse 19 intimate that they served the women in labor of the Egyptians, and that it is not likely that Pharaoh would have entrusted the execution of his tyrannical decree to Hebrew women—are examined by B. Dorsch in Syllog. vindic. in Exod. page 21. Furthermore, even if they had been Egyptian by origin, they could nevertheless have been converted to the faith of the Israelites; for Hebrew women would not have so easily entrusted themselves to midwives addicted to Egyptian idolatry. Finally, that those midwives were without faith or special help of God, by which they are said to have feared God in verse 17, is not admitted by Jerome in ch. 65 of Isaiah, nor by Rupert in book 1 on Exodus, ch. 7, because they assert that they were in a state of grace: Thomas will not admit it in the second part of the second part, q. 110, art. 3, supporting the opinion of Jerome; to whom Lyra also subscribes in his gloss, that these midwives were converted to the faith of the one God and the rite of the Hebrews. Tostatus says that they received a spiritual good and were saved: what of the fact that the Jesuit Pererius even contradicts Bellarmine, when he asserts that there was holy fear in them through grace infused into their minds, without the help of which they would by no means have committed themselves to such a manifest danger of life by that work of charity. Nor does Bellarmine's consequence stand on firm footing; whatever God rewards is a good moral work, uncontaminated by any sin, for God rewards even the virtues of the Gentiles directed toward the honesty of life with a temporal reward, yet Augustine teaches that all their works were sins, book 4 against Julian, ch. 3, and on the Palestinian acts, ch. 14: however much, he says, the works of infidels may be praised, we know the true sentence of the Apostle: everything that is not from faith is sin. With which Leo the Great agrees in sermon 20 on the fast of Pentecost, cf. B. Dorsch, loc. cit.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DIXIT AUTEM REX OBSTE- TRICIBUS EBRÆORUM.

Tertius hic gradus est pressuræ Israëliticæ, tendens ad masculæ prolis extirpationem. Cæte- rum Obstetricus illas duas oportet aut Principes fuiffe obstetricum, aut præfectas reliquis, ut Vata- blus notat, siquidem omnibus Ebræis mulieribus duæ sufficere minime potuerint. Ebræi nugantur, Jochabeth fuisse, ejusque filiam Miriam. Utrum autem Ebrææ fuerint, an Ægyptiæ, disquiritur: Posteriorem sententiam ideo urgent cum Hugone, Lyrano, & Oleastrio Pontificii moderni plerique, Tostatus, Pererius, Salianus & Cornel. a Lap. ut Bellarm. ut probent, gentiles sine fide aut speciali auxilio bonum opus morale nullo peccato contami- natum facere posse, quod cumprimis ab exemplo Ægyptiacarum obstetricum Bellarm. probare sa- tagit lib. V. de gratia & lib. arbit. cap. 9. At in- certum est, mulieres has Ægyptias fuisse. Ebræas eas faciunt cum Targum Hierosolym. & Rabbinis plerisque Aug. l. contra mendacium c. 15. Eman. Saa, Joh. Lorinus, Richardus & alii Pontif. quo etiam inclinant Trem. & Jun. ut & Rivetus, aliique. Neque vero vel argumento, vel testimonio solido probatum hactenus, quod fuerint Ægyptiæ. Jo- sephus lib. 2, c. 5. de mandato Obstetricibus dato nihil habet. Rationes autem, quas adferunt, qui Ægyptias statuunt, quod nempe ipsæ vers. 19. in- nuant se puerperis Ægyptiorum inservijsse, quodque verisimile non sit, Pharaonem tyrannici sui decreti executionem mulieribus Ebræis credidisse, exami- nat B. Dorsch. in Syllog. vindic. in Exod. pag. 21. Porro si maxime fuissent Ægyptiacæ origine, po- tuere tamen conversæ esse ad fidem Israëlitarum; non enim ita facile Ebrææ mulieres, idololatriæ Ægyptiacæ deditis obstetricibus se credidissent. Denique obstetrices illas sine fide aut speciali auxilio Dei fuisse, qua Deum timuisse dicuntur vers. 17. non admittet Hieron. in c. 65. Es. nec Rupertus l. 1. in Exod. cap. 7. quia asserunt illas in statu gratiæ fuisse: non admittet Thomas in secunda 2. q. 110. art. 3. Hieronymi sententiam adstruens; quibus etiam subscribit Lyranus in glossa, quod hæ obstetrices ad fidem unius Dei & ritum Ebræorum conversæ fuerint. Tostatus dicit, eas bonum spirituale accepisse & salvatas esse: quid quod Jesuita etiam Perer. Bel- larmino contradicat, dum asserit sanctum timorem in illis fuisse per interiorem animo infusam gratiam, qua nisi adjutæ fuissent, nequaquam seipsas in tam manifestum vitæ discrimen opere illo charitatis com- misissent. Nec consequentia Bellarmini firmo stat talo; quicquid Deus præmio afficit, id bonum opus morale est, nullo peccato contaminatum, nam & Gentilium virtutes ad honestatem vitæ directas Deus mercede temporali munerat, quorum tamen opera omnia peccata fuisse docet Aug. l. 4. contra Julian. c. 3. & de gestis Palæstinis c. 14. quantumli- bet, inquit, opera infidelium prædicentur, Apostoli sententiam veram novimus: omne, quod non est ex fi- de, peccatum est. Cui consonat Leo magnus serm. 20. de jejunio Pentecost. conf. B. Dorsch. l. c.

## 1:16
V. 16. AND THE TIME OF BIRTH SHALL HAVE ARRIVED. What is in the Hebrew as אבנים, seem to be the doors of the womb משבר. Thus the Vulgate with the LXX Interpreters. In Hebrew it is, when you see upon the אבנים by which name the Hebrews understand the stool of those giving birth with the Chaldean, nor does the word occur, except in Jer. 18:3, where it is used of the potter's wheel. Others here interpret it as the two hinges of the womb: in whichever way it is taken, the sense of the command is not obscure, namely that they should kill the fetus still clinging in the womb. Grotius approves the latter sense. What is in the Hebrew as אבנים seem to be the doors of the womb.

Latin:

V. 16. ET PARTVS TEMPVS ADVENERIT. Quod in Hebræo est אבנים, videntur esse fores uteri משבר. Ita Vulgata cum LXX. Interpretibus. In Ebr. est, cum videritis super אבנים quo nomine Ebræi sellam parturientium cum Chaldæo intelli- gunt, nec occurrit vocabulum, nisi Jer. 18, 3. ubi de sella figuli usurpatur. Alii hic interpretantur de duobus uteri cardinibus: utrovis accipiatur modo, sensus mandati haud obscurus est, ut nempe in ute- ro adhuc hærentem fœtum interficiant. Posterio- rem autem sensum probat Grotius. Quod in He- bræo est אבנים videntur esse fores uteri.

## 1:19
V. 19. FOR THEY HAVE THE KNOWLEDGE OF MIDWIFERY. In Hebrew it is: חיות they are lively, or life-giving, which Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, and B. Luther explain thus, that they are lively and vigorous, to which the Jerusalem Targum adds that they pray before their heavenly Father, and thus give birth before the midwife comes to them. Others interpret it thus, that the Hebrew women are life-givers, i.e., of infants, i.e., midwives, because midwives are so called by the Chaldeans, as Fagius testifies in his Commentary on the Targum Onkelos, who also understands the explanation of Onkelos in this way. Some interpret it as a lively and sagacious wit, by which method Cornelius a Lapide explains it to accommodate the Vulgate version. But the former interpretations are without doubt better, because it is not a question here of a lively wit but of strength and the knowledge of midwifery; meanwhile, those interpretations are easily reconciled: for if the Hebrew women were midwives to themselves, it is necessary that they had the knowledge and vigorous and robust strength.

But it is disputed here, on the occasion of the answer given by the midwives to the King concerning a lie, whether it is lawful in any case? Cassian in conference XVII, ch. 17, as also Bede on 1 Kings 21, affirm it, to whom Clement of Alexandria also seems to agree in book VII of the Stromata, as also Origen in book IV against Celsus, and among the more recent ones, Rupert of Deutz on this passage, as well as Hugo Grotius on the law of war and peace, book 3, ch. 1, no. 16, contending that that lie was lawful, because in such a case, where the life of an innocent person cannot otherwise be preserved, a falsehood can be spoken without sin, concerning whose opinion we have seen in the Annotations on Joshua 2:4. On the contrary, however, Augustine in his book against lying, ch. 10, Gregory in book 18 of the Morals, the Author of the Ordinary Gloss, as also Thomas in the second part of the second part, q. 110, art., as well as Lyra on this passage, assert that these midwives can be absolved neither from a lie nor from sin, and that every lie is a sin; however, Gregory the Great, Thomas, and Lyra establish that the lie of these midwives was only a venial sin. Alexander of Hales in his Summa, part 2, q. 139, considers a double cause of the lie in the midwives, one the compassion for the boys, the other the protection of their own life; with respect to the former, he asserts that this sin was venial, but with respect to the latter, a mortal sin, because they loved their own life inordinately and perversely; so also Nodinus, Tanner, Cornelius a Lapide, and most others. Some of our own refer this deed to human infirmities; others to personal deeds not indeed disapproved, but yet not to be imitated, nor proposed for imitation. Finally, others defend a middle opinion by distinguishing between the dissimulation of the truth and the pronunciation of a falsehood. They think that those midwives indeed dissembled something of the truth, but uttered nothing false: thus Tremellius and Junius judge that they spoke truly, and what is held in verses 17 and 18, that the midwives preserved the infants alive, they explain as concerning the outcome, namely, and the intention, but not concerning actual help given to the Hebrew women, so that they spoke the truth in part, but dissembled something of the truth lawfully and without a lie, to which opinion Dr. Walther also inclines in his Spongia Mosaica on this passage, referring this answer of the midwives to lawful simulations, provided that thereby neither the glory of God was detracted from, nor the safety of the neighbor, but rather it contributed to the safety of the infants; which opinion seems to be preferred, because the midwives are celebrated for having feared God, Exod. 1:17, and for this deed they received a reward from God, verse 21; if, however, they had lied, they could not have been proclaimed by the Holy Spirit as having the fear of God, nor would they have received a reward from God. Dr. Walther has dealt at length with this matter in the aforementioned place, where he weighs most of the examples usually brought forward for a lawful lie.

Latin:

V. 19. IPSÆ ENIM HABENT OBSTETRI- CANDI SCIENTIAM. In Ebr. est: חיות vivaces sunt, aut vivificantes, quod Aben-Ezra, Vatablus & B. Luth. ita explicant, quod vivaces & vegetæ sint vel robustæ, quibus ad- dit Targum Hieros. quod orent coram patre suo cæ- lesti, atque ita pariant, antequam obstetrix ad eas ve- niat. Alii sic interpretantur, quod mulieres Ebrææ sint vivificatrices sc. infantum, i. e. obstetrices, quia Chaldæis obstetrices ita vocantur teste Fagio in Comment. ad Targum Onkelos. qui ita etiam ex- plicationem Onkelosii intelligit. Nonnulli de vi- vaci & sagaci ingenio interpretantur, quo pacto ex- plicat Corn. a Lap. ut obstetricetur vulgatæ versio- ni. Sed priores interpretationes sine dubio melio- res sunt, quia non de vivaci ingenio sed de robore & notitia obstetricandi hic agitur, interim facile illæ interpretationes conciliantur: nam si obstetrices ipsæ sibi fuere Ebrææ, oportet ut scientiam habue- rint & vires vegetas ac robustas.

Disputatur autem hic occasione responsi ab obstetricibus Regi dati de mendacio, utrum id ali- quo casu licitum sit? Cassianus in collatione XVII. c. 17. ut & Beda in 1. Reg. 21. affirmant, quibus etiam annuere videtur Clem. Alex. l. VII. Stromat. ut & Orig. l. IV. contra Celsum, & e recentioribus Rupertus Thuitiensis in h. l. nec non Hugo Grotius de jure pac. & belli l. 3. c. 1. num. 16. contendens, mendacium illud licitum fuisse, quia in tali casu, ubi vita innocentis aliter conservari nequit, citra pecca- tum falsum dici queat, de cujus sententia vidimus in Annotat. ad Jos. 2, 4. Ex adverso vero Aug. lib. contra mendac. c. 10. Greg. lib. 18. Moral. Autor Glossæ ordin. ut & Thomas in sec. sec. qv. 110. art. nec non Lyranus ad h. l. obstetrices has neque a mendacio, neque a peccato absolvi posse, & omne men- dacium peccatum esse adserunt, harum tamen ob- stetricum mendacium peccatum veniale tantum fuisse Greg. M. Thomas & Lyranus statuunt. Alex. Alesius in summa part. 2. q. 139. in obstetricibus du- plicem mendacii causam considerat, unam puero- rum compassionem, alteram propriæ vitæ tuitionem; prioris respectu peccatum hoc veniale fuisse asserit, respectu vero posteriori peccatum mortale, quia vitam suam inordinate & perverse dilexerunt; sic etiam Nodinus, Tannerus, Corn. a Lap. & plerique alii. E nostratibus nonnulli referunt hoc factum ad infirmitates humanas; alii ad facta personalia non improbata quidem, sed tamen non imitanda, nec ad imitandum proposita. Denique alii mediam tuen- tur sententiam distinguendo inter veritatis dissi- mulationem & falsi pronunciationem. Obstetrices illas aliquid veri quidem dissimulasse, nihil tamen falsi protulisse: sic Trem. & Jun. vere eas locutas esse censent, quod autem vers. 17. & 18. habetur, obstetrices vivos conservasse natos, ita explicant de eventu nempe & consilio, non vero de actuali auxi- lio Ebræis mulieribus lato, ut ita ex parte verum di- xerint, aliquid autem veri licite ac sine mendacio dissimularint, in quam sententiam propendet etiam Dn. D. Walth. in Spong. Mos. ad h. l. ad licitas simulationes hoc responsum obstetricum referens, siquidem ideo nec Dei gloriæ quicquam deroga- tum fuerit, nec proximi saluti, imo ad salutem in- fantum id fecerit; quæ sententia præferenda vide- tur, quia celebrantur Obstetrices, quod Deum ti- muerint, Exod. 1, 17. & ob hoc factum præmium a Deo accepere vers. 21. si autem mentitæ fuissent, nec a timore Dei religioso prædicari potuissent a Spiri- tu S. nec præmium a Deo accepissent. Prolixe de hac materia egit D. Walth. l. c. ubi exempla plera- que pro mendacio licito adduci solita expendit.

## 1:21
V. 21. HE BUILT HOUSES FOR THEM) He increased their offspring, because they had spared the offspring of the Hebrews. Thus Ambrose rightly. Thus בנה is taken in Gen. 16:2 and 30:3, in which places the Greeks use the verb τεκνοποιεῖν, and thence בֵּן.

Paul Fagius, Robert Stephanus in the notes of Sebastian Castellio, Calvin, as well as Tremellius and Junius, and also our Brentius and Theod. Hackspan in his Philological and Theological notes on the Hebrews, understand that because the midwives, fearing God, did not kill their male offspring, it came to pass that the families of the Hebrews grew and were greatly increased. The masculine gender in the pronoun לָהֶם (to them) favors this. But since verse 20 has already dealt with the multiplication of the Hebrews, and what is explained here is the consequence not of the vivification of the male infants, but of the midwives' fear of the Lord, others interpret it concerning the midwives, that God built houses for them, and by an enallage familiar to the Hebrews, Ruth 1:13, 2 Kings 14:6, etc., they say the masculine is used for the feminine, which is the almost common explanation of the interpreters. Vatablus therefore thinks the masculine is used because women and families receive their name from men. Theod. Hackspan urges that it is not a miracle that is recounted here, but a divine blessing: whereas the childbirth of old midwives would be a miracle. He himself understands, however, that this argument can easily be met if it is said that houses were built for the midwives, not through their own childbirths, but in children and grandchildren. He therefore thinks that what primarily stands in the way of this diversity of gender is that it was Moses' intention to explain how the people grew. But although Moses explains that in this chapter, it still had to be proven that it is hinted at by these words. For not everything that is contained in that chapter signifies the same thing precisely, nor is that necessary. Therefore, he also prepares other reinforcements for this argument: Namely, that the cause of the new fury in Pharaoh is indicated here, which was not an increase in the family of the midwives, but the increased number of the Hebrews. This also follows, that it had already been said before that God did good to the midwives. To which, however, it may be answered: it is assumed without solid proof that the cause of the new fury and the more severe edict is presented in these words, when it is explained rather historically how God did good to the midwives, namely by building their houses. I confess, however, that the explanation of Brentius and Fagius seems sufficiently probable, and since an enallage is not easily to be admitted (even though the Chaldean and the LXX maintain it here) and the text is plain in the sources, with the proper meaning of the masculine pronoun retained, I judge that it should be preferred: Thus, therefore, the discourse flows: And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God (by not killing the males) and He made them (the Israelites) houses (furthermore He built up and multiplied their families), Pharaoh commanded all his people (that is, not only the midwives, but all the Egyptians should be intent on this, that the males should be taken away), every son that is born ye shall cast into the river. Thus the cause of the new edict, and of the same being made to the whole people, because he saw that the males were not being killed by the midwives, and that the families of the Israelites, which are built up especially through the males, were increasing daily, is indicated by Moses himself: and it is explained at the same time, what was said in the preceding verse, how the people were greatly strengthened, because, namely, the midwives did not obey the King, and God increased their families with a singular blessing.

But the common interpretation having been assumed, it is further discussed how the houses were built for the midwives, about which interpreters vary. August. followed the Greek ἐποίησαν ἑαυταῖς οἰκείας, as he himself read it, 'they made for themselves houses,' and thinks that they made fortified houses for themselves, so that they might protect themselves from the Egyptians; others say that the Israelite people built such houses for them. But how could they have protected themselves with houses against the King? Others refer it to Pharaoh, that he himself built houses for them, from which it would not be permitted for them to leave, so that, namely, there would be a need for the women of the Hebrews to be brought to them. But this is absurd, and it is not Pharaoh, but God, whom they feared, who is said to have built houses for them. What the Hebrews explain concerning the house of the priesthood and the Kingdom, because they imagine that the midwife was the mother of Aaron and Moses. Lyranus interprets it thus, that those midwives were received into the Hebrew people and joined in marriage to leading men. To which the Schol. of Job. Mariana also seems to lean regarding the lot given to the midwives among the Israelites; but Tostatus refutes this, because the Hebrews were cast out and held as slaves, and because in this way the midwives would have irritated Pharaoh more vehemently against themselves. Cornel. a L. also refutes it, because Moses does not say that God made houses for them among the Hebrews, but absolutely that He built houses for them. R. David Kimchi understands it thus, that God hid them from Pharaoh and placed them in safety. But that phrase is not used in that way, nor did God build earthly houses for them. Hieronymus and Rupertus and others explain it concerning spiritual and heavenly houses. But the Pontiffs themselves refute these, because 'to build houses' does not occur in the Old Testament in that sense. Others (to whom Grotius has been added) more correctly accept the phrase from the customary manner of speaking as referring to the building up of their families in the children born from them, with Hieronymus not denying it in Tradit. Ebr. on Gen. ch. 16, or with Theodoret regarding the matter of family affairs and temporal goods, how God is said to build houses in Ps. 127:1. And it seemed a reward worthy of piety that those who saved the offspring of the Hebrews should be increased with offspring, and therefore this opinion is preferred by most. See those various interpretations discussed by Fagius in this place, and Pererius.

But the Papists wrongly construct the merits of works from this, and some indeed attempt to carve out merits of eternal life from it with Pererius and Leonh. Marius, because it is said that God built houses for them and did them good because they feared God, which collection Thomas and Rupertus confirm with their explanation, because they understand heavenly mansions by 'houses.' But Cornel. a Lap. refutes this, because 'to build houses' does not signify in Scripture 'to give the reward of eternal life.' Cornelius adds that God in the Old Testament was not accustomed to express a heavenly reward and that the express promise of it is proper to the New Testament; but this is repugnant to Gen. 2:17, Lev. 18:5, Dan. 12:2, John 5:39, and is otherwise refuted among the Socinians. He would have spoken more correctly had he said that neither in the Old nor in the New Testament is any human work proposed as meritorious of eternal life; indeed, this χάρισμα is a gift of God purely gratuitous in Christ Jesus, Rom. 5, last verse. And there is no proportion between our works, even the most laborious of the most holy martyrs, and the glory of eternal life, Rom. 8:18. And therefore the collection of the Jesuit Pererius is to be rejected, because that fear of God proceeded from the grace of God, [and they] without doubt merited eternal life: because blessedness is his to whom God imputes righteousness without works, Rom. 4:6, and as we are justified δωρεὰν freely, τῇ χάριτι by grace through the redemption of Christ, Rom. 3:24, so also we are saved freely: not of works, lest any man should boast, Eph. 2:9, Rom. 11:6. And although fear proceeds from the grace of God, it is not therefore perfect, because it contracts imperfection from the proximate principle. But let the Jesuits first settle this among themselves. For Pererius and Marius say that that act of the midwives, the fear of God, proceeded from grace; Bellarmine, on the contrary, in book V de gratia et libero arbit. ch. 9, asserts that it was without grace and special help. Many others, therefore, among the Papists say that this work of the fear of God and of charity toward one's neighbor by the midwives earned this temporal reward, but not an eternal reward. Alexander Alesius says, that work was good, but not sufficient to merit glory because of a lack of charity, but because no good remains unrewarded, therefore the Lord rewarded that work on this earth. Alesius proves that, because in them there was only servile or human fear, by which they perhaps preferred to protect their present life rather than to merit eternal life, which does not stand with charity. How also many Papists assert that that deed, by which the midwives did not obey the tyranny of Pharaoh and helped the Hebrew women in childbirth, and did not kill the males, had been defiled by servile fear and illicit lying. But how could they have merited anything before God by a deed so defiled? And since all our righteousnesses are impure before God on account of the adhering stain of original sin and the imperfection with which they themselves labor, Is. 64:6, and if they come into contention with justice, they are mere σκύβαλα (refuse), Phil. 3:8, what remains but that we acknowledge that we can merit nothing before God, nay, if God should call us into judgment, that not even the most holy person could answer to a thousand ἐγκλήματα (charges), Job 9:3. Finally, even if we could do all things that God requires, we would still be servos ἀχρείους (unprofitable servants), Luke 17:10, because we only do what we ought. Therefore, he who does what he ought, as Christ teaches, merits nothing, for if he merited anything, he would not be ἀχρεῖος (unprofitable) to himself, in that he merits something for himself. Therefore, none of our works are meritorious, which are all owed, and besides that, imperfect and impure in every respect. Gregory the Great, in book 18 of his Morals, acknowledges this in this work of the midwives: that they themselves lied out of love for the present life; and so he wishes that the reward of kindness, which could have been bestowed upon them in eternal life, was diverted into a worldly recompense on account of the admitted guilt of the lie. In explaining this, Thomas himself is stuck: how could they have merited anything by the outward act of a lie? We answer, he says, they could not indeed merit an eternal reward, but perhaps some temporal reward, to the merit of which the deformity of that lie was not repugnant, just as it was repugnant to the merit of an eternal reward. But is it not most absurd to attribute the merit of a temporal reward to a lie? To this, whatever Pererius may say here in defense of Thomas, whose harsher words he acknowledges, Thomas attributes it to the fact that there is not as much repugnance to the merit of a temporal reward as there is a repugnance of a lie to an eternal reward. Cornelius acknowledges in this place that it is blasphemous to think, nay, even impossible and contrary to the nature of things, for God to approve or reward the act of a lie. He says, however, that God rewarded not the lie, but other acts of piety and fear of God. This we admit from that hypothesis by which it is established that the midwives lied here, just as Augustine answers in his book Against Lying, chapter 19, that the reward was given, not because they lied, but because they were merciful toward the people of God, so that in them it is not the deceit that is rewarded, but the benevolence and kindness of the mind, not the iniquity of the one lying. Nor, however, must it be admitted that the midwives merited that reward by that kindness of theirs, because that kindness was not pure, not even according to the Pontiff or Gregory the Great and Augustine, but was contaminated by servile fear. And therefore God does indeed reward virtues, even if they are stained by some mixture of filth; but those stains make the virtues less meritorious of divine reward. Cornelius a Lapide retorts against the nature of things that it is for a virtue to be stained by a vice, or to be judged by that most lucid eye of God, and to be held as a virtue and adorned with a reward, if it is stained. But how is it against nature for some vice to adhere to a virtue? Were not the virtues of the Gentiles contaminated by sins, inasmuch as they were not referred to their author, and although they seemed good in duty, they were judged as sin because the end was not right, according to Augustine, book 1, Against Julian, chapter 4. A virtue stained by a vice is not indeed held by the most lucid eye of God as a virtue absolutely, yet it is held as such as it is, that is, which does not have absolutely nothing of good quality: which, although it is not worthy of a reward by the Rule of justice, is affected with a reward by the divine goodness, just as Augustine, book 5, On the City of God, chapter 12, proves that the Romans, who referred everything to the desire for praise, received a reward from God for their praiseworthy deeds. But then, was not the lie, which the Papists attribute to the midwives, and that servile fear intimately involved in their good work, so that it affected the whole of it, and increased or contaminated it with some quality that is not good? Augustine says it was done by them at one time and in one cause mercifully and done deceitfully: that the lie was used as a means of executing an act of mercy, the lie done with the intention of helping. Therefore, the lie, if there was one, cannot be so separated from that deed that it is not involved in it, and good works are not explained by one act of the mind or affection, but by a series of circumstances and principles, and in them they are viewed by the most lucid eye of God.
