Nothing else is inferred, therefore, than that God does not reward vice, which is against Thomas, even if He rewards a deed which is contaminated by some vice: and that God does not act according to the tenor of justice when He rewards, but out of a singular motion of divine goodness: and so that a deed of such a kind is not meritorious, which is against the Pontiff and others, even if it receives a reward: because it receives a reward not according to justice, but through grace: not out of merit, but without any merit, whether because God promised it, or because it otherwise pleases Him to testify to His goodness in this way, which, when defects exist in good actions, does not immediately take away the whole, but tolerates it, and for the sake of eliciting a greater good, not only spares the lesser and that which is corrupted by defects, but even bestows some kind of rewards. Which in no way is repugnant to divine justice, because that reward does not concern the defects and vices, but that goodness to which the contamination from the viciousness of the proximate principle is sprinkled, since that goodness itself is derived from the first principle and has God as its author, who crowns nothing in us but His own gifts. If you say that God does not reward sins: I answer that this is true, insofar as sin is understood formally, because God abhors and punishes, He does not reward sin: But it is not true that God does not reward a work that is materially and by external act good in its own kind, even if it is contaminated by some vice, or is sin by accident. Civil virtues, even if they do not suffice before God, nor are they without sin, have many rewards, because God wishes the political state and human society to be preserved by this means; yet it does not follow from this that the virtues of the Gentiles are not sins, because whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14:23; nor does Bernard acknowledge that the virtues of the faithful are free from sin, sermon 5 on the words of Isaiah, for our justice, he says, if there is any humble justice, is perhaps right, but not pure, etc. Adrian of Utrecht, who was Roman Pontiff in the previous century, also acknowledges this in 4 Sentences, on the Sacrament of the Eucharist. fol. 20, where after he had said: our merits and preparation for the sacrament of the Eucharist are like a reed staff, which when someone has leaned upon it, it breaks and pierces the hand of the one leaning, and like a menstruous cloth: he adds; for we continually drip the pus of various crimes upon the cloth of a good life which we weave. Thus, therefore, according to Cornelius a Lapide, no one of the just would be held as just by that most lucid eye of God, or be adorned with a reward.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ÆDIFICAVIT EIS DOMOS) Sobolem earum auxit, quod Hebræi Soboli pepercissent. Ita Ambrosius re- cte. Sic בנה sumitur Gen. 16, 2. & 30, 3. quibus in locis Græ- ci utuntur verbo τεκνοποιεῖν, & inde בֵּן.

Paulus Fagius, Robertus Stephanus in Not. Se- bast. Castellio, Calvinus ut & Trem. & Jun. nec non Brentius noster ac Theod. Hakspan. in not. Philol. Theol. de Ebræis intelligunt, quod quia obstetrices, Deum timentes, non interfecere ipso- rum prolem masculam, factum sit, ut Ebræorum fa- miliæ creverint & valde adauctæ fuerint. Quibus favet genus masculinum in pronomine לָהֶם illis. Sed cum versus 20. jam egerit de multiplicatione Ebræorum, & consequens hic exponatur non vivi- ficationis infantum masculorum, sed timoris Do- mini obstetricum, alii de obstetricibus interpre- tantur, quod illis Deus domos ædificarit, & per- Enallagen Ebræis familiarem Ruth. 1, 13. 2. Reg. 14, 6. &c. masculinum dicunt positum pro fœmi- nino, quæ fere communis interpretum explicatio. Vatablus ideo masculinum adhibitum putat, quia fœminæ & familiæ a viris nomen accipiunt. Theod. Hackspan urget, quod non miraculum hic recen- seatur, sed benedictio divina: obstetricum autem ve- tularum partus miraculum sit. Huic tamen argu- mento facile occurri posse, ipse intelligit, si dica- tur, domus ædificatas esse obstetricibus, non per ipsarum partus, sed in liberis & nepotibus. Id ergo imprimis obstare huic diversitati generis putat, quod Mosis intentio fuerit edisserere, quemadmo- dum populus creverit. Sed quamvis id edisserat Mo- ses, in hoc capite, istis tamen verbis illud innui, probandum erat. Non enim omnia, quæ in illo capite habentur, idem præcise important, nec id necessum est. Suppetias ergo huic etiam argumen- to alias parat: Quod nempe novi furoris in Pharao- ne causa hic indicetur, quæ non augmentum fuit fa- miliæ obstetricum, sed auctus Hebræorum numerus. Succenturiat & hoc, quod antea dictum jam fuerit, quod Deus benefecerit obstetricibus. Ad quæ vero responderi poterit: assumi citra solidam probatio- nem, quod causa novi furoris, & severioris edicti verbis hisce exhibeatur, quum explicetur potius historice, quomodo Deus obstetricibus benefecerit, ædificando nempe domus ipsarum. Fateor tamen, satis probabilem videri Brentii & Fagii explicatio- nem, & quum non facile admittenda sit enallage, (etsi eam hic Chaldæus, & LXX. statuant) ac tex- tus planus in fontibus sit, retenta propria masculi- ni pronominis significatione, præferendam eandem censeo: Ita ergo fluit oratio: Et factum est, quia ti- muerunt obstetrices Deum, (non occidendo mascu- los) & fecit eis (Israelitis) domos (ædificavit porro ac multiplicavit eorum familias,) præcepit Pharao universo populo suo, (ut sc. non obstetrices tan- tum, sed universi Ægyptii in eo essent, ut masculi tollerentur) omnem filium natum in flumen proji- cietis. Sic causa novi edicti, ejusdemque ad populum universum facti, quod viderit non occidi ab obste- tricibus masculos, & indies augeri familias Israe- litarum, quæ per mares ædificantur maxime, a Mo- se ipso indicata: & explicatum simul, quod versu præ- cedente dictum, quomodo populus valde roboratus sit, quia sc. nec paruere Regi obstetrices, & singulari benedictione Deus eorum adauxit familias.

Assumta autem communi interpretatione, de ea porro disquiritur, Quomodo ædificatæ domus obstetricibus fuerint, de quo variant interpretes. Au- gust. Græcum ἐποίησαν ἑαυταῖς οἰκείας, ut ipse lege- bat, fecerunt sibi ipsis domos, secutus, putat, munitas domos sibi ipsis eas fecisse, ut se ab Ægyptiis tuerentur; alii dicunt Israeliticum populum tales domos illis ex- truxisse. Sed quomodo adversus Regem ædibus se tueri potuissent? Alii ad Pharaonem referunt, quod ipse domos eis extruxerit, unde exire illis non lice- ret, ut sc. opus esset, mulieres Ebræorum ad ipsas adduci. Sed hoc ineptum est, neque Pharao, sed Deus, quem timuerunt, dicitur ipsis domos ædifi- cæsse. Quod Ebræi de domo sacerdotii & Regni expli- cant, quia fingunt, obstetricem fuisse matrem Aaro- nis & Mosis. Lyranus sic interpretatur, quod fue- rint obstetrices illæ receptæ in populum Ebræum, & junctæ matrimonio viris primariis. Quo abire etiam videtur Schol. Job. Marianæ de sorte obstetri- cibus inter Israelitas data; sed id refellit Tostatus, quia Ebræi abjecti erant & quasi mancipia habe- bantur, & quia sic vehementius obstetrices irritas- sent contra se Pharaonem. Refellit & Cornel. a L. quia non ait Moses Deum fecisse eis domos inter Ebræos, sed absolute ædificasse illis domos. R. David Kimchi sic intelligit, quod absconderit eas Deus a Pharaone & in tuto collocarit. Sed illa phrasis ita non usurpatur, nec domos terrenas iis ædificavit Deus. De domibus spiritualibus & cælestibus Hie- ron. ac Rupertus, & alii explicant. Sed hos refel- lunt ipsimet Pontif. quia ædificare domos in V. T. eo sensu non occurrit. Rectius alii (quibus acces- sit Grotius) ex usitata loquendi ratione phrasin ac- cipiunt de ædificatis familiis earum in liberis ex iis- dem ortis, non abnuente Hieron. in Tradit. Ebr. ad Gen. c. 16. vel cum Theodoreto de argumento rei familiaris, & bonorum temporalium, quomodo Deus ædificare domos dicitur Ps. 127, 1. & dignum videbatur pietate præmium, quod, quæ proles E- bræorum servarunt, prole auctæ fuerint, ideoque hæc sententia a plerisque præfertur. Vid. varias illas interpretationes discuticus Fagius in h. l. & Perer.

Perperam autem Papistæ hinc extruunt operum merita, & nonnulli quidem vitæ æternæ merita inde exsculpere conantur cum Pererio & Leonh. Mario, quod dicatur Deus eis Domos ædificasse & benefecisse, quia Deum timuerunt, quam collectionem Thomas, & Rupertus sua explicatione firmant, quia per domos mansiones cœlestes intelligunt. Sed hoc refellit Cornel. a Lap. quia ædificare domos non significat in Scriptura, dare præmium vitæ æternæ. Addit Cornelius, Deum in V. T. non solere cœleste præmium exprimere ac promissionem illius expressam N. T. propriam esse; sed hoc repugnat Gen. 2, 17. Lev. 18, 5. Dan. 12, 2. Joh. 5, 39. & in Socinianis alias profligatur. Rectius dixisset, nec in Vet. nec in N. T. ullum opus humanum proponi ceu miritorium æternæ vitæ, imo hoc χάρισμα donum est Dei mere gratuitum in Christo Jesu Rom. 5. ult. & nulla proportio est inter opera nostra etiam laboriosissima Martyrum sanctissimorum, & gloriam æternæ vitæ Rom. 8, 18. Ideoque reprobanda Pererii Jesuitæ collectio, quia timor ille Dei profectus est ex gratia Dei, sine dubio meruerunt vitam æternam: quia beatitudo est ejus, cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus Rom. 4, 6. & ut justificamur δωρεὰν gratis, τῇ χάριτι ex gratia per redemptionem Christi Rom. 3, 24. sic etiam salvamur gratis: non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur Eph. 2, 9. Rom. 11, 6. Et quamvis timor proficiscatur ex gratia Dei, non tamen ideo perfectus est, quia imperfectionem a principio proximo contrahit. Transigant autem hic primum inter se Jesuitæ. Pererius enim & Marius dicunt, actum illum obstetricum timorem Dei ex gratia profectum fuisse, Bellarm. ex adverso l. V. de gratia & libero arbit. c. 9. sine gratia & speciali auxilio eundem fuisse, asserit. Alii proinde plerique e Pontif. opere hoc timoris Dei & charitatis proximi obstetrices promeruisse hanc mercedem temporalem ajunt, non autem mercedem æternam. Alex. Alesius, bonum fuit, inquit, illud opus, sed non sufficiens ad merendam gloriam propter defectum charitatis, sed quod nullum bonum irremuneratum manet, ideo Dominus illud opus remuneravit in hac terra. Probat illud Alesius, quia in ipsis fuit timor servilis vel humanus tantum, quo magis diligerent forte tueri præsentem vitam, quam mereri æternam, quod non stat cum charitate. Quomodo etiam plerique Pontif. factum illud, quo non paruerunt obstetrices tyrannidi Pharaonis & juvarunt mulieres Ebræas in partu, nec occiderunt masculos, conspurcatum fuisse timore servili & mendacio illicito asserunt. Quomodo autem facto taliter conspurcato mereri aliquid apud Deum potuissent? Et cum omnes nostræ justitiæ impuræ coram Deo sint propter adhærentem labem originalis maculæ & imperfectionis, qua ipsæ laborant Es. 64, 6. ac si in contentionem cum justitia veniant, σκύβαλα mera sint Phil. 3, 8. quid restat, quam ut agnoscamus, nos nihil mereri coram Deo posse, imo si in judicium nos vocet Deus, ad mille ἐγκλήματα ne minimum quidem vel sanctissimum quemque respondere posse, Job. 9, 3. Denique etiamsi omnia facere possemus, quæ requirit Deus, servos adhuc ἀχρείυς inutiles fore Luc. 17, 10. quia facimus ita tantum quod debemus. Qui ergo facit, quod debet, Christo docente, nihil meretur, nam si mereretur aliquid, non esset sibi ἀχρεῖος vel inutilis, eo quod sibi aliquid promereatur. Nulla itaque opera nostra meritoria sunt, quæ omnia debita, adhæc imperfecta & impura o- mnia sunt. Id in hoc obstetricum opere agnoscit Gregor. Magn. lib. 18. Moral. quod amore vitæ præ- sentis ipsæ mentitæ sint; adeoque vult mercedem beni- gnitatis, quæ eis poterat in æterna vita tribui, pro ad- missa culpa mendacii in terrenam esse repensationem declinatam. In quo explicando hæret ipse Thomas, quomodo actu exteriore mendacii potuerint aliquid mereri? Respondemus, inquit, non potuerunt qui- dem æternam remunerationem mereri, sed forte ali- quam remunerationem temporalem, cujus merito non repugnabat deformitas illius mendacii, sicut re- pugnabat merito remunerationis æternæ. At an- non absurdissimum est, mendacio tribuere remu- nerationis temporalis meritum? Cui, quicquid hic dicat Pererius pro Thoma, cujus verba duriora agnoscit, exculpando, Thomas tribuit, ob non tan- tam repugnantiam ad meritum remunerationis tem- poralis, quanta est repugnantia mendacii ad æter- nam remunerationem. Agnoscit Cornel. in h. l. blasphemum esse, cogitare, imo & impossibile & con- tra naturam rerum, Deum actum mendacii probare aut remunerare. Dicit autem, Deum præmiaffe non mendacium, sed alios pietatis & timoris Dei actus. Quod admittimus ex hypothesi illa, qua statuiter, mentitas hic fuisse obstetrices, uti Aug. re- spondet, lib. contra mendac. c. 19. præmium da- tum esse, non quia mentitæ sunt, sed quia in homines Dei misericordes fuerunt, ut ita non sit in iis remune- rata fallacia, sed benevolentia, benignitas mentis, non iniquitas mentientis. Neque tamen admitten- dum, benignitate illa sua præmium istud meruisse obstetrices, quia non fuit illa benignitas pura, ne secundum Pontif. quidem aut Gregorium M. & Aug. sed timore servili contaminata. Ideoque re- muneratur quidem Deus virtutes, licet aliqua sor- dium mixtura inquinatas; sed sordes illæ faciunt, quo minus virtutes meritoriæ sint remunerationis divinæ. Regerit Cornel. a Lapide contra naturam rerum hoc esse, ut virtus vitio inquinata sit, aut a lucidissimo illo Dei oculo judicetur, habeaturque vir- tus, ac mercede ornetur, si inquinata sit. Sed quo- modo contra naturam est, virtuti vitium aliquod adhærere? nonne virtutes gentilium peccatis conta- minatæ fuere, utpote quæ nec ad suum refereban- tur autorem, & quamvis officio videntur bonæ, ipso non recto fine peccatum erant judice Aug. lib. 1. contra Julian. cap. 4. Virtus vitio inquinata non habetur quidem a lucidissimo Dei oculo pro vir- tute absolute, habetur tamen talis qualis est, h. e. quæ non plane nihil habeat qualitatis bonæ: quæ quamvis ex Regula justitiæ digna præmio non sit, a divina bonitate præmio afficitur, uti Aug. lib. 5. de Civitat. Dei, cap. 12. probat, Romanos, qui omnia ad laudis cupiditatem retulere, ob facta laudabilia mercedem a Deo tulisse. Tum vero annon mendacium, quod obstetricibus tribuunt Papistæ, & timor ille servilis implicabatur intime bono ipsarum operi, ut illud totum affecerit, & qualitate aliqua non bona auxerit vel contamina- rit? Dicit Aug. fuisse ab illis uno tempore & in una causa factum misericorditer & factum fallaciter: mendacium ceu medium exequendi actum mise- ricordiæ fuisse usurpatum, mendacium animo sub- veniendi factum. Non igitur mendacium, si quod fuit, ita separari ab illo facto potest, ut ipsi non in- volvatur, & opera bona non uno actu mentis aut affectu, sed serie circumstantiarum & principiorum explicantur, & in illis a lucidissimo Dei oculo spe- ctantur. Nihil ergo aliud infertur, quam quod Deus non remuneretur vitium, quod contra Thomam est, etsi remuneretur factum, quod aliquo vitio contaminatum est: & quod Deus non secundum tenorem justitiæ agat, cum remuneratur, sed ex singulari motu bonitatis divinæ : adeoque quod fa- ctum ejusmodi non sit meritorium, quod est con- tra Pontif. cæteros, etsi remunerationem accipiat: quia remunerationem accipit non secundum ju- stitiam, sed per gratiam: non ex merito, sed citra omne meritum, sive quia promisit Deus, sive quia cæteroquin placet ipsi bonitatem suam ita testari, quæ defectibus existentibus in bonis actionibus non statim universa tollit, sed tolerat, & ad majus bonum eliciendum minori & defectibus corru- pto non tantum parcit, sed etiam aliqualia tribuit præmia. Quod nequaquam repugnat justitiæ di- vinæ, quia remuneratio ista non concernit defe- ctus & vitia, sed bonitatem illam, cui contamina- tio a vitiositate principii proximi adspersa est, cum ipsa bonitas a primo principio derivetur, ac Deum auctorem habeat, qui in nobis nihil nisi dona sua coronat. Si dicas, Deum non remunerari pecca- ta: Resp. id verum esse, quatenus peccatum intel- ligitur formaliter, quia abominatur & punit Deus non præmiat peccatum : Sed non verum est, De- um non remunerari opus suo genere materialiter & externo actu bonum, etsi aliquo vitio contami- natum, aut per accidens peccatum sit. Civiles virtutes, etsi apud Deum non sufficiant, neque sine peccato sint, habent multa præmia, quia Deus vult conservari hac ratione statum Politicum & so- cietatem humanam, non tamen inde conficitur, virtutes gentilium non esse peccata, quia quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est, Rom. 14, 23. neque peccato vacare fidelium virtutes agnoscit Bernh. serm. 5. de verbis Esaiæ, nostra enim, inquit, si qua est humilis justitia, recta forsitan, sed non pura &c. Agnoscit & Adrianus Trajectensis, qui superiori seculo Pontifex Rom. fuit in 4. sentent. de Sacra- mento Eucharist. fol. 20. ubi postquam dixisset; merita nostra & preparationem ad Eucharistiæ sacra- mentum esse velut baculum arundineum, cui dum quis innixus fuerit, confringitur & perforat ma- num innitentis, & quasi pannum menstruatæ: addit; jugiter enim supra pannum bonæ vitæ, quem texi- mus, justitiæ operibus stillamus saniem diversorum criminum. Ita ergo juxta Corn. a Lap. nemo ju- storum a lucidissimo illo Dei oculo pro justo ha- bendus, aut mercede ornandus esset.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

The birth of Moses, his drawing out of the waters, his royal upbringing, and his flight on account of the slaughter of the Egyptian.

Verse 1.

AFTER THIS A MAN WENT OUT.

Lyranus says that this happened after the commandment concerning the killing of the males. But in the Hebrew that 'AFTER THIS' is not present, and the verb is more correctly rendered in the pluperfect, 'and he had gone out': because Amram had already taken a wife some years before, and had begotten twin offspring before this edict about drowning the male offspring.

V. same [verse]. AND HE TOOK A WIFE OF HIS OWN LINEAGE.

IN the Hebrew it is: he took the daughter of Levi: Thus also is Jochebed, the mother of Moses, called, Num. 26, 59. Calvin maintains that Levi, the son of Jacob, was her parent, nor does he fear to say that Moses was born from an incestuous marriage, which would likewise have to be said of Aaron, if indeed Amram thus married the sister of his father. Andreas Rivetus laboriously attempts to defend Calvin on this passage against the Jesuits Corn. a Lap. and Leonh. Marius, who accuse him of impudence, error, immodesty, and ignorance, because he made a reproach against a holy man: Rivetus counters that Paulus Burgensis from the Pontificians, as also Alphonsus Tostatus, Augustinus Eugubinus, Oleastrius, Sanctes Pagninus, and Cardinal Cajetan, Benedictus Pererius admitting it, fostered the same opinion, namely that Levi was the father of Jochabed. But they nevertheless did not say that Moses was born of incest, nor does that follow according to their own mind from that hypothesis; for before the law of Moses described in Lev. 18, the Pontificians believe that the marriage of an aunt with a nephew was not forbidden and illicit, in which even if they themselves err, Calvin nevertheless without doubt affects the holy Amram with a graver reproach, because he believed such a marriage was prohibited, and yet determined that it was entered into by the same: even Rivetus himself, when he tried to excuse his teacher, accuses Amram of incest; certainly, he says, it is evident from Scripture that the marriage of an aunt with a nephew by a brother is placed among those things which are repugnant to decency, and were disapproved of even among the Canaanites themselves. What immodesty is it, therefore, if someone calls that incestuous cohabitation which the Holy Spirit judges to be such? But there is no need for us to impute that to Amram, or that with Bellarmine l. 1. de sacram. matrim. c. 27, we should determine that marriages of such a kind were lawful, and were not prohibited except by a positive law laid upon the Jews, because she is called the daughter of Levi, because she was of the Levites, or sprung from the stock of Levi; whence the Vulgate rightly rendered: and he took a wife of his own stock, and thus Vatablus, Pererius, Cornelius a Lapide, and others interpret it from the Pontificians, whom most of the Reformed and our own people support: and this is added peculiarly, so that it might be certain that the law concerning marrying those of the same tribe was then observed, and especially so that we might be more certain that Aaron and Moses were Levites by maternal as well as paternal descent. She was therefore the daughter of Levi, but as the daughters of Judah are spoken of, who are from that stock, not who were immediately procreated by the parent Judah: Especially, because the account of chronology also does not admit that it should be determined that Jochebeth was immediately procreated by Levi himself, the son of Jacob, unless something extraordinary and miraculous is determined, to which Rivetus also inclines, p. 38, Comm. in Exod.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Mosis nativitas, ex aquis eductio, Regia edu- catio, & propter Ægyptii cædem fuga.

Vers. 1.

EGRESSUS EST POSTHÆC VIR.

Id factum ait Lyran. post præceptum de masculis occidendis. Sed in Ebr. illud POSTHÆC non habetur ac verbum rectius in plusquamperfecto redditur, & egressus erat: quia Amram jam ante annos aliquot uxorem duxerat, & geminam pro- lem ante hoc de submergenda prole mascula edi- ctum procrearat.

V. eod. ET ACCEPIT UXOREM STIRPIS SUÆ.

IN Ebr. est: accepit filiam Levi: Sic etiam vo- catur Jochabet mater Mosis, Num. 26, 59. Illius parentem fuisse Levi, filium Jacobi, Calvinus sta- tuit, nec veretur dicere, Mosen ex incestuoso conju- gio prognatum esse, quod pariter de Aarone di- cendum esset, siquidem ita Amram duxerit soro- rem patris sui. Calvinum operose defendere co- natur Andreas Rivetus in h. l. adversus Jesuitas Corn. a Lap. & Leonh. Marium. qui impudentiæ erroris, immodestiæ, & ignorantiæ Calvinum argu- unt, quod convitium in sanctum virum fecerit: op- ponit Rivetus, quod eandem sententiam Paulus Burgensis e Pontif. ut & Alph. Tostatus, Aug. Eu- gub. Oleastrius, Sant. Pagninus & Cardin. Cajet. fatente Benedict. Pererio, foverint, quod nempe Levi pater fuerit Jochabedæ. Sed illi tamen non dixere, Mosen ex incesto genitum esse, nec id se- cundum mentem ipsorum ex ista hypothesi sequi- tur; ante Mosis enim legem Lev. 18. descriptam, credunt Pontif. matrimonium amitæ cum nepote non fuisse vetitum, & illicitum, in quo etsi errent ipsi, graviori tamen sine dubio Calvinus convitio sanctum Amramum afficit, quod prohibitum tale matrimonium credidit, & ab eodem tamen initum fuisse statuerit: ipse etiam Rivetus cum Præcepto- rem suum excusare conatus est, incestus arguit Amramum; certe, inquit, constat ex Scriptura, conjugium amitæ cum nepote ex fratre inter ea poni, quæ honestati repugnant, & in ipsis Cananæis im- probata fuerunt. Quænam igitur immodestia est, si quis incestum concubitum appellet eum, quem Spiri- tus Sanctus talem judicat? Sed non opus est, ut id imputemus Amramo, aut ut cum Bellarmino l. 1. de sacram. matrim. c. 27. matrimonia taliatum li- cita fuisse, nec nisi lege positiva Judæis lata prohibi- ta esse statuamus, quia filia Levi dicitur, quod Levi- tis fuerit, vel oriunda e stirpe Levi; unde recte Vulg. reddidit: & accepit uxorem stirpis suæ, atque ita e Pontif. interpretantur Vatablus, Perer. Corn. a Lap. & alii, quibus suffragantur e Reformatis plerique & nostrates: & additur hoc peculiariter, ut constaret tum legem observatam fuisse de ducendis contribu- libus, tum imprimis ut certiores essemus Aaronem & Mosen tam materno, quam paterno genere Levi- tas fuisse. Filia ergo Levi fuit, sed uti dicuntur filiæ Juda, quæ ex stirpe illa, non quæ immediate a Juda parente procreatæ sunt: Maxime, quia etiam Chro- nologiæ ratio non admittit, ut statuatur, Jochebeth immediate ab ipso Levi filio Jacobi procreatam fuisse, nisi aliquid extraordinarii & miraculosi sta- tuatur, quo etiam inclinat Rivetus p. 38. Comm. in Exod.

## 2:2
Verse 2. SEEING HIM ELEGANT SHE HID HIM THREE MONTHS. In Hebrew, that he himself was good, that is, beautiful. Josephus, book 2, ch. 5, describes his elegance at length; there was no spectator of forms so negligent who would not be stunned by the beauty of Moses, etc. Stephen, Acts 7:20, following the LXX Interpreters, calls him ἀστεῖον τῷ Θεῷ, which the Vulgate explained as pleasing to God. Beza, with the French Interpreter, rendered it divinely or divinely, that is, most beautiful, because by common Hebraism those things are called great to God which are the greatest, which interpretation of Beza, over the Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic, Ludovicus de Dieu approves in his notes on Acts 7:20. Extraordinary beauty, therefore, was given to him by God, which moved even the daughter of Pharaoh, with divine instinct added, to draw Moses from the waters and adopt him as her son. But it pleases Mr. Varenius in Decad. super Exod. p. 59, that by these words there is designated by Stephen also the eminence of the soul in a most beautiful body, and the excellence of his future dignity: that she saw that beauty both by intellect and sense, nay, that the pious mother recognized by peculiar revelation the gifts of his soul and the dignity of his future office. Yet it is not to be gathered from that beauty, with Ephrem the Syrian in his Oration on the Transfiguration of Christ, that Moses was sanctified in his mother's womb, because elegance of form does not argue the purity of the soul. But the things which are handed down here by Jarchi are trifles: whence did the mother see that he was good? Moses was born at the same time, the whole house was filled with an unusual light. This light does not shine from the light of Scripture, but from Rabbinic darkness. The hiding of the infant is attributed here to the mother, which the Apostle, Heb. 11:23, with the LXX Interpreters, attributes to both parents: but that could not be done by the mother alone without the parent knowing; and therefore it is attributed only to the mother, for the reason that that plan was first devised by the mother, who also took upon herself the care of executing it. Moreover, that hiding is said to be done by faith, Heb. 11, not because Amram received some oracle before the birth of the son concerning Moses as the liberator of his people, as Josephus reports, but because the pious parents clung to the general promises made by God, and placing their trust in God, did not fear the edict of the King. Theophylact adds in his Commentary on Heb. 11:23 that the parents wanted to expose the child when he was born, but that he smiled gently and for that reason was saved. But that does not fit so well with the eulogy of faith, through which they are said to have hidden the same.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VIDENS EUM ELEGANTEM AB- SCONDIT MENSIBUS TRIBUS. In Ebr. quod bonus ipse, id est, pulcher. Elegan- tiam ejus prolixe describit Josephus lib. 2. c. 5. nemo erat tam negligens formarum spectator, qui non aspe- cta Mosis pulchritudine obstupesceret &c. Stepha- nus Act. 7, 20. LXX. Interpretes secutus vocat ἀστεῖον τῷ Θεῷ, quod Vulgatus exposuit, gratus Deo. Beza cum Interprete Gallo, divinitus vel divi- ne, hoc est, maxime venustus reddidit, quia usitato Ebraismo magna Deo dicuntur, quæ maxima sunt, quam Bezæ interpretationem præ Vulgata, Eras- mo, Syro, Arabe & Æthiopico, probat Ludov. de Dieu ad Act. 7, 20. Extraordinaria ergo pulchri- tudo a Deo ipsi data, quæ commovit etiam filiam Pharaonis, accedente divino instinctu, ut Mosen aquis extraheret & pro filio adoptaret. Dn. Va- renio vero placet in Decad. super Exod. p. 59. his verbis designatam a Stephano etiam animæ in pul- cherrimo corpore eminentiam, dignitatisq́, futuræ ex- cellentiam: quod & intellectu & sensu videret illam pulchritudinem imo peculiari revelatione agnove- rit pia mater dotes animi & muneris futuri digni- tatem. Non tamen cum Ephremo Syro Orat. de transfiguratione Christi ex illa pulchritudine col- ligendum, Mosen in utero matris sanctificatum fuisse, quia elegantia formæ non arguit puritatem animæ. Nugæ autem sunt, quæ a Jarchio hic tra- duntur: unde vidit mater quod bonus esset? simul na- tus est Moses, tota domus luce insolita perfusa est. Non e luce Scripturæ micat hæc lux, sed e tenebris Rab- binicis. Matri autem tribuitur hic absconsio infantis, quam Apostolus Ebr. 11, 23. cum LXX. Interpretibus utrique parenti tribuit: sed a sola matre inscio parente illa fieri non potuit; ideoque matri tantum tribuitur, ideo quod consilium illud primo a matre excogitatum fuerit, cujus etiam exequendi curam in se suscepit. Cærerum fide dicitur facta illa absconsio Ebr. 11. non quod ora- culum aliquod Amram ante nativitatem filii de Mose gentis suæ liberatore acceperit, ut Josephus re- fert, sed quod adhæserint pii parentes generalibus promissionibus, a Deo factis, & in Deo fiduciam collocantes edictum Regis non timuerint. Theo- phylactus addit in Comment. ad Ebr. 11, 23. paren- tes voluisse exponere puerum cum natus est, sed illum blande risisse & ob id servatum fuisse. Sed id non adeo convenit elogio fidei, per quam eundem occultasse dicuntur.

## 2:3
Verse 3. AND WHEN THEY COULD NO LONGER HIDE HIM, etc.

But did the parents of Moses act rightly in complying in such a way with the King's manifestly impious edict? The Rabbis say they did so by a special divine mandate; but Scripture is silent about this; yet it does not seem to be doubted that this was undertaken by divine instinct or the suggestion of such a plan, because all the circumstances cry out that the whole matter was directed by the singular providence of God, and the faith of the parents of Moses is particularly commended by the Holy Spirit: therefore they did not do this out of dissent, or to comply with a tyrannical mandate, for if they had been required to suffocate their little son; but so that they themselves might escape the tyranny along with the infant; for without doubt a new search was instituted at that time, so that the infant could no longer be hidden, whence if they had kept him at home, they would have exposed both him and themselves to the most present danger of life. Therefore, the faithful parents of Moses are not to be accused of beastly cruelty with Calvin, nor is this deed to be disapproved as a sin of weakness, because they prudently chose the lesser of two proposed dangers, and they did not expose the infant so that he would perish, but so that he might be kept safe from the henchmen; therefore they exposed him in a well-fortified ark, and in a safe place, and in addition they added a guardian, his sister, who might look after him in some way: for the mother could secretly feed and clean him at night in a place so exposed, safe and nearby, and thus expect the help of God ἀπὸ μηχανῆς. Therefore they did not do it out of fear, but out of certain confidence. Nor is faith to be placed here in Josephus: as if they threw this ark into the middle of the river, for what would it have profited to station a sister as a guardian in that way? And it is a fable that the King's daughter ordered the ark to be pulled out by sending swimmers. Rivetus rightly warns that one should not judge the faith or constancy of the parents of Moses from this deed, but rather judge the deed from their faith, and therefore he not obscurely disapproves of the opinion of Calvin and others, by which they are accused of neglected duty, or are believed to have been overcome by excessive fear contrary to the testimony of Paul, judging that whatever they did here, they did by the inspiration and guidance of the divine Spirit.

Verse of the same.

FISCELLAM SCIRPEAM) The Greeks here preserve the Hebrew word. It signifies λάρνακα, which word Strabo uses in his narrative about Auge and Telephus. Simonides about Danae and Perseus. The words of Strabo, book XIII: Εὐριπίδης δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ Ἀλέω τῆς Αὔγης πατρὸς εἰς λάρνακα τὴν Αὐγὴν κατατεθεῖσαν ἅμα τῷ παιδὶ Τηλέφῳ, &c. Simonides: ὅτε λάρνακι ἐν δαιδαλέᾳ άνεμός βρόμῃ πνέων, κινηθεῖσα δὲ λίκνα δέματι ἔρειπεν &c. Scirpeam, that is, made of papyrus. Lucan, book IV: 'The Memphite boat is compared to thirsty papyrus.'

Latin:

Vers. 3. CUMQVE JAM CELARE NON POS- SENT &c.

Num vero recte fecere parentes Mosis, quod Edicto Regis manifeste impio ita morem gesse- rint? Rabbini e mandato divino peculiari hoc eos- dem fecisse dicunt; sed de eo Scriptura tacet; non tamen dubitandum videtur, instinctu divino vel suggestione talis consilii hoc susceptum esse, quia singulari providentia Dei rem omnem directam fuisse, omnes circumstantiæ clamitant, & fides pa- rentum Mosis peculiariter a Spiritu Sancto com- mendatur: non ergo hoc fecerunt ex dissidentia, aut ut morem gererent tyrannico mandato, si enim suffocasse filiolum debuissent; sed ut tyranni- dem ipsimet cum infantulo effugerent; sine dubio enim nova tunc instituta fuit inquisitio, ut am- plius infans occultari nequiverit, unde si domi eum servassent, & ipsum, & sese periculo vitæ præsen- tissimo exposuissent. Non ergo cum Calvino parentes Mosis fideles immanitatis ferinæ ar- guendi, aut factum hoc tanquam infirmitatis pec- catum improbandum, quia propositis duobus pe- riculis prudenter minus elegere, nec exposuerunt infantèm, ut periret, sed ut a satellitibus securus servaretur, ideo exposuerunt in arca bene munita, & in loco tuto, & custodem insuper addiderunt so- rorem, quæ eum utcunque curaret: nam poterat ita expositum loco tuto, ac vicino mater clam no- ctu alere, ac purgare, adeoque Dei auxilium ἀπὸ μηχανῆς expectare. Non ergo ex timore, sed ex certa fiducia id fecerunt. Neque enim Josepho fides hic adhibenda: quasi arcam hanc in medium flumen projecerint, quid enim ita profuisset, soro- rem custodem apponi? Et fabula est, filiam Regis missis natatoribus arcam extrahi jussisse. Recte Ri- vetus monet, non esse de parentum Mosis fide aut con- stantia ex hoc facto, sed de facto potius ex eorum fide judicandum, ideoque non obscure improbat Cal- vini & aliorum sententiam, qua neglecti officii ar- guuntur, aut metu nimio superati creduntur contra Pauli testimonium, Spiritus divini afflatu & guber- natione, quicquid hic fecerunt, fecisse censens.

Vers. eod.

FISCELLAM SCIRPEAM) vocem Hebræam servant hic Græci. Significat λάρνακα, qua voce utitur Strabo in nar- ratione de Auge & Telepho. Simonides de Danaë & Perseo. Strabonis verba lib. XIII. Εὐριπίδης δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ Ἀλέω τῆς Αὔγης πατρὸς εἰς λάρνακα τὴν Αὐγὴν κατατεθεῖσαν ἅμα τῷ παιδὶ Τη- λέφῳ, &c. Simonides: ὅτε λάρνακι ἐν δαιδαλέᾳ άνεμός βρόμῃ πνέων, κινηθεῖσα δὲ λίκνα δέματι ἔρειπεν &c. Scirpeam, id est, ex papyro. Luc. lib. IV. Conferitur bibula Memphitis cymba papyro.

## 2:5
Verse 5. PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER.

Josephus and Epiphanius, Heresy 77, name her Thermuthis; Artabanus, an ancient writer in Eusebius, book 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 4, as also the Alexandrian Chronicle, calls her Merris and her father Palmenothes, and her husband Cenephres, who reigned in the places around Memphis: Philo says she was Pharaoh's only heir, and without offspring; although long married, she then adopted Moses as her son. But these things are uncertain. It is probable that Moses' parents had explored the place to which that Princess was accustomed to come with her retinue, and therefore had exposed the son in a place where he could be seen by her as she came out, and by divine providence it then happened that she came out at that time.

Latin:

Vers. 5. FILIA PHARAONIS.

Josephus & Epiphan. Hæres. 77. nominant eam Termuthim; Artabanus, vetus Scriptor apud Euseb. l. 9. de præpar. Ev. c. 4. ut & Chronicon Alexandri- num appellat eam Merrim & Patrem Palmenothen, ac maritum Cenephium, qui in locis circa Memphim regnarit: Philo dicit, unicam fuisse Pharaonis hære- dem, & sine prole; licet diu nuptam, quæ deinde Mo- sen in filium adoptavit. Sed ista incerta sunt. Proba- bile est, explorasse parentes Mosis locum, in quem Princeps illa solebat cum comitatu suo accedere, itaque ibi exposuisse filium in locum, in quo ab egrediente videri posset, ac divina providentia tunc factum, ut isto tempore egrederetur.

## 2:10
Verse 10. WHOM SHE ADOPTED IN THE PLACE OF A SON.

God, in whose hand is the heart of the King, directed this, so that Moses might be educated in Egyptian wisdom, Acts 7:22. Otherwise, Pharaoh certainly would not have allowed this, unless the matter had been brought about by a peculiar divine direction. It appears, however, to be a fabrication that Josephus handed down, that the royal edict about casting out male children had been caused by some prediction about a certain boy, who was to be born of the Hebrews, who would bring destruction to the kingdom and the King. For thus, neither would Pharaoh's daughter have adopted Moses, being aware of that oracle, nor would Pharaoh have permitted it. Philo says that tutors were summoned for Moses: Greeks, who would teach him the liberal arts; Chaldeans, who would teach him the science of the stars; Assyrians, who would teach him their letters. But Cadmus, from whom the Greeks received letters, was much later than Moses, which Eusebius demonstrates in his book on the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3. Scripture says he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who had learned the greatest part of their wisdom from Jacob, Joseph, and the remaining Hebrews, inasmuch as they had had them as guests in their kingdom for more than a century, Ps. 105:22.

Verse of the same. AND SHE CALLED HIS NAME MOSES.

This is related concerning the infant, after he had already been weaned and brought to Pharaoh's daughter. Philo and Josephus, however, relate that she gave him the name after he was drawn by her from the waters; therefore, in the Mosaic narrative, some translate the present tense as the past, 'she had called'; thus it will agree with the account of Josephus, since it is likely that this name was imposed upon him from the extraction immediately when he was being extracted, and Pharaoh's daughter would not have left the infant without a name. But it is asked what kind of name it is; most of the ancients judge it to be Egyptian; thus Philo and Josephus, who observe that MO in Egyptian denotes water, and YSES, saved. Thus also Clement of Alexandria, who in book 1 of the Stromata notes that the Egyptians call water MOY, to whom Athanasius Kircher subscribes in his Prodromus. Therefore, he says, those who wish the name of Moses to be derived from the Hebrew word מֹשֶׁה err gravely; for he did not receive the name from his parents, nor from any other person of the Hebrew race, but from Pharaoh's daughter herself, who had no other language besides her native Egyptian. Hottinger also supports this in Exerc. Anti-Morin. p. 48, and most interpreters embrace that opinion. Others, however, even if they admit that an Egyptian woman gave an Egyptian name to the boy adopted by her, yet [maintain] that the name Moses is Hebrew, and translated from the Egyptian, of the same meaning as that original Coptic name. Thus Andreas Rivetus, who says it is not certain what that Egyptian name was. Nor does Aben-Ezra deny it, who thinks that the name of Moses had been interpreted from the Egyptian as MONIOS. But the text clearly indicates that Moses was called from מָשָׁה, he drew out, which is used for extraction from waters in Ps. 18:17, because this etymon is rendered in this place: she called him Moses, because she said: I drew him out מְשִׁיתִהוּ from the waters. Whence it is not to be doubted that the origin of that name is Hebrew, nor should another be sought in other languages, since Scripture so openly explains the reason for the name, nor is it likely, since the name was imposed upon him by the daughter of Pharaoh, and Moses himself here reports her very words, that he substituted another name and another reason for the name, since he always retained other proper names just as they were imposed, and did not translate them into another language, which he would have been much less likely to do in the case of his own name. That reasoning, that the daughter of Pharaoh had no other language than the Egyptian, enjoys no probability; indeed, it is more likely that she was not ignorant of the Hebrew language, and consequently gave the Hebrew boy a Hebrew name, even though it may have been that she drew it all the more willingly from the word מָשָׁה, and called him by it, because in the vernacular language also MOY denotes water: from this word alone, because the two final radicals are missing, and only one letter מ occurs in it, it cannot be derived, and how will they make it saved or extracted from the final syllable שׁה in the Coptic language, if they call it a compound name? Clement of Alexandria, in the place cited, relates that at his circumcision he received another name from his parents themselves, and was called Joachim: Rabbi Gedalia in Schalscheleth says that his father called him Chaber, his mother, Jekadiel, his sister, Jeder, and thus he was called by others by other names, which the Rabbis explain mystically, as Jerome notes in Tradit. Ebr. in the book of Chronicles says that Isabar Ali the Syrian was called Balthiel at his circumcision, that is, God deliver me; in the Sidra of the book of Chronicles he is said to be called Jamchil, he made to reign: Conf. Hotting. Hist. Orient. p. 12. but Scripture is silent as to what name he received at his circumcision, yet the name of Moses is not without an omen, because having been drawn out of the waters he was to lead the Israelites out of the waters of afflictions and from the Red Sea.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QUEM ILLA ADOPTAVIT IN LOCUM FILII.

Id direxit Deus, in cujus manu est cor Regis, ut in Ægyptia sapientia educaretur Moses, Actor. 7, 22. Alias certe id non admisisset Pharao, nisi pecu- liari directione divina res gesta esset. Apparet ta- men commentum esse, quod Josephus tradidit, edi- cto Regio de pueris masculis projiciendis, causam præbuisse aliquam prædictionem de puero quo- dam, ex Ebræis nascituro, qui regno & Regi per- niciem allaturus esset. Ita enim nec adoptasset Mo- sen filia Pharaonis, istius oraculi conscia, nec id Pharao concessisset. Philo Mosi accitos Præcepto- res dicit Græcos, qui liberales artes, Chaldæos, qui sideralem scientiam, Assyrios, qui suas literas eum docerent. At Cadmus, à quo Græci literas accepe- runt, multo posterior fuit Mose, quod demonstrat Euseb. lib. de præpar. Evang. c. 3. Spir. S. instructum dicit Sapientia omni Ægyptiorum, qui maximam partem Sapientiæ suæ à Jacobo, Josepho & reliquis Ebræis didicerant, utpote, quos ultra seculum in regno suo hospites habuerant Ps. 105, 22.

Vers. eod. VOCAVITQUE NOMEN EJUS MOSES.

Id refertur de infante, postquam jam ablacta- tus ad filiam Pharaonis adductus est. Philo tamen & Joseph. nomen eam ipsi dedisse referunt, postquam ab ea aquis extractus fuit, ideo in narratione Mosaica præsens nonnulli vertunt per præteritum, vocaverat; ita consonabit ea relationi Josephi, cum verisimile sit, ipsi hoc nomen ab extractione impo- situm statim cum extraheretur, nec sine nomine in- fantulum dimisisse filiam Pharaonis. Quale autem nomen sit, quæritur, Ægyptiacum esse plerique ve- teres censent; ita Philo & Josephus, qui observant, MO Ægyptiis aquam, & YSES, servatum, notare. Ita & Clem. Alexand. qui lib. 1. Stromat. aquam Æ- gyptios MOY vocare notat, quibus subscribit A- thanas. Kircher, in Prodrom. Copt. illi igitur, inquit, qui nomen Mosis ab Ebraica voce מֹשֶׁה deductum volunt, graviter errant; nomen namq; non à Parenti- bus, nec ab alio aliquo ex Ebræorum gente, sed ab ipsa Pharaonis filia accepit, quæ præter vernaculam Ægy- ptiacam linguam nullam aliam habebat. Cui suffra- gatur etiam Hottinger. Exerc. Anti-Morin. p. 48. & amplectuntur illam sententiam pleriq; Interpretes. Alii vero, etsi admittant, Ægyptiam mulierẽ puero à se adoptato nomen Ægyptium indidisse, nomen Mose tamen Ebræum esse, & ex Ægyptio translatũ, ejusdem significationis cum illo nomine originario Coptico. Ita And. Riv. qui non constare, ait, quodnam illud nomen Ægyptiacum fuerit. Nec abnuit Aben- Ezra, qui existimat, nomen Mosis interpretatum fuisse ex Ægyptio MONIOS. Sed textus clare indi- cat, Mose vocatum à מָשָׁה extraxit, quod de extra- ctione ex aquis usurpatur Pf. 18, 17. quia hoc Ety- mon redditur h. l. vocavit eum Mose, quia dixit: ex aquis מְשִׁיתִהוּ extraxi eum. Unde dubitandum non est, nominis illius originem Ebraicam esse, nec aliam in aliis linguis quæri debere, siquidem Scriptura tam aperte nominis rationem explicet, neque veri- simile est, cum nomen à filia Pharaonis sibi imposi- tum, & ipsa ejusdem verba Moses hîc referat, eum substituisse aliud nomen, aliamque nominis ratio- nem, cum nomina propria alias semper retinuerit, qualia imposita fuere, non vero in linguam aliam transfuderit, quod multo minus de suo nomine fa- cturus fuisset. Ratio illa, quod filia Pharaonis nul- lam aliam, quam Ægyptiacam linguam habuerit, probabilitate nulla gaudet, imo vero similius est, eandem non ignorasse Ebræam linguam, & puero Ebræo proinde nomen Ebræum imposuisse, etsi fieri potuerit, ut eo libentius à voce מָשָׁה extraxit, eundem appellarit, quod in lingua etiam vernacu- la MOY aquam notet: à sola voce hac, quia desunt duæ postremæ Radicales, nec nisi una litera מ in ea occurrit, derivari nequit, & quomodo è syllaba po- strema שׁה servatum vel extractum facient in lin- gua Coptica, si nomen compositum dicant? In Cir- cumcisione aliud nomen ipsum à parentibus acce- pisse, & Joachim appellatum esse, Clem. Alex. l. c. tradit: Rabbi Gedalia in Schalscheleth Patrem di- cit ipsum vocasse Chaber, matrem, Jekadiel, Soro- rem Jeder, atque ita ab aliis nominibus aliis appel- latum fuisse, quæ Rabb. mystice exponunt, notante Hieron- in Tradit. Ebr. in librum Paralipp. Isabar Ali Syrus vocatum in circumcisione fuisse dicit Balthiel, id est, libera me Deus; in Sidra libri Para- lipp. vocatus dicitur Jamchil, regnare fecit: Conf. Hotting. Hist. Orient. p. 12. sed Scriptura tacet, quodnam in circumcisione nomen acceperit, non autem omine caret Mosis nomen, quia ex aquis ex- tractus Israëlitas ex aquis afflictionum & è mari ru- bro educere debuit.

## 2:11
Verse 11. AFTER MOSES HAD GROWN.

Not only in age and stature, but also in wisdom, in power ἐν λόγοις καὶ ἔργοις, likewise in courtly dignity, and in the heroic magnitude of faith, Heb. 11, 25.

Verse same. HE WENT OUT TO HIS BROTHERS.

Having abandoned the court, which Stephanus revealed to have been done in the 40th year of his age, Acts 7:23, the Holy Spirit attributes this to the faith of Moses, Heb. 11:25, explaining more fully what kind of departure that was: that he no longer wished to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, but renounced such an adoption and dignity; that he joined himself to the Israelite people as the people of God; that he preferred to cleave to them, even though almost oppressed by servitude, rather than to enjoy the splendor of the royal court; that he judged he could no longer enjoy courtly pleasures without sin and recognized that those temporal delights would one day have to be exchanged for eternal punishments; that he believed in Christ the promised Messiah and preferred His reproaches far above the treasures of Egypt: cf. B. Rung. in h. l. To Rivetus it seems probable that Pharaoh’s daughter had already ceased to be among the living when Moses abandoned the court. But that does not accord with the text of the Apostle in Heb. 11, verse 24, because he preferred to be considered the son of the Israelite Church, which was most oppressed, rather than of the royal daughter of Pharaoh, which does not conflict with thanksgiving, but is a duty of piety, Luke 14, 16.

Verse same. AND HE SAW AN EGYPTIAN MAN &c.

Philo says that he was a taskmaster, which Rivetus does not prove, but it seems to be gathered not obscurely from the preceding words; he saw the burdens &c. when compared with Exodus 1, verse 11; that Egyptian, however, had ferociously struck an Israelite out of injustice someone, and indeed with a blow not light, but enormous, so that the striker, with the aggravating circumstances being weighed, had deserved the punishment of death, whence Moses, kindled with indignation, killed the robber, not by a word alone, which Clem. Alex. l. 1. Strom. says the mystics feel, as Peter did Ananias and Sapphira, Acts 5, 5. nor by employing the Tetragrammaton name, as R. Solomon trifles, but with a sword or some club or other instrument and with a strong blow, which the word נכה conveys, which is rendered by Luke Acts 7, 24. as πατάξειν, which is wont to be done with a huge pulsation not without noise and sound. But whether Moses sinned in this, is discussed. Some think he sinned, because he was a private person and, carried away by a desire for vengeance, did it, and therefore even fearfully looked this way and that in that matter, whether anyone saw him, and hid the one killed. To which Aug. agrees l. 22. against Faust. Manich. I find by consulting the eternal law that a man ought not to have been killed by Moses, who held no ordered authority, even if he were injurious and wicked: and Hilar. l. 5. de Trinit. who attributes this to emotion, and that Moses did not know the God of his fathers' blessings: add Oecumenius on the Epistle of Jude, who reports that the devil in the contest with Michael objected to him that the body of Moses was unworthy of burial, because he had killed an Egyptian.

2. Others say that it was indeed done by a private man, and without an extraordinary impulse, but without sin, either because Moses owed it to the common duty of humanity, as Ambros. l. 1. de offic. c. 36. judges, since he who does not repel an injury from a companion, if he can, is as much in fault as he who does it, or because he killed the Egyptian with the moderation of blameless defense, which is the opinion of Thomas 2. secundae qu. 6. art. 6. to the second, to which also Burgensis, Cajet. as well as Toletus, in Luc. 10. annot. 27. incline, because then there was no judge who could avert the injury, and the injury was present, and did not brook delay: whence it was Moses's duty to assist.

3. But because that is never turned to Moses's fault in Scripture, nay, the Protomartyr Stephen testifies that he was moved by God Acts 7, 25. 'he supposed that his brethren would have understood how that God by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not': there is no doubt that Moses did it from the consciousness of his vocation to deliver the people, and Stephen says openly: ἐποίησεν ἐκδίκησιν he did vengeance: but he would not have praised private vengeance; for this cannot be done lawfully, Rom. 12, 19. therefore he ought to be considered as a public person, equipped with authority for this deed extraordinarily by divine impulse to exercise just vengeance, as the future deliverer of the people, both of which is clear from the words of the Protomartyr. That example, therefore, was not common, but altogether singular, which is proposed for admiration, not for imitation, except by those who are impelled by the same Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 11. POSTQUAM CREVERAT MOSES.

Non ætate solum & Statura, sed Sapientia etiam, potentia ἐν λόγοις καὶ ἔργοις, dignitate item aulica, & magnitudine fidei heroica, Ebr. 11, 25.

Vers. eodem. EGRESSUS EST AD FRA- TRES SUOS.

Derelicta sc. aula, quod anno 40. ætatis factum esse, Stephanus aperuit, Act. 7, 23. fideig, Mosis ad- scribit Spir. S. Ebr. 11, 25. explicans uberius, qualis fuerit ille egressus, quod noluerit amplius filius vo- cari filiæ Pharaonis, sed adoptioni & dignitati tantæ renunciavit, quod populo Israelitico, ceu Dei po- pulo se aggregarit, quod illis adhærescere malue- rit, etsi servitute pene oppressis, quam aulæ regiæ splendore frui, quod voluptatibus aulicis sine pec- cato se amplius perfrui non posse judicarit & tem- porales illas delicias cum æternis suppliciis olim commutandas esse agnoverit, quod in Christum promissum Messiam crediderit, ejusque opprobria thesauris Ægyptiis longe prætulerit: conf. B. Rung. in h. l. Riveto probabile videtur filiam Pharaonis tum jam desuisse esse in vivis, cum Moses aulam deseruit. Sed id non congruit textui Apostoli Ebr. 11. vers. 24. quia maluit filius Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ maxime pres- sæ censeri, quam filiæ Pharaonis Regiæ, quod non pugnat cum gratitudine, sed officium est pietatis, Luc. 14, 16.

Vers. eodem. ET VIDIT VIRUM ÆGY- PTIUM &c.

Præfectum onerum fuisse Philo dicit, quod non probat Rivetus, sed videtur haud obscure col- ligi è verbis præcedentibus; vidit onera &c. col- latis cum Exod. 1. versu 11. ille vero Ægyptius per injuriam ferociter percusserat Israëlitam aliquem, & quidem percussione non levi, sed enor- mi, ita, ut percussor pensihabitis circumstantiis aggravantibus meritus fuerit mortis supplicium, unde indignatione accensus Moses latronem inter- fecit, non verbo solo, quod Clem. Alex. l. 1. Strom. mystas sentire ait, uti Petrus Ananiam & Saphiram, Act. 5, 5. nec adhibito nomine Tetragrammato, ut nugatur R. Salomo, sed gladio vel fuste aliquo aut alio instrumento ac percussione forti, quam infert verbum נכה, quod à Luca Act. 7, 24. redditur πα- τάξειν, quod ingenti pulsatione non absq; strepitu & sono fieri solet. Num vero peccarit in eo Moses, disquiritur. Peccasse nonnulli putant, quod priva- tus fuerit & vindictæ cupiditate abreptus id fecerit, ideoque etiam meticulofus ea in re huc illuc cir- cumspexerit, an aliquis eum videret, & occisum ab- sconderit. Quibus aunuit Aug. l. 22. contra Faust. Manich. Consulta æterna lege reperio, non debuisse hominem à Mose, qui nullam ordinatam potestatem gerebat, quamvis injuriosum & improbum, occidi: & Hilar. l. 5. de Trinit. qui affectui id tribuit, & quod nesciverit Moses Deum paternarum benedictionum: adde Oecumenium in Epistolam Judæ, qui tradit, diabolum in certamine cum Michaële ipsi objecisse Mosis corpus sepultura indignum esse, quod Ægy- ptium interfeeisset.

2. Alii ab homine privato quidem id factum dicunt, & citra extraordinarium impul- sum, sed absque peccato, sive quod ex communi humanitatis officio id debuerit Moses, uti Ambros. l. 1. de offic. c. 36. censet, quoniam qui non repellit à socio injuriam, si potest, tam est in vitio, quam ille, qui facit, sive quod cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ Ægyptium occiderit, quæ est Thomæ sententia 2. se- cundæ qu. 6. art. 6. ad secundum, quo etiam incli- nat Burgensis, Cajet. ut & Toletus, in Luc. 10. annot. 27. quia tunc non erat judex, qui posset injuriam avertere, & injuria erat præsens, nec moram patie- batur: unde Mosis fuit subvenire.

3. Sed quia nunquã id vitio Mosi vertitur in Scriptura, imo Protomar- tyr Stephanus à Deo motum fuisse testatur Act. 7, 25. existimabat autem intelligere fratres, quoniam Deus per manum ipsius daret salutem illis, at illi non intelle- xerunt: ex conscientia vocationis suæ, ad liberan- dum populum, id fecisse Mosen, dubitandum non est, & aperte dicit Stephanus: ἐποίησεν ἐκδίκησιν fe- cit vindictam: privatam autem vindictam, non lau- dasset utique; hæc enim legitime fieri non potest, Rom. 12, 19. ideo ut persona publica autoritate ad hoc facinus extraordinarie divino impulsu ad justam vindictam exercendam stipata considerari debet, ceu futurus liberator populi, quod utrumq; aper- tum est ex verbis Protomartyris. Exemplum ergo illud non fuit commune, sed prorsus singulare, quod ad admirationem proponitur, non ad imitationem, nisi eorum, qui eodem impelluntur Spiritu.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. HE HID THE EGYPTIAN HE HAD STRUCK.

He did it looking first this way and that, whence you may gather that he was as it were trembling about his deed, nor was he certain that he had been moved to it by GOD. Which is the reason why Calvin thinks that infirmity and weakness of faith were mixed with the extraordinary impulse, but Riv. does not approve of this, because what he could lawfully do, he also ought to have done cautiously, lest any sedition be stirred up, and he himself undergo the risk of his life. Faith is not repugnant to caution, nor must those things for which we are bound by faith always be done openly. Nor is circumspection always an argument of usurped power, for legitimate judges, when they fear a greater force, sometimes secretly execute punishment upon criminals. If you say, why did he look this way and that? lest anyone by chance should notice it, since, with Stephen as witness, he supposed and wished his brethren to understand that God by his hand would give them salvation, and had determined to give them here a specimen of future liberation? But he looked around at least, lest some Egyptian by chance or other adversary, by whom that matter might be betrayed before the King, should be present: he did not fear for himself from his brethren, for he undoubtedly had the one he was looking at (and perhaps others also) to whom the Egyptian had offered violence and whom he had delivered from his hand.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PERCUSSUM ÆGYPTIUM AB- SCONDIT.

Fecit id respiciens primum huc illuc, unde col- ligas, quasi de facto suo trepidarit, neq; certus fue- rit, se à DEO ad id permotum fuisse. Quæ causa est quod Calvinus motui extraordinario mixtam fuisse infirmitatem & fidei imbecillitatem existimet, sed id non probat Riv. quia quod licite facere potuit, caute etiam facere debuit, ne qua seditio excitaretur, & ipse capitis discrimen subiret. Fides cautioni non repugnat, nec semper aperte sunt facienda ea, ad quæ fide tenemur. Nec semper circumspectio ar- gumentum est usurpatæ potestatis, nam legitimi judices, cum verentur vim majorem, aliquando clam de reis supplicium sumunt. Si dicas, cur respe- xerit huc illuc? ne quis forte id adverteret, siquidem Stephano teste, existimarit, ac voluerit intelligere fratres, quod Deus per manum ipsius salutem illis da- ret, ac specimen futuræ liberationis hîc ipsis edere constituerit? Sed circumspexit saltem, ne quis Æ- gyptius forte aut alius adversarius, à quo coram Re- ge res illa proderetur, præsto esset: non à fratribus sibi metuit, nam illum inspectantem sine dubio ha- buit (& fortassis alios etiam) cui vim fecerat Ægy- ptius & quem è manu ejus liberarat.

## 2:12 Addition
On chapter 2:12, towards the end, at page 326, column b.

If anyone should say that death was unjustly inflicted for a simple striking, one responds with Augustine and Pererius that not everything that happened is narrated here: perhaps the Egyptian had nearly killed the Hebrew, and Moses could not repel him otherwise; or the Egyptian even rushed at Moses, who, repelling force with force, killed him. Lyranus notes that he killed him not only because of the striking, but also because of adultery, which Moses knew from those who were quarreling, which the Hebrews hand down, that the Hebrew struck by the Egyptian was the husband of Salomith, a most beautiful woman, whom he had defiled by fraud.

Latin:

Ad c. 2, 12. sub finem ad pag. 326. b.

Si quis dicat ob simplicem percussionem in- juste mortem inflictam, respondet cum August. Pe- rerius, non omnia, quæ acciderint hic narrari: fortassis Ægyptius Ebræum prope occiderat, nec aliter Moses repellere illum poterat; vel Ægy- ptius etiam in Mosen irruit, qui vim vi repellens occidit: Lyranus monet, interfecisse eum Mosen non tantum ob percussionem, sed & adulterium, quod ex iis altercantibus novit Moses, quod He- bræi tradant, Hebræum percussum ab Ægyptio fu- isse maritum Salomith mulieris pulcherrimæ, quam per fraudem vitiarit.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. TWO HEBREWS STRIVING. The word נצה signifies to fly, because one flew at the other, and it is used of a fight unto slaughter 2. Sam. 14, 6. Therefore the LXX. rendered it: διαπληκτιζομένως quarreling even to blows. Stephen Acts 7, 26. rendered it μαχομένως, which the Vulg. Erasm. Syrus and Arabs interpret as litigating. But Beza more correctly explained it as fighting, because it was a grave fight, in which they would have descended even to slaughter, had not Moses intervened, as is gathered from the emphasis of the Hebrew word.

Latin:

Vers. 13. DUOS EBRÆOS RIXANTES. Verbum נצה significat volare, quod involarit alter in alterum & de pugna ad cædem usurpatur 2. Sam. 14, 6. Ideo LXX. reddiderunt: διαπληκτιζο- μένως altercantes usque ad plagas. Stephanus Act. 7, 26. μαχομένως reddidit, quod Vulg. Erasm. Syrus & Arabs interpretantur, litigantes. Sed rectius Beza, pugnantes, exposuit, quia gravis pugna fuit, in qua ad cædem usque descendissent, nisi Moses interve- nisset, ut ex Emphasi vocis Ebrææ colligitur.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. WHO FLEEING &c. Although those things which Josephus and Philo report about the mind of Pharaoh being exacerbated against Moses, on account of the war bravely conducted against the Ethiopians, rest on no certainty, yet when the King saw that Moses had gone out, whom he had recognized as a prudent and strenuous man, and that he had killed an Egyptian to vindicate a Hebrew man, he suspected that Moses might be plotting something great, having seemed born for great things: therefore he pursued him.

The flight of Moses is here ascribed to fear, Heb. 11:27. Yet he is said to have left Egypt by faith, not fearing the wrath of the King. Some therefore explain this passage as referring to a simulated fear, or one that was apparently such. But it is expressly held in the text: Moses feared, and the cause of the fear is added, the divulging of the slaughter. Others say that he did indeed fear with that fear which can fall even upon a constant man, but not with a vicious fear: and that he did not entirely collapse in spirit, or cast away the hope of liberating the Israelites. By others, the leaving of Egypt in Heb. 11 is understood of the departure from Egypt with the people, because, fearing nothing of the King's wrath, he then left Egypt with a strong spirit through faith, leading the Israelites away with him, as Lyranus, Tostatus, Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide, Pareus, Rivetus in this place, and Jacobus Capellus and B. Gerhard in the Epistle to the Hebrews explain. To this opinion it seems to favor, that it is added, seeing the invisible, as if to say he placed his confidence in the promises of GOD, even though he did not doubt in the least that Pharaoh would pursue him when he left Egypt. But because the Apostle places this proof of faith before the Passover, which was celebrated before Moses left Egypt, and immediately subjoins that to the leaving of the court and the visitation of the people of GOD, and the word κατέλειπεν seems to correspond more correctly to the flight from Egypt than to the leading out of the people, for then he had come into Egypt, not to remain there, but with the sole purpose that he might leave Egypt, or rather, that he might lead the people out from there, these things are more conveniently explained concerning the flight from Egypt after the slaughter of the Egyptian man; in which he was certainly not free from fear at first, in view of the tyranny and power of Pharaoh, who was seeking to kill Moses, and that before he cast himself into flight, so that he might take up the plan of flight. But he nevertheless raised his spirit afterwards in view of the divine promise and protection, so that he feared the king's wrath no longer from then on, lest, namely, he should be apprehended in his flight, relying on divine assistance, even though he was not ignorant that kings have long hands. In that first consternation, therefore, he feared, how has this word been made public? And it was a just and not imprudent fear, because from it he began the plan of flight, which was necessary and salutary for him. But when he was already undertaking his flight with the Goel, his Redeemer, as Leader and Companion, he promised himself a safe conduct through true confidence, fearing nothing from the fury of the earthly King, secure in heavenly grace, even though he was ignorant of where he might turn himself. Therefore, with a strong spirit in the very midst of flight and exile he was, as one who saw him (by faith) who is invisible: to which opinion the Greeks add their vote, Chrysost. Theodor. & Theoph. to whom also most recently Mr. Dr. Walther has acceded in his Homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews, having previously sent to the Harmony the defense regarding the leading of Israel out of Egypt.

It is evident, however, from this example that flight is not illicit in the heat of danger, contrary to what Tertullian argues in his published book on flight in persecution, denying that it is lawful for any reason; which opinion Peter Martyr is the author of having been embraced by some in the previous century in the letter which he wrote on that matter at the end of his Common Places. But not only Moses here, but also David fleeing from the face of Saul, Elijah fleeing from the tyranny of Ahab 1 Kings 19, the prophets hiding with Obadiah as fugitives 1 Kings 18, the disciples scattering when Stephen was stoned Acts 8, Paul escaping from Damascus ibid., Christ himself withdrawing often John 6:15, ch. 7:1, ch. 8:59, proved by their own example that flight is sometimes not illicit, which also Polycarp of Smyrna in Eusebius b. 4 ch. 15, Athanasius, whose Apology for his flight exists, about which Socrates b. 3 ch. 13, Ambrose in the same b. 5 ch. 11, Chrysostom in Sozomen b. 8 ch. 15. & others saved themselves: indeed, which Christ also commanded Matt. 10:13, ch. 24:16, which finally self-love requires, lest anyone by exposing himself to enemies become the cause of his own death: love of neighbor, to whom he can be useful if he snatches away his own life; love of enemies, lest an occasion of greater cruelty be given to them. But as for the ministers of the Church, one must distinguish between common and personal persecution; in the former one must endure, concerning which Aug. Epist. 180, so that, namely, the Pastor does not abandon the flock Zech. 12:17, for whom he is also bound to lay down his life John 10:11, so that, as Aug. says in the same place, he may kindle by the example of his passion those whom he cannot preserve longer by the speech of doctrine: in the latter, however, it is sometimes lawful to flee, just as Moses by withdrawing himself in flight consulted not so much for himself as for the people of God, if indeed he saw that he was not yet recognized by his brothers as a minister of GOD, destined for their liberation. Nor is flight to be seized rashly, but the mind is to be properly examined, the scope accurately weighed, so that, namely, we look to the glory of GOD and the salvation of the neighbor, not only our own preservation or advantage, lest we turn out like hirelings. Finally, let everyone think with Nazianzen Orat. 28: to me all the earth, and no earth is my fatherland, because our fatherland is Heaven, and the whole earth is held as a fatherland for me, if indeed I am a κοσμοπολίτης, a citizen of the world.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QUI FUGIENS &c. Quanquam nulla certitudine nitantur, quæ Jo- sephus & Philo de animo Pharaonis adversus Mo- sen exacerbato, propter bellum, contra Æthyopes fortiter administratum, tradunt, tamen cum vide- rit Rex egressum Mosen, quem virum prudentem & strenuum agnoverat, ad Israëllitas, & ad virum Ebræum vindicandum, Ægyptium occidisse, suspi- cabatur, ne quid magni moliretur Moses, ad magna quæque natus visus: ideo persecutus eundem est.

Fuga Mosis timori hîc adscribitur, Ebr. 11, 27. vero fide reliquisse dicitur Ægyptium, non metuens iram Regis. De metu ergo simulato, vel apparenter tali nonnulli hunc locum explicant. Sed diferte habe- tur in textu: timuit Moses, metusque causa additur, divulgatio cædis. Alii timuisse quidem ajunt eo metu, qui in hominem constantem etiam cadit, non autem metu vitioso: nec prorsus concidisse ani- mo, aut spem liberandi Israëlitas abjecisse. Ab aliis relictio Ægypti Ebr. 11. de egressu ex Ægypto cum populo intelligitur, quod nihil timens iram Regis fortis animo per fidem tum reliquerit Ægyptum, secum etiam abducens Israëlitas, ut explicant Ly- ranus, Tostatus, Perer. C. à Lap. Pareus, Riv. in h. l. & Jacobus Capellus ac B. Gerh. in Epist. ad Ebr. Cui sententiæ favere videtur, quod additur, videns in- visibilem, q. d. fiduciam suam collocavit in pro- missiones DEI, etsi Pharaonem sese persecuturum, cum Ægyptum relinqueret, minime dubitarit. Sed quia Apostolus hoc fidei documentum præmittit paschati, quod celebratum est antequam relinque- ret Ægyptum Moses, & subjungit statim illud reli- ctioni aulæ & visitationi populi DEI, ac verbum κατέλειπεν rectius fugæ ex Ægypto congruere vi- detur, quam eductioni populi, tum enim venerat in Ægyptum, non ut illic maneret, sed eo omnino fi- ne, ut Ægyptum relinqueret, vel potius, ut popu- lum inde educeret, convenientius de fuga ex Ægy- pto post cædem hominis Ægyptii hæc exponuntur; in qua primum utique metus expers non fuit intui- tu tyrannidis, ac potentiæ Pharaonis, qui quære- bat Mosen occidere, idque priusquam in fugam se conjiceret, ut consilium fugæ capesseret. Sed ere- xit tamen postea animum intuitu promissionis ac protectionis divinæ, ita, ut nihil deinceps amplius iram regis metueret, ne scil. in fuga apprehendere- tur, fretus παραςάσει divina, utut non ignoraret Regibus longas esse manus. In prima ergo illa con- sternatione timuit, quomodo palam factum est ver- bum istud? Et fuit metus justus nec imprudens, quia inde consilium cœpit de fuga sibi necessaria & sa- lutari. Cum autem fugam jam capesseret Duce atq; Comite Goële Redemptore suo, salvum conductum vera fiducia sibi pollicebatur, nihil metuens furore Regis terreni, securus de gratia cœlesti, etsi nescius esset, quo se converteret. Forti ergo animo in ipsa fuga & exilio fuit, ut qui videret eum (per fidem) qui est invisibilis: cui sententiæ calculum adjiciunt Græci, Chrysost. Theodor. & Theoph. cui accessit etiam novissime Dn. D. Waltherus in Homil. ad E- pist. Ebr. missa priori antea in Harmonia propugna- ta de eductione Israëlis ex Ægypto.

Patet autem hoc exemplo, fugam non esse illici- tam in periculo fervente, secus atque Tertull. dispu- tat, edito libro de fuga in persecutione, negans ulla ratione licitam esse; quam sententiam etiam non- nullos superiori seculo incrustasse Petrus Martyr Epistola, quam ea de re scripsit, ad calcem Loc. Com. autor est. At non tantum Moses hîc, sed & David à Saulis facie fugiens, Elias fugiens à tyran- nide Achabi 1. Reg. 19. Prophetæ latentes apud Ab- diam profugi 1. Reg. 18. discipuli lapidato Stepha- no diffugientes Act. 8. Paulus Damasco effugiens ibid. Christus ipse secedens sæpius Joh. 6, 15. c. 7, 1. c. 8, 59. exemplo suo probarunt, fugam quandoque non esse illicitam, qua etiam Polycarpus Smyrnen- sis apud Euseb. l. 4. c. 15. Athan. cujus extat Apolo- gia pro fuga, de qua Socrates l. 3. c. 13. Ambrof. apud eundem l. 5. c. 11. Chrysost. ap. Sozomen. lib. 8. c. 15. & alii se salvarunt: imo quam etiam mandavit Chri- stus Matth. 10, 13. c. 24, 16. quam requirit denique amor proprius, ne quis se inimicis objiciens mortis suæ causa existat: amor proximi, cui utilis, si animam suam eripiat, esse potest; amor hostium, ne illis oc- casio detur majoris crudelitatis. Quod vero ad ministros Ecclesiæ, distinguendum inter persecutio- nem communem, & personalem; in illa perduran- dum, quo de Aug. Epist. 180. ne scil. Pastor dere- linquat gregem Zach. 12. v. 17. pro quo etiam ani- mam ponere tenetur Johan. 10, 11. ut, quod Aug. l. c. ait, exemplo suæ passionis accendat, quos sermone doctrinæ diutius conservare non valet: in hac vero fu- gere licet quandoque, uti Moses fuga se subducen- do non tam sibi, quam populo Domini consuluit, siquidem videret se nondum à fratribus agnosci pro ministro DEI, ad eorum liberationem destina- to. Nec temere fuga arripienda, sed animus pro- be excutiendus, scopus accurate expendendus, ut scil. gloriam DEI & salutem proximi, non solam nostri conservationem, aut commodum spectemus, ne mercenariis similes evadamus. Denique cum Nazianzeno ita quisque sentiat Orat. 28. mihi omnis terra, & nulla terra patria est, quia patria nostra Cæ- lum est, & tota terra pro patria mihi habetur, siqui- dem κοσμοπολίτης mundi civis sim.

## 2:16
Verse 16. CONCERNING THE INFANTS OF THE HEBREWS.

It is to be believed that she recognized him not so much from the circumcision of the infant, as some wish, but from the cruel edict of her father.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DE INFANTIBUS EBRÆORUM.

Id non tam è circumcisione infantuli, quod non- nulli volunt, quam ex edicto patris crudeli ipsam agnovisse credendum est.

## 2:16
Ver. 16. TO THE PRIEST OF MIDIAN] Of the true GOD, such as Melchizedek also was. For idolatry had not yet spread so widely.

I. The Chaldean: To the Prince of Midian: Artabanus in Eusebius b. 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, last chapter, calls him King of Arabia; the word כֹּהֵן denotes not only a priest, but also a Prince 2 Sam. 8:18, ch. 20:16, 1 Kings 4:5. But the meaning of priest is more famous, and hardly any other occurs in Moses; then if he was a Prince, whose daughters pasture sheep and lead them to water, and how do the shepherds dare to repel them so insolently? Nor does the hospitality for Moses seem safe enough with a royal Satrap, while Pharaoh was everywhere demanding Moses for slaughter even with public diplomatic letters; which Mr. Varenius noted here. Most therefore, with the LXX Interpreters and others both Eastern and Western, think more correctly that he was a priest; but because that priest was in Midian, it seems to some that he worshipped idols, which however does not appear consistent with the piety and prudence of Moses, that he should have contracted an affinity with an idolatrous priest. Therefore Cyril b. 3 on Adoration in Spirit, as also Abulensis, think that he was immediately led to the knowledge of the true God when Moses came to

him. Others say he was converted afterwards when he came to Moses in the desert Exod. 18:10. Some think he was of those who still had the knowledge of the true God received from Abraham, even if mixed with many superstitions. If this is true, as it is accepted by Grotius, and appears probable, since Demetrius in Eusebius l. c. traces his origin from Abraham through Keturah, the worship of God must have been propagated in Midian by this priest, and perhaps because of that kinship of blood and knowledge of the true God, Moses preferred to betake himself there rather than to others, directed also by God because of the posterity of Abraham, the friend of God. For Midian was founded by a son of Abraham by Keturah of the same name, as Jerome notes on Hebrew places, and situated by the Red Sea in the territory of Amalek, it was nearest to one fleeing from Egypt. The land of Midian is called by the general name Ethiopia, just as the Arabs are also called Ethiopians, whence Moses' wife is called an Ethiopian, Num. 1:12.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SACERDOTI MADIAN] Veri DEI, qualis & Melchisedech. Nondum enim idololatria tam late se dif- fuderat.

I. Chaldæus: Principi Madian: Regem Ara- biæ vocat Artabanus apud Euseb. l. 9. de præparat. Evangel. cap. ult. vox כֹּהֵן non solum sacerdotem, sed & Principem notat 2. Sam. 8. vers. 18. cap. 20. 16. 1. Reg. 4, 5. Ast famosior est Sacerdotis significa- tio, & vix in Mose alia occurrit; Tum si Princeps hic fuit, qui ejus filiæ oves pascunt, & aquatum ducunt, & quomodo audent pastores easdem tam procaciter repellere? Neque videtur satis tutum Mosi hospitium apud Satrapen Regium, Pharaone ubique publicis etiam diplomatis Mo- sen ad cædem deposcente; quod hic monuit Dn. Varenius. Plerique ergo cum LXX. Interpp. aliisq; tum Orientalibus tum Occidentalibus rectius sacer- dotem fuisse putant; sed quia ille sacerdos in Mi- dian fuit, idola coluisse nonnullis videtur, quod vero pietati & prudentiæ Mosis haud apparet con- gruum, quod cum idololatra sacerdote affinitatem contraxerit. Idcirco Cyrill. l. 3. de adorat. in Spiri- tu, ut & Abulensis putant eundem ad veri Dei agni- tionem statim perductum fuisse, cum Moses ad

eundem veniret. Alii conversum dicunt postmodum cum ad Mosen veniret in deserto Exod. 18, 10. Nonnulli eum exillis fuisse arbitrantur, qui veri Dei notitiam ab Abrahamo acceptã adhuc habebant, etsi multis superstitionibus admixtã. Quod si verum, uti & à Grotio acceptatur, & probabile apparet, cum originem ejus ab Abrahamo ex Kethura deducat Demetrius apud Euseb. l. c. cultum Dei in Madian ab hoc sacerdote propagatum fuisse oportet, & fortassis ob cognationem illam sanguinis ac notitiam veri Dei Moses èò potius se recipere voluit, quam aliorumsum, directus etiam à Deo ob posteritatem Abrahæ amici Dei. Madian enim condita fuit à filio Abrahæ ex Kethura ejusdem nominis, notante Hieron. de locis Ebraicis, & sita ad mare rubrum in territorio Amalek, fugienti ex Ægypto proxima fuit. Terra Madian generali nomine Æthiopia vocatur, quemadmodum Arabes etiam Æthiopes dicuntur, unde Mosis uxor Æthiopissa appellata est, Num. 1, 12.

## 2:18
Ver. 18. TO RAGUEL HER FATHER) That is, grandfather, as is gathered from Num. 10:29. Compare what is in Gen. 24:48.

This man יתר had a triple name according to some: Raguel, Jethro, and Hobab. The Hebrews add yet a fourth name, Kenite, Judges 4:11. However, others think Raguel was the father of Jethro, who was otherwise called Hobab, which is the opinion of Abulensis, Junius, and Tremellius, as well as our blessed Glassius in his Sacred Grammar, p. 760. More correctly, Burgensis, Cajetan, and Oleastrius, as well as Calvin and others, say that Jethro and Raguel were the same person, the father-in-law of Moses; but they make Hobab the son of Raguel or Jethro and the brother of Zipporah: because Jethro seems to have returned to his own people in Midian after he had blessed Moses, but Hobab remained with him, and his descendants, the Kenites, dwelt among the Israelites. Therefore, those words in Numbers 10:29 are not to be rendered with Jun. and Tremellius: Moses had said to Hobab the son of Raguel the Midianite, the father-in-law of Moses, but [rather] the kinsman or relative of Moses; for that Raguel was the father of these seven daughters is openly asserted here in the book of Exodus 2:18, nor does the text in any way permit us to understand the grandfather by the name of father. For Sephora is also called his daughter, and he himself gives her in marriage to Moses, which is the duty of a father, if he survives.

Latin:

Vers. 18. AD RAGUELEM PATREM SUUM) Id est, avum, ut colligitur Num. 10. 29. Confer quod Gen. 24. 48.

Nomen huic יתר triplex juxta quosdam fuit, Raguel, Jethro & Hobab: Ebræi addunt adhuc quartum nomen, Kinæus, Judic. 4, 11. Cæterum alii Raguelem patrem fuisse Jethronis putant, qui alias Hobab dictus fuerit, quæ est sententia Abulensis, Junii & Tremellii, ut & B. Glassii nostri in Gramm. S. p. 760. Rectius Burgens. Cajet. & Oleastrius, nec non Calvinus & alii Jethronem & Raguelem ipsum Mosis socerum fuisse dicunt; Hobab vero Raguelis vel Jethronis filium & Zipporæ fratrem faciunt: quia Jethro videtur ad suos rediisse in Midian, postquam Mosi benedixisset, Jobab vero mansit penes ipsum, posteriq; ejus Cenei inter Israëlitas habitarunt. Verba ergo illa Num. 10, 29. non reddenda cum Jun. & Trem. sunt: dixerat Moses Chobabo filio Reguelis Midianitæ socero Mosis, sed soceri Mosis, vel cum Hieronymo, cognato aut affini Mosis, nam quod Raguel pater fuerit harum septem filiarum, aperte asseritut h. in l. Exod. 2. v. 18. nec textus ullatenus permittit, ut avum nomine patris intelligamus. Nam & Sephora filia ejus dicitur, & ipse elocat eam Mosi, quod Patris est officium, si superfit.

## 2:21
Verse 21. AND MOSES SWORE THAT HE WOULD DWELL WITH HIM.

The Vulgate wrongly rendered ויואל here as 'swore'; it occurs once in the sense of adjuring (but not swearing) in 1 Samuel 14:24, but it is constructed with an accusative, whereas it properly signifies 'willed,' as the Chaldean, the LXX interpreters, Vatablus, and most others have translated it.
