The sense is that Jethro wished to retain Moses, whom he saw to be prudent and energetic, with him under certain conditions, and that Moses consented to them. Nor could Moses have bound himself by an oath to dwell with him perpetually, since he knew he was destined to liberate his people.

Verse same. HE TOOK ZIPPORAH.

There is no necessity to say, with Philo and Nyssenus, that Zipporah was taken immediately, nor does that accord with the prudence of Jethro or Moses, or the honor of marriage. He dwelt in Midian for 40 years and there fathered two sons, and when he was returning to Egypt, he still had a little son who was uncircumcised.

Latin:

Vers. 21. JURAVIT ERGO MOSES QUOD HABITARET CUM EO.

Male Vulgata hîc ויואל reddidit juravit; adjurandi quidem significatu (non autem jurandi) occurrit semel 1. Sam. 14, 24. sed cum Accusativo constructum, proprie autem significat voluit, ut Chald. LXX. Interpp. Vatablus & plerique alii transtulere. Sensus est, quod voluerit Jethro Mosen, quem videbat prudentem atque strenuum, certis conditionibus secum retinere, quodque Moses in easdem consenserit. Neque vero juramento se adstringere poterat Moses, ut perpetuo cum eo habitaret, siquidem destinatum se noverat ad liberandum populum suum.

Vers. eod. ACCEPIT SEPHORAM.

Statim ductam fuisse Sephoram, ut cum Philone & Nysseno dicamus, nulla est necessitas, neq; id congruit Jethronis vel Mosis prudentiæ, aut matrimonii honestati. Habitavit in Midian 40. annis, duosque ibi suscepit filios, & cum Ægyptum repeteret, filiolum adhuc tenellũ incircumcisum habebat.

## 2:22
Verse 22. AND THE OTHER SHE BARE, etc.

These things concerning the other son of Moses are interpolations: for they are not found here in the source, but in Exodus 18:14, from which place they were transferred here by the Vulgate, or rather added by an alien hand. For the Hebrew codices agree in the omission of this verse, as do the Targum of Onkelos and Jonathan, and indeed even the edition of the Greek Bibles.

The Roman [edition], which relies on the most ancient Vatican codex, and others of both Bessarion and Cardinal Carafa, as the preface testifies, and does not observe a different reading in the notes. Lucas Brugensis suspects that it is perhaps read only in some Greek books: Isidorus Clarius does not admit that little verse in the Venetian Latin Bibles of the year 1551. Cajetan considers it superfluous; Johann Benedict, a Sorbonic theologian of Paris, as well as Vatablus and Stephanus, indeed retain the same, but marked with an obelus. Mariana is doubtful about the same, as is C. à Lap. Pererius acknowledges that those words are of Scripture, but not in this place, but in chapter 18. Finally, Bonfrerius suspects only that that little verse has fallen out, although Cardinal Bellarmine boldly affirms it, but not only do so many cited documents contradict him, but also the series of the historical narrative, since Eleazar was born only around the time of the calling of Moses made by GOD, which is manifest from chapter 5, and the name imposed upon him confirms. Therefore, B. Luther inserts that little verse only by parenthesis.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ALTERUM VERO PEPERIT, &c.

Hæc de altero Mosis filio, Embolimæa sunt: in fonte enim hîc non habentur, sed Exod. 18, 14. quo loco à Vulgato huc traducta sunt, aut potiùs manu aliena adjecta. Nam consentiunt Codd. Ebræi in omissione hujus versus & Targum Onkelos ac Jonath. imo etiam Editio Græcorum Bibliorum

Romana, quæ codice antiquissimo Vaticano, & aliis tum Bessarii, tum Cardin. Caraffe, teste præfatione, nititur, nec in notis diversam lectio- nem observat. Lucas Brugensis suspicatur tan- tum in nonnullis libris Græcis forte legi: Nec ad- mittit illum versiculum Isid. Clarius in Bibliis Ve- netis Latinis Anno 1551. Cajetan. habet pro su- perfluo, Johann. Bened. Parisiensis Theologus Sor- bonicus, ut & Vatablus ac Stephanus retinent qui- dem eundem, sed obelo notatum. Dubius est de eodem Mariana, ut & C. à Lap. Perer. agnoscit, ver- ba illa Scripturæ esse, sed non in h. l. sed capite 18. Denique Bonfrerius suspicatur solum, excidisse illum versiculum, Card. tamen Bellarm. audacter id affirmat, sed refragantur illi non tantum tot do- cumenta laudata, sed etiam series narrationis histo- ricæ, siquidem demum sub tempus vocationis Mo- sis à DEO factæ Eleazar natus sit, quod è c. 5. ma- nifestum est, nomenque ipsi impositum confirmat. Ideo B. Luth. versiculum illum per parenthesin tan- tum inserit.

## 2:23
Verse 23. HE DIED. Not that King under whom Moses was born, nor he under whom he had gone out of Egypt, but some successor of theirs: for Moses was 80 years old before he returned to Egypt from Midian. And since Pharaoh is said to have died here, it is manifest indeed that it is not one and the same Pharaoh who ordered the male offspring of the Jews to be submerged in the waters, and who was submerged in the sea.

Verse same. TO GOD] Whom most people then began to invoke, Num. 20:16, having abandoned the idols of Egypt, Ezek. 20:8. There is no doubt that many in such a great number of Israelites still clung to God: who therefore, pressed by tyranny, cried out more sharply to God, even if they had not ceased their prayers before, Isa. 26:16. For God always preserves a holy seed for Himself.

Latin:

Vers. 23. MORTUUS EST. Non Rex ille, sub quo Moses natus, nec is, sub quo exierat Ægypto, sed Successor eorum aliquis: erat enim Moses annorum 80. antequam in Ægyptum rediit ex Madian. Et quum hîc mor- tuus dicatur Pharao, manifestum utique est, non esse unum & eundem Pharaonem, qui masculam Judæorum prolem aquis submergi jussit, & qui mari submersus est.

Vers. eod. AD DEUM] Quem invocare tunc plerique cœperunt, Num. 20, 16. relictis idolis Ægypti, Ezech. 20, 8. Non dubium est, multos in tanto Israëlitarum numero Deo adhuc adhæsisse: qui proinde tyranni- de pressi acrius ad Deum vociferati sunt, etsi antea etiam preces non intermiserint, Esa. 26, 16. Semper enim Deus sibi servat sanctum semen.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. The Calling of Moses.

Verse 1. BUT MOSES WAS TENDING THE SHEEP OF JETHRO. It is evident from chapter 7 that Moses was then 80 years old, and therefore, just as he spent 40 years in courtly life, he similarly spent 40 years in pastoral life, and consumed the third forty-year period of his life in the leadership of the people, over whom he presided for 40 years in the desert. Great men devoted effort to the pastoral life: Abel in the first age, then Abraham and his descendants, and now also Moses: and God willed that he who was first a shepherd of sheep should then be appointed shepherd of His people, just as David was called from the pasturing of sheep to shepherd Jacob, the servant of GOD, Psalm 78:71, 2 Sam. 5:2. For the pastoral art, as Philo says, is a prelude to kingship, that is, to the governance of men, the most gentle flock. God also willed that Moses, accustomed to courtly life, should become accustomed to a completely contrary kind of life, and a harsher one, and that he who was to act in the desert for 40 whole years and was to be subjected to hard labors and burdens, should be prepared for that by the laborious service of pasturing sheep in the desert; he who had spent his life in the Egyptian court would now undergo for 40 years a life abominable to the Egyptians, so that by this very thing he might prove to his own people how alien he was to the customs of the Egyptians, even though he had lived in the court for so many years. God is also accustomed to accomplish great things through lowly instruments, so that the glory of the deeds done may be attributed to divine power, not to human authority. Interpreters are prolixly concerned about the studies of Moses during those 40 years in the land of Midian, but Scripture is silent. Philo teaches that he was devoted to philosophy, both theoretical and practical, yet it is to be believed that he was much more occupied with the contemplation of divine things. Pererius thinks that he then wrote the book of Job itself and the histories of Genesis. But it is more probable that these were committed to written monuments in the desert, which we have noted elsewhere.

Verse same. THE SHEEP OF JETHRO HIS FATHER-IN-LAW. Others wrongly read in the codices: of his kinsman, because Jethro was the father-in-law of Moses, who is also called Raguel in Exod. 2:21, and so the Chaldean, the LXX, Jerome against Helvidius, and the Roman Latin Edition here, as also in chapter 4:18.

Verse same. HE CAME TO MOUNT HOREB. The Protomartyr in Acts 7:30 says that an Angel appeared in the desert of Mount Sinai, who had his name from the סְנֶה bush, and was contiguous to Mount Horeb, as Adrichomius notes. For they were joined at the roots, and the eastern part was called Sinai, the western part Horeb. It is called the mountain of God, either by the customary Hebraism, because it was great, as in Ps. 36:7 mountains of God are mentioned, or by prolepsis, because, namely, the glory of GOD was revealed there, as the Chaldean Paraphrast explained. For on that mountain GOD appeared here to Moses in the bush, gave waters from the rock, Exod. 17:6, granted victory against Amalek through the prayers of Moses in chapter 17:10, promulgated the law in Exod. 19, and dealt with Moses for 40 days, and delivered to him the tablets of the law.

Latin:

CAPUT III. Vocatio Mosis.

Vers. 1. MOSES AUTEM PASCEBAT OVES JETHRO. MOsen tunc fuisse 80. annorum è cap. 7. constat, ideoque ut in aulica vita 40. ita similiter in pastoritia 40. annos transegit, tertiam vitæ quadra- genam in præfectura populi consumsit, cui per 40. annos in deserto præfuit. Vitæ pastoritiæ magni viri operam dedere, Abel in prima ætate, Abraham deinde & posteri ejus, nunc etiam Moses: & pasto- rem Deus primum ovium esse voluit, quem deinde pastorem populi sui constituit, uti David à pastura ovium vocatus est, ut pasceret Jacob servum DEI Psalm. 78, 71. 2. Sam. 5, 2. Est enim pastoralis ars, di- cente Philone, præludium ad regnum, hoc est, ad re- gimen hominum gregis mansuetissimi. Voluit etiam Deus, ut Moses aulicæ vitæ asfuetus, plane contrariœ vitæ generi, ac duriori asfuesceret, & qui in deser- to acturus per integros 40. annos duris laboribus & oneribus subjiciendus erat, ad id præpararetur pasturæ ovium laborioso in deserto servitio, qui in Ægyptia aula vitam transegerat, nunc vitam Ægy- ptiis abominabilem per 40. annos subiret, ut hoc ipso suis probaret, quam alienus esset ab Ægyptiorum moribus, utut in aula tot annis vixisset. Solet etiam Deus per instrumenta vilia res magnas efficere, ut divinæ potentiæ non hominum autoritati gloria rerum gestarum tribuatur. De studiis Mosis per istos 40. annos in terra Midian prolixe solliciti sunt Interpp. sed tacet Scriptura. Deditum fuisse Philosophiæ tum Theoreticæ, tum practicæ Philo docet, multo tamen magis vacasse ipsum rerum di- vinarum considerationi, credendum est. Pereriu st putat, tum ipsum librum Jobi & historiarum Geneseos conscripsisse. Sed probabilius est, in deserto hæc li- terarum monumentis consignata esse, quod alibi monuimus.

Vers. eod. OVES JETHRO SOCERI SUI. Male alii Codd. legunt : cognati sui, quia Jethro fuit socer Mosis, qui etiam Raguel dictus Exod. 2, 21. atque ita Chaldæus, LXX. Hieron. contra Helvidium & Romana Editio Latina hic, ut & c. 4, 18.

Vers. eod. VENIT AD MONTEM HOREB. Protomartyr Act. 7, 30. in deserto montis Si- na Angelum apparuisse dicit, qui à סְנֶה rubo no- men habuit, & contiguus fuit monti Horeb, no- tante Adrichomio. Cohæsere enim radicibus & pars orientalis dicta fuit Sinai, pars occidentalis Horeb. Mons Dei dicitur, sive Ebraismo consueto, quod fuerit magnus, ut Ps. 36, 7. montes Dei dicun- tur, seu per πρόληψιν, quia scil. ibi revelata est gloria DEI, ut exposuit Paraphrastes Chald. Nam in isto monte DEUS hîc Mosi in rubo apparuit, aquas ex petra dedit, Exod. 17, 6. victoriam contra Amalek precibus Mosis impertiit cap. 17, 10. legem promulgavit Exod. 19. & cum Mose per 40. dies egit, eique tabulas legis tradidit.

## 3:2
Verse 2. AND THE LORD APPEARED TO HIM IN A FLAME OF FIRE FROM THE MIDST OF A BUSH. In the Hebrew it is held, the Angel of the Lord appeared to him, (not indeed the Lord) with which the LXX, the Chaldeans, and Stephen, Acts 7:30, agree, so that there is no doubt that the Vulgate lies in error here: which no one among the Papists easily defends in this passage.

Concerning that bush and the vision, Philo says thus in book 1 of the Life of Moses; the bush there was a thorny and weak shrub, suddenly ignited without anyone applying fire, and entirely seized from the roots up to the top by a flame gushing forth in the manner of a fountain, and it remained whole and unharmed, as if it were not material for a fire, but were itself nourished by the fire. Artabanus also confirms to Eusebius in the last chapter of the Evangelical Preparation that that fire was ignited without anyone applying it, that the fire suddenly erupted from the earth and burned, although he fabulously adds that in that place no material suitable for a fire was found, and that Moses, having seen the fire, terrified, wished to take flight, just as Philo also says concerning the bush, that from the midst there shone forth a certain most beautiful form similar to nothing visible, clearly a divine image shining with most clear light. Cornelius à Lapide says it was not a true fire, but a specimen of fire and a fiery flame: but since this openly contradicts the text and parallel passages, he is then forced to acknowledge that it was a burning fire, but that its power was divinely restrained, so that it would not break forth in secondary action and consume the material, because with GOD withdrawing the concurrence for actual operation, even all the fire in hell could not ignite tow. It is certain that the bush remained unharmed, because Moses affirms it, and therefore Moses acknowledges a great vision, and venerates the peculiar presence of GOD in that place. That it was not God who appeared immediately, but an Angel in the name of God, the Pontiffs, Photinians, Arminians, and also our Calixtine innovators contend. Some Jews and the Photinian Enjedinus make a double vision, Θεοφανείαν and ἀγγελοφίαν: so that the Angel was indeed seen, but God spoke. Rivetus brings forward three other explanations: The first, common to the ancients and recent theologians; that God, who appeared in a visible form, was the second person of the Most Holy Trinity, the Son of GOD, who was about to assume flesh, and wished by this symbol, as it were, to prefigure the future incarnation: inasmuch as he is called the Angel of the covenant in Malachi 3, verse 1, the Angel Goël

Gen. 48. v. 16. The Angel, in whom is the name of the Lord, Exod. 23. v. 20. The Angel of the face of the Lord, Isa. 63. v. 9. and he led the people out of Egypt, Exod. 23. verse 20. 1 Cor. 10. v. 9. Jude verse 4. and he is called the Angel of the Lord, because he was sent by GOD the Father, and especially was to be sent in the fullness of time, for the sake of our redemption, which is the eternal counsel of GOD; therefore, for the sake of insinuating this, he willingly usurped the name of Angel in the Old Testament, so that, namely, the faith of the Fathers concerning the same might be confirmed: who also knew the same angel to be the redeemer, to be sent for the sake of redemption, and they professed that faith of theirs, Gen. 48. verse 16. Job 33. verse 23. seqq. Isa. 63. verse 9. Ludov. de Dieu explains this opinion more fully on Acts 6. v. 30., observing this particularly, that by ἐν χειρὶ ἀγγέλε, by the hand of the Angel, seen in the bush, GOD sent Moses as prince and Redeemer: It has, he says, here I know not what Emphasis in the word HAND, so that it does not seem to be omitted, for the sense is that GOD, when He sent Moses as Prince and Redeemer, committed the entire governance both of Moses and of the redemption to be performed through him, to the hands of this Angel: whence it is clearly evident that that Angel, who appeared in Exod. 3, and who is there several times called Jehovah and the GOD of the fathers, and who sends and instructs Moses, was not a created angel, but the Son of GOD Himself, through whose hands Stephen says the GOD of the fathers sent Moses. He also notes this, that in Exod. 23. v. 20. GOD says: I will send an Angel before thee, that it is the same as verse 14, my face shall go, and will lead you, because that angel is the angel of the face of the Lord, the very face of GOD, whom he who sees, sees the Father, John 14. verse 9. and who is the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, Heb. 1. 3. Thus therefore it is established how the Son of GOD is called an Angel, even though He is truly Jehovah Himself. The second exposition of Rivet is taken from Philo; that it was GOD who appeared, but was called an angel because He announced future things, which Rivet explains thus: because GOD manifested Himself by a visible sign, in the way that angels were accustomed to appear to men, therefore, on account of that external sign which GOD used for a time to reveal Himself to men, He was called an Angel. But if GOD is called an angel solely on account of the announcement of future things, it would be necessary for GOD the Father, as also the Holy Spirit, to be called an angel; indeed, the Holy Trinity is called an Angel, because it belongs to the whole Holy Trinity to announce future things. Rivet is therefore mistaken when he thinks that most of the ancients held this. He tries in vain to explain it thus, as if it were not simply on account of prophecy, but because GOD manifested Himself in a visible sign, as Angels are accustomed to appear. He is called an Angel, for both GOD the Father and the Holy Spirit manifested themselves at times by a visible sign: unless perhaps Rivet understands it thus (which however does not appear), that there was a certain Schema of habit, or some peculiar sign, by which created Angels were accustomed to appear, and that the Son of GOD assumed that habit and schema and sign, and is called an angel by that name, because He appeared in an angelic schema, that is, in such a one as Angels were accustomed to. We grant that this opinion of certain ancients is not inconsistent, yet it is not necessary that the exact same schema be posited, provided it was similar or analogous. Meanwhile, that Angels sometimes appeared in human form, and that the Son of GOD was seen in the same form as the attendant angels, though more august, is evident from the appearance to Abraham made in Genesis 18; which, as a prelude to the future incarnation, is to be believed, along with the Fathers of the Council of Antioch and other ancients, to have been assumed.

Rivet brings forward this explanation from Athan. Orat. 4. against the Arians: that GOD spoke in the angel, just as He also made words to Moses in the tabernacle from the pillar of cloud, and so GOD was present, and performed that speech immediately, even though He used the works of angels, and was seen in an angel. Blessed Dorsch. does not deny this opinion in the collation on the Council of Sirmium and the Apologetic judgment of Strasbourg against Latermann, explaining it thus: that the ὄραμα or vision which GOD exhibited to Moses is called an angel. But if Athanasius understood an angel, that is, a finite and complete Spirit, who was seen, and through whom GOD spoke, which is what Rivet wants, since by nature an angel is invisible, it would be necessary for the angel to have put on a visible form, in which case it would have to be said that GOD was united to the angel, and the angel in turn to the visible form, by a peculiar union; and so it is truly more akin to the truth that Athanasius, along with the other fathers, understood the angel seen as the angelic schema with which GOD was as it were clothed, just as He also willed to be covered by the pillar of cloud. But if you say that not the ὄραμα of the burning bush, but the habit in which He appeared, is called an angel, the name of angel, which belongs to a person, will be less conveniently attributed to an external form. Wherefore, without doubt, it is better to understand with Scripture the angel in whom the name of GOD is, that is, the uncreated angel, which will be explained more fully later: who, even if He was so named on account of the habit familiar to angels, yet the person appearing in the same is not to be confused with that external visible habit, because Angel is the name of a person. And Blessed Dorscheus himself proved in Vindiciae cap. 4. Exod. p. 45. that this Angel is called Jehovah and is that very one through whom Moses in Deut. 33. verse 16 blessed the Israelite people, that Christ Himself was tempted by the Israelites, Isa. 63. 1 Cor. 10. placed outside the order and hierarchy of finite angels; finally, that He is an infinite angel, and likewise that the appearing angel and the speaking Jehovah are one and the same person. Clement of Alexandria praised the opinion concerning the light formed in the burning bush, as the interpreter explained it, namely, that a formed light appeared, that is, reduced into the form of a man, which represented the incarnate divine Word.

Vers. eod.

THAT THE BUSH WAS BURNING AND WAS NOT CONSUMED] An image of the people of Israel. The wonderful interpretation of these words by Abarbanel and Rabbi Hiskuni, see in Menasseh’s Conciliator, page 96. The meaning of this symbol is handed down from Philo as follows: namely, that the fire denoted GOD, and the bush denoted the Jews, whom the Egyptians were setting on fire or afflicting, but not consuming; indeed, rendering them more splendid and stronger. Grotius adopted this explanation of the vision. The ancients also establish here a type both of the incarnation and of the conception of Christ. Regarding the former, they say it denotes the union and communication and περιχώρησιν [interpenetration] of the divine nature, which is shadowed by the fire, and the human nature, which is shadowed by the bush, with the latter remaining unharmed: because it preserves the unconsumed substance of our humanity even in the very flame of divinity, as Gregory the Great says. Regarding the latter, Gregory of Nyssa, in his Oration on the Nativity of Christ, makes such an application: as the bush kindles the fire, and is not burned, so the virgin both brings forth the light, and is not corrupted. These things do not please Rivet, without a doubt, because our orthodoxy is illustrated by this figure concerning the περιχωρήσει [interpenetration] and communication of the Deity in the human nature of Christ; therefore he says that these things, subtly devised, do not hit the mark. But Although the latter figure may be a little more strange, the former, however, concerning the mystery of the incarnation, which is more accepted in the Church, ought not to seem ἀλλότριον: because as the whole business of the leading out was a type of the spiritual leading out from the power of the infernal Pharaoh, so the appearance of the person who was to perform that work is certainly exhibited here in no strange manner, such as to foreshadow the mystery of the incarnation. I have descended, says the Son of GOD, who had lowered himself into the bush, that I may deliver them: because he himself, the incorporeal light and the true light, John 1:9, Heb. 1:3, Ezek. 1:4, was about to descend into the shoot from the root of Jesse, Isa. 11:1, about to assume human nature; which is compared to a green tree, Luke 23:31, that he might deliver us from spiritual captivity, Heb. 2:14.

Latin:

Vers. 2. APPARUITQUE EI DOMINUS IN FLAMMA IGNIS DE MEDIO RUBI. In Ebr. habetur, apparuit ei Angelus Domini, (non vero Dominus) cui consonant LXX. Chaldæi & Stephanus, Act. 7, 30. ut dubium non sit, Vulga- tam hîc in mendo cubare: quam non facile quis- quam è Pontificiis h. l. tuetur.

De rubo illo & visione ita Philo lib. 1. de vita Mosis; rubus ibi erat frutex spinosus & invalidus, nemine ignem admovente subito incensus est, corre- ptusque totus à radicibus usque ad cacumen flamma in morem fontis scatente, manebatque integer & illæsus, quasi non esset incendii materia, sed ipse ab igne ale- retur. Ignem illum nemine admovente incensum esse confirmat etiam Artabanus ad Eusebium de præparat. Evangel. cap. ult. ignem repente è terra erupisse arsisseque, etsi fabulose addat, eo in loco nullam materiam incendio aptam repertam esse, Mosemque viso igne territum fugam arripere voluisse, quemadmodum etiam Philo de rubo in- quit, quod è medio promicarit forma quædam pul- cherrima nulli visibili similis, divinum plane simula- crum luce fulgens clarissima. Cornelius à Lapide non ignem verum, sed specimen ignis & flammæ igneæ fuisse dicit: sed cum hoc aperte textui, & locis parallelis refragetur, agnoscere deinde co- gitur, ignem fuisse ardentem, sed vim ejus divini- tus inhibitam esse, ne actu secundo prorumperet, & materiam consumeret, quia DEO concursum subtrahente ad actualem operationem etiam totum ignem infernalem stupam accendere non posse. Id certum est, rubum illæsum mansisse, quia Mo- ses id affirmat, ideoque visionem magnam agno- scit Moses, & præsentiam DEI in loco illo pecu- liarem veneratur. Apparuisse non Deum imme- diate, sed Angelum DEI nomine Pontif. Photin. Armin. nec non Novatores nostri Calixtini con- tendunt. Judæi nonnulli & Enjedinus Photinia- nus geminam faciunt visionem, Θεοφανείαν, & ἀγ- γελοφίαν: ut Angelus quidem visus, Deus autem loquutus sit. Rivetus tres adfert alias explica- tiones: Primam communem veterum & recentio- rum Theologorum; Deum, qui apparuit in forma visibili, fuisse secundam Sacro-Sanct. Trinitatis per- sonam, Filium DEI, qui carnem erat assumturus, & hoc veluti Symbolo futuram incarnationem præsignificare voluerit: utpote qui vocatur An- gelus fœderis Malach. 3. versu 1. Angelus Goël

Gen. 48. v. 16. Angelus, in quo est nomen Domini, Exod. 23. v. 20. Angelus faciei Domini Esa. 63. v. 9. & populum eduxit ex Ægypto Exod. 23. versu 20. 1. Cor. 10. v. 9. Jud. vers. 4. atque Angelus dicitur Domini, quod à DEO Patre missus sit, ac imprimis in plenitudine temporis mittendus fuerit, redem- tionis nostræ gratia, quod æternum DEI consi- lium, insinuandi ergo Angeli nomen libenter usurpavit in Veteri Testamento, ut scilicet fides Patrum de eodem confirmaretur: qui cognove- re etiam eundem angelum redemtorem, redem- tionis causa mittendum, eamque fidem suam pro- fessi sunt Gen. 48. versu 16. Job. 33. versu 23. seqq. Esa. 63. vers. 9. Hanc sententiam uberius explicat Ludov. de Dieu ad Actor. 6. v. 30. id peculiariter observans, quod ἐν χειρὶ ἀγγέλε per manum An- geli, in rubo visi, DEUS Mosen principem, & Re- demtorem miscrit: habet, inquit, hic nescio quam Emphasin vox MANUS, ut omittenda non videa- tur, sensus enim est, DEUM, cum Mosen mitte- ret Principem & Redemtorem, & Mosis & re- demtionis, per eum præstandæ, regimen universum commisisse manibus hujus Angeli: unde liquido con- stat, Angelum istum, qui Exod. 3. apparuit, quiq; ibi aliquoties Jehova ac DEUS patrum nuncupatur, ac Mosen mittit & instruit, non fuisse Angelum creatum, sed ipsum Filium DEI, per cujus manus ait Stephanus DEUM Patrum misisse Mosen. Notat & hoc, quod Exod. 23. v. 20. dicat DEUS: Mittam ante te Angelum, id idem esse cum vers. 14. facies mea ibit, & ducet vos, quia angelus ille est angelus faciei Domini, ipsa facies DEI, quam qui videt, Patrem videt, Johan. 14. versu 9. quique est ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης ὴ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτᾶ, Ebr, 1, 3. Ita ergo constat, quomodo Filius DEI vocetur Angelus, etsi vere sit Jehovah ipse. Altera Riveti expositio est è Philone petita; DE- UM fuisse, qui apparuit, sed angelum vocatum, quia futura prænunciavit, quam ita explicat Rive- tus, quia DEUS sese signo visibili manifestavit, quomodo solebant angeli hominibus apparere, idcir- co propter signum illud externum, quo DEUS ad tempus utebatur, ut se hominibus patefaceret, ap- pellatum fuisse Angelum. Sed si ob solam futuro- rum prænunciationem DEUS angelus vocatur, DEUM patrem, ut & Spiritum Sanctum ange- lum dici oportet, imo S. S. Trinitas Angelus dici- tur, quia totius Sacro-Sanctæ Trinitatis est, futu- ra prænunciare. Fallitur ergo Rivetus, dum plerosque veterum ita statuere putat. Nequicquam vero explicare id ita conatur, quasi non propter prophetiam simpliciter, sed quia DEUS se in signo visibili manifestavit, ut solent Angeli apparere. An- gelus dicatur, nam & DEUS Pater & Spiritus Sanctus signo visibili manifestarunt se quando- que: nisi forte id ita intelligat Rivetus (quod ta- men non apparet) quod Schema quoddam habitus, vel signum quodcunque peculiare fuerit, quo Angeli creati apparere consueverunt, illumque habitum ac schema & signum istud assumsisse Filium DEI, atque eo nomine angelum dici, quod schemate an- gelico, hoc est, tali, quo solebant Angeli, appa- ruerit. Quam sententiam veterum quorundam non inconcinnain esse, largimur, neque tamen necessum est, ut idem prorsus schema statuatur, dummodo simile fuerit vel ἀνάλογον. Interim hu- mana specie apparuisse Angelos quandoque, & eadem cum angelis stipatoribus etsi augustiori vi- sum fuisse Filium DEI, ex apparitione Abrahæ fa- cta Genes. 18. constat; quam in præludium futuræ incarnationis assumtam cum Concilii Antiocheni Patribus & aliis veteribus credendum est.

tiam explicationem Riv. ex Athan. Orat. 4. con- tra Arrian. hanc adfert, DEUM in angelo locu- tum esse, quemadmodum etiam è columna nubis verba ad Mosen in tabernaculo faciebat, adeoque DEUM præsentem fuisse, & locutionem illam immedia- te operatum esse, etsi angeli opera usus, & in an- gelo visus fuerit. Non abnuit B. Dorsch. huic sententiæ in collatione ad Concil. Sirm. & Apol. judic. Argentorat. contra Latermann. ita eam explicans, quod ὄραμα sive visum illud, quod Mo- si exhibuit DEUS, angelus appelletur. Sed si Athan. angelum, hoc est, Spiritum finitum com- pletum intellexit, qui visus est, & per quem locu- tus est DEUS, quod Rivetus vult, cum natura angelus ἀόρατος sit, angelum formam visibilem induisse oportet, quo pacto DEUM angelo, & angelum vicissim formæ visibili unitum fuisse pecu- liari unione, dicendum erit; itaque vero magis affine est, Athanasium cum cæteris patribus ange- lum visum de angelico schemate, quo DEUS quasi amictus fuit, quemadmodum & columna nubis operiri voluit, intellexisse. Quod si non qui- dem ὄραμα rubi ardentis, sed habitum, in quo ap- paruit, dicas angelum vocatum, angeli nomen quod personæ est, minus convenienter tribue- tur externæ formæ. Quapropter sine dubio præ- stat cum Scriptura angelum intelligere, in quo no- men DEI est, hoc est, angelum increatum, quod postea plenius expedietur: qui etsi ob habitum, angelis familiarem, ita nuncupatus fuerit, non ta- men cum habitu illo externo visibili confundenda est persona in eodem apparens, quia Angelus no- men personæ est. Et probavit B. Dorscheus ipse in vindic. cap. 4. Exod. p. 45. Angelum hunc voca- ri Jehovam & esse illum ipsum, per quem Moses Deut. 33. verf. 16. populo Israëlitico benedixit, Chri- stum ipsum ab Israëlitis tentatum Esa. 63. 1. Cor. 10. extra ordinem & hierarchiam finitorum angelorum positum; denique angelum infinitum esse, Ange- lum item apparentem & Jehovam loquentem, unam eandemq; esse personam. Laudavit Clem. Alexandrin. sententiam de luce formata in rubo ar- dente, ut interpres eam exposuit, quod nempe ap- paruerit formata lux, id est, in formam hominis redacta, quæ Verbum divinum incarnatum repræ- sentavit.

Vers. eod.

QUOD RUBUS ARDERET ET NON COMBURERE- TUR] Imago populi Israëlitici. Mirabilis verborum istorum distractio Abar- banelis & Rabbi Hiskuni, vid. in Conciliat. Me- nassis pag. 96. Significatio hujus Symboli è Philone hæc traditur, ignem nempe notasse DEUM per Ægyptios, id est, rubum Judæos incendentem seu affli- gentem, sed non consumentem, imo splendidiores & fortiores eos reddentem. Quam visionis explica- tionem assumsit Grotius. Typum etiam veteres constituunt hîc cum incarnationis, tum conceptio- nis Christi. Quoad illam notatam ajunt unio- nem & communicationem ac περιχώρησιν divinæ naturæ, quæ igne & naturæ humanæ, quæ rubo adumbratur, hac illæsa manente: quia inconsum- tam humanitatis nostræ substantiam etiam in ipsa di- vinitatis flamma servat, dicente Gregor. M. Quod ad hanc attinet, Gregor. Nyssenus Orat. de Christi nativit, ejusmodi applicationem facit: ut frutex incendit ignem, & non crematur, sic virgo & lumen parit, & non corrumpitur. Non placent hæc Rive- to, sine dubio, quod illustretur Orthodoxia no- stra hac figura de περιχωρήσει & communicatione Deitatis in humana Christi natura; Ideo subtili- ter hæc excogitata scopum non attingere ait. Sed quanquam posterior figura paulo alienior sit, prior tamen de mysterio incarnationis, quæ magis in Eccle- sia recepta est, non videri debet ἀλλότριον: quia ut totum eductionis negotium typus erat spiritualis eductionis è potestate infernalis Pharaonis, ita ap- paritio personæ, quæ opus illud peragere debebat, non aliena certe ratione hîc talis exhibetur, quæ in- carnationis mysterium adumbret. Descendi, inquit Filius DEI, qui in rubum se dimiserat, ut liberem eos: quia descensurus erat ipse lux incorporea, & lumen verum, Joh. 1, 9. Ebr. 1, 3. Ezech. 1, 4. in Surculum è radice Jessea, Esa. XI, 1. humanam assumturus natu- ram; quæ ligno viridi confertur Luc. XXIII, 21. ut nos è spirituali captivitate liberaret, Ebr. II, 14.

## 3:4
Verse 4. HE CALLED HIM FROM THE MIDST OF THE BUSH] Verses are cited from a Greek tragedy about God: 'Do you not see him sometimes appearing as fire, unapproachable in its rush.' It was a persuasion of the Gentiles at that time that such a sight portended great glory to the one seeing it, as Josephus notes here.

Divine appearances proposed in the Holy Scriptures are not to be judged from comedies or fables: nor is it right to judge the meanings of divine visions from the persuasion of the Gentiles. It is established from the Holy Scriptures that GOD, for the sake of showing his majesty and severity, was accustomed to manifest himself in fire: which also happened, when no singular glory was signified to him to whom the vision occurred. For GOD is described as dwelling in unapproachable light, 1 Tim. 6:16, and as an inextinguishable fire, Deut. 4:24, Heb. 12:29.

Grotius, along with the Jews, Photinians, and Papists, believes that it was an uncreated Angel. Therefore, on chapter 4:27, TO THE MOUNTAIN OF GOD: Where God had appeared to Moses through an Angel. But the circumstances of the history demonstrate most clearly that the uncreated Angel was the Son of GOD. Moses, who described it, testifies that it was JEHOVAH who was seen here in the midst of the bush, v. 4. And the LORD seeing that he was going to look, called him from the midst of the bush. In the Hebrew it is, AND THE LORD SAW, and Elohim God called him from the midst of the bush. Therefore it was JEHOVAH Elohim who was seen and spoke in the midst of the bush. The same openly testifies that he is GOD, and not a minister of GOD. I am, he says v. 6, the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. Nor does Moses name him otherwise throughout the whole history than God: verse 6. Moses hid his face, for he did not dare to look upon God. And v. 13. Moses said to God. But lest Grotius interpret the name Elohim in these passages as an angel (although that plural word never denotes one angel), it is explained immediately that it was Jehovah the Lord, v. 7. To whom the LORD said. And v. 14. God said to Moses, I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, has sent me to you. And v. 16. and God said again to Moses: these things you shall say to the children of Israel, the Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you: this is my name forever, and this is my memorial unto generation and generation. And lest you doubt whether this is the very name of him who appeared, or rather of him in whose name he appeared, it is said again v. 16 explicitly, The Lord God of your fathers appeared to me, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, saying, visiting I have visited, etc. And so Moses himself testifies that in this whole conversation with Moses, the LORD himself always spoke: The Lord said to him: which is repeated quite often. It is never hinted that any angel minister was either seen here or spoke with Moses. The same inhabitant of the bush does not speak as a ministering person or a legate of GOD, but demonstrates that he is GOD himself, as much by the names as by the divine works and attributes claimed for himself: I have seen the affliction of the people of God, I have heard their cry, and knowing their pain I HAVE DESCENDED, that I may deliver them. The cry of the children of Israel has come TO ME: and I have seen their affliction, but I HAVE COME and I will send you to Pharaoh. Therefore that omniscient and most gracious God, who saw the affliction of his people, who heard their cry, who intimately knew their pain, as the only knower of hearts, to whom their cry reached, the same descended here, the same came here, the same appeared here, that he might send Moses, and that he might deliver his people, the same promises here to Moses: I WILL BE WITH THEE, and this you shall have as a sign that I have sent you: when you have led out my people, etc. Everyone sees that these are not the words of a ministering Angel, but of GOD himself. If this interlocutor of Moses is still called a ministering angel using the name of GOD, I will say with equal right that Moses himself did not see and converse with him, but someone in the name of Moses, sustaining the person of Moses, or some servant of Moses. Because it is as clear that the Lord was the other interlocutor as it is that Moses himself was the interlocutor here. Therefore Moses prayed for a blessing from this inhabitant of the bush, Deut. 33:16. Let the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the head of the Nazarite among his brothers. He recognized therefore the same God himself. For he prayed for a blessing from no one else but GOD. The Israelite Church recognized this, which celebrates in Isa. 63:11 this angel the redeemer as the Author of the leading out from Egypt: Whom Paul also hints was Christ the Son of GOD, 1 Cor. 10:4, 9.

And hence, because the matter is too manifest, the Fathers with great consensus hand down that the uncreated angel who appeared was the Son of GOD. In the first century, Clement of Rome, Pope, l. 5. Constit. Apost. c. 21. (whom, however, we bring forward only κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον against the Papists). In the second, Justin Martyr, Apol. 2 for the Christians and Dialogue with Trypho. Irenaeus, l. 4. cap. 17, 23, 37, 48. In the third, Tertullian, l. 3. against Marcion and against Praxeas, and the chorus of Antiochene Fathers in the Synod instituted against Samosatenus. In the fourth, Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. illumin. 10. Ambrose, book on the faith against the Arians, c. 8, and on Psalm 43. Hilary, books 4 and 12 on the Trinity. Eusebius, Demonstratio Evangelica, l. 5. c. 9, 10, 11. Chrysostom on Acts 7. Augustine, l. 2. on the Trinity, c. 18, and most others. So also from the Papists, Isidorus Clarius, Bishop of Fulgos, in the Scholia to this place, Alphonsus Salmero, Commentary on 1 Cor. 10, Disp. 17. Antonius Fernandius the Jesuit on the visions of the O.T. 17. p. 179. Johan. Nodinus Commentary on Exodus at this place. Andr. Masius Commentary on Joshua c. 5. p. 95. Emanuel Saa in notes at this place. Either the Lord in an Angel or Christ himself, who is the angel of the great counsel. Mariana in Schol. at this place. It was the Son of GOD, who spoke with Moses in human form, and was preparing himself by playful acts for true struggles: Thus Philo from the Jews. Moses sees a prodigious spectacle and as much as one might suspect, it was that vision, and the presence of him who is; he is truly called an Angel, for the reason that he was announcing certain things to come. And to this point tends what is held in the Targum, Ex. 2, 25. The subjection of the sons of Israel was known before the Lord, and he said to his WORD, that he might liberate them. For this hypostatic word is the Redeemer of the Israelites, who therefore appeared here to Moses, so that he might inaugurate the work of liberation. But especially clear in this matter is R. Moses Gerundensis, son of Nahman, who as a Jew is much more sharp-sighted here than Grotius as a Christian, praised by Masius, he wrote thus concerning the Angel seen here by Moses: That Angel, if we speak of the thing itself, is the redeemer Angel, of whom it is written: For my name is in him (Ex. 23, 20.) That, I say, angel, who was saying to Jacob, I am the God of Bethel. He of whom it was said: And God called to Moses from the bush. He is called an Angel, however, because he governs the world. For it is written: Jehovah (that is, the Lord GOD) brought us out of Egypt: and elsewhere: He sent his Angel, and brought us out of Egypt. Furthermore, it is written: And the Angel of his face saved them. Namely, that Angel who is the face of GOD; of whom it was said: My face shall go before and I will cause you to rest. Finally, that Angel is the one of whom the Prophet says: And suddenly the Lord, whom you seek, shall come to his temple; and the angel of the covenant, whom you desire. We have said more on this sentiment against the Socinians, Theol. natural. & revelat. c. 11. p. 360, against Calixtus, who even offers the herb to them, and D. Christian Drejer, a follower of the same, in Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica Sect. II. c. V. p. 977, and in our public lectures on θεοφανεία, or the appearances of the Son of GOD in the Old Testament.

Latin:

Verf. 4. VOCAVIT EUM DE MEDIO RUBI] Citan- tur versus ex Tragœdia Græca de Deo: Ὄυκ ὄιστα δ’ αὐτὸν ποτὲ μὲν ὡς πῦρ Φαίνεται Ἄπλατον ὁρμῇ. Tale visum videnti magnam gloriam portendere persuasio erat gentium eo tempore, ut hîc notat Josephus.

Non æstimandæ divinæ apparitiones in Scriptu- ris S. propositæ ex Comœdiis vel fabulis: nec signi- ficata visionum divinarum judicare fas est è persua- sione gentium. E S. Literis id constat, quod DEUS ostendendæ majestatis, & severitatis suæ causa, in igne sese manifestare consueverit: quod etiam fa- ctum, cum non significata illi, cui obtigit visio, glo- ria singularis. Describitur enim DEUS, ut habitans lucem inaccessam, 1. Tim. 6, 16. & ut ignis inextinguibi- lis, Deut. 4, 24. Ebr. 12, 29.

Angelum increatum fuisse, cum Judæis, Photi- nianis & Papistis credit Grotius. Ideo ad cap. 4, 27. IN MONTEM DEI: Ubi Deus per Angelum Mosi apparuerat. At Angelum increatum Filium DEI de- monstrant περιστάσεις Historiæ luculentissime. Mo- ses, qui eam descripsit, JEHOVAM fuisse, qui hîc in medio rubi visus est, testatur v. 4. Cernens autem DOMINUS, quod pergeret ad videndum, vocavit eum de medio rubi. In Ebræo est, ET VIDIT DO- MINUS, & vocavit eum Elohim Deus de medio ru- bi. JEHOVAH ergo Elohim fuit, qui in rubi me- dio visus est, & loquutus. Idem aperte se testatur esse DEUM, non vero DEI ministrum. Ego, inquit v. 6. sum Deus Patris tui, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Jacob. Nec aliter nominat ipsum Moses per universam historiam, quam Deum: verf. 6. Abscon- dit Moses faciem suam, non enim audebat aspicere con- tra Deum. Et v. 13. Ait Moses ad Deum. Ne vero in his nomen Elohim per angelum interpretetur Grotius, (quamvis nunquam vox illa pluralis unum angelum notet) explicatur id statim, quod fuerit Jehovah Dominus v. 7. Cui ait DOMINUS. Et v. 14. Dixit Deus ad Mosen, Ego sum, qui sum. Sic dices fi- liis Israël: QUI EST, misit me ad vos. Et v. 16. dixit- que iterum Deus ad Mosen: hæc dices filiis Israël, Domi- nus Deus Patrum vestrorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, & Deus Jacob misit me ad vos: hoc nomen mihi est in æternum, & hoc memoriale meum in generatio- nem & generationem. Ac ne dubites, sitne hoc ipsum ejus nomen, qui apparuit, an vero, cujus nomine apparuit, dicitur iterum v. 16. diferte, Dominus Deus Patrum vestrorum apparuit mihi, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Jacob, dicens, visitans visitavi, &c. Atq; ita in toto hoc colloquio cum Mose semper DOMINUM ipsum loquutum esse, perhibet ipse Moses: Dixit Dominus ad eum: quod sæpius repe- titur. Nunquam Angelus aliquis minister aut vi sus hic, aut loquutus cum Mose innuitur. Idem habitator rubi non loquitur ceu persona mini strans, vel legatus DEI, sed se DEUM esse ipsum met, uti nominibus, ita etiam operibus & attributis divinis sibi vindicatis demonstrat: Vidi afflictionem populi Dei, audivi clamorem ejus, & sciens dolorem ejus DESCENDI, ut liberem eum. Clamor filiorum Israël venit AD ME: vidique afflictionem eorum, sed VENI & mittam te ad Pharaonem. Deus ergo ille omniscius & gratiosissimus, qui populi sui affli- ctionem vidit, qui exaudivit clamorem ejus, qui intime dolorem ejus cognovit, ceu καρδιογνώσης unicus, ad quem clamor eorum pervenit, idem hîc descendit, idem hîc venit, idem hîc apparuit, ut mittat Mosen, & ut liberet populum suum, idem hîc pollicetur Mosi: EGO ERO TECUM, & hoc habebis signum, quod miserim te: cum eduxeris populum meum &c. Quæ non Angeli ministri, sed ipsius DEI esse nemo non videt. Si collocutor hic Mosis adhuc dicatur angelus minister nomine DEI usus, parili jure dicam ego, non Mosen ipsum vi- disse, & cum eo colloquutum esse, sed aliquem Mosis nomine, personam Mosis sustinentem, aut servum quendam Mosis. Quia tam clarum est, Dominum fuisse collocutorem alterum, quam quod Moses ipse hic colloquutor fuerit. Ideo Moses ab hoc habitatore rubi benedictionem preca- tus est Deut. 33, 6. Benedictio illius, qui apparuit in rubo, veniat super caput Joseph, & super verticem Nazaræi inter fratres suos. Agnovit ergo eundem ipsummet Deum. Non enim ab alio, quam DEO benedictionem precatus est. Agnovit id Ecclesia Israëlitica, quæ celebrat Esa. 63. v. 11. Angelum hunc redemptorem Autorem eductionis ex Ægypto: Quem etiam Paulus Christum DEI Filium fuisfe 1. Cor. 10, 4. 9. innuit.

Atque hinc, quia res nimis manifesta, magno consensu Patres angelum increatum Filium DEI apparuisfe, tradunt. In primo seculo Clemens Ro- manus Pontifex l. 5. Constit. Apost. c. 21. (quem tamen κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον solum adversus Pontificios adducimus.) In secundo Justinus Martyr Apol. 2. pro Christ. & Dial. cum Tryph. Irenæus l. 4. cap. 17. 23. 37. 48. In tertio Tertullianus l. 3. advers. Marc. & contra Prax. & chorus Patrum Antiochenorum in Synodo contra Samosatenum instituta. In quarto Cyrillus Hierosolymit. Catech. illumin. 10. Ambrosius lib. de fid. contr. Arian. c. 8. & in Psalm. 43. Hilarius lib. 4. & 12. de Trinit. Eusebius de- monstrat. Evang. l. 5. c. 9. 10. 11. Chrysostomus in 7. Actor. Augustin. l. 2. de Trinit. c. 18. & alii pleriq; omnes. Ita etiam è Papistis Isidorus Clarius Fulgos. Episc. in Scholiis ad h. l. Alphonsus Salmero Com- ment. in 1. Cor. 10. Disp. 17. Antonius Fernandius Je- suita de visionibus V. T. 17. p. 179. Johan. Nodinus Comment. in Exod. ad h. l. Andr. Masius Com- ment. in Jos. c. 5. p. 95. Emanuel Saa in notis ad h. l. Vel in Angelo Dominus vel Christus ipse, qui est magni consilii angelus. Mariana in Schol. h. l. DEI Filius erat, qui specie humana cum Mose loquebatur, se lu- dicris ad vera certamina comparabat: Ita è Judæis Philo. Videt Moses prodigiosum spectaculum & quan- tum quis suspicari possit, erat ea visio, atque præsentia ejus, qui est; vocatur vero Angelus, eo quod ventura qœdam denunciabat. Atque huc facit,quod in Tar- gum habetur, Ex. 2, 25. Nota fuit coram Domino sub- jectio filiorum Israël, & dixit ad VERBUM suum, ut liberaret eos. Hoc enim verbum hypostaticum est, Redemtor Israëlitarum, qui ideo hîc apparuit Mo- si, ut auspicaretur opus liberationis. Sed imprimis lu- culentus est hac in re R. Moses Gerundensis Nah- manni filius, qui Judæus multo quam Grotius Chri- stianus hic oculatior, laudatus à Masio, ita de An- gelo hîc Mosi viso scripsit: Iste Angelus, si rem ipsam dicamus, est Angelus redemptor, de quo scriptum est: Quoniam nomen meum in ipso est (Ex. 23, 20.) Ille, inquam, angelus, qui ad Jacob dicebat, Ego Deus Be- thel. Ille de quo dictum est: Et vocabat Mosen Deus de ru- bo. Vocatur autem Angelus, quia mundum gubernat. Scriptum enim est: Eduxit nos Jehovah (hoc est, Do- minus DEUS) ex Ægypto: & alibi: Misit Angelum suum, & eduxit nos ex Ægypto. Præterea scriptum est: Et Angelus faciei ejus salvos fecit ipsos. Nimi- rum ille Angelus, qui est DEI facies; de quo dictum est; Facies mea præibit & efficiam, ut quiescas. De- niǵ, ille Angelus est, de quo Vates: Et subito veniet ad templum suum Dominus, quem vos quæritis; & an- gelus fœderis, quem cupitis. Plura in hanc senten- tiam adversus Socinianos, Theol. natural. & revelat. c. 11. p. 360. adversus Calixtum herbam ipsis etiam porrigentem, & D. Christian. Drejer. asseclam ejusdem Harmonia Calixtino - Hæretica Sect. II. c. V. p. 977. & in prælectionibus publicis de θεο- φανείἀ seu apparitionibus Filii DEI in Vet. Test. diximus.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. LOOSE THE SHOE FROM OFF THY FEET] Pythagoras imitates this in Iamblichus, On His Life, Ch. XXIV. 'Sacrifice and worship unshod.' Marinus on Proclus: 'Loosing his shoes there, which he himself had, in the sight of those people, he greeted the God.' No feet pertain to religion. Persius on the Jewish kings: 'Where kings exercise the festive sabbaths with a bare foot.'

That command was partly to enjoin purity, because shoes are sewn from unclean skins, and partly, above all, to excite submission in Moses, who approached too boldly; which reason Eusebius, Hugo Victorinus, Rupertus, and many others observe. Which rite seems to descend from slaves; for these used to walk with bare feet, therefore to bare the feet was a sign of reverence and subjection, whence John 1:27, the forerunner introduces Jesus as Lord, and shod, and himself as a servant and unworthy to loose the latchet of his shoe; and the removal of the shoe was a symbol in the cession of a right, Deut. 25:9, Ruth 4:7. Conversely, the shoe denoted power, Psalm 59:10, cf. Exod. 30:19, Jos. 5:15, Ezech. 16:10, ch. 24:17, Luke 15:22. Pererius brings forward other reasons still, that this was done to show attention in the commissioned task, with all other thoughts and cares cast off, to commend sincerity in contemplating divine mysteries, with the shoes of human weakness or rashness rejected, to propose the holiness of the Church, which is figured by the bush, to be betrothed to Christ alone, etc. But these reasons do not reach the mark.

Nor indeed will the Ethiopians, to whom the power of approaching the temple is not given unless with bare feet, because they believe the temples are twins to this mountain, as Damian à Goës reports, or the discalced Franciscans, be able to prove their rite or order from this, because this was an external rite and a singular one, peculiarly commanded to Moses: and therefore it is mere superstition, and κακοζηλία (bad zeal), when religion is placed in the fact that one walks with bare feet or with windowed shoes. That is nowhere commanded; and since the Franciscans place merit in it besides, they are altogether impious toward Christ; of whom the distich is known: 'A knotted cord, a bare foot, a deceitful cowl, these three lead the barefoot brothers to hell.' More correctly, one might refer it to the barefoot sacred rites of the heathens, who, as Solinus testifies in book 15, entered the temple of Apollo barefoot, and to the institution of the ancient discalced or barefoot heretics in Jerome and Philastrius. or you might refer that ceremony to the superstition of the Turks who visit their sacred places with bare feet.

Vers. eod. THE PLACE WHEREON THOU STANDEST, IS HOLY GROUND. The Papists draw these words first to their superstition concerning the holiness of places. Bellarm. l. 3.

de cultu sanct. c. 5. proves from it that a consecrated temple is deservedly held to be holy and venerable, and endowed with a certain divine power, because the place of holy things is also holy, Exod. 3:5. And it is known what great superstitions are fostered in the Papacy concerning holy places, which have been or are believed to have been illustrated at some time by the presence or a divine miracle; likewise concerning pilgrimage to the holy land, to Mount Sinai, and other places which are held to be sacred by divine manifestation, in which they imagine a certain permanent holiness for themselves, even if they deceive themselves with nothing but fables or uncertain legends, as the shrine of Mary of Loreto is a document among countless others. Moreover, as no place is holy by its own nature above another, since the whole earth is the Lord's, but by divine election, which is a relative holiness, so GOD chooses certain places for himself in which he wills to be worshipped ordinarily, as was done in the O.T. when he had chosen Mount Sion, or extraordinarily by manifesting himself somewhere with an external sign of presence, which place is then sacred to men as long as the divine manifestation lasts, such as it was here on Mount Horeb; whence Moses was commanded to loose his shoes, that is, to approach reverently, because it was a holy place, in which, namely, the most holy GOD was manifesting his presence. Therefore these things do not help the Pontificians, who attribute a certain perennial or permanent holiness to places in which GOD manifested himself extraordinarily and only for a time, because with the sign of the divine presence ceasing, the relation also ceases, and the holiness of the place, which is only relative. Whence we read that places which were once sacred on account of a manifested presence became not only common thereafter, but also abominable, with Bethel turned into Beth-Aven, and the holy land of Palestine subjected to a curse, so that they oppose themselves to divine judgment who make a land so cursed sacred again by their superstition, by undertaking religious pilgrimages to it in the opinion of worship and merit. As for places which are consecrated to God for ordinary worship, they are indeed deservedly held sacred, lest they be polluted by profane actions, yet they do not attain true internal or inherent holiness, nor do they have holiness by ceremonial consecration, as is believed in the Papacy, since there exists no command or promise for it; and therefore they are only relatively sacred by reason of the actions which are celebrated in them, and consequently actions are not sanctified by the place, as Papists pretend, but the place is sanctified by the sacred actions and the worship which is performed in it.

Furthermore, the Papists snatch away the words of our text so that they may prove the worship of images, inasmuch as holy creatures are said to be holy on account of their relation to holy things, as in Exodus 3 a place is called holy on account of the presence of an angel. Thus Bellarmine, book II on images, chapter 12; Sanders, book I on images, chapter 1. But the argument is worthless: Whatever is sacred on account of a relation to holy things, that is also honorable and adorable on account of honorable things. Images of holy things are sacred, on account of their relation to the archetype. And therefore. Response. (1.) It is still a matter of controversy among the Papists themselves whether images are in any way to be worshipped properly, or rather only improperly and abusively; whether the act of adoration is terminated at the images, not only by reason of an external sign, but also by reason of internal submission and affection; likewise, whether images ought to be worshipped with the same worship as the exemplar, which and other things are highly doubtful among the iconolaters, concerning which see Tanner, Vol. 3 of Scholastic Theology, question 2, page 1365. (2.) It is a very different thing to be adorable and to be holy; for that is adorable, not which is endowed with any holiness, but which is holy with an uncreated and infinite holiness: although therefore holy images may in some way exist, or be able to be called so on account of a relation to an archetype, namely in such a way that they ought not to be profaned, and that they can produce or foster holy thoughts from the recollection of the word heard, they are nevertheless in no way an object of adoration directed, either directly or indirectly. (3.) The land is called holy on account of the presence of the Angel, but not because it contracted from that any quality or dignity of adorability: that sanctification of the place was temporary and transitory, and in no way directed toward exciting an affect of religion or devotion toward this place, and therefore Cajetan explains these things thus: That place is called holy in that it was dedicated by divine election to divine apparitions. (4.) Therefore the land is called holy, not on account of the mere presence of an angel, because since this angel is uncreated, he is nowhere not present, but as he himself indicates, on account of a singular revelation, because he consecrated this place for a divine manifestation. Therefore, the mere presence of even GOD, let alone a created angel, does not procure holiness for a place. (5.) Now if the land of the bush, however holy on account of the divine revelation made there, was not adorable, which Moses certainly did not adore, much less is the image of any saint adorable; because there the presence and manifestation of GOD, who is to be adored, was certain, but here, however, Papists are not certain about the presence of the person represented by the image in a singular way, and that those holy persons are adorable is repugnant to Scripture, Isa. 42, 8. Since therefore that station of the angel on Mount Horeb, even if we acknowledge him to have been GOD himself, did not cause it to be held as holy in that way, as Bellarmine wishes, i.e. adorable, it certainly cannot be inferred that there is a cult of images on account of a mere relation to saints, to whom adoration is not owed in themselves, since the archetype is not adorable, much less will his images be adorable.

Finally, Bellarmine also abuses this passage, Book II, on the images of the saints, ch. 27, for the adoration of the Lord's cross: if the place in which the angel stood, Exod. 3, is holy ground, why not more so the cross, where Christ stood, sprinkled with his blood? But Bellarmine is mistaken when he again confuses here what is holy and what is adorable, which two things are most distinct, and we rightly invert the argument, since the station of the uncreated Angel on the mountain did not make it adorable, the adhesion of Christ to the wood of the cross much less procured for this wood that holiness on account of which it might be adorable, since that station was made immediately from the will of GOD, but this affixing of Christ on the cross was done by the hands of the unjust, Acts 2, 23. That land was holy on account of the revelation made there, and it ought not to have been held as holy perpetually afterward, with the revelation ceasing: but concerning the wood of the holy cross, the Papists say that it is perpetually holy, even if Christ does not hang on it, nor is GOD peculiarly present at it. Finally, if mere presence infers adorability, what remains but that we say that all things (for GOD is present to all things) are adorable, which indeed does not seem absurd to Vasquez in 3rd part of Thomas, qu. 25, art. 6, p. 1077, that all things, even inanimate and irrational, can be rightly adored, but it is by far most absurd, and in the same society it is refuted by Tanner, Tom. 4, Disp. 5, p. 1414, namely, the Jesuitical abominations finally end up in this, that all things are defined as adorable, which perhaps ought not to seem strange concerning Vasquez, since the same Jesuit argues on p. 1077 that it is not a sin to adore a ray of light or an image of the crucifix, under which a demon lurks; which we have chastised elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SOLVE CALCEAMENTUM DE PEDIBUS TUIS] Pythagoras imitatur apud Jamblichum de vita ejus C. XXIV. Ἀνυπόδητⓔ θύε κὰι προσκύνει. Marinus de Proclo: ὑπο- λυσάμενⓔ αὐτόθι ἃ ἡ᾿ αὐτῷ ὑποδίματα ὁρώντων ἐκείνων, τὸν Θεὸν ἠσπάζετο. Nulli pedes ad religionem pertinent. Persius de regibus Judæis: Exercant ubi festa mero pede sabbata reges.

Mandatum illud fuit tum ad imperandam pu- ritatem, quia calcei ex pellibus immundis consu- untur, tum imprimis ad excitandam in Mose sub- missionem, qui audacius appropinquavit; quam rationem observant Euseb. Hugo Victorinus, Ru- pertus & plerique alii. Qui ritus à mancipiis descen- dere videtur; hæc enim nudis pedibus incedebant, ideo pedes nudare, signum erat reverentiæ & sub- jectionis, unde Joh. I, 27. πρωτοβαπτισὴς Jesum tanquam Dominum, & calceatum, se, tanquam servum & indignum, qui solvat corrigiam cal- ceamenti ejus introducit; & calcei detractio Sym- bolum fuit in cessione juris, Deut. 25, 9. Ruth. 4, 7. Ex adverso calceus potestatem notabat, Psalm. 59, 10. conf. Exod. 30, 19. Jos. 5, 15. Ezech. 16, 10. cap. 24, 17. Luc. 15, 22. Pererius alias adhuc adducit rationes, quod factum id sit ad ostendendam in commissio mu- nere, exutis omnibus aliis cogitationibus, curisœ́, at- tentionem, ad commendendam in mysteriis divinis con- templandis sinceritatem, rejectis calceamentis hu- manæ imbecillitatis aut temeritatis, ad proponen- dam Ecclesiæ, quæ rubo figurata, soli Christo despon- dendæ sanctitatem &c. Sed hæ rationes scopum non attingunt.

Neq; vero Æthiopes, quibus non datur pote- stas templum adeundi, nisi nudis pedibus, quod templa gemina credant huic monti, referente Da- miano à Goës, aut Franciscani discalceati suum ritum aut ordinem hinc probare poterunt, quia fuit hic ritus externus isque singularis, Mosi peculiariter mandatus: ideoq; mera est superstitio, & κακοζη- λία, cum religio in eo collocatur, ut nudatis pedi- bus aut fenestratis calceis incedatur. Nuspiam id præceptum; & cum Franciscani in eo præterea me- ritum collocant, impii omnino sunt in Christum; de quibus notum est distichon: Cordula nodosa, pes nudus, Cappa dolosa, Hæc tria nudipedes ducunt ad tartara fratres. Rectius ad nudipedalia sacra Ethnicorum, qui Apol- linis templum, Solino teste libr. 15. nudipedes in- gressi sunt, & ad veterum hæreticorum discalceato- rum vel nudipedum institutum apud Hieronym. & Philastr. aut ad Turcarum superstitionem nudis pe- dibus sacra sua visitantium, ceremoniam istam re- duces.

Vers. eod. LOCUS IN QUO STAS, TERRA SANCTA EST. Trahunt hæc verba Papistæ primo ad super- stitionem suam de locorum sanctitate. Bellarm. l. 3.

de cultu sanct. c. 5. probat inde, templum consecra- tum merito sanctum & venerabile haberi, ac divina quadam virtute præditum esse, quia locus rerum san- ctarum quoq́; sanctus est, Exod. 3, 5. Et notum est, quantæ superstitiones in Papatu foveantur de lo- cis sanctis, quæ præsentia vel miraculo divino ali- quando illustrata sunt, aut creduntur; de peregri- natione item ad terram sanctam, ad montem Sinai & alia loca, quæ manifestatione divina sacra haben- tur, in quibus permanentem quandam sanctitatem sibi imaginantur, etsi non nisi fabulis aut incertis legendis semetipsos decipiant, ut inter innumera alia documento est fanum Mariæ Lauretanæ. Cæterum ut locus nullus natura sua præ alio san- ctus est, cum terra universa Domini sit, sed electio- ne divina, quæ relativa sanctitas est, ita eligit DEUS loca sibi quædam, in quibus ordinarie coli vult, ut in V. T. factum, cum montem Sion elegerat, aut extraordinarie alicubi se manifestans externo præ sentiæ signo, qui locus tum hominibus sacer est, quamdiu durat manifestatio divina, qualis hîc erat in monte Horeb; unde jubebatur Moses calceamen- ta solvere, hoc est, reverenter accedere, quia locus sanctus erat, in quo sc. DEUS sanctissimus præsen- tiam suam manifestabat. Nihil ergo hæc juvant Pontificios, qui sanctitatem quandam perennem, aut permanentem affingunt locis, in quibus extra- ordinarie & ad tempus solum DEUS se manifestavit, quia cessante signo præsentiæ divinæ cessat etiam relatio, & sanctitas loci, quæ tantum relativa est. Unde loca, quæ ob præsentiam manifestatam sacra quondam fuerunt, non modo communia deinde, sed & abominabilia facta esse legimus, Bethele in Beth-Aven converso, terra sancta Palæstina male- dictioni subjecta, ut adeo judicio divino se oppo- nant, qui terram adeo maledictam sacram iterum superstitione sua faciunt, peregrinationibus reli- giosis ad eandem opinione cultus & meriti susce- ptis. Quod ad loca, quæ ad ordinarium cultum Deo consecrantur, ea sacra quidem habentur meri- to, ne actionibus profanis polluantur, non tamen sanctitatem veram consequuntur internam aut in- hærentem, nec consecratione ceremoniali, quod in Papatu creditur, sanctitatem habent, utpote cujus nullum extat vel mandatum vel promissum; ideo- que relative tantum sacra sunt ratione actionum, quæ in illis celebrantur, ac proinde non sanctifi- cantur actiones à loco, ut Papistæ fingunt, sed locus sanctificatur per actiones sacras & cultum, qui in eo peragitur.

Abripiunt præterea Papistæ verba textus no- stri eo, ut probent cultum imaginum, siquidem creaturæ sanctæ dicantur propter relationem ad res sanctas, uti Exod. 3. locus sanctus propter angeli præ- sentiam dicitur. Ita Bellarm. l. II. de imag. cap. 12. Sanderus l. I. de imag. c. 1. sed argumentum ficul- neum est: Quicquid sacrum est ob relationem ad res sanctas, illud etiam honorabile & adorabile est propter res honorabiles. Imagines rerum sancta- rum sacræ sunt, ob relationem ad archetypum. Ideoque. Resp. (1.) controversum adhuc es- se inter ipsos Pontificios, an imagines ullo modo proprie adorandæ sint, an vero tantum impro- prie & abusive; an actus adorationis terminetur ad imagines, non tantum ratione signi exterioris, sed etiam ratione internæ submissionis & affectus; item, an imagines simul cum exemplari eodem cultu debeant adorari, quæ & alia inter εἰκονολάτρας valde dubia sunt, de quibus Tannerus vid. Tom. 3. Theol. Schol. qv. 2. p. 1365. (2.) Maxime diversa sunt, adora- bile esse & sanctum esse; nam adorabile est, non quod quacunque sanctitate præditum, sed quod sanctum est sanctitate increata & infinita: etsi ergo sanctæ imagines aliquo modo sint, aut dici possint ob relationem ad archetypum, ita sc. quod profanari non debeant, quodq; sanctas cogitationes parere, vel fovere ex recordatione verbi auditi possint, non tamen ullo modo objectum adorationis sunt, in quod ea sive directè, sive indirectè feratur. (3.) Terra sancta dicitur ob præsentiam Angeli, non autem quod qualitatem aliquam aut ἀξίωμα adorabilitatis inde contraxerit: sanctificatio illa loci temporaria & transitoria fuit, & nullo modo directa ad affectum religionis aut devotionis erga h. l. excitandum, ideoque ita explicat hæc Cajetanus: Sanctus dicitur locus ille eo, quod divina electione dicatus est mons ille ad apparitiones divinas. (4.) Sancta ergo dicitur terra, non ob præsentiam nudam angeli, quia cum angelus hic increatus sit, nusquam non præsens est, sed uti ipse indicat, ob singularem revelationem, quod hunc locum consecrarit divinæ manifestationi. Nuda itaque præsentia ne quidem DEI, nedum angeli creati sanctitatem loco conciliat. (5.) Jam si terra rubi, utut sancta ob revelationem divinam illic factam, adorabilis non fuit, quam utiq; Moses non adoravit, multo minus imago sancti alicujus adorabilis est; quia ibi certa erat DEI præsentia & manifestatio, qui adorandus est, hîc vero de præsentia personæ per imaginem repræsentatæ singulari, certi non sunt Papistæ, illasq; personas sanctas adorabiles esse, Scripturæ repugnat Esa. 42, 8. Quum ergo statio illa angeli in monte Horeb, etsi eum DEUM ipsum fuisse agnoscamus, non fecerit, ut sanctus ea ratione haberetur, ut vult Bellarm. h.e. adorabilis, inferri utiq; non potest cultus imaginum ob nudam relationem ad sanctos, quibus ipsis non debetur adoratio, cum archetypus adorabilis non sit, multo minus imagines ejus erunt adorabiles.

Denique abutitur etiam hoc loco Bellarm. l. II. de sanctorum imag. c. 27. pro adoratione crucis dominicæ: si locus, in quo stetit angelus Exod. 3. terra sancta est, cur non magis crux, ubi stetit Christus, ejus sanguine respersa? Sed fallitur Bell. cum iterum hic sanctum & adorabile esse permutat, quæ duo distinctissima sunt, & invertimus argumentum merito, quum statio Angeli increati in monte eum non fecerit adorabilem, adhæsionem Christi ad lignum crucis multo minus huic ligno eam sanctitatem conciliasse, ob quam adorabile sit, siquidem illa statio facta sit immediate ex DEI voluntate, hæc vero affixio Christi in cruce per manus injustorum facta est Act. 2, 23. illa terra sancta erat ob revelationem ibi factam, neque postmodum perpetuo sancta haberi debuit, cessante revelatione: at de sanctæ crucis ligno Pap. ajunt, perpetuo illud sanctum esse, etiamsi Christus in illo non pendeat, nec ad illam DEUS peculiariter præsto sit. Denique si nuda præsentia inferat adorabilitatem, quid restat, quam ut dicamus, res omnes (omnibus enim DEUS præsto est) adorabiles esse, quod Vasquezio quidem absurdum non videtur in 3. part. Thom. qu. 25. art. 6. pag. 1077. res omnes, etiam inanimatas & irrationales rite adorari posse, sed absurdissimum longe est, & in eadem societate à Tannero refellitur Tom. 4. Disp. 5. p. 1414. sc. eo tandem abeunt abominationes Jesuiticæ, ut res omnes adorabiles definiantur, quod de Vasquezio forte mirum videri non debet, siquidem disputet idem Jesuita p. 1077. peccatum non esse, adorare radium luminis vel speciem crucifixi, sub qua dæmon delitescit; quod alias castigavimus.

## 3:6
Verse 6. I AM THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, THE GOD OF ISAAC, THE GOD OF JACOB.

Thus he calls himself both here and elsewhere throughout the Old Testament

GOD, because those Patriarchs were the immediate parents of the Israelite people, whose leader Moses stood forth, and to whom the whole Old Testament refers. To them also the land of Canaan had been solemnly promised; furthermore, GOD had shown himself to them especially familiar and beneficent, and had made the most significant promises to them, and what is chief, he had entered into a covenant of grace with them, that he would be their God, Gen. 17, etc. Whence Christ himself from these words proves, Matt. 22, 32, the resurrection of the dead, against the sect of the Sadducees: which for that reason can also be opposed to the Photinians, who deny that the resurrection was taught in the Old Testament; and also to Cardinal Perron, who denied that anything about the same was contained in the Pentateuch.

The nerve of the inference here is: Of whomsoever God is God, they live, because God is the God of the living, not of the dead, i.e., of whom it is completely finished by death. But God testified that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, after their deaths; therefore, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live even after their deaths. Moreover, the nerve and force of the proof is intended if it is observed that that formula of the covenant: I will be your GOD, promises and pledges the spiritual grace of GOD, not only that which is exhibited in the present life, but also that which is exhibited in the other, not temporary, but eternal. Therefore, those of whom GOD is the God, by the power of the covenant of grace, they live eternally. Which reasoning of the inference is especially to be observed here, because it was not about the immortality of the soul, but about the resurrection of the dead that was being discussed here: We do not indeed deny that the Sadducees denied the resurrection of the dead because they did not believe in a life after this life, but maintained that souls perish with the body, nay, that there are no finite spirits at all: and therefore, the life of souls having been proven to survive after this life, their τὸ πρῶτον ψεῦδος, from which the error of the denied resurrection resulted, had been overturned. But the Sadducees are more strongly constrained by the reasoning that not only were souls received into the covenant of grace, but the Patriarchs themselves; because the whole person was brought into the covenant of grace through a solemn sacrament; and therefore it was necessary that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob should live not only in respect of their souls, as if their bodies were to remain in perpetual death, but it is necessary that their bodies also be resurrected to life. Not to mention that souls have a propensity toward the body, and therefore if that propensity remains after this life, it must eventually be fulfilled, so that souls are transferred from the preternatural state of separation into the state to which they were originally ordained in nature, namely, to constitute one person with their own proper and organic bodies. Rivetus is not pleased with such an indirect inference, as he calls it, by which first the immortality of the soul, and consequently the resurrection of the bodies, would have been proven, because there should have been an easier deduction by which the Sadducees felt themselves caught, and which seemed so clear to others: and therefore he makes this the Lord's argumentation: These names, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, are names not of souls, but of the whole composite; since therefore, after those three had departed from life, GOD professed that He was their GOD, which manner of speaking implies special care, it follows that they are not held by GOD as dead, but only as sleeping: Therefore they must be awakened by Him who is their GOD to blessed immortality. But this collection from the name would perhaps have been too subtle and philosophical here: we have already shown another nerve of concluding, so that the argumentation from the divine covenant and the federal promise, to which this name GOD refers, and which is the first The origin of that appellation is, made to Abraham Gen. 17. Since therefore GOD testifies that this promise is still in force even after death, when after the death of that Patriarchal triad He professes Himself to be GOD, it is necessary that those Patriarchs turn out to be heirs of eternal life through the resurrection, and do not remain in eternal corruption. In which sense Chrysostom rightly says in ch. 22 of Matthew: Just as, he says, Adam even if he were still living after the sin, yet by the sentence pronounced by GOD, he was already dead; so on the contrary those Patriarchs even if they were dead, yet they lived by the divine promise of the resurrection. Therefore not undeservedly does R. Menasseh Ben-Israel acknowledge in book 1 of the resurrection of the dead, ch. 10, that the resurrection of the dead is proven from this passage, which he proves by the same reasoning that Christ used: GOD is not the GOD of the dead, but of the living, who exist: For if the dead were not to rise at all, they would truly not exist, and because they survive in respect of the soul, and live, in respect of the body it is necessary that they be about to be raised. Add that the federal promise made in the circumcision of the flesh, not of the soul alone, but of the whole person, is explained in such a way that it includes eternal life. Compare Rev. 22, 6. More fully on these matters see Blessed Gerhard in Common Places on death §. 144. and our Socinianism refuted, Art. on the resurrection of the dead.

Latin:

Vers. 6. EGO SUM DEUS ABRAHAM, DEUS ISAAC, DEUS JACOB.

Ita sese tum hîc, tum alibi passim in Vet. Test.

DEUS appellat, quia Patriarchæ illi parentes pro- ximi populi Israëlitici fuere, cujus Dux Moses ex- titit, & ad quem refertur totum Vet. Test. Illis etiam promissa solemniter fuerat terra Kanaan, ad- hæc exhibuerat iisdem sese imprimis familiarem ac beneficum DEUS, & promissiones maxime insi- gnes iisdem fecerat, & quod præcipuum est, fœdus gratiæ cum illis inierat, sese futurum Deum ipso- rum Gen. 17. &c. Unde Christus ipse ex his ver- bis probat Matth. 22, 32. resurrectionem mortuo- rum, adversus sectam Sadducæorum: quæ eo no- mine etiam Photinianis opponi possunt, infician- tibus resurrectionem in Vet. Test. traditam esse; nec non Perronio Cardinali, qui negabat, in Penta- teucho aliquid de eadem haberi.

Nervus illationis hic est: Quorumcunque Deus est Deus, illi vivunt, quia Deus est Deus viventi- um, non mortuorum, h. e. de quibus plane per mor- tem actum est. At Abrahæ, Isaaci, & Jacobi Deus se Deum esse, post fata ipsorum, testatus est; E. Abraham, Isaac & Jacob vivunt etiam post fata. Intenditur autem nervus & vis probandi, si obser- vetur, quod formula illa fœderis: Ego ero DEUS tuus, gratiam DEI spiritualem promittat & spon- deat, non solum quæ in præsenti vita, sed etiam quæ in altera exhibetur, non temporariam, sed æternam. Quorum ergo DEUS est DEUS, vi fœderis gratiæ, illi æternum vivunt. Quæ illatio- nis ratio imprimis hîc observanda, quia non de im- mortalitate animæ, sed de resurrectione mortuorum hic disquirebatur: Non equidem diffitemur, Sad- ducæos ideo resurrectionem mortuorum negasse, quia non credebant vitam post hanc vitam, sed ani- mas cum corpore interire, imo nullos prorsus esse spiritus finitos, statuebant: ideoque evicta anima- rum vita, superstite post hanc vitam, eversum erat τὸ πρῶτον ψεῦδος ipsorum, ex quo error negatæ re- surrectionis redundabat. Sed fortius constringun- tur Sadducæi, ea ratione, quod non solum animæ receptæ fuerint in fœdus gratiæ, sed ipsimet Patri- archæ; quia totum suppositum per sacramentum so- lemne fœderi gratiæ inferebatur; ideoq; non re- spectu solum animarum vivere oportuit Abra- hamum, Isaacum & Jacobum, ac si in mor- te perenni mansura essent corpora, sed ne- cessum est, ut corpora etiam resuscitentur ad vitam. Ne de eo dicamus, quod animæ propen- sionem ad corpus habeant, ideoque si post hanc vitam superet illa propensio, complenda aliquan- do sit, ita, ut animæ è statu præternaturali separa- tionis in statum, ad quem primo in natura institu- ta ordinatæ fuere, transferantur, ad constituen- dum nempe cum corporibus sibi propriis & orga- nicis unum suppositum. Riveto non placet talis, quam vocat, indirecta illatio, qua primum immor- talitas animæ, consequenter autem resurrectio cor- porum probata fuerit, quod facilior esse debuerit deductio, qua se captos senserunt Sadducæi, & quæ aliis visa fuit tam perspicua: ideoque hanc facit Domini argumentationem: Hæc nomina Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, nomina sunt non animorum, sed totius com- positi; cum ergo postquam tres illi è vita excesserunt, DEUS professus fuerit, se esse eorum DEUM, quæ loquendi ratio curam specialem innuit, consequens est, apud DEUM non haberi tanquam mortuos, sed tan- tum velut dormientes: Proinde excitandos esse ab eo, qui DEUS est illorum ad beatam immortalitatem. Sed hæc collectio à nomine forte nimis hîc arguta fuisset ac philosophica: monstravimus jam ali- um concludendi nervum, ut directa sit argumen- tatio à fœdere divino, & promissione fœderali, ad quam respicit hoc nomine DEUS, & quæ prima istius appellationis origo est, Abrahæ facta Genes. 17. Cum ergo etiam post mortem hanc promissionem adhuc vigere, testetur DEUS, ubi post mortem trigæ istius Patriarchalis se DEUM esse profitetur, necessum est, ut Patriarchæ isti hæredes evadant vitæ æternæ per resurrectionem, non vero in æter- na corruptione maneant. Quo sensu recte Chry- sostomus in c. 22. Matth. Quemadmodum, inquit, Adam etsi adhuc viveret post peccatum, sententia ta- men à DEO prolata, jam mortuus erat; sic contra Patriarchæ illi etsi mortui essent, divina tamen pro- missione resurrectionis vivebant. Ideo non imme- rito agnoscit R. Menasses Ben-Israël lib. 1. de resur- rect. mort. c. 10. resurrectionem mortuorum ex h. l. probari, quam eadem ratione, qua usus est Christus, probat: DEUS non est DEUS mortuorum, sed vi- vorum, qui existunt: Mortui enim si plane non re- surgerent, vere non essent, & quia supersunt animæ ratione, ac vivunt, corporis ratione resuscitatur iri eos oportet.
