Adde, quod promissio fœderalis in cir- cumcisione carnis, non animæ solum, sed toti per- sonæ facta ita explicetur, ut æternam vitam includat. Conf. Apoc. 22, 6. Plenius de his B. Gerhardus in Loc. Com. de morte §. 144. & Socinismus noster pro- fligatus, Art. de resurr. mort.

## 3:8
Verse 8. INTO A GOOD AND SPACIOUS LAND] Hecataeus says of the Jews: They occupy three million arourae of the best and most fertile land.

It is a doubt how it is said to be spacious, for Jerome to Dardanus says that Judea is small, which contained only about 42 miles in length, from Dan to Beersheba, and in width only 12 miles, from Joppa to Bethlehem. But it was spacious both in respect of the land of Goshen, which they had inhabited until then, which was quite narrow for such a multitude; and in respect of the Hebrew nation, because Judea was sufficient for it; and in respect of its capacity for convenience, since because of the fertility of the soil and the frequency of cities, 33 Kings lived in it, and 6 peoples are listed here; to whom elsewhere a seventh, the Girgashites, is added, omitted here, either because they submitted themselves voluntarily to the Hebrews, as the Rabbis wish, or because they are included under one of these: compare Josh. 12. Deut. 8, 7. ch. 11, 20.

Verse same. WHICH FLOWS WITH MILK AND HONEY.

The fertility of the land and the remarkable abundance of all things is noted. Num. 13, 28. ch. 16, 13. Jer. 11, 5. Ezek. 20, 6. under milk are included the necessities, under honey the delights of the region; for honey is accustomed to be used for any sweet and delightful thing, and therefore the abundance of milk and honey designates a region that is well-watered, fertile, and abounding in pastures for milk and flowers, from which, as Virgil speaks, the herds and flocks can distend their udders with milk and the bees their cells with liquid nectar. Milk and honey are the most ready foods, which have no need of preparation: and the most common, which serve not only adults, but those who are not capable of more solid food. The same proverb is used in Joel 3, 18 in a spiritual sense: The mountains shall drip sweetness and the hills shall flow with milk. Although that fertility of the land was indeed natural to that region, as Josephus and Borchard and Moses himself testify in Deut. 8, 7, there is nevertheless no doubt that it was greatly enriched by a divine gift for the sake of the Israelites, Lev. 25, 10. ch. 26, 3. Deut. 11, 13. Therefore, what Strabo in book 15 calls the soil of Jerusalem sterile, rocky, and arid, unless it was ignorance or malevolence, must be understood of the time following the devastation.

Latin:

Vers. 8. IN TERRAM BONAM ET SPATIOSAM] He- cætæus de Judæis ait: Τριακοσίας μυριάδας ἀρουρῶν σχεδὸν τῆς ἀρίστης καὶ παμφορωτάτης χώρας νέμονται.

Dubium est, quomodo spatiosa dicatur, Hie- ron. enim ad Dardanum, Judæam parvam esse di- cit, quæ in longitudine tantum 42. milliaria circiter continebat, à Dan ad Barseba, in latitudine tantum 12. milliaria, à Joppe ad Bethlehem. Sed spatiosa fuit tum respectu terræ Gosen, quam hactenus incolue- rant, quæ satis angusta pro tanta multitudine; tum respectu gentis Ebrææ, quod eidem sufficeret Judæa; tum respectu capacitatis commode, siquidem ob ubertatem soli, & frequentiam civitatum 33. Re- ges in ea vixerint, & 6. populi hic recenseantur; quibus alias septimus Gergeseorum annumeratur, hìc prætermissus, sive quod sponte se submiserint Ebræis, ut Rabbini volunt, seu quod sub uno ex istis comprehendantur: conf. Jos. 12. Deuter. 8, 7. cap. 11, 20.

Vers. eodem. QUÆ FLUIT LACTE ET MELLE.

Notatur terræ fertilitas & omnium rerum ab- undantia insignis. Num. 13, 28. c. 16, 13. Jerem. 11, 5. Ezech. 20, 6. sub lacte necessaria, sub melle deliciæ comprehenduntur regionis; mel enim pro quavis re dulci & delectabili usurpari consuevit, ideoque copia lactis & mellis designat regionem irriguam, fœ- cundam & lactis pascuis floribusque abundantem, ex quibus cum armenta & greges ubera lacte tum apes cellas suas liquido nectare, ut Virg. loquitur, di- stendere possint. Lac & mel cibi sunt paratissimi, qui opus non habent apparatu: & communissimi, qui non adultis tantum serviunt, sed iis, qui soli- dioris cibi capaces non sunt. Idem proverbium Joël 3, 18. sensu spirituali adhibetur: Stillabunt montes dulcedinem & colles fluent lacte. Etsi vero ubertas illa terræ regioni isti naturalis fuerit, teste Josepho & Borchardo ac Mose ipso Deut. 8, 7. non tamen dubium est, eam divino munere valde locu- pletatam fuisse in Israëlitarum gratiam, Levit. 25, 10. c. 26, 3. Deut. 11, 13. Quod ergo Strabo l. 15. sterile, & saxosum, & aridum Hierosolymæ solum nominat, nisi inscitia, aut malevolentia fuerit, de tempore deva- stationem sequuto intelligendum erit.

## 3:11
Verse 11. WHO AM I? Since Moses was not ignorant that he was divinely destined for this great work, these are not the words of one doubting, or refusing, but of one humbly confessing his own ineptitude, when he was comparing himself partly with GOD, whose messenger he was to be, partly with Pharaoh, to whom he is destined, and partly with the Israelite people, when he was being sent to lead out such a great multitude: Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and lead the children of Israel out of Egypt?

Latin:

Vers. 11. QUIS SUM EGO? Cum non ignaret Moses, se divinitus huic tanto operi destinatum, non dubitantis hæc verba funt, aut detrectantis, sed humiliter ineptitudinem suam confitentis, ubi componebat se partim cum DEO, cujus legatus esse debebat, partim cum Pha- raone, ad quem destinatur, partim cum populo Israëlitico, cum tantæ multitudini educendæ mit- tebatur: Quis sum ego, ut vadam ad Pharaonem, & educam filios Israël ex Ægypto?

## 3:12
AND THIS YOU SHALL HAVE AS A SIGN.

But how could the offering on that mountain be a sign to Moses of the exodus of the people, which was finally to take place after the exodus? Hugo Victorinus says the mission of Moses itself is the sign of liberation. Abulensis makes the burning bush the sign of the embassy of Moses. But in the text, the sacrifice is established as a sign of the exodus, because this sign refers not to antecedent things, but to consequent things, and therefore it is to be observed; not every confirmatory sign precedes in time and in completion the execution of the promise which it confirms, just as not every sign of threats precedes the completion of the threat, 1 Sam. 2:34, 1 Kings 22:25, 28, Jerem. 48:29; for we can also give assurance of antecedent things from consequent things, and since it is a matter of impiety and stubbornness not to believe GOD unless signs are seen, Matt. 12:37. GOD sometimes confirms the faith of His own in such a way that He simultaneously exercises it, so that they do not distrust the word, even if it is not confirmed by a present sign. The Scholastics distinguish between prognostic and rememorative signs, the former of which precede events, the latter follow them. It is more appropriate to this passage that others establish three kinds of signs: (1) those which precede the thing itself, such as the sign given to Gideon, Judg. 6; (2) those which accompany it, such as that which was given to the shepherds, Luke 2; (3) those which follow and prove it by the event, such as that which was given to Hezekiah, 2 Kings 19:29. For this sacrifice had to be not only a rememorative sign in the future, but also a βεβαιωτικὸν (confirmatory sign) in the present. Therefore, with respect to faith, which looks upon the promise, this sign must be understood, because Moses could be made more certain of the first promise of the exodus when another was added concerning the sacrifice on that mountain, as if GOD were saying: let this be a sign to you of what I promise, that you will sacrifice on this mountain with the Israelite people, that I will certainly lead you out with the people from Egypt. Although, therefore, the sacrifice is later in execution, it had to be prior in the faith and mind of Moses, just as the end, which is prior in intention, is posterior in execution, because the end of the exodus was the worship of GOD through sacrifice, or rather through service, as the Hebrew text has it, designated, the completion of which sign is had in Exod. 13:4. He received, therefore, the sign of his mission, the promise and assurance that he, together with the people, would serve GOD on Mount Sinai in thanksgiving for the liberation. Indeed, two things are to be considered in those words: the prophecy or promise, and the event of the same. The present sign was the prophecy and promise itself, insofar as it was a divine promise and prophecy; but the event was a confirmatory sign, yet only after the thing was fulfilled. Therefore, this offering or worship on that mountain could be considered a present sign, not as an event, which was still ἐκ τῶν μελλόντων (among the things to come), but as GOD promising the same, that promise of His made Moses certain. For thus, insofar as it was then promised by GOD, it was truly a sign of the divine will concerning the fulfilling of His decree; for he who wills the consequent also wills the necessary antecedent, and therefore, because GOD willed the consequent, the worship on this mountain, Moses could be certain that He also most strongly willed the exodus of the people. He who promises a triumph, promises victory.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET HOC HABEBIS SIGNUM.

Quomodo vero signum Mosi esse poterat eductionis populi oblatio in illo monte, quæ futura demum erat post eductionem? Hugo Victorinus si- gnum liberationis dicit esse ipsam missionem Mosis. Abulensis rubum ardentem signum facit legationis Mosis. Sed in textu immolatio signum constitui- tur eductionis, quia hoc signum refertur non ad antecedentia, sed ad consequentia, ideoque obser- vandum; non omne signum confirmativum præcedere tempore, & complemento executionem promissionis, quam firmat, actualem, sicut nec omne signum com- minationum antecedit complementum commina- tionis, 1. Sam. 2, 34. 1. Reg. 22, 25. 28. Jerem. 48. vers. 29. nam & ex consequentibus fidem facere possumus antecedentibus, & cum impietatis ac pervicaciæ sit, non credere DEO, nisi visis signis Matth. 12, 37. DEUS ita fidem confirmat quando- que suis, ut simul eandem exerceat, ut non diffidant verbo, etiamsi id signo præsenti confirmatum non sit. Scholastici distinguunt inter signa prognostica & rememorativa, quorum illa antecedunt eventus, hæc sequuntur. Magis congruit huic loco, quod tria alii signorum genera constituunt; (1.) eorum, quæ rem ipsam præcedunt, ut signum Gideoni datum, Judic. 6. (2.) eorum, quæ comitantur, quale erat, quod pastoribus dabatur, Luc. 2. (3.) eorum, quæ consequuntur, & ex eventu probant, quale erat, quod dabatur Ezechiæ, 2. Reg. 19, 29. Nam non tantum rememorativum signum in futuro, verum etiam βεβαιωτικὸν in præsenti esse debebat ista immola- tio. Quapropter respectu fidei, quæ intuetur pro- missionem, hoc signum intelligendum, quia certior de prima promissione eductionis fieri poterat Mo- ses, cum adderetur altera de immolatione in isto monte, quasi diceret DEUS: sit hoc signum tibi, quod promitto, te immolaturum in hoc monte cum po- pulo Israëlitico, quod te certo educturus cum populo sim ex Ægypto. Etsi ergo posterior sit immola- tio in executione, prior tamen in fide & mente Mo- sis esse debebat, prout finis, qui prior est in inten- tione, posterior est in executione, quia eductionis finis erat cultus DEI per immolationem, vel potius per servitutem, ut Ebr. textus habet, designatus, cujus signi complementum habetur Exod. 13, 4. Accepit ergo signum missionis suæ, promissionem & asseverationem, quod una cum populo in monte Sinai in gratiarum actionem pro liberatione DEO serviturus sit. Nimirum duo in illis verbis consi- deranda, prophetia vel promissio, & eventus ejusdem. Signum præsens fuit ipsa prophetia & promissio quatenus divina promissio & prophetia: Eventus vero fuit signum confirmativum, sed postquam res impleta est. Quapropter hæc oblatio, vel cul- tus in monte isto signum præsens haberi poterat, non qua eventum, qui adhuc ἐκ τῶν μελλόντων erat, sed qua DEUS promittens eundem, illa promissio- ne sua Mosen certum reddebat. Sic enim qua- tenus tum promittebatur à DEO, vere erat signum voluntatis divinæ, de implendo decreto suo; qui enim vult consequens, vult etiam antecedens ne- cessarium, ideoque quia DEUS consequens, cultum in hoc monte voluit, eductionem etiam populi eun- dem maxime velle certus esse poterat Moses. Qui promittit triumphum, promittit victoriam.

## 3:13
Ver. 13. WHAT IS HIS NAME?

Rivetus takes it as referring to instruction or commission, as to what that will be: but because GOD had already indicated the same before; you shall lead my people out of Egypt, this question is understood more simply and correctly regarding the name of GOD itself, because Moses sought some peculiar indication of the divine name, from which the divine embassy might be recognized. For although it is utterly false that Moses, polluted by Egyptian filth, was ignorant of the name of GOD, nor should it be admitted that Moses, out of some curiosity, desired to penetrate more deeply into the nature of GOD than his ancestors, he was nevertheless not beside the point in asking about a certain name to be indicated to the people, so that by that means also he might convince them of his authority. Men. Ben-Ismael in Conciliat. p. 104 says that when the Tetragrammaton name is revealed, since it represents ten illustrious lights, the Israelites would through them know GOD as if veiled. But these are Rabbinic trifles.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QUOD EST NOMEN EJUS?

Rivetus de instructione vel commissione acci- pit, quænam illa futura sit: sed quia jam antea ean- dem indicarat DEUS; educes populum meum ex Ægypto, simplicius, rectiusque de nomine ipso DEI hæc quæstio intelligitur, quod expetierit Moses aliquod indicium peculiare nominis divini, ex quo agnosci possit divina legatio. Quamvis enim oppido falsum sit, Mosen Ægyptiaca fœditate pol- lutum, nomen DEI ignorasse, neq; admitti debeat, Mosen ex curiositate aliqua cupiisse altius, quam majores, in DEI naturam penetrasse, non tamen præter rem de nomine certo, populo indicando quærebat, ut ea etiam ratione fidem sibi apud il- lum faceret. Men. Ben-Ismaël in Conciliat. p. 104. dicit, revelato nomine Tetragrammato cum id repræ- sentet decem illustres luces, per eas cognituros Israë- litas DEUM quasi velatum. Sed hæ Rabbinicæ af- faniæ sunt.

## 3:14
Ver. 14. I AM WHO I AM.

The word אהיה is a peculiar name of GOD, because to Moses asking what is the name of Him who appeared, the answer was: thus you shall say to the children of Israel: Ejeh has sent me to you. And therefore Justin in his Exhortatory Sermon to the Gentiles and Jerome in his Epistle to Marcellus acknowledge it as a name. B. Franzius in Orac. 103 not inappropriately renders it: he who is to be, which we treat more fully elsewhere against Crellius, who confuses the name Ejeh with the name Jehovah. Moreover, the name אהיה אשר אהיה implies these things, as the most accurate periphrasis of GOD handed down by GOD himself, when inquiry was made about GOD and the divine nature: (1.) the supreme substantiality of GOD. (2.) absolute incommutability. (3.) divine ἀυτουσίαν & ἀνθύπαρξιν. (4.) the simple being of GOD. (5.) the origin of created things from GOD. (6.) finally, the truth of GOD, which we proved in Theol. nat. & revel. p. 255. Add the testimonies of the Rabbis adduced on p. 262. & 264, as also the excellent sayings of the Fathers on p. 268 et seqq., which are also to be opposed to Smalcius, who in his response to one of the Sophisms of Ravensberger, p. 17, argues that the words: I will be who I will be, only denote that GOD is of such great and firm truth that what He has promised does not vanish in the least. But this name only secondarily implies divine truth, while primarily it expresses the immutability of essence itself, because GOD, as He does not change His essence, so He does not change His purpose. We have specifically refuted Smalcius on page 277; compare also Corn. à Lap. on this passage, who deals at length with this name.

Latin:

Vers. 14. EGO SUM QUI SUM.

Vox אהיה nomen DEI peculiare est, quia quærenti Mosi, quod sit nomen ei, qui apparuit, responsum est: sic dicas filiis Israël: Ejeh misit me ad vos. Ideoque id pro nomine agnoscit Justinus serm. exhortat. ad gentes, Hieron. Epist. ad Mar- cellum. B. Franzius Orac. 103. non incommode reddit: eriturus, quod contra Crellium, nomen E- jeh cum nomine Jehovah confundentem, alias fu- sius exequimur. Nomen autem אהיה אשר אהיה hæc importat, ceu accuratissima DEI periphrasis à DEO ipso tradita, cum de DEO & divina natura quæreretur: (1.) summam substantialitatem DEI. (2.) absolutam incommutabilitatem (3.) ἀυτουσίαν & ἀνθύπαρξιν divinam (4.) simplex DEI esse, (5.) originem rerum treatarum à DEO, (6.) de- nique veritatem DEI, quæ probavimus in Theol. nat. & revel. p. 255. Adde Rabbinorum testimonia adducta p. 262. & 264. ut & dicta Patrum egregia p. 268. seqq. quæ Smalcio etiam opponenda re- sponso ad par unum Sophismatum Ravensbergeri p. 17. disputanti verba: ero qui ero, tantum notare, quod DEUS sit tantæ & tam firmæ veritatis, ut quod promisit, minime evanescat. At nomen hoc verita- tem divinam tantum secundario infert, primario au- tem exprimit ipsam essentiæ immutabilitatem, quod DEUS, ut non mutat essentiam, ita nec mutet sen- tentiam. Smalcium peculiariter confutavimus pag. 277. conf. etiam prolixe de hoc nomine agens Corn. à Lap. in h. l.

## 3:15
Ver. 15. THE LORD GOD OF YOUR FATHERS.

He who previously called himself by the word Ejeh, now calls himself by the name Jehovah: Corn. à Lap. and Crellius the Photinian wish both names to be the same; but Crellius is mistaken in that he confuses the Tetragrammaton name with a verb of the third person in the future tense, and contends that it should be pronounced Jiveh or Jeheveh. That those names Jehovah and Ejeh are distinct is indicated by their origin, since one is from הוה and the other from הוה, by the punctuation in the sacred codex, and finally by their formation: whence they are listed as distinct names by Jerome and others.

Ver. same. THIS NAME IS MINE FOREVER. It shall be. Maimonides. Correctly. For in the priestly blessings in the temple that name יהוה was pronounced, which contains the force of that which preceded אשר אהיה, made according to the norm of human names, to which י is usually prefixed, the letter י in the middle between two ה being changed into ו, as often for the sake of euphony.

Here GOD claims for himself the Tetragrammaton name as his proper and eternal memorial; and therefore they err gravely, and oppose GOD himself, who contend that the Tetragrammaton name is attributed to creatures besides GOD, which is done by Jews and Arians to undermine the argument for the Deity of Christ, which is drawn from this name; by Arminians and Calixtines to maintain that the Deity of Christ is not clearly and brightly taught in the Old Testament; by Papists to argue that the name Jehovah, and divine worship, were exhibited to a created Angel when he sustained the person of GOD; which scope is also proposed by Socinians, who contend that the angels in the Old Testament sometimes sustained the person of GOD in such a way that they were honored and called by the name of GOD. Some among the Calvinists pour cold water on them, who, although they acknowledge this name to be proper to GOD, nevertheless assert that it was attributed somewhere to those who represented GOD. But especially impudent in this was Enjedin the Photinian, who with the Jews stubbornly contends that the name of Jehovah is attributed even to inanimate things, such as the altar of the covenant, Jerusalem, etc. We have expressly refuted them in Theol. Nat. & Rev. p. 278 et seqq., and thus we showed that the name of GOD, Jehovah, is a name grammatically proper, not appellative; and then also logically so proper to the supreme GOD that it belongs to Him alone and is incommunicable. Having discussed the examples which are adduced by Enjedin (whom the Arminians followed in their Apology) and having weighed especially the passage Jer. 33:16, on which they chiefly rely, we finally proved that the name Jehovah is neither attributed anywhere, nor can it be attributed, to angels as messengers, even if they perhaps sustain the person of GOD in some way. But the angel seen here in the burning bush was dealt with before, as also in Syst. Theol. Tom. 2, p. 145, 159. If nothing else were available for refuting them, they could be most solidly convinced from this passage. For the name which GOD, being asked about his own proper name, claims for himself, as his name forever, and a memorial to generations and generations, cannot belong to or be attributed to others outside of GOD: for if that name were communicated to others outside of GOD, it would not be the memorial of GOD forever: but GOD here testifies that the name Jehovah is so proper to himself, which he also professed in Isa. 42:8, Jer. 16:21. Therefore R. Mos. Maimonides in More Nebuch. p. I. c. 60. says that the name Jehovah is called שׁם המיוחר because it is a proper name and different from other names in this way, that it is proper to the divinity alone, and signifies nothing except the necessity of the divine existence; that all the names of the Creator are derived from effects except this one; that this name is a name appropriated to the most high Creator and for this reason is called Schem-Hamphorasch, that is, the exposed name, because it shows the essence of the Creator with a perfect signification, in which there is no equivocation. See Menass. Ben-Israel in Conciliat. ad Exod. 3. c. p. 98. & p. 104. who teaches from the Rabbis that this distinction exists between other names and the Tetragrammaton, that other names in Scripture are also attributed to other things; but that venerable name to God alone, and to no one else besides. Which Lyranus, Paulus Burgensis, Petrus Galatinus, Pagn. and others also acknowledge from the Papists.

Furthermore, if the name Tetragrammaton ought to have been carried down to the people and retained as the eternal memorial of GOD, it is false what the Jews trifle and what Grotius hints at here, that that name is ἀνέκφρατον, and that it ought not to have been uttered except by the Priests only in the solemn blessing in Num. VI. on the day of atonement; which superstition of the more recent Jews seems to have arisen from the pious opinion of the ancients concerning the name of GOD, that it, as the thing signified, because it expresses the incomprehensible essence of GOD, is truly ἀνέκφρατον. Concerning which we have spoken in Theol. Nat. & Revel. p. 324. R. Solomon is foolish, striving to prove these trifles from this passage, which is entirely contrary to them; this is my name לְעוֹלָם to be hidden: which ψευδερμηνεία (false interpretation) is strangled by the added ἐξήγησιν (explanation), and my memorial to generation and generation; from which it is clear that the word עוֹלָם denotes not concealment, but perpetuity. Nor does this perpetual memorial of GOD obscurely

They say that the vowels of the Tetragrammaton are now unknown, and that no certain pronunciation can be had. For just as it was revealed for this reason, that it might be acknowledged, adored, and celebrated, so also it was for that reason recorded in letters, not that it might be looked upon without understanding, but that it might be read and pronounced, as Mr. Dr. Walther says in Spicil. controvers. 6. p. 78, even if he otherwise favors the antagonists of the reading Jehovah. But how could it be read and pronounced if it did not have vowels, or if the same had been known to no one for so many centuries; and would not the sacred text be in infinite places either mutilated or corrupted if that name were either destitute of vowels, which are otherwise believed by some ἐκ τῆς ἐναντίας (from the contrary) to be coeval with their letters, or had alien points? Would not the sentence of Christ be false, that heaven and earth must sooner perish than one apex from the law, Matt. V, 18. If that which is chief in the law, and ought to have been the perpetual memorial of GOD himself, his own and most august name, has so perished that neither its complete Scripture nor its true reading survives anywhere through the course of so many centuries? Since divine providence, says Mr. Varenius in Decad. Exod. p. 101, has watched over the י and the μία κεραίᾳ (one tittle), it has altogether watched most especially for the name JEHOVAH, which he wished to be understood and discerned by us, so that we do not give the glory of this name to another. We pass over the fact that the periphrasis of GOD, Apoc. I, 8, confirms the customary reading, as well as those names composed from the initials of the Tetragrammaton, Jehonatan, Jehoram, Jehoshaphat, etc., which Fuller urges: concerning which and others, which make for the full decision of that controversy, we have spoken sufficiently in Theol. nat. & rev. p. 227 seqq. The trifles of the Cappellian secret having also been routed, which was done especially in the Critico sacro p. 331 sqq. With whose furtive colors, as Varenius says, they adorn their feathers everywhere, who think they cannot be masters unless they abort something against the reading JEHOVAH. But we prefer to adhere to the opinion of the pious Ancients, Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Jerome, Theodoret, and the great man Luther, as also Galatinus and Münster, and also the most learned Fagius, defended by our predecessors, Mr. Bugenhagen and Mr. Dr. Franz in Orac. 103, as also by our Blessed Gerhard, rather than to rise up with certain Neoteric Hebraists, Lyranus, Burgensis, Pagninus, Cevallerius, Mercerus, Buxtorf, Drusius, Amama. Rivetus himself disapproves of the zeal of Drusius, because he undeservedly stirred up such tragedies concerning this name in Comment. ad Ps. 110, 1. p. 430. To which the appendix of book 6 of the Misc. of Nicolaus Fuller responds expressly.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DOMINUS DEUS PATRUM VE- STRORUM.

Qui antea se voce Ejeh, jam nomine Jehovah appellat: idem nomen utrumque esse Corn. à Lap. & Crellius Photin. vult; sed fallitur in eo Crellius, quod nomen Tetragrammaton cum verbo tertiæ personæ in futuro confundat, & pronunciandum esse Jiveh aut Jeheveh contendat. Distincta esse illa nomina Jehovah & Ejeh tum origo indicat, cum alterum sit ab הוה alterum ab הוה cum pun- ctatio in codice sacro, tum denique formatio: un de ut distincta nomina recensentur ab Hieronymo & aliis.

Vers. eod. HOC NOMEN MIHI EST IN ÆTERNUM Erit. Maimonides. Recte. Nam in benedictionibus sacerdo talibus in templo pronunciatum fuit nomen illud יהוה, quo vim continet ejus, quod præcessit אשר אהיה factum a normam humanorum nominum, quibus י præponi solet, litera י media inter duo ה mutata in ו, ut sæpe εὐφωνίας caus

Vendicat hîc DEUS sibi nomen Tetragram maton ceu proprium & æternum memoriale; ideoqu graviter errant, Deoq; ipsi repugnant, qui conten dunt, nomen Tetragrammaton præter DEU tribui creaturis, quod à Judæis & Arrianis fit, ut argumentum Deitatis Christi, ab hoc nomine petitum, labefactent; ab Arminianis & Calixtinis, ut Deitatem Christi in Vet. Testam. clare ac luculenter traditam non esse obtineant; à Papistis, ut Angelo creato nomen Jehovah, & cultum divinum, cum DEI personam sustinuit, exhibitum esse, propugnent; qui scopus etiam Socinianis, contendenti- bus, angelos in Vet. Test. ita personam DEI sustinuisse quandoque, ut nomine DEI honorati & nuncupati fuerint, propositus est. Quibus frigidam suffundunt è Calvinianis nonnulli, qui etsi nomen hoc DEI proprium esse agnoscant, alicubi tamen illis, qui DEUM repræsentarunt, tributum fuisse asserunt. Sed imprimis in eo impudens fuit Enjedin. Photin. qui cum Judæis, rebus etiam inanimatis utpote aræ fœderis, Hierof. &c. nomen Jehovæ tribui, pervicaciter contendit. Quos ex professo confutavimus Theol. Nat. & Rev. p. 278. seqq. adeoque ostendimus nomen DEI Jehovah esse nomen Grammatice proprium non appellativum; tum vero etiam Logice ita proprium summo DEO esse, ut ipsi soli conveniat, & incommunicabile sit. Discussis exemplis, quæ ab Enjedino adducuntur (quem Arminiani in Apolog. secuti sunt) & expenso imprimis loco Jerem. 33, 16. quo præcipue nituntur, denique evicimus, nomen Jehova neque tribui uspiam, neque tribui posse angelis tanquam legatis, etsi personam DEI aliqua ratione forte sustineant. At de angelo hic in rubo ardente viso actum antea fuit, ut & in Syst. Theol. Tom. 2. p. 145. 159. Si nihil aliud istis refellendis suppeteret, ex h. l. convinci solidissime possent. Quod enim nomen DEUS, de proprio suo nomine quæsitus, sibi vendicat, ceu nomen suum in æternum, & memoriale in generationes & generationes, id aliis extra DEUM convenire aut tribui non potest: si enim nomen illud aliis extra DEUM communicaret, non esset memoriale DEI in æternum: at nomen Jehovah ita sibi proprium esse, DEUS hîc testatur, quod professus etiam est Esa. 42, 8. Jer. 16, 21. Ideo R. Mos. Maimonides in More Nebuch. p. I. c. 60. nomen Jehovah dicit vocatum שׁם המיוחר quod sit nomen proprium & à cæteris nominibus hoc pacto diversum, quod hoc soli divinitati proprium sit, nec quicquam nisi necessitatem existentiæ divinæ significet; omnia nomina creatoris ab effectibus derivata esse præter hoc unum; nomen hoc esse nomen appropriatum Creatori altissimo & propter hoc vocari Schem-Hamphorasch, id est, nomen expositum, quia ostendit essentiam Creatoris significatione perfecta, in qua non est æquivocatio. Vid. Menass. Ben-Israel in Conciliat. ad Exod. 3. c. p. 98. & p. 104. qui è Rabbinis docet, hoc discriminis inter alia nomina & Tetragrammaton intercedere, quod cætera nomina in Scriptura aliis quoq̃ rebus tribuantur; at venerabile illud nomen soli Deo, nec præterea cuiquam. Quod è Pontificiis agnoscunt quoque Lyranus, Paulus Burgensis, Petrus Galatinus, Pagn. & alii.

Porro si nomen Tetragrammaton ad populum deferri, & ceu memoriale DEI æternum retineri debuit, falsum est, quod nugantur Judæi quodq̃ hic innuit Grotius, nomen illud ἀνέκφρατον esse, nec nisi à Sacerdotibus tantum in solemni benedictione Num. VI. die expiationis proferri debuisse; quæ superstitio recentiorum Judæorum orta videtur è veterum pia de nomine DEI sententia, quod illud qua rem significatam, quia incomprehensibilem DEI essentiam exprimit, vere sit ἀνέκφρατον. De qua diximus Theol. Nat. & Revel. p. 324. Ineptus est R. Salomo ex h. l. nugas istas probare satagens, qui prorsus illis contrarius est; hoc est nomen meum לְעוֹלָם ad occultandum : quæ ψευδερμηνεία per ad- jectam ἐξήγησιν jugulatur, & memoriale meum in generationem & generationem; è qua liquet, voca- bulum עוֹלָם non occultationem, sed perpetuitatem notare. Nec obscure hoc perpetuum DEI me- moriale refellit illorum opinionem, qui nominis

Tetragrammati vocales nunc ignorari, nullamq; cer- tam pronunciationem haberi posse, ajunt. Quem- admodum enim propterea id revelatum est, ut agnosceretur, adoraretur & celebraretur, ita etiam ideo in literas relatum est, non ut sine intellectu aspice- retur, sed ut legeretur & pronunciaretur, ut ait Dn. D. Walth. in Spicil. controvers. 6. p. 78. etsi alias antagonistis lectionis Jehovah faveat. Quomodo autem legi & pronuntiari posset, si vocales non ha- beret, vel eædem per tot secula nemini certo co- gnitæ essent; & annon textus sacer in infinitis locis vel mutilus vel corruptus esset, si nomen illud vel vocalibus, quæ alias à nonnullis ἐκ τῆς ἐναντίας, coævæ literis suis creduntur, destitueretur, vel aliena puncta haberet? Annon falleret Christi sen- tentia, quod prius cœlum & terra perire debeant, quam apex ulius è lege Matth. V, 18. Si id, quod præcipuum in lege est, ac memoriale ipsius DEI perpetuum esse debuit, nomen ipsius proprium & maxime augustum ita interiit, ut nec Scriptura ejus integra, nec lectio vera uspiam supersit per tot seculorum decursus? Quum providentia divina, ait Dn. Varenius in Decad. Exod. p. 101. pro י & μία κεραίᾳ vigilaverit, omnino & pro nomine JEHO- VAH, quod à nobis intelligi, & discerni voluit, ita ut gloriam hujus nominis non demus alteri, maxime vigilavit. Tacemus, quod periphrasis DEI, Apoc. I, 8. lectionem usitatam confirmet, nec non nomi- na ista ex initialibus Tetragrammati composita Je- honatan, Jehoram, Jehoshaphat &c. quæ Fullerus urget: de quibus & aliis, quæ ad plenam contro- versiæ istius decisionem faciunt, affatim diximus Theol. nat. & rev. p. 227. seqq. Profligatis etiam næniis arcani Cappelliani, quod in Critico sacro im- primis factum p. 331. sqq. Cujus furtivis coloribus, Varenio dicente, passim plumas ornant, qui se Magi- stros esse non posse putant, nisi aliquid abortiant contra lectionem JEHOVAH. Malumus autem nos pio- rum Veterum Irenæi, Epiph. Hieron. Theod. & Me- galandri Lutheri, ut & Galatini & Münsteri, nec non Doctissimi Fagii sententiæ à prædecessoribus, Dn. Bugenhag. & Dn. D. Franzio Orac. 103. ut & à B. Gerhard. nostro propugnatæ adhærere, quam Neoreticis quibusdam Ebraïstis Lyrano, Burgensi, Pagnino, Cevallerio, Mercero, Buxtorf. Drusio, A- mame assurgere. Drusii Zelum improbat Rivetus ipse, quod immerito tantas excitarit tragœdias de hoc nomine in Comment. ad Pf. 110, 1. p. 430. Cui appendix libri 6. Misc. Nicol. Fulleri, ex professo respondit.

## 3:18
Verse 18. A JOURNEY OF THREE DAYS.

It is a doubt, with what truth do they seek a journey of three days, who are planning an all-out departure from the kingdom? Resp. Most say that the Israelites were not thus deserving, but only dissembled something which they were not bound to indicate. Not a lie, but a silence of the whole truth intervenes here, says Corn. à Lap. and with him not a few. For they were going to go on a journey of three days, and this they said: but they were going to go further into Canaan, and this they kept silent. But with such dissimulation, and mental reservation, the Jesuits are indeed accustomed to excuse their equivocations and mental reservations, which, however, no sensible person approves of in them, and therefore they could not be approved of in the Israelites either, for thus Pharaoh would have been circumvented, and it is a matter of religion for us not to attribute such counsels to GOD. GOD could indeed have commanded the dismissal of his people: the Israelites could also have rightfully demanded it, who had subjected themselves to the Kings of Egypt for a time only by the right of hospitality, and had lived there not as citizens, but as foreigners: but because God does not yet command that to Pharaoh, which the Israelites would certainly not have obtained from him, nay rather, material for greater cruelty would have been suggested: Therefore GOD for the first time wished only that to be requested which could be considered highly equitable by the judgment of Pharaoh himself, namely, that he should grant a three-day journey to the Israelites, nor did he hint anything more to Moses, which was to be sought from Pharaoh by the elders of the people in the first embassy: and that this was also done, the execution teaches in chapter 5, verse 3. Therefore, although Pharaoh replied: Why do you distract the people from their works, they answered nothing else; nor did Pharaoh understand the request as anything other than the granting of a three-day holiday from work for the sake of sacrifice, nor was anything else to be sought by Moses in that first expedition. For although GOD foresaw that this request, however equitable, and a short journey, to be undertaken for the sake of religion, which even the Gentiles willingly permitted to anyone, would be denied, he nevertheless wished it to be requested, not so that he might prepare a way for himself for the just punishment of Pharaoh, as Rivetus wishes, but so that he might show him his μακροθυμίαν (long-suffering), that he was willing to ask for his people at least some kind of holiday, when he could rightfully ask for a total dismissal and extort it by his own help. There is therefore no cause or suspicion of deceit here, as if, while only requesting leave for the sake of sacrificing, they had something else in their commands and in their mind; for they had nothing else in their commands to request in the first embassy, they had nothing else in their mind, nor if they had been dismissed for a three-day journey, would they have attempted anything else. For they knew that GOD knew a thousand ways of leading them out of Egypt, so that there was no need at all for evil intent or fraud: and those holidays having been obtained, without doubt GOD would have bent and directed Pharaoh, who was complying, in another way. But because he foresaw that Pharaoh would not permit it, he nevertheless wished to show by this illustrious example the ordinary process in softening the hearts of the impious, and his own long-suffering, so that in no way is the cause of hardening attributed to GOD himself. In which sense also the solution of Augustine is to be accepted, q. 13 in Exod., who answers that it is to be understood that, although GOD knew what He was about to do, since He foreknew that Pharaoh would not consent to dismiss the people, that was said first which would also have been done at the beginning if he had dismissed them, but that Pharaoh's contumacy had earned that all things should be done just as Scripture testifies; whose meaning Rivetus perverts, as if Augustine had intended that GOD had indeed proposed this end to Himself, namely the absolute liberation of the people, but had also instituted the method of the means, so that it might be done by degrees and with the intervention of Pharaoh's stubbornness. Augustine did not say that, but Calvin's absolute decree suggested that to Rivetus; GOD did not intend an absolute liberation, but first intended the offering of the people in the desert to be obtained from Pharaoh, so that by degrees He might dispose him toward the dismissal of the people, nor did He Himself institute the means in such a way that it should be done with the intervention of Pharaoh's stubbornness, because He wished it to be done otherwise, and with Pharaoh himself consenting, which can be called a consequent will: but because He foresaw Pharaoh's stubbornness, therefore by a consequent will He decreed to execute the liberation with a mighty hand, with those means applied by which Pharaoh was irritated more than he was bent toward obedience. For as the thing was done, and as it stands in the execution, so also it is to be believed that it was decreed.

Latin:

Vers. 18. VIAM TRIUM DIERUM.

Dubium est, qua veritate viam trium dierum petant, qui omnimodum è regno discessum moliuntur? Resp. plerique non meritos ita esse Israëlitas, sed tantum aliquid dissimulasse, quod indicare non te- nebantur. Non mendacium hîc, sed silentium in- tegræ veritatis intervenit, ait Corn. à Lap. & cum eo non nemo. Ituri namq; erant itinere trium die- rum, & hoc dixerunt: sed longius ituri erant in Canaan, & hoc tacuerunt. Sed tali dissimulatione, & reservato mentali suas æquivocationes, & refer- vata mentalia Jesuitæ excusare quidem solent, quæ vero nemo cordatus in iis probat, ideoque nec in Israëlitis illa probari possent, sic enim circumven- tus fuisset Pharao, cujusmodi consilia DEO tri- buere, religio nobis est. Poterat sane imperare DEUS dimissionem populi sui: poterant etiam il- lam jure requirere Israëlitae, qui hospitii solum ju- re ad tempus se Regibus Aegypti subjecerant, & ibi non velut municipes, sed seu peregrini habitarant: sed quia Deus id nondum imperat Pharaoni, quod ab ipso impetraturi utique non fuissent Israëlitae, quin majori potius saevitiei materia suggesta fuis- set: Idcirco DEUS prima vice hoc tantum postu- lari volebat, quod summe aequum, ipsius Pharaonis judicio, censeri poterat, ut nempe triduanum iter concederet Israëlitis, nec aliud amplius innuebat Mosi, quod cum senioribus populi à Pharaone ex- petendum prima legatione erat: atque id etiam fa- ctum esse, executio docet cap. 5, l. 3. Ideo quan- quam regeret Pharao: Quare solicitatis populum ab operibus suis, nihil aliud reposuerunt; nec aliter, quam de triduanis feriis operarum indulgendis sa- crificii causa, intelligebat Pharao petitum, neque aliud ista prima expeditione Mosi expetendum erat. Quamvis enim praeviderit DEUS hoc po- stulatum, utut aequissimum, iterque exiguum, reli- gionis causa, quam etiam gentiles libenter cuivis permittebant, suscipiendum, denegatum iri, peti tamen id voluit, non ut ad Pharaonis justam puni- tionem sibi viam praeparet, ut Rivet. vult, sed ut ei- dem μακροθυμίαν suam ostenderet, quod petere suos aliqualem saltim feriationem vellet, cum jure totalem dimissionem petere & suo auxilio extorque- re posset. Non ergo hic ulla causa, vel suspicio do- li est, quasi tantum commeatum sacrificandi causa petentes, aliud in mandatis & in animo habuerint; nihil enim aliud in mandatis habebant in prima le- gatione petere, nihil aliud in animo habebant, ne- que si dimissi ad iter triduanum fuissent, aliud mo- liti essent. Nam sciebant, novisse DEUM mille modos sese ex Aegypto educendi, ut dolo malo aut fraude opus sibi minime sit: & obtentis illis feriis, sine dubio DEUS Pharaonem morem gerentem aliter flexisset ac direxisset. Sed quia praevidebat, non permissurum Pharaonem, ostendere tamen voluit hoc illustri exemplo ordinarium processum in emolliendis impiorum animis, ac longanimita- tem suam, ne ullatenus DEO ipsi causa induratio- nis tribuatur. Quo sensu etiam accipienda solutio Augustini qv. 13. in Exod. qui respondet, intelligen- dum esse, quamvis DEUS sciret, quid esset facturus, quoniam praesciebat, non consensurum Pharaonem ad populum dimittendum, illud primo dictum esse, quod etiam primitus fieret, si ille dimitteret, Pharaonis au- tem contumaciam meruisse, ut sic fierent omnia, quem- admodum Scriptura testatur; cujus mentem per- vertit Rivetus, quasi id voluerit Aug. DEUM qui- dem sibi proposuisse hunc finem, nempe absolutam populi liberationem, sed rationem etiam mediorum instituisse, ut id fieret per gradus & interveniente Pharaonis pervicacia. Id non dixit Aug. sed sugge- sit id Riveto absolutum decretum Calvini; non intendebat absolutam liberationem DEUS, sed primum oblationem populi in deserto à Pharaone obtinendam intendebat, ut per gradus eundem ad populi dimissionem disponeret, neq; media ipse ita instituit, ut ea fieret interveniente Pharaonis per- vicacia, quia aliter, & Pharaone ipso annuente fieri illam volebat, quae voluntas antecedens dici potest: sed quia praevidit Pharaonis pervicaciam, ideo vo- luntate consequente liberationem manu valida exe- qui decrevit, illis adhibitis mediis, à quibus irrita- batur magis Pharao, quam ad obsequium flecteba- tur. Uti enim res gesta est, & in exequutione se ha- bet, ita etiam eam decretam fuisse credendum.

## 3:19
Ver. 19. UNLESS BY A MIGHTY HAND] Thus also

The Greeks [say] ἐὰν μὴ. And the sense requires it, as appears below 6, 1. It seems therefore that there was in the Hebrew בלא, not ולא, which would make a sense alien to the history. But a strong hand is to be understood as the slaying of the firstborn: the greatest vengeance, ἐκδίκησις μεγάλη, 7, 4.

The Hebrew text is again rashly corrected from the Latin and Greek. Which agrees perfectly with the history, if it be rendered AND NOT, or NOT EVEN by a strong hand, as Drusius observed in his notes on difficult places, and Amama, in his Censura of the Vulgate version on this passage, as also Mr. D. Varenius in Decad. Ex. p. 137. And the Tigurines translated it so, not being opposed by R. Aben-Ezra and R. Bechai, who render it, not even with a strong hand, or R. Mehir Arama and R. Mose Albelda, who likewise explain it, nor with a strong hand, although they understand it of Pharaoh, neither because of the strong hand which Pharaoh has; the latter understand it of the power of Israel, nor with a strong hand, that is, you will not shake off the yoke of Pharaoh by force: Both are wrong: for the discourse is about the hand of GOD, not about the hand of Pharaoh or the Israelites. The genuine sense is, that even with the strong hand of GOD approaching, Pharaoh would not let the people go, as far as it depended on him: to which the event is not dissonant: because not even thus did Pharaoh constantly indulge them, so that the Israelites might go out. For wishing to obtain permission from him, they could not, however grievously he himself was afflicted by the hand of GOD: and although at length Pharaoh let them go, willing or unwilling, with the plague still pressing upon his kingdom, yet the dismissal was by no means serious and constant; for when the plagues of the Lord ceased, when he understood that the Israelites had fled, he wished them to be brought back, and pursued them even to the borders of Egypt, until he himself with his whole army was drowned in the Red Sea. They were not therefore dismissed by him, but when he desired to retain them, and to restrain them within the limits of his kingdom with as much power as he could, they were liberated from his hand by divine power, Exod. 14, 30. Thus those whom the strong hand of GOD could not induce to a full dismissal by miraculous punishments, the same hand of GOD afflicted with supreme punishment, and cast into the Red Sea, for the sake both of liberating and confirming the people in the faith, and of demonstrating His justice. Exod. 5, 31. And thus Onkelos read and understood it, whom Fagius interprets in this way, nor even because of his presence, whose virtue is most strong. Thus Hiskuni and others, therefore there is no cause for suspicion of a corrupted Hebrew text. Nor is the strong hand rightly taken as the slaying of the firstborn alone, from which interpretation Grotius wished to reconcile a semblance to his suspicion, but all the miracles performed in Egypt by the strong hand, that is, by the omnipotent power of the Lord, for the sake of the dismissal of the people, are designated: as is manifest in Exod. c. 7, 4, and other places of Scripture, in which mention is made of the strong hand and the exalted arm by which the Israelites were led out, teach. For who will admit that nothing else is signified by them than the slaying of the firstborn? Cf. what Varenius says here in the cited place. Moreover, because GOD here testifies that He knows the stubbornness of Pharaoh, it must be false what Socinus contends in Præl. c. 8, that GOD is not prescient of future contingent things, especially sins. By which opinion a path is paved to Atheism and the denial of the providence of GOD. Thus we proceed: this foreknowledge and prediction of the stubbornness of Pharaoh is either certain and infallible, or doubtful and uncertain. If the latter, the certainty of the divine word will be endangered; if the former, the hypothesis of Socinus will be false. But it is better that Socinus be mistaken than the omniscient GOD, who is ignorant of how to be mistaken or to deceive. And therefore Tertullian rightly said in book 2 against Marcion: That the foreknowledge of GOD has as many witnesses as He made Prophets. See Vol. II. Syst. Theol. page 511.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NISI PER MANUM VALIDAM] Sic &

Græci ἐὰν μὴ. Et sensus id exigit, ut apparet infra 6, 1. Vi- detur ergo fuisse in Hebræo בלא, non ולא, quod sensum faceret ab historia alienum. Manus autem valida intelligen- da est occisio primogenitorum : ultio maxima, ἐκδίκησις μεγάλη, 7, 4.

Temere iterum corrigitur Ebræus textus è Latino & Græco. Qui optime consonat historiæ, si reddatur ET NE, vel NE QUIDEM per ma- num validam, ut observavit Drusius ad loca diffi- cil. & Amama, in Censur. Vulg. vers. ad h. l. ut & Dn. D. Varenius Decad. Ex. p. 137. & transtule- runt Tigurini, non abnuentibus R. Aben-Ezra, & R. Bechai, qui reddunt, ne quidem manu forti, aut R. Mehir Arama, & R. Mose Albelda, qui itidem exponunt, nec manu forti, etsi illi de Pharaone in- telligant, neque propter manum fortem, quam habet Pharao; hi de potentia Israëlis, nec manu forti, id est, per vim excutietis jugum Pharaonis: Utrique per- peram : de manu enim DEI, non de manu Pharao- nis sermo est, aut Israëlitarum. Sensus genuinus est, accedente etiam val da DEI manu haud dimissu- rum populum Pharaonem, quantum in ipso erit: cui non dissonat eventus : quia ne sic quidem in- dulsit constanter Pharao, ut exirent Israëlitæ. Li- centiam enim ab ipso volentes consequi, obtinere, utut gravissime manu DEI affligeretur ipse, non potuerunt : & quamvis tandem nolens volens dimise- rit eosdem Pharao, plaga adhuc incumbente regno suo, neutiquam tamen seria prorsus & constans fuit dimissio; cessantibus enim plagis Domini, cum au- fugisse Israëlitas intelligeret, retractos cupiebat, & ad fines usque Ægypti eosdem prosequebatur, do- nec manu valida ipse cum toto exercitu in mari rubro mergeretur. Non ergo ab ipso dimissi, sed quum retinere cuperet, & quanta valeret poten- tia, intra limites regni sui compescere, liberati sunt à manu ejus divina virtute, Exod. 14, 30. Ita quos manus valida DEI miraculosis pœnis ad plenam dimissionem inducere non poterat, illos eadem DEI manus supremo supplicio afficiebat, inq; ma- re rubrum præcipitabat, cum liberandi, & in fide confirmandi populi, tum demonstrandæ justitiæ suæ gratia. Exod. 5, 31. Atque ita legit & intellexit Onkelos, quem hoc modo interpretatur Fagius, neque etiam propter præsentiam ejus, cujus virtus for- tissima est. Sic Hiskuni & alii, Nulla ergo suspi- cionis textus Ebræi corrupti causa. Nec recte manus valida de sola occisione primogenitorum acci- pitur, à quo interpretamento speciem conciliare Grotius voluit suspicioni suæ, sed omnia miracula manu valida, hoc est, omnipotenti virtute Domini in Ægypto dimissionis populi ergo patrata, designan- tur : ut Exod. c. 7, 4. manifestum est, & alia Scri- pturæ loca, in quibus manus validæ & brachii ex- celsi, quo educti sunt Israëlitæ, mentio fit, docent. Ecquis enim admittet, illis aliud nihil, quam occi- sionem primogenitorum fignificari? Conf. quæ hic Varenius l. c. Cæterum quia DEUS hic testatur, se scire proterviam Pharaonis, falsum sit oportet, quod contendit Socinus in Præl. c. 8. DEUM præscium non esse futurorum contingentium, inprimis peccato- rum. Qua sententia via sternitur ad Atheismum, & negandam DEI providentiam. Ita procedimus : hæc præscientia, & prædictio pervicaciæ Pharaonis aut certa & infallibilis est, aut dubia & incerta. Si posterius, periclitabitur, verbi divini certitudo, si prius, falsa erit Socini hypothesis. Præstat autem falli Socinum quam DEUM omniscicium, falli & fallere nescium. Ideoque recte Tertull. l. 2. contra Marc. dixit : Præscientiam DEI tot habere testes, quot fecit Prophetas. Vid. Tom. II. Syst. Theol. pag. 511.

## 3:21
In the same verse. AND I WILL GIVE FAVOR TO THIS PEOPLE BEFORE THE EGYPTIANS] I will make them gracious. Verse 22. YOU SHALL SPOIL EGYPT.

The Hebrew word signifies you shall empty. Not robbery, but by the just title of a gift from GOD they obtained these things, because GOD gave them favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, so that they might obtain those things which they had indeed received as a loan, but by divine favor, they obtained them for the sake of remuneration. And the word שאל introduces a friendly and submissive petition 1 Sam. 1, 28; ch. 2, 20; 2 Kings 4, 3; ch. 6, 5. But these were the causes for God, (1.) regarding the Egyptians, that their luxury might be restrained, (2.) regarding the Israelites, that they might carry away some reward for their labors, concerning which Tertullian against Marcion ch. 14, the Hebrews were prompted not to fraud, but to the compensation of a reward, which they could not otherwise exact from their masters. Therefore Wisdom 10, 17, it is said, that He gave the just the reward of their labors, (3.) with respect to the divine counsel, in the construction of the tabernacle, so that the Egyptians, willing or unwilling, might also contribute some material for it, in place of gratitude, for the benefit granted to them; for the spoils of Egypt were converted into the structure of the tabernacle. It was not, therefore, theft which was committed by the Israelites, Exod. 11, 2. chap. 12, 35. 36. nor was there any dispensation here regarding the law of nature, as it seems to some; for a dispensation properly occurs when an act is permitted and approved which is adequately and according to all its conditions against the law; such was not the case here, which, as regards the material, seemed indeed contrary to the law of nature, yet is not so in reality, if the circumstances and conditions are attended to, because the Egyptian vessels were not entirely the property of others, but were for the Israelites in place of the wages owed, and destined by GOD, the Lord of all; and besides, the Egyptians were manifest enemies of the Israelites, whom it is not illicit to despoil. R. AbenEzra says thus concerning these things: There are those who argue that our Fathers were thieves; but do these not see that there was an express divine command for this matter: nor is there need here to ask, why? because God, as He created all things, freely gives wealth to whom He wills, taking it from one and bestowing it upon another; nor is there any fault here, because all that is of GOD.

Latin:

Vers. eodem. DABOQUE GRATIAM POPULO HUIC CORAM ÆGYPTIIS] Faciam eos gratiosos. Vers. 22. SPOLIABITIS ÆGYPTUM.

Vox Ebr. vacuabitis significat. Non rapina, sed justo donationis DEI titulo hæc consequeban- tur, quia gratiam DEUS dedit ipsis in oculis Æ- gyptiorum, ut ea obtinerent, quæ mutuo quidem acceperant, sed divina gratia, remunerationis ergo consequebantur. Et vox שאל amicam & submis- sam infert petitionem 1. Sam. 1, 28. cap. 2, 20. 2. Reg. 4, 3. cap. 6, 5. Causæ autem Deo hæ erant, (1.) quoad Ægyptios, ut luxus ipsorum coërceretur, (2.) quoad Israëlitas, ut laborum aliquam reportarent merce- dem, de quo Tertullianus contra Marcionem c. 14. instincti sunt Ebræi non ad fraudem, sed ad mercedis compensationem, quam alias à Dominatoribus exigere non poterant. Ideo Sapient. 10, 17. dicitur, justis mer- cedem laborum suorum dedisse, (3.) respectu divini consilii, in extructione tabernaculi, ut Ægyptii no- lentes volentes etiam materiam aliquam ad id con- tribuerent, gratitudinis loco, pro beneficio ipsis concesso; conversa enim sunt spolia Ægypti in stru- cturam tabernaculi. Non ergo furtum fuit, quod ab Israëlitis commissum est, Exod. 11, 2. cap. 12, 35. 36. neque etiam circa legem naturæ, quod nonnullis videtur, hic dispensatum est; nam dispensatio pro- prie sit, cum permittitur & approbatur actus, qui adæquate & secundum omnes suas conditiones contra legem est; talis hîc non fuit, qui, quoad materiale, legi quidem naturæ contrarius videba- tur, non tamen revera est, si circumstantiæ & con- ditiones attendantur, quia vasa Ægyptia non fue- runt omnino res alienæ, sed Israëlitis loco mercedis debitæ, & à DEO omnium Domino destinatæ; ac præterea Ægyptii hostes erant manifesti Israëlita- rum, quos spoliare illicitum non est. R. AbenEzra ita de hisce: Sunt qui arguunt, quod Patres nostri fu- res fuerint; sed annon hi vident, quod expressum fue- rit hujus rei mandatum divinum: nec opus est hic quæ- rere, quare? quia Deus uti omnia creavit, libere dat opes, cui vult, uni auferendo, alteri tribuendo; nec quicquam hic est culpæ, quia omne illud est DEI.

## 3:22 Addition
On Exodus 3, verse 22. BUT SHE SHALL ASK, etc.

The word שאל נא signifies a friendly and submissive request, so that it may advise that neighbors are to be addressed in a friendly manner. See 1 Sam. 1:18, ch. 2:20, Exod. 17, 2 Kings 4:3, ch. 6:5, Exod. 12:36.

Latin:

Ad Exod. 3. vers. 22. SED POSTULA- BIT &c.

Vox שאל נא amicam & submissam petitio- nem significat, ut moneat amice compellandos vi- cinos. Vid. 1. Sam. 1. v. 18. c. 2, 20. Exod. 17. 2. Reg. 4. v. 3. c. 6. v. 5. Exod. 12, 36.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

The confirmation of Moses by signs, the staff turned into a serpent, the leprous hand, the water changed into blood: The circumcision of his son.

Ver. 1.

NOR WILL THEY HEAR MY VOICE.

BUT the Lord had said in chap. 3, 18, they will obey your voice; how then does Moses still doubt, or did he not apply faith to the words of GOD? The answer is to be drawn from the text, in which a distinction is made between the Hebrew people and the elders among the people. For God had predicted that the elders would believe, but now Moses raises a doubt about the people themselves, whether they would believe; whose character he did not ignore as being quite slow in accepting such things by faith, and for that reason in v. 30 it is notably said that he performed those signs before the people, so that, namely, he might convince them of his calling. Add that Moses does not indeed distrust the words of the Lord, that the Israelites will eventually obey him, but [he doubts] if he would demonstrate the truth of the divine apparition by signs, and therefore these things are to be accepted with a limitation in this way: they will not believe my bare words, nor will they thus obey me, unless I demonstrate my mission with signs; whence GOD does not disapprove of the answer, but instructs him with signs, so that they may believe that Jehovah appeared to him v. 5.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Confirmatio Mosis per signa, baculum in ser- pentem versum, manum leprosam, aquam in sanguinem mutatam: Filii ejus circum- cisio.

Vers. 1.

NEQUE AUDIENT VOCEM MEAM.

AT dixerat Dominus cap. 3, 18. obedient voci tuæ; quî ergo adhuc ambigit Moses, aut num fidem DEI verbis non adhibuit? Responsio è tex- tu depromenda est, in quo distinguitur inter popu- lum Ebræum, & Seniores in populo. Prædixerat nem- pe Deus seniores credituros, nunc autem de po- pulo ipso dubium movet Moses, num crediturus sit; cujus ingenium non ignorabat admodum tar- dum in talibus fide suscipiendis, & ea de causa v. 30. notanter dicitur, quod signa ista fecerit coram po- pulo, ut sc. illi vocationem suam persuaderet. Adde quod non diffidat quidem Moses de verbis Domini, quod obedituri tandem sibi Israëlitæ sint, sed si si- gnis veritatem apparitionis divinæ demonstraret, ideoq; limitate hæc accipienda sunt hoc modo, non credent nudis meis verbis, nec ita mihi obsequentur, nisi signis demonstrem meam missionem; un- de DEUS responsum non improbat, sed signis eum instruit, ut credant, quod apparuerit ipsi Je- hovah v. 5.

## 4:2
Verse 2. CAST IT ON THE GROUND.

Miracles are extraordinary signs of the calling or doctrine of those who are sent out of the ordinary course, but because signs must correspond to the matter, R. Abraham thinks that the staff represented Pharaoh, who was like a flexible rod in the time of Joseph, but was afterwards turned into a serpent, lying in wait for the Hebrews. Lyranus, Abulensis, and Pererius more conveniently say that the Hebrew held a rod or scepter while Joseph was alive, which, after he died, when thrown down, turned into a snake, because they were hated by the Egyptians as if they were snakes, but now in the hand of Moses this snake turns back into a rod, because Moses brought liberty and dominion back to his people. Rivetus brings forward this allegory, that the rod, that is, the administration to which Moses was being called, seemed to him like a serpent at first, whence he fled from it. But it was not Moses, but the people, who were to be confirmed by those signs; therefore, the explanation of Lyranus is to be preferred, unless you prefer to say with B. Rungius that Moses seems similar to the cast-down staff when he was sent into exile, which indeed afterwards became a terror to his master. Bellarmine tries to prove from this passage that miracles are necessary for a new faith; because Moses said: they will not believe me, and God did not answer, they must believe, whether they want to or not, but gave him the power of performing miracles: whence he concludes that Luther was destitute of a calling to reform the Church, because he did not shine with miracles. But that example (1.) is entirely foreign to the state of the question concerning the truth of the faith and the Church, for these miracles were not performed on account of a new faith or religion, or for the demonstration of the Church, because the Jewish people neither doubted their faith nor were ignorant that they were the people of GOD and the true Church, but on account of liberation, so that they might believe that Moses was sent to lead out the people. Furthermore, however necessary miracles may be when those things which were previously established by GOD are to be abolished, or those things which were not previously handed down are to be established; they are, however, by no means necessary when only the state of the Church is to be amended, or divine worship is to be purged, which is evident even from the example of the pious Kings who restored the worship of GOD in the Jewish Church. Thirdly, not even this is to be conceded, that miracles are precisely necessary for every extraordinary calling. For John also was called out of the ordinary course, who yet performed no signs, as is expressly stated in John 10:41. Therefore, this example of Moses proves nothing, except that GOD sometimes adds miracles to an extraordinary calling, namely when it seems convenient or necessary to Him: but not that they are always necessary. For many causes can be given which teach that miracles were necessary at that time, whether we look at Moses, entirely unarmed and destitute of the strong hand which was required for liberation, still unknown and now an exile: or at the power and army of Pharaoh, or at the oppression and character of the people, who would have with difficulty given credence to mere words. (4.) It is a mere paralogism when Papists proceed from the mission of Moses to the Lutheran one. He was sent as a solemn legate of GOD to a gentile King, as a leader of the entire people of GOD, as a future political president and governor of the people, as a vindicator of liberty and a Savior, as a new Lawgiver, and finally as an ecumenical director of the Church. No one dreamed of such a thing regarding B. Luther: and although he instituted a reformation or purging of divine worship, he nevertheless willed it to be instituted only according to the norm of Holy Scripture, and by no means did he sanction new laws, which was done by Moses, who was called by GOD. (5.) It is therefore false that B. Luther handed down a new faith or a new worship, as he preached that eternal Gospel, Rev. 14:6, and vindicated it from the corruptions of the Papists, and required divine worship solely according to the norm of Scripture. Those things were perhaps new then in appearance, just as things that are renewed seem new, but they were not new in truth and in reality any more than the very doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, because Luther rested in Scripture alone, whence the Papists themselves call us, as if in ignominy, Scripturarians and Biblicists, and have not rarely confessed that the Augsburg Confession cannot be refuted from Holy Scriptures. (6.) Finally, the Jesuits are most mistaken in this, when they blather that we attribute an extraordinary calling to Luther; Luther himself appealed to an ordinary calling, both of the ecclesiastical ministry, by which he was called mediately to the office of teaching in the Wittenberg Church, in Comm. on the Epist. to the Galat. chap. 1. Vol. 4. Lat. Jen. fol. 8, and of the Academic Doctorate, by virtue of which he received the power of defending evangelical truth, of profligating vain and foreign doctrines, and indeed he was bound to this by oath, see Vol. 2. Jen. German, in the public admonition to the Wittenberg chapter, fol. 279, and also Vol. 5. in the explanation of Ps. 82. fol. 76, and in the gloss on the Imperial edict, Vol. same, fol. 320, as also in a certain Epistle in the same Vol. concerning secret preaching, fol. 553, and of the Theological profession, concerning which it is held in the statutes of Frederick the Wise as follows: it is yours to interpret the divine law and to teach the book of life. But although our people sometimes say that something extraordinary stands out in the calling of Luther, no one nevertheless attributes an immediate and extraordinary calling to him, just as he himself also protested about this matter, that he never boasted of an immediate calling, Epistle to the Senate of Mülhausen, Vol. 2. Jen. Germ. fol. 451. But that he says in some place that he has his Gospel from Christ alone, and said that he was certain in his cause by a higher testimony than human, and indeed called himself an evangelist, (see Epistle to Frederick the Elector, Vol. 2. Jen. Germ. fol. 57. & contra statum Clericorum fol. 107. as also against the King of England fol. 113.) it is manifest from his very own words, that he speaks only of the origin or certainty of his doctrine, namely that it is not human, but of Christ himself, nor is he certain of it through men, but through the sealing of the Holy Spirit himself. Therefore those things are not to be twisted either to an extraordinary calling or to an immediate revelation of doctrine. See more in the Tract of B. Nic. Hunnius on the Lutheran ministry, B. Gerhard, Tom. 6, Loc., and in Kesler, as also Mr. Dr. Müller in the German writings published for Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 2. PROJICE EAM IN TERRAM.

Miracula signa sunt extraordinaria vocationis aut doctrinae eorum, qui extra ordinem mittuntur, sed quia signa rei convenire debent, R. Abraham censet, baculum Pharaonem repraesentasse, qui fle- xilis virga instar fuit tempore Josephi, sed postea in ser- pentem versus est, insidiando Ebraeis. Convenientius Lyranus, Abulensis & Pererius, Ebraeus virgam sive sceptrum tenuisse ajunt, vivente Josepho, quo de- functo projecta virga in colubrum transiit, quia ex- osi fuere Aegyptiis, ac si colubri essent, nunc autem in manu Mosis hic coluber in virgam revertitur, quia Moses populo suo rursus libertatem ac domi- nationem attulit. Rivetus affert hanc allegoriam, quod virga, id est, administratio, ad quam Moses vo- cabatur, illi quasi serpens primum visa, unde fugit eam. Sed signis illis non Moses, verum populus confirmandus erat, ideo praeferenda Lyrani expli- catio, nisi malis cum B. Rungio dicere, Mosen simi- lem videri baculo projecto, cum mitteretur in exilium, qui vero hero suo terrori factus postea est. Bellarminus ex h. l. probare conatur, miracula esse necessaria ad novam fidem; quod Moses dixerit: non credent mihi, & Deus non respondit, debent credere, velint, no- lint, sed dederit ipsi potestatem miracula patrandi: unde colligit, Lutherum vocatione destitutum fuisse ad reformandam Ecclesiam, quia miraculis non cla- ruit. Verum exemplum illud (1.) ἀλλότριον pror- sus est à statu quaestionis de fidei & Ecclesiae veritate, non enim ob novam fidem vel religionem, aut ob Ecclesiae demonstrationem miracula haec fie- bant, quia nec dubitabat populus Judaicus de fi- de sua, nec ignorabat, se DEI populum esse, ve- ramque Ecclesiam, sed ob liberationem, ut crede- rent, Mosen missum esse ad educendum populum. Porro utut necessaria sint miracula, cum vel anti- quanda sunt ea, quae prius à DEO constituta sunt, vel stabilienda, quae prius tradita non sunt; neces- saria tamen minime sunt, cum emendandus solum status est Ecclesiae, aut repurgandus cultus divi- nus, quod vel exemplo piorum Regum constat, qui cultum DEI in Ecclesia Judaica restaurarunt. Tertio ne id quidem concedendum est, ad omnem vocationem extraordinariam praecise necessaria esse miracula. Nam & Johannes extra ordinem voca- batur, qui vero nulla signa edidit, ut expresse ha- betur Joh. 10, 41. nihil ergo hoc exemplum Mosis probat, nisi quod DEus addat quandoque miracula vocationi extraordinariae, tum nempe cum ipsi id videtur commodum aut necessarium: non vero quod semper illa necessaria sint. Nam dari possunt multae causae, quae tum necessaria miracula fuisse doceant, sive Mosen respiciamus inermem prorsus & manu valida, quae requirebatur ad liberationem, destitutum, adhuc ignotum jam atque exulem: seu Pharaonis potentiam & exercitum, seu populi pressuram & ingenium, qui aegre fidem nudis ver- bis adhibuisset. (4.) Paralogismus merus est, cum à Mosis missione ad Lutheranam Papistae procedunt. Ille missus fuit legatus solennis DEI ad Regem gentilem, ut ductor populi DEI universi, ut poli- ticus futurus praeses & gubernator populi, ut vin- dex libertatis ac Salvator, ut novus Legislator, de- nique ut Ecclesiae director oecumenicus. Tale quid de B. Luthero nemo somniavit: & quan- quam cultus divini reformationem vel repurga- tionem instituerit, eam tamen non nisi ad S. Scri- pturae normam institutam voluit, neutiquam ve- ro leges novas sancivit, quod à Mose θεοκλήτῳ factum. (5.) Falsum itaque est, quod B. Luther. novam fidem aut cultum novum tradiderit, utpo- te qui aeternum illud Evangelium praedicavit, A- pocal. 14, 6. & à corruptelis Papistarum vindica- vit, ac cultum divinum unice ad normam Scriptu- ræ exegit. Nova forte illa tum fuere xατα δόξαν, uti nova videntur, quæ renovantur, nova autem xατ' ἀλήθειαν & revera non magis fuere, quam ipsa doctrina Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quia in sola Scriptura S. acquievit Lutherus, unde ipsi- met Papistæ nos, quasi per ignominiam, Scriptu- rarios & Biblistas appellant, nec raro fassi sunt è Scripturis S. confessionem Augustanam refutari non posse. (6.) Denique falluntur in eo Jesuitæ maxime, cum nos extraordinariam vocationem Luthero tribuere blaterant; provocavit Luther. ipse ad ordinariam vocationem tum ministerii Ec- clesiastici, qua vocatus erat mediate ad officium docendi in Ecclesia Wittenbergensi, in Comm. in Epist. ad Galat. cap. 1. Tom. 4. Lat. Jen. fol. 8. tum Doctoratus Academici, vi cujus potestatem accepit, veritatem Evangelicam defendendi, doctrinas va- nas & peregrinas profligandi, imo jurejurando ad id adstrictus fuit, vid. Tom. 2. Jen. Germ. id admo- nitione publica ad capitulum Witteberg. fol. 279. nec non Tom. 5. in explic. Ps. 82. fol. 76. & in glossa super edictum Cæsar. Tom. eod. fol. 320. ut & Ep. quadam eod. Tom. de concionat. clancul. fol. 553. tum professionis Theologicæ, de qua in statutis Fride- rici Sapientis ita habetur: vestrum est interpretari le- gem divinam & librum vitæ docere. Quanquam vero noñunquam nostrates aliquid extraordinarii in vo- catione Lutheri eminere dicant, nemo tamen ipsi immediatam & extraordinariam vocationem tri- buit, quemadmodum etiam ipse hac de re protesta- tus est, se nunquam jactasse immediatam vocatio- nem, Epistola ad Senatum Mülhusinum Tom. 2. Jen. Germ. fol. 451. Quod autem alicubi Evange- lium suum se habere à solo Christo ait, seque superiori, quam humana testificatione in causa sua certum esse dixit, imo sese Evangelistam vocavit, (vid. Epist. ad Frid. Elect. Tom. 2. Jen. Germ. fol. 57. & contra statum Clericorum fol. 107. ut & contra Regem Angliæ fol. 113.) manifestum est ex ipsismet ver- bis ejus, quod tantum de origine aut certitudine do- ctrinæ suæ loquatur, quod nempe illa non humana sit, sed ipsius Christi, neque per homines de ea cer- tus sit, sed per ipsiusmet Spiritus S. obsignationem. Non ergo illa vel ad vocationem extraordinariam, vel ad revelationem doctrinæ immediatam detor- quenda sunt. Plur. vid. Tract. B. Nic. Hunnii de minist. Luther. B. Gerhard. Tom. 6. Loc. & apud Kesler. nec non Dn. D. Müllerum in Scriptis Germ. pro Luthero editis.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. I AM NOT ELOQUENT FROM YESTERDAY AND THE DAY BEFORE: AND SINCE THOU HAST SPOKEN TO THY SERVANT, I AM OF A MORE IMPEDED AND SLOWER TONGUE.) From yesterday and the day before, that is, until now. The Greeks, χθὲς xαὶ πρώην, use it only of a recent matter.

Those things are obscure, and carry with them the appearance as if Moses had become of impeded tongue from that, or as if terrified by this vision he had contracted a greater difficulty of speaking. In the source all things are clearer. It is a Hebraism, I am not a man of words, i.e., I am not eloquent, even from yesterday, even from the day before, i.e., I was never eloquent before this. Even from then you speaking, i.e., even from the time you have spoken to your servant, as if he were to say, I was never eloquent before, nor am I now. For I have not become more eloquent since you dealt with me. It is added, because I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue, that is, because by nature I am of an impeded tongue and slow to speak. Elsewhere those are called heavy of tongue whose words are not understood, Is. 3, 5. 6. Here, however, it signifies the same as what is said in Exod. 6, 2, that Moses was uncircumcised of lips, i.e., a stammerer. If you ask why God sent Moses, who was not eloquent, to such a employed an embassy, or did not entirely correct the defect of his tongue in himself, it seems that this was done partly with respect to the people, so that they would not ascribe the liberation to the eloquence of Moses, but to the power of GOD, who, as Theodoret says, chose even unlearned Apostles, through whom He converted the world: and partly with respect to Moses, to keep him in humility, and to render his brother Aaron, a colleague joined to him and not a little more eloquent, more acceptable, since, as Ausonius says, each took from the other what he lacked, and to teach Moses and Aaron to extend their right hands to each other, that is, to teach political and ecclesiastical leaders. But does not Stephen contradict these in Acts 7:22, when he says that Moses was powerful in words and works?

Response: Stephen does not deny that he was slow of speech, but he commends the wisdom and prudence of his discourse; for one who speaks slowly can also speak wisely and prudently, and thus be powerful in words. Those who are slow of speech are sometimes all the more effective in the power and force of their words, the more sparing and slow their tongue is. Is it doubtful whether, because someone is βραδύγλωττος (slow of tongue), he can reject a calling or ought to abandon sacred study? That excuse did not help Moses, just as a similar one did not help Jeremiah in chapter 1; but because the calling of these men was immediate and extraordinary, and furthermore could be adorned by an extraordinary collation of gifts, which are lacking today; therefore, if someone is clearly of an impeded tongue, and thus inept for the office of preaching, let him rely not so much on his own judgment as on that of others, lest perhaps occupied by carnal affection he withdraw himself under that pretext alone, and let him properly weigh the warning of Christ in Luke 9:62, so that he does not rashly draw back his hand, or do so with a wounded conscience. For although not all are equally fluent, what is looked for in sacred matters is not how much eloquence, but with how much evidence the mysteries of salvation are proposed: the power of the sacred ministry consists not in πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in ἀποδείξει πνεύματος κὶ δυνάμεως, in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, 1 Cor. 2. An infirm person does not care for an eloquent physician, but for one who heals. And although GOD today does not make men eloquent or more fluent through miracles, He nevertheless, as experience testifies, not rarely renders those who trust in Him and obey His calling eloquent, or at least powerful in words, beyond the expectation of men; for that promise has not yet expired, that GOD wishes to give σῶμα κὶ σοφίαν (a mouth and wisdom), Luke 21:15, Matt. 10:20, Luke 12:11.

Latin:

Vers. 10. NON SUM ELOQUENS AB HERI ET NUDIUS TERTIUS: ET EX QUO LOQUUTUS ES AD SERVUM TUUM, IMPEDITIORIS ET TAR- DIORIS LINGUÆ SUM.) Ab heri & nudius tertius, id est, hactenus. Græci, χθὲς xαὶ πρώην, de re tantum re- centi usurpant.

Obscura illa sunt, & præ se ferunt, ac si Moses ex eo factus sit impeditæ linguæ aut quasi territus hac vi- sione majorem contraxerit loquendi difficultatem. In fonte omnia clariora sunt. Ebraismus est, non sum vir verborum, i. e. non sum facundus, etiam ab heri, eti- am à nudius tertius, i. e. nunquam antehac eloquens fui. Etiam ex tunc te loqui, i. e. etiam ex quo locutus es ad servum tuum, quasi dicat, neǵ antea facundus unquam fui, neque jam sum. Non enim eloquentior evasi, ex quo egisti mecum. Additur, quia ore gra- vis & lingua gravis sum, id est, quia natura impedi- tæ linguæ sum & tardus ad loquendum. Alias gra- ves lingua dicuntur, quorum verba non intelliguntur Es. 3, 5. 6. Hìc vero idem significat quod Exod. 6, 2. dicitur Mosen præputiatum fuisse labiis, i. e. balbum. Si quæras, cur DEus Mosen indisertum ad tantam legationem adhibuerit, aut vitium linguæ non omnino in ipso emendavit, videtur id factum tum respectu populi, ne liberationem Mosis eloquen- tiæ adscriberet, sed DEI potentiæ, qui Theodo- reto dicente, Apostolos etiam indisertos elegit, per quos orbem convertit: tum respectu Mosis, ut in hu- militate ipsum contineret, eique adjunctum Col- legam fratrem Aaronem haud parum disertiorem magis gratum redderet, cum, quo caret alteruter, sumsit ab alterutro, ut loquitur Ausonius, & ut dex- tras sibi porrigere mutuas Mosen & Aaronem, id est, Politicos & Ecclesiasticos præsules doceret. Sed annon cum his pugnat Stephanus Actor. 7, 22. cum Mosen potentem fuisse dicit in verbis & operibus?

Resp. Stephanus non negat, tardum ad loquendum fuisse, sed sapientiam ac prudentiam orationis ejus commendat, potest autem, qui tarde etiam loqui- tur, sapienter & prudenter loqui, adeoque potens esse in verbis. Sunt quandoque tardiloqui eo effica- ciores in verborum δεινότητι, & potentia, quo par- cioris & tardioris sunt linguæ. Dubium est, an ex eo, quod quis sit βραδύγλωττος, respuere possit vocatio- nem, vel abjicere debeat studium sacrum? Non juvabat ea excusatio Mosen, uti nec similis Jeremiam cap. 1. sed quia horum vocatio immediata & extraordinaria erat, ac præterea ornari poterat extraordinaria do- norum collatione, quæ hodie deficiunt; ideo si pla- ne impeditæ linguæ quis sit, adeoque ineptus ad prædicandi munus in eo non tam suo quam alio- rum judicio nitatur, ne carnali forte affectu occupa- tus isto tantum prætextu se subducat, Christique monitum Luc. 9, 62. probe expendat, ne temere manum retrahat, aut cum vulnere conscientiæ. Nam etsi non omnes æque expediti sint, non spectatur in sacris, quanta eloquentia, sed quanta evidentia pro- ponantur salutis mysteria: non in πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπί- νης σοφίας λόγοις, persuasibilibus humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed in ἀποδείξει πνεύματος κὶ δυνάμεως de- monstratione Spiritus & virtutis vis sacri ministerii consistit 1. Cor. 2. Infirmus non curat medicum elo- quentem, sed sanantem. Et quanquam DEus hodie per miracula eloquentes aut expeditiores non red- dat, eos tamen, qui ipsi confidunt, & vocationi ejus morem gerunt, præter hominum expectationem non raro facundos, aut certe verbis potentes red- dit, teste experientia; nondum enim expiravit illa promissio, quod velit DEus dare σῶμα κὶ σοφίαν Luc. 21, 15. Matth. 10, 20. Luc. 12, 11.

## 4:11
Verse 11. WHO HAS MADE THE MUTE AND THE DEAF, THE SEEING AND THE BLIND?

These things are not attributed to God absolutely; He made the seeing through the primordial creation, for all things were created very good, and thus without any defect, which cannot be referred to creation, Gen. 1:31, Wis. 1:21. But He makes the blind, the deaf, and the mute because of transgression; for those things are from sin, and by the just judgment of God in a nature destitute, not instituted; which must be observed against the Materialists or those who seek such defects in the condition of matter, because God is said to have made the mute and the deaf. But since this Angel in the bush is still continuing the conversation with Moses, let us acknowledge that the same One said these things who through reparation did all things well, and in the days of His flesh made the deaf to hear and the mute to speak, Mark 7:33.
