Latin:

Vers. 11. QUIS FABRICATUS EST MUTUM ET SURDUM, VIDENTEM ET COECUM?

Hæc non παγίως Deo tribuuntur, videntem fe- cit per primævam creationem, omnia enim valde bo- na condita sunt, adeoque sine ullo defectu, qui ad creationem referri non potest, Gen. 1, 31. Sap. 1, 21. Cæcum autem, surdum & mutum facit ob transgres- sionem; nam illa à peccato sunt, justoque Dei judicio in natura destituta, non instituta; quod contra Ma- teriarios vel qui in materiæ conditione tales defe- ctus quærunt, quia DEus mutum & surdum fecisse dicitur, observandum. Cum vero hic Angelus in rubo adhuc colloquium cum Mose continuet, agnoscamus, eundem illum hæc dixisse, qui per re- parationem omnia bene fecit, & in diebus carnis suæ surdos fecit audire ac mutos loqui, Marc. 7, 33.

## 4:13
Verse 13. SEND, WHOM YOU WILL SEND.) The Greeks better: προχείρισαι δυνάμενον ἄλλον ὃν προχειριεῖς: that is, send someone who is fit to be sent. For שלח often signifies fitness to the Hebrews. The modesty of Moses, praised below in Num. 12:3, appears here; but he ought to have thought that those who are sent by God are also rendered fit by Him: which shone forth most in the Apostles.

The ancients took this as a sigh for the sending of the Messiah, whose proper name this was, ὁ ἐρχόμενος (the one who is to come).

Matth. 11, 3. So Justin, Tertullian, Cyprian, Eusebius. But those words are not of one praying, but of one deprecating, of one impatient, not of one making a vow: furthermore, they are uttered indefinitely, and therefore, as they cannot be restricted to a certain person (whence they are rashly restricted by Lyranus to Aaron, and by R. Solomon to Joshua who was to be sent), so they do not of themselves insinuate that Christ is to be sent, but they only mean this, that the Lord should rather send anyone else whatsoever. Nor indeed was the Messiah to be sent to lead the people out of Egyptian servitude, but to deliver them from infernal captivity. Finally, the Lord was angry because of this evasion, who certainly would not have been moved to anger in the least by a desire for the Messiah; and therefore we do not see why we should deem that sense probable with Cornelius, against the text, which Tostatus and Eugubinus from among the Papists rightly reject. But the LXX rightly expressed the sense: choose another who is able, whom you may send.

Latin:

Vers. 13. MITTE, QUEM MISSURUS ES.) Græci melius: προχείρισαι δυνάμενον ἄλλον ὃν προχειριεῖς: id est, mitte aliquem qui idoneus sit mitti. Nam שלח Hebræis sæpe quamvis aptitudinem significat. Apparet hîc modestia Mosis prædicata infra Num. 12, 3. sed cogitare debuit, qui à Deo mit- tuntur, ab eo & idoneos reddi: quod in Apostolis maxime emicuit.

Veteres id habuere pro suspirio mittendi Mef- siæ, cujus nomen hoc proprium erat, ὁ ἐρχόμενος.

Matth. 11, 3. ita Justinus, Tertull. Cypr. Euseb. Sed verba illa non precantis sunt, sed deprecantis, impatientis, non votum facientis: adhæc indefinite pro- feruntur, ideoque uti ad personam certam restrin- gi nequeunt, (unde temere à Lyrano ad Aaronem, à R. Salomone ad Josuam mittendum restringuntur) ita per se Christum mittendum non insinuant, sed id solum volunt, ut quemcunque potius alium mit- tat Dominus. Neque vero mittendus erat Messias, ut educeret populum è servitute Ægyptiaca: Sed ut liberaret è captivitate infernali. Denique iratus fuit Dominus ob hanc tergiversationem, qui certe per Messiæ desiderium ad iram minime commotus fuisset; ideoque non videmus, cur cum Cornelio sensum illum probabilem censere debeamus, invito textu, quem merito rejicit è Pontificiis Tostatus & Eugubinus. Recte autem sensum expressere LXX. elige alium, qui possit, quem mittas.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. THE LORD WAS ANGRY WITH MOSES.

Since the anger of the Lord presupposes a fault, Moses did not lack all fault, whom Basil, Jerome, and Gregory here absolve from sin. For although diffidence of oneself is not otherwise to be disapproved of, when it proceeds from true humility, yet where God calls, where He promises His presence, where He confirms it with miracles, the diffidence is untimely and vicious, and such pusillanimity and evasion is joined with some disobedience or refusal of obedience, which Abulensis, Cajetan, Cornelius, and most others acknowledge. But it is absurd what R. Solomon imagines, that Moses was passed over for the priestly dignity because of this evasion, and that it was bestowed upon his brother Aaron.

Vers. same. AARON YOUR BROTHER THE LEVITE I KNOW THAT HE IS ELOQUENT.) Thus interpreters or orators are wont to be added to legates of great authority. Moses is more excellent than Aaron, as much as the mind is than speech.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IRATUS DOMINUS IN MOSEN.

Cum ira Domini culpam præsupponat, non va- cavit omni culpa Moses, quem à peccato hîc absol- vunt Basil. Hieron. & Gregor. Nam etsi diffidentia sui improbanda alias non sit, cum ex vera humilitate proficiscitur, tamen ubi DEus vocat, ubi παράστασιν suam promittit, ubi miraculis eam confirmat, intempestiva & vitiosa est diffidentia, & pusillanimi- tas, ac tergiversatio talis cum aliqua inobedientia seu obedientiæ detrectatione conjuncta est, quod agnoscunt Abulensis, Cajet. Cornel. & plerique alii. Ineptum autem est, quod R. Salomo fingit, Mosen ob hanc tergiversationem sacerdotali dignitate præ- teritum, eamque Aaroni fratri delatam esse.

Vers. eod. AARON FRATER TUUS LEVITES SCIO QUOD ELOQUENS SIT.) Sic magnæ autoritis legatis addi interpretes aut oratores solent. Moses Aarone præstantior, quantum mens sermone.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. BUT YOU SHALL BE TO HIM IN THOSE THINGS WHICH PERTAIN TO GOD.) In Hebrew, you shall be to him for God, i.e., you shall have the right of the sword over him and others. For this name is never given to men, unless to signify the right of life and death. See below 7, 1.

The Latin version must therefore be corrected here from the Hebrew text, which yields no sense. But it does not appear whence this right of life and death can be proven from the Hebrew phrase? From the passage 7, 1, no such thing is gathered. The contrary is rather manifest from it; because the right of life and death over Pharaoh was not granted to Moses. And the name Elohim is also given to angels: but is the right of life and death therefore given to them also? That phrase therefore proves a peculiar divine authority and power, with which God armed Moses, both over Aaron, whose magistrate he was, demanding of him what he ought to speak to the people: the Chaldean renders it לְרַב for prince: and over Pharaoh, to whom he was as a God, not because he had the right of the sword over him, but because he performed a divine legation before him, and was to be heard as God; just as Exodus 7, the second verse, explains the former. Behold, I have given you as a God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your Prophet. You shall speak all things that I shall command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh. The Arabic interpretation of the Moors explains the word Elohim in the former place, Exod. 4, 16, as מַצלֹסא a teacher, an instructor; but in the latter place, Exod. 4, 16, as מַרְיא a Lord or president: it would have more correctly rendered it vice versa, instructor here, and Lord there. Because he had to instruct Pharaoh concerning the will of the Lord, but to Aaron, he was constituted Lord. The Vulgate is certainly obscure enough with the LXX Interpreters: the Hebrew is clear: you shall be to him for GOD, because Moses put words into the mouth of Aaron, but the latter was the Orator and interpreter of Moses, just as Moses was the Interpreter of GOD, for God acted immediately in this legation not with Aaron, but with Moses, but the latter was

He interpreted the will of God in the place of God for Aaron, so that he might report it to the people. Therefore, the Neophotinians wrongly infer from this that Moses is called the God of Aaron and thus Christ is called God, even if he is not God by nature. For Moses is not called the God of Aaron, but he was for Aaron לאלהים in the place of God or instead of God; but Christ is absolutely called GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 16. TU AUTEM ERIS EI IN HIS, QUÆ AD DEUM PERTINENT.) Hebraice tu eris ipsi in DEum, h. e. jus gladii habebis in ipsum & alios. Nunquam enim hoc nomen hominibus datur, nisi ad significandum jus vitæ ac necis. Vide infra 7, 1.

Corrigenda ergò hîc ex Ebræo textu Latina versio, quæ nullum reddit sensum. Non apparet autem, unde hoc jus vitæ & necis è phrasi Ebræa probari possit? E loco 7, 1. tale quid non colligitur. Contrarium potius ex eo manifestum; quia jus vitæ ac necis in Pharaonem Mosi concessum non erat. Et datur nomen Elohim etiam angelis: num vero illis etiam ideo datur vitæ ac necis jus? Probatur ergo phrasi illa peculiaris autoritas ac potestas divina, qua DEus Mosen armavit tum in Aaronem, cujus Magistratus erat, ipsi demandans, quæ ad populum loqui debeat: Chaldeus reddit לְרַב pro principe: Tum in Pharaonem, cui pro Deo erat, non quod jus gladii haberet in ipsum, sed quod divina legatione penes ipsum fungeretur, & ceu DEus audiendus esset; uti Exod. 7. versus secundus priorem explicat. Ecce dedi te Deum Pharaoni & Aaron frater tuus erit Propheta tuus. Tu loqueris omnia, quæ præcipiam tibi, & Aaron frater tuus loquetur ad Pharaonem. Interpretatio Arabica Maurorum explicat vocem Elohim priori loco Exod. 4, 16. מַצלֹסא doctorem, institutorem; posteriori vero loco Exod. 4, 16. מַרְיא Dominum vel præsidem: rectius vice versa hic institutorem, ibi Dominum reddidisset. Quia Pharaonem de voluntate Domini instituere debebat, Aaroni vero Dominus constitutus erat. Vulgata certe satis obscura est cum LXX. Interpretibus: Ebræa clara sunt: tu eris ei pro DEO, quia Moses ponebat verba in os Aaronis, hic autem erat Mosis Orator & interpres, quemadmodum Moses Interpres erat DEI, nam imediate agebat DEus in hac legatione non cum Aarone, sed cum Mose, hic autem erat

Aaroni loco DEI, & voluntatem DEI interpre- tabatur, ut illam ad populum referret. Perperam ergo hinc Neophotiniani colligunt, Mosen dici De- um Aaronis atque ita Christum Deum vocari, etsi na- tura Deus non sit. Non enim Moses dicitur Deus Aa- ronis, sed Aaroni לאלהים loco Dei vel pro Deo fuit; at Christus absolute dicitur DEUS.

## 4:17
Verse 17. IN WHICH YOU ARE TO DO SIGNS.

The rod was merely an instrument for performing miracles, used freely, in which there was no intrinsic efficacy for performing miracles, and therefore it contributed nothing, and it was an instrument not σύ- νεργον (cooperating), but παθητικὸν (passive), which you may not undeservedly compare with the clay used by Christ when he restored sight to the blind man, John 9:6. However, it is impious that Danaeus compares the flesh of Christ with the staff of Moses, since the flesh of Christ, even if it is called an instrument, ὄργανον (organ) by the Greek Fathers, is not ineffective, but endowed with infinite divine power, not separate, but ἐνυπόστατον (subsistent), not ἀεργὸν (inactive), but most highly ἐνεργητικὸν (active), as the very miracles of Christ testify, which he performed for his own honor, so that they might believe in him. Did Moses perform miracles for the honor of his staff? The Jews, however, trifle as is their custom, when they say that the name of four letters was inscribed on a quadrilateral staff, by the power of which miracles were performed, and they pretend that it grew in the garden of Jethro, which no one but Moses could pull up. The Egyptians were also foolish, who are said to have venerated that rod and to have placed a staff in the temple of Isis in its honor; see Eusebius, book 10, de praepar. Evang., last chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 17. IN QUO FACTURUS ES SIGNA.

Virga erat tantum instrumentum miraculorum patrandorum libere adhibitum, in qua nulla erat efficacia intrinseca ad miracula patranda, ideoque nil cooperabatur, eratque instrumentum non σύ- νεργον, sed παθητικὸν, quod cum luto à Christo ad- hibito, cum caeco visum restituit, non immerito compares Joh. 9, 6. Impium autem est, quod Da- naeus carnem Christi cum baculo Mosis confert, si- quidem caro Christi, etiamsi vocetur instrumen- tum, à Graecis Patribus ὄργανον, non inefficax sit, sed virtute divina infinita praeditum, non fejun- ctum, sed ἐνυπόστατον, non ἀεργὸν, sed maxime ἐνεργητικὸν, testibus ipsis Christi miraculis, quae in honorem proprium edidit, ut in se crederent. Num in honorem baculi sui miracula edidit Moses? Nu- gantur autem Judaei, pro more, cum baculo quadri- latero nomen quatuor literarum inscriptum fuisse di- cunt, cujus vi patrata sint miracula, eumque crevisse fingunt in horto Jethronis, quem praeter Mosen nemo evellere potuerit. Inepti etiam Aegyptii fuere, qui virgam illam venerati dicuntur & in templo Isidis baculum in honorem ejus reposuisse; vid. Euseb. lib. 10. de praepar. Evang. cap. ult.

## 4:19
Verse 19. ALL ARE DEAD WHO SEEK YOUR LIFE.

Since Moses knew nothing about his Israelites, as some suppose, so that there was a need for an extraordinary divine revelation, and yet the Midianites were not so far removed from the Egyptians, they infer from this that epistolary commerce was not yet in use at that time, which Rivetus also supports in this place. But that argument is shaky: for one could similarly conclude that there was absolutely no commerce between the Midianites and the Egyptians; for otherwise, even if not by letters, they could easily have learned the fate of the Israelites through messengers. And can it not be said that Moses learned other things about the Israelites within these 40 years, even if he was perhaps not entirely certain about this, whether all the enemies who were seeking his life had met their fate, and there was a need for him to be confirmed about that through an oracle? Let the Jew Apella believe that Moses, for 40 whole years, knew as little as the most ignorant people about what was happening in Egypt with the Israelites, which Rivetus affirms. That would be the mark of a man who was not touched by any care for his own people: and it cannot be presumed of Moses, who had already long ago known that deliverance was to be prepared for the people by his hand, as Stephen testifies in Acts 7:25.

Latin:

Vers. 19. MORTUI SUNT OMNES, QUI QUÆRUNT ANIMAM TUAM.

Cum nihil de Israëlitis suis resciverit Moses, quod opinantur nonnulli, ut opus fuerit extraor- dinaria divina revelatione, Midianitae vero ab Ae- gyptiis non adeo dissiti fuerint, colligunt inde, tunc in usu nondum fuisse commercia Epistolica, qui- bus etiam suffragatur Rivetus in h. l. Sed id argu- mentum vacillat: nam similiter concludi posset, nulla plane cum Aegyptiis Midianitis fuisse com- mercia; nam alias etsi non per literas, vel inter- nuncios facile sortem Israëlitarum experiri potuis- sent. Et annon Moses intra hos 40. annos alia de Israëlitis rescivisse dici potest, etiamsi de eo for- san non omnino certus fuerit, utrumne omnes ini- mici, qui animam ipsius quaerebant, fatis conces- sissent, opusque fuerit, eum de illo per oraculum confirmari? Per integros 40. annos Mosen juxta cum ignarissimis, quid in Aegypto gereretur cum Israëlitis, quod affirmat Rivetus, scivisse, credat Judaeus Apella. Id hominis foret, qui nulla suo- rum cura tangeretur: ac de Mose, qui jam olim cognoverat per manum suam salutem paratum iri populo, teste Stephano Actor. 7, 25. praesumi non potest.

## 4:20
Verse 20. ON AN ASS.

Because they could not be carried on one ass, it is to be understood distributively, that each one was placed on an ass.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ASINO.

Quia uno asino vehi non poterant, intelligen- dum est distributive, unumquemque asino impo- situm fuisse.

## 4:23
Verse 23. LET MY SON GO, THAT HE MAY SERVE ME.

That consequence seems doubtful; for if all the sons of GOD are to be let go, Christians will not be subject to secular powers, an argument which the Anabaptists have abused. But this was a peculiar son of GOD; for GOD had chosen the people of Israel as his firstborn son for this reason, that he had consecrated this one above all others to himself as his own possession, and wished to hand down his law to him and to reign in the same, whence this theocracy is not to be opposed to other kingdoms, nor should it be drawn into a precedent: for as in this people GOD reigned by himself immediately, namely by prescribing the manner and laws of government directly, by revealing his will concerning doubtful causes and cases, and by directing the whole people at his pleasure, Jud. 8:23, 1 Sam. 8:7, concerning which see Theodoret on 1 Kings, question 17. The Lord GOD fulfilled the office of Lord and King, but the Prophet was an administrator and as it were a certain prefect or leader and commander: in other kingdoms, however, GOD reigns through others, and therefore from this theocracy to any other polity [the argument does not follow].

Verse same. BEHOLD, I WILL SLAY THY SON, THY FIRSTBORN.

A certain person understands this concerning the firstborn son of Moses, but all interpreters with unanimous consent accept those words as concerning Pharaoh's son, which the same person acknowledges, nor are there solid reasons why one should depart from this consensus; indeed, it is manifest that GOD threatens Pharaoh with the slaying of his firstborn son for the reason that he himself refused to let go Israel, the firstborn son of GOD, but hardened his heart against GOD, even though he was confirmed by many miracles concerning the will of GOD. And those things cohere in the same speech, with which Moses was to address Pharaoh for the last time, after he had labored in vain to compel him to obedience by various miracles. Thus said Jehovah: Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I said to thee: let my son go, that he may serve me, but thou hast refused to let him go; behold, I will slay thy son, thy firstborn. Here the fault is designated, the stubborn reluctance of Pharaoh, by which he refused to let go the firstborn son of GOD, and the punishment for the fault is subjoined; behold, I will slay thy son, thy firstborn. If these last words are separated, as if they did not look to the speech to be held in the name of GOD before Pharaoh, that speech will be imperfect, and the fault will be indicated to Pharaoh in such a way, but the punishment will not be denounced. If those words are referred to the firstborn son of Moses, the punishment will be denounced to him alone abruptly, without any mention of the fault, both of which seem unusual. And although not only Pharaoh's firstborn was to be slain, but every firstborn in Egypt, yet to the King, who was especially at fault, that punishment was especially to be denounced which most affected him and his house. Nor did the blessed Brentius absurdly indicate that by the naming of Pharaoh's firstborn, the other firstborns were designated in a certain way: the positing of one is certainly not the negation of the other; indeed, just as the name of firstborn son is a collective noun when GOD thus names Israel his son, so nothing prevents it from being a collective noun also for the firstborn son of Pharaoh, and embracing every firstborn in Pharaoh's kingdom. If it be said that this does not pertain to the journey of Moses into Egypt. I reply: just as the repeated command, 'see that you do all the wonders,' pertained to that journey, so also the latest event contributed most to it, namely so that Moses might be confirmed in his journey, and not remain in any way doubtful about the success, for the previous sections have taught how much he hesitated and equivocated. If the Lord had only said that Pharaoh would be hardened and would resist and would not consent to the letting go of the people, Moses, who had previously resisted, would certainly have been rendered more and more doubtful in this embassy. For to what purpose is it needed, if the heart of Pharaoh is to be hardened, so that he does not let the people go? Therefore, it is not only necessary that we believe those words concerning the final plague, by which Pharaoh was to be compelled to obedience, were added by God: but it is also very likely that God dealt here with Moses at greater length, and that those things which are now set forth concisely, concerning the hardening and coercion of Pharaoh through the slaying of the firstborn with its circumstances and ends, had been more fully explained, and most of them had been commanded to him by GOD in detail, and a certain order of acting had been prescribed, because the mind of Moses had to be fortified against the stubbornness of the king, and he himself had to be fully instructed for such a great embassy, which was not to be conducted except according to the prescription of GOD. If GOD had here threatened the killing of Moses's own firstborn, on account of the omitted circumcision, it would have been very badly done by Moses, that he did not immediately upon hearing that threat institute the circumcision of his son, but that the Lord had to meet him and force him to it by the evil inflicted. Finally, that it was not the firstborn son of Moses, but the second-born who was circumcised by Zipporah, is the constant and unanimous opinion of the Interpreters.

Latin:

Vers. 23. DIMITTE FILIUM MEUM UT SERVIAT MIHI.

Consequentia illa dubia videtur, si enim omnes DEI filii dimittendi, Christiani secularibus pote- statibus non erunt obnoxii, quo argumento abusi sunt Anabaptistae. Sed peculiaris hic fuit DEI fi- lius; populum enim Israelis in filium primogeni- tum elegerat DEUS hac ratione, quod hunc prae aliis omnibus sibi in peculium consecrarit, ei le- gem suam tradere, inque eodem regnare voluerit, unde haec θεαρχία aliis regnis opponenda non est, nec in exemplum trahi debet: nam ut in hoc po- pulo DEUS per se immediate regnavit, modum nempe, ac leges regiminis ἀμέσως præscribendo, voluntatem de causis & casibus dubiis patefacien- do, populumque universum pro arbitrio dirigen- do, Jud. 8, 23. 1.Sam. 8, 7. de quo Theodor. ad 1. Reg. quæst. 17. Dominus DEUS Domini & Regis implevit munus, Propheta autem erat administer & velut quidam præfectus aut Dux & Imperator: in aliis vero regnis per alios regnat DEUS, ideoque ab hac θεαρχίᾳ ad aliam quamcunque politiam N. V. C.

Vers. eod. ECCE, EGO INTERFICIAM FILIUM TUUM PRIMOGENITUM.

De filio primogenito Mosis hæc intelligit ὁ δεῖνα, sed de Pharaonis filio illa omnes Interpp. unanimi con- sensu accipiunt, quod idem agnoscit, neque causæ solidæ sunt, cur ab hoc consensu discedatur, imo manifestum est, ideo DEUM minitari Pharaoni occifionem filii primogeniti, quod filium DEI pri- mogenitum Israelem ipse dimittere noluerit, sed corsuum adversus DEUM, utut multis miraculis de voluntate DEI confirmaretur, obdurarit. Et cohærent illa in eadem oratione, qua compellare Moses Pharaonem novissime debebat, postquam miraculis variis ad obsequium eum adigere frustra laborasset. Sic dixit Jehovah: filius meus primo- genitus est Israel, & dixi tibi: dimitte filium meum, ut serviat mihi, sed tu renuisti dimittere eum, ecce ego interficio filium tuum primogenitum. Designatur hîc culpa, pertinax Pharaonis reluctantia, qua di- mittendum filium DEI primogenitum, & subjun- gitur culpæ pœna; ecce, ego interficio filium tuum pri- mogenitum. Si separentur hæc postrema verba, quasi non spectarent ad sermonem nomine DEI coram Pharaone habendum, sermo ille imperfe- ctus erit, nec nisi culpa ita Pharaoni indicabitur, non autem pœna denunciabitur. Si referantur illa ad Mosis filium primogenitum, pœna ei solum denunciabitur ex abrupto, sine ulla culpæ men- tione, quod utrumque insolens videtur. Etsi au- tem non tantum Pharaonis primogenitus interfice- retur, sed omnis primogenitus in Ægypto, Regi tamen, qui in culpa præcipue erat, præcipue illa denuncianda erat pœna, quæ ipsum, & domum ejus maxime afficiebat. Nec absurde B. Brentius, pri- mogenito Pharaonis nominato designari certa ratio- ne cæteros primogenitos indicavit: unius certe po- sitio alterius non est negatio: imo ut collectivum nomen est filii primogeniti, cum DEUS ita filium suum nominat Israelem, ita nihil obstat, quin collectivum etiam nomen sit filii primogeniti Pha- raonis, omnemque primogenitum in Pharaonis re- gno complectatur. Si dicatur, non pertinere id ad iter Mosis in Ægyptum. Resp. ut ad illud pertinebat iteratum mandatum, vide, ut omnia ostenta facias, ita etiam novissimus eventus eo maxime faciebat, ut nempe Moses in itinere suo confirmaretur, nec ullatenus dubius hæreret de successu, quantopere enim hæsitaverit, & tergiversatus sit, superiora docuere. Si tantum dixisset Dominus Pharaonem induratum reluctaturum nec consensurum in dimissio- nem populi, Moses utiq;, qui antea reluctatus est, ma- gis magisque dubius redditus fuisset in hac legatio- ne. Ad quid enim ea opus, si indurandum cor Pha- raonis, ne dimittat populum? Ideo non tantum ne- cessum est, ut verba illa de novissima plaga, qua Pharao cogendus ad obsequium erat, adjecta cre- damus à Deo: sed valde etiam verisimile est, Deum hîc pluribus egisse cum Mose, & quæ nunc concise exponuntur, de induratione & coactione Pharao- nis per occisionem primogeniti cum suis circum- stantiis & finibus plenius fuisse exposita, & pleraque ei à DEO sigillatim mandata, certumque ordinem agendi præscriptum fuisse, quia muniendus erat Mosis animus adversus regis pervicaciam, & plene instruendus ipse erat ad tantam legationem, non nisi ex præscripto DEI gerendam. Si DEUS ipsius primogeniti Mosis occisionem, ob intermissam circumcisionem, hic minatus esset, pessime à Mose factum foret, quod non actutum audita illa comminatione circumcisionem filii instituerit, sed Dominus ei occurrere & malo illato ad eandem ipsum adigere debuerit. Denique non primogenitum Mosis filium, sed secundogenitum à Zippora circumcisum fuisse, constans & unanimis est Interpretum sententia.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. THE LORD MET HIM. Papistic interpreters say that he met him through an angel. But nothing is held in the text about an angel, even though the Chaldean and the LXX introduce an angel; the Lord could have met Moses in another way than through an angel, he could have met him immediately: therefore let it be a matter of religious scruple to define what Scripture does not define, and to introduce an angel where there is no mention of an Angel, but only of the Lord. Grotius has it thus:

LORD.) יְהוָה. Aquila: God; Symmachus and Theodotion: Lord. But the LXX [render it] more according to the sense than according to the word: angel. Concerning which matter it has been spoken of elsewhere by others and by us.

But this license was not to be excused. Because it is not within the right of an interpreter to substitute an Angel in place of Jehovah the most high GOD. Nor does it appear from the text that the Lord met him through an Angel. Therefore this sense was not to be feigned. Scripture is not of private interpretation. That it was Jehovah, not an Angel, who met him, verse 26 confirms again. For he did not have in his power to grant life to him whom the angel ought to have killed by command. Moreover, he is read to have desisted from killing Moses, his life having been granted to him, and he who previously wanted to kill him was appeased by his communion. And why does Grotius not suspect here, according to his custom, that it was formerly written אֱלֹהִים because the LXX rendered it angel? Let him therefore acknowledge that not every different interpretation of the LXX or others immediately introduces a different reading.

Vers. eod. AND HE WANTED TO KILL HIM. That the Lord wanted to kill Moses, not as Tertullian ch. 3 against the Jews and Augustine hold, whom someone supports, [but] that it was the son of Moses is evident from the text; for the pronoun refers to the preceding, and what need would there have been for Zipporah to perform the circumcision, unless Moses himself had been stuck in those straits, exposed to the danger of life? Furthermore, the name Spouse of Bloods is more conveniently attributed to Moses than to the infant. Who was as it were snatched from the danger of death by the blood of the son, of which later. Therefore Diodorus of Tarsus and Theodoret think that not the infant, but Moses himself was in danger of life. Which is also the opinion of most Interpreters. How he wanted to kill him matters little, because history is silent as to whether it was by an introduced sudden disease, or by suffocation, as it seemed to Tertullian, or indeed by a drawn sword, which pleases Theodoret and most others. But that he did not want it absolutely, nor even only by a will of a sign or a vain terror, as Rivet wants, but altogether seriously, the text itself teaches, even if the anger of the Lord was mitigated afterwards, when the son was circumcised: unless therefore he had been circumcised immediately, Moses would easily have been killed. But GOD directed these things in such a way that he both testified to his serious indignation on account of the omitted circumcision, and nevertheless preserved Moses. The cause therefore of this divine anger was not the abduction of the woman, as

Eusebius and Augustine think, or whatever else, but the omission of the circumcision of the son against the express divine constitution Genesis 17, 12, because after it was performed he dismissed Moses. Therefore that was not free from sin. For even if some wish it to have been omitted on account of his father-in-law and wife as being Gentiles, that nevertheless does not excuse Moses, that he neglected the law of GOD for their sake or for the sake of domestic peace: nor is it to be admitted at all, since circumcision pertained even to the Midianites, the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, and Zipporah was not ignorant of it, since it is said here that she herself circumcised the son.

Latin:

Vers. 24. OCCURRIT EI DOMINUS. Per angelum occurrisse, interpretes Papistici dicunt. Sed nihil de angelo in textu habetur, etsi Chaldæus, & LXX. angelum ingerant; potuit alia ratione Mosi, quam per angelum occurrere, potuit occurrere immediate: religio itaque sit definire, quod non definit Scriptura, & ingerere angelum, ubi nulla Angeli, sed Domini tantum mentio fit. Grotius ita habet:

DOMINUS.) יְהוָה. Aquila Θεὸς: Symmachus & Theodotion κύριος. At LXX. ad sensum magis, quam ad vocem ἄγγελος. De qua re alibi dictum ab aliis & nobis.

Quæ vero licentia excusanda non erat. Quia integrum non est interpreti, loco Jehovah summi DEI substituere Angelum. Neque è textu apparet, eidem occurrisse Dominum per Angelum. Fingendus ergo hic sensus non erat. Scriptura non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως. Jehovam, non Angelum fuisse, qui ei occurrit, vers. 26. iterum confirmat. Vitam enim ei donare, quem occidere ex mandato debuisset angelus, in potestate sua non habebat. Idem autem ab interficiendo Mose destitisse vita eidem donata per ejus communionem placatus legitur, qui interficere prius ipsum volebat. Et cur hic non pro more suo suspicatur Grotius, olim scriptum fuisse אֱלֹהִים quia LXX. reddidere ἄγγελος. Agnoscat itaque non quamvis diversam LXX. aut aliorum interpretationem diversam actutum inferre lectionem.

Vers. eod. ET VOLEBAT EUM OCCIDERE. Mosen Dominum occidere voluisse, non ut Tertull. cap. 3. contra Judæos & August. volunt, quibus suffragatur ὁ δεῖνα, Mosis filium è textu evidens; pronomen autem ad antecedentia se refert, & quid opus fuisset, ut Zippora perageret circumcisionem, nisi Moses ipse in istis angustiis hæsisset vitæ discrimini expositus? Porro nomen Sponsi Sanguinum convenientius Mosi, quam infanti tribuitur. Qui sanguine filii quasi ereptus è mortis discrimine, de quo postea. Ideo Diodor. Tarsens. & Theodoret. non infantem, sed Mosen ipsum in discrimine vitæ hæsisse censent. Quæ plerorumque etiam Interpp. est sententia. Quomodo voluerit occidere, parum refert, quia historia tacet, an morbo subitaneo immisso, aut præfocatione, ut Tertulliano visum, an vero gladio stricto, quod Theodoreto & plerisque aliis placet. Non autem absolute voluisse, nec etiam tantum voluntate figni aut inani terriculamento, ut Rivet. vult, sed serio omnino, textus ipse docet, etsi postmodum ira Domini mitigata fuerit, cum circumcideretur filius: nisi ergo circumcisus fuisset illico, facile interfectus fuisset Moses. Sed DEUS hæc ita direxit, ut & seriam testaretur indignationem, ob circumcisionem intermissam, & Mosen nihilominus sospitaret. Causa ergo fuit hujus iræ divinæ, non abductio mulieris, ut

Eusebius & Augustin. putant, aut quæcunque alia, sed intermissio circumcisionis filii adversus expressam constitutionem divinam Genes. 17, 12. quia post peractam eandem dimisit Mosen. Non ergo peccato illa vacabat. Etsi enim nonnulli eam intermissam velint ob socerum & uxorem ceu gentiles, id tamen neque excusat Mosen, quod in gratiam ipsorum aut pacis domesticæ causa legem DEI neglexerit: nec admittendum omnino est, siquidem etiam ad Midianitas Abrahæ ex Cethura posteros circumcisio pertinuerit, & Zippora ejus ignara non fuerit, cum hic dicatur ipsa filium circumcidisse.

## 4:25
Vers. 25. ZIPPORAH TOOK IMMEDIATELY A VERY SHARP STONE.

Augustine thinks that the knife was stone, so named from the material, who also thinks that such an instrument was necessarily used in the Sacrament of circumcision. Others say that a stone was used also by reason of the place, namely Arabia Petraea, in which there was a greater abundance of stones than of iron, so that stones were even sharpened like iron. But from a comparison with John 5, 2, it appears that knives were accustomed to be prepared from sharp stones, make for yourself stone knives. The LXX render it, stone swords, from a sharp stone, whence Andreas Masius in his Commentary teaches that the Israelites then used sharp stones after the example of Zipporah; for fragments of flint are also sometimes found no less suitable for cutting than knives of steel, and Lery is the author that the Brazilians also used sharp stones in making bows and clubs. However, such an instrument was not precisely necessary, because in the institution of circumcision in Genesis 17, it is not defined. The Jews in their constitutions decree thus: it is a precept that one be circumcised with iron, whether it be a knife or a razor. Concerning a case of necessity, however, they hand down thus: it is permitted to circumcise with anything, even with a stone and glass. Since therefore this was a case of necessity, it will be the same, whether he says a knife was used, or any instrument that was at hand.

Regarding the efficient cause of circumcision, the matter is plain from the text, namely that Zipporah performed it in this instance, a point which some Calvinists attempt to render doubtful in vain, lest they be forced to admit that a woman can administer baptism in a case of necessity, given that in such a case circumcision, in whose place baptism has succeeded, was administered by Zipporah. They say that Zipporah only procured the circumcision, but did not perform it herself, and that Moses performed it; but this openly contradicts the text; for not to mention that Moses, on account of that extreme anxiety and extreme danger of death, could not have performed that act, the Holy Spirit expressly attributes the act of circumcision itself to Zipporah; for the same reason that He attributes it to Abraham when he circumcised his sons, Gen. 17:23, ch. 21:4. Furthermore, it says that Zipporah took a knife and cut off the foreskin of her son; therefore she did not only procure that cutting off; finally, it is added in the text that she herself threw the cut-off foreskin at his feet, that is, at the feet of Moses. Therefore, not only do the Hebrews, R. Solomon, Aben-Ezra, and Bechai acknowledge that Zipporah herself performed the circumcision, but Calvin, Tremellius, Piscator, and other Reformed theologians also admit it, as does Rivetus himself in the earlier edition of his Commentary on Exodus.

But as for Calvin accusing Zipporah of rashness in this, he reveals his own rashness, because Zipporah appeased the wrath of the Lord with this act of hers, as is stated in the text, and He desisted from him. Whence the Rabbis acknowledge that the circumcision was lawfully performed by her, and thus in their traditions they propose this canon: all are fit to perform circumcision (in a case, to wit, of necessity), even a slave, a woman, and a minor, and an uncircumcised Israelite whose brothers have died from circumcision. Finally, it is evident from the example of Hebrew mothers that women also performed circumcision, 1 Maccab. 2, 62; 2 Maccab. 6, 16. Rivetus, however, betrayed the first lie of his error in these words: No necessity lies upon either a private person or a woman to usurp another's right in baptizing. Indeed, if the Calvinists believed in the necessity of baptism as a means, as they call it, which Christ delivered in John 3:5, they would judge more correctly here without doubt. Nor indeed do they usurp another's right who dispense the sacrament of baptism in a case of necessity; because the sacraments are goods of the Church, which, although it ordinarily provides for baptism through ministers of the word, in an extraordinary case does not reject others, because it is better for an unordained person to baptize out of order than for infants to be deprived of the Sacrament of regeneration.

Verse of the same. AND SHE CUT OFF THE FORESKIN OF HER SON.

Cajetan posits an enallage of number and thinks both sons were circumcised; most other interpreters understand it of the younger son. Dr. Sebastian Schmidt in his treatise on circumcision thinks the firstborn was circumcised here. It is more probable that the firstborn had already been circumcised before, and that Moses had not delayed the sacrament of circumcision for a whole year, whence Zipporah not only was not ignorant of the rite of that sacrament, but, moved by the very necessity of it, administered it herself. For if neither son had yet been circumcised, it would have been necessary for both to be circumcised here, which is abhorrent to the text. If it be asked: Why then did Moses not administer the circumcision of the younger son at the proper time, the text indicates no cause. But preparation for the journey and his own haste could have been the cause: yet he himself ought not to have neglected the commandment of GOD for this or any other cause, and because he had neglected it, the Lord was by no means willing to bear this in him, as the future lawgiver and guardian of the law, among the people of the Lord. What Cajetan says, that Zipporah as a Gentile woman wished to keep one of the sons in the rite of her own gentility, that is, uncircumcised, is sufficiently refuted by the act of circumcision, which she did not hesitate to perform herself, and by the religion and piety of Zipporah, which shines forth from this history.

Verse 25. AND SHE TOUCHED HIS FEET.

Some understand the feet here to be those of the angel who was pressing upon Moses, but from a false hypothesis, as if the Lord wished to kill Moses here through an angel. Others say the infant's feet were touched with blood. But most more correctly refer these things to Moses, to which, among the Papists, Oleastrius, Eugubinus, Saa, Pererius, as also Baradius, lib. 1, Itinerar. Israël. c. 17, subscribe. They understand that phrase, however, in such a way that she threw the foreskin at the feet of her husband Moses, which they explain in various ways. Those Papistical interpreters whom we mentioned think this act was done out of indignation, because Zipporah had need to shed blood; but even if she had done this indignantly, it can be explained in a better light, namely, that she was indignant because Moses had brought danger of life upon himself by the intermission of circumcision. Others say Zipporah moved the foreskin to Moses' feet, so that if indeed Moses were affected by a disease because he had not circumcised his son before at his appointed time, he might now be healed again by the application of the blood of circumcision. Cornelius à Lapide says that contact of the feet was made for the sake of reverence, such reverence as they are accustomed to show to the Pope by kissing his feet; and the LXX interpreters, as also the Chaldeans, seem to take it for a reverential contact, as it is said in the Targum Hierosolymitanum, that she applied the foreskin to the feet of the destroying angel, saying: my husband wished to circumcise, but his father-in-law did not permit it: now therefore be propitious on account of the blood of this circumcision to the sins of my husband. It seems simplest if it be said that she touched Moses' feet with the foreskin, so that she might show what she had brought upon herself by it, and might give him hope of liberation, namely, by the completion of that which the Lord required.

Verse of the same. A SPOUSE OF BLOODS ART THOU TO ME.

R. Abraham wishes these to be spoken to the circumcised boy as words of one coaxing, and that mothers thus called their newly circumcised sons their spouses; but that cannot be proven. Commonly they refer it to Moses; some, like Rabanus, as words of an indignant person, because he himself was the cause of the shedding of blood, which, however, we think is alien to the piety of Zipporah, because she herself did not abhor the act of circumcision. Others say that Zipporah indicated this: I see that you will be a laborious and bloody spouse to me, the omens testify to it: therefore let me go that I may return home. But this also is alien. Therefore, with Kimchi, and Fagius, and others, we say that Moses is so called because she had as it were redeemed him with the son's blood, which, had she not circumcised him, would have been the end of the husband's life. The word, therefore, is not one of indignation, but of thanksgiving, because she had as it were acquired her husband anew as a spouse, even though this redemption cost the son's blood. Thus any pious person in a bloody and sanguinary affliction, as for instance some martyr, can address Christ, without reproach by the word of faith: you are a spouse of bloods to me.

Verse of the same. BECAUSE OF THE CIRCUMCISION.

In Hebrew the plural number occurs, whence also the name of the sacrament of circumcision מולות (circumcisions) has stuck. Tremellius and Piscator refer this to the circumcisions of both sons: but since only one is circumcised here, others more correctly judge that the plural is used on account of the diverse acts of circumcision, with R. Bechai. Mr. Dr. Sebastian Schmidt refers it to the circumcision both internal spiritual and external corporal, Rom. 2:29. Most simply it is said that an enallage, not unusual for the Hebrews, occurs here.

Latin:

Vers. 25. TULIT ILLICO ZIPPORA ACUTISSIMAM PETRAM.

Cultrum fuisse petrinum à materia sic denominatum August. censet, qui etiam necessario tale instrumentum adhibitum putat in Sacramento circumcisionis. Alii petram usurpatam dicunt ratione loci etiam, Arabiæ nempe Petrææ, in qua major petrarum, quam ferri erat copia, ita ut petræ etiam instar ferri acuerentur. Sed è collatione Johann. 5, 2. apparet, cultros è petris acutis parari consuevisse, fac tibi cultros petrarum. LXX. reddunt, gladios petrinos, ex petra acuta, unde Andreas Masius in Commentar. acutis lapidibus Israelitas tunc usos fuisse ad exemplum Zipporæ docet; nam & reperiuntur quandoque silicum fragmenta non minus ad secandum apta, quam cultri è chalybe, & autor est Lerius, Brasilienses etiam in fabricandis arcubus & clavis acutis lapidibus usos esse. Non tamen necessarium fuit tale præcise instrumentum, quia in institutione circumcisionis Genes. 17. id definitum non est. Judæi in constitutionibus suis ita sanciunt: præceptum est, ut circumcidatur ferro, sive culter sit sive novacula. De casu tamen necessitatis sic tradunt: quacunque re circumcidere licet, etiam lapide & vitro. Quum ergo hic casus fuerit necessitatis, perinde erit, sive cultrum adhibitum dicat, sive quodvis instrumentum, quod in promtu fuit.

De causa autem efficiente circumcisionis è textu res plana est, quod nempe Zippora in hoc casu eam peregerit, quod frustra dubium reddere conantur Calviniani nonnulli, ne scilicet opus habeant admittere mulierem in casu necessitatis baptismum administrare posse, eo, quod in tali casu circumcisio, in cujus locum baptismus successit, à Zippora administrata fuerit. Dicunt, Zipporam procurasse tantum circumcisionem, non vero ipsam, sed Mosen eandem peregisse, verum hoc palam refragatur textui; nam ne dicamus, quod Moses ob illam summam anxietatem, & extremum mortis periculum, actum illum peragere nequiverit, tribuit Spiritus S. diserte Zipporæ ipsum circumcisionis actum; eadem ratione, uti Abrahamo illum tribuit, cum filios suos circumcidit Genes. 17, 23. cap. 21, 4. Adhæc dicit, sumpsisse Zipporam cultrum & abscidisse præputium filii, non ergo tantum procuravit eam abscissionem; denique additur in textu, quod abscissum præputium ipsa projecerit ad pedes ejus, hoc est, Mosis. Ideo non tantum Ebræi, R. Salomon, Aben-Ezra, Bechai agnoscunt, quod ipsa Zippora circumcisionem peregerit; sed fatentur etiam id Calvinus, Tremellius, Piscat. & alii Reformati, ut & Rivetus ipse in priori Editione Commentarii in Exod.

Quod vero Calvinus temeritatis in eo accusat Zipporam, temeritatem ipse prodit suam, quia Zippora placavit hoc facto suo iram Domini, ut habetur in textu, & destitit ab eo. Unde Rabbini agnoscunt licite factam ab ipsa circumcisionem, adeoque in traditionibus suis canonem hunc pro- ponunt: omnes apti sunt ad circumcisionem peragen- dam (in casu scil. necessitatis) etiam servus, mulier & minorennis & præputiatus Israëlita, cujus mortui sunt fratres ex circumcisione. Denique constat ex- emplo matrum Ebræarum, mulieres etiam cir- cumcisionem peregisse 1. Maccab. 2, 62. 2. Maccab. 6, 16. Prodidit autem πρῶτον ψεῦδος erroris sui Rivetus his verbis: Nulla incumbit necessitas, ut vel privatus vel fœmina baptizando alienum jus usurpet. Nimirum si necessitatem baptismi ratione medii, quam vocant, crederent Calviniani, quam Chri- stus tradidit Joh. 3, 5. rectius hîc fine dubio senti- rent. Nec vero jus alienum usurpant, qui in casu necessitatis sacramentum baptismi dispensant; quia sacramenta bona sunt Ecclesiæ, quæ etsi ordinarie baptismum procuret per ministros verbi, in casu tamen extraordinario alios non respuit, quia præ- stat, personam non ordinatam baptizare extra or- dinem, quam Sacramento regenerationis privari infantulos.

Vers. eod. CIRCUMCIDIT PRÆPUTIUM FILII SUI.

Cajetanus Enallagen numeri statuit & utrumque filium circumcisum putat; plerique alii interpre- tes de filio minori natu intelligunt. Dn. D. Se- bast. Schmidt tract. de circumcis. primogenitum cir- cumcisum hîc putat. Probabilius est, primoge- nitum jam antea circumcisum fuisse, nec distu- lisse Mosen per integrum annum sacramentum circumcisionis, unde Zippora ritum illius sacra- menti non modo non ignorabat, sed ipsa necessi- tate ejusdem mota administravit. Nam si neu- ter filius circumcisus adhuc fuisset, oportuisset omnino utrumque hic circumcidi, quod à textu abhorret. Si quæratur: Cur ergo minoris natu filii circumcisionem non justo tempore admini- stravit Moses, causam nullam textus indicat. Sed potuit præparatio ad iter, & festinatio ipsius in causa esse: non tamen ipse neglexisse debebat man- datum DEI seu ob hanc, seu ob aliam causam, & quia neglexerat, in ipso ceu futuro νομοθέτᾳ le- gisque custode, apud populum Domini, hoc fer- re minime volebat Dominus. Quod Cajetanus dicit Zipporam tanquam fœminam gentilem voluis- se unum ex filiis retinere in ritu gentilitatis suæ, hoc est, incircumcisum, id satis refellitur ex actu cir- cumcisionis, quem ipsa peragere non dubitavit, & ex religione ac pietate Zipporæ, quæ ex hac hi- storia elucet.

Vers. 25. TETIGITQUE PEDES EJUS.

Pedes hic intelligunt nonnulli, angeli, qui Mosi incumbebat, sed ex falsa hypothesi, quasi Do- minus per angelum occidere Mosen hic voluerit. Alii infantis pedes cruore tactos fuisse dicunt. Sed rectius plerique ad Mosen hæc referunt, quibus è Pontificiis Oleastrius, Eugub. Saa, Perer. ut & Ba- rad. lib. 1. Itinerar. Israël. c. 17. suffragantur. Phra- sin autem illam ita intelligunt, quod præputium ad pedes mariti Mosis projecerit, quod diversimode ex- plicant. Illi, quos diximus Papistici Interpp. fa- ctum hoc ex indignatione putant, quod Zippora opus habuerit sanguinem fundere; sed etiamsi in- dignabunda hoc fecisset, explicari in meliorem id partem potest, quod indignata nempe fuerit ideo, quod Moses sibi periculum vitæ accersiverit cir- cumcisionis intermissione. Alii dicunt Zipporam admovisse præputium pedibus Mosi, ut siquidem Moses affectus esset morbo propterea, quod non circumcidisset antea filium definito suo tempore, nunc iterum sanetur ex admotu sanguinis circum- cisionis. Cornel. à Lapid. contactum illum pedum reverentiæ caufa factum dicit, qualem reveren- tiam & ofculum pedum Papæ exhibere folent; & videntur LXX. Interpp. ut & Chaldæi pro reveren- tiali contactu habere, uti in Targum Hierofolym. dicitur, applicuiffe præputium ad pedes angeli deva- ftatoris, dicendo: fponfus meus volebat circumcidere, at focer ejus non permittebat: nunc E. propitius efto propter fanguinem circumcifionis iftius peccatis fponfi mei. Simpliciffimum videtur, fi dicatur tetigiffe pedes Mofis præputio, ut monftraret, quid illo fibi accerfiverit, & fpem faceret ipfi liberationis, expe- dito nempe illo, quod Dominus requirebat.

Verf. eod. SPONSUS SANGUINUM MI- HI ES.

Hæc ad puerum circumcifum dicta vult R. Abra- ham tanquam blandientis verba, & quod ita filios recens circumcifos matres appellarint fponfos fuos; fed id probari nequit. Communiter referunt id ad Mofen; nonnulli ut verba indignantis cum Ra- bano, quod ipfe caufa fuerit fundendi fangui- nem, quod vero nos à pietate Zipporæ alienum putamus, quia non abhorrebat ipfa ab actu circum- cifionis. Alii dicunt, id indigitaffe Zipporam: video te mihi fore fponfum laboriofum & fanguinari- um, teftantur de eo aufpicia: dimitte E. me ut domum redeam. Sed & hoc alienum eft. Proinde cum Kimchio, & Fagio, aliisque Mofen ita vocatum dici- mus, quod quafi redemerit eum filii fanguine, quem nifi circumcidiffet, actum fuiffet de vita Mariti. Vox ergo eft non indignationis, fed gratulationis, quod maritum quafi fponfum de novo fibi compa- rarit, etfi filii fanguine hæc redemtio conftiterit. Ita Chriftum quilibet pius in afflictione cruenta & fanguinaria, utpote Martyr aliquis, compellare poteft, citra exprobrationem verbo fidei: tu mihi fponfus fanguinum es.

Verf. eod. OB CIRCUMCISIONEM.

In Ebr. occurrit plur. numerus, unde etiam no- men hæfit facramento circumcifionis מולות (circumcifiones.) Tremell. & Pifcat. id referunt ad circumcifiones utriusque filii: fed cum unus tantum hîc circumcifus fit, alii rectius propter diverfos actus circumcifionis cum R. Bechai pluralem adhi- bitum cenfent. Dn. D. Sebaft. Schmidt refert illum ad circumcifionem tum internam Spiritualem, tum externam corporalem Rom. 2, 29. Simpliciffime di- citur, enallagen Ebræis non inufitatam hîc occur- rere.

## 4:26
Verse 26. AND SHE LET HIM GO, AFTER SHE HAD SAID, A BRIDEGROOM OF BLOODS BECAUSE OF THE CIRCUMCISION.) The sense in the Hebrew is easier: And she departed from him: (Zipporah from Moses) But she had said a bridegroom of bloods, because of the circumcisions, that is, because of the custom of circumcision, which seemed strange to the Midianite woman. See below 18, where Zipporah returns to her husband.

He rashly corrects the Vulgate, which correctly expressed the sense. It is not said that Zipporah departed from Moses, but the Lord. Which Grotius could have learned from the Hebrew text, if he had inspected the same here: because the verb is of the masculine, not the feminine gender. Without cause, therefore, is Zipporah accused of having deserted Moses because of the circumcision of her son. Nor is any such thing hinted at below in chapter 18; indeed, it is said there that Moses had sent his wife back to her ancestral home. Zipporah had been more correctly instructed concerning the true worship of God. Therefore she herself administered the sacrament of circumcision. Which she would by no means have done, if she had abhorred it so greatly.

Latin:

Verf. 26. ET DIMISIT EUM, POSTQUAM DIXE- RAT, SPONSUS SANGUINUM OB CIRCUMCISIO- NEM.) Senfus in Hebræo facilior: Et difceffit ab eo: (Se phora à Mofe) Dixerat autem fponfus fanguinum, ob circum- cifiones, id eft, ob morem circumcifionis, qui Madianitidi mirus videbatur. Vide infra 18. ubi Sephora ad maritum redit.

Temere corrigit Vulgatam, quæ fenfum recte expreffit. Non Sephora à Mofe difceffiffe, fed Do- minus dicitur. Quod ex Ebræo textu difcere potu- iffet Grotius, fi eundem hîc infpexiffet: quia ver- bum eft mafculini, non fæminini generis. Sine cau- fa ergo accufatur Sephora, quod ob circumcifio- nem filii Mofen deferuerit. Nec infra tale quid cap. 18. innuitur, imo dicitur ibi Mofes uxorem ad patri- os lares remififfe. Rectius inftituta fuit Sephora de vero Dei cultu. Ideo ipfa facramentum circumci- fionis adminiftravit. Quod minime feciffet, fi ab eadem tantopere abhorruiffet.

## 4:27
Verse 27. INTO THE MOUNT OF GOD.) Where GOD had appeared to Moses through an angel.

The name of GOD added is accustomed to bring about an increase; but that it is a surname for a thing most great and admirable, as R. Kimchi observes in Ps. 65, as the terror of God, i.e., the greatest.

Gen. 35, 5. fire of God Job 1, 16. etc. But B. Glaff. in Gramm. S. lib. III. part. I. c. 60. rightly warned that this meaning is only ἑπομένην or consequent: Πρώτως truly and primarily the proper meaning is retained. Thus it is certain that the mountain of God is here primarily named from the apparition of God made in that place. Therefore GOD appeared there, not indeed an angel merely representing the person of GOD. Concerning which it was spoken to chapter 3, 4. Therefore he ordered the shoe to be removed; which honor it is nowhere read that a created angel caused to be shown to himself.

Latin:

Verf. 27. IN MONTEM DEI.) Ubi DEUS per ange- lum Mofi apparuerat.

Solet nomen DEI additum ἄυξησιν inferre; fed cognomen effe rei maximæ & admirabilis, ut R. Kim- chi in Pf. 65. obfervatum, ut terror Dei, i.e. maximus

Gen. 35, 5. ignis Dei Job. 1, 16. &c. Recte autem mo- nuit B. Glaff. in Gramm. S. l. III. part. I. c. 60. hanc fignificationem tantum esse ἑπομένην seu consequen- tem: Πρώτως vero & primario retineri propriam significationem. Ita montem Dei hic primario ab apparitione Dei ibidem facta nominari certum est. Apparuit ergo ibi DEUS, non vero angelus solum personam DEI repræsentans. Quo de ad cap. 3, 4. dictum. Ideo calceamentum solvi jussit; quem ho- norem sibi angelum creatum exhiberi curasse, nu- spiam legitur.

## 4:29
Vers. 29. ELDERS.) In the number of the LXX. Exod. 24, 1. 9. Num. 11, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 29. SENIORES.) Numero LXX. Exod. 24, 1. 9. Numer. 11, 16.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

The legates of GOD Moses and Aaron are rejected by Pharaoh. The Israelites are more oppressed.

Vers. 1. MOSES AND AARON ENTERED.

It is a doubt, when GOD ordered in chapter 3, 18, you shall go, you and the elders of Israel, to the King of Egypt, why Moses and Aaron did not join the elders to themselves here? It is the opinion of Tostatus, Pererius, and Cornelius that they did not wish to be joined for fear of the tyrant. The Jews say that Aaron took their place. It is more correctly said that only the heads of the embassy are named here, the others are not excluded, nay, it is not obscurely hinted that they were present with Moses and Aaron, through the response of Pharaoh, go to your burdens: for these things could not be said to Moses and Aaron. We see, however, here that Moses by no means stirred up sedition under the pretext of religion, but solicited the King for the dismissal of the people. He was led, therefore, by a different Spirit than the Anabaptists, Zwinglians, and Papists, who not rarely oppose themselves to Princes under the pretext of religion, stir up sedition, or plot their extermination. How the Jesuits absolve subjects from the bonds of an oath, and defend the slaughter of Kings even in public writings, is known to the common people, whence the seditious genius, which Corn. Lapideus marks here in Calvin with a black coal, he ought to have sought altogether in his own bosom and that of his associates at the same time.

Vers. same. LET MY PEOPLE GO.

Josephus says that Moses revealed to the King that oracle which he received on Mount Sinai, and enumerated the prodigies given to him. Whatever may be the case regarding that, it is certain that only the sum of the matter is reported here, and that the legates altogether must have used a more prolix speech to the King.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

Legati DEI Moses & Aaron respuuntur à Pha- raone. Israelitæ magis premuntur.

Vers. 1. INGRESSI SUNT MOSES ET AARON.

DUbium est, cum jusserit DEUS cap. 3, 18. ibis tu & senes Israel ad Regem Ægypti, cur hic se- niores non adjunxerint sibi Moses & Aaron? No- luisse illos adjungi metu tyranni, Tostati, Pererii, & Cornelii est sententia. Judæi dicunt Aaronem eo- rum vicem subiisse. Rectius dicitur, hic nominari solum capita legationis, cæteros non excludi, imo haud obscure innui, quod adfuerint Mosi & Aaro- ni, per responsum Pharaonis, ite ad onera vestra: hæc enim Mosi & Aaroni dici non poterant. Vi- demus autem hic, Mosen neutiquam prætextu re- ligionis seditionem excitasse, sed Regem pro dimis- sione populi solicitasse. Alio ergo Spiritu duceba- tur, quam Anabaptistæ, Zwingliani & Papistæ, qui religionis obtentu Principibus non raro se oppo- nunt, seditionem excitant, aut exterminium eo- rum moliuntur. Quomodo Jesuitæ subditos à vin- culis juramenti absolvant, cædemque Regum Scri- ptis etiam publicis defensitent, in vulgus notum est, unde seditiosum genium, quem in Calvino hic atro carbone notat Corn. Lapideus, simul in sinu suo & sociorum quærere omnino debuisset.

Vers. eod. DIMITTE POPULUM MEUM.

Josephus dicit, Mosen Regi oraculum illud aperuisse, quod in monte Sina accepit, & pro- digia enumerasse sibi data. Quicquid de eo sit, certum est, summam hic tantum rei referri, ac prolixiori oratione omnino usos fuisse Legatos ad Regem.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. WHO IS THE LORD, THAT I SHOULD HEAR HIS VOICE, I DO NOT KNOW THE LORD.

This Cyclopean voice does not betray ἄγνοιαν or an all-encompassing ignorance of GOD, the knowledge of whom is inscribed in the hearts of all, so that it can by no means be entirely obliterated, since consciences accuse themselves, even of the most impious, up to the day of judgment, as the Apostle testifies Rom. 2, 14. Whence it is impossible for there to be speculative Atheists, destitute of all sense of divinity, concerning which we spoke in Tom. 2. Loc. p. 97. But it betrays a contempt of the true God: who is that Jehovah, I do not know the Lord, that is, I do not care for this Jehovah, whom you boast of; for words of knowledge among the Hebrews imply affection. And since Pharaoh served the Egyptian idols, he was not altogether destitute of every sense of divinity, even if he neither knew nor wished to know the true GOD. Therefore, he opposes himself to Jehovah, relying on his own power, perhaps also trusting in his own idols. Incorrectly, therefore, is it gathered from this that he was a mere Atheist. But that Hornejus, distinguishing with Thomas, says that GOD is known by Himself indeed, if we look at the thing in itself; but that to us it is not known by itself, but ought to be demonstrated from effects, that is partly absurd, because if it is known by itself, it must be known to us; for it is called known with respect to another to whom it is known: in itself nothing is known, even if it be knowable, but when it is called known, it is understood that it is known to another: it is partly contrary to Scripture, which asserts not only a natural knowledge of GOD that is acquired, but also an innate one, which is the remainder of the primeval knowledge of God inscribed upon the hearts of men at creation in the image of GOD, Rom. 1:21, ch. 2:14. It seems to Rivetus that Pharaoh had not heard that name Jehovah before, and he gathers this from this place, which we leave in its own place. The Egyptians could certainly have perceived the knowledge of Jehovah from the Israelite people, who in their midst served the true GOD, therefore they are all the more inexcusable. But these voices are more of extreme pride than of mere ignorance, therefore when the Legates again inculcated GOD of the Hebrews and appealed to his command, Pharaoh, having held that in contempt, accused the legates of GOD only of sedition, because they were the authors of disturbances among the people, ver. 4. But Cajetan rightly observes here that the Tetragrammaton name is not unutterable, because Moses and Aaron expressed it before Pharaoh, who himself also repeated it twice.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUIS EST DOMINUS, UT AU- DIAM VOCEM EJUS, NESCIO DOMI- NUM.

Hæc vox Cyclopica non prodit ἄγνοιαν vel omnimodam ignorantiam DEI, cujus notitia omni- um cordibus inscripta est, ut obliterari plane haud- quaquam possit, cum accusent se conscientiæ, etiam maxime impiorum usque ad diem judicii, teste A- postolo Rom. 2, 14. Unde impossibile est dari Athe- os speculative, sensu omni divinitatis destitutos, quo de Tom. 2. Loc. diximus p. 97. Sed contemtum veri Dei: quis est ille Jehovah, nescio Dominum, id est, non curo Jehovam istum, quem jactatis; verba enim notitiæ apud Ebræos affectum inferunt. Et cum idolis Ægyptiis servierit Pharao, omni utique sen- su divinitatis destitutus non fuit, etsi verum DE- um neque sciverit neque scire voluerit. Opponit E. se Jehovæ sua fretus potentia, forsan etiam ido- lis suis confisus. Perperam itaque hinc colligitur, eum mere Atheum fuisse. Quod vero Hornejus cum Thoma distinguens dicit, DEUM esse, per se quidem notum esse, si rem in se spectemus; no- bis autem id per se notum non esse, sed ex effectis demonstrari debere, id partim absurdum est, quia si per se notum id est, nobis notum sit oportet; notum enim dicitur respectu alterius, cui notum est: in se nihil notum est, etsi cognoscibile sit, sed cum notum dicitur, alteri notum id esse intelli- gitur: partim Scripturæ contrarium, quæ non tan- tum naturalem DEI notitiam ἐπίκτητον adserit, sed etiam ἔμφυτον, quæ residua est ex primæva θεογνω- σίᾳ in creatione ad imaginem DEI cordibus ho- minum inscripta, Rom. 1, 21. cap. 2, 14. Riveto vi- detur, quod nomen illud Jehóvah Pharao antea non audiverit, idque ex h. l. colligit, quod suo loco relinquimus. Potuere certe Ægyptii à po- pulo Israelitico notitiam Jehovæ percepisse, qui in medio eorum DEO vero serviebat, proinde eo magis sunt ἀναπολόγητοι. Voces autem hæ magis sunt extremæ superbiæ, quam meræ ignorantiæ, ideo cum iterum DEUM Ebræorum inculcarent & ad ejus mandatum provocarent Legati, illo sus- que deque habito Pharao legatos DEI solum seditionis accusavit, quod turbarum auctores essent in populo verf. 4. Recte autem obser- vat hîc Cajetanus, nomen Tetragrammaton non esse ἀνέκφραστον, quia Moses & Aaron ex- pressere illud coram Pharaone, qui & ipse illud bis repetiit.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. THAT WE MAY GO A JOURNEY OF THREE DAYS.) You have translated well, let it be permitted to us to go: for נֵלְכָה is often that of one praying.

Latin:

Vers. 3. UT EAMUS VIAM TRIUM DIERUM.) Bene verteris, liceat nobis ire: nam נֵלְכָה sæpe est pre- cantis.

## 5:5
Vers. 5. AND PHARAOH SAID.

To Moses and Aaron, but not, as Cornel. wishes, to the Prefects of the works. For here the response of Pharaoh, given to the Legates of GOD, is continued. Only in the following verse is the edict to the Prefects of the works subjoined. The Vulgate here has it less correctly, it is to be amended thus from the Hebrew: Behold, the people of the land are many now, and you have made them cease from their burdens. It is a wonder that Pharaoh did not immediately decree something harsher against Moses and Aaron; but that is to be attributed not to his clemency, but to divine providence, by which He so moderated his spirit that He kept him within the threats of words.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DIXITQUE PHARAO.

Ad Mosen & Aaronem, non autem, ut vult Cornel. ad Præfectos operum. Continuatur enim hîc responsio Pharaonis, Legatis DEI data. Sequenti demum versu subjungitur edictum ad præfectos operum. Vulgata hîc minus recte ha- bet, ita ex Ebræo emendanda: Ecce, multus nunc populus terræ, & fecistis eum cessare ab one- ribus suis. Mirum, quod nihil durius statue- rit actutum Pharao in Mosen & Aaronem; ve- rum id non ejus clementiæ, sed divinæ providen- tiæ acceptum ferendum, qua ita animum ejus moderatus est, ut eum intra minas verborum re- tinuerit.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. YOU SHALL NO MORE GIVE STRAW TO THE PEOPLE.

The use of straw was either for kindling a fire, as Bernhard thinks, or if the bricks were not fired, but hardened and dried by the sun, for mixing with the clay, so that the clayey material might be better bound together, on which clay Rivetus is prolix here.

Vers. eod. AS BEFORE.) From Symmachus, καθάπερ καὶ πρότερον: Well to the sense, although the Greeks also say χθὲς καὶ πρώην. But in a slightly different sense, as we just said.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NEQUAQUAM ULTRA DABITIS PALEAS POPULO.

Usus palearum fuit vel ad accendendum ignem, ut Bernhard. putat, vel si lateres non igne cocti, sed sole indurati & exiccati fuere, ad commixtio- nem cum luto, ut materia lutosa melius adstringe- retur, in quo luto prolixus hîc est Rivetus.

Vers. eod. SICUT PRIUS.) Ex Symmacho, καθάπερ καὶ πρότερον : Bene ad sensum, quanquam & Græci di- cunt χθὲς καὶ πρώην. Sed paulo alio sensu, ut modo di- ximus.

## 5:8
Vers. 8. FOR THEY ARE IDLE, AND THEREFORE THEY CRY OUT.) They are wanton from idleness. See what is at the beginning of this book.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VACANT ENIM, ET IDCIRCO VOCI- FERANTUR.) Otio lasciviunt. Vide quæ initio hujus libri.

## 5:16
Vers. 16. AND IT IS DEALT UNJUSTLY AGAINST THY PEOPLE.) In Hebrew, thy people sins: that is, your Egyptians do us an injury. For thus we are accustomed to speak when we complain about the Kings themselves, by way of pleasantry, as Aben-Ezra noted. The Greeks, neglecting this figure, ἀδικήσεις ἐν τὸν λαόν σε.

They do not explain the Hebrew text in the same way: Some with Grotius interpret: and thy people sins: Others explain: it is sinned against thy people. They call the Israelites the King's people, so that they may mitigate his spirit. Trem. and Jun. followed Aben-Ezra with Grotius, They wish them to be called Egyptians in this way, but they explain it thus: Thy servants are beaten, when the fault is of thy people, that is, of the Egyptians, who do not supply straw, and demand the former labor from us. But the former sense is simpler and flows from the words themselves: behold, thy servants are beaten with lashes, and thy people sins: for the overseers complain, and that they, the servants of the King, are beaten with lashes, and the people of the King, the Israelites, are held as sinners, or treated in the same way: for the name of sin among the Hebrews is accustomed to be taken for the punishment of sin. Whence the Vulgate correctly expresses the sense: and it is dealt unjustly against thy people: but B. Luther emphatically insinuates the Hebraism. Dein Volck muß Sünder seyn.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ET INJUSTE AGITUR CONTRA POPU- LUM TUUM.) Hebraice, peccat populus tuus: id est, in- juriam nobis faciunt Ægyptii tui. Sic enim solemus loqui, ubi de Regibus ipsis conquerimur, κατὰ χαριεντισμὸν, ut notavit Aben - Esdra. Græci neglecto hoc schemate, ἀδι- κήσεις ἐν τὸν λαόν σε.

Ebræum textum non eodem modo explicant: Nonnulli cum Grotio interpretantur: & peccat po- pulus tuus: Alii exponunt: peccatur in populum tuum. Israelitas vocant populum Regis, ut animum ejus mi- tigent. Trem. & Jun. cum Grot. Aben-Ezram secuti, Ægyptios sic vocari volunt, sed hoc modo expo- nunt: Servi tui cæduntur, cum culpa sit populi tui, id est, Ægyptiorum, qui stramen non suppeditant, & pristinum laborem à nobis exigunt. Sed prior sensus simplicior est & ex ipsis verbis fluit: en, famuli tui flagellis cædimur, & peccat populus tuus: queruntur enim Præfecti, & se famulos Regis flagellis cædi, & populum Regis Israelitas tanquam peccatores haberi, vel eodem modo tractari: nomen enim peccati apud Ebræos solet pro pœna peccati accipi. Unde sensum recte exprimit Vulgatus: & injuste agitur contra populum tuum: Ebraismum autem emphatice insinuat B. Luther. Dein Volck muß Sünder seyn.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. THEY SAW THEMSELVES IN EVIL.

Or that they (the Israelites) are in evil. It is hinted that only now at last did they perceive that their lot, or that of the people, was most miserable: for that is what the phrase, to be in evil, imports.

Latin:

Vers. 19. VIDERUNT SE IN MALO.

Vel eos (Israelitas) in malo esse. Innuitur, quod nunc demum senserint sortem suam, vel populi miserrimam esse: id enim phrasis, in malo esse, im- portat.

## 5:20
Vers. 20. GOING OUT FROM PHARAOH.

It is not understood as Moses and Aaron, as the words in the Vulgate sound, but the overseers of the children of Israel who had gone out from Pharaoh, who had pleaded the cause of the people in vain before Pharaoh. Therefore the overseers were coming to meet one another, going out from Pharaoh, and Moses and Aaron, who were standing opposite, were waiting for them as they were going out, as it appears, to this end, that they might learn how they had been received by the King, and what they had accomplished.

Latin:

Vers. 20. EGREDIENTES A PHARAO- NE.

Non intelligitur Moses & Aaron, ut in Vulgata verba sonant, sed præpositi filiorum Israel egressi à Pharaone sunt, qui causam populi nequicquam coram Pharaone perorarant. Veniebant ergo sibi invicem obviam Præfecti egredientes à Pharaone, ac Moses & Aaron, qui ex adverso stabant, ipsis egredientibus, præstolantes eosdem, ut apparet, hac fini, ut discerent, quomodo à Rege ipsi exce- pti fuerint, quidque effecerint.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. LET THE LORD SEE AND JUDGE.

These words seem to be those of people praying for evil, but from the Hebrew they can be rendered in the future, the Lord will look upon you, and will judge, so that they are the words of those denouncing divine judgment. The word for judging is used by the custom of the Hebrews by metonymy for vengeance, as Heb. 13, 4.

Vers. eod. YOU HAVE MADE OUR ODOR TO STINK BEFORE PHARAOH.) Thus are the authors of liberty accustomed to be received by ungrateful peoples, when successes are not according to their wish. See also below 14, 11.

In Hebrew, in the eyes, that is, in the sight of Pharaoh. A metaphor taken from natural things, which breathe an odor, whether to refresh or to offend the brain, which are transferred to morals, whether pleasing or odious, compare Gen. 34, 30. Whence Bernard, Sermon 71 on the Canticles: morals have their colors, they have also odors; color in the conscience, odor in reputation.

Latin:

Vers. 21. VIDEAT DOMINUS ET JUDI- CET.

Verba hæc videntur imprecantium esse, sed ex Ebræo reddi possunt in futuro, videbit Dominus super vos, & judicabit, ut sint verba denunciantium judicium divinum. Vox judicandi more Ebræo- rum per Metonymiam pro vindicta usurpatur, ut Ebr. 13, 4.

Vers. eod. FOETERE FECISTIS ODOREM NO- STRUM CORAM PHARAONE.) Ita ab ingratis popu- lis excipi solent libertatis auctores, ubi successus non sunt pro voto. Vide & infra 14, 11.

In Ebr. in oculis, id est, in conspectu Pharaonis. Metaphora à rebus naturalibus desumta, quæ odo- rem spirant, seu ut recreent, sive ut cerebrum of- fendant, quæ ad mores transferuntur, sive gratos sive odiosos, confer. Genes. 34, 30. Unde Bernhard. Serm. 71. in Cantic. habent mores suos colores, habent & odores; colorem in conscientia, odorem in fama.

## 5:22
Vers. 22. AND MOSES RETURNED TO THE LORD.

The LXX more correctly rendered it 'turned,' because in his prayers he turned himself in this necessity to the Lord.

Vers. eod. WHY HAVE YOU AFFLICTED THIS PEOPLE?

GOD is said to have afflicted the people, first (1.) συγ- χωρητικῶς or permissively, second (2.) ἀφορμητικῶς or occasionally, third (3.) κυβερνητικῶς by governing and setting a salutary goal, but not (4.) ἐνεργητικῶς by effecting, so that Pharaoh would afflict; for this is not attributed to God, but Pharaoh himself is established as the cause of that matter, who αὐτομάτως afflicted the people, as the words immediately joined have it: from the time I came to him, he has afflicted this people. Rivetus with his associates does not approve of this explanation as truly Catholic and analogous to the faith. He rejects the former members, explains the third differently, and especially assumes the fourth, which we exclude. To the first mode, therefore, he retorts: If he is said to have afflicted by permission, he must also be said to lie, because GOD permits this. But we do not posit permission alone, nor is the reason for permission always the same: things that are merely sins are permitted in one way, while things that also have the character of punishment, such as this affliction was, are permitted in another. To the second he retorts that it cannot be said that GOD gave the occasion for doing that which happens contrary to His counsel and will, because God is ignorant of nothing. But the knowledge of God is one thing, and the Will and counsel of God is another. However, it must not be granted to Rivetus that it was the will of God that Pharaoh should afflict the people more; for Rivetus himself acknowledges that that wicked affliction by Pharaoh proceeded from vengeance, ambition, and avarice; how then shall such counsel be attributed to God without crime? Wherefore it is one thing for God to have willed to permit the affliction of the people, and another for God to have willed the affliction itself. But as for the argument that all the evils which are inflicted upon us by men are governed by divine Providence, Soph. 1, 12, Amos 3, 6, we do not deny that, but from it, it is by no means to be inferred that this was the counsel and will of God, that the people should be afflicted and oppressed: since His counsel and will was rather that the people should be released: or that Pharaoh, in the way he exercised truculent cruelty, was an instrument of God, when he was rather an instrument of the devil. It is rightly said that God did not will to restrain the mind of Pharaoh, which was inclined to tyranny, so as to prevent him from following his own instinct. But this must be understood correctly; for even if He did not will to restrain him by force, or to compel him by irresistible operation, there is no doubt that He willed to restrain him by word and by reasons, because for that reason He sent His messengers to Pharaoh. Finally, what is added, that God by wondrous and ineffable modes according to the will of His good pleasure directed the mind of Pharaoh in a clearly contrary manner against the people and into their affliction, that is altogether alien to God. For God does not do one thing in words and intend another in His counsel; those wondrous and ineffable modes, because they are not read as revealed in the word of God, but are founded only in the hidden and absolute decree of Calvin, are deservedly rejected by us. That GOD most justly afflicted the people, whom Pharaoh was unjustly vexing, is ἐξαγώνιον. For the question is not about justice, but about the mode of divine concurrence with injustice, which must be defined from the word of God in such a way that God does not concur positively, whether by an effable or ineffable, or known, or wondrous and hidden reason, because God can in no way be the Author of sin: but that the malice be imputed to man, and only permission, coercion, governance, or the offering of some accidental occasion be left to God: there is no doubt that GOD is the cause of the evils of punishment, but since He does not inflict them by Himself and immediately, and the fault of men intervenes, through whom they are afflicted, it is necessary to remove that evil of fault altogether from God, so that God is neither the physical nor the moral cause of it, even if He is rightly established as the cause of punishment as a just judge.

Same verse. WHY HAVE YOU SENT ME?

Which words are not of contumacy or indignation, but of inquiry and prayer, as Augustine rightly says, qv. 14 in Exod., nay rather of boldness and confidence, with which Moses indeed demands liberation from God, and requires its maturation thus μετὰ παῥῥησίας, but he does not wickedly expostulate with God about that affliction of the people, because he was certain of the leading out of the people, having been confirmed by God Himself: but when this more grievous affliction of the people intervened, about which he had not been forewarned, Moses means to say this: to what end have you sent me, if they must only groan and perish under this pressure, and You will not hasten the liberation which You promised. Therefore, Calvin's sharper censure of Moses, the man of God, that he sought release from his office here, is not to be approved, being akin to the accusation of the Jews, who because of They trifle by saying that Moses was forbidden to enter the land of Canaan because of this reproach; whence Rivetus could not excuse his Calvin here, even though for his sake he snatched at a middle opinion, that the holy man suffered something human here, and that a certain struggle of faith is detected in him, which delay and the importunity of the people had excited. For to him who pours out his grief before God in prayers, and invokes His grace with confidence, and does not receive a rebuff from God nor is reproved, it is wrongly imputed, whether that he wishes to cast off his calling, or that he bears the divine delay impatiently.

Latin:

Vers. 22. REVERSUSQUE EST MOSES AD DOMINUM.

Rectius LXX. conversus, reddiderunt, quia in precibus convertit se in hac necessitate ad Do- minum.

Vers. eod. CUR AFFLIXISTI POPULUM ISTUM?

DEUS afflixisse populum dicitur tum (1.) συγ- χωρητικῶς sive permissive, tum (2.) ἀφορμητικῶς, sive occasionaliter, tum (3.) κυβερνητικῶς gubernan- do & metam præstituendo salutarem, non vero (4.) ἐνεργητικῶς efficiendo, ut Pharao affligeret; hoc enim non Deo tribuitur, sed ejus rei causa ipse Pha- rao constituitur, qui αὐτομάτως populum afflixit, ut verba immediate subjuncta habent, ex quo in- gressus sum ad eum, afflixit populum istum. Non pro- bat Rivetus cum sociis hanc explicationem vere Ca- tholicam, & fidei analogam. Priora membra re- probat, tertium aliter explicat, quartum imprimis assumit, quod nos excludimus. Ad primum ergo modum regerit: Si ob permissionem afflixisse dica- tur, etiam dicendus est mentiri, quia hoc permittit DEus. Sed non solam permissionem statuimus, nec permissionis eadem semper est ratio: aliter permit- tuntur ea, quæ peccata tantum sunt, aliter ea, quæ etiam rationem pœnæ habent, qualis hæc erat affli- ctio. Ad alterum regerit, dici non posse DEum dedis- se occasionem faciendi id, quod evenit præter ejus con- silium & voluntatem, quia Deus nihil ignorat. Sed aliud est notitia Dei, aliud Voluntas & consilium Dei. Fuisse autem hanc Dei voluntatem, ut Pharao ma- gis affligeret populum, Riveto concedendum non est; improbam enim illam Pharaonis afflictionem fuisse profectam è vindicta, ambitione & avaritia agnoscit ipse Rivetus, quomodo ergo tale consili- um Deo tribuetur sine crimine? Quapropter aliud est voluisse Deum permittere afflictionem populi, ali- ud voluisse Deum ipsammet afflictionem. Quod ve- ro urgetur, à divina Providentia gubernari mala omnia quæ nobis ab hominibus inferuntur Soph. 1, 12.
