Amos 3, 6. id non negamus, sed ex eo minime in- ferendum est Dei hoc consilium & hanc voluntatem fuisse, ut affligeretur & premeretur populus: siquidem consilium & voluntas ejus potius fuerit, ut dimit- teretur populus: aut Pharaonem, qua truculentam sævitiam exercebat, instrumentum Dei fuisse, cum ita potius fuerit instrumentum diaboli. Animum Pharaonis ad tyrannidem propensum noluisse De- um retinere, quo minus instinctum suum sequere- tur, recte dicitur. Sed dextre intelligendum est; etiamsi enim vi noluerit retinere, aut cogere ope- ratione irresistibili, verbo tamen & rationibus re- tinere voluisse, dubitandum non est, quia ideo Legatos suos ad Pharaonem misit. Denique quod additur, Deum miris & ineffabilibus modis pro volun- tate beneplaciti direxisse animum Pharaonis plane contraria ratione adversus populum & in afflictionem ejusdem, id à Deo prorsus alienum est. Non enim aliud verbis agit Deus, aliud consilio suo intendit; modi illi miri & ineffabiles, quia non in verbo Dei patefacti leguntur, sed in Calvini solum abscondi- to & absoluto decreto fundantur, merito à nobis reprobantur. Justissime populum afflixisse DEum, quem injuste vexabat Pharao, ἐξαγώνιον est. Non enim de justitia quæritur, sed de modo concursus divini ad injustitiam, qui è verbo Dei ita definien- dus est, ut non positive concurrat Deus, sive effabili sive ineffabili, sive nota, sive mira & abscondita ra- tione, quia Deus nullo modo Autor peccati esse potest: sed ut malitia homini imputetur, Deo so- lum permissio, coercitio, gubernatio aut accidentalis cujusdam occasionis oblatio relinquatur: malorum pœnæ causam esse DEUM nullum est dubium, sed cum ea non per se & immediate infligit, & hominum culpa intervenit, per quos affliguntur, malum illud culpæ à Deo prorsus removere oportet, ut neque physica, neque moralis causa ejusdem Deus sit, etiamsi pœnæ causa ceu justus judex recte con- stituatur.

Vers. eod. QUARE MISISTI ME?

Quæ verba non sunt contumaciæ vel indignatio- nis, sed inquisitionis & orationis, ut recte August. qv. 14. in Exod. imo παῥῥησίας & fiduciæ, qua nempe liberationem postulat Moses à Deo, ejusque ma- turationem ita μετὰ παῥῥησίας requirit, non autem de illa populi afflictione improbe cum Deo expo- stulat, quia certus erat de eductione populi à Deo ipso confirmatus: at cum interveniret hæc gravior populi afflictio, de qua præmonitus non erat, id dicere vult Moses: ad quid me misisti, si tantum ge- mendum & pereundum est ipsis sub hac pressura, nec quam promisisti, liberationem, maturabis. Non ergo probanda Calvini censura acrior in Mosen, Dei virum, quod absolutionem ab officio hic ex- petierit, gemina Judæorum accusationi, qui ob hanc exprobrationem Mosen prohibitum fuisse in- gredi in terram Canaan nugantur; unde Calvinum suum hîc excusare non potuit Rivetus, etsi in ejus gratiam mediam sententiam arripuerit, quod hu- mani aliquid hîc sanctus vir passus fuerit, & in eo lu- cta quædam fidei deprehendatur, quam mora & populi importunitas excitaverint. Qui enim in precibus effundit dolorem suum apud DEum, ejusque gra- tiam provocat, cum fiducia, nec à Deo repulsam fert aut reprobatur, illi perperam affingitur, sive quod abjicere velit vocationem suam, sive quod impatienter ferat moram divinam.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. Moses is encouraged anew, and through him the people. The genealogy of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.

Ver. 1. FOR BY A STRONG HAND HE SHALL LET THEM GO. A strong hand denotes power to the Hebrews, but understand it not as the strong hand of Pharaoh, but as the power and operation of the Lord, as is evident from a comparison with chap. 3, 20.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. Animatur de novo Moses, & per eum populus. Genealogia Ruben, Simeonis, & Levi.

Vers. 1. PER MANUM ENIM FORTEM DIMITTET EOS. Manus fortis Ebræis potentiam notat, intellige autem non manum fortem Pharaonis, sed po- tentiam & operationem Domini, ut è collatione cap. 3, 20. constat.

## 6:3
Ver. 3. WHO APPEARED TO ABRAHAM, ISAAC AND JACOB AS GOD ALMIGHTY.) As one who could perform promises.

AND MY NAME ADONAI I DID NOT MAKE KNOWN TO THEM.) Adonai for יהוה, as the Hebrews read, to preserve reverence for the principal name. The sense, however, as the coherence indicates, is: I did not show myself to be Him who would in reality fulfill the promises. For the word אהיה points to that, and from it יהוה was made: my words are things. Rabbi Solomon saw this.

Concerning the name יהוה, and its origin, pronunciation, signification, and the proper sense of this text, (because it flowed from there, and the completion of the treatment seemed to demand it) we have dealt fully at Gen. 2, 4, so that there is no need to add much here. It does not denote primarily Him who fulfills promises, or bestows being upon them. Primarily, by this word is expressed ὁ ἀυτοὼν, whom you would rightly call ἀυταυτὸν, or rather ἀυταυτώτατον.

These things, therefore, are not to be understood of the names אֵל שַׁדַּי & יהוה (which the Vulgate rendered by אֲדֹנָי, just as some explain these as the names themselves, Lucas Burgensis, Cornel. à Lapid., Brentius in part, Flacius, Osiander & Franzius; nor of the signification of these names, as Cajetan and others understand; nor of the public use of the name Jehovah, which sense pleased some, but of the things signified by those names. For it is false that the name Jehovah had not yet been made known to the Patriarchs until Moses, seeing that it is read very often in Genesis, even where the words of the Patriarchs are reported verbatim, e.g., of Abraham, Gen. 20, 5, chap. 24, 3, and of God Himself to the Patriarchs, Gen. 15, 7, c. 18, 14, c. 28, 13. and it is by no means to be believed that they had that word without its signification; nor is there any reason why the public use of this name should not have flourished before Moses; indeed, the Patriarchs are said to have preached in the name of Jehovah. Nor, indeed, are these things to be taken simply concerning the things signified, but κατά τι & συγκριτικῶς, namely, that God had hitherto demonstrated Himself to the Patriarchs as Almighty, but had not so explained the virtue of the name Jehovah. Some wish to imply here that the name Adonai was not revealed to the Patriarchs. But these only betray their ignorance of the Hebrew language, and do not deserve to be refuted: since the name יהוה is written here, even though the Vulgate expressed it by Adonai; my name Adonai I did not make known to them; who also did not attain the Hebrew diction in this, that he rendered it 'I did not make known,' like the Chaldean, whom R. S. Jarchi argues against on that account; since he ought to have interpreted it thus: I was not known to them by my name Jehovah. Others, therefore, understand this of the virtue of the name; as do some Rabbis, who confess that the name itself was indeed known to the Fathers before Moses, but that its efficacy and θαυματουργικὴν virtue became known only through Moses, who performed his miracles by it, with that name inscribed on the staff which he used as an instrument in performing miracles. Which opinion is no less ridiculous than it is superstitious. Hieronymus ab Oleastro invents a new interpretation of the name Jehovah: namely, that it should be derived from הוה to crush, rather than from הוה to be, and thus it signifies properly God, insofar as He is crushing, and slaying, and destroying, and changing evil events, so that this is the genuine understanding of those words: I was not seen by the Fathers by the name Jehovah, that is, of one laying waste, crushing, and destroying kingdoms and nations for your sake, as I will now show. But neither can that etymology be approved, since it is too evident that the name of God is more correctly deduced from הוה than from הוה, which, if not always, is certainly for the most part used in a bad sense; nor does the explanation of the passage agree with the truth; since God was also known as laying waste, destroying, and crushing in the flood, the overthrow of Sodom, etc. Some interpret the divine words thus: I am Jehovah, and I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, and I was not known to them only in the name Jehovah; which opinion Brentius mentions in his Commentary on this passage, but does not approve, saying, let him who wishes embrace it. We, however, cannot embrace the same; because he not only inserted the exclusive particle לבד (only) by private daring beyond necessity, but also departed from the text, in which the whole discourse teaches that not so much the names El Shaddai as the name Jehovah is regarded, and is particularly inculcated by God. Others interpret it concerning the public use of the name Jehovah: that this name was not so frequented before Moses as the name El Shaddai. But this contributes little to the speech or intention of God; nor does it agree with the words themselves, which speak of the Fathers Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, not of the people indiscriminately; nor finally can it be taught that the name El Shaddai was more frequently used than the name Jehovah before Moses. From Genesis it is certainly not clear. Whence therefore will it be proved? Some insert an exclusive, i.e., I appeared in God Almighty, & not only in the name Jehovah, but that insertion is too arbitrary and lacks precedent. Others more conveniently understand the last member interrogatively, i.e., and did I not indicate to them my name Jehovah, as the blessed Lord Dr. Dorsch in his dissertation on the name Jehovah p. 8 explains לא for הלא, is it not, from similar passages, Exod. 8:26, Job 3:12, Lam. 1:12. The more common interpretations are these: First, that a clearer knowledge was reserved for Mosaic times, as Augustine, Gregory the Great, Damascene, and the Ordinary Gloss explain & Pererius, which opinion even Brentius himself did not disapprove, inasmuch as the name Jehovah is the name of the divine essence, of which they maintain a clearer knowledge was revealed to Moses. Pelargus refers it to a clearer knowledge of the Word, that is, the Son of God, adducing for this purpose the Jerusalem paraphrase. The other interpretation is that the discourse is about experimental knowledge, that the preceding Patriarchs had not yet sufficiently perceived by experimental knowledge that God is Jehovah, that is, He who not only is Himself ὁ ἀυτὼν, but also gives being to His promises, and thus causes them to be true, as if to say, you shall know me, not only as ὄντα, but also as ἐσίοντα. Which explanation pleased R. Solomon, Fagius, Vatablus, Lippomannus, Junius, Tremellius, Amama, and of our own, the blessed Bugenhagen, the blessed Rungius, and the blessed Brentius himself, which as the most convenient loc. cit.

we have followed. Care must be taken here, however, lest with the Socinians the name Jehovah be established as denoting nothing other than truth and the certainty of divine promises; for although it sometimes implies that, and in this place is used for the same reason, it does not, however, express only the truth of God in His promises, nor does it have regard only to the works of GOD, of which God is the cause and author, as the being of beings, but primarily it designates the absolute being of God and the immutability of the divine essence, from which also immutable truth flows, as has been demonstrated more fully in the same place.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QUI APPARUIT ABRAHAMO, ISAACO ET JACOBO IN DEO OMNIPOTENTE.) Ut qui possem præstare promissa.

ET NOMEN MEUM ADONAI NON INDICAVI EIS.) Adonai pro יהוה, ut Hebræi legunt, ad servandam reverentiam nomini præcipuo. Sensus autem est, ut cohæ- rentia indicat, non ostendi me eum esse, qui reipsa promissa implerem. Eo enim spectat vox אהיה, & inde facta יהוה: verba mea res sunt. Vidit hoc Rabbi Salomo.

De nomine יהוה, ejusque origine, pronuncia- tione, significatione, & textus hujus proprio sensu, (quia inde fluebat, & tractationis complementum id exigere videbatur) plene egimus ad Genes. 2, 4. ut hîc multa addere opus non sit. Non notat præ- cipue eum, qui promissa implet, vel esse eis largitur. Primario exprimitur hac voce, ὁ ἀυτοὼν, quem ἀυ- ταυτὸν, vel potius ἀυταυτώτατον recte dixeris.

Hæc ergo intelligenda non sunt de nominibus אֵל שַׁדַּי & יהוה (quod reddidit Vulg. per אֲדֹנָי quemadmodum hæc de nominibus ipsis explicant nonnulli, Lucas Burgensis, Cornel. à Lapid. Brentius ex parte, Flacius, Osiander & Franzius; nec de signi- ficatione horum nominum, ut Cajetanus & alii in- telligunt; nec de publico nominis Jehovah usu, qui sensus quibusdam placuit, sed de rebus per no- mina illa significatis. Falsum enim est, nomen Je- hovah nondum indicatum fuisse Patriarchis usque ad Mosen, utpote quod in Genesi sæpius legitur, etiam ubi ἀυτολεξεὶ verba Patriarcharum referun- tur, v. g. Abrahami, Genes. 20, 5. cap. 24, 3. Deique ipsius ad Patriarchas Genes. 15, 7. c. 18, 14. c. 28, 13. & sine significatione vocem illam ipsos habuisse, nul- latenus credendum est; neque causa ulla subest, cur publicus nominis hujus usus non viguerit ante Mosen, imo Patriarchæ prædicasse dicuntur in no- mine Jehovah. Neque vero de rebus significatis hæc simpliciter accipienda, sed κατά τι & συγκριτικῶς, quod nempe magis DEus omnipotentem sese hacte- nus demonstrarit Patriarchis, non autem ita virtu- tem nominis Jehovah explicavit. Nonnulli nomen Adonai Patriarchis revelatum non fuisse, hic innui volunt. Sed hi ignorantiam Ebrææ linguæ tan- tum produnt, nec refutari merentur: quum hic nomen יהוה scriptum sit, etsi Vulgatus per Ado- nai expresserit; nomen meum Adonai non indicavi eis; qui etiam in eo assecutus non est dictionem E- bræam, quod reddiderit, non indicavi, ut Chal- dæus, quem eo nomine arguit R. S. Jarchi; quum ita interpretari debuerit, non cognitus sum eis nomi- ne meo Jehovah. Alii ergo intelligunt hoc de nomi- nis virtute; utpote Rabbini nonnulli, qui fatentur nomen ipsum quidem cognitum fuisse Patribus ante Mosen, sed efficaciam & virtutem ejus θαυμα- τουργικὴν per Mosen, qui per hoc sua ediderit mira- cula, nomine isto inscripto baculo, quo ceu instru- mento utebatur in patrandis miraculis, demum in- notuisse. Quae sententia non minus ridicula, quam superstitiosa est. Hieronymus ab Oleastro novam cominiscitur nominis Jehovah interpretationem: quod nempe ab הוה conterere potius, quam ab הוה esse, derivandum sit, adeoque significet proprie DEum, quatenus est conterens, & mactans, & destruens, malosque eventus immutans, ut sit hic germanus verborum illorum intellectus: Non vi- sus sum Patribus nomine Jehovah, id est, vastantis, conterentis, & destruentis regna & gentes propter vos, sicut nunc ostendam. Sed nec Etymologia illa pro- bari potest, quum nimis evidens sit, rectius ab הוה fuit, deduci nomen Dei, quam ab הוה quod si non semper, plerumque certe in malam partem usurpa- tur; nec explicatio loci congruit veritati; quan- doquidem DEus etiam ut vastans, perdens, conte- rens fuerit cognitus in diluvio, eversione Sodomae &c. Nonnulli sic interpretantur verba divina: Ego sum Jehovah, apparuique Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo, ut DEus omnipotens, & non tantummodo in nomine Je- hovah cognitus sum illis; quam sententiam comme- morat, non autem approbat Brentius in Com- ment. ad h. l. sed amplectatur eam, inquit, qui volet. Nos autem eandem amplecti non possumus; quia non tantum praeter necessitatem ausu privato inse- rit particulam exclusivam לבד tantum, sed & rece- dit a textu, in quo non tam nomina El Schaddai, quam nomen Jehovah respici, atque peculiariter a Deo inculcari, tota oratio edocet. Alii de nominis Jehovah publico usu interpretantur: quod non ita frequentatum fuerit nomen istud ante Mosen, quemadmodum nomen El Schaddai. Sed parum hoc facit ad orationem vel intentionem Dei; neque verbis ipsis congruit, quae loquuntur de Patribus Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, non de populo promiscue; nec denique doceri potest, magis usu frequenta- tum fuisse nomen El Schaddai, quam nomen Jeho- vah ante Mosen. E Genesi certe id non liquet. Unde ergo id probabitur? Nonnulli inserunt ex- clusivam h. m. ego apparui in Deo omnipotente, & non tantum in nomine Jehovah, sed illa infertio nimis arbitraria est & exemplo caret. Alii convenien- tius interrogative postremum membrum intelli- gunt h. m. & annon indicavi ipsis nomen meum Jehovah, uti B. Dn. D. Dorsch. in disp. de nomine Jehovah p. 8. לא explicat pro הלא nonne, e locis similibus, Exod. 8, 28. Job. 3, 29. Thren. 1, 12. Com- muniores interpretationes hae sunt: Primo quod cognitio clarior reservata fuerit Mosaicis tempori- bus, ut explicat Aug. Greg. M. Damasc. Glossa Or- din. & Perer. quam sententiam nec ipse Brentius improbavit, siquidem nomen Jehovah essentiae di- vinae nomen sit, cujus clariorem notitiam Mosi pa- tefactam fuisse statuunt. Pelargus refert ad clario- rem notitiam verbi, id est, Filii Dei, adducens eam in rem paraphrasin Hierosolym. Altera inter- pretatio est, quod de experimentali notitia sermo fit, quod nondum satis perceperint praedecessores Patriarchae notitia experimentali DEum esse Jeho- vam, hoc est, illum, qui non solum ipse est ὁ ἀυ- τοὼν, sed promissis etiam suis dat esse, adeoque facit ut verae sint, q. d. cognoscetis me, non solum ὄντα, sed & ἐσίοντα. Quae explicatio placuit R. Salomoni, Fagio, Vatablo, Lippomanno, Junio, Tremell. Amama, & e nostris B. Bugenhagio, B. Rungio, ipsique B. Brentio, quam ceu convenientissimam loc. cit.

sequuti sumus. Cavendum tamen hic erit, ne cum Socinianis statuatur nomen Jehovah nihil aliud, quam veritatem & promissionum divinarum certitu- dinem notare; nam quamvis eam quandoque infe- rat, & h. l. eadem ratione usurpetur, non tamen so- lam veritatem Dei in promissionibus ejus exprimit, nec solum respectum habet ad opera DEI, quorum DEus causa est, & auctor, ceu ens entium, sed in- primis absolutum esse Dei & immutabilitatem essentiæ divinæ, ex qua etiam immutabilis veritas fluit, desi- gnat, ut ibidem latius demonstratum est.

## 6:3 Addition
On chapter 6, verse 3, towards the end.

Gataker, in Adversaria Miscellanea, ch. 18, p. 180, praised the opinion of our blessed Dorscheus and approved it, supported by his own calculation as if by valid reasons. Nor does it seem to be rejected; both because the Fathers did not have the power of the name El Shaddai known by experimental knowledge any more than that of the name Jehovah, just as the same promises were bound to them in Gen. 17:1 ff. as were to this one in Gen. 15; and because those things which are repeated in verse 4 are joined with the promises along with the very manifestation of the name Jehovah in Gen. 15:7; and because God seems to have wished to enumerate here, not what He did not perform for the Fathers, but what He did perform in the revelations of His promises; and because it coheres cumulatively, not appositively, in verse 4 with verse 3, which the particle וגם also implies; and because there is thus greater emphasis in the divine speech, as if to say, I have alleged the names El Shaddai for the attestation of my infallibility: what then? So that nothing might be lacking, did I not also impress my own proper and incommunicable name upon their minds, so that they might understand that I am just as unlikely to be false in the things promised as I am unable to change my incommunicable name?

Latin:

Ad c. 6. v. 3. sub finem.

Sententiam B. Dorschei nostri laudavit, & cal- culo suo ceu validis rationibus fuffultam proba- vit Gatakerus Advers. Miscell. c. 18. p. 180. Nec ea rejicienda videtur; tum quia non magis nomi- nis El Schaddai vim experimentali notitia cogni- tam habuere Patres quam nominis Jehovah, quemadmodum illi eædem promissiones Gen. 17. v. 1. seqq. alligatæ, quæ huic Gen. 15. tum quod quæ vers. 4. repetuntur è promissionibus cum ipsa ma- nifestatione nominis Jehovah Gen. 15, 7. conjun- cta sint; tum quod videatur hic voluisse enumerare Deus, non quod non præstiterit Patribus, sed quod præstiterit in revelationibus promissionum sua- rum, tum quod cumulative, non appositive vers. 4. cum 3. cohæreat, quod & particula וגם innuit: tum quod emphasis ita major in oratione divina sit, q. d. Ego ad contestationem infallibilitatis meæ Patriarchis allegavi nomina El Schaddai: quid? ut nihil deeffet nomen meum proprium & incommunica- bile nonne etiam ipsorum animis impressi, ut intelli- gerent tam non futurum me falsum in rebus promissis, quam mutare nomen meum incommunicabile ne- queo?

## 6:4
Vers. 4. THAT I MIGHT GIVE TO THEM.] That is, to their posterity. For parents and children share names with one another: especially when it goes well with children on account of their parents.

Latin:

Vers. 4. UT DAREM EIS.] Id est, posteritati eorum. Communicant enim inter se nomina parentes & liberi: præ- sertim cum liberis bene fit ob parentes.

## 6:6
Vers. 6. FROM THE WORKHOUSE.

The Vulgate did not translate ergastulum well, because workhouses are places in which laborers are shut up who are destined and condemned to certain works, but that word is not used generally for every burdensome servitude. In the Hebrew it is, from under the burdens of the Egyptians.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DE ERGASTULO.

Non satis bene ergastulum dixit vulgatus, quia ergastula loca sunt, in quibus laborantes conclu- duntur, qui ad opera quædam destinati sunt, & da- mnati, non autem usurpatur illa vox generaliter pro omni onerosa servitute. In Ebr. est, de sub one- ribus Ægyptiorum.

## 6:8
Vers. 8. UPON WHICH I LIFTED UP MY HAND.

It is a Hebraism, and an oath is denoted, because those swearing were accustomed to perform an oath with hand lifted on high. Compare Gen. 14:22, Ezra 9:15, Deut. 32:4, Ps. 106:26, Ezek. 20:45, chap. 36:6, and Isa. 3:7, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SUPER QUEM LEVAVI MANUM MEAM.

Ebraismus est, ac notatur juramentum, quia ju- rantes solebant manu in altum sublata juramentum præstare. Conf. Genes. 14, 22. Esdr. 9, 15. Deut. 32, 4. Ps. 106, 26. Ezech. 20, 45. cap. 36, 6. & Es. 3, 7. 8.

## 6:9
Vers. 9. THEY DID NOT HEARKEN BECAUSE OF ANGUISH OF SPIRIT.

Whether because they were faint-hearted, as the LXX Interpreters rendered it, ἀπὸ τῆς ὀλιγοψυχίας, or because they were so pressed by labors that they could scarcely breathe, which cause excuses them to an extent, not entirely, because this was done not out of malice and obstinacy, but out of sorrow of mind and hard servitude, which infirmity is indeed deservedly reproved where one is so affected by present calamities that he does not look to the future, even though promised by God. Grotius has it thus in this place:

Vers. 9. THEY DID NOT HEARKEN BECAUSE OF ANGUISH OF SPIRIT.) Cicero in his first Philippic spoke of anguish of the breast, which explains poverty of spirit: But in this place anxiety is signified more, as the following things indicate. LXX: ἀπὸ τῆς ὀλιγοψυχίας. But another old version referred it to a bodily defect contracted from labors, saying ἀπὸ κολοβότητος πνεύματος, just as Plutarch in the life of Demosthenes: γλώττης ἀσάφεια καὶ πνεύματος κολοβότης ἐπιταράττουσα τὸν νοῦν τῶν λεγομένων.

Vers. eod. AND THE MOST HARD WORK.) Here the Samaritan Codices of this time add: And they said to Moses: desist from us, that we may serve the Egyptians, because it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert. The cause of this addition and many others is quite cold, because mention is made below of such things as having been said before. For this is taken from that which is below 14:12, as if either the individual sayings of everyone were recorded in histories, or there were no repetitions in them on occasion. These are foolish curiosities of those transcribing in great leisure.

Latin:

Vers. 9. NON ACQUIEVERUNT PRO- PTER ANGUSTIAM SPIRITUS.

Sive quia pusillanimes erant, ut LXX. Interpp. reddiderunt, ἀπὸ τῆς ὀλιγοψυχίας, seu quia ita premebantur laboribus, ut vix respirare possent, quæ causa excusat eosdem in tantum, non in totum, quia non ex malitia & pertinacia hoc factum, sed ex animi mœrore & dura servitute, quæ vero infir- mitas merito reprehenditur, ubi quis ita præsenti- bus afficitur calamitatibus, ut futura, etsi à Deo promissa non respiciat. Grotius ita h. l. habet:

Vers. 9. NON ACQUIEVERUNT PROPTER ANGU- STIAM SPIRITUS.) Angustias pectoris dixit prima Phi- lippica Cicero, quod explicat egestatem animi: Sed hoc loco magis anxietas significatur, ut sequentia indicant. LXX. ἀπὸ τῆς ὀλιγοψυχίας. At alia vetus versio ad corporis vitium ex laboribus contractum retulit, dicens ἀπὸ κολοβότητος πνεύ- ματος, sicut Plutarchus in vita Demosthenis : γλώττης ἀσά- φεια καὶ πνεύματος κολοβότης ἐπιταράττουσα τὸν νοῦν τῶν λε- γομένων.

Vers. eod. ET OPUS DURISSIMUM.) Hic addunt Co- dices Samaritani hujus temporis: Et dixerunt Mosi: desiste à nobis, ut serviamus Ægyptiis, quia melius est nobis servire Æy- ptiis, quam mori in deserto. Causa hujus additionis & multa- rum aliarum satis est frigida, quia infra talium ut ante dicto- rum fit mentio. Sumtum enim hoc ex eo quod infra 14, 12. quasi vero aut singula cujusque dicta in historiis referantur, aut nullæ sint in eis ex occasione ἐπάνοδοι. Hæ stultæ sunt in magno otio transcribentium περιεργίαι.

## 6:14
Vers. 14. THESE ARE THE HEADS &c.

The genealogy of Moses and Aaron is recited, both for the clarity and greater credibility of the history, and so that it might be established that Moses was elected the first leader of the people not from the firstborn Reuben or the second son of Jacob, but from the tribe of Levi, who was the third son, and especially so that it might be signified that the Priesthood was established in that tribe from Aaron down to the coming of the Messiah. It is gathered, moreover, from these names that the Hebrew language was retained in the race of Abraham, since all those names are Hebrew, and do not have certain or congruent meanings in other languages.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ISTI SUNT PRINCIPES &c.

Recitatur genealogia Mosis & Aaronis, tum ob historiæ perspicuitatem fidemque majorem, tum ut constaret, non ex primogenito Ruben aut secun- do filio Jacobi, sed ex tribu Levi, qui tertius erat fi- lius, primum Ducem populi Mosen electum, & præ- cipue, ut significaretur in illa tribu constitutum es- se Sacerdotium inde ab Aarone usque ad adventum Messia. Colligitur autem ex his nominibus, reten- tam fuisse linguam Ebræam, in genere Abrahami, siquidem illa omnia nomina Ebraica sint, nec in aliis linguis significata certa aut congrua habeant.

## 6:16
Ver. 16. AND THE YEARS OF THE LIFE OF LEVI WERE ONE HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SEVEN.

Levi therefore died 41 years before the birth of Moses. For since Levi was 4 years older than Joseph, Gen. 30, who was 39 years old when Jacob went down into Egypt, Gen. 41, and died in the 110th year of his age, it must be that Levi departed this life 23 years after the death of Joseph, and thus lived in Egypt for 94 years after the entry of Jacob. There remained therefore still 121 years after his death until the exodus from Egypt, which took place in the 80th year of the age of Moses; from which are gathered the 41 years of Levi until the birth of Moses.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ANNI AUTEM VITÆ LEVI FUE- RUNT CENTUM TRIGINTA SEPTEM.

Obiit ergo Levi annis 41. ante nativitatem Mo- sis. Cum enim Levi 4. annis senior fuerit Josepho, Genes. 30. qui 39. annos natus erat, cum Jacob in Ægyptum descenderet Genes. 41. obiitque anno ætatis suæ 110. oportet Levi vita excessisse 23. annis post obitum Josephi, adeoque in Ægypto post in- gressum Jacobi per 94. annos vixisse. Restabant ergo adhuc post mortem ejus 121. anni usque ad egressum ex Ægypto, qui factus est anno ætatis Mo- sis 80. unde colliguntur anni 41. Levi usque ad na- tivitatem Mosis.

## 6:20
Ver. 20. HIS PATERNAL COUSIN.) So also the Greeks: θυγατέρα τὲ ἀδελφὲ τὲ πατρὸς ἀυτὲ. In reality she was his paternal aunt, and the Hebrew word signifies that. Those changed it who always thought that what is forbidden by law was a sin. See what is said concerning the law of war and peace, book 2, chapter 4, § 14.

He had no sufficient cause here for abandoning, and—which he does tacitly—correcting the Vulgate version, unless perhaps he wished to gratify Bellarmine and other Papists by his advocacy for the Roman Pontiff, who dispenses in the degrees prohibited in Leviticus 18. For they are accustomed to use as a pretext this example of Amram, a holy man, because he married his paternal aunt, even though it was subsequently forbidden by law; therefore Grotius denies that it was a sin before that express law was established, who in the cited place on the law of peace and war also attempts to prove that it was once given in common to the human race to have two sisters in marriage at the same time, and teaches, according to the Apostolic canons (but adulterated ones), that whoever had married two sisters one after the other, or an ἀδελφιδῆν, that is, a brother's or sister's daughter, is only to be kept away from the clergy. So that, namely, the double dispensations made by the Pontiff might not be judged to have been made against the law of nature or divine constitution, given to the Hebrews, as he says in the same place, together with the law concerning worshipping God, administering justice, not shedding blood, not worshipping false gods, not seizing another's property. But as far as Amram is concerned here, whom most translate the Hebrew word דּוֹדָה as paternal aunt, they excuse him on the grounds that he was carried away by the common custom of the nations in disturbed times, as were other holy men, to whom God did not impute such things on account of their faith in the Messiah, and spared them until all things were better established through the renewed law. They do not, however, admit that marriage with a paternal aunt was permitted before the law. For this is not a positive law, but rests on natural law, Lev. 18:12: 'The nakedness of thy father's sister thou shalt not uncover: she is thy father's near kinswoman.' But it can be said that Jochebed was the daughter of a paternal aunt, born of the sister of the brother Amram, and a granddaughter of Levi, which degree of kinship in the equal collateral line is not prohibited by divine law, as the Vulgate rendered it 'his paternal cousin.' Because the name דּוֹד generally signifies relatives even in a further degree, as in Isaiah 5:1, the Messiah is called the 'beloved' (דּוֹד) of Isaiah, and more specifically in Jeremiah 32:12, Hanameel is called the 'paternal uncle' (דּוֹד) of Jeremiah, when he was the son of a paternal uncle, i.e., a paternal cousin, v. 8, 9. Thus Jochebed is called the daughter of Levi because she was his granddaughter, Exod. 2:1, Num. 27:9, since granddaughters are also called daughters, 2 Chron. 11:18. Concerning these and other degrees, which Grotius in the cited place said were prohibited only by positive law, along with the Papists, let B. Gerhard on Marriage, § 312, be seen at length. It is strange that Grotius did not hesitate to praise even that of Michael of Ephesus on the fifth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, l. c. 2. 13. For a brother to lie with a sister was from the beginning a matter indifferent, but with the law placed against such cohabitation, it now matters much whether the law is observed or not. If such incests are not against the law of nature, what finally will be against it? But Grotius fashions and refashions for himself the law of nature at will, as could be shown in many instances.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PATRUELEM SUAM.) Sic & Græci θυγα- τέρα τὲ ἀδελφὲ τὲ πατρὸς ἀυτὲ. Revera fuit Amita, idque vox Hebræa significat. Mutarunt, qui quod lege vetitum est, semper putarunt nefas fuisse. Vide, quæ dicta de jure belli ac pacis lib. 2. cap. 4. §. 14.

Non habuit hic causam sufficientem deserendi, & quod tacite facit, corrigendi vulgatam versio- nem, nisi cum Bellarmino aliisque Papistis gratifi- cari fortassis voluit advocatura sua Pontifici Roma- no, in gradibus Levit. 18. prohibitis dispensanti. Solent enim prætexere hoc Amrami viri sancti ex- emplum, quod amitinam duxerit, etsi lege id post- modum prohibitum; ideo id nefas fuisse ante sanci- tam illam expressam legem negat Grotius, qui loco dicto de jure pacis & belli probare hoc etiam cona- tur, in commune olim humano generi datum fuisse, duas eodem tempore in matrimonio habere Sorores, ac canonibus Apostolicis, (sed adulterinis) docet, duas sorores alteram post alteram qui duxisset, aut ἀδελφιδῆν, id est, fratris aut sororis filiam, tantum à Clero arceri. Ut scil. quæ à Pontifice factæ sunt ge- minæ dispensationes, ne factæ censeantur contra le- gem naturæ aut constitutionem divinam, Ebræis, ut ibidam ait, simul cum lege de Deo colendo, jure dicen- do, non fundendo sanguine, non colendis Diis falsis, non rapienda re aliena, datam. At quod Amramum hic attinet, qui vocem Ebræam דּוֹדָה amitam reddunt, plerique excusant eundem, quod rebus perturbatis communi gentium more abreptus fue- rit, ut sancti alii, quibus ob fidem in Messiam non imputavit talia DEus, atque pepercit, donec omnia melius constituerentur per innovatam legem. Non autem admittunt, ante legem concessum matri- monium cum amita fuisse. Non enim hæc lex posi- tiva est, sed naturali jure nititur Lev. 18, 12. Turpi- tudinem sororis Patris tui non discooperies, quia caro est Patris tui. Sed dici potest, Jochebed fuisse filiam amitæ ex Fratris Amram Sorore natam, & Neptem Levi, qui gradus cognationis in linea collaterali æquali secundus, jure divino non est prohibitus, ut reddidit Vulgatus Patruelem suam. Quia nomen דּוֹד gene- raliter cognatos etiam in gradu ulteriori significat, uti Esa. 5, 1. Messias Esaiæ, ac specialius Jerem. 32, 12. Hanameël Jeremiæ דּוֹד Patruus dicitur, cum hic fu- erit filius Patrui, h. e. Patruelis, v. 8. 9. Ita Jochebed filia Levi dicta, quod ejus Neptis fuerit Exod. 2, 1. Num. 27, 9. quum etiam neptes filiæ dicantur 2. Par. 11, 18. De his & aliis gradibus, quos Grotius lege solum positiva prohibitos cum Papistis l. c. dixit, prolixe videatur B. Gerhardus de Conjug. §. 312. Mirum, quod Grotius etiam illud Michaelis Ephesi ad quintum Nicomachiorum laudare non dubitarit l. c. 2. 13. Fratrem cum Sorore concumbere ab initio RES MEDIA erat, at lege adversus tales concubitus posi- ta jam multum refert, observetur lex necne? Si ince- stus tales non sunt contra legem naturæ, quid tan- dem ei adversum erit: Sed Grotius fingit, & refin- git sibi naturæ legem pro lubitu, ut multis ostendi posset.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

The rod turned into a serpent, Water into blood.

Ver. 1. BEHOLD, I HAVE MADE THEE A GOD TO PHARAOH.) There is here in the Hebrew the word אֱלֹהִים, which, as Kimchi notes, Kimchi and other Hebrews, whether it is taken of God, or of angels, or of men, signify judicial power. The sense therefore is, Moses was placed, that he might exercise divine judgments upon Pharaoh, as a king of the king himself. Onkelos translated it Prince: Jonathan, the fear of Pharaoh, as if he were God: Rabbi Solomon, judge, very well, namely, by the command of God, attested by great wonders.

We have spoken of this at chapter 4, 16. The word Elohim, because its root is no longer used in Hebraism, what it signifies is rightly learned from a cognate language retaining the same root, Arabic, in which it denotes to worship and adore. Hence אֱלָהּ a numen to be venerated. Just as also in the Ethiopian language GOD is called አምላኽ from the verb מלך which for them in Hiphil is σέβεσθαι to worship, Matt. 15, 9; λατρέυειν to serve, Luke 1, 24, according to Ludovicus de Dieu on this passage. Who also does not doubt that from this, King מֶלֶךְ is also said by the Hebrews, as if one who is worshipped by subjects like some earthly numen. Therefore, on account of a certain communication of honor and dignity, it is attributed to angels and magistrates, because they are as it were Gods, whom others ought to venerate and honor. In which way Jonathan did not badly render here the fear of Pharaoh. For Pharaoh ought to have revered and looked up to Moses, as a legate of GOD; whom he attested himself to be by great prodigies, not as his king, who might possess the right of the sword over him. This was not granted to Moses, over whom rather, as a subject, Pharaoh the King possessed the right of life and death, conversely. I do not know whether Grotius perhaps, with the Papists who are accustomed to compare the Pope with Moses, wishes by this paradox of his to establish the power of the Pope over kings and secular Princes, to whom he might be in the place of God, and ought to be looked up to for God. But I do not wish to examine those things more deeply just now. That the word אלהים denotes judge is from a false etymology of the name, as has been said elsewhere.

Moses is therefore called God not absolutely, but in respect to Pharaoh; furthermore, God constituted by God, whence it is clear that θεὸν λεγόμενον is understood; who is GOD προσηγορικῶς and appellatively, not Ὀσιοδῶς or essentially. Nor yet is it only indicated that in a certain respect he would be greater and stronger than Pharaoh the King himself, by reason of the Israelite people, who were otherwise subject to Pharaoh: But also, that he is to deal with Pharaoh, not as a man is accustomed to deal with a man, but as God is accustomed to deal with a man, i.e., Pharaoh can oppose nothing to you except human forces, but you will deal with him with divine forces; what I will against him, you will administer and execute. Therefore, those who explain the name Elohim as Prince do not grasp the emphasis of the phrase, nor is the word ever taken in that way. Nor indeed is it to be concluded from that, that the name Elohim is not proper to GOD; for although in a figurative sense it is also attributed to others besides God, it nevertheless remains proper to the true God in the proper sense, concerning which we have treated at greater length in Tom. 2 in Aug. Confess. when we dealt with this name Eloah. But what is added concerning Aaron: he shall be your Prophet, is to be understood not of a Prophet strictly so called, who reveals something from immediate divine inspiration, but by Prophet is understood Interpreter, just as the word Prophet is taken in 1 Corinthians. 14, 4. because just as Moses was constituted God of Pharaoh, that is, in the place of GOD, so Aaron was the Prophet of Moses before Pharaoh, that is, in the place of a Prophet, to whom Moses revealed those things which he received immediately from God, so that he might carry them to Pharaoh as the Interpreter of Moses: and because Moses had to be like God in this act, he had, as God called by likeness, also his Prophet Aaron, but likewise only through some likeness, just as GOD has his Prophets.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

Virga in serpentem versa, Aqua in sangui- nem.

Vers. 1. ECCE, CONSTITUI TE DEUM PHARAO- NIS.) Est hic in Ebræo vox אֱלֹהִים, quæ, ut notat Kimchi, Kimchi, aliique Hebræi, sive de Deo sumatur, sive de Ange- lis, sive de hominibus, judiciariam potestatem significat. Sensus ergo est, positum Mosen, ut judicia divina in Pharao- nem exerceat, velut rex regis ipsius. Onkelos Principem transtulit: Jonathan timorem Pharaonis, ac si DEus esset: Rabbi Salomo judicem, optime, scilicet Dei mandatu magnis præstigiis testato.

DIximus de hoc ad cap. 4, 16. Vox Elohim, quia radix ejus in Ebraïsmo usitata amplius non est, quid significet, ex lingua cognata, eandem ra- dicem retinente, Arabica, recte addiscitur, in qua colere & adorare ea notat. Hinc אֱלָהּ numen vene- randum. Quemadmodum etiam in Æthiopica lin- gua DEUS አምላኽ dicitur à verbo מלך quod ipsis in hiphil est σέβεσθαι colere Matth. 15, 9. λατρέυειν servire Luc. 1, 24. juxta Ludovic. de Dieu ad h. l. Qui etiam non dubitat Ebræis inde quoque Regem מֶלֶךְ dici, quasi qui à subditis veluti terrenum aliquod numen colitur. Ideo ob honoris & dignitatis commu- nicationem quandam tribuitur angelis & magistrati- bus, quod veluti Dii sint, quos alii venerari atque honorare debeant. Quo pacto non male hic Jo- nathan timorem Pharaonis reddidit. Debebat enim Pharao revereri ac suspicere Mosen, ceu legatum DEI; quem se magnis prodigiis testabatur, non tanquam regem suum, qui jus gladii in ipsum ob- tineret. Hoc Mosi concessum non fuit, in quem potius ceu subditum jus vitæ ac necis, vice versa, Pharao Rex obtinebat. Nescio anne Grotius for- tassis cum Papicolis, qui Pontificem cum Mose com- ponere solent, hoc paradoxo suo Papæ potestatem in reges ac Principes seculares, quibus in Deum sit, & pro Deo suspici debeat, stabilitam velit. Sed nolo ista nunc quidem penitius rimari. Vocem אלהים judicem notare, à falsa etymologia nomi- nis est, ut alias dictum.

Dicitur ergo Moses Deus non absolute, sed Pharaonis respectu; adhæc Deus constitutus à Deo, unde patet, θεὸν λεγόμενον intelligi; qui DEUS sit προσηγορικῶς & appellative, non Ὀσιοδῶς aut essen- tialiter. Nec tamen id tantum indigitatur, quod certo respectu major & fortior futurus sit ipso Pha- raone Rege, ratione populi Israelitici, qui alias Pharaoni subjectus erat: Sed etiam, quod cum Pharaone acturus sit, non ut solet homo cum ho- mine, sed ut solet Deus cum homine, q. d. Pha- rao tibi nihil opponere potest præter humanas vires, tu autem ages cum ipso viribus divinis, quod ego adver- sus eum volo, tu administrabis & exequeris. Non ergo assequuntur Emphasin Φράσεως, qui nomen Elohim de Principe explicant, nec ita vox uspiam sumitur. Neque vero ex eo concludendum, no- men Elohim DEI non esse proprium; nam quam- vis sensu figurato aliis præter Deum etiam tribua- tur, manet tamen proprium vero Deo sensu pro- prio, quo de Tom. 2. in Aug. Confess. cum de hoc nomine Eloah egimus, pluribus actum. Quod ve- ro additur de Aarone: erit Propheta tuus, intelli- gendum est non de Propheta rigorose ita dicto, qui ex immediata inspiratione divina aliquid re- velat, sed per Prophetam intelligitur Interpres, uti vox Prophetæ accipitur 1. Corinth. 14, 4. quia sicut Moses constituebatur Deus Pharaonis, hoc est, lo- co DEI, sic Aaron Propheta Mosis erat apud Pha- raonem, id est, loco Prophetæ, cui Moses ea, quæ à Deo immediate accepit, revelavit, ut ea tanquam Interpres Mosis ad Phraonem deferret: & quia Moses similis Deo in hoc actu esse debuit, habe- bat ut Deus per similitudinem nuncupatus etiam Prophetam suum Aaronem, sed itidem per aliquam tantum similitudinem, sicut DEus Prophetas suos habet.

## 7:3
Ver. 3. BUT I WILL HARDEN HIS HEART, AND I WILL MULTIPLY SIGNS.

The Calvinists strive to prove their crooked doctrine from these words, because the hardening of Pharaoh's heart is ascribed to GOD actively and positively, with Calvin leading the way, who in this place contends that God governed his heart in a certain secret way, and hardened it to stubbornness, for which Rivetus, instituting an Apology here against Cornel. a Lapide, weighs various modes brought forward for the understanding of this expression. The first is that by which they say God hardens through patience, which he denies can be applied to God, because a parent does not escape the accusation of malice if he acts of his own accord and willingly toward his son in such a way that he does those things from which he knows his destruction will follow, if however he does not think of that, but hopes for better things from his son, then he is indeed excused from malice, but not from imprudence and ignorance. Resp. Scripture itself testifies that it happens through the long-suffering of God that one treasures up for himself wrath according to the hardness of his heart, Rom. 2, 4. And to attribute to God that in great long-suffering he tolerates vessels of iniquity, which are rendered no better, but worse, Rom. 9, 22. Nor is there any doubt from this history that, through the patience of God by which he tolerated Pharaoh, he was hardened more and more. Although indeed God foresaw that very thing, he is not therefore to be said to have intended the hardening, since he intended rather the conversion, which Peter assigns as the cause of divine long-suffering and tolerance, 2 Epist. cap. 3, 9. Rivetus retorts, either GOD acting thus intends to punish or he does not intend; if he intends to punish: Therefore he willed that effect, namely the hardening; if he does not intend to punish; therefore he did not harden, because hardening is a punishment. Resp. He did not intend punishment, but the softening of Pharaoh, because for that reason he manifested himself to him so frequently by word and miracles, so that, the power of God being at last acknowledged, he might return to a sounder mind and dismiss the people. He is said, however, to have hardened Pharaoh by this patience of his, but accidentally; so that this may be clear, it must be observed that hardening is both a punishment and a sin: when therefore a man is hardened by the patient tolerance of God, the patience of God relates accidentally to the hardening as a sin: and thus far hardening is not yet considered as a punishment.

The second mode is permission, concerning which Rivetus reasons thus: GOD permits either willingly or unwillingly: to say the latter is to cast GOD down from His state. But if He permits hardening willingly; therefore GOD wills that to be done, which is done. Resp. God does not indeed permit it unwillingly, that is, forced, nor willingly and intending the hardening; but not-willingly, which is the middle and third [way] in this case: You are not a GOD who wills iniquity, Ps. 5, 4. It can also be said that God wills that to be done which is done, because He wills it permissively; but His will must be referred to the permission of the hardening, but not to the hardening itself; He permitted the hardening willingly, because He willed to permit it: but He did not will the hardening itself, but detested the same, and visited it with the most grievous punishment. The third mode is of positive concurrence and cooperation: namely, that God hardens by positively concurring and cooperating, which mode Rivetus does not reject, he only teaches that the same is also approved by Cornelius a Lapide, and Pineda on Job 8, 20. Num. 3. with these words of his adduced: I will harden, and as it is in Hebrew, I will aggravate or strengthen the heart of Pharaoh, [making it] hard, strong, able to resist, and by no means timid and soft. For this natural constancy and animosity, by which it came about that Pharaoh was tenacious of his purpose, and would not easily change it, was from God, the author of nature, but Pharaoh himself abused those as if they were weapons, so that he might resist his own creator. But this positive concurrence and We deem it impious to ascribe to God the cooperation, hardening, and aggravation of Pharaoh's heart, by which it was made hard, strong, and powerful to resist God. Nor is this hardness merely a natural constancy and spirit, but it is the very obstinacy and perversity of a proud mind in Pharaoh, which Rivetus acknowledges along with Cornelius: since, therefore, God is not the author of this perversity and pride, how does He positively concur and cooperate toward the hardness of heart or hardening, because He is the author of spirit and constancy? And the question here is not only about innate concupiscence and the disposition of corrupt nature, but about malicious hardening, which how can we ascribe to God actively and positively without blasphemy? It is no wonder that the Jesuits do this, who blow almost the same pipes as the Calvinists, and therefore cannot solidly refute them, see Tom. 2. Syst. Th. p. 346. The fourth method is the subtraction of grace, which would soften the heart, just as the sun hardens clay not by positively causing hardness, but by subtracting or drawing out the moisture that tempered and softened the clay. Thus Rivetus wishes God also to be said to harden, and he thinks that if this method is well understood, the matter is settled, because since man's heart is depraved by nature, and yet is moved by God in all its actions, if God does not remove the perversity of nature, which He is not bound to do, while God moves him, that motion, as it is from God, is good, but it proceeds from such a subject that is evil in itself; whatever evil is in that motion, and the more he is moved, the more he wallows in his sins. We respond: many things occur here that are false or at least suspect: for it is assumed (1.) grace, which softens the heart in the sense of the Calvinists, that is, irresistibly. However, for conversion and softening, there is no need for irresistible grace, and that which is required is absolutely denied to no one, and is not simply subtracted from anyone. Therefore (2.) it is false that God subtracted all grace from Pharaoh; since through the word and miracles He reminded him of his duty and exhibited His grace to him. (3.) Nor does that simile about the sun, which draws out moisture, fit; because God does not draw out if there is any good in man. (4.) The depravation of the heart in Pharaoh is not only to be viewed in terms of natural perversity, which is common to all men; but in terms of the voluntary σκληρότητος (hardness) contracted by his own fault.

The fifth method is the objection of occasions: to which Rivetus also refers from Pererius the Jesuit in ch. 11 of Exodus, that God does many things within that man who is being hardened, by which he becomes worse through his own vice: that He excites in him various affections and motions, whether of hope and confidence or of desire or anger: likewise that He sends in various imaginations and perplexed and doubtful thoughts, and even injects dreams and nocturnal visions, by which he, being too credulous, is incited and precipitated into evil. Similarly, Rivetus, following Pererius, maintains that God does many things externally around the same man, whether good or evil: good things such as admonitions, corrections, scourges, benefits: Evil things, or those which can incline toward evil and incline the mind to it, of such a kind are various objects of pleasures or honors, by which the already corrupt mind, despoiled of God's grace and help, is immediately affected and clings to them. But that God does these things or permits them to be done, knowing that the sinner will abuse them to the greater ruin and destruction of his own soul; which Rivetus judges to coincide clearly with Calvin's opinion. But that God excites evils, whether internally or externally, or that He objects anything with the end that the sinner might abuse it for his own ruin, is simply repugnant to the Holy Scriptures and to nature and divine goodness; since God can neither promote evil nor intend it, as He is supremely good, and therefore the occasions by which man abuses himself toward evil are not objected by God for the sake of evil. Nor is anything similar observed in the history of Pharaoh, for all things were directed toward softening Pharaoh's mind, which he himself was hardening by his own fault. Therefore, as to Pharaoh's hardening, its positive cause was then the Devil, whose work it is to blind the heart 2 Cor. 4:3, and to fill it with malice Acts 5:3, and to work in the children of disobedience Eph. 2:2, and then Pharaoh himself, as is asserted in Exod. 7:13, 22, ch. 8:19, Pharaoh's heart strengthened itself, and he did not listen to them; ch. 9:35, Pharaoh added to his sinning in his heart; ch. 13:15, it happened when Pharaoh had hardened himself; which Augustine also acknowledged in Sermon 88 de tempore, to whom the Calvinists appeal in vain; most certainly, he says, it must be believed that it was not God's violence, but his own iniquity and indomitable pride that caused Pharaoh to be hardened so many times against God's commandments. But because hardening is also sometimes attributed to God, both in this place and in Exod. 4:2, ch. 9:12, 33, ch. 10:27, ch. 11:10, Rom. 9:29, it must be observed that hardening is viewed either as a sin or as the punishment for sin: as it is a sin, it cannot be attributed to God, whether by reason of command, or by reason of good pleasure, or by reason of positive concurrence: whether morally or physically; since, as God is the cause of no sin, much less should He be constituted the cause of this most atrocious sin by any reason, inasmuch as He has most gravely prohibited it Psalm 95:8, of which He complained in Exod. 10:3, 4, by which man directly opposes himself to God by turning his back to Him Zech. 7:11, by turning away and stopping his ears Ps. 58:2, Is. 6:10, Zech. 7:11, by closing his eyes Is. 6:10, Matt. 13:15, by hardening his neck, Deut. 10:16, and his face Jer. 5:3, and his forehead Ezek. 2:4, and finally by making his heart itself firm and strengthening it against God Psalm 95:8. Which God also finally punishes most gravely: but of those whom God is the avenger, He is not the author.

But we shall take up the arguments of Cornelius, and we shall examine what Rivetus answers to them. This is the first, that God, having sent Moses, commanded Pharaoh ten times to dismiss the people; therefore He willed that he should let the people go. Therefore He did not will to harden him, so that he might retain the people; for this is properly to will, to will effectively that Pharaoh should not wish to dismiss the people: but to will that he should dismiss them, and to command that, and yet again effectively not to will it, and therefore to harden him, are manifestly in conflict with one another. Rivetus answers: To will effectively and properly is to bring that about. But God did not bring it about that Pharaoh should dismiss them; therefore He did not will it properly and effectively: it must be said, therefore, that God willed His people to be dismissed by Pharaoh and did not will it. He willed it by the will of command and approbation, He did not will it by the will of decree and efficiency; therefore He willed that Pharaoh should will it, that is, He commanded that he should will and do it, because he owed this. He did not, however, will to effect that in Pharaoh, and to move him effectively to that, but to leave his mind, averted from its duty, to itself and to deliver it to Satan to be hardened, and to effect in him those motions well and holily, which he nevertheless might infect evilly? But both antagonists are deceived when they assume that God only properly wills that which He actually effects, since God properly wills many things to be done which He Himself does not effect, and therefore, even if He did not effect that Pharaoh should dismiss the people, it must nevertheless be believed that He Himself seriously and by the will of His internal good pleasure willed that dismissal, because He commanded the same. The distinction of Rivetus between the will of command and approbation, and the will of decree and efficiency, in the Calvinian sense is false, absurd, and impious, as if God willed anything, that is, commanded and approved it extrinsically, which nevertheless He did not will internally, but of which He had rather decreed and willed the contrary by the will of decree and immutable efficiency: as, for instance, that He commanded the dismissal of the people, but had decreed to bring it about that he would not dismiss them, by leaving to himself his mind averse from its duty for that end, and by handing him over to Satan to be hardened, and by bringing about motions in Pharaoh which he would infect with evil. And this with GOD himself intending and doing it, so that he might infect it with evil. Which things are horrible and blasphemous. For there are no contrary wills in God, nor does he act one way externally and decree another way internally, and he performs what is to be done effectively, in wondrous and secret ways. Truly this is what the Calvinists want, as they sometimes openly betray their mind, which Rivetus hides here (1.) that God, by an ineffable counsel, wills that things which he does not want to happen, and forbids to be done, should happen for a different end; as Calvin has in his calumnies of a scoundrel p. 103. (2.) that the impious are so ruled by divine providence that they can effect nothing other than what God has decreed by his eternal and immutable counsel, Triglandius in Declarat. p. 14. (3.) Just as God deprives the reprobate of his grace, so that they cannot but sin, so he has also destined them to this condition, that they cannot but act according to their nature, nay, that the reprobate are constrained by the necessity of sinning, and thereby also of perishing from this ordination of GOD, and are so constrained that they cannot but sin and perish, Zanch. c. 11. de reprobat. qv. 2. Whence (4.) they teach that God wills sin by the will of his good pleasure, Bucanus in Loc. Com. p. 155. That God incites, seduces, draws, commands, hardens, sends deceptions to men for their wicked actions, and brings about what are grave sins. Petrus Martyr. in Jud. 3, 9. p. 45. That God impels to sins, which he forbids, by a secret reason; Piscat. Macov. & others; which are blasphemies and take away all religion. Cornelius rightly says: If it was the will of God to harden Pharaoh; therefore, conforming himself to it, he did not sin, for the will of God is the measure of every good will. But Rivetus answers in vain: that this is true concerning the will of God, insofar as it is taken for a precept, not concerning the will of decree and efficacy; for thus he who performs the will of God's decree will not sin, even if he contravenes the precept of God. Rivetus gives an example; are those who affixed Christ to the cross excused from sin because they did what God willed? But he presupposes his own impious dogma, that GOD willed that they should do this; whereas one must distinguish between the passion and the action; for even if he decreed that Christ should suffer, he did not, however, will that the Jews should affix him to the cross; but here let that saying of Prosper hold: The action displeased, the passion was welcome. For having foreseen the malice, hardening, and blinding of the Jews, by which they were about to drive Christ to the cross, he directed the crucifixion to a salutary end, beyond the intention of the Jews; but this is not to will effectively, much less to effect that which the impious Jews did. The second reason is, God punishes the reluctant Pharaoh most severely: but God is not the author of those things of which he is the avenger, as Fulgentius testifies l. 1. ad Monim. c. 3. Rivetus answers: that the very reluctance of Pharaoh, insofar as it is from God, is an avenging and a punishment of sin, but insofar as it is done by man, it is also a sin, and therefore the kinds of causes must be distinguished; insofar as God is the author of the hardening, God is not the avenger of it, but by it he avenges; insofar as man hardens himself, God is not the author of that hardening, insofar as it is a sin, but the avenger. I reply: different modes of consideration and respects or ends of hardening cannot make a non-sin out of a sin, or absolve anyone from the guilt of sin. Hardening remains a sin, even if it happens for the sake of punishment, or is sent; and he who hardens actively and positively is truly the cause of sin, whether he does it to punish, or for another reason. We certainly also distinguish hardening, insofar as it is a punishment and insofar as it is a sin, but we do not teach that God concurs positively and actively to hardening. But since the Calvinists say this,

they make God entirely the author of hardening, whatever ends or respects they may devise. We say that God concurs to hardening, when it is the punishment of sin, when he exhibits objects and the occasion of sinning, not for the sake of hardening, but for the sake of probation, leaves a man to his own hardness, withdraws his grace from him, nay, even hands him over to the power of Satan, who positively hardens the same. It is inept what Rivetus says, that hardening is a sin, insofar as it is from Pharaoh; but insofar as it is from GOD, it is not a sin, but the punishment of sin: for the nature of sin is not to be estimated from the efficient or final cause, but from the formal cause: sin is ἀνομία, from whomever it may finally proceed and with whatever intention or end it may be done. What is evil in itself and a fault, that is not permitted for any end, and from whatever agent it is done, or may be done, it is evil. The efficient and the end are external causes, the diversity of which does not make it so that sin or evil is not sin or evil.

The third argument is drawn from those passages in which hardening is attributed to Pharaoh. Rivetus answers: that he also attributes the guilt and the hardening to Pharaoh, nevertheless he also attributes the just hardening of Pharaoh to God without any guilt. But Scripture attributes it to God in one way, and to Pharaoh in another, to GOD permissively and indirectly, to Pharaoh effectively and directly. But as for what Rivetus says, that action and efficacy are joined with that divine permission concerning many actions contributing to it, if he understands the action and efficacy of God to flow positively into the hardening or to be done solely with that intention, that man should be hardened, he says this ἄτερ γραφῆς, nay, he contradicts Scripture: for that openly opposes Scripture which (even though he praises Bellarmine as a witness lib. 2. de amiss. gratiæ & Statu peccati c. 14.) asserts that God does not intend the conversion and repentance, but the punishment of those who are hardened. For although induration, when it is a punishment, is intended as a punishment, yet not every time God is said to indurate is the act of punishing referred to; often by reason of the occasion or by his tolerance and long-suffering or permission, he is understood to indurate: and where he deals with man through his word, he certainly intends his conversion: nor when induration is a punishment, i.e., when someone is deprived of the grace of God and is handed over to Satan, is God entirely absent from man, but rather by his admonitions and even by his very punishments and judgments he wishes the same to be recalled from his hardness; which is clearly evident by the example of the Jews, who were greatly blinded and indurated and bound in the power and snares of the devil, inasmuch as Christ still desired them to be gathered and converted, John 5:24, Matt. 23:37. Passive hardness or induration, as Rivetus defines it (called πώρωσις καρδίας in Mark 3:5), is a perverse affection gradually introduced, by which, with the mind and intelligence blinded, the will contracts obstinacy and forwardness, so that it not only does not yield to admonitions nor perceive them, but also morally cannot perceive and yield. But who would ascribe this so perverse affection to God as author, or admit that God concurs with it positively, directly, and effectively? Rivetus, however, with his Calvin, urges this argument especially: Whatever a just judge decrees, he wills effectively. But a just judge decrees a punishment; therefore, he wills it effectively. Now, blinding is a punishment decreed by God; therefore, God wills it effectively. Response: The sophism fails through ambiguity: because God is said to will effectively either what God himself brings about, which he wills, or also what he brings about irresistibly, or at least what he does not not-will, so that it may happen, even if he himself does not bring it about; for not everything which a judge decrees, even if he wills it effectively that it be done, does he himself do. He can also decree to permit something as a punishment, so that this or that may happen, and it may result in a penalty: it is not necessary that He should always positively influence a punishment, but then indeed God, which must be diligently observed, is to be regarded not only as a just judge, and by reason of His justice, but also as the Father of mercies, rich in compassion, and who in the midst of wrath remembers His mercy; therefore His manner and that of a judge are different when He inflicts punishment; for a judge only inflicts punishment so that a crime may be punished and the criminal may be chastised, but God, even if He punishes crimes and delivers the stubborn and hardened to the power of Satan, does not, however, entirely deprive them of grace while they are still on the way; for even those who, according to their hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up wrath for themselves, He invites with the riches of His goodness and forbearance and longsuffering, and wishes them to be led to repentance, even if they either do not care for it or do not understand it: Rom. 2, 4. Which is taught by the example of Pharaoh himself, Exod. 9, 16. Rom. 9, 17. For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power, as Paul has it; Or as I might make you see my patience, as it is held in Moses; Thus, therefore, God was showing the riches and power of His patience by this tolerance and preservation of Pharaoh. And since God testifies that He does this even against those who are hardened to the end that they may be led to conversion: it is not permitted to presume that a different decree exists in the divine mind against the same persons, unless God is to be accused of impious hypocrisy, from which impiety the Calvinists will not free themselves as long as they teach that the reprobate are called or hardened not so that they may be converted, but so that they may be punished, be further hardened, and perish, just as they are accustomed to assign a double end of calling according to the diversity of the elect and the reprobate, and Trigland revealed their mind in this way in Apolog. p. 38, 98. As regards the reprobate, God either does not call them at all, neither externally through the word, nor internally through the Spirit, or if He takes care that His word is announced to them externally, He does not move them internally and effectively through His Spirit so that they may receive the word and believe in it, but by a just judgment He blinds and hardens them, until at length they die in their sins and perish. And this much concerning hardening: see on this matter the Remonstrants in explic. c. 9. ad Rom. p. 146.

Latin:

Verf. 3. SED INDURABO COR EJUS, ET MULTIPLICABO SIGNA.

Calviniani ex hisce verbis σκολιοδοξίαν suam probare satagunt, quod DEO adscribatur induratio cordis Pharaonis active & positive, præeunte Calvino, qui in h. l. contendit, quod DEus cor ejus arcano quodam modo gubernarit, & ad pervicaciam obdurarit, pro quo Apologiam adversus Cornel. a Lapid. hîc instituens Rivetus varios modos ad istius locutionis intelligentiam adductos expendit. Primus est, quo Deum indurare dicunt per patientiam, quem Deo applicari posse negat, quia parens non fugit accusationem malitiæ, si sponte & volens ita se gerat erga filium, ut ea faciat, ex quibus novit secuturam ejus perditionem, si autem id non cogitet, sed meliora de filio speret, tum excusatur quidem a malitia, sed non ab imprudentia & ignorantia. Resp. Scripturam ipsam testari per Dei μακροθυμίαν fieri, ut quis secundum σκληρότητα cordis sui thesaurizet sibi iram Rom. 2, 4. Deoque tribuere, quod in magna μακροθυμίᾳ vasa iniquitatis toleret, quæ nihilo redduntur meliora, sed deteriora, Rom. 9, 22. Neque dubium est ex hac historia, per patientiam Dei, qua Pharaonem toleravit, ipsum magis magisque induratum fuisse. Quamvis vero Deus præviderit id ipsum, non tamen ideo dicendus est intendisse indurationem, quum intenderit potius conversionem, quam causam μακροθυμίας & tolerantiæ divinæ assignat Petrus 2. Epist. cap. 3, 9. Regerit Rivetus, aut DEUS ita se gerens intendit punire aut non intendit; si punire intendit: Ergo voluit effectum illum obdurationem nempe; si non intendit punire; ergo nec induravit, quia induratio est punitio. Resp. non intendebat punitionem, sed emollitionem Pharaonis, quia ideo verbo & miraculis se tam frequenter manifestabat ipsi, ut agnita tandem Dei potentia ad saniorem mentem rediret, populumque dimitteret. Dicitur tamen indurasse Pharaonem hac sua patientia, sed per accidens; quod ut constet, observandum, indurationem esse & pœnam & peccatum: cum ergo patienti tolerantia Dei homo induratur, Dei patientia per accidens sese habet ad indurationem ceu peccatum: & hactenus nondum ut pœna consideratur induratio.

Alter modus est permissio, de quo ita ratiocinatur Rivetus: DEUS permittit volens vel invitus: posterius dicere, est, DEum de statu suo dejicere. Si autem volens permittit indurationem; ergo id DEus vult fieri, quod fit. Resp. non invitus quidem permittit Deus, id est, coactus, neque volens & intendens obdurationem; sed non volens, quod medium est, & tertium in hac causa: DEUS non volens iniquitatem tu es, Psal. 5, 4. Dici etiam potest, Deum velle id fieri quod fit, quia vult permissive; sed voluntas ejus referenda est ad permissionem indurationis, non autem ad indurationem ipsam; Volens permisit indurationem, quia voluit permittere: non autem voluit indurationem ipsam, sed detestatus est eandem, & gravissimo affecit supplicio. Tertius modus est positivi concursus & cooperationis: quod nempe Deus induret positive concurrendo & cooperando, quem modum non reprobat Rivetus, solum docet, eundem etiam probari Cornelio Lapideo, & Pinedæ in Jobum 8, 20. Num. 3. his ejus verbis adductis: indurabo, & ut Ebraice est, aggravabo aut confortabo cor Pharaonis durum, forte, potens resistere, minimeq; timidum, & molle efficiam. Hæc enim naturalis constantia & animositas, qua fiebat, ut Pharao propositi sui esset tenax, nec facile illud mutaret, erat à Deo, auctore naturæ, sed ipse Pharao illa quasi armis, ut suo conditori resisteret, abutebatur. Hunc vero positivum concursum & cooperationem ac indurationem & aggravationem cordis Pharaonis, per quem id effectum fuerit du- rum, forte, potensque Deo resistere, Deo adscri- bere impium censemus. Nec vero durities est tan- tum naturalis constantia & animositas, sed est ipsa pertinacia & protervia animi superbi in Pharaone, quod cum Cornelio Rivetus agnoscit: cum ergo proterviæ & superbiæ istius Deus auctor non sit, quomodo ad duritiem cordis vel indurationem id- eo positive concurrit & cooperatur, quia animosi- tatis & constantiæ autor est? Neque solum de inna- ta concupiscentia & corruptæ naturæ indole, sed de malitiosa induratione hîc quæstio est, quam quomo- do Deo active & positive adscribere possumus ci- tra blasphemiam? Jesuitas id facere non mirum, qui easdem fere tibias inflant cum Calvinianis, ideoque solide refellere ipsos nequeunt, vid. Tom. 2. Syst. Th. p. 346. Quartus modus est subtractio gratiæ, quæ cor emolliret, sicuti sol indurat lutum non efficiendo positive duritiem, sed subtrahendo hu- morem sive exugendo, qui lutum temperabat, & molliebat;. Sic Deum etiam dici indurare Rivetus vult, & h. m. si bene intelligatur, rem confectam fo- re putat, quia cum hominis cor natura depravatum sit, in omnibus autem actionibus suis à Deo moveatur, si Deus non tollat naturæ perversitatem, quod non te- netur, dum eum movet Deus, motus ille, qua à Deo est, bonus est, sed à tali subjecto in se malo procedit, quicquid mali est in motu illo, & quo magis movetur, eo magis in peccatis suis volvitur. Respondemus; hîc multa occurrunt falsa vel suspecta saltem: nam assumitur (1.) gratia, quæ cor emolliat sensu Calvi- nianorum, id est, irresistibiliter. Ad conversionem autem & emollitionem non opus est gratia irreli- stibili, ea vero, quæ requiritur, nemini absolute denegatur, nemini simpliciter subtrahitur. Pro- inde (2.) falsum est, Deum omnem gratiam subtra- xisse Pharaoni; quum per verbum & miracula, ipsum officii commonefecerit, gratiamque suam ipsi exhibuerit. (3.) Neque simile illud convenit de sole, qui humorem exugit; quia Deus non exugit, si quid boni in homine est. (4.) Depravatio cor- dis in Pharaone non tantum spectanda ratione na- turalis perversitatis, quæ communis omnibus est ho- minibus; sed ratione voluntariæ σκληρότητος pro- pria ejus culpa contractæ.

Quintus modus est occasionum objectio: ad quas etiam refert Rivetus è Pererio Jesuita in c. 11. Exod. quod Deus multa faciat intra eum hominem, qui ob- duratur, quibus vitio suo fiat deterior: quod excitet in eo varios affectus & motus, vel spei atque fiduciæ vel cupiditatis vel iræ: varias item imaginationes & per- plexas & dubias cogitationes immittat, etiam somnia & visa nocturna injiciat, quibus ille nimio plus cre- dulus incitetur & precipitetur in malum. Similiter facere DEum circa hominem eundem exterius multa vel bona vel mala cum Pererio Rivetus statuit: bona ut sunt admonitiones, correctiones, flagella, beneficia: Mala vel quæ ad malum possint inclinare atq; eo incli- natura sint animum, cujusmodi sunt varia objecta voluptatum vel honorum, quibus jam corruptus ani- mus DeiƧ gratia & auxilio spoliatus protinus affentie- tur & adhærescit. Hæc autem DEum facere vel fieri permittere scientem peccatorem abusurum illis ad ma- jorem animæ suæ perniciem & exitium; quæ plane cum Calvini sententia coincidere judicat Rivetus. Sed quod mala sive interius sive exterius Deus ex- citet, aut quod objiciat quicquam eo fine, ut pec- cator eo abutatur ad suam perniciem, & scriptu- ræ S. & naturæ ac bonitati divinæ simpliciter repu- gnat; quandoquidem Deus nec promovere malum possit nec intendere ceu summe bonus, ideoque occasiones, quibus homo ad malum abutitur, à Deo non objiciuntur ad malum. Neque simile quid in historia Pharaonis observatur, omnia enim directa erant ad animum Pharaonis emolliendum, quem propria culpa ipse indurabat. Quod E. ad Pharaonis indurationem, positiva ejus causa tum Diabolus erat, cujus est excæcare cor 2. Cor. 4, 3. idque malitia implere Actor. 5, 3. & operari in filiis incredulitatis Ephes. 2, 2. tum Pharao ipse, ut asseritur Exod. 7, 13. 22. cap. 8, 19. roboravit se cor Pharaonis, & non audivit eos; cap. 9, 35. addidit Pharao ad peccandum cor suum; cap. 13, 15. factum est cum indurasset se Pharao; quod etiam agnovit Augustinus Serm. 88. de tempore, ad quem frustra provocant Calviniani; certissime, inquit, credendum, quod Pharaonem non DEI violentia, sed propria iniquitas & indomabilis superbia contra DEI præcepta toties fecit indurari. Quia vero induratio DEO etiam quandoque tribuitur, tum hoc in loco, tum Exod. 4, 2. cap. 9, 12. 33. cap. 10, 27. cap. 11, 10. Rom. 9, 29. observandum, quod induratio vel ut peccatum spectetur, vel ut pœna peccati: qua peccatum est, Deo tribui non potest sive ratione mandati, sive ratione beneplaciti, sive ratione concursus positivi: sive moraliter, sive physice; siquidem cum Deus nullius peccati causa sit, multo minus hujus tam atrocis peccati causa ulla ratione constitui debet, utpote quod prohibuit gravissime Psalm. 95, 8. de quo conquestus est Exod. 10, 3. 4. quo homo Deo sese directe opponit obvertendo ei tergum Zach. 7, 11. avertendo & obturando aures Pf. 58, 2. Es. 6, 10. Zach. 7, 11. occludendo oculos Es. 6, 10. Matth. 13, 15. indurando cervicem, Deuter. 10, 16. & faciem Jerem. 5, 3. frontemque Ezech. 2, 4. cor denique ipsum obfirmando, ac roborando adversus DEum Psalm. 95, 8. Quod tandem Deus etiam gravissime punit: quorum autem DEus ultor est, eorum autor non est.

Sed assumemus argumenta Cornelii, & quid ad illa respondeat Rivetus, dispiciemus. Primum hoc est, quod DEus misso Mose Pharaoni decies præcepit dimissionem populi; Ergo voluit, ut missum faceret populum. Non ergo obdurare eum voluit, ut populum retineret; hoc enim proprie velle est velle efficaciter, ut Pharao nolit populum dimittere: Velle autem ut dimittat, idque præcipere ac rursum efficaciter id nolle, ideoque obdurare, manifeste inter se pugnant. Respondet Rivetus; Velle efficaciter & proprie est illud efficere. At DEUS non effecit, ut dimitteret Pharao; E. non voluit proprie & efficaciter: dicendum ergo Deum voluisse populum suum à Pharaone dimitti & non voluisse. Voluisse voluntate mandati & approbationis, non voluisse voluntate decreti & efficientiæ; volebat E. id velle Pharaonem, id est, imperabat ut vellet & faceret, quia hoc debebat. Non volebat tamen id in Pharaone efficere, & eum ad id efficaciter movere, sed animum ab officio suo aversum sibi relinquere & Satanæ indurandum tradere & eos motus in illo efficere bene & sancte, quos tamen ille inficeret male? Sed falluntur utrique Antagonistæ cum assumunt, DEum id solum proprie velle, quod actu efficit, cum multa Deus proprie velit fieri, quæ ipse non efficit, ideoque etsi non effecerit, ut dimitteret Pharao populum, credendum tamen est, ipsum dimissionem illam serio & voluntate interni beneplaciti voluisse, quia imperavit eandem. Distinctio Riveti inter voluntatem mandati & approbationis, ac voluntatem decreti & efficientiæ sensu Calviniano falsa, absurda, & impia est, quasi DEus quicquam velit, id est, mandet, & approbet extrinsece, quod tamen interne non velit, sed cujus potius contrarium decreverit ac velit voluntate decreti & efficaciæ immutabili: utpote, quod man- darit dimissionem populi, decreverit autem efficere, ne dimitteret, animum ab officio suo aversum eo fine sibi relinquendo, eumq; Satanæ indurandum traden- do & motus in Pharaone efficiendo, quos ille inficeret male. Idque DEO ipso intendente & id agente, ut male inficeret. Quæ horrida sunt & blasphema. Nullæ enim in Deo contrariæ voluntates sunt, nec aliud externe agit, aliud interne decrevit, & ut fiat, efficaciter, miris & arcanis modis præstat. Nimi- rum id volunt Calviniani, ut aperte quandoque mentem produnt suam, quam hîc occultat Rive- tus (1.) Deum inenarrabili consilio quæ fieri non vult, & facere vetat, fieri velle in diversum finem; ut ha- bet Calvinus ad calumnias nebulonis p. 103. (2.) im- pios ita à divina providentia regi, ut nihil aliud effi- cere queant, quam quod Deus æterno suo & immuta- bili consilio decrevit, Triglandius in Declarat. p. 14. (3.) Deum uti sua gratia destituit reprobos, ut non possint non peccare, ita etiam eos ad hanc conditionem destinasse, ut non queant non facere ex sua natura, imo reprobos constringi necessitate peccandi, eoque & pereundi ex hac DEI ordinatione, atque ita constringi, ut nequeant non peccare atque perire, Zanch. c. 11. de reprobat. qv. 2. Unde (4.) docent, Deum velle pec- catum voluntate beneplaciti, Bucanus in Loc. Com. p. 155. Deum homines ad suas pravas actiones incita- re, seducere, trahere, jubere, indurare, deceptiones immittere, & quæ peccata gravia sunt, efficere. Pe- trus Martyr. in Jud. 3, 9. p. 45. Deum ad peccata, quæ prohibet, occulta ratione impellere; Piscat. Macov. & alii; quæ blasphemiæ sunt & omnem religio- nem tollunt. Recte Cornelius: Si Dei voluntas erat, obdurare Pharaonem; E. ei se conformans non peccabat, Dei enim voluntas omnis bonæ voluntatis est mensura. Nequicquam autem respondet Rivetus: id verum esse de voluntate Dei, quatenus pro præcepto accipitur, non de voluntate decreti & efficaciæ; nam ita qui voluntatem decreti Dei præstat, non peccabit, etsi præcepto Dei contraveniat. Dat exemplum Ri- vetus; an qui Christum cruci affixerunt, excusantur à peccato, quia fecerunt quod voluit Deus? Sed præ- supponit impium suum dogma, voluisse DEUM, ut hoc facerent; cum distinguendum sit inter passio- nem & actionem; etsi enim decreverit, ut Christus pateretur, non tamen voluit, ut Judæi ipsum cruci affigerent; sed hîc valeat illud Prosperi: Actio displicuit, passio grata fuit. Prævisa nempe malitia, induratione & excæcatio- ne Judæorum, qua Christum in crucem acturi erant, ad finem salutarem, præter intentionem Judæorum direxit crucifixionem; hoc vero non est velle effi- caciter, nedum efficere id quod fecerunt impii Ju- dæi. Altera ratio est, Deus reluctantem Pharaonem gravissime punit: at Deus non est autor eorum, quorum est ultor, teste Fulgentio l. 1. ad Monim. c. 3. Respon- det Rivetus: ipsam reluctationem Pharaonis, quate- nus est à Deo, esse ultionem, & pœnam peccati, qua- tenus autem fit ab homine, etiam peccatum esse, ideo- que distinguenda esse causarum genera; qua Deus est autor obdurationis, ejus Deus non est ultor, sed per eam ulciscitur; qua homo se obdurat, illius obdura- tionis Deus non est autor, qua peccatum est, sed ultor.
