Resp. diversi considerandi modi & respectus aut fi- nes indurationis non possunt è peccato non-pec- catum facere, aut aliquem à peccati culpa absolve- re. Manet induratio peccatum, etiamsi pœnæ causa fiat, aut immittatur; & qui indurat active ac positive, vere causa peccati est, sive id faciat ut puniat, sive alia ratione. Distinguimus sane & nos induratio- nem, qua est pœna & qua peccatum est, sed non do- cemus, Deum positive & active concurrere ad in- durationem. Hoc vero cum dicant Calviniani,

Deum omnino indurationis auctorem faciunt, quoscunque etiam fines, aut respectus excogitent. Nos ad indurationem, cum pœna est peccati, con- currere dicimus Deum, cum objecta & occasionem peccandi non indurationis, sed probationis causa exhibet, duritiei suæ hominem relinquit, gratiam ei subducit, imo in potestatem Satanæ etiam ipsum tra- dit, qui eundem positivè indurat. Ineptum est, quod dicit Rivetus, obdurationem esse peccatum, quate- nus est à Pharaone; sed quatenus à DEO, non esse pec- catum, sed pœnam peccati: nam peccati ratio non è causa efficiente aut finali æstimanda est, sed è causa formali: peccatum est ἀνομία, à quocunque tan- dem proficiscatur & quacunque intentione, aut fi- ne fiat. Quod in se malum est & culpa, id nec ullo fine licet, & à quocunque agente fit, vel fiat malum est. Efficiens & finis causæ externæ sunt, quorum diversitas non facit, ut peccatum aut malum non sit peccatum vel malum.

Tertium argumentum ex illis locis depromi- tur, quibus Pharaoni tribuitur induratio. Respon- det Rivetus: & se tribuere culpam & obdurationem Pharaoni, nihilominus Deo etiam tribuere justam Pharaonis obdurationem sine ulla culpa. Sed aliter Scriptura Deo, aliter Pharaoni eam tribuit, DEO permissive & indirecte, Pharaoni effective & directe. Quod vero Rivetus cum permissione illa divina conjunctam dicit actionem & efficaciam circa mul- tas actiones ad id facientes, si actionem Dei & ef- ficaciam influere positive in obdurationem vel ea intentione solum fieri, ut homo induretur, intelli- gat, ἄτερ γραφῆς id dicit, imo Scripturæ contradi- cit: id enim Scripturæ aperte refragatur, quod (etsi Bellarminum testem lib. 2. de amiss. gratiæ & Statu peccati c. 14. laudet) asserit, Deum non intendere conversionem & pœnitentiam, sed pœnam eorum, qui indurantur. Nam quamvis induratio, cum pœ- na est, ut pœna intendatur, tamen neque quoties indurare Deus dicitur, actus puniendi respicitur; sæpe occasionis ratione aut tolerantia, & longanimi- tate sua aut permissione indurare intelligitur: & ubi per verbum suum cum homine agit, conversionem utique ejusdem intendit: neque cum induratio pœna est, h. e. cum quis privatur Dei gratia, Sata- næque traditur, Deus homini prorsus deest, quin commonefactionibus & vel pœnis ipsis ac judiciis suis eundem revocatum velit à duritie sua; quod exemplo Judæorum, qui maxime excæcati, & in- durati, ac in potestate & laqueis diaboli constri- cti erant, luculenter constat, utpote quos Christus adhuc congregatos & conversos cupiebat Joh. 5. 24. Matth. 23, 37. Durities vel induratio passiva, uti definit eam Rivetus, (πώρωσις καρδίας Marc. 3, 5. dicta) perversus est affectus paulatim indu- ctus, quo excæcata mente & intelligentia Voluntas pertinaciam contrahit & proterviam, ita ut admoni- tionibus non solum nec cedat, nec eas sentiat, sed etiam sentire & cedere moraliter non possit. Quis vero hunc tam perversum affectum Deo auctori adscri- beret aut Deum ad eundem positive, directe & effi- caciter concurrere admittet? Urget autem Rive- tus cum Calvino suo hoc præcipue argumentum: Quicquid decernit justus judex, id vult efficaciter. Atqui pœnam decernit justus judex; E. eam vult efficaciter. Excæcatio autem est pœna à Deo decre- ta; E. eam vult DEUS efficaciter. Resp. fallit σό- φισμα ambiguitate: quia efficaciter velle dicitur, vel quod efficiat DEUS id ipsum, quod vult, vel etiam quod efficiat id irresistibiliter, faltim quod non nolit, ut id fiat, etiamsi ipse id non effi- ciat; nam non omnia, quæ decernit Judex, etsi velit etiam efficaciter, ut fiant, ipse facit. Decer- nere etiam potest in pœnam aliquid permittere, ut hoc vel illud fiat, & in supplicium cedat: non est necessum, ut positive semper influat in pœnam, tum vero Deus, quod diligenter observandum, non tantum ut justus judex, & ratione justitiæ suæ spe- ctandus est, sed etiam ut πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν mul- tus miseratione, & qui in media ira recordatur miseri- cordiæ suæ; ideo dispar ejus, & judicis ratio est, cum pœnam infligit; judex enim tantum infligit pœnam, ut delictum puniatur, & facinorosus plectatur, Deus vero etsi delicta puniat, & contumaces, atque indu- ratos potestati Satanæ tradat, non tamen omni o- mnino eos destituit gratia, cum adhuc in via sunt; nam & illos, qui secundum duritiem suam & ἀμετα- νόητον καρδίαν iram sibi thesaurizant, divitiis χρηστό- τητος καὶ ἀνοχῆς καὶ μακροθυμίας invitat & per- ductos vult εἰς μετάνοιαν, etiamsi illi id vel non cu- rent, vel non intelligant: Rom. 2, 4. Quod ex- emplo ipsius Pharaonis docetur Exod. 9, 16. Rom. 9, 17. In hoc ipsum servavi te, ut ostenderem virtutem meam, ut Paulus habet; Vel ut videre te facerem pa- tientiam meam, ut in Mose habetur; Ita ergo divi- tias & virtutem patientiæ Deus ostendebat hac to- lerantia, & conservatione Pharaonis. Et quum testetur hoc Deus se agere etiam adversus illos, qui indurati sunt eo fine, ut ad conversionem perducantur: aliud mente divina decretum esse adversus eosdem, præ- sumere non licet, nisi Deus ὑποκρίσεως impiæ ar- guendus sit, a qua impietate Calviniani sese non li- berabunt, quoad usque docebunt, reprobos vocari aut induratos non ut convertantur, sed ut puniantur, magis indurentur, & pereant, quemadmodum dupli- cem vocationis finem pro diversitate electorum & reproborum assignare solent, mentemque ipsorum ita prodidit Trigland. in Apolog. p. 38. 98. Reprobos quod attinet, eos Deus vel plane non vocat, neq; exter- ne per verbum, neque interne per Spiritum, vel si ex- terne verbum suum iis annunciari curat, interne eos efficaciter per Spiritum suum non movet, ut verbum re- cipiant eiǵ; credant, sed justo judicio eos excæcat, atque indurat, donec tandem in peccatis suis moriantur & pereant. Atque hæc de induratione: vid. de hac materia Remonstrantes in explic. c. 9. ad Rom. p. 146.

## 7:10
Vers. 10. AND AARON TOOK THE ROD BEFORE PHARAOH AND HIS SERVANTS, WHICH WAS TURNED INTO A SERPENT) See whether from this the custom of carrying a caduceus came first to the neighboring nations, and then to the Greeks and Romans.

Latin:

Vers. 10. TVLITQVE AARON VIRGAM CORAM PHARAONE ET SERVIS EJVS, QVÆ VERSA EST IN COLVBRVM) Vide an hinc ad finitimas primum gentes, de- inde ad Græcos Romanosque mos venerit legatis ferendi ca- duceum.

## 7:11
Vers. 11. BUT PHARAOH CALLED THE WISE MEN AND THE SORCERERS

The name of wise man is general, by which those skilled in secret things or in a marvelous and magical art are signified, whence by a general name a special one is added for the sake of explanation, mekhashphim, which the Vulgate declares by 'maleficos' (sorcerers), more correctly they are called 'Præstigiatores' (jugglers): Moses also adds the name hartummim, by which some say astrologers and soothsayers are designated, others say necromancers. The LXX rendered it: epaoidos, enchanters; Schindler interprets it as Magi. It is a foreign word, as Mercer notes, like many that have been adopted into the Hebrew language. Aquila interpreted it as kryphiastas, from the hidden art or hidden things which they performed. A fourth name is also added, lahatehem, but by it not the enchanters themselves, but their enchantments are expressed, as Sixtus Amama observes at this place. Most people, with Pliny, Justin, and Augustine, make Zoroaster the inventor of such arts, who lived in the time of Ninus and Abraham, nearly 600 years before Moses, and is believed by some to have been Ham, the son of Noah. The leaders of those Magi of Pharaoh were Jannes and Jambres, as the Apostle testifies in 2 Tim. 3, 8, which names the Apostle did not draw from an Apocryphal book, as Origen in Hom. 35

in Matthew maintains, but had from divine inspiration. Berosus in the fragments names one of these Cenchus. See also Philo, book 2, on the life of Moses.

Vers. same. THEY DID LIKEWISE.

Not that it was a true miracle, but something similar; for although some of the Pontiffs think that true miracles can be performed by a demon and by infidels, especially Maldonado in c. 7. Matth. v. 22, who brings forward Chrysostom, Jerome, Euthymius, and Theophylact to that opinion, to whom Toletus also seems akin in annot. in c. 3. Joh. ann. 2, and Pererius, although he speaks hesitantly and ambiguously in book 4 in Dan. disp. 3. Nevertheless, one must distinguish entirely between miracles which are truly such, and 'lying wonders' (terata pseudous), as Scripture calls those in 2 Thess. 2, 9, the miracles which the Anti-Christ was to perform, which the Papists themselves commonly maintain were to be very great; whence it can be gathered that if the greatest miracles of the Anti-Christ are themselves lying wonders, much more must the miracles of others, such as false prophets and infidels, Matth. 24, 24, be considered as such, therefore Bellarmine confesses that those even greatest miracles are done only apparently, book 4 de Eccles. c. 14, and most Papists with Thomas, part 1, q. 110, art. 4, refer to a true miracle as that which is done beyond the order of the whole created nature, therefore Corn. a Lap. at this place denies that true miracles can be performed by a demon, because they exceed all the power of nature and all the faculty of a creature. Which is most certain from the Scriptures, as they claim the power of performing miracles for GOD alone, Ps. 72, 18, Ps. 136, 4, and therefore they deny that there is any one like GOD who performs miracles, Exod. 15, 14, 15, and they require infinite power for miracles, Ps. 77, 14, 15, and thus from miracles they conclude an axiom of adoration, that one must believe in Him and adore that God who performs miracles, which argument Christ and the Evangelists themselves use when divine honor is claimed for Christ, Joh. 2, c. 5, c. 10, c. 15, c. 20, last verse. Wherefore, although the instruments of Satan sometimes perform wonderful things, they are nevertheless not true miracles, but only seem such as regards their external appearance, whether done through the illusions of the demon, when the eyes are dazzled or the imagination is deranged, so that one thinks he sees what in reality he does not see, since demons can variously move the imagination, and both disturb the organ of sight and change the external medium, etc. how Apollonius of Tyana raised a dead man, mocking the eyes of the spectators so that they thought him alive who was in reality dead: either by local motion, when, for example, they quickly bring some object from elsewhere and substitute it, so that they appear to have produced it or to have changed nature, in which manner it is likely that the Magi brought in serpents and withdrew rods by the help of a demon, so that it appeared that the rods had turned into snakes; or finally by applying active agents to passive ones, and mixing them through natural causes, the power of which demons have most thoroughly known; concerning which see Delrio, *de Magia* lib. 2. qu. 9., who refutes the opinion of Maldonatus. Gitb. Voet. *de sign. & mirac.* part. 2. *dispp. select.* &c.

Latin:

Vers. 11. VOCAVIT AVTEM PHARAO SAPIENTES AC MALEFICOS

Nomen sapientis generale est, quo significantur rerum arcanarum vel artis mirabilis & magicæ pe- riti, unde generali nomine fpeciale ἐξηγήσεως cau- sa subjungitur מְכַשְׁפִים quod per maleficos decla- rat Vulgatus, rectius Præstigiatores dicuntur: addit etiam Moses nomen חַרְטֻמִים quo genethliacos & ariolos nonnulli, alii necromanticos designari dicunt. LXX. reddiderunt: ἐπαοιδὸς incantatores, Schind- lerus Magos interpretatur. Vox peregrina est, no- tante Mercero, quales multæ in linguam Ebræam afcitæ. Aquila interpretatus est κρυφιασὰς ab ar- te occulta vel rebus occultis, quas efficiebant. Ad- ditur & quartum nomen לַהֲטֵיהֶם sed eo non ipsi incantatores, sed incantationes ipsorum exprimun- tur, ut observat Sixt. Amama ad h. l. Inventorem ta- lium artium pleriq; cum Plinio, Justino & August. fa- ciunt Zoroastrem, qui tempore Nini, & Abrahæ, 600. fere annis ante Mosen vixit, & a nonnullis creditur Cham fuisse Noæ filius. Principes istorum Magorum Pharaonis Jannes & Jambres fuere teste Apostolo 2. Tim. 3, 8. quæ nomina non ex libro A- pocrypho Apostolus hausit, ut Orig. Hom. 35.

in Matth. statuit, sed ex inspiratione divina habuit. Berosus in fragment. unum ex his Cenchum nominat. Vid. etiam Philo l. 2. de vit. Mos.

Vers. eod. FECERUNT SIMILITER.

Non quod verum miraculum fuerit, sed simile quid; etsi enim nonnulli e Pontif. arbitrentur, mi- racula vera a dæmone, & infidelibus fieri posse, imprimis vero Maldonado in c. 7. Matth. v. 22. qui adducit in eam sententiam Chrysostomum, Hieron. Euthymium & Theophylact. cui affinis videtur etiam Toletus annot. in c. 3. Joh. ann. 2. & Pererius, quan- quam is dubitanter loquatur, & ambigue l. 4. in Dan. disp. 3. Distinguendum tamen omnino in- ter miracula, quæ vere talia sint, & τέρατα ψεύδυς prodigia mendacii, ut scriptura vocat illa 2. Thes. 2, 9. miracula, quæ Anti-Christus patraturus erat, quæ maxima omnino futura ipsi Papistæ communiter statuunt; unde colligere licet, si miracula maxima Anti-Christi ipsius prodigia sunt mendacii, multo magis aliorum miracula, pseudoprophetarum pu- ta & infidelium, Matth. 24, 24. talia habenda erunt, ideo Bellarm. fatetur, apparenter tantum fieri illa et- iam maxima quæq; miracula lib. 4. de Eccles. c. 14. & Papistæ pleriq; cum Thoma part. 1. qv. 110. art. 4. ad verum miraculum referunt, ut fiat præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, ideo Corn. a Lap. in h. l. mira- cula vera negat a dæmone fieri posse, quia omnem naturæ vim, omnemque creaturæ facultatem supe- rant. Quod e Scripturis certissimum est, utpote quæ soli DEO vim miracula patrandi vindicant Ps. 72, 18. Ps. 136, 4. eoq; negant, ullum DEO similem es- se, qui miracula faciat Exod. 15, 14. 15. & infinitam virtutem ad miracula requirunt, Ps. 77, 14. 15. adeo- que ex miraculis axioma adorationis concludunt, in illa credendum esse, eumque Deum adorandum, qui miracula patrat, quo argumento Christus & Ev- angelistæ ipsi utuntur, cum Christo divinus honor vindicatur Joh. 2. c. 5. c. 10. c. 15. c. 20. vers. ult. Qua- propter etsi mira patrent quandoque instrumenta Satanæ, vera tamen non sunt miracula, sed tantum quoad externam apparentiam talia videntur, sive per præstigias dæmonis facta, cum oculi perstringuntur, aut phantasia dementatur, ut quis putet, se videre, quod revera non videt, siquidem phantasiam varie movere possint dæmones, tum organum visus tur- bare, tum exterius medium immutare &c. quomo- do Apollonius Thyaneus mortuum resuscitavit, il- ludens oculis spectatorum, ut vivum eum putarent, qui revera erat mortuus: seu per motum localem, cum v. g. celeriter rem aliquam aliunde adducunt, substituunt, ut produxisse aut naturam immutasse videantur, quo pacto adduxisse Magos serpentes, subtraxisse virgas ope dæmonis verisimile est, ut appareret, virgas in colubros transiisse; sive deniq; applicando activa passivis, eaque commiscendo per causas naturales, quarum virtutem dæmones peni- tissime cognitam habent; de quibus Delrio de Ma- gia lib. 2. qu. 9. qui Maldonati sententiam profligat. Gitb. Voet. de sign. & mirac. part. 2. dispp. select. &c.

## 7:12
v. 12. AND THEY CAST DOWN EVERY MAN HIS RODS WHICH WERE TURNED INTO DRAGONS.

It is asked whether they were true dragons or serpents or not? Justin, Tertullian, Nyssen, and Prosper think they were only illusions of the demon, to whom some of the Pontifical interpreters also seem to agree, as does Rivetus in this place. But because they are called serpents just as those which Moses and Aaron produced, and it must not be said that the eyes of Moses and Aaron were bewitched, for they would have detected those illusions, indeed the serpent of Aaron truly devoured the serpents of the magicians, for these were not illusions, or illusions, which no pious person will ascribe to the servants of God, with Theodoret and Augustine: Lyranus, Burgensis, Tostatus, Cajetan, Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus, and Bonfrerius more correctly determine that they were true serpents. But how were those serpents produced? Calvin says that God changed the rods of the Magicians into serpents, in order to harden Pharaoh. But this is impious and blasphemous, and by that reasoning God would have fought against Himself, since the serpents of the Magicians were devoured by the serpents of Moses. Cajetan thinks, with Thomas and Delrio, that there was a true conversion of the rods into true serpents, but that it was done by applying active agents to passive ones, with such promptness that whatever things are necessary for the alteration and generation of an animal from pre-existing matter were all done in the twinkling of an eye, so that when the rods were thrown down, true serpents were produced from them, provided that demons can produce imperfect animals of this kind from putrefied rods; Peter Martyr, Class 1, Commonplaces, ch. 9, inclines to this opinion. But those rods were not putrefied, and the distance between a rod and a serpent is so great that a serpent cannot be produced from a rod, nor is it permissible to feign that there is anything of a seminal nature in the rods from which serpents might arise when nature is excited, even if the artifice of a demon is added. And therefore it remains for us to say that these serpents were brought from elsewhere and suddenly and imperceptibly substituted by the demon in place of the staffs, which is the opinion of most interpreters; which God permitted to happen, but in such a way that in these wonders Moses might prevail, and divine power might shine forth, partly so that the fallacies and deceits of the Magicians, by which Pharaoh was seduced and confirmed in his hardness, might be exposed; and partly so that Moses himself might not be thought a Magician, but that it might be evident ὀφθαλμοφανῶς [before the eyes] that Moses was the antagonist, victor, and tamer of the Magicians, and the great servant and Prophet of GOD, as Chrysostom says. Homily 37 on the Acts of the Apostles speaks; for the magicians did indeed change, as Theodoret observes, rods into serpents, but the rod of Moses devoured their rods; they changed water into blood, but they could not reduce the blood to its former nature; they produced frogs, but they could not remove the annoyance and inconveniences of the frogs from the Egyptians, as Moses did: compare the disputations on Magic by Gisbertus Voetius. Rivetus indicates yet another distinction, that the demon only formed bodies similar to the bodies of serpents, which were indeed true bodies, but not animated, and that the demon supplied that deficiency by moving them as if they were true serpents. But since Scripture equally calls them serpents, those which were seen to have come forth from the hand of the Magicians and that one which Aaron truly produced, it is more correctly believed that they were true serpents, but not produced, rather brought from elsewhere.

Verse same. BUT AARON'S ROD DEVOURD THEIR RODS.

Aaron's rod, that is, the serpent into which Aaron's rod was converted, devoured the rods of the Magicians, that is, the serpents into which the rods of the Magicians appeared to be converted, by Metonymy. But from the fact that the rods are called serpents because they were previously rods, Cornelius wrongly concludes that bread in the Eucharist is also called so, which had been bread, even if it has been converted into the body of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:26, John 6:31; for as far as John ch. 6 is concerned, it does not deal with the matter or form of the Eucharistic sacrament, even if what is contained there is rightly applied to the efficacy of the Sacrament, as we showed in our Harmon. Anti-Calixt. p. 762, as being said of the spiritual perception of the Lord's body. As for the other passage, it is clear that it is called bread after the blessing because it remains bread, even if it is a communication of the body of Christ, and therefore transubstantiation is here assumed by Cornelius by a begging of the question, which cannot be proved from the words of the Supper. If these words were read in the words of institution: bread is converted into the body of Christ, just as it is openly said in this place, Aaron's rod was converted into a serpent, they could urge their Metonymy in the words of the Apostle. But the Papists themselves are not yet certain, and not even the popes and Papistic Councils have been able to define it; whether by transubstantiation, to which the Council of Trent inclines, or indeed by adduction, which they say was sanctioned in the Lateran Council, the body of Christ is present (concerning which disputes of theirs see our Exegetical work on the Augsburg Confession); so far is it from being the case that they can pronounce that the dogma of transubstantiation is clearly contained in the words of Christ.

Latin:

v. 12. PROJECERUNTQVE SINGULI VIR- GAS SUAS QVÆ VERSÆ SUNT IN DRA- CONES.

Quæritur, an veri dracones vel serpentes fue- rint, necne? Præstigias tantum fuisse dæmonis, Justi- nus, Tertull. Nyssenus, Prosper putant, quibus acce- dere etiam videntur nonnulli e Pontif. Interpreti- bus, ut & Rivetus in h. l. Sed quia æque Serpentes nominantur atque illi, quos Moses & Aaron pro- duxere, neque dicendum, Mosis & Aaronis o- culos fascinatos fuisse, quin præstigias illas dete- xissent, imo serpens Aaronis vere devoravit ser- pentes Magorum, hæ enim non fuere præstigiæ, aut illusiones, quas nemo pius servis Dei adscribet, cum Theodoreto, & Augustino: rectius Lyranus, Bur- gens. Tostat. Cajetan. Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus, Bonfrerius statuunt, veros fuisse serpentes. Quomodo autem serpentes illi producti? Calvinus dicit, Deum virgas Magorum in serpentes mutasse, ut Pharaonem obduraret. Sed hoc impium & blasphe- mum est, eaque ratione secum ipse pugnasset Deus, cum serpentes Magorum a serpentibus Mosis devo- rati sunt. Cajetanus existimat cum Thoma & Del- rione, veram fuisse conversionem virgarum in veros serpentes, sed factam applicando activa passivis, cum ea promtitudine, ut quæcunque necessaria sunt ad alterationem & ad generationem animalis ex præja- cente materia, ea omnia in ictu oculi facta fuerint, ita ut projectis virgis ex eis veri serpentes producti sint, siquidem dæmones imperfecta hujusmodi ani- malia ex putrefactis virgis producere possint; in quam sententiam Petrus Martyr. Classe 1. Loc. Com. c. 9. inclinat. Sed nec virgæ illæ putrefactæ sunt, & tanta est inter virgam & serpentem distantia, ut ex virga serpens produci nequeat, nec fingere lice- at aliquid seminei virgis inesse, unde oriantur ser- pentes natura excitata, etiamsi dæmonis accedat ar- tificium. Ideoque superest, ut dicamus, serpentes hosce aliunde adductos subito & imperceptibiliter loco baculorum substitutos esse a dæmone, quæ plerorumq; interpretum est sententia; quod permisit Deus fie- ri, sed ita, ut in hisce miris Moses superaret, & divi- na potentia effulgeret, partim ut detegerentur fal- laciæ Magorum & præstigiæ, a quibus seducebatur Pharao, & in duritie sua confirmabatur; partim ne Moses ipse putaretur Magus, sed ut ὀφθαλμοφα- νῶς constaret, Mosen Magorum antagonistam, vi- ctorem, & domitorem verum, magnumque DEI servum & Prophetam esse, ut Chrysost. Hom. 37. in Acta Apostolorum loquitur; nam mutabant magi quidem, quod Theod. observat, virgas in serpen- tes, sed virga Mosis virgas illorum devoravit, mu- tabant aquam in sanguinem, sed sanguinem in pri- orem naturam reducere non poterant, produxe- runt illi ranas, sed molestiam & incommoda rana- rum ab Ægyptiis auferre non poterant, sicut fecit Moses: conf. de Magia dispp. Gisberti Voetii. Rive- tus adhuc aliud discrimen indicat, dæmonem solum corpora similia corporibus serpentum efformasse, quæ vera quidem corpora fuerint, sed non animata, defe- ctum autem illum supplevisse dæmonem, illa movendo, ac si veri fuissent serpentes. Verum cum Scriptura æque serpentes vocet, qui visi sunt prodiiffe a Ma- gorum manu, atque illum, quem Aaron vere pro- duxit,, rectius creditur veros illos serpentes fuisse, sed non productos, verum aliunde adductos.

Vers. eod. SED DEVORAVIT VIRGA AARON VIRGAS EORUM.

Virga Aaronis, id est, serpens in quem virga Aaronis conversa fuit, devoravit virgas Magorum, id est, serpentes, in quos videbantur conversæ vir- gæ Magorum per Metonym. Inde vero quod vir- gæ serpentes vocentur, quia fuere antea virgæ, per- peram colligit Corn. in Eucharistia panem etiam ita vocari, qui fuerat panis, etsi conversus sit in corpus Christi 1. Cor. 11, 26. Joh. 6, 31. nam quod ad c. 6. Joh. attinet, non agi eodem de sacramenti Eucharistici materia aut forma, etsi quæ ibi habentur, rectè ad efficaciam Sacramenti applicentur, utpote dicta de Spirituali perceptione corporis Domini, in Harmon. Anti-Calixt. p. 762. ostendimus. Quod ad alterum locum, apertum est, panem vocari post benedictionem, quia panis manet, etsi sit commu- nicatio corporis Christi, ideoque transsubstantiatio per petitionem principii hic supponitur a Corne- lio, quæ e verbis cœnæ probari nequit. Si in verbis institutionis hæc legerentur : panis convertitur in corpus Christi, quemadmodum h. l. aperte dicitur, virga Aaronis conversa est in serpentem, urgere Metonymiam suam possent in verbis Apostoli. Sed Papistæ ipsi nondum certi sunt, ac ne pontifices qui- dem, & Concilia Papistica id definire potuerunt; an per transsubstantiationem, quo propendet Con- cil. Trident. an vero per adductionem, quod in La- teranens. Conc. sancitum esse ajunt, corpus Christi adfit (de quibus ipsorum litigiis vid. Exeget. nostra August. Conf.) tantum abest, ut luculenter in ver- bis Christi transsubstantiationis dogma haberi, pro- nunciare possint.

## 7:14
Verse WAS HEAVENED] In Greek, βεβάρηται ἡ καρδία τῶ φαραώ [the heart of Pharaoh was weighed down]. Pharaoh's heart had hardened itself beforehand. This very thing which Pharaoh had done within himself, GOD reveals to Moses. See soon 32. There was in Pharaoh, as Josephus notes, folly with wickedness and malice.

Latin:

Vers. INGRAVATVM EST] In Græco, βεβάρηται ἡ καρ- δία τῶ φαραώ. Præcessit obfirmavit se cor Pharaonis. Hoci- psum quod Pharao intra se fecerat, DEVS patefacit Mosi. Vi- de mox 32. Fuit in Pharaone, ut notat Josephus ἀφροσύνη με- τὰ πονηρίας κὰι κακίας.

## 7:17
Verse 17. BEHOLD I WILL STRIKE WITH THE ROD. Leonhard Marius in this place and other Papists conclude thus: since God worked miracles through staffs, we also can consecrate inanimate things, and use them in performing miracles with confidence in divine aid. But whatever may be the case regarding Marius's opinion, namely whether some internal power has been placed in inanimate things, by which they, as proper causes and reaching the effect, truly work miracles, in the affirmative of which question he will hardly have consenting associates, Lorinus on Acts ch. 5 v. 15, Estius, and others; the consequence itself is truly worthless: If God chose certain creatures as moral instruments in performing miracles; therefore also men without an institution or word of GOD can consecrate certain things for the use of performing miracles. Nor indeed does confidence have a place where no word of God is available, because faith and the word are related. Faith embraces and receives the word, the word begets faith. If men believe that they can instill a supernatural power into creatures by their own consecrations, that is manifest sacrilege, indeed a certain species of idolatry.

It is also inquired in this place whether a creature can concur in performing miracles as a physical efficient cause, at least an instrumental one, or in any respect whatsoever, in such a way, however, that a true and real influence in the act of the miracle is to be ascribed to it? The Scholastics and some Papists precisely deny this; see Wilh. Estius in 2. sentent. dist. 1. sect. 5, where he teaches that a creature in miracles behaves itself only by way of a moral instrument or a meritorious cause or a cause without which it would not be: and in 3. sentent. dist. 16. qv. 1. art. 3, where he contends that not even the soul of Christ could have concurred in the changing of the law of nature, except by way of prayer and intercession: and he attributes that opinion to Thomas. Rivet seizes upon this, distinguishing in this cause as follows: If a rational creature is an instrument, it cannot be done otherwise than insofar as it signifies by word that God is performing that miracle, or asks for it by prayer; but if it is an inanimate creature, it is only a sign of the thing to be effected or of the divine action, but does not itself properly operate. The same is the opinion of Gisbertus Voetius in part 2 of his selected disputations, page 973; he says that secondary causes cooperate and concur physically to the antecedents or preparations, and to the accompanying or consequent adjuncts, but by no means to the act of the miracle itself as such and formally so called: that angels and men perform miracles as moral causes, or rather as moral συνάιτια of an instrument; which he affirms especially also concerning Christ, as he is man, on page 989.

He asks, namely, whether Christ, according to his human nature or as he is man, is the author of a miracle? And he answers: it is denied, but he only is a minister, or delegated cause, and a moral instrument, as also on page 1011, where, regarding the opinion of Heinsius—that Christ’s εὐχαριστία, or εὐλογία, by which he blessed the loaves with prayers to the Father, was the cause of the multiplication of the loaves—he notes that the natures in Christ must be distinguished: that he blessed and gave thanks according to his human nature, and thus could have contributed to the production of the miracle by a ministerial and delegated power, as an instrument or minister, and by moral causality alone, namely by praying and by commanding in the name of GOD that the bread be multiplied. Although indeed an infinite power is required to perform miracles, and in every miracle it is necessary that something be made from nothing, whether there is no underlying matter at all, or whether there is in it no passive potency for the effect that is produced, whence it is claimed for divine power alone to call those things which are not, Rom. 4, 16. nevertheless, the θαυματουργικὴ (miracle-working) power is not to be denied to the human nature of Christ, nor are miracles to be ascribed to him only as a minister, or a delegated cause, or a moral instrument, since infinite power was communicated to him through the personal union, which we asserted expressly in the Examination of the doctrine concerning the person of Christ. Nor did Christ, as he is man, obtain miracles only by way of prayer, or concur in these miracles only morally, which he also performed in the days of his flesh according to his human nature, because in that way there would be no difference between the miracles of the saints and the miracles of Christ according to his human nature: but the same influx that the divine nature of Christ had through the infinite power essentially proper to itself, the human nature of Christ has through the same power personally communicated to it: whence the paralogism of Voetius vanishes into smoke: If Christ as man is the physical cause of miracles, there will be two omnipotences, two first causes, because there is only one infinite power belonging to Christ as God and man, which is proper to him as God κατ᾿ αὑτὸ (in itself), and belongs to him as Man κατ᾿ ἄλλο (through another), and by the grace of communication; but the influx of the same power, even if it happens in different ways, cannot produce two omnipotences or two first causes, since Christ performed miracles for his own honor, so that they might believe in him, and faith is directed toward Christ not only as he is God, but also as he is man, and his glory, by which he is to be pursued with the worship of adoration, must be rendered to Christ not only according to his divine nature, but also according to his human nature; and as he is mediator, he is to be religiously adored according to both natures: either it is necessary that the Calvinists detract from Christ, as he is mediator, this honor, or that they acknowledge that Christ, even as man, concurred in mediatorial works and in acts of miracle, not only morally, but physically, because the concurrence of a moral instrument does not imply a divine axiom or religious worship; in which matter the Calvinists themselves still contend among themselves, namely, whether Christ, as he is mediator, is the proper and direct cause of any miracle. Voetius denies it, because the formal reason by which he is mediator does not imply the proper cause of a miracle. But although it may be admitted that to be mediator is not, properly speaking, the formal reason for the operation of miracles, yet because infinite power is materially required for the mediator and for the fulfilling of that office, certainly by the power of that same [power] Christ as mediator was able to perform divine miracles; indeed, without divine miracles he could not execute that office. And since most Calvinists acknowledge that Christ as mediator is to be adored, whatever may be the case regarding the peculiar negative of Voetius, which is also that of Maccovius in his disputation on the mediator Christ, 56, which Maresius, Vol. 2, against Tirinus, page 1065, near the end, considers to be held as a paradox in the Reformed Churches, certainly because Christ as man is mediator, it is necessary that he be endowed with infinite power, even according to his human nature, such as without doubt it is, by which miracles are performed; for the glory of adoration altogether presupposes infinite power and majesty.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ECCE PERCVTIAM VIRGA. Leonh. Marius in h. l. & Papistæ alii ita colli- gunt: quum Deus operatus sit miracula per baculos, etiam nos consecrare posse res inanimatas, iisque uti in miraculis patrandis fiducia divini auxilii. Sed quic- quid sit de Marii sententia, utrum nempe rebus ina- nimatis vis aliqua interna indita sit, qua illæ tanquam causa propriæ, & effectum attingentes vere operentur miracula, in cujus quæstionis affirmativa vix con- sentientes habebit socios, Lorinum in c. 5. Act. v. 15. Estium, & alios; consequentia ipsa vere ficulnea est: Si Deus quasdam creaturas elegit in instrumenta mo- ralia in patrandis miraculis; E. etiam homines sine in- stitutione aut verbo DEI possunt res quasdam conse- crare in usum patrandorum miraculorum. Neque vero fiducia locum habet, ubi nullum Dei verbum suppetit, quia fides & verbum relata sunt. Fides verbum amplectitur & recipit, verbum fidem gi- gnit. Si homines suis consecrationibus vim super- naturalem creaturis indere se posse credunt, mani- festum id sacrilegium est, imo species quædam ido- lolatriæ.

Disquiritur etiam h. l. utrum creatura possit concurrere ad patrandamiracula tanquam cau- sa efficiens physica, saltim instrumentalis, aut quocunque respectu, ita tamen, ut influxus verus & realis in actu miraculi eidem adscribendus sit? Scholastici, & Pa- pistæ nonnulli præcise hoc negant, vid. Wilh. Estius in 2. sentent. dist. 1. sect. 5. ubi docet, creaturam in miraculis sese habere tantum per modum instrumen- ti moralis vel causæ meritoriæ aut sine qua non : & in 3. sentent. dist. 16. qv. 1. art. 3. ubi contendit, ne animam quidem Christi potuisse ad immutationem legis naturæ concurrere, nisi per modum orationis & intercessionis : eamque sententiam Thomæ tribuit. Arripit id Ri- vetus, ita in hac causa distinguens: Si creatura ratio- nalis sit instrumentum, aliter id fieri non posse, nisi qua- tenus verbo significat, Deum illud miraculum facere, vel oratione illud petit; si vero sit creatura inanimata, eam tantum esse signum rei efficiendæ aut actionis divinæ, non autem ipsam proprie operari. Eadem est sen- tentia Gisberti Voetii part. 2. dispp. select. pag. 973. causas secundas physice cooperari, & concurrere, ait, ad antecedentia aut præparatoria, & ad adjuncta conco- mitantia aut consequentia, minime autem ad ipsum a- ctum miraculi ut sic & formaliter ita dictum : angelos & homines facere miracula, ut causas morales, sive po- tius συνάιτια instrumenti moralia; quod imprimis etiam de Christo, qua homo est, affirmat pag. 989.

Quærit nempe an Christus secundum huma- nam naturam sive qua homo, sit autor mi- raculi ? Et respondet : negatur, sed tantum est minister, sive causa delegata, & instrumentum mo- rale, ut & pag. 1011. ubi ad sententiam Heinsii, quod Christi εὐχαριστία, seu εὐλογία, qua precibus ad Pa- trem benedixit panibus, fuerit causa multiplicationis panum, notat distinguendas esse naturas in Christo: benedixisse ipsum & gratias egisse secundum H. N. & sic concurrere potuisse ad productionem miraculi, po- testate ministeriali & delegata, tanquam instrumen- tum, aut ministrum, & sola causalitate morali, pre- cando scilicet, & nomine DEI jubendo, ut multiplica- retur panis. Quanquam vero ad miracula patran- da virtus infinita requiratur, & in omni miraculo ne- cessarium sit, aliquid fieri e nihilo, sive quod nulla omnino sit materia substrata, sive quod in ea nulla sit potentia passiva ad effectum, qui producitur, un- de soli divinæ virtuti vindicatur τὸ vocare ea, quæ non sunt Rom. 4, 16. non tamen deneganda humanæ naturæ Christi potestas θαυματουργικὴ, neq; tan- tum ipsi ut ministro, vel causæ delegatæ, aut instru- mento morali adscribenda sunt miracula, siquidem ipsi virtus infinita per unionem personalem com- municata sit, quod in Exam. doctrinæ de persona Christi ex professo asseruimus. Neque per mo- dum orationis tantum impetravit miracula Christus, qua homo est, aut moraliter solum concurrit in his miraculis, quæ etiam in diebus carnis patravit se- cundum humanam naturam, quia ita nulla foret differentia inter sanctorum miracula & miracula Christi secundum humanam naturam: sed quem in- fluxum habuit divina natura Christi per virtutem infinitam essentialiter sibi propriam, eundem ha- bet humana natura Christi per virtutem eandem personaliter sibi communicatam: unde in fumum abit paralogismus Voetii: Si Christus ut homo sit cau- sa physica miraculorum duo fore omnipotentia, duas causas primas, quia est una tantum virtus infinita Christo Deo & homini conveniens, quæ ipsi ut Deo propria est κατ᾿ αὑτὸ, ut Homini convenit κατ᾿ ἄλλο, & per communicationis gratiam; ejusdem autem virtutis influxus, etsi diverfimode fiat, duo omnipotentia, aut duas causas primas parere ne- quit, cum Christus miracula in sui ipsius honorem ediderit, ut in ipsum crederent, fides autem feratur in Christum non solum qua Deus est, sed etiam qua homo, neque gloria ejus, qua cultu adorationis prosequendus sit, juxta divinam tantum naturam, sed etiam secundum humanam naturam deferri de- beat Christo; & qua mediator est, secundum utramq; naturam religiose adorandus sit: aut necessum est, ut Calviniani detrahant Christo, ut mediator est, hunc honorem, aut ut agnoscant, Christum etiam ut hominem ad opera mediatoria & ad actus mira- culi concurrisse, non tantummodo moraliter, sed physice, quia moralis instrumenti concursus non in- fert axioma divinum aut cultum religiosum; qua in re Calviniani ipsi adhuc inter se concertant, nimi rum, utrum Christus, qua mediator est, propria & di- recta sit causa alicujus miraculi. Voetius negat, quia ratio formalis, qua mediator est, non infert cau- sam miraculi propriam. Etsi autem admitti possit, mediatorem esse, proprie non esse ipsam rationem formalem operationis miraculorum, quia tamen ad mediatorem & munus illud obeundum materia- liter requiritur potentia infinita, utique vi ejus- dem Christus ut mediator divina miracula patrare potuit, imo sine divinis miraculis munus istud exe- qui non valuit. Et cum pleriq; Calviniani agno- scant, Christum ut mediatorem adorandum esse, quic- quid sit de peculiari Voetii negativa, quæ etiam Maccovii est disp. de mediat. Christo 56. quam Maresius Tom. 2. contra Tirin. pag. 1065. sub fi- nem pro paradoxo in Ecclesiis Reformatis haberi cen- set, utique quia Christus ut homo mediator est, vir- tute infinita præditum esse oportet, etiam secun- dum humanam naturam, qualis sine dubio est, qua miracula patrantur; nam gloria adorationis omnino virtutem & majestatem infinitam supponit.

## 7:19
Verse 19. ALL THE POOLS OF WATERS.

In the Hebrew, all the gathering of waters: whence the Egyptians had need to dig the earth to elicit water. From which it is gathered that all the water which could be of use to them—of wells, fountains, and cisterns, and even of the sea itself—was turned into blood, so that they were tormented by thirst and the fish died. Which seems to be said also of the land of Goshen, but in such a way that it happened only to the Egyptians living there, as Josephus notes, who testifies that the waters were sweet and drinkable for the Hebrews, which contributed not a little to increasing the dignity of the miracle. Some maintain that in the land of Goshen the waters were nowhere changed, for the sake of the Israelites, and that the neighboring Egyptians used that benefit, so that, namely, there would be no need to establish another miracle here, concerning certain waters which remained for the Israelites, but were suddenly changed into blood for the Egyptians; to whom it at least does not seem to be asserted that a new miracle was performed every time a Hebrew drew water from the river. Compare what is said on chapter 9, verse 4. Furthermore, God seems to have converted the water into blood because the Egyptians had drowned the male infants of the Israelites in the waters, innocent blood, and had infected the waters with their blood. Concerning which Theodoret: that river changed into blood, as if it were complaining of the slaughter of the children committed by the Egyptians; which cause also seems to be designated in Wisdom 11:7-8. Nor do some observe inconveniently another cause, namely that in Egypt honors, all but divine, were superstitiously paid to the Nile, because by its overflowing the whole of Egypt was made fertile; see Solinus chapter 35 and Pliny book 8, chapter 46.

Latin:

Vers. 19. OMNES LACUS AQUARUM.

In Ebr. omnem congregationem aquarum: un- de opus habuere Ægyptii terram fodere ad elicien- dam aquam. Ex quo colligitur, omnem aquam, quæ usui esse poterat ipsis, puteorum, fontium & ci- sternarum, etiam maris ipsius in sanguinem versam, ut siti cruciarentur & pisces interirent. Quod vi- detur etiam de terra Gessen dicendum, sed ita, ut so- lis Ægyptiis ibi habitantibus id contigerit, notante Josepho, qui Ebræis aquas dulces ac potabiles fuisse te- statur, quod non parum fecit ad miraculi dignita- tem augendam. Nonnulli statuunt, in terra Gessen nullibi aquas immutatas fuisse, in gratiam Israelitarum, eoque beneficio vicinos Ægyptios usos esse, ne scil. opus habeatur aliud miraculum hîc constituere, de quibusdam aquis, quæ Israelitis remanserint, Ae- gyptiis autem subito in sanguinem mutatæ sint; qui- bus id saltem non videtur asserendum, novum subin- de miraculum factum fuisse, quotiescunq; Ebræus a- quam ex flumine hauriret. Conf. quæ ad c. 9. v. 4. Cæterum ideo Deus aquam in sanguinem convertisse videtur, quia Ægyptii aquis innocuum sanguinem, Israelitarum infantes masculos merserant, & sangui- ne ipsorum aquas infecerant. Quo de Theodo- retus: fluvius ille mutatus in sanguinem, velut conque- rebatur de cæde puerorum per Ægyptios commissa; quæ causa designari quoque videtur Sap. 11. v. 7. 8. Nec incommode aliam causam nonnulli observant, nempe quod in Ægypto honores, tantum non divi- ni, Nilo superstitiose delati fuerint, quod exunda- tione ejus tota Ægyptus fœcundaretur, vid. Solinus cap. 35. & Plinius l. 8. c. 46.

## 7:22
verse same. AND THE MAGICIANS DID LIKEWISE.

This is to be understood in a qualified sense, namely, that they acted similarly according to external appearance; for a demon cannot produce true blood. Because true blood is not generated except in an animal and by the natural power of the soul; therefore, it is to be judged that the Magi, by the help of the demon, did whatever they did not by the transubstantiation of waters into blood, but by the substitution of blood in place of water. A greater doubt is whence the water came to them, since every collection of waters had been turned into blood by Moses? Tostatus and Lyranus say that the water was carried away very quickly by the demon. But the Magi wished to appear to produce blood from the water which was at hand and which seemed to be water to everyone, and therefore the demons did not carry away the water, but rather withdrew the water that was present, substituting blood very quickly. Others, with Theodoret, judge that the water had been brought from a nearby sea, or with Augustine, that it had been brought from the land of Goshen. But that distance was too great, since the Magi wished to imitate Aaron from the temple: others say that some water was reserved for the Magi by divine providence; but it is more correctly established that the waters which were kept in earthen and metallic vessels were at hand, or were even offered to the Magi by Moses himself, because for Moses, just as for the other Hebrews, the water was not blood, but the usual water. Justin, Question 26 to the Orthodox, says they dug wells near the river and drew water from there, just as it is said of the Egyptians. Others establish it thus, that the river was first turned into blood while the King was watching, but not all other waters immediately, but after the Magi had attempted the same, and had shown it in some small stream, then God, through his servants, added as a punishment the corruption of all the waters.

Vers. 22. BY THEIR INCANTATIONS) And here the Egyptian word is לוט, which the LXX, having lived in Egypt, translate as ταῖς φαρμακίαις: others as ἐν ἠρεμαίοις, others as διὰ τῶν ἀποκρύφων, by secret arts, such as those of the magi were accustomed to be. Perhaps the Greek λιταὶ comes from Egypt.

Latin:

vers. eod. FECERUNTQUE SIMILITER MALEFICI.

Hoc secundum quid intelligendum, quod scil. secundum apparentiam externam similiter fece- rint; sanguinem enim verum producere dæmon non potest. quia verus sanguis non generatur, nisi in animali & virtute animæ naturali; non E. per transubstantiationem aquarum in sanguinem, sed per substitutionem sanguinis loco aquæ fecisse cen- sendi sunt Magi ope dæmonis, quicquid fecerunt. Dubium majus est, unde ipsis aqua obvenerit, cum omnis congregatio aquarum a Mose in sanguinem versa fuerit? Tostatus & Lyranus celerrime a dæmo- ne asportatam aquam fuisse dicunt. Sed ex aqua, quæ præsto erat, & aqua omnibus videbatur, vole- bant Magi videri sanguinem procreare, ideoq; non aquam asportarunt dæmones, sed aquam præsen- tem potius subtraxerunt, sanguinem celerrime sub- stituendo. Alii cum Theodoreto e mari vicino alla- tam fuisse aquam, aut cum Aug. e terra Gessen, ad- ductam censent. Sed ea nimis longe erat distan- tia, cum ex templo imitari voluerint magi Aaronem: alii pro Magis divina providentia aliquid aquæ re- servatum dicunt; sed rectius statuitur, aquas, quæ in vasibus testaceis ac metallicis servabantur, in promptu fuisse, aut oblatas etiam Magis esse ab ipso Mose, quia Mosi perinde ut aliis Ebræis aqua non erat sanguis, sed aqua solita. Justinus quæst. 26. ad Orthodoxos, fodisse eos puteos circa flumen, & hausisse inde aquam, quemadmodum id de Ægyptiis dicitur. Alii ita statuunt, flumen primum fuisse in sanguinem muta- tum inspectante Rege, sed non alias omnes aquas im- mediate, postquam autem Magi idem tentassent, & ostentassent in aliquo rivulo, tum Deum per servos suos addidisse in pœnam, corruptionem omnium a- quarum.

Vers. 22. INCANTATIONIBVS SVIS) Et hic vox Æ- gyptia est לוט, quem LXX. in Aegypto versati transferunt ταῖς φαρμακίαις: Alii ἐν ἠρεμαίοις, alii διὰ τῶν ἀποκρύφων, arca- nis artibus, quales magorum esse solebant. Forte λιταὶ Græcum ab Aegypto venit.

## 7:24
Vers. 24. BUT ALL THE EGYPTIANS DUG ROUND ABOUT THE RIVER FOR WATER, THAT THEY MIGHT DRINK.

They did not find water, but blood, yet through filtration, and as it were watery, from which those who lacked wine and milk relieved their thirst. Philo also thinks that water flowed abundantly from new veins opened by digging.

Latin:

Vers. 24. FODERUNT AUTEM OMNES ÆGYPTII PER CIRCUITUM FLUMINIS A- QUAM, UT BIBERENT.

Non inveniebant aquam, sed sanguinem, per colatum tamen, & quasi aqueum, ex quo siti suc- currerunt, qui vino & lacte carebant. Philo etiam e venis novis subfossione apertis aquam redundas- se, putat.

## 7:25
Vers. 25. AND SEVEN DAYS WERE FULFILLED.

Eusebius in the catena maintains that this indicates that seven days flowed from the first plague until the second. But others more correctly maintain with Philo that this plague lasted for a week, for if it had lasted only one day, what need would there have been to dig new wells in the circuit of the Nile?

Latin:

Vers. 25. IMPLETIQUE SUNT SEPTEM DIES.

Eusebius in catena statuit, id indicari, quod septem fluxerint dies, a prima plaga usq; ad secun- dam. Sed rectius alii per septiduum durasse hanc plagam cum Philone statuunt, nam si uno tantum durasset die, quid opus fuisset novos fodere puteos in circuitu Nili?

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. The plague of frogs, of lice, and of flies.

Latin:

CAPUT IIX. Ranarum plaga, Sciniphum, & Muscarum.

## 8:2
Vers. 2. I WILL SMITE ALL THY BORDERS WITH FROGS) Here too is the Egyptian word צפרדעים. It is a species of frog or something similar to frogs peculiar to Egypt, as toads are elsewhere. The name remains among the Arabs with the letter r removed.

By all the borders of Egypt are understood the entire regions of this kingdom, because the word גבל does not denote only a border properly so called, but also the space contained within the borders. They are punished, however, with aquatic and croaking frogs, who had drowned the infants of the Hebrews in the waters, and had cared less for their wailing than for the croaking of frogs.

Latin:

Vers. 2. PERCVTIAM OMNES TERMINOS RANIS) Est & hic Aegyptia vox צפרדעים. Genus est ranarum aut ranis simile Aegypto proprium, ut alibi rubetae. Manet nomen apud Arabes extrita r litera.

INtelliguntur per omnes Ægypti terminos regni hujus regiones universæ, quia vox גבל non terminum tantum proprie dictum notat, sed etiam spatium intra terminos comprehensum. Ranis autem aquatilibus & coaxantibus puniuntur, qui infantes Ebræorum aquis merserant, eorumque vagitus mi- nus quam coaxationem ranarum curarant.

## 8:3
v. 3. AND THE RIVER SHALL BRING FORTH FROGS.

In Hebrew the verb שרץ is emphatic, meaning it will breed abundantly, which signifies a multiplication of offspring like that of fish and frogs, which occurred most copiously.

v. eod. THEY SHALL ASCEND AND ENTER THY HOUSE.

They therefore change their native and natural seat, and whereas they live elsewhere in the waters, they are carried into a colony of air and earth, they ascend houses, or are propelled thither in whatever way, they infect all foods, all vessels, which punishment was not a little more grievous than the preceding; for they tormented all the senses: sight by their size and deformity and multitude; hearing by their croaking; taste by the defilement of food and drink, and when they leaped into the very mouths with the food; smell by the most foul stench, especially when they died; touch by the most annoying invasion and occupation of bodies in beds, at tables and chairs, concerning which see Josephus, book 2, chapter 5, and Philo in his book on the life of Moses, not to mention that some, with Pererius, believe those frogs were harmful and poisonous.

V. eod. AND INTO THE REMAINS OF THY FOODS.

The Hebrew signifies kneaded flour, whence the Chaldean: in thy bread-baskets, and the LXX ἐν τοῖς φυράμασί σε, in thy masses.

Latin:

v. 3. ET EBULLIET FLUVIUS RANAS.

In Ebr. emphaticum est verbum שרץ proli- ficabit, quod multiplicationem fœtus instar piscium & ranarum significat copiosissime factam.

v. eod. ASCENDENT ET INGREDJENTUR DOMUM TUAM.

Mutant ergo sedem natalem, & naturalem, & cum in aquis alias degant, in aëris & terræ colo- niam feruntur, domos ascendunt, aut quomodo- cunq; eò propelluntur, cibos omnes, vasa omnia inficiunt, quæ pœna haud parum gravior erat præ- cedente; omnes enim sensus cruciabant, visum ma- gnitudine & deformitate ac multitudine; auditum coaxatione; gustum esculentorum & potulentorum conspurcatione, & cum prosiliebant in ipsa ora cum cibis; odoratum deterrimo fœtore, maxime cum e- moriebantur; tactum corporum in lectis, mensis & sellis molestissima invasione & occupatione, quo de vid. Joseph. l. 2. c. 5. & Philo in lib. de vita Mosis, ut taceam, quod nonnulli cum Pererio credunt, ra- nas illas noxias & venenatas fuisse.

V. eod. ET IN RELIQUIAS CIBORUM TUORUM.

Ebræum significat farinam consper sam, unde Chaldæus: in panariis tuis, & LXX ἐν τοῖς φυρά- μασί σε, in massis tuis.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. AARON STRETCHED OUT HIS HANDS OVER THE WATERS.

It must be rendered: towards, or against the waters: for he was stationed not at the waters, but in the palace of Pharaoh Tanim.

Latin:

Vers. 6. EXTENDIT AARON MANUS SU- PER AQUAS.

Reddendum est: versus, vel contra aquas: erat enim non ad aquas, sed in Regia Pharaonis Tanim tum constitutus.

## 8:8
verf. 8. APPOINT UNTO ME WHEN I SHALL PRAY FOR THEE.

The Hebrew phrase is thus: glory over me, when I shall pray: To glory over someone is to usurp for oneself another's honor, to exalt oneself above him, so the sense would be: I could indeed reserve this glory for myself, that at what time and at what hour I wished, I might pray to God for thee; but I will yield this glory to thee, that thou mayest assign me a time, so that in this way the divine power may be the more illustrated by the concession. Others less aptly think it is a hypothetical concession, as if he said: if I do not remove the frogs at the time which thou shalt appoint, mock and insult me. For this phrase is not used in this way for insult, nor are there any traces of a condition here.

Latin:

verf. 8. CONSTITUE MIHI QUANDO DE- PRECER PRO TE.

Ebr. phrasis ita habet : gloriare super me, quando deprecer: Gloriari super aliquem est usurpare sibi alterius honorem, se supra ipsum efferre, ita sensus esset: poteram quidem hanc gloriam mihi reserva- re, ut quo tempore & qua hora vellem, Deum pro te rogarem; sed cedam tibi hanc gloriam, ut mihi as- signes tempus, ut ita magis a concessione illustrata fuerit divina potentia. Minus commode alii hy- potheticam esse concessionem putant, quasi diceret: si non amoverim ranas eo tempore, quod constitueris, illude & insulta mihi. Nam ita phrasis hæc non u- surpatur pro insultatione, neque ulla conditionis hîc vestigia sunt.

## 8:10
Vers. 10. WHO ANSWERED: TOMORROW.

Pharaoh does not ask that he be freed from the frogs in a moment, either because he believed that some delay should be granted to Moses, so that he might accomplish this business with God and obtain it by prayers, or because he wished to test whether the frogs would fail of their own accord, as if brought by some chance, not by extraordinary divine power, so that those illusions, if there were any, would cease in the meantime.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QUI RESPONDIT: CRAS.

Pharao non petit, ut in momento a ranis libe- retur, sive quod crediderit, concedendum esse Mosi aliquam moram, ut hoc negotium conficeret apud Deum, precibusque impetraret, seu quod experiri voluerit, an ranæ per se defecturæ sint, ceu casu ali- quo illatæ, non extraordinaria vi divina, ita ut præ- stigia illæ interea, si quæ fuerint, cessaturæ sint.

## 8:15
vers. 15. BUT PHARAOH SEEING THAT REST HAD BEEN GIVEN, HARDENED HIS HEART) God generally sends adversities to those whom He wishes to correct, and if they do not make right use of them, He leads them through prosperity.

Latin:

vers. 15. VIDENS AUTEM PHARAO, QVOD DATA ESSET REQVIES AGGRAVAVIT COR SVVM) Deus plerumque eis, quos corrigere vult, immittit adversa, quibus si non recte utantur, traducit eos per prospera.

## 8:16
v. 16. AND LET THERE BE SCINIPHES IN ALL THE LAND OF EGYPT) A softened pronunciation for the Greek σκνίφες, σκνῖπες, σκνῖπες; for it is written in so many ways. A kind of gnat, harmful to trees.

Fagius says the Hebrew word signifies certain kinds of small vermin, which are accustomed to be most hostile, injuring the skin, and penetrating the nostrils and ears. But it is asked, what kind it was? Pererius thinks it was a new animal then first produced by GOD, which is nevertheless designated here by a known name. The ancient Greeks understood it as gnats, which opinion Cornelius a Lapide prefers. But we acquiesce in the common explanation of the Hebrews, who interpret it as lice, whom Pagninus, Oleastrius, Cajetan, B. Luth., Jun., and Tremell. follow, as well as the French and Tigurine versions. Diodorus Siculus, book 3, chapter 3, recounts certain winged lice, which are generated in the bodies of old men among the Ethiopians, not only different in genus, but also horrible in appearance and remarkably deformed. Corn. a Lap. is in vain that lice are not generated from dust, but from the human body, because this was not an ordinary generation, but clearly extraordinary and miraculous.

Latin:

v. 16. ET SINT SCINIPHES IN VNIVERSA TERRA ÆGTPTI) Emollita pronunciatio pro Græco σκνίφες, σκνῖπες, σκνῖπες; nam tot modis scribitur. Culicum genus, arboribus infestum.

Fagius Ebr. vocem significare ait genera quæ- dam exiguarum bestiolarum, quæ infensissimæ esse so- lent, cutem lædentes, & nares atque aures penetran- tes. Quæritur autem, quale genus fuerit? Pererius animal novum tunc primum a DEO productum fu- isse censet, quod tamen noto nomine hic designe- tur. Græci Veteres de culicibus intellexere, quam sententiam præfert Cornelius a Lapide. Sed nos in communi Ebræorum explicatione acquiescimus, qui interpretantur pediculos, quos sequuntur Pagni- nus, Oleastrius, Cajetan. B. Luth. Jun. & Tremell. Gallica item & Tigurina versio. Diod. Siculus lib. 3. c. 3. recenset alatos quosdam pediculos, qui corporibus senum ingenerentur penes Aethiopes, non genere so- lum diversi, sed specie etiam horridi & insigniter deformes. Frustra est Corn. a Lap. pediculos non e pulvere, sed e corpore humano generari, quia hic non fuit ordinaria generatio, sed plane extraordi- naria & miraculosa.

## 8:18
Verse 18. THEY DID SO.

Namely, as regards the attempt and the customary mode or rite of incantations, in that they certainly employed their arts; but with vain effort: therefore this is not to be understood as regards the effect; because God finally wished to convince the lying Magicians of their impotence, that they avail nothing without His permission, and Pharaoh of His divine power, so that He might soften the hardness of his heart.

Latin:

Vers. 18. FECERUNT SIC.

Scil. quoad conatum, & consuetum incantatio- num modum vel ritum, quod nempe adhibuerint suas artes; sed irrito molimine: non ergo quoad effe- ctum hoc intelligendum; quia voluit tandem Deus mendaces Magos convincere de impotentia sua, quod nihil valeant sine sua permissione, Pharaonem autem de divina sua potentia, ut duritiem cordis e- jus emolliret.

## 8:19
Verse 19. THIS IS THE FINGER OF GOD) This miracle is from GOD, as the Chaldean explains here.

By the finger of God some understand the plague, with Corn. a Lap., but it is more correctly understood as the power of God, just as in Luke 11:16 the hypostatic power of God, the Holy Spirit, is called the finger of God, but the plague was an effect of the power of God: since the Magicians make mention of GOD here, yet had no knowledge of the true GOD, Lyranus wishes to understand the demons themselves by the word GOD. But the proper meaning of the word GOD must be retained; for they were compelled to acknowledge and profess the power of GOD, even if [they did not know] who that true [God] was. God may be, they may have been ignorant; for that they resist further from now on c. 9, 11. is not new, that those who have been overcome regarding the truth return to their nature, and proceed to θεομαχεῖν.

Latin:

vers. 19. DIGITVS DEI EST HIC) Hoc miraculum a DEO est, ut hic explicat Chaldæus.

Per digitum Dei nonnulli plagam intelligunt cum Corn. a Lap. sed rectius potentia Dei intelligi- tur, quemadmodum Luc. 11, 16. hypostatica Dei potentia Spiritus S. Dei digitus vocatur, plaga au- tem effectus erat potentiæ Dei: cum DEI mentio- nem hic faciant Magi, veri DEI tamen no- titiam nullam habuerint, Lyranus voce DEI dæmo- nesipsos intellexisse vult. Sed retinenda est significa- tio vocis DEI propria; coacti enim sunt agnoscere, & profiteri DEI potentiam, etsi quis ille verus Deus sit, ignorarint; nam utut resistant amplius de- inceps c. 9, 11. non novum est, eos, qui victi sunt de veritate, ad ingenium redire, ac pergere θεομαχεῖν.

## 8:21
Ver. 21. EVERY KIND OF FLIES] The word ערב which appears here is itself Egyptian, signifying κυνομυῖαν (dog-fly), as the LXX, Philo, and others translate. Those who have wished to refer this word to a Hebrew origin, some derive it from mixing, like this Latin [translator], others, with changed vowels, interpret it as a raven, like the old Samaritan interpreter.

Tremellius and Junius translate it: a collection; Arias: a mixture, because a collection of various small animals was designated, which Fagius rightly interprets as a crowd of various insects, from the force of the Hebrew word, as in Joel 1 and c. 2 it is read concerning a similar punishment and army of locusts, bruchi, and caterpillars, cf. Wisd. 16, 8. I would not, however, say with R. Solomon and others that the collection was of venomous serpents, scorpions, asps, lizards, etc., because the plague was sent not to destroy, but to vex the Egyptians. But they are foolish who, with R. Aben Ezra, snatch the word to refer to various species of wild beasts, lions, leopards, wolves, which opinion is wrongly attributed to Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 21. OMNE GENVS MVSCARVM] Vox ערב quæ hic apparet, est & ipsa Ægyptiaca κυνομυῖαν significans, ut ver- tunt LXX. Philo, alii. Qui ad Hebræam originem hanc vocem referre voluere, alii a miscendo eam derivant, ut hic Latinus, a- lii mutatis vocalibus corvum interpretantur, ut vetus interpres Samaritanus.

Trem. & Jun. vertunt, colluviem: Arias, mixtio- nem, quod variarum bestiolarum colluvies de- signata fuerit, quod de turba ex variis insectis recte interpretatur Fagius, e vi vocis Ebrææ, uti Joel. 1. & c. 2. de simili pœna & exercitu e locustis, bruchis & erucis legitur, conf. Sap. 16, 8. Non tamen dixerim cum R. Salomone & aliis, colluviem fuisse e venenatis serpentibus, Scorpionibus, aspidibus, lacertis &c. quia plaga immittebatur non ad perdendum, sed ad ve- xandum Ægyptios. Inepti autem sunt, qui ad varias species ferarum, leonum, pardorum, luporum, cum R. AbenEzra vocem abripiunt, quæ sententia perpe- ram Josepho tribuitur.

## 8:22
Ver. 22. AND I WILL MAKE WONDERFUL IN THAT DAY THE LAND OF GOSHEN.

Not only from this, but also from other plagues were the Israelites immune: yet he notes this particularly about this one, because such a separation and exemption could seem almost incredible on account of the multitude so filled with that collection, because it is said, the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled, and moreover the land itself, upon which they are. Then also, so that here again the finger of God might be made known, and more fully acknowledged, therefore the cause is added, that you may know that I am Jehovah in the midst of the earth. Chald. Princes in the midst of the earth.

Latin:

Vers. 22. FACIAMQVE MIRABILEM IN DIE ILLA TERRAM GESSEN.

Non tantum ab hac, sed etiam ab aliis plagis immunes erant Israëlitæ: peculiariter tamen id de hac notat, quod pene incredibilis videri posset talis separatio & exemtio propter multitudinem adeo refertam, colluviei istius, quia dicitur, replebuntur domus Ægyptiorum insuper & terra ipsa, supra quam ipsi sunt. Tum etiam, ut hic denuo digitus Dei in- notesceret, & plenius agnosceretur, ideo causa addi- tur, ut scias, quod ego Jehovah in medio terræ. Chald. Principes in medio terræ.

## 8:26
Ver. 26. FOR WE SHALL SACRIFICE THE ABOMINATION OF THE EGYPTIANS TO THE LORD OUR GOD) In Greek, τὰ γὰρ βδελύγματα τῶν Αἰγυπτίων θύσομεν κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ ὑμῶν. Do not interpret βδελύγματα as idols with some: for that term would suit neither this place nor this time; but understand this concerning the matter which is being discussed: we shall offer to God those things which the Egyptians consider it a sin to be killed and therefore to be consecrated to God. See above Gen. 43, v. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ABOMINATIONEM ENIM ÆGYPTI ORVM IMMOLABIMUS DOMINO DEO NOSTRO) Græce, τὰ γὰρ βδελύγματα τῶν Αἰγυπτίων θύσομεν κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ ὑμῶν. Noli interpretari cum quibusdam βδελύγματα idola: is enim sermo neque loco huic neque tempori conveniret; Sed intel- lige hoc de re de qua agitur: offeremus ea Deo, quæ occidi ac proinde Deo sacrari nefas habent Ægyptii. Vide supra Genes. 43. v. 32.

## 8:28
v. 28. NEVERTHELESS DO NOT GO FARTHER.

Rivetus observes that Moses is silent regarding this condition proposed by Pharaoh about not going further, for the reason that he neither wished to lie, nor was it the time to bring forth the counsel of GOD. But the counsel of God extended thus far, that the people should be dismissed for a time for sacrifices; but as for the plenary leading out, as it followed Pharaoh's stubborn refusal in the event, so in this order it also followed in the counsel of GOD, because the execution of a decree must be analogous to the decree itself.

Latin:

v. 28. VERUNTAMEN LONGIUS NON AB- EATIS.

Ad hanc conditionem a Pharaone proposi- tam de non ulterius pergendo, tacere Mosen, ea de causa, Rivetus observat, quod nec mentiri voluerit, nec tamen tempus fuerit, ut DEI consilium profer- ret. Sed consilium Dei hactenus eo usq; se porri- gebat, ut ad sacrificia ad tempus dimitteretur populus; quod vero ad plenariam eductionem attinet, ea uti seqvebatur præfractam recusationem Pharaonis in eventu, ita hoc ordine etiam illa in consilio DEI se- qvebantur, quia executio decreti analoga esse de- bet ipsi decreto.

## 8:32
Ver. 32. AND THE HEART OF PHARAOH WAS HARDENED) The Greeks are clearer here: καὶ ἐβάρυνε Φαραὼ τὴν καρδίαν ἀυτοῦ.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ET INGRAVATVM EST COR PHARAO- NIS) Clarius hic Græci: καὶ ἐβάρυνε Φαραὼ τὴν καρδίαν ἀυτοῦ.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. The plague on the cattle. The plague of ulcers and hail.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Pestis in jumentis. Ulcerum & grandinis plaga.

## 9:3
Ver. 3. BEHOLD MY HAND SHALL BE UPON THE FIELDS.

By hand is understood the power of God, which is said to be over some to save, over others to punish, see Deut. 2, v. 15; 2 Sam. 12, ver. 15, just as also the visitation of God is one of grace, another of wrath, and by this mention of the hand of God it is indicated that God immediately, not by the hand of Moses and Aaron, will send the plague, namely by infecting the air and bodies; finally, by the hand of GOD most interpreters here particularly understand the plague, which is also called the hand of the Lord in 2 Sam. 24, 14 and the word of the Lord in Num. 14, v. 12. But the general and received meaning of the word can be retained; for what kind of exertion of the hand of GOD this will be is specified afterwards by the mention of a very grievous plague.

ver. same. UPON THY FIELDS, AND UPON THE HORSES, &c.

Not that the fields themselves are infected, but that the plague was sent upon the horses & asses &c. in the fields, as the Hebrews rightly observe: whence the particle אל warns that the former is to be taken ἐξηγητικῶς [exegetically], upon the fields i.e. the horses, which is an obscure ἐξήγησις [exegesis]; it would be said more correctly, the fields infected κατά τι [in a certain way], because the horses & asses were being infected in the fields. But from the Hebrew the matter is plain, for it is not had, upon the fields, but, which are in the field, so that the distinction of the cattle in the field & those which were in the stables, which were not affected by this plague, might be indicated. Furthermore, sheep & oxen are mentioned, which the Egyptians reared, not for slaughter or eating; for they abhorred them Gen. 46. last, but for services, wool & merchandise.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ECCE MANUS MEA ERIT SUPER AGROS.

PER manum intelligitur potentia Dei, quæ super alios esse dicitur ad salvandum, super alios ad puniendum, vid. Deut. 2. v. 15. 2. Sam. 12. vers. 15. quemadmodum & visitatio Dei alia gratiæ est, alia iræ, & indicatur hac manus Dei mentione immedia- te Deum manu sua, non manuMosis & Aaronis, im- missurum pestem, inficiendo nempe aerem & corpo- ra; denique per manum DEI peculiariter ple- riqve Interpp. hic intelligunt pestem, quæ & manus Domini 2. Sam. 24, 14. & verbum Domini Num. 14. v. 12. dicatur. Sed potest generalis, & recepta si- gnificatio vocis retineri; qualis enim manus DEI exertio hæc futura sit, postea specificatur mentione pestis valde gravis.

vers. eod. SUPER AGROS TUOS, ET SU- PER EQUOS, &c.

Non quod agri ipsi infecti sint, sed quod equis & asinis &c. in agris pestis immissa, ut Ebræi recte ob- servant: unde particula אל priorem ἐξηγητικῶς accipiendam esse monet Corn. super agros i. e. equos, quæ obscura est ἐξήγησις; rectius diceretur, agros κατά τι infectos, quia equi & asini in agris inficie- bantur. Sed ex Ebræo res plana est, non enim ha- betur, super agros, sed, quæ in agro, ut discrimen in- digitetur pecorum in agro & , quæ in stabu- lis erant, quæ hac plaga non afficiebantur. Cæte- rum oves & boves commemorantur, quas Ægyptii nutriere, non ad mactationem aut esum; abhorre- bant enim ab iisdem Gen. 46. ult. sed ad servitia, la- nam & Mercimonia.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. THAT NOTHING AT ALL SHALL DIE OF THOSE THINGS, WHICH PERTAIN TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL.

Although some Egyptians dwelt with the Israelites in the land of Goshen, the plague of the Egyptians touched the cattle there, while the cattle of the Israelites were left safe, because the Lord did this miracle, that although they breathed the same air, they nevertheless remained immune from infection. And the same must be held regarding the other plagues, even regarding the conversion of water into blood, with Josephus, Philo & Tostatus agreeing, so that Rivetus is in vain, granting a peculiar privilege to the Egyptians in Goshen, namely that they used the benefit of the Israelites, while other Egyptians were laboring with thirst; for the plague is announced to all Egyptians generally: nor were those neighbors in Goshen kinder to the Israelites, but, as Rivetus confesses, more cruel.

Latin:

Vers. 4. UT NIHIL OMNINO PEREAT EX HIS, QUAE PERTINENT AD FILIOS IS- RAEL.

Etsi habitabant cum Israëlitis Ægyptii non- nulli in terra Gessen, pecudes tamen Aegyptiorum tangebat ibi plaga, salvis relictis pecudibus Israëli- tarum, quia Dominus faciebat hoc mirabile, quod etsi eundem aerem haurirent, immunes tamen ab infectione manserint. Atque idem de aliis plagis etiam de conversione aquæ in sanguinem pariter ha- bendum, annuente Josepho, Philone & Tostato, ut frustra Rivetus sit, Aegyptiis in Gessen privilegium peculiare concedens, quod nempe Israëlitarum be- neficio usi sint, aliis Ægyptiis siti laborantibus; pla- ga enim omnibus Aegyptiis generaliter indicitur: neque benigniores illi vicini in Gessen erant Israe- litis, sed fatente Riveto, crudeliores.

## 9:7
Vers. 7. AND PHARAOH SENT TO SEE,

Why now at last did Pharaoh send to explore that which they could already explore in the preceding plagues? That does not seem to have been done then, partly because the roads were impassable on account of the frogs, flies & lice; partly because Pharaoh himself had been so afflicted by those scourges that he could not think about that exploration.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET MISIT PHARAO AD VIDEN- DUM,

Cur nunc demum misit Pharao ad illud explo- randum, quod in plagis præcedentibus explorare jam poterant? Id tum non factum videtur, partim quod viæ ob ranas, muscas & sciniphes, imperviæ es- sent; partim quod Pharao ipse flagellis istis sic affli- ctus fuerit, ut de exploratione illa cogitare non pos- set.

## 9:8
v. 8. TAKE TO YOU THE FULL HANDS OF ASHES.

In the Heb. full of the furnace. Some understand the word פיח as white ash, which has not yet been fully turned into ash, with which half-dead coals are covered. But because that ash is not easily taken with the hands, it seems that ashes still hot are to be understood, so that the pustules, which form like ash from heat, may be signified. Thus the Egyptians, who had tortured the Hebrews with a brick furnace, are again tortured by the same.

v. same. AND LET MOSES SPRINKLE IT.

Some observe that both Moses & Aaron are commanded to take ash from the furnace, but that Moses alone had to sprinkle it into the air, because as Philo notes, the later & nobler signs were reserved for Moses, as being to be performed in fire, heaven & air, whereas the former were performed in the waters & earth by Aaron. But these do not seem solid enough, nay, whatever was done by Aaron was directed by the command of Moses, and therefore the distinction of the miracles of Aaron & Moses has no place; & just as both received the ashes, so Aaron was not commanded to receive them in vain, or he transferred them from his hand into the hand of Moses, but both sprinkled them into the air, even if mention is made only of Moses, as of him by whose nod & example it had to be sprinkled.

Latin:

v. 8. TOLLITE PLENAS MANUS CINERIS.

In Ebr. plenas fornacis. Vocem פיח intelligunt nonnulli de favilla alba, quæ nondum plane in cine- rem versa est, qua semimortui carbones contegun- tur. Sed quia favilla ista non facile capitur mani- bus, cineres potius adhuc calidi intelligendi viden- tur, ut significentur pustulæ, quæ instar cineris ex calore fiunt. Ita Ægyptii, qui Ebræos fornace late- ritia torserant, eadem iterum torquentur.

v. eod. ET SPARGAT ILLAM MOSES.

Observant nonnulli, quod uterque Moses & Aaron tollere e camino cinerem jubeatur, solus au- tem Moses in aerem eum spargere debuerit, quia ut Philo notat, posteriora & nobiliora signa Mosi re- servata fuerint, utpote in igne, cœlo & aere patranda, cum priora in aquis & terra peracta ab Aarone sint. Sed hæc satis solida non videntur, imo quæcunqve ab Aarone facta, jussu Mosis directa sunt, ideoq; di- stinctio miraculorum Aaronis & Mosis locum non habet; & quemadmodum uterq; cineres accepit, ita non frustra Aaron accipere jussus est, aut de manu sua in manum Mosis eosdem transfudit, sed uterqve sparsit in aerem, etsi Mosis tantum mentio fiat, tan- quam illius, cujus nutu & exempo spargi debuit.

## 9:9
v. 9. AND IT SHALL BECOME DUST.

It is to be retained here the statement those ashes into that those cast into the air were turned into dust, nor is there need that we should say with Rivetus that that dust had only the nature of a sign, and the air infected by a small amount of ash could certainly have easily infected another part of the air adjacent to it; indeed, God could have multiplied the evil in the air most easily, so that there is no need to abandon the letter of the text.

Latin:

v. 9. ET VERTETUR IN PULVEREM.

Retinendum hîc est τὸ ῥητὸν cineres illos in aerem projectos in pulverem conversos fuisse, nec opus est, ut cum Riveto signi tantum rationem pulve- rem illum habuisse dicamus,& potuit certe aer in- fectus ab exiguo cinere aliam aeris partem conti- guam facile inficere, imo multiplicare malum Deus in aere quam facillime potuit, ut non opus sit, lite- ram textus deserere.

## 9:11
Ver. 11. AND THE MAGICIANS COULD NOT STAND BEFORE MOSES BECAUSE OF THE ULCERS.

Rupert of Deutz notes here the third victory of Moses against the magicians. The first was when his serpent devoured the serpents of the magicians; the second when they could not produce lice for him; the third when they themselves are tormented with ulcers. Although they could not imitate the other signs either, but failed at the third, and produced nothing further. From these ulcers seems to have arisen the calumny that the Egyptians ejected the Jews because of scabies and leprosy, which, drawn from Manetho, Lysimachus, and Apion the Grammarian, was propagated by Trogus, Diodorus Siculus, and Tacitus, because they wished to shift the blame onto the Jews in a ridiculous manner and rub their own scabies off on them.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NEC POTERANT MALEFICI STA- RE CORAM MOSE PROPTER ULCERA.

Tertiam hic victoriam Mosis contra Magos notat Rupertus Tuitiensis. Prima erat cum serpens ejus devoraret serpentes Magorum;altera cum pedicu- los illi producere non possent; Tertia cum ulceribus ipsi cruciantur. Quanquam nec cætera signa imi- tari potuerint, sed in tertio defecerint, nullumque amplius ediderint. Ab ulceribus his enata vide- tur calumnia Ægyptiorum Judæos ob scabiem & le- pram ejectos esse, quæ ex Manethone, Lysimacho & Appione Grammatico hausta, propagata est a Trogo, Diodoro Siculo, & Tacito, quia ita culpam in Juæos ridicule convertere, suamque illis scabiem affrica- re voluerunt.

## 9:15
Ver. 15. NOW EXTENDING MY HAND I WILL SMITE THEE AND THY PEOPLE WITH PESTILENCE, AND THOU SHALT PERISH FROM THE EARTH) More correctly: Now if I had extended my hand, I would have smitten thee. And the following: But for this reason I have sustained thee, that I may show my strength.

There is a doubt here as to what is understood by pestilence, because it is not read that the people or Pharaoh himself were smitten with pestilence, so that Pharaoh perished from the earth, who was rather suffocated by the waters, whence some understand by pestilence the final plague: but in that way that saying will not fit: thou shalt perish from the earth; because, as has been said, Pharaoh did not perish by pestilence, nor is it certain that the firstborn perished by pestilence: therefore others say that every kind of destruction is designated by the name of pestilence, rendering it thus: I will add plagues to plagues, until thou art destroyed from the earth. Most, however, following the Chaldean, render the Hebrew words thus: And indeed if I had wished I could have killed thee with pestilence, and thou wouldst have perished from the earth; but for this reason I have placed thee and preserved thee, that I may show my fortitude. Which is the explanation of R. Solomon, if I had wished, when my hand was against thy cattle, I would have smitten thee and thy people with the beasts. As also our Grotius: to which also the interpretation of Tremellius and Junius tends: for it is as if, when I extended my hand, I would have smitten thee also, etc. Which interpretation Mr. D. Walther approves with his vote in his Harmony, as also Mr. Franzius in his Oracles, p. 290, and also Mr. D. Rungius in his Commentary on this passage, who nevertheless does not disapprove of that opinion by which these words are referred to a threatening of future punishments, so that the word pestilence in general denotes every calamity utterly destroying men; which also pleased Pelargus, because God indeed adds weight here to his command by the frequently repeated threatening of all the plagues, and especially of the slaughter which is to be feared from pestilence or similar evils.
