In whatever sense it is rendered, this at least is certain, that the divine grace is commended here, in that He still deigns to recall Pharaoh, so often warned by the threatening of punishment, to a sounder mind, so that there is no place for the Calvinian depravation, as if God, by an absolute decree, wished to preserve Pharaoh, whom He could have destroyed immediately, to this end, that by his hardening and punishment He might show a more illustrious example of His judgment in him, since the text and the entire history teach the exact opposite; nothing was done here by absolute decrees, but rather that God did this by His miracles and threatenings and punishments, that He might soften Pharaoh's heart, and that He preserved him for that very reason, that He might publicly and solemnly show an example of long-suffering in so hard a heart.

Latin:

verf. 15. NVNC EXTENDENS MANUM PERCUTI- AM TE ET POPULUM TUUM PESTE, PERIBISQVE DE TERRA) Rectius: Nunc si extendissem manum meam, percussissem te. Et sequentia: Verum ideo te sustentavi, ut o- stendam robur meum.

Dubium hîc est, quid per pestem intelligatur, quia populus vel Pharao ipse peste percussus non legitur, ut interierit Pharao de terra, qui aquis suf- focatus potius est, unde per pestem nonnulli pla- gam ultimam intelligunt:sed ita non congruet il- lud: peribis de terra; quia ut dictum, peste non in- teriit Pharao, neque constat, primogenitos peste interiisse: proinde alii nomine pestis designatum di- cunt omne excidii genus, h. m. reddentes: plagas plagis addam, donec excidaris de terra. Pleriq; au- tem Chaldæum sequentes verba Ebræa ita reddunt: Et quidem si voluissem potuissem te occidere peste, & pe- riisses de terra; verum ideo posui te & servavi te, ut o- stendam fortitudinem meam. Quæ explicatio R. Salomonis est, si voluissem, cum manus mea erat con- tra pecus tuum, percussissem te populumq; tuum cum bestiis. Ut & Grotii nostri: quo etiam abit Tremel- lii & Junii interpretatio: modo enim cum extendi ma- num meam, percussissem etiam te &c. Quam inter- pretationem calculo suo probat Dn. D. Waltherus in Harm. ut & Dn. Franzius in Oracul. p. 290. nec non Dn. D. Rungius Comm. in h. l. qui tamen illam non reprobat sententiam, qua verba hæc referun- tur ad comminationem futurorum suppliciorum, ut vox pestis in genere omnem calamitatem funditus homines delentem notet; quæ Pelargo etiam pla- cuit, quod nempe pondus hîc addat præcepto suo Deus, sæpius iterata comminatione omnium plaga- rum, & maxime internecionis, quæ a peste, aut a similibus malis metuenda. Quocunque sensu red- datur, id utique constat, commendari hìc divinam gratiam, quod adhuc dignetur comminatione sup- pliciiPharaonem toties monitum ad saniorem men- tem revocare, ut locus nullus sit depravationi Cal- vinianæ, quasi Deus absoluto decreto Pharaonem, quem statim poterat perdere, conservare voluerit, hoc fine, ut obduratione ejusdem, & pœna illustrius exemplum judicii sui in ipso ostenderet, siquidem contrarium prorsus doceat textus & universa histo- ria; nihil hic actum per absoluta decreta, imo Deum miraculis & comminationibus ac suppliciis suis hoc egisse, ut Pharaonis cor emolliret eumq; ob id et- iam conservasse, ut exemplum μακροθυμίας in corde tam duro publice ac solemniter ostenderet.

## 9:16
Ver. 16. BUT FOR THIS REASON I HAVE PLACED THEE, THAT I MAY SHOW IN THEE MY FORTITUDE.

The Hebrew text has it thus: and indeed for this reason I made thee stand, that I might make thee see my power. The Apostle in Rom. 9, v. 17, rendered it: that for this very thing I have raised thee up, that I may show in thee my virtue. The LXX Interpreters have: thou wast preserved, rendering the rest as they are brought forward by the Apostle, except that here it has my power, but the LXX has my strength. The Calvinists, as I said, seek here the patronage of their absolute decree, especially in the word I raised up, which the Apostle used, which Rivetus explains thus, that God created Pharaoh, raised him to the kingdom, and by commands and plagues excited his stubbornness, and therefore destined him for destruction. By which method are simultaneously comprehended all the false interpretations of other Calvinists, some of whom interpreted the word as to create, others to raise to royal dignity, others to irritate: But for the most part all with that reason and intention: that God intended this in Pharaoh by an absolute and simple decree in raising him up, that he himself might be destroyed and eternally reprobated. But in truth, neither the creation or production of Pharaoh has anything to do with the matter here, nor was there any mention made of his elevation to the kingdom, and it is clearly alien to divine justice for anyone to either create someone for that purpose, or to raise him to any dignity to the end that He might destroy and overthrow him: for God has no need of an ungodly man, Sirach 15:12, much less is it to be said that He excited Pharaoh's stubbornness by commands and plagues, as that which He wished to beat down most of all by them. Rivetus complains of the calumny of Pererius and Cornelius, that they impute to Calvin that God placed Pharaoh and made him so obstinate and hardened in malice, that by punishing him in many ways He might have the occasion of demonstrating His power: but what else is it, when Rivetus himself maintains that God excited Pharaoh, that is, created him, raised him to the kingdom, excited his stubbornness by commands and plagues, and therefore destined him for destruction: or when he praised the opinion of Estius: for this very thing, that is, to that end I placed and raised thee, preserved and promoted thee, namely, not only by permitting, but by working many things both within and without, and by presenting to the senses things which would be to thee an occasion of greater contumacy and hardness of heart, indeed he even approves the dogma of Thomas in his Commentary on chapter 9. Epist. ad Rom. bringing this interpretation, I have stirred you up into sin, so that you may become worse, which although Thomas explains permissively, he adds nevertheless with Rivet approving, that it seems to him that something more is to be understood, because, namely, by a certain interior instinct men are moved by GOD to good and to evil. What finally is it other, when Rivet asserts, from the mind of Paul, that that stirring up of Pharaoh ought to be understood concerning his hardening or stirring up into sin, so that he might become worse, as if v. 18, when the Apostle concludes, therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens; he looks in the former to the words of GOD, I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, but in the latter the Apostle seeks proof from the words of God spoken to Pharaoh: for this very thing I have stirred you up. Whence Rivet assigns a twofold cause for this denunciation, the first that terror might be struck into Pharaoh, because he with his tyranny is in the hand of GOD: the second that he might confirm Moses by this reason, lest he fear the ferocity of the tyrant; but the third, which is the principal one, that he might recall Pharaoh to a sounder mind, Rivet passes over dry-shod, nay he rejects in Lessius and Corn. a Lap. that God primarily intended the amendment and obedience of Pharaoh, and when he saw that he would effect nothing with his scourges, he determined nevertheless to proceed, because he foresaw from that at least this good would follow, that all might recognize the divine power; this, I say, Rivetus rejects, along with the entire School of Calvin, because, to wit, in his judgment it is not only absurd for GOD to be frustrated of his end, which he primarily intended, but also blasphemous; and therefore it will also be absurd and blasphemous to men that GOD created us in Adam for eternal life, as a primary end, because, to wit, GOD was frustrated of that end through the apostasy of man; it will be absurd and blasphemous that GOD wills the conversion and salvation of a sinful man who is not converted and saved; therefore it will be absurd and blasphemous that which GOD proposes to us to be believed, and for the non-belief of which he condemns man. Add that Rivetus approves in his calculation the explanation of Lessius, book on predestination, ch. 3. Sect. 3. Therefore I have stirred you up for my contest; finally, in explaining the opinion of the Apostle, Rivetus at length approves the same thing which he had said was falsely attributed to Calvin by Cornelius; it is manifest, he says, that the sense from the Apostle is this, that just as GOD by a just, though hidden, judgment stirred up and hardened Pharaoh, that in him he might show his power, and his name might be glorified by the nations; so also he can justly stir up and harden any sinners whatsoever with the same will and judgment to the same end, because as mercy depends on the free and gratuitous will of GOD, so also the abandonment of the sinner and the hardening of the same depends on the just power of GOD, who, bound to no one, can do of his own what he wills. But this impious dogma, and truly a devourer of salvation, as Tertullian loves to speak, has no support either in our Mosaic text or in the Pauline citation of the same.

For as far as Moses is concerned, he describes at length how GOD wished in various ways to soften the heart of Pharaoh, but was frustrated in this intention of his, just as Christ complains of the Jews in Matthew 23:37, which the blessed Franzius shows from the coherence of the text in Orac. l. c., and the Remonstrants also showed in Explic. dilucida ch. 9. Rom. p. 140 seqq. Then indeed (2.) especially in this place he proposed the threat of most grave punishments, and of the very destruction of Pharaoh and his people, so that he might finally comply and let the Israelites go, which was also rightly observed from the following verses 20 and 21. Our blessed Franzius; he who feared the word of Jehovah among the servants of Pharaoh, made his servants flee into the house: but he who did not set his heart to the word of Jehovah, left his servants and his cattle in the field; for from that it is clear that this was proposed to Pharaoh and the people to this end, that both Pharaoh and his servants might fear the Lord and have faith in his words, and that some of the Egyptians, having been converted, also feared the word of Jehovah, while the others, although they also ought to have set their heart to the word of Jehovah, did not set it. (3.) The direct end, therefore, of this preservation or tolerance of Pharaoh was this, that GOD might make him see, that is, acknowledge and venerate (for words of knowledge imply affection) the power of GOD, so that, to wit, once that was acknowledged, he might finally let the people go: he did not kill or remove Pharaoh immediately, but preserved him: but to what end? Not that he might punish him more severely afterwards, but as the words of GOD himself testify here, that he might lead him to the acknowledgment of his power, and that thus the name of GOD might be celebrated in the whole earth. The subordinate end (which they call the ultimate in a certain respect) is the conversion and salvation of Pharaoh; but the ultimate simply is the glory of GOD. (4) The words which follow confirm this further: you still exalt yourself, so that you do not let my people go, i.e., you are so reckless and unmoved, and do not yet fear for yourself concerning my power: whence it is evident that there is no need for us to say that the particle ὅπως does not denote a final cause here, but is taken only ἐκβατικῶς, because its primary αἰτιολογικὴ signification holds entirely, and the genuine end of the Pharaonic preservation, and that a twofold one, which we have mentioned, is expressed. (5.) The word העמדתיך is, I have made you stand, I have preserved you, as the LXX Interpreters render it, and the force of the word implies it, and the text itself, especially according to the συνέχειαν and the explanation of the preceding parts, handed down by the Chaldean, R. Solomon, Calvin himself, Tremellius, and Junius; therefore it is not an incitement to hardening or to destruction; but only the preservation and tolerance of the prevaricating Pharaoh is designated, who had deserved to be removed with the living creatures or in other plagues, but was borne with by GOD up to this point with great μακροθυμία, not so that he might be more hardened or punished more severely, but so that he himself might finally acknowledge the divine power, and by that reason the name of GOD might be rendered more illustrious. (6.) Nor does that Apostolic ἐξήγησιν imply anything else; because, not to mention what Calvin himself warns here, that the Apostles were not very anxious in reciting the words, but looked rather to the matter, the sense of the Apostle must in any case be explained in such a way that it does not differ from the Mosaic and Hebrew text, which the Chaldean, LXX, and other Interpreters most of them, because the word itself demands it, interpret it concerning preservation; Junius and Tremellius also explain it thus: I have stirred you up, that is, I have made you remain, or I willed you to remain a survivor. Cf. Ex. 21:21. Which explanation of the Apostolic word, consonant with the Mosaic word, Calvin himself approves: I have preserved you, or I willed you to remain a survivor, for the Hebrew word, which is transitive in Hiphil, is derived from עמד, which is to stand; since therefore he had moderated himself, GOD now assigns the cause of his tolerance, because if Pharaoh had fallen in one light battle, the glory of the victory would have been less celebrated. Which interpretation, finally, Rivetus himself acknowledges should not be rejected, provided that the hardening of Pharaoh and the patience of GOD are included. But just as it is certain that the patience of GOD is included in the word for rousing, if it is the same as what I have done, that you should remain, so it does not appear how the hardening of Pharaoh is included in this word from the intention of GOD who rouses or from His act. (7.) Since the Apostle utters the words thus: that I may show in you my power, which in Moses stand thus: that I may make you see my power, he does not depart from the sense of the words of Moses, for the words ἐν σοὶ repeated from the LXX Interpreters are to be accepted in the same sense which the authentic text of Moses conveys; and therefore GOD so showed His power in Pharaoh, that He desired not so much to others, as especially to him, that the same be demonstrated, and that he himself, through the recognition of it, be brought to a sounder mind and obedience for a more illustrious manifestation of His glory. And he could indeed have recognized, had he not hardened his heart, the power of the Lord from so many prodigies, so that he might understand that the GOD of Israel was the true GOD, who was revealing Himself to him by such illustrious miracles: indeed, his ministers also recognized the power of GOD, ch. 9, 20; ch. 10, 7; ch. 12, 38; Pharaoh himself also recognized it, ch. 8, 20; ch. 9, 27; ch. 10, 16; but he returned to his nature, and was hardened all the more by the same, certainly not by the decree or operation of GOD, who intended and was doing something entirely different, but by his own fault, by which he hardened his mind against the command of GOD. (8.) GOD was not only showing the power of His strength, but primarily also the virtue of His long-suffering and tolerance, because in great patience He sustained him, and proposed the word to him through His servants, even though because of the hardness of his persevering heart he was a vessel of wrath, Rom. 9, 22. For even to those who treasure up for themselves wrath against the day of wrath, that GOD shows the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering, and indeed to this end, that by his kindness he may lead them to repentance, the Apostle teaches in a clear voice Rom. 2, 4. (9.) It is therefore false, according to Paul's mind, that that excitation of Pharaoh concerning his hardening ought to be understood as intended by God; nor is it established that from these words of Moses, of which we are now speaking, the Apostle proves that God hardens whom he wills; for even if these things cohere in the Apostle's words, it is not however necessary that we should establish that an inference is made here from the Mosaic words, since no foundation has been laid before, either expressly or implicitly, for this hardening, unless perhaps that is sought in the tolerance of GOD, but Pharaoh was hardened quite accidentally and beyond the intention of GOD. Nor do the Remonstrants observe beside the point, p. 155. l. c. The word to harden is used for rejection, since up to this point it has been a matter of rejection from righteousness and adoption, and rejection and hardening seem to be used promiscuously Rom. 11, 7. 15, 25. whence the sense is, GOD rejects from righteousness whom he wills, and has mercy on whom he wills; it is not indicated, however, that he either rejects or has mercy by an absolute will, but the discourse is about a consequent will, which presupposes faith and infidelity, concerning which we have dealt at greater length in the Apostolic oracles and on Mal. 1, 3.

Rivetus objects that the Apostle wished by this example to show divine liberty in leaving the impious to themselves, and in destining them to just judgments, for his own glory; as if it were an end proposed to himself; but for this demonstration it is not sufficient if it is a matter only of what GOD spared Pharaoh, so that he might reserve him for the illustrating of his glory more, but it is necessary that the hardening of Pharaoh be included at the same time, namely that it depends on the just power of God, who, bound to no one, can do what he wills, which Rivetus thinks the example of the potter shows in particular. Resp. We deny that this liberty is demonstrated here by the example of Pharaoh; for the Apostle has not yet dealt with the absolute power of GOD, but with the ordinary process of GOD in assuming or rejecting men through faith or infidelity. And it is a begging of the question that GOD absolutely proposed this end to himself, and that whatever he did concerning Pharaoh was directed to this end, namely the illustration of the glory of his power; since GOD did this more, as the whole of history testifies, to illustrate the glory of his mercy than of his power to reprobate and to exercise his judgments; since he even tolerated this vessel of wrath with great long-suffering. Therefore, as far as the simile of the potter is concerned, it must be observed, (1.) the potter is not here called properly and immediately GOD himself, as some Calvinists wish, for thus the Apostle would have said: does not the potter have power, or would have testified by some other indication that he was speaking of the heavenly potter. Whence (2.) most all others acknowledge here a comparison of unequals, by which GOD is compared with the potter, his power over men his creatures, with the power of the potter over the clay; the protasis of which is v. 21. does not the potter have power &c. is free from doubt; but there is a great dispute about the apodosis. Most Calvinists, who defend absolute predestination, judge that there is a manifest anantapodoton in the words of the Apostle: and therefore they presume to supply an apodosis of their own; to wit: if the potter has such power over his clay, that from the same lump it is permitted to him to make a vessel for honor and dishonor, as it seems to him; surely much more does GOD have the power from the same lump to create man either for salvation or for death according to his good pleasure: indeed they proceed to the actual usurpation of this power; although it is not yet agreed among them; what ought to correspond to the word lump in the apodosis, whether man not yet created, or indeed created: if the former, whether to be created, according to the divine decree, or indeed only creatable, and considered in pure potentiality: if the latter, whether persisting in integrity, or indeed fallen into sin? But the anantapodoton is established here without any necessity, and that rendering is uncertain and dangerous, by which they supply at will, especially because of the right of dominion, which they claim for GOD as creator over the creature as absolute, and the exercise of this right, about which both they and the Scholastics dispute variously, whether GOD could by absolute dominion reprobate a creature deserving nothing to eternal destruction, indeed create it for damnation. Some with Peter of Ailly and Paul Ferry in the Specimen of the Orthodox Scholastic c. 28. as also Whitaker in his last lecture to the Cambridge Clergy assert, that there would be no injustice, if GOD were to punish some creature eternally without sin, about which Moses Amyraut disputes especially in Tract. de Prædest. c. 4. Sutlovius in vindic. c. 12. We say, he says, that the power of GOD over creatures rests on mere superiority, the excellence and eminence of the divine nature and dignity, from which it flows, that God can reprobate man, destine him to death, deny efficacious grace, impute another's sin, and punish because of it, and finally oblige to the impossible and afflict without demerit. See also Pareus in Iren. c. 28. Chamier. Tom. 3. lib. 7. cap. 1. Kekermannus lib. 3. Instit. cap. 24. Maccov. in Syst. p. 65. But this is repugnant to divine justice, to punish the innocent, Gen. 18, 25. to which place those things which Rivetus has in Exerc. pag. 554. can be compared; it is repugnant to divine goodness and mercy, to devote someone to extreme curses beyond merit, and to expose him to immense torments. Nor is there any reason for them to appeal to the τὸ ἀνυπεύθυνον (unaccountability) of divine power, which God possesses not from the benefit of creation, but from his ὑπεροχῇ (superiority) and eminence: for this cannot be separated from God's justice or mercy, both of which are essential to God; yet neither permits that such dire things be decreed against a creature without any merit, or that a rational creature be created for eternal torments. GOD is not to be considered by us with his omnipotence alone or the sublimity of his tremendous majesty, but with all his attributes, by which he describes himself in his Word, and thus it must be seen what he can do toward his creatures. And it is in vain that a distinction is made between the right of dominion and the right of judgment. For GOD is the Lord of his creatures, and therefore he has the right of dominion over them, because he is their creator, whence follows the right of legislation, and what depends upon that, the right of judgment, which derives its origin from the benefit of creation. Nor is the distinction between damnation and destruction of any moment, as if someone could be destined for destruction, and be affected by it without his own wrongdoing, but not so for damnation, on the grounds that the latter, as a judicial act, requires wrongdoing beforehand. The Remonstrants rightly judge that this fiction is too thin to be used in so grave a matter; for what does it matter to me if I am forced to endure the dire flames of infernal fire forever, whether that evil is inflicted as destruction, from the right of dominion, or as damnation from the right of judgment? This is to play in a matter so painful, just as if it were only a question of the death of fleas or the loss of a few needles, and not of the perdition of an eternal soul and body alike. Compare here Curcellaeus's Vindication against Amyraut. Then if that right of destining a creature to eternal flames without its wrongdoing is deduced from the benefit of creation, the evil to be inflicted will far exceed the good conferred, and consequently the right resulting from the good conferred: which in no way accords with divine justice. For the evil of eternal damnation or destruction is the greatest evil of man, because he himself is reduced to such a state that it would be better for him never to have existed. The analogy of the Apostle is not, therefore, to be extended so far as to include the power of creating an innocent man for damnation or destruction. Finally, even if it could be proven that GOD could create a man from the same lump of clay for salvation and eternal damnation, it has nevertheless been proven immediately that he does not actually exercise this power, nor does he wish to exercise it. (3.) If the Apostolic treatment is weighed more accurately, the ἀπόδοσις is not suppressed, but is expressly held in the text in agreement with the πρότασις, verses 22, 23; for this is the πρότασις: does not the potter have the power of fashioning a vessel for honor and dishonor from the same mass? The ἀπόδοσις, however, is as follows: but if GOD, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much long-suffering the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—understand, does he not have the power to do this? Thus the rendering will be complete: the sense, therefore, is, since the potter has the power of thus fashioning a vessel for dishonor, will not GOD have the power of showing wrath, so that his power may be made known against the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction—not which he himself created or fitted for destruction, but which have been fitted for destruction by their own fault, toward whom, although he can most justly show his wrath, he nevertheless still endures them with much long-suffering, waiting, namely, to see whether they are going to repent? For the Holy Spirit teaches most openly that this is the proper end of divine long-suffering and tolerance, Rom. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. And therefore (4.) by vessels of wrath fitted for destruction the Apostle does not understand men who are yet to be created or to be brought into the light by birth, but men already existing, brought to the use of reason, who have merited the wrath of GOD by their own actual sins, upon whom GOD could most deservedly pour out his wrath and whom he could immediately destroy: which are called κατηρτισμένα, fitted, prepared, not by GOD, for although the Apostle said of the vessels of mercy that GOD prepared them for glory, he did not add concerning the vessels of wrath that they were prepared by GOD. And the reason for the disparity is given here, because it is the proper work of GOD to do good, toward which he, being supremely good, inclines by his nature. But to punish is, as it were, alien and foreign, to which he is not driven except, in a certain way, unwillingly and by the wickedness of men. Furthermore, when GOD shows wrath to those who are fitted for destruction, that is, punishes them, he certainly did not himself fit them for destruction, for he does not hate his own work, nor does he pursue with wrath or punishment that which is his own work. Therefore they are said to treasure up wrath for themselves, Rom. 2, 5, which is to fit themselves for destruction, whom the Lord therefore seeks, Ezech. 33, 11: Why would they want to die? For although a man does not prepare himself for punishment by his own intention—nay, sinning, he wishes solely to indulge his desire so that he may always be able to sin with impunity—yet because by sinning he commits those things on account of which he brings destruction upon himself, he is rightly said to fit himself for destruction. Although, therefore, to destroy is the act of GOD the judge, to prepare oneself for perdition is the act of the sinning man. (5.) Thus, therefore, the matter stands: GOD made man a vessel fitted for receiving grace and blessing; indeed, he filled him with grace in his original creation, but man makes himself a vessel of sin and wrath, and although he has been restored through Christ so that he might become a vessel of mercy, yet by rejecting the Gospel and persevering in sins he remains under wrath, or rather, grace provokes wrath against him anew through sin. He becomes, therefore, by his own fault a vessel of wrath fitted for destruction, in which GOD could most deservedly show his wrath by punishing it immediately; for to show wrath is to punish exemplarily, since it is properly shown when punishments are inflicted, so that men may learn to tremble at the wrath of the Lord, and then the power of GOD, the executor of wrath, is notified when someone is punished with an exemplary judgment: which was finally done in Pharaoh. (6.) GOD does not wish to show his wrath and make known the power that executes wrath upon the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction by some absolute decree; but by this law and condition, if, namely, they have remained such, for it is therefore expressly added that he bears them with much long-suffering and thus awaits their amendment; for where amendment is awaited, there is no peremptory decree of precisely destroying, but only a conditional one, namely, if amendment does not follow; on the contrary, where there is a purpose of destroying ἀποτόμως, there neither long-suffering nor the expectation of amendment has any place. (7.) The sum, therefore, of the analogy adduced is this: the potter has the power of making a vessel for dishonor and honor from the same mass; why, therefore, should GOD not have the power of exemplarily punishing at last the vessels of wrath, which have prepared themselves for destruction by their own fault and are most worthy of the wrath of GOD, after he has endured them with great long-suffering and awaited their repentance? (8.) This, therefore, is what the Apostle taught by the example of Pharaoh and the analogy of the potter, that GOD can justly complain about the hardened, not vice versa that they can complain about GOD, because GOD, both by hardening judicially and by punishing exemplarily, does not deal except with those who are already children of wrath and have treasured up wrath for themselves for the day of just judgment and have fitted themselves for perdition, and thus have hardened themselves: but he deals with them even when he wishes to avenge their hardness and contumacy, by still tolerating them with great long-suffering. And therefore the Apostle responds to the proposed objection: GOD hardens not by a powerful infusion of hardness, but by tolerating contumacious men with gentleness and indulgence in much patience: just as was established by the example of Pharaoh. But he who is thus hardened can, with respect to him by whom he is said to be hardened, not be hardened, and, already hardened by his own fault, while he is patiently tolerated and awaited for repentance, he can repent; otherwise, he could not be said to be tolerated with much long-suffering. For it is not called tolerance in common usage where no means of escaping is given: GOD can therefore complain about the hardened and rebuke them on a double count: both that they are hardened and that they remain such. Nay, even if GOD were to harden them to the greatest degree, even in an irresistible manner, it is manifest that they are justly reproved, but that God can by no means be blamed; since He hardens only those who have already hardened themselves and obstinately treasure up wrath for themselves, and thus by their stubborn malice drive GOD to their own hardening. Thus, absolutely no support is left here for the patrons of an absolute decree.

Latin:

Vers. 16. IDCIRCO AUTEM POSUI TE, UT OSTENDAM IN TE FORTITUDINEM ME- AM.

Hebraeus textus ita habet: & profecto propter hoc feci te stare, ut videre te faciam potentiam meam. Apostolus Rom. 9. v. 17. reddidit: ὅτι εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε, quia in hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te virtutem meam. LXX. Interpp. habent: διετηρή- θης conservatus es, caetera ita reddentes, ut ab Apo- stolo adducuntur, nisi quod hic τὴν δύναμίν μου ha- beat, LXX. vero τὴν ἰσχύν μου. Calviniani, ut di- xi, absoluti sui decreti hic quaerunt patrocinium, maxime in verbo ἐξήγειρα, quo Apostolus usus est, quod explicat Rivetus ita, quod Deus Pharaonem creaverit, ad regnum evexerit, mandatis & plagis per- vicaciam ejus excitaverit, atq; ideo exitio destinaverit. Quo pacto simul comprehenduntur omnes aliorum Calvinianorum ψευδερμηνείαι, quorum nonnulli vocem interpretati sunt per creare, alii ad regiam dignitatem evehere, alii irritare: Sed ea ratione, & intentione plerique omnes: quod Deus absoluto & simplici decreto id intenderit in Pharaone excitando, ut ipse perderetur & aeternum reprobaretur. Verum enim vero neque creatio aut productio Pharaonis hic quicquam ad rem facit, neq; de evectione ad regnum ullo verbo facta est mentio, & plane alienum est a divina justitia, quenquam vel creare ad id, aut ad dignitatem aliquam evehere hac fini, ut eundem perdat atq; evertat: neq; enim improbo viro Deo opus est, Syr. 15, 12. multo minus dicendum, quod excita- rit Pharaonis pervicaciam per mandata & plagas, ut- pote quam per ea maxime retundere volebat. Que- ritur Rivetus de calumnia Pererii & Cornelii, quod Calvino imputent, Deum posuisse Pharaonem & fe- cisse sic obstinatum & obduratum in malitia, ut eum multifariam puniendo occasionem haberet demon- strandi potentiam suam: sed quid aliud est, cum Ri- vetus ipse statuit, quod Deus Pharaonem excitaverit, id est, creaverit, ad regnum evexerit, mandatis & plagis pervicaciam ejus excitaverit, atque ideo exitio destinaverit: aut cum Estii laudavit sententiam: in hoc ipsum, id est, in eum finem posui & excitavi te, ser- vavi atque promovi, videl. non solum permittan- do, sed multa tam intus, quam foris operando, sensi- busq; objiciendo, quae tibi futura essent occasio majoris contumaciae ac duritiei cordis, imo etiam Thomae ap- probat dogma in Comment. ad c. 9. Epist. ad Rom. hanc afferentis interpretationem, excitavi te in pec- catum, ut deterior fias, quod etsi permissive explicet Thomas, addit tamen approbante Riveto, sibi vi- deri aliquid amplius esse intelligendum, quia videl. in- stinctu quodam interiori moveantur homines a DEO ad bonum & ad malum. Quid denique aliud est, cum Rivetus, ex Pauli mente excitationem illam Pha- raonis de ejusdem induratione vel excitatione in pecca- tum, ut deterior fieret, intelligi debere, asserit, quasi v. 18. cum concludit Apostolus, itaque cujus vult mise- retur, & quem vult indurat; respiciat in priori ad verba DEI miserebor, cujus misertus fuero, in poste- riori autem ex verbis Dei ad Pharaonem dictis pro- bationem petat Apostolus: ad hoc ipsum excitavi te. Unde geminam Rivetus causam hujus denunciatio- nis assignat, primam ut Pharaoni terror incuteretur, quod cum sua tyrannide in manu DEI sit: secun- dam ut Mosen hac ratione confirmaret, ne ferociam tyranni metueret; tertiam vero, quae praecipua est, ut Pharaonem ad saniorem mentem revocaret, sicco pede praeterit, imo reprobat Riv. in Lessio & Corn. a Lap. quod Deus primario intenderit Pharaonis emen- dationem atq; obedientiam, & cum videret se flagellis suis nihil effecturum, statuerit tamen pergere, quia prævidebat inde faltim hoc boni consecuturum, ut omnes cognoscerent divinam potentiam, hoc inquam reprobat Rivetus, cum Schola universa Calvini, quia scil. ipsius judicio non absurdum tantum est DEUM frustrari suo fine, quem primario intende- rat, sed etiam blasphemum; ideoq; hominibus etiam istis absurdum & blasphemum erit, DEUM nos in Adamo ad æternam vitam, ceu primarium finem con- didifse, quia sc. DEUS fine illo frustratus est per apo- stasiam hominis; absurdum & blasphemum erit, DEUM velle hominis peccatoris conversionem & salu- tem, qui non convertitur & salvatur; absurdum er- go & blasphemum erit illud quod DEUS nobis cre- dendumproponit, & ob quod non creditum hominẽ damnat. Adde quod Rivetus calculo suo probet Lessii explicationem lib. de prædest. c. 3. Sect. 3. ideo te excitavi in certamen meum; denique in expli- canda sententia Apostoli idem prolixe appro- bat Rivetus, quod per calumniam Calvino affingi a Cornelio dixerat, manifestum est, inquit, sensum ex Apostolo hunc esse, quod quemadmodum DEUS justo, quamvis occulto judicio Pharaonem excitavit & indu- ravit, ut in eo ostenderet potentiam suam, & glorifica- retur nomen ejus a gentibus; sic etiam quosvis peccato- res eadem voluntate ac judicio in eundem finem excita- re & indurare juste potest, quia ut misericordia pendet a libera & gratuita DEI voluntate, sic quoque pecca- toris derelictio & ejusdem induratio a DEI justa pote- state pendet, qui nemini adstrictus de suo facere potest, quod vult. Sed dogma hoc impium, vereq; salutis devoratorium, ut Tertull. loqui amat, nihil præsidii vel in nostro textu Mosaico habet, vel in allegatio- ne ejusdem Paulina.

Nam quod ad Mosen attinet, prolixe is descri- bit, quomodo DEUS variis modis cor Pharaonis emol- lire voluerit, at hac intentione sua frustratus fuerit, æque uti de Judæis conqueritur Christus Matth. 23, 37. quæ ex textus cohærentia ostendit B. Franzius in Orac. l. c. ostenderunt quoque Remonstrantes in Explic. dilucida cap. 9. Rom. p. 140. seqq. Tum vero (2.) inprimis in h. l. ideo comminationem pœ- narum gravissimarum, ipsiusque perditionis Pha- raoni, & populo eius proposuit, ut tandem morem gereret, & Israelitas dimitteret, quod recte observa- vit etiam e versibus seqq. 20. & 21. B. noster Fran- zius; qui timuit verbum Jehove e servis Pharaonis, fu- gere fecit servos suos in domum: at qui non apposuit cor suum ad verbum Jehove, dereliquit servos & pecus suum in agro; ex eo enim liquet, eo fine hoc proposi- tum fuisse Pharaoni & populo, ut tum Pharao, tum servi ejus Dominum timerent, verbisq; ejus fidem haberent, tum conversos etiam quosdam ex Ægy- ptiis verbum Jehove timuisse, cæteros cum etiam cor suum apponere deberent ad verbum Jehovæ, non apposuisse. (3.) Finis itaque directus istius con- servationis vel tolerantiæ Pharaonis hic fuit, ut face- ret ipsum DEUS videre, id est, agnoscere ac venerari, (verba enim notitiæ affectum inferunt) potentiam DEI, quo scil. ea agnita populum tandem dimitte- ret: non interemit statim, aut sustulit Pharaonem, sed conservavit: sed quo fine? Non ut puniret ipsum deinde gravius, sed ut verba ipsius DEI hîc testantur, ut ipsum perduceret ad agnitionem poten- tiæ suæ, & ut ita nomen DEI in universa terra celebra- retur. Finis ergo subordinatus (ultimum vocant secundum quid) est conversio & salus Pharaonis; ultimus autem simpliciter est gloria DEI. (4) Verba, quæ sequuntur, id ulterius confirmant: adhuc tu te ipsum extollis, ut non dimittas populum meum, q. d. adeo tu temerarius es, & immo- tus, nec dum de potentia mea tibi metuis: unde con- stat, opus non esse, ut dicamus, particulam ὅπως hic non finalem causam notare, sed ἐκβατικῶς so- lum accipi, quia obtinet omnino primaria ejus si- gnificatio αἰτιολογικὴ, & finis conservationis Pha- raonicae genuinus, isque geminus, quem diximus, exprimitur. (5.) Verbum העמדתיך est, stare te feci, conservavi te, ut LXX. Interpp. reddunt, & vis vocis infert, textusq; ipse inprimis juxta συνέχειαν, & explicationem antecedentium, a Chaldaeo, R. Sa- lomone, Calvino ipso, Tremellio & Junio traditam; non excitatio ergo ad indurationem vel ad perditio- nem; sed conservatio solum & tolerantia prevari- cantis Pharaonis designatur, qui meritus erat, ut cum animantibus aut in aliis plagis tolleretur, sed magna μακροθυμία a DEO huc usque ferebatur, non ut magis obduraretur, aut gravius puniretur, sed ut ipse tandem divinam agnosceret potentiam, eaque ra- tione nomen DEI illustrius redderetur. (6.) Nec aliud ἐξήγησιν illud Apostolicum infert; quia, ne dicamus, quod hic Calvinus ipse monet, Apostolos in verbis recitandis non admodum fuisse anxios, sed rem potius spectasse, explicandus utique sensus Apostoli ita est, ut non discrepet a Mosaico, & E- braeo textu, quem Chaldaeus, LXX. & alii Interpp. plerique, quia verbum ipsum id postulat, de conser- vatione interpretantur, Jun. etiam & Trem. ita ex- ponunt: excitavi te, id est, feci, ut restares, vel volui te manere superstitem. Conf. Ex. 21, 21. Quam expli- cationem vocis Apostolicae verbo Mosaico confo- nam, Calvinus ipse probat: conservavi te, vel super- stitem manere volui, verbum enim Ebraicum, quod transitivum est in Hiphil, deducitur ab עמד, quod est stare; quoniam ergo sibi moderatus fuerat, DEUS nunc tolerantiae suae causam assignat, quia si uno levi prelio cecidisset Pharao, minus celebris fuisset victoriae gloria. Quam interpretationem denique Rivetus ipse agno- scit rejiciendam non esse, dummodo includatur indu- ratio Pharaonis & patientia DEI. Sed uti patien- tiam DEI includi verbo excitandi, si idem sit quod feci, ut restares, certum est, ita quomodo induratio Pharaonis ex intentione DEI excitantis vel actu ejus- dem huic verbo includatur, non apparet. (7.) Cum Apostolus verba ita effert: ut ostendam in te potentiam meam, quae apud Mosen sic habent: ut fa- ciam te videre potentiam meam, non abit a mente verborum Mosis, nam verba ἐν σοὶ e LXX. Inter- pretibus repetita, eodem sensu accipienda, quem textus authenticus Mosis infert; ideoq; sic ostendit DEUS in Pharaone suam potentiam, ut non tam a- liis, quam praecipue ipsi eandem demonstratam i- psumque per ejus agnitionem ad saniorem mentem & obedientiam ad illustriorem gloriae suae manife- stationem redactum cuperet. Et agnoscere sane poterat, nisi cor obfirmasset suum, potentiam Do- mini e tot prodigiis, ut DEUM Israelis verum DE- UM esse intelligeret, qui tam illustribus miraculis se ipsi patefaciebat: imo agnovere etiam Ministri ejus potentiam DEI cap. 9, 20. c. 10, 7. c. 12, 38. agno- vit & Pharao ipse cap. 8, 20. c. 9, 27. c. 10, 16. sed ad in- genium rediit, ac magis faltim induratus iisdem fuit, non utique DEI decreto aut operatione, qui prorsus aliud intendebat, & agebat, sed propria culpa, qua adversus DEI mandatum mentem ob- durabat. (8.) Non tantum ostendebat DEUS potentiam fortitudinis suae, sed inprimis etiam vir- tutem longanimitatis & tolerantiae suae, quia in multa patientia sustinuit ipsum, eique verbum per servos suos proposuit, etsi ob duritiem cordis sui perseve- rantem vas irae esset, Rom. 9, 22. Nam & illis, qui iram sibi in diem irae thesaurizant, divitias bonita- tis & patientiæ & longanimitatis DEUM oftende- re, & quidem hac fini, ut benignitate sua eos ad pœ- nitentiam perducat λευκάδι φωνῇ docet Apostolus Rom. 2, 4. (9.) Fallum itaque est, ex Pauli men- te, excitationem illam Pharaonis de ejusdem indura- tione a Deo intenta intelligi debere; neque constat, quod ex his Mosis verbis, de quibus nunc agimus, probet Apostolus, Deum indurare, quem vult; etsi enim hæc cohæreant in Apostoli verbis, non neces- sum tamen est, ut statuamus, illationem hîc fieri e verbis Mosaicis, siquidem nullum antea fundamen- tum jactum sit, vel expresse, vel implicite, hujus indu- rationis, nisi forte id quæratur in tolerantia DEI, sed perquam accidentaliter & præter intentionem DEI Pharao induratus fuit. Neque præter rem obser- vant Remonstrantes, p. 155. l. c. Verbum indurandi usurpari pro rejectione, siquidem hactenus de reje- ctione a justitia, &υἱοθεσίᾳ actum fuerit, & promi- scue usurpari videantur rejectio & induratio Rom. 11, 7. 15, 25. unde sensus est, rejicere DEUM a justitia, quos vult, misereri, quorum vult; non indicatur au- tem, quod absoluta voluntate vel rejiciat, vel mise- reatur, sed de voluntate consequente sermo est, quæ fi- dem & infidelitatem præsupponit, quo de pluribus in oraculis Apostolicis & ad Mal. 1, 3. egimus.

Objicit Rivetus, voluisse Apostolum hoc exem- plo ostendere libertatem divinam in impiis sibi relin- quendis, & ad justa judicia destinandis, ad gloriam su- am; tanquam ad finem sibi propositum; ad hanc au- tem demonstrationem non sufficere, si agatur tantum de eo, quod DEUS pepercerit Pharaoni, ut eum reser- varet illustrandæ magis gloriæ, sed necessum esse, ut in- duratio Pharaonis simul includatur, quod nempe a Dei justa potestate illa dependeat, qui nemini obstrictus fa- cere possit, quod vult, quod imprimis exemplum figuli ostendere putat Rivetus. Resp. negamus exemplo Pharaonis hîc libertatem istam demonstrari; hacte- nus enim nondum egit Apostolus de absoluta DEI potestate, sed de processu DEI ordinario in assumen- dis aut rejiciendis per fidem aut infidelitatem homi- nibus. Et petitio principii est, DEUM hunc sibi finem absolute proposuisse, & ad hunc finem dire- ctum fuisse, quicquid circa Pharaonem egit, nempe gloriæ potestatis suæ illustrationem; cum magis DEUS id egerit teste universa historia, ut illustraret gloriam suæ misericordiæ, quam potestatis reprobandi, & judicia sua exercendi; siquidem hoc etiam vas iræ magna tolerarit μακροθυμίᾳ. Quod ergo ad simile de figulo attinet, observandum, (1.) figulum hic non dici proprie & immediate DEUM ipsum, ut Calvi- niani nonnulli volunt, sic enim dixisset Apostolus: annon habet figulus potestatem, aut aliquo alio indicio testatus esset, se de cœlesti figulo loqui. Un- de (2.) plerique omnes cæteri agnoscunt hic com- parationem imparium, qua DEUS cum figulo, pote- stas ejus in homines creaturas suas, cum potestate figuli in lutum, comparatur; cujus πρότασις v. 21. annon habet figulus potestatem &c. dubio vacat; sed de ἀποδόσει maxima disputatio est. Plerique Calvi- niani, qui prædestinationem absolutam tuentur, ἀναν- ταπόδοτον manifestum esse in verbis Apostoli cen- sent: ideoq; ἀπόδοσιν de suo supplere præsumunt; h. m. si figulus eam habet potestatem in lutum suum, ut ex eadem massa ipsi liceat facere vas ad decus & dedecus, prout ipsi videtur; utiq; multo magis DEUS potestatem habet ex eadem massa condendi hominem sive ad salu- tem, sive ad mortem pro beneplacito: imo ad actua- lem potestatis hujus usurpationem procedunt; quanquam de eo adhuc inter ipsos non conveniat; quid vocabulo massæ in ἀποδόσει respondere debe- at, an homo nondum creatus, an vero creatus: si prius, anne creandus, juxta decretum divinum, an vero creabilis tantum, & in pura puta potentialitate consi- deratus: si posterius, anne perstans in integritate, an vero lapsus in peccatum? Sed τὸ ἀνανταπόδοτον hic statuitur citra ullam necessitatem, & incerta & pe- riculosa est illa redditio, qua supplent pro arbitrio, maxime propter jus dominii, quod DEO ut creato- ri in creaturam absolutum vindicant, jurisque hujus exercitium, de quo tum ipsi, tum Scholastici varie disputant, anne DEUS potuerit absoluto dominio ad æternum exitium creaturam nihil meritam reprobare, imo ad damnationem condere. Nonnulli cum Pe- tro de Aliaco & Paulo Ferrio in Specimine Scholasti- ci Orthodoxi c. 28. ut & Wittakero concion. ult ad Clerum Cantabrigiensem asserunt, nullam injustiti- am fore, si DEUS creaturam aliquam puniat æterna- liter sine peccato, de quo Moses Amyraldus cumpri- mis disputat Tract. de Prædest. c. 4. Sutlovius in vin- dic. c. 12. Dicimus, inquit, potestatem DEI in creatu- ras niti sola ὑπεροχῇ, excellentia & eminentia divinæ naturæ & dignitatis, ex qua fluit, ut Deus hominem reprobare, destinare ad mortem, gratiam efficacem de- negare, alienum peccatum imputare, & propter illud punire, deniq; ad impossibile obligare & affligere sine demerito possit. Vid. etiam Pareus in Iren. c. 28. Cha- mier. Tom. 3. lib. 7. cap. 1. Kekermannus lib. 3. Instit. cap. 24. Maccov. in Syst. p. 65. Sed repugnat hoc justitiæ divinæ, innocentem punire, Gen. 18, 25. ad quem locum conferri poterunt ea, quæ Rivetus habet in Exerc. pag. 554. repugnat divinæ bonitati & misericordiæ, præter meritum extremis diris devo- vere, & immensis cruciatibus aliquem exponere. Nec est quod provocent ad τὸ ἀνυπεύθυνον potesta- tis divinæ, quod Deus habeat non ex beneficio crea- tionis, sed ex ὑπεροχῇ & eminentia: hæc enim non potest sequestrari a DEI vel justitia vel misericordia, quæ utraque Deo essentialis est; neutra autem per- mittit, ut vel in creaturam præter meritum ullum tam dira statuantur, vel ad cruciatus æternos crea- tura rationalis condatur. DEUS non est confide- randus nobis, cum omnipotentia sua duntaxat aut sublimitate majestatis tremendæ, sed cum omnibus suis attributis, a quibus se in Verbo suo ipse descri- bit, & sic videndum, quid in creaturas possit. Et frustra distinguitur inter jus dominii, & jus judicii. DEUS enim Dominus creaturarum est, eoque & jus dominii in ipsas habet, quia earum creator, un- de sequitur jus νομοθεσίας, & quod inde depen- det, jus judicii, ex creationis beneficio ortum du- cere. Nec ullius momenti est distinctio inter da- mnationem & exitium, quasi possit aliquis exitio de- stinari, eoque affici citra ipsius maleficium, damna- tioni non item, eo quod hæc tanquam actus judicialis maleficium prærequirat. Recte judicant Remon- strantes, nimis dilutum hoc commentum esse, quam ut usurpetur in re tam gravi; quid enim mea refert, si cogar diras infernalis ignis flammas in æternum per- peti, seu illud malum ut exitium, ex jure dominii, sive ut damnatio ex jure judicii irrogetur? Ludere hoc est in materia tam dolorosa, perinde ac si tantum de mor- te pulicum, aut de damno aliquot acicularum ageretur, non autem de æternæ animæ juxta & corporis perditio- ne. Conf. hîc Curcellæi Vindic. contra Amyraldum. Tum si e beneficio creationis jus illud deducatur, creaturam citra maleficium ejus ad æternas flammas destinandi, malum inferendum longe excedet bo- num collatum, adeoque jus ex bono collato redun- dans: quod justitiæ divinæ nullatenus congruit. Malum enim æternæ damnationis seu exitii est summum hominis malum, quia in eum ipse redi- gitur statum, ut præstaret, ipsum esse nunquam ha- buisse. Non ergo similitudo Apostoli eo usque protrahenda, ut potestatem creandi hominem in- nocentem ad damnationem vel exitium includat. Denique etiamsi probari posset, DEUM posse ex eadem terræ gleba creare hominem ad salutem & damnationem æternam, non tamen actu ipso hanc potentiam eum usurpare aut usurpare velle, proba- tum illico est. (3.) Si accuratius tractatio Apo- stolica expendatur, ἀπόδοσις non subticetur, sed in textu expresse habetur τῇ προτάσει consentanea vers. 22. 23. nam πρότασις hæc est; annon habet po- testatem figulus condendi vas ad decus & dedecus ex ea- dem massa? ἀπόδοσις autem ita habet : quod si DEVS volens ostendere iram & notam facere poten- tiam suam, sustinuit multa longanimitate vasa iræ co- agmentata ad interitum, & ut notas faceret divitias gloriæ suæ erga vasa misericordiæ, quæ præparavit ad gloriam, subintellige, annon habet potestatem id fa- ciendi, sic plena erit redditio : sensus itaque est, cum figulus potestatem habeat ita condendi vas ad dedecus, annon DEUS potestatem habebit ostendendi iram, ut nota reddatur potentia sua adversus vasa iræ coag- mentata ad interitum, non quæ ipse ad interitum creavit, aut coagmentavit, sed quæ propria culpa coagmentata sunt ad interitum, in quæ ipse iram suam ostendere cum possit justissime, adhuc tamen multa longanimitate ea sustinet, expectans videl. an- ne pœnitentiam actura sint? Hunc enim μακρο- θυμίας & tolerantiæ divinæ proprium finem esse apertissime docet Spiritus S. Rom. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. Ideoque (4.) per vasa iræ coagmentata ad interitum non intelligit Apostolus homines, qui adhuc crean- di, aut per nativitatem in lucem producendi sunt, sed homines jam existentes ad rationis usum adductos, per peccata sua actualia iram DEI promeritos, in quos DEUS jure meritissimo iram effundere, quosque illico perdere possit : quæ dicuntur κατηρτισμένα, aptata, apparata, non a DEO, nam etsi Apostolus de misericordiæ vasis dixerit, quod DEUS ea præ- pararit ad gloriam, de iræ tamen vasis non addidit, quod a DEO præparata sint. Et ratio disparitatis hic datur, quia hoc proprium DEI opus est, benefa- cere, ad quod natura sua propendet summe bonus. Alienum vero & extraneum quasi est punire, ad quod non nisi invitus quodammodo & hominum im- probitate adigitur. Porro quum illis, qui aptati ad interitum sunt, iram ostendat DEUS, id est, puni- at eosdem, non utiq; ipse eos ad interitum aptavit, opus enim suum odio non habet, nec ira aut pœna prosequitur, qua est opus suum. Ideo di- cuntur ipsi sibi thesaurizare iram, Rom. 2, 5. quod est se aptare ad interitum, quos proinde quærit Dominus Ezech. 33, 11. Cur velint mori? Nam quamvis homo ex intentione sua se non præparet ad pœnam, imo peccans ad obsequendum affectui unice optet, ut impune semper peccare possit, tamē quia peccando ea committit, propter quæ interi- tum sibi accersit, coagmentare se ad interitum re- cte dicitur. Etsi ergo perdere actus sit DEI judi- cis, comparare tamen se ad perditionem est hominis peccantis. (5.) Ita ergo se res habet, DEUS fecit hominem vas aptatum recipiendæ gratiæ & benedi- ctioni, imo gratia implevit in primæva creatione, homo autem seipsum facit vas peccati & iræ, & quamvis reparatus per Christum sit, ut possit fieri vas misericordiæ, tamen Evangelium rejiciendo & in peccatis perseverando sub ira manet, aut gratia potius de novo iram sibi concitat per peccatum. Evadit ergo propria culpa vas iræ coagmentatum ad interitum, in quo DEUS jure meritissimo iram ostendere posset actutum id puniendo; nam often- ten- dere iram est punire exemplariter, siquidem ita pro- prie ostendatur, dum poenæ infliguntur, ut discant homines, ad iram Domini contremiscere, & tum notificatur potentia DEI, iræ executrix, cum judi- cio exemplari quis punitur: quod in Pharaone tan- dem factum est. (6.) Non per absolutum decretum quoddam vult DEUS ostendere iram suam, & potentiam iræ executricem notam facere in va- sa iræ apta ad interitum; sed hac lege atque condi- tione, si scil. talia manserint, nam ideo exserte ad- ditur, quod ea ferat multa longanimitate atque ita e- mendationem expectet; ubi enim emendatio ex- pectatur, ibi non est decretum peremtorium præcise perdendi, sed tantum conditionatum, tum nempe, si non sequatur emendatio; ex adverso, ubi proposi- tum est ἀποτόμως perdendi, ibi nec longanimitas, nec expectatio emendationis locum habet. (7.) Summa itaque similitudinis adductæ hæc est: figulus habet potestatem faciendi vas ad dedecus & de- cus ex eadem massa; quidni ergo DEUS potestatem habeat, vasa iræ, quæ sese ad interitum propria culpa compararunt, iræq́; DEI dignissuma sunt, exemplariter tandem puniendi, postquam illa magna longanimitate sustinuit, & resipiscentiam earum expectavit. (8.) Hoc ergo est, quod exemplo Pharaonis & simili figu- li docuit Apostolus, DEUM jure conqueri de indura- tis posse, non vice versa ipsos de DEO, quia DEUS tum indurando judicialiter, tum puniendo exemplar- ter non versatur nisi circa illos, qui jam ante sunt filii iræ, & sibi thesaurizarunt iram ad diem justi judicii séq́; ad perditionem aptarunt, adeoque semetipsos indu- rarunt: sed versatur circa eos etiam, quando vindi- care vult eorum duritiem & contumaciam, magna longanimitate adhuc eosdem tolerando. Ideoq; re- spondet Apostolus ad propositam objectionem: DEUM indurare non per potentem duritiei infusio- nem, sed per lenitatem & indulgentiam tolerando ho- mines contumaces in multa patientia: quemadmo- dum exemplo Pharaonis constitit. Qui autem ita induratur, potest respectu ejus, a quo indurari dici- tur, non indurari, & jam induratus suapte culpa, dum patienter toleratur, & ad resipiscentiam expectatur, resipiscere; alioqui enim non posset dici cum multa longanimitate tolerari. Non enim ex usu loquendi tolerantia vocatur, ubi non datur ullum evadendi medium: potest ergo duplici nomine DEUS de in- duratis conqueri, eosque increpare; & quod indu- rati sint, & quod tales maneant. Imo si maxime in- duraret DEUS eosdem, etiam modo irresistibili, ju- ste illos reprehendi, Deum autem neutiquam argui posse jure, in aprico est: Siquidem induret eos tantum, qui seipsos jam obdurarunt & obstinate sibi iram thesaurizant, adeoq; DEUM pervicaci malitia ad indurationem sui adigunt. Ita nihil prorsus hic relinquitur præsidii absoluti decreti Patronis.

## 9:18
ver. 18. VERY GREAT HAIL, SUCH AS HAS NOT BEEN IN EGYPT FROM THE DAY IT WAS FOUNDED.

In the Hebrew it is added: from the time it became a nation: which explains the preceding words, that the discourse is concerning that foundation and time from which it began to be inhabited: some understand this term as the time from which it was called Egypt. But this is absurd, since Moses writes in Hebrew, and the Hebrew name clung to this kingdom from Mizraim the son of Ham. Now Egypt began to be inhabited soon after the dispersion of the nations, and therefore it had already been inhabited for 617 years up to this plague. It is evident, however, from this that Egypt was not devoid of rain or hail, and therefore it must be understood κατά τι, and in a comparative sense, when in Deut. 11 Egypt is distinguished from the land of Canaan, because by the Nile led from thence be irrigated by canals; for unless rains or hail had fallen in that kingdom, a comparison could not be established in this place between the hail which fell before, and that which was sent by this plague.

Latin:

vers. 18. GRANDINEM MULTAM NIMIS, QUALIS NON FUIT IN ÆGYPTO A DIE QUA FUNDATA EST.

In Ebr. additur: ex quo fuit in gentem: quæ explicant præcedentia, quod de illa fundatione ac tempore sermo sit, ex quo habitari cœpit: non- nulli intelligunt istum terminum, ex quo vocata est Ægyptus. Sed hoc ineptum est, cum Ebraice scri- bat Moses, & a Mezrai filio Cham nomen Ebraicum huic regno hæserit. Cœpit autem Ægyptus ha- bitari mox a dispersione gentium, ideoque ad hanc usque plagam per 617. annos jam incolebatur. Pa- tet autem hinc Ægyptum non caruisse pluviis aut grandine, ideoque κατά τι, & sensu compa- rato intelligendum esse, cum Deut. 11. a terra Ca- naan distinguitur Ægyptus, quod Nilo ductis inde canalibus irrigata sit; nisi enim pluviae aut grandi- nes cecidissent in illo regno, comparatio hoc in lo- co institui non posset inter grandinem, quae antea cecidit, & quae hac plaga immissa est.

## 9:24
ver. 24. AND HAIL AND FIRE MINGLED TOGETHER WERE CARRIED.

In the Hebrew it was fire withdrawing itself, or received into the hail. In this, therefore, was the prodigy, that fire was mingled together with the hail and rain, ver. 34, and Wisd. 16:22, so that the earth and the other elements together raged against the Egyptians: the air through thunders and tempest and violent storms, water through hail, fire through lightnings, to which Artabanus reports that earthquakes were also joined; by which horrible plague both men and beasts perished in the fields, on the road, and in the river, and every herb of the field was struck, and every tree of the region was broken, so that even against their will the Egyptians recognized from this that they were θεομαχεῖν, fighting against nature and the Lord of the elements: which Pharaoh himself was therefore forced to confess: I have sinned even now, I and my people are wicked, pray to the Lord, that the thunders of GOD and the hail may cease: that I may let you go, and you shall by no means remain here any longer. In the Hebrew. and you shall not add to standing, that is, you shall no longer be detained, so that you cannot go a three days' journey into the desert to sacrifice to your GOD.

Latin:

vers. 24. ET GRANDO ET IGNIS MISTA PARITER FEREBANTUR.

In Ebr. erat ignis recipiens se, vel receptus in grandine. In eo ergo prodigium erat, quod simul cum grandine & pluvia ignis permifceretur vers. 34. & Sap. 16, 22. ut terra & simul elementa caetera in Ae- gyptios saevirent, aër per tonitrua & tempestatem ac procellas vehementes, aqua per grandinem, ignis per fulgura, quibus conjunctos etiam fuisse terrae motus Artabanus refert; qua horribili plaga tum homines & jumenta in agris, in itinere, & in flumi- ne periere, tum omnis herba agri percussa fuit, tum omne lignum regionis confractum, ut vel inviti a- gnoscerent inde Aegyptii, se θεομαχεῖν, naturae, & elementorum Domino reluctari: quod proinde coactus fuit ipse Pharao confiteri: peccavi etiam nunc ego & populus meus impii, orate Dominum, ut desinant tonitrua DEI & grando: ut dimittam vos, & nequa- quam hic ultra maneatis. In Ebr. & non addetis ad standum, id est, non amplius detinebimini, quo minus ad sacrificandum DEO Vestro iter tridui in desertum abire possitis.

## 9:29
ver. 29. WHEN I SHALL HAVE GONE OUT OF THE CITY.

Why did he wish to go out of the city to pray to the Lord? This was done, partly because the city was full of idols, which reason the Hebrews give, that by this method he wished to indicate that the worship of GOD must be separated from profane religion: partly because he sought a retreat to deal more familiarly with GOD, which was also done by Christ at times in prayers, and partly to teach also, since no one dared to go out during that horrible tempest, that he would be safe from it in the field under the protection of the GOD of Israel.

Ver. same. I WILL EXTEND MY PALMS TO THE LORD) A custom of those praying among almost all nations. Lucretius:

Nor to lie prostrate on the ground and spread out palms, Before the shrines of the Gods. Seneca in Oedipus: I testify that I may now lift to heaven my pure hands, fearing no crimes. Compare 1 Tim. 2:8. Tertullian in his Apology: Christians looking up thither with hands expanded. And against the Jews, He prayed with hands expanded. The same said, To open hands in the book on Baptism.

That is, I will pray: for prayers are signified metonymically by the extension of palms, because they are made with extended palms, Isa. 1:15, Ps. 141:2, 1 Tim. 2:11, whence Moses, praying for the people, lifted up his hands, Exod. 17:11. Now the causes of the elevation of hands in prayers can be given as these: (1.) That we may understand that the mind must be lifted up and directed toward God equally with the hands; for which end hands are also clasped, so that we may have the mind closed to all other things and intent solely on GOD, therefore Jeremiah exhorts in Lam. 3:41 that we lift up our hearts together with our hands to GOD. (2.) Because this gesture is that of a suppliant, of one asking and expecting aid, or alms, since the hand is the instrument by which we accept gifts. (3.) Because by the extension of the hand we offer ourselves to God and as it were surrender ourselves into His hand, as Tertullian explains in Apolog. c. 30, the very posture of the praying Christian is prepared for every punishment, i.e., praying, I am ready, strike if you wish, or at least have mercy; therefore prayers are also made with joined hands: which is the rite of those who humble themselves, as if with bound hands they present themselves as captives before the divine majesty. (4.) The ancients add also this reason, that by this gesture we as it were protest the merits of Christ crucified, and offer them to GOD the Father, for the hearing of our prayers. This reason does not please Rivetus, because he believes that rite to be older and used by those who never thought of the crucifixion of Christ. But it suffices that it took its origin from the Saints, to whom there is no doubt that the Spirit of the Lord, who was in the Patriarchs and Prophets, manifested the crucifixion of the Lord, 1 Pet. 1:11. And although this rite was also used among the Gentiles, as Homer testifies in Iliad 7, etc., yet we do not think it should be called natural with Rivetus, but we judge that it passed from the ancient Saints to the Gentiles, like many other things. The Fathers certainly refer this rite with great consensus to the crucifixion of Christ, not only Maximus of Turin, Homily 11 on the cross of the Lord: Therefore we are commanded to pray with hands lifted up, that by the very gesture of our limbs we may confess the passion of the Lord; but also St. Cyprian on the exhortation of Martyrs, Theodoret q. 35 in Exod., Gregory of Nyssa on the life of Moses, Jerome on Mark c. 11, Minutius Felix in Octavius, etc.

Latin:

vers. 29. CUM EGRESSUS FUERO DE UR- BE.

Cur egredi de urbe voluit oraturus Dominum? Factum id, tum quod plena urbs esset idolis, quam causam Ebraei reddunt, quod hac ratione indicatum voluerit, separandum esse cultum DEI a profana religione: tum quod secessum quaesiverit familiarius cum DEO agendi, quod etiam a Christo quandoque in precibus factum, tum ut doceret quoque, cum nemo auderet egredi durante horrenda ista tempe- state, se sub custodia DEI Israelis in agro tutum ab eadem fore.

Vers. eod. EXTENDAM PALMAS MEAS AD DO- MINVM) Mos orantium apud omnes fere gentes. Lucre- tius:

Nec procumbere humi prostratum & pandere palmas, Ante Deûm delubra. Seneca Oedipode: Testor licet jam tollere ad caelum pie Puras nec ulla scelera metuentes manus. Confer 1. Tim. 2, 8. Tertullianus Apologetico: Illuc suspicien- tes Christiani manibus expansis. Et adversus Judaeos, Expansis manibus orabat. Idem dixit, Manus aperire libro de Baptismo.

Id est, orabo: significantur enim per extensio- nem palmarum metonymice preces, quod fiant ex- tensis palmis Es. 1, 15. Ps. 141, 2. 1. Tim. 2, 11. unde Mo- ses pro populo orans manus elevavit, Exod. 17, 11. Causae autem elevationis manuum in precibus hae dari possunt: (1.) ut mentem pariter cum manibus ele- vandam, & intendendam in Deum esse, intelliga- mus; quo fine etiam manus complicantur, ut men- tem ad quaevis alia occlusam unice DEO intentam habeamus, ideo hortatur Jeremias Thren. 3, 41. ut cum manibus simul corda ad DEUM levemus. (2.) Quod gestus iste supplicis sit, petentis & expectantus opem, aut stipem, siquidem manus instrumentum sit, quo dona acceptamus. (3.) Quod extensione manus Deo nos offeramus & in mano quasi dedamus, ut Tertul. explicat in Apolog. c. 30. paratus est ad omne supplicium ipse habitus orantis Christiani q. d. o- rans, praesto sum, plecte si vis, aut certe miserere, ideo manibus etiam junctis preces fiunt: qui ritus eorum est, qui se humiliant, quasi ligatis manibus sistunt se captivos coram majestate divina. (4.) Ad- dunt veteres & hanc rationem, quod hoc gestu protestemur quasi merita Christi crucifixi, eaque DEO patri offeramus, ob precum nostrarum exau- ditionem. Non placet haec ratio Riveto, quod cre- dat ritum illum antiquiorem & usurpatum ab iis, qui de crucifixione Christi nunquam cogitarunt. Sed sufficit, quod a Sanctis originem traxerit, quibus crucifixionem Domini, Spiritum ipsius, qui in Pa- triarchis & Prophetis fuit, manifestasse dubium non est 1. Pet. 1, 11. Et quanquam penes Ethnicos etiam hic ritus usitatus fuerit, teste Homero Iliad. 7. &c. non tamen cum Riveto naturalem illum dicendum putamus, sed a Sanctis antiquis, ut multa alia, ad gentiles transiisse censemus. Referunt utique Pa- tres magno consensu ritum istum ad crucifixionem Christi, non tantum Maximus Taurinensis Homil. 11. de cruce Domini: Ideo manibus elevatis orare praeci- pimur, ut ipso quoque membrorum gestu passionem Domini fateamur; sed & S. Cyprianus de exhorta- tione Martyrum, Theodoretus qv. 35. in Exod. Greg. Nyff. de vita Mosis, Hieron. in Marc. 11. c. Minutius Felix in Octavio &c.

## 9:30
ver. 30. BUT I KNOW THAT BOTH YOU AND YOUR SERVANTS DO NOT YET FEAR THE LORD.

The Hebrew טרם denotes before, whence the Hebrews torment themselves concerning the sense, what these words mean: because before you fear the Lord. Interpreters rightly observe that this word with the future sometimes has the meaning which the Vulgate, Tremellius, and Junius have placed here: not yet, as if to say, that you are not yet, after so many plagues, truly humbled, and do not fear God, and that that repentance is only hypocritical, not true or solid, which Moses could partly gather from external signs, and partly and primarily had from divine revelation.

Latin:

vers. 30. NOVI AUTEM QUOD ET TU ET SERVI TUI NECDUM TIMEATIS DOMI- NUM.

Ebraeum טרם notat antequam, unde se Ebrai macerant circa sensum, quid haec sibi velint: quia antequam timeatis Dominum. Recte autem obser- vant Interpretes, vocem hanc cum futuro habere quan- doque significationem, quam hic posuit Vulg. Trem. & Jun. necdum, q. d. quod necdum, post tot plagas vere humiliatus sis, Deumque timeas, quodq; poe- nitentia illa tantum hypocritica sit, non vera aut so- lida, quod partim e signis externis colligere poterat Moses, partim & imprimis habebat ex revelatione divina.

## 9:32
ver. 32. THE WHEAT AND THE SPELT WERE NOT DAMAGED, BECAUSE THEY WERE LATE.

In the Hebrew, because they were dark, they were still hidden in the grass, they had not yet come forth, which indeed were later destroyed by the following plague; as is taught in chapter 10, verse 5. For between the wheat harvest and the barley harvest there was only the interval of the harvest. In comparison to the barley and the flax, which ascend into the stalk, they seemed as if they were hidden. See Drusius, as also Fuller, book III, Miscellanies, chapter 2.

Latin:

vers. 32. TRITICUM ET FAR NON SUNT LAESA, QUIA SEROTINAE ERANT.

In Ebr. quia erant tenebrosa, latebant adhuc in gramine, nondum prodierant, quae vero postmo- dum a plaga sequente perdita sunt; ut c. 10, 5. doce- tur. Nam inter messem triticeam & hordeaceam intervallum tantum messis erat. In comparatione ad hordeum & linum, quae in culmum ascendunt, quasi latere videbantur. Vid. Drusius, ut & Fullerus l. III. Miscellan. c. 2.

## 9:35
ver. 35. AND HIS HEART WAS HARDENED.) The Greeks, καὶ ἐβαρύνε Φαραὼ τὴν καρδίαν ἀυτᾶ.

In the Hebrew text itself, Pharaoh is accused, and the cause of the hardening is attributed to him: Pharaoh hardened his heart, because, namely, after so many signs were produced and so many plagues were sent, he could not be softened or repent, so that he rather hardened his heart all the more against GOD.

Latin:

vers. 35. ET INGRAVATUM EST COR EJVS.) Grae- ci, καὶ ἐβαρύνε Φαραὼ τὴν καρδίαν ἀυτᾶ.

In textu ipso Ebraeo accusatur Pharao, eiq; cau- sa tribuitur indurationis: aggravavit Pharao cor su- um, quod nempe tot signis editis, tot plagis immis- sis adeo emolliri non potuerit, aut resipiscere, ut magis potius cor suum adversus DEUM obdurarit.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

The plague of locusts. The Egyptian darkness.

ver. 1. FOR I HAVE HARDENED HIS HEART AND THE HEART OF HIS SERVANTS, THAT I MAY PERFORM THESE MY SIGNS IN HIM.

Rivetus gathers from these words that the signs were not produced so that the heart of Pharaoh might be hardened, but rather that it was hardened so that an occasion might be given for multiplying the signs. But Rivetus is mistaken in this, that he takes the words in an etiological sense, which are to be understood in an ecbatic sense; they are to be explained concerning the event, not indeed concerning the end; that is, that GOD did not intend that end by hardening the heart of Pharaoh, that He might perform still more signs, but that more signs were to be in the future, after the heart of Pharaoh had been hardened by the former ones. But as to what Rivetus says, that the manifestation of the glory of GOD is indeed the true final cause, this we admit in so far as it is understood of miracles and other works of GOD, but not with respect to sins or the hardening of Pharaoh; because even if GOD may elicit good even from evils, and order them for his immense power and goodness toward good, he does not however intend those evils to that end, that good may be elicited, or that the glory of GOD may be revealed, since there is no end of evil, but only of good, nor can GOD intend evil in any way, whether as some end, or as a means directed to an end. Rivetus again appeals to the words of the Apostle Rom. 9, 23. to show the riches of his mercy, which indicate the final cause. Resp. that that final cause of divine tolerance is indicated (as some wish) can be admitted, but not of the Pharaonic hardening, which is an effect by accident or rather an accidental event only of divine tolerance: nay, by those it is only taught that GOD has power, and of showing wrath after the μακροθυμία exhibited, in the vessels of wrath tolerated, and of showing the riches of mercy in the vessels of grace. Riv. still urges that we cannot say that GOD permits sins without any end, for this does not befit GOD. We answer: there is no end of evil, but we do not deny the end of divine permission concerning evil. Furthermore, when God permits evil for the sake of illustrating his glory, he has not however decreed or intended the evil, but what he foresaw would happen, he willed to permit, and to order to the glory of his name. For it is not to be thought that GOD catches at the material of punishment, namely guilt, but once guilt is posited, he orders it to the deserved punishment and his own glory. For to catch at the material of punishing is foreign both to the goodness of GOD and to the order of justice, which requires that punishment not be inflicted unless guilt is prior, and that punishment be on account of guilt, not guilt on account of punishment, and also to divine truth, because with so many plagues GOD urged Pharaoh to repentance, which signified that GOD seriously and from the heart desired his repentance and salvation. That, however, is very blasphemous, in Rivetus's judgment, to say that God desires something that does not happen, nay, which he predicted would not happen, and the contrary of which he declared he would do for his glory. Thus, therefore, it would be blasphemous to say that God seriously willed that the vineyard should bear grapes, which bore wild grapes Is. 5, 2. To will and desire that the impious one be converted, who is not converted Ezech. 18, 32. c. 33, 11. that they come to the knowledge of the truth, who do not come 1. Tim. 2, 4. it will be blasphemous that Christ willed that the hearers be saved, who were not saved, Joh. 5, 34. that the Jews be gathered, who were not gathered Matth. 23, 37. etc. Thus is surely taken away every preaching of the Gospel, every announcement of repentance, all promises are overturned, all exhortations are nothing, with respect to the reprobate, because for GOD to will that the reprobate obey, be converted, be saved, according to the Calvinists is blasphemous, and since GOD testifies to this so often in his word, nay, affirms it with an oath, even with respect to the wicked Ezech. 18, 33. he will only testify hypocritically and falsely, which is truly blasphemous. And to what end does GOD urge in the Gospel that they believe, whom he foresaw would never believe, nor does he will to believe! The Calvinists do not find here in the grove and temple of their dogma what to answer. Guilh. Pempe of Oxford in Vindic. of grace, says that GOD urges to that end, that the duty of the reprobate themselves may be declared, and what obedience is pleasing to GOD. But to urge is to declare duty, therefore he declares duty to that end, that he may declare duty, which Samuel Rutherford opposes to Pempe in the same (Calvin's) School Exerc. Apolog. for divine grace Exerc. 2. c. 2. p. 317. Others say that the reprobate are not properly and of themselves warned, but by concomitance, insofar as they are mixed with the elect by their external society. And therefore just as the nature of seeds does not intend the irrigation of rocks, so GOD, that the elect may obey and be saved, urged all in the Church, not for the sake of the reprobate: that these say something, but do not attain the whole truth, says Rutherford, because not by chance, but for a certain end GOD takes care that seed be scattered into stony hearts: the question therefore still remains, to what end does GOD urge the reprobate mixed with the elect? Here Rutherford thinks one must exclaim with pious ignorance, O the depth! Rom. 11. But this is not pious ignorance, but an impious dissimulation of the cause expressed by the Holy Spirit, or a reprobation, and a distortion of the Holy Spirit's exclamation; for the Apostle exclaims not about the end of the universal preaching of the Gospel, but about certain singular judgments of GOD, nay, not even about divine judgments only, but also about the depth of the riches, that is, the mercy of GOD; for by the word πλέτο Rom. 11, 33. the riches of mercy are indicated, as is clear partly from the συνεχεία of the preceding verse, partly from a comparison of the passage Eph. 2, 7. Nor does the Apostle marvel less at the depth of the mercy of GOD, of which he had treated at length, and which he still inculcates in the following verses, that no one deserves anything before GOD, all things are free gifts of divine mercy, than at the wisdom and knowledge of GOD or divine judgments. And Paul had openly expressed the end of the Evangelical proclamation, that namely the sound of the Apostles went out into all the world to that end, that all might be converted to Christ; because the end of the proclamation according to him is the faith of those to whom the word is preached, chap. 10, 17. 18. And for that reason also all are concluded under sin by the voice of the law, that according to the word of the Gospel God might have mercy on all Rom. 11, 32. the whole Scripture is in this, that sinners and the impious may be stirred up to repentance, and be converted to the Lord, this is the end of legal sermons, the same is the end of Evangelical sermons, this God intends by the preaching of repentance, and by the announcement of the remission of sins, this is the cause of Prophetic and Apostolic exhortations, and of the whole Scripture. S. for these things are written, that you may believe John 20, 21. This was the scope of Christ's sermons, I say these things to you that you may be saved, he says to the Jews themselves, even those who were not saved John 5, 34. Therefore God calls sinners that they may come, that they may enjoy his grace, he invites them to repent, he exhorts them not to harden their hearts, and he wills that all come to the knowledge of the truth, and be saved 2 Pet. 3, 9. 1 Tim. 2, 4. That end is not hidden, but is always inculcated throughout the whole Scripture: whence one must marvel at the stupidity and blindness of the Calvinists concerning that end, namely that GOD intends the obedience of the reprobate, so that not a syllable or iota is to be held in Scripture, which are the words of Rutherford page 318. And what then at last will be the end of the proclamation, when GOD exhorts the reprobate to repent or obey, if he does not seriously will that they obey or repent. Rutherford responds from the mind of the Calvinists, that GOD exhorts them to that end, namely, that they may be inexcusable, that Christ is set, that he may be a sign of contradiction, that he may be for a testimony to them, that they themselves may be hardened, that the glory of his power may be declared in the vessels of wrath. But these ends are only accidental with respect to the divine intention, and pertain rather to the ἐκβάσεις. But the proper and direct end is repentance, conversion and salvation, that they may not stop their ears or hearts, and that they may obey, and be converted, see from the innumerable passages Ps. 95, 8. Prov. 1, 23. 24. ch. 9, 4. Isa. 55, 1. seqq, ch. 65, 1. Ezek. 18, 32. ch. 33, 11. Matt. 11, 32. ch. 23, 37.

37. Luke 7:30. 1 Tim. 2:4. 2 Pet. 3:4. For there is no other word which is preached to the impious, nor other seed which is scattered into stony hearts, nor a different end of preaching or of the scattering of the seed, but one and the same end, namely that all may bear fruit, Luke 8. Indeed, since the reprobate are condemned for the reason that they do not believe, it is necessary that GOD intends and seriously wills that they themselves believe, and by no means wills that they do not believe.

For either that which the reprobate ought to believe is true, and for the non-belief of which they are condemned, that is, that GOD wills to forgive their sins, that Christ has acquired salvation for them; or it is not true, even though they ought to believe it, and are condemned for the non-belief of it. If that is true, then certainly GOD seriously wills to forgive their sins, and Christ truly acquired salvation for them: for He testifies so many times that He wills them to believe this, and therefore they are condemned because they do not believe.
