John 3:17. If that is not true; then GOD wills them to believe that which is not true, and condemns them because they do not believe that which is not true. Which impious paradox, utterly overturning divine truth, since it necessarily flows from the doctrine of Calvin, John Piscator undertook to defend in his collation with Vorstius, p. 31, and John Maccovius in Colleg. 6, dispp. misc. Disp. 4, who consequently contend that the object of faith is a falsehood, or the false. Rutherford indeed rejects and refutes this with several arguments, l. c. p. 223, because neither Theology nor truth allows it, since faith rests upon divine truth, under which nothing false can lie, and it would have to be believed, according to Piscator and Maccovius, that GOD speaks that which can be false, and that God wills us to believe falsehoods, which is absurd. But he cannot escape this paradox. For how can that which men are bound to believe be true, if the reprobate are bound to believe in Christ, that is, that Christ died for them, which the Reformed deny to be true. Whence Rutherford struggles greatly with our argument; that everyone is bound to believe what is true: but everyone is bound to believe that Christ died for him; therefore, that Christ died for everyone is true. He brings forward the response of Cameron from Tom. 2, praelect. in Matt. 16, ch. v. 27, p. 204, who distinguishes the major premise: That which everyone is bound to believe is true, either as things that are narrated are true, or as things that are predicted are true, or as they are promised; in the first and second way it is not true, because things narrated and predicted are true, whether you believe it or not: but as for things that are true as promises, there is no necessity for them to be so unless you have believed, indeed it is necessary that they not be so if you have not believed. Rutherford, however, rejects that response because it is falsely supposed that Christ died for all conditionally, whether they be elect or reprobate, but for the elect absolutely, which opinion of Cameron seems to Rutherford to be akin to heresy, p. 222. He also rejects the response of Piscator and Maccovius, which we mentioned. But he himself responds in three ways: (1.) he distinguishes believing: that it is taken in three ways, 1. for assenting to every word of GOD, and thus the revealed word of GOD is the object of faith, and therefore if the argument is formed thus: That is true to which everyone is bound to assent as to the revealed word of GOD: he says the major is true, but the minor is false, because the word of GOD is not that Christ died for me by name, with that intention and decree that He might save me. But if this is not the word of GOD, the elect will certainly believe it without the word of GOD: but what kind of faith is that without the word of GOD? He says:

the word of GOD reveals the complacency and approval of GOD, but not properly the intention and decree of God concerning this or that man being saved, unless we except certain Patriarchs, Apostles, etc. But there is not only a need that we believe that God approves and has complacency in him, if anyone believes, but it is necessary for saving faith that everyone believe that GOD wills to be propitious to him, that Christ died for him: even if individuals are not expressed in the Holy Scriptures, universal propositions are nevertheless held and must be held, under which any individual can subsume, since our assent ought to rest upon the word of GOD, and trust and application require a promise applicable to anyone. 2. He says that believing is to rest with a fiduciary act of the heart in Christ as a sufficient Savior: and thus the major, that everyone is bound to believe what is true, is false. But this is the very Maccovian and Piscatorian paradox, which while Rutherford tries to escape, he falls into it imprudently, only adorned with a new color, namely: for it is neither true nor false, but a good and salutary gift of GOD, which the heart and affections apprehend, and in no way an object of the mind: thus the sophist invents a middle between true and false, and confuses the object of faith with the act of faith; for the act of faith is a gift and work of GOD, John 6:29, but its object is the word of the Gospel, which certainly must be true. Furthermore, he sophistically opposes the heart to the mind: for that which is proposed in the Gospel, Christ with His merit, is the object of both the mind and the heart, who ought to be acknowledged by the mind and apprehended by the heart as our Redeemer and Savior, and therefore when this word concerning Christ is proposed to the mind, it is necessary that it be true, nor can any middle be assigned between true and false: indeed, I cannot be moved in my heart toward Christ as my Savior unless I understand with my mind and know from the word of GOD that Christ is my Savior. He assigns the third meaning of the word 'to believe' thus: to believe, he says, is to apprehend by sense and by consequence, and thus that everyone is bound to believe, that is, to gather from the sense of faith and from the fiducial act of faith as from a cause, that is, it is true: let the major premise now hold, I assume: but everyone is bound to believe, namely not by a formal fiducial act of faith or assent of the mind, but by the sense of faith and an evident gathering from a cause to conclude, that Christ by his own and God the Father's intention and counsel died for him: the minor premise is now openly false. For only believers are bound by such a sense to gather the intention of God and the eternal decree concerning themselves by name, for the rest are not bound to believe this, that is, to gather it; indeed, they would thus be obliged to nourish a vain and evanescent presumption and a shadowy and chimerical conjecture: therefore the major premise proceeds concerning the act of faith, both of the mind in assenting and of the fiducial embrace of the heart, which is properly faith: but the minor premise concerns the sense of faith and a certain practical gathering, which is improperly faith. There are therefore four terms in the syllogism. Thus far Rutherford, who truly does not speak strong things. We answer (1.) that to believe entails a formal fiducial act of faith with the assent of the mind, he would be a dullard who denies it: but to gather from the sense of faith and from the fiducial act of faith as from a cause, this is not to believe, but is a consequence of faith, or a reflex act of the believer, who knows or gathers that he believes, while he has the sense of faith. But here the matter is not concerning a reflex act, but a direct act, not concerning the sense of faith, but concerning faith itself or the fiducial act, whether that which everyone is bound to believe, and to apprehend by faith, be true? (2.) If saving faith is not gathered from the word of the Gospel, but from the fiducial act of faith, or arises from it, the principle of faith will now no longer be the word of God, but the act of our heart, which is Enthusiastic, nay, faith from faith, and thus it will arise from itself; thus the Calvinists either do not know what they are saying, or they do not derive their faith from the word of God, but from the proper sense of their own heart, which is a truly empty and evanescent presumption, and a shadowy and chimerical conjecture, which they substitute in place of the word of God and true faith. For the word of God is not true to them, but the sense of their own heart is true. (3.) Whence Rutherford himself is forced to acknowledge that this is a certain sense of faith and a practical collection, which he points out, but not truly faith, even if he improperly calls it faith, so that he may make sport. But that improper faith is nothing to the point, or to the argument proposed: for in the minor premise, to believe is taken in exactly the same way, namely for faith properly so called, not improperly spoken: which held thus: Everyone is bound to believe that Christ died for him; for everyone is bound to believe by a proper act of faith, both of the mind in assenting, and by the fiducial embrace of the heart: for we are saved by this faith, when the faithful man believes that Christ died for him, not only by the mind assenting to this Evangelical truth, but also by the heart embracing the merits of Christ, and fiducially applying them to himself: if this is not saving faith, in the Calvinist School, what then is the faith by which they wish to obtain salvation, I for my part do not see, or certainly, they will have no faith by their own principles, which is most true. (4.) It is a new paradox of Rutherford, which I do not know if any other Calvinists will approve, if indeed he does not include application in the essence of faith, but opines that it is the same effect inseparably accompanying faith, not a formal act of the same; in which, however, he is not consistent with himself, if indeed from 1 Tim. 1:15 he notes these three things in faith (1.) assent, by reason of which the Gospel is a faithful saying. (2.) confidence, the acquiescence of the heart, and leaning upon Christ, as upon the object which of confidence, and upon the promises, as the object by which, which is to him the formal reason of faith: and (3.) application, by which he believes that Christ came to save him. And yet leaning upon Christ and the acquiescence of the heart in him and the promises concerning him is the very application of the merits of Christ, which certainly is not a consequent, but the form of faith; for the Apostle did not describe his faith otherwise, whether here in 1. Tim. 1:15, or in Gal. 2:20, than that he believes that Christ is his Savior, that the Son of God loved him, and gave himself for him; and he speaks of saving faith, in which he himself lives, not indeed of faith properly so called. Nor indeed can I with true confidence of heart rest in Christ, unless I am certain that he is my Savior; or (1.) I lean upon Christ the Savior indefinitely without respect to the saved, which is absurd: for thus the relative would be separated from its correlate, or I lean (2.) upon the Savior of other believers, and thus I apply him to others, not to myself: which is likewise absurd: or (3.) as my Savior, and thus particular application is included in the quidditative concept of faith. If I say, (which Rutherford objects) it is sufficient that I by a formal act of faith fiducially rest in Christ, as a sufficient Savior of all believers, and then by a sense of faith believe that he is my Savior, I only deceive myself with a vain persuasion: for whence that sense of faith, that I may certainly believe that he is my Savior? For faith ought to rest upon the word, nor can there be a sense of faith, unless faith itself is present first; now indeed that Christ died, from intention, and eternal decree, so that he might save me, that, as Rutherford says, p. 302, is not an object of faith, neither written, nor is it in the word by consequence. He adds a limitation: unless some internal token in my conscience is added, from which, with the fiducial act of faith preceding, I may collect that. But if the fiducial act precedes, whence does it arise? for I can have no confidence in the grace of God, unless I am certain that God denies his grace to no one: a person guilty of lèse-majesté, says Rutherford himself, believes that the Prince is clement toward all who suppliantly deprecate his wrath, before he trusts that he is clement toward himself. But how can he believe that God is clement toward all unless he has that from the word; that God wishes to have mercy on all: which the antagonist contends is neither written nor in the word of God by consequence. And these things concerning the first response, by which the word believe was distinguished. The other concerns the word true, which Rutherford distinguishes on page 300. That everyone is bound to believe, that is, he says, true, Metaphysically and fundamentally, in itself and as to the event: I concede the major and then I deny the minor; for that Christ died for everyone is not true in itself fundamentally and Metaphysically, but false. But we respond that the argument thus still remains safe; for it is only responded to the conclusion sophistically: and it is pretended that the minor is denied, which held thus: everyone is bound to believe that Christ died for him; in which the word TRUE certainly does not occur. But the disputation is inept, when the conclusion is denied while both the major and minor are conceded. Rutherford adds; that everyone is bound to believe, that is true, not only Metaphysically but also morally and Theologically, as being revealed to the believer through the word of God, or through some evident token in the conscience, and thus the major is true and the minor still false; for that Christ died for everyone is not true Theologically, nor revealed to everyone, but only to the elect and indeed to the believer, that is, to one resting by a fiducial act upon Christ the Savior. We respond: again that the response is to the direct conclusion. Furthermore, those distinctions are mere τερατολογίαι: for the major premise is simply true, unless one wishes to depart into the opinion of Maccovius, from which Rhetorfortis recoils: That which everyone is bound to believe is true, from whatever principle that truth may finally depend. It ought, however, to depend upon divine revelation, or the word of God, because we acknowledge no other principle of truth in Theology besides the word of God. Furthermore, if this is not true Theologically, that Christ died for everyone; therefore it will be false Theologically; or if it is still maintained as true, how then? Is it Philosophically, or by what reason at last will it be said to be true? If it is not true Theologically; therefore it is not to be believed either; for nothing is to be believed in Theology, unless it be Theologically true. And this was his other response.

Thirdly, he responds by limiting the word EVERYONE: that indeed everyone burdened with the weight of sins is bound to believe, that is true: as if what others not burdened are bound to believe, is not true, seeing that when they are bound to believe that hell exists, that the final judgment will come, that is not true? It is true, and remains true, in itself, however he may be, to whom that is proposed to be believed. Furthermore, it is false that not all, but only those burdened with the weight of sins are bound to believe that Christ died for them; for in the Evangelical commands all are ordered to believe. Rhetorfortis replies that it is commanded to the others that they believe, but yet in a certain order. We respond: it is sufficient that faith is commanded to them: and what kind of faith, pray, will that be, which God demands from the reprobate, on account of the lack of which they are guilty of eternal condemnation? Rhetorfortis says he demands from them that they may assent to every word of God, and to the promises, and that they may rest with a fiducial act in Christ, the sufficient author of salvation, but in no way are they bound to believe that Christ died for them. But he thus contradicts himself and the truth openly: himself indeed; because just before on page 300 he had said that it was not revealed to everyone that Christ died for him, but only to the elect, and indeed to the believer; that is, as he himself explains, to one resting with a fiducial act in Christ the Savior: here, however, he confesses that it is required not only of the elect, but also of the reprobate, that they rest with a fiducial act in Christ the Savior. But he contradicts the truth, because he who is bound to rest with a fiducial act in Christ is bound to apply the merit of Christ to himself, and therefore to believe that Christ died for him, that Christ is his own Savior: for this application is the fiducial act proper and formal to saving faith. Finally, no one can confess himself to be liable to blame for a rejected promise made by word, if the mind of the speaker determines not to fulfill the promise to him, or rather, if he has determined by a certain decree, he who promises by word, that the promise should not pertain or could not pertain to him. And these things are for the sake of defending the famous anti-Calvinian syllogism, in which they remain constrained on all sides.

We shall now collect some flowers and emblems of this utterly hardened Calvinian ματαιολογίας (vain-talk), proposed in the words of Rutherford himself, such as (1.) that God intends the obedience of all who are called is not a saying of Jehovah. (2.) It is false that all in the visible Church are bound by Evangelical exhortations to believe that God intends their obedience; to which pertains (3.) that dictum: it is false that Christ intended by that saying: 'whoever will confess me before men, him I also will confess before the Father,' that Peter should obey and confess Christ: (4.) The intention of God is not revealed properly and infallibly, but is gathered from the command, as to what the intention of God was, which he says is the observation of Wilb. Twisse in his Vindications of grace against the Arminians, and approves it by his own calculation on page 223. (5.) Evangelical commands and promises do not express to the reprobate the intention of God that the reprobate should obey, but only reveal to them that holy concatenation, both between faith and their obligation to believe, and between faith and eternal life. (6.) That God, when he says: 'reprobate, believe and you shall be saved,' puts forward that it is his intention and decree that the reprobate should believe and be saved, puts forward a notable lie. (7.) Although God did not set Christ as the Savior of all, even of the reprobate, yet he rightly demands that they rest with their whole trust in the most sufficient Savior of all who believe, and they are rightly guilty, because they do not wish to surrender themselves to Christ, although Christ never decreed from eternity to embrace them. (8.) That God invites to the banquet very many whom he did not decree should come, and commands them to embrace Christ the Savior who was never destined for them by the eternal counsel of God. (9.) God can by absolute power forgive the sins of all without the satisfaction of Christ, which he asserts with Wilb. Twisse on p. 310. Finally (10.) nothing is falser than this, that no one is liable to blame for a rejected promise if the one promising has determined by a certain decree that the promise should not pertain to him, as Rutherford has on page 44. Which paradoxes all, as they flow from the common dogma of the Reformed concerning the absolute decree, so it is not to be doubted that pious Christians abhor those horrid hypotheses with their whole soul. We return to our passage and the explanation of Rivet; who says, the meaning of this passage is, that hitherto Pharaoh has not dismissed you, it was not done by chance, but by my counsel, nor was the liberation delayed because I did not wish to rescue you, but that I might liberate you more gloriously: for blame is not placed, with God intending something else, in such a way that it was necessary for him first to be frustrated in his primary end, so that from an event which he had not wished, he might take counsel for a new end: which things certainly cannot be thought of without insult to God. This is Rivet: But it is false (1.) that the counsel of God was that Pharaoh should not dismiss the people; the whole history, and so many repeated embassies of God sent to Pharaoh, and finally so many prodigies and portents teach the contrary, for what else did he seek by his embassies or urge by his portents, than that the people should be dismissed? (2.) It is false that the liberation of the people was delayed by God so that he might liberate them more gloriously, because this was done to lead Pharaoh to repentance, but he persisting in contumacy and the hardness of his heart, God directed all that to the glory of his name and a more glorious liberation of the people. (3.) Blame is not placed on Pharaoh by God intending or decreeing it, but by permitting it and directing it to an end glorious to himself. (4.) There is no insult to God, but the very truth of Scripture, that men often disregard the intention and counsel of God and resist it. See Prov. 1:25, Matt. 23:37, Luke 7:30, Acts 7:51, 13:45. And in this Scripture commends the mercy of God, but condemns the contumacy of men. (5.) Nor is it insulting to God that God takes counsel from an event which he did not wish, because he foreknows that event from eternity and thus directs it by his eternal counsel. Did he not, when he had created Adam for life, after he foresaw that he would fall, take up another counsel concerning the salvation of Adam, namely concerning the redemption of Adam through Christ the Savior? Finally, God did not enter into a counsel for a new end, but for other means; for when man did not aspire to salvation through the observance of the commands of God, as he ought to have, and fell from grace and salvation, did not God enter into a gracious counsel concerning his reparation through the seed of the woman? It is necessary that the Calvinists deny the Gospel and the Evangelical covenant if they deny these things. And these things concerning the present passage.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Plaga locustarum. Tenebrae Aegyptiaca.

vers. 1. EGO ENIM INDURAVI COR EJUS ET SERVORUM ILLIUS, UT FACIAM SI- GNA MEA HAEC IN EO.

Rivetus ex his verbis colligit, non ideo fuisse si- gna edita, ut aggravaretur cor Pharaonis, sed potius aggravatum fuisse, ut inde occasio daretur signorum multiplicandorum. Sed fallitur in eo Rivēt, quod verba αἰτιολογικῶς accipiat, quae intel- ligenda sunt ἐκβατικῶς; de eventu, non vero de fine explicanda; hoc est, quod non indurando cor Pharaonis DEUS finem illum intenderit, ut plura adhuc signa faceret, sed quod signa plura futura sint, postquam cor Pharaonis prioribus induratum tantum est. Quod vero dicit Rivetus, manifestatio- nem gloriæ DEI utique veram causam finalem esse, id admittimus, qua de miraculis, aliisque DEI ope- ribus intelligitur, non autem respectu peccatorum aut indurationis Pharaonis; quia etsi DEUS e malis etiam bonum eliciat, eaque pro immensa sua po- tentia & bonitate ad bonum ordinet, non tamen mala illa intendit eo fine, ut bonum eliciatur, aut ut gloria DEI patefiat, siquidem mali finis non sit, sed boni tantum, nec DEUS malum intendere possit ullatenus, sive tanquam finem aliquem, sive tanquam medium ad finem directum. Provocat iterum Rivetus ad verba Apostoli Rom. 9, 23. ut ostenderet divitias misericordiæ suæ, quæ indicent causam fina- lem. Resp. causam finalem illam tolerantiæ divinæ indicari, (ut nonnulli volunt) admitti potest, non autem indurationis Pharaonicæ, quæ effectus est per accidens vel potius eventus solum accidentalis divinæ tolerantiæ: imo illis solum docetur, DEUM potesta- tem habere, & ostendendi iram post μακροθυμίαν ex- hibitam, in toleratis iræ vasis, & ostendendi divitias mi- sericordiæ in vasis gratiæ. Urget adhuc Riv. non posse nos dicere, DEUM peccata permittere sine ullo fine, hoc enim DEO non convenire. Respondemus: mali fi- nis nullus est, sed permissionis divinæ circa malum fi- nem non inficiamur. Porro cum permittit Deus malum illustrandæ gloriæ suæ causa, non decrevit tamen aut intendit malum, sed quod prævidit even- turum, permittere voluit, atque ordinare ad nomi- nis sui gloriam. Neque enim censendum est, DE- UM captare supplicii materiam, culpam nempe, sed posita culpa ordinat eam ad meritam pœnam suiq; gloriam. Captare enim puniendi materiam alie- num est tum a bonitate DEI tum a justitiæ ordine, qui requirit, ut pœna non infligatur, nisi prævia cul- pa, & ut pœna sit propter culpam, non culpa pro- pter pœnam, tum a veritate divina, quia tot plagis Pharaonem hortatus ad pœnitentiam est DEUS, quæ significabant DEUM serio, & ex animo ejus resipiscentiam & salutem cupere. Id vero valde blasphemum, Riveto judice est, dicere, Deum aliquid cupere quod non eveniat, imo quod prædixit non e- venturum, & cujus contrarium ad gloriam suam fa- cere declaravit. Sic ergo blasphemum fuerit dice- re, Deum voluisse serio, ut vinea uvas ferret, quæ labru- scas tulit Es. 5, 2. Velle & cupere, ut convertatur impius, qui non convertitur Ezech. 18, 32. c. 33, 11. ut veniant ad agnitionem veritatis, qui non veniunt 1. Tim. 2, 4. blasphemum erit, Christum voluisse, ut salvarentur auditores, qui non salvati sunt, Joh. 5, 34. ut congregarentur Judæi, qui non congregati sunt Matth. 23, 37. &c. Sic tollitur profecto omnis prædicatio Evangelii, omnis annunciatio pœniten- tiæ, evertuntur omnes promissiones, nullæ sunt ex- hortationes omnes, respectu reproborum, quia DEUM velle, ut reprobi obediant, convertantur, salventur secundum Calvinianos blasphemum est, & cum id toties testetur in verbo suo DEUS, imo jurejurando affirmet, etiam respectu improborum Ezech. 18, 33. hypocritice ac falso tantum testabitur, quod vere blasphemum est. Et quo fine horta- tur DEUS in Evangelio, ut credant, quos nun- quam credituros præscivit, nec credere vult! Non inveniunt hic in luco & fano dogmatis sui Calviniani, quod respondeant. Guilh. Pempe Oxoniensis in Vindic. gratiæ, DEUM eo fine hor- tari dicit, ut reprobis declaretur ipsorum officium, & quæ sit grata DEO obedientia. Sed hortari est officium declarare, ergo declarat officium eo fi- ne, ut declaret officium, quod opponit Pempio Samuel Rhetorfortis in eadem (Calvini) Schola Exerc. Apolog. pro divina gratia Exerc. 2. c. 2. p. 317. Alii dicunt, reprobos non proprie & per se moneri, sed per concomitantiam, quatenus electis externa sua societate permiscentur. Ideoque sicut natura satorum non rupium intendit irrigationem, ita DEUM ut electi obediant & salventur, hortati omnes in Ecclesia, non reproborum causa: hos aliquid dicere, sed veritatem omnem non assequi, ait Rhetorfortis, quia non casu, sed certo fine DEUS semen curat spargendum in corda saxea: manet ergo adhuc quaestio, quo fine DEUS hortetur reprobos electis commixtos? Hic pia ignorantia exclamandum censet Rhetorfortis, o alti- tudo! Rom. 11. At haec non pia est ignorantia, sed impia causae a Spiritu S. expressae dissimulatio, vel reprobatio, & exclamationis Spiritus S. detorsio; nimirum exclamat Apostolus non de fine praedica- tionis Evangelii universalis, sed de singularibus qui- busdam judiciis DEI, imo nec de judiciis modo di- vinis, sed de altitudine etiam divitiarum, id est, mi- sericordiae DEI; nam per vocem πλέτο Rom. 11, 33. misericordiae divitiae indigitantur, ut partim e vers. praecedentis συνεχεία partim e collatione loci Eph. 2, 7. Patet; nec minus miratur Apostolus altitudinem misericordiae DEI, de qua prolixe egerat, quamque in subseqq. adhuc inculcat, quod nemo quicquam penes DEUM mereatur, omnia sint gratuita divi- nae misericordiae munera, quam sapientiae & scientiae DEI aut judiciorum divinorum. Et expresserat a- perte Paulus finem praeconii Evangelici, quod nem- pe exiverit Apostolorum sonus in omnem orbem eo fi- ne, ut omnes ad Christum converterentur; quia fi- nis praeconii juxta ipsum fides est eorum, quibus praedicatur verbum, cap. 10, 17. 18. Atque ea ratio- ne etiam omnes per vocem legis concluduntur sub peccato, ut secundum verbum Evangelii Deus mi- sereatur omnium Rom. 11, 32. tota Scriptura in eo est, ut excitentur peccatores atque impii ad poeni- tentiam, & convertantur ad Dominum, hic finis est concionum legalium, idem finis Evangelicarum concionum, hoc intendit per praedicationem poe- nitentiae Deus, & per annunciationem remissionis peccatorum, haec causa est exhortationum Prophe- ticarum & Apostolicarum, totiusq; Script. S. nam haec scripta sunt, ut credatis Joh. 20, 21. hic scopus e- rat concionum Christi, haec dico vobis ut salvemini, ait ad ipsos Judaeos, etiam illos, qui non salvabantur Joh. 5, 34. Ideo vocat Deus peccatores ut veniant, ut gratia sua fruantur, invitat ut resipiscant, horta- tur, ne corda obturent, omnesque vult ad agnitionem veritatis venire, ac salvari 2. Pet. 3, 9. 1. Tim. 2, 4. Fi- nis ille non absconditus est, sed per universam Scri- pturam semper inculcatur: unde stuporem & caeci- tatem Calvinianorum mirari oportet, de fine illo, quod nempe DEUS intendat reproborum obedientiam, ne Syllabam vel jota haberi in Scriptura, quae Rhetor- fortis verba sunt pag. 318. Et ecquis ergo tandem finis praeconii erit, cum hortatur DEUS reprobos, ut resipiscant aut obediant, si serio non velit ut obe- diant aut resipiscant. Respondet ex mente Cal- vinianorum Rhetorfortis, DEUM ipsos hortari eo sc. fine, ut inexcusabiles sint, poni Christum, ut sit signum contradictionis, ut sit iis in testimonium, ut indurentur ipsi, ut declaretur gloria potentiae in vasis irae. Sed hi fines accidentales tantum sunt respectu inten- tionis divinae, & ad ἐκβάσεις potius perti- nent. Finis autem proprius & directus est resi- piscentia, conversio & salus, ne obturent au- res vel corda, & ut obediant, & conver- tantur, vid. e locis innumeris Psal. 95, 8. Pro- verb. 1, 23. 24. cap. 9, 4. Esa. 55, 1. seqq, cap. 65, 1. Ezech. 18, 32. c. 33, 11. Matth. 11, 32. cap. 23. 37.

37. Luc. 7, 30. 1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 4. Non enim ali- ud verbum est, quod prædicatur impiis, nec aliud semen, quod spargitur in corda saxea, nec diversus finis prædicationis aut sparsonis seminis, sed unus idemque finis, ut nempe omnes fructum ferant, Luc. 8. Imo cum reprobi ob id, quod non credant, da- mnantur, necessum est, DEUM intendere, ac serio velle, ut ipsi credant, neutiquam velle, ut non cre- dant.

Nam aut verum est id, quod credere debent reprobi, & ob quod non creditum ipsi condemnan- tur, hoc est, quod DEUS ipsis velit peccata condona- re, quod Christus ipsis salutem acquisiverit; aut non est verum, etiamsi id credere debeant, & ob id non cre- ditum condemnentur. Si verum illud est, utique DEUS serio vult ipsis peccata condonare, vereque Christus acquisivit ipsis salutem: nam id ut credant ipsi, toties se velle testatur, & ideo condemnantur, quod non credant. Joh. 3, 17. Si id verum non est; ergo DEUS vult eos credere id quod non est verum, & condemnat ideo, quod non credant id, quod ve- rum non est. Quod impium παράδοξον divinam veritatem prorsus evertens cum necessario e do- ctrina Calvini fluat, defendendum sumpsit Joh. Pisca- tor collatione cum Vorstio p. 31. Joh. Maccov. Col- leg. 6. dispp. misc. Disp. 4. qui proinde contendunt, objectum fidei esse τὸ ψεῦδος, vel falsum. Quod reprobat quidem Rhetorfort. ac refellit aliquot ar- gumentis, l. c. p. 223. quod id nec Theologia, nec veritas patiatur, quia fides innititur veritati divinæ, cui nihil falsi subesse potest, & credendum ita fo- ret, juxta Piscat. & Maccovium, DEUM loqui id quod falsum esse potest, & Deum nos velle credere falsa, quod est absurdum. Sed non potest effugere hoc para- doxon. Nam quomodo verum esse potest illud, quod credere tenentur homines, si reprobi credere teneantur in Christum, id est, Christum pro se mortu- um esse, quod verum esse Reformati negant. Un- de valde se torquet Rhetorfort. in argumento no- stro; quod unusquisq́; tenetur credere, id est verum: at unusquisq́; tenetur credere Christum pro se mortuum esse; ergo Christum pro unoquoque mortuum esse, est verum. Responsionem adfert Cameronis e Tom. 2. prælect. in Matth. 16. cap. v. 27. p. 204. qui majo- rem distinguit: Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, vel quomodo vera sunt, quæ narrantur, vel quomodo vera sunt, quæ prædicantur, velut promit- tuuntur; Primo & secundo modo verum non est, quia narrata & prædicta sunt vera, sive credideris sive non: at quæ vera sunt, ut promissa, ea nihil necesse est es- se, nisi credideris, imo necesse est ea non esse, si non credi- deris. Reprobat autem responsionem illam Rhe- torfort. quod ita falso supponatur, Christum mortu- um esse pro omnibus conditionate, sive electi, sive repro- bi fuerint, pro electis vero absolute, quæ sententia Ca- meronis hæresi affinis Rhetorforti videtur p. 222. Reprobat etiam Piscatoris & Maccovii, quam dixi- mus, responsionem. Tribus autem modis ipse re- spondet: (1.) distinguit τὸ credere: tribus illud mo- dis sumi, 1. pro τῷ assentiri omni DEI verbo & sic verbum DEI revelatum esse fidei objectum, ideoq; si ita formetur argumentum: Illud est verum, cui unusquisque tenetur assentiri, tanquam DEI verbo revelato: majorem veram esse dicit, mino- rem autem falsam, quia verbum DEI non sit Chri- stum pro me nominatim mortuum esse, ea intentione & decreto ut me salvet. At si hoc non est DEI verbum, credet id utique electus sine DEI verbo: quæ autem illa fides est sine DEI verbo? Dicit:

verbum DEI revelat DEI complacentiam & approba- tionem, non vero proprie intentionem & decretum Dei, de hoc vel illo homine salvando, nisi excipiamus quos- dam Patriarchas, Apostolos &c. At non tantum o- pus est, ut credamus approbare Deum, & compla- centiam in eo habere, si quis credat, sed necessum est ad fidem salvificam, ut unusquisque credat, DEUM sibi propitium esse velle, Christum pro se mortuum esse: etsi ergo individua non exprimantur in S. lite- ris, universales tamen propositiones habentur & ha- beri necessum est, sub quibus subsumere possit quodlibet individuum, cum assensus noster verbo DEI niti debeat, & fiducia ac applicatio, promissio- nem applicabilem cuivis prærequirat. 2. Dicit, τὸ credere esse actu fiduciali cordis in Christum, ut suffi- cientem Salvatorem recumbere: & sic majorem, quod unusquisq́; tenetur credere, id est verum, falsam esse. At hoc est ipsum Maccovianum & Piscat. parado- xum, quod effugere dum Rhetorfort. conatur, im- prudens in id incidit, novo tantum subornatum co- lore h. m. nam nec est verum nec falsum, sed bonum & salutare DEI donum, quod cor & affectus apprehen- dunt, & nullo modo mentis objectum: sic medium fin- git sophista inter verum & falsum, & confundit fidei objectum cum fidei actu; nam fidei actus est donum & opus DEI Joh. 6, 29. at objectum ejus est verbum Evangelii, quod utique verum esse oportet. Por- ro sophistice cor opponit menti: nam & mentis ob- jectum & cordis est, quod in Evangelio proponi- tur, Christus cum merito suo, qui & mente agno- sci, & corde apprehendi debet, ut redemtor & Salvator noster, ideoque cum menti proponitur hoc verbum de Christo, necessum est, ut verum sit, nec potest inter verum & falsum medium aliquod assignari: imo non possum in Christum ut Salvato- rem meum ferri corde, nisi mente intelligam, ac sci- am e verbo DEI, Christum meum Salvatorem esse. Tertiam significationem vocis credere ita assignat: τὸ credere, inquit, est sensu & ex consequente appre- hendere, & sic quod unusquisq́; tenetur credere, id est, fidei sensu & ex fidei actu fiduciali tanquam ex causa colligere, id est verum: valeat jam major, assumo: atqui unusquisq́; tenetur credere nempe non formali fidei actu fiduciali aut mentis assensu, sed fidei sensu & collectione evidenti ex causa concludere, Christum ex sua & DEI patris intentione & consilio pro se mortuum esse: minor jam est aperte falsa. Soli enim cre- dentes tenentur tali sensu DEI intentionem & æter- num decretum circa se nominatim colligere, reliqui enim non tenentur id credere, hoc est, colligere, imo sic obligarentur alere inanem & evanidam præsumtio- nem & conjecturam umbratilem & Chymæricam: itaq́; major procedit de fidei actu tum mentis in assentiendo, tum fiduciali cordis amplexu, quæ proprie est fides: minor vero de sensu fidei & collectione quadam practica, quæ est improprie fides. Sunt itaque quatuor termini in Syllogi- smo. Hactenus Rhetorfortis, qui vero fortia non loquitur. Respondemus (1.) τὸ credere formalem fidei actum fiducialem cum mentis assensu inferre, bar- dus sit, qui neget: e fidei sensu autem, & ex fidei actu fiduciali tanquam ex causa colligere, hoc non est cre- dere, sed est consequens fidei, vel actus reflexo creden- tis, qui cognoscit, vel colligit se credere, dum fidei sensum habet. At hîc non de actu reflexo, sed de actu directo, non de fidei sensu, sed de fide ipsa sive actu fiduciali res est, an quod unusquisque te- netur credere, ac fide apprehendere, verum sit? (2.) Si fides salvifica non ex verbo Evangelii, sed ex fidei actu fiduciali colligitur, aut oritur, fidei principium jam non amplius erit verbum Dei, sed actus cordis nostri, quod est Enthusiasticum, imo fides ex fide, & ita ex se ipsa orietur; ita vel ne- sciunt Calvinistae, quid dicant, vel fidem suam non e verbo Dei deducunt, sed e proprio cordis sui sen- su, quae vere inanis & evanida praesumtio est, & conjectura umbratilis & chymerica, quam loco ver- bi Dei fideique verae substituunt. Verbum enim Dei ipsis verum non est, cordis autem proprii sensus verus est. (3.) Unde agnoscere cogitur ipse Rhe- torfortis, sensum fidei & collectionem quandam practicam hanc esse, quam indigitat, non vero fidem, etsi illam improprie fidem vocet, ut lusus faciat. At illa impropria fides nihil ad rhombum, vel ad ar- gumentum propositum: nam in minori τὸ credere eodem prorsus modo sumitur, pro fide nempe pro- pria, non improprie dicta: quae ita habebat: Chri- stum pro se mortuum esse, tenetur quisque credere; nam credere tenetur quisque actu proprio fidei tum mentis in assentiendo, tum fiduciali cordis amplexu: nam per hanc fidem salvamur, cum credit nempe homo fidelis Christum pro se mortuum esse, non tantum mente huic veritati Evangelicae assentien- do, sed corde etiam Christi merita amplectendo, sibique fiducialiter applicando: si haec non sit fides salvifica, in Schola Calviniana, quid ergo sit fides, qua salutem consequi velint, equidem non video, aut certe, fidem per sua principia nullam habe- bunt, quod verissimum est. (4.) Novum est pa- radoxon Rhetorfortis, quod nescio an quisquam aliorum Calvinianorum approbaturus sit, siquidem applictationem fidei essentiae non includat, sed opine- tur eundem esse effectum inseparabiliter fidem co- mitantem, non actum ejusdem formalem; in quo ve- ro sibi ipsi non constat, siquidem e 1. Tim. I, 15. tria haec in fide notet (1.) assensum, ratione cujus Evangelium fidus sermo. (2.) fiduciam, cordis ac- quiescentiam, & innixum in Christum, ut in fiduciae objectum quod, & in promissiones, ut objectum quo, quae est ipsi formalis fidei ratio: & (3.) applicatio- nem, qua credit Christum venisse ad salvandum se. Atqui innixus in Christo & acquiescentia cordis in ipso & promissionibus de ipso est ipsa applicatio meritorum Christi, quae certe non est consequens, sed forma fidei; neque enim aliter fidem suam sive hic 1. Tim. 1, 15. sive ad Gal. II, 20. descripsit Apo- stolus, quam quod credat, Christum esse suum Sal- vatorem, Filium Dei se dilexisse, & semetipsum tra- didisse pro se; & loquitur de fide salvifica, in qua vi- vit ipse, non vero de fide proprie dicta. Nec sane possum vera cordis fiducia recumbere in Chri- stum, nisi certus sim, eum esse meum Salvatorem; vel (1.) innitor Christo Salvatori indefinite sine re- spectu ad salvatos, quod absurdum: ita enim rela- tum a correlato suo separaretur, vel innitor (2.) Salvatori aliorum credentium, & sic applico eum aliis, non mihi: quod itidem est absurdum: vel (3.) tanquam meo Salvatori, & sic particularis applica- tio clauditur in conceptu quidditativo fidei. Si di- cam, (quod Rhetorfortis excipit) sufficit, me actu formali fidei fiducialiter recumbere in Christum, ut sufficientem Salvatorem omnium credentium, dein- de fidei sensu credere, esse meum Salvatorem, mei- psum tantum vana persuasione decipiam: nam un- de ille fidei sensus, ut certo credam, eum esse meum Salvatorem? debet enim fides niti verbo, neq; fidei sensus esse potest, nisi prius ipsa fides adsit; jam ve- ro quod Christus sit mortuus, ex intentione, & aeter- no decreto, ut me salvet, id, dicente Rhetorforti, p. 302. non est fidei objectum, neque scriptum, neque se- cundum consequentiam est in verbo. Addit ille limi- tationem: nisi accedat aliquod internum in conscien- tia mea τεκμήριον, ex quo praeeunte actu fiduciali fidei illud colligam. At si actus fiducialis præit, unde- nam ille oritur? nam nullam fiduciam habere pos- sum in gratiam Dei, nisi certus sim, Deum nemini gratiam suam denegare: reus læsæ Majestatis, inquit ipse Rhetorfortis, prius Principem clementem esse in omnes iram ipsius suppliciter deprecantes credit, quam erga se clementem esse confidit. At quomodo credere potest, Deum clementem in omnes esse nisi id ex verbo habeat; Deum velle omnium mise- reri: quod neque scriptum neque secundum con- sequentiam in verbo Dei haberi, antagonista con- tendit. Atque hæc de prima responsione, qua vox credere distinguebatur. Altera concernit vocem veri, quam distinguit Rhetorfort. pag. 300. Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est, inquit, verum, Metaphysice & fundamentaliter, in se & quoad eventum: concedo majorem & tum minorem pernego; Christum enim pro unoquoque mortuum esse in se fundamentaliter & Metaphysice non est ve- rum, sed falsum. Verum respondemus ita adhuc salvum manere argumentum; nam respondetur tantum ad conclusionem sophistice: & prætexitur negari minorem, quæ ita habebat: unusquisque te- netur credere Christum pro se mortuum esse; in qua utique vox VERI non occurrit. Inepta autem est disputatio, cum & majori & minore concessa negatur conclusio. Addit Rhetorfortis; quod unus- quisque tenetur credere, id est verum, non tantum Metaphysice sed & moraliter & Theologice, utpote credenti revelatum per Dei verbum, vel per evidens aliquod in conscientia τεκμήριον, & sic vera major & adhuc falsa minor; nam Christum pro unoquoque mortuum esse, non est verum Theologice, nec uni- cuique revelatum, sed tantum electo & quidem cre- denti, hoc est actu fiduciali recumbenti in Christum Salvatorem. Respondemus: iterum responsio- nem ad conclusionem directam esse. Deinde meræ sunt τερατολογίαι istæ distinctiunculæ: major enim simpliciter vera est, nisi quis in Maccovii sen- tentiam discedere velit, a qua abhorret Rhetor- fortis: Quod tenetur quisque credere verum est, ex quocunque tandem principio veritas illa depen- deat. Debet autem dependere ex revelatione di- vina, vel verbo Dei, quia nullum aliud veritatis principium in Theologia agnoscimus præter Dei verbum. Porro si verum hoc non est Theologice, quod Christus mortuus sit pro unoquoque; ergo Theologice id falsum erit; aut si adhuc verum sta- tuatur, quomodo ergo? num Philosophice, aut qua- nam denique ratione verum esse dicetur? Si non verum est Theologice; ergo nec credendum est; nihil enim credendum in Theologia, nisi quod Theologice verum sit. Et hæc erat altera ejus re- sponsio.

Tertio respondet limitando vocem UNUS- QUISQUE: quod nempe unusquisque oneratus pec- catorum pondere tenetur credere, id verum est: quasi quod alii non onerati credere tenentur, verum non sit, utpote cum tenentur credere, infernum esse, ju- dicium novissimum futurum, id verum non sit? verum est, & manet verum, in se, utcunque se ha- beat is, cui id credendum proponatur. Porro fal- sum est, non omnes, sed onustos pondere peccatorum tantum teneri credere, Christum pro se mortuum esse; nam in mandatis Evangelicis omnes jubentur cre- dere. Regerit Rhetorfortis cæteris mandari ut credant, sed certo tamen ordine. Respondemus: sufficit, quod ipsis demandetur fides: & qualisnam tandem erit fides illa, quam exigit Deus a repro- bis, propter cujus carentiam ipsi rei sunt æternæ condemnationis? Dicit Rhetorfort. exigere ab iis Deum, ut assentiantur omni Dei verbo, & pro- missionibus & ut recumbant actu fiduciali in Chri- stum, sufficientem salutis autorem, nullo vero modo teneri eos credere, Christum pro se mortuum esse. Sed ita tum sibi, tum veritati contradicit aperte: sibi quidem; quia proxime pag. 300. dixerat, non esse unicuique revelatum Christum esse pro se mor- tuum, sed tantum electo, & quidem credenti; hoc est, ut ipse explicat, actu fiduciali in Christo Servatore recumbenti: hic vero fatetur, non ab electis tantum, sed etiam a reprobis exigi, ut actu fiduciali in Chri- stum Salvatorem recumbant. Veritati autem, quia qui tenetur recumbere actu fiduciali in Christum, is tenetur meritum Christi sibi applicare, adeoque credere, Christum pro se mortuum esse, Christum suum esse Salvatorem: hæc enim applicatio est actus fiducialis salvificæ fidei proprius & formalis. De- nique nemo potest se fateri affinem culpæ ob re- pudiatam promissionem verbo factam, si mens di- centis statuit, illi promissionem non præstare, vel potius, si certo decreto statuerit, qui verbo promittit, ne promissio ad illum pertineat aut pertinere possit. Atque hæc pro vindicando celebri Syllogismo anti Calviniano, in quo undiquaque constricti hæ- rent.

Colligemus jam flosculos nonnullos & em- blemata hujus ματαιολογίας Calvinianæ prorsus obduratæ, verbis ipsius Rhetorfortis proposita, qualia sunt (1.) quod Deus intendat obedientiam omnium vocatorum, non est Jehove dictum. (2.) Falsum est teneri ex Evangelicis hortationibus omnes in Ecclesia visibili credere, Deum ipsorum obedien- tiam intendere; quo pertinet (3.) illud effatum: falsum est Christum intendisse dicto illo: qui me confitebitur coram hominibus, hunc etiam consite- bor coram Patre, ut Petrus obediret & Christum confiteretur: (4.) Intentio Dei non proprie revela- tur & infallibiliter, sed colligitur ex mandato, quæ fuerit intentio Dei, quam dicit Wilb. Twissii ob- servationem esse, in vindiciis gratiæ contra Armi- nianos & calculo suo approbat pag. 223. (5.) man- data & promissiones Evangelicæ Dei intentionem, ut reprobi obediant, reprobis non exprimunt, sed tantum iis revelant sanctam illam concatenationem, tum in- ter fidem & ipsorum credendi obligationem, tum in- ter fidem & vitam æternam. (6.) Deum, cum ait: reprobi credite & salvi eritis, hoc præ se ferre, suam esse intentionem & decretum, ut reprobi credant & salventur, præ se fert insigne mendacium. (7.) Quam- vis Deus non posuerit Christum Salvatorem omnium etiam reproborum, tamen jure exigit, ut tota fiducia recumbant in Salvatorem sufficientissimum omni- bus credentibus, & jure rei sunt, quia nolunt se dede- re Christo, quamvis Christus ipsos amplecti ab æter- no nunquam decreverit. (8.) Invitare Deum ad convivium quamplurimos, quos venire non decre- vit, & jubere amplecti Christum Salvatorem ipsis æterno Dei consilio nunquam destinatum. (9.) Po- test Deus absoluta potentia omnium condonare pec- cata citra Christi satisfactionem, quod cum Wilb. Twissio asserit p. 310. Denique (10.) nihil hoc fal- sius, neminem esse affinem culpæ ob repudiatam pro- missionem, si promittens statuit certo decreto ne pro- missio ad illum pertineat, ut habet Rhetorfort. pag. 44. Quæ paradoxa omnia, ut fluunt ex communi Reformatorum dogmate de absoluto decreto, ita non dubitandum est, pios Christianos ab horridis istis hypothesibus toto animo abhorrere. Rever- timur ad locum nostrum & explicationem Riveti; qui, sensus, inquit, hujus loci est, quod hactenus Pha- rao vos non dimisit, non casu factum est, sed meo con- silio, nec ideo dilata liberatio, quod eripere vos nolim, sed ut gloriosius vos liberem : non enim ponitur culpa, Deo aliud intendente, ita ut necesse fuerit eum prius frustrari primario fine suo, ut ex eventu, quem no- luisset, consilium caperet de novo fine : quæ certe sine Dei contumelia cogitari non possunt. Hæc Rive- tus : At falsum (1.) est, consilium Dei fuisse, ut Pharao non dimitteret populum ; contrarium tota historia, & tot iteratæ legationes Dei, ad Pharao- nem expeditæ, tot denique prodigia, & ostenta docent, quid enim aliud expetebat legationibus aut urgebat portentis suis, quam ut dimitteretur populus? Falsum (2.) est, a Deo dilatatam fuisse liberationem populi, ut liberaret eum gloriosius, quia factum hoc est, ut Pharaonem ad resipiscentiam perduceret, eo vero persistente in contumacia, & duritie cordis sui, direxit id omne Deus ad glo- riam nominis sui, & gloriosiorem liberationem populi. (3.) culpa non ponitur Pharaonis Deo eam intendente aut decernente, sed permittente & ad fi- nem dirigente sibi gloriosum. (4.) Nulla est Deo contumelia, sed ipsa Scripturæ veritas, quod inten- tionem & consilium Dei sæpe posthabeant homi- nes eique refragentur. Vid. Prov. 1, 25. Matth. 23, 37. Luc. 7, 30. Act. 6, 51. c, 13, 45. Atque in eo commendat Scriptura Dei misericordiam, damnat autem hominum contumaciam. (5.) Neque Deum ex eventu, quem noluit, consilium capere, contumeliosum Deo est, quia præscit eventum il- lum ab æterno & ita æterno consilio suo dirigit. An non cum Adamum ad vitam creasset, postquam ipsum lapsurum prævidit, consilium aliud de Ada- mi salute suscepit, de redemtione nempe Ada- mi per Christum Salvatorem? denique non con- silium de novo fine, sed de mediis aliis iniit Deus; cum enim per observantiam mandatorum Dei ad salutem, ut debuerat, non adspiraret homo, & gra- tia ac salute excidit, an non consilium iniit Deus gratiosum de ejusdem reparatione per semen mu- lieris? Evangelium & pactum Evangelicum neces- sum est, ut negent Calviniani, si hæc inficientur. Atque hæc de præsenti loco.

## 10:7
verse 7. DO YOU NOT SEE THAT EGYPT HAS PERISHED) Do you not yet see that Egypt has perished? namely, if it is handled in this way. Aquila well, ἄρα ὔπω οἶδας (do you not yet know).

Latin:

vers. 7. NONNE VIDES QVOD PERIERIT ÆGT- PTUS) Nondum vides periisse Ægyptum ? nempe, si ita agitur. Aquila bene, ἄρα ὔπω οἶδας.

## 10:10
Verse 10.

SO THE LORD AND WITH YOU.

As if it were said: May God so help you, as I shall dismiss you. It is not a rebuke, as most would have it, but a μυκτηρισμὸς, as Fagius rightly observes, or a mocking, the sense of which is this: If God does not help you any more than I am about to dismiss you on such a condition, He will indeed help you remarkably; that mocking is therefore joined with a notable contempt of God; it will be seen from this what God can do, if I dismiss you on the condition which you request.

verse of the same. TO WHOM IS IT DOUBTFUL) He has well expressed the sense of the word see, which is in Hebrew, that is, let anyone see.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

SIC DOMINUS ET VOBISCUM.

Quasi dicatur : Sic Deus adjuvet vos, sicut ego dimittam vos. Non est increpatio, ut plerique vo- lunt, sed μυκτηρισμὸς, ut recte observat Fagius, vel subsannatio, cujus hic sensus : Si non magis Deus vos adjuvet; quam ego vos tali conditione dimissu- rus sum, egregie profecto vos juvabit : conjuncta ergo illa subsannatio est cum insigni contemtu Dei; videbitur ex eo, quid possit Deus, si vos dimittam ea conditione, qua petitis.

vers. eod. CUI DUBIUM EST) Bene expressit sensum verbi videte, quod in Hebræo est, id est, quivis videat.

## 10:13
Verse 13. A SCORCHING WIND.

That is, not the south wind, as the LXX and Philo think, and Eugubinus especially contends; but the east wind, which was hot there, and scorching. Which is gathered from the opposite; for the wind, which in turn cast the locusts out of Egypt into the Red Sea, is called the west wind, verse 19. Moreover, the miracle was twofold, both that God suddenly stirred up such a great and hot wind, which blew through all of Egypt; and that He produced and blew upon an innumerable multitude of locusts, which it is likely were produced immediately, because such a great quantity appeared in a moment; for although locusts are sometimes brought by the wind, yet such a great and sudden collection was made, beyond the usual order of nature, as all the circumstances teach.

Latin:

Vers. 13. VENTUM URENTEM.

Id est, non australem, ut LXX. & Philo pu- tant, & Eugub. imprimis contendit; sed orientalem, qui ibi calidus erat, & urens. Quod colligitur ex opposito; nam ventus, qui locustas vicissim ejecit ex Ægypto in mare rubrum, vocatur occidentalis, vers. 19. Geminum autem fuit prodigium, tum quod subito Deus tantum tanque calidum ven- tum excitavit, qui totam Ægyptum perflaret; tum quod innumeram locustarum multitudinem pro- duxerit, & afflarit, quas immediate productas fu- isse, quia in momento tanta copia prodiere, veri- simile est; Etsi enim vento locustæ quandoque ad- ducantur, tamen tanta & tam subita collectio, præ- ter usitatam naturæ ordinem, facta fuit, ut omnes circumstantiæ docent.

## 10:13 Addition
To chapter 10, 13. towards the end. p. 362. b.

Although they are indeed said to have been brought by the wind, yet a part of them can be considered to have been created by GOD, if not all. The east wind could not have brought the locusts except from Arabia, where they are not found in such great numbers. Yet this wind could have been employed by God, being hot and dry, and thus suitable for the generation of locusts. All Hebrews understand the east wind. Because קדם is the East, so called because he who looks at the sun has the east before him, whence also the west is called אחור, because he has the same behind him: And thus Oleastrius, Cajetanus, Pagninus, Bonfrerius, Munsterus, Fagius, Vatablus, Drusius, Rivetus, and most others interpret this wind. Agatharcides on the Red Sea 5, 27, Diodorus book 3, number 13, and Strabo book 16 report that countless locusts were both brought and expelled by the wind. Exodus 10, v. 17. That death to page 363. a. Destruction or deadly plague 2. 2 Kings 4, 40. both because they were the death of trees and herbs, Ps. 78, v. 4, and because locusts induce famine, and because they infested not only fields but also men, invaded houses, beds, and food, and when trampled on the roads and turned into gore, they stirred up horror and stench. Nor do locusts harm only by biting, but they also burn by contact; their saliva is a poison to herbs, says Damir. Likewise, when dead, they infect the air with a foul odor, whence a most grievous pestilence follows. There is no animal more destructive, says Damir. See Bochart's Hierozoicon 2. 4. 8. 461. Perhaps these, armed with burning poison, ejaculated it upon the men themselves, as it is said in Wisdom 16, v. 9, the bite of locusts killed them.

Latin:

Ad cap. 10, 13. sub finem. p. 362. b.

Etsi vero a vento advectæ dicuntur, tamen pars earum à DEO creata censeri potest, si non omnes. Ventus orientalis non nisi ex Arabia lo- custas potuit advehere, ubi tanto numero illæ non inveniuntur. Adhiberi tamen a Deo potuit ven- tus hic, utpote calidus & ficcus, adeoque aptus locustarum generationi. Orientalem ventum E- bræi omnes intelligunt. Quia קדם est Oriens, sic dictus, quod qui solem respicit, ante se habet ori- entem, unde & occidens אחור dicitur, quod idem eum habeat post se: Atque ita ventum hunc acci- piunt Oleastrius, Cajetanus, Pagninus, Bonfre- rius, Munsterus, Fagius, Vatablus, Drusius, Rivetus & alii plerique. Locustas innumeras a vento & ad- vectas & expulsas referunt Agatharc. de mari rubro 5, 27. Diodor. l. 3. num. 13. Strabo lib. 16. Exod. 10. v. 17. Mortem istam ad pag. 363. a. Perniciem aut mortiferam plagam 2. Reg. 4, 40. tum quod mors fuerint arborum & herbarum Ps. 78. v. 4. tum quod famem inducant locustæ, tum quod non agros tantum sed etiam homines infe- starint, domos, lectos, cibos invaserint, in viis quoque conculcatæ & in saniem conversæ horro- rem & fœtorem excitarint. Nec solo morsu no- cent locustæ, sed & contactu adurunt; Saliva ea- rum virus est herbis, inquit Damir. Mortuæ item tetro odore aërem inficiunt, unde lues gravissima sequitur. Nullum est animal perniciosius, ait Da- mir. Vid. Bocharti Hierozoicon 2. 4. 8. 461. Forte hæ adurenti veneno armatæ illud in homines ipsos ejaculatæ sunt, uti Sap. 16. v. 9. dicitur locustarum morsus occiderunt eos.

## 10:14
Ver. 14. SUCH AS THERE HAVE NOT BEEN BEFORE THAT TIME NOR SHALL BE AFTERWARDS.

The passage Joel 1, 1. & 4. seems to conflict. But some there wish the army of the Chaldeans to be designated allegorically by the locusts, nor does the Prophet speak of Egypt, but of Judea, whereas these words of Moses must be understood in relation to Egypt.

Latin:

Verf. 14. QVALES ANTE ILLUD TEMPUS NON FUERUNT NEC POSTEA FUTURÆ SUNT.

Videtur repugnare locus Joel 1, 1. & 4. Sed ibi nonnulli exercitum Chaldæorum allegorice per locustas designatum volunt, neque loquitur Pro- pheta de Ægypto, sed de Judæa, hæc vero verba Mosis intelligenda sunt relate ad Ægyptum.

## 10:15
Ver. 15. WHATEVER FRUIT WAS ON THE TREES.

The Vulgate did not correctly render 'poma' [apples/fruits]: the noun פרי is more general, comprehending all fruits, both those that are in a tender shell and those in a hard one. But whence those fruits, if indeed all the trees had been broken by the hail? Here it must be said that every tree is spoken of by hyperbole, so that the greatest part of the trees had been destroyed, but those which remained were exposed to the locusts.

Latin:

Verf. 15. QUICQUID POMORUM IN ARBORI- BUS FUIT.

Non recte Vulg. poma reddidit: nomen פרי generalius est, fructus omnes tam qui tenero, quam qui duro cortice sunt, comprehendens. Sed unde illi fructus, siquidem arbores omnes a grandine con- fractæ fuerint? Hic dicendum videtur, omnem ar- borem dici per hyperbolen, ita ut maxima arbo- rum pars corrupta fuerit, quæ autem reliquæ man- serint, locustis sint expositæ.

## 10:16
Ver. 16. INTO THE RED SEA.

Corn. a Lap. and others wish the Red Sea to be named from the red sand which was at the bottom of the sea; Suidas reports that some attributed this name to it from the color of the wave itself. But because that sea is not red by nature, Brodaeus, with Agatharchides, denies that it is correctly called red; to whom it is answered by others that 'Red' here is not an appellative noun, but a proper one from Edom, or Esau, which is called ἐρυθρὸν [red] by the Greeks, and ἐρυθραῖον [Erythraean], because it looked toward τὸν ἐρυθρὸν [the red one], Gen. 36, 9. Exod. 23, 31. concerning which Nicol. Fuller, lib. 4. Miscell. c. 20. is especially to be consulted; there is no reason why we should seek another derivation; for Suidas also approved this opinion, as did Arrian, lib. 8. of the deeds of Alexander: where he says that this sea is called red from a red King who was first there. For that sea is the Idumean Sea itself. If the Palestinians were able to call the Mediterranean Sea, of which they were not masters for long nor for the most part, by their own name 'Palestinian,' why should the Edomites not also call the Arabian [Sea], which they held entirely for a very long time, by their own name 'Edomite'? But what, I ask, is 'Edomite' other than ἐρυθρὸν, ἐρυθραῖον, or 'Red,' except that the former is pronounced in Hebrew, the latter in Greek and Latin, says Fuller, l. c.

Latin:

Verf. 16. IN MARE RUBRUM.

Mare rubrum ab arena rubra, quæ in fundo maris fuerit Corn. a Lap. & alii dictum volunt; Sui- das refert nonnullos ex colore undæ ipsi hoc no- men tribuisse. Quia vero mare illud non rubet na- tura, Brodæus cum Agatarchide negat recte id ru- brum vocari; Quibus ab aliis respondetur Ru- brum hic non esse nomen appellativum, sed pro- prium ab Edom, vel Esavo, qui ἐρυθρὸν Græcis ἐρυ- θραῖον dictum, quod ser ad τὸν ἐρυθρὸν Rubrum illum spectarit Gen. 36, 9. Exod. 23, 31. de quo cumpri- mis videndus est Nicol. Fullerus lib. 4. Miscell. c. 20. non est cur aliam derivationem quæramus; hanc enim sententiam approbavit etiam Suidas, ut & Arrianus lib. 8. gestorum Alexandri: ubi ait, ru- brum hoc mare dici a rubro, primo ibidem Rege. Nam mare illud est ipsum mare Idumæum. Si Palæ- stini mare mediterraneum, cujus nec ita diu, neque magna ex parte Domini erant, nuncupare tamen no- mine suo quiverunt Palæstinum, quidni & Edomæi Arabicum, quod diutissime totum tenuerunt, nomi- ne, itidem suo nuncuparint Edomæum? At quid ob- secro aliud est Edomæum, quam ἐρυθρὸν, ἐρυθραῖον, vel Rubrum, nisi quod illud Hebraice enunciatur, hæc Græce Latineque ait Fuller. l. c.

## 10:19 Addition
To Exodus 10. 19. in the same place.

Moreover, the name of the Red Sea is not found here, but ים סוף, which the Hebrews explain as the sedgy or marshy or weedy sea, because there are many reeds on its shores; others explain it as the stormy sea, because סוף is also a storm, as Münsterus does. Malvenda renders it the sea of the end, because סוף is an end, as if to say that it has ends not far distant from itself, whereas the Ocean does not seem to have an end. But the former reason for the name is to be preferred. See Vatablus.

Latin:

Ad Exod. 10. 19. ibidem.

Cæterum non habetur hic maris rubri no- men, sed ים סוף, quod Ebræi mare caricosum, seu pamposum, vel algosum, quia ad ejus littora sunt plurima carecta, alii procellosum, quia סוף etiam est procella exponunt, ut Münsterus. Malvenda reddit mare termini, quia סוף est terminus, q. d. quod Terminos habet non procul à se distantes, cum Oceanus non videatur habere terminum. Sed præferenda prior nominis ratio. Vid. Vatabl.

## 10:20 Addition
To Exodus 10. v. 20. after the words and terrified them with specters. p. 363. b.

Lightfoot in this place thinks that those horrific specters of demons are hinted at in Ps. 78, 49, because they are mentioned by the Psalmist in the place of the plague of darkness, which is not named there. And from this, Pharaoh was greatly moved by this plague, who had hardened himself against the previous ones.

To the same verse towards the end.

In this dark three-day period, Lightfoot gathers from Ps. 105, v. 38, that the Israelites were circumcised in Egypt. They did not rebel: which is hinted at there as them having performed some special part of obedience, which was circumcision: for most of them had been circumcised in Egypt, Josh. 5, 9, but no uncircumcised person was admitted to the Passover, Exod. 12, 48. Furthermore, the people are said to be circumcised a second time in Josh. 5, and thus another general circumcision preceded it, which, since it was not done in the desert, must be said to have been done in Egypt, so that God enveloped the Egyptians in three days of darkness while the pain of circumcision afflicted the Israelites. However, the Israelites enjoyed light not only in the streets and squares, but also in their chambers, in the same house which they perhaps inhabited with the Egyptians, with GOD not denying his presence, which he withdrew from the Egyptians, to the eyes of the Hebrews, as Tirinus and Rivetus hold. Lyranus, however, gathers from chapter 9, verse 26, that those Egyptians who dwelt in Goshen were immune from those plagues, with the exception of the slaughter of the firstborn, by reason of that benefit of cohabitation with the children of Israel. But as for what Lyranus reports from the Rabbis, that during this three-day period the unbelieving Jews who were unwilling to depart from Egypt were struck down and buried in the earth, lest the Egyptians seeing them should say: 'They are struck down, just as we are,' it is frivolous and destitute of any authority of Scripture.

Latin:

Ad Exod. 10. v. 20. post verba illosque spectris perterruisse. pag. 363. b.

Horrifica illa spectra dæmonum innui Ps. 78, 49. censet Lightfoot in h. l. quod a Psalte loco plagæ tenebrarum memorentur, quæ non nomi- natur ibidem. Atque hinc Pharaonem plurimum commotum fuisse hac plaga, qui ad priores ob- duruit.

Ad versum eundem sub finem.

In hoc triduo tenebricoso circumcisos fuisse Israelitas in Ægypto colligit Lightfootus è Psal. 105. v. 38. Non rebellarunt : quod innuatur ibi specia- lem aliquam obedientiæ partem eos præstitisse, quæ fuerit circumcisio : plurimi enim eorum in Æ- gypto circumcisi fuerant, Jos. 5, 9. at nemo incir- cumcisus ad Pascha admissus est Exod. 12, 48. Præ- terea populum circumcisum dici secundo Jos. 5. adeoque antecessisse aliam generalem circumcisio- nem, quæ cum in deserto facta non sit, in Ægypto facta dicenda sit, ut ita Ægyptios Deus tenebris tri- duanis involverit, cum dolor circumcisionis Israëli- tas urgeret. Gaudebant autem Israelitæ luce non tantum in vicis & plateis, sed etiam in cubiculis suis, in eadem domo, quam cum Ægyptiis forte inco- lebant, DEO concursum suum, quem Ægyptiis subtrahebat, non denegante oculis Ebræorum, ut habet Tirinus, Rivetus. Lyranus autem Ægy- ptios illos, qui in Gosen habitabant, ex beneficio isto cohabitationis filiorum Israel à plagis immu- nes fuisse, excepta primogenitorum cæde è c. 9. v. 26. colligit. Cæterum quod e Rabinis tradit Lyranus, in hoc triduo percussos Judæos incre- dulos, qui de Ægypto recedere noluerint, & terra fuisse sepultos, ne Ægyptii videntes dicerent: Per- cussi sunt illi, sicut & nos, frivolum est, omnique au- toritate Scripturæ destituitur.

## 10:21
Ver. 21. SO THAT THEY MAY BE FELT.

The Chaldean rendered the words of the text otherwise: 'let there be darkness, even after the gloom of night has passed': others interpret it thus: 'let there be darkness, so that it may take away the darkness of the night,' because משד is to recede; but the verb is more correctly derived from משש, to feel, as Luther also rendered it; and it is a phrase taken from common usage, when the dark air appears so thick as if it could be felt; although Tostatus and Burgensis also observe not incorrectly that the darkness was truly palpable, because the air was so condensed and the clouds brought in were so thick that they could in some way be felt. However, those darknesses were not made only in the eyes of the Egyptians, as Jansenius thinks in his Commentary on ch. 17. Wisdom, as if only the Egyptians had been struck with blindness, like the Sodomites, because this would have been a certain blinding of the Egyptians, not a darkening of Egypt; but Moses expressly says that there was palpable darkness for the Egyptians, but light for the Hebrews; nor is an eclipse of the sun to be posited, with Philo, because the darkness lasted for three days and deprived only the Egyptians of light. The cause of the darkness, therefore, was clouds and very dense mists, and a compaction of the air so great that the rays of the sun could not penetrate; it may be added, however, that a foul gloom settled upon those lands, concerning which see the Book of Wisdom, ch. 17. The Lord threatened this punishment to the disobedient in Deut. 28. 29.

No one dared to move from their place in such great darkness, lest they run into precipices or specters, because the Egyptians thought that the whole order of the world was being overturned and disturbed by such unusual darkness; and the Book of Wisdom, ch. 17, v. 4, testifies that sounds disturbing them rang around them, and sad visions appeared in mournful forms, which Rivetus rashly says were only invented by that author for the sake of exaggeration; since there should be no doubt that in such great darkness demons or spirits of darkness presented sad phantasms to them and terrified them with specters.

However, it is gathered from this narrative that the Egyptians were deprived not only of heavenly light but also of borrowed light from fire or a candle. Philo says in his book on the life of Moses that the fire which we use was either extinguished by the disturbed air or overcome by the thickest darkness; the Book of Wisdom, in the same place, says: and no power of fire could provide them with light. Therefore, Cajetan falsely asserts that they used candles, for thus the punishment would not have been so great, nor the horror so intense, even if they had been deprived of the light of the sun for three days.

V. same. WHEREVER THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL DWELT THERE WAS LIGHT.

In the Hebrew there is emphasis, in their dwellings, so that it may be signified that there was light for the Hebrews even in the same house where there was darkness for the Egyptians, which increased the magnitude of the miracle, God extending solar rays to the Hebrews, but not likewise to their neighbors or cohabitants the Egyptians.

Latin:

Verf. 21. UT PALPARI POSSINT.

Verba textus aliter reddidit Chaldæus: sint tenebræ, etiam postquam præcessit caligo noctis: alii fic interpretantur: sint tenebræ, ut noctis tenebras au- ferant, quia משד est recedere; sed rectius verbum a משש palpare deducitur, ut reddidit etiam Luth. estque phrasis e vulgari consuetudine desumta, cum tenebrosus aer crassus adeo apparet, ac si palpari posset; quanquem non male etiam Tostatus & Bur- gens. observent, vere palpabiles fuisse tenebras, quod aer ita condensatus nebulæque objectæ tam crassæ fuerint, quæ quodammodo palpari possent. Non autem tenebræ illæ factæ tantum sunt in oculis Æ- gytiorum, ut Jansenius putat Comment. in 17. c. Sap. quasi Ægyptii tantum percussi fuerint cæci- tate, ut Sodomitæ, quia hæc excæcatio quædam fuisset Ægyptiorum, non obtenebratio Ægypti, Mo- ses vero diferte tenebras palpabiles dicit Ægyptiis fuisse, lucem vero Ebræis; neque Solis Eclipsis statuenda, cum Philone, quia tenebræ per triduum perdurarunt, & Ægyptios tantum luce privarunt. Causa itaque tenebrarum fuere nubes & nebulæ densissimæ, ac constipatio aeris tanta, ut radii solares penetrare non potuerint; addi tamen potest, te- tram caliginem ipsis terris incubasse, de quo vid. lib. Sap. c. 17. Pœnam hanc minatus est Dominus inobedientibus Deut. 28. 29.

Nemo audebat se loco movere in tantis tene- bris, ne in praecipitia, aut spectra incurreret, quia ex tam insolitis tenebris putabant Aegyptii totum mundi ordinem everti & conturbari; & testatur l. Sap. c. 17. 4. sonos conturbantes ipsos circumstre- puisse, & visa tristia flebilibus formis apparuisse, quae tantum ad exaggerationem ab autore illo fuisse conficta, temere dicit Rivetus; quum dubium esse non debeat, in tantis tenebris daemones seu Spiri- tus tenebrarum tristia phantasmata ipsis objecisse, illosque spectris perterruisse.

Colligitur autem ex hac narratione, quod non solum lumine caelesti, sed etiam mutuatitio ignis aut candelae privati fuerint Aegyptii. Philo dicit lib. de vita Mos. ignem, quo utimur vel aere turba- to fuisse extinctum, vel a crassissimis tenebris victum Lib. Sap. l. c. ait; & ignis quidem nulla vis poterat illis lumen praebere. Falso itaque Cajetanus candelis eos usos asserit, sic enim tanta non fuisset poena, nec tantus horror, etiamsi per tres dies lumine solis or- bati fuissent.

V. eod. UBICUNQUE HABITABANT FI- LII ISRAEL LUX ERAT.

In Ebr. emphasis est, in sedibus suis, ut signi- ficetur, in eadem etiam domo Ebraeis fuisse lucem, ubi Aegyptiis tenebrae erant, quod miraculi magni- tudinem augebat, Deo radios Solares porrigente ad Ebraeos, non item ad Aegyptios vicinos, aut cohabitantes.

## 10:24
V. 24. AND PHARAOH CALLED MOSES.

Some say this happened when the three days were completed and the darkness had been dispelled, along with Lyranus, Abulensis, Pererius, and Cornelius. But the text does not easily admit this, because the darkness still lasting compelled Pharaoh to agree to the dismissal of the whole people, and not to except anything but the sheep and the herds: for which reason it must be said that those shadows had not yet been entirely removed, but only in part; and Moses could walk in the darkness as in the light; indeed, for Moses the darkness was not darkness, but all things shone.

Latin:

V. 24. VOCAVITQVE PHARAO MOSEN.

Nonnulli hoc factum dicunt triduo expleto, tenebrisque discussis cum Lyrano, Abulensi, Pere- rio, & Cornelio. Sed non admittit hoc facile textus, quia tenebrae adhuc durantes compulerunt Pha- raonem, ut annueret in dimissionem populi uni- versi, nec nisi oves, & armenta exciperet: quapro- pter dicendum, tenebras illas nondum plane fuis- se ablatas, sed ex parte; & poterat Moses in tene- bris ambulare, ut in luce, imo Mosi tenebrae non erant tenebrae, sed lucebant omnia.

## 10:25
V. 25. WHICH WE MAY OFFER TO THE LORD.

In the Hebrew, and we will do: whence Papists gather that the word to do is the same as to sacrifice, so that from the words of institution DO THIS, they may carve out the Mass-sacrifice. But no place of Scripture can be produced, nor from the Old Testament itself, where the word עָשָׂה is placed absolutely to mean to sacrifice. But when it obtains that meaning, the word for sacrifice always either precedes or follows, so that it can be gathered from the text that the discourse is about a sacrifice, which is also manifest here; but no such thing occurs in the words of the institution of the Holy Supper, and therefore from the simple word, do, a sacrifice is ineptly concluded.

Latin:

V. 25. QVAE OFFERAMUS DOMINO.

In Ebr. & faciemus: Unde Papistae colligunt, verbum facere idem esse quod sacrificare, ut e ver- bis institutionis HOC FACITE, exsculpant Missaticum sacrificium. Verum nullus produci potest locus Scripturae, neque ex ipso V.T. ubi ver- bum עָשָׂה absolute positum sit sacrificare. Sed quum significationem illam obtinet, semper vox sacrifi- cii aut praecedit, aut sequitur; ut ex textu colligi possit, de sacrificio sermonem esse, quod etiam hic manifestum est; tale autem quid in verbis institu- tionis S. Coenae non occurrit, ideoque ex simplici verbo, facite, inepte sacrificium concluditur.

## 10:27
Vers. 27. BUT PHARAOH'S HEART WAS HARDENED.

This hardening was now judicial and penal, because when after so many exhortations, so many prodigies, so many punishments Pharaoh did not repent, God now hardened his heart, which was hard in itself and had developed a callus: not only occasionally, by removing, to wit, the most grievous plague of darkness and by urging through Moses the dismissal of both the Hebrews themselves and their cattle, but also by subtraction, by withdrawing grace from Pharaoh and leaving him to his own hardness, for He no longer deigned to address him with His word or through the calling of His servants, whence Moses says to him: I will not see your face again. Nor, however, should it be concluded from these words that Pharaoh is denied to have hardened himself, because he was hardened by God as it is said, because Pharaoh persisted in the hardness of his heart, which is sufficiently clear from the fact that he is already threatening death to Moses, from whom he had seen so many miracles, and whom he had previously begged to intercede with God, so that this death might be taken away from him.

Latin:

Vers. 27. INDURAVIT AUTEM COR PHARAONIS.

Haec induratio jam erat δικαστικὴ & poe- nalis, quia cum post tot exhortationes, tot pro- digia, tot supplicia non resipuerit Pharao, in- duravit jam Deus cor ipsius, quod in sese du- rum erat, & callum obduxerat: non tantum ἀφορμητικῶς occasionaliter amovendo scil. pla- gam tenebrarum gravissimam & urgendo per Mosen tum Ebraeorum ipsorum tum etiam peco- rum dimissionem, sed etiam ἀφαιρετικῶς, subtra- hendo Pharaoni gratiam & relinquendo ipsum suae duritiei, non enim amplius dignabatur eum verbo suo vel compellatione per servos suos, unde di- cit ei Moses: non videbo ultra faciem tuam. Ne- que tamen ex his verbis concludendum, Pharao- nem negari sese indurasse, quia a Deo induratus dicitur, quia Pharao perrexit in cordis sui duritie, quod satis ex eo liquet, quod etiam Mosi mortem jam minetur, a quo tot prodigia viderat, quemque antea orarat, intercederet apud Deum, ut auferre- tur abs se mors ista.

## 10:29
Verse 29. I WILL NOT SEE THY FACE AGAIN.

But at chapter 11, 4, he was present before Pharaoh again, and announced the final plague to him. Some reconcile these things in this way, that he did not wish to meet Pharaoh voluntarily anymore; but it does not appear that Pharaoh summoned Moses when the last plague was announced to him; indeed, it is manifest that Moses announced it to Pharaoh of his own accord. Therefore others say that Moses did not come into the sight of Pharaoh, but announced it through his servants or counselors; thus Rivetus. But this contradicts the text of the following chapter, verse 9: 'And he went out from Pharaoh in great anger.' He was therefore present before Pharaoh, and denounced the slaughter of the firstborn to him. Wherefore it is better that we say that the things which are related in the following chapter were both said to Moses by inspiration while he was still standing before Pharaoh, and were reported by Moses to Pharaoh, and that narration having been completed, Moses left Pharaoh with vehement agitation, and never saw his face again thereafter. Compare also those things which follow already at chapter 11, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 29. NON VIDEBO ULTRA FACIEM TUAM.

At cap. 11, 4. denuo adfuit Pharaoni, eique plagam novissimam indicavit. Hæc ita conciliant nonnulli, quod nolit amplius Pharaonem αὐτομά- τως convenire; verum non apparet, quod accersi- verit Pharao Mosen, cum ultima plaga ipsi indica- retur, imo Mosen Pharaoni eam indicasse ultro, manifestum est. Proinde alii dicunt, Mosen non venisse in conspectum Pharaonis, sed per servos aut consiliarios ejus illam indicasse; ita Rivetus. Sed hoc repugnat textui cap. sequentis v. 9. & exivit a Pharaone iratus nimis. Adfuit ergo coram Pha- raone, eique cædem primogenitorum denuncia- vit. Quapropter præstat, ut dicamus, quæ capite seq. referuntur, & Mosi per inspirationem dicta es- se, cum adhuc coram Pharaone consisteret, & a Mose Pharaoni relata fuisse, eaque narratione per- acta, Mosen cum vehementi commotione Pha- raonem reliquisse, neque amplius deinceps faciem ejus vidisse. Confer & ea, quæ ad c. 11. 1. jam se- quuntur.

## 10:29 Addition
To verse 29, towards the end. page 364. a.

Namely, until Pharaoh was compelled to summon him, and not merely to grant him departure from Egypt with the whole people, but to command it and to entreat it from him as if by request. There is therefore a prolepsis here with respect to the following chapter, or rather the words of chapter 11, 1, are to be rendered: For the Lord had said to Moses, that the Ju- nius, Tremellius, and Piscator render it as he had said: however, these words are not to be understood as being in the bush, as it seemed to some, as one may read in Polus. For the text clearly indicates that they were spoken only after the remaining plagues. Which is also observed in chapter 12, 1.

But as far as chapter 12, 31 is concerned, a distinction must be made between a voluntary approach, which Moses renounced, judging himself to be a profane and desperate King unworthy of being approached further, whom he knew would dismiss Israel ἑκοντ᾽ ἀεκόντι- γε θυμῷ without further solicitation: And between an approach that is demanded or obtained by request, concerning which chapter 12, verse 31 speaks. Thus Cornelius à Lapide and Menochius explain it here: I will not come to you of my own accord; I will not urge you, you will rather desire to see me, when you compel us to leave during the plague of the firstborn.

Latin:

Ad v. 29. sub finem. pag. 364. a.

Scilicet donec Pharao coactus fuit ipsum accer- sere, eique discessum ex Ægypto cum toto populo non concedere, sed imperare & ab eodem veluti precario efflagitare. Prolepsis ergo est hic respe- ctu capitis sequentis, aut potius verba cap. 11, 1. red- denda: Nam Dominus dixerat ad Mosen, uti Ju- nius, Tremellius, Piscator reddunt dixerat: non ta- men hæc dicta intelligenda sunt in rubo quod qui- busdam visum, uti legere est apud Polum. Nam post reliquas demum plagas dicta esse, luculenter textus indicat. Quod etiam cap. 12, 1. observatur.

Sed quod ad cap. 12, 31. attinet, distinguendum inter accessionem ultroneam, cui renunciavit Moses, se Regem phrophanum & desperatum indignum ju- dicare, quem ultra conveniat, quem ἑκοντ᾽ ἀεκόντι- γε θυμῷ sine ulteriori sollicitatione Israelem dimis- surum noverat: Et inter accessionem demandatam aut precario impetratam, de qua cap. 12. vers. 31. Sic Cornel à Lapid. & Menochius hic exponunt: Spon- te ad te non accedam; non urgebo, tu potius me vide- re desiderabis, quando in primogenitorum plaga nos exire compelles.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. The commanded despoiling, and the slaying of the firstborn.

Verse 1. AND HE SAID.
