Those words are to be understood either as an internal revelation of God, as we just said, or with Junius and Tremellius they are to be rendered in the pluperfect, 'and he had said': or causally, as the particle ו is sometimes taken, because he had said, so that these things may be referred to the preceding chapter as the cause of such boldness, why Moses had received that he would no longer deign to visit or address Pharaoh. Whence others not inconveniently read the first three verses as a parenthesis, so that verse 4, 'And Moses said,' coheres with the end of the preceding chapter: thus the matter will be resolved regarding the apparent contradiction in verse 29 of the preceding chapter.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Indicta spoliatio, & Primogenitorum occisio.

Vers. 1. ET DIXIT.

VErba illa vel de interna revelatione Dei, ut proxime diximus, intelligenda, vel cum Junio & Trem. in plusquamperfecto reddenda sunt, & dixerat: aut αἰτιολογικῶς, uti particula ו quandoque sumitur, quia dixerat, ut referantur hæc ad cap. præcedens, ceu causa tantæ παῤῥησίας, cur Moses receperit, se non amplius Pharaonem dignaturum visitatione, vel allocutione. Unde non incom- mode alii versus tres priores per parenthesin le- gunt, ut vers. 4. & ait Moses, cum fine capitis præ- cedentis cohæreat: sic res expedita erit, quoad con- tradictionem apparentem, vers. 29. cap. præce- dentis.

## 11:2
Verse 2. LET HIM ASK OF HIS NEIGHBOR.

In the Hebrew, 'from a neighbor'; vessels were not to be asked from friends only, but also from the masters whom the Hebrews perhaps served. Cornelius a Lapide thinks that the Israelites were ordered to ask for gold and silver vessels for this reason, that they needed them for sacrifice; he also adds garments, of which, however, nothing is held here in the Hebrew, even though the LXX add them from the following chapter, because they would have need of them for the sake of adornment at the solemn feast. But if God had commanded this, would He not have incited His people to a lie? There was no need for such a pretext, because God directed the hearts of the Egyptians so that they would not deny what was asked.

Latin:

Vers. 2. POSTULET AB AMICO SUO.

In Ebr. a proximo vel vicino; non ab amicis tantum vasa petenda erant, sed etiam a Dominis, quibus forte Ebræi serviebant. Corn. a Lap. hic ea ratione postulare jussos esse Israelitas vasa aurea & argentea existimat, quod illis indigerent ad sa- crificium, addit etiam vestes, de quibus vero hic in Ebræo nihil habetur, etsi LXX. eas adjiciant ex se- quenti capite, quod ornandi causa in festo solemni iisdem opus haberent. Sed si hoc jussisset Deus, an non an ad mendacium instinxisset populum suum? Non opus fuit tali prætextu, quia direxit Deus cor- da Ægyptiorum, ut non denegarent, quod postula- batur.

## 11:3
Verse 3. HE WILL GIVE FAVOR.

Since, therefore, God directed the hearts of the Egyptians so that they would gratify the Hebrews with vessels, the charge of theft (ἔγκλημα) cannot have a place here: for God wished not only to free his own people from tyranny, but also to provide for them and to grant them comforts for their poverty and need. And God must be considered here, not only as the supreme Lord of all things, whose is the earth and its fullness, but also as a just rewarder (ἀνταποδότης), who can demand from unjust masters the wages denied by them and pay them to his own, which the Lord performs justly, now in one way, now in another. He uses in this his own authority (αὐτεξοσίᾳ) and liberty. Therefore, Wis. 10:17 says: God sold the just the reward of their labors. The Egyptians also must be considered not only as debtors who had unjustly withheld wages from the Hebrews, but also as manifest enemies of the Jews, and since it is lawful to despoil such, there is no doubt that the Egyptians were justly despoiled. Augustine adds a third aspect of sacrilege in book 22 against Faustus, ch. 71. The Egyptians, he says, were sacrilegious and wicked, who, by using that gold—that is, God's creature—badly for the injury of the Creator, served their own idols, and had unjustly and vehemently afflicted foreign men with gratuitous labor. Therefore, both the Hebrews were worthy to be commanded such things, and the Egyptians to suffer such things. Wherefore, the blasphemy of the Manichaeans and Marcionites is to be detested, who impiously accused the God of the Old Testament, because of this command of his, as a promoter of frauds or thefts. Nor is there any reason for us to say with some that God dispensed here regarding the seventh commandment; since the present case does not fall under that commandment, nor were the Israelites obligated by it not to receive vessels from the Egyptians; for to demand and ask for wages, with the supreme Lord ordering and commanding it, and at the same time granting the favor so that it is not denied but rendered, is not to handle another's property against the will of the owner; but where there is no obligation, there is no place for a dispensation. Irenaeus beautifully says in book IV, ch. 49: the people were serving the Egyptians in the worst slavery, and when they exercised power over the sons of Israel and made their life hateful to them in hard works of clay and brick, what therefore was done unjustly if they took a few things from many, and those who could have had many possessions if they had not served them, and departed rich, having received very little wages for great slavery, departed needy: cf. Philo, book 1, On the Life of Moses. Yet there could be a doubt about the process, because they seemed to pretend, by divine command, as if they were asking for a loan at least, what they were about to take away. But because the most just and holy God himself prescribed the whole process, and no necessity demands that we say they used this scheme, that difficulty will be resolved if it is said that no such thing was prescribed to them that would bear the appearance of a lie, for what is rendered in the Vulgate in ch. 12:36, 'so that they lent to them,' is read in the Hebrew thus: 'and they made them ask'; which is that God gave such favor to the Israelites before the Egyptians that they voluntarily offered them their silver and gold vessels, inciting them to ask confidently for whatever they wanted, which was observed by Cajetan. But the Egyptians were not persuaded that the Israelites would depart entirely, never to return: nor had they received anything from the Israelites about that; although there could be a doubt even about these things, whether it was publicly known to all. Therefore they had no need of a lie or deceit to obtain those vessels, which Cornelius, in Jesuitical fashion, rubs off on them, that they astutely used the title of a loan, using it as a pretext for their just spoliation, yet without lying. But who are thus absolved from a lie? Let us hear: because, he says, they intended to return the loan, insofar as it was a loan; but because that loan was at the same time given to them by God, hence they intended to retain that same thing, not under the title of a loan, but of a gift. I would not reluctantly agree with Cornelius if I had learned equivocations in the Jesuit School. But whether one retains it under the title of a loan or a gift, he deceives; and when he asks for a loan but thinks to retain it, he lies; for he harbors one thing in his heart and testifies another with his words, and thus he deceived his neighbor through that equivocation of his. Tertullian, book 2 against Marcion, chapter 20, reports as if from ancient tradition that the Egyptians sent envoys to Moses and the Hebrews, who had crossed the Red Sea, to demand back those goods: but the Hebrews replied that they would return those vessels, provided that they themselves paid the wages for such a harsh and long servitude and so many labors; the sum of which, since it exceeded those gold and silver vessels, the Egyptians preferred to leave the vessels to them. But that tradition needs solid testimony. Therefore, let the credit rest with Tertullian. Josephus teaches that these were given to the Israelites so that they might depart more quickly, and because of their former familiarity. But Exodus 12:36 does not permit that, when they are said to have despoiled the Egyptians. And therefore one must insist on the former response, that nothing is held in the text about their having asked for them as a loan. Rivetus posits a dissimulation here, but says that nothing was said against the truth. For just as Moses wished to use the concession of leaving to offer sacrifice, so also the people wished to use the vessels and clothing of the Egyptians to the same end; the rest they hid from their enemies and committed the outcome to God, who, when He had declared the Egyptians to be enemies of His people, nay, His own, and was not yet willing for the people to reclaim their liberty and goods by arms, willed that they should use deceit against their defrauders. Thus Rivetus.

But let those who make God the author of sin, the Calvinists, impute the deceit to God: it is a matter of religion for us to presume such things about the most holy God. God did not command that they ask for the vessels as a loan with the purpose that they should use them for sacrifices, nor is there anything in Moses about this pretext, and therefore there is no place for deceit here: nay, a doubt still remains whether it was certain to the Israelites that they were leaving Egypt entirely: how then could they dissimulate about things concerning which nothing certain was known to them.

Finally, even if some dissimulation is admitted, deceit nevertheless should by no means be admitted, much less should it be conceded that deceit of such a kind was prescribed.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DABIT GRATIAM.

Cum ergo Deus corda direxerit Ægyptio- rum, ut vasa gratificarentur Ebræis, non potest hic furti ἔγκλημα locum habere: volebat enim Deus suos non liberare tantum a tyrannide, sed iisdem etiam providere, & egestatis, atque inopiæ solatia concedere. Et considerandus hic est Deus, non tantum, ut summus rerum omnium Dominus, cujus est terra & plenitudo ejus, sed etiam ut justus ἀνταποδότης, qui mercedem ab iniquis Dominis denegatam ab iisdem poscere, suisque rependere potest, quod modo hac, modo alia ratione, juste tamen præstat Dominus. Utitur in eo αὐτεξοσίᾳ & libertate sua. Ideo Sap. 10, 17. dicitur vendidit Deus justis mercedem laborum suorum. Ægyptii etiam considerari debent non tantum ut debitores, qui mercedem injuste detinuerant Ebræis, sed etiam ut manifesti hostes Judæorum, quales spoliare cum licitum sit, juste Ægyptios spoliatos fuisse, dubitandum non est. Addit August. tertium respe- ctum sacrilegii lib. 22. contra Faust. c. 71. Ægyptii, inquit, sacrilegi & iniqui erant, qui & auro illo, hoc est, Dei creatura male utentes ad creatoris in- juriam suis idolis serviebant, & homines peregrinos labore gratuito injuste & vehementer afflixerant. Digni ergo erant & Ebræi, quibus talia juberentur, & Ægyptii, qui talia paterentur. Quapropter de- testanda est Manichæorum blasphemia & Marcio- nitarum, qui Deum V. T. impie ceu fautorem fraudum aut furtorum accusabant, ex hoc ejus præcepto. Neque est quod dicamus cum qui- busdam Deum dispensasse hic circa septimum præce- ptum; siquidem casus præsens non cadat sub præ- ceptum illud, neque Israëlitæ per istud obligati fuerint, ne vasa ab Ægyptiis acciperent; merce- dem enim supremo Domino ordinante ac juben- te, simulque gratiam largiente, ut ea non denege- tur, sed reddatur, postulare, atque poscere, non est rem alienam invito Domino contrectare; ubi au- tem non est obligatio, ibi nec locum habet dispen- satio. Pulchre Irenæus lib. IV. c. 49. populus pessi- mam servitutem serviebat Ægyptiis, & cum illi po- testatem exercebant in filios Israel & in odium eis ad- ducebant vitam in operibus duris luto & latere, quid igitur injuste factum est, si ex multis pauca sumse- runt, & qui potuerunt multas substantias habere, si non serviissent eis, & divites abire, paucissimam mercedem pro magna servitute habentes, inopes abie- runt: conf. Philo lib. 1. de vit. Mos. De processu tamen dubium esse queat, quia videbantur præ se ferre ex mandato divino, ac si mutuo saltim peterent, quæ ablaturi erant. Sed quia totum processum Deus justissimus & sanctissimus ipse præscripsit, neque ulla postulat necessitas, ut dicamus, hoc schemate usos fuisse, difficultas illa expedietur, si dicatur tale quid ipsis præscriptum non fuisse, quod mendacii speciem præ se ferret, nam quod cap. 12, 36. in Vulgata redditur: ut commodarent eis, id in Ebræo ita legitur: & fecerunt petere eos; quod nempe gratiam Israëlitis dederit Deus tan- tam coram Ægyptiis, ut hi ultro obtulerint ipsis vasa sua argentea, & aurea, incitantes eosdem, ut confidenter peterent, quicquid vellent, quod Ca- jetano est observatum. Non vero persuasi erant Æ- gyptii, Israëlitas plane discessuros, nunquam rever- suros: neque de eo ab Israëlitis quicquam accepe- rant; quanquam & de his dubium esse queat, utrum id omnibus publice notum fuerit. Non ergo opus habebant mendacio, vel dolo vasa ista obtinere, quem Jesuitico more ipsis affricat Cornelius, quod astute titulo commodati usi sint, illum suæ spoliationi justæ prætexentes, neque tamen mentiti sint. Qui vero ita a mendacio absolvuntur? audiamus; quia com- modatum, inquit, in quantum commodatum erat, reddere intendebant; sed quia illud commodatum si- mul erat eis donatam a Deo, hinc illud idem retinere intendebant, non titulo commodati, sed donati. Assen- tirem non ægre Cornelio, si in Schola Jesuitica æ- quivocationes didicissem. Ast sive sub titulo com- modati sive donati quis id retineat, fallit; & cum commodato petit, at retinere cogitat, mentitur; aliud enim corde fovet, aliud verbis testatur, & ita decepit proximum per illam suam æquivocationem. Ter- tullian. lib. 2. contra Marcion. cap. 20. refert tan- quam ex antiqua traditione, quod Ægyptii ad Mosen & Ebræos, Mare rubrum transgressos, Le- gatos miserint, qui hæc bona repeterent: Ebræi au- tem responderint, se vasa illa reddituros, dummodo ipsi tam duræ & longæ servitutis & tot laborum mer- cedem solverint; cujus summa cum excederet vasa illa aurea & argentea, maluisse Ægyptios ipsis vasa relinquere. Sed ea traditio testimonio solido eget. Fides ergo esto penes Tertullianum. Jo- sephus docet, hæc Israëlitis donata esse, ut celerius discederent, & ob pristinam familiaritatem. Sed id non permittit Exod. 12, 36. cum spoliaffe dicun- tur Ægyptios. Ideoque priori responsioni in- sistendum, quod nihil in textu habeatur de eo, quod commodato petierint. Rivetus dissimula- tionem hic statuit, nihil autem dictum fuisse con- tra veritatem, ait. Nam quemadmodum Moses voluit uti concessione abeundi ad sacrificandum, sic etiam vasis & vestibus Ægyptiorum voluit uti populus in eundem finem, reliqua celarunt hostes suos & Deo commiserunt eventum, qui cum Ægy- ptios declarasset hostes populi sui, imo suos, nec adhuc vellet populum armis libertatem suam & bona repetere, voluit ut dolo contra fraudatores suos uterentur. Hæc Rivetus.

Sed dolum Deo imputent, qui Deum peccati autorem faciunt Calvinistæ: nobis religio est, talia de Deo sanctissimo præsumere. Non jussit Deus, ut commodato peterent vasa eo fine, ut ad sacrificia iis uterentur, nec de hoc prætextu quicquam in Mose habetur, ideoque dolo hic locus non est: imo dubium adhuc superest, an Israëlitis de omnimoda desertione Ægypti constiterit: quomodo ergo dis- simulare id poterant, de quibus nihil certi ipsis constabat.

Denique etsi admittatur aliqua dissimulatio, do- lus tamen nullatenus admitti debet, multo minus concedendum, dolum ejusmodi præscriptum fuisse.

## 11:4
Verse 4. AT MIDNIGHT I WILL GO OUT.

Some say this slaughter was done by a good angel, Pererius, Cornelius, Rivetus; others by an evil one, with Lyranus and Abulensis, ch. 12, 13. And it is likely that it was not just one angel, but several, because the slaughter was done throughout the whole kingdom of Egypt. Furthermore, here the Lord Himself makes Himself the author of the slaughter of the firstborn of Egypt, He who was the savior of the firstborn of His people. Cf. verses 12, 13, 14, 27, 29, whom the Targum calls THE WORD, and who according to the faith of the Israelite Church, Sirach 18, was ὁ παντοδύναμος λόγος τꭣ θεꭣ. But whether the ministry of angels, whether good or evil, intervened in that slaughter of the Egyptians and the preservation of the Israelites is doubtful. For no mention of an angel is made here: only in verse 13 is it commemorated, נגף למשחית, a plague for destruction. & v. 23, He will not allow DESTRUCTION, or a destroying plague, to come into the houses to kill, nor is anything else held in Ps. 78:49 than that מלאכי רעים (but not מלאכים רעים) were employed in these Egyptian plagues, with no restriction made to the slaughter of the firstborn, of which the Psalmist treats only afterwards. Whence the ministry of angels can be looked at in the preceding plagues of hail, thunders, and lightnings, etc. Add that God Himself, Gen. 19:14, is called המשחית or ὀλοθρευτὴς: from whom, however, if in this place because of v. 23 ὀλοθρευτὴς is distinguished, and that word המשחית is understood not in the abstract concerning destruction, but substantively concerning a destroying subject, or one devastating directly from God, or sent by Him, it would be clearly undoubted that it was an evil angel, since the Angel of the Lord is expressed by the same name in 1 Chron. 21:15, 16, who was a good angel. Nevertheless, I see no reason why one should depart from the more received opinion concerning the evil exterminating angel: whom God, the Savior of the Israelites, did not allow to touch their houses.

Latin:

Vers. 4. MEDIA NOCTE EGREDIAR.

Cædem hanc alii per angelum bonum factam dicunt Perer. Corn. Rivet. alii per malum, cum Lyrano, & Abul. c. 12, 13. Neque unum tantum angelum, sed plures, quia per totum Ægypti re- gnum cædes facta, ita fuisse vero simile est. Cæte- rum hic Dominus ipse se autorem facit cædis pri- mogenitorum Ægypti, qui servator primoge- nitorum populi fuit. Conf. vers. 12. 13. 14. 27. 29. quem Targum VERBUM vocat, quique se- cundum fidem Israëlitiæ Ecclesiæ Sir. 18. fuit ὁ παντοδύναμος λόγος τꭣ θεꭣ. Num autem Mini- sterium Angelorum sive bonorum sive malorum in illa & cæde Ægyptiorum, & conservatione Israe- litarum intervenerit, dubium est. Non enim hic mentio angeli fit: commemoratur solum v. 13. נגף למשחית plaga ad perditionem. & v. 23. non con- cedet PERDITIONEM, vel plagam perdentem, ut veniat in domus ad interficiendum, neque Ps. 78, 49. aliud quid habetur, quam quod מלאכי רעים (non autem מלאכים רעים) adhibiti in hisce pla- gis Ægyptiacis, nulla restrictione ad cædem primo- genitorum facta, de qua postmodum demum Psal- tes agit. Unde respici potest ministerium ange- lorum in præcedentibus plagis grandinis, toni- truorum & fulminum &c. Adde, quod Deus ipse Gen. 19, 14. המשחית vel ὀλοθρευτὴς dicatur: a quo tamen si hoc loco ob v. 23. ὀλοθρευτὴς distinguitur & vox illa המשחית non in abstracto de perditione, sed substantive de supposito perdente, vel vastante a Deo directo, vel immisso intelligatur, angelum malum eum fuisse, plane indubium foret, quum eodem nomine Angelus Domini exprimatur 1. Chron. 21, 15. 16. qui bonus fuit angelus. Nihil tamen causæ video, cur a receptiori de Angelo malo exterminatore sententia discedendum sit : quem Deus Israelitarum Sospitator eorum domus attingere non concessit.

## 11:5
Verse 5. EVERY FIRSTBORN.

By firstborn, some understand not only infants, but all who were the first-born of their parents, even if they were heads of families. Whence they conclude that Pharaoh, because he was not the firstborn, was not a case: nay, Abulensis adds that the name of firstborn includes females equally as males, and firstborn in respect to one or both parents. But it does not seem that this name should be extended that far, since the circumstances teach that infants are designated, and Theodoret rightly warns that the Egyptians were justly punished by the slaughter of the firstborn, for the reason that they had oppressed the firstborn people of God and killed their male offspring. But it is a doubt, how could innocent infants be punished without prejudice to the justice of God? Cornelius answers: God is the Lord of the guilty and the innocent, of life and of death, so that He does not unjustly take away life from the innocent, as Lord, but most justly takes away life from the guilty, as the avenger of evils. But divine power alone does not cause life to be justly taken from the innocent: for since punishment presupposes guilt, justice does not permit that where there is no guilt, punishment should be inflicted. More correctly, therefore, it is denied that the infants were innocent; for they were infected with original sin, and thus by nature children of wrath, and since they were a part of their rebellious fathers, in them the fathers themselves were justly punished.

Verse same. FROM THE FIRSTBORN OF PHARAOH, WHO SITS ON HIS THRONE)

That is, who was to sit, according to that law of nations, concerning which see the testimonies in the book On the Law of War and Peace, II, ch. 7, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. OMNE PRIMOGENITUM.

Per primogenitos nonnulli intelligunt non tantum infantes, sed omnes, qui primi nati e parentibus suis erant, etiamsi essent Patres-familias. Unde colligunt Pharaonem, quia casus non est, primogenitum non fuisse : imo addit Abulensis primogeniti nomen fœminas æque ac mares complecti & primogenitos sive unius, sive utriusque parentis respectu. Sed non videtur eo usque hoc nomen extendendum, cum circumstantiæ doceant, infantes designari, & recte moneat Theodoretes, juste puniri Ægyptios primogenitorum cæde, ideo, quod primogenitum Dei populum oppressissent & prolem masculam eorum interemerint. Dubium autem est, qui infantes innocentes puniri potuerint salva Dei justitia? Respondet Cornelius : Deus est fontium & infontium, vitæ & mortis Dominus, ut insontibus non injuste vitam adimat, ut Dominus, fontibus vero justissime vitam eripiat, ut vindex malorum. Verum sola divina potestas non facit, ut innocentibus vita juste adimatur : quum enim pœna culpam præsupponat, justitia non permittit, ut ubi culpa nulla est, pœna infligatur. Rectius ergo negatur, innocentes fuisse parvulos; erant enim originali peccato infecti, & ita natura iræ filii, & quum pars aliqua fuerit patrum rebellium, in illis juste Patres ipsi puniebantur.

Vers. eod. A PRIMOGENITO PHARAONIS, QVI SEDET IN SOLIO EJUS)

Id est, qui sessurus erat, ex jure illo gentium, de quo testimonia vide lib. de jure belli, & pacis II. c. 7, 13.

## 11:7
Verse 7. NOT A DOG SHALL GROWL FROM MAN EVEN TO BEAST) A proverbial expression.

The sense of the proverbial expression is: no man, no beast shall be harmed, so that there is need to growl, nor shall even a dog, which is accustomed to bark at the slightest noise, growl; for there shall be total peace among all.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NON MUTIET CANIS AB HOMINE USQVE AD PECUS) Proverbiale.

Sensus proverbialis loquutionis est; nemo hominum, nullum pecus lædetur, ut mutire opus habeat, nec canis quidem, qui minimo strepitu latrare solet, mutiet; summa enim pax apud omnes erit.

## 11:8
Verse 8. AND ALL THE PEOPLE WHO ARE SUBJECT TO THEE)

In Greek: καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαός σε ὧ͂ σύ ἀφηγῆ. The Hebrew word for word: Who are at thy feet. Agrætius, the services of servants are 'at the feet': unless perhaps here, before the change of one letter which is very similar, it was בדגליך, under thy banners.

Grotius suspects that perhaps it was written differently here in the past: But why should it not have been written as the Hebrew truth still has it, ברגליך, under thy feet? If the original text is to be changed or read otherwise according to anyone's suspicions, since those could be numberless, it will truly be a nose of wax, which the Papists desire, and some of them have not feared to pronounce the same. But what certainty of the principle of faith and of the highest, indeed the only, religion will then remain, since it is permitted to suspect other oracles of Scripture for a like reason?

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET OMNIS POPULUS, QVI SUBJECTUS EST TIBI)

Græce καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαός σε ὧ͂ σύ ἀφηγῆ. Hebræa verbotenus : Qui in pedibus tuis. Agrætius, circumpedes sunt officia servorum: nisi forte hic fuerit ante literæ unius valde similis factam mutationem בדגליך, sub vexillis tuis.

Grotius suspicatur, forte hic fuisse aliter olim scriptum : Sed cur non ita scriptum fuerit, uti etiamnum habet Ebræa veritas ברגליך sub pedibus tuis? Si juxta cujusvis suspiciones textus originalis immutandus, aut secus legendus, quum illæ innumeræ esse possint, vere nasus cereus erit, quod optant Papistæ, & de eodem pronunciare nonnulli ex ipsis haud veriti sunt. At quæ ita certitudo principii fidei & religionis summi, imo unici restabit, quum parili ratione suspicari de aliis Scripturæ oraculis liceat?

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. The Passover. The striking of the firstborn. Exodus. Verse 1. THE LORD ALSO SAID.

It seems it should be rendered in the pluperfect: he had said, or a hysteron proteron must be posited, because Moses wished to continue and complete the history of the plagues, even though these things had been said to him by the Lord before he announced the final plague to Pharaoh. For they are commanded

The Israelites were to take a lamb on the 10th day of the first month to be sacrificed on the 14th day: whence it seems to be concluded that these things were said before the tenth day, and before the slaughter made on the fifteenth day, indeed even before its announcement, which the slaughter of the firstborn immediately followed on the next middle night.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. Pascha. Percussio primogenitorum. Exodus. Vers. 1. DIXIT QVOQVE DOMINUS.

Reddendum videtur in plusquamperfecto: dixerat, vel ponenda ὑςερολογία, quia continuare & absolvere historiam plagarum volebat Moses, etsi hæc dicta ipsi fuerint a Domino antequam ultimam plagam Pharaoni denunciaret. Jubentur enim

Israelitæ die 10. mensis primi tollere agnum 14. die immolandum : unde concludendum videtur, quod hæc dicta fuerint ante decimum diem, & ante cædem decimo quinto die factam, imo ante ejus denunciationem, hanc etiam statim sequebatur nocte proxima media cædes primogenitorum.

## 12:2
Verse 2. THIS MONTH SHALL BE UNTO YOU THE BEGINNING OF MONTHS; IT SHALL BE THE FIRST MONTH OF THE YEAR TO YOU.

From this it is gathered that the month Nisan, so called by a Chaldean word, which corresponds to our March and in part also to April, which Josephus says was called Xanticus by the Greeks and Pharmuthi by the Egyptians, was the beginning of the year. The Hebrews called it אָבִיב, which word denotes a stalk with an ear, because in Egypt the barley was then in the ear, Exod. 9, 31. Furthermore, it could seem, from ch. 23, 16. (which not a few also judge) that Tisri was previously the first month, which word Josephus observes denotes the beginning to the Chaldeans; but in the Aruch, Tisri is derived from שׁרָה, to dissolve, because in it all sins were dissolved on the feast of atonement, nor is the month Tisri to be held as the first or the beginning of the year except in a certain sense and with a certain respect. Indeed, the common and political year did not begin from the autumnal equinox, but from that month Tisri, which corresponds to our September and October, in which Buxtorf notes in his Lexicon Talmudicum under the word Tisri that the entire Hebrew nation used to assemble; Jerome records in ch. 1 of Ezekiel that all Orientals consider the month of October as the first month of the year. And so thus began the distinction of the political or common year among the Jews, which began in the month of Tisri, and served for calculating jubilees, Lev. 25, 9, as well as for contracts and secular business, concerning which see Josephus, book 1, ch. 4, and of the ecclesiastical year, which began in the month of Nisan in memory of the liberation from Egypt: but the Hebrews received these names of the months from the Chaldeans during the Babylonian captivity: whereas otherwise they only indicated them according to the number of the months, the first, the second, etc. they indicated them, therefore these names are not read except in books written after the Babylonian captivity, such as in Zechariah, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.

Latin:

Vers. 2. MENSIS ISTE VOBIS PRINCIPIUM MEN- SIUM PRIMUS ERIT IN MENSIBUS ANNI.

Ex eo colligitur, quod Mensis Nisan, Chal- daica voce sic dictus, qui nostro Martio, ex parte etiam Aprili respondet, quem Josephus a Græcis Xanticum, ab Ægyptiis Pharmuti vocatum dicit, principium anni fuerit. Ebræi appellarunt אָבִיב, quæ vox culmum cum spica notat, quod in Ægypto tunc hordeum esset spicatum, Exod. 9, 31. Cæterum videri posset, e c. 23, 16. (quod etiam non pauci cen- sent) antea primum mensem fuisse Tisri, quam vocem Chaldæis initium notare observat Josephus; sed in Aruch, Tisri a שׁרָה disfolvit, derivatur, quod in eo disfoluta fuerint omnia peccata in festo expia- tionis, nec nisi secundum quid ac certo respectu mensis Tisri primus habendus vel anni initium. Nimirum annus communis & politicus non ab au- tumnali æquinoctio, sed ab isto mense Tisri, qui Septembri, & Octobri nostro respondet, inchoaba- tur apud Judæos, in quo universam nationem Ebræam convenire notat Buxtorf. in Lex. Talm. voce Tisri; omnes Orientales mensem Octobrem habere pro primo anni mense Hieron. tradit in c. 1. Ezech. Sic itaque cœpit discrimen anni politici vel commu- nis apud Judæos, qui mense Tisri inchoabatur, & serviebat jubilæis computandis Lev. 25, 9. ut & con- tractibus & negotiis secularibus, de quo vid. Joseph. lib. 1. c. 4. & anni Ecclesiastici, qui Mense Nisan in memoriam liberationis ex Ægypto cœpit: hæc ve- ro mensium nomina a Chaldæis in captivitate Baby- lonica accepere Ebræi : cum alias tantum secun- dum numerum mensium primum, secundum &c. indigitarint, ideo non leguntur ista nomina nisi in libris scriptis post captivitatem Babylonicam, utpote in Zacharia, Esdra, Nehem. & Esther.

## 12:2 Addition
To Exod. 12, 2. page 366. a.

This is according to the common opinion. Which is especially approved by Scaliger and his followers, and among the interpreters by Fagius, Vatablus, Junius, Ainsworth, Lightfoot, Mariana, Cornelius à Lapide, Bonfrerius, and add also Bochart. But that distinction of the civil and ecclesiastical year is not taken from the Sacred Scriptures; indeed, it should rather be reckoned among the inventions of the Jews, nor is a new beginning of the year instituted here, but since the Israelites in Egypt had to accommodate themselves to the laws of the kingdom in the counting of months, it is now recalled to the ancient custom of the Patriarchs. Concerning which we have expounded our Φροντίδας δευτέ- ρας in the Chronicle, in these later annotations on Exodus, Sect. 1. Quest. 5. page 38. Which observation concerning our sacred Chronicle will perhaps also have its use in other annotations.

Latin:

Ad Exod. 12, 2. pag. 366. a.

Hæc ex sententia vulgari. Quæ Scaligero & sectatoribus imprimis probata, & ex Interpreti- bus Fagio, Vatablo, Junio, Ainsworth, Ligtfoth, Mariana, Cornelio à Lapide, Bonfrerio, adde & Bochartum. Sed distinctio illa anni civilis & Ec- clesiastici non è Sacris deprompta, imo Judæorum potius commentis accensenda est, nec hic novum instituitur anni initium, sed cum in Ægypto Israe- litæ sese legibus regni accommodare debuerint in computo mensium, ad pristinum Patriarcharum morem jam revocatur. Quo de Φροντίδας δευτέ- ρας in Chronico, annotatis hisce in Exodum poste- riori, exposuimus, Sect. 1. Quæst. 5. pag. 38. Quæ observatio de Chronico nostro sacro forte etiam in aliis annotatis usum suum habitura est.

## 12:3
Verse 3. ON THE TENTH DAY OF THIS MONTH EVERY MAN SHALL TAKE A LAMB.

The lamb had to be separated four days before the immolation or slaughter, so that the Israelites might then compose themselves for the departure, and have it in readiness to celebrate the passover, indeed so that by the sight and voice of the lamb they might be warned of the imminent departure. However, it is doubtful whether this rite was always observed afterwards or whether it ought to have been observed, which Abulensis, Lyranus, and Pererius deny, and it is likewise denied by the Hebrews; nor does it seem that it could have been so observed, especially where they had to assemble at Jerusalem from all places, as was done under Josiah, 2 Chron. 35. It was a type of Christ, 1 Cor. 5, 7, who had to be, as it were, separated and sanctified for the slaughter for us, through the entry made into the city of Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, four days before the Lord's passion.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DECIMA DIE MENSIS HUJUS TOLLET UNUSQUISQUE AGNUM.

Separari debuit agnus quatriduo ante immola- tionem, vel mactationem, ut deinde se ad exitum componerent Israelitæ, illumque in promtu habe- rent ad pascha celebrandum, imo ut agni aspectu ac voce de exitu imminente monerentur. Dubium autem est, num semper postea hic ritus observatus fuerit aut observari debuerit, quod negat Abulensis, Lyranus & Pererius, & ab Ebræis pariter negatur; neque videtur ita observari potuisse, maxime, ubi Hierosolymam ex omnibus locis convenire de- buerunt, uti sub Josia factum, 2. Chron. 35. Typus erat Christi 1. Cor. 5, 7. qui separari quasi debebat, & sanctificari ad mactationem pro nobis, per in- gressum in urbem Jerusalem factum Dominica Pal- marum quatriduo ante passionem Domini.

## 12:5
Verse 5. A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH) שֶׂה signifies offspring of both the goat and the sheep kind.

Therefore it cannot be rendered by one Latin word. The LXX took the name more broadly as πρόβατον. תָּמִים is τέλειον in the LXX, others say ἄμωμον. In the same sense Lucian said ἐντελῆ θυσίαν concerning sacrifices. You have the explanation of this word in Lev. ch. 22, v. 22, 23, 24, Deut. 15, 21, ch. 17, v. 1. For the Latin here called a blemish a bodily defect, or disease, as it was in the Aedilitian edict. The Egyptians, as Chaeremon testifies, did not admit ὅσα δίδυμα, ἢ κατάσπιλα, ἢ ἑτερόχροα, ἢ παραλλάσσοντα τῇ μορφῇ. Porphyry, 2 On Abstinence: οὐδὲν γὰρ μᾶλλον ἕτω ἢ τὰ ἀνάπηρα θυτέον. The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Acharnians: and from him Suidas τὰ γὰρ κόλοβα ἐν ταῖς ἱερευγίας & θύειν, καὶ καθόλκ ὅπερ ἦ μὴ τέλεον καὶ ὑγιὲς ἐ θύεται τοῖς Θεοῖς, Athenaeus from the Aristotelian symposium: ἐδὲν κολοβὸν προσφέρομεν πρὸς τὰς Θεὲς, ἀλλὰ πάντα τέλεια καὶ ὅλα. Hence the custom of testing victims among Philo, among Aristotle, as Athenaeus praises in book XV, among Cicero in II against Rullus. Lucian on Sacrifices: 'Having crowned the animal and, long before that, having examined whether it is perfect, so that they might not slaughter and bring to the altar anything useless.'

Thus the Vulgate could indeed be excused here, had it not used the word for lamb in a special sense, and furthermore, because what is in the Hebrew, 'from the sheep, AND, that is, or (as the particle Vav is wont sometimes to be taken) from the goats you shall take'; thus, from ignorance of the use of this copulative particle in a disjunctive sense, which Theodoret observes here, he would have interpreted it according to which rite 'you shall take also a kid': from which version, as Steuchus admits, some falsely believed that two distinct sacrifices of a lamb and a kid were commanded here. The Chaldean and Greek Metaphrasts, and commentators both Rabbinical and others, observe that a sheep, or if anyone lacks one, a kid, ought to have been sacrificed alternatively. Therefore, Cajetan corrects the Vulgate here. The Hebrew words properly sound thus: 'It shall be a male animal, from the lambs or from the goats you shall take it.' Whence Burgensis wrongly denies that a kid was used in the absence of a lamb. Moreover, this was enjoined upon every head of a household, that he should take and slaughter a lamb; if, however, the family was not sufficient for the eating of the lamb, he joined himself to another, because the lamb had to be eaten whole. But why did God choose a lamb? That was not done because of the Egyptians, as Lyra wishes, because they worshipped Jupiter in the figure of a ram, for thus a calf or a ram would have had to be used; but because the lamb is a clean and simple animal, and it refers to the type of Christ, Is. 53:7. To which the tradition of the Hebrews contributes, that the Messiah, on the same day on which they themselves were liberated, would bring full liberty to the Hebrews from Egypt through the Passover. See Masius on Jos. 5:10. But understand that 'WITHOUT BLEMISH' refers to the blemish of deformity, lameness, or scab, not to a blemish of color, cf. Lev. 22:21, because it had to be a type of the holiness, innocence, and perfection of Christ, Is. 53, 1 Pet. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 5. AGNUS ABSQUE MACULA) שֶׂה tam de caprugno

quam de ovillo genere partum significat. Itaque una voce La- tina reddi nequit. LXX. laxius nomen sumpsere πρόβατον. תָּמִים τέλειον LXX. alii ἄμωμον. Eodem sensu ἐντελῆ θυσίαν dixit Lucianus de sacrificiis. Explicationem hujus vocis ha- bes Lev. cap. 22. v. 22. 23. 24. Deut. 15, 21. c. 17. v. 1. Ma- culam enim hic Latinus dixit corporis vitium, aut morbum, ut in Ædilitio erat edicto. Ægyptii, teste Chæremone, non admittebant ὅσα δίδυμα, ἢ κατάσπιλα, ἢ ἑτερόχροα, ἢ παραλ- λάσσοντα τῇ μορφῇ. Porphyrius 2. de Abstinentia : οὐδὲν γὰρ μᾶλλον ἕτω ἢ τὰ ἀνάπηρα θυτέον. Aristophanis Scholiaste ad Acharnenses: & ex eo Suidas τὰ γὰρ κόλοβα ἐν ταῖς ἱερευ- γίας & θύειν, καὶ καθόλκ ὅπερ ἦ μὴ τέλεον καὶ ὑγιὲς ἐ θύεται τοῖς Θεοῖς, Athenæus ex Aristotelico symposio : ἐδὲν κολοβὸν προσφέρομεν πρὸς τὰς Θεὲς, ἀλλὰ πάντα τέλεια καὶ ὅλα. Hinc mos probandi victimas apud Philonem, apud Aristotelem, laudante Athenæo lib. XV. apud Cic. II. contra Rullum. Lucianus de Sacrificiis : ςεφανώσαντες τὸ ζῶον καὶ πολύ γε πρότερον ἐξετάσαντες εἰ ἐντελὲς, ἵνα μηδὲ τῶν ἀχρήςων τι, κα- τασφάττωσι προσάγωσι τῷ βωμῷ.

Ita excusari quidem hic Vulgatus posset, nisi speciali significatu vocem agni adhibuisset, ac por- ro, quod in Ebræo habetur, quem ex ovibus, ET, id est, aut (uti solet particula Vav quandoque ac- cipi) ex capris accipietis; ita ex ignorantia usus hu- jus particulæ copulativæ, sensu disjunctivo, quem Theodoretus hic observat, interpretatus esset, juxta quem ritum tolletis & hædum: e qua versione saten- te Steucho, nonnulli duo distincta sacrificia agni, & hædi hic præcipi falso credidere. Chaldæi, & Græ- ci Metaphrastæ, ac commentatores tum Rabbinici, tum alii alternative ovem, aut si quis ea careat, hæ- dum immolari debuisse, observant. Ideo corrigit hic Vulgatam Cajetanus. Ebræa proprie ita sonant: Erit pecus mascula, ex agnis, aut ex hædis accipietis eam. Unde perperam negat Burgensis, in defectu agni adhibitum fuisse hædum. Unicuique autem Patrifamilias hoc injungebatur, ut agnum tolleret, & mactaret, si tamen familia non sufficiebat agni comestioni, alteri se jungebat, quia agnus integer erat comedendus. Cur autem agnum elegit Deus? Factum id non ob Ægyptios, ut Lyra vult, quod il- li Jovem in figura arietis coluerint, sic enim vitulus vel aries adhibendus fuisset; sed quia agnus est ani- mal mundum & simplex, & typum Christi refert Es. 53, 7. quo facit traditio Ebræorum, Messiam eo- dem die, quo ipsi liberati sunt, per Pascha ex Ægy- pto plenam libertatem Ebræis allaturum. Vid. Ma- sius in Jos. 5, 10. Illud vero ABSQVE MACULA intellige de macula deformitatis, claudicationis, sca- biei, non de macula coloris, conf. Lev. 22, 21. quia typus esse debebat sanctitatis, innocentiæ & perfectio- nis Christi Es. 53. 1. Pet. 2.

## 12:6
Verse 6.

AND YOU SHALL KEEP IT) So that its appearance might prepare men for the sacred rites. Cf. what we said at verse 3 regarding the reasons why it had to be separated four days before the slaughter.

Same verse. AND SHALL SLAUGHTER IT.

From this the Pontificals conclude that the Paschal lamb was a victim and its slaughter was an expiatory sacrifice, which they afterwards draw to the sacrament of the Supper, that it likewise is a sacrifice, provided that the Paschal lamb was a type of the Sacrament of the Supper. But the Pontificals have not yet given proof that the Paschal lamb was a type of the Holy Eucharist; the Fathers do indeed sometimes call it so, but improperly, because something similar was shadowed forth there of that which is exhibited in the Holy Supper, not by reason of slaughter and oblation, but by reason of eating, and our people also sometimes use the name of type here; others, however, deny that the proper definition of a type intervenes here, for although the Lord's Supper has succeeded into the place of the Paschal lamb, it has not succeeded as a body into the place of a figure, but the Paschal lamb was rather a type of Christ, slaughtered for us 1. Cor. 5:7, and therefore the blessed Chemnitius denies that the Paschal Lamb was a type of the Eucharist. Bellarmine, however, appeals against him to the passage 1 Cor. 5:7, but nothing else is taught there than what we have said, that the slaughter of the lamb was a type of the slaughter of Christ, which certainly does not take place in the Holy Supper, but was done once on the altar of the cross. Bellarmine urges those words: 'therefore let us feast in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth': but he does not prove, nor can he prove, that they are properly and directly the feast of the Eucharist to look, since it is rather intimated that the whole Christian life is figuratively represented by the seven days of unleavened bread through this Apostolic allegation, as Estius acknowledges in his Commentary. The sense is, he says, that a life of unleavened bread is deservedly required of you, since our Paschal lamb has been sacrificed, namely Christ sacrificed for us and offered on the altar of the cross, etc. Furthermore, even if it had been a type of the Eucharist, it is not therefore necessary that what is in the type must immediately be found also in the antitype. Finally, we deny that the Paschal lamb was a sacrifice in the true sense; for as to the word שָׁחַט which is used in this place, it is wrongly rendered by the Vulgate as 'sacrificed' [immolavit], since it generally denotes slaughtering and killing, not only of sacrificial victims, but also common and profane ones, just as the word θύω, and θυσία 1 Sam. 28, 24; Matt. 22, 4; Mark 14, 12; Luke 15, 23; so also the Hebrew word Num. 11, 2. Hos. 5, 2. Nor is the Paschal lamb called a sacrifice anywhere in the Scriptures; if mention of a sacrifice occurs anywhere, the discourse is about the sacrifices connected to this sacrament, but the Paschal lamb itself is not called a sacrifice. For the definition and nature of a sacrifice does not fit it: because in every sacrifice the thing that is slaughtered is offered to God, either in whole or in part. But the Paschal lamb was slaughtered not to be offered to God, but to be eaten, because while its blood was indeed sprinkled on the doorposts, the Israelites ate all of its flesh. And therefore it indeed had the nature of a sacrament, but by no means that of a sacrifice. Add that sacrifices had to be slaughtered by priests; but the slaughtering of the lamb was done not by priests—which Claudius Xanctes, Tostatus, and Serarius affirm in vain—but by the heads of families, as this Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges along with Philo and Suarez, refuting Abulensis and Serrarius; since in the first Passover priests had not yet been instituted, and in the ancient law the heads of families remained [the ones to do it] afterwards, which Lyranus also reports on book 2 of Chronicles ch. 30, and Cajetan, as well as Bellarmine, book 1 on the Mass, ch. 7, that the head of the family slaughtered it himself, and the rest of the family [did so] through the head of the family. Furthermore, sins were laid upon sacrifices, but not so upon the Paschal lamb. Sacrifices were burned in the courtyards of the temple upon the altar, and that with sacred fire. Which was not done in the case of the Paschal lamb; for it had to be roasted with fire. Finally, sacrifices were bound to a certain place, and were not to be offered except at Jerusalem. But the Passover or the Paschal lamb was not bound precisely to a certain place, or to the Jerusalem temple; indeed, it was celebrated in private houses. And therefore it is by no means to be admitted that the Paschal lamb was a sacrifice properly so called. Meanwhile, some of our side concede that something sacrificial obtained in this sacrament, on account of a certain analogy which intervenes with sacrifices, from which, however, a sacrifice properly so called, and an expiatory one at that, cannot be concluded. See B. Franzius in Schol. Sacrific., to whose arguments Cloppenburgius responds in vain in his Schola sacrific. p. 143.

Verse of the same.

AT EVENING) In the Hebrew, between the two evenings, that is, between the beginning and the end, around the tenth hour of the day.

Therefore not at night, as Lipp. wants, but the slaughtering took place about two hours before sunset, around sunset Matt. 14, 15, 23, because after sunset, when the 15th day began, the Paschal lamb was eaten. Josephus, book 16 of Antiquities, ch. 20, as also book 7 of the Jewish War, ch. 17, teaches that the lambs were slaughtered or killed from the ninth hour, i.e., our third hour post-meridian, until the 11th, because the rite of slaughtering, roasting, and eating lasted until then. See Cajetan, Perer. on this place, Masius on Josh. 5, 10, Jansenius in Concord. Evangel. ch. 145. Hence it is that the Jews, and Christ, are said to have celebrated the Passover sometimes on the 14th and sometimes on the 15th day among the Ancients. The Jews define this time between the two evenings as between the sun sitting on the western horizon and the sun's absence from our sight: But how could the lamb be killed, gutted, roasted, prepared, and eaten in this narrow space of time? It is added that in the inclination of Palestine under the elevation of the pole at 32, twilight lasts for a short time. But this time is BETWEEN EVENING AND EVENING, which is between the evening oblation and sunset: Thus clearly Josephus: ἐνςάσης ἑορτῆς πάσχα καλεῖται, καθ' ὃ θύεσα μὲν ἀπὸ ἐνάτης ὥρας μετὰ ἑνδεκάτην. See Exod. 29, 41.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET SERVABITIS EUM) Ut ejus aspectus homines sa- cris præpararet. Conf. quæ ad vers. 3. diximus, de causis, cur quatriduo ante immolationem separari debuerit.

Vers. eodem. IMMOLAVITQVE EUM.

Ex eo concludunt Pontif. agnum Paschalem fuisse victimam ejusque immolationem fuisse sa- crificium expiatorium, quod postea trahunt ad sa- cramentum Cœnæ, quod illud pariter sacrificium sit, siquidem agnus Paschalis typus fuerit Sacramenti Cœnæ. Verum nondum probatum dedere Pon- tificii agnum Paschalem typum fuisse S. Eucharistiæ; Vocant quidem ita quandoque Patres, sed ἀκύρως, quod simile quid ibi adumbratum fuerit ejus, quod exhibetur in S. cœna, non ratione immola- tionis & oblationis, sed ratione manducationis, & utuntur etiam hic typi nomine nonnunquam nostra- tes; alii tamen negant propriam typi rationem hic intervenire, etsi enim in locum agni Paschalis suc- cesserit Cœna Domini, non tamen tanquam cor- pus successit in locum figuræ, sed paschalis agnus ty- pus potius fuit Christi, pro nobis mactati 1. Cor. 5, 7. ideoque negat B. Chemnitius, Paschalem Agnum Eucharistiæ typum fuisse. Provocat autem adversus eum Bellarm. ad locum 1. Cor. 5, 7. sed ibi nihil aliud docetur, quam quod diximus, mactationem agni typum fuisse mactationis Christi, quæ certe non sit in S. cœna; sed facta semel est in ara crucis. Urget Bellarm. verba illa: itaque epulemur in azymis sinceritatis & veritatis: sed non probat, nec proba- re potest ea proprie & directe epulum Eucharistiæ spectare, cum potius vitam omnem Christianam figurate per azymorum septem dies hac allegatione Apostolica repræsentari innuatur, ut agnoscit Estius in Commentario. Sensus est, inquit, merito vitam azymam a vobis exigi, quandoquidem agnus noster Paschalis immolatus est, nempe Christus pro nobis immolatus & in ara crucis oblatus &c. Porro etiamsi fuisset typus Eucharistiæ, non tamen illico id quod in typo est, statim etiam in antitypo reperiri necessum est. Denique negamus, agnum Paschalem fuisse sacrificium veri nominis; nam quod ad verbum שָׁחַט quod h. l. adhibetur, id perperam a Vulg. redditur, immolavit, cum generaliter mactationem & jugulationem notet non tantum hostiarum, sed etiam communem & profanam uti verbum θύω, & θυσία 1. Sam. 28, 24. Matth. 22, 4. Marc. 14, 12. Luc. 15, 23. ita & vox Ebræa Num. 11, 2. Os. 5, 2. neque uspiam in scripturis agnus paschalis vocatur sacrificium; si alicubi sacrificii occurrit mentio, de sacrificiis, connexis huic sacramento, sermo est, non vero ipse agnus paschalis sacrificium nuncupatur. Neque enim convenit ei ratio & natura sacrificii: quia in omni sacrificio res, quæ mactatur, offertur Deo, vel in totum vel ex parte. Agnus autem paschalis mactabatur non ut offerretur Deo, sed ut manducaretur, quia sanguine quidem ipsius aspergebantur postes, carnem vero ejus totam manducabant Israelitæ. Ideoque sacramenti quidem rationem habebat, neutiquam autem sacrificii. Adde quod sacrificia a sacerdotibus mactari debuerint; at mactatio agni non a sacerdotibus, quod frustra Claudius Xanctes, Tostatus & Serarius affirmant, sed a Patribus-familias facta est, ut cum Philone, & Svarezio agnoscit hic Cornelius a Lapide, Abulensem & Serrarium refutans; Siquidem in primo Paschate Sacerdotes nondum instituti fuerint, & in jure antiquo patres-familias postea permanferint, quod tradit quoque Lyranus ad lib. 2. Paralipp. c. 30. & Cajetan. ut & Bellarm. lib. 1. de missa cap. 7. patrem-familias per se immolasse, reliquos familiæ per patrem-familias. Porro sacrificiis imponebantur peccata, non item agno Paschali. Sacrificia comburebantur in atriis templi super altari, idque igne sacro. Quod in agno Paschali non factum; is enim igne assandus erat. Denique sacrificia ad certum locum erant alligata, nec nisi Hierosolymis offerri debebant. At Pascha vel agnus Paschalis non alligabatur præcise ad certum locum, aut ad templum Hierosolymitanum, imo in ædibus privatis celebrabatur. Ideoque minime admittendum, agnum Paschalem fuisse proprie dictum sacrificium. Interea aliquid sacrificiale in sacramento hoc obtinuisse nonnulli nostrates concedunt, ob quandam analogiam, quæ intervenit cum sacrificiis, ex qua vero non potest proprie dictum sacrificium, idque expiatorium concludi. Vid. B. Franzius in Schol. Sacrific. cujus argumentis nequicquam Cloppenburgius in sua sacrific. Schola p. 143. respondet.

Vers. eod.

AD VESPERAM) In Hebræo, inter duas vesperas, id est, inter initium & finem, circa horam diei decimam.

Non ergo nocte, ut Lipp. vult, sed duabus circiter horis ante Solis occasum mactatio fiebat, circa occasum Solis Matth. 14, 15. 23. quia post occasum Solis cum inciperet 15. dies, comedebatur agnus Paschal. Josephus l. 16. Antiquitat. c. 20. ut & l. 7. de bell. Jud. cap. 17. docet, quod immolati fuerint agni vel mactati ab hora nona i. e. tertia nostra po- meridiana usque ad 11. quod nempe eo usque ritus mactationis, assationis, & manducationis durarit. Vid. Cajetan. Perer. in h. loc. Masius in Jos. 5, 10. Jansenius in Concord. Evangel. c. 145. Hinc est quod Judæi, & Christus quandoque 14. quandoque vero 15. die apud Veteres Pascha celebrasse, dican- tur. Judæi definiunt hoc tempus inter duas ve- speras, inter Solem Horizonti occiduo insidentem, & inter Solis a nostro conspectu absentiam: Sed quomo- do in hac angustia temporis agnus cædi, exenterari, assari, aptari, comedi potuit? Accedit quod in in- clinatione Palæstinæ sub elevatione poli 32. crepu- sculum exiguo duret tempore. Est autem tem- pus hoc INTER VESPERAM & VESPERAM, quod est inter oblationem Vespertinam, & Solis oc- casum: Ita manifeste Josephus: ἐνςάσης ἑορτῆς πάσχα καλεῖται, καθ' ὃ θύεσα μὲν ἀπὸ ἐνάτης ὥρας μετὰ ἑνδεκάτην. Vid. Exod. 29, 41.

## 12:7
Verse 7.

AND THEY SHALL TAKE OF THE BLOOD OF IT.

It is a doubt whether that ceremony was proper to this first Passover, or whether it was perpetual in every Passover? But the latter does not seem likely, because that smearing of blood was done in the first Passover on account of the passing of the striking angel, nor does it seem that this ceremony could have been observed so conveniently, especially since everyone gathered at Jerusalem for the sake of the Passover, and mention of its being used is made nowhere else. Since Riverus concedes this, it is manifest that the nature of a sacramental sign is wrongly placed in that ceremony, and that because of this smearing of blood the lamb is said figuratively to be the passing or transition, which the Calvinists contend.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET SUMENT DE SANGUINE EJUS.

Dubium est, utrum ceremonia illa propria fuerit huic primo Paschati, an vero perpetua in omni Paschate? Non videtur autem posterius verisimi- le, quia fiebat illa sanguinis illitio in primo Pascha- te ob transitum angeli percussoris, neque videtur adeo commode hæc ceremonia observari potuisse, præsertim quum Hierosolymam omnes Paschatis causa convenirent, neque uspiam alibi ejus adhi- bitæ mentio fit. Quod cum concedat Riverus, ma- nifestum est, perperam in ea ceremonia rationem signi sacramentalis collocari, & ob hanc sanguinis illitionem agnum transitum sive transitionem fi- gurate dici, quod contendunt Calviniani.

## 12:8
Verse 8.

ROASTED WITH FIRE) A spit of pomegranate wood, which is common in Egypt, as Pliny teaches us in book XIII, ch. 19, remained in use for this sacred purpose.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ASSAS IGNE) Veru mali Punicæ, quæ frequens Ægypto, ut nos Plinius docet lib. XIII. c. 19. in hujus sacri usu mansit.

## 12:9
Verse 9.

YOU SHALL NOT EAT ANY OF IT RAW NOR BOILED IN WATER.

Oleastrius gives this meaning: you shall not eat of it in pieces or cut up; so that he does not want it divided into pieces. But that the word נא signifies cut up could be proven by no example; furthermore, God commanded in plain words that the whole lamb be roasted: finally, it is manifest that what is forbidden by this interdict is not that it should only be boiled or that its roasting should be half-raw, but that the roasting should be perfect. He wanted the lamb to be roasted rather than boiled, both because of the speed of preparation, which was necessary in this haste, and because that method is believed to be the most ancient of all, and especially so that the nature of the type might be more congruent: since the true lamb to be sacrificed for us had to be roasted by the fire of divine wrath.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

NON COMEDETIS CRUDUM QUID NEC COCTA IN AQUA.

Oleastrius hunc sensum reddit: non comedetis ex eo frustum vel dissectum; ita ut nolit in frusta dividi. Sed vocem נא significare dissectum, nul- lo exemplo probari potuit; adhæc integrum agnum assari verbis apertis jussit Deus: denique manifestum est, id vetari hoc interdicto, ne solum elixetur aut semicruda sit illius assatio, sed ut assa- tio perfecta sit. Voluit autem assari agnum po- tius, quam elixari, tum ob celeritatem præpara- tionis, qua opus erat in hac festinatione, tum quod modus ille credatur omnium antiquissimus, tum imprimis ut typi ratio magis congrueret: siqui- dem verus agnus pro nobis mactandus igne iræ di- vinæ assari debuit.

## 12:10
Verse 10.

NOR SHALL ANYTHING OF IT REMAIN UNTIL MORNING; IF ANYTHING REMAINS, YOU SHALL BURN IT WITH FIRE) The Passover is a διαβατήριον to Philo. You may rightly translate this into Latin as 'for the way,' that is, for the sake of setting out, according to Festus. Moreover, in sacred rites, what is said here was also used by the Gentiles 'for the way.' Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 2: There was a sacrifice among the ancients which was called 'for the way'; in it, the custom was that if anything remained from the feast, it was to be consumed by fire. Hence the joke of Cato: for he used to say that a certain Albidius, who had eaten up his goods, and lastly had lost by fire the house which was left to him, had done it 'for the way,' because he had burned what he could not eat. It appears from this that the Passover has an eucharistic nature, the law of which is that nothing should remain until morning. Lev. 7:15, concerning other victims, it is burned if anything remains uneaten on the third day. Lev. 7, v. 17. Grotius gathers from this that the Passover has an eucharistic nature, the law of which is that nothing of it should remain until morning, Leviticus 7:13. On chapter 15:26, he notes that this feast is commemorative rather than a legal sacrifice. But just as we readily concede that it was not strictly a sacrifice, even though it had something sacrificial about it and approached eucharistic and even propitiatory sacrifices—whence Christ is said to be the Passover sacrificed for us, 1 Cor. 5:7—so it was not merely a commemorative feast, but a sacrament in the true sense and a means of applying grace. That the old sacraments conferred or exhibited grace, insofar as they were, as it were, pledges or even certain seals by which the divine promise was sealed and confirmed, by whose power and efficacy grace was conferred even then on account of the future passion of Christ, is acknowledged by the Jesuit Gregor de Valentia, Tom. IV, in Thomam, Disp. III, q. 3. It is advised, however, that nothing should remain, because God did not wish such things as were applied to sacred uses to be either corrupted or to pass into profane uses; for this reason God also expressly provided for this concerning all sacrifices in Leviticus 7. And this is the reason for the following caution, why it had to be burned with fire if anything had remained.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

NEC REMANEBIT QUICQVAM EX EO USQVE MANE; SI QVID RESIDUUM ERIT, IGNE COM- BURETIS) Pascha est διαβατήριον Philoni. Id recte Latine vertas, propter viam, id est, proficiscendi gratia, Festo inter- prete. In sacris autem propter viam etiam gentibus usur- patum quod hic dicitur. Macrob. Saturn. ll. cap. 2. Sacrificium apud veteres fuit, quod vocabatur propter viam; in eo mos erat, ut si quid ex epulis superfuisset, igne consu- meretur. Hinc Catonis jocus est: nam & Albidium quem- dam, qui sua bona comedisset, & novissime domum, quæ ei reliqua erat, incendio perdidisset, propter viam fecisse dicebat, quod comesse non potuerat, id combussisse. Apparet hinc Pa- scha naturam habere ἐυχαριςικῆ, cujus lex est, ne quid mane sit reliquum. Lev. 7, 15. de aliis victimis comburitur, si quid superest non comesum, die tertia. Lev. 7. v. 17. Colligit hinc Grotius, Pascha naturam babe- re εὐχαριστικῆ, cujus lex est, ne quid mane sit reli- quum Levit. 7, 13. Ad cap. 15, 26. notat, convi- vium id magis esse commemorativum, quam sacri- ficium legale. Sed uti facile concedimus, proprie sacrificium non fuisse, tametsi aliquid sacrificiale habuerit, & ad sacrificia Eucharistica, imo & pro- pitiatoria accesserit, unde Christus Pascha pro no- bis immolatum dicitur, 1. Cor. V, 7. ita non con- vivium tantum erat commemorativum, sed Sacra- mentum veri nominis, ac medium applicandi gra- tiam. Sacramenta vetera contulisse, sive exhibuis- se gratiam, quatenus fuerunt veluti pignora aut etiam sigilla quædam, quibus est obsignata & firma- ta divina promissio, cujus vi & efficacia confereba- tur etiam tunc gratia propter passionem Christi fu- turam, agnoscit e Jesuitis Gregor. de Valentia. Tom. IV. in Thomam Disp. III. q. 3. Monetur autem ideo, ne remaneat quicquam, quia nolebat Deus talia aut corrumpi, aut in profanos usus ce- dere, quæ ad Sacra adhibebantur: idcirco etiam de omnibus sacrificiis id diserte cavit Deus Lev. 7. Et hæc est ratio cautionis sequentis, cur igne com- burendum fuerit, si quid superfuisset.

## 12:11
Verse 11.

YOU SHALL GIRD YOUR LOINS) The things that are said in this clause, likewise the sprinkling of blood, were commanded only for that time; and therefore they are not repeated in the laws of the annual Passover.

Same verse.

FOR IT IS THE PASSOVER OF THE LORD.

The word Passover is taken in three ways: (1) of the passing over, (2) of the paschal lamb, and (3) of the feast of the Passover. Cornelius a Lapide wishes the lamb to be called the Passover, and when the victim of the Passover is understood, he holds it to be a proper, not a metonymical, expression. But his own view is consistent, if indeed he wishes the passing over to be signified by this word in this place, and notes that there was a threefold passing over here: first, of the destroying angel; second, of the Hebrews out of Egypt into Canaan; third, of the same through the Red Sea. Augustine, Tract. cap. 55 in John, understands this third one; but he rejects the second, as Philo, Josephus, and Nazianzen do, and wishes the passing over of the destroying angel to be designated. And it is rightly acknowledged that the word פֶסַח is taken properly here and denotes a passing over, and therefore the remaining significations must be foreign to this place; but which passing over is designated, there is no need for divination; for a declaration is added that it is the passing over of the Lord: and in the following verse it is explained what kind of passing over that is, so that there is no doubt that the passing over of the Lord through Egypt, when the firstborn were struck down, is noted.

Moreover, these words, 'it is the Passover of the Lord,' were suggested to Zwingli in a dream by a nocturnal monitor, about whom he himself professed in the 'Subsidium Eucharisticum' that he did not know whether he was black or white. Although it is not unknown what this phrase signifies in an adage, we have no doubt that that nocturnal monitor of Zwingli was truly a black spirit, not a white one; since those things were suggested to him for the depravation of the words of the Testament of Christ, namely, that the substantive verb IS in the sacramental proposition, 'this is my body,' ought to be taken significantly and figuratively in this sense: 'this signifies my body,' because, forsooth, this lamb is said to be the Passover, that is, to signify the passing over of the Lord. But thus, by the help of the Zwinglian monitor, not only the words of the Testament of Christ are perverted, but also these Mosaic words. For here (1) there is no mention of a lamb; for it is said simply פֶסַח הוּא לַיהוָה, the passing over itself of the Lord. Nor (2) is the substantive verb IS found here, about which Zwingli was anxious when taken tropically, because he had no example of it at hand until it was suggested by the nocturnal monitor. But how can a verb be modified or taken figuratively which is not in the text at all? That words which are understood in the mind should be modified is absurd, because a trope is an affection not of the concepts of the mind, but of words. (3) If you say that the word הוּא supplies its place: 'The Passover itself is Jehovah,' what has this to do with the modification of the words of the Supper? For there Zwingli was not anxious about the tropical meaning of the pronoun THIS, as Carlstadt had dreamed of depraving that, but about the tropical sense of the substantive verb IS. (4) There is no trope in the words of Moses: they are to be understood properly. For the reason is given why there is need for haste, the passing over itself of the Lord, that is, because a swift passing over through Egypt is instituted by the Lord, therefore there is need for haste, so that you may hasten out of Egypt, since the Egyptians themselves urged the people to leave the land quickly, verse 33. (5) That the paschal lamb is the Passover, or the passing over of the Lord, that is, as the Zwinglians interpret, to signify the passing over, is not said here, nor was this signification the cause of the haste. It is indeed said of the blood of the lamb that it is a sign for the Israelites in the houses in which they were, that they might be safe in them from the striking angel: but it is nowhere said that the lamb or even the eating of the lamb is a sign of the passing over or signified the passing over of the Lord. Nor does any reason for a sign occur in it; for in what does this formal aspect of signifying consist, and in what way does the lamb or the eating of the lamb signify the passing over? If the Calvinists say that the reason is given in the words why this ceremony was instituted by God, and to what end He willed that that lamb be slaughtered and so eaten by the Israelites, so that the sense is, according to the interpreter Rivetus, that the lamb or the eating of the lamb, insofar as it ought to be eaten in haste, is the Passover of the Lord, or rather by reason of the following ceremony explained in verse 12 (for I will pass through the land of Egypt, etc.), that therefore this is the sense: thus you ought to prepare and eat the lamb, because it is indeed that lamb of the Lord's passing over, that is, a sign of the passing over, or it will signify that passing over which was indeed destructive to the Egyptians, but pleasant to you. I reply: Although it may be admitted that the passing over is designated, by which the Lord passed by the houses of the Israelites, yet that its signification is fixed in these words, in the sacrament of the paschal lamb, that indeed had to be proven. Rivetus could not prove that: even if he were to summon verse 10, which is, however, as far as this reason is concerned, irrelevant, for this reason in these words, 'it is the Passover to the Lord,' refers itself to the preceding, not to the following; and it is manifest that the haste in the eating and in the departure, previously commanded, is illustrated by this reason of the Lord's passing over, who, passing quickly through Egypt, compelled the Egyptians, whose firstborn were being killed by this passing over, to urge the Israelites themselves to depart quickly. That, however, is too subtle, which is elicited from the word פסח, as Rivetus wishes, that it denotes to leap over, and is to be taken then of that passing over by which some things are passed by out of many, and are leaped over by not touching them, which then carries him away to the point that he fixes in it the nature of a sign, that the lamb is or signifies such a leaping over, and that Passover here is taken of the passing over by which the houses of the Israelites were leaped over. For פסח does not always denote such a passing over and passing by, by which some things are leaped over. See 1 Kings 18:20, Isaiah 30:5, and from it is derived the noun פסח, a lame person, who certainly was not so called from leaping over at intervals. Nor was that leaping over signified by the eating of the lamb, much less by the haste of the eating: nowhere certainly in that eating or haste is this method of signifying established. The slaughter was a sign of the slaughter of Christ 1 Cor. 5, 7. The eating is not a sign of the passing over, but a means of the sacramental perception of Christ the true lamb, to be slaughtered for us. The smearing of the doorposts done with the blood of the lamb was a figure of smearing the doorposts of the heart with the blood of Christ: which, although we do not deny that it was a sign of the Lord's passing over or passing by the smeared houses, yet that does nothing for this proposition, the passing over itself to the Lord, as if that method of signifying were handed down through the same, because there in the subject, when the Calvinists form a proposition from it, it is not the blood of the lamb smeared on the doorposts of the houses, but the lamb to be eaten, which word they extract from the words immediately preceding, and construct for the subject in this proposition. Nor is there agreement among the Calvinists as to where the analogy of the sign to the thing signified ought to be placed here between the lamb and the passing over or the transition, which Rivetus reports is explained differently by various people, with some referring it to the haste of the eating, others to something else. But he himself does not know where he ought to fix his foot; he says that all agree on this, that this ceremony was instituted in memory of that passing over, verses 25, 26, and 27, so that the proposition is to be understood in this sense: the lamb is the passing over; that is, the lamb is a memorial sign of the passing over. But the question is not about the ceremony instituted afterwards in memory of the passing over, which was finally done in the verses cited below, 25, 26, but about that proposition which is had in verse 11: for it is the Lord's Passover. Furthermore, because that passing over had not yet occurred in that first enunciation, how could it be said, that lamb is a memorial sign of the passing over: which, since Rivetus sees it to be inconvenient, he now changes that proposition, and perverts the present tense EST into a verb of future time: that lamb shall be for you the passing over, that is, it shall signify to you and call to memory the passing over. But in this way the discourse will not be about this first enunciation, nor about these present words of the Lord, but about the subsequent paschal feast, namely what the religion of the Passover feast was to signify in following times, as is had in verse 27. Besides, another proposition is had there, namely this: the victim is the Lord's passing over, about which there is no question, since in this: it is the Lord's Passover, the Calvinists seek their sacramental metonymy. Thus, therefore, that which Rivetus says all agree upon, he himself abandons, and trusts that he will bring a better explanation from verse 13: the blood of the lamb shall be for you for a sign; for these words, he says, explain the preceding ones and change the figurative locution into a proper one. But how can these words be considered exegetical, when the subject here is clearly one thing, namely blood, and the predicate likewise another: it shall be for a sign, and no mention of the passing over is made in this proposition. And what need is there for this locution to be changed into a proper one, when no impropriety is contained in it; for when I say, this passing over is the Lord's passing over, no place is left for a trope, no metonymy prevails. Rivetus insists, by comparing the proposition Gen. 17, 10, where it is said of circumcision: this is my covenant: which proposition he thinks is explained afterwards in verse 11 thus: and it shall be for a sign of the covenant, and from this he concludes that in the present case they are likewise equivalent: the lamb is the passing over, that is, it will confirm your faith concerning the promised passing over. But he is mistaken in that he considers that proposition, this is my covenant, to be improper and figurative, since circumcision, without a trope, is properly a covenant and a covenant of grace, not only a sign of the covenant: he is mistaken also in that the other proposition: And it shall be for a sign of the covenant, is taken for exegetical, when it is clearly different; for circumcision is called a covenant because it is considered as a whole, namely the entire sacrament of circumcision, and it is called a sign of the covenant as it is viewed in part, by reason of the external amputation of the foreskin. Finally, he is mistaken in that he compares those propositions about circumcision with these about the Paschal lamb; since they are most diverse. For in the former, the Lord's passing over itself, not the Paschal lamb itself, or the entire sacrament of the Paschal lamb, but that passing over is explained, and its speed and haste, and the cause of the same is declared; in the latter, the blood of the lamb is indeed not inappropriately called a sign of the passing over, but what is this to circumcision, which is a sign of the covenant; since the blood of the lamb pertained not so much to the substance of the sacrament itself as to the preparation, or to the sacrifice prior to the sacrament, as some explain: and it is called a sign of the passing over because it confirmed faith concerning the transition, of which later. Whence Rivetus's inference is null, when he concludes thus: Therefore the blood of the lamb is a sign, the passing over of God is the thing signified, and yet the lamb or the blood of the lamb is called the passing over; and thus the thing signified is said of the sign. He says indeed that nothing clearer can be said, nor a more apt example brought forward of that sacramental locution, that is, of sacramental metonymy. But where is either the lamb or the blood of the lamb called the passing over? Nowhere will that be shown. Then if the lamb is called the passing over in this place, as the Reformed commonly contend, how then is the blood of the lamb substituted in place of the lamb? Let us convince Rivetus from Rivetus himself. For that, according to him, is called the sign of the passing over in this place which the Israelites were commanded to eat: but they were commanded to eat the lamb, not the blood of the lamb; therefore. It is manifest, therefore, that Rivetus is forced to confuse the lamb to be eaten with the blood of the lamb, with which the doorposts were to be smeared. Finally, since that sprinkling of the doorposts with the blood of the lamb was not always done in the celebration of the Passover and the eating of the paschal lamb, according to Rivet's opinion; therefore, according to the same, the sacrament could not have been celebrated then, which, according to the Calvinists, has no place without the proper analogy of the sacrament, or that analogy between the blood of the lamb and the passing over will not have to be sought. If you insist, what then is the subject in this proposition: it is the Lord's Passover? I answer: It is assumed in this question that the proposition is held here in its entirety, and EST is of the third adjacent, as they call it; but even if we admit that to the greatest extent, that proposition must be supplied in such a way as is necessary in other demonstrative ones, to wit: that passing over is the passing over of the Lord about to strike, namely, Egypt, but about to save you, where it is manifest that no trope, no metonymy has any place. Most recently, it must be observed that the very disciples of Zwingli reject that explanation, as many, namely, as prefer that the trope in sacramental propositions be placed in the predicate rather than in the substantive verb EST, which is the opinion of the principal ones today; not to mention that some acknowledge that the copula is not capable of a trope, a thing which we have demonstrated at greater length in Stereom. contra Berg. p. 124.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

RENES VESTROS ACCINGETIS) Quæ hoc comma- te dicuntur, item, ut sanguinis aspersio tantum pro illo tem- pore imperata sunt: ideoque in legibus anniversarii Pascha- tis non repetuntur.

Vers. eod.

EST ENIM PHASE DOMINI.

Paschatis vox tribus modis accipitur (1.) de transitu, (2.) de agno Paschali, & (3.) de festo Pa- schatis. Cornel. a Lapide agnum dici Phase vult, & quum intelligitur hostia Paschatis, propriam es- se, non metonymicam locutionem. Sed sibi ipsi vis constat, siquidem & transitum hac voce si- gnificari h. l. velit, notetque triplicem fuisse hic transitum, primum angeli vastatoris, secundum Ebræorum ex Ægypto in Canaan, tertium eorun- dem per mare rubrum. Hunc tertium intellige- re August. Tract. cap. 55. in Johann. secundum vero Philonem, Josephum & Nazianzenum, utrumque reprobat, & transitum angeli vastatoris designari vult. Et recte agnoscitur, vocem פֶסַח hic proprie accipi, ac transitum notare, ideoque re- liquas significationes ab h. l. alienas esse oportet; quis autem transitus designetur, divinatione opus non est; additur enim declaratio, quod transitus sit Domini: & vers. seq. explicatur, qualis ille transi- tus sit, ut dubium non sit, notari transitum Domi- ni per Ægyptum, quum primogenita cæderentur.

Cæterum hæc verba: est phase Domini, suggessit nocturnus monitor Zwinglio in somno, de quo ipse, ater an albus fuerit, se nescire professus est in subsidio Euchar. Quæ phrasis, etsi quid signifi- cet in adagio, non incognitum sit, vere tamen atrum fuisse spiritum, non album monitorem illum nocturnum Zwinglii, dubium nobis nullum est; siquidem suggesta illa ipsi sint ad depravationem verborum Testamenti Christi, quod nempe ver- bum substantivum EST in propositione sacra- mentali, hoc est corpus meum, σημαντικῶς accipi debeat, & figurate hoc sensu, hoc significat corpus meum, quia scil. hic agnus dicitur esse phase, id est, significare transitum Domini. At sic pervertun- tur ope monitoris Zwingliani non solum verba Testamenti Christi, sed etiam hæc verba Mosaica. Nam hic (1.) nulla agni mentio est; simpliciter enim dicitur פֶסַח הוּא לַיהוָה transitus ipse Domini. Neque (2.) hic verbum substant. EST reperi- tur, de quo tropice accepto sollicitus erat Zwin- glius, quia nullum ejus exemplum in promptu ha- bebat, donec hoc fuggereretur a monitore no- cturno. At quî modificari poteft aut figurate ac- cipi verbum, quod in textu plane non habetur? Verba, quæ in mente fubintelliguntur, modifica- ri, ἄτοπον, quia tropus eft affectio non conce- ptuum mentis, sed verborum. (3.) Si dicas, vocem הוא ejus vicem fupplere : Pascha ipsum Jehovah, quid hoc ad modificationem verborum cœnæ? nam ibi non de pronominis HOC fignificatu tropico Zwinglius follicitus erat, uti Carolstadius de illo depravando fomniaverat, fed de verbi sub- stantivi EST sensu tropico. (4.) Nullus in ver- bis Mofis tropus: proprie illa intelligenda funt. Redditur enim caufa, cur festinatione opus fit, transitus ipse Domino, id est, quia a Domino insti- tuitur transitus celer per Ægyptum, ideo feftinato opus est, ut properetis ex Ægypto, fiquidem ipfi Ægyptii urserint populum exire e terra velociter verf. 33. (5.) Agnum paschalem esse Pascha, sive transitum Domini, id est, ut Zwingliani interpre- tantur, significare transitum, hic non dicitur, neque caufa hæc fignificatio erat festinationis. De fanguine quidem agni dicitur, quod fit fignum Israelitis in ædibus, in quibus erant, quod nempe in illis tuti esse possent ab angelo percuffore: at agnum vel etiam manducationem agni signum esse transitus aut fignificasse transitum Domini, nufpiam dicitur. Nec in eo ulla figni ratio occurrit; in quo enim confiftit hic formale fignandi, & quo pacto agnus vel manducatio agni fignificat tranfi- tum? Si dicant Calviniani, rationem in verbis red- di, cur hæc ceremonia instituta fuerit a Deo, & in quem finem voluerit agnum illum mactari & ab Israelitis ita comedi, ut fenfus fit interprete Riveto, agnum sive agni efum, quatenus comedi debet festi- nanter, esse Phase Domini, vel potius ratione fe- quentis ceremoniæ vers. 12. explicatæ (nam transi- bo in terra Ægypti &c.) fenfum ergo hunc esse, fic debetis præparare & comedere agnum, quia est nempe agnus ille transitus Domini, id est, fignum transitus aut fignabit transitum illum Ægyptiis qui- dem perniciofum, vobis autem jucundum. Refp. Quanquam admitti poffit, transitum defignari, quo præteriit Dominus domos Ifraelitarum, tamen illius fignificationem his verbis figi, in sacramento agni paschalis, id vero probandum erat. Non po- tuit id probare Rivetus: etiamfi accerferet verfum 10. qui vero quantum ad hanc rationem, alienus eft, hæc enim ratio in his verbis, est Phase Domino, refert sefe ad antecedentia, non ad consequentia; & manifestum est, festinationem in manducatio- ne, & in exitu antea præceptam hac ratione illu- strari a transitu Domini, qui celeriter per Ægy- ptum transiens compellebat Ægyptios, quorum primogenita interficiebantur hoc transitu, ut ipsi- met Ifraelitas urgerent exire velociter.
