In Ebr. Sileant ut lapis. LXX. ἀπολιθωθήτωσαν lapidescant. B. Luth. commodissime, daß Sie erstarren wie die Steine. Orat Moses, ne hoste

Ebræorum moveantur, sed ut conticescere cogan- tur, donec pertranseat populus Domini.

## 15:17
Verse 17. IN THE MOUNTAIN OF THINE INHERITANCE.

Thus he calls Mount Moriah or Zion, foreseeing in the spirit that the seat and inheritance of the Lord would one day be there: therefore the Chaldean expressed the sense, rendering it, the place of the Majesty of GOD, because Moses explains himself thus, while he adds: thy sanctuary, which is the name of the temple, in which the holy seat of GOD, the holy worship of GOD was to be performed, and sacrifices were to be offered. Moses therefore prophesies not only about the leading of the Lord on the way, which remained, very arduous and dangerous, but also about the introduction into the land of Canaan, and about the Republic and Church to be planted and established there. Cf. Ps. 132, 13. Ps. 80, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 17. IN MONTE HÆREDITATIS TUÆ.

Sic vocat montem Morija vel Zion, in spiri- tu prævidens ibi sedem & hæreditatem Domini aliquando futuram: ideo sensum expressit Chal- dæus, reddens, locum Majestatis DEI, quia expli- cat ita sese Moses, dum addit: sanctuarium tuum, quod est nomen templi, in quo sancta DEI sedes, sanctus DEI cultus peragendus, & sacrificia offe- renda erant. Vaticinatur ergo Moses non tantum de deductione Domini in via, quæ reliqua erat, val- de ardua & periculosa, sed de introductione etiam in terram Canaan, & de Rep. & Ecclesia ibi plantan- da & firmanda. Conf. Ps. 132, 13. Ps. 80, 9.

## 15:18
Verse 18. THE LORD SHALL REIGN FOR EVER AND BEYOND.

Thus the Vulgate, along with the LXX interpreters, is extremely inconvenient; for there is nothing beyond eternity; the Hebrew לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד denotes a simple eternity lacking an end, which in the Greek of the New Testament is expressed thus: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, and is correctly rendered by the Chaldean: in the ages of ages: by B. Luther, ever and eternally, which sense Lyranus, Cajetan, Lippomannus, and others acknowledge. There is therefore no need for the foreign glosses which the Papists seek out in order to defend the Vulgate, while some interpret it thus: The Lord shall reign throughout the whole present age and beyond, namely, through the future age: others say with Abulensis that the word 'and beyond' was added by hyperbole, which proceeded from ignorance of the Hebrew phrase. We subjoin the Jerusalem paraphrase. They said one to another: Come, let us offer a crown and place it upon the head of the REDEEMER, who transfers and is not transferred: who changes and is not changed: who is King of all Kings in this Age: and whose is the kingdom and the crown in the future age, and thus whose is the kingdom for the ages of ages.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DOMINUS REGNABIT IN Æ- TERNUM ET ULTRA.

Ita perquam incommode Vulgatus cum LXX. Interpp. ultra enim æternitatem nihil est; Ebræum לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד æternitatem simplicem notat sine caren- tem, quæ in Græco Novi Testamenti ita expri- mitur: εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, & à Chaldeo recte redditur: in secula seculorum: à B. Luthero immer und Ewig, quem sensum agnoscunt Lyranus, Ca- jetan. Lippomannus aliique. Non ergo opus est pe- regrinis Glossis, quas ut Vulgatam tueantur, con- quirunt Papistæ, dum alii sic interpretantur: Do- minus regnabit per totum præsens seculum & ultra, scil. per seculum futurum: alii dicunt cum Abulen- si, vocem & ultra per hyperbolen additam esse, quæ ex ignorantia phraseos Ebrææ profecta est. Sub- jungimus paraphrasin Hierosolym. Dixerunt al- ter ad alterum: Age offeramus coronam eamque impo- namus in Caput REDEMTORIS, qui transfert & non transfertur: qui mutat & non mutatur: qui est Rex omnium Regum in hoc Seculo: & cujus est regnum & corona in futuro seculo, & adeo cujus est regnum in secula seculorum.

## 15:20
MARY THE PROPHETESS.

Cornelius proves by a foolish argument that the name was corrupted by the Masoretes, namely because the LXX, the Latin, and the Syrian interpreters pronounce it otherwise, since it is known that they not rarely change vowels for the euphony of their own language: whence Matthew Galenus in Catechism 45 is vehemently mistaken when he confidently asserts that the name of the Virgin Mary is entirely different from the name of the sister of Aaron, because it is most certainly true that this name of the sister of Aaron was once read differently. But as far as the etymology and interpretation of this name are concerned, most render it 'salty sea,' against whom Angelus Caninius argues in his notes on the New Testament, ch. 13; others interpret it as 'drop of the sea,' whom Cornelius attacks undeservedly, because he himself thinks the name is compound and arises from מר mari; now it is known that מר signifies a drop of the sea: wherefore Cornelius ought rather to have refuted his own people, who most foolishly made 'star of the sea' out of it; nor does he himself bring forward a better interpretation, while he renders it 'Mistress of the sea,' for the reason that מר denotes Master. But thus he descends from the Hebrew language into the Chaldean, and converts Master into Mistress, when he sees that it does not fit for Mary to be called Mistress of the sea; and he labors in vain to claim for Mary the dominion of the sea; for he could bring forward nothing except a spurious passage of Epiphanius, namely a sermon on the praises of the Virgin, and Damascene, who is very unskilled in these matters, who also wished for Anna and Mary to signify the same thing, which is openly false. More correctly, Caninius derives it from רום to exalt, so that she may be noted as Eminent and Exalted, which derivation Schindler also approves, but others most conveniently seem to deduce it from מָרַר he was bitter, because the name Maria was imposed, because she was born at a time when the Egyptian servitude was very bitter.

Verse of the same. SISTER OF AARON.

She is called not the sister of Moses, but of Aaron, because Aaron was older by birth. Papists gather from this that she was unmarried, since she is not named after a husband; Josephus, however, handed down that she was married to Hur.

Verse of the same. WITH TIMBREL AND DANCES.

A chorus is a multitude of those singing or dancing: and that not only songs but also dances and saltations were accustomed to be instituted in honor of God is manifest both from this place and from 1 Sam. 18:7, 2 Sam. 6:14, Psalm 68:26. And Solomon notes in Eccl. 3:4 that there is a time to mourn, and a time to dance. Therefore, not all dances or saltations are prohibited. Rightly Blessed Luther in the Gospel on the Wedding in Cana: faith and charity are not shaken off by dancing, otherwise dances could not even be granted to infants. To the pure all things are pure, Tit. 1:15. Nor are dances prohibited, but circumscribed by the law of honesty in the laws of the Academy of Wittenberg, which Philippus inserted into his counsels, part 1, p. 187. Too rigid here are most of the Reformed, who refer dances to the vanities of the world and to the author Lucian. Philippus Marnixius, however, admits and defends them expressly in his Epist. illustr. Belg. nor does Alstedius simply disapprove in Casuali Theol. chap. 19; if a dance, he says, is governed by certain laws by the Magistrate, they can be granted. To say nothing of the fact that in England certain types of dances have even been sanctioned by decrees; in France and Belgium, dances of men and women together have been permitted, not only private, but also public. Nor could Gisbertus Voëtius simply disapprove of mixed dances of women with men, or the opinion of our B. Meisner asserted in part 1, Phil. Sobr. in disp. 1 concerning the vanities of the world to the 7th commandment, even though he compiled many things against dances according to his custom. He is certainly too rigid when he says in thesis 5: Let it be granted that in idea and abstractly a dance can be imagined or conceived which is separated from all evil, yet subjectively and in existence such is not given or does not exist. But what indeed will be able to be proved or admitted in the end, to which some defect cannot adhere subjectively and in existence? This is pharisaical precision, to use his word, and why does Voëtius himself observe and determine that in moral matters one should not go up to the line or point where good is distinguished from evil, but rather one should stop a little on this side of the line, if that pharisaical precision, as he calls it, is to be observed in all things? Rivetus must also be considered an excessively unfair and rigid Censor of dances when he praises the saying of someone as not inept: A dance is a circle whose center is the devil and whose circumference is his angels. He assumes, of course, what must never be granted, that the vice of lasciviousness is morally inseparable from dances, that there are no dances today in which there are not some incitements to lasciviousness, that they can never be performed, namely mixed dances of young men with virgins, without the danger of incontinence, and he confuses honest dances with comic and impudent movements or the insane runnings of Bacchantes: which is not surprising in him, since he also takes absolutely the saying of Solomon, by which he pronounced laughter to be madness, Eccl. 2:13, and drags it here; nay, he even drags the curse of Isa. 3:17 here by the neck. Concerning timbrels also in the use of sacred things and other musical instruments, the Calvinists of our churches stir up a dispute, as if they were contrary to Evangelical simplicity and had been abolished by Christ as ceremonies proper to the Old Testament; where we will not indeed with Corn. à Lap. urge that they were received before the ceremonial law, as this example testifies; but because they are freely called into use by the saints, and serve to excite souls to the praise of the Lord and to exultation in the Lord, which both this place teaches, and they have nowhere been prohibited by Christ or the Apostles, nay, they exhibit a figure of the music and joy of heaven, Rev. 5:8, no reason appears why they could not have been assumed by the Church of Christ as adiaphora by the right of Christian liberty, or why, once assumed, they should be abrogated for the sake of the gloomy and morose Calvinist spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 20. MARIA PROPHETISSA.

Nomen à Masoretis corruptum esse inepto argumento probat Cornel. quia scil. aliter pronun- tiant LXX. Latinus, & Syrus Interpretes, siquidem notum sit, eosdem ad suæ linguæ Euphaniam vo- cales non raro immutare: unde vehementer falli- tur Matthæus Galenus Catech. 45. cum nomen vir- ginis Mariæ beatæ prorsus diversum esse à nomine So- roris Aaronis, confidenter asserit, quia certo certius sit, hoc nomen sororis Aaronis olim secus lectum fuisse. Cæterum Etymon hujus nominis & interpretatio- nem quód attinet, plerique reddunt salsum mare, adversus quos disputat Angelus Caninius in locis N. T. c. 13. alii interpretantur stillam maris, quos immerito exagitat Corn. quia putat ipse nomen compositum esse, & à מר mari oriri; notum autem est, quod מר stillam maris significet: quapropter redarguere potius debebat Corn. suos, qui ineptif- sime ex eo stellam maris fecere; neque ipse melio- rem adfert interpretationem, dum reddit, Domi- nam maris, eo quod מר notet Magistrum. At ita ex Ebræa Lingua in Chaldæam descendit, & Magi- strum in Dominum convertit, quum videat non congruere Mariam dici Magistram maris; ac fru- stra laborat, ut Mariæ dominium maris vindicet; neque enim quicquam afferre potuit, nisi Epipha- nii spurium locum, sermonem nempe de laudibus virginis, & Damascenum in his valde imperitum, qui etiam voluit Annam & Mariam idem signifi- care, quod aperte falsum est. Rectius Caninius à רום exaltare derivat, ut Eminens & Excelsa note- tur, quam derivationem etiam probat Schindlerus sed commodissime alii a מָרַר amarus fuit, deducer videntur, quod nomen Mariæ impositum, quia e prognata tempore est, quo servitus Ægyptiaca val de amara fuit.

Vers. eod. SOROR AARONIS.

Non Mosis, sed Aaronis soror dicitur, quia Aaron major natu erat. Colligunt inde Papistæ eam innuptam fuisse, siquidem à Marito non de- nominêtur; Josephus tamen eam Bur nuptam fuisse tradidit.

Vers. eod. CUM TYMPANIS ET CHORIS.

Chorus multitudo est canentium vel saltantium: & in honorem DEI non cantica solum sed & cho- reas ac saltationes institui consuevisse tum ex h. l. tum è 1. Sam. 18, 7. 2. Sam. 6, 14. Psalm. 68, 26. ma- nifestum est. Et notat Salomo Eccl. 3, 4. tempus esse lugendi, tempus & saltandi. Non ergo choreæ aut saltationes omnes prohibitæ sunt. Recte Beat. Lutherus in Evang. de Nuptiis in Canaan: fides & charitas saltando non excutiuntur, alias ne quidem in infantibus choreæ concedi possent. Mundis omnia munda sunt Tit. 1, 15. Nec prohibitæ sunt, sed lege honestatis circumscriptæ saltationes in legib. Aca- demiæ Wittebergensis, quas inseruit Philippus consiliis suis parte 1. p. 187. Nimis rigidi hic sunt è Reformatis plerique, qui ad excelsa mundi & ad Lucianum auctorem choreas referunt. Admittit tamen eas & defendit ex professo Philippus Mar- nixius in Epist. illustr. Belg. nec Alstedius simpli- citer improbat in Casuali Theol. cap. 19. si chorea, inquit, certis legibus regantur à Magistratu, possunt concedi. Ut taceam, quod in Anglia decretis etiam sint sancita certa saltationum genera; in Gallia & Belgio permissæ etiam sint saltationes γυναικοανδρι- καὶ non privatæ solum, sed & publicæ. Nec impro- bare simpliciter potuit saltationes compositas fæmi- narum cum viris Gisbertus Voëtius, aut sententiam B. Meisneri nostri part. 1. Phil. Sobr. assertam in disp. 1. de Excelsis mundi ad præceptum 7. etsi mul- ta adversus choreas pro more suo compilarit. Ni- mium certe rigidus est, cum thesi 5. ait: Detur, in Idea & abstracte fingi posse aut concipi choream, quæ à malo omni sejuncta sit, non tamen subjective & in existentiâ talis ita datur aut existit. Quid vero ita tandem probari aut admitti poterit, cui non subjecti- ve & in existentia aliquis adhærere possit defectus? Est hæc pharisaica præcisitas, ut verbo eius utamur, & cur ipse Voëtius observat, ac statuit, in morali- bus non esse eundem usque ad lineam sive punctum, quo discriminatur bonum à malo, sed potius ab hac parte lineæ paululum subsistendum esse, si per omnia illa pharisaica præcisitas, quam vocat, observanda? Ni- mium iniquus, & rigidus Censor chorearum cen- sendus etiam est Rivetus, cum laudat cujusdam dictum, ceu non ineptum: Chorea est circulus, cujus centrum est diabolus, & circumferentia angeli ejus. Nimirum assumit, quod nunquam concedendum est, moraliter inseparabile esse vitium lasciviæ à cho- reis, nullas esse choreas hodie, in quibus non aliqua sint lasciviæ incitamenta, nunquam fieri posse eas, compo- sitas nempe adolescentum cum virginibus sine periculo incontinentiæ, ac honestas choreas confundit cum Comicis & impudicis motibus aut insanis Baccharum cursitationibus: quod non mirum in ipso, siqui- dem etiam Salomonis dictum, quo risum insaniam pronunciavit Eccl. 2, 13. absolute accipiat, atque huc abripiat; imo etiam maledictionem Esa. 3. v. 17. obtorto collo huc pertrahat. De tympanis etiam in usu sacrorum & aliis instrumentis Musicis litem movent Ecclesiæ nostræ Calviniani, ac si ea Evan- gelicæ simplicitati contrarientur, & à Christo aboli- ta sint, tanquam ceremoniæ Vet. Test. propriæ; ubi non quidem cum Corn. à Lap. id urgebiinus, quod ante legem ceremonialem, teste hoc exemplo, recepta fuerint; sed quia à sanctis in usum vocata libere sunt, & ad excitandos animos ad laudem Domini & tripudium in Domino faciunt, quod utrumque hic locus docet, nec uspiam à Christo vel Apostolis prohibita sunt, imo figuram exhibent Musicæ & lætitiæ cælestis, Apoc. 5, 8. nulla apparet ratio, cur ab Ecclesia Christi tanquam adiaphora non assumi jure libertatis Christianæ potuerint, aut cur assumta abrogari in gratiam spiritus Calviniani te- trici & morosi debeant.

## 15:21
Verse 21. TO WHOM HE SANG BEFORE.

Some maintain that Miriam sang the same song separately from the men and after the men, which they themselves had sung: but others, because in the Hebrew, as Vatablus notes with the Rabbis, it is, and he answered them, namely Moses and the other men, since לָהֶם is of the masculine gender, not the feminine, they establish here two choirs, one of women, the other of men standing opposite, and answering one another in turn, following Philo in his book on Agriculture; others with Oleaster think that while Moses sang the individual verses of the Canticle, the women took them up and sang them in like manner. However, the masculine suffix is not to be overlooked, nor the verb עָנָה, which is to sing in turns, or to answer by singing, or ἀμοίϐεσϑαι, so that it is implied that the men sang, and the women answered, with Moses leading the former, and Miriam the latter.

Latin:

Vers. 21. QUIBUS PRÆCINEBAT.

Mariam seorsim à viris & post viros cecinisse idem carmen, quod ipsi cecinerant, nonnulli vo- lunt: alii vero quia in Ebræo, uti Vatablus cum Rabbinis notat, est, & respondebat illis, Mosi scil. aliisque viris, siquidem לָהֶם non fœminei, sed masculini generis sit, duos choros, unum mulierum, alterum virorum ex adverso stantes, & alternis sibi respondentes hîc constituunt, præeunte Philone lib. de Agric. alii cum Oleastro putant, Mose præci- nente singulos versus Cantici mulieres excepisse ac similiter decantasse. Non autem insuper habendum affixum masculinum, neque verbum עָנָה, quod est alternis canere, vel canendo respondere, vel ἀμοίϐεσϑαι, ut ita innuatur cecinisse viros, respondisse mulieres, illis præcinente Mose, his Miriam.

## 15:22
Verse 22. MOSES BROUGHT ISRAEL FROM THE RED SEA.

Brought, i. e. transferred, or caused to set out; for thus the word is used transitively in Ps. 80:9, namely, he caused them to go out by his order and command; just as the LXX translate it ἐξῆρε, he took away, and therefore there is no need to understand that he carried them on his shoulders; for this is attributed to GOD alone, Deut. 32:12 and elsewhere. The desert of Shur, into which they set out, is that in which Hagar was found by the Angel, Gen. 16:7. It is called Ethan elsewhere; but this name is common, that one is proper, expressing a part of the desert of Ethan, see Num. 33:7. They are said, however, to have come to Marah, which is the fifth station in the desert, and it receives this name here by prolepsis, because the Israelites imposed it upon it afterwards from the bitter water.

Latin:

Vers. 22. TULIT MOSES ISRAEL DE MA- RI RUBRO.

Tulit, i. e. transtulit, vel proficisci fecit; sic enim transitive usurpatur vox Ps. 80, 9. jussu scil. & mandato suo exire fecit; uti LXX. ἐξῆρε sustulit, ideoque non opus est, ut humeris eosdem por- tasse intelligamus; hoc enim DEO soli tribuitur, Deut. 32, 12. & alias. Desertum Sur, in quod pro- fecti sunt, est illud, in quo Agar inventa est ab An- gelo, Gen. 16, 7. Vocatur alias Ethan; sed hoc nomen commune est, illud proprium, partem nempe deser- ti Ethan exprimens, vid. Num. 33, 7. Venisse autem dicuntur in Mara, quæ est quinta statio in deserto, & nomen hoc per prolepsin hîc sortitur, quod ab aqua amara ei postea imposuere Israëlitæ.

## 15:25
Verse 25. HE SHOWED HIM A TREE] Bitter, as the Hebrews say, so that the power of GOD might appear the more in the contrary effect.

In the Hebrew it is: he taught him a tree: from which, however, some wrongly conclude with Lyranus and Cajetan that this power of sweetening the water was natural to this tree, which opinion Drusius also embraces, that this tree made the waters sweet by a natural faculty, either by separating the burnt parts of the earth, by the admixture of which the bitter taste of the water is made; or by attracting and drawing to itself, and imbibing the bitter parts of the water: they appeal to the passage in Sirach 38:4. But there only the power of medicines, and the virtue of this tree, is referred to the same author, God, and it is not asserted that this was natural, just as that was. Abulensis, on the contrary, with Rashi, maintains that the tree was of itself bitter and deadly, but was made sweet and wholesome by divine power, and they commonly say it is called Adelpha, concerning which see Fagius in this place. It is usually applied to Christ, the tree of life, concerning which see Tertullian, book on Baptism, ch. 9. That tree was Christ, remedying the veins of a nature previously poisoned and bitter into the most wholesome waters of Baptism; and Theodoret, question 26 on Genesis: It is enough to have learned that through the tree the waters laid aside all bitterness, and this predicts our salvation. For also by the most wholesome tree of the cross, the bitter sea of the nations exchanged its bitterness for sweetness. Add also Gregory of Nyssa in the Catena: God could indeed have made the water potable by a word alone; but He willed to indicate the wood, so that He might insinuate a type of the life-giving cross. Cf. & Tert. lib. contra Jud. cap. 13. Orig. Homil. 7. in Exod. Ambr. de initiandis Minist. Cypr. lib. de Zelo & livore near the end teaches how the bitterness and anger are to be softened by the cross of Christ; if you take food and drink from the Sacrament of the cross, the wood which at Mara profited in an image for the sweetness of taste will profit you in truth for the softening of a hardened heart.

Verse same: THERE HE SET FOR HIM STATUTES AND ORDINANCES] The Hebrews understand this of the rest of the Sabbath, and of the honor of parents, and that because of those words, 'as the Lord thy God commanded thee,' which are found twice in Deut. 5, verses 12 and 15. Others also say that judgments were instituted then.

Judgments are without doubt older than Moses, since human society cannot consist without judgments: but Moses delivered a certain form of judgments. Nor was the commandment concerning the honor of parents delivered only then, which it is certain had already been sanctioned in Paradise, nay, even impressed upon nature itself. Therefore God, Gen. 2:24, in the institution of marriage: 'A man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife,' hinting at the commandment concerning the honor and love of parents, by which we are bound to cleave to them. But not even that concerning the rest of the Sabbath is so recent, as we shall say hereafter. But why does he not also bring forward other ceremonies, such as that of the red cow, and those which the Hebrews think were delivered there besides? But others more correctly say that a certain new form of polity was established here, and that the people were prepared by certain more general and easier laws as if by rudiments for the remaining mandates which were to follow. It may also perhaps be said that the commandments which were established are expressed in the following verse: 'If thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord, &c.' because he here only demanded obedience generally, to be sincerely rendered to his commandments, which he was about to prescribe specifically hereafter, with the addition of a promise of grace, of which they had now enjoyed a specimen in this miraculous healing of the waters.

Latin:

Vers. 25. OSTENDIT EI LIGNUM] Amarum, ut Hebræi ajunt, quo magis in effectu contrario virtus DEI appareret.

In Ebr. docuit eum lignum: Ex quo tamen perperam cum Lyrano & Cajetano colligunt non- nulli, vim istam dulcorandi aquam ligno huic fuisse naturalem, quam sententiam Drusius etiam am- plectitur, naturali facultate lignum hoc aquas fe- cisse dulces, vel secernendo adustas terræ partes, qua- rum admixtione fit amarus aquæ sapor; vel attra- bendo & alliciendo ad sese, imbibendoq́; amaras aquæ partes: provocant ad locum Syrac. 38, 4. Sed ibi so- lum vis medicamentorum, & ligni hujus virtus ad eundem auctorem Deum refertur, non vero asse- ritur, æque hanc, ut illam naturalem fuisse. Abulen- sis ex adverso cum Raschi lignum ex se amarum & mortiferum fuisse volunt, virtute divina autem fa- ctum dulce ac salutare, idque Adelpha nominatum vulgo dicunt, de quo vid. Fagius in h. l. Applicari id ad Christum lignum vitæ solet, de quo Tertull. lib. de Bapt. c. 9. Lignum illud erat Christus, venenatæ & amaræ retro naturæ venas in saluberrimas aquas Baptismi remedians; & Theodore tus qv. 26. in Genes. Satis est didicisse per lignum deposuisse aquas omnem tristitiam, & hoc nostram salutem predicit. Nam & saluberrimo ligno crucis amarum gentium pelagus dulcedinem cum tristitia commutavit. Adde & Greg. Nyssenum in Catena, poterat sane Deus solo verbo aquam potabilem facere; sed lignum voluit indicare, ut typum salutiferæ crucis insinuaret. Conf. & Tert. lib. contra Jud. cap. 13. Orig. Homil. 7. in Exod. Ambr. de initiandis Minist. Cypr. lib. de Zelo & livore sub finem docet, quomodo cruce Christi amarulentia & ira lenienda sit, si de Sacramento crucis cibum sumis & potum, lignum quod apud Mara pro- fecit in imagine ad saporis dulcedinem, tibi in veritate proficiet ad mulcendi pectoris lenitatem.

Vers. eod. IBI CONSTITUI EI PRÆCEPTA ATQUE INDICIA ] De Sabbati otio hoc accipiunt Hebræi, & de Pa- rentum honore, idque ob verba illa, sicut præcepit tibi Domi- nus Deus tuus: quæ bis reperiuntur Deut. 15. commate 12. & 15. Alii etiam judicia tunc ajunt instituta.

Judicia sine dubio Mose antiquiora sunt, quum sine Judiciis societas humana consistere ne- queat: sed certam judiciorum formam Moses tradi- dit. Neque Præceptum de Parentum honore tum demum traditum, quod in Paradiso jam sancitum, imo naturæ ipsi impressum fuisse certum est. Ideo Deus Genes. 2, 24. in Conjugii institutione: Relin- quet homo patrem suum & matrem, & adhærebit uxori suæ, subinnuens præceptum de honore & amore parentum, quo illis adhærere tenemur. Sed ne illud quidem de Sabbati otio adeo recens, ut de- inceps dicturi sumus. Cur vero non adducit etiam alias ceremonias, ut de vacca russa, & quas præ- terea ibi traditas Ebræi putant? Sed rectius alii no- vam quandam Politiæ formam hîc constitutam ajunt, & generalioribus quibusdam ac facilioribus legi- bus tanquam rudimentis ad reliqua mandata, quæ sequi debebant, fuisse præparatum populum. Dici etiam fortassis potest, quæ præcepta constituta fue- rint, versu sequenti exprimi: si audieris vocem Do- mini, &c. quod γενικῶς hîc tantum obedientiam po- stularit, præceptis suis, quæ deinceps εἰδικῶς erat præscripturus, sincere præstandam, addita promis- sione gratiæ, cujus nunc specimen hac miraculosa aquarum sanatione oculis usurparant.

## 15:26
Verse same. AND SHALT OBEY HIS MANDATES.] Given to Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, in which there was no law concerning sacrifices, which men found of their own accord. He looks to this place in Jerem. 7:22: 'For I did not speak with your fathers and did not command them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning the matter of burnt offerings and victims: but this word I commanded them, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God and you shall be my people, and walk in all the way that I have commanded you that it may be well with you.' It appears these were taken from here. 'In the day that I brought them out,' interpret as: 'when I had first brought them out.' The law concerning sacrifices (except for the Passover, which is a commemorative feast rather than a legal sacrifice) was not given, unless on the occasion of idolatry committed by the people. That disease could not be cured except by a heavy burden of rites, pertaining mostly to victims.

The fiction of the Jews concerning the seven commandments given to Noah, which in Seder Olam c. 5 they ridiculously construct from the words of Gen. 2:17, 'the Lord commanded, saying: Of every tree thou shalt eat, &c.,' Hugo more than once makes his own, who delights in the trifles of the Rabbis to a wonderful degree. These commandments are: 1. That they should not worship idols, 2. that they should not curse God or His holy name, 3. that they should not practice thefts or rapines, 4. that they should not shed human blood, 5. that they should not defile themselves with incestuous marriages when the human race was soon multiplied, 6. that they should create judges who should pronounce laws according to these commandments. And they say these were given to Adam, and repeated to Noah, and a 7th was added: that they should not eat a limb of a living animal. Episcopius is more correct, whom Grotius once valued highly, lib. 1. Instit. c. 8. Those, if you except the last, which is merely ceremonial, recognize the dictates of natural reason rather than commandments handed down by Cabala: and there were many more others to which the first man and his posterity were bound. But we have taught before that the law concerning sacrifices is not of human invention, but of divine tradition: nor does Jeremiah contradict: His words are to be taken according to a certain respect, and in a comparative sense: that he demanded not so much sacrifices as obedience, in the day of the bringing out from Egypt, by which is noted not the day itself, strictly, on which they went out, but the time of the legislation, which was done in the desert after the exit. For the day of the exit is accustomed to be taken with a certain latitude, so that it may also embrace the time immediately following, and especially the time of the promulgation of the law: because for this cause they had been brought out of Egypt. Cf. Jer. 31:32. Nothing is better known than that the adverb of negation is sometimes put for a comparative particle. See Gen. 45:8. Exod. 16, 8. Prov. 8, 10. That this also happens in similar subject matter, some observe from a comparison of Hos. 6, 6 and 1 Sam. 15, 22. That the people already had a law concerning sacrifices before it was reduced to a certain formula by Moses in a solemn manner, is apparent from the first command concerning leading out and dismissing the people: When you have brought my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice upon this mountain. Exod. 3, 12 and verse 18. You and the Elders of Israel shall go to the King of Egypt, and you shall say to him: We will go a journey of three days into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God. Therefore, the law concerning sacrifices was not given only afterwards on the occasion of idolatry committed by the people. And not only idolatry, but sins of every kind, not only of the people, but of any from among the people, were to be expiated by sacrifices. Nor did the multitude or number of rites contribute even to the least of sins, much less to the expiation of idolatry, the most grievous of all, inasmuch as they were to be expiated only by the blood of the Messiah who cleanses us from all sins, 1 John 1, 7, exhibited figuratively in piacular sacrifices, but apprehended by true faith by those to whom remission happens, Heb. 11, 4 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. eodem. ET OBEDIERIS MANDATIS EJUS.] Datıs Noæh, Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, in quibus non erat lex de sacrificiis, quæ sua sponte homines invenere. Respi- cit ad hunc locum Jerem. 7, 22. Quia non sum loquutus cum Patribus vestris & non præcepi eis in die, qua eduxi eos de terra Ægypti de verbo holocaustonatum & victimarum: sed hoc ver- bum præcepi eis dicens: Audite vocem meam, & ero vobis Deus & vos eritis mihi populus, & ambulate in omni via, quam mandavi vobis ut bene sit vobis. Apparet hæc hinc sumpta In die, qua eduxi, interpretare, cùm primùm eduxissem. Lex de sacrificiis (excepto Paschate, quod convivium magis est commemorativum, quam sacrificium legale) data non est, ni- si ex occasione idololatriæ à populo commissæ. Non poterat is morbus sanari nisi multo rituum, ad victimas maxime perti- nentium, onere.

Commentum Judæorum de septem Præceptis Noæ datis, quæ in Seder Olam c. 5. ridicule è verbis Gen. 2, 17. præcepit Dominus dicens: De omni arbore comedes &c. extruunt, non semel suum facit Hugo, qui nugis Rabbinorum mirum quantum delecta- tur. Præcepta hæc sunt: 1. Ne idola colant, 2. ne Deo aut sancto nomini ejus maledicant, 3. ne furta aut ra- pinas exerceant, 4. ne sanguinem humanum fundant, 5. ne multiplicato mox genere humano incestis se nu- ptiis fœdent, 6. ut Judices creent, qui jura secundum hæc præcepta dicant. Atque hæc Adamo data fuisse dicunt, & Noacho repetita, additumque 7. ne mem- brum vivi animalis comedant. Rectius Episcopius, quem magni fecit quondam Grotius lib. 1. Instit. c. 8. Illa, si postremum, quod mere ceremoniale, excipias, rationis naturalis dictamina potius agnoscit, quam præcepta per Cabalam tradita: multoq; plura alia fuis- se, ad quæ primus homo, ejusque posteri obligati fue- rint. Legem vero de sacrificiis non esse humanæ in- ventionis, sed divinæ traditionis, antea docuimus: nec contrariatur Jeremias: Ejus verba secundum quid, & sensu comparato accipienda: quod non tam sacrificia, quam obedientiam postularit, in die eductionis ex Ægypto, qua notatur non ἀποτόμως ipsa dies, quo egressi sunt, sed tempus νομοθεσίας, quæ post egressum in deserto facta. Solet enim dies eductionis cum latitudine quadam accipi, ut tem- pus etiam proximum complectatur, maxime ve- ro promulgationis legis: quia hujus causa ex Ægy- pto educti erant. Conf. Jer. 31. 32. Nihil notius, quam quod adverbium negandi quandoque pro com- parativa particula ponatur. Vid. Gen. 45, 8. Exod. 16, 8. Prov. 8, 10. Quod etiam in simili materia usu venire è collatione Hose. 6, 6. & 1. Sam. 15, 22. non- nulli observant. Legem autem de sacrificiis ha- buisse jam populum, antequam ea solemni ratione in formulam certam redigeretur à Mose, vel è pri- mo de educendo & dimittendo populo mandato apparet: Cum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto, immolabis super montem istum. Exod. 3, 12. & vers. 18. Ingredieris tu & Seniores Israël ad Regem Ægypti, & dices ad eum: Ibimus viam trium dierum in solitu- dine, ut immolemus Domino Deo nostro. Non ergo lex de sacrificiis postmodum demum occasione idololatriæ à populo commissæ, data. Nec tantum idololatria, sed omnis generis peccata, non po- puli tantum, sed quorumvis è populo, expianda erant sacrificiis. Neque vel ad minimum peccato- rum, nedum ad idololatrias omnium gravissimum expiandum, rituum sive multitudo sive numerus conferebat, utpote quæ non nisi sanguine Messiæ ab omnibus peccatis nos mundantis, 1. Joh. 1, 7. expian- da, in sacrificiis piacularibus figurate exhibito, at ve- ra fide ab iis, quibus contingit remissio, apprehen- so, Ebr. 11, 4. seqq.

## 15:27
Verse 27. AND THAT WHICH IS RIGHT, THOU SHALT DO BEFORE HIM] Sound reason itself teaches what is right in itself and everywhere.

These things are adapted to fostering Papal will-worships. God does not want His worship to depend on the dictate of our reason. He binds us to the norm of His law. Therefore, that which is RIGHT BEFORE THE LORD is not what reason perhaps dictates to us, but what God declares to be right. For it cannot be recognized unless God teaches it. And these things explain each other here: 'to hear the voice of the Lord,' and 'to do that which is right before him,' because not only is the voice of the Lord to be heard, but one must also work according to the same, just as the others declare each other: 'to obey his mandates,' and 'to keep all his commandments.' The mandate precedes, the observation of the mandate ought to follow. It is for GOD to command, but for man to execute the commands. 'Let not everyone do what seems right in his own eyes,' the Lord commands in Deut. 12:8, which is diametrically opposed to the glosses of Grotius. And in verse 32. Whatever I command you, you shall keep, so that you may do it; you shall not add to it, nor take away from it. Num. 15:39. Let them not follow their own thoughts and whorish eyes (reason wanders here and there, like the eyes of harlots, when it forms new cults according to the occasion), but mindful of the commandments of God, let them do them. Cf. Isa. 29:13. Matt. 15:9. Psalm 106:36. Isa. 1:12.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ET QUOD RECTUM EST, CORAM EO FECERIS] Quod per se & ubique rectum, ipsa docet sana ratio.

Hæc accommodata sunt fovendis ἐθελοθρησ- κείαις Papalibus. Non vult Deus cultum suum pen- dere à nostræ rationis dictamine. Ad normam le- gis suæ nos adstringit. Ideo RECTUM CO- RAM DOMINO non est, quod forte nobis ratio dictat, sed quod rectum esse Deus declarat. Non enim nisi Deo docente id agnosci potest. Et explicant hîc se mutuo illa, audire vocem Domini, & quod rectum est coram eo facere, quia non audienda tantum est vox Domini, sed juxta eandem etiam operandum est, uti & reliqua se invicem declarant, obedire mandatis ejus, & custodire omnia præcepta ipsius. Mandatum præcedit, sequi debet observatio man- dati. DEI est jubere, hominis autem exequi jussa. Non faciat unusquisque, quod in oculis suis rectum vi- detur, præcipit Dominus Deut. 12, 8. quod è Dia- metro glossæ Grotianæ repugnat. Et versu 32. Quicquid ego præcipio, custodietis, ut faciatis, non addes ad illud, neque diminueves ex eo. Num. 15. v. 39. Non sequantur cogitationes suas & oculos meretricios (ratio hinc inde vagatur, ut meretricum oculi, cum pro re nata novos efformat cultus,) sed memo- res præceptorum Dei, faciant illa. Conf. Esa. 29, 13. Matth. 15, 9. Psalm. 106, 36. Esa. 1, 12.

## 15:27
Vers. 28. TWELVE SPRINGS] For the number of the tribes, if you join the descendants of Joseph into one.

SEVENTY PALM TREES] For the number of the Elders. Christ observed the same numbers in the selection of his ministers.

Latin:

Vers. 28. DUODECIM FONTES] Pro numero tribuum, si Josephi posteros in unam conjungas.

SEPTUAGINTA PALMÆ] Pro numero Seniorum. Eosdem numeros in ministrorum suorum delectu servavit Christus.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. Murmuring. Manna, and Quails.

Ver. 1. INTO THE DESERT OF SIN.

Which was the eighth station; for the seventh was at the Red Sea, the journey having turned back to it, Num. 23 v. 10. That desert between the Red Sea and Mount Sinai is different from the desert of Sin, Num. 20 v. 1, ch. 34 v. 3, which is called Kadesh, in which the thirty-third station was.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. Murmur. Manna, & Coturnices.

Vers. 1. IN DESERTUM SIN.

Quae octava fuit mansio; septima enim ad mare rubrum fuit reflexo ad illud itinere, Num. 23 v. 10. Desertum illud inter mare rubrum & montem Sinai diversum est a deserto Sin, Num. 20. v. 1. c. 34. v. 3. quod Cades vocatur, in quo trigesima tertia mansio fuit.

## 16:4
Ver. 4. I WILL RAIN BREAD FOR YOU FROM HEAVEN.

It points to Manna, inasmuch as from it, when crushed, they made cakes of bread, Num. 11, 8. Concerning Manna, see the elegant treatise of our B. Walther, published on this subject.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PLUAM VOBIS PANES DE COELO.

Manna indigitat, utpote ex quo contuso tortulas panis faciebant, Num. 11, 8. De Manna vid. elegans Tractatus B. Waltheri nostri, de hoc argumento editus.

## 16:5
Ver. 5. ON THE SIXTH DAY THEY PREPARE WHAT THEY BRING IN.

Which they store in their tents, so that they may eat it on the following day, the Sabbath: from which it is evident that the law concerning the Sabbath was already in force at that time, concerning which see at Gen. 2, 3. Origen and Ambrose in the first chapter to the Corinthians, ch. 12, and others, do not wrongly deduce from this that the day on which Manna first rained was Sunday: for from this, the sixth day is the preparation of the Sabbath, for us the day of Friday.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DIE SEXTO PARENT, QUOD INFERANT.

Quod condant in tabernaculis, quo sequente die Sabbathi vescantur: unde constat, legem de Sabbatho tum jam viguisse, de quo ad Genes. 2, 3. Orig. & Ambrof. in priorem ad Corinth. 12. cap. aliique hinc non male deducunt diem, quo primum pluit Manna, fuisse Dominicum: ab hoc enim dies sexta est parasceve Sabbathi, nobis dies Veneris.

## 16:7
Ver. 7. I HAVE HEARD YOUR MURMURING AGAINST THE LORD.

The name of the Lord is not repeated merely for the sake of honor, or placed absolutely for the reciprocal, as the Jews and Photinians and Papists wish, but there underlies a mystery of the plurality of the divine persons when the Lord speaks of the Lord, just as when the Lord rains from the Lord, as we have observed at Gen. 19, 24 and elsewhere. The Lord in the pillar of cloud, to whom they were to approach, ver. 9, heard the murmuring against the Lord, i.e., the Son of GOD, the judge of all the earth, Gen. 18, 25, heard the murmuring against God the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 7. AUDIVI MURMUR VESTRUM CONTRA DOMINUM.

Non tantum honoris causa repetitur nomen Domini, aut absolutum ponitur pro reciproco, ut Judaei & Photiniani ac Papist. volunt, sed subest mysterium pluralitatis personarum divinarum cum Dominus de Domino loquitur, uti cum Dominus pluit a Domino, quemadmodum ad Gen. 19, 24. & alias observavimus. Dominus in columna nubis, ad quem accedere debebant vers. 9. audivit murmur contra Dominum, h. e. Filius DEI judex universae terrae Genes. 18, 25. murmur audivit contra Deum Patrem.

## 16:10
Ver. 10. THEY LOOKED TOWARD THE WILDERNESS.

Namely, outside the camp. There the glory of the Lord appeared, because Jehovah manifested Himself in the cloud in a most august splendor, but outside the camp, as if He were about to abandon the camp and leave the murmuring people. There is no reason why we should say with the Papist interpreters that an angel appeared in place of GOD, since it is said ῥητῶς and expressly that GOD Himself appeared.

Latin:

Vers. 10. RESPEXERUNT AD SOLITUDINEM.

Scilicet extra castra. Ibi apparuit gloria Domini, quia in splendore perquam augusto se manifestabat Jehova in nube, sed extra castra quasi castra deserturus & populum murmurantem relicturus esset. Non est, cur dicamus cum Papp. Interpp. Angelum vice DEI apparuisse, siquidem ῥητῶς ac diferte DEUS ipse apparuisse dicatur.

## 16:13
Ver. 13. THE QUAIL COMING UP] The Greeks, ὀρτυγομήτρα.

It is not, however, sufficiently ascertained whether it was that bird. The Rabbis Solomon and Kimchi are content to say a fat bird. But Jonathan, both here and in Psalm 105, interprets it as pheasants. Josephus notes that no such birds as are described here are found except at the Arabian Gulf, as a sign of a miracle. A coming or flying crowd of quails, for that name is taken collectively; which the Hebrews consider to be general, inasmuch as by it are comprehended quails, partridges, francolins, and pheasants. The more accepted opinion, however, is that quails are designated specifically. It is to be noted that the sending of quails was not continued every evening, as Manna rained from Heaven every morning for 40 years, but it happened only twice, namely in this place, and Num. 11 v. 31 at the graves of craving, which history is referred to in Ps. 78, 26 and 27, which is clearly different from this one of ours, as the circumstances show. For although a doubt may be raised from the fact that Moses, when GOD was promising meat there to the murmuring people, doubted and objected that for such a great number of six hundred thousand, flocks and herds and the fish of the sea would hardly suffice in that place Num. 11, 21. Yet it must be acknowledged that Moses had either already forgotten the previous miracle, which also happened to the disciples of Christ in the desert, or, which seems more likely, he doubted concerning the circumstance of time, because GOD had said that He would give meat for an entire month, since he had not seen meat given miraculously in such quantity and for such a multitude of people, not to mention that Moses also doubted at the waters of contradiction, even though he had seen many miracles in the waters.

Verse of the same. ALSO IN THE MORNING THE DEW LAY.

In Hebrew it was 'morning there was a lying down or a bed of dew,' so that the whole plain was as if covered with dew. Vatablus, with the Chaldean, renders it: 'there was a covering of dew.' He who takes the word 'dew' properly, along with certain Rabbis, Lyranus, Oleastrius, and Cajetan, [understands it] in such a way that it descended in the morning with the dew, and the dew covered the manna like a certain case both from below and from above; to which opinion B. Waltherus also added his support. Others, however, understand by the dew in this place the manna itself, which was similar to a dewy and liquid humor, but coagulated and frozen, concerning which it is held in verse 14 that it appeared in the likeness of hoarfrost, because as the sun grew hot the manna would liquefy and vanish, just as dew vanishes. For concerning this, that it appeared in the wilderness on the surface of the earth like dew and like hoarfrost, it is stated openly in verse 15 that when the children of Israel saw it, they called it manna. Therefore there is no reason to doubt that that same thing, which is said to have lain like dew and appeared on the earth in the likeness of hoarfrost, was the manna itself.

When therefore it is said in Num. 11, 9 that the manna descended with the dew, by the name of dew, hoarfrost is understood, but in this place only the similarity of the dew to the manna is designated. Which opinion of Philo, Josephus, Greg. Nyssenus, Tostatus, and Corn. à Lap. is not to be rejected, if it is correctly explained, i.e., if only it is not denied that the manna was of a singular substance different from the dew, so that the name of dew was attributed to it only by analogy. For it is absolutely certain that it was a peculiar and extraordinary food, therefore it had to be preserved as a miraculous and singular thing Exod. 16, 33, and the sweet and delightful taste itself, and the power and faculty of nourishing, sufficiently teach that it is different from dew and hoarfrost, to which it was only analogous by reason of shape, color, and thinness, because it could not withstand the heat of the sun like dew and hoarfrost, for which reason August. in quaest. in V. T. c. 20, says: 'this bread or food was not created by the law of the world, by the mixing of elements; but it came from above, provided by a spiritual reason.' But that the manna was enclosed by dew lying upon it and lying under it will be difficult to prove from the sacred scriptures, nor is the tradition of the Jews trustworthy in this matter: it is more likely that the hoarfrost or dew was like a certain clean linen cloth, upon which the manna lay Num. 11, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ASCENDENS COTURNIX] Graeci, ὀρτυγομήτρα.

Non tamen exploratum satis, an ea avis fuerit. Rabbini Salomo & Kimchi contenti sunt dicere avem pinguem. At Jonathan & hic & in Psalm. 105. phasianos interpretatur. Tales autem aves, quales hic describuntur, nullas nisi ad Arabicum sinum notat Josephus in signum miraculi. Veniens vel advolans turba coturnicum, nomen enim illud collective sumitur; quod Ebraei generale esse censent, utpote quo comprehendantur coturnices, perdices, attagines & phasiani. Receptior tamen sententia est, coturnices in specie designari. Id notandum est, non continuatam fuisse coturnicum immissionem quavis vespera, uti quovis mane de Coelo Manna pluit per 40. annos, sed bis tantum facta est, hoc nempe in loco, & Num. 11. v. 31. ad sepulchra concupiscentiae, quae historia respicitur Pf. 78, 26. & 27. quae alia plane est ab hac nostra, ut circumstantiae docent. Quanquam enim dubium moveri possit ex eo, quod Moses, cum ibi DEUS promitteret carnes populo murmuranti, dubitarit atque objecerit tanto numero sexcentorum millium greges & armenta ac pisces maris ibidem vix sufficere Num. 11, 21. Agnoscendum tamen est, Mosen vel oblivioni jam dedisse prius miraculum, quod etiam discipulis Christi accidit in deserto, vel quod potius videtur, dubitasse de temporis circumstantia, quod dixerit DEUS se car- nes daturum ad integrum mensem, quia in tanta quantitate & pro tanta multitudine populi non viderat datas miraculose carnes, ut taceam quod Moses ad aquas etiam contradictionis dubitarit, etsi miracula multa in aquis viderit.

Vers. eod. MANE QUOQUE ROS JACUIT.

In Ebr. mane fuit cubatio aut stratum roris, ut tota planities rore quasi strata fuerit. Vatablus cum Chaldao reddit: fuit operimentum roris. Qui roris vocem proprie accipit cum Rabbinis quibusdam, Lyrano, Oleastrio & Cajetano, ita, ut mane cum rore descenderit, & ros manna instar thecae cujusdam tam inferne quam superne operuerit; cui sententiae etiam calculum adjecit B. Waltherus. Alii tamen per rorem hoc in loco intelligunt ipsum manna, quod simile fuerit humori rorulento & liquido, sed coagulo, ac conglaciato, de quo vers. 14. habetur, quod in similitudinem pruinae apparuerit, quia sole calescente liquefcebat, & evanescebat manna, uti ros evanescit. Nam de hoc, quod roris instar in solitudine apparuit in superficie terrae & instar pruinae, dicitur aperte vers. 15. quod cum id vidissent filii Israel, manna id vocarint. Ideo dubitandum non est, quod idem illud, quod tanquam ros jacuisse dicitur, & in similitudine pruinae apparuit super terram, ipsum manna fuerit.

Cum ergo Num. 11, 9. dicitur, quod manna cum rore descenderit, roris nomine pruina intelligitur, hoc autem in loco similitudo tantum roris cum manna designatur. Quae sententia Philonis, Josephi, Greg. Nysseni, Tostati, Corn. à Lap. non improbanda, si recte explicetur, h. e. si modo non negetur, Manna singularis fuisse substantiae diversae à rore, ita, ut nomen roris ei solum per analogiam tributum sit. Nam certum omnino est, peculiarem fuisse & extraordinarium cibum, ideo tanquam res miraculosa & singularis asservari debuit Exod. 16, 33. & sapor ipse dulcis & delectabilis, ac vis & facultas nutriendi docet satis, diversum esse à rore ac pruina, cui solum analogum fuit ratione figurae, coloris ac tenuitatis, quod roris ac pruinae instar solis ardorem sustinere nequiverit, quo nomine August. in quaest. in V. T. c. 20. hic panis, inquit, aut cibus non mundi lege creatus est, commixtione elementorum; sed desuper venit spirituali ratione provisus. Rore autem incubo & succubo conclusum fuisse manna, è sacris litteris aegre probabitur, neque fida hac in re est Judaeorum traditio: vero similius est pruinam sive rorem fuisse instar linteaminis cujusdam mundi, cui incubabat Manna Num. 11, 9.

## 16:14
Verse 14. IT APPEARED IN THE WILDERNESS SMALL AND AS IF BEATEN WITH A PESTLE.

It did not appear in the camp, because they were filthy, but outside the camp verse 27. It is said to be 'as if beaten with a pestle,' because it fell down as if husked by pounding and stripped of its follicles, or rather, because it was like wheat from which the husk has been removed by a pestle. Therefore the Chaldean translates it: 'husked.' The LXX [translate it] λεπτον, 'fine.' In Num. 11, 8 it is said to have been like bdellium, where the LXX have 'like crystal.' Pagninus: 'like a pearl': yet it had to be subsequently beaten with a pestle or mill, so that it might be reduced to flour. From which both the agreement and the difference of this manna from common manna, such as is frequent in Poland and Prussia, and from medicinal manna, is evident. Franc. Vallesius in 'De S. Philof.' c. 57 wishes it to have been the same as the medicinal manna which we use for the sake of purging. But the difference is manifest, because this is a medicine, not food; it does not satiate, nor does it generate good blood, it is used only for purging, nor does it melt in the sun like the manna of the Hebrews. The agreement of the Polish manna is greater, which also falls there before sunrise with the dew, is gathered with a sieve, shaken out, pounded, mixed with water, from which porridge is made, so that it may analogously serve for the use of bread; which is likewise sweet and pleasant; yet it differs in this, that it does not melt in the sun, but is only dissolved, so that the grain or seed falls: and that it has a husk, unlike the manna of the Hebrews, and finally, it does not fall every day; not to mention the miracles in the manna of the Hebrews, about which later.

Latin:

Vers. 14. APPARUIT IN SOLITUDINE MINUTUM ET QUASI PILO TUSUM.

Non in castris apparuit, quia sordida erant, sed extra castra vers. 27. Dicitur quasi pilo tusum, quod quasi tunsione decorticatum, & folliculis suis exutum depluerit, vel potius, quod instar tritici, cui pilo cortex ablatus est, fuerit. Ideo Chaldaeus vertit, decorticatum. LXX. λεπτον, album. Num. 11, 8. dicitur bdellio simile fuisse, ubi LXX. habent, simile Crystallo. Pagnin. simile Margaritae: erat tamen deinceps pilo aut mola tundendum, ut in farinam redigeretur. E quibus & convenientia & differentia Manna hujus à Manna vulgari, quale in Polonia & Prussia frequens est, & à manna medicinali, constat. Franc. Vallesius de S. Philof. c. 57. vult, idem fuisse cum medico manna, quo purgandi gratia utimur. Sed differentia manifesta est, quia hoc medicamentum, non cibus est, non saturat, nec sanguinem bonum gignit, solum ad purgandum adhibetur, neque etiam ut manna Ebraeorum ad solem liquefcit. Major est convenientia Polonici mannæ, quod ibi etiam ante solis ortum depluit cum rore, cribro colligitur, excutitur, tunditur, aqua miscetur, ex quo pultes conficiuntur, ut in usum panum analogice cedere possit; quod dulce item est ac suave; in eo tamen differt, quod non li- quescat ad solem, sed tantum solvatur, ut granum, vel semen decidat: quodque folliculum habeat se- cus atque Ebræorum manna, denique non cadat singulis diebus; ut taceamus miracula in Ebræo- rum manna, de quibus postea.

## 16:15
Ver. 15. THEY SAID TO ONE ANOTHER MANHU, WHICH MEANS, WHAT IS THIS?] מָן for מָה is Egyptian, as Hiskuni notes. From that language the Hebrews still retained many things. Thus also the Greeks interpret, and Onkelos, and Jonathan. Josephus likewise, adding: according to our dialect, namely the Jerusalem dialect of his time, which had again drawn much from neighboring nations.

Thus also the Greeks Origen, Theodoret, and Cyril interpreted it in book 3 on John, ch. 34, and most others. Aben-Ezra, Rungius, Piscator, etc. Drusius similarly takes it for Egyptian at the difficult passage of Exodus. And Schindler notes in his Pentaglot Lexicon that the little word מָן is taken in that sense among the Chaldeans also, and likewise among the Arabs. But he adds that for them the pronoun מָן is interrogative, concerning a person, just as the Hebrew מִי who? therefore it cannot be used here for a thing. He prefers, therefore, to derive it from מָנַר he counted, whence the Hebrew מָן gift: so that it is a noun, as if to say, this gift which has been prepared and counted out divinely. For being ignorant of what it was, they called it by this general name, and by it they acknowledged it as a singular and extraordinary gift, in which way also the blessed Luther, Forster, Chytræus, Gesner, Avenarius, Walther, and others of ours explain it, as well as Oleastrius, Pagninus, as also Vatablus: Mercer, Calvin, Tremellius, Junius, Tossanus, Scaliger, Buxtorf, and likewise Marc. Marinus, Guido Fabricius, R. Mardochai Nathan, etc. And although the people had not yet thought of the partitive counting, about which it follows finally in verse 16, they nevertheless acknowledged that this food was given and distributed to them divinely. That the etymology of the word Man from מָנָה has a place in verse 31, Junius himself admits, and most of the remaining interpreters agree. Nor does Man, as a pronoun, occur in the Hebrew language. For that single passage Psalm 61:8 is irrelevant: because there Man is with a Patach, and is an imperative, not a pronoun.

Ver. same. FOR THEY DID NOT KNOW WHAT IT WAS] They marveled at the Vav of the letters inscribed in it: Thus the Hebrews. The multiplication of what was gathered to satiety for each family, the corruption of what was kept, its failure on the Sabbath, the taste by no means common, undoubtedly increased the miracle later, the works of God. Otherwise, all ancient and new writers testify that Manna is found in Arabia. Isidore calls it honey coagulated in Arabia, adhering to branches in the likeness of salt.

They are trifles that are peddled from the Hebrews about the inscription of the letter. That the rest are the works of GOD, which are not common, no one doubts. But this too is a work of GOD, that Manna was peculiarly prepared. For the common one, which he says is found in Arabia, differs greatly from this. Otherwise, there is a double common manna: Medicinal, having the power of purging, which no one would say was that of the Israelites: and edible, such as is also found in Poland and Bohemia, about which at verse 14, which is enclosed in a husk, whereas this lacked a husk, and was as if pounded with a hair, and covered with a new lid above, but below with frost, and thus placed as if between two layers of straw, as R. Solomon explains, and B. Walther tries to derive from the Hebrew text in De Mann. page 79, about which we spoke at verse 13. Therefore the Israelites marveled, saying, Man hu: and Moses testifies in Deut. 8:3, 16, that the Fathers of the Israelites did not know such bread. Which also, because it was singular, was ordered to be kept for a perpetual memory for posterity, Ex. 16:33. Nor is there any doubt that the munificence of GOD shines forth more if it is established that for the sake of His people He produced a new kind of food which is called the food of angels in Psalm 78:24, as if prepared or dispensed by their works. See August. Questions on the O.T. q. 20. Lyranus, Vatablus, Oleaster, Cajetanus, Cornel. à Lapide, and most of the Hebrews acknowledge this.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DIXERUNT AD INVICEM MANHU, QUOD SIGNIFICAT, QUID EST HOC?] מָן pro מָה est Ægy- ptiacum, ut notat Hiskuni. Ex eo sermone multa adhuc reti- nebant Hebræi. Sic & Græci interpretantur, & Onkelos, & Jonathan. Josephus itidem, addens: κατὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν διά- λεκτον, nempe Hierosolymitanam sui temporis, quæ multum à vicinis gentibus iterum traxerat.

Sic etiam interpretati sunt Græci Origenes, Theodoretus & Cyrillus l. 3. in Joh. c. 34. ac plerique alii. Aben-Ezra, Rungius, Piscator &c. Drusius si- militer id pro Ægyptiaco habet ad loc. diffic. Ex. Et accipi ea ratione voculam מָן apud Chaldæos eti- am, nec non apud Arabes notat Schindlerus in Lex. Pentaglott. Sed addit illis pronomen מָן esse inter- rogativum, de persona, sicut Ebræis מִי quis? non igitur de re posse hic usurpari. Mavult ergo à מָנַר numeravit, deducere, unde Ebr. מָן donum: ut no- men sit q. d. donum hoc quod præparatum est, & adnumeratum divinitus. Ignorantes enim quid esset, hoc generali nomine vocabant, eoque agno- scebant pro dono singulari, & extraordinario, quo pacto etiam explicant B. Lutherus, Forsterus, Chytræus, Gesnerus, Avenarius, Waltherus, & alii nostri, nec non Oleastrius, Pagninus, ut & Vatablus: Mercerus, Calvinus, Tremellius, Junius, Tossanus, Scaliger, Buxtorf. itemque Marc. Marinus, Guido Fabricius, R. Mardochai Nathan &c. Etsi autem de partitiva annumeratione tum nondum cogitarit populus, de qua demum v. 16. sequitur, divinitus tamen hunc cibum sibi dari, ac distribui agnosce- bant. Quod versu 31. Etymologia vocis Man à מָנָה locum habeat, fatetur ipse Junius, & consen- tiunt reliqui Interpp. plerique. Neque in lingua Ebræa Man, quod pronomen sit occurrit. Nam unicus ille locus Psalm. 61, 8. alienus est: quia ibi Man cum Patach, & Imperativus, non Pronomen est.

Vers. eodem. IGNORABANT ENIM, QUID ESSET] Mirabantur Vav literarum ei inscriptam: Sic Hebræi. Auxit postea miraculum multiplicatio collecti ad satietatem pro qua- que familia, corruptio asservati, deliquium ejus in Sabbatho, sapor minime Vulgaris, Dei haud dubie opera. Alioqui Man- na reperiri in Arabia omnes Veteres & Novi Scriptores testan- tur. Id Isidorus vocat mel in Arabia coagulatum ramis inhæ- rens in similitudinem salis.

Nugæ sunt, quæ ex Ebræis de litteræ inscri- ptione venditantur. Cætera DEI opera esse haud vulgaria, nemo dubitat. Sed & hoc DEI opus est, quod peculiariter præparatum Manna. Vulgare enim, quod in Arabia reperiri ait, maximopere ab hoc differt. Duplex alioqui est vulgare manna: Medicinale, vim purgandi habens, quale Israëli- tarum fuisse, nemo dixerit: & esculentum, quale etiam in Polonia, ac Bohemia reperitur, de quo ad v. 14. quod folliculo includitur, quum hoc follicu- lo caruerit, ac quasi pilo tusum, novoque opercu- lo tectum fuerit superius, inferius vero pruina, adeoque velut inter duo stramenta repositum, ut R. Salomo explicat, & ex Ebræo textu deducere conatur B. Walther. de Mann. pag. 79. de quo vero ad v. 13. diximus. Ideo mirabantur Israëlitæ dicen- tes, Man hu: ac Moses testatur Deut. 8, 3. 16. Israë- litarum Patres non novisse ejusmodi panem. Qu- etiam, quod singularis esset, in perpetuam memo- riam ad posteros adservari jubebatur, Ex. 16, 33. Ne- que dubium est magis resplendescere munificen- tiam DEI, si statuatur in populi sui gratiam novum genus cibi produxisse quod angelorum dicitur Psal. 78, 24. velut opera ipsorum præparatum, aut dis- pensatum. Vid. August. Quæst. ex V. T. q. 20. Agnoscunt id Lyranus, Vatablus, Oleaster, Cajetanus, Cornel. à Lapide & ex Ebræis plerique.

## 16:16
Ver. 16. AN OMER FOR EACH HEAD.

According to Villalpando, an omer was four pounds. Cornelius says it contained 8 pounds or 96 ounces, which portion would have sufficed for a daily ration even for the very voracious ancient and vigorous age. An omer is called the tenth part of an ephah: but an ephah contained three seahs, 18 cabs, 432 eggs, as the calculation is usually begun: whence an omer was 1 1/5 cabs and a fifth part of a cab or 43 1/5 eggs. But it is said in verses 17 and 18 that neither he who had gathered more had more, nor he who had gathered less had less: not that the overseers reduced the manna to equality in the distribution, as Dionysius and Eman. Saa wish, but that it happened thus by the secret direction of God, which Moses openly hints. But it seems here that the same measure was assigned to children and women as to men, because GOD adapted the manna to the stomach of each one and to the nutritive faculty, by which He testified that He provides for each one his sufficient measure of food. That which Corn. believes, that an angel condensed the manna into an omer for the more voracious, and rarefied it in others, is a fiction: nor does it rest on the truth of Scripture, that angels naturally formed the manna daily in the clouds from matter disposed for it. Nevertheless, that some ministry of angels intervened in the granting of manna can be gathered from Psalm 78:25 and Wisdom 16:10, where it is called the food of angels; although this is also explained by some according to the judgment of men, that it was held to be angelic food, just as it is permitted to say angelic and divine in the common way of speaking, because it was the most delicate, most pleasant, and most excellent food. Furthermore, authors count here 6 precepts and as many miracles concerning the manna: the first in the equality of the collection; (2) in the putrefaction, when it was kept until the next day. (3) in the liquefaction of it, which remained in the field, when that which was at home was hard; (4.) in the preservation of manna on the Sabbath day, (5.) in the duration of the same for many centuries, when it was kept in the sanctuary, (6.) in the continuous gift of manna, for 40 whole years, because it rained down every day as truly in autumn as in spring, as truly in summer as in winter, until the Israelites arrived in the land of Canaan and were able to eat of the fruits of the land: the Papists add another miracle situated in the taste from the book of Wisdom ch. 16, 20, namely that it offered every taste at will, which some extend so far that they imagine that manna was offered to the Israelites at will not only by reason of its accidents, but also as regards the substance of the food, so that if anyone desired, for example, an egg, or a chicken, and other meats, the manna supplied the place of an egg, chickens, or other meats, which fiction is approved by Claudius de Xaintes, Thomas Bofius, Greg. de Valentia, and upon it they build the portent of transubstantiation. Nor is Forsterus alien to that opinion concerning the variety of taste in sermon 53 on Exodus. But Cornel. himself refutes his own, and the contrary is manifestly clear from Moses; since he assigns a certain taste to the Manna, that its taste was like a wafer with honey Exod. 16, v. 31, which B. Waltherus of Nuremberg explains as 'von den Nurnbergischen Leck-Kuchen', B. Luth. renders it 'Semmel mit Honig', nor indeed would the people have desired meats, fish, melons, Num. 11, 4, if the taste and the power of all those things, manna would have provided according to the whim of anyone. For to say with Augustine, lib. 2. Retract. c. 19. and Abulensis, that it provided to the pious only that taste which they desired, is neither in any way probable, nor does it agree with the stated place in the Book of Wisdom. As regards the authority of Blessed Luther in the scholium on that passage, it is manifest that he is only explaining the words of that author, not however delivering his own mind. Nor, however, does he place every kind of taste in those words, but refers them to the varied manner of cooking, which Rivetus, arguing at length against Pappus (whom he says raves ridiculously here), does not disapprove; that, however, I refer, he says, to the varied manner of cooking, because it was either boiled, as if into a pottage, or made into cakes, or eaten as it fell, and thus was tempered to the desire.

Latin:

Vers. 16. GOMOR PER SINGULA CA- PITA.

Juxta Vilalpandum Gomor erant quatuor li- bræ. Cornelius dicit 8. libras seu 96. uncias conti- nuisse, quæ portio etiam valde edaci seculo prisco, & valido suffecerit ad diurnum victum. Gomer di- citur decima pars Ephæ: Epha autem continuit tria sata, 18. Cabos, ova 432. uti computus iniri so- let: unde Gomer fuerit 1 1/5. Kabi & quintæ Kabi partis vel ovorum 43 1/5. Dicitur autem v. 17. & 18. nec qui plus collegerat, habuisse amplius, nec qui mi- nus reperiisse minus: non quod præfecti ad æquali- tatem manna in distributione redegerint, ut Dio- nysius & Eman. Saa volunt, sed quod occulta dire- ctione Dei sic evenerit, quod Moses aperte innuit. Videtur autem hîc eadem mensura tam parvulis & fœminis, quam viris assignata, quod DEUS manna stomacho cujusvis attemperarit, & facul- tati nutritivæ, quo testatus est, se unicuique suffi- cientem suam mensuram cibi procurare. Quod Corn. credit, Angelum edacioribus manna in gomor condensasse, in aliis rarefecisse, commentum est: neque veritate Scripturæ nititur, quod angeli man- na quotidie in nubibus è materia ad id disposita natu- raliter efformarint. Aliquod tamen Angelorum ministerium in mannæ concessione intervenisse è Psalm. 78. v. 25. & Sap. 16. v. 10. ubi Angelorum esca dicitur, colligere est; quamvis hoc etiam à non- nullis explicetur κατὰ δόξαν secundum hominum judicium, quod pro angelico cibo habitum fuerit, uti nempe angelicum & divinum communi more loquendi dicere licet, quod delicatissimus, suavissi- mus, & præstantissimus cibus fuerit. Cæterum nu- merant hîc auctores 6. præcepta & totidem mira- cula circa manna: primum in collectionis æqualitate; (2.) in putrefactione, cum servabatur in alterū diem. (3.) in liquefactione ejus, quod in agro remanebat, cum illud durum esset, quod domi erat; (4.) in con- servatione mannæ in die Sabbathi, (5.) in duratione ejusdem per multa secula, cum in sancto asserva- tum fuit, (6.) in continua mannæ donatione, per inte- gros 40. annos, quod tam vere, quam autumno, tam æstate quam hyeme singulis diebus depluerit, donec Israëlitæ in terram Canaan devenerint, & de frugibus terræ comedere potuerint: addunt Pon- tificii aliud miraculum in sapore situm è libro Sap. c. 16, 20. quod nempe pro lubitu omnem saporem ex- hibuerit, quod eo usque nonnulli extendunt, ut non tantum ratione accidentium, sed etiam quoad substantiam cibi ad nutum manna exhibitum fuisse Israëlitis fingant, adeo, ut si quis e. c. ovum deside- raret, aut gallinam, aliasque carnes, manna ovi, gallinarum, aut aliarum carnium vicem suffecerit, quod commentum probant Claudius de Xaintes, Thomas Bofius, Greg. de Valentia, eique inædificant transsubstantiationis portentum. Neque ab illa sententia de varietate saporis Forsterus alienus est in concione 53. in Exod. Sed refellit suos ipse Cor- nel. & contrarium manifeste liquet è Mose; siqui- dem certum saporem Mannæ assignet, quod sapor ejus fuerit tanquam lagani cum melle Exod. 16. v. 31. quod B. Waltherus Norimbergensis explicat von den Nurnbergischen Leck-Kuchen, B. Luth. reddit Semmel mit Honig, neque sane populus carnes, pisces, pepones, Num. 11, 4. desiderasset, si saporem & vim istorum omnium præbuisset manna pro lu- bitu cujusvis. Nam cum Augustino lib. 2. Retract. c. 19. & Abulensi dicere, quod piis tantum illum sa- porem præbuerit, quem desiderabant, nec ullo mo- do probabile est, neque dicto libri sapientiæ loco congruit. B. Lutheri auctoritatem quod attinet in scholio ad istum locum, manifestum est, quod verba autoris istius tantum explicet, non autem mentem suam tradat. Neq; tamen omnigenum saporem in verbis illis ponit, sed ea ad variam ra- tionem coquendi refert, quod nec Rivetus prolixe contra Papp. (quos ridicule hic delirare ait,) disse- rens, improbat; id autem refero, inquit, ad variam rationem coquendi, quia vel elixabatur, quasi in pul- mentum vel in placentas conficiebatur, vel comedeba- tur, prout cadebat, & ita ad desiderium transtempera- batur.

## 16:23
Vers. 23. REST OF THE SABBATH.) Which from here went into the law. Previously observed without rest.

He imagines a Sabbath without rest: which is a σιδηρόξυλον. See what we say to v. 25 of ch. 15, and to Gen. 2, 3. We are also about to speak of it at Ex. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 23. REQUIES SABBATHI.) Quæ hinc in legem ivit. Antea observatum sine otio.

Fingit Sabbathum sine otio: quod est σιδη- ρόξυλον. Vid. quæ ad 15. v. 25. ad Gen. 2, 3. Dictu- ri etiam de eo sumus ad Ex. 20.

## 16:31
Vers. 31. IT WAS AS CORIANDER SEED.

Similar to coriander seed by reason of shape and quantity, because it was small and round, not by reason of color: for that seed is black, and therefore the comparison to the word added, white, is not to be drawn, by which color is expressed, as by that likeness shape and quantity were designated. It seems, therefore, to have been like grains of sugar. In the parallel passage Num. 11, 7, it is said to have been like coriander seed (in quantity and roundness) but like Bdellium (in quality or species of color), i.e., transparent like a pearl and a precious stone, but having grains fine and orbicular like the grains of coriander. Furthermore, since Manna is called 1 Cor. 10, 3, a spiritual food, and is explained according to a mystical signification, it is debated by Interpreters in this place whether manna was a figure of the Eucharistic bread? That it is called spiritual food on account of its mystical signification, but not because it was spiritual food by nature, is beyond controversy; nor is it called into doubt whether the mystical signification was explained by Christ in John 6, or whether manna was a figure of the body of Christ, insofar as it is given to us as spiritual nourishment; but whether it was also a figure of the Eucharistic bread? is debated, which not only the Papists affirm, but also our own people, with Cyril leading the way, lib. 4. in Joh. c. 16. See Blessed Gerb. de Cœna p. 17. Lombard lib. 4. sentent. dist. 8. Rivetus on the contrary and other Calvinists deny that the figures of the O.T. prefigured the sacraments of the New, and contend that both the sacraments of the Old as well as the New were instituted to signify one and the same thing, and to exhibit it to faith as if present, so that they were mutually antitypes to each other, that is, corresponding types; yet types of one and the same thing. But we have in this case the manifest authority of the Apostle 1 Cor. 10, 4, who, just as he calls the deduction through the Red Sea by the ministry of Moses a baptism under the cloud, compares it with our Baptism; so also he compares the food and drink given to the Israelites in the desert with the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, and teaches that those provided a certain figure of these. And Rivetus assumes a false, not conceded hypothesis, that the Sacraments of the N.T. are merely figures, and do not differ in substance from the Sacraments of the O.T. Therefore in Comment. p. 434, he says, the excellence of the Sacraments of the New Testament

above the Old is not that they contain the thing itself in themselves, while these only signified it; for both are signifying signs. Where it is manifest that he stops at mere signification, and leaves nothing to the Sacrament of the Eucharist which did not have a place in manna: manna, he says, was a symbol of the body of Christ to be crucified for us; the bread which we break is a symbol of the body of Christ delivered for us. But thus the Eucharist will have no more of signified truth than the Jews themselves had, nay, far less, for manna represented the body of Christ more clearly than other bread; and it had, as Rivetus admits, many prerogatives which the Eucharistic bread does not have; in which argument Rivetus twists himself: But in truth he does not find in what respect the excellence of manna over the Eucharistic bread derogates from the nature of the figure. For there is nothing in what he says, that in the Sacraments signs are to be considered not materially, but formally: and that the manner of signifying is to be taken from the institution itself, not from the nature of things: for in truth the Calvinists do not derive their Sacramental analogy from the words of institution, but from the nature of things, as they think, and from likeness; and since they place the form of the Sacrament in the signification itself, it is necessary that they confess either that manna had a different signification, and therefore not as excellent as the Eucharistic bread has, or that there is no formal prerogative of the Sacrament of the Eucharist over manna. Whence he had to have recourse to the more illustrious doctrine of the New Testament over the Old; but ἀπαιδεύτως: because the question is no longer about doctrine, but about the Sacraments and their prerogative in the New Testament over the figures of the Old Testament, which he could not show, nor will any of the Calvinists be able to, as long as they place the form of the Eucharistic Sacrament in the mere signification and adumbration of the body of Christ delivered for us.

Verse same. AS OF FINE FLOUR) ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν μέλιτι LXX. Now ἐγκρίδες, according to Athenaeus book 14, are a pastry boiled in oil. Aquila translates צפיחת as starch. Others prefer rice, which is the Arabic word ארזן. It is of the best juice, as Aben-Ezra notes and those who have traveled the East know.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ERAT QUASI SEMEN CORIAN- DRI.

Semini Coriandri simile ratione figuræ & quan- titatis, quia minutum & rotundum, non ratione colo- ris: Semen enim illud nigrum est, ideoq; comparatio ad vocem adjectam, album, non est trahenda, qua color exprimitur, ut similitudine ista figura & quan- titas designata erat. Simile ergo videtur granis sac- chari fuisse. In loco parallelo Num. 11, 7. dicitur fuisse sicut semen Coriandri (quantitate & rotundita- te) at sicut Bdellium (qualitate vel specie coloris) pellucidum sc. instar unionis, ac margaritæ, sed grana habens tenuia, & orbicularia instar grano- rum Coriandri. Cæterum cum Manna 1. Cor. 10. 3. & esca spiritualis dicatur, & juxta mysticam signifi- cationem exponatur, disquiritur ab Interpretibus h. l. num manna figura fuerit panis Eucharisti ci? Ob significationem mysticam escam spiritualem dici, non autem quod natura spiritualis cibus fuerit, ex- tra controversiam est; neque in dubium vocatur, si- gnificationem mysticam expositam esse a Christo Joh. 6. c. aut manna figuram fuisse corporis Christi, quatenus nobis datur in spirituale alimentum; sed an præterea etiam figura fuerit panis Eucharistici? disquiritur, quod affirmant non tantum Pontificii, sed etiam nostrates, præeunte Cyrillo lib. 4. in Joh. c. 16. Vid. B. Gerb. de Cœna p. 17. Lombardus lib. 4. sentent. dist. 8. Rivetus ex adverso & alii Calviniani negant, figuras V. T. sacramenta Novi præfiguras- se, & contendunt, utraq; tam Veteris quam Novi Sa- cramenta instituta fuisse, ut rem unam & eandem si- gnificarent, & fidei tanquam præsentem exhiberent, ita ut sibi fuerint mutuo antitypi, id est, typi correspon- dentes; rei tamen unius typi. Sed habemus in hac causa manifestam auctoritatem Apostoli 1. Cor. 10, 4. qui uti deductionem per mare rubrum per Mosis ministerium factam baptismum vocans sub nube, comparat cum nostro Baptismate; ita & cibum & potum Israelitis in deserto datum componit cum sacramento corporis & sanguinis Christi, ac docet, illa figuram quandam horum præbere. Et assumit Rivetus falsam, non concessam hypothesin, Sacra- menta N. T. esse meras tantum figuras, nec differre substantia a Sacramentis V. T. Ideo in Comment. P. 434. ait, præstantia Sacramentorum Nov. Test.

supra Vetera non est, quod illa rem ipsam in se contine- ant, haec autem tantum singnificarint; utraq; enim sunt signa significantia. Ubi manifestum est ipsum in mera significatione sistere, nihilq; Sacramento Evcha- ristiae relinquere, quod in manna locum non habue- rit: manna, inquit, fuit symbolum corporis Christi pro nobis crucifigendi; panis, quem frangimus, est symbo- lum corporis Christi pro nobis traditi. At ita Evcha- ristia non plus veritatis significatae habebit, quam ipsi Judaei habuerint, imo longe minus, manna enim clarius repraesentabat corpus Christi, quam alius panis; & multas, fatente Riveto, habuit praerogativas quas panis Evcharist. non habet; in quo argumento torquet sese Rivetus: Sed revera non invenit, in quonam excellentian mannae prae pane Evcharistico in figurae ratione deroget. Nihil enim est, quod ait, in Sacramentis signa consideranda esse non materiali- ter, sed formaliter: & significandi rationem ex ipsa in- stitutione, non ex rerum natura desumendam esse: nam revera Calviniani suam analogiam Sacramentariam non ex verbis institutionis depromunt, sed e rerum, uti putant, natura, & similitudine; & cum formam Sacramenti collocent in ipsa significatione, neces- sum est fateantur, aut diversam significationem manna habuisse, eoque non tam praestantem, quam habet panis Evcharistic9, aut nullam Sacramenti Ev- charistiae praerogativam formalem esse prae manna. Unde recurrere necessum habuit ad doctrinam illu- striorem Novi Test. prae Veteri; sed ἀπαιδεύτως: quia non jam quaestio est de doctrina, sed de Sacramentis eorumq; praerogativa in Novo Test. prae figuris Ve- teris Test. quam nullam monstrare potuit, aut quis- quam Calvinianorum poterit, quoad usq; formam Sacramenti Evcharistici in sola significatione & adum- bratione corporis Christi pro nobis traditi colloca- bunt.

Vers. eod. QVASI SIMILAE) ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν μέλιτι LXX. Sunt autem ἐγκρίδες teste Athenaeo lib. 14. πεμμάτιον ἑψόμε- νον ἐν ἐλαίῳ. Aquila צפיחת vertit ἄμυλον. Oryzan malunt alii, quae vox Arabica ארזן. Succi est optimi, ut notat Aben- esdra & norunt qui Orientem lustrarunt.

## 16:34
Verse 34. AND AARON PLACED IT IN THE TABERNACLE TO BE KEPT.

These things are said proleptically, because at that time the tabernacle had not yet been constructed; nor should it be maintained, with Lyranus and others, that the Hebrews had a certain small tabernacle before that great one was built. For what is read in chapter 33, verse 7, concerning the tent of meeting outside the camp, is extraneous; since that was only erected at Horeb, and it is a manifest indication of historical prolepsis that the manna had to be stored before the Lord, or before the testimony; for the ark of the covenant was certainly not yet constructed at that time.

Latin:

Versus 34. POSUITQUE ILLUD AARON IN TA- BERNACULO RESERVANDUM.
