Tantæ molis erat Romanum condere Papam. At Apostolus omnem animam potestatibus eminenti- bus subjicit Rom. 13, 1. Ideoque nec Pontificem ab hac subjectione eximit, neque apparet, in quonam dignitas regia inferior hodie sit, quam olim fuerit, nisi quod ausint Pontifices Reges omnes deprimere infra infimos ordinis apud se Sacerdotalis missifices. Alii cum Ascanio, Martinengo ideo regale Sacerdoti- um N. T. tribui dicunt, quod sit tempus gratiæ, Veteri autem regnum Sacerdotale, quod fuerit tempus justitiæ. Sed superflua & superstitiosa est illa vocabularum aucupatio, siquidem Petrus ver- bis Apostoli usus sit ex editione LXX. Interpre- tum. S. Johannes vero Apoc. 1, 6. c. 5, 10. cum nos Reges & Sacerdotes factos dicit, dignitatem Regiam anteposuit Sacerdotali; unde Esthius ipse in 1. Petr. 2, argumentum hoc evanescere dicit, quod statuen- dum putant nonnulli in discrimine Sacerdotii Ve- teris & Novi, refellens non Martinengum tantum, sed Hugonem Cardinalem, Thomam Anglicanum & alios.

Grotius ad verba hæc ita habet:

IN REGNUM SACERDOTALE) Græci inversa constructione βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα: ut 1. Pet. 2, 9. In Hebræo: regnum Sacerdotum. Chaldæus interpretatur reges & sa- cerdotes, ut Apoc. 5, 10. quæ idem alibi 1, 6. extulit βασιλέαν καὶ ἱερεῖς. Omnes Israëlitæ reges aliquatenus ante reges con- stitutos. Sacerdotes autem in Paschate. Philo tertio de Mose: ἐν τῷ πάσχα σύμπαν τὸ ἔθνος ἱερᾶται. Christiani reges, quod devicerint carnem, peccatum, mundum, diabolum; sacerdotes precibus, eleemosynis, martyrio in re aut propo- sito.

R. Qui vero omnis Israelitæ Reges fuerint, quum habuerint caput, & ducem suum? Qui sacer- dotes in Paschate? quum Pascha, Grotio autore, con- vivium solum fuerit Eucharisticum, neque sacrifi- cium haberi debeat? Christiani, inquit, reges, quod devicerint carnem, peccatum, mundum, Diabolum: Sa- cerdotes precibus, eleemosynis, martyrio in re aut propo- sito. Omittit præcipua, ceu sunt fides, per quam Deo sistunt sacrificium Christi, & obedientia, cujus respectu semetipsos Deo exhibent hostias viventes Rom. 12, 1. Sed cur non Israelitis etiam ista tribuit? Cau- sa in promptu est, quia non nisi carnalia de illis sapit, & quoad spiritualia illa ingens discrimen assignat in- ter Israelitas & Christianos, Socini ut & Pelagii secu- tus ductum. Quo de alias. Petrus certe eadem ratione, & ex hoc ipso loco non βασίλειον ἱεράτευ- μα facit 1. Epist. 2, 9. qua Judæi in id electi dicuntur: nec Christianos tantum merito suo Christus βασι- λεῖς καὶ ἱερεῖς fecit Apoc. 1, 6. imo uti dilexit omnes, & omnes a peccato sanguine suo lavit, in quoscunque in- de a lapsu Protoplastorum peccatum pervaserat: Ita etiam omnes, quantum ad virtutem & efficaciam meriti nec non quantum ad propositum & intentio- nem etiam promerentis, regnum & sacerdotes Dei facti sunt. Ideo in cælis a quatuor animalibus & 24. Senioribus nomine omnium Electorum, sive Ju- dæi, sive Christiani sint, sive sub V. T. vixerint, sive sub Novo, celebratur Christus, quod fecerit ipsos Deo reges & Sacerdotes. Apoc. 5, 10.

## 19:8
vers. 8. AND ALL THE PEOPLE ANSWERED TOGETHER.

That is, with one voice or common consent, because the will of the Lord had been indicated to the elders, who, having called together the whole congregation of the people, explained the same, and from common consent, indeed even with the whole assembly acclaiming, we will do everything that the Lord has spoken, their pledge having been received by Moses, and Moses reported the same to the Lord.

Latin:

vers. 8. RESPONDITQUE OMNIS POPU- LUS SIMUL.

Hoc est, una voce vel communi consensu, quod senioribus indicata fuerit voluntas Domini, qui convocata tota populi congregatione eandem exposuerint, atq; ex communi consensu, imo etiam acclamante cœtu universo, omne quod locutus est Dominus, faciemus, sponsione ipsorum percepta ad Mosen, & Moses eandem ad Dominum retulerit.

## 19:9
vers. 9. I WILL COME TO THEE IN THE DARKNESS OF A CLOUD.

In Hebrew in the density of a cloud, or in a dense cloud. It is not understood as the cloud which accompanied the Israelites by day, because that rested upon the camps of the Israelites, nor was it called a dark or dense cloud: but this one stood upon Mount Sinai: Moreover, this apparition was made so that authority and reverence might be reconciled to the ministry of Moses, and the promulgated law might be received as divine 1. Thess. 2, 12.

Latin:

vers. 9. JAM VENIAM AD TE IN CALIGI- NE NUBIS.

In Ebr. in densitate nubis, vel in densa nube. Non intelligitur nubes, quæ interdiu comitata est Israelitas, quia illa Israelitarum castris incumbebat, neque nubes caliginosa aut densa vocata est: hæc vero subsistebat in monte Sinai: Facta autem hæc apparitio est, ut conciliaretur Mosis ministerio au- ctoritas & reverentia, ac lex promulgata suscipere- tur, ceu divina 1. Thess. 2, 12.

## 19:10
vers. 10. SANCTIFY THEM TODAY AND TOMORROW.

That sanctification is separation for sacred uses is very well known. Here, however, its cause was required both continence, so that they might abstain from their wives for three days, and the washing of bodies and garments, and the purification of the camp, with a religious expectation of the Lord. Papists conclude from this continence the celibacy of the Ministers of the Church, because they judge that they are polluted by marriage. But first, they ought to have known that these things were merely ceremonial and symbolic, and intended nothing else than that their minds should be called away from all things that are earthly and pertain to this life; and that they do not suppose or imply any legal pollution in the use of marriage, which is never reckoned among legal pollutions, but just as in fasting we abstain from food and drink, not as from things polluted or polluting, but which do not so much conduce to more intense spiritual meditation; so also this abstinence was required when that admirable Θεοφανεια was imminent. Although some believe that this prohibition does not concern married men, or is to be referred only to a woman suffering from her period, and legally unclean. Furthermore, it is rashly supposed that the ministers of the Church are continuously occupied with sacred things, or even that they are called away from sacred things by the use of marriage as an order instituted by God; indeed, since the Pontificians make the husband and wife the matter of the sacrament of matrimony, and constitute the conjunction of man and wife as the form, it is so far from being the case that they can say that ministers are called away from sacred things by the sacrament of matrimony, that they must even admit that they administer the sacrament of matrimony in it, see Bellarmine, book 2, on Matrimony, ch. 5 and 6. Finally, if the administration of sacred things had been hindered by such use in the Old Testament, it should not be judged that the same is done in the New, because the holiness of Christians does not consist in these external and ceremonial things, but in internal purification and sanctification.

Latin:

vers. 10. SANCTIFICA ILLOS HODIE ET CRAS.

Sanctificationem separationem esse ad sacros usus, notissimum est. Hic autem requirebatur ejus causa tum continentia, ut nempe per triduum ab uxoribus abstinerent, tum lotio corporum & vestium, tum pur- gatio castrorum, cum religiosa expectatione Domi- ni. Papistæ ex hac continentia concludunt cœlibatum Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, quod nempe ipsos pollui ma- trimonio censeant. At primum quidem scire de- bebant, hæc mere ceremonialia esse, & Symbolica, neq; aliud intendisse, quam ut mentes avocarentur ab omnibus, quæ terrena sunt & ad hanc vitam spe- ctant; neque legalem aliquam pollutionem in usu connubii supponere aut inferre, qui nunquam ac- censetur legalibus pollutionibus, sed quemadmodum in jejunio a cibo & potu abstinemus, non tanquam a rebus pollutis aut polluentibus, sed quæ spirituali meditationi intensiori non adeo conducant; ita et- iam hanc abstinentiam, cum admiranda illa Θεοφα- νεια immineret, requisitam fuisse. Quamvis nonnul- li credant, prohibitionem hanc non concernere conjugatos, aut referendam tantum ad mulierem menstruo laborantem, & immundam legaliter. Por- ro temere supponitur, ministros Ecclesiæ continuo sacris vacare, aut etiam a sacris, per usum connubii ceu ordinis a Deo instituti, revocari; imo cum Pon- tificii maritum & uxorem materiam faciant sacra- menti matrimonii, & formam conjunctionem viri & uxoris constituant, tantum abest, ut dicere possint a- vocari ministros per sacramentum matrimonii a rebus sacris, ut fateri etiam habeant, administrare eos in eo sacramentum matrimonii, vid. Bell. lib. 2. de Matrim. c. 5. & 6. Denique si maxime in Veteri Testamento sacrarum procuratio impedita fuisset tali usu, non tamen idem in Novo fieri censendum esset, quia sanctitas Christianorum non consistit in externis istis, & ceremonialibus, sed in interna puri- ficatione & sanctificatione.

## 19:11
ver. 11. THE LORD WILL DESCEND.

It is not an enallage of person, as Cornelius wants, the second for the first; I will descend: God the Father speaks of God the Son, who was about to descend, not by a change of place, but by a revelation of His presence, as He is the one by whom the law was promulgated.

Latin:

vers. 11. DESCENDET DOMINUS.

Non est enallage personæ, ut Cornelius vult, se- cundæ pro prima; descendam ego: Loquitur Deus Pater de Deo Filio, qui descensurus erat, non muta- tione loci, sed revelatione præsentiæ suæ, utpote a quo lex promulgata est.

## 19:12
ver. 12. TAKE HEED THAT YOU DO NOT ASCEND THE MOUNTAIN, NOR TOUCH ITS BORDERS.

That was prohibited for the sake of reverence and humility, since it is not permitted even to approach Kings or Princes for those who are not called. Therefore, what is added in ver. 13, when the trumpet begins to sound, then they shall ascend the mountain, does not conflict with this interdict. The LXX add: When the voices and trumpets and clouds have departed from the mountain, then they shall ascend the mountain. But those things are not found in the sources, nor was there any doubt that, especially when that divine manifestation ceased, the way to the mountain was open to anyone. Therefore, they were only forbidden to touch the borders of the mountain out of curiosity. But when the sign was given by God, they were called to the same place by God, but only to the foot of the mountain, v. 17, and therefore not even then were they to cross the boundaries, which had been defined by some external sign or obstacle placed toward the foot of the mountain, because the whole mountain was smoking with fire, Deut. 5, 4. Whence the Apostle explained another reason for the access to Mount Zion, which is spiritual and open to all, Heb. 12, 18. But the Papists very badly distort these things to the access to the Holy Scriptures, as if it were denied to the people, with Innocent III leading the way, Epist. to the Metz, book V. Decretal. Tit. 7, cap. 12. The beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned, that is, let no simple and unlearned person presume to reach the subtlety of Holy Scripture. That apocalyptic beast did not observe that access was prohibited to both men and beasts. Whence Scripture should not be granted even to the priests and Bishops themselves, unless perhaps they are to be reckoned neither as men nor as beasts, but as vipers and Dragons. We have an interdict given to all concerning touching the mountain: no interdict is found concerning reading the Scriptures, indeed all are rather invited to read them. John 5, 39. Luke 16, 29. 1 Pet. 1, 19. But the Holy Spirit warns, even to the Bishops and Pontiffs themselves, that they must be handled reverently and soberly, lest they think παρ᾿ ὅ δεῖ φρονεῖν. Rom. 12, 3, ver. 13. OR MAN] In Hebrew איש, but the Chaldean interprets that well as אנשא. So also the LXX, ἐάντε ἄνθρωπος. It is frequent among all nations to use a masculine noun for a common one.

Latin:

vers. 12. CAVETE NE ASCENDATIS IN MONTEM, NEC TANGATIS FINES ILLIUS.

Prohibitum id reverentiæ & humilitatis causa, si- quidem nec ad Reges aut Principes accedere liceat eis, qui non vocantur. Quod ergo vers. 13. subji- citur, cum cœperit clangere buccina, tunc ascendant in montem, non pugnat cum hoc interdicto. LXX. ad- dunt: Cum voces & tubæ, & nubes discesserint ex mon- te, tum illi ascendent in montem. Sed ea non haben- tur in fontibus, nec dubium erat, cessante illa præ- fertim divina manifestatione, cuilibet patere adi- tum ad montem. Ex curiositate itaque tangere fi- nes montis tantum vetabantur. Cum autem signum datum a Deo, vocabantur eodem a Deo, sed tantum ad radicem montis v. 17. ideoque ne tum quidem ter- minos, quos aliquo externo signo vel obstaculo ob- jecto versus radicem montis definitos fuisse, tran- scendere debuere, quia totus mons igne fumabat, Deut. 5, 4. Unde Apostolus aliam rationem expli- cuit accessus ad montem Sion spiritualem, qui o- mnibus patet, Ebr. 12, 18. Pessime autem hæc de- torquent Papistæ ad accessum ad Scripturas S. quasi populo is denegatus sit, præeunte Innocentio III. E- pist. ad Metens. l. V. Decretal. Tit. 7. cap. 12. Bestia, quæ tetigerit montem, lapidetur, hoc est, simplex & indoctus aliquis non præsumat ad subtilitatem Scri- pturæ S. pertingere. Non observavit bestia illa Apocalyptica, tum hominibus tum jumen- tis prohibitum fuisse accessum. Unde nec ipsis facerdotibus ac Episcopis concedenda fuerit Scriptu- ra, nisi forte illi nec hominibus accensendi, nec be- stiis, sed viperis & Draconibus. De monte attingendo interdictum habemus, omnibus datum: de Scriptu- ris legendis nullum reperitur interdictum, imo o- mnes potius ad easdem legendas invitantur. Job. 5, 39. Luc. 16, 29. 1. Pet. 1, 19. Quas vero reverenter & sobrie tractandas esse, ab ipsis etiam Episcopis, & Pontificibus, ne sapiant παρ᾿ ὅ δεῖ φρονεῖν Spiritus S. monet. Rom. 12. 3, vers. 13. SIVE HOMO] In Hebræo איש, sed id Chaldæus bene interpretatur per אנשא Sic & LXX. ἐάντε ἄνθρω- πος. Masculinum nomen pro communi usurpare frequens apud omnes gentes.

## 19:13
ver. same. AND WHEN THE TRUMPET SHALL BEGIN TO SOUND.

In Hebrew, when the trumpet shall have drawn out or the sound shall be more prolonged. Joel 2, 5. The Chaldean and LXX render the opposite sense, when it shall have been withdrawn or ceased. Although most make this trumpet angelic, with the Chaldean and LXX, i.e., an angel striking the air so that it might emit a sound: nevertheless, some understand it properly of the sound of a horn or trumpet, by which the people were to be moved by Moses so that they might approach the mountain, which Rivetus prefers; the Jews dream that the horn of the ram which was sacrificed in place of Isaac was used. But it is more probable that the sign was given by God Himself, and indeed through an angelic trumpet, and it is more convenient to the majesty of the revelation, and it is not obscurely indicated in v. 16, the same trumpet, at whose hearing the people are reported to have feared and Moses himself to have led them out from the place of the camp, verse 17. The herald of God was summoning not only the people, but Moses himself, and the sound of the trumpet was the sign of his calling.

Latin:

vers. eod. ET CUM COEPERIT CLANGE- RE BUCCINA.

In Hebr. cum protraxerit buccina vel sonus erit protractior. Joel. 2, 5. Contrarium sensum reddunt Chald. & LXX. cum subtractus fuerit seu cessaverit. Buccinam hanc etsi pleriq; angelicam, cum Chald. & LXX. faciunt, angelo sc. aerem collidente, ut sonum ederet: Nonnulli tamen proprie intelligunt de fono cornu seu buccinæ, quo populus a Mose moveri de- buit, ut accederet ad montem, quod præfert Rive- tus; Judæi somniant adhibitum cornu arietis, qui loco Isaaci immolatus fuit. Sed a Deo ipso fignum datum fuisse, & quidem per buccinam angelicam probabi- lius est, ac majestati revelationis convenientius, & haud obscure indigitatur v. 16. eadem buccina, ut- pote ad cujus auditum timuisse populus ac Moses ipsum de loco castrorum eduxisse refertur vers. 17. Præco Dei convocabat non populum tantum, sed ipsum etiam Mosen, ejusq; vocationis signum erat sonus buccinæ.

## 19:15
ver. 15. DO NOT APPROACH YOUR WIVES] The Romans would say to be in a chaste state. This part of sanctification. 1 Sam. 21, 5. 1 Cor. 7, 5. Chaeremon the Stoic about the Egyptian Priests: ἀπέχοντο κὶ ὁμιλίας γυναικείας. See also Servius on the third Eclogue, and Porphyry on Abstinence, book two.

Latin:

vers. 15. NE APPROPINQUARFTIS UXORIBUS VE- STRIS] In casto esse dicerent Romani. Pars hæc sanctificatio- nis. 1. Sam. 21, 5. 1. Cor. 7, 5. Chæremon Stoicus de Ægyptiis Sacerdotibus: ἀπέχοντο κὶ ὁμιλίας γυναικείας. Vide & Ser- vium in Eclogam tertiam, & Porphyrium de Abstinentia se- cundo.

## 19:18
ver. 18. AND EVERY MOUNTAIN SHALL BE TERRIBLE.

In the Hebrew text it is, and the mountain trembled, whence without doubt it was terrible: which the Vulgate expressed as a consequence. For it did not always render words word for word. And therefore there is no reason for us to concede to Cornelius that the Hebrew Codex formerly read otherwise, with which this Chaldean version agrees. They count here seven terrible things on the mountain: 1. The whole mountain was trembling, 2. it was burning with fire and smoke, 3. The thunders and lightnings were dreadful. 4. There was a very thick darkness, 5. there was rain and a storm, Heb. 12, 18. 6. The sound of a trumpet was blaring, 7. an angel was proclaiming the Decalogue with a trumpet-like and horrible voice. But concerning an angel promulgating the Decalogue, nothing is held in the text, nor is it indicated that it was proclaimed with a trumpet-like voice. GOD himself, with the voice of majesty, which the people feared to hear further, promulgated it Exod. 20, 1. 19. Deut. 5, 25. 26. The Apostle indicated this from a special revelation of the Holy Spirit, Heb. 12, 21. That Moses himself trembled on account of this terrible vision, and he teaches that these things pertained to this, that it might be indicated that the law strikes terror and horror into all, just as the Gospel on the contrary brings grace, which was acquired by the blood of Christ the Mediator, who speaks better things. v. 24. Whence the allegorical sense, which the Papists note here, that the thunder signifies the terror of the preaching of the Gospel, cannot be proven. For the Apostle opposes these things, he does not compose the thunder and the voice of the Gospel, which he teaches to be sweet and full of grace.

Latin:

vers. 18. ERITQUE OMNIS MONS TERRI- BILIS.

In Ebræo textu est, & contremuit mons, unde dubio procul terribilis fuit: quod consequens ex- pressit Vulgata. Non enim semper κατὰ πόδα red- didit verba. Ideoque non est quod concedamus Cornelio, aliter habuisse olim Ebræum Codicem, cui consonat hic Chaldæus. Numerant hic septem terri- bilia in monte: 1. Totus mons tremebat, 2. igne & fumo ardebat, 3. Horrenda erant tonitrua, & ful- gura. Erat caligo densissima, 5. erat pluvia & pro- cella, Ebr. 12, 18. 6. Sonus buccinæ perstrepebat, 7. angelus voce tubali & horribili Decalogum procla- mabat. Sed de angelo Decalogum promulgante, nihil in textu habetur, neq; voce tubali proclama- tum esse indicatur. DEUS ipse voce majestatis, quam porro audire populus verebatur, promulga- vit Exod. 20, 1. 19. Deut. 5, 25. 26. Apostolus e pecu- liari S. S. revelatione indicavit Ebr. 12, 21. Mosen ipsum ob visionem hanc terribilem contremuisse, docetq; hæc eo pertinuisse, ut indicaretur legem o- mnibus terrorem & horrorem incutere, uti Evan- gelium ex adverso gratiam adfert, quæ sanguine Christi Mediatoris κρείττονα λαλῦντι acquisita est. v. 24. Unde probari nequit allegoricus sensus, quem hic Papistæ notant, tonitru significare terrorem præ- dicationis Evangelii. Nam opponit hæc Apostolus, non componit tonitru & vocem Evangelii, quam suavem & gratiæ plenam esse docet.

## 19:19
ver. 19. THE PRIESTS ALSO) That is, the firstborn. See Num. 3.

Latin:

vers. 19. SACERDOTES QVOQVE) Id est, primogeni- ti. Vide Num. 3.

## 19:19
MOSES SPOKE AND GOD ANSWERED HIM.

It is manifest that these things cannot be understood concerning the promulgation of the law, in which GOD did not speak, nor did Moses answer, but he was attending with the people. Junius conjectures that Moses expressed his consternation to the Lord, ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος, Heb. 12:21, and was raised up by the Lord's response. There is no need for such divination. What the Lord said to him, Moses himself indicates in v. 21. He repeats, namely, the prohibition against crossing the boundaries, lest they perish through rash curiosity: and thus that discourse of the history is continued in v. 23, 24, 25.

Latin:

MOSES LOQUEBATUR ET DEUS RE- SPONDEBAT EI.

Manifestum est hæc de promulgatione legis in- telligi non posse, in qua non DEUS loquebatur, nec respondebat Moses, sed cum populo attende- bat. Junius conjectat Mosen consternationem su- am exposuisse Domino ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος, Ebr. 12,21. & responso Domini erectum fuisse. Non opus tali divinatione. Quid dixerit ei Dominus, Moses ipse indicat v. 21. Repetit nempe prohibitio- nem de transiliendis terminis, ne curiositate teme- raria pereant: atque ita continuatur διαλογισμὸς ille historiæ v. 23. 24. 25.

## 19:20
v. 20. AND THE LORD DESCENDED.

But Cornelius understands it thus, that he descended further to the very summit of the mountain: as if he had previously stood only in the air, as though raised up above the mountain, and in that sense it is said in v. 18 that he descended upon the mountain. Others more simply render it in the pluperfect: But the Lord had descended, i.e., already before v. 18, or let it be understood previously in v. 18 concerning the descent onto verse 20 concerning the descent in the perfect act, and the end of the motion, which is with regard to the signs of presence, but not with regard to true motion, which does not befit God. Cornelius rashly substitutes an angel in the place of God, against the clear letter of the history.

Latin:

v. 20. DESCENDITQUE DOMINUS.

At Cornelius ita accipit, quod ulterius descen- derit ad ipsum verticem montis : ut prius tantum in aere, quasi sursum elevatus super montem constiterit, eoq; sensu descendisse super montem v. 18. dicatur. Simplicius alii reddunt in plusquamperfecto : De- scenderat autem Dominus scil. jam ante v. 18. vel in- telligatur prius v. 18. de descensu in montem: hoc ve- ro versu 20. de descensu in actu perfecto, & termino mo- tus,quod ad signa præsentiæ, non vero quoad verum motum,qui Deo non convenit. Temere Corneli- us Dei loco surrogat angelum, adversus apertam hi- storiæ literam.

## 19:22
v. 22. THE PRIESTS ALSO WHO APPROACH THE LORD.

The firstborn of the families are rightly understood, in whose power was the dignity of the priesthood: for Aaron and his sons had not yet been assumed. Cf. Exod. 24:5, ch. 19:22. There is therefore no reason why we should understand the sons of Aaron with Augustine by prolepsis, as if they are called priests, not because they were such already, but because they were to be such. For the firstborn administered the sacred rites until the Levites were assumed: because the Lord had consecrated them to himself, Ex. 13:2, Num. 8:16. To approach the Lord here is not to draw near to the place of the Lord's appearance, but it is a periphrasis of the office; whose duty, namely, it is to approach the Lord. But the Vulgate is deservedly corrected here, and the text is rendered thus with Tremellius and Junius: Neither even the priests themselves, i.e., even if they otherwise approach the Lord and sanctify themselves for that purpose or are accustomed to sanctify themselves, yet it will not be permitted for them now to draw near. Which sense v. 20 confirms.

v. same. LEST HE STRIKE THEM.

In Hebrew, lest perhaps, which is not of one doubting, but of one asserting eventually, he may divide among them. Aquila descends to διακόψῃ: For some separation is indicated by the killing, which alone the Vulgate and other interpreters express. The LXX, ἀπαλλάξῃ, may destroy. Symmachus, διαφθείρῃ, may ruin; but separation or division, whether from the people, or of the soul from the body, as dichotomy is taken in Matt. 24, which Rivetus understands, taking the place in 1 Sam. 6:8 in the same way, that Jehovah had made a division in Uzzah, that is, had separated the soul of Uzzah by killing him.

Latin:

v. 22. SACERDOTES QUOQUE QUI AC- CEDUNT AD DOMINUM.

Recte intelliguntur primogeniti familiarum, penes quos erat sacerdotii ἀξίωμα: nondum enim Aaron cum filiis assumti erant. Conf. Exod. 24,5. c. 19,22.Non ergo est, quod filios Aaronis cum Au- gust. per πρόληψιν intelligamus, quasi Sacerdotes dicantur, non quod tales jam erant, sed quia tales futuri erant. Primogeniti enim administrarunt sacra, donec Levitæ assumerentur : quia consecra- verat illos sibiDominus Ex. 13,2. Num. 8,16. Accede- re ad Dominum hic non est ad locum apparitionis Domini appropinquare, sed περίφρασις est officii; quorum scilicet munus est accedere ad Dominum. Merito autem emendatur hic Vulgata, ac textus ita redditur cum Trem. & Junio : Nec etiam ipsi sacerdo- tes, q. d. etsi illi alias accedant ad Dominum & se ad id sanctificent vel sanctificare soleant, nec ipsis ta- men licitum nunc erit appropinquare. Quem sen- sum firmat v. 20.

vers. eod. NE PERCUTIAT EOS.

In Ebr. ne forte, quod non dubitantis, sed e- ventualiter asseverantis est, dividat in eis. Aquila διακόψῃ descendit: Nam aliqua separatio indicatur per occisionem, quam solam Vulg. & alii Interpp. exprimunt. LXX. ἀπαλλάξῃ interimat. Symmachus διαφθείρῃ disperdat; separatio vel divisio autem vel a populo, vel animæ a corpore, uti διχοτομία acci- pitur Matth. 24. quem Rivetus intelligit, eodem modo locum 1. Sam. 6,8. accipiens, quod divisiffet Jehovah divisionem in Uza, id est, separasset ani- mam Uza, interficiendo eum.

## 19:24
v. 24. LEST THEY CROSS THE BOUNDARIES NOR ASCEND] The Greeks, καὶ βιαζέσθωσαν ἀναβῆναι, very well. And to this refers what we read in Matt. 11:12, Luke 16:16. What was once not permitted on the mountain, that is now permitted into heaven. The property of the word הרס is to break through.

Latin:

vers. 24. NE TRANSEANT TERMINOS NEC ASCEN- DANT] Græci καὶ βιαζέσθωσαν ἀναβῆναι, optime. Et huc respicit quod legimus Matth. 11, 12. Luc 16,16. Quod olim in montem non licuit, id nunc in cœlum licet. Proprietas vocis הרס est perrumpere.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX. Promulgation of the Law.

v. 1. AND THE LORD SPOKE) Through an angel, Acts 7:38. To whom other lesser angels were present, whence the law is said to have been given through angels by Josephus, Heb. 1:1, 2:2.

Nowhere is it read that God used an angel as a herald in the promulgation of the law; Moses proclaims with a loud voice that GOD himself promulgated the law and proposed it in person: Moses ascended the mountain to God, not to an Angel; God, not an Angel, called out to him, ch. 19:23. And when he had reported the words of the Lord to the people, and in turn the response of the people to the Lord, which certainly the Lord did not receive through an angel, v. 7 seqq., God himself promises that he will descend in a cloud, not through an angel: Now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, that the people may hear me speaking to you, and believe you forever. Nor is there any doubt that GOD himself descended onto the mountain, for which reason he wished it to be so carefully guarded that no one from the people should ascend the mountain, nor touch its boundaries. Whence the whole mountain is said to have smoked, when the Lord descended in fire, and the people are warned not to dare to cross the boundaries to see the LORD, lest the great multitude perish. Furthermore, Moses was speaking and GOD was answering him, as the words of the text have it in v. 19. Therefore, the same Lord who descended onto the mountain spoke all the words of the law, and not an Angel of the Lord in his place. chap. 20, 15. Then if the Angel had spoken thus: I am the Lord thy GOD, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt: thou shalt have no other Gods before me: would not that Angel, speaking in the place of GOD, have been able to be considered as one who must be held in the place of GOD and worshipped alone? Angels never speak in such a way: It is so far from the case that an angel should be thrust into this most solemn appearance of GOD and substituted in the place of God. He appears, he speaks, who binds the Israelites to the religion and worship of himself alone. The Lord God is strong, a Jealous one, verse 5. Therefore the people could not hear this λαλιὰν of Jehovah himself, they had need of Moses as a mediator, who might deal with GOD, not through an angel minister as mediator, but immediately. Speak thou to us and we will hear, let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die. And Moses is said to have approached the darkness in which GOD was, not a ψιλός angel. He who appears here claims for himself names, attributes, works, and axioms that are entirely divine, and those incommunicable. But that angels exercised play-acting, and that the incommunicable name of GOD was communicated to them, will never be proven: nor such a representation, in which a creature attributes to itself all things that are of God. Legates of Kings representing persons are not accustomed to usurp the name of the king, or to attribute royal honors to themselves: nor has it ever been heard that a Legate represented any King in a conjugal office, or in other incommunicable matters, says Andr. Rivetus in his Commentary on Hosea, ch. 12, p. 369. Similarly, Deut. 4, 12, Jehovah is said to have spoken from the midst of the fire, not an angel, and in this the excellence of the people is established above all the nations of the earth, verse 32. Ask of the days of old, which were before thee from the day that GOD created man upon the earth, from the one end of heaven unto the other, if such a thing as this has ever happened, or if it has ever been known, that a people should hear the voice of GOD speaking from the midst of the fire, as thou hast heard and lived. And v. 16. Out of heaven he made thee to hear his voice, that he might instruct thee, and upon earth he showed thee his great fire, and thou heardest his words from the midst of the fire, because he loved thy Fathers, etc.

But for the sake of the Socinians and the Papists, and indeed even the Jews, as it appears, Grotius chose this gloss: who also, as witnessed by Manasseh Ben Israel in Conciliat. quest. ch. 18, on Exodus, deny that God descended into the cloud. Therefore, with the Papists, he wants a certain primary angel to be the herald here, whom they call Michael. Stephen says nothing of the sort in Acts 7:38, that Moses was with an angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai: but he does not say that that angel was a minister. That it was Jehovah himself has already been demonstrated. Therefore, the Angel Jehovah was the Lord: who was none other than the Son of God: that angel who had appeared in the bush, whom Stephen had introduced in v. 30, 35. Therefore Jehovah, in promulgating the law, speaks of Jehovah Ex. 20, 7. which is an indication of distinct divine persons. And the law in the hand of the mediator (the Fathers understand the Son of GOD by great consensus, who is the ONE mediator of GOD and men) διαταγεὶς δι᾽ ἀγγέλων ordained among the angels, (as διὰ is accepted in Rom. 4, 11. 1. Tim. 2, 2. Heb. 7, 9.) is said by the Apostle Gal. 3, 19. to be a διαταγὴ to GOD and the mediator the Son of God, in whose hand it was ordained: but the ministry is attributed to the Angels, who were the attendants of the Son of GOD. THE LORD came from Sinai and rose from Seir for them: he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of saints (the LXX render it Angels) Deut. 33, 2. And thus the law was received εἰς διαταγὰς (that is, ἐν διαταγαῖς) of angels Acts 7, 52. among the arranged, and well-placed ranks of them standing by their Commander, and attending him for the sake of majesty.

Chrysostom, hom. XVII. on the Acts of the Apostles, accurately distinguishes between the angel who gave the law, and the angels through whose ministry the law was received. You who have received the law by the dispositions of Angels, and have not kept it. What is this? Some think he is saying that which was ordained by the Angels. But it is not so; for where did Angels appear ordaining the law? But he calls the law that was handed down to him through the Angel who appeared to him in the bush the disposed law. This is Chrysostom: distinguishing νομοθεσίαν or the promulgation of the law, from the ordination by the disposition of the law. He ascribes the former to the angel who testified: I am the GOD of Abraham etc., and thus to the Son of God: but he attributes the latter to the ministering angels. So Antonio Fernandes, Doctor of Coimbra; that on Gal. 3. The law was ordained by Angels in the hand of the mediator, does not signify that the Angels gave the law, but that they exhibited their ministry there: for it is certain that trumpets sounded, fires flashed, thunders were heard, and these very things were done by the ministry of the Angels, nor did Paul mean anything else. I pass over the explanation of Ludovicus de Dieu in the Acts of the Apostles p. 78, who understands by διαταγὴν ἀγγέλων a decree of the senate, in which the Son of God was the president.

In the same sense the word spoken δι᾿ ἀγγέλων, if it be understood of the law, can be accepted in Heb. 2, 2. the word promulgated among the angels: among the clangor and sound of the angels, which Paul compares with signs and wonders, and various mighty works, among which is the announced Gospel; so that regard is had not to the author promulgating, but to the circumstances and signs by which both promulgations were made. Because of those trumpets, and thunders, and the remaining signs, the angels were administering, says Theophylact. Thus also Chrysostom accepts it concerning other angelic acts in the place cited. What then shall we say? Angels were present then, to whom the nation was entrusted, and they played with trumpets and did other things, namely fire and darkness. Although there is no need to accept λόγον concerning the law, as we showed when we disputed about these passages against D. Drejer in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony Sect. III. c. V. page 980. Which is also noted by Chrysostom in the place cited. The passage Heb. 1, 1. does nothing to the matter: it is not denied there that GOD spoke of old through the Son; it is only taught that most recently he manifested himself through the Son, i.e., manifested in the flesh. Let those things which were said in the place cited p. 990 be compared.

verse same. AND THE LORD SPOKE ALL THESE WORDS. Moses is undoubtedly prefacing these things, so that he might procure the highest authority for the law, which was promulgated by the Lord himself, with the whole people listening, and might teach that the same one, who in the primeval creation inscribed the law directly upon the heart of man, now, after it had been not a little obliterated in all men by the fall and among the Israelites because of their association with the Egyptians, wished to promulgate it with his own voice in a solemn manner. The word הדברים denotes these words, which are called the words of the ten-fold covenant in chapter 34, 28, whence the name decalogue. For the ten commandments were promulgated here, which are repeated in Deut. 5, 6, seqq., and are said to be inscribed on tablets in Ex. 34, 28. Deut. 4, 13. c. 5, 23. c. 10, 4. Concerning the explanation of which these rules are wont to be noted. (1.) That all virtues and all vices ought to be reduced to the Decalogue. (2.) That all those things which are contained in Moses, the Prophets, as well as the writings of the N.T., which are moral, serve to explain its commandments. (3.) That not only the exterior works which are named are hinted at, but at the same time the interior ones are indicated, even if they are not expressly named. (4.) That the obedience owed to the law is not to be estimated from the natural powers still remaining after the fall, but from the powers granted in the state of integrity. (5.) That the affirmation of the commandments at the same time includes the contrary negation. (6.) That species are comprehended in the genus, related species and the universal genus in the principal species: that the prohibited cause is understood in the prohibited effect, and the correlate in the related. (7.) That some things are contained in them as principles in conclusions, some things as conclusions in their principles. (8.) That the same virtue can be referred to different precepts of the Decalogue for different ends and respects; and those which are similar to these, the reason for which is the perfection of the Decalogue and the interpretation of the same delivered by the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, and the very condition of the precepts. For neither can the good prescribed by the law be performed unless the contrary evil is avoided: nor does the Law require external obedience of the body, but primarily internal obedience of the heart. For God in the law commands not only the hand, or other external members, but also the heart and the whole man; nor does He demand just any kind of compliance, but perfect and consummate, which is most well-known even from the summary complex of the Law in Matt. 22, 27, that we should love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Whence the Socinians and Papists strike against the very principles, when they estimate the precepts of the Law after the manner of the Pharisees only according to the external bark of the letter, understand most things only of external obedience, and dream that far more perfect moral precepts were delivered in the New Testament. It is also manifest from these things that, when we wish to distinguish those who divide these ten words only into two tables, namely concerning the love of God and of the neighbor, otherwise and more minutely than they were distributed by God, the rules of accurate distribution can scarcely be observed, but the same are distinguished only κατά τι, inasmuch as we teach that in the first table both private worship of God is directed, by which our heart is informed concerning trust and fear, and the tongue, the most noble instrument of man, by which he is distinguished from brutes, is informed with the honor of confession and praise, and public worship concerning sanctification prescribed by God: in the second table our duties with respect to the neighbor are prescribed and directed, both external, partly special regarding those in whom there is the relation of father and son, partly general, regarding the neighbor's life, marriage, faculties, and reputation: and then internal, as far as the concupiscence of the heart is concerned. Rivetus praises the disposition of Thomas, 1. secundae qu. 100. artic. 5. Just as in human society two things are required, how one ought to conduct himself toward him who presides over the community, and then toward others who live in the same society; so the first three precepts treat of the love of GOD, and order man toward GOD according to faithfulness, reverence, and service, so that he may not transfer the sovereignty of GOD to another, that he may not commit anything injurious against Him, and that he may serve GOD, to whom he owes all things. The remaining precepts order man toward his neighbor, of whom there are some to whom we owe special gratitude on account of benefits; all however, to whom we ought not to do harm, either by deed, or by heart, or by mouth: now it is possible to do harm to a neighbor by deed in three ways, either in his person by killing him, or in a person joined to him, as regards the procreation of offspring: or in the goods of fortune as they are called; harm is done by mouth through detraction: by heart through concupiscence, for all of which remedies are prescribed in the commandments in the second table. In which distribution, although Rivetus says it is not badly handed down, we observe that he himself departs from the other Reformed, who refer four commandments to the first table, indeed even from himself, since a little before he had followed them: and that that arrangement is to be admitted only in a certain respect and for a certain reason; for one does not sin against the fifth, sixth, and seventh commandments by deed alone, but also by mouth and by heart. Therefore, only the divine distribution of the words of the law is accurate, by which the Law is distributed into ten words or commandments by the most wise Legislator.

Latin:

CAPUT XX. Legis Promulgatio.

vers. 1. LOCVTVSQVE EST DOMINVS) Per ange- lum Act. 7,38. Cui alii minores angeli aderant,unde per ange- los data lex dicitur Josepho, Hebr. 1,1. 2,2.

NUsquam legitur Deus in promulgatione legis Angelo præcone usus; DEUM ipsum legem promulgasse, & αὐτοπροσώπως eandem propo- suisse Moses λευκάδι φωνῇ proclamat: Ad Deum, non ad Angelum Moses ascendit in montem; Deus non Angelus ipsi acclamavit cap. 19, 23. Et cum populo verba Domini, & Domino vicissim responsum populi retulisset, quod certe Dominus per angelum non accepit v. 7. seqq. Deus ipse pro- mittit, se descensurum in nube, non per angelum: Jam nunc veniam ad te in caligine nubis, ut audiat po- pulus loquentem ad te, & credat tibi in perpetuum. Neque dubium est, DEUM ipsum in montem de- scendisse, quapropter tantopere cautum voluit, ne quis ascendat in montem, nec fines ejus tangat ex populo. Unde mons fumasse totus dicitur, cùm Do- minus in igne descendit, moneturque populus, ne au- sit transcendere terminos ad videndum DOMINUM, ne pereat plurima multitudo. Porro Moses loque- batur & DEUS respondebat ei, uti habent verba tex- tus v. 19. Idem ergo Dominus, qui descendit in montem, locutus est cunctos legis sermones, non vero ipsius loco Angelus Domini. cap. 20, 15. Tum si ita locutus esset Angelus: Ego sum Dominus DEUS tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti: non habebis Deos a- lienos coram me: annon Angelus ille loco DEI lo- quens loco DEI habendus, & colendus solus cen- seri potuisset? Nunquam ita loquuntur Angeli: Tantum abest, ut huic tam solemnissimæ apparatio- ni DEI ingerendus sit, Deique loco substituendus angelus. Is apparet, is loquitur, qui ad sui unius religionem, & cultum adstringit Israelitas. Do- minus Deus fortis, Zelotes vers. 5. Ideo λαλιὰν hanc ipsius Jehove audire non poterat populus, me- diatore Mose opus habebat, qui cum DEO, non per mediatorem angelum ministrum, sed immedia- te ageret. Loquere tu nobis & audiemus, non loqua- tur nobis Dominus, ne forte moriamur. Et acces- sisse dicitur Moses ad caliginem, in qua erat DEUS, non angelus ψιλός. Vindicat sibi, qui hic apparet, nomina, attributa, opera, & axiomata prorsus divina, eaque ἀκοινώνητα. Sed histrioniam exercuisse an- gelos, & DEI incommunicabile nomen ipsis com- municasse, nunquam probabitur: nec talem repræ- sentationem, in qua creatura omnia, quæ Dei sunt, sibi attribuat. Non solent Legati Regum personas repræsentantes vel regis nomen usurpare, vel regios honores sibi attribuere: nec unquam auditum est, Le- gatum Regem aliquem repræsentasse in officio conju- gali, aut aliis rebus incommunicabilibus, ait Andr. Ri- vetus Comment. in Hoseam c. 12. p. 369. Simi- liter Deut. 4, 12. Jehovah loquutus dicitur de medio ignis, non angelus, & in eo ἐξοχὴ populi constitui- tur præ omnibus terræ nationibus vers. 32. Inter- roga de diebus antiquis, qui fuerint ante te ex die, quo creavit DEUS hominem super terram, a summo cælo usque ad summum ejus, si facta est aliquando hujusmodi res, aut unquam cognitum est, ut audiret populus vocem DEI loquentis de medio ignis, sicut tu audisti & vixisti. Et v. 16. De cælo te fe- cit audire vocem suam, ut doceret te, & de terra ostendit tibi ignem suum maximum, & audisti verba illius de medio ignis, quia dilexit Patres tuos &c.

In gratiam autem Socinianorum & Pontificio- rum, imo etiam Judæorum, ut apparet, elegit Grotius hanc glossam: qui etiam, teste Manasse Ben Israel in Conciliat. quæst. c. 18. in Exod. negant, Deum in nu- bem descendisse. Ideo cum Papistis angelum quendam primarium hic præconem vult, quem illi Michaelem dicunt. Nihil tale Stephanus Actor. 7, 38. Mosen cum angelo fuisse, qui ei locutus est in monte Sina, ait: An- gelum vero illum ministrum fuisse non ait. Jeho- vam ipsum fuisse, jam demonstratum. Angelus ergo Jehovah Dominus erat: qui nullus alius, quam Filius Dei: angelus ille, qui in rubo apparuerat, quem Ste- phanus v. 30. 35. introduxerat. Ideo Jehovah legem promulgans, de Jehovah loquitur Ex. 20, 7. quod in- dicium est distinctarum personarum divinarum. Et lex in manu mediatoris (Filium DEI magno consen- su Patres intelligunt, qui UNUS mediator DEI est, & hominum) διαταγεὶς δι᾽ ἀγγέλων ordinata inter an- gelos, (uti διὰ accipitur Rom. 4, 11. 1. Tim. 2, 2. Ebr. 7, 9.) Apostolo dicitur Gal. 3, 19. διαταγὴ DEO & me- diatori Filio Dei, in cujus manu ordinata est, tribuitur: Angelis autem ministerium, qui stipatores erant Filii DEI. DOMINUS de Sinai venit & ortus est e Seir eis: illuxit e monte Paran, & venit cum decem millibus sanctorum (Ἀγγέλων reddunt LXX.) Deut. 33, 2. Atque ita εἰς διαταγὰς (hoc est, ἐν διαταγαῖς) ἀγγέλων lex accepta Act. 7, 52. inter disposita, be- neque collocata eorum agmina Imperatori suo ad- stantia, eumque majestatis causa stipantia.

Chrystost. hom. XVII. in Act. Apost. accurate distinguit inter angelum, qui legem dedit, & angelos, per quorum ministerium lex accepta est. Qui accepistis legem per dispositiones Angelorum, nec servastis. Quid est hoc? Quidam putant, eum dicere illam, quæ ordi- nata fuit ab Angelis. Non est autem sic; ubi enim Angeli apparuerunt ordinantes legem? Sed disposi- tam legem dicit eam, quæ illi tradita fuit per Angelum, qui illi apparuit in rubo. Hæc Chrysostomus: νομο- θεσίαν vel legis promulgationem, ordinationem a dispositione legis distinguens. Illam angelo ad- scribat, qui testatus est: Ego sum DEUS Abraham &c. adeoq; Filio Dei: hanc vero tribuit angelis mi- nistris. Ita Antonius Fernandius Conimbricensis Doctor; illud ad Gal. 3. Lex ordinata est per Angelos in manu mediatoris, non significat, Angelos dedisse le- gem, sed suum ibi exhibuisse ministerium: nam constat insonuisse tubas, micuisse ignes, audita tonitrua, & hæc ipsa Angelorum ministerio facta, nec aliud vo- luisse Paulum. Taceo explicationem Ludovici de Dieu in Act. Apost. p. 78. per διαταγὴν ἀγγέλων de- cretum senatus, in quo præses fuerit Filius Dei, intelli- gentis.

Eodem sensu δι᾿ ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος, si de lege intelligatur, accipi potest Ebr. 2, 2. inter an- gelos promulgatus sermo: inter clangorem sonumq; angelorum, quem confert Paulus cum σημείοις τε καὶ τέρασι, καὶ ποικίλαις δυνάμεσι, inter quæ est Evangelium annunciatum; ut non ad autorem pro- mulgantem, sed ad circumstantias & signa, quibus facta utraq; promulgatio, respectus habeatur. Ob tubas illas, & tonitrua & reliqua signa administrabant angeli, ait Theophylactus. Sic etiam de aliis actibus angelicis accipit Chrysost. h. in l. Quid ergo dice- mus? aderant tunc angeli, quibus gens fuit credita, & tubis canebant & alia faciebant, nempe ignem & cali- ginem. Quanquam de lege opus non sit accipere λόγον, uti cum de his locis contra D. Drejerum di- sputavimus Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica Sect. III. c. V. pag. 980. ostendimus. Quod etiam notatum Chrysostomo in h.l. Locus Ebr. 1, 1. nil ad rem facit: non negatur ibi DEUM per Filium olim locutum esse; solum novissime per Filium, in carne sc. manife- statum sese manifestasse docetur. Conferantur, quæ loc. cit. p. 990. dicta.

vers. eod. LOCUTUSQUE EST DOMINUS CUNCTOS SERMONES HOS. Præfatus sine dubio hæc Moses est, ut autori- tatem legi summam conciliaret, quæ ab ipso Do- mino, audiente universo populo promulgata est, ac doceret eundem, qui in primæva creatione le- gem ἀμέσως insculpsit cordi hominis, eam nunc, postquam per lapsum in omnibus hominibus ac penes Israelitas propter consuetudinem cum Æ- gyptiis non parum obliterata, αὐτοφώνως solenni ratione promulgare voluisse. Vox הדברים no- tat verba hæc, quæ cap. 34, 28. dicuntur verba fœderis decem, unde nomen δεκαλόγꙋ. Nam promulgata hic sunt decem præcepta, quæ Deut. 5, 6, seqq. repe- tita, & Ex. 34, 28. Deut. 4, 13. c. 5, 23. c. 10, 4. tabulis inscripta dicuntur. De quorum explicatione no- tari solent hæ regulæ. (1.) Reduci ad Decalogum debe- re omnes virtutes, & vitia omnia. (2.) Ad explican- da ejus præcepta facere omnia ea, quæ in Mose, Prophe- tis, ut & Scriptis N. T. continentur, moralia. (3.) Non extariora solum opera innui, quæ nominantur, sed si- mul interiora indicari, etsi non expressè nominentur. (4.) Obedientiam legi debitam non æstimandam esse ex viribus naturalibus post lapsum adhuc reliquis, sed ex viribus in statu integritatis concessis. (5.) Affirmatio- nem præceptorum simul contrariam negationem inclu- dere. (6.) In genere comprehendi species, in præcipua specie cognatas species & universum genus: in effectu pro- hibito intelligi prohibitam causam, in relato corre- latum. (7.) Quædam contineri in iis tanquam princi- pia in conclusionibus, quædam tanquam conclusiones in principiis suis. (8.) Ob diversos fines & respectus eandem virtutem ad diversa præcepta Decalogi refer- ri posse; & quæ his similes sunt, quarum ratio est per- fectio Decalogi & interpretatio ejusdem a Spir. S. tradita in Scripturis, & ipsa præceptorum conditio. Neq; enim bonum a lege præscriptū præstari potest, nisi malum contrarium caveatur: nec externam cor- poris, sed imprimis internam cordis Lex requirit o- bedientiam. Non enim manui solū, vel aliis externis membris, sed cordi etiam ac toti homini, Deus in lege præcipit; neque qualecunque solum obsequium, sed perfectum & consummatum postulat, quod vel e summaria complexione Legis Matth. 22, 27. ut dili- gamus Deum ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & ex totis viribus, & proximum sicut nosmetipsos, notissimum est. Unde in ipsa principia impingunt Sociniani, & Pontificii, cum Legis præcepta Pharisæorum mo- re juxta externam corticem literæ tantum æstimant, de externa solum obedientia pleraq; intelligunt, ac longe perfectiora moralia præcepta in N. T. tradita es- se somniant. Manifestum etiam ex hisce est, cum aliter & minutius, quam a Deo decem hæc verba distributa sunt, qui solum in tabulas duas, de dile- ctione nempe Dei & proximi, eadem diremit, di- spefcere volumus, accuratæ distributionis regulas vix observari posse, sed κατά τι tantum eadem di- scriminari, utpote cum docemus in prima tabula & privatum Dei cultum dirigi, qua cor nostrum de fiducia & timore, lingua instrumentum hominis nobilissimum, quo a brutis discernitur, confessionis & laudis honore, informatur, & publicum de sanctifi- catione a Deo præscripta: in secunda tabula officia nostra respectu proximi cum externa, partim spe- cialia quoad eos, in quibus est relatio patris & fi- lii, partim generalia, qua proximi vitam, conjugium, facultates, ac famam: tum interna, quantum ad concupiscentiam cordis, præscribi atque dirigi. Ri- vetus laudat Thomæ dispositionem 1. secundæ qu. 100. artic. 5. Quemadmodum in humana commu- nitate duo requiruntur, quomodo se quis ad eum qui præest communitati, deinde ad alios, qui in eadem so- cietate versantur, gerere debeat; Sic tria prima præ- cepta agere de dilectione DEI, & hominem ordinare ad DEUM juxta fidelitatem, reverentiam, & famula- tum, ne DEI principatum in alium transferat, ne in eum injuriosum aliquid committat, & DEO serviat, cui omnia debet. Reliqua præcepta hominem ad proximum ordinare, quorum nonnulli sunt, quibus gratitudinem specialem debemus ob beneficia: omnes autem, quibus nocere non debemus, vel opere, vel corde, vel ore: contingere autem opere tripliciter nocere pro- ximo, vel in persona sua ipsum occidendo, vel in persona conjuncta, quantum ad prolis procreationem: vel in bo- nis fortunæ ut vocant; ore fieri nocumentum per detra- ctionem: corde per concupiscentiam, quibus omnibus in præceptis in secunda tabula remedia præscribuntur. In qua distributione, cum eam non male traditam dicat Rivetus, observamus abire ipsum a cæteris Refor- matis, qui quatuor præcepta ad primam tabulam re- ferunt, imo etiam a seipso, cum paulo antea eos se- quutus fuerit: & dispositionem illam secundum quid ac certa ratione itidem solum admittendam esse; nec enim opere solum peccatur contra quintum, sex- tum & septimum præceptum, sed ore etiam atq; corde. Proinde solam divinam verborum legis distribu- tionem accuratam esse, qua in decem verba vel præ- cepta Lex distribuitur a Legislatore sapientissimo.

## 20:2
ver. 2. I AM THE LORD THY GOD, WHO BROUGHT THEE OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT.

Some, along with Burgensis, make these words the general prologue of the Decalogue; others claim them for the first commandment, along with the Targum of Jonathan, the Hebrews, Josephus, and Philo, as Martyr does in his Commonplaces and Sohnius in his Disputations, fol. 167. But they are more correctly held to be the affirmative part of the first commandment, as to who is to be worshipped as the true God, to which the negative is subordinated, concerning not having strange gods, which means that no one else besides and beyond Jehovah Elohim the Lord God ought to be worshipped as the true God: to which opinion the blessed Gerhard, in Deut. ch. 5, p. 252, professes that he does not wish to move a dispute rashly, and observes that for that reason God himself shows by the example of the first commandment that in the explanation of the remaining commandments, negative commandments are contained in the affirmative ones, and affirmative in the negative ones. And thus the first commandment is explained in the Symbolic book of our Churches, the Larger Catechism of the blessed Luther (in Form. Conc. p. 404.) It means exactly the same thing: See to it that you establish that I alone am your God, and do not attempt to seek another outside of me at all. Moreover, the words of Christ in Mark 12:29 favor this opinion, by which he makes this the first of all commandments: The Lord thy God is one Lord. Nor is there any reason for Burgensis and Rivetus to say that there is not a preceptive locution here, but only an indicative one; for the words subjoined, thou shalt have no other gods before me, teach that it is not only indicated that Jehovah is our Lord God, but at the same time it is also commanded that he be acknowledged and worshipped as the one Lord and one God. For not only the affirmative part, but the negative part joined to it, renders the full sense of the commandment: from which the preceptive locution is to be sought. Although by that very fact, when God indicates this in the first place in the promulgation of the commandments, I am the Lord thy God, everyone understands that it is commanded that we acknowledge him as our God. But as for what is said a little later, I am the Lord thy God, a jealous God, it is manifest there that a threatening and a promise are subjoined to the first commandment, such as are also held in others, which nevertheless are not incorrectly used by the blessed Luther as a general appendix to the commandments, because all things overflow from the first commandment; its observance is the observance of all, its violation is the violation of all. To which it contributes that Clement of Alexandria, in Strom. book 6, asserts that in the first commandment both the worship of the one true God is commanded and idolatry is forbidden, of which the former pertains to the affirmative part, the latter to the negative part of the first commandment. R. Moses Maimonides and other teachers of the Hebrews in the first house of the affirmative commandments, which is the house of divine worship, likewise make these words the first commandment, I am the Lord thy God, just as they constitute the following words as the first in the first house of the negative ones: Thou shalt have no other gods before me. To which R. Chasdai, and at the same time Episcopius in his Institutes, book 3, Sect. 2, ch. 1, object in vain that those words, I am the Lord thy God, are the root and principle of all the commandments; for that it is the first commandment, and that it is the principle and root of the rest, are not opposites. Nor is what Episcopius says to be admitted, that God did not command this to be believed, but caused it to be known and understood by his works, that he is the Lord and God of his people: for works are rashly opposed to the word, as they are used to confirm the word of God, and although the knowledge which is had from works may precede the knowledge of the word, it is by no means to be denied that God in his word and law has demanded his own recognition, and thus it is commanded in the law that we believe Jehovah to be our God. For even to love God, as he is God, or as he is the highest good, is natural, according to Episcopius, and yet there is no doubt that the love of God is commanded by divine law, Deut. 6:5, ch. 10:12, even if Episcopius doubts whether this is a special commandment, but that is beside the point, for even if it is not a distinct commandment in the Decalogue, but is contained under the first, as many others are, it is nevertheless to be held as a special commandment, to which not even this is an obstacle, that the love of GOD diffuses and exerts itself through all the commandments, and that there is a certain sum of the commandments in the first table, indeed of all simply, from which love of God the love of neighbor overflows, and we love God while we love our neighbor. For other things also, which have been commanded to us in the first commandment, diffuse themselves in such a way, such as fear, obedience, and the worship of God: because the love of neighbor also overflows from the fear, obedience, and worship of GOD. Nor indeed (as Episcopius wishes) do the fear and love of GOD merely constitute the manner in which all the commandments are to be observed, or are they only an impelling reason for the observation of all the commandments, but they are also special virtues pertaining to the first commandment. Although these words were uttered in such a way that they seem to concern only the Israelites, nevertheless, just like the other commandments, they pertain to all and oblige all, even if they were promulgated to the Israelites alone, and some things specially suit them: and therefore one must distinguish the substantial things of the commandments, and the circumstantial or accidental things: and likewise the moral things, which are common to all, and the ceremonial things, which are proper to the Israelites. Wherefore, however the Israelites may be addressed here, and they alone were led out of Egypt, and were the people of the Lord, whose God He confirmed Himself to be by entering into a peculiar covenant, and ordained for them the Sacrament of circumcision, through which He received the same into grace, this promise having been made, I am thy God: there is nevertheless no doubt that these words: I am the Lord thy God, in the Decalogue, just as those which indisputably present the precepts of the law, concern all men, whether they be taken as a general prologue to the Decalogue, or as the first commandment, or a part of the same. In these, therefore, it is commanded, by force of coherence with the negative joined thereto, that (1.) we believe that God exists, (2.) that we believe that God is one, (3.) that we believe Jehovah Elohim is one in essence, three in persons, (4.) that we worship Him as our God, that is, faith in the existence of GOD is required Heb. 11,6. knowledge of God Jer. 9, 14. knowledge and faith of the unity of essence, and also of the Trinity of persons John 17, 3. for he does not acknowledge the true God, who does not acknowledge Him who alone is the true God, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which here in the Decalogue is commanded, but its explanation is handed down throughout the symbols of the Prophetic and Apostolic faith. Finally, the worship of this true GOD; inasmuch as we are commanded by the first precept both to acknowledge and to worship Him; who is also called by the axiom of worship אלה, as if it were σεβάσμιον: to which worship pertains (1.) love on account of divine grace, Deut. 6, 5. (2.) fear on account of justice Deut. 6, 12. chap. 10, 20. Assuredly God proposes Himself as the highest good, the Being of beings, our most generous benefactor God, and therefore requires that we love Him in that manner; He presents Himself as the supreme Lord, and therefore requires that we fear Him Mal. 1, 6. (3.) Trust by which present goods, (4.) hope, by which future ones, on account of the truth of the promises, because He is our God, and indeed always wills to be the same. (5.) Patience in adversities on account of God's ἀυτεξυσίαν, and most free will. (6.) Humility on account of God's sublimity, which the name Jehovah embraces in its entirety, because indeed He Himself not only gives to all things and to His promises to be, Exod. 1, 1. But is ἀυτοὼν, and ἀυτεξύσιον, depends on nothing, but all things depend on Him. (7.) Obedience on account of God's lordship and power Deut. 26, 17.

Therefore, on the contrary, there is prohibited (1.) The atheism of those who have no God through ἀγνωσίᾳ and affected ignorance. (2.) Those who do not acknowledge God, such as He has revealed Himself, whether as to Essence, or essential attributes, or the mystery of the divine persons, who are the one God in essence, or as to the divine will. (3.) Those who do not worship God as God, either because they devise another worship, or because they neglect or deny the commanded worship, inasmuch as they (1.) do not love God as God, to which pertains hatred of God, and feigned, not sincere, love. (2.) Do not fear God, to which look contempt and carnal security, as well as servile fear. (3.) Do not trust in God, where there is distrust, doubt, hypocritical trust. (4.) Those who do not hope in God, whence comes despair, and doubt by deliberation. (5.) Do not patiently commit and submit themselves to God, whence comes impatience, and murmuring of the heart against GOD, restlessness of heart, rashness. (6.) They do not humble themselves before God as is fitting, whence comes pride, and feigned humility. (7.) They do not obey God, whence comes disobedience, and violation of God's commandments. But concerning these and others, the moralists.

verse 2. WHO BROUGHT THEE OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT) Great benefits ought to win over authority for the one commanding.

This illustrious benefit shown to the people is proposed, not so much to win authority for the Legislator, as so that they may understand from this notable work, conspicuous by so many proofs of omnipotence and divine glory, which true God they ought to acknowledge, and from this benefit of redemption from Egyptian servitude, learn both to place their confidence in Him, and to show Him worship and obedience, and that they are bound to these things. And yet it is not to be gathered from this that only the Israelites were bound by the law promulgated on Mount Sinai; which Pererius wishes in Diss. VI. on chap. 2 to the Romans. For since natural notices are in all men τῇ φύσει, which are called the work of the law Rom. 2, 15, this law, which is their public and solemn declaration, pertains equally to all, and it is to be believed that those whom those bind, the law also binds. Furthermore, since the transgression of the law is punished in all, even in the Gentiles Lev. 18, 22. Rom. 1, 28. certainly it is necessary that the law bind all to observance, whom it binds to punishment. Whence the Apostle testifies that by the law every mouth is stopped and the whole world becomes guilty before God, Rom. 3, 19. which would not be, if the Mosaic law bound only the Jews. Although therefore the Ministry of Moses was restricted to the Israelites, yet the moral laws promulgated immediately by GOD and consigned to letters by Moses pertain to all. Nor did the Blessed Luther think otherwise, when in the Preface to Vol. V. of the O.T. Tom. III. Jena. Germ. fol. 7. he says: I say that these precepts of the decalogue must be kept, not because Moses handed them down, which pertained only to that people, but because all men have these notices impressed upon nature, with which Moses also agrees. For it is one thing to speak of the ministry of Moses, which is special, another of the use of the Mosaic laws, which is common. Which, however, are not to be accepted as if the law of the Decalogue binds all only insofar as those things which are natural are handed down in it, not insofar as they are solemnly promulgated by God, which seems to be the opinion of certain Scholastics and of Dominicus a Soto, as well as of Hieronymus Zanchius on the work of Redemption book I. chap. 12. and of Musculus in Common Places, or according to natural obligation only, not also, as they say, divine. For that promulgation, although it may seem to have been made only to the Israelites, yet it was not made only on account of the Israelites; just as also the many Prophetic promises concerning Christ were made to the Israelites, but not on account of them alone: but as Holy Scripture, which is divided into Law and Gospel, pertains to all, so both the moral law and the Gospel concern all men. Therefore in the New Testament, moral laws are not promulgated anew to the Gentiles, but are repeated from Moses, and prescribed to all, and therefore they are taught to pertain to the Gentiles equally as to the Jews, and the Mosaic law is inculcated by Christ Himself to all, inasmuch as it binds all, and the sum of the moral law comprised by Christ in the love of GOD and neighbor Matth. 22, 40. concerns even the Gentiles themselves Rom. 13, 9. James 2, 8. every mouth is stopped by the law. Rom. 3, 9. Scripture has concluded all under sin, by the testimony of the same Apostle Gal. 3, 22. Finally, the Law ought to have been a schoolmaster to Christ not only for the Jews, but also for the Gentiles, verse 24. therefore St. Augustine. to a Jew asking, why do you hold the Old Testament, whose precept you do not keep, in book X. against Faustus, chap. 2. replied, that the precepts of living (that is, moral ones) are kept by Christians even from the BOOKS themselves (of the O.T.): but the precepts of the victim to be sacrificed, that is, the ceremonial ones, were then rightly observed when those things which are now revealed were being announced. And Bellarmine himself argues in book IV. on Justification, chap. 6. against Dominicus a Soto, that the law, even insofar as it was handed down by Moses, binds us, which opinion Pareus also acknowledges to be the better and safer one in his response to Bellarmine, book 1.

Nor is there any reason why one should think with Rivet that there is no difference in the matter between those opinions, but only in the manner of speaking: for the reason that it is agreed among all that the moral precepts, which are contained in the law, are of perpetual observance among Christians, and are binding, insofar as they are moral: meanwhile he thinks that the precepts, as given by Moses, did not so much bind the Gentiles, or those who were in the world who worshipped God, in which point he certainly does not have Bellarmine and others agreeing with him; whence he himself later acknowledged a real disagreement: and he prefers that opinion which affirms that the Mosaic law did not bind others than the Israelites, and thus contradicts the others who say it bound others. He urges this reason, that a law not promulgated does not bind: But the Decalogue was promulgated to the Israelites alone. But that reason is εὐδιάλυτος. For not only the Israelites but many foreigners mixed with the assembly of the Israelites were present at this promulgation, and it was done with such sublimity and Majesty, which could spread and penetrate through the whole world, with the fame of the miracles, which for that reason were precursors to it; and this was also the will and intention of God the legislator, that the solemn promulgation and the law of the Decalogue itself should be divulged to others, and observed by all Gentiles, even if it were not explained to all, except through natural law alone. But Rivetus insists: that the law of Moses was not only a declaration of the law of nature, but also preceptive, that is, that in it was added the force of a new precept, in which was also mixed some merely constitutive precept. Resp. That constitutive precept was not new, but obtained from the foundation of the world, and was propagated from the very first parents to their descendants, even if that precept concerning the sanctification of the seventh day was not necessary by nature, but defined only by the will of the Legislator. Then if a new obligation of the precepts of the Decalogue was contracted, by the force of that external precept then solemnly made, certainly the same will either not concern the Israelites alone, or if it pertains to them alone, it will not regard Christians, which, since the latter is absurd and contrary to Scripture, as we have shown, one must admit that that new obligation did not pertain to the Israelites alone; where Rivetus indeed slips into asserting that the law, insofar as it was delivered by Moses, no longer obligates Christians: But if Christians are not obligated by the Mosaic Moral law, it will have to be said that, as far as moral matters are concerned, they are obligated only by the law of nature, or certainly Christ himself must be constituted as a new νομοθέτης, which the Reformed reject in Papists and Socinians.

And this controversy, whether Christians are obligated by the Mosaic moral law, not only by the law of nature, by which it is agreed that even Gentiles knowing nothing of Christ are obligated, is not of such light or small moment, because the error of the Antinomians easily insinuates itself unless it is rightly decided: nor is it enough (as Rivetus thinks) that it be taught that all faithful Christians are subject to the rule, direction, authority, and obligation of the moral law; if he understands only the obligation and direction common to Gentiles and Christians, which is, namely, that of the law of nature, and does not admit that the peculiar obligation of the Mosaic moral law, by force of the divine promulgation of the law made by living voice and written letter in the Holy Scriptures, binds Christians. For thus the Mosaic law will clearly not pertain to Christians, because it does not obligate them through divine promulgation, which is said to regard the Jews alone, nor through the publication or promulgation of Christ, because it was not the office of Christ to promulgate a law either new or anew, but to fulfill the law and provide Redemption. Therefore, Rivetus does not remove the difficulty by a distinction of the word as if it were all in the word 'insofar as' (quatenus), which, if it is taken reduplicatively, may rightly be said that the law insofar as it is delivered by Moses does not obligate us; if it is understood relatively concerning the law which was delivered by Moses, then its obligation cannot be denied regarding us. For there is no need for that determination of the ministry of Moses: The question is, whether the law also insofar as it is promulgated by GOD obligates us, or indeed only insofar as it is inscribed in nature? nay, if we rightly weigh the matter, the moral law was not promulgated through the ministry of Moses, but immediately through the Son of GOD himself: for it was neither uttered to the people by Moses with a living voice, nor inscribed on stone tablets by his ministry, but the Son of GOD brought it forth ἀυτοφώνως, and inscribed it on the same tablets ἀμέσως and with his own hand, so to speak, or by the finger of the Spirit. The subtlety, therefore, sought in the ὁμωνυμία of the word is nothing.

Wherefore in the end he seeks a solution to the difficulty, namely that Moses proposed the law to Israel for some other end than that for which it is now proposed; namely, that he might terrify the Israelites and keep them under some pedagogical servitude until Christ should restore liberty to those believing through faith: since it is certain that the law is not given to us in such a way under the Gospel. Resp. Concerning the moral law, the matter is: which is not comprised under the Gospel, but is ἀντιδιῃρημένως distinct from it, yet it obligates those who are under the Gospel or enjoy Evangelical grace: nor is there a difference in this regarding the faithful of the ancient time before Christ, and now after Christ has been exhibited; because Evangelical grace was not lacking to them, nay, we believe that we are saved in the same manner through the grace of our Lord as they were. Acts 15:10. Nor did the moral law as such obligate the ancient faithful otherwise than Christians. As for those two ends of the Mosaic law, namely of terrifying and keeping under pedagogical servitude: those are not the primary and proper ends of the law, but secondary or accidental. For the law was given εἰς ζωὴν, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 7:10, which is therefore called holy and just and good in verse 12. And these things belong to the law by itself. But that it terrifies, that it keeps under servitude, this is by accident, whether you look at the Israelites or us in the New Testament: nor does it only terrify and keep under servitude, but it condemns and brings death: but by accident, as the law which was given εἰς ζωὴν for life, was found to be εἰς θάνατον for death, as the same Apostle has in Rom. 7:10. Nor did the pedagogy which the moral law provided to the Israelites regarding Christ pertain only to them, but the moral law is still a παιδαγωγὸς εἰς χριστὸν, ἵνα ἐκ πίσεως δικαιωθῶμεν, as the same Apostle testifies in Galatians 3:24. Thus far, therefore, again no difference is detected regarding the Israelites and Christians. If you say with Rivetus: but the moral law insofar as it was delivered by Moses was abrogated among Christians: we do not deny that it is sometimes commonly said to be abrogated, but that it is not explained in the same way. Rivetus, with whom we are dealing here, says it is abrogated in three ways. He calls the first way this: Insofar as it was the law of the Old Testament and of Moses, or by reason of the ministry, not by reason of the matter. For the law remains, but is administered otherwise, because we have nothing more in common with Moses, but with Christ, who in the Gospel proposed the remission of sins, from which we could not be justified by the law of Moses, and commended and confirmed the manner of life to be instituted after our renewal, which was indeed taken from Moses. Resp. There is no need here for a commemoration of the ministry; nor should the minister, but the principal cause, be regarded; indeed, Moses does not intervene in the promulgation itself, as far as the moral law originally promulgated is concerned, even though he later historically repeated the promulgation in Deuteronomy 5. But as far as the matter is concerned, when he says the law remains, he understands it either as doctrine or under the aspect of law and legal obligation. There is no doubt that the doctrine of the law remains: which no one can deny was delivered by God immediately, and not only repeated frequently by Moses, but also by the Prophets, and indeed by Christ also and the Apostles: but the question is concerning the law under the aspect of law and legal obligation, and Rivetus himself distinguishes the Moral law declared by Moses and the Prophets (add also Christ and the Apostles), insofar as it is such, that is, declarative of the eternal and natural law, and insofar as it was constitutive of a special obligation. In the former way it is obvious that it is proposed to us: but he warns thus, that a purely declarative law has the nature of doctrine rather than of a precept: however, divine doctrine can never be deprived of its authority and truth, and therefore a purely declarative law can never be abrogated or lose its force, because it is a lamp and a light, which always illuminates in the same way. In the latter way, therefore, it ought to be viewed here: but Rivetus says that the Mosaic law was established as a law of special obligation only among the Israelite people; which we admit regarding the ceremonial and forensic [law]; but we do not concede it at all regarding the moral [law]. For by that reasoning the Mosaic moral law would in no way obligate Christians; and thus they would be obligated to obedience only by the law of nature, as far as moral matters are concerned, which is inconvenient and contrary to the Scriptures. Nothing, therefore, would be common to us with Moses, as far as the moral law is concerned: and there will be clearly no obligation of it as far as we are concerned. For that Christ commended a way of instituting life taken from Moses, all Reformed [theologians] acknowledge that this was not done by way of a new promulgation of the Mosaic law, so as to obligate us, otherwise not obligated to the Mosaic law. The second way of the abrogated Mosaic law is explained by Rivetus as follows: namely, insofar as the law held all who do not observe it under a curse, which curse Christ took away from the law, when by fulfilling it and receiving the curse into himself, it is henceforth to us like a serpent whose poison has been removed, Galat. 3, then by renewing our hearts and bending them to obedience, that indeed sincere even if not perfect in all degrees. But by that reasoning the law is not more abrogated for us than for the Israelites; for Christ fulfilled the law for them too, and received the curse of the law into himself; yet that innovation of hearts is not the very removal of the curse of the law, but a consequence of it: because we are not freed from the curse through renewal, but through justification, and the application of the liberation made through Christ, which comes to us in that [justification]. The third way is this, that the law is now not burdensome to true Christians, because its severity has been removed through Christ; but that situation held equally for faithful Israelites, as far as the Mosaic moral law was concerned: such as David, Josiah, and others: for was the severity of the law removed through Christ for us alone? What then is this distinction? In sum, says Rivetus, the law is not proposed to us, as was done by Moses, as a condition preceding the right to life, which is to be performed by us before we have that right, but as a condition following a contract, which is otherwise valid in itself, [and] nevertheless obligates to a certain recognition, as it is in contracts in which some estate or possession is given in such a way that he to whom it is given is truly the owner of the estate; he is nevertheless obligated to what they call homages, and some services. But was the moral law given to the Israelites for any other reason? was it for them a condition preceding the right to life otherwise than if someone wished to obtain life through the law? Such is the law still for all who wish to be justified through the law; for it requires perfect obedience from all who wish to acquire a right to life through the observation of the law.
