Furthermore, the diverse ends of the law are thus opposed to each other: the first and proper one, which however had a place only in the instituted nature in the state of integrity, where it was for our first parents as a condition preceding the right to life: which condition, since it found no place after the fall, hence the other and same (as far as the law is concerned) accidental end of the law is pedagogical, that through it we may be led and compelled to Christ, who fulfilled the law for us: to those justified by whose obedience the Mosaic moral law is surely also to be proposed, as a condition following that gracious contract, if it is permitted to speak so, entered into between GOD and men through Christ the mediator, in which they are received into grace, obligating us to obedience, not for the sake of meriting anything, but for the sake of recognition and gratitude; where the Mosaic moral law also entirely obligates the faithful to obedience, in that it is a divine law, promulgated to all in the person of the Israelites and those who were with them, just as the Paradisiacal law concerning the tree of knowledge was promulgated to all men in our first parents, and would have obligated all if they had not merited ejection from Paradise. If you say that our people also sometimes say that the moral law has been abrogated as far as justification, as far as the curse, as far as the rigor of exaction: we certainly admit that: but that is only ἀκυρολογία: They acknowledge that it is not abrogated as far as obligation: for we are still debtors to the law, Rom. 8, verse 2. Furthermore, if we wish to speak accurately, the moral law has not been abrogated. For the duties of the law are to direct and to obligate to observance, which still remain. It is indeed rightly said that justification is not from the law, that the faithful are immune from the curse, [and] that the works of the pious, even if they are not perfect in every way, please GOD; yet speaking precisely, there is no abrogation of the law here. Not by reason of justification: because there was never any justification from the law after the fall, and therefore the law cannot be said to be abrogated by reason of justification. The law was indeed given for life: but that life is not from the law after the fall, or that the law does not justify, is not an abrogation of the law, but our prevarication causes that, while the authority of the law remains. In the state of integrity the law could give life, now it cannot; not because anything has been lost to the law, which is the immutable rule of divine justice, but because we have fallen away from the integrity with which we were created. Therefore, a change did not happen in the law, but in us. It is said that a weakening was made διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς Rom. 8, 3. but since our flesh could not render the law itself weak, that is to be understood concerning the hindered fruit and primary end of the law with respect to us, because of the flesh, and concupiscence, and the force and guilt of sin, which is common to all. The law cannot give life Gal. 3, 21. for the reason that it cannot be fulfilled by us. That, therefore, is to be taken κατά τι with respect to us. Therefore the law is not said to be dead or abrogated, but we are dead to the law Rom. 3, 31. 7, 4. Nor is the moral law rightly said to be abrogated by reason of the curse. There is a twofold kind of men: some are believers and pious: others are unbelievers and impious: Who will deny that these are under the curse of the law? For the wrath of God remains upon them, John 3, 17. 36. The curse, therefore, of the Mosaic law has not been abrogated, nor its condemnation, because it is exercised against the impious. As for the faithful, for them indeed there is no curse, Rom. 8, 1, but for that reason the law cannot be said to be abrogated. For it ought not to have yielded to the pious in curse, but in life. What of the fact that the pious observe the law, and render satisfaction to it not in their own person, but in Christ the Mediator: and that the curse of the law has not properly been abrogated, but relaxed by dispensation, and transferred to Christ, who for us was made a curse Gal. 3, 13. That penal sanction remains, Cursed &c. Deuter. 27, 26, which nevertheless does not press upon us, inasmuch as Christ sustained it in our place. Finally, neither by reason of rigorous exaction is the moral law accurately said to be abrogated; For that rigor of exaction remains for the law, even if the Gospel shows him who satisfied the rigorous exaction of the law in full, through whom the faithful are indeed freed from the rigor of exaction, but nothing is lost to the law in this. Therefore here again there is some change with respect to us, but none with respect to the moral law. For the law requires from us perfect observance most strictly, which because we are unable to perform for the same, we apprehend by faith in the Gospel Christ, who performed that same obedience for us in all ways and respects most absolute: and furthermore, being justified, through his obedience, with the help of the Holy Spirit we show obedience to the law, as much as the condition of our infirmity permits, which obedience, having proceeded from faith, is pleasing and acceptable to GOD through Christ, even if it is by no means perfect, provided it is offered only with a sincere and ἀνυποκρίτῳ [unfeigned] heart. And this much concerning the obligation of the law.

Latin:

vers. 2. EGO SUM DEUS TUUS, QUI E- DUXI TE DE TERRA ÆGYPTI.

Hæc verba proœmium generale Decalogi faci- unt nonnulli cum Burgensi, alii pro primo præcepto venditant cum Targum Jonathanis, Ebræis, Josepho & Philone, utpote Martyr in Loc. communibus & Sohnius in Disp. fol. 167. Sed rectius habentur pro parte affirmativa primi præcepti, quis pro vero Deo colendus, cui negativa subjicitur, de non habendis diis alienis, quod nempe nulli alii extra, & præter Jeho- vam Elohim Dominum Deum, pro vero Deo coli debeant: cui sententiæ nolle se temere litem movere, profitetur B. Gerhardus in Deut. 5. c. pag. 252. & ob- servat, quod ea ratione Deus ipse exemplo primi præcepti ostendat, quod in explicatione reliquo- rum præceptorum in affirmativis negativa, & in ne- gativis affirmativa præcepta contineantur. Atque ita explicatur primum præceptum in libro Sym- bolico Ecclesiarum nostrarum Catechismo Majori B. Lutheri (in Form. Conc. p. 404.) Idem plane vult dicere: Hoc vide cures, ut me solum Deum tuum esse statuas, nec omnino extra me alium quærere coneris. Favent autem huic Sententiæ verba Christi Marc. 12, 29. quibus πρῶτον πασῶν ἐντολῶν primum omni- um præceptum hoc facit, Dominus Deus tuus Dominus unus est. Nec est, quod dicat Burgensis, ac Rivetus, non haberi hic locutionem præceptivam, sed tantum indicativam; namque non solum indicari hoc, quod Jehovah Dominus Deus noster, sed simul etiam præcipi, ut pro Domino uno, ac Deo uno agnosca- tur & colatur, verba subjuncta docent, non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Plenum enim sensum præ- cepti reddit non sola pars affirmativa, sed quæ ei jungitur negativa: e qua petenda est præceptiva locutio. Quamvis eo ipso cum Deus primo loco hoc indicat, in promulgatione præceptorum, Ego Dominus Deus tuus, quisque intelligat, præcipi, agnoscamus eum pro Deo nostro. Quod autem paulo post itidem dicitur: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, æmulator, ibi manifestum est, comminationem & promissionem subjungi primi præcepti, quales etiam in aliis habentur, quæ tamen non inrecte a B. Luthero, ceu generalis præceptorum appendix adhibetur, quia e primo præcepto redundant o- mnia, ejus observatio est omnium observatio, violatio est violatio omnium. Quo facit, quod Clemens Alexandr. l. 6. Strom. primo præcepto & mandari cultum unius veri Dei & vetari idololatri- am asserit, quorum illud ad partem affirmativam, hoc ad negativam primi præcepti pertinet. R. Moses Maimonid. & alii Ebræorum Magistri in prima domo præceptorum affirmativorum, quæ est domus divini cultus primum præceptum faciunt itidem hæc verba, Ego sum Dominus DEUS tuus, quemadmodum primum in prima domo negativo- rum constituunt verba sequentia: Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Quibus frustra R. Chasdai, ac simul Episcopius in instit. lib. 3. Sect. 2. c. 1. hoc op- ponunt, quod illa verba, Ego sum Dominus DEUS tuus, radix & principium sint omnium præcepto- rum; nam primum præceptum esse, & reliquorum esse principium, & radicem, non sunt opposita. Nec ad- mittendum quod Episcopius ait, Deum hoc non cre- di jussisse, sed cognosci ac sciri fecisse operibus suis, se Do- minum esse ac Deum populi sui: nam opera temere op- ponuntur verbo, utpote quæ ad verbum Dei confir- mandum adhibita sunt, & quamvis notitia, quæ ex operibus habetur, notitiam verbi antevertere pos- sit, negandum tamen minime est, Deum in verbo ac lege sua postulasse sui agnitionem, adeoque manda- tum esse in lege, ut Jehovam Deum nostrum creda- mus. Nam & amare Deum, ut Deus est, vel ut summum bonum est, naturale est, secundum Episco- pium, nec tamen dubium est, dilectionem Dei lege di- vina præceptam esse, Deut. 6, 5. c. 10, 12. etsi an hoc spe- ciale præceptum sit, ambigat Episcopius, sed præter rem, nam utut non distinctum sit in Decalogo præ- ceptum, sed sub primo, ut alia multa contineatur, speciale tamen præceptum habendum, cui ne id quidem officit, quod dilectio DEI per omnia præ- cepta se diffundat, atq; exerat, & summa quædam præceptorum sit in prima tabula, imo omnium sim- pliciter, qua ex dilectione DEI redundat dilectio proximi, ac Deum diligimus, dum proximum dili- gimus. Nam & alia, quæ in primo nobis deman- data sunt præcepto, ita se diffundunt, utpote timor, obsequium, & cultus Dei: quia etiam e timore, obe- dientia, & cultu DEI amor proximi redundat. Nec vero (quod Episcopius vult) timor & amor DEI tantum modum constituunt, quo præcepta omnia ob- servanda, aut ratio solum sunt impellens ad præcepto- rum omnium observationem, sed virtutes etiam sunt speciales ad primum præceptum pertinentes. Quan- quam autem verba hæc ita prolata sint, ut concer- nere solum Israelitas videantur, tamen, æque uti cæ- tera præcepta ad omnes pertinent, omnesque obli- gant, etiamsi illa solis Israelitis promulgata sint, ac nonnulla eisdem specialiter conveniant: ideoque distinguenda sunt τὰ συστατικὰ substantialia, & τὰ περιστατικὰ vel accidentalia præceptorum: itemq; moralia, quæ omnibus communia, & ceremonialia, quæ Israelitis propria. Quapropter utut compel- lentur hic Israelitæ, illique soli ex Ægypto deducti, & populus Domini fuerint, quorum Deum sese esse peculiari fœdere inito confirmavit, ac Sacra- mentum circumcisionis ipsi ordinavit, per quod in gratiam eosdem recipiebat, hac facta promis- sione, Ego Deus tuus: nullum tamen dubium est, hæc verba: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, in Decalo- go perinde uti ea, quæ ἀναντιῤῥήτως præcepta legis exhibent, omnes homines concernere, sive ut proœmium generale Decalogi, sive ut primum præ- ceptum, aut pars ejusdem accipiantur. In his ergo præcipitur, vi cohærentiæ cum negativa subjuncta, ut (1.) Deum esse credamus (2.) ut unum esse De- um credamus, (3.) ut credamus Jehovam Elohim unum essentia, trinum personis, (4.) ut eum ceu Deum nostrum colamus, hoc est, requiritur fides existentia DEI Ebr. 11,6. cognitio Dei Jer. 9, 14. cogni- tio ac fides unitatis essentiæ, nec non Trinitatis perso- narum Joh. 17, 3. non enim agnoscit verum Deum, qui non agnoscit eum, qui solus est verus Deus, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. quod hic in Deca- logo præcipitur, explicatio vero ejus in Symbolis Propheticæ & Apostolicæ fidei passim traditur. De- niq; cultus hujus veri DEI; utpote quem & agno- scere & colere primo præcepto jubemur; qui etiam a cultus axiomate אלה dicitur, quasi σεβάσμιον : ad quem cultum pertinet (1.) dilectio ob divinam gratiam, Deut. 6,5. (2.) timor ob justitiam Deut. 6, 12. cap. 10,20. Nimirum proponit se Deus ceu sum- mum bonum, Ens entium, liberalissimum benefa- ctorem Deum nostrum, eoque requirit, ut se ea ra- tione diligamus; sistit se ceu supremum Dominum, ideoque requirit, ut se timeamus Mal. 1. 6. (3.) Fiducia qua bona præsentia, (4.) spes, qua futura,ob promissionum veritatem, quia est Deus noster, uti- que idem esse semper vult. (5.) Patientia in ad- versis ob Dei ἀυτεξυσίαν, & liberrimam volunta- tem. (6.) Humilitas ob Dei sublimitatem, quæ omnia nomen Jehovah complectitur, quod nempe ipse non tantum omnibus rebus, ac promissis suis esse det, Exod. 1,1. Sed ἀυτοὼν, & ἀυτεξύσιον sit, a nullo dependeat,ab ipso vero dependeant omnia. (7.) Obedientia ob Dei dominium & potestatem Deut. 26, 17.

Prohibetur ergo ex adverso (1.) Atheismus eorum, qui nullum Deum habent ἀγνωσίᾳ & igno- rantia affectata. (2.) Qui Deum non agnoscunt, qualem se patefecit, qua Essentiam, seu essentialia attributa, aut personarum divinarum mysterium, quæ sunt ipse unus essentia Deus, aut qua voluntatem di- vinam. (3.) Qui Deum non ut Deum colunt,seu quod alium cultum excogitent, seu quod cultum deman- datum negligant,aut denegent, utpote qui Deum (1.) non diligunt ut Deum, quo pertinet odium Dei, & amor simulatus, non sincerus. (2.) Deum non timent, quo spectant contemtus & securitas carnalis, nec non timor servilis. (3.) Deo non confidunt, ubi diffidentia, dubitatio, fiducia hypocritica. (4.) Qui in Deum nonsperant,unde desperatio,& dubita- tio deliberatione. (5.) Deo patienter se non com- mittunt, & submittunt, unde impatientia, & mur- muratio cordis adversus DEUM, inquietudo cordis, temeritas. (6.) Coram Deo non humiliant sese ut par est,unde superbia,& humilitas simulata. (7.) Deo non obediunt,unde inobedientia,& mandatorum Dei violatio. Sed de his & aliis moralistæ.

vers. 2. QUI EDUXI TE DE TERRA ÆGYPTI) Ma- gna beneficia autoritatem conciliare debent præcipienti.

Hoc illustre beneficium populo exhibitum proponitur, non tam ut autoritatem Legislatori conciliet, quam ut quem verum Deum agnoscere debeant, ex hoc insigni opere, tot documentis o- mnipotentiæ ac gloriæ divinæ conspicuo, intelli- gant, & ab hoc redemtionis e servitute Ægyptiaca beneficio, tum confidentiam in ipsum collocare, tum cultum & obedientiam ei exhibere,atque ad ea se obligari discant. Nec tamen inde colligendum, solos Israelitas per legem in monte Sinai promulgatam obligatos fuisse; quod vult Pererius Diss. VI. in cap.2. ad Rom. Nam quum notitiæ naturales omnibus ho- minib9 τῇ φύσει insint,quæ opus legis dicuntur Rom. 2,15. lex ista,quæ publica & solennis earum declara- tio est, ad omnes pariter pertinet, & quos illæ obli- gant,hos etiam legem obligare,credendum est.Por- ro quum legis transgressio in omnibus,etiam genti- bus puniatur Lev.18,22. Rom.1,28.utiq; legem omnes oportet obligare ad observationem, quos obligat ad pœnam. Unde Apostolus testatur per legem omni- um os obstrui & reum fieri totum mundum Deo, Rom. 3, 19. quod non esset, si lex Mosaica solos Judæos obligaret. Etsi ergo Ministerium Mosis restrictum fuerit ad Israëlitas, leges tamen morales a DEO a- μέσως promulgatæ a Mose literis consignatæ ad o- mnes pertinent. Nec aliud B. Luther. sensit, cum in Præf. in lib. V. T. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. fol. 7. ait: Dico servanda esse hæc decalogi præcepta, non quia Mo- ses ea tradidit, quod ad illum populum tantum perti- nebat, sed quia has notitias naturæ impressas omnes ho- mines habent, cum quibus etiam Moses congruit. A- liud nempe est, loqui de Mosis ministerio, quod spe- ciale, aliud de legum Mosaicarum usu, qui communis est. Quæ tamen eo accipienda non sunt, ac si lex Decalogi solum omnes obliget, quatenus in eadem tradita ea, quæ naturalia sunt, non quatenus a Deo so- lenniter promulgata, quæ Scholasticorum quorundam & Dominici a Soto, nec non Hieronymi Zanchii de op. Red. l. I. cap. 12. & Musculi in LL. CC. videtur sententia, vel secundum obligationem naturalem solum, non etiam, ut loquuntur, divinam. Nam promulgatio illa etsi Israëlitis solum facta videatur, non tamen solum facta est propter Israëlitas; quem- admodum etiam promissiones Propheticæ de Chri- sto plurimæ ad Israëlitas, non autem propter eos solos factæ sunt: sed uti Scriptura Sacra, quæ in Le- gem & Evangelium dispescitur, ad omnes pertinet, ita tam lex moralis, quam Evangelium omnes con- cernit homines. Ideo in Novo Testam. leges mo- rales non de novo promulgantur gentibus, sed e Mose repetuntur, & omnibus præscribuntur, ideoq; ad gentes æque, ac Judæos pertinere docentur, & a Christo ipso lex Mosaica omnibus inculcatur, ut- pote quæ omnes obliget, ac summa legis moralis di- lectione DEI ac proximi a Christo comprehensa Matth. 22, 40. ipsos etiam gentiles concernit Rom. 13, 9. Jac. 2, 8. omnibus os per legem obstruitur. Rom. 3, 9. Scriptura omnes conclusit sub peccatum, teste eodem Apostolo Gal. 3, 22. Denique non tantum Judæis, sed gentibus etiam debuit Lex esse pædagogus ad Christum, vers. 24. ideo S. Augustin. Judæo in- terroganti, cur tenes Vetus Testamentum, cujus præ- ceptum non servas l. X. contra Faust. c. 2. respondit, servari a Christianis etiam ex ipsis LIBRIS (V.T.) præcepta vitæ agendæ (hoc est, moralia:) præcepta vero victimæ sacrificandæ, hoc est, ceremonialia tunc recte fuisse observata, cum prænunciabantur ista, quæ nunc revelata sunt. Et Bellarminus ipse disputat l. IV. de Justif. cap. 6. adversus Dominicum a Soto, le- gem etiam, quatenus a Mose tradita, nos obligare, quam sententiam etiam potiorem ac tutiorem esse a- gnoscit Pareus in resp. ad Bell. l. 1.

Neque est quod cum Riveto quis censeat, inter istas sententias non esse in re aliquod discrimen, sed in modo solum loquendi: eo quod inter omnes conveniat, moralia, quæ in lege continentur, esse perpetuæ obser- vationis apud Christianos, & obligare, quatenus sint moralia: interim præcepta, qua data a Mose non tam obligasse gentiles, vel si qui in orbe erant, qui Deum colerent, existimat, in quo certe Bellarm. & a- lios consentientes non habet; unde ipse postmo- dum agnovit realem dissensum: atque illam præfert sententiam, qua legem Mosaicam non obligasse alios, quam Israëlitas, affirmat, adeoq; cæteris, qui alios obligasse ajunt, contradicit. Rationem hanc ur- get, quod lex non promulgata non obliget: Promul- gatus autem Decalogus sit solis Israëlitis. At ea ratio est εὐδιάλυτος. Nam nec solum Israëlitæ sed mul- ti peregrini cœtui Israëlitarum admixti aderant huic promulgationi, & facta ea est tanta sublimi- tate, ac Majestate, quæ per orbem universum per- crebescere, ac penetrare poterat, cum miraculo- rum fama, quæ ideo prævia eidem erant; atque hæc etiam Dei legislatoris voluntas, ac intentio fuit, ut solennis promulgatio, ac lex ipsa Decalogi ad alios divulgaretur, & ab omnibus gentilibus servaretur, etsi non explicaretur omnibus, nisi per jus tantum naturale. At instat Rivetus : legem illam Mosis non tantum fuisse legis naturæ declarationem, sed etiam præceptivam, id est, in ea additam fuisse vim novi præcepti, in qua etiam admixtum aliquod præ- ceptum mere constitutivum. Resp. Illud præce- ptum constitutivum non novum fuit, sed inde ab orbe condito obtinuit, & ab ipsis primis pa- rentibus ad posteros propagatum fuit, etsi præ- ceptum illud de sanctificatione septimæ diei naturâ non fuerit necessaria, sed ex voluntate tantum Legislatoris definita. Tum si nova contracta fuit obligatio præceptorum Decalogi, ex vi ex- ternæ illius præceptionis solenniter tunc factæ, cer- te eadem aut non solos Israelitas concernet, aut si eos solos attinet, ad Christianos non specta- bit, quod posterius quum absurdum & Scriptu- ræ adversum sit, ut ostendimus, fateri oportet non solos Israelitas attinuisse novam illam obliga- tionem; ubi Rivetus quidem eo labitur, ut asse- rat, legem quatenus per Mosen tradita fuit, non am- plius obligare Christianos: Sed si lege Morali Mosai- ca non obligantur Christiani, dicendum erit, quod quantum ad moralia, sola naturæ lege obligentur, aut certe Christus ipse novus νομοθέτης constituen- dus erit, quod in Papistis, & Socinianis reprobant Reformati.

Atque hæc controversia, anne lege morali Mo- saica Christiani obligentur, non solum lege naturæ, qua etiam gentiles obligari nihil de Christo sci- entes, constat, non adeo levis aut exigui mo- menti est, quia facile error Antinomorum sete in- gerit, nisi ea recte decidatur: neque satis est (quod existimat Rivetus) quod doceatur omnes Chri- stianos fideles legis moralis regulæ, directioni, im- perio & obligationi subjectos esse; si obligationem & directionem communem gentilibus & Christia- nis, quæ scil. legis naturæ est, tantum intelligat, nec admittat peculiarem obligationem legis mora- lis Mosaicæ, ex vi divinæ promulgationis legis, vo- ce viva, & litera scripta in S. literis factæ Christia- nos obstringere. Ita enim lex Mosaica plane non attinebit Christianos, quia nec per divinam promulgationem eos obligat, quæ ad solos Judæos spectare dicitur, neque per publicationem aut pro- mulgationem Christi, quia Christi munus non fuit legem vel novam vel de novo promulgare, sed legem implere, ac Redemtionem præstare. Non ergo distinctione vocis difficultatem tollit Rivetus quasi ea tota sit in voce quatenus, quæ si redu- plicative accipiatur, recte dicatur, legem quate- nus est à Mose tradita nos non obligare; si relative intelligatur de lege, quæ à Mose tradita est, tum non posse ejus obligationem quoad nos negari. Nam non opus est illa ministerii Mosis determinatione: Quæstio est, utrum lex etiam quatenus à DEO pro- mulgata nos obliget, an vero solum, qua naturæ inscripta? imo si recte rem expendemus, pro- mulgata lex moralis non fuit per Mosis ministe- rium, sed immediate per ipsum Filium DEI: nam neque viva voce prolata ad populum per Mosen, ne- que tabulis lepideis inscripta ejus ministerio, sed protulit eam ἀυτοφώνως Filius DEI, tabulis ean- dem inscripsit ἀμέσως ac manu propria, ut ita lo- quamur, vel digito Spiritus. Subtilitas ergo, in vo- cis ὁμωνυμίᾳ quæsita, nulla est.

Quapropter in fine quærit difficultatis solutio- nem, Mosen scilicet alio aliquo fine Israeli pro- posuisse legem, quam quo nunc proponatur; nempe ut terreret Israelitas, & eos sub aliqua servitute pæda- gogica contineret, donec Christus libertatem per fi- dem credentibus restitueret: siquidem certum sit, tali modo nobis non dari legem sub Evangelio. Resp. de lege morali res est: quæ sub Evangelio com- prehensa non est, sed ἀντιδιῃρημένως ab eodem distincta, illos tamen, qui sub Evangelio sunt, vel gratia Evangelica fruuntur, obligat: nec in eo, quoad fideles antiqui temporis ante Christum, & nunc post exhibitum Christum differentia est; quia illis gratia Evangelica non defuit, imo cre- dimus nos ad eundem modum per gratiam Domi- ni nostri salvari, quemadmodum ipsos. Actor. 15, 10. Nec lex moralis, qua talis aliter obligavit fi- deles priscos, quam Christianos. Quod ergo duos illos fines legis Mosaicæ, terrendi scilicet & sub servitute pedagogica continendi, attinet: non illi fines legis primarii ac proprii sunt, sed se- cundarii, vel accidentales. Nam data lex fuit εἰς ζωὴν teste Apostolo Rom. VII, 10. quæ ideo sancta & justa & bona dicitur vers. 12. Atque hæc legi per se conveniunt. Quod autem terret, quod sub servitute continet, hoc ex accidenti est, sive Israelitas, sive nos in Nov. Testam. spectes: ne- que tantum terret, ac sub servitute continet, sed condemnat & mortem affert: sed ex accidenti, qua lex quæ εἰς ζωὴν ad vitam data, inventa est esse εἰς θάνατον ad mortem, ut idem Apostolus habet Rom. 7, 10. Nec pædagogia, quam præstabat Is- raelitis ad Christum lex moralis, tantum ad il- los pertinebat, sed etiam lex moralis παιδαγω- γὸς adhuc est εἰς χριστὸν, ἵνα ἐκ πίσεως δικαιωθῶ- μεν teste eodem Apostolo Galat. 3, 24. Hactenus ergo iterum nulla deprehenditur, quoad Israeli- tas & Christianos, differentia. Si dicas cum Ri- veto: atqui lex moralis quatenus à Mose tradita, abrogata fuit penes Christianos: non diffitemur vulgo abrogatam nonnunquam dici, sed non eo- dem modo id explicari. Rivetus quicum nobis hic res est, tribus modis abrogatam dicit. Primum modum hunc dicit: Quatenus fuit lex Vet. Testam. & Mosis vel ratione ministerii, non ratione materiæ. Manet enim lex, sed aliter administrata, quia cum Mose nobis nihil amplius est commune, sed cum Chri- sto, qui in Evangelio remissionem peccatorum, à qui- bus per legem Mosis non poteramus justificari, pro- posuit, & rationem vitæ instituendæ post renovatio- nem nostram à Mose quidem desumtam commenda- vit & confirmavit. Resp. Ministerii commemo- ratione hic opus non est; nec minister, sed cau- sa princeps spectari debet, imo minister in ipsa promulgatione non intervenit Moses, quantum ad legem moralem primitus promulgatam attinet, et- si promulgationem postea historice repetierit Deu- ter. 5. Quod vero ad materiam attinet, cum manere legem dicit, vel intelligit eam, ut doctrinam, vel sub ratione legis, & legalis obligationis. Doctrinam legis manere dubium nullum est: quam à Deo ἀμέσως traditam, non à Mose crebrius tantum re- petitam, sed etiam à Prophetis, imo à Christo quo- que & Apostolis, nemo inficiari potest: sed de lege sub ratione legis & legalis obligationis quæstio est, & distinguit ipse Rivetus legem Moralem à Mose & Prophetis (adde etiam Christo & Apostolis) decla- ratam, quatenus talis, id est, æternæ legis & naturalis declarativa est, & quatenus constitutiva fuit specialis obligationis. Priori modo eam nobis proponi ἐξα- γώνιον est: sed ita monet, legem pure declarativam potius habere rationem doctrinæ quam præcepti: do- ctrina autem divina nunquam potest sua autoritate & veritate privari, nec proinde lex pure declarativa unquam potest abrogari aut vim suam amittere, quia est lucerna & lux, quæ semper eodem modo illumi- nat. Posteriori ergo modo spectari hic debet : sed tantum in populo Israelitico constitutam fuisse spe- cialis obligationis legem Mosaicam dicit Rivetus; quod de ceremoniali & forensi admittimus; de mo- rali autem minime concedimus. Nam ea ratione nullatenus obligaret lex moralis Mosaica Christia- nos; adeoque sola naturæ lege obligarentur illi ad obedientiam, quantum ad moralia, quod in- conveniens & Scripturis adversum est. Nihil ergo nobis cum Mose commune fuerit, quoad le- gem moralem : & nulla plane ejus erit quoad nos obligatio. Nam quod Christus vitæ instituendæ rationem è Mose desumptam commendarit, id non per modum novæ promulgationis legis Mosai- cæ, ut nos obligaret, alioquin ad legem Mosaicam non obligatos, factum esse omnes agnoscunt Re- formati. Alter modus abrogatæ legis Mosaicæ à Riveto ita exponitur : quatenus nempe lex omnes, qui eam non observant, sub maledicto detinebat, quam ma- ledictionem legi ademerit Christus, cum eam implen- do & maledictionem in se recipiendo, ut nobis dein- ceps sit instar serpentis, cui ademptum sit venenum, Galat. 3. tum corda nostra innovando & flectendo ad obedientiam sinceram illam quidem etsi non omnibus gradibus perfectam. Sed ea ratione lex non abro- gata magis nobis, quam Israelitis; nam & pro il- lis legem implevit Christus, ac maledictionem le- gis in se recepit; Innovatio tamen illa cordium non est ipsa maledictionis legis ablatio, sed ejusdem con- sequens: quia non per renovationem à maledictio- ne liberamur, sed per justificationem, ac liberatio- nis per Christum factæ, quæ in illa nobis obtingit, applicationem. Tertius modus hic est, quod lex nunc Christia- nis veris non sit onerosa, quia severitas ejus per Chri- stum sublata; sed illud penes Israelitas fideles pa- riter sese habebat, quantum ad legem moralem Mo- saicam : utpote Davidem, Josiam & alios : num enim nobis solis sublata legis severitas per Chri- stum ? Quid ergo hoc discriminis ? In summa, inquit Rivetus, lex non proponitur nobis, quemad- modum à Mose factum est, tanquam conditio ante- cedens jus ad vitam, quæ sit nobis præstanda, pri- usquam jus illud habeamus, sed tanquam conditio contractum subsequens, quod ex se alioqui validus est, nihilominus obligat ad recognitionem quandam, ut sit in contractibus, in quibus fundus aliquis aut possessio ita datur, ut, cui datur, sit vere dominus fundi; obligatur nihilominus ad homagia quæ vo- cant, & servitia nonnulla. Verum num alia ra- tione lex moralis data Israelitis ? anne ipsis erat conditio antecedens jus ad vitam aliter quam si per le- gem vitam quis consequi vellet ? qualis lex ad- huc omnibus est, qui per legem justificari volunt; requirit enim ab omnibus obedientiam perfectam, qui per legis observationem jus ad vitam acqui- rere volunt. Adhæc opponuntur ita sibi diversi fines legis : primus & proprius, qui tamen non nisi in natura instituta locum habuit in statu integrita- tis, ubi ut conditio antecedens jus ad vitam ea pri- mis parentibus fuit : quæ conditio quum post lapsum locum non invenit, hinc alter idem- que (quantum ad legem) accidentarius finis legis est pædagogicus, quod per eandem deducamur, & compellamur ad Christum, qui pro nobis legem implevit : cujus obedientia justificatis lex mora- lis Mosaica utique etiam proponenda est, tanquam conditio contractum illum gratiosum, si ita loqui li- ceat, inter DEUM & homines per Christum me- diatorem, in quo illi in gratiam recipiuntur, ini- tum consequens, obligans nos ad obedientiam, non aliquid promerendi ergo, sed recognitionis, & gratitudinis causa; ubi lex moralis Mosaica omni- no etiam fideles obligat ad obedientiam, eo quod lex divina sit, omnibus in persona Israelitarum & qui illis aderant, promulgata, quemadmodum lex Paradisiaca de arbore cognitionis in protopla- stis omnibus hominibus promulgata fuit, omnes- que obligasset si ejectionem è Paradiso non meru- issent. Si dicas, nonnunquam etiam nostrates dicere ab- rogatam esse legem moralem quoad justificationem, quoad maledictionem, quoad rigorem exactionis : fatemur id sane: sed ea ἀκυρολογία solum est: A- gnoscunt illi non abrogatam quoad obligationem : Nos enim adhuc debitores esse legis Rom. 8. vers. 2. Cæterum si accurate loqui velimus, lex moralis abrogata non est. Legis enim officia sunt dirigere & obligare ad observantiam, quæ adhuc manent. Recte quidem dicitur, justificationem non esse ex lege, fideles immunes esse à maledictione, opera pio- rum licet usque quaque perfecta non sint, DEO pla- cere; exquisite tamen loquendo, nulla hic est le- gis abrogatio. Non ratione justificationis : quia nulla unquam post lapsum fuit ex lege justifica- tio, ideoque lex dici nequit ratione justificatio- nis abrogata. Data quidem est lex ad vitam : sed quod ex lege vita post lapsum non est, vel quod lex non justificat, non est abrogatio legis, sed nostra id facit prævaricatio, manente legis autoritate. In statu integritatis lex poterat vitam dare, nunc non potest; non quod legi, quæ est immutabilis justitiæ divinæ regula, aliquid deces- serit, sed quod nos ab integritate concreata defe- cerimus. Non ergo in lege mutatio accidit, sed in nobis. Dicitur infirmatio facta διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς Rom. 8, 3. sed quum caro nostra legem in se non potuerit infirmam reddere, de impedito legis fructu & fine primario respectu nostri, ob carnem, & con- cupiscentiam, ac peccati, quod omnibus commu- ne, vim & reatum, id intelligendum. Lex vivificare non potest Gal. 3, 21. ideo, quia impleri à nobis non potest. Id ergo κατά τι respectu nostri accipien- dum. Ideo non lex mortua vel abrogata dicitur, sed nos mortui legi Rom. 3, 31. 7, 4. Nec ratione maledi- ctionis lex moralis abrogata recte dicitur. Duplex hominum genus : alii credentes sunt, & pii : alii infideles, & impii: Hos sub maledicto legis esse quis inficiabitur ? Ira enim Dei manet super ipsos, Job. 3, 17. 36. Maledictio ergo legis Mosaicæ abrogata non est, aut condemnatio, quia exercetur adversus impios. Quod ad fideles, illis quidem maledictio nulla est, Rom. 8, 1. sed ideo lex abrogata dici non potest. Non enim cedere debuit piis in maledicti- onem, sed vitam. Quid quod pii observent legem, eidemque satisfactionem præstent non in persona propria, sed in Christo Mediatore : quodque ma- ledictio legis proprie non abrogata sit, sed relaxata per dispensationem, ac translata in Christum, qui pro nobis factus est maledictum Gal. 3, 13. Manet illa pœnalis sanctio Maledictus &c. Deuter. 27, 26. quæ tamen nos non premit, siquidem eam Christus no- stri loco sustinuerit. Denique nec ratione rigoro- sæ exactionis lex moralis accurate abrogata dicitur; Manet namque legi rigor ille exactionis, etsi Ev- angelium monstret eum, qui rigorosæ exactioni le- gis ex asse satisfecit, per quem fideles quidem libe- rantur à rigore exactionis, sed legi nihil in eo dece- dit. Ergo hîc iterum aliqua respectu nostri, nulla autem respectu legis moralis est mutatio. Lex enim requirit à nobis observantiam perfectam rigidiffime, quam quia præstare eidem non vale- mus, Christum, qui eandem pro nobis præstitit obedientiam modis numerisque omnibus abfolu- tiffimam, in Evangelio nobis propofitum fide apprehendimus: ac porro justificati, per ejus obedientiam, adjutu Spiritus S. legi obfequium, quantum infirmitatis ratio nostræ permittit, ex- hibemus, quod obfequium ex fide profectum DEO per Christum gratum & acceptum est, etsi perfectum minime fit, dum solum animo fincero & ἀνυποκρίτῳ præstetur. Atque hæc de legis ob- ligatione.

## 20:3
Vers. 3. YOU SHALL HAVE NO OTHER GODS BEFORE ME.) That is, besides me: πλὴν ἐμὲ [except me]. In which sense this עַל־פָּנַי [before my face] is used elsewhere as אִם־פָּנַי [before my face] 2 Sam. 3:13 & 35. Moreover, it is a πλεονασμὸς [pleonasm] frequent among the Hebrews, as ἕτερος εἰ μὴ [another if not] 1 Cor. 3:11.

It is not a pleonasm, but imports a singular emphasis: nor is it taken exceptively, as if it were 'besides me,' as the Greeks and Chaldeans explained it: but as the Hebrew word ordinarily sounds, 'upon or at my faces,' that is, 'before me,' just as the Vulgate and some Greek codices [render it] πρὸ πρόσωπόν με [before my face]. For it is not forbidden only that we should not have other gods besides GOD: or that we should not have [them] with GOD, as some render it, 'you shall not have other gods with me,' as that אִתִּי [with me] is held in Exod. 20:32, but it is notably said 'before me': partly so that alien gods may be universally excluded, whether they are subordinated or coordinated to GOD: for all those are worshipped with divine honor before GOD: partly so that they may be implied to be worshipped, as it were, in reproach of GOD before his very sight, as many as are worshipped outside the true GOD; which is indicated to be yielded to the one GOD with so much the greater contempt and to provoke him to jealousy. If any wife should testify conjugal love to another in the sight of her husband, that certainly tends to the greater contempt of the spouse. And therefore some render it thus: 'you shall not have before me,' that is, while I am watching, since nothing of those things which you do escapes me, do not bring into my sight alien gods, as if they were rivals, so as to provoke me to anger and jealousy. Now they are called אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים [other gods], who, namely, are assumed outside and besides יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים [Jehovah Elohim], as is evident from the preceding affirmative member; and since the verb יִהְיֶ [shall be] is singular, 'there shall not be to you other ELOHIM,' it is taken either distributively, 'there shall not be to you any of the alien gods,' or κατὰ μίμησιν [by imitation] of the true GOD, who is Elohim: because his worshippers attribute the name and honor proper to him who alone is the true GOD, Jehovah Elohim, to an alien god, Psalm 81:10. Furthermore, the word 'alien' and 'strange' is used, 'there shall not be in you אֵל זָר [a strange god],' LXX. θεὸς πρόσφατος [a new god], and you shall not bow yourself לְאֵל נֵכָר [to a strange god]. LXX. θεῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ [to a strange god]. For he who is other than the true GOD is truly a strange GOD, and since the true GOD has revealed himself peculiarly to the Israelites: any stranger, whom the fathers did not know, who did not reveal himself to them, is not the true GOD, Dan. 12:37. Therefore, idolatry is prohibited by this negative Precept, by which divine glory is attributed to others besides GOD, or to one who is not that Jehovah Elohim, and he is set in the sight of GOD, or before GOD, and is honored as a GOD, or [the person] acknowledges that one true GOD at the same time (and with him worships an idol). If the whole precept is viewed, as both an affirmative and a negative part, it is repugnant to idolatry taken γενικῶς [generally], by which, namely, the true GOD is not held for GOD or is not worshipped as is right with divine worship, or another, who is not GOD, is worshipped as God. Whence idolatry is usually distinguished, which is by reason of the object, and which is committed by reason of the mode, when that is religiously worshipped which is not the true GOD; and that either when we think it is GOD κατὰ δόξαν [according to opinion] from our own judgment, so that we believe it is altogether GOD: or when it is worshipped as GOD κατ' ἀλήθειαν [in truth] indeed or in reality, but we do not think that we are worshipping it as God; when religious worship is claimed for one to whom it does not belong, whether that worship be religious by its nature, or by rite and custom. Which is to be observed against the Papists, who require that we should hold [it] for GOD, and believe and think that we are honoring [it] with divine worship or as GOD proper. And yet it was idolatry when religious worship was offered to creatures, as to the calf, even if it was not offered as to GOD by the Israelites, Exod. 32:4, under the leadership of Aaron, as also 1 Kings 12:28, under the leadership of Jeroboam, who certainly did not believe the calf was GOD and yet were truly idolaters. Which must also be held concerning Micah, Judg. 17:3. Compare Acts 7:41, 1 Cor. 10:7. Add that the Gentiles also, whom they worshipped religiously, did not hold the images for the supreme GOD, yet they were truly idolaters. Next, idolatry is committed by reason of the mode, when the true GOD is indeed worshipped, but not divinely, that is, as he himself commanded and prescribed, whether without a command through ἐθελοθρησκείαν [will-worship] or against a command or the prescribed form of worship: although even such worship, which is undertaken without a command as religious worship, by that very fact tends against the command of GOD, by which we are forbidden to devise divine worship from our own ingenuity, which is to play the harlot after one's own inventions and the thoughts of one's own heart, and thus to commit idolatry, Numb. 15:39, Psalm 106:36, from which head the Papists are again convicted of idolatries, who have devised various and almost innumerable ἐθελοθρησκείας [will-worships].

Idolatry is also usually distinguished into the grosser sort, such as when the fictions of the Gentiles are held for GOD, or fictitious gods devised by them, or creatures created by GOD, the sun, stars, plants, animals, men living or dead, or even things made by art, graven images and other images: and the more subtle sort; to which they refer heresies of every kind concerning the essence and will of GOD, false worships and ἐθελοθρησκείας [will-worships], because thus GOD is not worshipped divinely, and when divine honor of confidence, fear, love, hope, obedience is attributed to others rather than to GOD, or is communicated to others, by which pact Satan is worshipped as GOD by this age, when obedience is rendered to him more, 2 Cor. 4:4, the belly of the Pseudo-Apostles, Phil. 3:19, the gold of the avaricious is called GOD, Job 31:2, the pleasure of the Epicureans, 2 Tim. 3:4, and the Mammon of those who place their trust in riches, Matt. 6:24, etc. When therefore the Apostle says that an idol is nothing in the world, 1 Cor. 8:4, it is to be observed that the name of an idol is concrete, and signifies both the material, the thing itself which is worshipped, whether it be real or fictitious, which by an extrinsic denomination, so to speak, of our intellect and will is an idol; and the formal, namely an act of the mind, such as some opinion about an object with the attribution of divine excellence; or of the will, such as submission and veneration. Although therefore as regards the material, an idol is not nothing, if it be a true entity, some creature, yet it is nothing in the world formally, because outside of our fiction it is not in reality GOD, but is only feigned to be GOD.

The question is asked here: Are Jews and Turks or Mohammedans also deservedly accused of idolatry? This does not seem so to Calixtus, Exercitat. de DEO & attrib.

1. That the Jews so abhor idolatry that they do not even tolerate images: and that Joseph Scaliger, Elench. trihær. cap. XVI., testifies that the Jews were most alien to all idolatry under the later temple, and still are: and that the Mahumedans adore none except one GOD the creator, C. Azoar. XXV., and that they bear nothing more painfully than images and statues, so much so that they do not mark their coins with images, but with certain letters. Although, however, they are not guilty of that gross idolatry which is found among the gentiles and pagans, they cannot nevertheless be absolved from idolatry, because they do not have as the true GOD Him who alone is the true GOD, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and they fashion for themselves another idol, which is nothing in the world, which they worship as GOD, namely a GOD who is one, as in essence, so in person, such as the GOD of dreams is a mere and vain Idol of the human brain. 2. He who does not honor the Son, he does not honor the Father either, and thus does not honor the true GOD, and is truly an idolater, John V, 23. 1 John II, 23. cap. V, 20, 21. Whence the orthodox Fathers argued that the Arians were idolaters, as is most well known, and in the Apology of the Augustan Confession they are called idolaters who do not acknowledge the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of the same divine essence. Conf. B. Luther, Tom. VIII. Jenens. German. in Conc. Isleb. fol. 287. and de verb. noviss. Dav. fol. 155. Add that the Jews assert that the divine name and religious worship were deservedly attributed to created angels, and that the Turks adore their Mahomet, and invoke saints, concerning which see Epimetr. Syncret. Calixt. p. 357.

3. The Calixtines also raise a doubt concerning the Papists: for they desire to absolve them also from idolatry, so that they may be able to cultivate spiritual communion with them, and therefore they pronounce the public worship of the Papacy to be immune from idolatry: But the Missals, Marialia, Rationalia, and other such public writings of the Papacy, fortified with public Papal diplomas, along with the daily practice in all temples and chapels, easily convince them, nor is the Mariolatry, angelolatry, Hagiolatry, Iconolatry, Artolatry, and lipsanolatry of the Papists unknown to anyone, concerning which see Disp. 3. de glor. DEI B. Gerhard, not to mention that they attribute to angels the essential name of GOD, Jehovah, and divine worship, and also the Missatic idolatries and almost innumerable idolatrous superstitions which are in the Papacy. 4. Nor is there any reason for them to say, with Marius in this place, that the Pontificians worship the Saints, not as the highest GOD, but as ministers and intercessors; for religious worship is indivisible, nor does it admit of degrees, and thus it can by no means be attributed to creatures: and that the Papists worship the saints not only as intercessors, but also as bestowers of bodily and spiritual benefits, nay, attribute to them καρδιογνωσίαν and other divine attributes, swear by them, place trust in them, and consecrate temples and altars and feasts to them, B. Gerhard, art. de mort. §. 435. Schröder, Apodix. de Sanct. and others have sufficiently demonstrated: Conf. Tom. II. Syst. Theol. pag. 265.

5. Now there can be no doubt concerning the idolatry of the Socinians, who not only worship a different GOD than that one true GOD, since they do not have Jehovah Elohim, GOD the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit for the true GOD, but the idol of their own heart, a GOD who is only one in person, but also venerate Christ, whom they hold to be a mere man as to nature and essence, with divine honor, and contend that divine worship was offered to angels in the Old Testament. Concerning whom at length

6. Theol. natural. & revel. p. 543. We also showed in Tom. II. Syst. p. 253. that the Arminians, and also the Calvinists, imagine a divine majesty which is the foundation of adoration, other than the infinite and immense Majesty of the one GOD, which can be read there. 7. But they in vain cast the crime of idolatry upon our Churches, as if we held Christ according to his human nature to be God, because we indeed profess, with Scripture and antiquity, that the Deity is communicated to the human nature, yet we do not make the human nature GOD, nor do we say that divine glory belongs to it, except in so far as it subsists in the person of the Son of GOD, and constitutes one ὑφιςάμενον with the Son of GOD, and therefore we by no means worship some other being outside of GOD in a divine manner, or transfer divine worship to another: for the human nature is not outside the Son of GOD, but has been assumed into the hypostasis of the Son, and thus into the fellowship of the Holy Trinity, not as a diverse person, but as the nature of the Son of GOD himself, proper through personal union.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NON HAEBIS DEOS ALIENOS CORAM ME.) Id est, præter me: πλὴν ἐμὲ. Quo sensu hic עַל־פָּנַי eodem alibi אִם־פָּנַי 2. Sam. 3, 13. & 35. Est autem πλεονα- σμὸς Hebræis frequens, ut ἕτερος εἰ μὴ. 1. Corinth. 3, 11.

Non Pleonasmus est, sed fingularem ἔμφασιν importat: neque accipitur exceptive, quasi sit præter me, ut Græci & Chald. expofuere: sed pro- ut sonat vox Ebræa ordinarie, super vel ad facies meas, id est, coram me, quemadmodum Vulgata & Græci nonnulli Codd. πρὸ πρόσωπόν με. Non enim vetatur solum, ne præter DEUM alios Deos habeamus: aut ne cum DEO, ut reddunt non- nulli, non habebis mecum Deus alios, prout Exod. 20, 32. habetur illud אִתִּי mecum, sed notanter di- citur coram me: partim ut universaliter Dii alieni excludantur, five qui fubordinantur, five qui co- ordinantur DEO: omnes enim illi coram DEO di- vini coluntur honore: partim ut quasi in oppro- brium DEI coram ipsius conspectu coli innuantur, quotquot extra verum DEUM coluntur; quod tanto majori contemtui uni DEO cedere eumque ad zelum provocare indicatur. Si quæ conjux in conspectu mariti sui, alteri connubialem teste- tur amorem, id utique ad majorem conjugis ver- git contemtum. Ideoque ita reddunt nonnulli: non habebis coram me, id est, me spectante, cum ni- hil quidquam eorum, quæ facis, me lateat, non ad- ducas in conspectum meum Deos alienos, velut quos- dam rivales, ut me ad iram & zelum provoces. Dicuntur autem אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים Dii alii, qui scil. extra & præter יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים, ut è præce- denti membro affirmativo constat, affumuntur; & cum verbum singulare sit יִהְיֶ non ERIT tibi ELO- HIM alii, id vel distributive accipitur, non erit ti- bi ullus ex Diis alienis, vel κατὰ μίμησιν veri DEI, qui est Elohim: quia DEO alieno nomen & hono- rem ei, qui solus est verus DEUS, Jehovah Elo- him, proprium tribuunt ejus cultores Psalm. 81, 10. Adhibetur porro vox alienus & extraneus non erit in te אֵל זָר Deus alienus LXX. θεὸς πρόσφατος recens, nec incurvabis te לְאֵל נֵכָר Deo extraneo. LXX. θεῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ. Nam qui alius est à vero DEO, vere alienus est DEUS, & quum DEUS ve- rus se patefecerit peculiariter Israelitis: extraneus quicunque, quem non noverunt patres, qui illis se non patefecit, non est verus DEUS, Dan. 12, 37. Prohibetur ergo hoc Præcepto negativo ido- lolatria, qua alii præter DEUM, vel qui non est ille Jehovah Elohim gloria divina tribuitur, isque in conspectu DEI, vel coram DEO statuitur, & ut DEus honoratur, seu agnoscatur simul ille unus verus DEus (& cum illo idolum colatur.) Si in- tegrum spectetur præceptum, qua partem affirman- tem simul ac negantem, Idololatriæ γενικῶς ac- cepta eidem repugnat, qua nempe DEUS verus non habetur pro DEO vel non colitur, prout par est, divino cultu, aut alius, qui non est DEUS, pro Deo colitur. Unde distingui solet idolola- tria, quæ est ratione objecti, & quæ committitur ratione modi, quando id religiofe colitur, quod non est verus DEUS; idque vel cum id ut DEUS κατὰ δόξαν ex sententia nostra, ut nempe omni- no putemus id esse DEUM : vel cum id ut DEUS colitur κατ' ἀλήθειαν quidem vel revera, non au- tem existimemus, nos id ut DEum colere; cum religiosus cultus vindicatur ei, cui non competit, sive is cultus natura sua religiosus sit, sive ex ritu & consuetudine. Quod contra Pontificios observan- dum, qui requirunt, ut pro DEO habeamus, & cultu divino seu DEO proprio honorare nos cre- damus, & existimemus. Atqui idololatria erat, cum creaturæ, utpote vitulo delatus est cultus re- ligiosus, etsi non ut DEO delatus ab Israelitis Exod. 32, 4. Aarone duce, ut & 1. Reg. 12, 28. duce Jero- boamo, qui certe non credebant vitulum esse DEum & tamen vere idololatræ erant. Quod etiam de Micha habendum Jud. 17, 3. Conf. Actor. 7, 41. 1. Corinth. 10, 7. Adde quod gentiles quo- que imagines, quas religiose coluere, non pro summo DEO habuerint, vere tamen idololatræ fuerint. Deinde committitur idololatria ratio- ne modi, quando DEus verus colitur quidem, sed non divine, hoc est, ut ipse jussit, ac præscripsit, sive citra mandatum per ἐθελοθρησκείαν sive con- tra mandatum aut formam cultus præscriptam: quanquam & cultus ejusmodi, qui citra manda- tum suscipitnr ceu cultus religiosus, eo ipso con- tra mandatum DEI vergat, quo vetamur ex pro- prio ingenio cultum divinum excogitare, quod est scortari post adinventiones proprias, & cogitata cordis sui, adeoque idololatriam committere, Nu- mer. 15, 39. Psalm. 106, 36. ex quo capite iterum Pa- pistæ idololatrias convincuntur, qui varias & in- numeras propemodum ἐθελοθρησκείας excogita- runt.

Distingui etiam solet Idololatria in crassiorem, qualis est cum pro DEO habentur commenta gentilium, seu Dii fictitii ab ipsis excogitati, vel creaturæ à DEO conditæ, sol, stellæ, frutices, ani- mantia, homines vivi, aut demortui, vel etiam arte facta, sculptilia & imagines aliæ: & subtilio- rem; ad quam referunt omnis generis hæreses de DEI essentia, & voluntate, falsos cultus & ἐθε- λοθρησκείας, quia ita DEUS non divine colitur, & cum honor divinus confidentiæ, timoris, di- lectionis, spei, obedientiæ aliis potius quam DEO tribuitur, aut cum aliis communicatur, quo pacto Satanas ut DEUS ab hoc seculo colitur, cum ei magis obsequium præstatur 2. Corinth. 4, 4. ven- ter Pseudo - Apostolorum Philipp. 3, 19. aurum ava- rorum DEUS dicitur Job. 31. 2. voluptas Epicuræo- rum 2. Timoth. 3, 4. ac Mammon eorum, qui fi- duciam in divitiis collocant Matth. 6, 24. &c. Quum ergo Apostolus idolum nihil esse dicit in mun- do 1. Corinth. 8, 4. observandum, nomen idoli con- cretum esse, ac dicere tum materiale, ipsam rem quæ colitur, sive ea vera sit, sive ficta, quæ per denominationem extrinsecam, ut ita dicam, intelle- ctus & voluntatis nostræ idolum sit; tum formale, actum nempe mentis, qualis est opinio aliqua de objecto cum conciliatione excellentiæ divinæ; vel voluntatis, qualis est submissio & veneratio. Li- cet ergo quoad materiale idolum non sit nihil, si sit ens verum, creatura aliqua tamen nil est in mun- do formaliter, quia extra fictionem nostram revera id non est DEUS, sed fingitur solum esse DEUS.

Quæritur hîc: Anne Judæi etiam ac Turcæ vel Mahumetani merito idololatrias postulentur? Non id videtur Calixto Exercitat. de DEO & attrib.

div. quod Judæi adeo abhorreant ab idololatria, ut ne imagines tolerent: quodque Joseph. Scaliger Elench. trihær. cap. XVI. testetur, Judæos ab omni idololatria alienissimos sub posteriore templo fuisse, & adhuc esse: & quod Mahumedani nullum adorent præter unum DEUM creatorem C. Azoar. XXV. quodque nihil ægrius ferant, quam imagines & statuas, adeo ut nec nummos suos imaginibus, sed certis literis insigniant. Quamvis vero crassæ istius idololatriæ, quæ apud gentiles & paganos reperitur, rei non sint, non tamen ab idololatria absolvi possunt, quia non habent pro vero DEO eum, qui solus verus est DEUS, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, & aliud idolum sibi fingunt, quod nihil est in mundo, quod pro DEO colunt, nempe DEUM, qui unus, ut essentia, ita persona sit, qualis DEUS fomnium merum & vanum Idolum cerebri humani est. Qui non honorat Filium, ille nec Patrem honorat, adeoque non honorat verum DEUM, ac vere idololatra est Johann. V, 23. 1. Johann. II, 23. cap. V, 20. 21. unde Patres orthodoxi Arianos idololatrias arguerunt, uti notissimum est, & in Apologia August. Confess. idololatræ dicuntur, qui non agnoscunt Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum esse ejusdem divinæ essentiæ. Conf. B. Lutherus Tom. VIII. Jenens. German. in Conc. Isleb. fol. 287. & de verb. noviss. Dav. fol. 155. Adde quod Judæi angelis creatis nomen divinum & cultum religiosum merito tributum esse asserant, quodque Turcæ & Mahumetem suum adorent, & sanctos invocent, de quibus vid. Epimetr. Syncret. Calixt. p. 357.

Dubium etiam de Papistis movent Calixtini: nam & illos ab idololatria absolvere cupiunt, ut cum iis communionem colere queant spiritualem, ideoque publicum cultum Papatus ab idololatria immunem esse pronunciant: Sed facile convincunt eos Missalia, Marialia, Rationalia & id genus alia scripta Papatus publica, publicis diplomatibus Papalibus munita cum praxi quotidiana in templis & sacellis omnibus, nec ulli ignota est Papistarum Mariolatria, angelolatria, Hagiolatria, Iconolatria, Artolatria, lipsanolatria, de quibus vide Disp. 3. de glor. DEI B. Gerhard. ut taceamus, quod angelis nomen DEI essentiale Jehovah & cultum divinum tribuant, nec non idololatrias Missaticas & superstitiones idololatricas propemodum innumeras, quæ in Papatu sunt. Nec est quod dicant, cum Mario in h. l. quod Pontificii Sanctos colant, non ut summum DEUM, sed ut ministros & intercessores; nam cultus religiosus indivisibilis est, nec gradus admittit, adeoque nullo pacto tribui creaturis potest: & colere Papistas sanctos non solum ut intercessores; sed etiam ut largitores beneficiorum corporalium, & spiritualium, imo tribuere eis καρδιογνωσίαν & alia attributa divina, per eosdem jurare, fiduciam in eos collocare, templa & altaria & festa iis consecrare B. Gerhard. art. de mort. §. 435. Schröder. Apodix. de Sanct. & alii satis demonstrarunt: Conf. Tom. II. Syst. Theol. pag. 265.

Jam de Socinianorum idololatria dubium esse non potest, qui non tantum alium DEUM colunt, quam unum illum verum DEUM, cum non Jehovam Elohim DEUM Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. habeant pro vero DEO, sed idolum cordis sui, DEUM, qui persona unus tantum est, sed etiam Christum, quem nudum hominem, quantum ad naturam & essentiam habent, honore divino venerantur, angelisque cultum divinum delatum esse in Vet. Testam. contendunt. De quibus prolixe

Theol. natural. & revel. p. 543. Arminianos etiam, nec non Calvinianos majestatem divinam, quæ adorationis fundamentum sit aliam ab infinita & immensa DEI unius Majestate comminisci osten- dimus Tom. II. Syst. p. 253. quæ illic legi possunt. Nequicquam autem ipsi Ecclesiis nostris idolola- triæ crimen impingunt, quasi Christum secundum humanam naturam pro Deo habeamus, quia Dei- tatem quidem communicatam humanæ naturæ cum Scriptura & antiquitate profitemur, non ta- men humanam naturam DEUM facimus, nec glo- riam ei divinam convenire dicimus, nisi qua in per- sona Filii DEI subsistit, & cum Filio DEI unum ὑφιςάμενον constituit, ideoque ita neutiquam ali- um quendam extra DEUM divino modo colimus, aut cultum divinum ad alium transferimus: nam humana natura non est extra DEI Filium, sed as- sumta est in hypostasin Filii, adeoque in consorti- um S. S. Trinitatis, non ceu persona diversa, sed ceu natura ipsius Filii DEI, per unionem persona- lem propria.

## 20:4
8. Vers. 4. THOU SHALT NOT MAKE UNTO THEE A GRAVEN IMAGE.) An eminent image.

9. Calvin, lib. II. inst. cap. 8. §. 13., the Heidelberg Catechism, quest. 93., and Ursinus in his explanation, and other Reformed, constitute the second commandment here, and they bring into that opinion Origen, lib. III. harm. 8. in Ex., Nazianzen in his poems, Jerome and Ambrose in their Commentaries on Ephesians VI., and Chrysostom, hom. 49. in Matthew. Although, however, some of the Reformed do not wish to litigate contentiously about it, such as Calvin, Ursinus, and Musculus, yet most of them so adhere to that opinion that they accuse our people of wicked mutilation, and even of sacrilege, because they wish the prohibition concerning graven images to be included under the first commandment concerning not having strange Gods, and therefore omit it in the Catechism: such as Innocent Gentillet in Apol. pro Christ. c. II. cap. de Imag., the Anhaltines in Apol. contra quosdam Nobil. fol. 28., the Neo-Marburgers in resp. Apol. fol. III., and also Rivetus: who likewise imputes sacrilege to us and the Pontificians here, Expl. Dec. pag. 3. Although he defends his Ursinus (entirely beside the point) against B. Gerhard, as if the blessed man had attributed to him that he peddled that distinction of the first and second commandment as necessary, whereas he himself rather judged that one should not fight odiously about the change of words. But although such particulars about graven images and idols are not proposed to simpler people in the Catechism, sacrilege is not therefore committed. B. Luther used a summary. And the commandments were recited by the Apostle with some omitted in Romans 13:9. Will the Calvinists argue against him too? I add that the words are left entire in the Bibles, and the same are not omitted by our people in the explanations of the Decalogue; only in the compendious recitation of the commandments for the more unlearned are those things which were added for the sake of explanation especially on account of the Jews not recited. But as for the commemoration of them regarding all the words, while the Calvinists strive to foist it upon the Church as necessary, they not only undermine Christian liberty, but they also act primarily to establish their own iconoclasm and to eliminate Luther's Catechism from the Church by undermining it. And although this law should not be held with certain Jesuits as merely positive, pertaining only to the Jews, nor do we think with B. Chemnitz that there is anything ceremonial in this commandment, namely that the use of all images whatsoever was forbidden to the Jews, even outside of worship, yet it cannot at least be denied that the Jews were very prone to figure GOD under some image and to worship Him in it, which

calf-worship and many other things teach, whence they were not only frequently recalled from that idolatry by the Prophets, but here also, in the very promulgation of the moral law, God specifically willed this to be forbidden to them. Thus far, therefore, we think that this was inserted primarily for the sake of the Jews as Φιλειδώλων. Moreover, it is manifest from the very words of the Decalogue that these things are added, not so that images of the Deity himself are simply prohibited, but so that images which are made for the sake of religious worship are forbidden; for that reason it is added, you shall not bow down to them, nor serve them: which words contain a limitation of the preceding. Which is confirmed primarily from Deut. 4:16. For there, images of man, bird, and fish are also prohibited: which certainly were not prohibited except by reason of the vicious end of idolatrous worship: and it is also forbidden to lift up the eyes to heaven, to the sun, the moon, and other stars, which is certainly not to be understood simply, but as the added declaration holds, lest you be impelled to bow down to them and serve them. How, therefore, it is forbidden to lift up the eyes and look at the sun and the moon, in that same manner it is forbidden to make images. But that is not prohibited except by reason of that vicious end. Add also Leviticus 26:1-2, where for the same reason the erection of a statue is also prohibited, which cannot be understood otherwise than concerning the idolatrous erection of a statue, for otherwise it was not illicit (Genesis 28:18, ch. 31:45, ch. 35:14, Joshua 24:20, 1 Samuel 7:12).

Furthermore, this interdict is added as a special one and as an appendix to the general prohibition of idolatry, and therefore it must be explained from its intent, and since that forbids that strange gods be held, this likewise must be accepted in that sense, that images not be worshipped as gods, or made for the sake of religious worship: for the opposition of the true God and strange gods is to be noted: whence it is certain that they are prohibited for that reason, in that they are strange gods, but not that they are prohibited simply. The force of which argument Rivetus admits in his explanation. Decalogue, page 40, for he himself concludes thus: For since that commandment follows the prohibition of strange gods, by which all idolatry in general is comprehended, which is committed as often as something is attributed to GOD which pertains to HIM, whether by thought, or by words, or by gestures, and deeds, as we showed before, here GOD willed to prohibit that species of idolatry by which idolaters professed in some figure or corporeal effigy that they were worshipping some deity. Rightly, therefore, is a distinction made between images and idols, between εἰκονοποιΐαν and εἰδωλοποιΐαν. For it is nowhere prohibited to make images; but that it is prohibited here and elsewhere throughout to make an image for idolatry and religious worship is undoubted. Ursinus laughs at the distinction, because εἴδωλον is nothing other than an image; but even if this be true, if you look at the etymology, yet by the usage of Scripture and the Church there is no idol except that which is set forth for worship, whether an idol is erected in the heart or is constituted otherwise. Therefore, sacred images, which exhibit sacred things, and idolatrous ones, which represent idols or fictitious GODS, or whose representation is idolatrous, as when in the Papacy they exhibit and represent Mary in the likeness of GOD, must be distinguished first. We acknowledge that these are prohibited. But as for those which are indeed sacred, but neither produce scandal by their representation nor are set forth for worship, they are not forbidden and can have their use not only for ordering, but also for teaching, reminding, and testifying. For what writing does for those who read, a picture does for the unlearned who see it, as Gregory the Great says, lib. 9, Epist. 9. If, however, it is asked concerning images representing the Deity himself, as it is certain that GOD κατ᾿ ὀυsίαν cannot or ought not to be expressed by any image or likeness, which therefore is forbidden by divine law, no one denies, so if, in the way GOD has exhibited himself κατ᾿ ὀικονομίαν, ὀπτασίαν, or ἐπιφάνειαν, it is shadowed forth by painting or sculpture, it cannot be judged contrary to the command of GOD: because nothing else is then exhibited than the history of that apparition or manifestation by which GOD himself deigned to reveal himself; concerning which, if it is permitted to form an idea and image in the conception of the mind (without which it cannot even be read and considered), no sane person will deny that the same can equally be set before the eyes by a painting or a sculpted image without transgression; as for example when the apparition is exhibited (Daniel 7:24, or Matthew 3:16, or that which occurred in the Johannine Apocalypse, and similar ones, which are described in Scripture): which pictures and images, therefore, there is no doubt can be set up in temples also for the sake of history, memory, and doctrine. For neither in this commandment nor elsewhere is representation prohibited, but worship and adoration, nor is GOD represented by himself in that way, but that by which GOD at some time willed to be manifested. Therefore we approve that of Gregory, lib. 9, Epist. 1: If anyone wishes to make images, do not forbid it at all: but avoid by all means worshipping images. Which Rivetus also professed when he inquired in his explanation of the Decalogue, page 40, as to which images are prohibited by this commandment, approving the opinion of Vasquez, that the sense of this prohibition is that it is not only not permitted to worship an image instead of GOD, but also not to worship the true GOD in any likeness of him: where among other things he also has this: We concede that by the words of the law not every εἰκονοποιΐαν is absolutely prohibited, but only that which is referred to worship and religion. And that is rightly urged against other Pontificians, as much the old scholastics as the more recent ones, who said that this alone was prohibited, that images should not be worshipped after the manner of the Gentiles as gods, but that not every worship and adoration of images was prohibited: Because GOD simply prohibited worshipping images, not only worshipping them after the manner of the Gentiles. Therefore, Vasquez rightly acknowledges in Disputation 104, chapter, that it is also forbidden to worship GOD in an image. That it was merely ceremonial and positive, and concerned the Jews alone, Vasquez falsely asserts. For even in the New Testament we are forbidden to adore GOD in images, Acts 17:29, nor is there anything that compels us to restrict this part of the Decalogue to the Jews alone, in which the Ancients acknowledge everything except the determination of the Sabbath to be moral, Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 31, Augustine, book 19, against Faustus, chapter 18, and Epistle 119, chapter 12. Yet it must not be maintained with the Calvinists that the precept concerning not fashioning or sculpting images of the deity is natural, which Rivetus contends; for it is one thing to fashion an image of the deity, another to adore the deity in an image: since GOD can be depicted by some image, by which He Himself has manifested, even if the image is not adored, or GOD in the image. Nor could Rivetus deny that GOD appeared in Daniel 7. Revelation 5, in human form, although he refers that not so much to signify the person of GOD the Father Himself, as His operation, which also concerning the apparition

lest the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. But even if the person himself is not noted by that image, but only the effects, it is nevertheless clear that those images can be lawfully painted, since indeed that history of the apparition is shadowed forth or exhibited: Whence Rivetus confesses that images are lawful which are fashioned outside of temples, without danger of idolatry, superstition, and scandal, for historical or symbolic use, or for honest adornment. He also complains that some deal with the Reformed as if they had to do with Jews or Mahometans, who admit no images of living things at all. Meanwhile, he himself agitates against our people concerning images of the Holy Trinity, when God the Father is painted in the figure of an old man, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, the Son of God in the form of the body which He assumed, and against us, no less than the Pontificians, he urges the words spoken against the idolatry of the Gentiles in Romans 1:23: they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, because they attempt to fashion the divine glory and majesty through the image of an old man; but these are calumnies which he has poured out against his conscience. For he knew well that we do not thus fashion the essence of God with the Gentiles, nor the divine majesty and glory, but only represent the apparition by which God exhibited Himself. But when the Reformed conceive this in their mind, do they also change the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of a mortal man? They certainly cannot read and conceive the history of the manifestation of God in the form of the Ancient of Days without conceiving the image of an old man; for what else are intelligible species than internal images of things? Nor is there any reason for him to say that this cannot be blamed, because this natural necessity is imposed upon us, that we understand through species and images: but that pictures are prohibited. For if by such a conceived image, which he says is necessary, the glory of God is not changed into the image of man, then certainly it will not be done by such a painted or sculpted image, if idolatry and the opinion of the expressed divine essence itself be absent. But that such images are prohibited by divine law is a mere begging of the question, which here proves to us only the ἑαυτομαχίαν (self-contradiction) of Rivetus: because he himself conceded that for symbolic use, if the sin of idolatry, superstition, and scandal is absent, images are lawful: why then are those images not lawful which are exhibited in the Scriptures, even concerning God Himself? But what he says, that it is one thing if those visions are read or recited to us separately and insofar as they are formed within us through some intelligible species, and another if they are jointly sculpted by the hand of man and given the name of the Trinity, is of no moment. For if mention is made at the same time of the Ancient of Days from Dan. VII and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and of Christ θεανθρώπως (as God-man) from Holy Scripture, must one not present those images to the mind at the same time? What images, therefore, are conceived in the mind at the same time without sin, why should they not be exhibited at the same time without sin when depicted on a board? But an excessive fervor against innocent and mnemonic images seems to have so occupied Rivetus that, although he said he did not wish to move a controversy concerning Christ Himself insofar as He was made man, whether He could be painted, yet he soon pronounced that it was not far removed from the Papistic rite, by which the idols of the Gentiles are imitated, that our people paint the Elector of Saxony and Luther, one on the right side, the other on the left, prostrate before the image of the crucifix. Thus, the Reformed cannot even bear the image of the crucifix, or hold the adoration of the crucifix shadowed forth to be ἀνεπίληπτον (irreproachable): Indeed, with their Beza, they intimate that they detest the image of the crucifix from their heart, which ought to be strongly impressed upon the mind of the faithful. But what is the reason that the Reformed can bear the image of the crucified Christ on coins and gold and silver vessels, but refuse to bear them in temples, and are untimely reformers of temples? Or are they perhaps drawn away by the cursed hunger for gold from the zeal against images on coins, with which they boil against images in temples? And whence will they prove that the same are lawful outside of temples, but not in temples, so that they are placed in them outside of worship? Rivetus brings forward this cause, that the law concerning images, since it looks to religion, must also be restricted to it: He also pretends scandal and the alienation of Jews and Mahometans, and the greatest danger, indeed the ruin of the simpler folk, because many are drawn to superstition, and idolaters are confirmed in their obstinacy. But does religion flourish only in the temple? Should not account also be taken of it outside the temple? If the law prohibits religious images, that is, those erected for the sake of religion, as Rivetus says, how does he call those religious which we tolerate outside of worship? They are religious, he says, when they are seen in a temple, provided they are accommodated to adoration, or in a private oratory, and men are intent upon them when they pray. But that mode accommodated to adoration is not affixed to them by the place, say a temple or a private oratory, nor can such a material or sensible mode be designated, nor does it have a place among us. That in the Papacy they are considered accommodated to the adoration of images is caused by an erroneous opinion and persuasion, not sticking in the boards or walls, but in the hearts of those given over to superstition; from whom, and specifically from the Jesuit Vasquez, Rivetus drew this restriction of the mode accommodated to adoration; with which superstition we have no commerce: we who admit neither the adoration of God in images, nor an intention directed toward images, nor a mode accommodated to adoration, while we leave a place for images for the sake of adornment, memory, symbol, or even for the sake of stirring up affection. Scandal, both among infidels and idolaters as well as among the weak, is scandal taken, not given, and arises from images by accident, provided they are not scandalously adorned. Therefore, according to the counsel of B. Luther, idolatry and false opinion must be overturned from the minds, and the people must be rightly informed concerning images, and no danger will remain; which counsel of B. Luther, as Rivetus himself praised, so he was forced to acknowledge that the procedure of his Carlstadt, by which he tumultuously cast statues out of the temples, was deservedly condemned by Luther (such is the power of truth); furthermore, concerning the abolishing of images which are painted or sculpted in such a form or appearance that they cannot be looked upon by honest eyes, but especially those whose very appearance provokes to idolatry, we do not disagree, as he observes from the Montbéliard Colloquy, provided that the abolition of them is done not by private counsel, but by the authority of pious Magistrates. We add that it is necessary that it be done in an orderly fashion without tumult and scandal, with the doctrine of faith preserved and Christian liberty unharmed.

If, however, the Reformed still urge the abrogation of all sacred images from the temples as necessary by the force of a commandment, let them teach by what words sacred images are prohibited in the temple, outside the reason for worship? or where have Christ or the Apostles in the New Testament reproved the same, and commanded them to be abolished from the temples? Here certainly not the painting of images, but their worship is prohibited: and not in the temple alone, but simply, without mention of place, it is commanded that images not be made for the purpose that they be adored. In the earlier centuries, indeed, images were not in use in the worship of God: but since the Gentiles worshipped deities in idols, Christians abstained from idols, lest they seem to have a likeness with the pagans, whence also the Ancients were more ill-disposed toward images, because those who were converted from the Gentiles wished to worship the true God in images, being accustomed to idols, as B. Chemnitius observes p. 4. Exam. Concil. Trid. de imag. p. 26. nor were images received into temples until Constantine, and not even those of Christ: yet B. Chemnit. shows p. 28 that the historical use was not rejected on that account in the primitive Church. But with the idols of the Gentiles destroyed, and peace restored to the Churches under Constantine, and afterwards the use of historical images began to be more frequent among Christians, and when panegyrical solemnities concerning the passions of the martyrs were frequented and temples began to be adorned more splendidly, images were also received into them, namely around the year 380, whence Gregory of Nyssa makes mention of them, and among the Latins, Paulinus and Prudentius: Cyril, however, when Julian objected to Christians that they adored the image of the cross, in book 6, asserted the historical use of images excellently, which was also done by Gregory the Great, whom furthermore the 6th universal Synod around the year 680 confirmed. But when images had begun to be adored among the Latins, the Greeks attacked their adoration by the demolition of images. Whence horrible and bloody struggles arose: concerning which see the aforementioned B. Chemn. Therefore, in the ancient Church, the use of images of the passion of Christ, and of the Lord's cross and similar things, was not prohibited: until the Iconoclasts, led by Leo the Isaurian in the year of Christ 725, ordered that images which had begun to be worshipped be removed, so that the Saracens might not have a pretext to write against the Christians; his son Constantine Copronymus then followed in the year 753, and in the Synod of Constantinople prohibited images from being made. On account of which a tumult arose in the previous century, namely in the year of Christ 1522, when B. Luther was staying in Patmos, Carlstadt, a wild man in whom there was no indication of the Spirit but manifest signs of impiety, as Philip testifies in his Epistle to Myconius, stirred up the mob here in Wittenberg, casting statues out of the temple by a private and rash act, as Hieronymus Schurff, Tom. II. Jen. Germ. Luther. fol. 24, and Joh. Schleid. l. 3. Comment. hist. have reported. Whose disciples and followers, the Reformers not only of temples and Sacraments but also of purer doctrine, whom we designate as Zwinglio-Calvinists, even now do not endure sacred images in temples with a calm mind, and desire them to have rather a likeness to Jewish Synagogues and Saracen shrines, petulantly reproaching us beyond our merit, because our temples, if they are adorned with memorial and symbolic images without superstition and idolatry, are similar to the temples of idolaters.

Nor does Canon 36 of the Council of Elvira help them: It has pleased that there should not be pictures in Churches, lest what is worshipped and adored be depicted on walls. For it is manifest that not all images are prohibited there, but those which are displayed for the sake of worship and adoration, lest what is depicted on walls be worshipped. Which does not differ from the opinion of Gregory the Great, l. 9. Ep. 1: If anyone wishes to make images, by no means forbid it, but avoid the adoration of images in every way. Therefore, in Canon 60 of the same Council, it is defined: If anyone has broken idols, and has been killed there, because it is not written in the Gospel, nor is it found to have ever been done by the Apostles, it has pleased that he not be received into the number of martyrs. Those Fathers therefore admit that it is not in the New Testament written that images, even if they have been prostituted to idolatry, must be abolished, nor was that done by the Apostles, because, namely, idolatry can cease while images remain. For an idol is nothing in the world, as the Apostle testifies. Therefore, idolatrous worship must be abrogated, nor can images which were once prostituted to worship do harm. If, however, the scandal cannot be removed unless those also are removed, we do not deny that they are rightly removed by public authority. Therefore, images and idols differ greatly, even when they do not differ materially. The molten oxen in the temple of Solomon did not displease the Lord; the calves in Dan and Bethel did displease Him. He tolerated the bronze serpent when it was not prostituted to worship, which He Himself had ordered to be made for the sake of looking at it; but when they offered incense to it, Hezekiah rightly removed it, he did not tolerate it. 2 Kings 18:4. GOD Himself had ordered the Cherubim to be placed at the ark of the covenant; He would by no means have allowed them to be adored. If images had been simply prohibited in temples, neither these nor others divinely ordained or admitted in the tabernacle or the temple of Solomon would have existed. Where one must wonder at Rivetus, that he denies the bronze serpent and the Cherubim were images, because they were hieroglyphic types, Explic. Decalog. 51, as if these were opposites and a type could not be an image. The author of Wisdom, ch. 14, 11, 12, does indeed call idols scandals, but of the foolish. Therefore, to the wise and rightly informed, they are not a scandal.
