Crocius in consid. Triad. cap. 12, appeals primarily to the passage Deut. 4:15, that the cause of the prohibition of an image of God holds place even outside the case of worship, and therefore that prohibition must be understood absolutely. He posits a twofold cause: 1. because no likeness of GOD was seen, 2. lest souls be corrupted. But that law deals with an image representing God according to His essence, so that they do not believe God to be similar to the image of created things, namely of a husband or a woman, or a beast, or the Sun, or the Moon, by expressing Him, but that they know and acknowledge the Creator to be most distantly distinct from the creatures which He created, and that He cannot be represented by any image of a created thing as far as His essence is concerned, nor should they worship and revere God in such likenesses. Therefore, God did not there present Himself to be seen by the idol-loving people in any likeness, lest such likenesses shadowing forth God should attribute to Him such an essence, and thus they be deceived by error and their souls be corrupted. But that symbolic images of God, expressing the operations or hypostases of God, not His essence, are simply prohibited even outside the context of worship does not appear from that passage: nor are those things which could then be snares of error to a people prone to idolatry, Deut. 12, 20, a scandal and incitement to all, or ought they to be considered simply prohibited for that reason.

Crocius still insists, gathering from Hos. 2, v. 2 as follows: Just as it is not enough for a husband if he casts out his wife from his lusts and wandering loves, and furthermore turns away from her: so it is not enough for God if He roots out adulteries, that is, secret loves from the midst of the breasts, that is, from the heart of the people, unless He also removes from their eyes the incitements to fornication. What good man, says Rivetus in the cited place, p. 47, would want his otherwise chaste wife to walk about in harlot's attire, or to have the signs of a brothel painted in his house? What, therefore, is the Christian prudence of those Evangelicals who fill their churches with images in such a way that they do not differ from the idolatrous temples of the Papists? But they assume that images are in themselves incitements to idolatry: that images in our churches are harlot's adornment, that they are signs of Papistic idolatry, which is false and slanderous. We do not admit or approve of such things, even if we do tolerate historical and symbolic images. For a man who is naturally lascivious, association with a beautiful woman can be an incitement, which to another who is studious of chastity is not an incitement at all. An ornament used by a harlot for the sake of lasciviousness can be used and worn by a chaste virgin without lasciviousness.

Wherefore our Churches rightly hold a middle ground between idolaters and iconoclasts: not indeed adoring images with the Papists, nor simply abolishing them from temples with the Calvinists, but bearing them for the sake of history, memory, or ornament, if superstition be absent, and placing their use among things indifferent.

Therefore, as far as the worship of images is concerned, it is most manifest from the words of the law that the religious worship of any images whatsoever is simply prohibited. For God simply counts the use of likenesses for worship, when the Divine Being is worshipped in them, among strange gods: and He prohibits it in such a way that there is no room for evasion or exception, as has been rightly observed by the blessed Chemnitz, Part 4, Examination of the Council of Trent, on images, p. 21. For first, He counts the graven and molten image, a statue placed or an erected stone formed or fashioned into some image. And by the general word Themunah, that is, a likeness or image, expressing and representing some species by any figure whatsoever, in any way, and painted or made from any material. Deut. 4, He calls it Samel, that is, a figure, effigy, or form. Secondly, He enumerates the things whose likeness or image He forbids to be proposed or used for worship in such a way that there is no room for exception: for He says of those things which are either in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or which are under the waters, or which are under the earth. Now, God, the Angels, and the Spirits of the blessed are in heaven; demons are under the earth; the bodies of the dead are also under the earth. The rest, which are fixed in the sky, which are in the air, which are in the waters, which are on the earth, are evident in themselves. Therefore, He prohibits making, proposing, or using for worship not only images of idols and demons (1 Cor. 8), nor only of irrational creatures, but also of Angels, of the spirits of the just who are in heaven, and of deceased men whose bodies are under the earth; and the law of GOD does not want even the image of God Himself to be made, proposed, and used for worship: for our GOD is in heaven. And the law prohibits the image of that which is in heaven from being made for worship. And Deuteronomy 4. The reason is added: you heard the voice of His words, but you did not see any likeness when the Lord spoke to us from the midst of the fire. Thirdly, He prohibits every kind of religious worship with two words, when He says: You shall not adore nor worship them, by the first of which, which signifies bowing down, He embraces all external gestures and rites of worship; by the second, the internal affections and devotions of worship. And the Book of Wisdom, chapter 14, and the Prophets throughout (Is. 44, c. 46, Jer. 10, Ezech. 6, c. 14, Os. 11, and elsewhere) describe those external acts of worship with bowings, genuflections, prostrations of the body, extensions of the hands, kissings, sacrifices, incense, frankincense, libations, adornment of gold, purple, etc., carrying about, invocations, supplications, vows, desire, love, devotion, hope, trust, fear, etc. Fourthly, lest anyone evade these things as if only the worship which is exhibited to the material or form of the likenesses themselves were prohibited: Scripture shows that even when those acts of worship of images are referred to the prototype, whether to things signified by the images or to God, they are nevertheless called the worship of strange gods. Which the blessed Chemnitz demonstrates with examples from Scripture, such as when first Thare

300 years after the flood is said to have sacrificed to strange gods (Jos. 24), that is, the Ur of the Chaldeans, when they worshipped God in fire, for the Fathers were not so inept as to think that the divine essence was the element of fire: and afterwards Laban (Gen. 31), as also Micah (Jud. 17) and the Danites (ch. 8), who venerated Teraphim, or statues fashioned into the image of human form, not as if they believed that the divine essence was a statue fashioned from wood, but because they were persuaded that God is rightly worshipped in such a likeness: which also appears in the calf-worship of the Israelites (Exod. 32). Wherefore God then prolixly and clearly prohibited that images or statues be made for the worship of religion, lest either creatures or God Himself be worshipped in them, which prohibition is repeated in Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 5, ch. 12.

Andradius is truly inept when he contends that in the Old Testament, while Christ was not yet incarnate, it was not permitted to worship the invisible God in a visible image, but now, after God has been manifested in the flesh, Christ may be lawfully and rightly worshipped through images: for the law concerning graven things and images not being worshipped is moral, and binds everyone: therefore, when St. John (1 Epist. 5:20) had said that the Son of God has come and has given us a mind that we may know the true God, he adds, little children, beware of idols or likenesses, using the word εἴδωλον, which the Greeks used here. And throughout the New Testament, idolatry is most gravely prohibited and condemned. Rom. 1:20, 1 Cor. 10:7, Gal. 5:21. Nor did the worship of images have any other origin than from the pagans, whose idolatry consisted for a great part in the adoration and worship of images, likenesses, and statues, where indeed superstitious and idolatrous worship was added to the political use of images among the heathens. For although in ancient times no nations worshipped deities without likenesses, just as Herodotus teaches that the Persians erected statues to their gods, and Augustine (l. 4, de Civ. Dei, cap. 31) observes from Varro that the Romans worshipped gods without a likeness for more than one hundred and seventy years, yet in later times the nations bound their whole religion and the entire worship of gods to likenesses, concerning which see Clem. Alex. (exhortation to the gentiles), Arnobius (book 6 against the gentiles), Euseb. (book 3 on the preparation for the Gospel). How Hermes called visible and tangible likenesses of this kind the bodies of gods, because he believed that spirits were invisibly joined to visible things through a certain art, see Aug. bk. 8 de C. D. ch. 23. Which they worshipped with sacrifices, crowns, candles, adorations, fasts, feasts, lustral water, and carrying about: just as the Jews worshipped their idols and the Papists today worship statues and images, so much so that Lud. Vives admits that no difference can be shown, except that the Papists have merely changed the names and titles. See B. Chemn. loc. cit. p. 17. B. Schröder. Apodixi de imaginib. as also Polydor. Vergil. bk. 6 de invent. rerum ch. 13. bk. 2 ch. 23. bk. 5 ch. 3. And the Gentiles likewise used this pretext, with which the Papists paint their idolatry, that they do not offer these honors to the likenesses, but to the gods whose appearance they represent, as Cassander teaches from Arnobius and Lactantius in his refutation to art. 21. August. Conf. Johannes Ferus in chapter 17 of Acts acknowledges that they had the intention of offering worship to the true God through idols and images. Moreover, heretics also preceded the Papists; Simon Magus, who handed over the image of his prostitute Selene to his followers to be worshipped: the followers of Basilides, who used invocations of images, as Irenaeus testifies in bk. 1 ch. 23. The Carpocratians, or Gnostics, whom Irenaeus notes worshipped images, even the form of Christ, in chapter 24. And Epiphanius T. 1 bk. 1 heresy 27. How constantly the pious Ancients contradicted the worship of images can be taught even from the Pontifical writers themselves. The worship of likenesses, says Polydore Vergil in bk. 6 ch. 13, almost all the ancient Fathers, as witnessed by They condemned [it] with Jerome, for fear of idolatry: but Cassander declares from Origen how much the Ancients at the beginning of the Church abhorred all veneration of images, and teaches more fully that at the beginning of Christianity not even the use of images was admitted because of hatred of Paganism, and for fear of idolatry: But afterwards in the age of Ambrose, Nyssen, and Prudentius, pictures were received in temples, where that danger of adoration and worship was less or was feared: and that in the age of Gregory it was still the opinion of the Church that pictures were to be honored, not indeed that they should be worshipped and adored, but that the unlearned, by looking at pictures, just as by reading books, might be reminded of historical events and be incited to piety. But how the seeds of image worship were already scattered in the time of Gregory, and how Gregory himself, although he did not wish images to be adored, nevertheless adored Christ before an image, and from there a progression was made to the worship of images, and how Damascenus propagated the same, and others sanctioned it, the blessed Chemnitz learnedly teaches in the aforementioned place, p. 35. Regarding the progress of that superstition, Cassander in the same place further teaches: But when sharp contentions had arisen among the Greeks, with some breaking all images, and others ordering them to be worshipped and adored, the Roman Church entirely condemned the breaking, and judged that the true use of the Roman Church, already received through almost the whole world, should be retained; Which custom the Roman Church, which equally disapproved of the breaking and the adoration, the Gallican and German Churches stoutly defended for several centuries, so much so that when some decrees about adoring images had been issued in the Nicene Synod under Constantine and Irene, and a copy of that Synod had been brought to the Synod of Frankfurt, and had been diligently read by the order of Charlemagne, at which Synod Roman Legates were also present, by the highest consensus of the Fathers that Greek Synod, in the part where it judged that images should be adored, was disapproved and condemned, as something that was opposed not only to the divine scriptures and the ancient tradition of the Fathers, but also to the custom of the Roman Church, which condemnation was also inserted into the acts and chapters of that Frankfurt Synod, and on that matter four books were written under the title of Charles himself, of which Hincmar the Bishop makes mention, and a copy of them still exists today in the Vatican Library and in some places in Gaul, which books diligently refute the arguments of the Oriental Fathers, and sharply defend what had been the opinion of the Roman Church until then. These things [are from] Cassander, concerning which the blessed Chemnitz is also to be consulted: who hands down not a few things about the seventh Iconolatric Synod: and observes from Acts chapter 6 that there were those in the Synod itself who judged that the historical use of images should be received, but their adoration should be refused, but the better part was overcome by the majority, and concerning the Frankfurt [Synod] he shows that those who wrote the lives of the Popes rashly, with its acts suppressed, feigned that the seventh Iconolatric Synod and the adoration of images were received and approved there, when other serious historians, such as Eginhard, Regino, Adon, Ammonius, Blendus, Aventinus, and Hincmar testify to the contrary, and the books of Charles on images, published in Gaul by Bishop Tilius, convict those Papist writers of the manifest crime of forgery: and furthermore he deals with the struggle of Claudius and Jonas, in the year of our Lord 840, how the former criticized the worship of images in the Italian Churches outside the Frankfurt Synod (although he also leaned toward abolishing images), but the latter fell into the distinction of the seventh Pseudo-Synod concerning the adoration of latria and dulia, and began to cloak the adoration of images: and how the German and Gallic Churches long abhorred the adoration of images, and how an inclination was attempted, and what struggles prevailed in the Greek Church, and after that seventh Iconolatric Synod, but finally the adoration of images prevailed, so much so that Zonaras and Nicetas write that it was held as a heresy in their times if anyone did not adore images. Cassander in the aforementioned place teaches that the Germans, even in the age of Frederick Barbarossa, in the year 1160, disapproved of the adoration of images: Although indeed in the Roman Church the Scholastic writers, as they are called, not only attributed to images an honorary adoration of external reverence, as the Greeks did, but argued that images should be worshipped with the same adoration as their prototypes, such as Thomas, Bonaventura, and the remaining Sententiaries and Summists, yet Durandus of Saint-Pourçain pronounced this to be false, and contended that images are not adored properly, but only abusively and improperly, which opinion Raphael de Latorre, a Spanish Dominican, in his Summa on Religion, quest. 94, art. 16, Disp. 6, attributes also to Gerson the Elder, Olcot, Pico della Mirandola, and teaches that Alfonso à Castro also inclines toward it; because they judge that images are incapable of adoration which terminates in them truly, but because they refer to things worthy of adoration, which are adored through remembrance in the presence of images, therefore they are said to be adored abusively and improperly. But although that Raphael calls this opinion (of those Catholics of his) rash, which savors of heresy, and approves the opinion of Thomas in opposition: yet he was by no means able to prove it to all recent Roman Catholics, as even that Dominican observed. Not to those who say that images should be adored with an inferior or honorary adoration, with Ambrosius Catharinus and Martinus Peresius: Nor to those who, with Nicolaus Sanderus, Cardinal Bellarmine, and Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi, Franc. They attribute to the image, according to Suarez, a twofold adoration: one by which it is worshipped in itself as an object, which is by an inferior adoration, the other by which the exemplar is worshipped in the image: just as an ambassador is worshipped either in his own person, or the King in the ambassador: nor finally according to Vasquez, who denies that an image is to be worshipped in itself, even though external signs of honor, such as genuflection and kissing, can be performed before it: indeed he contends that an inanimate or irrational thing is not capable in itself of honor, worship, and adoration, and that he who shows a sign of submission to an image out of a true affection of servitude, commits in itself a crime and superstition, and is an idolater or εἰκονόδουλον: that the reason is one thing in an ambassador as in a living image, and another in an inanimate thing, into which no dignity is derived from the exemplar, and therefore no adoration can be deferred to it. He feigns, however, nonetheless, that the image of God and of Christ is worshipped with latria, which is truly and properly latria, not by reason of any dignity which may be in the image itself, but because the image together with the prototype constitutes one object of adoration, or an integral and proximate term of adoration, so that images are not worshipped except with the exemplar and out of affection toward it: and thus he teaches that the image of Christ is worshipped with latria, not in itself, but accidentally, insofar as one speaks of images in themselves: finally he even proceeds to this, that any thing in the world is to be worshipped with divine adoration on account of a certain relation and conjunction with God. Thus they destroy themselves with mutual contradictions, and while they strive to cloak idolatry with the τερατολογίαις of distinctions, they only betray it the more. But Iconolatry remains, or the worshipping of an image with divine honor, which represents God, whether with respect to the prototype, or whether the prototype is worshipped by the image, or whether the image is worshipped with the prototype, as one object of adoration, with divine honor. What is more, Vasquez goes so far as to call false the opinion of Antisiodorensis, Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure, Marsilius Adrianus of Utrecht, and later the Roman Pontiff, that no one can be excused from the sin of idolatry, who, by apparitions in which he sees the form of a crucifix or another of Christ offered to him, absolutely gives divine honors, thinking, since the outward work of religion is directed by the intention of the mind, that he can be excused from the crime of idolatry who, in the form of a crucifix under which a demon may be lurking, adores God; and that nothing stands in the way of it being lawful to adore God in any thing in the world by its own nature: Whence Rivetus not undeservedly exclaims concerning the Papists: O holy nations, for whom these deities are born in gardens. Certainly the Jesuits, relying on this doctrine of theirs, can adore their vegetables and cabbages in their gardens with religious worship, nay, even a dunghill, and indeed every thing in which something can be conceived that is of God.

But were those disputes settled in the Tridentine Synod, or were the superstitions abolished? Certainly, such varied writings on that subject of images were in that conventicle, Petr. Suavis relates that the Fathers were not agreed as to what should be established concerning the worship of images: therefore, as B. Chemnitius observes, they proposed their opinion in ambiguous words; they say that due honor and veneration should be imparted to them; but they do not define what that due honor is; nor do they dare to establish religious adoration, and they deny that trust is to be FIXED in images: they say only that the honor which is exhibited to them is referred to the prototypes which they represent, so that through the images which we kiss and before which we uncover our heads and prostrate ourselves, we adore Christ: and they studiously approve the decrees of the second Nicene Synod; the Tridentines do not recount the gross superstitions, the worship of invocation and adoration of images, in their decree: but because they nevertheless wish them to be retained, they command such veneration as was defined in the seventh synod. What this truly is can easily be judged from a few flowers: such as the decree there: That sacred images are to be honored, venerated, saluted, embraced, kissed, worshipped, and adored: that Leontius's saying is praised: When I have an image of Christ, I seem to hold and adore Christ himself through it, and Manzoni's prayer to the image of Christ: Lord, who givest grace to the saints, look upon me; that a disease was repelled by an image being placed on the painful spot: likewise that a certain John said: If anyone looking at and adoring an image of Christ should say: This is Christ, he does not sin: Which and many other things brought forward by B. Chemnitius are truly idolatrous. When the Archbishop of Mainz understood this well, he decreed in the Provincial Synod to the contrary in the year 1549, Can. 41, 42, in Binius, Vol. 4, p. 2, fol. 258, that images in temples are to be tolerated not for adoration, but for memory. Similarly, the Roman Catholics (for so they were called among us at that meeting) involved their opinion in general terms in the recent Colloquy of Thorn in the year 1645, that the sacred images of God and the saints, because of the spiritual connection (which they have to God and the saints) and the excellence participated in from thence, are usefully and piously in the honor and veneration of the faithful. But because they constituted the Council of Trent, which approved the Pseudo-Synod of Nicaea in this cause, as the principle of the liquidation, as they called it, of Catholic doctrine, they are to be held equal to it in the matter of idolatry, provided they have not declared themselves better. Bellarminus, indeed, the hyperaspist of that same Council, seems to have declared himself more conveniently in this, that he does not attribute to the image the same honor which he attributes to the exemplar, lib. 2 de imag. cap. 20, but he understands that worship which is due to images by itself and properly, not as they act as a substitute for the exemplar: and he makes that worship indeed imperfect, but he judges that it pertains analogically and reductively to the species of that which is due to the exemplar: but he wishes the image to be worshipped by accident with the same kind of worship with which the exemplar itself is worshipped, namely when we consider the exemplar as it objectively shines in the image, and we venerate it thus represented and as it were clothed by the image, just as he who adores a King clothed, adores at the same time the King and his clothes: But what is that excellence of clothing to which worship is exhibited by the intention and submission of the mind, or of the image (which he very ineptly calls the clothing of God) so that religious worship is deferred to the same? If an image is not more properly adored, as it acts as a substitute for the prototype, than the clothing with which a King is dressed, no one, unless he carries his brain in his heel, will admit that an image is properly adored. For is the King's shoe properly worshipped with the worship that is deferred to the King? Concerning the Pope's shoe, when they kiss it, the Pope's flatterers may perhaps have said that, although the Pope himself, if he is wise, would not bear it with an even mind, that no other kind of honor is deferred to him than to his shoe, and that his shoe is properly worshipped with him with the same kind of honor, with this only difference, that that honor is due to the Pope by itself, but to his shoe only by accident, yet not improperly, but properly exhibited. If with others, such as Guilhelm. Estius, Alphons. a Castro, etc. you except that images are not adored in themselves, but all their veneration is referred to the prototypes, Bellarminus contradicts, since some worship is due even to the image itself, and therefore the same worship which is Christ's is to be deferred to the image of Christ reductively, the Thomists and the theologians commonly (the Pontificians) contradict, whose constant opinion, according to Azorius lib. 9. Inst. cap. 6. artic. 3. is this, that the image is honored with the same worship with which that of which it is an image is honored, which he wishes to be also the mind of the Council of Trent: nor will the idolatry be excused; for even he who adores God in images is pronounced an idolater here. And all iconolaters could have excused their idolatry by that reasoning, just as the moscholaters in Exod. 32. verse 4, because they did not worship the calf, but God in the calf. The Israelites, because they venerated the God of Israel through Baal, Hos. 2. verses 16, 17, etc. Add that to images, as practice testifies, divine and religious honor is deferred in the Papacy: because they honor them by dedicating them, by imposing the name of the prototype, by expecting the bestowal of all benefits from them, by adorning them with garlands and crowns, by appointing priests for them, by kissing, by supplicating, by addressing, by lighting candles, by sacrificing, etc. Bellarmine himself wishes that honor, which is owed to them in themselves and properly, to be analogically the same as that which is owed to the prototype: which, however, must be religious and worship of the first table: for it is not civil, nor worship pertaining to the second Table. But that there are degrees in religious worship, one being perfect, another imperfect and analogical, is repugnant to sound Theology. As the essence, so also the divine and religious glory is ἀμέριςος: and there is only one religious adoration, proper to GOD alone, ἀκοινώνητος to others outside of God, who does not wish to give his glory to another, Isa. 42. verse 6, and forbids by this precept the deferring of adoration to images. Whence the Walenburg brothers, since they understand that all religious adoration of images is prohibited here, seek other escapes, namely that it is forbidden to worship images for their own sake, as if they themselves were alive, or those that represent a falsehood, not to adore in the image him who truly is, because GOD himself wished to be honored in the ark, book 12 de unit. Eccles. cap. 37. num. 11. But such a distinction or limitation is not found in the text and so he inveighs precariously and rashly. Nor were the Israelites so foolish that they worshipped the image of the calf, which Aaron had formed, for its own sake, or as if it were alive, or even so profane that they worshipped in the calf another than the GOD of Abraham, who had led them out of Egypt; yet this was true idolatry the ark, even if invocation took place near the ark; which, however, was not directed to the ark itself, neither by itself, nor by accident. And so the Walenburgs find a new κρησφύγετον by corrupting the sacred text thus: You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of THEM (namely, the false gods, of whom he had spoken before) which (namely, the false Deity) is in heaven above, and which is in the earth beneath, nor of those which are in the waters: so that, namely, only the images of false gods are prohibited, because heathendom worshipped three species of false gods: in the heavens the sun, Jupiter, etc.; on earth plants, various animals; in the waters Neptune and others. But this is foolish. Those good brothers did not examine the Hebrew text, perhaps they could not even examine it. For in it that pronoun OF THEM is not contained. Therefore it cannot be referred to the false gods, who precede. Nor does the pronoun אשׁר look to a false Deity, but to those things which are subsequently added, which are in the heavens, in the earth, etc. Finally, not only the likeness of false gods is prohibited, but of all those things which are in heaven, in the earth, and in the waters. Is not GOD in heaven, are not angels and saints in heaven? Whose images, at any rate, when they are prepared for worship, are prohibited. That not only the images of false gods, but whatever simulacra are prohibited here, Salmero on Rom. 3, Vasquez lib. 2 de adorat. Disputat. 4. C. L. with Origen of Alexandria, Paludanus, and others establish: and Jacob Tirinus acknowledges on this passage that this law pertains to images of either the true GOD or of creatures when they are worshipped, and there is a danger of idolatry.

Gregorius de Valentia tries to escape idolatry in this way in Tome 3, Disputation 6, Question 2, that idolatry is a cult by which divine honor is attributed to some creature, just as to GOD; but there is no need for that assumption; for were those not idolaters who attributed divine honor, for example, of sacrifice, to someone other than the true GOD, even if they did not hold him for the GOD Creator of heaven and earth? Therefore the Valentian acts just as if someone were to define adultery as intercourse with another who is not a spouse, as if with a spouse: as if she is not an adulteress who has intercourse with another, while they do not hold him for a spouse, but only for that, who prostitutes herself to another as if to a spouse. For idolatry is spiritual fornication.

Verse of the same. NEITHER ANY LIKENESS WHICH IS IN HEAVEN ABOVE, AND WHICH IS IN THE EARTH BENEATH, NOR OF THOSE WHICH ARE IN THE WATERS UNDER THE EARTH.) The Greek Interpreters and Philo seem to have accepted this as if the pictures of animals were also forbidden. But the Chaldean and the Jews take the Vav, which is in the text, ἐξηγητικῶς, namely so that the sense is that eminent images are forbidden, those which have the form of animals, under which the Hebrews also include the stars. Waters are said to be under the earth, because GOD excavated the earth, so that waters might be contained there. Psalm 104, verse 6, and the Hebrews there. See our annotations to book 1 for the Truth of the Christian Religion around the beginning.

reptiles were made? Are not all idols, whether painted or sculpted, prohibited? But why does he disapprove of the opinion of the Alexandrian or Greek Interpreters of the Hebrews and the Vulgate (for this one agrees), why does he disapprove of the opinion of Philo, in the book on the Embassy, μὴ ἄγαλμα, μὴ ξόανον, μὴ γραφὴν, not an effigy, not a simulacrum, not a painting. That Philo in the book on the Giants says that statuary and painting were excluded by Moses from the Republic is not to be approved at all. Just as a graven image, so also an image is not prohibited, unless it is set up for idolatrous worship. But let Grotius, who fosters this with the modern Hebrews and Greeks, explain to us the mystery of his distinction. That was done in the explanation of the Decalogue. To take it ἐξηγητικῶς as the Hebrews do, so that it is understood that not all graven images are prohibited, like the golden vine which was in the temple, but those which bore the likeness of some animal. But why would animal-bearing graven images be prohibited, and these indeed alone? Are there animals in Heaven? (stars by Grotius Expl. Dec. p. 33. are included under the name of living creatures, because they have their own motion, who will not laugh?) Or are there no other figures and names imposed on the stars than those of living creatures? Are only living creatures on earth forbidden to be worshipped and represented for worship? Thus would it have been permitted to exhibit the Sun and Moon and inanimate things, without violation of this precept? That the first men raised monuments, a tree, a log, a stone to those whom they held as Gods, that they believed by a magical rite that an ethereal Spirit was drawn into those images by the polytheists, and that this opinion had already prevailed among the peoples of the East, that does not prove that GOD by this edict of his inhibited either all things or only those sculpted things having the form of some animal: εἰδωλολατρεία, which GOD prohibited entirely, could have been much broader, whether it was in use then, or was to be in the future, or can be. Therefore, he is to be judged to have prohibited not only graven images, but any images whatsoever for the sake of worship.

But that Grotius thinks that not only the veneration of graven images was prohibited to the Hebrews, but their entire manufacture, Expl. Dec. p. 32, in that he himself falls into the error of Philo, as if Moses proscribed the art of statuary from the Republic, and how do those agree with the forms of the Cherubim, which are judged to have exhibited living creatures, with the forms of oxen in the molten sea and others, which GOD willed to be made just as much as the golden vine? This is what Tertullian observed, Lib. 2 against Marc. chap. 22. The golden Cherubim and Seraphim, in the figured example of the ark, certainly a simple ornament, accommodated to the platform, having causes far different from the condition of idolatry, FOR WHICH a likeness is prohibited, do not seem to conflict with the law of the likeness of prohibited things, the state of likeness not being found in that, FOR WHICH the likeness is prohibited. Indeed, those which were set up for worship are ordered to be abolished, Exod. 34, verse 13, Numer. 33, verse 52. Deuteronomy 7, verse 5. But if the intention of worship or the danger was absent, images, whether sculpted or painted, were not prohibited. Grotius raves along with the Jews themselves when he says that it was forbidden for the Jews to have sculpted or prominent images of living creatures not only in the temple, but in any other place whatsoever. Was not the prominent image of Caesar on the coin, which neither the Jews abhorred, nor Christ himself in Matthew 22? Such are the ravings of a man, because God, contrary to this law, as the founder of the law, by his own right, ordered Cherubim, winged figures with human faces, to be placed in the very inner sanctuary of the temple, and a bronze serpent to be erected. God does not contradict himself: nor if that Zealot had so gravely prohibited all sculpture, and every cast image, or as Grotius speaks, every prominent image, would the author himself have been in placing the Cherubim in the temple, and in erecting the bronze Serpent. It is a double point that he adds concerning Solomon's bronze basin with the addition of oxen and lions, that it was done either at GOD's command (to wit, against the law, as an exception is made to a rule) or, if it did not have GOD's permission, that it was a beginning and a certain step toward other things in which he sinned afterward, which latter opinion he says pleases the Hebrews more. Thus it pleases him to lick the spit of every Hebrew. That was not against the law of GOD, much less the beginning of idolatry: nay, all those things which Solomon does, he received from David his parent, who testifies that he received the pattern of them all from the hand of the Lord 1 Paral. 29. verse 19. Grotius thinks that these things concerning graven images were forbidden from the same class, which by their nature are not illicit, as are most things in the law of Moses: But he is greatly mistaken here: because this precept is of the moral law; nay, the highest and first precept of the first table, by which idolatry is prohibited. And therefore images of every kind, whether carved or cast, whether incised or painted, whether of living creatures or of animate things, whether they be in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters, in so far as they are set forth for worship, and are made for that cause, are forbidden here. Nor can a distinction be feigned here, or by any probable reason be made, between paintings and incised forms of living creatures and graven images. Which Grotius could have learned from Clement of Alexandria V. Strom., where he says that Moses openly said that one ought not to make any graven or cast, or fashioned or painted image or likeness, so that we might not attend to sensible things. Grotius acknowledges that not all paintings are forbidden, on account of the standards of the Hebrews displaying a man, an ox, a lion, an eagle. Yet he acknowledges all those are forbidden which idolaters used for their worship Levit. 26. verse 1. Numer. 33. verse 52. Which he also says concerning incised figures. But in this case there is no different reason for graven images, nor can one be given. But as for his denying that this concerns paintings or incised forms of living creatures, he denies it against the text. Which prohibits every image, every likeness made for the sake of worship. For the added words teach that it is forbidden in that respect: Thou shalt not adore them. Therefore images are not prohibited otherwise than in so far as they are adored. What the Christian Church held against the Iconoclasts: that it admits not only painted images, but also those standing in the Church, Grotius confesses; who therefore also makes this law concerning graven images and images merely positive, and perverts it in the said manner, lest the same superstitious and idolatrous worship of images be convicted in the Papacy. If Christians were not bound by other laws of the Hebrews that are in position, neither were they by this one, and it is in vain that it is opposed to the Pontificians. Thus, wherever he believed the occasion allowed, Hugo, playing the Pope, wished to succor the Pontificians, although for the most part by doing otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NON FACIES TIBI SCULPTILE.) Imagi- nem eminentem.

Præceptum hic secundum constituunt Calvinus lib. II. inst. cap. 8. §. 13. Catech. Heidelb. quæst. 93. & Ursin. in explic. aliiqve Reformati, atque in eam sententiam adducunt Orig. lib. III. harm. 8. in Ex. Naz. in carm. Hieron. & Ambrof. in Comment. ad Ephes. VI. Chrysost. hom. 49. in Matth. Quanquam vero nonnulli ex Reformatis nolint contentiose de eo litigare, utpote Calvinus, Ursinus, Musculus, tamen adeo inhærent plerique illi sententiæ, ut nostrates nefariæ mutilationis, & sacrilegii etiam arguant, quod interdictum de sculptilibus sub pri- mo præcepto de non habendis Diis alienis compre- hensum velint, ideoque illud in Catechesi omittant: utpote Innocent. Gentillet. in Apol. pro Christ. c. II. cap. de Imag. Anhaldini in Apol. contra quosdam Nobil. fol. 28. Neo-Marpurg. in resp. Apol. fol. III. etiam Rivetus: qui sacrilegium itidem nobis & Pontificiis hic imputat, Expl. Dec. pag. 3. Etsi Ursi- num suum (præter rem omnino) adversus B. Ger- hard. tueatur, quasi illi tribuerit ὁ μακαρίτης, quod distinctionem illam primi & secundi præcepti ceu ne- cessariam venditarit, quam ipse potius de mutatio- ne verborum non odiose esse pugnandum censue- rit. At quamvis simplicioribus ejusmodi specia- lia de sculptilibus & imaginibus in Catechesi non proponantur, ideo tamen haud committitur sacri- legium. Usus B. Lutherus est συντομῇ̃. Et reci- tata præcepta sunt ab Apostolo nonnullis omissis Roman. 12, 9. num & illum arguent Calviniani? Addo quod in Bibliis integræ relinquantur verba, eademque in explicationibus Decalogi non præ- termittantur à nostris, solum in compendiosa re- citatione præceptorum rudioribus ea, quæ expli- cationis causa ob Judæos maxime addita sunt, non recitantur. Eorum vero commemorationem quo- ad omnia verba, dum ceu necessariam Ecclesiæ obtrudere satagunt Calviniani, non libertatem modo Christianam labefactant, sed id imprimis etiam agunt, ut εἰκονοκλασίαν suam statuminent, ac Lutheri Catechesin per cuniculos ex Ecclesia eliminent. Quanquam vero non habenda sit hæc lex cum quibusdam Jesuitis pro mere positiva, ad Judæos solum pertinente, neque cum B. Chemni- tio censeamus ceremoniale quid in hoc præcepto reperiri, nempe quod Judæis interdictum fuerit omni omnino imaginum usu, etiam extracultum, negari tamen saltim id non poterit, Judæos valde proclives fuisse ad DEUM sub imagine aliqua figurandum & in illa adorandum, quod

μοσχολατρεία & multa alia docent, unde non tantum à Prophetis ab ea idololatria revocaban- tur frequenter, sed hic etiam in ipsa legis mora- lis promulgatione Deus peculiariter hanc ipsis interdictam voluit. Hactenus ergo Judæorum imprimis ceu Φιλειδώλων causa ea inserta esse exi- stimamus. Cæterum ex verbis ipsis Decalogi manifestum est, addi hæc, non ut prohibean- tur simpliciter imagines ipsius Numinis, sed ut imagines, quæ religiosi cultus gratia fiunt, ve- tentur; Nam ideo additur, non adorabis ea, ne- que coles: quæ verba limitationem præcedenti- um continent. Quod imprimis è Deuter. 4, 16. confirmatur. Nam ibi prohibentur etiam homi- nis, volucris, piscis, imagines: quæ certe non ni- si ratione vitiosi finis cultus idololatrici prohibi- tæ: ac vetitum etiam est, attollere oculos in cælum, ad solem, Lunam, & alias stellas, quod utique non simpliciter intelligendum, sed quemadmo- dum addita declaratio habet, ne impulsus adores ea & colas. Quomodo ergo prohibitum est ocu- los attollere & aspicere Solem & Lunam, eo eti- am pacto prohibitum est imagines facere. At id non nisi ratione finis illius vitiosi prohibitum. Adde etiam Levit. XXVI, 1. 2. ubi eadem ratione etiam prohibetur erectio statuæ, quod aliter intel- ligi nequit, nisi de idololatrica statuæ erectione, alias enim id non erat illicitum Genes. XXVIII, 18. cap. XXXI, 45. cap. XXXV, 14. Jos. XXIV, 20. 1. Sa- muel. VII, 12.

Porro additur hoc interdictum ceu speciale & tanquam appendix ad generalem idololatriæ pro- hibitionem, ideoque ex ejus mente explican- dum est, & quum illud vetet, ne dii alieni ha- beantur, hoc itidem in eam sententiam accipi- endum, ne imagines ut dii colantur, aut cultus religiosi causa fiant: Notanda enim oppositio Dei veri & Deorum alienorum: unde constat ea ratione prohiberi, qua sunt Dii alieni, non au- tem simpliciter easdem prohibitas esse. Cujus argumenti vim admittit Rivetus explicat. Decal. pag. 40. ita enim ipse concludit: Nam quum præ- ceptum illud sequatur prohibitionem alienorum Deo- rum, qua comprehenditur omnis idololatria in ge- nere, quæ committitur, quoties creaturæ aliquid tribuitur, quod ad DEUM pertinet, sive cogita- tione, sive verbis, sive gestibus, & factis, ut an- tea ostendimus, hic DEus prohibere voluit eam ido- lolatriæ speciem, qua in figura aliqua aut effigie corporea profitebantur Idololatræ, se numen aliquod colere. Recte ergo distinguitur inter imagines, & idola, inter εἰκονοποιΐαν & εἰδωλοποιΐαν. Ima- gines enim facere nuspiam prohibitum est; fa- cere autem imaginem ad Idololatriam & cultum religiosum hîc & alibi passim prohiberi indubium est. Ridet Ursinus distinctionem, quia εἴδωλον nihil aliud sit quam imago; sed etsi hoc verum sit, si etymon spectes, usu tamen Scripturæ, & Ecclesiæ nullum est idolum, nisi quod ad cul- tum prostat, sive in corde erigatur idolum, si- ve alias constituatur. Distinguendæ ergo im- primis sunt imagines sacræ, quæ res sacras exhi- bent, & idololatricæ, quæ idola vel DEOS fi- ctitios repræsentant, vel quorum repræsentatio idololatrica est, ut cum in Papatu Mariam instar DEI exhibent, & repræsentant. Has prohibi- tas esse agnoscimus. Quod vero ad illas atti- net, quæ sacræ quidem sunt, sed nec repræsen- tatione sua scandalum pariunt, nec ad cultum prostant, eæ nec vetitæ sunt & usum suum non ordinandi solum, sed & docendi, commonefaciendi, testificandi habere possunt. Quod enim legenti- bus Scriptura, hoc idiotis cernentibus pictura præ- stat, dicente Gregor. M. lib. IX. Epist. 9. Si autem de imaginibus quæratur, Numen ipsum repræ- sentantibus, uti certum est DEUM κατ᾿ ὀυsίαν nulla imagine aut similitudine exprimi posse, aut debere, quod proinde lege divina interdictum esse, nemo diffitetur, ita si, quomodo κατ᾿ ὀικο- νομίαν, ὀπτασίαν, vel ἐπιφάνειαν sese exhibue- rit DEUS, pictura aut sculptura adumbretur, non id mandato DEI contrarium censeri poterit: quia nihil aliud tum exhibetur, quam historia illius apparitionis, vel manifestationis, qua DE- US ipse se patefacere dignatus est; de qua si animi conceptu ideam, & imaginem formare licet (si- ne qua utique ea ne legi quidem ac considerari potest) nemo sanus inficiabitur, pictura aut scul- pturæ imagine eandem pariter oculis sisti citra prævaricationem posse; utpote cum verb. grat. exhibetur apparitio Dan. VII, 24. aut Matth. III, 16. vel in Apocalypsi Johannea facta, & similes, quæ in Scriptura descriptæ sunt: quas proinde pi- cturas & imagines in templis quoque sisti posse hi- storiæ, memoriæ & doctrinæ causa, dubitandum non est. Nam neque in hoc præcepto nec alibi prohibetur repræsentatio, sed cultus, & adoratio, nec ea ratione repræsentatur DEUS per se, sed id, quo aliquando manifestari voluit DEUS. Ideo probamus illud Gregorii lib. IX. Epist. I. Si quis imagines facere voluerit, minime prohibe: adora- re vero imagines omnibus modis devita. Quod pro- fessus etiam est Rivetus, cum disquisivit in expli- cat. Decalog. pag. 40. quænam imagines hoc præ- cepto prohibeantur, Vasquezii sententiam ap- probans, prohibitionis hujus sensum esse, non so- lum non licere colere imaginem pro DEO, sed eti- am verum DEUM in aliqua ejus similitudine ado- rare: ubi inter alia etiam ita habet: Concedi- mus verbis legis non absolute prohiberi omnem εἰκο- νοποιΐαν, sed eam tantum, quæ ad cultum & re- ligionem refertur. Atque id recte adversus Pon- tificios alios urgetur, utpote tam veteres scho- lasticos, quam recentiores, qui hoc solum pro- hibitum fuisse dixerunt, ne imagines more gen- tilium tanquam dii adorentur, non autem quem- libet cultum & adorationem imaginum prohibitam esse: Quia DEUS simpliciter prohibuit adorare imagines, non solum adorare eas more gentilium. Ideo merito agnoscit Vasquez Disputat. CIV. cap. etiam interdictum esse DEUM in imagine adora- re. Quod vero ceremoniale tantum ac positi- vum fuisse, & ad Judæos solum spectasse falso ad- serit Vasquez. Nam in Novo etiam Testamen- to in imaginibus DEUM adorare vetamur Actor. XVII, 29. nec est quicquam, quod cogat hanc Decalogi partem ad Judæos solum restringe- re, in quo Veteres omnia præter Sabbati de- terminationem moralia esse agnoscunt, Iren. lib. IV. cap. 31. Augustin. lib. XIX. contra Faust. cap. 18. & Epist. CXIX. cap. 12. Non tamen cum Calvinia- nis statuendum, præceptum de non fingendis vel sculpendis imaginibus numinis naturale esse, quod Rivetus contendit; nam aliud est imaginem finge- re numinis, aliud in imagine adorare numen: quum pingi possit DEUS aliqua imagine, qua se ex- hibuit ipse, tametsi non adoretur imago, aut DEUS in imagine. Nec enim diffiteri potuit Rivetus, apparuisse DEUM Dan. VII. Apocal. V. in specie humana, licet id non tam ad signifi- candam DEI Patris personam ipsam, quam ejus operationem referat, quod etiam de apparitio-

ne Spirit. Sanct. in specie columbæ At etiam non ipsa persona, sed effectus illa imagine solum notarentur, liquet tamen imagi- nes illas licite pingi posse, cum nempe historia illa apparitionis adumbratur, vel exhibetur: Un- de fatetur Rivetus licitas esse imagines, quæ ex- tra templa, citra periculum idololatriæ, supersti- tionis & scandali, ad usum historicum, aut Sym- bolicum, vel ad ornatum honestum effinguntur. Queritur etiam, quod ita nonnulli cum Refor- matis agant, ac si res sibi cum Judæis aut Ma- humetanis esset, qui nullas prorsus rerum viven- tium imagines admittunt. Interea exagitat ipse nostros ob imagines de S. Trinitate, cum DEus Pater in figura senis, Spiritus S. in forma colum- bæ, Filius DEI in forma corporis, quod assumsit, pingitur, & adversus nos non minus quam Pon- tificios urget verba in Ethnicorum idololatriam di- cta Roman. 1, 23. mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis DEI in efformatam imaginem mortalis hominis, quod gloriam, & majestatem divinam per imagi- nem hominis senis effingere conentur; sed calumniæ hæ sunt, quas adversus conscientiam effudit. Noverat enim probe, nos nec essentiam DEI cum gentibus ita efformare, nec majestatem & gloriam divinam, sed solum repræsentare ap- paritionem, qua DEUS sese ipsum exhibuit. Hanc vero cum animo concipiunt suo Reforma- ti, num etiam gloriam incorruptibilis DEI in imaginem hominis mortalis commutant? Le- gere certe & concipere historiam manifestatio- nis DEI in forma antiqui dierum non possunt, quin imaginem concipiant hominis senis; quid enim aliud species intelligibiles sunt, quam in- ternæ rerum imagines? Nec est, quod dicat, culpari id non posse, quia necessitas hæc naturalis imposita nobis, ut per species & imagines intellige- mus: Picturas autem prohibitas esse. Nam si tali concepta imagine, quam necessariam dicit, non mutatur gloria DEI in imaginem hominis, utique nec picta vel sculpta ejusmodi imagine id fiet, si absit idololatria, ac opinio expressæ ipsi- us essentiæ divinæ. Prohibitas autem esse lege divina tales imagines mera est petitio principii, quæ ἑαυτομαχίαν Riveti hic nobis tantum pro- bat: quia concessit ipse ad usum symbolicum, si peccatum idololatriæ, superstitionis, & scandali ab- sit, licitas esse imagines: quidni ergo licitæ illæ imagines, quæ in Scripturis exhibitæ sunt, eti- am de ipse DEO? Quod autem dicit aliud esse, si visiones illæ seorsim & quatenus nobis leguntur aut recitantur per aliquas species intelligibiles in- terius nobis efformentur, aliud si conjunctim ho- minis manu sculpantur, & Trinitatis nomine do- nentur, nullius est momenti. Nam si simul & antiqui dierum è Dan. VII. & Spiritus Sanct. in spe- cie columbæ visi, & Christi θεανθρώπως mentio fiat ex Sacra Scriptura, annon simul animo illas imagines sistere oportet? Quæ ergo simul sine peccato animo concipiuntur imagines, quidni simul citra peccatum in tabula depictæ exhibe- antur? Sed nimius adversus imagines innocen- tes, ac mnemoneuticas fervor adeo occupasse videtur Rivetum, ut quum de ipsomet Christo quatenus homo factus est, an pingi potuerit, con- troversiam se non movere velle dixerit, mox ta- men à ritu Papistico, quo idola gentium imitan- tur, illud non longe abesse pronunciarit, quod no- strates Electorem Saxoniæ & Lutherum pingunt unum à dextro, alterum à sinistro latere, pro- cumbentes coram imagine crucifixi. Sic ne cru- cifixi imaginem quidem ferre , aut adorationem crucifixi adumbratam ἀνεπίληπτον habere pof- funt Reformati : Imo cum Beza suo imaginem cru- cifixi ex animo se detestari innuunt , quæ omnino menti fidelium fortiter imprimi debet. Quid autem causæ , quod Christi crucifixi imaginem in nummis & vafis aureis , atque argenteis ferre pof- fint , in templis autem ferre renuant Reformati , & reformatores templorum intempestivi ? aut num auri sacra fame forte abstrahuntur à Zelo adversus imagines in nummis , quo effervescunt adversus imagines in templis ? Et unde proba- bunt , licitas easdem esse extra templa , non item in templis , ut extra cultum in iis collocen- tur. Causam adfert Rivetus hanc, quod lex de ima- ginibus , quum ad religionem spectet , ad eam etiam restringenda sit : Prætexit etiam scandalum & alie- nationem Judæorum & Mahometanorum , ac ma- ximum periculum , imo perniciem simpliciorum , quod nempe multi ad superstitionem trahantur , idololatræ vero in pertinacia sua confirmentur. At num religio tantum in templo viget? annon eti- am ejusdem extra templum habenda ratio ? Si religiosas imagines prohibet lex , id est , religio- nis causa erectas , quod ait Rivetus , quomodo religiosas dicit eas, quas toleramus extra cultum? Religiosæ , inquit , sunt , cum visuntur in templo , modo adorationi accommodato , vel in privato ora- torio , & homines intenti sunt in eas cum precan- tur. Sed modus ille adorationi accommodatus affixus ipsis non est à loco , templo puta aut pri- vato oratorio , nec modus ejusmodi materialis , aut sensibilis designari potest , aut penes nos lo- cum habet. Quod in Papatu censeantur accom- modatæ ad adorationem imaginum , facit erronea opinio , & persuasio, non in tabulis vel parieti- bus , sed in cordibus ipsorum superstitioni de- ditis hærens ; à quibus, & nominatim Jesuita Vas- quezio hanc restrictionem modi ad adorationem accommodati hausit Rivetus; qua cum superstitio- ne nihil nobis est commercii : qui nec adoratio- nem DEI in imaginibus , aut intentionem directam ad imagines , nec modum adorationi accommoda- tum admittimus , cum imaginibus ornatus , me- moriæ , symboli vel etiam affectus ciendi causa lo- cum relinquimus. Scandalum cum apud infide- les , & idololatras tum penes infirmos est scan- dalum acceptum non datum , & per accidens oritur ab imaginibus , modo illæ non sint scandalose adornatæ. Evertenda ergo de consilio B. Luthe- ri est idololatria & falsa opinio è mentibus , ac recte informandus de imaginibus populus , & nullum supererit periculum , quod consilium B. Luther. uti laudavit Rivetus ipse , ita processum Carolstadii sui , quo tumultuose statuas è tem- plis ejecit , à Luthero merito damnatum esse, agnoscere coactus fuit , ( quæ vis veritatis ) de cætero de abolendis imaginibus , quæ ea forma aut specie pictæ vel sculptæ sunt , ut oculis honestis conspici non possint , sed imprimis quarum aspe- ctus ipse ad idololatriam provocat , nos non dif- sentire è colloquio Montispurgensi observans , modo abolitio illarum non privato consilio , sed au- toritate piorum Magistratuum fiat. Addimus , opus esse , ut fiat ordinate citra tumultum , ac scandalum , salva fidei doctrina , illasa libertate Christiana.

Si autem abrogationem omnium imaginum sacra- rum è templis , ceu necessariam , vi præcepti , ad- huc urgeant Reformati , doceant quibus verbis imagines sacræ in templo prohibitæ sint , extra cultus rationem? aut ubi Christus, vel Apostoli in Nov. Testam. easdem reprobarint, atque e templis aboleri praeceperint? Hic certe non imaginum pi- ctura, sed cultus prohibetur: nec in templo solum, sed simpliciter, citra loci mentionem praecipitur, ne fiant imagines eo fine ut adorentur. In prioribus quidem seculis non in usu fuerunt imagines in cul- tu Dei: sed quum gentiles in simulacris numina co- lerent, abstinebant Christiani a simulacris, ne cum paganis similitudinem habere viderentur, unde etiam Veteres imaginibus iniquiores fuere, quod qui ex gentibus converterentur, verum Deum in ima- ginibus colere vellent, simulacris assueti, ut observat B. Chemnitius p. 4. Exam. Concil. Trid. de imag. p. 26. nec receptae imagines in templa usque ad Con- stantinum, ac ne Christi quidem: non rejectum ta- men propterea historicum usum in primitiva Eccle- sia B. Chemnit. ostendit p. 28. Sed destructis idolis gentium, & pace Ecclesiis sub Constantino red- dita, & postea frequentior coepit inter Christianos usus esse historicarum imaginum, & cum Panegy- ricae solennitates de martyrum passionibus fre- quentatae & templa splendidius exornari coepere, in iisdem etiam receptae imagines sunt, utpote cir- ca annum 380. unde Gregorius Nyssenus earum me- minit, & apud Latinos Paulinus & Prudentius: Cy- rillus vero cum Julianus Christianis objiceret, quod imaginem crucis adorarent lib. 6. adseruit ima- ginum usum historicum praeclare, quod etiam a Gregor. M. factum, quem porro 6. Synodus univer- salis circa annum 680. confirmavit. Cum autem adorari imagines penes Latinos coepissent, Graeci de- molitione imaginum adorationem earum adorti sunt. Unde horribilia & cruenta certamina exorta: de quibus l. c. B. Chemn. Ideo in antiqua Ecclesia usus imaginum Christi passionis, & crucis Dominicae ac similium prohibitus non fuit: donec Iconoclastae duce Leone Isaurico Anno Christi 725. imagines co- li ceptas tolli jussere, ne Saraceni haberent, unde Christianis dicam scriberent, sequutus deinde Fi- lius Constantinus Copronymus An. 753. in Constan- tinopol. Synodo imagines fieri prohibuit. Qua- rum causa tumultum superiori seculo, anno nempe Christi 1522. cum B. Luther. in Pathmo ageret, hic Wittebergae commota plebe Carlstadius, homo fe- rus, in quo nulla significatio Spiritus, sed manifesta impietatis signa fuerunt, teste Philippo Epist. ad My- con. excitavit, ausu privato & temerario statuas e templo ejiciens, ut Hieronym. Schurff. Tom. II. Jen. Germ. Luther. fol. 24. Joh. Schleid. l. 3. Comment. hist. perhibuere. Cujus discipuli, & sectatores, Reformatores non modo templorum & Sacramen- torum, sed etiam doctrinae purioris, Zwingliano- Calvinistas indigitamus, etiamnum aequo animo sacras imagines in templis haud sustinent, eadem- que Synagogis Judaicis & Saracenicis fanis gemina potius habere cupiunt, nobis praeter meritum pe- tulanter exprobrantes, quod templa nostra, si ima- ginibus memorialibus, & Symbolicis citra supersti- tionem & idololatriam exornentur, templus idolola- trarum similia sint.

Neque juvat eos Canon 36. Concilii Illiberitani: Placuit picturas in Ecclesiis esse non debere, ne quod colitur & adoratur, in parietibus depingatur. Ma- nifestum enim est ibi non prohiberi omnes imagi- nes, sed eas, quae cultus & adorationis causa pro- stant, ne quod in parietibus depictum est, colatur. Quod non discrepat a Greg. M. sententia l. 9. Ep. 1. Si quis imagines facere voluerit, minime prohibe, adorare vero imagines omnibus modis devita. Ideo in Can. 60. ejusdem Concilii definitur: Si quis ido- la fregerit, & ibidem fuerit occisus, quia in Evange- lio non est scriptum, neque invenitur ab Apostolis un- quam factum, placuit in numerum eum non recipi martyrum. Fatentur ergo Patres illi, non esse in Nov. Testam. scriptum imagines etsi ad idololatriam prostititerint, abolendas esse, neque ab Apostolis id fa- ctum esse, quia scilicet idololatria cessare potest, ma- nentibus imaginibus. Idolum enim nil est in mundo, teste Apostolo. Abrogandus ergo cultus idolola- tricus, nec nocere possunt imagines, quæ olim ad cultum prostituere. Si tamen scandalum tolli non possit, nisi illæ etiam tollantur, autoritate publica easdem recte tolli, non diffitemur. Multum er- go differunt imagines & idola, etiam cum materia- liter non differunt. Boves fusiles in templo Salo- monis non displicuerunt Domino, displicuerunt vituli in Dan & Bethel. Serpentem æneum, cum ad cultum non prostaret, tolerabat, quem aspectus causa fieri ipse jusserat; at cum ei suffitum facerent, merito Ezechias tollebat, non tolerabat. 2. Reg. 18, 4. Cherubinos ad aram fœderis locari jusserat DE- US ipse, adorari neutiquam admisisset. Si simpli- citer prohibitæ fuissent imagines in templis, nec istæ, nec aliæ divinitus ordinatæ vel admissæ in ta- bernaculo, vel templo Salomonico fuissent. Ubi mirari oportet Rivetum, quod neget serpentem æne- um & Cherubinos imagines fuisse, quia typi fuerint hieroglyphici, Explic. Decalog. 51. quasi hæc op- posita sint ac typus nequeat esse imago. Vocat quidem auctor Sapientiæ cap. 14, 11. 12. Idola scan- dala, sed ἀφρόνων. Sapientibus ergo & recte infor- matis scandalo non sunt.

Crocius in consid. Triad. cap. 12. provocat im- primis ad locum Deut. 4, 15. quod prohibitionis ima- ginis Dei causa etiam extra casum cultus locum ha- beat, ideoque prohibitio illa absolute intelligenda sit. Causam autem geminam ponit 1. quia DEI nulla visa similitudo, 2. ne corrumpantur animæ. At lex illa agit de imagine Deum κατ’ οὐσίαν referente, ne Deum rerum creatarum imagine, mariti nempe vel fœminæ, vel jumenti vel Solis, vel Lunæ ex- primendo, similem esse credant, sed creatorem à creaturis, quas condidit, longissime distinctum esse, nec ulla rei creatæ imagine, quantum ad essen- tiam referri posse, sciant & agnoscant, nec in si- militudinibus ejusmodi Deum colant, ac revere- antur. Ideo nulla similitudine illic Deus visen- dum se præbuit populo Φιλειδώλῳ, ne tales simili- tudines adumbrantes Deo essentiam ejusmodi tri- buant, adeoque errore decipiantur, & corrumpan- tur animæ ipsorum. Sed imagines Dei symbolicas operationes vel ὑπόστασιας Dei, non essentiam ejus exprimentes, simpliciter prohibitas esse etiam ex- tra rationem cultus ex eo loco non apparet: neque quæ populo in idololatriam proclivi tum esse po- terant errorum tendiculæ Deuter. 12, 20. omnibus scandalo, & irritamento sunt, aut simpliciter ideo prohibita censeri debent.

Instat adhuc Crocius ex Os. 2. v. 2. ita colligens: Quemadmodum marito non satis est si uxorem li- bidinibus & amoribus vagis ejiciat, eamque porro aversetur: ita Deo non satis est, si adulteria, id est, occultos amores è medio uberum, id est, è corde populi extirpet, nisi ab oculis quoque removeat scortationum irritamenta. Quis vir bonus, inquit Rivetus l. c. p. 47. vellet uxorem suam alioqui castam habitu me- retricio incedere, aut in domo sua insignia lupanaris depingi. Quæ igitur Christiana prudentia eorum Evangelicorum, qui templa ita imaginibus replent, ut à templis idololatricis Papistarum non differant? Sed assumunt illi, imagines per se esse irritamenta idoloplatriæ: imagines in templis nostris esse orna- tum meretricium, esse insignia idololatrias Papisticæ, quod falsum, & calumniosum. Ea, quæ talia sunt, non admittimus, nec probamus: etsi imagines historicas, & symbolicas feramus. Potest homini natura lascivo conversatio cum formosa muliere irritamentum esse, quæ alii castitatis studioso irritamentum minime fit. Ornatus à meretrice aliquando lasciviæ causa adhibitus à virgine casta adhiberi & usurpari potest, citra lasciviam.

Quapropter inter idololatras & iconoclastas medium recte tenent Ecclesiæ nostræ: non adorantes quidem cum Papistis imagines, nec simpliciter è templis cum Calvinianis abolentes, sed easdem historiæ, memoriæ, vel ornatus causa, si superstitio absit, ferentes, & inter adiaphora, vel indifferentia usum earum collocantes.

Quod ergo ad imaginum cultum attinet, simpliciter prohiberi imaginum quarumvis cultum religiosum, è verbis legis manifestissimum est. Deus enim usum simulacrorum ad cultum, cum in illis Numen colitur, simpliciter numerat inter deos alienos: & ita prohibet, ut nullus elusioni aut exceptioni sit locus, ut recte observatum B. Chemn. Part. 4. Exam. Conc. Trid. de imag. p. 21. Primum enim numerat sculptile & fusile, statuam positam seu erectum lapidem ad imaginem aliquam formatum vel fabricatum. Et generali vocabulo Themunah, hoc est, similitudinem seu imaginem, exprimentem & repræsentantem qualicunque effigie speciem aliquam, quocunque modo, & ex quacunque materia pictam vel effectam. Deut. 4. vocat Samel, id est, figuram, effigiem, seu formam. Secundo res, quarum similitudinem seu imaginem ad cultum proponi aut usurpari vetat, ita enumerat, ut nullus exceptioni locus sit: dicit enim eorum, quæ vel in cœlis supra, vel in terra deorsum, vel quæ sub aquis, vel quæ sub terra sunt. Sunt autem in cœlo Deus, Angeli & Spiritus beatorum, sub terra sunt dæmones; Sunt etiam sub terra corpora mortuorum. Reliqua, quæ cœlo affixa, quæ in aëre, quæ in aquis, in terra sunt, per se patent. Prohibet igitur ad cultum facere, proponere, aut usurpare, non tantum imagines idolorum & dæmoniorum 1. Cor. 8. nec tantum irrationalium creaturarum, verum etiam Angelorum Spirituum justorum, qui in cœlis sunt, & hominum defunctorum, quorum corpora sub terra sunt, & ne ipsius quidem Dei imaginem ad cultum fieri, proponi & usurpari vult lex DEI: DEUS enim noster in cœlo est. Et lex prohibet ejus, quod in cœlo est, imaginem ad cultum fieri. Et Deuteron. 4. ratio additur, vocem verborum ejus audivistis, non autem vidistis simulacrum aliquod, quando de medio ignis nobis locutus est Dominus. Tertio duobus vocabulis prohibet omne genus cultuum religiosorum, cum inquit: Non adorabis nec coles ea, quorum altero, quod incurvationem significat, omnes externos gestus, & ritus cultuum: altero interiores affectiones & devotiones cultuum complectitur. Et cultus illos exteriores Liber Sapientiæ cap. 14. ac Prophetæ passim Es. 44. c. 46. Jer. 10. Ezech. 6. c. 14. Os. 11. & c. describunt incurvationibus, geniculationibus, provolutionibus corporis, manuum extensionibus, exosculationibus, sacrificiis, incenso, thure, libationibus, ornatu auri, purpuræ & c. circumgestationibus, invocationibus, supplicationibus, votis, desiderio, amore, devotione, spe, fiducia, metu & c. Quarto, ne quis hæc ita eludat, quasi tantum prohibeatur cultus, qui ipsi materiæ vel formæ simulacrorum exhibetur: ostendit Scriptura, etiam quando cultus illi imaginum ad prototypum, sive an res per imagines significatas sive ad Deum referuntur, tamen appellari cultum deorum alienorum. Quod demonstrat B. Chemnitius exemplis Scripturæ, utpote cum primum Thare

300. annis post diluvium sacrificasse dicitur Diis ali- enis Jos. 24. h. e. Ur Chaldæorum, cum in igne Deum coluere, non enim adeo ineptos fuisse Patres, ut exi- stimarent essentiam divinam esse elementum ignis: & postea Labani, Genes. 31. ut & Miche Jud. 17. ac Da- nitarum cap. 8. qui Teraphim, seu statuas ad imagi- nem formæ humanæ fabricatas venerati sunt, non quasi crederent, quasi essentia divina esset statua ex ligna formata, sed quod persuasi fuerint, Deum in tali simulacro recte coli: quod etiam in μοσχολα- τρείᾳ Israelitarum Exod. 32. apparet. Quapropter Deus tum prolixe ac luculenter prohibuit, ne fie- rent imagines aut statuæ ad cultum religionis, ne in illis vel creaturæ, vel ipse Deus coleretur, quod in- terdictum repetitur Levit. 26. Deuter. 5. c. 12.

Ineptus vero est Andradius, cum contendit, in Veteri quidem Testam. cum Christus nondum esset in- carnatus, non licuisse Deum invisibilem in imagine vi- sibili colere, nunc vero postquam Deus manifestatus est in carne, licite & recte Christum per imagines coli: nam lex de sculptilibus & imaginibus non colendis moralis est, & omnes obligat: ideo cum S. Johannes 1. Epist. 5, 20. dixisset, Filium Dei venisse, & dedisse no- bis mentem, ut cognoscamus verum Deum, addit, fili- oli cavete ab idolis vel simulacris, vocem εἴδωλον ad- hibens, qua Græci hic usi sunt. Et passim in N. T. idololatria gravissime prohibetur, ac damnatur. Rom. 1, 20. 1. Cor. 10, 7. Gal. 5, 21. Nec aliunde ortum habuit imaginum cultus, quam à paganis, quorum idololatria magnam partem in imaginum, simula- crorum & statuarum adoratione & cultu consiste- bat, ubi nempe ad politicum imaginum usum apud Ethnicos superstitiosus, & idololatricus cultus acce- debat. Etsi enim antiquitus nullæ gentes numina absque simulacris colerent, quemadmodum Persas statuas Diis suis erexisse Herodotus docet, & Roma- nos plusquam centum & septuaginta annos deos si- ne simulacro coluisse, ex Varrone observat August. l. 4. de Civ. Dei cap. 31. posteris tamen temporibus totam religionem & universum deorum cultum gentes ad simulacra alligarunt, de quo Clem. Alex. orat. ad gentes, Arnobius lib. 6. contra gentes, Eu- seb. lib. 3. de præpar. Evangel. Quomodo Hermes visibilia & contrectabilia ejusmodi simulacra corpora deorum, dixerit, quod Spiritus invisibiliter per artem quandam visibilibus rebus copulati crediderit, vide Aug. l. 8. de C. D. c. 23. Quæ sacrificiis, coronis, ce- reis, adorationibus, jejuniis, festis, aqua lustrali, cir- cumgestatione, coluere: perinde uti Judæi sua idola venerati sunt hodieque Pontificii statuas & imagines venerantur, adeo ut fateatur Lud. Vives non posse discrimen ostendi, nisi quod nomina tantum & titulos mutarint Pontificii. Vid. B. Chemn. loc. cit. pag. 17. B. Schröder. Apodixi de imaginib. ut & Polydor. Vergil. l. 6. de invent. rerum c. 13. L. 2. c. 23. l. 5. c. 3. & utebantur itidem hoc colore gentiles, quo suam idololatriam pingunt Papistæ, se honores istos non si- mulacris, sed diis, quorum speciem repræsentant, de- ferre, uti ex Arnob. & Lactant. docet Cassander in consut. ad art. 21. August. Conf. Animum ipsis fuisse vero Deo cultum exhibere per idola & imagines agno- scit Job. Ferus in cap. 17. Actor. Præiverunt autem Papistis etiam hæretici; Simon Magus, qui secta- toribus suis scorti sui Selenes imaginem adorandam tradidit: Basilidis sectatores, qui imaginum invo- cationibus usi, teste Iren. l. 1. c. 23. Carpocratiani, vel Gnostici, quos imagines, etiam formam Christi, co- luisse notat Iren. cap. 24. Et Epiph. T. 1. l. 1. hær. 27. Quam constanter autem pii Veteres imaginum cultui contradixerint, vel ex ipsis scriptoribus Pon- tificiis doceri potest. Simulacrorum cultum, inquit Polyd. Vergil. l. 6. c. 13. omnes fere Veteres Patres teste Hieronymo damnabant, ob metum idololatriae: Cassander autem ex Origene declarat, quantum Veteres initio Ecclesiae ab omni veneratione imaginum abhorruerint, docetque uberius, initio Christianismi ne usum quidem imaginum admissum fuisse odio Paganismi, & ob metum idololatriae: Postea vero aetate Ambrosii, Nysseni, Prudentii picturas in templis receptas fuisse, ubi periculum illud adorationis & cultus minus erat aut timebatur: & Gregorii adhuc aetate Ecclesiae sententiam fuisse, ideo honorari picturas, non quidem ut colantur & adorentur, sed ut imperiti picturis inspiciendis, haud aliter ac libris legendis rerum gestarum admonerentur, & ad pietatem incitarentur. Quomodo autem semina imaginum cultus Gregorii tempore jam sparsa, ac Gregorius ipse, licet imagines adorari nollet, tamen ante imaginem Christum adorarit, & inde progressio facta sit ad imaginum cultum, eundemque Damascenus propagarit, aliique sanciverint, erudite docet B. Chemnit. l. c. p. 35. De progressu illius superstitionis Cassander u. s. porro docet: Cum autem apud Graecos acres contentiones extitissent, aliis imagines omnes confringentibus, aliis coli & adorari jubentibus, Ecclesiam Romanam confractionem omnino damnasse, usum verum Ecclesiae Romanae & per totum fere orbem jam receptum retinendum censuisse; Quam consuetudinem Romana Ecclesia, quae pariter confractionem & adorationem improbavit, Gallicanae & Germanicae Ecclesiae aliquot seculis fortiter tutatae sunt, usque adeo, ut cum in Synodo Nicena sub Constantino & Irene de imaginibus adorandis aliquot decreta edita fuissent, atque exemplar illius Synodi ad Francofurtensem Synodum allatum, jussu Caroli M. diligenter lectum fuisset, cui Synodo etiam Legati Romani interfuere, summo Patrum consensu Graeca illa Synodus, qua parte imagines adorandas censebat, improbata & damnata fuerit, ut quae non modo divinis literis & antiquae Patrum traditioni, sed etiam consuetudini Romanae Ecclesiae adversaretur, quae damnatio etiam actis, & capitibus illius Francofurt. Synodi inserta fuit, atque ea de re Caroli ipsius titulo, quatuor libri conscripti fuere, quorum Hincmarus Episcopus meminit & eorum exemplum hodieque in Bibliotheca Vaticana & nonnullis Galliae locis extat, qui libri & rationes Orientalium Patrum diligenter confutant, & quae hactenus fuerat Ecclesiae Romanae sententia, acriter defendunt. Haec Cassander, de quibus etiam B. Chemnitius conferendus: qui de septima Iconolatrica Synodo non pauca tradit: & ex Actor. cap. 6. observat, fuisse in ipsa Synodo, qui historicum usum imaginum recipiendum, orationem vero earum recusandam esse, judicarent, sed meliorem partem victam a majori, & de Francofurtensi ostendit temere eos, qui vitas Pontificum scripsere, suppressis illius actis finxisse, ibi septimam Iconolatricam Synodum & adorationem imaginum receptam & approbatam fuisse, quum alii graves Historici, ut Eginardus, Regino, Adon, Ammonius, Blendus, Aventinus, Hincmarius contrarium testentur, & libri Caroli de imaginibus in Galliis a Tilio Episcopo editi illos Pontificios scriptores de crimine falsi manifesto convincant: ac porro de certamine agit Claudii & Jonae, An. Dom. 840. quomodo ille cultum imaginum in Italicis Ecclesiis extra Francofurt. Synodum reprehenderit (licet etiam ad abolendas imagines declinarit) hic vero delapsus fuerit ad septimae Pseudo-Synodi distinctionem de adoratione latriae & duliae, atque imaginum adorationem palliare ceperit: quodque Ecclesiae Germanicae, & Gallicae diu abhorruerint ab adoratione imaginum, & quomodo tentata fuerit inclinatio, ac quae certamina in Ecclesia Graeca, & post septimam illam Iconolatricam Synodum vi- guerint, at prævaluerit tandem adoratio imagi- num, adeo ut Zonaras, & Nicetas scribant pro hære- si suis temporibus habitum, si quis non adoraret ima- gines. Cassander u. s. docet Germanos adhuc ætate Friderici Barbarossæ, Anno 1160. imaginum adora- tionem improbasse: Quanquam vero in Ecclesia Romana Scriptores Scholastici, quos vocant, non tantum sicut Græci honorariam adorationem exter- næ reverentiæ imaginibus tribuerint, sed imagines eadem adoratione, qua prototypa colendas esse dispu- tarint, utpote Thomas, Bonaventura, & reliqui Sen- tentiarii & Summistæ, Durandus tamen de San- cto Porciano hoc falsum esse pronunciavit, atque imagines non adorari proprie, sed abusive tantum & improprie, contendit, quam sententiam Raphael de Latorre, Hispanus Dominicanus in summa de Religione quæst. 94. art. 16. Disp. 6. tribuit etiam Gersoni Majori, Olcoto, Pico Mirandulano, & in eam inclinare etiam Alphonsum à Castro, docet; quod censeant imagines incapaces esse adorationis, quæ ad eas terminetur verè, sed quia res referunt ado- ratione dignas, quæ per recordationem in præsen- tia imaginum adorantur, ideo abusive & improprie dici adorari. Etsi autem Raphael ille hanc senten- tiam (istorum Catholicorum suorum) temerariam dicat, quæ hæresin sapiat, ac ex adverso Thomæ sen- tentiam probet: Ea tamen quod Dominicanus eti- am ille observavit, omnibus se probare minime potuit Romano-Catholicis recentioribus. Non illis, qui imagines adoratione inferiori vel honoraria adorandas esse ajunt, cum Ambrosio Catharino, & Martino Peresio: Nec istis, qui cum Nicol. Sande- ro, Card. Bellarmino, Alberto Pio, Carporum co- mite, Franc. Suarezio imagini duplicem tribuunt adorationem: unam qua in se colitur tanquam obje- ctum, quod inferiori adoratione, alteram qua exem- plar in imagine colitur: quemadmodum legatus vel in persona propria colitur, vel Rex in legato: nec denique Vasquezio, qui imaginem per se negat ado- randam esse, etsi coram ea externa signa honoris, ut genuflexio, & deosculatio fieri possint: imo con- tendit, rem inanimaem sive irrationalem capacem non esse secundum se honoris cultus & adorationis, il- lumque qui notam exhibet submissionis imagini ex ve- ro affectu servitutis, secundum se committere crimen & superstitionem, & esse idololatram aut εἰκονόδουλον: Aliam esse rationem in legato ceu in imagine viva, aliam in re inanima, in quam nulla derivatur ab ex- emplari dignitas, ideoque nec adoratio ei deferri potest. Fingit autem nihilominus, adorari imaginem Dei, & Christi latria, quæ vere & proprie sit latria, non ratione dignitatis alicujus, quæ in ipsa imagine sit, sed quia imago cum prototypo constituit unum adora- tionis objectum, vel integrum & proximum adora- tionis terminum, ita ut imagines non nisi cum exem- plari & ex affectu erga illud adorentur: adeoque do- cet imaginem Christi adorari latria, non per se, sed per accidens, quatenus de imaginibus quis loquitur secundum se: denique eo etiam progreditur, quam- libet rem mundi divina adoratione propter quandam habitudinem & conjunctionem cum Deo adorandam esse. Ita mutuis contradictionibus se conficiunt, & dum distinctionum τερατολογίαις palliare idolo- latriam satagunt, magis solum eam produnt. Ma- net autem Iconolatria, sive imaginem divino ho- nore colam, quæ repræsentat DEum, vel respectu prototypi, sive imagine prototypum colatur, sive cum prototypo imago, ceu unum adorationis objectum, divi- no honore adoretur. Quid quod eo abeat Vasquez, ut falsam dicat Antisiodorensis, Alexandri de Ales, Bonaventuræ, Marsilii Adriani Ultrajectani, post- ea Romani Pontificis, sententiam, nullum posse à peccato idololatriæ excusari, qui apparitionibus, in quibus speciem crucifixi, vel aliam Christi sibi videt offerri, absolute divinos honores desert, existimans, quum ex intentione animi opus exterius religionis dirigatur, posse ab idololatriæ crimine excusari, qui in specie crucifixi, sub qua Dæmon delitescat, Deum adoret; nec quicquam obstare, quo minus suapte natura in qualibet re mundi DEum adorare liceat: Unde de Papistis non immerito exclamat Rivetus: ô Sanctæ gentes, quibus hæc nascuntur in hortis Numina. Certe Jesuitæ freti hac sua doctrina possunt olera sua & brassicas in hortis suis religioso cultu adorare, imo & sterquilinium, adeoque rem omnem, in qua potest aliquid concipi, quod DEI sit.

Num vero in Tridentina Synodo lites illæ compositæ, aut superstitiones abrogatæ? scripta utique tam varia in illa materia de imaginibus in isto conciliabulo fuisse Petr. Suavis narrat, ut quid constituendum de cultu imaginum sit, Paterculis non constiterit: ideo verbis ambiguis, ut observat B. Chemnitius, sententiam suam proposuere, debitum honorem & venerationem eis impertiendam dicunt; non autem quis debitus ille honor sit, definiunt; nec adorationem religiosam audent statuere, ac fiduciam in imaginibus esse FIGENDAM negant: solum honorem, qui illis exhibetur, ad prototypa, quæ illæ repræsentant, referri ajunt, ita ut per imagines quas osculamur & coram quibus caput aperimus, & procumbimus, Christum adoremus: & secundæ synodi Nicenæ decreta approbant studiosé, crassas superstitiones, cultus invocationis & adorationis imaginum in decreto suo non recensent Tridentini: sed quia tamen retineri illas volunt, præcipiunt talem venerationem, sicut in septima synodo definita est. Qualis væro hæc sit, è flosculis nonnullis facile judicari potest: utpote quod decretum ibi: Sacras imagines honorandas, venerandas, salutandas, amplectendas, osculandas, colendas & adorandas esse: quod laudetur Leontii dictum: Quando imaginem Christi habeo, per eam Christum ipsum me tenere, & adorare videor, & Manzonis precatio ad imaginem Christi: Domine, qui das sanctis gratiam, respice me; quod imagine loco dolenti imposita morbus repulsus sit: item quod Johannes quidam dixit: Si quis imaginem Christi adspiciens, & adorans, dixerit: Hic est Christus, non peccet: Quæ & alia multa à B. Chemnitio adducta vere idololatrica sunt. Quod quum probe intellexerit Archi-Episcopus Moguntinus, in Provinciali Synodo ex adverso decernebat Anno 1549. Can. 41. 42. apud Binium Tom. 4. p. 2. fol. 258. imagines in templis non ad adorationem, sed ad memoriam tolerandas esse. Similiter involvebant generalibus terminis suam sententiam Romano-Catholici (sic enim ut vocarentur inter nos tum conventum) in Colloquio Thoruniensi nupero Anno 1645. sacras DEI & sanctorum imagines propter spiritualem (quam ad DEum & sanctos habent) connexionem participatamque inde excellentiam utiliter & pie in honore & veneratione fidelium esse. Sed quia principium liquidationis, ut vocabant, doctrinæ Catholicæ constituebant Tridentinum concilium, quod Pseudo-Synodum Nicenam probavit in hac causa, parilis cum illa idololatriæ rei habendi, siquidem melius se non declararint.
