Bellarminus quidem Concilii ejusdem hyperaspistes in eo videtur se declarasse convenientius, quod imagini non eundem honorem, quem exemplari tribuit lib. 2. de imag. cap. 20. sed inteligit cultum illum, qui per se & proprie imaginibus debetur, non qua vicem gerunt exemplaris: & cultum quidem illum imperfectum facit, sed analogice tamen & reductive ad speciem ejus, qui debetur exemplari, pertinere censet: at per accidens imaginem eodem genere cultus, quo exemplar ipsum colitur, coli vult, nempe cum consideramus exemplar, ut objective relucet in ima- gine, & ipsum sic repræsentatum & quasi vestitum imagine veneramur, sicut qui adorat Regem vestitum, adorat simul Regem & vestes: Sed quænam est illa excellentia vestitus, cui animi intentione ac sub- missione cultus exhibeatur, aut imaginis (quam vero ineptissime vestem DEI vocat) ut eidem re- ligiosus cultus deferatur? Si non magis proprie adoratur imago, qua vicem refert prototypi, quam vestitus, quo Rex indutus est, nemo, nisi qui cerebrum in calcaneo gerit, imaginem pro- prie adorari admittet. Num enim calceus Regis proprie colitur eo cultu, qui Regi defertur? de calceo Pontificis cum eum osculantur id forsan adulatores Pontificis dixerint, quamvis nec id æquo animo Pontifex, si sapit, laturus sit, sibi non aliud honoris genus, quam calceo suo de- ferri, & proprie eodem genere honoris calce- um suum secum coli, hoc solum discrimine, quod per se ille honor Pontifici debeatur, calceo autem ipsius per accidens solum, non tamen improprie, sed proprie exhibeatur. Si cum aliis, utpote Guil- helm. Estio, Alphons. a Castro &c. excipias imagines non in se ipsis adorari, sed ad prototypa referri earum omnem venerationem, contradicit Bellarminus, si- quidem imagini etiam ipsi aliquis cultus debeatur, ad- eoque imagini Christi reductive idem cultus, qui Christi est, deferendus sit, contradicunt Thomistæ & Theologi communiter (Pontificii) quorun. con- stans secundum Azorium lib. 9. Inst. cap. 6. artic. 3. hæc est sententia, imaginem eodem cultu honorari, quo id, cujus est imago, qui eam vult etiam esse Concilii Tridentini mentem: nec excusabitur ido- lolatria; nam etiam is, qui in imaginibus adorat DEUM idololatra hic pronunciatur. Et excusa- re ea ratione potuissent omnes εἰκονολάτραι suam idololatriam utpote μοσχολάτραι Exod. 32. vers. 4. quod non vitulum, sed in vitulo DEUM co- lerent. Israelitæ quod per Baalem DEUM Isra- elis venerarentur Hos. 2. vers. 16. 17. &c. Adde quod imaginibus, teste praxi, in Papatu honor divinus & religiosus deferatur: quia honorant il- las dedicando, prototypi nomen imponendo, cun- ctorum beneficiorum largitionem ab illis expectando, sertis & coronis ornando, sacrificulos præficiendo, osculando, supplicando, alloquendo, cereos accen- dendo, sacrificando &c. Bellarmin. ipse honorem illum, qui iisdem per se & proprie debetur, vult esse analogice eundem cum illo, qui prototypo debe- tur: quem tamen religiosum esse, ac primæ tabu- læ cultum oportet: non enim civilis est, aut cultus ad secundam Tabulam pertinens. At gradus esse in cultu Religioso, alium esse perfectum, alium imperfectum, & analogicum repugnat sanæ Theo- logiæ. Ut essentia, ita & gloria divina ac reli- giosa est ἀμέριςος: & unica est tantum adoratio religiosa, soli DEO propria, aliis extra Deum ἀκοινώνητος, qui gloriam suam alteri dare non vult Esa. 42. vers. 6. & imaginibus adorationem deferre hoc præcepto vetat. Unde Fratres Wa- lenburgici, quum intelligant adorationem omnem re- ligiosam imaginum hic prohibitam, alia effugia quærunt, nempe vetitum esse imagines coli pro- pter se ipsas, quasi ipsæ vivant, aut quæ falsum re- præsentant, non adorare in imagine eum, qui ve- re est, quia DEUS ipse voluerit in arca honorari libr. 12. de unit. Eccles. cap. 37. num. 11. Sed ta- lis distinctio aut limitatio non reperitur in textu adeoque precario ac temere invehitur. Nec adeo inepti erant Israelitæ, ut imaginem vituli, quem formarat Aaron, propter se ipsam adora- rent, aut quasi ipsa viveret, vel etiam adeo prophani, ut alium, quam DEUM Abrahæ, qui eos eduxerat ex Ægypto, in vitulo adora- rent, vera tamen hæc idololatria erat, hac lege prohibita. Neque vero in arca DEUS adorari voluit, etsi penes arcam invocatio fieret; quæ ta- men ad arcam ipsam non dirigebatur, nec per se, nec per accidens. Itaque novum κρησφύγε- τον inveniunt Walenburg. textum sacrum ita cor- rumpendo: Non facies tibi sculptile, neque ul- lam similitudinem EORUM (videl. falsorum Deo- rum, de quibus antea loquutus fuerat) quæ (nim. falsa Deitas) est in cœlo desuper, & quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis: ut scilic. falsorum tantum Deorum imagines prohibeantur, quia gentilitas tres species falsorum Deorum adora- rit, in cœlis solem, Jovem &c. in terra plantas, animalia diversa: in aquis Neptunum & alios. Sed hoc ineptum est. Boni illi fratres textum Ebræum non inspexerunt, forte nec inspicere potuerunt. Nam in illo pronomen illud EO- RUM non habetur. Non ergo ad falsos Deos, qui præcedunt, referri potest. Nec pronomen אשׁר respicit falsam Deitatem, sed ea, quæ dein- de subduntur, quæ in cœlis, in terra &c. De- nique non tantum similitudo falsorum Deorum prohibetur, sed omnium eorum, quæ in cœlo, in terra & in aquis sunt. Annon in cœlo DEUS est, annon angeli & sancti sunt in cœlo? Quo- rum utique imagines, quum ad cultum paran- tur, prohibitæ sunt. Non falsorum tantum Deo- rum imagines, sed quæcunque simulacra hîc pro- hibita esse Salmero in Rom. 3. Vasquez lib. 2. de adorat. Disputat. 4. C. L. cum Origene Alexandr. Paludano & aliis statuunt: & ad imagines seu DEI veri seu creaturarum cum adorantur, & pericu- lum idololatriæ est, hanc legem pertinere agnoscit Jacob Tirinus ad h. l.

Gregorius de Valentia ita effugere conatur ido- lolatriam Tomo 3. Disputat. 6. Quæst. 2. quod idololatriæ cultus sit, quo honor divinus tribuitur creaturæ alicui, sicut DEO; at illo affumento opus non est; Num enim illi idololatræ non fue- re, qui honorem divinum verb. gr. Sacrificii alii quam DEO vero tribuerunt, etsi non haberent eum pro DEO Creatore cœli & terræ? Perinde ergo agit Valentianus, ac si quis adulterium defi- niret concubitum cum altero qui non sit conjux, tanquam cum conjuge: quasi adultera non sit, quæ commisceatur alteri, dum eum non habeant pro conjuge, sed eo tantum, quæ alteri ceu conjugi se prostituit. Idololatria enim est fornicatio spiri- tualis.

Vers. eod. NEQUE OMNEM SIMILITUDINEM QUÆ EST IN CŒLO DESUPER, ET QUÆ IN TERRA DEORSUM, NEC EORUM QUÆ SUNT IN AQUIS SUB TERRA.) Græci Interpp. & Philo hoc ita videntur accepisse, quasi & picturæ animalium vetarentur. At Chaldæus & Judæi Vav, quod in textu est, sumunt ἐξηγητικῶς, nempe ut sensus sit, vetari imagines eminentes eas, quæ formam habeant animalium, sub quibus Hebræi & astra comprehendunt. Aquæ sub terra esse dicuntur, quia DEus terram excavavit, ut ibi aquæ continerentur. Psalm. 104. vers. 6. & ibi Hebræi. Vide annotata nostra ad lib. 1. pro Veritate Religion. Christianæ circa initium.

ptilia fierent? Nonne omnia idola sive picta, sive sculpta, prohibita sunt? Cur vero Ebræorum Alexandrinorum seu Græcorum Interpp. & Vulgatæ (hæc enim consonat) cur Philonis improbat sententiam, libr. de Legat. μὴ ἄγαλμα, μὴ ξόανον, μὴ γραφὴν, non effigiem, non simulacrum, non picturam. Quod Philo lib. de Gigantibus statuariam & pictoriam à Mose è Republ. exclusam dicit, minime probandum. Uti sculptile ita & imago non prohibetur, nisi qua idololatrico cultui prostat. Sed explicet nobis distinctionis suæ mysterium, quod hic fovet Grotius cum Ebræis & Græcis modernis. Factum id in explic. Decalogi. Ἐξηγητικῶς accipere Hebræos, ut intelligatur, non omnia sculptilia prohiberi, ut vitem auream, quæ in templo fuit, sed quæ similitudinem alicujus animalis referrent. Cur vero prohiberentur sculptilia animalia referentia, & hæc quidem solum? An in Cœlo animalia sunt? (sidera à Grotio Expl. Dec. p. 33. animantium nomine comprehendi, quia motum suum habent, quis non ridebit?) Aut nullæ aliæ quam animantium figuræ & nomina astris imposita? Num in terris tantum animantia vetantur adorari & ad cultum repræsentari? Sic Solem & Lunam exhibere licuisset & res inanimatas, citra violationem hujus præcepti? Quod monumenta, arborem, stipitem, saxum primi homines iis, quos pro Diis habebant, excitarint, quod magico ritu crediderint, Spiritum æthereum in eas imagines deduci ὁι πολύθεοι, quodque hæc opinio apud Orientis populos jam invaluerit, id non probat, DEUM edicto hoc suo vel omnia vel sola etiam sculpta animalis alicujus formam habentia inhibuisse: Longe latius potuit εἰδωλολατρεία, quam omnem DEus prohibuit, sive quæ tum in usu fuit, sive quæ deinceps futura erat, aut esse potest. Proinde non sculptilia tantum, sed imagines quascunque cultus causa fieri prohibuisse censendus est.

Quod autem Grotius putat, non venerationem tantum sculptilium prohibitam Ebræis, sed omnem eorum fabricam Expl. Decal. p. 32. eo in Philonis errorem incidit ipse, quasi statuariam artem proscripserit Moses è Republica, & quomodo illa cum formis Cherubinis, quæ animantia exhibuisse censentur, cum bovium formis in mari æneo & aliis conveniunt, quæ æque, uti vitem auream, fieri DEus voluit? Hoc est, quod observavit Tertull. Lib. 2. contra Marc. cap. 22. Cherubim & Seraphim aurea in arcæ figuratum exemplum, certe simplex ornamentum, accommodata suggestui longe diversas habendo causas ab idololatriæ conditione, OB QUAM similitudo prohibetur, non videntur similitudinem prohibitarum legi refragari non in eo similitudinis statu deprehensa, OB QUEM similitudo prohibetur. Aboleri quidem jubentur, quæ ad cultum prostabant Exod. 34. vers. 13. Numer. 33. vers. 52. Deuter. 7. vers. 5. sed si cultus intentio aut periculum aberat, non prohibebantur sive sculptæ, sive pictæ imagines. Delirat Grotius cum ipsis Judæis, cum non in templo tantum, sed quovis alio in loco habere sculptas vel eminentes animantium imagines Judæis interdictum ait. Annon eminens imago erat Cæsaris in nummo, quam nec Judæi abhorrebant, neque Christus ipse Matth. 22. Talia deliria hominis sunt, quod DEus contra hanc legem, ceu legis conditor, suo jure, in templi ipso penetrali locari jusserit Cherubinos, alatas humano effigies vultu, ac erigi serpentem æneum. Non contrariatur sibi ipsi DEus: neque si tam graviter Zelotes ille omnem sculpturam prohibuisset, omnemque fusam imaginem, vel uti Grotius loquitur, omnem imaginem eminentem, autor ipse fuisset locando- rum in templo Cherubinorum, erigendique Ser- pentis aenei. Geminum est, quod de Salomonis labro aeneo adjectis bovibus & leonibus adjicit, id aut DEO factum praecipiente (scil. contra legem, ut fit exceptio a regula) aut si DEI veniam non ha- buit, initium fuisse & gradum quendam ad alia, quae peccavit postea, quam posteriorem sententiam magis Hebraeis placere ait. Ita placet ipsi, nullum non Hebraeorum sputum lingere. Non erat id con- tra legem DEI, multo minus initium idololatriae: imo omnia illa, quae facit Salomo, a Davide Pa- rente accepit, qui eorum omnium typum a manu Domini se accepisse testatur 1. Paral. 29. vers. 19. Putat Grotius, haec de sculptilibus interdicta esse ex eodem genere, quae natura sua illicita non sunt, uti pleraque in Mosis lege: At fallitur hic maxi- mopere: quia praeceptum hoc legis est moralis; imo praeceptum summum & primum tabulae primae, quo idololatria prohibita. Ideoque omnis ge- neris imagines sive sculptae sive fusae, sive incisae, sive pictae, seu animantium seu rerum animata- rum, sive in coelo, sive in terra, sive in aquis sint, qua cultui prostant, ejusque causa fiunt, hic interdictae. Neque discrimen hic fingi vel ulla probabili ratione potest, inter picturas & incisas formas animantium & inter sculptilia. Quod e Clemente Alexandrino didicisse poterat Grotius V. Strom. ubi ait, Mosen aperte dixisse, nullum opor- tere sculptilem vel fusilem, vel fictam vel pictam ima- ginem simulacrumve facere, ut sensilia minime at- tenderemus. Non omnes picturas vetitas, ob ve- xilla Hebraeorum hominem, taurum, leonem, aqui- lam praeferentia, agnoscit Grotius. Omnes tamen illas vetitas, quibus idololatrae ad cultum suum ute- bantur Levit. 26. vers. 1. Numer. 33. vers. 52. Quod & de figuris incisis dicit. At sculptilium hac in causa nulla est, nec dari potest diversa ratio. Quod vero negat, hic de picturis aut formis in- cisis animantium agi, contra textum negat. Qui omnem imaginem, omnem similitudinem cultus cau- sa factam prohibet. Nam eo respectu vetari ad- jecta verba docent: Non adorabis ea. Non ergo aliter prohibitae imagines, quam quatenus ado- rantur. Quod contra Iconoclastas tenuit Chri- stiana Ecclesia: uti non imagines pictas, modo, sed & extantes in Ecclesia admissas fatetur Grotius; Qui ideo etiam hanc legem de sculptilibus & imaginibus & mere positivam facit, & dicto mo- do pervertit, ne eadem cultus imaginum supersti- tiosus & idololatricus in Papatu convincatur. Si Christiani uti aliis ταῖς ἐν θέσει Hebraeorum legibus obligati non fuere, ita neque hac, frustra ea Pon- tificiis opponitur. Ita nusquam non, ubi occa- sionem ferre credidit, Pontificiis succurrere, quamvis plerumque aliud agendo, voluit Hugo Papizans.

## 20:5
Verse 5. THOU SHALT NOT ADORE THEM NOR WORSHIP THEM.

This is a restriction of the preceding words: Thou shalt not make for thyself a graven image, nor the likeness of them, to wit, that thou shouldst bow thyself to them, or worship them, that is, that thou shouldst offer religious worship to it, whether by external signification or by internal veneration: as is evident from Levit. 26. verse 3. Therefore, the manufacture, painting, or use is not simply prohibited, which the Calvinists with the recent Jews desire (who are so superstitious, as Münster notes on this passage, that they feel that even if a thorn has been stuck in one's feet before an image, no one ought to bow down to extract it, etc.), but the religious worship of images: Whence this precept is not positive, pertaining only to the Jews, which Vasquez and some other Pontificians think, but moral and universal: nor does it constitute a distinct commandment in the Decalogue, as most of the Reformed desire, but it pertains to the preceding one concerning not having strange gods, to which the special prohibition of worshipping images altogether looks as to a general prohibition of strange Gods. For it is undoubted that all idolatry whatsoever is prohibited by the first precept. Since therefore the worship of images, or of GOD in images, is idolatry, how can it be denied that the prohibition of the same is to be referred to the first precept, therefore this first precept is thus explained in verse 23. You shall not make with me gods of silver, neither shall you make to yourselves gods of gold. Levit. 19. verse 4. You shall not turn yourselves to idols, nor make to yourselves molten gods: I am Jehovah your GOD. Clement of Alexandria lib. 2. Strom. agrees, Augustin. Epist. 119. to Jan. lib. 3. Conf. cap. 8. as also Quæst. 71. in Exod. Hieronym. de celebr Paschat. Eucher. in Epist. Rom. Beda in h. l. Bernhard. Lyran. Hugo Cardinalis, and others, and from the Reformed Oecolamp. lib. de conf. auric. fol. 116. Hemming. in Euch. Class. 2. Loco de Lege Martyr. Class. 2. LL. CC. cap. 14. Szegedin. in loc. p. 50. &c. Moreover, this special prohibition was added, for this reason primarily, because the Jews had lived in the midst of the Gentiles who were addicted to the worship of images and they themselves were greatly inclined to the same. Conf. Jos. 24. verse 4. Exod. 32. Now to Grotius.

Verse the same. THOU SHALT NOT ADORE THEM.) The Hebrew word signifies a gesture indicative of honor. Even if another has made such likenesses, thou shalt exhibit no honor to it with whatever mind at last: which was accustomed to be done among the Hebrews by a bowed body. These are cautions against contagions from the Gentiles.

NOR WORSHIP THEM.) With victims, libation, incense. For these are referred to עבד.

It separates, as is manifest, this clause from the preceding one, so that it may constitute distinct precepts, as if all graven images or images were first simply prohibited, and then truly, if any have been made or exist, they are said not to be affected by any gesture of honor, much less to be worshipped with victims, libations, or incense. But these are badly torn apart and divided into two or more precepts: since the making of graven images, indeed of any images whatsoever, is indeed prohibited, but only with a certain respect: namely, that they should not be adored or worshipped. Let no one make for himself an image to adore or worship; Grotius does not dare to affirm that all images are prohibited for the sake of ornament, history, or doctrine, although he asserts this regarding carved or prominent ones with some Jews. The ἐξήγησις or repetition of the preceding interdict is explicit here: Do not adore them. Which the opposition also of the true God and of foreign gods confirms: namely, that they are prohibited only insofar as they are foreign gods. As also that addition, BEFORE ME. Images can therefore be had, provided they are not had BEFORE GOD: provided they are not worshipped with divine honor. Add the parallel passage Levit. 16, 1. I am the Lord your God: You shall not make for yourselves an idol and a graven image, nor shall you erect pillars, nor shall you place a notable stone in your land, that you may adore it. This is a clear explanation of the divine interdict: You shall not make an idol or a graven image, that you may not adore it. And the erection of a stone as a testimony was not prohibited, but only that which was done for worship. Wherefore neither is that to be admitted, that it was lawful by this commandment to show worship to images, with whatever intention it might be done: Why might it not have been lawful to show some reverence to the image of an honored person, without violation of the commandment of the first table? For civil or respectful honor does not pertain to the first table: but religious honor does. This, when offered to another than the one GOD, is forbidden; but that has no commerce with the first table of the law. Grotius is therefore fed here on Jewish fables, from which he could derive no conviction other than from the ravings of the Jews. But in this place, he says in his explanation of the Decalogue, p. 36, undoubtedly every act is signified by which honor is accustomed to be shown; just as elsewhere the Hebrews are forbidden to use the names of false gods, Exod. 23, verse 13. (which, however, is to be understood only by reason of approval, not by reason of any mention whatsoever, since they are not passed over in silence in Scripture itself, but are mentioned everywhere, nay, it is hinted at by that phrase, 'neither shall an abomination be heard out of your mouth.' For thus we speak of those things which we most abhor, because we do not wish to pollute our lips with the mention of them. Which litotes is called extenuation: Compare Eph. 5. 3, regarding the phrase, and Deut. 7. 26, regarding the thing, and regarding both the phrase and the thing itself, Hos. 2. v. 7.) So also we are forbidden to show any sign of honor to images, with whatever intention it might be done, as Moses of Coucy notes in the 19th prohibitive commandment. We do not envy Grotius such witnesses: who delights in these triflers exceedingly. But these things tend again to this, that those commandments are held to be merely positive, and that Christians are no longer believed to be bound by them, lest Papal Idolatry should shine through, and be judged contrary to the law of the first table. Which the things he added to the aforementioned explanation teach. Moreover, regarding this Commandment about not bending the body before images, since it is of POSITIVE Law, the Hebrews deny that foreigners, however pious, such as Naaman, were bound by it. These, as blind guides, are little to be heeded. But Naaman, however

that a Gentile worshipped in the house of Rimmon, and that he begged pardon for that fault, which is observed by more accurate Critics and Interpreters to be found only in 2 Kings 5, verse 18, is entirely contrary to the Grotian hypothesis: For if he begged pardon for that act, he certainly believed himself to be bound by this commandment. But let Grotius continue: Nor indeed did the ancient Christians believe themselves to be bound by it indiscriminately, but only insofar as there was in the testimony of honor shown before an image the veneration of a false deity, which is evil in itself and in every way; which can be understood from the place in Job just indicated to us, namely 31. 26, and the place in Acts 10. 25, from that history which we just premised regarding Nazianzen. Nothing else is understood from it than that the worship of others besides God, and even the very ceremonies by which false deities were worshipped, were condemned. Moreover, just as Christians did not believe themselves to be bound indiscriminately not to have images; so neither did they judge that it was written for the Jews, and they thought that only worship was forbidden. The history from Nazianzen tends to this, and what Grotius observed there besides, p. 31. Christians also did not consider it contrary to their religion to bow down before the images of Emperors. But after Julian had ordered the images of false gods to be added to his own images, the more prudent thought it better to tolerate any evils than to bow down there. Gregory Nazianzen narrates this. Tertullian to Scapula: We worship the Emperor, therefore, in the way that is both lawful for us and expedient for him, as a man second to God, and having obtained whatever he has from God, and being less than GOD alone. The same against the Gentiles: Tempering the majesty of Caesar below God, I commend him more to God, to whom alone I subject him. I subject him, however, to whom I do not equate him, and soon: I will plainly call the emperor Lord, but when I am not forced to call him Lord in the place of God. This commandment, of which we have treated until now, both Philo and the Christians who followed him call τὸ περὶ μοναρχίας, concerning the rule of one, or also καθαίρεσιν τῆς πολυθεΐας, concerning the destruction of the multitude of gods. Wherefore they did not hold this law to be positive, but moral and perpetual: and they believed only the commandment concerning the Sabbath in the Decalogue to be of positive law. Among all those ten Commandments, says Augustine, Epist. 119. c. 12, ONLY that which is placed concerning the Sabbath is commanded to be observed figuratively. -- The other commandments there, however, we observe properly, as they are commandments, without any figurative meaning. For we have also clearly learned not to worship idols. Nor does Irenaeus think otherwise, lib. 4. c. 31. He says those commandments similarly remain with us, and he calls them natural, and literal, and common to all. But even the Jews themselves deny that this commandment concerning images is positive, and given to them alone. For thus they interpret the first commandment of the Noachides concerning external worship, where it forbids the worship of stones, stocks, statues, images, angels, stars, and other creatures, which are held either as the supreme deity or as an intermediary to the supreme. See Maimonides in More Nebuch. part I. c. 36, and the tract on idolatry, c. 2. sect. 1 and 2. Selden on the law of nature and nations according to the laws of the Hebrews, lib. 2. c. 1, 2, and 6. If they acknowledged it to be positive and given to them alone, they would not blame other nations for the worship of images, nor could they blame them. Most Papists also acknowledge that the 10 commandments of the Decalogue are moral and of natural law. Roman Catechism, part 3, cap. 1, fol. 2. Thomas 1. 2. quest. 100. art. 1. Whence Puteanus l. 2. quest. 94. note 2. For there are ten commandments of the Decalogue and all these are of natural law, even the commandment concerning the sanctifying of the Sabbath, at least according to its substance. But if the worship of GOD in images was forbidden to the Jews alone, why were the Gentiles punished on account of the same? Why was the Israelite people punished before the law was established, when they worshipped the true GOD in the golden calf? Those who follow the banner of Calvin are hostile to images above others today. Among them, however, there are not wanting those who acknowledge that the use of images is forbidden here for the reason that they are worshipped. Rivetus in Explicat. Decal. p. 35. He forbids images of all things (which are in Heaven, on earth, in the waters) to be made to the end that they may represent God to themselves, and worship Him externally in these visible things. Nor does Rivetus deny that certain sensible things were proposed to the Israelites, through which they might be moved to the worship and adoration of GOD, as if by His institution they were present: he only denies that such things were either worshipped or could have been worshipped without idolatry, and he teaches that in the Decalogue, which is common to all, images for worship are forbidden, and therefore Christians ought to abstain from them, p. 39. But Grotius wishes the use of graven images to be simply forbidden, but to the Hebrews only, and for special reasons. That he gratifies Papistic idolatry in this is manifest from Vasquez the Jesuit, Tom. I. Comment. in 3. part. Thom. disput. 104, whose words I transcribe. Because, he says, although the use, or rather the worship of images was forbidden by the Mosaic law, it does not follow that it was therefore forbidden by natural law, and consequently, since it was a ceremonial prohibition, it ought to have ceased at the time of the Evangelical law; and that which is otherwise lawful and honest by natural law, such as to paint images and to use them for adoration, ought to have a place in the Evangelical law. Therefore he observes here (in expl. Dec. p. 36.) that it was long disputed in the East, and not without sedition, whether it was right in places of prayer to bow the body before the images of Christ or the saints in their honor, which he says is called by the Greeks σχετικὴν προσκύνησιν, i.e., a sign of love and reverence towards men eminent for holiness. And although he acknowledges that it long seemed to Germany and France to be evil, or not to be free from the appearance of evil, as from the Synods of Frankfurt and Paris,

In the times of Charlemagne and his children, it appears, he nevertheless undertakes the defense of the Greeks against the Westerners, and concedes the danger of evil only in this relative worship (σχετικῆ προσκυνήσει), but does not acknowledge it as evil in itself. He notes that in those Synods the Greeks were treated rather harshly, because the Western Bishops interpreted the opinion of the Greeks expressed in the second Nicene Synod in a harsher sense than it actually was, deceived by the acts of the Nicene Synod not being translated so faithfully into Latin, inasmuch as they took the words of Constantine, Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, in a clearly inverted sense, as if he had asserted for images the adoration of latria, which is owed to the Holy Trinity. But John Daillé cuts the nerve of these in his book 4 on images, chapter 4. and 5, when he called into doubt the reliability of the Greek codices here, and proved their disagreement with other examples, indeed, he showed in reality that opinion approved at Nicaea, that, namely, images of the Trinity are to be adored with the same adoration as the Prototypes, as Rivet testifies in his discussion on Grotius (Grotian. discuss. διαλύσει) page 36. Nor, while listing the species of idolatry (εἰδωλολατρείας), which the Hebrews call strange worship (עברה זרה), does he count adoration: he only commemorates these three, sacrifices, libations, and incense, which are held by the Hebrews to be worship alien to the law or idolatry, when they are not applied to the honor of the true GOD: he also defines idolatry no otherwise than whatever is raised beyond the measure of human honor to the likeness of divine sublimity, as Tertullian speaks: whereas on the contrary it is certain from Rabbi Moses Maimonides on Idolatry, chapter 3, section 6, and the Talmudists in Sanhedrin, chapter 7, section 6, that the Rabbis list four acts of foreign worship: altar or sacrifice (מזבח), libation (המנסך), incense (הַמְקַטֵּר), and adoration (השתחויה). Although in the Papacy not only adoration, but the other acts also are performed to images, as experience testifies. Nor indeed is it only idolatry when that which is not God is worshipped as God, but also when God is not worshipped in a divine and appropriate manner; otherwise the Israelites would not have been idolaters when they worshipped God in the calf (Exodus 32:4, 1 Kings 12:28), for they did not hold the calf to be the supreme God himself: or Micah in his idols worshipping the God of Israel (Judges 17:3, etc.); nor the Gentiles, of whom Augustine notes in his Enarrations on Psalm 113, verse 13, that some said: I worship neither an idol nor a demon, but I look upon the bodily effigy as a sign of that thing which I ought to worship. But Grotius does not hesitate to undertake the defense of the Gentiles, praising in his discussion the dissertation of Tyrius on images, for that reason, without doubt, that in it there are some things held in common with the Papal practice, inasmuch as, when he says in the Dissertation, 38. nature has no need of statues in themselves, nor of images, but since the condition of mortals is very weak, and the earth is as far removed from the divine as it is from Heaven, it devised for itself signs of this kind, to which it attributed both the names and titles of the gods. Similarly, the Jesuits describe idolatry: Gregor de Valentia, disputation 6, method 2, question 2, that it is properly when divine honor is attributed to some creature, just as to God, so that they conclude that Roman Catholics are not idolaters, since they honor images in such a way that they nevertheless by no means apply divine honor to the creature as to God, since they venerate both the images of Christ and of the saints, but not as God. Although the Papists differ greatly among themselves on this. For Gretser does not hesitate to contend that the cross of the Lord is to be worshipped with latria (book 1 on the cross, chapter 49). Vasquez, however, goes so far as to affirm that any inanimate thing whatsoever can by right of nature be adored as an image of GOD, indeed even a straw and a ray of the sun, under which the Devil might hide, if it is thought to be Christ (book 2 on adoration, chapter 4; book 3, Disputation 1, chapter 8). Martin Bresser, likewise a Jesuit, in book 5 on conscience, chapter 12, finally argues that it is not a sin to adore the Devil in the case that he should appear in the form of a crucifix, because not even then would the Devil be adored, but Christ himself.

Verse same. I AM THE LORD GOD STRONG JEALOUS) Impatient of a rival, like a husband. UNTO THE THIRD AND FOURTH GENERATION) From the children of descendants, as happened in the Babylonian deportation. v. 6. UNTO THOUSANDS) Not a thousand, but many thousands: thus it is shown how much more generous GOD is in doing good than in punishing.

This threatening and promise, although it pertains to all the commandments (Exodus 34:6), is added to the first, because this is the source, and foundation, and head of the rest. The zeal of God, however, partly implies Charity, as Theodoret interprets in this place, by which He does not permit the soul, as if it were His bride and wife, to be taken from Him: partly jealousy, and anger, because, namely, out of sincere love toward us He cannot bear that we should adhere to others through spiritual fornication, and so His anger flares up against such people. Nor yet is a carnal affection or perturbation to be attributed to God for this reason. For this must be understood in a manner worthy of God (θεοπρεπῶς). Augustine against Adimantus: The zeal of God signifies not a torment of the mind, but a most tranquil and most sincere justice, by which He does not allow the soul to commit fornication with impunity. But He is said to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and upon the third and upon the fourth (in Hebrew), that is, upon the grandsons and great-grandsons, hating them, which the Chaldean refers to these, but others to the fathers themselves, and that more correctly, as appears from chapter 34:7, Jeremiah 32:18. Diodorus of Tarsus, Severus, and Theodoret understand it exclusively, that the children, grandsons, and great-grandsons are punished, not the fathers themselves: but that it should be accepted inclusively is rightly taught by Augustine in Questions on the Old and New Testament, chapter 14, Chrysostom on Psalm 84, Leo in Epistle 86, Gregory the Great, book 15 of Morals, chapter 22. Nor does it seem to be called into doubt with Cornelius and Marius whether the sins of immediate parents pass into their children: since examples and experience testify that this happens not rarely, and divine justice does not permit the sins of parents to be punished in children, of which the children are in no way participants, Ezekiel 18:20, in which, however, the reason of God is one thing, and the reason of the Magistrate is another. To this person that prescribed law is given, the children shall not be put to death for the parents Deut. 24, 16. God, however, cannot be bound to this, but acts by his own authority, as he knows it to be fitting for the common salvation and the own salvation of any persons, as far as temporal punishments or calamities are concerned, since with him no one is absolutely innocent Ex. 34, 8. But concerning eternal ones, that authentic [word] remains: The soul that has sinned, it shall die. There is therefore no reason why this threat should be restricted, with Greg. M. l. 15. Mor. c. 31., to Original sin; indeed, it is manifest that actual sins are being dealt with here: One must only distinguish between common and personal sins, and likewise between temporal and eternal punishment. Conf. Num. 14, 33. 1. Sam. 15, 2. Matth. 23. To this also pertains the fact that children, when grace has been withdrawn from their parents, on account of their own fault, by the removal of the means of salvation, are consequently also deprived of the means of grace.

But how is it a punishment to dead parents that a son suffers? Resp. It is a punishment to them insofar as it was foretold by God, whence they are not without fear concerning the future lot of their children in life. It should be noted, however, that what are punishments to parents can be suitable trials and medicines for children, if these are pious. Add also this, that God is speaking here of what men deserve in punishments, and what he can justly do, yet he does not bind himself so as not to show himself kind toward the descendants of the impious: Whence the children of impious parents are not rarely read to have obtained grace, as Hezekiah, Josiah, and others are examples.

AND I WILL SHOW MERCY UNTO THOUSANDS. Not in view of the merits of the Fathers, as Marius wishes, which are none Gen. 32. verse 10. Psalm. 143. v. 2. Es. 65. verse 6. Dan. 9. verse 4. But by the power of grace and of gratuitous promise, and on account of the Messiah, in whom alone we are beloved, and in grace before God Eph. 1 verse 6. Rom. 5. vers. 15. in whose promise the saints placed their confidence of being heard in their prayers, Exod. 32. v. 13. 2. Chron. 6. vers. 42. Psalm. 132. vers. 10. Dan. 9. verse 17. For God in judicial visitation punishes iniquities out of justice, but in gracious visitation rewards the pious and their posterity out of mercy, lest anyone with the proud Pharisees urge the rule: the consequences of contraries are contrary: because these contraries are not in the same degree. He also posits an unequal limit to that visitation: so that we may know that although justice and mercy are equal in Him, yet by reason of the effects, mercy extends itself beyond justice.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NON ADORABIS EA NEQUE COLES.

Haec restrictio verborum praecedentium est: Non facies tibi sculptile, neque similitudinem eorum, scil. ut te iis incurves, aut ea colas, hoc est, religio- sum cultum sive externa significatione, sive in- terna veneratione ei deferas: quemadmodum e Levit. 26. vers. 3. constat. Non ergo prohibetur simpliciter fabrica, pictura, aut usus, quod Cal- viniani cum recentioribus Judaeis volunt (qui adeo superstitiosi sunt, notante Münstero ad h. l. ut etiam cum spina pedibus infixa fuerit ante imaginem, neminem incurvari debere ad illam extrahendam fentiant &c.) sed cultus imaginum religiosus: Un- de præceptum hoc non est positivum, ad Judæos tantum pertinens, quod Vasquetz, & alii Pon- tificii nonnulli putant, sed morale & universale: neque distinctum in Decalogo mandatum con- stituit, ut plerique Reformati volunt, sed ad præ- cedens de non habendis diis alienis pertinet, qua ad generalem alienorum Deorum prohibitionem speciale interdictum colendarum imaginum omni- no spectat. Omnem enim prorsus idololatri- am primo præcepto esse prohibitam, indubium est. Quum ergo cultus imaginum, aut DEI in imaginibus idololatria sit, quomodo negari po- test ejusdem prohibitionem ad primum præce- ptum referendum esse, ideo ita primum hoc præ- ceptum explicatur vers. 23. Non facietis mecum deos argenteos neque deos aureos facietis vobis. Le- vit. 19. vers. 4. Non convertetis vos ad idola, neque facietis vobis deos fusiles: Ego Jehovah DEUS ve- ster. Annuunt Clemens Alexandr. lib. 2. Strom. Au- gustin. Epist. 119. ad Jan. lib. 3. Conf. cap. 8. ut & Quæst. 71. in Exod. Hieronym. de celebr Paschat. Eucher. in Epist. Rom. Beda in h. l. Bernhard. Ly- ran. Hugo Cardinalis, & alii, & e Reformatis Oe- colamp. lib. de conf. auric. fol. 116. Hemming. in Euch. Class. 2. Loco de Lege Martyr. Class. 2. LL. CC. cap. 14. Szegedin. in loc. p. 50. &c. Addita autem hæc specialis prohibitio est, ea imprimis de causa, quia Judæi egerant in medio gentilium cul- tui imaginum addictorum & ipsi ad eundem valde inclinabant. Conf. Jos. 24. vers. 4. Exod. 32. Jam ad Grotium.

Vers. eod. NON ADORABIS EA.) Vox Hebræa ge- stum honoris indicem significat. Etiamsi talia simulacra ali- us fecerit, nullum qualicunque tandem animo honorem ei exhibebis: quod curvato corpore apud Hebræos fieri sole- bat. Hæ cautiones sunt adversus contagia ex gentibus.

NEQUE COLES.) Victimlis, libamine, incenso. Hæc enim ad עבד referuntur.

Separat, uti manifestum est, hoc comma à præcedenti, ut distincta præcepta constituat ac si sculptilia vel imagines omnes primum simpliciter prohibitæ, tum vero, si quæ factæ sint aut existant, nullo honoris gestu afficiendæ dicantur, nedum vi- ctimis, libamine, incenso, colendæ. Sed male dis- cerpuntur, & in duo aut plura præcepta dividun- tur ista: quum sculptilium, imo quarumcunque ima- ginum fabrica prohiheatur quidem, sed solum cer- to respectu: ne scil. adorentur aut colantur. Ne quis faciat sibi imaginem ad adorandum vel co- lendum; ornatus, historiæ, doctrinæ causa prohibi- tas esse imagines omnes, nec Grotius affirmare audet, licet de sculptis vel eminentibus cum Judæis nonnullis id asserat. Diserta hîc est ἐξήγησις vel re- petitio interdicti præcedentis: Ne adores eas. Quam oppositio etiam Dei veri & Deorum alienorum confirmat: prohibitas nempe tantum esse, qua Dii alieni sunt. Ut & προσθήκη illa, PENES ME. Haberi ergo possunt imagines, modo non ha- beantur PENES DEUM: modo non honore di- vino colantur. Adde locum parallelum Levit. 16, 1. Ego Dominus Deus vester: Non faciatis vobis ido- lum & sculptile, nec titulos erigatis, nec insignem la- pidem ponetis in terra vestra, ut adoretis eum. Lucu- lenta hæc explicatio est interdicti divini: Non fa- cietis idolum aut sculptile, ne adoretis illud. Et erectio lapidis in testimonium facta non erat prohibita, sed ea solum, quæ in cultum fiebat Jos. 22. vers. 10. ita nullum est dubium licitas fuisse in alios usus ima- gines, etiam eminentes, modo non exponerentur cultui. Quapropter nec id admittendum, imagi- nibus nullum per hoc præceptum, qualicunque tandem fieret animo, exhibere licuisse cultum : Quidni ima- gini personæ honoratæ licuisset aliquam reveren- tiam exhibere, citra violationem præcepti tabulæ primæ? Non enim pertinet honor civilis aut officio- sus ad tabulam primam: sed religiosus. Hic eadem deferri alii, quam uni DEO vetatur; illi vero cum prima legis tabula nihil commercii. Judaicis ergo commentis hic pascitur Grotius, quibus neque aliunde, quam e Judæorum deliriis, fidem concilia- re potuit. Hoc vero loco, ait in explic. Decal. p. 36. haud dubie significatur omnis actus, quo honos habitus demonstrari solet; sicut enim alibi vetantur Hebræi, nomina usurpare Deorum falsorum Exod. 23. vers. 13. (quod vero ratione approbationis itidem solum in- telligendum, non ratione cujusvis commemoratio- nis, quum in ipsa Scriptura non taceantur, sed pas- sim commemorentur, imo phrasi illa, neque audietur ex ore vestro abominatio, innuitur. Sic enim de iis loquimur, quæ maxime abominamur, quod earum mentione labia nostra polluere nolimus. Quæ λι- τότης extenuatio dicitur : Conf. Eph. 5. 3. qua phrasin, & Deut. 7, 26. qua rem, & quoad phrasin pariter ac rem ipsam Hos. 2. v. 7.) Ita etiam imaginibus ullum signum honoris, quocunque tandem animo id fieret, ex- hibere prohibemur, uti notat Moses de Cotzi præcepto vetante 19. Non invidemus Grotio testes ejus- modi : qui nugatoribus istis delectatur maximo- pere. Tendunt autem hæc iterum eo, ut ista tan- tum præcepta positiva habeantur, neque jam illis ob- ligari credantur Christiani, ne pelluceat Idololatria Papalis, legique primæ tabulæ adversa judicetur. Quod ea, quæ explicationi prædictæ subjunxit, do- cent. Cæterum hoc Præcepto de non flectendo apud imagines corpore, cum CONSTITUTI sit Juris, alienigenas, quantumvis pios, ut Nahamanen, ne- gant obligatos fuisse Ebræi. Hi tanquam cæci Du- ctores parum curandi. Nahamanem autem adhuc

Ethnicum adorasse in domo Rimmon, eamque cul- pam deprecari, quod solum e 2. Reg. 5. versu 18. haberi, accuratioribus Criticis & Interpp. obser- vatum, Grotianæ hypothesi prorsus adversatur: Si enim ille culpam deprecatus est ejus rei, præce- pto hoc se obligari utique credidit. Sed pergat Gro- tius : Neg, vero indistincte se eo obligari credidere Chri- stiani Veteres, sed tantum, quatenus in testimonio ha- biti honoris apud imaginem inerat falsi numinis vene- ratio, quæ per se & omnimodo mala est; quod intelligi potest ex loco Jobi modo nobis indicato, scil. 31, 26. & loco Act. 10, 25. ex ea historia, quam de Nazian- zeno modo præmisimus. Nihil aliud inde intelligi- tur, quam quod aliorum cultus præter Deum, ipsæ- que etiam ceremoniæ, quibus colebantur falsa nu- mina, damnatæ. Cæterum uti non indistincte se ad non habendum imagines obligari haud credide- runt Christiani; sic neque id Judæis scriptum cen- suere, cultumque solum interdictum existimarunt. Eo tendit etiam historia e Nazianzeno, & quæ præ- terea ibi observavit Grotius p. 31. Etiam coram ima- ginibus Imperatorum procumbere non alienum a sua religione arbitrati sunt Christiani. At postquam suis imaginibus falsorum Deorum imagines addi jusserat Julianus, prudentiores mala quævis potius toleranda duxere, quam ut ibi procumberent. Narrat Grego- rius Nazianzenus. Tertullianus ad Scapulam : Co- limus ergo Imperatorem sic, quomodo & nobis licet, & ipsi expedit, ut hominem a Deo secundum, & quic- quid est a Deo consequutam & solo DEO minorem. Idem adversus gentes : Temperans majestatem Cæsa- ris infra Deum magis illum commendo Deo, cui soli subjicio. Subjicio autem, cui non adæquo, & mox : di- cam plane imperatorem Dominum, sed quando non cogor, ut Dominum Dei vice dicam. Hoc præceptum, de quo hucusque egimus, & Philo, & eum secuti Chri- stiani vocant τὸ περὶ μοναρχίας, de unius imperio, aut etiam καθαίρεσιν τῆς πολυθεΐας, de destructione mul- titudinis Deorum. Quapropter legem hanc non pro positiva habuere, sed pro morali & perpetua: solumq; præceptum de Sabbatho in Decalogo constituti juris crediderunt. Inter illa omnia decem Præcepta, ait Augustinus Epist. 119. c. 12. SOLUM ibi, quod de Sabbatho positum est, figurate observandum præcipi- tur. -- Cætera tamen ibi præcepta proprie, sicut præ- cepta sunt, sine ulla figurata significatione observamus. Nam & idola non colere, manifeste didicimus. Nec aliter Irenæus lib. 4. c. 31. Præcepta illa dicit similiter permanere apud nos, eaque vocat naturalia, & litera- lia & communia omnium. Sed & Judæi ipsi negant, præceptum hoc de imaginibus positivum esse, sibiq; solis datum. Ita enim interpretantur præceptum Noachidarum primum de cultu externo, ubi inter- dicit saxorum, stipitum, statuarum, imaginum, an- gelorum, astrorum, aliarum creaturarum cultu, qua vel pro numine summo habentur, vel pro intermedio ad summum. Videatur Maimonides in More Ne- buch. part. I. c. 36. & tract. de idololatr. c. 2. sect. 1. & 2. Seldenus de jure natur. & gent. ad leges Ebr. lib. 2. c. 1. 2. & 6. Si id pro positivo sibi solis dato agnoscerent, non culparent gentes alias propter imaginum cultum, neque culpare possent. Agno- scunt etiam Papistæ plerique, præcepta Decalogi 10. moralia esse ac juris naturalis. Catechism. Rom. part. 3. cap. 1. fol. 2. Thomas 1. 2. quæst. 100. art. 1. Unde Puteanus l. 2. quæst. 94. not. 2. Sunt enim de- cem præcepta Decalogi & hæc omnia sunt juris natu- ralis, etiam præceptum de sabbatho sanctificando sal- tem secundum substantiam. Quod si cultus DEI in imaginibus Judæis solum interdictus, quî pro- pter eundem gentes punitæ? quî populus Israeli- ticus ante legem constitutam, cum in vitulo aureo DEUM verum coleret? Infesti sunt præ aliis ho- die imaginibus, qui Calvini vexillum sequuntur. Inter eos tamen non desunt, qui imaginum usum ea ratione hic interdictum, qua coluntur, agno- scant. Rivetus in Explicat. Decal. p. 35. Quorum omniam, (quæ in Cœlo, in terrà, in aquis sunt) imagines fieri prohibet in eum finem, ut sibi Deum repræsentent, & in his visibilibus externe colant. Neque negat Rivetus, proposita Israelitis fuisse sensibilia quædam, per quæ ad cultum & adorationem DEI, tanquam ex instituto ejus præsentia moveren- tur: negat solum, talia aut adorata fuisse aut sine ido- lolatria adorari potuisse, docetque in Decalogo omni- bus communi prohiberi imagines ad cultum, ideo ab iis abstinere debere Christianos p. 39. Sed Grotius sim- pliciter interdictum usum sculptilium vult, verum Ebræis tantum, & ob speciales causas. Idololatriæ Papisticæ hæc ipsum gratificari e Vasquezio Jesuita Tom. I. Comment. in 3. part. Thom. disput. 104. manifestum est, cujus verba adscribo. Quia, inquit, quamvis usus, imo cultus imaginum lege Mosaica pro- hibitus fuerit, non ideo jure naturali vetitum fuisse sequitur, ac proinde cum fuerit ceremonialis prohibi- tio, tempore legis Evangelicæ debuit cessare; atque id, quod alias jure naturali licitum & honestum est, ut imagines depingere, & illis uti ad adorationem, in le- ge Evangelica locum habere debet. Ideo observat hic (in expl. Dec. p. 36.) diu in Oriente, nec sine seditione disputatum esse, an rectum esset in precationum locis in honorem aut Christi aut sanctorum, coram eorum ima- ginibus flectere corpora, quod σχετικὴν προσκύνησιν i. e. signum amoris & reverentiæ erga viros sanctimo- nia eminentes a Græcis vocari ait. Et quanquam agno- scat, Germaniæ & Galliæ diu visum id malo, aut mali specie non carere, ut ex Francof. & Parisiensi Synodis,

Caroli M. liberorumque ejus temporibus habitis, ap- paret, patrocinium tamen Græcorum adversus Oc- cidentales suscipit, ac periculum solum mali in hac σχετικῆ προσκυνήσει concedit, eam vero per se malam non agnoscit. Notat, in illis Synodis inclementius tractatos Græcos, quod occidentales Episcopi senten- tiam Græcorum expressam in Nicena Synodo secunda in duriorem partem, quam ipsa erat, interpretaren- tur, decepti actis Nicenæ Synodi in Latinum non ita fideliter versis, utpote quod Constantini Constantiæ Cyri Episcopi verba sensu plane inverso acceperint, quasi latriæ adorationem, quæ S. Trinitati debetur, imaginibus asseruerit. Sed his nervum incidit Joh. Dallæus lib. 4. de imagin. c. 4. & 5. cum fidem Græ- corum hodiernorum Codicum hic in dubium vo- cavit, eorumque cum aliis dissensum exemplis pro- bavit, imo reipsa sententiam illam Nicææ approbatam, quod, nempe Trinitatis imagines eadem adora- tione cum Prototypis adorandæ sint, ostendit, Riveto in Grotian. discuss. διαλύσει pag. 36. teste. Neque εἰδωλολατρείας, quam Ebræi עברה זרה vocant, species recensens, aannumerat adorationem: solum tria hæc, sacrificia, libamina, suffitus ab Ebræis cultum a lege alienum vel idololatriam habita, cum non in veri DEI honorem adhibentur commemo- rat: idololatriam etiam non aliter definit, quam quicquid ultra humani honoris modum ad instar di- vinæ sublimitatis attollitur, uti Tertullianus loqui- tur: quum ex adverso e R. Mose Maimonide de Idol. c. 3. f. 6. ac Thalmudicis in Sanhedrim c. 7. sect. 6. certum sit, Rabbinos quatuor actus cultus peregrini recensere מזבח altare seu sacrificium המנסך libationem, המקטר suffitum, & השתחויה adorationem. Quanquam in Papatu non adoratio solum, sed cæteri etiam actus imaginibus fiant, ut experientia testatur. Nec vero idololatria tantum est, cum ut Deus colitur non Deus, sed etiam cum Deus non colitur modo divino eique competente, alias idololatræ non fuissent Israelitæ, cum Deum in vitulo colerent Exod. 32, 4. 1. Reg. 12, 28. non enim vitulum habebant pro ipso summo Deo: aut Micha in simulacris suis Deum Israelis colens Jud. 17, 3. &c. nec gentiles, de quibus Augustin. notat in Enarr. Psalm. 113. v. 13. quod nonnulli dixerint: nec simulacrum, nec Dæmonium colo, sed effigiem cor- poralem ejus rei signum intueor, quam colere debeo. Sed Gentilium patrocinium suscipere non dubi- tat Grotius, laudans in discuss. Tyrii dissertationem de imaginibus, ea, sine dubio, de causa, quod in illa habeantur gemina praxi Papali nonnulla, utpote, cum Deorum, inquit Dissert. 38. naturæ nec statuis per se, nec imaginibus opus est, sed cum infirma sit op- pido mortalium conditio, tantumque a divina, quan- tum a Cœlo terra recedat, signa ejusmodi excogitavit sibi, quibus & nomina Deorum & nuncupationes tri- buerit. Similiter describunt Jesuitæ idololatriam: Gregor. de Valent. disp. 6. m. 2. q. 2. quod proprie sit, cum creaturæ alicui divinus honor tribuitur, sicut Deo, ut concludant, Romano - Catholicos Idolo- latras non esse, cum sic honorent imagines, ut ta- men minime creaturæ adhibeant divinum hono- rem, sicut Deo, cum venerentur tum Christi, tum sanctorum imagines, sed non, sicut Deum. Quan- quam in eo maximopere inter se discrepent Papi- stæ. Gretserus enim non dubitat contendere cru- cem Domini colendam esse latria lib. 1. de cruce c. 49. Vasquez autem eo quoque abit, ut affirmet, rem quamlibet inanimatam jure naturæ tanquam DEI imaginem posse adorari, imo festucam ac radium solis quoque, sub quo Diabolus lateat, si putetur esse Christus lib. 2. de adorat. 4. c. 4. l. 3. Disp. 1. c. 8. Martinus Bresserus itidem Jesuita lib. 5. de consc. c. 12. dispu- tet denique, peccatum non esse, adorare Diabolum casu quo appareret specie crucifixi, quia nec tum Dia- bolus, sed ipse Christus adoraretur.

Vers. eod. EGO SUM DOMINUS DEUS FORTIS ZE- LOTES) Confortis impatiens, ut mariti. IN TERTIAM ET QVARTAM GENERATIONEM) Ex filiis posterorum, ut factum in Babylonica deportatione. v. 6. IN MILLIA) Non mille, sed multa millia: ita osten- ditur, quanto largior sit DEUS in benefaciendo, quam in pu- niendo.

Hæc comminatio & promissio etsi ad omnia præcepta pertineat Ex. 34. v. 6. ad primum addita, quia hoc fons est, & fundamentum, ac caput reli- quorum. Zelus autem Dei partim Charitatem in- nuit, Theodor. in h. l. interprete, qua animam, qua- si sponsam suam & uxorem, sibi adimi non permit- tit: partim zelotypiam, atque iram, quod nempe ex sincero amore erga nos ferre nequeat, ut spirituali fornicatione aliis adhæreanus, adeoque ira adver- sus tales excandescat. Nec tamen ideo carnalis affectus, vel perturbatio Deo tribuenda. Nam θεο- πρεπῶς hoc intelligendum. August. contr. Adi- mant. Zelus Dei non cruciatum animi, sed tranquillissi- mam sincerissimamque justitiam significat, qua animam impune non sinit fornicari. Visitare autem dicitur iniquitatem Patrum super filios & super tertianos & super quartanos (in Ebræo) h. e. in nepotes & abne- potes, odio habentes se, quod Chald. ad hosce refert, alii vero ad ipsos Patres, idque rectius, ut e cap. 34, 7. Jer. 32, 18. apparet. Diodor. Tarsensis, Severus, & Theodor. exclusive intelligunt, quod filii nepotes & abnepotes, non patres ipsi puniantur: sed inclusive id accipiendum esse merito docent Aug. in qq. V. & N. T. c. 14. Chrys. in Ps. 84. Leo Epist. 86. Greg. M. l. 15. Moral. c. 22. Neque vero in dubium vocandum cum Cornelio & Mario videtur, num parentum pro- ximorum peccata in liberos transeant: quum non ra- ro id evenire exempla, & experientia testentur, ne- que justitia divina permittat puniri in liberis paren- tum peccata, quorum nullo pacto participes sunt liberi, Ez. 18, 20. in quo tamen alia Dei, alia Magi- stratus est ratio. Huic illud jus præscriptum est, non occidentur filii pro parentibus Deut. 24, 16. Deus au- tem ad id astringi nequit, sed ἀυτεξουσίως agit, prout saluti communi, & propriæ quorumvis congruum id novit, quantum ad pœnas vel calamitates tem- porales, siquidem apud ipsum nemo prorsus innocens sit Ex. 34, 8. De æternis vero manet authentica illa: Anima quæ peccaverit, morietur. Non ergo est, quod restringatur hæc comminatio cum Greg. M. l. 15. Mor. c. 31. ad peccatum Originale, imo manifestum est de actualibus hic agi: Distinguendum modo in- ter peccata communia & personalia, pœnam item tem- poralem & æternam. Conf. Num. 14, 33. 1. Sam. 15, 2. Matth. 23. Huc etiam pertinet, quod liberi, quando parentibus gratia subtracta est, ob ipsorum culpam, mediorum salutis ablatione, consequenter etiam gratiæ mediis destituantur.

Sed quomodo parentibus mortuis id pœna est, quod patitur filius? Resp. Pœna est ipsis quatenus prædicta a Deo, unde non sine metu de forte libero- rum futura in vita sunt. Notandum tamen, quod quæ parentibus pœna sunt, filiis probationes & medi- cinæ, accommoda esse possint, si hi pii sint. Adde & hoc, quod Deus hic de eo loquatur, quod homines mereantur in pœnis, & quid juste facere possit, non tamen alliget se, quo minus erga impiorum poste- ros se benignum præstet: Unde impiorum paren- tum filii non raro gratiam consequuti leguntur, uti exemplo sunt Ezechias, Josias, & alii.

ET FACIAM MISERICORDIAM IN MILLIA. Non intuitu meritorum Patrum, uti Marius vult, quæ nulla sunt Gen. 32. vers. 10. Psalm. 143. v. 2. Es. 65. vers. 6. Dan. 9. vers. 4. Sed vi gratiæ & pro- missionis gratuitæ, ac propter Messiam, in quo uno sumus dilecti, & in gratia penes Deum Eph. 1 versu 6. Rom. 5. vers. 15. in cujus promissionem san- cti in precibus suis fiduciam exauditionis loca- runt, Exod. 32. v. 13. 2. Par. 6. vers. 42. Psalm. 132. vers. 10. Dan. 9. versu 17. Deus enim in judiciali visitatione iniquitates punit ex justitia, sed in visi- tatione gratiosa pios, & eorum posteritatem re- muneratur ex misericordia, ne quis cum superbis Pharisæis regulam urgeat: contrariorum contraria sunt consequentia: quia hæc contraria non sunt in eodem gradu. Inæqualem etiam ponit illius visita- tionis terminum: ut sciamus etsi in ipso æqualis sit justitia & misericordia, ratione tamen effectuum mi- sericordiam sese extendere ultra justitiam.

## 20:7
Vers. 7. THOU SHALT NOT TAKE) Namely, into thy mouth. But that is done not only by the proper name of GOD expressed, but also by any word whatsoever by which God is understood. This is not to be taken only concerning the name of God, but concerning all that by which God has revealed Himself, just as by the name of God it is accustomed to be understood, whatever of the Essence and will of God has been revealed in His word, Joh. 17. v. 6. and the very essence and Majesty of the Lord Psalm. 8. v. 2. therefore the Jews wrongly take this concerning the name Jehovah, as if its pronunciation were forbidden. Some say that it is forbidden here that the name of God be attributed to idols, which in Scripture are called vanity: Tertull. de idol. c. 20. Cyrill. l. 4. in Joh. in which manner indeed the name of God is profaned, but since this is idolatry, it pertains properly to the first commandment.

IN VAIN) That is, thou shalt not swear falsely, for לַשָּׁוְא and בַשֶּׁקֶר are the same, as appears in the ninth commandment when this chapter of Exodus is compared with the other of Deuteronomy, where the Greeks place in both places μαρτυρίαν ψευδῆ.

Thus Grotius restricts this only to perjury and a false oath, and that with the Socinians, which was also done by the Chaldean and Josephus. But although that is included here Lev. 19. v. 12. Matth. 5. v. 33. yet any rash or vain oath is here generally forbidden: as לַשּׁוְא is according to vanity, that is, vainly, lightly. LXX. ἐπὶ ματαίῳ in a vain matter. For that Hebrew word is so taken Mal. 3, 14. Jer. 4, 30. Psalm. 127. vers. 2. Whence the Socinians are mistaken, when they gather from this word that it was only forbidden to swear falsely and mendaciously, but not to swear without cause. See what we have said to Deut. 6. vers. 13. Nor indeed is any oath whatsoever simply and absolutely forbidden, as the Essenes thought; since God Himself in doubtful matters willed the oath to be the end of controversies Exod. 22. v. 2. Heb. 6. v. 16. and commanded to swear by His name, namely when the glory of GOD and the salvation of one's neighbor demands it, Deut. 6, 13. c. 10. v. 20.

Nor is a vain oath forbidden only by this interdict, but by this named species of the abuse of the divine name, immediately forbidden, consequently any abuse is forbidden. Just as in most commandments some one species of a grosser offense is expressed, so that the abomination of the remaining sins before the judgment of God may be shown: So here in the contrary manner, under the lesser, the greater is proposed to be thought of; because men think themselves innocent in the vain and idle usurpation of the divine name, therefore it is easily understood that by that being forbidden, the profanation and blasphemy of the divine name is more forbidden. One sins therefore against this commandment when the name of the Lord is taken in vain, not so much in the heart, when one thinks less reverently of God, or blasphemous thoughts occur to us, for these pertain to the first commandment, when God is not worshipped as God: as with the mouth, because the word נָשָׂא to take is accepted as the taking of the name of God into the mouth Psalm. 6, 4. Psalm. 50, 16. From which places it is gathered that there is a certain ellipsis here, to be supplied thus: Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord into thy mouth, so that this commandment properly curbs the tongue, and casts a bolt upon the mouth, in those things which concern the name of the Lord, against which interdict one sins not only in an oath, in the name of false gods Zeph. 1, 7. or by creatures Matth. 5, 34. or lightly without urgent necessity deposited Hos. 4, 16. Jam. 5, 12. or in an unjust cause, against truth or conscience Is. 48. v. 1. Jer. 4, 2. when impious or even impossible things are confirmed by an oath Matth. 14, 6. or those things which, having been confirmed by an oath, are not performed, if they can be done without prejudice to piety Jos. 9, 20. but also when in any way the name of God is not rightly usurped, which happens both in sins of commission, when we abuse the name of God, or profane and blaspheme it, and in sins of omission, when we do not invoke, adore, or celebrate it, as is fitting. Therefore perjuries and false swearings, futile adjurations, vain attestations of God, rash devotions, as also vain and illicit vows, concerning things not in our power, pertain here: as well as any abuse of the divine name, curses, blasphemies, execrations, imprecations, illicit consecrations, and blessings, incantations, and witchcrafts, auguries, and whatever magical superstitions. Lev. 20, 6. Deut. 18, 13. Likewise lies and deceits, and any deceptions which are done under the pretext of the name and word of God Jer. 14, 14. 15. irreverence of the Divine name, Epicurean discourses about God, jocose and ridiculous interpretations of the words of Scripture, heresies, and corruptions of the divine word, etc. Furthermore, the omission of the holy usurpation of the name of God, such as invocation, adoration, thanksgiving, confession, when it is required, as also the glorification of God, and also the confession of sin, which is required for the honor of God, when it is suppressed Psal. 30, 2. Prov. 28, 13. likewise when we are remiss and cold in prayers, we do not pray rightly, we are lazy in the praise of God, or not devout etc. Finally, when the abuse of the divine name is not hindered, and just and due zeal is not applied for the glory of the divine name etc. All of which are forbidden by this commandment. On the other hand, the religious use of the divine name is commanded in invocation, thanksgiving, preaching, confession of sins, confession of heavenly doctrine, blessing, celebration, etc., and specifically in an oath. Indeed, no command is given here (which the Jews seem to wish, when they number this among the affirmative precepts) that we must swear by the name of the Lord, Deut. 6, v. 13. But that when necessity demands it, we should perform oaths only in the name of the Lord, which sense some Rabbis acknowledge. Therefore, the act of swearing is not good in itself, but by hypothesis, if it be necessary: nor is it to be sought for its own sake, but because of the lack of other proof, Heb. 6, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NON ASSUMES) Nempe in os tuum. Id autem fit non tantum proprio DEI nomine expresso, sed etiam quovis vocabulo, quo Deus intelligitur. Non tantum de nomine Dei hoc accipiendum, sed de omni illo quo Deus se patefecit, quemad- modum nomine Dei solet intelligi, quicquid de Dei Essentia & voluntate in verbo ejus patefactum est, Joh. 17. v. 6. & essentia ipsa & Majestas Domini Psalm. 8. v. 2. ideo perperam Judæi hoc de nomine Jehovah accipiunt, quasi ejus pronunciatio vetetur. Nonnulli hic prohiberi dicunt, ne nomen Dei tribuatur idolis, quæ in Scriptura vanitas dicuntur: Tertull. de idol. c. 20. Cyrill. l. 4. in Joh. quo pacto sane prophanatur nomen Dei, sed quum hæc sit ido- lolatria, ad primum præceptum proprie pertinet.

IN VANUM) Id est falso non pejerabis, idem enim est לַשָּׁוְא & בַשֶּׁקֶר ut in præcepto nono apparet collato hoc Exodi capite cum altero Devteronomii, ubi Græci ponunt utroque loco μαρτυρίαν ψευδῆ.

Ita tantum ad perjurium & falsum juramen- tum restringit hoc Grotius, idque cum Socinianis, quod & a Chaldæo & Josepho factum. Sed quamvis id hic comprehendatur Lev. 19. v. 12. Matth. 5. v. 33. tamen quodvis temerarium vel vanum jura- mentum hic generatim prohibetur: uti לַשּׁוְא est secundum vanitatem, id est vane, leviter. LXX. ἐπὶ ματαίῳ in re vana. Nam ita vox illa Ebræa accipi- tur Mal. 3, 14. Jer. 4, 30. Psalm. 127. vers. 2. Unde falluntur Sociniani, cum solum prohibitum fuisse jurare falso, atque mendaciter, non autem sine cau- sa jurare, ex hac voce colligunt. Vid. quæ ad Deut. 6. vers. 13. diximus. Neque vero simpliciter & ab- solute prohibetur juramentum quodvis, ut Essæi pu- tarunt; Siquidem Deus ipse in dubiis juramentum finem controversiarum esse voluerit Exod. 22. v. 2. Ebr. 6. v. 16. & per nomen suum jurare jusserit, quan- do nempe id gloria DEI, & salus proximi postulat, Devt. 6, 13. c. 10. v. 20.

Neque solum hoc interdicto vanum juramen- tum prohibetur, sed nominata hac specie abusus nominis divini, immediate prohibita, consequenter quivis abusus prohibetur. Quemadmodum in plerisque præceptis una aliqua species crassioris delicti exprimitur, ut abominatio reliquorum pec- catorum coram Dei judicio ostendatur: Ita hic contrario modo sub minori majus cogitandum pro- ponitur; quia homines in vana & otiosa usurpa- tione nominis divini se insontes cogitant, ideo ea prohibita facile intelligitur magis prohibitam esse nominis divini prophanationem & blasphemiam. Pec- catur ergo adversus hoc præceptum, quando no- men Domini assumitur in vanum, non tam corde, cum minus reverenter de Deo cogitatur, aut blasphe- mæ cogitationes nobis incidunt, hæc enim ad pri- mum præceptum pertinent, cum Deus non ut Deus colitur: quam ore, quia verbum נָשָׂא assumere de assumtione nominis Dei in os accipitur Psalm. 6, 4. Psalm. 50, 16. Ex quibus locis colligitur, ellipsin quandam hic esse, ita supplendam: Non assumes no- men Domini in os tuum, ut hoc præceptum linguam proprie frænet, & ori repagulum injiciat, in iis, quæ nomen Domini concernunt, adversus quod interdictum peccatur non modo in juramento, in nomine falsorum deorum Zeph. 1, 7. aut per creaturas Matth. 5, 34. aut leviter citra urgentem necessita- tem deposito Hos. 4, 16. Jac. 5, 12. aut in causa inju- sta, contra veritatem aut conscientiam Es. 48. v. 1. Jer. 4, 2. cum impia vel etiam impossibilia juramen- to confirmantur Matth. 14, 6. aut quæ juramento confirmata non præstantur, si salva pietate fieri pos- sint Jos. 9, 20. sed etiam cum quocunque modo nomen Dei non recte usurpatur, quod fit tum in peccatis commissionis, cum abutimur nomine Dei, aut id pro- phanamus & blasphemamus, tum in peccatis omis- sionis, cum illud non invocamus, adoramus, cele- bramus, ut par est. Pertinent ergo huc perjuria & pejerationes, futiles dejerationes, vanæ Dei attestatio- nes, temerariæ devotiones, ut & vota vana, & illicita, de rebus non sitis in potestate nostra: nec non quivis abusus nominis divini, maledictiones, bla- sphemationes, execrationes, imprecationes, illicitæ consecrationes, ac benedictiones, incantationes, & veneficia, auguria, & quæcunque Magicæ superstitio- nes. Lev. 20, 6. Deut. 18, 13. Mendacia item & doli, ac deceptiones quævis, quæ sub prætextu nominis & verbi divini fiunt Jer. 14, 14. 15. irreverentia no- minis Divini, Epicurei sermones de Deo, jocosæ & ridiculæ verborum Scripturæ interpretationes, hæreses, & corruptelæ verbi divini, &c. Adhæc usurpationis nominis Dei sanctæ intermissio, utpote invocationis, adorationis, gratiarum actionis, confessionis, cum ea requiritur, ut & glorificationis Dei, nec non con- fessionis peccati, quæ requiritur in honorem Dei, cum ea supprimitur Psal. 30, 2. Prov. 28, 13. item cum in precibus sumus remissi & frigidi, non recte pre- camur, pigri sumus in laude Dei, aut non devoti &c. Denique cum non impeditur abusus nominis di- vini, non adhibetur zelus justus ac debitus pro glo- ria divini nominis &c. Quæ omnia hoc præcepto vetantur. Ex adverso vero præcipitur religiosus usus nominis divini in invocatione, gratiarum actione, præ- dicatione, confessione peccatorum, confessione doctri- næ cœlestis, benedictione, celebratione &c. & in specie in juramento. Non est quidem præceptum hic da- tum (quod videntur Judæi velle, cum præceptis af- firmativis hoc annumerant) ut per nomen Domi- ni juremus Deut. 6. v. 13. Sed ut quando necessitas exigit, nonnisi in nomine Domini juramenta præste- mus, quem sensum agnoscunt Rabbini nonnulli. Jurandi ergo actus non per se bonus, sed ex hypothe- si, si necessarius sit: nec per se appetendus, sed ob de- fectum alterius probationis Ebr. 6, 17.

## 20:8
Vers. 8. SANCTIFY) You shall worship holily by giving thanks to GOD, because He created men and the world for the sake of men.

Not only by giving thanks, much less only for the work of creation, since thanks are to be given to God for all benefits, and especially for spiritual ones, and on the Sabbath the spiritual and heavenly concession of the eternal Sabbath ought to be celebrated; but also by praying, and by invoking the name of the Lord, and by performing other spiritual works which contribute to the celebration of the Sabbath.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SANCTIFICES) Sancte colas gratias agendo DEO, quod homines & mundum hominum causa condiderit.

Non tantum gratias agendo, nedum solum pro opere creationis, siquidem pro omnibus beneficiis, & imprimis spiritualibus gratiæ Deo agendæ sint, & in Sabbato spiritualis & cœlestis æterni Sabbati con- cessio celebrari debeat; sed etiam precando, & nomen Domini invocando, aliaque spiritualia opera, quæ ad Sabbati celebrationem faciunt, peragendo.

## 20:10
Vers. 10. ANY WORK) The servant as we said above, where the Passover was being discussed. Concerning this rigid rest of the Jewish Sabbath, see Dio Cassius, Seneca in Augustine, the poets of the Satires and Epigrams, and after them Rutilius.

YOUR SON AND YOUR DAUGHTER) At that age which is governed by the commands of parents.

THE STRANGER WHO IS WITHIN YOUR GATES) No foreigners are held by that law of Sabbath rest, except by reason of cohabitation with the Israelites: for it would have disturbed the civil order, and brought loss to the Israelites, if others living among them had been permitted to do work.

Latin:

Vers. 10. OMNE OPUS) Famulum ut supra diximus, ubi de Paschate agebatur. De hac rigida quiete Sabbati Ju- daici vide Dionem Cassium, Senecam apud Augustinum, Poe- tas Satyrarum & Epigrammatum, post eos Rutilium.

FILIUS TUUS ET FILIA TUA) In ea ætate, quæ pa- rentum imperiis gubernatur.

ADVENA QVI EST INTRA PORTAS TUAS) Nulli extranei lege ista otii Sabbatici tenentur, nisi ex coha- bitatione cum Israelitis: turbasset enim ordinem civilem, & damnum attulisset Israelitis, si alii inter ipsos viventes per- missi essent opus facere.

## 20:11
Verf. 11. HEAVEN AND EARTH) This universe, as at the beginning of Genesis. AND ALL THINGS THAT ARE IN THEM) Herbs, trees, animals. THEREFORE THE LORD BLESSED THE SABBATH DAY AND SANCTIFIED IT) And for that reason, since there was also a need for the leisure of some day to temper servile works, this day, as being specially dedicated to God from the beginning, was preferred to others. Leisure, however, well befits the Heptad, which is "a virgin and motherless," as Philo speaks, and the writer of the Theologumena Arithmeticae. See also Capella.

He distinguishes, along with the Jews and especially R. Judah Barbefalbele and R. Ephraim in Keli Jakar, the cause of worship and leisure: as he declared himself more clearly in the explanation of the Decalogue, page 40. That holy worship has as its cause the created world; the leisure, which is immediately commanded, the Egyptian servitude. The former pertains to the human race; the latter to the Hebrews alone, Exod. 21, 13, which is also the opinion of Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 30, and Eusebius, History, chapter 4. The latter [is] in the same place; In which [matters] and others, which are handed down there concerning the Sabbath, not one error lies hidden. First, that he refers the leisure of the Sabbath to the Hebrews alone. One had to distinguish the moral leisure of the Sabbath from the ceremonial. For the moral is perpetual, and looks to all; but the ceremonial is temporary and proper to the Israelite people. Although, therefore, we can easily concede that there is something ceremonial in this precept, even as regards the leisure prescribed on this Sabbath, as far as the rigor of the leisure is concerned—to which, indeed, the "deuteroses" (traditions) of the Jews added much, to which they were not bound by divine constitution, as is known even from the Evangelical history: yet it is moral that we ought to rest on the Sabbath from ordinary and servile labors, but in such a way that works of necessity, piety, and charity are not considered excluded. The rigor of the rest prescribed to the Jews is detected in the prohibition of a journey for the sake of transacting private business, Exod. 16, v. 29, 30, and the kindling of a fire, Exod. 35, v. 3, and the carrying of a burden, Jer. 17, v. 21, Nehem. 13, v. 15, 16, 17, all of which we acknowledge to have been temporary and proper to the Jews. But this is perpetual and looks to all, that some day in the week be sacred, on which both beasts and men cease somewhat from the burden of labors. Which was prescribed not to the Hebrews only, but to all. Because God willed the Sabbath to be kept by all. But what else is the Sabbath than "anapausis," a cessation from the labor of the body, and rest, if you look at the etymon of the word? Remember, says Jehovah, that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall work and do all your works. But on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God: you shall do no work in it. Nowhere is this restricted to the Jews. Nor is it abrogated in the New Testament: as far as the moral [part] is concerned, which we have mentioned. And it flourished before the Israelites were chosen as the people of God, indeed from the very origin of the world, Gen. 2, 1. Furthermore, the cause is also general, looking to all. Because it is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. For in six days the Lord God made heaven and earth. Therefore Christians also are obligated to rest, so that then they themselves may cease from the works of servants, and also allow their own to rest. Christ says the Sabbath was made for man, not for the Jew only, Mark 2, v. 22. Then if this is moral, that some time be peculiarly consecrated to divine worship, it will also be moral that during that time we rest from labors, as being those by which the external worship of God is hindered. The sanctification of the Sabbath is divine, both segregative from profane use and consecrative to sacred uses. Therefore both sanctifications are prescribed to us also; nor can the latter be without the former. Therefore Chrysostom called this law of the Sabbath immovable for Christians: Hom. 4 in Matth. Lest, therefore, those things happen to us, let us prescribe this law to ourselves as immovable, and not to us only, but also to our spouses and our children, so that we may place this one day of the whole week, on which we gather to listen, entirely in the mention of those things which are said. Which truly cannot be done unless we cease from profane works and make our own cease.

Secondly, Grotius does not correctly explain the blessing of the seventh day made by God at the beginning of the world, Gen. 2, as if worship were commanded there, but not leisure. But that God so sanctified this day from the beginning that He also sanctioned leisure and cessation from common works, the words of Moses do not obscurely teach, Gen. 2, v. 2, 3. And God completed on the seventh day His work which He had made: and RESTED on the seventh day from all the work which He had performed. And He blessed the seventh day: and sanctified it: BECAUSE in it He HAD CEASED from all His work which God created to make. Thus, therefore, He sanctified the seventh day, that He willed it to be worshipped holily, and that on it one should CEASE from every profane work, in memory of the created world and of the rest or cessation of God from the work of creation, celebrated on this day. And thus the supreme lawgiver explains it most clearly, Exod. 20, verse 21. Remember, that you SANCTIFY the Sabbath day. Six days YOU SHALL WORK, and do all your works. But on the seventh day is the SABBATH (rest or cessation) of the Lord your God, you shall do no work in it. -- For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them and RESTED on the seventh day. THEREFORE the Lord blessed the Sabbath day, and sanctified it. Who now does not see that the Lord so blessed and sanctified the seventh day, that man might then be free for holy worship on it, and indeed REST from all his work. And that was done THEREFORE, because God RESTED on that day. For these things are composed among themselves: in six days God made heaven and earth and all things that are in them; And: six days you shall work, and do all your works: Likewise, On the seventh day the Lord RESTED: And, on the seventh day YOU SHALL REST, nor shall you do any work in it. And by that reasoning it is taught here with a loud voice that God blessed this day from the beginning, and sanctified it, namely on account of the rest from profane and common works alike, and pious worship. For Grotius cannot deny that that primordial sanctification is referred to in the words of the Decalogue. And he seems to refer to this, he says in Explic. Decal. p. 40, in Deuteronomy Moses, when to the words Φύλαξαι τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν Σαββάτων ἁγιάζειν ἀυτὴν he adds, ὃν τρόπον ἐνετείλατό σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σε: namely already long ago from the beginning of the world. In the same manner, therefore, from the beginning of the world, when God sanctified this day, HE COMMANDED it to be celebrated, just as he later demanded it here in the law. But in the law he not only demanded pious worship, but also rest or cessation from all our work. Wherefore from the beginning of the world he already required on this day, along with worship, cessation from all work. Nor should it be passed over that Grotius himself praises the observation of the Hebrews; that this day was chosen for rest, because God had rested on it, and from the beginning had dedicated the same to joy and the memory of creation. But Maimonides (says Grotius Explic. Decal. p. 42) and other Hebrews distinguish very well the reason why REST was commanded, and why ON THIS DAY. The former reason is openly expressed in Deuteronomy: namely because, having been liberated by divine aid from Egypt, they ought to consider how harsh the servitude was, and consequently to treat servants and others committed to their authority humanely. The latter is in this place (Exod. 20. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God) by which it is signified that since any day could be taken for rest, this one was chosen by God, because from the beginning it had already been dedicated to joy and thanks for the creation of the world, and God himself had ceased to create the things of this world on that day: Whence the name Sabbath. Thus Isaac Arania, and others. These are Grotius's words. If this day was chosen for REST, because from the beginning it had been dedicated to joy and memory, it was certainly dedicated to the memory of the Lord's REST and to rest from common works, in memory of the CESSATION and REST of the Lord from his works, whence it obtained the name of Sabbath. Nor is the opinion of the Hebrews otherwise, as we shall say later. Furthermore, since Ex. 16. v. 24. The Sabbath, as a day already celebrated among the Jews before the law was given, is mentioned in these words: this is what Jehovah proclaimed, rest is the Sabbath made for Jehovah tomorrow, what you are to cook, cook today, it is manifest that this day was already then known and celebrated, not only for religious worship, but also for vacation from work and rest: since for its celebration they were also required to rest in the gathering of Manna. An argument is also usually sought from the history of the flood Gen. 8. v. 10. that Noah waited seven days after the diminution of the waters, before he sent out the dove for the first time, and then waited another seven days again, because on that day the kindness of GOD was explored by Noah, on which they worshipped God singularly in the ark, on that day they awaited rest from the troubles of the flood, on which, resting themselves from other cares, they devoted themselves SOLELY to the worship of God. But the proof from Heb. 4. v. 3. 4. is stronger.
