The Apostle teaches that those words I swore in my anger, if they shall enter into my rest, were uttered when works had already been completed from the foundation of the world, having adduced the passage Gen. 2. for he said in a certain place concerning the seventh day thus: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works: he shows that the promise of rest made, included in the commination of exclusion from rest made to the incredulous, cannot be understood of the rest of the Sabbath, because already with the works of God completed from the foundations of the world having been laid, GOD had rested on the seventh day. Whence it is clear that the rest of the Sabbath, according to the Apostle, began from the completion of the works of God after the sixth day: which is Rivet's argument in Explic. Decal. page 119. which he defends against Gomarus in the Appendix subjoined there in chapter 3. page 130. seqq. The same is confirmed also by the very appellation of the Sabbath, for what else is the Sabbath than rest, and the day of the Sabbath, than a day consecrated to rest? Since therefore the Sabbath was from the beginning of the world Gen. 2. v. 2. it is necessary to confess that not only the worship of God flourished on that day from the creation of the world; but also the very leisure and rest from labors.

And this seems to be the opinion of all, both ancients and moderns, who acknowledge that the Sabbath was celebrated from the origin of the world, which seemed so to most. Concerning the institution and origin of the Sabbath, indeed, certain divisions of opinion are found: which some refer finally to the law, but others deduce from the first origin of the world: which controversy occurred between Fr. Gomarus and Andreas Rivetus in Explic. Decal. and Antonius Walæus in LL. CC., the former defending the novelty of the Sabbath, the latter its antiquity: But I do not find anyone besides Grotius who separated leisure from common works from the law or celebration of the Sabbath from the worship of God: all constitute the Sabbath, whenever it was instituted or began to be observed, as a day of both pious worship and leisure, or rest from profane things, and they wish it to have been instituted and observed for that reason. Grotius alone is peculiar here. Most derive the religious leisure of the Sabbath from the sanctification of the seventh day of creation. From the Hebrews, Philo lib. 3. de vit. Mos. says the day of the Sabbath has a privilege from nature, from which the birthday of the world was made. Josephus deduces its rest from the primeval sanctification of the Sabbath in Genesis 2, Antiquit. l. 1. c. 2. And thus Moses says that the whole world and all things contained in the world were made in six days; but on the seventh GOD rested and ceased from works. Wherefore we also celebrate recreation from labors through that day, calling it the Sabbath. The inference made with the word wherefore teaches that he connects the very calling of the Jews with the first sanctification of the Sabbath and the rest of God. Isaac Atias the Jew, in the treasury published at Venice in the year 1627, teaches that this was known even to the Gentiles, and impressed upon their hearts concerning the Sabbath day, part 1. number 157. Clemens Alexandr. observes that not only the Hebrews, but also the Greeks knew the seventh day to be sacred, lib. 5. Stromat., and Grotius confesses, from Clement and Eusebius in the Praeparatio, and likewise from the verses of Hesiod, that this veneration of the Sabbath reached the nations also. But that they believed it was destined only for worship, and not for leisure and rest, can be taught neither from Clement nor from others. Eusebius lib. 13. Evang. praeparat. proves the sanctity of the seventh day from Plato, Homer, Callimachus, and the eulogies of Solon. Josephus l. 2. contr. Appion. confirms that this vacation or rest of the seventh day is comprehensive: That there is no city anywhere of Greeks or Barbarians, nor any nation, to which the custom of the week, in which the Jews WERE AT LEISURE, has not reached. Which was also observed by Philo lib. 2. de Vit. Mos. Our law admonishes everyone of their duty: Barbarians, Greeks, inhabitants of the continent as well as of the islands, Westerners and Easterners, Europeans and Asians, the whole habitable world even to the furthest limits. For who does not honor that sacred day recurring through individual weeks? To which it contributes that the Ancients, before the method of calculating by years and months had been invented, distinguished the spaces of time by weeks, as Salmasius observed from the Chronological works of Georgius Syncellus: whence Rivetus, since all nations from every age have acknowledged this revolution of seven days, concludes that its origin could have had no other source than the inveterate opinion that the world was created in six days, and that on the seventh there was a cessation from work, so that it is most likely that after this first week the following one was numbered in this way, and the rest in succession, and that this obtained among all nations. Therefore Augustinus Steuchus, Eugubinus, in his Cosmopoeia on chapter 2 of Genesis, observes that the seventh day was then sanctified and afterwards held by all nations as venerable and sacred.

If it pleases you to hear the opinion of the ancient Fathers, Chrysostom, homily 9 on chapter 2 of Genesis, concerning the sanctification and rest of the seventh day, says: 'Already from the beginning God insinuates this doctrine to us, teaching that in the complete cycle of a week one whole day is to be set apart and reserved for spiritual work.' Tertullian, Apology chapter 16, reports concerning the Gentiles that they decreed the day of Saturn for leisure and feasting, deviating themselves in the Jewish manner; whence, if one compares book 1 to the nations chapter 13, it is gathered that they were idle on the Sabbath day, which for them was Saturn's day; which the Romans therefore considered less suitable for conducting business, as appears from Tibullus book 1, Eclogue 3, and Ovid, book 1 of the Art of Love. The same Tertullian, book 4 against the Jews, observes that the Jews say that from the BEGINNING God sanctified the seventh day, by resting from all the works which He made, and from that point also that Moses said to the people: Remember the Sabbath day; and from his own opinion in book 4 against Marcion, ch. 12, he teaches that Christ Himself made the Sabbath day, holy from the beginning by the blessing of the Father, more holy by His own benefaction. Theodoret, to the adds these things, in which he demonstrated that He did not think that day useless for creating, but established it as accommodated for rest. Augustine, Epistle 86 to Casulanus, derives the vacation from there from the sanctification of the seventh day. But the fact that some of the Fathers seem to derive the Sabbath from the Mosaic law—Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Eusebius, Damascenus, to whose opinion Gomarus appeals along with Abulensis—is to be understood either concerning the rigor sanctioned in the law and the Mosaic ceremonies, or certainly it looks not to the negation of that primordial sanctification, but to the renewal of the same.

Among the Papists, the Reformed, and the Orthodox, the matter is placed almost beyond the hazard of controversy, since the Papists—if you except Tostatus, Catharinus, Genebrardus, Cornelius a Lapide, Salianus, Emanuel Saa, and others—and the Reformed also—besides Gomarus, most of them, Zwingli, Calvin, Beza, Martyr, Pelican, Bullinger, Bucanus, Zanchius, Ursinus, Gualtherus, Aretius, Bertram, Mercer, Fagius, Junius, Marloratus, Pareus, Zepperus, Fecqvernekinus, Martin, Alsted, and those who cite them, Rivetus and Walaeus, and others—unanimously acknowledge that the rest of the Sabbath day has its origin from the institution made on the seventh day of creation. Which is also the opinion of our own B. Luther, Chemnitz, Gerhard, Franzius, etc. is the unanimous opinion: Some of whom also prove the same from the added mnemonic particle: Remember the Sabbath day, that you may sanctify it: because God wished by the same to remind the ancients of its institution: Thus Bullinger in chapter 12 of Matthew.

and Chemnitz in Exposition of the Decalogue. What of the fact that some Jews today also confess that the Sabbath was observed before the law by Abraham and other Patriarchs; which opinion Menasse Ben-Israel defends in problem 8 concerning creation, and indeed not only by the sanctification of the divine name, but also by vacation from labors, who also brings forward an argument for this matter from Schemot Rabba, that Moses asked Pharaoh in Egypt to permit the afflicted people to cease from labors for one day, and that having obtained this, he chose the Sabbath by tradition. And these things concerning the second.

Thirdly, he cannot be absolved from error, because Grotius denies that the Lord's Day was substituted in the place of the Sabbath, without doubt to gratify the Anabaptists, who judge the precept concerning the Sabbath to be entirely abolished, so that by the force of Christian liberty they think any works are lawful on any day, since the Socinians, the necessary associates of Grotius, seem to go off to that as well. These things being known, Grotius writes in Explanation of the Decalogue, p. 41, they refute those who think that the first day of the week, i.e., the Lord's Day, was substituted in the place of the Sabbath. For nowhere is mention made of that thing by Christ, nowhere by the Apostles. And when the Apostle says that Christians are not to be judged for Sabbaths or new moons, Col. 2:16, he shows that they are free from that law of resting, which liberty would be nothing if the day had been changed while the law remained. But these things are contrary to the common opinion and religion of Christians, and if they do not abolish all worship of the Lord's Day, they certainly expose it to the lust of anyone. Although Grotius professes that Christians by voluntary consent used that day on which Christ had risen for their assemblies, and that it is not for those living socially to violate such consent when it has passed into a custom, yet petulant minds will not allow themselves to be restrained by voluntary consent or custom and rite alone, if a divine precept is lacking, but will convert liberty into license, which the bands of Anabaptists sufficiently teach. But then Grotius thinks that that custom did not enjoin rest further than as it was necessary for holding assemblies. Beyond this, he will hardly permit anyone to be bound on our Sabbath day to vacation from the works of servants, pleading the cause of the Anabaptistic confusion of days. For thus, because assemblies can be held on every day, and rest is necessary for holding assemblies, we will be no more bound to rest on the Lord's Day than on other days, as one might please. Therefore, no difference of days will remain at all, none will be to be consecrated peculiarly to GOD by divine law: The precept concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath will have been utterly abrogated, both as to the peculiar worship of God and as to the cessation from common works. We have thus to what end the superior Grotian hypotheses were directed: namely, that the advocate of a most wretched cause might be able to help the Socinians and Anabaptists. If the Sabbath day is abrogated, and the Lord's Day not substituted in its place, what remains but to say that no day of the week is dedicated to God? But the precept concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath is not merely ceremonial, but since it is a part of the Decalogue, and all ten precepts concern all men, and none looks to the Jews alone, it contains something moral which is of perpetual right, otherwise there will not be ten, but only nine precepts of the divine tables which will be incumbent upon us, nor will the whole law be inscribed in us by the Holy Spirit in hearts of flesh, which was inscribed on tables of stone, 2 Cor. 3:3. Certainly the sanctification which is commanded on this day is not something ceremonial, but moral: not abolished by the death of Christ, but restored: Nor is the vacation or breathing of sons and servants merely ceremonial, but has something moral in itself: just as the example of GOD Himself, who rested from His works, does not at all pertain to ceremonies, or to mere shadows of future things, nor should the ends of rest, the consideration of the works of God and the celebration of the same, be referred to that. Furthermore, how sacrosanct this commandment should be held by us, let that great Nota bene of the most excellent and greatest legislator God teach us: REMEMBER, that you may keep the Sabbath day holy, which recalls to memory the ancient institution, made from the foundation of the world, and therefore it is to be religiously observed by us all, no less under the New than the Old Testament. The reason also, which God subjoined, concerns all men, that in six days God worked, on the seventh he rested, and therefore blessed it, and sanctified the same: For this memorial of the hexaemeron of creation, and of the day of the Lord's rest, is given no less to us than to the Jews: This example of God binds us no less than the Jews to the observation of the seventh day, when we have done our works for six days; for our sake no less than for the sake of the Jews did God bless the seventh day, and sanctified it as a day of Sabbath and of rest. Although it is indeed ceremonial that the Sabbath day was to be dedicated to the worship of God and to rest, yet this pertains to the substance of the commandment, and it is moral, that when we have worked for six days, we ought to be free for GOD on the seventh, and thus consecrate one of the seven days to the external worship of GOD. And this is what Chrysostom observed in homily 10 on chapter 2 of Genesis. Now from here from the beginning GOD insinuates this doctrine to us, teaching IN THE CIRCLE OF THE WEEK ONE WHOLE DAY to be set apart and reserved for spiritual operation.

And how can the operation of six days exist, unless it is interrupted and terminated by the seventh day of rest? If it is denied that one day from the cycle of the week is to be consecrated to worship and rest, by the force of the divine precept concerning the Sabbath, then certainly no certain number or cycle of days will be able to be limited by any divine precept, since there was no mention of any other number anywhere in any other precept, and consequently it will be permitted to choose either the twentieth or the fiftieth or certainly any one at all, and thus it will be entirely free for anyone to choose whichever he wishes, without the violation of any divine precept. All indeed admit this, that by the force of this precept, some certain time is destined for sacred worship. Although they disagree about whether it follows from the force and analogy of this precept that one day from the cycle of seven days should be observed, with a few thinking that only some time should be destined for sacred worship indeterminately, and that the seventh day is not precisely inferred by this precept: yet all admit by the force of the precept that a certain time is owed to divine worship: and they say that this is inscribed in nature, that some time ought to be consecrated to worship, and they make this the moral part of this precept: which consequently could never be abrogated. Grotius, thinking otherwise, is left alone here with his Anabaptists. Nor should it be doubted, in the New Testament, that the seventh day was defined in place of the seventh day of creation, the Lord's day of the resurrection, and thus one day out of the week was retained, by the force of the divine precept, the Lord's day alone being substituted for the day of the Sabbath; whence it is again confirmed that this must be acknowledged by us also as invariable and moral in this precept, namely that one of the seven days ought to be sacred to GOD, because the Church of the New Testament has so judged, nor has anyone been found, or will ever be found, who dares or is able to attempt any public change here. For that which binds the whole Church from the foundation of the world until the consummation of the age, both under the Old and the New Testament, both before the law, and under the law, and after the ceremonial law was abrogated, that is to be held as moral and perpetual.

It is indeed disputed whether Christ substituted the day we call the Lord's day, or whether, as is pleasing to most, this was done by the Apostles, but all easily agree on this, that the observance of the Lord's day did not prevail by custom alone or human constitution, but was sanctioned by some divine institution: since those things which the Apostles sanctioned by Apostolic authority are to be held as divine institutions. Concerning which dispute Walæus may be read in his dissertation on the Sabbath, where he attributes the former opinion to Eusebius, Cyril of Alexandria, Justin, Fr. Junius, Piscator, and Perkins, and thinks the latter is more received, and he himself follows it. However, those opinions seem to be able to be reconciled without difficulty, if it is said that Christ indeed consecrated this day by his resurrection which took place on this day and by his example, when he appeared to the Disciples on the same day, except Thomas, and afterwards on the other seventh day after eight days he again showed himself, with Thomas present, John 20:19, 26; and on the same day he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the gathered Apostles, Acts 2 (although Walæus strives to render all those things doubtful), and in Revelation 1:10 by the consensus of all the first day of the week is called ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, as if, if not expressly sanctioned by the Lord, it was nevertheless consecrated by his example. But the Apostles, by the divine authority in which they excelled, when previously the first day of the week was celebrated as a feast in honor of the Lord's resurrection and appearance, as well as the Spirit sent down from heaven (for it is not to be believed that no certain day in those of the Christians of the New Testament was sanctified by firstfruits or that the Sabbath was celebrated with the Jews before the day of the Lord's resurrection), subsequently sanctified this first day of the week and instituted it as the ordinary Sabbath of the Christians. And therefore rightly Augustine, Homily 15 on the words of the Apostles: The Lord's resurrection promised us an eternal day, and consecrated for us the Lord's day, which is called the Lord's day, because he rose on that day. And Epistle 119 to Januarius, chapter 13: The Lord's day was declared to Christians, not to the Jews, by the resurrection of the Lord, and from that time it began to have its festivity. Cyril, book 12 on John, chapter 38. Note that he did not simply narrate the matter, but added diligently, after eight days, and with all gathered in one place: Therefore the eighth day must be the Lord's day: for on the first of the Sabbaths he appeared to the others, that is, on the Lord's day; afterwards on the eighth day in succession, with both extremes counted, the disciples gathered again, with Thomas present, in a similar way see the Lord. Rightly, therefore, holy congregations are held in the churches on the eighth day. Nor indeed can any beginning of an institution made by the Church be designated or brought forward, nor could an institution made after the departure of the Apostles have bound the Church throughout the whole world, as it is certain to no one, as history testifies, that the whole Church was bound to the observance of the Lord's day up to this day. What is held concerning τῇ μίᾳ τῶν Σαββάτων in Acts 20:7, on which the disciples gathered to break bread, Grotius himself understands as the Lord's day, and it is so accepted by most; by Justin in Dialogue with Trypho, by Chrysostom in this place, by Augustine, Theophylact, and Bede, since in the manner of the Hebrews ONE is used for FIRST, Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1. Compare Genesis 1:12. That day was therefore then an ordinary assembly by Apostolic institution. So 1 Corinthians 16:2: But concerning the collections which are made for the Saints, as I have ORDAINED for the churches of Galatia, so also do you. On the ONE OF THE SABBATH let each one of you store up by himself. On the first day of the week, as Beza rendered it. Chrysostom: On the one of the Sabbath, that is, on the Lord's day, let each one store up by himself, putting away what has pleased him well. See how he also exhorts from the time: for the day was suitable for bringing them to almsgiving: for remember, he says, what things you have obtained on that day: for ineffable goods and the root and beginning of our life were made in it. But not for this reason alone is the time suitable for exercising kindness with a prompt and eager mind, but also because it has rest and relaxation and immunity and freedom from labors. For a mind freed from labors is rendered more ready and more apt for mercy. Furthermore, communicating with the venerable and immortal things also brings and commits great eagerness of mind; therefore, let each one of you, not simply this one or that one, but each one, whether he be poor, or rich, or man, or woman, or slave, or free, store it up with himself: he did not say, carry it into the Church, lest they blush on account of the small amount, but when they have increased the contribution by collections made little by little, when I have arrived, then let him show it. In the meantime, he says, store it up with yourself and make your house a church, a little chest, a treasury: be a guardian of the sacred money, a steward of the poor appointed by yourself. Thus far Chrysostom. Jerome likewise explains the collection to be instituted on the Lord's day, but in such a way that it may be done publicly, and be carried into the Church on individual Lord's days; just as in Jewish Synagogues collections were made publicly on Sabbaths, and even now are done among us on Lord's days: which custom Justin, Apol. II, teaches was also received in the Ancient Church. Thus, therefore, by Apostolic ordination the Lord's day was already designated for holding public assemblies: for which reason it was also specifically called κυριακὴ, because it was consecrated to the Lord: although afterwards by the edict of Constantine the Great, as is known from Eusebius's Oration on the praises of Constantine, the observance of the Lord's day was confirmed: as it was already received before throughout the Christian world, and was frequented by common use among the Romans and Greeks and other peoples: so that it could not acknowledge any other than an Apostolic origin, according to the Rule of Augustine, De Bapt. cap. XXIV. What the universal Church holds, and was not instituted by Councils, but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by no other than Apostolic authority.

Nor is there any reason for Grotius to object to the observance of the Sabbath, which, since it was sacred and solemn along with the Lord's day in the ancient Church, from which it cannot be judged that these were substituted by the Apostles in its place: Because even if the Sabbath was also sacred, and for that reason those days were held as brothers, it was not, however, equally sacred and solemn among Christians as the first day of the week, but only a preparation for the solemn holiday of the Lord's day was made on it, nor was there a cessation from ordinary works on the Sabbath in the same way, nor was it celebrated with such solemnity as the ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, as is gathered from Eusebius, lib. IV. de Vit. Constant. cap. 18. Indeed, it was reprobated among the Ebionites, among other things, that they celebrated the Sabbath day and the Lord's day similarly, as witnessed by Eusebius, lib. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 21. And it was decreed in the Council of Laodicea, can. XXIX, that Christians ought not to Judaize and be idle on the Sabbath, but should work on that day; but preferring the Lord's day, they should be idle if they can, as Christians: but if they are found to be Judaizing, let them be anathema before Christ. The Constitutions of the Apostles, by which it is commanded that no one should work on the Sabbath, but should be free for the study of piety, are of no authority, much less Apostolic, being spurious and adulterated, to which Grotius therefore appealed here in vain. But what Col. 2:16 commands, that no one should judge us in food, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, does not abolish the moral precept concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath, but what was ceremonial in it, and belonged to the shadow of things to come: such as is not the cessation from ordinary labors, and divine worship, and a certain day of the week consecrated to the same. Nor is that liberty to be valued as nothing because we still restrict the cessation and worship to a certain day: since no little has been remitted from the rigor of the law concerning the Sabbath, which obtained among the Jews, as previously observed. Add that the laws binding the Jews to certain times looked then to a part of divine worship; but among Christians the observance of a certain day does not constitute a part of worship, but was decreed only for the sake of order, as a certain circumstance of worship: since otherwise it is permitted to worship God in this way at all times, nor are we precisely bound to days, as the Jews are, so that anyone could deservedly judge us for it: which is contrary to Christian liberty. Let Jerome's Comm. l. III. in Gal. IV. be compared. Concerning the Sabbath against the Jews, Fr. Spanheim, l. III. dubior. Evang. dub. XIV. et seqq., can be read.

Latin:

Verf. 11. COELUM ET TERRAM) Univerfum hoc, ut initio Geneseos. ET OMNIA QUAE IN EIS SUNT) Herbas, arbores, animalia. IDCIRCO BENEDIXIT DOMINUS DIEM SABBATHI ET SANCTIFICAVIT EUM) Ac propterea cum etiam ad temperandas ferviles operas diei alicujus otio opus esset, hic dies, ut ab initio specialiter Deo dicatus, prælatus est aliis. Bene autem convenit otium Heptadi, quæ παρθένος καὶ ἀμήτωρ ut Philo loquitur, & scriptor θεολογυμένων τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς. Vide & Capellam.

Distinguit cum Judæis & imprimis R. Juda Barbefalbele & R. Ephraim in Keli jacar, cultus & otii causam: ut in explic. Decal. luculentiùs se declaravit pag. 40. Sanctus ille cultus causam habet mundum conditum: otium, quod mox præcipitur, Ægyptiacam servitutem. Illud ad genus humanum pertinet; hoc ad Ebræos solos Exod. 21, 13. quæ & Irenæi sententia lib. 4. cap. 30. & Eusebii Histor. cap. 4. Hæc ibidem; In quibus vero & aliis, quæ illic tradita de Sabbato sunt, non unus latet error. Primum, quod Sabbati otium ad solos Ebræos referat. Distinguendum erat otium Sabbati morale a ceremoniali. Morale enim perpetuum est, & ad omnes spectat: ceremoniale vero temporarium & populo Israelitico proprium. Etsi ergo concedere facile possimus; esse aliquid ceremoniale in hoc præcepto, etiam quantum ad otium præscriptum in hoc Sabbatho, quoad rigorem otii, cui vero δευτερώσεις Judæorum multum addidere, ad quod divina constitutione adstricti non erant, uti vel ex historia Evangelica notum est: Id tamen morale est, quod in Sabbatho ab ordinariis & servilibus laboribus quiescere debeamus, sed ita, ut necessitatis, pietatis & charitatis opera exclusa non censeantur. Rigor requiei Judæis præscriptæ deprehenditur in interdicto itineris negotii privati expediundi causa Exod. 16. v. 29. 30. & accensionis ignis Exod. 35. v. 3. & portationis oneris Jer. 17. v. 21. Nehem. 13. v. 15. 16. 17. quæ omnia temporaria & Judæorum propria fuisse, agnoscimus. Sed hoc perpetuum & ad omnes spectat, quod dies aliqua in septimana sacra sit, qua & jumenta & homines nonnihil a laborum onere cessant. Quod non Ebræis tantum præscriptum, sed omnibus. Quia Sabbathum Deus servari ab omnibus voluit. Quid vero aliud est Sabbathum, quam ἀνάπαυσις cessatio a labore corporis, & quies, si vocis Etymon aspicias? Memento, inquit Jehovah, ut diem Sabbathi sanctifices. Sex diebus operaberis & facies omnia opera tua. Septimo autem die Sabbathum Domini Dei tui est: non facies omne opus in eo. Nuspiam hoc ad Judæos restringitur. Nec in Nov. Testam. abrogatur: quantum ad morale, quod diximus. Et viguit, antequam Israelitæ in populum Dei eligerentur, imo inde ab origine mundi Gen. 2, 1. Porro causa etiam generalis est, ad omnes spectans. Quia Sabbathum Domini DEI tui est. Sex enim diebus fecit Dominus Deus cælum & terram. Ideo Christiani etiam obligantur ad requiem, ut tum ipsi ab operibus famulis cessent, tum etiam quiescere sinant suos. Christus Sabbathum propter hominem factum dicit, non propter Judæum tantum Marc. 2. v. 22. Tum si morale hoc est, ut tempus aliquod peculiariter cultui divino consecretur, morale etiam erit hoc, ut tempore illo quiescamus a laboribus, utpote quibus cultus DEI externus impeditur. Sanctificatio Sabbathi divina est tum segregativa ab usu prophano, tum consecrativa ad usus sacros. Utraque ergo etiam nobis sanctificatio præscripta est; neque hæc sine illa esse potest. Ideo Chrysostomus legem hanc Sabbathi Christianis immobilem dixit: Hom. 4 in Matth. Ne igitur ista nobis contingant, legem hanc nobis prescribamus immobilem, nec nobis modo, sed conjugibus etiam, liberisque nostris, ut unum hunc totius hebdomadis diem, quo ad audien- dum concurritur, totum in eorum, quæ dicuntur, mentione ponamus. Quod fieri profecto nequit, nisi ab operibus prophanis cessemus, nostrosque cessare faciamus.

Secundo non recte explicat Grotius benedictio- nem diei septimæ a Deo sub initium mundi factam Gen. 2. quasi cultus ibi præceptus fuerit, non autem otium. Sed DEUM ita ab initio sanctificasse hanc diem, ut otium etiam sanci verit & cessationem ab operibus communibus, non obscure verba Mosis docent Gen. 2. v. 2. 3. Complevitque DEUS die septi- mo opus suum, quod fecerat: & REQVIEVIT die septimo ab universo opere, quod patraverat. Et benedixit diei septimo: Et sanctificavit illum: QVIA in ipso CESSAVERAT ab omni opere suo, quod creavit DEUS, ut faceret. Ita ergo sanctificavit septimam diem, ut eum sancte coli, eoque ab opere omni profano CESSARI vellet, in me- moriam mundi conditi, & quietis vel cessationis Dei ab opere creationis, hac die celebratæ. At- que ita luculentissime explicat id supremus νομο- θέτης Exod. 20. versu 21. Memento, ut diem Sab- bathi SANCTIFICES. Sex diebus OPERA- BERIS, & facies omnia opera tua. Septimo au- tem die SABBATHUM (quies vel cessatio) Domini DEI tui est, non facies omne opus tuum in eo. -- Sex enim diebus fecit Dominus cœlum & ter- ram & mare & omnia, quæ in eis sunt & RE- QVIEVIT in die septimo. ID CIRCO benedi- xit Dominus diei Sabbathi, & sanctificavit eum. Quis jam non videt, benedixisse ita & sanctificasse Do- minum septimum diem, ut tum sancto cultui va- caret homo eodem, tum vero QVIESCERET ab omni opere suo. Idque IDCIRCO factum, quod Deus illo die REQVIEVERIT. Com- ponuntur enim hæc inter se, sex diebus Deus fecit cœlum, & terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt; Et: sex diebus operaberis, & facies omnia opera tua: Item, Septimo die REQVIEVIT Dominus: Et, septimo die QVIESCES, nec facies omne opus tuum in eo. At- que ea ratione Deum ab initio benedixisse huic diei, eumque sanctificasse, nimirum ob otium pa- riter ab operibus prophanis, & communibus, & cultum pium, sonora voce hic docetur. Non enim negare potest Grotius, primævam illam san- ctificationem in verbis Decalogi respici. Et huc respicere videtur, inquit in Explic. Decal. p. 40. in Deuteronomio Moses, cum ad verba Φύλαξαι τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν Σαββάτων ἁγιάζειν ἀυτὴν addit, ὃν τρόπον ἐνετείλατό σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σε: nimirum jam olim ab orbis initio. Ad eundem ergo modum ab orbis initio, cum sanctificavit Deus hunc diem, PRÆCEPIT eundem celebrari, sicut in lege postmodum hic demandavit. At in lege non solum demandavit cultum pium, sed & otium vel cessatio- nem ab omni opere nostro. Quapropter ab initio orbis jam cum cultu requisivit hoc die cessationem ab omni opere. Nec prætereundum est, quod Gro- tius ipse laudet Ebræorum observationem; diem hunc electum fuisse ad quietem, quia Deus eo quieve- rat, & ab initio eundem gaudio & memoriæ creatio- nis dicaverat. Optime autem Maimonides (inquit Grotius Explic. Decal. p. 42.) & Ebræi alii distin- guunt causam, cur QVIES imperata sit, & cur Hoc DIE. Prior causa in Devteronomio aperte ex- primitur: nempe quia liberati ope divina ex Ægypto cogitare debeant, quam dura esset servitus, ac proinde servos aliosque suo imperio traditos humane tractare. Posterior hoc loco (Exod. 20. Septimo autem die Sabbathum Domini Dei tui est) quo significatur, cum ad quietem quilibet posset sumi dies, hunc a Deo electum, quod ab initio jam dicatus esset gaudio & gratæ de orbe condito memoriæ, atque ipse DEUS res hujus mundi condere eo die desisset: Unde Sabbatho nomen. Sic Isaacus Arania, aliique. Hæc Grotius. Si electus hic dies ad QVIETEM, quod ab initio gaudio & memoriæ dicatus esset, memoriæ utique QVIETIS Domini & quieti ab operibus commu- nibus dicatus fuit, in memoriam CESSATIO- NIS & QVIETIS Domini ab operibus suis, unde nomen Sabbathi obtinuit. Nec alia Ebræo- rum sententia, ut postea dicemus. Porro cum Ex. 16. v. 24. Sabbathi, tanquam diei inter Judæos jam celebris ante latam legem mentio fit his ver- bis: illud est, quod edixit Jehovah, quies Sabbathum factum est Jehovæ cras, quod cocturi estis, coquite hodie, manifestum est, notam celebremque jam tum fuisse hanc diem, non solum ob cultum reli- giosum, sed etiam ob vacationem ab opere & quie- tem: quum ob ejus celebrationem quiescere etiam eadem in Manna colligendo debuerint. Solet etiam argumentum peti ex historia diluvii Gen. 8. v. 10. quod Noah septem dies expectarit post aquarum diminutionem, antequam prima vice columbam emitteret, ac deinde alios iterum septem expecta- rit dies, quod eo die explorata a Noah fuerit DEI benignitas, quo singulariter Deum in arca cole- bant, eo die expectarint quietem a diluvii mole- stiis, quo ab aliis ipsi quiescentes curis, se SOLI Dei cultui manciparunt. Sed firmior est probatio ex Ebr. 4. v. 3. 4. Docet Apostolus verba illa juravi in ira mea, si ingressuri sunt in requiem meam, pro- latam esse, cum opera ab institutione mundi jam essent perfecta, adducto loco Gen. 2. dixit enim in quo- dam loco de septima die sic: Et requievit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis: ostendit promis- sionem de requie factam inclusam comminationi exclusionis a requie factæ incredulis, non posse intelligi de requie Sabbathi, quia jam operibus Dei perfectis a jactis mundi fundamentis DEUS quieverat septimo die. Unde liquet, quietem Sab- bathi secundum Apostolum incepisse a perfectio- ne operum Dei post sextum diem: quod est Rive- ti argumentum in Explic. Decal. pag. 119. quod in Appendice ibi subjuncta cap. 3. pag. 130. seqq. ad- versus Gomarum defendit. Idem ab ipsa quoque Sabbathi appellatione confirmatur, quid enim aliud Sabbathum est, quam requies, & Sabbathi dies, quam dies quieti consecrata? Quum ergo Sab- bathum ab initio mundi fuerit Gen. 2. v. 2. non so- lum cultum Dei die illo a conditu mundi viguisse; sed ipsum otium & quietem a laboribus, fateri ne- cessum est.

Atque hæc omnium, cum veterum, tum re- centiorum sententia esse videtur, qui Sabbathum ab origine mundi celebratum agnoscunt, quod pleris- que ita visum fuit. De institutione sane Sabbathi atque origine divortia quædam reperiuntur senten- tiarum: quam alii ad legem demum referunt, alii vero a prima mundi origine deducunt: quæ contro- versia cum Fr. Gomaro intercessit Andreæ Riveto in Explic. Decal. & Antonio Walæo in LL. CC. illo cum Joh. Prideaux Sabbathi novitatem, his anti- quitatem propugnantibus: Sed quenquam præter Grotium in Sabbathi lege, aut celebratione a cultu Dei otium ab operibus communibus sequestrasse, non invenio: omnes Sabbathum, quandocunque illud institutum fuerit, aut observari cœperit, & cultus pii, & otii, vel quietis a profanis diem consti- tuunt, eaque ratione institutum & observatum vo- lunt. Unus Grotius hic peculiaris est. Plerique otium Sabbathi religiosum a sanctificatione septi- mæ creationis diei derivant. Ex Ebræis Philo lib. 3. de vit. Mos. diem Sabbathi a natura ait habere pri- vilegium, ex quo mundo natalis factus est. Josephus a primæva sanctificatione Sabbathi Genes. 2. ejus quietem deducit, Antiquit. l. 1. c. 2. Atque ita mun- dum sex diebus universum & omnia, quæ mundo con- tinentur, Moses facta esse dicit; Septima autem re- quievisse DEUM & ab operibus cessasse. Quam- obrem etiam nos recreationem a laboribus per eum diem celebramus, appellantes eum Sabbathum. Illa- tio voce quamobrem facta docet connectere ipsam vocationem Judæorum cum prima Sabbathi sancti- ficatione & quiete Dei. Isaacus Atias Judæus in the- sauro Venetiis Anno 1627. edito docet, Ethnicis etiam id notum fuisse, ac in ipsorum cordibus impres- sum de Sabbathi feria, part. 1. numer. 157. Clemens Alexandr. non solum Ebræos, verum etiam Græ- cos septimum diem sacrum scivisse lib. 5. Stromat. observat, eamque Sabbathi venerationem ad gen- tes quoque pervenisse, e Clemente & Eusebio in præparatione, Hesiodi item versibus fatetur Gro- tius. Quod autem solum cultui sacrum, non au- tem otio & quieti destinatum crediderint, neque Clemente, neque ex aliis doceri potest. Eusebius lib. 13. Evang. præparat. ex Platone, Homero, Cal- limacho & Solonis elogiis Septimæ diei sanctita- tem probat. Hanc vero vacationem vel quietem diei septimæ complecti Josephus l. 2. contr. Appion. confirmat: Nullam esse uspiam civitatem Græco- rum aut Barbarorum, nec ullam gentem, ad quam se- ptimanæ, in qua Judæi VACABANT, consuetudo non pervenerit. Quod etiam observatum Philoni lib. 2. de Vit. Mos. Nostrum jus omnes admonet offi- cii: Barbaros, Græcos, continentis æque ac insularum incolas, Occidentales & Orientales, Europæos atque Asiaticos, totum orbem habitabilem usque ad extre- mos terminos. Quis enim sacrum illum diem per sin- gulas hebdomades recurrentem non honorat? Quo facit, quod Veteres, priusquam ratio computan- di per annos & menses inventa esset, temporum spatia per septimanas distinxerint, uti e Chronologi- cis Georgii Syncelli observavit Salmasius: unde Ri- vetus, quum omnes nationes ab omni ævo hanc septem dierum revolutionem agnoverint, colligit, originem ejus aliam non habere potuisse, quam inveteratam opinionem, quod sex diebus mundus creatus fuerit, & septimo cessatum ab opere, ut ita verosimillimum sit, post hanc primam hebdoma- dem sequentem ita fuisse numeratam, & reliquas deinceps, idque ita apud omnes nationes obti- nuisse. Ideo Augustinus Steuchus, Eugubinus in Cosmopœia ad c. 2. Gen. & sanctificatum tunc fuisse diem septimum & habitum postea apud omnes gen- tes venerabilem & sacrum, observat.

Patrum antiquorum sententiam si audire pla- cet, Chrysostom. hom. 9. in cap. 2. Gen. de sanctifica- tione & requie diei septimæ, Jam hinc ab initio, ait, doctrinam hanc nobis insinuat Deus, erudiens, in cir- culo integro hebdomadis diem unum integrum segre- gandum & reponendum in spiritualem operationem. Tertullianus Apol. cap. 16. perhibet de Ethnicis, quod diem Saturni otio & victui decreverint ex- orbitantes & ipsi Judaico more; unde si confe- ratur l. 1. ad gentes cap. 13. colligitur, eosdem die Sabbathi, qui ipsis Saturni erat, feriatos esse; Quem ideo rebus gerendis minus aptum existimarunt Ro- mani, ut e Tibullo l. 1. Eclog. 3. & Ovid. lib. 1. de arte amandi apparet. Idem Tertullianus lib. 4. adversus Judæos observat, Judæos dicere, quod a PRI- MORDIO Deus sanctificavit diem septimum, requiescendo ab omnibus operibus, quæ fecit, & inde etiam Mosen dixisse ad populum : Mementote diei Sabbathi ; & ex propria sententia lib. 4. adversus Marcion. c. 12. Christum ipsum, docet, Sabbathi diem benedictione Patris a primordio sanctum bene- factione sua effecisse sanctiorem. Theodoretius ad ver- ba, Et benedixit Deus diei septimæ & sanctificavit eam, hæc addit, in quo demonstravit, quod illum di- em non inutilem putabat ad creandum, sed ad quietem accommodatam statuit. Augustin. Epist. 86. ad Casulan. vacationem inde a sanctificatione diei septi- mæ repetit. Quod vero nonnulli e Patribus Sab- bathum e lege Mosaica deducere videntur, Justinus, Ireneus, Tertullianus, Eusebius, Damascenus, ad quorum sententiam cum Abulensi provocat Goma- rus, id vel de rigore in lege sancito & ceremoniis Mo- saicis intelligendum, vel certe non ad negationem sanctificationis illius primævæ, sed ad ejusdem in- novationem spectat.

Inter Pontificios, Reformatos & Orthodoxos res extra controversiæ fere aleam posita est, quum Pontificii, si Tostatum excipias, Catharinus, Gene- brardus, Cornelius a Lapide, Salianus, Emanuel Saa, alii: Reformati etiam, præter Gomarum, plerique, Zwinglius, Calvinus, Beza, Martyr, Pelicanus, Bullinger, Bucanus, Zanchius, Ursinus, Gualtherus, Aretius, Bertramus, Mercerus, Fagius, Junius, Marloratus, Pareus, Zepperus, Fecqvernekinus, Martinus, Alstedius, & qui hos adducunt, Rive- tus, & Walæus, aliique, ὁμοθυμαδὸν agnoscant, quietem diei Sabbathi originem habere ab institutione septimo creationis die facta. Quæ nostrorum quo- que B. Lutheri, Chemnitii, Gerhardi, Franzii &c. unanimis est sententia: Quorum nonnulli eandem etiam probant ex addita particula μνημονευτικῇ : Memento diei Sabbathi, ut ipsum sanctifices: quod eadem Deus veteres commonefacere ipsius insti- tutionis voluerit: Ita Bullingerus in cap. 12. Matth.

& Chemnitius in Expos. Decal. Quid quod Judæi quoque nonnulli hodie fateantur Sabbathum ante legem ab Abraham aliisque Patriarchis cultum esse; quam sententiam Menasse Ben-Israel probl. 8. de creatione propugnat, & quidem non tantum san- ctificatione nominis divini, sed etiam vacatione a laboribus, qui etiam eam in rem argumentum ad- ducit e Schemot Rabba, Mosen petiisse a Pharaone in Ægypto, ut afflicto populo permitteret unum diem cessare a laboribus, eoꝙ́ impetrato ex traditione elegisse Sabbathum. Atque hæc de secundo.

Tertio, ab errore absolvi non potest, quod negat Grotius, diem Dominicam surrogatam esse in locum Sabbathi, sine dubio, ut Anabaptistis gratifi- cetur, qui præceptum de Sabbatho plane abolitum censent, adeo, ut vi libertatis Christianæ quævis opera quovis die licita existiment, siquidem eo etiam abire videntur Sociniani, Grotii necessarii. Hæc cognita, scribit Grotius in Explic. Decal. p. 41. refellunt eos, qui μίαν σαββάτων i. e. diem Dominicam surrogatam putant in locum Sabbathi. Nusquam enim ejus rei a Christo, nusquam ab Apostolis facta mentio. Et Apostolus cum dicit, non damnandos Christianos ob Sabbatha aut interlunia Col. 2, 16. liberos eos esse ostendit ab illa otiandi lege, quæ libertas nihili esset, si manente lege mutatus esset dies. Quæ vero commu- ni Christianorum sententiæ & religioni refragan- tur, omnemque cultum diei Dominicæ si non tol- lunt, cujusvis certe libidini exponunt. Quamvis vero consensu voluntario Christianos diem illum, quo Christus resurrexerat, ad suos cœtus usurpasse, talem etiam consensum, ubi in morem abiit, violare, non esse socialiter viventium profiteatur Grotius, solo tamen consensu voluntario aut more ac ritu petulantia ingenia coërceri se non patientur, si præceptum desit divinum, quin libertatem in licentiam convertant, quod manipuli Anabaptistarum sat docent. Tum vero morem illum otium non ultra indixisse arbitratur Grotius, quam quatenus ad cœtus agendos erat necessarium. Extra hoc nostro Sabbathi die quenquam obstringi ad vacationem ab operibus famulis, haud permittet, confusionis dierum Anabaptisticæ causam perorans. Sic enim quia singulis diebus cœtus agi possunt, & ad cœtus agendos otium est necessarium, non magis adstringemur feriari die Dominico, quam aliis, quibus libuerit, diebus. Nulla ergo plane supererit dierum differentia, nullus DEO erit peculiariter consecrandus ex lege divina: Abrogatum penitus fuerit præceptum de sanctificatione Sabbathi, tum qua cultum Dei peculiarem, tum qua cessationem ab operibus communibus. Habemus ita, quorsum superiores hypotheses Grotianæ directæ fuerint: ut nempe Socinianos & Anabaptistas juvare posset advocatus causæ pessimæ. Si abrogatus est dies Sabbathi, nec in ejus locum surrogatus dies Dominicus, quid restat, quam ut dicatur, nullum diem Septimanæ Deo dicatum esse? At præceptum de sanctificatione Sabbathi non est mere ceremoniale, sed quum pars Decalogi sit, & omnia decem Præcepta concernant omnes homines, nullum ad solos spectet Judæos, morale quid continet, quod perpetui juris est, alias non decem, sed novem tantum erunt tabularum divinarum præcepta, quæ nobis incumbent, neque lex integra inscribetur nobis per S. S. in cordibus carneis, quæ in tabulis lapideis inscripta erat 2. Cor. 3, 3. Sanctificatio certe, quæ hoc die præcipitur, non est quid ceremoniale, sed morale: non per mortem Christi abolita, sed restaurata: Neque vacatio vel respiratio filiorum & servorum mere ceremonialis est, sed morale quid in se habet: quemadmodum exemplum ipsum DEI, qui ab operibus suis quievit, haudquaquam ad ceremonias pertinet, vel ad umbras meras rerum futurarum, nec fines quietis, consideratio operum Dei & celebratio ejusdem, eo referri debet. Porro quam sacrosanctum nobis hoc præceptum habendum sit, magnum illud Nota bene Dei legislatoris O. M. edoceat: MEMENTO, ut diem Sabbathi sanctifices, quod in memoriam revocat veterem institutionem, ab orbis conditu factam, adeoque nobis omnibus religiose observandum est, non minus sub Novo, quam Vet. Testam. Ratio etiam, quam subjunxit Deus, concernit omnes homines, quod sex diebus Deus operatus sit, septimo quieverit, eique idcirco benedixerit, & sanctificavit eundem: Non enim minus nobis, quam Judæis hoc memoriale datur, de hexaëmero creationis, & die quietis Domini: Non minus nos, quam Judæos hoc exemplum Dei adstringit ad observationem diei septimæ, ubi sex diebus opera nostra fecerimus; non minus nostri, quam Judæorum causa benedixit Deus septimæ diei, eamque sanctificavit in diem Sabbathi, & quietis. Quamvis vero ceremoniale sit, quod dies Sabbathi dicanda fuerit cultui Dei & quieti, hoc tamen ad præcepti substantiam pertinet, ac morale est, quod quum sex diebus operati fuerimus, septimo DEO vacare debeamus, adeoque unum e septem diebus DEI externo cultui consecrare. Atque hoc est, quod observavit Chrysostomus hom. 10. in c. 2. Gen. Jam hinc ab initio doctrinam hanc nobis insinuat DEUS, erudiens IN CIRCULO HEBDOMADÆ DIEM UNUM integrum segregandum & seponendum in spiritualem operationem.

Et quomodo sex dierum operatio esse potest, nisi a septimo quietis die intercidatur ac terminetur? Si negetur, unum diem a circulo hebdomadæ cul- tui & quieti consecrandum esse, vi præcepti divini de Sabbatho, utique nullus certus dierum numerus aut circulus limitari poterit ex ullo præcepto di- vino, siquidem nullius alterius numeri ullibi in ullo alio præcepto mentio fuit, ac proinde vel vicesimum vel quinquagesimum vel certe unum- quemque licebit eligere, atque ita cuivis etiam in- tegrum erit eligere, quemcunque velit, sine ullius præcepti divini violatione. Id sane fatentur omnes, vi præcepti hujus, certum aliquod tem- pus sacro cultui destinatum esse. Quamvis de eo, an ex vi, & analogia hujus præcepti consequens sit, ut unus dies e circulo septem dierum observetur, discrepent, paucis quibusdam aliquod solum tem- pus cultui sacro destinandum esse indeterminate, non præcise septimum diem præcepto hoc infer- ri, censentibus : omnes tamen ex vi præcepti cer- tum tempus cultui divino deberi admittunt : idque naturæ inscriptum ajunt, quod aliquod tempus ad cultum consecrari debeat, & hoc morale hujus præcepti faciunt : quod proinde nunquam abro- gari potuit. Grotius secus sapiens cum Anaba- ptistis suis solus hic relinquitur. Neque dubi- tari debet, in Nov. Test. septimum diem defini- tum esse loco septimi creationis diei, Domini- cum resurrectionis diem, adeoque retentum unum e septimana diem, vi præcepti divini, solam sur- rogatum in diem Sabbathi diem Dominicum; un- de iterum confirmatur, hoc pro invariabili & morali hujus præcepti nobis quoque agnosccn- dum, quod nempe unus e septem diebus sacer DEO esse debeat, quia Ecclesia Nov. Test. ita cen- suit, nec repertus est, aut reperietur unquam, qui mutationem aliquam publicam hic moliri ausit, aut valeat. Quod enim totam Ecclesiam inde ab orbis con- ditu usque ad consummationem seculi obligat, cum Ve- teris, tum Nov. Test. tum ante legem, tum sub lege, tum post abrogatam legem ceremonialem, id pro mo- rali & perpetuo habendum est.

Disputatur quidem de eo, anne Christus sur- rogarit diem Dominicum, quem vocamus, an vero, quod plerisque placet, ab Apostolis hoc factum, sed conveniunt in eo facile omnes, quod non sola consuetudine aut humana constitutione invaluerit Dominicæ diei observatio, sed aliqua institutio- ne divina sancita sit : siquidem ea, quæ Apo- stoli Apostolica autoritate sanciverunt, pro di- vinis institutis habenda sint. De qua disputa- tione Walæus legi potest dissert. de Sabbath. ubi priorem sententiam Eusebio, Cyrillo Alexandrino, Justino, Fr. Junio, Piscatovi & Perkipso tribuit, al- teram receptiorem esse putat, eamque sequitur ipse. Videntur autem conciliari haud difficulter posse illæ sententiæ, si dicatur, Christum quidem resur- rectione sua hac die facta & exemplo suo hanc diem consecrasse, cum eadem Discipulis apparuerit, excepto Thoma, & postmodum altera septima- na post octo dies iterum, Thoma præsente, ea- dem se exhibuerit Joh. 20, 19. 26. eadem etiam die S. S. in Apostolos congregatos effuderit Act. II. (quamvis ista omnia dubia reddere satagat Wa- læus) ac Apoc. 1, 10 omnium consensu ἡμέρα κυ- ριακὴ primus hebdomadis dies nuncupetur, utpo- te à Domino, si non expresse sancitus, exemplo tamen ejus consecratus. Apostolos vero divina, qua pollebant, autoritate, quum antea in hono- rem Dominicæ resurrectionis & apparitionis, nec non demissi de cœlo Spiritus S. festus ageretur pri- mus septimanæ dies (non enim credendum diem nullum certum in illis Christianorum Nov. Test. primitiis sanctificatum aut Sabbathum cum Ju- dæis præ die resurrectionis Dominicæ celebra- tum) deinceps hunc primum hebdomadæ diem sanctivisse, & instituisse in Sabbathum Christiano- rum ordinarium. Ideoque recte Augustinus hom. XV. de verbis Apostol. Domini suscitatio promisit nobis æternum diem, & consecravit nobis diem Dominicum, qui Dominicus vocatur, quia eo die resurrexit. Et Epist. CXIX. ad Januar. cap. 13. Dies Dominicus non Judæis, sed Christia- nis resurrectione Domini declaratus est, & ex illo ha- bere cœpit festivitatem suam. Cyrillus lib. XII. in Joh. cap. 38. Adverte, quod non simpliciter rem enarravit, sed addidit diligenter, post octo dies, & omnibus unum in locum congregatis: Diem igitur octavum Dominicum diem esse necesse est: nam una Sabbathorum cæteris apparuit, id est, die Domini- co; die postea deinceps octavo, utrisque connume ra- tis extremis congregati rursum discipuli, Thoma præ- sente, simili modo Dominum vident. Jure igitur sanctæ congregationes die octavo in Ecclesiis fiunt. Nec vero ullum initium institutionis ab Ecclesia factæ designari aut adferri potest, aut institutio post Apostolorum excessum facta obligare po- tuit totum per orbem Ecclesiam, uti ad obser- vationem diei Dominicæ totam Ecclesiam de- vinctam ad hunc diem fuisse, nemini dubium, teste historia. Quod de τῇ μίᾳ τῶν Σαββάτων Actor. 20, 7. qua discipuli convenerunt ad fran- gendum panem, habetur, Grotius ipse de die Do- minico intelligit, & a plerisque ita acicipitur; Justi- no in Dial. c. Tryph. Chrysostomo in h. l. Augu- stino Theophyl. Beda, quum Ebræorum more UNA pro PRIMA usurpetur, Matth. 28, 1. Marc. 16, 2. Luc. 24, 1. Conf. Gen. 1, 12. Fuit ergo ille dies tum conventus ordinarius institu- to Apostolico. Ita 1. Cor. 16, 2. De collectis au- tem, quæ fiunt in Sanctos, sicut ORDINAVI Ec- clesiis Galatiæ, ita & vos facite. Per UNAM SABBATHI unusquisque vestrum apud se reponat. Primo quoque die hebdomadis, ut Beza reddidit. Chrysostomus: Per unum Sabbathi, hoc est, die Do- minico unusquisque apud se reponat, recondens, quod ei bene placuerit. Vide, quomodo etiam adhorta- tur a tempore: dies enim erat idoneus adeos addu- cendos ad Eleemosynam: recordemini enim, inquit, quænam eo die consequuti estis: bona enim ineffa- bilia & radix & initium vitæ nostræ in eo facta sunt. Non hac autem sola ratione aptum est tem- pus ad benignitatem prompto & alacri animo exer- cendam, sed &, quod habet quietem ac remissionem immunitatemque & vacationem a laboribus. Nam animo a laboribus libera redditur expeditior, & aptior ad misericordiam. Adhæc autem veneran- dis quoque ac immortalibus communicare magnam affert & committit animi alacritatem; in ea ergo unusquisque vestrum, non simpliciter hic aut ille, sed unusquisque, sive sit pauper, sive dives, sive vir, sive mulier, sive servus, sive liber apud se reponat: non dixit, ferat in Ecclesiam, ne propter paucita- tem erubescant, sed quum, quæ paulatim fiunt, collectionibus auxerint collationem, quum acces- sero, tunc ostendat. Interim, inquit, apud te re- pone & domum tuam fac Ecclesiam, arculam, ga- zophylacium: esto custos sacræ pecuniæ a teipso ordi- natus dispensator pauperum. Hactenus Chry- sostomus. Hieronymus pariter de collectione die Dominica instituenda explicat, sed ita, ut publice fiat, & in Ecclesiam singulis Dominicis diebus deferatur; quemadmodum in Synago- gis Judaicis publice in Sabbathis collectæ fie- bant, bant, atque etiamnum apud nos fiunt in diebus Dominicis: quam etiam consuetudinem receptam fuisse in Veteri Ecclesia Justinus Apol. II. docet. Sic ergo Apostolica ordinatione dies Dominica jam destinata fuit habendis publicis conventibus: ideo etiam peculiariter κυριακὴ dicta, quod Domino consecrata: licet postmodum Constantini M. edicto, ut ex Orat. Eusebii de laudibus Constant. notum est, diei Dominicæ observatio confirmata fuerit: utpote quæ antea jam recepta per orbem Christianum erat, ac penes Romanos & Græcos, aliosque populos communi usu frequentata: ut aliam, quam Apostolicam originem agnoscere non potuerit, secundum Regulam Augustini de Bapt. cap. XXIV. Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi autoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur.

Nec est, quod Grotius opponat Sabbathi observationem, quæ cum die Dominica sacra & solemnis fuerit in antiqua Ecclesia, unde hæc in illius locum ab Apostolis surrogata censeri non possit: Quia etsi Sabbathum etiam sacrum fuerit, eoque nomine dies isti fratres habiti sint, non tamen æque sacrum, & solemne penes Christianos erat, ac dies primus Septimanæ, sed fiebat solum in eodem præparatio ad Dominicæ diei solemnem feriam, non perinde erat in Sabbatho vacatio ab ordinariis operibus, nec ea solemnitate celebrabatur, uti ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, quemadmodum ex Eusebio lib. IV. de Vit. Constant. cap. 18. colligitur. Imo reprobabatur in Ebionitis inter alia etiam hoc, quod diem Sabbathi & diem Dominicum similiter celebrarint, teste Eusebio lib. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 21. Sanciebaturque in Laodiceno Concilio can. XXIX. non oportet Christianos Judaizare & in Sabbatho otiari, sed ipsos eo die operari; diem autem Dominicum præferentes otiari, si modo possint, ut Christianos: quod si inventi fuerint, ut Judaizantes, sint anathema apud Christum. Constitutiones Apostolorum, quibus jubetur, ne laboret quis Sabbatho, sed vacet doctrinæ pietatis, nullius autoritatis sunt, nedum Apostolicæ, utpote nothæ & adulterinæ, ad quas hic proinde frustra provocavit Grotius. Quod vero Col. 2, 16. præcepit, ne quis nos judicet in cibo, aut in potu aut in parte diei festi, vel novilunii vel Sabbathorum, quæ sunt umbra futurorum, non tollit morale præcepti de sanctificatione Sabbathi, sed quod in illo ceremoniale erat, & ad umbram futurorum pertinebat: quale non est vacatio a laboribus ordinariis, & cultus divinus, certusque Septimanæ dies eidem consecratus. Neque vero ideo nihil æstimanda illa libertas, quod adhuc vacationem, & cultum certæ diei adstringimus: siquidem a rigore legis de Sabbatho non parum remissum sit, qui inter Judæos obtinebat, ut antea observatum. Adde, quod leges Judæos ad certa tempora adstringentes, ad divini cultus partem tunc spectarent; penes Christianos vero diei certæ observatio non partem cultus constituat, sed ordinis causa sancita solum sit, ceu cultus quædam circumstantia: siquidem alias omni tempore Deum ita colere liceat, nec præcise nos, uti Judæi, ad dies alligati simus, ut quis nos ideo judicare merito possit: quod libertati Christianæ refragatur. Conferatur Hieronymi Comm. l. III. in Gal. IV. De Sabbatho contra Judæos disserens legi potest Fr. Spanhemius l. III. dubior. Evang. dub. XIV. feqq.

## 20:12
vers. 12. HONOUR) Both by other signs of reverence, and by providing for them what is necessary for life, which is comprehended under the word τιμῆς, as 1 Tim. 5:3, 17. The Hebrews say that a son ought even to work in a mill to provide for his parents.

YOUR FATHER AND YOUR MOTHER) as earthly GODS, from whom you draw your origin.

THAT YOU MAY BE LONG-LIVED.

In the explanation of the Decalogue, that we may insert this here from the annotations of Grotius, he observes that the law in direct words promises only temporal happiness, the precept of which is longevity: and that it is promised generally to those keeping the law, Lev. 18, etc., and here specifically added to this precept. But that hypothesis smacks of Socinianism: that only temporal happiness, and not eternal, is promised in the law. Christ taught otherwise, Luke 10:28. Do this, and you shall live. For the question there was about ETERNAL LIFE, v. 26. Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? The Apostle taught otherwise, Gal. 3:12. But the law is not of faith, but he who does them shall live in them. Where the discourse is about the promise of the law and eternal life. The Scribes and Pharisees themselves were sounder in this cause than our Hugo, who otherwise willingly Judaizes. For the lawyer, questioning Christ about obtaining eternal life, when the supreme interpreter of the law replied, what is written in the law, how do you read? what indeed must be done according to the law, not so that one may obtain a long life, but that he may possess an eternal one, he replied without hesitation the sum of the law: You shall love your Lord God with all your heart, etc., adorned with this eulogy by Christ: you have answered rightly, do this, and you shall live. Therefore, it was not a doubt among the lawyers then that eternal life was promised in the law. To which it contributes that even in the Onkelos version the promise of the law, Lev. 18:5, Which if a man do, he shall live in them, is explained concerning eternal life. And the Sadducees and some atheists are still condemned today by the remaining Jews, on account of this dogma, which the Socinians borrowed from them, that all the promises and blessings which await the observers of the law are temporal, and that neither punishment nor reward of the future life is expressed in the law: See Menasse Ben-Israel de resurrect. mortuor. c. 7, 46. What? That they even wish those words, that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days Deut. 22, 7, to be understood concerning the future world, which is good in all respects, since longevity of life does not befall all who observe the law here: And that thou mayest prolong thy days, viz. in the world, which is most perfectly long; in Menasse Ben-Israel c. 11, 69. Although indeed some of the Jews clearly denied that eternal life was promised in the law, and observed that the Prophets speak more clearly concerning the same, they did not however assert that the law by direct words promises only temporal happiness: As here Menasse Ben-Israel did not follow the Sadducean opinion of Grotius, when he praised him c. 13. p. 91. More correctly Aben-Ezra, whom Menasse likewise praises, [held] that future blessedness had been left to be DEDUCED by the learned and wise from various places of the LAW: however much it may seem to the unlearned to promise only temporal goods. If it can be deduced from various places of the law, it is necessary that the same is promised directly, albeit in less perspicuous words, and not to all, in the law. The Arminians are also sounder in this cause than Grotius, whom he is accustomed to applaud, since they do not entirely deny that special promises and eternal goods are contained even in the ceremonial laws, which pertain entirely to the Mosaic covenant, as witnessed by Episcopius Lib. III. Instit. Theol. Sect. IV. cap. I. The Transylvanian Anti-Trinitarians, Fr. Davidis and Georg. Blandrata, are sounder, who in refut. Majoris de Trinit. I. 6. have these things: Nor yet on that account do we despoil the Saints of the O. Testament of the spiritual riches of the Son of God; For as there is one and the same Church of the Elect from the foundation of the world even to the end, so there is the same and common salvation for all. The same God the Father, the same Saviour Messiah, the same Spirit, the same life, and inheritance, there is no difference in substance, but in mode, measure and degree of the manifestation of the Messiah, and of Salvation. Nor do Jerome or Augustine support Grotius, as he himself thinks. For although Jerome, in Book II of his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, assigns the promises to the Law, and in Dialogue I against the Pelagians seems to deny against Pelagius that the kingdom of heaven was promised in the Old Testament, and asserts that it was first proclaimed in the Gospel by John; yet these things, so as not to contradict himself, must be understood in a qualified sense, namely, concerning the clear and manifest, and therefore public, proclamation of the kingdom of heaven: furthermore, they must be explained in so far as the refutation of the opposing opinion of Pelagius requires, who ascribed those promises to the Old Testament in order to assert that eternal life was to be obtained through the Law. For Pelagius taught that many before the coming of Christ had been saved through the Law without the grace of Christ, and with that intention, under the title of εὐλογιῶν or Testimonies in chapter 23, he defined that the kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament, as Augustine testifies in On the Acts of the Pelagians, ch. 5, just as Coelestinus said, that the Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.

What is to be held concerning the opinion of Jerome must also be held concerning that of St. Augustine: who furthermore observes that the Old Testament is spoken of in two ways: In one way, according to the authority of the divine Scriptures: which God established on Mount Sinai with the carnal people and which has earthly promises, but in such a way that while it promises earthly things more openly, it nevertheless promises spiritual and heavenly things symbolically: In another way, according to the most common custom of speaking, by which all the canonical Scriptures before the incarnation of the Lord are reckoned under the designation of the Old Testament: in which sense he acknowledges that heavenly things were also openly promised in the Old Testament. See ch. 5 of On the Acts of the Pelagians. Jerome certainly acknowledged that the saints in the Old Testament were justified by the faith of Christ. Therefore, he did not deny them knowledge and saving faith, nor did he absolutely establish John as the first proclaimer of the kingdom of heaven. He writes in Book I, on ch. 2 to the Galatians, that the saints who were of old were justified by the faith of Christ, inasmuch as Abraham saw the day of Christ and rejoiced. And Moses esteemed the reproach of Christ as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. For he looked to the REWARD. And Isaiah saw the glory of Christ, as the Evangelist John records. And Jude says of all in general: I wish to remind you, knowing all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed those who did not believe a second time. Whence it is not so much the works of the Law that are condemned, as those who trust that they can be justified by works alone. And Book II, on ch. 4: For just as all die in the first-formed Adam, not yet born; so also all, even those who were born before the coming of Christ, are made alive in the second Adam. And thus it happens that we have served the Law in the Fathers, and they are saved by grace in the sons. This understanding agrees with the Catholic Church: which asserts one providence for both the Old and New Testaments; nor does it distinguish in time those whom it has joined in condition. We are all built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Jesus Christ our Lord as the cornerstone containing us, who made both one, and breaking down the middle wall of partition, destroyed the enmity of both peoples in his flesh, and changed the difficulty of the ancient Law with the integrity of the evangelical doctrines. Truly in Christ we are all one bread and two agreeing upon the earth. And just as we are founded upon the Prophets, so also the Patriarchs stood upon the foundation of the Apostles. Augustine, Book I against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, ch. 21: However much you may proclaim the ancient righteous to have been of virtue, it did not make them saved, except for the FAITH of the mediator, who shed his blood for the remission of sins. -- This you do not want, enemies of the grace of Christ, that the ancients be believed to be saved by the same grace of Jesus Christ, but you divide the times according to Pelagius, as if for the men of the two previous times, namely before the Law and under the Law, the blood of Jesus Christ was not necessary, emptying what was said, for there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. And Book I of On the Merits and Remission of Sins, ch. 11: The grace of the Savior alone destroyed the kingdom of death in any man, which worked also in the ancient saints, whoever, before Christ came in the flesh, nevertheless belonged to his helping grace, not to the letter of the Law, which could only command, NOT HELP. For this was HIDDEN in the Old Testament according to the most just dispensation of times, which is now revealed in the New. See concerning the opinion of Augustine, Vossius, Response to the judgment of Herm. Ravensperg, ch. XXIII, and Book III of the History of the Pelagians, part II, thesis X.

Latin:

vers. 12. HONORA) Tum aliis reverentiæ signis, tum ad vitam necessaria illis exhibendo, quod sub voce τιμῆς comprehenditur, ut 1. Tim. 5, 3. 17. Ajunt Hebræi, vel in pistrino laborare filium debere, ut subveniat parentibus.

PATREM TUUM ET MATREM TUAM) ut terre- stres DEOS, a quibus originem trahitis.

UT SIS LONGÆVUS.

In explicatione Decalogi, ut hoc annotatis Grotianis hic inferamus, observat, legem verbis di- rectis felicitatem temporalem tantum promittere, cu- jus præceptum sit longævitas: eamque generaliter pro- mitti legem servantibus Lev. 18. &c. hic peculiariter huic præcepto adjici. Sed hypothesis illa Socinis- mum redolet: in lege solum temporalem felicitatem, non vero æternam promitti. Aliud Christus docuit Luc. 10, 28. Hoc fac, & vives. Quærebatur enim ibi de VITA ÆTERNA v. 26. Magister, quid fa- ciendo vitam æternam possidebo? Aliud Apostolus Gal. 3, 12. Lex autem non ex fide est, sed qui fecerit ea, vivet in illis. Ubi de legis promissione, & vita æter- na sermo est. Saniores fuere ipsimet Scribæ, & Pharisæi in hac causa nostro Hugone, qui alias li- benter Judaizat. Legisperitus enim Christum de consequenda vita æterna interrogans, cum repo- neret summus legis interpres, in lege quid scriptum est, quomodo legis? quid nempe faciendum sit juxta legem, non ut longævam quis consequatur vitam, sed ut æternam possideat, sine cunctatione repo- suit summam legis: Diliges Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo &c. elogio hoc a Christo exornatus: recte re- spondisti, hoc fac, & vives. Tum ergo hoc penes legisperitos dubium non fuit, in lege vitam æter- nam promissam esse. Quo facit, quod etiam in versione Onkelos legis promissio Lev. 18, 5. Quæ faciens homo, vivet in eis, de vita æterna explicetur. Et damnantur adhuc hodie Sadducæi & athei non- nulli a Judæis reliquis, ob hoc dogma, quod ab ipsis mutuo sumfere Sociniani, omnes promissiones & benedictiones, quæ manent cultores legis, tempora- les, neque illam vel pœnam, vel præmium vitæ futuræ in lege expressum esse: Vid. Menasse Ben-Israel de resur- rect. mortuor. c. 7, 46. Quid? quod verba etiam illa, ut bene sit tibi, & prolongare facias dies Deut. 22, 7. intelligenda esse velint de mundo futuro, qui per omnia bonus est, siquidem non omnibus legem obser- vantibus longævitas vitæ hic obtingat: Et prolongare facias dies, sc. in mundo, qui perfectissime longus est; apud Menasse Ben-Israel c. 11, 69. Quanquam ve- ro nonnulli e Judæis clare vitam æternam lege pro- missam negarint, ac Prophetas clarius de eadem loqui observarint, non tamen legem verbis directis solam temporalem felicitatem promittere asseruere: Ut hic Menasse Ben-Israel Sadducæam Grotii opi- nionem assequutus non fuerit, cum eum laudavit c. 13. p. 91. Rectius Aben-Ezra, quem itidem lau- dat Menasse, futuram beatitudinem relictam fuisse doctis & sapientibus ERVENDAM ex variis LE- GIS locis: utut imperitis videatur tantum tempora- lia bona promittere. Si erui potest e variis legis lo- cis, necessum est, eandem directe, etsi minus per- spicuis, nec omnibus verbis promissam esse in le- ge. Saniores etiam in hac causa Grotio sunt Ar- miniani, quibus applaudere consuevit, siquidem legibus ceremonialibus, quæ ad pactum Mosaicum omnino pertinent, specialia etiam promissa & æ- terna bona contineri, non inficientur penitus, te- ste Episcopio Lib. III. Instit. Theol. Sect. IV. cap. I. Saniores Anti-Trinitarii Transylvani, Fr. Davi- dis, & Georg. Blandrata, qui in refut. Majoris de Trinit. I. 6. illa habent: Neque tamen propterea San- ctos V. Test. spiritualibus divitiis Filii Dei spoliamus; Nam ut una eademque a condito mundo ad finem usq; Electorum Ecclesia est, ita eadem & communis omni- um salus. Idem Deus Pater, idem Servator Messias, idem Spiritus, eadem vita, & hæreditas, in substan- tia discrimen non est, sed in modo, mensura & gradu patefactionis Messia, & Salutis. Neque pro Grotio faciunt Hieronymus, aut Augustinus, uti ipse putat. Etsi enim Hieronymus lib. II. Comment. in Epist. ad Gal. promissiones legi assignet, ac Dial. I. contr. Pelag. videatur negare contra Pelagium regnum Cælorum in V. T. repromitti, primumque in Evangelio per Johannem id prædicari, asserat; hæc tamen, nec sibi ipsi adversetur, secundum quid intelligenda sunt, nimirum de claro & luculento, eoque publico præconio regni Cælorum: adhæc ita explicanda, quatenus oppositæ Pelagii sententiæ confutatio requirit, qui Veteri Testamento promissiones illas adscribebat, ut vitam æternam per legem obtinendam assereret. Docebat enim Pelagius, multos ante adventum Christi per legem fuisse salvatos sine gratia Christi, eaque intentione εὐλογιῶν sive Testimoniorum titulo cap. 23. definivit, regnum cælorum etiam in V. T. promissum, teste Augustino de gestis Palest. c. 5. perinde ut Cœlestinus dixit, legem sic mittere ad regnum, quemadmodum Evangelium.

Quod de Hieronymi, idem etiam de S. Augustini sententia habendum: qui præterea observat, Vetus Testamentum duobus modis dici: Uno modo, secundum divinarum Scripturarum autoritatem: quod in monte Sinai pepigit Deus cum populo carnali & promissiones terrenas habet, sed ita ut apertius quidem terrena promittat, Symbolice tamen spiritualia quoque ac cælestia: Altero modo secundum loquendi consuetudinem vulgatissimam, qua universæ Scripturæ Canonicæ ante incarnationem Domini ministrante Vet. Testam. appellatione censeatur: quo sensu in Vet. Test. aperte etiam promissa esse cælestia agnoscit. Vid. c. 5. de gestis Palæstin. Hieronymus certe agnovit, sanctos in V. T. ex fide Christi justificatos. Notitiam ergo & fidem salutarem ipsis non denegavit, neque absolute primum regni Cælorum præconem Johannem constituit. Sanctos, scribit l. 1. in c. 2. ad Galat. qui antiquitus fuerunt, ex fide Christi justificatos, siquidem Abrahamus vidit diem Christi, & lætatus est. Et Moses majores divitias æstimavit thesauro Ægyptiorum improprium Christi. Aspiciebat enim in REMUNERATIONEM. Et Esaias vidit gloriam Christi, ut Johannes Evangelista commemorat. Et Judas de omnibus generaliter: Commonere, inquit, vos volo, scientes semel omnia, quoniam Jesus populum de terra Ægypti salvans, secundo eos, qui non crediderunt, perdidit. Unde non tam legis opera damnantur, quam hi, qui tantum ex operibus se justificari posse confidunt. Et l. II. in c. 4. Quomodo enim omnes in Protoplasto Adamo nec dum nati moriuntur: ita & omnes, etiam hi, qui ante adventum Christi nati sunt, in secundo Adam vivificantur. Atque ita sit, ut nos legi servierimus in Patribus, & illi gratia salventur in filiis. Iste intellectus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ convenit: quæ & Veteris & Novi Testamenti unam asserit providentiam; nec distinguit in tempore, quos conditione sociavit. Omnes ædificati sumus super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, continente nos angulari lapide Jesu Christo, Domino nostro, qui fecit utraque unum, & medium parietem dissipans inimicitiam utriusque populi in sua carne destruxit, & antiquæ legis difficultatem Evangelicorum dogmatum integritate mutavit. Vere in Christo omnes unus panis sumus & duo consentimus super terram. Et quomodo nos super Prophetas fundati sumus: ita & Patriarchæ in Apostolorum fundamine constiterunt. Augustinus lib. I. contr. duas Epist. Pelag. c. 21. Quantælibet fuisse virtutis antiquos justos prædices, non eos salvos fecit, nisi FIDES mediatoris, qui in remissionem peccatorum sanguinem fudit. -- Hoc vos non vultis, inimici gratiæ Christi, ut eadem gratia Jesu Christi salvi credantur antiqui, sed distribui- tis tempora secundum Pelagium, quasi hominibus duorum superiorum temporum, ante legem sc. & in lege sanguis Jesu Christi non fuerit necessarius, eva- cuantes quod dictum est, unus enim Deus, unus media- tor Dei & hominum, homo Jesus Christus. Et lib. I. de peccat. merit. & remiss. c. II. Regnum mortis sola in quolibet homine destruxit gratia Salvatoris, quæ ope- rata est etiam in antiquis sanctis, quicunque antequam in carne Christus veniret, ad ejus tamen adjuvantem gratiam, non legis literam, quæ jubere tantum, NON ADJUVARE poterat, pertinebant. Hoc namque OCCULTABATUR in V. T. pro tempo- rum dispensatione justissima, quod nunc revelatur in Novo. Vid. de sententia Augustini Vossius respons. ad judic. Herm. Ravensperg. c. XXIII. & l. III. Hi- stor. Pelag. part. II. th. X.

## 20:13
Verse 13. THOU SHALT NOT KILL) This order has been changed from the order which is in Deuteronomy. For both Philo and Tertullian teach us in more than one place that the Greek Codices had the prohibition of adultery placed before that of murder. Marriage is the foundation of all civil society.

There is no reason why we should say the order of the Commandments is changed here. The Hebrew Codices in this place all agree to one. The Law in Deuteronomy also observes the same order. Josephus observes the same in Book III of the Antiquities, ch. 6. Matthew observes the same in chapter 19, 18. Chrysostom observes the same at the beginning of chapter 5 of Ephesians, and others, as Grotius admits. That the Greeks change the order in this place can have arisen from elsewhere than from the reading of the Codices of the Hebrews which they had. And the Greek Codices are to be believed corrupted rather than the Hebrew source, which here is perfectly consistent with itself in Exodus just as in Deuteronomy. Since Grotius does not pretend any corruption in this latter place, just as the Greeks also agree with the Hebrews, why then does he pretend that the order of the Commandments was different in Exodus than it was repeated in Deuteronomy? He also acknowledges that the ancients not rarely cite them in that order: but he says they cite the same from Deuteronomy, in his Explication. Decal. p. 45. as if Moses had ordered the precepts there otherwise than in Exodus. He brings forward Philo and Tertullian as having read it as the Greeks had it, and it is neither a wonder, nor does it prejudice the Hebrew source in any way. Which could likewise be said of the repetition made in Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20; for the Evangelists are accustomed to follow the Greek translation; unless it were too manifest there that the order of the precepts of the Decalogue was not observed: for in the last place the precept concerning honoring parents is recounted, which is the first in the second table. If marriage is the foundation of civil society, the preservation of life is the foundation of marriage. If many Hebrew women preferred the chastity of life, did the supreme legislator therefore place the precept concerning not committing adultery in the prior place? The custody of eternal salvation, which is endangered by unchastity, is altogether to be preferred to temporal life. But the most wise lawgiver wished it to be provided first for life, then for marriage, afterwards for goods, and finally for the reputation of one's neighbor. An injury which is inflicted upon a neighbor by reason of his own person is more grave than that which is inflicted by reason of a person joined to him: that which is inflicted upon life itself, than that which is inflicted upon the life of a partner.

Latin:

Vers. 13. NON OCCIDES) Mutatus hic ordo ad ordi- nem, quæ in Deuteronomio. Nam Græcos Codices adulte- rii interdictionem ante illam homicidii positam habuisse & Philo, & Tertullianus non uno loco nos docent. Matrimo- nium totius civilis societatis fundamentum est.

Nihil causæ est, cur ordinem Præceptorum hic mutatum dicamus. Consentiunt Ebræi Codices hoc loco ad unum omnes. Eundem etiam ordi- nem observat lex in Deuteronomio. Eundem ob- servat Josephus lib. III. Ant. c. 6. Eundem Matthæus cap. 19, 18. Eundem Chrysostomus ad initium cap. 5. Ephes. & alii, fatente Grotio. Quod Græci mu- tent ordinem in hoc loco, aliunde ortum esse po- test, quam ex lectione Codicum, quos habuere, Ebræorum. Et corrupti potius credendi Græci Codices, quam fons Ebræus, qui hic sibi apprime constat in Exodo pariter, & Deuteronomio. Quo posteriori loco nullam corruptelam quum fingat Grotius, quemadmodum etiam Græci consonant Ebræis, cur ergo secus habuisse ordinem Præcepto- rum in Exodo fingit, quam repetitus fuerit in Deute- ronomio? Veteres etiam agnoscit non raro adducere eo ordine: sed e Deuteronomio eundem adducere ait, in Explic. Decal. p. 45. ac si aliter Moses illic ordi- nasset præcepta, quam in Exodo. Philonem & Tertullianum producit ita legisse, ut Græci habe- bant, neque mirum est, neque Ebræo fonti quic- quam præjudicat. Quod de repetitione Marc. 10, 19. Luc. 18, 20. facta pariter dici posset; Solent enim Evangelistæ Græcam translationem sequi; nisi manifestum illic nimis esset, haud observatum or- dinem præceptorum Decalogi: Ultimo enim loco præceptum de honorandis Parentibus recensetur, quod in tabula secunda primum est. Si matrimo- nium fundamentum est civilis societatis, conser- vatio vitæ matrimonii est fundamentum. Si pu- dicitiam vitæ multæ Ebræorum mulieres prætule- re, num ideo priori loco Præceptum de non mœ- chando locavit summus legislator? Præferenda omnino vitæ temporali custodia salutis æternæ, quæ per impudicitiam periclitatur. Cautum au- tem voluit ὁ νομοθέτης sapientissimus primum vi- tæ, tum conjugio, postmodum bonis, denique famæ proximi. Injuria quæ proximo infertur ratione personæ propriæ gravior est, quam quæ ratione personæ conjunctæ: quæ vitæ infertur ipsi, quam quæ vitæ sociæ.

## 20:14
