verse 14. THOU SHALT NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.

A new error reveals itself in the Grotian Explanation of the Decalogue concerning this precept, in that he denies that all illicit Venus is prohibited by it. For although we may easily grant that the word נאף is properly used for adultery, and it may be conceded that it occurs in that sense alone among the Hebrews, and for that reason it has been rendered thus by Greek, Latin, and other interpreters, nevertheless the genus itself is prohibited under a special interdict, and by the name of adultery, synecdochically, every illicit lust included, which the explanation of Christ in Matt. 5:28 clearly confirms. Therefore, adultery and fornication are joined in Matt. 15:19, whence Aben-Ezra rightly observed that every illicit sexual act is included by that word, even whoredom. But here Grotius is again seduced by the Socinian spirit: whence he thinks too abjectly of the Decalogue, nor does he allow it to be a summary collection of moral virtues and vices or a perfect rule of justice; nay, he thinks it was not at all necessary in so brief a Decalogue to mention all the crimes that were to be forbidden thereafter, that it was enough for those things to be touched upon which would most harm piety or human society. Which might be admitted regarding a specific enumeration of crimes: but because he does not grant the Decalogue even a generic collection of all crimes, it is manifest that he is sailing in the wind for Socinus. Therefore he does not approve the opinion of the Jews, who, according to Philo, referred whatever is in the law of Moses to these ten heads, unless in this sense, not that those things were contained in these words (by virtue of them being contained in them) but that what we have here pertains to certain kinds of actions, to which the rest could be referred for the sake of aiding the memory: that they had another meaning, however, is clear from the example of Aben-Ezra already adduced. Add that he judges it more credible, for the sake of the Anabaptists and Socinus, that something was added to the law by Christ than that it was merely vindicated from a perverse interpretation in Matt. 5, which chapter, however, John testifies was given not to provide law, but to provide grace and truth, and in that way opposes it to Moses in chapter 1:17. The law was perfect in itself, admitting neither addition nor subtraction. Ps. 19:8, Deut. 4:2, ch. 12:32. Therefore, no additions to the law should be invented. The summary of the law, which by Christ's testimony was the love of God with all the heart, all the soul, and of one's neighbor as of oneself, argues for that perfection to which nothing further can be added. For what could be required above and beyond that supreme degree of love for God and neighbor? And therefore theologians observe the rule that there is more in the Decalogue than is said; since it designates the species with the genus, the genus with the species; the part with the whole, the whole with the part; the cause with the effect, the effect with the cause; the consequent with the antecedent, the affirmation with the negation, the correlate with the relatum, and vice versa. Whence Augustine, Book II, Quest. 71 on Exodus, to the question, whether fornication is held under the name of adultery? If, he says, by the name of theft one rightly understands every illicit usurpation of another's property—for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery, but certainly intended the whole to be understood from the part, whatever is illicitly taken of a neighbor's goods—then surely by the name of adultery every illicit intercourse and the unlawful use of those members must be understood to be forbidden. The cause, however, for the use of the word נָאַף rather than זָנָה seems to some to be the custom of Scripture, which often applies more serious crimes for the sake of greater horror, not excluding but including the lighter ones, since the legislator, by the proposition of the grosser species, intended to render hateful all those things which are either incentives to, or appendices of, more serious sins, or are otherwise related or akin to them.

Latin:

vers. 14. NON MOECHABERIS.

Novus error in Explicatione Grotiana De- calogi circa hoc præceptum se prodit, quod neget omnem Venerem illicitam eo prohiberi. Quanquam enim facile largiamur, vocem נאף de adulterio proprie adhiberi, & apud Ebræos solo illo sensu occurrere concedi possit, eoque id a Græcis, Lati- nis & aliis Interpretibus sic redditum sit, sub spe- ciali tamen interdicto genus ipsum prohibitum, & adulterii nomine Synecdochice omnis illicita libido comprehensa, quod Christi explicatio Matth. 5 28. luculenter confirmat. Ideo μοιχεῖαι & πορ- νεῖαι conjunguntur Matth. 15, 19. unde recte Aben- Ezra omnem illicitam Venerem illa voce com- prehendi, etiam scortationem, observavit. Sedu- ctus autem hic denuo est Grotius a Sociniano spi- ritu: Unde nimis abjecte de Decalogo sentit, neque eundem summariam virtutum & vitiorum mora- lium complexionem aut perfectam Justitiae regulam esse patitur: imo nihil necesse fuisse censet; in tam brevi Decalogo omnia crimina, quæ post interdicen- da erant, memorare, satis fuisse attingi ea, quæ aut pie- tatem aut societatem humanam maxime læderent. Quod de specifica criminum enumeratione admit- ti posset: Sed quia nec genericam complexionem omnium criminum Decalogo concedit, Socino ipsum velificari manifestum est. Ideo non pro- bat Judæorum sententiam, qui juxta Philonem, quæcunque in Mosis lege sunt, ad hæc decem Capita re- ferebant, nisi eo sensu, non quod illa his verbis inessent (virtute illis continerentur) sed quod quæ hic habe- mus, ad genera quædam actionum pertineant, ad quæ referri memoriæ adjuvandæ causa possent cætera: Quibus vero aliam mentem fuisse, vel exemplo Aben-Ezræ jam adducto liquet. Adde, quod in Anabaptistarum & Socini gratiam magis credibile judicet, additum aliquid esse legi a Christo, quam a prava duntaxat interpretatione eam vindicatam esse Matth. 5. cap. quem vero non ut legem daret, sed gratiam & veritatem præstaret, Johannes testatur, eoque pacto Mosi opponit cap. 1, 17. Lex in se per- fecta fuit, nec additionem, nec detractionem ad- mittens. Psal. 19, 8. Deut. 4, 2. cap. 12, 32. Nulla ergo fingi debent legis additamenta. Summa etiam legis, quæ Christo teste fuit dilectio Dei ex toto corde, tota anima, & proximi, sicut nostri ipso- rummet, eam perfectionem arguit, cui nihil in- super adjici possit. Quid enim exigi supra & præ- ter illum supremum gradum dilectionis DEI & proximi queat? Ideoque Regulam observant Theologi, plus in Decalogo esse, quam dici; cum ge- nere speciem, cum specie genus; cum toto partem, cum parte totum; cum effectu causam, cum causa effe- ctum; cum antecedente consequens, cum negatione affirmationem, cum relato correlatum, & vice versa designare. Unde Augustinus l. II. Quæst. 71. in Exod. ad quæstionem, utrum mæchiæ nomine fornicatio teneatur? Si furti nomine, inquit, bene intelligitur omnis illicita usurpatio rei alienæ, non enim rapinam permisit, qui furtum prohibuit, sed utiq; a parte totum intelligi voluit, quicquid illicite rerum proximi aufer- tur: profecto & nomine mæchiæ omnis illicitus concu- bitus atque illorum membrorum non legitimus usus prohibitus debet intelligi. Causa autem adhibiti potius verbi נָאַף quam זָנָה videtur quibusdam consuetudo Scripturæ, graviora sæpe crimina im- pingentis ad majorem horrorem, non exclusis sedinclu- sis levibus, quum legislator crassioris speciei pro- positione illa omnia exosa voluerit reddere, quæ vel incentiva sunt, vel appendices graviorum pec- catorum, vel cæteroquin illis cognata, aut affinia.

## 20:16
verse 16. THOU SHALT NOT SPEAK FALSE TESTIMONY AGAINST THY NEIGHBOR) In the Hebrew: thou shalt not answer: because those who were adjured and interrogated were giving testimony.

Regarding the neighbor, who he is, Grotius in his explanation of the Decalogue, p. 47, has this: The neighbor here is a fellow Israelite, as appears from examining the passage Exod. 2:13 and Lev. 19:18. To whom is opposed ὁ ἐχθρὸς, that is, the enemy. See Matt. 5:43. In the Gospel, the neighbor is any human being, as in Luke 10:33 and following, which was also the case before the law of Moses, Gen. 11:3.

The former gloss is merely Jewish and Socinian. The moral law was not prescribed only for Israelites,

Nor did Israelites alone sin against this law when they spoke false testimony against another Israelite; others also sin when they speak false testimony against anyone whatsoever. Shall we believe it was permitted for Israelites to speak false testimony without prejudice to the Decalogue, provided they did not speak it against an Israelite? That it was permitted against an enemy, as is hinted here by Grotius? Was it at least forbidden to covet the wife of an Israelite, or his house, or other things, Ex. 20:17? Was it forbidden only to kill an Israelite, Ex. 21:14? And so in other cases, as the same word for neighbor occurs in the law? Absurd. Which Augustine urges in Book 1 of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 30. Whoever thinks that the Apostle (who repeats the Mosaic law) did not give a commandment concerning every man is forced to confess what is most absurd and most wicked, that it seemed to the Apostle (Moses) that it was not a sin if someone committed adultery with the wife of a non-Christian (Israelite) or an enemy, or killed him, or coveted his property. But if it is the mark of a madman to say this, it is manifest that every man is to be considered a neighbor: because evil is to be done to no one. Therefore, just as in Gen. 11:3, 7, Exod. 11:2, Lev. 20:20, and elsewhere throughout, the word רֵעַ denotes any neighbor whatsoever, so also in the Decalogue. Nor was that opposition of neighbor and enemy taken from the law in Matt. 5:43, but it pertained to the Pharisaic δευτερώσεις or corruptions of the law. For where in the law is it prescribed: Thou shalt love thy neighbor and hate thine enemy? It is too manifest that this is a Pharisaic addition. Nor indeed is the neighbor in the Gospel only any man whatsoever, but according to the undoubted interpretation of Christ, which is superior to every exception, in Luke 10:33 ff., the neighbor in the law itself, Lev. 19:18, is to be understood in this way, of which Christ convinces the lawyer, and in that very point Grotius, who Judaizes: who likewise understands only the Israelite in that place. The word רֵעַ denotes a companion from רָעָה, he grazed, as if one who grazes together with another; but we are all grazed together by God, the earth feeds all at once: we are all neighbors, if not by race, then by nature and pasture. Therefore Augustine, Epist. LII to Macedonius: The neighbor in this place is to be weighed not by the proximity of blood, but by the society of reason, in which all men are companions. For if the account of money makes companions, how much more the account of nature, common by the law not of trading, but of birth. The Greeks render πλησίον from πέλας, by which is denoted any neighbor, any man. The Targum חַבֵר, which likewise denotes any companion, is explained not only of Israelites, but of anyone, even enemies, in the law, Exod. 23, 4. Nor does the Decalogue, to whose summary it pertains that we should love our neighbor as ourselves, look to Israelites alone, but to all men; and the words themselves imply this: Where Augustine excellently teaches again in his book On True Religion: It is inhuman not to love in a man what is human, but to love what is a son, what is a kinsman; for this is not to love that in him which pertains to God, but to love that which pertains to oneself. Let a man love his neighbor as himself. For certainly no one is a father to himself, no one is a son, or a relative, or anything of this kind, but only a man. Therefore, he who loves someone as himself ought to love in him that which he himself is. And this interpretation was placed beyond the hazard of doubt among Christians; nor was it controversial among the sounder Jews: as is evident from Justin's Dialogue with Trypho, πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ ὁμοιοπαθὲς καὶ λογικὸν ζῶον ἄνθρωπος, and from the explanation of the Rabbis, in the Targum in the notes to the Chaldean paraphrase of Lev. 19, 18. But Grotius preferred the clear interpretation of the sounder Rabbis, the orthodox Fathers, the Mosaic law, and Christ himself, to that of Socinus

& to abandon the Pharisaical depravity of the Anabaptists.

Latin:

vers. 16. NON LOQVERIS CONTRA PROXIMUM TUUM FALSUM TESTIMONIUM) In Hebræo: non re- spondebis: quia adjurati, & interrogati perhibebant testimo- nium.

De Proximo, quis ille sit, Grotius in explica- tione Decalogi p. 47. ita habet: Proximus hic est popularis Israelita, ut apparet expenso loco Exod. 2, 13. & Lev. 19, 18. Cui opponitur ὁ ἐχθρὸς, ho- stis scil. V. Matth. 43. In Evangelio proximus est homo quivis, ut Luc. 10, 33. ac seqq. quod & ante Mosis legem Gen. 11, 3.

Glossa prior mere Judaica est & Sociniana. Lex moralis non tantum Israelitis præscripta,

Nec Israelitae solum peccabant contra hanc legem, cum contra Israelitam alium falsum dicebant testi- monium, peccant etiam alii, cum dicunt falsum testimonium contra quemcunque. Num crede- mus licuisse Israelitis dicere falsum testimonium salvo Decalogo, modo non dixerint contra Israe- litam? Licuisse contra hostem, ut hic a Grotio innuitur? Num saltem prohibitum concupiscere uxorem Israelitae, aut domum, aut alia, Ex. 20, 17. num prohibitum tantum occidere Israelitam Ex. 21, 14. & sic in aliis, uti eadem proximi vox occur- rit in lege? Absurdum. Quod urget Augustinus l. 1. de doctr. Christian. c. 30. Quisquis arbitratur, non de omni homine Apostolum (qui legem Mosai- cam repetit) praecepisse, fateri cogitur, quod absur- dissimum & sceleratissimum est, visum fuisse Apostolo (Mosi) non esse peccatum, si quis aut non Christiani (Israelitae) aut inimici adulteraverit uxorem, aut eum occiderit, aut ejus rem cupiverit. Quod si dementis est dicere, manifestum est, omnem hominem proximum deputandum esse: quia erga neminem operandum est malum. Proinde uti Gen. 11, 3. 7. Exod. 11, 2. Lev. 20, 20. & alibi passim vox רֵעַ quemcunque proxi- mum notat, ita etiam in Decalogo. Nec opposi- tio illa Proximi & hostis e lege petita est Matth. 5, 43. sed ad δευτερώσεις vel corruptelas legis Phari- saicas pertinebat. Ubi enim in lege praescriptum: Diliges proximum tuum & odio habebis inimicum tuum? Nimis manifestum hic est additamentum Pharisaicum. Neque vero in Evangelio solum proximus est homo quilibet, sed juxta indubitatam omnique exceptione superiorem interpretatio- nem Christi Luc. 10, 33. seqq. in ipsa lege ita in- telligendus proximus Lev. 19, 18. quo de convin- cit legisperitum Christus, & in ipso Grotium Ju- daizantem: qui perinde illic loci solum Israelitam intelligit. Vox רֵעַ Socium notat a רָעָה pavit, quasi qui cum alio simul pascitur; at omnes simul pascimur a Deo, omnes alit simul terra: proximi sumus omnes, si non gente, natura, & pastura. Ideo Augustinus Epist. LII. ad Maced. Proximus hoc loco non sanguinis propinquitate, sed rationis so- cietate pensandus est, in qua socii sunt omnes homines. Nam si pecuniae ratio socios facit, quanto magis ratio naturae, non negotiandi, sed nascendi lege communis. Graeci reddunt πλησίον a πέλας, quo notatur quili- bet propinquus, quivis homo. Targum חַבֵר quod itidem quemvis socium denotat, nec de solis Israe- litis, sed quibusvis, etiam hostibus in lege id ex- plicatur Exod. 23, 4. nec ad solos Israelitas, sed omnes homines Decalogus, ad cujus summam per- tinet, ut proximum sicut nos ipsos diligamus, spe- ctat; idque verba ipsa inferunt: Ubi praeclare iterum Augustinus l. de ver. religion. docet: In- humanum est non amare in homine, quod homo est, sed amare, quod filius est, quod cognatus; hoc est enim non amare illud in eo, quod ad Deum pertinet, sed amare illud, quod ad se pertinet. Diligat homo proximum, tanquam seipsum. Certe enim sibi ipsi nemo est Pater, nemo est filius, aut affinis aut aliquis hujusmodi, sed tantum homo. Qui ergo diligit ali- quem, tanquam seipsum, hoc in eo diligere debet, quod sibi ipse est. Atque haec interpretatio penes Chri- stianos extra dubitationis aleam posita fuit; ne- que apud saniores Judaeos controversa: ut e Ju- stini Dial. cum Tryph. patet, πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ ὁμοιοπαθὲς καὶ λογικὸν ζῶον ἄνθρω- πος, & ex Rabbinorum explicatione, apud Tar- gum in notis ad paraphr. Chaldaic. Lev. 19, 18. Sed Grotius maluit Rabbinorum saniorum, Pa- trum orthodoxorum, legis Mosaicae, ipsius Chri- sti luculentam interpretationem, quam Socini

& Anabaptistarum Pharisaicam depravationem relinquere.

## 20:17
ver. 17. THOU SHALT NOT COVET) In this place in Hebrew it is לא תחמד, in Deuteronomy תתאוה. That word signifies also deceitful acts, by which another's property is misappropriated, and, in a more sublime sense, appetite also. Because the Hebrews for the most part neglected this sense, Christ therefore shows that such an appetite is not only displeasing to God, but also, if it is fostered, liable to hell.

Grotius does not express whether God intended here that more sublime sense, which he mentions, and to which the Hebrews ought to have attended, or otherwise? However, in his Explanation of the Decalogue, p. 48, he sufficiently hints at what is designated by concupiscence in this law: Therefore, in the Old Testament, by those Hebrew words which we have mentioned, it is generally signified not only motions, but a permanent purpose and intent. See Mich. III. But Grotius acknowledges that the more sublime sense asserted by Christ is not derived from the law, but considers it an addition to the law: since Christ not only prohibited the purpose and machination of a deliberate will, but also commanded that motions be suppressed as soon as they are felt, by avoiding all occasions by which they can be nourished, Matt. 5. But that sense, which Christ brought back into the light and asserted, is no other than that which was insinuated by the supreme Legislator himself, and which ought to have been attended to by all in the law already proposed. This is taught by the words of the Decalogue, the scope of Christ's sermon, and the analogy of the whole law. For in the Decalogue, there is used not only the word חמד, which is to desire something from the heart, with consent and with work fervent in the matter, but also תתאוה, which is, he made himself to covet, he incited himself to covet, by which the supreme Legislator refutes depraved motions and even depraved concupiscence habitually inherent in us from our origin, James 1:14, Matt. 15:19, and thus the very corruption of human nature: as it is truly sin and ἀνομία, and yet it does not fight except against this precept of the law. But it is repugnant to be ἀνομία and to be repugnant to no Precept of the Decalogue. Nor indeed was Christ's scope to enrich the law with certain additions, but to vindicate the same against manifest corruptions, such as, for example, that concerning having hatred for an enemy, likewise as if only adultery were prohibited by the law, only external homicide, etc. Finally, not only a permanent purpose and intent is prohibited by this law, which Grotius defends for the sake of the Socinians and Papists, but also any προπάθεια whatsoever, and Paul taught that depraved concupiscence itself is from the law itself, Rom. 7:13. Whence Augustine, book I, de nupt. & concup. c. 29. He does much good who does what is written, 'go not after thy concupiscences,' but he does not perfect it; because he does not fulfill what is written, 'thou shalt not covet,' so that we, understanding that we lie in this disease, might seek the grace of medicine, and in that precept might know both what we ought to strive to perfect in this mortality, and to what that most blessed immortality can be reached by us: for unless it were to be perfected at some time, it would never be commanded. Grotius himself praises a remarkable warning from the first book of Porphyry on abstinence, that one must abstain not only from deeds, not only from deliberate counsels and diseases of the mind, but also from the very habits themselves. After you have abstained from deeds, you must also abstain from HABITS, and especially from the very diseases of the mind. For what does it profit to abstain from deeds, if you remain bound to the causes from which they proceed? He adds: Those philosophers (Aelian, Porphyry, etc.) see more in this part than the teachers of the Jews, who were in Christ's time, and a little before, and after him: who, because no punishment was attached in this place (Ex. 20:16) or elsewhere to the THOUGHT of misappropriating a wife or another's property, held this more for a certain moral opinion, such as there are many in Proverbs, than for a divine precept. And so they deny that one sins by the will alone: instructed by such teachers, Paul would not have believed that he sinned by coveting, unless a more exact consideration of the LAW had persuaded him of it, Rom. 7:13. But if in this place that from which Porphyry wished one to abstain is prohibited, then the very motions of the mind, not only a permanent purpose and intent, are prohibited. Grotius believes that that philosopher saw more here from the light of nature than the Jews could have had from the law itself. But he is just as blind as the teachers of the Jews, who did not err from the more sublime sense of the law because they believed no punishment was attached to this precept: for the punishment of the general curse is, and concerns the violation of all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. 27:26, or because they did not hold this precept of the Decalogue for a precept, but because they did not penetrate its sense, by whom Paul, being instructed, likewise did not believe that one sins by coveting. But if the Apostle was persuaded of it by a MORE EXACT consideration of the Law, it must certainly be held in the law itself when more exactly considered, and it will not be to be held as an addition brought in by Christ. Nor does Paul condemn only the purpose of a deliberate will, but the very depraved motions and the law of sin adhering in our members, that innate depraved concupiscence, the indwelling ἁμαρτία, that evil which is present: as is manifest.

Furthermore, neither can that be proven, which Grotius says, that such an appetite is liable to hell only IF IT IS FOSTERED. For if that appetite is in itself displeasing to God, which he acknowledges, and it is ἀνομία and ἁμαρτία, it will be in itself and by itself liable to hell. For the wages of sin is death, Rom. 6:23. And Grotius confesses in his Explic. Decal. p. 48, that Christ commanded that motions be suppressed as soon as they are felt, by avoiding all occasions by which they could be nourished, and to add hell as a punishment to those acting otherwise, Matt. 5:28, where he acknowledges that the discourse is about the very motions of concupiscence: For I say to you: That everyone who shall look at a woman to covet her, has already committed adultery with her in his heart, etc. Justin says to Zen. and Seren. that appetite is forbidden to us by Christ as if it were smoke. Nor is that Papistic hypothesis about sins venial by their nature from anywhere else than from Judaism. But he also reveals another error here, that in the Old Law the punishment of Gehenna is nowhere revealed; nay, that the law of Moses dictates no punishment for such offenses. That he has this from the Jews, he does not deny: for he adds: this is also noted by the Masters. Let him therefore have those blind Doctors as his Masters. But what wonder, if Aben-Ezra, David Kimchi, and even Josephus judged that no punishment was dictated for counsel and wicked intent, or even for sacrilegious thoughts, since they did not even consider them as sin: denying that one can sin by will alone: but that Grotius, who considers them as sins, and confesses that the Philosophers themselves saw more here than those Masters of the Jews, should still appeal to the Masters of the Jews in this, that the law of Moses reveals no punishment for such offenses, that indeed one must wonder at. For these are related, guilt and punishment: as he himself argued elsewhere against Socinus, and all guilt of itself brings about punishment. Has he retracted that in Defens. fid. Cathol. de satisf. Christi c. III. p. 50. That he who sins deserves punishment, and is therefore punishable, this follows necessarily from the very relation of sin and the sinner to a superior, and is properly NATURAL? And that a punishment is dictated for all offenses in the law, which can be denied with the appearance of truth, when everyone is pronounced cursed who has not remained in ALL things which are written in the book of the law. Which curse certainly includes eternal punishment at the same time. As death, which is the wages of sin, also includes eternal death at the same time, Rom. 6, 23. For he who offends in one, is guilty of all, Jac. II. Since the infinite justice of God is injured by any sin whatsoever, it is no wonder that any sin whatsoever of itself deserves eternal punishment.

But he appeals in vain to the Ancients, Tertullian, Justin, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius. They do not say, as the cited passages show, that anything more perfect was commanded here by Christ than in the law: Tertullian says only that we have come to know innocence through faith, as revealed by a perfect Teacher; the others assert only that the very thought and movements of illicit concupiscence were restrained by that command about not desiring a woman; they by no means affirm that those things were not prohibited in the law. If this commandment seemed both new and grave to the Jews, it seemed so because of a corrupted sense of the law, which Grotius himself admits was not understood by them. But when Tryphon, the most learned of them, said to Justin, 'But those precepts of yours in the Gospel I know to be so great and wonderful that I think no one can observe them,' he did not speak badly so far; nor does that help Grotius at all. Since Paul testifies that the law likewise can be kept by no one, Rom. 8, 9. But Grotius contradicted him very badly, and ineptly opposed to him that saying of Christ in Matthew 19:26: 'With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.' For by what means will he confirm that the law, as it has been explained by Christ, can be kept by us? It is possible for God that it be performed in us by the imputation of the perfect Justice of Christ, which Scripture teaches is impossible for us to perform by the perfect observation of the law. But that the law can be performed by any of us, neither Christ nor any of the Apostles ever taught: rather, the unique Teacher wished to lead that young man to acknowledge his own ἀδυναμίαν (inability), Matthew 19:18 seqq. Moreover, he now wishes to show that possibility

Grotius, instructed in the School of Socinus, as it appears, or because he loves antiquity, [is a follower] of Pelagius, the predecessor of Socinus. Namely, of eternal life (I present his words from the Explanation of the Decalogue, p. 49): 'Christ obtained for those believing in him a more certain faith and a much greater Spirit than had ever been given, and then indeed he also gave us a most absolute example by his cross: and nothing is so hard at the beginning that it does not become easy by practice.' By this habit of resisting, it happens little by little that those movements, as if defeated, do not dare to rise again. This is that beautiful victory through faith, of which 1 John 5:4 treats. These things are entirely Pelagian and Socinian, diametrically contrary to Scripture. Faith in eternal life was equally certain to the Ancients, and equally obtained for believers of the Old Testament by Christ: because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13:8. And we believe that we are saved by the grace of our Lord, just as they were, Acts 15:10. The ancient faithful had the Spirit not only of revelation, as the Socinians wish, but also of sealing, and they ought to have attributed him equally to Christ, as having been obtained by him. See Augustine, Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, book III, ch. 4. 'Therefore, in the time of the Old Testament, let us say that the Holy Spirit (these are the words of the Bishop of Hippo) was in those who even then were children of promise according to Isaac, not only as a helper, which those (the Pelagians) think is sufficient for their dogma, but also as a giver of virtue, etc.' Now, indeed, Christ did not only give us an example by his cross, but he merited justice and salvation, which Grotius himself demonstrated elsewhere against Socinus in his Defense of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ. For Christ undertakes, as Augustine has it in book XIV against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 14, our punishment without guilt, so that from there he might dissolve our guilt and also end our punishment. Concerning the Pelagians, see the book On the Grace of Christ against the Pelagians and Caelestius, ch. II. They (the Pelagians) are accustomed to say that Christ provided us with help in that for not sinning, because by living justly himself, and by teaching justly, he left an example. Lately, to make faith in eternal life [the means] so that we can observe the precepts of the Gospel, which are greater than the precepts of the law, and to defeat even depraved movements so that they do not dare to rise again, and that this is the righteousness of faith celebrated in the Scriptures, is the ἄκρομα (teaching) of the Socinian School, indeed the πρῶτον ψεῦδος (first lie) of the errors of that heresy, which we refuted in Socinianism Overthrown, Section 1, member 2, question 5.

Latin:

verf. 17. NON CONCUPISCES) In hoc loco Hebraice לא תחמד, in Deuteronomio תתאוה. Significat ea vox & actus dolosos, quibus alienum intervertitur, &, sensu subli- miore appetitus etiam. Hunc sensum quia ferme neglige- bant Hebræi, ideo Christus ostendit, talem appetitum non modo Deo displicere, sed &c, si foveatur, gehennæ obnoxium.

Non exprimit Grotius, sensumne illum, quem dicit, sublimiorem hic intenderit Deus, & attendere debuerint Ebræi, an secus? Satis autem in Decal. explic. p. 48. innuit, quid hac in lege per concupi- scentiam designetur: Ideo in Veteri fœdere vocibus illis Ebræis, quas diximus, plerumque non motus solos, sed permanens studium propositumque significari. Vid. Mich. III. Sensum vero sublimiorem a Christo as- fertum, non e lege derivatum agnoscit, sed pro le- gis additamento habet Grotius: cum non tantum voluntatis deliberatæ propositum ac machinationem prohibuit Christus, sed & præcepit motus simul atque sentiuntur, opprimi, vitando occasiones omnes, quibus ali possunt Matth. 5. Sed sensus ille, quem Chri- stus produxit denuo in apricum, & asseruit, non est alius, quam qui ab ipso Legislatore summo insinua- tus fuit, & in lege jam propositus ab omnibus at- tendi debuit. Quod docent verba Decalogi, sco- pus concionis Christi, & analogia totius legis. In De- calogo enim ideo adhibetur non tantum verbum חמד quod est, ex animo aliquid desiderare, cum con- sensu & opere in rem ferventi, sed etiam תתאוה, quod est, seipsum fecit concupiscere, seipsum irrita- vit ad concupiscendum, quo motus pravos & concu- piscentiam etiam pravam habitualiter ob origine nobis inhærentem Jac. 1, 14. Matth. 15, 19. adeoque ipsam naturæ humanæ corruptionem redarguit supre- mus Legislator: utpote quæ vere peccatum ac ἀνο- μία est, nec tamen nisi contra hoc legis præceptum militat. Repugnat autem ἀνομίαν esse, & nulli Deca- logi Præcepto repugnare. Nec vero Christi scopus fuit legem additamentis quibusdam locupletare, sed eandem adversus manifestas corruptelas, qua- lis v. g. illa erat de odio habendo hoste, item ac si solum adulterium lege prohibitum fuerit, solum externum homicidium &c. vindicare. Denique non permanens solum studium propositumq́; lege hac prohiberi, quod in gratiam Socinianorum & Papistarum propugnat Grotius, sed etiam προπάθειαν quamvis, ipsamque pravam concupiscentiam ex ipsa lege Paulus docuit Rom. 7, 13. Unde Augustinus lib. I. de nupt. & con- cup. c. 29. Multum boni facit, qui facit, quod scri- ptum est, post concupiscentias tuas ne eas, sed non per- ficit; quia non implet, quod scriptum est, non concupi- sces, ut nos in hoc morbo jacere intelligentes medicinæ gratiam quæreremus, & in eo præcepto sciremus, & quæ debeamus in hac mortalitate perficiendo conari, & quo possit a nobis illa immortalitate beatissima per- veniri: nisi enim quandoque perficiendum esset, nun- quam jubendum esset. Laudat ipse Grotius e Porphy- rii libro de abstinentia primo monitum præclarum, quod non tantum a factis, non solum a deliberatis con- siliis animique morbis, sed ab ipsis etiam moribus pror- sus abstinendum sit. Postquam autem factis abstinue- ris, abstinendum & MORIBUS, ac maxime ipsis animi morbis. Quid enim prodest factis abstinere, si causis, unde ea procedunt, adstrictus maneas? Addit: Plus videre hac in parte isti Philosophi, (Ælianus, Porphyrius &c.) quam Judæorum Magistri, qui Christi tempore, & paulo ante, ac post eum fuere: qui ideo, quod pœna nulla hoc loco (Ex. 20, 16.) alibi- ve COGITATIONI intervertendæ uxoris, reive alienæ apposita est, magis pro sententia quadam morali, quales in Proverbiis multæ sunt, quam pro divino præcepto hoc habuere. Itaque negant, peccari sola vo- luntate: talibus Magistris institutus Paulus non credi- disset peccare concupiscendo, nisi exactior LEGIS consideratio ei id persuasisset Rom. 7, 13. At si hoc lo- co id, a quo Porphyrius abstineri voluit, prohibe- tur, ipsi utique motus animi, non solum permanens studium propositumque prohibentur. Plus hic vi- dit Philosophus ille e naturæ lumine, quam ex ipsa lege habere potuisse Judæos credit Grotius. Sed æque cæcus, ac Magistri Judæorum, qui non ideo errabant a sublimiore sensu legis, quod pœnam nul- lam crederent appositam huic præcepto: pœna enim maledictionis generalis est, & concernit violatio- nem omnium, quæ in libro legis scripta sunt Deut. 27, 26. aut quod hoc præceptum Decalogi non ha- buerint pro præcepto, sed quod sensum ejus non pe- netraverint, a quibus Paulus institutus, pariter non credidit, peccari concupiscendo. Si autem Apostolo ab EXACTIORI Legis consideratione id per- suasum, oportet utique in lege ipsa exactius con- siderata hoc haberi, non vero pro additamento a Christo invecto id habendum erit. Nec vero Pau- lus solum voluntatis deliberatæ propositum damnat, sed motus ipsos pravos ac legem peccati in membris no- stris hærentem, connatam illam pravam concupi- scentiam, inhabitantem ἁμαρτίαν, malum illud παρακείμενον: uti manifestum.

Porro nec id probari potest, quod Grotius talem appetitum gehennæ obnoxium solum dicat. Si FOVEATUR. Nam si Deo appetitus ille in se dis- plicet, quod agnoscit, & ἀνομία & ἁμαρτία est, in se ac per se gehennæ obnoxius erit. Peccati enim stipendium mors est Rom. 6, 23. Et fatetur in Explic. Decal. p. 48. Grotius, Christum præcepisse motus simul atque sentiuntur opprimi, vitando occasiones omnes, quibus alii possent, ac pœnam aliter agentibus addere gehennam, Matth. 5, 28. ubi agnoscit de ipsis motibus concupiscentiæ sermonem esse: Ego enim dico vobis: Quia omnis, qui videbit mulierem ad con- cupiscendum eam, jam mœchatus est eam in corde suo &c. Primum appetitus veluti fumum a Christo no- bis interdici Justinus ad Zen. & Seren. ait. Neque aliunde, quam e Judaismo est illa, de peccatis natura sua venialibus, hypothesis Papistica. Sed & alium hic prodit errorem, in lege Veteri pœnam gehennæ nuspiam proditam; imo talibus delictis nullam pœ- nam legem Mosis dictare. Quod a Judæis se habere, non diffitetur: Addit enim: id etiam a Magistris notatum. Habeat ergo cæcos illos Doctores Ma- gistros suos. At quid mirum, si Aben-Ezra, David Kimchi, Josephus etiam pœnam consilio & propo- sito pravo, cogitatis etiam sacrilegis nullam dictam censuerint, quum ne quidem pro peccato illa ha- buerint: sola voluntate peccari negando: quod au- tem Grotius, qui ea pro peccatis habet, & Philo- sophos ipsos plus hic vidisse Judæorum istis Magi- stris fatetur, adhuc tamen ad Judæorum Magistros in eo provocet, quod nullam pœnam talibus deli- ctis lex Mosis prodat, id vero mirari oportet. Sunt enim hæc relata, culpa & pœna: uti ipse alias con- tra Socinum disputavit, omnisque culpa per se pœ- nam infert. Num retractavit illud defens. fid. Ca- thol. de satisf. Christi c. III. p. 50. Quod is, qui de- linquit, pœnam meretur, eoque punibilis est, hoc ex ipsa peccati & peccatoris ad superiorem relatione necessa- rio sequitur, & proprie NATURALE est? Et pœ- nam omnibus delictis dictam esse in lege, qua veri specie negari potest, quum maledictus pronuncie- tur omnis ille, qui non permanserit in OMNIBUS, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis. Quæ certe maledictio æternam pœnam simul complectitur. Uti mors, quæ peccati stipendium, mortem etiam æternam simul comprehendit, Rom. 6, 23. Qui enim in uno offenderit, reus est omnium Jac. II. Quum infini- ta Dei Justitia lædatur quovis peccato, non mirum, quodvis peccatum per se mereri æternam pœnam.

Nequicquam vero provocat ad Veteres, Tertullianum, Justinum, Athenagoram, Clem. Alexandr. Lactantium. Non illi perfectius hic quid a Christo, quam in lege præceptum, adductis locis, ajunt: Tertullianus solum per fidem nos innocentiam novisse dicit, ut a perfecto Magistro revelatum; cæteri solum cogitationem ipsam motusque illicitæ concupiscentiæ illo de fœmina non appetenda, compefci afferunt; in lege autem illa prohibita non fuisse, minime affirmant. Si novum simul & grave visum Judæis hoc præceptum, ita visum ob corruptum legis sensum, quam ab ipsis non intellectam fatetur ipse Grotius. Cum autem Justino doctissimus illorum Tryphon, vestra autem illa, dixit, in Evangelio præcepta adeo scio esse magna & mirabilia, ut putem, neminem ea posse observare; hactenus non male dixit, Nec Grotium id quicquam juvat. Siquidem Paulus testetur, legem itidem servari a nemine posse, Rom. 8, 9. Pessime autem illi contradixit Grotius, & inepte opposuit illud Christi Matth. 19, 26. Apud homines hoc impossibile est, apud Deum autem omnia possibilia sunt. Eo enim legem, prout a Christo explicata est, servari a nobis posse, quo pacto confirmabit? Possibile Deo est, ut in nobis præstetur imputatione perfectæ Christi Justitiæ, quod ut a nobis præstetur observatione legis perfecta, nobis impossibile esse, Scriptura docet. Sed legem præstari a quoquam nostrum posse, neque Christus, neque Apostolorum ullus unquam docuit: ad ἀδυναμίαν potius suam agnoscendam Magister unicus juvenem illum deductum cupiebat Matth. 19, 18. seqq. Cæterum possibilitatem nunc illam monstrare vult

Grotius, in Schola Socini, ut apparet, instructus, aut cum antiquitatem amet, Pelagii Prædecessoris Socini. Vitæ scil. æternæ (verba ejus exhibeo e Decal. explic. p. 49.) certiorem fidem & Spiritum multo majorem, quam datus unquam fuerat, in se credentibus Christus impetravit, tum vero & cruce sua exemplum nobis absolutissimum dedit: nihilque tam durum initio est, quod non exercendo facile fiat. Hac repugnandi consuetudine fit paulatim, ut motus illi, velut debellati, non audeant resurgere. Hæc est pulcra illa per fidem victoria, de qua agit Joh. Epist. 1. c. 5, 4. Quæ prorsus Pelagiana & Sociniana sunt, Scripturæ καδδιάμετρον contraria. Vitæ æternæ fides æque certa fuit Veteribus, æque impetrata credentibus V. T. a Christo: quia Jesus Christus heri, hodie, idem & in secula Ebr. 13, 8. Et credimus, gratia Domini nostri salvari, quemadmodum & illi Actor. 15, 10. Spiritum non revelationis tantum, quod Socinistæ volunt, sed obsignationis quoque habuere fideles antiqui, eumque pariter Christo acceptum ferre debuere, utpote ab ipso impetratum. Vid. August. contra duas Epistol. Pelag. l. III. c. 4. Tempore igitur V. T. Spiritum S. (verba Hipponensis Episcopi sunt) in eis, qui etiam tunc secundum Isaac promissionis filii erant, non solum adjutorem, quod isti (Pelagiani) suo dogmati sufficere existimant, verum etiam largitorem dicamus fuisse virtutis &c. Jam vero cruce sua Christus non exemplum nobis dedit solum, sed promeruit justitiam & salutem, quod alias contra Socinum demonstravit ipse Grotius defensione fidei Catholicæ de satisf. Christi. Suscipit enim Christus, ut Augustinus habet l. XIV. contr. Faust. Manich. c. 14. sine reatu supplicium nostrum, ut inde solveret reatum nostrum & finiret etiam supplicium nostrum. De Pelagianis v. l. de grat. Christi contr. Pelag. & Cœlest. c. II. Solent (Pelagiani) dicere, nobis in eo Christum ad non peccandum præbuisse adjutorium, quia juste ipse vivendo, justeque docendo reliquit exemplum. Novissime vitæ æternæ fidem facere, ut possimus præcepta Evangelii majora legis præceptis observare, motus etiam pravos ita de- bellare, ut resurgere non audeant, eamque esse fidei ju- stitiam in Scripturis decantatam ἄκρομα est Scho- læ Socinianæ, imo πρῶτον ψεῦδος errorum hære- seos istius, quod nos confutavimus Socinismo pro- fligato Sect. 1. membr. 2. qv. 5.

## 20:18
verse 18. HE SAW VOICES) He heard. For the word 'seeing' is used for every sense.

Latin:

vers. 18. VIDEBAT VOCES) Audiebat. De omni enim sensu usurpatur vox videndi.

## 20:19
verse 19. LET NOT THE LORD SPEAK, LEST PERCHANCE WE DIE.

The Israelites request that they might hear the will and commands of the Lord through the intervention of Moses, not immediately: because they could not endure GOD speaking ἀμέσως (directly), being greatly terrified and shaken with fear when they saw the voices, and the lamps, and the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain. But Moses himself was also terrified, which, although it is not related in the history, the Apostle handed down to memory in Heb. 12:21: 'And so fearful was the sight, Moses said, I am terrified and trembling.' These things testify to the rigor, terror, and curse of the law, which no one, not even Moses himself, can endure because of the infirmity of the flesh, from which horror and fear, indeed despair, must arise, unless another intervenes who averts these things. Although, therefore, the People wished to interpose Moses because of that fear, the fear and horror proper to him teach that Moses was not equal to enduring and averting that terror: for which reason it is reported that GOD himself gave this most gracious response to the people through Moses, Deut. 18:16, 17: 'As you asked of the Lord your GOD in Horeb, when the assembly was gathered: and you said: I will not hear again the voice of the Lord my GOD, and I will not see this great fire anymore, lest I die: And the Lord said to me (says Moses) They have spoken all things well: I will raise up a Prophet for them from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them all things that I shall command him.' Which speak of Christ the Mediator, and promise him, Acts 3:27, ch. 7:37. From this passage, therefore, and the promise concerning Christ, the present history is to be supplemented: that then on Mount Horeb, when the people were already beholding death and seeking the intervention of Moses, while Moses himself was trembling greatly and fearing, the mediation of Christ was promised, without which no one can bear the wrath of GOD and the curse of the law. Compare what we have said regarding that passage. Well, says the Lord, have they spoken; because he who approaches me without a mediator approaches a consuming fire: especially if he hears nothing else than the voice of the law, which can do nothing but terrify and condemn the sinner. Wherefore I will give them a Mediator, who may place himself in the middle, expiate sin, and announce to them the Gospel concerning the remission of sins and the eternity of life; as Osiander paraphrases that passage.

Latin:

vers. 19. NON LOQUATUR DOMINUS, NE FORTE MORIAMUR.

Expetunt Israëlitæ, ut Mose interveniente au- diant voluntatem & mandata Domini, non imme- diate: quod DEUM ἀμέσως loquentem ferre non sustineant, cum viderent voces, & lampades, & so- nitum buccinæ montemque fumantem admodum perterriti, ac pavore concussi. Sed & Moses ipse perterritus fuit, quod etsi in historia non referatur, memoriæ prodidit Apostolus Ebr. 12, 21. καὶ ὕτω Φοβερὸν ἧν τὸ Φανταζόμενον, μωσῆς εἶπεν, ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος. Quæ legis rigorem, terrorem, ac maledictionem, quam nemo, ac nec Moses ipse ob carnis infirmitatem sustinere potest, testantur, unde oriri oportet horrorem ac timorem, imo desperationem, nisi alius intercedat, qui hæc aver- tat. Etsi ergo Populus Mosen ex isto pavore in- terponere voluerit, Mosen tamen non fuisse parem sustinendo ac avertendo terrori, timor ac horror ejusdem proprius docet: quapropter DEUS ipse hoc responsum gratiosissimum po- pulo per Mosen dedisse refertur Deut. 18, 16. 17. ut petijsti a Domino DEO tuo in Horeb, quando con- cio congregata fuit: atque dixisti: ultra non audiam vocem Domini DEI mei, & ignem hunc maxi- mum amplius non videbo, ne moriar: Et ait Do- minus mihi (ait Moses) Bene omnia sunt loquuti: Prophetam suscitabo eis de medio fratrum suorum, similem tui, & ponam verba mea in ore ejus, loque- turque ad eos omnia, quæ præcepero illi. Quæ de Christo Mediatore loquuntur, eumque promit- tunt Actor. 3, 27. cap. 7, 37. Ex hoc loco ergo & promissione de Christo supplenda est præsens historia: quod tum in monte Horeb jam popu- lo mortem me tuenti, & interventionem Mosis expetenti, quum Moses ipse tremeret admodum ac timeret, Christi mediatio promissa sit, sine qua nemo iram DEI ac maledictionem legis fer- re queat. Confer. quæ ad istum locum dixi- mus. Bene, inquit Dominus, sunt loquuti; quia qui sine mediatore ad me accedit, ad ignem consu- mentem accedit: præsertim si nihil aliud audiat, quam vocem legis, quæ non nisi terrere, & damna- re peccatorem potest. Quare Mediatorem illis da- bo, qui se interponat medium, peccatum expiet, & Evangelium de remissione peccatorum ac vitæ æter- nitate ipsis annuntiet; ut locum illum παραφράζει Osiander.

## 20:20
Vers. 20. AND MOSES SAID TO THE PEOPLE, DO NOT FEAR.

After the announcement of that Evangelical Promise, these things were, without doubt, said to the people: otherwise they would have been said in vain. Because without the Gospel, the law works nothing but terror. He added the reason for the coming of the Lord, with such a horrendous display: for the Lord came to test you. This testing was of the examination of conscience, of recognition, of infirmity, of sin and demerit, of the sense of wrath and curse, and of refuge to the grace promised in Christ the mediator, and of the flight from sin obtained by the same, and of the zeal for new obedience. Therefore there is added an explanation, and, that is, that his terror might be among you, and you might not sin, that henceforth having done penance you might flee from sin, with trembling and horror.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ET AIT MOSES AD POPULUM, NOLITE TIMERE.

Post annuntiationem Promissionis illius Ev- angelicæ hæc, sine dubio, dicta ad populum: alias frustra dicta forent. Quia sine Evange- lio lex non nisi terrorem operatur. Addidit causam adventus Domini, cum tam horrendo apparatu: ut enim probaret vos, venit Dominus. Probatio hæc fuit examinis conscientiæ, agnitio- nis, infirmitatis, peccati & demeriti, sensus iræ & maledictionis & refugii ad gratiam in Christo mediatore promissam, eademque obtenta fugæ peccati, & studii novæ obedientiæ. Ideo addi- tur ἐπεξήγησις, &, id est, ut terror illius esset in vobis, & non peccaretis, ut deinceps acta poenitentia pec- catum fugeretis, cum tremore & horrore.

## 20:24
Vers. 24.

YOU SHALL MAKE AN ALTAR OF EARTH FOR ME] Of green turf, as Ovid, Silius, and other poets speak. It is the custom for those making a journey to build such altars as being makeshift.

What have poets to do here? Are the ceremonial laws of Moses to be explained from them? The custom of travelers is likewise irrelevant here: because the Israelites were neither to imitate the custom of others, nor did the altars of the Gentiles have any commerce with the altars of the Hebrews. Furthermore, because God forbade them to have silver and golden gods, he now demands not a golden or silver, but only an earthen altar for the offering of burnt offerings and peace offerings. And therefore he also did not want altars to be made of hewn stones, if they should wish to make them of stone at all, v. 25. by which he testified that there was no need for external apparatus and ornament for his worship, and that he is delighted by simplicity, and that he might withdraw the people from silver in worship and ritual, lest they believe that some divinity lay hidden in gold, silver, or marble, Daniel VI. although afterwards in the description of the tabernacle he commanded that everything be done not without singular apparatus and ornament, for a certain reason, namely as a type and foreshadowing of spiritual things, and especially of future things, because all things had their mystical significance. Furthermore, he also wished to teach in this way that he looks at the victims rather than the altars, and is more delighted by the faith of those offering than by the price and splendor of the altars. Moreover, he also warns that the use of those altars would not be perpetual, but that just as they are easily constructed from earth and rough stones, so they would easily be destroyed; indeed, he wanted them constructed from earth or unpolished stones for this reason, so that wherever the Lord might wish, the occasion for building an altar for him would be at hand.

A doubt arises, however, as to how this command of the Lord concerning the altar of burnt offerings stands with the divine command and construction in Exod. 27, where it is ordered at length how the altar of burnt offerings is to be constructed, which was to be fabricated from shittim wood, not from earth or stones, which was to be covered with bronze plates on the outside and inside, so that it would not be damaged by fire: Some, because this altar had to be hollow inside v. 8, say that it had to be filled up to the middle either with earth, with Abulensis and Richard, or with unhewn and unpolished stone, with Ribera, by the force of this command in Exod. 20, 24, 25, and that Moses and Solomon did so 1 Macc. 4, 56. In this altar, therefore, the structure of stones three cubits high, according to Cornelius à Lapide, rose to the middle, that is, to a cubit and a half, then the area of the grate was placed upon it, on which, with fire placed underneath, the meat was burned: but it was surrounded by shittim boards covered with bronze. Rivetus explains this opinion in this way on Exod. 27. Since the altar was hollow beyond its own sides, he says that certain walls were built from the bottom to the top from clayey earth, or from bricks or stones, so that they were like another earthen or stone altar enclosed by bronze: but in this opinion, that which is said about the wall being made either of bricks or of clay seems inconvenient and little probable to him: for since the altar had to be portable, it would have been very inconvenient to tear down old walls and build new ones everywhere. Add that in this way this command concerning an earthen and stone altar would not have been satisfied, because here the discourse is not about walls alone, but about the whole altar: nor could an altar of shittim wood be called an altar built of earth or of stones because of earth heaped in or stones placed upon it or even brick walls. And therefore it is more correctly observed that this which is commanded concerning building an altar of earth or unpolished stones must have been understood of altars outside the tabernacle before the temple, which had to be built by tumultuous work for the use of a few days, and destroyed after use. Which is also noted in the Osiandrine and Vinarie Paraphrase. Osiander notes that Christ's humanity was thus foreshadowed, which was of the earth. For man is earth: because of him our works are acceptable to God. Heb. 13, 10. But if (so his Paraphrase has it at v. 25) anywhere outside the sacred tabernacle, having been ordered by my special command, you shall have made a stone altar, you shall not build it for me of hewn stones: for if you have lifted your tool over it, that is, as soon as you have undertaken to polish those stones with iron instruments, that altar will immediately be polluted by you, by this very excessive and untimely zeal of yours, so that neither the altar nor the victims will be acceptable to me. Moses ordered such an altar to be made even after the tabernacle was erected in the land of Canaan, Deut. ch. 27, which command of Moses Joshua fulfilled, ch. 8. But God signified that it does not please him that human industry should test its powers in adorning the worship of God (outside the prescription of his own word). Thus Osiander. Compare also 1 Kings 18, 31; Judges 13, 29. What cause is more correctly maintained than the Grotian one, concerning the old law: for what do the laws of the Gentiles have to do with divine laws in ceremonial matters? But Grotius holds it thus: Ver. 25. IF INDEED YOU LIFT UP YOUR TOOL UPON IT, IT SHALL BE POLLUTED] It is an old law that iron be removed from sacred things, which Cicero follows in his own laws. Hecataeus concerning the Jerusalem Temple: Ἐν ᾧ βωμός ἐστι τετράγωνος, ἐκ ἐν τμητῶν ἀλλ̓ ἐκ τῶν ἀργῶν λίθων ὕτω συγκείμενος. Ver. 26. YOU SHALL NOT GO UP BY STEPS TO MY ALTAR] Something similar exists in the old Roman Pontifical law, from which Servius cites this for the 4th book of the Aeneid: Among the ancients, it was not permitted to climb stairs of more than three steps, unless they were Greek, so that no part of one's feet or carriage might be seen underneath, and therefore not by more steps, but by three, so that the double effort of the ascent would not cause the garment to be lifted up, or the legs to be bared. For that reason they are also called Greek stairs, because they are constructed in such a way that they are closed on every side by the joining of boards, so that they do not allow a view of any part of the body. These things could have proceeded from excessive affectation. It is our task to examine the causes, according to the guidance of Scripture. But Moses adds here, as follows: LEST YOUR NAKEDNESS BE REVEALED. For the priests wore linen breeches, which only extended as far as the knees: and thus the sacrificing priest was barefoot, Ex. 28, 42. Some wish this precept to have been established on account of the impure rites of Priapus, to which the Jews were very prone 1 Kings 15, 12. 13. (the idol of the Moabites, when the Hebrews were about to pass through the land of the Moabites. Whence they were also solicited by them to this cult. Num. 25.) in which the Gentiles exposed their private parts to the people. Thus Thomas, Lyranus, Villalpandus. Whence some make a peculiar precept comprised in these words: you shall not reveal your nakedness; but they contain the cause of the precept, not a peculiar precept. And in those abominable rites, those shameful acts were prohibited without steps. Therefore, God wished here only to remind the Israelites of reverence, chastity, and honesty in celebrating sacred rites, so that sacred things might be treated reverently and holily; as Jerome observes in his letter to Fabiola, ch. 28, 42. But how does it agree with this precept that in Ex. 27, 1, the altar was required to be three cubits high, which is a height so great that no one could conveniently minister at the altar without steps: and that in 2 Chron. 4, 1, Solomon is said to have made a bronze altar of ten cubits in height, for the ascending of which steps were certainly necessary? Abulensis and Ribera respond that there were no wooden or stone steps there, but a continuous ascent from the ground, which gradually and uniformly rose aloft, so that in the ascent no exposure was to be feared, which we concede regarding the altar of the tabernacle. But as for Solomon's bronze altar, others respond: that one had to ascend to the substructures by steps, but not from there to the altar itself. That height, however, 2 Par. 4, designated, was a superstructure of the wall and the altar. But in that way, nakedness would have been revealed in the ascent of the substructures. And therefore it is more correctly answered that this precept was temporal, also adapted to the time of the pilgrimage: and furthermore, that the Solomonic steps were so wide and magnificent that the entire lower part of the garment was also covered by the steps, so that those things which nature wishes to be hidden could not be seen. Finally, that a remedy was also applied, because the priests under the law used breeches and drawers, as Jerome noted in the place cited. Rupert gives a moral application: do not make steps on the altar of your heart, that is, do not be exalted because of your progress, otherwise your nakedness will be revealed: because the pride of the mind is accompanied by the shame of the flesh.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ALTARE DE TERRA FACIETIS MIHI] Cespide de viridi, ut Ovidius, Silius & Poëtæ alii loquuntur. Tales aras utpote subitarias struere mos iter facientibus.

Quid huc Poëtæ faciant? Num ex illis leges Mosis ceremoniales explicandæ? Mos iter facien- tium hîc itidem alienus: quia nec aliorum morem Israëlitæ imitari debebant, nec aræ gentilium com- mercii quicquam cum aris Ebræorum habebant. Cæterum quia vetabat Deus, ne habeant Deos ar- genteos & aureos, jam non aureum vel argenteum, sed terreum solum postulat altare ad oblationem holocaustorum, & victimarum pacificarum. Ideoque etiam non ex sectis lapidibus fieri voluit altaria, si omnino lapidea facere velint v. 25. quo non opus esse externo apparatu, & ornatu ad cultum suum testaretur, seque delectari simplicitate, & ut argen- tum cultu rituque populum abstraheret, ne in au- ro, argento vel marmore aliquid latere numinis crederent Daniel. VI. etsi deinceps in descriptione tabernaculi non sine apparatu & ornatu singulari cuncta fieri præceperit, ob certam causam typum nempe & adumbrationem rerum spiritualium, im- primis vero futurarum, quia omnia habebant suam significationem mysticam. Porro docere etiam ita voluit, se victimas potius, quam altaria intueri, ma- gisque fide offerentium, quam pretio ac splendore altarium delectari. Adhæc monere quoque altarium illorum usum non fore perpetuum, sed ut è terra scabrisque lapidibus facile construuntur, ita facile eadem destructum iri; imo ideo è terra aut lapidi- bus non politis ea construi voluit, ut ubique cum voluerit Dominus, occasio ipsi altare extruendi in promptu esset.

Dubium autem oritur, quomodo hoc præ- ceptum Domini de altari holocaustorum consti- stat cum præcepto & constructione divina Exod. 27. ubi prolixe ordinatur, quomodo construendum altare holocaustorum sit, quod de lignis Setim fa- bricandum erat, non de terra, vel lapidibus, quæ æneis tabulis exterius & interius tegenda, ne ab igne læderentur: Nonnulli, quia hoc altare interius cavum esse debebat v. 8. vel terra cum Abulensi, & Richardo, vel lapide insecto & impolito cum Ribera id usque ad medietatem implendum fuisse dicunt, vi hujus præcepti Exod. 20, 24. 25. idque ita Mosen & Salomonem fecisse 1. Macc. 4, 56. In altari ergo hoc alto tres cubitos lapidum structura, secundum Cornelium à Lapide ad dimidium, id est, ad cubi- tum cum dimidio ascendebat, deinde illi superpo- nebatur area craticulæ, in qua igne supposito car- nes cremabantur: circumcirca vero ambiebatur tabulis Setim ære obductis. Quam sententiam ita explicat Rivetus ad Exod. 27. Cum altare cavum es- set ultra ipsius latera, parietes quosdam ab uno ad summum ex terra argillosa, vel ex lateribus aut la- pidibus exstructos fuisse, ut essent velut aliud alta- re terreum, aut lapideum æneo inclusum: in qua vero sententia id ipsi incommodum, & parum pro- babile videtur, quod dicitur de pariete vel ex late- ribus, vel ex argilla conficiendo: cum enim porta- tile esse deberet altare, valde incommodum fuisset veteres parietes diruere; & novos ubique extruere Adde, quod ita huic præcepto de altari terreo, & lapideo non satisfactum fuisset, quia hic non de pa- rietibus solum, sed integro altari sermo est: nec al- tare de ligno Setim ob terram ingestam vel lapide impositos aut etiam parietes lateritios dici pote- rat altare è terra vel è lapidibus extructum. Ideoque rectius observatur hoc, quod præcipitur de altari construendo è terra aut lapidibus impolitis, intel- ligendum fuisse de altaribus extra tabernaculum ante templum, quæ opere tumultuario debuerunt construi ad usum paucorum dierum, & post usum destrui. Quod etiam in Paraphrasi Osiandrina & Vinariensi annotatum. Christi humanitatem ita ad- umbratam esse, quæ de terra fuit, Osiander notat. Homo ènim terra est: propter ipsum nostra opera Deo sunt accepta. Ebr. 13, 10. Quod si vero (Sic ha- bet Paraphrasis ejus ad v. 25.) alicubi extra taber- naculum sacrum, speciali mandato meo id jussus, al- tare lapideum feceris, mihi non ædificabis illud de se- ctis lapidibus: si enim levaveris cultrum tuum super illud, id est, quam primum ferreis instrumentis lapi- des illos poliendos susceperis, statim altare illud per te, hoc ipso nimio & intempestivo studio tuo polluetur, ita, ut neq́ altare neq́ victimæ mihi sint gratæ futuræ. Tale altare etiam post erectum tabernaculum fie- ri jussit in terra Chanaan Moses Deut. c. 27. quod Mosis mandatum implevit Josua c. 8. significavit a. Deus, sibi non placere, ut industria humana suas vires in cultu Dei ornando (extra præscriptum ipsius ver- bi) experiatur. Hæc Osiander. Conf. etiam 1. Reg. 18, 31. Jud. 13, 29. Quæ causa rectius se habet, quam Grotiana, de lege veteri: quid enim leges gentilium ad leges divinas in ceremonialibus? Sic autem Gro- tius habet: Vers. 25. SI ENIM LEVAVERIS CULTRUM SUPER EO POLLUETUR] Ferrum à Sacris amoveri vetus lex est, quam sequitur in suis legibus Cicero. Hecatæus de Templo Hiero- solymitano: Ἐν ᾧ βωμός ἐστι τετράγωνος, ἐκ ἐν τμητῶν ἀλλ̓ ἐκ τῶν ἀργῶν λίθων ὕτω συγκείμενος. Vers. 26. NON ASCENDES PER GRADUS AD AL- TARE MEUM] Simile aliquid in jure Pontificio Romano vetere, ex quo Servius hoc adfert ad IV. Æneidos: Apud vete- res scalas plus tribus gradibus, nisi Græcas, scandere non licebat, ne ulla pars pedum ejus currumve subter conspiceretur, eoq́ nec pluribus gradibus, sed tribus, ut ascensu duplices nisus non pate- rentur extolli vestem, aut nudare crura. Nam ideo & Græca sca- læ dicuntur, quia ita fabricantur, ut omni ex parte compagine tabularum clausæ sint, ne aspectum ad corporis aliquam partem admittant. Potuerunt hæc ἐ κακοζηλία proficisci. Nostrum est scrutari causas, juxta Scripturæ ductum. Addit autem hic Moses, uti sequitur: NE REVELETUR TURPITUDO TUA. Gestabant enim Sacerdotes subligacula linea, quæ tantum ad genua usque porrigebantur: adeoq; pedibus nudis erat Sacerdos sacrificans, Ex. 28, 42. Nonnulli hoc præceptum sancitum volunt ob im- pura Priapi sacra, in quæ valde proclives Judæi erant 1. Reg. 15, 12. 13. (Moabitarum idoli, quum per Moabitidem transituri essent Ebræi. Unde etiam ab iisdem ad hunc cultum solicitati sunt. Num. 25.) in quibus sua pudenda Gentiles populo denuda- bant. Ita Thomas, Lyranus, Vilalpand. Unde pe- culiare præceptum quidam faciunt hisce verbis comprehensum: non reveles turpitudinem tuam; sed ea causam præcepti continent, non peculiare præ- ceptum. Et in nefandis illis sacris sine gradibus pro- hibebantur ista turpia. Itaque hic solum reverentiæ, castitatis & honestatis Israëlitas in celebrandis sacris commonefacere voluit Deus, ut sacra reverenter & sancte tractarentur; uti observat Hieronymus ad Fa- biol. Conf. cap. 28, 42. At quomodo huic præcepto convenit, quod Ex. 27, 1. altare tres cubitos altum esse debuit, quæ altitudo tanta, ut nemo altari commode sine gradi- bus ministrare potuerit: quodq; 2. Paral. 4, 1. Salomo dicitur altare æneum decem cubitorum altitudinis fecisse, ad quod conscendendum gradibus utique opus fuit? Respondent Abulensis & Ribera, non li- gneos, aut lapideos ibi gradus fuisse, sed continuum ascensum de terra, qui paulatim uniformiter sub- latus sit in altum, ut in ascensu nulla metuenda fue- rit denudatio, quod de altari tabernaculi concedi- mus. Quod vero ad Salomonis aeneum altare, respon- dent alii: ad substructiones per gradus ascenden- dum fuisse, non autem inde ad ipsum altare. Illam vero altitudinem 2. Par. 4. designatam, fuisse su- perstructionem parietis & altaris. Sed ita turpitu- do revelata fuisset in ascensu substructionum. Ideo- que rectius respondetur, hoc praeceptum temporale fuisse etiam accommodatum peregrinationis tempo- ri: ac praeterea gradus Salomoneos fuisse adeo latos & magnificos, ut tota vestis inferior pars etiam gradibus clauderetur, ne videri possent, quae natu- ra vult occultari. Denique remedium etiam adhibi- tum fuisse, quia Sacerdotes usi sub lege braccis & fe- moralibus, uti notavit l. c. Hieronymus. Rupertus tradit moralem applicationem: in altari cordis tui non facias gradus, id est, non extollaris de profectibus tuis, alioqui revelabitur turpitudo tua: quia super- biam mentis comitatur contumelia carnis.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. Concerning slaves, homicides, kidnapping, curses against parents, the punishment of retaliation.

Ver. 1. THESE ARE THE JUDGMENTS.

Judicial precepts in chapters 21, 22, 23, to which, however, in chapter 23 some ceremonial ones are also added: but the denomination is made from the more important.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. De mancipiis, homicidiis, plagio, parentum ma- ledictis, poena talionis.

Vers. 1. HAEC SUNT JUDICIA.

Praecepta judicialia capp. 21. 22. 23. quibus tamen cap. 23. quaedam etiam ceremonialia subjuncta: sed a potiori sit denominatio.

## 21:2
Ver. 2. IF YOU BUY A HEBREW SERVANT] Adjudged because of theft. Junius and Tremellius expand: Whether he, pressed by poverty, sold himself or his children, as below v. 7 and Deut. 15, 12, or was sold by others in the name of theft according to the law below 22, 3.

Ver. same. HE SHALL SERVE YOU SIX YEARS, IN THE SEVENTH HE SHALL GO OUT FREE FOR NOTHING.

Some understand this and the parallel passage in Deut. 15, v. 12, concerning the Sabbatical year or the year of remission. Thus also our blessed Gerhard in his Commentary on Deuteronomy, p. 939, that this year was holy and solemn, which brought both the relaxation of debts and the cessation from work, plowing, sowing, planting, harvesting, and vintage: and therefore it is likely that in the same year in which the remission of debts took place, this manumission of servants also had to take place. (2.) Debts were real obligations, servitudes were personal obligations: as therefore in that Sabbatical year a remission of real obligations was made, so also it is likely that in the same year a remission of personal obligations was made through the manumission of servants. They observe, therefore, that in Deut. 15 the constitutions concerning the remission of debts and the manumission of servants are also joined. But Augustine, Question XXII on Deuteronomy, is more correct. He did not want these purchased ones to be dismissed in the year of remission, which it was necessary to observe as every seventh year by all, but in the seventh year of his purchase, in whatever year that seventh year of theirs might occur. The words of the law are clear: He shall serve you six years, in the seventh he shall go out. And Deut. 15, 12: if your Hebrew brother or Hebrew sister (sister) sells himself to you, and he shall serve you six years, in the seventh year you shall dismiss him free. Compare Jer. 34, 12, etc. Whence Piscator on Deut. 15 rightly contradicts his own: In that seventh year you shall dismiss him free: THAT WORD is referred by OUR interpreters to the year of intermission, which was mentioned in the preceding: but the text contradicts this exposition, which expressly says that he ought to serve for six years, which is found below v. 18 and Jer. 34, 14. Therefore I judge that this word should be expunged, and it should be translated simply in the seventh year, namely, of his servitude, which the article ה denotes in the Hebrew. Nor indeed can those words, he shall serve you for six years, be taken in such a way as to mean the whole of that time which remains of the six years, up to the seventh year. For the letter speaks clearly about six years to be spent in servitude. Therefore he was not to be dismissed if he served only a year or two, even if the Sabbatical year fell within it: and the seventh year of manumission refers itself to those six years of servitude. The reason for the passage in Leviticus 25, 39 is different, where the discourse is about the Jubilee year, not the Sabbatical. Add that the reason demands it, added in Deut. 15, 18: Because according to those, he shall serve you for SIX YEARS as the wage of a hireling. Which words, even if Andreas Rivetus on Ex. 21, p. 8, thinks they mean only this, that he who served you as a servant bound by necessary servitude, his servitude was much heavier than that of a hireling. Therefore he is worthy of a double wage, namely, manumission and gifts; and although various explanations are brought forward by the blessed Gerhard, besides which Cornelius has handed down another, rendering it with the LXX interpreters as for six years with an annual wage, that is, that he should serve you as a hireling, to whom you would have had to pay an annual wage every year, yet the blessed Gerhard, p. 942, acknowledges, and rightly, that the simplest exposition is that which is gathered from Isaiah 16, 14 and 25, 16. He says that hired servants among the Hebrews were accustomed to hire out their services for three years. It is said, therefore, that such a purchased servant served for a double wage or double the wage of a hireling, because he had served for twice as long a time as a hireling was accustomed to serve, and therefore he also ought to receive a double wage when a comparison is made to the wage of a hireling. The sense, therefore, is: Even if you have given such a purchased servant a double wage, namely, and freedom and a gift, yet let this not seem harsh to you, nor ought you to grieve or be indignant at his freedom, because since he has served you for six years, even double the wages of a hireling is owed to him by right. Compare what B. Gerhard has on page 911. Rivetus also supports this, l. c. p. 5. He could not detain him against his will after six years of servitude had been completed; but the master was obliged to manumit him, and that without receiving any price, freely. He derives the reason for this institution from chapter 31 of Genesis, because Jacob served six years for the flock of Laban and in the seventh obtained his dignity. In which there is indeed some analogy; but the true cause is to be deduced from the reason for the Sabbaths, because in the seventh year by the institution of GOD all things that had been in the labor of the earth rested; God also willed that slaves be freed and rest from labor, so that that rest might be prefigured which God had willed to shadow forth by the Sabbath. See what is at Deut. 15, 18. Grotius, who here is of the same opinion as us.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SI EMERIS SERVUM HEBRAEUM] Ex causa furti addictum. Junius & Tremellius ampliant: Sive is pauper- tate pressus se aut liberos venderet, ut infra v. 7. & Deut. 15, 12. sive ab aliis furti nomine venderetur ex lege infra 22, 3.

Vers. eod. SEX ANNOS SERVIET TIBI, IN SEPTI- MO EGREDIETUR LIBER GRATIS.

De anno Sabbatico vel remissionis intelligunt nonnulli hunc & parallelum locum Deut. 15. v. 12. Sic etiam B. Gerhardus noster Comment. in Deut. p. 939. quod hic annus fuerit sacer, & solemnis, qui & debitorum relaxationem & cessationem ab ope- re, aratione, satione, plantatione, messe ac vinde- mia attulit: adeoque verisimile sit eodem anno, quo remissio debitorum fiebat, etiam hanc servorum manumissionem fieri debuisse. (2.) Debita erant obli- gationes reales, servitutes obligationes personales: ut ergo in anno illo Sabbatico obligationum rea- lium facta fuit remissio, ita quoque eodem remissio- nem obligationum personalium per manumissio- nem servorum factam fuisse, verisimile est. Obser- vant ideo etiam Deut. 15. constitutiones de remis- sione debitorum, & de manumissione servorum conjungi. Sed rectius Augustinus q. XXII. in Deut. Hos emtos non anno remissionis dimitti voluit, quem septimum quemque observari oportebat ab omnibus, sed anno septimo emtionis ejus, quotocunque anno illo- rum septimus iste annus occurreret. Verba legis lu- culenta sunt: Sex annos serviet tibi, in septimo egre- dietur. Et Deut. 15, 12. si vendiderit se tibi frater tuus Ebraeus aut Ebraea (soror) & sex annos serviet tibi, in septimo anno dimittes eum liberum. Conf. Jer. 34, 12. &c. Unde suis hic merito contradicit Piscator ad Deut. 15. Anno illo septimo dimittes eum liberum: Vox ILLA a NOSTRIS interpp. re- fertur ad annum intermissionis, cujus facta est men- tio in praecedentibus: sed huic expositioni textus refra- gatur, qui expresse dicit, servire illum debere sex an- nis, id quod reperitur infra v. 18. & Jer. 34, 14. Itaque judico vocem hanc expungendam, & simpliciter vertendum anno v. septimo sc. servitutis suae, id, quod in Hebraeo notat articulus ה. Nec vero verba illa sex annis tibi serviet, ita accipi possunt, toto illo tempore, quod de sex annis superest, usque ad annum septimum. Nam litera σαφῶς loquitur de sex annis in servitute consumendis. Non ergo dimittendus erat, si tantum annum vel biennium serviit, etiamsi incideret Sabbaticus annus: & septimus manumissionis annus ad sex illos servitutis se refert. Alia ratio est loci Levit. 25, 39. ubi de Jubilaeo anno, non de Sabbatico sermo est. Adde quod ratio id poscat Deut. 15, 18. addita: Quoniam juxta illa mercedem mercenarii per SEX ANNOS serviet tibi. Quae verba etsi Andr. Rivetus ad Ex. 21. p. 8. hoc tantum sibi velle censeat, qui tibi ut servus necessaria servitute addictus servivit, ejus multo gravior fuit servitus, quam mercenaria. Ideo duplici mercede digna est nempe manumissione, & muneribus; ac à B. Gerhardo variae adferantur explicationes, praeter quas aliam adhuc tradidit Cornelius, reddens cum LXX. Interpp. per sex annos annua mercede, id est, ut mercenarius, cui mercedem annuam quotannis persolvere debuisses, tibi serviret, agnoscit tamen B. Gerhard. p. 942. & merito simplicissimam esse illam expositionem, quae colligitur ex Esa. 16, 14. c. 25, 16. Servi, inquit, mercenarii apud Hebraeos operas suas locare solebant ad tres annos. Dicitur ergo emtitius ejusmodi servus duplici mercede vel duplo mercedis mercenarii serviisse, quia bis tanto tempore servierat, quam mercenarius servire solebat, ac proinde etiam duplicem mercedem ad mercenarii mercedem comparatione facta accipere debebat. Sensus ergo est: Etsi dederis emtitio istiusmodi servo duplicem mercedem, videl. & libertatem & donativum, non tamen hoc tibi durum videatur, nec vel dolere, vel indignari debes de ejus libertate, quia cum per sex annos tibi servierit, etiam duplum mercedis mercenarii ipsi jure debetur. Conf. quae habet B. Gerhard. pag. 911. Suffragatur etiam Rivetus l. c. p. 5. Non poterat invitum detinere post sex annos servitutis exactos; sed manumittere debebat eum Dominus, idque nullo accepto pretio gratis. Hujus instituti causam ex cap. 31. Genes. arcessit, quia Jacob sex annos servivit pro grege Labani & septimo dignitatem adeptus est. In quo quidem est aliqua analogia; sed vera causa deducenda est ex ratione Sabbatorum, quia anno septimo ex DEI instituto omnes, quae in labore fuerant terrae, quiescebant; Deus etiam voluit mancipia liberari & à labore quiescere, ut praefiguraretur requies illa, quam Sabbatho Deus voluerat adumbrare. Vid. quae ad Deut. 15, 18. Grotius, qui hîc nobis est ὁμόψηφος.

## 21:3
Verse 3.

WITH WHATEVER CLOTHING HE HAD ENTERED, WITH SUCH LET HIM GO OUT] In the Hebrew: If he shall have entered in his body, in his body he shall go out: where the LXX rightly interpret 'in his body' as 'alone'. For it is opposed to that which follows concerning one having a wife and children.

The Vulgate is deservedly corrected. For the Hebrew word does not denote clothing, but body, and the opposition sufficiently teaches that it is not a matter of clothing. Nor did it matter much that the exit be arranged by the clothing with which he had entered: Therefore Oleaster rightly observes: To come in his body is for the Hebrews to come alone.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

CUM QUALI VESTE INTRAVERAT, CUM TALI EXEAT] In Hebraeo: Si in corpore suo ingressus fuerit, in corpore suo egredietur: ubi in corpore suo bene LXX. interpretantur solus. Opponitur enim id ei, quod sequitur de habente uxorem & liberos.

Merito corrigitur Vulgata. Non enim vox Ebraea vestem notat, sed corpus, docetque satis oppositio, non agi de veste. Nec multum referebat disponi exitum à veste, cum qua intraverat: Ideo Oleastr. recte observat: Venire in corpore suo Hebraeis est venire solum.

## 21:4
Verse 4.

BUT IF THE MASTER SHALL HAVE GIVEN HIM A WIFE] From foreign slave women.

THE WOMAN AND CHILDREN SHALL BE THE MASTER'S] For servile marriages were dissolved by the will of the Master.

It is not a matter here of the dissolution of the bond of matrimony, nor was it in the will of the Master: For those whom God has joined, let no man separate, Matt. 19, 6. which axiom, or its [derivation] from the primordial matrimonial law, Christ deduced without the distinction of status and condition obliging. Moreover, since the wife was a foreigner, and perpetually enslaved to the master, it is no wonder that divorce is permitted here, inasmuch as marriage with a foreigner was not pleasing to God, Deut. 21, 14. Neh. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SIN VERO DOMINUS DEDERIT EI UXOREM] Ex ancillis extraneis.

MULIER ET LIBERI ERUNT DOMINI SUI] Serviles enim nuptiae voluntate Domini solvebantur.

Non hic de solutione vinculi matrimonii agitur, nec in voluntate Domini erat eadem: Quos enim Deus conjunxit, homo non separet, Matth. 19, 6. quod axioma, vel ejus è lege matrimoniali primaeva, sine status & conditionis discrimine obligante Chri- stus deduxit. Cæterum, quum uxor fuerit alie- nigena, & in perpetuum hero mancipata, non mirum permitti hîc divortium, siquidem Deo gra- tum non fuerit cum alienigena matrimonium, Deut. 21, 14. Neh. 13.

## 21:5
Vers. 5. IF THE SERVANT SHALL SAY I LOVE MY MASTER, TO THE DOOR &c.

Such a servant was to be brought not to the door of the tabernacle, or the gate of the city, but to the door of his master's house. Yet that matter had to be carried out by the authority of the Magistrate. Therefore the master is ordered to bring him first to the Gods, or magistrates. That piercing of the ear, however, and the affixing to the door of the house was not done to him as a punishment or a certain confusion, because he did not wish to use the benefit of the law, Deut. 25, 7. as Theodoret, Lyranus, Abulensis, and Cajetan wish, but as a sign of perpetual servitude in this house, which Theodoret likewise observes; the awl denotes the obligation: the piercing of the ear, obedience; the door, the zeal for serving in entering and exiting; and by this very act the servant testified that he wished to be affixed to this door, and to recede from it no more. Moreover, this matter was a figure of the Messiah, who had his ear pierced, Psalm 40, 7. and devoted himself to servitude for his whole life, that he might free us from perpetual servitude, to which we are devoted for our whole life, Heb. 2, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SI DIXERIT SERVUS DILIGO DOMI- NUM, AD OSTIUM &c.

Talis servus adducendus erat non ad ostium tabernaculi, vel portam civitatis, sed ad ostium do- mus heri sui. Peragi tamen res ea debebat autorita- te Magistratus.
