Ideo herus eum prius ad Deos, vel magistratus deducere jubetur. Illa autem au- ris perforatio, & ad januam domus affixio non in pœ- nam aut confusionem quandam ipsi fiebat, eo quod beneficio legis uti noluerit, Deut. 25, 7. ut cum Theo- doreto Lyranus, Abulens. Cajetan. volunt, sed in signum perpetuæ servitutis in hac domo, quod obser- vat itidem Theodor. subula notat obligationem: per- foratio auris obedientiam, janua studium inserviendi in introeundo & exeundo, ac testabatur hoc ipso servus, se velle huic januæ affixum esse, nec ab ea amplius recedere. Erat autem hæc res figura Messia, qui aurem perforatam habuit Psalm. 40, 7. & servituti se per totam vitam addixit, ut nos à per- petua servitute liberaret, cui per totam vitam addi- cti sumus Ebr. 2, 14.

## 21:6
Vers. 6.

GODS] Thus judges are called by the Hebrews, as those who exercise the judgments of the law in the place of God. And those who had bought their dignity with money are called by the witticism golden and silver Gods.

FOR EVER] Half a century in Latin, that is, fifty years. See Jerome on Gal. 4. עֹלָם signifies duration, as much as the subject matter allows. Furthermore, such a servant could be freed by an instrument of manumission, or by redemption. He was also freed by the death of the Master, even if the master had left a son.

Most interpreters explain the words 'for ever' as 'until the Jubilee year,' comparing here Lev. 25, 39. 40. with Targum Jonathan and R. Solomon. But in Leviticus it is not a question of a servant who chose to live in perpetual servitude, but one who sold himself to a Master because of poverty, and recovered the liberty he had sold in the Jubilee year: the former, because he preferred to be a perpetual servant rather than be manumitted by his Master, was not released in the Jubilee year. Inasmuch as servitude pleased him more than liberty. And therefore these words FOR EVER seem to be understood as the days of his life. For if only two years remained until the Jubilee, when he himself devoted himself to perpetual servitude, and therefore had his ear pierced, was he to be released after the two years had elapsed, and would it be said of him because of that two-year servitude, and he shall be a servant for ever? And therefore rightly Piscator in his scholia on Deut. 15, 17. Some explain these things as if it were said, until the year of the Jubilee, which explanation they wish to confirm from a comparison of the words, Levit. 25, 40. But in my judgment, the discourse there is about the jubilee year which might fall within any one of those six years which a Hebrew slave is otherwise bound to serve. However, in the case of one who, when it was permitted for him to leave servitude in the seventh year, did not wish to use that benefit, but preferred to remain in servitude, I do not think the benefit of the Jubilee year had any place. Therefore, I judge that those words, a slave of the age, in this passage are to be explained as if it were said a perpetual slave, who, namely, is bound to serve until the end of his life; in which meaning this expression is found 1 Sam. 1, 22. Likewise chap. 27, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

DIIS] Sic ab Hebræis vocantur judices, ut qui divina vice judicia legis exerceant. Et qui pecunia dignitatem emissent, vocantur dicterio Dii aurei, & argentei.

IN SECULUM] Semiseculum Latinè, id est, annos quin- quaginta. Vid. Hieronym. ad Gal. 4. עֹלָם durationem signi- ficat, quantam fert materia subjecti. Liberari præterea po- terat servus talis instrumento manumissionis, aut redemtio- ne. Liberabatur & morte Domini, quamvis dominus filium reliquiffet.

Verba in seculum plerique interpp. exponunt, usque ad annum Jobelæum, conferentes hic Lev. 25, 39. 40. cum Targ. Jonath. & R. Salomon. Sed in Levitico agitur non de servo, qui vivere elegit per- petuam servitutem, sed qui ob egestatem se vendidit Domino, & Jobelæo anno libertatem, quam ven- diderat, recuperabat: ille quia perpetuus servus esse maluit, quam manumitti à Domino, in anno Jo- belæo non dimittebatur. Siquidem servitus ipsi præ libertate placuerit. Ideoque intelligi hæc ver- ba IN SECULUM videntur de diebus vitæ. Quod si enim duo solum restitissent anni ad Jobe- læum, cum ipse se perpetuæ servituti addixit, & ideo aurem sibi perforari curavit, num ille elapso bien- nio dimittendus erat, num dicetur ob biennii illius servitutem de eo, & erit servus in seculum? Ideoque recte Piscator in schol. ad Deut. 15, 17. Quidam hæc exponunt, ac si dicatur, usque ad annum Jubi- læi, quam expositionem volunt confirmare ex colla- tione verborum, Levit. 25, 40. Sed meo judicio ser- mo ibi est de anno jubilæo, qui inciderit in unum ali- quem è sex illis annis, quos alias servus Hebræus ser- vire tenetur. In eo autem, qui, cum ei è servitute exire liceret anno septimo, beneficio illo noluit uti, sed in ser- vitute manere maluit, non puto beneficium anni Ju- bilæi locum habuisse. Itaque verba ista servus sæcu- li hoc loco sic exponenda judico, ac si dicatur servus perpetuus, qui scil. servire tenetur usque ad finem vitæ suæ; in qua significatione locutio hæc reperitur 1. Sam. 1, 22. Item cap. 27, 12.

## 21:7
Vers. 7.

IF ANYONE SHALL HAVE SOLD HIS DAUGHTER] This was granted to the father in extreme necessity: not to the daughter herself. And this is understood of a daughter who is still under age. Puberty itself, no less than manumission by instrument, redemption, the Jubilee, or the death of the master, even if she had a son, dissolved this servitude: nor did the piercing of the ear pertain to this.

SHE SHALL NOT GO OUT AS THE MAIDSERVANTS ARE ACCUSTOMED TO GO OUT] In the Hebrew: as the slaves are accustomed to go out: that is, her master shall not use her labor outside the house, as is usually done with slaves, but will keep her at home honestly and modestly. Thus the writer of the Hiskuni.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

SI QUIS VENDIDERIT FILIAM SUAM] Patri id concessum in summa necessitate: non ipsi filiæ. Et intelligitur hoc de filia adhuc impubere. Ipsa pubertas non minus, quam manumissio per instrumentum, redemtio, Jubilæus, aut mors Domini, quamvis & filium haberet, hanc servitutem solvebat: neque auris perforatio ad hanc pertinebat.

NON EGREDIETUR SICUT ANCILLÆ EXIRE CONSVEVERUNT] In Hebræo: sicut servi exire consveverunt: id est, non utetur Dominus ejus opera extra domum, ut servis fieri solet, sed domi eam honeste pudiceque continebit. Ita scriptor Hiskuni.

## 21:8
Vers. 8.

IF SHE SHALL DISPLEASE THE EYES OF HER MASTER, TO WHOM SHE HAD BEEN DELIVERED, HE SHALL LET HER GO] In the Hebrew, if he neither betrothed her (to himself, namely, or to his son) nor caused her to be redeemed. For after the negative, the Hebrew for 'nor' is placed. The girl always had the right of redeeming herself, if the means existed. As many sixths were deducted from the price as the years she had served.

The Vulgate was entirely to be corrected here: which Osiander amends otherwise: That he may not betroth her, he shall cause her to be redeemed. But thus the particle Vav is omitted: therefore the explanation of Grotius is to be preferred. Compare verse 10.

BUT HE SHALL NOT HAVE THE POWER OF SELLING TO A FOREIGN PEOPLE] A foreign people is understood here as anyone who is not of the house of the buyer. For a Hebrew slave could not be sold even to other nations, as Josephus notes in Antiquities of the Jews, book XVI, where he blames Herod because he had decreed the contrary. In a similar sense, the word 'people' is taken in Deut. 17, 16. The word 'strangers,' however, has different meanings depending on the subject matter.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

SI DISPLICUERIT OCULIS DOMINI SUI, CUI TRADITA FUERAT, DIMITTET EAM] In Hebræo, si nec desponsavit eam (sibi sc. aut filio) nec redimi eam fecit. Et enim post non Hebræis pro nec ponitur. Puellæ semper jus erat se redimendi, si facultas esset. Tot sextæ de pretio deducebantur, quot annos servierat.

Omnino corrigenda hîc erat Vulgata: quam aliter emendat Osiander: Ut non despondeat eam, redimi faciet eam. Sed ita omittitur particula Vav: præferenda ergo Grotiana explicatio. Confer. vers. 10.

POPVLO AUTEM ALIENO VENDENDI NON HABEBIT POTESTATEM] Populus alienus hîc intelligitur quilibet, qui non sit de domo emtoris. Nam aliis gentibus ne servus quidem Hebræus vendi poterat, ut notat Josephus Antiqv. Histor. lib. XVI. ubi Herodem culpat, quod contrarium statuerit. Pari sensu vox populi sumitur Deut. 17, 16. Extranei autem vox pro re subjecta diversas habet significationes.

## 21:9
Vers. 9.

HE SHALL DO TO HER ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM OF DAUGHTERS] In Hebrew: according to the time of daughters he shall do to her. For thus the word משפט is often taken. He shall betroth her to his son at that age at which fathers are accustomed to look out for marriages for their daughters, so that she may be neither too young nor past her prime.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

JUXTA MOREM FILIARUM FACIET EI] Hebraice: secundum tempus filiarum faciet ei. Nam ita משפט sæpe sumitur. Despondebit eam filio suo ea ætate, qua patres filiabus de nuptiis prospicere solent, ut nec sit ἄωρος, nec ὑπέρακμος.

## 21:10
BUT IF HE SHALL HAVE TAKEN ANOTHER FOR HIM] The word 'for him' is redundant here. The meaning is, if he shall have taken another wife besides, supply 'the son.' Thus the Hebrews and Greeks.

NUPTIAS] In Hebrew her flesh, that is, food, as the Chaldean interprets it here. And the Greeks mean this when they say τὰ δέοντα.

PRETIUM PUDICITIÆ] The Greeks rightly [say] τὴν ὁμιλίαν αὐτῆς. Thus Aben-Ezra, R. Levi, Solomon, Kimchi & Moses of Coucy, some of whom add, in their own times; which custom has interpreted, as was later placed in the law of Solon: τρὶς ἑκάστου μηνός. Regarding which law Plutarch [says]: Καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὴ γίγνοιντο παῖδες, ἀλλὰ τιμή τις ἀνδρὸς αὕτη πρὸς σώφρονα γυναῖκα κὰι φιλοφροσύνη πολλὰ τῶν συλλεγομένων ἑκάστοτε δυσχερῶν ἀφαιροῦσα κὰι τᾷς διαφορᾷς οὐκ ἐώσα παντάπασιν ἀποτραχύνειν. What Plutarch called φιλοφροσύνη here, the Apostle calls εὔνοια in 1 Cor. VII, 3. Every husband owes these three things expressly to his wife by divine law. The wise men have added not badly to these, that he should take care of her when sick, free her if by chance she is a captive, bury her when dead, provide for the widow regarding a dwelling and food, and that a daughter should live from her father's goods until she marries.

Osiander does not understand this law concerning the case of a second wife being brought in, but if he has taken another while this one is left or neglected. But he shall not have the power of selling her to a foreign PEOPLE (thus he rendered it), if he has despised her, Heb. in dealing treacherously with her: that is, he ought not to sell her deceitfully and maliciously to foreigners, so that by this means he might free himself from the trouble (of providing for the girl's marriage): for thus he would commit a malicious fraud, and act with deceit. But if he has betrothed her to his son, because he sees that she is an honest girl of liberal character, he shall do for her according to the custom of daughters: that is, he shall also give her a dowry, and shall treat her no differently than if he had given a daughter in marriage: without regard to the fact that she had been a slave. But if he does not wish to betroth her to his son, but has taken another wife for him, so that the girl has clearly fallen from that hope, then he shall provide for the girl's marriage, and shall not deny her clothing and the price of her chastity: in Hebrew, he shall not diminish her remnants (or food), covering, and dowry, that is, then he shall give her so much, from which she may have sustenance for some weeks or months, if she marries some other man: furthermore he shall give her garments, a bed, and a dowry, which bridegrooms were accustomed to give to their wives after intercourse: so that she may (being endowed in this way) find an honest bridegroom. Thus far the Osiandrine paraphrase things more correctly: Whom Fagius preceded with the Chaldean: If he shall have taken another also for her (thus the Targum renders it) that is, if beyond her he shall have also brought in another, whom he may join in marriage to his son, she shall not on that account be held in a lower place, nay, as far as sustenance, clothing, and also the conjugal debt pertains, nothing shall be subtracted from her.

Vers. 10.

Latin:

QVOD SI ALTERAM EI ACCEPERIT] Abundat hîc ei. Sensus est, si alteram præterea uxorem duxerit, supple filius. Ita Hebræi & Græci.

NUPTIAS] Hebraice carnem ejus, id est, alimenta, ut hîc Chaldæus interpretatur. Et hoc Græci volunt, cum dicunt τὰ δέοντα.

PRETIUM PUDICITIÆ] Græci recte τὴν ὁμιλίαν αὐτῆς. Sic Aben-Ezdra, R. Levi, Salomo, Kimchi & Moses de Kotzi, quorum quidam adjiciunt, suis temporibus; quod consuetudo interpretata est, ut in Solonis postea lege positum: τρὶς ἑκάσυ μηνός. Ad quam legem Plutarchus: Καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὴ γίγνοιντο παῖδες, ἀλλὰ τιμή τις ἀνδρὸς αὕτη πρὸς σώφρονα γυναῖκα κὰι φιλοφροσύνη πολλὰ τῶν συλλεγομένων ἑκάσοτε δυσχε- ρῶν ἀφαιρῦσα κὰι τᾷς διαφορᾷς ἐκ ἐώσα παντάπασιν ἀποτρα- χύνειν. Quod hic φιλοφροσύνην dixit Plutarchus, idem Apostolus εὔνοιαν 1. Cor. VII, 3. Tria hæc expresse debet vir quisque uxori ex lege divina. His adjecere sapientes non male, ut ægrotæ curam habeat, liberet si forte captivam, sepeliat mortuam, viduæ prospiciat de domicilio & alimentis, & ut ex paternis bonis vivat filia, donec nubat.

Osiander hanc legem non de casu superinductæ alterius conjugis intelligit, sed si alteram acceperit filio ista relicta vel posthabita. POPULO autem alieno (sic reddidit) vendendi eam non habebit potestatem, si spreverit eam, Ebr. in prævaricando in ea: id est, non debet dolose & malitiose eam alienigenis vendere, ut hac ratione se à molestia (prospiciendi puellæ de conjugio) liberet: ita enim dolum malum committeret, & fraude ageret. Sin autem filio suo desponderit eam, quia videt esse honestam, & liberalis ingenii puellam, juxta morem filiarum faciet ei: id est, dabit ei etiam dotem, eamque non aliter tractabit, ac si filiam elocasset: non habita ratione quod serva fuerit. Quod si filio eam despondere nolit, sed alteram ei acceperit uxorem, ita ut ea spe puella plane exciderit, tum providebit puellæ nuptias, & vestimentum & pretium pudicitiæ non negabit: Hebraicè, reliquias, (seu victum) operimentum & dotem non diminuet, id est, tum dabit ei tantum, unde aliquod septima- nas aut menses victum habeat, si alicui alii nupserit : præterea dabit illi vestes, lectum & dotem, quam solebant sponsi post concubitum uxoribus suis da- re : ut possit (hoc modo dotata) honestum spon- sum invenire. Hactenus Osiandrina paraphrasis : Sed rectius Grotius hæc interpretatur : Cui præivit Fagius cum Chaldæo : Si aliam quoque acceperit illi (sic reddit Targum) id est, si ultra ipsam aliam quoque superinduxerit, quam filio suo matrimo- nio jungat, non propterea illa viliori loco habeatur, imo quod alimentum, vestitum, & debitum quoque conju- gale attinet, nihil illi subtrahatur.

Vers. 10.

## 21:11
IF HE SHALL NOT HAVE DONE THESE THREE THINGS] That is, if he shall not have betrothed her to himself, nor to his son, nor have allowed her to be redeemed. Others explain it thus: If these three things, which were previously owed to her, namely sustenance, clothing, and the conjugal debt, are subtracted from her on account of another woman being brought in: But the preceding things are rather being looked at, as Fagius observed from the Hebrews, whom Grotius has deservedly followed here. HE SHALL GO OUT FREE WITHOUT MONEY] At the time of puberty, and indeed with gifts according to the law Deut. 15, 14.

Latin:

SI TRIA ISTA NON FECERIT] Id est, si eam non de- sponderit sibi, nec filio, nec redimi sit passus. Alii ita explicant: Si tria ista, quæ antea ei de- bebantur, victus nempe, vestitus, & debitum con- jugale, ei propter aliam superinductam subtrahan- tur : Sed respiciuntur potius superiora, ut ex Ebræis observavit Fagius, quem merito hic sequutus est Grotius. EGREDIETUR GRATIS ABSQVE PECUNIA] Tem- pore pubertatis, & quidem cum donis ex lege Deut. 15, 14.

## 21:12
Vers. 12.

HE WHO SHALL STRIKE A MAN, WILLING TO KILL] 'Willing to kill' is not to be added, which is neither in the Hebrew, nor in the Greek. And the Talmudic law has it otherwise, so that the will to strike with death following is sufficient. For as Seneca says, he ought to have been entirely unwilling, who is defended by imprudence. Furthermore, the law, and custom, and equity have added exceptions to the law, if the wounded person has fared better after some time, so that it can be believed he died more from the negligence of doctors or his own than from the wound, or if the slaughter was committed in a crowd, and the certain author is not known: for in these cases the punishment is diminished.

He rightly corrects the Vulgate Latin interpreter from the Hebrew, with which the Greek also agrees. Who therefore will be able to defend the decree of the Council of Trent concerning the Vulgate version not being rejected under any pretext? Sixtinus ab Amama gathers in Anti-Barb. ad h. l. from this version that it seems to follow that he who has struck another, or injured him, not indeed with the intention of killing, but only of injuring, even if death follows immediately, is not guilty of death, nor held for homicide. If that were to prevail, the hope of impunity would always entice wicked men to homicides, pretexts would never be lacking. And who would be the judge here? Whence Cajetanus: The law weighs the effect of the death that followed from the striking, not caring whether he struck with the intention of killing, or only with the intention of striking. And deservedly, for strikes are not measured. And Oleastrius, The law is set, he says, in general, so that every striker, whether he intends to kill, OR NOT, and the one struck has died, such a one was to be punished with death: but immediately exceptions are placed against this law.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

QVI PERCVSSERIT HOMINEM, VOLENS OC- CIDERE] Non addendum volens occidere, quod nec in He- bræo est, nec in Græco. Et aliter habet jus Thalmudicum, ut sufficiat voluntas percutiendi cum morte sequuta. Nam ut ait Seneca, ex toto noluisse debet, qui imprudentia defendi- tur. Cæterum lex, & mos, & æquitas exceptiones legi ad- didere, si vulneratus aliquo tempore melius se habuerit, ut cre- di possit magis medicorum aut sua negligentia mortuus, quam ex vulnere, aut si in turba facta sit cædes, nec sciatur certus au- tor : in his enim minuitur pœna.

Recte corrigit Latinum interpretem Vulga- tum ex Ebræo, cui Græca etiam consonat. Quier- go tueri poterit Concilii Tridentini decretum de vulgata versione nullo prætextu rejicienda ? Six- tinus ab Amama colligit in Anti-Barb. ad h. l. ex hac versione videri sequi, eum, qui percusserit alium, vel læserit non quidem animo occidendi, sed tantum lædendi, etsi mors è vestigio subsequatur, non esse reum mortis, nec teneri homicidii. Id si obtineret, sem- per impunitatis spes nefarios homines ad homici- dia prolectaret, nunquam prætextus deessent. Et quis hic judex esset? Unde Cajetanus: Pensat lex effectum secutæ mortis ex percussione, non curan- do, an ille percusserit animo occidendi, an v. per- cutiendi animo duntaxat. Et merito, percussio- nes enim non mensurantur. Et Oleastrius, Poni- tur lex, inquit, in communi, ut omnis percutiens, sive intendat occidere, SIVE NON, & percussus fuerit mortuus, talis morte erat plectendus : sed statim ponuntur exceptiones ab hac lege.

## 21:13
HE WHO HAS NOT LAIN IN WAIT) Where there is a light fault. An officer of the magistrates is not bound to flee, who has killed a guilty person resisting, nor a master who has killed a disciple, or a father who has killed a son while punishing him, nor if anyone has killed him who, having been warned, has approached a place to which it was not permitted for him to approach. If an uncircumcised stranger had committed anything of this kind through a light fault, he was not condemned to death by the judges, but the avenger of blood was to be avoided by him: for asylums were not open to him, namely if he had killed a Hebrew.

Latin:

QVI NON EST INSIDIATUS) Ubi est levis culpa. Fugere non tenetur magistratuum apparitor, qui reum resistentem, nec magister, qui discipulum, aut Pa- ter, qui filium castigans occiderit, nec si quis eum, qui mo- nitus ad locum, quo accedere ipsi non licebat, accesserit. In- circumcisus advena si quid tale per levem culpam admisisset, à judicibus ad mortem non damnabatur, sed cavendus ei erat vindex sanguinis : asyla enim ei non patebant, nempe si He- bræum occidisset.

## 21:14
Vers. 14.

THOU SHALT TAKE HIM FROM MY ALTAR) The Hebrews understand the contrary, that the altar was a refuge for those who had committed φόνον ἀκούσιον, as it was among almost all nations. But among the Hebrews they could not remain there, but were to be led to a city of refuge.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

AB ALTARI MEO AVELLES EUM) Ex contrario intelligunt Hebræi altare pro perfugio fuisse iis, qui φόνον ἀ- κούσιον commisissent, ut ferme apud omnes gentes. Verum apud Hebræos ibi morari non poterant, sed deducendi erant ad urbem perfugii.

## 21:15
Vers. 15.

HE WHO SHALL STRIKE HIS FATHER OR MOTHER, LET HIM DIE THE DEATH) By strangulation.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QVI PERCVSSERIT PATREM SUUM AUT MA- TREM, MORTE MORIATUR) Strangulatione.

## 21:16
AND HE SHALL HAVE SOLD HIM] In Hebrew: whether he shall have sold him, or he shall have been found with him. For the copula there, as often, is put for a disjunctive. The sense is that kidnapping is a capital crime, whether the kidnapper has alienated the stolen person or not. Death, where it is said without addition, understand as strangulation; where it is added, his blood be upon him, as stoning.

Latin:

ET VENDIDERIT EUM] In Hebræo: sive vendiderit eum, sive apud eum inventus fuerit. Nam copula ibi, ut sæpe pro disjunctiva ponitur. Sensus est plagium esse capitale, sive plagiarius subreptum alienaverit, sive non. Mortem, ubi sine additamento dicitur, intellige strangulationem, ubi additur, sanguis ejus super ipso, lapidationem.

## 21:19
Verse 19.

YET SO THAT HE SHALL RESTORE HIS LABOR AND EXPENSES FOR PHYSICIANS] Five kinds of injuries to a man are reported by the Hebrews: loss of a limb, confinement to bed, pain, medical treatment, and insult.

Latin:

Verf. 19.

ITA TAMEN, UT OPERAS EJUS ET IMPENSAS IN MEDICOS RESTITVAT] Injuriæ in hominem quinque ab Hebræis genera referuntur: amissio membri, decubitus, dolor, medicatio, contumelia.

## 21:21
Vers. 21.

PECUNIA ILLIUS EST (HIS MONEY IT IS)] Possession. PAVPERI QVI HABITAT TECVM (TO THE POOR WHO DWELLS WITH THEE)] The word 'poor' here does not restrict the law, but is placed as an example, because it mostly happens that they are more in need of the help of others.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

PECUNIA ILLIUS EST] Possessio. PAVPERI QVI HABITAT TECUM] Vox pauperis hic non restringit legem, sed exempli causa posita est, quia plerum- que ita accidit, ut illi magis egeant opis alienæ.

## 21:22
Verse 22.

BUT SHE HERSELF SHALL HAVE LIVED] In Hebrew ולא יהיה אסון And there shall not be death. And in the following verse: ואם אסון יהיה if there shall be death. Which seems to be understood as, if there shall be death of either the mother or the infant, although the Masters of the Hebrews accept it only concerning the mother. But the Greeks read in both places אסמון: For they translate it ἐξεικονισμένον, and distinguish between an abortion of a fetus already having human form, and one not having it, so that the former makes it a capital crime, but the latter does not, following in that matter the laws of the Greeks, which were then in force also in Egypt. Aristotle, Politics VII, 16: "Before sensation and life have been generated, abortion should be brought about; for the holy and the not-holy is determined by sensation and life." Thus also Hippocrates felt; nor does Augustine interpret this passage otherwise in Question LXXXVI on Exodus. But for Christians, to use the words of Tertullian in his Apologeticus, it is not permitted to dissolve even that which is conceived in the womb, while the blood is still being fashioned into a human being. It is a hastening of homicide to prevent birth. Nor does it matter whether one snatches away a soul already born, or disturbs one being born. He is a man who is to be: even every fruit is already in the seed. The same Tertullian has similar things in his Exhortation to Chastity near the end, and in On the Veiling of Virgins.

AND THE ARBITERS SHALL HAVE JUDGED] In Hebrew: in judges, that is, by the judgment of the judges.

Whatever may be the case regarding the laws of the Greeks and Egyptians in this matter, whatever regarding Aristotle's Politics VII, 16 and the opinion of Hippocrates, the divine law here does not distinguish, but whether it be the destruction of the mother or of the fetus, (as Grotius rightly says) it wills that a soul be rendered for a soul; which is present when conception takes place. Therefore Tertullian rightly observes in Apologeticus, ch. 8: To us (Christians), homicide being once forbidden, it is not permitted to dissolve even that which is conceived in the womb, while the blood is still being fashioned into a human being. It is a hastening of homicide to prevent birth. Nor does it matter whether one snatches away a soul already born, or disturbs one being born. He is a man who is to be: even every fruit is already in the seed. And that the soul is in the seed, Gregory of Nyssa demonstrated with thirteen invincible arguments in his book On the Making of Man, ch. 28 and 29. Which we have brought forward in the Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica, Sect. 2, page 528, seqq. But the LXX Interpreters must be acknowledged here, as elsewhere in many places, as a παρόραμα (oversight), and not a different reading to be invented without necessity. The Vulgate likewise should have been corrected, which restricts it only to the death of the mother: since the infanticide was as guilty as the matricide, as Cajetan, Cornelius à Lapide, and Grotius admit.

Latin:

Verf. 22.

SED IPSA VIXERIT] Hebraice ולא יהיה אסון Et non fuerit mors. Et versu sequente: ואם אסון יהיה si fuerit mors. Quod videtur intelligendum, si fuerit mors aut matris aut infantis, quanquam de matre tantum accipiant Hebræorum Magistri. At Græci legerunt utroque loco אסמון: Vertunt enim ἐξεικονισμένον, distinguuntque inter abortum partus humanam jam figuram habentis, & non habentis, ut ille capitale faciat, non vero hic, sequuti ea in re Græcorum leges, quæ tunc & in Ægypto vigebant. Aristoteles Politicorum VII, 16. Πρὶν αἴσθησιν ἐγγενέσθαι καὶ ζωὴν, ἐμποιεῖσθαι δεῖ τὴν ἀμβλωσιν· τὸ γὰρ ὅσιον καὶ τὸ μὴ διωρισμένον τῇ αἰσθήσει καὶ τῷ ζῆν. Sic & Hippocrates sensit: nec aliter hunc locum interpretatur Augustinus quæst. LXXXVI. ad Exodum. At Christianis, ut Tertulliani utar verbis in Apologetico, etiam conceptum utero, dum adhuc sanguis in hominem deliberatur, dissolvere non licet. Homicidii festinatio est prohibere nasci. Nec refert natam quis eripiat animam, an nascentem disturbet. Homo est & qui futurus est: etiam fructus omnis jam in semine est. Paria habet idem Tertullianus in exhortatione castitatis circa finem, & de Virginibus velandis.

ET ARBITRI JUDICAVERINT] In Hebræo: in judicibus, id est, judicum arbitratu.

Quicquid sit de Græcorum & Ægyptiorum legibus hac in causa, quicquid de Aristotelis Politicorum VII, 16. & Hippocratis sententia, lex divina hic non distinguit, sed sive exitium sit, sive matris, sive fœtus, (ut recte Grotius) animam vult pro anima reddi; Quæ adest, cum conceptio fit. Ideo recte observat Tertullianus in Apologet. cap. 8. Nobis (Christianis) homicidio semel interdicto, etiam conceptum utero, dum adhuc sanguis in hominem deliberatur, dissolvere non licet. Homicidii festinatio est prohibere nasci. Nec refert natam quis eripiat animam, an nascentem disturbet. Homo est & qui futurus est: etiam fructus omnis jam in semine est. Et animam in semine esse præclare Gregorius Nyssenus XIII. rationibus invictis demonstravit lib. de opific. hominis cap. 28. & 29. Quas adduximus Harmonia Calixtino-Hæret. Sect. 2. pag. 528. seqq. LXX. vero Interpp. hic agnoscendum, ut alibi passim παρόραμα, non vero fingenda citra necessitatem diversa lectio. Vulgatus pariter castigandus erat, qui tantum ad mortem matris restringit: cum infanticida tam reus fuerit, quam matricida, ut fatetur Cajetanus, Cornelius à Lapide & Grotius.

## 21:24
Verse 24.

EYE FOR EYE, TOOTH FOR TOOTH.

Although the Karaites take these literally, other Hebrews nevertheless admit that they cannot be taken in a literal sense, whence Paulus Fagius observes on Deut. 9: This law of retaliation, according to Rabbi Kanam, as he is cited by Bachai, was never observed; for he says that it is evident from tradition, beyond Scripture, that it is not an eye for an eye, but a pecuniary estimation of the eye should be rendered. Otherwise, indeed, the law would not be satisfied, which says, just as he gave a blemish to a man, so let it be given to the author, Levit. 14. Now it is clear Exod. 21. that he who caused the damage is bound to satisfy the injured party regarding interest and expense for physicians. But if an eye were to be gouged out for an eye from the author, who would satisfy him? There is also another of a more tender constitution than he who was injured, who might similarly meet death from an equal wound. Therefore, it is impossible that a wound and injury equal in all respects be inflicted upon the author. Wherefore this constitution is to be accepted in a proverbial sense, namely, that the damage ought to be estimated by the judges, as to how much should be given for an eye or a tooth knocked out.

Latin:

Verf. 24.

OCULUM PRO OCULO, DENTEM PRO DENTE.

Etsi Caræi hæc ad literam accipiant, alii tamen Ebræi fatentur non posse ea literali sensu accipi, unde Paulus Fagius ad Deuter. 9. observat: Hæc lex talionis autore Rabbi Kanam, ut à Bachai citatur, nunquam est observata; Nam præter Scripturam ex traditione ait constare, quod non oculus pro oculo, sed æstimatio oculi pecuniaria reddatur. Alioqui enim legi non fa- tisfieret, quæ ait, quemadmodum dedit maculam in hominem, sic detur in autorem Levit. 14. jam patet Exod. 21. quod de intereffe & sumtu in medicos satis- facere læso, qui damnum dedit, tenetur. Quod si au- tori oculus pro oculo effoderetur, quis illi satisfaceret? Est & alius tenerioris constitutionis, quam ille, qui læsus est, qui ex æquali vulnere similiter mortem obie- rit. Propterea fieri non potest, ut per omnia vulnus & læsio æqualis autori infligatur. Quæpropter sensu proverbiali accipienda hæc constitutio, quod scil. da- mnum æstimari debeat à judicibus, quantum pro ocu- lo vel dente excusso dandum sit.

## 21:27
Vers. 27. HE SHALL LIKEWISE LET THEM GO FREE] This law concerning liberty, on account of a broken limb, was of benefit to circumcised servants, not others. Others from the nations were not set free except by a price given, or through an instrument of manumission.

Junius, on the contrary, restricts it to foreigners: and leaves the action of retaliation to Hebrew servants from the common law, Lev. 24, 19. But Rivetus more correctly determines that the present law, because there is no exception of the condition of foreigners and natives, is common.

Latin:

Vers. 27. SIMILITER DIMITTET EOS LIBEROS] Hæc lex de libertate, ob membrum ruptum, servis circumcisis proderat, non aliis. Alii ex gentibus non nisi pretio dato, aut per instru- mentum manumissionis liberabantur.

Junius contra ad alienigenas restringit: & Ebræis servis actionem talionis relinquit è lege communi Lev. 24, 19. At Rivetus legem præsen- tem, quia nulla exceptio conditionis alienigena- rum & indigenarum sit, communem esse, rectius statuit.

## 21:29
Vers. 29. BUT IF THE OX WERE WONT TO PUSH WITH HIS HORN IN TIME PAST] An ox accustomed to push with its horn, as the words of the XII Tables have it, reported in the Institutes, title 'If a quadruped'.

AND HATH KILLED] It is another thing if it has done harm with tooth or foot: which are unusual.

AND HAVE TESTIFIED TO HIS OWNER] They have interposed a denunciation of damage not yet done, to speak in the Roman manner: see law 'Qui foveas', § 1, Digest, ad legem Aquiliam.

AND SHALL HAVE KILLED HIS OWNER] In the Hebrew: and his owner shall die. Gross negligence is punished by death. But if the heirs wish, redemption is permitted here. Therefore it is not said, dying he shall die, that is, he shall be altogether affected by death.

Not if the heirs wish: for it was not placed in their discretion: but if the owner of the brute cannot be solidly convicted of gross negligence, as Mr. Varenius rightly observes against Raschi and Aben-Ezra, whom Grotius followed here.

Latin:

Vers. 29. QVOD SI BOS CORNUPETA FUERIT AB HERI ET NUDIVS TERTIUS] Bos cornu petere solitus, ut verba ha- bent XII. Tabularum relata in Institutiones tit. Si quadrupes.

OCCIDERITQVE] Aliud si dente aut pede nocuerit: quæ infolita.

ET CONTESTATI SINT DOMINUM EJUS] Denun- tiationem interposuerint damni infecti, ut Romano loquar more: vide l. Qui foveas. §. 1. D. ad l. Aquil.

ET DOMINUM EJUS OCCIDERIT] In Hebræo: & Dominus ejus moriatur. Culpa lata morte punitur. Sed si hæ- redes velint, permittitur hic redemtio. Ideo non dictum est, moriendo moritur, id est, omnino morte afficietur.

Non si hæredes velint: in eorum enim arbitrio id non fuit positum: sed si Dominus bruti non possit solide de lata culpa convinci, ut contra Raschi & Aben- Esdr. quos sequutus hîc Grotius est, recte observat Dn. Varenius.

## 21:32
Vers. 32. THIRTY SHEKELS] Half the valuation of a free man. See what [is written] at Matt. 26, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 32. TRIGINTA SICLOS) Dimidium æstimationis hominis liberi. Vide quæ ad Matth. 26, 15.

## 21:33
Vers. 33. IF A MAN SHALL OPEN A PIT AND DIG] If another could not foresee the pit, as the law 'Qui foveas' says, Digest, ad legem Aquiliam.

Latin:

Vers. 33. SI QVIS APERUERIT CISTERNAM ET FO- DERIT) Si alius foveam providere non potuerit, ut ait l. Qui foveas. D. ad l. Aquil.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. Concerning theft, rape, idolatry.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII. De furto, stupro, idolatria.

## 22:2
Vers. 2. IF A THIEF BREAKING INTO A HOUSE, OR DIGGING] A burglar in Latin.

AND HAVING RECEIVED A WOUND HE SHALL HAVE DIED) Maimonides notes that he can only be wounded in such a way if he does not flee, or if witnesses cannot be had. See what we have written on this matter in book II of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 1, §. XII, and in the Annotations. If witnesses are present, he is now equated to a daytime thief.

The reason for the disparity between a nocturnal and a daytime thief is that the force and intention of the nocturnal one are uncertain, whether he comes even to kill, and because at night if thieves are encountered, they are accustomed to rage for slaughter, and because they can neither be distinguished, nor repelled, nor apprehended securely.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SI EFFRINGENS FVR DOMVM, SIVE EF- FODIENS) Directarius Latine.

ET ACCEPTO VULNERE MORTVVS FVERIT) Vul- nerari eum ita demum posse si non fugiat, aut testes haberi non possint, notat Maimonides. Vide quæ nos hac de re lib. II. de Jure belli ac pacis cap. 1. §. XII. & in Annotatis. Si testes ad- sint, jam diurno furi æquiparatur.

Ratio disparitatis inter furem nocturnum & diurnum est, quod nocturni vis & intentio incerta, anne etiam ad occidendum veniat, quodque noctu si offendantur, ad cædem furere soleant fures, & quod nec dignosci, nec repelli secure aut appre- hendi possint.

## 22:3
Verse 3. HE SHALL BE SOLD) Into servitude not longer than six years: but shorter if before that his labors had been worth as much as the thing stolen; for he could not be retained in servitude on account of a debt of a fine. This is to be understood of males; for females were not adjudged for theft. Josephus, book XVI of the Antiquities of the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VENVNDABITVR) Ad servitutem non longio- rem sexennio: contractiorem vero si ante operæ ejus tantum valuisssent quantum res furto sublata; nam ob mulctæ debitum in servitute retineri non poterat. Intelligendum hoc de mari- bus; fœminæ enim ob furtum non addicebantur. Josephus li- bro XVI. Antiquæ Historiæ.

## 22:4
Verse 4. IF IT SHALL BE FOUND WITH HIM WHO STOLE IT, WHETHER OX, OR ASS, OR SHEEP) In the Hebrew: If in finding it shall have been found in his hand the theft: that is, if the theft has come to notice not by his own voluntary confession, as is prescribed in Leviticus VI, but in another way. For he who reports himself, and has not killed or sold what he has stolen, is not held to double restitution.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SI INVENTVM FVERIT APVD EVM, QVI FVRATVS EST VIVENS SIVE BOS, SIVE ASINVS, SIVE OVIS) In Hebræo: Si inveniendo inven- tum fuerit in manu ejus furtum: id est, si furtum non ipsius voluntaria confessione, ut præcipitur Levit. VI. sed alio modo ad notitiam pervenerit. Nam qui se defert, neque oc- cidit, aut vendidit quod furatus est, non tenetur duplione.

## 22:6
Verse 6. IF FIRE GOING FORTH SHALL HAVE FOUND THORNS] If anyone has set fire to his own stubble or thorns for the purpose of burning it, and the fire has wandered further and progressed and damaged another's crop or vineyard. These are the words of the law, 'He who kills', §. 'in this', Digest, ad legem Aquiliam.

HE SHALL RESTORE THE DAMAGE, WHO SHALL HAVE KINDLED THE FIRE] Since he ought to have either extinguished the fire or fortified it so that it would not wander, says the law, 'If a slave', §. 'if a fornicator', Digest, ad legem Aquiliam. He is in fault who has not taken care that the fire should not proceed further, says the law, 'He who kills', §. 'in this', Digest, on that title.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SI EGRESSUS IGNIS INVENERIT SPINAS] Si quis in stipulam suam vel in spinam comburendae ejus causa ignem immiserit, & ulterius evagatus & progressus ignis alie- nam segetem, vel vineam laeserit. Verba sunt l. Qui occidit. §. in hac D. ad l. Aquiliam.

REDDET DAMNUM, QVI IGNEM SUCCENDERIT] Cum deberet vel ignem exstinguere, vel ita munire ne evage- tur, ait l. Si servus §. si fornicarius. D. ad l. Aquiliam. In cri- mine est, qui non observavit, ne ignis longius procederet, ait l. Qui occidit §. in hac D. eo tit.

## 22:8
Verse 8. TO THE GODS) To the three judges upon whom hands were laid.

THAT HE SHALL NOT HAVE EXTENDED HIS HAND INTO THE PROPERTY OF HIS NEIGHBOR] To extend the hand is to seize.

Latin:

Vers. 8. AD DEOS] Ad tres judices quibus manus impo- sita.

QVOD NON EXTENDERIT MANUM IN REM PROXIMI SUI] Extendere manum est arripere.

## 22:9
Verse 9.

TO THE GODS) Thus are the supreme judges called, such as Moses and, in his absence, Aaron and Hur. Below 24, 14. Afterwards the Senators of the Sanhedrin, who formerly judged these cases. But as the number of lawsuits grew, it was introduced later that three upon whom hands had been laid by the Sanhedrin could judge concerning them.

AND IF THEY SHALL HAVE JUDGED, HE SHALL RESTORE DOUBLE TO HIS NEIGHBOR] Namely the depositary, if deceit was present, or the depositor if he has brought an unjust action. For it is unjust for a depositary to be held for mere accident. See the Institutes, 'By what modes an obligation is contracted by a thing'.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

AD DEOS] Ita vocantur summi judices, qualis Moses & eo absente Aaron & Hur. Infra 24, 14. Postea Senatores Sy- nedrii, qui olim his de causis judicavere. Sed crescente litium numero introductum ferius, ut tres quibus impositae à Synedrio manus, judicare de iis possent.

ET SI ILLI JVDICAVERINT, DUPLUM RESTI- TUET PROXIMO SUO] Nempe depositarius, si dolus ad- fuerit, depositor si iniquam actionem intenderit. Nam de me- ro casu teneri depositarium iniquum est. Vide institutiones. Quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio.

## 22:10
OR CAPTURED BY THE ENEMY] For he who has received a thing on loan is not responsible for the incursions of enemies: provided, of course, that he has used the loaned thing according to the instructions: which the Hebrews add here. So also Gaius, l. In rebus commodatis. D. commodati. Add l. Si ut certe §. quod vero. D. eodem tit. And Instit. Quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio §. 2.

Latin:

VEL CAPTUM AB HOSTIBUS] Hostium enim incursus non praestat is, qui rem commodatam accepit: nempe si re commodata ex praescripto fuerit usus: quod hic addunt Hebraei. Ita & Cajus l. In rebus commoda- tis. D. commodati. Adde l. Si ut certe §. quod vero. D. eodem tit. Et Instit. Quibus modis re contrahitur obliga- tio §. 2.

## 22:12
BUT IF IT SHALL HAVE BEEN TAKEN BY THEFT, HE SHALL RESTORE THE DAMAGE TO THE OWNER] Namely if gross negligence was present, which is not far from deceit.

Others wish for restitution to be assigned to him who has been convicted of theft. But there is no word had here concerning that. Nor is it right to force an alien subject upon the text. There are, to be sure, three cases regarding a deposit: (1.) Of fraud: thus the depositary is held to return double. (2.) Of negligence, thus he shall return the simple amount: (3.) If the thing was taken secretly and by stealth, he shall be innocent.

Latin:

QVOD SI FURTO ABLATVM FUERIT, RESTI- TUET DAMNUM DOMINO] Nempe si lata culpa adfue- rit, quae à dolo non longe abest.

Alii restitutionem assignari ei volunt, qui furti convictus fuerit. Sed de eo hic nullum habe- tur verbum. Neque fas est textui alienum subje- ctum ingerere. Triplex scilicet est circa depositum casus: (1.) Fraudis: sic depositarius tenetur ad du- plum reddendum. (2.) Negligentiae, ita reddet simplum: (3.) Si res secreto, & furtim sublata, in- nocens erit.

## 22:15
Verse 15.

BUT IF THE OWNER WAS PRESENT, HE SHALL NOT RESTORE] For the owner could also have applied diligence. Such is the case of a common friend invited to dinner, and silver borrowed for that purpose, in the said law, In rebus.

ESPECIALLY IF IT HAD COME HIRED FOR THE WAGES OF HIS WORK] There is another reading here in the Hebrew: If the hireling himself came for his wages. In Greek: ἐὰν δὲ μισθωτὸς ᾖ, ἔσται αὐτῷ ἀντὶ τῆς μισθῷ αὐτῷ. That is, if he who guards the thing has stipulated for wages for the guarding, he shall now be liable for the loss on account of those wages: he shall be held even for an accident, whether the owner was present or was not present. See law 1, section saepe evenit, Digest, on deposit; and Mynsinger on the said title of the Institutes, Quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio, section Praeterea & ii.

In the Hebrew there is another distinction: if it is hired for wages, let him come for his wages, that is, beyond the wages for which it was hired, there is no need to pay anything more, as Fagius rightly says. Namely, if the owner, the lessor, was present when that evil happened. For either he himself saw that it could not have been averted by human diligence, or if he could have, since the owner himself being present did not avert it, he deservedly suffers the detriment of the duty not performed. But if it seems harsh that he who received something on loan should be held to the restitution of the thing that perished, when he used no deceit, as is decreed in verse 14, this political constitution was enacted to avoid deceits and to sharpen diligence in guarding the property of others: since a borrowed thing must be cared for as one's own; and because the utility from the borrowed thing returns to the borrower, it is not inequitable that he should also bear the loss, lest the lender suffer detriment on account of his service.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QVOD SI IMPRAESENTIARUM DOMINUS FUE- RIT, NON RESTITUET] Poterat enim & Dominus adhibere diligentiam. Talis est casus communi amico ad coenam invitato, & in id commodato argento, in d. l. In rebus.

MAXIME SI CONDUCTUM VENERAT PRO MERCEDE OPERIS SUI] Alia hic sententia in Hebraeo: Si mercenarius ipse venit propter mercedem suam. Graece: ἐὰν δὲ μισθωτὸς ᾖ, ἔσται αὐτῷ ἀντὶ τῆς μισθῷ αὐτῷ. Id est, si is, qui custodit rem, pro custodia mercedem sit stipulatus, jam in damnum veniet propter illam mercedem: tenebitur etiam de casu, sive dominus adfuerit, sive non adfuerit. Vide l. 1. §. saepe evenit. D. depositi; & Mynsingerum ad dictum tit. Instit. Quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio. §. Praeterea & ii.

In Ebraeo alia est distinctio: si mercede con- ductum est, veniat pro mercede sua, id est, praeter mercedem, qua conductum nihil amplius solvere opus habeat, ut recte Fagius. Si scil. Dominus locator praesens fuerit, quando malum illud acci- dit. Nam aut ipse vidit id humana diligentia aver- ti non potuisse, aut si potuit, quum Dominus ipse praesens non averterit, detrimentum merito pati- tur officii non praestiti. Quod si autem durum vi- deatur, eum, qui mutuo aliquid accepit, ad restitu- tionem teneri rei, quae periit, cum nullo usus est dolo, ut v. 14. decernitur, politica haec constitutio sancita est ad cavendos dolos, & acuendam diligen- tiam in custodiendis alienis: quum commodata res curanda sit, ceu propria; & quia è commodata uti- litas redit ad commodatarium, non iniquum est, eum damnum quoque praestare, ne commodans propter officium sentiat detrimentum.

## 22:16
Verse 16. IF HE SHALL SEDUCE

He has enticed without force: LXX. ἐὰν ἀπατήσῃ τις παρθένον. For this species of the deed differs from that which is in Deut. 22, 28. 29. There, marriage is imposed with a fine. Here, the option of a fine or marriage is given to the father of the virgin.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SI SEDUXERIT]

Pellexerit fine vi: LXX. ἐὰν ἀπατήσῃ τις παρθένον. Differt enim hæc facti species ab illa, quæ est Deu- teron. 22, 28. 29. Ibi matrimonium cum mulcta imponitur. Hic patri virginis optio datur mulctæ, aut matrimonii.

## 22:17
Verse 17. IF THE FATHER OF THE VIRGIN SHALL REFUSE TO GIVE HER, HE SHALL PAY MONEY.

Nor does Deut. 22, 29 treat of a woman forced by violence, which Grotius seems to hint at here; because force pertains to rape. But this treats of a virgin seduced by flattering words, not yet betrothed, if the seducer has slept with her, or defiled her, which was provided for in verse 16, that he should endow her and have her as his wife, i.e., that he cannot demand a dowry from his father-in-law, but is bound to provide a dowry for the virgin he corrupted from his own means, and nevertheless take her as his wife: But if the father of the virgin shall refuse to give his daughter to the seducer (perhaps a dissolute and clearly wicked man), the seducer shall pay (more correctly, shall give) to the corrupted virgin money according to the measure of the dowry which virgins are accustomed to receive, that is, he shall count out as much money as is usually given as a dowry to such a virgin. It seems it can be gathered from this that the dissent of the parent of a seduced woman annuls the marriage, even if it was consummated by carnal copulation. But concerning that case when matrimonial consent and mutual betrothal is confirmed by carnal copulation, a clear provision is had in Deut. 22, 28. If a man finds (or has approached) some virgin girl who does not yet have a betrothed; and seizing her (the LXX have βιασάμενος as if it were a matter of violent rape, but the word is more general, and violent rape was punished not by a fine, but by death,) has lain with her, and the matter has come to judgment (in Hebrew, and they have been found or detected, that is, when the deed cannot be denied) he who has slept with her shall give to the father of the girl 50 shekels of silver, and he shall nevertheless have her as his wife: because he has humbled or defiled her: he shall not be able to dismiss her by a bill of divorce, all the days of his life. Whence Cypraus, chapter 10, on the law of marriages, §. 11. page 474, warns that according to the Mosaic law, as also the laws of the Athenians, he who has defiled a virgin ought to marry her, whether the parents of the seducer agree or not: provided the parents of the seduced woman do not refuse to give her to him. However, the dissent of the parents of the seduced woman does not indeed simply cause the marriage, which is confirmed by carnal copulation, to be invalid, yet it could hitherto annul it according to the custom of the Jewish polity, because marriages were then also dissolved by a bill of divorce. Osiander also notes in this the difference of our laws: Modern laws do not compel a seducer to marry the one he has defiled, if he did not promise marriage: but yet if one is a good and just man, he will not disdain to join her to himself in marriage, since he has taken away the girl's greatest ornament, her virginity: But the Mosaic law concerning marrying the seduced woman can be understood with the condition, where, namely, the seducer had promised marriage to her whom he defiled, or with whom he has lain.

For the rest, matrimonial consent, confirmed by carnal copulation, makes a marriage valid, even if the parents do not consent. The consent of parents is indeed required by the force of divine law for marriage, nor can a marriage that is entered into without the consent of parents be considered legitimate in all ways, but it does not pertain to the very substance and essentials of a marriage, which can be valid without the consent of parents, if the principal contracting parties, as are the bridegroom and bride, consent, and carnal copulation has followed: indeed, according to the very institution of marriage in Genesis 2, 24, a man is bound to leave father and mother, and cleave to his wife; and thus, by that very sentence of God, as noted by the blessed Hunnius, conjugal love is preferred to the love of children toward parents: and it is observed in the Harmonia of Chemnitius. Lyserus on Matthew 5, 31, [argues that] even if he enters into marriage through fornication, it cannot nevertheless be dissolved, because that case does not conflict with the SUBSTANCE of marriage. And our people agree on this, as can be seen in the blessed Luther, Vol. VI, Wittenberg, fol. 266, Vol. 5, Jena, fol. 237, Vol. V, Altenburg, fol. 376, in the book on matrimonial matters. Philippus, Laws on Marriage, title on the Consent of Parents. Chytræus, on Leviticus 18 and 19, book on clandestine betrothals, p. 616. Johannes Brentius in the Catechism and Apology of the Confession of Württemberg, article on Marriage, likewise the Theologians of Tübingen (with the Jurisconsults) in a response of the month of April, the year 1624, who, citing Johannes Harprecht on the rubric of the Institutes on marriage, n. 126, teach that before subsequent copulation and priestly blessing, carnal copulation or intercourse simply makes all betrothals—whether pure, conditional, sworn, or unsworn, not previously dissolved—indissoluble. The unanimous opinion of Wittenberg. The faculty is found in Dedekennus, part III, fol. 441, and in the Theological Consultations of Wittenberg, book 4, p. 23. The Theological Faculty of Rostock in Dedekennus, book 1, fol. 436. The blessed Balduinus in Cases of Conscience. The blessed Hülsemann in the extended Breviary, page 433. The blessed Danhawerus in the book of open conscience, page 812. Among the Jurisconsults, one should confer especially with the blessed D. Carpzovius, Jurisprudence of the Consistory, book II, Title VI, definition LX, and Forensic Jurisprudence, part IV, constitution XX, def. 15. Johannes Schneidewinus on book 1 of the Institutes, part II, Title 10, n. 35. When intercourse has followed clandestine betrothals, then it must be concluded that by the authority of the parents such marriages, already consummated, cannot be rescinded. And the same is observed and pronounced in our Consistories. For in this case it must be considered that a greater scandal may be avoided, and the greatest injury would then be done to the defiled and deserted woman. Joachim à Beust, treatise on the law of marriages, chapter 47, p. 184. If, however, the matter were not intact, for instance when intercourse has intervened, then whether the children are minors or of age, a consummated marriage cannot be rescinded, even if the parents have not consented to them, C. cum causa de raptoribus, see also Paul. Cypræus de jure connub. cap. 10. §. 10. 11. Harprechtus correctly again loc. c. n. 130. Illicit intercourse does not indeed make an illicit marriage valid, but it does bring it about that it cannot be dissolved: both because carnal union purifies every defect, and because many things are hindered from being contracted which, once contracted, are not dissolved.

If any things seem to present a contrary opinion among our countrymen, it must be observed that the state of the case, when they argue for the necessity of parental consent, is directed primarily against the Tridentine decree, which maintains that clandestine marriages entered into without parental consent are not LEGITIMATE: and that it is one thing not to be legitimate, and another not to be valid: and our people easily agree on this, that parents can be compelled to bring forward reasons for a refused consent, and that judges of matrimonial causes or supreme magistrates can take their place and have the power to enable children to enter into marriage when parents deny consent to honest marriages of their children without cause: that matrimonial contracts between the contracting parties must be entirely voluntary, and their most free consent is required: that paternal power consists in piety, not in cruelty: likewise we use this law, so that well-harmonized marriages may not be disturbed by the right of paternal power: and B. Luther has warned most gravely everywhere about the abuse of paternal power in denying consent, and finally the paternal power itself remains, even if in such a case, when carnal union has occurred, the right regarding the marriage of children expires through their fault, nor can paternal power remove that right which others have acquired over a son through a union of that kind. See Cypraeus c. 10. §. 11. n. 6. & Constit. Elect. Saxon. Ecclesit. tit. Von Ehegelübnissen. Add that Harprecht at the beginning of the title de nupt. §. 108. demonstrates that by Canon law it is not denied that the consent of parents is necessary in contracting a marriage, but that this only indicates that a marriage contracted against the authority and consent of parents is not to be dissolved if it has been consummated by coitus, and that this entirely agrees with civil law, having adduced §. 122. and the following with many supporting opinions; in which manner also Klingius de caus. matrimon lib. 24. testifies that Canonists and Theologians agree in this, that if carnal copulation has followed, the marriage is not to be separated, however much the consent of parents may have been lacking.

Abulensis distinguishes those laws, the present one of Exod. 22, 17. and that which is read in Deut. 22, 28, in this way: that here the discourse is about a girl who, seduced by blandishments, consented of her own accord to the defilement: but in Deuteronomy about her to whom force was applied. Similarly Menochius, & Malvenda at Deut. 22. This case differs from that of Exod. 22, 16. where it is a matter of coitus not extorted by force, but obtained by fraud, blandishments, and promises of marriage. Here, however, he circumvented her, imprudent, without a promise, by jest, wine, or cunning: but without consent, which the word 'to seize' signifies. Wherefore there only a dowry is prescribed, here a fine is imposed in addition to the dowry. But that difference cannot be firmly taught from the text: for the word 'to seize' does not immediately imply violence: and force pertains to rape, which was punished with a capital penalty. To Andreas Rivetus at Exod. 22. v. 17. that seems to be the difference; that in the law which is held here (Exod. 22.) it is a matter of a virgin whom a youth has enticed under the pretext of future nuptials: but in Deut. of her to whom someone, having seized the opportunity, has brought injury: in which, although he did not properly apply force, yet he did not use persuasion, but defiled her having seized her in the very act, though she was not resisting. For here he uses the word for enticing or alluring, but in Deuteronomy he uses the word for seizing: so that in the former act we understand a specious persuasion, but in the latter a present assault, by which, as if having seized the opportunity, someone brought injury: in which case, because of the injury brought upon the parent, the defiler paid fifty shekels, and was furthermore bound to marry the defiled woman, without hope of divorce, or in such a way that he could not divorce her under any pretext. In the former case, however, which is treated here, he who had enticed her was bound to marry the girl, but the parent could resist the marriage, and compel the defiler to pay such a dowry as would befit the girl's condition.

But the answer of B. Gerhard in his commentary on the passage of Deut. seems simpler: that the law is the same in both places, but is explained more fully in Deuteronomy: and thus two things are added which had been omitted here: The first is that the defiler was compelled to endow the virgin ACCORDING TO THE PROPORTION OF HER STATUS and to pay her such a sum of money as she would have received from her father in place of a dowry: The second, that he also had to give fifty shekels to the father of the defiled woman because of the trampled paternal authority and the violated chastity of the girl; whom he could not furthermore dismiss from himself by a bill of divorce all the days of his life. In this place of Exodus, however, there is held to be a certain limitation, which is to be understood in the law of Deuteronomy: He shall have her as a wife: if, that is, the father of the defiled woman wished to give her: for he could give or refuse: and therefore fifty shekels were paid to the father, so that he might the better be able to marry off or support his daughter, now already defiled, to another, if he denied her to the defiler. As these things are very correctly stated, so Rivetus's opinion about the different cases seems not inappropriate, because it is likely that the most wise legislator imposed a heavier penalty on one seizing a girl than on one inducing her with bland words: in this, however, I would not agree with Rivetus, that he thinks it is a matter here of one who was not necessarily compelled to marry the girl, even if the father of the defiled woman did not refuse: For it is added expressly: And he shall have her as a wife: But in our judgment, the difference is to be placed in this, that the defiler seizing the girl could never dismiss her all the days of his life, but had to retain her perpetually: which is not added here, nor does it seem to be understood in that case where she was deflowered having been induced merely by bland words. For the guilt then was also in her, because she allowed herself to be seduced.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SI PATER VIRGINIS DARE NOLUERIT, REDDET PECUNIAM.

Neque Deuter. 22, 29. de vi compressa agitur, quod innuere hic videtur Grotius; quia vis ad ra- ptum pertinet. Agitur autem hic de virgine verbis blandis seducta, nec dum desponsata, si seductor dormierit cum ea, seu vitiaverit eam, quod de v. 16. dispositum erat, ut dotet eam, habeatq́; eam uxorem, h. e. non posse ipsum a socero dotem exigere, sed teneri, ut de suis facultatibus virgini a se corruptæ dotem constituat, & nihilominus eam in uxorem ducat: Si vero pater virginis filiam suam stupratori (homini fortasse dissoluto & plane nequam) da- re noluerit, reddet (rectius dabit) stuprator virgini corruptæ pecuniam juxta modum dotis, quam virgi- nes accipere consueverunt, id est, tantum pecuniæ numerabit, quantum ejusmodi virgini per dotem dari solet. Videtur hinc colligi posse, dissensum Pa- rentis stupratæ tollere matrimonium, utut copula carnali consummatum. Sed de eo casu cum consensus matrimonialis & mutua desponsatio firmatur co- pula carnali, dispositio clara habetur Deut. 22, 28. Si invenerit (vel adortus fuerit) vir puellam ali- quam virginem, quæ non habet adhuc sponsum; & apprehendens eam (LXX. habent βιασάμενος ac si de stupro violento agatur, sed generalior est vox, & violentum stuprum non mulcta, sed morte pu- niebatur,) concubuerit cum illa, & res ad judicium venerit (in Ebr. & inventi vel deprehensi fuerint, id est, cum factum negari non poterit) dabit qui dor- mierit cum ea patri puellæ 50. siclos argenti, & habe- bit eam nihilominus uxorem: quia humiliavit seu constupravit illam: non poterit per libellum repu- dii dimittere eam, cunctis diebus vitæ suæ. Unde Cypraus cap. 10. de jure connubior. §. 11. pag. 474. monet, quod juxta legem Mosaicam, ut & Athe- niensium jura, qui virginem vitiarit, eam ducere debuerit, sive Parentes stupratoris annuerint, sive non: dummodo stupratæ Parentes ipsam ei dare non re- nuant. Dissensus autem Parentum stupratæ non ef- ficit quidem simpliciter, quo minus ratum sit con- jugium, quod copula carnali firmatum, hactenus ta- men pro more politiæ Judaicæ id tollere poterat, quia per libellum repudii tum etiam dissolveban- tur matrimonia. Notat etiam in eo Osiander diver- sitatem nostrarum legum: Hodierna jura non cogunt stupratorem, ut a se vitiatam ducat, si matrimonium non promisit: sed tamen si quis est vir bonus & æquus, non dedignabitur eam sibi matrimonio jungere, cum summum puellæ ornamentum virginitatem abstule- rit: Ast lex Mosaica de ducenda stuprata intelligi potest cum conditione, ubi nempe stuprator matri- monium promiserit illi, quam vitiavit, vel cum qua concubuit.

De cætero consensus matrimonialis, firmatus carnali copula, ratum facit matrimo- nium, etiamsi parentes non consentiant. Requi- ritur quidem consensus Parentum vi legis divinæ, ad matrimonium, nec omnibus modis legitimum haberi potest conjugium, quod extra Parentum consensum initur, sed non pertinet ad ipsam sub- stantiam & essentialia conjugii, quod ratum esse potest, citra consensum Parentum, si partes contra- hentes principales, ceu sunt Sponsus & Sponsa, con- sentiant, accesseritque copula carnalis: imo secun- dum ipsam matrimonii institutionem Genes. 2, 24. relinquere tenetur vir patrem & matrem, & uxori suæ adhærere; adeoque præfertur per ipsam sententiam Dei notante B. Hunnio amor conjugalis dilectioni liberorum erga parentes: & observatur in Harm. Chemnit. Lyser. ad Matth. 5, 31. etiamsi per scortationem conjugium ineat, non posse tamen id dissolvi, quia casus ille non pugnat cum matrimonii SUBSTANTIA. Atque in eo consentiunt nostrates, ut videre est apud B. Luther. T. VI. Witeberg. fol. 266. Tom. 5. Jenensi fol. 237. Tom. V. Altenb. fol. 376. libr. de matrimonialibus. Philipp. LL. de Conjug. tit. de Consens. Parent. Chytræum, ad Levit. 18. & 19. lib. Sponsal. clandestin. p. 616. Joh. Brentium in Catechet. & Apolog. Confess. Wurtenb. art. de Conjugio, Theologos item Tubing. (cum JCtis) in respons. Mens. April. Anno 1624. qui citante Joh. Harprechto ad rubr. instit. de nupt. n. 126. docent, quod ante copulationem subsequentem & benedictionem Sacerdotalem omnia sponsalia sive pura, sive conditionata, sive jurata, sive injurata, prius non dissoluta, simpliciter faciat indissolubilia concubitus sive copula carnalis. Ὁμοψηφία Witeb. Facult. habetur apud Dedekenn. part. III. fol. 441. & in Consil. Theol. Witteb. l. 4. p. 23. Facult. Theol. Rostoch. apud Dedekenn. lib. 1. fol. 436. B. Balduini in cas. Consc. B. Hülsemann. in Breviar. extenso pag. 433. B. Danhaw. lib. consc. apert. pag. 812. E JCtis conferatur imprimis B. D. Carpzovius Jurisprud. Consist. lib. II. Tit. VI. defin. LX. & Jurisprud. forens. part. IV. constit. XX. def. 15. Joh. Schneidewinus ad lib. 1. instit. part. II. Tit. 10. n. 35. Quando ad clandestina sponsalia accessit concubitus, tunc concludendum est, autoritate Parentum hujusmodi conjugia jam consummata rescindi non posse. Et idem servatur & pronunciatur in Consistoriis nostris. Hoc enim casu considerandum est, ut majus scandalum vitetur, & maxima tunc fieret injuria vitiatæ, & desertæ mulieri. Joachim. à Beust. tract. de jure connubior. cap. 47. p. 184. Si autem res non esset integra, puta quando intervenisset concubitus, tunc sive liberi sint minorennes, sive majorennes, conjugium consummatum non potest rescindi, etiamsi parentes in illos non consenserint C. cum causa de raptoribus, vid. & Paul. Cypræus de jure connub. cap. 10. §. 10. 11. Recte iterum Harprechtus loc. c. n. 130. Illicitus concubitus non facit quidem ut matrimonium illicitum convalescat, sed tamen efficit, ne dirimi queat: tum quod copula carnalis omne vitium purificet, tum quod multa impediantur contrahenda, quæ jam contracta non solvuntur.

Si quæ contrariam mentem præ se ferre videantur apud nostrates, observandum, quod status causæ, cum pro necessitate consensus parentum disputant, directus sit imprimis contra decretum Tridentinum, quod nempe clandestina matrimonia sine parentum consensu inita LEGITIMA non sint: quodque aliud sit, non esse legitimum, aliud non esse ratum: & facile in eo consentiant nostri, parentes ad causas recusati consensus proferendas adigi posse, & judices causarum matrimonialium vel Magistratus supremos in eorum locum succedere, ac potestatem liberis ineundi matrimonium facere posse parentibus citra causam consensum denegantibus honestis matrimoniis liberorum: contractus matrimoniales inter partes contrahentes omnino debere esse voluntarios, & consensum earum requiri liberrimum: patriam potestatem in pietate, non in atrocitate consistere: item hoc jure utimur, ne bene concordantia matrimonia jure patriæ potestatis turbentur: & de abusu paternæ potestatis in denegando consensu passim B. Lutherus gravissime monuit,ac manet denique ipsa patria potestas, etiamsi in tali casu, cum copula carnalis accessit, jus in libe- rorum nuptias culpa eorum expiret, neque toller potestas patria potest jus illud, quod alii per ejus modi copulationem in filium adepti sunt. Vid. Cy præus c. 10. §. 11. n. 6. & Constit. Elect. Saxon. Ecclesit. tit. Von Ehegelübnissen. Adde quod Harprecht ad princip. tit. de nupt. §. 108. demonstret jure Canonico non negari parentum consensum contrahen do matrimonio esse necessarium, sed hoc tantum indi cari, matrimonium contra parentum autoritatem & consensum contractum non esse dirimendum, si conca bitu fuerit consummatum, idque cum civili jure omni no congruere, adductis §. 122. seqq. plurimis suffra giis; quo pacto etiam Klingius de caus. matrimon lib. 24. testatur, quod Canonistæ & Theologi in ec consentiant, si copula carnalis subsecuta sit, matrimo- nium non esse separandum, utcunque consensus paren- tum defuerit.

Abulensis leges illas, præsentem Exod. 22, 17. & eam, quæ Deut. 22, 28. legitur, ita distinguit: quod hîc sermo sit de puella, quæ blanditiis seducta ultro in stuprum consensit: in Deuter. vero de ea, cui vis illata est. Similiter Menochius, & Malvenda ad Deut. 22. Hic casus differt ab illo Exod. 22, 16. ubi agitur de concubitu non vi extorto, sed fraude, blan- ditiis, promissis matrimonii impetrato. Hic autem eam imprudentem, citra sponsionem, joco, vino, aut astu circumveniebat: sed sine consensu, quod verbum apprehendendi significat. Quamobrem illic sola dos, hic præter dotem mulcta indicitur. Sed è textu ea differentia firmiter doceri non potest: neque enim verbum apprehendendi statim violentiam in- fert: & vis ad raptum pertinet, qui pœna capitali puniebatur. Andreæ Riveto ad Exod. 22. v. 17. ea videtur esse differentia; quod in lege, quæ hic ha- betur (Exod. 22.) agatur de virgine, quam juvenis pellexerit obtentu nuptiarum futurarum: in Deut. autem de ea, cui quis occasione arrepta vitium intu- lerit: in quo etsi vim non adhibuerit proprie, ta- men non usus est suasione, sed ipso facto prehensam, non tamen resistentem stupravit. Hic enim verbo pelliciendi, aut alliciendi, in Deuter. autem prehen- dendi utitur: ut in priori facto speciosam persuasio- nem intelligamus, in posteriori autem præsentem impetum, quo velut occasione arrepta quis vi- tium intulit: quo casu, propter injuriam parenti illatam pendebat stuprator quinquaginta siclos, & insuper tenebatur vitiatam ducere, sine spe repu- dii, vel ita, ut nullo prætextu eam potuerit repu- diare. In priori autem casu, de quo hic agitur, te- nebatur puellam ducere, qui pellexerat, sed parens poterat matrimonio resistere, & cogere stuprato- rem ad dotem numerandam talem, qualis puellæ conditioni conveniret.

Simplicior autem videtur B. Gerhardō alio- rum responsio, in comment. ad loc. Deut. legem utrobiq; eandem esse, sed plenius explicari in Deu- teronomio: adeoque duo addi, quæ hîc prætermissa erant: Primum est, quod virginem PRO RA- TIONE STATUS dotare eique tantam pecu- niæ summam, quantam dotis loco à patre accepis- set, numerare coactus fuerit stuprator: Alterum, quod etiam patri constupratæ propter conculca- tam patriam autoritatem & violatam puellæ pudi- citiam quinquaginta siclos dare debuerit; quam præterea non potuit per libellum repudii à se di- mittere omnibus diebus vitæ suæ. In hoc Exodi loco tamen haberi limitationem quandam, quæ ad Deuter. legem subintelligenda: Habebit eam uxo- rem: si sc. stupratæ pater eam dare voluerit: poterat enim dare, vel renuere: atque ideo quinquaginta sicli pendebantur patri, ut eo melius filiam jam am constupratam alteri elocare vel sustentare posset, si stupratori eam denegaret. Quæ uti sese rectis- sime habent, ita non inconcinna videtur Riveti de casibus diversis sententia, quia verisimile est legis- latorem sapientissimum graviori pœna affecisse apprehendentem puellam, quam blandis verbis in- ducentem: in eo tamen non annuerim Riveto, quod putet hîc de eo agi, qui non adactus fuerit neces- sario ad puellam ducendam, etiamsi Pater stupratæ non renuerit: Additur enim expresse: Habeatque eam in uxorem: Sed in eo locanda, nostro judicio, est differentia, quod stuprator apprehendens puel- lam nunquam eam omnibus diebus vitæ dimittere potuerit, sed eam perpetuo retinere debuerit: quod hîc additum non est, neque in eo casu, quo blandis saltim verbis inducta fuit deflorata, subin- telligendum videtur. Culpa enim tunc in ipsa etiam fuit, quod seduci se passa sit.

MALEFICOS (SORCERERS)] LXX. φαρμακοὺς (sorcerers). But in Hebrew the word is feminine, not because the same thing is not to be punished in men, but because the female sex is more prone to this crime. NOR SHALL YOU OPPRESS WITH USURY] This commandment binds not only the creditor, but also the scribe, the guarantors, and the witnesses of the contract. Moreover, usury is called נֶשֶׁךְ, because like the bite of a serpent, it proceeds from a small beginning to an immense size.

Regarding the first fruits, which were offered from fruits already perfectly processed, finally from the second day of the solemnity of Pentecost, Levit. 23, 15. Num. 28, 26. Deuter. 16, 9. chap. 18. v. 4. chap. 26. ver. 10. Mr. Varenius accepts this here on page 355.

Vers. 29.

DECIMAS TUAS ET PRIMITIAS TUAS] Plenitudi- nem & lachrymam tuam: id est, primitias frugis maturescen- tis, aut rerum liquidarum, ut vini & olei.

De primitiis, quæ de fructibus perfecte jam elaboratis offerebantur demum ab altero solemni- tatis Pentecostes Levit. 23, 15. Num. 28, 26. Deuter. 16, 9. cap. 18. v. 4. c. 26. vers. 10. accipit Dn. Varen. hîc pag. 355.

CHAPTER XXIII. Laws given to judges. Feasts. The angel as guide.

Ver. 1.

In Hebrew: You shall not lift up a report of vanity, whether by spreading a vain report about a neighbor, or by admitting it in judgment.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII. Leges judicibus datæ. Festa. Angelus ductor.

Vers. 1.

In Ebr. Non levabis rumorem vanitatis sive spar- gendo vanum rumorem de proximo, sive admit- tendo in judicio.

## 23:3
Ver. 3.

THOU SHALT NOT PITY THE POOR IN JUDGMENT] For a false appearance of mercy, or even such a hunting for fame, imposes upon many. Quintilian XII, 7. Both kinds of ambition must indeed be removed, whether by selling one's services to the powerful against the humble, or that other more boastful one, of raising up the lesser against dignity. For fortune does not make causes either just or unjust. The same, IV, 1. For pity alone inclines even a just judge. There are not a few judges who, to use the words of Terence, add to the poor out of pity. Therefore Philo says that here is required τὸ ἀνένδοτον πρὸς ἱκεσίας καὶ οἴκτους.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

PAUPERIS QVOQVE NON MISEREBERIS IN JUDICIO] Imponit enim multis falsa species misericordiæ, aut etiam famæ talis aucupatio. Quintilianus XII, 7. Sum- movendum vero utrumque est ambitus genus vel potentibus con- tra humiles venditando operam, vel illud etiam jactantius, mi- nores utique contra dignitatem attollendi. Non enim fortuna causas vel justas vel injustas facit. Idem IV, 1. Nam sola rectum quoque judicem inclinat miseratio. Sunt non pauci Judices, qui ut Terentianis utar verbis, propter misericordiam addunt pauperi. Propterea Philo requiri hîc ait τὸ ἀνένδοτον πρὸς ἱκεσίας καὶ οἴκτους.

Verse 9.

## 23:10
Verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

## 23:11
THOU SHALT MAKE THE LAND TO REST, THAT THE POOR MAY EAT.

Why the land had to rest, a triple cause can be given elsewhere: 1. that the Hebrews might be admonished of clemency toward inanimate things, and from excessive care for life, and from avarice might be led away. This is the moral use. 2. That the land in the seventh year of rest, having resumed its vigor, might thereafter be more fertile: this is the natural use. 3. That the seventh year of rest might be a memorial of the creation of the earth, just as the seventh day also was: which use was symbolic. Here, however, this reason is urged, that the poor may eat and rejoice in the fruits of the field: which use is political.

But what could the poor eat if the land rested? Some think that the land could and should have been sown in the Sabbatical year, but that the crops should not have been harvested. But the words command that they make the land rest, Lev. 25, 4. In the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath for the land: you shall not sow your field. Cf. Joseph. lib. XII. Antiq. cap. 4. l. 14. cap. 7. l. 15. c. 4. Wherefore it must be said that it happened by a special divine blessing that a harvest grew without the sowing of crops. It could certainly have happened easily that, the harvest having been made in the preceding spring, many seeds having fallen here and there and at random through the fields during the following hot summer, since in Judea rains are rare in the time of summer, they hardened, and with the rains approaching toward autumn, they took root in the ground, and then burst forth into stalks and ears. Therefore it is said Lev. 25, 5. That which the soil produces of its own accord, you shall not reap.

It must be observed, however, that while the owners of the fields are indeed prohibited from the harvest, they are not entirely deprived of the fruits of that year, provided they do not claim them for themselves alone and do not collect them to be stored, Levit. 25, 5. Ordinarily, all fruits were to be left for the poor, the widows, and the strangers: but if the produce of the land had been abundant, even the head of the household could claim something for himself for the sustenance of his own dependents. 2. Therefore, no Jew was barred by religion from these fruits born spontaneously in the seventh year, and consequently even the owner of the land and his household could pick them, just as anyone else could, but only for daily uses and necessities, not for storing for the future, as is done in the harvest, the vintage, and the annual collection of fruits, as B. Gerhard notes, Comment. in Deut. 15. p. 917. From which one may gather the power of the divine blessing, which was exerted even in the Sabbatical year while the land was resting. Nor is it only about fields that we are dealing here, but also about orchards, vineyards, and olive groves: for the vine, the olive, and other fruit-bearing trees, even if no cultivation is applied for one year, bear fruit, and often in greater quantity: especially the wine-grape vine, which if it is left for one year unpruned, extends its branches and brings forth more grapes. Therefore it is no wonder if the poor had from such things wherewith to provide for their need. From the remainder, however, which fell to the ground, the beasts of the field also had what they might eat.

Vers. 11.

BUT IN THE SEVENTH YEAR YOU SHALL LET IT REST) Tacitus on the customs of the Jews, Hist. V. The seventh year also is given to idleness. What the Sabbath day is to men, that the seventh year is to the land. It has been said by Philo.

Latin:

REQUIESCERE FACIES TERRAM, UT COMEDANT PAUPERES.

Cur terra requiescere debuerit, triplex alias causa reddi potest: 1. ut Ebræi clementiæ admo- nerentur erga inanima, & à nimia vitæ cura, & a- varitia abducerentur. Qui est usus moralis. 2. Ut terra septimo quietis anno q. resumto vigore feracior deinde esset: qui est usus naturalis. 3. Ut septimus quietis annus memoriale esset creationis terræ, uti & erat dies septimus: qui usus erat symbolicus. Hic vero urgetur hæc causa, ut comedant pauperes, fructibusque agri gaudeant: qui usus est politicus.

Quid verò comedere pauperes poterant, si terra quievit? Nonnulli putant terram & anno Sabbatico seri potuisse, & debuisse, non autem fruges colligi debuisse. Sed verba præcipiunt, ut requiescere faciant terram, Lev. 25, 4. Septimo anno Sabbatum erit terræ: agrum non seres. Conf. Joseph. lib. XII. Antiq. cap. 4. l. 14. cap. 7. l. 15. c. 4. Quapropter dicendum peculiari divina benedictione factum, ut sine frugum semente messis nasceretur. Fieri sane potuit facile, ut facta messe præcedenti vere, multa sparsim & temere per agros delapsa semina per sequentem æstatem fervidam, cum in Judæa tempore æstatis raræ sint pluviæ, indurescerent, & accedentibus, sub autumnum pluviis, radices in terra agerent, ac deinde in culmos, spicasque erumperent. Ideo dicitur Lev. 25, 5. Quæ sponte gignet humus, non metes.

Observandum autem prohiberi quidem dominis agrorum messem, sed non privari eos plane fructibus illius anni, dummodo eos non vendicent sibi solis eosque non colligant servandos, Levit. 25, 5. Ordinarie omnes fruges pauperibus, viduis & peregrinis erant relinquendæ: quod si vero proventus terræ fuissent copiosi, etiam paterfamilias ad suorum domesticorum sustentationem, ex illis quidpiam sibi poterit vendicare. 2. Nullus ergo religione Judæus ab hisce frugibus septimo anno sponte natis arcebatur, ac proinde etiam fundi dominus ejusque domestici potuerunt eos carpere, sicut & quivis alius, sed ad quotidianos usus & necessitates duntaxat, non ad recondendum in futurum, ut fit in messe, vindemia & annua fructuum collectione, uti notat B. Gerhard. Comment. in Deut. 15. p. 917. Unde colligere licet vim divinæ benedictionis, quæ etiam anno Sabbatico exerta quiescente terra. Nec vero solum de agris hic agitur, sed etiam de frutetiis, vinetis, & olivetis: vitis autem, oliva, & aliæ arbores fructiferæ, etiamsi anno uno nihil culturæ adhibeatur, fructum ferunt, & sæpe majori quantitate: præsertim vitis vinifera, quæ si anno uno dimittatur non putata, extendit palmites suas, & plures uvas affert. Itaque non mirum est, si ex talibus pauperes habuerint, unde inopiæ suæ consulerent. Ex reliquo autem quod in terram cadebat, habebant etiam quod comederent bestiæ agri.

Vers. 11.

ANNO AVTEM SEPTIMO DIMITTET EAM) Tacitus de Judæis moribus Hist. V. Septimum quoque annum ignaviæ datum. Quod Sabbati dies hominibus, hoc annus septimus terræ. Dictum est Philonis.

## 23:13
Vers. 13.

YOU SHALL NOT SWEAR BY THE NAME OF FOREIGN GODS, NOR SHALL IT BE HEARD FROM YOUR MOUTH] It was not permitted to them even to pronounce the name of false Gods, so that they might be further removed from veneration. Therefore, instead of בעל שמין they said בעל זבוב, instead of בית אל they said בית און, and so in the rest.
