Du- bium etiam movetur, quum Moses fœdus nominet, qui Paulus Testamentum substituerit? sed nomen E- bræum generale est, quod non solum pro fœdere inter partes cum mutua sponsione, & restipulatione, sed etiam pro declaratione voluntatis aut promissionis, quæ ab uno proficiscitur, accipitur : neque ob- stat, quo minus una & eadem conventio & fœdus & testamentum simul sit, hoc est, ut confœderatio inter duas partes sub certis conditionibus : & unius nihilominus dispositio testamentaria acceden- te morte; maxime si talis conditio ponatur, quæ ab ipso testatore in aliqua parte impleatur, quod hic factum est.

ET AIT, HIC EST SANGVIS FOEDE- RIS, QVOD PEPIGIT DOMINVS VOBIS- CVM.

Similis est locutio Christi, cum in S. Euchari- stiae institutione, Hoc, ait, est sanguis Meus Novi Testa- menti, ideoque uti Moses sanguinem vere praesen- tem, non significationem vel typum sanguinis istis verbis indicat, ac de sanguine victimarum, qui tum effundebatur sine figura, ac proprie verba ejus ac- cipienda, ita Christus pariter sanguinem suum vere praesentem esse testatur, non tantum significari, aut typum ejus, vel figuram exhiberi, & de sanguine, uti verba sonant, quem effudit in remissionem peccato- rum loquitur, quae citra tropum & figuram, ne per- vertantur verba tropisque pro lubitu nostro detor- queantur, & ambigua reddantur, omnino accipien- da sunt. Si Vetus Testamentum sanguine vero vi- ctimarum, quae referebant Christum, sancitum, No- vum utique Testamentum non tantum figura san- guinis, sed ipsissimo Christi sanguine, qui per victi- marum sanguinem adumbratus est, sancitum esse intelligendum, quum Christus id totidem verbis aperte testetur, iisq; ad hanc Vet. Foederis confir- mationem respiciat, similibus verbis utens, ut sen- sum non diversum, sed eundem subesse certiores redderemur. Quam vere ergo sanguine typico conspersus illic fuit populus, tam vere etiam dispen- satur nobis in S. Coena sanguis Christi, & quidem juxta Christi mandatum, Bibite, hoc est sanguis me- us, ore percipiendus.

Nec ullius momenti est Riveti exceptio; quod ita consecuturum sit, uti visibili modo aspergebatur vitulorum sanguis, aspersionem sanguinis Christi etiam visibilem, imo ipsum sanguinem Christi signum esse, quemadmodum sanguis vitulorum signum fuit. Nam to visibile esse accidens est; sed veritas praesentis san- guinis ad substantiam rei pertinet, ad materiam nempe, quae populo communicata, & de veritate ac substantia tantum sonant verba Mosis, Hic est san- guis foederis, non de accidentibus sanguinis, quod fuerit visibilis, quod corruptibilis &c. quapropter a veritate substantialis praesentiae sanguinis victimarum in Vet. Foedere ad veritatem praesentiae substantialis sanguinis Christi in N. T. recte procedit consequen- tia, non item ab accidentibus, quae variare possunt. Neque sanguis vitulorum signum tantum foederis, sed medium fuit fanciendi & confirmandi ejusdem: quod de sanguine Christi omnino etiam creden- dum, quo & in effusione ejusdem sancitum foedus gratiae, & in dispensatione in S. Eucharistia confir- matur, & nobis non per ἀπουσίαν ejusdem, sed per veram realem & substantialem παρουσίαν, quam ver- ba Christi veracicissima testantur: Hoc est sanguis meus N. T. &c.

Verf. eod.

SUPER CVNCTIS SERMONIBUS HIS.

Hos sermones perperam restringit Rivetus ad praecepta divina exclusis promissis. Falluntur, in- quit in h. l. p. 127. qui haec super omnibq verbis his de pro- missionibus divinis intelligunt, hac ratione confirman- dis, quia manifeste referuntur ad praecepta, quae ex li- bro recitabantur, a quorum observatione, velut condi- tione a parte populi necessaria foedus illud pendebat. E- rat enim liber praeceptorum non promissionum. Tunc enim sub V. T. conditio legis servandae proponebatur; quae sub novo non exigitur, sed in Christo pro no- bis praestita annunciatur & fide recipitur. Sed fallitur vehementer Rivetus: quia sermones in libro sanguine asperso a Mose propositi non mi- nus promissiones continebant, quam præcepta; & veluti foedus a parte Israelitici populi conditionem obedientiæ includebat, sic obligabat se Deus hoc fœdere, quod populi hujus Deus esse velit, ei bene- facturus hîc & in æternum. Et quanquam conditio illa perfectæ obedientiæ impleri haud potuerit, pro- missiones tamen ideo negandæ non sunt obedientiæ factæ divinitus; quia infidelitas hominum fidem Dei non evacuat Rom. 3, 4. ut taceam, quod lex pædagogus fuerit ad Christum; in quo habemus τὸ πλήρωμα νόμꙋ Rom. 10, 4. quodque libro legis & sermonibus illis comprehensâ etiam fuerint ea, quibus Christus figurabatur, uti confirmatio fœderis sanguine victima- rum facta, & ipsa sanguinis victimarum effusio nihil aliud erant, quam adumbratio & typus eorum, quo- rum corpus & substantiam habemus in Christo Col. 2. Erat aspersio ista, inquit Pelargus in h. l. admoni- tio tacita conditionis humanæ, immundos esse nos omnes natura, deinde futuræ expiationis per Christum; & symbolum certissimum fœderis, quod Deus initurus esset nobiscum altari nostro Christi sanguine asperso Es. 63, 2. 3. & nobis ipsius sanguine ablutis.

## 24:10
ver. 10. AND THEY SAW THE GOD OF ISRAEL) A certain very bright form, as it were of a man turning his back. The Chaldean, the glory of God; in Greek, τὸν τόπον, ὗ ἐςήκει ὁ Θεός.

Be it so, that God was seen in a form of such a kind, as Tostatus wishes, that He appeared in the form of a bright cloud, others in a human form in the likeness of a magnificent Prince and King Legislator, who was seen to have feet, and under them a sapphire footstool, or as Grotius wishes, a floor worthy of such a walker (which human form, however, although it is approved by Lyranus, Cajetanus, Pradus, and Cornelius, does not sufficiently agree with Deut. 4:15). Therefore, He who appeared was not an Angel, but Jehovah Himself, the God of Israel. Which we have already shown that the whole context of the text cries out.

AND UNDER HIS FEET) As if a floor worthy of such a walker. ver. 11. AND UPON THEM, WHO HAD WITHDRAWN AFAR OFF FROM THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL) The Hebrew Codex says upon the separated, that is, the elect, as the Greeks rightly took it, τῶν ἐπιλέκτων τῆ Iσραὴλ, as are Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the LXX. Ez. 42:6. אציל which word is of the same origin as this name, is translated ἐξέχοντο. HE LAID HIS HAND) That is, He did them no harm. Thus the same expression is taken in Esth. 2:21. In the Greek it is, 8 διεφώνησεν ὐδὲ εἷς, that is, not one of them was missing, as in Num. 31:49, 8 διαπεφώνηκεν ἀπ᾿ ἀυτῶν ὐδὲ εἷς, in the same sense, yet with a different Hebrew word. And again another Hebrew name is in Ez. 37:11, διαπεφω- νήκαμεν, that is, we have perished. But it is not without cause that this was added, because the opinion of those times was accepted that such visions do not happen unless to those about to die immediately. See Jud. 13:22. ver. 19. COVERING HIM WITH A CLOUD) As His minister, as Maimonides explains. For in the Synagogue the החזנים are accustomed to be covered, who are called Ἀζανῖται by Epiphanius, to whom correspond in the Church the Deacons wearing a stole: The cloud here signifies the weakness of our intellect concerning divine things.

Latin:

vers. 10. ET VIDERUNT DEUM ISRAEL) Formam quandam valde lucidam velut hominis tergum obvertentis. Chaldæus, gloriam Dei, Græce τὸν τόπον, ὗ ἐςήκει ὁ Θεός.

Sit ita, visum Deum fuisse in forma ejusmodi, uti Tostatus vult, in forma lucidæ nubis apparuisse, alii in forma humana in speciem magnifici Principis, & Regis Legislatoris, qui visus sit habere pedes, & sub iis Sapphirinum scabellum, vel ut vult Grotius, solum tanto incessore dignum, (quæ tamen hominis forma, etsi Lyrano, Cajetano, Prado, Cornelio probetur, non satis convenit cum Deut. 4, 15.) Non ergo qui appa- ruit, Angelus fuit, sed Jehovah ipse, Deus Israel. Quod totam textus συνέχειαν clamare jam ostendi- mus.

ET SUB PEDIBUS EJUS) Quasi solum dignum tanto incessore. vers. 11. NEC SUPER EOS, QVI PROCVL RECES- SERANT DE FILIIS ISRAEL) Hebræus Codex super sepa- ratos, id est, electos, ut Græci recte sumfere, τῶν ἐπιλέκτων τῆ Iσραὴλ, ut sunt Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, & LXX. Ez. 42, 6. אציל quod verbum est ejusdem originis, cujus hoc no- men, vertitur ἐξέχοντο. MISIT MANUM SVAM) Id est, nihil illis nocuit. Sic eadem locutio sumitur Esth. 2, 21. In Græco est, 8 διεφώνησεν ὐδὲ εἷς, id est, nemo eorum desideratus est, ut Num. 31, 49. 8 διαπε- φώνηκεν ἀπ᾿ ἀυτῶν ὐδὲ εἷς, sensu eodem, alio tamen verbo He- bræo. Et rursus aliud nomen Hebræum est Ez. 37, 11. διαπεφω- νήκαμεν, id est, periimus. Non autem sine causa id additum, quia recepta erat opinio illorum temporum, talia visa non ob- tingere, nisi jamjam morituris. Vid. Jud. 13, 22. vers. 19. TEGENS ILLUM NVBE) Tanquam ministrum suum, ut exponit Maimonides. Solent enim in Synagoga o- periri החזנים, qui Epiphanio Ἀζανῖται, quibus respondent in Ecclesiæ Diaconi ferentes orarium: Nubes hic significat im- becillitatem intellectus nostri circa divina.

## 25:1 Argument
PART III. OF EXODUS, POETIC, ON THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE TABERNACLE. CHAPTER XXV. On the offering of gifts, the ark of the covenant, the table, and the candlestick.

Latin:

PARS III. EXODI ΠΟΙΗΤΙ- KH DE TABERNACULI CONSTRUCTIONE. CAPUT XXV. De oblatione donorum, arcæ fœderis, mensæ, & candelabro.

## 25:2
Ver. 2. THAT THEY TAKE FOR ME FIRSTFRUITS) תרומה here are not firstfruits, but a spontaneously made offering. ver. 4. HYACINTH AND PURPLE AND SCARLET TWICE DYED AND BYSSUS] Four colors as images of the four elements; scarlet of fire, hyacinth of air, purple of the sea, byssus of the earth. As the innermost sanctuary of the supercelestial world, so the greatest part of the temple bore the image of the visible world: the seven lamps as the planets: the twelve loaves as symbols of the Zodiac. See what is said at Matt. 27:50.

Grotius, having followed the Jews, as appears from R. Menasseh Ben Israel the conciliator in Exodus at chapter XX, question 30, makes the four colors images of the four Elements in the veils, the seven lamps symbols of the Planets, and the twelve loaves of proposition symbols of the Zodiac. But I fear that he can prove these expositions of symbols to the Reader: about which he was not even anxious; thinking perhaps that it was enough for Grotius to state those things. This declaration is too philosophical. What do the Lamps have to do with the Planets, of which recent Astronomer observers now count not just seven, but add more? What do the loaves of proposition have to do with the signs of the Zodiac, or the colors in the veils with the four Elements? More rightly at Matt. 27:51, Grotius acknowledges that these could have had another signification proper to the Israelites. Nor are they said badly to have designated the loaves as the bread of life, by which the Church is continually fed, Christ, so that there were twelve for the twelve tribes of the Israelites, because He pertains to all. The seven lamps can signify the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit, or His perfect illumination, since that number is of perfection. But to examine these things more exquisitely now is not our purpose. Concerning the structure of the tabernacle, see Richard of St. Victor, book on the Tabernacle; Ribera, book V on the Temple; Villalpandus in the description of the temple. Concerning the symbolic signification, see Beda and Pelargus in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VT TOLLANT MIHI PRIMITIAS) תרומה hic non sunt primitiæ, sed sponte facta oblatio. vers. 4. HTACINTHVM ET PVRPVVRAM COC- CVMQVE BIS TINCTVM ET BTSSVM] Quatuor co- lores in velis quatuor elementorum imagines; coccinum ignis, hyacinthus aeris, purpura maris, byssus telluris. V enim intimum adytum mundi supercœlestis, ita templi pars maxima mundi aspectabilis ferebat imaginem: septem lychni planetarum: Duodecim panes Zodiaci Symbola. Vide quæ ad Matth. 27, 50.

Grotius Judæos sequutus, ut e R. Menass. Ben Israel conciliatore in Exod. ad cap. XX. quæst. 30. apparet, quatuor colores in velis quatuor Elementorum imagines, septem lychnos Planetarum, duodecim panes propositionis Zodiaci Symbola facit. Vereor autem, ut probare possit Lectori has Symbolorum expositiones: de quo etiam sollicitus non fuit; ratus forte, satis esse, ista statuere Grotium. Nimis Philosophica hæc est declaratio. Quid Lychni ad Planetas, quorum nunc non septem tantum numerant, sed plures addunt nuperi observatores Astronomi? Quid panes propositionis ad signa Zodiaci, aut colores in velis ad quatuor Elementa? Rectius ad Matth. 27, 51. agnoscit Grotius, potuisse hac aliam Israelitis propriam habere significationem. Nec male panes designasse dicuntur panem vitæ, quo Ecclesia jugiter pascitur, Christum, ut duodecim fuerint ob duodecim tribus Israelitarum, quod is ad omnes pertineat. Septem lychni dona Septiformia Spiritus S. vel perfectam ejus illuminationem, quum numerus ille perfectionis sit, significare possunt. Sed hæc nunc rimari exquisitius, nostri non est instituti. De tabernaculi structura vid. Richard. Victor. l. de Tabern. Riber. l. V. de Templo, Villalpand. in descript. templi. De Symbolica significatione Beda & Pelargus in h. l.

## 25:5
Ver. 5. AND SHITTIM WOOD) Σήπτα in Symmachus, Ζήτινον δένδρον in Dioscorides, سنط in the Arabs, as Salmasius noted in his commentary on Cebes.

The LXX Interpreters rendered here ξύλα ἄσηπτα, incorruptible wood, as in Is. 41:19, πύξον, Boxwood; Theodotion and Jerome, thorn: The Samaritan and Chaldean Paraphrasts retained the Hebrew word; the Syrian interpreted it here, as also Jonathan the Chaldean in Is. 41:19, by אָש כַרעָא which the Latin Interpreter of the Syrian translation explained as Eberium: The Persian renders it שִמְשָר. The Arab סנט אר from Santo wood, as the Latin Interpreter translates; which seems to be from the Hebrew שִטָה, so that this might be from the unused root שוט. Commonly the Hebrews and our own judge it to have been a species of Cedar, and that a most noble one, concerning which Jerome at Joel 3. It is, however, a kind of tree in the desert, similar to a white thorn in color and leaves, though not in size. Otherwise they are such large trees that very wide planks are cut from them; and the wood is very strong, and of incredible lightness and beauty, so that the wealthiest and most studious men even make from them the vessels of wine presses, which they call ἄρσενας καὶ θηλύας; which woods are not found in cultivated places, and on Roman soil, apart from the wilderness of Arabia. See more about these in Buxtorf, Histor. arc. fœd. c. 4. p. 49. seqq. Aben Ezra thinks these trees grew around Mount Sinai: others judge they were brought from Egypt, because Ex. 35, 24 it is hinted that everyone brought the woods that were at hand to him: which would not have been necessary if forests of such wood had been in the desert. Whence Rivetus gathers at Ex. 25. that the Hebrews had with them planks of that select and exquisite wood, which, after they had arrived in the promised land, they might use for some work fashioned with skill and exquisite art, which they later offered for the use of the sanctuary.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET LIGNA SETIM) Σήπτα Symmacho, Dioscoridi Ζήτινον δένδρον, سنط Arabibus, ut notavit ad Cebetem Salmasius.

LXX. Interpp. reddidere hîc ξύλα ἄσηπτα, ligna imputribilia, ut Es. 41, 19. πύξον Buxum, Theodotio & Hieronymus spinam: Samaritanus & Chaldæi Paraphrastæ retinuere Ebræam vocem, Syrus interpretatus est hîc, ut & Jonathan Chaldæus Es. 41, 19. per אָש כַרעָא quod Latinus Syræ translationis Interpres exposuit Eberium: Persicus reddit שִמְשָר. Arabs סנט אר ex ligno Santo, ut Interpres Latinus vertit; quod videtur ex Ebræo שִטָה esse, ut hoc a radice inusitata שוט sit. Communiter Ebræi & nostri Cedri speciem fuisse, eamq; nobilissimam censent, de qua Hieronymus ad Joel. 3. Est autem genus arboris in eremo, spinæ albæ simile, colore & foliis, non magnitudine. Alioquin tam grandes arbores sunt, ut latissima ex illis tabulata cædantur; lignumque fortissimum est, & incredibilis levitatis ac pulchritudinis, ita ut ex his etiam vasa torcularium, quæ ἄρσενας καὶ θηλύας vocant, ditissimi quisq; & studiosissimi faciant; quæ ligna in locis cultis, & in Romano solo, absque Arabiæ solitudine non inveniuntur. Videantur de his plura apud Buxtorfium Histor. arc. fœd. c. 4. p. 49. seqq. Aben Ezra putat, circa montem Sinai hæc ligna crevisse: alii ex Ægypto allata censent, quia Ex. 35, 24. innuatur unumquemque ea, quæ præsto erant ipsi ligna attulisse: quo opus non fuisset, si talis ligni sylvæ in diserto fuissent. Unde colligit Rivetus ad Ex. 25. Ebræos secum habuisse ligni illius selecti & exquisiti tabulas, quibus postquam pervenissent in terram promissam, uterentur ad scitum aliquod & arte exquisita elaboratum opus, quas postea in usum sanctuarii obtulerint.

## 25:8
vers. 8. AND THEY SHALL MAKE ME A SANCTUARY.

A tabernacle, which may be, as it were, a holy temple, in which sacred rites and sacrifices may be performed to me, and as it were my house, in which I may be worshipped, sought, and found with solemn and public cult. For although the Lord is in need of no house Es. 66, 1. 2. nor does He dwell in temples made by hands Act. 7, 48. c. 17, 24. yet He commands a tabernacle to be built for Himself, not so that He may play with the Israelites as Sebastian Franck blasphemed; nor so that He may look to His own convenience, as the Manichaeans raved, in Augustine book against Adamantius c. 10. but so that He may reveal His majesty as if in a visible sign, and join Himself more closely to those by whom He wishes to be acknowledged and worshipped, and may insinuate something μυστικώτερον (more mystical) about Christ, who was to σκηνώσα (dwell) among us, as if by a type: just as the tabernacle itself was an image of Christ, whose material was from men, namely the flesh of men assumed from man, but the form or divinity itself was begotten by the Father from eternity, and finally that it may remind individuals to attend to the preservation of the Ecclesiastical ministry, as here Pelargus. Therefore He asks for a Theruma from His people, i.e., a gift, which may be lifted up on high, waved, and exhibited to the sight of all, according to the custom used by the nation, and that it be spontaneous, and accommodating itself to the ability of individuals, He wishes both precious and common things to be offered, namely from the Egyptian spoils. Concerning whose mystical signification Bede c. 3. All these things, which the Lord commanded to be offered to Him materially by the former people for the making of a sanctuary, we also who desire to be spiritual children of Israel, that is, imitators of the people of God who sees, ought to offer with spiritual understanding, insofar as through such voluntary oblations we ourselves may deserve to make a sanctuary for Him in us, and He may deign to consecrate a dwelling for Himself in the midst of us, that is, in our heart. To whom indeed we offer gold, when we shine with the clarity of true wisdom, which is in right faith: silver, when there is also confession by our mouth unto salvation: bronze, when we rejoice to spread the same faith by public preaching: hyacinth, when we lift up our hearts: purple, when we subject the body to passion: twice-dyed scarlet, when we burn with a twofold love, that is, of God and neighbor: fine linen, when we feel the chastity of the flesh: goats' hair, when we put on the habit of penitence and mourning: rams' skins dyed red, when we see the teachers of the Lord's flock themselves baptized in their own blood: violet skins, when we hope that after death we shall have spiritual bodies in heaven: acacia wood, when, having conquered the thickets of sins, we serve the Lord alone with clean flesh and soul: oil for preparing the lamps, when we shine with the fruits of charity and mercy: aromatics, ointment, and incense of good odor, when we spread the reputation of our good action far and wide to many as an example of living well: onyx stones and gems to adorn the Ephod, when we proclaim with worthy praise the miracles of the saints, by which they adorned thoughts devoted to God and works of virtues, and we assume these for the aid of our faith, where there is need, etc. Origen homily 9. Faith, he says, can be compared to gold, the word of preaching to silver, patience to bronze, knowledge to incorruptible woods, virginity to fine linen, the glory of confession to scarlet, the vigor of charity to purple, the hope of the kingdom of heaven to hyacinth.

verse of the same. I WILL DWELL IN THE MIDST OF THEM) Thence I will give answers. Below 22.

Latin:

vers. 8. FACIENTQUE MIHI SANCTUARIUM.

Tabernaculum, quod sit, quasi templum sanctum, in quo mihi sacra & sacrificia peragantur, & quasi domus mea, in qua solemni & publico cultu colar, quærar, & inveniar. Quanquam enim dominus nullius domus indigus sit Es. 66, 1. 2. nec in templ manu factis habitat Act. 7, 48. c. 17, 24. jubet tame sibi tabernaculum construi, non ut ludat Israëlitas ut Sebast. Francus blasphemavit; nec ut commodum suum spectet, ut Manichæi delirarunt, apud August libr. contr. Adamant. c. 10. sed ut visibili velut in dicio suam patefaciat majestatem, ac se propiu conjungat iis, a quibus agnosci ac coli vult, ac μυστικώτερον aliquid de Christo, qui inter nos σκηνώσα debebat, quasi typo insinuet: quemadmodum ta bernaculum ipsum Christi erat imago, cujus materia ex hominibus, caro nempe hominum ex homine assumta, forma autem aut divinitas ipsa a Patre ab æterno genita, & ministerii tandem Ecclesiastici con servationem incumbere singulis commoneat, ut hic Pelargus. Itaq; a populo suo omni poscit Theruma, h. e. donum, quod in altum tollatur, ventiletur, omniumq; conspectui, ritu gentis usitato, exhibeatur, idque spontaneum, & facultati singulorum se accommodans pretiosa simul & communia offerri vult, ex spoliis nempe Ægyptiacis. De quorum mystica significatione Beda c. 3. Cuncta hæc, quæ Dominus sibi a priore populo ad faciendum sanctuarium materialiter offerri præcepit, nos quoque qui spirituales filii Israël, hoc est, imitatores Dei videntis populi esse desideramus, spirituali intelligentia debemus offerre, quatenus per hujusmodi oblationes voluntarias & ipsi sanctuarium ei in nobis facere mereamur, & ipse in medio nostrûm habitare, hoc est, in corde nostro mansionem sibi consecrare dignetur. Cui videlicet aurum offerimus, cum claritate veræ sapientiæ, quæ est in fide recta, resplendemus: argentum, cum & ore nostro confessio sit ad salutem: æs, cum eandem fidem publica prædicatione divulgare gaudemus: hyacinthum, cum sursum corda levamus: purpuram, cum corpus passioni subjicimus: coccum bis tinctum, cum gemino, hoc est, Dei & proximi amore flagramus: byssum, cum carnis castitatem sentimus: pilos caprarum, cum habitum pœnitentiæ ac lučtus induimus: pelles arietum rubricatas, cum ipsos dominici gregis doctores suo sanguine baptisatos videmus: pelles janthinas, cum nos post mortem spiritualia in cœlis corpora habituros esse speramus: ligna Sittim, cum expugnatis peccatorum spinetis munda carne, & anima Domino soli servimus: oleum ad luminaria concinnanda, cum fructibus charitatis & misericordiæ refulgemus: aromata, unguentum & thymiama boni odoris, cum opinionem bonæ nostræ actionis multis ad exemplum bene vivendi longe lateq; diffundimus: lapides onychinos & gemmas ad ornandum Ephod, cum miracula sanctorum, quibus cogitationes Deo devotas & opera virtutum ornavere, digna laude prædicamus, atq; hæc in adjutorium fidei nostræ, ubi opus, assumimus &c. Origenes homil. 9. Fides, ait, auro conferri potest, sermo prædicationis argento, patientia æri, lignis imputribilibus scientia, bysso virginitas, cocco confessionis gloria, purpuræ charitatis vigor, hyacintho spes regni cœlorum.

vers. eod. HABITABO IN MEDIO EORUM) Inde responsa dabo. Infra 22.

## 25:9
verse 9. ACCORDING TO ALL THE LIKENESS OF THE TABERNACLE WHICH I WILL SHOW THEE.

The Lord showed its idea to Moses on the mountain: according to the likeness of which all things were to be accurately formed, both to warn that in the worship of God what is uniquely prescribed by the law must be observed, and nothing is to be instituted by one's own judgment or ἐϑελοθρησκείᾳ (will-worship); and to teach that these were copies, and shadows of heavenly things, which were formed by Moses Heb. 8, 5. which were ἐπεράνια (heavenly things) then hidden with God in the secret of His majesty, to be manifested one day in Christ. And therefore the pious

Fathers, with the Scripture of the N.T. leading the way and especially the Epistle to the Hebrews, were compelled to elicit these from those types and shadows. Thus Cyril teaches that the ark signified Christ in John book 4 c. 28. Gregory homily last in Ez. Rupert. and others, which the Pontificians wrongly draw to designate the Virgin Mary: Bede c. 4. says the ark made of acacia wood signifies the Lord's body consisting of members, lacking every stain of vices; the length of the ark the long-suffering patience of our redeemer; the breadth, the amplitude of charity, with which He wished to come to us, and to dwell among us; the height, the hope of future sublimity. That the Ark of the Covenant is Christ is manifest from Rev. 11, 19; where Corn. a Lap. acknowledges that Christ is exhibited. The ark consisted of incorruptible woods: so the flesh of Christ is incorruptible Ps. 16: it was covered with gold on the inside: the flesh of Christ shines with the fullness of divine majesty entirely Col. 2, 9. The ark kept the tablets of the law. Christ always had the law in His heart, and kept it holily Psalm 40, 6. Beside the ark, manna and the rod of Aaron were stored, by which the word of the Gospel and the Priesthood of Christ were foreshadowed. In the ark was the mercy seat: in Christ we have the true propitiation 1 John 2, 2. Two Cherubim above the Ark looking at each other mutually, and looking at the ark, are the two Testaments, Old and New, which are directed toward Christ, and look at each other mutually, and declare Him. Most of which Cornelius l. c. observed in the same way, with the Holy Fathers leading the way. But what he brings from St. Ambrose Sermon 22, comparing the blessed Virgin with the ark, does not receive a type of the ark, but only a bare comparison: such as is also that of Jerome to Eustochium on virginity. The spouse of Christ is the ark of the covenant, gilded inside and outside, the guardian of the law of the Lord. Just as in that there was nothing else except the tablets of the testament, so in you let there be no thought from without. Upon this mercy seat, as if upon the Cherubim, the Lord wishes to sit. Augustine, in Exod. q. 105, hands down another meaning or allegorical explanation, that the ark signifies the Secret of God; but that the mercy seat is placed upon the ark, in which the law was, he explains thus: that because we break the law and are in need of the mercy of God, which might blot out the crimes committed against the law, there is need of a mercy seat, so that God may be propitiated. Thus also Rivetus: since the law needed a covering by which our transgressions might be covered, that covering was placed upon the ark, which is aptly named the mercy seat, because God did not wish our offenses to be covered by any other reason than that propitiation which Christ alone provided, and alone could provide.

Latin:

vers. 9. JUXTA OMNEM SIMILITUDINEM TABERNACULI QUOD OSTENDAM TIBI.

Ideam ejus ostendit Dominus Mosi in monte: ad cujus instar accurate omnia efformanda erant, tum ut moneret, in cultu Dei unice præscriptum legis observandum, nec proprio arbitrio vel ἐϑελοθρησκείᾳ quicquam instituendum esse; tum ut doceret, exemplaria hæc esse, & umbras rerum cœlestium, quæ formabantur a Mose Ebr. 8, 5. quæ ἐπεράνια tum apud Deum in secreto majestatis recondita, olim in Christo manifestanda erant. Ideoque pii

Patres præeunte Scriptura N. T. & imprimis Epi- stola ad Ebræos hæc e typis & umbris illis eruere fa- tegerunt. Sic arcam Christum fignificasse docet Cyrillus in Joh. l. 4. c. 28. Gregor. homil. ult. in Ez. Rupert. & alii, quam perperam trahunt ad Mariam virginem designandam Pontificii: Beda c. 4. arcam de lignis Sittim factam dicit fignificare corpus Domini- cum ex membris constans, omni vitiorum labe carenti- bus; longitudinem arcæ longanimem redemtoris nostri patientiam; latitudinem,amplitudinem charitatis,qua ad nos venire,interǫ,nos habitare voluit; altitudinem spem futuræ sublimitatis. Arcam Testamenti Chri- stum esse ex Ap. 11, 19. manifestum est; ubi Corn. a Lap. agnoscit Christum esse exhibitum. Arca consta- bat lignis imputribilibus: ita caro Christi imputribilis est Pf. 16: illa auro intrinfecus obducta: caro Christi majestatis divinæ plenitudine splendet tota Col. 2, 9. Arca asservabat tabulas legis. Christus legem sem- per in corde habuit,sancteque custodivit Psal. 40,6. Juxta arcam manna, & virga Aaronis recondeban- tur,quibus verbum Evangelii & Sacerdotium Christi adumbratum. In arca erat propitiatorium : in Christo habemus propitiationem veram 1. Joh. 2, 2. Duo Cherubim suprà Arcam se respicientes mutuo, & arcam intuentes,duo Testamenta sunt, Vetus, & Novum,quæ ad Christum directa sunt, seq; mutuo respiciunt, & declarant. Quæ pleraq; Cornelius l. c. præeuntibus S. Patribus itidem observavit. Quod autem e S. Ambrof. Serm. 22. Virginem bea- tam comparante cum arca adducit,non typum arcæ, sed nudam tantùm comparationem resipit: qualis et- iam illa Hieronymi est ad Eustoch. de virg. Sponsa Christi est arcatestamenti, intrinfecus & extrinfecus deaurata, custos legis Domini. Sicut in illa nihil ali- ud fuit,nisi tabulæ testamenti,ita in te nullus sit extrin- secus cogitatus. Super hoc propitiatorium, quasi super Cherubim sedere vult Dominus. Aliam significatio- nem,vel allegoricam explicationem tradit Augustin. in Exod. q. 105. quod arca significet Dei Secretum; quod autem super arcam, in qua lex fuit, propitiatori- um locatur,ita explicat,quod quia legem frangimus,& misericordia Dei indigemus, quæ adversus legem com- missa crimina deleat,opus sit propitiatorio,ut Deus pro- pitietur. Sic etiam Rivetus: cum lex operimento in- digeret, quo transgressiones nostræ tegerentur,apposi- tum fuit arcæ tegumentum illud, quod propitiatorium apposite nominatur, quia non alia ratione tegi voluit Deus offensas nostras, nisi ea propitiatione, quam unus Christus præstitit, & solus præstare potuit.

## 25:16
vers. 16. AND YOU SHALL PUT INTO THE ARK THE TESTIMONY WHICH I SHALL GIVE YOU] The Decalogue. See above, 16, 34. The ark, however, took the place of all the images which the nations had.

Certainly God did not wish the ark to be fashioned for the sake of the images of the Gentiles, or of the nations themselves, but to prefigure the mysteries of the New Testament. Cf. Rom. 3, 25. Heb. 4, 16. c. 9, 4. 9. Rev. 12, 19. But it seems to conflict with these things which are held here concerning the fashioning of the ark, that in Deut. 10, 1, Moses is commanded to make an ark, into which, descending from the mountain, he replaced the tablets v. 3. Whence R. Solomon thinks there was a double ark, namely this Mosaic one, which was accustomed to go out with the Israelites into war: and another which Bezaleel made, because work on the tabernacle was finally labored upon after the day of atonements: And that this very one did not go out into war except in the time of Eli, when it was captured, and that in that Mosaic one were the fragments of the Tablets, the Agadah taught, in the book Tanchuma, R. Moses Bar Nachman observes. But R. Aben-Ezra explained the passage of Deut. 10, 1. 5, as did the just now praised Nachmanides concerning the Ark of Bezaleel. Make for yourself an ark, i.e., you shall take care to make that Moses, however, when he had descended from the mountain, he says here that he had deposited the tablets in the tent of meeting, until the ark and the tabernacle had been made. Others, however, such as Lyra, Pellican, Junius and Tremellius, Diodati, the Dutch, as well as Abarbanel, say that the ark of Moses was indeed a different one, made of mere wood (Deut. 10:1), but for that purpose only, that the tablets of the law might be kept in it until the ark of Bezalel was completed; but not for the continuous use of the Israelites. For they argue that only one ark of this kind was made, in which both the whole and the broken tablets were, which always went in the middle of the Israelite camp, and was not taken into battle except once in the time of Eli: which opinion Buxtorf proves with various arguments from Abarbanel, and refutes the contrary reasons of those who affirm that there was a double ark, one of Bezalel and one of Moses, and that the latter was accustomed to be led into battle by the Israelites, in Hist. arc. Foed. c. 3. There is no mention except of one ark (Ex. 25:10, ch. 35:10, 40:1). And the Kohathites, whose duty it was to carry the vessels of the sanctuary, carried only one (Num. 4:5, 6), nor is it read that more than one ark went before the Israelites (Num. 10:33), nor was it introduced into the holy of holies except once (1 Kings 8:1). Compare what is said at Num. 2:17. Those who observe that Paul is not speaking of the skēnē or tabernacle, in which both the manna was to be kept (Ex. 16:34) and Aaron's rod was deposited (Num. 17:4), correctly explain what is said in Heb. 9:4, that besides the tablets of the law, the manna and Aaron's rod also seem to be placed in the ark.

Latin:

vers. 16. PONESQVE IN ARCA TESTIFICATIO- NEM QVAM DABO TIBI] Decalogum. Vide supra, 16,34. Arca autem vicem præstitit omnium imaginum, quas habe- bant gentes.

Non certe in gratiam imaginum gentilium, aut ipsarum gentium Deus arcam fabricari voluit, sed ad figuranda mysteria Novi Testamenti. Conf. Rom.3,25. Ebr. 4,16. c. 9,4.9. Apoc. 12,19. Pugnare autem videtur cum his,quæ de arca fabricanda hic habentur, quod Deut. 10, 1. Moses facere jubetur arcam, in quam e monte descendens tabulas reposuit v. 3. unde R. Salomo geminam putat esse arcam, hanc sc. Mosaicam,quæ solita fuerit cum Israëlitis egredi in bellum : & alteram quam fecit Bezaleel, quia in opere tabernaculi demum laboratum fuerit post diem expiationum : Et hanc ipsam non egressam esse in bellum nisi tempore Eli, cum capta est, inque illa Mosaica fragmenta fuisse Tabularum, Agadam do- cuisse, in libro Tanchuma, R. Moses Bar Nachman observat. Sed locum Deut. 10,1.5. exposuit R. Aben- Ezra, ut & laudatus modo Nachmanides de Arca Bezaleelis. Fac tibi arcam, i. e. facere curabis: Mosen autem cum descendisset e monte, tabulas in tento- rio conventus reposuisse hic ait, donec facta esset arca & tabernaculum. Alii vero, utpote Lyræ, Pelicanus, Junius & Tremellius, Deodatus, Belgæ, ut & Abarbanel arcam Mosis quidem aliam fuisse ajunt e mero ligno factam Deut. 10, 1. sed eo tantum fine, ut tabulæ legis in ea asservarentur, donec arca Bezaleelis absoluta esset; non autem pro usu continuo Israelitarum. Hujusmodi enim arcam non nisi unam factam esse, in qua tam integræ quam fractæ tabulæ fuerint, quæ semper in medio castrorum Israeliticorum profe- cta, nec nisi Eli tempore semel in bellum ducta fue- rit: quam sententiam ex Abarbenele variis argu- mentis probat, contrariasque rationes eorum, qui geminam fuisse arcam, alteram Bezaleelis, alteram Mosis, & hanc in bellum ab Israelitis educi solitam affirmant, diluit Buxtorfius in Hist. arc. Fœd. c. 3. Non sit mentio nisi unius arcæ Ex. 25, 10. c. 35, 10. 40, 1. Et Kehatitæ, quorum officium fuit portare vasa sanctuarii, non nisi unam portarunt Num. 4, 5. 6. nec nisi una arca legitur profecta ante Israelitas Num. 10, 33. non nisi in sanctum sanctorum introducta 1. Reg. 8, 1. Conf. quæ dicta ad Num. 2, 17, Quod Ebr. 9, 4. Vi- dentur in arca præter tabulas legis etiam locari Manna, & virga Aaronis, recte explicant, qui non de σκηνῆ seu tabernaculo Paulum loqui observant, in quo & Manna asservandum erat Ex. 16, 34. & virga Aaronis reposita fuit Num. 17, 4.

## 25:17
verse 17. YOU SHALL ALSO MAKE A MERCY SEAT.

The LXX [translate it as] hilastērion, epithema, a mercy seat, a lid. Thomas, Cajetan, Delrio, and Castrius in Lamentations 2:1 think that the mercy seat was elevated and lifted up on high by the Cherubim above the ark, because it was the seat of God, so that the ark was his footstool. But others more correctly, with the LXX interpreters, epithema or a covering placed upon it, with Josephus (Ant. bk. 3, ch. 6), establish that it was a lid not protruding in any part, and as it is called in v. 20 a lid or covering, immediately touching and covering the ark, and that it was made of pure gold, because otherwise the ark would have been open and gaping; which is the opinion of Abulensis, Alcafar, Ribera, Cornelius, Rivetus, and Pelargus: and therefore Rivetus observes with Cornelius that the ark is called the footstool of God sitting on the mercy seat, insofar as the mercy seat enclosed the Cherubim, on whose wings God sat, Ps. 98. Furthermore, that the ark and the mercy seat were not in the second temple, but were carried away by the King of the Chaldeans along with the other instruments of the house of God, is evident from 2 Chron. 36:18 and 4 Esdras (which some Papists call canonical, ch. 10:22), which are said by Cyril of Jerusalem (Catech. Illuminat.) and in the Second Council of Nicaea (art. 5) to have been crushed and trampled by Nebuchadnezzar; because those types were gradually to be abolished, and oracles were to cease, and the ark of the Lord is no longer to be remembered (Jer. 3:16). Thus, the story that is commemorated in 2 Macc. 2:5 about the ark being taken away by Jeremiah at the time of the captivity and kept in a cave is a fable, as Galatinus (bk. 4, de arc. Cath. verit. c. 9) and Villalpandus (in Ez. tom. 2, P. 2, c. 70) acknowledge with the Jews themselves, that it was not in the second temple, even if he trifles here that it will appear again at the end of the world after the conversion of the Jews. The mercy seat, just like the ark, was a type of Christ, as the Apostle teaches (Rom. 3:25), Cyril (de incarn. unig. c. 3), Gregory the Great (in Ez. 6), Rupert, Bede, and others: and Barradius (T. II. Harmon. bk. 3, ch. 14) concurs that Christ was signified by both the ark and the mercy seat. That it was golden was to refer to the Deity of Christ; it covered the ark, in which the law was, because the law, dwelling before the eyes of God without a covering, subjects us to wrath and curse; therefore God interposed Christ as a covering between his seat and

the law, to show that he did not wish to take account of the accusing law: that lid was the mercy seat, because in Christ we have propitiation: there also was the Oracle (Num. 7, last verse), because Christ is the oracle of the Father. The Chaldean rendered it, 'I will appoint my word there for you,' which is to be understood of Christ, the exaggeltikos [proclaiming] Word of the eternal Father.

Latin:

vers. 17. FACIES ET PROPITIATORIUM.

LXX. ἱλαστήριον ἐπίθεμα propitiatorium opercu- lum. Thomas, Cajetan. Delrio, & Castrius in Thren. 2, 1. propitiatorium elevatum, & in altum a Cheru- binis sublatum fuisse supra arcam putant, quia fuerit sedes Dei, ita ut arca scabellum esset pedum ejus. Sed rectius alii cum LXX. Interpp. ἐπίθεμα vel su- perpositum, cum Josepho l. 3. Ant. c. 6. tegmen nulla ex parte prominens, & uti v. 20. operculum seu tegumen- tum vocatur, immediate arcam tangentem, & tegen- tem, tabulam fuisse ex puro auro factam statuunt, quia alioqui arca fuisset aperta & hiasset; quæ Abulensis, Alcafar. Ribera, Cornelii, Riveti, & Pelargi est senten- tia: ideoq; observat cum Cornel. Rivetus, arcam Scabellum dictum Dei in propitiatorio sedentis, qua- tenus propitiatorium inclusit Cherubinos, in quorum alis sedebat Deus, Ps. 98. Cæterum uti arcam & pro- pitiatorium in templo secundo non fuisse, sed a Re- ge Chaldæorum cum aliis instrumentis domus Dei ablata esse, e 2. Chron. 36, 18. & lib. 4. Esdr. Pontifi- ciis nonnullis Canonico c. 10, 22. constat, quæ a Ne- bucadnezare contrita & conculcata, Cyrill. Hieros. Catech. Illuminat. & in II. Synod. Nicæn. art. 5. di- cuntur; quia paulatim typi illi abolendi essent, & oracula cessare deberent, neque arca Domini com- memoranda amplius sit Jer. 3, 16. ita fabula est, quod 2. Macc. 2, 5. de arca tempore captivitatis a Jeremia subducta & in spelunca asservata commemoratur, uti agnoscunt cum Judæis ipsis Galatin. l. 4. de arc. Cath. verit. c. 9. Villalpandus in Ez. tom. 2. P. 2. c. 70. eandem in templo secundo non fuisse, etsi hic nuge- tur, etiam in fine mundi post Judæorum conversio- nem apparituram. Fuit autem propitiatorium, æque ut arca, typus Christi, docente Apostolo Rom. 3, 25. Cyrillo de incarn. unig. c. 3. Gregor. M. in Ez. 6. Ruperto, Beda, & aliis: & suffragatur Barradius, T. II. Harmon. l. 3. c. 14. quod Christus & arca & propitia- torio significatus fuerit. Quod aureum fuit, ad refe- rendam Christi Deitatem, arcam, in qua lex erat, te- gebat, quia lex sine operimento ante oculos Dei versans iræ & maledictioni nos subjicit, ideo Chri- stum ceu operimentum inter sedem suam, &

legem interposuit Deus, ut ostenderet, se legis accu- santis rationem habere non velle : operculum illud erat propitiatorium, quia in Christo habemus propi- tiationem : ibi etiam erat Oraculum Num. 7. ult. quia Christus est oraculum Patris. Chald. reddidit,statu- am ibi verbum meum tibi, quod de Christo intelligen- dum, ἐξαγγελτικῷ Patris æterni λόγῳ.

## 25:18
verse 18. YOU SHALL ALSO MAKE TWO GOLDEN CHERUBIM, AND THEY SHALL BE BEATEN WORK) Angels in the form of calves, presiding over sterility and fertility, and that in memory of Joseph. He who compares Ezek. 1:10 and 10:14 will see that what I say is true. For what is shor in that place is kerub in this place. See what [was said] above on Gen. 49:6. From this arose what we shall have below concerning the calf, and in the history of Jeroboam, which has its origin from Joseph. This is the principal form: but it seems that it had the face of a man, eagle's wings, and a lion's mane, which are the four panim, phaseis [faces] of Ezekiel, who calls that composite form sometimes chayot, as in 1:5, sometimes demut, as in 10:15. These four forms signify nothing else than what God explains below in 34:6, when he says that he appeared to Moses sitting on the Cherubim, namely, that he is swift to do good, but slow to vengeance. The man is a symbol of goodness: the eagle of swiftness: the lion of vengeance: the ox-feet of slowness; whence the Greek 'with an ox's foot'. Philo not badly says that the goodness and power of God are signified.

What was the point of displaying the memory of Joseph, and the sterile and fertile years, at the Ark of the Covenant, and in the very Cherubim? Where Scripture presents angels in the form of calves, and establishes them as presidents of sterility and fertility? Ez. 1, 10. It is uncertain whether the same figures were displayed here on the mercy seat, nor does that new opinion of Jerome Prado, which Grotius seems to have followed, that those four animals did not represent four different species, of which one had the head of an ox, another of a man, a third of a lion, and the fourth of an eagle, but rather four different parts of a composite form, so that the face was indeed that of a man, the wings were eagle-like, the manes were those of a lion, and the feet were those of an ox, prove itself to other Papists, especially Sanctius and Alcazar. Josephus maintains that the Cherubim on the mercy seat were new winged animals, never seen by any man, represented here, Ant. l. 3. Ant. c. 6. In much the same way, some Greeks also made the Cherubim placed before Paradise into bugbears and terrors and specters, with no appearance of truth, rendering the most noble place infamous with specters or monstrous birds. It is the common opinion that the angels placed before Paradise and those figured at the Ark of the Covenant are the same, whom Philo, Clement of Alexandria, Athanasius, Origen, Chrysostom, Augustine, Theodoret, and others have observed were called Cherubim from the multitude of wisdom or knowledge, although the etymology and the reason for the name are quite uncertain among the Hebrews. But as for the form in which the Cherubim on the mercy seat were figured, although there are not wanting those who assert a calf-like form, chiefly on the argument that Jeroboam therefore placed two calves in different parts of the kingdom in imitation of the Mosaic Cherubim; others, however, assign to them a quadruple face from Ezekiel, but most attribute a human face to them: who defend themselves by the prescription of years, the consent of the universal Church, and the dignity and sweetness of the human figure; since indeed they are commonly accustomed to be painted or sculpted in that way. This is also supported by the derivation from the Chaldean כרייא which denotes a boy with the prefix כ of likeness. Those seem to act more correctly who leave a matter not expressed in the Scriptures in the middle. We spoke about the Cherubim at Gen. 3, v. 22. Mr. Dr. Dorscheus compares the visions of the Cherubim among themselves in his septenary of singular angelic dissertations, dissert. 3. & having shown their analogy, he concludes thus not inelegantly: These Cherubim, whom Adam had first feared when seen at the garden of Paradise, soon had worshipped with pious observance as interpreters of the divine will, whom Moses had observed when seen in the most serene sight of the divine majesty (Exod. 24), whom Isaiah had heard and seen singing the Trisagion in a Seraphic and flaming form, whom Ezekiel had admired in the diverse appearance of winged animals, in the circle of fiery wheels, in the beauty of the sapphire throne, whom Daniel had noticed in great number trembling with all their souls before the most holy judge, whom John for eternal ages, had again perceived; whose images God had dedicated in the inner sanctuaries of the temple or tabernacle, most frequent by express word—these, I say, the Cherubim, diffused throughout the world, in the perpetual sight of divine happiness, joyfully guard our infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, the Republic, the Church, the family, individuals, the universe, virtue, studies, works, and all our counsels, and fortify them with the strongest protection against the adversaries of the Spirit. Thus far Dr. Dorscheus.

Latin:

verf. 18. DUOS QUOQUE CHERUBIM AUREOS, ET PRODUCTILES FACIES) Angelos μοσχομόρφες, sterilita- tis & fœcunditatis præsides, idque in Josephi memoriam. Vi- debit verum esse quod dico qui contulerit Ezech. 1, 10. & 10, 14. Nam quod illo loco est שׁור, hoc loco est כרוב. Vide quæ supra Gen. 49, 6. Hinc natum quod infra de vitulo habe- bimus, & in Jeroboami historia, cui origo a Josepho. Haec præcipua forma : sed videtur ei vultus fuisse hominis , alæ aquilinæ, leonis jubæ, quæ sunt quatuor פנים, φάσεις Ezechieli, qui compositam illam formam modo חיות, ut 1, 5. modo דמות vocat, ut 10, 15. Hæ quatuor formæ non a- liud significant, quam quod Deus Mosi visus insidere Cheru- binis voce explicat infra 34, 6. esse nimirum celerem se ad be- nefacta: tardum ad vindictam. Homo bonitatis symbolum: aquila celeritatis: leo vindictæ: pedes bovini tarditatis; unde Græcum βοείῳ ποδὶ. Philo non male fignificari ait Dei ἀγαθό- τητα καὶ ἐξουσίαν.

Quid memoriam Josephi, & annos steriles ac fœ- cundos attinebat, ad arcam fœderis, & in ipsis Che- rubim exhibere? Ubi Angelos in vitulorum forma sistit Scriptura, & Præsides sterilitatis & fœcunditatis constituit? Ez. 1, 10. easdem figuras, quas hic in pro- pitiatorio exhiberi, incertum, neque illa Hieronymi Pradi, quam secutus videtur Grotius, nova opinio, quod quatuor illa animalia non quatuor diversas species, quarum una caput bovis, altera hominis, ter- tia Leonis, quarta aquilæ haberet, sed quatuor diver- sas partes compositæ formæ exhibuerint, ut vultus qui- dem hominis, alæ vero aquilinæ, jubæ autem Leonis fuerint, & pedes bovis, aliis se probat Papistis, præci- pue Sanctio & Alcafari. Josephus vult, Cherubim in propitiatorio animalia volucria nova fuisse, a nullo unquam homine conspecta, hic repræsentata l. 3. Ant. c. 6. ita ferme etiam Græci nonnulli μορμολύ- κεια & terriculamenta, ac Spectra fecerunt Cheru- binos ante paradisum locatos, nulla veri specie, lo- cum nobilissimum Spectris infamem reddentes, aut monstrosis volucribus. Angelos ante Paradisum loca- tos, eosdemq́; ad arcam fœderis figuratos esse commu- nis est sententia, quos Cherubim a Sapientiæ vel Scien- tiæ multitudine dictos Philo, Clem. Alex. Athan. O- rig. Chrys. Aug. Theod. & alii observarunt, quan- quam etymologia, & ratio nominis admodum in- certa penes Hebræos sit. Formam autem quod attinet, qua figurati fuerint Cherubim in propitiatorio, etsi non desint, qui vitulinam, eo præcipue argumento, quod ideo Jerobeam etiam vitulos duos in diversis regni partibus ad imitationem Cherubinorum Mo- saicorum collocarit, adstruant; alii tamen quadru- plicem faciem ex Ezechiele ipsis assignant, plerique vero humanam tribuunt iisdem faciem: qui se an- norum præscriptione, universæ Ecclesiæ consensu, & dignitate, suavitateq; figuræ humanæ tuentur; fi- quidem communiter ita pingifculpive soleant. Qui- bus etiam patrocinatur derivatio a Chaldæo כרייא quod puerum notat cum præfixo כ similitudinis. Re- ctius videntur agere, qui rem in Scripturis non ex- pressam in medio relinquunt. Diximus de Che- rubim ad c. 3. Gen. v. 22. Visiones Cherubinorum confert Dn. D. Dorsheus inter sese in septenario sin- gular. Angelic. dissert. 3. & monstrata earum analo- gia non ineleganti sic concludit: Hi Cherubini, quos ad hortum Paradisi visos Adamus primum timuerat, mox tanquam interpretes voluntatis divinæ pia observantia coluerat, quos Moses in sere- nissimo divinæ majestatis conspectos (Exod. 24.) observaverat, quos Esaias Seraphico, flam- mantiq́; Schemate trisagium cantantes audiverat, vi- deratque, quos Ezechiel in animalium alatorum di- versa facie, in ignearum rotarum circulo, in throni Sap- phirini pulchritudine admiratus fuerat, quos Daniel magno numero coram sanctissimo judice totis mentibus horrentes animadverterat, quos Johannes in contem- platione perpetuæ gloriæ, & illo in æterna secula nictu iterum deprehenderat, quorum imagines in adytis tem- pli, aut tabernaculi frequentissimas verbo expresso Deus dedicaverat, hi, inquam, Cherubini per orbem diffusi, perpetuo divinæ felicitatis aspectu læti infantiam, pueritiam, adolescentiam, juventam, senectam, Remp. Ecclesiam, familiam, singulos, universos, virtutem, stu- dia, opera, consilia nostra omnia tuèntur, ac fortissimo præsidio contra adversarios Spiritus muniunt. Ha- ctenus Du. Dorscheus.

## 25:23
ver. 23. YOU SHALL MAKE A TABLE OF ACACIA WOOD] Such as the Delphic one was: whence also other similar tables received the name.

That table was not in the holy of holies, where the ark and the mercy seat were, but in the holy place or the court of the priests, into which the people did not enter: on which were placed the loaves of proposition, v. 30, in Hebrew called the loaves of the faces, whence Num. 4:7 it is called the table of the faces: concerning the preparation of which loaves Lev. 24:30, and since vessels were made for the use of this table Exod. 37:16, the same are here recounted at the same time: namely (1.) the dishes, in Hebrew קְעָרֹת, by which Villalpandus, book 4, on the temple, ch. 57, understands golden bowls, upon which the individual loaves were placed. Pagninus, Arias, Tremellius, and Junius translate them as platters, in which the bread was shaped, so that they might be equal among themselves. Vatablus notes that they were certain concave vessels in which the loaves were placed. (2.) The phials: כַּפּוֹת, Pagninus renders as spoons, Vatablus as censers, in which incense was placed, to be put upon the individual loaves, Lev. 24:7. (3.) The censers: in Hebrew קְשׂוֹת: Pagninus translates as middle reeds, Tremellius and Junius as platters, Vatablus as covers and bowls, with which the loaves were covered or enclosed, so that they might be kept pure, whence Num. 4:7 they are called the platters of the covering; and Tremellius notes that R. Jehudah explains it thus. (4.) The cups, מְנַקִּיּוֹת, Junius and Tremellius render as snuffers, that is, instruments for cleaning the table; the name properly signifies cleaning-tools: others are said to have been forks, with which the bread was cleaned, so that it might not become moldy: Cornelius reports that some understand them as vessels with which wine was poured out, but he falsely alleges Vatablus for that opinion, who understands them as bowls with which the loaves were covered: nor is it sufficiently certain that libations were made on the table of the loaves.

Moreover, this table signified, as Beda notes in ch. 6, the Holy Scripture composed of the strong words and acts of the Holy Fathers, which suggests to us the food of salvation and life: which has length, implying the perseverance of the religion we have begun; breadth, implying the amplitude of charity; height, implying the hope of perpetual reward. Nor does the type of the spiritual table displease Pelargus or Rivetus, on which the Gospel of Christ and his benefits are proposed to us, which refresh the soul, just as Christ confers the blessedness of celestial life upon the table, Luke 22:30, so that in the duodenary number of the loaves there is an allusion to the 12 tribes of Israel, and all believers, whom he feeds with his word. In the Old Testament, indeed, only the priests ate of the loaves of proposition, Lev. 24:9, except that necessity excused David, 1 Kings 21:6. Matt. 21:23. But in the New, no one is to be repelled, since we are all a chosen race, a royal priesthood, 1 Pet. 2:9.

Latin:

vers. 23. FACIES ET MENSAM DE LIGNIS SETIM] Qualis Delphica fuit : unde & aliæ similes mensæ nomen ac- cepere.

Mensa illa non in sancto sanctorum fuit, ubi ar- ca erat, & propitiatorium, sed in sancto sive atrio sa- cerdotum, in quod populus non ingrediebatur: in qua ponebantur panes propositionis v. 30. in Ebr. panes facierum dicti, unde Num. 4, 7. vocatur men- sa facierum : de quorum panum confectione Lev. 24, 30. & quum in usum hujus mensæ facta fuerint vasa Exod. 37, 16. eadem hic simul recensentur : utpote (1.) acetabula in Ebr. קְעָרֹת, per quæ Vi- lalpand. l. 4. de templ. c. 57. intelligit crateres aureos, quibus singuli panes imponebantur. Pagninus, Arias, Tremell. & Junius vertunt scutellas, in quibus efformati panis, ut æquales essent inter se. Vata- blus vasa quædam concava fuisse notat, in quibus impositi panes. (2.) Phialas : כַּפּוֹת Cochlearia Pa- gninus, thuribula reddit Vatablus, in quibus pone- batur thus, singulis panibus imponendum Lev. 24, 7. (3.) Thuribula : in Ebr. קְשׂוֹת : Pagninus vertit medios calamos, Tremell. & Junius scutellas, Vata- blus opercula, & crateres, quibus panes tegebantur, aut concludebantur, ut servarentur puri, unde Num. 4, 7. vocantur Scutellæ tegminis; atq; ita expo- nere R. Jehudam notat Tremell. (4.) Cyathos, מְנַקִּיּוֹת Jun. & Tremell. scopulas reddunt, id est, repurgan- dæ mensæ instrumenta; Nomen proprie significat emundatoria: alii furculas fuisse dicuntur, quibus pa- nis purgaretur, ne mucidus fiat : Cornelius refert nonnullos vasa, quibus vinum libabatur, intelligere, sed falso in eam sententiam Vatablum allegat, qui crateres intelligit, quibus panes tegebantur: neq; sa- tis constat, libamina in mensa panum facta.

Significabat autem hæc mensa notante Beda c. 6. Scripturam S. de fortibus S. Patrum verbis, actibus- que compactam, quæ nobis cibum salutis, ac vitæ sugge- rit : quæ babeat longitudinem, cum perseverantiam no- bis cœptæ religionis, latitudinem, cum amplitudinem charitatis, altitudinem, cum spem perpetuæ remunera- tionis insinuat. Nec displicet Pelargo, aut Riveto ty- pus de mensa spirituali, in qua Evangelium Christi, ejusque beneficia nobis proponuntur, quæ animum reficiunt, quemadmodum cœlestis vitæ beatitudinem Christus mensæ confert Luc. 22, 30. ut in duodenario panum numero allusio sit ad 12. tribus Israelis, & o- mnes credentes, quos verbo suo pascit. In V. qui- dem Test. propositionum panibus vescebantur soli Sacerdotes, Lev. 24, 9. nisi quod necessitas excusabat Davidem 1. Reg. 21, 6. Matth. 21, 23. in Novo vero ne- mo repellendus, cum omnes simus genus electum, regale Sacerdotium 1. Pet. 2, 9.

## 25:31
ver. 31. YOU SHALL MAKE) So also the Greeks, with אֶת understood before the name of the lampstand: Likewise the Chaldean, the Syrian, the LXX, Jerome in his books, and many Rabbis. Therefore the letter Jod, which is placed in the second position in this verb, is redundant. I think that arose from two readings, of which one had תַּעֲשֶׂה, as if God were speaking to Moses, the other יעשׂו, as if about a craftsman. Just as below v. 39 and ch. 26:31. For he who commands it to be done, and he who executes the commands, both make it. Hecataeus mentions the lampstand placed in the Jerusalem Temple in Josephus against Apion, book 1.

ver. same. YOU SHALL MAKE A LAMPSTAND OF BEATEN WORK.

The holy place had these three things: namely, the altar of incense and the table, which was placed at its northern or left side, and also the lampstand, which was placed at the southern or right side: by which they say three ways of living are designated: that which is placed in the contemplation of divine things, that which is in the action of sacred things, and that which is in the light and coruscation of good works. The lamps of this lampstand illuminated the holy place, but only at night, Ex. 27:21. Mystically, the lampstand is Christ according to Gregory the Great, illuminating all things; according to others, the Church, which brings light to the world, Apoc. 1, last; or the doctrine of the Church, as it pleases others. The seven lamps are the teachers, who shine forth throughout the night of the present age by their doctrine and life. The many branches shadow forth the various ranks of ministers. The ornaments on the branches, or the calyxes, figure spiritual things, whether ordinary or extraordinary. By the cups suitable for containing liquid, the capacity for containing doctrine could be shadowed forth: by the spheres, the roundness and perfection of both doctrine and life; by the flowers, the grace and alacrity of the ministers: the snuffers and extinguishers, their offices, who, even if they are established in the last place in the Church, are nevertheless not useless for preserving the purity of the divine light. Some say these are the disputations and explanations by which errors are removed and light is restored to the truth. This lampstand illuminated the table, the altar, and the whole holy place, because the faith and doctrine of the Church ought to illuminate and direct the works of mercy, prayers, and all the sacred things of the faithful in this life, etc.

Latin:

vers. 31. FACIES) Sic & Græci, subaudito אֶת ante nomen candelabri : Item Chaldæus, Syrus, LXX. Hieronymus in libris & Rabbini multi. Ergo litera Jod, quæ in hoc verbo secundo loco ponitur, abundat. Puto id natum ex duabus lectionibus, quarum altera habebat תַּעֲשֶׂה, velut ad Mosem loquente Deo, alia יעשׂו, velut de fabro. Quo- modo infra v. 39. & c. 26, 31. Nam facit & qui jubet fieri, & qui jussa exequitur. Candelabri in Templo Hierosolymitano po- siti meminit Hecatæus apud Josephum contra Appionem I.

vers. eod. FACIES ET CANDELABRUM DUCTILE.

Sanctum hæc tria habebat : sc. altare thymiamatis & mensam, quæ illi erat ad latus septentrionale vel sinistrum collocata, nec non candelabrum, quod po- situm erat ad latus meridionale, seu dextrum : qui- bus tres vivendi rationes dicunt designatas, eam quæ in contemplatione divinorum, eam quæ in actio- ne sacrorum, & eam, quæ in luce, ac coruscatione bono- rum operum posita est. Lucernæ hujus candelabri sanctum illuminabant, sed noctu tantum Ex. 27, 21. Mystice candelabrum est Christus secundum Gregor. M. omnia illuminans, secundum alios Ecclesia, quæ lucem præfert mundo, Apoc. 1, ult. vel doctrina Ec- clesiæ, ut aliis placet. Septem lucernæ sunt doctores, qui tota nocte præsentis seculi doctrina & vita præ- lucent. Rami plures varios ministrorum gradus adumbrant. Ornamenta in ramis, seu calamidona figurant spiritualia, seu ordinaria, seu extraordina- ria. Scyphis ad continendum liquorem aptis capaci- tas adumbrari potuit doctrinam continendi : Sphæ- rulis rotunditas & perfectio tam doctrinæ, quam vi- tæ; floribus Ministrantium gratia & alacritas : emun- ctoria & extinctoria eorum officia, qui etsi in Ecclesia sint postremo loco constituti, ad servandam tamen divinæ lucis puritatem non sunt inutiles. Nonnulli dicunt ea esse disputationes, & explicationes, qui- bus errores auferuntur, & sua veritati lux redditur. Candelabrum hoc illuminabat mensam, altare, to- tumque Sanctum, quia fides & doctrina Ecclesiæ il- luminare & dirigere debet opera misericordiæ, ora- tiones, omniaque fidelium sacra in hac vita &c.

## 25:39
v. 39. A TALENT OF GOLD.

The weight of the lampstand with its instruments was a talent of gold. Which contained 3000 shekels, Ex. 38:25. A shekel, however, contained four drachmas, that is, four Hungarian gold pieces, Ex. 30:13, and therefore a talent was worth 12,000 Hungarian gold pieces, or one hundred and twenty pounds of gold.

Latin:

v. 39. TALENTUM AURI.

Pondus candelabri cum suis instrumentis talen- tum erat auri. Quod continebat 3000. siclorum Ex. 38, 25. Siclus autem quatuor drachmas contine- bat, h. e. quatuor aureos ungaricos, Ex. 30, 13. ideoq; talentum valebat 12000. aureis ungaricis, vel cen- tum viginti auri libris.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI. The form of the tabernacle.

v. 1. MOREOVER, THOU SHALT MAKE THE TABERNACLE

The tabernacle was, according to Josephus, a kind of mobile and portable temple, walking with the Hebrews through the desert; after the form of which the temple of Solomon was subsequently constructed. And it was made of boards of Shittim wood gilded (each of which had two silver bases), so that the entrance lay toward the East: and it was covered both above and on the sides with veils; first with ten curtains, which were spread out in the manner of a tent. Secondly with 2. coverings, or haircloth rugs, thirdly with skins of rams dyed red, fourthly with violet skins against rains and storms, which are therefore called the roof in v. 14, into which light was admitted through the front door, because it had no window. Before the tabernacle was the court, both the outer one of the people and the inner one of the priests, in which was the bronze laver and the altar of burnt offerings. In the tabernacle itself, however, and in its front part, was the altar of incense, and to the right side of the same the golden candlestick, to the left the table of showbread: but in its inner part, namely the holy of holies, was the ark having within itself the tables of the law, and above itself the mercy seat, which two Cherubim veiled.

Now this tabernacle signified the Church, both militant on earth and triumphant in heaven, whose accurate μηχανὴ denotes the perpetual care of God building the Church, the construction according to the pattern shown by God, which is inculcated three times, warned that all things in the Church are to be arranged according to the prescriptions of the heavenly architect, not according to the inventions or discoveries of men. The standing boards inserted into silver bases are the true members of the Church, which are like columns in the temple of God, Rev. 3:12, leaning upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Eph. 2:20. To this pertains what Arias noted in his book on Noah, that the boards represented the human stature clothed in a long garment, the hinges the legs or the bones of the legs, the bases the feet of the human body, so that the very appearance might immediately suggest certain σκιάσματα (shadows) of living columns. That whole structure, suitably erected and joined together through joints and seams, represented the mystical body of Christ, Eph. 4:11. But the fact that its parts could easily be joined and separated signified that the faithful in the tabernacle of the body (which must both be laid aside and erected) are away from the Lord while on pilgrimage, until they arrive at the stable kingdom in heaven, 2 Cor. 5:4, 2 Pet. 1:13. The bars are the teachers, whom God gave for the joining together of the saints, Eph. 4:2. The curtain by which the structure was adorned on the inner side and covered above, made of twisted fine linen with the figures of Cherubim, had the same signification of the Church, insofar as it is crowded with a multitude of angels, Heb. 1:14. The triple covering protecting the tabernacle and the linen curtain signified the wonderful protection of the Church against all kinds of storms, which is safer under the guardianship of the Lamb than the tabernacle was under the covering of skins. The splendor of the curtains, which, according to Josephus, was so great from the threads of fine linen, hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and twice-dyed colors, and the most elegant figures of the Cherubim, that they shone no differently than heaven itself, foreshadowed the splendor of the Church, which it scatters through doctrine and heavenly gifts. The parts of the tabernacle, distinguished by the interposition of a veil, were not two contiguous dwellings, but one continuous work, so that we might understand that the Church of the Jews and Gentiles is fitted into one spiritual building; yet a certain veil was interposed, which the condition of that time demanded, so that that old Church might be distinguished from the Gentiles by legal ceremonies as if by some interposed wall, which having been dissipated by the coming of Christ, the veil was torn, Luke 23:45, and the partition destroyed, Eph. 2:14. The High Priest entered the Holy of Holies once every year with the blood of victims to denote Christ's entry into heaven through His own blood, Heb. 9:7. The distinction which was made by the veil was an image of the distinction between the Church militant and triumphant: the former is holy at least by imputation and inchoation; the latter is holy by perfection and supreme integrity in heaven. And because heaven is foreshadowed by the Holy of Holies, in which is the ark and the true mercy seat, Christ, Rev. 11:19, to which access was not open except to the high priest; it was taught that the way is not opened except through our high priest through the veil of His flesh and by the sacrifice of His own body, Heb. 9:11, ch. 10:19, 20. That veil also, which distinguished the sanctuary from the holy place, signified that those who are still outside the veil, that is, not yet received into heaven, behold God and the future goods which are in the Holy of Holies, that is, in heaven, only through faith and enigmatic knowledge, 2 Cor. 5. The other veil at the door of the tabernacle warned that the people ought not to inquire too curiously into the mysteries of God, nor to meddle with or intrude upon the mysteries of the sacred rites which were committed peculiarly to the priests and Levites. The outer court of the people represented the rudiments of those beginning, in which also was the altar of burnt offerings, which noted the mortification of the flesh, and the bronze laver, which noted the sacrament of Baptism instituted by Christ for the washing away of sins. The inner court of the Priests, to which those made spiritual priests through Christ and washed by His blood are admitted, Rev. 1:5, so that they may offer spiritual incense, Rev. 5:8, 10, enjoy the table of the Lord, Matt. 8:11, Luke 1:417, and be more and more illuminated by the light of doctrine and heavenly wisdom, until that heavenly morning star, Christ Jesus, rises upon them with full radiance and illuminates them with the light of glory, 2 Pet. 1:19, Rev. 22:5, 16, ch. 21:23, when indeed they are admitted into the Holy of Holies: in which are the Cherubim, that is, the holy angels, and the mercy seat, and the ark of the covenant, Christ fully manifests Himself. Compare Bede, book on the Tabernacle; Rabanus on this passage; as also Isidore in Ex. 28 and 49; Gregory the Great, book 28 of Morals, ch. 9; Rupert, book 4, ch. 12.

verse same. VARIATAS OPERE PLUMARIO FACIES (YOU SHALL MAKE THEM WITH EMBROIDERED WORK)] The Greeks more simply εργασία ὑφάντε, that is, just as garments are made from silk, as Aben Ezra speaks on this passage.

The Vulgate omits the word Cherubim, which is in the Hebrew, and is not neglected by the Chaldean, the LXX, or Pagninus: because those curtains were required to be filled with figures of Cherubim.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI. Forma tabernaculi.

v. 1. TABERNACULUM VERO ITA FACIES.

Tabernaculum erat quasi templum mobile Jose- pho autore ac portatile, ambulans cum Ebræis per desertum ; ad cujus formam postmodum templum Salomonis constructum est. Eratq; illud factum ex tabulis lignorum Setim inauratis, (quæ singulæ binas habebant bases argenteas) ita ut ad Orientem pate- ret aditus : ac tam superne tegebatur, quam ad late- ra quatuor velis; primo decem cortinis, quæ in mo- dum tentorii expansæ erant. Secundo 2. sagis, sive stragulis cilicinis, tertio pellibus arietum rubricatis, quarto pellibus janthinis contra pluvias, & procellas, quæ tectum ideo vocantur v. 14. in quod lumen an- terius per ostium admissum, quia fenestram non ha- bebat. Ante tabernaculum erat atrium tum exterius populi, tum interius sacerdotum, in quo labrum æne- um & altare holocaustorum erat. In tabernaculo vero ipso ejusq; parte priori erat altare thymiamatis & ad latus dextrum ejusdem Candelabrum aureum, ad sini- strum mensa panum propositionis : in interiori vero e- jus parte sancto nempe sanctorum erat arca habens intra se tabulas legis supra se propitiatorium, quod ve- labant duo Cherubim.

Significabat autem hoc tabernaculum Ec- clesiam, tum militantem in terris tum triumphan- tem in cœlis, cujus accurata μηχανὴ perpetuam Dei curam ædificantis Ecclesiam notat, extructio ad exemplar, a Deo ostensum, quæ trina vice incul- catur, omnia ad cælestis architecti præscripta, non ad hominum commenta, vel inventa in Ecclesia esse disponenda monebat. Asseres stantes basibus ar- genteis immissi veræ sunt Ecclesiæ membra, quæ ve- lut columnæ in templo Dei sunt, Apoc. 3, 12. innixa basi Apostolorum & Prophetarum Eph. 2, 20. Quo facit, quod Arias in libr. de Noah notarit, quod af- seres humanam repræsentarint staturam longa veste in- dutam, cardines crura sive crurum ossa, bases humani corporis pedes, ut ipse aspectus statim viventium colu- mnarum exhiberi quædam σκιάσματα, innueret. Totum illud tabulatum congruenter erectum & coagmentatum per compages, & commissuras com- pactum figurabat corpus Christi mysticum Eph. 4, 11. Quod autem partes ejus facile conjungi possent, & disjungi, significabat fideles in corporis tabernacu- lo, (quod & deponendum & erigendum est) pere- gre abesse a Domino, donec ad regnum stabile per- veniat in cœlis 2. Cor. 5, 4. 2. Petr. 1, 13. Vectes sunt doctores, quos dedit Deus ad coagmentationem sanctorum Eph. 4, 2. Tentorium quo tabulatum ab interiori parte ornabatur, & superius operiebatur, ex bysso retorta cum Cherubinorum figuris ean- dem habebat Ecclesiæ significationem, quatenus il- la stipatur angelorum multitudine Ebr: 1, 14. Tegu- mentum triplex operiens tabernaculum & aulæum byssinum, significabat mirabilem Ecclesiæ prote- ctionem contra omnis generis tempestates, quæ ma- gis tuta est sub tutela agni, quam tabernaculum erat sub tegumento vellerum. Aulæorum splendor, qui ex filis byssinis, hyacinthinis, purpureis, coccineis, dibaphis, figurisque elegantissimis Cherubinorum tantus erat, Josepho teste, ut non aliter, quam cælum ipsum fulserint splendorem Ecclesiæ, quem per do- ctrinam & charismata cœlestia spargit, adumbrabat. Tabernaculi partes per veli interpositionem distin- ctæ non erant duo contigua domicilia, sed unum continuum opus, ut intelligeremus Ecclesiam Ju- dæorum & gentium in unum spirituale ædificium a- ptari, velum tamen quoddam interpositum erat, quod illius temporis ratio postulabat, ut vetus illa Ecclesia legalibus ceremoniis quasi maceria aliqua interposita a gentibus distingueretur, quibus dissi- patis per adventum Christi velum scissum Luc. 23, 45. & interstitium dirutum est Eph. 2, 14. Sanctum Sanctorum quotannis semel cum victimarum san- guine ingrediebatur Pontifex ad denotandum Chri- sti ingressum in cœlum, per sanguinem proprium Ebr. 9, 7. Distinctio quæ per velum fiebat, imago erat di- stinctionis Ecclesiæ militantis & triumphantis: illa imputatione & inchoatione saltem sancta est; hæc perfectione & integritate summa in cœlis. Et quia per sanctum sanctorum cœlum adumbratum, in quo est arca, & propitiatorium verum Christus Ap. 11, 19. ad quod non patebat aditus nisi summo sacerdoti; viam non nisi per pontificem nostrum per velum carnis ejus & vi sacrificii corporis ipsius, patefieri, docebatur, Ebr. 9, 11. c. 10, 19. 20. Significabat etiam velũ illud, quod sanctuarium a sancto distinguebat, eos, qui adhuc sunt extra velum, id est, nondum sunt in cœlum recepti, per fidem tantum, & ænigma- ticam cognitionem speculari Deum, & futura bo- na, quæ sunt in sancto sanctorum, id est, in cælo 2. Cor. 5. Velum alterum ad ostium tabernaculi monebat, populum in mysteria Dei curiosius inquirere non debere, nec mysteriis sacrorum, quæ sacerdotibus & Levitis peculiäriter commissa erant, sese immi- scere, aut ingerere. Atrium populi exterius incipi- entium rudimenta referebat, in quo & altare holo- caustorum erat, quod carnis mortificationem, & la- brum æneum, quod sacramentum Baptismi ad ablu- tionem peccatorum a Christo institutum notabat. Atrium Sacerdotum interius, ad quod facti per Chri- stum Sacerdotes spirituales sanguine ejus abluti ad- mittuntur Ap. 1, 5. ut offerant thymiamata spiritua- lia Ap. 5, 8. 10. fruantur mensa Domini, Matth. 8, 11. Luc. 1. 417. & magis, magisq; illuminentur doctrina & sapientiae coelestis luce, donec phosphorus ille coelestis Christus Jesus plena jubare ipsis exoriatur, & luce gloriae eosdem collustret 2. Pet. 1, 19. Ap. 22, 5. 16. c. 21, 23. cum nempe in sanctum sanctorum admit- tentur: in quo Cherubini sunt, id est, angeli sancti, & propitiatorium, atq; arca foederis, Christus sese plene manifestat. Conf. Beda libr. de tabernac. Raban. in h. l. ut & Isidor. in Ex. 28. & 49. Gregor. M. l. 28. Mor. c. 9. Rupertus l. 4. c. 12.

vers. eod. VARIATAS OPERE PLUMARIO FACIES] Graeci simplicius εργασία ὑφάντε, id est, sicut vestes e serico fiunt, ut Abenesdra loquitur ad h. l.

Vulgata omittit vocem Cherubim, quae in E- braeo habetur, & a Chald. LXX. Pagnino neglecta non est: quia aulaea illa figuris Cherubim referta es- se debebant.

## 26:5
verse 5. ITA INSERTAS UT ANSA CONTRA ANSA VENIAT, ET ALTERA ALTERI POSSIT APTARI (SO INSERTED THAT LOOP COMES AGAINST LOOP, AND ONE MAY BE FITTED TO THE OTHER)] He explains how those five curtains were to be connected when they stopped from their journey. The Greeks: ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς μέρους εἰς τὴν συμβολήν. In the old Samaritan it was, as the Greeks report: διαδεχόμεναι συμβολαὶ μία πρὸς μίαν ἀντιπροσώπως κατὰ τὸ προσέχον ἀλλήλαις, clearly enough.

Latin:

vers. 5. ITA INSERTAS UT ANSA CONTRA AN- SAM VENIAT, ET ALTERA ALTERI POSSIT APTA- RI) Exponit quomodo cortinae illae quinae ubi ab itinere ces- sabatur, connecti debuerint. Graeci: ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς μέρους εἰς τὴν συμβολήν. In Samaritano veteri fuit, ut Graeci referunt: δια- δεχόμεναι συμβολαὶ μία πρὸς μίαν ἀντιπροσώπως κατὰ τὸ προσ- έχον ἀλλήλαις, satis perspicue.

## 26:17
verse 17. DUAE INCASTRATURAE FIENT (TWO TENONS SHALL BE MADE)] That is, hinges, as the Chaldean and Syrian here. The LXX said ἀγκωνίσκους, as ἀγκῶνας 2 Chron. 9:18. But Symmachus says κατοχᾶς (fastenings).

Latin:

vers. 17. DUAE INCASTRATURAE FIENT) Id est, car- dines, ut hic Chaldaeus & Syrus. LXX. dixere ἀγκωνίσκους, ut ἀγκῶνας 2. Par. 9, 18. At Symmachus κατοχᾶς.

## 26:33
verse 33. QUO ET SANCTUARIUM ET SANCTUARII SANCTVARIA DIVIDENTUR (BY WHICH BOTH THE SANCTUARY AND THE HOLY OF HOLIES SHALL BE DIVIDED)] In Greek ἀναμέσον τοῦ ἁγίε κὴ ἀναμέσον τοῦ ἁγίε τῶν ἁγίων. Compare Heb. 9:23 and what was said on that place of Matthew which we just cited.

Latin:

vers. 33. QUO ET SANCTUARIUM ET SANCTUARII SANCTVARIA DIVIDENTUR) Graece ἀναμέσον τοῦ ἁγίε κὴ ἀναμέσον τοῦ ἁγίε τῶν ἁγίων. Confer Hebr. 9, 23. & quae di- cta ad eum quem modo citavimus Matthaei locum.

## 26:36
ver. 36. YOU SHALL MAKE A SCREEN. The Vulgate has not rendered it sufficiently well; for מסך is rather a veil or a curtain. Josephus says that it descended only to half the height of the columns, so as to provide an entrance for the priests and to admit the light of the sun: because there were no windows in the tabernacle, since it was covered on all sides.

Latin:

vers. 36. FACIES ET TFNTORIUM. Vulgata non satis commode reddidit; Nam מסך velum potius vel aulaeum est. Quod ad dimidi- am tantum columnarum partem descendisse ait Jo- sephus, ut ingressum praeberet Sacerdotibus, lumen- que Solis immitteret : quia in tabernaculo nullae erant fenestrae, siquidem id undique tectum fuerit.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII.

The altar of burnt offerings, and the court.

ver. 1. YOU SHALL MAKE AN ALTAR OF ACACIA WOOD) We produced the passage of Hecataeus concerning this altar of burnt offerings above 20, 25.

This altar was for burnt offerings, not to be placed in the tabernacle, but before it in the court under the open sky, on account of the fire and the odor of the victims: but the altar of incense was in the holy place, to burn incense upon it morning and evening to God. It was to be constructed of acacia wood, but which was to be covered with bronze plates inside and out, so that it would not be damaged by the fire. This altar foreshadowed Christ, whose human nature is compared to incorruptible acacia wood, just as Christ calls himself a green tree in Luke 23:31, and was not to see corruption, Ps. 16:10. The Papists foolishly imagine here a type of a wooden cross, which they trifle is free from corruption.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII.

Altare holocaustorum, & atrium.

vers. 1. FACIES ET ALTARE DE LIGNIS SETIM) Locum Hecataei de hoc altari holocaustorum supra produxi- mus 20, 25.

ALtare hoc erat holocaustorum, non in taberna- culo, sed ante illud in atrio collocandum sub dio, propter ignem & nidorem victimarum: thy- miamatis vero altare in sancto erat, ad adolendum in eo mane & vesperi thymiama Deo. De lignis Se- tim illud construendum, sed quae aeneis tabulis inte- rius & exterius obducenda, ne igne laederentur. Quod altare Christum adumbrabat, cujus humana natura lignis Setim imputribilibus comparatur, uti Christus lignum viride se vocat Luc. 23. 31. ac corru- ptionem videre non debuit Ps. 16, 10. Inepte Pa- pistae hic typum crucis lignea fingunt, quam corru- ptionis expertem esse nugantur.

## 27:2
V. 2. AND THE HORNS SHALL BE UPON THE FOUR CORNERS FROM ITSELF.

Horns or small columns shall go up from the four corners, as Osiander holds; the word קרן in general is something pointed upwards, whence it is also taken for rays. Some gather from Josephus that there were no horns, such as bulls have, but that the corners of the altar are taken for horns. Since it is otherwise difficult, in the judgment of Rivetus, to perceive how Jo- by and others could have grasped the horns of the altar, especially that one which was ten cubits high. But that is not difficult for us: because they could ascend the altar by stairs, in order to grasp the horns: and therefore we do not think there is a reason why we should depart from the more usual meaning of the word and the common opinion concerning the horns. They certainly could not be bound to the corners of the lambs Ps. 118, 27.

Latin:

V. 2. CORNUA AUTEM PER QUATUOR ANGULOS EX IPSO ERUNT.
