Cornua aut columnulae egredientur sursum ex quatuor angulis, ut habet Osiander; vox קרן in ge- nere est, aliquid acuminatum in altum, unde etiam pro radiis accipitur. Non fuisse cornua, qualia tauri sunt, sed angulos altaris pro cornibus accipi nonnulli e Josepho colligunt. Siquidem diffici- le alias, Riveto judice, sit percipere quomodo Jo- ab & alii potuerint apprehendere cornua altaris, il- lius præfertim, quod decem cubitos altum esset. Sed id difficile nobis non est: quia per scalas altare a- scendere poterant, ut cornua apprehenderent: id- eoque non arbitramur causam esse, cur ab usitatiori vocis significatione & communi sententia de corni- bus discedamus. Ligari certe ad angulos non po- tuere agni Ps. 118, 27.

## 27:3
ver. 3. AND YOU SHALL MAKE FOR ITS USES POTS TO RECEIVE THE ASHES, AND TONGS AND FLESH-HOOKS AND FIRE-PANS.

These things in Hebrew are thus, according to the interpreter Pagninus and Montanus: And you shall make its pots (lebetes) for removing the ashes (removing its ashes. Osiander with the Vulgate renders and explains, for receiving into those pots the ashes which remained from the burnt wood and sacrifices) and its shovels (Osiander, shovels) and its sprinkling vessels (Montanus, bowls; Osiander renders its basins, which the Vulgate rashly omitted) and its tridents (in the Vulgate they are rendered flesh-hooks) and its fire-pans. Cornelius, however, excuses the Vulgate in vain, because not all the vessels are enumerated in the Hebrew, and therefore Jerome did not bind himself to the Hebrew enumeration of the vessels, but indifferently expressed some, with the clause added, and the other vessels: but he omitted the phials: because he named them in their proper place, ch. 25, 29. But what things are omitted here in the Hebrew, Cornelius does not indicate; nor is that added clause found in the Latin: and it is the duty of a good interpreter to render the original text faithfully. The pots are designated not so much for receiving as for taking up and carrying away the ashes. The shovels for sweeping the ashes into a heap. The Vulgate wrongly substituted tongs. For יעים are shovels. Bowls or basins were used for receiving the blood of the victims, as R. Solomon observes. The LXX have Φιάλας αὐτõ. Cajetan, wash-basins. But those were distinct

Phials, ch. 25, 29, which were stored on the table of showbread (not on the altar of burnt offerings), which Cornelius rashly and inconveniently asserts were transferred from there when there was need for them for libations on the altar of burnt offerings: for those were used for incense, but these were used for receiving blood. Furthermore, the tridents were used for extracting meat from the cauldrons and pots, 1 Sam. 2. Whence the LXX called them κρεάγρας, the Vulgate, flesh-hooks. Lyranus says the flesh-hooks were used for extracting meat from the cauldron, and for placing upon the altar those things which were burned there. Finally, the fire-pans were vessels or instruments for taking up coals. The LXX rendered them πυρεῖα. Lyranus holds that they were vessels in which live coals were taken from the altar of burnt offerings, to be carried inside the tabernacle to burn incense. Tremellius and Junius render them its tongs, which are for use in taking fire from the hearth. For to the Hebrews מחתת from חתה is to take, for example, fire from a hearth or pyre.

Latin:

vers. 3. FACIESQUE IN EJUS USUS LEBE- TES AD SUSCIPIENDOS CINERES, ET FOR- CIPES ATQUE FUSCINULAS ET IGNIUM RECEPTACULA.

Hæc in Ebræo ita habent, interprete Pagnino & Montano: Et facies ollas ejus (lebetes) ad excine- randum illud (removendum cinerem ejus. Osian- der cum Vulgata reddit & exponit, ad suscipiendas in eas ollas cineres, qui de lignis, sacrificiis combustis remanebant) & scopas ejus (Osiander palas,) & aspersoria (Montanus crateres, Osiander reddit pel- ves ejus, quæ temere omisit vulgata) & tridentes e- jus (in vulgata redduntur fuscinulæ) & receptacula ejus. Nequicquam autem excusat Vulgatam Cor- pelius, quod in Ebræo non omnia vasa recensean- tur, ideoque Hieronymus se non astrinxerit Ebrææ vasorum enumerationi, sed indifferenter aliqua ex- presserit addita clausula, & cætera vasa: Phialas autem omiserit: quia nominavit eas in propria sede cap. 25, 29. Verum quæ hic omissa in Ebræo sint, non indicat Cornelius; neque clausula illa addita reperitur in Latino: & Interpretis boni est fideliter textum originalem reddere. Ollæ non tam ad sus- cipiendos, quam ad tollendos & auferendos cineres designantur. Scopæ ad cineres in cumulum ver- rendos. Vulgata perperam forcipes substituit. יעים enim sunt scopæ, Crateres vel pelves ad exci- piendum victimarum sanguinem adhibebantur, ob- servante R. Salomone. LXX. habent Φιάλας αὐτõ. Cajetanus malluvias. Distinctæ autem erant illæ

Phialæ c. 25, 29. quæ in mensa panum propositionis (non in altari holocaustorum) reponebantur, quas inde transsumtas fuisse, quando iis opus erat ad liban- dum in altari holocaustorum, temere & inconvenien- ter asserit Cornelius: illæ enim ad thura, hæ vero ad sanguinem excipiendum adhibitæ sunt. Porro tridentes ad carnes ex ahenis, & ossis extrahendas adhibebantur 1. Sam. 2. Unde κρεάγρας dixere LXX. fuscinulas Vulgata. Lyran. fuscinulas dicit usurpatas ad extrahendum carnes de caldario, & ad ponendum super altare ea, quæ ibi cremabantur. Denique receptacula ignium vasa vel instrumenta erant ad capiendas prunas. LXX. πυρεῖα reddi- dere. Lyranus vult fuisse vasa, in quibus de altari holocausti accepti carbones vivi, ut deferrentur in- tra tabernaculum, ad cremandum thymiama. Tre- mell. & Junius reddunt forcipes ejus, qui ad ignem de foco capiendum usui sunt. Nam Ebræis מחתת a חתה capio est, ignem puta de foco vel pyra.

## 27:4
Ver. 4. YOU SHALL MAKE ALL THE VESSELS OF BRASS) So also the Greeks. The particle כל therefore is redundant here, either in the Scripture or in the sense, as also below v. 19.

ver. same. AND A GRATE IN THE MANNER OF A BRASS NET.

The altar had something above the middle surrounding the frame; below this surrounding part, a certain grate, made like a net of brass, surrounded the altar: the upper part retained the name of the altar, the lower was called the grate in the middle height of the altar, and it was as it were a hearth, upon which fire and wood and victims were placed, so that the ashes might fall down through the holes of that net.

Latin:

Vers. 4. OMNIA VASA EX ÆRE FABRICABIS) Sic & Græci. Abundat ergo hic particula כל aut in Scriptura, aut in sensu, ut & infra v. 19.

vers. eod. CRATICULAMQUE IN MODUM RETIS ÆNEAM.

Altare supra medietatem habebat quiddam ambiens aram, infra hunc ambitum craticula qua- dam quasi rete ex ære facta circundabat aram: supe- rior pars nomen altaris retinebat, inferior craticula vocabatur in media altaris altitudine, eratq; quasi focus, super quo ignis & ligna & victimæ impone- rentur, ut per retis illius foramina cineres decide- rent.

## 27:8
Ver. 8. YOU SHALL NOT MAKE IT SOLID BUT EMPTY AND HOLLOW INSIDE.

Because this altar was hollow, some say it was filled with earth or stones: others think that within its sides certain walls were to be built of clayey earth, or bricks or stones, so that it might be like an earthen or stone altar. Namely, they think it was like a certain small square furnace divided in two by a brass net, the upper part of which would hold fire, wood, and victims within its capacity, while the lower part, empty down to the ground, would receive the embers and falling ashes, concerning which we spoke at Exod. 20, 24; it is left as an inconvenience that the old walls would always be torn down and new ones built everywhere, whenever the altar had to be carried from place to place. And therefore the opinion of others seems preferable, that that bronze net was so arranged that it received the fire and ashes while the walls of the altar remained untouched, so that it did not touch them immediately, but remained as it were suspended, by which means there would be no danger from the fire to the beams or wooden planks: which, even if they were encased in bronze, it was nevertheless necessary to take precautions lest the bronze should become inflamed, or melt, and the beams thus be set on fire. It can also be said that a small altar, or bronze hearth, hung within the grate itself, suspended in the middle of the altar by chains tied to its four horns, to which hearth wood and fire were applied, so that it would not damage the altar. Finally, it seems to some that it also had a window on the eastern side, through which the ashes were to be extracted, and the wood placed upon the small altar or hearth.

Latin:

Vers. 8. NON SOLIDVM SED INANE ET CAVVM INTRINSECUS FACIES ILLUD.

Quia cavum altare hoc fuit, nonnulli terra vel lapidibus repletum dicunt: alii intra latera ejusdem parietes quosdam ex terra argillosa, vel lateribus aut lapidibus extruendos putant, ut esset velut altare terreum aut lapideum. Scilicet fuisse id putant instar exiguæ cujusdam fornacis quadratæ bipartito per æneum rete divisæ, cujus pars superior ignem intra suam capacitatem, ligna victimasque, inferior autem usque ad solum vacua favillas exciperet, cineresque defluentes, de quo ad Exod. 20, 24. diximus, incommodum id relinqui, ut veteres parietes semper diruerentur, & novi ubique extruerentur, cum hinc inde portandum esset altare. Ideoque præferenda videtur aliorum sententia, quod rete illud æneum ita fuerit dispositum, ut ignem & cineres susceperit intactis parietibus altaris, ut illos non immediatè tangeret, sed quasi pensile maneret, quo ita nullum periculum esset ab igne asseribus vel tabulis ligneis: quæ etsi ære inclusæ essent, præcaveri tamen oportebat, ne æs inflammaretur, aut liquesceret, asseresque sic incenderentur. Dici etiam potest in ipsa craticula pependisse arulam, seu focum æneum in medio altaris catenis suspensum ad quatuor ejusdem cornua alligatis, cui foco ligna & ignis apponerentur, ne altare læderet. Denique id fenestram etiam habuisse nonnullis videtur ad latus orientale, per quam cineres extrahendi fuerunt, & ligna super arulam seu focum ponenda.

## 27:9
verse 9. YOU SHALL MAKE THE COURT OF THE TABERNACLE.

The court (in Greek αὐλὴ) by which the tabernacle was enclosed on every side, though not in such a way that it occupied the precise center, because it rose above the court, so that the people outside the court could in a certain way see it. The use of the court was so that the Priests and Levites might perform sacred rites there, slaughter victims, and teach, and so that the people might station themselves there as if for a common assembly, to be present at the sacrifices, to hear the word of God, and to pray. In the temple of Solomon there were distinct courts for the Priests and the people; in the tabernacle there was only one, but there were undoubtedly distinct stations within it, so that the Priests and Levites stood apart, while the people remained in the front part near the altar of burnt offerings. The significance of the court pertains to the Church, in which ministers of the word, and hearers, and hypocrites mixed with the pious are found; for this reason, because the assembly of the Church was there, it was so greatly desired by David, Ps. 65:5, Ps. 84:3, 11. It was extended outside the tabernacle, so that it might be indicated that God would gather a Church from the nations outside the people of the Jews. Its expansion figured the amplitude of the Church, Is. 60:4, 5. The lattice walls signified the liberal communion of all sacred things, because in the Church of Christ the mysteries are celebrated publicly; the veil hung at the entrance warned that access to the Church is not open to all, but to the penitent, and to those who do not reject the Lord's calling; and also that there is a need for reverence toward sacred things and sobriety in handling the mysteries of God. That all things were square represented the firmness, solidity, and perfection of the holy city of God, just as in Rev. 21:16, similar things are held regarding the heavenly Jerusalem.

In this court teaching was done, and prayers were made, and sacrifices were offered: in this court also (in the later temple) Christ walked and taught: for it was a place of prayer for the people, and of sermons, and it is called the temple by the Evangelists and Josephus.

For Christ never entered the tabernacle or the holy place, for it was permitted only to the Aaronic priests to enter this. In this court they feasted, eating the peace offerings before the Lord. At the door of this court, women after childbirth, lepers, and other unclean persons were purified and expiated. However, it was not permitted for any of the unclean or the Gentiles to enter this court under penalty of death: whence Herod built another outermost court for the Gentiles and the unclean, so that they themselves could be present at the sacred rites and sacrifices from a distance.

vers. eod. TENTORIA) In the Hebrew [it is] 'fundas', that is, curtains distinguished by openings, which would bar entry, not the view. The Chaldean also understood it thus.

Latin:

vers. 9. FACIES ET ATRIUM TABERNACULI.

Atrium (Græcis αὐλὴ) quo tabernaculum ab omni parte inclusum, non tamen ita ut hoc præcise medium occuparet, quod supra atrium eminebat, ut populus extra atrium quodammodo illud videre possit. Usus atrii fuit, ut Sacerdotes, & Levitæ sacra istic obirent, victimas mactarent, docerent, ac populus ibi tanquam ad communem conventum se sisteret, sacrificiis præsto futurus, verbum Dei auditurus, & oraturus. In templo Salomonis distincta fuere pro Sacerdotibus & populo atria; in tabernaculo unicum tantum, sed distinctæ sine dubio in eodem stationes, ut seorsim Sacerdotes & Levitæ starent, juxta altare holocaustorum populo in parte anteriore manente. Atrii significatio ad Ecclesiam pertinet, in qua verbi ministri, & auditores, & hypocritæ piis admixti dantur; ideo quia illic conventus erat Ecclesiæ, desiderabatur id tantopere a Davide Ps. 65, 5. Ps. 84, 3. 11. Protendebatur illud extra tabernaculum, ut indicaretur Deum Ecclesiam ex gentibus extra Judæorum populum collecturum. Dilatatio ejus figurabat Ecclesiæ amplitudinem Es. 60, 4. 5. Parietes ocellati significabant liberalem sacrorum omnium communionem, quia in Ecclesia Christi publica celebrantur mysteria; velum oftio appensum monebat, non omnibus patere aditum ad Ecclesiam, sed pœnitentibus, & Domini vocationem non reprobantibus; opus etiam esse reverentia ad sacra & sobrietate in tractandis Dei mysteriis. Quod omnia fuerunt quadrata, firmitatem, soliditatem & perfectionem sanctæ civitatis Dei referebat, uti Ap. 21, 16, etiam de Hierôsolyma cœlesti similia habentur.

In hoc atrio docebatur, & orationes fiebant, offerebanturque saerificia: in hoc atrio etiam, (in templo posteriori) versatus est & docuit Christus: erat enim id locus orationis populo, & concionum, & ab Evangelistis ac Josepho templum vocatur.

Nec enim unquam ingressus est Christus tabernaculum vel sanctum, hoc enim solis Sacerdotibus Aaronitis ingredi licebat. In hoc atrio epulabantur comedentes victimas pacificas coram Domino. Ad ostium hujus atrii puerperæ, leprosi, aliique immundi lustrabantur & expiabantur. Nulli autem immundorum vel gentilium licebat intrare hoc atrium sub pœna mortis: unde Herodes aliud atrium extimum pro gentilibus & immundis ædificavit, ut ipsi eminus interesse possent sacris & sacrificiis.

vers. eod. TENTORIA) In Hebræo fundas, id est, cortinas foraminibus distinctas, quæ aditum arcerent, non aspectum. Sic sumsit & Chaldæus.

## 27:17
vers. 17. THEY SHALL BE CLAD WITH SILVER PLATES.

In the Hebrew there is not the word צפה, which is to cover, as [it is used] of the ark and the table covered and overlaid with silver plates, but חשק, which is to gird, [meaning] that these columns were surrounded by thin silver plates like threads, so that a circle was left with a space in the middle between the circles, which is as it were openwork, as Cornelius acknowledges here along with Abulensis. Furthermore, the columns of the court adorned with silver rings signified the ornaments and gifts which God distributes to those who teach, and who ought to be like columns in the Church. The bronze bases teach that the Church is fortified against the assaults of Satan: the fine linen curtains [teach] that it is purified through faith in Christ, whiter than snow, Ps. 51, Is. 1.

Latin:

vers. 17. VESTITÆ ERUNT ARGENTEIS LAMINIS.

In Hebræo non est verbum צפה, quod est operire, uti de arca & mensa laminis argenteis operta & obducta, sed חשק quod est cingere, quod columnæ hæ tenuibus argenti laminis instar filorum circumdatæ essent, ut gyrum spatio medio inter gyros vacuo relicto, quod est quasi opus interrasile, ut agnoscit hic cum Abulensi Cornelius. Cæterum columnæ atrii ornatæ argenteis circulis significabant ornamenta & dona, quæ distribuit Deus iis, qui docent, & columnarum instar esse debent in Ecclesia. Bases æneæ docent Ecclesiam firmatam esse contra insultus Satanæ: Cortinæ byssinæ purgatam eam esse per fidem in Christum supra nivem Ps. 51. Es. 1.

## 27:21
vers. 21. IN THE TABERNACLE OF THE TESTIMONY.

But in the Hebrew it is מועד from יעד, to meet. The Vulgate therefore confuses that noun with עדות, testimony, having followed the LXX interpreters.

WHICH IS HUNG BEFORE THE TESTIMONY.

This testimony is the ark containing the testimony by metonymy, that is, the law.

THAT IT MAY SHINE UNTIL MORNING] In the Hebrew: from evening until morning: for in the morning it was extinguished, 1 Sam. 3:3. Hecataeus, however, thought otherwise: 'upon these there is a light that is unquenchable both by night and by day.' Such was the lamp in the temple of Ammon, according to Plutarch, [explaining] why the oracles failed.

Here is explained what was said in v. 20, that it should burn ALWAYS, namely, in the night time. Therefore Cajetan and Lipom. say falsely that the lamps also burned by day. See Lev. 24:3, 1 Sam. 3:3, 2 Chron. 13:1. It is signified that only in the night of this age do we need living lamps, [that is,] teachers, Ap. 21:23. But the lamps had to shine always: because God does not want the light of the Gospel to be extinguished in the Church in the darkness of this life. And just as the high priest poured in oil so that they would not be extinguished, so the Son of God, with the oil of the Holy Spirit poured in, supplies strength to the ministers and gives increase to their labors, so that the Gospel may not be preached in vain, and so that it may not finally be completely extinguished in the Church.

Latin:

vers. 21. IN TABERNACULO TESTIMONII.

Sed in Ebræo est מועד a יעד convenire. Confundit ergo Vulgatus nomen illud cum עדות testimonium, sequutus LXX. Interpp.

QUOD OPPANSUM EST TESTIMONIO.

Hoc testimonium est arca continens testimonium per metonymiam, id est, legem.

VT USQUE MANE LVCEAT] In Ebræo: a vespera ad mane: nam mane exstinguebatur 1. Sam. 3, 3. Aliter tamen existimavit Hecatæus, ἐπὶ τούτων φῶς ἐστιν ἀναπόσβεστον καὶ τὰς νύκτας, καὶ τὰς ἡμέρας. Talis fuit lychnus in templo Ammonis teste Plutarcho, cur oracula defecerint.

Hic explicatur, quod v. 20. dictum erat, ut ardeat SEMPER, scil. nocturno tempore. Falso ergo Cajetan. & Lipom. ajunt, Lucernas etiam de die arsisse. Vid. Levit. 24, 3. 1. Sam. 3, 3. 2. Par. 13, 1. significatur sola nocte hujus seculi lucernis vivis, doctoribus nos indigere Ap. 21, 23. Semper autem lucere debebant lucernæ: quia non vult Deus, ut lux Evangelii in caligine hujus vitæ in Ecclesia extinguatur. Et uti summus Sacerdos oleum infundebat, ne exstinguerentur, sic Filius Dei oleo S. S. infuso & ministris vires suppeditat, & ipsorum laboribus dat incrementum, ne frustra prædicetur Evangelium, neve tandem in Ecclesia plane extinguatur.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII. Priestly Vestments.

Vers. 1. TAKE UNTO THEE ALSO AARON.

The Lord speaks and commands these things: because the calling of ministers ought to be from God: and this indeed was immediately from God, because the beginning of the ordinary priesthood was taking place in the instituting of the people of GOD Ebr. 5, 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII. Vestitus Sacerdotalis.

Vers. 1. APPLICA QUOQUE AD TE AARON.

HÆc Dominus loquitur & præcepit: quia vocatio ministrorum a Deo esse debet: & hic quidem immediate erat a Deo, quia initium sacerdotii ordinarii fiebat in populo DEI instituendo Ebr. 5, 1.

## 28:2
v. 2. AND YOU SHALL MAKE A HOLY GARMENT.

In Hebrew: Garments of holiness or holy garments. By them glory and beauty, dignity and authority were gathered for Aaron. And this was the more important reason for the sacred garments: the other was that the Priests might be reminded of the holiness of their office and that they ought always to bear in their mind the memory of the people. Add also the type of Christ. For the splendid clothing of the Priest figured the majesty and mighty works of Christ: the garments of other priests expressed our spiritual adornment Col. 3, 12. Apoc. 1, 6.

Latin:

v. 2. FACIESQUE VESTEM SANCTAM.

In Ebræo: Vestes sanctitatis vel sanctas. Con- ciliabatur Aaroni illis gloria & decor, dignitas & au- toritas. Atq; hæc vestium sacrarum potior causa erat: altera ut monerentur Sacerdotes de sanctitate muneris sui & quod gerere semper in animo debeant memoriam populi. Adde etiam typum Christi. Splendidus enim Sacerdotis vestitus majestatem & virtutes Christi figurabat: Sacerdotum aliorum ve- stes ornatum nostrum spiritualem exprimebant Col. 3, 12. Apoc. 1, 6.

## 28:4
verf. 4. BREASTPIECE, EPHOD, TUNIC AND CHECKERED COAT, TURBAN AND SASH.

It is more correctly rendered as breastpiece חשׁן: LXX. peristhithion; R. Solomon said it was an ornament over the region of the heart. Josephus, however, interpreted it as logion l. 3. Ant. c. 8. ephod LXX. and Josephus epomis, Aquila ependyma, from aphad to gird, to put on over: Vulg. superhumerale, understand the tunic as the outer one, others render it a mantle, the Greeks ton podere, which is a garment let down to the ankles. Checkered coat Pagninus interpreted as a tunic woven with Phrygian work, others as eyelet-work. LXX. chiton kosymboton a tunic drawn tight with knots: an inner linen garment, which was an ornament of the head, is rendered by others as diadema hieratikon. SASH LXX. zone. Jerome to Fabiola also calls it a Cingulum and Zona. Lev. 8, 7. 8. 9. these are recounted in reverse order: for here the beginning is made from the outer things, but there from the inner things, which was the order of clothing the Priest: for first he put on the breeches, over which he threw the linen tunic, which the sash tightened, over this he put on another. But in the description he rightly begins with the more noble, because it was not yet a matter of clothing the priest. But Cornelius wrongly concludes from the pedagogy of the O. T. that such priestly ornaments are also to be used in the N. T., because they were instituted by God there, but nowhere here; those were typical, which ceased when the antitype succeeded: there the proper adornment of the priests was used, in the N. T. there are no longer priests properly so called, who offer sacrifices; which order the Papists have invented without Scripture, nay, against Scripture, which acknowledges no other than the one N. T. priest. The argument of Cornelius therefore is to be corrected thus: If in the O. T. the external adornment of the priests was so great, much greater will be the internal and spiritual adornment of the high Priest Christ: If there the Priests were to be adorned with holy garments, certainly here the ministers of the word ought to be conspicuous by true holiness: concerning which Celestine the Roman Pontiff Ep. 2 to the Gauls c. 1. we are to be distinguished from the common people or others by doctrine not by dress, by conversation not by habit, by purity of mind not by attire. Meanwhile, the moral remains, that ministers of the word ought to appear decently and honestly in the Holy Ministry, which is to be observed against Zwinglian and Anabaptist levity. Their sarcasm is unworthy, that when we use peculiar garments in the celebration of the Sacrament we are acting out a play, or imitating the Jews, or even the Heathens. For in honor of the Sacraments and to excite the reverence and devotion of the people, such garments are used in our Churches out of Christian liberty without any superstition, or kakozelian: since all things in the Church ought to be done according to order and decency. Rivetus certainly does not disapprove of the linen garments which the ministers in England put on in this place, provided they are not for the imitation of the Jews, and for some mystical signification, but only for some distinction, and those are not established as necessary, but as indifferent. Verse of the same. CIDARIM) A small cap. Jerome on Zechariah: Thus also some Greeks [call it] πίλιον, others a mitre. Thus the flamens had a pileus on their head, in which there was a short rod, having a bit of wool on top, which, since they could not carry it through the heat, they began to bind their heads with a thread only: for it had been forbidden for them to walk with their heads completely bare. Thus Servius on the 8th Aeneid. He has something of it also on the tenth. It is to be noted, however, that the ornaments of the Pontifex Maximus were σύςοιχα [congruent] with the ornaments of the Temple. The four colors are the same. Seven garments, if you count the plate, for the seven lamps. Twelve gems for the twelve loaves. But with these ornaments that Pontifex did not go outside the city, except in the gravest danger, as in the times of Alexander the Great.

Latin:

verf. 4. RATIONALE, SUPERHUMERA- LE, TUNICAM ET LINEAM STRICTAM, CIDARIM ET BALTHEUM.

Rectius חשׁן pectorale redditur: LXX. περι- στήθιον; R. Salomo dicebat esse ornamentum e regione cordis. Josephus tamen λόγιον interpretatus est l. 3. Ant. c. 8. אפד LXX. & Josephus ἐπώμιδα, Aquila ἐπένδυμα, ab אפד cingo, superinduo: Vulg. superhu- merale, tunicam intellige exteriorem, alii pallium red- dunt, Græci τὴν ποδήρη, quæ vestis est usque ad talos demissa. Lineam frictam Pagninus tunicam opere phrygionico contextam interpretatus est, alii ocella- tam. LXX. χιτῶνα κοσυμβωτὸν tunicam nodis substri- ctam: lineum vestimentum interius, quod capitis ornamentum fuit, redditur ab aliis διάδημα ἱερατι-κόν. BALTHEUS LXX. ζώνη. Hieronym. ad Fa- biol. etiam Cingulum & Zona vocatur. Lev. 8, 7. 8. 9. hæc ordine inverso recensentur: hic enim initium fit ab exterioribus, ibi autem ab interioribus, qui fuit ordo vestiendi Sacerdotem: primo enim induebat femoralia, super quæ injiciebat lineam tunicam, quam zona stringebat, huic superinduebat aliam. Sed in descriptione recte incipit a nobilioribus, quia nondum agebatur de sacerdote vestiendo. Male autem Cornelius concludit e pædagogia V. T. ejus- modi ornamenta sacerdotalia etiam in N. T. adhi- benda esse, quia illic a Deo instituta, hic nuspiam; illa typica erant, quæ cessarunt antitypo succedente: illic ornatus sacerdotum proprius adhibitus, in N. T. non amplius sunt sacerdotes proprie dicti, qui offerant sacrificia; quem ordinem ἄτερ γραφῆς, imo contra Scripturam, quæ non nisi unicum N. T. sacerdotem agnoscit, Pontificii commenti sunt. Ar- gumentum ergo Cornelii ita corrigendum: Si in V. T. tantus fuit externus sacerdotum ornatus, mul- to major erit internus & spiritualis summi Sacerdo- tis Christi ornatus: Si illic sanctis vestibus ornandi fuere Sacerdotes, utique hic verbi ministri sanctitate vera debent esse conspicui: de quo Cæle- stinus Pontifex Rom. Ep. 2. ad Gall. c. 1. discernendi a plebe vel cæteris sumus doctrina non veste, conversatio- ne non habitu, mentis puritate non cultu. Manet in- terim morale, decenter & honeste debere ministros ver- bi apparere in S. Ministerio, quod contra levitatem Zwinglianam & Anabaptisticam observandum. In- dignus eorum Sarcasmus est, quod cum vestes pe- culiares in Sacramenti celebratione adhibemus hi- strioniam exerceamus, aut Judæos imitemur, vel etiam Ethnicos. In honorem enim Sacramento- rum & ad excitandam reverentiam & devotionem populi ex libertate Christiana ejusmodi vestimenta adhibentur in nostris Ecclesiis citra ullam supersti- tionem, vel κακοζηλίαν: quum omnia in Ecclesia κατὰ τάξιν καὶ ἐυσχημοσύνην fieri debeant. Ri- vetus certe lineas vestes quas superinduunt in Anglia ministri non improbat hoc loco, dummodo non ad imitationem sint Judæorum, & ad mysticam ali- quam significationem, sed tantum ad aliquam di- stinctionem, nec necessaria illa statuantur, sed indif- ferentia. Vers. eod. CIDARIM) Pileolum Hieronymus ad Zacha- riam: Sic & Græci quidam πίλιον, alii mitram. Sic flamines in capite pileum habebant, in quo erat brevis virga, desuper habens lance aliquid, quod cum per astus portare non possent, filo tantum capita religare cœperunt: nam nudis penitus eos capitibus incede- ve, nefas fuerat. ItaServius ad 8.Æneid.Habet ejus aliquid &ad decimum. Notandum vero Pontificis maximi ornamenta fuif- se σύςοιχα Templi ornamentis. Colores quatuor iidem. Se- ptem vestimenta, si laminam annumeres, pro septem lychnis. Duodecim gemmæ pro duodecim panibus. Cum his autem ornamentis Pontifex ille non procedebat extra urbem, nisi in gravissimo periculo, ut Alexandri Macedonis temporibus.

## 28:6
V. 6. AND THEY SHALL MAKE THE EPHODS OF GOLD AND HYACINTH &c.

There was another linen ephod, which others ministering in sacred things wore, such as his mother gave to Samuel every year: another of gold and hyacinth &c. proper to the High Priest: concerning which Jerome to Fabiola. A plate of gold, that is, the threads are stretched with wonderful thinness, from which cut threads are twisted, with a woof of three colors, hyacinth, scarlet, purple, and with a linen warp, and a small cloak of wonderful beauty is made, striking the eyes with its brightness. What the form of the garment was, as Vatablus notes, it was the outermost and very short, which lacked sleeves, and in a way tightened and constricted the inner looseness of the garments. It was not, therefore, let down to the ankles, as some wish. Josephus calls it ἔνδυμα τῶ σέρνω, a garment of the chest; Philo, book 2 on the Monarchy, Ὕφασμα θορακοειδὲς, a pectoral texture in the likeness of a breastplate. It seems to have covered the chest with one part of itself, and the back of the Pontifex with the other, down to the girdle. Two gems on each shoulder, according to Josephus, served in place of clasps, by which the epomis was to be connected. Moreover, by the various material of the sacred garments, various gifts of the Holy Spirit were signified; furthermore, by gold, the knowledge of divine things; by hyacinth, heavenly thoughts; by purple, the fight even unto blood; by scarlet, which imitates fire with its heat, burning charity; by fine linen, perfect chastity are designated.

Latin:

V. 6. FACIENT AUTEM SUPERHUME- RALIA DE AURO ET HYACINTHO &c.

Ephod fuit aliud lineum, quod alii sacris mini- strantes gestarunt, quale Samueli quotannis mater dedit: aliud de auro & hyacintho &c.summoSacer- doti proprium: de quo Hieronym. ad Fabiol. Auri la- mina, id est, braccè mira tenuitate tenduntur, ex qui- bus secta fila torquentur, cum subtegmine trium colo- rum hyacinthi, cocci, purpuræ, & cum stamine byssino, & efficitur palliolum miræ pulchritudinis, perstringens fulgore oculos. Qua forma vestis erat, notante Va- tablo, extima brevissima, quæ manicis carebat, & quodammodo arctabat, & constringebat laxitatem interiorem vestium. Non ergo dimittebatur ad ta- los, quod nonnulli volunt. Josephus vocat ἔνδυμα τῶ σέρνω pectoris indumentum: Philo l. 2. de Mo- narch. Ὕφασμα θορακοειδὲς textum pectorale tho- racis specie. Texisse ulla sui parte videtur pectus, altera tergum Pontificis usq; ad cincturam. Duæ gemmæ in utroque humero secundum Josephum fibularum vice fuere, quibus Epomis connectere- tur. Varia autem vestium sacrarum materia signi- ficata fuere varia S. S. dona, adhæc auro divinarum rerum cognitio, hyacintho cœlestes cogitationes, purpurapugna usque ad sanguinem, cocco qui ignem calore imitatur, ardens charitas, bysso perfecta casti- stas designantur.

## 28:9
v. 9. TWO ONYX STONES. LXX. λίθος σμαράγδε. Jerome to Fabiola. The stones, he says, which in Hebrew are Soham, are translated by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion as Onyx, by the LXX as Emerald; Josephus calls them Sardonyx, agreeing with the Hebrew and Aquila, so as to demonstrate either the color of the stones or their native land. Jerome seems to hold the Sardonyx and Onyx as the same, which gems others distinguish. Arias Montanus judges these stones, from the Chaldean and Arabic version, to have been Beryls, which are similar to the Emerald in violet or sky-blue color. Thus one can scarcely establish anything certain, because among the Jews the names of gems are very uncertain.

YOU SHALL ENGRAVE ON THEM THE NAMES OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL. It seems that the names of the children of Israel, not of the tribes, are indicated. Whence Abulensis thinks that the names of Manasseh and Ephraim were not engraved, but the name of Joseph and Levi, which was otherwise omitted in certain acts. But because afterwards in v. 21 individual stones are said to correspond to the names of individuals, through the 12 tribes, among which the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim certainly were, and the tribes themselves are not rarely designated by the name of the children of Israel, nay, Aaron, as one born from the tribe of Levi, represented his tribe by himself, I would rather subscribe to others who understand the names of the tribes here with Josephus, book 3, ch. 2. And not only the first element of the name, but THE NAMES THEMSELVES, because the words of the Lord demand that. Therefore it was necessary for those gems to be large, which would hold so many names. And the inscription of the names was made according to the natural order of the children of Israel. Concerning those stones, Josephus from tradition, book 3, Ant. ch. 9. From the small stones, he says, which the pontiff wore on his shoulders, one used to shine whenever a sacrifice had been offered, the one that occupied the right shoulder, and it emitted such brightness that it was seen even by those looking from afar, and that contrary to nature and its own custom.

Latin:

v. 9. DUOS LAPIDES ONYCHINOS. LXX. λίθος σμαράγδε. Hieronym. ad Fabiol. Lapides, inquit, qui Ebraice Soham, ab Aquila, Sym- macho & Theodotione Onychini, a LXX. Smaragdini transferuntur, Josephus Sardonychas vocat, cumEbreo Aquilaque consentiens, ut vel colorem lapidum vel pa- triam demonstraret. Pro iisdem habere videtur Hie- ron. Sardonychon & Onychan, quas gemmas alii di- stinguunt. AriasMontanus hos lapides ex versione Chald. & Arab. Beryllos fuisse censet, qui Smaragdo similes coloris violacei, vel cœrulæi sunt. Ita vix certi quid statuere licet, quia apud Judæos valde in- certa sunt gemmarum nomina.

SCULPES IN EIS NOMINA FILIORUM ISRAEL. Filiorum Israel non tribuum nomina indigita- ri videntur. Unde Abulensis insculpta non fuisse nomina Manasse & Ephraim, sed nomen Joseph & Levi, quod alias in quibusdam actibus omittebatur, existimat. Sed quia postea v. 21. singuli lapides di- cuntur respondere nominibus singulorum, per 12. tribus, inter quas Manassis, & Ephraimi tribus omni- no fuere, ac nomine filiorum Israel tribus ipse non raro designantur, imo Aaren ceu ex tribu Levi ori- undus per se suam tribum repræsentabat, malim aliis subscribere, qui tribuum nomina hîcintelli- gunt cum Josepho l. 3. c. 2. Neque solum primum nominis elementum, sed NOMINA IPSA, quia id verba Domini poscunt. Ideo magnas opor- tuit illas gemmas esse, quæ tot nomina caperent. Et inscriptio nominum facta est secundum ordi- nem naturalem filiorum Israel. De lapidibus illis Josephus ex traditione l. 3. Ant. c. 9. Ex lapillis, inquit, quos pontifex in humeris gestabat, mi- cabat alter quoties litatum esset, is qui dextrum hume- rum occupabat, tantumq́; fulgorem emittebat, ut procul etiam intuentibus conspiceretur, idq́; præter naturam & suam consuetudinem.

## 28:11
verse 11. ENGRAVING OF A GEM-CUTTER) LXX. γλύμμα σφραγῖδος, that is, in the way in which the gems of signet rings are accustomed to be carved. To engrave is properly ἐκτύπων, to carve is ἐντύπων: but these are accustomed to be confused.

Latin:

verf. 11. CÆLATVRA GEMMARII) LXX. γλύμμα σφραγῖδος, id est, eo modo quo gemmæ annulorum signato- riorum scalpi solent. Cælare proprie ἐκτύπων, scalpere ἐντύ- πων: sed solent ista confundi.

## 28:12
verse 12. A MEMORIAL FOR THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL.

That the children of Israel might be called to memory, not before the Pontiff, as Oleaster seems to have wished, nor before the people, unless in such a way that they themselves understood that they were as if set before GOD, which however is only a consequence, but (as to the immediate sense) that they might be called to memory and commended to God Himself, as is held concerning the rainbow in Gen. 9:13, concerning which Jerome in the place cited. The Pontiff carried the names of the tribes on his shoulders, that he might offer and commend the tribe of Israel to God, as if that sculpture were speaking thus: I commend to you, O Lord, the tribe of Reuben and the rest. The words of v. 12 infer that: And Aaron shall carry their names before the Lord, upon both shoulders, for a remembrance. Compare 5:29, Lev. 2:2. It is signified that the High Priest sets us before God by name, and for his love towards us commends us, signified, to the memory and thanks of GOD the Father; not that anything could fall out of the divine memory, but that God is not willing to show us grace except through the intervening mediation of Christ, and does that at his intercession, which those who remember their own are accustomed to do. Christ also carries the faithful on his shoulders and sustains them and the whole Church, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against it, Matthew 16:16.

Latin:

verf. 12. MEMORIALE FILIIS ISRAEL.

Ut in memoriam revocarentur filii Israel non penes Pontificem, ut Oleaster videtur voluisse, nec penes populum, nisi ita, ut intelligerent ipsi se quasi coram DEO sisti, quod tamen consequens tantum est, sed (quod ad sensum immediatum) ut Deo ipsi in memoriam revocarentur & commendarentur, uti de iride habetur Gen. 9,13. quo de Hieron. l. c. Por- tabat Pontifex nomina tribuum in humeris, ut tribus Israel Deo offerret & commendaret, quasi illa sculptura sic loqueretur: Commendo tibi Domine tribum Ruben & cæteras. Id inferunt verba v. 12. Portabitq; Aaron nomina eorum coram Domino, super utrumque hume- rum, ob recordationem. Conf. 5,29. Lev. 2,2. Signi- ficatum summum Pontificem nos Deo nominatim sistere, ac pro amore suo adversus nos memoriæ & gratiæ DEI Patris nos significatum commendare; non quod excidere quid divinæ memoriæ posset, sed quod Deus non nisi interveniente Christi me- diatione nobis gratiam exhibere velit, atq; id ad ejus intercessionem faciat, quod solent qui suorum meminerunt. Portat etiam Christus humeris suis fideles & sustinet eosdem ac totam Ecclesiam, ne portæ inferorum prævaleant adversus eam Matth. 16,16.

## 28:15
verse 15. YOU SHALL ALSO MAKE A BREASTPLATE OF JUDGMENT.

LXX. τὸ λογεῖον τῶν κρίσεων: Tremellius & Junius, the sacred breastplate of judgment, because the Priest wore it when consulting GOD to answer concerning the law, to which the explanations of the Rabbis also tend. Epiphanius published a booklet about the gems, which here assigns to each of the sons of Israel his own stone in this breastplate: to Reuben the Sardius, to Simeon the Topaz, to Levi the Emerald, to Judah the Carbuncle, to Dan the Sapphire: to Naphtali the Jasper: to Gad the Ligure: to Asher the Agate: to Issachar the Amethyst: to Zebulun the Chrysolite: to Joseph the Beryl: to Benjamin the Onyx.

Latin:

verf. 15. RATIONALE QVOQUE JUDICII FACIES.

LXX. τὸ λογεῖον τῶν κρίσεων: Tremell. & Ju- nius sacrum pectorale juris, quia id induebat Sacer- dos consulentibus DEUM de jure responsurum, quo etiam abeunt Rabbinorum explicationes. De gemmis Epiphan. libellum edidit, qui hìc unicuiq; ex filiis Israel suum assignat in hoc pectorali lapi- dem: Rubeni Sardium, Simeoni Topazium, Levi Smaragdum, Judæ Carbunculum, Dan Saphirum: Naphtali Jaspidem: Gado Ligurium: Asser Acha- tem: Issacharo Amethystum: Zebuloni Chrysolithum: Josepho Beryllum: Benjamino Onychinum.

## 28:17
verf. 17. AND YOU SHALL SET IN IT FOUR ROWS OF STONES.

The four rows of gems are the four cardinal virtues, says St. Jerome to Fabiola. Bede, however, says that the three stones in each row are the three Theological virtues. But since these gems all adorned the High Priest, who bore the type of Christ, they are to be believed to have designated the perfection of all virtues in him. Similar are the 12 gems adorning the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem, Apoc. 21:19, by which the 12 Apostles are signified, as is hinted in v. 14: whose names they bore: whence, because these gems in this place bear the names of the tribes of Israel, the virtues of these gems are accustomed to be compared by interpreters with the sons of Israel, which, however, all shine forth most perfectly in the High Priest alone.

IN THE FIRST ROW SHALL BE A SARDIUS STONE AND A TOPAZ AND AN EMERALD.

In the first row or rather order, interpreters easily agree, and these three gems are found, although in a different order, also in Apoc. 21. The Sardius, translucent with the appearance of fire, in which a blood-red color is seen along with the fiery color, by which it strikes terror into wild beasts, Christ's fiery love and the bloody passion redundant from it, which can strike terror into the demon himself Gen. 3, 15. In color, according to Pliny b. 37, ch. 6, it is similar to clear and transparent flesh, so that human flesh seems to be converted into a transparent and shining gem, which can be referred to the incarnation of the Son of GOD of Christ. And since it heals wounds according to Epiphanius in his book on gems, and stops blood flowing from anywhere, as Boethius testifies, it shadows forth the power of the passion of Christ, by which our wounds are healed Is. 53, 7. and the blood is stopped, which we ought to have shed for our sins. The topaz is partly blue, partly golden in color, and it flames more intensely while it is struck by the rays of the Sun, as Ambrose has it in this place, ch. 18. It refers to the heavenly and golden holiness of Christ, which shone more and more inflamed when it felt and experienced the rays of divine wrath in the great passion. The topaz is said to repress the passions of the soul, frenzy, sadness, anger, lust: but a far more certain and effective power of repressing the passions of the soul belongs to Christ and the merit of his obedience; The flashing Emerald in Hebrew, is most green, so much so that it imbues even herbs and the air with its greenness: and therefore it so refreshes the sight that the eyes cannot be sated by its contemplation. Which things agree with the perennial and most beautiful greenness of the virtues of Christ, by which the faithful and the blessed can never be sated: whose stupendous constancy and brazen patience flourished on the cross. For emeralds are said to be related to air: whence mirrors were made from them. Is not the cross of Christ indeed the clearest mirror of divine Wisdom, charity, and all virtues? Amulets against poisons are made from emeralds: is not the passion of Christ a most present antidote against the poisons of Satan?

Latin:

verf. 17. PONESQUE IN EO QUATUOR ORDINES LAPIDUM.

Quatuor ordines gemmarum sunt quatuor vir- tutes cardinales, ait S. Hieron. ad Fabiol. Beda vero, tres lapides, inquit, in singulis ordinibus sunt tres vir- tutes Theologicæ. Sed quum hæ gemmæ universæ or- narint Pontificem, qui Christi typum gerebat, per- fectionem omnium virtutum in eo designasse cre- dendæ sunt. Similes sunt gemmæ 12. fundamenta cœlestis Hierosolymæ exornantes Ap. 21,19. quibus 12. Apostolos significatos v. 14. innuitur: quorum nomina referebant: unde quia hæ gemmæ hoc loco nomina tribuum Israelis gerunt, cum filiis Israel conferri solent virtutes harum gemmarum ab in- terpp. quæ vero universæ in solo summo Pontifice perfectissimæ elucent.

IN PRIMO VERSU ERIT LAPIS SARDIUS ET TOPAZIUS ET SMARAGDUS.

In primo versu vel potius ordine facile conve- niunt interpp. & reperiuntur hæ tres gemmæ, licet alio ordine, etiam Apoc. 21. Sardius ignis specie translucens, in quo cum igneo colore sanguineus conspicitur, quo feris terrorem incutit, Christi igneum amorem & inde redundantem cruentam pas- sionem exprimit, quæ dæmoni ipsi terrorẽ incutere potest Gen. 3, 15. Colore, secundum Plinium l. 37. c. 6. similis est carni perspicuæ ac pellucidæ, ita ut caro hu- mana in gemmam pellucidam & splendentem vi- deatur conversa, quod ad Filii DEI ἐνανθρώπησιν & gloriam majestatis in carne Christi relucentem referri possit. Et cum vulneribus medeatur secun- dum Epiphan. l. de gemmis, & sanguinem undecunq; fluentem sistat, Boethio teste, vim passionis Christi, qua sanantur vulnera nostra Es. 53, 7. & sanguis sisti- tur, quem ob peccata profundere debebamus, ad- umbrat. Topazius partim cœruleo, partim aureo est colore, atq; flammeseit impensius, dum radiis Solis verberatur, ut habet Ambrosius in h. l. c. 18. sanctita- tem cœlestem & auream Christi refert, quæ magis ma- gisque inflammata coruscavit, cum iræ divinæ radios in passione magna sensit & expertus est. Compri- mere dicitur topazius animæ passiones phrenesin, tristitiam, iram, luxuriam: at longe certior & effica- cior vis comprimendi animæ passiones Christo, ejusque obedientiæ merito convenit; Smaragdus fulgurans Ebraice, maxime viret, adeo ut virore suo etiam herbas & aërem imbuat: ideoque visum ita recreat, ut nec satiari oculi ejus intuitu possint. Quæ virori perenni & pulchertimo virtutum Christi conveniunt, quo nunquam exatiari fideles ac beati possint: cujus stupenda constantia & ænea patientia in cruce viruit. Æri enim Smaragdi dicuntur af- fines: unde ex iis fiebant specula. Annon vero crux Christi clarissimum speculum divinæ Sapientiæ, charitatis , & virtutum omnium? Ex Smaragdis fiunt amuleta contra venena: annon passio Christi contra venena Satanæ antidotum est præsentissi- mum?

## 28:18
verse 18. IN THE SECOND A CARBUNCLE, A SAPPHIRE AND A JASPER) Carbuncle ἄνθραξ LXX. whom Chrysostom follows in his oration on the Old & N. T. that there is one God.

In the Hebrew in the third place is יהלם, by which name the Adamant comes, as Lexicographers note, also among the Chaldeans מכקלום because it breaks all stones; or because it cannot be broken or tamed, from הלם he broke by metaphrasis, as Schindler has it in his Pentaglot Lexicon. Therefore there is no reason for Corn. a Lap. to inquire why the Adamant is omitted in the breastplate? whose reasons are frivolous: For what he asks: whence could the poor Hebrews procure for themselves in Egypt an adamant, upon which the name Judah could be inscribed? The answer is easy; He who gave them favor before the Egyptians, so that they could receive and carry away other treasures from there Ex. 11, 2. why could he not also provide for them in the same way regarding the most precious gems? and that they were not so poor, the collection of a huge sum of gold and other gems sufficiently teaches. Moreover the CARBUNCLE, in Greek ἄνθραξ a burning coal, refers to its appearance, and it does not feel the power of fire, to which the Chalcedony seems to correspond in the Apocalypse, similar to it in color, it denotes Christ the light of the world illuminating and inflaming him, who was able to overcome the fire of divine wrath, and averted the same from the whole human race. The brightness of the carbuncle, says Isidore b. 12, ch. 13, is not overcome even by night, ignited in color it shines like a coal in the darkness; Thus Christ the true light shines in the darkness John 1, 4. The carbuncle is said to shine more when thrown into sharp vinegar, and it burns when sprinkled with water, according to Pliny: thus the charity of Christ burned more in the waters of passions and tribulations, where he was given vinegar to drink: when he himself prayed for sinners, even for those who had driven him to the cross. The pious ancients compare the incarnate Word to a burning coal to explain also the communication of Idioms. Justin q. 44 to the Orthodox. Cyril b. on the incarnation of the word & others. The SAPPHIRE is blue Exod. 24, 10. and shines with golden dots like stars, and sparks according to Pliny & Isidore. Our Sapphires seem to be hyacinths rather than the Sapphires of the ancients, which were once called the gem of gems; such as the supreme Judges of the Egyptians once wore from their neck, upon which TRUTH was inscribed, as Aelian testifies b. 14, ch. 34. According to Galen & Dioscorides, taken internally it helps those struck by a Scorpion, according to Nyssen in Canticles Orat. 14, it sharpens the sight, according to Albert the Great it is valid against Melancholy: Christ is blue like a sapphire, because he shines with the immense sea of heavenly light with heavenly serenity, majesty and blessedness with golden dots of burning Charity, he heals the wounds of the infernal scorpion, sharpens the eyes of faith, drives away the melancholy of the mind &c. The ADAMANT, the most excellent of gems, surpasses the others in splendor and strength, whose invincible power, however, a despiser of the two most violent things of nature, iron and fire, is broken by goat's blood: finally in medicine it makes most effective poisons void, drives away madness, and expels vain fears from the mind, as Pliny says. Which things shadow forth the excellence, splendor, strength and spiritual virtue of Christ, who allowed himself to be as it were broken for our sins, when the just died for the unjust, 1. Pet. 3, 18.

Latin:

vers. 18. IN SECVNDO CARBVNCVLVS, SAPHIRVS ET JASPIS) Carbunculus ἄνθραξ LXX. quos sequitur Chry- sostomus oratione Vet. & N. T. unum esse Deum.

In Ebræo loco tertio est יהלם, quo nomine Adamas venit, notantibus Lexicographis, etiam a- pud Chaldæos מכקלום quia lapides omnes fran- git; vel quia frangi aut domari nequit, ab הלם fregit per metaphrasin, ut habet Schindlerus in Lexi- co Pentaglotto. Ideo non est quod disquirat Corn. a Lap. cur Adamas prætermittatur in rationali? cu- jus rationes frivolæ sunt: Nam quod quærit: unde pauperes Ebræi tantum Adamantem, cui nomen Jehu- da inscribi possit, in Ægypto sibi comparare potuerunt? Facilis est responsio; Qui ipsis gratiam dedit coram Ægyptiis, ut alios thesauros inde accipere ac repor- tare potuerint Ex. 11, 2. quidni etiam de gemmis pretiosissimis itidem prospicere potuerit? nec adeo pauperes fuisse, ingentis summæ auri, & aliarum gemmarum collatio satis docet. Cæterum CAR- BUNCULUS, Græce ἄνθραξ carbo ignitus ejus spe- ciem refert, & vim ignis non sentit, cui videtur in Apocal. respondere Chalcidoneus colore ipsi similis, Christum lucem mundi eum illuminantem & inflam- mantem notat, qui ignem iræ divinæ superare valuit, eandemque a toto genere humano avertit. Car- bunculi fulgor, inquit Isidor. l. 12. c. 13. nec nocte vin- citur, colore ignitus ut carbo lucet in tenebris; Sic Christus lux vera in tenebris lucet Joh. 1, 4.. Magis splendescere carbunculus dicitur in acetum acre injectus, & inardescit aquis perfusus, Autore Plinio: sic magis exarsit charitas Christi in passionum & tribulationum aquis, ubi aceto potatus est: quando pro peccatoribus ipse oravit, etiam iis, qui ipsum in crucem egerant. Verbum incarnatum ignito carboni comparant ad explicandam etiam commu- nicationem Idiomatum pii veteres. Justinus q. 44. ad Orthod. Cyrillus l. de incarn. verbi & alii. SA- PHIRUS cæruleus est Exod. 24, 10. & aureis pun- stis q. stellis collucet, & scintillis secundum Plin. & Isi- dor. Nostri Sapphiri potius hyacinthi videntur quam veterum Sapphiri, quæ gemmæ gemmarum olim ap- pellatæ; quales Ægyptii Judices summi quondam e collo gestabant, quibus insculpta erat VERITAS teste Æliano l. 14. c. 34. Secundum Galen. & Dio- scorid. haustus percussis a Scorpione prodest, secundum Nyssen. in Cantic. Orat. 14. visum acuit, secundum Albertum M. contra Melancholiam valet: Christus instar Sapphiri cæruleus est, quia lucis cœlestis im- mensum pelagus cœlesti serenitate, majestate & bea- titudine aureis punctis collucet ardentis Charitatis, sanatscorpionis infernalis plagas, acuit oculos fidei, pellit melancholiam animi &c. ADAMAS præ- stantissima gemmarum cæteras splendore ac fortitu- dine superat, cujus tamen invicta vis duarum violen- tissimarum naturæ rerum ferri, ignisque contemtrix hircino rumpitur sanguine: denique in medicina ef- ficacissima venena irrita facit, lymphationes abigit, me- tusque vanos expellit a mente dicente Plinio. Quæ præstantiam, splendorem, fortitudinem & virtutem Spiritualem Christi adumbrant, qui pro peccatis nostris se quasi disrumpi permisit, cum justus pro injustis mortuus, 1. Petr. 3, 18.

## 28:19
verse 19. IN THE THIRD A LIGURE, AN AGATE AND AN AMETHYST) Lyncurius. Chrysostom has Hyacinth here.

What is to be understood by the ligure, or as Jerome otherwise calls it the lyncurium, no one would rashly say, even if the LXX also rendered it so. Jerome Epist. to Fabiola. I wonder enough, he says, why the hyacinth, a most precious stone, is not placed in this number, unless perhaps it is the lyncurium by another name, searching those who have written about the natures of stones and gems, I could hardly find the lyncurium. Some indeed report that it is coagulated from the urine of a lynx. Francis Rueus says it is amber distilling from a pine tree, others make it electrum, but they do not refer to the gem. Therefore we assume the hyacinth, which is also mentioned in the Apocalypse; and it easily agrees with the Greek λιγυρὸν, which is sweet and pleasant, because it is pleasant to the eyes on account of its violet brightness, just as Josephus also commends the ligure for its admirable beauty. For the hyacinth is violet, and of a heavenly color like the sapphire, and the flower which is likewise called by this name. Thus is signified the wondrous meekness and sweetness of Christ. The hyacinth of the ancients used to cure the plague and poisonous diseases, and for that reason it was accustomed to be hung from the neck in the region of the heart, as Rueus notes, it strengthened the body and brought about joy: which things mystically befit Christ. The AGATE is of wondrous variety in color, especially of a black color intersected with white spots, it is of value; according to Ans. Boethius, book 2 on gems, ch. 97, it opposes pestiferous poisons, and refreshes the heart, and protects against every kind of contagion. Some think it corresponds to the Chrysoprase in Apoc. 21, which with its pallor kindles toward blackness with golden drops likewise intervening. It refers to the golden wisdom of Christ, joined with sharpness against heretics and the impious; by which the heart is refreshed, and poisons are resisted. The AMETHYST is purple, rose-colored and violet, gently pouring forth little flames, a symbol of modesty, which is the purple of virtue according to Ambrose, because as purple covers, clothes, and adorns them, and it is thus considered by the Greeks to be called ἀμέθυςτος, because it wards off drunkenness; it befits the humility and moderation of Christ and the priestly purple, by whose virtue we resist not only drunkenness, but any depraved desires and vices whatsoever, lest the soul be made drunk.

Latin:

verf. 19. IN TERTIO LIGURIVS, ACHATES ET AME- THISTVS) Lyncurius. Hic Hyacinthum habet Chrysosto- mus.

Quid per ligurium, vel ut Hieron. alias vocat lyncurium intelligendum sit, nemo temere dixerit, etsi etiam LXX. ita reddiderint. Hieron. Epist. ad Fabiol. Satis, inquit, miror, cur hyacinthus pretiosissi- mus lapis in horum numero non ponatur, nisi forte ipse est alio nomine lyncurius, scrutans eos, qui de lapidum scripsere naturis, atque gemmarum lyncurium inveni- re haud potui. Tradunt quidem nonnulli eum ex lyncis urina coagulari. Franc. Rueus Succinum esse dicit ex pino arbore destillans, alii electrum fa- ciunt, sed ea gemmam non referunt. Ideo hyacin- thum assumimus, quæ etiam in Apocal. commemo- ratur; & cum Græco λιγυρὸν, quod est suave, & ju- cundum, quia ob fulgorem violaceum jucundus est oculis, facile consonat, quemadmodum & Josephus ligurium ab admiranda pulchritudine commendat. Est enim hyacinthus violaceus, & cœlestis coloris in- star Sapphiri, & floris, qui hoc itidem vocatur no- mine. Designatur ita eodem mira Christi man- suetudo, & suavitas. Hyacinthus Veterum pesti & venenatis morbis medebatur, ideoque a collo sus- pendi solebat e regione cordis, notante Rueo, robora- bat corpus ac lætitiam conciliabat: quæ Christo my- sttice conveniunt. ACHATES miræ est in colore varietatis, nigri inprimis coloris albis intersecta ma- culis, in pretio est; secundum Ans. Boethium l. 2. de gemmis c. 97. venenis pestiferis adversatur, & cor re- creat, & adversus omne contagii genus tuetur. Non- nulli censent Ap. 21. Chrysoprasium respondere, qui pallore suo ad nigredinem accendit guttis aureis itidem intervenientibus. Refert auream Christi sapientiam, cum acredine in hæreticos, & impios conjuncta; qua cor recreatur, & venenis resistitur. AMETHYSTUS purpureus est, roseus & violaceus, leniter flammulas fundens, modestiæ Symbolum, quæ purpura virtutis est secundum Ambrosium, quia ut purpura eas tegit, vestit, ornat, & dicta ita Græcis ἀμέθυςτος censetur, quod Ebrietatem arceat; convenit Christi humilitati, & moderationi ac pur- puræ Sacerdotali, cujus virtute non ebrietati tantum, sed quibusvis pravis concupiscentiis & vitiis resisti- mus, ne anima inebrietur.

## 28:20
verse 20. IN THE FOURTH CHRYSOLITE, ONYCHINUS, AND BERYL) Chrysolite to Chrysostom is beryl.

JASPIS) Onyx according to Chrysostom. In this review of stones, Josephus agrees with Jerome in The Jewish War 5, 15.

In the last place is held יָשְׁפֵה, which Pagninus, Osiander, and others, along with the lexicographers, acknowledge to be Jasper. Chrysolite is partly of a golden color, partly of a sea color, or it even makes gold appear white with a certain silvery aspect, which Pliny says are the best: Boethius notes that the Oriental ones glow like the purest gold; it is effective against diseases of the chest and pusillanimity; by its white color it shadows forth holiness, by its golden color the royal Majesty and glory of Christ, who supplies and offers strength and grace and hope to any timid and pusillanimous person. 1 John 2:1. ONYCHINUS, the most excellent species of which they call Sardonyx (occurring in Rev. ch. 21), is so called because it reddens like a Sardius and whitens like an Onyx, just as in Christ redness and whiteness are joined, Cant. 6:10. Andreas Baccus in his treatise on the 12 gems writes that Onyx, when brought to the eyes, draws out depraved humors and strengthens the sight: just as from Christ is the strength of our eyes, Rev. 3:18. The most excellent Jasper is green, having red or bloody spots, or some purple: as Albertus Magnus and Pliny acknowledge, and it is very firm: by which the perpetual greenness of Christ and his blood, and his firmness, are designated; and as Jasper is an amulet against poisons, wards off epilepsy, and stops the flow of blood and menses: so in Christ we have a remedy against poisons and diseases, as also against impure and carnal actions and thoughts: as Jasper promotes the birth of women, so Christ promotes good works, etc.

Latin:

vers. 20. IN QVARTO CHRTSOLITH. ONYCHINVS, ET BERILLVS) Chrysolithus Chrysostomo beryllus.

JASPIS) Onύχιον Chrysostomo. In hac lapidum recen- sione cum Hieronymo congruit Josephus Belli Judaici 5, 15.

Postremo loco habetur יָשְׁפֵה quem Jaspidem esse cum Lexicographis Pagninus, Osiander & alii agnoscunt. Chrysolitus partim aurei, partim ma- rini coloris est, vel etiam aurum albicare quadam ar- genti facie facit, quos optimos Plin. dicit: Orienta- les purissimi auri instar rutilare notat Boetius, valet contra pectoris morbos, & pusillanimitatem; †albo colore sanctitatem,aureo regiam Majestatem & glo- riam Christi adumbrat, qui timido, & pusillanimi cuivis robur & gratiam & spem sufficit ac præbet. 1.Ioh.2,1.ONYCHINUS,cujus speciem præstantissi- mam dicunt Sardonychen (in Apoc. occurrentem c. 21.) ita vocatum,quod rubescat ut Sardius,candescat ut Onyx, quemadmodum in Christo rubedo & can- dor sociantur Cant. 6,10. Andreas Baccus tract. de 12. gemm.Script.Onychen tradit oculis admotum pra- vos humores educere, ac visum confirmare : uti a Christo est oculorum nostrorum robur Apoc. 3, 18. JASPIS præstantissima est viridis, habens maculas ru- beas, sive sanguineas,vel quidquam purpuræ: ut Al- bert. M. & Plin. agnoscunt, estque firmissima: quo Christi viror perpetuus & sanguis ejus luteus,ac fir- mitudo ipsius designatur; & ut Jaspis amuletum est contra venena,Epilepsiam arcet, & fluxum sangui- nis ac menstrua sistit: ita in Christo habemus reme- dium contra venena & morbos, ut & impuras & carnales actiones & cogitationes: ut partum mulie- rum Jaspis; ita Christus bonorum operum promo- vet &c.

## 28:29
v. 29. AND AARON SHALL BEAR THE NAMES OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL IN THE BREASTPLATE OF JUDGMENT.

Not seals and hieroglyphic-like marks, as Hieronymus Prado wishes, but names, as the text clearly prescribes. He was to bear the names of the children of Israel not only upon his shoulders but on his breast, so that it might be noted that our high Priest Christ bears us not only by his power, but also carries us on his breast and embraces us with the most ardent affection of his heart: This breastplate was affixed to the tunic of the Ephod, so that the breastplate could not be removed unless the tunic was removed: thus the faithful are so bound to Christ that nothing can separate them from him. Rom. 8.

Latin:

v.29. PORTABITQUE AARON NOMINA FILIORUM ISRAEL IN RATIONALI JUDI- CII.

Non sigilla ac hieroglyphicas veluti notas,ut Hie- ron.Prado vult,sed nomina,ut text9 luculenter præ- scribit. Non tantum super humeros, sed in pectore gestare nomina debebat filiorum Israel,ut notaretur summum Pontificem nostrum Christum non tantum potentia sua nos ferre,sed etiam pectore suo gerere, & ardentissimo cordis affectu nos complecti: Affi- xum erat hoc pectorale tunicæ Ephod, ut nisi tuni- ca deposita pectorale deponi non potuerit: sic fide- les Christo ita velut alligati sunt, ut nihil eos ab ipso separare possit. Rom. 8.

## 28:30
Vers. 30. DOCTRINE AND TRUTH) Δήλωσιν xąi ἀλήθειαν. Literally: lights and integrity, φωτισμὸς xąi τελειώσεις: as both Aquila and Theodotion have it. In a teacher, such as the high Priest ought to be above others, two things are required: knowledge and purity of life. Hence the Egyptians took the custom of hanging a necklace on the high Judge, which they called ἀλήθειαν. Diodorus Siculus says it was made of very precious gems, Aelianus says of Sapphire. We have cited the places in the first book on the truth of the Christian Religion. Urim and Thummim were consulted by a King or Prince in matters pertaining most to the public state, or by the Sanhedrin in the most difficult controversies of law.

Therefore the Vulgate wrongly interprets Urim and Thummim as doctrine and truth: but Cajetan, Martin Delrio in his Disquisitiones Magicae, book 4, ch. 1, Oleaster on this passage, and Riebera on Malachi 2, as well as Arias Montanus, more correctly render them as fires or illuminations and perfections. For that is what the Hebrew words themselves signify. But Bellarmine is inept, who derives אוּרִים from יוֹרֶה, which in Hiphil is הוֹרָה (he taught), and even more ineptly, that he derives תֻּמִּים from אָמַן (he was truthful); book 4, On the Pontiff, ch. 3, which we leave to the grammarians to attack. Aquila rendered it Φωτισμὸς καὶ τελειώσεις, Lev. 8:8, and it is certain that the Hebrew words cannot be rendered otherwise, by the force of the etymology. To which the interpretations of most others also go. The Arab rendered it אלאואר ואלצחאיד (elucidations and certainties). The Syrian בְּהִירָא וַשׁלְמָא (lucid and perfect); the Samaritan, elucidations and perfections. B. Luth. Light and Right, Tusius, the Persian Metaphrast, and the Talmudists retain the Hebrew word with Onkelos. But it is the most inept of all that the Papists conclude from this: because the Pontiff of the Old Testament had doctrine and truth in his breastplate; therefore the Pope, when he teaches the Church, cannot err. From the staff to the corner. From the Pontiff of the Old Testament to the Roman Pope; from the responses promised divinely through Urim and Thummim in the breastplate to the responses to be drawn from the chest of the Roman Pontiff's breast, to whom no promise of immediate revelation was made: from the decisions of doubtful cases to the decision of questions of faith. For Grotius rightly acknowledges that this revelation occurred only in doubtful cases. Add that the one inquiring there was the high Priest himself, to whom the response was returned by God through Urim and Thummim, concerning which R. Levi Ben Gerson says: all this served to excite prophecy, therefore Urim and Thummim were not consulted except through the Priest. But the Papists constitute the Roman Pontiff not as one inquiring about controversies, but as one giving oracles to inquiries. Therefore these differ as much as heaven and earth.

But as to how responses were given by God through Urim and Thummim, opinions vary. Some asserted that it was done by a voice uttered and heard by the Priest, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Zoma ch. 7. Most, however, believed that they were given in the stones of the breastplate and the letters inscribed on them, so that those letters either flowed into the order in which they ought to be read, or stood out externally, or it was secretly inspired into the mind and soul of the Priest how they ought to be joined, concerning which see at length Buxtorf in History of Urim and Thummim, ch. 4.

But the authors also make it uncertain what is designated by Urim and Thummim, or what they properly were. Concerning which R. David Kimchi says nothing is certain. Cornelius a Lapide thinks those two names, Urim and Thummim, were inscribed on the breastplate, so that God would reveal things not through them, but while he wore them on the breastplate, concerning which he was consulted through the Pontiff. Nor is Calvin alien to that opinion, R. Solomon and Nachmanides, Baal Hatturim, R. Bechai, R. Isaac Arama, Elias Misrachi, Abarbanel, and others; especially the Cabbalists think that the writing of the name יהוה existed on the breastplate, which Jonathan also indicates in his paraphrase, which has this on this passage. In them was engraved and set forth that great and holy Name of GOD, by which three hundred and ten worlds, or ages, were created, and which was also engraved and set forth upon the foundation stone, through which the Lord of the World sealed the door of the great Abyss from the beginning: Whoever utters that holy Name in a time of calamity is delivered, and hidden things are revealed through it. Add the book Zohar on Exodus f. 105. col. 4. edit. Cremon. URIM are the secret of the shining mirror, and this is the engraving of the letters of that holy name through the mystery of the forty-two letters, by which the Worlds were created, and which were impressed upon it; THUMMIM are the secret of those letters, which were contained in the place of the non-shining mirror, and this consisted of seventy-two letters, the engravings of that mystical holy Name of God. And all these are called URIM and THUMMIM. Finally, R. Abraham Seba the Spaniard in Tzeror Hammor testifies that the greater part of the Sages, whom he calls Cabbalistic, agree that they were holy names. Which opinion seems very plausible to R. Levi Ben Gerson, etc. R. Aben Ezra assigns here not the Tetragrammaton name, but something else fashioned by the work of an artisan, whose meaning R. Azarias explains thus: that he thought Urim and Thummim were something similar to those figures or instruments which the Astro- words for knowing the thought of him who asks: to which opinion Christ. a Castro also seems to return, that Urim and Thummim are Teraphim, two small images through which God gave answers, which were called Urim for clarity and Thummim for truth, Com. in Min. Proph. l. 3. c. 3. Arias Montanus, however, in his Apparatus, thinks that something polished like a mirror was given to Moses, which was to be inserted between both parts of the breastplate through an open side, and was kept there. Others finally, in our judgment the best of all, wish them to be nothing other than the twelve stones themselves arranged in the breastplate, which contained the names of the tribes of Israel, since in the recapitulation Ex. 39, 8, where even the most minute things are not neglected, Urim and Thummim are not specially commemorated, but only the stones themselves, just as on the contrary in Lev. 8, 8 there is no mention of the stones, but only Urim and Thummim are named. Moreover, according to those authors, those stones were called by these names because of the singular use for which they were divinely destined, because God gave answers through their extraordinary coruscation or scintillation, or the prominence of the inscribed letters of the names, of which those that contained the answer would shine above the rest, or through an illumination of the intellect of him who, wearing those gems, invoked God and sought an answer, made according to the covenant and promise of God the institutor (which opinion is approved by Chrysost. orat. 4. contra Jud., Delrio, Serarius, Ribera, and Salianus in Annal. T. 2. ad ann. 2544. Sect. 550. and following, as also by Rivet in Comm. super h. l.), or finally by any other reason through those gems, not by some physical force, but according to an institution of GOD now unknown to us, He gave answers, both clear and certain, complete and perfect. Fagius in the Chaldaic Paraphrase agrees with this opinion. Onkelos with Brentius on this passage, as also Franc. Vatablus, R. Azarias in Meor Enajim c. 50, says: it seems to me very credible that they were the stones of the breastplate themselves, placed within its folds. I am moved to this opinion: first, because those stones are called אבני מלואים, stones of fillings, because they were: מלאות את החושן, filling the breastplate; furthermore, we know that the answer came forth from the stones and their letters, etc. Moreover, the High Priest with Urim and Thummim was a figure of Christ, through whom we have illumination and true perfection, John 1, 16, 18, and in whom shines the truth and clarity which is the fulfillment of the law.

Latin:

Vers. 30. DOCTRINAM ET VERITATEM) Δήλωσιν xąi ἀλήθειαν. Ad verbum: lumina & integritatem, φωτισμὸς xąi τελειώσεις: quomodo & Aquila & Theodotion. In do- ctore, qualis esse debebat supra alios summus Sacerdos, duo requiruntur,scientia & vitæ puritas. Hinc Ægyptii sumsere morem summo Judici appendendi monile, quod vocabant ἀλήθειαν. Id ex gemmis pretiosis admodum fuisse ait Dio- dorus Siculus, ex Sapphiro Ælianus. Loca attulimus ad 1. librum de veritate Religionis Christianæ. Consulebatur V- rim &Thummim aRege autPrincipe in rebus ad statum publi- cum maxime pertinentibus, aut a Synedrio in difficillimis de jure controversiis.

Perperam ergo Vulgata Urim & Thummim interpretatur doctrinam & veritatem: Cajetanus ve- ro, Martin. Delrio disquis. Magic. l. 4.c. 1. Oleaster ad h. l. Riebera ad Malach. 2. ut & Ariasmont. re- ctius ignes seu illuminationes & perfectiones reddunt. Id enim significant ipsæ voces Ebrææ. Ineptus vero est Bellarmin. qui אוּרִים a יוֹרֶה quod in Hiphil est הוֹרָה docuit, deducit, & longe adhuc ineptior, quod תֻּמִּים ab אָמַן verax fuit, deri- vet; l. 4. de Pontif. c. 3. quæ exagitanda Gramma- ticis relinquimus. Aquila reddidit Φωτισμὸς καὶ τελειώσεις Lev. 8, 8. certumque est, voces Ebræas aliter reddi non posse, vi Etymi. Quo abeunt et- iam plerorumque interpretationes. Arabs reddi- dit אלאואר ואלצחאיד dilucidationes & certitudines. Syrus בְּהִירָא וַשׁלְמָא lucidum & perfectum; Samaritanus,elucidationes, & perfectio- nes B. Luth. Licht und Recht, Tusius, Metaphrastes Persicus, & Talmudistæ retinent cum Onkelosio vo- cem Ebræam. Sed id omnium est ineptissimum, quod Papistæ ex eo concludunt: quia Pontifex V.T. in pectorali habuit doctrinam & veritatem; E. Papa cum Ecclesiam docet, errare non potest. A baculo ad angulum. A Pontifice V.T. ad Romanum Papam; a re- sponsis divinitus promissis per Urim & Thummim in pe- ctorali ad responsa e scrinio pectoris Pontificis Romani depromenda, cui nulla immediatæ revelationis facta promissio : a decisionibus casuum dubiorum ad decisio- nem quæstionum fidei. Nam recte agnoscit Grotius in causis dubiis hanc revelationem tantum obtigisse. Adde quod interrogans illic fuerit ipse Sacerdos summus, cui responsum a Deo reddebatur per Urim & Thummim, de quo R. Levi Ben Gerson : totum hoc inserviebat ad excitandam prophetiam, idcirco non consulebantur Urim & Thummim, nisi per Sacerdo- tem. Pontificii autem Romanum Pontificem con- stituunt, non interrogantem de controversiis, sed ad interrogationes oracula reddentem. Toto ergo cœlo hæc distant

Quomodo autem a Deo responsa data fuerint per Urim & Thummim, sententiæ variant. Nonnulli per vocem editam, & a Sacerdote auditam, factum id asseruerunt, in Talmud Hierosolymitano Zoma c. 7. Plerique tamen omnes data fuisse in lapidibus pecto- ralis, & literis illis insculptis, crediderunt, ita ut lite- ræ illæ vel confluxerint in ordinem, quo legi debe- bant, vel exterius prominuerint, vel occulte Sacer- dotis menti & animo inspiratum fuerit, quomodo conjungi debeant, de quo prolixe vid. Buxtorf. in Hist. Urim & Thummim c. 4.

Sed & illud incertum reddunt Autores, quid per Urim & Thummim designetur; vel quid proprie illa fuerint. De quo nihil constare, ait R. David Kimchi. Cornelius a Lapide putat illa ipsa duo no- mina Urim & Thummim inscripta fuisse rationali, ut non per ea, sed dum illa gereret in rationali, Deus revelaret, de quibus consulebatur per Pontificem. Nec alienus ab ea sententia est Calvinus, R. Salomo & Nachmannides, Baal Hatturim, R. Bechai, R. Isaac Arama, Elias Misrachi, Abarbaneel, & alii, inprimis Cabbalistæ existimant nominis יהוה Scripturam extitisse in pectorali, quod indicat etiam Jonathan in paraphrasi, quæ ita habet ad h. l. In eis insculptum erat, & expositum Nomen illud DEI magnum & san- ctum, quo creati sunt trecenti & decem mundi, vel sœcu- la, quodq́; sculptum, & expositum quoq́; erat in lapide fundationis, per quem Dominus Mundi obsignavit osti- um Abyssi magnæ a principio : Quisquis profert illud Nomen sanctum tempore calamitatis, liberatur, & oc- culta per illud revelantur. Adde librum Zohar in E- xodum f. 105. col. 4. edit. Cremon. URIM sunt se- cretum speculi lucentis, & hoc est sculptura literarum nominis illius sancti per mysterium quadraginta dua- rum literarum, quibus creati sunt Mundi, quæq́; impres- sæ fuerunt in eo; THUMMIM sunt secretum illarum literarum, quæ comprehensæ fuerunt in loco speculi non lucentis, & hoc constabat Septuaginta duabus literis, sculpturis illius Nominis Dei sancti mystici. Et omnia hæc vocantur URIM, & THUMMIM. Deniq; testan- tur R. Abraham Seba Hispan. in Tzeror Hammor majorem partem Sapientum, quos vocat Cabbalistico- rum consentire, quod fuerint nomina sancta. Quæ sententia R. Levi Ben Gerson valde plausibilis vide- tur &c. R. Aben Ezra non nomen Tetragramma- tum, sed aliud quid opera artificis elaboratum hî c affignat, cujus mentem R. Azarias ita explicat, quod existimarit, Urim & Thummim simile quid fuisse illis figuris vel instrumentis, quæ faciunt Astro- logi ad sciendum cogitationem ejus, qui interrogat: Quo fere redire etiam videtur Christ. a Castro sen- tentia, quod Urim & Thumim sint Teraphim duo parvula simulacra, per quæ Deus responsa dederit, quæ Urim dicta ob perspicuitatem & Thumim ob veritatem, Com. in Min. Proph. l. 3. c. 3. Proleg. Ari- asmont. vero in apparatu censet aliquid tersum specu- li instar datum fuisse Mosi, quod inter utramq́; partem rationalis per latus apertum inferendum fuerit, ibique servatum sit. Alii denique omnium optime, no- stro judicio, nihil aliud esse volunt, quam ipsos lapi- des duodecim in pectorali dispositos, qui nomina tribu- um Israelis continebant, quandoquidem in α̉νακε- Φαλαιώσει Ex. 39, 8. ubi minutissima etiam haud negliguntur, specialiter non commemorentur Urim, & Thummim, sed ipsi saltim lapides, uti contra Lev. 8, 8. nulla lapidum mentio sit, sed nominatur tantum Urim & Thummim. Dicti autem fuere, secundum illos autores, isti lapides his nominibus, propter usum singularem, cui divinitus destinati, quod Deus per eorundem sive extraordinariam coruscationem, aut scintillationem, vel eminentiam literarum insculpto- rum nominum, quarum eæ, quæ responsum contine- rent, fulgerent supra reliquas, sive per illuminatio- nem intellectus illius, qui gemmas istas gestans Deum invocabat, & responsum petebat, factam ex pacto & promissione Dei institutoris (quæ sententia sese probat Chrysost. orat. 4. contra Jud. Delrioni, Sera- rio, Rieberæ & Saliano in Annal. T. 2. ad ann. 2544. Sect. 550. & seqq. ut & Riveto in Comm. super h. l.) sive deniq; alia quacunq; ratione per illas gemmas, non vi quadam physica, sed juxta institutionem DEI nobis jam incognitam, responsa dederit, & perspicua, & certa, completa, atque perfecta. Cui sententiæ accedit Fagius in Chaldaicam Paraph. Onkelos cum Brentio in h. l. ut & Franc. Vatablus, R. Azarias in Meor Enajim c. 50. valde, inquit, credibile mihi vi- detur fuisse lapides pectoralis ipsos, inditos intra du- plicationes ejus. Movet me ad hanc sententiam: pri- mo quod Lapides illi vocantur אבני מלואים Lapi- des impletionum, quia fuerunt: מלאות את החושן implentes pectorale, adhæc novimus responsum egres- sum esse ex lapidibus, & literis illorum &c. Cæterum Pontifex cum Urim & Thummim figura erat Chri- sti, per quem illuminationem, & perfectionem ve- ram habemus Joh. 1, 16. 18. & in quo relucet veritas & claritas, quæ legis complementum est.

## 28:31
verse 31. YOU SHALL ALSO MAKE THE ROBE OF THE EPHOD.

LXX. ὑποδύτην ποδήρη. The material was silk or wool of a hyacinth color. In terms of form, it corresponded almost to the Roman praetexta, or a garment reaching down to the ankles below the knees without sleeves, of whole and seamless work, except that an opening or hole was left through which the head of the Priest was to be passed; at the bottom edge were arranged alternately pomegranates and golden bells, not golden globes as Ecclus. 45, 11 has with the LXX, but of hyacinth and purple, to which, however, golden threads could have been mixed.

Latin:

vers. 31. FACIES ET TUNICAM SUPER- HUMERALIS.

LXX. ὑποδύτην ποδήρη. Materia fuit sericum vel lana hyacinthini coloris. Formæ ratione re- spondebat fere prætextæ Romanorum, aut vesti ta- lari ultra genua descendenti sine manicis, opere in- tegro, & inconsutili, nisi quod relinquebatur os, sive foramen, quo caput Sacerdotis erat traducendum; in ima pene disposita erant alternis mala punica & tintinnabula aurea, non item globuli aurei ut Eccef. 45, 11. cum LXX. habet, sed ex hyacintho, & diba- pho, cui tamen admixta esse potuere fila aurea.

## 28:33
verse 33. AT THE FEET OF THE SAME ROBE, AND ROUND ABOUT) In the LXX, ὑπο τό κράσπεδον τὲ ἱερέως τὸ λεγόμενον λῶμα. And the LXX do not only translate it thus, which here is שול, but also פּאמה, which is below 39, 31. I would believe that this word is also Egyptian.

Latin:

vers. 33. AD PEDES EJUSDEM TUNICÆ, ET PER CIRCVITVM) In LXX. ὑπο τό κράσπεδον τὲ ἱερέως τὸ λε- γόμενον λῶμα. Neque tantum sic transferunt LXX. quod hic est שול, sed & פּאמה, quod est infra 39, 31. Crediderim & hanc vocem esse Ægyptiacam.

## 28:34
