See what we said above at 20, 5, and what we said about the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 13, § 1, and 21, § 14. Add Plutarch in Pericles not far from the end.

Let those things be compared which we also have said above concerning these matters at Exodus 20:5, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

MISERICORS ET CLEMENS, PATIENS ET MUL- TÆ MISERIATIONIS AC VERAX, QUI CUSTODIS MISERICORDIAM IN MILLIA, QUI AUFERS INI- QUITATEM, SCELERA ATQUE PECCATA] In He- bræo, custodit & aufert: multis autem verbis exprimuntur proprietates Dei beneficæ, quod illæ in Deo multum præva- leant: Jerem. 2, 13. Ideo dicunt Hebræi מדות, sive pro- prietates Dei esse 13. in quibus una tantum sit vindicativa.

NULLUSQUE APUD TE PER SE INNOCENS EST] Græcum: καὶ ὀυ καθαριεῖ τὸν ἔνοχον. In Hebræo: purificando non purificabit, i. e. non parcet, ut hic Chaldæus, nempe contumaci. Tertull. 2. adversus Marcionem: Deus mitior pro rebus edomitis, qui retro austerior pro indomitis.

Malvenda reddidit vacuando non vacuabit. Lud. de Dieu refert ad bonitatem Dei, quia נקה evacuabitur Zach. 5, 3. Omnis jurans evacuabitur, id est, prorsus succidetur, & Es. 3, 26. vacua in terris sedebit, id est, prorsus desolata. Ita hîc evacuando non evacuabit, non prorsus succidet, sed puniet tan- tum in 3. & 4. generationem. Ita Jerem. 30, 11. cap. 46, 28. Caftigabo te ad judicium, id est, moderate, & fuccidendo non fuccidam te, ubi idem verbum, quod hîc habetur. Jonath. perdendo non perdam te. Illam vero interpretationem, nequaquam te ha- bebo impunem, rejicit etiam Mercerus, quia mani- fefta hîc oppofitio inter clementiam, qua erga fuos, & feveritatem, qua erga hoftes ufuruf effet. Conf. Num. 14, 18. Plerique tamen ita exponunt, ut Vulgatæ facile congruat. Innocentem faciendo non innocentem faciet, habet Vatabl. & Oleastr. Pu- rificando non purificabit Montan. abfolvendo non ab- folvet Syr. Pagn. Jun. Tremell. Supplent autem fon- tem vel reum, vel eos, qui non refipifcunt. Qui fen- fus fequentibus congruit.

Verf. eod.

IN TERTIAM ET QUARTAM PROGENIEM] Non in omnibus criminibus, fed in iis, quæ in Dei majeftatem directe feruntur. Qualia funt imprimis defectio a Deo, & cultus falforum Deorum. In iis enim puniendis Deus non illo tantum judiciali, fed & dominico in pofteros jure uti- tur. Vide quæ fupra 20, 5. & quæ diximus de Jure belli ac pacis libro 2. cap. 13. §. 1. & 21. §. 14. Adde Plutarchum in Pe- ricle non longe a fine.

Conferantur, quæ & nos de hifce ad Exod. 20, 5. 6. fupra diximus.

## 34:10
Ver. 10.

WHICH HAVE NEVER BEEN SEEN UPON THE EARTH] The Greeks: ἃ ὀὐ γέγονεν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ. In the Hebrew: which have not been created in all the earth. For divine miracles are as it were certain creations.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

QUÆ NUNQUAM VISA SUNT SUPER TERRAM] Græci: ἃ ὀὐ γέγονεν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ. In Hebræo: quæ non creata funt in omni terra. Miracula enim divina velut crea- tiones quædam funt.

## 34:13
Ver. 13.

DESTROY THEIR ALTARS: BREAK DOWN THE STATUES] Namely in the places which will be under your dominion, as Moses of Coucy explains, and Augustine on Deut. 7:5.

BREAK DOWN THE STATUES] Columns placed separately outside of buildings.

Latin:

Verf. 13.

ARAS EORUM DESTRUE: CONFRINGE STATU- AS] Nempe in locis, quæ veftræ erunt ditionis, ut Mofes de Kotzi explicat, ac Auguftinus ad Deut. 7, 5.

CONFRINGE STATUAS] Columnas feorfim extra ædi- ficia pofitas.

## 34:16
Ver. 16.

NEITHER SHALT THOU TAKE A WIFE FROM THEIR DAUGHTERS FOR THY SONS.

Marriages with the Canaanite nations are prohibited because of the danger of seduction to idolatry, which was likewise done in Deut. 7:3, which is deservedly extended also to other idolatrous nations, by parity of reasoning, with the Holy Spirit Himself as interpreter, 1 Kings 11:11, Ezra 9:1, namely to the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, and Egyptians; if, however, they themselves wished to pass over to the religion of Israel, it was lawful to marry them, even from the Canaanites, but after the first invasion of the Canaanites, for in this, women as well as men had to be slaughtered. As Salmon married Rahab the Canaanite, Matt. 1:5; David married Maachah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, likewise of the Canaanite race, 2 Sam. 3:3; Samson married a Philistine, Judg. 16:1; Boaz married Ruth the Moabitess, Ruth 4:13: and in Deut. 21:12 it is permitted to Israelites to marry women captured in war. Furthermore, it is clear from this passage and similar ones, Deut. 8:3, Jer. 29:6, that it pertains to parents to give their children in marriage, and thus marriages without the consent of parents are void, which is to be noted against the definition of the Council of Trent, session 24. Compare the Examination of the Council of Trent by B. Chemnitz. Furthermore, from this law the Papists conclude that marriages contracted with infidels, as also with heretics, can be annulled, namely because of the danger of seduction, Bonfrère on this passage, Marius on Deuteronomy 7. Concerning which John Dueveldorp, in a special book on not entering into marriage with infidels, proceeding so far as to assert that the union of all those who are joined in our churches is illicit, and praising Gentian Hervet, who asserts that little children begotten from such an illicit union sustain some other penalty beyond the penalty of loss if they die before baptism, in the Paedagogus of Clement of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 8.

But just as the law concerning the complete extirpation of the Canaanites was clearly special; so also the law concerning pronouncing marriages with Gentile women void, just as Ezra chapters 9 and 10 explained this law, was judicial, pertaining to the polity of the Hebrews in the Old Testament, not obligating Christians in the New Testament because the middle wall of partition has been destroyed, Eph. 2:14. Since Christ and the Apostles admit only one cause for divorce, namely adultery, nor does Paul pronounce a marriage already contracted with an infidel void, 1 Cor. 6:12. See B. Gerhard on marriage § 392.

If faith is to be placed in Jerome on chapter 4 of Hosea; it seems to me for that reason the people of Israel made for themselves a calf's head in the wilderness, which they might worship, and Jeroboam the son of Nebat fashioned golden calves, so that what they had learned in Egypt, Ἄπιν καὶ Μνεῦιν, who are worshipped under the figure of oxen, to be gods, this they might preserve in their superstition. Which most acknowledge regarding the golden calf of Aaron, even if it pleases some to say that the calves of Jeroboam were constructed rather in imitation of the Cherubim, which were on the mercy seat. Although indeed Selden in 'De Dis Syris' wishes the calf not to have been Apis or Mnevis, but a gilded ox accustomed to be shown in the disappearance and finding of Osiris, Syntagm. 1, c. 4, about which Plutarch writes in his booklet on Isis; yet the same Selden acknowledges on page 140 that Apis and Mnevis were both living oxen worshipped by the Egyptians with the highest honor. That the worship of oxen among the Egyptians was indeed most ancient is gathered from Gen. 43:31: The Egyptians cannot eat bread with the Hebrews; where Onkelos adds this reason: because the cattle, which the Egyptians worship, the Hebrews eat. And from Exod. 8:26: 'We shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to the Lord our God, but even if we should sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians in their eyes, would they not stone us?' Where it is manifest that the apotheosis of oxen, sheep, and other animals flourished then among the Egyptians. Eusebius traces the worship of Apis and Mnevis from King Aeth, who held the kingdom in the time of Isaac, nay, he reports from Manetho the priest that under King Chous, the second dynasty after the flood, Apis and Mnevis and the Mendesian goat were elevated to gods.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

NEC UXOREM DE FILIABUS EARUM ACCIPIES FILIIS TUIS.

Prohibentur conjugia cum gentibus Cananæis ob periculum feductionis ad idololatriam, quod Deut. 7, 3. itidem factum eft, quod merito etiam ad alias gentes idololatricas, ex paritate rationis, in- terprete ipfo Spir. Sancto, 1. Reg. 11, 11. Esdr. 9, 1. ex- tenditur, utpote ad Moabitidas, Ammonitidas, Idu- mæas, Ægyptias; fi tamen ipfæ ad religionem Ifraël tranfire vellent, licitum erat eas ducere, etiam è Cananæis, fed post primam Cananæorum invafio- nem, nam in hac fœmina æque, ac viri trucidari debuere. Uti Salmon Rahab Cananæam Matth. 1, 5. David Maacham filiam Tholmai regis Gefur iti- dem è Cananæorum genere, 2. Sam. 3, 3. Simfon Philiftæam Judic. 16, 1. Booz Ruth Moabitidem, Ruth. 4, 13. duxit: & Deut. 21, 12. permiffum eft Ifraëlitis bello captas mulieres ducere. Cæterum liquet ex hoc loco & fimilibus, Deut. 8, 3. Jer. 29, 6. quod ad parentes fpectet elocare liberos, adeoque irrita fint conjugia, fine parentum confenfu, quod contra definitionem Conc. Trident. feff. 24. notan- dum. Conf. Exam. Concil. Trident. B. Chemnitii. Porro ex hac lege concludunt Pontificii, matrimo- nia cum infidelibus, ut & hæreticis contracta irritari poffe, ob periculum nempe feductionis, Bonfr. in h. l. Marius in Deuteron. 7. Quo de Joh. Duevel- dorp. peculiari libro de Matrimonio non in- eundo cum infidelibus, eo procedens, ut illici- tam effe copulam omnium eorum, qui in Eccle- fiis noftris copulantur, & Gentianum Hervetum, laudans, parvulos ex tali illicita copula procreatos ultra pœnam damni etiam aliam aliquam pœnam fuftinere, fi ante baptismum decedant, afferen- tem in Pædag. Clem. Alexand libr. 2. cap. 8.

sed uti lex de Canaanis penitus extirpandis plane spe- cialis erat; ita etiam lex de irritis pronunciandis ma- trimoniis cum foeminis gentilibus, quemadmodum hanc legem exposuit Esdr. capp. 9. 10. judicialis fuit ad Politiam Ebræorum in Vet. Testamento pertinens, Christianos in N. Testam. non obligans ob destru- ctum parietem intergerinum, Eph. 2, 14. siquidem Christus & Apostoli unicam causam divortii ad- mittant, nempe adulterium, neque Paulus matri- monium jam contractum cum infideli pronunciat irritum, 1. Hoseæ; videtur id circo mihi populus Israël in solitudine fecisse sibi vitu- li caput, quod coleret, & Jerobeam Filius Nabat vi- tulos aureos fabricatus, ut quod in Ægypto didicerant, Ἄπιν καὶ Μνεῦιν, qui sub figura Boum coluntur, esse Deos, hoc in sua superstitione servarent. Quod ple- rique de vitulo aureo Aaronis agnoscunt, etsi Jero- boami vitulos quibusdam ad imitationem Cherubi- norum potius exstructos dicere libeat, qui in pro- pitiatorio erant. Quanquam vero Seldenus de Dis Syris vitulum non fuisse Apin aut Mnevin velit, sed Bovem deauratum in Osiridis ἀφανισμῷ, & εὑρέσει ostendi solitum, Syntagm. 1, c. 4. quo de Plutarchus libello de Iside; Apin tamen & Mnevin summo ho- nore Ægyptiis cultos Boves fuisse utrosque vivos, idem Seldenus agnoscit pag. 140. Cultum sane boum apud Ægyptios antiquissimum fuisse è Gen. 43, 31. colligitur: Non possunt Ægyptii cum Ebræis comede- re panem; ubi Onkelos causam subnectit hanc: eo quod pecus, quod Ægyptii colunt, Ebræi comedunt. Et ex Exod. 8, 26. Quantam abominationem Ægy- ptiorum sacrificaremus Domino Deo nostro, sed & si sacrificaremus abominationem Ægyptiorum in ocu- lis eorum, nonne lapidarent nos? Ubi manifestum, apotheosin, boum, ovium, aliorumque animalium vi- guisse tum apud Ægyptios. Eusebius à Rege Afeth, qui Isaaci tempore regnum obtinuit, Apis & Mne- vis cultum deducit, imo sub Choo Rege, secunda post diluvium Dynastia, Apin & Mnevim & Mendesium caprum in Deos relatos ex Manethone Sacerdote tradit.

## 34:26
Verse 26.

THE FIRST FRUITS OF THE PRODUCE OF YOUR LAND YOU SHALL OFFER, IN THE HOUSE OF THE LORD YOUR GOD] You shall carry them into the holy house, carrying them on your shoulders in memory of the Egyptian servitude. Maimonides notes that this was done. Add Deut. 26:2.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

PRIMITIAS FRUGUM TERRÆ TUÆ OFFERES, IN DOMO DOMINI DEI TUI] Feres in ædem sacram, succollando in memoriam servitutis Ægyptiæ. Ita factum notat Maimonides. Adde Deut. 26, 2.

## 34:28
Verse 28.

AND HE WROTE ON THE TABLETS THE WORDS OF THE COVENANT, THE TEN.

This is to be understood concerning GOD, with whom Moses made [the covenant], not concerning Moses, and therefore the verb is to be referred to the more remote noun: because it is certain that in the later tablets GOD himself wrote the words of the law immediately, Exod. 34:10, Deut. 10:4.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ET SCRIPSIT IN TABULIS VERBA FOEDERIS DECEM.

De DEO hoc intelligendum, cum quo Moses fecit, non de Mose, adeoque ad nomen remotius re- ferendum est verbum: quia certum est in posterio- ribus tabulis DEUM ipsum immediate verba legis scripsisse, Exod. 34, 10. Deut. 10, 4.

## 34:29
Verse 29.

AND WHEN MOSES DESCENDED FROM MOUNT SINAI] Chrysostom cites this passage in Greek at 2 Cor. 3.

HE DID NOT KNOW THAT HIS FACE WAS HORNED] The LXX: 'that the appearance of the color of his face was glorified.' And shortly after: 'the appearance of the color of his face was glorified.' Because the word קָרַן, from which קֶרֶן (horn) comes, also signifies to radiate. Paul favors this Greek interpretation, 2 Cor. 3:8 and following, where he names it the 'glory of the face' and shows that Moses used a veil to cover it. There is nothing, however, that forbids believing that those rays rose up in the shape of horns, and from that it happened that Mnevis, who was worshipped among the Egyptians with horns, is believed by Aben-Ezra himself at the head of Exodus 2 to be none other than Moses, just as Justin Martyr, or whoever is the author of the Admonition to the Greeks, where in Diodorus Siculus it is Mnevis, put Moses. In which passage the same writer has 'engraphois' instead of 'agepantois', and 'hikanotatoi' instead of 'koinotatoi', with a better sense. Surely Moses was another Joseph, the shepherd of the people. Joseph, however, as we have said, was signified by the name and figure of an ox. But God, when He performed this in Moses, seems to have looked toward the worship of the Calf, as if He were saying: 'You want something bull-shaped. Have it, and test whether you can bear it.' In Macrobius, book 1 of the Saturnalia, ch. 21, at Heliopolis a bull was consecrated to the sun, which they call Noton. Read Mnevis.

But Grotius still fights for the Mosaic horns, bringing forward another reason for them. Namely, that Moses was another Joseph, the shepherd of the people. Joseph, however, as we have said, is signified by the name and figure of an ox. One must be too sharp to penetrate the force of the consequence: Joseph was signified by the figure of an ox. Therefore, Moses killed with bovine horns. Finally, he proposes a conjecture as to why this form was granted to Moses: 'But God, when He performed this in Moses, seems to have looked toward the worship of the Calf, as if He were saying, you want something bull-shaped. Have it and test whether you can bear it.' To have brought these forward is to have solidly refuted them. Steuchus, Bishop of Xifam, observed that we laugh and the Jews themselves execrate whenever they see Moses depicted in our temples with a horned face, as if we thought him some kind of devil. Thomas in 2 Cor. 3 and Sixtus Senensis in book 5 of the Bibliotheca, annot. f. 6, also reject the Vulgate here. Bellarmino on the Triumphant Church, ch. 2. Benedictus, and others.

He wishes to defend the horned Moses of the Vulgate Interpreter. He acknowledges that the word קָרַן also signifies to radiate, and that the LXX rendered it so: with which Jonathan exactly agrees; and that Paul favors this interpretation, 2 Cor. 3:8 ff., where he names it the 'glory of the face' and shows that Moses used a veil to cover it. All of which clearly confirm the genuine sense. And yet he strives to defend the horns of the Vulgate. But by what reasoning? There is nothing, he says, that forbids believing that those rays rose up in the shape of horns, and from that it happened that Mnevis, who was worshipped among the Egyptians with horns, is believed by Aben-Ezra himself at the head of Exodus 2 to be none other than Moses. But shall we derive the splendor with which the face of Moses radiated from the idolatry of the Egyptians? Many things are assumed here without proof. That the Egyptians worshipped Moses, whom they rather detested: That the Egyptians heard about the horns of Moses when he had been with God in the desert, and wished to pursue that glory of Moses with worship: that Mnevis is Moses himself: and that he was taken for Moses by Aben-Ezra because of the horns, etc., as if Aben-Ezra could not have looked to other things: to say nothing of how it could be certain to Aben-Ezra that rays of the shining face of Moses rose up in the form of horns? The Egyptians worshipped Mnevis before the face of Moses radiated: when the golden calf was cast in imitation of that Egyptian worship, if Hier-

Latin:

Vers. 29.

CUMQUE DESCENDERET MOSES DE MON- TE SINAI] Citat hunc locum Græce Chrysostomus ad 2. Cor. 3.

IGNORABAT, QUOD CORNUTA ESSET FACIES SUA] LXX. ὅτι δεδόξασται ἡ ὄψις τῆ χρώ- ματος τῆ προσώπυ ἀυτὲ. Et mox: ἦν δεδοξασμένη ἡ ὄψις τῆ χρώματος τῆ προσώπυ ἀυτῆ. Quia vox קָרַן, unde קֶרֶן cornu, radiare etiam significat. Favet huic Græcæ inter- pretationi Paulus, 2. Cor. 3, 8. & sequentibus, ubi δόξαν προσ ώπε nominat, & ad eam tegendam velo usum Mosem often- dit. Nihil tamen est, quod vetet credere, radios illos surre- xisse in cornuum speciem, indeque factum, ut Mneves, qui apud Ægyptios cum cornubus colebatur, ipsi Aben-Esdræ ad caput Exod. 2. credatur esse non alius à Mose, sicut & Justi- nus Martyr, aut quisquis est scriptor Admonitionis ad Græ- cos, ubi in Diodoro Siculo est Μνεύτην, posuit Mosen. Quo in loco idem scriptor pro ἀγεπάντοις habet ἐγγράφοις, & pro κοινότατοι habet ἱκανώτατοι, sensu meliore. Nimirum Mo- ses alter erat Josephus populi pastor. Josephus autem, ut dixi- mus, bovis nomine ac figura significatus. Videtur autem Deus, cum in Mose hoc præstitit, respexisse ad Vituli cultum, quasi diceret: Vultis aliquid ταυρόμορφον. Habete, & expe- rimini an ferre possitis. Apud Macrobium primo Saturna- lium c. 21. apud Heliopolim taurum soli consecratum, quem Noton cognominant. Lege Mnevin.

Sed pugnat Grotius adhuc pro cornibus Mo- saicis aliam eorum afferens rationem. Nimirum Moses alter erat Josephus, populi Pastor. Josephus au- tem, ut diximus, bovis nomine ac figura significatur. Nimis acutum esse oportet, qui vim penetret con- sequentiæ: Josephus fuit bovis figura significatus. E. Moses cornibus bovinis mactavit. Conjecturam de- nique proponit, cur hæc forma conciliata sit Mosi: Videtur autem Deus, cum in Mose hoc præstitit, re- spexisse ad vituli cultum, quasi diceret, vultus aliquid ταυρόμορφον. Habete & experimini, an ferre possitis. Quæ adduxisse, est solide refutasse. Ridere nos & execrari ipsos Judæos, quoties Mosen in templis nostris cornuta facie depictum vident, quasi nos eum dia- bolum quendam esse putemus, observavit Steuchus Xifamensis Episcopus. Vulgatam etiam hic repro- bant Thomas in 2. Cor. 3. Sixtus Senensis lib. 5. Bibl. annot. f. 6. Bellarminus de Eccles. triumph. cap. 2. Benedictus, & alii.

Cornutum Mosen Vulgarii Interpretis tueri vult. Agnoscit vocem קָרַן significare etiam radia- re, & LXX. ita reddidisse: quibus exacte consonat Jonathan; & favere huic interpretationi Paulum, 2. Cor. 3, 8. feqq. ubi δόξαν προσώπυ nominat, & ad eam tegendam velo usum Mosen ostendit. Quæ omnia luculenter sensum genuinum confirmant. Et tamen cornua Vulgatæ defendere annititur. Qua vero ratione? Nihil est, inquit, quod vetet credere, radios illos surrexisse in cornuum speciem, indeque factum, ut Mneves, qui apud Ægyptios cum cornibus colebatur, ipsi Aben-Esdræ ad cap. Exod. 2. credatur esse non alius à Mose. At num ab Ægyptiorum ido- lolatria splendorem, quo radiavit facies Mosis, di- fcemus? Multa hic precario assumuntur. Ægyptios coluisse Mosen, quem detestati potius sunt: Ægy- ptios de cornibus Mosis, cum in deserto apud Deum egisset, inaudisse, eamque gloriam Mosis cultu pro- sequi voluisse: Mnevem esse ipsum Mosen: & pro Mose ab Aben-Esdra habitum ob cornua &c. ac si non alia respicere potuerit Aben-Esdra: ut ta- ceam, unde Aben-Esdræ constare potuerit, quod sub cornuum forma radii splendentis faciei Mosis sur- rexerint? Mnevin coluere Ægyptii, antequam Mo- sis facies radiaret: quum vitulus aureus conflatus fuerit ad imitationem cultus illius Ægyptii, si Hie-

## 35:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXV. The contribution of the Israelites.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXV. Israelitarum contributio.

## 35:3
Verse 3. YOU SHALL NOT KINDLE A FIRE IN ALL YOUR DWELLINGS ON THE SABBATH DAY] From this, drawing an argument from the light to the grave, i.e., from the lesser to the greater, the teachers of the Hebrews taught that public punishments are not to be carried out on the Sabbath.

The kindling of fire for cooking food is prohibited, Ex. 16:24, as are other servile tasks, such as the gathering of wood, Num. 15, the carrying of burdens, Jer. 17:21, Neh. 13:15, 19, and traveling for the sake of business, Ex. 16:29, are prohibited. Works of necessity, however, were excepted, such as when a fire had to be kindled because of the cold, or to provide light (which the Rabbis also prohibited too superstitiously), or when resisting an enemy, 2 Macc. 2:41, such as also the watering of cattle, their rescue if they have fallen into a pit, Matt. 12, Mark 2, Luke 6, and works of charity, such as the preparation of medicines, food, and the cooking of broths for the use of the sick, etc. Furthermore, that not all things which were prohibited on the Sabbath were also prohibited on the greater feast days outside the Sabbath is clear from the fact that those things which pertained to either buying or cooking food were permitted on feast days, Exod. 12, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NON SUCCENDETIS IGNEM IN OMNI- BUS HABITACULIS VESTRIS PER DIEM SABBA- TI] Hinc ducto argumento à levi ad grave, i. e. à minori ad majus, docuere Hebræorum magistri, pœnas publicas in Sab- batis non exercendas.

Prohibetur succensio ignis ad coquendum ci- bum Ex. 16, 24. ut & alia servilia munera, utpo- te lignorum collectio, Num. 15. onerum bajulatio, Jer. 17, 21. Nehem. 13, 15. 19. iter faciendum negotiorum causa, Ex. 16, 29. prohibita sunt. Opera tamen ex- cipiebantur necessitatis, quale erat, quum ob bru- mam ignis accendendus erat, vel ad præbendum lu- men (quod nimis superstitiose etiam Rabbini pro- hibebant) cum hosti resistendum 2. Maccab. 2, 41. qualia etiam pecorum adaquatio, eorum si in fove- am inciderint, eductio Matth. 12. Marc. 2. Luc. 6. & opera Charitatis, utpote præparatio pharmacorum, ciborum, & jusculorum ad ægrorum usus coctio &c. Cæterum non omnia, quæ in Sabbatho prohibe- bantur, etiam diebus festis majoribus prohibita fuisse extra Sabbatum inde liquet, quod quæ ad cibos seu emendos, seu coquendos spectabant permissa fuerint festis diebus Exod. 12, 16.

## 35:21
Verse 21.

WITH A MOST READY AND DEVOTED MIND) In the Hebrew: whom his heart lifted up, whom his Spirit made willing (the Chaldean says 'filled'). Those who are high-hearted and full of Spirit are called liberal.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

MENTE PROMTISSIMA ATQVE DEVOTA) In Hebræo: quem extulit cor suum, quem spontaneum fecit (Chaldæus implevit) Spiritus ejus. Celsi corde, & pleni Spiritu dicuntur liberales.

## 35:22
Verse 22.

BRACELETS) כומז, if we believe the Hebrews, is neither a bracelet, nor, as the Latin translates elsewhere, a small lamprey, but a woman's undergarment usually adorned with gold and gems.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

DEXTRALIA) כומז, si Hebræis credimus, neque dextrale est, neque ut alibi Latinus vertit, murænula, sed subligar muliebre auro plerumque & gemmis ornatum.

## 36:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVI. The construction of the Tabernacle.

Verse 1.

THAT THEY MIGHT KNOW HOW TO WORK SKILLFULLY THE THINGS WHICH ARE NECESSARY FOR THE USES OF THE SANCTUARY) In the Hebrew: For the work of the ministry of holiness. The Septuagint: πάντα τὰ ἔργα κατὰ ἅγια καθήκοντα, where you might read more correctly: πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἅγια κατὰ τὰ καθήκοντα, especially since some books have the last three words, but with ἅγια omitted.

Verse the same. AND WHAT THE LORD COMMANDED.

ALthough these things have already been recounted above, here they are nevertheless repeated anew in the execution of the command. Nor is that prolixity idle. [For it shows how obediently the Israelites procured everything that pertained to the worship of GOD, and how much God values true worship instituted by Himself: and furthermore, that composition of the tabernacle was a shadowy sermon concerning the Son of GOD about to be incarnate and to intercede with the Father for the human race. Whence this commemoration ought not to seem useless to us either. Cornelius alleges here the own baseness of his interpreter at verse 14, writing thus: Our interpreter in this repetition does not render word for word, but the sense, and briefly embraces the Hebrew repetition, and also fetches certain things by way of explanation from what was said above: For this is permitted to the liberty, talent, and disposition of the interpreter. But these things were to be censured and amended, not indeed commended or excused. For who will approve of such license in the translation of Holy Scripture, by which some things are omitted, and others are added to the text?

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVI. Tabernaculi constructio.

Vers. 1.

UT SCIRENT FABRE OPERARI QVÆ IN USUS SANCTVARII NECESSARIA SUNT) In Hebræo: Ad opus ministerii sanctimoniæ. LXX. πάντα τὰ ἔργα κατὰ ἅγια καθήκοντα, ubi rectius legas; πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἅγια κατὰ τὰ καθήκοντα Præsertim cum tres postremas voces, sed omisso ἅγια, habeant libri aliqui.

Vers. eod. ET QUÆ PRÆCEPIT DOMINUS.

ETsi hæc superius jam recensita sint, hîc tamen denuo illa in exequutione præcepti repetuntur. Nec otiosa est ista prolixitas. [Ostendit enim quam obedienter Israëlitæ omnia, quæ ad cultum DEI pertinebant, procurarint, & quanti faciat Deus cultum verum à seipso institutum: ac fuit præterea illa tabernaculi compositio umbratilis concio de Filio DEI incarnando & intercessuro apud Patrem pro genere humano. Unde nec nobis hæc commemoratio frustranea videri debet. Allegat hic propriam turpitudinem interpretis sui Cornelius ad v. 14. ita scribens: Noster interpres in hac repetitione non reddit verbum verbo, sed sensum, repetitionemque Hebræam breviter complectitur, quædam etiam per explicationem è supra dictis accersit: Hoc enim permittitur libertati, ingenio & dispositioni interpretis. Sed hæc reprehendenda & emendanda, non vero commendanda, aut excusanda erant. Quis enim talem licentiam in Scripturæ S. translatione probabit, qua nonnulla omittuntur, alia adjiciuntur textui?

## 36:6
NEITHER MAN, NOR WOMAN SHOULD OFFER ANYTHING MORE FOR THE WORK OF THE SANCTUARY) Moses did what was the duty of a wise Prince by imposing a limit on the completion of things.

Latin:

NEC VIR, NEC MULIER QVICQVAM OFFERAT ULTRA IN OPERE SANCTUARII) Fecit Moses quod sapientis erat Principis modum imponendo rerum confectioni.

## 36:8
Ver. 8.

AND ALL THE WISE-HEARTED MEN MADE TO FINISH THE WORK OF THE TABERNACLE) There is a transposition here in the Greek: for those things follow here which in the Hebrew and Latin make ch. 39, up to v. 30. Then furthermore those things which we have here in the Hebrew and Latin up to verse 37. Afterwards certain additions and verse 21 of ch. 38. Then chapter XXXVII, where at the beginning certain things are missing in the Greek. To the end of that chapter is added the mention of the laver. After that, those things which are for us in ch. XXXVIII, 24 to the end. Then after certain additions follow those things which we have in XXXIX, 31 to the very end. But the last chapter of the book is in the Greeks as it is in the Hebrews and Latins. Furthermore, there is a wonderful discrepancy in the particles of these parts.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

FECERUNTQVE OMNES CORDE SAPIENTES AD EXPLENDUM OPUS TABERNACULI) Est hic transpositio in Græco: sequuntur enim hic illa quæ in Hebræo ac Latino faciunt c. 39. usque ad v. 30. Deinde porro ea, quæ in Hebræo & Latino hic habemus ad versum 37. Postea additamenta quædam & versus 21. c. 38. Inde caput XXXVII. ubi in initio quædam desunt in Græco. Fini ejus capitis addita labri mentio. Post id ea quæ sunt nobis cap. XXXIIX. 24. ad finem. Deinde post additamenta quædam sequuntur ea, quæ habemus XXXIX. 31. ad finem usque. Caput vero libri ultimum in Græcis est, ut in Hebræis & Latinis Præterea in harum partium particulis mira discrepantia.

## 37:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVII. The construction of the ark of the covenant. Of the table, of the candlestick. Of the altar of incense, and the composition of the incense.

AND BEZALEEL MADE THE ARK.

IN this chapter, it treats first of those things which were to be placed inside the Holy of Holies, then of those which were to be placed in the holy place. How the ark of the covenant was prepared, the mercy seat with the Cherubim: likewise the golden table, the golden candlestick, and also the altar of incense, as well as the oil of sanctification and the sacred incense.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVII. Arcæ fœderis fabrica. Mensæ candelabri. Aræ thymiamatis, & compositio thymiamatis.

FECIT AUTEM BEZALEEL ET ARCAM.

IN hoc capite primum de iis agitur, quæ intrà Sanctum Sanctorum, deinde de his, quæ in loco sancto collocari debebant. Quomodo parata arca fœderis, propitiatorium cum Cherubim: Mensa item aurea, candelabrum aureum, nec non altar thymiamatis, ut & oleum sanctificationis & thymia ma sacrum.

## 38:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVIII. The construction of the altar of burnt offering, of the bronze laver, and of the court. The sum of the expenses.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIIX. Fabrica altaris holocausti, Labri ænei, & atrii. Summa impensarum.

## 38:8
Ver. 8. HE ALSO MADE THE BRONZE LAVER WITH ITS BASE.

IN this chapter are recounted those things which were to be placed outside the tabernacle, namely the altar of burnt offerings, the bronze laver, and the court of the tabernacle with its veil. The craftsmen are commended, and the huge weight of gold, silver, and bronze spent on the tabernacle is enumerated. The bronze laver is said to have been prepared from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle: Tremellius and Junius render it as steel with Kimchi, but the common opinion is better, because the material of steel easily contracts rust if water is kept in it, and therefore it was less suitable for that basin destined for washings. And R. Abraham Ben-Ezra is the authority that bronze mirrors were in use among Jewish women: which were also not unusual among other nations, as Pliny testifies, book XXXIII, ch. 19, book XXXIV, ch. 17.

Ver. same. WHICH KEPT WATCH AT THE DOOR OF THE TABERNACLE]

Namely by turns, not the same ones perpetually: as also the men. Num. 3:25. These women, having renounced the care of their own adornment, brought their instruments for sacred uses. See what is at Luke 2:37.

Those women, according to the Hebrew text, are said to have gathered in troops at the door of the tabernacle, because they betook themselves there with wonderful alacrity and in competition, and brought their mirrors, as Philo relates in book III of the Life of Moses. Whence it is rashly snatched away by the Papists and Grotius to women serving the tabernacle in a certain order, for which ministry there was no need when the tabernacle was not yet erected, and why would those women at least have contributed mirrors, who were serving the tabernacle, and not others? But it is not unlike the truth, as some advise, that that laver was not cast entirely from the mirrors, but that they were inserted and woven into it all around, for the sake of elegance and splendor, just as golden cups are inlaid with diamonds.

Latin:

Vers. 8. FECIT ET LABRUM ÆNEUM CUM BASI SUA.

HOc capite recensentur, quæ extra tabernacu- lum collocanda erant, altare nempe holocau- storum, labrum æneum & atrium tabernaculi cum velo suo. Commendantur artifices, & enumeratur ingens pondus auri, argenti & æris in tabernacu- lum insumti. De speculis mulierum, quæ excuba- bant in ostio tabernaculi, labrum æneum paratum dicitur: Chalybeum id quidem cum Kimchio red- dunt Tremellius & Junius, sed præstat communis sententia, quia chalybis materia facile contrahit rubiginem, si in ea aqua asservatur, adeoque ad con- cham illam lotionibus destinatam minus idonea erat. Et specula ænea Judæis mulieribus in usu fuisse autor est R. Abraham Ben-Ezra: quæ etiam apud alias gentes non inusitata, teste Plinio libr. XXXIII. c. 19. libr. XXXIV. c. 17.

Vers. eod. QVÆ EXCVBABANT IN OSTIO TABERNACU- LI]

Nempe per vices, non eædem perpetuo: ut & viri. Num. III, 25. Hæ mulieres abdicata cultus sui cura, instrumenta sua in sacros usus adferebant. Vide quæ ad Lucam II, 37.

Mulieres illæ juxta Ebræum textum dicuntur turmatim concurrisse ad ostium tabernaculi, quod mira alacritate, ac certatim eo se contulerint, & specula sua attulerint, ut refert Philo lib. III. de vita Mosis. Unde temere ad mulieres id abripitur à Pontificiis & Grotio ordine certo tabernaculo in- servientes, quo ministerio tabernaculo tum non- dum erecto opus non erat, & cur illæ saltem mulie- res contulissent specula, quæ inserviebant taberna- culo, non aliæ? Non autem absimile vero est, quod nonnulli monent, labrum illud non conflatum fuisse ex speculis totum, sed ea circumcirca ipsi fuisse in- serta & intexta, elegantiæ & splendoris gratia, uti calices aurei intexuntur adamantibus.

## 38:10
Ver. 10. TWENTY BRONZE PILLARS WITH THEIR BASES.

The Vulgate is wrong in this way. For in the Hebrew it is held thus: Twenty pillars with their bronze bases: for the bases, not the pillars, were bronze. So also in verse 12, in the Vulgate, 'ten pillars with BRONZE bases' is rashly added. For it is not held in the original text that the pillars were bronze: as the pillars of the tabernacle, so also those of the court were not bronze, but wooden, made of cedar or of Shittim wood, as Philo rightly observed, whom Cornelius rashly contradicts, contending that these were bronze based on the erroneous Vulgate version in chapter 38, 10, 12.

Vers. 10. THE CAPITALS OF THE PILLARS)

Hooks to which the skin was flayed from the cattle, called וָוִים from a figure similar to the letter of that name.

Latin:

Vers. 10. COLUMNÆ ÆNEÆ VIGINTI CUM BA- SIBUS SUIS.

Perperam ita Vulgata. Nam in Ebræo sic habetur: Columnæ viginti cum basibus suis æneis: bases enim, non columnæ fuerunt æneæ. Sic etiam vers. 12. in Vulgata temere additur columnæ decem cum basibus ÆNEÆ. Non enim in Originali textu habetur, quod æneæ fuerint columnæ: Ut ta- bernaculi columnæ, ita & atrii non æneæ fuere, sed ligneæ è cedro factæ, vel lignis Setim, ut recte observavit Philo, cui temere contradicit Cornelius, has æneas fuisse ex erronea versione vulgata c. 38, 10. 12. contendens.

Vers. 10. CAPITA COLUMNARUM)

Unci ad quos pecudibus cutis detrahebatur, dicti וָוִים a figura simili ejus nominis literæ.

## 38:24
Vers. 24. AND WHAT WAS OFFERED IN DONATIONS.

In the Hebrew: And it was to be moved or lifted. Therefore, it does not concern all donations, but the תנופה, the elevation, or voluntary offering, which was to be moved before the Lord toward the four corners of the world, according to the customary manner of the Levites.

ACCORDING TO THE MEASURE OF THE SANCTUARY.

In the Hebrew: according to the shekel of the Sanctuary. The sum is 29 Kikar (in the Vulgate, talents) and 730 shekels. According to the calculation of Georgius Agricola in his book on the price of metals, 29 Kikar of gold make 664,912 Hungarian florins, since indeed one Kikar or talent corresponds to 22,928 Hungarian florins, which we call Ducats. Let 730 shekels be added, which correspond to 5,579 Hungarian gold pieces; the total sum of gold is 670,491. To which are added one hundred talents of silver, worth 203,600 Hungarian florins, and seventy talents of bronze, which make 2,036 Hungarian [florins] according to the same calculation. When these are taken collectively, there result about 18 tons of gold, as we call them. A smaller sum, however, results according to a truer calculation: about eight tons of gold. For a talent contains 3,000 shekels, from which result 87,730 gold shekels, and since the proportion of gold to silver is now about twelvefold, these are equivalent to 1,052,760 silver shekels, which make 526,380 imperials or thalers, which they call Joachimsthalers. The sum of silver shekels is 301,775, which make 150,887 and a half imperials, and together with the gold 677,267 and a half Joachimsthalers: if bronze is added to these, the value of which is less certain due to the uncertain quality of the bronze, the sum will approach nearly 8 tons of gold. Retaining Agricola's calculation of the bronze, so that its value was 4,072 thalers: to which the sums of gold and silver being added, there result 681,339 Joachimsthalers, but 778,673 Meissen florins. From which it is to be gathered how generous the divine blessing was upon the people even in Egyptian pressures, how liberal their contribution to sacred things, and how magnificent the structure of this portable temple. And yet other things have not yet come into the census, namely, those most precious gems which were applied to the garments of the High Priest. But that a talent contains 3,000 shekels is sufficiently manifest in this place: because those who were counted here were 603,550 in number. and since each one paid half a shekel, there result from that 301,775 shekels, which the Holy Spirit sets forth in this way, that they were 100 talents and 1,775 shekels: from which it is left that one hundred talents make 300,000 shekels, and therefore one talent will be 3,000 shekels. And since in Ez. 25, 12 a mina is said to have contained 60 shekels, a talent ought to have had 50 minas.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET QUOD OBLATUM EST IN DONA- RIIS.

In Ebræo: Et fuit movenda vel levanda. Non ergo de omnibus donariis, sed de תנופה, elevatione, seu voluntaria oblatione, quæ coram Domino mo- venda erat versus quatuor mundi plagas, more Le- vitarum consueto, agitur.

AD MENSURAM SANCTUARII.

In Ebræo: ad siclum Sanctuarii. Summa 29. Kikar (in vulg. talentorum) & 730. siclorum. Juxta computum Georgii Agricolæ in libro de pretio Me- tallor. auri, 29. Kikar efficiunt florenos Ungari- cos 664912. uti nempe uni Kikar vel talento re- spondent 22928. floreni Ungarici, quos Ducatos vocamus. Addantur sicli 730. qui respondent Ungaricis aureis 5579. tota summa auri est 670491. Quibus accedunt argenti talenta centum, 203600. florenos Ungaricos valentia, & septuaginta talen- ta æris, quæ efficiunt juxta eundem computum 2036. Ungaricos. Quibus collectim acceptis prodeunt circiter 18. tonnæ auri, quas vocamus. Minor tamen summa juxta veriorem computum prodit: octo circiter tonnarum auri. Nam talen- tum continet 3000. siclos, unde prodeunt aurei sicli 87730. & quum proportio auri ad argentum nunc sit duodecupla circiter, æquivalent hi siclis argenti 1052760. qui efficiunt 526380. imperiales vel thaleros, quos Joachimicos nuncupant. Ar- genti summa siclorum est 301775. qui faciunt im- periales 150887. ac dimidium, ac cum auro con- junctim 677267. Joachimicos & dimidium: qui- bus si æs addatur, cujus valor ob incertam æris præstantiam minus certus est, summa accedet pro- pemodum ad 8. tonnas auri. Retenta Agricolæ computatione æris, ut valor ejus fuerit 4072. tale- rorum: quibus summæ auri & argenti additis prodeunt 681339. Joachimici, floreni verò Misni- ci 778673. Unde colligere est quam larga fuerit populi in Ægyptiacis etiam pressuris divina bene- dictio, quam liberalis ejusdem ad res sacras colla- tio, & quam magnifica templi istius portatilis stru- ctura. Nec tamen adhuc in censum venerunt alia, sc. gemmæ istæ pretiosissimæ, quæ ad vestes Pontificis adhibitæ fuere. Quod autem talentum contineat 3000. siclos, satis manifestum hoc loco: quia qui hîc censi sunt fuere numero 603550. & quum unusquisq; solverit dimidium siclum, prode- unt inde 301775. sicli, quos ita effert Spiritus S. quod fuerint 100. talenta & 1775. sicli: unde relin- quitur, centum talenta efficere 300000. siclos, ideoque unum talentum erit 3000. siclorum. Et quum Ez. 25, 12. mina 60. siclos continuisse dicatur, talentum oportuit habuisse 50. minas.

## 38:25
Ver. 25. BUT IT WAS OFFERED BY THOSE WHO PASSED TO THE NUMBER.

The Vulgate wrongly renders it thus, as if gold had been offered according to the number of persons, for its offering was purely voluntary: but concerning the silver it is said that they contributed according to the number of persons, namely half a shekel for each head: nor can the Papists excuse the Vulgate: because it itself clearly distinguishes the offering of silver, adding about it thus: THERE WERE BESIDES one hundred talents of silver. The Hebrew text, on the contrary, has it thus, as Cornelius admits: And the silver (namely the number or weight) from those numbered of the Synagogue (was) one hundred talents, one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five according to the weight of the sanctuary, half a shekel for each head (they offered). And so I also read in the Chaldean, the LXX, and as Cornelius acknowledges, it is recognized by the Hebrews, as also by Tostatus and Lipomanus. It is added: who were passing to the registered (that is, who were being registered) from twenty years and above, (of whom there were) six hundred thousand, three thousand, five hundred and fifty. And one hundred Kikar of silver were spent in casting the bases of the sanctuary, and the bases of the veil, one hundred (those) bases were made from one hundred Kikar. For each base had a Kikar. And from one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five (shekels) he made the hooks of the columns, (from which hooks the curtains hung) and he covered their heads (of the columns) and filleted them (that is, he overlaid them with silver, for the sake of ornament, the heads of the columns: and he made silver threads or silver rings, which, surrounding the columns, were an ornament to them.) as Osiander rightly corrects the Vulgate.

Latin:

Vers. 25. OBLATUM AUTEM EST AB HIS, QUI TRANSIERUNT AD NUMERUM.

Perperam Vulgata ita reddit, ac si aurum ob- latum fuerit ad numerum personarum, nam ejus oblatio fuit mere voluntaria: de argento vero dici- tur, quod juxta numerum personarum contulerint dimidium nempe siclum capita singula: nec excu- sare possunt Vulgatam Papistæ: quia distinguit ipsa aperte oblationem argenti, de ea ita subjungens: Fuerunt PRÆTEREA centum talenta argenti. Ebræus contra textus ita habet, fatente Cornelio: Et argenti (sc. numerus vel pondus) à numeratis Synagogæ (fuit) centum talenta, mille septingenti se- ptuaginta quinq; juxta pondus sanctuarii, dimidium sicli singula capita (obtulerunt.) Atque ita etiam legi in Chald. LXX. & ab Ebræis, ut & à Tostato & Lipo- manno agnoscit Cornelius. Additur: qui transibant ad recensitos (id est, qui recensebantur) à viginti annis & supra, (quorum fuerunt) sexcenta millia, tria millia, quingenti & quinquaginta. Et insumpta sunt centum Kikar argenti in fundendis basibus san- ctuarii, & basibus veli, centum (illæ) bases fiebant de centum Kikar. Kikar enim qualibet basis habe- bat. Et de mille septingentis, & septuaginta quinque (siclis) fecit clavos columnarum, (ex quibus clavis cortinæ pendebant) & operuit capita earum (co- lumnarum) & filavit eas (id est, argento obduxit, ornatus gratia, capita columnarum: fecitque ar- gentea fila seu argenteos circulos, quæ, ambientes columnas, ornamento ipsis essent.) ut recte emen- dat Vulg. Osiander.

## 38:29
Ver. 29. ALSO OF BRONZE WERE OFFERED SEVENTY TALENTS, TWO THOUSAND AND FOUR HUNDRED SHEKELS.

There is a great error of calculation here in the Vulgate. Which Cajetan, Lipomanus, and Vatablus acknowledged, but the new correctors established by Papal authority did not amend, and Grotius passed over. They, from the Hebrew with the LXX and the Chaldean, read 70 talents and two thousand and four hundred shekels, just as B. Luther also translated. But because in that way more talents of silver would have been offered than of bronze, and 60 bronze columns could not have been made with so little bronze, along with the bases, altars, and bronze instruments in chapter 27, 10, the Hebrew text seems to be read and understood by Marius and Cornelius thus: there were offered of bronze 70 talents and two thousand (namely talents, as the Hebrews are accustomed to place the greater number after the lesser) and 400 shekels, so that there were 2,070 talents with 400 shekels, which sum ascends, according to the calculation of Marius, to 258,766 pounds and eight ounces: since there are 12 ounces to a pound, to transport which weight, if 3,000 pounds are given to each wagon or transport carriage, about 86 wagons would be required; or if 2,500 pounds are carried by a wagon, one hundred wagons would be needed. Whence, since at least 6 wagons were given to the Gershonites and Merarites to carry the vessels of the tabernacle in Num. 7, 3, Cornelius thinks the rest were imposed on others or carried by the Levites themselves: for which difficulty there is no need, if the common reading is retained, which the Hebrew punctuation suggests concerning 70 talents and 2,400 shekels. For six wagons are abundantly sufficient to transport those. And Cornelius falsely assumes from the Vulgate version of this chapter 38, 10 and 12 that the columns themselves were also of bronze, of which there is nothing in the Hebrew text. Wherefore there is no reason why one should depart from the common reading, indeed since the Athnach accent makes a manifest distinction of the 70 talents from the remaining numbers, which refer to the shekels, it must be said that the offering of bronze was only 70 talents and 2,400 shekels, therefore the bronze was also not distributed per capita (which is said of the silver) but was תנופה an elevation or voluntary offering, from which it is said here that only the bases of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation were made, and the bronze altar, and the bronze grate which was for it, and all the vessels of the altar, with no mention of the columns made even in the Vulgate version itself.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ÆRIS QUOQUE OBLATA SUNT TA- LENTA SEPTUAGINTA, DUO MILLIA ET QUADRINGENTI SUPRA SICLI.

Grandis hic est error calculi in Vulgata. Quem agnovit Cajetanus, Lipomanus ac Vatablus, sed non emendarunt novi correctores autoritate Pontifi- cia constituti, ac præteriit Grotius. Illi ex E- bræo cum LXX. & Chaldæo legunt 70. talenta & duo millia & quadringentos siclos, quemadmodum etiam transtulit B. Lutherus. Quia vero ita plu- ra fuissent talenta argenti oblata, quam æris, & tam pauco ære 60. columnæ æneæ confici non po- tuere, cum basibus, altaribus, & instrumentis æneis cap. 27, 10. Mario & Cornelio ita legendus & acci- piendus videtur textus Ebræus, oblata sunt æris ta- lenta 70. & duo millia (sc. talenta, uti solent Ebræi majorem numerum postponere minori) & 400. sicli, ut fuerint 2070. talenta cum 400. siclis, quæ summa ascendit, juxta calculum Marii ad 258766. libras & uncias octo: cum libræ 12. unciarum sunt, cui ponderi vehendo, si dentur singulis plaustris vel vectoriis curribus libræ 3000. plaustra 86. cir- citer requirentur; vel si 2500. libræ, vehantur plau- stro, centum opus fuerit plaustris. Unde quum saltim 6. plaustra Gersonitis & Maranitis data sint ad vehenda vasa tabernaculi Num. 7, 3. aliis impo- sita, aut ab ipsis Levitis portata reliqua censet Cor- nelius: qua vero difficultate opus non est, si commu- nis lectio retineatur, quam interpunctio Ebræa suggerit de 70. talentis & 2400. siclis. Ad ea enim subvehenda abunde sufficiunt sex plaustra. Et falso supponit Cornelius è versione vulgata cap. hujus 38, 10. & 12. columnas ipsas æneas etiam fuisse, quo de in Ebræo textu nihil habetur. Quapropter non est causa, cur à communi lectione discedatur, imo cum accentus Athnach manifestam faciat ta- lentorum 70. distinctionem à reliquis numeris, qui ad siclos referuntur, dicendum quod æris oblatio 70. talentorum tantum fuerit & siclorum 2400. ideo etiam non per capita distributum fuit æs (quod de argento dicitur) sed erat תנופה elevatio seu voluntaria oblatio, è qua hic dicuntur solum factæ bases ostii tabernaculi conventus, & altare æne- um, & cribrum æneum, quod erat ei, & omnia vasa altaris, nulla mentione columnarum facta etiam in ipsa vulgata versione.

## 39:1 Argument
CHAP. XXXIX. The making of the Priestly vestments, and the offering of all things that were prepared.

Latin:

CAP. XXXIX. Confectio vestitus Sacerdotalis, & oblatio omni- um, quæ pansa erant.

## 39:15
Vers. 15. THEY MADE UPON THE BREASTPLATE ALSO CHAINS.

These verses 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 are more concise, and they omit not a few things which are contained in the Hebrew truth. Indeed, besides the contraction of others, in v. 18 the material of three verses is comprised by the Vulgate interpreter. But those things are rightly amended by Osiander, and have been properly translated by B. Luther. Furthermore, since no mention is made of Urim and Thummim, it is not without reason concluded that they were nothing other than the arrangements of the gems in the breastplate.

Latin:

Vers. 15. FECERUNT IN RATIONALI ET CA- TENULAS.

VErsus hi 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. contractiores sunt, nec pauca omittunt, quæ in Ebræa veri- tate habentur. Siquidem præter aliorum contra- ctionem in v. 18. trium versuum materia compre- hensa sit à Vulgario interprete. Recte autem emendantur illa ab Osiandro, & probe translata sunt à B. Luthero. Cæterum cum nulla mentio fiat Urim & Thumim, non immerito colligitur, ea nihil aliud fuisse, quam dispositiones gemmarum in pectorali.

## 39:29
Vers. 29. AND THEY WROTE UPON IT WITH THE WORK OF AN ENGRAVER IN STONE

Such as ἔντυπα are accustomed to be. For which reason Salmasius, a man of the greatest reading, thinks that here in the LXX it should be read, not ἐκτετυπωμένα, but ἐντετυπωμένα.

Latin:

Vers. 29. SCRIPSERUNTQVE IN EA OPERE GEMMARIO)

Qualia solent esse ἔντυπα. Quam ob causam hic in LXX. vir maximæ lectionis Salmasius legendum putat, non ἐκτετυ- πωμένα, sed ἐντετυπωμένα.

## 39:31
Ver. 31. THE WORK OF THE TABERNACLE AND OF THE TENT OF THE TESTIMONY WAS THEREFORE FINISHED.

In Hebrew: The whole work of the dwelling (namely) of the tabernacle of the congregation was therefore finished: that is, whatever was required for the structure of the divine dwelling, together with all the furnishings. Moreover, the children of Israel are said to have made everything which God had commanded Moses, because it was done at the expense and in the name of the children of Israel, and the Israelites made it through their craftsmen. For what anyone does through another, he is seen to have done by himself.

Latin:

Vers. 31. PERFECTUM EST IGITUR OMNE OPUS TABERNACULI ET TECTI TESTI- MONII.

In Ebræo: Perfectum est igitur omne opus ha- bitaculi (nimirum) tabernaculi congregationis : id est, quicquid ad structuram habitaculi divini re- quirebatur, una cum tota supellectile. Fecisse autem dicuntur filii Israël cuncta, quæ præceperat Deus Mosi, quia sumtibus, & nomine filiorum Israel ea facta sunt, & Israëlitæ ea fecerunt per artifices suos. Quod enim quis per alium facit, per seipsum fecisse videtur.

## 39:42
Ver. 42. THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL OFFERED. The children of Israel did more correctly. For it is a matter of the making of the vestments, not the offering.

Latin:

Vers. 42. OBTULERUNT FILII ISRAEL. Rectius fecerunt filii Israël. Nam de vestium confectione, non oblatione agitur.

## 39:43
Ver. 43. AND WHEN MOSES SAW ALL THAT WAS FINISHED, HE BLESSED THEM.

In Hebrew: And Moses saw all the work (of the tabernacle) and behold they had done it (plainly) just as the Lord had commanded, so they had done, and he blessed them, i.e., not the tabernacle and its parts, concerning the consecration and sanctification of which the following chapter treats. But the Israelites, both the craftsmen who had faithfully performed their duty, and the whole people who had contributed generously and had willingly promoted the work: having prayed for divine blessing and reward for them.

Latin:

Vers. 43. QUÆ POSTQUAM MOSES CUNCTA VIDIT COMPLETA, BENEDIXIT EIS.

In Ebræo: Et vidit Moses omne opus (taber- naculi) & ecce fecerant id (plane) sicut præceperat Dominus, ita fecerant, & benedixit eis, sc. non taber- naculo & partibus ejus, de quorum consecratione & sanctificatione sequenti capite agitur. Sed Israë- litis tam artificibus, qui officio suo fideliter erant perfuncti, quam toti populo, qui large contulerat, opusque ultro promoverat: divinam ipsis precatus benedictionem & remunerationem.

## 40:1 Argument
CHAPTER XL. The erection of the tabernacle, and its inauguration to the glory of the Lord.

Ver. 1. AND THE LORD SPOKE.

The erection of the tabernacle is commanded here by GOD, the manner, order, and time in which He willed it to be done, so that nothing might be undertaken by human judgment, which having been completed according to the prescription of GOD, the inauguration of the tabernacle was made, with the glory of the Lord descending in a cloud and filling it.

Latin:

CAPUT XL. Erectio tabernaculi, ejusque ad gloriam Domi- ni inauguratio.

Vers. 1. LOQVUTUSQUE EST DOMINUS.

Præcipitur hîc à DEO erectio tabernaculi, mo- dus, ordo & tempus, quo id fieri voluit, ne quid hu- mano arbitrio susciperetur, quibus ex præscripto DEI completis inauguratio facta est tabernaculi, gloria Domini in nube descendente, illudque re- plente.

## 40:2
Ver. 2. IN THE FIRST MONTH ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE MONTH.

Afterwards in v. 15 it is held: In the first month of the second year, namely after the exit from Egypt: Therefore almost an entire year had passed, namely with 14 days subtracted, before the tabernacle was erected. The chronotaxis according to Rivetus is as follows: From the 15th day of the departure to the promulgation of the law on Mount Sinai, 50 days had elapsed. Then Moses was on the mountain for six days, but outside the cloud with others: soon he remained fasting for 40 days inside the cloud with God, which having been completed when he had descended, he spent 36 days because of the idolatry of the people, partly in carrying the smaller tabernacle out of the camp, partly in punishing the people and instructing them more frequently: and after another forty days he spent time with GOD on the mountain fasting, until the tenth day of the seventh month, at which time, descending from the mountain with the second tablets, he brought full reconciliation to the people, in memory of which the feast of atonement was celebrated every year. But from the day of atonement until the first month of the following year, five and a half months elapsed, during which they were occupied in the numbering, the contribution of the people, and the construction of the tabernacle, and its various furnishings. That first month is Nisan, which corresponds partly to our March, partly to April: and the erection of the tabernacle was a symbol of the conception of Christ, by which the tabernacle of his body was erected for him, which he filled with the fullness of his divinity Coloss. II, 19, which the Church celebrates as having happened on March 25th.

Latin:

Vers. 2. MENSE PRIMO PRIMA DIE MENSIS.

Postea v. 15. habetur Mense primo secundi, an- ni scil. post exitum ex Ægypto: Lapsus ergo pene integer annus erat demtis scil. 14. diebus, antequam erigeretur tabernaculum. Chronotaxis secundum Rivetum ita habet: A 15. die egressus ad legis pro- mulgationem in monte Sina effluxerant 50. dies. Inde Moses sex diebus in monte fuit, sed extra nu- bem cum aliis: mox 40. diebus jejunus intra nu- bem mansit cum Deo, quibus exactis cum descen- disset, ob idololatriam populi 36. dies impendit partim tabernaculo minori è castris efferendo, partim castigando populo, eoque sæpius instruendo: ac post alteram quadragenam dierum cum DEO transegit in monte jejunus, usque ad Mensis septi- mi diem decimam, quo tempore cum secundis ta- bulis è monte descendens plenam reconciliatio- nem attulit populo, in cujus memoriam festum ex- piationis singulis annis celebratum fuit. A die au- tem expiationis usque ad primum mensem anni sequentis effluxerunt quinque Menses cum dimi- dio, quibus occupati fuerunt in numeratione, con- tributione populi, & constructione tabernaculi, variæque ejusdem supellectilis. Mensis ille primus Nisan est, qui partim Martio, partim Aprili nostro respondet: fuitque erectio tabernaculi Symbolum conceptionis Christi, qua erectum ei tabernaculum corporis, quod implevit plenitudine divinitatis suae Coloss. II, 19. quam 25. Martii factam celebrat Ecclesia.

## 40:13
Verse 13.

AND MAY THEIR ANOINTING INTO THE ETERNAL PRIESTHOOD PROFIT) It is enough that they were anointed, so that there is no need for their descendants to be anointed: for whom it sufficed to be ἀπὸ τῶν τῶν χρισῶν ἱερέων γένος, 2 Macc. 1:10. It is otherwise for the High Priests above 29:29, 30:30, Lev. 4:3 and 21:10. Except also that priest who accompanied the camp, an exhorter to virtue. For it was the custom for him to be anointed for this very thing: But Josephus teaches us that these anointings also ceased to be performed while the second Temple stood, namely because that primitive oil from which the anointing was to be made had perished. From that, two ceremonies remained from antiquity, through which the High Priests were inaugurated, being clothed in the garments for seven days, and a sacrifice dedicated to that matter.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ET UNCTIO EORVM IN SACERDOTIVM AETER- NVM PROFICIAT) Satis est illos fuisse unctos, ut opus non sit & posteros ungi: quibus sufficiebat esse ἀπὸ τῶν τῶν χρισῶν ἱερέων γένος, 2. Macc. 1, 10. Aliud in summis Sacer- dotibus supra 29, 29. 30, 30. Levit. 4, 3. & 21, 10. Excipe & eum Sacerdotem, qui castra comitabatur, hortator ad virtu- tem. Eum enim ad hoc ipsum ungi mos habuit: Sed & has unctiones fieri desiisse stante Templo secundo, docet nos Jo- sephus, nimirum quia oleum illud primitivum unde unctio fieri debebat, interciderat. Ex eo duae ex antiquo restitere ceremoniae, per quas summi Sacerdotes inaugurarentur, se- ptenis diebus vestium indutus, & sacrificium ei rei dicatum.

## 40:24
Verse 24. OVER AGAINST THE VEIL.

This golden altar was not inside the holy of holies, as Origen hom. 9 in Levit. and August. q. 173 maintain, but outside it: because it had to be placed before the veil, that is, in front of the veil Exod. 30:6, and when the order of the tabernacle is described here, Moses is said to have placed the ark in the Holy of Holies, and to have hung the veil before it, but afterwards he is said to have placed the table and the lampstand, and the altar of incense over against the veil: and therefore the altar was thus before the veil with the table and the lampstand: inasmuch as the priest had to burn incense on it daily c. 21:8, therefore Josephus lib. III c. 7 and l. VIII c. 2, Hieron., Beda lib. III de Tabern. c. 11 and 12, Theophyl. in Ebr. 9, and others acknowledge that that altar was outside the Holy of Holies; nor is anything else implied in Ebr. 9:3. For the Holy of Holies had that Θυμιατήριον not within itself, but outside the veil facing it, so that, namely, the incense might evaporate towards the oracle; and therefore it is called the altar of the oracle, 1 Kings 6:22, as being that which for that reason was contiguous to the oracle: in the Hebrew it is called l. c. the altar to the oracle, which the LXX translate as the altar before the face of the oracle.

Latin:

Vers. 24. CONTRA VELUM.

Altare hoc aureum non erat intra sanctum sanctorum, ut Origen. hom. 9. in Levit. & August. q. 173. volunt, sed extra illud: quia poni debebat coram velo, id est, ante velum Exod. 30, 6. & quum hîc describatur ordo tabernaculi, Moses arcam quidem dicitur posuisse in Sancto Sanctorum, & appendisse ante eam velum, postea vero mensam & candelabrum, & altare thymiamatis contra velum collocasse dicitur: ideoq; sic altare erat ante velum cum mensa & candelabro: siquidem quotidie in eo adolere debebat sacerdos c. 21, 8. ideo Josephus lib. III. c. 7. & l. VIII. c. 2. Hieron. Beda lib. III. de Ta- bern. c. 11. & 12. Theophyl. in Ebr. 9. aliique agno- scunt altare illud extra Sanctum Sanctorum fuisse; nec aliud innuitur Ebr. 9, 3. Nam Sanctum Sancto- rum habuit Θυμιατήριον illud non intra se, sed extra velum sibi obversum, ut scil. incensum evaporaret versus oraculum; atque ideo dicitur altare oraculi, 1. Reg. 6, 22. utpote quod ob eam causam oraculo contiguum erat: in Ebraeo vocatur l. c. altare ad oraculum, quod LXX. vertunt altare ante faciem oraculi.

## 40:28
Verse 28. AND MOSES AND AARON WASHED.

Moses is joined to Aaron in this washing, as long as he was performing the office of priest, before, namely, he had fully consecrated Aaron and his sons.

Latin:

Vers. 28. LAVERUNTQUE MOSES AC AARON.

Moses jungitur Aaroni in hac lotione, quamdiu munus obibat Sacerdotis, priusquam scil. Aaronem, & filios ejus plene consecrasset.

## 40:31
Verse 31. AFTER ALL THINGS WERE FINISHED.

In the Hebrew v. 33 (for the old interpreter contracted many things again) it is read: And Moses finished all the work. For the sense of the Vulgate is imperfect.

Latin:

Vers. 31. POSTQUAM OMNIA PERFE- CTA SUNT.

In Ebraeo v. 33. (nam contraxit iterum multa vetus interpres) legitur; Et consummavit Moses omne opus. Sensus enim Vulg. imperfectus est.

## 40:33
Verse 33. BECAUSE THE CLOUD HAD COVERED ALL THINGS.

These are redundant, and are not found in the Hebrew text. They smack of a pleonasm. But those things on the other hand are missing, or are not rendered so clearly in the Vulgate, which the Hebrew text adds here: And the glory of the Lord had filled the tabernacle; which glory of GOD some understand as the splendid cloud itself: but because it is distinguished from the cloud, an extraordinary manifestation of glory must be posited here, or at least an extraordinary splendor of the cloud, on account of which not even Moses could enter the tabernacle. Conf. 1 Kings 8:21. Which things exhibit a type of Christ, whose tabernacle of the body the glory of GOD and the whole fullness of the divinity fills: and they are a symbol of the presence of God in the Church, because He wishes to be present there by His grace, to forgive sins, to hear prayers, and to adorn and crown the faithful with His blessing.

Latin:

Vers. 33. QUIA CUNCTA NUBES OPE- RUERAT.

Haec redundant, & non habentur in textu E- braeo. Pleonasmum sapiunt. Illa autem contra de- sunt, vel non ita clare redduntur in Vulgata, quae hîc addit textus Ebraeus: Et gloria Domini imple- verat tabernaculum; quam DEI gloriam nonnulli de ipsa nube splendida intelligunt: sed quia à nube distinguitur, extraordinaria manifestatio gloriae hîc statuenda, vel certe extraordinarius splendor nubis, ob quem ne Moses quidem ingredi taber- naculum potuit. Conf. 1. Reg. 8, 21. Quae typum ex- hibent Christi, cujus tabernaculum corporis glo- ria DEI & tota divinitatis plenitudo implet: & sym- bolum sunt praesentiae Dei in Ecclesia, quod ibi gra- tia sua praesto esse, peccata condonare, preces exaudire, ac benedictione sua fideles ornare ac coronare velit.

## 40:34
Ver. 34. IF AT ANY TIME THE CLOUD LEFT THE TABERNACLE.

In Hebrew: when the cloud was lifted: so also the LXX. ἡνίκα δ' ἂν ἀνέβη, when it ascended. It is one thing to leave the tabernacle, another to be lifted above the tabernacle. Thus it continues with the Vulgate: THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SET FORTH BY THEIR TROOPS. In the Hebrew it is: in all their journeyings, which is far different, because it is implied only that they undertook no journey unless the cloud being raised on high indicated it.

Latin:

Vers. 34. SI QUANDO NUBES TABER- NACULUM DESEREBAT.

In Ebraeo: cum elevabatur nubes: ita & LXX. ἡνί- κα δ' ἂν ἀνέβη, quando ascendebat. Aliud est dese- rere tabernaculum, aliud elevari supra tabernacu- lum. Sic cum Vulgata pergit: PROFICISCEBANTUR FILII ISRAEL PER TURMAS SUAS. In Ebræo est: in omnibus profectionibus suis, quod longe aliud est, quia innuitur id solum, quod nullam susceperint profectionem, nisi nube in sublime elevata id indicaretur.

## 40:35
Vers. 35. IF IT HUNG ABOVE, THEY REMAINED IN THE SAME PLACE. In the Hebrew the sense is clear: if it was not raised (higher than usual) they remained in the same place until the day on which it was raised: for the cloud of the Lord rested (from above) by day upon the tabernacle, and fire by night.

Latin:

Vers. 35. SI PENDEBAT DESUPER, MANEBANT IN EODEM LOCO. In Ebræo sensus luculentus est: si non elevabatur (altius solito) manebant in eodem loco usque ad diem, quo elevaretur: nubes quippe Domini incubabat (superne) per diem tabernaculo, & ignis in nocte.

## 40:36
Vers. 36. AND FIRE BY NIGHT) The same cloud became fiery at night. The cloud was a protection against the heat: the fire was an aid against the darkness. The cloud is a vehicle of God, Ps. 104, 3, and in Hesiod ἠέρα ἑσσάμενοι. Fire is a symbol of the divine nature, according to Porphyry.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ET IGNIS IN NOCTE) Eadem nubes nocte ignescebat. Nubes protectio contra ardorem: ignis auxilium contra tenebras. Nubes vehiculum Dei Ps. 104, 3. & apud Hesiodum ἠέρα ἑσσάμενοι. Ignis naturæ divinæ Symbolum, teste Porphyrio.

# Leviticus

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ANNO AD LEV

PREF

The book of Leviticus, called in Hebrew from the initial word ויקרא Vajikra, has been illustrated after Justin Martyr and Apollinaris, the teacher of Jerome, praised by him himself, and cited in the Douay Bibles, especially by Hesychius, a Jerusalem Presbyter, in the year 400, who in book VII provided mainly mystical explanations, and by Victorinus of Piacenza the Martyr (whose explanation Jerome likewise praised) around the year 470, and also by Rodulphus Flaviacensis in the year 910. And these among the ancient Doctors devoted effort to the explanation of Leviticus. The material concerning sacrifices throughout the whole of Leviticus was illustrated by Triphon, a disciple of Origen, in the year 230. Among the Scholastics, there are celebrated among the interpreters of this book Nicolaus Trivetus, who wrote a Postilla on it in the year 1400, and Rupertus Rosens the Englishman, author of the Scholastic Postilla in the year 1420. Among the Papists, Lorinus, and Joh. Serarius; among the Reformed disciples of Calvin, Willet; among our own, B. Franzius; besides those who wrote on the Pentateuch, Corn. à Lapide, Bonfrer, Calvin, Franc. Junius, Pelargus, B. Chytraeus, Marbachius, etc.

Now this book describes the sacrifices and duties of the Levites, and it treats first of sacrifices up to chapter 8. Then of the priests and Levites, or of the persons offering sacrifices and serving in them, and of their preparation and arrangement up to chapter 23. Finally, of the times destined for oblation, feast days, where it also treats of the Jubilee years and vows from chapter 23 to the end: or, if one prefers to distribute this book with Pelargus, it treats 1. of things, namely sacrifices, in seven chapters; either voluntary, such as the burnt offering in chapter 1, the Mincha or meal offering in chapter 2, the peace or Eucharistic offering in chapter 3; or necessary, such as the ἱλαστικοῖς, both for chatan sins in chapter 4 and for Ascham trespasses in chapter 5, and concerning the rites to be observed in sacrifices in chapters 6 and 7. It treats 2. of persons, namely priests and Levites, and of those unclean from eating, childbirth, leprosy, and the issue of seed, up to chapter 16. Namely, first of the priests, and their inauguration in chapter 8, and their function in chapter 9, and concerning the transgression of Nadab and Abihu in chapter 10, then of the whole people, whom God willed to be bound to a choice in animals regarding food and contact: therefore concerning animals

It is so: that symbol of the presence of GOD by day reflected the appearance of a dense cloud; but by night it shone with fire, so that in the desert even the night was illuminated: and thus it provided both the use of a daytime shade and a nocturnal light, yet by its motion and rest it simultaneously prescribed to the Israelites the time for moving camp or resting. Now it was signified by the shadowy cloud and light what God promised to us in Christ, Isa. 4, 3, who is for us a shade by day from the heat, and a light in the darkness of night: who, like a cloud of grace, mitigates the heat of the wrath of GOD and of temptations, and with his light dispels all darkness, showing us the way and leading us, until we arrive at the heavenly Canaan, and he is about to illuminate us eternally with the splendor of his glory: to whom be praise and honor for ever and ever, Amen.

Latin:

ANNO AD LEV

PRÆF

LIber Leviticus, Ebraïce ab initiali voce ויקרא Vajikra dictus illustratus est post Justinum Martyrem & Apollinarem Hieronymi præceptorem, ab ipso laudatum, & in Duacensibus Bibliis adductos, imprimis ab Hesychio, Presbytero Hierosolymitano, Ann. 400. qui lib. VII. explanationes mysticas præcipue tradidit, & à Victorino Pisatiensi Martyre (cujus explanationem laudavit itidem Hieronymus) circa Ann. 470. nec non Rodulph. Flaviacens. Ann. 910. Atque hi inter veteres Dd. operam contulerunt ad explicationem Levitici. Materiam de Sacrificiis per totum Leviticum tract. de qualitate Sacrificiorum illustravit Triphon Origenis discipulus Anno 230. E Scholasticis celebrantur inter libri hujus Interpp. Nicolaus Trivetus, qui Postillam in eundem scripsit Anno 1400. & Rupertus Rosens Anglus, Postillæ Scholasticæ Autor Ann. 1420. E Pontificiis Lorinus, & Joh. Serarius, è Reformatis Calvini discipulis Willetus, è nostris B. Franzius præter illos, qui in Pentateuchum scripsere Corn. à Lapide, Bonfrer. Calvinum, Franc. Junium, Pelargum, B. Chytraum, Marbachium &c.

Describit autem liber hic Levitarum sacrificia & munia, & de Sacrificiis agit primum usque ad cap. 8. Dehinc de Sacerdotibus & Levitis, seu de personis sacrificia offerentibus, iisque inservientibus, ac præparatione ac dispositione earum usque ad cap. 23. Postremo de temporibus oblationi destinatis, diebus festis, ubi etiam de annis Jobeleis, & votis à c. 23. usque ad finem: aut, si quis malit hunc librum distribuere cum Pelargo, agit 1. de rebus, sacrificiis nempe, capp. septem; vel voluntariis, utpote de holocausto c. 1. Mincha, vel sacrificio cibario c. 2. pacificatorio vel Eucharistico c. 3. vel necessariis, utpote ἱλαστικοῖς tum pro chatan peccatis cap. 4. tum pro Ascham delictis c. 5. deque ritibus in Sacrificiis observandis c. 6. & 7. Agit. 2. de personis, Sacerdotibus puta & Levitis, immundis ex esu, puerperio, lepra, & effusione feminis usq; ad c. 16. Nimirum primum de Sacerdotibus, eorumque tum inauguratione c. 8. tum functione c. 9. & circa eam Nadab & Abihu prævaricatione cap. 10. tum de populo toto, quem ad delectum adstrictum voluit Deus in animalibus quoad cibum & contractum: Ideo de animalibus

Ita est : Symbolum illud præsentiæ DEI per diem speciem densæ nubis referebat ; noctu vero igne coruscabat , ita , ut in deserto nox etiam illu- minaretur : adeoque & usum diurni umbraculi & nocturni luminis præbebat , motu tamen suo & quie- te Israëlitus simul præscribebat tempus movendi ca- stra aut quiescendi. Significatum autem umbra- tili nube & luce fuit , quod promisit Deus nobis in Christo , Esa. 4, 3. qui nobis umbraculum interdiu ab æstu , & lumen in tenebris nocturnis : qui ceu nubes gratiæ æstum iræ DEI & tentationum mitigat , & luce sua tenebras omnes discutit , nobis viam monstrans , & nos deducens , donec in cælestem Ca- naan perveniamus , gloriæque suæ splendore nos æter- num illuminaturus est : cui sit laus & honor in secu- lorum secula , Amen.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Notes on Leviticus
In the name of Jesus. Notes on Leviticus.

Latin:

I. N. J. NOTATA IN LEVITICUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
Preface.

pure and impure things, ch. 11; then concerning women after childbirth, ch. 12; then concerning lepers, ch. 13 and 14; then concerning those with issues, ch. 15. Finally, it deals with actions partly necessary, such as expiation, ch. 16, 17; the avoidance of incest, ch. 18; the observation of various laws, ch. 19 and 20; and specifically regarding priests, ch. 21, 22; and the celebration of feast days, ch. 23; and certain ceremonies, ch. 24; and the Sabbatical and Jubilee years, ch. 25, to which finally, ch. 26, promises and threats are subjoined: partly voluntary, such as vows, and the redemption of them and of tithes, ch. 27.

Moreover, Leviticus was dictated at the twelfth station of the Hebrews in the tabernacle newly built, ch. 1, 1, in the first month of the second year of the exodus: in which one month the entire book was composed: yet these precepts were not given all at once but successively on distinct days, ch. 9, 1; ch. 10, 1, 2; ch. 16, 1.

Furthermore, that we may offer a foretaste concerning sacrifices, which are the principal subject matter of the book, there are three names of sacrifices especially. The first is general, קרבן Corban, which is also read in Mark 7:11. It is δῶρον in Josephus, Antiquities book 4, ch. 4, and Matthew 15:5, a gift or offering, from קרב, he approached: although it is also used for the sacred treasury in Josephus, book 2 of the Wars, ch. 8, and Matthew 27:6. The other two are special, namely זבח, a slaughtered sacrifice, from זבח, he slaughtered, and מנחה, or oblation, from מנח; the former denotes a sacrifice from animals, the latter from the fruits of the earth.

For the MATTER from which it was permitted to offer sacrifices were either animals, or quadrupeds, as among the larger ones, a calf, a bullock, an ox, a cow; among the smaller ones, from the goat kind, a he-goat and a kid; from the sheep, a lamb and a ram; or birds, turtledoves, young pigeons, etc.; or fruits, whether of liquids, wine and oil, or of dry things, such as were incense, salt, grain, fruits of trees, bread, fine flour, etc. Therefore they are called victims, by which God wished to be propitiated, not by human flesh: in the slaughter of which He took no pleasure: whatever of idolatry and impiety of the Gentiles formerly seemed to be, receiving ἀνθρωποφαγίαν (cannibalism); as is evident in Caelius, ch. 12, book 6 of Antiquae Lectiones, as from the history of the Athenians, Romans (Macrobius, book 3, ch. 7, Saturnalia), Egyptians (Diodorus, book 1, ch. 7; Alexander, book 6, ch. 26; Polydore Vergil, book 5, ch. 8), and Carthaginians (in Plutarch in his book on superstition) is clear: just as also the madness of certain Israelites (2 Kings 28:10; Jeremiah 32:35) went so far that they sacrificed their own sons, in the valley of Ben-Hinnom, to the idol Moloch, that is, in the interpretation of Caelius, Saturn, which Ahaz is read to have done, 2 Chron. 28. But it did not require the sacrifice of just any animals: not of horses, which the Mysians once sacrificed, as Alexander testifies in book 2, chapter 22, which the Romans also sacrificed to their Mars, as Plutarch recounts in his Roman Questions, and which the Goths also sacrificed when about to go to war, as Johannes Magnus commemorates in book 1, chapter 13; not of donkeys, whose slaughter is said to have been acceptable to Apollo according to Callimachus, Pindar in the Pythian Odes, and Caelius in book 30, chapter 21; not of mules, which the Romans similarly employed, as Alexander testifies in book 5, chapter 21; not of pigs, which were called the beginnings of gentile sacrifices according to Varro, book 2, chapter 4, of rural affairs: but neither of fish, from which we read that the gentiles also abstained, whose proverb is found in Plutarch in his Symposiacs. ἰχθύων θύσιμος ἐδεὶς ἐδὲ ἱερεύσιμός ἐσι: much less did He declare that bears, wolves, lions, or similar creatures from among the wild and untamed animals would be a sacrifice pleasing to Him: but rather that He desired only those that were clean, and likewise only those that were tamer and more gentle, both for the integrity and perfection of the Antitype, and to signify the purity of our own souls, which is always more acceptable to God than all sacrifices: a fact which the Philosopher recognized from natural light, saying in his Rhetoric: ἐχ’ εἰκὸν τὸν θεὸν χαίρειν ταῖς δαπάναις τῶν θυόντων· ἀλλὰ ταῖς ἐυσεβείαις τῶν θυόντων. It is not consistent that God should be delighted by the expenses of sacrifices more than by the piety of those who sacrifice. And Zaleucus, the lawgiver of the Locrians: 8 θεραπεύεται ὁ Θεὸς δαπάναις, ἀλλὰ ἀρετῇ κ καὶ προαιρέσει τῶν κα- λῶν ἔργων καὶ δικαίων. διὸ ἕκασον δεῖ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι κὴ πράξει καὶ προαιρέσει τὸν μέλλοντα ἔσεσθαι θεοφι- λῆ, that is: God is not worshipped with many expenses: but rather with virtue and the pursuit of good and just works. Therefore, everyone who wishes to be dear to God ought to be good both in action and in will.

The principal end of the Levitical sacrifices was the foreshadowing of the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, of which they were visible and real sermons, a fact which B. Franzius confirmed in his Schol. Sacrif. Disp. IV, from the sacrifices offered in the family of Adam after the promulgation of the Gospel, Heb. 11:3, from the sacrifices of Abraham, and also from the testimony of David, Ps. 110, Isa. 35, Daniel ch. 9:24, and the explanation of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chaps. 7, 8, 9, 10. To these are added others handed down in the New Testament concerning the sacrifice of Christ, which are like a brilliant commentary on the Levitical doctrine of sacrifices. Concerning which St. Augustine, in his book On Faith to Peter, ch. 2, says: in the sacrifices of carnal victims, which the Holy Trinity itself, which is the one God of the New and Old Testament, commanded our Fathers to offer, the most grateful gift of that sacrifice was signified, which the only Son of GOD, according to the flesh, would mercifully offer for us. But He Himself, according to the doctrine of the Apostle, offered Himself for us as an offering to God for a sweet-smelling savor. He is the true God and High Priest: who for us, not in the blood of bulls and goats, but through His own blood, entered once into the Holy Places. This is what that High Priest signified at that time, who entered into the Holy of Holies with the blood of goats. This, therefore, is He who in Himself alone possessed everything that He knew to be necessary for the effect of our redemption, being the same, namely, Priest and sacrifice, the same God and temple, the Priest through whom we are reconciled, the sacrifice of reconciliation, the temple in which we are reconciled, the God to whom we are reconciled, yet He is the sole Priest, sacrifice, and temple, and all these things God according to the form of a servant.

The secondary ends are others with respect to God, in that they were testimonies of honor, worship, obedience, and thanksgiving toward God, and visible works of external confession: with respect to the people, in that they were the nerves and bonds of sacred assemblies, the discipline and pedagogy of the Jews, the means of Levitical cleansing, the images of true and internal worship, and the signs and tokens of spiritual sacrifices for the Church; with respect to the ministry, the subsidies and stipends of the Levites.

These species of sacrifices are found: First, by a general distribution, sacrifices can be divided into burnt offerings, meal offerings, and propitiatory offerings for sins and trespasses, as well as Eucharistic offerings, specifically so called. The first species of them is called עֹלָה from lifting up or ascending, because it was lifted up upon the altar, and its odor ascended on high before the Lord.
