The LXX render it ὁλοκαύτωμα and ὁλόκαυsον, because the whole was burned; it is also called אִשֶּׁה, Levit. 1:5, a fire-offering or burnt offering, as also כָּלִיל, consumed, absolute, because the whole had to be consumed by fire, and nothing remained except the skin, which fell to the Priest. It was made from quadrupeds, an ox, a calf, a ram, a goat, or from birds, a turtledove and a pigeon, and it was offered both on individual days, morning and evening, which is called עֹלַה תָּמִים, the continual sacrifice, ὁλοκαύτωμα ἐνδελεχισμῦ, in a yearling lamb with fine flour and oil: and also on the Sabbath, on which twice as much was to be offered as in the continual sacrifice, or on the New Moon, on which were to be offered two bullocks, one ram, seven unblemished yearling lambs, three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, by which was figured the unblemished Lamb of God to be offered for us on the altar of the cross, 1 Pet. 1:18, Rev. 13:8, which sacrifice is to be recalled in the memory of the continual sacrifice, the fruit of which endures forever. Secondly, the propitiatory sacrifice was twofold: one for a sin committed through ignorance, חַטָּאת, περὶ ἁμαρτίας, Lev. 4. Which likewise foreshadowed the sacrifice of Christ offered for our sins, Ps. 40:7, Rom. 8:3, περὶ ἁμαρτίας. And of this sacrifice there were again two kinds. For the priests were permitted to eat the flesh of those whose blood was not brought into the tabernacle, Lev. 6. But the skin and head of those whose blood was brought into the holy of holies were burned outside the camp, nor was it permitted to eat anything of them; which foreshadowed that Christ was to be offered outside Jerusalem, Heb. 13, 10. The other propitiatory sacrifice was the victim for a fault committed ἐκ προαιρέσεως אָשָׁם Lev. 6, 5. c. 7, 1. which is likewise applied to Christ, Isa. 53, 9. when he shall make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. Conf. 2 Cor. 5, 21. To these was added thirdly מִנְחָה a gift, a meat offering, of inanimate things, fine flour, bread, fruits, salt, wine, oil, to be added to all burnt offerings, and of whatever cattle, in part and by a certain rule, (of which later), it was a type of the true bread of heaven, John 6. who, anointed with the oil of gladness, Ps. 45, 8. offered the incense of prayers and tears to the Father, Heb. 5. v. 7. Fourthly, the sacrifice of peace offerings, or Eucharistic שְׁלָמִים was offered in testimony of gratitude, and of a vow for peace or safety. For it was twofold, both of gratitude for a benefit received, and of a vow for obtaining peace and safety; in which oxen, sheep, or goats were accustomed to be offered. It was also a type of Christ: for no thanksgiving or prayer is pleasing to God, except in the sacrifice of Christ, who, sanctifying himself for us, by his own completed Eucharist and prayer, uniquely, perfectly holy and religious, has sanctified all our thanksgiving and prayer.

Furthermore, the special offerings are those which follow: (1.) The offering of firstfruits, and of firstborn, whether by the prescription of the law, Exod. 22. Num. 5. or by spontaneous vow, Num. 18. (2.) The offering of tithes, or the tenth part of all fruits collected both from the earth and from the cattle. (3.) The annual sacrifice of atonement כִּפֻּר, by which the High Priest made atonement for himself, the tabernacle of the testimony, the altar of incense, and the whole people, Lev. 16. (4.) The sacrifice of purification, by which women after childbirth, Lev. 12, 6. 8, as also those polluted by menstruation, Lev. 15, 29, and likewise lepers, Lev. 14, 10. 21. 22, and men with an issue of seed, c. 12, 14, were purified. (5.) The sacrifice of consecration, by which the Priests were inaugurated, Exod. 29, Lev. 8. Which prefigured the atonement made by the blood of Christ, and the consecration of this our High Priest. Some add the Paschal lamb, and likewise the rite of the red heifer; but the former was a Sacrament, not a sacrifice, the latter was merely a παρασκευὴ for Levitical cleansing.

Moreover, such varied Sacrifices were employed, both so that the people, bound to a certain norm of external worship, might be restrained and kept in their duty by these as it were bonds of obedience until the coming of the Messiah, and so that by the variety of the Sacrifices the variety of the benefits of the Messiah might be set more clearly before their eyes as if by types and images, and so that this diversity, multitude, and constant repetition of Sacrifices might publicly testify that the worshippers of such rites were never rendered perfect unless another thing were added, the expiatory sacrifice of Christ, which by one offering would perfect all, Heb. 9, 25, ch. 10, 11. The perfect sacrifice of Christ, as Lyranus says, could not be sufficiently represented by one or a few imperfect ones, and therefore it was figured by many, just as the divine perfection, being unique, was represented variously and manifoldly in the perfections of creatures.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO.

puris & impuris c. 11. tum de puerperis c. 12. tum de leprosis c. 13. & 14. tum de feminifluis c. 15. Agit 3. de- nique de actionibus partim necessariis , utpote ex- piatione c. 16. 17. vitatione incestus c. 18. observatione variarum legum c. 19. & 20. & in specie quoad Sacer- dotes c. 21. 22. ac festorum dierum celebrationem c. 23. & ceremonias quasdam c. 24. annosque Sabbaticos & Jobelæos c. 25. quibus denique c. 26. promissiones & comminationes subjunguntur : partim voluntariis , ceu sunt vota , eorumq; ac decimarum redemptio c. 27.

Cæterum dictatus est Leviticus in duodecima Ebræorum statione in tabernaculo recens fabrefacto c. 1, 1. anni secundi egressus mense primo : quo uno mense integer liber concinnatus : non tamen simul sed successive distinctis diebus hæc præcepta data sunt c. 9, 1. c. 10, 1. 2. c. 16, 1.

Porro ut de Sacrificiis , quæ præcipua libri ma- teria sunt , aliquid prælibemus , nomina Sacrificio- rum tria potissimum sunt. Primum Generale est קרבן Corban , quod etiam legitur Marc. 7, 11. Est δῶρον apud Josephum l. 4. Antiq. c. 4. & Matth. 15, 5. munus vel donum à קרב appropinquavit : licet etiam de thesauro sacro adhibeatur apud Joseph. lib. II. de Bell. c. 8. & Matth. 27, 6. Cætera duo specialia sunt, utpote זבח Sacrificium mactatum , à זבח mactavit , & מנחה vel oblatio , à מנח , quorum illud sacrificium ex animalibus : hoc ex terræ frugibus notat.

MATERIA enim , ex quibus sacrificia lice- bat offerre , erant vel animalia , aut quadrupedia , ut de majoribus vitulus , juvencus , bos , vacca , de mino- ribus ex genere caprarum , hircus & hædus , ex ovium , agnus , & aries ; aut volatilia , turtures , pulli colum- barum &c. vel fructus , sive de liquidis , vino & oleo , sive de aridis , qualia erant thus , sal , granum , arbo- rum fructus , panis , simila &c. Nominantur ergo victimæ , quibus sibi volebat litari Deus non ex hu- manis carnibus : quarum mactatione minime gau- debat : quicquid idolomaniæ & impietatis gentili- um quondam videbatur , ἀνθρωποφαγίαν recipien- tium ; apud Cælium cap. 12, l. 6. antiquar. Lect. ut ex Atheniensium , Romanorum , ( Macrob. lib. 3. c. 7. Saturn. ) Ægyptiorum ( Diod. lib. 1. cap. 7. Alex. lib. 6. cap. 26. Polyd. Virgil. lib. 5. c. 8. ) & Carthagi- niensium ( apud Plutarch. in lib. de superstitione ) historia patet : quemadmodum & Israë观点tarum quorundam furor ( 2. Reg. 28, 10. Jerem. 32, 35. ) il- luc abiit, ut filios mactarent suos, in valle Ben-Hin- non, Idolo Moloch, hoc est, interprete Cælio Sa- turno, quod fecisse legitur Ahaz 2. Par. 28. Sed nec quorumvis animalium mactationem requirebat: non equorum, quos Mysi quondam immolabant, Alexandr. teste l. 2. cap. 22. quos Romani etiam Marti suo, recitante Plutarcho in quæstionibus Romanis, quos & Gothi in bellum processuri ma- ctabant, ut commemorat Joh. Magn. l. 1. cap. 13. non asinorum, quorum jugulatio Apollini fertur accepta fuisse à Callimacho, Pindaro in Pythiis & Cælio lib. 30. cap. 21. non mulorum, quos Romani similiter adhibuerunt, Alexandro teste lib. 5. c. 21. non porcorum, qui gentilium sacrificiorum initia dicebantur juxta Varronem lib. 2. cap. 4. rei rusticæ: sed nec piscium, à quibus gentiles etiam abstinuisse legimus, quorum proverbium apud Plutarch. in Symposiac. ἰχθύων θύσιμος ἐδεὶς ἐδὲ ἱερεύσιμός ἐσι: multo minùs vero urforum, luporum, leonum, aut si- milium, ex feris indomitisq; animantibus, victimam sibi fore gratam denunciavit: verum ut mundorum duntaxat, ita & mansuetiorum, benigniorumq́, tantum, cum ad Antitypi integritatem atque perfectionem, tum ad animorum nostrorum puritatem significan- dam, quæ omnibus victimis Deo semper est acce- ptior: id quod ex naturali luce agnovit Philosophus, dicens in Rhetoricis: ἐχ’ εἰκὸν τὸν θεὸν χαίρειν ταῖς δαπάναις τῶν θυόντων· ἀλλὰ ταῖς ἐυσεβείαις τῶν θυόντων. Non est consentaneum delectari Deum sum- ptibus sacrificiorum magis, quam pietate sacrificantium. Et Zaleucus Locrensium Nomotheta: 8 θεραπεύεται ὁ Θεὸς δαπάναις, ἀλλὰ ἀρετῇ κ καὶ προαιρέσει τῶν κα- λῶν ἔργων καὶ δικαίων. διὸ ἕκασον δεῖ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι κὴ πράξει καὶ προαιρέσει τὸν μέλλοντα ἔσεσθαι θεοφι- λῆ, id est: Non colitur Deus impensis multis: verum virtute & studio bonorum justorumq́ operum. Proin- de unumquemq́, oportet esse bonum & actione, & vo- luntate, qui vult Deo carus esse.

Finis præcipuus Sacrificiorum Leviticorum erat adumbratio Sacrificii Christi propitiatorii, cujus visibiles & reales conciones erant, quod è sacrificiis in Adami familia post Evangelii pro- mulgationem oblatis, Ebr. 11, 3. è sacrificiis Abra- hami, nec non è testimonio Davidis Psal. 110. Esa. 35. Daniel. cap. 9, 24. & explicatione Epistolæ ad Ebr. capp. 7. 8. 9. 10. confirmavit B. Franzius Schol. Sa- crif. Disp. IV. Quibus alia accedunt in N. Test. de Sacrificio Christi tradita, quæ instar luculenti commentarii sunt doctrinæ Leviticæ de Sacrifi- ciis. De quo S. Augustinus lib. de Fide ad Petrum c. 2. in sacrificiis carnalium victimarum, quæ ipsa sibi sancta Trinitas, quæ unus est Deus Novi & Veteris Testamenti, à Patribus nostris præcipiebat offerri, illius Sacrificii significabatur gratissimum munus, quod pro nobis seipsum solus DEI Filius secundum carnem esset misericorditer oblaturus. Ipse autem secundum Apostoli doctrinam obtulit semetipsum pro nobis hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis. Ipse verus Deus & Pontifex: qui pro nobis non in sanguine tau- rorum & hircorum, sed per sanguinem suum semel introivit in Sancta. Quod tunc Pontifex ille signi- ficabat, qui cum sanguine hircorum in Sancta San- ctorum introibat. Iste igitur est, qui in se uno totum, quod esse necessarium ad redemptionis nostræ sciebat effectum, idem sc. Sacerdos & sacrificium, idem Deus & templum, Sacerdos per quem sumus reconciliati, Sacrificium reconciliationis, Templum in quo reconci- liati, Deus cui reconciliati, solus tamen Sacerdos, Sa- crificium & Templum, & hæc omnia Deus secundum formam servi.

Fines Secundarii sunt alii respectu Dei, quod fue- rint testimonia honoris, cultus, obsequii & grati- tudinis erga Deum, & externæ confessionis opera visibilia: respectu populi quod nervi & vincula con- gressuumSacrorum,disciplina & pædagogia Judæo- rum, media Leviticæ mundationis, imagines vero- rum & internorum cultuum, & spiritualium sacrifi- ciorum signa & tesseræ Ecclesiæ; respectu ministerii, subsidia & stipendia Levitarum.

Species Sacrificiorum hæ reperiuntur: Pri- mum generali distributione sacrificia dividi pos- sunt in holocausta, cibaria, & propitiatoria pro pecca- tis & delictis, ut & Eucharistica, peculiariter ita nuncupata. Prima eorum species dicitur עֹלָה ab elevando, vel ascendendo, quia levabatur super alta- re, & odor ejus ascendebat in altum coram Domi- no. LXX. reddunt ὁλοκαύτωμα, & ὁλόκαυsον, quia totum cremabatur; vocatur etiam אִשֶּׁה Levit. I, 5. ignitum, vel incensum, ut & כָּלִיל consumatum, ab- solutum, quia totum igne debebat absumi, néc quic- quam reliquum manebat, præter pellem, quæ Sa- cerdoti cedebat. Fiebat ex quadrupedibus, bove, vitulo, ariete, capro, hirco, vel ex avibus, turture, & columba, & offerebatur tum singulis diebus mane & vesperi, quod dicitur עֹלַה תָּמִים sacrificium juge, ὁλοκαύτωμα ἐνδελεχισμῦ, in agno anniculo cum si- mila & oleo: tum in Sabbatho, quo duplo plus, quam in jugi sacrificio offerendum erat, vel in Neo- menia, qua offerendi erant duo juvenci, aries unus, agni anniculi immaculati septem, tres decimæ E- phæ similæ, oleo permistæ, quo figuratus fuit agnus Dei immaculatus pro nobis in ara crucis of- ferendus, 1. Petr. 1, 18. Apocal. 13, 8. quod sacrifi- cium jugi memoria recolendum, cujus fructus in perpetuum durat. Secundo sacrificium propitiato- rium geminum erat: unum pro peccato per igno- rantiam commisso חַטָּאת περὶ ἁμαρτίας, Lev. 4. Quod itidem sacrificium Christi adumbravit pro peccatis nostris oblatum Ps. 40, 7. Rom. 8, 3. περὶ ἁμαρτίας. Atque hujus sacrificii iterum duæ erant species. Nam quorum sanguis non inferebatur in tabernaculum, eorum carnibus vesci licebat sacer- dotibus Lev. 6. Quorum autem sanguis in sanctum sanctorum inferebatur, eorum pellis, caput extra castra cremabantur, nec licebat quicquam de iis edere; quæ Christum extra Hierosolymam offe- rendum adumbrabant, Ebr. 13, 10. Alterum pro- pitiatorium sacrificium hostia erat pro delicto ἐκ προαιρέσεως commisso אָשָׁם Lev. 6, 5. c. 7, 1. quæ Christo itidem aptatur Esa. 53, 9. cum posuerit ani- mam suam pro delicto, videbit semen. Conf. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Quibus accedebat tertio מִנְחָה munus, sacrifi- cium cibarium, de rebus inanimis, simila, pane, fru- gibus, sale, vino, oleo, omnibus holocaustis, & quarumcunque pecudum, ex parte ac certa ratione, (de quo postea) addendum, erat typus veri cælo- rum panis, Joh. 6. qui oleo lætitiæ unctus, Ps. 45, 8. thus precum & fletuum Patri obtulit, Ebr. 5. v. 7. Quarto sacrificium pacificorum, seu Eucharisticum שְׁלָמִים in testimonium gratitudinis, & voti pro pa- ce vel salute offerebatur. Erat enim duplex, tum gratitudinis pro beneficio, accepto, tum voti pro pace ac salute consequenda; in quo boves, oves aut capræ offerri solebant. Typus etiam fuit Christi: nulla enim vel gratiarum actio, vel preca- tio grata est Deo, nisi in sacrificio Christi, qui se- metipsum sanctificans pro nobis consummata sua Eucharıstia & oratione unice perfecte sancta, & re- ligiosa nostram omnem gratiarum actionem & precationem sanctificavit.

Speciales porro oblationes sunt, quæ sequun- tur: (1.) Oblatio primitiarum, & primogenitorum, sive ex legis præscripto, Exod. 22. Num. 5. sive ex vo- to spontaneo, Num. 18. (2.) Oblatio Decimarum, seu partis decimæ omnium fructuum tum ex terra, tum ex pecudibus collectorum. (3.) Sacrificium ex- piationis anniversarium כִּפֻּר, quo Pontifex seipsum, tabernaculum testimonii, altare thymiamatis, to- tumq; populum expiabat Lev. 16. (4.) Sacrificium purgationis, quo puerperæ Levit. 12, 6. 8. ut & men- struo pollutæ Lev. 15, 29. nec non leprosi, Levit. 14, 10. 21. 22. seminiflui viri, c. 12, 14. purgabantur. (5.) Sa- crificium consecrationis, quo Sacerdotes inaugura- bantur Exod. 29. Lev. 8. Quæ expiationem sangui- ne Christi factam, & consecrationem hujus Pontifi- cis nostri figurabant. Addunt nonnulli agnum Pa- schalem, itemque ritum vaccæ russæ; sed ille Sacra- mentum erat, non sacrificium, hic παρασκευὴ so- lum ad mundationem Leviticam fuit.

Adhibebantur autem tam varia Sacrificia, tum ut populus ad certam cultuum externorum nor- mam alligatus, his quasi vinculis obedientiæ con- strictus coërceretur & contineretur in officio usque ad Messiæ adventum, tum ut varietate Sacrificio- rum varietas beneficiorum Messiæ, veluti typis & imaginibus ante oculos illustrior poneretur, tum ut hæc diversitas, multitudo, & assidua repetitio Sa- crificiorum publice testaretur, nunquam perfectos reddi hujusmodi rituum cultores, nisi aliud acce- deret, expiatorium Christi sacrificium, quod una oblatione perficeret omnes, Ebr. 9, 25. cap. 10, 11. Perfectum Christi sacrificium, ut Lyranus ait, non potuit per unum, vel pauca imperfecta sufficienter repræsentari, ideoque per multa figurabatur, sicut perfectio divina unica existens in perfectionibus creaturarum varie & multipliciter repræsentabatur.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. OF LEVITICUS, CONCERNING THINGS, OR SACRIFICES. CHAPTER I. CONCERNING BURNT OFFERINGS.

Ver. 1. CONCERNING THE TABERNACLE OF THE TESTIMONY.

What tabernacle of the testimony Moses understands is clear from the last chapter, last verse, of the preceding book. For these cohere immediately, and the discourse is about that tabernacle which had just then been erected: and therefore there is no doubt that the Lord spoke here from the mercy seat, because not only had the tabernacle been erected, but the mercy seat had also been placed within it. Just as He spoke before of the cloud, and made mention of the door of the Mosaic tabernacle, Exod. 33, 9, so now He is said to speak from the tabernacle of the testimony, from the mercy seat, Exod. 25, 22.

Ver. same.

Latin:

PARS I. LEVITICI, DE REBUS, VEL SACRIFICIIS. CAPUT I. DE HOLOCAUSTIS.

Vers. 1. DE TABERNACULO TESTIMONII.

QUodnam tabernaculum testimonii Moses in- telligat, è præcedentis libri cap. ult. vers. ult. patet. Nam cohærent hæc immediate, ac de eo ta- bernaculo sermo est, quod jamjam erectum erat: ideoque dubium nullum est, de propitiatorio hîc lo- quutum esse Dominum, quia jam non erectum tan- tum erat tabernaculum, sed etiam in eo collocatum propitiatorium. Ut antea de nube loquebatur, & de ostio tabernaculi Mosaici verba fecit, Exod. 33, 9. ita nunc è tabernaculo testimonii loquutus dicitur, è propitiatorio Exod. 25, 22.

Vers. eod.

## 1:1
Ver. 1. CONCERNING OXEN AND SHEEP) In every law of victims you may see God content with animals that are very easily obtained: oxen, sheep, kids, small birds: and if anyone had no abundance of these, with food or fine flour.

However, burnt offerings are not to be confused with the Mincha, concerning which in ch. 2. The matter of the burnt offerings is defined here: concerning oxen and sheep in this place, concerning goats v. 10, and from birds the dove and turtledove, v. 14, which were chosen as being more tame, and which could be obtained with less difficulty, and which conveniently figure Christ: for in the ox, labor is shadowed forth; in the sheep, innocence; in the goat, fortitude; in the dove, meekness; in the turtledove, the love of Christ. See Theodor., Cyrill., Procopius, etc. Christ was offered in the ox because of the power of the cross, in the lamb because of innocence, in the ram because of headship, in the he-goat because of the likeness of the flesh of sin, in the turtledove and dove because of God and man, because the Mediator of God and man was shown in the conjunction of two substances, as from Isidore of Seville in c. 1 of Lev. Pelargus: because in the turtledove a close conjunction with God is observed. He offers to GOD a calf, says Origen in hom. 2, who overcomes the pride of the flesh with labor: a sheep, who corrects the irrational motions of anger; a kid, who overcomes lasciviousness; a pair of turtledoves, who joins his mind to the word of God as to a spouse; young birds, who imitates the dove-like eyes of the bride. Furthermore, the Vulgate is to be corrected here: which reads thus: a man, who shall offer of you a sacrifice to the Lord from the cattle, that is, from two, and sheep offering victims: whereas in the Hebrew, Chaldean, and LXX it is so held, as Bonfrerius admits: A man, when he shall offer of you an oblation to the Lord, from the beasts, from the oxen and sheep you shall offer your oblation: which sense is full, that when they wished to offer any quadruped animal, they could offer no other than from the oxen and sheep, which the Jesuit acknowledges to be the sense of this place entirely; but so that the word צאן may promiscuously include sheep and goats, just as the Greek word προϐάτων is also taken; and this for the sake of reconciliation with v. 10. Therefore you shall not slaughter human victims: (because there was only one human victim to be slaughtered, CHRIST.) Nor were dogs, pigs, donkeys, and other unclean animals of that kind to be offered: lest the dignity of the sacrifices be endangered: (because Christ, whose types the sacrifices were, was the most pure victim.) You shall not offer beasts, boars, wolves, foxes: (because Christ was not wild, or ferocious, nor forced: but with a most mild spirit he spontaneously undertook the death to be endured for us). But someone is said to OFFER a victim, both because he offers it at the door of the tabernacle, in which way it is accepted in v. 3. that is, he hands it into the hands of the Priests; and because he takes care that it be offered, or sacrificed, through the Priest: which is the sense of this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 1. DE BOBVS ET OVIBUS) In omni lege victi- mali videas Deum contentum animantibus parabilibus val- de, bobus, ovibus, hædis, aviculis: & si cui nec horum esset copia, cibo, vel simila.

Non confundenda tamen holocausta cum Mincha, de quo cap. 2. Materia holocaustorum hîc definitur: de bobus & ovibus h. l. de capris v. 10. & ex avibus columba, & turture, v. 14. quæ electa sunt, ceu mansuetiora, & quæ minori difficultate haberi possint, ac Christum commode figurent: in bove enim labor, in ove innocentia, in capro forti- tudo, in columba mansuetudo, in turture amor Christi adumbratur. Vid. Theodor. Cyrill. Proco- pius, &c. Oblatus est Christus in bove propter virtu- tem crucis, in agno propter innocentiam, in ariete propter principatum, in hirco propter similitudinem carnis peccati, in turture & columba propter Deum & hominem, quia Mediator Dei & hominis in dua- rum substantiarum conjunctione ostendebatur, ut ex Isidor. Hisp. in c. 1. Lev. Pelargus: quia in turture arcta cum Deo conjunctio spectatur. Offert DEO vitulum, ait Origenes hom. 2. qui carnis super- biam labore vincit: ovem, qui irrationales iræ motus corrigit; hædum, qui lasciviam superat, par turtu- rum, qui verbo Dei ut conjugi mentem suam sociat; pullos, qui oculos columbinos sponsæ imitatur. Cæte- rum corrigenda hîc Vulgata: quæ sic habet: ho- mo, qui obtulerit ex vobis hostiam Domino de peco- ribus, id est, de duobus, & ovibus offerens victimas: quum in Ebræo, Chaldæo, & LXX. ita habeatur, fa- tente Bonfrerio: Homo, quum obtulerit ex vobis ob- lationem Domini, de bestiis, de bobus & ovibus offe- retis oblationem vestram: qui sensus est plenus, quod cum aliquod animal quadrupes offerre voluerint, non aliud offerre queant, quam ex bobus & ovibus, quem omnino hujus loci sensum esse agnoscit Jesuita; sed ut vox צאן promiscue oves & capras comprehen- dat, uti vox Græca προϐάτων etiam accipitur; idque ob conciliationem cum v. 10. Non ergo mactabitis humanas hostias: (quia unica tantum erat mactan- da humana hostia, CHRISTUS.) Neque canes, por- ci, asini, aliaque id genus immunda animalia offeren- da erant: ne sacrificiorum dignitas periclitetur: (quia Christus, cujus typi erant sacrificia, mundis- sima hostia fuit.) Non offeras bestias, apros, lupos, vulpes: (quia Christus non ferus fuit, aut trucu- lentus, nec coactus: sed mitissimo animo mortem perferendam sponte pro nobis suscepit). OFFER- RE autem aliquis dicitur hostiam, tum quod ad ostium tabernaculi offerat, quo pacto accipitur v. 3. h. e. in manus Sacerdotum tradat; tum quod per Sa- cerdotem offerri, seu immolari curet: qui sensus est hujus loci.

## 1:2
A MAN, WHO SHALL OFFER OF YOU A SACRIFICE TO THE LORD) A private person, namely, of his own will, not by the precept of the law. See Deut. 23, 22.

Nor is there anything in the text about the sacrifice of a private person only, nor about a voluntary one: for where are other rites prescribed for burnt offerings to be offered by public persons? Furthermore, that לִרְצֹנוֹ is indeed rendered by Vatablus and Tremellius, ver. 3, according to his will, but the Chaldean, LXX, and B. Luther, along with the Vulgate, explain it—and rightly so—as for his favor before the LORD, i.e., to be reconciled to Him: as it is immediately taken in the following verse. Cf. Isa. 56, 7, c. 61, 2, Jer. 6, 20.

Latin:

HOMO, QVI OBTVLERIT EX VOBIS HOSTIAM DOMINO) Privatus nempe suapte voluntate, non ex præce- pto legis. Vid. Deut. 23, 22.

Nec de privati tantum hostia quicquam in tex- tu, nec de voluntaria habetur: Ubi enim holocau- stis à personis publicis offerendis alii præscripti ri- tus? Porro illud לִרְצֹנוֹ à Vatablo & Tremellio reddi- tur quidem vers. 3. secundum voluntatem suam, sed Chald. LXX. B. Lutherus cum Vulgato exponunt, idque recte, ad favorem ejus coram DOMINO, scil. sibi conciliandum: uti versu sequenti statim acci- pitur. Conf. Esa. 56, 7. c. 61, 2. Jer. 6, 20.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. MALE] The Egyptian priests also, as Chæremon testifies, τῶν βοῶν τὰς θηλείας παρητεῖτο.

By a male without blemish is without doubt denoted the strength of Christ, and that he himself is immaculate, in whom there is no stain of sin, Is. 53, 9. 2 Cor. 5, 21. He shall offer a male, not a female, not a lame, blind, or scabby beast: but one that lacks every reproach. For although Christ, who was to expiate the sins of the World, was to be the seed of a WOMAN, Gen. 3, 15, yet not a female (the most holy virgin Mary) but the son of the virgin himself expiated sins with his own blood. And the same was so subject to no vice: that he neither committed sin, nor was guile found in his mouth, 1 Pet. 2, 23.

HE SHALL OFFER AT THE DOOR OF THE TABERNACLE. He shall offer by handing it into the hands of the Priest at the door of the tabernacle, that is, of the courtyard: because private individuals did not enter the courtyard itself, in which the Priests sacrificed, just as Josephus reports concerning the temple, to which the tabernacle was similar, l. 8. Ant. c. 2. he then surrounded the Temple with a certain partition of three cubits in height to exclude the profane multitude, and to admit only the priests. Moreover, the sacrifices were to be brought to the DOOR OF THE TABERNACLE, because the Tabernacle was the visible seat of the majesty of God, and a type of the visible Church, Num. 7, 8. by which symbol, or rather certain pledge, he signified a closer conversation with men, and the ὁμοσχηνίαν, or dwelling together, of his Son with mortals in one scene, so that we might be taught primarily, that outside the true Church and without that unique propitiatory of Christ, no worships, introduced with whatever intention, are acceptable to God, Lev. 17, 8. Exod. 20, 24. Deut. 12, 13. 14.

TO APPEASE THE LORD FOR HIMSELF) In Hebrew, according to his will before the Lord, that is, whenever he wishes to approach God.

Heb. for his good pleasure before the Lord (See what we said at v. 1) that is, so that that victim may be pleasing to GOD. For those things which were offered elsewhere than at the door of this Tabernacle, the Lord abhorred them. Because God does not wish to be worshipped in any other way than that which He prescribed in His word: and he who in the assembly of heretics, Jews, or Gentiles, that is, elsewhere than in the Church of Christ, of which the tabernacle was a type, hopes that he can offer worship pleasing to God: he is entirely mistaken; as Osiander holds here.

Latin:

Vers. 3. MASCVLVM] Ægyptii quoque Sacerdotes teste Chæremone, τῶν βοῶν τὰς θηλείας παρητεῖτο.

Per masculum immaculatum sine dubio deno- tatur Christi robur, & quod ipse immaculatus sit, in quo nulla peccati labes, Es. 53, 9. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Mascu- lum offeret, non fœminam, non pecus claudum, cœ- cum, scabiosum: sed quod omni reprehensione ca- reat. Etsi enim, qui expiare debebat Mundi pecca- ta, MULIERIS semen futurus erat Christus, Genes. 3, 15. tamen non fœmina (virgo sanctissima Maria) sed ipsius virginis filius expiavit suo sanguine pec- cata. Et idem adeo nulli vitio fuit obnoxius: ut peccatum nec fecerit, nec sit inventus dolus in ore ejus, 1. Petr. 2, 23.

OFFERET AD OSTIUM TABERNACULI. Offeret tradendo in manus Sacerdotis ad ostium tabernaculi, id est, atrii: quia atrium ipsum, in quo Sacerdotes sacrificabant, non ingrediebantur priva- ti, quemadmodum de templo, cui simile erat taber- naculum, perhibet Josephus l. 8. Ant. c. 2. circum- dedit deinde Templo septum quoddam trium cubito- rum altitudine exclusurum profanam multitudi- nem, & solos sacerdotes admissurum. Adducenda autem erant sacrificia ad OSTIUM TABERNA- CULI, quia Tabernaculum sedes erat adspectabi- lis majestatis Dei, & typus Ecclesiæ visibilis, Num. 7, 8. quo veluti symbolo, imo pignore certo pro- piorem conversationem cum hominibus, Filiique sui cum mortalibus ὁμοσχηνίαν, vel contubernium in una scena exhibebat, ut doceremur imprimis, extra Ecclesiam veram & sine illo propitiatorio unico Christi, nullos, quacunque intentione introductos cultus Deo acceptos esse, Levit. 17, 8. Exod. 20, 24. Deut. 12, 13. 14.

AD PLACANDVM SIBI DOMINVM) In Hebræo ad suam voluntatem coram Domino, id est, quandocunque voluerit ad Deum accedere.

Ebr. in beneplacitum ejus coram Domino (Vid. quæ ad v. 1. diximus) id est, ut hostia illa sit grata DEO. Quæ enim alibi, quam ad ostium hujus Tabernaculi offerebantur, eas abominabatur Dominus. Quia Deus non vult alio modo coli, quam eo, quem in suo verbo præscripsit: & qui in cœtu hæreticorum, Judæorum, aut Ethnicorum, hoc est, alibi, quam in Christi Ecclesia, cujus typus fuit tabernaculum, sperat se Deo cultum placentem præstare posse: is toto cœlo errat; ut hîc Osiander habet.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. AND HE SHALL LAY HIS HAND UPON THE HEAD OF THE VICTIM) For this custom, there was a custom among the Greeks of pouring wine between the horns of the victim. Mention is made in Virgil, Ovid, and others.

That custom has nothing to do with this sacred rite of χειροθεσία [laying on of hands], which was done to signify both a spontaneous offering, and the transfer of guilt and punishment onto the head of the victim, and true reconciliation. For the laying on of hands was a symbol of this. The Jews themselves are forced to acknowledge, in this and other rites, the substitution of the victim in the place of those offering. R. Menasse Ben-Israel, Conciliat. in Levit.

quest. 1. p. 185. Just as when Isaac was already bound for immolation, the Lord substituted a ram for him, and thus wished to be satisfied: so also it behooves the one sacrificing to think that he himself has deserved by his sins against God the death with which the animal is afflicted. And for the triple sin, of deeds, of words, of thoughts, the law commands a man to lay hands upon the beast to be immolated, to confess his offenses with his voice, and to burn the entrails and kidneys of the beast, the former of which expiates sins committed in act, the second in words, the third in thoughts, so that it behooves a man to think that he has deserved the death with which he afflicts the beast, which is laid upon the ground, beheaded, and burned, as a symbol of the quadruple death with which the senate was accustomed to punish the guilty, namely, stoning, strangulation, beheading, and burning: as R. Isaac Arama and other authors have also noted. This is Menasse.

Whence, since the modern Rabbis do not commonly understand the true cause of that matter, the mystery of the transfer of the guilt and punishment of the human race onto the Messiah, the expiatory sacrifice of the whole world, nor do they wish to understand it from the most clear oracles of Scripture, and primarily Is. 53, it is no wonder that they torment themselves so much on this subject, as to how guilt could be transferred to victims, or the reconciliation of God be brought about through the offering of victims? The Kabbalists indeed acknowledge that through the sacrifice God was reconciled to sinners, and even that influxes of heavenly grace were attracted; R. Moses Gerundensis, R. Solomon Levi, R. Jehuda Levita: but how the spiritual cause, God, is coupled to men through living creatures and bodily sacrifices, they confess they cannot explain, as R. Menasse observed in the cited place. They also acknowledge this, that if Adam had not sinned, the divinity would always have been present to the human race, and therefore there would have been no need for sacrifices: indeed it seems absurd, as Aben-Ezra notes, the same Manasse observing, that man, made in the image of God so that he might be joined to Him, should have need of irrational animals: but when God saw that he was not attaining the end for the sake of which he was created, God ordained sacrifices, so that by this means the sinner might receive heavenly grace, and once the forgiveness of the offense was obtained, a remedy for the infirmities of the soul might remain, according to the words of Lev. 4, 2. Moreover, some acknowledge that sacrifices were not ordained because the Israelites, born and raised among the barbarous nation of the Egyptians, had imbibed the gentile customs of sacrificing from demons; which opinion of R. Moses Maimonides is refuted by R. Moses Gerundensis and R. Solomon in Dibre Salomo, asking: If that worship was only pretended, and God aimed at something else, why were there so many precepts concerning it, so many ceremonies: especially since both Cain and Abel, before any idolatry had invaded the world, sacrificed, and afterwards Noah, whose odor was so pleasing to God that He swore He would never again destroy the world with waters. R. Menasse Ben-Israel notes four sacrifices before the law was given. The first of Adam, concerning which nothing is indeed mentioned in the Holy Scriptures, yet it is the common consensus of the wise that he sacrificed: the second of Abel: the third of Noah: the fourth of Abraham, when a ram was substituted for Isaac to be immolated. If therefore sacrifices had no place before the fall, and began immediately after the fall, if they were ordained for reconciling man to God and expiating sins, if it is absurd that God be reconciled by the victims of living creatures, and that the sins of beasts be expiated through those external sacrifices, if nevertheless it must be believed in sacrifices that the beast takes the place, and that the guilt and punishment of the man is imposed upon it, who does not perceive that another mystery was shadowed forth by the sacrifices, namely, concerning the reconciliation of man with God, through the transfer of guilt and punishment, and the satisfaction of divine justice to be rendered through the offering of Christ, who, as Isaiah 53 testifies, had to lay down his soul as a sacrifice for us, especially since the Levitical sacrifices could not be brought to an end except through the sacrifice of Christ, Dan. 9, 27. and a clear figure, and an image of that Levitical sacrificial victim, have existed on account of their manifold agreement, and have been able, as Scripture itself interprets, to place that as it were before the eyes and exhibit it to the life. For just as sins were laid upon the Levitical sacrifices, which was especially conspicuous in the solemn anniversary sacrifice, Lev. 16, 21. 22. so our sins were laid upon Christ, Isa. 53. ver. 9. as those were slaughtered, Levit. 3. v. 2. so Christ had to be slaughtered on the altar of the cross, Isa. 53, 7. 8. as the victims were spread out, that is to say, with their legs parted and their whole body expanded, they were slaughtered, as Villalpandus notes in book III de templ. 37. so Christ, slaughtered on the cross, was as it were an expanded victim, and in like manner stretched out, who in every victim was represented as if a living image of the crucified. As their blood had to be poured out and sprinkled before the Lord, Lev. 3, 3. chap. 4, 5. 6. 7. so by the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, which he had to pour out for us, we were to be sprinkled, Isa. 52, 15. c. 53, 11. 1. Pet. 1, 3. as the expiation of sins was made ὡς ἐν τύπῳ through the Levitical sacrifices: so κατ' ἀλήθειαν the sins of the whole world were expiated through the sacrifice of Christ, Isa. 53, 6. 7. Dan. 9, 24. by the virtue of which the sacrifices, performed by faith, reconciled the offerers to God; whom otherwise these animal victims could by no means have appeased, as the Jewish teachers freely admit. Therefore the sacrifices were so various and manifold, not only so that if God had handed down only one kind of sacrifice to the Israelites, they, weary of the perpetual repetition of the same, might easily slip into the impious rites of the Gentiles, but so that by such a variety of sacred rites the many and various benefits of the death of Christ might be depicted, and so that the multitude and variety of the Levitical sacrifices might admonish the Israelites that no Levitical offering truly expiated sins before God, but that all sacrifices looked toward that one sacrifice of the High Priest, by which he blotted out the sins of the whole world. And to that end the sacrifices were also so often iterated and repeated, so that it might be signified that they did not of themselves expiate sins, nor perfect and consummate those who offered, that is, did not of themselves bring a perfect and complete liberation from sin, nor true and perfect righteousness to those offering, but were shadows of the one body of Christ to be offered once for us on the altar of the cross Heb. 10. Which is the reason why sacrifices were not pleasing to God of themselves, or by the work performed, or by the faith in the Jews so offering them, as mere abominations Is. 1. And God testified, Jer. 7, 22. I did not command your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices (namely, by this opinion, that they are worship of God in themselves, and obtain or merit the remission of sins, even if the sacrificers are without true repentance, and give free rein to all wickedness) but I commanded them this word, saying, hear my voice and I will be your God &c. And thus far R. Moses the Egyptian rightly determines that sacrifice was not commanded by the Lord for its own sake, and therefore he willed that it should be done neither often, nor everywhere, nor by everyone, but only in the temple by the priests. Whence also Corn. a Lap. is to be corrected, who, at verse 3, brings forward that the proper end of a burnt offering was to worship God, but not to appease Him, against the most open text of verse 3, TO APPEASE THE LORD FOR HIMSELF; where it is not indicated that appeasement follows beyond the intention of the offerer (which is also false, because sacrifices were not pleasing by the work performed, but by the faith with which they were offered), but the end and intention for which they ought to have been offered, namely to appease the Lord, is expressly designated, and it is added in verse 4, and it shall be acceptable FOR ATONEMENT, which Cornelius Lapideus perverts, as if he made it only for the atonement of temporal punishment and the purification of legal uncleanness, or averted guilt and eternal punishment through the contrition and charity of the offerer: because guilt and eternal punishment cannot be averted except by the virtue of the sacrifice of Christ, to be apprehended by the offerers by true faith alone, John 1, 29. 1 John 2, 2. Rom. 3, 25.

same verse. AND HE SHALL LAY HIS HAND.

Namely he, who takes care that a burnt offering be offered for himself, and for whose atonement it ought to profit: for these things cohere thus: He shall lay his hands upon the head of the victim, and the victim shall be acceptable (it shall be accepted and pleasing) and profiting for his atonement (who offered it), that is, then his sin shall be atoned for, and he himself reconciled to God through faith in Him, who will offer Himself on the cross to the Father. Namely, he who took care that a victim be offered for himself signified, by this gesture of the laying on of his hands, that he was laying his sins upon this victim Lev. 16. For the true atonement, which is shadowed here, was made on the cross through Christ, in whom it is necessary for us to lay our sins by faith, as they laid the hands of the victim upon Him.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PONETQVE MANVM SVPER CAPVT HOSTIÆ) Pro hoc more mos erat apud Græcos vinum fundendi inter cornua victimæ. Mentio apud Virgilium, Ovidium, alios.

Nihil illi mori commercii cum hoc sacro ritu χειροθεσίας, quæ facta ad significandum tum oblationem spontaneam, tum translationem culpæ & pœnæ in caput victimæ, tum reconciliationem veram. Hujus enim Symbolum erat manuum impositio. Agnoscere coguntur ipsimet Judæi, in hoc, & aliis ritibus surrogationem victimæ in locum offerentium. R. Menasse Ben-Israël Conciliat. in Levit.

quæst. 1. p. 185. Quemadmodum Isaaco jam ad immolationem ligato, Dominus arietem eidem substituit, atque ita sibi satisfieri voluit: ita & sacrificantem cogitare oportet, ipsum se peccatis adversus Deum meruisse mortem, qua animal afficitur. Et pro triplici peccato, operum, verborum, cogitationum, lex hominem immolandæ pecudi manus imponere, delicta sua voce confiteri, & interiora, ac renes pecudis comburere jubet, quorum prius peccata actu, alterum verbis, tertium cogitationibus commissa expiat, ita ut hominem cogitare oporteat, se meritum esse mortem, qua bestiam afficit, quæ humi sternitur, decollatur ac comburitur, in Symbolum quadruplicis mortis, qua animadvertere in reos senatus solebat, nimirum lapidationis, strangulationis, decollationis, & combustionis: uti notavereunt quoque R. Isaac Arama, aliique autores. Hæc Menasse.

Unde quum veram illius rei causam, mysterium translationis culpæ & pœnæ generis humani in Sacrificium expiatorium totius mundi Messiam, communiter non intelligant Rabbini hodierni, nec intelligere è luculentissimis Scripturæ oraculis, & imprimis Es. 53. velint, mirum non est, quod tantopere in hac materia se torqueant, quo pacto transferri culpa in victimas, aut Dei reconciliatio per oblationem hostiarum fieri potuerit? Agnoscunt sane Cabbalistæ per Sacrificium Deum reconciliatum fuisse peccatoribus, imo etiam attractos cælestis gratiæ influxus; R. Mose Gerundensis, R. Salomo Levi, R. Jehuda Levita: sed quomodo causa spiritualis Deus copuletur hominibus per animantes, & sacrificia corporalia, fatentur, se explicare non posse, ut loco laudato observavit R. Menasse. Agnoscunt & hoc, nisi Adam peccavisset, semper divinitatem humano generi affuturam fuisse, idcoque opus sacrificiis non futurum fuisse: imo absurdum videtur Aben-Ezræ notante eodem Manasse, hominem factum ad imaginem Dei, ut ei conjungatur, opus habere animalibus rationis expertibus: sed quum videret Deus, eum non attingere finem, cujus gratia creatus erat, ordinasse Deum sacrificia, ut hac ratione peccator cælestem gratiam reciperet, ac impetrata delicti venia remedium superesset infirmitatum animæ, secun- dum verba Lev. 4, 2. Agnoscunt insuper nonnulli, sacrificia non ideo ordinata, quod Israëlitæ inter barbaram Ægyptiorum gentem nati atque educati, gentiles mores sacrificandi a dæmonibus hauserint; quam R. Mosis Maimonidis opinionem refellit R. Mo- ses Gerundensis, & R. Selomoh in Dibre Salomo, quæ- rentes: Si cultus ille tantum prætendebatur, & Deus alio tendebat, cur tot præcepta circa eum, tot ceremo- niæ fuerint: præsertim cum & Cain & Habel, prius- quam idololatria ulla mundum invasisset, sacrifica- verint, & postea Noah, cujus odor Deo tam gratus fue- rat, ut jurarit, se nunquam deinceps aquis mundum perditurum. R. Menasse Ben-Israel quatuor notat Sacrificia ante datam legem. Primum Adami, de quo nihil quidem in S. literis memoratur, commu- nis tamen sapientum consensus sit, eum sacrificasse: alterum Habelis: tertium Noachi: quartum Abraha- mi, quando Isaaco immolando substitutus est aries. Si ergo Sacrificia ante lapsum locum non habue- runt, ac statim post lapsum cœperunt, si ordinata sunt ad hominem Deo reconciliandum, & expian- da peccata, si Deum animantium hostiis conciliari, & per illa externa sacrificia bestiarum peccata ex- piari absurdum, si nihilominus bestiam locum sup- plere, atque illi hujus culpam & pœnam imponi, in sacrificiis credendum, ecquis non deprehendit, aliud mysterium sacrificiis adumbratum, de hominis nempe cum Deo conciliatione, per culpæ & pœnæ translationem, ac satisfactionem justitiæ divinæ per Christi oblationem præstandam, qui Esa. 53. teste, animam suam ponere debuit sacrificium pro nobis ma- xime, quum non nisi per sacrificium Christi finis af- ferri Leviticis Sacrificiis potuerit Dan. 9, 27. & il- lustris figura, & imago Sacrificii illius hostiæ Levi- ticæ, ob multivariam convenientiam, extiterint, istudq; veluti πρὸς ὄμμα ποιῆν, & ad vivum exhibe- re, Scriptura ipsa interprete potuerint. Ut enim sa- crificiis Leviticis peccata imponebantur, quod in- primis in anniversario solemni sacrificio conspi- cuum erat, Lev. 16, 21. 22. sic peccata nostra Christo imposita sunt, Esa. 53. vers. 9. ut illa mactata sunt, Levit. 3. v. 2. ita Christus in ara crucis mactari de- buit, Esa. 53, 7. 8. ut victimæ expansæ, divarica- tis scilicet cruribus & toto corpore earum ex- panso jugulabantur, notante Vilalpando lib. III. de templ. 37. ita Christus in cruce mactatus, quasi vi- ctima expansus est, & pari modo distentus, qui in qualibet hostia ceu imagine viva crucifixus repræ- sentatus fuit. Ut sanguis illorum fundendus, & co- ram Domino spargendus erat, Lev. 3, 3. cap. 4, 5. 6. 7. ita aspersione sanguinis Christi, quem fundere pro nobis debuit, aspergendieramus, Esa. 52, 15. c. 53, 11. 1. Petr. 1, 3. ut expiatio peccatorum facta ὡς ἐν τύπῳ per sacrificia Levitica: sic κατ' ἀλήθειαν expiata sunt totius mundi peccata per sacrificium Christi Es. 53, 6. 7. Dan. 9, 24. cujus virtute sacrificia, fide peracta, reconciliabant offerentes Deo; quem cæteroquin istæ animantium victimæ minime placare potuissent, Judæorum Magistris ultro fatentibus. Ideo tam varia & multiplicia fuere sacrificia, non tantum, ne si unum solum sacrificii genus Israëlitis tradidisset Deus, per- tæsi ejusdem perpetua repetitione facile ad impia gentilium sacra delaberentur, sed ut tanta varietate sacrorum multa & varia beneficia mortis Christi de- pingerentur, & ut multitudo & varietas Leviticorum Sacrificiorum admoneret Israëlitas, nullam Leviti- cam oblationem vere expiare corā Deo peccata, sed omnia sacrificia respicere unicum illud Sumi Sacer- dotis sacrificium, quo totius mundi peccata dele- vit. Atque eo fine Sacrificia etiam toties iterata, & repetita sunt, ut significaretur, ea per se non expiare peccata, nec perficere, & consummare offerentes, hoc est, non perfectam & integram liberationem a peccato, nec veram & perfectam justitiam per se af- ferre offerentibus, sed umbras esse unius corporis Chri- sti semel pro nobis in ara crucis offerendi Ebr. 10. Quæ causa est, cur sacrificia Deo non placuerint per se, vel ex opere operato, sive fide offerentis, sed re- probata a Deo in Judæis ita offerentibus fuerint, ceu meræ abominationes Es. 1. testatusque Deus, Jer. 7, 22. non præcepi Patribus vestris in die, qua eduxi eos de terra Ægypti, de holocaustis & victimis (hac sc. opi- nione, quod sint cultus Dei per se se, & impetrent, aut mereantur remissionem peccatorum, etiamsi sacri- ficatores sint sine vera pœnitentia, & omnibus scele- ribus frenos laxent) sed hoc verbum præcepi eis, di- cens, audite vocem meam & ero vobis Deus &c. Atq; hactenus recte R. Moses Ægyptius statuit sacrificium non propter se a Domino imperatum, ideoq; voluisse eum, ut nec sæpe, nec ubiq; nec ab omnibus fieret, verum in templo tantum a sacerdotibus. Unde castigandus etiam Corn. a Lap. ad v. 3. holocausti finem proprium fuisse colere Deum, non autem eum placare, contra apertissimum textum v. 3. AD PLACANDUM SI- BI DOMINUM, adferens; ubi non quod præter intentionem offerentis sequatur placatio (quod falsum etiam est, quia non ex opere operato placebant sacrificia, sed qua fide offerebantur) indicatur, sed qua fini & intentione offerri debuerint, nimirum ad placandum Dominum, expresse designatur, additur- que v. 4. & acceptabilis erit IN EXPIATIONEM, quod pervertit Cornelius Lapideus, quasi tantum ad expiationem pœnæ temporalis, & purgationem immun- ditiei legalis fecerit, aut culpam & pœnam æternam ex contritione & charitate offerentis averterit: quia cul- pa & pœna æterna averti non potest nisi sacrificii Christi virtute, unice vera fide ab offerentibus ap- prehendendi, Joh. 1, 29. 1. Joh. 2, 2. Rom. 3, 25.

vers. eod. PONETQVE MANUM.

Scilicet is, qui holocaustum pro se offerri cu- rat, & in cujus expiationem id proficere debet: hæc enim ita cohærent: Ponet manus super caput hostiæ, & acceptabilis (accepta & grata erit) hostia atque in expiationem ejus (qui eam obtulit) proficiens, id est, tum erit ejus peccatum expiatum, & ipse Deo re- conciliatus per fidem in eum, qui seipsum in cru- cem offeret Patri. Nimirum significabat is, qui of- ferri curabat hostiam pro se, hoc impositionis ma- nuum suarum gestu, se peccata sua huic hostiæ impo- nere Lev. 16. Vera enim expiatio, quæ hic adumbra- tur, facta est in cruce per Christum, in quem oportet nos fide ponere peccata nostra, ut illi manus victi- mæ imponebant.

## 1:4
Same verse. FOR EXPIATION] לכפר which is translated into Latin as to expiate, here it is to commend someone to GOD.

The force of the Hebrew word is perverted, and it does not appear why it should not denote expiation here, as the Vulgate rendered it and as it is accepted everywhere. Indeed, it is taught in verse 9 that a burnt offering is to be offered for a sweet-smelling savor. Nor is it to be doubted that that sacrifice was made for the expiation of sins: Grotius ought to have considered what he had argued against Socinus concerning the emphasis of the word כפר, in De Satisfactione, ch. 10, p. 139. Socinus acknowledges no satisfaction in the expiatory sacrifices. And yet the word itself for atoning, or expiating, properly signifies nothing other than to pay the penalty, and the authors cited by us, when they wish to paraphrase 'to expiate,' say: to give blood for blood, life for life, soul for soul; to buy something with blood, to obtain salvation through the death of another. Nor do the Hebrew words differ from this. For Caphar or Kipper is not only to cover, but also to redeem (Exod. 21, 30; Psalm 49, 8) and to appease (Gen. 32, 10), and from there, furthermore, to expiate. Expiation is attributed first to the victims, as appears in Heb. 9, 13, 23. Then to the priest on account of the victims which he presents, as often in LEVITICUS. Finally to God admitting that expiation. Therefore כפר is not to commend someone to God, an example of whose meaning cannot be brought forward, but to expiate. Grotius, however, wished to gratify by this meaning of the word, introduced both by the Vulgate interpreter, who in other places not rarely interprets the Hebrew word as 'he will pray for him,' and especially by Socinus, who attacks the satisfaction of Christ. How changed from that one!

Latin:

Vers. eod. IN EXPIATIONEM] לכפר quod Latine vertitur expiare, hic est DEO aliquem commendare.

Pervertitur vis vocis Ebrææ, quæ cur non expiationem hic denotet, uti Vulgatus reddidit & passim accipitur, non apparet. Imo holocaustum in odorem quietis offerendum v. 9. docetur. Neque dubitandum est sacrificium illud ad expiationem peccatorum fecisse: Cogitasse debebat Grotius, quæ de Emphasi vocis כפר contra Socinum disputarat, de Satisf. c. 10. p. 139. Satisfactionem nullam Socinus in sacris expiatoriis agnoscit. Atqui vox ipsa piandi, sive expiandi nihil aliud proprie significat, quam luere, passimque autores a nobis citati cum expiare volunt περιφράζειν, dicunt dare sanguinem pro sanguine, vitam pro vita, animam pro anima: sanguine aliquid emere, morte alterius salutem consequi. Neque voces Ebrææ hinc dissident. Nam Caphar vel Kipper non modo est tegere, sed & redimere Exod. 21, 30. Psalm. 49, 8. & placare Genes. 32, 10. atque inde porro expiare. Tribuitur autem expiatio primo victimis, ut apparet Hebr. 9, 13. 23. Deinde sacerdoti propter victimas, quas exhibet, ut sæpe in LEVITICO. Postremo etiam Deo istam luitionem admittenti. Non ergo כפר est Deo aliquem commendare, cujus significatio- nis exemplum adferri nequit, sed expiare. Gratifi- cari autem voluit Grotius hac vocis significatione invecta tum Vulgato interpreti, qui aliis in locis non raro vocem Ebræam interpretatur, rogabit pro eo, tum maxime Socino satisfactionem Christi impu- gnanti. Quantum mutatus ab illo!

## 1:5
AND HE SHALL SLAUGHTER.

The priest, not the offerer. For although no mention of a priest is made here, yet from that rule, the subject is such as is permitted to be by the predicate, it is to be gathered that these things are to be understood not of the offerer, but of the priest, just as the Holy Spirit not rarely leaves the omitted subject to be gathered from the quality of the predicate Gen. 24, 31. 32.

6. 2. Sam. 15. 27. 2. Kings 23, 29. There are indeed not lacking those who gather from ch. 8, 14. 18. that it was done by the offerers also: but there is nothing else held there than that Aaron and his sons, when an offering had to be made for them, had to lay their hands upon the victim, but not that they had to perform the offering: which in their consecration to the priesthood was done by Moses himself, by divine command, he taking on the parts of the priest, so that they might first be consecrated as priests: whose duty it was thereafter to slaughter the victims Ex. 29, 10. the sprinkling of blood, the cutting into pieces 2. Chron. 29, 34. the burning. Furthermore, Oleaster rightly observes in this place, and from him Bonfrerius, that one reason for the laying on of hands is not to be assigned specifically in the individual kinds of sacrifices, even if this one reason can be given in general, namely that the victim in any kind of sacrifice should take the place of the offerer, yet in the individual kinds of sacrifices this reason is to be accommodated specifically in such a way that it respects the intrinsic end of any sacrifice. And so in a burnt offering, by this laying on of hands, the offerer testified that he and all his things were God's, and ought to be spent in His service, and that he was substituting this victim in his own place, which would signify that very thing by its assumption; which Vatablus also indicates here concerning the burnt offering. In peace offerings, the offerer substituted the victim in his own place, so that by his own humiliation and mortification before God he might pray for salvation and prosperity, which salvation and prosperity would then return to the offerer by the participation of the same victim. In the sacrifice for sin, as I said, he substituted the victim for himself into the death merited by his sins, and derived into it all the punishments of his sins, which he signified by this laying on of hands; as Bonfrerius here. Which things fit Christ, whose figure all sacrifices were, very well: who, having been substituted in our place, first, when He was made a burnt offering for us, offered Himself entirely and His whole life in service and obedience even unto death, and the death of the cross, kindled by the fire of love, to God the Father. Then as a true Mincha and bread of heaven, anointed with the oil of gladness, He willed to offer the incense of prayers and tears to God the Father for us Heb. 5, 7. and obtained for us all the good things which we ask John 16, 23. Furthermore, as a peace offering, He succeeded into our place, and by His humiliation and delivery into death, He restored the glory to the Father, which we violated by robbery, and merited peace for us with God. Finally, as a propitiatory sacrifice for sin and transgression, he had to be sacrificed in our place, so that he might render us immune from guilt and punishment. Is. 53. Rom. 4, 15.

AND THE SONS OF AARON SHALL OFFER.

More correctly, they shall bring, namely the priests, pouring out the blood of that calf, or more correctly: sprinkling it upon the altar, not in one place only, but around the circuit of the altar, which altar is before the door of the tabernacle. For the altar of burnt offerings was placed before the gilded tabernacle in the courtyard. Thus the virtue of the blood of Christ is to be sprinkled through the preaching of the Gospel to all regions of the world among all nations. And the skin of the sacrifice having been removed: Because Christ not only hung naked on the cross, but was also stripped of all human protection, etc.

Latin:

IMMOLABITQUE.

Sacerdos, non offerens. Nam licet nulla Sa- cerdotis hic facta mentio, ex regula tamen illa, tale est subjectum, quale permittitur esse a prædicato, colligere est, non de offerente, sed sacerdote hæc intelligenda esse, uti non raro subjectum omissum ex prædicati qualitate colligendum relinquit Sp. S. Gen. 24, 31. 32.

6. 2. Sam. 15. 27. 2. Reg. 23, 29. Non desunt quidem, qui e c. 8, 14. 18. colligant, id ab offerentibus etiam factum: sed ibi nihil aliud habetur, quam quod Aaron & filii ejus, cum pro iisdem fieri debuit oblatio, manus suas imponere hostiæ debuerint, non vero quod ob- lationem peragere: quæ in consecratione eorum ad Sacerdotium a Mose ipso, divino mandato fiebat, partes Sacerdotis subeunte, ut sc. illi primum in Sa- cerdotes consecrarentur: quorum vero deinceps, erat hostiarum jugulatio Ex. 29, 10. aspersio sanguinis, ὀρθοτομία 2. Chron. 29, 34. incensio. Porro recte obser- vat Oleaster h. l. & ex eo Bonfrerig, non unam in specie in singulissacrificiorum generibus assignandam esse rationem impositionis manuum, etsi una hæc in genere ratio dari possit, videlicet ut victima in quacunque sacrificii specie offerentis locum sustineret, in singulis tamen sacrificiorum generibus speciatim hanc rationem ita accommodandam esse, ut respiciat finem intrinsecum cujusvis sacrificii. Itaque in holocausto hac manus impositione testabatur offerens se suaque omnia Dei esse, in ejusque obsequium impendi debere, suoque loco victimam hanc substituere, quæ id ipsum sui assumtione significaret; quod ipsum etiam de holocausto indicat hic Vatablus. In pacificis victimam suo loco offerens supponebat, ut sui humiliatione & coram Deo mortificatione salutem & prosperitatem deprecaretur, quæ deinde salus & prosperitas ad offerentem ejusdem victimæ participatione rediret. In Sacrificio pro peccato, ut dixi, victimam pro se in mortem a se peccatis commeritam substituebat, in eamque omnes peccatorum suorum pœnas derivabat, quod hac manus impositione significabat; ut hic Bonfrerius. Quæ Christo, cujus figura erant omnia sacrificia, optime conveniunt: qui in nostri locum surrogatus primo, cum holocaustum factus pro nobis, se totum vitamque suam universam in obsequium & obedientiam usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis igne amoris succensus, Deo Patri obtulit. Deinde tanquam verum Mincha & cœlorum panis oleo lætitiæ unctus thus precum & fletuum Deo Patri pro nobis offerre voluit Ebr. 5, 7. nobisque consequutus est omnia, quæ petimus, bona Joh. 16, 23. Porro ceu victima pacifica in nostri locum successit sui humiliatione, & in mortem traditione gloriam Patri, quam per rapinam violavimus, restituit, & pacem nobis apud Deum promeruit. Denique velut hostia propitiatoria pro peccato & delicto immolari debuit, nostri loco, ut nos a culpa & pœna immunes redderet Es. 53. Rom. 4, 15.

ET OFFERENT FILII AARONIS.

Rectius adferent, Sacerdotes scilicet, sanguinem ejus vituli fundentes, rectius: spargentes eum super altare, non uno tantum in loco: sed per altaris circuitum, quod altare est ante ostium tabernaculi. Altare enim holocaustorum ante tabernaculum inaura tum erat collocatum in atrio. Sic virtus sanguinis Christi spargenda est per prædicationem Evangelii, ad omnes Mundi plagas inter omnes Gentes. Detractaque pelle hostiæ: Quia Christus non modo nudus in cruce pependit: sed spoliatus etiam omni humano præsidio &c.

## 1:5
ver. 5. A CALF. Heb. son of a bovine. Mention of the bovine was made in v. 3. Here, therefore, it is explained that it ought not to be aged, but younger: which was also required to be immaculate: and Philo observes in his book on Victims, since animals to be sacrificed had to be whole, uninjured in all parts, and lacking in defects and blemishes, it was the duty of the priests to examine them from head to heel before the sacrifice. Moreover, Christ was signified as immune from every stain, sacrificed in the flower of youth. Cyril, book 15, on Adoration in Spirit and Truth.

ver. same. POURING OUT HIS BLOOD. The reason is held in Heb. 9, 22. Abulensis teaches that by a continuous miracle all the blood exhaled immediately, because otherwise, when many victims were sacrificed at the same time, it would have induced an intolerable stench: Cornelius notes from Aristeas that Solomon met this inconvenience through pools, conduits, and underground channels, through which the blood would be emitted and washed away by water poured over it. But why should we not believe that some remedy was also applied by Moses, so that there might be no need for a miracle of that kind?

Latin:

vers. 5. VITULUM. Ebr. filium bovis. Bovis mentio v. 3. facta. Hic ergo explicatur, quod non annosus, sed junior esse debeat: qui & immaculatus requirebatur: & obser- vat Philo lib. de Victim. quum animalia immolanda integra, illæsa partibus omnibus, vitiis, nævisq; ca- rentia esse debuerint, sacerdotum fuisse, ea ante im- molationem a capite ad calcem scrutari. Significa- tus autem est Christus ab omni labe immunis, in flo- re juventutis immolatus. Cyrill. l. 15. de ador. in Spir. & Verit.

vers. eod. SANGUINEM EJUS FUNDEN- TES. Causa habetur Ebr. 9, 22. Per miraculum conti- nuum omnem sanguinem mox exhalasse, Abulensis docet, quia alioquin fœtorem intolerabilem, cum multæ victimæ simul immolatæ sunt, induxisset: cui incomodo Salomonem occurrisse per piscinas, mea- tus, & canales subterraneos, per quos sanguis emitte- retur, & aqua superfusa abstergeretur ex Aristea no- tat Cornelius. Sed cur non credamus etiam aliquod remedium adhibitum a Mose, ne opus sit continuo ejusmodi miraculo?

## 1:5 Addition
On Leviticus 1:5, towards the end of the verse. p. 470. a.

They poured out the blood, as it were, asking that GOD might accept it in place of the blood of him who was offering. Bonfrerius notes here a double custom of pouring blood at the base: 1. immediately at the base, namely in sacrifices for sin and guilt. See Lev. 5:9. 2. mediately, when it was poured along the walls of the altar and flowed down from there to the base, namely in burnt offerings and peace offerings.

Latin:

Ad Levit. 1, 5. sub finem versus. p. 470. a.

Sanguinem fundebant q. rogantes, ut DEUS illum loco sanguinis ejus, qui offerebat, acciperet. Notat autem hic morem duplicem fundendi san- guinem ad basin Bonfrerius 1. immediate ad basin nempe in sacrificiis pro peccato, & delicto. Vid. Lev. 5, 9. 2. mediate cum per altaris parietes funde- batur indeque decurrebat ad basin, nempe in holo- caustis & pacificis.

## 1:6
Ver. 6. AND THE SKIN HAVING BEEN REMOVED] All things are naked to God. This rite signifies this, therefore the writer to the Hebrews 4, 13 said τετραχηλισμένα, wishing to signify naked and open. For the removal of the skin began from the neck.

The skin fell to the Priests, Lev. 8, 7, whence some gather that it was also their duty to remove the skin, whom, however, the Levites helped in a case of necessity, 2 Chron. 29, 34.

THEY SHALL CUT THE LIMBS INTO PIECES] The priests, 2 Chron. 29, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DETRACTAQUE PELLE] Deo nuda omnia. Id ritus hic significat, ideo τετραχηλισμένα dixit scriptor ad Hebræos 4, 13. nuda & aperta volens significare. A collo enim incipiebat pellis detractio.

Pellis cedebat Sacerdotibus Lev. 8, 7. unde col- ligunt nonnulli, quod eorum fuerit etiam pellem detrahere, quos tamen Levitæ in casu necessitatis ad- juverint 2. Par. 29, 34.

ARTUS IN FRUSTA CONCIDENT] Sacerdotes 2. Par. 29, 24.

## 1:6 Addition
On verse 6, after the passage 2 Chronicles 29:34. p. same.

Interpreters provide still other reasons why the skins were to be removed, namely for the cleanliness of the sacrifice, and because it was, as it were, the food of GOD and, as it were, a banquet, whence the altar is the table of the Lord. Therefore, things that were not accustomed to be eaten by men also had to be separated from the victims, such as feathers, the bladder, etc. See Bonfrerius and Tirinus.

Latin:

Ad v. 6. post locum 2. Par. 29, 34. p. ead.

Causas adhuc alias cur detrahendæ pelles reddunt interpp. nempe ob mundiciem sacrificii, & quod id fuerit q. cibus DEI, & q. convivium, unde altare mensa Domini. Quæ ergo ab hominibus edi non consuevere, à victimis etiam separari debebant, ut pluma, vesica, &c. Vid. Bonf. & Tirin.

## 1:7
FIRE] From heaven, below 9, 24.

Latin:

IGNEM] De cœlo infra 9, 24.

## 1:8
Ver. 8. AND ALL THINGS WHICH ADHERE TO THE LIVER] Rather the trunk of the body. For that is פגר.

Vatablus notes that the Hebrew word signifies the fat or that caul which is placed over the liver. Aben Ezra likewise explains it as fat with the Chaldean, and thus also the LXX render it τὸ στέαρ: and B. Luth. 'das Fette'. Buxtorff says the intestines are denoted. In Avenarius' Lexicon, the heart, liver, lung, and spleen are all called by this name when joined together. He judges it not inappropriately explained as entrails. Forster, however, in his Lexicon thinks it signifies the trunk. It does not occur except in v. 12 and ch. 8, 10. Although, however, the whole body of the calf, together with the head, was placed upon the wood, it was nevertheless sufficient that those parts be named here about which there could be doubt, but concerning the rest of the flesh it is manifest that it all had to be burned in the burnt offering: and therefore it seems that that fat or that caul, which is found placed over the liver, was placed in the place of decapitation to cover it when the head was placed on the fire to be burned; but the rest of the body, together with the intestines and legs, though all were washed first, was placed on the fire after the cremation of the head. Conf. R. David Kimchi in the book of Roots and Paul Fagius in this place. And therefore the intestines and feet of the victim were washed with water: because Christ brought no impurity to his passion: And the Priest burned everything, likewise signifying Christ, who offered himself, and was both victim and priest. Moreover, the burning of the Sacrifice by heavenly fire shadowed forth both the divine wrath, which is a consuming fire, Deut. 4, in the most bitter passion of Christ, and the most ardent love of Christ toward the human race, out of which he willed to undergo the passion. Truly the fire of divine wrath would not have consumed this sacrifice at all, had it not been kindled by that flame of Christ's love, by which the wrath was to be turned into this substitute victim. John 10, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET CUNCTA QUÆ ADHÆRENT JECORI] Imo truncum corporis. Id enim est פגר.

Vatablus notat vocem Ebræam significare adi- pem seu reticulum illud, quod super hepar positum est. AbenEzra adipem itidem exponit cum Chald. atque ita etiam LXX. τὸ στέαρ reddunt: & B. Luth. das Fette. Buxtorffius intestina notari ait. Ave- nario in Lexico cor, jecur, pulmo, & lien hæc omnia conjuncta hoc vocantur nomine. Non inconve- nienter pro extis exponi censet. Forsterus tamen in Lex. truncum significare putat. Non occurrit ni- si v. 12. & c. 8, 10. Etsi autem totum corpus vituli, una cum capite impositum fuerit super ligna, satis tamen erat partes illas hic nominari, de quibus du- bium esse poterat, de reliqua autem carne manife- stum est, eam omnem in holocausto comburi de- buisse: ideoque videtur, adipem illum vel reticu- lum istud, quod super epar positum invenitur, im- positum fuisse loco decollationis ad tegendumi- psum, quando caput incendendum igni imponeba- tur; reliquum vero corpus una cum intestinis & cru- ribus, prius tamen omnibus lotis, igni impositum post capitis cremationem. Conf. R. David Kimchi in libr. Radic. & Paul. Fagius in h. l. Atque ideo intestina & pedes hostiæ lavabantur aqua: quia Christus nihil impuritatis ad passionem suam at- tulit: Et adolebat omnia Sacerdos, itidem Christum significans, qui seipsum obtulit, & hostia fuit & sa- cerdos. Combustio autem Sacrificii igne cœlesti facta, cum iram divinam, quæ ignis consumens est, Deut 4. in acerbissima Christi passione, tum arden- tissimum amorem Christi erga genus humanum, ex quo passionem subire voluit, adumbrabat. Nimi- rum ignis divinæ iræ minime consumssisset hoc sa- crificium, nisi amoris Christi flamma ille, qua ira in hanc succedaneam hostiam convertenda erat, ac- census fuisset. Joh. 10, 18.

## 1:9
Ver. 9.

ON THE BURNT OFFERING] Concerning the burnt offerings of the Jews, see the excellent passage of Theophrastus, which is in Porphyry, book two of On Abstinence: and Eusebius in the Preparation for the Gospel. Servius, on the second Georgic, says that sometimes entire victims were sacrificed, and he cites a verse of Virgil: And he places the solid entrails of bulls upon the flames. The same Servius is at that passage, which is in the sixth book of the Aeneid. Therefore, solid entrails signifies a burnt offering. Seneca in Oedipus: And he burns solid cattle. Porphyry mentions the ancient burnt offering among the Cyprians. Herodotus, concerning the Egyptians, book II: leading the animal to the altar, they burn a pyre. Then, having poured wine upon it and called upon God, they slaughter it. The same in Polymnia: but Eumilcas at that time was sacrificing and performing rites upon a great pyre, burning whole bodies. But the nations, with the offices of divinity distributed, consecrated burnt offerings to the gods below, as to those who consume all things: the Hebrews referred all things to one God, as the Lord of life and death in burnt offerings, and in other matters as the giver of good things, hostile to vices, and most worthy of praise. For you will see sacrifices referred to these heads. Porphyry, book II of On Abstinence, says thus: one must sacrifice to the gods for three reasons. Either for honor, or for thanks, or for the need of good things. And shortly after: we honor the gods either seeking that the turning away of evils and the provision of good things may come to us, or trusting in good, or that we may obtain some benefit, or according to the simple appreciation of their good nature. But just as the ends of sacrifices are diverse, which you may find both in Arnobius and in Iamblichus, and partly in Macrobius, book III. of the Saturnalia, from Trebatius, so too are the rites, which either came from the Hebrews to other nations, or, which is more credible, were used by the Syrians and Egyptians and corrected by the Hebrews, and used by other nations without that amendment. Servius on the third Aeneid: Moreover, these are animal victims which are only sacrificed, and the meat profits the Priests. (These are shelamim). Elsewhere it signifies only that blood is poured onto the altars, as the bowls of blood and of the sacred: (asham and hattat) elsewhere a part of the body: as, And the entrails into the false Porricia into the waves. (todah Levit. 22, 29.) Elsewhere entire victims, as And he places the solid entrails of bulls upon the flames. That is, olah, for olah among other things signifies to consume: whence this sacrifice is also called a whole burnt offering. Add what we will bring forward below, Levit. 17, 11. It is wonderful how the most ancient sacred rites agree among themselves. Moreover, to all the sacred rites of the Hebrews there were attached their own formulas of praises, prayers, and blessings, whence Theophrastus says of them: calling upon God through prayers.

Three things are to be noted here. The first is that Grotius, neither in burnt offerings nor in other sacrifices, when he relates their ends and uses, ever mentions their principal scope, that they were shadows of things to come and prefigured the sacrifice of Christ: but he is entirely silent about it, and pursues only moral matters or moral ends. He ought not to have forgotten that of Jerome to Paulinus: In Leviticus, INDIVIDUAL SACRIFICES, indeed almost individual syllables and garments, Aaron and the whole Levitical order breathe heavenly Sacraments. And what Augustine inculcates, book 10 of The City of God, ch. 20: The ancient sacrifices of the saints were manifold and various signs of the one true sacrifice of Christ, since for this one thing very many things are figured, just as if one thing were said in many words, so that it might be highly commended without weariness. And book 20 against Faustus, ch. 18. The Hebrews, in the victims of cattle which they offered, in many and various ways, as is worthy of such a matter, celebrated by prophecy the future victim which Christ offered. The second is that he explains the sacrifices, their causes, ends, and rites from profane histories and Poets, when they treat of the sacred rites of the nations, and thus judges divine laws from the sacrifices of the Gentiles, which we have already criticized in him before. Hence he seeks the ends of sacrifices from Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Macrobius, and narrates sacred rites from Virgil, Servius, and others. And such authors in explaining divine laws in Grotius play both parts, as it is said. Excellent interpreters of Holy Scripture indeed! I would not indeed deny that Jewish rites can sometimes take light even from exotic writers, where they describe the rites of the Jews, but that divine laws must be explained from profane institutions and rites, and their causes and ends, that is not to be conceded at all: For one must not learn from the ape of God, the Devil, what God intended, or how divine laws are to be understood, since he, as the father of lies, has depraved them at will, and has introduced that κακοζηλίαν (bad zeal) of the Gentiles into the sacred things of the Jews only for the purpose of obscuring, mocking, and agitating, or blaspheming them. Grotius, however, seems to imitate Julian, who, as Cyril testifies (l. 3. contr. Julian.), said that the sacred things of the Jews differ in nothing from those of the Gentiles: whereas they differ in all causes, and especially in the efficient and final. The pious and the impious do the same things; they are to be distinguished not by their deeds, but by their causes, warns August. Ep. 48. Conf. the same in l. 22. contra Faust. c. 16. where he distinguishes the sacrifices of the Hebrews from those of the Pagans. The third point, in which the πρῶτον ψεῦδος (first falsehood) consists, is also joined with impiety and absurdity: namely, that Grotius deems it more credible that the rites of the Jews in sacrifices draw their origin from the Syrians and Egyptians, and were only corrected by the Hebrews, whereas they are usurped by other nations without that amendment. For shall we believe that God took his most holy institutions, which he himself profusely sanctioned and willed to be written down for religious observation through the inspiration of his divinity, by mutual exchange from the idolatry of the Syrians and Egyptians? For the Hebrews did not assume them at will, or amend them once assumed, but all and each were prescribed divinely in the law, and had to be observed most exactly according to its norm. And were not sacrifices offered by the Patriarchs immediately after the promise concerning the Messiah was promulgated, as is evident concerning Abel (Gen. 4, Heb. 11, 3)? From which foundation Menasse Ben Israel observed that Moses Gerundensis refuted the Grotian opinion in Moses Maimonides (Quæst. 1. in Levit.). How, however, similar ceremonies were transferred to other nations from the Hebrews through perverse imitation or rather the diabolical perversion of divine institutions, the Fathers, Justin Martyr, Augustine, Eusebius, and others, have taught at length. From this Grotian principle it will now be possible to judge what should be held concerning his study, however laborious and erudite it may be, while he gathers from a great number of profane authors, for the sake of explaining the sacred things of the Jews, whatever he happens to have observed. Let it suffice to have warned of this once, so that such things may not delay us hereafter.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

IN HOLOCAUSTUM] De holocaustis Judæorum vide egregium locum Theophrasti, qui est apud Porphyrium se- cundo de Abstinentia: Eusebium ἐν προπαρασκευῇ. Integras interdum victimas immolari ait Servius ad II. Georgicon, ad- fertque Virgilii versum: Et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis. Ad quem locum, qui est in sexto Æneidos idem Servius. Er- go solida viscera holocaustum significat. Seneca in Oedipo- de: Solidasque pecudes urit. Holocaufti veteris apud Cy- prios meminit Porphyrius. Herodotus de Ægyptiis libro II. ἀγαγόντες τὸ κτῆνος πρὸς τὸν βωμὸν πυρὰν καῖεσι. ἔπειτα δὲ ἐπ' ἀυτὲ οἶνον ἐπισπείσαντες καὶ ἐπικαλέσαντες τὸν Θεὸν σφάζεσι. Idem Polymnia : ὁ δὲ ἐυμίλκας ἐν τότῳ τῷ χρό- νῳ ἐθύετο καὶ ἐκαλλιερεῖτο ἐπὶ πυρῆς μεγάλης, σώματα ὅλα καταγίζων. Sed gentes distribvtis divinitatis officiis holo- causta diis inferis, ut cuncta absumentibus, sacrabant: He- bræi cuncta ad unum referebant Deum, ut vitæ necisque Do- minum in holocaustis, in cæteris ut ad bonorum datorem, vi- tiis infestum, laude dignissimum. Ad hæc enim capita vi- debis sacrificia referri. Porphyrius II. περὶ ἀποχῆς fic ait: τριῶν ἕνεκα θυτέον θεοῖς. ἢ γὰρ διὰ τιμὴν, ἢ διὰ χάριν ἢ διὰ χρείαν τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Et mox: τιμῶμεν δὲ τὲς θεὸς ἢ κακῶν μὲν ἀποτροπὴν, ἀγαθῶν δὲ παρασκευὴν ἡμῖν γενέσθαι ζητῶντες, ἢ πεποιθότες εὖ, ἢ ἵνα τύχωμεν ὠφελείας τινὸς, ἢ κατὰ τὴν ψι- λὴν τὴν τῆς ἀγαθῆς ἀυτῶν ἕξεως ἐκτίμησιν. Sicut autem fines sacrificiorum diversi sunt, quos & apud Arnobium & apud Jamblichum reperias, partim & apud Macrobium III. Satur- nalium, ex Trebatio, ita & ritus, qui aut ab Hebræis ad gentes alias venere, aut quod credibilius est, à Syris & Ægyptiis usur- pati correcti sunt ab Hebræis & ab aliis gentibus sine ea emen- datione usurpati. Servius ad III. Æneidos; Sunt autem hæ animales hostiæ quæ tantum immolantur, & caro Sacerdotibus proficit. (hæc sunt שלמים) Alibi tantum sanguinem in aras fundi significat, ut sanguinis & sacri pateras: (אשם & חטאת) alibi partem corporis: ut, Extaque falfos Porrici- am in fluctus. (תודה Levit. 22, 29.) Alibi integras victimas, ut Et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis. Id est, עלה nam עלה inter alia consumere significat: unde & κάρπωμα vocatur hoc sacrificium. Adde quæ adferemus in- fra Levit. 17, 11. Mirum est, quam vetustissima sacra inter se congruant. Omnibus autem sacris Hebræorum suæ aderant formulæ laudum, precum, benedictionum, unde de iis Theo- phrastus: διὰ τῶν ἐυχῶν θεοκλυτῶντες.

Tria hic monenda. Primum est, quod Gro- tius nec in holocaustis, nec in sacrificiis aliis, cum fi- nes & usus eorum refert, præcipuum eorum scopum, quod umbræ fuerint futurorum & Christi sacrificium præfigurarint, uspiam commemoret: Sed de eo prorsus sileat, & moralia solum aut morales fines sectetur. Non dememinisse debuisset illius Hiero- nymi ad Paulin. In Levitico SINGULA SACRIFI- CIA, imo singulæ pene Syllabæ & vestes, Aaron & totus ordo Leviticus spirant cælestia Sacramenta. Et quod inculcat. Augustinus lib. 10. de C. D. c. 20. U- nius vere sacrificii Christi multiplicia variaque signa erant sacrificia prisca sanctorum, cum ob hoc unum permulta figurentur, tanquam verbis multis res una diceretur, ut sine fastidio multum commendaretur. Et libr. 20. contra Faustum c. 18. Ebræi in victimis pe- cudum, quas offerebant, multis & variis modis, sicut re tanta dignum, prophetiā celebrabant futuræ victimæ, quam Christus obtulit. Alterum est, quod sacrificia, eorum causas, fines & ritus e prophanis historiis, & Poetis, cum de gentium sacris agunt, explicet, adeo- que e gentilium sacrificiis de legibus divinis judi- cet, quod antea in ipso jam reprehendimus. Hinc a Porphyrio, Jamblicho, Macrobio fines sa- crificiorum petit, e Virgilio, Servio, aliisque ri- tus sacros enarrat.
