Et tales autores in explican- dis legibus divinis apud Grotium utramq;, quod dicitur, faciunt paginam. Egregii profecto S. literarum Interpretes! Non equidem nega- rim, posse ritus Judaicos etiam ab exoticis quando- que lucem capere Scriptoribus, ubi Judæorum ritus describunt,sed leges divinas ex institutis & riti- bus prophanis,eorumq́; causis & finibus explicandas ef- se,id minime concedendum: Non enim a Dei simia, Diabolo discendum,quid Deus intenderit,aut quo- modo leges divinæ intelligendæ sint,quum is, ceu pater mendacii,easdem pro lubitu depravarit, nec nisi obscurandis,illudendis,& exagitandis,aut blas- phemandis sacris Judæorum illam Gentilium κακο- ζηλίαν invexerit. Imitari autem Julianum videtur Grotius, qui Cyrillo l. 3. contr. Julian. teste, Judæo- rum sacra nihil a gentilibus differre dixit: quum causis tamen omnibus differant, & imprimis effi- cienti ac finali. Cumpii & impii eadem faciunt,non factis,sed causis discernendi sunt, monet August. Ep. 48. Conf. idem l. 22. contra Faust. c. 16. ubi sacrifi- cia Ebræorum a Paganis distinguit. Tertium, in quo πρῶτον ψεῦδος consistit, cum impietate & ab- surditate etiam conjunctum est: quod nempe Gro- tius credibilius censeat, ritus Judæorum in sacrificiis a Syris & Ægyptiis originem trahere,correćtos solum esse ab Ebræis,quum ab aliis gentibus sine emendatione illa usurpentur. Num enim Deum sanctissima sua in- stituta, quæ ipse prolixe sancivit & conscribi in reli- giosam observationem per inspirationem numinis sui voluit, credemus ab idololatria Syrorum & Ægy- ptiorum mutuo sumpsisse? Non enim ea pro lubitu Ebræi assumserunt, aut assumta emendarunt, sed o- mnia & singula divinitus in lege præscripta sunt, & juxta ejus normam exactissime observari debue- runt. Et annon a Patriarchis statim post promul- gatam promissionem de Messia oblata sacrificia, uti de Abele constat Gen. 4. Ebr. 11, 3? E quo funda- mento Grotianam sententiam in Mose Maimonide, Mosen Gerundensem refutasse observavit Menasse Ben Israel Quæst. 1. in Levit. Quomodo autem ad alias gentes ab Ebræis similes Ceremoniæ ex prava imitatione vel diabolica potius institutorum divi- norum perversione traductæ sunt, prolixe docuere Patres, Justinus Martyr, Augustinus, Eusebius, alii. Ex isto principio Grotiano jam judicari poterit, quid haberi debeat de studio ejusdem quantumvis operoso, atque erudito,dum ex prophanis autori- bus magno numero, ad sacra Judæorum explican- da,congerit,quæcunque forte observavit. Quod hic semel monuisse sufficiat, ne talia nos deinceps remorentur.

## 1:9
AND A SWEET SAVOR TO THE LORD.

Not that God was delighted by the smell of flesh: but that, putting on the shadow of the passion of his Son, he was delighted by that satisfaction: so that for the sake of Christ then to come, he might forgive sins: just as now, with Christ revealed, he is appeased toward us for the sake of the same through his death, which is always in the sight of God the Father, as Osiander says here. Conf. Eph. 5, 2.

Latin:

ET SUAVEM ODOREM DOMINO.

Non quod Deus nidore carnium delectaretur: sed quod induens umbram passionis Filii sui, ea sa- tisfactione delectaretur: ut propter Christum tum venturum,condonaret peccata: sicut nunc revelato Christo propter eundem nobis placatur per ipsius mortem,quæ semper est in conspectu Dei Patris, ut hîc Osiander. Conf. Eph. 5,2.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. BUT THEY SHALL POUR ITS BLOOD UPON THE ALTAR] See what is at Exod. 29, 16.

Not upon the grated hearth, for thus the blood would have extinguished the fire, but it had to be poured upon the sides of the altar, or the walls round about v. 5. 11. 15.

TO THE NORTH.

The altar of burnt offerings was at the door to the south. Therefore, in order that the immolation might take place before the door, it had to be done at the northern side of the altar: by which it was signified, according to Cyril, that Christ's passion would profit the Gentiles: because Judea was to the South, whence the Gentiles, opposed to the Jews, were signified by the North. Osiander has this to say about this rite: The victim was slaughtered not on the southern side, but on the northern: so that it might be signified that the people of the Old Testament did not yet have the full revelation of the light of the Gospel: which is rightly compared to the meridian Sun, in respect to the shadows of the Law.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SANGUINEM VERO ILLIUS FUNDENT SUPER ALTARE] Vide quod Exod. 29,16.

Non super craticulam reticulatam, sic enim ignem exstinxisset sanguis, sed super latera altaris, vel parietes circumcirca v. 5. 11. 15. fundi debuit.

AD AQUILONEM.

Altare holocaustorum ostio erat ad meridiem. Ut ergo coram ostio fieret immolatio,ad latus aqui- lonare altaris fieri debuit: quo significatum, autore Cyrillo, Christi passionem gentibus profuturam: quia Judæa ad Austrum fuit, unde gentes Judæis opposi- tæ per Aquilonem significatæ. Osiander de hoc ritu ita habet: Mactabatur hostia non in latere meridiona- li,sed aquilonari: ut significaretur: populum Vet. Test. nondum habere plenam revelationem lucis Evangelii: quæ meridiano Soli recte comparatur, respectu umbra- rum Legis.

## 1:14 Addition
On verse 14, IF OF THE BIRDS, at page 471. b.

Partridges were not used because they are more wild; ducks and hens, because they fed on unclean nourishment; turtledoves in their mature age, pigeons in their tender age, as being thus most excellent, as Bochart notes in his Hierozoicon.

Latin:

Ad v. 14. SI DE AVIBUS ad pag. 471. b.

Perdices non adhibebantur, quod magis sylvestres, anates & gallinæ, quod vescebantur immundo nutrimento, turtures, in matura, columbæ in tenera ætate, utpote ita maxime præstantes, notante Bocharto in Hierozoico.

## 1:15
ver. 15. WITH THE HEAD WRUNG TO THE NECK) Not only in burnt offerings, but in all sacrifices, the bodies of the birds were left connected at the neck. Abulensis and Osiander think the neck was opened by being twisted with the nail; which is also the opinion of the Rabbis. But Bonfrerius notes that the force of the Hebrew word is this, not that the head should be twisted off, but that it should be wrung to the neck, in almost the same way in which we slaughter hens and fatted birds, and indeed also sheep, by wringing the head to the neck, so that a free place may be open for inflicting the wound in the throat, not with the nail, but with iron: just as in c. 5, 8, to wring to the wings is to wring as far as the wings. The rest, however, sufficiently indicate that a cut had to be applied, yet the head was not to be separated from the neck, the danger of which thing, however, would have existed entirely in that contortion of Abulensis. In the Hebrew and Chaldean also, it is held there as 'against his neck or nape'. Add, since such a contortion often extinguishes the bird, and the blood cools immediately upon death, so that consequently it is also extracted with more difficulty, unless the blood is drawn out together with the soul, it would have happened that much blood would have remained in the veins, which the Jews especially avoided. The head, however, should not have been broken off, partly because of the figure of the passion of Christ, partly because of the foreshadowing of his mystical body, which is never separated from its head: concerning which Greg. M. hom. 1. in h.l. says the head of the turtledove once cut remained attached to the body, because Christ indeed suffered for us, but he was not separated from us through the passion, but rather he joined us to himself. Therefore, Piscator wrongly inserted Rabbinical nails into the text, and renders it 'split the head with the nail of his finger': he also interpreted wrongly concerning the throwing away of the head in v. 16: 'and he shall have taken away his head': but the head should not have been cast away, and indeed not even separated from the trunk, but the discourse is about the vesicle of the throat being thrown away. It is asked, however, why offerings had to be made from turtledoves, etc., and not from other birds, hens, partridges, etc. Resp. Lyran. The other birds are either more wild, or if they are domestic, they feed on unclean nourishment, such as hens and ducks. The turtledove signifies the chastity of Christ; the dove, which lacks gall, his sweetness or meekness.

Latin:

vers. 15. RETORTO AD COLLUM CAPITE) Non in holocaustis tantum, sed in omnibus sacrificiis avium corpora collo connexa relinquebantur. Abulensis & Osiander putant ungue contortum collum apertum; quæ Rabbinorum etiam senten- tia est. Sed Bonfrerius notat vim vocis Ebrææ hanc esse,non ut caput contorqueretur, sed ad collum re- torqueretur,eo fere modo,quo gallinas & altilia ju- gulamus, imo & oves, retorquendo in collum ca- put,ut in gutture vulneri inferendo liber locus pa- teat,non ungue,sed ferro: uti c.5, 8. retorquere ad pennulas est retorquere usq; ad alas. Cætera vero satis indicant sectionem fuisse adhibendam, non ta- men caput a collo separandum, cujus tamen rei pe- riculum omnino fuisset in illa Abulensis contorsio- ne. In Ebræo etiam & Chaldeo ibi habetur contra collum vel cervicem ejus. Adde,cum talis contorsio avem sæpenumero extinguat, ac per mortem statim sanguis frigescat, ut proinde etiam difficilius extra- hatur,nisi sanguis simul cum anima educatur, sutu- rum fuisset,ut multum sanguinis in venis remansis- set,quod maxime Judæi cavebant. Abrumpi autem caput non debuit partim ob figuram passionisChri- sti, partim ob adumbrationem corporis ejusdem mystici,quod a capite suo nunquam separatur: quo de Greg.M. hom. 1. in h.l. caput turturis incisum olim inhesit corpori,quia pro nobis quidem passus est Chri- stus, sed a nobis per passionem separatus non est, quin imo nos sibi conjunxit. Perperam ergo Piscator tex- tui Rabbinicos ungues inseruit,redditque den Kopff mit dem Nagel seines Fingers zerspalten: perperam etiam de projectione capitis v. 16. interpretatus est: und er seinen Kopff wird weggethan haben: non vero abjici caput debuit,ac ne separari quidem a trunco, sed de vesicula gutturis projicienda sermo est. Quæ- ritur autem cur de turturibus &c. non de aliis avi- bus, gallinis,perdicibus &c. oblationes fieri debue- rint. Resp. Lyran. Cæteræ aves vel sunt magis sylve- stres,vel si sunt domesticæ, vescuntur immundo nu- trimento, ut gallinæ, anates. Turtur significat Christi castitatem, columba, quæ felle caret ejus dulcedinem, vel mansuetudinem.

## 1:16
v. 16. BUT THE VESICLE OF THE THROAT.

Vatablus rendered the word מְרֵאתוֹ as 'stomach', but the Chaldean and Vulgate more correctly explained it as the vesicle of the throat: as did also Theodoret, Φύσαν, that is, a follicle; Aquila, σιτίζεαν, that is, the alimentary part: which receives food and communicates it to the remaining parts of the body; and the LXX, πρόλοβον, that is, the vesicle of the throat, so called from the follicle λόβῳ, which first receives the food eaten from the throat. If the stomach or the body of the sheep itself, from which the head was not to be torn off, was to be cast away, what then was to be sacrificed? God did not wish the vesicle of the throat to be burned, because it is unclean, and for the detestation of gluttony: for the pleasure of food is not felt except in the mouth and this vesicle: as Cyril warns, he also reproves soft feathers and delicate garments.

Latin:

v. 16. VESICULAM VERO GUTTURIS.

Vatablus ventriculum reddidit vocem מְרֵאתוֹ, sed Chald. & Vulg. rectius vesiculam gutturis expo- suere: uti & Theodor. Φύσαν id est, folliculum, A- quila σιτίζεαν,id est,alimentarem partem: quæ ré- cipit cibum eumq; reliquis corporis partibus com- municat, & LXX. πρόλοβον, hoc est, vesiculam gut- turis a folliculo λόβῳ ita dictam,qui primus cibum a gutture comestum recipit. Si ventriculus vel cor- pus ipsum ovis, a quo abrumpendum caput non e- rat, projiciendum, quid ergo immolandum erat? Noluit autem Deus vesicam gutturis incendi, quia immunda est, & ad ingluviai detestationem: cibi enim voluptas non sentitur,nisi in ore & hac vesica: monen- te Cyrillo, plumas etiam molles, vestes delicatas re- probat.

## 1:17
vers. 17. HE SHALL NOT CUT.

He was to tear the wings, not cut them, because although Christ endured the most bitter pains in his passion, yet his body was not dissected into pieces.

Latin:

vers. 17. NON SECABIT.

Alas scindere,non secare debebat,quia etsiChri- stus in passione acerbissimos dolores sustinuit, non tamen corpus ejus in frusta dissectum fuit.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

Mincha, or the flour sacrifice.

Vers. HIS OFFERING SHALL BE FINE FLOUR, AND HE SHALL POUR OIL UPON IT, AND PUT FRANKINCENSE] Virgil in the 6th Aeneid: - - - - - - heaped up are burned Frankincense gifts, feasts, bowls with poured oil. The High Priest offered daily Marad.

The Mincha was threefold: fine flour, of baked breads either in an oven, or in a frying pan, or on a griddle, and of ears of grain: which are added, so that the poorer might not lack what to offer.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Mincha, seu sacrificium ferreum.

Vers. SIMILA ERIT EJUS OBLATIO, FUNDET- QUE SUPER EAM OLEUM, ET PONET THUS] Vir- gilius in 6. Æneidos: - - - - - - congesta cremantur Thurea dona, dapes, fuso crateres olivo. Pontifex Maximus quotidie offerebat Marad.

Mincha triplex erat : simila, panum coctorum seu in clibano, seu in sartagine, seu in craticula, & spicarum : quæ adduntur, ne pauperioribus desit, quod offerant.

## 2:2
verse 2. AND SHALL PLACE A MEMORIAL.

More correctly: he shall burn the memorial, by which God is as it were reminded, so that He may have merciful regard for the offerer.

FOR A SAVOR.

In Hebrew אשֶה is an ignition, or a burnt offering, or a holocaust, but in a certain sense: namely, in that some part of it, a handful, or as much as could be taken by the hand, was burned in memory of the whole gift, because by that it was signified that the whole mass of flour, or of breads, or of fruits was consecrated to God. Therefore, v. 3 and 10, the whole offering is called a Holy of Holies, because the remainder had to be eaten only by the Priests and in the holy place of the court of the tabernacle, Levit. 6, 16, whereas from other common Sacrifices they could eat even at home, and the wives, children, and servants of the priests were not excluded from eating them. Moreover, there had to be added to this offering oil, by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit were noted; frankincense, by which the fragrance of prayers; and salt, which is called of the covenant v. 13, by which the memory and constancy of God's covenant, because salt preserves from putrefaction and is a symbol of perpetuity. Num. 18, 12. From this mandate concerning Salt, Christ warned in Mark 9, 49. so that we may be compared to the eternal and incorruptible observance of the covenant, by the example of offerings, which without salt are ungrateful. Leaven, however, v. 11, as a symbol of corruption and sin 1 Cor. 5, 8, and honey as a symbol of pleasure and delights were excluded. See Procopius and Rupertus.

But this is to be understood concerning the voluntary gift, which alone is treated in this chapter. For in Eucharistic sacrifices leavened cakes were used, Lev. 7, 13, and leavened breads in the offering of firstfruits c. 23, 20. Thus also this is to be understood concerning the voluntary gift of a sweet savor, what is commanded concerning the savor and frankincense: for it had to be done otherwise if at any time the gift was one recalling the memory of iniquity, as Num. 5, v. 16. Which had to lack oil and frankincense, because in sin there is nothing that can be pleasing. Let us now hear Grotius.

Latin:

vers. 2. ET PONET MEMORIALE.

Rectius : adolebit memoriale, quo Deus ad- moneatur quasi, ut offerentis clementer rationem habeat.

IN ODOREM.

In Ebr. אשֶה ignitio, vel oblatio ignita, vel ho- locaustum, sed secundum quid : qua nempe aliquid ejus, pugillus, vel quantum manu capi poterat, cre- mabatur in memoriam totius muneris, quia totam similæ, vel panum, vel frugum massam Deo conse- crari eo significabatur. Ideo v. 3. & 10. Sanctum San- ctorum dicitur tota oblatio, quia reliquum non nisi a Sacerdotibus & in loco sancto comedi debebat atrii tabernaculi Levit. 6, 16. quum ex aliis communibus Sacrificiis etiam domi vesci potuerint, uxores quo- que, liberi, ac domestici sacerdotum ab eorum esu exclusi non fuerint. Addi autem huic oblationi de- buit oleum, quo Spirit. S. dona, thus, quo precum fra- grantia, & sal, quod vocatur fœderis v. 13. quo me- moria & constantia fœderis Dei, quia sal a putrefa- ctione præservat, & perpetuitatis symbolum est, no- tabatur. Num. 18, 12. Ex hoc mandato de Sale Chri- stus monuit Marc. 9, 49. ut ad æternam & incorru- ptam fœderis observationem comparemur, obla- tionum exemplo, quæ sine sale ingratæ sunt. Fer- mentum vero v. 11. ceu symbolum corruptionis & peccati 1. Cor. 5, 8. & mel ceu Symbolum voluptatis & deliciarum excludebatur. Vid. Procopig & Rupertus.

De munere autem voluntario, quo de tantum in hoc capite agitur, id accipiendum. Nam in Euchari- sticis sacrificiis collyræ fermentatæ adhibitæ sunt Lev. 7, 13. & panes fermentati in oblatione primitiarum c. 23, 20. Sic etiam de munere voluntario odoris grati hoc intelligendum, quod de odore, ac thure præci- pitur : secus enim id fieri oportuit, si quando munus fuit memoriam iniquitatis revocans, ut Num. 5. v. 16. Quod oleo & thure carere debuit, quia in peccato nihil est quod gratum esse possit. Audiamus jam Grotium.

## 2:3 Addition
On chapter 2, verse 3, SHALL AARON. at page 472. a.

Namely, for eating, Lev. 6:16; understand this of the solitary Mincha; for what was joined to other sacrifices was burned, see Leviticus 23:13. The reason is added: MOST HOLY, and therefore not to be eaten except by the Priests. This sacrifice was therefore instituted partly for the sake of the poor, so that the means to offer might not fail them; partly for the sake of the Priests, so that they might have bread; partly also for the sake of the Lord, so that God, the giver of them, might be worshipped also with the fruits of the earth. Menochius adds, regarding verse 1, that the sacrifice was, as it were, a banquet prepared for GOD: whence there was in it bread, wine, and salt, Numbers 15:4, 10, and here in verse 13; partly to foreshadow Christ, who is the true bread of life.

Latin:

Ad cap. 2. vers. 3. ERIT AARON. ad pag. 472. a.

Nempe ad comedendum Lev. 6. v. 16. intellige de Mincha solitario; nam quod aliis sacrificiis adjunctum erat cremabatur, vid. Levit. 23. versu 13. Additur ratio: SANCTUM SANCTORUM, ideoque non comedendum, nisi à Sacerdotibus. Institutum itaque hoc sacrificium partim pro pauperibus, ne illos offerendi facultas deficeret, partim ob Sacerdotes, ut haberent panem: partim etiam ob Dominum, ut terræ quoque frugibus Deus earum dator coleretur. Addit Menochius circa vers. 1. quod sacrificium fuerit q. convivium DEO instructum: unde in eo fuerit panis, vinum & Sal, Numer. 15. versu. 47. 10. & hic versu 13. partim ob Christum adumbrandum, qui verus panis vitæ.

## 2:4
WITHOUT LEAVEN ] See what we said above Ex. 12, 15. Except the Sacrifice of thanksgiving, in which it was permitted to offer common food, that is, leavened. Below 7, 13.

It is also to be observed that fine flour and oil were also accustomed to be offered separately, as a peculiar Sacrifice with frankincense, which besides were also offered jointly with oxen, goats, and sheep, which were offered as a holocaust or peace offerings, and were accustomed to be added to them as supplements, together with wine, Num. 15. There, only a part was cast into the fire, the rest belonged to the Priest: here, however, those things which accompanied the holocaust were entirely burned. See Josephus, book 3, Antiquities, c. 10.

Verse 4. BAKED IN AN OVEN ] Mola, toasted spelt. Festus. Pliny, book 18, 2, says it was decreed by Numa that spelt was not pure for divine service unless toasted.

Latin:

ABSQUE FERMENTO ] Vide quod supra diximus Ex. 12, 15. Excipe Sacrificium gratiarum actionis, in quo licebat offerre victum familiarem, id est, fermentatum. Infra 7, 13.

Id etiam observandum, quod simila & oleum etiam offerri consueverint seorsim, ceu peculiare Sa- crificium cum thure, quæ præterea quoque conjun- ctim cum bobus, capris, ovibus, quæ offerebantur in holocaustum, vel pacifica oblata sunt, illisq; ceu addi- tamenta solita sunt adjici, una cum vino Num. 15. Illic pars tantum in ignem conjiciebatur, reliqua Sacer- dotis erant : hic vero ea, quæ holocaustum comita- bantur, tota cremabantur. Vid. Joseph. l. 3. Antiq. c. 10.

Vers. 4. COCTUM IN CLIBANO ] Mola, far tostum. Festus. Plinius libro 18, 2. a Numa statutum, ait, non esse far purum ad rem divinam, nisi tostum.

## 2:9
verse 9. HE WHO SHALL HAVE OFFERED IT. More correctly, shall have brought it to the altar. HE SHALL TAKE.

He shall lift up on high the memorial from the sacrifice, that is, he shall lift up some part of the cake in the usual manner, and afterwards by offering it he will remind God with this offering, so that He may mercifully regard the offerer, and he shall burn (that particle) upon the altar.

Latin:

vers. 9. QUI CUM OBTULERIT EAM. Rectius attulerit eam ad altare. TOLLET.

Levabit in altum memoriale de sacrificio, id est, partem aliquam placentæ sursum levabit more soli- to, & postea eam offerendo Deum oblatione hac admonebit, ut offerentem clementer respiciat, & adolebit (sic particulam illam) super altare.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. AND OF HONEY] Because honey was used in the λεοντικοῖς [leontic] rites, as Porphyry teaches us in his 'On the Cave of the Nymphs'. Those rites, however, were of Mithras, as you will see if you look at the same Porphyry in the fourth book of 'On Abstinence', and the Scholiast of Papinius at the end of the first book of the Thebaid. Interpretation adds figs and dates to honey. The mystical sense is that excessive pleasures are displeasing to God. Theophrastus wrongly thinks honey was mixed into the sacrifices of the Hebrews. Plutarch is better in his 'Symposiacs' regarding these same Hebrews: μέλι δ' προσφέρουσι ταῖς ἱερεργίαις [and they offer honey in their sacred rites].

It is more correctly said that the exclusion of honey served as a reminder of the true and perpetual sweetness of heavenly foods, and especially of the living bread, Christ (John 6), which degenerates into no bitterness and lasts without any loathing (1 Pet. 2:3; Ps. 19:11), whereas, by contrast, cooked honey contracts acidity, ferments the bread to which it is mixed, and smells foul when burnt; and also a reminder of the bitterness of the passions and life of Christ, in which there is not a γλυκύπικρον [bittersweet], as in ours, or bittersweet, but mere bitterness without the honey of pleasure.

Latin:

Vers. 11. AC MELLIS] Quia mel usurpabatur in Sacris λεοντικοῖς, ut nos docet Porphyrius ad antrum Nympharum. Ea autem sacra erant Mithræ, ut videbis, si nspicias eundem porphyrium quarto de abstinentia, & Scholiasten Papini ad finem primi Thebaidos. Melli interpretatio accenset ficus & dactylos. Mysticus sensus, displicere Deo nimias volupta- tes. Male Theophrastus mel sacris Hebræorum admixtum putat. Melius Plutarchus Symposiacis de iisdem Hebræis : μέλι δ' προσφέρουσι ταῖς ἱερεργίαις.

Rectius exclusio mellis dicitur admonuisse de vera & perpetua ciborum cœlestium, imprimis vero panis vivi Christi Joh. 6. dulcedine, quæ in nullam degenerat amaritiem, & sine omni durat fastidio 1. Petr. 2, 3. Ps. 19, 11. cum ex adverso mel coctum aco- rem contrahat, & panem, cui miscetur, fermentet, & combustum fœteat : nec non de acerbitate passionum & vitæ Christi, in qua non γλυκύπικρον ut in nostra, vel dulcamarum, sed mera amaritudo sine melle vo- luptatis.

## 2:12
vers. 12. YOU SHALL OFFER THEM ONLY AS FIRST FRUITS AND GIFTS.

For the use of the Priests, that is, it will indeed be permitted to offer leavened breads to the Lord for the food of the Priests (Lev. 2:3) and a cake of leavened bread for the sake of gratitude for the sustenance of the Priests and for the use of the banquet which was celebrated after the sacrifice was completed, Lev. 7.

BUT THEY SHALL NOT BE PLACED UPON THE ALTAR AS A SWEET-SMELLING SAVOR.

That is, in the sacrifices, however, nothing of the sort shall be burned to the Lord on the altar, and thus neither leaven nor honey shall be used. For since such sacrifices foreshadow Christ, in whom no leaven of corrupt morals has been found, leaven is rightly removed from such a sacrifice. And because honey is indeed sweet at first, but when taken in large amounts in food it increases bile and causes bitterness; whereas Christ, however often and much he is grasped and consumed by faith, becomes sweeter to believers day by day: he would not have been rightly foreshadowed by honey; wherefore honey is rightly removed from such sacrifices.

Latin:

vers. 12. PRIMITIAS TANTUM EORUM OFFERETIS AC MUNERA.

In usum Sacerdotum, id est, licebit quidem & pa- nes fermentatos offerre Domino in cibum Sacerdo- tum (Lev. 2, 3.) & crustulam panis fermentati grati- tudinis ergo pro alimento Sacerdotum & ad usum convivii, quod, peracto sacro, celebrabatur, Lev. 7.

SUPER ALTARE VERO NON IMPONEN- TUR IN ODOREM SUAVITATIS.

Id est, in Sacrificiis vero nihil tale Domino in al- tari cremetur, adeoq; sic neq; fermentum, neq; mel adhibeatur. Cum enim talia Sacrificia Christum adumbrent, in quo nec fermentum corruptorum morum ullum est repertum, recte fermentum a tali sacrificio removetur. Et quia mel initio quidem dulce est : sed multum in cibo sumtum bilem auget & amaritudinem efficit : Christus vero, quantumvis sæpe multumque fide apprehensus & comestus, in- dies credentibus magis dulcescat : non fuisset recte adumbratus melle : quare mel recte a talibus sacri- ficiis removetur.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. WHATEVER YOU OFFER OF SACRIFICE] He translates from the Greek θυσία [sacrifice]: which word in this place signifies not bloody victims, but offerings made of fine flour. In the Hebrew קרבן [korban], as at the beginning of the chapter. See what is said on Mark 9:49. The Greeks called such things πόπανα [popana] and ψαιςὰ [psaista], to which you see oil mixed in Porphyry's 'On Abstinence', book two. The Latins called them 'liba' from 'libando' [to pour a libation]. A part of these was burned upon the altar: above 9. Menander in 'The Dissembler': Ὁ λιβανωτὸς ἐυσεβὴς καὶ τὸ πόπανον. Τῦτ᾽ ἔλαβεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ ἅπαν τεθέν [The frankincense is pious, and the cake; God received this, all placed upon the fire].

YOU SHALL SEASON WITH SALT) Hence 'mola salsa' [salted meal], which is also 'casta' [pure]. Servius on the 8th Eclogue, on the 2nd Aeneid, likewise on the 4th and on the last of the same work. Pliny, dealing with salt in book 31, ch. 7: 'Its authority is understood most of all in sacred rites, since none are performed without salted meal.' Salt signifies a covenant (2 Chron. 13:5). Hence the 'Salt of the Covenant' in this very place, namely, because of its durability. Philosophers also understand salt as the soul, the preserver of the body: Varro, Philo, Porphyry.

Christ is also noted here as the heavenly Salt, because by his grace he seasons both bodies and souls and preserves them for eternity, so that they may arrive at immortal life: without which salt no gift is pleasing to God. Cf. Paul Fagius on this passage. Salt is also a symbol of wisdom and discretion, which is needed in every gift and work. Finally, salt is a symbol of ἀφθαρσίας [incorruptibility] (Mark 9:49, 50). All of which can be referred to the 'Mincha' or sacrifice of Christ. For that offering is full of the grace of seasoning us for life, and it is seasoned with the salt of wisdom and justice, subject to no decay or corruption; and it perfects forever those who are sanctified (Heb. 10:14). The 'Mincha' is Christ's flesh prepared in the oven or womb of the Blessed Virgin: fried in the frying pan of the passion: dead on the gridiron of the cross; so that it may provide us with pleasing sustenance in the Holy Supper and the Word of the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QUIDQUID OBTULERIS SACRIFICII ] Vertit ex Græco θυσία : quæ vox hoc loco non cruentas victi- mas, sed oblata ex simila significat. In Hebræo קרבן, ut ini- tio capitis. Vide quæ ad Marcum 9, 49. Græci talia vocabant πόπανα & ψαιςὰ, quibus admixtum oleum vides, apud Por- phyrium de Abstinentia secundo. Latini a libando liba di- xere. Horum pars adolebatur super altare : supra 9. Menander Discolo : Ὁ λιβανωτὸς ἐυσεβὴς καὶ τὸ πόπανον. Τῦτ᾽ ἔλαβεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ ἅπαν τεθέν.

SALE CONDIES) Inde mola salsa, quæ & casta. Ser- vius ad 8. Eclogam, ad 2. Æneid. item ad 4. & ad ult. ejusdem operis. Plinius de Sale agens lib. 31. c. 7. Maxime tamen in sacris intelligitur auctoritas, quando nulla conficiuntur sine mola salsa. Sal fœdus significat 2. Paral. 13, 5. Hinc Sal fœ- deris hoc ipso loco nim. ob diuturnitatem. Philosophi per salem etiam animam intelligunt, corporis conservatricem : Varro, Philo, Porphyrius.

Notatur & hic Christus Sal cœlestis, quia sua gratia tam corpora, quam animas condit, & servat æternitati, ut perveniant ad vitam immortalem : si- ne quo sale nullum munus Deo gratum est. Conf. Paul. Fagius in h. l. Sal etiam Symbolum est sapien- tiæ & discretionis, qua in omni munere & opere opus est. Sal denique est ἀφθαρσίας Symbolum Marc. 9, 49, 50. Quæ omnia ad Mincha vel sacrificium Christi referre licet. Nam oblatio illa plena est gratia con- diendi nos ad vitam, & condita est sale sapientiæ & justitiæ, nulli labi aut corruptioni obnoxia ; con- summatq; in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur Ebr. 10, 14. Mincha est Christi caro in clibano vel utero B. Virginis parata : in sartagine passionis frixa : in craticula crucis mortua ; ut gratum nobis præbeat in S. cœna & Verbo Evangelii alimentum.

## 2:14
v. 14. THE GIFT OF THE FIRST FRUITS.

Such as was offered at Passover from the first fruits of the barley harvest; just as the first fruits of the loaves from the wheat harvest were to be offered to GOD at the feast of Pentecost, and the first fruits of all produce at the feast of Tabernacles (Lev. 23:15, 17; Exod. 23:16, 19). The first fruits of the produce at Passover is Christ rising at Passover as if the firstborn of the dead, says Cyril.

Jerusalem [Targum]: it is not about those, but only about voluntary gifts.

Latin:

v. 14. MUNUS PRIMARUM FRUGUM.

Quale offerebatur in Paschate de primitiis frugum messis hordeaceæ ; ut primitiæ panum ex messis triticea in Pentecoste festo, & primitiæ fru- gum omnium in festo tabernaculorum DEO offer- ri debebant Levit. 23, 15. 17. Exod. 23, 16. 19. Pri- mitiæ frugum in Paschate est Christus resurgens in Pa- schate quasi primogenitus mortuorum, ait Cyrillus

Hieros. non de illis, sed de voluntariis tantum do- nis agitur.

## 2:16
verse 16. ALL THE FRANKINCENSE.

The final words of the chapter are missing here in the Vulgate: This is an ignited (or Sacrifice, accepted) to the Lord.

Latin:

vers. 16. TOTUM THUS.

Verba postrema Capitis hîc desunt in Vulga- ta: Hoc est ignitum (seu Sacrificium, acceptum) Do- mino.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. The Peace Offering.

verse 1. BUT IF THE PEACE OFFERING.

Which is designated here as threefold: of oxen, of sheep, and of goats, where God claims for Himself all the fat and the blood. And this is the summary of this chapter. Regarding the peace offering, Grotius says thus: שלמים from שלום, which is Peace: but Servius on the fourth Georgics teaches us that peace is also used by the Latins for a benefit. By the Chaldeans this sacrifice is called a sanctificatory, as by the Greeks τελεστικὸν: by the Hebrews by another name תודר, that is, τελείωσις: Now these were of three kinds: תודר αἴνεσις, for a benefit received, the fulfillment of a vow, or of mere liberality, as can be seen below 7, 12. Regarding these, it was permitted after the blood was poured out for private individuals, who had offered them, and their wives and children to feast, as a sign of friendship with God. That was not permitted in the offering of fine flour, because that was among the Sacerdotal privileges: nor in victims for sin and guilt, lest they rejoice over the fault. For the same reason the Pontiff's victim is burned. Below 4, 12.

Paul Fagius has dealt at length with the word שלמים at this place. Furthermore, the rite of sprinkling blood upon the altar indicated that without the shedding of the blood of Christ no sacrifice is pleasing or fruitful to God, Heb. 9, 14. 22. Therefore, it is shown here how our spiritual sacrifices ought to be instituted: 1. By the laying on of hands, i.e., that with the spiritual right hand of faith we transfer all our sins onto Christ. 2. By the sprinkling of blood, or confidence in the merit and efficacy of the death and blood of Christ. 3. By the mortification of the flesh, or of all desires and affections. 4. By consideration of the scope and end, to which alone all things must be referred. Gregory the Great, homily 25 on the Gospel: By the precept of the law, the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in the sacrifice. For in the tail is the end of the body: and he sacrifices well, who leads the sacrifice of a good work up to the end of the required action. Therefore it is prohibited in verse 17. eating of blood, so that they might think how great that future price of blood for the sins of the World would be, and abstain from blood at least for so long until that which was shown in type was completed by the deed. See Augustine, book 32, chapter 13 against Faustus. Nor was the fat to be eaten, so that they might be warned about abstinence from pleasures, temperance, and frugality, and might acknowledge that not vile and abject things, but all that is fat and choice should be offered to God, and that they might look toward the better and more excellent sacrifice of Christ, and also to the feast of fat things prepared by Him, Isa. 25, 6. Nor indeed was all fat forbidden to the Jews, but only that of goats, sheep, and oxen, as Josephus notes in book 3, chapter 10, that is, of those animals which can be offered to God. Compare Lev. 7, 21. But regarding other clean animals, which could not be offered to God, that was nowhere prohibited. Only the fat was forbidden from those which surrounds and covers or hides the vital organs, verse 3. that is, those vital interior parts, the heart, liver, lungs, kidneys, intestines, not that which is mixed throughout the flesh. Now our spiritual Eucharistic sacrifices (after the peace sacrifice of Christ) are here adumbrated, when we offer ourselves to God in obedience to His will, Rom. 12; when we are prepared to undergo even death for His name, 2 Tim. 4; when we celebrate God with praises, by commemorating the benefits bestowed upon us by Him, both spiritual and corporal, Hos. 14, Heb. 13; when we contribute liberally from our resources either to feed the ministers of the Church, Phil. 4, or to support the poor, Heb. 13.

Latin:

CAPUT III. Hostia Pacifica.

vers. 1. QUOD SI HOSTIA PACIFICORUM.

QUæ triplex designatur h. l. Bovis, Ovium, & Capræ, ubi adipem omnem & sanguinem Deus sibi deposcit. Atque hæc est capitis hujus summa. De hostia pacifica ita Grotius: שלמים a שלום, quod est Pax: sed pacem pro be- neficio poni etiam Latinis docet nos Servius ad IV. Georgi- con. Chaldæis hoc sacrum dicitur sanctificatorium, ut Græ- cis τελεστικὸν: Hebræis alio nomine תודר, id est, τελείωσις: Erant autem hæc trium generum תודר αἴνεσις, ob acce- ptum beneficium, voti solutio, aut meræ liberalitatis, ut vide- re est infra 7, 12. de his licebat post effusum sanguinem priva- tis, qui obtulerant, eorumque uxoribus & liberis epulari, in signum amicitiæ cum Deo. Id in oblatione similæ non li- cebat, quia id inter privilegia erat Sacerdotalia: nec in victi- mis pro peccato ac delicto, ne de culpa lætarentur. Eadem de causa Pontificis victima comburitur. Infra 4, 12.

De voce שלמים prolixe Paul. Fagius ad h. l. egit. Cæterum sanguinis spargendi super altare ritus indicabat, sine sanguinis Christi effusione nullum Deo gratum aut fructuosum esse sacrificium Ebr. 9, 14. 22. Exhibetur ergo hîc, quomodo sacrificia no- stra spiritualia institui debeant, 1. impositione manu- um, h. e. ut spirituali fidei dextra peccata nostra in Christum transferamus omnia. 2. Aspersione san- guinis, sive fiducia meriti & efficacia mortis sangui- nisq; Christi. 3. Mortificatione carnis, sive cupidi- tatum, & affectuum omnium. 4. Consideratio- ne scopi & finis, ad quem unum referenda omnia. Gregor. M. hom. 25. super Evangel. Præcepto legis cauda hostiæ in sacrificio offerri jubetur. In cauda quippe finis est corporis: & ille bene immolat, qui sacri- ficium boni operis usq; ad finem debitæ perducit actio- nis. Ideo prohibetur v. 17. esus sanguinis, ut cogi- tarent, quantum illud futurum sanguinis pretium pro peccatis Mundi, & tamdiu saltem abstinerent a sanguine, donec opere compleretur, quod in typo ostensum est. Vid. August. l. 32. c. Faust. c. 13. Nec adipe vescendum erat, ut monerentur de abstinentia a voluptatibus, temperantia & frugalitate, agnosce- rent Deo non vilia & abjecta, sed pinguia & opima quæque offerenda esse, & ad meliorem ac præstan- tiorem Christi hostiam respicerent, nec non ad con- vivium pinguium ab ipso paratum Es. 25, 6. Nec vero adeps omnis interdictus Judæis, sed solum ca- prinus, ovinus, & bovinus, ut Joseph. l. 3. c. 10. notat, hoc est, illorum animalium, quæ Deo offerri pos- sunt. Conf. Lev. 7, 21. De aliis vero mundis animali- bus, quæ Deo offerri non poterant, id nuspiam pro- hibitum. Solum vetabatur de illis adeps, qui am- bit & contegit vel operit vitalia v. 3. hoc est, partes il- las vitales interiores, cor, hepar, pulmonem, renes, ilia, non qui carni passim immiscetur. Spirituales autem hostiæ nostræ Eucharisticæ hic adumbratæ (post sa- crificium Christi pacificum) sunt, quando nos ipsos Deo offerimus in obsequium voluntatis ejus Rom. 12. quando parati sumus, pro ipsius nomine etiam mortem subire 2. Tim. 4. quando Deum laudibus celebramus, commemorando ipsius in nos collata, tam spiritualia, quam corporalia beneficia Ose. 14. Ebr. 13. quando de nostris facultatibus liberaliter contribuimus vel ad alendos ministros Ecclesiæ Phil. 4. vel ad fovendos pauperes Hebr. 13.

## 3:1 Addition
On chapter 3, towards the end, p. 474. a.

Modern Jews, with Willet as witness, maintain that the eating of fat is prohibited in general. But what was caught by hunting could be eaten, with the blood only excepted, Deuteronomy 17, but not the fat; and why would the restriction of certain animals be applied in Leviticus 7, the fat of the sheep and the ox and the goat, if all fat were prohibited? It is therefore a mere superstition of the Jews that they do not eat fat.

Latin:

Ad cap. 3. sub finem p. 474. a.

Judæi moderni Willeto teste esum adipis in universum prohibitum volunt. At captum venatione comedi poterat, sanguine solum excepto Deuteronom. 17. non autem adipe, & cur restrictio certorum animantium adhiberetur Levit. 7. Adipem ovis & bovis & capræ, si adeps omnis prohibitus esset? Est ergo hæc mera superstitio Judæorum, quod adipem non comedant.

## 3:2
verse 2. AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE TABERNACLE OF THE TESTIMONY.

Not at the right side of the court looking toward the North, where the burnt offering was to be sacrificed c. 1, 11. & the sacrifices for sin and guilt c. 6, 25. c. 7, 2. c. 14, 13. but at the eastern part of the court, where the entrance of the tabernacle was Ex. 27, 16. c. 28, 15. which place was less holy, because the ashes of the altar were cast into that part to be carried outside, just as our Eucharistic sacrifices are also far less holy than the expiatory sacrifice of Christ, which was figured more by the sacrifices for sin and guilt than by the victims of peace offerings. Whence also those are everywhere called holy of holies: therefore the sacrifice for guilt had to be sacrificed in the same place as the victim for sin, for the reason that it pertained equally to the priest, and they were holy of holies, neither of which suits the Eucharistic victims: which also for that reason had to be sacrificed near the entrance of the court, because in the very entrance the fat of the victim and the breast had to be placed upon the hands of him who was offering the victim to be sacrificed, so that he himself might offer them, and the Priest might thus receive them from his hands to offer the same to God. chap. 7, 30.

Latin:

vers. 2. IN INTROITUTABERNACULI TESTIMONII.

Non ad latus atrii dextrum ad Aquilonem re- spiciens, ubi holocaustum immolandum c. 1, 11. & sacrificia pro peccato & delicto c. 6, 25. c. 7, 2. c. 14, 13. sed ad partem orientalem atrii, ubi introitus erat tabernaculi Ex. 27, 16. c. 28, 15. qui locus minus san- ctus erat, quia in illam partem conjiciebantur alta- ris cineres forâs exportandi, quemadmodum etiam Eucharistica nostra sacrificia longe minus sancta sunt, quam expiatorium Christi sacrificium, quod sacrificiis pro peccato & delicto magis figuratum fuit, quam pacificorum victimis. Unde etiam illa sancta sanctorum passim dicuntur: ideo eodem loco sacrificium pro delicto, quo hostia pro peccato immo- lari debuit, ex ea ratione, quia æque ad sacerdotem pertinebat, & sancta sanctorum erant, quorum neu- trum hostiæ Eucharisticæ convenit: quæ etiam ideo juxta introitum atrii immolari debebat, quia in ipso introitu debebat manibus illius, qui offerebat hosti- am immolandam, imponi adeps hostiæ & pectulcu- lum, ut offerat ea ipse, & è manibus ejus ita accipiat illa Sacerdos Deo eadem oblaturus. cap. 7, 30.

## 3:3
vers. 3. THE FAT THAT COVERETH THE INWARDS, &c.

He speaks of a double fat or grease, namely of that which covers the intestines, and this the more learned Hebrews wish to be properly called חלב Cheleb, fat, namely fat separated from the flesh, which we can call lard, in German Schmarleib. And of that which adheres to the intestines, which fat they feel is properly called שומן Schomen in the Scriptures, which is namely joined to the flesh; and thus they distinguish between Cheleb and Schomen. Which observation is of P. Fagius in this place.

Latin:

vers. 3. ADIPEM QUI OPERIT VITALIA, &c.

De duplici loquitur adipe seu pinguedine, nem- pe de eo qui operit intestina, & hunc doctiores He- bræi proprie חלב Cheleb, adipem dici volunt, pingue- dinem scilicet separatam a carne, quam nos axun- giam appellare possumus, germanice Schmarleib. Atq; de eo, qui adhæret intestinis, quam pinguedi- nem שומן Schomen in Scripturis proprie dici senti- unt, quæ scilicet conjuncta est carni; atq; ita distin- guunt inter Cheleb & Schomen. Quæ observatio est P. Fagii in h. l.

## 3:4
vers. 4. AND THE CAUL ABOVE THE LIVER.

The Hebrews, as the same Fagius notes, say it is the red flesh encompassing the liver, which is as it were an abundance of the liver, according to the interpretation of the name, having the appearance of fat. The Jews commonly interpret it as das roth Fleisch. Now as to what is added: Which is upon the liver, R. David Kimchi says it means the same as if one read עם הכבד that is, with the liver, so that the preposition על upon has there the force of the preposition עם with. And it is implied that he ought to take away some small portion of flesh also from the liver together with the caul. This is Fagius.

Latin:

vers. 4. ET RETICULUM JECORIS.

Ebræi notante eodem Fagio, dicunt esse rubeam carnem epar complectentem, quæ quasi epatis abun- dantia est, juxta nominis interpretationem, spe- ciem habens pinguedinis. Judæi vulgo das roth Fleisch interpretantur. Jam quod additur: Quod est super Jecur, R. David Kimchi idem valere dicit, ac si legatur עם הכבד id est, cum jecore, ut Præpositio על super habeat ibi vim Præpositionis עם cum. Et innuatur, quod portiunculam aliquam carnis etiam de epate una cum reticulo auferre debeat. Hæc Fagius.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. AND THEY SHALL BURN THEM UPON THE ALTAR ] Which the Latins render as exta. Servius on the 1st Georgic. The mystical sense is that desires are to be killed in honor of God, the instruments of which are the fat, the kidneys, the liver.

UPON THE BURNT OFFERING.

Literally it is upon the burnt offering, which they interpret as with the burnt offering. Or, after that continual burnt offering, which was offered daily, so that it implies that that continual burnt offering ought to precede all other sacrifices. And thus also R. Solomon explains it. Which sense the LXX also have, who read ἐπὶ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα, upon the burnt offerings. If the Vulgate Version is retained, in holocaustum, this name is not to be understood in a special sense, as burnt offerings are distinguished from other sacrifices, but generally, so that all these things may be entirely consumed by fire.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ADOLEBUNTQVE EA SVPER ALTARE ] Quod reddere exta Latinis. Servius ad 1. Georgicon. My- sticus sensus est, interimendas in Dei honorem cupidines, qua- rum instrumenta adeps, renes, jecur.

IN HOLOCAUSTUM.

Ad literam est super holocaustum, quod inter- pretantur cum holocausto. Vel, post holocaustum illud juge, quod quotidie offerebatur, ut innuat holocau- stum illud juge omnia alia sacrificia antecedere de- bere. Atque ita etiam R. Salomo exponit. Quem sensum & LXX. habent, qui legunt ἐπὶ τὰ ὁλοκαυ- τώματα, super holocausta. Si retineatur Vulg. Ver- sio, in holocaustum, non intelligendum erit hoc no- men sensu speciali, uti ab aliis sacrificiis holocausta distinguuntur, sed generaliter, ita ut integre hæc o- mnia igne absumantur.

## 3:9
Vers. 9. THE WHOLE RUMP WITH THE KIDNEYS] Which are the offa penita according to Festus. But those things which are not commanded here to be burned, they fell to the Priest below 7, 31. Thus among the Greeks: it was the law that the priest should take the remains of the sacrifice, says the Scholiast on the Plutus. Soon after: the skin and the limbs, which the same Scholiast on the Peace calls first-fruits. Among the Hebrews, the head and jaw, the right shoulder from the feet, and the stomach from the body fell to the Priest. It was not permitted to redeem them: it is signified that words, acts, and appetites are to be consecrated to God.

Osiander rightly corrects the Vulgate here, with Bonfrerius not denying it: For with the kidneys, in the Hebrew it is from the region of the backbone, or that which looks or is joined to the spine. Cajetan also thinks the tail in oxen and goats was offered in the sacrifices of peace offerings, but ἄτερ γραφῆς and contrary to Josephus, book 3, chapter 10. In a lamb or sheep, the tail was full of fat and delicate, not so in an ox or goat. But God wanted the best to be offered to Him.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CAUDAM TOTAM CVM RENIBVS] Quæ offa penita apud Festum. Quæ autem hic non jubentur adoleri, ea cedebant Sacerdoti infra 7, 31. Sic apud Græcos: νόμος ἧν τὰ ὑπολειπόμενα τῆς θυσίας τὸν ἱερέα λαμβάνειν, ait Scholiastes ad Plutum. Mox: τὸ δέρμα καὶ τὰ κῶλα, quas idem Scholiastes ad Pacem vocat ἀπαρχάς. Apud Hebræos cedebant Sacerdoti de capite maxilla, de pedibus armus de- xter, de corpore stomachus. Ea redimere non licebat: signi- ficatur sacrandos Deo sermones, actus, appetitus.

Corrigit hic merito Osiander, non abnu- ente Bonfrerio, Vulgatam: Pro cum renibus in Ebræo est e regione spinæ dorsi, sive quæ respicit aut juncta est spinæ dorsi. Caudam etiam in bobus & capris in hostiis pacificorum oblatam putat Cajetan. sed ἄτερ γραφῆς & contra Joseph l. 3. c. 10. In agno vel ove cauda plena erat pinguedine & delicata, non item in bove vel capra. Optima autem sibi Deus offerri voluit.

## 3:16
verse 16. ALL THE FAT SHALL BE THE LORD'S. Because below in chapter 7 it is said, you shall not eat the fat of the sheep, and of the ox, and of the goat, some conclude that the fats of others were permitted: And what would have been done with the fat of clean animals slaughtered in houses, if they could neither eat it nor sell it to the Gentiles? Therefore, they restrict this law to sacrificial animals, to the fat of the ox, sheep, and goat, with Lyranus, Estius, or even to those which were actually sacrificed with Menochius from Lev. 7:25. Therefore, 'all the fat' is to be referred to the aforementioned, i.e., all the fat mentioned above, as Bonfrer notes. Fat is the best portion of the victim, and most suitable for burning on the altar: therefore it had to yield to God and be burned: and it was taught thus, according to Estius, that life and all sufficiency are from God to us: because fat demonstrates the abundance of nourishment; and it warned us that we ought to flee lasciviousness.

Latin:

vers. 16. OMNIS ADEPS DOMINI ERIT. Quia infra c. 7. dicitur, adipem ovis, & bovis, & capræ non comedetis, colligunt nonnulli aliorum adi- pes concessos fuisse: Et quid factum fuisset de adipe mundorum in domibus mactatorum, si nec edere poterant, nec gentibus vendere? Restringunt ergo hanc legem ad animalia immolatitia, ad adipem bovis, ovis, & capræ, cum Lyrano, Estio, vel etiam ad ea, quæ actu immolabantur cum Menochio e Lev. 7,25. omnis ergo adeps referendus ad superiora h. m. omnis adeps supra dictus, ut notat Bonfrer. A- deps optima est hostiæ portio, & aptissimus ad com- burendum in altari : ideo Deo cedere & comburi debuit: & docebatur ita, secundum Estium, a Deo nobis esse vitam, & omnem sufficientiam: quia a- deps demonstrat nutrimenti abundantiam; ac mo- nebat nos fugere debere lasciviam.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. The sacrifice for the sin of ignorance.

verse 1. THE SOUL THAT SHALL SIN THROUGH IGNORANCE. First, the sacrifice for the sin of the Priest, which was a calf; 2. of the people, which was likewise a calf; 3. of a Prince, which was a goat; 4. of any commoner, which was a goat or a sheep. THROUGH IGNORANCE) ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ Aquila. The LXX less properly ἀκουσίως. Indeed, every δι᾽ ἀγνοίας is ἀκούσιον: but not the reverse. CAUSING THE PEOPLE TO SIN] Leading the people into error by doctrine or example. See 1 Paral. 21:3, where there is the same form of speech. WHICH HE COMMANDED THAT THEY SHOULD NOT BE DONE] Contrary to the forbidding precepts, which are לֹא תֵעָשֶׂנָה to the Hebrews. For if anything had been omitted through mere error of those things which are commanded, that could still be fulfilled. The same form of speech is in 13, 22, and 27 of this chapter. Although things omitted by error can sometimes be fulfilled otherwise, if the omission here and now is contrary to divine law, the sin of omission also had to be expiated. Verse 3. CALF] In grave sins a light victim, lest it be believed that a great expense had obtained forgiveness, an opinion which Plato criticizes in the Greeks. Compare what is below 9:8.

Most understand this of the High Priest, because it is said, 'who is anointed': and thus there will be no law concerning the expiation of other priests. However, although the inferior priests were not anointed with the solemn anointing, they can nevertheless be called anointed by the general acceptance of the word. The high priest is anointed with pure oil, the others with mixed blood, as Fagius notes on Lev. 6. Compare chapter 6:14.

CAUSING THE PEOPLE TO SIN. The Hebrew words can also be taken in this way, if he has committed such a sin as is wont to be committed by any one of the people, as Vatablus observes with Fagius. However, the former sense seems preferable concerning a sin that provides scandal: for what sin of a priest will there be otherwise that is not also wont to be committed by others? And Fagius notes that the Hebrews also prefer this, whom B. Luther has also followed.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. Hostia pro peccato Ignorantiæ.

vers. 1. ANIMA QUÆ PECCAVERIT PER IGNORANTIAM. Primum hostia pro peccato Sacerdotis, quæ erat vitulus, 2. populi, quæ itidem vitulus. 3. Princi- pis, quæ hircus. 4. Plebeji alicujus, quæ capra, vel ovis erat. PER IGNORANTIAM) ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ Aquila. LXX. minus proprie ἀκουσίως. Est quidem omne δι᾽ ἀγνοίας ἀκούσιον: at non contra. DELINQVERE FACIENS POPVLVM ] Doctrina aut exemplo populum in errorem inducens. Vid. 1. Paral. 21, 3. ubi idem loquendi genus. QUÆ PRÆCEPIT VT NON FIERENT ] Contra præcepta vetantia, quæ לֹא תֵעָשֶׂנָה Hebræis. Nam si quid per errorem merum omissum esset eorum quæ juben- tur, id adhuc impleri poterat. Idem loquendi genus 13. & 22. & 27. hoc capite. Etsi per errorem omissa quandoq; impleri alias possint, si tamen omissio hic & nunc facta divinæ legi contraria sit, peccatum omissionis expiandum etiam erat. Vers. 3. VITVLVM ] In gravibus peccatis levis victima, ne sumtus magnus impetrasse veniam crederetur, quam opi- nionem in Græcis Plato reprehendit. Conf. quod infra 9, 8.

De summo Sacerdote intelligunt plerique, quia dicitur, qui unctus est : & ita nulla erit lex de expia- tione aliorum Sacerdotum. Cæterum licet Sacer- dotes inferiores solemni unctione minime uncti fuerint, generali tamen vocis acceptione uncti dici possunt. Unctus summus sacerdos est oleo puro, cæte- ri misto sanguine notante Fagio ad Lev. 6. Conf. c. 6,14.

DELINQUERE FACIENS POPULUM. Ebræa etiam accipi ita possunt, si tale admise- rit peccatum, quale admitti solet ab uno quovis e popu- lo, ut Vatablus cum Fagio observat. Prior tamen sen- sus præferendus videtur de peccato, quod scanda- lum præbet : quodnam enim peccatum alias erit Sacerdotis, quod non etiam admitti soleat ab aliis. Atque istum etiam præferre Ebræos notat Fagius, quem sequutus etiam est B. Lutherus.

## 4:4
verse 4. AND HE SHALL SACRIFICE IT TO THE LORD. He shall cause it to be sacrificed through another, namely the Priest: For what one does through another, he is thought to have done by himself.

Latin:

vers. 4. ET IMMOLABIT EUM DOMINO. Immolare faciet per alium nempe Sacerdotem: Nam quod quis per alium facit, per seipsum fecisse putatur.

## 4:10
verse 10. AS IT IS OFFERED FROM THE CALF OF THE SACRIFICE OF PEACE OFFERINGS. In Hebrew, 'as it is wont to be lifted from the ox (offered) in a sacrifice of retribution.' This sacrifice seems in some way mixed from an expiatory and a remuneratory, or retributory sacrifice: not that our works (by which we testify our gratitude to God) do anything toward the expiation of sins before God: but that we may be admonished of the gratitude which we owe to the Son of God sacrificed for us.

Latin:

vers. 10. SICUT OFFERTUR DE VITVLO HOSTIÆ PACIFICORUM. In Ebr. sicut levari solet de bove (oblato) in sa- crificium retributionis. Hoc sacrificium quodammo- do mixtum videtur ex Sacrificio expiatorio & re- muneratorio, seu retributorio: non quod nostra opera (quibus gratitudinem nostram Deo testa- mur) aliquid faciant ad expiationem peccatorum coram Deo : sed ut admoneamur de gratitudine, quam Filio Dei pro nobis immolato debemus.

## 4:12
verse 12. OUTSIDE THE CAMP. This which also had to be done in the sins of the whole people: so that the whole calf offered for sin should be burned not on the altar, but outside the camp: for thus it is indicated that the sins of the Priest are equal to the sins of the whole people, and that the whole camp of the people is contaminated by them: so that horror might be struck into the priests for a greater detestation and caution or flight from sin, and so that the sins of the priests might not harm the people, because this ceremony is a certain silent prayer that those sins might not touch the camp, but being driven out, might be abolished with the victim. Moreover, the satisfactory passion of Christ was especially foreshadowed outside the camp, by whose virtue the expiation of the priests and the people was made, Heb. 13:12.

Latin:

vers. 12. EXTRA CASTRA. Id quod etiam fieri debuit in peccatis totius po- puli: ut totus vitulus pro peccato oblatus non in al- tari, sed extra castra combureretur: ita enim indi- catum peccata Sacerdotis æquari peccatis totius popu- li, iisque castra tota populi contaminari: ut horror Sacerdotibus incuteretur ad majorem peccati de- testationem, & cautionem vel fugam, ac ne peccata Sacerdotum populum læderent, quia ceremonia hæc tacita quædam oratio, ne peccata illa tangerent castra, sed extra ea profligata aboleantur cum victi- ma. Adumbrata autem fuit imprimis passio Chri- sti satisfactoria extra castra, cujus virtute fiebat Sa- cerdotum & populi expiatio Ebr. 13, 12.

## 4:13
Verse 13. IF THE WHOLE CONGREGATION OF ISRAEL] πᾶσα συναγωγὴ Ἰσραήλ. LXX. The whole people, while they were wont to be gathered. The senate of the seventy men later filled its place, and therefore is bound by this law. However, error in the Sanhedrin is excused, because it has no other leader to follow: but in individuals it is not, because they ought to acquiesce to the judgment of the Sanhedrin, for the sake of peace, concerning which matter the law is Deut. 17:8 and following. But because it is not thought that graver sins can fall upon the High Priest and the senate, therefore there is only an expiation of ignorance for them.

It is false that graver sins do not fall upon the Pontiff and the Senate. The calf-worship of Aaron, to say nothing of other things, taught otherwise. Grotius seems to want to veil the infallibility of the Pontiff here, when he decides not alone, but with some council. However, the significance of the rites was rather this: (1.) That the blood of Christ would be sufficiently shed and efficiently profitable. Perfection is indicated by the number seven, and sufficiency in the sprinkling of blood against the veil of the sanctuary, because it was necessary for the horns of the altar of incense to be smeared with it, admonished that the incense of our prayer must be sprinkled with the blood and merit of Christ, John 16:23. The horns of the sacrificial altar also had to be imbued with blood, so that it might be noted that sin, death, and all enmity would be overcome by the victorious horns of the Cross of Christ. That the victim had to be carried outside the camp noted the foulness of sin, and the place of the sacrifice of Christ, Heb. 13:12.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SI OMNIS TVRBA ISRAEL] πᾶσα συνα- γωγὴ Ἰσραήλ. LXX. Populus omnis, dum is congregati sole- bat. Ejus locum postea implevit senatus LXX. virûm, ac propterea hac lege tenetur. Excusatur autem error in Syne- drio, quia neminem alium ducem habet, quem sequatur: in singulis autem non, quia acquiescere debent judicio synedrii, pacis causa, qua de re lex est Deut. 17, 8. & seqq. Quia vero in Pontificem Maximum & senatum non putantur ca- dere posse peccata graviora, ideo sola pro illis expiatio sit ignorantæ.

Falsum, non cadere peccata graviora in Ponti- ficem & Senatum. Aliud μοσχολατρεία Aaronis, ut alia jam taceamus, docuit. Velisicari hîc videtur Grotius infallibilitati Pontificis, cum non solus, sed cum concilio aliquo decernit. Cæterum significatio rituum potior hæc erat (1.) Christi sanguinem suffi- cienter fundendum & efficienter profaturum. Perfe- Etio numero septenario indicata, & sufficientia in spar- sione sanguinis contra velum sanctuarii, quod cornua altaris suffitorii eo illini oportuit, admonuit, oratio- nis nostræ thus sanguine & merito Christi esse asper- gendum Joh. 16, 23. Aræ victimariæ cornua etiam san- guine erant imbuenda, ut notaretur Crucis Christi victricibus cornibus peccatum, mortem & omnem inimicitiam superatum iri. Quod extra castra vi- ctima efferenda, notabat fœditatem peccati, & lo- cum sacrificii Christi Ebr. 13, 12.

## 4:13 Addition
On chapter 4, verse 13, AND IF THE WHOLE CONGREGATION.

An example is 2 Chronicles 29:23. When a matter is hidden, see what is to be done in Numbers 5:6, 7. For the sin of communion, see Proverbs 28:17, Isaiah 1:15, chapter 58:7, Ezekiel 22:16.

Latin:

Ad cap. 4. versu 13. QUOD SI OMNIS TURBA.

Exemplum est 2. Chron. 29. vers. 23. Cum res occulta est, quid sit faciendum vid. Num. 5. vers. 6. 7. Communionis peccatum vid. Proverb. 28. vers. 17. Es. 1, 15. cap. 58, 7. Ezech. 22. versu. 16.

## 4:22
Ver. 22. IF A PRINCE SHALL SIN] ὁ ἄρχων, that is to say, a king, interrex, or ethnarch: in war, for instance, where there is no opportunity to consult the Sanhedrin.

Latin:

Vers. 22. SI PECCAVERIT PRINCEPS] ὁ ἄρχων, ni- mirum rex, interrex, vel ethnarcha: in bello puta, ubi Syne- drii consulendi non est copia.

## 4:24 Addition
On chapter 4, verse 24, page 474, column b. BURNT OFFERING.

Namely, the continual [offering] according to Malvenda, concerning which Exodus 29, verse 38. That it is so called by antonomasia; the reason added: BECAUSE IT IS FOR SIN, or a victim for sin, or it pertains to what follows, therefore it will touch, as it is sometimes taken in an illative sense, therefore: or to what precedes, that it is to be sacrificed in the place of burnt offerings, because it is a victim for sin.

Latin:

Ad cap. 4. versu 24. pagina 474. b. HOLOCAUSTUM.

Scilic. juge secundum Malvendam, de quo Exod. 29. vers. 38. Quod ita per ἀντονομασίαν vocetur; Ratio addita: QUIA PRO PECCATO EST, vel victima pro peccato, aut pertinet ad fequentia, ideo tinget, uti quandoque accipitur sensu illativo, ideo: vel ad præcedentia, quod immolanda sit in loco holocaustorum, quia hostia est pro peccato.

## 4:25
Ver. 25. TOUCHING THE HORNS OF THE ALTAR OF BURNT OFFERING. Touching, or smearing with blood the horns, not of the altar of incense, which was done in the sacrifice for the sin of the Priest, v. 7, but of the altar of burnt offering. For the offices of the Ministers of the Church and of the Political Magistrate are distinct.

Latin:

vers. 25. TANGENS CORNUA ALTARIS HOLOCAUSTI. Tangens, sive illinens sanguine cornua non alta- ris thymiamatis, quod fiebat in hostia pro peccato Sacerdotis v. 7. sed altaris holocausti. Distincta sunt namque officia Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, & Magistratus Politici.

## 4:26 Addition
Verse 25. AND IT SHALL BE FORGIVEN HIM.

This is not to be understood only of legal expiation, or only of the condonation of punishment in this life with Estius, but of the non-imputation of sin; but that remission, as Lyranus admits, was made not by the virtue of the sacrifice itself (ex opere operato) but by the devotion and prayer of the priest and the offerer, which were made in the faith of Christ who was to come.

Latin:

Versu 25. ET DIMITTETUR EI.

Hoc non tantum de expiatione legali intelligendum, aut solum de condonatione pœnæ in hac vita cum Estio, sed de non imputatione peccati; sed remissio illa, fatente Lyrano, fiebat non virtute ipsius sacrificii (ex opere operato) sed devotione & oratione Sacerdotis & offerentis, quæ fiebant in fide Christi venturi.

## 4:35 Addition
Verse 35. FOR A BURNT OFFERING.

For a burnt sacrifice, as Pagninus, Mercerus, Tirinus, Luther. For burnt offerings were always joined to sacrifices for sin, whether parts of the same sacrifice were taken to be applied to a burnt offering, or another [offering] which was offered as a burnt offering. Thus above 3, 5, and chapter 5, 12, as Junius and Malvenda, who also explains; over the burnt offerings of the Lord, or beyond, besides the whole burnt offerings. The Chaldean, Syrian, Arab; over the whole burnt offering, that is, together with other offerings; Fagius after that burnt offering, which was accustomed to be offered daily. Piscator, however, rendered it, as they are consumed by fire and burned for Jehovah.

Latin:

Vers. 35. IN INCENSUM.

In Sacrificium ignitum, ut Pagninus, Mercerus, Tirinus, Lutherus. Nam sacrificiis pro peccato semper adjungebantur holocausta, sive partes ejusdem sacrificii ad holocaustum adhiberentur exceptæ, sive aliud, quod in holocaustum offerretur. Sic supra 3, 5. & cap. 5, 12. ut Junius & Mal- venda, qui etiam exponit; super incensa Domini, vel ultra, præter holocausta. Chaldæus, Syrus, Arabs; super holocaustum, id est, una cum aliis oblationi- bus; Fagius post incensum illud, quod quotidie of- ferri solebat. Piscator vero reddidit, prout igne cor- sumta adolentur Iehovæ.

## 5:1
Ver. 1. IF A SOUL SHALL SIN] חטא is sin, a fault in omitting; אשם is a transgression in committing; that which is done with deceit is פשע: but it appears below in 5 that אשם and חטא are often confused. Moreover, even he who doubted whether he had sinned was bound by this law. For in doubtful matters the safer part is to be taken, nor does abundant caution do harm.

The terms חטאה and אשם are not distinguished in the same way by interpreters. The Hebrews say the former is when one sins against affirmative precepts, of which they count as many as there are bones in the human body, namely 248. The latter (delictum), however, is that which is against negative ones, of which they assign as many as there are days in the year, 365; the sum of which together is 613, which they encompass arithmetically with the word תריג. Paul Fagius and others understand by the name of sin, sins of omission; but by the name of delict, sins of commission, which Augustine (Quaest. 20) and Gregory (Hom. 21 in Ezech.) invert; the latter also adds another distinction: that sin is in the deed, delict is in the thought. Procopius and Jerome, Corn. a Lap. say that sin is what is committed knowingly, delict what is committed unknowingly, which the LXX call πλημμέλειαν, as if it were πλὴν μέλειαν. And Vatablus also understands a lesser sin in this way. But it seems this should rather be inverted, since in ch. 4 it is treated of sins committed through error by the word חטאת, but of graver sins by the word אשם used in ch. 5, 15. And therefore we here more willingly accede to the explanation of the Hebrews and Grotius than to Cornelius.

And Bonfrerius also adds his vote to this opinion, along with Josephus (b. 3, ch. 10) and Philo: who, however, by no means concedes that these words are used promiscuously when there is talk of sacrifices, even if perhaps they are used promiscuously in Hebrew when they are taken for a crime and the commission of a crime: yet with this caution added, that even then sin is never called a delict, nor is 'to commit a delict' put for 'to sin' in Hebrew, unless when sin, by reason of supervening knowledge, passes to some extent into the condition of a delict, which happens when he who had committed it through ignorance recognizes that he had acted against the law of God (ch. 4, 13, 22, 27). Bonfrerius nevertheless refers some things among delicts because of the gravity of what was done through ignorance, namely those committed regarding divine things: and against Cornel. and others he observes that they do not correctly say with Augustine that πλημμέλειαν is as if it were πλὴν μέλειαν, 'beyond care,' but that it is deduced from πλὴν and μέλος, as if it were said; beyond measure and harmony, so that whatever is admitted that is incongruous, unrefined, or indecorous is called πλημμέλεια; or at least that it is said to be 'beyond care,' which happens out of contempt and lack of care for the divine name.

HEARING THE VOICE OF THE SWEARER] Of the adjurer: that is, if anyone, having been warned, suppresses the truth. See Prov. 29, 24 and what is at Matt. 26, 63, where this matter is treated at length. The conjunction here has the force of an example placed under its genus. In Latin it would be well rendered by 'for example.' For if the judge had seen the crime, he would abstain from judging, so that he might give testimony.

Augustine understands it of him who has heard the voice of one swearing falsely and has not indicated it: others of him who has heard an execration, or something worthy of an execration: that Grotian explanation concerning the adjuration of the judge is also that of the Chaldean, Vatablus, Lyranus, Oleaster, Arias Montanus, Sa, Tirinus, Estius, and Villalpando in Is. 17, just as Origen, Procopius, Hesychius, Radulphus, and Abulensis agree with Augustine. Cornelius and the Rabbis prefer to take it of one hearing the voice of one swearing falsely and abusing the name of God. Which opinion the Junio-Tremellius notes rightly prefer for the reasons they allege. But because all the attached laws speak of one sinning through ignorance and of private sins, and an offering is commanded to all in common: furthermore, because the law of that falsehood, whether pronounced in judgment or outside of judgment, is set forth below in v. 20 and following, it seems rather to be treated here of him who does not correct a neighbor who is blaspheming, but through industry or imprudence conceals his sin; thus this is a law concerning the correction of a neighbor, as below in 19, 17.

The Jewish people had to abstain from the contact of all unclean things, or immediately wash themselves with water and purify themselves: if they had not done that, a delict was committed. That signified that Christians ought to guard themselves from every pollution of sins with the utmost zeal. And in the law many things were pronounced unclean to the Jews which nevertheless were not unclean by their own nature before GOD, so that GOD might in this way reproach the human race with its own spiritual uncleanness: whereby it happens that to a man polluted by sins even things that are clean in themselves yield to uncleanness, so that he is considered contaminated before GOD by their use, when he does not use them rightly out of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 1. SI PECCAVERIT ANIMA] Peccatum חטא culpa in omittendo, אשם delictum in committendo; quod dolo sit est פשע : sed אשם & חטא sæpe confundi apparet infra 5. Tenebatur autem hac lege etiam qui dubita- bat an peccasset. In dubiis enim sumenda pars tutior, neque nocet abundans cautio.

Non eodem modo ab Interpp. distinguuntur חטאה & אשם. Ebræi illud dicunt esse, cùm pec- catur contra præcepta affirmativa, quorum tot nu- merant, quot sunt ossa in humano corpore nempe 248. Hoc vero (delictum) quod est contra negativa, quorum tot assignant, quot sunt dies in anno 365. quorum summa conjunctim est 613. quam voce תריג Arithmetice complectuntur. Paul. Fagius, & alii peccati nomine peccata omissionis; delicti au- tem nomine peccata commissionis intelligunt, quod invertunt August. quæst. 20. & Gregor. hom. 21. in Ezech. qui vero etiam aliam addit distinctionem: Peccatum in opere esse delictum in cogitatione. Proco- pius & Hieronymus, Corn. a Lap. Peccatum dicunt, quod scienter, delictum quod ignoranter committi- tur, quod LXX. vocent πλημμέλειαν quasi πλὴν μέ- λειαν. Atque ita etiam minus peccatum intelligit Vatablus. Sed invertendum potius hoc videtur, siquidem c. 4. de peccatis ex errore commissis actum sit voce חטאת, de peccatis vero gravioribus voce אשם adhibita c. 5, 15. Ideoq; Ebræorum & Grotii ex- plicationi hic libentius accedimus, quam Cornelio.

Et huic quoque sententiæ calculum adjicit cum Josepho l. 3. c. 10. & Philone, Bonfrerius: qui ve- ro minime concedit promiscue has voces usurpari, cum de hostiis sermo est, etsi forte promiscue usur- pentur in Ebræo, cum pro crimine & criminis com- missione accipiuntur : addita tamen hac cautela, quod tum quoque nunquam peccatum vocetur de- lictum, neque pro peccare ponatur delinquere in E- bræo, nisi cum peccatum ratione supervenientis no- titiæ in delicti quadantenus conditionem transeat, quod sit, cum id commissum, & se contra legem Dei egisse agnoscit, qui per ignorantiam id commiserat c. 4, 13. 22. 27. Nonnulla tamen inter delicta refert Bonfrer. ob gravitatem per ignorantiam factam, quæ sc. circa res divinas commissa : & adversus Cor- nel. & alios observat πλημμέλειαν eos non recte cum Augustino dicere quasi πλὴν μέλειαν præter curam, sed deduci a πλὴν & μέλος quasi dicatur; præter modum & concentum, ita ut quicquid incon- cinnum, inconditum, indecorum admittitur, πλημμέ- λεια dicatur; aut certe præter curam dici; quod ex contemtu & fine cura nominis divini fiat.

AVDIENS VOCEM JVRANTIS ] Adjurantis : id est, si quis monitus verum suppresserit. Vid. Prov. 29, 24. & quæ ad Matth. 26, 63. ubi late hac de re. Conjunctio hic vim ha- bet exempli positi sub genere suo. Latine per puta bene red- deretur. Nam Judex si crimen vidisset, judicatu abstinebat, ut testimonium diceret.

August. de eo intelligit, qui audierit vocem pe- jerantis, nec indicavit: alii de eo, qui execrationem, vel aliquid execratione dignum audierit: Grotiana illa explicatio de judicis adjuratione est etiam Chal- dæi, Vatabli, Lyrani, Oleastri, Ariæmontani, Sa, Tirini, Estii, Vilalpandi in Es. 17. uti cum Augustino faciunt Origenes, Procopius, Hesychius, Radulph. Abulens. Cor- nel. & Rabbini, qui de audiente vocem pejerantis & nomine Dei abutentis accipere malunt. Quam sententiam merito præferunt notæ Junio-Tremell. ob rationes quas allegant. Sed quia adjunctæ le- ges omnes de peccante per ignorantiam, & de pri- vatis peccatis loquuntur, communisque omnibus imperatur oblatio: præterea quia falsitatis illius cum in judicio, tum extra judicium pronunciatæ lex ponitur infr. v. 20. & seqq. potius de eo hîc vi- detur agi, qui non corrigit proximum blaspheman- tem, sed de industria vel imprudentia peccatum ejus dissimulat, est itaque hic lex de correptione proximi, ut infra 19, 17.

Populus Judaicus a contactu omnium rerum immundarum abstinere, aut mox sese aqua abluere, & purgare debebat: id nisi fecisset, delictum erat commissum. Id significabat, Christianos sibi ab o- mni pollutione peccatorum cavere summo studio debere. Et in lege multa pronuntiabantur immun- da Judæis, quæ tamen sua natura non erant immun- da coram DEO, ut DEUS hoc modo humano gene- ri immundiciem ipsius spiritualem exprobraret: qua fit ut homini peccatis polluto etiam res per se mundæ cedant ad immundiciem, ut eorum usu co- ram DEO contaminatus censeatur, quando iis non ex fide recte utitur.

## 5:3 Addition
Verse 3. AND IT HAS BEEN HIDDEN AND HE HAS KNOWN IT AFTERWARDS, HE SHALL BE GUILTY OF SIN.

In the Hebrew it is: And it has been hidden from him, as the LXX, Chaldean, Mercer, and others render it (that is, if he is polluted by contact ignorantly and imprudently) and he (afterwards) knew and sinned, that is, he incurred guilt. Junius, Tremellius, and also Piscator render it, whether it has been hidden from him or he himself has known it, he is nevertheless guilty. But the former explanation is closer to the words of the Hebrew text. Furthermore, Lyranus wrongly judged that the sacrifice was not determined here but left to the discretion of the Priest, since divine worship has been restricted solely to the discretion and command of God: and afterwards, verse 6, we read that the sacrifice is expressly defined, as Menochius admits. It differs from that which occurs in verse 17: For this deals with sin which is committed ignorantly from contact with unclean things: but that deals with other sins which are committed imprudently besides this case.

Latin:

Vers. 3. OBLITAQUE COGNOVERIT POST- EA, SUBJACEBIT DELICTO.

In Ebræo est: Et absconditum fuerit ab eo, ut LXX. Cald. Mercer. & alii reddunt. (id est, si igno- rans & imprudens contactu polluitur) & ipse (post- ea) scivit & deliquit, id est, delictum incurrit. Junius, Tremellius, ut & Piscat. reddunt, sive abdi- tum fuerit ab eo, sive ipse noverit, reus tamen est. Sed prior explicatio verbis textus Ebræi propior est. Cæterum sacrificium hic non determinari sed ar- bitrio Sacerdotis relinqui perperam Lyranus cen- suit, quum cultus divinus unice ad arbitrium & mandatum Dei restrictus fuerit: & postea vers. 6. exprefse sacrificium id definitum legamus, fatente Menochio. Differt ab eo, quod vers. 17. occur- rit: Nam hic de peccato, quod ex immundorum con- tactu ignoranter committitur: ibi vero de peccatis aliis, quæ præter hunc casum imprudenter commit- tuntur, agitur.

## 5:4
Ver. 4. AND SHALL HAVE BROUGHT FORTH WITH HIS LIPS] Otherwise an oath was not considered to bind.

THAT HE MIGHT EITHER DO SOME EVIL] Understand it of harm permitted by law: as of the demand for retaliation, or vengeance on a murderer.

Greg., Cajetan, Vatablus, and Estius do not well explain that 'doing evil' as fasting: because the opposite, 'doing good,' is not taken here in a moral sense. Cornelius acknowledges this and interprets it of just affliction, e.g., when parents swear that they will punish their children. We prefer here the Grotian exposition. An evil of fault is not the matter of an oath.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET PROTVLERIT LABIIS SVIS] Aliter non censebatur obligare jusjurandum.

VT VEL MALE QVID FACERET] intellige de no- cumento lege permisso: ut de postulatione talionis, vindi- cta in homicidam.

Non bene illud male facere de jejunio Greg. Ca- jetan. Vatabl. Estius explicant: quia oppositum be- nefacere sensu morali hic non accipitur. Agnoscit id Cornel. & de justa afflictione, v. c. cum parentes jurant se castigaturos liberos, interpretatur. Præfe- rimus nos hic expositionem Grotianam. Malum culpæ non est materia juramenti.

## 5:5
Ver. 5.

LET HIM DO PENANCE FOR THE SIN] In Hebrew: And she (the soul) shall confess that in which she has sinned: Thus also the Greeks ἐξαγορεύσει τὴν ἁμαρτίαν: But to that confession was added this clause: Behold, I repent and am ashamed of my works, I will never return to that thing. The dying did the same. In the sacred τελεστικοῖς there was no confession of a fault, but prayers, thanks, praises.

Whence the Papists attempt to elicit their Sacramental confession. But concerning confession in the Vulgate, which is authentic to them, not a word is held: and although confession is required in the Hebrew source, that confession was nevertheless most distinct from the sacramental confession of the Papists: For neither was a special enumeration of all sins with aggravating circumstances required, but rather in the annual public and common Sacrifice described in Lev. 16, expiation was performed by a general confession of all sins being made: nor was that confession either sacramental or meritorious, or made for the sake of satisfaction to be imposed by a priest to redeem punishment in this or the future age, which the Papists boast of regarding their confession: But so that with true repentance for sin, by the divinely ordained Sacrifice offered through faith in the antitype Christ, and his expiatory Sacrifice, they might obtain remission of sin. And the Pontificians themselves contend that the sacrament of penance was instituted only after the resurrection of Christ and that a special enumeration of sins was required, and Toletus proves with many testimonies in his tract on Confession that the purpose of confessing was not necessary in the old law. Add what the gloss has in c. utrum sola dist. 1. de pœnit. Sins are not forgiven by contrition of heart, nor by confession of mouth, but only by the grace of God.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

AGAT POENITENTIAM PRO PECCATO] In He- bræo: Et confessa fuerit (anima) id in quod peccavit: Sic & Græci ἐξαγορεύσει τὴν ἁμαρτίαν: Sed illi confessioni ade- rat hæc clausula: Ecce pœnitet me & pudet me operum meo- rum, nunquam revertar ad istam rem. Idem faciebant mo- rituri. In Sacris τελεστικοῖς non erat delicti confessio, sed preces, gratiæ, laudes.

Unde Papistæ confessionem suam Sacramen- talem elicere conantur. Sed de Confessione in vul- gata, quæ ipsis authentica est, ne gry habetur: & li- cet confessio in Ebræo fonte requiratur, maxime tamen distincta fuit illa confessio a Papicolarum Sa- cramentali confessione: Nam nec omnium peccato- rum specialis enumeratio cum circumstantiis aggra- vantibus requisita fuit, quin potius in anniversario publico & communi Sacrificio Lev. 16. descripto o- mnium peccatorum generali confessione facta ex- piatio peragebatur: neque confessio illa vel Sacra- mentalis vel meritoria fuit vel ob satisfactionem a Sa- cerdote imponendam ad redimendam pœnam in hoc vel futuro seculo facta, quod de sua confessione jactitant Papistæ: Sed ut vera pœnitudine ob pec- catum oblato Sacrificio divinitus ordinato per fi- dem in antitypum Christum, ejusque Sacrificium expiatorium remissionem peccati conseque- rentur. Et contendunt Pontificii ipsimet post resurrectionem Christi demum Sacramen- tum pœnitentiæ institutum ac specialem pec- catorum enumerationem requisitam esse, probatq; Toletus multis testimoniis tract. de Confess. proposi- tum confitendi non fuisse necessarium in veteri le- ge.
