Adde quod habet glossa c. utrum sola dist. 1. de pœnit. Nec cordis contritione, nec oris confessione pec- cata admittuntur, sed tantum gratia Dei.

## 5:5 Addition
To verse 5, after the end of the notes.

Fagius indeed brings forward the formula of confession which the Hebrews teach, וידוי של דברים, the confession of words, which was done in a solemn manner and with certain words: He says, he used to lay his hands between the horns of the victim to be sacrificed, and said אנא השם וגו׳ I beseech, O Lord, I have sinned, I have done iniquitously, and I have transgressed before you, I have done thus and thus: Behold, I repent, and I am ashamed of my works: I will never return to that thing. But Oleaster says, I do not know whether this mode of confessing was invented by modern Hebrews or whether they had it from tradition. Furthermore, it must be understood that there was need for confession also in other sacrifices for sin, even if it is not expressed. And the Hebrews rightly note, which was also observed by Fagius, that sacrifices were of no avail by themselves, nor did they expiate sins, without repentance and confession, according to Numbers 5, 6, 7. But repentance, which was neither sacramental nor meritorious, and required faith in the Messiah shadowed forth through the sacrifices, if it was to be true and pleasing to God for the remission of sins, Hebrews 11, 4, et seqq.

Latin:

Ad v. 5. post finem notarum.

Adducit quidem Fagius formulam confes- sionis, quam Ebræi docent וידוי של דברים confessio verborum, quod fieret more solemni, & certis verbis: Manus, inquit, imponebat inter cornua ho- stidæ immolandæ, & dicebat אנא השם וגו׳ Obse- cro, ô Domine, peccavi, inique egi, & prævaricatus sum coram te, sic, & sic feci: Ecce pœnitet me, & pudet me operum meorum: nunquam revertar ad istam rem. Sed Oleaster, nescio, inquit, an hic confitendi modus à modernis Ebræis confictus sit, an habuerint ex tradi- tione. Cæterum confessione opus fuisse etiam in aliis sacrificiis pro peccato intelligendum, etiamsi non exprimatur. Et recte Ebræi notant, quod Fagio etiam observatum, nihil profuisse sacrificia per se, neque expiasse peccata, sine pœnitentia & confessione, juxta Num. 5, 6. 7. Quæ vero neque Sacramentalis, neque meritoria erat, & fidem in Messiam per sacrificia adumbratum requirebat pœnitentia, si vera & DEO grata esse debebat ad remissionem peccatorum Ebr. 11, 4. seqq.

## 5:7
v. 7. LET IT NOT BE COMPLETELY SEVERED.

Why the head was not to be severed, Fagius rightly observes, because it was done for the sake of a mystery, that although Christ, who was foreshadowed in all the Sacrifices, shed his blood in death for our sins, his head was nevertheless not torn from his body, that is, even though he died, yet he did not perish in death, but lifted his head from death into eternal life, nor will he ever be torn from his body, which is the Church. This is the greatest consolation of all the pious. For whether one is living and afflicted or dying is extinguished, let him trust well, because the head is not torn away from its members.

Latin:

v. 7. NON PENITUS ABRUMPATUR.

Cur non abrumpendum fuerit caput, recte observat Fagius, quod id mysterii causa factum, quod licet Christus, qui in omnibus Sacrificiis ad- umbratus fuit, sanguinem suum in morte pro pec- catis nostris effuderit, caput tamen ejus non est avulsum a corpore, hoc est, etsi mortuus est, tamen non periit in morte, sed sustulit caput e morte in perpetuam vitam, nec avelletur unquam a corpore suo, quod est Ecclesia. Hæc est maxima consola- tio omnium piorum. Sive enim quis vivus affli- gatur, sive moriens extinguatur, bene confidat, quia caput non est avulsum a membris suis.

## 5:8
CHAPTER V. Sacrifices for sins arising from silence of truth, uncleanness, error, an oath, abuse of sacred things, ignorance.

Latin:

CAPUT V. Hostiæ pro peccatis ex Silentio Veritatis, immun- ditia, errore, juramento, sacrorum abusu, ignorantia.

## 5:11
Vers. 11. BUT IF HIS HAND CANNOT AFFORD TWO TURTLEDOVES OR TWO YOUNG PIGEONS, HE SHALL OFFER FOR HIS SIN THE TENTH PART OF AN EPHA OF FINE FLOUR] Porphyry 2. περὶ ἀποχῆς; the divinity looks more to the character of those who sacrifice than to the number of those being sacrificed. Persius Sat. 2. A mind with justice and right combined, the holy recesses of the soul, and a breast imbued with noble honor: this I grant to bring to the temples, and I will make atonement with meal.

HE SHALL NOT PUT OIL UPON IT, NOR SHALL HE PUT ANY FRANKINCENSE THEREON] As in mourning, he shall abstain from ornaments and perfumes. Compare Num. 5, 15.

Oil is the medium of light and the symbol of joy; it is signified, therefore, that the sinner is devoid of both light and joy before the remission of sin. Frankincense, however, is not admitted, so that it may be designated that the sin does not smell good, but very badly, as Cyril and Theodoret note; but not as Radulphus wishes, that here prayer with confidence is lacking, as if the sinner ought not to ask for pardon with a free brow because he does not exhibit a worthy satisfaction, which cause Cornelius alleges: for this is contrary to Scripture Matt. 21, 21. Mark 11, 24. John 16, 23. James 1, 6. 7. 1 John 1, 8. nor does the pardon of sin depend upon our own, which is nothing, but solely upon the satisfaction of Christ; which is most worthy, because it is most perfect.

Latin:

Vers. 11. QVOD SI NON QVIVERIT MANUS EJVS DVOS OFFERRE TVRTVRES AVT DVOS PVLLOS COLVMBARVM, OFFERET PRO PECCATO SVO SIMILÆ PARTEM EPHI DECIMAM] Porphyrius 2. περὶ ἀποχῆς· μᾶλλον τὸ δαιμόνιον πρὸς τὸ τῶν θυόντων ἦθος ἢ πρὸς τὸ τῶν θυομένων πλῆθος βλέπει. Persius Sat. 2. Compositum jus fasque animi, sanctosque recessus Mentis & incoctum generoso pectus honesto: Hoc cedo ut admoveam templis & farre litabo.

NON MITTET IN EAM OLEVM, NEC THVRIS ALIQVID IMPONET] Vt in luctu, ornamentis & odoramentis abstinebit. Conf. Num. 5,15.

Oleum lucis est medium & lætitiæ symbolum, significatur ergo peccatorem & lucis & lætitiæ expertem esse ante remissionem peccati. Thus vero non admittitur, ut peccatum non bene olere, sed pessime, designetur, notante Cyrillo & Theodor. non autem ut Radulph. vult, quod hic desit oratio cum fiducia, quasi peccator libera fronte veniam petere non debeat, quia dignam non exhibet satisfactionem, quam causam Cornelius allegat : Hoc enim refragatur Scripturæ Matth. 21, 21. Marc. 11, 24. Joh. 16, 23. Jac. 1,6. 7. 1. Joh. 1, 8. neq; venia peccati a nostra, quæ nulla est, sed unice a Christi satisfactione dependet; quæ dignissima, quia perfectissima.

## 5:12
Vers. 12. FOR A MEMORIAL OF HIM WHO SHALL OFFER] So that he who has offered, mindful of this, may take heed for himself in the future.

In Hebrew it is: for a memorial (not of the offerer, but) of it, that is, of the offering, so that God may deign to look graciously upon him because of the offering of Christ, which it foreshadowed, and to forgive the sin to the one offering the victim.

Latin:

Vers. 12. IN MONVMENTVM EJVS QVI OBTVLERIT] Vt qui obtulit hujus memor in posterum sibi caveat.

In Ebr. est : in memoriale ( non offerentis, sed ) ejus, id est, oblationis, ut Deus eum ob oblationem Christi, quam adumbrabat, gratiose respicere, ac peccatum offerenti hostiam condonare dignetur.

## 5:15
Vers. 15. IF ANY ONE PREVARICATING THE CEREMONIES] For 'prevaricating' in Hebrew it is כי תמעל מעל. Among certain Greeks, παραβῇ παραβάσει. For here מעל is taken in a broader sense, so as to include even a fault without deceit. And so the LXX elsewhere translate it παραβαίνειν, elsewhere πλημμελεῖν. But this concerns a sin against a commanding law: as the opposition of verse 17 shows.

WHICH CAN BE BOUGHT FOR TWO SICKLES] In Hebrew it is: according to your estimation of the money of the Shekels: where Aben-Ezra says, at least two: for because the dual number has a place in few words among the Hebrews, therefore among them, as among other nations, the plural number is content with the meaning of two. Thus, ordered to be free after years, he becomes free after a biennium by Roman law, l. Libertas in fine. D. de manumissis testamento. And given a condition, do that in days, if nothing else has been added, the condition must be fulfilled in two days, l. inter D. de verb. signif.

There is no reason, therefore, for Cornelius to correct the Hebrew reading, as if it should be read in the dual שקלים, not as the text has it, in the plural. In the Greek, 50 shekels are held, but against the faith of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Latin copies, and quite inconveniently, because a ram could be bought for two shekels, but not a bull for 50 shekels. Therefore, the Roman and Royal Greek editions lack any number here.

Latin:

Vers. 15. SI PRÆVARICANS CEREMONIAS] Pro prævaricans in Hebræo est כי תמעל מעל Apud Græcos quosdam παραβῇ παραβάσει. Largiore enim significatu hic מעל sumitur, ut & culpam sine dolo comprehendat. Itaque & LXX. alibi vertunt παραβαίνειν, alibi πλημμελεῖν. Agitur autem hic de peccato contra legem jubentem : ut ostendit oppositio commatis. 17.

QVI EMI POTEST DVOBVS SICLIS) In Hebræo est : secundum æstimationem tuam pecuniæ Siclorum : ubi Aben-Esdra, minimum duorum: quia enim dualis numerus in paucis vocibus locum habet apud Hebræos, ideo apud eos, ut apud gentes alias, pluralis numerus duorum significatione contentus est. Sic post annos liber esse jussus, post biennium liber fit Romano jure l. Libertas in fine. D. de manumissis testamento. Et data conditione, illud facito in diebus, si nihil præterea fuisse adjectum, in biduo conditionem impleri oportet l. inter D. de verb. signif.

Non ergo est, quod Ebræam lectionem corrigat Cornelius, q. in duali legendum esset שקלים non uti textus habet, in plurali. In Græco 50. sicli habentur, sed contra fidem Ebræorum, Chald. & Latin. exemplarium, & inconvenienter prorsus, quia aries duobus siclis emi poterat, 50. siclis vero non aries, sed bos emebatur. Ideo Græcæ editiones Roman. & Regia carent hic omni numero.

## 5:19 Addition
To chapter 5, verse 22, page 475, column b.

They ask here why confession and sacrifice are required in this place, since such persons were unclean until evening and were purified by washing, Leviticus 11 and Numbers 19. Ainsworth answers from Maimonides and R. Solomon that this deals with one who, being unclean, either came into the sanctuary or ate of holy things, namely, ignorantly. For since the law strikes with excision one who does this knowingly, it sufficiently implies that a sacrifice is to be offered by him who did this ignorantly. But it can be said that there was need for a sacrifice when one had neglected to wash and purify oneself. Moreover, our pollution from the sins of others was primarily signified. 1 Timothy 5, verse 22.

Latin:

Ad cap. 5. v. 22. pag. 475. b.

Quærunt hic, cur confessio & sacrificium hoc loco requiratur, quum tales immundi fuerint ad vesperam: & ablutione purgati sint Levit. 11. & Num. 19. Respondet Ainsvvorth ex Maimonide, & R. Salom. hic de eo agi, qui immundus existens vel in sanctuarium venit, vel de rebus sanctis comedit, nempe ignoranter. Quum enim lex scienter hoc agentem excisione mactet, satis innuit sacrificium ab eo offerendum, qui hoc ignorans fecerit. Sed dici potest, tum sacrificio opus fuisse, cum abluere sese & purgare quis intermiserat. Significata autem imprimis fuit pollutio nostra ex peccatis alienis. 1. Timoth. 5. vers. 22.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. The victim for perjury, the laws of the holocaust, of the perpetual fire, the rites of individual sacrifices and the victim in the consecration of priests, and its sacrificial portion.

Vers. 1. HAVING CONTEMNED THE LORD) The leader and president of human society. See Num. 5, 6.

Contempt is understood not as formal, but as interpretative, proceeding not from mere malice, but from infirmity; therefore it could be expiated by restitution and sacrifice: but he who openly contemned the Lord was to be killed, Num. 15, 30. See there Abulensis quest. 43. and Estius, and Cornelius here.

, is considered to despise; he who does not think of the presence, omniscience, and vengeance of God: to despise the Lord, who does not obey His commandments.

The Vulgate departs from the source: rendering it thus, the soul that has sinned, and by despising the Lord has denied to his neighbor a deposit. In the Hebrew it is: the soul, that has sinned, and has committed a transgression against the Lord (which is a kind of sin committed from certain knowledge, to which are subjoined for example some species) and has denied to his neighbor his deposit.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. Hostia properjurio, Leges holocausti, Ignis perpetui, ritus singulorum Sacrificiorum & victimæ in consecratione Sacerdotum, ejusque hosticum.

Vers. 1. CONTEMTO DOMINO) Societatis humanæ ductore & præside. Vide Num. 5, 6.

COntemtus intelligitur non formalis, sed interpretativus, non ex mera malitia, sed infirmitate profectus, ideo restitutione & sacrificio expiari poterat : qui vero aperte contemnebat Dominum, occidendus erat Num. 15,30. Vid. ibidem Abulensis quæst. 43. & Estius, ac Cornelius hic.

, contemnere censetur; qui non cogitat Dei praesen- tiam, omniscientiam, & vindictam: contemnere Dominum, qui praeceptis ejus non paret.

Vulgata a fonte recedit: ita reddens, anima quae peccaverit, & contempto Domino negaverit proxi- mo suo depositum. In Ebraeo est: anima, quae pecca- verit, & praevaricata fuerit praevaricationem in Do- minum (quod genus est peccati ex certa scientia commissi, cui subjunguntur exempli gratia nonnul- lae species) & negaverit proximo suo depositum ejus.

## 6:2
Ver. 2. THE DEPOSIT WHICH HAD BEEN ENTRUSTED TO HIS FAITH. The Latin omitted here what is in the Hebrew ובתשומת יד in the placing of the hand. Some Greeks: ἐν πίσωσι χειρος. LXX. ἤ περὶ κοινωνίας. Thus also Kimchi on Exod. 23, 1. correctly. See Jerem. 50, 15. Gal. 2, 9.

The Vulgate is deservedly criticized for the omission: The placing of the hand. The Chaldean rendered it the partnership of the hand. It is understood as common business; i.e., if he denied that money had been given to him for the sake of common business, as Kimchi explains.

OR HAS COMMITTED EXTORTION) The word עשק is ἀναγκασμὸς, where someone is forced to pay what he does not owe. It is distinguished from גזל both here and in Ecclesiastes 5, 7, so that for the Latins it is extortion from the force of seized goods. See what was said on Luke 3, 14.

The Vulgate is correctly amended, the word עשק brings in oppression and fraud, Ef. 18, 28. Pf. 73. 8. And therefore it is not badly explained here by Grotius. Vatablus, however, distinguishes these two, גזל and עשק, in that the former denotes force, the latter fraud. If he denied (this he correctly repeats ἀπὸ κοινῶ) that he had extorted money by force, or had occupied the goods of his neighbor by fraud. So also B. Luther. Which explanation is more convenient: because by those two ways violence and fraud are exhausted.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DEPOSITVM QVOD FIDEI EJVS CRE- DITVM FVERAT. Omisit hic Latinus, quod in Hebraeo est ובתשומת יד in positione manus. Quidam Graeci: ἐν πίσωσι χειρος. LXX. ἤ περὶ κοινωνίας. Sic & Kimchi ad Exod. 23, 1. recte. Vid. Jerem. 50, 15. Gal. 2, 9.

Merito taxatur Vulgata, ob omissionem: Po- sitionem manus. Chald. reddidit societatem manus. Intelligitur communis negotiatio; q. d. si negaverit datam sibi fuisse pecuniam negotiationis communis causa, ut Kimchius explicat.

AVT CALVMNIAM FECERIT) Vox עשק ἀναγ- κασμὸς est, ubi quis cogitur solvere, quod non debet. Di- stinguitur a גזל & hic & Ecclesiastae 5, 7. ita ut Latinis con- cussio a vi bonorum raptorum. Vide quae dicta ad Lucam, 3, 14.

Recte emendatur Vulgata, vox עשק oppressio- nem & fraudem infert Ef. 18, 28. Pf. 73. 8. Ideoq; non male hic explicatur a Grotio. Vatablus tamen duo haec גזל & עשק ita distinguit, quod illud vim, hoc fraudem notet. Si negaverit (hoc recte ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetit) se vi pecuniam extorsisse, vel bona proximi sui occupasse fraude. Sic etiam B. Luthe- rus. Quae explicatio convenientior est: quia duo- bus illis modis violentia & fraudulentia exhauritur.

## 6:5
Ver. 5. THE FIFTH PART BESIDES) For an expiation. Maimonides.

The fifth part was not given in expiation: But for the sake of expiation a sacrifice for guilt was ordained, v. 6, 7. For expiation could not be made before GOD with money. Yet there was sanctioned, besides the restitution, a fifth part of what was taken, both for the injury and for the damage which the Lord had suffered from the lack of his property.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QVINTAM INSUPER PARTEM) Pro expia- tione. Maimonides.

Non dabatur pars quinta in expiatione: Sed expiationis causa ordinata erat hostia pro delicto v. 6, 7. Pecunia enim fieri non poterat expiatio coram DEO. Sancita tamen fuit praeter restitutionem pars quinta ablati tum pro injuria, tum pro damno, quod ex carentia rei suae passus erat Dominus.

## 6:6
ver. 6. BUT FOR HIS SIN HE SHALL OFFER A RAM.

In sins through ignorance a commoner [offered] a goat, but here anyone, even a commoner, in sins committed knowingly had to offer a ram, because these are graver. These are general laws, concerning everyone, therefore there is no reason for Cornelius to say that there is no mention made of the Priest, the Prince, and the whole people, because it is supposed that these would not sin from knowledge: for under the general word: IF A SOUL, i.e., a man, whoever he may be, has sinned (where mention is made specifically of the soul, because it is the proper and principal cause of sin) even Priests and princes are included: whom He willed to be equal in punishment to those to whom they were not superior in virtue.

ACCORDING TO THE ESTIMATION AND MEASURE OF THE OFFENSE) For ביום he reads כרם For רם is often estimation. But the Greeks [read] as we now have in the Hebrew: and they explain ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐλεγχθῇ, as soon as he has recognized that he has sinned. Well.

Latin:

vers. 6. PRO PECCATO AUTEM SUO OF- FERET ARIETEM.

In peccatis per ignorantiam plebejus capram, hic vero quilibet, etiam plebejus in peccatis scien- tialiter commissis arietem offerre debuit, quia haec graviora. Generales hae sunt leges, omnes concer- nentes, ideo non est quod Cornelius dicat. Sacerdo- tis, Principis, totiusq; populi nullam factam mentio- nem, quia supponatur hos ex scientia non esse peccatu- ros: sub generali enim voce: SI ANIMA, h.e. homo, quicunque ille sit, peccaverit (ubi animae peculiari- ter mentio fit, quia causa est propria & praecipua peccati) comprehenduntur etiam Sacerdotes & principes: quos pares voluit esse in poena iis, quibus virtute non fuere superiores.

JVXTA AESTIMATIONEM MENSVRAMQVE DE- LICTI) Pro ביום legit כרם Nam רם saepe est aestimatio. At Graeci ita ut nunc in Hebraeo habemus: & explicant ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐλεγχθῇ, cum primum peccasse se cognoverit. Bene.

## 6:9
v. 9. THIS IS THE LAW OF THE BURNT OFFERING.

Sc. the continual [offering], which was offered daily morning and evening, Num. 28. 3. That for the expiation of nocturnal sins, this for diurnal.

ALL NIGHT.

In the burning upon the altar it had to be, as it is in the Hebrew, all night the burnt offering, whence the Priest had to watch through the whole night, who would successively place and arrange the parts of the burnt offering on the altar, so that thus they might be consumed gradually all night: for the successive passion of the Son of God to be continually shadowed forth. Which, however, the law commanded only concerning the continual Sacrifice, as Hesychius, Tostatus, and Hugo Victor acknowledge, and this is not to be established concerning all [sacrifices], as Radulphus wished. And how, if all sacrifices were to be burned successively on the altar in this way, would the altar of burnt offerings have sufficed for the sacrifices of the whole people?

ought to be, had been ordained elsewhere, also v. 18. Regarding the following constitutions and the use of these ceremonies, the Osiandrine Paraphrase rightly holds: if by chance a garment has been sprinkled with the blood of that sacrifice, those little drops of blood adhering to the garment shall not be carried out of the tabernacle into a profane place; but that garment shall be washed in a holy place, that is, in the tabernacle. But the earthen vessel in which the flesh of this sacrifice was cooked shall be broken, so that it cannot be transferred to profane uses; but if it is a bronze vessel, it shall at least be scoured and washed with water, so that nothing of the holy remains adhering to it may afterwards be profaned by chance. By these ceremonies, the inestimable price of the blood of Christ and his passion is commended to us, which are in no way to be profaned. But the blood of Christ is carried out into a profane place, and his sacrifice is profaned by those who think that even outside the Church of Christ, among Turks, Jews, and Gentiles, there is remission of sins if they lead an honest external life; likewise by those who, while they magnificently proclaim the blood of Christ with their words, lead a profane and wicked life, and who rave against their neighbor with harsh execrations through the passion of Christ.

Latin:

v. 9. HAEC EST LEX HOLOCAUSTI.

Sc. jugis, quod mane & vesperi quotidie offe- rebatur Num. 28. 3. Illud pro nocturnis, hoc pro di- urnis peccatis expiandis.

TOTA NOCTE.

In adustione super altare debuit esse, ut in Ebr. est, tota nocte holocaustum, unde vigilare Sacerdos per totam noctem debuit, qui partes holocausti successive poneret & disponeret in altari, ut sic sen- sim tota nocte cremarentur: ad successivam passio- nem Filii Dei jugiter adumbrandam. Quod ta- men tantum de jugi Sacrificio lex præcepit, ut He- sych. Tostat. Hugo Victor. agnoscunt, idq; non de o- mnibus, quod Radulphus voluit, statuendum. Et quomodo si omnia sacrificia ita successive in altari cremanda, suffecisset altare holocaustorum ad sa- crificia per universum populum?

debeat, alias sancitum erat, etiam v. 18. De sequen- tibus constitutionibus & harum ceremoniarum usu recte Paraphrasis Osiandrina habet, si de sanguine il- lius sacrificii fortè vestis fuerit aspersa: non efferentur guttulæ illæ sanguinis vesti inhærentes extra taber- naculum in locum prophanum: Sed lavabitur vestis illa in loco sancto, id est in tabernaculo. Vas autem fictile, in quo cocta est caro hujus sacrificii,confringetur: ne ad profanos usus transferri possit, quod si vas æ- neum fuerit, saltem defricabitur, & lavabitur aqua, ne quid sanctarum reliquiarum adhærens postea forte prophanetur. Commendatur nobis his ce- remoniis inestimabile pretium sanguinis Christi & passionis ejus: quæ nullo modo sunt prophananda. Effertur autem sanguis Christi in locum propha- num, & prophanatur ejus sacrificium ab iis,qui pu- tant, etiam extra Ecclesiam Christi apud Turcas, Judæos, & Ethnicos esse remissionem peccatorum, si honestam externam conversationem ducant: item illi, qui cum sanguinem Christi verbis magni- fice prædicant, prophanam & sceleratam vitam a- gunt, & qui per passionem Christi duris execratio- nibus in proximum debachantur.

## 6:12
Vers. 12. IT SHALL ALWAYS BURN) It shall not be extinguished, the Hebrew Codex has. ὁμῦ σβεσθήσεται. Virgil in Aeneid 2: 'And the eternal fire from the innermost shrines he brings forth.' Where Servius: The fire of Vesta is eternal. See what we have noted on Mark 9:49.

The fire that fell from heaven (Lev. 9:20, ch. 16:1, Num. 3:4, ch. 26:61) had to be perpetually cherished and preserved on the altar. Which the Gentiles imitated only by the impulse of the demon, who is the ape of God and of divine worship; whence among the Romans the care of nourishing the fire was entrusted to the Vestals, as Alexander testifies, book 5, ch. 12.

The celestial fire signified the fire by which the sacrifice of Christ was consumed, both of divine love toward the human race and of burning wrath against sin, so that with the latter expiated, the former might obtain salvation. The fire had to be perpetually cherished because the virtue of the passion of Christ, like a perpetual fire, should be a perpetual food for our souls, and the purity of the word of the cross should always be kept warm, burn, and shine in us.

Latin:

Vers. 12. SEMPER ARDEBIT) Non extinguetur, habet Hebreus Codex. ὁμῦ σβεσθήσεται. Virgilius in 2. Æn. Æternumque adytis effert penetralibus ignem. Vbi Servius: Vestæ ignis æternus est. Vide quæ notavimus ad Marcum 9, 49.

Ignis cœlitus delapsus Lev. 9, 20. c. 16, 1. Num. 3, 4. c. 26, 61. perpetuò foveri & conservari debebat in altari. Quod gentiles non nisi impulsu dæmo- nis, qui simia est Dei & divini cultus, imitati sunt: Vnde apud Romanos Vestalibus cura ignis nutrien- di demandata teste Alexund. l. 5. c. 12.

Ignis cœlestis notabat ignem, quo consumtum est sacrificium Christi tum amoris divini erga genus humanum, tum iræ flagrantis adversus peccatum, ut hoc expiato, illud salutem consequeretur. Perpe- tuo fovendus erat ignis, quod virtus passionis Chri- sti instar perpetui ignis animis nostris perpetuum sit pabulum, & semper in nobis fervari, ardere, & lu- cere debeat puritas verbi crucis.

## 6:14
vers. 14. THIS IS THE LAW OF THE SACRIFICE AND OF THE LIBATIONS.

In the Hebrew it is, this is the Law of the Mincha or of the flour sacrifice. Whence, in order to reconcile the Vulgate with the source, Cornelius wishes the word ET to be taken exegetically, and he derives Libamina forcedly from liba and breads.

Latin:

vers. 14. HÆC EST LEX SACRIFICII ET LIBAMENTORUM.

In Ebræo est, hæc Lex Mincha vel sacrificii far- rei. Unde ut conciliet cum fonte Vulgatam Corne- lius, vocem ET ἐξηγητικῶς accipi vult, & Libamen- ta coactè a libis & panibus deducit.

## 6:14 Addition
To chapter 6, verse 14, towards the end, at page 477, column a.

This deals with the sacrifice of fine flour (not as an accessory to the daily burnt offering, but) as a solitary one, of which above in chapter 2. Why then is it repeated here? The answer is, so that the difference may be indicated when it was offered by someone from the people (for then a part fell to the Priests for food) and when by a Priest. For then the whole was burned on the altar.

Latin:

Ad cap. 6. v. 14. sub finem. ad pag. 477. a.

Agitur hic de sacrificio similæ (non accessorio jugi holocausto, sed) solitario, de quo supra cap. 2. Cur ergo hic repetitur? Respond. ut indicetur dif- ferentia cum à quopiam è populo offerretur (tunc enim pars Sacerdotibus cedebat in cibum) & cum à Sacerdote. Nam tum totum in altari cremabatur.

## 6:18
ver. 18. EVERYONE WHO TOUCHES THEM SHALL BE SANCTIFIED.

Namely, as much the fine flour offered with oil and frankincense, as the sacrifices offered for guilt and for sin.

SHALL BE SANCTIFIED.

That is, let him take care that he be holy, not polluted. The sacrifice of the Mincha designates Christ. He was a sacrifice on the cross: but in the Lord's Supper He is our food. Let only the Priests eat of it, that is: Christians: for these are priests before God 1 Pet. 2. And let only the males eat of it, not that women are not co-heirs of grace 1 Pet. 3. (for in Christ there is neither male nor female Gal. 3.) but that it may be signified that Christ pertains to those who do not allow themselves to be driven hither and thither, inconstant in various opinions of doctrines: But have determined to persevere manfully in sound doctrine and piety, even with danger to their lives, through the grace of God. Moreover, let the Lord's Supper be celebrated in a holy place, that is, among the faithful who are true members of the Church of Christ: not in the conventicles of Heretics. Leaven signifies the corruptions of heavenly doctrine and the impurity of morals: from both of which let Christians beware as diligently as possible, as Osiander rightly says here.

Latin:

vers. 18. OMNIS QUI TETIGERIT ILLA SANCTIFICABITUR.

Scilicet tam similam cum oleo & thure obla- tam, quam hostias pro delicto, & pro peccato oblatas.

SANCTIFICABITUR.

Id est, curet ut sit sanctus, non pollutus. Sacrifi- cium Minchæ Christum designat. Is in cruce fuit sa- crificium: sed in Cœna Domini est cibus noster. De eo vescantur soli Sacerdotes, id est: Christiani: hi enim sunt Sacerdotes coram Deo 1. Petr. 2. Et ve- scantur eo masculi soli, non quod fœminæ non sint cohæredes gratiæ 1. Petr. 3. (in Christo enim non est masculus, nec fæmina Gal. 3.) verum ut significetur, ad eos pertinere Christum, qui non inconstantes variis doctrinarum opinionibus huc illuc impelli se patiuntur: Sed viriliter in sana doctrina & pieta- te, etiam cum vitæ periculo, per gratiam Dei perse- verare constituerunt. In loco autem sacro, hoc est, inter fideles vera Ecclesiæ Christi membra, celebre- tur cœna Domini: non in conventiculis Hæreti- corum. Fermentum corruptelas doctrinæ cœlestis & morum impuritatem significat: ab utrisq; sibi Christiani quam diligentissime caveant, ut hîc recte Osiander.

## 6:25 Addition
Verse 25. IN THE PLACE WHERE IT IS OFFERED.

Lyranus advises that this is not to be understood as the offering of a burnt offering for burning, which took place upon the altar, but for slaughtering, which took place in the courtyard before the altar. In the place: namely, from the northern side, says Ainsworth, (see ch. 1, 11.) it signifies that Christ was to be killed in Jerusalem and on Mount Zion, which was on the sides of the North, Psalm 48:2 (which, however, is not proven by Cocceius regarding the location of Mount Zion) and Mount Calvary, where Christ was crucified, was on the side of Jerusalem towards the north and west.

Latin:

Vers. 25. IN LOCO UBI OFFERTUR.

Lyranus monet, non esse intelligendum de oblatione holocausti ad incendendum, quæ fiebat super altare, sed ad immolandum, quæ fiebat in atrio ante altare. In loco: nempe à latere septentrionali, ait Ainsworthus, (vide c. 1, 11.) significat Christum in Hierosolyma & monte Sionis occidendum, qui erat in lateribus Aquilonis Psalm. 68, 2. (quod tamen de montis Sionis situ Coccejo non probatur) & mons Calvariæ, ubi Christus crucifixus erat, a parte Hierosolymæ versus septentrionem & occidentem.

## 6:30
Vers. 30. IT SHALL BE BURNED WITH FIRE.

Victims of this kind were to be entirely burned, whose blood was brought into the tabernacle, which was done in the victim for the sins of the Priest and the people (ch. 4:6, 18); but it was burned outside the camp (ch. 4:12, 21; Heb. 13:11).

Latin:

Vers. 30. COMBURETUR IGNI.

Ejusmodi hostiæ totæ cremandæ erant; qua- rum sanguis inferebatur in tabernaculum, quod fa- ctum est in hostia pro peccatis Sacerdotis & populi c. 4, 6. 18. cremabatur autem extra castra c. 4, 12. 21. Ebr. 13, 11.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

## 7:2 Addition
To chapter 7, verse 2. HE SHALL SLAUGHTER. p. 477. b.

Münster notes that the rites of the trespass offering omitted earlier are described here: and he observes that nothing from the sacrifices for sin and trespass fell to those offering them, up to verse 7, which, with Lyranus as authority, was done to signify that they ought to be distanced from the sin committed, by guarding against relapse.

Latin:

Ad cap. 7. vers. 2. MACTABIT. p. 477. b.

Describi hic ritus delicti prius omissos notat Münsterus: & nihil cessisse offerentibus ex hostiis pro peccato, & delicto ad vers. 7. observat quod Lyrano autore factum, ut designaretur, quod elongari debeant a peccato perpetrato, cavendo à recidiva.

## 7:10 Addition
Verse 10. EQUAL MEASURE.

In Hebrew: every one shall be as his brother: that is, whoever among the sons of Aaron shall sacrifice, the reserved Mincha sacrifices shall fall to the same, as Osiander, and Cornel. à Lapide, Menochius, and Willet say, but not as if the raw [portion] had been the offering priest's, v. 9, but the cooked [portion] common to all, as Oleaster, Cajetan, and Sa wish. For where would this be said?

Latin:

Vers. 10. MENSURA ÆQUA.

In Ebræo: omnis ut frater suus erit: id est, quicunque ex filiis Aaron sacrificabit, eidem cedent reservata sacrificia Mincha, ut Osiander, & Cornel. à Lapide, Menochius, Willetus, non autem, quasi crudum quidem offerentis Sacerdotis fuisset v. 9. Coctum autem commune omnibus, ut Oleaster, Cajetanus, Sa volunt. Ubi enim hoc dicetur?

## 7:13 Addition
Verse 13. ALSO LEAVENED BREAD.

And yet leaven is forbidden in chapter 2, verse 11. I respond: it is forbidden to be placed on the altar, as Fagius and Lyranus [say], but here the bread was prepared only for the eating of the priests and others who were feeding on the remains of this sacrifice. Moreover, it had to be leavened; because our joys must be mixed with sorrow. Psalm 73, verse 21.

Latin:

Vers. 13. PANES QUOQUE FERMENTATOS.

Atqui fermentum prohibetur cap. 2. versu 11. Respond. prohibetur imponi altari, ut Fagius & Lyran. hic autem panis tantum ad esum Sacerdotum & aliorum, qui sacrificii hujus reliquiis vescebantur paratus. Fermentatus autem debebat esse; quia gaudia nostra cum dolore miscenda. Psal. 73. vers. 21.

## 7:16
Vers. 16. IF ANYONE SHALL OFFER A SACRIFICE BY VOW OR VOLUNTARILY) εὐχὴ ἡ ἑκύσιον LXX. whether by a preceding obligation of a vow, or from mere liberality. The former is called נדר, the latter נדבה from the verb נדב, which is to give. Therefore נדבה is translated δῶμα Deut. 23, 24. 2 Chron. 31, 14. And thus Maimonides distinguishes in Maase Karbanoth, who also notes this, that where נדבה is said without anything added, a burnt offering is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SI VOTO VEL SPONTE QVISPIAM OB- TVLERIT HOSTIAM) εὐχὴ ἡ ἑκύσιον LXX. siye præce- dente voti obligatione, sive ex mera liberalitate. Illud נדר vocatur, hoc נדבה a verbo נדב, quod est donare. Ita- que נדבה δῶμα vertitur Devter. 23, 24. 2. Paral. 31, 14. Et sic distinguit Maimonides in Maase Karbanoth, qui & hoc notat, ubi nullo addito נדבה dicitur, intelligi holocaustum.

## 7:17
vers. 17. AS FOR SIN AND FOR GUILT] See above 3:1.

The rites of the sacrifices for guilt, and of the peace offerings; the prohibition of fat and blood.

Latin:

vers. 17. SICUT PRO PECCATO ATQUE DELICTO] Vide supra 3, 1.

Ritus hostiarum pro delicto, & pacificorum; susque adipis & sanguinis prohibitio.

## 7:17 Addition
Verse 17. WHATEVER THE THIRD

That which was found remaining from the sacrifices on the third day had to be consumed, both because in those hot regions it could easily putrefy, and so that it might be signified that the body of Christ, rising on the third day, abolishes the legal sacrifices, as Ainsworth holds.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QUICQUID TERTIUS INVENERIT.

Id absumendum erat, quod tertio die inveniebatur residuum adhuc sacrificiis, tum, quia in calidis illis regionibus facile putrescere poterat, tum ut significaretur corpus Christi tertio die resurgens abolere legalia sacrificia, ut habet Ainsworthus.

## 7:19 Addition
Verse 19. THE FLESH THAT SHALL TOUCH ANY UNCLEAN THING SHALL NOT BE EATEN BUT SHALL BE BURNED WITH FIRE.

Flesh, namely, remaining from the sacrifices of retribution, as Münster, Lyranus, and Osiander [say], flesh offered to God. For it was permitted to eat other, non-sacred flesh, even if it had touched something unclean. Deut. 12:15, 22.

Latin:

Vers. 19. CARO QUÆ TETIGERIT ALIQUID IMMUNDUM NON COMEDETUR SED COMBURETUR IGNI.

Caro scil. reliqua de sacrificiis retributionis, ut Münsterus, Lyranus, Osiander, Caro Deo oblata. Nam alia carne non sacra, etiamsi quid immundi tetigerit, licebat vesci. Deut. 12, 15. 22.

## 7:23
Vers. 23. YOU SHALL NOT EAT THE FAT OF THE SHEEP AND OF THE OX AND OF THE GOAT) Because it harms the stomach. Maimonides.

That God was solicitous in these Levitical and Ceremonial laws about the diet to be observed in food for the sake of preserving health, let Apella the Jew believe, Maimonides, and whoever else he may be; it is also strange that Grotius believes it: who is everywhere solicitous about natural causes in these matters. Thus v. 26, he thinks that a natural cause underlies the interdict, why the blood of other animals is forbidden, but not that of fish: because the blood of fish does not equally inflame bodies: and so in other matters here and there. As if God were acting as a physician here, and proposing a Dietetic (which Porphyry opined), when He is occupied in establishing Ecclesiastical and Ceremonial institutions proper to the Jewish people. Others more correctly teach that the fat of the sheep, ox, and goat is not to be eaten, because those three were to be sacrificed to God, whence He also wished to claim their fat for Himself, even if they are slaughtered at home for food. But they could eat the fat of other animals which were not sacrificed to GOD, such as the deer, the buffalo, etc., which were clean for food but not for sacrifice. Then indeed the most holy legislator wished to exclude from the mysteries the sense of our own flesh, whose vice is figured by fat, and whose motion, whose vice is figured by blood, and warned that, being led away from carnal things and fixed in spirit upon spiritual things, having never entered into counsel with flesh and blood, we should offer ourselves wholly to God, Gal. 1, 16. Furthermore, because fat, as also blood, is the soul ver. 26. THE PRIEST WHO OFFERS IT SHALL EAT IT.

The sacrifice belonged by right only to the one offering it, who nevertheless could call his children, the males, to eat of it v. 29, by which it was signified that it is the duty of the Priestly office to blot out the sins of the people with their prayers and offerings, and to eat, that is, to consume: Theodor. in this place. Conf. c. 10, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ADIPEM OVIS ET BOVIS ET CAPRÆ NON COMEDETIS) Quia nocet stomacho. Maimo- nides.

LEgibus hisce Leviticis & Ceremonialibus De- um solicitum fuisse, de diæta in victu observan- da ad sanitatem tuendam, credat Judæus Apella, Mai- monides, & quisquis ille sit; mirum etiam credere Grotiurn: qui passim de causis naturalibus in hisce solicitus est. Ita v.26.causam naturalem subesse inter- dicto,cur sanguis aliorum animantium, non autem pi- scium vetitus sit, existimat hanc: quia non æque in- flammat corpora piscium sanguis: atque ita in aliis hinc inde. Quasi Deus hîc medicum ageret, & Dieteticum proponeret, (quod Porphyrius opinatus est) cum in sanciendis Ecclesiasticis & Ceremonia- libus populo Judaico propriis institutis occupatur. Rectius alii adipem ovis, bovis & capræ non come- dendum docent, qui ailla tria Deo immolanda, un- de etiam eorum adipem sibi deposcere voluit, etiamsi domi mactentur ad esum. Adipem vero aliorum animalium, quæ DEO non immolaban- tur, comedere poterant, utpote cervi, bubali &c. quæ munda erant ad esum non autem ad sacrifici- um. Tum vero carnis etiam nostræ sensum, cujus vitium adipe, motumque, cujus vitium sanguine figuratur, a mysteriis voluit seclusum sanctissimus legislator, monuitque, ut a carnalibus abducti, & in spiritualia animis defixi, consilio cum carne & sanguine nunquam inito, totos nos Deo offera- mus, Gal. 1, 16. Porro quia adeps, ut & sanguis, ani- vers. 26. SACERDOS QUI OFFERT COME- DET EAM.

Ad solum offerentem jure pertinebat hostia, qui tamen advocare poterat ad esum ejusdem libe- ros, masculos v. 29. quo significatum fuit, muneris Sacerdotalis esse precibus & oblationibus suis pec- cata populi delere, & comedere, id est, consumere: Theodor. h. l. Conf. c. 10,17.

## 7:26
Vers. 26. YOU SHALL NOT EAT THE BLOOD OF ANY ANIMAL, AS WELL OF BIRDS AS OF CATTLE] The word בהמה extends more broadly than cattle; it signifies all things that walk upon the earth. And hence the Hebrews understood that the blood of fish was not forbidden. See Moses of Coucy in the prohibitive precept 137. Hence it appears that a natural cause underlies the interdict. For the blood of fish does not inflame bodies equally. Plutarch on the eating of flesh, second: οἱ δὲ ὕθεσι συῶν ἐπιτόκων ἐναλλόμενοι καὶ λακτίζοντες, ἵνα αἷμα καὶ γάλα καὶ λύτρον ἐμβρύων ὁμοῦ συμ φθαρέντων ἐν ὠδῖσιν ἀναδεύσαντες (ὦ Ζεῦ καθάρσιε) φάγωσι τῦ ζώε τὸ μάλιςα φλεγμαῖνον.

It is not without reason that the Vulgate is castigated. We easily concede that fish are not easily included by the word בהמה. But as for that cause of the permitted blood of fish, which we touched upon just now from Grotius, whence, I pray, will it be taught? Should it not rather be said, as we just warned, that the cause is that God did not ordain fish for sacrifice: because the blood of those animals which were to be sacrificed to God ought not to have been eaten. But why God did not choose fish for Himself, Cornelius a Lapide brings forward various reasons on Lev. 1, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 26. SANGVINEM QVOQVE OMNIS ANI- MALIS NON SVMETIS IN CIBO, TAM DE AVI- BVS, QVAM DE PECORIBUS] Vox בהמה latius pa- tet, quem pecora; significat omnia, quæ super terram ince- dunt. Et hinc intellexere Hebræi, piscium sanguinem non esse vetitum. Vide Mosen de Kotzi præcepto vetante 137. Hinc apparet causam naturalem subesse interdicto. Non æque enim inflammat corpora piscium sanguis. Plutarchus de car- nium esu secundo: οἱ δὲ ὕθεσι συῶν ἐπιτόκων ἐναλλόμενοι καὶ λακτίζοντες, ἵνα αἷμα καὶ γάλα καὶ λύτρον ἐμβρύων ὁμοῦ συμ φθαρέντων ἐν ὠδῖσιν ἀναδεύσαντες (ὦ Ζεῦ καθάρσιε) φάγωσι τῦ ζώε τὸ μάλιςα φλεγμαῖνον.

Non abs re castigatur Vulgata. Pisces etiam voce בהמה haud includi facile concedimus. Sed quod causa illa sit concessi sanguinis piscium, quam proxime e Grotio attigimus, unde obsecro docebi- tur? Annon potius dicendum, ut modo monuimus, eam esse causam, quod pisces Deus non ordinarit in sacrificium: quia sanguis eorum animantium, quæ sacrificari Deo debebant, comedi non debuerit. Cur autem Deus pisces sibi non delegerit, rationes varias adducit Cornel. a Lapide ad Lev. 1,2.

## 7:27
v. 27. WHATEVER TOUCHES ITS FLESH SHALL BE SANCTIFIED.

The Chaldean renders it, everyone who shall touch it, shall be holy. But because it is subjoined, if his garment shall have been sprinkled with its blood, it shall be washed in a holy place, it seems rather to be indicated, whatever the sacrifice shall have touched, that it will be sanctified: for that which is unclean not to touch it is a symbol of life, therefore He forbade the eating of both, so that we might acknowledge God as the author of life, and be deterred from all injury, especially from homicide. Beautifully Jerome Ep. 128 to Fabiola: Priests offer the fat from salutary victims, the breast and the right arm are taken for food: Sense is in the heart, the heart in the breast, pleasure according to the physicists is in the liver. After, therefore, they have made a fat holocaust, and have burned the concupiscence of lust with the fire of the Spirit, they receive the breast and the arm as a reward. In the breast, pure thoughts, knowledge of the law, the truth of dogmas: in the arm, good works, and the fight against the devil, and the armed hand, so that what they have conceived in the mind, they may prove by example. By the rite of elevation and agitation v. 34, they were admonished of the exaltation of Christ John 3, 14. c. 12, 32. and of the preaching of the Gospel to be brought forth into all the corners of the world. The remaining meats of the Peace Offering are permitted to those offering, so that, cleansed by the water of expiation, they might prepare a feast from it, and be taught concerning the purgation of their sins, and also concerning the spiritual eating of the lamb to be sacrificed on the altar of the cross. The blood of fish, however, is not forbidden as that of birds and cattle, because God had destined these for sacrifices, but no fish: whence the blood of those was given to expiate on the altar for souls (but not the blood of fish) Lev. 17, 11. and so it was a matter of piety to hold in value the blood, which was a symbol of purification in the blood of Christ. These ceremonial laws do not bind us in the N.T., even if for the sake of the scandal of the Jews the law concerning not eating blood was kept for a time, because it seemed so to the Holy Spirit Acts 15, 29.

Latin:

v. 27. QUICQUID TETIGERIT CARNIS EJUS SANCTIFICABITUR.

Chaldæus reddit, omnis qui tetigerit, sanctus erit. Sed quia subjungitur, si de sanguine illius vestis fuerit aspersa, lavabitur in loco sancto, videtur po- tius indicatum, quicquid tetigerit sacrificium, te san- ctificatum iri: nam quod immundus id tangere non næ vitæque Symbolum est, idcirco esum utriusq prohibuit, ut autorem vitæ Deum agnoscamus, a injuria omni, imprimis ab homicidio deterreamu Pulchre Hieronymus Ep. 128. ad Fabiolam : De v ctimis salutaribus adipem offerunt Sacerdotes, pectu & brachium dextrum in cibum accipiuntur : Sensus e in corde, cor in pectore, voluptas secundum Physicos e in jecore. Postquam ergo pingue holocaustum fece rint, & concupiscentiam libidinis igne Spiritus crema verint, pectus & brachium accipiunt in præmium. I pectore mundas cogitationes, legis notitiam, dogmatun veritatem: in brachio bona opera, & pugnam contr diabolum, & armatam manum, ut quod mente conce perint, exemplo probent. Ritu autem elevationis & agitationis v.34. admoniti sunt de exaltatione Chri sti Joh. 3,14. c.12,32. & de prædicatione Evangelii in omnes mundi angulos proferenda. Reliquæ Sa crificii Pacifici carnes permittuntur offerentibus,u aqua expiationis mundati convivium inde quod dam parent, & de purgatione peccatorum suo rum, nec non de spirituali esu agni immolandi in ara crucis edocerentur. Piscium vero sanguis vetitus non est uti volucrium, & pecorum, quia hæc in sa crificia destinarat Deus, nullum autem piscem: un de sanguis istorum data est ad expiandum in altari pro anim abus (non autem piscium sanguis) Lev. 17, 11. adeoq; pietatis erat, in pretio habere sanguinem, qui Symbolum erat purificationis in sanguine Chri sti. Non obligant autem nos hæc ceremonialia in N. T. etsi ob scandalum Judæorum ad tempus lex de non comedendo sanguine servata fuerit, quia ita visum Spiritui S. Act. 15,29.

## 8:1 Argument
PART II. OF LEVITICUS, CONCERNING PERSONS. CHAPTER VIII. The anointing of the Priests and the Tabernacle.

Latin:

PARS II. LEVITICI, DE PER- SONIS. CAPUT VIII. Sacerdotum & Tabernaculi unctio.

## 8:10
v. 10. AND WHEN THE SANCTIFIER HAD SPRINKLED THE ALTAR SEVEN TIMES, HE ANOINTED IT AND ALL ITS VESSELS.

This altar, therefore, was not finally sanctified with its vessels on that day on which the Princes of Israel offered their gifts, Num. 7, 1. as Tremellius and Junius judged at that place. But how the altar ought to have been consecrated and sanctified had been handed down in Exod. 29, 36. 37.

Latin:

v. 10. CUMQUE SANCTIFICANS ASPER- SISSET ALTARE SEPTEM VICIBUS UNXIT ILLUD ET OMNIA VASA EJUS.

Non ergo demum sanctificatum hoc altare fuit cum vasibus suis isto die, quoPrincipes Israelis munera sua obtulerunt, Num. 7, 1. uti Tremell. & Junius ad illum locum censuere. Quomodo au- tem consecrari & sanctificari debuerit altare, tradi- tum erat Exod. 29,36. 37.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. HE ANOINTED HIM] As one who had been made a god by God, both of the people and of Aaron, Ex. 4, 16. Moses the perfect one: Aaron the one progressing, according to Philo.

Moses anointed Aaron because he was a Prophet of the Lord: but Prophets were accustomed to perform this duty also extraordinarily; by whom also Kings were anointed, when God chose someone out of the ordinary, or finally appointed him through a Prophet. 1 Sam. 10, 1. c. 16, 13. 2 Reg. 9, 1. 3. 6. 1 Reg. 19, 15. 2 Reg. 8, 18. Otherwise, when a King had already been appointed, or it was certain about a future King, the High Priests exercised this office, 1 Reg. 1, 30. 34. 39. 2 Par. 32, 2. Since, therefore, no Priest had yet been anointed, Moses performed that anointing out of the ordinary, not as a god made by God, or as a Magistrate: for it is not the duty of a Prince to anoint Priests; but as a Prophet of the Lord.

Aaron, however, had to be washed, so that he might be warned that such a High Priest was being appointed, who himself had need of purification, and could in no way expiate the sins of others, and therefore that there was still another High Priest, according to the order of Melchizedek, who expiates the same. Ps. 110, 4. Heb. 2, 17. He had to be adorned with sacred clothing, because it is not permitted for him, deformed by sins, to come into the sight of God without the holy garment of the innocence of Christ, whose breast alone shines with clarity and integrity (denoted by Urim and Thummim). Cf. Hieron. in Epist. ad Fabiol. Moreover, from the fact that Moses is said to have offered a victim, v. 14, some gather that he was the same Priest, and they wish this to be indicated in Ps. 99, 6, from which the Papists gather that pastors are called not by the Magistrate, but by the Pontiff, just as Aaron was called by Moses, see Bellarm. l. 1. de Cler. c. 7. but the consequence from the calling of Aaron, which was done by the immediate command of God, to the calling of today is futile: Nor is there any doubt that Moses held the Political Principate: But that he himself was a Priest, and the highest one at that, is established by no document. For it is one thing to undergo certain Priestly acts, another to be a Priest. For the former was done formerly by the firstborn and by certain others, such as Prophets and men of God, to whom it was committed beyond the order by a special divine mandate for the occasion: and thus it could have been done by Moses even before the Levitical Priesthood was instituted, by the command of God, even if he himself was not a Priest. Abulensis from this very passage v. 25 proves that Moses was not a Priest, because otherwise he would have received the breast with the right shoulder. Regarding Ps. 99, 6, we shall see there.

Latin:

Vers. 12. VNXIT EVM] Vt qui a Deo deus factus esset, tum populi, tum Aaronis, Ex. 4, 16. Moses ὁ τέλειος: Aaron ὁ προκόπτων Philoni.

Unxit Moses Aaronem, quia Propheta Domi- ni fuit: Prophetæ vero folebant hoc etiam munere fungi extraordinarie; a quibus etiam Reges ungeban- tur, cum Deus extra ordinem aliquem eligeret, aut per Prophetam demum constitueret. 1. Sam. 10, 1. c. 16, 13. 2. Reg. 9, 1. 3. 6. 1. Reg. 19, 15. 2. Reg. 8, 18. Alias ubi Rex constitutus jam erat, aut de futuro Rege constabat, Pontifices hoc officium exercebant, 1. Reg. 1, 30. 34. 39. 2. Par. 32, 2. Quum ergo nullus Sacerdos adhuc unctus esset, Moses extra ordinem eam un- ctionem peregit, non ceu Deus a Deo factus, seu Ma- gistratus: Principis enim hoc non est, Sacerdotes ungere; Sed ceu Propheta Domini.

Lavandus autem erat Aaron, ut moneretur ejusmodi constitui Pontificem, qui ipse purgatione opus habeat, & nequicquam aliorum possit expiare peccata, ideo alium adhuc esse Pontificem, secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech, qui expiat eadem. Ps. 110, 4. Ebr. 2, 17. Vestitu sacro ornandus erat, quod ipsi peccatis deformato in conspectum Dei fine ve- ste sancta innocentiæ Christi prodire non liceat, cu- jus solius pectus claritate & integritate (per Urim & Thummim notata) nitet. Conf. Hieron. in Epist. ad Fabiol. Cæterum ex eo, quod victimam obtulis- se dicitur Moses, v. 14. colligunt nonnulli eundem Sacerdotem fuisse, idque indicari volunt Psal. 99, 6. e quo colligunt Pontificii, pastores non a Magistratu, sed a Pontifice vocari, uti Aaron a Mose vocatus est, vid. Bellarm. l. 1. de Cler. c. 7. sed futilis est conse- quentia a vocatione Aaronis, quæ Dei jussu imme- diato facta, ad hodiernam vocationem: Neque du- bium est Mosen Principatum Politicum gessisse: Ipsum autem Sacerdotem fuisse eumque summum, nullo documento constat. Nam aliud est, actus quosdam Sacerdotales subire, aliud Sacerdotem es- se. Prius enim factum olim erat a primogenitis & ab aliis quibusdam, utpote Prophetis & viris Dei, quibus id præter ordinem mandato divino speciali pro re nata committebatur: adeoque a Mose etiam ante institutum Leviticum Sacerdotium fieri po- tuit, jussu Dei, etsi ipse Sacerdos non fuerit. Abu- lensis ex hoc ipso loco v. 25. probat Mosen non fuis- se Sacerdotem, quia alias accepisset pectusculum cum armo dextro. De Ps. 99, 6. ibi visuri sumus.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. Aaron's offering, and blessing.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Aaronis oblatio, & benedictio.

## 9:1 Addition
To chapter 9, verse 1. ON THE EIGHTH DAY. page 478. b.

Viz. from the consecration of Aaron Exod. 29. v. 30. Levit. 8. vers. 33. Ezech. 43. v. 27. Ainsworth explains the reason: Most living creatures were in a state of uncleanness and imperfection for seven days, and in the eighth were perfect, as infants Levit. 12. v. 2. 3. beasts Levit. 22. vers. 27. the unclean from leprosy, flux, &c. Levit. 14. v. 8. 9. 10. & 15, 13. 14. Num. 6, v. 9. 10. Likewise the Priests before the eighth day were not admitted to minister: By which was shadowed the day of Christ, who by rising on the day after the Sabbath, sanctified the Church and the ministry, &c.

Latin:

Ad cap. 9. versu 1. OCTAVO DIE. pag. 478. b.

Scil. a consecratione Aaronis Exod. 29. v. 30. Levit. 8. vers. 33. Ezech. 43. v. 27. Causam exponit Ainsworthus: Animantia pleraque in immunditia & imperfecto statu erant per septem dies, & in octavo perfecta, ut infantes Levit. 12. v. 2. 3. bestiæ Levit. 22. vers. 27. immundi ex lepra, fluxu, &c. Levit. 14. v. 8. 9. 10. & 15, 13. 14. Num. 6, v. 9. 10. Pariter Sacerdotes ante octavum diem non erant admissi ad ministrandum: Quo adumbratus est dies Christi, qui resurgendo postridie Sabbati, sanctificavit Ecclesiam & ministerium, &c.

## 9:2
Ver. 2. A CALF FOR SIN) In memory of the calf worship.

It is absurd, nay, impious to say, that God himself wished to celebrate the memory of idolatrous worship with a sacrifice. Nor indeed did the Lord command Aaron here to expiate the sin of μοσχολατρείας [calf-worship] by the offering of a calf for sin, because this was common to every High Priest, when he offered for sin, to sacrifice a calf Lev. 4, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VITULUM PRO PECCATO) In memoriam cultus vituli.

ABsurdum, imo dictu impium est, Deum ipsum sacrificio memoriam cultus idololatrici cele- brare voluisse. Nec vero Aaronem hic expiare pec- catum μοσχολατρείας oblatione vituli pro peccato jussit Dominus, quia hoc commune erat omni Pon- tifici, cum pro peccato offerret, vitulum sacrificare Lev. 4, 3.

## 9:3 Addition
Vers. 3. A GOAT.

A fetid animal to denote the stench of sin, as Lyranus notes. And yet c. 4. a calf was commanded to be offered for sin, viz. when the Priest was included in the community of the people. Here, however, the people are taken separately from the Priest. Or it must be said that the calf was offered for a certain and determined sin, the goat for uncertain and indeterminate sins, as Bonfrerius has warned.

Latin:

Vers. 3. HIRCUM.

Animal fœtidum ad denotandum fœtorem peccati, notante Lyrano. Atqui c. 4. vitulus pro peccato offerri jubebatur scil. cum Sacerdos in communitate populi includebatur. Hic vero populus separatim a Sacerdote sumitur. Aut dicendum vitulum oblatum pro peccato certo, & determinato, hircum pro peccatis incertis, & indeterminatis, ut Bonfre- rius monuit.

## 9:7
Ver. 7. MAKE ATONEMENT FOR THYSELF AND FOR THE PEOPLE) בעד in this place, as also 2 Chron. 30, 18. for that which is for the most part על as above 10, 20. 26. 51. and elsewhere.

This is noted in Heb. 7, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 7. DEPRECARE PRO TE ET PRO POPULO) בעד hoc loco, ut & 2. Par. 30, 18. pro eo quod plerumque על ut supra 10, 20. 26. 51. & alibi.

Notatur hoc Ebr. 7, 26.

## 9:10
Ver. 10. HE BURNED. He placed upon the altar to be burned, as Lyr. and Menochius, or it is a πρόληψις [anticipation]. See v. 24. so also v. 13. 17. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ADOLEVIT. Imposuit altari adolenda, ut Lyr. & Meno- chius, vel πρόληψις est. Vid. v. 24. sic & v. 13. 17. 20.

## 9:16 Addition
Vers. 16. ALL OF WHICH HE BURNED UPON THE ALTAR.

That Aaron first offers sacrifices to expiate his own sins teaches that, although he bore the type of Christ (insofar as he later sacrificed for the people), he was nevertheless not himself the true expiator of sins: but that another was to be expected (THE SON OF GOD) pure from all sin: for whom there would be no need to offer first for his own, and then finally for the sins of others, Heb. 5 & 7, as Osiander holds. For when Aaron is said to have burned these sacrifices, it must be understood that he prepared them, the pile of wood having been made, the victims dismembered, and everything duly ordered, so that they would only have to be set on fire afterwards by the Lord: which is also read to have been done.

Latin:

Vers. 16. QUÆ OMNIA SUPER ALTA- RI CREMAVIT.

Quod Aaron prius pro suis peccatis expiandis sacrificia offert, docet, tametsi gereret typum Christi (quatenus pro populo postea immolavit) tamen non fuisse ipsum verum peccatorum expiatorem: sed ex- pectandum fuisse alium (FILIUM DEI) purum ab omni peccato: cui non opus esset, prius pro suis, dein- de demum pro alienis peccatis offerre Hebr. 5. & 7. ut Osiander habet. Cum enim Aaron cremasse sacri- ficia hæc dicitur, sentiendum est, quod ea præparave- rit, strue lignorum facta, dimembratis hostiis, & omnibus rite ordinatis, ut tantum incendenda post- ea essent a Domino: quod & factum legitur.

## 9:17
Ver. 17. WITHOUT THE CEREMONIES OF THE BURNT OFFERING.

In Hebrew. Besides the burnt offering, which was accustomed to be offered every day, as Vatabl. i.e., all these sacrifices of Aaron did not hinder the offering of the daily burnt offering.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ABSQUE CEREMONIIS HOLO- CAUSTI.

In Ebr. Præter holocaustum, quod singulis die- bus offerri solebat, ut Vatabl. q. d. omnia hæc Aa- ronis sacrificia non impediebant oblationem holo- causti jugis.

## 9:22 Addition
Vers. 22. EXTENDING HIS HAND TO THE PEOPLE HE BLESSED THEM.

Lifting his hand, he pronounced the blessing commanded in Num. 6. In which he was a type of Christ, as the true and supreme Priest, who was sent by the Father to abolish the curse through his cross and bring the blessing, Gen. 22, Acts 3, Luke 24, verse 50. He is said to have extended or lifted his hand, not HANDS; because even if he lifted both hands, he nevertheless lifted his right hand higher than his left.

Latin:

Vers. 22. EXTENDENS MANUM AD PO- PULUM BENEDIXIT EI.

Elevans manum pronunciavit benedictionem Num. 6. demandatam. In quo typus Christi fuit, ceu veri & summi Sacerdotis, qui missus a Patre, ut per crucem suam maledictionem aboleret, & benedictionem adferret Genes. 22. Actor. 3. Luc. 24. vers. 50. Manum extendisse vel elevasse dicitur, non MANUS; quia etsi manum utramque eleva- ret, manum tamen dextram altius elevabat, quam sinistram.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. MOSES. Lyranus teaches that Moses entered, both to teach Aaron the manner of offering incense, and to pray with Aaron for the giving of fire.

THE GLORY OF THE LORD APPEARED. Concerning the fire sent by God, Cornelius and Menochius, but others, with Malvenda, more correctly understand it as the presence of God in the cloud. Compare Ex. 40, 34.

Latin:

Vers. 23. MOSES. Lyranus Mosen intrasse docet, tum ut Aaro- nem doceret modum offerendi thymiamatis, tum ut cum Aarone oraret pro datione ignis.

APPARUIT GLORIA DOMINI. De igne a Deo misso Cornel. & Menochius, sed rectius de præsentia Dei in nube alii intelligunt cum Malvenda. Conf. Ex. 40,34.

## 9:24
vers. 24. FIRE. The fire descending from heaven was a sign of divine acceptance. See Gen. 4.4. 1 Kings 18, 38. 1 Chron. 21, 26. 2 Chron. 7, 1. Which fire they were obliged to use ever after and to preserve it for that purpose, and to nourish it with wood kindled, Lev. 6, 12.

FROM THE LORD. In Hebrew: from the faces of the Lord: from the mercy seat, where then for the first time God established a visible proof of His presence, as Malvenda and Junius see. Lev. 10, 2.

Latin:

vers. 24. IGNIS. Ignis de cœlo descendens signum erat divinæ acceptationis. V. Gen. 4.4. 1. Reg. 18,38. 1. Par. 21,26. 2. Par. 7, 1. Quo igne semper deinceps uti atque eo fine eundem asservare debuerunt, lignisq; accensis nutrire Lev. 6, 12.

A DOMINO. In Ebr. a faciebus Domini: a propitiatorio, ubi tunc primum Deus statuit aspectabile præsentiæ suæ documentum, ut Malv. & Jun. vid. Lev. 10, 2.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. The death of Nadab and Abihu.

Latin:

CAPUT X. Nadab & Abiu interitus.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. AND FIRE COMING OUT FROM THE LORD DEVOURED THEM, AND THEY DIED.) Namely, the fire burned them inwardly even to death: for the bodies remained and were carried outside the camp, as follows. And from this the Hebrews took the custom that where the penalty of fire is in the law, they would pour molten lead into the mouth of the condemned, by which he would perish, burned from within.

Latin:

Vers. 2. EGRESSVSQVE IGNIS A DOMINO DE- VORAVIT EOS, ET MORTUI SVNT.) Nempe intus eos ussit ignis ad mortem usque: nam corpora mansere & extra castra deportata sunt, ut sequitur. Et hinc Hebræi mo- rem sumsere, ut ubi poena ignis est in lege, plumbum fervens damnato in os funderent, quo intus ustus periret.

## 10:3
v. 3. THIS IS WHAT HE SPOKE. The Papists observe that it is not found where God said these things, and they allege this in support of traditions: but although we do not deny that in that age things were handed down by word of mouth which do not exist written in so many words, these words, however, do not favor unwritten tradition at all; for are not those things written here which Moses asserts the Lord said? If, therefore, they were not found written elsewhere, they are nevertheless recited here. But the Hebrews say they are contained in Ex. 19, 22. 'But also the priests, who are brought near to the Lord, let them sanctify themselves; lest perhaps Jehovah destroy them.' Others wish to refer to the passage Exod. 29, 43. But it can be said that these things were spoken to Moses here, or inspired in him; therefore they are not things said long ago or previously, but things which he had just received from the Lord are being reported.

Latin:

v. 3. HOC EST QUOD LOQUUTUS EST. Non reperiri, ubi hæc dixerit Deus, Pontificii observant, atque id in subsidium traditionum allegant: sed etsi ætate ista tradita viva voce, quæ tot verbis scripta non extent, haud negemus, hac ta- men verba traditioni non scriptæ nihil favent; an- non enim illa scripta hic habentur, quæ dixisse Do- minum perhibet Moses? Si ergo maxime alias scri- pta non reperirentur, hic tamen ea recitantur. Di- cunt autem Ebræi ea haberi Ex. 19, 22. Sed & Sacer- dotes, qui applicati sunt ad Dominum, sanctificent se; ne forte Jehovah dissipet eos. Alii respici volunt lo- cum Exod. 29, 43. Sed dici potest, hæc ad Mosen hic dicta, vel eidem inspirata esse; non ergo olim, vel antea dicta, sed quæ jam acceperat a Domino, re- ferri.

## 10:5
vers. 5. CLOTHED, From this Lyranus gathers that they were saved, see 2 Kings 13.

Latin:

vers. 5. VESTITOS, Ex hoc colligit Lyran. eos salvatos, vid. 2. Reg. 13.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. DO NOT UNCOVER YOUR HEADS) The Gentiles used to take off their hats and go with torn clothes. But the Talmudists in this place and below 21, 10, understand it as forbidden to let the hair grow long, from Ez. 44, 20. For the High Priest always, for others during the time of their service. But it is said to be grown long for those who let their hair grow for 30 days.

Others more correctly, do not shave your hair, as was done in mourning, Job 1, 20. Jer. 7, 29. Mic. 1, 16. just as the shaving of the beard is a sign of mourning, Jer. 41, 25. thus Drusius, Ainsworth, Malvenda. Namely, that they should not dishonor them, by whose punishment God was sanctified, as Augustine, question 32.

YOUR BRETHREN AND ALL THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL SHALL LAMENT) That is, although they may mourn, do not follow their example. Just as by Roman law enemies or those condemned for treason are not accustomed to be mourned, law 'Liberorum' § 3, Digest 'de his qui notantur infamia': so in Hebrew law, those whom God had slain.

Latin:

Vers. 6. CAPITA VESTRA NOLITE NVDARE) Gen- tes pileos deponebant, & ibant vestibus scisis. At Thal- mudici hoc loco & infra 21, 10. intelligunt vetitum comam promittere, ex Ez. 44, 20. Summo Pontifici semper, cæteris tempore ἐφημερίας. Promittere autem eis dicitur, qui per 30. dies comam alit.

Rectius alii, ne radatis capillos, ut in luctu fa- ctum Job. 1, 20. Jer. 7, 29. Mich. 1, 16. uti & rasio bar- bæ signum luctus Jer. 41, 25. sic Drusius, Ainsvvorth, Malvenda. Ne sc. deslererent eos, quorum pœna Deus erat sanctificatus, ut August. qu. 32.

FRATRES VESTRI ET OMNIS DOMVS ISRAEL PLANGANT) Id est, quamvis illi lugeant, vos eorum ex- emplar ne sequimini. Sicut Romano jure non solent lugeri hostes, vel perduellionis damnati l. Liberorum §. 3. D. de his qui notantur infamia: ita in Hebræo jure ii quos Deus interfecerat.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. YOU SHALL NOT DRINK WINE AND EVERYTHING THAT CAN INTOXICATE, YOU AND YOUR SONS, WHEN YOU ENTER THE TABERNACLE] That is, while you wear the stole. Josephus, Chæremon on the Egyptians: 'And this time, whenever they were about to perform some sacred rite, they would set aside a number of days, some forty-two, others more, others fewer, but never less than seven,' Hecatæus, when he had dealt with the Jewish Temple: 'They spend their days in it, and the priests perform certain purifications, and they do not drink wine at all in the temple.' The reason for wine being forbidden at that time is so that the use of reason may remain intact, and the incentives of lust may be absent. The same Chæremon, produced by Porphyry in On Abstinence 4, brings forward these reasons why the Egyptian priests abstained from wine.

It is added for this reason, that you may have knowledge, i.e., I have forbidden wine for this reason, that you may be able to discern and judge rightly, and remain consistent in your administration, as Lyranus says. Vers. 11. AND TEACH THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL ALL MY STATUTES] Namely, those which pertained to the ceremonies. For this care belonged properly to the Priests. BY THE HAND OF MOSES] that is, my hand. It is common for the Hebrews to place a noun in place of a pronoun. Vers. 12. EAT IT WITHOUT LEAVEN. In the Hebrew: Eat it as unleavened cakes, that is, made into unleavened masses. See ch. 6, 16; ch. 2, 10. Moses here repeats the law given before, lest the Priests, struck by present grief, should forget or neglect the commands of God, as Ainsworth says here. Vers. 17. WHY HAVE YOU NOT EATEN? They ought to have eaten this goat. Lev. 6, 16. Since they could not do so because of their grief, they judged it should be burned. V. 19. HOW COULD I HAVE EATEN? To Willet, this seems to be a mitigation of the crime rather than a just defense: for as to what is added, that Moses received it, he thinks with Borrhæus that he tolerated that infirmity out of human compassion. Furthermore, from this passage he concludes with Calvin (although it is not explained above, where the law of the sacrifice for sin is delivered, nor elsewhere) that the flesh of the victim for sin had to be eaten on the same day it was offered, and the remains burned: otherwise there would have been no reason why Aaron, on the same day the flesh was sacrificed, should have burned it or excused himself from eating it, if the eating could have been deferred to another day.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VINUM ET OMNE QVOD INEBRIARE POTEST NON BIBETIS TV ET FILII TVI QVAN- DO INTRATIS IN TABERNACVLVM] Id est, dum stolam feretis. Josephus, Chæremon de Ægyptiis: ὁ δὲ χρό- νος ὗτος ὁπότε συντελεῖν τι περὶ τὴν ἱερὰν μέλλοιεν θρησκείαν προλαμβάνων ἡμερῶν ἀριθμὸν, οἱ μὲν δυοῖν καὶ τετταράκοντα, οἱ δὲ τούτων πλείες, οἱ δὲ ἐλάττες, ὐδέποτε μὲν τις τῶν ἑπτὰ λει- πομένας, Hecatæus cum de Templo Judaico egisset: διατρί- βυσι δ᾽ ἐν ἀυτῷ καὶ τὰς ἡμέρας ἱερεῖς τινας ἁγνείας τινὰς ἁγνέυοντες, καὶ τὸ παράπαν οἶνον ὐ πίνοντες ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ. Cau- sa vini eo tempore interdicti, ut & rationis usus constet, & absint libidinis incitamenta. Quas causas cur Ægyptii Sa- cerdotes vino abstinuerint, adfert idem ille Chæremon pro- ductus a Porphyrio de Abstinentia 4.

Ideo additur, ut habeatis scientiam, q. d. Ideo interdixi vinum, ut recte discernere possitis & judi- care, & vobis ipsis in administratione constare, ut Lyranus. Vers. 11. DOCEATISQVE FILIOS ISRAEL OMNIA LEGITIMA MEA] Nempe ea quæ ad ceremonias pertine- bant. Hæc enim cura proprie erat Sacerdotum. PER MANVM MOTSI] id est, meam. Frequens Hebræis nomen ponere pro pronomine. vers. 12. COMEDITE ILLUD ABSQUE FER- MENTO. In Ebr. Comedite eam massas, id est, factam in massas infermentatas. Vid. c. 6, 16. c. 2, 10. Legem ante datam Moses hic repetit, ne Sacerdotes præsenti dolore perculsi mandata Dei obliviscerentur, aut negligerent, ut hic Ainsworth. vers. 17. CUR NON COMEDISTIS? Hircum hunc comedere debebant. Lev. 6, 16. quod cum præ mœrore non possent, comburen- dum censebant. v. 19. QUOMODO POTUI COMEDERE? Hæc Willeto videtur potius mitigatio criminis, quam justa defensio: Nam quod additur, Mosen eam recepisse, humana commiseratione tolerasse eam infirmitatem cum Borrhai censet. Cæterum ex hoc loco colligit cum Calvino (etsi nec supra, ubi lex traditur hostiæ pro peccato, nec alibi id expli- cetur) carnes victimæ pro peccato eadem die, qua fuerat oblata, fuisse comedendas, & reliquias con- cremandas: alias non fuisset ratio, cur vel Aaron ea- dem die, qua fuerant immolatæ carnes, illas com- bussisset aut se ab iis comedendis excusasset, si come- stio in alterum diem potuisset differri.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

The distinction between clean and unclean animals.

vers. 1. TO MOSES AND AARON.

Because the knowledge of these pertains both to the Magistrate regarding civil use, and to the Priest regarding sacrifices. V. 3. WHICH HAS A DIVIDED HOOF] Many of these things taken from the Egyptians have natural causes, based on good or bad food, as Maimonides notes. Chæremon, in Porphyry on the Egyptian Priests: 'They abstained from all fish and from four-footed animals that are solid-hoofed or many-cleft or not horned. And of birds, those that are carnivorous.' Where he says 'not horned,' it means the same as solid-hoofed. For they have solid hooves, which are not horned, as Pliny testifies in book 11, who also adds: 'a solid hoof and a two-horned animal do not exist.' The same author notes that copulation occurs only during the day for all those that have a solid hoof, and that their offspring are less numerous: book 10. Porphyry says it was forbidden for the Jews to eat any of the solid-hoofed animals. That the sacrifices were transferred from the Egyptians to the Hebrews is false. Nor can it be proven that God looked to natural causes of good or bad food in them. No faith is due to Maimonides and other Rabbis who are blind in these matters. Beyond the most free will of the Supreme Legislator, if no cause can be brought forward, this must be left to divine wisdom, which did nothing rashly, even if we do not attain the reason for its institutions. Thus, when in v. 7 the Hebrews were ordered to abstain from eating swine, our author betakes himself to the Egyptians, and rather to Tacitus or Plutarch, because the abundance of food, since pork is very sweet, causes scabies, and so on in other cases. If all these things were proven from the divine Pandects, they would deservedly obtain belief. To discuss the reasons for divine institutions from foreign philosophers and historians is to play with a serious, nay, a divine matter. I would not deny that in the concession of animals for food, all things were ordained and distinguished appropriately to nature, if indeed those are forbidden to be eaten which are poisonous by their own nature, such as reptiles, or which feed on unclean foods, such as pigs and hoopoes, bats, owls and eagle-owls, etc.; yet there is no doubt that the primary cause in most cases was symbolic, so that by the division of the hoof the distinction between good and evil might be noted, and by rumination the application of known good to action, (Augustine on Psalm 47. Rumination denotes repeated cognition, or meditation on that which has been heard. Cf. Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 11.) Unclean animals signified the uncleanness of vices, of which they are symbols, so that the people, accustomed to bodily cleanliness, might be called away from the uncleanness of idolaters and their unclean sacrifices, and, being stirred up, might rise to the cleanliness of the mind. Pelargus is correct on this passage, p. 104, that the uncleanness of individuals is not to be estimated merely from the harm and unwholesomeness of the food, but because they displayed certain marks either in the members of their bodies or in the seeking of their sustenance, which would warn men of vices. An argument for the special providence and care of God is shown to be singular toward the bodies as well as the souls of the pious: the former, so that they might not be easily harmed by any promiscuous eating; the latter, so that they might strive for purity and, when they hear that they must abstain from those things which lack cloven hooves, which do not ruminate, which live by plunder, which are savage and monstrous, they might determine that they are being called from rapine, avarice, lust, monstrosity, and intemperance to justice, moderation, clemency, sobriety, and faith. Concerning which Novatian, book on Jewish foods, chapter 3, in the works of Tertullian, p. 653 in my edition: In animals, human morals and acts and wills are depicted. They are clean if they ruminate, i.e., if they always have the divine precepts in their mouth as if it were food; they cleave the hoof if they complete the journeys of life with a firm step of innocence, justice, and every virtue. For of those which divide the foot into two hooves, the gait is always robust, while the slippery part is supported by the foundation of the other hoof and is held in the tracks by solidity. Thus, those who do neither are unclean: those whose gait is not firm in virtues, nor is the food of divine precepts ground in the mouth by any rumination; for even those who do one but not the other are not clean, while they are weak in the other, nor are they perfect in both. But these are either those doing both, like the faithful, who are clean; or one, like the Jews and heretics, who are defiled; or neither, like the Gentiles, who are consequently unclean. Thus, in animals, a kind of mirror of human life has been established by the law, in which they may consider the images of the sanctions, so that whatever vicious things are committed by men against nature may be condemned all the more, while they are blamed even when established naturally in cattle. Who, a little later, also discourses thus in particular on the symbolic significance of some: For what does the law want for itself when it says, 'You shall not eat the camel,' except that by the example of the animal it condemns a life that is weak and twisted with crimes? Or when it prohibits the pig from being taken as food, it certainly reproves a life that is muddy and miry and rejoicing in the filth of vices, placing its good not in the generosity of the mind, but in the flesh alone; or when it [prohibits] the hare, it accuses men who have transformed themselves into women. Who would make the body of a weasel his food? But it reproves thefts. Who a lizard? But it hates the uncertain variety of life. Who a gecko? But it execrates spots, those seeking prey from the death of another. Who a raven? But it execrates crafty wills. Who a sparrow? When it forbids it, it rebukes intemperance; when the owl, it hates those who flee from the light of truth. When the swan, the proud of high neck; when the plover, the too garrulous intemperance of the tongue; when the bat, those seeking the shadows of night as well as of error. These things Novatian. Which Isidore repeats. Theodoret, chapter 11 on Leviticus, says of birds that those are unclean which are rapacious, which feed on corpses, and which rejoice in darkness: so that we may be instructed to abstain from them and similar things. As for ruminating animals having a cloven hoof, Cyril, chapter 9 against Julian, teaches that to ruminate is a symbol of prudence, and to divide the foot is for those who discern good from evil in action. See more on these matters in Clement of Alexandria, book 2, Paedagogus; Origen on this passage; Cyril, book 14 on Adoration; Eusebius, book 8 of the Preparation for the Gospel; Augustine against Adimantus, chapter 15. Nor is it said without reason that God intended, even in the very use of foods, an exercise for His people, both of obedience in honor of God who so commands, and of temperance. There were added, says Novatian again, chapter 4, also other causes by which many kinds of foods were taken away from the Jews, not so that those things might be condemned, but so that they might be restrained to serve one GOD: because for this purpose, frugality became those who were chosen, and temperance of the gullet, which is always found to be a neighbor to religion, or rather (if I may say so) its blood relation and kinsman. For luxury is an enemy to holiness. Which this glutton of antiquity should not have neglected here. But he philosophizes only about diet and natural causes, or Egyptian rites from exotic writers, paying little attention to what Novatian warned here in chapter 2: In the first place, that must be posited, that the law is spiritual, which if they deny is spiritual, they are certainly BLASPHEMING. If, avoiding blasphemy, they confess it is spiritual, let them read it spiritually. For divine things must be received divinely, and holy things must certainly be asserted holily. Moreover, a grave fault is branded if earthly and human doctrine is presented for sacred and spiritual scriptures, which must be guarded against so that it does not happen. These are the words of Novatian, which we not undeservedly oppose to Grotius. The whole treatise of Novatian is worthy to be weighed here. Tertullian also wrote a book on clean and unclean animals, but it is now missing. Concerning fish, Theodoret, question 11 on Leviticus, says thus: Those which are endowed with scales and fins, these swim upon the waters. But those which are not of this kind wallow downward and on the ground (clinging to the bottom). They are clean, therefore, who do not apply their soul to earthly things, but, endowed with the fins of faith, are surrounded by the ornament of virtue: for what a scale is in fish, this is faith among men. Cf. also Origen, homily 7 on Leviticus. Whoever desires more specific details will be able to approach Pelargus, among others, in his commentary on this passage. Regarding swine, if we listen to Plutarch, he accuses the Jews in Sympos. book 4, 4. 5. because they abstain from them, not indeed out of disgust, but rather revering swine as teachers of plowing. But he does them an injustice: since the supreme legislator taught by this symbol that one must abstain from voracity (which is its characteristic), from delicacies and the enticements of gluttony (since swine's flesh is sweet): and also that one must avoid the impudence and impurity depicted by this animal, Prov. 11, 22. 2 Pet. 2, 22.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Animalium mundorum & immundorum di- stinctio.

vers. 1. AD MOSEN ET AARON.

QUia horum cognitio spectat tum ad Magistra- tum quoad civilem usum, tum ad Sacerdotem quoad sacrificia v. 3. QVOD HABET DIVISAM VNGVLAM) Multa ho- rum ab Ægyptiis translata causas habent naturales, ex bono vel malo alimento, ut notat Maimonides. Chærem. apud Porphyrium de Sacerdotibus Ægyptiis: ἰχθύων τε ἀπείχοντο πάντων καὶ τετραπόδων ὅσα μώνυχα ἢ πολυσχιδῆ ἢ μὴ κε- ρασφόρα. Πτηνῶν δὲ ὅσα σαρκοφάγα. Ubi quod ait non cor- nigera, idem valet quod solidungula. Nam solidas habent ungulas, quæ non sunt cornigera, teste Plinio libro 11. qui & addit: solida ungula, & bicorne nullum. Idem notat coitum tota die esse tantum iis omnibus quibus solida ungula: & foe- tus minus numerosos: libro 10. Porphyrius vetitum ait Ju- dæis vesci τί τῶν μωνύχων ζώων. Ab Ægyptiis translata sacrificia ad Ebræos, falsum est. Neq; probari potest, causas in iisdem naturales Deum spectasse boni malive alimenti.
