Maimonidæ aliisque Rabbinis cæcis in hisce Do- ctoribus, fides debetur nulla. Præter liberrimam Supremi Legislatoris voluntatem, si nulla adferri queat causa, sapientiæ divinæ hoc relinquendum, quæ nihil temere egit, etsi non assequamur institu- torum ejus rationem. Ita cum v. 7. suis esu abstinere jussi sunt Ebræi, ad Ægyptios se recepit noster, & ad Tacitum vel Plutarchum potius, quod abundantia alimenti, quia caro suilla suavissima, scabiem faciat, atque ita in aliis. Quæ omnia si e Pandectis divinis probarentur, fidem merito impetrarent. E Philo- sophis & Historicis extraneis de rationibus divino- rum institutorum disserere, est in re seria, imo divi- na ludere. Non negarim in concessione animan- tium ad esum omnia apposite ad naturam sancita, & discreta esse, siquidem ea edi vetentur, quæ vel na- tura sua venenosa sunt, uti reptilia, vel immundis ci- bis vescuntur, ut porci & upupæ, vespertiliones, noctuæ & bubones &c. dubium tamen non est, causam po- tissimam in plerisque fuisse Symbolican, ut divisio- ne ungulæ notaretur discretio boni & mali, rumi- natione applicatio boni cogniti ad operationem, (August. in Ps. 47. ruminatio designat iteratam co- gnitionem, seu meditationem ejus, quod auditum. Conf. Iren. l. 5. c. 11.) immunda animalia significa- rent immunditiem vitiorum, quorum symbola sunt, ut corporali munditiei assuefactus populus ab im- mundiciis idololatrarum, eorumque immundis sa- crificiis avocaretur, & ad mundiciem mentis exci- tatus assurgeret. Recte Pelargus in h. l. p. 104. im- mundiciem singulorum non a noxa & insalubritate cibi tantum æstimandam: sed quia vel aliquas in cor- porum membris vel in quærendo victu notas prætule- runt, quæ vitiorum admonerent homines. Providentiæ & curæ Dei specialis argumentum monstrari singula- re erga piorum tum corpora, tum animos: illa, ne quovis & promiscuo esu facile lædantur: hos, ut puri- tati studeant & ubi abstinendum ab iis audiunt, quæ divisis carent ungulis, quæ non ruminant, quæ ex ra- pto vivunt, quæ sæva sunt atque immania: a rapina, avaritia, libidine, immanitate & intemperantia ad justitiam, moderationem, clementiam, sobrietatem & fidem vocari se statuant. Quo de Novatianus lib. de cibis Judaic. c. 3. in operibus Tertull. p. mihi 653. In animalibus mores depinguntur humani & actus & voluntates Mundi, si ruminent, i. e. in ore semper ha- beant quasi cibum præcepta divina: ungulam findunt, si firmo gradu innocentiæ, justitiæ, omnisque virtutis vita itinera conficiant. Eorum enim, quæ in duas ungulas pedem dividunt, robustus semper incessus, dum lubricum partis alterius ungulæ firmamento fulcitur, & in vestigiis soliditate retinetur. Sic qui neutrum faciunt, immundi sunt: quorum nec in virtutibus fir- mus ingressus est, nec divinorum præceptorum in ore ullius ruminationis teritur cibus: nam & qui alterum faciunt, nec ipsi mundi, dum sunt ex altero debiles, nec in utroq; perfecti. Hi autem sunt aut utrumq; facien- tes, ut fideles, qui mundi: aut alterum, ut Judæi & hæ- retici, qui sunt inquinati: aut neutrum, ut Ethnici, qui sunt consequenter immundi. Ita in animalibus per legem quasi quoddam humanæ vitæ speculum constitu- tum est, in quo imagines sanctionum considerent, ut plus vitiosa quæque hominibus contra naturam com- missa damnentur, dum etiam naturaliter in pecoribus constituta culpantur. Qui paulo etiam post in spe- cie de nonnullorum Symbolica significatione ita disserit; Quid enim vult sibi lex, cum dicit, Camelum non manducabitis, nisi quoniam de exemplo animalis vitam damnat enervem & criminibus tortuosam. Aut cum suem cibo prohibet assumi, reprehendit uti- que cænosam & luteam & gaudentem vitiorum sor- dibus vitam, bonum suum non in animi generositate, sed in sola carne ponentem: aut cum leporem, accusat reformatos in fæminam viros. Quis mustelæ corpus sibi cibum faciat? Sed furta reprehendit. Quis lacertam? sed odit vitæ incertam varietatem. Quis stellionem? Sed maculas execratur, prædam de aliena morte quæ- rentes. Quis corvum? Sed versutas execratur volunta- tes. Quis passerem? cum eum interdicit, intempe- rantiam coarguit: quando noctuam, odit lucifugas ve- ritatis. Quando cygnum, cervicis altæ superbos: quan- do charadrium, garrulam nimis linguæ intemperan- tiam: quando vespertilionem, quærentes tenebras no- ctis simul atque erroris. Hæc Novatianus. Quæ Isidorus repetit. Theodoreto c. 11. in Lev. de volucribus di- cit, illas esse immundas, quæ sunt rapaces, quæ cadave- ribus pascuntur & gaudent tenebris: quo erudiamur, ut abstineamus ab illis & similibus. Quod ad rumi- nantia animalia, ungulam divisam habentia Cyrillus c. 9. contr. Julian. ruminare docet prudentiæ esse Symbolum, pedem dividere, qui in actione bonum a malo discernunt. Plura de hisce vid. apud Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Pædagog. Origenem in h. l. Cyrillum l. 14. de adoratione. Euseb. 8. de Præpar. Evang. Augustin. contr. Adim. c. 15. Nec præter rem dicitur, inten- to- disse Deum etiam in ipso ciborum usu exercitium populi sui tum obedientiae in honorem Dei ita juben- tis, tum temperantiae. Accesserunt, inquit iterum Novatianus c. 4. & aliae causae, quibus multa a Judaeis ciborum genera tollerentur, non ut illa damnarentur, sed ut isti coercerentur servituri uni DEO: quia ad hoc assumtos frugalitas decebat, & gula temperantia, quae semper religioni deprehenditur esse vicina, imo (ut ita dixerim) consanguinea potius atq; cognata. Sancti- tati enim inimica est luxuria. Quae antiquita- tis heluo neglexisse hic non debuerat. Sed ille philosophatur tantum de diaeta & causis naturali- bus, aut sacris Aegyptiacis e Scriptoribus exoticis: parum attendens, quod Novatianus hic monuit c. 2. In primis illud collocandum, legem spiritualem esse, quam si spiritualem negant, utique BLASPHE- MANT. Si devitantes blasphemiam spiritualem con- fitentur, spiritualiter legant. Divina enim divine sunt accipienda & sancta sancte utiq; asserenda. Caeterum culpa gravis inuritur, si terrestris & humana sacris & spiritualibus literis doctrina praestatur, quod ut ne fiat, cavendum est. Haec Novatianus, quae non immerito Grotio opponimus. Dignus est totus Novatiani tra- ctatus, qui hic expendatur. Scripsit & Tertullianus librum de animalibus mundis & immundis, sed qui nunc desideratur. De piscibus Theodoretes qu. 11. in Lev. ita: Qui squamis & pinnis praediti sunt, hi a- quas supernatant. Qui vero non sunt ejusmodi, deorsum & humi voluntantur (fundo adhaerentes.) Mundi sunt igitur, qui animam ad terrena non appellunt, sed pinnis fidei praediti ornamento virtutis ambiuntur: Quod e- nim in piscibus est squama, hoc apud homines est fides. Conf. & Origenes hom. 7. in Lev. Specialiora qui desiderat, Pelargum praeter alios adire poterit Commentario in h. l. De Porcis Plutarchum si audia- mus, Judaeos arguit in Sympos. l. 4, 4. 5. quod absti- neant iisdem, non quidem fastidientes, sed colentes magis sues, ut arandi magistras. Sed injuriam facit ipsis: siquidem summus legislator hoc symbolo do- cuerit, voracitate (quae suum est) deliciis & gulaee irri- tamentis (quum suavis sit caro suilla) abstinendum esse: vitandam etiam impudentiam ac impuri- tatem hoc animali depictam, Prov. 11, 22. 2. Pet. 2, 22.

## 11:3
Verse same. AND CHEWETH THE CUD) The fat of ruminants is healthy, according to Pliny book 28, ch. 9. Hence the ruminal sacrifices among the Coruncani, as Pliny records in book 8.

Latin:

Vers. eod. ET RVMINAT) Ruminantium saevum salu- bre, Plinio teste libro 28. c. 9. hinc ruminales hostiae apud Coruncanum, memorante Plinio libro 8.

## 11:4
Verse 4. AS THE CAMEL) The camel has a cloven foot with a small division. Pliny book 11.

The camel is a symbol of stupidity, Matt. 14, 24; the hare of fear, Prov. 30, 6; the rabbit of frauds, Esth. 16, 5; the pig of filth and impurity, 2 Pet. 2, 22. See Rabanus on Deut. 14, 7. The camel is contrary to wisdom, the hare as a timid creature is contrary to fortitude; the rock-badger, as rapacious, is contrary to justice; the pig is contrary to chastity. Compare also Hesychius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SICVT CAMELVS) Camelo bisulcus pes di- scrimine exiguo. Plin. lib. 11.

Camelus est symbolum stuporis Matth. 14, 24. lepus timoris Prov. 30, 6. cuniculus fraudum Esth. 16, 5. porcus sordium & impuritatis 2. Pet. 2, 22. Vid. Rabanus in Deut. 14, 7. Camelus contrarius est sapien- tiae, lepus ut timidus fortitudini contrarius est; choero- gryllus, ut rapax, justitiae, porcus castitati contrarius est. Conf. & Hesychius in h. l.

## 11:7
Verse 7. SWINE) The Egyptians also abstained from this, as Herodotus mentions. Among Anaxandrides, someone giving a reason why he refuses to serve with the Egyptians: Οὐκ ἐσθίεις ὗειν᾽ ἐγὼ δὲ γ' ἥδομαι Μάλισα τύτοις. Tacitus thinks the cause is that the animal is prone to mange. I think it is truer that in those places much swine's flesh is eaten, which the comic poet Plato and the prince Gaius in Philo said was most sweet, and that the abundance of food causes mange. For Plutarch also, inquiring into the cause of this abstinence, says that for those who drink swine's milk, ἐξανθεῖν τὰ σώματα λέπραν καὶ ψω- ρικὰς τραχύτητας. Moreover, there is mention of this Jewish custom, besides those I have mentioned, in Juvenal and Macrobius, and Porphyry, On Abstinence, in the second book at the end and in the fourth.

They give reasons for this ceremonial law, partly physical—not only fear of leprosy, about which Plutarch and Manetho in Aelian 10, 16, and R. Bechai speak—but also the filthiness of pigs, because the law prohibits all uncleanness, as Maimonides holds; and partly moral. Thus Bochart in Hierozoicon from Clement of Alexandria and

Lactantius. He taught that impure men are to be avoided, and that one must abstain from sins and impurities.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SVS) Et hac Aegyptii abstinebant, ut meminit Herodotus. Apud Anaxandridem quidam rationem reddens cur Aegyptiorum commilitium detrectet: Οὐκ ἐσθίεις ὗειν᾽ ἐγὼ δὲ γ' ἥδομαι Μάλισα τύτοις. Causam putat Tacitus quod scabie obnoxium id animal. Ve- rius puto, quod illis in locis multa comesta caro suilla, quam suavissimam esse dixit Plato comicus, & Cajus princeps apud Philonem, abundantia alimenti scabiem faciat. Nam & Plutarchus in causam hujus abstinentiae inquirens, ait iis qui lac suillum bibunt, ἐξανθεῖν τὰ σώματα λέπραν καὶ ψω- ρικὰς τραχύτητας. Moris autem hujus Judaici, praeter eos quos dixi, mentio apud Juvenalem & Macrobium, & Por- phyrium de Abstinentia secundo in fine & quarto.

Causas hujus legis ceremonialis reddunt par- tim Physicas, non tantum metum a lepra, de quo Plutarch. & Manetho in AElian. 10, 16. & R. Bechai. Sed etiam sorditiem porcorum, quia lex omnem immunditiem prohibet, ut habet Maimon. partim morales. Ita Bochard. in Hierozoic. e Clem. Alex. &

Lactant. Docuit vitandos impuros homines, & à peccatis atque immunditiis abstinendum.

## 11:9
Verse 9. EVERYTHING THAT HAS FINS AND SCALES, BOTH IN THE SEA AND IN THE RIVERS AND PONDS, YOU SHALL EAT) Fish that were not scaly, so that they might not be polluted, [was] the law of Numa according to Pliny, book 32, chapter 2. In Festus also, among the goods which it is permitted to offer, [are] fish, which also have scales, except for the parrotfish. Porphyry on the Jews: ἀπηγόρευτο ὑὸς ἐųίειν ἢ ἰχθύων τῶν ἀφολιδώτων ἃ σελάχια καλοῦσιν ἕλληνες. Yet I learn from the same Pliny, book 31, verse 8, that the Jews made garum from fish lacking scales.

Fish lacking fins or scales, such as eels, are too moist, viscous, and unhealthy; for small scales and fins are indicators of dryness. Gregory, book 5, Morals, chapter 6. Fish that have fins are accustomed to making leaps above the water. Therefore, those who are fortified by the rigor of virtue and do not admit the appetite for secular occupation have scales: but those who seek the secret of contemplation, and float above the waves of secular cares, and who know how to ascend to heavenly things by the leaps of the mind, have fins. B. Luther on Deuteronomy 14 understands by fins the doctrine of faith, which rules and drives hearts in this world by the word of God, and by scales the adornments or fruits of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 9. OMNE QVOD HABET PINNVLAS ET SQVAMMAS TAM IN MARI QVAM IN FLUMI- NIBUS ET STAGNIS COMEDETIS) Pisces qui squam- mosi non essent, ne pollucerentur, lex Numæ apud Plinium lib. 32. c. 2. In Festo quoque inter merces quas pollucere li- ceat, pisces, quibus & squamma, præter scarum. Porphyrius de Judæis: ἀπηγόρευτο ὑὸς ἐųίειν ἢ ἰχθύων τῶν ἀφολιδώτων ἃ σελάχια καλοῦσιν ἕλληνες. Judæos tamen garum fecisse ex piscibus squamma carentibus disco ex eodem Plinio lib. 31. versu 8.

Pisces carentes pinnulis vel squamis, ut anguil- læ, nimis humidi, viscosi & insalubres sunt, squamu- læ enim & pinnæ siccitatis sunt indices. Gregor. l. 5. moral. c. 6. Pisces qui pinnulas habent, saltus super aquas dare solent. Sqammas ergo habent, qui rigore virtutis muniti secularis occupationis appetitum non admittunt: Pinnulas vero, qui secretum contempla- tionis petunt, & undis secularium curarum superna- tant: quique mentis saltibus ad superna conscendere sciunt. B. Luther. in Deuter. 14. per pinnas intelli- git doctrinam fidei, quæ verbo Dei regit & agit corda in hoc mundo, per sqamas ornatus seu fru- ctus fidei.

## 11:13
Verse 13. THESE ARE THEY WHICH OF THE BIRDS YOU SHALL NOT EAT) All forbidden birds are both birds of prey and devourers of other birds.

Of the forbidden birds, some are birds of prey, thieves, predators; 2. some live on carcasses, they are carnivores; 3. some dwell in unclean places, they feed on serpents; 4. some are voracious, given to insatiable gluttony; 5. some love the night and solitude, fleeing the light and the sight of men; 6. some are high-flying, etc. The birds of prey warn that God hates rapacity; the carnivores, cruelty and the oppression of the poor. Those that delight in unclean places [warn] that impurity is to be avoided. The light-shunning ones [warn] that the works of darkness are to be fled: the high-flying ones [warn] that we ought not to be wise above what is necessary. Radolphus in this place observes the vices which were signified by each one: The eagle denotes the pride of the powerful, Ezekiel 17, verse 17. Griffins signify the cruelty of the powerful. The osprey, which is not of such strength, but is nevertheless a predator, signifies those who are violent toward the poor. The kite signifies the snares of the powerful. The vulture, haunting camps and carcasses, signifies those who are, as it were, the vultures of princes and courts, for the purpose of despoiling others with their help. Ravens are those who feed on the deaths of others. The ostrich, which is similar to the heron in feathers but not in flight, Job 39:16, denotes hypocrites who harm others under the guise of religion. The owl, seeing sharply at night, denotes those who are wise in evil. The gull, being amphibious, signifies soldiers who, as if dry and celibate on land, as being lacking a wife, are nevertheless tossed about by the waters and currents of wandering luxury. The hawk, a bird of prey, which when it has been tamed serves its owners for plunder and robbery, signifies servants who plunder the poor at the nod of their masters. The eagle-owl signifies those who, filled with the foulest crimes, flee the light and men. The cormorant signifies those who are absorbed by the pleasures of the flesh. The ibis signifies those who are unjust and cruel toward themselves, that is, their bodies and souls. The swan signifies those who boast of mere clothes and earthly affluence. The pelican signifies insatiable avarice. The porphyrio signifies the contumacious, who receive nothing unless it is steeped in the water of their own will and delight. The stork signifies stupidity for grasping heavenly things. The plover, a garrulous bird, signifies loquacity: the hoopoe, simulating a groan in its song among the dung, signifies the sadness of the world, for into this, and into the filth and sorrows of the world, delights and joy end. The bat signifies secular knowledge, wise only in natural and earthly things. They are also forbidden for the sake of health: for example, those whose flesh is very hard and difficult to digest, or too moist, concerning which see Thomas, book 2, question 102, article 6. Birds are forbidden to the Jews, some being birds of prey, which are of excessive dryness, and some being aquatic birds because of an excess of humidity. But those that are more temperate are permitted to them, such as hens, partridges, and others of this kind. Furthermore, because the Hebrews and interpreters vary greatly in explaining the names of the animals and birds, if anyone wishes to survey that variety ὡς ἐν συνόψει (as in a summary), let him see the synopsis of the Critics and Interpreters of Matthew Poole on this chapter. We supersede those works, since no certainty can be had concerning most of them, and through the variety of these opinions, where there is no definition, we are rendered more alone and more uncertain.

Latin:

Vers. 13. HÆC SUNT QVÆ DE AVIBUS COME- DERE NON DEBETIS) Omnes aves vetitæ & rapaces sunt & aliarum avium voratrices.

Ex prohibitis avibus quædam rapaces sunt, fu- races, prædatrices, 2. quædam cadaveribus vičti- tant, sunt carnivoræ, 3. quædam habitant in locis immundis, serpentibus vescuntur, 4. quædam vo- races replendæ ingluviei deditæ, 5. quædam noctem & solitudinem amant fugientes lucem & conspectum hominum, 6. quædam altivolæ &c. Rapaces mo- nent, Deum odio habere rapacitatem, carnivoræ crudelitatem, & pauperum oppressionem. Quæ locis immundis delectantur, immunditiem vitan- dam esse. Lucifugæ opera tenebrarum esse fugien- da: altivolæ non debere nos nimis altum sapere. Radolphus in h. l. observat vitia, quæ significata fuerint per singulas: Aquila notat potentium su- perbiam Ezech. 17. v. 17. Gryphes significant poten- tium crudelitatem. Halicetus, qui non est tantis vi- ribus, sed tamen prædo, significat violentos in pau- peres. Milvus significat potentium insidias. Vul- tur castra & cadavera affectans significat eos, qui quasi vultures Principum & aularum sunt asseclæ, ad hoc, ut eorum ope alios exspolient. Corvi sunt, qui mortibus pascuntur alienis. Struthio, qui he- rodio similis est pennis, sed non volatu Job. 39, 16. notathypocritas, qui sub religionis specie aliis no- cent. Noctua noctu acutum cernens, notat sa- pientes in malo. Larus amphibius significat mili- tes, qui in terra quasi aridi & cælibes, utpote uxo- re carentes, vagæ tamen luxuriæ aquis & fluxu vo- lutantur. Accipiter rapax, qui ubi mansuefactus est, possessoribus ad prædas & rapinas servit, signi- ficat famulos ad dominorum nutum pauperes de- prædantes. Bubo significat eos, qui fœdissimis sce- leribus oppleti lucem & homines fugiunt. Mergu- lus significat eos, qui voluptatibus carnis absorben- tur. Ibis significat eos, qui in se, id est, corpora & animas suas, iniqui & crudeles sunt. Cygnus signifi- cat eos, qui de solis vestibus & terrena affluentia gloriantur. Onocrotalus significat avaritiã inex- plebilem. Porphyrio significat contumaces, qui ni- hil nisi tinctum aqua propriæ voluntatis & delecta- tionis suscipiunt. Ciconia significat stoliditatem ad capienda cœlestia. Charadrius avis garrula signifi- cat loquacitatem: Upupa gemitum in cantu inter stercora simulans significat tristitiam seculi, in hanc enim atque in sordes & dolores seculi deliciæ & læ- titia desinunt. Vespertilio significat secularem sci- entiam, sola naturalia & terrena sapientem. Pro- hibitæ sunt etiam sanitatis causa : v. g. quarum ca- ro dura admodum & concoctu difficilis est, aut nimis humida, de quo Thoen. lib. 2. quæst. 102. art. 6. Prohibita sunt Judæis aves, quædam rapaces, quæ sunt nimiæ siccitatis, & quædam aves aquaticæ pro- pter excessum humiditatis. Concessæ autem sunt eis magis temperatæ, sicut gallinæ, perdices & alia hu- jusmodi. Cæterum quia variant admodum Ebræi & Interpp. in nominibus animantium, & avium ex- plicandis, si quis illam varietatem ὡς ἐν συνόψει lu- strare velit, videat synopsin Criticorum ac Interpp. Matth. Poli in hoc caput. Nos illa opera super- sedemus, siquidem de plerisque nulla haberi possit certitudo, & per varietatem istarum sententiarum, ubi nulla est definitio magis solum magisque incer- ti reddamur.

## 11:17
Verse 17. AND THE IBIS) So the Greeks. But the Rabbis wish it to be the bird which is called 'Chus' in the Paduan field. Interpreters vary in a wonderful way in these names, so that there are few about whose meaning they agree.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET IBIN) Sic Græci. At Rabbini eam avem esse volunt quæ in agro Patavino Chus dicitur. Mirum in modum in his nominibus variant interpretes, ita ut pauca sint de quorum significatu conveniat.

## 11:34
Verse 34. IF WATER HAS BEEN POURED UPON IT) Namely, which has been touched by unclean food: for that water is unclean, and makes other things unclean.

Latin:

Vers. 34. SI FUSA FUERIT SUPER EUM AQUA) Nempe quæ immundo cibo contacta fuerit: Illa enim aqua immunda sit, & immunda facit alia.

## 11:35
Verse 35. WHETHER OVENS OR POT-STANDS SHALL BE DESTROYED) Better, others: the oven and the hearth shall be torn down. The interpretation concludes from the greater to the lesser that earthen vessels into which an unclean animal has fallen are to be broken, as that in which there is less loss.

Latin:

Vers. 35. SIVE CLIBANI SIVE CHYTROPODES DE- STRUENTUR) Melius alii: furnus & focus diruentur. A majori ad minus collegit interpretatio frangenda vasa ficti- lia in quæ ceciderit animal immundum, ut in quo minus sit damni.

## 11:36
BUT FOUNTAINS AND CISTERNS AND EVERY GATHERING OF WATERS SHALL BE CLEAN) Because of the scarcity of those things in those places.

Latin:

FONTES VERO ET CISTERNÆ ET OMNIS A- QVARUM CONGREGATIO MUNDA ERIT) Ob ea- rum rerum in illis locis infrequentiam.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. The purification of a woman in childbed.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. Puerperæ purificatio.

## 12:2
Verse 2. HAVING RECEIVED SEED. Here it is tacitly implied that a woman would also give birth without seed, as Galen, lib. 7 de A. C. V. c. 2, and Helvicus in the Giessen Disputations believe.

SHE SHALL BE UNCLEAN) This also has a natural cause in those places, from whence it reached other nations as well. Euripides mentions it in Iphigenia in Tauris. There was also mention of it in the books of Chrysippus.

THE DAYS OF HER MENSTRUAL SEPARATION] That is, in such a way that she also makes others unclean by her touch.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SUSCEPTO SEMINE. HIc innui tacite mulierem etiam parituram si- ne semine Galat. l. 7. de A. C. V. c. 2. & Helvi- cius in Disput. Gieffens. censent.

IMMUNDA ERIT) Habet & hoc causam naturalem il- lis in locis, unde ad alias etiam gentes pervenit. Meminit Euripides Iphigenia in Tauris. Fuit & in Chrysippi libris ejus mentio.

JUSTA DIES SEPARATIONIS MENSTRUÆ] Id est, ita ut & alios contactu suo impuret.

## 12:4
Verse 4. THIRTY-THREE DAYS] Censorinus adds a few days: A pregnant woman does not go into the temple before the fortieth day. He adds the reason: And after birth, most women who have given birth are heavier, and sometimes do not contain their blood. During these days after those first seven, the woman in childbed only abstains from the sanctuary.

Latin:

Vers. 4. TRIGINTA TRIBUS DIEBUS] Censorinus aliquot dies adjicit: Prægnans ante diem quadragesimum non prodit in fanum. Causam addit: Et post partum pleræque fœ- tæ graviores sunt, nec sanguinem interdum continent. His die- bus post septem illos primos, puerpera tantum a sanctuario abstinet.

## 12:5
Verse 5. SIXTY-SIX DAYS) The number of days is doubled for her who has been delivered of a child of the female sex. Not without cause: for those who bear females are less warm, and therefore they are also purged more slowly. The same is the reason why fetuses of the female gender are perfected more slowly in the womb, which is noted by Aristotle in History of Animals 6, 22 and 7, 3. Whence also Hippocrates, περὶ φύσιος παιδιό. For the cleansing happens to women after childbirth for the most part, in the case of a girl in forty-two days: thus the longest time is complete. It would be without danger even in twenty-five days if she were cleansed. But in the case of a boy, the cleansing happens in thirty days. Thus the longest time is complete. It would be without danger even in twenty days if she were cleansed. Soon he repeats the same: history, the cleansing of the lochia, that in the case of a girl it happens in forty-two days, but in the case of a boy in thirty days, the longest time.

He again draws the cause solely from Physics, having dismissed the genuine one, which is most proper and mystical to this Levitical and Ceremonial constitution. But the principal cause is from the uncleanness of sins, which he implies

Hiero-Psaltes Ps. 51, v. 7. Behold, I was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. And therefore Pelargus rightly: This chapter pertains to the consideration of original sin, which in the birth of all and everyone so exerts itself, that it not only condemns every carnally born and not spiritually reborn person to eternal damnation and death, but also renders the parents themselves guilty before God. Hence also the reason why the double time of the woman's impurity, when she had brought forth a female child, was prescribed, can be drawn out solidly: That which is brought from the physical sciences is not solid enough, as can be gathered from those things which Cornelius à Lapide philosophizes about these matters in this place. But from the Scriptures the matter is manifest, namely that through this sex the sin, which is propagated through generation, was introduced: Concerning which Rupertus says: Rightly does both the written law and the natural law burden the female more than the male, because clearly in the approach of sin, through which death entered into the world, the female stood closer to that reptilian vessel of the Devil, from whence he hissed the poison of our impurity, than the man. For not the woman through the man, but the man through the woman was polluted by the lie of the Devil. See 1 Tim. 2:14.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SEXAGINTA SEX DIEBUS) Duplicatur nu- merus dierum in ea, quæ fœminini sexus partu soluta est. Non sine causa : nam minus calent αἱ θηλύτοκοι, eoque & tardius purgantur. Eadem causa est, cur in utero fœtus fœminini ge- neris perficiantur serius, quod notatum Aristoteli de Histo- ria animantium 6, 22. & 7, 3. Unde & Hippoc. περὶ φύσιος παιδιό. καὶ γὰρ ἡ κάθαρσις γίνεται τῇσι γυναιξὶ μετὰ τὸν τόκον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ, ἐπὶ μὲν τῇ κούρῃ ἡμέρῃσι τεσσαράκοντα καὶ δύο: ἔτως ἡ χρονιωτάτη τελείη. ἀκίνδυνος δ' ἂν εἴη, καὶ ἐν εἴκοσι, καὶ πέντε ἡμέρῃσιν εἰ καθαίροιτο. ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ κούρῳ ἡ κάθαρσις γίνεται ἡμέρῃσι τριάκοντα. ὕτως ἡ χρονιωτάτη τελείη. ἀκίνδυνος δ' ἂν εἴη καὶ ἐν εἴκοσιν ἡμέρῃσιν εἰ καθαίροιτο. Mox idem repetit: ἱστο- ρίη, ἡ κάθαρσις τῶν λοχίων, ὅτι ἐπὶ μὲν τῇ κούρῃ γίνεται ἐν τεσ- σαράκοντα καὶ δυοῖν ἡμέρῃσιν, ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ κούρῳ ἐν τριάκοντα ἡμέρῃσιν ἡ χρονιωτάτη.

Causam iterum è Physica solum eruit, missa genuina, huic constitutioni Leviticæ & Ceremo- niali maxime propria & mystica. Sed præcipua causa est ab immundicie peccatorum, quam innuit

Hiero-Psaltes Pf. 51. v. 7. Ecce in iniquitatibus con- ceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Id- eoque recte Pelargus: Pertinet hoc caput ad peccati originalis considerationem, quod in omnium & singu- lorum ortu ita se exerit, ut non modo omnem carna- liter natum & non spiritualiter renatum damnationi, mortique addicat aeterne, sed parentes etiam ipsos co- ram Deo reos statuat. Hinc etiam causa, cur duplum impuritatis mulieris, cum enixa sexus foeminei par- tum fuerat, præscriptum tempus, depromi potest solida: Quæ è Physicis adfertur, solida fatis non est, uti ex iis, quæ de his philosophatur Cornelius à Lapide h. l. colligere est. Sed è Scripturis res manifesta est, quod nempe per hunc sexum pecca- tum, quod per generationem propagatur, inve- ctum sit: Quo de Rupertus: Recte tam scripta lex, quam naturalis foeminam plus, quam masculum gra- vat, quia videlicet in accessu peccati, per quod mors intravit in mundum, reptili illi vasculo Diaboli, unde venenum immunditiæ nostræ principium ille sibilavit, propior foemina stetit, quam Vir. Nam non per vi- rum mulier, sed per mulierem Vir mendacio Diaboli pollutus. Vid. 1. Timoth. 2, 14.

## 12:6
Verse 6. SHE SHALL BRING A LAMB. This offering was made partly for gratitude for fertility, preserved health, and a happy birth: partly for the expiation of menstrual impurity: and partly also for the sake of a vow for the happy upbringing of the offspring.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DEFERT AGNUM. Fiebat hæc oblatio tum ob gratitudinem pro fœ- cunditate, conservata valetudine & felici partu: tum ob expiationem impuritatis menstruæ: tum eti- am voti causa pro felici partus educatione prolis.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. The leprosy of men and garments.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. Lepra hominum & vestimentorum.

## 13:2
Verse 2. A MAN IN WHOSE SKIN AND FLESH THERE HAS ARISEN A DIFFERENT COLOR) Josephus discourses excellently on these laws against Apion in the first book, where he refutes the fables of the Egyptians about Moses being driven out because of leprosy: 'For he forbade those who have leprosy either to remain in the city or to dwell in a village, but to walk alone with torn garments; and he does not consider the one who touches them or is under the same roof to be clean. And indeed, even if the disease is healed and he recovers his natural state, he enjoins certain purifications, washings in spring waters, and the shaving of all hair, and commands that after performing many and various sacrifices, then he may enter into the holy city.' The same writer has similar things in his Antiquities of the Jews, book 3, chapter 5. However, the Hebrews believe that the leprosy of houses and garments was found only in Judea.

Leprosy warned of the spiritual contagion of the mind, the will, and all the affections, and of the anger of God against sins, who, as Augustine says, often strikes leprosy with leprosy, that is, the harm with punishment, and of His grace, bestowed upon us in Christ, by whose power all things, even incurable diseases, and indeed the spiritual plague itself, are healed. Therefore, so many lepers were healed by Christ in the days of his flesh, so that we might be warned that He came into the world for the sake of curing the spiritual leprosy with which we are all infected: Since neither from leprosy, nor from any disease could there be restoration, unless Christ had taken away the cause of the disease, sin. Matt. 8:17; Luke 17:12. The state and habit of the leper was miserable: 1. The garments had to be torn. 2. The head uncovered. 3. The mouth veiled. 4. The dwelling remote. 5. The sign of the disease public. By which qualities the condition of those laboring under spiritual leprosy is depicted: whose garments are torn and loose, because they lack the garment of righteousness, and as for the head, with the girdle of truth, they are naked of the gifts of the Holy Spirit and full of all confusion (Ezek. 16:7); they never have a mouth open for prayers and the celebration of the divine name, and their breath is foul (Rom. 5:14); furthermore, their habitation is separated, because they are excluded from the kingdom of God (Gal. 5:21). Finally, their voice is a perpetual cry concerning the torment of the soul (Luke 16:24). Nor was the leprosy of garments without its significance: For it warned (1) that the virus of the ancient serpent had been so powerful that it infected sentient and insentient things alike. (2) That he who is abandoned by the grace of the Holy Spirit is, not only in mind but even in his very clothing, impure and cursed (Deut. 28). (3) That there is such care for our kind by God that He is concerned even about garments, how they might be cleansed and freed from the stain. (4.) If a garment, warp, or woof is infected with leprosy, it had to be burned with fire: how much more must man be burned with eternal fire, unless he is expiated by the Blood of Christ. Leprosy was nowhere so abominable, as Josephus testifies, as in Judea, in which alone the balsam that cures leprosy and wounds was born: In the Church alone is the abomination of sin recognized, and medicine against sin is had. The leprosy of a house denotes that all impurity, perverse doctrine, and the conversation of the wicked must be fled (1 Cor. 6:17; Jer. 31:9; Tit. 3:10). Cf. Jerome, Vol. 9, quest. 39.

Latin:

Vers. 2. HOMO IN CUJUS CUTE ET CARNE OR- TUS FUIT DIVERSUS COLOR) Præclare de his legibus disserit Josephus contra Appionem primo, ubi refutat Ægy- ptiorum fabulas de Mose ob lepram exacto: τοῖς γὰρ λε- πρῶσιν ἀπείρηκε, μήτε μένειν ἐν τῇ πόλει, μητ' ἐν κώμῃ κατοι- κεῖν, ἀλλὰ μόνος περιπατεῖν κατεσχισμένυς τὰ ἱμάτια· καὶ τὸν ἁψάμενον αὐτῶν ἢ ὁμώροφον γενόμενον, ὐ καθαρὸν ἡγεῖται. καὶ μὴν κἂν θεραπευθῇ τὸ νόσημα, καὶ τὴν αὐτῷ φύσιν ἀπολάβη προσέρηκέ τινας ἁγνείας, καθαρμᾶς πηγαίων ὑδάτων λυτροῖς καὶ ξυρήσεις πάσης τριχὸς, πολλὰς τε κελεύει, μὴν παντοίας ἐπιτελέ- σαντα θυσίας, τότε παρελθεῖν εἰς τὴν ἱερὰν πόλιν. Similia habet idem Scriptor Historiæ antiquæ libr. 3. cap. 5. Censent autem Hebræi lepram domuum & vestium repertam in sola Judæa.

LEpra monebat de Spirituali contagione men- tis, voluntatis, omnium affectuum, de ira DEI adversus peccata, qui Augustino dicente, lepram ple- rumque percutit lepra, hoc est, noxam pœna, & de ipsius gratia, nobis in Christo præstita, cujus vir- tute omnes, incurabiles etiam morbi, nec non ipsa lues spiritualis sanantur. Ideo tot leprosi à Chri- sto sanati sunt in diebus carnis ejus, ut spiritualis lepræ, qua infecti sumus omnes, curandæ causa ipsum in mundum venisse, moneremur: Siquidem nec à lepra, nec ab ullo morbo daretur restitutio, nisi causam morbi, peccatum, sustulisset Christus Matth. 8. v. 17. Luc. 17. v. 12. Status & habitus le- prosi fuit miserabilis, 1. vestium oportuit esse dif- solutum, 2. Caput detectum. 3. Os velatum. 4. Do- micilium remotum, 5. indicium morbi publicum. Quibus qualitatibus pingitur conditio lepra spiri- tuali laborantium: quorum vestimenta lacera, & dissoluta, quia carent veste justitiæ, & quod ad caput, cinctu balthei veritatis, nudi sunt à donis S. S. & omni confusione pleni Ezech. 16, 7, os nun- quam habent ad preces ac celebrationem nominis divini apertum, fœtidusque illorum halitus est Rom. 5. v. 14. habitatio insuper sejuncta, quia ex- clufi sunt à regno DEI Galat. 5. v. 21. Vox denique perpetua & clamor de animi cruciatu Luc. 16. v. 24. Nec fignificatione sua caruit lepra vestium: Monebat enim (1.) ita potens fuisse antiqui serpen- tis virus, ut sensata, & insensibilia pariter infece- rit. (2.) Eum, qui S. S. derelinquatur gratia, non animo duntaxat, sed vestitu etiam ipso impurum & maledictum esse Deuter. 28. (3.) Tantarn generis nostri curam esse DEO, ut etiam de vestibus so- licitus sit, quomodo mundari & à labe liberari queant. (4.) Si vestis, stamen, subtegmen lepra in- fectum, igne fuit exurendum: quanto magis ho- mo igne æterno exurendus, nisi expietur Christi Sanguine. Lepra nuspiam tam abominabilis, te- ste Josepho, ut in Judæa, in qua sola nascebatur bal- samus lepram curans & vulnera: In sola Ecclesia agnoscitur abominatio peccati, habeturque medi- cina contra peccatum. Lepra domus notat omnem impuritatem, doctrinam perversam, conversatio- nem malorum fugiendam esse 1. Cor. 6, 17. Jer. 31, 9. Tit. 3, 10. Conf. Hieron. Tom. 9. quæst. 39.

## 13:3
Verse 3. AND THE HAIR HAS TURNED WHITE) For they were bound to leave the hair in the ulcer, so that the increase or decrease of the evil could be discerned.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET PILOS IN ALBUM MUTATOS COLO- REM) Tenebantur enim pilos in ulcere relinquere, ut digno- sci posset incrementum aut decrementum mali.

## 13:4-6
Verse 4, 6. OUTSIDE THE CAMP) And after the land was possessed, outside the cities, which had succeeded to the place of the camps.

According to Menochius and Cornelius, this is another species of leprosy, which is considered to be the cleanest, that is, the least contagious scabies. Lyranus says that leprosy is spoken of equivocally, because it appears as such. To others, to flourish is to spread itself, or to creep, Mercerus, Chaldean, Arabic, Ainsworth.

Latin:

Vers. 4. 6. EXTRA CASTRA) Et post terram possessam, extra urbes, quæ in castrorum locum successerant.

Juxta Menoch. & Cornelium hæc alia species le- præ, quæ mundissima dicitur habenda, hoc est minime contagiosa scabies. Lyran. æquivoce le- pram dici ait, quod talis videtur. Aliis florere est diffundere sese, vel serpere, Mercero, Chald. Arab. Ainsworth.

## 13:9
Verse 9. BECAUSE IT IS A SCAB) Theodotion: ekbrasma. Jerome on Nahum 2: ekbrasmos, an ebullition, which is said more significantly in Greek: since ekbrasmos is used in such matters when that which was hidden within breaks out onto the surface: whence also the pimples which are born on the lips after sickness are called ekbrasmata. These pimples are such that they do not harm by spreading, which leprosy does.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVIA SCABIES EST) Theodotion ἔκβρασμα. Hieronymus ad Nahum. 2. ἔκβρασμός ebullitio quæ fignifican- tius in Græco dicitur: fiquidem ἔκβρασμός in istiusmodi rebus ponitur, cum quod latebat intrinsecus, erumpit in faciem: unde papulæ quoque, quæ post ægrotationem nascuntur in labiis, vo- cantur ἐκβράσματα. Hæ papulæ tales sunt, ut transitione non noceant, quod facit Lepra.

## 13:12
Verse 12. BUT IF THE LEPROSY SPREADS ABROAD IN THE SKIN) Leprosy that does not spread is more stubborn, just as narrow rivers are deeper.

Latin:

Vers. 12. SIN AUTEM EFFLORUERIT DISCUR- RENS LEPRA IN CUTE) Lepra non diffuens pertina- cior, ut flumina areta sunt profundiora.

## 13:51
IF THE LEPROSY IS PERSISTENT] LXX. ἔμμονος. Others from the ancient Samaritan φιλόλεσκος. Thus, that is, מאור is dominant among the Arabs.

Valesius denies that the leprosy about which Moses speaks in this chapter is the same as the leprosy of other regions: he maintains it is not one disease, but various defects of the skin, vitiligo, scabies, elephantiasis, achor, alopecia, or ophiasis. Their leprosy was in the skin, in garments, and in houses, and was curable: The leprosy of others was in the flesh, not in garments, and incurable: That was not so much a natural disease as a divine plague: which Theodoret says was sent by special providence to the sinning Jews. Therefore, the leprosy pertained to the Priest, not to the physician, inasmuch as the Priest had to judge it, not as a disease, but as a legal uncleanness. And the parts were to be anointed with blood and oil, Levit. 14, v. 14, so that it might be established that leprosy is cured only by divine power, not by medical art: which teaches that leprosy is relieved by bloodletting: but here blood was to be added, as Abarbenel noted. Oil was added, by which it might be taught that after punishments have been given and repentance performed, the oil of intellect and wisdom would never be lacking to those members, as Muis observed from the same Abarbenel and Isaac Karo.

Latin:

SI LEPRA PERSEVERANS EST] LXX. ἔμμονος. Alii ex vetere Samaritano φιλόλεσκος. ita مارت id est, מאור est dominans Arabibus.

Lepram, de qua in hoc capite Moses, negat Valesius eandem esse cum lepra aliarum regionum: vult non unum esse morbum, sed varia vitia cutis, vitiliginem, scabiem, elephantiasin, achorem, alo- peciam, vel ophiasin. Illorum lepra in cute, in ve- stibus & ædibus, & curabilis fuit: Aliorum lepra in carne, non in vestibus, & incurabilis: Illa non tam morbus fuit naturalis quam plaga divina: quam peculiari providentia Judæis peccantibus imissam ait Theodorei. Ideo ad Sacerdotem pertinebat lepra, non ad medicum, utpote quam dijudicare debebat Sacerdos, non ut morbum, sed ut immunditiem legalem. Et inungendæ erant partes sanguine & oleo Levit. 14. v. 14. ut constaret, lepram divinitus tantum curari, non arte medica : quæ docet lepram sanguinis missione levari : at hic sanguis adden- dus erat, ut notavit Abarbenel. Oleum addebatur, quo doceretur, post datas pœnas actamque pœni- tentiam membris illis oleum intellectus & sapien- tiæ nunquam defuturum, ut ex eodem Abarb. & Isaaco Karo observavit Muis.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. The expiation of leprosy; as also concerning the leprosy of a house.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. Lepræ expiatio; ut & de lepræ domus.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. CEDAR WOOD AND SCARLET AND HYSSOP) Leprosy is a punishment for pride, as appears in Miriam, Moses' sister, Gehazi, and Uzziah. The cedar signifies this pride: the scarlet, or crimson, sin; and the hyssop the opposite virtue, ταπεινόφροσύνην (humility). For hyssop grows on the ground and has a purgative power, as Porphyry teaches in the fourth book of On Abstinence, that it was believed by the Egyptians according to Chaeremon.

Latin:

Vers. 4. LIGNVM CEDRINVM VERMICVLVM- QVE ET HYSSOPVM) Lepra superbiæ pœna, ut apparet in Mariamme Mosis sorore, Giezi, Ozia. Hanc superbiam cedrus significat : vermiculus, sive coccinum, peccatum, & hyssopus oppositam virtutem ταπεινόφροσύνην. Humi enim na- scitur, & vim habet purgatricem hyssopus, ut Ægyptiis credi- tum ex Chæremone docet Porphyrius de Abstinentia quarto.

## 14:7
Vers. 7. SEVEN TIMES) Which number makes for perfection. See also below 51.

The mystical significance of the rites of expiation is not to be neglected: 1 Cor. 10, 11. For the merit of Christ's passion was foreshadowed: whose two natures, according to Hesychius, the two birds denoted—the immortal one, that which was let go free; the mortal one, that which was to be sacrificed. The sprinkler [signified] the word of the Gospel, the scarlet the passion of Christ, the cedar wood his ἀφθαρσίαν (incorruptibility), the sprinkling the act of ministry by which we are sprinkled with the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1, 2; Psalm 51, 9. The sevenfold iteration signified our perfection in Christ; the living waters, the waters of baptism tinctured and reddened with the blood of Christ; the shaving of the hair, the mortification of the flesh; the new garments, the newness of life, Eph. 4, 24. Cf. Cyril, book 8 on Leviticus; Theodoret, question 19.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SEPTIES) Qui numerus perfectioni facer. Vide & infra 51.

Significatio rituum expiationis mystica non ne- gligenda : 1. Cor. 10, 11. Adumbratum enim passio- nis Christi meritum : cujus naturas duas secundum Hesychium duæ aves, immortalem ea, quæ libera di- missa, mortalem, quæ immolanda erat, notabant. Aspergillum verbum Evangelii, Coccinum passionem Christi, lignum cedrinum ἀφθαρσίαν ejus, aspersio actum ministerii, quo sanguine Christi aspergimur 1. Petr. 1, 2. Psalm. 51, 9. Septenaria iteratio perfe- ctionem nostram in Christo, aquæ viventes, aquas baptismi sanguine Christi tinctas, & purpuratas, rasura pilorum mortificationem carnis, vestes no- væ, novitatem vitæ Ephes. 4, 24. figurarunt. Conf. Cyrill. l. 8. in Levit. Theodor. quæst. 19.

## 14:14
Vers. 14. UPON THE TIP OF THE EAR AND THE THUMB OF THE HAND.

This signified that both the ear and the hand are sanctified by the blood of Christ, and that he is now again free to hear and do divine things, whereas before he could not approach sacred places. Cf. what is said on chapter 13, v. 46.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SUPER EXTREMUM AURICU- LÆ ET POLLICEM MANUS.

Hoc significabat sanguine Christi sanctificari & aurem, & manum, eumque jam iterum liberum ef- se ad audienda & facienda divina, cum antea non poterat loca sacra adire. Conf. quæ ad cap. 13. v. 46.

## 14:17
Vers. 17. AND UPON THE BLOOD.

The Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Arabic [translate] 'upon the place of the blood,' where the blood is placed, as is explained in verse 28. Menochius [says] 'upon the blood,' as if the ears and thumbs were acted upon. Others [say] 'beyond or besides the blood of the sacrifice,' Pagninus, Sam. q.d. Those parts are to be anointed not only with blood, but also with oil.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET SUPER SANGUINEM.

Septuag. Syrus & Arabs super locum sanguinis, ubi sanguis positus est, ut exponitur vers. 28. Menochius super sanguinem quasi actæ sunt aures, & pollices. Alii ultra vel præter sanguinem hostiæ Pagn. Sam. q. d. Partes illæ non solum sanguine, sed etiam oleo ungentur.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. The expiation of a flux of seed and of a menstruous woman.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. Seminisflui & menstruosæ expiatio.

## 15:2
Vers. 2. A MAN WHO SUFFERS A FLUX OF SEED) Whose semen flows perpetually, he is unclean while that infirmity remains. There are, however, three kinds of it expressed here in the Hebrew, by way of a drop, by way of saliva, and by way of a thicker coagulum, which are to the Rabbis טפה ריר עב. It should be known, however, that in the regions of Syria and neighboring places, τὴν γονόρῥοιαν (gonorrhea) has no less a contagious harm than τὰ ἔμμηνα (menstruation), whence these things are constrained by laws which do not depart far from the laws of leprosy. Even beds, seats, and tables which they have touched are held to be impure.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VIR QVI PATITVR FLVXVM SEMINIS) Cujus genitura perpetuo effluit, immundus est, dum manet id vitium. Sunt autem hic in Hebræo expressa tria ejus gene- ra, per modum stillæ, per modum salivæ, per crassius coagu- lum, quæ Rabbinis טפה ריר עב. Sciendum autem in Syriæ locis & vicinis non minus τὴν γονόρῥοιαν quam τὰ ἔμ- μηνα habere aliquid contagio nocens, unde ista legibus, quæ a lepræ legibus non longe abeunt, constringuntur. Etiam le- cti, sedes, mensæ, quas contigerint, pro impuris habentur.

## 15:16
Vers. 16. A MAN FROM WHOM SEED OF COPULATION GOES OUT) that is, erupts. He is unclean until evening. That is called קרי (keri), a species of which is ὀνειρωγμός (nocturnal emission). Chaeremon on the Egyptian priests: 'But if it should ever happen that one has a nocturnal emission, they immediately cleansed the body with a bath.'

Latin:

Vers. 16. VIR DE QVO EGREDITVR SEMEN COI- TVS) id est erumpit. Is ad vesperam immundus est. Id di- citur קרי, cujus species ὀνειρωγμός. Chæremon de Ægyptio- rum Sacerdotibus : εἰ δέ ποτε συμβαίη κὰι ὀνειρώττειν, παρα- χρῆμα ἀπεκάθαιρον λουτρῷ τὸ σῶμα.

## 15:18
Vers. 18. THE WOMAN WITH WHOM HE SHALL HAVE LAIN) Namely, on that day, he to whom such a thing happens, which must be repeated from the preceding. But it is the custom for Greek and Roman women to take a bath after any kind of Venus, to which Josephus also wishes to draw this law. Theano was more correct, who said that a woman is immediately clean after the intercourse of her husband.

Regarding these laws, Theodoret rightly says in Quest. 20 on Leviticus: Through natural things He instructed us about the vices of the mind, and from them He taught us how atrocious these are, and with how much zeal they are to be shunned. So that, namely, we may recognize the foulness of our stain, repress the pride of the heart, beware of spiritual uncleanness, and contemplate the punishments established for the impure, Rom. 1:24, 28; 1 Cor. 6:10; Gal. 5:21; Apoc. 22:15; that we may possess our vessel with sanctification and honor, 1 Thess. 4:4. Let us allow ourselves to be cleansed by the seed of the divine word and the precious blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:23; 1 John 1:7. Let us keep our spirit, and soul, and body blameless for the coming of Christ, 1 Thess. 5:23. Procopius says, in Christ we obtain purity, but water is required. Indeed, the coming of Christ is predicted to us in this place, while it is pronounced that the man is unclean until the evening.

Latin:

Vers. 18. MULIER CVM QVA COIERIT) Nempe eo die is cui tale quid evenit, quod repetendum ex præcedenti- bus. At Græcis & Romanis foeminis mos aquam sumere post qualemcunque Venerem, quo & hanc legem vult trahere Josephus. Rectius Theano quæ foeminam a maritu sui con- gressu statim puram esse dicebat.

De legibus hisce recte Theodoretius quæst. 20. in Levit. Per naturalia nos instruxit de vitiis animi atq; ex illis nos docuit, hæc quam sint atrocia, quanto stu- dio fugienda. Ut nempe labis nostræ fœditatem agnoscamus, superbiam cordis reprimamus, spiri- tualem immunditiem caveamus, poenas impuris constitutas intueamur, Rom. 1, 24. 28. 1, Cor. 6, 10. Galat. 5, 21. Apocal. 22, 15. vas nostrum cum sancti- ficatione, & honore possideamus, 1. Theffal. 4, 4. Semine verbi divini ac pretioso sanguine Christi nos mundari sinamus 1. Petr. 1, 23. 1. Joh. 1, 7. Spiri- tum, & animam & corpus inculpate in adventum Christi servemus 1. Thessal. 5, 23. Procopius, in Christo, inquit, consequimur puritatem, sed aqua re- quiritur. Christi vero adventus nobis predicitur hoc loco, dum pronunciatur vir esse immundus usque ad vesperam.

## 15:24
Vers. 24. UNCLEAN.

The same, chapter 18, v. 19, with a more serious penalty, if, namely, within that seven-day period, the flow having now ceased, or even through imprudence, he has lain with her: but he who has done this knowingly and prudently is to be put to death. Levit. 20:18.

Latin:

Vers. 24. IMMUNDUS.

Idem cap. 18. v. 19. fine graviori poena, si scil. in- tra illud septiduum jam cessante fluxu, vel etiam per imprudentiam coierit: at qui sciens prudens hoc fe- cerit, occidendus. Levit. 20, 18.

## 15:31
Vers. 31. YOU SHALL TEACH SO THAT THEY MAY AVOID UNCLEANNESS.

In Hebrew: You shall separate from their uncleannesses. The Hiphil form intends the meaning: i.e., you shall take care that they are separated as much as possible from all uncleanness.

Latin:

Vers. 31. DOCEBITIS UT CAVEANT IM- MUNDITIEM.

In Ebr. Separabitis ab immunditiis suis. Forma Hiphil significatum intendit: q. d. curabitis ut quam maxime separentur ab omni immunditia.

## 16:1 Argument
PART III. OF LEVITICUS, CONCERNING ACTIONS. CHAPTER XVI. The day of the great atonement.

Latin:

PARS III. LEVITICI, DE ACTI- ONIBVS. CAPUT XVI. Dies expiationis magnæ.

## 16:2
Vers. 2. UPON THE ORACLE.

THAT IS, upon the propitiatory. The oracle is taken from that part of the ark from which the voice of the speaking GOD was heard, which was the entire golden plate and the cover of the ark. The propitiatory is described in Exodus as being of the purest gold, holding two cubits and a half in length, and a cubit and a half in breadth, with the Cherubim and with the promise of GOD that He would speak from there. The LXX call it there, and Josephus besides, ἐπίθεμα, that is, a thing placed upon, namely, upon the ark, of which it was the cover, which force the word כפרת Chapporeth has, from כפר Caphar, which generally means to cover and to overlay, and to shut; but in Piel, Chipper means to atone, and to purge, and as it were to hide uncleanness and error. From the said Greek words, it is also named ἱλαστήριον, which sounds as propitiatory to the Latins. Philo joins both names, ἐπίθεμα τῆς κιβωτῦ, the cover of the ark, and ἱλαστήριον, because it was τῆς ἵλεω δυνάμεως τὸ ἐπίθεμα τῆς κιβωτῦ, the cover of the propitiation of the ark itself. There, on both sides, were the Cherubim with wings expanded, upon which God, sitting, was said to deliver oracles. The propitiatory was immediately and very closely placed upon the ark, touching and covering it itself, for this is what the name of a covering or lid denotes, and otherwise the ark would have been open, which was neither fitting in itself, and it would have been exposed to dust, and it would have been necessary for the raised plate to be supported by small columns or long hinges, since the small and slender wings of the Cherubim would not suffice for this support, of which, however, there is no mention of such supports. But so that the ark might be considered the footstool of GOD, it was enough if it were conceived as sitting upon the wings of the Cherubim, with which they, with their own bodies also, covered the propitiatory, which has the nature of a footstool, with one standing to the South, the other to the North, which was the width of the ark; but the sides of the length, the eastern and western, were veiled by their wings expanded toward each other, with the face of one turned toward the other toward the propitiatory, just as when two men look at each other, and hold hands: for thus, I say, the two Cherubim having their faces turned toward each other, toward the mercy seat, with wing expanded, touched the expanded wing of the other on both sides. Therefore, when the name of the oracle is spoken of concerning the mercy seat, it is not taken precisely for the said golden table, but insofar as it included the Cherubim with their wings, who were also entirely golden, like it, and produced from the same by hammering, and therefore called 'produced' [productiles], and being made from the mercy seat itself, or from the table, they were considered to be one thing in the category of art with the mercy seat and the table, that is, one entire throne, of which the wings resting on the table were as it were the seat, the table as it were the footstool, and God would speak from the wings of the Cherubim, and consequently from the mercy seat, as from an oracle, because the mercy seat, or the often-named table, was the base and support of the Cherubim, and therefore of the throne of God, and the footstool of his feet. In the temple of Solomon, the Cherubim which he made were not turned toward each other, but were contiguous and lateral, and both had their faces turned toward the East, their backs toward the West, nor did they surround the ark or the mercy seat, but they expanded their wings across the entire breadth of the Holy of Holies, although one with the extremity of his one wing touched the southern wall, and the other, contiguous to him, with the extremity of his also touched the opposite northern one. Solomon made the same, besides these Cherubim, others at the altar of incense similar to them, which would veil the altar, just as the aforementioned ones in the said manner veiled the ark. And thus, with ours which Moses made, there were triple Cherubim in the temple. But Paul speaks of ours when he writes that they were overshadowing the mercy seat. Finally, the Mosaic Cherubim were entirely golden; the others were of gilded olive wood.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SUPER ORACULUM.

ID est, super propitiatorium. De illa parte arcæ sumitur oraculum, è qua vox loquentis DEI au- diebatur, quæ fuit tabula aurea tota arcæque oper- culum. Describitur in Exodo propitiatorium de auro mundissimo, duos cubitos, & dimidium te- nens longitudinis, & cubitum, ac semissem latitu- dinis, cum Cherubim & cum promisso DEI, quod inde loqueretur. Vocant ibi LXX. prætereaque Josephus, ἐπίθεμα, id est, suppositum nempe super arcam, cujus erat operculum, quam vim habet כפרת Chapporeth, à כפר Caphar quod valet ge- neraliter tegere & operire, ac occludere; in Piel ve- ro Chipper expiare, atque purgare, & quasi immun- ditiem atque erratum abscondere. A dictis Græ- cis nominatur quoque ἱλαστήριον quod Latinis pro- pitiatorium sonat. Philo utrumque nomen con- jungit ἐπίθεμα τῆς κιβωτῦ operculum arcæ, & ἱλαστήριον, quia esset τῆς ἵλεω δυνάμεως τὸ ἐπίθε- μα τῆς κιβωτῦ propitiationis arcæ ipsius opercu- lum. Ibi ex utraque parte Cherubim alis erant expanfis, quibus insidens Deus, dicebatur oracu- la edere. Erat propitiatorium immediate ac pro- xime impositum arcæ, tangens tegensque ipsam, hoc enim denotat nomen tegumenti, sive operculi, & alioquin aperta fuisset arca, quod nec decebat per se, & pulveribus exposita esset, & elevatam tabulam oportuisset columellis aut cardinibus lon- gis fulciri, cum ad hoc alæ Cherubim parvæ graci- lesque non sufficerent, de quibus tamen fulcris nulla mentio. Ut autem arca censeretur scabellum pedum DEI, satis erat si conciperetur sedens super alis Cherubim, quibus illi cum suismet etiam cor- poribus, tegebant propitiatorium, quod habet rationem scabelli, uno consistente ad Meridiem, altero ad Septentrionem, quæ erat latitudo arcæ; latera vero longitudinis orientale, & occidentale, per suas alas expansas ad invicem velantibus, facie alterius ad alterum obversa versus propitiatorium, perinde, ut cum duo homines aspiciunt sese invi- cem, tenentque manibus: sic enim, inquam, duo- rum Cherubim facies habentium versas ad invi- cem, versus propitiatorium, ala expansa, alterius alam expansam contigebat ab utroque latere. Igi- tur cum de propitiatorio nomen oraculi dicitur, non accipitur præcise pro dicta tabula aurea, sed quatenus complectebatur Cherubim cum alis suis, qui toti etiam aurei, sicut illa, & ex eodem produ- cti per malleationem, ideoque vocati productiles, factique ex propitiatorio ipso, sive ex tabula, unum quid censebantur esse in genere artis cum propitia- torio, ac tabula, id est, thronus unus, ac integer, cujus quasi sedes essent alæ insistentes tabulæ, ta- bula veluti scabellum, & Deus loqueretur ex alis Cherubim, & consequenter ex propitiatorio, tan- quam ex oraculo, quia propitiatorium, sive sæpe nominata tabula, erat basis atque sustentaculum Cherubim, ac proinde throni Dei, ac scabellum pedum ejus. In templo Salomonis Cherubim, quos fecit, non erant obversi sibi, sed contigui, & laterales, faciesque versas habebant ambo ad Orientem, tergum ad Occidentem, nec arcam pro- pitiatoriumve ambibant, sed per latitudinem omnem Sancti Sanctorum expandebant alas, licet unus extremitate alæ unius suæ parietem meridio- nalem tangeret, alter ei contiguus, extremitate etiam suæ oppositum septentrionalem. Fecit idem Salomon, præter istos Cherubim, alios ad altare thymiamatis similes, qui velarent altare, quemad- modum jam dicti dicto modo velabant arcam. At- que ita cum nostris, quos fecit Moses, triplices erant Cherubim in templo. De nostris autem lo- quitur Paulus, cum scribit, quod erant obumbran- tia propitiatorium. Denique Mosaici Cherubim erant aurei toti; alii ex ligno olivarum deaurato.

## 16:4
Verse 4. HE SHALL BE CLOTHED WITH A LINEN TUNIC] Thus the priests of Ammon according to Silius: Their bodies are veiled in linen. The snow-white color is proper for sacred rites among all nations. Plato, Laws 12. Cicero, Laws 2. It is to be noted, however, that the High Priest on the Day of Atonement did not have all the ornaments customary to him, but only such as the other priests had, as if in mourning.

Latin:

Vers. 4. TVNICA LINEA VESTIETVR] Sic Ammo- nis Sacerdotes apud Silium: Velantur corpora lino. Niveus color sacris proprius apud gentes omnes. Plato de le- gibus 12. Cicero de legibus 2. Notandum autem summum Sa- cerdotem in die Expiationis non omnia habuisse solita sibi ornamenta, sed tantum qualia habebant Sacerdotes alii, tan- quam in mœrore.

## 16:9
Verse 9. FOR THE SCAPEGOAT] From the Greek ἀποπομπαίῳ, which the LXX have, and from there the Greek Christians often. The word is composed of עז, which signifies a he-goat or she-goat, and אזל which is to go away, whence others translate it ἀπερχόμενον, LXX Leviticus 19:26. διεσσαλμένον εἰς ἄφεσιν. Aquila: ἀπολελυμένον εἰς τὴν ἄρημον.

Mercer, Fagius, Vatablus, and Menochius prove this. It does not please Bochart, in Hierozoicon I. 65. Others take the word Azazel as the proper name of a mountain, such as R. Solomon, Aben-Ezra, and Kimchi according to Fagius and Mercer, as also the Arabs in Bochart, so that the sense might be, the other lot for Hazazel, that is, for a mountain, or for the goat, to be sent into the mountain Hazazel. But this gloss is forced, and there is no mention of such a mountain anywhere in the descriptions of regions or in the Holy Scriptures. Whence Bochart prefers to derive the word from the Arabic 'Azala', to remove or separate: so that the goat kept may be said to be for Azazel πρὸς ἀναχωρήσεις, that is, so that it may be led into a remote and separated place of the desert, verse 22. To us, the common notion is approved, whence the Greeks also said ἄφετον ζῶον, that is, a dismissed, free animal, and ἀποπομπαῖον not as a driver away of evils, as the Greeks called their gods ἀποπομπαίους, ἀποτροπαίους, ἀλεξικάκους, but because it was sent out into the desert. But concerning the signification of this scapegoat, Grotius continues thus:

This goat signified here that those sins expiated by the victim do not return into the sight of God. Josephus calls it ἀποτροπιασμὸν. But the Hebrews understand this of sins to which neither the penalty of death nor of excision is added. For these, even if they escape the judges, are not expiated except through heavy afflictions. But what the divine writer to the Hebrews says in 10:2, that a conscience of sin remained in the Hebrews after that sacrifice was performed, understand that they had often relapsed into the same or similar sins, which fragility the law does not take away, promising earthly things, but the word and Spirit of the Gospel does.

An overly meager explanation of the principal sacrifice. As to the signification, it is certain that by the goat ἀποπομπαῖον, as the LXX render the Hebrew word as if composed of עֵז (goat) and אָזַל (to go away), and as indicated by Aquila's ἀπολελυμένον εἰς τὴν ἄρημον, it is signified that expiated sins do not return into the sight of God; but it is passed over in silence, which is the principal thing here in the figure of the goat, that the expiation was made through the substitution of the goat in the place of the people, and the imputation of sins made to the goat, and also the payment for them in place of the people, by which the Satisfaction of the Messiah was foreshadowed, as one who had to be substituted in place of the human race, to take the sin of the whole world upon himself, and to pay the penalty for it in our stead, as we have both from the very Mosaic description of this sacrifice, and from the Prophetic declaration in Isaiah chapter 53, and especially from the explanation in the New Testament, John 1:29 and Hebrews 9, etc. Which we have asserted elsewhere against Socinus: indeed, since they were asserted by Grotius himself in his Defense of the Catholic Faith, they should not have been wrapped in such deep silence here, unless he had wished to sail in favor of the Socinians. Grotius argued there in chapter 10, page 123, that the death of a beast was substituted for the death of a man, having adduced three passages. First, from Deuteronomy 21, where it is ordained that if a murderer is not found, the people are to be expiated by a slaughtered beast, and the word of expiation in verse 8 is explained: Expiate your people, O God, and do not impute innocent blood: because otherwise the land could not be expiated from shed blood, except by the blood of the shedder, Numbers 35:27. Second, from Leviticus 17:11: The soul of every flesh is in the blood: I have indeed destined it for you on the altar, to make expiation for your souls. For it is the blood that makes expiation for the soul. Item thirdly from Leviticus 10:17, where the victim is said to bear the iniquities of the guilty, and by that phrase the payment of the penalty is brought in, Grotius taught. He concludes in the cited place: From these things which we have said, it is now clear how the victims for sin in the Old Covenant expiated sins, namely by moving God to remit the carnal penalty, and that through a certain satisfaction. But what the types performed carnally, this ὁ ἀντίτυπος (antitype) Christ performs spiritually, what the types did in certain transgressions only, this Christ does in all, namely by moving God to remit the spiritual penalty, and that through a most perfect satisfaction. For there is always more, not less, in the thing designated by the type than in the type, as reason shows. These and many other things formerly in the cited book Grotius. But now, when he is occupied in the proper seat of this doctrine, in the types and figures, described primarily in Leviticus, throughout the whole book, he did not make even a word of mention of that typical adumbration, let alone of the antitype, namely the satisfaction of Christ, whether in explaining this anniversary sacrifice, or in declaring the mystical signification of others. He sticks only to natural or moral things. Regarding this sublime antitype, he is more mute, as it is said, than a fish.

Furthermore, as to the sins for which expiation was made by this solemn sacrifice, he acquiesces to the tradition of the more recent Hebrews, that it was made only for those to which the penalty of death or ἐξελοθρεύσεως (extermination) was added, which, even if they escape the judges, he says are not expiated except through heavy miseries; but where is there an exception in the Scriptures? Since, however, the law excepts nothing, it is not for us to restrict it. ALL the iniquities of the children of Israel were reckoned to the goat and imposed upon it, AND ALL THEIR TRANSGRESSIONS, and their sins, and the goat bore ALL THEIR iniquities into a solitary land, Levit. 16:21. Therefore all iniquities, all transgressions and sins were expiated through him. What is more evident than this universality? For the universal particle is used absolutely without restriction, and sins are distributed into species, and all species of sins are thus comprehended. The Greeks recount ἀνομίας, ἀδικίας, ἁμαρτίας here, says Grotius on v. 21. The last of these, חטאת, seems to signify those which are not done deliberately: the other two, those which are done deliberately: the former, that is, עונת, against prohibiting laws, the latter, פשעים, against commanding ones; but all sins are comprehended in these species. For they are either done deliberately or not deliberately: either against prohibiting laws, or against commanding ones. Grotius indeed adds a restriction, but in such a way, however, that those for which a penalty, such as we have mentioned, is expressly appointed, are not comprehended. But that has no foundation in this text; indeed, it openly contradicts it, because ALL (which universal note Grotius omitted) INIQUITIES, ALL TRANSGRESSIONS, ALL SINS, are said here to be expiated, not just some. Nor is it true that secret sins had to be expiated through grievous hardships. For as many Israelites as applied to themselves by true faith the expiation of the Messiah, shadowed forth in this type, obtained the remission of sins: therefore they had no need of expiation through hardships. Nor are hardships sent to penitents for the expiation of sins. They are not τιμωρίαι (punishments), but δοκιμασίαι (trials) of the faithful.

Thirdly, Grotius supposes that a carnal penalty was remitted by the intervention of expiation through sacrifices, which we have already heard him openly asserting, and that therefore the pardon of only some sins was obtained by them: But this is false. For those expiations availed for the remission of sins, which is repeated very often in Leviticus. Moreover, when God remits sins, He pardons not only the carnal penalty, but especially the eternal one. They were true expiations, as they are very frequently called. But when sins are expiated, every penalty is remitted. Although, indeed, the sacrifices did not expiate by their own power, yet this effect is not to be denied to them, insofar as they had a relation to the antitype of the expiatory Christ, by whose power they provided the expiation of sins when they were offered with true faith. The goat for Azazel carried all sins into the desert, so that it might be signified that those sins expiated by the victim do not return into the sight of God, as Grotius holds here. But those things which are so expiated that they do not return into the sight of God, it must be that not their carnal, but especially their eternal punishment has been remitted. It is also false that the laws given in sacrifices were for the pardoning of forensic punishments in a political judgment. For they did not work expiation in the forum of the earth, but in the forum of heaven. Grotius thought that violent death, which transgressors had deserved, and which God in the Hebrew Republic ordinarily exacted through Judges, since it was a theocracy, just as a King is otherwise accustomed to exact punishments through Judges, had been pardoned in certain transgressions, an expiation having been made through sacrifices, as can be seen from c. 10 de Satisfact. p. 121. But sacrifices were ordained for obtaining the remission of sins in the divine forum, not indeed in a political judgment. For the pardoning of eternal punishment, not indeed of temporal. That will be shown by no testimony or document from the Scriptures, that temporal forensic punishment to be inflicted by Judges was remitted through the offering of sacrifices. Just as the Gospel does not abolish the Polity, so neither do the sacrifices, which were appendices of the Gospel in the Old Testament, or a certain living Evangelical sermon.

Therefore, what is said fourthly in Heb. 10:2, that a conscience of sin remained after that expiation was performed, Grotius indeed rightly refers to the Hebrews who had often relapsed into the same or similar sins, but he does not satisfy the Apostolic intention: which is to demonstrate the necessity of the sacrifice of Christ, that the ancient sacrifices could not by themselves take away sins, but expiated solely by the virtue of the sacrifice of Christ, and prefigured it. For they were repeated more often for this reason, because they served to designate the abolition of sins to be done once, if indeed it were useful that the commemoration of sins be repeated again and again, and that the fame of a huge benefit to be expected by all should increase through continued sacrifices. If the Israelites had been freed from the conscience of sins by those Levitical sacrifices by themselves, there would certainly have been no need for their repetition, just as the sacrifice of Christ is not repeated, which, having been performed once, purged consciences from all sin.

But that Grotius thinks fifthly that the law could not take away that frailty, lest the Hebrews relapse into the same or similar sins, because it promised earthly things, again betrays a Socinian hypothesis, as if the promise of eternal goods were sufficient for us to avoid sins, or for that frailty to be taken away through it, and it had no place in that law. But how innumerable are those to whom it is certainly known about eternal life, from divine promises, who do not abstain from sins? nay, not even the faithful, who not only have certain knowledge of the future life, but have also been confirmed concerning its inheritance through the earnest of the Spirit, are so exempt from this frailty that they do not stumble in many things, James 3:2, of which indeed the Israelites were not so destitute, that through those very sacrifices the Evangelical promises were, as it were, placed before their eyes, and exhibited as in a type: and even in that scapegoat they could have confirmed their faith, and conceived hope of grace and life through the promises of the remission of sins, and the expiation made by these. In explaining which figure the Ancients devoted effort: Justin Martyr in Dialog. with Trypho, p. 291. The scapegoat was a designation of the coming of Christ, when the Elders and Priests, laying their hands upon him and punishing him with death, sent him forth as a scapegoat and one averting miseries; he was made an offering for all sinners wishing to repent through penance, who are devoted to the faith of Jesus. Cyril against Julian, book 9, Vol. 6, page 311 in my edition. Two goats are taken, not as if there were two Christs, or two Sons according to some, but rather because it was necessary that the same one be sacrificed for us, and indeed die according to the flesh; but live according to the Spirit. For that one, most worthy of all, died for all, and the death of Christ was the dissolution of death. And afterwards: if the blood of bulls and goats does not suffice to wash away sin, why does the Lawgiver say that he is to make atonement for the sins from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, and from their injustices? Did he therefore err in his words? Far from it. What then was the meaning? It is indeed manifest and clear to all that the truth shines forth not in the figures, but in the things signified by them. For Christ is that immaculate sacrifice, that pure victim, by whose death for us according to the flesh, we have become scapegoats, that is, we have departed from death and corruption. By his blood, however, we have been redeemed, and freed from all uncleanness, justified freely by his grace, as it is written, and have obtained the grace by which the memory of sins has been blotted out through the mercy of God. Theodoret, question 22 on Leviticus. Let no one think it absurd that the goats prefigure the passion of Christ, since John himself called him the lamb, but let him consider rather that he offered himself not only for the just, but also for sinners. Hesychius is more prolix in his Commentary on this passage. He warns that there is much here that the intention of the teacher at the same time and it is necessary for the listener, so that he may not depart from that which is right, because the mysteries which the law now expounds are very great, and some stumble in them, being ignorant of the power of the words. And after a great deal, fol. 101. Therefore, the goat signifies that Christ is present with all. For just as he was sacrificed in the first instance through the flesh; so now he is said to be living on account of his divinity. But because he is one and impassible and passible, the Priest necessarily lays hands upon the living one, so that by the laying on of hands it may be shown that the living, impassible, and immortal Word of God took upon himself this sacrifice for us in the flesh. Rightly, therefore, did the Priest pronounce the iniquities and injustices and sins upon him. This is he of whom Isaiah spoke: Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? Calling the Son the arm of the Lord, consubstantial with the Father, concerning whom he also added the things that follow: He himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows. But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. Thus he openly bore our sins and injustices and iniquities upon himself: And therefore, according to the LXX, he says, he shall lay them upon the head of the living goat: for this is a figure of the fact that Christ also permitted a crown of thorns to be placed upon his head, because sins are accustomed to be received in thorns. Hesychius also applies this, which is said, he shall do this once in the year, because it had to be offered once to exhaust the sins of many: and provoking to the testimony of Christ in John 5: If you believed Moses, you would surely have believed me also, for he wrote of me: he adds this: But what and where (he wrote) Christ did not add, because whatever things are mystical, whatever things are high, whatever things are divine, these were spoken of Christ by Moses in shadows and figures and images. If Grotius had considered this, he would not have neglected to search for Christ in Moses.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CAPRO EMISSARIO] Ex Græco ἀποπομπαίῳ, quod LXX. habent, & inde Christiani Græci sæpe. Vox composita ex עז, quod caprum capramve significat, & אזל quod est abire, unde alii vertere ἀπερχόμενον, LXX. Levitici 19, 26. διεσσαλμένον εἰς ἄφεσιν. Aquila: ἀπολελυμένον εἰς τὴν ἔρημον.

Probant id Mercerus, Fagius, Vatablus, Me- nochius. Non placet Bochardo, in Hieroz. I. 65. Alii pro nomine proprio montis habent vocem A- zazel, utpote R. Salomo, Aben-Ezr. & Kimchi apud Fagium, & Mercerum, ut & Arabes in Bo- chardo, ut sensus sit, sortem alteram pro Haza- zel, id est, monte, vel pro Capro, in montem Hazazel mittendo. Sed hæc glossa coacta est, nec uspiam talis montis mentio in descriptionibus re- gionum, vel in S. literis facta. Unde Bochardus mavult deducere vocem ex Arabico Azala remo- vere, vel separare: ut sic hircus servatus dicatur ad Azazel πρὸς ἀναχωρήσεις, id est, ut in locum deser- ti remotum & separatum deducatur vers. 22. No- bis probatur communis notio, unde Græci ἄφε- τον ζῶον etiam dixerunt, id est, dimissum, liberum animal, & ἀποπομπαῖον non ceu malorum depul- sorem, ut Græci Deos suos ἀποπομπαίους, ἀπο- τροπαίους, ἀλεξικάκους dixere, sed quod emittere- tur in desertum. De significatione autem hujus hirci emissarii ita pergit Grotius:

Significabat hîc hircus peccata illa per victimam expiata non redire in conspectum Dei. ἀποτροπιασμὸν id vocat Jo- sephus. Id autem intelligunt Hebræi de peccatis, quibus ne- que mortis neque ἐξολοθρεύσεως pœna est addita. Hæc enim, etiamsi Judices lateant, non expiari, nisi per ærumnas graves. Quod autem dicit divinus ad Hebræos Scriptor 10. 2. mansis- se in Ebræis post sacrum illud peractum conscientiam peccati, intellige, relapsos illos sæpe in eadem aut paria peccata, quam fragilitatem lex non aufert, terrena pollicens, sed verbum & Spiritus Evangelii.

Nimis jejuna præcipui sacrificii explicatio. Quod primum ad significationem, certum est, per hircum ἀποπομπαῖον, ut vocem Ebræam reddunt LXX. quasi compositam ex עֵז hircus & אָזַל abi- re, Aquilæ ἀπολελυμένον εἰς τὴν ἔρημον indicatum, peccata expiata non redire in conspectum Dei, sed tacetur, quod hîc præcipuum est in figura hirci, quod expiatio facta fuerit per surrogationem hirci in locum populi, & imputationem peccatorum hirco factam, nec non luitionem pro iisdem vice populi, qua adumbrata Satisfactio Messiæ, utpote qui in vicem humani generis surrogari, peccatum totius mundi in se suscipere, ac pœnam pro eodem luere nostri loco debuerit, ut habemus cum ex ipsa Mo- saica sacrificii hujus descriptione, tum ex Prophe- tica declaratione Es. 53. cap. tum imprimis è Nov. Testam. explicatione Johann. 1. v. 29. & Ebr. 9. &c. Quæ alias adversus Socinum asseruimus: imo quum ab ipso Grotio asserta in defens. Cathol. fidei sint, hîc nisi Socinianis velificari voluisset tam al- to silentio involvi minime debuissent. Disputa- vit ibi Grotius cap. 10. p. 123. mortem pecudis homi- nis morti surrogatam fuisse, adductis tribus locis. Primo è Deut. 21. ubi constituitur, ut homicida non reperto populus expietur pecude cæsa, & vox expia- tionis v. 8. explicatur: Expia populum tuum Deus, & ne imputes sanguinem innocentem: quia alias non potuit terra expiari à sanguine effuso, nisi per san- guinem effusoris Num. 35, 27. Secundo è Levit. 17, 11. Anima cujusque carnis in sanguine est: Ego vero destinavi vobis eum in altari, ad expiationem fa- ciendam pro animabus vestris. Nam sanguis est, qui pro anima expiationem facit. Item tertio è Levit. 10, 17. ubi victima dicitur reorum iniquitates portare, eaque phrasi luitionem pœnæ inferri, docuit Grotius. Concludit loco laudato: Ex his quæ dixi- mus, perspicuum jam est, quomodo victimæ pro pecca- to in Veteri fœdere peccata expiarint, nimirum De- um movendo, ut pœnam carnalem remitteret, idque per satisfactionem quandam. Quod autem typi præ- stiterunt carnaliter, hoc ὁ ἀντίτυπος Christus præ- stat spiritualiter, quod typi in quibusdam tantum de- lictis, id Christus in omnibus, Deum scilicet movendo, ut spiritualem pœnam remittat, idque per satisfactionem perfectissimam. Plus enim non minus semper est in re typo designata, quam in typo, ut ratio monstrat. Hæc & plura alia quondam libro citato Grotius. Nunc vero ubi in propria sede hujus doctrinæ, in typis & figuris, Levitico imprimis descriptis occupatur, per totum librum, ne verbo quidem istius typicæ adumbrationis, nedum antitypi, satisfactionis nem- pe Christi, mentionem fecit, sive in hoc explican- do anniversario sacrificio, sive in aliorum mystica significatione declaranda. Hæret solum in natu- ralibus vel moralibus. De hoc sublimi antitypo ma- gis mutus est, quod dicitur, quam piscis.
