Porro quod ad peccata, pro quibus hoc solemni Sacrificio expiatio fiebat, Hebræorum recentio- rum acquiescit traditioni, quod pro iis solum facta, quibus mortis vel ἐξελοθρεύσεως exterminationis pœ- na est addita, quæ etiamsi judices lateant, non nisi per ærumnas graves expiata, dicit; at ubi in Scripturis habetur exceptio? Cum vero lex nihil excipit, no- strum non est, eandem restringere. Accensebantur hirco & imponebantur OMNES iniquitates filio- rum Israel, & UNIVERSA DELICTA, atque peccata eorum, portavitque hircus OMNES INI- eorum in terram folitariam Levit. 16. v. 21. Omnes ergo iniquitates, univerfa delicta & peccata expiata funt per ipfum. Quid evidentius hac univerfalitate? Nam & univerfalis particula abfo- lute adhibetur citra reftrictionem, & peccata di- ftribuuntur in fpecies, omnesque adeo peccatorum fpecies comprehenduntur. Græci ἀνομίας, ἀδικίας, ἁμαρτίας hic recenfent, inquit Grotius ad v. 21. Ho- rum poftremum חטאת ea fignificare videtur, quæ non deliberato fiunt: Cætera duo ea quæ deliberato: prius illud, id eft, עונת contra leges vetantes, pofte- rius פשעים contra jubentes; At his fpeciebus omnia comprehenduntur peccata. Nam aut fiunt deliberato aut non deliberato: aut contra leges ve- tantes, aut contra jubentes. Addit quidem reftri- ctionem Grotius, fed ita tamen, ut non comprehen- dantur ea, quibus pœna, qualem diximus, diferte ap- pofita eft. Sed ea nullum habet in hoc textu funda- mentum, imo refragatur eidem palam, quia O- MNES (quam univerfalem notam omifit Grotius) INIQVITATES, OMNIA DELICTA, OMNIA PECCATA, non aliqua tantum expiari hîc dicun- tur. Nec verum eft, per ærumnas graves occulta pec- cata expiari debuiffe. Confequebantur enim Ifrae- litæ, quotquot vera fide applicabant fibi expiatio- nem Meffiæ, in hoc typo adumbratam, remiffionem peccatorum: non ergo opus habebant expiatio- ne per ærumnas. Neque ærumnæ ad expiationem peccatorum immittuntur pœnitentibus. Non τι- μωρίαι funt, fed δοκιμασίαι fidelium.

Tertio fupponit Grotius, carnalem pœnam re- miffam interventu expiationis per facrificia, quod eti- am aperte afferentem jam audivimus, ideoque nonnullorum folum peccatorum veniam iisdem impetratam: Sed id falfum eft. Nam faciebant ex- piationes illæ ad remiffionem peccatorum, quod fæpius in Levitico repetitur. Cum autem peccata remittit, pœnam non folum carnalem, fed impri- mis æternam condonat Deus. Erant veræ expia- tiones, uti vocantur frequentiffime. At cum expi- antur peccata, pœna omnis remittitur. Quanquam vero non virtute propria expiarent facrificia, non tamen effectus hic illis denegandus, qua relationem habebant ad antitypum Chrifti expiatorium, cujus virtute præftabant expiationem peccatorum, cum vera fide offerebantur. Portabat omnia peccata hircus Azazel in defertum, ut fignificaretur, non redire peccata illa per victimam expiata, in confpectum Dei, ut hîc habet Grotius. Quæ vero ita expiata, ut non redeant in confpectum Dei, eorum non carnalem, fed imprimis æternam pœnam remif- fam effe oportet. Falfum etiam eft, leges in facri- ficiis datas effe ad condonandas pœnas forenfes in ju- dicio Politico. Non enim operabantur expiatio- nem in foro foli, fed in foro poli. Exiftimavit Grotius, mortem violentam, quam promeriti trans- greffores fuere, quamq; in Republ. Ebræa Deus per Ju- dices, quum ea ϑεοκρατεία fuerit, ordinarie exegerit, uti alias Rex pœnas per Judices exigere folet, condona- tam fuiffe in quibusdam delictis, facta per facrificia expiatione, ut è c. 10. de Satisfact. p. 121. videre eft. Sed facrificia ordinata erant ad impetrandam re- miffionem peccatorum in foro divino, non vero in judicio Politico. Ad pœnam condonandam æter- nam, non vero ad temporalem. Nullo id è Scriptu- ris teftimonio aut documento oftendetur, pœnam temporalem forenfem à Judicibus infligendam per fa- crificiorum oblationem remiffam fuiffe. Uti Evange- lium non abolet Politiam, ita nec facrificia, quæ erant Evangelii in Vet. Teft. appendices, aut viva quædam concio Evangelica.

Quod ergo quarto Ebr. 10, 2. remanfiffe confcien- tia peccati dicitur, post peractam illam expiationem, id recte quidem Grotius refert ad Hebræos in eadem aut paria peccata sæpe relapsos, sed non satisfacit in- tentioni Apostolicæ: quæ est demonstrare necessita- tem sacrificii Christi, quod antiqua sacrificia per se nequiverint peccata tollere, sed expiarint unice virtute sacrificii Christi, illudque præfigurarint. Id- eo enim repetebantur sæpius, quod fecerint ad de- signandam peccatorum abolitionem semel facien- dam, siquidem utile fuerit, commemorationem pec- catorum identidem repeti, & ingentis beneficii omni- busque expectandi famam continuatis sacrificiis crebrescere. Si sacrificiis illis Leviticis per se ex- oluti essent peccatorum conscientia Israelitæ, non opus utique fuisset eorum repetitione, sicut Chri- sti sacrificium non repetitur, quod semel peractum conscientias ab omni peccato purgavit.

Quod autem quinto fragilitatem illam, ne re- laberentur Hebræi in eadem aut paria peccata, legem auferre non potuisse, quia terrena pollicebatur, existi- mat Grotius, Socinianam iterum prodit hypothe- sin, quasi sufficiat bonorum æternorum pollicitatio ad id, ut peccata vitemus, aut per eandem fragilitas illa tollatur, neque in lege illa locum habuerit. At quam innumeri sunt, quibus certo constat de æter- na vita, è promissionibus divinis, qui à peccatis non abstinent? imo ne fideles quidem, qui non solum certam notitiam habent futuræ vitæ, sed etiam per arrhabonem Spiritus de ejus hæreditate confirmati sunt, ita ab hac fragilitate exemti sunt, ut non labantur in multis Jac. 3, 2. cujus vero adeo expertes non fuere Israelitæ, ut per ipsa quoque sacrificia iisdem Evangelicæ promissiones quasi πρὸς ὄμμα ponerentur, & ὡς ἐν τύπῳ exhiberen- tur: atque in hirco etiam illo ἀποπομπαίῳ fidem suam firmare potuerint, & spem gratiæ & vitæ con- cipere per promissa remissionis peccatorum, & ex- piationis his facta. In qua figura explicanda Vete- res operam navarunt: Justinus Martyr in Dialog. cum Tryph. pag. 291. Hircus emissarius adventus Christi designatio erat, cum eum veluti emissarium at- que ærumnas avertentem emiserunt Seniores & Sacer- dotes manus illi inferentes & morte eum mulctantes, oblatio is factus est pro cunctis per pœnitentiam respi- scere volentibus peccatoribus, qui Jesu fidei sunt addicti. Cyrillus contra Julian. cap. 9. Tom. 6. pag. mih. 311. Duo hirci assumuntur, non tanquam duo Christi sint, aut duo juxta nonnullos Filii, sed potius, quod opor- tebat eundem immolari pro nobis, & mori quidem se- cundum carnem; vivere autem secundum Spiritum. Mortuus enim est pro omnibus unus ille, omnium di- gnissimus, & Christi mors solutio mortis fuit. Et postea; si taurorum & hircorum sanguis non sufficit ad eluendam peccatum, cur Legislator ait, quod ex- piaturus sit pro peccatis ab immundiciis filiorum Is- rael, & ab injustitiis eorum? An igitur in verbis er- ravit? Absit. Quinam ergo sensus fuit? Manife- stum est sane, & clarum omnibus, quod veritas ne- quaquam in figuris, sed in rebus per eas significatis elu- cet. Christus enim est immaculatum illud sacrificium, pura illa victima, qua mortua pro nobis secundum car- nem, facti sumus emissarii, h. e. à morte & corruptio- ne recessimus. Ejus autem sanguine redemti sumus, & omni immunditia liberati, justificati gratis per gra- tiam ipsius, ut scriptum est, & gratiam, qua deleta est peccatorum memoria per Dei misericordiam conse- quuti. Theodoretius quæst. 22. in Lev. Nemo existi- met ineptum, hircos præfigurare passionem Christi, cum ipsum Johannes appellavit agnum, sed perpendat po- tius, quod non pro justis tantum, sed & pro peccatori- bus seipsum obtulerit. Prolixior est Hesychius in Com. in h. l. Multa, præmonet, hic intentio docentis simul & audientis est necessaria, ut non recedat ab eo, quod rectum est, quia maxima sunt mysteria ea, quæ nunc exponit lex, & quidam in ipsis offendunt, ignorantes virtutem dictorum. Et post bene multa fol. 101. Ergo cum omnibus præsentem Christum esse significat hircus. Quemadmodum enim per carnem in primo immolabatur; sic nunc vivens propter divinitatem dicitur. Sed quia unus & impassibilis & passibilis est, necessario & viventi manus Sacerdos imponit, ut manus impositione ostendatur, quia vivens verbum Dei impassibile, immortale, hoc pro nobis carne suscipiens sacrificium suscepit. Recte ergo in ipso iniquitates & injustitias & peccata Sacerdos pronunciavit. Hic est, de quo Esaias dicebat: Domine quis credidit auditui nostro? Et brachium Domini cui revelatum est? Brachium Domini filium appellans, Patri consubstantialem, de quo & ea, quæ sequuntur, subdidit: Languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portavit. Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra. Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum & livore ejus sanati sumus. Sic aperte super se peccata nostra & injustitias & iniquitates portavit: Et propterea secundum LXX. ait, imponet eos super caput hædi vivi: hujus enim figura est, quod & ex spinis coronam imponi capiti suo Christus permisit, quia in spinis peccata solent accipi. Applicat etiam hoc Hesychius, quod dicitur, semel in anno faciet hoc, quod semel offerri debuerit ad multorum exhaurienda peccata: & ad testimonium Christi Joh. 5. provocans: Si credideritis Mosi, credideritis utiq; & mihi, de me enim ille scripsit: hæc subjicit: Quid autem & ubi (scripserit) non addidit Christus, quia quæcunque mystica, quæcunque alta, quæcunque divina sunt, hæc de Christo à Mose umbris & figuris, ac imaginibus dicebantur. Hoc si pensi habuisset Grotius, Christum in Mose scrutari non neglexisset.

## 16:12
Verse 12. HE SHALL ENTER BEYOND THE VEIL INTO THE HOLY) Beyond the second veil into the Holy of Holies. Philo, 2 de Monarchia, Origen, 9 ad Levit., make mention of this censer.

Latin:

Vers. 12. VLTRA VELUM INTRABIT IN SANCTA) Vltra velum secundum in Sancta Sanctorum. Philo 2. de Monarchia, Origenes 9. ad Levit. meminere hujus foculi.

## 16:14
Verse 14. HE SHALL ALSO TAKE OF THE BLOOD OF THE CALF, AND SHALL SPRINKLE WITH HIS FINGER] You may observe something similar among the Romans in Zosimus, and in Prudentius's hymn on St. Romanus.

Latin:

Vers. 14. TOLLET QVOQVE DE SANGVINE VITULI, ET ASPERGET DIGITO] Simile quid apud Romanos observes in Zosimo, & in Prudentii hymno de S. Romano.

## 16:17
Verse 17. NO MAN) Namely, of those who were allowed to enter the Temple at other times, that is, the Priests and Levites.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NULLUS HOMINUM) Eorum scilicet quibus aliis temporibus ingredi Ædem licebat, id est, Sacerdotum & Levitarum.

## 16:18
v. 18. he shall make request as much for himself as for the people v. 24. Why then in the conclusion of the chapter v. 30. is it said, on this day there shall be your expiation and cleansing from all your sins, and v. 32. 33. the Priest, who shall have been anointed, shall make expiation and shall make expiation for the sanctuary and the tabernacle of the Testimony and the altar, the PRIESTS also and the WHOLE PEOPLE. Since he understands here in the conclusion that the word כפר ought to be rendered expiation, why did he not render it so in the very description of this expiatory sacrifice? This whole constitution teaches, with the addition of the observation and custom of the people, and the Apostolic declaration in Heb. 9 and 10, that that day was not considered so much a feast of prayer as a solemn expiation through the sacrifices prescribed there, not to mention that כפר nowhere denotes prayer and supplications alone. I see that our B. Franzius also observed this error of the Vulgate Version in Disp. de sacrif. 15. th. 4. Whose words I am pleased to append here (p. 591.) Hence in Leviticus 16. (where it treats of the universal Sacrifice for sins) although the old interpreter sometimes translates it by TO REQUEST, yet sometimes, as in verses 30. 32. 33. he is forced, even against his will, to retain the original nomenclature of expiating, and to translate it by TO EXPIATE. For he saw that that translation could not be Catholic, especially because, moreover, the words for expiating and cleansing are interchanged in Levit. 16: and regard is had solely to those annual ceremonies accustomed to be used every year on the tenth day of the seventh month, through which such a most solemn expiation was made, which indeed did not lack prayers, yet in the meantime was not accomplished by prayers alone. The more recent Jews indeed have such formulas, for good weather, for the preservation of the scepter of Judah, so that no one among the people might be in need, so that God might not hear the foolish prayers of men, which can be read in Fagius, but from where, I ask, will it be taught that such were either sanctioned or used in the time of Moses.

Latin:

v. 18. rogabit tam pro se, quam pro populo v. 24. Cur ergo in conclusione capitis v. 30. dicitur, in hac die erit expiatio vestri atq; mundatio ab omnibus peccatis vestris, & v. 32. 33. expiabit autem Sacerdos, qui un- ctus fuerit & expiabit sanctuarium & tabernaculum Testimonii atque altare, SACERDOTES quoque & UNIVERSUM POPULUM. Quum hic in con- clusione intelligat, vocem כפר reddi debere expia- tionem, cur in ipsa descriptione sacrificii expiatorii hujus non ita reddidit? Tota haec constitutio do- cet, accedente quoque observatione & consuetu- dine populi, & Apostolica declaratione Ebr. 9. & 10. non habitum esse illum diem tam precationis fe- stum, quam solemnis expiationis per sacrificia ibi praescripta, ut taceam, quod כפר nuspiam solam orationem & preces denotet. Video observasse etiam hunc errorem Vulgatae Versionis B. Franzium nostrum Disp. de sacrif. 15. th. 4. Cujus verba hic subjicere jam placet (p. 591.) Hinc Levitici 16. (ubi agitur de Sacrificio pro peccatis universali) etsi inter- dum vetus interpres convertit, per ROGARE, tamen interdum, ut vers. 30. 32. 33. pristinam expiandi no- menclationem retinere, & per τὸ EXPIARE conver- tere vel invitus cogitur. Vidit enim Catholicam esse non posse illam conversionem, praesertim quod insuper permutantur Levit. 16. expiandi & mundandi vocabu- la: Uniceque habetur respectus ad ceremonias illas an- niversarias die decimo septimi mensis quotannis adhi- bere solitas, per quas talis fieret solemnissima expiatio, quae quidem precibus non carebat, interim tamen solis precibus non perficiebatur. Recentiores sane Judaei tales formulas habent, pro bono aere, pro conser- vatione sceptri Juda, ne quis in populo egeret, ne Deus stultas hominum preces audiret, quae legi apud Fagium possunt, sed tales Mosis tempore aut sancitas, aut adhibitas fuisse, unde, obsecro, do- cebitur.

## 16:21
Verse 21. THE INIQUITIES OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL AND ALL THEIR OFFENSES AND SINS) The Greeks, ἀνομίας, ἀδικίας, ἁμαρτίας. The last of these, חַטָּאת, seems to signify those things which are done not deliberately: the other two, those which are done deliberately: the former, that is עָוֹן, against laws that forbid, the latter פִּשְׁעֵיהֶם against those that command, but yet in such a way that those things for which a penalty, such as we have mentioned, is expressly appointed are not included.

Latin:

Vers. 21. INIQVITATES FILIORUM ISRAEL ET VNIVERSA DELICTA ATQVE PECCATA EORUM) Græci, ἀνομίας, ἀδικίας, ἁμαρτίας. Horum postremum חַטָּאת ea significare videtur, quæ non deliberato fiunt: cætera duo ea quæ deliberato: prius illud, id est עָוֹן contra leges vetantes, posterius פִּשְׁעֵיהֶם contra jubentes, sed ita tamen, ut non comprehendantur ea quibus pœna qualem diximus diferte apposita est.

## 16:22
Verse 22. AND SHALL BE SENT AWAY INTO THE DESERT] Where it was cast down from a mountain.

What he had previously opposed to Socinus, having sought it from the Jews, while he was still defending the cause of the Catholic faith against him, concerning the Satisfaction of Christ, ch. 1, p. 14. Nor is there any reason for Socinus to object that this scapegoat was not accustomed to be killed: and that the shedding of blood or death is required for the remission of sins. For although Scripture does not expressly state that this very goat was cast down from a high place in the desert and thus given to death, the Hebrew interpreters agree that it was; for if it were not, what else did that driving away into the vast wilderness threaten but a death that was by no means natural, either from hunger or from the tearing of wild beasts? These are the words of Grotius in the same place. The Hebrews, according to Fagius: This goat was cast down from Mount Azazel, while he who had led it away held in his hand a crimson thread, which had been tied to the horn of the goat. Which (as they report) if they had God propitious and forgiving them their sins, was accustomed to turn immediately into whiteness, which was a sign of grace and benevolence: But if not, the thread remained crimson and was not changed, which signified that God was angry with them

God, as one who did not wish to forgive them their sins. But when the crimson thread had become white, the horn which they had with them sounded immediately, which, when others stationed and arranged not far from that order as far as the city of Jerusalem heard, they themselves also immediately sounded their horns, which they had prepared for this purpose as well, so that in a very short time, within almost an hour, this sound was heard not only in Jerusalem, but in the whole land of Israel. By which means the whole people knew that God was propitious and appeased toward them, so that they might be stirred up to praise, celebrate, and sanctify the name of God. But if the crimson thread was not changed, which was a sign of an angry and offended GOD, the horns were silent, and no sound rang through the land. And then the whole people were bound to be sad for the entire year, to do penance, and by prayers and fasts to appease and reconcile God to themselves again. The Talmudists write in Joma, ch. 4, fol. 39. The Masters taught that 40 years before the desolation of the temple (at which time Christ suffered) the lot no longer ascended into the right hand, nor did the crimson tongue turn white, nor did the evening lamp shine any longer, and the doors of the temple opened of their own accord. Indeed, by the death of Christ, all power was taken away from the legal sacrifices, the light of knowledge was extinguished in that nation, and not only the temple, but also heaven, hitherto closed to the Gentiles, then finally began to open; then also the veil of the temple was torn, as Bochart has it in Hier. l. 2. 54. 657. Others, as noted by Menochius and Tirinus, say that this goat was devoured in the desert by wild beasts, so that it might pay the penalties of the people. Guilb. Estius provides this application regarding the two goats: The former, which was sacrificed and in the tabernacle, signified Christ having suffered in the city at the clamors of the Jews: the latter, which was sent out into the desert to be devoured by wild beasts, Christ having suffered and been crucified outside the city, and that by the hands of Gentiles as if they were wild and barbarous men.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET DIMISSUS FUERIT IN DESERTO] Ubi de monte præcipitabatur.

Quod è Judæis petitum antehac opposuerat Socino, cum causam adhuc fidei Catholicæ contra ipsum defenderet, de Satisf. Christi c. 1. p. 14. Nec est, quod objiciat Socinus, ἀποπομπαῖον hunc hircum interimi non solitum: ad peccatorum autem remissionem fusionem sanguinis sive mortem requiri. Nam hunc ipsum hircum de loco sublimi præcipitatum in deserto, atque ita neci datum, etsi Scriptura diferte non prodit, Hebræi Interpretes consentiunt, quod ut non esset, quid tamen aliud illa in vastam solitudinem abactio quam mortem minime naturalem, aut ex fame aut ex ferarum laniatibus minabatur? Hæc ibidem Grotius. Ebræi apud Fagium: Hircus hic ex monte Azazel præcipitabatur, tenente interim eo, per quem abductus erat manu sua filum rubicundum, quod ac cornu capri alligatum erat. Quod (ut illi referunt) si Deum propitium atque remittentem ipsis peccata sua haberent, mox in albedinem, quod gratiæ ac benevolentiæ signum erat, converti solebat: Sin, filum manebat rubicundum, nec mutabatur, quod ipsis iratum

Deum, ut qui ipsi peccata eorum remittere nollet, significabat. Ubi vero filum rubicundum album factum esset, ilico Cornu, quod secum habebant sonabat, quod ubi alii non procul ab eo ordine Hierosolymam urbem usque constituti ac subornati audirent, statim & ipsi cornibus suis, quæ in hunc usum quoque comparata habebant, sonuerunt, ita ut brevissimo tempore intra horam fere non Hierosolymis tantum, sed in tota terra Israel sonus iste audiretur. Quo ista ratione universus populus sciret, sibi Deum propitium & placatum esse, ut ad laudandum, celebrandum, ac sanctificandum nomen Dei excitaretur. Sin vero filum rubicundum non mutaretur, quod irati & offensi DEI signum erat, silebant cornua, nullusq; sonus terram personabat. Et tum universus populus per totum annum tristari, pœnitentiam agere, atque precibus ac jejuniis Deum sibi rursus placare, ac reconciliare tenebatur. Talmudici scribunt in Joma cap. 4. fol. 39. Magistri docuerunt 40. annis ante templi desolationem (quo tempore Christus passus est) non adscendisse amplius sortem in manum dextram, neque linguam coccineam exalbuisse, neque lucernam vespertinam amplius arsesse, & templi fores per se patuisse. Nimirum morte Christi legalibus sacrificiis omnis virtus ademta, lumen cognitionis in ea gente extinctum, nec templum solum, sed & cœlum hactenus clausum gentibus, tum demum patere cœpit, tunc & velum templi scissum est, ut habet Bochard. in Hier. l. 2. 54. 657. Alii, notante Menochio, & Tirino, hunc caprum devoratum in deserto à feris ajunt, ut pœnas populi lueret. Guilb. Estius de hircis duobus hanc tradit applicationem: Priorem, qui immolatus & in tabernaculo, Christum significasse passum in civitate clamoribus Judæorum: posteriorem, qui emissus in desertum devorandus à feris, Christum passum & crucifixum extra urbem, idque manibus gentilium tanquam ferorum ac barbarorum hominum.

## 16:24
Vers. 24. AS MUCH FOR HIMSELF, AS FOR THE PEOPLE] For good weather, for good government, and so that prayers made for the sake of private utility might not be heard against the public. Thus Christians prayed for all Emperors for a long life, a secure empire, a safe home, strong armies, a faithful senate, an upright people, a quiet world, as Tertullian speaks in his Apologeticus.

In Hebrew it is וכפר & he shall make atonement for himself and for the people. The Vulgate version must therefore be corrected here. Nor does that prayer for good weather, for good government, etc., have anything to do with the matter here, where the subject is the expiation of crimes and the propitiation of God. Shall we believe that on that great day of atonement the Priest was more concerned in the offering of victims for good weather and government than for the reconciliation of the people and the obtaining of saving grace? He could have been more correctly informed by the Jews themselves: whose solemn formula of confession on the day of atonement, recited by the Priest, was this: O Lord, they have sinned, they have acted wickedly, they have transgressed before you, your people, the house of Israel, I beseech you O Lord, forgive now the sins and iniquities and transgressions by which they have sinned, acted wickedly, and transgressed before you, your people, the house of Israel: As it is written in the law of Moses your servant, because on this day he shall make atonement for us, that he may cleanse you and you may be clean from all your iniquities before the Lord. If room is left for the Grotian glosses and the Vulgate version of the word כפר, there will have been no atonement for the sins of the High Priest and his house, nor any atonement for the sins of the people made in the Holy of Holies: it must be said that only the sanctuary and the altar were cleansed from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, where v. 16. & 17. that word is rendered by the Latin Interpreter as He shall make atonement; whereas at other times that word is rendered HE SHALL PRAY for himself and his house v. 6. he shall pour out prayers over it v. 10. he shall ask for himself, and his house, and for the whole assembly of Israel v. 17. he prays for himself

Latin:

Vers. 24. TAM PRO SE, QVAM PRO POPULO] Pro bono aëre, pro bono regimine, & ne exaudirentur preces privatæ utilitatis causa factæ contra publicam. Sic Christiani orabant pro omnibus Imperatoribus vitam prolixam, imperium securum, domum tutam, exercitus fortes, senatum fidelem, populum probum, orbem quietum, ut Tertullianus in Apologetico loquitur.

In Ebræo est וכפר & expiabit pro se & pro populo. Corrigenda ergo hîc vulgata versio. Nec quicquam ad rem illa oratio hîc facit pro bono aëre, pro bono regimine &c. ubi de criminibus expiandis, Deoque propitiando res est. Credemusne in die illo magno expiationis solicitum fuisse magis pro aëre & regimine bono Sacerdotem in oblatione hostiarum, quam pro reconciliatione populi & gratia salvifica impetranda? Rectius informari poterat ab ipsis Judæis: quorum hæc erat solennis in die expiationis confessionis formula, à Sacerdote recitata: O Domine, peccarunt, inique egerunt, prævaricati sunt coram te populus tuus, domus Israel, obsecro Domine, remitte nunc peccata & iniquitates & prævaricationes, quibus peccaverunt, inique egerunt & prævaricati sunt coram te populus tuus, domus Israel: Sicut scriptum est in lege Mosis servi tui, quoniam in die isto expiationem faciet pro nobis, ut emundet vos & ab omnibus iniquitatibus vestris coram Domino mundi sitis. Grotianæ glossæ & versioni vocis כפר vulgati si locus relinquatur, nulla expiatio peccatorum summi Sacerdotis, & domus ejus, nulla etiam expiatio peccatorum populi in sancto Sanctorum facta erit: solum expiatum dicendum sanctuarium & altare ab îmundiciis filiorum Israel, ubi v. 16. & 17. vox illa redditur à Latino Interprete per Expiabit; quum alias reddatur vox ista ORABIT pro se ex sua domo v. 6. fundet preces super eo v. 10. rogabit pro se, & domo sua, & pro universo cætu Israel v. 17. orat pro se

## 16:27
Vers. 27. THEY SHALL CARRY OUTSIDE THE CAMP AND THEY SHALL BURN WITH FIRE) That signified that every memory of crimes of that kind, for which expiation was established, was cast far away by God.

Who therefore would have signified only the remission of a carnal punishment, and not indeed of that graver eternal one? Nor should the meaning handed down by the Apostle have been neglected here, by which this Ceremony also referred to the expiation made through Christ. Heb. 13, 11. For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the holy places by the High Priest for sin, are burned outside the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us go forth therefore outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For he refers there to this constitution in Levit. 16, 27. But Grotius preferred to compare the interpretation of divine institutions to Poets and profane Historians, rather than to the holy men of God carried along by the Holy Spirit, nay, he even attempted to render the interpretation of the latter, which is God-breathed, ambiguous or to obscure it by the sayings of the former.

Latin:

Vers. 27. APPORTABUNT FORAS CASTRA ET COM passent IGNE) Id significabat, omnem memoriam criminum ejus generis, quibus expiatio constituta erat, a Deo longe projectam.

Qui ergo tantum carnalis poenae, non vero gra- vioris illius sempiternae condonationem significa- set? Neque negligi hic debuit significatio ab Aposto- lo tradita, qua expiationem per Christum factam haec quoque Ceremonia referebat. Ebr. 13, 11. Quo- rum animalium infertur sanguis pro peccato in sancta per Pontificem, horum corpora cremantur extra castra. Propter quod & Jesus, ut sanctificaret per suum san- guinem populum, extra portam passus est. Exeamus igitur extra castra, improperium ejus portantes. Re- spicit enim ibi hanc constitutionem Levit. 16, 27. Sed Grotius maluit conferre ad interpretationem institutorum divinorum Poetas, Historicos propha- nos, quam sanctos Dei viros ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερομένους, imo per illorum dicta horum interpre- tationem θεόπνευστον non raro ambiguam reddere conatus est, aut obscurare.

## 16:28
Vers. 28. WHOEVER SHALL BURN THEM SHALL WASH HIS GARMENTS) Similar to below in Numbers 19, 1. so also among the nations, expiatory victims were believed to pollute those who had touched them. Porphyry on Abstinence, book two: For all the theologians agreed in this, that one must not touch the victims in expiatory sacrifices, and that one must use purifications. For let no one go into the city, nor into his own house, without first having cleansed his clothes and body in rivers or a spring, they say, so that even those whom they permitted to sacrifice, they commanded to abstain from the things sacrificed in these rites.

Latin:

Vers. 28. QVICUMQVE COMBUSSERIT EA LAVA- BIT VESTIMENTA SUA) Simile infra Numerorum 19, 1. sic & apud gentes victimae ἀποτρόπαιαι polluere credeban- tur, qui eas attigissent. Porphyrius de Abstinentia secundo: πάντες γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ ὡμολόγησαν οἱ θεολόγοι, ὡς ὔτε ἁπτέον ἐν τοῖς ἀποτροπαίοις θυσίαις τῶν θυομένων, καθαρσίοις τε χρηστέον. μὴ γὰρ ἴοι τις εἰς ἄστυ, μηδ' εἰς οἶκον ἴδιον, μὴ πρότε- ρον ἐσθῆτα καὶ σῶμα ποταμοῖς ἢ πηγῇ ἀποκαθήρας, Φασὶν, ὥςτε καὶ οἷς ἐπέτρεψαν θύειν, ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν θυομένων τύτοις πα- ρήγγειλαν.

## 16:32
Vers. 32. THE PRIEST WHO SHALL HAVE BEEN ANOINTED] The High Priest, that is. See what is above on Exodus 40, 13.

Concerning this goat we proposed some things in an Academic program, which I am pleased to add here. And it holds thus: Truly memorable, and most astonishing, if there ever was any spectacle in the Church of the Old Testament exhibiting the antitypes of the true things, which was presented annually to the whole people on the solemn feast of expiation, described most exquisitely according to the tenor of the Divine command in Levit. 16. The High Priest had to be prepared above all things for such sacred, such admirable expiatory rites, to have his hands and feet washed, to be clothed in sacred garments, and to be expiated by a young bull and a ram, the former offered as a Sacrifice for sin, the latter as a burnt offering. But if we examine the sacred rites themselves, for the sake of which this preparation was required, the mere consideration of them strikes the mind with admiration, so that it is no wonder that those who then witnessed them with their eyes, emaciated by fasts (and agitated by the conscience of their sins), were even turned into stupor. They were forced to bring these two goats for a Sacrifice for sin, these were presented before the Lord at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, a Lot was cast upon both, with the name of Jehovah inscribed on one, and Azazel on the other, and whose Lot, while the High Priest drew both, bore the name of the Lord, he was to be slaughtered, but the other was to be sent away alive into the desert: But neither was a common slaughter to be performed there, nor this a common sending away. For the blood of that one was brought into the Holy of Holies itself, the entrance to which was open to no one except the High Priest, and not even to him, except on this Solemnity, so that he might sprinkle it seven times toward the mercy seat to the east, but with a covering of vapor and a cloud of incense kindled, lest he be consumed by the sight of it. But the live goat was set before the Lord, and prayers were poured out over him with great devotion. But also with both hands placed upon the head of the goat, the Pontiff confessed all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions and sins, which he prayed down upon its head, and thus, properly laden with all the sins of the whole people, he finally sent away that goat, through a man prepared for it, as a certain scapegoat into the desert. These spectacles were not, however, mute; rather, there was a diligent instruction delivered concerning the purpose of this sacrifice, especially by the High Priest, who, if credence is to be given to the teachers of the Jews, ought not to have moved even a cubit on the day before that festival, but instructed the other priests whom he had with him concerning it throughout the whole night. All these things were a shadow of good things to come, as the Apostle testifies; and just as those whose craft it is to make signs out of bronze and to cast statues, before they produce the true work of bronze, or of silver or gold, first form a clay model to the likeness of the future image, not because the model is necessary, but until the work, which is the principal thing, is completed, the same is also to be understood here, as Origen very well advised in Sermon 10 on Leviticus, and with him Cyril in book 9 against Julian. The narrowness of the page does not permit me to unweave every detail; but it will be worth the effort to indicate, rather than explain, only those things which seem to regard the impending birthday festival. Which, however, it is pleasing to propose not so much in our own words as in the words of the Doctors of the Church, which strike the mind with joy and gravity alike. Nor without reason does St. Cyril here advise in his Epistle to Bishop Acacius that it is altogether fitting that, looking upon these shadows, we exclaim: Who is wise, and understands these things? Who is discerning, and knows them? Let us look first at the linen tunic with which the High Priest was to be clothed: concerning which Origen says in Homily IX: Linen arises from the earth; therefore the true High Priest, Christ, is clothed in a sanctified linen tunic when He takes on the nature of an earthly body. For of the body it is said, that it is earth, and into earth it will go. Wishing therefore my Lord and Savior to raise up this, which had gone into the earth, he took on an earthly body, that he might carry it, raised from the earth, to heaven. The tunic of Christ's flesh had indeed been sanctified: for it was not conceived from the seed of a man, but generated from the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, that not only a goat ought to have been offered, but also a calf, Hesychius (lib. 5 in Levit. ad h.l.) judges that the admirable legislator prefigured different things in different ways. For because Christ arose from the Jews according to the flesh, who lived under the yoke of the law, the sacrifice of a calf is rightly named. For a calf is compared to the legal yoke, and to the work and justice pertaining to it, accustomed to pull the yoke, and thus to work the earth. But because, according to the fact that he was incarnate, he was made a goat from the common mass, therefore he is again called a goat. But as for the distinction of the two goats, which St. Augustine (lib. 3, Quæst. sup. Levit. cap. 51) warns must not be treated negligently in allegorical signification, there is no reason for us to be occupied with the impiety of Julian, who cavils that the goat lacking the sign was sent away to a certain demon called ἀποπομπαῖος, which St. Cyril (lib. 9, contra eum, as also Epist. XXXIX ad Acac.) has abundantly refuted; nor should ears be lent here to Origen, who 'Origenizes' about the dismissed Barabbas and the slain Christ; leading into the desert those doing well, because they are the lot of the Lord, and those doing evil, because they are their own lot; about the two who hung at the right and left at the time of Christ's cross, the one made the lot of the Lord, the other the lot of the apopompaeus, and led away into the desert of hell; about Christ triumphing over contrary powers, the spirits of wickedness, and making the strong one of the apopompaeus, by leading them to the desert, but rendering the strong one of the Lord his own Church. Nor can we accede to the explanation of Justin, about the twofold advent of Christ shadowed here (Dial. cum Tryph. p. 201), or to Isidore, who thinks a twofold people is signified, namely of Jews and Gentiles, both burdened with the mass of sin. More elegant is the opinion of Theodoret (Quæst. 22 in Levit.), Hesychius, and Cyril of Alexandria, that a twofold nature is designated in Christ. Let us consider, says Cyril in the cited epistle, Emmanuel in the slaughtered goat, having indeed suffered the death of the flesh, but for the destruction of death and sin. For he was free among the dead, that is, immune from sin, and not liable with us to the sentence of death. Let us see the same also in the other goat, namely the living and dismissed one, even if he suffered humanly, yet he did not suffer divinely, and meanwhile, while he dies in the flesh, he is the victor of death. The same Cyril (lib. IX, c.) reveals another enigma of the twin goat. Jul. that is, that the immolated goat shadowed forth Christ, but the one that was dismissed alive shadowed forth the human race. The only-begotten was made in our likeness, he was among the goats, he sustained the death hanging over us, that he might release us from death and corruption. And again: Christ is the immolated Sacrifice, and by no means a profane victim, by whose death for us according to the flesh, we have been made ἀποπομπαῖοι, that is, we have departed from sin and corruption, and have been redeemed by his blood, and freed from all uncleanness. But we shall best call both goats a Sacrament of Christ, according to the χειραγωγίαν of Isaiah ch. LIII and St. Paul Heb. IX, as one who takes upon himself, carries, and expiates the sins of the whole human race in the manner of an ἀποπομπαία, which were imposed upon his head and as it were reckoned to him, and who undergoes death for sins and offers himself to GOD in an odor of fragrance, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 32. SACERDOS QUI VNCTVS FUERIT] Sum- mus scilicet. Vide quae supra Exodi 40, 13.

De hirco hoc nonnulla proposuimus in pro- grammate Academico, quae hic addere placet. Ita autem illud habet: Memorabile profecto, ac per- quam stupendum, si quod unquam in Ecclesia Ve- teris Testamenti ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν exhiben- te Spectaculum fuit, quod in solenni expiationis festo quotannis universo populo sistebatur, juxta tenorem mandati Divini Levit. 16. exquisitissime descriptum. Præparari Sacerdos summus debuit ante omnia, ad tam sacra, tam admiranda piacu- laria, manus pedesque abluendus, vestibus sacris induendus, ac juvenco atque ariete, illo in Sacri- ficium pro peccato, hoc in holocaustum oblato, expiandus. Quod si Sacra ipsa, quorum causa hæc parasceve requisita, lustremus, sola eorum consideratio admiratione percellit animos, ut mirum haud sit illos, qui oculis tum præsentes ea usurparunt, jejuniis maceratos, (ac conscientia peccatorum suorum exagitatos) vel in stuporem conversos. Adducere cogebantur isti hircos duos in Sacrificium pro peccato, hi sistebantur coram Domino in ostio tabernaculi testimonii, super utrumque Sors mittebatur, alteri Jehovah, alteri Azahel inscripto nomine, & cujus Sors, dum extraheret utrumque Sacerdos Summus, Do- mini nomen referebat, is mactandus erat, alter vero vivus emittendus in desertum: Sed nec illic vulgaris mactatio, neque hæc communis emissio peragenda. Istius enim sanguis in ipsum Sanctum Sanctorum, cujus aditus nemini nisi Summo Sa- cerdoti, ac nec huic quidem, præterquam in hac Solennitate, patebat, inferebatur, ut è regione propitiatorii, septies ad orientem eum asper- geret, at operto vapore, ac nebula accensi thy- miamatis oraculo, ne intuitu ejus consumeretur. Vivus autem hircus coram Domino statuebatur, precesque super eum magna devotione fundeban- tur. Sed & posita manu utraque super caput hir- ci, confitebatur Pontifex omnes iniquitates filio- rum Israel, & universa delicta atque peccata ejus, quæ imprecabatur capiti ejus, atque ita probe o- nustum peccatis omnibus universi populi dimit- tebat demum per hominem paratum, hircum il- lum, ceu κάθαρμα quoddam in desertum. Non autem muta fuere ista Spectacula, quin potius de fine hujus sacrificii sedula tradita informatio à Summo imprimis Sacerdote, qui si Magistris Judæorum fides adhibenda, ne cubitum quidem pridie illius festi sese conferre debuit, sed per to- tam noctem cæteros, quos secum habebat sacer- dotes, de illo instruxit. Umbra hæc omnia fue- re bonorum futurorum, teste Apostolo, & sicuti hi, quibus artificium est, signa ex ære facere, & sta- tuas fundere solent, antequam verum opus æris pro- ducant, aut argenti vel auri, figmentum prius lute ad similitudinem futuræ imaginis formant, non quod figmentum necessarium sit, sed usque quo opus, quod principale est, expleatur, idem etiam hic intelligen- dum, optime monuit Origenes Serm. 10. in Le- vit. & cum eo Cyrillus lib. 9. contr. Julian. Re- texere singula chartæ angustia haud permittit; sed solum quæ imminentem Festivitatem Ge- nethliacam spectare videntur, indicare potius, quam explicare operæ erit pretium. Quæ ta- men non tam nostris, quam Ecclesiæ Docto- rum verbis, animos jucunditate pariter ac gra- vitate magis percellentibus, proponere juvat. Nec immerito hic monet S. Cyrillus Epistola ad Acacium Episcopum, convenire omnino, ut umbras has intuentes exclamemus: Quis Sapiens, & in- telligit hæc; quis intelligens, & cognoscit ista? Spe- ctemus primum tunicam lineam, qua induendus erat Sacerdos Summus: qua de Origenes hom. IX. Linum de terra oritur; tunica ergo sanctificata li- nea induitur verus Pontifex Christus, cum natu- ram terreni corporis sumit. De corpore enim di- citur, quia terra sit, & in terram ibit. Volens ergo Dominus & Salvator meus hoc, quod in terram iërat, suscitare, terrenum suscepit corpus, ut id elevatum de terra portaret ad cœlum. Sanctificata vero erat tu- nica carnis Christi: non enim erat ex semine viri con- cepta, sed ex Sancto Spiritu generata. Porro quod non hircus solum offerri debuit, sed & vitulus, in di- versis diversa præfigurasse admirandum legislatorem, censet Hesychius lib. 5. in Levit. ad h.l. Quia enim Christus de Judæis secundum carnem, qui sub jugo legis vivebant, ortus est, recte vituli sacrificium nomi- natur. Legali enim jugo, & pertinenti ad eum ope- rationi, & justitiæ vitulus comparatur, jugum con- suetus trahere, atque ita terram operari. Quia au- tem secundum quod incarnatus erat, de communi mas- sa hircus factus est, propterea rursus hircus appella- tur. Quod vero ad hircorum duorum distinctio- nem, quam in allegorica significatione non negligen- ter tractandam esse monet S. Augustin. lib. 3. Quæst. sup. Levit. cap. 51. non est quod in impietate Ju- liani, hircum signaculo carentem Dæmoni cuidam ἀποπομπαίῳ dimissum cavillantis, occupemur, quam S. Cyrill. lib. 9. ei oppositò, ut & Epist. XXXIX. ad Acac. abunde profligavit; nec Origeni aures hîce præbendæ, qui Ωριγενίζει de dimisso Bar- raba, & occiso Christo; debene agentibus, quod sors Domini sint, male agentibus, quod sors propria sint, ducens in eremum; de duobus, qui tempore crucis Christi ad dextram & sinistram pependerunt, illo forte Domini, hoc forte apopompæi facto, & in ere- mum abducto inferni; de Christo potestates contrari- as, spiritus nequitiæ triumphante, ac fortem apopom- pæi faciente, traducendo eos ad eremum, fortem autem domini Ecclesiam suam reddente. Nec Justini acce- dere possumus explicationi, de gemino adventu Christi hîce adumbrato Dial. cum Tryph. p. 201. aut Isidoro, geminum significari populum existimanti, Judæorum scil. & gentium, utrumque peccati mole onustum. Concinnoior est Theodoreti Quæst. 22. in Levit. Hesychii, & Cyrilli Alexandr. sententia, gemi- nam in Christo naturam designari. Consideremus, inquit Cyrillus Epist. citata, in mactato capro Ema- nuelem, mortem quidem carnis passum, verum ad de- structionem mortis & peccati. Erat enim inter mor- tuos liber, hoc est, immunis à peccato, nec obnoxius nobiscum mortis sententiæ. Videamus eundem & in altero capro, vivente videlicet, ac dimisso, etsi hu- manitus passum, divinitus tamen non passum, & in- terea dum in carne moritur, mortis victorem. Ali- ud ænigma hirci gemini aperit idem Cyrillus lib. IX. c. Jul. quod scil. hircus immolatus Christum, qui vero vivus dimittebatur, genus humanum ad- umbrarit. Factus est unigenitus in specie nostra, ha- bus inter hædos, nobis impendentem sustinuit mor- tem, ut nos à morte & corruptione emitteret. Atque iterum: Christus est immolatum Sacrificium, & mi- nime prophana victima, quo mortuo pro nobis secun- dum carnem, facti sumus ἀποπομπαῖοι, hoc est, recessimus à peccato & corruptione, & illius sanguine redemti sumus, & ab omni immunditie liberati. O- ptime autem juxta χειραγωγίαν Esaiæ cap. LIII. & S. Pauli Ebr. IX. utrumque hircum Sacramentum dicemus Christi, ut peccata totius humani generis ad instar ἀποπομπαίας in sese suspicientis, portan- tis, expiantis, quæ capiti ejus imposita, & veluti annumerata sunt, & pro peccatis mortem sub- euntis seque offerentis DEO in odorem fragran- tiæ &c.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII. The place of sacrifice, and the reason for the forbidden eating of blood.

the decision of the whole matter and of the true doctrine concerning sacrifices, F. Socinus passed over: how much more is it to be blamed in Grotius, that, when he is occupied with the Levitical sacrifices, and has been brought to this passage, he has completely wrapped its chief force in silence: whence light could have been brought to this whole book. The words of this authentic text are as follows: The soul of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you, that upon the altar you may make atonement in it for your souls, and the blood may be for an atonement of the soul. Where it is first to be observed, the word

that כפר cannot in this matter be rendered to pray, to entreat, as the Vulgate has often rendered it, nor to commend some thing to God, as Grotius contends it should be rendered toward the beginning of the book on Leviticus 1, 4; for blood does not pray, or entreat for us, it does not commend us to God. Nor is that attributed to blood here, but as the Vulgate has rendered it in this conviction, atonement is claimed for it. Therefore, according to this general Mosaic maxim as a norm and rule of sacrifices, the word must be rendered in other places also not by prayed, but by made atonement, where indeed it deals with individual sacrifices specifically, Lev. ch. 3, 4, 5, 16, etc. Just as the same word is also applied to the complete rites of sacrifices, to which the notion of praying certainly cannot be attributed.

Then indeed it is clear from this authentic text, whence the force of atonement belongs to the blood of cattle? namely, that it has the same from this divine ordination, but not of itself. The soul of the flesh is in the blood, I HAVE GIVEN IT to you upon the altar TO ATONE FOR your SOUL, the blood itself atones: Naturally, thence the blood has the force of atoning: because by the will and ordination of God the soul of the flesh or of the beast, which is in the blood, is given with the blood for the soul of the sinner, and in place of the same, so that thus the soul of the beast itself may suffer in place of the soul of sinners, and by suffering may satisfy for the sin, not αὐτοενεργητικῶς, but by the virtue of the Antitype here shadowed forth, whose soul was given for our soul for the atonement of sins and satisfaction for us, whose blood atones for the sins of the whole world. The LXX express the substitution of the beast in place of man by the little word ἀντὶ, which is in place of or instead of: ἐξιλάσασθαι περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν: for its blood shall make atonement instead of the soul. Concerning which Eusebius, l. c. demonstr. Evangelic., that Moses has here most clearly taught how a soul is to be offered to God instead of a soul. And again: For clearly instead of the human soul the blood of the slaughtered animals is of a nature to make atonement. Which particle is used also of Christ giving his soul a ransom instead of many, Matt. 20, 28, Mark 10, 45, and a ransom instead of all, 1 Tim. 2, 6. For as often as that particle is applied to persons, it is Grotius's rule in De Satisf. Christi ch. 9, p. 116, it signifies that one has succeeded into the place of another. And therefore Grotius has professed above (book on Satisf. Christi ch. 10, p. 123) that in atonement the death of the beast is substituted for the death of man, and that this is manifest from the fact that in Leviticus 17, 11, blood was given to make atonement for the souls of sinners. Why then is he now completely silent about it? Which he had taught from the very exotic sources in the cited book, Pliny, who said that there is thanks for the beast in the placating of the Gods: Ovid: that men are reconciled to God through victims, in which matter p. 130 he thought it especially to be noted, that very often, when it deals with expiatory sacrifices, mention is made of blood, because by the most ancient law of God spoken to Noah in Genesis 9, 4, and thence propagated to all peoples, blood is in place of the soul, and for that reason is called by the name of soul. Hence that of Virgil: By blood must a return be sought, and by a soul must one make atonement. Explaining which words from Trebatius, Macrobius says that those victims were called animal sacrifices. Sins themselves are properly said to be piari, that is, to be expiated: Either by paying the debted penalty, or by something else, which succeeds into the place of the debted penalty. As see in Virgil: - - And they will expiate the guilt of the wretched with death. That is, they will cause them to be expiated. Pliny: Wars are accustomed to expiate the luxury of the people. Cicero: The immortal Gods have expiated your crimes in our soldiers. In the same author it is often to expiate crimes by punishment: and in Sallust, to expiate slaughter with slaughter, blood with blood. Indeed, the word punishment itself was first in sacred matters, whence it was transferred to penalties. But in sacrifices to expiate is to pay by the succession of another thing into the place of the debted penalty. Hence Plautus: Must an expiatory sacrifice be made for me because of your stupidity, That you may submit my back as a substitute for your stupidity. Hence the author of the Distichs, which bear the name of Cato, says: Since you are yourself guilty, why does a victim die for you? Where for you, is in your place. And likewise he says that those who offer victims hope for their own safety by the death of another. Hence piacula are properly the sacrifices themselves: Let these be the first expiatory sacrifices. Virg. 6. And no expiatory sacrifices will release you. Horace: which also Ovid calls piamina: The Roman Fathers called Februa piamina. The force of which word he himself soon expresses, by which our crimes are expiated. Improperly, piacula are the crimes, on account of which expiatory sacrifices are owed; as Servius rightly says on that of Virgil: He deferred the committed expiatory sacrifices to late death. And a little later: From these it is manifest that sacred lustral rites or expiatory offerings pertained to placating the deity, and thus obtaining impunity for things committed before. Which Pliny expresses thus: An old opinion prevailed in ancient times, that all things were februa, by which the CONSCIENCES OF EVIL-DOERS WERE PURGED, AND SINS WERE BLOTTED OUT. Caesar explains the reason while dealing with the Gauls: They believe that unless the life of a man is rendered for the life of men, the divine will of the immortal gods cannot be appeased. Which Grotius sets forth more extensively there, finally concluding thus on p. 135. Moreover, that custom of the nations in expiating sins by the slaughter of men or cattle brings no little light to understanding the very nature of expiatory sacrifice and the proper terms of that subject. And this labor can be the less despised, because Socinus says that the Baptist, when he called Christ the Lamb of God, had regard to sacrifices in general, by which it was believed that sins were expiated not only among the Hebrews, but also among the Gentiles. Nor indeed is it to be doubted, when the divine writer to the Hebrews most often uses the Greek words καταρίζειν and ἁγιάζειν in this very argument of expiatory sacrifice, that he used them in the sense which the Greek language had received. Which he most recently urges effectively against Socinus thus on p. 139. Socinus denies that God is appeased by expiatory sacrifices. But the writers cited above by us testify to the contrary, who use the word for appeasing to express those sacrifices: whence also that phrase arose, placed in the said passage to the Hebrews, ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας, to appease sins, that is, by appeasing God to expiate sins. Socinus acknowledges no satisfaction in expiatory sacrifices. And yet the very word for atoning or expiating signifies properly nothing else than to pay: and the authors cited by us everywhere, when they wish to express expiating, say περικαθάιζειν, to give blood for blood, life for life, soul for soul: to buy something with blood, to obtain salvation by the death of another. Nor do the Hebrew words differ here. For Caphar and Kipper is not only to cover, but also to redeem, Exod. 21:30, Ps. 49:8, and to appease, Gen. 32:20, and from there furthermore to expiate. Chitta is to pay, Gen. 31:39. Whence this also began to be used to signify expiation. All these things Grotius in the same place. But now as if led by repentance for those things, lest by the word of that substitution he makes mention of placation, of satisfaction, and indeed never refers back to this book opposed to Socinus, just as on the other hand he is not infrequently accustomed to refer back to those things which he elsewhere handed down as acceptable to Socinus among the Anabaptists.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII. Locus Sacrificii, & causa vetiti esus sanguinis.

decisio totius negotii & veræ doctrinæ de sacrificiis, præterierit F. Socinus: quanto magis reprehenden- dum in Grotio, quod, cum in Leviticis sacrificiis occupetur, & ad hunc locum delatus fuerit, vim ejus præcipuam silentio plane involverit: Unde toti huic libro lux conciliari poterat. Verba hu- jus authenticæ ita habent: Anima carnis in sangui- ne est: & ego dedi illum vobis, ut super altare in eo ex- pietis pro animabus vestris, & sanguis pro animæ pia- culo sit. Ubi id primum observandum, vocem

כפר non posse in hac materia reddi orare, rogare, ut Vulgatus sæpe reddidit, non commendare rem ali- quam Deo, uti sub initium libri ad Levit. 1, 4. red- dendam esse Grotius contendit; Sanguis enim non orat, aut rogat pro nobis, non commendat nos Deo. Nec id sanguini hic tribuitur, sed ut hic convictus Vulgatus reddidit, expiatio ei vindicatur. Juxta ergo hanc maximam generalem Mosaicam ceu normam & regulam sacrificiorum reddendum verbum erit in aliis etiam locis non per rogavit, sed ex piavit, ubi nempe de sacrificiis singulis in specie agitur Lev. c. 3. 4. 5. 16. &c. Quemadmodum etiam ritibus integris sacrificiorum eadem vox applica- tur, quibus certe rogandi notio tribui non potest.

Tum vero patet ex hac authentica, unde expiatio- nis vis sanguini pecudum conveniat? quod nempe ex ordinatione hac divina eandem habeat, non autem per se. Anima carnis est in sanguine, EGO DEDI ILLUM vobis super altare ad EXPIANDAM ANI- MAM vestram, sanguis ipse expiat: Nimirum in- de sanguis expiandi vim habet: quia ex volunta- te & ordinatione Dei anima carnis seu pecoris, quæ est in sanguine, cum sanguine datur pro anima pec- catoris, & loco ejusdem, ut ita anima ipsa pecoris pa- tiatur loco animæ peccatorum, & patiendo satisfa- ciat pro peccato, non αὐτοενεργητικῶς, sed virtute Antitypi hic adumbrati, cujus anima data est pro nostra anima ad expiationem peccatorum & satis- factionem pro nobis, cujus sanguis expiat totius mundi peccata. LXX. surrogationem pecoris loco ho- minis vocula ἀντὶ exprimunt, quæ est vice vel loco: ἐξιλάσασθαι περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν: τὸ γὰρ αἷμα ἀυτᾶ ἀντὶ ψυχῆς ἐξιλάσεται. Quo de Eusebius l. c. de- monstr. Evangelic. quod Moses hic luculentissime docuerit, quomodo offerenda Deo ψυχὴ ἀντὶ ψυ- χῆς. Et rursus: Σαφῶς γὰρ ἀντὶ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς τὸ τῶν σφαγιαζομένων ζώων αἷμα φύσιν ἐξιλάσκεσθαι. Quæ particula adhibetur etiam de Christo animam suam dante λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν so- lutionis pretium loco multorum, Matth. 20, 28. Marc. 10, 45. & ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων 1. Tim. 2, 6. Quo- ties enim personis applicatur ea particula, Grotii re- gula est de Satisf. Christi cap. 9. p. 116. significat alte- rum successisse in locum alterius. Ideoque Grotius professus est supra (lib. de Satisf. Christi c. 10. p. 123.) quod in expiatione mors pecudis morti hominis surro- getur, idque manifestum esse ex eo, quod Levit. 17, 11, sanguis datus sit ad expiationem faciendam pro ani- mabus peccatorum. Cur ergo nunc de eo penitus silet? Quod ex ipsis quoque exoticis libro citato docuerat, Plinio, qui pecori gratiam esse dixit in Deorum placamentis: Ovidio: per victimas homines Deo conciliari, in quam rem p. 130. imprimis notan- dum duxit, sæpissime, cum de sacris expiatoriis agitur, sanguinis fieri mentionem, quia ex vetustissima Dei le- ge Noacho dicta Genes. 9, 4. atque inde ad populos omnes propagata sanguis est vice animæ, ac propterea animæ nomine appellatur. Hinc illud Virgilii: Sanguine quærendus reditus, animaque litandum. Quæ verba explicans ex Trebatio Macrobius, eas ho- stias ait animales fuisse appellatas. Piari proprie di- cuntur ipsa peccata, hoc est, lui: Sive solvendo pœnam debitam, sive aliud, quod poenæ debitæ in locum suc- cedit. Ut ecce apud Virgilium: - - Et culpam miserorum morte piabunt. Hoc est, efficient, ut luantur. Plinius: Luxum populi expiare solent bella. Cicero: Tua scelera Dii immor- tales in nostros milites expiaverunt. Apud eundem sæpe est scelera supplicio expiare: & apud Sallustium, cædem cæde, sanguinem sanguine expiare. Imo & sup- plicii vox primum in sacris fuit, unde ad pœnas trans- lata est. Sed in sacrificiis piare est luere per successionem rei alterius in locum pœnæ debitæ. Hinc Plautus: Men' piaculum oportet fieri propter stultitiam tu- am, Ut meum tergum stultitiæ tuæ subdas succedaneum. Hinc autor Distichorum, quæ Catonis nomen præse- runt, ait: Cum sis ipse nocens, moritur cur victima pro te? Ubi pro te, est tuo loco. Atque itidem eos, qui victimas offerunt, ait morte alterius suam salutem sperare. Hinc piacula proprie ipsa sacrificia: Ea prima piacula sunto. Virg. 6. Teque piacula nulla resolvent. Horatius: quæ & piamina Ovidio: Februa Romani dixere piamina Patres. Cujus vocis vim ipse mox exprimit, quo crimina no- stra piantur. Improprie piacula crimina, propter quæ piacula debentur; ut recte Servius ad illud Virgilii: Distulit in seram commissa piacula mortem. Et paulo post: Ex his manifesto apparet, sacra lustra- lia sive piamenta pertinuisse ad placandum numen, & sic impetrandam impunitatem ante commissorum. Quod Plinius ita exprimit: Vetus priscis temporibus opinio obtinuit, februa esse omnia, quibus malefa- ctorum CONSCIENTIÆ PURGARENTUR, DE- LERENTURQUE PECCATA. Causam explicat Cæsar de Gallis agens: Pro vita hominum nisi vita hominis reddatur, non posse Deorum immortalium numen PLACARI arbitrantur. Quod prolixius ibi exequitur Grotius, tandem ita concludens p. 135. Cæterum mos ille gentium in expiandis peccatis hominum aut pecudum mactatione non parum adfert lucis ad intelligendam ipsam sacrificii expiatorii na- turam & vocabula propria ejus argumenti. Eoque minus sperni potest hic labor, quod dicat Socinus, Ba- ptistam, cum Christum agnum Dei appellavit, ad sa- crificia in universum respexisse, quibus non solum apud Hebræos, sed & apud Gentes peccata expiari crede- bantur. Neque vero dubitandum est, cum in hoc ipso Sacrificii expiatorii argumento voces Græcas καταρί- ζειν & ἁγιάζειν sæpissime usurpat divinus Scriptor apud Ebræos, quin eo sensu usurpaverit, quem Græ- ca lingua receperat. Quæ novissime adversus So- cinum efficaciter ita urget p. 139. Negat Socinus, pla- cari Deum sacris expiatoriis. At contrarium testan- tur Scriptores supra à nobis allegati, qui placandi vo- cem ad exprimenda ea sacra usurpant: unde & illa nata est phrasis in dicto loco ad Hebræos posita ἱλάσκε- σθαι ἁμαρτίας, placare peccata, id est, placando DE- UM peccata expiare. Satisfactionem nullam Soci- nus in sacris expiatoriis agnoscit. Atqui vox ipsa piandi sive expiandi nihil aliud proprie significat, quam luere: passimque autores à nobis citati, cum ex- piare volunt περικαθάιζειν, dicunt, dare sanguinem pro sanguine, vitam pro vita, animam pro anima: San- guine aliquid emere, morte alterius salutem consequi. Neque voces Ebrææ hic dissident. Nam Caphar & Kipper non modo est tegere, sed & redimere Exod. 21, 30. Ps. 49, 8. & placare Genes. 32, 20. atque inde porro expiare. Chitta est luere Genes. 31, 39. Unde & hoc cœ- pit ad expiationem significandam usurpari. Hæc omnia ibidem Grotius. Nunc vero quasi pœnitu- dine istorum ductus, ne verbo istius surrogationis, placationis, satisfactionis mentionem facit, ac ne re- mittit quidem unquam ad hunc Socino oppositum librum, uti ex adverso non raro ad ea, quæ Socino in Anabaptistis grata alibi abs se tradita, remittere consvevit.

## 17:3
Vers. 3. IF HE SHALL KILL AN OX OR A SHEEP, OR A GOAT) Namely, an offering to the Lord, which is here sub-understood from the following verse, καθ' ὑπόζευγμα, or by trajection.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SI OCCIDERIT BOVEM AVT OVEM, SIVE CAPRAM) Nempe oblationem Domino, quod ex versu sequenti hic subintelligitur, καθ' ὑπόζευγμα, aut per trajectionem.

## 17:4
Vers. 4. AND SHALL NOT OFFER IT AT THE DOOR OF THE TABERNACLE] What the LXX add here, ὡς τε ποιῆσαι αὐτὸ εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα ἢ σωτήριον κυρίῳ δεκτὸν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, should have been placed after those words ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς: and then follow: καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τῆς σκηνῆς τῆ μαρτυρίς μὴ ἐνέγκῃ αὐτὸ, ὥς τε προσενέγκαι δῶρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπέναντι τῆς σκηνῆς κυρίε, κὴι λογισθήσεται τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ αἷμα. But two versions have been confused: one which had applied a convenient interpretation to those general words, the other which followed the Hebrew κατὰ πόδας: whence the second repetition is empty, which also flowed from the Greek LXX into the Samaritan. For the Samaritan codices which we now have were made according to Greek exemplars, from the time when the Samaritans were forced by Justinian to accept Christianity.

The ordinary place of offering was the tabernacle. Yet the sacrifices of Samuel (1 Sam. 16 and 17), of David (1 Paral. 21), of Elijah (1 Kings 18) are not to be condemned, provided that they offered them elsewhere either by a peculiar command or by divine impulse.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET NON OBTULERIT AD OSTIUM TA- BERNACULI ] Quod hic addunt LXX. ὡς τε ποιῆσαι αὐτὸ εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα ἢ σωτήριον κυρίῳ δεκτὸν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, poni debuerat post illa ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς: & deinde se- qui: καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τῆς σκηνῆς τῆ μαρτυρίς μὴ ἐνέγκῃ αὐτὸ, ὥς τε προσενέγκαι δῶρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπέναντι τῆς σκηνῆς κυρίε, κὴι λογισθήσεται τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ αἷμα. Sed con- fulæ sunt duæ versiones: altera quæ interpretamentum com- modum generalibus illis verbis adhibuerat, altera quæ He- bræum κατὰ πόδας sequebatur: unde secunda repetitio in- anis, quæ & ex Græco LXX. in Samaritanum fluxit. Nam Samaritani quos nunc habemus codices facti sunt ad Græca exemplaria, ex quo Samaritani ab Justiniano coacti sunt su- scipere Christianismum.

LOcus ordinarius oblationis erat tabernaculum. Non damnanda tamen Sacrificia Samuelis 1. Sam. 16. & 17. Davidis 1. Paral. 21. Eliæ 1. Reg. 18. siquidem illi vel mandato peculiari, vel impulsu di- vino alibi ea obtulerint.

## 17:7
Vers. 7. THEY SHALL NO MORE SACRIFICE THEIR HOSTS TO DEMONS) Namely, to the τραγομόρφοις (goat-formed ones), which are שעירים to the Hebrews, whence perhaps the name of Satyrs. Thus also the Chaldean understood it here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NEQVAQVAM ULTRA IMMOLABUNT HOSTIAS SUAS DÆMONIBUS ) Nempe τραγομόρφοις, qui Hebræis שעירים, unde forte nomen Satyrorum. Sic & Chaldæus hic accepit.

## 17:10
Vers. 10. AND OF THE STRANGERS, WHO SOJOURN AMONG THEM) For this commandment is among those which were given to the sons of Noah: as we said at Genesis 6, 4.

I WILL SET MY FACE AGAINST THAT SOUL] I will be vehemently angry with him. Thus also below 20, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET DE ADVENIS, QVI PEREGRINANTUR INTER EOS) Est enim hoc præceptum inter ea quæ Noæli- beris sunt data: ut diximus ad Geneseos 6, 4.

OBFIRMABO FACIEM MEAM CONTRA ANI- MAM ILLIVS] Irascar illi vehementer. Sic & infra 20,3.

## 17:11
Vers. 11. FOR THE SOUL OF THE FLESH IS IN THE BLOOD) See what is above at Genesis 9, 4. Hence Macrobius (Saturn. 3, c. 5) explains animal hosts from that of Virgil, 'With blood you have appeased the winds,' and from what follows, 'And by blood must a return be sought, and with a soul must you propitiate.' To which place Servius: 'The skill of Pontifical Law seems indeed to have made mention of an animal host, when he says: "and with a soul must you propitiate" (Argolica); for he said both soul and to propitiate, using a pontifical word.' Likewise to the third of the Aeneid: 'A soul is never without blood.' And to the beginning of the fourth: 'In the blood is the soul.' And afterwards: 'For there are two kinds of hosts: one in which the will of GOD is sought through the entrails, the other in which the soul alone is consecrated to GOD.' Whence also the aruspices call them animal hosts. And to that of the fifth Aeneid: 'He would give a better soul for the death of Dares.' For he gives an animal host. And in book IX: 'He vomits his purple soul,' according to those who say that the soul is blood. And in book X. at the end: In arms he pours out his soul in surging gore, the seat of which most wish to be the blood. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call that by which the body lives and feels נפש, by which we understand חיות. Philo: αἷμα τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσία ζωτικῆς, καὶ πνεῦμα τῆς ψυχῆς ουσία λογικῆς.

THAT UPON THE ALTAR YOU MAY MAKE EXPIATION FOR YOUR SOULS) Ovid, Fasti VII. This soul we give to you in place of a better one.

He philosophizes there (on Gen. 9:4) likewise only about the soul in the blood, that blood is to the vital soul what oil is to a lamp, from Plutarch and others. Here, however, he brings together poets and other exotic authors for the matter; he sticks to the bark, he scorns the kernel, like a stork licking only the vessel, not reaching the porridge. For this authentic text is most famous, especially in Ecclesiastical Agendas and Mosaic Pontifical law. Which brings light to the expiatory figures. But about this, our author is completely mute in this place, like a Serapian frog. He seems to have treated sacred things not with a sacred mind, but with a profane one, since he heaps up nothing but the sayings of profane authors, however they may have occurred, whether Trojan or Rutulian, they are held by him with no distinction. Our blessed Frantzius, loc. cit., reproves, and not undeservedly, that in Socinus, because that most illustrious passage Lev. 17:11, from which perhaps the Apostle derived that summary of his in Heb. 9:22, without the shedding of blood there is no remission, since in this passage of Lev. 17:11 is situated the greatest part and

Latin:

Vers. 11. QVIA ANIMA CARNIS IN SANGUINE EST) Vide quæ supra Geneseos 9, 4. Hinc animales hostias exponit Macrobius Saturn. 3. c. 5. ex illo Virgilii, Sanguine placastis ventos. & eo quod sequitur, Sanguine quærendi reditus, animaque litandum. Ad quem locum Servius: Videtur sane peritia Juris Pontifica- lis animalis hostiæ mentionem fecisse, cum dicit: animaque li- tandum Argolica; nam & animam dixit & litare, verbo pon- tificali usus. Item ad III. Æneidos: Anima sine sanguine nun- quam est. Et ad initium quarti: In sanguine anima est. Et postea: Duo enim genera hostiarum sunt: unum in quo volun- tas DEI per exta exquiritur, alterum in quo sola anima DEO sacratur. Vnde etiam aruspices animales hostias appellant. Et ad quinti Æneidos illud: Meliorem animam pro morte Da- retis. Nam animalem hostiam dat Et libro IX. Purpuream vo- mit ille animam, secundum eos qui animam sanguinem dicunt. Et libro X. in fine: In arma undanti cruore animam diffundit, cujus sedem plerique sanguinem esse volunt. Hebræorum mos est id quo corpus veget ac sentit vocare נפש, quo intelli- gimus חיות. Philo : αἷμα τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσία ζωτικῆς, καὶ πνεῦμα τῆς ψυχῆς ουσία λογικῆς.

VT SUPER ALTARE IN EO EXPIETIS PRO ANI- MABUS VESTRIS) Ovidius Fastorum VII. Hanc animam vobis pro meliore damus.

Philosophatur ibi (ad Genes. 9, 4.) itidem so- lum de anima in sanguine, quod animæ vitali san- guis id sit, quod oleum lychno, ex Plutarcho, & aliis. Hic vero Poetas & alios exoticos in rem confert; In cortice hæret, nucleum spernit, in- star ciconiæ vas tantum lambens, pultem non attingens. Celeberrima enim imprimis est hæc authentica in Agendis bisse Ecclesiasticis & jure Pon- tificali Mosaico. Quæ lucem adfert figuris expi- atoriis. De quo vero mutus plane est hoc loco Noster, instar ranæ Serapiæ. Sacra non sacra mente videtur tractasse, sed prophana, quum nil nisi prophanorum autorum dicta congerat, quomodocunque obvenerint, Tros Rutulique fuant, ipsi nullo discrimine habentur. Reprehendit, nec immerito id in Socino B. Frantzius noster loc. cit. quod locum illustrissimum Levit. 17, 11. ex quo for- san suum illud derivavit compendium Apostolus Ebr. 9, 22. sine sanguinis effusione non fit remissio, cum in hoc loco Levit. 17, 11. sita sit maxima pars &

## 17:15
Verse 15. THE SOUL THAT SHALL HAVE EATEN THAT WHICH DIED OF ITSELF) From this Pythagoras took the idea of abstaining from θνησείδιων κρεῶν (flesh of animals that died of themselves). Laertius, Aelian 4. 17, and Iamblichus make mention of this. It was not permitted for the Flaminica to have shoes made from animals that died of themselves. Now, those are called morticina which were made from cattle that died of their own accord. Thus Servius on Aeneid IV: but Porphyry also teaches us in book 3 of On Abstinence from Animal Food that others abstained from animals that died of themselves, and in book 4 he specifically reported the same thing about those who were initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries. Besides these, the Hebrews counted among the θνησιμαίοις (carrion) living creatures not rightly slaughtered, according to the law of Deuteronomy 12:15. Maimonides provides a medical reason for this law, saying that θνησιμαĩα (carrion) are digested with difficulty.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ANIMA QVÆ COMEDERIT MORTICI- NVM) Hinc sumsit Pythagoras θνησείδιων κρεῶν ἀπέχεσθαι. Meminere Laertius, Ælianus 4. 17. & Jamblichus. Flaminicæ non licebat foleas morticinas habere. Morticinæ autem di- cuntur, quæ de pecudibus sua sponte mortuis fiebant. Ita Servius ad IV. Æneidos: sed & alios a morticinis abstinuisse docet nos Porphyrius libro 3. de Abstinentia ab animalibus, qui & libro 4. idem speciatim prodidit de iis, qui Eleusiniis initiabantur. Hebræi præter has θνησιμαίοις accensebant animantes non rite jugulatas, ex lege Deuteronomii 12, 15. Causam hujus legis affert medicam Maimonides, dicens θνη- σιμαĩα difficulter concoqui.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

Illicit marriages.

Verse 1. HE SHALL LIVE IN THEM) A long life. The Chaldean here. BUT Christ explains it concerning eternal life in Luke 10, and Paul in Galatians 3, and indeed the Chaldean also in this place. Which we have already noted before, and it was observed by R. Menasseh Ben Israel in On the Resurrection of the Dead, book 1, chapter 10, p. 72. Toward the end of Deuteronomy it is read: Set your heart unto all those things which I testify among you this day, etc., because it is not a vain thing for you, for that is your life and through this thing you shall prolong your days upon the land. By these words it is shown that there is a double reward: Spiritual, because that is your life. As it is also said elsewhere: And you shall keep my statutes and my judgments, because a man shall do them and shall live in them. There is no doubt that that life is not bodily life: for he who observes the precepts of the law diligently does not prolong his life any longer than any Gentile whatsoever. For thus the divine Onkelos explains that ויחי בהון לחיי עלמי (and he shall live in them to eternal life.) The other, bodily reward, is soon declared by those words, and through this thing you shall prolong your days upon the land. Wherefore souls also are immortal, because a Spiritual reward is promised to them here.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

Conjugia illicita.

Vers. 1. VIVET IN EIS Vitam longam. Chaldæus hic. AT de vita æterna explicat Christus Luc. 10. & Paulus Gal. 3. imo etiam Chaldæus hoc in loco. Quod antea jam notavimus, & R. Menassi Ben Is- rael observatum fuit de resurrect. mortuor. lib. 1. cap. 10. p. 72. Circa finem Deuteronomii legitur: Ad- jicite animum vestrum ad omnia illa, quæ ego commen- do vobis hodie &c. quia non est res inanis vobis, nam illa vita vestra & hac re prolongabitis dies super ter- ram. His verbis ostenditur, quod duplex præmium sit: Spirituale, quia illa est vestra vita. Uti etiam alibi di- citur: Et custodietis mandata mea, & præcepta mea, quia faciet homo illa, & vivet cum illis. Non dubium est, quin ea vita, non sit vita corporalis: nam qui obser- vat sedulo præcepta legis, non diutius protollit vitam, quam gentilis quilibet. Ita enim divinus Anquelos illud explicat ויחי בהון לחיי עלמי & vivent cum il- lis vitam æternam.) Alterum præmium corporale mox declaratur illis verbis, & hac re prolongabitis dies ve- stros super terram. Quare animæ etiam sunt immor- tales, quia hic præmium eis Spirituale promittitur.

## 18:3
Verse 3. I AM THE LORD YOUR GOD) To whom belongs the right of enacting laws. Where the divine law speaks, let human customs be silent.

Latin:

Vers. 3. EGO DOMINVS DEVS VESTER) Cui jus le- ges ferendi. Vbi loquitur lex divina, sileant mores humani.

## 18:6
Verse 6. NONE OF YOU SHALL APPROACH TO ANY THAT IS NEAR OF KIN TO HIM) This is not to be taken so generally as the Greek Christians did, whose opinion on this matter Basil explains to Diodorus, but of those women who are included in the following words. See what we have said in book 2 of On the Law of War and Peace, chapter 5, § 13.

TURPITUDE) ערוה, that is, nakedness; the Hebrews call those parts which are shameful when naked. Therefore the LXX [use] ἀσχημοσύνην (shamefulness). Paul, 1 Cor. 12:23, [uses] τὰ ἀσχήμονα (the uncomely parts).

Latin:

Vers. 6. AD PROXIMAM SANGVINIS SVI NON AC- CEDET) Non hoc ita generaliter sumendum, ut fecere Græ- ci Christiani, quorum hac de re sententiam explicat Basilius ad Diodorum, sed de iis feminis, quæ sunt comprehensæ verbis sequentibus. Vide quæ a nobis dicta libro 2. de Jure belli ac pacis cap. 5. §. 13.

TVRPITVDINEM) ערוה, id est, nuditatem Hebræi vo- cant partes quæ nudæ dedecent. Ideo LXX. ἀσχημοσύνην. Paulus 1. Cor. 12, 23. τὰ ἀσχήμονα.

## 18:8
FOR IT IS THY FATHER'S NAKEDNESS) The father has uncovered.

Latin:

TVRPITVDO ENIM PATRIS TVI EST) Pater nu- davit.

## 18:9
Verse 9. WHICH IS BORN AT HOME OR ABROAD] That is, whether the mother bore her from your father, or from another marriage, which is to be taken similarly regarding the father, so that not only sisters from both parents, but also from one, are understood to be prohibited, as the Chaldean [says] here. Some interpret 'born abroad' as born from fornication.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVÆ DOMI VEL FORIS GENITA EST] Id est, sive mater eam genuerit ex tuo patre, sive ex alio matri- monio, quod similiter de patre sumendum, ut non tantum sorores ex utroque parente, sed & ex altero prohibitæ intelli- gantur, ut hîc Chaldæus. Foris genitam quidam interpre- tantur ex stupro.

## 18:11
Vers. 11. THE NAKEDNESS OF THE DAUGHTER OF THY FATHER'S WIFE THOU SHALT NOT UNCOVER] There is present in the Hebrew 'of the daughter of thy Father': but because concerning a sister by the same father, as the LXX speak here, it was sufficiently provided for above in verse 9, therefore the Sadducees took the word מולדת here concerning the stepdaughter of the Father, whom the Father had adopted, just as I have noted that ילד and γεννᾶν are sometimes taken at Luke 3. Indeed, even by Roman law we are forbidden to marry sisters made so by adoption, as long as the adoption remains, l. per adoptionem. D. de Ritu nuptiarum. Institutionibus de nuptiis. §. Inter eas.

This constitution was exposed to many Disputations, from which some among the Calvinists, J. Piscator the Theologian, and Antonius Matthæus the Jurist, and among the Papists Steph. Menochius the Jesuit, and then also among our own, Dn. D. Dan. Cramerus, have disapproved of the marriage of step-siblings; but above others, a friend of mine, while he lived, M. Sam. Bohl, disputed fervently against it from the sources at the Academy of Rostock, in his tract against the Marriage of Step-siblings, and likewise in his Vindications, and his very brief Response to the necessary Defense. But what Dn. D. J. Cothmannus, of pious memory, argued against the same for the sake of asserting the common opinion in his Necessary defense, and brief Refutation, he responded very briefly. I say the common opinion: since the marriage of step-siblings is not only lawful by civil and Canon law, but is also defended by theologians with great consensus as being in no way prohibited by divine law. Moreover, those who judge that this is prohibited by this constitution, you may see departing into three different opinions. The first is that it is absolutely prohibited: The second, that it is restricted and in a certain case, namely when a new offspring of the Parents intervenes in the marriage of the step-siblings. The others defend the former; M. Bohl alone defends the latter, rendering the text thus: The nakedness of the daughter of thy Father's wife (which wife bears to thy Father) this one being thy sister, do not uncover her nakedness. The third, therefore, is that of Grotius here, who likewise explains the law with the Sadducees in a certain case, namely if the Father has adopted the stepdaughter, and proves that adoption by the force of civil law is an impediment to marriage. But whatever may be the case regarding civil law, how, I ask, will it be proved that the marriage of step-siblings is forbidden here by divine law, if the Father has adopted the stepdaughter? That the word מולדת is to be understood concerning adoption will be taught by no example from the Scriptures, which rather, by the force of its origin and the usage of Scripture, implies generation: as Grotius himself confesses, that in the Hebrew there is present 'OF THE DAUGHTER of thy Father'. The Vulgate renders it, 'WHOM SHE HAS BORNE to thy Father'. The principal objection of Grotius, as well as of the others, is that a new interdict is held here in v. 11, which was not yet made in v. 9, lest a tautology be established in these prohibited degrees. But it is answered that not every repetition is a tautology, but that which is done without reason and is idle. Moreover, the causes of the repetition are brought forward, both a more express declaration, so that a special law in v. 11 might be added to the general law in v. 9, and the severity of the prohibition on account of the frequency of such marriages among the Egyptians and Canaanites. Bohlius himself indeed admits the repetition of the same in the same verse: he who urged this so sharply, NEVER, NEVER, NEVER in the law of Moses in the promulgation of different laws is the same law repeated, de matrim. Comprivign. fol. 67. But a little before, in v. 9, he asserted that three different sisters are described, p. 65, and explained them in such a way that he had need to admit a repetition: I say therefore 1. The daughter of my Father is my Sister, who has one Father and a different mother with me. 2. The daughter of my mother is a sister, who has one and the same mother with me, although a different Father. 3.
