The daughter of the mother of the parent at home is the daughter of my mother and Father. But the daughter of the mother of the parent abroad is that which HAS JUST BEEN DESCRIBED, my sister, who has one mother with me, but not a Father. But she had already been mentioned, and called the daughter of my mother. Here therefore, according to that Bohlian explanation, the same law, the same interdict is repeated, and that in the same verse. Furthermore, those who establish a special repetition in v. 11 say that it does not treat of a step-sibling here, taken from another wife, but of a son born from this very marriage, who is prohibited from marrying the daughter of his mother brought into the paternal home, because it is a kinship, or a kinswoman of the Father, i.e., made his nearest kinswoman through the marriage of the mother, and she has succeeded into the place of a daughter, and is a sister of that Son by the same mother, as is explained in Gerhard de Conjug. §. 357. or concerning the daughter of kinship or paternal birth not to be married, who is a sister by the same father, as she is called here by the LXX Interpreters and is rendered by the Blessed Luther, 'die deinem Vater gebohren ist', which sense seems to others more convenient than the former. Some, however, do not think there is any need for a repetition to be posited here: where a triple opinion again occurs. The first is that of Ludov. de Dieu in his animadversions on this passage, p. 89. Diffe- rentiam nos hanc statuimus. V.9. the matter concerns the son of a second marriage, who is prohibited from marriage with a half-sister from a first marriage, whether she be the daughter of the father, i.e., whom the father had by a deceased spouse, or the daughter of the mother, i.e., whom his mother had conceived by a deceased husband. But v. 11 concerns the son of a first marriage, who is prohibited from marriage, not with a stepdaughter, but with a half-sister from a second marriage, whom his stepmother bore to his own father, who is therefore called the daughter of the wife of thy father, that is, of the stepmother, (for uxor Patris among the Hebrews is a description of a stepmother) but in such a way that she is also said to be born of thy father, so that a stepdaughter may not be understood. Although indeed one follows from the other, it is nevertheless not entirely the same, for since the son of a second marriage cannot call his father's deceased wife from a first marriage his stepmother, but only her whom the father marries in a second marriage, some distinction is deservedly established here. For since the son of a second marriage could have said, 'This daughter, whom my father begot from a prior marriage, is from such a mother as I have never acknowledged as a mother, neither by the law of nature nor by civil law, seeing that she died before I was born. Therefore, her marriage is lawful for me.' God forbids this to happen in v. 9, because, he says, she is the daughter of your father. But since the son of a first marriage could have retorted that his mother is indeed called a stepmother by civil law, yet that he has a different relationship with her than the son of a second marriage, and that marriage with the sister of the prior marriage is forbidden to him, because she would necessarily exceed him in age, whereas he would exceed the sister of the later marriage in age: God forbids this marriage also in v. 11, for the same reason as the former, because she is the daughter of your father, and thus a sister. Another opinion is that in this verse marriage with the daughter of a sister ὁμοπατρίας or ὁμομητρίας is forbidden, namely the second degree in the unequal collateral line (just as in v. 10 immediately preceding, the second degree in the direct line was forbidden), so that no one may join to himself a granddaughter from a sister ἑτεροθαλεῖ: since a granddaughter is also called a daughter by the Hebrews. But the third opinion is this, namely that in this eleventh verse marriage with a full sister ἀυτοκασιγνήτης is forbidden; but in the ninth verse, marriage with a sister ὁμοπατρίας or ὁμομητρίας: by which arrangement there will be no need for that Bohlian repetition. Which opinion is not disapproved of by our blessed Gerhard, and has been adopted by Luc. Osiander in his Paraphrase: For he rendered it thus: 'The nakedness of the daughter of your father's wife, whom she bore to your father, and is your sister (by father and mother) you shall not uncover:' (that is, you shall not marry a full sister, who is your sister by reason of both parents.) He explained the ninth verse thus: 'The nakedness of your sister, whether by your mother, who was born at home or abroad, you shall not uncover,' i.e., you shall not marry her whom your father begot by another wife than your mother (for she is said to be born at home), nor shall you marry her whom your mother bore by another man before she married your father: for she is said to be born abroad. But if a full sister is considered to be described as 'the daughter of your mother, WHOM SHE BORE AT HOME,' why could the 'daughter of your father's wife, whom she bore to him as your father' not be described in the same way?

The difficulty which is raised from the word מוֹלֶדֶת is not resolved in one way. For some render it as a noun of kinship or generation, which meaning of the word cannot be denied with any appearance of truth. See Gen. 24, 4. Num. 10, 30. Esth. 2, 10. etc. 'DAUGHTER OF YOUR FATHER'S WIFE OF THE KINSHIP OF YOUR FATHER.' Junius and Tremellius render it, 'DAUGHTER BORN OF YOUR STEPMOTHER, A KINSWOMAN OF YOUR FATHER,' but Piscator advises that it ought rather to be rendered 'OF YOUR FATHER'S KINSWOMAN,' who, namely, was rendered a kinswoman to him through the marriage of your mother: Others explain it as generation or NATIVITY or paternal offspring. For which it seems to make that, in Ezech. 16, 4, the word is rendered by the LXX as γένεσις, and can be taken concerning birth or nativity, and that in Gen. 43, 7

it is held thus; 'That man asked us diligently, and about our מולדתנו offspring, our children, sons or daughters.' For Joseph inquired about these; the father's lineage was sufficiently known to him, the sons who had sold him were sufficiently known. He wanted to be informed about the grandchildren. Genesis 48, 6, מולדתך אשר הולדת 'your offspring, which you have begotten; your children,' as Ariasmontanus renders it. The LXX, τὰ δὲ ἔκγονα, ἃ ἐὰν γεννήσῃς. Others take it as a verb, and render it: 'WHICH IS BEGOTTEN TO YOUR FATHER,' or 'BORN of your father,' the Chaldean, Arab, R. Aben-Ezra, Pagninus, Ariasmontanus, B. Luther. With whom the LXX Interpreters agree regarding the matter, ὁμοπατρία ἀδελφή σου ἔστιν, which is indeed begotten by the father; And the Vulgate, 'WHOM SHE BORE to your father.' Those therefore who explained it passively seem either to have read מוּלֶדֶת in the passive for מוֹלֶדֶת or to have rendered it according to the sense, not the word. But if it is the Active Hiphil here, and the daughter of the wife of my father begetting to my father is understood, it will not immediately be a step-sister, whom a half-sister could also be understood to be here, indeed the pronoun אשר could be understood, which is not rarely omitted, so that the sense here might be, 'the nakedness of the daughter of your father's wife אשר מולדת אביך whom (the daughter) your father's wife bore to your father, your sister, do not uncover her nakedness;' as the Vulgate rendered it, 'whom she bore to your father.' And similarly v. 9, 'whom she bore (your mother) at home or abroad;' which is not badly explained, whether she was born legitimately or illegitimately, whether in marriage or outside of it, as Radolphus, Lyranus, Abulensis, B. Gerhard interpret.

The principal argument which is urged against the marriage of step-siblings is this: Whatever person I cannot marry as a blood relative, I am also unable to marry the immediate blood relative of that person. But I cannot marry the new offspring of new parents, because he is a blood relative to me. Therefore, I cannot marry his sister either. But the major proposition is not simply true; since it is not permitted to marry even my paternal aunt as a blood relative, Lev. 18, 2. Whose daughter, however, who is her immediate blood relative, it is not forbidden to marry by divine or civil law. The opposing party indeed says that this is forbidden by divine law, but in that they are contradicted by theologians and all jurists, nor can anything be brought forward by which it might be solidly taught that this is forbidden. Similarly, I cannot marry my brother's wife, and yet it is not forbidden to marry her immediate blood relative, namely the sister of a sister-in-law. The major proposition, therefore, cannot be accepted absolutely. The blessed Chemnitius warned of this in Loci Communes, part III, p. 545. Certain Popes wrongly understood that prohibition, that no one should approach his near of kin, as if one must abstain from all blood relatives as far as kinship can be known. But the emphasis of the Hebrew words shows that it is forbidden for anyone to marry a relative who approaches closely to his own flesh, or it is forbidden to marry the flesh of his flesh, that is, one who is either propagated from my flesh, or from whose flesh I have been propagated, or who has been propagated with me from the same flesh. The blessed Chemnitius then adds: From this, a judgment can also be formed concerning affinity, insofar as marriages are also prohibited in that. A husband and wife are one flesh. Therefore, to both there is שאר, that is, he has the remains of his flesh in the relatives of his spouse, and that affinity is a closeness forbidden to him. This is from the blessed Chemnitius. But between step-siblings there is only affinity in the broad sense. A new offspring cannot reconcile for them either a mutual communion of blood between themselves, because no new generation occurs between them, and therefore no new communion of blood can arise, or even affinity strictly so called. For this is a bond of persons contracted by new marriages, which definition does not fit step-siblings, with a new offspring being added. Step-siblings indeed with a new offspring are one flesh or blood relations, but compared among themselves they are not either blood relations or affines properly speaking, just as before birth, so also after birth. Then if a marriage has been celebrated between step-siblings, where no new fetus existed on the part of the parties, which indeed is later obtained by divine blessing, certainly according to that opinion that marriage would have to be dissolved, as being nefarious; which is just as inconvenient, as it is absurd, that by a new birth a new communion of blood is reconciled for the parents, or an affinity impeding marriages. Grotius on v. 6 thus limits the Rule: He shall not approach his near of kin, this is not to be taken so generally, as the Greek Christians did, whose opinion on this matter Basil explains to Diodorus, but concerning those women who are included in the following words: So also Radulphus Comment. on this place. A man is not prohibited from approaching any relative whatsoever, but only her whom the following discourse will determine. Which we admit at least in such a way that it is understood that these prohibitions pertain not only to persons expressly named, but also to degrees equally distant, lest some ὑπεξέλόν τι be fostered here. For the Papists, whom Grotius willingly gratifies, are accustomed to defend this hypothesis; that those persons who are not expressed here, their marriages are not prohibited, so that, of course, it may be intact for their Pope to dispense by the intervention of money in degrees which are firmly inferred from analogy to be prohibited by divine law. But where there is the same reason, there is the same law. Concerning which see D. Gerhard on marriage §. 275.

Latin:

Vers. 11. TVRPITVDINEM FILLÆ VXORIS PATRIS TUI NON DISCOOPERIES] Adest in Hebræo natæ Patris tui: quia vero περὶ ὁμοπατρίας ἀδελφῆς, ut hic loquuntur LXX. satis cautum erat supra 9. ideo Sadducæi vocem מולדת hic sumebant de Patris privigna, quam Pater ad- optasset, quomodo & ילד & γεννᾶν sumi interdum notavi mus ad Luc. 3. Sane & Romano jure vetamur, Sorores per adoptionem factas ducere, quamdiu manet adoptio l. per ad- optionem. D. de Ritu nuptiarum. Institutionibus de nuptiis. §. Inter eas.

Constitutio hæc multis Disputationibus exposi- ta fuit, è qua matrimonium comprivignorum è Calvi- nianis nonnulli J. Piscator Theologus, & Antonius Matthæus JCtus, è Pontificiis Steph. Menochius Jesui- ta, tum è nostris quoque Dn. D. Dan. Cramerus re- probarunt, sed præ aliis fervide adversus illud è fontibus disputavit in Acad. Rostochiensi amicus, dum viveret, mihi intimus M. Sam. Bohl. tract. con- tra Matrimonium Comprivign. Vindiciis item, & Responso breviss. ad necessariam Defens. Quod vero contra eundem pro adserenda communi sen- tentia propugnavit Dn. D. J. Cothmannus p. m. Ne- cessaria defensione, & Refutatione brevi resp. breviss. Communem dico sententiam: Siquidem Compri- vignorum matrimonium non jure civili, & Canoni- co solum licitum sit, sed a Theologis etiam ceu jure divino minime prohibitum magno consensu defen- datur. Cæterum qui hac constitutione id prohibe- ri censent, in tres diversas videas abire sententias. Prima est, quod absolute id prohibeatur: Altera, quod restricte & in certo casu, cum nempe novus par- tus Parentum intercedit comprivignorum matrimo- nio. Priorem cæteri; Posteriorem solus M. Bohl. de- fendit, textum ita reddens; Nuditatem filiæ uxoris Patris tui (quæ uxor Patri tuo parit) hæc cum sit soror tua, noli detegere nuditatem ejus. Tertia ergo hic est Grotii, qui certo itidem casu, si nempe Privignam Pa- ter adoptarit, cum Sadducæis legem explicat, & ad- optionem vi juris civilis impedimentum matrimonii es- se probat. Sed quicquid de jure civili sit, divino ju- re hic comprivignorum matrimonium, si Pater ad- optarit privignam, interdici, quomodo obsecro probabitur? Vocem מולדת de adoptione intelli- gendam esse, nullo exemplo e Scripturis docebitur, quæ potius, vi originis & usus Scripturæ generatio- nem infert: uti Grotius ipse fatetur, in Ebræo adesse NATÆ Patris tui. Vulgatus reddit, quam PEPERIT Patri tuo. Præcipua ut Grotii, ita & reliquorum ob- jectio est, quod novum hic interdictum v. 11. habea- tur, quod v. 9. factum nondum sit, ne tautologia in his gradibus prohibitis constituatur. Respondetur au- tem, non omnem repetitionem esse ταυτολογίαν, sed quæ citra rationem fit & otiosa est. Causæ autem repetitionis adferuntur tum expressior declaratio, ut ad legem generalem v. 9. accederet specialis v. 11. tum prohibitionis severitas ob frequentiam talium nuptia- arum inter Ægyptios & Cananæos. Repetitionem ejusdem versu eodem sane admittit ipse Bohlius: qui tam acriter hoc ursit, NUNQUAM, NUNQUAM, NUN- QUAM in lege Mosis in diversarum legum promulgatio- ne lex eadem repetitur, de matrim. Comprivign. fol. 67. Paulo ante autem v. 9. tres describi sorores diver- sas asseruit p. 65. atque ita easdem explicavit, ut ad- mittere repetitionem opus habuerit: Dico ergo 1. Filia Patris mei est Soror mea, quæ mecum habet unum Patrem & aliam matrem. 2. Filia matris meæ est so- ror, quæ mecum unam eandemq; habet matrem, quam- vis diversum Patrem. 3. Filia matris Parentis domi est filia matris & Patris mei. Filia autem matris paren- tis foras est ea, QUÆ MODO DESCRIPTA est, soror mea, quæ mecum unam habet matrem, sed non Patrem. At ea commemorata jam erat, & dicta filia matris meæ. Hic ergo secundum Bohlianam illam explicationem eadem lex, idem interdictum repe- titur, idque eodem versu. Porro qui repetitionem specialem v. 11. constituunt, non de privigno hic agi dicunt, ex alia uxore suscepto, sed de filio ex hoc ipso matrimonio genito, qui prohibeatur ducere filiam ma- tris suæ paternæ domui illatam, quod sit cognatio, sive cognata Patris, h. e. per conjugium matris facta ejus- dem cognata proxima, & in filiæ locum successerit, so- rorq; sit Filii illius ὁμομήτριος, ut explicatur apud Gerhardum de Conjug. §. 357. vel de filia cognationis sive nativitatis paternæ non ducenda, quæ soror est ὁμοπάτρια, ut vocatur hic a LXX. Interpp. & a B. Luthero redditur, die deinem Vater gebohren ist, qui sensus priori aliis videtur commodior. Nonnulli ta- men haud opus esse putant, ut hic repetitio statua- tur: ubi triplex iterum occurrit sententia. Prima est Ludov. de Dieu in animadvers. ad h. l. p. 89. Diffe- rentiam nos hanc statuimus. V.9. agitur de filio secun- darum nuptiarum, cui prohibetur conjugium cum di- midia Sorore ex primis nuptiis, sive ea sit filia Patris, i. e. quam Pater ex defuncta conjuge, sive filia matris, i. e. quam mater ejus ex defuncto marito susceperit. At v. 11. agitur de filio primarum nuptiarum, cui prohibetur conjugium, non cum privigna, sed cum dimidia sorore ex secundis nuptiis, quam noverca ejus Patri ipsius pe- perit, que ideo vocatur filia uxoris Patris tui, id est, noverce, (nam uxor Patris apud Ebræos descriptio est noverca) sed sic ut eadem dicatur nata ex Patre tuo, ut ne privigna intelligatur. Etsi vero unum ex altero se- quatur, non tamen esse prorsus idem, quum enim filiǫ se- cundarum nuptiarum defunctam Patris ex primis nu- ptiis uxorem non possit novercam suam dicere, sed eam tantum, quam Pater secundis nuptiis ducit, discrimen hic aliquod merito statuitur. Quoniam enim secunda- rum nuptiarum filius dicere potuisset, hæc filia, quam Pater meus ex priori conjugio suscepit, ex tali matre est, quam ego nec lege nature, nec civili lege matrem un- quam agnovi, quippe ante me natum defunctam. Ergo licitum mihi est ejus conjugium. Vetat id Deus v. 9. fieri, quia, inquit, est Patris tui filia: At quoniam primarum nuptiarum filius regerere potuisset, matrem quidem sibi novercam lege civili dici, aliter tamen secum, quam cum filio secundarum nuptiarum rem habere, huic cum sorore prioris conjugii interdictum esse matrimoni- um, quod hæc illum necessario ætate vinceret, se vero Sororem posterioris conjugii ætate superare: Vetat De- us v. 11. & hoc conjugium, ob eandem causam, ob quam prius, quia nata Patris tui est, tumque Soror. Altera vero sententia est, quod hoc versu prohibeatur con- jugium cum Sororis ὁμοπατρίας vel ὁμομητρίας filia, secundus nempe gradus in linea collaterali inæquali (uti v. 10. immediate præcedenti prohibebatur se- cundus gradus in linea recta) ne quis neptem sibi ex So- rore ἑτεροθαλεῖ jungat: quum neptis etiam Ebræis di- catur filia. Tertia autem sententia est hæc, quod nem- pe Sororis Germanæ ἀυτοκασιγνήτης hic versu unde- cimo; versu autem nono sororis ὁμοπατρίας vel ὁμο- μητρίας conjugium interdictum sit: Quo pacto nec Bohliana illa repetitione opus erit. Quæ sententia B. Gerhardonoftro haud improbatur, & à Luc. Osi- andro in Paraphrasi assumta est: Sic enim reddidit: Turpitudinem filiæ uxoris Patris tui, quam peperit Pa- tri tuo, & est soror tua (ex Patre & matre) non revela- bis: (id est, non duces germanam sororem, quæ utriusque Parentis ratione soror tua sit.) Versum no- num ita exposuit: Turpitudinem sororis tuæ sive ex matre, quæ domi vel foris genita est, non revelabis, i. e. non duces eam, quam Pater tuus ex alia uxore, quam ex matre tua genuit, (ea enim domi genita dicitur, nec eam duces, quam mater tua ex alio Viro, antequam Patri tuo nupsit, genuit: ea enim foris genita dicitur) quod si soror Germana censetur ita describi filia ma- tris tuæ, QUAM PEPERIT DOMI, quidni ita de- scribi posset Filia uxoris Patris tui, quam ipsi ut Pa- tri tuo peperit?

Difficultas, quæ movetur è voce מוֹלֶדֶת non uno modo expeditur. Alii enim reddunt, ut nomen cognationis vel generationis, quæ significatio vocis nulla veri specie negari potest. V. Gen. 24, 4. Num. 10, 30. Esth. 2, 10. &c. FILIÆ UXORIS PATRIS TUI CO- GNATIONIS PATRIS TUI. Junius & Tremellius red- dunt, FILIÆ NATÆ EX NOVERCA TUA COGNATA PATRIS TUI, sed Piscator monet, reddi potius de- bere COGNATÆ PATRIS TUI, quæ scil. reddita est ei cognata per conjugium matris tuæ: Alii expo- nunt generationis sive NATIVITATIS vel prolis PATERNÆ. Pro quibus videtur id facere, quod E- zech. 16, 4. vox ea redditur à LXX. γένεσις, & de geni- tura vel nativitate accipi possit, quodque Gen. 43, 7.

ita habeatur; Diligenter quærebat vir ille de nobis, & מולדתנו prole nostra, liberis nostris, filiis vel filiabus. De his enim Joseph inquisivit; prosapia Patris ipsi satis nota erat, satis noti filii qui ipsum vendiderant. De nepotibus informari volebat Genes. 48, 6. מולדתך אשר הולדת proles tua, quam tu gene- rasti; liberi tui, uti reddit Ariasmontan. LXX. τὰ δὲ ἔκγονα, ἃ ἐὰν γεννήσῃς. Alii pro verbo habent, redduntque: QUÆ GENITA EST PATRI TUO, vel NATÆ Patris tui, Chaldæus, Arabs, R. Aben-Ezra, Pagninus, Ariasmontanus, B. Lutherus. Quibus consonant quoad rem LXX. Interpp. ὁμο- πατρία ἀδελφή σου ἔστιν, quæ utique genita est à Patre; Et vulgata, QUAM PEPERIT Patri tuo. Qui ergo passive exposuerunt, vel legisse videntur pro מוֹלֶדֶת in passivo מוּלֶדֶת vel ad sensum, non ad vocem reddidisse. Quod si Activum Hiphil hîc sit, & filia uxoris Patris mei generantis Patri meo intelligatur, non actutum erit comprivigna, quam intelligi hic etiam possit soror homopatria, imo sub- intelligi possit pronomen אשר quod non raro sub- auditur, ut sensus hic sit, nuditatem filiæ uxoris Pa- tris tui אשר מולדת אביך quam (filiam) peperit Pa- tri tuo Soror tua illa, noli detegere nuditatem ejus; uti reddidit Vulgata, quam peperit Patri tuo. Ac simi- liter v. 9. quam peperit (mater tua) domi vel foras; Quod non male explicatur, sive legitime nata sit, sive illegitime, sive in matrimonio, sive extra, uti Radol- phus, Lyranus, Abulensis, B. Gerhard. interpretantur.

Ratio palmaria, quæ adversus Comprivignorum matrimonium urgetur, hæc est: Quamcunque per- sonam, ut consanguineam ducere non possum, istius per- sonæ immediatam consanguineam etiam ducere ne- queo. At novum partum novorum Parentum ego du- cere non possum, quia est mihi consanguineus. E. nec ejus sororem ducere possum. Sed major propositio non est simpliciter vera; siquidem & amitam meam, ut consanguineam non liceat ducere Lev. 18, 2. Cu- jus tamen filiam ipsi immediate consanguineam du- cere vetitum non est jure divino aut civili. Dicit qui- dem pars adversa, vetitum id esse jure divino, sed in eo Theologis contradicitur, & JCtis omnibus, nec quic- quam adferri potest, quo id vetitum esse solide do- ceatur. Similiter fratris mei uxorem ducere nequeo, & tamen immediate consanguineam illi, Sororem nempe fratriæ ducere, vetitum non est. Major ergo propositio absolute accipi non potest. Monuit de eo B. Chemnitius LL. CC. part. III. p. 545. Pontifices quidam prohibitionem illam, quod nullus ad proximam carnis suæ accedere debuerit, male intellexerunt, quasi ab omnibus Consanguineis, quousque cognatio cognosci potest, abstinendum. Sed emphasis vocabulorum Ebræ- orum ostendit, prohiberi, ne quis ducat propinquam, quæ proxime carni suæ appropinquet, vel prohiberi carnem carnis suæ, h. e. quæ vel ex mea carne propaga- ta est, vel ex cujus carne ego propagatus sum, vel quæ mecum ex eadem carne propagata est. Addit deinde B. Chemnitius: Hinc etiam judicium sumi potest de affinitate, quatenus etiam in illa sint nuptiæ prohibi- tæ. Vir & uxor sunt una caro. E. utrique est שאר, h. e. habet reliquias carnis suæ in conjugis cognatis & illa affinitas, propinquitas est ipsi prohibita. Hæc B. Chemnitius. At inter comprivignos est tantum late dicta affinitas. Novus partus non pot- est illis conciliare vel sanguinis inter se mutuam communionem, quia inter ipsos nova non acce- dit generatio, ideoque nec nova sanguinis oriri potest communio, vel etiam affinitatem stricte ita dictam. Hæc enim vinculum est personarum nuvis nuptiis contractum, quæ definitio non convenit comprivignis, novo accedente partu. Comprivigni quidem cum novo partu sunt una caro vel Consangui- nei, sed inter se collati non sunt vel consanguinei vel affines proprie loquendo, sicut ante partum, ita eti- am post partum. Tum si nuptiæ celebratæ sint inter comprivignos, ubi nullus partium extitit novus fœtus, qui vero postea divina benedictione conse- quatur, utique juxta istam sententiam dissolven- dum foret illud matrimonium, tanquam nefarium; quod perinde inconveniens, uti absurdum est, per novum partum parentum novam conciliari sangui- nis comunionem, aut affinitatem nuptias impedi- entem. Grotius ad v. 6. ita limitat Regulam: Ad pro- ximam sanguinis sui non accedet, non hoc ita generali- ter sumendum, ut fecere Græci Christiani, quorum hac de re sententiam explicat Basilius ad Diodorum, sed de iis fœminis, quæ sunt comprehensæ verbis sequentibus: Sic etiam Radulphus Coñent. in h. l. Non prohibetur homo ad quamlibet propinquam accedere, sed ad eam solum, quam sequens sermo determinabit. Quod ta- men ita saltem admittimus, ut intelligatur, prohi- bitiones hasce non tantum ad personas nominatim expressas, sed etiam ad gradus æque distantes pertine- re, ne ὑπεξέλόν τι hîc foveatur. Solent enim Pontifi- cii, quibus lubenter gratificatur Grotius, tueri hanc hypothesin; quæ personæ non sint hic expressæ, earum nuptias prohibitas non esse, ut nimirum Pontifici suo integrum sit in gradibus, quos lege divina prohi- bitos esse, ex analogia firmiter colligitur, interven- tu pecuniæ dispensare. At ubi par ratio, ibi idem jus. Quo de vid. D. Gerhard. de conjug. §. 275.

## 18:18
Verse 18. THOU SHALT NOT TAKE A WIFE'S SISTER TO HER, TO VEX HER, TO UNCOVER HER NAKEDNESS, BESIDE THE OTHER IN HER LIFETIME) He takes the word 'rival' here improperly for another spouse: whom the Greeks here more happily call ἀντίζηλον. It had gone badly for Jacob in that. Just as the hatreds of brothers are said to be the sharpest, so also are the rivalries of sisters. The Pesikta not undeservedly criticizes here the opinion of the Karaites, who wanted it to be forbidden here to have two wives at the same time, because 'sister' often signifies among the Hebrews some other thing of the same kind. And that opinion has been renewed in our own century by men not unlearned, namely because they do not want anything to be forbidden in the Gospel which was permitted in the Law: for the refuting of whom, those things which were said in the book on the Law of War and Peace II. c. 5. §. 9. will suffice. The law in Deuteronomy is clear enough, permitting multiple wives. Custom, the best interpreter of the law, is added.

That opinion of the Karaites does not seem so worthy of rejection: that simultaneous bigamy is prohibited here. For it cannot be denied that 'sister' often signifies to the Hebrews some other thing of the same kind. See Gen. 26, 31. Ex. 26, 3. Ez. 1, 9. 23. c. 3, 13. Joel 2, 8. But that not a sister properly so called, but another spouse is designated here, seems to be able to be inferred from this: First, because it is not said, as in the preceding, 'thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy wife's sister,' but simply, 'thou shalt not take a wife to a sister' (one wife to another). Then because the reason is not added, which is added in nefarious or incestuous marriages: 'she is thy wife's flesh,' or 'this is a wickedness,' or similar. Whence it appears that the prohibitions of another kind follow here, and that the former ones concerning incestuous marriages have already been dispatched, just as also those which follow are all of another kind. Furthermore, it is not simply prohibited to take a wife to her sister, but in her lifetime. But it is never lawful to marry a sister of one's wife properly so called. Moreover, the added cause 'to vex' is general, and pertains to simultaneous polygamy. For then the other wife murmurs and is afflicted when another is brought in over her, whether she be a sister or any other woman. For in general, the second wives of polygamists are described as being rivals and accustomed to cause distress 1 Sam. 1, 6. But when a sister is married after the wife has died, how can the sister be afflicted, who has already passed away? Added to this is the fact that marriage with a wife's sister had already been prohibited by parity of reason in verse 16: 'thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife, because it is thy brother's nakedness.' For the closeness of flesh is exactly the same in a brother's wife and in a wife's sister. Finally, because polygamy is nowhere else prohibited in the divine law, except for the King in Deut. 17, 6, which however Christ in Matt. 19, 2 and the Apostle in 1 Cor. 6, 16, ch. 7, 5 teach is prohibited to all, it seems to be inferred that it is prohibited by this law. Which reasons, certainly not to be despised for this opinion, that simultaneous polygamy is prohibited by these words, can be urged. Which I see is also defended by Junius and Tremellius on this place. Nor do the authors of the Notes added to the Belgian Bibles disapprove of it.

Although we are unwilling to stubbornly oppose others who understand 'sister' here properly so called, we can by no means rise to support Grotius, because simultaneous polygamy is not prohibited in the law. That the opinion itself, that nothing is forbidden in the Gospel which was permitted in the Law, does not please him, is not surprising, because it has long since pleased him more to agree with Socinus and the Anabaptists. What he argued in book II of the Law of War and Peace, ch. V, §. 9, comes down to this: from the first condition, by which GOD assigned to one male only one female, it appears indeed that it is best and most pleasing to God, and from this it follows that it was always excellent and praiseworthy, yet not so that it would be a wickedness to do otherwise. But that Christ forbade what GOD had joined by institution to be separated by man, by taking from that which is best and most acceptable to God the most worthy matter for the new law. But how will it be proven that a new law has been established here? Or that a law concerning the union of one man and one woman had not been sanctioned before the Gospel? Something other than the primordial law is taught by the commandment in the Decalogue: You shall not commit adultery, and something other is taught by this law in Leviticus 18:18, as has already been shown. And in Malachi 2:14-15, most think that everyone is openly rebuked who, by acting perfidiously against the wife of his youth, brings another in over her, since God made one out of two for the sake of seeking offspring. Christ does not sanction a new law; he refers the Pharisees back to the primordial one. His words are clear, Matthew 19:4: Have you not read that he who made man from the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, AND THEY SHALL BE TWO IN ONE FLESH. The question was one of law, whether it was permitted by divine law for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatsoever? He therefore recalls them to the original sanction. He does not establish a new law, but wishes the matter to be decided by the most ancient law. THEREFORE THEY ARE NO LONGER TWO, BUT ONE FLESH. What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder. If he had introduced a new law, the Pharisees would have immediately opposed him and would have considered him an innovator. Add that Christ testifies with a resounding voice, FROM THE BEGINNING IT WAS NOT SO. That Moses indeed permitted the dismissal of wives on account of the σκληροκαρδιαν (hardness of heart) of the Jews; but from the beginning, by the force of the first constitution, it was not so. The very words themselves, which are brought forward from Genesis 2:24, are cited by Christ as a divine institution, FOR THIS REASON A MAN SHALL LEAVE father and mother AND SHALL CLEAVE to his wife. Which have the force of commanding; just as the rest also; AND THEY SHALL BE two into one flesh; from which Christ seeks the decision: Therefore they are not two, but one flesh. And further: What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder. If this conclusion must be held as a commandment, it is necessary that the premises from which it is deduced also obtain the force of a commandment. Therefore, God did not wish only to testify what is best and most pleasing to himself, otherwise the same would have to be said of Christ also, that he did not prescribe a law, but only testified to that, whose words are no more than those which he brought from Moses, are imperative. It is too clear to teach that Christ, what was lawful FROM THE BEGINNING, what was less so. And unless the law of marriage was established there, it will nowhere be established. Which is absurd. Therefore, with great consensus, the Doctors of the Church here fix the matrimonial law. Ignatius in Epist were given at the beginning of creation. Fulgent. de stat. vid. Epist. 2: Marriage is not from the dregs of sin, but from the institution of God. Chrys. ad Matth. XX. hom. LXIII. confirms this at length: See the wisdom of the Master, who, when asked if it were lawful, lest they be disturbed, brought forward the ancient opinion, placed the confirmation from Scripture, showing that this is the COMMAND of God and the Father of all. For he did not say, because he made only one man and one woman, but also, because he ORDERED that one should be joined to one. For if he had wished another wife also to be taken, he would have fashioned many women for the one man created. But now, by the knot of creation and SANCTION, he taught thoroughly that one must be joined to one perpetually and never be rescinded. This LAW, therefore, although it may seem to be promulgated by me now, was nevertheless most diligently SANCTIONED from the beginning of time. And a little later: Then, the ancient Law having been read through, which persists firm as much in words as in things, and relies on the authority of the lawgiver, he also interprets and sanctioned the law with great power. Thus he shows that divorce is both against nature and against the law. Against nature, indeed, because flesh is cut; but against the law, because when God has joined and ordered not to separate, you yourselves have dared to act against the PRECEPTS OF GOD. He adds a reason, which we also add here: But if Christ had been opposed to the O.T., he certainly would not have contended for Moses, nor would he have confirmed those things which were once done from the beginning, nor would he have striven to show that his own things agree with the ancient ones. Similarly, Jerome in h.l. says that the NATURAL LAW and the first opinion of God are here opposed to the second, which was granted not by the will of God, but by the necessity of those sinning. And certainly the Lord, he says, had not brought forward HIS OWN OPINION, but had remembered the COMMANDMENT of God of the old history. And Augustine l. 19. contra Faustum c. 29: Thus the Lord declared by the testimony of the same law what the LAW both commanded the good and permitted to the hard. Ambrose lib. 1. de Abraam c. 4. indeed brings forward in excuse of Abraham's deed, that he took a handmaid, because before the law of Moses adultery does not seem to have been forbidden: God, he says, although he praised marriage in Paradise, had not condemned adultery. But he does not acquiesce in this defense, he brings forward others; that he did it not from any heat of wandering lust, but from a desire of seeking posterity, when there was a scarcity of the human race after the flood, as also of religion, and indeed with the wife herself as author: Nay, Ambrose added that God had imposed penance for this deed upon Abraham, and for that reason had also demanded circumcision. It is not idle that after this God, because he approved his other works, said to him for the penance of this deed: I am God, walk before me, and be without complaint, irreprehensible, so that your wife may not complain of you, nor anyone reproach your deeds. Is not circumcision of the flesh evidently a precept of chastity, so that one may cut away the lust of the flesh and restrain desires untamed by luxury and lasciviousness? For by the word of circumcision it is prescribed that the stench of all impurity be wiped away, and the incentive of lust be taken away. Ambrose also added a third defense: Those things which Abraham did, to conceive offspring from a handmaid, are in figure and spoken according to allegory. Let us recognize, therefore, that since these things which happened in figure were not a crime for them; they will be for us, if we are unwilling to avoid those things written for our correction.

Grotius appeals to the law in Deuteronomy c. 21, 15, which he thinks is clear enough, and to custom as the best interpreter of the law. But that law is not so clear for simultaneous polygamy: It can be taken as successive. If a man has had two wives successively, one having died or been divorced. Nor is polygamy approved there, but only a case is formed, that being posited. A case, however, can be decided, even if the fact which is supposed is not approved. For he who disposes concerning the consequent does not immediately approve the antecedent. God disposed concerning not bringing the hire of a harlot into the treasury, Deut. 23, 8. Did he therefore hold the harlot's gain as valid, or sanction it? Thus, for one wishing to dismiss a wife, he prescribed a mode, not in approval of divorce as if it were legitimate, but in moderation of an evil thing tolerated because of the hardness of hearts. Furthermore, although God tolerated the custom of polygamy, both for the multiplication of the posterity of Abraham, and for the hardness of the heart of the Jews, it does not follow that it was lawful, so far is it from the case that the primordial law should therefore be called into doubt or denied. What if, even with a peculiar divine dispensation posited regarding the indulgence of several wives, which some establish, the ancient law is not denied, but supposed. For around that primordial law a dispensation would then have been made.

As to Deut. 17, 16. 17. polygamy is prohibited there, not permitted: The King shall not multiply wives to himself. Now he who takes more than one, certainly multiplies wives; so that there is no distinction between polygamy and the multiplication of wives, which Augustine q. 27. in Deuter. and Drusius ad loca difficil. c. 77. hand down. The invention of the Hebrews, that eighteen wives were permitted to the King, but he should not have taken more, when Grotius, the Advocate of Polygamy, approves it, how will he convince one of it from divine law or the better antiquity of the Hebrews? For R. Solomon is from the more recent ones, whom Lyranus alleges here. And what, pray, is the analogy or reason in that number?

If examples and custom ought to interpret the law, they must be lawful and approved. Those things, however, which are repugnant to the express letter of the law cannot be held as an interpretation of the law. That holy men had more than one wife does not abolish the primordial law, nor does it prove that polygamy was once lawful. Otherwise, it would have to be established that it was also lawful then to marry two sisters, by the example of the holy Patriarch Jacob. Which marriage is prohibited here as nefarious. For a certain and clear law ought not to be impugned or disturbed by doubtful examples. There are those who say that the Patriarchs had a certain peculiar divine dispensation, with Justin, Dialogue with Trypho, p. 291. The Patriarchs did not have multiple wives as fornicators, but it was a certain economy and arrangement. Whether that dispensation was proper to the Patriarchs, which seems so to some, and indeed in such a way that it was either inspired to individuals, or once inspired, became known to the subsequent ones: Or whether it was common to the Jewish people at that age, or as others wish, even to other nations: which latter opinion seems to have been Augustine's, book XVI of The City of God, chapter 38, at that time no law prohibited having many wives for the sake of multiplying posterity. He does not deny the primordial and most ancient law, but it was held as if it were nothing in that age, on account of a common dispensation. And book XXII against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 42. Some sins are against nature, others against custom, others against a precept. If you consult nature, the Fathers used multiple women not for the sake of lust, but for the sake of procreation: if custom, at that time and in those places it was done. If a precept, it was prohibited by no law.

Nor does Chrysostom deny it, Homily 56 on Matthew. One must not judge the Fathers by our own reasoning. For then it was permitted, now it is not permitted. To others, however, it seems that a divine dispensation did not intervene here, but a mere tolerance and permission, namely that God, in holy men, tolerated this flaw just as He did others, and that they themselves did not sin against the divine law so much from choice as from ignorance of the true sense of the primeval divine law, by which custom, received by the whole world, with God tolerating and overlooking it, they saw polygamy, and having illustrious promises concerning the multiplication of seed, they held polygamy to be a middle and indifferent thing. I do not deny, says Ambrose, Book 1 on Abraham, ch. 4, that Abraham took a son from his handmaid, so that you may know that Abraham was not of some superior nature or substance, but one from the number and fragility of all men, and finally he was called from the region of the Chaldeans, whom we have learned were intent on vain superstition more than others. Both opinions, both concerning dispensation and concerning bare permission, are so arranged that they seem to be able to be supported by probable reasoning, yet neither is free from its own difficulty. For if polygamy is prohibited by the law of nature, as most wish, how could it be granted as free, which was illicit by the law of nature? If a dispensation concerning the primeval law was made immediately after polygamy was introduced for the multiplication of the human race, and that universally, what was the point of sanctioning that law from the beginning, and immediately dispensing with it universally for several centuries? But if it was only tolerated because of the ignorance of the holy men, how could men familiar with God and specially illuminated by the Holy Spirit be ignorant of the primordial law, which is clear enough, or be left in that ignorance, so that God did not inform His people more correctly for so many centuries? If the first law was unknown to the Patriarchs, could not, and should not, the sense of the law repeated by Moses, both general and that which was specifically given to the King in Deut. 17, have been known to David? I confess that, having duly weighed the arguments on both sides, I here seize upon the suspension of judgment: yet I incline more to that opinion which recognizes a divine dispensation here, which I see has pleased great men: which Bellarmine also rightly calls common. But that a special dispensation may be asserted as far as the Patriarchs and other men of God are concerned, to which the judgment of Blessed Luther also seems to return, when he reckons such marriages of the Patriarchs among heroic movements, that is, arising from a peculiar divine impulse; but as far as the rest of the Israelites, who were destitute of that special dispensation, a certain divine permission seems to be established, as regards the faithful indeed with a gracious non-imputation in the court of heaven on account of ignorance and common error, joined with repentance and general expiation of sins, even of hidden ones and those of ignorance; but as regards the rest, with a tolerance of them in the court of earth and in the polity, so that they might not be punished with a peculiar penalty, or be cast out from the people of God: just as God is said to have permitted divorce, not by approving it, but by tolerating it in the political court, on account of the hardness of heart, and for a certain political end, namely, that greater evils might be avoided.

As concerns the passage 2 Sam. 12, 8, the wives of Saul are not said there to be given to David for marriage, since it is nowhere read that he joined them to himself in matrimony, nor could he join them without incest, Lev. 18, 15, but as regards lordship: because to give or to be in the bosom does not always imply conjugal society. 1 Kings 1, 20, Ps. 35, 13, Ps. 79, 12, Is. 65, 7, Luke 6, 38, nor does that giving immediately imply legitimate usurpation, since the word of giving is also used in tolerance, Gen. 20, 6, Judg. 11, 9.

Grotius further urges that a method is prescribed even for one wishing to dismiss a wife, and no one is prevented from marrying a dismissed woman except him who dismissed her, and the priest. Deut. 24, 4. But whence is it proved that it was lawful for a married man to superinduce a dismissed woman upon his wife: which we have taught is contrary to this law, Lev. 18, 18.

He also wishes to prove his opinion from the nature of marriage; Marriage, he says, we consider to be naturally such a cohabitation of a male with a female, which constitutes the female as if under the eyes and custody of the male; for such a partnership can be seen even in certain mute animals. But in man, as he is an animal using reason, faith has been added to this, by which the female binds herself to the male. Nor does nature seem to require anything else for marriage to subsist. But why does he neglect the Justinian definition, Instit. de patr. potest. § 2. Matrimony is the conjunction of a man and a woman, containing an undivided society of life, and which theologians gather from Matt. 19, 9, 1 Cor. 6, 2, that it is an undivided conjunction of one man and one woman into one flesh, for the sake of both generating offspring and avoiding fornication. Why does he only mention the faith by which the female binds herself to the male? Is not faith reciprocal in marriage, as regards the bond and the conjugal debt, 1 Cor. 7, 4? Can a man perhaps be one of many women, with the nature of marriage safe: but one woman cannot be a woman of many men? They will be two in one flesh, Christ gathers from the law of marriage equally concerning the husband and the wife, Matt. 19. And the Apostle urges reciprocity here, 1 Cor. 7, 4. The woman does not have power over her own body, but the husband. Likewise also the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife. Bellarmine indeed wishes to introduce a certain disparity, when he argues that God can dispense concerning the polygamy of one man with several wives, but not of one woman with several men, De Sacr. matr. l. c. 11. But Sanzbietz and Coning do not admit that disparity, and assert that God can, without violation of the law of nature, grant even to a woman that she may marry several men at the same time. But this is by the way.

Finally, Grotius appeals to the custom of peoples, because polygamy flourished among the Persians, Indians, and others. Among the Egyptians, only the priests were restricted to the marriage of one woman: but divine law proves that custom to be illicit. Grotius has not yet taught that it is agreeable to the law of nature. The Germans are praised by Tacitus in his De moribus Germanorum because they were content with single wives; Cecrops is praised because, among the Athenians, as Athenaeus testifies, μίαν ἑνὶ ἔζευξεν, he coupled one woman to one husband; the Romans were always monogamous, and by the praetor's edict they marked with infamy anyone who had two marriages established at the same time, lib. I. ff. de his qui not. inf. & l. 2. C. de inc. & inut. nupt. Neither kingdoms nor marriage torches know how to bear a partner: says Seneca in Agamemnon. Those who thought or acted otherwise are to be judged to have deviated from the law of nature rather than to have followed it. It is natural, according to Michael of Ephesus on Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 3, τὸ παρὰ τοῖς πλείστοις καὶ ἀδιαστρόφοις καὶ μετὰ φύσιν ἔχωσιν, which prevails among the majority who are not corrupt but are in accordance with nature. For that law also, 'thou shalt not commit adultery,' repeated on Mount Sinai, was inscribed at the beginning of nature along with the remaining laws of the Decalogue, the remnants of which some nations have held more reverently than others.

Latin:

Vers. 18. SOROREM UXORIS TUÆ IN PELLICA- TUM ILLIUS NON ACCIPIES, NEC REVELABIS TURPITUDINEM EJUS, ADHUC ILLA VIVENTE) Pellicem hic improprie sumit pro altera conjuge: quam Græ- ci hic felicius ἀντίζηλον vocant. Jacobo id male cesserat. Sicut acerrima dicuntur esse fratrum odia, sic & æmulationes soro- rum. Reprehendit hic Pesiĉtha non immerito Caraitarum sententiam, qui volebant vetari hic, duas habere eodem tem- pore uxores, quia Soror sæpe apud Hebræos alterum aliquid ejusdem generis significat. Eamque sententiam & nostro seculo renovarunt viri non ineruditi, nempe quia nolunt quicquam in Evangelio esse vetitum, quod in lege licuerit: quibus refellendis sufficient, quæ dicta in libro de Jure Belli ac Pacis II. c. 5. §. 9. Lex in Deuteronimo satis clara est, plures uxores permittens. Accedit optima legis interpres con- suetudo.

Non videtur adeo reprobanda Caraitarum illa sententia: quod bigamia hic prohibeatur simultanea. Nam negari non potest sororem Ebræis sæpe alte- rum aliquid ejusdem generis significare. Vid. Gen. 26, 31. Ex. 26, 3. Ez. 1, 9. 23. c. 3, 13. Joel. 2, 8. Hic autem non sororem proprie ita dictam, sed aliam conjugem designari, inde colligi posse videtur: Primo quod non, ut in antecedentibus, dicatur, nuditatem soro- ris uxoris tuæ non deteges, sed simpliciter, uxorem ad Sororem (aliam uxorem ad aliam) non accipies. Tum quod non addatur ratio, quæ in nefariis aut ince- stuosis nuptiis adjecta est: caro uxoris tuæ est, aut ne- fas hoc est, aut similis. Unde apparet, hîc alterius ge- neris interdicta sequi, ac priora de nuptiis incestuosis jam expedita esse, quemadmodum etiam ea, quæ se- quuntur, omnia alterius generis sunt. Adhæc non simpliciter prohibetur affumi uxor ad sororem e- jus, sed בחייה in vita ejus. At sororem uxoris pro- prie dictam nunquam fas est ducere. Porro adjecta causa לצרר ad lacessendum generalis est, & ad polyga- miam simultaneam pertinet. Nam tum murmurat & affligitur altera uxor, cum altera superinducitur, si- ve sit soror, sive quacunq́ alia. In genere enim uxores secundæ Polygamorum describuntur, quod æmulæ sint & angere soleant 1. Sam. I, 6. Cum vero defun- cta uxore soror ejus ducitur, quomodo soror affligi potest, quæ jam diem obiit? Accedit, quod conju- gium cum sorore uxoris jam prohibitum fuerit ex paritate rationis vers. 16. nuditatem fratria tuæ non retegito, quia nuditas fratris tui est. Eadem enim omnino est carnis propinquitas in uxore fratris, & in uxoris sorore. Denique quia alias nuspiam in le- ge divina interdicta polygamia, nisi Regi Deut. 17, 6. quam tamen omnibus interdictam Christus Matth. 19, 2. & Apostolus 1. Corinth. 6, 16. cap. 7, 5. do- cent, colligi videtur, hac lege eandem prohi- bitam. Quae rationes, non sane contemnendae pro hac sententia, quod his polygamia simulta- nea prohibeatur, urgeri possunt. Quam etiam propugnari à Junio & Tremellio in h. l. video. Nec improbant eandem Notarum Bibliis Belgicis ad- ditarum autores.

Quanquam vero aliis Sororem proprie dictam hic intelligentibus refragari morose nolimus, Gro- tio tamen assurgere nequaquam possumus, quod in lege non sit prohibita polygamia simultanea. Quod autem ipsi sententia illa, nihil quicquam Evangelio vetitum esse, quod in lege licuerit, non placeat, mirum non est, quia placuit jam pridem ipsi potius, quod Socino & Anabaptistis. Quae lib. II. de jure Pacis & belli cap. V. §. 9. disputavit, huc redeunt, ex prima conditione, qua uni mari foe- minam non nisi unam DEUS attribuit, id apparere quidem, quod optimum sit Deoque gratissimum, & hinc sequi, semper id fuisse egregium ac lauda- bile, non tamen, ut aliter facere nefas esset. Chri- stum vero quod DEUS institutione conjunxerat, id ab homine separari vetuisse, ex eo, quod optimum Deoque acceptissimum est, dignissimam lege nova de- sumendo materiam. At quomodo probabitur, no- vam hic legem constitutam esse? aut legem de uni- us Viri & unius mulieris copula ante Evangelium non sancitam fuisse? Aliud praeter legem primor- dialem Decalogo praeceptum: Non moechaberis, ali- ud haec lex Levit. XVIII, 18. uti jam ostensum, do- cet. Et Mal. 2, 14. 15. censent plerique, palam repre- bendi omnem, qui perfide agendo contra uxorem pu- bertatis suae aliam ei superinducit, siquidem Deus ex duobus ad semen quaerendum unum fecerit. Non no- vam legem Christus sancit; ad primordialem Phari- saeos remittit. Clara sunt ejus verba, Matth. 19, 4. Non legistis, quia qui fecit hominem ab initio, masculum & foeminam fecit eos, & dixit: Propter hoc dimittet ho- mo Patrem & matrem, & adhaerebit uxori suae, ET ERUNT DUO IN CARNE UNA. Quaestio erat juris, an liceret jure divino homini dimittere suam uxo- rem quacunque ex causa? Revocat ergo eos ad prima- vam sanctionem. Non novam legem constituit, sed ex lege antiquissima rem decidi vult. ITAQUE JAM NON SUNT DUO, SED UNA CARO. Quod ergo Deus conjunxit, homo non separet. Si novam legem in- vexisset, actutum sese opposuissent Pharisaei, eum- que pro Novatore habuissent. Adde quod Christus sonora voce testetur, AB INITIO NON FUIT SIC. Permisisse Mosen quidem ob σκληροκαρδιαν Judae- orum dimissionem uxorum; sed ab initio, vigore primae constitutionis, sic non fuisse. Verba etiam ipsa, quae è Genes. 2, 24. adducuntur, ceu institutio divina à Christo adferuntur, PROPTER HOC DIMIT- TET homo Patrem & Matrem & ADHAEREBIT uxo- ri suae. Quae vim imperandi habent; quemad- modum etiam reliqua; & ERUNT duo in carnem unam; unde decisionem petit Christus: Itaque non sunt duo, sed una caro. Et porro: Quod ergo Deus conjunxit, homo non separet. Si haec conclusio haberi debet pro praecepto, necessum est, ut praemissa, unde illa deducitur, etiam vim praecepti obtineant. Non ergo DEUS solum testari voluit, quod optimum sibique gratissimum sit, alias idem de Christo etiam dicendum fuerit, quod non legem praescripserit, sed id solum testatus sit, cujus verba non magis, quam quæ e Mose adduxit, imperativa sint. Nimis luculentum est, docere Christum, quod AB INI- TIO licitum fuerit, quod minus. Et nisi illic lex matrimonii sancita sit, nuspiam eadem sancita erit. Quod absurdum. Ideo magno consensu hic Ec- clesiæ Doctores legem matrimonialem figunt. Ignatius in Epist. ad Antioch. una uni viro non plu- res datæ sunt in exordio creaturæ. Fulgent. de stat. vid. Epist. 2. Connubium non est ex colluvione pec- cati, sed ex institutione Dei. Chrys. ad Matth. XX. hom. LXIII. prolixe hoc confirmat: Vide Magistri sapientiam, qui cum interrogatus esset, si liceret, ne conturbarentur, antiquam sententiam proferret, confirmationem a Scriptura posuit, ostendens Dei & Patris omnium id esse MANDATUM. Non enim dixit, quia virum & mulierem unam solum- modo fecit, verum etiam, quia JUSSIT, ut unus uni conjungatur. Nam si voluisset alteram etiam condu- ci uxorem, uni viro creato multas conformasset mu- lieres. Nunc autem ut creationis & SANCTIO- NIS nodo unam uni perpetuo conjungi & nunquam rescindi oportere perdocuit. Hæc ergo LEX etsi mo- do a me promulgari videatur, diligentissime tamen a principio temporum SANCITA EST. Et paulo post: Deinde prisca jam perlecta Lege; quæ tam ver- bis, quam rebus firma persistit, & autoritate latoris nititur, magna jam cum potestate ille quoque & inter- pretatur & legem sanxit. Ita ostendit & præter na- turam & contra legem esse repudium. Præter natu- ram quidem, quia caro inciditur: contra legem au- tem, quia cum Deus conjunxerit ac jusserit non se- parare, ipsi contra PRÆCEPTA DEI facere ausi estis. Addit rationem, quam hic etiam addimus: Atqui si oppositus Christus V. T. fuisset, non decer- tasset certe pro Mose, neque ea, quæ semel a principio facta fuerunt, confirmasset, nec sua priscis convenire studuisset ostendere. Similiter Hieronymus in h. l. NATURALEM LEGEM primamque Dei sen- tentiam secundæ hic opponi, ait, quæ non voluntate Dei, sed peccantium necessitate concessa est. Et certe Dominus, inquit, non PROPRIAM SENTEN- TIAM tulerat, sed veteris historiæ MANDATO- RUM Dei fuerat recordatus. Et Augustinus l. 19. contra Faustum c. 29. Ita Dominus quid LEX & bonis PRÆCIPERET & duris permitteret, ejusdem legis testimonio declaravit. Ambrosius lib. 1. de Abraam c. 4. adfert quidem in excusationem facti Abrahami, quod ancillam duxerit, quod ante legem Mosis adulterium non videatur interdi- ctum: Deus inquit, in Paradiso licet conjugium laudaverit, non adulterium damnaverat. Sed huic defensioni non acquiescit, alias adducit; quod non ardore aliquo vagæ libidinis, sed studio quærendæ po- steritatis, quum raritas esset humani generis, post dilu- vium, ut & religionis, id fecerit, & autore quidem uxore ipsa: Imo addidit Ambrosius, pœnitentiam hujus facti Deum Abrahamo injunxisse, ac circum- cisionem ideo etiam demandasse. Non otiosum est, quod posthac Deus statim quia alia ejus opera pro- baret, pro hujus facti pœnitentia dixit illi: Ego sum Deus, emerere in conspectu meo, & esto sine querela, irreprehensibilis, ut de te uxor non queratur, nec quisquam tua facta reprehendat. Nonne evidenter circumcisio carnis præceptum est castimoniæ, ut ali- quis resecet libidinem carnis & indomitas luxu ac lascivia refrenet cupiditates? Etenim circumcisio- nis vocabulo id præscribitur, ut omnis impuritatis fœtor abstergatur, & incentivum libidinis aufera- tur. Addidit etiam tertiam defensionem Ambro- sius: Illa quæ gessit Abraham, ut de ancilla susciperet sobolem, in figura sunt & secundum allegoriam dicta. Agnoscamus ergo, quoniam hæc quæ in figura con- tingebant, illis crimini non erant; nobis autem erunt, si ad correptionem nostram scripta cavere nolimus.

Provocat Grotius ad legem Deuteronomio c. 21, 15. quam satis claram esse putat, & ad consue- tudinem legis optimam interpretem. At lex illa non ita clara est pro πολυγαμίᾳ simultanea: Accipi po- test de successiva. Si habuerit homo duas uxores suc- cessive, altera defuncta vel repudiata. Neq; ibi pro- batur πολυγαμία, sed casus solum formatur, ea po- sita. Decidi autem casus potest, etsi factum, quod supponitur, non approbetur. Non enim qui de con- sequente disponit, statim antecedens approbat. Dispo- suit Deus de meretricio non inferendo ærario Deut. 23, 8. Num ideo quæstum meretricium ratum ha- buit, aut sancivit? Ita dimittere volenti uxorem mo- dum præscripsit, non in divortii ceu legitimi appro- bationem, sed in rei malæ propter duritiem cordium toleratæ moderationem. Porro etsi toleravit Deus po- lygamiæ consuetudinem, tum ob posteritatis Abrahæ multiplicationem, tum ob cordis Judæorum duritiem, non tamen eam licitam fuisse sequitur, tantum abest, ut lex primordialis ideo in dubium revocari aut negari debeat. Quid quod posita etiam pecu- liari dispensatione divina, quoad indulgentiam plu- rium uxorum, quam nonnulli statuunt, lex antiqua non negetur, sed supponatur. Circa enim legem istam primævam facta tum fuerit dispensatio.

Quod ad Deut. 17, 16. 17. prohibetur ibi poly- gamia, non permittitur: Rex non multiplicabit sibi uxores. Jam qui plures una ducit, multiplicat utiq; uxores; ut nulla sit distinctio inter polygamiam & multiplicationem uxorum, quam Augustinus q. 27. in Deuter. & Drusius ad loca difficil. c. 77. tradunt. Commentum Ebræorum, quod Regi octodecim per- missæ fuerint uxores, plures autem ducere non debue- rit, cum approbat Polygamiæ Advocatus Grotius, quomodo ei e lege divina aut antiquitate meliori Ebræorum fidem faciet? R. Salomo enim e recen- tioribus est, quem Lyranus hic allegat. Et quænam sodes, in illo numero analogia vel ratio est?

Exempla & consuetudo si legem interpretari debeant, licita & probata sint oportet. Ea vero quæ legis expressæ repugnant literæ, pro interpre- tatione legis haberi non possunt. Quod viri sancti plures una uxores habuerint, non tollit legem pri- mordialem, nec probat, licitam fuisse olim polyga- miam. Alias etiam licitum tum fuisse, duas sorores ducere, exemplo S. Patriarchæ Jacobi, statuendum foret. Quod conjugium ceu nefarium hic prohi- betur. Non enim ab exemplis dubiis lex certa & lu- culenta impugnari aut solicitari debet. Sunt, qui di- cunt, Patriarchas peculiarem quandam divinam dis- pensationem habuisse, cum Justin. Dial. cum Tryph. p. 291. Non tanquam fornicantes Patriarchæ habue- runt plures uxores, sed œconomia quædam id atq; dis- positio fuit. Sive dispensatio illa Patriarchis propria fuerit, quod nonnullis videtur, & quidem ita, ut aut singulis inspirata fuerit, aut semel inspirata priori- bus innotuerit subsequentibus: Sive communis fuerit illa ætate populo Judaico, aut quod alii vo- lunt, etiam gentibus aliis: quæ postrema sententia videtur Augustini fuisse l. XVI. de C. D. c. 38. eo tempore multiplicandæ posteritatis causa multas habe- re uxores nulla Lex prohibebat. Non negat legem primævam & antiquissimam, sed ea ista ætate quasi nulla habebatur, ob communem dispensationem. Et l. XXII. contra Faustum Manich. c. 42. Peccata alia sunt contra naturam, alia contra morem, alia contra præceptum. Si naturam consulas, Patres non lasciviendi, sed generandi causa pluribus mulieribus utebantur: si morem, illo tempore & illis locis id fa- citabatur. Si præceptum, nulla lege prohibebatur.

Nec abnuit Chrysostomus hom. 56. in Matth. Non est judicandum de Patribus pro nostra ratione. Tunc enim licebat, nunc non licet. Aliis tamen vi- detur, non dispensationem divinam hic intervenis- se, sed meram tolerantiam & permissionem, quod nempe Deus in sanctis viris uti alios nævos, ita hunc quoque tolerarit, quodque ipsi non tam ἐκ προαιρέ- σεως adversus legem divinam peccarint, quam ex ignorantia veri sensus divinæ legis primævæ, qua consuetudine totius orbis receptam, Deo tolerante ac dissimulante, videbant polygamiam, & illustres de multiplicatione seminis habebant promissiones, polygamiam pro re media & indifferente habue- rint. Non abnuo, inquit Ambrosius lib. I. de Abrah. c. 4. quod Abraham de ancilla susceperit filium, ut co- gnoscas, quoniam non superioris cujusdam naturæ aut substantiæ fuit Abraham, sed unus e numero & fra- gilitate universorum hominum, deniq́; & de regione Chaldæorum vocatus est, quos superstitione vana in- tentos esse magis, quam cæteros accepimus. Utraque sententia tum de dispensatione, tum de nuda per- missione ita comparata est, ut probabili ratione vi- deatur sustineri posse, difficultate tamen sua neu- tra careat. Nam si lege naturæ prohibita est poly- gamia, quod plerique volunt, quomodo ut liberum concedi potuit, quod lege naturæ illicitum fuit? Si dispensatio circa legem primævam facta est inde statim ab invecta ob multiplicationem generis hu- mani polygamia, eaque universalis, quid attinebat legem illam sancire ab initio, & actutum circa ean- dem universaliter per complura secula dispensare? Si vero ob ignorantiam sanctorum tolerata solum fuit, quomodo viri Dei familiares & Sp. S. pecu- liariter illuminati legem primordialem satis lucu- lentam ignorare potuere, aut in illa ignorantia re- linqui, ut Deus per tot secula populum suum non informarit rectius? Si lex prima ignorata Patriar- chis, annon Davidi legis a Mose repetitæ sensus, cum generalis, tum ejus, quæ speciatim Regi tradi- ta erat Deut. 17. cognitus esse potuit, atque debuit? Fateor rationibus in utramque partem probe ex- pensis me τὸ ἐπέχειν hic arripere: magis tamen in illam inclinare sententiam, quæ dispensationem di- vinam hic agnoscat, quam magnis Viris placuisse video: quam etiam Bellarminus recte communem vocat. Sed ut specialis, quantum ad Patriarchas aliosque Dei viros, dispensatio adseratur, quo etiam redire videtur B. Lutheri ἐπίκρισις, cum motibus Heroicis talia Patriarcharum conjugia accenset, h. e. ex impulsu peculiari divino oriundis; quantum vero ad cæteros Israelitas ea speciali dispensatione destitutos, permissio quædam divina statuenda vide- tur, quoad fideles quidem cum gratiosa non imputa- tione in foro poli ob ignorantiam & errorem com- munem, cum pœnitentia & expiatione peccatorum generali, etiam occultorum & ignorantiæ in ipsis con- junctum; quoad reliquos vero cum tolerantia eo- rundem in foro soli & politia, ne peculiari pœna plectcrentur, aut e populo Dei ejicerentur: uti permisisse dicitur Deus divortium, non approban- do, sed in foro Politico id tolerando, ob cordis du- ritiem, certoque fine Politico, ut sc. majora evita- rentur mala.

Locum 2. Sam. 12, 8. quod concernit, non ibi datæ uxores Saulis dicuntur Davidi quoad conju- gium, quum nuspiam eas matrimonio sibi copulas- se legatur, nec citra incestum copulare potuerit Lev. 18, 15. sed quoad dominium: quia dare vel esse in sinu non semper conjugalem societatem infert. 1. Reg. 1, 20. Psal. 35, 13. Ps. 79, 12. Es. 65, 7. Luc. 6, 38. nec datio illa legitimam usurpationem statim in- ferat, fiquidem etiam verbum dandi in tolerantia adhibeatur Gen. 20, 6. Jud. 11, 9.

Urget præterea Grotius, quod etiam dimittere uxorem volenti modus præscribatur, nec dimissam ducere quisquam impediatur præter eum, qui dimi- sit, & sacerdotem. Deut. 24, 4. Sed unde probabi- tur, quod licitum fuerit conjugato superinducere uxori suæ dimissam: quod refragari legi huic Lev. 18, 18. docuimus.

E natura etiam conjugii sententiam suam pro- bare vult; Conjugium, inquit, naturaliter esse existi- mamus talem cohabitationem maris cum fœmina, quæ fœminam constituat quasi sub oculis & custodia maris; nam tale consortium & in mutis animantibus quibusdam videre est. In homine vero qua ani- mans est utens ratione, ad hoc accessit fides, qua se fœ- mina mari obstringit. Nec aliud, ut conjugium subsistat, natura videtur requirere. Sed cur defini- tionem Justinianeam negligit, Instit. de patr. potest. §. 2. Matrimonium est viri & mulieris conjunctio, individuam vitæ societatem continens, & quam Theologi e Matth. 19, 9. 1. Cor. 6, 2. colligunt, quod sit unius maris & unius fœminæ in carnem in- dividua conjunctio, tum prolis generandæ, tum scor- tationis vitandæ gratia. Cur fidem tantum comme- morat, qua se fœmina mari obstringit? Annon est reciproca in conjugio fides, quoad viculum & debitum conjugale 1. Cor. 7, 4. Num forte vir po- test quidem unus esse multarum mulierum, salva natura conjugii: Una autem mulier non potest es- se multivira? Erunt duo in carnem unam, colligit Christus e lege connubii æqualiter de marito & uxore Matth. 19. Et reciprocationem hic ur- get Apostolus 1. Cor. 7, 4. Mulier sui corporis potestatem non habet, sed vir. Similiter autem & vir sui corporis potestatem non habet, sed mulier. Disparitatem quandam invehere vult quidem Bel- larminus, cum disputat, Deum dispensare posse cir- ca polygamiam unius viri cum pluribus uxoribus, non autem unius uxoris cum pluribus viris de Sacr. matr. l. c. 11. Sed Sanzbietz & Coning. eam dispa- ritatem non admittunt, Deumque posse citra legis naturæ violationem etiam mulieri concedere, ut pluribus viris simul nubat, asserunt. Sed hoc ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ.

Denique ad populorum consuetudinem pro- vocat Grotius, quod apud Persas, Indos, alios poly- gamia viguerit. Apud Ægyptios soli Sacerdotes unius fœminæ conjugio adstricti fuerint: sed eam consuetudinem illicitam esse lex divina convincit. Legi naturæ consentaneum esse, nondum docuit Grotius. Laudantur Germani Tacito de moribus Germanor. quod singulis uxoribus contenti fue- rint; laudatur Cecroes, quod apud Athenienses, teste Athenæo, μίαν ἑνὶ ἔζευξεν unam fœminam uni mari- to copularit; Romani semper monogami fuere, ac prætoris edicto infamia notarunt, qui binas nuptias in eodem tempore constitutas habuisset lib. I. ff. de his qui not. inf. & l. 2. C. de inc. & inut. nupt. Nec regna socium, nec ferre tadæ sciunt: ait Seneca in Agamemn. Qui secus senserunt vel egerunt, a lege naturæ exorbitasse potius, quam eandem se- quutos esse judicandi sunt. Naturale est juxta Michaelem Ephesium ad Nicom. c. 3. τὸ παρὰ τοῖς πλείστοις καὶ ἀδιαστρόφοις καὶ μετὰ φύσιν ἔχωσιν, quod apud plerosque non corruptos, sed naturæ conve- nienter se habentes obtinet. Nam & illa lex, non mœchaberis in monte Sinai repetita naturæ initio insculpta fuit cum reliquis Decalogi legibus, cu- jus reliquias alii aliis inter gentes reverentius ha- buere.

## 18:21
Verse 21.

THAT HE MAY BE CONSECRATED TO THE IDOL MOLOCH) By fire. See what will be said in Deuteronomy 18, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

VT CONSECRETVR IDOLO MOLOCH) Per ignem. Vide quæ dicentur Deuteronomii 18, 10.

## 18:23
Verse 23.

BECAUSE IT IS A CRIME) In Hebrew, confusion, most aptly. It is not merely an abomination, as were those which preceded, but an effusion of alien seed into a human womb, from which monsters are born.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

QVIA SCELVS EST) Hebraice, confusio, optime. Non abominatio tantum est, ut quæ præcessere, sed in uterum humanum effusio γονῆς ἀλλογενῆς, unde portenta nascuntur.

## 18:24
Verse 24.

IN ALL THESE, BY WHICH ALL THE NATIONS HAVE BEEN CONTAMINATED.) Refer this regarding the contamination of the Nations to those final things, or if you wish, add also the incests of the law of nations. For there are also incests of civil law forbidden for this reason, that the excessive proximity of permitted things might not lead to illicit ones. See what we have said in the place already mentioned.

That it does not refer only to those final things, as Grotius wishes with the Papists (see Cornel. a Lap. here), but that it pertains to all these laws, is manifest from the fact that even from the beginning of those laws such things are premised v. 2. Speak to the Children of Israel and you shall say to them, I am the Lord your God; According to the custom of the land of Egypt, in which you have dwelt, you shall not do, and according to the manner of the region of Canaan, into which I am about to bring you, you shall not act, nor shall you walk in their statutes. Afterwards, toward the end, the Lord concludes universally: Nor be polluted in ALL THESE, by which all the nations have been contaminated, which I will cast out before your sight, and by which the land is polluted, whose crimes I will visit, so that it may vomit out its inhabitants. Keep my statutes and judgments, and do not do any of these abominations, as much the native as the foreigner who dwells among you. For all the inhabitants of the land have done these execrations. Every soul that shall do any of THESE ABOMINATIONS, shall perish from the midst of your people. In sum, the entire chapter is occupied in prohibiting the abominations of the gentiles, and it tends to this, that all those things which are prohibited here should be fled from as abominations. Add that in Lev. ch. 20, such threats are added again to those prohibited degrees. Whence Bellarmine confesses that this exception, which Grotius also used here, that the threats in this place pertain only to the final prohibitions, does not seem sufficiently solid: de matr. c. 27. There is no distinction of Grotius between the degrees of consanguinity and affinity, which he hands down in the cited place, that the prohibition of the former was commended to the Hebrews together with the law concerning worshipping God, speaking the law, not shedding blood, not worshipping false Gods, not seizing another's property, and that that law is common to men and rests upon natural honesty: but that as regards these (degrees of affinity) the laws are not likewise common, as they contain more of a precaution. For the universal sentence of the Lord intercedes against this opinion, by which ALL those are condemned as profane abominations.

That two sisters were joined to Jacob was extraordinary. Since he had known one sister substituted for him by fraud, but had given his word to the other, it was done without doubt with divine dispensation intervening, so that he should neither have to dismiss the former, nor violate the word given to the latter, and then to take their handmaids, because God had determined to build the house of Jacob through those two sisters and their handmaids, and to propagate those XII notable Israelite tribes. Augustine excuses Jacob thus in book XVI de C. D. c. XXXIIX. Whence it happened to him to have four women, from whom he procreated twelve sons and one daughter, while he coveted none of them illicitly, the divine Scripture indicates. For he had come to take one, but when one had been substituted for the other for him, he did not dismiss her either, whom he had unknowingly used in the night, lest he seem to have held her in mockery: and from that time, since no law prohibited having multiple wives for the sake of multiplying posterity, he also took her, to whom alone he had already given assurance of a future marriage. When she was sterile, she deservedly gave her handmaid, from whom she herself might receive children. Which also her elder sister, although she had given birth, imitated, since she desired to multiply offspring, and accomplished. Jacob is not read to have sought any, except one: nor did he use many, except for the duty of begetting offspring preserved by conjugal right: so that he would not even do this, unless his wives, who had legitimate power over the body of their husband, had demanded it be done. He says that no law then prohibited multiple wives, consequently to his hypothesis: because he establishes a general divine dispensation of the primordial law. But this is more conveniently referred to a special dispensation by the Blessed Luther, Comment. on Gen. 29. There are heroic examples, and there are moral ones; Laws and customs are simply to be observed, nor is any transgression to be borne, lest confusion arise. Heroic examples are those which do not accord with the laws. For often a heroic man, whom God has inspired with a singular divine power, breaks through and shatters the rule. But he does not leave behind him an example. Moral ones, laws and rights are to be observed and examples followed. But in heroic ones there is no consequence, no example is valid, unless it is in all things similar. If you are similar to Jacob, if such a case, such an occasion and necessity should occur, then it will be permitted to you also, what was permitted to Jacob. If you are not in all things similar to Jacob, you will have to stand by the law and common customs. As regards Amram, Jochebed, whom he married, is called דּוֹדַת Exod. 6, 20. not in a special sense, as if she were an aunt or father's sister, which is against the law Lev. 18, 2. but in a general sense, so that a kinship is indeed designated, but in a further degree, (Compare Is. 1, 1. Jer. 32, 12.) because she was a cousin, born from a father's sister, as the LXX Interpreters and the Vulgate render, θυγατέρα ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ πατρὸς, his paternal cousin: not a daughter to Levi, but a granddaughter, who is also sometimes called a daughter by the Hebrews. See what we have noted on that passage Exod. 6, 20.

The Apostolic Canons have been sufficiently convicted of forgery; therefore, that which c. 18 says, that one marrying two sisters or the daughter of a brother or sister is only barred from the clergy, ought to be considered of no authority. Those canons are rejected even by the Papists of more refined taste. By Gelasius with 70 Bishops, C. sancta dist. XVI, the book of Apostolic Canons is apocryphal. Others say they were corrupted by heretics, and some even that they are supposititious. Whence therefore could Grotius be certain that this one, which he cites, was not supposititious or corrupted? Baronius at the year 102, § 17, approves only those which were either received by the Fathers among other canons of Councils, or confirmed by Papal authority, or passed into common use of Ecclesiastical Discipline. By themselves, therefore, they are furnished with no authority. Nor is the Council of Elvira of great authority, which in Canon LX excludes one from communion only for five years if anyone has married his sister-in-law after the death of his wife. Bellarmine himself proves that this Council erred frequently, l. II. de imag. c. 9, inasmuch as it denies absolution to the lapsed, prohibits pictures in temples, etc. To which we oppose the Council of Auxerre, which in Can. XXX condemns such marriages as illicit: It is NOT PERMITTED to marry two sisters, if one has died, to take the other in marriage. Thus, therefore, Grotius has been cast down from the defenses of a very bad cause: which he undertook to plead, without a doubt, so that he might enter into good favor with the Roman Pontiff, who claims for himself the right of dispensing in the degrees prohibited here, and not rarely has even dispensed for the sake of the holy penny; and might encrust the opinion of the Council of Trent, which in Session XXIV, Canon III, thundered thus: if anyone shall say that the Church cannot dispense in certain degrees of consanguinity and affinity, which are expressed in Leviticus, let him be anathema. Hence he also borrowed his arguments from Cardinal Bellarmine, who in chapter XXVII of De matrimonio contends that only marriages in the first degree of consanguinity, both in the direct and in the collateral line, and in the first degree of affinity in the direct line only, are forbidden by the law of nature. But to this incomparable defender (as he is called by Cornelius a Lapide) of the (Roman) faith, the truth itself, which is its force and evidence, has wrung out this confession: That general proposition in Lev. XVIII. TO THE NEAR OF HIS BLOOD LET NO ONE APPROACH, embraces the LAW OF NATURE, and therefore the word TURPITUDE is repeated in INDIVIDUAL precepts, because it is base to contract marriage with a kinswoman, since NATURE itself dictates that a certain reverence is owed to them, with which carnal copulation conflicts, and because those nations without any discrimination (perhaps because they did not have a Pope dispensing, for in that Bellarmine fixes the discrimination) were mingling with their kinsfolk, they were undoubtedly sinning IN INDIVIDUAL cases against the LAW OF NATURE, and therefore were deservedly punished. But we do not think it necessary (which is to be diligently noted) that it be proven strictly: that all those degrees prohibited in this chapter XVIII are forbidden by the law of nature, which is merely natural and impressed by nature upon the minds of all, provided that it be obtained that they are forbidden by divine law, not one special and proper to the Jews, but common and binding all men, which no one except God alone can relax or dispense. For Grotius denies this here; for even if it were granted that these prohibitions do not come from the mere law of nature, they can nevertheless be seen to have gone into prohibition by a precept of divine will, nor is such a precept of a kind that binds only the Hebrews, but one that binds all men, as it seems to be gathered from the words of God in Lev. 18, 24. 25. 27. For if the Canaanites and their neighbors sinned by doing such things, it follows that an ancient law preceded, which, since it is not merely natural, it remains that it was given by God, either to them specifically (which is not likely, nor do the words sufficiently support it) or to the human race, either in the primeval constitution or in the restoration after the fall. Which Grotius deduces in the same place from the fact that even in the New Testament Paul so severely detests the marriage of a stepson with a stepmother in 1 Cor. 5, 1, on the argument that such a mixture is held to be impure even by profane Gentiles, which common estimation, if it did not have its origin from a necessary dictate of nature, it follows entirely that it descends from an ancient tradition which flowed from some precept.
