With these things thus argued, where Grotius ought to have brought forth his opinion, how much they used the word nefas concerning such things. Therefore also the sin was imputed to the Canaanites, which however Grotius restricts to intercourse with parents, with sisters, with the wives of others, thinking the other laws were added only for the protection and safeguarding of these.

And from these, as I think, can be understood the distinction which he applied here to our text, between incest of the law of nations and of civil law (of the Hebrew people) lest the excessive proximity of lawful things lead to illicit ones, who furthermore from the incests of the law of nations, which he estimated from a certain primeval law given to Adam, undoubtedly also distinguished the incests of the law of nature, for example, of a son with his mother and a father with his daughter. But just as the law concerning worshipping God, not shedding blood, not seizing the property of another, was not given from without, but was inscribed on the inner tablets of the heart from the beginning, so not only the old fame concerning divine law, but the law of nature itself is wont to be alleged in those incests, both by the Fathers and even among profane authors themselves: Ambrose, dissuading the marriage of a brother with a sister's daughter, lib. 8. Epist. 66. It is forbidden, he says, by the law of nature, it is forbidden by the law which is in the hearts of individuals. There is, says Augustine, l. 16. de C. D. c. 16., I know not how, in human modesty something NATURAL and praiseworthy, so that it restrains itself from her to whom it owes reverent honor because of kinship, although it is a more general lust, concerning which we see even modesty itself blushing in marital chastity. It has been observed by Alex. ab Alex. lib. I. gen. dier. c. 24. that almost all the Greeks thought it an ABOMINATION for those born of the same parent to be held together in incestuous marriages. Papinianus, l. etiam si Concubinam 56. ff. de vit. nupt., defined that incest is committed if anyone has a sister's daughter as a concubine, just as Anastasius, l. ab incestis 9. c. de incest. & inut. nupt., called the marrying of a brother's daughter or a sister's daughter or one who had once cohabited with a brother by marriage right an ABOMINABLE license: and the Emperor Zeno, l. Nefandissimum. 2. c. si nuptiæ ex rescripto, called the marriage of a brother, sister, and daughter an ABOMINABLE crime. But in the judgment of Grotius, it was not forbidden even for the Hebrews to marry a brother's daughter, and before the times of the law it was permitted even for the Hebrews to marry a paternal aunt: nor was there a prohibition given in common (before the civil law of the Hebrews) to the human race against having two sisters in marriage at the same time: nor was the marriage void if anyone among Christians, after the death of his wife, marries her sister, or joins to himself a brother's daughter; since this, according to him, is prohibited only by civil law (of the Hebrews), by which Christians are not bound. lib. II. de jure pacis & belli c. V. §. XIV. But against these and similar things, the clear letter concerning incests and abominable marriages, on account of which the earth even vomited out the nations, which therefore ought to have been contrary to the law of nations, then St. John also openly protests in Matt. XIV, 4. Mark 6, 18. οὐκ ἔξεστί σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, by which that matter is condemned as illicit. Whence Bellarmine himself designated the marriage incestuous, Chap. XX, 21. It is known that Daniel Hoffmann, a theologian of Helmstedt, formerly, and recently Christopher Joachim Bucholtz, Professor of Law in the Academy of Rinteln, on the occasion of a certain Prince of the Holy Roman Empire marrying his wife's sister in the year 1652, attempted to defend such nuptials as being in no way contrary to divine and natural law; but just as Dr. Heinrich Heshusius, Superintendent, with the ministers of Hildesheim, sufficiently responded to Hoffmann, with the approval of the Theological College of Jena in its judgment, so also can those things which the Rinteln Professor has again brought onto the stage of the learned world be easily satisfied. See B. Gerhard, loc. cit. on Marriage, § 347.

it appears (for he is sufficiently slippery in this matter) that he says natural reason alone, without an express law, forbids parents and children from being joined; perhaps agreeing here with Cardinal Cajetan, who argued that only the marriage of a son with his mother and a father with his daughter is prohibited by natural law, and that the Roman Pontiff can grant dispensations in other cases; inasmuch as the cohabitation of a brother with a sister was FROM THE BEGINNING a MIDDLE thing, according to Michael of Ephesus on the fifth book of the Nicomachean Ethics. Grotius may teach: but in the case of relatives by marriage who are in the direct line, and likewise in the first degree of blood relatives in the collateral line, which is accustomed to be called the second degree because of the origin from a common stock, he wishes that modesty intervenes because of the very recent natural image of the parents in the children, so that nature, if it does not command, at least dictates more honestly that one should abstain from those marriages: And he states, not obscurely, with the Hebrews that those laws, and the law that brothers should not be mixed with sisters, were given to Adam himself along with the law concerning worshipping God; even if that is not narrated by Moses in its proper place, inasmuch as there was an ancient report among the Gentiles concerning a divine law against that kind of marriage, whence also

Whoever flatters those doing evil, places a cushion under the head or elbow of the one lying down, says Gregory the Great, book 18, chapter 4, so that he who ought to have been rebuked for his fault, supported by praises in it, may rest softly. They daub the wall, says Gregory the Great again, which is repeated from the same chapter, Sunt nonnulli, dist. 46, who flatter those committing sins, so that those acting perversely may build, and those flattering may make it as it were clean. Compare on this case the very recent alternating writings of Mr. Dr. Aegidius Strauch and Dr. Bucholz.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

IN OMNIBUS HIS, QVIBVS CONTAMINATÆ SVNT VNIVERSÆ GENTES.) Hoc de contaminatione Gentium refer ad postrema illa, aut si vis, adde & incestus juris gentium. Sunt enim & incestus juris civilis ideo vetiti, ne nimia licitorum vicinitas ad illicita duceret. Vide quæ nos dicto jam loco.

Ad postrema solum illa non referri, quod cum Pontificiis vult Grotius, (vid. Cornel. a Lap. hic) sed ad leges has omnes pertinere inde manifestum est, quod & ab initio earum legum talia præmittuntur v. 2. Loquere Filiis Israel & dices ad eos, Ego Dominus Deus vester; Juxta consuetudinem terræ Ægypti, in qua habitastis, non faciatis, & juxta morem regionis Canaan, ad quam ego introducturus sum vos, non agetis, nec in legitimis eorum ambulabitis. Postea sub finem universaliter concludit Dominus: Nec polluamini in OMNIBUS HIS, quibus contaminatæ sunt universæ gentes, quas ego ejiciam ante conspectum vestrum, & quibus polluta est terra, cujus ego scelera visitabo, ut evomat habitatores suos. Custodite legitima mea, atque judicia, & non faciatis ex OMNIBUS abominationibus istis, tam indigena, quam exoticus, qui peregrinantur apud vos. OMNES enim execrationes fecerunt accolæ terræ. Omnis anima, quæ fecerit ex ABOMINATIONIBUS HIS QVIPPIAM, peribit de medio populi tui. Summa, universum caput occupatum est in abominationibus gentilium prohibendis eoque tendit, ut illa omnia ceu abominationes fugiantur, quæ hie prohibentur. Adde, quod Lev. 20. cap. istis gradibus prohibitis denuo comminationes ejusmodi adjiciantur. Unde fatetur Bellarminus, exceptionem istam, qua Grotius usus hic etiam est, quod comminationes ad postrema solum interdicta hoc in loco pertineant, non videri satis solidam: de matr. c. 27. Nulla est distinctio Grotii inter gradus consanguinitatis & affinitatis, quam loco citato tradit, quod illorum prohibitio Ebræis simul cum lege de Deo colendo, jure dicendo, non fundendo sanguine, non colendis Diis falsis, non rapienda re aliena commendata sit, eamque legem esse hominibus communem & honestate naturali niti: at quoad hos (affinitatis gradus) leges non item communes esse, ut quæ cautionem magis contineant. Huic enim opinioni intercedit universalis sententia Domini, qua OMNIA illa ceu abominationes profanæ damnantur.

Quod Jacobo sorores duæ junctæ, extraordinarium. Quum alteram sororem per fraudem sibi suppositam cognovisset, alteri autem fidem dedisset, sine dubio divina dispensatione interveniente factum, ut nec illam dimittere debuerit, neque huic datam fidem violare, tum utriusǫ ancillam assumere, quód constituisset Deus, per duas illas Sorores & ancillas earum domum Jacobi ædificare, ac XII. illas insignes Israeliticas tribus propagare. Augustinus Jacobum ita excusat l. XVI. de C. D. c. XXXIIX. Unde autem illi acciderit, quatuor habere fæminas, de quibus duodecim filios & unam filiam procreavit, cum earum nullam concupisceret illicite, divina Scriptura indicat. Ad unam quippe accipiendam venerat, sed cum illi altera pro altera supposita fuisset, nec ipsam dimisit, qua nesciens fuerat usus in nocte, ne ludibrio eam videretur habuisse: & ex eo tempore quoniam multiplicandæ posteritatis causa plures uxores lex nulla prohibebat, accepit etiam il- lam, cui uni jam futuri conjugii fidem fecerat. Quæ cum esset sterilis, ancillam suam, de qua filios ipsa su- sciperet, merito dedit. Quod etiam major Soror ejus, quamvis peperisset, imitata, quoniam multiplicare prolem cupiebat, effecit. Nullam Jacob legitur petiisse, præter unam: nec usus plurimis, nisi gignendæ prolis officio conjugali jure servato: ut neque hoc faceret, nisi uxores ejus id fieri flagitassent, quæ corporis viri sui habebant legitimam potestatem. Plures uxores legem nullam tum prohibuisse consequenter hypothesi suæ dicit: quia divinam generalem dispensationem legis primævæ statuit. Sed convenientius ad spe- cialem dispensationem hoc refertur a B. Luthero, Comment. in Gen. 29. Alia sunt exempla heroi- ca, alia moralia; Leges & mores simpliciter sunt ser- vandi, nec ferenda est ulla transgressio, ne fiat confu- sio. Heroica exempla sunt, quæ non congruunt cum legibus. Sæpe enim vir heroicus, quem Deus singulari numine afflavit, perrumpit & frangit regulam. Sed non relinquit post se exemplum. Moralia, leges & ju- ra sunt servanda & exempla sequenda. Sed in heroi- cis nulla est consequentia, nullum exemplum valet, nisi sit per omnia simile. Si fueris similis Jacob, si talis ca- sus, talis occasio & necessitas inciderit, tum & tibi li- cebit, quod Jacob licuit. Si non fueris per omnia si- milis Jacob, standum tibi erit in lege & moribus communibus. Amramum quod attinet, dicitur Jocha- bed, quam duxit, דּוֹדַת Exod. 6, 20. non sensu speciali, quasi amita vel Patris soror fuerit, quod contra legem Lev. 18, 2. sed generali, ut cognatio quidem, sed in gradu ulteriori designetur, (Confer. Es. 5, 1. Jer. 32, 12.) quod fuerit amitæ filia, ex Pa- tris sorore nata, ut LXX. Interpp. & Vulgata red- dunt, θυγατέρα ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ πατρὸς, Patruelem suam: Levi non filia, sed neptis, quæ etiam filia Ebræis quandoque dicitur. Vide, quæ ad locum illum Exod. 6, 20. notavimus.

Canones Apostolici νοθείας satis convicti sunt; Nullius ergo autoritatis censeri debet, quod c. 18. duas Sorores aut ἀδελφιδῆν fratris aut soro- ris filiam ducens a Clero tantum arcetur. Canones illi ab ipsis Pontificiis emunctioris naris rejiciun- tur. Gelasio cum LXX. Episcopis C. sancta dist. XVI. liber Canonum Apostolicorum Apocryphus est. Alii corruptos eos ab hæreticis, nonnullos etiam supposititios esse dicunt. Unde ergo certus esse po- tuit Grotius, hunc, quem citat, non fuisse supposi- titium, aut corruptum? Baronius ad ann. CII. §. 17. illos tantum probat, qui vel a Patribus inter alios Conciliorum canones recepti, vel Pontificia autori- tate firmati, aut in communem usum Ecclesiasticæ Disciplinæ transivere. Per se igitur autoritate nulla instructi sunt. Neque magnæ authoritatis est con- cilium Eliberinum, quod Canone LX. a commu- nione tantum ad quinquennium excludit, si quis post obitum uxoris suæ Sororem duxerit. Bellarminus ipse Concilium hoc frequenter errasse l. II. de imag. c. 9. probat, utpote quod lapsis absolutionem dene- get, picturas in templis prohibeat &c. Cui oppo- nimus Antisidorense, quod Can. XXX. ceu illicitas damnat ejusmodi nuptias: Non LICET duas So- rores ducere, si una mortua fuerit, alteram in conju- gium accipere. Ita ergo a præsidiis causæ pessimæ dejectus est Grotius: quam dubio procul ideo agendam suscepit, ut apud Pontificem Romanum bonam iniret gratiam, qui in gradibus hic pro- hibitis dispensandi jus sibi vindicat, nec raro etiam dispensavit sancti denarii causa; ac Tri- dentin. Concilii sententiam incrustaret, quod Sessione XXIV. Canone III. ita fulminavit: si quis dixerit, Ecclesiam non posse in quibusdam gra- dibus consanguinitatis & affinitatis, qui in Levit. ex- primuntur, dispensare, anathema esto. Hinc argumen- ta sua etiam a Cardinali Bellarm. mutuo sumfit, qui c. XXVII. de matrim. contendit, jure naturæ inter- dicta solum esse conjugia in primo gradu consangui- nitatis tam in recta, quam in transversa linea, & in primo gradu affinitatis in linea recta tantum. Cui vero incomparabili, uti a Cornelio a Lapide vocatur, fi- dei (Romanæ) hyperaspistæ veritas ipsa, quæ vis & evidentia ejus est, hanc confessionem expressit: Propositio illa generalis Lev. XVIII. AD PROXI- MAM SANGUINIS SUI NEMO ACCE- DAT, JUS NATURÆ complectitur, & ideo etiam in SINGULIS præceptis repetitur vocabu- lum TURPITUDO, quia turpe est, cum cogna- ta matrimonium contrahere, cum NATURA ipsa dictet, reverentiam quandam illis deberi, cum qua pugnat copula carnalis, & quia gentes illæ sine ullo dele- ctu (forte quod non haberent Pontificem dispen- santem, in eo enim delectum figit Bellarminus) mi- scebantur consanguineis, peccabant haud dubie IN SINGULIS contra JUS NATURÆ, & ideo me- rito puniebantur. Non autem opus esse censemus, (quod sedulo notandum) ut ἀπότομως hoc evinca- tur: gradus omnes illos prohibitos hoc cap. XIIX. lege naturæ, quæ mere naturalis omniumque mentibus natura impressa sit, vetitos, dummodo id obtinea- tur lege divina, non speciali & Judæorum propria, sed communi & omnes homines adstringente, quam nemo præter unum Deum relaxare, aut dispensare possit, interdictos. Id enim hic inficiatur Grotius; Nam etiam concesso, a mero jure naturæ non venire hac interdicta, videri tamen possunt præcepto divinæ vo- luntatis hæc ivisse in vetitum, neque enim tale id esse præceptum, quod solos Ebræos adstringat, sed quod ho- mines universos, colligi videtur e Dei verbis Lev. 18, 24. 25. 27. Nam si Cananæi eorumq; vicini peccarunt talia faciendo, sequitur, ut lex antiqua præcesserit, quæ cum mere naturalis non sit, restat, ut a Deo data sit, aut ipsis peculiariter (quod non est verisimile, nec satis ferunt verba) aut humano generi, sive in primæ- va constitutione, sive in reparatione post lapsum. Quod ibidem deducit Grotius ex eo, quod etiam in N. T. Paulus conjugium privigni cum Noverca tam severe detestetur 1. Cor. V, 1. eo argumento, quod talis commixtio impura etiam a profanis Genti- bus habeatur, quæ communis existimatio si a necessa- rio naturæ dictato originem non habuit, omnino se- quitur, ut descendat ex veteri traditione, quæ a præ- cepto aliquo manavit. His ita disputatis, ubi senten- tiam suam promere debuit Grotius, quantum ap- vocem nefas de talibus usurparint. Ideo etiam pecca- tum imputatum Cananæis, quod tamen restringit Grotius ad concubitum cum Parentibus, cum soro- ribus, cum nuptis alienis, cæteras leges solum in προφυλακὴν & præmunimentum harum adjectas, existimans.

Et ex his, uti arbitror, intelligi potest distin- ctio, quam hic ad textum nostrum adhibuit, inter incestus juris gentium & juris civilis (populi Ebræi) ne nimia licitorum vicinitas ad illicita deducat, qui porro ab incestibus juris gentium, quos e primæva quadam lege Adamo data æstimavit, incestus etiam juris naturæ sine dubio distinxit, puta filii cum matre & Patris cum filia. Sed uti lex de Deo colen- do, non fundendo sanguine, non rapienda re aliena, non data extrinfecus, sed inscripta interioribus cor- dis tabulis ab initio fuit, ita non fama solum vetus de lege divina, sed ipsa lex naturæ in illis incestibus cum a Patribus, tum & penes ipsos prophanos au- tores allegari solet: Ambrosius conjugium fratris cum sororis filia dissuadens lib. 8. Epist. 66. Interdi- ctum, inquit, est naturæ jure, interdictum est lege, quæ est in cordibus singulorum. Inest, inquit Augu- stinus l. 16. de C. D. c. 16. nescio quomodo humana verecundia quiddam NATURALE atque lauda- bile, ut cui debet causa propinquitatis verecundum honorem, ab ea contineat, quamvis generaliorem ta- men libidinem, de qua erubescere videmus & ipsam pudicitiam conjugalem. Omnes fere Græcos NE- FANDUM putasse, eodem Parente genitos invicem incestis nuptiis detinere Alex. ab Alex. lib. I. gen. dier. c. 24. observatum. Papinianus l. etiam si Con- cubinam 56. ff. de vit. nupt. incestum committi, si quis sororis filiam concubinam habeat, definivit, quemadmodum Anastasius l. ab incestis 9. c. de in- ceft. & inut. nupt. fratris filiam vel sororis vel eam, quæ cum fratre nuptiali jure quondam cohabitarat, ducere NEFANDAM licentiam: & Zeno Impe- rator l. Nefandissimum. 2. c. si nuptiæ ex rescripto, Nefandissimum scelus fratris sororis & filiæ nuptia- rum dixit. Grotio autem judice, nec Ebræis quidem filiam fratris ducere vetitum est, ac ante legis tempora licuisse etiam Ebræis amitam ducere: neque in commu- ne datum (ante legem civilem Ebræorum) huma- no generi interdictum de non habendis eodem tempo- re in matrimonio Sororibus duabus: nec irritum fuisse conjugium, si quis inter Christianos post obitum uxo- ris suæ Sororem ejus ducat, aut fratris filiam sibi jun- gat; fiquidem hoc jure solum civili (Ebræorum) prohibitum, secundum ipsum, sit, quo Christiani non obstringantur. lib. II. de jure pacis & belli c. V. §. XIV. Quibus vero & similibus clara litera de incestibus & conjugiis nefariis, ob quæ etiam gentes terra expuerit, quæ proinde juri gentium adversa esse oportuit, tum S. Johannes quoque aperte re- clamat Matth. XIV, 4. Marc. 6, 18. 8κ ἔξεςί σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τῶ ἀδελφῶ σε, quibus eares, tan- quam illicita impro batur. Unde Bellarminus ipse conjugium incestum indigitavit, Cap. XX, 21. Notum est, quod Daniel Hoffmannus Helmstæd. Theologus olim, & nuper Christophorus Joachim Bucholtz in Acad. Rintelens. Juris Professor occa- sione Principis cujusdam S. R. I. sororem uxoris ducentis Anno 1652. nuptias ejusmodi, ceu juri divino ac naturali minime adversas defendere conati sint, sed uti Hoffmanno D. Heinricus Hes- husius Supersntendens cum Ministris Hildesien- sibus sufficienter, approbante Collegio Theo- logico Jenensi in judicio suo, responsum: ita illis etiam, quæ Rintelensis Professor denuo in proscenium orbis literati produxit, facile satisfieri potest. Vid. B. Gerhard. LL. CC. de Conjug. §. 347.

paret, (satis enim lubricus in eo est) Parentes & liberos solum sine expressa lege RATIONEM NA- TURALEM jungi fatis vetare, ait; forte cum Cardinali Cajetano hic faciens, qui jure naturæ pro- hiberi tantum conjugium Filii cum matre & Patris cum filia, in cæteris dispensare posse Rom. Pontificem, disputavit; fiquidem fratris cum Sorore concubitum AB INITIO rem MEDIAM fuisse e Mich. Ephes. ad V. Nicomach. doceat Grotius: in affinibus vero, qui in recto sunt limite, item in sanguinis gradu transversorum primo, qui ob ortum a stirpe commu- ni secundus dici solet, ob recentem admodum paren- tum in liberis imaginem naturalem verecundia in- tercedere velit, ut natura si non præcipiat, certe hone- stius dictet, abstinendum esse ab illis matrimoniis: Easq, leges, & ne fratres Sororibus misceantur, simul cum lege de Deo colendo ipsi Adamo datas cum Ebræ- is haud obscure statuit; etsi id a Mose narratum suo loco non sit, fiquidem fama vetus apud Gentiles fuerit de lege divina adversus id genus conjugia, unde &

Quisquis male agentibus adulatur, pulvillum sub ca- pite vel cubito jacentis ponit, ait Gregor. M. l. 18. c. 4. ut qui corripi ex culpa debuerat, in ea fultus laudibus molliter quiescat. Parietem liniunt, ait iterum Gre- gorius M. quod ex eodem repetitur c. Sunt nonnulli. dist. 46. qui peccata perpetrantibus adulantur, ut illi, perverse agentes ædificent, illi adulantes quasi niti- dum reddant. Confer de hoc casu scripta amœbæa Dn. D. Ægid. Strauchii & D. Bucholz. nuper- rima.

## 18:30
Verse 30. KEEP MY COMMANDMENTS) In Hebrew: Keep my keeping. Just as also below, 22, 9, where the LXX [say]: φυλάξονται τὸ φύλαγμά με. The Hebrews draw this to the opinions received in interpreting the law, so that no one may depart from them out of love for private opinion. I would rather think this is hinted at, that not only those things which are of natural law are to be kept, but also those which, like outworks, by their interposition remove natural law further from contempt. Thus among Christians, canons are called προφυλακὴ of divine laws.

Latin:

Vers. 30. CVSTODITE MANDATA MEA) In He- bræo: Custodite custodiam meam. Quomodo & infra, 22, 9. ubi LXX. φυλάξονται τὸ φύλαγμά με. Trahunt hoc Hebræi ad receptas in lege interpretanda sententias, ne quis ab eis privatæ opinionis amore discedat. Ego potius putem hoc innui, non modo servanda, quæ juris sunt naturalis, sed & ea, quæ velut antemuralia interjectu suo jus naturale longius a contemtu semovent. Sic apud Christianos, canones προφυ- λακὴ vocantur θείων νόμων.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. Various Moral and Ceremonial [Precepts].

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. Varia Moralia, & Ceremonialia.

## 19:2
Verse 2.

BE YE HOLY) This chapter comprehends almost all the duties of man.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SANCTI ESTOTE) Caput hoc omnia ferme officia ho- minis comprehendit.

## 19:3
Verse 3.

EVERY ONE SHALL FEAR HIS FATHER OR HIS MOTHER) In Hebrew the mother is placed first, because naturally the father is feared more. And because naturally the mother is loved more, therefore in honor, that is, love, the father is placed in the first position.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VNVSQVISQVE PATREM SVVM AVT MA- TREM SVAM TIMEAT) In Hebræo mater proponitur, quia naturaliter magis timetur pater. Et quia naturaliter mater amatur magis, ideo in honore, id est, amore, pater prio- re loco ponitur.

## 19:7
Verse 7. IT SHALL BE PROFANE) More correctly, it shall be profane, i.e., ἄδυτόν ἐςι, as the LXX translate very well here. Your sacrifice shall be void: it will profit you nothing: this law is opposed to the custom of the nations, who used to make περικόμματα from victims.

Latin:

Vers. 7. PROFANVS ERIT) Rectius profanum erit, i. e. ἄδυτόν ἐςι, ut optime hic vertunt LXX. Sacrificium tuum erit irritum: nihil tibi proderit: opposita hæc lex mori gen- tium, quæ de victimis faciebant περικόμματα.

## 19:9
Verse 9.

YOU SHALL NOT REAP TO THE VERY SURFACE OF THE EARTH) In Hebrew, You shall not finish by reaping the corner of your field: That is, you shall leave some corner of the sown field unreaped or ungathered. That corner, according to custom, was the sixtieth part.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

NON TONDEBIS VSQVE AD SOLVM SVPERFI- CIEM TERRÆ) In Hebræo, Non consummabis metendo angulum agri tui: Id est, angulum aliquem agri consiti relin- ques indemessum vel indecerptum. Is angulus ex moribus erat pars sexagesima.

## 19:11
Verse 11.

YOU SHALL NOT STEAL) This happens not only when someone steals goods from another, but when someone sees or knows [it], and is silent.

YOU SHALL NOT LIE) In the Hebrew: You shall not deny, namely a deposit. Here also are those who see, or know, and are silent: nor do they help with their testimony him who is being defrauded.

NOR SHALL ANYONE DECEIVE HIS NEIGHBOR) תשקרו, which is here in the Hebrew, they interpret as demanding what is not owed.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

NON FACIETIS FVRTVM) Id fit non tantum, cum quis alteri bona subtrahit, sed cum quis videt, aut novit, & tacet.

NON MENTIEMINI) In Hebræo: Non negabitis, nem- pe depositum. Etiam hic fontes habentur, qui vident, aut norunt, & tacent: neque testimonio juvant eum, qui frau- datur.

NEC DECIPIET VNVSQVISQVE PROXIMUM SV- VM) תשקרו, quod hic est in Hebræo interpretantur poscere non debitum.

## 19:13
Vers. 13. YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT EXTORTION AGAINST YOUR NEIGHBOR) תעשק, which is here in the Hebrew, they wish to be properly to retain what you owe to another.

NOR SHALL YOU OPPRESS HIM BY FORCE) תגזל is what the Romans call the violence of stolen goods.

Latin:

Vers. 13. NON FACIES CALVMNIAM PROXIMO TVO) תעשק, quod hîc in Hebræo est, proprie esse volunt re- tinere, quod alteri debeas.

NEC VI OPPRIMES EVM) תגזל est, quod Romani vim bonorum raptorum vocant.

## 19:14
Vers. 14.

NOR SHALL YOU PLACE A STUMBLING BLOCK BEFORE THE BLIND) This law includes all who give bad advice, especially to the simpler-minded.

Augustine, sermon 38 to the brothers in the desert: You curse the deaf when you do not know how to give counsel because of their ignorance; you place a stumbling block before the blind when you show false things as true. Gregory the Great in the Pastoral Rule: To curse the deaf is to disparage one who is absent and not hearing; to place a stumbling block before the blind is to do a thing that is indeed discreet, but nevertheless to provide an occasion of scandal to one who does not have the light of discretion.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

NEC CORAM CÆCO PONES OFFENDICVLVM) Comprehendit hæc lex omnes, qui mala dant consilia, præ- sertim simplicioribus.

AUgustinus serm. 38. ad fratr. in Eremo: Tunc surdo maledicitis, quando consilium propter igno- rantem dare nescitis; tunc cæco offendiculum ponitis, quando falsa pro veris ostenditis. Gregor. M. in Pa- stur. Surdo maledicere, est absenti & non audienti derogare: coram cæco offendiculum ponere est dis- cretam quidem rem agere, sed tamen ei, qui lumen discretionum non habet, scandali occasionem præbere.

## 19:15
Vers. 15.

NOR SHALL YOU JUDGE UNJUSTLY) So that a sentence passed by a judge through an error of law that is not controversial could be revoked by him.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

NEC INJVSTE JVDICABIS) Ita ut sententia per erro- rem juris non controversi a judice lata revocari ab ipso posset.

## 19:16
Vers. 16. YOU SHALL NOT STAND AGAINST THE BLOOD OF YOUR NEIGHBOR) That is, you shall not suffer an innocent person to be killed by force or by the appearance of a trial, if you can free him by aid or testimony. Thus Moses of Coucy, Maimonides, and others. The Hebrews understand neighbor here, as in all the laws of Moses, to be only an Israelite or a foreigner subject to the law.

Latin:

Vers. 16. NON STABIS CONTRA SANGVINEM PROXIMI TVI) Id est, non patieris innocentem per vim aut judicii specie interimi, si eum liberare auxilio aut testi- monio possis. Sic Moses de Kotzi, Maimonides & alii. Pro- ximum hîc, ut & in omnibus Mosis legibus, Israëlitam so- lum aut extraneum legi subjectum intelligunt Hebræi.

## 19:17
YOU SHALL NOT HATE YOUR BROTHER IN YOUR HEART) So that you do not pursue private revenge outside of permitted cases.

It is evident from this that for the Jews in the Old Testament not only the external action, e.g., of homicide or injury, as the Socinians wish with the Jews, but also the internal action, such as that of hatred, was forbidden; see Matthew 5:23. Cassian, book 8 on the Capital Vices, chapter 14.

Latin:

NON ODERIS FRATREM TVVM IN CORDE) Vt ultioni privatæ studeas extra casus permissos.

Patet hinc Judæis in V. Test. non tantum actio- nem externam v. c. homicidii aut læsionis, ut cum Ju- dæis Sociniani volunt, sed etiam internam, qualis est odii, vetitam fuisse, vid. Matth. 5, 23. Cassian. l. 8. de Capital. vitiis c. 14.

## 19:17 Addition
To c. 19. 17. p. 497. DO NOT HAVE SIN UPON HIM.

So also the LXX, Chald., Syr., Ar., Munster, Luth., Tigur., Piscator, Castal., and Chazkuni: do not suffer sin on account of this, or do not bear sin for his sake; and Ainsworth teaches that the words signify this properly and customarily from Lev. 22:9, Num. 18:32. See other translations in Pole's Synopsis.

Latin:

Ad c. 19. 17. pag. 497. NE HABEAS SUPER ILLO PECCATUM.

Ita etiam LXX. Chald. Syr. Ar. Munsterus, Luth. Tigur. Piscator. Castal. & Chazkuni: ne hinc peccatum luas, vel ne portes propter ipsum pecca- tum; idque proprie & usitate verba significare è Lev. 22, 9. Num. 18, 32. Ainsworth. docet. Alias translationes vid. apud Polum Synopsi.

## 19:18
Verse 18.

DO NOT SEEK REVENGE) The word which has a place here, נקם, properly, as the Hebrews intend, is when someone denies a benefit to another because of an injury received,

From this the law of retaliation, Num. 35, 19. Deut. 19, 12, is to be explained, namely that in retaliation one should not seek revenge, but only one's own right, so that justice may be satisfied; since neither private nor public vengeance, if one seeks it out of rancor, is lawful. Matt. 5, 39. Rom. 12, 19. seqq.

NOR SHALL YOU BE MINDFUL OF AN INJURY) This word is נטר, which they say applies to one who indeed gives a benefit, but with the addition of a reproach for an injury received long ago.

OF YOUR CITIZENS) Of those who live subject to the law. And thus the word עמית, which follows here, is accustomed to be taken in the law. Before the law, it was understood of any man whatsoever, as Gen. 11, 3. Exod. 2, 13. 11, 2. Naturally, as the multitude and malice of men grew, written laws were made which would provide at least for citizens, and sometimes for those nations with whom commerce was necessary. See what Hermachus has on this matter in Porphyry, book one, On Abstinence from Animal Food.

The meaning of the divine law is perverted, in the Jewish manner which Christ rebuked in Matt. 5, 43, which we are taught by Christ's clear interpretation in Luke 10, 36, is to be understood not of citizens and nations with whom the Jews had dealings, but of any NEIGHBOR whatsoever, and every man joined by common creation, and likewise by common redemption and grace. We are taught that the love of even an enemy was commanded by Moses in Exod. 23, 4. Every man is a neighbor to man, nor is any distance of race to be thought of where there is a common nature, says Augustine in Ps. 118. Conc. 8. and Sermon 59 on the season: we are all neighbors by the condition of earthly birth, and also by the hope of the heavenly inheritance.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

NON QVÆRAS VLTIONEM) Verbum quod hic נקם locum habet proprie, ut Hebræi volunt, cum quis ob acceptam injuriam beneficium alteri negat,

Explicanda inde lex talionis, Num. 35,19. Deut. 19, 12. ut nempe in talione non quærat quis ultio- nem, sed tantum jus suum, ut justitiæ satisfiat; si- quidem nec privata, nec publica vindicta, si eam ex rancore quis petat, licita sit. Matth. 5, 39. Rom. 12, 19. seqq.

NEC MEMOR ERIS INJVRIA) Hoc verbum est נטר, quod in eum ajunt competere, qui beneficium dat quidem, sed addita exprobratione ob acceptam olim injuriam.

CIVIVM TVORVM) Eorum, qui legi subjecti vivunt. Et ita vox עמית, quæ hic sequitur in lege sumi solet. Ante le- gem de quovis homine intelligebatur, ut Genes. 11, 3. Exod. 2, 13. 11, 2. Nimirum crescente hominum multitudine & malitia, leges scriptæ sunt, quæ civibus saltem consulerent, interdum & iis gentibus, quibuscum necessaria erant com- mercia. Vide quæ hac de re habet Hermachus apud Porphy- rium libro primo de Abstinentia ab animalibus.

Pervertitur, more Judaico, quem Christus ca- stigavit Matth. 5, 43. sententia legis divinæ, quam non de civibus & gentibus, quarum commercio utebantur Judæi, sed de quovis PROXIMO, omni- que homine communi creatione, communi item redemtione, ac gratia conjuncto intelligendam es- se, luculenta Christi interpretatione docemur Luc. 10, 36. Inimici etiam dilectionem a Mose præce- ptam esse docemur Exod. 23, 4. Omnis homo est ho- mini proximus, nec ulla cogitanda est longinquitas generis, ubi est natura communis, ait Augustinus in Ps. 118. Conc. 8. & Serm. 59. de tempore: omnes proximi sumus conditione terrenæ nativitatis, & etiam spe cælestis hæreditatis.

## 19:19
Verse 19.

YOU SHALL NOT SOW YOUR FIELD WITH DIVERSE SEED) What is said here of the field has a place also in the vineyard, Deut. 29, 9. Maimonides notes that the Egyptians used both mixtures for many magical purposes. The Hebrews teach that in a mystical sense, schisms are forbidden here. And he has excellently joined two prohibitions: that heterogeneous things should not be mixed, and that homogeneous things should not be divided.

A GARMENT, WHICH IS WOVEN OF TWO, YOU SHALL NOT PUT ON) There is here, if I am not mistaken, an Egyptian word, שעטנז, which the Hebrews interpret as being of wool and linen. Thus the Romans believed that if a Flaminica were found to have had a woolen tunic sewn with linen, a sin had been committed for that reason. Servius teaches this on the last book of the Aeneid. All these things commend that which is unadulterated.

I have frequently warned, says Theodoret, quest. 27, that intellectual things, which pertain to the soul, are taught through sensible things. But here one is warned especially not to mix false doctrine with true, nor to sell secular life under a religious habit, nor hidden malice under an external veil. Wool, because it is coarser, signifies a visible work; linen, because it is finer, signifies hidden malice: therefore, they put on a garment woven of wool and linen who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts, Ps. 27. Radulph.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

AGRVM TVVM NON SERES DIVERSO SEMI- NE) Quod hic in arvo dicitur, idem in vinea locum habet Deut. 29, 9. Vtraque mixtura usos ad multa magica Ægy- ptios notat Maimonides. Sensu mystico schismata hic vetari tradunt Hebræi. Et egregie conjunxit duo interdicta, ne commisceantur ἑτερογένεα, ne dividantur ὁμογένεα.

VESTE, QVÆ EX DVOBVS TEXTA EST, NON INDVERIS) Est hic vox, ni fallor, Ægyptiaca שעטנז, quam Hebræi interpretantur, ex lana & lino. Sic Romani credidere, si Flaminica inventa esset tunicam laneam lino ha- buisse consutam, ob eam causam piaculum esse commissum. Docet id Servius ad ultimum Æneidos. Hæc omnia com- mendant τὸ ἀκίβδηλον.

Frequenter admonui, inquit Theodoret. quæst. 27. per sensibilia doceri intellectualia, quæ spectant ad animum. Monetur autem hic imprimis, ne do- ctrinam falsam cum vera misceamus, nec vitam se- cularem religioso habitu, malitiam occultam ex- terno velamine venditemus. Lana, quia crassior, opus visibile, linum, quia subtilius est, occultam malitiam significat: vestem ergo ex lana & lino contextam induunt, qui loquuntur pacem cum proximo suo, mala autem in cordibus eorum, Psal. 27. Radulph.

## 19:20
Verse 20.

ETIAM NVBILIS) In the Hebrew, betrothed. The Greeks mean the same when they say Διαπεφυλαγμένη ἀνθρώπῳ. The Hebrews wish it to be understood here as a semi-free handmaid by the master's indulgence, such as those of free status among the Romans.

VAPVLABVNT) In the Hebrew, a scourging. The sense is that she herself shall be scourged, namely with a bull's pizzle; for the man is expiated by a victim, as will be said presently. That punishment seemed sufficient:

No action is given from this act, just as there is none for him who has been harmed by the oath of testimony or of deposit. See above VI.

BECAUSE SHE WAS NOT FREE) The marriages of slave women are not fully marriages, nor are betrothals fully betrothals. Maimonides.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ETIAM NVBILIS) In Hebræo desponsata. Græci idem volunt, cum dicunt Διαπεφυλαγμένη ἀνθρώπῳ. Agi hic volunt Hebræi de Ancilla semilibera domini indultu, quales statu liberi apud Romanos.

VAPVLABVNT) In Hebræo vapulatio. Sensus est ipsa vapulabit, nervo nempe bubulo; nam vir victima expiatur, ut jam dicetur. Ea animadversio sufficere visa:

nulla ex hoc facto actio datur, sicut nec ei qui laesus est jura- mento testimonii aut depositi. Vide supra VI.

QVIA NON FVIT LIBERA) Ancillarum nuptiae non plene nuptiae sunt, nec sponsalia plene sponsalia. Maimo- nides.

## 19:23
Vers. 23.

YOU SHALL REMOVE THEIR FORESKINS) By the name of foreskin the Hebrews call whatever is removed as useless.

FRUITS WHICH GERMINATE SHALL BE UNCLEAN TO YOU) For three years: which is added in the Hebrew. The first fruits of uncultivated fields have something wild and unhealthy. Many precepts consult for health. The fruits of the fourth year are to be dedicated to God: finally, those of the fifth are profitable to the Lord. Maimonides adds that this law is opposed to the customs of idolaters.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

AVFERETIS PRAEPVTIA EORVM) Praeputii nomine vocant Hebraei quicquid ut inutile aufertur.

POMA QVAE GERMINANT IMMVNDA ERVNT VOBIS) Per tres annos: quod additur in Hebraeo. Primi agrorum incultorum fructus ferum aliquid habent & insa- lubre. Multa praecepta valetudini consulunt. Quarti anni fructus Deo dicantur: quinti demum Domino prosunt. Maimonides addit legem hanc oppositam moribus idolola- trarum.

## 19:25
Vers. 25.

BUT IN THE FIFTH YEAR YOU SHALL EAT THE FRUITS) With three witnesses being present, so that it may be established that the law has been fulfilled.

God did not wish to consult nature here alone: that law had its own significance. Radulphus says this about it: The earth is the soul of each person, into which fruit-bearing trees, that is, the plantations of virtues, are to be planted: yet no one ought to rejoice in the fruits of these as they first appear, nor congratulate himself, before the foreskin of admiration, Φιλαυτίας [self-love] and Φιλοδοξίας [love of glory] is removed, and good works are done out of pure love of God, and for the sake of God's glory alone.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

QVINTO AVTEM ANNO COMEDETIS FRV- CTVS) Tribus adhibitis testibus, ut constare possit de im- pleta lege.

Non hic solum naturae consulere voluit Deus: habuit lex illa suam significationem. Radulphus ita de ea: Terra est cujusq; anima, in quam arbores fru- ctiferae, h. e. virtutum plantaria inserenda sunt: de harum tamen fructibus primum se proferentibus ne- mo gaudere, nec sibi gratulari debet, priusquam prae- putium admirationis, Φιλαυτίας & Φιλοδοξίας aufe- ratur, & puro amore Dei, ac propter solam Dei glo- riam bona fiant opera.

## 19:26
Vers. 26.

YOU SHALL NOT EAT WITH THE BLOOD) Namely, victims. They are forbidden to be eaten as long as the blood has not been poured out from the basins and removed. Thus Jonathan and Maimonides. The reason for the prohibition is that profane nations used to feast near the blood, thinking it to be food for demons: concerning which matter see the nekyia of Homer. It seems that among the Egyptians רום meant something else, namely either a mountain or a roof, or both. For other Greek versions have, ἐπὶ τῶν ὀρέων [on the mountains], others ἐπὶ τῶ δώματι [on the roof]. The custom of sacrificing and at the same time eating the victims in high places and those closer to the sky is most ancient, as the history of Abraham also teaches us, and Strabo. But it was forbidden by law to prevent schisms.

This is not the proper reason why the eating of blood is forbidden, which has been done quite frequently, Gen. 9, 4. Lev. 3, 17. c. 7, 26. c. 13, 10. Deut. 12, 16. c. 15, 23. God gave another reason in Lev. 17, 11, and a twofold one at that: one physical and natural, because the soul of the flesh is in the blood, lest the soul itself seem to be eaten with the blood; the other Levitical and ceremonial, because God gave the blood on the altar for the soul of sins to make atonement. Although it may be said that this is the one and only cause or reason for the divine interdict: but that the fact that the soul of the flesh is in the blood ought to be considered the reason for the reason. Therefore, what He reserved for Himself for atonement, He did not want to be eaten by men. We care little what the cause of error was for the Greeks here: they were not adorning their version from the Egyptian but from the Hebrew language. But that Abraham sacrificed in high places before a specifically certain place for sacrifices was defined, was not done because he believed high places were closer to Heaven; for he knew well that God is not encompassed by place: but because sacred things ought to be considered removed from men and profane actions, and far more sublime than them, and because the mind must be elevated into heaven, with thought and devotion lifted from earthly things by sublimity and altitude. But it was forbidden by law, not to prevent schisms, but for the observance of the divine sanction, by which divine worship was restricted to a certain place, where God had fixed the memory of His name, which He later willed to be the Jerusalem temple because of the antitype, namely the sacrifice of Christ, to be offered there in the future, concerning which one should read the blessed Frantzius in Schol. sacrific.

YOU SHALL NOT USE AUGURY NOR OBSERVE DREAMS) The first word which is נחש the LXX translate by ὀιωνίζεσθαι. The Hebrew and Greek word signifies, similar to the Latin augurari, not by origin but by usage, to catch at any omen whatsoever, for instance from sneezing, from the twitching of an eye, from a broken shoelace, from the name of a person who meets us. The other word they translate by ὀρνιθοσκοπεῖν, which properly pertains to auspices. The Hebrew word seems derived from clouds. God has often signified His will through dreams: but not through those omens, or through auspices. See the excellent history in Josephus concerning Mosollamus the Jew, a mocker of the auspice caught by the Greeks. Furthermore, R. Levi rightly notes that natural prognostications are not forbidden here.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

NON COMEDETIS CVM SANGVINE) Nempe vi- ctimas. Ea vetantur edi, quamdiu sanguis e pelvibus ef- fusus ablatusque non est. Ita Jonathan & Maimonides. Causa vetandi, quod profanae nationes apud sanguinem epu- larentur, eum pro alimento esse Daemonibus putantes: qua de re vide νεκυίαν Homeri. Videtur apud Aegyptios רום ali- ud significasse, nempe aut montem aut solarium, aut utrum- que. Nam Graecae versiones aliae habent, ἐπὶ τῶν ὀρέων, aliae ἐπὶ τῶ δώματι. Mos sacrificandi ac simul victimas eden- di in locis excelsis & coelo propioribus antiquissimus est, ut & Abrahami historia nos docet, & Strabo. Vetitus autem le- ge ad impedienda schismata.

Non haec est propria causa, cur vetatur esus san- guinis, quod crebriuscule factum, Gen. 9, 4. Lev. 3, 17. c. 7, 26. c. 13, 10. Deut. 12, 16. c. 15, 23. Aliam reddidit Deus Lev. 17, 11. eamque geminam, aliam Physicam & naturalem, quod anima carnis sit in sanguine, ne cum sanguine anima ipsa comedi vi- deatur; aliam Leviticam & Ceremonialem, quod sanguinem in altare dederit Deus pro anima pecca- torum ad expiandum. Quanquam dici possit, hanc unam solum causam vel rationem interdicti divini esse: id vero quod anima carnis in sanguine sit, ra- tionem rationis haberi debere. Quod ergo sibi re- servavit ad expiationem, comedi ab hominibus noluit. Quae Graecis hic errandi causa fuerit, pa- rum curamus: Non ex Aegyptiaca sed Ebrea lin- gua versionem suam adornabant. Quod Autem Abraham in excelsis locis ante definitum peculiari- ter certum sacrificiorum locum sacrificavit, non fa- ctum, quod Coelo propiora crediderit excelsa; Deum enim loco non ambiri probe noverat: sed quod sa- cra ab hominibus & actionibus prophanis semota esse, iisque longa sublimiora censeri debeant, & quod mens elevanda sit in coelum, sublimitate & altitudine cogitationem ac devotionis a terrenis eve- cta. Vetitum vero lege id est, non ad impedienda schismata, sed observantiam divinae sanctionis, qua restrictus fuit cultus divinus ad certum locum, ubi Deus memoriam fixerat nominis sui, quem Hiero- solymitanum templum postmodum esse voluit pro- pter antitypum, Christi nempe sacrificium, ibi olim offerendum, quo de legendus B. Frantzius in Schol. sacrific.

NON AVGVRABIMINI NEC OBSERVABITIS SO- MNIA) Prius verbum quod est נחש per ὀιωνίζεσθαι vertunt LXX. Significat autem vox Hebræa & Græca similis La- tinæ augurari, non ex origine, sed ex usu omen qualecunque captare, puta ex sternutatione, ex oculi subsultu, ex corrigia rupta, ex nomine hominis, qui nobis occurrat. Alterum au- tem verbum vertunt per ὀρνιθοσκοπεῖν, quod proprie ad au- spicia pertinet. Videtur verbum Hebræum ductum a nu- bibus. Deus per somnia voluntatem suam sæpe significa- vit: non autem per illa omina, aut per auspicia. Vide egre- giam de Mosollamo Judæo auspicii a Græcis captati irrisore historiam apud Josephum. Cæterum φυσικὰς προγνώσεις hîc non vetari recte notat R. Levi.

## 19:27
Verse 27.

NOR SHALL YOU CLIP THE HAIR IN A ROUND) Which custom the Greek scholia note here to be that of the Saracens. Wherefore Choerilus, when in the verses that are in Josephus he called the Jews τροχοκόραδας, confused them, as a Greek man, with the Arabs their neighbors, and then their fellow soldiers. Herodotus in Thalia concerning the Arabs: they cut their hair in a circle, shaving around the temples. Plutarch also in Theseus says: the Arabs used to cut the front part of the head. Which agrees with that which Theodorus Mopsuestenus says: the Saracens, leaving the hair on the back part, only cut off the part on the forehead, who are those now called Gentiles. The Hebrews say the same concerning the Amorites. Moreover, that the name here in Greek for rounded hair is σισόη, Hesychius teaches us was customary for the Phaselitans.

Concerning this passage, and who the τροχοκόυριδες of Choerilus are, see our B. Dorschæus, Syn. Theol. Zach. p. 22, 23, of the former edition.

NOR SHALL YOU SHAVE THE BEARD) So also Phesictha: and among the Greeks, Hesychius. Cyprian also in book III of Testimonies proves from this that the beard is not to be plucked. In the Hebrew it is: You shall not corrupt the extremity of your beard. To shave the beard is the custom of the Babylonian priests. See the epistle which is called Jeremiah's, without Baruch's.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

NEQVE IN ROTVNDVM ATTONDEBITIS CO- MAM) Quem morem esse Sarracenorum notant hîc scholia Græca. Quare Chœrilus cum in versibus, qui apud Jose- phum sunt Judæos dixit τροχοκόραδας, confudit eos, ut ho- mo Græcus, cum Arabibus vicinis eorum, & tunc commili- tibus. Herodotus Thalia de Arabibus: κείρονται δὲ ὑπο- τρόχαλα περιξυρῦντες τὸς κροτάφυς. Etiam Plutarchus in Theseo ait: οἱ Ἀραβες ἐκείροντο τῆς κεφαλῆς τὸ πρόσθεν. Quod convenit cum eo, quod dicit Theodorus Mopsueste- nus: οἱ Σαρακηνοὶ τὴν κόμην κατὰ τὸ ὄπισθεν μέρος ἐῶντες μόνον ἀποκείρονται τὸ μέρος τὸ ἐπὶ τὸ μέτωπον οἵ εἰσιν οἳ νῦν λεγόμενοι Γεντίλιοι. Idem de Amorrhæis dicunt Hebræi. Quod autem hic in Græco nomen est comæ rotundatæ σισόη Phaselitis usitatum fuisse docet nos Hesychius.

De hoc loco, & quinam τροχοκόυριδες Chœri- li sint, vid. B. Dorschæus noster Syn. Theol. Zach. p. 22. 23. prior. edit.

NEC RADETIS BARBAM) Sic & Phesictha: & inter Græcos Hesychius. Cyprianus quoque libro III. Testimo- niorum hinc probat, barbam non vellendam. In Hebræo est: Non corrumpes extremitatem barbæ tuæ. Barbam radere mos Babyloniorum Sacerdotum. Vide epistolam quæ Jere- miæ dicitur sine Baruchi.

## 19:27 Addition
Vers. 27. NOR SHALL YOU SHAVE YOUR BEARD p. 498. b. after the annotations of Grotius.

This is therefore prohibited not so much because it would argue for effeminacy, because it is not effeminacy but superstition that is prohibited here, as because this was accustomed to be done in honor of idols, Baruch 6, where the Egyptian priests and others performed sacred rites only with a shaved beard; see Lev. 21:5. The heathens consecrated their beard and first down to their gods: see Suetonius on Nero, c. 12. And this was done by the heathens especially at funerals, whence also in the following verses in this place the incision for the dead is prohibited, which is likewise prohibited together with baldness in Deut. 14, v. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 27. NEC RADETIS BARBAM p. 498. b. post annot. Grotii.

Prohibitum ergo hoc non tam quod molli- tiem argueret, quia non mollities, sed superstitio hic prohibetur, quam quod hoc fieri consueverit in honorem idolorum Baruch. 6. ubi sacrificuli Ægyptii & alii nonnisi abrasa barba sacra facie- bant, vid. Lev. 21, 5. Barbam & primam lanuginem Diis suis consecrabant Ethnici: vid. Sueton. de Neron. c. 12. Et imprimis in funeribus hoc ab Eth- nicis fiebat, unde etiam v. seqq. hoc in loco prohi- bita incisio pro mortuo, quæ similiter una cum cal- vitio prohibetur Deut. 14. v. 1.

## 19:28
Verse 28.

YOU SHALL NOT INCISE YOUR FLESH FOR THE DEAD) He took נפש for a corpse, and it is said to have been the custom of the Amorites to mourn for the dead by incising the body. You could take נפש for blood, so that an incision drawing blood is forbidden, which the pagans used, as—those whom Bellona, with slashed arms, moves in a savage way. Which words of Lucan are in the first book: and the Gauls, concerning whom Martial: The white arms are less mangled by savage knives, when the inspired crowd rages in Phrygian modes. See concerning this custom 1 Kings 18:28 and Jeremiah 16:6. The custom remains even now among certain barbarian peoples. Others say here that it concerns the laceration which is done by the nails: Deuteronomy 14, that which is done by knives.

NOR SHALL YOU MAKE ANY FIGURES OR STIGMATA FOR YOURSELVES) With points pricked into the skin, as Horace says: The Talmud, under the title concerning the Sanhedrin, notes that it was customary for this to be done with ink or antimony. Moreover, with such points on the forehead or hand, the names of gods were written, or the number of the names, or hieroglyphic marks of the gods. See the Apocalypse, chapter 13, at the end. The same was also done with a heated iron. Philo: concerning those who brand themselves for the service of man-made things with a heated iron.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

SUPER MORTVO NON INCIDETIS CARNEM VESTRAM) Sumsit נפש pro cadavere, diciturque mos fu- isse Amorrhæorum lugere mortuos inciso corpore. Possis su- mere נפש pro sanguine, ut vetetur incisio sanguinem elici- ens quo pagani utebantur, ut - - quos sectis Bellona lacertis Sæva movet. Quæ verba Lucani sunt primo: & Galli, de quibus Mar- tialis: Alba minus sævis lacerantur brachia cultris, Cum furit ad Porygos, enthea turba modos. Vide de hoc more 1. Reg. 18, 28. & Jerem. 16, 6. 15. mos & nunc manet apud quasdam barbaras gentes. Alii hîc ajunt agi de laceratione, quæ fit per ungues: Deuteron. 14. de ea quæ fit per cultros.

NEQVE FIGVRAS ALIQVAS AVT STIGMATA FACIETIS VOBIS) Victuris in cute punctis, ut ait Hora- tius: Atramento aut stibio id fieri solitum notat Thalmud ti- tulo de Synedrio. Talibus autem punctis in fronte, aut manu scribebantur nomina Deorum, aut numerus nominum, aut hieroglyphicæ Deorum notæ. Vide Apocalypsin cap. 13. in fine. Idem & ferro ignito fiebat. Philo: περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰς δυλείαν τῶν χειροκμήτων ἑαυτὸς καταστιζόντων σιδήρῳ πεπυρωμένῳ.

## 19:28 Addition
To v. 28. Those words: YOU SHALL NOT MAKE INCISIONS IN YOUR FLESH FOR THE DEAD, ibid. after the annotations of Grotius.

Where nephesh is taken for blood, it will not be easily taught. And what sense is there in 'you shall not make incisions in your flesh for blood'? Nor is nephesh a corpse, but a soul, as Vatabl., Munst., Oleaster, Syr., and Ainsw. have rendered it; it was done in honor of the soul of the deceased, and as an argument of grief, as Mariana and Menochius hold; or they even believed it was beneficial to the soul departing from the body. Varro says that women were accustomed to lacerate their faces in funerals and mourning so that, by showing blood, they might satisfy the shades, says Servius on Aeneid 3. Some of the barbarians also defile their own bodies by cutting off their noses, ears, and other parts, thinking that they are in some way gratifying the deceased. Plutarch in Cons. ad Apoll. Thus the Scythians, according to Herodotus, book 4, no. 7.

On those words: NEITHER SHALL YOU MAKE ANY FIGURES OR STIGMATA FOR YOURSELVES, after Grotius's annotation.

Dievius notes that these were made with a chisel. Fagius and Münster observe that the Gentiles used to carve figures of letters into their flesh and fill them with some color, so that those scars would always be seen: and Maimonides notes that they thus marked themselves for idolatry. Bonfrerius, however, prefers to understand it as referring to stigmata branded for the sake of a funeral, even though no mention of this custom is made among Greek or Latin writers, because all of these were long after those times.

Latin:

Ad v. 28. Verba illa: SUPER MORTUO NON INCIDETIS CARNEM VESTRAM, ib. post annot. Grotii.

Ubi נפש pro sanguine sumatur, non facile do- cebitur. Et quis senius, super sanguine non incide- tis carnem vestram? Neque נפש cadaver est, sed anima, uti reddidit Vatabl. Munst. Oleaster, Syr. Ainsw. in honorem animæ defuncti id fiebat, & mœroris argumentum, ut Mariana, & Menochius habent; vel etiam id animæ è corpore abeunti prodesse credebant. Varro dicit mulieres in exe- quiis & luctu ideo solitas ora lacerare, ut sanguine ostenso inferis satisfaciant ait Servius 3. Æneid. Qui- dam barbarorum etiam corpora sua naribus, au- ribus, aliisque partibus amputandis fœdant, gra- tificari se aliquo modo defunctis putantes. Plu- tarch. in Cons. ad Apoll. Ita Scythæ teste Herod. lib. 4. num. 7.

Ad illa verba: NEQUE FIGURAS ALIQUAS AUT STIGMATA FACIETIS VOBIS, post annotatum Grotianum.

Scalpro hæc facta Dievius notat. Fagius & Münsterus sculpsisse observant gentiles in carne sua literarum figuras, easque aliquo colore supplevisse, ut cicatrices illæ semper viderentur: Atque ita se ad idololat转换为riam signasse notat Maimonides. Bonfre- rius vero mavult de stigmatis, causa funeris inustis accipere, etsi nulla hujus moris mentio fiat apud scri- ptores Græcos vel Latinos, quod hi omnes his tem- poribus dudum posteriores fuerint.

## 19:29
Verse 29.

DO NOT PROSTITUTE YOUR DAUGHTER) That this was done in honor of the gods by the Babylonians and neighboring peoples, you may learn from Herodotus book I, Strabo book XVI, and that epistle which is ascribed to Jeremiah: where ropes are signs of a votive obligation, just as elsewhere of surrender, 1 Kings 20:31. This custom came from the Phoenicians to the Cyprians: therefore it is added here: Lest the land be contaminated, and be filled with wickedness.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

NE PROSTITVAS FILIAM TVAM) Quod in hono- rem deorum factum a Babyloniis & vicinis gentibus discas ex Herodoti libro I. Strabone libro XVI. epistola illa quæ Jeremiæ ascribitur: ubi funes sunt signa votivæ obligationis, sicut alibi deditionis 1. Reg. 20, 31. Hic mos a Phœnicibus ad Cyprios devenit: ideo hîc additur: Ne contaminetur terra, & impleatur piaculo.

## 19:30
Verse 30.

DO NOT POLLUTE MY SANCTUARY) This holiness pertained not only to the temple, but also on account of the temple to the whole city of Jerusalem: in which no one was buried except David: the body of a dead person did not remain through the night: bones were not carried through it: no one dwelt there unless he had accepted the law: there were no paradises or gardens.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

SANCTVARIVM MEVM NE POLLVITE) Hæc sanctitas non ad templum tantum, sed & ob templum ad to- tam urbem Hierosolymorum pertinuit: in qua nemo sepul- tus præter Davidem: non manebat per noctem corpus mor- tui: non transferebantur per eam ossa: non habitabat quisquam nisi qui legem suscepisset: Nulli erant Paradisi hortive.

## 19:31
Verse 31.

AE MAGOS) In Hebrew אבות, elsewhere more fully אובות. The LXX derive this from אוב, which signifies a skin, Job 32:19, and by translation a belly, whence they translate ἐγγαστριμύθους, which word is also found in Galen in the Glosses of Hippocrates. Sophocles called them τερατομάντεις. That is more correct than what others translate as θελητάς from the verb אבה.

AB ARIOLIS) Ἐπαοιδoῖς οὐ προσκολληθήσεσθε. He understands those who promised that they could send and drive away diseases by incantations. Sophocles, Polybius, physicians, and above all Homer mention them. The name comes from the notable knowledge which they peddled. But the Rabbis derive it from an animal, whose bones, taken between the teeth, they claim those diviners used to predict the future. They describe that animal in such a way that it seems clearly the same as that which is called by the Scythians Boramet, a ζώόφυτον ἀμυνόμορϕον.

Latin:

Verf. 31.

AE MAGOS) In Hebræo אבות, alibi plenius אובות. Id LXX. derivant ab אוב, quod utrem fignificat Job. 32, 19. & per translationem ventrem, unde vertunt ἐγγαστριμύθες, quæ vox & apud Galenum in Gloffis Hippocratis. τερατομάν- τεις dixit Sophocles. Id rectius quam quod alii θελητάς ver- tunt a verbo אבה.

AB ARIOLIS) Ἐπαοιδoῖς ὀ προσκολληθήσεσθε. Eos in- telligit, qui carminibus se posse morbos immittere ac depel- lere pollicebantur. Meminere Sophocles, Polybius, Medici & ante omnes Homerus. Nomen ab insigni Scientia quam venditabant. At Rabbini ab animali id deducunt, cujus offibus inter dentes sumtis divinaculos illos futura prædi- xisse volunt. Id animal ita describunt, ut plane idem videatur cum eo, quod Scythis Boramet dicitur, ζώόφυτον ἀμυνόμορϕον.

## 19:35
Verse 35. IN REGULA) In a measuring rod, or in the measurement of a field.

Latin:

Verf. 35. IN REGULA) In decempeda, sive in agri men- fione.

## 19:36
Verse 36. JUSTUS MODIUS) Epha: for dry things.

ÆQVVS SEXTARIUS) Hin: for liquids. This word arrived at Athens from the Phoenicians. Half of it is ἡ μίνη, as Eustathius notes.

Latin:

Verf. 36. JUSTUS MODIUS) Epha : in aridis.

ÆQVVS SEXTARIUS) Hin : in liquidis. Vox hæc a Phœnicibus Athenas pervenit. Dimidium ejus ἡ μίνη, ut no- tat Eustathius.

## 20:1 Argument
CAP. XX. The punishment for the worship of Moloch, magic, cursing of parents, and illicit intercourse.

Latin:

CAP. XX. Pœna cultus Moloch, Magiæ, Maledictionis Pa- rentum, & coitus illiciti.

## 20:3
Verse 3.

ET EGO PONAM FACIEM MEAM) That is, if the matter does not come to the judges, or the judges neglect it; I will punish by כרת, that is, premature death.

CONTAMINAVERIT SANCTUARIUM MEUM) He contaminates, that is, he despises the sanctuary, who sacrifices in another place.

ET POLLUERIT NOMEN SANCTUM MEUM) He is said to pollute the name of God who worships another.

Latin:

Verf. 3.

ET EGO PONAM FACIEM MEAM) Id est, si res ad Judices non devenerit, aut judices neglexerint; ego puniam per כרת, id est, mortem immaturam.

CONTAMINAVERIT SANCTUARIUM MEUM) Contaminat, id est, contemnit sanctuarium, qui alio in loco sacrificat.

ET POLLUERIT NOMEN SANCTUM MEUM) Polluere nomen Dei dicitur, qui alium colit.

## 20:4
Verse 4. DIMISERIT HOMINEM) He who does not punish one devoted to death by law is called an obdurator, סעד in Chaldean, חזק according to Maimonides.

Latin:

Verf. 4. DIMISERIT HOMINEM) Qui non punit lege devotum morti, is dicitur obfirmator, סעד Chaldæo, חזק Maimonidæ.

## 20:11
HE WHO SHALL HAVE SLEPT WITH HIS STEPMOTHER) Not all incest was punished by death, but those for which it is added here or elsewhere.

Latin:

Verf. 11. QVI DORMIERIT CVM NOVERCA) Non omnes incestus morte puniebantur, sed ii, quibus id hic aut alibi additur.

## 20:20
THEY SHALL DIE WITHOUT CHILDREN) ערירים: Thus also the Greeks ἄτεκνοι. Rightly, as appears in Gen. 15, 2. But the Sadducees read עררים and interpreted it as, they shall die naked, so that the punishment might correspond to the fault.

The Samaritan Pentateuch has nothing by which it might prefer itself to the sources: and it is deservedly abandoned here by Grotius because of the discrepancy from the Hebrew: with which the Greeks and the Vulgate agree. That word ערירי also perhaps could be rendered destroyed, because the root is ערר, he destroyed, demolished, laid waste, as also ערער signifies destroyed, demolished, and indeed with a violent destruction, and miserable. Therefore, what is said in v. 20 ערירים ימתו, that is expressed simply in v. 21 ערירים יהיו, that they are to be destroyed and ought to perish by a miserable death. Bellarmine, ch. 27, on matrimony, takes it thus, that their sons are not to be inscribed in the genealogies. But because it is said, they shall bear their sin: Likewise they shall die, a heavier punishment is designated; namely, that they are to be taken from the midst by the Magistrate, so that children may not be born from them, if that word is rendered WITHOUT CHILDREN, or that they ought to perish by a miserable and violently destructive death (whatever that kind of punishment may finally have been among the Hebrews, for not all are known).

Latin:

Verf. 20. ABSQVE LIBERIS MORIENTUR) ערירים: Sic & Græci ἄτεκνοι. Recte, ut apparet Gen. 15, 2. At Sadducæi legere עררים & interpretati sunt, nudi morientur, ut pœna culpæ respondeat.

P Entateuchus Samaritanorum non habet, quo se fontibus præferat: & merito hic deseritur a GVotio ob discrepantiam ab Ebreo: Cui consonant Græci & Vulgatus. Illud autem ערירי etiam reddi fortassis poterit destructi, quia ערר radix est, destru- xit, diruit, depopulatus est, uti etiam ערער destructum, dirutum, & quidem vehementi destructione, ac mise- rum significat. Ideo quod v. 20. dicitur ערירים ימתו id effertur simpliciter v. 21. ערירים יהיו quod destru- endi sint atq; misera morte perire debeant. Bellarmin. c. 27. de matrim. ita accipit, quod Filii illorum non sint in genealogiis adscribendi. Sed quia dicitur, pec- catum suum portabunt: Item morientur, gravior pœna designatur; quod nempe sint per Magistra- tum e medio tollendi, ne ex illis nascantur liberi, si vox illa reddatur SINE LIBERIS, aut quod mor- te misera & vehementer destructiva (quodcunque tandem illud apud Ebræos supplicii genus fuerit, non enim omnia nota sunt) interire debeant.

## 20:20 Addition
On chapter 20, verse 20, page 499, a, towards the end of the chapter.

Which latter opinion is more consistent, even though the LXX, R. Solomon in Lyranus, the Vulgate, Pagninus, Arias-Montanus, B. Luther, Junius & Tremellius, and Piscator translate it as 'without children,' which Osiander explains simply as the deprivation of divine blessing and childlessness, Brentius as that they will not beget children, or if they do beget them, they are not to be held as legitimate, in which way also Augustine, Quest. 76 in Leviticus, Procopius, Hesychius, the interlinear gloss, and Cajetan understand it as the denial of succession to children. Others, however, interpret it with Piscator, Cornel. à Lapide, and Menochius as follows: they will not be allowed to remain in this wickedness until they can have children, but they will be killed. It is certain from the following verse that the punishment designated here by this phrase is: ערירים ימתו, and that the punishment is to be inflicted rather by the Magistrate, to whom the execution of these laws and punishments is prescribed, than to be brought about immediately by God: and the word ערירי, even if in Gen. 15:2 it may denote 'childless,' yet in Jeremiah, chapter 22, verse 30, it cannot have that meaning: as is stated there. Compare here the Blessed Hülseman, Breviar. Extens. cap. 21, thes. 9, p. 426. B. Gerhard, de conjug. §. 269 & 309.

Latin:

Ad cap. 20. versu 20. pag. 499. a. sub finem capitis.

Quæ posterior sententia magis congruit, etsi LXX. R. Salomo apud Lyran. Vulgat. Pagnin. Arias- Montan. B. Lutherus, Junius & Tremellius, Piscator vertant, fine liberis, quod Osiander de privatione benedictionis divinæ, & ἀτεκνίᾳ simpliciter expli- cat, Brentius quod non sint liberos procreaturi, aut si procreabunt, illi non sint legitimi habendi, quo pacto etiam Augustinus quæst. 76. in Levit. Procopius, Hesychius, glossa interlinearis, & Cajetan. de dene- ganda liberis successione accipiunt. Alii autem ita cum Piscatore, Cornel. à Lapide & Menochio inter- pretantur: non sinentur in hoc scelere permanere, do- nec liberos habere possint, sed occidentur. Certum est è versu sequenti, pœnam hic designatam esse ista phrasi: ערירים ימתו, & pœnam potius à Magi- stratu, cui præscribitur legum harum & pœnarum exequutio, infligendam, quam immediate à Deo inferendam: & vox ערירי etsi Gen. 15, 2. ἄτεκνον notet, apud Jeremiam tamen cap. 22. versu 30. eum sensum habere nequit: ut illic dictum. Conf. hic Beat. Hülseman. Breviar. Extens. cap. 21. thes. 9. p. 426. B. Gerhard. de conjug. §. 269. & 309.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. Mourning and marriages of the Priests.

Verse 1.

LET NOT THE PRIEST BE DEFILED AMONG THE DEAD OF HIS CITIZENS) Let him not be present at a funeral unless of those very closely related, which follows. It was also not permitted for him to reside in burial grounds. The high priest is permitted to be present at no funeral under 10.

He adds, however, an exception there from the Hebrews: If the high priest had found someone unburied on the road. For he was able to bury him. Moses of Coucy, in the prohibitive precept 237.

Verse the same.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. Luctus & conjugia Sacerdotum.

Verf. 1.

NE CONTAMINETVR SACERDOS IN MORTI- BVS CIVIVM SVORVM) Ne intersit funeri nisi valde propinqui, quod sequitur. In sepulchretis quoque ei resi- dere non licebat. Pontifex maximus nulli funeri interesse permittitur infra 10.

ADdit tamen ibi exceptionem ex Ebræis: Si quem Pontifex maximus in via inhumatum re- periffet. Eum enim humare poterat. Moses de Kotzi præcepto vetante 237.

Verf. eod.

## 21:1 Addition
On Leviticus chapter 21, verse 1. LET NOT THE PRIEST BE DEFILED AMONG THE DEAD OF HIS PEOPLE.

In the Hebrew it is לנפש, which some render as 'over a corpse.' But 'soul' is nowhere taken in the Scriptures for a corpse: however, it denotes a human being by synecdoche: that the Priest should not defile himself over a human being, which Mercerus and Mariana understand of an inferior Priest, because they would thus contract an impurity that would hinder them from the Ministry of the tabernacle; if, that is, there were those among the common people who would take care of the funeral, though in a case of necessity Priests are bound to bury the dead, as Polus notes from Muis. And it was lawful for them without distinction to enter for a deceased Father and mother or a blood relative, but not for the High Priest, because he was constantly occupied in the worship of God, and there was no one who could take his place if he were defiled, as Münster observes.

Latin:

Ad Levit. cap. 21. versu 1. NE CONTAMINETUR SACERDOS IN MORTIBUS CIVIUM SUORUM.

In Ebræo est לנפש quod reddunt nonnulli super cadavere. Sed anima nuspiam accipitur in Scripturis pro cadavere: hominem autem Synecdo- chice notat: ne contaminet se super homine scilic. Sacerdos, quod de inferiori Sacerdote Mercerus & Mariana intelligunt, quod ita contraherent im- munditiem eos à Ministerio tabernaculi impe- dientem; si scil. adessent, qui funus curarent è po- pularibus, in casu autem necessitatis tenentur Sacer- dotes mortuum sepelire, ut è Muisio Polus notat. Et ad defunctum Patrem & matrem vel consan- guineum integrum erat illis citra differentiam in- gredi, non tamen summo Sacerdoti, quia is jugiter in cultu Dei occupabatur, nec erat qui ejus vices suppleret, si contaminaretur ipse, ut observat Münsterus.

## 21:7
A HARLOT AND A VILE PROSTITUTE) These hardly differ among themselves. But in the Hebrew the second word is חללה, which the LXX translate as βεβηλωμένην. By זונה here the Hebrews understand all foreign women, likewise those who have had intercourse with those with whom marriage is forbidden by divine law: but by חללה, women born or descended from one who is forbidden to the Priests. But Josephus by זונה understands more simply her who has prostituted herself: by חללה those who are hardly believed to be chaste, such as maidservants, captives, tavern-keepers, stable-girls.

NOR HER WHO HAS BEEN REPUDIATED BY HER HUSBAND) She who has taken the shoe off a kinsman is considered by the same law as this one: from the law which is in Deut. 25, 9.

Latin:

SCORTVM ET VILE PROSTIBVLVM) Vix diffe- runt hæc inter se. At in Hebræo secunda vox est חללה, quod βεβηλωμένην vertunt LXX. Hebræi per זונה hic intelli- gunt omnes externas feminas, item eas, quæ concubuissent cum iis, quibuscum nuptiæ divino jure interdictæ sunt: per חללה vero feminas natas ortasve ex ea, quæ Sacerdotibus interdicta est. At Josephus per זונה simplicius intelligit eam, quæ prostituerit: per חללה eas, quæ castæ vix creduntur, quales sunt ancillæ, captivæ, cauponæ, stabulariæ.

NEC EAM, QVÆ REPVDĨATA EST A MARITO) Pari cum hac jure censetur ea, quæ affini calceum exuit: ex lege, quæ est Deut. 25, 9.

## 21:9
Verse 9. THE PRIEST'S DAUGHTER) Married or betrothed to someone. Thus the Rabbis understand.

SHALL BE BURNED WITH FIRE) Namely, by being cast into the body, as we said above: but his corrupter was accustomed to be strangled.

Combustion, if you listen to the Hebrews, was done with hot lead, inserted into the mouth opened by forceps to burn the viscera and intestines, which they call the combustion of the soul: but bodies were also burned by a fire kindled with wood or bundles. They used to burn one lying with his daughter, with the daughter of his daughter, with the daughter of his son, with the daughter of his wife, with the son of his son, with the daughter of the daughter of his wife, with his mother-in-law, with the mother of his mother-in-law, with the mother of his father-in-law while his wife was still living. Suffocation or strangulation was done by a cloth. They would lower those who were being strangled into the ground, up to their knees: afterwards they would wrap a cloth around the neck, which was pulled by two people from both sides, until the guilty party breathed out his soul. The cloth was buried at the same time as the guilty party was buried.

Latin:

Vers. 9. SACERDOTIS FILIA) Nupta aut desponsata alicui. Sic Rabbini intelligunt.

FLAMMIS EXVRETVR) Nempe in corpus immissis, ut diximus supra: Corruptor autem ejus strangulari solebat.

Combustio, si Hebræos audias, fiebat calido plum- bo, in os forcipe apertum ad viscera & intestina comburenda immisso, quam animæ combustionem vocant: Comburebantur autem etiam corpora igne lignis vel fasciculis accenso. Comburebant ve- ro concumbentem cum filia sua, cum filia filiæ suæ, cum filia filii sui, cum filia uxoris suæ, cum filio filii sui, cum filia filiæ uxoris suæ, cum socru sua, cum matre socrus suæ, cum matre soceri sui vivente ad- huc uxore sua. Suffocatio vel strangulatio fiebat per sudarium. Deprimebant eos, qui strangulabantur in imo, usque ad poplites eorum: post collo cir- cumdabant sudarium, quod utrumque a duobus trahebatur, usque dum reus animam efflaret. Suda- rium sepeliebatur simul, cum reus sepeliebatur.

## 21:9 Addition
On verse 9, towards the end of Grotius's annotation, p. 499. b.

That restriction of the Rabbis, approved by Grotius, to the daughter of a Priest MARRIED or betrothed to someone is not correct: for in the text there is no exception: since it was a perpetual law, and there would be no difference between the daughter of a Priest and another, who (if such) was to be stoned, Exod. 22, Deut. 22, as Polus points out from Lyranus.

Latin:

Ad vers. 9. sub finem annot. Grotii, p. 499. b.

Non recte se habet illa Rabbinorum Grotio probata restrictio ad filiam Sacerdotis NUPTAM aut desponsatam alicui: in textu enim nulla est ex- ceptio: cum perpetua lex esset, nec differentia fo- ret inter filiam Sacerdotis, & alterius, quæ (si talis) lapidanda erat, Exod. 22. Deut. 22. ut e Lyrano Po- lus advertit.

## 21:10
Ver. 10. HE SHALL NOT REND HIS GARMENTS) Namely, at a funeral. See what was said at Matt. 26, 65.

Latin:

Vers. 10. VESTIMENTA NON SCINDET) Nempe in funere. Vide quæ ad Matth. 26, 65. dicta.

## 21:11
Ver. 11. HE SHALL NOT GO IN TO ANY DEAD BODY) A Cretan priest in Euripides, describing his rites, says: Καὶ νεκροθήκης 8 χριμπτόμενος. Porphyry, 2. On Abstinence: Καὶ οἱ τῶν τῇδε ἱερεῖς καὶ ἱεροσκόποι καὶ τάφων ἀπέχεσθαι κελεύεσι· αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀνδρῶν ἀνοσίων καὶ ἐμμήνων καὶ συνυσιῶν καὶ θεᾶς ἤδη αἰσχρᾶς καὶ πενθικῆς. Thus the Flamen Dialis would never enter a place where there was a tomb, and would never touch a dead body. Gellius 10, 15. Servius on the 3rd Aeneid: It had been a Roman custom for a branch of cypress to be placed before a house of mourning, so that no Pontiff might be defiled by entering through ignorance. Book 6, on Aeneas: He had been defiled by the death of Palinurus. The same in the Fulda Manuscript on the 1st Aeneid: It is provided that a priest shall not enter a house in which there has been a funeral within five days. And on the 11th Aeneid: It was a Roman custom that those defiled by a funeral should not sacrifice at all. Tacitus, Annals 1. Nor that an Emperor, endowed with the augurate and most ancient ceremonies, should have had to touch funeral rites. The Hebrews add an exception, if the High Priest had found someone unburied on the road. For he was able to bury him. Moses of Coucy, in the prohibitive commandment 237. The same was noted by Servius on the 6th Aeneid from Roman Pontifical Law in these words: Although it was forbidden for Pontiffs to see a corpse, yet it seemed more forbidden if they left it unburied.

Latin:

Vers. 11. AD OMNEM MORTVVM NON INGRE- DIETVR) Sacerdos Cratensis apud Euripidem suos ritus de- scribens ait: Καὶ νεκροθήκης 8 χριμπτόμενος. Porphyrius 2. de Abstinentia: Καὶ οἱ τῶν τῇδε ἱερεῖς καὶ ἱεροσκόποι καὶ τά- φων ἀπέχεσθαι κελεύεσι· αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀνδρῶν ἀνοσίων καὶ ἐμμή- νων καὶ συνυσιῶν καὶ θεᾶς ἤδη αἰσχρᾶς καὶ πενθικῆς. Sic Fla- men dialis locum in quo bustum esset, nunquam ingredieba- tur, mortuum nunquam attingebat. Gellius 10,15. Servius ad 3. Æneidos: Moris Romani fuerat, ramum cupressi ante do- mum funestam poni, ne quisquam Pontifex per ignorantiam pollueretur ingressus. Lib. 6. de Ænea: Funestatus fuerat morte Palinuri. Idem in Manuscripto Fuldenfi ad 1. Æneidos: Cautum est, ne Sacerdos ejus domum ingrediatur, in qua ante quintum diem funus fuerit. Et ad 11. Æneidos: Consuetudo Romana fuit, ut polluti funere minime sacrificarent. Tacitus Annalium 1. Neque Imperatorem auguratu & vetustissimis cœ- remoniis præditum, attrectare feralia debuisse. Exceptionem addunt Hebræi, si quem Pontifex maximus in via inhuma- tum reperisset. Eum enim humare poterat. Moses de Ko- tzi præcepto vetante 237. Idem ex Jure Pontificio Romano notavit Servius ad 6. Æneidos his verbis: Cum Pontificibus nefas esset cadaver videre, tamen magis nefas visum fuerit, si in- sepultum relinquerent.

## 21:12
Ver. 12. THE OIL OF THE HOLY ANOINTING) In Hebrew, נזר שמן משחת, the holy oil, the anointed of God, the LXX. That נזר is translated as ἁγίασμα below 25, 5. 2 Kings 11, 13. Ps. 89, 40. Ps. 132, 18. Zech. 7, 3. More properly ἀφόρισμα, Exod. 39, 30.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OLEVM SANCTÆ VNCTIONIS) In Hebræo, נזר שמן משחת τὸ ἅγιον ἔλαιον, τὸ χρισὸν τῶ Θεᾶ, LXX. illud נזר ἁγίασμα vertitur infra 25, 5. 2. Reg. 11, 13. Ps. 89, 40. Ps. 132, 18. Zach. 7, 3. Magis proprie ἀφόρισμα, Exod. 39, 30.

## 21:13
Ver. 13. HE SHALL TAKE A WIFE IN HER VIRGINITY) Most people understand this of the High Priest: but Ezekiel 44, 22 teaches us that it is to be understood of any priest. Therefore, this is to be connected with the beginning of the chapter, so that what began to be said about the High Priest in verse 10 may be taken parenthetically, and the discourse may return to where it had digressed. Demosthenes in 'Against Neaera' says that after the times of Theseus, a king was made by the Athenians for the sake of sacred rites only, and adds: Τὸν μὲν βασιλέα ὁ δῆμος ᾑρεῖτο ἐκ προκρίτων κατ᾿ ἀνδραγαθίαν χειροτονῶν. Τῇ δὲ γυναικὶ αὐτῷ νομον ἔθετο ἁγνὴν εἶναι καὶ μὴ ἐπιμεμιγμένην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρθένον γαμεῖν. Where also note that ἁγνὴν, which follows here concerning his people, so that this Attic Law, like many others, came to the Athenians from the Phoenicians, and to them from the Hebrews.

The discourse is about the High Priest. He is not commanded to take a wife. For nothing forbade him from remaining celibate. And it could happen that the High Priest, before he was chosen, had taken a widow left by a priest, as is prescribed in Ezekiel 44, 22. But when a virgin is spoken of, the Hebrews understand a girl not younger than twelve years, nor older than twelve years and a half, and who has not been betrothed to another. Nor was it permitted for him to take more wives. If he had taken two, he would have had to divorce one before the day The tenth Tisn, otherwise he could not have performed the solemn sacrifice. These are called ἄγραφα. It was permitted to the other Priests to marry widows and several wives, provided they abstained from harlots, and those repudiated and profaned, i.e., those who had suffered defilement in any way (they were called חללות by the Hebrews). Cyril, book XII, on adoration. By this was signified the marriage of the Pontiff with a virgin, that Christ would not dwell spiritually with impious and corrupt souls, but with the most chaste and pure as if they were virgins, and would render them fruitful, and call them joined to Himself by birth.

Latin:

Vers. 13. VIRGINEM DVCET VXOREM) Hæc plerique de Pontifice maximo intelligunt: at de quovis sacerdote intel- ligenda docet nos Ezechiel 44, 22. Quare connectenda hæc cum initio capitis, ut quæ de Pontifice maximo dici cœ- pere commate 10. sumantur παρενθετικῶς, redeatque unde di- gressa erat oratio. Demosthenes in Neæram post Thesei tempora regem ab Atheniensibus factum ait sacrorum causa tantum, additque: Τὸν μὲν βασιλέα ὁ δῆμος ᾑρεῖτο ἐκ προ- κρίτων κατ᾿ ἀνδραγαθίαν χειροτονῶν. Τῇ δὲ γυναικὶ αὐτῷ νομον ἔθετο ἁγνὴν εἶναι καὶ μὴ ἐπιμεμιγμένην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ, ἀλλὰ παρθένον γαμεῖν. Vbi & illud nota ἁγνὴν, quod hic sequitur de populo suo, ut omnino Jus id Atticum, ut multa alia, ad Athenienses a Phœnicibus, ad hos ab Hebræis venerit.

De Pontifice sermo est. Non jubetur ducere uxorem. Cælibem enim manere, nihil vetabat. Et fieri potuit, ut Pontifex antequam eligeretur, vi- duam a Sacerdote relictam, ut Ezech. 44, 22. præscribitur, duxisset. Virgo autem, cum dici- tur, Ebræi puellam intelligunt non minorem an- nis duodecim, nec majorem annis duodecim cum dimidio, & quæ alteri desponsata non fuerit. Nec plures ei licuisse uxores ducere. Si duas duxerit, alteram abdicare debuisse ante diem decimum Tisn, alioquin solenne sacrificium eum peragere non potuisse. Quæ ἄγραφα dicun- tur. Cæteris Sacerdotibus licebat ducere viduas & plures uxores, dummodo a meretricibus, & re- pudiatis & profanatis, h. e. stuprum quacunque ra- tione passis (diebantur Ebræis חללות) abstine- rent. Cyrillus l. XII. de adorat. Significabatur per hoc conjugium Pontificis cum virgine, quod Chri- stus non cum impiis & corruptis animis, sed cum ca- stissimis, & purissimis tanquam virginibus spiritua- liter versaretur, easque fœcundas redderet, ac sibi ge- nere junctas appelleret.

## 21:17
Verse 17. HE WHO HAS A BLEMISH. Rightly [does] Theodoret, quest. XXX in Levit., [say] that voluntary passions are prohibited through affections not voluntarily assumed.
