For the blindness of the eyes signifies a lack of knowledge; the amputation of the ear, disobedience; the removal of the nose, the deprivation of the faculty of discernment; the cutting off of the hand, sloth in acting: he is hunchbacked whom earthly solicitude weighs down, so that he never looks upon heavenly things: he is blear-eyed whose sense and mind nature does not empty, but the depravity of his conduct confuses: he has a white spot who, attributing to himself the brightness of justice or wisdom, excludes himself through arrogance from the light of heavenly knowledge: he has a constant scab, whom the petulance of the flesh dominates: an impetigo, whom avarice [dominates]: he is a hernia-sufferer who carries in hidden places, i.e., in his mind, the weight of filth. Gregory the Great, part I, Pastoral, last chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QVI HABUERIT MACULAM. Recte Theodoreti. quæst. XXX. in Levit. per affectiones non sponte susceptas prohiberi volunta- rias passiones. Oculorum enim cæcatio significat cognoscendi inopiam; auris amputatio inobedien- tiam: naris ablatio, facultatis discernendi privatio- nem: manus abscissio, in agendo socordiam: Gibbo- sus est, quem terrena solicitudo deprimit, ne un- quam superna respiciat: lippus est, cujus sensum & mentem natura non evacuat, sed conversationis pravitas confundit: albuginem habet, qui cando- rem justitiæ vel sapientiæ sibi tribuens a luce su- pernæ cognitionis se per arrogantiam excludit: jugem habet scabiem, cui carnis petulantia domina- tur: impetiginem, cui avaritia: herniofus est, qui in abditis, i. e. in mente, pondus turpitudinis gestat. Gregor. M. part. I. Pastor. c. ult.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. Foreigners and the unclean are barred from the eating of victims. Which must be without blemish.

Latin:

CAP. XXII. Alienigena & immundi ab esu victimarum ar- centur. Quæ immaculatæ esse debent.

## 22:4
Verse 4. HE WHO HAS BEEN LEPROUS. Here are enumerated those who are to be recognized as unclean, namely: 1. The leper, i.e., according to the interpreter Procopius, he who is entirely lacking in virtue and is useless. 2. One suffering from a flux, i.e., he who allows the powers of his mind to flow away uselessly, and does not use them for those things which we know to be honest and pious. 3. He who has touched a corpse, i.e., according to Dionysius, he who delights in the fading and transitory things of this age. 4. He who has suffered a nocturnal pollution, which St. Gregory explains as lust. 5. He who has touched a reptile, or any animal or unclean person, which Procopius interprets as one who carries the poison of asps on his lips, or fraudulently imposes upon the simpler ones. 6. He who has eaten what died of itself or was torn by a beast, i.e., he who has grown completely cold, and is not known by a fervent spirit, or who has become the food of the devil according to the allegory of the ancients. He wishes all these to be removed from the eating of sacred things, however much they may have originated from the priestly race and family: and he expressly denounces the penalty of death to the transgressors.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVI FUERIT LEPROSUS. REcensentur hic, qui pro immundis agnoscen- di, nempe 1. leprosus h. e. interprete Procopio, qui prorsus caret virtute & inutilis est. 2. Fluxu la- borans, h. e. qui mentis vires patitur effluere inu- tiliter, nec utitur ad eas res quas honestas & pias novimus. 3. Qui attigit cadaver, h. e. juxta Diony- sium, qui evanidis & transitoriis hujus seculi dele- ctatur. 4. Qui nocturnam passus est pollutionem, quam de libidine exponit D. Gregorius. 5. Qui attigit re- ptile, aut quodvis animal vel hominem immun- dum, quod Procopius interpretatur de eo, qui vene- num aspidum gerit in labiis suis, aut simplicioribus fraudulenter imponit. 6. Qui comedit mortici- nium aut raptum a bestia, h. e. qui penitus refrixit, nec fervido spiritu cognoscitur, aut qui diaboli factus est cibus juxta allegoriam veterum. Hos omnes ab esu sacrorum remotos vult, quantumvis ex genere & familia sacerdotali oriundos: & mor- tis pœnam expresse denunciat transgressoribus.

## 22:9
Verse 9. LET THEM KEEP MY PRECEPTS) It is 'my charges' in the Hebrew, that is, let them perform their functions. They began these functions in the seventeenth year of their age. Josephus is the witness in book XV of the Antiquities of History.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CVSTODIANT PRÆCEPTA MEA) Custodias meas est in Hebræo, id est, functiones obeant. Eas functiones in- choabant ætatis anno XVII. Testis Josephus libro XV. Anti- quæ Historiæ.

## 22:10
Verse 10. THE SOJOURNER OF THE PRIEST) תושב is here called a pierced servant, and is opposed to a servant bound only for six years, who is here called שכיר, because he differs little from a hireling. Thus the Heracleotae called servants δωροφόρους ἀφερόντες τὸ πικρὸν τῆς προσηγορίας, says Athenaeus VI, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 10. INQVILINVS SACERDOTIS( תושב hic dicitur servus perforatus, & opponitur servo non nisi ad sexennium obligato, qui hic dicitur שכיר, quia parum distat a mer- cenario. Sic Heracleotæ servos appellabant δωροφόρους ἀφερόντες τὸ πικρὸν τῆς προσηγορίας ait Athenæus VI, 18.

## 22:22
Verse 22. IF IT SHALL BE BLIND) Either completely, or in one eye: which also was observed by the Egyptians, notes Chaeremon in Porphyry, On Abstinence, book four.

IF WITH A BROKEN FOOT) The LXX here put συντετριμμένον. Pliny VIII. 43 [notes] that calves brought to the altar on the shoulders of a man do not offer a sacrifice: just as the gods are not appeased by a limping [victim], nor by another's victim.

IF HAVING A SCAR) In the Hebrew חרוץ. The LXX translate it γλωσσότμητοι. Servius notes that it was observed that victims should not have a split tongue, on that line of Aeneid VI, 'chosen according to custom, the two-year-olds.' But the Hebrews by חרוץ in this place understand that which has torn eyelids, ears, and nostrils.

Latin:

Vers. 22. SI CÆCVM FVERIT) Vel planè, vel oculo altero: quod & Ægyptiis observatum notat Chæremon apud Porphyrium de abstinentia quarto.

SI FRACTO PEDE) שבור συντετριμμένον ponunt hic LXX. Plinius VIII. 43. Vitulos ad aram humeris hominis allatos non litare: sicut nec claudicante, nec aliena hostia deos placari.

SI CICATRICEM HABENS) In Hebræo חרוץ. γλωσ- σότμητοι vertunt LXX. observatum ne victimæ linguam fis- sam haberent notat Servius ad illud Æneidos VI. lectas de more bidentes. At Hebræi per חרוץ hoc loco intelligunt id, cui descissæ palpebræ, aures & nares.

## 22:23
Verse 23. WITH EAR AND TAIL AMPUTATED) ὠτότμητον ἢ κολοβόκερκον [say] the LXX. Servius in the said place (Aen. VI) says it was observed that they should not have a pointed tail. Pliny, book VIII, ch. XLV, says the test of victims in a calf is that the tail should touch the joint of the hock. See what is above at XII. 5. Isidore of Seville referred these allegorically to men in ch. XXI of Leviticus. A blemished or variegated animal, he says, is rejected from Sacrifice, that is, men in whom there is a diversity of sins, and who are changed now into lust and greed, now into various crimes. A blind animal is indeed rejected, that is, one who neither sees God nor does His works: also a broken one, or one vexed and bruised by carnal vices. One having a scar is also rejected, who does not deplore the wounds of his sins with a worthy satisfaction of penance, but still carries the sign of the old disease inwardly through the desires of pleasure. One with an amputated tongue is also rejected, who does not confess the Lord nor meditate on the divine law. One having a papule is rejected, who boils with the itch of lust and the heat of concupiscence. Similarly, one with a scab, who completes the sin of the flesh by the contagion of the act. Now, one having an impetigo represents the collection of heretics, which frequently immerses itself into the body of the Church, and like an impetigo, causes a bruise. Furthermore, those with an amputated ear are those who do not obey the word of God, by not doing what is just. But he who has an amputated tail is he who does not complete the good which he begins with a persevering end. A defect or one with amputated testicles signifies those who, although they are men in body, are effeminated by the practice of filth. Philo also noted in his booklet on sacrifices that men are admonished by these symbols, as it were, that as often as they approach the altars, whether to name vows or to pay them, they should bring no vice and no disease into their soul, but should strive entirely to present it bright and immaculate in the sight of God, lest He turn away from what He has seen. Certainly Paul alluded to this in Rom. 12:1-2, beseeching by the mercies of God that we present our bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is our rational worship.

Latin:

Vers. 23. AVRE ET CAVDA AMPVTATIS) ὠτότμητον ἢ κολο- βόκερκον LXX. Servius dicto loco (Aen. VI) observatum ait, ne habeant caudam aculeatam. Plinius libr. IIX. c. XLV. vi- ctimarum probationem in vitulo ait esse, ut articulum suffra- ginis cauda contingat. Vide quæ supra XII. 5. Isidorus Hispalens. hæc allegorice retulit ad ho- mines in c. XXI. Lev. Rejicitur, inquit, a Sacrificio maculatum animal, vel varium, id est, homines, in quibus diversitas est peccatorum, & nunc in libidine & cupiditate, nunc in diversis criminibus demutan- tur. Rejicitur quidem & cæcum animal, id est, qui nec Deum videt, nec opera ejus facit: fractum quoque sive vitiis carnalibus vexatum & collisum. Rejici- tur & cicatricem habens, qui non digna satisfactione pœnitentiæ, vulnera peccatorum deplorat, sed adhuc veteris morbi fignum per desideria voluptatis inte- rius gestat. Reprobatur & lingua amputatum, qui Dominum non confitetur neque divinam legem medi- tatur. Rejicitur & papulam habens, qui pruritu libidinis & ardore concupiscentiarum exæstuat. Si- militer & scabiosum, qui peccatum carnis perficit contagione operis. Jam vero impetiginem habens, hæreticorum figurat collectionem, quæ frequenter se in Ecclesiæ corpus immergit, & ut impetigo livorem facit. Porro aure amputati sunt, qui verbo Dei non obediunt, non faciendo, quæ justa sunt. Qui vero caudam habet amputatam, ille est, qui bonum, quod incipit, perseveranti fine non perficit. Defectum vel testiculis amputatum, significat eos, qui cum corpore viri sint, turpitudinis usu effœminantur. Philo etiam in libello de victimis annotavit, sub- moneri his quasi symbolis homines, ut quoties ac- cedunt ad altaria vel nuncupati vota vel redditu- ri, nullum vitium, nullumque morbum afferant in anima, sed conentur omnino nitidam & immacula- tam in conspectu Dei producere, ne visam aversé- tur. Certe Paulus huc allusit ad Rom. 12. v. 1.2. precatus per miserationes Dei, ut sistamus corpora nostra hostiam vivam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, ra- tionalem illum cultum nostrum.

## 22:24
Vers. 24. AND IN YOUR LAND YOU SHALL BY NO MEANS DO THIS) Do not castrate either a man or any animal. Thus the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET IN TERRA VESTRA HÆC OMNINO NE FACIATIS) Ne castretis aut hominem aut animal ullum. Ita Hebræi.

## 22:25
Vers. 25. FROM THE HAND OF A FOREIGNER YOU SHALL NOT OFFER BREAD) Understand bread here, not sacrifices or μαννὰ, but properly those loaves, namely τῆς προθέσεως, which the Hebrews themselves had to sow, themselves to reap, themselves to grind, and themselves to bake, as Jerome teaches us on Malachi 1. But the Talmudists connect these with the preceding, and note that defective sacrifices are not to be accepted even then, when they are offered by a foreigner. That a sacrifice is called the food of God is not without example.

Latin:

Vers. 25. DE MANV ALIENIGENÆ NON AVFERETIS PA- NES) Panes hic intellige, non victimas, aut μαννὰ, sed proprie panes illos, nempe τῆς προθέσεως, quos Hebræi ipsi ferere, ipsi demetere, ipsi molere, ipsi coquere debebant, ut nos docet Hieronymus ad Malachiam 1. At Thalmudici cum superioribus hæc connectunt, & notant victimas vitio- sas ne tum quidem accipiendas, ubi ab alienigena offeruntur. Victimam Dei cibum vocari non caret exemplo.

## 22:25 Addition
On chapter 22, verse 25, after Grotius's annotation, page 500. b.

Lyranus, Menochius, Tirinus, and Estius explain 'breads' generally as sacrifices, which could not be offered by foreigners immediately (even if, mediately, money provided by Gentiles for victims was offered for them), but it will not be easily shown that 'breads' in general denote sacrifices.

Latin:

Ad cap. 22. versu 25. post annotatum Grotii pag. 500. b.

Panes generaliter de sacrificiis exponunt Ly- ran. Menochius, Tirinus, Estius, quæ offerri non poterant ab alienigenis immediate (etsi mediate ad victimas præbita a gentilibus pecunia offerretur pro iisdem) sed non facile docebitur panes in ge- nere notare sacrificia.

## 22:27
Vers. 27. BUT ON THE EIGHTH DAY AND THEREAFTER THEY MAY BE OFFERED TO THE LORD) Pliny, book VIII, ch. 3, says the offspring of cattle is pure for sacrifice on the seventh day.

Latin:

Vers. 27. DIE AVTEM OCTAVO ET DEINCEPS OFFERRI POTERVNT DOMINO) Plinius lib. VIII. c. 3. pecoris fœtum sacrificio purum dicit die septimo.

## 22:27 Addition
On verse 27, after Grotius's annotation.

Better reasons render others. The Hebrews themselves on account of

Saying that the Sabbath was made for this, because it provides strength and perfection to all things, and to Christians: by which he mystically hinted that Christ would not suffer death in infancy or childhood, but in perfect manhood, as Fagius holds.

Latin:

Ad vers. 27. post annot. Grotii.

Meliores rationes reddunt alii. Ebræi ipsi ob

Sabbatum id factum dicentes, quod præstet rebus omnibus robur, & perfectionem, & Christiani: quibus mystice innuebat Christum non passurum mor- tem in infantia aut pueritia, sed in perfecta virili æta- te, ut habet Fagius.

## 22:28
Vers. 28. THEY SHALL NOT BE SACRIFICED ON THE SAME DAY WITH THEIR YOUNG) They shall not be killed: for שחט is taken for any kind of killing. The Greeks say ἐ σφάξεις. The reason for the law is that both affection and the power of imagination exist even in them. Porphyry on Moses: ὧδε νεοττοῖς ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ νομοθέτης τὰς γονέας συν νεξαιρεῖν. However, this law speaks neither of wild animals nor of birds. There is another law concerning chicks that are being brooded, Deuteronomy 22:6.

Latin:

Vers. 28. NON IMMOLABVNTVR VNA DIE CVM FOE- TIBVS SVIS) Non occidentur: nam שחט de quavis occifione sumitur. Græci ἐ σφάξεις. Causa legis, quia & στοργὴ & vis imaginatrix etiam in illis est. Porphyrius de Mofe: ὧδε νεοττοῖς ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ νομοθέτης τὰς γονέας συν νεξαιρεῖν. Attamen hæc lex neque de feris neque de avibus loquitur. Est lex alia de pullis quibus incubatur, Deute- ronomii 22, 6.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAP. XXIII. Solemnities of the Feasts.

Latin:

CAP. XXIII. Solemnitates Festorum.

## 23:10 Addition
To chapter 23, verse 10. WHEN YOU HAVE ENTERED.

Whence it is gathered that these ceremonial feasts and laws did not bind the Hebrews in the desert.

Latin:

Ad cap. 23. vers. 10. CUM INGRESSI.

Unde colligitur festa & leges istas ceremonia- les Ebræos non obligasse in deserto.

## 23:14
Verse 14.

AND IN ALL YOUR DWELLINGS) That is, even outside the promised land. This is special to this precept, accompanied by a prayer for the future harvest.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

CVNCTISQVE HABITACVLIS VESTRIS) Id est, et- iam extra terram promissam. Id speciale huic præcepto, comitante prece pro futura messe.

## 23:15
Verse 15.

YOU SHALL COUNT SEVEN WEEKS FROM THE DAY AFTER THE SABBATH.

Not from the day the Paschal lamb was slaughtered, as not a few of the ancients believed, but from the day of the offering of the sheaf, that is, the second day of the Paschal solemnity, those seven weeks are to be computed. The text is clear: You shall count from the morrow, i.e., the second day of the Sabbath, the day after the Passover, or the first day from the day on which you brought the sheaf of the elevation of unleavened bread, seven full weeks. If, therefore, the beginning of the computation is made inclusive of the day of the offering of the sheaf, Pentecost will fall on the sixth day of the third month; if exclusive, on the seventh, which Josephus adopts in Antiquities, book III, chapter V. Hence the calendars of the Jews varied, though the latter is preferred by others: who observe that, unless the computation of 50 days begins after the day of the offering of the sheaf, that original Pentecost, which followed Christ's passion and resurrection, would not have fallen on a Sunday. This feast is called

חַג שָׁבֻעוֹת the feast of weeks, Deut. 16:9, Mark 12:31, because the solemnity of the harvest of firstfruits was distant from the Passover by seven weeks, Exod. 34:22, so named because after the harvest was already completed, two loaves of firstfruits from the new grain were offered at this feast, Lev. 23:17; in the New Testament it is called πεντηκοστὴ and ἑορτὴ τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς, because seven weeks make 49 days, whence it was celebrated on the fiftieth day from the feast of the Passover. The Hebrews, as Josephus testifies, called it Asartha from עֲצֶרֶת an assembly and congregation, because on that day all were accustomed to gather.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

SEPTEM HEBDOMADES NVMERABIS AB ALTERA DIE SABBATI.

Non a die mactati agni Paschalis, ut veterum non pauci crediderunt, sed a die oblationis manipu- li, h. e. secundo paschalis solemnitatis die, septem il- læ hebdomadæ computandæ. Textus clarus est: Numerabitis a crastino, i. e. altero die Sabbati postridie Paschatis, sive diei primæ a die qua addu- xistis manipulum elevationis azymorum, septem hebdomadas plenas. Quod si ergo a die oblationis ma- nipuli inclusive initium computationis fiat, incidet Pentecoste in diem sextam mensis tertii, si exclusive, in septimam, quam assumit Josephus l. III. Antiqq. c. V. Unde Calendaria Judæorum variata, posterius tamen ex aliis placet: qui observant, nisi compu- tatio 50. dierum incipiat post diem oblationis mani- puli, Pentecosten illam primævam, quæ Christi passionem & resurrectionem sequuta est, non inci- disse in diem Dominicam. Vocatur festum hoc

חַג שָׁבֻעוֹת festum hebdomadum Deut. 16, 9. Marc. 12, 31. quia per septem hebdomadas a paschate distabat solemnitas messis primitiarum Exod. 24, 36. ita nuncupata: quia post messem jam peractam in hoc festo offerebantur duo panes primitiarum e recenti frumento Lev. 23, 17. in N. T. vocatur πεν- τηκοστὴ & ἑορτὴ τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς, quia septem septi- manæ efficiunt 49. dies, unde quinquagesimo die a festo Paschatis celebrabatur. Ebræi, teste Josepho, vocarunt Asarthan ab עֲצֶרֶת cœtus & congregatio, quod eo die omnes convenire consueverint.

## 23:17
Verse 17.

LOAVES OF FIRSTFRUITS) Thanksgiving for the harvest.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

PANES PRIMITIARVM) Gratiarum actio pro messe.

## 23:21
Verse 21.

IT SHALL BE A PERPETUAL STATUTE.

An explanation is added: In your generations. Therefore, this is not to be applied to Christians along with the Ebionites, who asserted that they were bound to observe both the Old and New Testaments. For the feasts of the Jews were abrogated in the New Testament, Rom. 14, Gal. 4:10, Col. 2:16. And therefore, the defined עוֹלָם, whose limit was hidden, is understood as lasting while the Jewish polity endured.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

LEGITIMUM SEMPITERNUM ERIT.

Additur explicatio: In generationibus vestris. Non ergo ad Christianos hoc trahendum cum Ebioni- tis, qui eosdem & Vet. & N. T. servare teneri asse- rebant. Festa enim Judæorum abrogata sunt in N. T. Rom. 14. Gal. 4, 10. Col. 2, 16. Ideoque defi- nitum עוֹלָם cujus terminus absconditus erat, intel- ligitur, dum duraret Politia Judaica.

## 23:24
Verse 24.

A MEMORIAL OF BLOWING OF TRUMPETS) A sign of joy on account of Isaac being delivered from death: whence also a ram was then sacrificed. In that deliverance, however, the future deliverance through the Messiah was understood. Zech. 9:14.

Grotius therefore acknowledged here that in Zechariah ch. 9 there is a prophecy concerning the deliverance of Christ. Why, then, did he twist it there into an entirely different sense concerning the deliverance from Antiochus?

Latin:

Vers. 24.

MEMORIALE CLANGENTIBVS TVBIS) Signum gaudii ob Isaacum a morte liberatum: unde & aries tunc mactabatur. In ea autem liberatione intelligebatur libe- ratio futura per Messiam. Zach. 9, 14.

Agnovit ergo hic Grotius, apud Zachariam c. 9. de liberatione Christi vaticinium haberi. Cur ergo id in alium plane sensum de liberatione ab An- tiocho illic detorsit?

## 23:27
Verse 27.

ON THE TENTH DAY OF THIS SEVENTH MONTH) To avert diseases, which are frequent in autumn.

The cause of the feast of atonement was not the averting of bodily diseases, nor the remembrance of the forgiveness of the calf-worship, as the Jews and Grotius with them trifle, but the foreshadowing of the atonement for the sin of the whole world, which was expected to come through Christ, as the Apostle teaches in Heb. 9 and 10, and as Isaiah taught in the Old Testament in ch. 53, and as is manifest from a comparison of the institution of this feast described in ch. 16. See what was said there against Grotius.

Verse of the same.

AND YOU SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS) By fasting and other signs of grieving, at the time when God had forgiven the crime of the calf-worship.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

DECIMO DIE MENSIS HVJVS SEPTIMI) At aver- tendos morbos, qui in autumno frequentes.

Festi expiationis causa, non aversio morbo- rum corporalium, non recordatio condonationis μοσχολατρείας, ut Judæi & cum ipsis Grotius nugan- tur, sed adumbratio expiationis peccati totius mun- di, quæ per Christum futura expectabatur, ut docet Apostolus Ebr. 9. & 10. & docuit in V. T. Esaias c. 53. & e collatione institutionis hujus festi c. 16. descri- ptæ manifestum est. Vid. quæ ibi adversus Gro- tium dicta.

Verse 36.

Vers. 36.

## 23:40
Verse 40.

FRUIT OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL TREE) That is, the fruits most common in that land, and which keep their freshness for a long time. Maimonides. Josephus: ἐκ φοινίκων καὶ κιτρίων. A similar thing among the Athenians is the ὀσχοφορία. The interpreter of Nicander, Aristodemus in Athenaeus, and others make mention of it. Such branches themselves are the εἰρεσιώνη to the Greeks, which word Josephus also uses here. In Hebrew, the fruit of the honored tree (Targ. tree of citrons), branches (or curvatures, Targ. spatulas and fronds) of palms (they bore the form of a scepter with leaves still hiding in the shoot), a branch of a dense tree, or of dense fronds (others a branch of tangled wood, Targ. myrtles), and willows of the brook. From the branches of the palm, myrtle, and willow they prepared a bundle, which they carried in the right hand, and the citron indeed in the left hand, and they carried them around in the morning, nor did they take food before they had carried them around while the temple was standing; they did this for seven days (except for this, only on the first) and on the seventh they shouted from Psalm CXIIX, 25. אָנָּא יְהוָה הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא אָנָּא יְהוָה הַצְלִיחָה נָּא I beseech Thee O Lord, save I pray, I beseech Thee O Lord, prosper I pray! Whence they called the bundle itself Hosanna, and לוּלָב a spatula from the principal part, which is the palm frond, having the appearance of a scepter. They also called the seventh day the great Hosanna, indeed they even name the formulas of prayers thus in ritual books; הוֹשַׁעֲנוֹת לְסֻכּוֹת the formulas of hymns used in the feast of tabernacles are so called. Likewise the Hosanna of the first day. The Hosanna of the second day, etc. See Angelus Caninius, Disquisitions on this word. In the Chaldean paraphrase of the book of Esther, these things are contained: On the 25th. Of the month of Tishri they shaded the dark parts of the roofs of their houses in gardens and cut down branches of dates, and took cedars, and cut chilfna (which some call willow, others rosemary, others sedge) and made for themselves Hosanna, and read in their books and prayed and rejoicing they rejoiced with Hosanna and sang and exulted like kids. In the prayers still accepted today for that feast, there is a huge heap of the names of God and to each one is sung in response: Hosanna for your sake Lord of Lords Hosanna, etc. Then a great number of those things which are attributed to God is recited, such as for your truth, Hosanna, for your covenant, Hosanna, etc. After this, a great collection of those things which they desire to be saved is enumerated, such as the chosen temple Hosanna, Mount Moriah, Hosanna, etc., then they return to the ἀυτονομασίας of God, such as Lord Savior, Hosanna, Redeemer, and Savior, Hosanna, etc. Then again to various matters and to themselves adorned with various titles. Finally, the form of the song is changed in this manner: I beseech thee, redeem the branch of thy planting, to which is sung in response, And Hosanna; I beseech thee, look upon the covenant: of thy rings; and Hosanna, etc. Lastly, it returns to the first form, except that the members are longer, and that in this manner: On account of him who is perfect in his generations, delivered because of the multitude of his righteousnesses, snatched from the coming flood of the deluge, and there is sung in response, Hosanna and Hosanna, because thou art our Father! And this little response is increased again a little while later.

Hoshana and Hoshana and Hatzlicha na in this manner, there is no measure and no end, but all things resound, clamor, and echo Hosanna, especially on the seventh day of that feast. There is no doubt that many things were added to this Litany by later writers, as Andr. Osiander observes in book III, annotations to chapter 36 of his Harmony. Most, however, believe it was already accepted in the time of Christ, whence, near the coming of Christ, outside the time of the feast of tabernacles, some from divine instinct repeat their Hosanna from the same, or rather from Ps. 118:25, and thus exhibit to him the honor owed to God alone (Mark 10:7), and for that reason give thanks to the Son of God, who had come into the tabernacle of his body (Matt. 21:8, 9).

Latin:

Vers. 40.

FRVCTVS ARBORIS PVLCHERRIMÆ) Id est, fru- ctus maxime obvios in illa terra, & qui virorem diu conser- vent. Maimonides. Josephus: ἐκ φοινίκων καὶ κιτρίων. Simi- lis apud Athenienses ὀσχοφορία. Meminere interpres Ni- candri, Aristodemus apud Athenæum, & alii. Ipsi rami ta- les εἰρεσιώνη Græcis, qua voce & hic Josephus utitur. In Ebr. fructus arboris honoratæ (Targ. arbo- ris citrorum) ramos, (vel curvitates, Targ. spatulas ac frondes) palmarum (referebant formam sceptri foliis adhuc in surculo delitescentibus) ramum ar- boris densæ, vel densarum frondium (alii ramum li- gni complicati, Targ. myrtos) & salices torrentis. Ex ramis palmæ, myrti, & salicis parabant fascicu- lum, quem dextra, citrinum vero sinistra manu ge- stabant, & circumferebant mane, nec cibum capie- bant, priusquam circumportaverint stante templo; septem diebus id agebant (extra hoc primo tan- tum) & septimo acclamabant e Psal. CXIIX, 25. אָנָּא יְהוָה הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא אָנָּא יְהוָה הַצְלִיחָה נָּא Ob- secro Domine, salva quæso, obsecro Domine, prospera quæso! Unde fasciculum ipsum vocabant Hosanna, & לוּלָב Spatulam a præcipuo, quod est frons palmæ, sce- ptri habens speciem. Vocabant etiam diem septimum Hosanna magnum, imo etiam formulas precationum ita nuncupant in ritualibus libris הוֹשַׁעֲנוֹת לְסֻכּוֹת formulæ hymnorum usitatæ in festo tabernaculorum dicuntur. Item Hosanna primi diei. Hosanna secundæ diei &c. Vid. Angel. Caninii Disquisit. in hac voce. In paraphrasi Chald. libr. Esther. hæc habentur: Die 25. Mensis Thisri inumbrabant opaca tectorum do- muum suarum in hortis & præcidebant ramos dacty- lorum, & sumebant cedros, & incidebant chilfna (quam alii salicem, alii rosmarinum, alii carices di- cunt) & faciebant sibi ipsis Hosianna, & legebant in li- bris suis & orabant & gaudentes gaudebant cum Ho- sianna & cantabant & exultabant sicut hædi. In pre- cationibus adhuc hodie receptis illo festo habetur in- gens acervus nominum Dei & ad singula succinitur: Hosanna propter te Dominum Dominorum Hosanna &c. Deinde recensetur magnus eorum, quæ Deo attri- buuntur numerus, ut propter veritatem tuam, Ho- sanna propter testamentum tuum, Hosanna &c. Posthæc enumeratur magna congeries earum rerum, quas salvari cupiunt, ut templum electum Hosanna, montem Moria, Hosanna &c. tum redeunt ad ἀυ- τονομασίας Dei, ut Domine Salvator, Hosanna, re- demtor, & Salvator, Hosanna &c. tum iterum ad varias res & seipsos variis appellationibus ornatos. Tandem mutatur forma cantionis ad hunc modum: Quæso redime surculum plantationis tuæ, cui succini- tur Et Hosanna; Quæso respice ad fœdus: annuli tui; & Hosanna &c. Postremo reditur ad primam for- mam, nisi quod membra sunt longiora, idque ad hunc modum: Propter integrum in generationibus suis, li- beratum ob multitudinem justitiarum suarum, ere- ptum ab inundatione veniente diluvio, & succi- nitur Hosanna & Hosanna, quia Pater noster tu es! Et hæc succentiuncula aliquanto post iterum augetur

הוֹשַׁעְנָא וְהוֹשַׁעְנָא וְהַצְלִיחָה נָא ad hunc modum Deniǵ, nullus neǵ, est modus neǵ, finis, sed omnia concrepant, perstrepunt & reboant Hosanna, maxi- me septimo ejus diei festo. Non dubium est huic Li- taniæ multa fuisse a recentioribus adjecta, ut ob- servat Andr. Osiander. l. III. annot. ad c. 36. Har- mon. eam tamen tempore Christi jam receptam fuisse plerique censent, unde sub adventum Christi extra tempus festi tabernaculorum ex eadem suum Hosianna, vel potius ex Ps. CXIIX, 25. nonnulli ex instinctu divino ingeminant, eique ita honorem soli Deo debitum Marc. 10, 7. exhibent, Filioque Dei, qui in tabernaculum venerat corporis sui, ea ratione gratulantur Matth. 21, 8. 9.

## 23:40 Addition
To verse 40, towards the end of our annotations, page 502, a.

Most interpreters here agree with the Hebrews that a new and peculiar rite is commanded in this verse besides the making of the tabernacles. Such a rite, however, is said to have been: The Jews made a bundle out of these four (or rather out of three, namely from the branches of palm, myrtle, and willow: for they carried the citron fruit in their left hand) which they carried in the morning for seven days. To Junius, however, it seems that the material for the huts is explained here, and not a new ceremony.

Latin:

Ad vers. 40. sub finem annot. nostrorum. pag. 502. a.

Consentiunt hic plerique interpp. cum Ebræis hoc versu præcipi novum & peculiarem ritum præter confectionem tabernaculorum. Ritus au- tem talis dicitur fuisse: Faciebant Judæi fascicu- lum ex istis quatuor (vel potius ex tribus, nempe ex ramis palmæ, myrthi & salicis: nam pomum citri- num sinistra manu gerebant) quem mane gesta- bant per septem dies. Junio tamen videtur hic ex- plicari materiam tuguriorum, non vero novam ce- remoniam.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAP. XXIV. The rites of preparing the lamps and the loaves of proposition. The punishments for blasphemers and for retaliation.

Latin:

CAP. XXIV. Ritus concinnandi lucernas, & panes propositio- nis. Pœnæ blasphemorum, & talionis.

## 24:2
Ver. 2. TO PREPARE THE LAMPS CONTINUALLY.

The lamps in the golden candlestick are understood, for no other lamps placed separately from the candlestick in the tabernacle are considered. That they are to be prepared continually, Lorinus understands in this way, that it had to be done twice daily, morning and evening (Ex. 30:7, 8), and therefore with Lipomannus and Cajetan he establishes a perpetual light: but others more correctly hold that those lamps shone only at night, not during the day, as Beda (III, on the Tabernacle, c. 1), Lyranus, Oleaster, Joh. Benedictus, and Cornel. a Lap. on Exod. 27, as well as Saa on Lev. 24:2, establish, which Lorinus reports to be also the opinion of Jerome, Hugo, and Rupert, where Josephus is also cited (book III, Antiq. c. 10), who teaches that three had to shine for God throughout the whole day, and the rest were lit in the evening, with which Comestor agrees in Schol. Histor. on Exod. book 62. Rickelius on Ex. 27:21, because he had not seen the tabernacle, but only the temple, argues not undeservedly that Scripture makes no mention of any lamp shining during the day, but simply asserts that the lamp was lit in the evening and shone until morning, as is expressly held in Ex. 27:21. Cf. 1 Sam. 3:3, 2 Chron. 13:11. That phrase, therefore, that it may burn ALWAYS (Ex. 27:21), is to be taken as meaning that 'always' is the same as 'every night.' For the priests lit the lamps in the evening so that they would burn all night, but in the morning they extinguished, cleaned, arranged, and poured oil into them. And that is what the passage in Exod. 30:7, 8 implies, which Lorinus therefore urges in vain for a perpetual light: 'And Aaron shall burn incense upon them, sweet-smelling in the morning. When he shall arrange the lamps, he shall burn it. And when he shall place them at evening, he shall burn incense.' In the source it is 'morning, morning' (that is, every morning) when he shall make the lamps beautiful (i.e., when he shall have cleaned them, which used to be done in the morning) and when he shall make them burn, 'at evening' (that is, when he shall light the lamps, which was done in the evening) so that they might illuminate the tabernacle all night.

Latin:

Vers. 2. AD CONCINNANDAS LUCER- NAS JUGITER.

Lucernæ in candelabro aureo intelliguntur, non enim respiciuntur aliæ lucernæ in tabernaculo seorsim collocatæ a candelabro. Quod jugiter concinnandæ sint, intelligit Lorinus hoc modo, quod bis quotidie id fieri debuerit mane & vesperi Ex. 30, 7. 8. ideoque cum Lipomanno & Cajetano perpetuum lumen statuit: Sed rectius alii noctu duntaxat lucernas illas luxisse, non interdiu, cum Beda III. de Tabern. c. 1. Lyrano, Oleastrio, Joh. Benedicto, Cornel. a Lap. in Exod. 27. ut & Saa ad Lev. 24, 2. statuunt, quam etiam Hieronymi, Hu- gonis & Ruperti sententiam esse tradit Lorinus, ubi adducitur etiam Josephus l. III. Antiq. c. 10. tres per totam diem Deo lucere debuisse, reliquas sub vesperam accendi, docet, cui consentiunt Comestor in Schol. Histor. in Exod. l. 62. Rickelius in Ex. 27, 21. quod non viderit tabernaculum, sed solum templum, urgetque non immerito, quod Scriptura nullam faciat mentionem lucernæ alicujus per diem lucentis, sed simpliciter asserat lucernam ve- spere accensam fuisse & luxisse usque ad mane, ut ex- presse habetur Ex. 23, 21. Conf. 1. Sam. 3, 3. 2. Par. 13, 11. Illud ergo ut ardeat SEMPER Ex. 27, 21. ita accipiendum, ut semper idem sit, quod singulis noctibus. Vespere enim accendebant Sacerdotes lucernas, ut tota nocte arderent, mane vero eas ex- tinguebant, mundabant, componebant, & oleum infundebant. Atque id infert locus Exod. 30, 7. 8. quem proinde frustra pro lumine perpetuo urget Lorinus. Et adolebit incensum super eos Aaron, sua- ve fragrans mane. Quando componet lucernas, ac- cendet illud. Et quando collocabit eas ad vesperam, uret thymiama. In fonte est mane, mane, (id est, sin- gulis matutinis) cum pulchras faciet lucernas (h. e. quum mundaverit eas, quod solebat mane fieri) & cum accendere faciet, ad vesperam (id est, cum accendet lucernas, quod vesperi fiebat) ut tota no- cte tabernaculum illuminarent.

## 24:5
Ver. 5.

TWELVE LOAVES) חַלּוֹת are cakes. But the Greek word ἄρτοι also extends to them.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

DVODECIM PANES) חַלּוֹת sunt Placentæ. Sed vox Græca ἄρτοι etiam ad eas se extendit.

## 24:7 Addition
To chapter 24, verse 7. THAT THE BREAD MAY BE FOR A MEMORIAL OF THE OFFERING.

Vatablus advises: since the bread could not be burned upon the bread, the incense was there for the whole week: but on the Sabbath day the bread was eaten, and the incense was burned. In the Hebrew it is, that it may be for bread or upon the bread as a memorial to be consumed by fire, that is, the bread will truly be burned.

Latin:

Ad cap. 24. versu 7. UT SIT PANIS IN MONIMENTUM OB- LATIONIS.

Vatablus monet: quum non potuerit adoleri panis super panem, thus fuisse per totam hebdoma- dam: die Sabbathi autem panem comestum, thus ac- censum fuisse. In Ebræo est, ut sit pro pane vel super panem in memoriale igne absumendum, id est, vere panis cremabitur.

## 24:11
Ver. 11.

AND WHEN HE HAD BLASPHEMED THE NAME AND CURSED IT) In the Hebrew in the former place is יִקֹב, which the Chaldean explains as פּרֵשׁ, i.e., he explicitly uttered. The Greeks say ἐπονομάσας. Understand 'the name' as that most holy one, here to the Greeks τὸ ὄνομα, for that aggravates the guilt. And so, below, the punishment of him who in any way curses God is arbitrary according to the measure of the guilt: for him who has pronounced that name, the punishment is death (vv. 15, 16). Grotius understands this only of that most holy name יהוה: he asserts, following the superstition of the Hebrews, that this aggravates the guilt. Therefore, at v. 16, he notes that for those who had cursed without that name being expressed, the punishment was scourging. But that distinction is not held in the text, which Grotius gathers in vain from a comparison of v. 15 and 16. In the former it is said, 'The man who shall curse his God shall bear his sin.' In the latter: 'He who shall blaspheme the name of the Lord shall die the death.' There is no mention here of the name Jehovah. And is the name of the Lord not blasphemed even if the tetragrammaton name is not expressed? Yet the punishment for blasphemy of the name of the Lord in general is established as death. And therefore it is out of the mere superstition of the Jews that they interpret blasphemy only regarding the tetragrammaton name, with this rule given: 'No blasphemer is guilty of stoning until he has expressed the proper name of God, את המיוחד, as it stands in his Scripture.' Ludov. de Dieu observes that the superstition even reached the point that in Sanhedrin c. 7 it is read: 'He who curses his father and his mother is not guilty unless he has cursed them by the tetragrammaton name, which is שמהמיוחד, the proper name; if he curses by בכנוי, by a surname, such as שדי, etc., R. Meir condemns him, but the sages acquit him.' Will Grotius also nod to those sages here?

Latin:

Vers. 11.

CVMQVE BLASPHEMASSET NOMEN ET MA- LEDIXISSET EI) In Hebræo priori loco est יִקֹב, quod Chaldæus explicat, פּרֵשׁ, i. e. diserte extulit. Græci ἐπονο- μάσας. Nomen intellige illud sanctissimum, Græcis hic τὸ ὄνομα, id enim gravat culpam. Itaque infra ejus qui quo- quo modo Deo maledicit pœna est arbitraria pro modo cul- pæ: qui illo nomine pronuntiato, pœna mortis. 15. 16. De nomine illo sanctissimo יהוה id solum intel- ligit Grotius : id enim gravare culpam, Ebræorum superstitionem sequutus asserit. Ideo ad v. 16. ad- vertit, in eos, qui maledixissent, non expresso illo no- mine, pœnam fuisse verberum. At illa distinctio in textu non habetur: quam nequicquam e collatione v. 15. 16. colligit Grotius. Illo dicitur, Homo qui maledixerit Deo suo, portabit peccatum suum. Hoc: qui blasphemaverit nomen Domini, morte morietur. Nulla hic nominis Jehovah mentio. Et annon blasphematur nomen Domini etiam non expresso nomine tetragrammato? Blasphemiæ autem no- minis Domini in genere pœna statuitur mors. Ideoque ex mera superstitione Judæorum est, quod de nomine tetragrammato solum blasphemiam interpretentur, hac data regula: Nullus maledicus reus est lapidationis, donec expresserit nomen Dei proprium את המיוחד sicut se habet in Scriptura sua. Observat Ludov. de Dieu, eo etiam venisse supersti- tionem, ut in Sanhedrim c. 7. legatur: Qui maledi- cit Patri suo & matri suæ, non sit reus, nisi quum ma- ledixerit ipsis per nomen tetragrammaton, quod est שמהמיוחד nomen proprium; si maledicat בכנוי per cognomen, utpote שדי &c. R. Meir. ipsum conde- mnat, ac sapientes absolvunt. Num & hic sapienti- bus illis annuet Grotius?

## 24:14
Ver. 14.

OUTSIDE THE CAMP) For the stoning did not take place in the place of judgment. AND LET ALL WHO HEARD LAY THEIR HANDS UPON HIS HEAD) Because his people are expiated by his death as if by a victim. Oleaster gives the reason for this, that just as he, for whose sin the sacrifice was offered, had to lay his hand upon the head of the victim, because his sin was being punished, so the same must also be held regarding those who had heard the blasphemy, which was signified by this imposition of hands as some sin of theirs. But since one who hears blasphemy is not immediately presumed to consent, unless perhaps he approves by remaining silent, others more correctly judge that they laid their hands upon the head of the guilty party as a testimony of the deed and an approval of the punishment. Lyranus adds that they were accustomed to say: Your malice has led you to death, not us.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

EXTRA CASTRA) Neque enim fiebat lapidatio in loco judicii. ET PONANT OMNES QVI AUDIERUNT MA- NUS SVAS SVPER CAPVT EJVS) Quia populus ejus morte tanquam victima expiatur. Causam hujus reddit Oleaster, quod sicut is, pro cujus peccato offerebatur hostia, debebat po- nere manum super caput hostiæ, quia peccatum ejus puniebatur, ita idem quoq; habendum de illis, qui blasphemiam audierant, quod significatum hac manuum impositione aliquod eorum peccatum. Sed quum non præsumatur is statim consentire, qui blasphemiam audit, nisi forte tacendo appro- bet, rectius alii eos in testimonium facti & appro- bationem supplicii manus capiti rei censentur im- posuisse. Addit Lyranus eos dicere solitos: Ma- litia tua te adduxit ad mortem, non nos.

## 24:14 Addition
To verse 14, towards the end of the annotations, p. 502, b.

They not only placed their hands upon the head of the one to be stoned as witnesses, protesting that they wished, if they were testifying falsely, that the blood of the innocent would fall back upon their own heads: but they also prayed by this rite that God would devolve the guilt of the sin onto that man, and not strike the people because of his crime: and they professed that he was to be slaughtered as a piacular victim, so that he might expiate heaven and earth filled with such great blasphemy.

Latin:

Ad v. 14. sub finem annotat. p. 502. b.

Non solum tanquam testes ponebant manus super caput lapidandi, q. protestantes, velle se, si falsa testarentur, ut sanguis innocentis in ipsorum caput redundaret: sed precabantur etiam hoc ritu, ut Deus in eum hominem peccati culpam devolveret, nec populum propter ejus scelus attereret: & pro- fitebantur illum tanquam victimam piacularem mactandum, ut cœlum & terram tanta blasphe- mia impletam piaret.

## 24:16
Verse 16.

HE WHO BLASPHEMES THE NAME OF THE LORD) That name. In the Hebrew it is, shall have pronounced, the Chaldean likewise as above, and the Greeks ὀνομάζων. But from that which precedes it is understood as cursing. For those who had cursed without that name being expressed, the penalty was stripes.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

QVI BLASPHEMAVERIT NOMEN DOMINI) No- men illud. In Hebræo est, pronuntiaverit, Chaldæus itidem ut supra, & Græci ὀνομάζων. Sed ex eo quod præcedit intel- ligitur maledicendo. In eos qui maledixissent non illo no- mine expresso, pœna erat verberum.

## 24:18
Verse 18.

HE SHALL RENDER A SUBSTITUTE) That is, an animal of the same kind. In the Hebrew there is only what follows, life for life. But it was the custom to give a price for an animal. Note, however, that a dumb animal is redeemed as a possessed thing: but a man, who possesses all things, is not redeemed, but a killing is compensated by a killing. By so much, even in the judgment of God, is a man of more value.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

REDDET VICARIAM) Id est, paris generis animal. In Hebræo est tantum quod sequitur, animam pro anima. Sed mos erat pro animali dare pretium. Nota vero redimi animal mutum ut rem possessam: Hominem vero qui omnia possidet non redimi, sed cædem cæde pensari. Tanto, etiam Deo judice, pluris est homo.

Verse 19.

## 25:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXV. Of the Sabbatical and Jubilee years.

Latin:

CAPUT XXV. Anni Sabbatici, & Jobelæi.

## 25:4
Verse 4.

BUT IN THE SEVENTH YEAR THERE SHALL BE A SABBATH OF THE LAND, A RESTING OF THE LORD) In that year, they say, debts were also remitted, unless it had been agreed that the obligation should last until the Jubilee: and that this very thing was held as agreed upon, if the pledge had been returned according to the law. Exodus 22:16. Alexander the Great granted the Jews the right to use their own laws, adding τὸ ἕβδομον ἔτος ἀνείσφορον εἶναι. By the constitution concerning the Sabbatical year, first, the fertility of the fields was provided for by the interposition of the rest of the land. 2. It was intended as a reminder, as the Hebrews note, and from them Paulus Fagius, that the rich should consider the needs of the poor, and since they themselves in the seventh year are anxiously mindful that the poor are always held in that care, who never sow or reap. 3. The Sabbatical year reminded [them] of the Sabbath of remission, and of the liberty to be expected in Christ, as Procopius notes: as also 4. of the eternal Sabbath, Is. 65, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SEPTIMO AVTEM ANNO SABBATVM ERIT TERRÆ, REQVIETIONIS DOMINI) Eo anno etiam remissa ajunt debita, nisi de quibus convenisset ut ad Jubilæ- um duraret obligatio: id ipsum autem pro convento haberi, si pignus redditum esset ex lege. Exodi 22, 16. Alexander Magnus cum Judæis concessit suis uti legibus, addit τὸ ἕβ- δομον ἔτος ἀνείσφορον εἶναι. Per constitutionem de anno Sabbatico primo fertilitati agrorum consulebatur interposita terræ quiete. 2. Monebatur, notantibus Hebræis, & ex iis Paulo Fagio, ut divites pauperum necessitates cogitarent, & cum ipsi septimo anno solicite sint recordarentur pauperes semper cura illa teneri, qui nunquam serant, aut metant. 3. Annus Sabbaticus commonuit de Sabbato remissionis, & libertatis ex- pectandæ in Christo, notante Procopio: ut & 4. de sempiterno Sabbato Es. 65, 17.

Vers. 5.

GRAPES OF THY FIRST FRUITS) Some Greeks [read] τῆς ναζιραίας, from the Hebrew, namely נָזִיר, of that land which has rested, as Pliny speaks. The Samaritan, as the Greeks citing it [say], [reads] τῶν χέρσων, well: for οἱ χέρσοι are uncultivated fields. The LXX, not badly, [read] τῆ ἁγιάσματος, of the land at that time set apart from use, which is often designated by the word ἁγιάζειν, and is the proper meaning of the Hebrew נוזר.

Vers. 5.

UVAS PRIMITIARVM TVARUM) Quidam Græci τῆς ναζιραίας, ex Hebræo nempe נָזִיר, terræ illius requietæ, ut Plinius loquitur. Samaritanus Græcis citantibus τῶν χέρσων bene: sunt enim οἱ χέρσοι agri inculti. LXX. non male τῆ ἁγιάσματος, terræ eo tempore sepositæ extra usum, quod sæpe designatur voce ἁγιάζειν, & propria est significa- tio Hebræi נוזר.

Vers. 8.

WEEKS) The word is found both in Aristotle, Politics 5, and in Varro.

## 25:10
Vers. 10.

REMISSION TO ALL THE INHABITANTS OF THY LAND) A remedy for the inequality which bad fortune had introduced.

A MAN SHALL RETURN UNTO HIS POSSESSION) For the Israelites were usufructuaries, or feudatories, God or His law being the lord. Below v. 23, 38, 42, 55. Diodorus, in book 40, dealing with the Jews, says that it was not permitted to sell their own inheritances.

The Hebrews think the Jubilee year is named from the Arabic word Jobel, which denotes a ram's horn: whence Aquila rendered it 'horned'. See other derivations, if you please, in Pelargus on this passage, where he also recounts the reasons for the Jubilee year: (1) the preservation of the genealogy, lineage, and place of the Messiah, with the distinction of tribes, families, and possessions being guarded: (2) of Jewish chronology, since sales were instituted according to the Jubilees. (3) That this law might be a certain sinew of humanity, beneficence, and frugality. (4) That the coming of Christ might be expressed by certain signs, as it were, whose ministry chronologists observe to fall in the thirtieth Mosaic Jubilee. (5) That the true Jubilee of the Gospel might be foreshadowed, Acts 13, 38; John 8, 36; Gal. 3, 13; ch. 4, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

REMISSIONEM CVNCTIS HABITATORIBVS TERRÆ TVÆ) Συστάχθειαν, medicam inæqualitatis quam mala fortuna induxerat.

REVERTETUR HOMO AD POSSESSIONEM SV- AM) Erant enim Israelitæ usufructuarii, sive feudatarii, Deus sive lex ejus dominus. Infra v. 23. 38. 42. 55. Diodorus libro 40. de Judæis agens, dicit non licuisse τὺς ἰδίυς κλήρες πωλεῖν.

Annum Jobeleum Ebræi dictum putant a Jo- bel verbo Arabico, quod cornu arietinum notat: unde Aquila id reddidit κερατίνην. Alias derivatio- nes vide sis apud Pelargum in h. l. ubi causas etiam anni Jobelei recenset: (1) conservationem Genea- logiæ, stirpis & loci Messiæ, custodita tribuum ac fa- miliarum ac possessionum distinctione: (2) Chro- nologiæ Judaicæ, cum venditiones juxta Jobeleos institutæ sint. (3) Ut lex ista nervus esset quidam humanitatis, beneficentiæ, & frugalitatis. (4) Ut adventus Christi notis quasi quibusdam exprimere- tur, cujus ministerium in trigesimum Jobeleum Mo- saicum incidere Chronologi observant. (5) Ut Jo- beleus verus Evangelii adumbraretur, Actor. 13, 38. Joh. 8, 36. Gal. 3, 13. c. 4, 6.

## 25:10 Addition
To chapter 25, verse 10. THE FIFTIETH YEAR.

The question here is: whether the Jubilee year was in reality the forty-ninth or the fiftieth? Gerhard Mercator and Scaliger, along with Hugo the Cardinal and Lyranus, establish the former; Eusebius, Bede, Torniellus, Salianus, Serarius, Cornelius à Lapide, and Bonfrerius establish the latter, because 1. it is expressly called the fiftieth year, not counting the preceding Jubilee, for thus that year would be counted twice, as the last of the former and the first of the following. 2. Just as the seventh day of the week, excluding the previous Sabbath, is not the eighth including it: so the 50th year is to be assumed excluding the year of the previous Jubilee, not including it. 3. Otherwise, verse 11, about omitting sowing etc., would be repeated in vain if the Jubilee always fell in a Sabbatical year. 4. Otherwise, the greatest confusion would be introduced into the Chronicles of the Jews, who hold 50 complete years for a Jubilee. These are their arguments, which Pole exhibits concisely in his Synopsis Critica & Interpretum, p. 607. He adds a doubt from Bonfrerius, which he solves with his words: One thing stands in the way (which seems to have drawn them into the opposite opinion), namely, the difficulty of the harvest, which would arise if the Sabbatical year and the Jubilee followed one another continuously. Resp. God could easily have remedied that inconvenience if He had then imparted the blessing of four years as He had promised for three, verse 21.

Latin:

Ad cap. 25. versu 10. ANNUM QUINQUAGESIMUM.

Quæritur hic: utrum annus Jubilæus fuerit reipsa quadragesimus nonus, an quinquagesimus? Prius statuunt Gerh. Mercator & Scaliger cum Hugone Cardinali, & Lyrano; posterius Eusebius, Beda, Torniellus, Salianus, Serarius, Cornelius à Lapide, Bonfrerius, quia 1. diserte vocatur annus quinquagesimus, non annumerato præcedente Jubilæo, sic enim annus iste bis numeraretur, ut ultimus prioris, & primus sequentis. 2. Sicut se- ptimus dies hebdomadæ, excluso priore Sabbato, non octavus eo incluso: ita annus 50. prioris Ju- bilæi anno excluso, non incluso, assumendus est. 3. Alias frustra repeteretur v. 11. omittendam semen- tem &c. si Jubilæus semper in annum Sabbaticum incideret. 4. Alias confusio summa induceretur in Chronica Judæorum, qui 50. annos completos pro Jubilæo habent. Hæc illi, συνοπτικῶς ea exhiben- te Polo in Synopsi Crit. & Interpp. p. 607. Addit è Bonfrerio dubium, quod verbis ejus solvit: Uni- cum obstat (quod illos videtur in contrariam senten- tiam pertraxisse) nempe, annonæ difficultas, quæ na- sceretur, si annus Sabbaticus & Jubilæus sibi conti- nenter succederent. Resp. Facile potuit Deus illi in- commodo mederi, si tunc benedictionem impertiret quatuor annorum ut trium promiserat vers. 21.

YE SHALL NOT OPPRESS) 'Let not a man oppress his neighbor,' LXX. From the preceding it appears that this law pertains to preserving equality between the movable thing sold and the price of the thing. Thus Moses of Kotzi on the commandment, ch. 82. See what we [wrote] in book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 12, 11. Equality, however, was accustomed to be viewed in such a way that what was below the sixth part of the just price was disregarded.

Ita Moses de Kotzi ad præceptum jubens c. 82. Vide quæ nos libro 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 12, 11. Æqualitas autem ita spectari solita est, ut quod infra sextam partem erat pretii justi insuper haberetur.

CONTRIBVLES VESTROS) Jus hoc advenæ non pro- derat.

AND YOU SHALL RECEIVE HIM AS A SOJOURNER AND A STRANGER) Translate: help him (as also) a stranger and a sojourner, who shall live with you. Here and below 47, the ו in ותושב is explanatory, which becomes manifest below 14, 45. It signifies, however, one who, having renounced idolatry and depraved morals, worshipped God, although not with Jewish rites, as the Chaldean shows here. If you ought to have pity on a foreigner, much more so on your fellow countryman. To such foreigners something of alms was owed, but not likewise a portion of the tithes, the gleaning, and other things.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAP. XXVI.

Promises made to the obedient, threats made to the disobedient.

Ver. 1.

A FIGURED STONE) Namely with pictures, which the Hebrew word indicates: that was forbidden even outside of pillars, not as evil in itself, but as used by the Canaanites in the worship of idols.

Images, carved figures, and stones are not absolutely prohibited, but those which are erected for the sake of adoration. Neither shall you set up a figured stone in your land, THAT YOU MAY WORSHIP it. Therefore this cause is added, why one should serve wooden and stone idols: Because I am Jehovah your God. Compare Is. 42, 8. If everything that was used in the worship of idols were simply prohibited, what at last will remain? For almost nothing is not snatched into abuse in the worship of idols.

Latin:

CAP. XXVI.

Promissiones obedientibus, comminationes in- obedientibus factæ.

Vers. 1.

INSIGNEM LAPIDEM) Nempe picturis, quod Hebræa vox indicat: vetitum id etiam extra columnas non ut per se malum, sed ut à Cananæis in idolorum cultu usur- patum.

Non prohibentur imagines, sculptilia, lapides absolutè, sed qua eriguntur adorationis causa. Nec insignem lapidem ponetis in terra vestra, UT AD- ORETIS eum. Ideo additur causa hæc, cur idolis ligneis & lapideis serviendum sit: Quia ego sum Jehovah vester. Confer Es. 42, 8. Si omne illud sim- pliciter prohiberetur, quod in idolorum cultu usur- patum, quid tandem reliquum erit: Fere enim ni- hil non in idolorum cultu in abusum abripitur.

## 26:12
Ver. 12. I WILL WALK AMONG YOU. It concerns a gracious presence. Cocceius in the last of Moses §. 1556. rightly translates this passage thus: And I will give my tabernacle in the midst of you, and my soul shall not abhor you, and (then afterwards) I will walk in the midst of you, taking it concerning the incarnation of the Son of God. Compare Deut. 33, 3. and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 12. AMBULABO INTER VOS. De gratiosa præsentia agitur. Coccejus in ul- tim. Mos. §. 1556. καλῶς locum hunc ita vertit: Et dabo tabernaculum meum in medio vestri, & non abominabitur anima mea vos, & (tum deinde) am- bulabo in medio vestri, de ἐνσαρκώσει Filii Dei ac- cipiens. Conf. Deut. 33, 3. & quæ ibi dicta.

Verse 13.

THAT YOU MIGHT WALK ERECT) As free men, not accustomed to the yoke. It is a Greek proverb, Οὔποτε δουλεία κεφαλὴ ἐυθεῖα πέφυκεν, Ἀλλ' αἰεὶ σκολιὴ, κ' ἀυχένα λοξὸν ἔχουσα

Latin:

Vers. 13.

VT INCEDERETIS ERECTI) Vt homines liberi, non assueti jugo. Græcum Proverbium est, Οὔποτε δουλεία κεφαλὴ ἐυθεῖα πέφυκεν, Ἀλλ' αἰεὶ σκολιὴ, κ' ἀυχένα λοξὸν ἔχουσα

## 26:25
Verse 25.

PESTILENCE) He translates the word מור and the Greek λοιμὸν well, according to frequent usage, concerning which see Matthew 24:7.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

PESTILENTIAM) Bene vertit vocem מור & Græ- cam λοιμὸν ex usu frequenti, de quo ad Matth. 24, 7.

## 26:30
Verse 30.

YOUR HIGH PLACES) It was the custom of those nations to sacrifice ἐπὶ ὑψηλοτάτων ὀρέων (on the highest mountains). Herodotus, Clio. See what is above at 19:26 and Numbers 33:52.

AND I WILL BREAK YOUR IMAGES) חמנים. If anyone considers Isaiah 17:8 and Ezekiel 6:4, they seem to have been not so much images as places, namely those in which sacred fires were made, which the origin seems to signify: πυρανθεῖα (fire-altars) to Strabo in book 15, πυρεῖα (fire-temples) to others. Some think both the name and the institution came from Ammon, who is חם to the Hebrews. Let us consider whether the god Omanus and King Achaemenes were named from this word. Rabbi Beckai says that those first fires were not idolatrous, but were instituted to give thanks to God for the sun. Soon, because of the evil usage that followed, they were forbidden, as were many other things. A clear description of such a πυρεῖον (fire-temple) is in book 1 of Procopius's Persian Wars, as a fuller edition exists in the Vatican codex: Ἐτύγχανε δὲ ὁ χοσρόης ἐξ Ἀσσυρίων εἰς χωρίον Αρδαβιγάνων ἤκων πρὸς βοῤῥᾶν ἄνεμον, ἔνθεν διενοεῖτο εἰς τὴν Ῥωμαίων ἀρχὴν Διὰ περσαρμενίων ἐσβάλλειν. Τὸ μέγα πυρεῖον

It is there that the Persians worship the gods most, where indeed the Magi, keeping the fire unquenched, perform all other things with precision, and use an oracle for the greatest of matters. You have another description of the fire-temples in Benjamin, where he describes Chenarafam, and says that it is called by the fire אלהותא, that is, divinity. See also Theodoret 10, 29, 30, and History V, 38. Teixera also says that in his time this custom remained among certain Persians.

It seems to Grotius from Is. 17:8, Ez. 6:4, that it can be gathered that the חמנים were not so much idols as places. But those are distinguished here and in Ezekiel from the high places. 'I will destroy your high places, and I will break your idols.' Therefore it does not seem to have been necessary that he should depart from the Vulgate here. If you say that the origin of the word seems to signify places in which sacred fires were made, called πυραθεῖα by Strabo in book XV, and πυρεῖα by others. I reply: since חמן is said from חמם, to be hot, and חמה is the Sun, and they interpret it as a solar place, and an idol built in an open place receiving the heat of the sun, likewise a temple of Hammon, which others call a heliocaminus, as Avenarius notes. That it came from Ammon, from whom the Hebrews think both the name and the institution of חם came, we leave to its own place. There are those who say that in the Egyptian language Ammon is called Jupiter. 34. It is held, 'they tore down before him the altars of the Baalim and the חמנים, the idols which were sacred to him,' where the Rabbis understand an image of the sun, or idols or enclosures and πυραθεῖα sacred to the Sun: just as they wish it to be designated in this place as dedicated to the honor of the Sun. Added here are במות, the high places, in which the Persians (as witnessed by Herodotus in Clio), and other Asiatics and Jews, performed sacred rites to Jupiter; whence, according to Hesychius, he is called ἐπάκριος ζεύς. Grotius also leaves it to be considered here whether from this word חמן the god Omam, and the King Ochamanes, were named. Thus Scaliger entirely opined, nor did Selden deny it, observing that Amanus and Omanus were called the Sun, just as Anaitis was the Moon, book II, Syntagm. c. 8. In vain, therefore, is Grotius, when he observes from R. Bechanus that those first fires were not idolatrous, but instituted to give thanks to God for the Sun. Soon, from the evil use that followed, they were forbidden, like many other things. For those πυρεῖα sacred to the Sun, or because the Persians worshipped the sun in fire, just as Grotius also notes from Benjamin, that the fire was called אלהותא, divinity; how will they be able to be excused, or who finally instituted fires to give thanks to GOD, even if this too would have been damnable and idolatrous as ἐθελοθρησκεία? The Persians certainly invoked fire in every sacrifice, and seem to have worshipped it above other gods, as witnessed by Strabo, 'and thus, sacrificing, they pray to fire as the first god.' Among the Chaldeans, the cult of fire was most ancient, if faith is to be given to the Hebrews, which they held as a symbol of the Sun, and by that name worshipped it religiously; whence the Hebrews also take that אור of the Chaldeans in Gen. 11 for their god, Fire, and say that Abraham, who refused to bring worship to the sun and fire, was thrown into chains, despoiled of his goods, and banished by the King to the borders of Syria: which R. Moses Maimon. in More Nebuch. book III, chapter 29, according to the Arabic text, he cites in the 2nd book on the cult of the Nabatheans: See Hottinger, book 1, on the use of Oriental languages, chapter 8, page 291. In Pirke Eliez. chapter 26, Abraham is said to have been thrown into the middle of a fiery furnace, but snatched away by the King of glory according to that in Gen. 15, 'I am the Lord, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.' Although Aben-Ezra more correctly takes אור as the name of a city and the native soil of Abraham, which Josephus calls ὀρὴν, yet the conjecture of those who opine that that city obtained that name because Fire was worshipped there as a Deity, according to the religion of the Zabaeans, does not seem vain. But these things are said by the way.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

Ezech. 6, 4. non tam simulacra quam loca fuisse videntur, nempe in quibus sacri ignes facti, quod origo videtur significare: πυρανθεῖα Straboni libro 15. πυρεῖα aliis. Τὸ μέγα πυρεῖον

Bechani ob-servat, primos ignes istos non fuisse idololatricos, sedinstitutos ad Deo gratias agendas pro Sole. Mox exmalo usu sequuto vetitos, ut multa alia. MosesMaimon. in More Nebuch. lib. III, cap. 29. juxta Ara-bicum textum 2. libro de cultu Nabatheorum adducit: Vid. Hottinger. lib. 1. de usu linguar. Oriental. cap. 8.pag. 291. In Pirke Eliez. cap. 26. in medium fornacisignitæ conjectus dicitur Abraham, sed a Rege gloriæereptus juxta illud Gen. 15. ego sum Dominus, quieduxi te ex Ur Chaldeorum. Quanquam vero אורpro nomine urbis & natali solo Abrahi rectius acci-piat Aben-Ezra, quam ὀρὴν vocat Josephus, non va-na tamen videtur illorum conjectura, qui autu-mant, id nominis urbem illam consequutam, quodibi Ignis pro Numine coleretur, juxta Zabaorum re-ligionem. ## 26:37
Vers. 37.

THEY SHALL FALL EVERY ONE UPON HIS BROTHERS AS IF FLEEING FROM BATTLES) Understand 'brothers' as fellow countrymen. This is wont to happen in battles, where ranks are disordered, so that fellow soldiers are overwhelmed by fellow soldiers. But the Rabbis interpret באחין as 'by brotherly crime': that is, the sin of one party will be imputed to all who did not resist according to the mutual oaths made on the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal. See what we have brought forward in book II of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 21, § 11, and in the Annotations.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

CORRVENT SINGVLI SUPER FRATRES SVOS QVASI BELLA FVGIENTES) Fratres intellige populares. Solet id fieri in præliis, ubi turbati sunt ordines, ut commilites a commilitibus obruantur. At Rabbini באחין interpretantur fraterno crimine: id est, unius partis delictum omnibus imputabitur, qui non obstiterint secundum mutuas jurationes factas in montibus Garizim & Hebal. Vide quæ allata a nobis libro II. de jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 21. §. 11. & in Annotatis.

## 27:21
Ver. 21.

AND THE CONSECRATED POSSESSION) Better the LXX: ὥσπερ ἡ γῆ ἀφωρισμένη, as land captured from enemies, and devoted to God, and thus placed outside of commerce, which is called חרם, or ἀνάθεμα. See what is below 28.

Latin:

## 27:29
Ver. 29.

AND EVERY CONSECRATION WHICH IS OFFERED BY MAN, SHALL NOT BE REDEEMED, BUT SHALL SURELY DIE) Concerning man, that is, concerning enemies, or deserters from the military: for in other cases this law has no place. See examples Num. 21, 2. Josh. 17.

Junius inserts 'beast': Every devoted beast which is devoted by man. But in the Hebrew there is no mention of a beast. And it is held from men, as v. 28. ἀπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων; not ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων, as the LXX rendered it. Therefore it is a question of not redeeming the anathema of a human person. Which some judge God to have permitted, not approved (as with divorces). Capella on the vow of Jephthah §. 8. brings forward these causes of the law: 1. That He might show Himself to be the Lord of life and death. 2. That He might deter parents from severe curses. 3. That He might prefigure Christ, who is חרם, a curse for us. Whence that custom seems to have come down to the Gentiles. Cloppenburg in Spicilig. Schol. Sacrif. p. 218. wishes this law to be a bond, by which they were devoted by anathema with a just zeal for God on account of some crime, so that they might not escape, whom God wished to be punished, as 2 Chron. 15. 1 Kings 2. Deut. 21, 18. 27. And therefore it pertains to the coercive power of the Magistrate, yet so that the works of the Priests intervened for its execution, to whom belonged the cognizance of vows and the right, property, and Dominion of things sacred to God by חרם. Num. 18, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ET OMNIS CONSECRATIO QUÆ OFFERTUR AB HOMINE, NON REDIMETUR, SED MORTE MORIETUR) De homine, id est, de hostibus, aut militiæ desertoribus: nam in aliis hæc lex locum non habet. Exempla vide Num. 21, 2. Jos. 17.

Bestiam ingerit Junius: Omnis bestia devota quæ devovetur ab homine. Sed in Ebr. nulla bestiæ mentio est. Et habetur ex hominibus, ut v. 28. ἀπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων; non ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων, uti LXX. reddidere. Agitur ergo de non redimendo anathemate personæ humanæ. Quod permisisse Deum non probasse (uti repudia) nonnulli censent. Capella de voto Jepthth. §. 8. causas legis has adfert: 1. ut se esse vitæ & necis Dominum ostenderet. 2. Ut absterreret parentes a severis diris. 3. Ut præfiguraret Christum, qui est חרם κατάρα pro nobis. Unde ad Ethnicos mos ille devenisse videtur. Cloppenburg. in Spicilig. Schol. Sacrif. p. 218. legem hanc esse vult vinculum, quo justo Zelo Dei propter crimen aliquod devovebantur anathemate, ne elaberentur, quos Deus punitos vellet, ut 2. Chron. 15. 1. Reg. 2. Deut. 21, 18. 27. Ideoque spectare ad potestatem coercitivam Magistratus, ita tamen ut ad ejus exequutionem intervenirent opera Sacerdotum, ad quos pertinebat votorum cognitio rerumque Deo per חרם sacrarum jus, proprietas, & Dominium. Num. 18, 14.

## 27:32
Vers. 32.

WHICH PASS UNDER THE SHEPHERD'S ROD) The lambs used to pass through the door of the fold, where their mother sheep stood: and the tither marked every tenth one.

Tithes are demanded many times, Ex. 22, 29. & 23, 19. Num. 18, 24. partly for the preservation of the Ecclesiastical ministry: partly in testimony of confession and thanksgiving: partly as an admonition of beneficence. And there were three kinds of them: one, which from the fruits and cattle fell to the Levitical order, Deut. 24, 28. Num. 18. another, which was paid to the Priests, which they called second tithes: a third kind, from all the produce of the earth, to be distributed as alms among the poor, strangers, widows, and orphans, concerning which Deut. 26, 12.

dum. For if it had been free either to exchange the cattle, or to redeem them, no fat, healthy, and sound animal would ever have come to the Levites: just as GOD complains in Malachi: that a blind, maimed, lame, and sickly animal is offered to Him, 1. c. v. 8. Thus Pelargus, with B. Chytraeus leading the way.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

QVÆ SVB PASTORIS VIRGA TRANSEUNT) Transibant agni per ostium caulæ, ubi ovis eorum mater stabat: & decimum quemque signabat decimator.

Multoties decimæ exiguntur, Ex. 22, 29. & 23, 19. Num. 18, 24. tum ad conservationem ministerii Ec- clesiastici: tum in testificationem confessionis ac gratitudinis: tum in admonitionem beneficentiæ. Et tria illarum erant genera: unum, quod ex frugi- bus & pecoribus cedebat ordini Levitico, Deut. 24, 28. Num. 18. alterum, quod Sacerdotibus exsolveba- tur, quas decimas δευτεροδεκάδας appellabant: ter- tium genus, ex omnibus terræ nascentibus, ad elee- mosynas distribuendas inter pauperes, peregrinos, viduas, & orphanos, de quibus Deut. 26, 12.

dum. Si enim liberum fuisset aut commutare pe- cus, aut redimere, nullum unquam animal pingue, vegetumque, integrumque venisset ad Levitas: si- cut apud Malachiam queritur DEUS: cœcum, muti- lum, claudum, & languidum pecus sibi offerri, 1. c. v. 8. Hæc Pelargus, præeunte B. Chytreo.

## 27:34
Verse 34.

THESE ARE THE COMMANDMENTS WHICH THE LORD COMMANDED TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL ON MOUNT SINAI.

God commands, however, in this place, that tithes from the land be paid, or redeemed by the owner at a set price, with a fifth part added: not so that the Levites may make a profit from another's loss: but so that the cunning and frauds of those changing grain into money may be countered. But as for those things from living creatures, which He willed to be returned simply from the herd or flock, without exchange or redemption: if anyone does otherwise, He orders him to suffer the loss of the exchange, so that both may fall to the Lord. Where He applies a remedy to avarice and greed quite conveniently. Namely, concerning the instituting and exercising of divine worship, by which both the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ is graphically depicted, and our Eucharistic offerings are shadowed forth, so that with due thanksgiving, the propagation of the Gospel, sincere piety of life, patience, and beneficence toward our neighbor, we may show ourselves grateful to our God for His immense goodness. May God of all grace grant this through Christ our mediator by the power of the Holy Spirit, blessed for ever, Amen.

Latin:

Versus 34.

HÆC SUNT PRÆCEPTA, QUÆ MAN- DAVIT DOMINUS MOYSI AD FILIOS IS- RAEL IN MONTE SINAI.

Præcipit autem hoc loco Deus, ut decimæ ex terra solvantur, aut pretio taxato, & quinta superad- dita, a possessore redimantur: non ut Levitæ ex alie- no damno lucrum faciant: sed ut astutiæ, & frumen- tum in pecuniam mutantium fraudibus, occurratur. Quæ vero ex animantibus, armento vel grege sim- pliciter reddi voluit, sine permutatione ac redem- tione: si quis secus faxit, eum jacturam permutatio- nis pati jubet, ut utrumq; cedat Domino. Ubi ava- ritiæ ac sordibus remedium adhibet sat commo- De instituendo nempe & exercendo cultu divi- no, quibus tum Christi sacrificium propitiatorium graphice depictum, tum oblationes nostræ Euchari- sticæ adumbratæ, ut debita gratiarum actione, Evan- gelii propagatione, sincera vitæ pietate, patientia, & erga proximum beneficentia Deo nostro pro im- mensa bonitate gratos nos exhibeamus. Quod faxit Deus omnis gratiæ per Christum mediatorem no- strum virtute Spiritus S. benedictus in Secula, Amen.

# Numbers

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOK OF NUMBERS, PREFACE.

Just as the authority of the Legislator, both the primary Triune GOD and the secondary Moses, was legitimized in GENESIS and EXODUS up to chapter 20: the Law itself was proposed from chapter 20 of Exodus to the end of Leviticus: so now the people themselves had to be distributed into certain classes, which arrangement, and the military movement of those arranged in the desert, the book of NUMBERS exhibits: and finally, for the people who had arisen or were newly born after the old generation had perished in the desert, or were born and grown in the desert, the Law had to be repeated and explained, which was done in DEUTERONOMY. The present book obtains its name among the Hebrews partly from וידבר חומש, both from the initial word וידבר and He spoke, and especially from the more significant word of the first verse במדבר in the desert: which briefly comprises the SUM of the book, as we have already said: because although some things done in the desert are described in Exodus and Leviticus, those were the acts of only one year, these of only one month, but here the acts done IN THE DESERT over 39 years are described: partly when it is called אלה פקודים the book of numbers, and also ספר הפקודים the book of reviews, it is designated by the Greeks by the name ἀριθμοὶ, and likewise by the Latins by the name of Numbers, because it has this peculiar feature compared to the remaining Mosaic books, that it is occupied in a great part with the review and number, as much of persons, for instance of warriors, firstborn, Levites, of numbers in the consecration of the tabernacle and altar, as also of the Old from chapter 1 to 26. & then of the new people after the death of the Fathers in the desert, as of the stations, and of the possessions in the desert during the time of the pilgrimage, and teaches how they had to have in count those things which pertained to the journey, whence it can be called the ITINERARY of the Israelites. Therefore Abuiensis says: It is called more from the numbers, he says, than from the rest which are in it; since there is nothing by which this book differs more specially from the others than by the numbers. For in it three things are described, from which it could have taken its name: namely, precepts, enumerations, and histories of times: it was not fitting to name it from the precepts: for none are treated here, except certain judicial and ceremonial ones. But it should not have been called from the judicial ones, because more are handed down in Deuteronomy: nor from the ceremonial ones, because these are treated principally in Leviticus. It should not have taken its name from the histories either, because those are contained in the other books as well: Therefore only the enumerations remain, from which this book could be named by way of distinction. Among the interpreters, besides those who wrote on the whole Bible or the Old Testament or the Pentateuch alone, there occur few who have devoted effort to this book alone: Jerome commemorates Hippolytus, who flourished in the year 220, because he adorned one book on Numbers. Cajetan also exists on Numbers; as does Job. Wolsius. In the Douay Bibles, Acacius, from the year 350, and Severianus from the year 400, who contributed some things on Genesis and Numbers; Greg. Nyssenus in the year 380, who contributed on Exodus and Numbers, and Apollinaris the younger in the year 380, who contributed some things on Leviticus and Numbers, are cited.

Moreover, some assign the order with respect to the preceding book as follows: that in Leviticus the rationale of divine worship and political government is ordered by certain specific degrees and classes, by which there may be a seat also for the new Church and the doctrine resounding in it concerning GOD and the promised Messiah. But since the duties, consecration, and confirmation of the Levites and Priests are no less described in the same, the order is more correctly sought from the Chronology, because what was dictated and recorded in Leviticus after the tabernacle was erected, concerning which there is mention in Exodus, in the first month of the second year from the exodus, is followed by the numbering of the people in the desert, at the beginning of the second month, which this book describes, and thus it contains the deeds of 38 years and 9 months, namely from the first day of the second month in the second year of the exodus, up to the first day of the eleventh month in the fortieth year after the exodus; so that therefore in Genesis there especially stands out and shines forth the promise concerning CHRIST the blessed seed, delivered to Adam and Abraham, and the History of the Creation of the World, and of the Church miraculously founded, propagated, and defended by GOD from that time on from the beginning: in Exodus, the LAW of GOD, or the promulgation of the DECALOGUE on Mount Sinai, and the constitution of the Jewish Church and Polity: in Leviticus, the Laws concerning sacrifices, which are types of the sacrifice and benefits of Christ and of spiritual offerings accepted by God through Christ: in Deuteronomy, a copious and clear narration of the Decalogue: so in Numbers, the History of the wondrous government of the people of Israel, wandering for thirty-nine years in the desert, is recited.

It is distributed, however, according to a dichotomy or by reason of the subject matter, as was done by the Blessed Gerhard in his Exegesis of Holy Scripture, because it describes the journey of the Israelites through the desert, and both its preceding preparation and its subsequent station, on which occasion examples of obedience honored with rewards, or of disobedience visited with punishments, are introduced, or by reason of Chronology, by Dr. Pelargus, because it first delivers those things which were done in the desert up to the 40th year, c. 19. Then in the remainder, those things which followed in the fortieth year. To others, a trichotomy is pleasing, with Abulensis, because first the just disposition for the departure of the Israelites up to c. 10, then the departure from Mount Sinai to the wilderness of Moab up to c. 23. and it pursues the history of the deeds which happened during the time of that pilgrimage, finally it exhibits the plan of approaching the land of promise, and the nearest stations, where they already reached the borders or the land of Canaan itself, up to the end of the book. Some assign three parts of the book according to three deserts: referring the history to the desert of Sinai from c. 1 to 10. To the desert of Kadesh, which is considered great (Deut. 1, 19) from c. 10 to 20. To the desert of the Moabites from c. 29 to the end of the book. Others make 4 Sections, so that the first is the review of the people and its tribes up to c. 4, the second the commemoration of certain laws up to c. 10. The third the historical relation of various deeds up to c. 28. Finally, the fourth exhibits mixed together both the designation of certain ceremonial laws and of histories, which distribution we prefer to the others, because the laws which are delivered from c. 5 to 10 do not pertain so much to the preparation for the departure as they are of perpetual observance. Therefore, let the first part be called arithmetical, the enumerator: the second legislative, the ordainer of certain laws: the third historical, the commemorator of deeds: the last part mixed, partly legal concerning sacrifices, the celebration of the seventh month, the rendering of vows, partly historical concerning the slaughter of the Midianites, partly genealogical, by which the lot of the two and a half tribes, and after the stations are reviewed, the possession of the remaining tribes and the decision of the complaint of the sons of Manasseh in the final chapters.

Latin:

ANNOTATA AD LIBRVM NVMERORVM, PRÆFATIO.

UTi Legislatoris tum primarii DEI Triunius tum secundarii Mosis autoritas in GENESI & EXODO us- que ad c. 20. legitimata: Lex ipsa a c. 20. Exodi usq; ad finem Levitici pro- posita est: ita nunc distribuendus e- rat populus ipse in certas classes, quam ordinatio- nem, & ordinatorum castrensem in deserto cir- cumductionem exhibet NUMERORUM liber: ac denique populo post veterem in deserto pro- stratum exorto seu novello, vel in deserto nato & adulto Lex repetenda erat, & explicanda, quod in DEUTERONOMIO factum.
