vers. 4. THIS IS THE CULT. In the Hebrew it is not cult, but ministry. For the function of the Kohathites is designated. Which is likewise observed in v. 28 concerning the cult of the Gershonites. Whence v. 15, These are the burdens of the sons of Kohath; and v. 24, This is the office of the family of the Gershonites.

Latin:

vers. 4. HIC EST CVLTVS. In Ebræo non cultus est, sed ministerium. Designatur enim functio Caathitarum. Quod pariter observatum v. 28. de cultu Gersonitarum. Vnde v. 15. Ista sunt onera filiorum Caath; & v. 24. Hoc est officium familiæ Gersonitarum.

## 4:5
Vers. 5. AARON AND HIS SONS. The sons of Aaron also entered the holy of holies, but only when the camps were to be moved to take them down, but not when they were fixed, so as to minister in it, Lev. 16, Heb. 9, 7, which was fitting only for the high Priest. Because then the economy of the presence of God withdrew itself to the ark of the covenant. Therefore access was open to the other Priests, who took down the veil which divided the holy from the holy of holies, and wrapped the ark and the Cherubim in it, and similarly wrapped the table and the altar and the lampstand with a scarlet cloak, which were in the holy place, which it was not permitted even for the Levites to touch or see under penalty of death. But the Kohathites prepared those things veiled. Then the Gershonites approached, folding up and carrying out their curtains and veils. Finally the Merarites were present, dissolving and exporting the columns and boards of the tabernacle. In the erection there was the opposite order.

In the Hebrew it is, and they shall place the staves. There was no need for them to insert the staves into the ark, because they had already been inserted into it, and were never pulled out, Ex. 25, 15. The Vulgate must therefore be corrected here, which Cornelius cannot help: They shall insert, namely, onto their shoulders. Did they insert the staves onto their shoulders? Therefore to place the staves, that is, they were ordered to fit them, so that the ark could be carried. But they had to extend the hyacinthine cloak, i.e., one of the silk curtains, in which among others the hyacinthine or yellow color stands out, over the ark already covered with the veil and the skins of bulls, so that from this more splendid covering the Israelites might recognize where the ark of the covenant was being carried.

Latin:

Vers. 5. AARON ET FILII EJVS. Ingrediebantur & filii Aaron sanctum sanctorum, sed tantum quando movenda erant castra ad illa deponenda, non vero cum fixa illa erant, ut in eo ministrarent, Lev. 16. Ebr. 9, 7. quod soli summo Pontifici conveniebat. Quia tunc subducebat se οἰκονομία præsentiæ Dei ad arcam fœderis. Ideo aditus patebat Sacerdotibus cæteris, qui deponebant velum, quod sanctum a sancto sanctorum dividebat, eiq; involvebat arcam & Cherubim, ac pallio coccineo similiter mensam involvebat & altare & candelabrum, quæ erant in sancto, quæ ne Levitis quidem tangere, aut videre licebat sub pœna mortis. Ea autem velata parabant Caathitæ. Deinde accedebant Gersonitæ convolventes & efferentes suas cortinas & vela. Postremo Meraritæ aderant, columnas & tabulas tabernaculi dissolventes, & exportantes. In erectione contrarius ordo erat.

In Ebr. est, & ponent vectes. Non opus erat, ut inducerent vectes in arcam, quia jam in eam in- ducti erant, & nunquam extrahebantur, Ex. 25, 15. Corrigenda ergo hic Vulgata, quam juvare non po- test Cornelius : Inducent nempe in humeros. Num vectes in humeros inducebant? Ponere ergo vectes, hoc est, aptare jubebantur, ut portari possit arca. Extendere autem debebant pallium hyacinthinum, h. e. unam ex cortinis sericis, in qua inter alios emi- neat hyacinthinus seu flaveus color, super arcam jam velo & taurorum pellibus contectam, ut ex hoc splendidiore tegumento agnoscerent Israelitae, ubi locorum portaretur arca foederis.

## 4:7
ver. 7. AND THEY SHALL PLACE WITH IT THE CENSERS AND THE MORTARS.

In Hebrew, bowls or large platters and censers. Fine flour for the mincha or cereal offering was received in the bowls; incense was kept in the censers, which was to be burned with the sacrifices; cups and bowls were used for pouring out libations or rather drink offerings, such as oil or wine.

Latin:

vers. 7. ET PONENT CUM EA THURI- BULA ET MORTARIOLA.

In Ebr. Scutellas, vel patinas amplas & thuribu- la. Scutellis excipiebatur simila pro mincha sive far- reo sacrificio, in thuribulis thus asservabatur, quod cum sacrificiis adolendum erat; cyathi & crateres adhibebantur ad liba vel potius libamenta funden- da, puta oleum vel vinum.

## 4:10
Ver. 10. AND THEY SHALL INSERT THE POLES.

There were no poles on the lampstand. Others render the words of the original text thus: And they shall place upon a yoke or such an instrument, by which they may be conveniently transported from place to place. For מוט has its name from motion. Tremellius: thus they shall place upon the carrying poles. So also v. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET INDUCENT VECTES.

In candelabro non erant vectes. Verba tex- tus originalis ita reddunt alii, Et ponent super jugum vel tale instrumentum, quo commode de loco in locum transportari possint. Nam מוט a motione nomen habet. Tremellius: sic imponent palangis. Sic & v. 12.

## 4:11
ver. 11. A COVERING OF VIOLET SKINS.

In Hebrew it is a covering of badger skin, which is also to be observed in v. 12, 14. The GOLDEN altar, that is, of incense, which was constructed of shittim wood but overlaid with gold, was to be wrapped or covered with a covering of badger skins.

Latin:

vers. 11. OPERIMENTUM JANTHINARUM PELLIUM.

In Ebr. est operimentum pellis taxi, quod & v. 12. 14. observandum. Altare AUREUM, id est, thymiamatis, quod e lignis Setim constructum, sed auro obductum, erat involvendum vel insternen- dum operimentum de pellibus taxorum.

## 4:13
ver. 13. THEY SHALL CLEANSE THE ALTAR OF ASHES.

The altar of burnt offerings, which had to be cleansed both on account of the victims burned upon it at Sinai (for after the departure from Sinai they did not sacrifice in the desert) and on account of the wood by which the sacred fire was to be kept alive, Lev. 6, 12.

Latin:

vers. 13. ALTARE MUNDABUNT CINERE.

Holocaustorum altare, quod tum victimarum in eo combustarum in Sina (nam post egressum ex Si- na non sacrificarunt in deserto) tum lignorum causa, quibus fovendus erat ignis sacer Lev. 6, 12. mun- dandum erat.

## 4:13 Addition
To vers. 13. AND THEY SHALL WRAP IT IN A PURPLE CLOTH.

In the Hebrew: Of the dust. A sign of this shame and misery. And dust was the food of the serpent, which was fitting for her, who was enticed by the serpent's temptations, as Ainsworth notes.

More correctly, they shall spread over: namely, the purple curtain, in which the purple color stood out above others, which according to Lyranus was made for the altar, so that it might be signified that the fire lay hidden beneath it, which, once given divinely, was to be diligently preserved: and as Ainsworth notes, so that its dignity might be signified through the blood of Christ, whence also the scarlet cloth was covered. Compare Matt. 27:28 with Mark 15:17 and John 19, verse 2.

Latin:

Ad vers. 13. ET INVOLVENT ILLUD PURPUREO VESTI- MENTO.

In Ebræo: De pulvere. Signum hoc turpitu- dinis, & miseriæ. Et pulvis cibus serpentis ei con- veniebat, quæ serpentis tentationibus pellecta, mo- nente Ainsvvortho.

Rectius insternent: Cortinæ nempe purpu- reæ, in qua purpureus color præ aliis eminebat, quod secundum Lyranum altari factum, ut desi- gnaretur, quod ignis sub eo lateret, qui semel datus divinitus diligenter asservandus erat: & Ainsvvor- tho notante, ut dignitas ejus per sanguinem Christi si- gnificaretur, unde & tabula coccinea tegebatur. Conf. Matth. 27, 28. cum Marc. 15, 17. & Johann. 19. versu 2.

## 4:14
Ver. 14. FLESH-HOOKS AND TRIDENTS, HOOKS.

In Hebrew, for these three there is one word, signifying tongs or flesh-hooks, by which meats are extracted from the cauldron.

AND FIRE-PANS.

Shovels, by which we remove coals and ashes from the hearth: in the Hebrew there are also bowls, which are here incorrectly omitted by the Vulgate.

Latin:

Vers. 14. FUSCINULAS AC TRIDENTES, UNCINOS.

In Ebr. pro his tribus una vox est, Forcipes, vel κρεάγρας, quibus carnes ex lebete extrahuntur, si- gnificans.

ET BATILLA.

Palas, quibus prunas & cinerem e foco remo- vemus: in Ebraeo habentur & phialae, quae hic per- peram omittuntur a Vulgata.

## 4:15
AND LET THEM NOT TOUCH THE VESSELS OF THE SANCTUARY.

In Hebrew: He shall not touch the holiness, or any holy thing. Junius observes here that the ark itself was also carried by the Levites, but only until the priests, having increased in number, could carry it, Deut. 31, 9. For that it was the duty of the priests afterwards, all the examples of the histories teach, in the books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings. But how did the Kohathites, who carried them, not touch them? They were not to touch them immediately, and those things which were covered, and therefore they touched only the coverings, and they could not even look upon the things that were covered without danger of life. The priests had to cover them first, v. 19, 20.

a hyacinthine leather covering, and they shall place it upon the carrying poles. That this is ancient appears both from the ancient Samaritan and from Origen, Homily 4 on Numbers.

Grotius renders no reason for the corrupted Hebrew text: he decides solely by authority, it seems entirely. For the fact that the LXX, that the Samaritan Codex, that Origen here refer to certain words, or rather an entire verse, which is not held in the Hebrew, cannot be taken as a reason. Why should we posit that the verse was omitted in our Hebrew Codices, and not believe rather that it was wrongly assumed in the edition of the LXX? Grotius acknowledges that not all editions in the LXX version contain it. However, it is not surprising if some do, because Origen followed his own reading of the LXX Codex, or those who edited Origen, and because the Samaritan, variously interpolated according to the Codex of the LXX Interpreters, also retained it. It is likely that this patch was sewn onto the LXX Interpreters. A certain codex, since their editions vary, was added by some sciolist who thought that the mention of the bronze laver and its base should not have been omitted, or by way of explanation, he added these things in Greek: They shall also take a purple garment and cover the laver and its basin, and they shall cast it into the covering of hyacinthine skins and place it upon the pole. But there is no need for these, since the bronze laver and other things were already included under the general designation of ALL THE INSTRUMENTS in v. 14. Certainly, all the Hebrew Codices, the Chaldean paraphrases, the Vulgate Latin version, and some editions of the LXX Interpreters agree here, in which there is no trace of that verse. And therefore there can be no suspicion of corruption of the sources. Grotius acknowledges in v. 25 that some things not at all necessary were inserted into the Samaritan Codex, e.g., Num. 10:5. He will never prove such a thing about the Hebrew Codex.

Latin:

vers. 15. ET NON TANGANT VASA SAN- CTUARII.

In Ebr. Non tanget sanctitatem, vel ullam rem sanctam. Observat hic Junius deportatam fuisse etiam ipsam arcam a Levitis, sed donec Sacerdotes numero aucti eam deportare possent Deut. 31, 9. nam Sacerdotum postea fuisse, omnia historiarum ex- empla docent, in libris Jehoschuae, Judicum, Sche- muelis, & Regum. Quomodo autem non attin- gebant Cahathitae quae deportabant? Non attinge- re debebant immediate, & quae tecta, ideoque at- tingebant solum opercula, ac ne aspicere quidem poterant quae tecta sine periculo vitae. Sacerdotes prius tegere debebant v. 19. 20.

λυμμα δερμάτινον ὑακίνθινον καὶ ἐπιθήσουσιν ἐπὶ ἀναφορεῖς. Ve- tus esse hoc apparet tum ex Samaritano antiquo, tum ex Ori- gene Homilia 4. ad Numeros.

Rationem nullam reddit Grotius corrupti textus Ebraici : Solum pro autoritate decernit, omnino videtur. Nam quod LXX. quod Samari- tanus Codex, quod Origenes verba quædam, vel in- tegrum potius versiculum hîc referant, qui non ha- betur in Ebræo, pro ratione haberi non potest. Cur omissum in nostris Codicibus Ebræis statuamus ver- sum, & non credamus potius in editione LXX. eun- dem perperam assumtum ? Non habere eum omnes editiones in LXX. versione, agnoscit Grotius. Mi- rum autem non est, si aliquæ habeant, quod Origenes sequutus lectionem suam Codicis LXX. sive qui O- rigenem edidere, quodque Samaritanus ad Codi- cem LXX. Interpp. varie interpolatus, eundem etiam retinuere. Verisimile est, assutam hanc la- ciniam ad LXX. Interpp. Codicem quendam, quum varient illorum editiones, a sciolo quodam, qui pu- tarit non prætermittendam fuisse commemoratio- nem labri ænei, & baseos ejusdem, eam adjecerit, aut explicationis instar, Græce hæc addidit : Accipi- ent quoque vestem purpuream & tegent labrum, & ba- sin ejus, & injicient illud in operimentum pellium hya- cinthinarum & imponent super vectem. Quibus vero opus non est, quum labrum etiam æneum, & alia sub generali designatione OMNIUM INSTRU- MENTORUM v. 14. jam comprehensa fuerint. Consentiunt certe hic Ebræi Codices universi, para- phrases Chaldææ, Vulgata Latina versio & editio- nes nonnullæ LXX. Interpp. in quibus versus illius nullum est vestigium. Ideoque nulla esse potest corruptionis fontium suspicio. Inserta Codici Samaritano nonnulla minime neceffaria agnoscit v. 25. Grotius, v. g. Num. 10,5. De Ebræo Codice tale quid nunquam probabit.

## 4:16
v. 16. OVER WHOM WAS ELEAZAR. He was appointed over the Kohathites, just as Ithamar, the younger son of Aaron, was over the Gershonites and Merarites, but in such a way that he simultaneously performed the duty of general Superintendent of all. TO WHOSE CARE PERTAINS THE OIL, THE INCENSE AND THE SACRIFICE. Mincha in Hebrew, which is always (daily) offered. It was Eleazar's duty to take care of the oil for the lamps, the aromatic incense, the fine flour and the frankincense: from which material the daily sacrifice was made. Furthermore, the sacred vessels were committed to his care as Prefect of the Kohathites. That the care of the fine flour, wine, frankincense, oil, and aromatics was later distributed among the Levites can be gathered from 1 Chron. 9:29.

Latin:

vers. 16. SUPER QUOS ERAT ELEAZAR. Erat is super Caathitas constitutus, uti Gerfo- nitis & Meraritis præerat Ithamar, junior Aaronis filius, sed ita ut simul generalis omnium Superinten- dentis munere fungeretur. AD CUJUS CURAM PERTINET OLEUM, INCENSUM ET SACRIFICIUM. Mincha in Ebr. quod semper (quotidie) offer- tur. Eleazari erat curare oleum lucernarum, in- censum aromaticum, similam & thus : de qua mate- ria quotidie sacrificium fiebat. Præterea e- rant ejus curæ ceu Præfecti Caathitarum vasa sacra commissa. Curam similæ, vini, thuris, olei & aroma- tum postea in Levitas distributum fuisse e 1. Paral. 9, 29. colligere est.

## 4:18
v. 18. DO NOT DESTROY THE PEOPLE OF KOHATH. That is, take care that by your carelessness and negligence (if you do not yourselves wrap the sacred parts of the tabernacle, but expose them naked to be seen by the Kohathites) it does not happen that the family of the Kohathites is cut off by the Lord: but do this for them so that they may live and not die, that is, you take care that they do not incur the danger of death if they touch, Hebr. if they approach the holy of holies, that is, the most holy things, so that they see them naked. For it usually happens that he who is negligent in his calling destroys others with himself, as Osiander has in this place.

Latin:

vers. 18. NOLITE PERDERE POPULUM CAATH. Id est, cavete, ne vestra incuria & negligentia (si non ipsi involvatis sacras tabernaculi partes : sed nudas Caathitis conspiciendas objiciatis) fiat, ut fa- milia Caathitarum a Domino excidatur : sed hoc faci- te eis ut vivant & non moriantur, id est, vos curate, ne periculum vitæ incurrant, si tetigerint, Hebr. si ac- cefferint ad sancta sanctorum, id est, sanctissima, ut ea nuda adspiciant. Fieri enim solet, ut qui in sua vo- catione est negligens, alios secum perdat, ut habet Osiander h. l.

## 4:18 Addition
vers. 18. HE SHALL UNCOVER HER HEAD.

The priest, namely, as Lyranus notes. And this 1. for greater confusion, and so that, stunned by this, she might confess. This was shameful, 1 Cor. 11:5, 6. 2. So that she might understand that all things are naked and open before God. 3. Since it was a judgment concerning chastity, it was not fitting for her to have the insignia of modesty. In capital cases, the heads of the accused were uncovered. 4. This is a sign of grief, Lev. 21:10. 5. It was an indication that it was in her own power either to condemn or to absolve herself. A covered head was a sign of subjection, 1 Cor. 11:5, 6, 7, 10. Which causes Poole collected in this place from Bonfrerius, Menochius, and Ainsworth.

Latin:

vers. 18. DISCOOPERIT CAPUT EJUS.

Sacerdos scil. ut notat Lyranus. Idque 1. ad majorem confusionem, & ut ex hoc stupefacta con- fiteretur. Probrosum hoc erat 1. Corinth. 11, 5. 6. 2. ut intelligat omnia nuda & aperta esse coram Deo. 3. Cum judicium esset de pudicitia, non decebat eam habere pudoris insignia. In causis capitalibus de- nudabantur reorum capita. 4. Signum hoc do- loris Lev. 21, 10. 5. Indicium erat, in sua potestate esse seipsam aut condemnare aut absolvere. Oper- tum caput subjectionis erat indicium 1. Cor. 11, 5. 6. 7. 10. Quas causas ex Bonfrerio, Menochio & Ains- vvortho collegit Polus h. 1.

## 4:25
v. 25. HYACINTHINE COVERING. The Hebrews here have מכסה which is usually translated as κάλυμμα, that is, a covering. But the ancient Codices had מסכך instead of מסך which is expanded, ἐπίσπαστον. And thus some Greek Codices from the Samaritan. Thus also the Hebrew Codices which we now have in Samaritan script.

Certain Greek Codices with the Samaritan, whether they are from the Greeks, as others not without reason judge, or those particular Greek Codices were interpolated from the Samaritan, cannot prejudice the consensus of the Hebrew Codices, nor is there any necessity here for which we are forced to say the Hebrew source is corrupted. If as often as the Samaritan, or even some Greeks disagree, the Hebrew source is to be judged to lie in a fault, what at last will remain uncorrupted, and what certainty and truth will be left in the Hebrew Truth? But thus in these and other places not only the Hebrew text but also the Vulgate consonant with it will be corrupted: which is against the Tridentine decree.

Latin:

Vers. 25. VELAMEN !JANTHINUM) Hebræi hic ha- bent מכסה quod κάλυμμα solet verti, id est opercu- lum. At vetusti Codices habuere מסכך pro מסך quod est expansum, ἐπίσπαστον. Et sic Græci quidam Codices ex Samaritano. Sic & quos nunc habemus Codices Hebræi Sa- maritana litera.

Græcorum Codices quidam cum Samarita- no, sive illi ex Græcis, ut alii non abs re censent, feu Græci illi particulares Codd. e Samaritano in- terpolati sint, non possunt præjudicare consensui Ebræorum Codicum, nec ulla hic necessitas, ob quamEbræum fontem corruptum dicere cogamur. Si toties, quoties Samaritanus, vel etiam Græci non- nulli discrepant, fons Ebræus in mendo cubare cen- seatur, quid tandem supererit incorruptum, & quæ- nam relinquetur in Ebraica Veritate certitudo & veritas? Sic vero in his aliisque locis non Ebræus tantum textus sed & vulgata illi consonans corrupta erit: quod est contra Tridentinum decretum.

## 4:32
v. 32. THEY SHALL RECEIVE BY NUMBER] Under inventory.

Tremellius rendered: You shall recount by name the instruments of the observation of their burden, that is, whatever you shall hand over to them to be carried or kept, have them listed one by one in an index and described, and commit them to them from the copy, as Junius has in this place.

PART II. DIRECTIVE.

Prescribing laws, both regarding persons to be observed concerning the holiness of the camps with respect to the unclean, whether bodily or spiritual uncleanness ch. 5, or singularly holy ones, such as the Nazirites and Priests ch. 6, and the princes of Israel offering ch. 7, and also the Levites to be consecrated ch. 8, and also regarding things, such as the Paschal solemnity and the departure ch. 9, and the silver trumpets ordered for that purpose ch. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 32. AD NUMERUM ACCIPIENT] Sub inven- tario.

Tremellius reddidit: Nominatim recensetote instrumenta observationis oneris eorum, id est, quæcunque illis deportanda servandave tradetis, ea sigillatim relata in indicem, descriptaque habetote, eisq; ex antigrapho committite, ut habet Junius h. l.

PARS II. ΔΙΑΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ.

Leges præscribens, tum qua personas de sanctimonia castrorum observanda re- spectu immundarum, qua immunditi- em corporalem vel spiritualem cap. 5. vel singulariter sanctarum, utpote Nazi- ræorum & Sacerdotum c. 6. & principum Israelis offerentium c. 7. nec non Levita- rum consecrandorum c. 8. tum qua res, ut- pote solemnitatem Paschalem & profectio- nem c. 9. & tubas ideo ordinatas argen- teas c. 10.

## 4:44 Addition
To vers. 44. THREE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED.

Thus, out of 6200 Merarites (Num. 3:34), more than half were robust and fit for this ministry: in which the singular Providence of GOD shines forth, because the greatest burdens were to be imposed upon them, as Ainsworth observes.

Latin:

Ad vers. 44. TRIA MILLIA DU- CENTI.

Ita ex 6200. Meraritis Num. 3, 34. plus quam pars dimidia robusti erant, & apti ad hoc ministe- rium: in quo singularis DEI elucet Providentia, quia his maxima onera imponenda essent, obser- vante Ainsvvortho.

## 4:47 Addition
To vers. 47. FOR THE SERVICE OF THE TABERNACLE AND TO CARRY THE BURDENS.

Chap. 6. v. 18. p. 515. a. after our notes.

Regarding the opinion of Cyril, however, to which Fagius and Oleaster accede, it must be noted that it is more likely that the demon transferred this rite to his own sacred rites, which we have observed more than once regarding others. For it is not sufficiently established that that rite prevailed among the Gentiles before Moses.

In Hebrew: to serve the service of service, and the service of the burden. These were the two kinds of Levite ministry: namely, serving the Priests in the erected Tabernacle, and when it was necessary to set out, carrying the same.

Latin:

Ad vers. 47. AD MINISTERIUM TABER- NACULI ET ONERA POR- TANDA.

Cap. 6. v. 18. p. 515. a. post notas nostras.

De sententia tamen Cyrilli, cui accedit Fagius & Oleastr. id monendum, verisimilius esse dæmo- nem hunc ritum ad sua sacra transtulisse, quod non semel de aliis observavimus. Non enim satis con- stat, ritum illum ante Mosen obtinuisse penes gen- tiles.

In Ebræo: ad servire servitutem servitii, & ser- vitutem oneris. Duo hæc erant Levitarum mini- sterii genera : nempe serviendi Sacerdotibus in Ta- bernaculo erecto, & quum proficiscendum esset, deportandi idipsum.

## 5:2
Ver. 2. THEY SHALL CAST OUT OF THE CAMP EVERY LEPER.

The leper was exiled from the camp along with the one having an issue, until they were healed, and were received back following a purification according to Lev. 14, 15, yet without the sacrifices, which were not performed in the desert, Am. 5, 25; Acts 7, 42. Those defiled by a dead body purified themselves for certain days, and after the seventh day, without any other ceremony, they returned to the camp. We are taught that the wicked, who are truly unclean, must be cast out of the Church by excommunication until they perform penance. Isidore: Lepers, heretics, those unstable in thought, unclean in deed, are to be separated from the camp of the Church as if defiled and diseased, lest by the contagion of their morals they pollute the life of the innocent.

Latin:

Vers. 2. EJICIENT DE CASTRIS OMNEM LEPROSUM.

LEprosus a castris exulabat cum feminifluo, donec sanarentur, & prævia lustratione juxta Lev. 14, 15. sine tamen sacrificiis, quæ non fiebant in deserto Am. 5, 25. Act. 7, 42. reciperentur. Polluti super mor- tuo certis diebus se lustrabant, & post septimum di- em, sine alia ceremonia ad castra redibant. Doce- mur, ex Ecclesia sceleratos, qui vere immundi sunt, ejiciendos esse, per excommunicationem, donec pœnitentiam agant. Isidorus: Leprosi, hæretici, flu- xi cogitatione, immundi opere, ut tanquam coinquinati & morbidi a castris Ecclesiæ separentur, ne cogitatione morum suorum vitam polluant innocentium.

## 5:2 Addition
To chap. 5, 2. near the end of the annotation, p. 512. b.

Just as soldiers, having heard the trumpet, would rise for the departure, so this Prayer excited GOD, that He might arise and set out with them, and deign to be present with them everywhere by His gracious presence, cf. Ps. 3, 8. Ps. 7, 7. Ps. 10, 12. Ps. 35, 2. Ps. 74, 22. Ps. 82, 5. Therefore the name of Jehovah is not attributed to the ark as the Socinians and Drusius in Os. p. 74 wish. But Moses addresses GOD Himself, sitting above the Cherubim of that ark 1. Sam. 4, 4. 1. Par. 13, 6. Exod. 25, 22. chap. 20, 24. Deut. 12, 5. For it is 1. a prayer. But God alone is worshipped. 2. directed to Him who rises and returns: which is attributed to God by anthropopathy Gen. 18, 10. Ps. 87, 8. Isa. 2, 19. Hos. 5, 14. & c. 3. poured out then, when the ark was already setting out, or when it was already resting. But it would be absurd to say to one already setting out, arise: to one already resting, return. 4. It is requested that the enemies be scattered, which only God can perform Ps. 18, 7. Add here the Prophetic explanation of Ps. 132, 7. Arise O Lord: you and the ark of your sanctification. To arise signifies to exercise power, to declare His presence by the very act. To return is to become propitious, and as it were to take care as a head of a household in the house of his own. But who would attribute these things to the ark?

Lyranus, Munsterus, Fagius, and Vatablus rightly observe here from R. Solomon that there were three camps: namely, the camp of GOD, the camp of the Levites, and the camp of Israel. Lepers were kept away from all, the impure through a flux were excluded from the first two: but one polluted on account of a corpse was kept away only from the tabernacle of the Church.

Latin:

Ad cap. 5, 2. sub finem annot. p. 512. b.

Ut milites audita tuba surgebant ad profe- ctionem, ita DEUM excitabat hæc Oratio, ut exur- geret, & cum iisdem proficisceretur, ac gratiosa præsentia ubique ipsis adesse dignaretur, conf. Psal. 3, 8. Psalm. 7, 7. Ps. 10, 12. Ps. 35, 2. Ps. 74, 22. Ps. 82, 5. Non ergo arcæ tribuitur Jehovæ nomen uti volunt Sociniani, & Drusius in Os. p. 74. Sed Moses allo- quitur ipsum DEUM, super Cherubim illius arcæ sedentem 1. Sam. 4, 4. 1. Par. 13, 6. Exod. 25, 22. cap. 20, 24. Deuteronom. 12, 5. Est enim 1. precatio. At so- lus Deus adoratur. 2. ad eum directa, qui surgit & revertitur: quod Deo per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν tribui- tur Genes. 18, 10. Psal. 87, 8. Esa. 2, 19. Os. 5, 14. & c. 3. fusa tunc, quando jam proficiscebatur arca, aut quando jam quiescebat. At inepte diceretur jam proficiscenti, surge: jam quiescenti redi. 4. Pe- titur ut dispergantur inimici, quod nonnisi Deus præ- stare potest Psalm. 18, 7. Adde hic explicationem Propheticam Psalm. 132, 7. Surge Domine: tu & arca sanctificationis tuæ. Surgere significat potentiam exercere, ipso facto declarare præsentiam suam. Reverti est propitium fieri, ac velut Patremfamilias in domo suorum curam gerere. Hæc autem quis tribuet arcæ?

Recte autem hic observat e R. Salom. Lyra- nus, Munsterus, Fagius, Vatablus, tria fuisse castra: Castra nempe DEI, castra Levitarum, & castra Israel. Leprosi ab omnibus arcebantur, impuri per fluxum a primis duobus excludebantur : pol- lutus vero propter cadaver solum a tabernaculo Ecclesiæ arcebatur.

## 5:3
Ver. 3. WHEN I HAVE DWELT AMONG YOU) LXX. ἐν ὇ῖς ἐγὼ καταγίνομαι ἐν αὐτοῖς. In the Hebrew word for word: in whose midst I, where for I, the Chaldean placed שכינתי, my tabernacling. This word signifies the special and permanent care of God.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CVM HABITAVERIM VOBISCUM) LXX. ἐν ὇ῖς ἐγὼ καταγίνομαι ἐν αὐτοῖς. In Hebræo ad verbum: in quorum medio ego, ubi pro ego, Chaldæus posuit שכינתי, ἡ ἐμὴ σκήνωσις. Significat hæc vox curam Dei specialem & permanentem.

## 5:6
Ver. 6. CONCERNING ALL THE SINS WHICH ARE WONT TO HAPPEN TO MEN) LXX. τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων. The Chaldean understood it as concerning a lie: in the way the word מעל is often wont to be taken. Nor does the Chaldean take it so only here, but also in Josh. 22, 20; Ezekiel 17, 20. Understand, however, a sworn lie: for in theft and robbery the simple amount was restored. But if the sin were in sacred things, a fifth part was added: Lev. 5, v. 15; and an oath is a sacred thing.

Latin:

Vers. 6. EX OMNIBUS PECCATIS QVÆ SOLENT HOMINIBUS ACCIDERE) LXX. τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῶν ἀν- θρωπίνων. Chaldæus de mendacio intellexit: quomodo sæ- pe vox מעל sumi solet. Neque hic tantum Chaldæus sic sumit, sed & Jos. 22, 20. Ezechielis 17, 20. Intellige autem mendacium juratum: nam in furto & rapina simplum resti- tuebatur. Si autem in sacris peccatum esset, accedebat quin- ta: Lev. 5. v. 15. juramentum autem res sacra est.

## 5:6 Addition
To v. 6. to the note of Grotius. In the same place.

The subject here is offenses or injuries against a neighbor, committed by fraudulently and knowingly usurping his property, as is sufficiently clear from v. 7 and 8. Cf. Lev. 6, 2. where this law is explained more plainly. The sense is: whoever has stolen something, or extorted it by force, and has returned it of his own accord, shall not be compelled, except to simple restitution. But if he has sworn falsely, and has been convicted that he took the thing, he shall restore the thing, and add a fifth part, because he perjured himself: as Munsterus and Fagius have noted.

Latin:

Ad v. 6. ad notam Grotii. Ibidem.

Agitur hic de delictis sive injuriis in proxi- mum, res ejus fraudulenter & scienter usurpando commissis, ut satis patet ex v. 7. & 8. Conf. Levit. 6, 2. ubi hæc lex planius explicatur. Sensus est: qui aliquid furripuerit, aut vi extorserit, & sua sponte id reddiderit, non cogetur, nisi ad sim- plicem restitutionem. Quod si falso juraverit, & convictus fuerit, quod rem abstulit, restituet rem, & quintam partem addet, quia pejeravit: ut Mün- sterus & Fagius notarunt.

## 5:7
CHAPTER V. The removal of the unclean, offerings, and the law of jealousy.

Latin:

CAPUT V. Immundorum remotio, oblationes & lex zelo- typiæ.

## 5:7
Ver. 7. THEY SHALL CONFESS THEIR SIN.

The Papists gain nothing from this for the specific confession of sins. For it is not a question here of the enumeration of all and individual sins and all circumstances. However, that we can confess some sins that torment the conscience, no one doubts.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CONFITEBUNTUR PECCATUM SUUM.

Nihil inde lucrantur Pontificii pro confessio- ne specifica peccatorum. Non enim agitur hîc de enumeratione omnium & singulorum peccato- rum omniumq; circumstantiarum. Nonnulla au- tem peccata, conscientiam torquentia confiteri nos posse, nemo ambigit.

## 5:8
Vers. 8. BUT IF THERE BE NO ONE TO RECEIVE) In Hebrew: If there be no kinsman to whom it may be restored: that is, if neither he who suffered the loss is alive, nor does he have heirs: which is to be understood concerning proselytes: for an Israelite could not lack an heir. The Hebrews note here that the sin is not forgiven unless restitution has been made and pardon sought. It was wisely ordained, lest anyone by any chance profit from a crime.

Osiander rightly warns here: Those who today wish to return unjustly acquired goods should return them to those whom they defrauded, or to their kinsmen, or finally contribute them to the maintenance of the ministry and the poor. The ram of expiation looked toward the satisfaction of Christ, to which the warning of the Hebrews should be referred, that Israelites in these and other expiatory sacrifices, for example, when a ram was being led to death, ought to have prayed thus: O Lord, I am guilty of death, but because Thou dost not desire the death of a sinner, accept for me this ram, which I sacrifice to Thee.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SIN AUTEM NON FUERIT QVI RECI- PIAT) In Ebr. Si nullus sit propinquus, cui restituatur: id est, si nec is vivat qui damnum passus est, nec habeat heredes: quod intelligendum de proselytis]: nam Israëlitae heres de- esse non poterat. Notant hic Hebræi non dimitti peccatum, nisi restitutione facta, & petita venia. Provide autem con- stitutum, ne quis ullo casu quid ex delicto lucretur.

Merito hic monet Osiander: Qui hodie inju- ste acquisita reddere volent, reddant iis, quos de- fraudarunt, aut eorum propinquis, aut deniq; con- ferent ad conservationem ministerii & pauperum. Aries expiationis respiciebat satisfactionem Christi, quo referendum Ebræorum monitum, quod Israe- litæ in his & aliis sacrificiis expiatoriis v. c. cum ad mortem ducebatur aries, ita precari debuerint: O Domine ego sum reus mortis, verum quia non vis mor- tem peccatoris, accipe pro me hunc arietem, quem tibi immolo.

## 5:9 Addition
Verf. 9. ALL THE FIRST FRUITS.

In Hebrew, all things to be lifted, or every elevation: by elevation, however, he understands primarily the firstfruits, and besides these the breast and the shoulder of the peace offering, which also fell to the Priest, and which are not rarely called Theruma.

Latin:

Verf. 9. OMNES PRIMITIÆ.

In Ebr. omnes levandæ, vel omnis elevatio : per elevationem autem intelligit imprimis primitias, & præterea pectus & armum pacificum, quæ etiam Sacerdoti cedebant, quæque non raro vocantur Theruma.

## 5:10
v. 10. WHATEVER IS OFFERED INTO THE SANCTUARY BY INDIVIDUALS AND IS HANDED TO THE HANDS OF THE PRIEST, SHALL BE HIS. Cornelius rightly corrects the Vulgate here. For the Hebrew words are thus: whatever each one has sanctified (to the Lord) shall be his (it shall be in the power of the offerer, so that what he sanctifies, he may give to the priest, to whomever he wishes) and whatever is handed in this way to the hands of the Priest, shall be his, to whom it was handed by the offerer, as observed by Osiander. Not everything that was brought into the sanctuary or tabernacle was the Priest's. For some things were given into the treasury, indeed even into the hands of the Priests for the use of the temple or tabernacle, which certainly did not fall to the Priest for his own uses.

Latin:

v. 10. QUICQUID IN SANCTUARIUM OF- FERTUR A SINGULIS ET TRADITUR MA- NIBUS SACERDOTIS, IPSIUS ERIT. Corrigit hic merito Vulgatam Cornelius. Nam Ebræa ita habent: quod quisq́; sanctificaverit (Domi- no) suum erit (in potestate erit offerentis, ut id quod sanctificat, det sacerdoti, cuicunq; voluerit) & quic- quid hoc modo traditur manibus Sacerdotis, ipsius erit, cui ab offerente est traditum, ut observatum O- siandro. Non omne quod in sanctuarium vel ta- bernaculum afferebatur, Sacerdotis erat. Nam- da bantur aliqua in gazophylacium, imo etiam in ma- nus Sacerdotum ad usum templi, vel tabernaculi, quæ Sacerdoti utique in usus ejus non cedebant.

## 5:12
Vers. 12. IF THE WIFE HAS GONE ASTRAY) Namely, she who for some time has been alone with a man not her husband.

Latin:

Vers. 12. UXOR ERRAVERIT) Quæ scilicet tempore ali- quanto cum viro non suo sola fuerit.

## 5:13
AND HAS SLEPT) For, or has slept: that is, where there is either suspicion or crime.

Latin:

ET DORMIERIT) Pro, vel dormierit: id est, ubi vel su- spicio est, vel crimen.

## 5:15
NOR SHALL HE PUT FRANKINCENSE UPON IT) As in mourning. Thus also oil and frankincense were absent from every sacrifice for sin. Leviticus 5, verse 11.

The mystical significance is not to be neglected: For since oil signifies the Holy Spirit, and frankincense prayers: God does not wish oil and frankincense to be applied, warning that those who are polluted by such shameful acts, before they perform penance, neither have the Holy Spirit nor can they pray rightly, even if they perform external divine worship, as others do. As Osiander observed in this place. Furthermore, that law of jealousy provided for the safety of spouses, so that it would not be lawful for a husband, because of blind suspicions, to rage against his wife at his own whim, and it also warned about the preservation of chastity, since God wished adulteries to be punished most severely, and finally about the jealousy of God against the spiritual adultery of the worship of idols. Concerning this law and the circumstances of its process, see the discussion here at length by Dr. Varenius.

Latin:

NEC IMPONET THUS) Vt in mœrore. Sic & ab omni sacrificio pro peccato aberant oleum & thus. Levitici 5. vers. 11.

Non negligenda significatio mystica: Quùm enim oleum Spiritum Sanctum significet, & thus pre- ces: non vult Deus adhiberi oleum & thus, admo- nens, quod qui talibus flagitiis polluti sunt, prius- quam pœnitentiam agant, nec Spiritum Sanctum ha- beant, nec rite orare possint, etiam si externos cultus divinos exerceant, ut alii. Uti observavit Osiander in h.l. Cæterum lex illa Zelotypias tum incolu- mitati conjugum consulebat, ne marito liceret, pro- pter cæcas suspiciones pro suo arbitratu in uxorem sævire, tum vero monebat de castitatis conservatio- ne, quum Deus gravissime punita voluerit adulte- ria, denique de zelotypia Dei adversus spirituale ad- ulterium idolorum cultum. De hac lege & circum- stantiis ejusdem processus vid. hic prolixe agens Dn. D. Varenius.

## 5:16
Vers. 16. HE SHALL NOT POUR OIL UPON HER) As it is an aid to beauty.

Latin:

Vers. 16. NON FUNDET SUPER EAM OLEUM) Quippe formæ adminiculum.

## 5:17
Vers. 17. AND HE SHALL TAKE HOLY WATER) We ought not to be surprised if God, among His own people, in a crime of the most serious nature and of the most difficult proof, brought about something miraculous, when similar things appeared also among other nations, which for the most part lived innocently. Polemon in his book on the wonders of Sicily, where he speaks of the craters of the Palici: they receive a tablet having a declaration for those swearing concerning what they demand the oath. And the one swearing, brandishing a branch, holy, pure, and wearing a single tunic, touching the crater, recites the oath from a dictation, and if he confirms the stated oaths, he departs home unharmed. But the transgressor of the gods dies on the spot. In the wonders which circulate under the name of Aristotle, we read the same thing about the matter: there is also an oath which is thought to be holy there; for whatever one swears,

τις, γράψας εἰς πινακίδιον, ἐμβάλλει εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ· καὶ μὲν εὐ- ένορκῇ, ἐπιπολάζει τὸ πινακίδιον. ἐὰν δὲ μὴ εὐορκῇ, τὸ μὲν πι- νακίδιον βαρὺ γενόμενον, ἀφανίζεσθαί φασι, τὸν δὲ αἴθραπον πίμ- πρασθαι. Add Diodorus Siculus in book 2. Pliny has a similar account, though elsewhere, in book 31, chapter 2. The river Olachas in Bithynia washes Briatium: this is the name of both the Temple and the God, in whose whirlpool those who swear falsely are said to suffer as if from a burning flame. Porphyry, in his book on that subject, reported the same regarding the Styx: οἱ πάντες δὲ ὕδωρ ἰσόρησαν τὴν Στύγα ἐπίγειον, φύσιν ἔχον ἀμύνεσθαι τὺς κατʼ αὐτᾶ ψευδῶς ὀμόσαι τολμήσαντας. Solinus on the springs of ancient Sardinia: They are effective for convicting thieves: for whoever denies a theft involving an oath touches his eyes with the waters; where there is no perjury, he sees more clearly: if perfidy denies it, the crime is uncovered by blindness, and, deprived of sight, he confesses his misdeed in darkness. Achilles Statius imitated these true things in his fables in book 7, chapter 20, and Eustathius in books 7 and 11.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ASSVMETQVE AQVAM SANCTAM) Mi- rari non debemus si Deus in suo populo in gravissimo & dif- ficillimæ probationis crimine miri aliquid effecerit, cum & apud alias gentes, quæ ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον innocenter vivebant, similia apparuerint. Polemon in libro de miris Siciliæ, ubi de crateribus Palicorum: οἱ δὲ δέχονται γραμμάτιον ἔχοντες ἀγορευσιν τοῖς ὁρκυμένοις περὶ ὧν ἀπαιτῦσι τὸν ὅρκον. ὁ δὲ ὁρκύμενος θαλλὸν κραδαίνων, ἐσέμμενο͂, ἅζωτο͂, καὶ μονοχί- των, ἐφαπτόμενο͂ τῦ κρατῆρο͂ ἐξ ὑποβολῆς διεῖσι τὸν ὅρκον, καὶ ἂν μὲν ἐμπεδώσει τὺς ῥηθέντας ὅρκυς, ἀσίνης ἄπεισιν ὄικαδε. πα- ραβάτης δὲ γενόμενο͂ τῶν θεῶν ἐμποδὼν τελευτᾷ. In mirabili- bus quæ Aristotelis nomen circumferunt, eadem de re sic legi- mus: ἔσι δὲ καὶ ὅρκο͂ ὃς ἅγιο͂ ἀυτὸθι δοκεῖ εἶναι· ὅσα γὰρ ὄμνυσι

τις, γράψας εἰς πινακίδιον, ἐμβάλλει εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ· καὶ μὲν εὐ- ένορκῇ, ἐπιπολάζει τὸ πινακίδιον. ἐὰν δὲ μὴ εὐορκῇ, τὸ μὲν πι- νακίδιον βαρὺ γενόμενον,ἀφανίζεσθαί φασι, τὸν δὲ αἴθραπον πίμ- πρασθαι. Adde Diodorum Siculum libro 2. Simile sed alibi habet Plinius libro 31. cap. 2. Amnis Olachas in Bithynia Bria- tium alluit: hoc est & Templo & Deo nomen, cujus gurgite per- juri notantur pati velut flammam urentem. Porphyrius de Styge idem prodidit libro ejus argumenti: οἱ πάντες δὲ ὕδωρ ἰσόρησαν τὴν Στύγα ἐπίγειον, φύσιν ἔχον ἀμύνεσθαι τὺς κατʼ αὐτᾶ ψευδῶς ὀμόσαι τολμήσαντας. Solinus de veteris Sar- diniæ fontibus: Coarguendis valent furibus: nam quisquis Sacramentoraptum negat, lumina aquis attrectat: ubi perju- rium non est, cernit clarius: Si perfidia abnuit, detegitur faci- nus cæcitate, & captus oculis admissum tenebris fatetur. Imi- tati hæc vera in fabulis suis Achilles Statius libro 7. cap. 20. & Eustathius lib. 7. & 11.

Vers. 3. THEY SHALL ABSTAIN FROM WINE AND EVERYTHING THAT CAN INTOXICATE) Plutarch reported in Symposiacs 4 that what was votive was penal.

## 6:5
CHAPTER VI.

The Nazariteship, and ecclesiastical blessing.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Nazaræatus, & benedictio Ecclesiastica.

## 6:5
Vers. 5. NO RAZOR SHALL PASS OVER HIS HEAD) To grow the hair is a sign of a vow. Tacitus in Germania called the habit of the mouth votive and bound to virtue. The reason for the similarity is in the fact that long hair is a burden: so also is a vow. Thus also ropes are signs of a vow, because both bind.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NOVACULA NON TRANSIBIT PER CA- PUT EJUS) Comam alere voti signum. Votivum obliga- tumque virtuti oris habitum dixit Tacitus in Germania. Ra- tio similitudinis in eo, quod coma longa onus est: sic & vo- tum. Ita & funes voti signa, quia utrumque ligat.

## 6:7
Vers. 7. HE SHALL NOT BE DEFILED EVEN UPON THE DEATH OF HIS FATHER, AND MOTHER, AND BROTHER, AND SISTER) Clearly like the High Priest, to whom the Nazarite is equal during the time of his purity.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NE SUPER PATRIS QUIDEM, ET MA- TRIS ET FRATRIS SORORISQVE FVNERE CON- TAMINABITVR) Plane ut Pontifex maximus, cui Nazaræus tempore castus sui æquatur.

## 6:8
Vers. 8. ALL THE DAYS OF HIS SEPARATION HE SHALL BE HOLY TO THE LORD) So that if any pollution had intervened, the votive days were to be repeated.

Latin:

Vers. 8. OMNIBUS DIEBUS SEPARATIONIS SUÆ SANCTUS ERIT DOMINO) Ita ut si qua intervenisset pollutio, repetendi essent votivi dies.

## 6:18
Vers. 18. THEN THE NAZARITE SHALL BE SHAVED BEFORE THE DOOR OF THE TABERNACLE) While the Temple was standing and while living in Palestine, the vow had to be completed in the Temple, as Paul did in Acts 21:26. The vows of Samson and John the Baptist were of another kind, perpetual, by a singular command, yet drawing many things from the Nazariteship.

AND TAKE HIS HAIR AND PUT IT UPON THE FIRE) The Greeks also used to consecrate hair to the gods, as Achilles did to Spercheius: Earinus to Aesculapius, others to others, about whom the poets are to be consulted.

Concerning the vow of the Nazariteship: (1) we observe the word: which signifies one separated from others, either by religion or a singular vow or by dignity and a crown or kingdom. (2) This discourse is about the votive Nazariteship: which, since it was twofold, temporary, such as Paul's was in Acts 21, verse 25, and perpetual, such as Samson's in Judges 13, verse 7, here it treats of the temporary one, when someone for a time separated himself from the common life of men, and abstained from wine and strong drink, and nourished his hair, so that by this sign he might show that he was separated from the cultivation of the body and other delights. In wine luxury is prohibited, in strong drink every earthly pleasure. For strong drink is made from a diverse kind: thus pleasure arises from a diverse passion of vices; for those men drink wine and strong drink who, in order to deceive men, pretend to have certain shadows and images of virtues; they eat raisins, so that they may take glory from men. But those men drink vinegar who, after the holiness of life, slip into the filth of past vices and are delighted by the corruption of old wickedness. Then they are commanded to nourish their hair and keep the locks of their head unshorn: for which thing there is a twofold reason: the one because of the mystery, that while the hair was being nourished, it might be signified that virtues also were to be increased. Gregor. lib. 2. Mor. cap. 26. the other, that it might turn those who had been led away from errors and the superstitions of the Egyptians to better things. (For thus Cyril: The most foolish nation of the Gentiles, he says, following their own customs, and living after the manner of dumb animals, they offered their hair to demons, permitting it to be nourished (ἀνίησαν κόμην δαιμονίοις ἀυτὸν σκη- πτόμενοι τρέφειν ατῷ, sometimes indeed they offered it to Nymphs, whom they called Oreads, sometimes to a river, when it seemed good, καὶ λατρείας ἦν τρόπῷ τὸ χρῆμα ἀυτοῖς, which thing was held by them as a religion. Moses therefore, most wise, or rather God through Moses, when he understood that the Hebrews could not easily lay aside the errors which they had imbibed in Egypt, decided to institute similar rites. Gradually separating them from their ancient errors: by which rites they might worship not demons any longer, but God omnipotent, as if under a shadow and figure, or also, that he might warn that excessive cultivation of the body ought to be alien, for the tonsure has some degree of neatness 1. Cor. 11.) (3) It was the law that one should not enter over a dead person, where the Hebrews observe that defilement is incurred over a dead person in three ways, (1) when a corpse or even bones found in a field are touched, (2) when one has gone to a funeral, or into a house in which a dead person lies, or one who is breathing his last, (3) if one touches any of his vessels Num. 19, 10.

(4) As regards its use, this rite did not merit the remission of sins, nor did it appease the wrath of God, but it was (1) an exercise of temperance, (2) a preparation for meditation and devotion, (3) a confession of the faith of Israel, to whom this rite had been delivered, (4) a type of Christ, who is the chief Nazarite not by letter or ceremonies, because he drank wine, but by spirit, namely, separated from the human race, and consecrated and clean from all sin, and in whom there is nothing that is not holy, so that through him all may be sanctified. Whom the other Nazarites, especially Samuel 1 Sam. 1 and Samson, signified.

(5) The abuse of the Papists: who strive to establish their monastic vows from these vows, such as Seb. Barrad., Corn. a Lap., and others. Cornelius compares his religious, who are by no means religious, with the Nazarites (1) by reason of their profession and separation from the common life of men, but the thing itself speaks that that separation is rather a twin to the sect of the Pharisees than to the institution of the Nazarites. If impure celibacy, feigned poverty, and blind obedience testify to a Nazariteship, then indeed the vow of the Monks will truly be a Nazariteship. Concerning almost all of them it is true, as Cornelius does not deny, what Prosper says in de vit. contemplativ.: they live secularly in religion, they seek the opinion of virtue instead of virtue, they preach great things and do not do them, they accuse vices and do not lay them aside, they pretend to be displeased with themselves publicly for what they commit secretly. And what, I ask, was the analogy of the monastic life with the vows of the Nazarites? The vows of the Nazarites were approved by God, but where is the fictitious religion of the Monks either holy or approved, which cannot but greatly displease God? Because it places a state of perfection in human traditions, and in indifferent things seeks the worship of God, the remission of sins, and the merit of eternal life, and impiously detracts from the satisfaction and merit of Christ. Furthermore, in the vows of the Nazarites, all things were contrary to the monastic profession. For they lived in marriage, and had their own possessions, nor were they bound to the obedience of any Abbot or Prior, nor were they Hermits or Cenobites, as the Monks are, but they lived in the midst of the people. Moreover, the Pontifical Monks correspond neither to the native Nazarites nor to the votive ones. Not to the former, because they are not such by divine edict, nor by the legitimate naming of parents, and approved by God; indeed, sons often put on the cowl against the will of their parents. Not to the latter, because their profession was temporary, the Monks' is perpetual. The θρησκεία of the Nazarites was restrained within a few institutions; they were to nourish their hair, to avoid the vine and what comes from the vine, and to abstain from contact with corpses. The πολιτεία of the Monks is occupied not only about innumerable things, but also about all other things, and in studies that are entirely contrary. Tonsure is among the laws of Monasticism, although it is contrary to the prohibition which is in Lev. 21, 5. The gain from corpses and their preparation and burial is huge, the use of grapes and wine is most free, which monastic families have not yet forbidden to themselves. The Nazarites were sacred to God alone, the Monks to men, whose rules they profess, whom they venerate as patrons, indeed even as tutelary deities, from whom they borrow their name, institutions, way of life, dress, badge, and other things of that kind, to whom they dedicate their life, studies, worship, and indeed themselves as if they were slaves. Hence so many families, and families not only different, but also adverse, and utterly at odds with one another by contrary studies, whose rivalries, quarrels, contentions, and dissensions are known to the world. There is hardly a number for those who do not do this one thing.

(2) By reason of abstinence from wine and grapes, because they ought to abstain not only from wine, but from everything that could disturb or defile the mind, and provide even a remote occasion for gluttony and other sins. But Cornelius speaks cautiously about the obligation. For he did not dare to affirm that they actually abstain. Nowhere, however, is abstinence from wine commanded; indeed, the Apostle ordered Timothy, who was not a little more religious than the impure order of Monks, to drink wine for the sake of his health.

(3) By reason of the prohibition of mourning, because they ought to cut off affections toward parents. But just as abstinence from wicked desires, so also the mortification of wicked affections is commanded not to Monks, whom Scripture does not know, but to all Christians, Gal. 5, 16. 24. Col. 3, 5. seqq. Eph. 4, 22. We shall grant them, however, with Pelargus, that glorious title of the Nazarite sectaries, of whom Philastrius says: The heresy of the Nazarites is that which receives the law and the Prophets, yet affirms that one must live carnally, and suspects that all justification consists in carnal observance: of whom also Epiph. Tom. I. These modern Nazarites say the same: they observe circumcision and the Sabbath: these observe traditions and innumerable rites. They acknowledge Moses, and that he received the law from God: But they say the books of the law are forged and fictitious: These acknowledge the scripture to be sacred: But meanwhile they proclaim it imperfect, obscure, and mutilated, and appeal to another unwritten word. Concerning them also St. Jerome, tom. 2: While they wish to be Jews and Christians, they are neither religious nor Christians; of these also it will be rightly said: while they wish to be Jesuits and Christians, they are neither Jesuits nor Christians, but Esauites, but Jebusites. Laonicus Chalcondytes also noted in book 7, Ναζηραίες, a certain kind of monks or ἱερέων among the Turks, which seems to have proceeded likewise from the κακοζηλίᾳ of the ancient Nazarites. Whether the Jesuits themselves wish to be referred to their census, let them see; it is confessed that the vows of the Nazarites pertained to the legal pedagogy, and that there was no place for them except while the tabernacle and temple were standing. If those things still obtain today, then the cleansings which Moses prescribed in this place, and the offerings of the Levitical sacrifices, will have to be instituted according to the tenor of the divine law, which no one would say, for the temple has been destroyed, the sacrifices have ceased, the Jewish Synagogue has been buried, and those old institutions ought no more to be restored through monasticism than through other Levitical ceremonies, which today are not only dead, but deadly, not only empty, but also pernicious.

Although indeed Paul in Acts 21 still made such a vow of the ancient Nazariteship, yet it was both singular, and done by the counsel of James the Bishop of Jerusalem, in order to appease the weak Jews, who had embraced the Gospel, but still clung to Mosaic rites, and it was done while the Jewish Synagogue was not yet fully buried, which in any case had to be buried with honor.

(5) Regarding the Ecclesiastical tonsure. Cornelius says that its use was taken from the Nazarites, and that by that sign they warn that vices must be cut away and that they ought to be stripped of the crimes of the flesh, as if of hair, as Isidore testifies in De divinis officiis; nay, and in memory of the crown of thorns of Christ, monks are to be shorn into a crown in this way, as Bede testifies in book 5 of the History of the English, chapter 22. Finally, the shaving of the head is a warning and a symbol of one who is mourning and grieving, and also of one who is chaste and adorned with the ornament of modesty, as well as one who despises earthly things and meditates on heavenly ones. But these things are not proper to monks, but belong to all the faithful: to cut away vices, to carry about the memory of the passion of Christ, to mourn for sins and scandals, to study chastity, to despise earthly things, to meditate on heavenly ones: And that monks excel in these things above others will be taught at the Greek Calends. Nor is the tonsure, which they make the sign of these things, only for monks, but for any clerics whatsoever. But to the Nazarites, whom they wish to be the image of monks, the tonsure did not belong, but long hair. The Nazarite sanctification consisted mostly in the nourishing of long hair, as Cornelius says; cutting and shaving had a place when they were defiled, which could happen from the mere presence of a corpse, or if someone died in their presence, because they had to be immune from all contamination, whence they were defiled, whether by chance some corpse or bones had fallen upon them, or they themselves had been brought by chance into the house of one dead or dying, so that it might be noted that they ought to be most remote from all sin (of which a corpse was an image), even casual and surreptitious, and even another's; therefore on the same day on which he became defiled, the head had to be shaved, and thus the purification had to be done for seven continuous days according to the prescription of the law, and on the seventh day the head had to be shaved again (although the Hebrews and Vatablus think that this shaving ought to have been done only on this seventh day, and not likewise on the first); and that institution concerned only temporary Nazarites. For the heads of perpetual Nazarites were never shaved, however they were defiled. For all things prescribed in this chapter, as Cornelius says, only concern the Nazarite who is such for a certain time, as is evident in verses 4, 5, 6, 13, 18. What then do these things have to do with perpetual monks, who always wear a shaved and shorn head, and do not nourish long hair like the Nazarites? What does that tonsure of the monks, which they institute for the sake of religion, have in common with the shaving of the head, which had to be done on account of defilement by temporary Nazarites? But enough of these.

Latin:

Vers. 18. TVNC RADETUR NAZARÆUS ANTE OSTIVM TABERNACULI) Stante Templo & in Palæsti- na viventibus, in Templo complendum erat votum, ut fecit Paulus Actor. 21. vers. 26. Samsonis & Joannis Baptistæ vota alterius erant generis, perpetua, ex præcepto singulari, multa tamen trahentes a Nazaræatu.

TOLLEQVE CAPILLOS EJUS ET PONET SUPER IGNEM) Etiam Græci comas diis sacrabanr, ut Achilles Sperchio: Earinus Æsculapio, alii aliis, de quibus videndi Poëtæ.

Circa votum Nazaræatus: (1) vocem observa- mus: quæ significat separatum ab aliis, vel reli- gione aut voto singulari vel dignitate & corona seu regno. (2) De Nazaræatu votivo hic sermo est: qui quum duplex fuerit, temporarius, qualis Pauli erat Act. 21. vers. 25. & perpetuus, qualis Samsonis Jud. 13. v. 7. hic de temporario agitur, cum quis ad tem- pus separabat sese a communi hominum vita, & a vino & sicera abstinebat, ac crines alebat, ut hoc signo ostenderet se a cultu corporis, aliisque deli- ciis separatum esse. In vino luxuria prohibetur, in sicera omnis voluptas terrena. Sicera enim ex diverso conficitur genere: Sic voluptas ex diversa oritur vitiorum passione; Illi enim vinum, & sice- ram bibunt, qui ad decipiendos homines umbras quasdam & imagines simulant habere virtutum; uva passa illi vescuntur, ut gloriam capiant ab homi- nibus. Acetum autem hi bibunt, qui post vitæ san- ctitatem in sordes præteritorum vitiorum labuntur, & corruptione veteris nequitiæ delectantur. Dein- de comam nutrire crinesque capitis intonsos serva- re jubentur: cujus rei duplex ratio: altera pro- pter mysterium, ut dum coma aleretur, virtutes quo- que augendas esse significaretur. Gregor. lib. 2. Mor. cap. 26. altera, ut ab erroribus & Ægyptiorum su- perstitionibus abductos ad meliora converteret. (Ita enim Cyrillus: Gentilium, inquit, dementissima na- tio, suas consuetudines sequuti, mutarumque pecudum more viventes, offerebant comam dæmoniis, eam nutriri permittentes, (ἀνίησαν κόμην δαιμονίοις ἀυτὸν σκη- πτόμενοι τρέφειν ατῷ, alias quidem Nymphis, quas O- reades appellabant, alias fluvio, cum visum esset, offere- bant, καὶ λατρείας ἦν τρόπῷ τὸ χρῆμα ἀυτοῖς, quæ res ipsis pro religione habebatur. Moses itaq́; sapien- tissimus, imo vero Deus per Mosen, cum intelligeret, non facile Hebræos, quos in Ægypto errores imbibissent, de- ponere posse, similes ritus instituere decrevit. Sensim eos a priscis erroribus absjungens: quibus ritibus non dæmones ultra, sed Deum omnipotentem quasi sub um- bra & figura colerent, vel etiam, ut moneret, nimium corporis cultum oportere esse alienum, habet enim ali- quid nitoris tonsura 1. Cor. 11.) (3) Lex erat, ne super mortuum ingrederetur, ubi observant Ebræi, super mortuo tribus modis contaminationem fieri, (1) cum cadaver aut ossa etiam in agro reperta tangun- tur, (2) cum itum ad exequias, vel in domum, in qua mortuus jacet, aut animam agens, (3) si aliqua ejus vasa contingat Num. 19, 10.

(4) Usum ejus quod attinet, non merebatur hic ritus remissionem peccatorum, nec placabat iram Dei, sed erat (1) exercitium temperantiæ, (2) præpa- ratio ad meditationem & devotionem, (3) Confessio fidei Israelis, cui hic ritus traditus erat, (4) typus Christi, qui est præcipuus Nazaræus non litera, seu ceremo- niis, quia bibit vinum, sed spiritu, videl. segregatus ex genere humano, & consecratus ac mundus ab o- mni peccato, & in quo nihil non sanctum, ut pro- pter eum omnes sanctificentur. Quem cæteri Naza- ræi imprimis Samuel 1. Sam. 1. & Samson significa- runt.

(5) Abusum Papistarum: qui vota sua monasti- ca ab his votis stabilire satagunt, utpote Seb. Barrad. Corn. a Lap. & alii. Confert religiosos suos mini- me religiosos Cornelius cum Nazaræis (1) ratione professionis & separationis a communi hominum vi- ta, sed res ipsa loquitur separationem illam potius geminam esse Pharisæorum sectæ, quam Nazaræo- rum instituto. Si impurus cælibatus, paupertas si- mulata & obedientia cæca Nazaræatum testantur, sa- ne Monachorum votum vere erit Nazaræatus. De plerisq; omnibus verum est, non diffitente Corne- lio, quod ait Prosper de vit. contemplativ. in religio- ne seculariter vivunt, opinionem virtutis pro virtute quærunt, prædicant magna, nec faciunt, accusant vitia, nec deponunt, publice displicere sibi simulant, quod oc- culte committunt. Et quænam, obsecro, vitæ mo- nasticæ cum Nazaræorum votis analogia fuit? Na- zaræorum vota approbata erant a Deo, ubi vero vel sanctita, vel approbata Monachorum fictitia religio, quæ non potest non Deo maximopere displicere? Quia statum perfectionis in humanis traditionibus ponit, & in rebus adiaphoris cultum Dei, remissio- nem peccatorum, ac meritum æternæ vitæ quærit, Christi satisfactioni & merito impie detrahit. Porro in Nazaræorum votis Monasticæ professioni omnia contraria fuerunt. Illi enim in conjugio vivebant, & possessiones proprias habebant, nec ad obedien- tiam Abbatis, aut Prioris alicujus adstricti, nec vel Eremitæ vel Cænobitæ fuerunt, uti Monachi, sed in medio populi vivebant. Adhæc Monachi Pontificii neq; nativis Nazaræis respondent, nec votivis. Non illis, quia nec divino edicto tales sunt, neque nun- cupatione parentum legitima, Deoque probata, imo invitis parentibus sæpe filii cucullum induunt. Non his, quia ipsorum professio temporaria erat, Monachorum perpetua. Naziræorum θρησκεία coercebatur intra pauca instituta, illis coma erat alenda, vitis & quæ a vite vitanda, & a contactu cadaverum abstinendum. Monachorum πολιτεία non tantum circa innumera occupatur, sed & circa alia omnia, & in studiis contrariis prorsus. Tonsura inter Monachatus Leges est, quamvis contraria in- terdicto, quod Lev. 21, 5. Quæstus ex cadaveribus & illorum pollinctura & sepultura ingens, uvarum & vini usus liberrimus, quem familiæ monasticæ sibi nondum interdixere. Naziræi Deo soli sacri erant, Monachi hominibus, quorum regulas profitentur, quos patronos venerantur, imo velut tutelaria nu- mina, a quibus nomen, instituta, vitæ genus, vestem, tesseram, & aliud id genus mutuantur, quibus vita, studia, cultum, imo seipsos velut mancipia addi- cunt. Hinc tot familiæ, & familiæ non diversæ duntaxat, sed & adversæ, & δὶς διὰ πασῶν a se invi- cem contrariis studiis dissidentes, quarum æmula- tiones, rixæ, contentiones, dissidia orbi nota. Nu- merus vix illis, qui non hoc unum agunt.

(2) Ratione abstinentiæ a vino, & acinis, quod non a vino tantum, sed omni eo, quod mentem tur- bare vel inquinare, & vel remotam occasionem gu- læ aliisque peccatis præbare posset, abstinere debe- ant. Sed caute loquitur Cornelius de debito. Nam quod revera abstineant, affirmare ausus non fuit. Nullibi tamen præcepta est abstinentia a vino, imo Timotheum qui haud paulo religiosior fuit impuro Monachorum ordine, jussit Apostolus vinum vale- tudinis causa bibere.

(3) Ratione interdicti luctus, quod affectus er- ga parentes truncare debeant. Ast uti abstinentia a pravis cupiditatibus, ita & pravorum affectuum mortificatio non Monachis, quos ignorat Scriptura, sed omnibus Christianis demandata est, Gal. 5, 16. 24. Col. 3, 5. seqq. Eph. 4, 22. Largiemur tamen ipsis cum Pelargo gloriosum illud Nazaræorum sectariorum ti- tulum, de quibus Philastrius. Nazaræorum hære- sis est, quæ legem & Prophetas recipit, carnaliter tamen vivendum affirmat, omnemq; justificationem in carnali observantia consistere suspicatur: de quibus etiam E- piph. Tom. I. Dicunt idem Nazaræi isti hodierni: cir- cumcisionem illi observant & Sabbathum: hi tradi- tiones, ritusq; innumerabiles. Mosen illi confiten- tur, & quod legem a Deo acceperit: Sed libros legis fictos dicunt & commentitios: Hi scripturam confi- tentur, esse sacram: Sed interim imperfectam, ob- scuram, mutilamque clamitant & ad aliud verbum non scriptum provocant. De illis quoque D. Hie- ronymus tom. 2. Dum volunt Judæi esse, & Christia- ni, nec religiosi sunt, nec Christiani; de his etiam recte dicetur: dum volunt Jesuitæ esse, & Christiani, nec Jesuitæ sunt nec Christiani, sed Esauitæ, sed Jebusitæ. Notavit & Laonicus Chalcondytes l. 7. Ναζηραίες ge- nus quoddam Monachorum vel ἱερέων apud Tur- cas, quod ex κακοζηλίᾳ Veterum Nazaræorum iti- dem profectum videtur. Num in illorum censum referri velint Monachi, Jesuitæ ipsi viderint, id in confesso est, Nazaræorum vota ad legalem pædago- giam pertinuisse, nec locum istis, nisi stante taberna- culo & templo fuisse. Si hodie adhuc illa obti- nent, etiam mundationes, quas præscripsit Moses hoc loco, & oblationes sacrificiorum Leviticorum juxta divinæ legis tenorem instituendæ erunt, quod nemo dixerit, destructum enim est templum, cessa- runt sacrificia, sepulta est Synagoga Judaica, nec magis restitui debent per Monachatum illa vetera instituta, quam per alias Leviticas ceremonias, quæ hodie non mortuæ tantum sunt, sed mortiferæ, non inanes solum, sed & pernitiosæ.

Quanquam vero Paulus Act. 21. adhuc tale Nazaræatus veteris votum fecerit, tamen id & singulare fuit, & consilio Jacobi Episcopi Hierosolymitani factum, ut Judæos infirmos, qui amplexi erant Evangelium, sed adhuc Mosaicis ritibus inhærebant, placaret, & factum est Synagoga Judaica nondum plane sepulta, quæ utique cum honore sepelienda erat.

(5) Ratione tonsuræ Ecclesiasticæ. Ejus usum a Nazaræis cepisse dicit Cornelius, eoque signo monere, vitia resecanda esse & criminibus carnis, quasi crinibus exui eos oportere, teste Isidoro de div. offic. imo & in memoriam spineæ coronæ Christi sic in coronam attondendos esse Monachos, teste Beda l. 5. de gest. Angl. c. 22. Denique capitis abrasionem monitionem, & symbolum esse lugentis & mœrentis, nec non casti, & ornatu pudicitiæ exornati, ut & terrena contemnentis, & cœlestia meditantis. At hæc non Monachorum propria sunt, sed omnibus fidelibus competunt vitia resecare, memoriam passionis Christi circumferre, ob peccata & scandala lugere, castitati studere, terrena contemnere, cœlestia meditari: Et præ aliis in hisce eminere Monachos ad Calendas Græcas docebitur. Neque solum tonsura, quam horum signum faciunt, Monachorum est, sed clericorum quorumvis. Nazaræis vero, quos imaginem Monachorum esse volunt, tonsura non conveniebat, sed coma. Sanctificatio Nazaræa maxime sita erat in cæsarie alenda, dicente Cornelio, tonsio & rasio locum habebat, cum polluebantur, quod e sola præsentia cadaveris fieri poterat, vel si quis coram eis moreretur, quia immunes esse debebant ab omni contaminatione, unde polluebantur, sive in ipsos casu aliquod cadaver vel ossa incidissent, sive ipsi in domum mortui aut animam agentis fortuito delati essent, ut notaretur, ab omni peccato (cujus imago erat cadaver) etiam casuali & subreptitio, etiam alieno remotissimos eos esse oportere, ideo eadem die, qua pollutus fiebat, radendum erat caput, atq; ita purgatio fieri debuit continuis septem diebus juxta legis præscriptum, & septimo iterum radendum erat caput (etsi Ebræi & Vatablus solum hoc septimo, non item primo rationem fieri debuisse, censeant) atq; illud institutum tantum concernebat temporales Nazaræos. Perpetuis enim Nazaræis caput nunquam radebatur, quomodocunq; polluerentur. Omnia enim hoc capite præscripta, dicente Cornelio, tantum spectant Nazaræum, qui talis est ad certum tempus, ut patet v. 4. 5. 6. 13. 18. Quid ergo hæc ad Monachos perpetuos, perpetuo caput rasum & tonsum gerentes, non vero comam Nazaræorum instar alentes? Quid tonsura illa Monachorum, quam religionis causa instituunt, cum rasione capitis, quæ ob pollutionem fieri debebat penes Nazaræos temporarios, commercii habet? Sed hæc de istis.

## 6:21
Ver. 21. THIS IS THE LAW OF THE NAZARITE, WHEN HE SHALL HAVE VOWED HIS OBLATION TO THE LORD IN THE TIME OF HIS CONSECRATION.

The Hebrew is to be rendered thus, not 'when he shall have vowed', but 'who shall have vowed his oblation to the Lord, concerning his separation'. That is, he who has vowed to God that he will observe the ceremonies of the Nazarites for a certain time, and afterwards will sacrifice to God in the aforementioned and prescribed manner, shall do this. For he who has bound himself by a vow to the observances of the Nazarites, by the same reason has also bound himself to the subsequent sacrifices. Which sense, how Cornelius extracts it from the Vulgate, let him be seen himself.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ISTA EST LEX NAZAREI, CUM VOVERIT OBLATIONEM SUAM DOMINO TEMPORE CONSECRATIONIS SUÆ.

Ebræa ita reddenda, non cum voverit, sed qui voverit oblationem suam Domino, super separatione sua. Id est, hæc faciet, qui vovit Deo se ad certum tempus Nazaræorum ceremonias observaturum, & postea Deo prædicto & statuto modo sacrificaturum. Qui enim ad Nazaræorum observationes sese adstrinxit voto, is eadem ratione etiam ad subsequentia sacrificia sese alligavit. Quem sensum, quomodo ex Vulgata extrudat Cornelius, ipse videatur.

## 6:22
Ver. 22. ACCORDING TO WHAT HE HAD VOWED IN HIS MIND, SO SHALL HE DO UNTO THE COMPLETION OF HIS SANCTIFICATION.

In the Hebrew there is nothing about perfection, whence Papists rashly carve out a state of perfection from this passage. The words sound thus: According to his vow, which he has vowed, so shall he do concerning the law of his separation (or abstinence), that is, if he has vowed anything extraordinarily, besides the aforementioned sacrifices, to which he is bound by law, he shall also perform that, so that he may fulfill his vow. Now, when the time of the vow was completed, the Nazarites were required to offer four kinds of sacrifices, two of which, as Osiander warns (the one offered for sin, the other as a burnt offering), signified that even in our good works there is need for the remission of sins, because they are never so perfect that they are not in some way stained by some contagion of sin: the third, the thank-offering, reminds us of thanksgiving towards God: because He has given us the Holy Spirit, who works in us, so that we may will and perform some good: the meal offering, however, shows that we have need to eat Christ often in the holy supper and to drink His blood there: by which we may walk in newness of life, and always make greater progress in it. But that various sacrifices also had to be offered when a Nazarite had been defiled over a dead person, the same Osiander of ours rightly warned about that, that so many sacrifices for one, and indeed, as it seems, not a heinous sin, teach that the Levitical sacrifices could not (by their own power or virtue) expiate the sins of the people, and therefore there was need for the most perfect sacrifice of Christ, which was prefigured by them.

Latin:

Verf. 22. JUXTA QVOD MENTE DE-VOVERAT, ITA FACIET AD PERFE-CTIONEM SANCTIFICATIONIS SUÆ.

In Ebræo nihil de perfectione, unde ex hoc lo-co temere Papistæ statum perfectionis exsculpunt.Verba ita sonant: Juxta votum suum, quod vovit, sicfaciet super lege separationis ( seu abstinentiæ) suæ,id est, si quid extraordinarie voverit, præter supracommemorata sacrificia, ad quæ lege adstringi-tur, etiam id præstabit, ut votum suum impleat.Offerre autem completo voti tempore necessumhabuerunt Nazaræi quatuor genera sarificiorum,quorum duo, monente Osiandro, (hoc pro pec-cato, illud in holocaustum oblatum) significabant,etiam in bonis nostris operibus opus esse remissionempeccatorum, quod nunquam sint ita perfecta, quinaliqua peccati contagione quodammodo macu-lentur: tertium sacrificium retributorium, admo-net nos de gratiarum actione erga Deum: quod do-narit nobis Spriritum sanctum, qui agit in nobis, utvelimus & perficiamus aliquid boni: sacrificiumvero cibarium ostendit, nos habere opus, ut sæpeChristum in cœna sacra manducemus ejusq; san-guinem ibidem bibamus: quo in novitate vitæ am-bulare, & in ea semper majores progressus facerequeamus. Quod autem varia etiam sacrificia, cumsuper mortuo pollutus fuerat Nazareus, offerendafuerint, de eo recte idem Osiander noster monuit,tot sacrificia pro uno, & quidem, ut videtur, non atrocipeccato, docere, Levitica Sacrificia non potuisse (ἀυτο-ενεργητικῶς vel virtute propria) expiare peccata populiadeoł opus fuisse perfectissimo Christi sacrificio, quodab illis præfiguratum fuit.

## 6:23
Ver. 23. THUS SHALL YOU BLESS] Standing, with hands expanded, in a clear voice.

The following points are to be observed concerning this solemn ecclesiastical blessing: (1) The principal author is GOD, who prescribed it and entrusted it to the high priest Aaron through Moses: Speak to Aaron and his sons, just as He promulgated the other laws through Moses, whom He set over the people as commander and as it were king, who ought to be the lawgiver here, and to whom the right of νομοθεσίας (legislation) belongs: Thus He did not give this law concerning the blessing immediately to Aaron, but ordered Moses to deliver the same to Aaron. Since, therefore, the formula was prescribed by God Himself, it was deservedly held in high esteem among the Israelites, and consequently, in later times, it ought not to have been changed by substituting another name in place of the tetragrammaton, as will be said later. (2) The ministerial cause of the blessing to be recited is named as Aaron, whence it is called the εὐλογία Ἀαρὼν (blessing of Aaron) in Sirach 36:9. and his sons, to whom the priesthood had already been committed, to which it pertained not only to teach and to sacrifice, but also to pray and to bless, 2 Chronicles 30:27; Sirach 45:19. Moreover, the high priest was in this a type and figure of Christ, the unique High Priest of the New Testament; as Aaron, after completing his duties in teaching and sacrificing, before he dismissed the people, imparted the blessing to them, so Christ, after completing His ministry on earth and His sacrifice on the cross, before He dismissed His disciples, wished to confer a blessing upon them, which in all likelihood extends to all, both Jews, Acts 3:25, and Gentiles, Genesis 12:3, Galatians 3:14. (3) The ceremonies which are employed in this blessing. Grotius indicates three, that it was done standing, with hands outstretched, and in a clear voice. The Hebrews, from whom Grotius has these, add three others: that this blessing be uttered in the holy tongue, that the face be directed toward the people, and that the tetragrammaton name of GOD be expressed at each of the blessings, which otherwise it was a religious duty for them not to utter. Cf. Drusius on Numbers.

p. 371. P. Fagius advises that that expansion of the hands was done in such a way that they not only prayed with hands spread toward heaven for the fulfillment of those blessings (which elevation of the hands was a reminder of lifting the soul to God, Ps. 25:1, Ps. 68:4, Ps. 118:6), but they also expanded or stretched out their hands over the people, Lev. 5:22, Syr. 50:22, as if they were about to impose them upon the heads of the universal Church, and to deposit into the Church itself the grace received from heaven by their hands (this χειροθεσία intervening). This ministry of theirs was by no means fruitless, because God willed to impart those blessings through it, as the words of the promise have this annexed: I am about to bless them, i.e., I will bring it about that they have neither prayed in vain nor placed my name upon the people and announced my grace to them, whence even now the priestly blessing is to be esteemed most highly, as August. advises in the questions. from the O. & N. T. Cons. Syr. 36:19, c. 3:11, Matth. 10, 12, yet it was not a true χειροθεσία, but an analogue, representing the same, when the blessing was made to the whole people. But when it was conferred upon one single person, it is perhaps not to be denied that the imposition of hands was employed. Which Junius & Tremellius v. 27 render thus: And imposing (hands) on the children of Israel (they shall invoke) my name, does not agree with the authentic text, in which mention is made of neither hands nor invocation. They are commanded to place the name of the Lord upon the children of Israel; they are not commanded to impose hands upon them. But that phrase, to place the name of the Lord upon someone, is the same as to bless someone in the name of the Lord: as is evident from a comparison of Deut. 6:18, c. 21:5, c. 28:10, 2 Sam. 6:8: whence also the name of the Lord is said to be placed in the tabernacle & temple, because the preaching & invocation of the name of the Lord and the blessing made in the same to them 1 Kings 9:3, c. 14:21, 2 Kings 21:4, 2 Chron. 33:7. It also pertains to the rites, which was observed by Weidner in loc. fidei Christ. praecip. tr. 1. The Priest, blessing someone with these blessings, held both palms stretched out before his face, but when he said LORD, he raised the first three fingers, namely the thumb, the index, and the middle finger of each hand, higher, and with the word Lord thus spoken, he relaxed the fingers as before. Which he indeed employs to signify the mystery of the H. H. Trinity: What could be allegorized better by the elevation of three fingers than the excellence of the Trinity? But that meaning will be proven with difficulty from the testimonies of the Rabbis. Some gather from Ps. 67:8 that when the Priests said in this blessing: The Lord bless thee, the people responded from true faith: Blessed be God to us, our God, may God bless us.

(4.) The frequency of this blessing. It seems probable to some that it was pronounced every day morning & evening, when sacrifices were offered in the congregation of the Church, as often, namely, as the Priests dismissed the people. Which is still piously employed in our Church, provided it does not pertain to the Levitical ceremonies, but to the promise concerning the gracious presence of God in the Church, Ex. 20:24. But the rashness of the Jews cannot be excused, in that they dared to change this blessing prescribed by GOD himself out of mere superstition, and in place of the name τετραγραμμάτε or the words הקדוש ברוך הוא that Holy One blessed be He, to substitute, as Reuchlin notes in Cabal., or as is held in Pesickta, and has been adduced by Drusius in Comment. in Num. 25, to use the word Adonai or another name (in their opinion) holier than it.

(5.) The mystery of the H. H. Trinity designated in that solemn blessing. Which the Jews indeed deny, the Socinians laugh at (Smal. contr. Schopper. p. 13 & others), and some Calvinists also agitate, and especially Danaeus in Comm. in h. l. Lombard. dist. 6. p. 42. But it is confirmed not obscurely (1.) By the triple repetition of the name Jehovah, because it was to be recited in this blessing not once or twice, or four times or more, but three times. Since this is not without a mystery, nor can another be solidly brought from Scripture if you depart from the mystery of the H. H. Trinity, there is no doubt that it is designated here. Since no apex in such a succinct & nervous blessing should be superfluous. (2.) By the manner of the predicate. For that Lord, from whom the blessing is both to be vowed & obtained, is pointed out in this solemn blessing, and his name is placed upon the children of Israel. But the Father, Son & H. S. are Jehovah or the Lord, from whom the blessing is to be vowed & obtained; E. the Father, Son & H. S. are pointed out in the solemn blessing, and the name of the Father, Son & H. S. is placed upon the children of Israel. All those testimonies which prove the mystery of the H. H. Trinity confirm the minor, concerning which see Tom. 3. System. Theolog. (3.) By the consideration of the distinct members of the blessing.
