The Hebrew 'teruah' denotes a cut and broken sound, now raised, now depressed, which is distinguished from a plain and steady one, and it was a sign of moving the camps (the Vulgate then calls it a howling), so that at the first blast the first camps of Judah with Issachar and Zebulun, at the second Reuben with Simeon and Gad, at the third Ephraim with Manasseh and Benjamin, at the fourth Dan with Asher and Naphtali would move their camps: compare chapter 2. It seems, however, that at that time only a single trumpet blast was issued; but when it was necessary to go out to war, both trumpets howled, to speak with the Vulgate, verse 9.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SI AVTEM PROLIXIOR ATQVE CONCISVS CLANGOR INCREPUERIT MOVERUNT CASTRA]

Sic apud veteres Romanos alius erat tubæ sonus ad pugnam, alius ad receptum: quod discrimen posteris temporibus male omissum docet Procopius Gothicorum II.

Ebr. תרועה sonitum incisum & confractum, modo elatum, modo depressum, notat, qui distinguitur a plano, & æquabili, & signum erat movendorum castrorum (Vulg. vocat deinde ululatum) ut ad primum clangorem primi Juda cum Issaschar, & Zabulon, ad secundum Ruben cum Simeone & Gad, ad tertium Ephraim cum Menasse & Benjamin, ad quartum Dan cum Aser & Naphthali castra sua moverent: conf. cap. 2. videtur autem tum unica tuba solum clangor editus: cum vero exeundum fuit ad bellum, ambæ tubæ ululabant, ut cum Vulgata loquamur vers. 9.

## 10:10
Verse 10.

IF AT ANY TIME YOU SHALL HAVE A FEAST. The discourse is about a public feast: but about a sacred and solemn one, which was made from peace offerings, or which was made with a preceding sacrifice, and which concluded it, such as was also in the consecration of kings, and thanksgiving for a notable victory, etc. In the Hebrew, Chaldean, and LXX interpreters' version, it is 'in the day of your gladness': but a denunciation of the feasts is added (for which also the day of the Sabbath is to be reserved) and of the calends or new moons, in which they did not indeed cease from servile works, yet special victims were offered, and thus it was a peculiar solemnity. Psalm 80:4 teaches that a sacred feast is denoted.

Verse the same.

I THE LORD YOUR GOD] Here the Samaritan codex has inserted certain things that are not at all necessary, taken from Deuteronomy 6:1, as Procopius of Gaza noted long ago regarding that place in Deuteronomy.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

SI QUANDO HABEBITIS EPULUM. De publico epulo sermo est: Sed de sacro & solemni, quod ex hostiis pacificis, vel quod prævio sacrificio fiebat, illudque claudebat, quale etiam fuit in consecratione Regum, & gratiarum actio- ne pro insigni victoria &c. In Ebr. Chald. & LXX. Interpp. versione est, in die lætitiæ vestræ: Sed addita denunciatio festorum (ad quæ etiam Sabbati dies reservanda) & calendarum seu Neo- meniorum, in quibus non cessabant quidem ab operibus servilibus, offerebantur tamen speciales victimæ, adeoque peculiaris erat solemnitas. Psal. 80, 4. docet sacrum epulum notari.

Vers. eod.

EGO DOMINUS DEUS VESTER] Hic inserta quæ- dam habet codex Samaritanus minime necessaria desumta, ex Deuteronom. 6, 1. ut jampridem ad eum Deuteronomii lo- cum notavit Procopius Gazæus.

## 10:11
Ver. 11.

IN THE SECOND YEAR, IN THE SECOND MONTH, ON THE TWENTIETH DAY OF THE MONTH, THE CLOUD WAS LIFTED. Up to this point, therefore, the Israelites were at Mount Sinai, to which they came on the 1st day of the 2nd month of the 1st year of the exodus from Egypt, Exod. 19, 1. Wherefore, within this time up to the 20th day of the 2nd month of the second year, which is not yet a full year (ten days are still lacking), all those things were done which are related from chapter 19 of Exodus up to this place through Exodus, Leviticus, and the Book of Numbers; namely, the moral, ceremonial, and forensic laws were delivered, the tabernacle was fashioned and erected, the priests were consecrated, the people were numbered, the Levites were selected, the camps were ordered, and thus at Mount Sinai, both the Church and the Republic of the Hebrews were formed, just as in Zion the doctrine of the Gospel was promulgated and the Christian Church was formed, Acts 2, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ANNO SECUNDO MENSE SECUNDO VIGESIMO DIE MENSIS ELEVATA EST NUBES. Huc usque ergo Israelitæ fuere ad montem Sinai, quo venerunt 1. die Mensis 2. anni 1. exitus ex Ægypto Exod. 19, 1. Quapropter intra hoc tempus usque ad 20. diem Mensis 2. anni secun- di, quod nondum est integri anni (desunt adhuc decem dies) ea omnia gesta, quæ inde a cap. 19. Exod. usque ad hunc locum referuntur per Exodum & Leviticum, & Librum Numerorum; traditæ nempe leges morales, ceremoniales, & forenses, fabrefactum & erectum tabernaculum, consecrati Sacerdotes, numeratus populus, selecti Levitæ, or- dinata castra, adeoque ad montem Sinai, forma- ta tam Ecclesia quam Resp. Ebræorum, quemad- modum in Sion promulgata doctrina Evangelii, & formata Ecclesia Christiana Act. 2, 1.

## 10:12
ver. 12.

THE CLOUD RESTED IN THE WILDERNESS OF PARAN.

This station was the thirteenth. This wilderness of Paran, in itself one, comprised many other partial ones, in which the Israelites had two different dwelling places up to Sin, which also was a part of that wilderness, where the thirty-third dwelling place was, Num. 33, 35. That wilderness of Paran is described by those who have surveyed it as most vast, extended from Mount Sinai to Kadesh-barnea by a journey of eleven days, broken, dry, waterless, sterile, and unplowable, almost destitute of herbs and trees, with sheer cliffs and mountains, rough and horrid, in which the Israelites were to dwell for 38 years. See Adrichomius and Bochart. It is a figure of our calamity, who are wandering through the wilderness of this world.

Latin:

vers. 12.

RECUBUIT NUBES IN SOLITUDINE PHARAN.

Statio hæc fuit decima tertia. Hoc deser- tum Pharan in se unum multa alia partialia com- plexum, in quibus duas diversas mansiones ha- buere Israelitæ usque in Sin, quæ etiam erat pars istius deserti, ubi trigesima tertia mansio fuit Num. 33, 35. Desertum illud Pharan describitur ab illis qui illud lustrarunt, ceu amplissimum, extensum a monte Sinai usque ad Cadesbarne per iter un- decim dierum, lacerum, siccum, inraquosum, sterile, & inarabile, herbis & arboribus pene de- stitutum, præruptis rupibus & montibus, asperum atque horridum, in quo per 38. annos Israelitis commorandum erat. Vid. Adrichomius, & Bo- chardus. Figura est calamitatis nostræ, qui pere- grinamur per desertum hujus mundi.

## 10:15
Ver. 15.

IN THE TRIBE OF THE CHILDREN OF ISSACHAR WAS THE PRINCE) That this passage and the one above in chapter 2 may be understood, it must be known that the army of the Israelites had been divided into four columns. Each column consisted of three tribes. The tribe of Judah held the leadership of the first column with a standard having the figure of a lion. Reuben of the second column, with the standard of a man. Ephraim of the third, with the standard of an ox. Dan of the fourth, with the standard of an eagle. These four great standards are called here דגלי מחנת, camp standards, τάγματα παρεμβολῆς in Greek, corresponding to the eagles of the Romans. Furthermore, just as the Roman cohorts had their own proper signs, so also did those tribes here which did not have the leadership of a column. Those signs are called here מטו, as if you would say a staff, and from those signs the same name adhered to the tribes themselves. The LXX call these signs δυνάμεις.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

IN TRIBV FILIORUM ISASCHAR FUIT PRIN- CEPS) Ut hic locus & is qui supra est capite 2. intelligatur, sciendum est exercitum Israëlitarum in quatuor agmina fuif- se partitum. Agmen quodque trium erat tribuum. Ductum primi agminis obtinebat tribus Juda cum vexillo figuram ha- bente Leonis. Secundi agminis Ruben, vexillo hominis. Tertii Ephraim, vexillo bovis. Quarti Dan, vexillo aquilæ. Hæc quatuor magna vexilla dicuntur hic דגלי מחנת ve- xilla castrensia, τάγματα παρεμβολῆς Græce, respondentia aquilis Romanorum. Præterea sicut cohortes Romanæ sua propria habebant signa, ita & hic tribus illæ quæ ductum agminis non habebant. Ea signa vocantur hic מטו quasi baculum dicas, & ex iis signis ipsis tribubus idem nomen ad- hæsit. LXX. hæc signa vocant δυνάμεις.

Vers. 31. YOU WILL BE OUR GUIDE) He translated the sense well: in the Hebrew, You will be for us instead of eyes. See Job 29, 15. It is the wisdom of a Commander to have those who are knowledgeable of the routes, and to redeem them at a great price.

## 10:35
Vers. 39. AND WHEN IT WAS LIFTED UP) That the inverted נ is placed here and at the beginning of the following chapter in the Hebrew text signifies nothing other than a matter to be noted exceptionally and to be fixed in the memory. Thus also the letters in the text are often somewhat larger.

PART III. OF THE HISTORICAL BOOK.

I. Describing the journey according to eight murmurings, of which 1. from weariness of the journey, 2. from weariness of the Manna c. 11. 3. from emulation of Moses c. 12. 4. from diffidence after the exploration of the land of future possession c. 13. whose punishment c. 14. with the condonation of the intervening sacrifices, with the observance of the law following, for the cause of which some things c. 15. were handed down. 5. From envy of the leadership of Moses and the Priesthood of Aaron c. 16. 6. From indignation on account of the severe vengeance of the rebellion: the consequence of which was both the confirmation of the Priesthood to Aaron by the flowering rod, c. 17. and the distinction of the Priests and Levites, c. 18. and the institution of the water of purification, c. 19. 7. From lack of water, c. 20. the consequence of which is the death of Aaron and the introduction of his successor etc. 8. From weariness of the way and contempt of the Manna: the consequence of which is the journey up to the borders of the promised land and the defeat of Sihon and Og c. 21. II. The removal of the obstacles to entry by Balaam c. 22. 23. 24. and the spiritual and carnal fornication with the Midianites c. 25. III. The recounting of the new generation of Israelites, c. 26. where there is a disposition concerning the successions of the heirs. c. 27.

PARS III. LIBRI ΙΣΤΟΡΙΚΗ.

I. Profectionem describens juxta octo murmurationes, quarum 1. ex tædio iti- neris, 2. ex tædio Mannæ c. 11. 3. ex æ- mulatione Mosis c. 12. 4. ex diffidentia post explorationem terræ futuræ pos- sessionis c. 13. cujus pœna c. 14. cum con- donatione intervenientibus sacrificiis, consequente legis observatione, quo- rum causa nonnulla c. 15. tradita. 5. Ex invidentia principatus Mosis & Pontifi- catus Aaronis c. 16. 6. Ex indignatione ob severam rebellionis ultionem: cujus consequens tum Sacerdotii Aaroni per virgam florentem confirmatio, c. 17. tum Sacerdotum & Levitarum discre- tio, c. 18. tum aquæ lustralis institutio, c. 19. 7. Ex penuria aquæ, c. 20. cujus consequentia mors Aaronis & successo- ris introductio &c. 8. ## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. The twofold murmur of the Jews, primarily of those desiring meat and the ordination of the LXX Elders.

Vers. 1. MEANWHILE A MURMUR OF THE PEOPLE AROSE AS OF THOSE GRIEVING.

The Hebrews מתאננים which is here, distinguish from מתאבלים, as noted by the learned Dr. Varenius, on this passage, because the latter are those who reveal grief by signs of clothes and gestures, the former those who press deep sorrow in their heart: which fits this place perfectly, where there is no sign of external complaint. For there is another murmuring, about which it follows in vers. 4. 5., which was made with the rest in c. 12, 2. c. 14, 2. c. 16, 3. c. 17, 6. c. 20, 3. c. 21, 5. by complaint: but this one seems to have been merely mental, known only to GOD, and punished by the same, and soon restrained by panegyric prayers, yet so that fire consumed the extremity of the camps: (by which name the learned Dr. Varenius understands the principal ones of the camps from a comparison of Genesis 19, 4. Judges 8, 7., which we leave in its place) whence the place was called Taberah. The particle ו therefore in verse 4 is to be rendered by 'but', not by 'indeed' as in the Vulgate, lest one and the same murmuring be judged, since it was made in a different way and in different places.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Murmur Judæorum geminum, imprimis carnes desiderantium & ordinatio LXX. Seniorum.

Vers. 1. INTEREA ORTUM EST MURMUR POPULI QUASI DOLENTIUM.

EBræi מתאננים quod hic est, distinguunt à מתאבלים, notante D. D. Varenio, ad h. l. quod hi sint luctum vestium, gestuumque signis prodentes, illi altum dolorem corde prementes : quod huic loco apprime convenit, ubi nullum externæ oblo- cutionis signum. Alia enim est murmuratio, de qua vers. 4. 5. sequitur, quæ cum cæteris cap. 12, 2. cap. 14, 2. cap. 16, 3. cap. 17, 6. cap. 20, 3. cap. 21, 5. obloquutione facta : hæc autem mere mentalis fuisse videtur, soli DEO cognita, & ab eodem punita, precibusque panegyricis mox cohibita, sic tamen ut ignis consumserit extremitatem castro- rum: (quo nomine Dn. D. Varenius primarios quosque castrorum è collatione Genes. 19, 4. Jud. 8, 7. intelligit, quod suo loco relinquimus) unde locus dictus Tabhera. Particula ergo ו versu 4. per autem reddenda est, non cum Vulgata per quippe, ne una eademque murmuratio censeatur, quum diverso modo, & diversis locis facta sit.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. MOSES PRAYED TO THE LORD) An image of Christ in this matter. See soon 12, 13. 14, 19. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ORAVIT MOSES AD DOMINVM) Christi hac in re imago. Vide mox 12, 13. 14, 19. & alibi.

## 11:4
Vers. 4. THE MIXED MULTITUDE INDEED) Whom the Greeks call ἐπιμίκτους, many from Egypt, many had joined themselves to the Hebrews on the journey. See the Egyptian writers in Josephus against Apion.

Verse of the same. WHO WILL GIVE US FLESH TO EAT.

Regarding this murmuring, a doubt arises, which I nowhere find resolved, that is not slight, from Psalm 78:20. For in that place they are introduced speaking thus: Can GOD prepare a table in the wilderness? Because he struck the rock and the waters flowed, and the torrents flooded. Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people? Yet he had already given bread a year before, namely Manna, and with it had sustained the people. Indeed, he had also given flesh, for the sake of which they murmured here in particular, which happened before the rock was struck providing them water: as is evident from a comparison of chapters 16 and 17 of Exodus, and the sequence of the history. How then could the Israelites call into question the power of GOD in providing flesh and bread, when they had already experienced it in reality? how, having instituted a comparison of the miraculous provision of water and the exhibition of bread and flesh in the desert, could they diminish that benefit of extraordinary drink, as already received, and yet argue that this miracle of extraordinary feeding was impossible to perform, if indeed they had been fed miraculously with bread and flesh before they were given drink from the rock? It cannot be said here with Aben-Ezra that Scripture in Psalm 78:20 speaks confusedly, because those reasonings of the Israelites tempting and soliciting divine power regarding the provision of food are recounted in such a way that such things could in no way have come into their minds unless the lack of water had first been supplied by the striking of the rock. Wherefore one or the other must necessarily be said: either that they desired a more sumptuous table than that which had already been prepared for them from quails, Exodus 16, with which they had already been fed before the rock was struck, such as they denied could be spread for them in the desert: or since, from those things which follow in the Psalm, it seems sufficiently evident that God, by the repeated sending of quails, and continued for an entire month, fulfilled their desires and demonstrated his power, about which Moses himself was in some measure solicitous here in verse 22, it must be determined that these forgetful gluttons had forgotten the prior provision of quails, or certainly did not believe that God, who was still continuously supplying them with water flowing miraculously, even if he had fed them with quail flesh for perhaps a single meal, could by his power not bring it about that for a long time flesh could be provided to such a multitude of men in that horrid desert. Who therefore, to demonstrate his power, provided them quails not for one day, nor two, or five or ten, nor even twenty, but up to a month of days, and until the flesh turned to nausea for them, verse 19. Compare Psalm 78:29-30. Meanwhile, as far as bread is concerned, we readily grant that they, led by a nausea for the heavenly Manna, desired wheaten bread, the desire for which the Lord did not deign to grant them, but rather struck them with a plague on account of their contempt for the heavenly bread and their tempting of divine power. Whence in the Psalm, verse 20, by the word לחם, wheaten bread, such as they had eaten before in Egypt, is denoted, as Simon de Muis rightly observes. Compare Numbers 21:5. Therefore not the words

The verses of Asaph 23, 24, 25 teach that the Lord gave them the desired bread when He provided Manna, because they had already been fed by it for a year, nor is it right to admit a confusion of history here; but they describe the long-suffering of God, in that He not only still granted angelic bread from heaven to a murmuring and extremely perverse people, but also abundantly satisfied their desires and pleasure with more delicate meat, even though He finally, struck by anger, struck the leaders among the people v. 26, 30. Num. 11, 33.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VULGUS QUIPPE PROMISCUUM) Quos Graeci ἐπιμίκτους vocant, multi ex Aegypto, multi in itinere se Hebraeis aggregaverant. Vide Aegyptios Scriptores apud Jo- sephum contra Appionem.

Vers. eod. QUIS DABIT NOBIS AD VE- SCENDUM CARNES.

De hac murmuratione dubium, quod nuspi- am invenio expeditum non leve oritur e Psalm. 78, 20. Nam in illa ita loquentes introducuntur: Numquid poterit DEUS parare mensam in deserto? Quoniam percussit petram & fluxerunt aquae, & tor- rentes inundaverunt. Numquid & panem poterit dare, aut parare mensam populo suo? At dederat jam, ante annum, panem, Manna nempe, eoque sustentarat populum. Imo dederat & carnes, qua- rum causa hic imprimis murmuratum, quod fa- ctum, antequam percuteretur petra aquam illis praebens: ut e cap. 16. & 17. Exodi collatione, & historiae serie constat. Quomodo ergo in dubi- um vocare poterant Israëlitae DEI potentiam in subministrandis carnibus, & pane, qui eam exper- ti jam reapse erant? quomodo instituta compara- tione miraculosae praebitionis aquae, & exhibitio- nis panis, & carnis in deserto, illud potationis extra- ordinariae beneficium, ceu jam acceptum, extenua- re, hoc autem cibationis extraordinariae miraculum, ceu factu impossibile, arguere poterant, siquidem prius pane & carnibus cibati miraculose, quam e pe- tra potati fuerint? Dici hic non potest cum Aben- Ezra, Scripturam Ps. 78, 20. confuse loqui, quia ita re- censentur illae ratiocinationes Israëlitarum divinam potentiam tentantium & solicitantium circa prae- bitionem cibi, ut nullo modo talia ipsis in mentem venire potuerint, nisi prius aquae defectus supple- tus fuisset petrae percussione. Quapropter alteru- trum dicendum necessario est, vel quod lautiorem mensam desiderarint, quam quae parata ipsis jam e coturnicibus erat, Exod. 16. quibus ante percussam petram cibati jam fuerant, qualem in deserto sibi sterni posse negarint: vel quum ex iis, quae in Psalmo sequuntur, satis constare videatur, Deum immisione coturnicum iterata, & per integrum mensem continuata, desideria ipsorum implevisse, ac potentiam suam, de qua hic v. 22. Moses ipse aliqua ratione solicitus fuit, demonstrasse, statuendum, de- licatulis istis obliviosis hic memoria excidisse prio- rem coturnicum praebitionem, aut certe non cre- didisse ipsos, Deum, qui continuo ipsis adhuc aquam miraculosae fluentem sufficiebat, etsi ad unicam forte coenam carnibus coturnicum sese cibarit, haud efficere virtute sua posse, ut diuturno tempo- re tantae hominum multitudini in horrido isto de- serto carnes praebeantur. Qui proinde demon- strandae suae potentiae coturnices ipsis praebuit non uno die, nec duobus, vel quinq; aut decem, nec viginti quidem, sed usq; ad mensem dierum, & usq; dum car- nes ipsis verterentur in nauseam v. 19. Conf. Psal. 78, 29. 30. Interim, quod ad panem attinet, largimur facile, eos Manna coelestis nausea ductos fru- mentaceum panem desiderasse, cujus vero deside- rii ipsos compotes reddere non dignatus est Do- minus, quin plaga potius percussit eosdem ob con- temtum coelestis panis, & tentationem potentiae divinae. Unde in Psalmo vers. 20. voce לחם pa- nem frumentaceum, qualem in Aegypto antehac comederant, notari, Simon de Muis recte ob- servat. Conf. Numer. XXI, 5. Non ergo verba

Assaphi vers. 23. 24. 25. docent, quod panem desi- deratum ipsis dederit dominus, cum Manna præ- buit, quia eo jam per annum cibati erant, neque eti- am historiæ confusionem hic admittere fas est; sed Dei describunt μακροθυμίαν, quod murmuranti & extreme perverso populo non tantum adhuc de cœlo angelicum panem concesserit, sed carne etiam delicatiori abunde desideria, & voluptatem ipso- rum exsatiarit, etsi tandem ira percitus primores in populo percusserit v. 26. 30. Num. 11, 33.

## 11:7 Addition
To chapter 11, verse 7, page 529, column a. AND THE MANNA WAS AS CORIANDER SEED, THE COLOR OF BDELLIUM.

Latin:

Ad cap. 11. vers. 7. pag. 529. a. ERAT AUTEM MAN QUASI SEMEN CO- RIANDRI COLORIS BDELLII.

## 11:8
Vers. 8. OF THE TASTE AS OF OIL BREAD. Exod. 16, 32. mention is also made of the taste of honey: Nowhere, however, is it held that the people had the taste of every kind of food in the Manna, and what Lyranus says with the Jews, that it tasted of fish when they desired fish, is a fable, even if an ancient one, as the witness of Wis. 16, 20, the contrary of which is sufficiently clear from this defined species of taste and from the desire for fish, cucumbers, and other foods.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SAPORIS QVASI PANIS OLEATI. Exod. 16, 32. etiam Saporis mellis mentio fit: Nus- piam autem habetur, quod omnis generis ciborum saporem in Manna habuerit populus, & quod cum Judæis Lyranus ait, pisces sapuerit, quando pisces de- siderarunt, cujus fabulæ etsi antiquæ teste Sap. 16, 20. contrarium satis ex hac definita saporis specie & ex desiderio piscium, cucumerum, aliorumque ciborum patet.

## 11:14 Addition
Verse 14. SHALL HAVE STIRRED UP THE HUSBAND.

The former refers to the form alone: For coriander seed is of a black color: because it was round and small, like that seed: But its color was like Bdellium: which Pliny, book 12, chapter 9.

This law was permitted to men, not to women, according to Aben Ezra: Estius gives the reason: 1. Lest the authority of the husband be diminished. 2. Women are too prone to such suspicions. 3. Because it is more harmed, as he testifies in ch. 9, that it is clear and white. And that the Greek Scholiast hinted that Jonathan, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered Bdellium as aromatic is implied. And thus the Samaritans, Montanus, Junius, and Tremellius, along with the Chaldean and Jerome and the new interpreters, translate it with great consensus. However, this does not please Bochart. He prefers to translate it as a white pearl. Because bdellium is usually almost black, and is not rounded into grains, but into lumps. For the pearl, he brings forward these points in his Hierozoicon: 1. The land of Havilah (in which is בדולח, Gen. 2.) is that part of Arabia from which pearls are extracted, as we have clearly proven in our Paradise. 2. Manna was white, Exod. 16, 14. (as all write, and as is evident from αὐτοψίᾳ,) and round; which two things are most significant in a pearl. 3. Thus the ancients. So the Talmudists explain in Joma, cap. 8. fol. 73. a כמרגלית that is, as a pearl. And Baal hatturim on Gen. 2. says that the species of Manna is attributed to bedolach, Num. 11. because precious stones and pearls descended with the Manna. Thus the various versions of the Arabs. Thus Saadias, and Kimchi in his Lexicon, and Benjamin, and the Author of the history of the second Temple throughout. 5. The reason for the name agrees, בדלח for בדולה (as ה is wont to be put for ו.) If you grant this, or that the final is paragogic, it will be from בדל to separate and segregate: i.e., excellent.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CONCITAVERIT VIRUM.

Prius illud refertur ad formam solam : Nam co- riandri semen nigri est coloris : quod rotundum & minutum fuerit, ut semen illud: Color autem ejus fuit instar Bdellii : quod Plinius libr. 12. cap. 9.

Permissa hæc lex viris, non fœminis, secun- dum Aben. Ezram : Causam reddit Estius 1. Ne au- toritas viri imminueretur. 2. Mulieres ad tales su- spiciones nimis pronæ sunt. 3. Quia magis læditur cap. 9. testatur, lucidum & album esse. Et Bdellium aromaticum post Jonath. Aquil. Symmach. Theodot. reddidisse innuit Scholion Græcum. Atque ita vertunt Samar. Montanus, Junius, Tremell. cum Chald. & Hieron. novique Interpp. magno consensu. Non autem id placet Bocharto. Mavult Margaritam albam vertere. Quia bdellium fere nigrum esse solet, nec in grana rotundatur, sed in grumos. Pro margarita hæc affert in Hierozoico: 1. Terra Havilah (in qua בדולח, Gen. 2.) est ea pars Arabiæ, ex qua margaritæ eruuntur, ut plane probavimus in Paradiso. 2. Manna album erat, Exod. 16, 14. (ut omnes scribunt, & ex αὐτοψίᾳ patet,) & rotundum; quæ duo in margarita maxime insignia. 3. ita veteres. Sic Talmudici explicant in Joma, cap. 8. fol. 73. a כמרגלית id est ut margaritam. Et Baal hatturim ad Gen. 2. dicit Mannæ speciem bedolach tribui, Num. 11. quia pretiosi lapides & margaritæ cum Manna descendebant. Ita Arabum varia versiones. Ita Saadias, & Kimchi in Lexico, & Benjamin, & Autor historiæ Templi secundi passim. 5. Convenit ratio nominis, בדלח pro בדולה (ut solet ה pro ו poni.) Hoc si dederis, aut finale esse paragogicum, erit a בדל separare & segregare: q. d. eximium.

## 11:15
Vers. 15. LEST I BE AFFLICTED WITH SUCH EVILS) In the Hebrew it is now, ואל אראה ברעתי Greek: ἵνα μὴ ἴδω τὴν κάκωσίν με. But it was once ברעתך κάκωσίν σε, that you are treated badly: But because that sounded too harsh regarding God, it was therefore changed by later ones, as were certain other things.

But whence is it certain here that it was once written thus? What is this license, or audacity, of arguing against the Hebrew Codices without any reason, at least, because it pleases? The Hebrews, Greeks, Latins, and others agree: and yet an Aristarchus dreams of corruption. Nor does he bring forth any cause for his suspicion: so that it is clear to everyone that, beyond the merit of the original Hebrew text, he is intent most of all on dislodging it from its standing. Aben-Ezra himself indeed admits here: there is no need for a correction by the scribes.

Latin:

Vers. 15. NE TANTIS AFFICIAR MALIS) In Hebræo nunc est, ואל אראה ברעתי Græce : ἵνα μὴ ἴδω τὴν κά- κωσίν με. Sed fuit olim ברעתך κάκωσίν σε, te male tra- ctari: Sed quia id de Deo sonabat durius, ideo a posteriori- bus mutatum est, ut & alia quædam.

Unde vero hîc constat, quod olim sic scriptum fuerit? Quænam hæc licentia, vel audacia, Ebræos Codd. arguendi sine ulla ratione, saltem, quia id placet. Ebræi, Græci, Latini aliique consentiunt: & somniat tamen Aristarchus corruptionem. Neque ullam promit causam suspicionis suæ: ut nemini non pateat, quod præter meritum textus Origina- lis Ebræi, in id intentus sit maxime, ut eundem gra- du suo deturbet. Aben-Ezra sanè ipse hîc fatetur: non est opus correctione scribarum.

## 11:16
Vers. 16. SEVENTY MEN OF THE ELDERS OF ISRAEL, WHOM YOU KNOW THAT THEY ARE ELDERS OF THE PEOPLE AND MASTERS] They had already had a certain inspection over the people in Egypt Exod. 24, 4, 9, comparing the passages Exod. 1, 11, III, 16, V, 6. That number had pleased because just as many children of Jacob had come into Egypt, and from that there arose also among the exiled Hebrews in Egypt, and elsewhere, a college of equal number. These, however, of whom it is treated in this place, were hitherto presiding over the council of the LXX, not with the power of judging, which they soon receive, and they become אלהים i.e., gods.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SEPTUAGINTA VIROS DE SENIBUS ISRA- EL, QVOS TV NOSTI QVOD SENES POPULI SINT AC MAGISTRI ] Inspectionem quandam in populum jam in Ægypto habuerant Exod. 24, 4. 9. collatis locis Exod. I, 11. III, 16. V, 6. Placuerat is numerus, quod totidem Jacobi li- beri in Ægyptum venissent, ex eoque extitit etiam apud exu- les Hebræos in Ægypto, & alibi paris numeri collegium. Hi autem de quibus h. l. agitur, LXX. consilio hactenus præe- rant, non judicandi potestate, quam mox accipiunt, fiuntque אלהים i. e. dii.

## 11:16 Addition
On Num. 11. v. 16. after the note of Grotius.

That such a college of LXX. or rather LXXII. men, into which six were chosen from every tribe, the Israelites had in Egypt cannot be gathered from those places Ex. 1, 3. 4. However, that Moses instituted a similar one in the desert by the counsel of Jethro, as far as the number and general end, so that he might be relieved, is evident from c. 19. This, however, was new, because it was instituted by the immediate command of God and at a different time: not that the former were already dead, and consumed by fire, as R. Solomon and Drusius wish, but that the former helped him only in civil matters, whereas these in spiritual ones, whence these had need of the Prophetic Spirit: or that until now both greater causes, and those which concerned God and the worship of God, were always referred to Moses, and that the final appeal was always to him, to which three things, so that the burden might be made lighter for him, these LXX. were now to be chosen to be carried and expedited: who constituted the Sanhedrin, and had continuous successions afterwards in the land of Canaan.

Latin:

Ad Numer. 11. v. 16. post notam Grotii.

Tale collegium LXX. vel potius LXXII. virorum in quod sex de quavis tribu delecti fuerint, in Ægypto habuisse Israelitas ex istis locis Ex. 1, 3. 4. colligi non potest. Instituisse autem ex consilio Jethronis Mosen in deserto simile, quantum ad numerum & finem generalem, ut sublevaretur e cap. 19. constat. Hoc tamen novum fuit, quod ex immediato Dei mandato & diverso tempore institutum: non quod priores jam mortui, & igne absorpti, ut R. Salomo vult, & Drusius, sed quod priores sive in civilibus tantum negotiis ipsum juvarent, hi vero in spiritualibus, unde his Spiritu Prophetico opus fuit: sive quod ad Mosen hactenus semper, & majores causæ, & quæ Deum, Deique cultum spectabant, relatæ fuerint, quodque ad eum ultima semper fuerit appellatio, ad quæ tria cum Mose, ut levius ipsi redderetur onus, ferenda & expedienda, jam LXX. hi eligendi erant: qui Synedrium constituere, & continuas postea successiones habuere in terra Canaan.

## 11:17
Vers. 17. THAT THEY MAY SUSTAIN WITH YOU THE BURDEN OF THE PEOPLE] Rabbi Juda explains אתך which is translated here as with you, as by your example, in such a way as you have done.

Latin:

Vers. 17. VT SVSTENTENT TECVM ONVS PO- PVLI ] Rabbi Juda אתך quod hîc tecum vertitur explicat, exemplo tuo, ita ut tu fecisti.

## 11:20
Vers. 20. EVEN TO A MONTH OF DAYS) That is, a full month. Thus δύο ἔτη ἡμερῶν, are two full years 1 Macc. 1, 30.

LET IT BE TURNED INTO NAUSEA) The Greeks, εἰς χολέραν: namely just as they translate זר as bitterness in Isaiah 28, 21. And these indeed derive it from זור, which signifies alienation. But Symmachus from זרר which is to scatter. For he translates it ἀπεψίαν, which is accustomed to follow excessive gluttony, and to spread the remains of poorly digested food through the body: whence also follows that which the Greeks and the Latin said, bile and nausea. Tertullian on fasts joined both: by digesting the quails even to cholera.

Latin:

Vers. 20. VSQVE AD MENSEM DIERUM) Id est, mensem exactum. Sic δύο ἔτη ἡμερῶν, sunt duo anni pleni 1. Macc. 1, 30.

VERTATVR IN NAVSEAM) Græci, εἰς χολέραν: nempe sicut זר πικρίαν vertunt Esaiæ 28, 21. Et hi quidem a זור derivant, quod abalienationem significat. At Symma- chus a זרר quod est dispergere. Vertit enim ἀπεψίαν, quæ nimiam voracitatem consequi solet, cibique male cocti reli- quias per corp9 diffundere: unde & illud sequitur, quod dixere Græci & Latinus, bilis ac nausea. Tertullian. de jejuniis utrum- que conjunxit: usque ad choleram ortygometras cruditando.

## 11:25
Vers. 25. NOR DID THEY CEASE ANY MORE) The Hebrew agrees with the Greek here: ἐκ ἔτι προσέθεντο. After that time they did not have the prophetic spirit, which God had given them only once, so that it might add to them the authority necessary for the new power: See a similar case 1 Sam. 10, 10. Indeed, as Maimonides notes, some generally had the prophetic spirit, others at long intervals, others once.

The Vulgate Latin version must therefore be corrected here. For the contrary exists in the authentic text, namely that they did indeed prophesy then, but did not continue afterwards.

Latin:

Vers. 25. NEC VLTRA CESSAVERVNT) Hebræum cum Græco hic convenit: ἐκ ἔτι προσέθεντο. Post id tem- pus non habuere spiritum propheticum, quem semel tantum illis Deus dederat, ut auctoritatem novæ potestati necessari- am ipsis adderet: Vid. simile 1. Sam. 10, 10. Nimirum, ut no- tat Maimonides, alii plerumque habuere spiritum propheti- cum, alii ex longis intervallis, alii semel.

Emendanda itaque hic Vulg. versio Lat. Con- trarium enim in textu authentico extat, quod nem- pe prophetarint quidem tunc, sed postmodum non perrexerint.

## 11:26
Vers. 26. TWO MEN Eldad and Medad belonged to the number of LXX defined in v. 16. Therefore they did not increase the same, which has seemed rash to some. Grotius says that the LXX were chosen because just as many children of Jacob came into Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 26. DUO VIRI Eldad & Medad pertine- bant ad numerum LXX. definitum v. 16. Non er- go eundem auxerunt, quod nonnullis temere vi- sum. Grotius LXX. fuisse delectos ait, quod toti- dem Jacobi filii in Ægyptum venerint.

## 11:28
Ver. 28. MY LORD MOSES FORBID THEM) See a similar passage in Luke 9, 49.

Latin:

Vers. 28. DOMINE MI MOSES PROHIBE EOS) Si- mile vid. Luc. 9, 49.

## 11:29
WOULD THAT ALL THE PEOPLE MIGHT PROPHESY) Moses, being very good, was free from all envy, belonging entirely to God and to the people.

We have dealt with this vow in a certain Academic program, which it will be worth the effort to append here. It reads as follows: Would that all might prophesy! It was the vow of the greatest of the Prophets in the Old Testament, S. Moses, whom Jerome in Galatians 1, 1 teaches was not only a Prophet but also an Apostle, just as the Hebrews handed down that among the Prophets themselves, and the holy men of God, some were considered both Prophets and Apostles: and whom Gregory the Great, homily XVI on Ezekiel, did not hesitate to prefer in the knowledge of God to Abraham, the Coryphaeus of the Patriarchs, the Father of believers, the Friend of God. That Mosaic vow is referred to in Numbers 11, 29 in these very words: Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his spirit? The occasion of the vow was this: The people had murmured against their leader Moses, and having despised the heavenly food, had desired the meats and onions of Egypt, not without tears, and with such contention that the greatest of men complained before God: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is heavy for me. That was certainly not out of despair, as Cornelius a Lapide introduces his own Popes here, Pius V and Clement VIII, who, in the manner of the Hebrew High Priest Caiaphas, prophesied unknowingly that they could scarcely save their own souls in the Roman Pontificate, the former of whom used to say: when I was a religious (therefore he subsequently ceased to be a religious) I hoped well for the salvation of my soul; having been made a Cardinal I feared; now having been created Pope I almost despair. For although the greatest of men was vehemently disturbed in spirit on account of the huge tumult and sedition of such a multitude—three hundred thousand men—and of their very stiff-necked, brazen, nay, adamantine front, and suffered something human on account of the infirmity with which he was surrounded as a man, yet there is no reason why we should render an ambiguous eulogy of the same man, either regarding his reverence toward God or his meekness toward the people, for which he obtained praise from God himself, that he was the meekest of all men, or brand him with the mark of pusillanimity, unworthy of a heroic spirit, much less imagine that he was like one in despair, which is not to be presumed of this Secretary of divine wisdom, as Cornelius calls him. For the wise man, as Seneca holds regarding the wise man, is removed by a greater interval from the contact of those below than that any harmful force could carry its strength to him: just as heavenly things escape human hands, and nothing is harmed to the divinity by those who fashion temples or idols: so whatever is attempted against the wise man impudently, petulantly, or proudly, is attempted in vain. To those most ardent prayers of the Man of God, afflicted on all sides, the Lord not only satisfied the whole multitude of the people with meat in the horrid desert, not for one day, not for two, not for five, not for ten, but for a whole month by a stupendous miracle, but also, intending to lighten the burden of the government of his servant, he ordered seventy men to be gathered for him, Elders, not so much in age as in prudence and experience and probity of life, masters of the people, or those worthy to be such, and having been brought to the door of the tabernacle, where the Lord presented himself, he filled them with the gifts of the Spirit, having taken them from the spirit of Moses, so that together with Moses they might sustain the burden of government. Which was done without the diminution of the Mosaic gifts, through the communication of similar gifts: not otherwise than when light is taken from a candle, when another is lit, the light of the other is not diminished, but is increased and multiplied, which was observed by Theodoret and Augustine, and expressed by the Targum thus: I will increase of the spirit which is upon you, and I will place it upon them. It happened, however, when the Spirit had rested upon them, and the Elders, brought out to the door of the tabernacle, were prophesying, that two from the number of the seventy men remained in the camp, namely Eldad and Medad: upon whom the Spirit likewise rested, since they too had been enrolled and destined for government, although it is not clear for what reason they did not go out to the tabernacle: Who, stirred by the Spirit, likewise prophesied in the camp. When this was reported to Moses by a boy or minister, and Joshua wished it to be inhibited, the man of God burst out in these words: Why, he said, are you jealous for me? for the asserting and defending of my authority? Who would grant that all the people might prophesy? So far am I from envying them this gift of the Spirit, that I wish from my heart that all Israelites were adorned with a similar gift: What the meaning of this wish is, what gifts of the Spirit are understood, and what kind of prophecy, is not the same opinion among interpreters. That those gifts are granted which the rulers of the people have need of, cannot be doubted, such as the prudence of governing, wisdom, and counsel for resolving doubts not only of law and justice, but also of religion and ceremonies, which were accustomed to be brought to Moses, and also the mighty works necessary for government. Which some wish to be included under the name of prophecy, adding to them moreover the knowledge of hidden things, for deciding lawsuits and hidden causes, the foreknowledge of future things, for either approaching or guarding against them, and warding them off from the people, and finally the impulse and motion toward the praises of God and hymns, since singers and psalmists are also distinguished by the name of Prophets, and are said to prophesy on harps, psalteries, and cymbals, 1 Paral. 16. Although indeed all those things are most rightly referred to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, whom they acknowledge as the author, it is not to be thought that all those things are included by the word prophesying in the Mosaic wish. Which Cornelius a Lapide rashly confuses, since the gifts of the Spirit and Prophecy differ, as genus and species, broader and narrower. Therefore he does not fear to prefer here to the authentic text (which is the stupidity of the Papists, after they allowed their mind to be bewitched by the Tridentine decrees) the παρόραμα of the Vulgate, where, concerning the elders who had gone out to the tabernacle, it translated the Hebrew words as they prophesied, AND DID NOT CEASE FURTHER, which render the contrary sense entirely, namely that they prophesied only on that day, and not further, AND DID NOT ADD FURTHER, which even the LXX interpreters, Theodoret, and Vatablus retained, leaning upon this confusion as a certain fulcrum: namely that these seventy elders were in continuous need of the spirit, although not as regards the praises of God and song, yet as regards other parts of it, for government and for deciding lawsuits; and thus they always had the prophetic Spirit, as if prepared for them in habit and assisting, although they did not always prophesy in act, but only then when they had to answer the questions of the people: Perhaps, just as the Roman Pontiff always has the infallible Spirit prepared in habit and assisting, even if he does not always use it in the same act, but sometimes has to admit that he is destitute of the actual motion of the same, which he professed to the Legates of the King of Spain in the controversy concerning the immaculate conception of the virgin: But just as the Jesuit does not piously enough remove devotion to the praises of God and hymns from the gifts of the Spirit necessary for government, as if those who sit at the key of government have less need of them, so he wrongly requires in them the gift of prophecy, or the Prophetic Spirit in deciding questions: since the rulers of the people are not, or ought not to be, Prophets immediately, and that impulse which is attributed to these Elders when they are said to have prophesied was extraordinary; nor was any promise of the perpetual assistance of the Prophetic Spirit handed down to them, nor is any trace of it found here. That assertion is rash,

that God spoke to them inwardly, always, when they had to answer the questions of the people, and inspired what was to be said or done, just as He inspired the Prophets with the things which they had to say or do. Concerning which neither a trace nor a footprint is found in the text, or elsewhere in scripture, as far as these seventy Elders are concerned. The single word of prophesying is had here, mention is made of a single prophetic act, nor are they said to have prophesied anywhere else. Nor are the Pontificians certain about Prophecy in the first act: whether it is a certain quality, or a habit, which Jacob Bonfrerius says theologians generally deny in this place, or whether it only says a divine deputation to receive the prophetic light? although the same man inclines to this, that these elders always remained prophets in the first act not by reason of any habit, but because by reason of divine deputation to the acts of prophesying that Spirit would return from time to time at intervals. But what else do they have to bring forward for that opinion, besides the erroneous Vulgate translation, in which it is held, but contrary to the original text, they prophesied, AND DID NOT CEASE FURTHER, about which we have already spoken. And yet they build upon this rash persuasion the dogma concerning the infallibility of councils: although they conclude, moreover, very ignorantly from a Council convened by God Himself, and instructed by the Spirit present with God in an illustrious Φανερώσει, to councils gathered by Papal authority; and also from the gifts of government granted to individual rulers (which rendered neither individuals nor the whole body infallible in pronouncing, even if they were a great help to them) to the gift of infallibility in all things, from counsel and wisdom in those matters which pertain to policy, whether civil or ecclesiastical, to judgment, power, and the faculty of knowing in controversies of faith. And how infallible was the judgment of the LXX Elders in the great Sanhedrin, or the condemnation of Christ, which Cornelius affirms was made by them, let him teach? What kind of ἀκρισία (lack of judgment) is detected even in Rob. Bellarm. lib. IV. de R. P. cap. 24. and his hyperaspist I. Gretser, as also in Joh. Lorinus on this passage, when they prove from the present place that all Bishops receive jurisdiction from the Pope, when neither was Moses a Pontiff, nor were the LXX elders Bishops; nor did these Elders receive jurisdiction from Moses; but they were instructed by God with the spirit of counsel and prudence, after the likeness of Moses. No less in vain is Oleaster, in favor of traditions, asserting that the true understanding was handed down to these elders by Moses, which he had received on Mount Sinai, and that it was communicated by them further to the Prophets, and from these to the Men of the Great Synagogue: which is a fiction of the Hebrews, and is nowhere found in the Scriptures. This Spirit pertained to the good of others, as Lorinus not badly says, so that they could be rightly ruled with prudence, counsel, doctrine, knowledge of law and religion, and a clear understanding of doubtful matters: but that he says a certain faculty of prophesying was granted at the same time, i.e., either of celebrating divine praises in a singular manner, or of better understanding the divine letters, or sometimes even of prophesying, or of rushing forcefully upon enemies, as was done by Saul, and that the gift of sanctifying grace, or its increase, was added at the same time, is ἄγραφον (unwritten) and merely precarious. That one act of prophesying does not make Prophets, just as the one prophecy of Caiaphas did not in the least make him a prophet. It was only an indication of the Spirit received, which then exerted itself in them by prophesying, but it is not read that it exerted itself to that extent afterwards: Namely, what pleases Bonfrerius, that they should both sing divine praises and declare certain hidden things, so that both by the very manner of speech and by their outward demeanor it might sufficiently appear that they were moved by a certain divine spirit, just as we also read concerning Saul: But Bonfrerius acknowledges that there ceased in them the spirit, regarding that unusual manner of prophesying, by which they were seized on that first occasion, so that they appeared as if possessed, and less in control of themselves, although he asserts, misled by the common translation, that they did not lack divine illuminations in judging and instructing the people, and he thinks, quite absurdly with Oleaster, that the sense of the Hebrew source is likewise included in the same word, even though they are contrary. However, Cornelius restricts this act of prophesying—without cause and contrary to the more famous meaning of the word—to enthusiasm in celebrating the praises of God, appealing to the Abulensis; who, however, acknowledges that those prophesying at the same time brought forth some things about future events or certain hidden truths; thus the Rabbis, with the Jerusalem Targum, rashly define those hidden and future things, while Scripture is silent, especially regarding those two prophesying in the camp, because they prophesied—as Serarius brings forward the words of the Paraphrast in lib. 1. in Jos. cap. 7. quaest. 4.—about the death of Moses, and the succession of Joshua in the leadership, and the quails that were to fly in, and about the punishment to be taken by the Israelites, and also about Gog and Magog being defeated by Christ at the end of the world. Others say the Elders prophesied about that which pertained to the government of the people: but this is asserted ἄτερ γραφῆς. However, the oracles of Eldad and Medad can hardly be entirely hidden from the Papists, since in the book of Hermas, authentic to them, which is inscribed The Shepherd, chapter II, it is held thus: The Lord is near to those who turn to Him, as it is written in Eldad and Medad, who prophesied in the wilderness to the people: which Cornelius also does not reject. But let them feed themselves as they wish on the fodder of that shepherd, and on spurious writings. We do not concern ourselves with those. Scripture expresses that the LXX prophesied, and that those two prophesied, since six from each tribe, and thus seventy-two, had been deputed; and it implies that all prophesied in such a way that they were recognized as prophesying. But what either the former or the latter prophesied, it does not express. Nor is it therefore our place to define that. That, however, would be worthy of a question, although entirely neglected by the Papist interpreters whom we have seen: Why did Moses wish that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them His Spirit? That the Spirit of the Lord is to be given to all is certainly to be wished (although the Chaldean takes this part of the wish even concerning the Spirit of Prophecy): but indeed, that all should prophesy, and that such a multitude should be carried away by a prophetic Spirit and driven by enthusiasm, is it to be believed that Moses knew this? Where this is primarily to be observed, that the wish is general, and that the word of prophesying, which is in itself common, is not to be restricted according to the mind of Moses either to the foretelling of future things or other hidden matters, which no man could penetrate without a new revelation from God, or to that manner of prophesying which is apparent and reveals itself through external signs; since all the people are rightly said to prophesy; even if they do not all prophesy in the same way, or conduct themselves in the act of prophesying; but some prophesy by singing hymns and praises of God, others by interpreting the word of God, others by foretelling future events, revealing hidden things, and others by performing other prophetic acts. And it may be considered that Moses, the great Prophet, because of his familiar conversation with God and the more abundant illumination of the Spirit of Prophecy, with which he was endowed above others, was not ignorant of that outpouring

of the Spirit, which the Lord predicted through Joel chapter II, and that he had at the same time included the same in his wish: O that that blessed time might approach, in which all the people will prophesy! In which the Lord is about to give His Spirit to all! In which the Spirit may be poured out upon all flesh! That the most clear-sighted of those who saw the Old Testament truly saw in the spirit and longed for those blessed times, many other things establish, such as the prediction concerning the spiritual circumcision of Israel and his seed, Deuteronomy 30:6, the final prophetic blessing upon the Israelite virtues in the last chapter of Deuteronomy, and the admiration of that same blessedness: Blessed are you, O Israel, who is like you, O people, who are saved in the Lord? etc., and then primarily the stirring up of the nations, Deuteronomy 32:43, explained in Romans 15:10, Rejoice, O nations, with His people; would that those times might shine forth, in which, with the people of the Lord, the nations also, alien from Israel, might rejoice in sweet harmony and concert, with unanimous heart, and celebrate God, and prophesy with hymns, and songs, and lyres, and psalteries? That a man θεήλατον had embraced this sentiment in his mind with a general wish is now confirmed all the more abundantly, because I see that the pious ancients also judged the same, Cyril of Jerusalem, and of Alexandria, Theodoret, and Procopius; the former of whom took the words of Moses prophetically, as if to say, Moses: Now indeed a particular grace has occurred (regarding those seventy elders) but at some time there will be a copious donation: For it was indicated, he says, that which was to be, or was to be fulfilled at Pentecost among us, that is, in Jerusalem, where Cyril was preaching.

Which we celebrate even now daily in the Church with a grateful mind, we who are now also rendered partakers of the Mosaic wish in this Zion of ours, when the elders, instructed by the Spirit of the Lord πίονι μέτρῳ, not in age, but in doctrine and virtue, who prophesy not in the camps, or in the tabernacle of Israel, but in the great house of God, the Church of the living God, not privately, but publicly, in Temples and Schools, exercise the gifts of the Spirit, received from the Spirit of Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, singing and interpreting the Word of God with hymns, and prayers, and sermons, and readings, and bringing forth its hidden senses: we point out our Candidates, excellently versed in divinely inspired doctrine, also sufficiently conspicuous for their merits in the Church of God, etc.

Latin:

QVIS TRIBVAT, VT OMNIS POPVLVS PROPHE- TET) Moses ut valde bonus ab omni vacabat invidia, Dei totus & populi.

De hoc voto egimus in programmate quodam Academico, quod operæ prætium erit hic subjun- gere. Sic autem habet: Utinam omnes prophetarent! Votum fuit maxi- mi Prophetarum in Vet. Testamento, S. Mosis, quem Hieronymus in Galat. I, 1. non Prophetam tan- tum, sed & Apostolum fuisse docet, quemadmodum Ebræi inter ipsos Prophetas, & sanctos Dei viros quosdam & Prophetas & Apostolos habitos tradide- re: quemque Gregor. M. homil. XVI. in Ezech. in scientia Dei, Abrahamo Patriarcharum Coryphæo, credentium Patri, Dei Amico, præferre non dubi- tavit. Refertur autem votum illud Mosaicum Nu- mer. 11, 29. his omnino verbis: Quis tribuat, ut omnis populus prophetet, & det eis Dominus spiritum suum? Occasio voti hæc erat: Murmurarat populus ad- versus Ducem Mosen, contemtoque cibo cœlesti, carnes ac cepas Ægypti desiderarat, non sine lacry- mis, tantaque contentione, ut vir summus penes Deum quereretur: Non possum solus sustinere omnem hunc populum, quia gravis est mihi. Non id sane ex desperatione, uti Pontifices hic suos introducit Cor- nelius Lapideus, Pium V. & Clementem IIX. qui sese in Pontificatu Romano animas suas vix salvare pos- se, Cajaphæ Pontificis Ebræi more, nescii prophe- tarunt, quorum prior ille dicere consueverat: cum essem religiosus, (deinceps ergo religiosus esse desiit) sperabam bene de salute animæ; Cardinalis factus ex- timui; Nunc Pontifex creatus pene despero. Quan- quam enim animo vehementer, ob tantæ multitu- dinis, tricefies centenorum hominum millium, eo- rumque duræ admodum cervicis, & æneæ, imo a- damantinæ frontis, ingentem tumultum & seditio- nem, perturbatus fuerit Maximus virorum, & hu- mani aliquid, ob infirmitatem, qua circumdatus, ut homo, erat, passus sit, non tamen est, quod eidem vel reverentiæ adversus Deum, vel mansuetudinis erga populum, cujus laudem à Deo ipso adeptus est, quod super omnes homines fuerit mitissimus, elo- gium ambiguum reddamus, aut pusillanimitatis, Heroico spiritu indignæ notam inuramus, nedum desperabundo eum similem fuisse existimemus, quod de hoc sapientiæ divinæ Secretario, quem Cor- nelius vocat, præsumendum non est. Sapiens enim, ut Seneca in sapiente habet, majore intervallo conta- ctu inferiorum abductus est, quam ut ulla vis noxia ad illum vires suas perferat: uti cœlestia humanas manus effugiunt, & ab his, qui templa, aut simulacra con- flant, nil divinitati nocetur: ita quicquid sit in sapien- tem proterve, petulanter, superbe, frustra tentatur. Ad istas ergo Viri Dei undiquaque afflicti preces ardentissimas, tum carnibus universum populi multitudinem, non uno die, non duobus, non quinque, non decem, sed integro mense stupen- do miraculo, saturavit in horrido deserto Domi- nus, tum onus etiam regiminis servi sui levaturus, jussit sibi congregari septuaginta viros Seniores, non tam ætate, quam prudentia & experientia, at- que vitæ probitate, Magistros populi, vel dignos, qui tales essent, adductosque ad ostium taberna- culi, cui se præsentem sistebat Dominus, acceptis de spiritu Mosis donis Spiritus implevit, ut una cum Mose onus gubernationis sustentarent. Quod sine donorum Mosaicorum imminutione factum, per similium donorum communicationem: non secus at- que luce à candela sumta, cum accenditur alia, non imminuitur lux alteri, sed augetur & multi- plicatur, quod Theodoreto, & Augustino observa- tum, & à Targum ita expressum: augebo de spiritu, qui est super te, & ponam super eos. Accidit au- tem, quum requievisset in illis Spiritus, & pro- phetarent Seniores ad ostium tabernaculi edu- cti, ut duo è numero septuaginta virorum in ca- stris remanserint, nimirum Eldad, & Medad: su- per quos pariter requievit Spiritus, siquidem & ipsi descripti, ac regimini destinati fuerint, etsi non constat, qua de causa non exierint ad tabernacu- lum: Qui agitati à Spiritu in castris similiter pro- phetarunt. Quod ubi Mosi per puerum, vel Mini- strum nunciaretur, & inhibitum vellet Josua, in hæc verba prorupit vir Dei: Quid, inquit, æmula- ris pro me? pro asserenda & tuenda autoritate mea? Quis tribuat, ut omnis populus prophetet? Adeo non invideo illis donum hoc Spiritus, ut ex animo exo- ptem omnes Israelites simili dono exornari: Quæ voti hujus sententia sit, quæ dona intelligantur Spi- ritus, & cujusmodi prophetia, non eadem mens est interpretum. Dona ea concessa esse, quibus re- ctores populi opus habent, dubitari nequit, qualia sunt prudentia regendi, sapientia, & consilium ad dubia non modo juris & justitiæ, sed religionis etiam, & ceremoniarum, quæ ad Mosen deferri so- lebant, expediunda, nec non virtutes ad regimen necessariæ. Quæ nomine prophetiæ etiam com- prehendi nonnulli volunt, iisdem insuper adden- tes occultorum cognitionem, ad decidendas lites & causas occultas, futurorum prænotionem, ad ea vel accessenda, vel præcavenda, & arcenda à populo, impulsum denique ac motionem ad Dei laudes, & hy- mnos, quum Cantores etiam, ac Psalmistà Prophe- tarum nomine insigniantur, & prophetare in cytha- ris, Psalteriis, & cymbalis dicantur, 1. Paral. 16. Quanquam vero illa omnia ad dona Spiritus S. quem autorem agnoscunt, referantur rectissime, non tamen verbo prophetandi in voto Mosaico ea omnia concludi existimandum. Quæ temere con- fundit Cornelius à Lapide, quum differant Spiritus dona & Prophetia, ceu genus & species, latius & an- gustius. Ideo authentico textui non veretur hic præferre, (qui stupor est Papistarum, postquam per Tridentina decreta sibi mentem excantari passi sunt) παρόραμα vulgarii, ubi de senibus ad taber- naculum egressis, verba Ebræa transtulit prophe- taverunt, NEC ULTRA CESSAVERUNT, quæ contrarium prorsus sensum reddunt, quod nempe illo die tantum prophetarint, non ultra, NEC ADDIDERUNT ULTRA, quem etiam LXX. interpretes, Theodoretus & Vatablus retinuerunt, huic confusioni ceu fulcro cuidam innixus: quod nempe spiritu, licet non quoad Dei laudes, & cantum, tamen quoad alias ejus partes continuo indiguerint hi septuaginta senes, ad regimen, & ad lites decidendas; adeoque semper habuerint Spiritum propheticum, quasi in habitu sibi paratum, & assistentem, licet actu non semper prophetarint, sed tunc tantum cum quæ- stionibus populi respondere debuerunt: Forte, sicut semper in habitu paratum, & assistentem habet Spiritum infallibilem Romanus Pontifex, utut eo- dem actu non utatur semper, sed actuali motione ejusdem se destitui fateri quandoque necessum ha- beat, quod in controversia de immaculata virgi- nis conceptione, Legatis Regis Hispaniarum pro- fessus est: Sed uti à donis Spiritus, ad regimen ne- cessariis, non satis pie Jesuita removet devotionem ad laudes Dei & hymnos, quasi opus illa minus ha- beant, qui ad clavem gubernationis sedent, ita do- num prophetiæ, vel Spiritum Propheticum in quæ- stionibus decidendis, perperam in illis requirit: quum Rectores populi non actutum sint, aut esse debeant Prophetæ, & extraordinarius ille fuerit im- pulsus,qui hisce Senioribus tribuitur, cum prophe- tasse dicuntur; neque de perpetua Spiritus Prophe- tici assistentia promissio ulla ipsis tradita sit, nec a- pex ullus hic habeatur. Temeraria est illa assertio,

Deum eis interius, semper, cum quæstionibus populi respondendum fuit, loquutum esse, ac inspirasse, quid dicendum, vel agendum esset, perinde ut inspiravit Prophetis ea, quæ dicere, vel agere debebant. De quo nec vola, nec vestigium in textu, aut alias in scriptu- ra, quantum ad hos septuaginta Seniores, depre- henditur. Unicum prophetandi verbum hîc ha- betur, de unico actu prophetico mentio sit, nec uspiam alias prophetasse dicuntur. Neque de Pro- phetia in actu primo certi sunt Pontificii : utrum ea qualitas quædam, aut habitus sit, quod fere Theo- logos negare ait Jacob Bonfrerius in h. l. an vero solum dicat deputationem divinam ad recipiendum lumen propheticum? quamvis eo inclinet idem, quod hi senes semper manserint in actu primo pro- phetæ non ratione alicujus habitus, sed quod ratione deputationis divinæ ad prophetandi actus subinde per intervalla is Spiritus rediret. Quid vero pro ista sententia adferre aliud habent, præter erroneam translationem vulgatam, in qua habetur, sed refra- gante textu originali prophetaverunt, NEC UL- TRA CESSAVERUNT, de qua jam ante dixi- mus. Et superstruunt tamen huic persuasioni te- merariæ dogma de infallibilitate conciliorum: quamvis insuper perquam imperite à Concilio à Deo ipso convocato, & Spiritu à Deo, illustri Φανερώσει præsente, instructo, ad concilia Papali autoritate congregata; nec non à donis regiminis singulis recto- ribus concessis (quæ nec singulos, nec universos in pronunciando infallibiles reddidere, etsi magno adjumento ipsis fuerint) ad donum infallibilita- tis in universis, à consilio & sapientia in iis, quæ ad Politiam sive civilem, sive Ecclesiasticam perti- nent, ad judicium, vim & facultatem cognoscendi in controversiis fidei, concludant. Et quam infallibile judicium Seniorum LXX. in magno Synedrio fue- rit vel condemnatio Christi, quam ab ipsis factam esse Cornelius affirmat, edoceat? Qualis ἀκρισία etiam in Rob. Bellarm. lib. IV. de R. P. cap. 24. ejus hyperaspista I. Gretsero, ut & Joh. Lorino in h. l. de- prehenditur, cum è præsenti loco probant, omnes Episcopos à Papa Jurisdictionem accipere, quum nec Moses Pontifex fuerit, nec LXX. senes Episcopi; neque Jurisdictionem à Mose hi Seniores accepe- rint; sed spiritu consilii, & Prudentiæ, ad instar Mosis, instructi fuerint à Deo. Non minus frustra est Oleaster, in gratiam traditionum, afferens, tra- ditam istis senibus veram intelligentiam à Mose, quam in Monte Sinai acceperat, eamque ab ipsis porro Prophetis, ab his Viris Synagogæ M. comu- nicatam: quod ab Ebræorum commento est, nec uspiam in Scripturis invenitur. Pertinebat hic Spi- ritus ad bonum aliorum, ut non male Lorinus, ut re- cte regi possent cum prudentia, consilio, doctrina, no- titia juris & religionis, perspicaci dubiorum scientia: quod autem concessam simul ait facultatem quandam prophetandi, i. e. vel celebrandi laudes divinas, modo quodam singulari, vel divinas literas melius intelligen- di, vel interdum etiam vaticinandi, vel irruendi for- titer in inimicos, ut à Saule factum, & adjectum una sanctificantis gratiæ munus, aut incrementum, ἄγραφον est, & mere precarium. Unus ille pro- phetandi actus non facit Prophetas, uti vaticina- tio una Cajaphæ eum prophetam minime fecit. Erat tantum indicium accepti Spiritus, qui tum in iis se exerebat vaticinando, postea autem sese exe- ruisse eatenus non legitur: Scilicet, quod Bonfre- rio placet, ut & divinas laudes canerent, & abdita quædam enunciarent, ut tum ipso orationis modo, tum exteriore habitu satis appareret, ipsos divino quodam spiritu agi, quemadmodum & de Saule legimus: Cessasse autem in iis agnoscit Bonfrerius spiritum, quoad modum illum insolentem prophetandi, quo prima illa vice correpti fuerunt, ut quasi Entheati, & minus sui compotes apparerent, etsi in judicanda, & instituenda plebe, divinis illustrationibus non caruisse, seductus vulgata translatione, asserat, cujus pariter, & Ebræi fontis sensum, ut contrarii sint, eadem voce comprehensum, cum Oleastro perabsurde existimat. Quam interpretationem duriorem esse fatetur Lorinus: sensui Cajetani, & Pagnini acquiescens, quod non amplius addiderint vaticinari, & causam reddit ex Theodoreto: quia non vaticinandi, sed gubernandi causa proponebantur, etsi neget, ablatum spiritum prophetiæ, utpote quo per totum regimen indiguerunt, confundens donum Spiritus cum actu prophetandi. Actum autem hunc prophetandi, ut citra causam & contra significationem vocis famosiorem restringit Cornelius ad Enthusiasmum in laudibus Dei celebrandis, ad Abulensem provocans; qui vero simul de futuris, aut veritatibus quibusdam absconditis nonnulla protulisse vaticinantes agnoscit; sic temere abscondita & futura illa, tacente scriptura, definiunt cum Targum Hierosolymitano Rabbini, maxime quoad duos illos in castris prophetantes, quod nempe de Mosis morte, & Josuæ in principatu successione, & coturnicibus advolaturis, de supplicio ab Israelitis sumendo, item de Gog & Magog in fine mundi à Christo debellandis, uti Paraphrastæ verba adducit Serarius lib. 1. in Jos. cap. 7. quæst. 4. vaticinati sint. Alii prophetasse Seniores de eo ajunt, quod ad gubernationem populi pertinebat: sed hoc ἄτερ γραφῆς asseritur. Papistas autem vix latere omnino possunt oracula Eldad & Medad, quum in libro Hermæ, ipsis authentico, qui Pastor inscribitur cap. II. ita habeatur: Prope est Dominus his qui se ad eum convertunt, sicut scriptum est in Eldad & Medad, qui vaticinati sunt in solitudine populo: quæ etiam non rejicit Cornelius. Sed pascant illi sese ut velint pastoris istius pabulis, & scriptis spuriis. Nos ea non moramur. Scriptura vaticinatos esse LXX. vaticinatos & duos illos, quum è singulis tribubus sex, adeoque LXXII. deputati fuerint, exprimit: omnesque ita vaticinatos, ut vaticinantes agnoscerentur, innuit. Quid vero sive illi, sive isti vaticinati sint, non exprimit. Nec nostrum ergo est illud definire. Id vero quæstione dignum foret, etsi ab interpp. quos vidimus, Papisticis, prorsus neglectum: Qui voverit Moses, ut prophetet omnis populus, & det eis Dominus Spiritum suum? Spiritum Domini dari omnibus vovendum utique, (quamvis de Spiritu Prophetiæ etiam hanc voti partem accipiat Chaldæus): at vero prophetent omnes, ac Spiritu prophetico abrepti, Enthusiasmo agatur tanta multitudo, num novisse Mosen credendum? Ubi hoc imprimis observandum, votum generale esse, neque verbum prophetandi, quod in se commune, vel ad vaticinationem de rebus futuris, aut aliis absconditis, quas hominum nullus, citra novam Dei revelationem penetrare queat, vel modum illum prophetandi apparentem, & per externa indicia sese prodentem restringendum ex mente Mosis esse; quum populus omnis prophetare recte dicatur; etiamsi non omnes eadem ratione vaticinentur, aut in actu prophetandi sese gerant; sed alii prophetent hymnos & laudes Dei decantando, alii verbum Dei interpretando, alii futura prænunciando, abscondita revelando, alii alia prophetica peragendo. Et censeri queat, Mosen Prophetam magnum, mysteriorum Novi Testamenti ob familiarem cum Deo conversationem, & Spiritus Prophetiæ uberiorem illuminationem, quo præ aliis instructus fuit, haud ignarum ejus effusionis

Spiritus, quam per Joelem cap. II. prædixit Dominus, eandem voto suo complexum simul fuisse : O utinam beatum illud tempus appropinquet, quo populus omnis prophetabit! quo Dominus omnibus Spiritum suum daturus est! Quo effundatur Spiritus super omnem carnem! Vidisse sane in spiritu, & exoptasse videntium Vet. Test. oculatissimum beata illa tempora, tum alia multa stabiliunt, utpote prædictio de spirituali circumcisione Israelis, & seminis ejus Deuter. 30, 6. benedictio Prophetica novissima virtutibus Israeliticis Deuter. ultimo, facta, & admiratio beatitudinis ejusdem: Beatus es tu Israel, quis similis tui popule, qui salvaris in Domino? &c. tum imprimis excitatio gentium Deuter. 32, 43. ab Apostolo de Vocatione atque illuminatione gentium sub Nov. Test. Rom. 15, 10. exposita, Lætamini gentes cum plebe ejus; utinam tempora illa affulgeant, quibus cum populo Domini gentes etiam alienæ ab Israele suavi harmonia, & concentu, corde unanimi lætentur, Deumque celebrent, & hymnis, ac canticis, Cytharis, atq; Psalteriis prophetent? Quam sententiam voto generali Virum θεήλατον animo complexum fuisse jam eo uberius confirmat, quod videam pios veteres idem etiam censuisse, Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum, & Alexandrinum, Theodoretum, & Procopium; quorum prior Mosis verba prophetice accepit, q. d. Moses; Nunc quidem particularis contigit gratia (quoad istos LXX. senes) sed aliquando copiosa erit donatio: Indicabatur enim, inquit, id quod futurum, vel complendum erat in Pentecoste apud nos, id est, in Hierusalem, ubi Cyrillus concionabatur.

Quod completum etiamnum quotidie in Ecclesia grata mente celebramus, qui voti Mosaici compotes jam quoque peculiariter in hac Sione nostra reddimur, cum Spiritus Domini πίονι μέτρῳ instructos, senes, non ætate, sed doctrina & virtute, qui prophetant non in castris, aut in tabernaculo Israelis, sed in domo Dei magna, Ecclesia Dei viventis, non privatim, sed publice, in Templis, & Scholis, dona Spiritus, à Mosis, Prophetarum & Apostolorum Spiritu accepta, exerunt, hymnis, & orationibus, concionibus, & lectionibus, Verbum Dei decantantes, & interpretantes, abditosque ejus sensus proferentes: Candidatos Nostros indigitamus, in doctrina divinitus inspirata egregie versatos, meritis etiam in Ecclesiam Dei satis conspicuos, &c.

## 11:31 Addition
On v. 31. BUT A WIND &c.

That this mission of quails is different from that in Exod. 16. is evident from the place and time: because that one occurred in the desert of Sin at the eighth station, this one at the thirteenth station at the graves of craving: that one occurred in the first year of the exodus on the 15th day of the second month, before they had come to Sinai, when manna was given; this one in the second year, after Manna had been exhibited, and after the departure from Mount Sinai Num. 33, 16. Compare c. 10, 11. Cornelius a Lapide notes that God gave the quails, both because they abound in the Arabian Gulf, and because their flesh is excellent and delicate. Although indeed some say that the flesh of quails is to be condemned, because they also feed on poisons, because Hellebore is their food according to Aristotle, l. de plant. c. 5. and Galen to Piso, and they alone besides man are subject to the falling sickness, and so are considered unwholesome by Pliny 10, 23. and Solinus; yet Aristotle himself commends quails, and compares them to partridges, and Bochart in Hierozoicon 2. 1. 16. teaches that the quail is of good juice, and of excellent flavor, and useful to those who are well, from Rasis tract. 3. l. 10. de carnib. volatib. and Ibnezohar l. de alimentis. Nicol. Maffa in Epist. Medicin. apud Gesner. says, Averroes wonderfully praises the flesh of quails. Athenaeus lists them among the more sumptuous dishes of the table. Finally, Philo testifies that quails were a delicacy to the Jews. And not only does the quail not infect man with the disease from which it suffers, but the brain of a quail is a powerful amulet against it, according to Galen. But if the eating of quails were less healthy, it should be known 1. that it was not an ordinary food. 2. that God could easily have removed, by a miracle, whatever was harmful.

Latin:

Ad v. 31. VENTUS AUTEM &c.

Hanc coturnicum missionem diversam esse ab illa Exod. 16. e loco & tempore constat: quia illa in deserto Sin octava mansione, hæc in mansione decima tertia in sepulchris concupiscentiæ: illa anno primo egressus die 15. mensis secundi, antequam in Sinai venissent, cum daretur manna, contigit; hæc anno secundo, post exhibitum Manna, & post excessum e monte Sinai Num. 33, 16. Conf. c. 10, 11. Coturnices dedisse Deum Corn. a Lap. notat, tum quia abundant in sinu Arabico, tum quia caro earum excellens & delicata est. Quanquam vero nonnulli coturnices mensis damnari dicant, quod & venenis vescantur, quia Elleborus earum cibus teste Aristot. l. de plant. c. 5. & Galeno ad Pisonem, & comitialem morbum solæ præter hominem sentiant, adeoque insalubres habentur a Plinio 10, 23. & Solino; Aristoteles tamen ipse coturnices commendat, & perdicibus comparat, & Bochartus in Hie- roz. 2. 1. 16. coturnicem esse boni succi, & egregii saporis, ac valentibus utilem, e Rasis tract. 3. l. 10. de carnib. volatib. & Ibnezohar l. de alimentis docet. Nicol. Maffa in Epist. Medicin. apud Gesner. Averroes, inquit, mirifice coturnicum carnem laudat. Athenæus inter lautiora mensæ fercula recenset. Testatur denique Philo coturnices in deliciis fuisse Judæis. Nec solum coturnix morbi, quo laborat contagione hominem non inficit, sed adversus illum potens est amuletum coturnicis cerebrum teste Galeno. Quod si esus coturnicum esset minus salubris, sciendum 1. non fuisse cibum ordinarium. 2. facile Deum potuisse per miraculum, quicquid erat noxium, eximere.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

The murmur of Miriam, and her punishment.

Verse 1.

BECAUSE OF HIS ETHIOPIAN WIFE) Namely, because they wanted him, having dismissed the foreign woman, to become the husband of some Israelite woman, for which reason they also contumeliously call her an Ethiopian instead of a Midianite: wrongly; for since she had submitted herself to the law, she was to be held as an Israelite, like Rahab and Ruth.

Tostatus gives this reason for the murmuring, that Zipporah, the wife of Moses, was preferred over Miriam. Lyranus, that he had separated himself from his wife as regards the marriage bed; so also the Arab. But that cause seems to be hinted at in the text, that he had taken a foreign woman, as Oleaster, Fagius, Vatablus, and others maintain. Furthermore, without insult, the wife of Moses could be called כושית even if she were a Midianite; because not only the Ethiopia of the Abyssinians, or India, but Arabia also was called Cushaea. And the Midianites were also called Cushites, not because they were born from Cush, but because they occupied a part of the region of Cush, as Junius, Piscator, Ainsworth, and Mariana [maintain] from Gen. 10:7 and chapter 25:2. Indeed, כוש in the Scriptures [does not mean] Ethiopia as [it does for] the Hebrews, Greeks, Philo, Josephus, and most of the Fathers think, but Bochart proves it is Arabia: 1. from Hab. 3:7, where Cush and Midian are placed as equivalents; 2. from Job 28:19, where the topaz of Cush is of Arabia, which was very well known, whereas none of the ancients knew of an Ethiopian one; 3. from Ezek. 29:10, 'I will make the land of Egypt desolate from the tower of Syene' (this was the boundary of Egypt towards Ethiopia, says Pliny 5.9, and Solinus 35, and Strabo book 17, Josephus on the Jewish War 5.1) 'even unto the border of it' of Arabia, by which the part of Egypt most remote from Ethiopia is bounded. 4. From Ezek. 30:9, 'After I have set a fire in Egypt, messengers shall go forth in ships to Cush,' i.e., Arabia, into which they often travel by ships through the Red Sea, but by no means to Ethiopia, into which one cannot even sail up the Nile because of the cataracts near Syene. (5.) From 2 Kings 19:9, where Tirhakah the King comes unexpectedly, certainly not from Ethiopia, from where he could not have betaken himself unless Egypt had been subdued, and from 2. Chron. 14:9, ch. 21:16, where the Arabs are said to be neighbors to the Cushites. See also Zeph. 3:10, Isa. 18:1. These things Bochart in Phaleg, book 4, ch. 2, p. 238, who also wishes the word כושי in Jer. 13:23 to denote not an Ethiopian, but an Arab, because the Arabs also are of a blackish and swarthy color, as the eyewitness Ludovico de Varthema testifies in his Navigations, book 1, ch. 8. Compare Cant. 1:5. Which opinion of Bochart we leave in its own place. For it is not to be rashly denied that the word כושי denotes an Ethiopian somewhere. It is a fable that Josephus says Tharbis, the daughter of the King of Egypt, was married by Moses: for his wife was Zipporah, as Augustine, Theodoret, the Hebrews, and others commonly acknowledge, of whom this passage treats. Compare B. Walther, Harmony on this passage.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

Murmur Mirjam, ejusque pœna.

Vers. 1.

PROPTER VXOREM EJVS ÆTHIOPISSAM) Nempe quod vellent eum dimissa extranea maritum Israelitidis alicujus fieri, quare & contumeliose pro Madianitide appellant Æthiopissam: male; nam cum ea legi se subjecisset habenda erat pro Israelitide ut Rahab & Ruth.

TOstatus hanc causam reddit murmuris, quod Sephora uxor Mosis Mariæ præferri voluerit. Lyranus quod ab uxore se quantum ad torum separarit; Sic & Arabs. Sed causa illa videtur in textu innui, quod alienigenam duxerit, ut Oleastr. Fag. Vatablus & alii volunt. Cæterum citra contumeliam uxor Mosis כושית etsi Madianitis, dici poterat; quia non Æthiopia solum Abassinorum, vel India, sed Arabia Chusæa etiam dicta. Et vocati quoque Madianitæ sunt Chusitæ, non quod ex Chus prognati, sed quia obtinebant partem regionis Chusi ut Junius, Piscator. Ainswort. Mariana è Gen. 10, 7. cap. 25, 2. Imo כוש in Sacris non Æthiopiam ut Ebr. Græci, Philo, Josephus & plerique Patres putant, sed Arabiam esse Bochart. probat 1. ex Hab. 3, 7. ubi Chuz & Midian ponuntur ut ἰσοδύναμα 2. è Job. 28, 19. ubi Topazius כוש Arabiæ, quæ notissi- ma erat, cum Æthiopicæ nullus veterum, 3. ex Ez. 29, 10. Desolabo terram Ægypti à turri Syenes (is ter- minus erat Ægypti versus Æthiopiam, ait Plinius 5, 9. & Solinus 35. ac Strabo l. 17. Joseph. de B. J. 5, 1.) usque ad terminum ejus Arabiæ, qua terminatur Ægypti pars ab Æthiopia remotissima. 4. Ex Ez. 30, 9. Postquam immisero ignem in Ægyptum, pro- dibunt nuncii navibus ad Chuz, i. e. Arabiam, in quam navibus per mare rubrum sæpe commeant, ad Æthiopiam nequaquam, in quam ne per Ni- lum quidem adversum navigatur propter catara- ctas prope Syenem. (5.) Ex 2. Reg. 19, 9. ubi Tira- ka Rex improviso venit, non certe ex Æthiopia, unde se conferre non potuit nisi subacta Ægypto, & ex 2. Par. 14, 9. c. 21, 16. ubi Arabes finitimi Chitæis dicuntur. Vid. & Soph. III, 10. Es. 18, 1. Hæc Bochart. in Phaleg. IV. 2. c. 238. qui etiam Jer. 13, 23. Vocem כושי non Æthiopem, sed Arabem notare vult, quia & Arabes coloris sunt nigricantis & subfusci, ut testis est αὐτόπτης Ludov. Vartomannus Navigat. lib. I. c. 8. Conf. Cant. 1, 5. Quam Bocharti senten- tiam suo relinquimus loco. Non enim temere ne- gandum voce כושי Æthiopem alicubi notari. Fa- bula est, quod Tharbam filiam Regis Ægypti à Mo- se ductam Josephus ait: Fuit enim uxor ejus Zippo- ra ut August. Theodor. Ebræi, aliique communiter agnoscunt, de qua hic agitur. Conf. B. Walther. Harm. ad h. l.

## 12:3
Verse 3.

THE MEEKEST MAN] He reads ענו, not עני, as some Hebrews do. And with him the Greeks here and the Samaritan, Bemidbar Rabba, Aben Ezra, Kimchi. The reason is given why God believed the injury to Moses should be avenged, because he himself was most gentle in bearing his own injuries. These are rudiments towards the Gospel.

That reading is rightly preferred, to which the Hebrew Codices also agree.
