But what is said about rudiments towards the Gospel smacks of Socinianism: as if there were other precepts of the New Testament here, and others had been of the Old, regarding the vengeance of injuries or the tolerance of them. It certainly does not fit Moses, since by the law he prohibited vengeance and anger against a neighbor and another private person, Lev. 19:17, 18, not only against Israelites but also strangers, v. 34, and commanded not to leave even an enemy's beast of burden under its load, but to help it, Exod. 21:3, 4, 5, and to do good to enemies, which the Apostle proves from Deut. 33:36 and Prov. 25:21, Rom. 12:20. Nor does that causal connection, which is found in the Vulgate version, occur in the Hebrew source: nor was the gentleness of Moses the cause of vengeance for God.

Although the word ענו is indeed retained, it is nevertheless more correctly explained with B. Luther as referring to the affliction of Moses, that he was indeed the most afflicted of all: rather than about meekness, that he was the meekest of all: since the word ענו is used in that sense in Ps. 9:13, Psalm 22:27, Ps. 76:10, Isa. 11:4, Zech. 9:8, and the discourse is about the affliction of Moses, by the force of the context; about which also in the preceding chapter, Num. 11:14, 15. Nor is it so fitting that Moses himself should have attributed this eulogy to himself, that he was the meekest of all, such as holy men are not read to have proclaimed about themselves, so much so that they rather modestly extenuated those things which they could have proclaimed in themselves: whence also that doubt, which some raise here, how Moses wrote such a great eulogy about himself, expires: which Tostatus attributes to divine instinct with Rickelius, since he could not know the hearts of others without revelation: others say this was added by another hagiographer writer, who arranged the Diaries of Moses, or by Ezra, with Hugo and Cornelius à Lapide. For whom there is no need, if you interpret it with B. Luther, Forster, Osiander, and others as the affliction of Moses. How often Moses was otherwise moved to anger is evident from many places: See Exod. 11:8, ch. 16:20, ch. 32:19, Lev. 10:15, Num. 16:15, ch. 20:10, 11. (Compare Ps. 106, 32. 33.) chap. 31, 14. which was not always just, or sufficiently moderate.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VIR MITISSIMVS] Legit ענו non עני, ut Hebræi quidam. Et cum ipso Græci hic & Samaritanus, Bemidbar Rabba, Abenesdra, Kimchi. Causa redditur, cur Deus inju- riam Mosis ulciscendam crediderit, quia ipse in suis injuriis ferendis erat lenissimus. Rudimenta hæc sunt ad Evange- lium.

Recte præfertur illa lectio, cui etiam Codi- ces Ebræi consentiunt. Sed quod de rudimentis ad Evangelium dicitur, Socinismum sapit: quasi alia præcepta Novi Testamenti hic sint, alia fuerint Ve- teris, qua ultionem injuriarum, vel tolerantiam ea- rum. Mosi certe id non congruit, siquidem lege prohibuerit vindictam et iram adversus proximum, aliumque privatum Levit. 19, 17. 18. non solum ad- versus Israelitas, sed etiam peregrinos v. 34. jusse- ritque jumentum etiam inimici sub onere non re- linquere, sed eidem succurrere Exod. 21, 3. 4. 5. ac benefacere inimicis, quod è Deut. 33, 36. ac Prov. 25, 21. probat Apostolus Rom. 12, 20. Neque causalis ille nexus, qui in vulgata versione habetur, in fon- te Ebræo occurrit: nec lenitas Mosis Deo causa fuit ultionis.

Quanquam vero retineatur vox ענו, ea ta- men rectius exponitur cum B. Luthero, de afflictio- ne Mosis, quod nempe fuerit omnium afflictissimus: quam de mansuetudine, quod omnium mitissimus fuerit: siquidem eo sensu adhibeatur vox ענו Ps. 9, 13. Psalm. 22, 27. Ps. 76, 10. Es. 11, 4. Zach. 9, 8. & de afflictione Mosis sermo est, vi contextus; de qua etiam cap. præcedente Num. 11, 14. 15. Neque adeo convenit, ut Moses ipse sibi hoc elogium, quod omnium fuerit mitissimus, tribuerit, qualia sancti vi- ri de sese prædicasse adeo non leguntur, ut extenu- arint potius modeste ea, quæ prædicare in semet- ipsis poterant: unde etiam dubium illud, quod hic movent nonnulli, quomodo Moses tantum elo- gium de se scripserit, expirat: quod Tostatus instin- ctui divino cum Rickelio tribuit, siquidem sine reve- latione aliorum corda scire non potuerit: alii addi- tum hoc ab alio Scriptore hagiographo, qui Diaria Mosis digesserit, vel ab Esdra, cum Hugone & Cor nelio à Lapide ajunt. Quibus opus non est, si cum B. Luthero, Forstero, Osiandro, aliis de afflictione Mosis interpreteris. Quam sæpe alias Moses ad iram commotus fuerit, è multis locis constat: Vid. Exod. 11, 8. cap. 16, 20. cap. 32, 19. Levit. 10, 15. Num. 16, 15. cap. 20, 10. 11. (Conf. Ps. 106, 32. 33.) cap. 31, 14. quæ non semper justa, aut moderata satis fuit.

## 12:6
Verse 6.

IN A VISION) Namely enigmatic, where one thing is seen and another is signified, as elsewhere chariots, elsewhere bones in Ezekiel, and other things in other Prophets.

THROUGH A DREAM) Which themselves were also for the most part αἰνιγματώδη [enigmatic], such as Jacob's ladder, Pharaoh's cows, the ash-cake in the history of Gideon, the statue of Nebuchadnezzar.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

IN VISIONE) Nempe ænigmatica, ubi aliud videtur, aliud significatur, ut alibi currus, alibi ossa apud Ezechielem, & alia apud Prophetas alios.

PER SOMNIVM) Quæ & ipsa plerumque erant αἰνίγμα- τώδη, ut scala Jacobi, boves Pharaonis, panis subcinericius in Gedeonis historia, statua Nabuchodonosori.

## 12:8
Verse 8.

FOR MOUTH TO MOUTH I SPEAK TO HIM) I openly signify my decrees to him, as a friend is accustomed to do to a friend.

VISION] Open, that is to say, ἐν εἴδει [in form] in Greek, so that it may be distinguished from that which preceded. Such was that vision in Ex. 34, 4, whence the LXX here [say] καὶ τὴν δόξαν κυρίου εἶδε [and he saw the glory of the Lord].

OPENLY, AND NOT BY ENIGMAS AND FIGURES HE SEES THE LORD) That is, as appears from the above, by ecstasies or dreams exhibiting one thing and hiding another. The Hebrews say that the privilege which is treated here was given to Moses for the reason that, out of reverence, he had shrunk from seeing God appearing to him in an Angel, Exod. 3, 6. A similar distinction of dreams [is found] in Artemidorus: for he says that some are θεορεματικὰ [theorematic], which offer future things just as they will be, others ἀλληγορικὰ [allegorical], which [do so] through figures.

In the Hebrew it is: in a vision & not by enigmas AND THE FORM OF THE LORD he sees: so that the triple excellence of this Prophet may be noted: (1.) that the Lord speaks with him mouth to mouth, (2.) that it is in an open vision, not enigmatic like others, (3.) that he sees also THE FORM or likeness of the Lord: which, wrongly denied by the Vulgate, Grotius does not notice, praising the comment of the Hebrews that these privileges were given to Moses for the reason that, out of reverence, he had shrunk from seeing God appearing to him in an Angel, Exod. 3, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ORE ENIM AD OS LOQVOR EI) Aperte mea de- creta ipsi significo, ut amicus amico solet.

VISIONE] Aperta scilicet, ἐν εἴδει Græce, ut distinguatur ab eo quod præcessit. Talis illa visio Ex. 34, 4. unde LXX. hîc καὶ τὴν δόξαν κυρίου εἶδε.

PALAM, ET NON PER ÆNIGMATA ET FIGU- RAS DOMINUM VIDET) Id est, ut ex superioribus ap- paret per ἐκτασίας aut somnia aliud exhibentia, aliud occul- tantia. Privilegium autem, de quo hîc agitur, datum Mosi ajunt Hebræi pro eo, quod præ reverentia Deum in Angelo sibi apparentem videre defugerit Exod. 3, 6. Simile discri- men somniorum apud Artemidorum: ait enim alia esse θεορε- ματικὰ, quæ futuras res ita ut erunt offerunt, alia ἀλληγορικὰ, quæ per figuras.

In Ebr. est: in visione & non per ænigmata ET SPECIEM DOMINI videt: ut triplex ἐξοχὴ hujus Prophetæ notetur: (1.) quod ore ad os lo- quatur cum eo Dominus, (2.) quod in visione aper- ta, non ut alii ænigmatica, (3.) quod videat eti- am SPECIEM vel similitudinem Domini: quod perperam negatum à Vulgata, non advertit Gro- tius, Ebræorum laudans commentum, quod privi- legia hæc Mosi data pro eo, quod præ reverentia Deum in Angelo sibi apparentem videre defuge- rit, Exod. 3, 6.

## 12:10
Verse 10.

LEPROSY) The proper punishment for pride and evil-speaking, as we shall say elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

LEPRA) Pœna propria superbiæ & maledicentiæ, ut alibi dicemus.

## 12:12
Verse 12.

LET HER NOT BE AS ONE DEAD, AND AS AN ABORTIVE] And it is redundant: The sense is, let her not be like a putrefied fetus, which comes out of the womb consumed by half of itself. There was here in ancient codices אמנו of our mother and בשרנו of our flesh, not badly, because as she is the same mother as Moses and Aaron, so also in a certain way the flesh: But it flows better, what is now read comparatively.

Grotius does not teach whence he has that ancient reading: Nor do we acknowledge here that αὐτὸς ἔφα. It is well, however, that he shows favor to our codices, and prefers them; but by what right he dares to prefer new ones to ancient ones, let him see to that himself.

But they are referred entirely in the sources to the fetus dead in the womb, and to the protasis of the comparison, which in our version have been referred to the apodosis, and to Miriam herself; and what Aaron anticipated with prayers that it might not happen, in her case they sound as if that had already been done.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

NE FIAT HÆC QVASI MORTVA, ET VT AB- ORTIVUM] Et abundat: Sensus est, ne sit similis fœtui pu- trefacto, qui dimidia sui parte consumptus ex utero exit. Fuit hîc in antiquis Codicibus אמנו matris nostræ & בשרנו carnis nostræ, non male, quia ut mater Mariæ eadem, quæ Mosi & Aaroni, ita & caro quodammodo: Sed melius fluit, quod nunc legitur comparative.

Non docet Grotius, unde habeat illam anti- quam lectionem: Nec agnoscimus hîc illud αὐτὸς ἔφα. Bene tamen, quod gratiam facit Codicibus nostris, eosque præferat; quo jure autem antiquis novos præferre ausit, ipse viderit.

Ad fœtum autem in utero mortuum omnino re- feruntur in fontibus, & ad protasin comparatio- nis, quæ ad apodosin in nostra versione relata sunt, & ad ipsam Miriam; quodque Aharon precibus præoccupavit ne fieret, in illa ita sonant, ac si jam factum id esset.

## 12:14
Verse 14.

IF HER FATHER HAD SPIT IN HER FACE] Allegorical for to rebuke severely.

LET HER BE SEPARATED SEVEN DAYS OUTSIDE THE CAMP] To this example are instituted the excommunications by the synagogue, and among Christians by the Church.

They do not dare to approach the Father before the seventh day, how much less to me? as Fagius, Vatablus, Piscator, Junius.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

SI PATER SPUISSET IN FACIEM EJUS] Allego- ricum pro graviter increpare.

SEPARETUR SEPTEM DIEBUS EXTRA CASTRA] Ad hoc exemplum instituti ἀφορισμοὶ a synagoga, & inter Christianos ab Ecclesia.

Non audent accedere ad Patrem ante septimum diem, quanto minus ad me? ut Fagius Vatabl. Piscat. Jun.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. Spies sent, and having returned they stir up murmuring.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. Exploratores missi, & reversi murmur ex- citant.

## 13:16
Verse 17.

TO VIEW THE LAND] Concerning the spies see what was said in De Jure Belli ac Pacis book III, ch. 4, 18. Moreover, you have an excellent form of those things which are accustomed to be commanded to spies in the following. Lyranus and Tostatus think that the permissive mandate concerning the exploration in v. 3, to which the people gave occasion in Deut. 1:22, is to be accepted. But it is an express commandment of God, and God wished thus to provide for the infirmity and diffidence of the people: but that people allowed itself to be precipitated into diffidence more by the explorers. Which happened by accident. Compare Theodoret, q. 85.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

AD CONSIDERANDAM TERRAM] De explorato- ribus vide quæ dicta de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. III. c. 4, 18. For- mam autem eorum, quæ mandari exploratoribus solent, egre- giam habes in sequentibus. Permissive mandatum de exploratione v. 3. cui populus occasionem dedit Deut. 1, 22. accipien- dum esse Lyranus, & Tostatus putant. Sed expressa est Dei præceptio, & voluit Deus infirmitati, & dif- fidentiæ populi sic consulere: sed ille se ab explora- toribus magis passus est in diffidentiam præcipitari. Quod ex accidenti evenit. Confer. Theodor. q. 85.

## 13:20 Addition
On verse 21. SIX HUNDRED THOUSAND.

Latin:

Ad verf. 21. SEXCENTA MILLIA.

## 13:22
Verse 23.

BEFORE TANIM] So both the Chaldean and the Greeks. Namely, the letter צ is translated sometimes by S and sometimes by T, as צינ [Sin] is Sinæ, צור [Tzor] is Sarra and Tyrus. Moreover, the omission of the guttural in pronunciation is very frequent. See what is at Matthew 1:21.

SONS OF ENAC] To the Greeks, the Inachidae. For it is established that they came from the East into Greece in the most ancient times.

So also the city of Zoan is called by historians among the principal cities of Egypt, by the name Tanis: with whose antiquity Hebron is here compared. This city, therefore, is the most ancient of all and the first after the flood expressed in Scripture, built three years before Babylon: just as Zoan, which together with Heliopolis and Memphis now constitutes one city called Al-Kair, having 15 miles in circumference, has turned into the greatest city of all.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ANTE TANIM] Sic & Chaldæus & Græci. Nempe צ modo per S modo per T vertitur, ut צינ Sinæ, צור Sarra & Tyrus. Gutturalis autem omissio in pronunciatione perfre- quens. Vide quæ ad Matth. 1, 21.

FILII ENAC) Græcis Inachidæ. Eos enim antiquissimis temporibus ab Oriente in Græciam venisse constat.

Sic etiam vocatur ab Historicis Soan urbs inter præcipuas Ægypti, nomine Tanis: cum cujus vetu- state hìc Ebron comparatur. Hæc ergo civitas omnium antiquissima & prima à diluvio in script. expressa, triennio ante Babylonem ædificata: uti Zohan, quæ cum Heliopoli, & Memphi jam unam constituit civitatem Al-Kair dictam 15. miliaria in ambitu habentem in omnium maximam civitatem evasit.

## 13:23 Addition
On Num. 13. v. 24. A BRANCH WITH A GRAPE. at page 533. a.

On grapes and clusters of huge size, Pliny, book 14, 1. In inner Asia, grapes grow the size of a cow's udder, of a pot, or even of an infant child. Strabo, book 2, records clusters of two-foot size, with Pliny in the aforementioned place as authority. Again, at Rome, one vine shaded the open-air walkways in the porticoes of Livia with its shady coverings, and the same was fruitful with twelve amphorae of must. There is no reason for Bonfrerius to say that it cannot easily be discerned here whether two men carried the vine branch and the cluster of grapes at the same time, or whether they took turns in carrying that burden, as Philo in his Life of Moses intended; because when the branch is said to be carried between two, it is implied that they carried it at the same time. Compare Serarius on Joshua, chapter 19, question 2.

Latin:

Ad Num. 13. v. 24. PALMITEM CUM UVA. ad pag. 533. a.

De uvis & botris ingentis magnitudinis Plinius l. 14, 1. In interiori Asia nascuntur uvæ magnitudine uberis vaccini, ollæ, imo pueri infantis. Botros bipedali magnitudine commemorat Strabo l. 2. Plinio l. c. autore. Rursus Romæ una vitis in Liviæ porticibus subdiales deambulationes umbrosis operculis opacabat, eademque duodenis musti amphoris fœcunda. Non est quod Bonfrerius dicat, non facile hic discerni posse, an duo vini palmitem & botrum uvarum portantes simul gestarint, an vero vicissim ejus oneri gestando successerint, ut Philo de vita Mosis voluit? quia quum inter duos portatus dicatur palmes, simul ipsos portasse eundem innuitur. Conf. Serar. in Jos. cap. 19. quæst. 2.

## 13:26 Addition
Verse 27. KADESH.

That is, Kadesh-barnea, from where they had been sent, Deut. 1, 19. It is distinguished from the other Kadesh (lest it be confused with Tostatus) because that other one was in the desert of Zin, Num. 20, 1; ch. 27, 14; ch. 33, 36; Deut. 33, 51, in which was the 33rd encampment in the 40th year of the exodus. But this one was in the desert of Paran, to which they came immediately from Mount Sinai, and it was the immediate border of Judea, Num. 34, 4, since Idumea lay between the other Kadesh and Judea. This name Kadesh-barnea also had, according to Adrichomius and Torniellus, the name Rithmah, Num. 33, 48.

Of armed men, with women, servants, and Egyptians not counted, which number easily grew to three million. Augustine, in Questions on Numbers 19, maintains that those words are those of one inquiring rather than one doubting, and Bonfrerius, Estius, and Malvenda make them only those of one wondering, which was also the opinion of Rambam, R. Simeon, and Oleaster. But the reasoning seems to introduce doubt: how can meat be provided for such a multitude for an entire month? Moses also begins, says our Osiander, while he is among a people who were then incredulous, to doubt somewhat the power of God. And so R. Akiva among Lyranus, Cornelius a Lapide, and Muis. Therefore the Lord says: is the Lord's hand, he says, shortened? However, Moses is not punished here, as in Num. 20, where he openly testified to his lack of faith before the Israelites and with great scandal to them, because God visits public sins differently than secret ones, and these proceeded from mere perturbation and thoughtlessness.

Latin:

Vers. 27. CADES.

Id est Cadesbarnes, unde missi erant Deut. 1, 19. Distinguitur ab altero Cades (ne cum Tostato confundatur) quia alterum illud in deserto Sin fuit, Num. 20, 1. cap. 27, 14. cap. 33, 36. Deut. 33, 51. in quo fuit 33. mansio sub annum exitus 40. Hoc vero in deserto Paran, quo venerunt statim a monte Sinai, eratque terminus immediatus Judææ Num. 34, 4. quum inter alterum Cades & Judæam intercesserit Idumæa. Nomen etiam hoc Cadesbarne juxta Adrichomium & Torniell. habuit Rethma. Num. 33, 48.

Virorum armatorum, mulieribus, servis, & Ægyptiis non annumeratis, qui numerus facile excrefcebat ad trigesies centena millia. Verba autem illa quærentis potius, quam diffidentis esse vult August. quæst. in Numer. 19. eademque admirantis solum facit Bonfrerius, Estius, Malvenda, quæ Rambam, R. Simeonis & Oleastrii etiam sententia fuit. Sed ratiocinatio dubitationem inferre videtur, quomodo per integrum fensum tantæ multitudini carnibus prospici possit? Incipit & Moses, inquit Osiander noster, dum versatur in populo tum incredulo, de potentia Dei subdubitare. Atque ita R. Aquiba apud Lyranum, Cornelius a Lapide & Muis. Ideo Dominus: nunquid, inquit, manus Domini invalida est? Non autem hic punitus Moses, ut Num. 20. ubi palam coram Israelitis, & magno cum scandalo eorum diffidentiam suam testatus in simili est, quia aliter peccata publica aliter secreta visitat Deus, & ex mera perturbatione & inconsideratione hæc profecta.

## 13:29
Verse 30. AMONG THESE CALEB QUIETING THE MURMUR OF THE PEOPLE.

Caleb alone did this, for Joshua, as a minister of Moses, would have been suspected, who nevertheless was later a supporter to Caleb in encouraging the people, chapter 14:6 ff., even though he rendered equal thanks with him, when the people wished to stone them both.

Latin:

Vers. 30. INTER HÆC CALEB COMPE- SCENS MURMUR POPULI.

Solus id fecit Caleb, Josua enim ceu minister Mo- sis suspectus fuisset, qui tamen postea parastates in erigendo populo Calebo fuit cap. 14, 6. seqq. etsi parilem cum ipso gratiam retulerit, quum utrum- que populus lapidare voluerit.

## 13:29 Addition
On verse 30. toward the end, note.

The word סח is written with a large ס to indicate the difficulty of restraining.

Latin:

Ad verf. 30. sub finem notar.

Verbum סח cum ס majusculo scribitur ad indicandam difficultatem compescendi.

## 13:33
Verse 34. AND GOING EVEN TO THE TORRENT OF THE GRAPE] An anticipation of a name given afterwards, as the following verses explain: and Deut. 1:24.

In this tract around the city of Rehob, situated in the borders of Syria at the roots of Mount Lebanon, the most famous wine, the Bibline and the Chalybonian, was praised by the ancient Greeks. Vines of stupendous size are also recounted by Pliny, Natural History, book 14, chapter 1, and Strabo in Geography, book 2; but they do not reach the example of this, where the strength of two men was necessary to carry one cluster. Concerning the mystical signification, see Augustine, vol. 10, sermon 100, de tempore.

Latin:

Vers. 34. PERGENTESQVE VSQVE AD TORREN- TEM BOTRI] Anticipatio nominis post dati, ut explicant sequentia: & Deut. 1, 24.

In hoc tractu circa urbem Rechob in finibus Sy- riæ ad radices montis Libani sitam vinum celeber- rimum Biblium, & Chelboniticum à Græcis antiquis deprædicatum. Recensentur & à Plinio lib. 14. nat. hist. cap. 1. ac Strabone in Geograph. lib. 2. vites stu- pendæ amplitudinis; sed ad hoc non accedunt ex- emplum, ubi duorum virorum necessariæ fuere vi- res ad unum portandum botrum. De mystica signi- ficatione vid. August. tom. 10. serm. 100. de tempore.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. The Lord is appeased by Moses, but the Israelites are led to death in the desert: who, not having listened to God, also fight unsuccessfully.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. Placatus à Mose Dominus, sed Israelites in de- serto morti adducti: qui Deo non audito, etiam pugnant infeliciter.

## 14:4
Verse 4. INTO EGYPT.

Behold the stupidity? Who would have provided provisions for those returning? Or would the Lord have rained Manna upon rebels? How would they have crossed the Red Sea? How would hostile nations have permitted them to pass through their territories?

Latin:

Vers. 4. IN ÆGYPTUM.

EN stoliditatem? Quis revertentibus præbuis- set annonam? an rebellibus Dominus pluisset Manna? quomodo mare rubrum transmisissent? Quomodo gentes hostiles eos per suos fines trans- ire permisissent?

## 14:6
Verse 6. THEY RENT THEIR GARMENTS.

What the custom of the ancients was, in blasphemy, in sedition of the people, and in mourning, as noted by Fagius and Drusius.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SCIDERUNT VESTIMENTA.

Quis mos veterum fuit, in blasphemia, in sedi- tione populi, & in luctu, notante Fagio & Drusio.

## 14:6 Addition
On chapter 14, 6. toward the end, note.

All these things concurred in this place. But the tearing, as Fagius notes, was done on the outer garment, which it was being broken downwards to some extent, so that that broken part was left hanging for several days.

Latin:

Ad cap. 14, 6. sub finem not.

Hæc omnia concurrebant hoc loco. Fiebat autem scissio, Fagio notante, in veste exteriori, quæ deorsum aliquo usque rumpebatur, ita ut pars illa ru- pta ad aliquot dies pendula relinqueretur.

## 14:9
Verse 9.

ALL DEFENSE] In Hebrew metaphorically, Shadow. See Luke 1:35.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

OMNE PRÆSIDIUM] In Hebræo methaphorice, Vmbra. Vide Luc. 1, 35.

## 14:9 Addition
On verse 9, after the notes of Grotius.

Other passages are more correctly compared, where the word shadow implies protection and defense, Psalm 12:1 and 121:5, Isaiah 30:2, chapter 49:2, chapter 51:16. Osiander explains: the Lord has now taken away from them the spirit of resistance, counsel, and success. Thus the Chaldean and the Syrian: their strength or vigor has departed. Compare Joshua 2. Bonfrer understands it of God: because it follows, God is with us, as if to say, they lack God as a protector, who had hitherto preserved them, while their iniquities were not yet complete.

Latin:

Ad vers. 9. post not. Grotii.

Rectius conferuntur alia loca, ubi vox um- bræ protectionem & præsidium infert Psalm. 12, 1. & 121, 5. Esa. 30, 2. cap. 49, 2. cap. 51, 16. Osiander explicat, Dominus jam illis animum resistendi, con- silium & successus ademit. Ita Chaldæus & Syrus: recessit fortitudo vel robur eorum. Conf. Jos. 2. Bonfrer. de Deo intelligit: quia sequitur, Deus no- biscum, q. d. illi Deo protectore carent, qui hacte- nus eos conservarat, dum iniquitates eorum non- dum completæ essent.

## 14:16
Verse 16. FOR WHICH HE HAD SWORN] In Hebrew, which he swore to them, ἣν ὤμοσεν αὐτοῖς. But it is to be noted that God swore this to the Israelite people, who are always considered the same, not to these or those of the people. Wherefore God fully fulfilled this oath in the times of Joshua. See below 30, and what we have noted concerning the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 13, section 4, paragraph 4.

But why does God threaten what He foreknew He would never bring into effect? This was done so that both the gravity of the people's sin, and the power of God punishing and the gentleness of Him forgiving, and the efficacy of pious intercession might be manifest: in which sense Origen, considering Moses as a type of Christ, Homily 8 on Numbers, says: This threatening is not anger, but prophecy. Concerning the ten temptations, of which mention is made in verse 22, see Paul Fagius in the Chaldean Paraphrase.

Latin:

Vers. 16. PRO QVO JURAVERAT] Hebraice, quam juravit eis, ἣν ὤμοσεν αὐτοῖς. Sed notandum jurasse hoc De- um Israëlitico populo, qui semper idem censetur, non his vel illis de populo. Quare juramentum hoc plene implevit De- us Josuæ temporibus. Vide infra 30. & quæ notata nobis de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. 2. c. 13. 4. §. 4.

Cur autem Deus minatur, quod præscivit se nun- quam in effectum producturum? Factum id ut pa- teret tum peccati populi gravitas, tum Dei ulciscen- tis potestas, & ignoscentis lenitas, tum intercessio- nis piæ efficacitas: quo sensu Origenes Mosen ceu typum Christi considerans Homil. 8. in Num. Com- minatio hæc, inquit, non est iracundia, sed prophetia. phetia. De decem tentationibus, quarum mentio fit v. 22. vid. Paul Fagius in Paraphr. Chald.

## 14:17
Verse 17. LET IT BE MAGNIFIED. In the word יגדל there is a large letter, perhaps for the emphasis of the magnificence of God, as Malvenda says.

Latin:

Verf. 17. MAGNIFICETUR. In verbo יגדל litera magna est, forte ad em- phasin magnificentiæ Dei, ut Malvenda.

## 14:17 Addition
On verse 17, towards the end of the note.

Buxtorf, in his Masoretic Commentary, says that it is indicated by a larger ' [yod]; because if the people tempted God even ten times (which the letter ' is worth), or murmured against him ten times more, yet the clemency and grace of God ought to overcome the ingratitude of the people even ten times over, so that he might not kill them in the desert.

Latin:

Ad vers. 17. sub finem not.

Buxtorf. in Comment. Masor. per majuscu- lum ' indicari ait; quod si vel decem (quod litera ' valet) tentationibus Deum populus tentaret, aut decuplo plus adversus eum murmuraret, Dei tamen clementiam, & gratiam vel decies superare debere populi ingratitudinem, ne eum in deserto occidat.

## 14:18
Verse 18. WHO VISITS. Ludovicus de Dieu here and in Exodus 34:7 renders it: by emptying he will not empty, visiting the sins of the fathers, i.e., even when He is angry and punishes, He does not however cut them off entirely, but only to the third or fourth generation. For Moses opposes these words to an angry God, and one threatening destruction, so that he may remind Him of His goodness. Compare Jeremiah 32, chapter 46:28. It can, however, be said for the common explanation, which I do not easily abandon, that Moses does not pray that the sin remain unpunished, but that God, while punishing the principal authors of the crime in justice, may remember His mercy, and not destroy the whole people.

Latin:

Verf. 18. QUI VISITAS. Ludovic. de Dieu hîc & Exod. 34, 7. reddit, eva- cuando non evacuabit visitans peccata patrum, i. e. eti- am quando succenset, & punit, non tamen pror- sum succidit, sed in tertiam tantum, aut quartam generationem. Opponit enim hæc verba Moses irato Deo, & internecionem minanti, ut eam bo- nitatis suæ commonefaciat. Conf. Jerem. 32. cap. 46, 28. Dici tamen pro communi explicatione, quam non facile desero, potest, quod Moses non oret, ut peccatum maneat impunitum, sed ut Deus in ju- stitia puniens præcipuos sceleris autores, mise- ricordiæ suæ reminiscatur, nec totum populum deleat.

## 14:24
Verse 24. HE HAS FOLLOWED ME) He has fulfilled after me: which the Chaldean interprets as having perfectly followed the fear, that is, religion toward God.

Latin:

Verf. 24. SECUTUS EST ME) Implevit post me: quod Chaldæus interpretatur perfecte secutus est timorem, id est, re- ligionem in Deum.

## 14:25
Verse 25. BECAUSE THE AMALEKITE AND THE CANAANITE DWELL IN THE VALLEYS.

Thus in verse 45, they are said to dwell in the mountain, namely, as regards a firm and stable seat. But here it concerns a military encampment to hinder the Israelites.

MOVE TOMORROW. That is, hereafter, as in Exod. 13, 14. because they remained in Kadesh for many days, Deut. 1, 46. chap. 2, 1. Malvenda, who lived on the mountain, explains it thus, that he had previously occupied and taken possession of that mountain before the Israelites, from verse 43.

Latin:

Verf. 25. QUONIAM AMALECITES ET CANANEUS HABITANT IN VALLIBUS.

Ita v. 45. in monte habitare dicuntur, scil. quoad firmam & stabilem sedem. Hìc vero de habitatio- ne castrensi ad præpediendum Israelitas agitur.

CRAS MOVETE. Id est, posthæc, ut Exod. 13, 14. quia manserunt in Cades multis diebus, Deut. 1, 46. cap. 2, 1. Malven- da illa, qui habitabat in monte, ita explicat, qui prius ante Israelitas montem illum insederat, & occupa- verat è verf. 43.

## 14:30
Verse 30. THAT I MIGHT MAKE YOU DWELL] 'You' is to be referred to the whole people, without restriction of time. See similar passages in On the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chap. 9, § 3.

Latin:

Verf. 30. VT HABITARE VOS FACEREM] Vos ad totum populum referendum est, sine temporis restrictione. Loca similia vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. 2. c. 9. §. 3.

## 14:30 Addition
On verse 30, EXCEPT CALEB.

But Phinehas also entered: who was already over 20 years old, because in Numbers 31 he is sent into war with the vessels and trumpets, which were not entrusted before the 30th year, Numbers 4:3. I answer: The tribe of Levi is excepted, as from it no one was sent to explore, Numbers 13:4, nor is anyone read to have murmured. Also, this punishment was only for the murmurers, verse 28. Compare here the blessed D. Georg König, Vindiciae loc. cit. page 527, where he also treated of the age of Phinehas extended to 300 years by a singular divine blessing.

Latin:

Ad v. 30. PRÆTER CALEB.

At Pinehas etiam ingressus: qui jam ultra 20. annos fuit: quia Num. 31. mittitur in bellum, cum vasis, & tubis, quæ non committebantur ante 30. an- num. Num. 4, 3. Resp. Tribus Levi excipitur, ut e qua nec missus ullus ad explorandum. Num. 13, 4. neque ullus murmurasse legitur. Pœna eti- am hæc sola murmurantium fuit vers. 28. Confer. hic B. D. Georg König. vindic. loc. cit pag. 527. ubi etiam de Pineæ ætate ad 300. annos benedictione divi- na singulari producta egit.

## 14:33
Verse 33. YOUR CHILDREN SHALL BE WANDERERS] Because of the sins of the parents, the children are exiled. The same happened when Nebuchadnezzar deported them.

Latin:

Verf. 33. FILII VESTRI ERUNT VAGI] Ob peccata parentum exulant liberi. Idem evenit Nabuchodonosoro deportante.

## 14:34
Verse 34. A YEAR FOR A DAY] Thus Ezech. 4, 6.

Latin:

Verf. 34. ANNUS PRO DIE] Sic Ezech. 4, 6.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. What burnt offerings and other sacrifices those who have entered the land ought to offer, both strangers and Israelites: and concerning first fruits, and sacrifices for sins of ignorance, and transgressions. The stoning of the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath. The fringes and ribbons of the Hebrews ordained as a reminder of the law.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. Quænam ingressi in terram offerre debeant ho- locausta, & alia sacrificia, tam peregrini quam Israelitæ: & de primitiis, ac sacrificiis pro peccatis ignorantiæ, & delictis. Lapida- tio viri, qui in Sabbato ligna collegit. Fimbriæ ac vittæ Ebræorum in commonitionem legis ordinatæ.

## 15:1 Addition
On chapter 15, verse 1, SPOKE.

To Bonfrer and Cornelius a Lapide it is probable that these precepts were given on Mount Sinai, and are narrated here out of order, especially because they could not have long lacked the ashes of the red heifer, on account of the frequent purifications to be performed with it.

Latin:

Ad cap. 15. v. 1. LOCUTUS EST.

Bonfrerio & Cornelio a Lapide probabile est, hæc præcepta in monte Sinai data esse, & hic extra ordinem narrari, imprimis, quia cinere vaccæ rufæ diu carere non potuerint, ob crebras purificatio- nes eo faciendas.

## 15:4
Verse 4. HE SHALL OFFER] No victim without salted meal and wine: Thus also among the Greeks: For a sacrifice is as it were a banquet, and is called the food of the Lord below 28, 2.

Others give this as a more important reason, that the Lord wished to teach ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (as in a type) that Christ, having been made a victim on the altar of the cross, would be perpetual food and drink for all the faithful, John 4 and 6. Nor is a moral reason added without cause, as to what kind of good works ought to be: through a similar purity of mind, or intention, or even spiritual knowledge, through oil charity and mercy, through wine spiritual grace and the internal joy of the heart or the communication of the passion of Christ, as the ordinary gloss has it from the Fathers. That which is held in Num. 28, 2, my oblation, MY BREAD, although some wish it to be said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (anthropopathically), so that God might testify to his affection toward our works flowing from faith, not that he demanded sacrifices for food, or for the sake of a banquet, yet they think not without cause that that metaphor looks rather to that heavenly bread, by which our souls are to be refreshed, John 6, and denotes the fruit and efficacy of the passion and death of Christ. Osiander interprets 'my bread' as 'my offerings by fire', that is, the offerings which I commanded to be offered, by which I feed the fire of the sacrifices.

Latin:

Verf. 4. OFFERRET] Nulla victima sine mola salsa, & vino: Sic & apud Græcos: Est enim sacrificium quasi convivium, vocatur- que cibus Domini infra 28, 2.

POtiorem alii causam hanc dant, quod ὡς ἐν τύ- πῳ docere voluerit Dominus, Christum in ara crucis victimam factum universis fidelibus peren- nem cibum potumque fore Joh. 4. & 6. Nec abs re moralis causa additur, qualia opera bona esse debe- ant: per similem puritatam mentis, vel intentionis, aut spiritualem etiam scientiam, per oleum charita- tem & misericordiam, per vinum gratiam spiritua- lem & internam cordis jucunditatem vel commu- nicationem passionis Christi, uti è Patribus glossa ordinaria habet. Quod Num. 28, 2. habetur, obla- tionem meam, PANEM MEUM, quamvis nonnul- li ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dictum velint, ut affectum erga opera nostra ex fide profluentia testaretur Deus, non ut sacrificia in cibum postularet, aut convivii causa, metaphoram tamen illam respicere potius panem illum cœlestem, quo animæ nostræ reficien- dæ sunt Joh. 6. fructumque ac efficaciam passionis & mortis Christi denotare, non citra causam exi- stimant. Osiander panem meum ad ignita mea in- terpretatur, id est, oblationes, quas præcepi offeren- das, quo alo sacrificiorum ignem.

## 15:13
Vers. 13.

AS WELL NATIVES AS STRANGERS SHALL OFFER SACRIFICES BY THE SAME RITE) By strangers in this place, the Hebrews understand those who had subjected themselves to the Law. For to others, only burnt offerings were permitted, and indeed without a libation.

The Vulgate is to be corrected here: which, having omitted verses 12, 14, and 16, took only some things from verse 15; such license does not deserve an excuse even in the translating of profane authors. Furthermore, that the same right is attributed to proselytes is to be understood regarding right in sacred matters, not in political ones, since strangers did not have the same rights or privileges as the Israelites, Levit. 25, 25.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

TAM INDIGENÆ QVAM PEREGRINI EODEM RITU OFFERENT SACRIFICIA) Peregrinos h. l. intelligunt Hebræi, qui legi se subjecerant. Nam aliis holocausta tantum permissa & quidem sine libamine.

Corrigenda hic Vulgata: quæ v. 12. 14. 16. omissis, è v. 15. nonnulla tantum assumsit, qualis licentia ne quidem in prophanis autoribus transferendis excusationem meretur. Cæterum quod idem jus proselytis tribuitur, de jure in rebus sacris non in politicis intelligendum, cum non habuerint peregrini cum Israëlitis eadem vel jura, vel privilegia, Levit. 25, 25.

## 15:20
Vers. 20. AS OF THE THRESHING FLOORS) Concerning wheat, barley, wine, figs, pomegranates, olives, dates.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SICUT DE AREIS) De tritico, hordeo vineto, ficubus, malis punicis, olivis, dactylis.

## 15:20 Addition
Verse 20, AS FROM THE THRESHING FLOORS, after the notes of Grotius, page 534, a.

Understand it not as regards quantity, but as regards the rite of offering, Leviticus 2:14, and that just as those firstfruits were offered to the priests, and nothing of them was burned on the altar, so also these are to be offered.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SICUT DE AREIS, post Grot. notas pag. 534. a.

Intellige non quoad quantitatem, sed quoad offerendi ritum Lev. 2, 14. & quod sicut illæ primi- tiæ, Sacerdotibus offerebantur, nec quicquam ea- rum in altari cremabatur, ita & hæ offerendæ sint.

## 15:21
Vers. 21. THROUGH IGNORANCE.

Such sins were expiated, but those which were committed with a high hand, for those souls were to be cut off, v. 26, 31; that is, the transgressors were to be punished with death: an example of which matter is subjoined in him who had gathered sticks on the Sabbath; and so that the Israelites would not be unmindful of the laws of the Lord, especially also concerning the Sabbath, they were commanded to make peculiar memorials for themselves, v. 38. Grotius therefore rashly restricts sins committed THROUGH PRIDE, which the Chaldean explained as בריש, as if you would say 'headily' or 'brainily,' to those where someone stubbornly denies that there is a God or a law given by God. Who, however, afterwards acknowledges that he who, having been warned, continues to commit sin against the law is called by the same name. Nor is it proven by a comparison with Deut. 13, 13. Jos. 22, 31. 33. it can, that what was said about the extermination of transgressors in verse 30 is to be understood such that he who thus offends God is not led to the judges, but is killed by those who catch him in the crime, as Zimri was by Phinehas; and his goods are to become an ἀνάθεμα (anathema). Nothing of the sort is taught in those places. Nor do they doubt Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed III. 41, such is the authority for us that we determine that faith must be given to one affirming something beyond the divine law. This finally is also to be observed: that while that political punishment of excision had to be undergone by such transgressors, they were nevertheless not excluded from sacrifices and the fruit of them for the expiating of their sins in divine judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 21. PER IGNORANTIAM.

Talia peccata expiabantur, quæ vero elata manu committebantur, ob illa exscindendæ erant animæ v. 26. 31. hoc est prævaricatores morte puniendi: cujus rei exemplum subjungitur in eo, qui Sabbato ligna collegerat; & ne legum Domini maxime etiam de Sabbato immemores essent Israëlitæ, memorialia peculiaria sibi facere jubebantur v. 38. Temere ergo restringit Grotius peccata per SUPERBIAM, quæ Chald. exposuit בריש q. d. capitose, cerebrose patrata, ad ea, cum præfracte quis negat esse Deum aut legem à Deo datam. Qui tamen postea agnoscit eodem nomine appellari, qui monitus in legem committere pergit. Neque probari è collatione Deut. 13, 13. Jos. 22, 31. 33. id potest, quæ de exterminatione transgressorum dicta vers. 30. intelligenda esse, ut qui sic Deum offendit, non ducatur ad judices, sed occidatur ab iis, qui eum in crimine deprehendunt, ut à Phinea Zambris; Bona autem ejus fiant ἀνάθεμα. Nihil tale illis locis docetur. Nec Maimonidis Duce dubitant. III. 41. tanta nobis est autoritas, ut præter legem divinam aliquid affirmanti fidem habendam statuamus. Id denique etiam observandum: excisionis illam pœnam politicam talibus transgressoribus quidem subeundam fuisse: non tamen exclusos fuisse eosdem à sacrificiis, & fructu eorum ad expiandum peccata ipsorum, in judicio divino.

## 15:21
SO ALSO OF THE DOUGH) In the Hebrew it is עריס, which signifies φύραμα (mixture/dough), and חלה which signifies a cake, κολλύραν (a loaf).

Latin:

ITA ET DE PULMENTIS) In Hebræo est עריס, quod φύραμα significat, & חלה quod placentam κολλύραν.

## 15:30
Vers. 30.

WHICH THROUGH PRIDE] In the Hebrew: with a high hand, for which the Chaldean placed בריש, as if you would say 'headily' or 'brainily.' Understand it of him who stubbornly denies that there is a God, or a law given by God, which the following words indicate. By the same name is called he who, having been warned, continues to commit sin against the law.

SHALL PERISH FROM HIS PEOPLE) In the Hebrew הכרת תכרת, he shall be exterminated by extermination: ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἡ ψυχὴ ἐκείνη ἐκ τῶ λαῶ αὐτῆς (that soul shall be cut off from his people) in the Greek. That expression elsewhere indicates destruction to be inflicted by God. Furthermore, here, from a comparison of the place Deut. 13, 13 and Joshua 22, 31.33, it is to be understood in this way: that he who thus offends God is not led to the judges, but is killed by those who catch him in the crime, as Zimri was by Phinehas; and his goods are to become an ἀνάθεμα (anathema). Thus Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed III. 41. Add what we have said in the book De Jure Belli ac Pacis, Chapter 20, § 9.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

QUÆ PER SUPERBIAM] In Hebræo: in manu excelsa, pro quo Chaldæus posuit בריש, quasi dicas capitose, cerebrose. Intellige de eo, qui præfracte negat esse Deum, aut legem a Deo datam, quo indicant sequentia. Eodem nomine appellatur qui monitus in legem committere pergit.

PERIBIT DE POPULO SUO) In Hebr. הכרת תכרת exterminio exterminabitur: ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἡ ψυχὴ ἐκείνη ἐκ τῶ λαῶ αὐτῆς Græcis. Ea locutio alibi interitum a Deo infligendum indicat. Cæterum hic ex collatione loci Deut. 13, 13. Josuæ 22, 31.33. intelligenda hoc modo, ut qui sic Deum offendit non ducatur ad judices, sed occidatur ab iis qui eum in crimine deprehendunt, ut a Phinea Zambris: Bona autem ejus fiant ἀνάθεμα. Sic Maimonides Duce dubitantium III. 41. Adde quæ diximus de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro II. Cap. 20. §. 9.

## 15:34
Vers. 34.

WHAT THEY OUGHT TO DO CONCERNING HIM.

With what kind of punishment they ought to affect him. For a law had already been passed concerning the death to be inflicted upon such persons, Exod. 35, 2. But because there were diverse capital punishments, namely suffocation or strangulation, burning, hanging, stoning, they wished to be informed concerning him, with what kind of punishment the violator of the Sabbath is to be affected: and the penalty of stoning was divinely dictated for him, which was considered the most severe, just as suffocation was held to be the lightest. Whence the gravity of this crime, the violation of the Sabbath, shines forth: because it was to be punished with the same kind of punishment as all other most severe crimes. For idolaters were stoned, Levit. 20,

Latin:

Vers. 34.

QUID SUPER EO FACERE DEBERENT.

Quo genere supplicii eum deberent afficere. De morte enim talibus inferenda lex jam erat lata Exod. 35, 2. Quia vero diversa erant capitalia supplicia, suffocatio nempe seu strangulatio, combustio, suspensio, lapidatio, de eo informari volebant, quonam genere supplicii afficiendus sit Sabbati violator: & lapidationis pœna illi divinitus dictata est, quæ censebatur gravissima, uti suffocatio pro levissima habita est. Unde gravitas hujus delicti, violationis Sabbati elusescit: quod eodem supplicii genere puniendum, quo gravissima quæque alia delicta. Nam lapidabantur idololatræ Levit. 20,

## 15:38
Ver. 38.

THAT THEY MAY MAKE FOR THEMSELVES FRINGES BY THE CORNERS OF THE CLOAK) See Deut. 22, 12. and on Matth. 9, 20.

Concerning these, Fagius thus from the Hebrews in this place: ציצית is as it were a lock of the head, they are twisted threads, or the extremity of a garment, i.e., that which is left after the weaving in the cloth, and which hangs from it, is called ציצית (in which opinion is also R. David Kimchi.) And Scripture commanded to hang ציצית on the hem of the garment, which is so called by them, because it bears the form of branches, on account of many threads joined together. However, threads sewn onto the hem of a garment, which are not woven, are called גדלים, which word is placed in Deuter. 22. Some of ours have thought that ציצית were, to the Hebrews, what the Evangelists call phylacteries from the Greek verb φυλάττω, that is, I guard, because by them it was signified that the divine commandments were to be held in memory, and diligently guarded. Therefore, throughout the whole hem of the garment, a fringe of this hyacinthine, that is, sky-blue color, extended itself, which is called in Hebrew ציצית; furthermore, what is said: 'And let them make for themselves ציצית or a fringe upon the wings,' i.e., the hems, or extremities which are understood by the wings of their garments, from this, because it is said in the plural 'of garments,' some gather, and wish, that this ought to be referred to all garments, even inner ones, not only that outer one, so that everywhere, putting on any garment whatsoever, they might be reminded of the commandments of God. A certain trace of this ceremony still appears among the Jews, for they have among their other garments, one not unlike a breastplate, except that it lacks sleeves, which they use daily in their prayers, and they put it on over all other garments. And they call it ארבע כנפות and that on account of the four corners which it has, for it is square, in which corners hang ציצית, that is, those twisted threads, which they themselves commonly name Zotten. It is wonderful how much they attribute to this garment, as if it had some singular power against יצההרע, that is, evil, or that depraved concupiscence. Whence it is that those among them who wish to be considered more religious than the rest, perpetually wear it under other garments. This Fagius alleging Arba turim, in the tract Orech chaim at the eleventh sign. The Hebrews therefore had to sew fringes thread by thread to the extremity of their outer garments, which were quadrangular cloaks: just as we see fringes or remaining threads standing out at the extremities of fabrics, upon these fringes they induced, and extended all around a פתיל hyacinthine thread, that is, of a heavenly and violet color. But fringes or threads in them are not the same as Φυλακτήρια: as August. and others have wished, because phylacteries were plates or small membranes, and were worn on the head, but fringes consisted of cloths and were the extreme parts of garments. Hieronymus in c. 23. Matth. gives the reason for the law, that this was done for the Jewish people to be distinguished, so that just as circumcision on bodies was a sign of the Jewish nation, so also the garment might have some difference. The principal reason added here is, that these little wings and shaggy extremities of garments ought to have been for them both documents, so that they would perpetually present to their eyes the memory of the divine commandments, and distractions, so that they might lead their senses away from every kind of superstition and error. Therefore the fringes

The Jews in the time of Christ magnified Matt. 23, 13. so that, namely, they might be believed to be more observant of the divine commandments.

Latin:

Verf. 38.

UT FACIANT SIBI FIMBRIAS PER ANGULOS PALLII) Vide Deut. 22, 12. & ad Matth. 9, 20.

De his ita ex Ebræis Fagius h. l. ציצית est tanquam cincinnus capitis, sunt quæ fila retorta, vel extremitas vestis, h. e. id quod relinquitur post texturam in panno, quodq; pendet ab illo, vocatur ציצית (in qua sententia est & R. David Kimchi.) Præcepitque Scriptura suspendere ציצית in ora vestimenti, quod sic vocatur ab eis, quod rami formam præ se ferat, propter multa fila commissa. Veruntamen fila assuta in ora vestimenti, quæ non sunt texta, vocantur גדלים quæ vox ponitur Deuter. 22. Quidam ex nostris putarunt ציצית, Hebræis fuisse, quod Evangelistæ vocant, phylacteria à Græco verbo φυλάττω, id est, custodio, quia per ea significaretur, divina mandata memoria esse tenenda, & diligenter custodienda. Igitur per totam vestimenti oram fimbria hujus hyacinthini, id est, cœrulei coloris se porrigebat, quæ vocatur Hebraice ציצית; porro quod dicitur: Et faciant sibi ציצית vel fimbriam super alas, h. e. oras, sive extremitates quæ per alas intelliguntur vestimentorum suorum, ex hoc quia pluraliter dicitur vestimentorum, quidam colligunt, & volunt, hoc referri debere ad omnes vestes, etiam interiores, non exteriorem illam tantum, ut ita ubique, quamcunque inducentes vestem admonerentur mandatorum Dei. Hujus ceremoniæ adhuc vestigium quoddam apparet apud Judæos, habent enim inter cæteras vestes suas, quandam non dissimilem thoraci, nisi quod manicis caret, qua utuntur quotidie in precibus suis, eamque induunt super omnes alias vestes. Illamque vocant ארבע כנפות idque propter quatuor angulos, quos habet, est enim quadrata, in quibus angulis pendent ציצית, id est, fila illa retorta, quæ ipsi Zotten vulgo nominant. Mirum est, quantum tribuant huic vesti, quasi singularem vim quandam habeat contra יצההרע, id est, malum, sive pravam illam concupiscentiam. Unde est, quod qui inter illos cæteris religiosiores haberi volunt, perpetuo eam sub aliis vestibus gestant. Hæc Fagius allegans Arba turim, in tract. Orech chaim signo undecimo. Debebant ergo Ebræi extremitati vestium extimarum, quæ pallia quadrangula fuere fimbrias filatim assuere: quomodo in extremitatibus telarum fimbrias sive fila reliqua extare videmus, super has fimbrias inducebant, & extendebant circumcirca פתיל filum hyacinthinum, id est, coloris cœlestis & violacei. Non sunt autem fimbriæ aut fila in iis idem quod Φυλακτήρια: uti August. & alii voluere, quia phylacteria laminæ aut membranulæ erant, & in capite gestabantur, fimbriæ vero ex pannis constabant & extremæ erant vestium partes. Rationem legis reddit Hieronym. in c. 23. Matth. quod factum id sit ad populum Judaicum dignoscendum, ut quomodo in corporibus circumcisio signum Judaicæ gentis erat, ita & vestis haberet aliquam differentiam. Præcipua ratio hic addita est, quod nempe pennulæ istæ & villosæ vestium extremitates debuerint ipsis esse tum documenta, ut oculis ipsorum perpetuo objicerent memoriam mandatorum divinorum, tum avocamenta, ut abducerent eorum sensus ab omni superstitionum & errorum genere. Fimbrias ergo

Judæi tempore Christi magnificabant Matth. 23, 13. uti scil. magis observantes mandatorum divinorum crederentur.

## 15:39
Verse 39.

AND THAT THEY MAY NOT FOLLOW THEIR OWN THOUGHTS AND EYES) In the Hebrew: Do not inquire after your heart and after your eyes, by following which you would commit fornication. Heart and eyes signify the desire of the mind. To inquire here is διακρίνειν, to curiously and boldly dispute about the reason for the law, and not to be willing to obey unless it is understood. Which thing, as they say, led Solomon by certain steps into grave sins, when, having taken foreign wives, he had nevertheless easily believed that he would avoid the cause of the law, that is, idolatry. This is what Philo says against Flaccus, that even those things which seem the least of the law must be solicitously observed: διὰ τὸ καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν οἰκοδομημάτων ὑφαιρέσει ἑνὸς κὰι τὰ ἔτι παγίως ἑσάναι δοκῦντα συμπίπτειν πρὸς τὸ κενωθὲν χαλώμενα κὰι καταῥῥέοντα. Tacitus says well in book I of his histories: If it is permitted to individuals to question where they are commanded, obedience perishing, authority also falls. The same in book of histories 2. he blames the soldiers, who preferred to interpret the commands of their leaders rather than execute them. We shall have an example in the following chapter, זנה which the Latin translates as to commit fornication, in a metaphorical sense is to break the bond of the covenant with God, which is done most of all by the worship of idols.

Yet this happens also by other sins: and not only is Idolatry prohibited here, or even an inquiry into the reason for the law; but also that we should not, having neglected the divine law, leave room for the vicious thoughts of the heart, or even for the lusts of the eyes: or interpret the law itself in such a way as we ourselves wish.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

NEC SEQVANTUR COGITATIONES SUAS ET OCULOS) In Hebræo: Non inquiratis post cor vestrum & post oculos vestros, quos sequentes fornicaremini. Cor & oculi significant animi lubitum. Inquirere hic est διακρίνειν cu- riose & audacter disputare de ratione legis, neque nisi ea in- tellecta velle obedire. Quæ res Solomonem, ut ajunt, per gradus quosdam in gravia induxit peccata, cum ductis uxo- ribus externis facile tamen se causam legis, id est, idololatri- am vitaturum credidisset. Hoc est, quod Philo ait adversus Flaccum, etiam quæ minima videantur legis, sollicite servan- da: διὰ τὸ καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν οἰκοδομημάτων ὑφαιρέσει ἑνὸς κὰι τὰ ἔτι παγίως ἑσάναι δοκῦντα συμπίπτειν πρὸς τὸ κενωθὲν χαλώμενα κὰι καταῥῥέοντα. Bene Tacitus historiarum li- bro I. Si ubi jubeantur, quærere singulis liceat, pereunte ob- sequio etiam imperium intercidit. Idem libro histor. 2. cul- pat milites, qui jussa ducum interpretari quam exequi mal- lent. Exemplum habebimus capite sequenti, זנה quod per fornicari vertit Latinus, in sensu metaphorico est fœderis cum Deo vinculum abrumpere, quod maxime sit idolorum cultu.

Fit tamen id etiam aliis peccatis : nec solum Ido- lolatria hîc prohibetur, aut etiam inquisitio de ra- tione legis; sed ne posthabita lege divina vitiosis cordis cogitationibus, vel etiam concupiscentiis oculorum locum relinquamus: aut legem ipsam sic interpretemur, prout ipsimet optamus.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. The sedition of Korah, and the punishment.

Verse 1.

NOW BEHOLD KORAH) In the Greek: κὰι ἐλάλησε Κορέ. In the Hebrew: and Korah took, namely those about whom it is treated in the following verse. Korah, as the firstborn, claimed for himself the right of sacrificing by ancient law. See below 3.

OF THE SONS OF REUBEN) Who could not digest that the right of the Priesthood had been taken away from Reuben, as the firstborn of Jacob.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. Seditio Coræ, & pœna.

Vers. 1.

ECCE AUTEM CORE) In Græco: κὰι ἐλάλησε Κορέ. In Hebræo: & assumsit Core, nempe illos, de quibus agitur Commate sequenti. Core ut primogenitus veteri jure sacrifi- candi jus sibi vindicabat. Vid. infra 3.

DE FILIIS RUBEN) Qui concoquere non poterant Ru- beni, ut Jacobi primogenito, ablatum jus Sacerdotii.

## 16:2
Verse 2.

PRINCES OF THE ASSEMBLY) In Hebrew, prince of the gathering: ἀρχηγοὶ συναγωγῆς in the Greek. This gathering is a number of men, a thousand, or a hundred. See above Exod. 18, 2.

WHO AT THE TIME OF THE COUNCIL WERE CALLED BY NAME] Just as in the tribes they are called קריאי העדה ἐπίκλητοι τῆς συναγωγῆς, the eminent among their own, Num. 1, 16. So also in the thousand-man cohorts and in the centuries. For the number of two hundred and fifty sufficiently prevents this passage from being understood as the Sanhedrin of LXX men. Korah partly gathered those who were heads of cohorts, partly those who were of great value in authority among their own. The former is indicated by the first, the latter by the second, and therefore to the latter is added ἄνδρες ὀνοματοὶ, which is an epexegesis of the word ἐπίκλητος, which is also attributed to more noble days below 28, 18. 25. 29, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

PROCERES SYNAGOGÆ) Hebraice princeps cætus: ἀρχηγοὶ συναγωγῆς in Græco. Cœtus hic est numerus ho- minum mille, aut centum. Vide supra Exod. 18, 2.

QUI TEMPORE CONCILII PER NOMINA VO- CABANTUR] Sicut in tribubus dicuntur קריאי העדה ἐπίκλητοι τῆς συναγωγῆς, eximii inter suos, Num. 1, 16. Sic & in millenariis cohortibus & in centuriis. Nam ne de Sy- nedrio LXX. virum intelligi hic locus possit, satis impedit numerus ducentorum quinquaginta. Core partim collegit eos qui capita erant cohortium, partim eos, qui autoritate apud suos plurimum valebant. Illud prioribus, hoc poste- rioribus indicatur, ideoque additur posterioribus ἄνδρες ὀνο- ματοὶ, quæ ἐπεξήγησις est vocis ἐπίκλητος, quæ & diebus no- bilioribus tribuitur infra 28, 18. 25. 29, 1.

## 16:9
Verse 9. THAT YOU MIGHT SERVE HIM.

This is explained concerning sacrifices in the German version. But those belonged only to the priests and the sons of Aaron, not to the rest. Nor is there anything in the source text here regarding sacrifices.

Latin:

Vers. 9. UT SERVIRETIS EI.

DE Sacrificiis hoc in versione Germ. explicatur. Sed ea Sacerdotum tantum & Aronidarum erant, non cæterorum. Nec in fonte quicquam de Sacrificiis hic habetur.

## 16:14
Verse 14.

WILL YOU ALSO GOUGE OUT OUR EYES) To use illusions in the censers.

Some Hebrews explain this concerning the illusions and fascination of the whole multitude, or even of the elders of Israel, asking whether you wish to gouge out their eyes so that they do not see how you have dealt with them: others interpret this concerning the spies, asking whether you wish to take away the eyes of these men, so that they do not condemn what ought to be condemned? Others explain it thus: even if you gouge out our eyes, we will not come to you: See Fagius on this passage. There is no talk here of illusions in the censers: nor are the seditious speaking of the fascination of their own eyes, as the Vulgate rendered it, but they say, do you wish to gouge out the eyes OF THESE MEN, as the Chaldean also interpreted it, and thus, if they are not speaking of the spies, they imply that which they saw with their own eyes, the deformity of the land: do you wish to fascinate the eyes of these (pointing demonstratively to all of them), so that they do not see your wickedness, or, do you think all are so blinded by your illusions that they do not understand your palpable imposture?

Latin:

Vers. 14.

AN ET OCULOS NOSTROS VIS ERUERE) Præ- stigiis uti in thuribulis.

De præstigiis & fascinatione universæ multitudi- nis, vel etiam seniorum Israel Ebræi nonnulli expo- nunt, num illis vis oculos eruere, ut non videant, quomodo cum ea egeris: alii de exploratoribus h. m. interpretantur, nunquid oculos adimere viris istis vis, ne damnent, quæ forent damnanda? alii sic exponunt: etiamsi nobis oculos eruas, non veniemus ad te: Vid. Fagius in h. l. De præstigiis in thuribulis hîc sermo non est: neque de fascinatio- ne oculorum suorum loquuntur seditiosi, ut Vulgat. reddidit, sed num oculos, inquiunt, ISTORUM VI- RORUM, uti Chald. etiam interpretatus est, vis eruere, adeoque si non de exploratoribus agant, quod oculis suis viderunt terræ difformitatem, id innuunt: num vis istis (δεικτικῶς monstrando uni- versos) oculos fascinare, ne videant tuam nequi- tiam, vel, an putas omnes tuis præstigiis ita excæ- catos, ut palpabilem tuam imposturam non intel- ligant?

## 16:15
Verse 15.

THAT I HAVE NOT TAKEN EVEN A DONKEY FROM THEM) Nothing is to be changed. See a similar protestation in 1 Sam. 12:3. The LXX, however, read אלא חמוד ἐπιθύμημα αὐτῶν ὐδενὸς ἕιληφα. And the Samaritan Codex of the Christians followed them, as it often does.

Grotius rightly departs here from his Capellus, whose suspicion concerning the corrupted Hebrew text Buxtorf also refutes in his Vindiciae, p. 540, not only from the consensus of the Chaldean Paraphrast and others, but also from a collation of that passage in 1 Sam. 12:3, observing furthermore that this passage is one of those 13 which the ancient Hebrews wrote were intentionally changed by the LXX interpreters, so that, for instance, the nations would not seize upon this phrase as a cause for caviling, as if he had played with an equivocation, saying: Perhaps he took no donkey, but something else, from which it is clear that a reading already existed here in the Greek, and was thence introduced into the Samaritan text; the Hebrew reading, on the contrary, is approved.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

QVOD NE ASELLUM QVIDEM UNQVAM AC- CEPERIM AB EIS) Nihil mutandum. Vide similem obtestationem 1. Sam. 12,3. LXX. tamen legerunt אלא חמוד ἐπιθύμημα αὐτῶν ὐδενὸς ἕιληφα. Et eos sequutus, ut sæpe, Sa- maritanus Christianorum Codex.

Merito hic à Capello suo discedit Grotius, cujus suspicionem de textu Ebræo corrupto di- luit etiam Buxtorffius in vindic. p. 540. non mo- do è consensu Paraphrastæ Chaldæi, & aliorum, sed etiam è collatione loci istius 1. Sam. 12, 3. ob- servans insuper, quod hic locus unus sit ex illis 13. quos Ebræi veteres scripserunt studio à LXX. in- terpp. esse mutatos, ne vid. gentes ex hac phrasi causam cavillandi arriperent, quasi æquivocatione lusisset, dicentes: Asinum forte nullius accepit, sed aliquid aliud, unde liquet, jam olim hinc lectio- nem in Græcis extitisse, & inde in Samariticum textum illatum esse; lectionem è contrario He- bræam approbatam.

## 16:16 Addition
On chapter 16, verse 16, BEFORE THE LORD, at page 535, b.

Bonfrer thinks this was not done in the tabernacle, but outside the tabernacle, because the tabernacle could not hold 250 men.

Latin:

Ad cap. 16. vers. 16. CORAM DOMINO. ad pag. 535. b.

Non id in tabernaculo factum, sed extra ta- bernaculum putat Bonfrer. quod tabernaculum vi- ros 250. capere nequiverit.

## 16:21
Verse 21.

SEPARATE YOURSELVES FROM THE MIDST OF THIS CONGREGATION) It is the duty of good subjects to separate themselves from the seditious.

That separation was made for the sake of a punishment to be inflicted only upon the accomplices of the guilt, not indeed for the sake of avoiding the guilt.

Latin:

Verf. 21.

SEPARARAMINI DE MEDIO CONGREGATIONIS HUJUS) Bonorum subditorum est segregare se a seditiosis.

Segregatio illa fiebat ob pœnam non nisi cul- pæ complicibus infligendam, non vero ob culpam evitandam.

## 16:30
Verse 30.

BUT IF THE LORD SHALL HAVE MADE A NEW THING] The Hebrews, if the Lord shall have created a creation. For they read אם בריא יברא: But the Greeks read: אם בארה יבאר ἀλλ’ ἢ ἐν χάσματι δείξει Κύριος. For באר is translated to declare, and בארה, to be the same as באר, the plural בארות shows, pits, cisterns. Moreover, that χάσματι should be read in the LXX, not φάσματι as some books have, both the older books and Augustine in his questions on this passage show.

Latin:

Verf. 30.

SIN AUTEM NOVAM REM FECERIT DOMI- NVS] Hebræi, si creationem creaverit Dominus. Legunt enim אם בריא יברא : At Græci legerunt : אם בארה יבאר ἀλλ’ ἢ ἐν χάσματι δείξει Κύριος. Nam באר ver- titur διασαφεῖν, & בארה, idem esse, quod באר mon- strat plurale בארות, φρέατα λάκκοι. Legendum autem in LXX. χάσματι, non ut quidam libri habent φάσματι, ostendunt & libri antiquiores, & Augustinus in quæstioni- bus ad hunc locum.

## 16:32
Ver. 32.

HE SWALLOWED THEM UP WITH THEIR TABERNACLES, AND ALL THEIR SUBSTANCE.

A doubt is raised by some, whether Korah himself was among those whom the earth swallowed, or not? Since mention is made only of Dathan and Abiram in v. 25 and 27. Deut. 11, 6. Psalm 106, 17. and Josephus, book 4, ch. 3, teaches that Korah was not swallowed by the earth, but by fire: which is also the opinion of Cajetan, Fr. Junius, Dn. D. Varenius, and certain others: But since Korah was the ringleader in this sedition, and Moses dealt with him especially concerning it v. 5 and 8, to whom the others are joined as to a head under the name of his assembly or faction v. 5 and 6, 10, 11, 16, and he ordered the people to separate no less from the tabernacles of Korah than from the rest v. 24, from whom also the people are said to have separated themselves v. 22, and the earth swallowed these with their tabernacles v. 32, it is manifest that Korah cannot be exempted from this destruction, of whom express mention is made v. 32. Nor indeed can Korah be numbered among those who were consumed by fire: for their number, precisely defined as 250 men, is openly distinguished from Korah and the remaining leaders and authors of the sedition v. 1 and v. 32 and 35. Add that the passage concerning Korah being taken away with Dathan and Abiram by the earth, while the fire killed those 250 men, is clearer than the sun, Numbers 26, 10, in twisting which the authors of the contrary opinion are occupied in vain, since in the source, not only according to the distinction of the accents, but by an open conjunction in the accusative case, the earth opening its mouth is said to have swallowed Korah just as much as Dathan and Abiram, whence Abulensis, Torniellus, Bonfrer, Cornel. à Lapid., and most others They commonly teach that Korah himself was also swallowed by the earth, along with all his household, as is held in v. 32, with the exception, however, of his sons, who were not partners in that sedition. Num. 26, 11. Nor does it hinder that in v. 25, 27, only Dathan and Abiram are named. For Moses had no need to summon Korah, who was already present, to whom Moses had already reproached the sedition as the ringleader in v. 8 and 11, nor is the placement of these in Deut. 11, 6 and Ps. 106, 17 an exclusion of others: just as On, listed in Num. 16, 1 among the first authors of the sedition, is not therefore to be exempted from destruction and punishment because no mention of him is made afterwards, either in the reproach of the guilt or in the execution of the punishment, and because he is likewise passed over in parallel passages: since there is no doubt that he, as equal to the others in guilt, was also equal to them in punishment.

INTO HELL (שאול, εἰς ᾅδꙋ, supply places. The word, both Hebrew and Greek, is properly said of the body, and signifies places that are within the earth, as for the most part graves, withdrawn from the sight of men, whence the name ἀϊδὲς: thence, by a translation made to the human soul, as we are accustomed to take words from known things to signify things unknown to us, it is put for that region which is known to God, unknown to us, which preserves human spirits until the time of judgment, both of those who lived well and of those who lived badly. For there is no distinction of that matter in this word, which will become more manifest to him who has read our notes on Matt. 11, 23; Luke 16, 23; 23, 43.

We admit that both words are used of the body, so that it denotes a grave: nor is there any doubt about that. But that it is said to be designated by that word as a common region of souls is asserted ἄτερ γραφῆς (without Scripture). Grotius repeats this on Luke 16, 23. The rich man was indeed ἐν ᾅδη (in Hades), but Lazarus was also ἐν ᾅδη, with the regions of ᾅδꙋ (Hades) separated. For both Paradise and Gehenna, or as the Greeks used to speak, the Elysian fields and Tartarus, are in ᾅδꙋ. I would have wished that Grotius had proved that from the Scriptures. But I see no book brought forward from the Biblical Code. He cites at least Virgil, Diphilus, Sophocles, Diodorus Siculus, Plato, Plutarch, Iamblichus, and among the Jews, Josephus, and among the Christians, Tertullian and Ambrose. But what did the heathens know about the receptacles of souls, and whether the region of the brute and the damned is common, distinguished by its own chambers? But because Josephus used that word ᾅδꙋ generally, and Tertullian used the word for the underworld in his book De Anima, is a common region of souls, both of the faithful and the unfaithful, therefore established in Scripture? For the question here is about the sense of Scripture. Ambrose speaks of the philosophers and uses their language in his book De bono mortis, ch. 10. It had been enough to say to them (the philosophers) that souls liberated from bodies sought ᾅδην, i.e., a place that is not seen, which place we call hell in Latin. He does indeed add, finally, that Scripture also calls those habitations storehouses of souls: but he does not add that Scripture designates Paradise by the name ᾅδꙋ just as it does Gehenna: Grotius therefore is in vain on Luke 23, 43, explaining the words κατέβη εἰς ᾅδꙋ (he descended into Hades), which he thinks were added to the creed, from that passage of Luke: If Christ's soul, he says, was in Paradise, it follows that it was ἐν ᾅδη. For just as the words παραδείσꙋ (of Paradise) and γεέννης (of Gehenna) signify a distinct lot of the good and the bad, so ᾅδης (Hades) commonly designates the state of souls separated from the body and is opposed both to this life and to the resurrection, in which way the Holy Scriptures also use שאול. He did not prove this from the Holy Scriptures. The words of Jacob in Gen. 37, 35 do not teach this. Some accept them as referring to the grave, or by explaining the preposition אל with R. Solomon as BECAUSE, as it is accepted in this way in 1 Sam. 2, 27 and 2 Sam. 13, 16: I shall go down mourning into the grave BECAUSE OF my son torn by wild beasts: or by explaining it simply in that way, with Christoph. à Castro in Baruch, p. 497: I shall not cease to mourn until you commit me to burial. Others wish the word שׁאול here to be taken for the state of death, not because a peculiar receptacle of souls is designated into which all souls commonly tend after death, but because death itself and the state of death in general is sometimes expressed by that word, as is manifest in Psalm 89, 49: Who is the man who shall live and not see death, shall deliver his soul from the hand of hell? where the same thing is expressed in both members of the verse, in the manner of Scripture, by emphatic repetition. Job 7, 9: As the cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to the underworld does not ascend. But why the verb καταβαίνων (descending) is then used, Grotius gives not a bad reason for that, that the Greek language received it to signify the condition of separated souls for no other reason than that, just as the body, after it descends into the grave, is no longer seen, so also the soul having slipped out of the body. But the Apostolic Creed cannot be explained concerning the state of death: because a peculiar article is held in it concerning the death of Christ: DEAD; BURIED, DESCENDED INTO HELL. Nor does the soul of Christ come into the state or region of separated souls only after burial. If, therefore, that were signified, the descent into hell should have been placed before the burial. And who does not know that death brings this about, that he who dies is in the state of the dead, whoever that may be after death? The mention of this matter in the short Creed would therefore have been superfluous. But Grotius, on the contrary, says it was not superfluous. For since there were various opinions among the Pagans concerning the state of souls after this life, it was relevant to the matter to teach men by Christ's example ὡς ὑφέσηκεν ἡ ψυχὴ τῶν ἀποθανόντων (that the soul of those who have died subsists), i.e., that souls are not extinguished with bodies, but are preserved in unseen places. But that the soul was not extinguished was already sufficiently taught by the profession of the resurrection, because that could not happen unless the soul had resumed the body and Christ had been brought to life. If the soul were extinguished with the body, how would the resurrection happen? Then indeed, that the soul of Christ remained surviving in death, the commendation of the same into the hands of God the Father, and the promise made to the thief: Today you will be with me in Paradise, sufficiently confirms. And since in the Creed we believe in the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life for the sake of that matter; in order to teach that the soul is not extinguished with the body, there was no need for that very obscure addition or peculiar article concerning the descent into hell: What of the fact that that descent into hell is proper and peculiar to Christ, and not indeed common to other men: that that descent into hell followed the burial of Christ, and that Christ, having been ζωοποιηθεὶς vivified in spirit, descended into hell, as is gathered from 1 Peter 3:18 and the series of the articles of the Creed. Because after burial he could not descend into hell unless vivified. Descending therefore, he first demonstrated himself alive to those in the underworld, afterwards he showed himself revived to men; finally to those above in Heaven through his glorious ascension, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth, Phil. 2:10.

Latin:

Verf. 32.

DEVORAVIT ILLOS CUM TABERNA- CULIS SUIS, ET UNIVERSA SUBSTAN- TIA EORUM.

Dubium à nonnullis movetur, an inter istos, quos terra absorpsit, Coreb ipse fuerit, nec ne? si- quidem Dathani, & Abiram solum mentio fiat v. 25. & 27. Deut. 11, 6. Psal. 106, 17. & Joseph. l. 4. c. 3. Coreh non terra, sed incendio absorptum doceat: quæ etiam est Cajetani, Fr. Junii, Dn. D. Varenii & aliorum quorundam sententia: Sed quum Core primipilus in hac seditione fuerit, eumque impri- mis de eadem convenerit Moses v. 5. & 8. cui cæ- teri tanquam capiti sub nomine cœtus seu factio- nis ejus adjunguntur v. 5. & 6. 10. 11. 16. ac separari jusserit populum non minus à Coreh, quam reli- quorum tabernaculis v. 24. à quibus etiam sese v. 22. separasse dicitur populus, atque hos cum taber- naculis suis devoravit terra v. 32. manifestum est Core ab hoc exitio non posse eximi, cujus expref- sa mentio fit v. 32. Nec vero Core inter eos nume- rari potest, qui igne absumti sunt: nam eorum numerus præcise definitus 250. virorum à Core, & reliquis primoribus seditionis autoribus aperte discriminatur v. 1. & v. 32. & 35. Adde quod sole clarior sit locus de Cora cum Dathan & Abiramo, terra abrepto cum ignis interficeret illos 250. vi- ros, Numer. 26, 10. in quo torquendo nequic- quam contrariæ sententiæ autores occupantur, quum in fonte non juxta distinctionem accentuum tantum, sed apertam in casu accusativo conjunctio- nem terra aperiens os suum Corahum æque ac Da- than, & Abiram devorasse dicitur, unde Abulensis, Torniellus, Bonfrer. Cornel. à Lapid. & plerique alii communiter ipsum etiam Corachum à terra devo- ratum docent, cum omnibus domesticis ut v. 32. habetur, exceptis tamen filiis, qui seditionis istius consortes non fuere. Num. 26, 11. Nec officit, quod v. 25, 27. soli nominentur Dathan, & Abiram. Co- ram enim non opus habebat advocare Moses, qui jam præsens erat, cui etiam exprobrarat jam Moses seditionem ceu antesignano v. 8. & 11, neque isto- rum Deut. 11, 6. & Ps. 106, 17. positio est aliorum ex- clusio: uti nec On Num. 16, 1. inter autores seditio- nis primos recensitus, ideo ab exitio & supplicio eximendus est, quod postmodum nulla ejus facta sit mentio, sive in exprobratione culpæ sive in exe- quutione pœnæ, quodque in locis parallelis idem pariter prætereatur: quum dubium nullum sit, eum ceu parem cæteris in culpa, parem ipsis quoque fuisse in pœna.

IN INFERNUM (שאלה, εἰς ᾅδꙋ, supple loca. Vox tum Ebræa, tum Græca de corpore proprie dicitur, & loca signifi- cat, quæ intra terram sunt, ut plerumque sepulcra, visui homi- num subducta, unde nomen ἀϊδὲς: inde ad animum huma- num facta translatione, ut solemus a rebus notis vocabula sumere ad significandas res nobis ignotas, pro ea regione po- nitur, quæ Deo cognita, incognita nobis, spiritus humanos ad tempus judicii servat, tum eorum, qui bene, tum eorum qui male vixerunt. Nullum enim in hac voce est ejus rei di- scrimen, quod manifestius fiet ei, qui nostra legerit ad Matth. 11, 23. Luc. 16, 23. 23, 43.

Vocem utramque de corpore usurpari, ut sepul- crum notet, admittimus: neque de eo dubium est. At quod de regione animarum communi dicitur ea voce designata, ἄτερ γραφῆς asseritur. Repetit id Grotius ad Luc. 16, 23. Fuit quidem Dives ἐν ᾅδη, sed fuit ἐν ᾅδη etiam Lazarus disterminatis ᾅδꙋ regioni- bus. Nam & Paradisius & Gehenna, sive ut loque- bantur Græci, Elysii, Tartara sunt in ᾅδη. Vel- lem probasset id Grotius è Scripturis. Sed nullum è Codice Biblico librum adductum video. Virgi- lium saltem, Diphiluni, Sophoclem, Diodorum Si- culum, Platonem, Plutarchum, Jamblichum ad- fert, & è Judæis Josephum, è Christianis Tertullianum & Ambrosium. Sed quid Ethnici scivere de ani- marum receptaculis, & an brutorum & damna- torum regio communis sit, conclavibus propriis distincta? Sed quod voce illa ᾅδꙋ generaliter usus est Josephus, & voce inferorum Tertullianus l. de ani- ma, num ideo communis regio animarum cum fide- lium, tum infidelium in Scriptura constituitur? De Scripturæ sensu enim hîc quæritur. Ambrosius de Philosophis loquitur, eorumque lingua utitur libro de bon. mort. X. Satis fuerat, dixisse illis (Phi- losophis) quod liberatæ animæ corporibus ᾅδην pete- rent, i. e. locum, qui non videtur, quem locum La- tine infernum dicimus. Addit quidem, denique & Scriptura habitacula illa animarum promptuaria no- minat: non autem addit, Scripturam ᾅδꙋ nomi- ne æque Paradisum, uti gehennam designare: Ne- quicquam ergo Grotius ad Luc. 23, 43. verba κα- τέβη εἰς ᾅδꙋ, quæ symbolo adscripta putat, è loco illo Lucæ explicat: Si Christi anima, inquit, fuit in παραδείσῳ, sequitur eam fuisse ἐν ᾅδη. Nam sicut παραδείσꙋ & γεέννης vocabula distinctam bonorum malorumque sortem significant, ita ᾅδης communiter designat statum animarum à corpore separatarum opponiturque tum vitæ huic; tum resurrectioni, quo modo & שאול usurpant S. literæ. Non probavit hoc è S. literis. Verba Jacobi Genes. 37, 35. id non do- cent. Ea de sepulcro accipiunt nonnulli, vel præ- positionem אל cum R. Salomone PROPTER ex- ponentes, uti 1. Sam. 2, 27. 2. Sam. 13, 16. accipitur hoc pacto, descendam lugens in sepulcrum PRO- PTER filium meum à feris laniatum: vel simplici- ter ita exponentes, cum Christoph. à Castro in Ba- rotius ruch. p. 497. lugere non desinam, donec me sepulturæ manderis. Alii vocem שׁאול hîc pro statu mortis accipi volunt, non quod peculiare animarum re- ceptaculum designetur, in quod comūniter omnes animæ tendant post mortem, sed quod mors ipsa & status mortis in genere voce illa quandoque expri- matur, uti Psalm. 89, 49. manifestum est : Quis est homo, qui vivet & non videbit mortem, eruet ani- mam suam de manu inferni? ubi utroque membro versus idem, more Scripturæ, emphatica repe- titione exprimitur. Job. 7, 9. Sicut consumitur nu- bes & pertransit, sic qui descenderit ad inferos, non ascendit. Cur autem verbum καταβαίνων tum ad- hibeatur, rationem non male reddit Grotius istam, quod Græcus sermo ad animorum separatorum con- ditionem significandam id receperit non alia de cau- sa, nisi quod quemadmodum corpus, postquam in se- pulcrum descendit, amplius non conspicitur, ita & animus è corpore elapsus. De statu vero mortis ex- plicari non potest Symbolum Apostolicum : quia peculiaris in eo habetur articulus de morte Chri- sti : MORTUUS; SEPULTUS, DESCENDIT AD INFEROS. Nec post sepulturam demum anima Christi in statum aut regionem separatarum animarum venit. Si ergo id significaretur, præ- mitti descensus ad inferos sepulturæ debuisset. Et quis nescit, mortem inferre hoc, ut qui mo- ritur, in statu mortuorum sit, quicunque ille tan- dem sit post mortem ? Supervacua ergo fuisset in Symbolo brevi hujus rei mentio. At Grotius con- tra non fuisse supervacuam. Nam cum inter Pa- ganos variæ essent de animarum statu post hanc vitam sententiæ, ad rem pertinebat, Christi exemplo docere homines, ὡς ὑφέσηκεν ἡ ψυχὴ τῶν ἀποθανόντων, i. e. non extingui cum corporibus animas, sed asser- vari in locis inconspicuis. Sed animam non extin- ctam fuisse satis jam docebatur professione resurre- ctionis, quia ea fieri non potuit, nisi anima corpus resumpsisset, Christusque vivificatus fuisset. Si ani- ma extingueretur cum corpore, quomodo fieret resurrectio ? Tum vero animam Christi supersti- tem mansisse in morte, commendatio ejusdem in manus Dei Patris, & promissio latroni facta : Ho- die mecum eris in Paradiso, satis confirmat.
