XIII. From the desert of Sinai, they arrived by a continuous three-day journey into the desert of Paran, Num. 10, 12. 33, at Kibroth-Hattavah, Luther: to the graves of lust, v. 16. Here, where they encamped for 23 days, they were struck by divine fire, from which that place obtained the name Taberah. Cf. Num. 11, 1. Ps. 78, 19. Where also the sanhedrin of the LXX elders was joined to Moses, Num. 11, 10, and quails were given not for one day, but for an entire month.

XIV. Hazeroth, v. 17. Here, and c. 11, 35, where Miriam, struck with leprosy, stayed for some days until she was cleansed. XV. Rithmah, in the desert of Paran, v. 18. Here, and c. 12, 16, near Kadesh Barnea, c. 13, 26, from where 12 scouts were sent out, which happened in the fifth month. In the sixth month, the scouts having returned and the people having been incited and deterred by them, and attempting a return to Egypt, God threatened destruction, with Joshua and Caleb alone excepted. Num. 14, 1. c. 26, 64. c. 32, 10. Ten scouts were extinguished by sudden death, c. 14, 36.

XVI. From Kadesh Barnea, they returned again into the desert according to the command of the Lord toward the Red Sea, and they circled the mountains of Seir and Edom for 37 whole years, within which space of time that whole assembly of rebels was extinguished, and they had seventeen stations in that circuit: for they arrived first at Rimmon-Parez, v. 19. Here, then XVII. at Libnah, v. 20. After, XVIII. at Rissah, v. 21. Further, XIX. at Kehelathah, v. 22. Thence XX. at the mountains of Shapher, v. 23. Furthermore, XXI. at Haradah, v. 24. XXII. at Makheloth, v. 25. XXIII. at Tahath, v. 26. XXIV. at Tarah, v. 27. XXV. at Mithkah, v. 28. XXVI. at Hashmonah, v. 29. XXVII. at Moseroth, v. 30. XXVIII. at Bene-Jaakan, v. 31. (which place is called in Deut. 10, 7 by the name Beeroth Bene Jaakan, because there are the wells of the sons of Jaakan.) Afterwards they proceeded to XXIX. Hor-Hagidgad, v. 32. (Cf. Deut. 10, 7.) From there they came to XXX. at Jotbathah, v. 33. (which region was irrigated by streams of water, Deut. 10, 7.) They also had station XXXI. at Hebronah, v. 34, and XXXII. at Ezion-geber, v. 35, which is near Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of the Edomites.

And these were those 17 stations, until they completed the said circuit from Kadesh Barnea as far as Ezion-geber, from the North to the South, and having traveled the very shore of the Red Sea, and in turn returned into the desert of Zin, and thus they identified the XXXIII. station at Kadesh, v. 36. 37. 38. Cf. Num. 20, 1. Jud. 11, 17. At Kadesh, I say, of Zin, in the extreme borders of Idumea, Num. 20, 14. 15, toward Ezion-geber and the Red Sea, v. 37. Here, Deut. 2, 8. (not Kadesh Barnea, which was situated on the southern border of Canaan, Num. 34, 4. Jos. 15, 3.) where Miriam died, Num. 20, verse 1.

XXXIV. They arrived at Mount Hor, v. 37. Here, where Aaron died, v. 38, and King Arad, who fought against them, having been defeated, v. 40. Here and 21, 1, they set out (having left the straight road leading to Idumea) to the Eastern side, circling the land of the Edomites, Num. 21, 4. Deut. 2, 8, and thus they arrived at XXXV. Zalmonah, v. 41. Here, which name clung to this station from the IMAGE of the bronze serpent, Num. 21. XXXVI. The station was Punon, v. 42. Here. XXXVII. Oboth, v. 43. (c. 21, 10.) XXXVIII. Ije-Abarim at the border of the Moabites, v. 44, in that desert, namely, which is before the sight of the Moabites from the rising of the sun, c. 21, 11, and is called the desert of Moab, Deut. 2, 8. Cf. Jud. 11, 18. XXXIX. Departing thence, when God forbade them to engage in war with the Moabites (Num. 21, 12. Deut. 2, 8.), they crossed the valley or torrent of Zered, and came to Dibon-Gad, v. 45. Here. XL. Thence to Almon-Diblathaim, v. 46, which is also Beth-Diblathaim in the desert of Moab, Jer. 48, 22. Ez. 6, 14. But when God forbade them to act hostilely toward the Ammonites, and ordered that they cross the river Arnon, which then separated the Moabites and the Amorites, Num. 21, 13. Deut. 2, 24, having set out from Beer, they encamped in the mountains of Abarim before Nebo, which was the XLI. station, v. 47. Here, and when Sihon denied them passage through the extremities of his region, which the Edomites and Moabites had granted, they defeated him in war; the King of Bashan also engaging with them, they occupied his region, he himself having been overcome. Finally, they encamped in the plains of the Moabites, on this side of the ford of Jericho, v. 48. 49. Here c. 22, 1. Which station of theirs was the XLII. and last, at Shittim, c. 25, 1, or Abel-Shittim, v. 49. Here, where they remained until, having set out from there under Joshua, they arrived at the Jordan, Jos. 3, 1.

Vers. 30. AND FROM MOSEROTH THEY ENCAMPED IN BENE-JAAKAN) In Bene-Jaakan there were wells, whence this place is more fully called בְאֵרֹת בְנֵי־יַעֲקָן; but a completely contrary journey is described for us in Deut. 10, 6. 7. Truly, we shall say that those two verses were placed there by the error of a copyist when we have come to that place. Let those things also be seen there which are to be said by us concerning that place. For there is no need for that desperate hiding-place to which Grotius often retreats. There are those who say that in Deut. 10, 7 it is said that the Israelites arrived thence at Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah at Jotbathah, so that the word THENCE refers not to Moserah, but to Beeroth; so that, namely, they indeed arrived at Moserah from Beeroth, but having first traveled through Gudgodah, or Hor-Hagidgad, Jotbathah, and the remaining intervening stations. See other reconciliations at the cited place.

Ver. 51. WHEN YOU SHALL HAVE CROSSED THE JORDAN. The river Jordan derives its name from two fountains and streams, Jor and Dan, which rise not far from the city of Dan, which was formerly Lais, afterwards Caesarea Philippi, and finally called Panas, at the roots of Lebanon, and joining near that city they form the Jordan. It is almost the only river of the promised land, very famous in Scripture. Concerning which Jerome says: The river Jordan, dividing Judea, Arabia, and Aulon, which flowing as far as the Dead Sea after many circuits, near Jericho, mixed with the dead sea, loses its name. It is a pleasant river, and as far as the situation of the places allows, it is ambitious, as Pliny speaks, and offering itself to the inhabitants as if unwilling, it seeks by nature the dire Asphaltite lake, by which it is finally drunk up, and loses its praised waters mixed with pestilential ones. Therefore, where the first opportunity of the valleys was, it pours itself into the lake of Gennesaret, 16 miles in length, 6 in breadth, with seven pleasant towns around it, thence gliding through a most pleasant valley, it tends toward the sea of the desert. And a little above the mouth, where it flowed with a very wide and very deep channel, the Israelites crossed, Jos. 3.

Vers. 55. AS NAILS IN YOUR EYES) Better: goads, namely for sinning, σκόλοπες in Greek. In your eyes i.e. when you shall look upon them and their rites. LANCES IN YOUR SIDES) In Greek, βολίδες. The lethal reed sticks in the side. Grave evils will come forth to you from thence.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIII. Mansiones 42. IsraëBackgroundlitarum. De excindendis Cananæis, eorumque idolis.

Vers. 1. HÆ SUNT MANSIONES FILIO- RUM ISRAEL. EXplicat has mansiones 42. Hieronymus ad Fa- biolam tract. peculiari mystice, qui videatur. I. Ramesses: Exod. 12, 37. Quo collocati erant a Jo- sepho Gen. 47, 11. eoque convenerant omnes inter Ægyptios, ad conquirendum stipulam dispersi Ex. 5,12. non minus quam illi, qui cum Ægyptiis mixti habitabant c. 3,22. II. Succoth v. 5. hic: Ex. 13,20. ubi mandata illis Moses dedit de ritu Paschatos annuo, & consecratione primogenitorum. III. Etham in ex- tremitate deserti v. 6. quo perducti columna ignis, & nubis præeunte, Ex. 13, 20. 21. IV. Pi-Hahiroth in- ter Migdolum & mare e regione Baal-Zephon v. 7. hic, ubi Pharao cum exercitu suo eos assecutus est, ac traducti ipsi sunt per mare Erythræum in deser- tum Etham Ex. 14. & Cantico, quod omnium primum & antiquissimum est, Ex. 15,1. Ap.15,3. Deum victo- riæ autorem celebrarunt. Quod Ebræi ajunt men- sis 1. d. 21. postremo sc. azymorum factum, quo con- vocatio sancta ex Dei instituto Exod. 12, 16. habenda erat. Inde continuo tridui itinere d. 22. 23. 24. per desertum Etham processerunt, aquam non inveni- entes v. 8. hic, Ex. 15,22. donec V. in Mara aquas a- maras reperirent, quas vero dulces reddidit Moses Ex. 15,23. VI. In Elim erant 12. fontes aquarum & LXX. palmæ,ubi castrametati sunt Israëlitæ v. 9.hic, Ex. 15,27. VII. Ad mare Erythræum v. 10. hic. VIII. Desertum Sinis inter Elima & Sinai, quo pervenerunt die 15. Mensis 2. ubi coturnices vesperi, & manna tempore matutino acceperunt Exod. 16. IX. Dophka v. 12. hic. X. Alus v. 13. XI. Raphidim, ubi e Petra aqua subministrata v. 14. hic, cum mur- muraret populus, unde Meriba & Massa nomen lo- co datum. Conf. Ex. 17, Deut. 9, 21. Ps. 78, 16, 20. Ps. 105,41. & Amalekitas populo lasso occurrentes, & in postremo agmine debilitate affectos cædentes Josua devicit Ex. 17,8. Deut. 25,17. XII. Desertum Sinai,ubi mense tertio die tertio castrametati, e re- gione montis Horeb per integrum pene annum commorati sunt, quia anno 2. ab exitu, Mens. 2. d. 20. inde moverunt Num. 10, 11. 12. Illic enim lex promulgata Ex. 19. 20. 21. 22. 23. Deut. 4, 13. 14. per 10.dies, & noctes Moses in monte cumDeo fuit, Ex. 24,9. Deut. 9, 9. & de structura tabernaculi, Sa- cerdotibus, & sacrificiis mandata, Ex. 25. 26. 27. 28. 29. 30. 31. proposita accepit. Quarto mense finitis illis 40. diebus tabulas legis manu Dei fabre- factas, & digito Dei scriptas ob μοσχολατρείαν po- puli confregit Moses Ex. 32. postea Dei precibus re- conciliati jussu, alias tabulas dolavit, & 40. diebus iterum in monte commoratus Decalogum denuo a Deo ipso tabulis inscriptum e monte reportavit, Ex. 34. ac mandata divina imprimis de Sabbati ob- servatione & oblatione ad opus tabernaculi proposuit, c. 35. quæ contributio facta c. 36, 6. 38, 24. opusque primo hujus anni qui erat a mundo condito 2514. semestri, cum apparatu eo pertinente, fabricatum est Ex. 36. 37. 38. unde anno secundo exodi Mensis primi die primo postquam mandatum expressum de eo acceperat Moses, tabernaculum erectum gloriaq; Dei impletum est, Ex. 40. e quo leges illas Deus Mosi per intervalla tradidit, quæ in 7. prioribus Le- vitici capp. descriptæ sunt. Eodem anno mense primo Israëlitæ a Deo moniti secundum Pascha cele- brarunt ad vesperam diei decimi quarti.

XIII. E deserto Sinai continuo tridui itinere in desertum Paran pervenerunt Num. 10, 12. 33. in Ki- brot-Hattavah, Luther. zu den Lustgräbern v. 16. hic, ubi per 23. dies castrametati, divino igne percussi, ex quo locus ille nomen Taberæ adeptus est. Conf. Num. 11, 1. Ps. 78, 19. ubi etiam Mosi synedrium LXX. seniorum adjunctum, Num. 11, 10. & coturnices non ad unum diem, sed mensem integrum dati.

XIV. Hazeroth v. 17. hîc & c. 11, 35. ubi Miriam lepra percussa aliquos dies, donec mundaretur, sub- stitere. XV. Rethmæ, in deserto Paran v. 18. hic & c. 12, 16. juxta Kadesch Barnea c. 13, 26. unde explora- tores 12. emissi sunt, quod factum est Mense quinto. Sexto reversis exploratoribus populo per eosdem irritato, & absterrito reditum in Ægyptum moli- ente, Deus exitium Josua & Calebo solum exceptis, minatus est. Num. 14, 1. c. 26, 64. c. 32, 10. decem exploratoribus subita morte extinctis c. 14, 36.

XVI. E Kades Barnea in desertum iterum juxta præceptum Domini versus mare rubrum reversi montana Seiris & Idumæam per integros 37. annos circuiverunt, intra quod temporis spatium totus ille rebellium cœtus extinctus est, habueruntq: sta- tiones septendecim in illo circuitu: pervenerunt enim primum in Rimmon--Parez: v. 19. hic, tum XVII. in Libna v. 20. post XIIX. in Rissa v. 21. ulterius XIX. in Kehelata v. 22. Inde XX. in montana Sapher v. 23. Porro XXI. in Harada v. 24. XXII. in Makeloth v. 25. XXIII. In Thahath v. 26. XXIV. in Thara, v. 27. XXV. in Mithka v. 28. XXVI. in Hashmona. v. 29. XXVII. In Moseroth. v. 30. XXIIX. in Bne-Jaakon. v. 31. (qui locus Devt. 10, 7. vocatur nomine Beerot Bne Jaakan, quod ibi putei filiorum Jaakan.) Post- modum perrexerunt XXIX. Hor - Gidgad vers. 32. (Conf. Devt. 10, 7.) Ex eo venerunt XXX. in Jotha- tha v. 33. (quæ regio erat irrigua fluminibus aqua- rum Deut. 10, 7.) stationem etiam habuerunt XXXI. in Hebrona. v. 34. & XXXII. in Ezeongaber v. 35. quæ est prope Elothas, ad littus maris rubri, in terra Edo- mæorum.

Atq; hæ fuerunt illæ 17. stationes, donec cir- cuitum dictum a Kades Barnea usque ad Ezion-ga- ber, ab Aquilone ad Meridiem, & ipsum maris rubri litus profecti, absolverent, & vicissim in desertum Sin reverterentur, adeoque XXXIII. stationem in Kadesch nancidentifierentur. v. 36. 37. 38. Conf. Num. 20, 1. Jud. 11, 17. In Kades, inquam, Zinis in extremis Idumeæ finibus, Num. 20, 14. 15. versus Ezion-gaber, & mare rubrum, v. 37. hic, Deut. 2, 8. (non Kades Barnea, quæ in confinio australi Cananeæ sita erat Num. 34, 4. Jos. 15, 3.) ubi mortua est Miriam Num. 20. versu 1.

XXXIV. Pervenerunt ad montem Horeb v. 37. hîc, ubi Aaron mortuus est, v. 38. & Rege Arad, qui contra eos pugnavit, devicto v. 40. hîc & 21, 1. profe- cti sunt (relicta via recta, ad Idumeam ducente) ad latus Orientale, terram Edomæorum circumeuntes. Num. 21, 4. Deut. 2, 8. adeoq; pervenerunt XXXV. Thalmonam, v. 41. hîc, quod nomen ab IMAGINE serpentis ænei hæsit huic stationi, Num. 21. XXXVI. Statio fuit Phænon v. 42. hîc XXXVII. Oboth. v. 43. (c. 21, 10.) XXXIIX. Ije-Abarim ad terminum Moabi- tarum v. 44. in illo sc. deserto, quod est ante conspe- ctum Moabitarum ab ortu Solis c. 21, 11. & desertum Moab appellatur Deut. 2, 8. Conf. Jud. 11, 18. XXXIX. Inde discedentes cum prohiberet Deus, ne bellum cum Moabitis misceant (Num. 21, 12. Deut. 2, 8.) Zeredum vallem, vel torrentem transie- runt, & venerunt in Dibon-Gad. v. 45. hîc. XL. Inde in Almon-Diblathaim v. 46. quæ & Beth-Diblathaim in Moabi deserto Jer. 48, 22. Ez. 6, 14. Quum vero Deus vetaret, ne cum Ammonitis ho- stiliter agerent, & juberet, ut fluvium Arnonis, qui tum Moabitas & Amoræos disterminabat, transi- rent, Num. 21, 13. Deut. 2, 24. Beerum profecti in mon- tibus Abarim ante Nebuntem consederunt, quæ erat XLI. mansio v. 47. hîc, & quum Sihon illis transitum per extrema regionis suæ denegaret, quem Edomæi & Moabitæ concesserant, bello eum devicerunt; Re- ge etiam Basanis cum illis congrediente regionem e- jus, ipso superato, occuparunt. Tandem castrametati sunt in campestribus Moa- bitarum, cis vadum Jerichuntinum v. 48. 49. hîc c. 22, 1. Quæ statio eorum fuit XLII. & ultima, in Sittim c. 25, 1. vel Abel-Sittim v. 49. hîc, ubi permanserunt, donec sub Josua profecti inde, ad Jordanem perve- nerunt Jos. 3, 1.

Vers. 30. ET DE MOSEROTH CASTRAMETATI SVNT IN BENE-JAACAN) In Bene-Jaacan erant putei, unde plenius hic locus vocatur בְאֵרֹת בְנֵי־יַעֲקָן; sed contrarium plane iter describitur nobis Deut. 10, 6. 7. verum ea duo commata exscriptoris errore ibi posita dicemus, ubi ad eum locum ventum fuerit. Videantur autem illic etiam, quæ ad illum lo- cum a nobis dicenda sunt. Non enim opus illo de- sperato κρησφυγέτῳ, ad quod se sæpe recipit Gro- tius. Sunt, qui dicant, Deut. 10, 7. inde Gutgodam, & Gutgoda Jhobacham Israelitas pervenisse dici, ita ut τὸ INDE non ad Moseram, sed ad Beeroth referatur; ut nempe a Beeroth Moseram pervenerint quidem, sed peragrata prius Gutgoda, sive Hor-hagidgad, Jot- batha, & reliquis interjectis stationibus. Alias con- ciliationes vide loco citato.

Vers. 51. QVANDO TRANSIERITIS JOR- DANEM. Nomen habet fluvius Jordanis a duobus fonti- bus & rivis, Jor, & Dan, qui non procul ab urbe Dan, quæ prius Lais, postea Cæsarea Philippi, deniq; Pan- tas dicta ad radices Libani oriuntur, & prope eam urbem coeuntes Jordanem efficiunt. Qui fere uni- cus est terræ promissæ fluvius in Scriptura valde ce- lebris. De quo Hieronym. Jordanis fluvius dividens Judæam, Arabiam & Aulonem, qui usq́; ad mare mor- tuum fluens post multos circuitus, juxta Hiericho mor- tuo commixtus mari nomen amittit. Amnis amænus, & quatenus locorum situs patitur, ambitiosus est, ut Plinius loquitur, accolisque se præbens velut invitus Asphaltitem lacum dirum natura petit, a quo postremo ebibitur, aquasq́; laudatas perdit pestilentibus mixtas. Ergo ubi prima convallium fuit occasio in lacum se fun- dit Genesarum, 16. miliar. longitudinis, 6. latitudinis, amænis circum septem oppidis, inde per amœnissimam vallem delabens, ad mare deserti tendit. Et paulo su- pra ostium, ubi latissimo & profundissimo alveo fluebat, transierunt Israelitæ, Jos. 3.

Vers. 55. QVASI CLAVI IN OCULIS VESTRIS) Me- lius stimuli, nempe ad peccandum, σκόλοπες Græci. In ocu- lis vestris i. e. cum ipsos ipsorumque ritus conspicietis. LANCEÆ IN LATERIBVS) Græci, βολίδες. Hæret la- teri lethalis arundo. Gravia mala inde vobis exvenient.

## 33:1 Addition
On chapter 33, verse 1. THESE ARE THE JOURNEYS.

We add what Fagius has here: The Jews console themselves miserably, because these departures give them hope of a future redemption. And they say that Moses described them so diligently to indicate that, just as once the children of Israel, having gone out of Egypt, after a long journey, after frequent changes of places and the hardships of the way, finally came to the promised land; so too it would be that the Jews, finally after many tribulations, would be led back into their own land through their Messiah, whom they still miserably await. Would that they would weigh what one of their ancient Rabbis, namely, R. Moses Hadarschen, said most truly, קודם שנולד מוליך ישראל בגלות האחרון נולד הגואל, Before he was born who led Israel into the last captivity, the Redeemer was born. These are the words of Fagius.

Latin:

Ad cap. 33. vers. 1. HÆ SUNT MANSIONES.

Addimus quæ hic habet Fagius: Misere consolantur se Judæi, quod hæ profectiones spem illis faciant redemtionis futuræ. Et dicunt Mosen eas tam diligenter descripsisse ad indicandum, quod sicut olim filii Israel egressi ex Ægypto, post longam profectionem, post crebras locorum mutationes & itineris molestias tandem ad terram promissam venerint; ita quoque fore, ut Judæi tandem post multas tribulationes, in suam terram reducantur per Messiam suum, quem misere etiamnum expectant. Utinam expenderent quod quidam ex veteribus RR. eorum nempe, R. Moses Hadarschen, verissime dixit, קודם שנולד מוליך ישראל בגלות האחרון נולד הגואל, Antequam natus est, qui redegit Israel in captivitatem novissimam, natus est Redemptor. Hæc Fagius.

## 33:52 Addition
Verse 52. DESTROY THE HIGH PLACES. at page 550. b.

The high places are either hills and elevated places where they consecrated groves to their gods and shrines in their midst; or, as Fagius prefers, columns, signs, and pillars upon which they erected images of the gods so that they might appear more venerable. As the LXX rendered it, στήλας, columns. Moreover, they worshipped GODS on the summit of mountains, Deut. 12, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 52. EXCELSA VASTATE. ad pag. 550. b.

Excelsa vel sunt colles, editique loci, ubi diis suis lucos, & in eorum medio delubra consecrabant; vel ut Fagius mavult, columnæ, signa, tituli, super quos Deorum imagines erigebant, ut venerabiliores viderentur. Uti LXX. reddidere στήλας columnas. DEOS autem colebant in cacumine montium Deut. 12, 2.

## 34:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIV. The situation, boundaries, and distributors of the land of Canaan.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIV. Terræ Canaan situs, limites, & distributores.

## 34:4 Addition
On chapter 34, verse 4. BY THE ASCENT OF SCORPION. at page 551. a.

It is more correctly taken as the name of the place, Ackrabbim, as B. Luther rendered it: and Lyranus, Tostatus, Vatabl., Montanus, Mercerus, Estius, Menochius, and others admit this, with Jerome leading the way. Cf. Jud. 1, the last, which they think was named from a multitude of scorpions. See Deut. 18, 15. Hence the region or city of Idumea nearby, Acrabatena, 1 Maccab. 5, verse 3.

Latin:

Ad cap. 34. vers. 4. PER ASCENSUM SCORPIONIS. ad pag. 551. a.

Rectius ut nomen loci accipitur Ackrabbim, ut B. Lutherus reddidit: & fatentur, præeunte Hieronymo, Lyranus, Tostatus, Vatabl. Montanus, Mercerus, Estius, Menochius, & alii. Conf. Jud. 1. ult. quem a scorpionum multitudine dictum putant. Vid. Deut. 18, 15. inde regio, vel urbs Idumææ vicina Acrabatena 1. Maccab. 5. vers. 3.

## 34:5
Vers. 5. BY THE CIRCUIT THE BORDER) An oblique boundary. To the south of Judea lie Idumea, Moab, and Egypt. Vers. 11. TO THE SEA OF CENERETH) Concerning which see at Matt. 14, 34. It was once a portion of the kingdom of the Amorites. Vers. 17. ELEAZAR THE PRIEST.

The Priest was employed in the partition of the land for a singular reason (since otherwise the duties of the Chair and the Court ought not to be mixed, Luke 12, 13. 14.) and that is: (1) On account of the type of Christ, to whom the spiritual inheritance of his children pertains. (2) On account of equity regarding the remaining Priests and Levites, to whom, although they had no inheritance, yet some portion from each of the tribes fell. (3) On account of counsel to be provided when a difficulty arose, which the Priest received from God. (4) For the sake of piety, so that that whole action might be begun with an invocation of the divine name and ended with thanksgiving. Cf. Pelargus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PER GYRVM TERMINVS) Limes obliquus. Ad austrum Judææ objacent Idumæa, Moabitis, Ægyptus. Vers. 11. AD MARE CENERETH) De quo vide ad Matth. 14, 34. Fuit olim portio regni Amorrhæorum. Vers. 17. ELEAZAR SACERDOS.

ADhibitus Sacerdos fuit in partitione terræ sin- gulari de causa (quum alias Cathedræ & Curiæ munia miscenda non sint Luc. 12, 13. 14.) idq; (1) ob typum Christi, ad quem spiritualis pertinet filiorum suorum hæreditas. (2) Ob æquitatem quoad Sacer- dotes reliquos, & Levitas, quibus etsi nulla hæredi- tas, pars tamen aliqua ex singulis tribubus cedebat. (3) Ob consilium incidente difficultate subministran- dum, quod Sacerdos a Deo accipiebat. (4) Pietatis causa, ut tota illa actio invocatione nominis divini inchoaretur, & gratiarum actione terminaretur. Conf. Pelargus in h. l.

## 34:7 Addition
Verse 7. THE HIGHEST MOUNTAIN.

In Hebrew, Mount Hor: where some understand that Mount Hor on which Aaron died, with Munster; but Bonfrer rejects this because that was to the South and near the Idumeans, not to the North, Num. 33, verses 37, 38. And therefore Ainsworth and Bonfrerius think that another mountain, also called Hor, is designated, which they think is Mount Hermon called by various names, Deut. 3, verse 9. Or they explain 'mountain mountain' as the highest mountain, or they wish it to be called Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, as two ridges and peaks of the same mountain. For this, by a long stretch, closed the Northern border of the promised land.

Latin:

Vers. 7. MONTEM ALTISSIMUM.

In Ebr. Mons Hor: ubi nonnulli intelligunt montem illum Hor, in quo Aaron mortuus, cum Münstero: quod vero reprobat Bonfrer. quia ille ad Austrum erat & prope Idumæos, non ad Septentrionem Num. 33. vers. 37. 38. Ideoque montem alium etiam Hor dictum Ainsworthus, Bonfrerius ipsum montem Hermon variis nominibus appellatum designari putant, Deut. 3. vers. 9. vel etiam montem montem explicant de altissimo monte, aut ita dictum Libanum & Anti-Libanum volunt, ceu duo ejusdem montis juga, & vertices. Hic enim longo tractu Borealem terræ promissæ oram claudebat.

## 35:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXV. The cities of the Levites, and of refuge.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXV. Urbes Levitarum, & refugii.

## 35:5
Vers. 5. AND OUTSIDE THE SUBURBS) A space of a thousand cubits, an accession to the cities. They were called Levitical cities, not because only Levites dwelt in them, but because there the youth were educated in the studies of the liberal disciplines and arts, and the law of God was diligently expounded in the synagogues.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET FORIS SVBVRBANA) Spatium mille cu- bitorum, accessio urbium. Urbes Leviticæ dicebantur, non quod soli Le- vitæ in iis habitarent, sed quod ibi juventus in stu- diis liberalium disciplinarum & artium erudiretur, & in Synagogis lex Dei diligenter exponeretur.

## 35:6
Vers. 6. SIX SHALL BE FOR THE AID OF FUGITIVES) Natural equity is the cause of this institution. Therefore, places of refuge were open even to strangers. The roads were leveled, and there were stones as an indication of the road. Learned men accompanied the fugitive, who might mitigate the avenger with gentle words, if by chance they encountered him. The place of refuge itself was abundant in waters; it was forbidden to manufacture weapons there: he who had fled had to seek a living for himself by some craft. No one was prevented from fleeing, whatever the homicide might have been. But the accused was led under guard from the city of refuge to the judges of the place where the homicide had been committed. If evil intent appeared, he was punished: if it were an accident or a light fault, he was led back under guard to the city of refuge. Cf. Deut. 4, 42. 9, 2. & seqq. Jos. 20. Even besides these, other cities of the Levites were available for refuge for those who wished: if anything of such a kind happened to a Priest, the basilica of the temple served as an asylum. Even among the Greeks, accidental cases were expiated by exile, as Claudius Saturninus proves by the example of Phoenix from Homer, I. Aut facta §. Eventus D. de Pœnis. Add the exiles of Cephalus and Hercules in Apollodorus. Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animals, book one: 'since the lawgivers did not establish involuntary homicide without any penalty, so that they might not give any pretext to those who voluntarily choose to imitate the deeds of those who act involuntarily.' Soon the same author well distinguishes involuntary acts: 'some arising from a cause that is unforeseen and unguardable by human nature, others from our own negligence.' The law which we are treating here looks to the latter kind.

Through asylums, the immoderate fervor of vengeance is restrained, a certain hope of life is left to miserable accused persons, and equity and circumspection are commended to judges; but especially, the indulgence of our supreme Pontiff Christ is typically shadowed forth, by whose death we have obtained life and eternal immunity. See concerning Asylums, which Grotius has here in part recounted, more prolixly expounded from Paul Fagius according to the mind of the Hebrews, in Pelargus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SEX ERVNT IN FVGITIVORVM AVXI- LIA) Naturalis æquitas hujus instituti causa. Ideo perfu- gia etiam advenis patebant. Viæ erant complanatæ, & la- pides pro viæ indicio. Comitabantur fugientem viri eru- diti, qui vindicem, si forte in eum incidissent, blandis verbis mitigarent. Locus ipse perfugii aquis abundans, arma ibi fabricare vetitum: opificio aliquo vitam sibi quærere debe- bat is qui perfugerat. Nemo fugere impediebatur qualecun- que fuisset homicidium. Sed cum præsidio ex urbe perfugii reus deducebatur ad judices loci, ubi homicidium erat per- petratum. Si appareret malum consilium, puniebatur: sin casus aut levis culpa, sub præsidio in perfugii urbem reduce- batur. Conf. Devt. 4, 42. 9, 2. & seqq. Jos. 20. Etiam extra has aliæ Levitarum urbes volentibus pro perfugio erant: Sa- cerdoti si quid tale evenisset, pro asylo erat templi basilica. Etiam apud Græcos exilio fortuiti casus luebantur, ut ex- emplo Phœnicis ex Homero probat Claudius Saturninus I. Aut facta §. Eventus D. de Pœnis. Adde exilia Cephali & Herculis ap. Apollodorum. Porphyr. de Abstinentia ab ani- mantibus primo: ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸν ἀκούσιον φόνον ἐκ ἔξω πάσης ζη- μίας κατέστησαν οἱ νομοθέται, ὅπως μηδεμίαν ἐνδῶσι πρόφα- σιν τοῖς ἑκουσίως τὰ τῶν ἀκουσίως δρώντων ἔργα μιμεῖσθαι προ- αιρεμένοις. Mox idem ἀκούσια bene distinguit: τῶν μὲν παρὰ τὴν ἀσάθμητον αἰτίαν καὶ ἀφύλακτον γιγνομένων ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει, τῶν δὲ παρὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀμέλειαν. Ad posterius ge- nus spectat lex quam hic tractamus.

Per asyla immoderatus vindictæ fervor est co- hibitus, miseris reis spes quædam vitæ relicta, judi- cibus æquitas, & circumspectio commendata; im- primis vero typice indulgentia summi nostriPontifi- cis Christi adumbrata, cujus morte vitam consecuti sumus, & immunitatem sempiternam. Vide de Asy- lis,quæ hic ex parte recensuit Grotius, prolixius e Paulo Fagio ex mente Ebræorum exposita,apud Pe- largum in h. l.

## 35:16
Vers. 16. IF ANYONE SHALL HAVE STRUCK WITH IRON) It is the custom of the Hebrews to circumlocute a matter with many words. The sense is that the penalty of death is for anyone who has killed a man with any weapon whatsoever (as the Romans use that word in law, Hi qui D. ad l. Juliam de vi publica). From the weapon, evil intent is presumed, unless the contrary appears.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SI QVIS FERRO PERCVSSERIT) Mos He- bræorum multis verbis rem circumloqui. Sensus est, mortis esse pœnam qualicunque telo (ut Romani eam vocem usur- pant l. Hi qui D. ad l. Juliam de vi publica) quis hominem occiderit. Ex telo præsumitur malum consilium, nisi contra- rium appareat.

## 35:17
Vers. 17. IF HE SHALL HAVE THROWN A STONE, AND THE BLOW SHALL HAVE OCCURRED) In the Hebrew: If he shall have struck him with a manual stone from which one might die. The Greeks mean the same: λίθῳ ἐν ᾧ ἀποθανεῖται ἐν αὐτῷ πατάξῃ αὐτὸν. A manual stone is one that fills the hand, not a small pebble, such as is prohibited in the new work in the law concerning the ward. §. Meminisse: concerning the notification of new works.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SI LAPIDEM JECERIT, ET ICTVS OC- CVBVERIT) In Hebræo: Si lapide manuali unde quis mori possit, eum percusserit. Idem volunt Græci: λίθῳ ἐν ᾧ ἀποθα- νεῖται ἐν αὐτῷ πατάξῃ αὐτὸν. Lapis manualis est qui ma- num impleat, non lapillus, quali opus novum prohibetur l. de pupillo. §. Meminisse: de operis Novi nunciatione.

## 35:19
V. 19. THE KINSMAN OF THE SLAIN) In Hebrew גאל הדם the avenger of blood: In Greek, ὁ ἀγχιστεύων τὸ αἷμα. The Hebrews understand the nearest by blood.

Latin:

V. 19. PROPINQVVS OCCISI) Hebraice גאל הדם vindex sanguinis: Græce, ὁ ἀγχιστεύων τὸ αἷμα. Proximum sanguine intelligunt Hebræi.

## 35:21
Vers. 21. THE INNOCENT SHALL BE DELIVERED FROM THE HAND OF THE AVENGER) In the Hebrew: And the assembly shall have absolved the homicide from the power of him who goes to avenge the slaughter, he shall be brought back, &c. Assembly in Hebrew עדה, in Greek συναγωγή. Now עדה is for the Hebrews almost the same as the crowd for the Latins. Ulpian in the law Præter D. concerning the violence of plundered goods, denies that two are properly called a crowd: but he says that if there shall be ten or fifteen men, it is called a crowd. Thus the Hebrews call a number of men above ten עדה. But so that nothing should be lacking to the just number, they took here three times seven, and appointed so many judges of homicides in the cities, and of other matters not excepted from the Sanhedrin. Formerly, however, the whole people of the place used to judge: just as also for some time the whole people was in place of the Sanhedrin, with Moses teaching them.

Latin:

Vers. 21. LIBERABITVR INNOCENS DE VLTORIS MANV) In Hebræo: Et conventus absolverit homicidam a potestate ejus, qui ultum it cædem, reducetur, &c. Conventus Hebraice עדה, Græce συναγωγή. Est autem עדה Hebræis ferme idem quod turba Latinis. Ulpianus in l. Præter D. de vi bonorum raptorum, negat duos turbam proprie dici: sed si decem fuerint aut quindecim homines turbam ait dici. Sic Hebræi עדה vocant numerum hominum supra decem. Ne quid autem ad numerum justum deesset, sumserunt hic ter septem, & tot constituerunt in urbibus judices homici- diorum, rerumque aliarum non exceptarum Synedrio. Olim vero totus loci populus judicabat: sicut & pro Syne- drio aliquamdiu fuit populus omnis Mose eum edocente.

## 35:26
Vers. 26. HE WHO SHALL HAVE KILLED HIM SHALL BE WITHOUT GUILT) Not only the kinsman, but anyone. Custom has interpreted this passage in this way from what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ABSQVE NOXA ERIT QVI EVM OCCI- DERIT) Non propinquus tantum, sed quivis. Ita consue- tudo hunc locum interpretata est ex sequentibus.

## 35:27
Vers. 27. UNTIL THE HIGH PRIEST WHO HAS BEEN ANOINTED WITH OIL SHALL DIE) The high priest ought to have been a most holy man, and was believed to be such: now God is accustomed to forgive the sins of others on account of evils piously endured by holy men. See Ezek. ch. 5, and those things which we have gathered pertaining to this at Matt. 20, 28. Then indeed the kinsmen had great consolation for their grief in such great public mourning. The accused was also restored at that time to his goods and honors. And because the high priest was the expiator of such faults, therefore neither to him, if he had committed homicide, was a return given, nor to him who had killed him.

The principal reason, which we have mentioned, concerning the typical foreshadowing of Christ the High Priest, is neglected, concerning which Theodoret, quest. 51. The death of the High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek was the resolution of human sin: he brought back into Paradise those who were exiles from there.

Latin:

Vers. 27. DONEC SACERDOS MAGNVS QVI OLEO VNCTVS EST MORIATVR) Sacerdos magnus homo sanctissimus esse debebat, & talis credebatur: solet autem Deus ob mala a viris sanctis pie tolerata aliorum peccatis ignoscere. Vid. Ezech. c. 5. & quæ huc pertinentia conges- fimus ad Matth. 20, 28. Tum vero propinqui luctus sui so- latium magnum habebant in luctu publico tanto. Restitue- batur autem tunc reus etiam ad bona & honores. Et quia Sacerdos magnus expiator erat talium culparum, ideo nec ipsi, si homicidium fecisset, dabatur reditus, nec ei qui ipsum occidisset.

Negligitur præcipua, quam diximus, ratio de adumbratione ChristiPontificis typica, de qua Theo- doretus quæst. 51. Mors Pontificis secundum ordinem Melchisedech erat humani peccati exsolutio: ille redu- xit in Paradisum eos qui illinc exulabant.

## 35:28
Vers. 28. FOR THE FUGITIVE OUGHT TO HAVE REMAINED IN THE CITY UNTIL THE DEATH OF THE PRIEST) In the Hebrew, he shall remain, that is, he would have remained. For because the Hebrews do not have an optative and potential mood, they use the indicative for it. But he would have remained is similar to that Virgilian one: At tu dictis Albane maneres.

There was also some trace of this custom among the nations. For in the Arician Temple a fugitive was freed from flight by the death of the Priest. Witness Servius on the 6th of the Aeneid.

Latin:

Vers. 28. DEBVERAT ENIM PROFVGVS VSQVE AD MORTEM PONTIFICIS IN VRBE RESIDERE) In Hebræo, manebit, id est, mansisset. Quia enim Hebræi modum optantem & potentialem non habent, utuntur pro eo indicativo. Mansisset autem est simile isti Virgiliano: At tu dictis Albane maneres.

Fuit & hujus moris vestigium aliquod apud gentes. Nam in Templo Aricino fugitivus morte Sacerdotis a fuga libe- rabatur. Testis Servius ad 6. Æneidos.

## 35:30
Vers. 30. AT THE TESTIMONY OF ONE NO ONE SHALL BE CONDEMNED) To death, that is.

Latin:

Vers. 30. AD VNIVS TESTIMONIVM NVLLVS CONDEMNABITVR) Ad mortem scilicet.

## 35:31
Vers. 31. YOU SHALL NOT ACCEPT A PRICE) For the retaliation of a wound a fine could be accepted, not for the punishment of homicide.

Latin:

Vers. 31. NON ACCIPIETIS PRETIVM) Pro vulne- ris talione mulcta accipi poterat, non pro pœna homicidii.

## 35:32
Vers. 32. EXILES AND FUGITIVES BEFORE THE DEATH OF THE PRIEST SHALL BY NO MEANS BE ABLE TO RETURN TO THEIR CITIES) The sense is less full. But in the Hebrew: Do not accept a redemption (that is, a fine or money offered to the judge) so that he may flee to his city of refuge, so that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the Priest. In the Greek: ᾧ λήψεσθε λύτρα τοῦ φυγεῖν εἰς πόλιν τῶν φυγαδευτηρίων, τοῦ πάλιν κατοικεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἕως ἂν ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ μέγας. The omitted disjunctive particle made the passage more obscure, which also happens in other places. The sense is, by no payment of a fine, by no bribe, may you be led to the ends, so that he who has been brought to judgment from the city of refuge under public protection, if it is recognized that he committed homicide deliberately, may be sent back to the city of refuge, or so that to him who is in the city of refuge, it may be permitted to dwell elsewhere before the death of the high priest.

Latin:

Vers. 32. EXVLES ET PROFVGI ANTE MORTEM PONTIFICIS NVLLO MODO IN VRBES SVAS RE- VERTI POTERVNT) Sensus minus plenus. At in He- bræo: Ne accipiatis redemtionem (id est, mulctam aut pecu- niam judici oblatam) ut fugiat ad sui receptus urbem, ut re- vertatur ad habitandum in terra ante mortem Sacerdotis. In Græco: ᾧ λήψεσθε λύτρα τοῦ φυγεῖν εἰς πόλιν τῶν φυγαδευ- τηρίων, τοῦ πάλιν κατοικεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἕως ἂν ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ μέγας. Locum obscuriorem fecit omissa particula dis- junctiva, quod & aliis locis evenit. Sensus est, nulla mulctæ persolutione, nulla mercede perduci te fines, ut is qui ab ur- be receptus sub præsidio publico ad judicium perductus est, si cognoscatur deliberato fecisse homicidium, remittatur ad urbem receptus, aut ut ei qui est in urbe receptus, permitta- tur alibi habitare ante mortem Pontificis maximi.

## 36:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVI. The law concerning not mixing families.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVI. Lex de non commiscendis familiis.

## 36:6
Vers. 6. ONLY THAT TO THEIR OWN TRIBES OF MEN) Nay, and to their own family. The Greeks: ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν. See what we said above concerning the word 27 משפחה, 11. So also in the law of the Jubilee, Leviticus 25, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 6. TANTVM VT SVÆ TRIBVS HOMINIBVS) Imo, & suæ familiæ. Græci: ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν. Vide quæ supra diximus de voce 27 משפחה, 11. Sic & in lege Jubilæi, Levitici 25, 10.

## 36:8
Vers. 8. FOR ALL THE MEN SHALL TAKE WIVES OF THEIR OWN TRIBE AND KIN) Another sense

Of the law. The Hebrew words: Every daughter, who succeeds to an inheritance in any family of the Israelites, shall be wife to someone who is of the origin of the same paternal family. In Greek, not badly: πᾶσα θυγάτηρ ἀγχιστεύεσα κληρονομίαν ἐκ τῶν φυλῶν ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἑνὶ τῶν ἐκ τῶ δήμυ τῶ πατρὸς ἀυτῆς ἔσονται γυναῖκες. This law reached the Athenians through the Phoenicians. בת יורשת נחלה is in Greek ἐπίκληρος, a daughter who is the sole heir. The law is in Sopater and in Diodorus Siculus, book 12. τῇ ἐπικλήρῳ ἐπιδικαζέσθω ὁ ἀγχιστεύς. Donatus on Terence expressed it thus: Let the orphan marry the nearest relative: let the nearest relative marry the orphan, it is an Attic law. See many things which we have brought from the Greeks and Terence to this matter at Matthew, book 16. ἀγχιστεύς is הנחל, whence the LXX made the verb ἀγχιστεύειν. The Hebrews are mistaken who think this law was temporary before possessions were established. Josephus says otherwise in two places: the writer of Tobit says otherwise, 6. v. 13. 14. 15. 7, 14. where σοὶ ἐπιβάλλει ἡ κληρονομία ἀυτῆς is לך משפט הנחלה.

Most understand the law restrictively concerning daughters who have their own fiefs: whence Burgensis, Cajetan, and Masius reject the Vulgate on chapter 17 of Joshua. Yet John Tarnovius in Exercitat. Bibl. book 1, p. 34, contends at length that it should be explained generally. Thummius in Disputat. on chapter 1 of Matthew, and Walther in Harm., who reduced to a summary what was brought forward by them, so that indeed in verse 7 a reason is given why daughters must marry into the family of their paternal tribe, if indeed the possession of the sons of Israel is not to be transferred from tribe to tribe, and in verses 8 and 9 the same is declared in this way: Every man shall contract a marriage in the possession of his tribe, and therefore, by force of the things related, every female shall marry in the possession of her tribe.

Latin:

Vers. 8. OMNES ENIM VIRI DVCENT VXORES DE TRIBV ET COGNATIONE SVA) Alius sensus

Legis. Verba Hebræa: Omnis filia, quæ fuccedit in hæreditatem in familia quacunque Ifraelitarum, alicui, qui fit originis familiæ ejusdem paternæ uxor erit. Græce non male: πᾶσα θυγάτηρ ἀγχιστεύεσα κληρονομίαν ἐκ τῶν φυλῶν ὑιῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἑνὶ τῶν ἐκ τῶ δήμυ τῶ πατρὸς ἀυτῆς ἔσονται γυναῖκες. Hæc lex per Phœnicas ad Athenienses pervenit. בת יורשת נחלה est Græce ἐπίκληρος, filia hæres unica. Lex est apud Sopatrum & apud Diodorum Siculum l. 12. τῇ ἐπικλήρῳ ἐπιδικαζέσθω ὁ ἀγχιστεύς. Donatus ad Terentium sic expreffit: Orba proximo nubat: orbam proximus ducat, lex Attica est. Vid. multa quæ ex Græcis & Terentio ad hanc rem attulimus ad Matth. l. 16. ἀγχιστεύς est הנחל, unde verbum ἀγχιστεύειν fecere LXX. Falluntur Hebræi qui putant hanc legem fuisse temporariam ante stabilitas possessiones. Aliter Josephus duobus locis: aliter Tobiæ scriptor 6. v. 13. 14. 15. 7,14. ubi σοὶ ἐπιβάλλει ἡ κληρονομία ἀυτῆς est לך משפט הנחלה.

REstrictè intelligunt legem plerique de filiabus, quæ propria feuda habent: unde Vulgatam rejiciunt Burgenfis, Cajetanus, & Masius ad cap. 17. Josuæ. Generaliter tamen eam explicandam prolixe contendit Joh. Tarnovius in Exercitat. Bibl. l. 1. p. 34. Thummius Disputat. in cap. 1. Matth. & Waltherus in Harm. qui in summam redegit, quæ ab illis adducta sunt, ut nempe versu 7. ratio reddita sit, cur in familia tribus paternæ nubere filiæ debeant, siquidem possessio filiorum Israel a tribu in tribum transferenda non sit, ac versu 8. & 9. eadem declaretur hoc modo: Omnis vir in possessione tribus suæ conjugium contrahet, & proinde, ex vi relatorum, omnis fœmella in possessione tribus suæ nubet.

# Deuteronomy

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. IN THE YEAR FROM THE SECOND PRESS

This book is called by the LXX δευτερονόμιον in the inscription and Deut. 17, 18, not because it contains a δεύτερον νόμον, a second and new law, but from the adverb δεύτερον, because the law is sanctioned again in the same, as Theodoret notes, q. 1, as is had in Deut. 1, 5. Moses began to explain the law; whence it is said the law was explained A SECOND TIME.

Irenaeus calls it a recapitulation of the law, c. 4, 1. Theodoret a recapitulation of those things which were sanctioned by law and done in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. B. Luther, T. 3. Lat. p. 65, a compendium of all Moses and a summary of the whole law, and the wisdom of the people of Israel, in which, those things which pertain to the Levites and Priests being omitted, only those things are taught which are necessary for the people to know. The Hebrews call it משנה התורה, a repetition of the law, from Deut. 17, 18, Jos. 8, 32, or simply משנה; yet it is not a bare repetition, but at the same time an explanation. B. Luther observes here that it is rightly called a most copious and rich explanation of the Decalogue. They also call it ספר תוכחות, the book of reproofs, as Fagius and Münster note, because the Israelitic people are rebuked in it with harsh words.

But this repetition was made by Moses, who was about to die, not only because all the old men who had heard the first promulgation of the law after leaving Egypt were already dead, Num. 14, whence he entered into a new covenant with the new people, Deut. c. 29, v. 1. But also because Moses, about to bid them farewell, wished to leave this as a Testament, and to impress the law more deeply upon them by this repetition, for which reason he also commended it to new Kings. They observe especially that the name איש, from an idiom of the holy language, is general and collective, and signifies any man or woman; and that the word דבק is properly used of the closest union of man and woman in marriage, Gen. 2, 24, Matth. 19, 5, and that it was always observed in such a way that they married only within their tribes, and indeed their families, nor can the contrary be proven by even one example, if only it is noted that that law pertained neither to the Levites nor to the Kings, but to private individuals. But not in vain was the determination added to the words, every daughter v. 8, inheriting an inheritance from the tribes of the sons of Israel; which are certainly definitive, and define the subject, so that it cannot be taken generally, but they are to be explained not only of an inheritance actually present, but also of a future one, for if any inheritance should fall to one after marriage, the transfer from family to family is equally to be feared as if it happened before marriage was entered into. But also concerning the examples, there is a very great doubt whether marriages were always entered into in the same family, outside of the tribe of Levi and royal persons. But these things are about the book of Numbers: May the author of every number, with whom is the number of our months, grant that we may be found in the number of those marked from the tribes of the sons of Israel, and may we celebrate God among the innumerable heavenly hosts, without number, and without days. Amen!

Latin:

I. N ANNO A DEVTERO PRÆLO

VOcatur liber hic a LXX. δευτερονόμιον in ἐπιγραφῇ & Deut. 17, 18. non quod δεύτερον νόμον secundam & novam legem contineat, sed ab adverbio δεύτερον, quod denuo in eodem lex sanciatur notante Theod. q. 1. ut habetur Deut. 1, 5. Cœpit Moses explanare legem; unde dicitur SECVNDO explicata lex.

Irenæus vocat recapitulationem legis c. 4, 1. Theodoretius recapitulationem eorum, quæ lege sancita sunt & gesta in Exodo, Levitico & Numeris. B. Lutherus T. 3. Lat. p. 65. Compendium totius Mosis & summam totius legis, & sapientiam populi Israel, in quo prætermissis illis, quæ ad Levitas & Sacerdotes pertinent, tantum ea docentur, quæ populo scitu sunt necessaria. Hebræi משנה התורה iterationem legis e Deut. 17, 18. Jos. 8, 32 vel simpliciter משנה vocant; non tamen est nuda repetitio, sed simul explicatio. Recte dici explanationem Decalogi plane copiosissimam & locupletissimam, observat hic B. Lutherus. Vocant & ספר תוכחות librum reprehensionum notante Fagia, & Münstero, quia duris verbis in eodem objurgatur populus Israeliticus.

Facta autem hæc repetitio a Mose jamjam morituro, non modo quia senes omnes, qui ex Ægypto egressi primam legis promulgationem audierant, mortui jam erant Num. 14. unde cum populo novo novum fœdus iniit Deut c. 29. v. 1. Sed etiam quia Moses ipsis jam valedicturus hoc veluti Testamentum relinquere, legemque hac repetitione profundius ipsis imprimere voluit, ob quam causam etiam novis Regibus eam commen- Observant imprimis, nomen איש ex idiotismo lin- guæ sanctæ generale & collectivum esse, & significa- re quemlibet virum aut fœminam; & verbum דבק proprie de arctissima viri & fœminæ συζυγίᾳ in ma- trimonio usurpari Gen. 2, 24. Matth. 19, 5. quodque semper id ita observatum fuerit, ut tantum intra tribus suas, imo & familias nupserint, neq; contrari- um vel uno exemplo probari possit, si modo note- tur, legem istam neq; ad Levitas, neq; ad Reges, sed ad privatos pertinuisse. Sed non frustra ad verba, omnis filia v. 8. addita est determinatio, hæreditans hæreditatem de tribubus filiorum Israel; quæ utique ὁριστικὰ sunt, ac subjectum definiunt, quo minus ge- neraliter id accipi possit, explicanda autem sunt non de hæreditate actu præsente tantum, sed etiam de futura, si qua enim post matrimonium obtinge- ret hæreditas, æque metuenda translatio de familia in familiam, ac si evenerit ante initum matrimoni- um. Sed & de exemplis valde magnum dubium est, num perpetuo in eadem familia inita sint matrimo- nia, extra tribum Levi & personas regias. Sed hæc de Numerorum libro: Concedat omnis numeri au- ctor, apud quem numerus est mensium nostrorum, ut in numero signatorum ex tribubus filiorum Israel in- veniamur, Deumq; inter cœlestes turmas innume- rabiles, sine numero, & sine dierum celebremus. A- men!

## 1:1 Introduction: N. 7. Notes on Deuteronomy, Colloquium
N. 7. NOTES ON DEUTERONOMY, COLLOQUIUM.

gives c. 17, 18. and orders it to be read to the whole people in every seventh year of remission c. 31, 10. Interpreters of Deuteronomy in the Douay Bibles cited are Nicetas and Gilbertus: Of the more recent ones, there exist on this book B. Luther, B. Gerhard, B. Franzius and Johannes Wolfius, and on the last of Moses, Joh. Coccejus.

The time when it was delivered is the 40th year of the exodus from Egypt, the 120th and final year of Moses, shortly after the death of Aaron, which occurred in the same year in the fifth month Num. 20, 28. c. 33, 38. after the victory over Og and Sihon, after the prophecy of Balaam, the slaughter of Beelphegor, the census of the people, the Midianite war and other things which, having been done after the death of Aaron, are recounted from Num. 20 onwards. For Moses began to speak these things on the 1st day of the 11th month of the 40th year from the exodus Deut. 1, 3. and then immediately to commit them to writing shortly before his death, so that this book might comprise the history of a few days from the beginning of the eleventh month until the middle of the twelfth. For on the 14th day of the 1st month of the 41st year the Hebrews already celebrated the Passover in the land of Canaan Jos. 5, 10. having been circumcised before the crossing of the Jordan, which they undertook only after the 30 days of mourning were completed.

Whence Franc. Junius distributes the book according to days into 7 parts: (1) He presents the history of the first day of the 11th month c. 1, 2, 3, 4. (2) The history of the second up to c. 11. (3) of four days from c. 12 to 26. (4) The history of one day c. 27, 28. (5) likewise of one day c. 29, 30. (6) likewise of one day c. 31, 32, 33. (7) The history of the 30 days of mourning c. 34. However, four parts are constituted by Concinnjus. The first is παρασκευαστικὴ, to which we refer the historical repetition of all the benefits bestowed upon the people, as also the punishments inflicted upon the disobedient, ch. 1. 2. 3, as well as the exhortation deduced therefrom to the observance of God's covenant, ch. 4. The second, the exegetical part, first contains a repetition of the law, both moral, up to ch. 12, as being the history of the promulgation of the Decalogue, ch. 5, with an addition of an explanation of this, regarding the first commandment, about having one God, ch. 6, and that we should not venerate foreign gods and thus have no commerce or covenant with idolaters, ch. 7; for which purpose the entire journey through the desert is recalled to the Israelites' memory, with its temptations and benefits, and a dissuasion from ingratitude, ch. 8. and of the gratuitous mercy of God, that not on account of their own righteousness—since the people had rather provoked the Lord's anger more often by their rebellion—but by the grace of God alone was the promised land granted to them, ch. 9; as well as the divine benefits in the restoration of the tables of the law, the calling of the new High Priest and the Levites, and the reconciliation of the whole people, with an exhortation to the love of God and of one's neighbor, ch. 10, having brought forward various arguments, ch. 11; then of the ceremonial and forensic laws up to ch. 26. And indeed, first, as regards ecclesiastical matters: (1) Concerning the place of divine worship, that idols, altars, and statues be abandoned, and the place destined by God be observed, with the avoidance of all affected piety and will-worship, ch. 12. (2) Concerning the ministers: that seducers be guarded against and removed, and apostates be punished, ch. 13; that the mourning of the Gentiles be not observed, nor clean and unclean things be held indiscriminately with them; and that tithes be paid to the Levites destined by God for the ministry, ch. 14. (3) Concerning certain ceremonial matters in the Church to strengthen charity among the Israelites: such as the year of the remission of servitudes, and what is to be consecrated to God himself, and as firstborn to God, ch. 15; and the feasts to be celebrated in honor of God, ch. 16. For the sake of these observances, the duties and requirements of the Magistrate are set forth, ch. 17. (4) The sustenance of the Priests, regarding the avoidance of sorcerers, with the promise of the great Prophet, the Teacher of all, ch. 18. Then, as regards political matters: namely, 1. concerning the cities of refuge, ch. 19; 2. concerning matters of war, ch. 20; 3. concerning undiscovered homicides, bigamy, and the corpses of those hanged, ch. 21; 4. concerning certain economic and matrimonial matters, ch. 22, 23, and 24. (5) Concerning lawsuits and vengeance, ch. 25; containing partly the promises and curses, which are the hedge of the law, ch. 26, 27, 28, 29, 30. For they are first made more certain and are confirmed concerning the entry into the promised land, when the firstfruits and tithes are required to be paid in it with thanksgiving and public joy, and the exaltation of the people is promised, ch. 26. Then, by certain symbols and a solemn attestation, curses are proclaimed concerning special transgressions, ch. 27; and blessings are subjoined, made for those who will observe the law, along with curses for any transgressors whatsoever, ch. 28. Thirdly, the solemn renewal of the covenant made in the land of Moab is exhibited, ch. 29. Finally, an Evangelical Sermon is subjoined, concerning spiritual circumcision by the word of faith, and life, and salvation, so that we may be led to the fullness of the law, which is Christ, as the Apostle interprets in Rom. 10, ch. 30. The third part, the prophetic, then exhibits the final prophecy of Moses, ch. 31, 32, then the prophetic blessing, ch. 33. The fourth and last, the historical, deals with the death and burial of Moses and the mourning of the people, ch. 34.

Furthermore, Grotius speaks neither piously nor reverently of Deuteronomy, almost at the beginning of his explanation of the Decalogue; 'It must be known,' he says, 'that the words which are held in this place in Exodus were brought forth by the Angel in the name of God: but those which are in Deut. 5 are of Moses, referring to the same things from memory, and indeed with such freedom that he sometimes transposes words, exchanges some with others of the same meaning, omits some things sufficiently known from the former, and adds others, by way of interpretation. For Deuteronomy, or as Philo speaks, Epinomis, is nothing other than the law and history summarized and repeated for the sake of those who had not been present at the promulgation of the law and those events.' The freedom of changing words also appears to a not un-diligent reader of other places of the holy Scripture, as Gen. 17, 4 compared with 7; Gen. 24, 17 compared with 43; Exod. 11, 4 compared with 12, 28; Exod. 32, 11 and following compared with Deut. 9, 27 and following. This observation, however, pertains to this: that in the holy scriptures we should not be most superstitious word-hunters, like certain Jews, who dream that those words which are in Exodus and those which are in Deuteronomy were spoken at one and the same point in time, and likewise, where there is a transposition in inverted order, that those things which had been said earlier were also said later, and that the later ones, containing the same sense, were also said earlier. There are enough miracles in the sacred histories that there is no need to invent new ones without necessity and for no use. Thus far Grotius. We do not patronize the trifles or dreams of the Jews: yet we cannot approve that those who diligently observe the words of Holy Scripture and investigate the causes of the permutations, as well as the reasons for the omissions, should be held as superstitious word-hunters, because that can be done without superstition, and should not be considered word-hunting. In the holy scriptures we recognize not little words, but the words of the almighty God, which ought to be considered more powerful and more worthy than heaven and earth, because, as Christ testifies, heaven and earth must sooner pass away than even one iota or one apex perish from the word of God. But while Grotius asserts that Moses refers to the words from memory (not brought forth in the name of God, but by God himself, as demonstrated in its place), he testifies not obscurely that he does not believe that Deuteronomy was written down by the dictation of the Holy Spirit. For that which is referred to from memory, and as it comes to mind, is drawn from memory, is neither dictated by the Holy Spirit, nor consigned to letters through divine inspiration. How then will this Scripture be divinely inspired, or have proceeded from Moses through the impulse of the Holy Spirit, or as Peter speaks, 'borne along by the Holy Spirit' 2 Ep. 1, 21. But perhaps it is not a wonder that these things are handed down in this way by Grotius, since he denies that other historical books, which are held in the Hebrew Code, even had need to be dictated by the Holy Spirit, or were dictated by the same. Let those things which we said in the preliminary Diatribe be compared.

N. 7. OTATA AD ONOMIUM, OQUIUM.

dat c. 17,18. & quolibet septimo remissionis anno toti populo prælegi jubet c. 31, 10. Interpp. Devteronomii in Bibliis Duacensibus adducuntur Nicetas & Gil- bertus: E recentioribus extant in hunc librum B. Lutherus, B. Gerhardus, B. Franzius & Johannes Wol- fius, in ultima Mosis Joh. Coccejus.

Tempus quo tradita, est annus 40. exitus ex Ægypto, annus Mosis 120. & ultimus, paulo post mor- tem Aaronis, quæ eodem anno contigit mense quin- to Num. 20, 28. c. 33, 38. post victoriam Og & Sihon, post prophetiam Balaam, cladem Beelphegor, cen- sum populi, bellum Madianiticum & alia, quæ post mortem Aaronis gesta, inde a Num. 20. recensentur. Cœpit enim hæc Moses dicere mense 11. anni 40. ab exitu prima die mensis Deut. 13. ac deinde statim scripto consignare paulo ante mortem, ut pauco- rum dierum historiam complectatur hic liber ab initio mensis undecimi, usque ad medium 12. Nam anni 41. die 14. Mensis 1. jam pascha celebrarunt in terra Canaan Ebræi Jos. 5,10. ante circumcisi post transi- tum Jordanis, quem expletis 30. diebus luctus de- mum suscepere.

Unde distribuit librum juxta dies Franc. Ju- nius in 7. partes: (1) Historiam exhibet diei primi Mensis 11. c. 1. 2. 3. 4. (2) Historiam secundi usq; ad c. 11. (3) quatuor dierum a c. 12. ad 26. (4) Histo- riam unius diei c. 27. 28. (5) itidem unius diei c. 29. 30. (6) itidem unius diei c. 31. 32. 33. (7) Histori- am luctus 30. dierum c. 34. Concinnjus autem qua- tuor partes constituuntur. Prima est παρασκευαστι- κὴ, ad quam referimus historicam repetitionem omnium beneficiorum populo præstitorum, ut & suppliciorum inobedientibus irrogatorum c. 1. 2. 3 nec non exhortationem inde deductam ad fœderis Dei observationem c. 4. Altera ἐξηγητικὴ primo con- tinet repetitionem legis tum moralis usque ad c. 12 utpote historiæ promulgati Decalog. c. 5. addita hu- jus explicatione, quoad primum præceptum, de ha- bendo uno Deo cap. 6. & ne deos alienos veneremur adeoque nullum cum idololatris commercium aut fœdus habeamus c. 7. qua fini in memoriam revo- catur Israëlitis universa deserti via cum tentationi- bus & beneficiis ac dehortatione ab ingratitudine c. 8. & gratuita Dei misericordia, quod non propter justitiam suam, quum iram potius Domini sæpius provocarit populus rebellione sua, sed sola Dei gratia terra promissa ipsis concedatur c. 9. nec non ἐυεργεσίαι divinæ in tabularum legis reparatione, novi Pontificis & Levitarum vocatione, totiusque po- puli reconciliatione, cum exhortatione ad dilectio- nem Dei, & proximi c. 10. adductis variis argu- mentis c. 11. tum ceremonialis & forensium usque ad 26. Et quidem primo quantum ad Ecclesiastica (1.) Quoad locum divini cultus, ut ἐιδωλεῖα, aræ, statuæ relinquantur, locus a Deo destinatus observetur, cum vitatione omnis κακοζηλίας, & ἐθελοθρησκείας c. 12. (2) quoad ministros: ut seductores caveantur, & tollantur, apostatæ puniantur, c. 13. gentilium lu- ctus non observetur, nec cum iis promiscue mun- da, & immunda habeantur: utque decimæ Levitis ad ministerium à Deo destinatis pendantur c. 14. (3.) quoad ceremonialia quædam in Ecclesia ad charitatem inter Israëlitas firmandam: utpote an- num remissionis servitutum, & erga Deum ipsum & qua primogenita Deo consecranda, c. 15. & fe- sta in honorem Dei celebranda c. 16. Quarum ob- servationum gratia Magistratus officia & requisita sistuntur c. 17. (4) Sacerdotum sustentationem, quoad præstigiatorum vitationem, cum promissio- ne magni Prophetæ omnium Doctoris c. 18. Dein- de quantum ad Politica: utpote 1. de civitatibus refugii c. 19, 2. de rebus bellicis c. 20, 3. de homici- diis incompertis, digamia, & suspensorum cadave- ribus, c. 21, 4. de Oeconomicis & matrimonialibus quibusdam c. 22, 23. & 24. (5) De litigiis & vindicta c. 25. partim promissiones & comminationes, quæ sunt sepimentum legis cap. 26. 27. 28. 29. 30. continens. Nam certiores primum redduntur, & confirman- tur de ingressu in terram promissam, cum postulan- tur in eadem primitiæ & decimæ cum Eucharistia & publica lætitia exolvendæ, & promittitur populi exaltatio c. 26. Tum Symbolis certis, & contesta- tione solemni proclamantur maledictiones de spe- cialibus transgressionibus, cap. 27. & benedictiones subjunguntur legem observaturis factæ, cum male- dictionibus prævaricatorum quorumvis c. 28. Ter- tio solemnis fœderis renovatio in terra Moabitica facta c. 29. exhibetur. Denique subjungitur Concio Evangelica, de circumcisione spirituali verbo fidei, & vita, ac salute, ut ad πλήρωμα legis, quod est Chri- stus interprete Apostolo Rom. 10. deducamur. c, 30. Tertia pars προφητικὴ tum vaticinium Mosis no- vissimum c. 31. 32. tum benedictionem Propheticam c. 33. exhibens. Quarta & ultima ἱστορικὴ de morte & sepultura Mosis & luctu populi agit c. 34.

Porro de Deuteronomio nec pie, nec reveren- ter sane loquitur Grotius in explicatione Decalogi fere sub initium; Sciendum est, inquit, quæ in Exo- do hoc loco habentur verba, per Angelum Dei nomine prolata: quæ vero sunt Deut. 5. esse Mosis eadem me- moriter referentis, & quidem ea libertate, ut voces transponat interdum, quasdam cum idem significan- tibus commutet, omittat quædam satis nota ex prio- ribus, addat alia, interpretamenti vice. Est enim Deuteronomium, sive ut Philo loquitur Epinomis, ni- hil aliud quam lex & historia summatim repetita in eorum gratiam, qui promulgationi legis rebusque illis non interfuerant. Permutandi verba libertas, & aliis in locis sacræ Scripturæ non indiligenti ejus lecto- ri apparet, ut Gen. 17, 4. collato 7. Gen. 24, 17. colla- to 43. Exod. 11, 4. collato 12, 28. Exod. 32, 11. & seqq. collato Deut. 9, 27. & seqq. Pertinet autem hæc ob- servatio eo, ne in sacris literis superstitiosissimus vo- cularum aucupes, ut Judæi quidam, qui & illa quæ in Exodo sunt, & quæ in Deuteronomio sunt verba pariter uno eodemque puncto temporis prolata, simul- que ubi transpositio est inverso ordine, quæ prius di- cta fuerant dicta & posterius, posteriora sensum eun- dem continentia prius etiam dicta somniant. Satis multa sunt in sacris historiis miracula, ut nova extra necessitatem, nullique usui comminisci nihil sit opus. Hactenus Grotius. Non patrocinamur nugis vel somniis Judæorum: non tamen probare possumus superstitiosos haberi vocularum aucupes, qui verba Scripturæ S. diligenter observant, ac permutatio- num causas, nec non omissionum rationes indagant, quod citra superstitionem fieri potest, neque pro aucupio vocularum habendum. In sacris literis non voculas, sed verba omnipotentis Dei, quæ cœ- lo terraque potentiora, ac digniora censeri debent, agnoscimus, | quia Christo teste cœlum & terram prius interire oportet, quam vel jota unum & apex unus de verbo Dei pereat. Dum vero Mosen me- moriter verba (non nomine Dei, sed à Deo ipso, ut suo loco demonstratum, prolata) referre asse- rit Grotius, haud obscure testatur, se non crede- re, dictante Spiritu Sancto, Deuteronomion perscriptum esse. Quod enim memoriter refer- tur, ac prout succurrit, ex memoria depromitur, id nec à Spiritu S. dictatur, nec per θεοπνευσίαν literis consignatur. Quomodo ergo hæc Scriptura θεό- πνευστος erit, aut è Mose profecta per impulsum S. S. vel ut Petr. loquitur Φερομένῳ ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε 2. Ep. 1, 21. Sed non mirum fortassis, hæc ita à Grotio tradi, quum neget alios libros historicos, qui in Codice Ebræo habentur, vel opus habuisse, ut à S. S. dictarentur, vel ab eodem dictatos esse. Con- ferantur, quæ in præliminari Diatrib. diximus.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. THE PREPARATORY PART OF DEUTERONOMY. CHAPTER I. A repetition of those things which happened in the desert, and the punishment of the people.

Ver. 1. THESE ARE THE WORDS WHICH MOSES SPOKE TO ALL ISRAEL) This book is משנה a repetition of the principal laws and admonitions for the sake of those who, at the time the law was promulgated, were either not yet born or, by reason of their age, were incapable of understanding. At the same time, Moses gives an account of the actions of God and of his own.

IN this chapter is contained a summary repetition of the deeds from the encampment at Horeb up to the encampment at Kadesh-barnea, a space of two years. But how could Moses speak these words to all Israel, of whom there were so many myriads, Num. 26? It is not to be thought that this was done by a miracle, as Abulensis, Bonfrerius, Cornelius, and Tirinus suggest, so that the voice of Moses could be heard by all, but it is more likely that these things were spoken to the princes and heads of families, and by them conveyed to the people, perhaps even immediately committed to writing, so that all things could be more correctly conveyed to all.

BEYOND THE JORDAN.

But Moses was not to cross the Jordan, Deut. 31. ver. 2. Response of Cornelius: perhaps Moses wrote this on this side of the Jordan, and he who compiled these journals, while already in Canaan, substituted 'beyond the Jordan' for it. But no change is to be conceded to authentic Scripture in any respect. The word בְּעֵבֶר, as Vatablus notes, signifies both beyond and on this side, so that it cannot be judged which meaning prevails except from the position of the speaker and the listener. Others interpret it as at the crossing, in the crossing, or Jordan.

OVER AGAINST THE RED SEA.

Over against, not as the LXX, near: for the plains of Moab are very far distant from the Red Sea. Others make Suph the name of a certain region, but it is more correctly rendered sea of reeds or weedy or red by the Targum and LXX. There was the beginning, but the plains of Moab were the end of the pilgrimage.

BETWEEN PHARAN AND TOPHEL, AND LABAN AND HAZEROTH.

The latter name, as an appellative, the LXX rendered ἀυλῶν, a pipe. But all are proper names; not of the places in which the Israelites had sinned, as the Targums wish, but pertaining to the topography of that place where these things were said, even if those names do not occur elsewhere. Pharan is the southern boundary, Tophel the northern, Laban the western, Hazeroth the eastern, where the thirteenth station of the Israelites was, Num. 33, 17.

Latin:

PARS I. DEVTERONOMII ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΙΚΗ. CAPUT I. Repetitio eorum quæ in deserto acciderunt, & pœnæ populi.

Vers. 1. HÆC SVNT VERBA QVÆ LOQVVTVS EST MOSES AD OMNEM ISRAEL) Est hic liber משנה repetitio præcipuarum legum, ac monitorum in eo- rum gratiam, qui tempore promulgatæ legis aut nondum na- ti, aut per ætatem intelligendi incapaces fuerant. Simul ratio- nem reddit Moses actionum Dei & suarum.

IN hoc capite habetur summaria repetitio gesto- rum à mansione in Horeb, usque ad mansionem in Cadesbarne spatio duorum annorum. Quomodo vero hæc verba ad omnem Israël loqui potuit Moses, cujus tot myriades Num. 26. Non per miraculum id factum putandum cum Abulens. Bonfrer. Cornel. Tirino, quod vox Mosis ab omni- bus audiri potuit, sed verosimilius est, Principi- bus, & capitibus familiarum hæc dicta, ab iis ad po- pulum delata, forte etiam actutum scripto com- prehensa, ut omnia ad omnes rectius deferri po- tuerint.

TRANS JORDANEM.

At Moses transire Jordanem non debuit Deut. 31. vers. 2. Resp. Cornel. forte Moses stripsit cis Jordanem, & qui hæc diaria digessit, in Canaan jam consistens, pro eo substituit trans Jordanem. Sed non concedenda Scripturæ authenticæ in ullo mu- tatio. Vox בְּעֵבֶר notante Vatablo notat & ultra & citra, ut non nisi ex loco loquentis, & audientis judicari possit, utra significatio obtineat. Alii in- terpretantur ad transitum in transitu, vel è latere Jordanis.

CONTRA MARE RVBRVM.

E regione, non ut LXX, prope: nam campe- stria Moab longissimè distant à mari rubro. Alii Suph faciunt nomen certæ regionis, sed rectius redditur mare junci aut algosum vel rubrum à Targ. & LXX. Ibi fuit initium, campestria Moab vero terminus peregrinationis.

INTER PHARAN ET TOPHEL, ET LABAN ET HASEROT.

Nomen posterius, ut appellativum reddide- re LXX. ἀυλῶν tibiam. Sed omnia sunt propria; non locorum, in quibus peccarant Israëlitæ, uti Targu- mim volunt, sed ad τοπογραφίαν istius loci, ubi hæc dicta, facientium, etsi nomina illa alias non occur- rant, Pharan est terminus meridianus, septentriona- lis Tophel, Occidentalis Laban, Orientalis Hazeroth, ubi fuit decima tertia mansio Israëletarum N. 33, 17.

## 1:2
v. 2. ELEVEN DAYS. The time when Moses spoke these things is not defined, but the place, the distance of a journey of eleven days from Horeb, as the Targum rendered it: By the way of Mount Seir. From Sinai to Kadesh-barnea there are 17 leagues of one hour; from Kadesh-barnea to the plains of Moab there are 34 leagues, as is evident from the maps of Adrichomius: therefore from Sinai to Moab there are 51 leagues: wherefore if you cover four and a half leagues each day, you will come in eleven days from Sinai to these plains of Moab, so Abulensis, and from him Cornelius.

Latin:

v. 2. VNDECIM DIEBUS. Non definitur tempus, quo hæc loquutus est Moses, sed locus, distantia itineris undecim dierum ab Horeb, ut Targum reddidit: Per viam montis Seir. A Sina usque ad Cadesbarne sunt 17. leucæ unius ho- ræ; à Cadesbarne usque ad campestria Moab sunt 34. leucæ, ut patet ex tabulis Adrichomii: à Sina er- go ad Moab sunt 51. leucæ: quare si quolibet die conficias quatuor leucas cum dimidia, undecim diebus venies à Sina usque ad hæc campestria Mo- ab, ita Abulensis, & ex eo Cornelius.

## 1:3
v. 3. IN THE FORTIETH YEAR. Not from the return of the spies to Moses, as Dionysius the Carthusian, but from the departure of the Israelites out of Egypt.

Latin:

v. 3. QVADRAGESIMO ANNO. Non à reditu exploratorum ad Mosen, ut Dio- nys. Carth. sed ab exitu Israëletarum ex Ægypto.

## 1:4
Verf. 4. WHO DWELT IN ASHTAROTH) See what we shall say at Jud. 2, 13. Ashtaroth are the highest mountains of the Amorites, so called from the fact that sheep, which are called עַשְׁתְּרֹת, frequently graze there, Deut. 7, 13. as Paul Fagius holds here. Just as also Bashan is the name of a pasture mountain, from which that region was named. The things which Grotius says at Jud. 2, 13. are different, which we examine there.

AND IN EDREI.

In the Hebrew that AND is not had. Nor did Og dwell in both places, in Ashtaroth and Edrei, but in the former place. It must therefore be referred to HE SMOTE, so that the place where Og was smitten is designated as Edrei, Num. 21, 33. Deut. 3, 1. It was a city in the region of Og near the lake of Gadara, Deut. 3, 10. Jos. 13, 13. Hos. 13, 2.

Latin:

Verf. 4. QVI MANSIT IN ASTAROTH) Vide, quæ dicemus ad Jud. 2, 13. Ashtaroth sunt montes Amorrhæorum altissimi, ex eo sic dicti, quod oves, quæ עַשְׁתְּרֹת vocantur, frequenter ibi pascantur, Deut. 7, 13. ut habet hic Paul. Fagius. Sicut etiam Basan est nomen montis pascui, unde regio illa denominata est. Quæ Gro- tius ad Jud. 2, 13. diversa sunt, quæ illic expendimus.

ET IN EDREI.

In Ebræo non habetur illud ET. Neque ha- bitavit Og utrobique in Astaroth, & Edrei, sed in priori loco. Referendum ergo ad PERCVSSIT, ut locus, ubi Ogh percussus est, designetur Edrei Num. 21, 33. Deut. 3, 1. Fuit civitas in regione Og vicina lacui Gadareno, Deut. 3, 10. Jos. 13, 13. Os. 13, 2.

## 1:5
v. 5. AND MOSES BEGAN TO EXPLAIN THE LAW AND TO SAY.

Which explanation begins finally at c. 5. A narrative is premised, however, concerning the deeds done in the desert, and an exhortation, as was warned in the preface.

Latin:

v. 5. CEPITQVE MOSES EXPLANARE LEGEM ET DICERE.

Quæ explanatio incipit demum c. 5. Præmit- titur autem narratio de rebus gestis in deserto, & exhortatio, ut in procœmio monitum.

## 1:6
v. 6. IT IS SUFFICIENT FOR YOU THAT YOU HAVE STAYED AT THIS MOUNTAIN.

They had dwelt at Mount Horeb for almost an entire year, namely from the third month of the 1st year until the 2nd month of the 2nd year, during which space of time they had received the law, had built the tabernacle of the covenant, had established the priesthood and the polity, and had organized the people by standards and ranks Exod. 19. verse 1. Num. 10, 11. Deut. 1. 2.

Latin:

v. 6. SVFFICIT VOBIS, QVOD IN HOC MONTE MANSISTIS.

Habitarant in Monte Horeb ferme per an- num integrum, à mense sc. tertio anni 1. usque ad mensem 2. anni 2. quo temporis spatio legem ac- ceperant, tabernaculum fœderis extruxerant, Sa- cerdotium, & politiam constituerant, populum per vexilla & acies ordinaverant Exod. 19. vers. 1. Num. 10, 11. Deut. 1. 2.

## 1:7
v. 7. TO THE MOUNTAIN OF THE AMORITES

To the mountainous country, or region, as in v. 2. by Mount Seir the whole region of the Edomites is designated. AND TO ALL THE NEIGHBORS, more correctly to all its neighboring lands THE LAND OF THE CANAANITES, AND OF LEBANON AS FAR AS THE GREAT RIVER EUPHRATES.

Understand: Setting out to the land, proceed to the land of the Canaanite, that is, of the Canaanites. The discourse is about those who are situated in the low and western part of Palestine toward the sea toward the North Deut. 3, 25. as far as the Euphrates, the boundary toward the East, see Exod. 23. v. 31. Num. 34, 7. But there the boundaries of the promised land do not extend as far as the Euphrates, as in this place and Jos. 1, 4. Augustine, Questions on Joshua c. 21, says that a double land was promised to the Hebrews, one, which was hereditary, defined by stricter boundaries from Dan to Beersheba, and from the entrance of Hamath to the river of Egypt, the other as far as the Euphrates, which was only tributary or subject to tax to the Hebrews under David and Solomon 2. Sam. 8. v. 3. 1. Paral. 18. v. 3. 1. Kings 4. v. 21. But from Gen. 15, 18. it is evident that the inheritance was promised as far as the Euphrates, but under the condition if they remained in the faith and worship of GOD, Deut. 19, 8. which, because they did not fulfill, that expansion of boundaries did indeed begin to be fulfilled under David and Solomon, but because of the frequent defections of the people they did not possess those regions fully and quietly as far as the Euphrates, and they did not even fully possess those narrower boundaries, since they could never exterminate all the Canaanites: See Josephus, book 6. Antiquities c. 50. Jerome, Epistle 129. and on Ez. 9. Masius on Jos. 1.

Latin:

v. 7. AD MONTEM AMORRHÆORUM

Ad montana, seu regionem, uti v. 2. per montem Seir tota Idumæorum regio designata. ET AD OMNES VICINOS, rectius ad omnia vicina ejus TERRAM CANANÆORUM, ET LI- BANI USQUE AD FLUMEN MAGNUM EUPHRATEM.

Subint. Ad terram proficiscentes pergite ad ter- ram Cananæi, h. e. Cananæorum. Sermo est de iis, qui in ima, & occidentali Palæstinæ parte ad mare versus Aquilonem siti Deut. 3, 25. usque ad Eu- phratem terminum versus Orientem, vid. Exod. 23. v. 31. Num. 34, 7. At ibi non usque ad Euphratem porriguntur termini promissæ terræ, uti hoc loco & Jos. 1, 4. Augustinus qq. in Jos. c. 21. duplicem ter- ram Ebræis promissam fuisse dicit, unam, q. hære- ditariam strictioribus terminis definitam à Dan usque ad Bersabe, & ab introitu Emath, usque ad rivum Ægypti, alteram usque ad Euphratem, quæ erat tantum tributaria seu vectigalis Ebræis sub Davide & Salomone 2. Sam. 8. v. 3. 1. Paral. 18. v. 3. 1. Reg. 4. v. 21. Sed è Gen. 15, 18. patet hæreditatem promissam fuisse usque ad Euphratem, verum sub conditione si in fide & cultu DEI permanerent, Deut. 19, 8. quam quia non implevere, cœpit qui- dem illa terminorum dilatatio sub Davide, & Sa- lomone impleri, sed ob defectiones crebras popu- li non possederunt illas regiones plene & quiete usque ad Euphratem, ac ne angustiores quidem il- los terminos plenè possederunt, cum nunquam omnes Cananæos exterminare potuerint: V. Jo- seph. l. 6. Antiq. c. 50. Hier. Ep. 129. & in Ez. 9. Masius in Jos. 1.

## 1:8
v. 8. THAT HE MIGHT GIVE IT TO THEM, AND TO THEIR SEED.

The Vau here is to be taken exegetically, that is, to their seed. For the Patriarchs themselves did not possess the promised land Lev. 11. v. 13.

Latin:

v. 8. UT DARET ILLAM EIS, ET SE- MINI EORUM.

Vau hic exegeticè accipiendum, id est, semi- ni eorum. Non enim Patriarchæ ipsi possederunt terram promissam Lev. 11. v. 13.

## 1:13
Verse 13. WISE AND KNOWLEDGEABLE) More correctly, and prudent. He is wise who has learned: he is prudent who knows how to use it: Thus both are said of Joseph Gen. 41, 39. The Hebrews say that in addition to these, there are required in a judge humility, the fear of God, hatred of avarice, love of truth, philanthropy, a good reputation, a vigorous age, and honest wealth.

Moses is said to have proposed this counsel to the people. But in Num. 11 it is said that he proposed it to God: Why have you laid the burden of all this people upon me? Answer: When he said this to God in Num. 11, the inferior judges had already been appointed long before; therefore these are different histories.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SAPIENTES ET GNAROS) Rectius, & pru- dentes. Sapiens est, qui didicit: prudens, qui uti novit: Ita- que de Josepho utrumque dicitur Gen. 41, 39. Requiri præ- ter hæc in judice ajunt Hebræi ταπεινοφροσύνην, timorem Dei, odium avaritiæ, amorem veri, φιλανθρωπίαν, bonam famam, ætatem vegetam, opes honestas.

Hoc consilium Moses dicitur populo propo- fuisse. At Num. 11. dicitur Deo id proposuisse: Cur imposuisti pondus universi populi super me? Respons. Quando hoc Deo dixit Num. 11. jam pridem con- stituti erant judices inferiores, diversæ ergo sunt hæ historiæ.

## 1:16
Vers. 16. AND DEANS) The word ושטריכם is missing here, which the Greeks here called γραμματοεισαγωγεις to the judges, elsewhere γραμματεῖς. Prov. 6, 7. LXX. ἀναγκάζοντα. Aquila, an enforcer. Under that name are included bailiffs and others who appear before magistrates and execute their orders and sentences. David de Pomis calls them in French Geollires, putting the species for the genus. They were taken from the Levites, 1 Chron. 16, 11 and Neh. 8.

The Vulgate is rightly criticized because it omitted the word ושטרים. Although it seems to have explained it rather paraphrastically as those who would teach you individual things: whence Pererius, with Augustine, book 18 de Civ. D. ch. 39, understands those who taught letters. But what have they to do with judgments? Eugubinus and Lipomanus wish scribes, perhaps Notaries, Actuaries, to be designated. Carol. Sigon. de Republ. Hebr. ch. 7, [thinks they were] those who were over the judges, because in the Hebrew text they are called prefects of the tribes; therefore, appeals were made to them from the inferior judges, and these were over the whole tribe, whereas the others only had a certain number of men under them, according to B. Gerhard, who also observes from Josh. 23, verse 2, that among the Israelites in every city there were four grades of offices. First, זקנים Elders or Senate, for the mild name Senate comes from Elders.
