Secondly, רָאשֵׁי אָבוֹת heads of Fathers, the primates of individual tribes, the first and more eminent in the city, Tribunes. Thirdly, שׁוֹפְטִים Judges, who knew and declared the law. Fourthly, שֹׁטְרִים Apparitors, who executed judged matters and compelled the people to the observance of precepts with a staff and a thong.

Such as the Hebrews say were sought from the Levites, as Fagius also notes from 2 Chron. 19, verse 11 and Neh. 8, 11.

The Levites, he says, because they did not have an inheritance with the remaining tribes, were therefore considered ministers of both sacred and profane matters. From this it is also gathered how excellent a thing it is to act as a minister of public law, since the principal tribe was deputed for this; but it cannot be carved out from those passages that they were ministers of profane matters, nor should faith be rashly given to the Jews, since nowhere are the Levites read to have been deputed by God to profane matters, but always to sacred matters.

Latin:

Vers. 16. AC DECANOS) Desideratur hic ושטריכם quod hic γραμματοεισαγωγεις τοῖς κρίταις dixere Græci, ali- bi γραμματεῖς. Prov. 6, 7. LXX. ἀναγκάζοντα. Aquila ἐκβια- στήν. Sub eo nomine comprehenduntur viatores, & alii qui ap- parent magistratibus, & eorum jussa ac sententias exsequun- tur. David de Pomis Gallice Geollires dicit, speciem ponens pro genere. Sumebantur e Levitis 1. Par. 16, 11. & Neh. 8.

Recte taxatur Vulgata, quod omiserit vocem ושטרים. Quamvis eam paraphrasticè potius ita exposuisse videatur, qui docerent vos singula: unde Pererius cum August. l. 18. de Civ. D. cap. 39. eos, qui docerent literas, intelligit. Sed quid illis cum judiciis? Eugubinus & Lipomanus scribas, forte Notarios, Actuarios designari volunt. Carol. Si- gon. de Republ. Hebr. c. 7. eos, qui judicibus præ- fuerint, quia in textu Ebræo dicuntur præfecti tri- bubus, ad eos ergo ab inferioribus judicibus pro- vocatum fuit, & hi integræ tribui præfuerunt, cum reliqui solum certum numerum hominum sub se habuerint, judice B. Gerhardi, qui etiam ob- servat ex Jos. 23. versu 2. apud Israëlitas in qualibet urbe fuisse quatuor officiorum gradus. Primo זקנים Senes vel Senatus, nam à Senibus nomen mite Senatus habet. Secundo רָאשֵׁי אָבוֹת capita Pa- trum, singularum tribuum primates, primi & e- minentiores in urbe, Tribuni. Tertio שׁוֹפְטִים Judices, qui jus noverant & dicebant. Quarto שֹׁטְרִים Apparitores, qui res judicatas exequeban- tur, & baculo ac loro populum cogebant ad obser- vantiam præceptorum.

Quales è Levitis petitos Ebræi dicunt, notan- te etiam Fagio è 2, Paral. 19. vers. 11. & Neh. 8, 11.

Levitæ, inquit, quia non habebant hæreditatem cum reliquis tribubus, ideo habiti sunt tam rei sacræ quam prophanæ ministri. Hinc etiam colligitur, quam egre- gia res sit publici juris ministrum agere, quum ad hoc præcipua tribus fuerit deputata; sed id ex illis locis exsculpi non potest, rei prophanæ ministros illos fuiffe, nec temere Judæis habenda fides, quum nuspiam Levitæ rei prophanæ, semper rei sacræ à Deo deputati legantur.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. THERE SHALL BE NO DISTINCTION OF PERSONS) In Hebrew: you shall not acknowledge faces. Face, that is, those things which appear in a man and do not pertain to the case.

Fagius rightly [notes] at this place: Face, because it is most evident in the human body, therefore by its appellation all evident, apparent, and personal things are understood, for instance, friendship, wealth, power, wisdom, and other things of that kind.

BRING TO ME) That is, to Moses my Prophet, who will answer in my name. See Exod. 18. v. 22.

Nay, these words are of Moses himself, not of God, as Grotius has hallucinated. Moses therefore ordered the more serious cases to be brought to himself, because he had free recourse to God, as Dionysius [notes] here.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NULLA ERIT DISTANTIA PERSONA- RUM) In Hebræo: non agnoscetis facies. Faciem, id est ea, quæ in homine apparent, & ad causam non faciunt.

Recte Fagius h. l. Facies, quia maxime patet in corpore humano, ideo ejus appellatione omnia pa- tentia, apparentia, & personalia illa, puta amicitia, opulentia, potentia, sapientia, & id genus alia intelli- guntur.

REFERTE AD ME) Id est, ad Mosen Prophetam me- um, qui meo nomine respondebit. Vide Exod. 18. v. 22.

Imo verba hæc ipsius Mosis sunt, non Dei, ut hallucinatus est Grotius. Ad se ergo referri ju- bebat Moses graviores causas, quia habebat libe- rum recursum ad Deum, ut hic Dionysius.

## 1:19
Vers. 19.

AND WHEN WE HAD COME TO KADESH BARNEA) He names the places where the warnings had been made.

For this place is near Canaan, only the mountain of Idumea lies between. Therefore, from there spies were sent to invade it immediately. Which is said to have been done from Paran in Num. 13, 1. For this is the name of the desert in which Kadesh-barnea was.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

CUMQUE VENISSEMUS IN CADES BARNE) Lo- ca nominat, ubi monitiones factæ erant.

Nam hic locus est juxta Canaan, tantum in- terest mons Idumææ. Ideo exinde missi sunt ex- ploratores, ad eam statim invadendum. Quod ex Pharan factum dicitur Num. 13, 1. Hoc enim est deserti nomen, in quo Cadesbarnea erat.

## 1:22
Vers. 22. LET US SEND MEN.

Num. 13, 3. Jehovah said: Send: Doubtless the Hebrews had requested it: Moses asked the Lord, who responded by way of τροποφορίαν [accommodation]: Send, which word is to be taken permissively, not preceptively. For out of incredulity, diffidence, and carnal prudence they requested that spies be sent, when they ought to have relied on divine promises and followed GOD (preceding in the pillar of cloud and fire) without hesitation.

Latin:

Vers. 22. MITTAMUS VIROS.

Num. 13, 3. Jehovah dixit: Mitte: Nimirum Ebræi postularant id: Moses Dominum rogavit, qui per τροποφορίαν respondit: Mitte, quod ver- bum permissive, non præceptive accipiendum. Nam ex incredulitate, diffidentia & carnali pru- dentia exploratores mitti petebant, quum niti di- vinis promissionibus, ac DEUM, (præceden- tem in columna nubis & ignis) sine cunctatione sequi debuissent.

## 1:25
Vers. 25. THE LAND IS GOOD.

Here the spies first commended it, but afterwards they added that they had seen in it the sons of Anakim Num. 13. v. 23. 28. therefore there v. 32. they are said to have brought an evil report about the land, which, however, Joshua and Caleb refuted. Num. 14. v. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 25. BONA EST TERRA.

Hic commendarunt primum eam explora- tores, sed postea addidere se vidisse in ea filios E- nakim Num. 13. v. 23. 28. ideo ibi v. 32. malam fa- mam de terra induxisse dicuntur, quam tamen di- luit Josua & Caleb. Num. 14. v. 7.

## 1:27
Vers. 27. THE LORD HATES US) A harmful persuasion that one is hated by God.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ODIT NOS DOMINUS) Noxia persuasio Deo se credere exosum.

## 1:28
Vers. 28. FORTIFIED UP TO HEAVEN.

Surrounded and fortified with very high walls. LXX. τετειχισμέναι. It is a hyperbole. See Gen. 10, verse 4. Deut. 9, verse 1. Jud. 7, verse 12. Psalm 107, verse 26. Is. 14, verse 14. John 21, the last, and on that passage Augustine, tractate 124 on John.

Latin:

Vers. 28. AD COELUM USQUE MU- NITÆ.

Muris altissimis vallatæ, & munitæ. LXX. τετειχισμέναι. Est hyperbole. V. Gen. 10. vers. 4. Deut. 9. vers. 1. Jud. 7. vers. 12. Psalm. 107. vers. 26. Es. 14. vers. 14. Joh. 21. ult. & ad illum locum August. tr. 124. in Joh.

## 1:36
Vers. 36. EXCEPT CALEB.

Namely, Caleb alone, as one of the people led out of Egypt, entered the promised land. Joshua, however, as the leader of the people, verse 38; whence both are joined in Num. 32, v. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 36. PRÆTER CALEB.

Scil. solus Caleb, ut unus è populo educto ex Ægypto, ingressus est terram promissam. Josua autem, ut Ductor populi vers. 38. unde uterque con- jungitur Num. 32. v. 12.

## 1:37
Vers. 37. YOU WILL ENTER BY NIGHT.

What Moses relates here as said to him by God was not said then, when the people murmured, nor in that place, but at the waters of contention, Num. 20, v. 22. He says, however, 'The Lord was angry with me also ON ACCOUNT OF you,' not excluding his own lack of faith, but referring to the occasion through which he fell into it, i.e., by your incredulity and importunate clamors you caused me also to begin to doubt. Compare Num. 14, 13. Psalm 106, v. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 37. NOCTU INGREDIERIS.

Quæ hic sibi à Deo dicta refert Moses, non tum dicta, cum populus murmuravit, nec eo in loco, sed ad aquas contradictionis Num. 20. v. 22 Dicit autem, mihi quoque iratus Dominus PRO- PTER vos, non excludens suam diffidentiam, sed referens occasionem, per quam in eam prolapsus est, q. d. vestra incredulitate & importunis clamo- ribus effecistis, ut ipse quoque dubitare inciperem. Conf. Num. 14, 13. Psalm. 106. v. 32.

## 1:39
Vers. 39. AND THE CHILDREN WHO TODAY DO NOT KNOW THE DISTANCE BETWEEN GOOD AND EVIL] This is what is said in Jonah, who do not know what is between the right hand and the left: Homer in the Odyssey γ — οἶδα ἕκασα Ἐσθλά τε καὶ τὰ χέρεια· πάροιθε δέ τε νήπιος ἦα. A more adult age is called that which knows how to reject evil and choose good. Isaiah 7, v. 14, 15, 16.

Furthermore, Moses does not free infants from original sin, but from actual sins, as far as that degree which is in adults who sin with προαίρεσις. For actual sins also proceed from them, Gen. 6, v. 5. It is one thing to be ignorant of sin, another not to have sin. 1 Tim. 1, 13. Luke 12, 47. For infants do not even know that they live, and yet they live.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ET FILII QUI HODIE BONI AC MALI IGNORANT DISTANTIAM] Hoc est quod in Jona di- citur, qui nesciunt quid sit inter dextram & sinistram: Ho- merus Odysseæ γ — οἶδα ἕκασα Ἐσθλά τε καὶ τὰ χέρεια· πάροιθε δέ τε νήπιος ἦα. Ætas adultior dicitur ea, quæ novit malum rejicere, bonum vero eligere. Esaiæ 7. v. 14. 15. 16.

Cæterum non liberat Moses infantes à pec- cato originali, sed ab actualibus, quoad eum gra- dum, qui est in adultis cum προαιρέσει peccantibus. Nam & actualia peccata ab iis proveniunt Gen. 6, v. 5. Aliud est nescire peccatum, aliud peccatum non habere. 1. Tim. 1, 13. Luc. 12, 47. Nam nec se vivere sciunt infantes, & tamen vivunt.

## 1:46
Vers. 46. YOU SAT THEREFORE IN KADESH BARNEA FOR A LONG TIME.

In the Hebrew it is added 'according to the days which you stayed.' Vatablus understands it thus: You stayed there for as many days after the return of the spies as you had been there before it. The Hebrews in Seder Olam, Abul., Genebr.: as many as in all the remaining encampments, that is, 19 years, Deut. 2, v. 14. Others gather from Num. 13 that they barely stayed there for 40 days, and were ordered to migrate from there immediately after the return of the spies. The words in the source can be taken according to the customary Hebraism as a repetition and an indeterminate explanation of that which had preceded, 'many days'.

Latin:

Vers. 46. SEDISTIS ERGO IN CADES BARNE MULTO TEMPORE.

In Ebr. additur secundum dies, quibus mansi- stis. Vatablus id ita intelligit. Tot diebus post regres- sum exploratorum ibi mansistis, quot ante eundem ibi fueratis. Ebræi in Seder Olam, Abul. Genebr. quot in reliquis omnibus mansionibus, hoc est 19. annis Deut. 2. v. 14. Alii ex Num. 13. colligunt, quod vix 40. dies ibi substiterint, & post reditum explora- torum statim inde migrari jussi fuerint. Verba in fonte accipi possunt juxta Ebraïsmum usitatum ut repetitio, & explicatio indeterminata illius quod præcesserat, diebus multis.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. The passage through the Esavites: the prohibition of fighting against Moab and Ammon. The conquest of King Sihon.

v. 1. WE COMPASSED MOUNT SEIR. That is: Edom, which is called a mountain, because it is high and mountainous Obad. v. 3. 9.

A LONG TIME. In Hebrew, many days: namely, thirty-eight years v. 14. until they should gradually perish, who had been led out of Egypt.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Transitus per Esavitas: prohibitio pugnæ con- tra Moab & Ammon. Expugnatio re- gis Sehon.

v. 1. CIRCUIVIMUS MONTEM SEIR. ID est: Idumæam, quæ mons dicitur, quia alta & montosa Obad. v. 3. 9.

LONGO TEMPORE. In Ebræo multis diebus: triginta scil. octo an- nis v. 14. donec sensim perirent, qui ex Ægypto e- ducti erant.

## 2:3
v. 3. GO TOWARD THE NORTH. Toward the North, to the promised land, which is Northern with respect to Edom, which you have compassed for a long time toward the South and the West. The sense therefore is, as rightly B. Gerh. p. 72. Just as setting out from Kadesh-barnea you left the promised land behind you, departing from it: so now again you should turn your journey back to it. Turn yourselves therefore to the North, so that leaving the Edomites on the left, and the Moabites and Ammonites (who dwell to the East of the promised land) on the right, you may proceed by a straight path to the Amorites, whom having overcome in war, turned toward the West, you may ascend through the Jordan into the promised land. That Mount Seir, which the Israelites had hitherto for a long time compassed, runs toward the south and west, from it they were ordered to deflect their way toward the North, which the promised land faced. Conf. Münsterus in h. l.

Latin:

v. 3. ITE CONTRA AQVILONEM. Ad Aquilonem, ad terram promissam, quæ est Aquilonaris respectu Idumææ, quam circuïstis longo tempore versus Meridiem & Occidentem. Sensus ergo est, ut recte B. Gerh. p. 72. Sicut à Cadesbarnea proficiscentes terram promissam à tergo reliquistis, ab ea discedentes: ita nunc rursus ad eam iter reflectatis. Convertite igitur vos ad Aquilo- nem, ut relictis Idumæis à sinistris, ac Moabitis & Ammonitis (qui ad Orientem promissæ terræ ha- bitant) à dextris recta via proficiscamini ad A- morrhæos, quibus bello superatis ad Occidentem versi per Jordanem in terram promissam ascenda- tis. Mons ille Seir, quem Israëlitæ hactenus lon- go tempore circumiverant, versus meridiem & occidentem excurrit, ab eo viam Aquilonem ver- sus deflectere jussi sunt, quem spectabat terra pro- missa. Conf. Münsterus in h. l.

## 2:4
v. 4. YE ARE TO PASS THROUGH THE COAST OF YOUR BRETHREN THE CHILDREN OF ESAU.

They had indeed refused them passage before Num. 20, 21. But from this passage and v. 8. and 29. it is clear that they finally granted the same to them through the extremities of their region, as Abul. and Cornel. hold. When they were standing in Kadesh on the borders of the Edomites and Amorites, from where they could pass to the Amorites by a shortcut, the Edomites resisted, but now after that very long circuit, when they seek passage from the border of the Edomites and Moabites, terrified by the miracles among the Israelite people, even if not by the ordinary and public way, at least they permitted passage through the extremities of Edom. Conf. Jud. 11. v. 17.

Latin:

v. 4. TRANSIDITIS PER TERMINOS FRATRUM VESTRORUM FILIORUM ESAU.

Negarant quidem illi antea transitum Num. 20, 21. Sed ex hoc loco & v. 8. ac 29. liquet, quod eundem tandem concesserint illis per extrema re- gionis suæ, ut habet Abul. & Cornel. Cum in Cades confiniis Idumæorum & Amorrhæorum consiste- rent, unde ad Amorrhæos compendio transire po- terant, restitere Idumæi, at nunc post longissimum illum circuitum, ubi a confinio Idumæorum & Moabitarum transitum petunt, territi miraculis in populo Israëlitico, etsi non per viam ordinariam & publicam, saltim per extremitates Idumææ transitum permisere. Conf. Jud. 11. v. 17.

## 2:5
Vers. 5. I HAVE GIVEN MOUNT SEIR TO ESAU FOR A POSSESSION) The measure of the sins of the Idumean nation was not yet filled.

They are forbidden to attack the Idumeans with war, because He had given them Mount Seir for a possession. This command was not only for a certain time, as the wars of David and others teach 2 Sam. 8 v. 14, Is. 60 v. 10, although God did not give Idumea to the Israelites for an inheritance in that manner even in his time, as He did the land of Canaan, so that they might possess it by absolute dominion, whence the Idumeans also shook off the yoke again after 120 years 2 Kings 8 v. 20, Gen. 27 v. 40. But it was also restricted to certain persons. The Amalekites indeed were also of the descendants of Esau Gen. 36, 12. But since they attacked the Israelites beyond all merit, they had to be destroyed at the special command of GOD Exod. 17 verse 13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IN POSSESSIONEM ESAU DEDI MONTEM SEIR) Nondum impleta erat mensura peccatorum gentis Idumææ.

Vetantur bello aggredi Idumæos, quia ipsis montem Seir in possessionem dederat. Præce- ptum hoc non tantum certi temporis fuit, ut Davidis & alia bella docent 2. Sam. 8. v. 14. Es. 60. v. 10. quamvis nec illius tempore Israëlitıs Idumæ- am in hæreditatem eo modo dedit Deus, ut ter- ram Canaan, ut eam mero imperio possiderent, unde & Idumæi jugum post 120. annos iterum ex- cussere 2. Reg. 8. v. 20. Gen. 27. v. 40. Sed etiam ad certas restrictum erat personas. Amalekitæ sane etiam erant è posteris Esavi Gen. 36, 12. Sed quum præter omne meritum aggressi Israëlitas sunt, ad speciale mandatum DEI deleri debuere Exod. 17. versu 13.

## 2:6
Vers. 6.

YOU SHALL BUY FOOD FROM THEM WITH MONEY, AND YOU SHALL EAT.

This seems to be contrary to the words of Moses Deut. 29, 5, you have not eaten bread, to wit, besides the manna. But those words speak of the whole people, meanwhile, those who were in more opulent circumstances, or more delicate, not content with that common food of all, even though it could be prepared at will even for pleasure, seem to have used other foods, and to have either bought them from neighboring nations, or obtained them by hunting Jos. 1, 11. see Andr. Mas. on Jos. 1, 11. Abulens. in Ex. 16 q. 12. Pererius in Exod. 13 Disp. 1. Lorinus in Sap. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

CIBOS EMETIS AB EIS PECUNIA, ET COMEDETIS.

Id adversari videtur verbis Mosis Deut. 29, 5. panem non comedistis scil. præter manna. Sed illa de populo universo loquuntur, interim, qui in eo lautiori erant fortuna, vel delicatiores, illo com- muni omnium cibo, etsi pro lubitu præparari etiam ad voluptatem potuerit, non contenti, videntur aliis cibis usi, eosque vel à vicinis gentibus emisse, vel venatione accepisse Jos. 1, 11. vid. Andr. Mas. ad Jos. 1, 11. Abulens. in Ex. 16. q. 12. Pererius in Exod. 13. Disp. 1. Lorinus in Sap. 16.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. HE HAS KNOWN YOUR JOURNEY) The Greeks in the Imperative, διάγνωθι, remember.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NOVIT ITER TUUM) Græci in Imperativo, διάγνωθι, reminiscere.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. FROM ELATH, FROM ASION GABER.

The Greeks called Elath Hexopolis, or the city of the heroes: Josephus writes that Ezion-geber was called Berenice.

Vers. 8. I HAVE GIVEN AR TO THE CHILDREN OF LOT FOR A POSSESSION.

Ar is not Aroer, as the LXX say, because the tribe of Gad built this Num. 32, 34, but it is the metropolis of the Moabites, situated on a high rock by the torrent Arnon.

They are forbidden to fight against the Moabites, as being the sons of Lot, whence in Num. 25, v. 2, vengeance was to be taken upon them in such a way, however, that they were not to be expelled from their region.

Latin:

Vers. 8. DE ELATH, DE ASION GA- BER.

Elath Hexopolin dixere Græci, vel Heroum civitatem: Hezion Geberi Josephus Berenicem vo- catam fuisse scribit.

Vers. 8. FILIIS LOTH TRADIDI AR IN POSSESSIONEM.

Ar non est Aroër, ut LXX. quia hanc tribus Gad ædificavit Num. 32, 34. sed metropolis Moa- bitarum, sita in excelsa rupe ad torrentem Arnon.

Prohibentur pugnare contra Moabitas, utpote Lothi filios, unde Num. 25, v. 2. vindicta de illis ita sumenda erat, ut tamen è regione sua non expelle- rentur.

## 2:10
Vers. 10. THE EMIM WERE THE FORMER INHABITANTS THEREOF.

Of the land of the Moabites. The Emim are called terrible giants on account of their immense stature, from אימה, as Jerome in Questions on Genesis 14 and the Chaldean [Targum] say, or from אמה, a cubit, as if to say, men of cubits, as Oleaster says. See Gen. 14, v. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 10. EMIM PRIMI FUERUNT HA- BITATORES EJUS.

Terræ Moabitarum. Emim Gigantes terribi- les ob immanem proceritatem ab אימה terra ut Hieron. in Quæst. in Genes. 14. & Chald. vel ab אמה cubitus, q. d. viri cubitorum, ut Oleaster, di- cuntur. V. Gen. 14. v. 5.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. AS TALL AS THE ANAKIM, AS IF GIANTS, THEY WERE ACCOUNTED] The sense is: Just as the Inachidae were called Rephaim, so also were these. The Emim were considered nearly equal to the Rephaim. I say Inachidae with the Greeks, to whom they came, whom Cicero, Pollux, and others call ἄνακας. Just as also an armed woman, called Pallas by the Greeks, was called in the Tyrian language ὄγκα ענק. The word Rephaim seems to be of the primeval language, which Symmachus is accustomed to translate as θεομάχους, others as τιτᾶνας, others as γίγαντας or γηγενεῖς. The most ancient trace of the name seems to be in the Raphaneae of Syria, and some other places of almost the same sound.

The Rephaim here and in Gen. 14, v. 4, are so called from the first giant Rapha, their parent, 1 Chron. 20, 6, just as the Anakim are from Anak, Josh. 15, 13. Others say they were so called because they make men faint and strike them with their immense stature. Masius on Josh. 12, 4, with R. Nachman, thinks it is a surname of the Hivites.

Latin:

Vers. 11. TAM EXCELSUS UT DE ENACIM PRO- PE, QVASI GIGANTES, CREDERENTUR] Sensus est : Sicut Inachidæ dicebantur Rephaini, sic & isti. Emim habe- bantur suppares Rephainis. Inachidas dico cum Græcis, ad quos illi advenere, quos ἄνακας vocant Cicero, Pollux, alii. Sicut & femina armata, Pallas dicta Græcis, lingua Tyria ὄγκα ענק dicebatur. Rephaim vox videtur esse lin- guæ primævæ, quam Symmachus solet vertere θεομάχους, alii τιτᾶνας, alii γίγαντας aut γηγενεῖς. Nominis vetustissimum vestigium esse videtur in Raphaneis Syriæ, & aliis aliquot locis paris ferme soni.

Raphaim hic & Gen. 14. v. 4. à primo gigan- te Rapha parente dicti 1. Par. 20, 6. uti Enakim ab Enak Jos. 15, 13. Alii sic vocatos ajunt, quod remif- fos faciant homines & immani statura percelle- rent. Masius ad Jos. 12, 4. cum R. Nachman co- gnomen Hevæorum esse putat.

## 2:12
Vers. 12.

BUT THE HORITES ALSO DWELT IN SEIR BEFORETIME.

of Seir, whom Masius in the cited place thinks were Troglodytes, so called from their caverns.

AS ISRAEL DID UNTO THE LAND OF HIS POSSESSION.

In that which was on this side of the Jordan, which they occupied while Moses was still alive, having expelled the Amorites. There is no need, therefore, to say with Masius that this clause was added by Joshua, or even by Ezra.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

IN SEIR AUTEM PRIUS HABITAVE- RUNT HORRHÆI.

tana Seir, quos Masius l. c. Trogloditas fuisse putat, ita dictos à cavernis.

SICUT FECIT ISRAEL IN TERRA POSSESSIONIS SUÆ.

In ea, quæ cis Jordanem erat, quam vivente adhuc Mose expulsis Amorrhæis occuparunt. Non ergo opus est, ut cum Masio dicatur, hanc clausulam à Josua, vel etiam ab Esdra adjectam esse.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. MEN OF WAR) Thus are those called who have completed their twentieth year of age.

Thus Fagius explains it according to the opinion of the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 14. HOMINUM BELLATORUM) Ita vocantur, qui vigesimum ætatis annum expleverunt.

Sic explicat Fagius ex mente Ebræorum.

## 2:19
Ver. 19. FOR I WILL NOT GIVE THEE OF THE LAND OF THE CHILDREN OF AMMON, BECAUSE I HAVE GIVEN IT UNTO THE CHILDREN OF LOTH FOR A POSSESSION.

But was not a portion of that land given to the tribe of Gad, Jos. 13. v. 25? Moses is speaking of the land of Ammon, which they still possessed at that time, not that which had long since been snatched from them by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and later passed to the Israelites, Jud. 11. v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NON ENIM DABO TIBI DE TERRA FILIORUM AMMON, QVIA FI- LIIS LOTH DEDI EAM IN POSSESSIO- NEM.

At annon data istius terræ portio tribui Gad Jos. 13. v. 25. Loquitur Moses de terra Ammon, quam isto tempore adhuc possidebant, non quæ jam pri- dem à Sihone Amorrhæorum rege ipsis erepta, post Israëlitis cessit Jud. 11. v. 15.

## 2:20
v. 20. WHOM THE AMMONITES CALL ZOMZOMMIM.

They are called in Gen. 14. v. 15 Zuzim, that is, robust: but Zomzommim denotes the wicked from זמה a crime, likewise the famous, who are in the mouths and reputation of men, as the Chaldean rendered it, the observed: from which it is gathered that the Ammonites and Moabites formerly used the Hebrew language just as the Hebrews did; for Zuzim, Zomzommim, and Emim, verse 11, are Hebrew names, provided that Lot was of the family of Eber. Grotius is therefore mistaken, who thinks they used another language. Compare with the annotations to verse 11 those things which he handed down on Genesis 11, verse 1.

Latin:

v. 20. QVOS AMMONITÆ VOCANT ZOMZOMMIM.

Dicuntur illi Gen. 14. v. 15. Zuzim, id est, ro- busti: Zonzommim vero notat flagitiosos à זמה facinus, item famosos, qui sunt in ore & reputatio- ne hominum, uti Chaldæus reddidit spectatos: unde colligitur Ammonitas, & Moabitas æque usos fuisse quondam Ebræa lingua, ut Ebræos; Zuzim enim, Zomzomimm. & Emim vers. 11. nomina sunt Ebraica, siquidem Loth è familia Eberi fuerit. Fallitur er- go Grotius, qui putat eos alia lingua usos. Conf. cum annot. ad vers. 11. ea quæ tradidit ad Genes. 11. versu 1.

## 2:23
Vers. 23. THE HIVITES ALSO WHO DWELT IN HAZERIM EVEN UNTO GAZA.

Hazerim are a people distinct from the Hivites, who were in the land of Canaan, Jos. 13. v. 13. The Targum rendered it Hivites. Regarding the LXX ἐζαιοι, some take Hazarim as an appellative, IN VILLAGES. But it is a place to the south of the promised land. For by these two boundaries, Hazerim and Gaza, the southern region of Palestine is described from the east even unto the west.

Vers. 23. CAPHTORIM) So both the Chaldean and the Greeks. In the Hebrew: כפתרים of which I think the city Caparorsa was one. See Ptolemy.

Moses implies this: Just as the Hivites were expelled by the Caphtorim, the Horites by the Edomites, the Rephaim by the Ammonites, even though there were not a few of the children of Anakim who were twins, so also do not doubt that the Philistines can be expelled by you. But Caphtorim are wrongly rendered Cappadocians by the LXX and the Vulgate. For these are situated in Asia Minor on the continent by the Euxine Sea, descended from Japheth, Joseph. b. 1. antiq. c. 6. Caphtorim were born from Mizraim, the son of Ham. They joined themselves with the Philistines in such a way that they were considered as one people, Gen. 10, 14. Compare Jerem. 47, verse 4, Am. 9, verse 7.

Latin:

Vers. 23. HEVÆOS QVOQVE QVI HA- BITABANT IN HASERIN USQVE GALAAD.

Haarim distincti sunt populi ab Hevæis, qui fuerunt in terra Canaan Jos. 13. v. 13. Targum red- didit Hevæos. Ad LXX. ἐζαιοι Hazarim nonnulli ut appellativum accipiunt, IN VILIIS. Sed est locus ad meridiem terræ promissæ. Nam pen duos hosce terminos Chazerim & Assah describi- tur meridionalis plaga Palæstinæ ab oriente usque ad occidentem.

Vers. 23. CAPPADOCES) Sic & Chaldæus & Græci. In Hebræo: כפתרים quorum fuisse puto urbem Caparorsam Vide Ptolomæum.

Id innuit Moses: Sicut Hevæi expulsi sunt à Caphtorim, Horræi ab Idumæis, Rephaim ab Ammonitis, etsi fuerint filiis Enakim gemini non pauci, sic etiam Palæstinos à vobis expelli posse, ne dubitetis. Male autem redduntur Caphtharim Cappadoces à LXX. & Vulg. Hi enim siti sunt in Asia minori in continente ad Pontum Euxinum oriundi à Japhet, Joseph. l. 1. antiqu. c. 6. Caphtho- rim à Mefraim filio Cham prognati. Cum Phili- stæis se ita conjunxerunt, ut pro uno populo cen- serentur Gen. 10, 14. Conf. Jerem. 47. versu 4. Am. 9. vers. 7.

## 2:25
Vers. 25. I WILL BEGIN TO SEND THE TERROR) Such as the Greeks call Panic.

Vers. same. WHO DWELT UNDER ALL HEAVEN.

R. Solomon, as Münster notes, imagines that during the victory over Sihon and Og the sun stood still as in the time of Joshua, and that from there the terror was under all heaven. But the word ALL must be taken conveniently, as Oleaster advises, concerning all to whom the fame of those events penetrated, especially the Canaanites who were to be conquered by the Israelites.

Latin:

Vers. 25. INCIPIAM MITTERE TERROREM) Qua- lem Græci Panicum vocant.

Vers. eod. QVI HABITABANT SUB OMNI CŒ- LO.

R. Salomo notante Münstero fingit in victo- ria de Sihon & Og stetisse Solem sicut tempore Jo- suæ, atque inde terrorem fuisse sub omni cælo. Sed commode accipienda vox OMNIS, ut monet Oleaster, de omnibus ad quos fama rerum istarum penetravit, cumprimis Cananæis ab Israëlitis ex- pugnandis.

## 2:26
Vers. 26. WITH PEACEABLE WORDS. These might appear simulated. Because GOD had commanded to destroy all the inhabitants of the land Num. 33. v. 52. But this commandment struck the Canaanites across the Jordan v. 51. The kingdom of Sihon was outside the promised land, therefore Moses offers peace first, and that partly so that the King's obstinacy, and partly so that a just cause for waging war might be brought to light. And that all these things were directed by the secret instinct of God is clear from v. 30.

GIVE WATER FOR MONEY. Thence is to be explained Num. 21, 22. We will not drink waters from the wells, to wit, for free. See Aug. b. 4. questions in Numbers q. 37.

Latin:

Vers. 26. VERBIS PACIFICIS. Videri hæc possint simulata. Quia DEUS præceperat omnes habitatores terræ delere Num. 33. v. 52. Sed hoc præceptum Cananæos trans Jor- danem feriebat v. 51. Regnum Sihonis erat extra terram promissam, ideo pacem prius offert Moses, idque partim, ut Regis pertinacia, partim ut justa belligerandi causa in lucem produceretur. Et di- recta hæc omnia fuisse arcano Dei instinctu, è v. 30. liquet.

AQVAM PECUNIA TRIBUE. Inde explicandum Num. 21, 22. Non bibemus aquas ex puteis scil. gratis. V. Aug. l. 4. qq. in Nu- mer. q. 37.

## 2:29
Vers. 29. AND THE MOABITES. These had previously granted passage not by the public road, but through the extremities. Compare Jud. 11, 7. and when they saw King Sihon being slain, they began to fear for themselves, thence they called Balaam to curse. Num. 22, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ET MOABITÆ. Hi prius transitum non per viam publicam, sed per extremitates concessere. Conf. Jud. 11, 7. & cum viderent Regem Sihon cædi, ceperunt sibi metuere, inde Balaamum vocarunt ad maledicen- dum. Num. 22, 5.

## 2:30
Vers. 30. BECAUSE THE LORD THY GOD HAD HARDENED HIS SPIRIT.

Hardening is attributed to God not as the hardness of heart is a fault, but as the hardening is a punishment for a preceding fault Num. 21, 26. Lev. 18, 28. And God is said to harden here by withdrawing grace and by casting in a motion and fear of the Hebrews, lest they occupy the kingdom under the guise of passage. See what we said concerning the hardening of Pharaoh at Exod. 7. and following.

Vers. same. AS THOU SEEST THIS DAY.

In Hebrew, as is this day, which Hebraism Fagius and Münster correctly explain: as this day testifies, or, as is known to all.

Latin:

Vers. 30. QVIA INDURAVERAT DOMINUS DEUS TUUS SPIRITUM EJUS.

Tribuitur induratio Deo non qua durities cordis est culpa, sed qua induratio est antegressæ culpæ pœna Num. 21, 26. Lev. 18, 28. Et indurare hic dicitur Deus subducendo gratiam & injiciendo motum, ac formidinem Ebræorum, ne specie transi- tus regnum occupent. Vid. quæ de Pharaonis in- duratione ad Exod. 7. seqq. diximus.

Vers. eod. SICUT NUNC VIDES.

In Ebr. ut est dies hæc, quem Ebraismum Fa- gius & Münsterus recte explicant: ut testatur dies ista, vel, ut omnibus notum est.

## 2:30 Addition
On Deuteronomy 2, verse 30, after the note on page 557. a.

Episcopius has this to say about this passage in book 4 of his Theological Institutions, chapter 14, page 391. That hardening was not an action whose effect or necessary consequence was some sin which Sihon, King of Heshbon, committed; but only a divine action by which a certain panic terror and dread was injected into the King, as is indicated in verse 25, by which it then came about that, bereft of sound counsel and providing little prudently for his Kingdom and the security of his Kingdom, he preferred to refuse the passage to the people of God stubbornly, having rejected the peaceful words which he was using and the fair conditions which he was offering to obtain it, rather than to permit it prudently. For (as the Poet rightly says) fear, a bad interpreter of things, drew every counsel along a worse path. That refusal of passage was not properly a sin, but only a certain not very sound and ill-considered action, born from a panic fear injected by GOD, which was an occasion that God wished to use to strip that King of his kingdom and to transfer his kingdom to His own people: who would doubt that it is lawful for GOD to do this on any occasion? These are the words of Episcopius.

Latin:

Ad Devteronom. 2. versu 30. post notam pagin. 557. a.

Episcopius de hoc loco ita habet libro 4. institutionum Theologicarum capite 14. pagina 391. Induratio ista non fuit actio, cujus vel effectus vel necessarium consequens fuit peccatum aliquod, quod commisit Sihon Rex Hesbon; sed tantum actio divina, qua Panicus quidam terror ac pavor Regi, injectus fuit, ut indicatur versu 25. quo deinde factum fuit, ut sano consilio destitutus, parumque prudenter Regno & Regni sui securitati providens, transitum populo Dei, rejectis pacificis verbis, quibus utebatur, & æquis conditionibus, quas offerebat ad eum impetrandum, præfracte negare quam prudenter permittere voluerit. Nam (ut recte Poeta) malus interpres rerum metus omne trahebat Consilium pejore via. Negatio ista transitus peccatum proprie non erat, sed tantum parum sana & inconsulta quædam actio, ex Panica a DEO injecta formidine nata, quæ occasio fuit, qua Deus uti voluit ad Regem istum exuendum regno suo, & regnum ejus transferendum ad populum suum: quod quin DEO qualibet occasione liceat facere, quis dubitet? Hæc Episcopius.

## 2:31
Vers. 31. BEHOLD I HAVE BEGUN TO DELIVER UNTO THEE] In the Hebrew, before thee, that is, that it may be in thy power.

It is a Hebraism, says Fagius, to be before someone, for, to be in the power and at the disposal of someone.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ECCE CŒPI TIBI TRADERE] In Hebræo, coram te, id est, ut tuæ sit potestatis.

Ebraismus est, inquit Fagius, coram aliquo esse, pro, in potestate, & arbitrio alicujus esse.

## 2:34
Vers. 34. MEN AND WOMEN AND LITTLE ONES.

According to the express commandment Deut. 20. v. 16. Already in the time of Abraham they had deserved destruction. Gen. 15. v. 16. Therefore there is no cruelty here, but the just judgment of God.

Latin:

Vers. 34. VIRIS AC MULIERIBUS ET PARVULIS.

Juxta mandatum expressum Deut. 20. v. 16. Jam Abrahæ tempore internecionem meriti erant. Gen. 15. v. 16. Nulla ergo hic crudelitas, sed ju- stum Dei judicium.

## 2:37
WHICH ARE ADJACENT TO THE TORRENT JABBOK.

Where Jacob wrestled with the Angel Gen. 32. v. 22. and which pertains to the children of Ammon. Rabbi Solomon, as noted by Münster, explains דּ for אֲשֶׁר so that the sense may be, everything which is next to the torrent Jabbok.

Latin:

Vers. 37. QVÆ ADJACENT TORREN- TI JEBOC.

Ubi Jacob luctatus est cum Angelo Genes. 32. v. 22. & quæ pertinet ad filios Ammon. R. Salomo, notante Münstero explicat דּ pro אֲשֶׁר ut sen- sus sit, omne, quod est juxta torrentem Jaboc.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

The battle against King Og: the exclusion of Moses from the land of Canaan, and the confirmation of Joshua as his successor.

IN EDREI.

By the name of the city the whole neighboring region is designated. Luther: near Edrei. They had received a command concerning that matter Num. 21.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Pugna contra Regem Og: exclusio Mosis à ter- ra Canaan, & confirmatio Josuæ suc- cessoris.

Vers. 1. IN EDREI.

NOmine urbis tota vicina regio designatur. Luth. bey Edrei. Mandatum ea de re accepe- rant Num. 21.

## 3:3
AND WE SMOTE THEM] Aquila: we devoted to destruction. Thus we destroyed, as those peoples are wont to be destroyed who have been made חרם ἀνάθεμα (anathema).

Latin:

Vers. 3. PERCUSSIMUSQVE EOS] Aquila ἀναθεμα- τίσαμεν. Ita delevimus, ut solent deleri illi populi, qui facti sunt חרם ἀνάθεμα.

## 3:4
WASTING ALL HIS CITIES AT ONE TIME.

In the Hebrew: And we took all his cities at that time. There was not a city which we did not take from them. Sixty cities (v. 1. Kings 4. v. 13.) Every cord, חֶבֶל (hebel) a small cord is taken for a region, because formerly they used to measure fields with cords: whence the cord of the Lord

Jacob Deut. 32, 9. See Ps. 77, 55. 61. Zeph. 2, 5. 7. Mich. 2, 5. The LXX here render it τὰ περίχωρα (the surrounding region), Argob, of King Og (who dwelt) in Bashan. He ruled also over the Amorites v. 8. He is called however King of Bashan, because he had the seat of his kingdom in that region. Bashan was a most fertile region on this side of the Jordan from the sources of the river, up to the torrent Jabbok, having obtained its name from its fertility. Argob is the name of the city which Jair stormed, after the Bashanites had repaired it after the times of Moses 1. Kings 4. verse 13.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VASTANTES CUNCTAS CIVI- TATES ILLIUS UNO TEMPORE.

In Ebræo: Et cepimus omnes urbes ejus in tem- pore isto. Non fuit urbs, quam non cepimus ab eis. Sexaginta urbes (v. 1. Reg. 4. v. 13.) Omnem funem, חֶבֶל funiculus pro regione sumitur, quia olim funibus agros metiebantur: unde funiculus Domini

Jacob Deut. 32, 9. Vid. Pf. 77, 55. 61. Zeph. 2, 5. 7. Mich. 2, 5. LXX. hic reddunt τὰ περίχωρα vicinam regionem, Argob, regis Og (qui habitabat) in Ba- san. Imperabat ille etiam Amorrhæis v. 8. Voca- tur autem Bafanis Rex, quia in illa regione sedem regni habuit. Bafan fuit uberrima regio cis Jor- danem à fontibus fluminis, usque ad torrentem Ja- bock, à fertilitate nomen adepta. Argob nomen urbis est, quam Jair expugnavit, postquam eam Bafanæi post tempora Mofis reparassent 1. Reg. 4. versu 13.

## 3:6
BUT THE CATTLE AND THE SPOILS OF THE CITIES WE PLUNDERED.

That was done without doubt by a special concession of GOD, and extraordinarily, that He allowed the Israelites those cattle in Bashan, for according to the divine law the cattle were not to be spared Deut. 20. verse 14. unless perhaps it should be said that that law concerns the Canaanites dwelling across the Jordan, but not the kingdom of Bashan on this side of the Jordan.

Latin:

Vers. 6. JUMENTA AUTEM ET SPOLIA URBIUM DIRIPUIMUS.

Factum id sine dubio ex peculiari DEI conces- sione, & extraordinarie, quod Israëlitus jumenta il- la in Bafan indulserit, nam juxta legem divinam nec jumentis parcendum fuit Deut. 20. vers. 14. nisi fortasse dicendum, quod lex illa concernat Ca- nanæos trans Jordanem habitantes, non vero re- gnum Bafan cis Jordanem.

## 3:8
Verse 8. FROM THE TORRENT ARNON EVEN UNTO MOUNT HERMON.

Concerning Arnon, ch. 2, v. 24. Hermon is a part of Mount Gilead, by reason of which Gilead is joined with Lebanon: therefore it is called both a part of Mount Gilead and a part of Mount Lebanon. It is called from חרם, destroyed, because on account of the snow it is rigid, vast, and uncultivated. Because it was to the East of the holy land, it is used for the east, Psalm 89, verse 13.

Latin:

Vers. 8. A TORRENTE ARNON USQVE AD MONTEM HERMON.

De Arnon c. 2. v. 24. Hermon est pars mon- tis Gilead, ratione cujus Gilead cum Libano jungi- tur: ideo & pars montis Gilead, & pars montis Libani dicitur. Dicitur à חרם perditus, quia ob ni- vem rigidus, vastus & incultus est. Quia fuit ad Orientem terræ sanctæ, pro oriente usurpatur Pfalm. 89. vers. 13.

## 3:9
Verse the same. WHICH THE SIDONIANS CALL SARION AND THE AMORITES SANIR.

Moses Gerundensis notes that the name Sanir in the Canaanite language signifies snow. Whence the Chaldean interprets it as snowy. Hermon and Senir are joined in 1 Chron. 5, v. 23, Cant. 4, v. 8, whether the Vau is taken exegetically, or whether distinct parts of the same mountain had distinct names. Zidon was a city of Phoenicia lying beyond Lebanon on the western shore of Palestine, distant 200 stadia from Tyre, famous for the invention of glass and precious linens.

Latin:

Vers. eod. QVEM SIDONII SARION VOCANT ET AMORRHÆI SANIR.

Nomen Sanir in lingua Canan. nivem signi- ficare Mose Gerund. notat. Unde Chald. nivosum in- terpretatur. Conjungitur Hermon & Senir 1. Par. 5. v. 23, Cant. 4. v. 8, Sive quod Vau ἐξηγητικῶς ac- cipiatur, sive quod distinctæ partes ejusdem montis distincta nomina habuerint. Zidon urbs fuit Phœ- nices trans Libanon in occiduo Palæstinæ littore jacens à Tyro 200. stadiis distans, vitri inventione & pretiosis linteis celebris.

## 3:11
Verse 11. FOR ONLY OG REMAINED OF THE RACE OF THE GIANTS.

In that region, namely, on this side of the Jordan, no one of the race of the Rephaim, as it is held in the Hebrew, had remained: but beyond the Jordan, giants were found even afterwards, not only of the race of the Anakim, but also descending from Rapha, 2 Sam. 21, 16, 1 Chron. 20, v. 6.

Verse the same. IN RABBATH.

This was the metropolis of the Ammonites, situated at the river Jabbok, 2 Sam. 12, v. 26, which, having been conquered by Ptolemy Philadelphus, was afterwards called Philadelphia.

Verse the same. THE LENGTH OF NINE CUBITS) Maimonides thinks he was six cubits. For beds are accustomed to be made a third part longer than men.

Philalpandus understands it of a funeral bed or bier, because they were accustomed to place corpses on an earthen crate and burn them among piles of aromatics, 2 Chron. 16, v. 14. But it is more correctly understood as an ordinary bed, named here for this purpose, that from it the tallness and stature of Og might be estimated. Augustine, book 15, De Civitate Dei, ch. 9, reports that he saw on the Utican shore a molar tooth of a man that would equal a hundred of ours. Pliny reports, book 7, concerning a body found in Crete of 46 cubits. Which we leave in the middle. It is nonsense what R. Solomon says: that Og remained a survivor from those giants whom Chedorlaomer conquered, Gen. 14, 14. For thus he would have lived more than 400 years; which others invent far more ineptly, that he was of the number of those who lived before the flood Gen. 6. and standing on the highest mountain, escaped the waters of the flood.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SOLUS QVIPPE OG RESTITERAT DE STIRPE GIGANTUM.

In illa sc. regione cis Jordanem nullus de ge- nere Rephaim, ut in Ebræo habetur, remanserat: trans Jordanem vero Gigantes deinceps etiam re- perti sunt, non solum ex genere Enakim, sed etiam è Rapha descendentes 2. Sam. 21, 16. 1. Par. 20. v. 6.

Vers. eod. IN RABBATH.

Fuit hæc metropolis Ammonitarum sita ad flu- men Jabock 2. Sam. 12. v. 26. quæ à Ptolomæo Phi- ladelpho expugnata, Philadelphia postea nuncu- pata.

Vers. eod. NOVEM CUBITORUM LONGITUDO EJUS) Fuisse ipsum fexcubitalem putat Maimonides. Lectos enim tertia parte longiores hominibus fieri solere.

Philalpandus de lecto funebri sive feretro intel- ligit, quia solebant cadavera in crate terrea reponi, & inter aromatum strues comburi 1. Par. 16. v. 14. Sed rectius lectus usualis intelligitur, hic eo fine nominatus, ut inde Ogi proceritas, & statura æsti- metur. August. l. 15. de C. D. c. 9. perhibet se in Uticensi littore vidisse molarem dentem hominis, qui nostros centum adæquaret. Plinius refert. l. 7. de cor- pore Cretæ invento 46. cubitorum. Quod in me- dio relinquimus. Nugæ sunt, quod R. Salomo ait: Ogum superstitem mansisse ab illis gigantibus, quos Kedorlaomor vicit Gen. 14, 14. Sic enim vixisset plus- quam 400. annos; quod alii longe ineptius fingunt, eum ex illorum numero fuisse, qui ante diluvium vixere Gen. 6. & in altissimo monte consistentem, aquas diluvii evasisse.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. AND WE POSSESSED THE LAND AT THAT TIME FROM AROER, WHICH IS UPON THE BANK OF THE TORRENT ARNON UNTO THE MIDDLE PART OF MOUNT GALAAD.

In Hebrew: And that land we obtained by hereditary right at that time, from Aroer, which is upon or near the torrent Arnon and half of Mount Gilead. Bonfrerius acknowledges that the Vulgate version here departs from the Hebrew text. The author of the Vulgate version judged that it was Moses's purpose to indicate the boundaries of the land occupied by Israel on this side of the Jordan. But Bonfrerius rightly points out that this does not seem to be the mind of the Holy Scriptures, since it notes only one boundary, Aroer, whereas the Israelites extended beyond the middle part of Mount Gilead into the rest of its part, and the land of the Bashanites. He tries in vain to defend it with new punctuation or by a colon added to the word 'unto'. Because that 'UNTO' is not in the source, nor is a colon found in the Vulgate editions. But as to what he objects against the Hebrew text, that the Reubenites cannot be said to have possessed either Mount Gilead or the Gileadite land, because no part of Mount Gilead lay adjacent to their region. He answers. Moses says that he gave to Reuben and Gad the cities not only of Mount Gilead, but of all that land from Aroer. And Bonfrerius answers himself, although less properly, that the region of the Reubenites and generally whatever was possessed by the Israelites across the Jordan comes under the name of the land of Gilead, because their region was also not far from Mount Gilead.

Latin:

Vers. 12. TERRAMQVE POSSEDIMUS TEMPORE ILLO AB AROER, QVÆ EST SUPER RIPAM TORRENTIS AR- NON USQUE AD MEDIAM PARTEM MONTIS GALAAD.

In Ebr. Et terram istam hæreditario jure conse- cuti sumus in tempore isto, ab Aroër, quæ est super vel juxta torrentem Arnon & dimidium montis Gi- lead. Agnoscit Bonfrerius versionem Vulgatam hic discedere à textu Ebræo. Versionis Vulgatæ autor judicavit propositum fuisse Mosi terminos terræ cis Jordanem ab Israële occupatæ indicare. Sed recte monet Bonfrerius, non videri hanc mentem S. S. quum unum tantum terminum Aroer notet, siquidem Israëlitæ ultra dimidiam partem montis Gilead vid. in reliquam ejus partem, & Ba- sanitarum terram excurrebant. Frustra autem tueri nova interpunctione vel per colon adjectum ad vocem usque conatur. Quia nec in fonte illud USQUE habetur, nec colon in Vulgat. editioni- bus reperitur. Quod autem Ebræo textui obji- cit, Rubenitas non posse dici vel montem Galaad, vel terram Galaaditidem possedisse, quia nihil montis Galaad eorum regioni adjacuit. Resp. Civitates non tantum montis Galaad; sed totius istius terræ ab Aroer ait Moses, se dedisse Ruben & Gad. Et respondet sibi ipsi Bonfrerius, subinde licet minus proprie, Rubenitarum regio & universim quicquid ab Israëlitis trans Jordanem possessum est, nomine ter- ræ Galaad venire, propterea quod etiam eorum regio non procul a monte Galaad abesset.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. LAND OF GIANTS. So called either because King Bashan was a survivor of the giants, or because giants had previously inhabited it.

Latin:

Vers. 13. TERRA GIGANTUM. Sic dicta sive quod Basan Rex superstes fue- rit è gigantibus, sive quod in ea prius gigantes habitarint.

## 3:14
Vers. 14. JAIR SON OF MANASSEH. 'Son' is taken here for descendant. He was a Manassite not by the paternal line, because he is referred to the tribe of Judah 1 Chron. 2. v. 20. But by the maternal, having been begotten, namely, from the daughter of Machir. Compare here Num. 32. v. 41.

Vers. eod. UNTO THIS PRESENT DAY. Abulensis thinks these were added by Ezra, because these things happened shortly before the death of Moses, but from a false hypothesis, that Ezra restored the Bible consumed by fire. Cornel. à Lapide answers that it is not necessary to say this, since three or more months flowed from these events to the death of Moses: and if these were added by another, they should be considered added not by Ezra, but by him who later arranged these Diaries of Moses. It will be said more correctly that such things were inserted (if they were inserted) by him by whom the last chapter was added. For Moses did not only write Diaries, but adorned the entire history, and the whole book, at the dictation of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 14. JAIR FILIUS MANASSE. Filius pro postero hic accipitur. Manasseus fuit non ex linea paterna, quia ad tribum Juda re- fertur 1. Par. 2. v. 20. Sed materna, susceptus scil. ex filia Machir. Conf. hic Num. 32. v. 41.

Vers. eod. USQUE IN PRÆSENTEM DIEM. Addita hæc ab Esdra Abulensis putat, quia pau- lo ante mortem Mosis hæc contigerint, sed ex fal- sa hypothesi, quod Esdras Biblia incendio absumta restaurarit. Respondet Cornel. à Lapid. non neces- sum esse hoc dicere, siquidem tres & plures menses ab hisce gestis ad mortem Mosis fluxerint: & si addita hæc ab alio, non ab Esdra, sed ab eo, qui hæc Diaria Mosis postea digesserit, addida censen- da sint. Rectius ab illo talia inserta (si inserta) à quo ultimum caput adjectum est, dicentur. Nam Moses non Diaria tantum conscripsit, sed inte- gram historiam, totumque librum, dictante Sp. S. adornavit.

## 3:15
Vers. 15. I ALSO GAVE GALAAD TO MACHIR. Since he had already given a part of the Gileadite region to the Reubenites and Gadites in v. 13, the remainder of Gilead is understood here, which had not yet been occupied by them; by Machir his descendants are understood. For Machir had already died.

Latin:

Vers. 15. MACHIR QVOQVE DEDI GA- LAAD. Quum partem Gileaditicæ regionis Rube- nitis & Gaditis jam tum dederit v. 13. residuum Gi- leadis hic intelligitur, quod ab illis nondum occu- patum erat; per Machir intelliguntur ipsius posteri. Machir enim jam obierat.

## 3:17
Vers. 17. AND THE BOUNDARIES OF CENERETH UNTO THE SEA OF THE DESERT, WHICH IS MOST SALT. In Hebrew: And the boundary (namely, of the Jordan) from Kinnereth and unto the sea of the plain (or desert) the salt sea. Num. 34. verse 11. John 13. verse 20. the boundaries are set from Kinnereth unto Pisgah. The Jordan, that famous river of Palestine, passes through the sea of Kinnereth, and empties itself into the salt sea. Kinnereth was a city in the tribe of Naphtali, which Herod adorned, and in honor of Caesar named Tiberias: whence the name was obtained by the surrounding region, and also by the lake. Gennesaret Luke 5. v. 1. Joseph. l. 18. c. 3. The sea of the plain or of the fields is the dead sea, so called because it washes some notable plain, or rather the sea of the desert, because the most pleasant region of the Pentapolis Gen. 13. v. 10. was reduced to a wilderness after the conflagration, whence Adrichomius and Bochardus observed that everything round about for five leagues is squalid and sterile. It is also called the dead sea, because fish, if any flow into it, soon die, because on account of the heavenly burning there is greater saltiness in it than in the Mediterranean sea.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET TERMINOS CENERETH USQUE AD MARE DESERTI, QUOD EST SALSISSIMUM. In Ebr. Et terminum (scil. Jordanis) à Kin- nereth & usque ad mare planitiei (vel deserti) ma- re salis. Num. 34. versu 11. Johann. 13. versu 20. statuuntur termini à Kinnereth usque ad Pisga. Jor- danis celebris ille Palæstinæ fluvius transit per mare Kinnereth, & exonerat se in mare salsum. Kinereth urbs fuit in tribu Naphthali, quam Hero- des ornavit, & in honorem Cæsaris Tiberiadem nominavit: unde nomen tum circumjacens regio. tum etiam lacus obtinuit. Genesareth Luc. 5. v. 1. Joseph. l. 18. c. 3. Mare planitiei vel campestrium est mare mortuum ita dictum, quia insignem aliquam planitiem alluit, vel potius mare deserti, quia regio amœnissima Pentapoleos Genes. 13. v. 10. post in- cendium in solitudinem redacta, unde Adricho- mius & Bochardus ad quinque leucas omnia circum- circa squalere, & sterilia esse observarent. Dici- tur etiam mare mortuum, quia pisces, si qui in illud fluxerint, mox emoriuntur, quia ob cœlestem exustionem in eo major salsedo, quam in mari mediterraneo.

## 3:18
Ver. 18.

ARMED, GO BEFORE YOUR BRETHREN, THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL, ALL MEN OF VALOR.

In Hebrew, girded with swords, armed at the loins, as the Targum rendered it: Cf. Josh. 6, ver. 13, all men of strength from the age of 20, namely, to 50. All were required to be fed and prepared for this expedition, yet only some were chosen afterwards from them, namely 40,000; the rest were left at home for the protection of the family and the cultivation of the fields.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

EXPEDITI PRÆCEDITE FRATRES VESTROS, FILIOS ISRAEL, OMNES VI- RI ROBUSTI.

In Ebr. accincti gladiis, ad lumbos armati, ut Targum reddidit: Conf. Jos. 6. v. 13. omnes viri ro- boris ab anno 20. scil. ad 50. Omnes debebant esse pransi, & parati ad hanc expeditionem, delecti ta- men postea tantum aliqui sunt ex iis, nempe 40000. reliqui ad protectionem familiæ, & agro- rum culturam domi relicti.

## 3:20
Ver. 20. UNTIL THE LORD GIVES REST TO YOUR BRETHREN. Abulensis and Cornelius à Lapide think that the Reubenites and Gadites returned to their own lands only after the distribution of the land was completed, that is, after 14 years. But it should rather be said that they were dismissed after seven years, namely, after the Canaanites had been defeated, for whose expulsion they had brought aid to the other tribes. Which is clear from Num. 32, ver. 21, 22.

Latin:

Vers. 20. DONEC REQUIEM TRIBUAT DOMINUS FRATRIBUS SUIS. Post distributionem terræ peractam demum rediisse Rubenitas & Gaditas ad sua, h. e. post 14. annos putat Abulens. & Cornel. à Lap. Sed dicen- dum potius dimissos esse post septennium postquam nempe Cananæi debellati fuere, quorum ejicien- dorum gratia cæteris tribubus suppetias tulerant. Quod luculentum est è Num. 32. v. 21. 22.

## 3:23
ver. 23. AND I BESOUGHT) חנן signifies a suppliant prayer. See Prov. 26, ver. 25. The word in the reciprocal conjugation ואתחנן denotes to pray for grace. Targ. Jonathan: I sought mercies before the Lord. Why did Moses so greatly desire to see this land? Because it not only provided a home for the Patriarchs, his progenitors, but it was also the future seat of the Church; indeed, the Messiah was to arise, preach, and carry out the work of redemption in it. Although he himself had already heard before that he would not see the land of Canaan, yet either out of human infirmity or out of confidence in that grace still to be obtained, because such threats usually have the condition of repentance connected to them (Jer. 18, ver. 7), he asks for it as a suppliant.

Latin:

vers. 23. PRECATUSQUE SUM) חנן significat, suppli- cem precationem. Vid. Prov. 26. vers. 25. Verbum in conjugatione reciproca ואתחנן notat orare gratiam. Targ. Jonath. quæsivi misera- tiones coram Domino. Cur tantopere desideravit Moses videre hanc terram? Quia hospitium ea non solum Patriarchis progenitoribus præbuit, sed eriam sedes futura Ecclesiæ, imo in ea oriturus prædicaturus, & redemptionis opus exequuturus erat Messias. Quamvis vero jam ante ipse audie- rit, se non visurum terram Canaan, tamen vel ex infirmitate humana, vel ex fiducia gratiæ istius ad- huc impetrandæ, quia comminationes ejusmodi solent habere connexam pœnitentiæ conditionem Jer. 18. v. 7. id supplex petit.

## 3:25
Ver. 25. AND THIS GOODLY MOUNTAIN AND LEBANON. Some think the Vau is exegetical, meaning this goodly mountain, namely, Lebanon; others understand by the goodly mountain Mount Moriah, on which Abraham offered his son, on which Zion and Jerusalem were to be built, and they judge that by Lebanon the temple built from the woods of Lebanon is designated, which is called the house of the Forest of Lebanon, 1 Kings 7, 2. Thus Targ. Jonathan: Make me see this good mountain; in which Jerusalem is built, and Mount Lebanon, in which the שכינת Divinity is to dwell. Others, because Zion or the temple had not yet been built at that time, judge that the southern boundary of that land is indicated by the mountain (some point out the mountains of Bethel, which Adrichomius praises) and the northern by Lebanon.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ET MONTEM ISTUM EGRE- GIUM ET LIBANUM. Nonnulli Vau exegeticum esse arbitrantur montem istum egregium, sc. Libanum, alii per mon- tem egregium montem Moriah, in quo Abraham filium suum obtulit, in quo ædificanda Sion & Je- rusalem intelligunt, & per Libanum templum è lignis Libani extructum designari censent, quod vocatur domus Sylvæ Libani 1. Reg. 7, 2. Ita Targ. Jonathan: Fac me videre montem bonum hunc; in quo ædificata Jerusalem, & montem Libanum, in quo habitatura est שכינת Divinitas. Alii, quia non- dum Zion vel templum extructa tum erant, termi- num terræ illius australem notari censent per montem (nonnulli montes Bethelis indigitant, quos deprædi- cat Adrichomius) septentrionalem v. per Libanum.

## 3:26
v. 26. AND HE SAID TO ME, IT IS ENOUGH FOR THEE. In Hebrew there is a vau, which is rightly rendered here adversatively: but much for thee, that is, let it be enough for thee, or because regard is had for the prayers, you have asked me enough:

Cease now to pray, you will not enter the land of Canaan, to which sentence the following words, do not add to speak to me about this matter, are favorable, or because it is implied that enough benefits have already been bestowed upon him. God often mercifully denies to the pious what He grants in anger to the impious, as Augustine says in Psalm 85. Sacred history teaches that Moses, even though he was excluded from the promised land with Aaron, nevertheless had many prerogatives over him: (1.) that he entered into a part of the land on this side of the Jordan in Gilead, (2.) that he defeated Og and Sihon, and assigned those kingdoms to his own people, (3.) that he received the blessing of Balaam, (4.) that he destroyed the Midianites, (5.) that he beheld the whole land from nearby.

Latin:

v. 26. ET DIXIT MIHI, SUFFICIT TIBI. In Ebr. est vau, quod recte adversative hic red- ditur: sed multum tibi, h. e. satis esto tibi, sive quod habeatur respectus ad preces, satis rogasti me:

precari nunc define, non intrabis in terram Cana- an, cui sententiáe sequentia verba, ne addas loqui ad me de re ista, favent, sive quod innuatur sat benefi- ciorum ipsi præstitum esse. Deus sæpe misericordi- ter negat piis, quod iratus concedit impiis, dicente August. in Psal. 85. Historia sacra docet, Mosen, etsi exclusus à terra promissa cum Aarone fuerit, multas tamen præ eo habuisse prærogativas (1.) quod in parte terræ cis Jordanem in Galaaditidem ingressus sit, (2.) quod debellarit Og & Sihon, & regna illa suis assignarit, (3.) quod acceperit benedictum Bileami, (4.) quod Midianitas de- leverit, (5.) quod è propinquo totam terram con- spexerit.

## 3:27
verse 27. ASCEND THE TOP OF PISGAH.

Pisgah is a mountain sloping toward the eastern part of the Dead Sea, or the Salt Sea, or rather the summit and peak of that mountain which was called Nebo, at which place Moses also died, Deut. 34. A part of the mountains of Abarim, Num. 27, 12. Whence also Moses ascended into the mountains of Abarim, and specifically onto Mount Nebo, and to the peak of that mountain called Pisgah, and there he was to survey Canaan with his eyes, not that he could behold the whole of it with his eyes from the highest peak: for it had to be surveyed from the southern boundary to the northern, and from the eastern to the western, which could not be done from a mountain, however high, but because God miraculously showed him that whole land, and supernaturally elevated his visual faculty.

Latin:

vers. 27. ASCENDE CACVMEN PHAS- GÆ.

Pisga est mons acclivis ad orientalem partem maris mortui, vel salsi, vel potius cacumen ac fasti- gium montis illius, quid dicebatur Nebo, quo loco etiam Moses mortuus Deut. 34. Pars montium A- barim Num. 27, 12. Vnde & in montes Abarim, & in specie in montem Nebo, & in fastigium illius montis Pisga dictum Moses ascendit, ibique Cana- an oculis perlustrare debuit, non quod è summo cacumine totam oculis suis intueri poterit: nam perlustranda erat à termino Australi ad Aquilona- rem, & Orientali ad Occidentalem, quod à mon- te, utut summo, fieri non potuit, sed quod Deus miraculosè totam terram illam ipsi exhibuerit, ac facultatem visivam supernaturaliter elevarit.

## 3:28
Verse 28. COMMAND JOSHUA) It is the mark of a good Prince also to instruct his successor with good precepts, but not to seek glory for himself through a very poor comparison.

Indeed, these things were done by a special divine mandate. By which Joshua was to be comforted and strengthened, because he had seen that the Canaanites possessed most fortified cities, and some even endowed with giant-like strength.

CHAPTER IV.

Exhortation to obedience. Cities of refuge beyond the Jordan.

Latin:

Vers. 28. PRÆCIPE JOSVÆ) Boni Principis est etiam successorem bonis præceptis instruere, non autem ex deter- rima comparatione gloriam sibi quærere.

Imo hæc speciali mandato divino gesta sunt. Quo confortandus & corroborandus erat Josua, quia viderat Cananæos urbes possidere munitissimas, quosdam etiam giganteo præditos robore.

CAPVT IV.

Adhortatio an obedientiam. Asyla trans Jordanem.

## 4:1 Argument
verse 1. THAT DOING THEM, YOU MAY LIVE.

Concerning the present, long, and prosperous life, Saccinianus, Cornel. a Lapide, and Grotius understand it, but that this must be accepted as concerning eternal life is manifest from a comparison of Lev. 18, 5 and Luke 10, 25. Dionysius the Carthusian at this place says that under such promises and rewards, spiritual goods and eternal and heavenly rewards are to be understood principally. What of the fact that Leonh. Mar. from these passages, as Cornel. from Lev. 18, 5, concludes that the reborn can acquire eternal life for themselves through the fulfillment of the law. Whence it ought to deal with eternal life. Which, however, cannot be concluded from them, unless it is demonstrated that the law can be perfectly fulfilled by us, which is entirely against the Apostle, Rom. 8, 3, chapter 7, 14.

Latin:

vers. 1. UT FACIENS EA, VIVAS.

DE vita præsenti, diuturna & prospera Sacinia- ni, Cornel. à Lapide & Grotius intelligunt, sed de æterna hoc accipiendum esse vita, è collatio- ne Lev. 18, 5. Luc. 10, 25. manifestum est. Dionys. Carthus. ad h. l. sub talibus promissis ac præmiis intelligenda sunt principaliter bona spiritualia, & æterna atque cœlestia præmia. Quid quod Leonh. Mar. ex his locis, ut Cornel. è Lev. 18, 5. colligat, renatos per legis impletionem vitam æternam sibi acquirere posse. Vnde ea de vita æterna agere o- portet. Quod tamen concludi ex iis nequit, nisi domonstretur, legem à nobis perfecté impleri posse, quod omnino est contra Apostolum. Rom. 8, 3. cap. 7, 14.

## 4:2
Verse 2. YOU SHALL NOT ADD TO THE WORD WHICH I SPEAK TO YOU, NOR SHALL YOU TAKE AWAY FROM IT) This saying is not opposed to traditions interpreting the Scripture, nor to human precepts hedging the law. To diminish is not to do what is commanded: to add is to do otherwise than is commanded, below 12, 32.

Who could doubt that these things are handed down for the sake of the Papists, who defend their traditions? For they are accustomed to use both exceptions: when we urge the classic passage for the perfection of Holy Scripture, they claim that only contrary traditions are prohibited, not indeed those by which Scripture is explained, and that these things concern the perfect observation of the law, so that nothing is omitted or done otherwise than commanded, not the perfection of the law itself. Both of which have been solidly refuted by our people in the Papists. For God wills that nothing be added to the law, nothing taken away, not only what is contrary, but also what is different: because He willed the law to be the unique and adequate norm of worship and religion: nor does He permit religion or worship to be fashioned from one's own ingenuity, but by this very fact, that He binds the people to the law alone, He prohibits and forbids it. And what he taught here concerning the law, the same he most severely inculcated concerning the other books of Holy Scripture toward the end of the entire Scripture, Apoc. 22, as a sort of colophon to the perfection of the Holy letters, which ought now to be held equally as the unique norm and rule of faith and religion after the completed Canon of Scripture; but he excluded all traditions, by whatever name they may come, from this axiom. To which opinion the ancients were also accustomed to urge the Apostle's anathema, Gal. 1, 8, which was said not only of him who preached contrary things, but of him who preached OTHER & DIFFERENT things. Chrysostom, hom. 1 in Epist. ad Gal.: He did not say, if they preached contrary things, or overturned the whole Gospel, but if they even preached Christ BEYOND the Gospel which you have received, and if they weakened ANYTHING, let them be anathema. Theophylact follows Chrysostom: For he did not imply, if they preached only contrary things, but if they preached that which is beyond what we preach, that is, if they added any little thing themselves, let them be subject to execration. Whence St. Augustine, lib. 3 contra literas Petil. cap. 6: If anyone, whether concerning Christ, or concerning His Church, or concerning any other thing whatsoever that pertains to our faith and life, I will not say if we, but altogether, as he safely added, if an Angel from Heaven should announce to you beyond what you have received in the legal and Evangelical Scriptures, let him be anathema. Nor indeed is an addition made only when contrary things are taught, but by the weakening of those things which have been set down. For contrary things repel and overturn one another. But here the people are forbidden to add anything to the law, or to add thereto. Therefore St. Ambrose, de Parad. cap. 12, most rightly says: We ought to join nothing to the command of God, even for the sake of caution. For if you either add or subtract anything, it is PREVARICATION. Basil calls it infidelity, false testimony, and sacrilege if anyone adds or takes away anything. It would be an argument of infidelity, he says in Serm. de fid. Confess. (his words properly sound as apostasy, Φανερὰ ἔκπτωσις τῆς πίστεως) and a most certain sign of pride, if anyone wishes to reject anything of those things which are written, or to introduce those things which are not written. And in brev. qu. qu. 98: A leader ought to be disposed toward GOD as a minister of Christ and a steward of the mysteries of God, fearing lest he either say or institute anything BEYOND the will of GOD certainly expressed IN THE SCRIPTURES, and be found a FALSE witness or a SACRILEGIOUS person in that which he either introduces as alien to the Doctrine of the Lord, or omits anything of the decrees of GOD.

Nor does the Papistical distinction of traditions, those interpreting Scripture and those added to the Scriptures, help Grotius or other Innovators here: because an indubitable and infallible interpretation of Scripture is not to be taken from tradition, but from Scripture itself, which alone is the authentic and ἀνυπεύθυνος interpreter of itself. For the Holy letters are to be explained by the same Spirit by which they were inspired, 2 Pet. 1, 21. Nor can any such infallible ἐξηγητικὴ tradition be shown. The consensus of the Fathers is only a testimony of faith and religion, and obtains only human authority, and thus cannot be held as an infallible norm, or be considered of divine authority, or as a principle of faith. It is a topical argument, not an apodictic one: not rarely fallible and subject to exceptions, by no means infallible and ἀνυπεύθυνον, and above every exception. Let him be heard here Augustine, Epistle 112 to Paulinus. If things are confirmed by the clear authority of the divine Scriptures, that is to say, those which are called Canonical in the Church, they must be believed without any hesitation. But as for other witnesses or testimonies, by which one is persuaded that something ought to be believed, it is permitted to you to believe or not to believe, according to how you weigh the merit of the one advising you to be convinced, whether he has it or does not have it.

What Grotius says concerning human laws that are wise in divine matters: those pertain either to external polity, order, and ecclesiastical decorum, or to the substance of divine worship and to religion. All these are excluded, because nothing is to be added to divine laws concerning the worship of God. Therefore, for the sake of explanation, the exclusive particle is added in the Vulgate version, which is authentic for Papists, in the parallel text of Deut. 4:2: 'What I command you, this ONLY do to the LORD, neither add anything, nor diminish.' Now, no one denies that those laws of the former kind are lawful, but they are only of human authority, and do not apply here. Blessed Gerhard has satisfied the various exceptions of the Papists in his Commentary on this passage.

But as for the other exception, that it is a question here of the perfect observation of the law, not of the perfection of the law itself, although it is certain that the law requires perfect obedience, so that we neither diminish anything by not doing what is commanded, nor add anything by doing it otherwise than it was commanded, yet this is not properly or primarily indicated here by those words of adding and diminishing; and besides, what else does that obligation to observe the law in such a way that nothing is done or omitted otherwise than it is commanded argue, if not the perfection of the law itself? For to what rule are we so bound that it is not right to diminish or omit anything, nor to add or do otherwise than it commands, unless it must be entirely perfect, 'admitting in no way any addition or subtraction,' as Varinus defines a rule. Therefore, it is not even a rule unless it is perfect. For a rule, as Theophylact has it in chapter 2 to the Philippians, and a plumb line, has neither addition nor subtraction. Nor indeed can we set before ourselves the divine law, as a perfect norm, for perfect observation, and constitute it as our goal, unless we hold the divine law to be a perfect norm. Therefore, not the least among the Papists acknowledge that the perfection of the law is asserted here. Alphonsus Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, on this passage: 'Here the law is commended for its perfection, because to what is perfect nothing can be added, nor should anything be taken away, as is evident.' Francis Vatablus on this passage: 'Moses complains, therefore, that nothing is to be added or taken away from the words of God, lest the precepts of God not be kept, because the traditions of men added to the word of God are an obstacle to their being kept.' For precepts turn a man away from the truth, Titus 1:14.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NON ADDETIS AD VERBUM, QUOD VOBIS LOQVOR, NEC AVFERETIS EX EO) Hoc dictum neque traditionibus scriptum interpretantibus, neque Præceptis humanis legem sepientibus repugnat. Diminuere est, non facere quod jubetur: addere, aliter quam jussum est, facere, infra 12, 32.

Hæc in gratiam Pontificiorum, traditiones suas propugnantium tradi ecquis ambigat? Solent enim illi utraque exceptione uti, cum pro perfectione Scri- pturæ S. locum Classicum urgemus, tum quod tra- ditiones solum contrariæ, non vero illæ, quibus Scriptura explicatur, prohibitæ sint, tum quod de observatione legis perfectà, ne quicquam omittatur, aut aliter, quam jussum est, fiat, non de ipsa perfe- ctione legis, hæc agant. Quæ vero utraque à nostris solide profligata in Papistis est. Nihil enim addi, nihil demi legi vult Deus, non modo, quod con- trarium sit, sed etiam quod diversum sit: quia le- gem unicam & adæquatam cultus & religionis nor- mam esse voluit: neque ex proprio ingenio con- fingi religionem, aut cultum permittit, sed hoc ipso, quod ad solam legem adstringit populum, prohi- bet ac interdicit. Et quod de lege hic præcepit, idem de Scripturæ S. aliis libris sub finem universæ Scripturæ Apoc. 22. severissime inculcavit hoc quasi colophone perfectionem S. literarum, quæ pariter pro unica fidei & religionis norma atque regula post absolutum Canonem Scripturæ nunc haberi debeat; traditiones vero omnes, quocunque nomine veniant, ab hoc axiomate exclusit. In quam sententiam etiam veteres anathema Apo- stoli Gal. 1, 8. urgere consveverunt, quod dictum est, non modo illi, qui contraria prædicarit, sed qui ALIA & DIVERSA. Chrysostomus hom. 1. in Epist. ad Gal. Neque dixit, si contraria annuncia- verint, aut totum Evangelium everterint, verum si vel PAULUM evangelizaverint PRÆTER Evangelium, quod accepistis, & si QUIDVIS labefa- ctarint, anathema sint. Chrysostomum sequitur Theophylactus: Neque enim, si contraria solum prædicaverint, intulit, sed si Evangelizaverint id, præ- ter quod ipsi Evangelizamus, hoc est, si plusculum quidpiam ipsi adjecerint, execrationi subdantur. Unde S. Augustinus lib. 3. contra literas Petil. cap. 6. Si quis de Christo, sive de ejus Ecclesia, sive de alia quacunque re, quæ pertinet ad fidem, vitamque no- stram, non dicam, si nos, sed omnino, quæ securus adje- cit, si Angelus de Cælo vobis annunciaverit, præter- quam quod in Scripturis legalibus, & Evangelicis ac- cepistis, anathema esto. Nec vero additio tum fit, cum contraria docentur, sed eorum, quæ posita sunt, la- befactatio. Pellunt enim se mutuo, adque evertunt contraria. Hic vero prohibetur populus aliquid addere legi, vel insuper adjicere. Ideo rectissime S. Ambrosius de Parad. cap. 12. Nihil vel cautionis gratia jungere debemus mandato Dei. Si quid enim vel addas, vel detrahas, PRÆVARICATIO est. Basilius infidelitatem falsumque testimonium & sacri- legium dicit, si quis aliquid addat, aut demat. Infide- litatis argumentum fuerit, ait Serm. de fid. Confess. (verba ejus apostasiam proprie sonant, Φανερὰ ἔκπτωσις τῆς πίστεως) & superbiæ signum certissimum, si quis eorum, quæ scripta sunt, aliquid rejicere velit, aut eorum, quæ non sunt scripta, introducere. Et in brev. qu. qu. 98: Erga DEUM Præpositus anima- tus esse debet tanquam minister Christi, & dispensator mysteriorum Dei, metuens, ne quid PRÆTER vo- luntatem DEI IN SCRIPTURIS certo expressam vel dicat, vel instituat, & inveniatur FALSUS testis, aut SACRILEGUS in eo, quod aut inducit alienum à Doctrina Domini, aut aliquid placitorum DEI omittit.

Neque juvat hic Grotium, aut alios Novatores Papistica distinctio traditionum, Scripturam inter- pretantium, & ad Scripturas adjectarum: quia in- terpretatio Scripturæ indubitata & infallibilis non è traditione, sed ex ipsa Scriptura desumen- da, quæ sola est authentica & ἀνυπεύθυνος sui ipsi- us interpres. Eodem enim Spiritu explicandæ sunt S. literæ, quo inspiratæ sunt 2. Petr. 1, 21. Neque ulla monstrari potest infallibilis ejusmodi traditio ἐξηγητικὴ. Consensus Patrum testimonium est solum fidei & religionis, & autoritatem humanam tantum obtinet, adeoque non pro norma infallibili haberi, aut divinæ authoritatis, vel pro principio fidei censeri potest. Topicum est argumentum, non apodicticum: Fallibile non raro atque exceptioni- bus obnoxium, neutiquam infallibile & ἀνυπεύ- θυνον, omnique exceptione superius. Audiatur hic Augustinus Epist. 112. ad Paulin. Si divinarum Scripturarum, earum scil. quæ Canonicæ in Ecclesia nominantur, perspicua firmantur autoritate, sine ulla dubitatione credendum est. Aliis vero testibus vel testimoniis, quibus aliquid credendum esse suadetur, tibi credere vel non credere liceat, quantum meriti ea admonentem ad faciendam fidem vel habere vel non habere perpenderis.

Quod de legibus humanis divinam sapientibus dicit Grotius: illæ vel ad externam politiam, ordi- nem & εὐσχημοσύνην Ecclesiasticam pertinent, vel ad cultus divini substantiam, & ad religionem. Hæ omnes exclusæ sunt, quia nihil addendum est divi- nis legibus de cultu Dei. Ideo additur, ἐξηγήσεως causa, in Vulgata versione, Papistis authentica, particula exclusiva in textu parallelo Deut. 16, 32. Quod præcipio tibi, hoc TANTUM facito DO- MINO, nec addas quicquam, nec minuas. Illas autem prioris generis leges licitas esse nemo ne- gat, sed eæ humanæ tantum sunt autoritatis, nec huc faciunt. Exceptionibus Pontificiorum va- riis satisfecit B. Gerhardus in Comment. ad h. l.

Quod vero ad alteram exceptionem, quod de observatione perfecta legis hic agatur, non de ipsa legis perfectione, tametsi certum sit, legem requi- rere perfectam obedientiam, ita ut nec diminua- mus quicquam non faciendo, quod jubetur, nec ad- damus, aliter, quam jussum est, faciendo, id tamen hic proprie aut primo verbis illis addendi & dimi- nuendi non indigitatur, ac præterea obligatio ista ad legem ea ratione observandam, ne quid aliter, quam præceptum est, fiat, aut omittatur, quid ali- ud arguit, quam ipsam legis perfectionem? Ad quam enim regulam ita adstringimur, ut neque di- minuere fas sit aliquid vel prætermittere, neque ad- dere, aut aliter facere, quam illa jubet, eam omni- no perfectam esse oportet, πᾶσαν πρόθεσιν ἡ ἀ- φαίρεσιν μηδαμῶς ἐπιδεχόμενον, uti Varinus regu- lam definit. Quapropter ne regula quidem est nisi perfecta sit. Regula enim, ut habet Theophylactus in c. 2. ad Phil. & amussis neque appositionem habet, neque ablationem. Neque vero possumus legem di- vinam, ut perfectam normam, ad observationem perfectam nobis unice præfigere, scopumque no- strum constituere, nisi legem divinam pro norma perfecta habeamus. Ideo agnoscunt Papistarum non postremi, hic perfectionem legis adstrui. Al- phonsus Tostatus Abulensis Episcopus in h. l. Hic commendatur lex à perfectione, quia perfecto nec ad- di potest, nec auferri debet, ut patet. Franc. Vatablus in h. l. Causatur Moses, ideo nihil esse addendum vel demendum verbis Dei, ne non serventur præcepta Dei, quod traditiones hominum verbo Dei additæ ob- staculo sint, ne serventur. Præcepta enim hominem avertunt à veritate Tit. 1, 14.

## 4:3
verse 3. AGAINST BEEL-PEOR.

They say this idol of the Moabites is so called because they would open their posteriors before it, or relieve their bowels in its honor. Jerome on Isaiah 25, Hosea 4 and 9. He teaches that it is Priapus, and that it was worshipped especially by women. See 1 Kings 15:13. It is also called simply Peor, Joshua 22:17. Selden, On the Syrian Gods, book 1, chapter 5, calls the Rabbinical accounts of that obscene worship of Peor 'nonsense, nonsense'; he also denies that Priapus is the same as Peor. It is believed that this idol was worshipped in the fornication with the daughters of the Moabites, Numbers 25:1, done in honor of this idol, or at least so that the Israelites might possess those harlots. Let what we have said about this idol on Numbers 23:18 be compared.

Latin:

vers. 3. CONTRA BEEL-PHEGOR.

Hoc idolum Moabitarum ita vocatum ajunt, quod coram eo פוערין aperirent rs, sive foramen po- dicis & ventrem exonerarent in ejus honorem. Hier. in Es. 25. Os. 4. & 9. Priapum id esse, atque à mulieribus imprimis cultum fuisse docet. Vid. 1. Reg. 15, 13. Vocatur & simpliciter Peor, Jos. 22, 17. Selden. de Dis Syris lib. 1. c. 5. liras liras dicit Rabbinicas de cultu illo Peoris obscœno: negat etiam Priapum eundem esse cum Peor. Fornicatio cum filiabus Moabitarum Num. 25, 1. in hono- rem hujus idoli facta, vel certe ut scortis illis poti- rentur Israëlitæ, idolum istud cultum creditur. Conferantur quæ de hoc idolo diximus ad Num. 23, 18.

## 4:6
Verse 6. LET THEM SAY, BEHOLD A WISE PEOPLE) The judgment is to be made from the laws concerning peoples: an ancient oracle,

Only the Chaldeans obtained wisdom, and the Hebrews, / Reverencing the self-begotten King God purely. Verse 8. AND JUST JUDGMENTS] 'krimata' or 'mishpatim' are called here the laws concerning contracts, most suitable to equity.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DICANT, EN POPULUS SAPIENS) Ex Le- gibus de populis sit judicium: oraculum vetus,

Μοῦνοι Χαλδαῖοι σοφίαν λάχον, ἠδ' ἄῤ Ἑϐραῖοι, Αὐτογένεθλον ἄνακτα σεϐαζόμενοι Θεὸν ἁγνῶς. Vers. 8. JUSTAQUE JUDICIA] κρίματα sive מִשְׁפָּטִים dicuntur hic leges de contractibus, æquitati convenien- tissimæ.

## 4:15
Verse 15. YOU SAW NO LIKENESS) Empedocles opposes images for the same reason: 'For it is not adorned with a human head according to its limbs, / Nor do two branches spring from its back,' etc. Ammonius cites this on Aristotle's 'On Interpretation'. Tacitus, Histories 5: 'The Jews understand only with the mind, and as one deity. They consider those profane who fashion images of God out of mortal materials in the likeness of men.'
