The same about the Germans: 'Nor do they think it consistent with the greatness of the heavenly beings to simulate them in any human form.' The reason for Numa is the same for why he abolished images, as Plutarch teaches: 'For he (namely Pythagoras) did not suppose the first principle to be sensible or subject to passion, but invisible and incorruptible and intelligible,' etc. Antiphanes on God: 'He is known from an image, he is not seen by the eyes, he resembles nothing. Therefore no one can learn him from an image.' Xenophon of Colophon: 'One God is greatest among gods and men, / In no way like to mortals in body, nor in thought.' The same: 'But if oxen and lions had hands, / Or could draw with their hands and perform works as men do,' etc.

Latin:

Vers. 15. NON VIDISTIS ALIQVAM SIMILITU- DINEM) Eadem ratione imagines oppugnat Empedocles: Οὔτε γὰρ ἀνδρομέῃ κεφαλῇ κατὰ γυῖακέκασται, Οὐ μὲν ἀπαὶ νώτων γε δύο κλάδοι ἀΐσσουσι, &c. Citat Ammonius ad Aristotelem περὶ ἑρμηνείας. Tacitus Hist. V. Iudæi mente sola, unumque numen intelligunt. Profa- nos qui Deum imagines, mortalibus materiis, in speciem homi- num effingunt. Idem de Germanis: Neque in ullam humani oris speciem assimulare ex magnitudine cælestium arbitrantur. Par causa Numæ cur simulacra sustulerit, docente Plutar- cho: Οὔτε γὰρ ἐκεῖνος (nempe Pythagoras) αἰσθητὸν ἢ πα- θητὸν, ἀόρατον δὲ καὶ ἀκήρατον καὶ νοητὸν ὑπελάμϐανεν εἶναι τὸ πρῶτον &c. Antiphanes de Deo: ἀπὸ εἰκόνΘ- ἐ γνωρίζεται, ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐχ ὁρᾶται, ὐδενὶ ἔοικε. διόπερ αὐτὸν ὐδεὶς ἐκμαθεῖν ἐξ εἰκόνΘ- δύναται. Xenophanes Colophonius: Εἷς Θεός ἔντε θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισι μέγιστος Οὔτι δέμας θνητοῖσιν ὁμοίϊος, ὐδὲ νόημα. Idem: Ἀλλ' εἴτοι χεῖρας εἶχον βόες ἠδὲ λέοντες, Ἢ γράψαι χείρεσσικαὶ ἔργα τελεῖν ἅπερ ἄνδρες, &c.

## 4:19
Verse 19. ADORE THEM AND WORSHIP THEM) The Greeks: πλανηθεὶς προσκυνήσῃς. So also the Chaldean in this place. Others no less probably: Cast yourself down and bow yourself, with 'and' placed instead of 'or': that is, not only should you not prostrate your whole body, but you should not even incline your body, which is less. Namely, lest by such gestures the Jews might gradually be led to worship those things instead of God. See Job 31:26, 27.

WHICH THE LORD THY GOD HATH CREATED FOR THE SERVICE OF ALL NATIONS THAT ARE UNDER THE HEAVEN) The Latin here added 'for the service,' lest they be thought to have been given for worship. The LXX follow the Hebrew: ἃ ἀπένειμε ὁ κύριος ὁ Θεός σε αὐτὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι τοῖς ὑποκάτω τᾶ ὐρανᾶ. Nor is it true that it was added by them to provide light: which the Talmudists say, perhaps deceived by other versions. For the ancient Christians consistently read it thus, and being brought to this passage, said that the worship of the stars was permitted to the nations before the times of the Gospel: for Justin adds in his Dialogue with Trypho, εἰς τὸ προσκυνεῖν αὐτόν. Such as Clement and others have: among whom either the word 'gave' is to be interpreted as 'to allow,' just as Paul says that God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways, because clearly God by no law repressed that custom after it had once prevailed, or it is to be understood as having excused them in those less correctly instituted, not because they worshipped the stars, but because they worshipped God as powerful in the stars, which, however, He forbade to the Israelites because of the danger: just as we dissuade those whom we hold especially dear not only from harmful things but from those that could harm.

Grotius rightly notes that in the Hebrew, 'FOR THE SERVICE' is not contained; but he says it was added by the Latin, lest they be thought to have been given for worship: for which insertion there was no need: for worship had been prohibited by the words immediately preceding: lest perhaps when you lift up your eyes to Heaven you see the Sun and the Moon and all the stars of Heaven and, deceived by error, adore them, and worship them.

But that addition of the Hebrews to provide light he rightly disapproves, from the Hebrew text, the version of the LXX interpreters, and the constant reading of the ancients. For in the Hebrew there is only חלק, 'he has divided': R. Hiscuni therefore adds of his own that, 'TO ILLUMINATE THEM': with this gloss rendered: he divided, so that as if by divided time they might provide light to individual nations and provinces: for certain stars shine in some regions, and not in others, lest the stars provide light to all nations at the same time. But it is said simply that God divided or distributed the stars to the nations, so that the use might be understood, which is commended in

in Genesis, that they may be for signs, and for seasons, and for years, and for days, which common use of them the people of God have with all nations, as Augustine has in Q. 6 on Deuteronomy. B. Luther, because the word חלק also denotes 'he flattered,' explains it thus in Tom. 3, p. 344. The metaphor is taken from a little child flattering upon the knees, as if he were to say, what God flattered to the nations, because He wished to fawn upon and flatter the nations, which He would entice to Himself by the goodness and benefits of the stars.

But to Grotius, in whom we truly cannot approve that, for the sake of the Papists, as it appears, he brings forward the Φιλειδώλων ancients, who, being brought forward in this place, said that the worship of the stars was permitted to the nations before the times of the Gospel, and explains and holds that opinion as settled, so that he not obscurely pleads the cause of the Pontificians at the same time. That erroneous opinion should perhaps have been imputed not so much to the ancient Christians as to the Rabbis. For thus R. Moses Gerundensis thinks, that regard is had here to the idolatry of the Gentiles, of whom some worshipped this, others that star as a tutelary God. Nor are those things Justin's, which Grotius brings forward from Justin's Dial. with Trypho, but those of Trypho the Jew; beware of saying the Sun and Moon: which it is written were permitted by God to the nations, that they might worship them as Gods: ἅ γέγραπται, τοῖς ἔθνεσι συγκεχω- ρηκέναι τὸν Θεὸν ὡς Θεὸς προσκυνεῖν: although Trypho himself also confesses that the Holy Spirit pronounces a dire curse upon those who make and worship idols. Grotius consulted Justin poorly here: I find nothing of the sort even in Clement (I think the Alexandrian is indicated), who rather went off into entirely different things here: Indeed, in the case of Augustine (whom, however, Grotius did not bring forward), Q. VI. in Deuteronomy, something analogous is read, but neither does he speak of the stars distributed to the Gentiles for adoration by divine permission, much less of the divine foreknowledge of the idolatry of the Gentiles: It is not said so, he says, as if God commanded them to be worshipped by the nations, and not to be worshipped by His own people alone: but it is said either so, because God foresaw that the nations would exhibit worship to these celestial bodies and yet, foreseeing this, created them: whereas He foresaw that His own people would be such as would not worship them: Or it is said DISTRIBUTED, so that the use may be understood, which is commended in Genesis, etc., which have been brought forward above. In vain, therefore, does Grotius sweat in recalling the sayings of the Fathers to a good mind, since he could bring forward no one who said that the worship of the stars was permitted to the Gentiles before the times of the Gospel. Nor is there a sound mind here in Grotius himself: Among the Ancients, he says, the word DEDIT must either be interpreted as 'to allow,' just as Paul says that God allowed the nations to go in their own ways, because, namely, God did not repress that custom by any law, after it had once prevailed: or it must be understood as having excused them in those less correctly instituted, not that they worshipped the stars, but that they worshipped God as powerful in the stars, which, however, He forbade to the Israelites themselves, because of the danger. Just as those whom we hold exceptionally dear, we dissuade not only from harmful things, but from those which can harm. These are the words of Grotius. But the word which the LXX use, ἀπένειμε, is not DEDIT, which is sometimes used for PERMISIT, or SIVIT. It is one thing, therefore, that God divided the stars to the nations, which implies use and ministry and thus divine ordination, and another that He allowed the nations to go in their own ways, which designates only the permission of sin. And it is false that God did not repress by any law that custom, which he ought rather to have called idolatry. For He repressed astrolatry by Moses by this very law: which law certainly did not bind the Jews alone, even if it was given and promulgated among them alone, but, like other moral laws, all men. And for that reason it was solemnly repeated, because the moral law, inscribed upon nature, had been almost obliterated and extinguished by contrary sins and customs. Nor did the Fathers ever excuse in the Gentiles, as being less correctly instituted, the fact that they worshipped God in the stars; for thus they would have confirmed them in the same error, nay, in idolatry; which was not only forbidden to the Israelites here, but to all men. For the moral law binds all. Nor was this interdiction made only because of the danger of idolatry, but as a species of idolatry: since God did not wish to be worshipped in the stars or other creatures by anyone; and those who worship Him in them, because they do not worship GOD in a divine way or in the way prescribed by GOD, are condemned for idolatry: as is demonstrated at length elsewhere against the similar idolatry of the Papists. Let the Angelolatry of Dr. Stephan Clotzius be compared for that matter, and other Disputations of ours instituted against the Pontificians. For Grotius plays the Papist here not obscurely, or he gratifies them with a welcome service.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ADORES EA ET COLAS) Græci: πλανηθεὶς προσκυνήσῃς. Sic & Chaldæus hoc loco. Alii non minus probabiliter: Dejicias te & incurves te, posito & pro aut: id est, non modo non toto corpore procumbas, sed nec inclines corpus, quod minus est. Nempe ne talibus gestibus paula- tim eo adducerentur Judæi, ut pro Deo ista colerent. Vide Jobum 31, 26. 27.

QUÆ CREAVIT DOMINUS DEUS TUUS IN MI- NISTERIUM CUNCTIS GENTIBUS QUÆ SUB CŒ- LO SUNT) Latinus hîc addidit in ministerium, ne data ad cultum putarentur. LXX. Hebræum sequuntur: ἃ ἀπένειμε ὁ κύριος ὁ Θεός σε αὐτὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι τοῖς ὑποκάτω τᾶ ὐρανᾶ. Neque verum est adjectum ab iis ad lumen præbendum: quod ajunt Thalmudici, decepti forte ab aliis versionibus. Nam constanter ita legere Christiani veteres, & hoc loco adducti dixere gentibus ante Evangelii tempora permissum cultum astrorum: addit enim Justinus Dialogo cum Tryphone, εἰς τὸ προσκυνεῖν αὐτόν. Qualia habent & Clemens & alii: apud quos aut verbum dedit interpretandum per sinere, sicut Pau- lus dicit Deum sivisse gentes ire in viis suis, quia scilicet Deus nulla lege morem illum postquam semel invaluerat repres- sit, aut intelligendum excusasse in illis minus recte institutis, non quod astra colerent, sed quod Deum in astris potentem, quod ipsum tamen Israëlitis interdixit ob periculum: sicut quos eximie caros habemus, eos non a noxiis tantum rebus sed ab iis quæ nocere possent, dehortamur.

Recte notat Grotius, in Ebræo illud, IN MI- NISTERIUM non haberi; Additum autem ait à Latino esse, ne data ad cultum putarentur: qua vero ἐπεμϐολῇ opus non erat: Cultus enim prohibitus fuerat verbis immediate præcedentibus: ne forte elevatis oculis in Cœlum videas Solem & Lunam & omnia astra Cœli & errore deceptus, adores ea, & colas.

Προσθήκην vero illam Ebræorum ad lumen præbendum merito improbat, è textu Ebræo, ver- sione LXX. interpp. & constanti lectione veterum. In Ebræo enim tantum est חלק partitus est: De suo ergo addit R. Hiscuni illud, AD ILLUMI- NANDUM EOS: hac reddita glossa: divisit, ut quasi partito tempore singulis gentibus & provinciis lumen præbeant: quædam enim astra nonnullis regio- nibus lucent, aliis non item, ne eodem tempore omni- bus gentibus astra lumen præbeant. Sed simpliciter dicitur, quod partitus sit Deus gentibus stellas, aut di- stribuerit, ut intelligeretur usus, qui commendatur in

Genesi, ut sint in signis, & in temporibus & in annis & in diebus, quem usum in eis communem habet populus Dei cum omnibus gentibus, ut habet Augustinus Q. 6. in Deuteronom. B. Lutherus verbum חלק quia notat etiam blanditus est, ita explicat Tom. 3. p. 344. Metaphora sumpta est à filiolo super genua abblandien- te, quasi dicat, quæ blandificavit Deus gentibus, quod adulari & blandiri vellet Gentibus, quas ad se allice- ret bonitate & beneficiis stellarum.

Sed ad Grotium, in quo vero probare non possumus, quod in gratiam, uti apparet, Papista- rum Φιλειδώλων veteres adducat, qui hoc loco ad- ducti, dixerint, gentibus ante Evangelii tempora per- missum astrorum cultum, illamque sententiam ita ex- plicet, ratamque habeat, ut haut obscure Pontifi- ciorum causam simul agat. Non tam Christianis ve- teribus, quam Rabbinis forte erronea illa opinio imputanda fuerat. Sic enim R. Moses Gerundensis arbitratur, respectum hic haberi ad Gentilium idolo- latriam, quorum alii hoc, alii aliud sidus tanquam tu- telarem Deum coluerunt. Nec Justini illa sunt, quæ è Justini Dial. cum Tryph. adfert Grotius, sed Try- phonis Judæi; Solem & Lunam dicere, caveas: quæ scriptum est à Deo gentibus permissa esse, ut tanquam Deos adorarent: ἅ γέγραπται, τοῖς ἔθνεσι συγκεχω- ρηκέναι τὸν Θεὸν ὡς Θεὸς προσκυνεῖν: quanquam & Trypho ipse fateatur, Spiritum S. execrationem di- ram indicere Idola facientibus & adorantibus. Malè hic consuluit Justinum Grotius: Nihil etiam tale in Clemente (Alexandrinum indigitari puto) reperio, qui potius in diversa omnia hic abiit: Penes Au- gustinum quidem, (quem vero non adduxit Gro- tius) Q. VI. in Deuteronom. aliquid analogi legitur, sed neque is de distributis syderibus gentilibus ad adorationem per divinam permissionem, nedum de præscientia divina idololatriæ gentilium loquitur: Non ita dictum est, inquit, tanquam Deus præcepit ea coli à gentibus, à solo autem populo suo non coli: sed aut ita dictum est, quod Deus præsciverit, gentes cul- turam exhibituras his cælestibus & tamen hoc præsci- ens, creaverit eas: cum vero populum suum futurum esse præsciverit, qui ista non coleret: Aut DISTRI- BUET dictum est, ut intelligatur usus, qui commen- datur in Genesi &c. quæ supra adducta sunt. Fru- stra ergo sudat Grotius in revocandis Patrum di- ctis ad bonam mentem, quum neminem, qui Gen- tibus ante Evangelii tempora permissum astrorum cultum dixerit, adferre potuerit. Neque sana mens hic Grotio ipsi est: Apud Veteres, ait, aut interpre- tandum verbum DEDIT, per sinere, sicut Paulus dicit, Deum sivisse gentes ire in viis suis, quia sc. Deus nulla lege morem illum, postquam semel in value- rat, repressit: aut intelligendum excusasse in illis mi- nus recte institutis, non quod astra colerent, sed quod Deum in astris potentem, quod ipsum tamen Israëlitis interdixit, ob periculum. Sicut quos eximie caros habemus, eos non à noxiis tantum rebus, sed ab iis quæ nocere possunt, dehortamur. Hæc Grotius. At ver- bum, quod LXX. adhibent, ἀπένειμε, non est DE- DIT, quod pro PERMISIT quandoque adhibe- tur, seu SIVIT. Aliud ergo, divisisse Deum syde- ra gentibus, quod usum & ministerium adeoque di- vinam ordinationem infert, aliud sivisse gentes in viis suis ire, quod peccati permissionem solum designat. Et falsum est, Deum nulla lege morem illum, quem idololatriam potius dicere debebat, repressisse. Nam hac ipsa lege repressit astrolatri- am per Mosen: quæ sane lex non Judæos solum obligabat, etsi inter hos solos data & promulgata, sed uti cæteræ morales leges, omnes homines. Atque ideo solemniter repetita, quod contrariis peccatis & consuetudinibus lex moralis, naturæ insculpta, pene obliterata fuerit, atque exincta. Neque excusarunt uspiam Patres in gentilibus, ut- pote minus recte institutis, quod Deum in astris co- luerint; sic enim confirmassent eosdem in errore, imo idololatria; quæ non Israëlitis tantum hic in- terdicta, sed omnibus hominibus. Lex enim mo- ralis omnes obligat. Neque solum ob periculum ido- lolatriæ, hæc interdictio facta, sed ceu idololatriæ species: siquidem in astris, aut creaturis aliis Deus à nullo coli voluerit; & qui ipsum in illis colunt, eo quod non divino, vel à DEO præscripto modo DEUM colat, idololatrias damnatur: uti alias ad- versus Papistarum similem idololatriam prolixe demonstratur. Conferatur eam in rem Angelola- tria Dn. D. Stephani Clotzii, & aliæ nostrorum Dispp. contra Pontificios institutæ. Papizat enim hic non obscure Grotius, aut gratam ipsis operam gratificatur.

## 4:25
Ver. 25. AND YOU SHALL HAVE REMAINED IN THE LAND) For about eight hundred years. For the Hebrews agree that these things are to be referred to the times of Shalmaneser and Nebuchadnezzar.

QUICKLY) After the measure of sins has been filled.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ET MORATI FUERITIS IN TERRA) Ad annos serme octingentos. Nam ad Salmanasaris & Nabu- chodonosori tempora hæc referenda consentiunt Hebræi.

CITO) Post impletam peccatorum mensuram.

## 4:29
Ver. 29. AND WHEN YOU SHALL SEEK THERE THE LORD YOUR GOD) God always forgives the Hebrew people when led to repentance, but not always individuals.

The Novatian and Socinian dogma of uncertainty concerning divine grace, nay, a pit of despair. For if God does not forgive the guilt of those led to repentance, no one will be able to be certain of the forgiveness of sins and the grace of GOD: all sinners will have to doubt, nay, to despair of the remission of sins. But God protests against this, and even affirms with an oath, that He does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he should turn and live: on whatever day he shall turn from his wickedness, He has declared that He is prepared to receive him back into grace: Ezek. 18 and 33. To those who are in danger of despair, (these are the words of Augustine, tr. 33 in John) what does He say? On whatever day the wicked shall have turned, I will forget all his iniquity. For the sake of those, therefore, who are in danger of despair, He has proposed a covenant of indulgence. Therefore Tertullian, in his book on repentance, chapter 4, excellently invites us to salvation with a reward, even swearing; saying, 'I live': He desires to be believed. O blessed are we, for whose sake GOD swears! O most miserable, if we do not believe the Lord even when He swears! We have expressly refuted that heresy in our Disputation on the Augustan Confession at Rostock, article XII, which may be consulted here.

Latin:

Vers. 29. CUMQVE QUÆSIERIS IBI DOMINUM DEUM TUUM) Populo Hebræo ducto pœnitentia Deus semper ignoscit, singulis non semper.

Dogma Novatianum, & Socinisticum incerti- tudinis de divina gratia, imo desperationis bara- thrum. Si enim Deus pœnitentia ductorum cul- pæ non ignoscit, nemo de peccatorum venia & gratia DEI certus esse poterit: Peccatoribus o- mnibus de remissione peccatorum dubitandum, imo desperandum erit. At protestatur contra Deus, & jurejurando etiam affirmat, se nolle mor- tem impii, sed ut convertatur ac vivat: In quacun- que die se ab impietate sua avertet, in gratiam eundem se recipere paratum esse declaravit: Ezech. 18. & 33. Illis, qui desperatione periclitantur, (verba sunt Au- gustini tr. 33. in Joh.) quid dicit? In quacunque die impius conversus fuerit, omnis iniquitatis ejus oblivi- scar. Propter illos ergo, qui desperatione pericli- tantur, proposuit indulgentiæ pactum. Ideo præ- clare Tertullianus lib. de pœnit, cap. 4. invitat præ- mio salutem, jurans etiam; Vivo, dicens: cupit cre- di sibi. O beatos nos, quorum causa DEUS jurat! O miserrimos, sinec juranti Domino credimus! Ex professo hæresin illam profligavimus Disp. in August. Confess. Rostochiensibus art. XII. quæ hic conferantur.

## 4:34
verse 34. BY THE BATTLE. He is not speaking of the war against Amalek. Because the matter concerns things done in Egypt, not in the desert. He points to the battle against the Egyptians, of which Exodus 14:14 and 15:3 speak.

Latin:

vers. 34. PER PUGNAM. Non de bello contra Amalek loquitur. Quia res est de rebus in Ægypto, non in deserto gestis. Pugnam adversus Ægyptios, de qua Exod. 14, 14. c. 15. 3. indigitat.

## 4:39
Verse 39. GOD IN HEAVEN ABOVE, AND ON THE EARTH BENEATH) One governing all things.

Latin:

Vers. 39. DEUS IN COELO SURSUM, ET IN TER- RA DEORSUM) Unus cuncta gubernans.

## 4:40
verse 40. AND THAT YOU MAY REMAIN FOR A LONG TIME UPON THE EARTH. In Hebrew: ALL THE DAYS: LXX: μακροήμεροι long-lived. Some understand this as all the days of anyone's life: but it concerns the perennial habitation of the Israelites in the land of Canaan. For unless they had provoked the wrath of GOD against themselves by their sins, they could have dwelt in the land of Canaan even to the present day.

PART II. EXEGESIS OF DEUTERONOMY, Concerning both the repetitions of the laws and the promises and threatenings.

Latin:

vers. 40. ET PERMANEAS MULTO TEMPORE SUPER TERRAM. In Ebr. OMNIBUS DIEBUS: LXX. μα- κροήμεροι longævi. Omnes dies vitæ cujusvis in- telligunt nonnulli: sed de perenni habitatione Israëlitarum in terra Canaan agitur. Nisi enim peccatis suis iram DEI in se concitassent, in terra Canaan usque in præsentem diem habitare po- tuissent.

PARS II. DEVTERONOMII ΕΞΗΓΗΤΙΚΗ, Tum repetitionum legum tum promis- sionum & comminationum.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. Repetition and explanation of the Decalogue.

Latin:

CAPUT V. Repetitio & explicatio Decalogi.

## 5:4
Ver. 4. FACE TO FACE SPOKE TO US) Just as men are accustomed to converse with men: which refers to the distinct perception of voices: not to anything visible. For they saw nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 4. FACIE AD FACIEM LOCUTUS EST NO- BIS) Ita ut homines cum hominibus colloquentes solent: quod refer ad vocum perceptionem distinctam: non ad con- spicuum aliquid. Nihil enim viderunt.

## 5:6
Ver. 6. I THE LORD THY GOD) Moses was content here to relate the sense. The words themselves are in Exodus. See that passage and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 6. EGO DOMINUS DEUS TUUS) Sensum con- tentus est hic referre Moses. Verba ipsa sunt in Exodo. Quem locum vide & ibi dicta.

## 5:12
Ver. 12. OBSERVE THE SABBATH DAY THAT THOU MAYEST SANCTIFY IT, AS THE LORD THY GOD COMMANDED THEE) The words of Moses are interposed. And he commanded, understand on Mount Sinai, in the words which are in Exodus. And this is the reason why Moses did not mention creation here, referring the hearers to that which had been written down. But the other reason, not then expressed, but which could be understood to some extent from the words of GOD, he thought should be expressed more clearly, that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest.

The people are recalled there to the primeval institution of the Sabbath, which we are taught by this repetition was therefore made in Gen. 2:3. What Grotius produced here, alien to the rule in the explanation of the Decalogue, we have recalled to the rule of truth at chapter 20 of Exodus. That the law of the calling had no place before the promulgation of the Decalogue, he drew from the Jews, who in Bereshith Rabba say: that Abraham did not observe the Sabbath. Furthermore, the hypothesis that for the Hebrews only leisure and cessation from servile works is prescribed here, and not acts of positive religion or divine worship, was borrowed from the Papists, which Cajetan on Thomas 2, qu. 122, art. 4, Schvvarez lib. 2, de Fest. Observ. c. 1, n. 3, f. 153, and Jacob Bonfrerius on Exod. 20:8, 9, defend. That the Lord's Day was substituted by the Church in place of the Sabbath, Grotius has from the same Bonfrerius: whom B. Gerhardus in his Commentary on chapter V of Deuteronomy, p. 315, refutes in such a way that he teaches this was done by the Apostles. in chapter V of Deuteronomy, p. 315, refutes, so as to teach that this was done by the Apostles. If Bonfrerius, says our B. Gerhardus, according to the Jesuitical style, understands the Roman Pontiff, we deny that the Lord's Day was substituted by him in place of the Sabbath. We maintain that this was done rather by the Apostles. For that the Apostles observed the first day of the week in celebrating assemblies can be gathered from Acts 20:7 and 2 Cor. 16:2, where μία σαββάτων is the first day of the week. Thence by John that day is called ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, Apoc. 1:10. Finally, that Grotius acknowledges nothing moral in the Sabbath, he owes to the Anabaptists and the Photinians, about whom B. Gerhardus speaks in the cited Commentary, p. 308. The Photinians say that the Sabbath was abrogated in the New Testament in such a way that nothing, and thus not even the moral part, remained. But we have treated those matters there more fully along with other things pertaining to the Decalogue.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OBSERVA DIEM SABBATI UT SANCTI- FICES EUM, SICUT PRÆCEPIT TIBI DOMINUS DEUS TUUS) Verba Mofis interposita. Et præcepit, intel- lige in monte Sinai, verbis quæ in Exodo. Et hæc est causa cur hic creationis non meminerit Moses, auditores ad id quod perscriptum erat rejiciens. Causam autem alteram tunc non expressam, sed quæ ex verbis DEI intelligi aliquatenus po- terat, manifestius exprimendam duxit, ut requiescat servus tu- us, & ancilla tua.

REvocatur ibi populus ad primævam Sabbati institutionem, quam proinde Gen. 2, 3. factam esse hac repetitione docemur. Quæ hic à regula aliena in explicatione Decalogi particulariter tra- dita Grotius prodidit ad cap. 20. Exodi ad regulam veritatis revocavimus. Vocationis legem locum non habuisse ante Decalogi promulgationem, à Judæis hausit, qui in Bereschith Rabba ajunt: Abraha- mum non observasse Sabbatum. Cæterum Ebræis otium solum & cessationem ab operibus servilibus hic præscribi, non vero actus religionis positivæ vel cultus divini, à Papistis mutuata est hypothesis, quam Ca- jetanus in Thomam 2. qu. 122. art. 4. Schvvarez lib. 2. de Fest. Observ. c. 1. n. 3. f. 153. Jacob Bon- frerius ad Exod. 20, 8. 9. propugnant. Ab Ec- clesia in Sabbati locum suffectum esse diem Domini- cum, ab eodem Bonfrerio habet Grotius: quem ita è nostris B. Gerhardus Comment. in cap. V. Deut. p. 315. refellit, ut ab Apostolis hoc factum esse doceat. Si Bonfrerius, inquit B. Gerhardus no- ster, juxta stylum Jesuîticum, intelligit Pontificem Romanum, negamus ab illo in Sabbati locum suffe- ctum esse diem Dominicum. Ab Apostolis potiuss hoc factum esse statuimus. Quod enim Apostoli pri- mum Septimanæ diem in celebrandis conventibus ob- servaverint, colligi potest ex Actor. 20, 7. & 2. Cor. 16, 2. ubi μία σαββάτων est primus septimanæ dies. Inde à Johanne dies iste vocatur ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, Apoc. 1, 10. Denique quod nihil in Sabbato morale a- gnoscat Grotius, Anabaptistis debet, & Photinia- nis, de quibus B. Gerhardus in laudato Comment. p. 308. Photiniani Sabbatum in Nov. Test. ea ratio- ne abrogatum esse dicunt, ut nihil, & sic nec morale remanserit. Sed illa ibi cum aliis ad Decalogum pertinentibus fusius exequuti sumus.

## 5:16
Ver. 16. THAT THOU MAYEST LIVE A LONG TIME) A reward is usually added to commanding precepts. A punishment to forbidding ones. Aben-Ezra.

Latin:

Vers. 16. UT LONGO TEMPORE VIVAS) Præmium addi solet præceptis jubentibus. Vetantibus pœna. Aben- Esdra.

## 5:18
Ver. 18. FALSE TESTIMONY) שֶׁקֶר which is in Exodus is explained by שָׁוְא; in both there is a signification of falsehood.

Latin:

Vers. 18. FALSUM TESTIMONIUM) שֶׁקֶר quod est in Exodo explicatur per שָׁוְא, in utroque est falsi signifi- catio.

## 5:20
Ver. 20. THOU SHALT NOT COVET) Or thou shalt not desire. For חָמַד and אָוָה have the same value. See here what we observed regarding the parallel passage of Exodus. Grotius himself also acknowledged the difference there. There is no reason for us to repeat those things.

Latin:

Vers. 20. NON CONCUPISCES) Sive non desiderabis Idem enim valent חָמַד & אָוָה. Vide hic, quæ ad Exodi locum parallelum ob- servavimus. Discrimen etiam ipse Grotius illic agnovit. Non est, quod ea repetamus.

## 5:22
Ver. 22. THESE WORDS THE LORD SPOKE) He did not say, All these words, as in Exodus 20, because here he did not express the individual words, but the sense.

Latin:

Vers. 22. HÆC VERBA LOCUTUS EST DOMINUS Non dixit, Hæc verba omnia, ut Exodi 20. quia hic non vo ces singulas, sed sensum expressit.

## 5:29
Ver. 29. O THAT THERE WERE SUCH A HEART IN THEM) Maimonides notes from these words that God does not wish to move the wills of men in the way in which He acts through natural causes, but by enticing and persuading: and he adds the passages Deuteronomy 11:20, chapter 30:13.

Latin:

Vers. 29. QUIS DET TALEM EOS HABERE MEN TEM) Notat ex his verbis Maimonides, nolle Deum eo mo do quo per causas naturales agit movere hominum volunta tes, sed alliciendo, suadendoque: additque loca Deuteron. 11 20. c. 30, 13.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. The Lord is to be loved with all the heart.

ver. 1. PRECEPTS, AND CEREMONIES AND JUDGMENTS.

Lyranus not incorrectly understands moral precepts by the word מצות (Gr. commandments), ceremonial ones by חקים (statutes), and forensic ones by משפטים (judgments).

Latin:

CAPUT VI. Dominus ex toto corde diligendus.

vers. 1. PRÆCEPTA, ET CEREMONIA ATQUE JUDICIA.

LYranus per vocem מצות (Gr. ἐντολαὶ) præcepta moralia, per חקים τὰ δικαιώματα ceremonialia, per, משפטים κρίματα forensia non male intelligit.

## 6:3
ver. 3. A LAND FLOWING WITH MILK AND HONEY.

It can be taken literally, that there the udders of cows drip with abundant milk, and a store of honey flows down from the combs. Cf. Deut. 32, 1. Sam. 14, 25. Ezek. 20, 6. 15. For Jerome, who saw it, testifies that nothing is richer than the land of promise, at chapter 5 of Isaiah and Ezek. 20. Therefore, regard is had at once to rich pastures and frequent swarms of bees; indeed, since milk serves for necessity, but honey for delights and pleasure, it is not obscurely hinted that there is an abundance both of those things which are necessary and those which make for pleasure, all of which are supplied in such plenty that they seem to flow like fountains.

ver. 4. HEAR O ISRAEL THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE GOD.

Why the letter ע in the word שמע (hear) and the letter ד in אחד (one) are written as large letters, see Buxtorf in Comment. Masor. p. 159. Concerning the Unity of the divine essence, it has been treated most extensively in Tom. 2, in Aug. Conf., against the polytheism of the Gentiles and Socinians, as well as against others who deny it directly or indirectly, in Tom. 2, System. Theol. We do not wish to do what has been done. It was shown there that this law concerning worshipping and adoring one God alone did not pertain only to the Old Testament, which is a fiction of the Socinians that is truly irrational and atheological. Christ repeats this law in the New Testament and inculcates it most especially as a commandment of the highest necessity and as the chief one, Mark 12, 29, nor did He come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, Matt. 5, 12. Just as no one can be God by nature except Jehovah, so no one else is to be held or worshipped as God, or pursued with the divine honor of adoration, outside of and besides Jehovah the one God. However, this divine unity is not to be opposed to the Trinity of persons, as the Jews and Anti-Trinitarians do, because it is not explained here who that one Jehovah God is—whether the Father alone, or the Son and Holy Spirit with the Father—but it is taught that Jehovah is one God. But in other documents of Scripture it is clearly demonstrated that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are that one Jehovah, concerning which see Tom. III, System. Theolog. Some also prove the mystery of the Holy Trinity from the three names LORD GOD THY LORD is one, which Helvicus proves from the Jews themselves in Vind. Loc. Script. p. 175, and from the book Racanath, as also from the book Zohar, Galat. l. 2. de arc. Cath. Verit. cap. 1, Morneus de verit. rel. Christ. c. 6, Paul. Weidner. in loc. fid. præcip. tr. 1. v. 138. Cf. B. Gerhard. Disp. de Benedict. Eccles. Num. 6, 8. 53.

Latin:

vers. 3. TERRAM LACTE ET MELLE FLUENTEM.

Potest accipi proprie, quod ibi ubera vaccarum plena lac destillent, & mellis copia ex favis defluat. Conf. Deut. 32, 1. 1. Sam. 14, 25. Ezech. 20, 6. 15. Nihil enim terra promissionis pinguius esse testatur Hieronymus, qui eam vidit, ad cap. 5. Es. & Ezech. 20. Ad pascua ergo opima & frequentia apum examina simul respectus habetur, imo cum lac necessitati, mel autem delitiis & voluptati inserviat, haud obscure innuitur abundantia tum eorum, quæ necessaria sunt, tum quæ ad voluptatem faciunt, quæ omnia tanta suppetant copia, ut instar fontium fluere videantur.

veri. 4. AUDI ISRAEL DOMINUS DEUS NOSTER DEUS UNUS EST.

Cur in voce שמע audi litera ע & in אחד litera ד litera majuscula sit, vid. Buxtorf. in Comment. Mosor. p. 159. De Unitate essentiæ divinæ in Tom. 2. in Aug. Conf. fusissime adversus πολυθεϊαν gentilium & Socinianorum, tum adversus alios, qui eam directe vel indirecte negant, Tom. 2. System. Theol. actum est. Nolumus τὸ πραχθὸν πράττειν. Non solum ad Vet. Test. hanc legem de uno solo Deo colendo, & adorando pertinuisse, quod commentum est Socinianorum vere ἄλογον & ἀθεόλογον, illic ostensum. Repetit hanc legem Christus in N. Test. & vel maxime ceu præceptum observatu summe necessarium, ac præcipuum inculcat Marc. 12, 29. nec venit, ut legem solveret sed ut impleret Matth. 5, 12. Ut nunquam alius potest esse natura Deus præter Jehovam, ita nunquam alius habendus aut colendus, ut Deus, aut divino adorationis honore prosequendus, extra & præter Jehovam Deum unum. Non autem cum Judæis, & Anti-Trinitariis opponenda hæc unitas divina personarum Trinitati, quia hic non quis sit ille Jehovah unus Deus, solusne Pater, an cum Patre Filius, & Sp. S. explicatur, sed quod Jehovah unus Deus sit, docetur. In aliis autem Scripturæ documentis Patrem, Filium & Sp. S. esse unum illum Jehovam liquido demonstratur, de quibus vid. Tom. III. System. Theolog. Etiam e trinis nominibus DOMINUS DEUS TUUS DOMINUS unus est, nonnulli S. S. Trinitatis mysterium probant, quod ex ipsis Judæis Helvicus in Vind. Loc. Script. p. 175. & è libro Racanath, ut & è libro Zohar Galat. l. 2. de arc. Cath. Verit. cap. 1. Morneus de verit. rel. Christ. c. 6. Paul. Weidner. in loc. fid. præcip. tr. 1. v. 138. probant. Conf. B. Gerhard. Disp. de Benedict. Eccles. Num. 6, 8. 53.

## 6:5
Ver. 5. THOU SHALT LOVE THE LORD THY GOD WITH ALL THY HEART AND WITH ALL THY SOUL, AND WITH ALL THY STRENGTH) See what is at Matt. 22, 37. Some worship God for fear of punishment: others for the reward promised in the law: the best out of love, as Abraham did: therefore he was called the friend of God, Is. 41, 8.

The particle Vau is omitted, which here is illative: Therefore thou shalt love; and thus this commandment is deduced from the former ones, that God is to be loved with all the heart because He is the Lord, because He is our GOD, because He is one, for therefore we ought also to place all the trust of our heart in that one Lord our God, and embrace Him alone with the highest love. Impiously, therefore, does Molanus argue in Pract. Theol. tract. 3. cap. 16. Concl. 1. n. 11. that it is a matter of honesty, not of necessity, that we love God above all things. Also to be rejected are the corruptions of Tirinus and Bonfrerius, that the highest love of ours ought not to be intensive and extensive, much less continuous, but only appreciative or comparative, nor is a supernatural act of love commanded in the law, such that we prefer God to all created things. For the words themselves sufficiently testify that a supreme, most intensive, and continuous love of God is required, which, even if they say it belongs to the comprehensor and not the wayfarer, God nevertheless rightly demands from wayfarers if they wish to aspire to life through the fulfillment of the law. For it is required that we love God WITH ALL OUR HEART, that is, in such a way that the will is carried toward God with its entire impetus, and all the affections of the heart are pure, holy, and directed toward the love of God alone; for by the name of heart the will is denoted, as in Deut. 4:29, Jos. 22:5, because just as life proceeds from the heart, so operation proceeds from the will, which Lyranus admits; the heart is put for the will, because just as the heart moves the other members, so the will moves the other faculties of the soul. WITH ALL OUR SOUL, that is, in such a way that our sensitive appetite adheres uniquely to God, and our whole life is consecrated to God. Soul denotes the sensitive life, whose property is ἐπιθύμησις Gen. 23:8, c. 34:3, and it is taken for life in Exod. 4:19, c. 21:23. WITH ALL OUR MIND, or διανοίᾳ which is added in Mark 12:13, Luke 10:27, συνέσει in Mark 12:33, that is, in such a way that we direct all our thoughts uniquely to GOD. For by the name of mind the intellect is expressed, τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν: because διάνοια is explained by σύνεσιν. WITH ALL OUR STRENGTH, that is, in such a way that we direct and consecrate all the powers of soul and body, the lower and external senses, speech, and all our members, whatever we have and can do, to the love of God and the obedience flowing from that love. Which word is added ἐκ περισσίας, so that the highest and most intensive degree of love may be indicated. Burgensis in c. 21 does not dissent from this interpretation. Matthew. Therefore, although those four are not always joined, as in Mark 12:13, Luke 10:27, but sometimes three, as in this place, sometimes only two, from all the heart and from all the soul, Deut. 10:12, c. 11:13, c. 13:3, c. 26:16, c. 30:6, Jos. 22:5, the Papists nevertheless acknowledge that the same meaning is conveyed, for he who names the whole heart does not exclude the intellect, the will, and the remaining powers, but embraces them together, so that the rest may be seen to be added for the sake of a fuller declaration. Augustine teaches that this degree of love is required in these things, l. 1 de doctr. Christ. c. 22, when he says, with all the heart, with all the soul, with all the mind, he leaves no part of our life which ought to be vacant and, as it were, give place so that it might wish to enjoy another thing, but whatever else comes into the mind to be loved, let it be snatched to that place where the whole impetus of love runs. The other Fathers agree with this, see Basil in Ps. 44, Theod. quaest. 3 in Deut.

etc. Although indeed it is said of Hezekiah 2 Kings 20:2 and of Josiah c. 23:25 that they loved God with all their heart; it must be noted, however, that this phrase obtains a double meaning in the Scriptures; first, to denote in the precepts the rigorously perfect love which the law requires, but then to designate a sincere and ἀνυπόκριτον love, which is commended in those examples of the pious, although it was not without flaws, as is evident in Hezekiah, who acknowledged his sins Isa. 39:17, and in Josiah, who, having fallen gravely, waged war against the King of Egypt and died in the same. Add that those eulogies are attributed to them συγκριτικῶς and κατὰ τὶ, because with a burning zeal of piety they abolished idols and restored the worship of God with a more ardent affection of heart than any others. Therefore they cannot be taken ἁπλῶς and absolutely.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DILIGES DOMINUM DEUM TVVM EX TOTO CORDE TUO ET EX TOTA ANIMA TVA, ET EX TOTA FORTITVDINE TUA) Vide quæ ad Matth. 22, 37. Deum colunt quidam metu pœnæ: alii ob mercedem in lege promissam: optimi ex amore, ut fecit Abrahamus: ideo dictus amicus Dei, Es. 41, 8.

Omittitur particula Vau, quæ hic est illativa: Itaque diliges; adeoque deducitur hoc præceptum è prioribus, diligendum esse Deum ex toto corde, quia est Dominus, quia DEUS noster, quia unus est, nam ideo etiam in uno illo Domino Deo nostro omnem fiduciam cordis collocare, ipsumque unum summo amore complecti debemus. Impie ergo disputat Molanus in Pract. Theol. tract. 3. cap. 16. Concl. 1. n. 11. de honestate non de necessitate esse, ut Deum super omnia diligamus. Reprobandæ etiam corruptelæ Tirini, & Bonfrerii, summum debere amorem nostrum esse non intensive & ex- tensive, multo minus continue, sed appreciative so- lum vel comparative, nec præcipi in lege actum di- lectionis supernaturalem, ut Deum rebus omnibus creatis anteferamus. Nam verba ipsa satis testan- tur summam, intensissimam & continuam dile- ctionem Dei requiri, quam etsi comprehensoris, non viatoris esse dicant, jure tamen Deus postulat à viatoribus, si per legis impletionem ad vitam ad- spirare velint. Requiritur enim ut Deum diliga- mus EX TOTO CORDE, hoc est, ita ut volun- tas toto impetu in Deum feratur, ac omnes cordis affectus puri, sancti, & in solius Dei dilectionem directi sint, cordis enim nomine voluntas notatur, ut Deut. 4, 29. Jos. 22, 5. quia ut ex corde procedit vita, ita ex voluntate operatio, quod fatetur Lyra- nus; Cor ponitur pro voluntate, quia sicut cor movet alia membra, sic voluntas movet alias animæ potentias. EX TOTA ANIMA, hoc est, ita ut appetitus no- ster sensitivus Deo unice adhæreat, ac tota nostra vi- ta Deo consecretur. Anima vitam sensitivam no- tat, cujus est ἐπιθύμησις Gen. 23, 8. c. 34, 3. & pro vi- ta accipitur Exod. 4, 19. c. 21, 23. EX TOTA MENTE, vel διανοίᾳ quæ additur Marc. 12, 13. Luc. 10, 27. συνέσει Marc. 12, 33. hoc est, ita ut omnes nostras cogitationes ad DEUM dirigamus unice. Mentis enim nomine exprimitur intellectus τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν: quia διάνοια per σύνεσιν exponitur. EX TOTA FORTITUDINE, hoc est, ita ut omnes animæ & corporis vires, sensus inferiores & exterio- res, sermonem, & omnia membra, quicquid habe- mus, & possumus ad dilectionem Dei & obedien- tiam ex dilectione promanantem, dirigamus, ac consecremus. Quæ vox additur ἐκ περισσίας, ut summus & intensissimus dilectionis gradus indigi- tetur. Cui interpretationi non abnuit Burgensis in c. 21. Matth. utut ergo non semper illa quatuor conjungantur, ut Marc. 12, 13. Luc. 10, 27. sed mo- do tria, uti hoc loco, modo duo tantum ex toto cor- de & ex tota anima Deut. 10, 12. c. 11, 13. c. 13, 3. c. 26, 16. c. 30, 6. Jos. 22, 5. agnoscunt tamen Pontificii eandem sententiam inferri, nam qui totum cor nominat, intellectum, voluntatem, & reliquas vi- res non excludit, sed simul complectitur, ut cære- ra videri possint uberioris declarationis gratia ad- di. Hunc dilectionis gradum in hisce requiri do- cet August. l. 1. de doctr. Christ. c. 22. cum ait, to- to corde, tota anima, tota mente, nullam vitæ nostræ partem relinquit, quæ vacare debeat, & quasi locum dare, ut alia re velit frui, sed quicquid aliud diligen- dum venerit in animum, illuc rapiatur, quo totus di- lectionis impetus currit. Cui consonant Patres cæ- teri, vid. Basil. in Ps. 44. Theod. quæst. 3. in Deut.

&c. Quanquam vero de Ezechia 2. Reg. 20, 2. & de Josia c. 23, 25. dicatur, quod toto corde Deum di- lexerint; notandum tamen, eam phrasin duplicem in Scripturis obtinere significationem; primum rigorose perfectam dilectionem, quam lex requirit, in præceptis notare, tum vero sinceram, & ἀνυπό- κριτον dilectionem designare, quæ in exemplis illis piorum commendatur, quamvis nævis non caruerit, ut in Ezechia patet, qui peccata sua agno- vit Esa. 39, 17. & in Josia, qui graviter lapsus Æ- gyptio Regi bellum movit, in eodem occubuit. Adde, quod συγκριτικῶς & κατὰ τὶ illa elogia ipsis tribuantur, quod flagranti pietatis zelo idola ab- rogarint & cultum Dei ardentiore cordis affectu quam ulli alii restaurarint. Non ergo ἁπλῶς & ab- solute accipi possunt.

## 6:7
verse 7. AND YOU SHALL TELL THEM TO YOUR CHILDREN.

Hebrew שנן in Piel denotes to sharpen, Deut. 32:4, Ps. 64:4, Ps. 140:4, which, just as a sword, while it is being sharpened, is pushed more often against the whetstone so that it may strike and pierce more, so the commandments are to be sharpened and inculcated with the greatest zeal frequently, so that they may penetrate minds as if they were piercing with a sharp edge.

Latin:

vers. 7. ET NARRABIS EA FILIIS TUIS.

Ebr. שנן in Piel notat acuere Deut. 32, 4. Pf. 64,4. Pf. 140, 4. quod sicut gladius, dum acui- tur, sæpius ad cotem impellitur, ut magis feriat ac pungat, ita mandata acuenda, summoque studio inculcanda sint frequenter, ut penetrent animos, ac si acumine pungerent.

## 6:8
Verse 8.

AND YOU SHALL BIND THEM AS A SIGN ON YOUR HAND, AND THEY SHALL BE AND SHALL BE MOVED BETWEEN YOUR EYES] They shall be for you as spectacles: for that is what the word טוטפת signifies. See whether the Latin wrote, they shall not be moved. For in the Greek it is ἀσάλευτα.

The Jews understand all these things literally, and think that the upper hand or arm is denoted, binding Phylacteries to the left arm, and also membranes or plates marked with minute characters and enclosed in leather to the forehead. They think these are called here by the name טוטפת, (they also call them Thephitim, which they used in their prayers, concerning which see Moses of Coucy in Fagius on c. 13 Ex.) which Arias and Pagninus explain as frontals, others as nose-jewels, the LXX as ἀσάλευτα, they shall be immovable before your eyes. The Vulgate as they shall be moved before your eyes, which some reconcile in this way, that the law ought not to be removed from the eyes, and thus it ought always to be present or moved before the eyes. Those who reject Jewish superstition also explain the signs on the hand, forehead, and doorposts of houses as the words sound, from the Ancients Justin Dial. with Trypho, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact on Matthew 23, as also Osiander in the Paraphrase on this place. This, he says, was a pedagogy by which the Jews were kept in their duty, just as GOD also commanded them to wear certain monuments on the corners of their garments, by which, looking at them, they would be reminded of the observance of the commandments, concerning which fringes Num. 15:38, Deut. 22:12, which Christ joins with phylacteries in Matthew 23:5. Scaliger in Trihaer. Elench. c. 8 thinks that Christ himself wore phylacteries because of the divine ordinance, but how could the law be inscribed on the doorposts of houses, which, as Augustine warns, qu. 17 in Deut., according to the propriety of the words, no Israelite is recorded to have done, because no one can, unless perhaps he divides the words of the Lord through many parts of his house. How also could the whole law have been contained in such membranes, which are to be placed between the eyes? The Lord speaks openly of a sign and a memorial. Compare Exod. 13:9. For those things are said to be written in the hands which are before the eyes, Isa. 49, 16. 17. They are also said to be written, of which there is a perpetual remembrance, Mal. 3, 16. Nor is anything else indicated than that the commandments ought to have been perpetually before them: as Lyranus rightly says: You shall bind them for a sign, on your hand, that is, in your works, because the hand is the organ of organs, which ought to be done out of charity. And they shall be and shall move before your eyes, that is, they shall in no way be forgotten by you, just as a man does not forget a thing which is hung before his eyes, and you shall write them on the threshold of your house, that is, entering the house, and going out, you shall remember the love of God. See especially a similar passage, Prov. 7, 3. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET LIGABIS EOS TANQVAM SIGNVM IN MA- NV TVA, ERVNTQVE ET MOVEBVNTVR INTER OCVLOS TVOS] Erunt vobis pro conspicillis: id enim significat vox טוטפת. Vide an Latinus scripserit, non movebuntur. Nam in Græco est ἀσάλευτα.

Hæc omnia Judæi ad literam intelligunt, & manum superiorem vel brachium notari putant, Φυλακτήρια brachio sinistro alligantes, nec non membranulas vel laminas minutis characteribus signatas & corio inclusas fronti. Has nomine טוטפת hic vocari putant, (vocant & Thephitim quod in orationibus iis utebantur, de quibus vid. Mose de Cotzi apud Fagium in c. 13. Ex.) quod ex- ponit Arias & Pagnin. frontalia, alii monilia nasi, LXX. ἀσάλευτα erunt immobilia ante oculos tuos. Vulg. movebuntur ante oculos tuos, quæ ita nonnulli conciliant, quod lex non debeat ab oculis removeri, adeoque semper versari aut mo- veri debeat ante oculos. De signis in manu, fronte, & postibus ædium, prout verba sonant, ex- plicant etiam, qui superstitionem Judaicam reji- ciunt, è Veteribus Justinus Dial. cum Tryph. Chrysost. Euthym. Theophyl. in Matth. 23. ut & Osiander in Paraphr. h. l. Fuit hæc, inquit, pæda- gogia, qua continerentur Judæi in officio, sicut etiam jussit DEUS in angulis vestium gestare certa aliqua monumenta, quibus intuentes admonerentur de ob- servatione mandatorum, de quibus fimbriis Num. 15, 38. Deut. 22, 12. quas Christus cum phylacte- riis conjungit Matth. 23, 5. Scaliger in Trihær. Elench. c. 8. putat, Christum ipsum propter di- vinam ordinationem phylacteria gestasse, sed quomodo lex potuit inscribi postibus ædium, quod monente Augustino, qu. 17. in Deut. se- cundum proprietatem nemo Israëlitarum fecisse com- memoratur, quia nec quisquam potest, nisi forte di- vidat verba Domini per multas partes domus suæ. Quomodo etiam lex tota membranulis ejusmodi, quæ inter oculos collocentur, comprehendi po- tuisset? Loquitur Dominus aperte de signo & memoriali. Conf. Exod. 13, 9. Nam ea dicuntur in manibus scripta, quæ oculis obversantur Esa. 49, 16. 17. dicuntur etiam scripta, quorum est per- petua recordatio Malach. 3, 16. Nec aliud quid- quam indicatur, quam quod præcepta ipsis debue- rint perpetuo obversari: ut recte Lyranus: Li- gabis ea in signum, in manu, hoc est, in operibus tuis, quia manus est organum organorum, quæ debent fieri ex charitate. Eruntque & movebuntur an- te oculos tuos, hoc est, nullo modo erunt tibi oblivioni, sicut homo non obliviscitur rei, quæ ante oculos ejus appenditur, scribesque ea in limi- ne domus tuæ, hoc est, intrans domum, & exiens recordaberis de Dei dilectione. Vide imprimis si- milem locum Prov. 7, 3. 4.

Concerning those Tephillin as also concerning the Sisith, Deut. 22. verse 12. Episcopius treats at length in his Instit. lib. 3. cap. 1. num. 13. & num. 15. pages 62. 63.

Latin:

Ad Deut. 6, 8. post notam p. 663. b.

## 6:11
Ver. 11.

VINEYARDS AND OLIVE GROVES WHICH YOU DID NOT PLANT] According to the Greek proverb, Ἄλλοι μὲν σπείρεσ᾽, ἄλλοι δ᾽ αὖ ἀμήσονται.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

VINETA ET OLIVETA QVÆ NON PLANTASTI] Secundum Græcum proverbium, Ἄλλοι μὲν σπείρεσ᾽, ἄλλοι δ᾽ αὖ ἀμήσονται.

## 6:13
ver. 13.

YOU SHALL FEAR THE LORD YOUR GOD, AND HIM ONLY SHALL YOU SERVE.

In the Hebrew the exclusive particle is not added, which, however, having been added by the LXX and the Vulgate, the text is by no means falsified, as the Papists say, rashly accusing Luther of falsification on account of the addition of the exclusive particle in Romans 3:28. Christ himself brought it in that manner, 'and him only shall you serve' (Matthew 4:10). Grotius teaches in his annotations on the Gospels, p. 51, that the interpreters added it to express the meaning so much more clearly, and that the very order of the words demanded that the LXX add this 'only' here; for it is not written (Grotius continues) ותעבדו, which would have been 'and him you shall serve,' but ואתו תעבד, which clearly contains an emphasis that cannot be understood in the Greek words except by living pronunciation: and therefore something had to be added by which the reader might be admonished of this emphasis. For there is a silent reference to what had preceded in the same chapter, verse 4, that God is one. Wherefore Josephus also did not hesitate to add the same word in explaining this commandment, saying, 'that God is one, and him only to be worshipped.' Add that in the passage of Deuteronomy it follows continuously: 'You shall not follow other gods.' And Samuel, inculcating this commandment to the people, had expressly said, 'and him alone serve' (1 Samuel 7:3). Crellius also acknowledged this in his Commentary on Matthew 4, p. 249. For when in those places in Moses it is commanded that the Israelites worship God, and serve him, the force of the words is such that other gods are excluded from this worship, as is clearly seen from the words of the following chapter, Deuteronomy 6. For we read there: 'You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him, and shall swear by his name. You shall not go after other gods of all the nations, etc.' Add that Crellius admits that Deuteronomy 6:5, that greatest and chief commandment of the whole law: 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc.,' rests upon the unity of God as a foundation, because since there is only one God, the whole affection of the heart is to be turned to him ALONE, and he alone is to be worshipped, or concerning God and his Attributes. Divin. c. 17. p. 117. And this is what Francis Davidis rightly and deservedly urges against Faustus Socinus in the Disputation concerning the invocation of Christ, that the commandment of God stands severely that outside of God the creator of heaven and earth no one is to be invoked; which F. Socinus himself also conceded several times, although afterwards he contended that it was only commanded that God be worshipped and God alone be served (which indeed suffices for us here), but not that God alone is to be invoked. Hence the argument of Francis Davidis against Socinus in the aforementioned Disputation, chapter 17, part 7, p. 149, is invincible: God alone, who brought Israel out of Egypt, is to be worshipped. Christ is to be worshipped. Therefore, Christ is that sole God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

verse 13. YOU SHALL SWEAR BY HIS NAME.

In Hebrew, 'in his name,' LXX, 'upon his name.' It is not an absolute commandment but a hypothetical one, if, namely, the glory of God and the salvation of one's neighbor require an oath: so that we swear not otherwise than in the name of God, as Aben Ezra admits, who alone is the omniscient knower of hearts, the highest truth, the highest justice. And therefore it is not permitted to swear by creatures, with the Pharisees, or by the names of saints, with the Papists (concerning which Thomas 2, 2. q. 89. art. 6), for thus one sins against this commandment. And the Jesuits themselves, Bellarmine, Bonfrerius, and others, acknowledge that an oath is an act of worship, which honor they admit belongs to God alone. Add the prohibition of Christ that we should not swear by creatures, Matthew 5:3 and James 5:12, and also Jeremiah 5:7, 'they swear by gods that are not gods.' Nor is there any reason to object to the oath by the 'fear of Isaac' (Genesis 31:52), or by the 'life of Pharaoh' (Genesis 42:15). For there, by the 'fear of Isaac,' God himself is understood, whom Isaac worshipped and feared, compare Isaiah 8:13. But here it is not an oath but only an adjuration: and by that same reasoning we are also accustomed to adjure by the Gospel or the truth of the Gospel, where we swear by God. But when the formula is used: 'so help me God and his holy Gospel,' we do not swear by the Gospel, but the sense of the formula is this, that God may help me by the holy Gospels. Therefore, there is no reason for Rivetus to argue against this formula in his Explanation of the Decalogue, p. 88, as if the same contained remnants of Papist superstition. He should rather have seen how Calvin could be excused in his Harmony on Matthew 23:16 ff., when he does not disapprove of all oaths conceived by creatures, but only those which ascribe to creatures what belongs to God, whom Spanhemius could not defend, part 2, Dub. 124. §. 9. Christ teaches that only oaths conceived by the temple and the altar redound upon themselves and are binding, but he does not approve of them; rather, he censures them as hypocritical and insulting in themselves. Nor indeed are all things lawful to be done, which are binding after they have been done.

An oath, if it is to be defined in general, is a confirmation of speech by the attestation of God. Some add an execration, so that God is called upon either openly or tacitly as a judge decreeing punishment for perjury, not only as a witness. But there is not an execration in every oath. God also swears, but without an execration. They say indeed that God does not swear, but is only introduced as if swearing, when he promises more assertively. But Peter attributes both a promise and an oath to God (Acts 2:30), as does Paul (Hebrews 6:16), where these two are proposed as distinct. God therefore swears, although he cannot perform an execratory oath, which looks to a superior who can destroy, and belongs only to him who can sin and perjure himself. Whence one must distinguish between a simple oath and an execratory one. But since it is commanded here that you shall swear in the name of the Lord, it is manifest that an oath is lawful. The Essenes seem to have forbidden every oath. See Josephus, book 2 of the Jewish War, ch. 7, which is also attributed to the Manichaeans, but Augustine reports that they swore by the Paraclete. Pelagius contends that the oath was forbidden in the New Testament in his Epistle to Demetrias, in Jerome, Vol. 2 of his works, p. 20; see also Vol. 4 of Jerome, to Caelestius, p. 63. The Anabaptists follow him in the Emden Colloquy, who nevertheless in the Frankenthal Colloquy, art. 11, having abandoned that error, declared themselves more correctly, that only vain, futile, and rash oaths are to be disapproved. The Socinians indeed admit that it is lawful for a Christian to swear, but not that it is lawful in such a way as it was once lawful in the Old Testament, namely to swear for any cause whatever, provided one did not commit perjury. They contend this for the reason that they may maintain that Christ added something to this precept, which not only was not understood by the Pharisees, but which was not even signified by the words of the law, namely that one should not swear rashly or irreverently. Maldonatus also goes in this direction in chapter 5 of Matthew. But Schwarz rightly observes, Vol. 2 of Religion, book 1, on oaths, ch. 2, that it was a false opinion of the Jews (in the time of the New Testament, of the Pharisees) that there is no sin in swearing, provided perjury is avoided. Christ was not a new lawgiver, nor did the law, which is a perfect rule of justice, need any addition, but there was need for a cleansing from Pharisaical corruptions. The precept about not taking the name of the Lord in vain forbids not only perjury, but also any vain and rash oath whatsoever, just as the word שָׁוְא denotes not only what is false and deceitful, but whatever is vain, useless, and trivial, Ps. 127:2, Jer. 4:30, Mal. 3:14; therefore these three things are required for an oath, Jer. 4:2: you shall swear truly, that is, without pretense and simulation and fraud; rightly: that is, not by a rash and precipitate chance, but where necessity demands; and justly, that is, in matters that are just and lawful, and worthy to be confirmed by an oath. Add the interpretation of the Hierosolymitan Psalter Ps. 15, 4. and Sirach ch. 23, 10. 17.

As for the words of Christ in Matt. 5, 34. (to which those of James ch. 5, 20. are twin), they do not pertain to perfecting the law of Moses but to amending the corruption of the Pharisees, and they do not simply prohibit an oath, as Basil in Ps. 15, Chrysostom in Homily XVII on Matthew, and Theophylact on ch. V of Matthew seem to have understood it; to which opinion regarding the oath prohibited in the N.T., Sixtus of Siena in Book VI of his Bibliotheca Sancta, annotation 26, has brought forward Athanasius, Epiphanius, and Hilary. But most of those might perhaps be explained more kindly. Not only in the O.T. but also in the N.T. did pious and holy men swear. Rom. 1, 9. ch. 9, 2. 1 Cor. 15, 31. Heb. 1, 20. Gal. 1, 20. Phil. 1, 8. 1 Thess. 2, 5. 2 Thess. 2, 1. And there are prophecies concerning oaths in the time of the N.T. Is. 45, 24. Jer. 12, 16. Grotius in Book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, ch. 13, replies that it is not the assertory oath, but the promissory one, that is forbidden by Christ. But not every promissory oath is illicit: otherwise all contracts in civil society would easily have to be abolished, nor would Kings and Princes be able to make mutual pacts, nor subjects perform homage or bind their faith by oath, and therefore promissory oaths are by no means forbidden: concerning which it must be observed that they are also made regarding future things: nor is the outcome always in the hand of those who promise; by them the infallible outcome of the promised thing is not so much asserted as the purpose and will of the promisor is established. Nor do the words of Christ admit this restriction. For it would have to be proven that the Pharisees, against whom Christ acts, did not recognize perjury except in promises confirmed by oath, and not likewise in sworn assertions and testimonies, and indeed that they did not look further into the law concerning the avoidance of perjuries. Others therefore (2.) think that Christ did not prohibit the oath simply and absolutely, but the oblique and indirect formulas of an oath: by which the Pharisees thought that they were not held by great religion to perform what they had promised, or that they did not sin gravely if, under such formulas, they asserted things that were trivial, without directly using the name of God. (3.) It is better to say that all oaths regarding a useless and unnecessary matter, performed in any way, transgress against the command of God. Wherefore, levity and rashness in oaths are forbidden, whether the name of God is used directly or indirectly. Hence this explanation and vindication of the law by Christ is opposed to two Pharisaical corruptions: (1.) that it is not an oath, nor does it oblige one to perjury, where the name of God is not used directly, such as when they swore by the temple or by the altar. Where the Pharisees, because of avarice, preferred the gold and gifts of the temple, and the sacrifices, to the temple and the altar. Matt. 23, 16. et seqq. For even when one swears by creatures, one swears obliquely, indirectly, relatively, and implicitly by God. Concerning which B. Luther in his Enarratio of the Second Commandment, Vol. II, Wittenberg, says: he who swears by those things which are of God, or applied to Him, always also swears by God, from whom, in whom, and for whom are all things. (2.) That only perjuries are forbidden, but not any rash oaths whatsoever. And therefore Christ warns that one should not swear ὅλως at all; so that that word AT ALL is to be referred to the subject matter, that one should not swear either directly or indirectly in common speech, where business can be transacted by simple affirmation or negation. Therefore that word ὅλως does not import that it is not lawful to swear at any time or in any case. The bad habit of swearing out of levity is prohibited; an oath that is incumbent out of necessity is not prohibited.

An oath, therefore, is either lawful or illicit. Lawful is that which does not fight against the word of God, and is not undertaken rashly, but out of necessity, and only regarding true things that are certainly known. It is illicit either by reason of the manner, when the oath is not made according to the word of God, by the name of God, but by creatures, just as the Papists swear by the holy angels and relics, or by reason of the object for the sake of which the oath is made: when it is undertaken regarding false, or impossible, or uncertain, or illicit, or trivial and futile things. Lawful oaths, which do not impinge upon the love of God and neighbor, must be kept entirely, even if extorted by force or fraud, or made to a robber or an enemy, Lev. 19, 11. Matt. 5, 34. But illicit ones, made through error or infirmity, or in any way whatsoever, which cannot be kept without offense to the glory of God and the salvation of the neighbor, must by no means be kept, lest sin be heaped upon sin: because he who keeps an illicit oath sins twice, once by swearing wrongly, and again by keeping what was wrongly sworn, whence the rules: in evil promises rescind your faith: What is wrongly sworn is kept worse. Therefore David rightly did not keep the oath emitted out of excessive fervor to destroy the whole house of Nabal. 1 Sam. 25, 21.

The Scholastics observe that one sins against the commandment concerning the oath in six ways: 1. when one knowingly swears what is false, 2. when one deceitfully swears what is true which is thought to be false, 3. when one ignorantly swears what is false which is believed to be true, 4. When a promise confirmed by oath is not kept. 5. When one swears to what is illicit. 6. When one swears indiscreetly or rashly. Add 7. when one swears by creatures, or idols, not by the name of God. But it is another thing in an execratory oath, by which we devote and as it were pledge ourselves or our own, which we hold dear, to God as judge, if we knowingly and prudently deceive: for thus one does not swear by creatures, but only faith is added to our speech with some obtestation. See Job 31, 16. et seqq. Ps. 7, 5. 6. 8. When one swears equivocally, or with a reserved mental condition. For the Jesuits err gravely when they patronize equivocal oaths, concerning which see B. Meisner. Disputation on Jesuitical equivocations. Toletus, Instruction for Priests, Book IV, ch. 21, argues that sometimes, though not always, a man is bound not only to swear according to his own mind, but also according to the mind of others, that is, to use the common meaning which the hearer conceives in his mind, and not to use any equivocation: yet sometimes he is not bound, but it is lawful to use equivocation and to deceive the hearer. Likewise, if a husband asks his wife if she is an adulteress, she can say 'I am not,' even if it were true, by understanding 'so that I may reveal it to you.' Similarly, one who is compelled to swear that he will take someone as his spouse can swear that he will take her, if it pleases him afterwards. And ch. 20, that a man captured by robbers can swear equivocally, by reason of compulsion, by saying: 'I swear that I will give,' and within himself, 'if it pleases me,' and then he is not bound, because he did not swear absolutely that he would give. You may find similar things in Sanchez, Navarrus, Gregory of Valencia, Suarez, Lessius, and others. But Scripture forbids lying and deceit entirely, especially in oaths: Leviticus 19:11, Jeremiah 9:8, Psalm 12:4, Psalm 15:3, 5, Ephesians 4:25. By what appearance of truth can it be denied that lying and deceit intervene in such equivocations? The Jesuits deny this under the pretext that the one equivocating does not utter a falsehood with the intention of deceiving, but out of a desire to preserve himself, and blameless they call this protection: but this scheme is vain. For whoever speaks one thing and suppresses another in his heart, or thinks otherwise than he speaks, he certainly deceives another, and intends to deceive by his speech. For that which he says, he does not bring forth with any other mind than to generate a different opinion in the mind of another, which is to deceive. Whatever end, therefore, they may establish, whether to escape danger or any other, the means is deceit, because they intend to achieve their end by deceiving: which is against the rule of the Apostle, Rom. 3:8, namely, to remove a physical evil by an ethical evil, to wit, a lie and perjury: and thus it is not an innocent, but a most blameworthy and reprehensible protection. Nor indeed can a limitation reserved in the mind, added to what is uttered, make a true proposition in the sight of God or in the sense of the speaker, nor suffice to exclude a lie. For truth and falsehood concern justice and injustice, which is directed outward and toward one's neighbor: they are not, therefore, to be estimated from those things which are cherished and retained in the mind, but from those which are brought forth in speech. Moreover, it is clear even from the logicians that no limitation is to be admitted which cannot be elicited from the varied signification of words, or from an ambiguous composition of a sentence, or from a diverse arrangement of circumstances, or from the scope and occasion of the speaker. But a mental supplement exhibits nothing of the sort. It is not, therefore, a limitation; but deceit and simulation. But neither are equivocations properly of this kind: because that equivocal sense does not reside in simple terms, nor in complex ones, but only in the mind and in those things which are reserved in the mind. What is more, a mental reservation contradicts that which is uttered by words, it does not limit it, nor does it present it veiled by words sounding ὁμωνύμως: e.g., if it is asked: are you a Jesuit? and it is answered, I am not, by an open denial, while in the mind a limitation is hidden (so called ψευδωνύμως), namely, so that I may tell you: it is manifest that if this reservation is joined to the first response, it will result not in a limitation of the same, but in a completely contradictory proposition, to wit: I am indeed a Jesuit, but I am not bound to tell you: or if a traitor or assassin is asked whether he came for regicide or clandestine plots, and he answers that he did not come, with a mental reservation, that he did not come by carriage, or did not come from Prussia, or did not come on the Kalends of March, or with the intention of betraying himself to the Magistrate, etc., and if an oath is required, he performs it according to his mental restrictions, even if he appears to perform it according to the sense of the questioner: is this not deceit, a lie, perjury, mockery of the Magistrate, a denial against his conscience of that about which he is asked? because the question was not about the manner of arrival, or the place or other causes, but about that end of the arrival which the words most openly indicate. And therefore a diverse respect does not exclude contradiction, a lie, or perjury, because that respect is neither attended to on the part of the questioner or proponent, nor is it perceived in the response or oath. Furthermore, Scripture openly condemns those who feel one thing in their heart and speak another with their mouth, and it wills that we commend ourselves not only before God, but also in the conscience of all men in the manifestation of the truth. Jer. 9:8. 2 Cor. 4:2. But the Bishop of Antwerp, Malderus, in his tract on the abuse of mental restrictions, acknowledges and confirms this, that it is against truthfulness to correct the falsehood of an enunciation with the poultice of a mental restriction, and that this speech, mixed from a mental and an exterior verbal part, is against simplicity and sincerity, and is not speaking the truth with one's neighbor, but lying with a lie reheated in the mind. And how will an oath be the end of all controversy among men, as it ought to be, Heb. 6:16, if there can be a place for such equivocations and lies in an oath? Will not lawsuits thus be multiplied to infinity, since there is nothing from which the other party can be certain of the other's faith, and not only must commerce thus be disturbed among men, but also God's counsel for ending lawsuits by an oath be rendered completely void. But if it is permitted to make an openly false enunciation true by an added limitation, which each person may conceive in his mind at will, laws against lying and perjury will have been enacted in vain, for it will not be easy to find one who could not fashion such a limitation in his mind. Judgments will be in vain, the counsels of Princes will be in vain, nor will the Pope himself be able to consult with his own, or pronounce anything in a judgment where votes or testimonies must be employed, without it being eluded by this Jesuitical artifice, if there is a place for such mental reservations and restrictions; indeed, no case could be given in which one could not either deny the truth or assert the false without a lie and perjury, and thus public faith will perish, the dignity and security of the highest heads will perish, all commerce will perish, with truth and sincerity perishing. And shall we not believe that the martyrs were foolish and most injurious to heavenly truth and to themselves, because they did not withdraw themselves from tortures and cruel death by this artifice? For if they had been wise in the Jesuitical way, that safeguard of innocent protection remained for them? But they did not wish to delude God and men with equivocations in the Jesuitical manner, in order to escape dangers.

Nor is there any reason for the Jesuits to try to escape by the distinction between a competent and an incompetent judge. For if the judge is not competent, it will indeed be permissible to say that one is not bound to answer; but when someone gives a response, whether the judge is competent or not, he ought to answer from the truth, especially when an oath is employed. And the Jesuits not only teach that he who is questioned unjustly or not according to the order of law, even if he is guilty of a crime, can elude the judge through certain amphibologies, by saying, I do not know, namely, so that I may tell you, I do not remember, namely, to tell you. Tolet. l. c. Lessius l. II. c. 31. dubit. 3. n. 8. Greg. de Valent. Tom. III. Disp. V. q. 13. punct. 2. But some even establish that even then, when the accused is questioned juridically, he does not sin mortally if he even denies the truth before the judge. See Lessius, loc. cit., no. 16, who observes that Petrus Navarrus and Eman. a Saa also hold the same in the entry 'Reus', as well as certain other more recent authors. Add Toletus, lib. IV, instr. sac., c. 58. And there was published by an English priest a booklet on the art of equivocating, previously approved by the Archpriest of England, Blackwell, and the provincial, Henry Garnett, in which it is taught how the subjects of the Queen of England, when asked whether they had received Papist ministers into their hospitality, or whether Romans had gone abroad, or whether they had seen this or that person, might safely respond by retaining within themselves a mental proposition: 'I have not seen,' that is, by the beatific vision, or 'I have not come from there' so that I might infect this city with the plague; which Andreas Eudemon-Joannes approves in his Apology for Garnett, and makes Abraham, Christ, and the Apostles the authors of this discipline, pp. 30, 44. In which booklet is also praised the oath of Francis Tresham, which, having been convicted of the Spanish conspiracy against the King of England, he gave while dying, that he had not seen Garnett for sixteen years, under this equivocation, that he had not seen him at Rome or Venice, pp. 89, 133. The perjury of the Jesuit Garnett and his horrible execration concerning the conspiracy to remove the King and the Parliament of England by means of gunpowder barrels placed under the assembly, by which he eluded the supreme and legitimate Magistrate, may be seen in the action concerning the treason of the kingdom of England against Garnet and his associates, page 101. Which arts are so detestable that even the more sincere Papists themselves have rejected them, even though Navarrus in C. Humanæ Aures 22. q. 5. derives them from his Great Patriarch Francis, who, when asked by officers pursuing a murderer whether he had passed that way where Francis was, put his hands inside his sleeves and answered that he had not passed this way, tacitly implying he had not passed through those sleeves. Therefore Malderus rejects those mental reservations in Navarrus, Sanchez, Valencia, Toledo, Suarez, etc., showing clearly that there is no externally uttered speech which, although otherwise false, can be verified by the mere addition of a mental restriction, tract. de abus. restrict. mental. Paulus Laymann also refutes the same, l. IV. Theol. moral. c. 13. But above all, Joseph Barnes, whom the Theological Faculty of Paris approved by its judgment, rejects and refutes them in his lengthy Commentary on equivocation. Compare Thomas Morton, Apolog. Cathol. l. II. c. 13. B. Meisner, disp. de æquiv. Papist, held in the year 1613.

Latin:

vers. 13.

DOMINUM DEUM TUUM TIMEBIS, ET ILLI SOLI SERVIES.

In Ebr. non addita est exclusiva, qua tamen à LXX. & Vulg. addita textum minime falsatum dicunt Pontificii, Lutherum ob additionem par- ticulæ exclusivæ Rom. 3, 28. falsationis temere ar- guentes. Adduxit Christus ipse eo modo καὶ ἀυ- τῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις Matth. 4, 10. Interpretes eam ad sententiam tanto clarius exprimendam addidisse, do- cet Grotius in annot. ad Evang. p. 51. ipsum etiam verborum ordinem exegisse, ut illud μόνῳ hic ad- jicerent LXX. neque enim, (pergit Grotius) scriptum est ותעבדו quod fuisset καὶ ἀυτῷ λατρεύσεις, sed ואתו תעבד quod plane emphasin continet, quæ in Græcis verbis intelligi non potest, nisi viva pronun- ciatione: ideoque addendum aliquid fuit, quo lector ejus ἐμφάσεως admoneretur. Est enim tacita relatio ad id quod eodem capite commate 4. præcesserat, Deum unum esse. Quare nec Josephus dubitavit eandem vo- cem in præcepto hoc explicando adjicere, ὅτι Θεός ἐσιν εἷς, inquiens, καὶ τῦτον σέβεσθαι μόνον. Adde quod in Deuteronomii loco sequitur continuo: non sectabe- ris Deos alienos. Et Samuel hoc præceptum populo inculcans diserte dixerat ולו לבדו & ei soli servi- te 1. Sam. 7. 3. Quod agnovit etiam Crellius in Com- ment. super Matth. 4. p. 249. Etenim cum illis apud Mosen locis præcipitur, ut Israëlite Deum adorent, & ipsi servant, ea verborum vis est, ut excludantur ab hoc cultu alii Dii, quemadmodum ex seqq. c. 6. Deut. verbis liquido cernitur. Ita enim ibi legimus: Domi- num Deum tuum timebis, & illi servies, & per no- men illius jurabis. Non ibitis post Deos alienos cunctarum gentium &c. Adde quod Crellius fa- teatur Deut. 6. 5. maximum illud ac præcipuum legis universæ mandatum: Diliges Dominum Deum tu- um ex toto corde &c. Unitate Dei ceu fundamento niti, quod cum unus tantum Deus sit in eum UNUM totus cordis affectus convertendus unusque colendus sit, vel de Deo & Attrib. Divin. c. 17. p. 117. Atque hoc est, quod jure meritoque urget Franc. Davidis ad- versus Faust. Socin. in Disputatione de invocatio- ne Christi, quod mandatum Dei severe extet, extra Deum creatorem cœli & terræ neminem invocandum esse; quod concessit etiam ipsi aliquoties F. Soci- nus, etsi postmodum solum Deum adorandum, soli Deo serviendum tantum præceptum esse (quod qui- dem hic nobis sufficit) contenderit, non autem so- lum Deum invocandum esse. Hinc invictum est ar- gumentum Franc. Davidis advers. Socin. in Disp. prædict. cap. 17. part. 7. p. 149. Solus Deus, qui edu- xit Israëlem ex Ægypto adorandus est. Christus ad- orandus est. E. est Christus solus ille Deus, qui eduxit Israëlem ex Ægypto.

vers. 13. PER NOMEN ILLIUS JURA- BIS.

In Ebr. in nomine ejus, LXX. ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτῶ. Non est præceptum absolutum sed hypotheti- cum, si scil. gloria Dei, & salus proximi juramen- tum exigat: ut tum non aliter, quam in nomine Dei juremus, ut fatetur Aben Esdra, qui solus est omni- scius καρδιογνώστης, summa veritas, summa justitia. Ideoque per creaturas, cum Pharisæis, aut per san- ctorum nomina cum Papistis (de quo Thomas 2, 2. q. 89. art. 6. minime licet jurare, sic enim peccatur contra hoc præceptum. Et agnoscunt ipsimet Je- suitæ Bellarminus, Bonfrerius, aliique juramentum esse actum latriæ, quem honorem soli Deo conveni- re fatentur. Adde prohibitionem Christi ne per crea- turas juremus, Matth. 5, 3. & Jac. 5. 12. nec non Jer. 5, 7. jurant per Deos qui non sunt Dii.
