Lev. 25, 2. Whence Josephus called it the Sabbatical year from the rest of the fields; because real debts were to be remitted to a needy neighbor in the same, as is held here v. 2.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. Sabbatismus annorum. Primogenita Do- mino sacra.

Vers. 1. SEPTIMO ANNO] Quod hîc in Hebræo est מִקֵּץ sonat quidem a fine: sed Hebræis etiam initium finis dicitur. Itaque מִקֵּץ per ἀρχὴ interdum vertitur Græcis.

S Ensum esse, septimo quoque anno, vers. 9. docet. Dicitur enim מִקֵּץ in extremo, vel a fine alicujus anni fieri, phrasi Ebræa, quod fit appetente illo an- no. Conf. cap. 14, 28. Jer. 34, 14. Nam duplex est ex- tremum, initii nempe, & finis. Vocatur exinde an- nus remissionis שְׁמִטָּה, quia terræ cultura quie- scebant in eodem Exod. 23, 20. Lev. 25, 2. Unde Jose- phus eum annum Sabbaticum nuncupavit a quiete agrorum; quia debita realia proximo egenti re- mittenda erant eodem, ut hic habetur v. 2.

## 15:2
Vers. 2. HE TO WHOM SOMETHING IS OWED BY A FRIEND, OR BY HIS NEIGHBOR AND BROTHER, SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO DEMAND IT BACK) Not even after the year has passed, unless a clause perpetuating it has been added to the contract.

But in that way no one would easily have given anything as a loan without this clause, and by that agreement all would have been obligated to pay back the debt. And indeed, that it was permitted to demand debts after the year had passed, Burgensis, Toffanus, as well as Piscator, suppose; Cajetan thinks the word שְׁמִטָּה denotes only a withdrawal, not a remission: But just as the release of the land and the manumission of slaves had been decreed as plenary, so also was the remission of the debt, nor was it permitted ever to demand it again; but that had a place only in a loan for consumption, not in a loan for use, not in a debt from a sale, and from an injury, from a thing received: nor in any loan whatsoever, but one given for the sake of poverty, not if someone had borrowed money for the sake of carrying on trade, or buying something, or redeeming his own possession, ver. 4. 7. This was granted only to the needy: therefore those who had contracted debts, if they acquired anything from which they could pay the debt in the Sabbatical year, did not enjoy it. Ps. 37, 21. It was not lawful only to extort the repayment of a loan from the needy, Exod. 21, 26. Nor was that without just reason, lest, to wit, the poor Jews, pressed by that exaction, should flee from their own land, in which the worship of God flourished, to the lands of the Gentiles, as Dionysius observes; and the law of charity demands that we should assist the needy, Luke 6, 35, and God compensated that beneficence with a most bountiful blessing: Finally, that year of remission was a figure of the total remission of all debts of guilt, which is made to us by God, who we are by no means able to pay, and of the deletion of the handwriting which was against us, made through Christ, Coloss. 2, 14. Esa. 61, 1. 2. Cor. 6, 2. Esa. 63, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 2. CVI DEBETVR ALIQVID AB AMICO, VEL PROXIMO AC FRATRE SVO REPÈTERE NON POTERIT) Ne exacto quidem anno, nisi clausula perpe- tuans adjecta sit contractui.

At ita nemo facile mutuo aliquid dedisset, ci- tra hanc clausulam, eoque pacto omnes reddere de- bitum obligati fuissent. Et sane exacto anno exige- re licuisse debita cum Judæis Burgensis, Toffanus, ut & Piscator autumant; Cajetanus vocem שְׁמִטָּה subtractionem tantum, non remissionem notare putat: Verum ut plenaria sancita erat terræ dimissio & ser- vorum manumissio, ita etiam debiti remissio, nec li- cebat unquam iterum exigere; sed id locum tan- tum habebat in mutuo, non in commodato, non in debito ex venditione, & injuria, ex re accepta: nec in mutuo quovis, sed egestatis causa dato, non si quis mercaturae exercendae, vel aliquid emendi vel pos- sessionem suam redimendi causa mutuum accepis- set vers. 4. 7. Solis etiam egenis hoc indultum est: ideo illi, qui nomina contraxerant, si quid ac- quirerent, unde anno Sabbatice exolvere debitum possent, eo non fruebantur. Ps. 37, 21. Solum fas non erat, extorquere ab egeno mutui restitutio- nem Exod. 21, 26. Neque id destituebatur justa ra- tione, ne scil. Judaei pauperes illa exactione pressi e terra sua, in qua cultus Dei viguit, ad terras gentili- um confugerent, uti observat Dionys. & charitatis lex postulat, ut egenis subveniamus, Luc. 6, 35. eam- que beneficentiam Deus largissima benedictione compensabat: Denique annus ille remissionis figura erat remissionis totalis omnium debitorum culpae, quae nobis a Deo fit, qui solvendo minime sumus, & deletionis chirographi, quod adversus nos erat, per Christum factae Coloss. 2, 14. Esa. 61, 1. 2. Cor. 6, 2. Esa. 63, 4.

## 15:3
Vers. 3. FROM A FOREIGNER AND A SOJOURNER YOU SHALL EXACT) It is one word in Hebrew נכרי. In Greek τὸν ἀλλότριον ἀπαιτήσεις. These words signify not an idolater, but an uncircumcised person who lived among the Israelites, as can be seen in Ex. 12, 42. Lev. 22, 25. To such inhabitants were owed, because of the kinship of the human race, those things which are of natural law: not, however, those which are of greater goodness, such as the corner of the field, the gleaning, the gathering of grapes, the left-over berries, the tithes: which this law wishes to be shown to fellow-citizens and circumcised proselytes, who are equal to fellow-citizens in this matter.

The circumcised proselytes do not seem to have been entirely equal, but inferior to the Jews regarding privileges and public dignities. Whence Abulensis against Lyranus and the interlinear Gloss rightly teaches that this benefit of not exacting a loan did not pertain to foreign proselytes, even if they had approached the Jewish religion and lived among the Jews: Since they were not even freed from the personal debt of servitude in the Sabbatical year, Lev. 25, 41. Deut. 14, 12. Jer. 34, 14, and therefore it is likely that they were not freed from real debts either. Which opinion is also approved by our blessed Gerhard in his Commentary on this place, p. 910. But those places do not deal with the seventh Sabbatical year, but Levit. 25, 41 deals with the Jubilee year; Deuter. 14, 12, however, deals with the seventh year of servitude, whence even for Hebrews manumission was not granted there in the Sabbatical year. And therefore it is more correctly urged that this privilege of manumission in the seventh year of servitude was openly granted to the HEBREWS, as also in Exod. 21, 2, and is nowhere extended to proselytes, and that privileges are of strict interpretation, and not without cause does the Holy Scripture name the Hebrew servant, by which name the Proselyte does not come. Rightly Rivetus in Ex. 21, p. 6: We are taught from the sacred scriptures that this law is a privilege granted to the Hebrews alone. For when the Israelites had slaves from foreigners and strangers, they were not bound to deal with them in the same way, as is clear from Levit. chap. 25, 45 and 46: these, he says, you shall have as servants, and you shall transmit them by hereditary right to your descendants, and you shall possess them forever; but your brothers, the children of Israel, you shall not oppress by power. There are, however, some who think that the servitude of foreigners was also dissolved in the Jubilee year, at whose arrival Jerome, chap. 1. Epist. to the Galatians, believes that every harsh condition was accustomed to be dissolved, dealing at the same time with the bringing of Ammonites and Moabites into the Church. The same is expressly taught by Nicetas, the scholiast of Nazianzen, on oration 44, but nothing of the sort can be gathered from the words of the law; nor is there any example by which it could be proven that it was customary among the Hebrews; nay, the law speaks of foreign servants as of things whose possession was perpetual and about to pass to heirs: and whatever is said about them indicates the true nature of absolute dominion. But over a Hebrew servant there was not absolute dominion, but only usufruct, so that he was not properly a servant, but rather as a hireling. For Fabius, book 5, rightly distinguishes & 7. between serving and being a servant, that is, between perpetual servile labors and the right, so to speak, and the conditions of servants; for he writes that those who were bound, who gave their labor to creditors, indeed served, but were not servants.

Latin:

Vers. 3. A PEREGRINO ET ADVENA EXIGES) Una vox est in Hebraeo נכרי. Graece τὸν ἀλλότριον ἀπαιτήσεις. Eae voces significant non idololatram, sed incircumcisum, qui inter Israelitas vivebat, ut videre est Ex. 12, 42. Lev. 22, 25. Ta- libus incolis debebantur ob humani generis cognationem ea, quae sunt juris naturalis: non etiam ea, quae majoris sunt bonitatis, ut angulus agri, racematio, spicilegium, acini relicti, decimae: quae lex ista exhiberi vult popularibus, & proselytis circumcisis, qui popularibus hac in re pares.

Non videntur omnino pares fuisse proselyti cir- cumcisi, sed inferiores Judaeis quoad privilegia, & di- gnitates publicas. Unde Abulens. contra Lyran. & Gloss. interlin. recte hoc beneficium non exactio- nis mutui, non spectasse ad peregrinos proselytos, etsi ad religionem Judaicam accesserint, & inter Judaeos habitarint, docet: Siquidem illi nec a debi- to servitutis personali liberati fuerint anno Sabba- tico Lev. 25, 41. Deut. 14, 12. Jer. 34, 14. ideoque nec a debitis realibus eos liberatos esse, verisimile est. Quam sententiam etiam approbat B. Gerhardus noster in Comm. ad h. l. p. 910. sed non agitur illis locis de anno septimo Sabbatice, sed Levit. 25, 41. de anno Jobeleo. Deuter. 14, 12. vero de anno septi- mo servitutis, unde nec Ebraeis ibi anno Sabbatice manumissio indulgebatur. Ideoque rectius id urge- tur, quod hoc privilegium manumissionis septi- mo anno servitutis EBRAEIS tributum aperte sit, ut & Exod. 21, 2. nuspiam vero extendatur ad prose- lytos, quodque privilegia strictae sint interpretatio- nis, nec absque causa S. S. nominet servum Ebraeum, quo nomine non venit Proselytus. Recte Rivetus in Ex. 21. p. 6. Hanc legem esse privilegium solis Ebraeis concessum ex sacris literis docemur. Nam cum Israeli- tae ab extraneis & peregrinis haberent mancipia, non tenebantur eodem modo cum illis agere, ut patet ex Levit. cap. 25, 45. & 46. hos, inquit habebitis fa- mulos, & haereditario jure transmittetis ad posteros, ac possidebitis in perpetuum; fratres autem vestros filios Israel ne opprimatis per potentiam. Sunt tamen qui putant servitutem etiam alienigenarum solutam fuisse anno Jubilaeo, cujus adventu Hieron. cap. 1. Epist. ad Gal. omnem duram conditionem solvi consue- visse credit, agens simul de Ammonitis & Moabitis in Ecclesiam adducendis. Idem expresse docet Nicetas Nazianzeni Scholiastes ad orationem 44. sed nihil tale colligi potest ex verbis legis; neque exemplum aliquod habetur, quo probari posset, usitatum fuisse apud Ebraeos; quinimo de servis alienigenis loquitur lex tanquam de rebus, quarum perpetua erat possessio, & ad haeredes transitura: & quaecunque de iis dicuntur, indicant veram ratio- nem dominii absoluti. At in Ebraeum servum non e- rat absolutum dominium, sed ususfructus tantum, ita ut proprie servus non esset, sed potius tanquam mercenarius. Recte enim distinguit Fabius l. 5. & 7. inter servire & servum esse, hoc est, inter operas perpetuas serviles & inter jus, ut ita loquamur, & conditiones servorum; addictos enim, qui operas creditoribus dabant, scribit serviisse quidem, sed servos non fuisse.

## 15:4
Vers. 4. AND THERE SHALL BE NO NEEDY AND BEGGAR AMONG YOU.

These words contain not a promise, as Abulensis, Cajetan, Oleaster, Paludanus wish, but a precept, that they should not suffer anyone to be in need, but should assist the poor, v. 7, 8, as Estius, Bonfrer, Cornelius à Lapide, Marius, Hervæus, Tirinus, etc., acknowledge; to which what is said in v. 11 is not repugnant: The poor shall not cease out of the land of your habitation: because by this very thing it is taught that the occasion for beneficence will never be lacking to them, which is a stimulus for exercising the same. See 1 John 3, 17. The Hebrews in v. 11 say this is the meaning: I know that you will not obey me with a perfect heart, and therefore my blessing will be diminished from you, and there will be poor with you continually. And indeed God certainly willed and commanded that there should be no needy person among them. But did everyone always obey, so that no poor person was found? However, the vow of poverty and the order of mendicant monks is overturned by this precept. For by the force of this law, mendicancy is prohibited in a well-constituted Republic, not indeed that it is a sin to beg when necessity urges, but that God wished that those who were begging should be assisted, so that they would not have to beg. But mendicant monks do this studiously, so that they may be and remain beggars. We know that mendicancy is not approved by God from the fact that He commands it to be abolished through the beneficence of the rich. But things that do not please God should not be vowed: therefore voluntary poverty should not be vowed to God.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET OMNINO INDIGUS ET MENDICUS NON ERIT INTER VOS.

Non promissionem ut Abulensis, Cajetan. Oleast. Paludan. volunt, sed præceptum hæc verba continent, ne patiantur quemquam egere, sed subveniant pauperibus v. 7. 8. uti agnoscunt Estius, Bonfrer. Cornel. à Lapide, Marius, Hervæus, Tirinus &c. cui non repugnat, quod dicitur v. 11. Non deerunt pauperes in terra habitationis tuæ: quia hoc ipso docetur, non defuturam ipsis unquam occasionem beneficentiæ, quæ stimulus est eidem exercendæ. Vid. 1. Joh. 3, 17. Ebræi in v. 11. dicunt hunc esse sensum: scio quod non perfecto corde mihi parebitis, & ideo minuetur à vobis mea benedictio, eruntque jugiter pauperes vobiscum. Et sane voluit quidem Deus, ac præcepit, ne esset egenus inter ipsos. Sed num ideo obsequuti omnes semper, ut nullus inventus sit pauper? Evertitur autem ex hoc præcepto votum paupertatis, & ordo mendicantium Monachorum. Prohibetur enim, vi hujus legis, in bene constituta Rep. mendicitas, non quidem quod mendicare, urgente necessitate, peccatum sit, sed quod mendicantibus subveniri voluerit Deus, ne mendicarent. At monachi mendicantes hoc studiose agunt, ut sint, & maneant mendici. Non probari Deo mendicitatem, ex eo cognoscimus, quod eam per beneficentiam divitum aboleri jubet. Non autem vovenda, quæ Deo non placent: ideo paupertas voluntaria voveri Deo non debet.

## 15:8
Verse 8. AND YOU SHALL LEND] Under a pledge. For that is what the Hebrew word conveys.

Indeed, even without a pledge. Deut. 24, 12. For we must not close our hand to the poor man, of whom we are treating here, in his necessity, even if he does not have a pledge. Matt. 5, 42. Luke 6, 35. 1 John 3, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET DABIS MVTVVM] Sub pignore. Id enim fert vox Hebræa.

Imo etiam absque pignore. Deut. 24, 12. Pauperi enim, de quo hic agitur, manum claudere non debemus in necessitate, etiamsi pignus non habeat. Matth. 5, 42. Luc. 6, 35. 1. Joh. 3, 17.

## 15:11
Verse 11. THERE WILL NOT BE WANTING POOR] See the note on Matt. 26, 11.

THAT YOU MAY OPEN YOUR HAND TO YOUR BROTHER WHO IS NEEDY AND POOR] These are not added to the noun 'brother', but are distinguished by a copulative conjunction in the Hebrew: so that the best order is shown, that first liberality should be exercised toward him who is most closely related by blood, with whom Isaiah 58, 7 agrees; then that it should be given to him who is extremely miserable; and finally to any man of slender fortune and who is asking for help.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NON DEERUNT PAVPERES] Vid. ad Matth. 26, 11.

UT APERIAS MANUM FRATRI TUO EGENO ET PAVPERI] Non sunt ista adjecta nomini fratris, sed per copulativam conjunctionem distincta in Hebræo: ita ut ordo ostendatur optimus, ut primum liberalitas exerceatur in eum, qui maximè propinquus est sanguine, quicum convenit Esaias 58, 7. deinde ut detur ei, qui miser sit admodum, postremo quivis tenuis fortunæ homini & auxilium postulanti.

## 15:12
Verse 12. WHEN YOUR HEBREW BROTHER OR HEBREW WOMAN HAS BEEN SOLD TO YOU] So also the Greeks: ἐὰν δὲ πραθῇ σοι. Understand this whether by his own action, or by another to whom the right has been acquired, namely by adjudication on account of theft. But 'to you' is well said. For he could not be sold to a foreigner, as Josephus notes in Antiquities 15. The same applies to those bound for a crime, and to those born as house-slaves from a Hebrew. There was a different law for those who were captured in war, sold by the Canaanites, or born from them. For the servitude of these, if the master willed it, was perpetual, unless they lost some of their principal members by being injured by the master.

HE SHALL SERVE YOU] Or your predecessor. For the times are continued between the predecessor and the buyer.

Latin:

Vers. 12. CUM TIBI VENDITUS FUERIT FRATER TVUS HEBRÆUS VEL HEBRÆA] Sic & Græci: ἐὰν δὲ πραθῇ σοι. Intellige sive suo facto, sive ab alio cui jus quæsitum fuerit, addictione scilicet ob furtum. Bene autem tibi. Nam extraneo vendi non poterat, ut Josephus notat Antiquæ Historiæ 15. Idem de nexis ob noxam, & de vernis natis ex Hebræo. Aliud jus in iis, qui bello capti, venditi a Cananæis, aut ab iis nati. Horum enim, Domino volente, perpetua erat servitus, nisi a Domino læsi aliquod membrorum præcipuorum amitterent.

SERVIERIT TIBI] Vel auctori tuo. Nam inter auctorem & emtorem continuantur tempora.

## 15:18
Verse 18. BECAUSE ACCORDING TO THE WAGE OF A HIRED SERVANT HE HAS SERVED YOU SIX YEARS] Better in the Hebrew: because a double wage of a hired servant, supply, is owed to him: he shall serve you for six years. Hired servants used to hire out their services for three years, Is. 16, 14. Let it not be burdensome to you to dismiss a slave in the seventh year free with gifts. Think of what you would have given to a hired servant for three years: and think that this one has served you for twice that amount of time, and you will find that you have made much profit.

Regarding this passage, let those things be seen which we said on Ex. 21, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QUONIAM JUXTA MERCEDEM MERCENARII SEX ANNOS SERVIVIT TIBI] Melius in Hebræo: quia duplex Merces mercenarii, supple, illi debetur: servibit tibi sex annis. Mercenarii in triennium operas locabant Es. 16, 14. Ne grave tibi sit servum anno septimo liberum cum donis dimittere. Cogita quid mercenario per triennium daturus fueris: & cogita hunc alterum tantum temporis tibi inservijsse, & invenies te multum lucri fecisse.

De hoc loco videantur, quæ ad Ex. 21, 2. diximus.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. Three Feasts to be observed. Just judges to be appointed.

Verse 1. AND YOU SHALL SACRIFICE THE PASSOVER TO THE LORD YOUR GOD FROM THE SHEEP AND FROM THE OXEN] In the Hebrew: You shall sacrifice to the Lord your God the Passover, a sheep and an ox;

which must be understood distinctly: as on the day of the Passover, and the paschal victim is to be sacrificed, a lamb or a kid, and besides that ὁλοκαυτώματα, as on other days according to the law of Levit. 6,12. The passage 2 Paralip. 30,15 makes this manifest in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Likewise R. Solomon h. l. Maimonides in קרבן חפסח.

Since in Exod. 12, 3 it is commanded that a lamb be sacrificed at the Passover, it seems that this does not treat of the first day of the paschal solemnity, but in general of all seven days of the same, in which burnt offerings and sacrifices were offered, Levit. 23, 8. Numer. 28, 20. For by the name Phase some understand the whole seven-day paschal period. More correctly, therefore, the Hebrew words are translated thus: you shall sacrifice the Phase (the paschal lamb) of the sheep and of the oxen, which were used for sacrifices. The Chaldean rendered it from the sons of the sheep, and holy victims from the oxen. The name אביב (which is a reed, at the top of which is an ear, LXX τῶν νέων, i.e., of new fruits) which Pagninus and Arias rashly confuse as a Hebrew and appellative noun with the Chaldean name and proper noun of the fifth month, Ab, which corresponds to July, as if this had been the month of new fruits among the Jews. In Judea, the crops ripened in the month of Nisan, which corresponded to March or April, and began from the new moon which immediately precedes or follows the vernal equinox, at which time the sun is as close to the zenith of the Palestinians as it is to us at the time of the solstice, and the heat for them then is as great as it is for us in the dog days, Jos. 3, 15. chap. 4, 19. chap. 5, 10.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. Tria Festa observanda. Judices justi constituendi.

Vers. 1. IMMOLABISQUE PHASE DOMINO DEO TVO DE OVIBUS ET DE BOBUS] In Hebræo: Immolabis Domino Deo tuo Pascha, ovem & bovem;

quæ distinctè accipienda: ut die paschatis, & paschalis victima immoletur, agnus sive hœdus, & præterea ὁλοκαυτώματα, ut aliis diebus ex lege Levit. 6,12. manifestum id facit locus 2. Paralip. 30,15. in Hebræo, Græco & Latino. Item R. Salomo h. l. Maimonides in קרבן חפסח.

QUum Exod. 12, 3. in paschate agnus immolari præcipiatur, videtur hic non de prima solemnitatis paschalis die, sed in genere de totis septem ejusdem diebus, in quibus holocausta & sacrificia offerebantur, agi Levit. 23, 8. Numer. 28. 20. Nomine enim Phase intelligunt nonnulli totum Septiduum paschale. Rectius ergo Ebræa ita vertuntur: immolabis Phase (agnum Paschalem) ovem & bovem, quæ ad sacrificia adhibebantur. Chald. reddidit de filiis ovium, & victimas sanctas de bobus. Nomen אביב (quod est calamus, in cujus summitate spica est, LXX. τῶν νέων novarum scil. frugum) quod Ebræum & appellativum temere confundit Pagninus & Arias cum nomine Chaldeo & proprio mensis quinti Ab, qui respondet Julio, quasi hic apud Judæos fuerit mensis novarum frugum. In Judæa fruges maturuere mense Nisan, qui Martio, vel Aprili respondebat, & initium capiebat à novilunio, quod proxime præcedit, aut sequitur æquinoctium vernum, quo tempore Sol vertici Palæstinorum tam propinquus est, quam nobis tempore solstitii, & tantus illis tunc calor, quantus nobis diebus canicularibus Jos. 3, 15. cap. 4, 19. cap. 5, 10.

## 16:5 Addition
On Deut. 16. v. 5. YOU WILL NOT BE ABLE IN ANY OF THE CITIES &c.

Bochart in Hieroz. 1. 2. 50. 572. reports that a certain learned man thinks that it was possible to slaughter and eat anywhere even while Jerusalem was standing: To whom, however, he rightly opposes these two things: 1. Then the males are commanded in vain to come annually to Jerusalem, Exod. 23. v. 17. & 34. v. 23., and those who were on a remote journey in the first month, to come in the second month. 2. And God would protect His cities by a miracle in vain, while they were flowing into Jerusalem according to Exod. 34. verse 24. The narrowness of time and place is objected in vain, as if so many thousands of lambs could not be set and offered at one altar between the two evenings. For it is clear that the atrium of the temple was very wide from 1 Kings 8. v. 63. & 2 Chron. 5. v. 6. And the altar in the second temple was as wide as it was long, 50 cubits, according to Josephus, De Bell. 6, 6. But not whole lambs were placed on that altar, but only the fat of the entrails, and the blood was poured at the base. Very many and ready priests were occupied for four hours in offering these. And Maimonides teaches that the fat of the lambs could be burned throughout the whole night.

Latin:

Ad Deut. 16. v. 5. NON POTERIS IN QUALIBET URBIUM &c.

Bochartus in Hieroz. 1. 2. 50. 572. refert virum quendam doctum putare, potuisse ubivis mactari, & comedi etiam stante Jerusalem : Cui vero recte hæc duo opponit : 1. Tum frustra mares juben- tur quotannis venire Hieros. Exod. 23. v. 17. & 34. v. 23. &, qui primo mense erant in via remo- ta, venire mense secundo. 2. Et frustra Deus per miraculum urbes suas servaret, dum juxta Exod. 34. vers. 24. Hierosolymam confluerent. Temporis & loci angustia frustra objicitur, quasi inter duas vesperas non potuerint tot agnorum millia ad unum altare sisti & offerri. Nam templi atrium latissimum fuisse patet ex 1. Reg. 8. v. 63. & 2. Paral. 5. v. 6. Et altare in secundo templo fuit tam latum quam longum cubitis 50. teste Josepho de Bell. 6, 6. In illud autem altare non toti agni, sed solum exto- rum adipes imponebantur, & sanguis fundebatur ad basin. Quibus offerendis vacabant plurimi & expediti sacerdotes per horas quatuor. Et agni adi- pes tota nocte adoleri potuisse docet Maimonides.

## 16:7
Vers. 7. AND RISING IN THE MORNING.

In the morning, namely, after the seven days of the Paschal solemnity were finished, which were to be observed according to Exod. 34, 18, and not the morning after the first most solemn day, as Dionysius, Abulensis, Lyranus, and Cajetan wish, who understand this of those who came from other cities. For even for these, all the feast days were to be completed, as is clear from Luke 2, 43. On the seventh day a solemn assembly took place, which, called by the name of a gathering, was a type of the gathering of the nations.

Latin:

Vers. 7. MANEQUE CONSVRGENS.

Mane scil. post finitas septem dies solennitatis Paschalis, quæ observandæ erant Exod. 34, 18. non vero mane post diem primam maxime solemnem, ut Dionys. Abulens. Lyran. & Cajetan. volunt, qui id intelligunt de illis, qui ex aliis urbibus venerunt. Nam & his complendi erant dies festi omnes, ut è Luc. 2, 43. liquet. Septima die fiebat solemnis congregatio, quæ nomine collecta dicta, typus fuit collectionis gentium.

## 16:8
Vers. 8. SIX DAYS YOU SHALL EAT UNLEAVENED BREAD AND ON THE SEVENTH DAY, BECAUSE IT IS THE GATHERING OF THE LORD YOUR GOD, YOU SHALL DO NO WORK.

The seventh day is not to be excluded, as is clear from verses 3 and 4; for seven days you shall eat bread of affliction without leaven (which was a memorial of the affliction in Egypt) and the seventh day shall be a gathering of the Lord, because in his honor they gathered solemnly and immediately to sing praises and offer sacrifices to him. The Chaldean: on the seventh day is a congregation before Jehovah. The sense, therefore, is: Six days you shall eat unleavened bread (but you shall not be idle on these six days, but on the first more solemn one); but on the seventh day, besides the eating of unleavened bread, you shall also refrain from work, because it is a feast of the congregation. And now it will be permissible to take the words thus: Six days (which will follow that first solemn one, in which you will sacrifice the phase, in which he had already warned that leaven was not to be eaten) you shall likewise eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh (which will be the last of them) you shall also observe this, that you do no work on it.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SEX DIEBUS COMEDES AZYMA ET IN DIE SEPTIMA, QUIA COLLECTA EST DOMINI DEI TUI, NON FACIES OPUS.

Septimus dies non excludendus, ut è vers. 3. & 4. liquet, septem diebus comedes absque fermento panem afflictionis (qui memoriale erat afflictionis in Ægypto) & erit septima dies collecta Domini, quia in ejus honorem solemniter, & confestim conveniebant ad decantandas laudes & sacrificia ei offerenda. Chald. die septima congregatio est coram Jehovah. Sensus ergo est: Sex diebus comedes azyma, (sed non vacabis istis sex diebus, sed prima solemniori) Septimo autem die præter azymorum manducationem etiam vacabis ab opere, quia est festum congregationis. Et jam ita accipere licebit verba: Sex diebus (quæ sequentur primam illam solemnem, in qua phase immolabis, in qua non comedendum esse fermentum, antea jam monuerat) itidem azyma comedes, & in septima (quæ erit illarum ultima) illud etiam observabis, ut nullum opus eodem facias.

## 16:9
Vers. 9. FROM THE DAY THAT YOU PUT THE SICKLE TO THE CORN.

Not everyone put the sickle to the crops on one day: this must therefore be understood of that putting in which was enjoined by law, at least so that the first fruits might be offered to the Lord. And therefore he rightly paraphrases

the Chaldean: at the beginning of the sickle, when the sheaf of elevation is reaped, that is, from the second day of unleavened bread, on which the first harvest and the offering of the sheaf took place: from which the first fruits of the crops are cut to offer the sheaf of the Lord, by which offering the whole harvest was sanctified, Levit. 23, 4. Even if in some places of Palestine the crops had scarcely ripened around the time of the Passover: whence the sheaf of fruits had to be brought from the vicinity, from the region of Jericho, in which the crops ripened almost 15 days earlier, whereas in the Jerusalem soil, according to Josephus. If the ears had not yet reached full maturity, they were parched with fire and crushed, Levit. 2, 14. chap. 23, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 9. AB EA DIE, QUA FALCEM IN SEGETEM MISERIS.

Non omnes una die falcem mittebant in segetes: intelligendum ergo hoc de illa immissione, quæ injuncta lege erat, saltim ut Domino primitiæ offerrentur. Ideoque recte παραφράζει

Chaldæus: principio falcis, cum demetitur mani- pulus elevationis, hoc est, à secundo die azymo- rum, quo fiebat prima messio, & oblatio mani- puli: à quo primitiæ frugum abscinduntur ad of- ferendum manipulum Domini, per quam oblatio- nem tota messis sanctificabatur Levit. 23, 4. Eti- amsi in nonnullis locis Palæstinæ circa tempus Pa- schatos fruges vix dum maturuere: Unde mani- pulus frugum è vicinia afferendus erat è regione Jerichontica, in qua fere 15. diebus ante maturesce- bant segetes, quum in solo Hierosolymitano, te- ste Josepho. Si ad plenam maturitatem nondum pervenissent spicæ, torrebantur igni, & contun- debantur Levit. 2, 14. cap. 23, 14.

## 16:10
Vers. 10.

A VOLUNTARY OFFERING OF YOUR HAND)

In Greek καθὼς ἡ χείρ σε ἰσχύει. The word which is here in Hebrew מסת is not properly Hebrew, but Chaldean, meaning exactly the same as the Hebrew די, which Hebrew word is translated from the Chaldean by מסת Exod. 2, 4. Prov. 30, 8. Thus also R. Solomon and Kimchi interpret this passage, most excellently: For the sense is, that everyone should give in the Sabbatical year as much as suffices for a voluntary offering. That, however, which suffices, τὸ ἱκανὸν, as the Greeks are accustomed to translate די, is to be understood as the means granted by God, as follows in the text.

Grotius is correct in this. The Vulgate did not translate the Hebrew word מסת in this place: just as it also did not render certain words in Gen. 25, 7, ch. 44, 7, Lev. 5, 7, 11, as also Deut. 4, 12, Jud. 4, 4, 1 Sam. 17, 13, 2 Kings 18, 17. Therefore, the word Missa cannot be derived from this passage, nor can the meaning of a spontaneous offering have a place here: since the word נדבה signifies that. See Num. 29, 39, Amos 4, 5, Lev. 22, 18, ch. 23, 38, Exod. 35, 27. The word מסת itself is either Chaldean, or if it is Hebrew, it is of the number of those which are common to the Hebrews and Chaldeans. The Chaldean מסת is די or sufficiency, as Grotius has rightly observed. See Deut. 15, 8, Lev. 5, 7, ch. 12, 8, 2 Sam. last, 16, Gen. 33, 9. The sense in this place is: according to your sufficiency shall be the spontaneous offering, etc. Thus the word מִסַּת also occurs in the Chaldean in the absolute state. See 2 Samuel 7, 28. Moreover, every offering was required to be spontaneous Num. 28, 27. But here is understood the non-due [offering], by which they were offered spontaneously beyond the ordinary and due sacrifices Deut. 22, 1, from which spontaneous offerings feasts were made before the Lord, even for servants, Levites, strangers, the lowly, and widows, in memory not of the exodus from Egypt, which was celebrated through the solemnities of the paschal lamb, but of the miserable and servile state in Egypt. Votive offerings, which in their root, or in the taking of the vow, were spontaneous, were to be entirely consecrated to God, and fell to the Priests by law, so that nothing at all from them returned to those who offered.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

OBLATIONEM SPONTANEAM MANUS TUÆ)

Græce καθὼς ἡ χείρ σε ἰσχύει. Vox quæ hic est in Hebræo מסת non Hebraica est proprie, sed Chaldaica, plane idem valens quod Hebræo די, quæ vox Hebræa à Chaldæo per מסת transfertur Exod. 2, 4. Prov. 30, 8. Sic & R. Sa- lomo & Kimchi hoc loco interpretantur, optime: Sensus enim est, ut det quisque anno Sabbatco quantum sufficit vo- luntariæ oblationi. Illud autem quod sufficit, τὸ ἱκανὸν, ut Græci די solent vertere, intelligendum pro facultatibus à Deo concessis, ut in textu sequitur.

Recte hæc Grotius. Vulgata Ebræam vocem מסת h. l. non transtulit: quemadmodum & Genes. 25, 7. cap. 44, 7. Levit. 5, 7. 11. aliquas voces non reddidit, ut & Deuter. 4, 12. Jud. 4, 4. 1. Sam. 17, 13. 2. Reg. 18, 17. Non potest ergo ex hoc loco vox Missa deduci, vel etiam spontaneæ oblationis significatio locum habere: quum eam significet vox נדבה. Vide Num. 29, 39. Amos. 4, 5. Lev. 22, 18. c. 23, 38. Exod. 35, 27. ipsa vox מסת vel Chal- daica, vel si Ebræa, ex harum numero est, quæ E- bræis, & Chaldæis sunt communes. Chald. מסת est די vel sufficientia, ut probe observavit Grotius. Vid. Deuter. 15, 8. Levit. 5, 7. c. 12, 8. 2. Sam. ult. 16. Genes. 33, 9. Sensus h. l. est: juxta sufficientiam tuam erit spontanea oblatio, &c. Ita vox מִסַּת apud Chald. etiam in statu absoluto occurrit. Vid. 2. Sa- muel. 7, 28. Cæterum omnis oblatio spontanea esse debebat Num. 28, 27. Sed hîc intelligitur indebita, qua præter ordinaria & debita sacrificia sponte of- ferebantur Deut. 22, 1. è quibus oblationibus spon- taneis epulæ fiebant coram Domino, etiam servis, Levitis, advenis, pusillis, viduis, in memoriam non eductionis ex Ægypto, quæ celebrabatur per sole- mnitates agni paschalis, sed miseri, & servilis status in Ægypto. Oblationes votivæ, quæ in sua radice, seu in voti susceptione erant spontaneæ, Deo penitus consecrandæ erant, ac Sacerdotibus ex lege cede- bant, ita ut nihil quicquam ex illis ad offerentes rediret.

## 16:13
Verse 13. YOU SHALL ALSO CELEBRATE THE SOLEMNITY OF TABERNACLES.

Which was thus called חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת the festival of tabernacles, in Greek σκηνοπηγία, because they had tabernacles under the open sky for the seven days of this festival, that is, temporary dwellings, little houses made from trees, in which they slept and rested, and that in memory of the state that, having gone out of Egypt, they lived in tabernacles in the desert for 40 years, and as a foreshadowing of our sojourn in the earthly and fragile tabernacle of our body, until we are introduced into the promised heavenly inheritance. 2 Corinthians 5, Heb. 11. It was to be celebrated on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, called by the Hebrews תִּשְׁרִי, for seven days. The first and last, however, were more solemn, in which they rested from all works, and held public assemblies, Levit. 23:39. The last day of the Feast is called the great one, John 7, 37. Some say that the eighth day, that is, the 22nd of the month Tishri, was also solemn, and that it was called the gathering. See B. Meisner, Preface to the Festival Gospels.

WHEN YOU HAVE GATHERED FROM THE THRESHING FLOOR AND WINEPRESS YOUR FRUITS) For ἑορτὴ σκηνοπηγίας is ἑορτὴ συντελείας in the LXX. Aquila calls it συλλογῆς: Symmachus, of the gathered fruits, συγκομιδῆς: Exod. 23, 16. The word σκηνοπηγίας is also found in Plutarch’s Symposiacs, where he treats of the rites of the Jews; he also calls it θυρσοφορίαν.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SOLENNITATEM QUOQUE TA- BERNACULORUM CELEBRABIS.

Quæ ita dicebatur חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת festivitas ta- bernaculorum, Græce σκηνοπηγία, quod sub dio habuerint per septiduum hujus festi tabernacula, hoc est, habitationes tumultuarias, domunculas ex arboribus confectas, in quibus cubabant & dor- miebant, idque in memoriam status, quod egressi ex Ægypto 40. annis in tabernaculis habitarint in de- serto, & adumbrationem commorationis nostræ in terreno, & fragili corporis nostri tabernaculo, donec in promissam hæreditatem cœlestem intro- ducamur. 2. Corinth. 5. Ebr. 11. Celebranda erat die decimo quinto Mensis septimi Ebræis dicti תִּשְׁרִי per septem dies. Primus tamen & ulti- mus erant solemniores, in quibus quiescebant ab operibus omnibus, & conventus publicos age- bant Levit. 23, 39. ultima diei Festi vocatur magna, Joh. 7, 37. Nonnulli octavam diem, hoc est, 22. mensis Thisri etiam solemnem dicunt fuisse, illam- que vocatam collectionem. Vid. B. Meisner. Præfat. in Evang. fest.

QVANDO COLLEGERIS DE AREA ET TOR- CVLARI FRVGES TVAS) Nam ἑορτὴ σκηνοπηγίας est ἑορτὴ συντελείας LXX. Aquilæ συλλογῆς : Symmacho συγκο- μιδῆς collectarum frugum: Exod. 23, 16. σκηνοπηγίας vox est etiam apud Plutarchum Symposiacis, ubi de Judæorum agit ritibus; vocat & θυρσοφορίαν.

## 16:16 Addition
On verse 16. EVERY MALE.

Joseph Mede, Dissert. 45, notes that all males within the years of service are understood, that is, the twentieth (see Num. 1. v. 2. 3.) and the fiftieth. But why not the females? He answers: 1. Their infirmity stood in the way: they were unequal to such a journey. 2. The danger to chastity in such a great gathering. 3. The care of the house and children in the absence of the fathers. Others add: as a type of the Messiah. Regarding that IN THE PLACE, the same Mede has it thus: There was one temple, and one place designated for sacrifices and prayer, as a type of the one Christ the mediator. But there were 400 synagogues in Jerusalem for hearing the law.

On the same verse. HE SHALL NOT APPEAR BEFORE THE LORD EMPTY.

The Jews were accustomed, as Mede says here again, in any of these three festivals to offer their elevations, and firstfruits, and tithes, and voluntary offerings, as the season of the year allowed. In the feast of the Passover, besides the sheaf of grain, I believe they offered the firstborn and the tithes of the cattle, for the best things were owed to God, such as those born in the spring time. In the feast of Pentecost, besides the two loaves, they paid the tithes of the grain, as much as they had threshed, and a voluntary offering, Deut. 16. v. 10. And since this feast is the end of the harvest, in its mention occur the commandments about leaving the gleanings, etc. In the feast of Tabernacles they offered the firstfruits and tithes of wine and oil, and the remains of the tithes of the threshing floor, namely, of the threshed grain. Hence 2 Chron. 31. verse 7. They began to place the heaps in the third month, that is, in the feast of Pentecost, and they finished in the seventh month, that is, in the feast of Tabernacles.

Latin:

Ad vers. 16. OMNE MASCULINUM.

Joseph. Medus Dissert. 45. notat intelligi omnes mares intra annos servitii, hoc est, vicesi- mum (vide Num. 1. v. 2. 3.) & quinquagesimum. Sed cur non fæminæ? Resp. obstabat 1. earum in- firmitas : tanto itineri impares erant, 2. pericu- lum castitatis in tanto concursu. 3. Cura domus & liberorum in absentia Patrum. Alii addunt in typum Messiæ. Ad illud IN LOCO, idem Medus ita habet : Unum erat templum, & unus locus sacri- ficiis & orationi designatus, in typum unius Christi mediatoris. At audiendæ legi erant 400. Synagogæ in Hierosolyma.

Ad vers. eund. NON APPAREBIT CORAM DOMINO VACUUS.

Solebant Judæi ut hic iterum Medus in aliquo horum trium festorum offerre elevationes suas, & primitias, & decimas, & sponte oblata, prout tempestas anni ferebat. In festo Paschatis, præ- ter manipulum frugum obtulisse credo primoge- nita & decimas pecorum, Deo enim debebantur optima, qualia erant verno tempore nata. In fe- sto Pentecostes, præter duos panes, solvebant deci- mas frumenti, quantum trituraverant, & oblatio- nem spontaneam, Deut. 16. v. 10. Et cum hoc fe- stum sit finis messis, in ejus mentione occurrunt præcepta de relinquendis spicis, &c. In festo Ta- bernaculorum offerebant primitias & decimas vini & olei, & reliquias decimarum areæ, nempe fru- menti triturati. Hinc 2. Chron. 31. vers. 7. Acer- vos ponere cœperunt tertio mense, id est, in festo Pentecostes, & desierunt septimo mense, id est, in festo Tabernaculorum.

## 16:18
Verse 18.

YOU SHALL APPOINT JUDGES AND MAGISTRATES IN ALL YOUR GATES) Two scribes were present with them: as many criers: as many collectors of alms. Disciples sat at their feet, so that they might learn the law by practice itself, and be substituted in the place of those dying or decrepit. Eunuchs were not permitted to judge: for they are believed to be more cruel, even by Aristotle. Claudian in the first book against Eutropius: All monsters yielded to the eunuch consul. Then: Add that a eunuch is moved by no piety, nor does he care for his race or birth. Clemency is for all towards their own kind, and bonds of loss bind their spirits.

Concerning these, compare what we have brought forward from Paul Fagius on chapter XVII. Judgments were in the gates both so that access might be open to all, and so that more solemn contracts might be known to all: and so that those who exercised judgment in the sight of all might the more guard against injustice.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

JVDICES ET MAGISTRATVS CONSTITVES IN OMNIBVS PORTIS TVIS) His aderant duo scribæ: præ- cones totidem: totidem Eleemosynæ collectores. Ad pedes sedebant discipuli, ut ipso usu jus addiscerent, & in morienti- um aut decrepitorum locum surrogarentur. Eunuchi non permittebantur judicare: creduntur enim crudeliores, etiam Aristoteli. Claudianus primo in Eutropium: Omnia cesserunt eunucho consule monstra. Deinde: Adde quod eunuchus nulla pietate movetur, Nec generi natúve cavet. Clementia cunctis In similes, animosque ligant consortia damni.

De his confer, quæ ad cap. XVII. è Paul. Fagio adduximus. In portis erant judicia tum ut omnibus accessus pateret, tum ut solemniores contractus omnibus innotescerent: tum ut illi, qui judicium in conspectu omnium exercebant, eo magis ab inju- stitia caverent.

## 16:21
Verse 21. YOU SHALL NOT PLANT A GROVE) Hecataeus on Jerusalem: there is no planting at all there that is woody or anything of that sort. This is also the opposite of the custom of idolaters, who had groves near their temples. See 1 Kings 15, 13.

See Philo Judaeus, On Monarchy II, near the beginning. Jerome on chapters 7 and 32 of Jeremiah. This Gentile error occupied all the provinces, so that they would sacrifice victims at the heads of fountains and most pleasant groves, and the religion of every wicked superstition was preserved. See concerning groves in Lipsius on Tacitus, Germania.

Latin:

Vers. 21. NON PLANTABIS LVCVM) Hecatæus de Hierosolymis: ὠδὲ φύτευμα παντελῶς ὀδὲν οἶτ' ἀλσῶδες ἤ τι τοιῦτον. Oppositum & hoc mori idololatrarum, qui apud templa lucos habebant. Vid. 1. Reg. 15, 13.

Vid. Philo Jud. de Monarch. II. sub initium. Hieronym. ad cap. 7. & 32. Jerem. Gentilis hic er- ror omnes Provincias occupavit, ut ad capita fontium lucosque amœnissimos victimas immo- larent, & omnis pravæ superstitionis religio ser- varetur. Vid. de lucis apud Lipsium ad Tacit. German.

## 16:21 Addition
On Deut. 16. v. 21. at the end note on p. 579. a.

The Rabbis accepted this for this reason also, so that not only would no tree, but not even any stake be found in the courtyard. Because in the text it is read כל־עץ, and the whole circuit of the temple and the walkway had nothing but a pavement covered with stones. Moreover, this pertained to a greater detestation of clandestine idolatry. Cf. 2 Kings 23:6.

Latin:

Ad Deut. 16. v. 21. sub finem notar. ad p. 579. a.

Rabbini id eo etiam accepere, ne non modo arbor ulla, sed ne quidem palus ullus in atrio repe- riretur. Quia in textu legitur כל־עץ, totusque templi ambitus, & peripatus non nisi lapidibus stratum pavimentum haberet. Pertinebat autem id ad majorem idololatriæ sublucanæ detestationem. Conf. 2. Reg. 23. v. 6.

## 16:22
Verse 22. A STATUE] A huge stone, as a monument to some history, at which a gathering used to take place. That was permitted before the law. Gen. 28, 18; ch. 31, 52.

Fagius more correctly explains what kind of statues were prohibited: a statue is one single and large stone, which stood out between the altar and the grove, on which the mystagogues of the idols stood and recited their songs with voice and musical instruments, as Moses Nachmani is the author. The legislator Moses forbids such a statue, even though Jacob in the 32nd chapter of Genesis erected a statue, for the Lord had not yet forbidden it.

Latin:

Vers. 22. STATUAM] Lapidem ingentem, in historiæ ali- cujus monumentum, ad quem concursus fieri solebat. Id ante legem licuit. Gen. 28, 18. c. 31, 52.

Quales statuæ prohibitæ rectius explicat Fagi- us: statua lapis unus est & grandis, qui inter alta- re & lucum prominebat, in quo idolorum mystago- gi constituti suas cantiones voce & instrumentis mu- sicis recitarunt, ut autor est Moses Nachmanni. Talem statuam vetat legislator Moses, etsi Jacob 32. cap. Genes. statuam erexerit, nondum enim Dominus prohibuerat.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII. The victim to be chosen. Idolatry to be punished. The priest to be consulted. The Royal Law.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII. Hostia deligenda. Idololatria punienda. Sa- cerdos consulendus. Lex Regia.

## 17:2
THEY TRANSGRESS HIS COVENANT) Those are said to transgress the covenant who fall away from religion. Compare Heb. 10, 29.

Latin:

TRANSGREDIANTUR PACTUM ILLIUS) Trans- gredi pactum dicuntur, qui a religione deficiunt. Confer Hebr. 10, 29.

## 17:3
Verse 3.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

## 17:5
Vers. 5. AT THE GATES OF THY CITY] To the judges of any city, in the number of 23 or at least 21. For to them belonged the cognizance of crimes, except for those which were reserved for the Sanhedrin, such as false prophecy and the crime of an entire tribe. It is otherwise in the case of one soliciting to new gods. For he was not led to the judges.

On the contrary, he was led to the judges. For judgments were exercised in the gates, and not far from there was the place where evildoers were punished. Therefore, it is commanded here that those who have abandoned divine worship and have begun to adore the stars of heaven, or demons, or other things of that kind, be diligently sought out from all places, and that these be led to the cities where justice is accustomed to be exercised and the wicked punished, so that there, with all the people gathered, they may be condemned by the vote of all and slaughtered by the hand of all, as Fagius observes here, who also notes an emphasis in the words, concerning which God commanded nothing, from R. Bechai. For it may happen that one, warned by the miracle of the Sun as the chief ornament of nature, might adore the Creator GOD in the sun, which reason might seem pious, but because GOD did not command it, it is impious.

Latin:

Vers. 5. AD PORTAS CIVITATIS TUÆ] Ad judices urbis cujusque, numero 23. aut minimum 21. Nam ad hos spectabat cognitio de criminibus, extra ea quæ excepta erant Synedrio, qualia erant Pseudoprophetia, & crimen totius tribus. Aliud in sollicitante ad Deos novos. Is enim ad judices non ducebatur.

Imo ducebatur ad judices. In portis enim judicia exercebantur, inde non procul erat locus, ubi malefici puniebantur. Ideo jubetur hic, ut omnibus è locis diligenter perquirantur, qui di- vinum cultum reliquerunt, cœlique sydera, aut dæmones, aut id genus alia adorare ceperunt, hi- que ad urbes deducantur, ubi jus exerceri & sce- lerati plecti solent, ut ibi omni populo collecto omnium suffragio condemnentur omniumque ma- nu trucidentur, ut hic observat Fagius, qui no- tat etiam emphasin in verbis, de quibus Deus nihil præcepit, e R. Bechai. Nam fieri potest, ut mira- culo Solis ceu præcipuo naturæ ornamento admo- nitus in sole opificem DEUM adoret, quæ ratio pia videri possit, sed quia DEUS eam non præcepit, impia est.

## 17:6
Vers. 6. AT THE MOUTH OF TWO OR THREE WITNESSES] Of good reputation. In Hebrew custom, those who do not have the use of reason, boys before the age of 13, thieves even after restitution, those who live by gambling, tax collectors who exact more than is just, goat-herds, and if there are any others who do things that are worthy of stripes, do not have the right of testimony. Those who are very close relatives, or intimate friends, or enemies of either of the parties can also be rejected.

Latin:

Vers. 6. IN ORE DUORUM AUT TRIUM TESTI- UM] Bonæ famæ. Jus testimonii moribus Hebræis non ha- bent amentes, pueri ante annum 13. fures etiam post restitu- tionem, qui de alea victitant, publicani qui plus æquo exi- gunt, caprarii, & si qui alii ea factitant quæ verberibus digna sunt. Rejici etiam possunt qui valde propinqui, aut familia- res, aut inimici sunt partium alteri.

## 17:7
Vers. 7.

THE HAND OF THE WITNESSES FIRST SHALL KILL

HIM. In the Sanhedrin, the method of stoning is written thus, as Fagius notes here: The condemned man, naked with his hands bound, was placed at the precipice of the place of stoning, near whom the witnesses stood from behind with their eyes covered: The first pushed the one to be punished from behind and caused him to fall headlong. If he was still breathing after the fall, another rolled a large stone upon him. Furthermore, if he were not completely extinguished even by this, the multitude heaped stones upon him. This atrocity of punishments is commanded in this case, so that it may be a more effective example for avoiding that crime.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

MANUS TESTIUM PRIMA INTERFI- CIET EUM.

In Sanhedrin ratio lapidationis hæc scribitur notante hic Fagio: Damnatus nudus ligatis mani- bus in præcipitium loci dilapidationis constituebatur, cui testes à tergo obtectis oculis astabant : Prior ple- ctendum à tergo protrusit ac præcipitem dedit. Si delapsus adhuc spirabat, alter grandem lapidem in eum provolvit. Porro si ne sic quidem penitus exstinctus esset, multitudo lapides in eum aggerebat. Hæc atro- citas suppliciorum in hoc præcipitur, quo sit exemplum efficacius ejus facinoris cavendi.

## 17:8
Vers. 8.

IF YOU SHALL PERCEIVE A JUDGMENT TO BE DIFFICULT AND AMBIGUOUS AMONG YOU) That this law is to be understood as all the more necessary because the cohesion of all the Israelites depends upon it, as Maimonides has often noted. In the Greek: ἐὰν δὲ ἀδυνατήσῃ ἀπὸ σῦ ῥῆμα ἐν κρίσῃ. For they often translate פלא as ἀδυνατεῖν. The sense is: where some controversy has occurred that is too obscure for it to be clear to all the magistrates of any city. It is not a question of fact, but of law, that is being treated here. The causes of obscurity that human laws have, divine laws enunciated in a human manner do not avoid; partly because of words or phrases that are ambiguous, which are many in all languages, and very many in the Hebrew; partly because where laws speak generally, it is disputed which rarer species of facts ought to be excepted; partly because where they speak specifically, it is not always clear whether the law stays within that species, or whether it ought to be extended to those things which seem equal: and there are many other causes why the same words are not accepted in the same way by all, some being more obtuse, others more subtle than is necessary.

It does not seem to be a question of the ambiguity of divine law. For divine laws, which were sufficiently clear to the Jews to whom they were delivered, are not to be judged from the ambiguity or obscurity of human laws, even if now, being ignorant of ancient customs, they are sometimes ambiguous to us. But it is about difficult cases which did not seem to be decided by express law. And therefore such more difficult and obscure causes were to be referred to the supreme tribunal, of which there were 70 assessors, and two judges, one supreme called the Nasi, the president, the other an inferior vicar of that one if absent or hindered by illness, Jerem. 52, 24. And not only private persons, but also public ones, the inferior judges themselves, were commanded to flee to it in more difficult causes. And they were questions of fact, not of law, when the judgment was ambiguous between BLOOD AND BLOOD, that is, not between pure and impure blood, of the polluted and the clean, as Targ. Jonath. and R. Salomon [say], but as Cajetan, Vatabl., Lyran., and Abulens. [say], if the homicide is ambiguous, or the quality of the homicide, with some asserting that it is voluntary, to be punished by death, others that it is accidental, and therefore that the right of asylum belongs to the homicide, which sense Grotius does not seem to reject; likewise between CAUSE AND CAUSE, that is, in civil causes (as the former were criminal), whether the cause is just or unjust, because of ambiguous circumstances; between PLAGUE AND PLAGUE, the Hebrew word Lev. 13, 4 denotes a plague of leprosy, as before criminal and civil causes, thus here Ecclesiastical causes, concerning the judgment of leprosy and other Ecclesiastical matters, are noted. Fagius, however, refers all these things which are recounted in this place to political judgments. If it should be difficult for you to explain, that is, if a minor judge does not know how to decide concerning a controversy, which the Hebraism calls דבר למשפט, that is, a word or matter of judgment. Between blood and blood, that is, the innocent and one to be condemned for a capital crime. Between cause and cause, that is, a pecuniary lawsuit and those of lesser moment. And between the plague of leprosy etc., that is, a bruise and a wound. Grotius agrees with the former opinion, which we judge not to be disapproved. For he has it thus here:

BETWEEN BLOOD AND BLOOD) Whether the slaughter of this or that kind deserves a place of refuge, or does not deserve it. For there are many degrees in guilt: it is broad, medium, or minimal.

CAUSE AND CAUSE] This is to be understood concerning pecuniary lawsuits and concerning verbal injuries, the penalty for which was arbitrary: and in one and the same kind, because of the τὸ ἀόριστον (indeterminacy) of the law, it could probably be judged that a greater penalty should be imposed by one, and a lesser by another. What is called דין κρίσις (judgment) here, is called ריב ἀντιλογία (controversy) below 25, 1.

LEPROSY AND LEPROSY] The word נגע is indeed used, which in Hebrew is sufficiently general, which signifies every more serious evil, which the Greek interpreters often call μάστιγα (scourge), as do the writers of the New Testament, Mark 3:10, ch. 5:29, 34, Luke 7:21. But ἀντονομασικῶς (by antonomasia) it signifies leprosy, and in that sense it is taken fifty times in one chapter, Leviticus XIII. And physicians often doubt whether the leprosy which has these or those marks is or is not a contagion to be feared.

AND OF THE JUDGES WITHIN THY GATES) In the tribunals of individual cities, which were in the gates among the Hebrews and their neighbors, as appears in Gen. 34:20, Ruth 4:1, 2, Prov. 22:22, ch. 31:23, 31.

THOU SHALT SEE THE WORDS VARY) The Hebrew: words of contentions: that is, if the contention of the judges proceeds so far that a minority party wishes to maintain its opinion against the majority, and a certain schism could arise among those differing in opinion that would distract that city and its neighbors. For this law was given to prevent schisms.

ARISE AND GO UP TO THE PLACE WHICH THE LORD THY GOD SHALL CHOOSE) That is, in the earliest times in Shiloh, Josh. 18:1, 22:12, Judg. 18:31, 20:18, 18, 1 Kings 1:3, Jer. 7:12, 26:6. After the times of David, Jerusalem. 1 Kings 8:2, 2 Chron. 6:7, and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

SI DIFFICILE ET AMBIGUUM APUD TE JUDI- CIUM ESSE PERSPEXERIS) Hanc legem intelligi tanto magis opus, quod ab ea pendeat coagmentatio omnium Israëlitarum, ut sæpe notavit Maimonides. In Græco: ἐὰν δὲ ἀδυνατήσῃ ἀπὸ σῦ ῥῆμα ἐν κρίσῃ. Nam פלא ἀδυνατεῖν sæpe vertunt. Sensus est: ubi controversia aliqua inciderit obscurior, quam ut de ea omnibus urbis alicujus magistrati- bus liqueat. Non de facti, sed de juris quæstionibus hic agi- tur. Quas obscuritatis causas habent leges humanæ, eas di- vinæ humano modo enunciatæ non evitant; partim ob vo- ces aut locutiones πολυσήμυς, quæ sunt in omnibus linguis multæ, in Hebraica plurimæ; partim quia ubi leges loquun- tur generaliter, disputatur quæ factorum species rariores ex- cipi debeant; partim quia ubi loquuntur specialiter, non semper in aperto est, an lex intra eam stet speciem, an vero ad ea quæ paria videntur debeat extendi: multæque aliæ sunt causæ, cur eadem verba non ab omnibus, aliis crassio- ribus, aliis, quam opus est, subtilioribus, eodem modo acci- piantur.

Non videtur de ambiguitate legis divinæ agi. Non enim ex humanarum legum ambiguitate, aut obscuritate judicandæ sunt divinæ leges, quæ luculentæ satis fuere Judæis, quibus traditæ, etsi nunc nobis consuetudinum veterum ignaris, quan- doque ambiguæ sint. Sed de cafibus difficilibus, qui expressa lege non videbantur decisi. Ideoque ad tribunal summum tales causæ difficiliores & obscu- riores deferendæ erant, cujus LXX. erant adsef- sores, ac duo judices, unus summus נשיא præla- tus dictus, alter inferior istius absentis, vel mor- bo impediti vicarius Jerem. 52, 24. Nec solum pri- vatæ personæ, sed etiam publicæ ipsimet inferiores judices in causis difficultioribus eo confugere ju- bebantur. Et Quæstiones facti, non juris erant, cum inter SANGUINEM, ET SANGUINEM ambiguum erat judicium, hoc est, non inter san- guinem purum & impurum, polluti & mundi, ut Targ. Jonath. & R. Salomon. sed ut Cajetan. Vatabl. Lyran. & Abulens. si ambiguum sit homicidium, vel qualitas homicidii, aliis adserentibus illud esse voluntarium, morte puniendum, aliis esse casua- le, adeoque homicidæ jus asyli competere, quem sensum non videtur respuere Grotius; item inter CAUSAM, ET CAUSAM, id est, in causis ci- vilibus (uti priores erant criminales,) sitne causa justa an injusta, ob circumstantias ambiguas; inter PLAGAM, & PLAGAM, vox Ebræa Lev. 13, 4. pla- gam lepræ notat, ut ante causæ criminales & civiles, ita hic causæ Ecclesiasticæ, dijudicationem lepræ & aliarum rerum Ecclesiasticarum concernentes notantur. Fagius tamen ad politica judicia hæc, quæ h. l. recenfentur refert omnia. Si difficilis ex- plicatu tibi fuerit, hoc est, si judex minor nescit de controversia statuere, quam Hebraïsmus vo- cat דבר למשפט, id est, verbum sive rem judi- cii. Inter sanguinem & sanguinem, hoc est, inno- centem, & damnandum crimine capitali. Inter causam, & causam, hoc est, litem pecuniariam, & quæ minoris momenti. Et inter plagam lepræ &c. hoc est, livorem, & vulnus. Priori sententiæ ac- cedit Grotius, quam non improbandam censemus. Ita enim hic habet:

INTER SANGVINEM ET SANGVINEM) An cædes hujus vel illius generis mereatur locum receptus, an non me- reatur. Nam in culpa multi sunt gradus: est lata, media, mi- nima.

CAVSAM ET CAVSAM] Intelligendum hoc de litibus pecuniariis, & de verborum injuriis, quorum pœna erat ar- bitraria: & in uno eodemque genere propter legis τὸ ἀόριστον poterat probabiliter ab altero major, ab altero minor irrogan- da censeri. Quod hî̂c dicitur דין κρίσις infra 25, 1. dicitur ריב ἀντιλογία,

LEPRAM ET LEPRAM] Est quidem vox נגע quæ in Hebræo est satis generalis, quæ omne gravius malum signifi- cat, quod μάστιγα sæpe vocant Græci interpretes, ut & Novi Fœderis scriptores Marc. 3, 10. c. 5, 29. 34. Luc. 7, 21. Sed ἀντονομασικῶς lepram significat, eoque sensu quinquagies su- mitur in uno capite Levit. XIII. sæpe & medici dubitant, le- pra quæ has aut illas habet notas, sit an non sit contagio me- tuenda.

ET JVDICUM INTRA PORTAS TVAS] In urbium singularum tribunalibus, quæ in portis erant morte Hebræo- rum & vicinorum, ut apparet Gen. 34, 20. Ruth. 4, 1. 2. Prov. 22, 22. C. 31, 23. 31.

VIDERIS VERBA VARIARI) Hebræum: serba con- temtionum: id est, si eo usque procedat judicum contentio, ut pars minor tueri sententiam suam velit contra majorem, & in- ter diversa sentientes scissura quædam civitatem illam ac vici- nas distractura oriri possit. Ad schismata enim præcavenda data est hæc lex.

SVRGE ET ASCENDE AD LOCUM QVEM ELE- GERIT DOMINUS DEUS TVVS) Id est, primis tempo- ribus in Silo Jof. 18, 1. 22, 12. Jud. 18, 31. 20, 18, 18. 1. Reg. 1, 3. Jerem. 7, 12. 26, 6. Post Davidis tempora Hierosolyma. 1. Reg. 8, 2. Paral. 6, 7. & alibi.

## 17:9
Ver. 9.

AND THOU SHALT COME TO THE PRIESTS OF THE LEVITICAL KIND) So also in the Greek πρὸς τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοὺς Λευίτας (to the priests the Levites). But you will rightly understand both the Priests and the Levites, who, because they had abundant leisure, diligently learned not only all the law, but also medicine and other arts, as did the Egyptian Priests: and therefore in the first centuries the Senate was accustomed to choose the LXX men mostly from them, as being more learned: whence also here the senate is to be understood as being from the better part. Philo in the book on the Life of Moses: συνήδρευον οἱ ἱερεῖς (the priests sat in council): and in the book on Constituting a Prince: ὅταν ἐν ἀμαυρᾶν ποιῆται τὴν ἀντίληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων ἀσάφεια κὰι πολὺ σκότο ἀπεργαζομένων, παραγτέον τὰς κρίσεις κὰι ἀναπεμπέτω πρὸς ἀκριβεσέρους δικασάς. ἔτοι δὲ τίνες ἂν εἶεν ἡ̓ ἱερεῖς κὰι ὁ τῶν ἱερέων ἔξαρχος ἡγεμών; (When obscurity makes the perception of matters dim and produces much darkness, judgments must be brought forward and sent up to more accurate judges. And who would these be but the priests and the leader who is the chief of the priests?) Josephus against Apion II: κὰι γὰρ ἐπόπται πάντων κὰι δικασαὶ τῶν ἀμφισβητυμένων οἱ ἱερεῖς ἐτάχθησαν (For the priests were appointed as overseers of all things and judges of disputed matters). Excessive wealth and thence luxury and laziness caused it to be that often afterwards there were more learned men in other tribes, and therefore, with the Priests and Levites passed over, and indeed sometimes with the High Priest passed over, they were co-opted into the senate by the senators. Thus Maimonides in the book יד החזקה (Yad HaHazakah) under the Title concerning the Sanhedrin, chapter 11. But here account is taken of better times, when the Priests and Levites were such as they ought to be. When therefore such a controversy had arisen that would lead one or more cities into dissension, the dissenters were ordered to go to the Priests and Levites, who were in the Senate, and were considered the most learned. If they satisfied them, either by the weight of reasons or by testifying that the matter was defined in this or that way in customs and adjudicated cases, it was well. But if there was nothing of that kind, the same learned men referred the reasons of both parties to the Sanhedrin, and answered according to its decree, which thereafter stood in the place of law. If in serious controversies it was customary for Christians to consult the Roman Synod, likewise consisting of LXX Bishops, formerly the best and most skilled in divine matters.

AND TO THE JUDGE) That 'and' here is to be taken for 'or', as often elsewhere: a locution also used by the Latins, as Servius proves on that line of Aeneid II: 'They order to precipitate and to burn with placed flames.' Citing also that: 'Others roll a huge stone, and the spokes of wheels, etc.'

He shows what follows below 12. Thus Exod. XXI, 15. & 17. for ו the Latin translator put 'or'. And the conjunction is to be taken in that way in Num. XXX, 5. 6. & Matth. XII, 37. Judges, when they are spoken of with the number of a multitude, can rightly be understood as either those of the civil tribunals, or even the highest senators, as Deut. 1, 16. c. XVI, 18. c. XIX, 17. 18. c. XXI, 2. But where it is placed in the singular number, it is accustomed to signify an interrex divinely appointed, such as those who are named in the book שפטים. Such interreges also existed among the Tyrians by the same name שפטים, which name Josephus, translating the Acts of the Tyrians into Greek in his first book against Apion, translates as δικαστάς (judges). For after the Kings Ithobalus and Baalem, he says thus: 'After him, judges were appointed and they judged, Ecnibalus son of Baslachus for two months, Chelbes son of Abdaeus for ten months, Abbarus the high priest for three months, Mytgonus and Gerasastus the son of Abdelim for six years.' From the Tyrians the same name came to the Carthaginians, the leaders of the Tyrians, among whom the highest magistrates were called Suffetes, as Festus teaches us from Calidius. I have called it the highest magistracy with Livy, who also elsewhere says their power was like that of a consul. 'Suffetes' for שפטים is either from a softer pronunciation, such as that of the Ephraimites in Jud. XII, 6, or corrupted by Latin writers. But those שפטים among the Hebrews were clearly similar to the Roman interreges, and later to the dictators, and they did not differ from the Hebrew Kings in any respect, except that they did not have a bodyguard and royal pomp: and for that reason they did not exact tributes or taxes. Otherwise they were, as Josephus speaks, ἡγεμόνες ἀυτοκράτορες (sovereign leaders). Therefore they are also called kings in Jud. IX, 6, 'they made Abimelech King,' that is, a δικαστήν (judge); Jud. XVIII, 1, 'when Samson was dead; in those days there was no King in Israel': that is, no δικαστής (judge). And just as Kings had the right of execution without a Sanhedrin, as the Talmudic title concerning the King teaches and 2 Sam. 1, 15. and other places, so also these δικασταὶ or interreges, as appears from the example of Gideon Jud. 8, 16. 17. and Jephthah Jud. 12, 6, which are rightly noted by Abarbanel at the beginning of the book of Judges. But such δικασταὶ, since they were given by God, and for that reason endowed with prophetic gifts, whence Josephus is accustomed to call them Prophets, could safely be consulted: but because such were not to be at all times (for this is what is meant by what is added, 'who shall be in that time,' that is, if there shall be any), God willed that the Sanhedrin be consulted instead of them, composed of most learned men, referring to the whole people.

WHO SHALL TELL THEE THE SENTENCE OF JUDGMENT] Either from a certain tradition known to them, or from a decree of the Sanhedrin, if the matter had not been defined before.

Grotius wished to sail his own Roman course here. But the nature of this constitution is far different from that of a Roman Council. For that was sanctioned by divine authority, by virtue of which the Priests and Levites were to be approached: That this [Council] enjoys authority peculiar above other places or councils, and that the same was divinely sanctioned, not even Grotius dared to say. There, the matter concerned judicial cases: here, controversies of faith and religion are ventilated. There, not only Priests, but Judges also were consulted, which Moses expressly added: and thus it was some judgment consisting of different Ecclesiastical and Political persons at the same time: Here, however, the Synod is bare, and they contend that it ought to consist of Bishops alone. For that Grotius wishes the particle AND in those words, AND TO THE JUDGE, to be taken for OR, that is merely precarious. He proves it from Virgil. Truly excellent! Is the Hebrew style of the Holy Spirit to be learned from Virgil? The Judge is joined here with the Priests, not separated. Nor ought one to understand by 'Judge' here precisely an INTERREX, a Dictator, or the highest Magistrate, as he wishes 'Suffetes' to be called for שפטים among the Tyrians, just as those are called Judges who succeeded Joshua in the government: as if those δικασταὶ, like Prophets endowed by GOD with prophetic gifts, who could safely be consulted, because they were not to be at all times, the Sanhedrin ought to have been consulted instead of them, by virtue of the constitution. It is not a matter of Judges of the kind who were once to be like Kings, but general laws are prescribed, which also concern earlier times, before the Judges obtained the government. The name of Judge, therefore, here extends more broadly: nor is the same power attributed here to the Sanhedrin as is to those Prophets, who were equipped with judicial and, as it were, royal authority. to be consulted in place of such a Prophet. The judgment of the Prophets, who were moved by the Holy Spirit, was infallible in such matters. Which cannot be said of the Sanhedrin. Which Grotius himself ought to have acknowledged. Therefore, he says, the law does not permit everyone to follow the interpretation of the law which he wishes and to make it certain by some probable color: but it establishes a rule necessary for preserving unity: And you shall do (thus he renders the words of the Hebrew text) according to the word of the matter which he shall announce to you (someone, namely, of the priests, or if they are absent, someone of the Levites) from that very place which the Lord shall have chosen: (that is, according to the opinion of that assembly which was first at Shiloh, then at Jerusalem) and take heed that you do according to all their instructions, according to the word of the law (that is, the interpretation of the law) which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, that is, the prescription which judges ought to follow in judging) you shall do, and you shall not turn aside from that which they shall indicate to you, to the right or to the left. Grotius now continues: Therefore the Sanhedrin could not err, either in testifying to ancient tradition, or in explaining the law, and its own opinion. IT COULD indeed, IT COULD: even if, the matter being better known afterwards, for instance, being warned by very pious and learned men, the Senators might see that they had strayed from the true sense of the law: once the law was revealed, there was a method for expiating the error, Lev. 4, 13. But individuals were commanded not to believe everything that the Sanhedrin might say, but not to act against it, not to teach against it. Grotius therefore gains little from the Sanhedrin, or that judgment, for the Roman Pontiff and the infallible judgment of his Council. He adds indeed: in matters of great moment it could certainly not happen that the Sanhedrin, composed from the beginning of the best men and continued by perpetual co-optation, could be deceived: unless by the long lapse of centuries, and corrupted discipline, which if it had happened, God, loving unity, was going to answer to admonish or convince them through Urim and Thummim, or was going to raise up some Prophet noble for true miracles, and finally was going to give the Messiah himself, greater than Moses, upon whose sending the authority of the Sanhedrin vanished. But if the Sanhedrin, instituted by God himself, could slip even in matters of great moment through the lapse of centuries and corrupted discipline, how is the Sanhedrin, or a Council convened by the Roman Pope and confirmed by his authority, to be judged immune from lapse and error, whose institution certainly cannot be referred to God as its author in the way that the institution of that Jewish one can. Unless perhaps Grotius, in order to foist upon us as God's answer, which might be in place of Urim and Thummim or the voice of the Prophets, that which the Roman Pontiff brings forth from the cabinet of his own breast; which we shall then hold in that place, when it shall be demonstrated from the word of God that it is to be held as such, which we expect at the Greek Calends. In vain, therefore, does the Jesuit Francis Costerus in Apolog. 2 against Gomarus conclude from this passage: That with the opinions of the Scriptures and of domestic priests varying, one had to go from them to the supreme tribunal of the Jewish people, i.e., to the supreme Pontiff, so that one had to acquiesce absolutely and simply in his opinion: and that the same ought still to have a place in the N. T., and therefore that an absolute and supreme Judgment belongs to the Roman Pontiff. In vain also do Bellarmine, Stapleton, and Cornelius à Lapide strive to carve out the infallible judgment of the Roman Pontiff from this. To say nothing of the fact that the Church of the Old Testament, enclosed within the narrow limits of the Jewish land, is the Church of the New Testament, diffused throughout the whole world, there the Sanhedrin and Judge could be approached, but here it is impossible for one Judge, as for instance the Pontiff, whether alone or even with his council, to define and decide all causes throughout the whole world, just as it is equally impossible to refer all causes to the same one: This certainly is certain, that the Hebrew Pontiff was a type not of the Roman Pontiff, but of the one Christ, who alone is truly ecumenical, and entirely ἀνυπεύθυνος. And that the Pontiffs of the Old Testament were not infallible is evident from the Prophets themselves as authors, Isa. 28, 6, Jerem. 7, 4, chap. 8, 18, and is known from the examples of Aaron, Uriah, Pashhur, Caiaphas, and Hannah. Nor should this be passed over, that this judgment was restricted to the divine law, and that one had to acquiesce in its sentence and decision not absolutely, but insofar as they pronounced according to the law, verse 10, concerning which we shall now see.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

VENIESQVE AD SACERDOTES LEVITICI GE- NERIS) Sic & in Græco πρὸς τοὺς ἱερεῖς τοὺς Λευίτας. Sed bene intelliges tum Sacerdotes tum Levitas, qui quod pingue haberent otium, non tantum omnia legis, sed & medicinæ, aliarumque artium diligenter ediscebant, ut & Ægyptii Sacer- dotes: ideoque primis seculis ex illis, ut eruditioribus, Sena- tus LXX. virum legi maxime solebat: unde & hic ex potiori parte senatus, ille intelligendus est. Philo libro de Vita Mo- sis: συνήδρευον οἱ ἱερεῖς: & in libro de Principe constituen- do: ὅταν ἐν ἀμαυρᾶν ποιῆται τὴν ἀντίληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων ἀσάφεια κὰι πολὺ σκότο ἀπεργαζομένων, παραγτέον τὰς κρίσεις κὰι ἀναπεμπέτω πρὸς ἀκριβεσέρους δικασάς. ἔτοι δὲ τίνες ἂν εἶεν ἡ̓ ἱερεῖς κὰι ὁ τῶν ἱερέων ἔξαρχος ἡγεμών; Jose- phus adversus Appionem II. κὰι γὰρ ἐπόπται πάντων κὰι δικασαὶ τῶν ἀμφισβητυμένων οἱ ἱερεῖς ἐτάχθησαν. Opes ni- miæ & inde luxus ac pigritia effecere, ut sæpe postea erudi- tiores essent in tribubus aliis, ac propterea, & Sacerdotibus & Levitis prætetitis, imo interdum præterito & summo Sa- cerdote, a senatoribus in senatum cooptarentur. Ita Mai- monides libro יד החזקה Titulo de Synedrio, cap. 11. Hic vero ratio habetur meliorum temporum, cum Sacerdo- tes & Levitæ essent quales esse debebant. Cum ergo talis orta esset controversia civitatem unam pluresve in dissidium perductura, jubebantur ire dissentientes ad Sacerdotes & Levitas, qui in Senatu erant, & eruditissimi habeban- tur. Qui si ipsis satisfecissent, aut rationum pondere, aut testando, rem hoc vel illo modo in moribus ac rebus ju- dicatis definitam, recte. Sin tale nihil erat, iidem viri eru- diti rationes partis utriusque referebant ad Synedrium, & ex ejus decreto respondebant, quod in posterum legis erat loco. Si a Christianis in gravibus controversiis consuli solebat Synodus Romana ex LXX. itidem Episcopis con- stans, olim optimis & rerum divinarum peritissimis.

ET AD JVDICEM) Illud & hic sumendum pro vel, ut sæpe alibi: locutione & Latinis usitata, ut probat Servius ad illud Æneid. II. Præcipitare jubent subjectisque urere flammis. Allegans & illud: Saxum ingens volvunt alii, radiosque rotarum, &c.

Ostendit quod sequitur infra 12. Sic Exod. XXI, 15. & 17. pro ו Latinus posuit vel. Et ita sumenda copula Num. XXX, 5. 6. & Matth. XII, 37. Judices cum multitudinis numero dicuntur, recte intelligi possunt vel illi urbanorum tribuna- lium, vel summi etiam senatores, ut Deut. 1, 16. c. XVI, 18. c. XIX, 17. 18. c. XXI, 2. Vbi autem in Singulari ponitur nu- mero, solet significari interrex divinitus constitutus, quales sunt qui nominantur in libro שפטים. Tales interreges & apud Tyrios fuere eodem nomine שפטים, quod no- men Josephus Acta Tyriorum in Græcum vertens adversus Appionem libro priore vertit δικαστάς. Nam post Itho- balum & Baalem Reges, sic ait: μετὰ τοῦτον δικασταὶ κατε- στάθησαν καὶ ἐδίκασαν ἀυτοὶ, Ἐκνίβαλος Βασλάχου μῆνας δύο, Χέλβης Ἀβδαίου μῆνας δέκα, Ἀββαρος ἀρχιερεὺς μῆνας τρεῖς, Μύτγονος καὶ Γεράσσατος τοῦ Ἀβδηλίμου δικασταὶ ἔτη ἕξ. A Tyriis idem nomen venit ad Carthaginenses Tyriorum tra- duces, apud quos summi magistratus dicti Suffetes, ut ex Ca- lidio nos docet Festus. Summum Magistratum dixi cum Livio, qui & alibi eorum imperium ait fuisse velut consula- re. Suffetes pro שפטים est aut ex molliori pronuntia- tione, qualis erat Ephræthæorum Jud. XII, 6. aut corruptum per Latinos scriptores. Isti vero apud Hebræos שפטים plane similes erant Romanis interregibus, ac postea dictato- ribus, neque a Regibus Hebræis ulla re differebant, præter quod satellitium & pompam regiam non habebant: ac pro- pterea nec tributa nec vectigalia exigebant. Cæterum erant, ut Josephus loquitur, ἡγεμόνες ἀυτοκράτορες. Itaque & reges vocantur Jud. IX, 6. constituerunt Regem Abimelech, id est, δικαστὴν Jud. XVIII, 1. mortuo Samsone; in diebus illis non erat Rex in Israël: id est δικαστής. Ac sicut Reges abs- que Synedrio jus interficiendi habebant, ut docet Talmudi- cus titulus de Rege & 2. Sam. 1,15. & loca alia, sic & isti δι- κασταὶ sive interreges, ut apparet exemplo Gedeonis Jud. 8, 16. 17. & Jephtæ Jud. 12, 6. quæ recte notata Abarbaneli ad initium libri judicum. Tales autem δικασταὶ, cum a Deo dati essent, ac ob id donis instructi propheticis, unde & Pro- phetas eos vocare solet Josephus, tuto sane consuli poterant: sed quia non omni tempore tales erant futuri (hoc enim vult quod adjicitur, qui erit illo tempore, id est, si quis erit) voluit Deus pro illis consuli Synedrium, compositum ex hominibus eruditissimis, totum populum referens.

QVI INDICABVNT TIBI JVDICII VERITATEM] Aut ex traditione certa ipsis cognita, aut ex decreto Synedrii, si res non ante fuerat definita.

Velificari Romæ suæ hîc voluit Grotius. At longe alia hujusce constitutionis, alia Romani Conci- lii est ratio. Illa enim autoritate divina sancita est, vi cujus adeundi erant Sacerdotes & Levitæ: Hoc peculiari præ aliis locis aut Conciliis gaudere au- toritate, eademque divinitus sancita, nec ipse Grotius ausus fuit dicere. Ibi de causis Judicialibus agebatur: hic ventilantur controversiæ fidei & religio- nis. Ibi non Sacerdotes solum, sed Judices etiam con- sulebantur, quod diserte addidit Moses: adeoque fuit constitutum aliquod judicium è diversis per- sonis Ecclesiasticis & Politicis simul constans: Hic ve- ro Synodus nuda est, eandemque è solis Episcopis constare debere, contendunt. Quod enim Gro- tius ad verba illa, ET AD JUDICEM, particulam ET vult accipi pro VEL, id mere precarium est. Probat id è Virgilio. Egregie profecto! Nimirum Spiritus sancti stylus Ebræus è Virgilio discendus erit? Conjungitur hîc Judex cum Sacerdotibus, non sequestratur. Neque per Judicem hîc præ- cise INTERREGEM Dictatorem, aut summum Magistratum, uti SUFFITES pro שפטים apud Ty- rios dictos vult, intelligi oportet, prout Judices di- cti sunt, qui Josuæ in regimine succefferunt: quasi δικασταὶ illi ceu Prophetæ à DEO donis instructi Pro- pheticis, qui tuto consuli poterant, quia omni tempore non erant futuri, pro illis consuli debuerit Synedri- um, vi constitutionis. Non agitur de Judicibus illis, qui olim Regum instar futuri erant, sed præ- scribuntur leges generales, quæ etiam tempora an- teriora concernunt, priusquam Judices regimen obtinebant. Judicis ergo nomen hîc latius patet: neque eadem hîc Synedrio, quæ Prophetis illis ju- diciaria, & velut regia autoritate stipatis, tribuitur potestas. Synedrium loco talis Prophetæ consuli De- um voluisse, gratis dicitur. Prophetarum judici- um, qui à Spiritu S. agitabantur, erat in talibus in- fallibile. Quod de Synedrio dici nequit. Quod agnoscere debuit Grotius ipse.
