Non ergo, inquit, cuig; permittit lex, legis interpretationem, quam vult, sequi & aliquo probabili colore certam facere: sed re- gulam statuit necessariam servandæ unitati: Et faci- es (sic reddit verba textus Ebræi) secundum sermo- nem verbi, quod annunciabit tibi (aliquis scil. sa- cerdotum, aut si ii absint, aliquis Levitarum) è loco ipso, quem elegerit Dominus: (id est, de sententia consessus ejus, qui Siloæ fuit primo, deinde Hierosoly- mis) & attende, ut facias secundum omnia ipsorum documenta, secundum sermonem legis (id est, in- terpretationem legis) quam te docebunt, & secun- dum judicium, quod tibi dicent, id est, præscri- ptum, quod in judicando sequi judices debeant) fa- cies neque deflectes ab eo, quod tibi indicabunt, ad dextram, aut sinistram. Pergit nunc Grotius: Ergo Synedrium errare non poterat, aut in testanda traditione veteri, aut in explicanda lege, & sua sen- tentia. POTERAT sane, POTERAT: etsi re postea melius cognita, puta per homines valde pios & eruditos commoniti Senatores viderent, se à vero sensu legis aberrasse: prodita lege erat ratio errorem expiandi, Lev. 4, 13. At singulis, non credere omnia, quæ Synedrium diceret, imperabatur, sed non contra agere, non contra docere. Parum ergo lucratur à Sy- nedrio, vel judicio isto Grotius pro Rom. Pont. & Concilii ejusdem judicio infallibili. Addit qui- dem: in rebus magni momenti fieri sane non poterat, ut Synedrium, ab initio compositum ex viris optimis & perpetua cooptatione continuatum falli posset: nisi lon- go seculorum lapsu, corruptaq; disciplina, quod si eve- nisset, Deus, amans unitatis ad eos admonendos aut con- vincendos responsurus erat per Urim & Thumim, vel excitaturus erat Prophetam aliquem veris miraculis nobilem, & postremo daturus Messiam ipsum, Mose majorem, quo misso autoritas Synedrii evanuit. Sed si Synedrium ab ipso Deo institutum seculorum lapsu corruptaque disciplina etiam in rebus magni momenti labi potuit, quomodo à lapsu & errore immune judicaturus Synedrium, vel Concilium à Papa Romano coactum, ejusque autoritate fir- matum, cujus institutio certe ad Deum autorem ita referri non potest, ut Judaici illius institutio. Nisi forte Grotius, ut Dei responsum, quod loco U- rim & Thumim vel vocis Prophetarum sit, nobis obtrudat, quod è scrinio pectoris sui promit Ro- manus Pontifex; quod nos tum eo loco habituri sumus, cum è verbo Dei pro tali habendum de- monstrabitur, quod ad Calendas Græcas expecta- mus. Nequicquam ergo Francisc. Costerus Jesuita Apolog. 2. contr. Gomar. ex hoc loco concludit: Variantibus Scripturarum & Sacerdotum domesti- corum sententiis, eundum fuisse ab illis ad supremum Judaici populi tribunal, vid. ad summum Pontificem, ita ut in sententia ejus absolute & simpliciter acquie- scendum fuerit: idemq; adhuc in N. T. locum habere debere, ac proinde absolutum & supremum Judicium Romano Pontifici competere. Nequicquam etiam Bellarminus, Stapletonus, Cornelius à Lapid. infalli- bile Rom. P. judicium hinc exsculpere satagunt. Ut taceam, quod Ecclesiæ Veteris Testamenti in- tra angustos Judaicæ terræ limites conclusa, Ecclesia Nov. Testam. intra totum orbem diffusa sit, ibi adiri potuerit Synedrium & Judex, hic vero uni Judici, utpote Pontifici, sive soli, sive cum suo etiam concilio hoc impossibile sit, causas omnes per totum orbem terrarum definire, ac decidere, æque uti impossibile est omnes causas ad eundem deferre: Id certe constat, quod Pontifex Ebræus non Romani Pontificis, sed unius Christi fuerit typus, qui solus vere œcumenicus est, & prorsus ἀνυπεύθυνος. Et Pontifices Vet. Testament. non fuisse infallibiles, cum Prophetis ipsis autoribus constat Esa. 28, 6. Jerem. 7, 4. cap. 8, 18. tum ab exemplis Aaronis, Uriæ, Pasuris, Caiphæ & Hannæ notum est. Neque hoc prætereundum, quod adstrictum fuerit hoc judicium ad legem divinam, quodque ejus sententiæ & decisioni acquiescendum fuerit non absolute, sed quatenus secundum legem pronunciabant vers. 10. de quo nunc videbimus.

Vers. 10.

AND YOU SHALL DO WHATEVER THEY WHO PRESIDE OVER THE PLACE WHICH THE LORD SHALL HAVE CHOSEN SHALL SAY) Because the Sanhedrin was to endure perpetually, but not those interreges, therefore he fixes his speech especially on them.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET FACIES QUODCUNQVE DIXERINT QVI PRÆSVNT LOCO QVEM ELEGERIT DOMINUS) Quia Synedrium perpetuo erat duraturum, non autem interreges illi, ideo in illis maxime sermonem figit.

## 17:11
AND THEY SHALL HAVE TAUGHT YOU ACCORDING TO HIS LAW, AND YOU SHALL FOLLOW THEIR SENTENCE, AND YOU SHALL NOT DECLINE TO THE RIGHT NOR TO THE LEFT] The Greeks better: καὶ φυλάξῃ ποιῆσαι πάντα ὅσα ἂν νομοθετηθῇ σοι. Κατὰ τὸν νόμον καὶ κατὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἣν ἂν εἴπωσί σοι ποιήσεις· ἐκ ἐκκλινεῖς ἀπὸ ῥήματος ὗ ἐὰν ἀναγγείλωσί σοι δεξιὰ ἠδὲ ἀριστερά. For that 'according to the law' is not a restrictive precept, as if individuals were then only obliged to obey the decree of the Sanhedrin if the Sanhedrin should answer in accordance with the law: for that would have been to submit the interpretation to the judgment of each person, and therefore to give occasion for dissensions, to prevent which this law was placed. The whole passage stands thus in the Hebrew word for word: And you shall do according to the word (for mouth signifies word) of the matter which he shall announce to you (someone, namely, of the priests, or if they are absent, one of the Levites) from the very place which the Lord shall choose: that is, according to the opinion of his assembly, which, as we have said, was first at Shiloh, then at Jerusalem) and you shall take heed to do according to all their instructions, according to the word of the law (that is, the interpretation of the law) which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you (that is, the prescription which judges ought to follow in judging) you shall do, and you shall not turn aside from that which they shall indicate to you to the right hand or to the left. Therefore the law does not permit everyone to follow the interpretation of the law which he wishes, and to form a sect under some plausible pretext: but it establishes a rule necessary for preserving unity. Therefore, could the Sanhedrin not err, either in testifying to the ancient tradition, or in explaining the law according to its own opinion? It could indeed, it could: and if, the matter being later better understood, for instance, being warned by very pious and learned men, the senators saw that they had strayed from the true sense of the law, there was a method provided by law for expiating the error. Levit. 4, 13. But individuals were commanded not to believe everything that the Sanhedrin might say, but not to act against it, not to teach against it. See Josephus in this place and Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed 3, 41, and the book Manoim chapter 50, § 4, and Moses of Coucy in the 46th mandatory precept. For those things which could be called into controversy, such as: whether a little bird should be cut in this or that way: what calculation should be entered into for the Passover: whether a slightly greater or lesser penalty should be imposed for this fault, and others of that kind: in which it did not matter so much what was done, as it mattered to preserve the structure of the Hebrew body without any schism. In matters of great importance, it could certainly not happen that the Sanhedrin, composed from the beginning of the best and most learned men and continued by perpetual co-optation, could be deceived, unless by the long lapse of centuries and corrupted discipline: but if that had happened, God, loving unity, was going to answer to admonish or convince them through Urim and Thummim, or was going to raise up some prophet noble with true miracles, and finally was going to give the Messiah himself, greater than Moses, upon whose sending the authority of the Sanhedrin vanished. It is to be noted furthermore that some decrees of the senate, whether made for interpreting the law or for fortifying it, vanished, not only if the Senate had changed its opinion before the custom was received everywhere, but even if the people did not bear them from the beginning, or if they fell into disuse.

This gloss likewise favors the desperate Papist cause: For it has already been said that Fr. Costerus understands these things thus, and others likewise. Thus, in particular, Cornel. à Lapide interprets it, and brings forward the very same reasoning that Grotius does here: Estius also interprets it thus, and others. And for its sake he even corrects the Vulgate version itself, declares that the Greek translation is better, and renders the Hebrew words thus: You shall attend, that you may do according to all their documents, according to the word of the law (that is, the interpretation of the law) which THEY shall teach you. But although we may readily grant that the sentence of the Sanhedrin was not subject to the whim of any individual, and indeed that the authority of the Sanhedrin, which is to be held in reverence by all, is sanctioned here, yet blind obedience is not prescribed, such that if something openly contrary to the law were defined, they should embrace it; nor is the Sanhedrin pronounced absolutely infallible here, just as the blind Jews contend that the sentences of the Rabbis, even if they pronounce that the left is the right, are to be followed and accepted. Whence even the sounder among the Papists acknowledge that the Sanhedrin was bound to the divine law, and ought to have elicited the true sentence from it, and was not to be heard otherwise than when it decreed nothing contrary to the divine law; and not a few explain the words 'according to the laws,' as they sound, as referring to the very letter of the law, not to a Synodal interpretation, or at least to a sense consistent with the law and born from the law, and not indeed to one dissenting from it or brought into the law. Hieronymus ab Oleastro: It is not free for judges to judge as they wish, but according to the laws, and they must be obeyed when they have judged according to them. Cardinal Cajetanus: In Hebrew it is held 'upon the mouth of the law, which they shall teach you': for unless it corresponds to the mouth of the divine law, what the priests teach and judge in ambiguous matters is not supported by divine authority. Alphonsus Tostatus observes two conditions here: The first is that they judge according to truth: The second, that they judge according to the law: and he adds: Therefore it seems that if they have judged against the truth, or against the law, one must not consent to them. And thus also the ordinary gloss on this passage: It is not said there that you should obey, unless they have taught you according to the law. Dionysius Carthusianus limits it thus, that a sentence contrary to the law was indeed not to be held as true and just, so that one should consent to it in mind, yet the penalty or damage of that sentence should have been tolerated by an innocent person who could not appeal to a higher judge. Cornelius à Lapide certainly seems to be fighting with himself here. For when he has contended that these words are to be taken assertively, as if he were saying that subjects ought to acquiesce and presuppose that the judgment of the priests and the Pontiff has been rendered according to the law of God, he soon corrects himself, however, with these words: Understand, unless it is manifestly perceived to the contrary, namely, that the Pontiff judges expressly outside the law and perverts the law: For then one had to obey not him, but the law of God. He acknowledges, therefore, that the words are to be understood conditionally and restrictively: and Cornelius proves this hypothetical sense also from the versions: and equally from the source itself. This sense is evident from the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Septuagint, which have it thus: You shall do what they have taught according to the mouth of the law, that is, according to the law, from the law which they have taught you. He could have added the Vulgate version: And they shall teach you ACCORDING TO HIS LAW. What of the fact that Grotius acknowledges that the Sanhedrin could have erred, that it was not commanded to individuals to believe everything that the Sanhedrin said, but only not to act against it, not to teach against it, whence there is nothing here for the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff. Every magistrate has that power of sanctioning public doctrine, or what ought to be taught publicly, so that it is not permitted for private individuals to act or teach against it; but is every magistrate therefore infallible?

So that it may be more correctly understood concerning the judgments among the Jewish people, I shall append what Paul Fagius notes about them from the Hebrews on Deuteronomy 16:13. שׁוֹפְטִים are judges, who determine a case or judgment; שׁוֹטְרִים are those who rule over the people and execute the commands of the judges with a rod and a scourge. And he who is the highest among all the judges is called נָשִׂיא, that is, a prelate, and מוּפְלָא, that is, an excellent one. And he is in the place of Moses our teacher, to whom there were 70 Elders, from whom came the סַנְהֶדְרִין; but in every Israelite city there was a Sanhedrin, that is, a Council, Senate, or small Consistory, which consisted of 23 Sages, and was located at the gate of the city. And in their presence sat three orders of disciples of the sages, who would succeed into the place of the judges who were departing, those who were the closest. But in a city in which there were not one hundred and twenty men, a Sanhedrin was not located in it. There also stood before the Sanhedrin two Scribes, one on the right, the other on the left. One wrote the words of those who judged that the accused should be released. The other, however, wrote the words of those who judged that he should be condemned. Likewise two heralds, two who were contending in the judgment, two witnesses, and two of their adversaries, and two collectors of alms. Furthermore, if any city did not have one hundred and twenty men, only three judges were appointed in it. But only priests, Levites, and the more noble Israelites, who were worthy to receive the priesthood and who were clean from all bodily vices, were chosen into the great and small Consistory. And these had to be wise men, wealthy, skilled in the art of Magic, so that they might know how to destroy Magic, and knowledgeable in seventy languages, so that a Judge, who was from the Sanhedrin, would have no need to hear anything from the mouth of an interpreter. Furthermore, no one who was too worn out by old age was received into the Sanhedrin, nor a Eunuch, and that on account of cruelty, nor anyone unless he had children, so that he might be the more merciful. But neither was a King admitted into the Sanhedrin, for the reason that it is forbidden to contend with him. A high priest, however, was received, provided he was endowed with wisdom. The judges also had to be wise and magnanimous men, namely to deliver him who suffers violence from the hand of the violent one, likewise the poor, the oppressed, and those who fear God, and they should not gape after avarice to collect money, but should be truthful men, far from lies, and who pursue justice.

Latin:

ET DOCUERUNT TE JUXTA LEGEM EJUS, SEQUERISQUE SENTENTIAM EORUM, NEC DECLINABIS AD DEXTRAM NEC AD SINISTRAM] Melius Græci: καὶ φυλάξῃ ποιῆσαι πάντα ὅσα ἂν νομοθετηθῇ σοι. Κατὰ τὸν νόμον καὶ κατὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἣν ἂν εἴπωσί σοι ποιήσεις· ἐκ ἐκκλινεῖς ἀπὸ ῥήματος ὗ ἐὰν ἀναγγείλωσί σοι δεξιὰ ἠδὲ ἀριστερά. Non enim est illud juxta legem adstrictivum præcepti, quasi tum demum obligentur singuli parere decreto Synedrii, si Synedrium congruentia legi respondeat: id enim fuerat interpretationem cujusque arbitrio submittere, ac proinde dare occasionem dissidiis, quibus cavendis hæc lex posita est. Totus locus sic habet in Hebræo verbotenus: Et facies secundum sermonem (os enim sermonem significat) verbi quod annuntiabit tibi (aliquis scil. Sacerdotum, aut si ii absint, aliquis Levitarum) e loco ipso quem elegerit Dominus: id est, de sententia consessus ejus, qui, ut diximus, Siloæ fuit primo, deinde Hierosolymis) & attendes ut facias secundum omnia ipsorum documenta, secundum sermonem legis (id est, interpretationem legis) quam te docebunt, & secundum judicium quod tibi dicent (id est, præscriptum quod in judicando sequi judices debeant) facies, neque deflectes ab eo quod tibi indicabunt ad dextram aut sinistram. Non ergo cuique permittit lex legis interpretationem quam vult sequi, & aliquo probabili colore sectam facere: sed regulam statuit necessariam servandæ unitati. Ergo Synedrium errare non poterat, aut in testanda traditione Veteri, aut in explicanda lege e sua sententia? Poterat sane, poterat: & si re postea melius cognita, puta per homines valde pios & eruditos commoniti senatores viderent se a vero sensu legis aberrasse, prodita lege erat ratio errorem expiandi. Levit. 4, 13. At singulis, non credere omnia quæ Synedrium diceret, imperabatur, sed non contra agere, non contra docere. Vide Josephum h. l. & Maimoniden Ductore Dubitantium 3, 41. & libro Manoim cap. 50. §. 4. & Mosen de Kotzi præcepto jubente XLVI. Quæ enim in controversiam vocari poterant, qualia erant: An avicula hoc vel illo modo esset discindenda: quæ ineunda supputatio ad Pascha: an huic culpæ paulo major vel minor esset imponenda pœna, & ejus generis alia: in quibus non tanti referebat utrum fieret, quanti erat servare compagem Hebraici corporis sine ullo divortio. In rebus magni momenti fieri sane non poterat, ut Synedrium ab initio compositum ex viris optimis & eruditissimis & perpetua cooptatione continuatum falli posset, nisi longo sæculorum lapsu, corruptaque disciplina: quod si evenisset, Deus amans unitatis, ad eos admonendos aut convincendos responsurus erat per Urim & Thummim, vel excitaturus erat Prophetam aliquem veris miraculis nobilem, & postremo daturus Messiam ipsum Mose majorem, quo misso auctoritas Synedrii evanuit. Notandum præterea scita senatus nonnulla sive legi interpretandæ, sive præmuniendæ facta evanuisse, non modo si Senatus ante receptum ubique morem sententiam mutasset, verum etiam si vel ab initio populus ea non ferret, vel si irent in desuetudinem.

Favet hac glossa itidem causae desperatae Pa- pisticae: Sic enim haec intelligere Fr. Costerum, sic alios jam dictum est. Sic imprimis Cornel. à La- pid. interpretatur, eandemque omnino rationem adfert, quam hîc Grotius: Sic interpretatur eti- am Estius, & alii. Et in ejus gratiam ipsam etiam Vulgatam versionem corrigit, Graecam translatio- nem melius se habere pronunciat, & verba Ebraea ita reddit: Attendes, ut facias secundum omnia ipsorum documenta, secundum sermonem legis (id est, interpretationem legis) quam TE docebunt. Sed quanquam facile largiamur, non subjectam fuisse Synedrii sententiam cujusque arbitrio, imo auto- ritatem Synedrii, quae omnibus reverenter haben- da, hîc sancitam, non tamen caeca obedientia prae- scribitur, ut si aliquid aperte contrarium legi de- finitum fuerit, amplecterentur; aut absolute hîc infallibile pronunciatur Synedrium, quemadmo- dum caeci Judaei Rabbinorum sententias, etiam- si pronuncient, sinistram dextram esse, sequendas & suscipiendas esse contendunt. Unde & Syne- drium ad legem divinam adstrictum fuisse, atque ex illa eruere veram sententiam debuisse, neque ali- ter, quam qua legi divinae nihil contrarii decernebat, audiendum fuisse, saniores è Papistis agnoscunt, neque pauci verba secundum leges, uti sonant, de ipsa legis litera, non de interpretatione Synodica, vel certe de sensu legi consentaneo, & in lege enato, non vero de dissentaneo, aut in legem illato, explicant. Hieronymus ab Oleastro: Non est judicibus liberum judicare, ut volunt, sed juxta leges, & illis parendum, cum secundum eas judicaverint. Cardinal. Cajeta- nus: Hebraice habetur super os legis, quod doce- bunt te: nisi enim divinae legis ori congruat, tam quod docent, quam quod judicant Sacerdotes in ambi- guis, divina non est fultum autoritate. Alphonsus Tostatus duas hîc conditiones observat: Prima est, ut judicent secundum veritatem: Secunda, ut judicent secundum legem: & addit: Ergo videtur, quod si judi- caverint contra veritatem, vel contra legem, non est iis consentiendum. Atque ita etiam glossa or- dinaria in h. l. Non dicitur ibi, ut obedias, nisi do- cuerint te juxta legem. Dionysius Carthusianus limi- tat ita, quod sententia contraria legi tenenda qui- dem non fuerit, ut vera & justa, ut ei mente con- sentiretur, poena tamen aut damnum sententiae illius tolerari debuerit ab innocente, qui non potuerit ad altiorem judicem provocare. Cornelius certe Lapi- deus hîc ἑαυτομαχεῖν videtur. Nam quum conten- derit assertive haec verba accipienda esse, quasi dicat, subditi acquiescere debent & praesupponere, Sacerdo- tum & Pontificis judicium latum esse juxta legem Dei, mox tamen corrigit sese, hisce verbis: Intel- lige, nisi manifeste cernatur contrarium, scil. quod Pon- tifex expresse citra legem judicet, legemque pervertat: Tum enim non illi, sed legi Dei obediendum erat. A- gnoscit ergo, verba esse conditionaliter & restricti- ve intelligenda: atque hunc sensum hypotheticum probat etiam Cornelius è versionibus: aeque & ex fonte ipso. Patet hic sensus ex Ebraeo, Chaldaeo & Septuaginta, qui sic habent: Facies, quod docue- rint ad os legis, id est, juxta legem, ex lege, quam docuerint te. Addere poterat vulgatam versionem: Et docuerint te JUXTA LEGEM EJUS. Quid quod Grotius agnoscat potuisse Synedrium erra- re, quod singulis imperatum non fuerit credere o- mnia, quae Synedrium diceret, sed solum non contra agere, non contra docere, unde nihil hinc pro infalli- bilitate Romani Pontificis. Habet quivis Magi- stratus potestatem illam sanciendi doctrinam pu- blicam, vel quod doceri publice debeat, ita ut contra agere aut ducere privatis integrum non fit; num vero ideo quivis Magistratus infallibi- lis est?

Ut rectius de judiciis constet in populo Judai- co, subjiciam quæ de iis annotat ex Ebræis Paul. Fagius ad Deuter. 16, 13. שׁוֹפְטִים sunt ju- dices, qui determinant causam sive judicium; שׁוֹטְרִים sunt qui dominantur populo & exequun- tur mandata judicum cum virga & flagello. Et qui summus est inter omnes Judices, is vocatur נָשִׂיא id est, prælatus & מוּפְלָא id est, excel- lens. Atque is est loco Mosis Magistri nostri, cui fuerunt LXX. Seniores, à quibus venerunt סַנְהֶדְרִין; in qualibet autem civitate Israëlitica erat Sanhe- drim, id est, Concilium, Senatus sive Consisto- rium parvum, quod constabat 23. Sapientibus, eratque collocatum in porta civitatis. Et in con- spectu eorum sedebant tres ordines discipulorum sapientum, qui in locum judicium decedentium succedebant, ii qui erant propinquiores. In civitate vero, in quo non erant centum & viginti homines, non collocabatur in ea Sanhedrim. Sta- bant quoque coram Sanhedrim duo Scribæ, unus ad dextram, alter ad sinistram. Unus scribebat ver- ba eorum, qui dimittendum reum judicabant. Alter vero scribebat verba eorum, qui eum da- mnandum censebant. Duo item præcones, duo qui in judicio contendebant, duo testes, & duo eo- rum adversarii, atque duo collectores eleemosynæ. Porro si qua civitas non habebat centum & viginti ho- mines, constituebantur in ea tantum tres judices. Adlegebantur autem in Consistorium magnum, & parvum tantum Sacerdotes Levitæ, & Israëlitæ nobi- liores, qui digni erant ad suscipiendum Sacerdo- tium, quique mundi erant ab omnibus vitiis corporis. Atque hi debebant esse viri sapientes, divites, periti artis Magicæ, ut scirent destruere Magiam, gnari septuaginta linguarum, ita ut Ju- dex, qui ex Sanhedrim erat, non opus haberet ali- quid audire ex ore interpretis. Nec porro in San- hedrim recipiebatur, qui nimis senio confectus erat, nec Eunuchus, idque propter crudelitatem, neque nisi cui essent liberi, quo eo magis misericors esset. Sed nec Rex in Sanhedrim admittebatur, eo quod pro- hibitum sit contendere cum eo. Sacerdos vero ma- gnus recipiebatur, modo sapientia præditus esset. Ju- dices quoque esse debebant viri sapientes & ma- gnanimi ad liberandum scil. eum, qui vim pati- tur, de manu violanti, pauperes item oppressos atque timentes Deum, neque inhient avaritiæ ad colligendam pecuniam, sed sint viri veraces, alieni à mendaciis & qui justitiam sectentur.

## 17:12
Vers. 12.

BUT WHOEVER SHALL ACT PROUDLY, REFUSING TO OBEY] In Greek, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὃς ἂν ποιήσῃ ἐν ὑπερηφανίᾳ ὥστε μὴ ὑπακοῦσαι. That word to act proudly or to act in pride, in Hebrew is בְּזָדוֹן which signifies rashness. Nor is it poorly translated as ἰταμίαν by the Greeks in Jerem. 49, 15. It is certainly rashness in matters that admit of dispute to love one's own opinions so pertinaciously that on account of them peace is broken, which cannot be maintained among men except through a certain authority presiding over all. God, however, rarely performs miracles: for the most part He preserves human affairs by means congruent with human nature. That description of pride, however, does not apply to everyone, but only to those who impose upon themselves the role of teacher and distract the people. Such a one is called in the Talmudic books זָקֵן הַמּוֹרֵא an elder, that is, a contumacious doctor. The doctors were not except those older than 40 years.

BY THE COMMAND OF THE PRIEST WHO AT THAT TIME MINISTERS TO THE LORD THY GOD] Who is about to say what has been accepted, or will consult the Sanhedrin, and will answer according to its decree: as has already been said above,

AND BY THE DECREE OF THE JUDGE] In the Hebrew: or of the judge. And the Greeks, ἢ τῷ κριτῇ: who did not badly add from the preceding, ὃς ἂν ᾖ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις, that is, if anyone such shall have been given by God in your time. For God does not always give such ones.

THAT MAN SHALL DIE] A heavy penalty, but to avoid the most heavy danger of all. That we may apply this to Christian times, that statement of Augustine is appropriate, Question on Deuteronomy, book 5, chapter 38. Excommunication now does in the Church what killing did then. And on faith and works, chapter 6. Phinehas the Priest pierced adulterers found together with an avenging sword. Which certainly has been signified to be something to be done at this time by degradations and excommunications.

AND YOU SHALL REMOVE THE EVIL FROM ISRAEL] Thus you will prevent schism, a huge evil. For the same reason, the investigation concerning a False Prophet was permitted only to the Sanhedrin, and the penalty was signified to all cities by letters.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

QVI AVTEM SVPERBIERIT, NOLENS OBEDI- RE] Græce, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὃς ἂν ποιήσῃ ἐν ὑπερηφανίᾳ ὥστε μὴ ὑπακοῦσαι. Vox illa superbire aut facere in superbia, in He- bræo est בְּזָדוֹן quod temeritatem significat. Nec male ἰτα- μίαν vertitur Græcis Jerem. 49, 15. Temeritas certe est in re- bus disputationem recipientibus tam pertinaciter amare suas sententias, ut propterea pax rumpatur, quæ nisi per auctori- tatem quandam omnibus præsidentem retineri nequit huma- nitus. Deus autem miracula raro facit: plerumque res hu- manas conservat modis humanæ naturæ congruentibus. Su- perbiæ vero illud elogium non omnibus convenit, sed iis de- mum, qui doctoris sibi personam imponunt, & populum di- strahunt. Talis qui est, vocatur in Thalmudicis libris זָקֵן הַמּוֹרֵא senex, id est, doctor contumax. Doctores non erant nisi majores 40. annis.

SACERDOTIS IMPERIO QVI EO TEMPORE MI- NISTRAT DOMINO DEO TVO] Qui dicturus est, quid sit receptum, aut Synedrium consulet, & ex ejus decreto re- spondebit: ut jam supra dictum est,

ET DECRETO JUDICIS] In Hebræo: vel judicis. Et Græci, ἢ τῷ κριτῇ: qui non male addiderunt ex supe- rioribus, ὃς ἂν ᾖ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις, id est, fi quis tuo tempore talis a Deo datus fuerit. Non enim semper tales dat Deus.

MORIETUR HOMO ILLE] Gravis pœna, sed ad vi- tandum periculum omnium gravissimum. Ad Christiana tempora ut hoc applicemus, appositum est Augustini illud quæstion. super Deuteron. lib. 5. cap. 38. Hoc nunc agit in Ec- clesia excommunicatio, quod agebat tunc interfectio. Et de fide, & operibus cap. 6. Phinees Sacerdos adulteros simul inventos ferro ultore confixit. Quod utique degradationibus & excom- municationibus significatum est esse faciendum hoc tempore.

ET AVFERES MALVM DE ISRAEL] Sic impedies schisma, ingens malum. Eadem de causa cognitio de Pseu- dopropheta soli Synedrio permissa, & pœna per literas omni- bus civitatibus significata.

## 17:13
AND ALL THE PEOPLE HEARING SHALL FEAR, SO THAT NO ONE HENCEFORTH SHALL SWELL WITH PRIDE] He will take care not to make himself the author of a doctrine disapproved by public authority, and consequently a leader of factions. For this is זָדָוֹן, as we have already said. See Josephus, and the commanding precepts.

Latin:

CUNCTUSQVE POPULUS AUDIENS TIMEBIT, UT NULLUS DEINCEPS INTVMESCAT SVPERBIA] Cavebit se facere auctorem dogmatis, publica auctori- tate improbati, ac proinde partium ducem. Hoc enim est זָדָוֹן, ut jam diximus. Vide Josephum, & præcepta jubentia.

## 17:14
Verse 14. AND YOU SHALL SAY: I WILL SET A KING OVER ME] It was therefore permitted for them to seek a King, but not at the time when they had an interrex appointed by God. Moreover, the laws concerning the King, the temple, and the destruction of the Amalekites pertain to the times of the possessed land. And it was necessary for a King to be appointed before the place for the temple was looked for; lest a civil war should arise on that account from the contention of the tribes.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ET DIXERIS: CONSTITUAM SUPER ME REGEM] Licebat ergo ipsis Regem expetere, sed non quo tempore, interregem habebant a Deo constitutum. Leges autem de Rege, de templo & excidio Amalecitarum pertinent ad tempora possessæ terræ. Et opus erat Regem constitui, antequam locus templo dispiceretur; ne ex contentione tri- buum bellum ob id civile nasceretur.

## 17:15
WHOM THE LORD YOUR GOD SHALL CHOOSE] Shall have approved through a Prophet. Thus Saul and David were anointed through Samuel: Solomon through Nathan, and in Solomon all his descendants. For in him the kingdom was made hereditary by that law which the Franks call Salic. Before, it was personal.

FROM THE NUMBER OF YOUR BRETHREN] Masters vary in the interpretation of this passage. The more accepted opinion is that it sufficed that he was born from the lawful marriage of a Hebrew mother: And thus believed those who called Agrippa the younger their brother.

Verse 15. YOU SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO MAKE A MAN OF ANOTHER NATION KING] The Zealots wrongly drew this to mean that it was not permitted to obey foreign kings. The law deals with voluntary election; not with that which necessity has imposed. See Jeremiah 38, 17. Ezekiel 17, 12. 13. 14. 15. See on the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 4, § 14, and what pertains to Matthew 22, verse 17.

Latin:

QVEM DOMINUS DEUS TUUS ELEGE- RIT] Approbaverit per Prophetam. Sic per Samuelem unctus Saul & David: per Nathanem Solomon, & in Solo- mone omnes ejus posteri. In ipso enim regnum factum est successorium ea lege, quam Franci Salicam vocant. Ante erat personale.

DE NUMERO FRATRUM TVORUM] Variant Ma- gistri in hujus loci interpretatione. Receptior sententia est suffecisse ut ex justis nuptiis matris Hebrææ natus esset: Atque ita credidere illi qui Agrippam minorem fratrem su- um dixere.

Vers. 15. NON POTERIS ALTERIUS GEN- TIS HOMINEM REGEM FACERE] Male hoc Zelotæ eo trahebant, quasi externis regibus parere non liceret. Lex agit de voluntaria electione; non de eo quod indixit necessitas. Vid. Jerem. 38, 17. Ezech. 17, 12. 13. 14. 15. Vid. de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 2. cap. 4. §. 14. & quæ ad Matth. 22. vers. 17.

## 17:16
Verse 16. HE SHALL NOT MULTIPLY HORSES FOR HIMSELF] In Judea there was a plenty of donkeys: a lack of horses. And so even the leading men were carried on donkeys, Judges 10, verse 4. C. 12. V. 14. 1 Chronicles 27, verse 30. God forbids the King to bring many horses into his kingdom, lest, namely, the people should become accustomed to horses from that.

NOR SHALL HE BRING BACK THE PEOPLE INTO EGYPT BY THE NUMBER OF CAVALRY RAISED] Better in the Hebrew: Lest he make the people return into Egypt to have many horses. Make the people return, that is, give an occasion to the common people to seek an Egyptian habitation for the sake of many horses instead of the promised land, and to migrate there for the love of horses. For Egypt is fertile in horses, 1 Kings 10, 28. But for many reasons God did not want the Israelites to fix their habitation in Egypt. Exodus 14, 13. below 28, 68. This is to be understood of that time when it was permitted for them to dwell in the promised land: for once expelled from there, it was permitted to seek a seat of exile as much in Egypt as elsewhere, as many wise men proved they felt by their own example. Therefore he adds by the same way.

Latin:

Vers. 16. NON MULTIPLICABIT SIBI EQVOS] In Judæa asinorum erat copia: equorum inopia. Itaque & viri principes asinis vehebantur Jud. 10. vers. 4. C. 12. V. 14. 1. Paral. 27. vers. 30. Vetat Deus Regem multos equos in regnum suum accersere, ne scilicet inde populus equis as- suesceret.

NEC REDUCET POPULUM IN ÆGYPTVM EQVI- TATUS NUMERO SUBLEVATUS] Melius in Hebræo: Ne redire faciat populum in Ægyptum ad multos equos ha- bendos. Redire faciat populum, id est, occasionem det po- pularium multis pro terra promissa expetendi habitationem Ægyptiacam, & eo migrandi amore equorum. Nam Ægy- ptus equis ferax 1. Reg. 10, 28. multis autem de causis nole- bat Deus Israëlitas habitationem in Ægypto figere. Exod. 14, 13. infra 28, 68. Intelligendum hoc de eo tempore, quo in terra promissa habitare ipsis licebat: nam inde expulsis tam in Ægypto quam alibi exilii sedem licuit quærere, ut multi sapientes exemplo suo sentire se probarunt. Ideo addit per eandem viam.

## 17:17
Verse 17. HE SHALL NOT HAVE MANY WIVES] As many Kings in the East, for the sake of pride, took away many thousands of women useless to them from the honest uses of others, the authority of the wise permitted the King to have up to eighteen.

NOR IMMENSE WEIGHTS OF SILVER AND GOLD] In treasuries, namely. By a similar counsel, Lycurgus attributed so much land to the Kings, ὥσε μὴ ἐνδεῖαι τῶν μετρίων, μήτε πλύτῳ ὑπερφέρειν. He adds the reason: ἐ γὰρ ἐβουλήθη ὕτε τοῖς βασιλεῦσι τυραννικὸν Φρόνημα παραστῆσαι, ὅτε τοῖς πολίταις Φθόνον ἐμποιῆσαι τῆς δυνάμεως. This is what follows here: Nor let his heart be lifted up in pride above his brethren. In Judea, no treasuries except those dedicated to God. Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 12. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NON HABEDIT UXORES PLURIMAS] Ut multi in Oriente Reges multa millia fœminarum ipsis inu- tilia, aliorum honestis usibus subtrahebant fastus causa, sapi- entum auctoritas permisit Regi habere ad octodecim.

NEQVE ARGENTI ET AURI IMMENSA PON- DERA] In thesauris scilicet Pari consilio Lycurgus tantum terræ Regibus attribuit, ὥσε μὴ ἐνδεῖαι τῶν μετρίων, μήτε πλύ- τῳ ὑπερφέρειν. Causam addit: ἐ γὰρ ἐβουλήθη ὕτε τοῖς βασιλεῦσι τυραννικὸν Φρόνημα παραστῆσαι, ὅτε τοῖς πολίταις Φθόνον ἐμποιῆσαι τῆς δυνάμεως. Hoc est quod hic seque- tur: Nec elevetur cor ejus in superbiam supra fratres suos. In Judæa nulli thesauri nisi Deo dicati. Josephus Antiquæ Hi- storiæ 12. 12.

## 17:18
Vers. 18. HE SHALL WRITE FOR HIMSELF A COPY OF THIS LAW) You would more correctly translate מִשְׁנֶה as a copy. For he was required to write out the whole Pentateuch, first so that any Israelite might have it, and then again, so that the King might have it: so that he would know the law he must follow in both private and public affairs. Thus he was also required to read it

both privately for himself, and in the Temple, with the people listening, so that the people would know that no one is exempt from the law.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DESCRIBET TIBI DEVTERONOMIVM) Rectius מִשְׁנֶה exemplum verteris. Totum enim Pen- tateuchum tenebatur describere, primum ut Israëlita quivis, deinde iterum, ut Rex: ut sciret & in privatis & in publicis negotiis legem sibi sequendam. Sic & legere eam debebat

& sibi privatim, & in Templo, audiente populo, ut sciret po- pulus neminem a lege excipi.

## 17:20
Vers. 20. SO THAT HE MAY REIGN A LONG TIME, HE AND HIS CHILDREN OVER ISRAEL] Which happened to David, not to Saul.

Regarding the Royal Law prescribed by Moses, these things are to be noted: (1.) Concerning the appointment of a King. That is not commanded, but permitted in this place, as can be gathered from a comparison with 1 Sam. 8, verse 7; and the Hebrews themselves teach that this is not a command here, but a prophecy. Cf. Augustine, quest. 26 in Deuteronomy. Schickard in Jure Reg. page 19 wishes this to be a command to choose a King. He proves it from R. Nachmoni, that R. Jehuda said that three things were enjoined upon the Israelites upon their entry into the land of Canaan: (1.) The extirpation of the memory of Amalek. (2.) The appointment of a King. (3.) The building of the house of the sanctuary. Which R. Moses Maimonides also relates, Vol. 2, Halacha Melachim, chap. 1, but the building of the house of the sanctuary is nowhere read to be commanded in the law of Moses. Furthermore, others also deny that the appointment of a King was commanded. R. Bechai on Parashah Shofetim, chap. 6: It was not the will of GOD that there should be a King in Israel other than Himself. It is written (Hos. 13, verse 11) I give you a King in my anger, that is Saul the first King, and I take him away in my fury, that is Zedekiah the last King. R. Nachmoni thinks that this conflicts with the liberty of the Jewish people. R. Levi Ben Gerson argues from the outcome that little good, but a great deal of evil, happened to this people because of kings. Moreover, they urge 1 Sam. 8, verse 6, that the act of the people requesting a King was displeasing to Samuel. He would not have dissuaded them so strongly if it had pleased the divine will. On the contrary, Schickard urges that it is a command: By setting you shall set. But it can be answered: These things are also correctly understood concerning the certainty of a future appointment, in a prophetic sense, not a preceptive one: or rather, it is not commanded that they choose a King, but where God has chosen a King, they shall set only him. The Lord's election, however, was made either by the voice of the Prophet or by the indication of URIM, as Aben-Ezra notes.

(2.) Concerning the Royal lineage, that he was to be chosen from his brothers or the Israelites, both so that he might love his subjects more, protect his native soil, and especially defend the ancestral religion, and because the Messiah, the true King of Israel, had to arise from the Israelites according to the flesh, Gen. 49, verse 10. (3.) Concerning Polygamy. It was not granted to the King, as indeed Augustine thinks in quest. 27 in Deuteronomy, distinguishing between polygamy and the multiplication of wives, but it is rather to be considered entirely forbidden by the force of the original institution in Gen. 2. For David's example does not create a rule. He was a man according to God's heart regarding the exercise of religion, 1 Sam. 13, verse 14; 2 Kings 22, verse 2, yet he was not without his own flaws in the meantime. Nor, however, is polygamy only prohibited, but Kings are recalled from all illicit pleasure in such a way that it does not befit them. Cf. Prov. 2, verse 16; chap. 9, verse 13; chap. 30, last verse. For chastity, and the avoidance of all whoredom and impurity, is most fitting for Kings. Sardanapalus, who sees those reveling in the company of women with that prefect, rightly denies that he can obey them. Justin, book 1.

(4) Concerning the prohibition of the multiplication of gold and silver and of avarice, which is to be understood as relative, so that he does not place his trust in them, become puffed up in spirit, and be entangled in unnecessary wars. Thus also the prohibition of hippomania, or the multiplication of horses, is likewise to be understood as relative, so that he does not trust in such defenses, or be led into pride, lest, supported by the number of his cavalry, he wage war on his neighbors and lead the people back into Egypt, which reason is added in the text, according to the Vulgate version, as some explain, which however Grotius not undeservedly amends here from the authentic text, rendering the Hebrew text with the Hebrews Cajetan and Vatablus thus: that he may not cause the people to return into Egypt that he may multiply horses, that is, that he may not buy many horses for himself, so that he is prohibited, both that the King may not multiply horses for himself, and that he may not permit the people to return into Egypt and procure horses for themselves there, since he would be very prone to the customs and vices of the Egyptians, and could easily be imbued with their vicious customs by those dealings. This is not to be understood concerning the return of the whole people into Egypt, but that that indiscriminate journeying and trading into Egypt should not be granted. One species is named, but the same reason applies to others, for as the multitude of horses is hitherto prohibited, so that the King may not place his trust in them, so likewise the multiplication of other things, in which protection and strength are confidently placed, must be considered interdicted. A king is not saved by many, and a giant shall not be saved in the multitude of his strength. A horse is a fallacious thing for safety, and he shall not be saved in the multitude of his strength. Some in chariots and in horses, but we will remember the name of our Lord, Isa. 31, 1. Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, hoping in horses, and having confidence upon chariots, because they are many, and upon horsemen, because they are very strong, and have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, and have not sought the Lord. Egypt is man and not God, and their horses flesh and not Spirit. Conf. Ezek. 17, verse 15. For the same reason horses are named, which were more noble in Egypt, so that the Israelites might not be permitted to go down into Egypt for their sake. But the reason is similar if they return there for the sake of other trade, and because it was specially forbidden to them that they should not be eager for a multitude of horses, hence they are rebuked in Isa. 2, verse 8, because, having forgotten their God, they had filled the land with horses. Because the cavalry of Egypt was famous and the most noble horses could be procured from it, he did not want the King to be delighted by their abundance, or the subjects to be captured by love and desire for the region. And the Jews were otherwise very studious of their own country, so that they did not easily grant travels to anyone. The Jews alone, says Cunaeus, lib. 1 de Rep. Hebr. cap. 4, content within the borders of their own land with those riches which nature produced for them, led their life far from trade: For they did not cross the seas, nor did they visit foreigners, nor were they visited by them. To which the divine command contributes. Jehovah has declared to you, says Moses, you shall not dare to return by this way ever. Cornelius says that it is nowhere written when and where God commanded this. B. Taddelius in tract. Rex Israel thef. 22, refers him to Exod. 14, verse 13. Certainly, for the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall not dare to see forever. He says that, as the words themselves teach, Moses looked to this. For although you may object that those Egyptians are meant who were pursuing as enemies, yet nothing prevents you from translating it thus: certainly, the Egyptians whom you saw, you shall not see again forever. For why should they meditate on apostasy, and seem now and at any moment about to relapse to the Egyptians, says Moses, STAND, for neither now nor ever will any return to the Egyptians be open to you. But God does not there act as a lawgiver or prescribe a law about not returning to Egypt. But he raises them up against the power of the enemies by the confidence of the destruction of the same. This command is more rightly elicited from our text, so that the words may be rendered in the present tense. Even now also Jehovah declares to you, you shall not dare to return by this way ever. To which Moses looks in Deuteronomy 28, verse 8. Of which (land) the Lord said (and declared) to you, that you should see it no more. (5.) Concerning the study of the law or Holy Scripture, which is especially commended to the King. For God does not bar the King as a layman from the reading of Scripture, as the Papists forbid the same to laymen: But he inculcates it highly to Kings: Just as it was also said to Joshua, cap. 1, verse 8. The volume of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night. To which end he wished to require here that the King should describe the law for himself and read in it all the days of his life, verse 18, 19. It is doubtful what is understood by the copy of this law. Some understand only the Decalogue repeated in Deuteronomy, because Joshua is read to have written the copy of the law upon stones, cap. 8, verse 32. But because the precept is added that he should read in it all the days of his life, others deny that the Decalogue alone is rightly looked to, of whom however some wish only Deuteronomy, others all the books of Moses to be denoted by that word; which latter Grotius assumes with the Jews, following their traditions, according to whom indeed the copy of the law ought to be explained as a double of the law, or a twofold law, so that, namely, the King may have two copies of the law, not as the Chaldean rendered it, a copy of the law. Whence is that of R. Solomon: The King had two books of the law, one which was stored and kept in the archives, and another which went out and came in with him. In which manner Schickard Reg. cap. 2, page 31, expressly judges it to be commanded here, by the force of the word copy, that the King should describe two copies of the law with his own hand, citing to that opinion Maimon. Hal. Melach. cap. 3, where Schickard also describes at length the book of the law in respect to 1. the material, which ought to have been parchment. 2. The distribution of the columns. 3. The ink. 4. The prototype, which was kept by the Levites in the sanctuary. 5. The letters. 6. The correction. 7. The binding. Fagius from the Hebrews observes a limitation. That if he does not have the law described beforehand, after he has been made King, he is bound to describe two books of the law. One which he may store in his treasury, another which he may continually have with him, whether he goes out to war, or sits in judgment, or at a banquet, etc. See also Sanhedrim Coccej. cap. 2. Philo also handed this down in his book on the creation of a Prince. That the King ought to have written out the law with his own hand, so that the divine precepts might be more firmly fixed in the mind through writing, which easily slip away through mere reading. But what does not seem so to Lyranus, if indeed the King is said to have done that which he does through others, if however that is to be admitted, it is without doubt to be understood only of an adult King, since Joash at seven years old could hardly have written out the whole Pentateuch with his own hand, 2 Kings 11:21. But, as I have said, it pleases others that here not the Pentateuch in its entirety, but Deuteronomy is commanded to be written out. For thus they render מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה, the reception of the law. B. Luther, diß andere Gesetzk, and they wish this to be indicated by the pronoun הַזֹּאת, this very law, which he repeats, and now near to death prescribes anew to Israel, and Abulensis gives the reason in this place: Deuteronomy inculcates the fear of God more than Exodus or Leviticus. For it is an ardent and perpetual sermon of Moses inciting the Hebrews to the worship of God. Which opinion B. Gerhard also approves. Moreover, the law had to be written out from that exemplar which was in the sight of the Levitical priests, because, as Fagius notes, the Mosaic books were deposited at the side of the ark, and their custody was entrusted to the Levites, Deuteronomy 31:24. (6.) On avoiding pride. Lest his heart be lifted up in pride above his brothers. By which words arrogance and elation of mind are forbidden, and clemency, humility, and gentleness are commended to those in the highest positions. Therefore David so detested arrogance that he did not hesitate to profess, Psalm 101:5.

I will not be able to endure one who is haughty of eyes and swollen in spirit. The Kings of Israel are praised because they were εὐπρόσιτοι (accessible); the Persian pride is reproved, which caused their King to be ἀπρόσιτος (inaccessible), nor was it permitted for anyone to see him, as is evident from the history of Esther. Among the Persians, says Justin, book 1, the person of the King is hidden under the guise of Majesty. The voice of the Emperor Musumuli Al. is also commended in the Proverbs: The worst of men, whom men fear, cannot establish an empire, who prefer to be feared than to be loved. Augustine, book 5, de Civ. Dei 24, says that Kings would be happy if they were not puffed up by honors and obsequies, if they remembered that they are men, if they acted for the majesty and praise of GOD. A prince should know how to rule over men, so that he may think of himself as inferior to GOD and also that he himself is a man.

Latin:

Vers. 20. UT LONGO TEMPORE REGNET IPSE ET FILII EJUS SUPER ISRAEL] Quod Davidi contigit, non Sauli.

De Jure Regio à Mose præscripto hæc no- tanda (1.) de Regis constitutione. Illa non præci- pitur, sed permittitur hoc loco, ut è collatione 1. Sam. 8. vers. 7. colligere est; & docent Ebræi ipsi, hic non esse mandatum, sed vaticinium. Conf. Augustin. quæst. 26. in Deuteronom. Schickardus in Jure Reg. pag. 19. hic vult mandatum esse eligere Regem. Probat è R. Nachmoni, quod R. Jehuda dixerit, tres res injunctas esse Israelitis ad ingres- sum in terram Canaan: (1.) extirpationem memoriæ Amaleck. (2.) Constitutionem Regis. (3.) Ædifi- cationem domus sanctuarii. Quæ etiam tradit R. Moses Maimonid. Tom. 2. Halacha Melachim cap. 1. sed nuspiam legitur præcepta ædificatio domus sanctuarii in lege Mosis. Porro etiam Regis constitutionem demandatam esse negant alii. R. Bechai ad Parfch. Schoph. cap. 6. Non erat voluntas DEI, ut esset Rex in Israel alius, quam ipsemet. Scriptum est (Hof. 13. vers. 11.) do tibi Regem in ira mea, is est Saul Rex primus, & aufero in furore meo, is est Zidkias Rex ultimus. R. Nachmoni censet, id pugnare cum libertate po- puli Judaici. R. Levi Ben Gerson ab eventu ar- guit, parum boni, mali vero plurimum ob reges huic populo contigisse. Urgent insuper 1. Sam. 8. vers. 6. quod Samuel populi Regem petentis factum detectetur. Non tantopere eos dehortatus fuisset, si divinæ voluntati placuisset. Ex adverso urget Schickardus mandatum esse: Ponendo pones. Ve- rum responderi potest: Hæc etiam recte accipi de certitudine futuræ constitutionis, sensu propheti- co: non præceptivo: aut potius, non præcipi, ut Regem eligant, sed ubi Deus elegerit Regem, eum tantum ponent. Electio autem Domini facta est vel per vocem Prophetæ, vel indicio URIM, ut notat Aben - Ezra.

(2.) De Regia prosapia è fratribus vel Israeli- tis eum eligendum fuisse, tum ut eo magis sub- ditos diligeret, natale solum tueretur, ac impri- mis avitam religionem propugnaret, tum quia Messias Rex verus Israel ex Israëlitis secundum carnem oriri debuit, Genes. 49. vers. 10. (3.) De Polygamia. Non concessa illa Regi, uti quidem Augustinus putat quæst. 27. in Deuteronom. Di- stinguens inter polygamiam & uxorum multiplica- tionem, sed interdicta omnis potius censenda est, vi primævæ institutionis Genes. 2. Davidis enim exemplum non parit regulam. Fuit vir se- cundum Cor Dei quoad religionis exercitium 1. Sam. 13. vers. 14. 2. Reg. 22. vers. 2. suis interim non ca- ruit nævis. Nec tamen polygamia solum prohi- betur, sed ab omni illicita voluptate ita revocantur Reges, quod ea ipsos non deceat. Conf. Prov. 2. vers. 16. cap. 9. vers. 13. cap. 30. vers. ult. Castitas enim, omnisque scortationis & impuritatis vitatio Re- gibus maxime convenit. Sardanapalus, qui cum præfecto illo videt in fœminarum consortio lasci- vientes, merito se illis parere posse negat. Justin. lib. 1.

(4) De interdicto multiplicationis auri & argen- ti ac Φιλαργυρίας, quod accipiendum id fit κατὰ τί, ne fiduciam in illa collocet, animo efferatur, & bellis non necessariis implicetur. Sic & ἱππο- μανίας, vel multiplicationis equorum interdictum itidem secundum quid accipiendum, ne in præ- sidiis talibus confidat, aut in superbiam deduca- tur, ne equitatus numero sublevatus vicinis bel- lum inferat, populumque in Ægyptum reducat, quæ ratio in textu additur, juxta vulgatam versionem, quemadmodum nonnulli explicant, quam tamen non immerito ex textu authentico hic emendat Grotius, cum Ebræis Cajetano & Vatablo textum Ebræum sic reddens: ne reverti faciat populum in Ægyptum ut multiplicet equos, hoc est, ut multos equos sibi coëmat, ut ita prohibeatur, tum ne Rex sibi equos multiplicet, tum ne populo permittat, ut in Ægyptum redeat, atque equos sibi illic comparet, siquidem is pronus admodum fuerit ad mores & vitia Ægyptiorum, & commerciis illis facile vitiosis eorum moribus imbui potuisset. Non de reditu totius populi in Ægyptum hæc accipienda, sed ne promiscue illa in Ægyptum profectio & negotiatio concedatur. Nominatur una species, sed de aliis eadem ratio, nam uti multitudine equorum hactenus prohibetur, ne in eadem fiduciam Rex collocet, ita similiter aliarum rerum multiplicatio, in quibus præsidium & robur confidenter ponitur, interdicta censenda. Non salvatur Rex per multos, & gigas non salvabitur in multitudine virtutis suæ. Fallax equus ad salutem, in multitudine virtutis suæ non salvabitur. Hi in curribus & in equis, nos autem nominis Domini nostri recordabimur Esa. 31, 1. Væ qui descendunt in Ægyptum ad auxilium in equis sperantes, & habentes fiduciam super quadrigas, quia multæ sunt, & super equitibus, quia prævalidi nimis, & non sunt confisi super sanctum Israëlis, & Dominum non requisiverunt. Ægyptus homo & non Deus, & equi eorum caro, & non Spiritus. Conf. Ezech. 17. verf. 15. Eadem ratione nominantur equi, qui generosiores in Ægypto erant, ne eorum gratia in Ægyptum descendere permittantur Israëlitæ. Sed similis ratio est, si aliorum commerciorum gratia eo redeant, ac quia specialiter illis interdictum, ne equorum multitudini studeant, inde reprehenduntur Esa. 2. verf. 8. quod Dei sui obliti, terram equis implevissent. Equitatus Ægypti quia erat celebris & generosissimi ex ea equi comparari poterant, noluit Regem eorum copia delectari, vel subditos amore & desiderio regionis capi. Et fuere patriæ suæ Judæi alias studiosissimi, ut peregrinationes non facile cuivis concesserint. Soli Judæi, inquit Cunæus, lib. 1. de Rep. Hebr. cap. 4. intra suæ terræ fines illis contenti opibus, quas illis natura producebat, vitam procul commerciis agitavere: Non enim maria transibant neque exteros visebant, neque ab his visebantur. Quo facit mandatum divinum. Edixit Jehovah vobis, inquit Moses, non audebis reverti per hanc viam unquam. Cornelius quando & ubi hoc præceperit Deus, nuspiam scriptum esse ait. B. Taddelius in tract. Rex Israel thef. 22. temittit eum ad Exod. 14. verf. 13. Certe כי quos videtis Ægyptios hodie, non audetis videre in æternum. Omnino ait, quod verba ipsa docent, huc respexit Mose. Licet enim objicias, Ægyptios intelligi illos, qui ceu hostes insequebantur, tamen nihil obstat, quo minus ita vertas, certe, quos vidistis Ægyptios, non videbitis rursum in æternum. Cur enim ἀποστασίαν meditarentur, & jam jamque ad Ægyptios relapsuri viderentur, inquit Mose, STATE, neque enim nunc vel olim ullus patebit vobis ad Ægyptios reditus. Sed ibi Deus non agit νομοθέτην aut legem præscribit de non redeundo in Ægyptum. Sed erigit eos adversus hostium potentiam fiducia interitus eorundem. Rectius è nostro textu hoc mandatum eruitur, ut verba reddantur in præsenti. Etiam num quoque edicit tibi Jehovah, non audebis reverti per viam hanc unquam. Quo respicit Mose Deuteronom. 28. verf. 8. De qua (terra) dixit (ve- edixit) tibi Dominus, ut eam amplius non videas, (5.) De studio legis vel Scripturæ S. quod imprimis Regi commendatur. Non enim arcet Deus Re- gem ceu Laicum à Scripturæ lectione, quemad- modum Pontificii Laicis eandem interdicunt: Sed inculcat eam summopere Regibus : Sicuti etiam Josuæ dictum cap. 1. vers. 8. Non recedet vo- lumen legis ab ore tuo, sed meditaberis in eo diebus ac noctibus. Qua fini requirere hic voluit, ut Rex sibi describat legem & in ea omnibus diebus vitæ suæ legat vers. 18. 19. Dubium est quidnam per מִשְׁנֵה legis hujus intelligatur. Nonnulli solum Decalogum in Devteronomio repetitum intelli- gunt, quia Josua מִשְׁנֵה legis super lapides scri- psisse legitur cap. 8. vers. 32. Sed quia additur præ- ceptum, ut legat omnibus diebus vitæ suæ in ea, alii negant, rectius tantum Decalogum respici, è qui- bus tamen nonnulli solum Deuteronomium, alii omnes libros Mosis ea voce notari volunt; quod po- sterius cum Judæis assumit Grotius traditiones eo- rum sectatus, juxta quos vero מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה exponi deberet duplum legis, vel duplex lex, ut scil. Rex duo legis exemplaria habeat, non ut Chal- dæus reddidit exemplar legis. Unde est illud R. Salomonis : Habebat Rex duos libros legis, unum qui repositus asservabatur in archivis, & alium qui exibat & introibat cum eo. Quo pacto Schickar- dm tractat. de Jur. Reg. cap. 2. pag. 31. diserte hic præceptum esse censet, vi vocis מִשְׁנֵה, ut Rex bi- na legis exemplaria propria manu describat, addu- cens in eam sententiam Maimon. Hal. Melach. cap. 3. ubi etiam prolixe Schickardus describit le- gis librum ratione 1. materiæ, quæ debuerit esse membrana. 2. Distributionis cortinarum. 3. Atra- menti. 4. Prototypi, quod asservatum à Levitis in sanctuario. 5. Literarum. 6. Correctionis. 7. Ligatu- ræ. Fagius ex Ebræis limitationem observat. Quod si antea non habeat descriptam legem, postquam Rex factus est, tenetur duos libros legis describere. Alterum quem reponat in suo thesauro, alterum quem jugiter secum habeat, sive egrediatur ad bellum, sive sedeat in judicio, sive in convivio &c. Vid. etiam Sanhe- drim Coccej. cap. 2. Tradidit & Philo l. de creat. Princip. Regem debuisse propria manu legem descri- bere, ut divina præcepta per scriptionem magis animo infigerentur, quæ nuda lectione facile effluant. Quod vero Lyrano non videtur, siquidem Rex id fecisse dicatur, quod per alios faciat, si tamen id admitten- dum sit, sine dubio de Rege adulto solum intelli- gendum, quum Joas septennis Pentateuchum to- tum propria manu describere haud potuerit 2. Reg. 11. v. 21. Verum, ut dixi, aliis placet hic non pen- tatevchum universim, sed Deuteronomion descri- bendum præcipi. Sic enim reddunt מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה receptio legis. B. Lutherus, diß andere Gesetzk, atque id indicari volunt pronomine הַזֹּאת hanc ipsam legem, quam repetit, & Israeli morti jam vicinus de- nuo præscribit, causamque reddit Abulensis h. l. Deuteronomium magis inculcat timorem Dei quam Exodus, aut Leviticus. Est enim ardens & perpe- tua Concio Mosis incitans Hebræos ad cultum DEI. Quam sententiam etiam approbat B. Gerhardus. Describi autem lex debuit ex eo exemplari, quod erat in conspectu Sacerdotum Leviticorum, quia in latere arcæ, notante Fagio, repositi fuere libri Mo- saici, eorumque custodia Levitis fuit commendata Deuter. 31. v. 24. (6.) De vitanda superbia. Ne ef- feratur cor ejus in superbia super fratres suos. Qui- bus verbis fastus & elatio animi prohibetur, cle- mentia, humilitas, & mansuetudo summis capiti- bus commendatur. Ideo fastum ita detestatus est David, ut profiteri non dubitarit Psalm. 101. vers. 5.

Elatum oculis & tumentem animo ipsum non potero ferre. Laudantur Reges Israel, quod εὐπρόσιτοι fuerint: reprobatur fastus Persicus, qui fecit, ut Rex eorum esset ἀπρόσιτος, neque cuivis eum videre licuerit, ut ex historia Esther constat. Apud Persas, inquit, Justinus lib. 1. Regis persona sub specie Majestatis occulitur. Commendatur etiam Impe- ratoris Musumuli Al. vox in Proverbiis: Pessimus hominum, quem timent homines, stabilire imperi- um nequeunt, qui metui, quam amari malunt. Au- gustinus lib. 5. de Civ. Dei 24. Felices fore Reges, ait; si honoribus & obsequiis non extollantur, si se esse ho- mines meminerint, si ad DEI majestatem & laudem agant. Princeps ut hominibus se imperare norit, ut se DEO inferiorem & seipsum quoque hominem esse cogitet.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

Offerings fall to the Priests and Levites as a possession. The abomination of the nations is forbidden. A great Prophet is promised.

Verse 1. THEY SHALL EAT THE SACRIFICES OF THE LORD AND HIS OFFERINGS. In Hebrew, the ignitions of Jehovah and his inheritance they shall eat; ignitions, that is, sacrifices. For not all sacrifices, but only burnt offerings were entirely consumed by fire; in peace offerings, only the shoulder and the breast were given to the Priest. From the victim for sin, the whole flesh fell to him. By the inheritance of the Lord, they understand the firstfruits and tithes, which He had given as a proper and hereditary possession, in which the Levites participated.

Latin:

CAPUT XIIX.

Sacerdotibus & Levitis pro possessione cedunt oblationes. Prohibita abominatio gentium. Magnus Propheta promissus.

Vers. 1. SACRIFICIA DOMINI ET OBLA- TIONES EJUS COMEDENT. IN Ebr. ignitiones Jehovah & hæreditatem ejus co- medent; ignitiones, id est, sacrificia. Non enim omnia sacrificia, sed holocausta solum tota igni ab- sumebantur, in hostia pacifica armus solum & pectus dabatur Sacerdoti. E victima pro peccato tota ca- ro ipsi obveniebat. Per hæreditatem Domini intel- ligunt primitias & decimas, quas dederat velut pro- priam & hæreditariam possessionem, de qua Levi- tæ participabant.

## 18:3
Verse 3. THEY SHALL GIVE THE PRIEST THE SHOULDER AND THE STOMACH. In Hebrew, the arm, and the jaws, and the stomach. Paulus Fagius on the Chaldean Paraphrase at this place: The animal has three principal parts, the head, the feet, and the trunk of the body, and from each, something is ordered to be given to the offering Priest; from the feet, the right shoulder; from the head, both jaws with the tongue included, as they think; and from the body, the stomach, or as others lead, the pouch in which the milk necessary for the fetus is collected. Therefore, by the fleece of the sheep is understood the wool which is shorn from the sheep every year. The Rabbis, however, fixed the measure so that one part is given out of sixty. This is Fagius. Isidore in allegories: the breast is given to the Priest so that he may have pure thought and knowledge of doctrine; the right arm so that he may have good works and proceed with an armed hand to the battle against the Devil, and that what he has conceived in his heart, he may perfect by the example of works. The jaw is also given from the private [animal], so that he may excel in eloquence; the belly is also given, so that he may extinguish luxury and despise gluttony.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DABUNT SACERTOTI ARMUM AC VENTRICULUM. In Ebr. brachium, & maxillas & ventriculum. Paulus Fagius ad Chald. Paraphr. h. l. Habet pe- cus tres præcipuas partes, caput, pedes, & trun- cum corpus, & de qualibet Sacerdoti offerenti ali- quid dari jubetur, de pedibus armus dexter, de capi- te utraque maxilla cum inclusa lingua ut putant, & de corpore stomachus, aut ut alii ducunt, Sacculus, in quo colligitur lac fœtui necessarium. Proinde per vellus ovium intelligitur lana, quæ singulis annis de- tondetur ab ovibus. Mensuram vero taxaverunt Rabbini, ut de sexaginta partibus una detur. Hæc Fagius. Isidor. in allegor. pectus datur Sacerdoti, ut cogitationem mundam, & doctrinæ habeat noti- tiam: brachium dextrum ut bona opera habeat & ad pugnam contra Diabolum armata manu proce- dat, & quod corde conceperit, operum exemplo per- ficiat. Datur & de privato maxilla, ut eloquentia polleat, datur & venter, ut luxuriam extinguat & gulam contemnat.

## 18:3 Addition
To chapter 18, verse 3, page 585, column a, after our annotation.

The Vulgate interpreter truncated this precept, who recounts only two, namely the shoulder and the stomach: whereas the Hebrew, Chaldean, and the LXX add a third one besides, namely τὰ σιαγόνια, that is, the jaws or the head. The reason for the precept is not obscure. The best things are owed to God and his ministers. The best things are the head with the jaws, which has the brain and the tongue, that is, it is the seat of reason and the instrument of eloquence; the breast, in which the heart is, is the source of life. The right shoulder is the organ of fortitude and strength and of all brave actions. Perhaps God wished to signify by this: that those are finally his true ministers whose thoughts, words, and deeds agree with their heart; or who excel others in industry, eloquence, and life and deserve to be commended, as Episcopius says in Book 3 of his Theological Institutions, chapter 5, number 30, page 89.

Latin:

Ad cap. 18. v. 3. p. 585. a. post annotat. nostra.

Præceptum hoc truncavit vulgatus interpres, qui nonnisi duo recenset, armum scilicet ac ven- triculum: cum Hebræa, Chaldæa & LXX. tertium insuper addant, videlicet τὰ σιαγόνια, id est, ma- xillas seu caput. Ratio præcepti non est obscu- ra. Optima Deo & ministris ejus debentur. Optima sunt caput cum maxillis, quod cerebrum & linguam habet, id est, rationis sedes, & elo- quentiæ instrumentum est; pectus, in quo cor, vitæ fons est. Armus dexter fortitudinis ac ro- boris actionumque omnium fortium organum. Forte eo significatum voluit Deus; Istos demum esse veros ministros suos, quorum cogitata, dicta, ac facta cum corde conveniunt; aut qui industria, elo- quentia, & vita cæteris antestant & commendari merentur, ut ait Episcopius lib. 3. Instit. Theol. c. 5. n. 30. p. 89.

## 18:4
Verse 4. THE FIRSTFRUITS OF THE CORN, OF THE WINE AND OF THE OIL) ראשית in Hebrew, elsewhere תרומה which the Greeks translate ἀφαίρεμα. They were given before the tithe, and it had to be no less than the sixtieth part of the fruits.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PRIMITIAS FRUMENTI, VINI ET OLEI) ראשית in Hebræo, alibi תרומה quod Græci ver- tunt ἀφαίρεμα. Dabantur ante decimam, debebatque non minus esse parte fructuum sexagesima.

## 18:4 Addition
To verse 4, in the same place. Verse 4. AND THE PART OF THE WOOLS FROM THE SHEARING OF THE SHEEP.

Indeed, God wished for his ministers to be provided for liberally, not only regarding food, but also regarding clothing. Moreover, they are called the firstfruits of the shearings, not the first wools that fall off at any shearing, as the Hebrews ineptly seem to wish: but those which are shorn first every year. For the text expressly deals with annual fruits and revenues, as is manifest from the firstfruits of the grain, wine, and oil, to which the firstfruits of the shorn wools are added. They wish for wool to be understood only as that which is shorn from sheep, and is suitable and fit for cloth to be made from it. No wonder. For there is wool only in sheep: other quadrupeds have either hair or bristles. There is no doubt that goats are included under sheep. And because the word for firstfruits does not denote a certain quantity, the Rabbis defined it as the sixtieth part of the shorn wools. As Episcopius has it in the place cited.

Latin:

ad vers. 4. ibidem. vers. 4. ET LANARUM PARTEM EX OVIUM TONSURA.

Nempe ministris suis non de victu tantum, sed & de vestitu prospectum liberaliter voluit Deus. Primitiæ autem tonsurarum vocantur, non primæ lanæ quæ ad quamlibet tonsionem de- cidunt, uti inepte velle videntur Ebræi: sed quæ quotannis primæ detondentur. Diserte enim in tæxtu agitur de annuis fructibus & proventibus, uti ex primitiis frumenti, vini, olei, quibus primi- tiæ lanarum detonsarum accensentur, manife- stum est. Lanam autem intelligi tantum eam volunt, quæ ovibus detondetur, & idonea atque apta est, ut ex ea pannus fiat. Nil mirum. Est enim in solis ovibus lana: cæteræ quadrupedes aut pilos aut setas habent. Sub ovibus autem capras com- prehendi non est dubium. Et quia primitiarum vox certam quantitatem non denotat, eam Sexa- gesima lanarum detonsarum parte definiverunt Rabbini. Ut l. c. habet Episcopius.

## 18:5
Verse 5. THAT HE MAY STAND AND MINISTER TO THE NAME OF THE LORD, HE AND HIS SONS) Since they were few in number, they all ministered together. After there was a great multitude of Priests, classes and turns were wisely instituted by David, 1 Chronicles 24. See what is at Luke 1, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5. VT STET ET MINISTRET NOMINI DO- MINI IPSE ET FILII EJVS) Cum pauci essent numero, si- mul omnes ministrabant. Postquam magna fuit Sacerdo- tum multitudo, sapienter a Davide institutæ classes & vices 1. Paral. 24. Vide quæ ad Lucam 1, 5.

## 18:6
Verse 6. IF A LEVITE SHALL COME OUT OF ONE OF THY CITIES. Certain cities had been designated for the Levites through all the tribes, Numbers 35, 2; Joshua 21, 23. If, therefore, any of them should betake himself from there to the place of the ark out of a desire for divine worship, so that he might minister there, he was to be admitted to the dwelling and the ministry of sacred worship by virtue of this institution, and there he received the same portion as the others. For although the Levites actually ministering did not have a part of the sacrifices, otherwise than Jerome and ab Oleastro think: for the burnt offerings were indeed entirely burned, from the sacrifices for sin or for a male, only the males among the Priests participated, from the peace offerings only the shoulder, both jaws, and the breast fell to the Priests and their households: Levites could indeed be invited by those offering to approach the feasts instituted from sacrificial meats, but that any part of those victims was assigned to them equally as to the Priests is not handed down in the Scriptures: yet it is gathered from equity itself that food was supplied to them from the sacred treasury of the temple, and it can be confirmed from this passage, which some accept in such a way that, beyond that part which was owed to the Levites in their city from the produce of tithes and first fruits, some portion likewise fell to them, as to others ministering at the tabernacle or temple. Others, however, with Pagninus, render the same thus: besides his sales made to the Fathers, or besides things possessed by sale from the Fathers, so that by sales possessions are metonymically noted, as also B. Luther: Über das er hat von dem verkaufften Guth seiner Våter. For although the Levites did not possess lands for agriculture, vineyards, or olive groves, they nevertheless had their cities, in which they could possess houses, feed flocks and herds, and possess other movables either received from parents by hereditary right or bought for a price, and indeed even fields for grazing near the cities for the fodder of their beasts of burden, Jeremiah 32, 7. Which could be enriched when God blessed those portions which returned to them from tithes and firstfruits.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SI EXIERIT LEVITES EX UNA URBIUM TUARUM. Designatæ erant Levitis urbes certæ per omnes tribus Numer. 35, 2. Jos. 31, 23. Si ergo quis eo- rum inde ad locum arcæ studio cultus divini se con- tulerit, ut ibi ministret, ad habitaculum & cultus sacri ministerium admittendus erat, vi hujus in- stitutionis, ibique accipiebat partem eandem, quam cæteri. Etsi enim Levitæ actu ministrantes sacrificiorum partem non habebant, secus atque Hieronym. ab Oleastro putat: holocausta quippe tota cremabantur, ex sacrificiis pro peccato vel masculo soli masculi de Sacerdotibus participabant, ex hostiis pacificis armus, utraque maxilla & pe- ctus solum Sacerdotibus, & eorum domesticis ce- debant: ad epulas ex carnibus sacrificalibus insti- tutas ab offerentibus invitati accedere quidem po- tuere Levitæ, sed illis æque ac Sacerdotibus victi- marum illarum partem aliquam assignatam fuisse, in Scripturis non traditur: Alimenta tamen iis ex sacro templi ærario subministrata fuisse ex æqui- tate ipsa colligitur, & ex hoc loco confirmari potest, quem nonnulli sic accipiunt, quod ultra illam partem, quæ Levitis in civitate sua de pro- ventu decimarum ac primitiarum debebatur, ali- qua portio similiter, ut aliis à tabernaculo vel templo ministrantibus obtigerit. Alii vero cum Pagnino sic eundem reddunt: præter venditiones suas factas Patribus, vel præter res venditione pof- sessas à Patribus, ut per venditiones metonymice notentur possessiones, uti etiam B. Luther. Über das er hat von dem verkaufften Guth seiner Våter. Quamvis enim fundos ad agriculturam, vineæ, oliveta Levitæ non possiderent, habebant tamen urbes suas, in quibus domos possidere poterant, greges & armenta alere, aliaque mobilia vel à parentibus jure hæreditario accepta, vel pretio empta possidere, imo & juxta urbes agros compa- scuos, ad jumentorum pabula habebant Jerem. 32, 7. Quæ locupletari poterant, cum benedixit De- us portionibus istis, quæ ex decimis & primitiis ad eos redibant.

## 18:8
Verse 8. EXCEPT THAT WHICH IS OWED TO HIM IN HIS CITY FROM HIS PATERNAL SUCCESSION) For the Levites could acquire for themselves some movable goods in those cities, the mention of which is in Numbers 35. The suburban fields of those cities which I mentioned were of the whole tribe, and not alienable.

Latin:

Vers. 8. EXCEPTO EO QVOD IN URBE SUA EX PATERNA EI SUCCESSIONE DEBETUR) Poterant enim Levitæ bona aliqua mobilia sibi comparare in urbibus illis, quarum mentio Num. 35. Suburbani illarum quas dixi urbium agri tribus erant totius, & non alienabiles.

## 18:10
Vers. 10. NOR SHALL THERE BE FOUND AMONG YOU ANY ONE WHO MAKES HIS SON OR HIS DAUGHTER PASS THROUGH THE FIRE] Thus also the LXX, οὐχ εὑρεθήσεται ἐν σοὶ περικαθαίρων τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ ἐν πυρί: Whence it appears that מעביר in this place is taken by the interpreters in a milder sense, although otherwise the word is ambiguous, and can also denote killing, as appears in Ezekiel 16, verses 20, 21. Where for the same are placed ותזבחים and ותעביר, and there is added לאכול to sacrifice: which three words you may find in the same meaning in the same Ezekiel 23, v. 37, 38, 39. From which places and Psalm 106, 37, where there is ויזבחו, and most clearly Jeremiah 19, 5, where there is לשרף to burn, it appears that the Canaanites and their neighbors were accustomed to put their children to death in honor of their gods. Thus history testifies in 2 Kings 17, v. 31, that the Sepharvites gave their children to be burned by fire in honor of Adrammelech and Anammelech. The Canaanites especially worshipped Moloch, and in imitation of them, not rarely the Hebrews. Amos 5, v. 26, compared with Acts 7, v. 43, shows this. Leviticus 18, v. 21. That the Canaanites were called both by themselves and by their neighbors those who are Phoenicians to the Greeks, has been shown at Matthew 15, v. 22. There is no doubt that Moloch is Saturn, whose star is even now called by that name by the Hebrews: namely, because of the seven stars by which mortals are ruled, the star of Saturn is carried in the highest orbit and with the greatest power, as Tacitus speaks in History 5. This name was given to that star from a King whose name was Χ; but who, as preeminent among Kings, was called ἀντονομασικῶς מלך. Philo of Byblos relates from Sanchuniathon, the most ancient writer of Phoenician affairs, that it was the custom of the nations of that region that when the greatest public calamities were feared, the Kings of the peoples would put to death the son whom they loved most to appease the wrath of the gods. And indeed this sacrifice was not performed by a common death, but by a solemn and ancient ceremony. That the Phoenician King, who after death was consecrated by his people into the Star of Saturn (for the Phoenicians, to use the words of Philo, ἐξαιρέτως ἀπὸ τῶν σφετέρων βασιλέων τοῖς κοσμικοῖς στοιχείοις τὰς ὀνομασίας ἐπέθεσαν), when the greatest danger from war was impending, having placed his only son, whom he had, upon the altar with royal ceremony and sacrificed him there, averted the public destruction by a domestic one. In which place It is written by Philo of Byblos: 'Cronus, whom the Phoenicians call Israel,' where certain eminent men think that Israel is named for Abraham, and that the history of the sacrificed Isaac is indicated with some corruption. But it seems more credible to me that the copyist of Eusebius, who recites the words of Philo of Byblos, erred; for where 'Il' was written, he thought it was an abbreviation for 'Israel,' such as often occurs in the manuscripts of Greek Christians. For that King, who was consecrated by his people into that most high star, had the name 'Il'—just as Enoch had the name 'Idris'—as Philo himself teaches us from Sanchuniathon in these words: 'Il, who is also Cronus.' For the Syrians pronounced what the Hebrews call 'El' as 'Ail,' just as also in Ezekiel 30:11 and 32:21, of which prophet many things incline toward the Syrian dialect. But because that King was believed to have greatly deserved well of his country by sacrificing his son, therefore those who were afterwards in similar danger sacrificed their own children to that same King, who had been elevated among the gods under the name of that star. Porphyry teaches this from the same Sanchuniathon and his interpreter Philo of Byblos, whom he cites in the second book of 'On Abstinence': 'The Phoenicians,' he says, 'in the greatest dangers from war, famine, or pestilence, would sacrifice to Saturn one of their dearest, chosen by public vote for that purpose.' Porphyry adds that the history of Sanchuniathon was full of such victims. That 'Il,' as I said, was called 'Melech' antonomastically, which the Hebrews now express with other words, and was formerly expressed with other sounds, sometimes even with the addition 'Molech,' as in Amos 5:25, where the LXX have 'the tabernacle of Moloch,' Aquila 'Melchom,' just as the Syrian and Arab have placed in Acts 7:43: So also Jeremiah 49:3. But Symmachus, where the LXX have 'Moloch,' translates it either as 'king' or 'ruler.' Giving children to Moloch in Leviticus 20:2 seems correctly understood as burning, because the penalty of death is added there, which is not the case here, nor in Leviticus 18:21. Sophocles in 'Andromeda':

For it is the law among the barbarians to sacrifice the human race to Cronus from the beginning.

Josephus on Ahaz: 'He burned his own son according to the customs of the Canaanites.' Jerome also mentions this custom in his commentary on Jeremiah 7:37. Curtius teaches us that the chief of the Phoenicians or Canaanites were the Tyrians, among whom it was a most ancient custom to sacrifice a free-born boy, and he says the Carthaginians performed this sacrifice, handed down by their founders [namely, the Tyrians], until the destruction of their city. The Carthaginians are Poeni, that is, Phoenicians: just as in Horace, both Poenus is a Syrophoenician and a Libyphoenician. Ennius on the Poeni:

The Poeni were accustomed to sacrifice their boys.

Plato in 'Minos': 'For us, the law is not to sacrifice humans, but it is unholy. But the Carthaginians sacrifice them, as if it were holy and lawful for them; and these are some of their own sons to Cronus, as perhaps you have heard.'
