Justin from Trogus, book 18, on the same Carthaginians: 'When among other evils they were also suffering from a plague, they used a bloody religion of sacrifices and crime as a remedy: for they sacrificed men as victims: and they brought infants (an age which even provokes the mercy of enemies) to the altars, seeking the peace of the gods with the blood of those for whose life the gods are most accustomed to be asked.' Plutarch has the same about them in his book 'On Superstition.' But Silius Italicus:

It was the custom among the peoples whom the stranger Dido founded to seek favor from the gods with slaughter, and to place small children—unspeakable to say—upon the blazing altars.

Lactantius, book 1, chapter 31. Pescenius Festus in his book of history 'per saturam' reports that the Carthaginians were accustomed to sacrifice human victims to Saturn, and when they had been defeated by Agathocles, King of the Sicilians, they thought the God was angry with them: therefore, to pay the atonement more diligently, they sacrificed two hundred sons of nobles. Minucius in 'Octavius': 'In some parts of Africa, infants were sacrificed to Saturn by their parents, with caresses and a kiss suppressing their crying, so that a weeping victim might not be sacrificed.' Augustine, 'City of God' 7, chapter 19: 'Therefore, by some, boys were accustomed to be sacrificed to Saturn, as by the Poeni.' Tertullian, 'Scorpiace': 'It was permitted in the world that the Saturn of the Africans be appeased by human victims.' The same in his 'Apology': 'Since Saturn did not spare his own children, he persisted in not sparing strangers, whom indeed their own parents offered, and willingly responded, and caressed the infants so that they would not be sacrificed while weeping.' Where note that point consistent with the history of the Tyrians, that Saturn did not spare his own children, namely because he himself sacrificed them: whence he is said by the Greeks to have eaten them, who took the ambiguous word 'le-ekol,' which signifies both to eat and to consume by fire, in that more common sense. Diodorus Siculus explains the custom of this sacrifice thus. He says that at Carthage there was a bronze statue of Saturn (such as the Jews affirm the Moloch of the Canaanites to have been) which had hands turned upward toward the ground, but under which there was fire: all Spaniards testify that such statues were found in those islands of America which face Africa, and, as is credible, the inhabitants and rites were received from there, which could be confirmed by other evidence if it were necessary. The Jews add that while the boy was being burned, the spectators would make noise with dances and drums, so that the wailing would not be heard: which very thing the Jew Benjamin records was done on an island in the Indian Ocean, which he calls Chenaragam, having received the rite, as is credible, from the Tyrians, who sailed that ocean long ago. Also on the island of Crete there were many Phoenician colonies: among which was Citrium. Here too boys were sacrificed, and indeed to Saturn, Ister revealed in his collection of Cretan sacred rites, as Porphyry testifies. Hence Athenagoras: 'The Phoenicians and Cretans worshipped Cronus with child-slaughter.' These are the 'child-slaughtering rites': which the writer of Wisdom mentions in 14:23, on account of which the same writer calls those who held the promised land before the Hebrews, 'merciless slayers of children' in 12:5. Philo on the same in his book 'On Abraham': 'But they considered barbaric customs with much child-slaughter as a holy and God-pleasing work.' Procopius is witness that such rites remained among the Blemmyes, who lived between the Arabian Gulf and the Nile, until the times of Justinian. Concerning the Dumæti in Arabia, you have the same in Porphyry. The Hebrews, having imitated these in their often corrupt customs, especially in Topheth, which is also the valley of the sons of Hinnom, 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chronicles 28:3, Jeremiah 7:31, 19:5. Therefore, that in other times or places children were only led through the fire by their parents or purified by fire, is a vestige and imitation of a most savage custom: such temperaments or σοφὰ φάρμακα (wise remedies) a later age has found everywhere. Thus, in Laodicea of Syria, Porphyry teaches in the aforementioned book that a hind was substituted for the sacrifice of a virgin: in Cyprus, an ox for a man: in Egypt, wax figures made in the human likeness. Thus the Pelasgians once sacrificed a man to Saturn according to an ancient oracle: Καὶ κεφαλὰς Κρονίδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα (And send heads to the son of Cronus and to the father, O lights). Later there existed those who said they could be discharged if they threw a torch. Ovid, Lactantius, and Macrobius mention this, who also commemorates other similar amendments of sacrifices in book 1 of the Saturnalia. chapter 7. Arnobius, narrating the same matter, says that the custom was changed by them through a cunning fraud and the ambiguity of names. Thus, instead of real men, you have men made of straw thrown into the Tiber in Ovid’s Fasti, book 5. Something similar also happened among the Phoenicians. For when an ancient oracle commanded boys to be העביר באש (passed through the fire), and for a long time that ambiguous word had been accepted in the sense of consuming, a kinder interpretation wished for Moloch or Saturn to be satisfied by the body being led through the flame, as Tertullian speaks, where he describes the rites of the Valentinians drawn from pagan superstition. Ferdinand Mendes Pinto, the Portuguese, narrates that he saw the same custom of passing boys through the fire on the maritime coast of Asiatic India, a custom accepted, as is credible, also by the Phoenicians. For in the Indian island of Chenaraga, that Benjamin whom I mentioned says he found both rites: both that of burning sons, and the other of purifying them by leading them through the fire. Maimonides likewise, thinking more correctly than other Jews, acknowledges both customs in his section on idolatry, chapter 6. Thus also Rabbi Simeon in the book Jaikuth. The custom of passing through the fire came through the Phoenicians into Sicily (for Scylax and others teach us that the Phoenicians were in Sicily), and from there to Rome. Varro, in the Scholiast of Horace: The Palilia are both private and public among the rustics, so that when they have thrown stubble with hay, they jump over a great fire, believing themselves to be purified by these Palilia. The same custom remained for a long time in Africa, as witnessed by Leo Africanus, nor did it pass into Brazil from elsewhere, as I think. Whether Christians received it from the Africans or from the Romans can be doubted: but Chrysostom in his sermon on the Nativity of St. John, Theodoret on the last book of Kings chapter 16, and the Synod in Trullo, Canon 65, mention and condemn it. And it is more truly treated here because of those things which we have already said.

Grotius observes here, among other things, that the Canaanites especially worshipped Moloch and that the Hebrews also did so not infrequently in imitation of them, which he shows from Amos 5:25, Acts 7:43, Leviticus 18:21. But that Moloch was Saturn, which name was given to that star by a certain king of the Phoenicians who sacrificed his son to avert a public calamity, called Ἴλ, but who was called מלך (Melech) ἀντονομασικῶς (by antonomasia) as an eminent one among kings, he teaches from Sanchuniathon and others. You may read things similar to these in Eusebius, book 4 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 7, who also makes Saturn a king of Phoenicia, who after his death was enrolled in the number of the gods and believed to have migrated into the star of Saturn, but to whom his wife Anobreth sacrificed her only son, whom she had conceived by Saturn. Whence the poets attribute to Saturn that he devours his own sons. Concerning which some things are also found in Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius, and Orosius about children sacrificed to Saturn. Ludovicus de Dieu on Leviticus.

20, 2. He says that the idol of the Ammonites from 1 Kings 2, 5 was already known to the Israelites in the desert, when they had gone out from Egypt, which is clear from that passage in Leviticus 20, 2. Moreover, that the Egyptians called Mars thus, to whom Saturn was called Ρηφαν. This idolatry seems to have been propagated from the Ammonites to the Phoenicians, Punics, and Canaanites, and from these to the Israelites. Compare 1 Chron. 18, 21; Deut. 12, 31; 2 Kings 23, 13; Jer. 49, 1; Amos 1, 16; Ps. 105, 35. And it is probable that it proceeded from the κακοζηλία (misguided zeal) of the immolation of the Son commanded to Abraham, which the Ammonites had heard from Lot, and the idol was named Moloch, because that god was believed to be the king of the other gods, and was conspicuous in royal attire, as the Hebrews observed, with Lyranus in Leviticus 18 as witness. Although John Selden in Syntagma lib. 1 de Diis Syris cap. 6, p. 198, makes that feral cult, which was performed by the slaughter of boys, much older, according to Suidas and Aben Batrich. inasmuch as it had already begun under the beginnings of Hellenism or the age of Sheruch. But let philologists discuss these things.

Verse same. OR WHO CONSULTS DIVINERS] In Greek, μαντευόμενος μαντείαν. A species of this is βελομαντεία (belomancy), concerning which we shall speak at Ezekiel 21, where קסם קסמים is as it is here. In Hebrew, divining divinations. It is not about those who seek, but those who render divinations. Luther renders it 'Weissage' (soothsayer). Glossa ordinaria: Diviners go around altars with wicked prayers and seek divination in the entrails of animals.

AND OBSERVES DREAMS. Thus the Vulgate referred the word מעונן here and in Leviticus 19, 26 and 2 Chronicles 33, 6 to dreams; the Chaldean, 'observing days'; B. Luther, 'Tagewehler' (day-chooser); Osiand. wishes to denote those who promise that they will cure men or beasts with certain incantations.

AND AUGURIES. Thus some Hebrews: he who notices the flight and chirping of birds; B. Luth., 'der auf Vogelgeschrey achtet' (he who heeds bird-cries). But B. Gerhard rightly observes that similar superstitious divinations of a future thing are also noted, which were snatched by the vigilant from any thing whatsoever, such as, for example, auspices, extispicy, tripudia, solistima, judicial astrology, hydromancy by water, oenomancy by wine, coskinomancy by a sieve, lecanomancy by a basin, gastromancy by belly-shaped vials full of water, dactylomancy by rings, catoptromancy by mirrors, cleidomancy by a key, chiromancy by inspection of the hands, pyromancy by inspection of fire, capnomancy by inspection of smoke, libanomancy by inspection of incense, spodomancy by the ashes of sacrifices, ceromancy from melted wax, daphnomancy from the burning of laurel, geomancy from the inspection of certain figures marked out on the ground, all superstitious lots and other illicit divinations of this kind, as also all superstitious things accustomed to be sought from various things, such as from the meeting of an Ethiopian, a hare, an old woman, some ill-omened beast, etc., from the stumbling of feet on a threshold, from the noise of a door, from the ringing of ears, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 10. NEC INVENIATVR IN TE QVI LU- STRET FILIUM SUUM AUT FILIAM PER IGNEM] Sic & LXX. ὐχ ἐυρεθήσεται ἐν σοὶ περικαθαίρων τὸν ὑἱὸν ἀυτῦ κὰι τὴν θυγατέρα ἀυτῦ ἐν πυρί: Unde apparet מעביר hoc loco sumtum ab interpretibus in sensu molliore, cum ali- oqui vox sit ambigua, & interfectionem quoque notare pos- sit, ut apparet Ezech. 16. versu 20. 21. Vbi pro eodem po- nuntur ותזבחים & ותעביר, additurque לאכול immolare: quæ tria verba in eodem significatu reperias apud eundem Ezechielem 23. v. 37. 38. 39. Ex quibus locis & Psalm. 106, 37. ubi est ויזבחו, & apertissime Jerem. 19, 5. ubi est לשרף com- burere, apparet Cananæos & eorum vicinos solitos morti dare liberos suos in Deorum suorum honorem. Ita Sephar- væos in honorem Adramelechi & Hanamelechi liberos suos igni comburendos dedisse testatur historia 2. Reg. 17. v. 31. Cananæi maxime Molochum colebant, & eorum imitatio- ne non raro Hebræi. Ostendit id Amos 5. v. 26. collatus cum Act. 7. v. 43. Levit. 18. v. 21. Cananæos & sibi & vici- nis dictos, qui Phœnices Græcis, ostensum est ad Matth. 15. v. 22. Moloch non dubitandum quin sit Saturnus, cujus stel- la & nunc eo nomine ab Hebræis vocatur: nimirum quod e septem sideribus, queis mortales reguntur, altissimo orbe & præcipua potentia stella Saturni feratur, ut loquitur Tacitus Hist. 5. Nomen hoc ei astro datum a Rege cui nomen Χ; sed qui, ut eximius inter Reges, ἀντονομασικῶς dictus מלך. Narrat ex Sanchuniathone antiquissimo rerum Phœnices scriptore Philo Byblius, morem fuisse gentibus illius tra- ctus, ut cum maximæ calamitates publicæ metuerentur, po- pulorum Reges filium, quem diligerent maxime, morti darent ad placandam deorum iram. Neque vero communi morte, sed solenni veterique ceremonia hoc sacrificium peractum. Ei mori obsequentem Regem Phœnicum, qui post mortem in Sidus Saturni a suis fuit consecratus (nam Phœnices, ut Philonis utar verbis, ἐξαιρέτως ἀπὸ τῶν σφετέρων βασιλέων τοῖς κοσμικοῖς στοιχείοις τὰς ὀνομασίας ἐπέθεσαν) cum ma- ximum ex bello periculum immineret, filio quem habe- bat unicum regio cultu in aram imposito atque inibi sacri- ficato publicum exitium domestico avertisse. Quo in loco Philonis Byblii scribitur: Κρόνον ὃν οἱ Φοίνικες Ἰσραὴλ προσ- αγορεύουσι, ubi quidam viri egregii Ἰσραὴλ pro Abrahamo nominatum, & Isaaci immolati historiam cùm quadam de- pravatione indicari existimant. At credibilius mihi vide- tur exscriptorem Eusebii, qui Philonis Byblii verba recitat, errasse, qui ubi Ἶλ erat scriptum, putavit compendium esse pro Ἰσραὴλ, quale sæpe in manuscriptis Græcorum Christia- norum occurrit. Regi enim illi, qui in sidus illud altissimum consecratus a suis est, nomen fuisse Ἶλ, ut Enocho nomen יהוד, ipse ille Philo ex Sanchuniathone nos docet his ver- bis: Ἶλον τὸν καὶ κρόνον. Syri enim id quod Hebræi dicunt אל pronuntiabant איל, quomodo & Ezechiel 30. v. 11. c. 32. vers. 21. cujus Prophetæ multa ad Syriacam dialectum declinant. Quia vero Rex ille patriam filio immolato ma- xime demeritus credebatur, ideo qui in simili periculo post- ea erant, eidem illi Regi in deos sub astri illius nomine re- lato suos liberos sacrificabant. Docet hoc ex eodem San- chuniathone & ejus interprete Philone Byblio, quos aucto- res laudat Porphyrius περὶ ἀποχῆς secundo: Phœnices, in- quit, in maximis periculis ex bello, frugum inopia, pestilen- tia, carissimorum aliquem publicis suffragiis ad id delectum sacrificabant Saturno. Addit Porphyrius talium victimarum plenam fuisse Sanchuniathonis historiam. Is autem Ἶλ, ut di- xi ἀντονομαστικῶς מלך dictus, quod aliis nunc Hebræi ef- ferunt, aliis vocibus olim efferebatur, aliquando & cum ad- ditamento מלכם, ut in Amoso 5. vers. 25. ubi LXX. τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ Μολὸχ, Aquila Μελχὸμ, quomodo, & Syrus & Arabs in Actis 7. v. 43. posuere: Sic & Jerem. 49, 3. At Symmachus ubi LXX. habent Μολόχ, vertit aut βασιλέα, aut ἄρχοντα. Dare filios Molocho Levitici 20. vers. 2. recte vi- detur de combustione accipi, quia mortis pœna ibi additur, quæ hîc non est, nec Levitici 18. v. 21. Sophocles Andromeda:

Νόμος γάρ ἐστι τοῖσι βαρβάροις Κρόνῳ Θυηπολεῖν βρότειον ἀρχῆθεν γένος.

Josephus de Achazo: ἴδιον ὡλοκάυτωσε παῖδα κατὰ τὰ Κα- ναναίων ἤθη meminit ejus moris & Hieronymus ad Jerem. 7. vers. 37. Phœnicum sive Cananæorum præcipui Tyrii, apud quos vetustissimum fuisse morem, immolare puerum Ingenu- um, docet nos Curtius, aitque sacrum Carthaginienses a con- ditotibus [Tyriis scilicet] traditum usque ad excidium urbis suæ fecisse. Carthaginienses Pœni, id est, Φοίνικες: sicut Ho- ratio uterque Pœnus est Syrophœnix & Libyphœnix. Ennius de Pœnis:

Pœni sunt soliti sos sacrificare puellos.

Plato Minoe: ἡμῖν μὲν ὀ νόμος ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπους θύειν, ἀλλ' ἀνόσιον. Καρχηδόνιοι δὲ θύουσι, ὡς ὅσιον ὃν καὶ νόμιμον ἀυτοῖς; καὶ ταῦτα ἔνιοι ἀυτῶν ὑιεῖς τῷ Κρόνῳ ὡς ἴσως καὶ ἀκήκοας. Justi- nus ex Trogo libro 18. de Carthaginiensibus eisdem: Cum inter cætera mala etiam peste laborarent, cruenta sacrorum religione & scelere pro remedio usi sunt: quippe homines, ut vi- ctimas immolabant: & impuberes (quæ ætas etiam hostium misericordiam provocat) aris admovebant, pacem deorum san- guine eorum exposcentes, pro quorum vita dii rogari maxime so- lent. Idem de iis habet Plutarchus libro de superstitione. Si- lius autem Italicus:

Mos fuit in populis quos condidit advena Dido Poscere cæde deos veniam, ac flagrantibus aris Infandum dictu parvos imponere natos.

Lactantius libro 1. cap. 31. Pescenius Festus in libro Histor. per saturam refert, Carthaginienses Saturno humanas hostias solitos immolare, & cum victi essent ab Agathocle Rege Siculorum, ira- tum sibi Deum putavisse: itaque ut diligentiùs piaculum solve- rent, ducentos nobilium filios immolasse. Minutius Octavio: Saturno in nonnullis Africæ partibus a parentibus infantes im- molabantur, blanditiis & osculo comprimente vagitum, ne fle- bilis hostia immoletur. Augustinus de Civit. Dei 7. c. 19. Ideo a quibusdam pueri Saturno soliti sunt immolari, ut a Pœnis. Tertullianus Scorpiace: Afrorum Saturnum bominum victi- ma placari apud sæculum licuit. Idem Apologetico: Cum propriis filiis Saturnus non pepercerit, extraneis utique non parcendo perseverabat, quos quidem ipsi parentes sui offere- bant, & libenter respondebant, & infantibus blandiebantur, ne lacrymantes immolarentur. Vbi nota illud historiæ Tyrio- rum congruens, Saturnum suis liberis non pepercisse, nimi- rum quod eos ipse immolaverit: unde eos comedisse dicitur a Græcis, qui vocem ambiguam לאכול, quæ & comedere & igne consumere significat, usitatiore illo sensu accepere. Morem ejus sacrificii sic explicat Siculus Diodorus. Ait Carthagine æneam fuisse Saturni statuam: (qualem scilicet & Molochi apud Cananæos fuisse Judæi affirmant) quæ ma- nus haberet supinas supra terram, sed quibus ignis subesset: cujusmodi statuas omnes Hispani testantur repertas in illis Americæ insulis, quæ Africam contra spectant, &, ut credi- cred- bile est, inde habitatores & ritus accepere, quod aliis quoque indiciis, si id opus esset, posset confirmari. Addunt Judæi, dum comburebatur puer, choreis ac tympanis circumstre- puisse spectatores, ne ploratus exaudiretur: quod ipsum in maris Indici insula, quam Chenaragam vocat, factitatum me- morat Judæus Benjamin, accepto, ut credibile est, a Tyriis, qui eum Oceanum jam olim navigarunt, ritu. Etiam in Creta insula plurimæ Phœnicum coloniæ: inter quas Citri- um. Hic quoque sacrificatos pueros, & quidem Saturno, Ister in collectione Creticorum sacrorum prodidit, testante Porphyrio. Hinc Athenagoras: Φοίνικες καὶ Κρῆτες τὸν Κρό- νον ἐν ταῖς τεκνοφονίαις ἐθρήσκευον. Hæ sunt τεκνοφόνοι τε- λεταί: quarum meminit Scriptor Sapientiæ 14. v. 23. propter quas illos qui terram promissam Hebræis ante Hebræos tenu- ere, idem Scriptor vocat τέκνων φονέας ἀνελεήμονας 12, 5. Philo de iisdem libro de Abrahamo: βαρβαρικὰ δὲ ἔθη με- τὰ πολλῇ παιδοκτονίαν ὡς ὅσιον ἔργον καὶ θεοφιλὲς προσέδοξεν. Apud Blemyas qui inter Arabicum sinum ac Nilum cole- bant, talia sacra ad Justiniani mansisse tempora, testis est Pro- copius. De Dumætiis in Arabia idem apud Porphyrium ha- bes. Hos imitati sæpe corruptis moribus Hebræi, maxime in Topheth, quæ & vallis filiorum Hinnom, 2. Reg. 23. v. 2. 2. Paral. 28. vers. 3. Jerem. 7. v. 31. 19. v. 5. Quod ergo aliis temporibus aut locis liberi a parentibus tantum per ignem traducti aut igne lustrati sunt, vestigium est & imitatio sæ- vissimi moris: qualia temperamenta aut σοφὰ φάρμακα pas- sim ferior ætas invenit. Sic in Laodicea Syriæ pro virginis sacrificio cervam substitutam docet Porphyrius dicto jam li- bro: in Cypro pro homine bovem: in Ægypto cereos factos ad humanam effigiem. Sic Pelasgi olim Saturno hominem sacrificabant ex oraculo veteri: Καὶ κεφαλὰς Κρονίδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα. Postea extitere qui dixere defungi eos posse si facem jacerent. Meminere Ovidius, Lactantius, Macrobius, qui & alias simi- les sacrificiorum emendationes commemorat lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. 7. Arnobius eandem rem narrans, ait ab eis morem fraude callidula & nominum ambiguitate mutatum. Sic pro hominibus veris nudos in Tiberim homines stramineos habes apud Ovidium Fastorum 5. Tale aliquid & apud Phœ- nicas accidit. Cum enim oraculum vetus juberet pueros העביר באש, diuque verbum illud ambiguum acceptum esset in sensu consumendi, benignior interpretatio Molochum sive Saturnum contentum esse voluit, traducto corpore flam- ma, ut Tertullianus loquitur, ubi Valentini ritus e paganica superstitione haustos describit. Eundem morem trajiciendi per ignem pueros vidisse se in ora Indiæ Asiaticæ maritima narrat Ferdinandus Mendes Pinto Lusitanus, acceptum ut credibile est, & hunc a Phœnicibus. Nam in Chenaraga In- diæ insula, is quem dixi Benjamin repertum dicit ritum utrumque, & comburendi filios, & alterum eos lustrandi per ignem traductos. Maimonides itidem, rectius quam Judæi alii sapiens, utrumque morem agnoscit de idololatria sectio- ne 3. cap. 6. Sic & Rabbi Simeon libro Jaikuth. Venit mos trajiciendi per ignem per Phœnicas in Siciliam, [nam Phœni- cas in Sicilia fuisse Scylax & alii nos docent) inde Romam. Varro apud Scholiasten Horatii: Palilia tam privata quam publica sunt apud rusticos, ut cum fœno conjectis stipulis ignem magnum transiliant, bis Palilibus se expiari credentes. Man- sit idem mos diu in Africa teste Leone Afro, nec aliunde, ut puto, in Brasiliam transiit. Ab Afris an a Romanis Christia- ni acceperint, dubitari potest: Sed memorant & damnant Chrysostomus in Nativitate S. Johannis, Theodoretus in ul- timum librum Regum cap. 16. Synodus in Trullo Canone 65. Et de hoc more hîc agi verius ob ea quæ jam diximus.

Observat hîc inter alia Grotius, Cananæos ma- xime Molochum coluisse & eorum imitatione Ebræos quoque non raro, quod ex Amos. 5, 25. Actor. 7, 43. Levit. 18, 21. ostendit. Molochum autem fuisse Sa- turnum, quod nomen ei astro à Phœnicum rege quo- dam qui filium calamitatem publicam avertendi cau- sa immolavit, Ἴλ dicto, sed qui ἀντονομασικῶς, ut eximius inter reges מלך nuncupatus fuit, è Sanchu- niathone, & aliis docet. Gemina his legas apud Eu- se bium 4. de præpar. Evangel. cap. 7. qui Saturnum etiam facit Phœniciæ regem, qui post mortem in Deorum numerum relatus, in sidus Saturni com- migrasse creditus fuerit, sed cui Anobreth conjux ejus filium unicum, quem ex Saturno susceperat, immolarit. Unde Poetæ Saturno tribuunt, quod filios suos devoret. Quo de etiam apud Clement. A- lex. Lactant. Orosium reperiuntur nonnulla de libe- ris Saturno immolatis. Ludovicus de Dieu ad Levit.

20, 2. dicit fuisse idolum Ammonitarum e 1. Reg. 2, 5. notum jam Israelitis in deserto, quum ex Ægypto egressi essent, quod ex isto loco Levit. 20, 2. liqueat. Ægyptios autem sic vocasse Martem, quibus Saturnus Ρηφαν dictus fuerit. Videtur hæc idololatria ab Ammonitis ad Phœnices, Pœnos, & ad Cananæos, ab his ad Israelitas propagata. Conf. 1. Chron. 18, 21. Deuter. 12, 31. 2. Reg, 23, 13. Jer. 49, 1. Amos. 1, 16. Ps. 105, 35, Et probabile est per κακοζηλίαν demandatæ Abrahamo immolationis Filii, quam Ammonitæ a Lotho audiverant, eandem profectam esse, idolumque Moloch nominatum, quod Deus ille cæterorum Deorum rex crederetur, & regio habitu conspicuus fuerit, ut Ebræi observarunt, Lyrano in Levit. 18. teste. Quanquam multo antiquiorem feralem illum, qui puerorum mactatione præstabatur, cultum e Suida, Aben Batrich faciat Joh. Seldenus Syntag. lib. 1. de Diis Syris cap. 6. p. 198. utpote sub initiis Hellenismi aut Sheruchi ævo jam cœptum. Sed hæc Philologi discutiant.

Vers. eod. AVT QVI ARIOLOS SCISCITETVR] Græce, μαντευόμενος μαντείαν. Hujus species βελομαντεία, de qua dicemus ad Ezech. 21. ubi קסם קסמים ut hic. In Ebr. divinans divinationes. Non de quærentibus, sed reddentibus divinationes agitur. Luth. reddit Weissage. Glossa ordinaria: Arioli circumeunt aras nefandis precibus & divinationem in extis animalium quærunt.

ET OBSERVET SOMNIA. Ita Vulgat. vocem מעונן hic & Levit. 19, 26. 2. Paral. 33, 6. ad somnia retulit; Chald. observans dies, B. Luther. Tagewehler, Osiand. eos notari vult, qui certis incantationibus homines, aut jumenta se curaturos promittunt.

ATQVE AVGVRIA, Sic Ebræi nonnulli: qui avium volatum & garritum advertit, B. Luth. der auf Vogelgeschrey achtet. Recte autem observat B. Gerhard. etiam similes rei futuræ divinationes superstitiosas notari, quæ ex quacunque re a vigilantibus captabantur, quales sunt v. g. auspicia, extispicia, tripudia, solistima, Astrologia judiciaria, hydromantia per aquam, œnomantia per vinum, Coskinomantia per cribrum, lecanomantia per pelvim, gastromantia per phialas ventricosas aqua plenas, dactylomantia per annulos, catophomantia per specula, clidomantia per clavem, chiromantia per inspectionem manuum, pyromantia per inspectionem ignis, capnomantia per inspectionem fumi, libanomantia per inspectionem thuris, spodonomantia per cineres sacrificiorum, ceromantia ex cera liquata, daphnomantia ex lauri adustione, geomantia ex certarum figurarum in solo dispunctarum inspectione, fortes omnes superstitiosæ & hujusmodi aliæ divinationes illicitæ, ut & superstitiosa omnia ex variis rebus peti solita, utpote ex occursu Æthiopis, leporis, vetulæ, bestiæ alicujus infaustæ &c. ex pedum in limine offensione, ex ostii strepitu, ex aurium tinnitu &c,

## 18:11
Verse 11. NOR BE A SORCERER NOR AN ENCHANTER] In Greek, ἐπαείδων ἐπαοιδήν. חבר חבר, which is here, is also found in Ps. 58, where it treats of that which is in Virgil: 'by singing the snake is broken.' Pliny, book 28, verse 2: Many believe that the works of potters are broken in such a way, and not a few also that serpents themselves are charmed back. And that this is one of those understood, and that even in nocturnal quiet they are drawn by the song of the Marsi. The Hebrews render the word מכשף as a prestidigitator, such as the magi were in Egypt, Exod. 7, 11. Luther, 'ein Zauberer' (a sorcerer). חֹבֵר חָבֶר is 'joining a society,' who with his incantations gathers many animals (serpents, scorpions) into one place, Psalm 58, 6; Proverb 25, 24; Isaiah 47, 9, 12. The Rabbis, a conjurer of demons; Luther, 'einen Beschwerer' (an exorcist/conjurer).

The Hebrew word אוב denotes a bottle or small flask. Whence they say it is applied to those who seem to speak with a dull voice as if from a bottle or a cage; the Hebrews thus: אוב is he between whose thighs a dead person ascends and sits, or speaking from between his armpits in a very low voice, as if it proceeded from the lower parts of the earth. The LXX render it ἐγγαστριμύθους (ventriloquists). Tertullian, lib. 4 adv. Marc. Vulgate, 'consulting a Python.' Pythons are so called from the Pythian woman, from whose private parts an unclean demon is said to have given responses, and they are called so both those who had a demon in their belly giving responses, and the demons themselves speaking from the belly's hovel, Levit. 18, 31; Acts 16, 16. See Chrysostom, hom. 29 in 1 Corinth.; Fagius in the notes of the Chaldean paraphrase, Levit. 19, 31.

NOR DIVINERS.

The Hebrew word ידעני does not denote him who consults diviners, but the diviner himself. LXX, τερατοσκόπον (observer of portents) and interpreter: Luther, 'ein Zeichendeuter' (a sign-interpreter), who conjectures future things from superstitious signs and conjectures of things, inasmuch as he divines from the inspection of a horoscope, the crackling of laurel, the lines of the hands, or similar things, as our blessed Gerhard does here.

AND SEEK TRUTH FROM THE DEAD.

Thus according to the Hebrew text, the Chaldean, the LXX, the Vulgate, Luther, and others. But those who seek from the dead are necromancers, who, after they have macerated themselves, betake themselves to cemeteries and, oppressed by sleep next to the bones of the dead, proclaim that they see wonderful things in dreams, or even evoke shadows or the dead for the sake of inquiring something.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NEC SIT MALEFICVS NEC INCANTATOR) Græce ἐπαείδων ἐπαοιδήν. חבר חבר, quod hic est etiam Ps. 58. reperitur, ubi de eo agitur quod apud Virgilium est, cantando rumpitur anguis. Plinius libro 28. vers. 2. Figulinarum opera multi rumpi credunt tali modo, non pauci etiam serpentes ipsos recantare. Et hunc unum esse ex ipsis intellectum, contrahique Marsorum cantu etiam in nocturna quiete. Vocem מכשף Ebræi præstigiatorcm reddunt, quales magi erant in Ægypto Exod. 7, 11. Lutherus, ein Zauberer. חֹבֵר חָבֶר est consocians societatem, qui conjurationibus suis multa animalia (serpentes, scorpiones, in unum locum congregat Psalm. 58, 6. Proverb. 25, 24. Esa. 47, 9. 12. Rabbini conjuratorem Dæmonum, Lutherus einen Beschwerer.

Vox Ebr. אוב utrum seu lagunculam notat. Un- de de iis adhiberi ajunt, qui obtusa voce tanquam ex laguncula aut cavea loqui videantur, Ebræi ita: אוב est, inter cujus femora afcendit & sedet mortuus, vel inter axillas ejus loquens admodum submissa vo- ce, ac si ex inferioribus terræ ea prodiret. LXX. ἐγγα- στριμύθες (ventriloquos) reddunt. Tertullian. lib. 4. adv. Marc. Vulgat. consulens Pythonem. Pythones à Pythia muliere dicuntur, ex cujus pudendis im- mundus dæmon responsa dedisse dicitur, & vocantur ita tum ii qui in ventre dæmonem responsa dantem haberent, tum ipsi dæmones ex ventris gurgustio loquentes Levit. 18, 31. Actor. 16, 16. Vid. Chryso- stom. hom. 29. in 1. Corinth. Fagius in not. paraphr. Chald. Levit. 19, 31.

NEC DIVINOS.

Vox Ebræa ידעני non eum notat, qui consulit divinos, sed divinum ipsum. LXX. τερατοσκόπον portentorum inspectorem & interpretem: Lutherus, ein Zeichendeuter, qui ex superstitiosis rerum notis & conjecturis res futuras conjectat, utpote qui ex horoscopi inspectione, lauri crepitu, manuum linea- mentis vel similibus divinat, uti hic Gerhardus no- ster ὁ μακαρίτης.

ET QUÆRAT A MORTUIS VERITA- TEM.

Ita juxta Ebræum textum Chald. LXX. Vulgatus, Lutherus, aliique. Quærentes autem à mortuis sunt necromantæ, qui postquam se macerarunt, ad cœ- miteria se conferunt & juxta ossa mortuorum sopo- re oppressi mira se in somniis videre prædicant, vel etiam umbras aut mortuos aliquid indagandi ergo evocant.

## 18:14
BUT YOU HAVE BEEN INSTRUCTED OTHERWISE BY GOD.

Hebrew. To be translated thus: As for you, however (here is the royal accent Zakeph Gadol), Jehovah your God does not permit you, to wit, to do so.

Latin:

TU AUTEM A DEO ALITER INSTI- TUTUS ES.

Ebr. Ita vertenda: Ad te autem quod attinet (hic est accentus Regius Zakeph Gadol) non sic permit- tit tibi Jehovah Deus tuus scil. facere.

## 18:15
Verse 15. A PROPHET FROM AMONG YOU AND FROM YOUR BRETHREN, LIKE ME, WILL GOD RAISE UP

Often, to be sure, where great necessity or evident utility has demanded it: but when he says, like me, he does not speak of the office of νομοθέτε [lawgiver], but of the Prophetic [office], and the word 'like' denotes a certain community of name and authority, not an equality in every respect, as appears below in 34, v. 10.

HIM YOU SHALL HEAR] Obey him in all things, even if he should command something against the law. For God can change the law in whatever part He wishes, at whatever time He wishes. And because all the marks of a true Prophet, concerning which it will be treated below, agree in Jesus of Nazareth, therefore he had to be obeyed, even if he had not been the promised Messiah, Acts 3, 23.

A detestable depravation of the illustrious prophecy concerning Christ. For a certain SINGULAR Prophet is promised here: it is not, in truth, a matter of a Prophet being raised up now and then, one after another. Therefore it is said μοναδικῶς [singularly], GOD will raise up A PROPHET. And indeed an eminent or great Prophet, not inferior to Moses. For the particle LIKE ought to retain its full force, nor is it from the propriety of that word that we should depart, since God peculiarly promises such a one as Moses was. For by community of name and Prophetic authority all Prophets sent by God were like Moses: nor is that anything singular, as the words in this place demand when accepted in their proper sense. Now since in Deuteronomy 34, 10 it is held that there has not arisen any more a Prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, Fagius himself concludes this in his annotations on the Chaldaic paraphrase. although otherwise not entirely alien to that Grotian ψευδερμηνείᾳ [false interpretation], that the present passage cannot be understood of any other of the Prophets, who in all ages in

Israel, and all who were inferior to Moses, were more properly understood than of Christ our Savior, who was not only equal to Moses, but surpassed him by many parasangs. Indeed, the Jews themselves, as Fagius adds, testify and hold in the articles of their faith that Moses is the Father of all the Prophets preceding him, following him, and existing in his own time, so that no one of the Prophets was more worthy or more excellent than he. And Fagius excellently observes that, although Moses had some parts in common with other Prophets, there were nevertheless parts of the Mosaic office which Christ alone equaled, nay, surpassed: inasmuch as Moses was raised up as a Prophet and the first leader of the people, who acknowledged no superior, who observed no one among the Fathers as greater than himself. Therefore, according to the promises made to the Patriarchs, he led the people into the covenant and partly into the promised land. This manner of likeness neither Ezra and Zerubbabel, the leaders of the people from Babylon, nor the judge Samuel and the same Prophet, nor even the Prophet David attained. Christ alone in these gifts is equal or rather greater than Moses. Christ alone in this part, just as Moses was raised up, was a great Prophet and a reconciler of the people with God, who looks to no other example and to no predecessor.

Furthermore, if we look at the occasion of the prophecy, the people had asked of the Lord that He might speak to them through a mediator, either because, terrified by the voice of the law, they desired in silence and in the innermost affection of their heart, besides Moses, whom they then desired as an intermediary, that at long last that promised Shiloh and blessed seed might also be sent, in whom they hoped for ἀνάπαυσιν (rest), or because God promised them more ample things, which is His Φιλανθρωπία (love for mankind), than they dared to ask expressly. So that that saying, AS YOU ASKED of the Lord your God, is understood not so much from the mind of those praying as from the will of the God who hears, and of the Holy Spirit sighing within them, who forms for us ἄᄚητα (inexpressible) sighs within us, Rom. 8:26. Let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die, they said, Exod. 20:19, praying, of course, that the Lord might not speak to them in such a way that they must perish. The Lord, however, heard this in such a way that He promised that He would speak to them so that they would not die, but through His word would obtain life. Fagius subscribes again to this reasoning, which is the force and evidence of truth: Although this passage pertains somewhat to the Prophets of all ages, yet the WHOLE promise (and it ought to be viewed as a whole, not indeed as some part considered separately), if you consider the cause, is fulfilled in ONE Christ. For there is no one, except Christ, who can remove from the mind the terrors conceived concerning the law of the Lord, as the people demanded. As often as the ancients asked for redemption, the remission of sins, and the renewal of the broken covenant, they always asked in a hidden way for Christ. The people standing at Mount Sinai asked for a word of solace from the Lord through a mediator: for they were deprecating the word of the law, by which they had been cast into deadly terrors. When, therefore, the people at Mount Horeb were praying not to hear the voice of GOD any more (that is, that terrible and killing one) but were asking for a Mediator, the Lord answered and said to Moses: They have done well in this, that they have spoken: I will raise up a Prophet among them: as if He were saying, The people indeed pray well, but not you, but another, whom I shall raise up, will fulfill their desires. And he is our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, blessed for ever and ever. Cf. B. Chemnitz, chap. 46, Harmonia Evangelica. And Grotius himself acknowledged at Matt. 17:5 this συνέχειαν (continuity) in the Mosaic text: It is to be noted, he says, what follows in Moses: as if it were said: you yourselves asked that God should not deal with you with those signs that make for terror. God performs

what you wished. The Word was made flesh, etc. To these let there now be added that divine universal command: HIM YOU SHALL HEAR, which at the same time tacitly involves the promise of life, as is manifest from comparison: The people said, I will not hear the voice of the Lord my God anymore, lest I die: Moses, by the inspiration of God, answers: The Lord your God will raise up a Prophet for you. Him you shall hear, understand: and you shall not die, nay, you shall live. Similarly, it is evident from the opposition in v. 19: Whoever will not hear his words, which he will speak in my name, I will be the avenger. For just as vengeance and punishment are declared for the disobedient, so grace and life are declared for the obedient. Now who is he, who alone is to be heard by all, unless it be he whom God Himself proclaimed from Heaven as to be heard with a similar voice, HEAR HIM, Matt. 17, which could seem to be taken as if from that oracle, or at least points a finger to this oracle. Indeed, as Grotius admits, l.c., they are the very words of Moses, Deut. 18:15. אליו תשמען (To him you shall listen). Who is he, whose word alone, if it is heard, brings life; if it is despised, brings punishment and death, unless it be he who testifies, the words that I speak are Spirit and life, John 6:63. He who will keep my word will not see death forever, John 8:51. And again, chap. 12:47: If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him. Nor, moreover, should the observation of our blessed Luther be held in low esteem, that it is said here, I will put my words in his mouth: that we are not only sent here from Moses to Christ, to whom Moses hands over the torch as it were, but that that Prophet is about to promulgate a different word than was the word of the law, which God is only then about to put into his mouth. But there is no other word beyond the word of Moses, except the word of the Gospel. See B. Luther, Vol. III, Germ. Jenens. fol. 126. who rightly says that this is the principal passage of the whole of Deuteronomy, indeed of the whole Mosaic Pentateuch, and a clearly expressed prophecy concerning Christ as the new Teacher and Mediator.

All of which things become clearer, if the interpretation of the N. T., certainly ἀνυπεύθυνος and superior to every exception, should be added. For Christ himself also not obscurely looks back to this passage in John 5, verse 16 [sic]: If you believed Moses, you would believe Me also; for he wrote of me, and both Stephen the protomartyr in Acts 7, v. 37, and Peter, the leader of the Apostles, in Acts 3, v. 21, 22, most explicitly explained this one oracle concerning Christ, so that no doubt can remain for Christians concerning it, and it would even be a sin to understand it otherwise: since in that way one would openly contradict the Holy Spirit. Then indeed individual words of the oracle are also read clearly applied to Christ in the New Testament: who is that promised Prophet in Matt. 21, v. 11, the great Prophet in Luke 7, v. 16, the Prophet powerful in deed and word before God and all the people (as Moses was) in Luke 24, v. 19, the Prophet who was to come in John 6, v. 14, whom GOD raised up, in Acts 3, v. 26, chap. 5, v. 30, chap. 13, v. 23. according to the promise made to the Fathers, v. 32, 33. (Peter in Acts 3 and Paul in Acts 13 use the word ἀναστήσας, which is read here among the LXX Interpreters.) Raised up from the Jewish nation, and from his brethren, Rom. 1, 3, chap. 9, 5, from the midst of his brethren, Luke 7, 16, A great Prophet has risen among us. A Prophet of such a kind as Moses was, Heb. 3, verse 12, in whose mouth God placed his words, and who spoke, in the name of God, his Father, all things which he commanded him. Conf. John 7, 17, chap. 8, 27, 29. As the Father taught me, these things I speak. v. 40, chap. 12, 49. I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. verse 50. The things which I speak, as the Father gave to me, so I speak. chap. 5, verse 13. But I in the name of my Father: that Prophet, whom all are bound to hear, who do not wish to perish Matth. 17, 5. He who does not listen to Him, let him be rooted out from the people, God exists as an avenger Joh. 12, 48. Luc. 3, 16. Joh. 3, 36.

Nor was this a matter of doubt among the ancient Jews, that the promise was made here concerning Christ: which appears not only from those passages by which they seem to have had regard to this oracle, Matth. 21, 11. Luc. 7, 16. Joh. 6, 14., but especially from the cited discourse of Peter and Stephen, who assume and urge it as ὁμολογουμένως certain, and as a κυρίαν δόξαν, about which no one would doubt, Acts 3 and 7. In Midrash Kohelet on Eccles. 1, these things are read: What is that which was the same that shall be? It is read that R. Berachias said in the name of Isaac, just as the first redeemer was, i.e., Moses, so shall the last Redeemer be, i.e., the Messiah. The Muhammadans themselves acknowledge and profess that Jesus is the Great Prophet, being more clear-sighted in this part than the Christian Grotius; who, having set all these aside, preferred to be wise for himself or rather to gratify his Papists, and with Lyranus, Tostatus, Oleaster, Corn. a Lapide, Jacobus Bonfrerius, Tirinus, and Marius, to take this passage concerning the Prophets in general.

But he who wished to be considered most observant of antiquity ought rather to have listened to the Fathers, who interpret the oracle solely concerning Christ: Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho, Tertullian in book 4 against Marcion, Lactantius in book 4 of his Institutes, ch. 17, Eusebius of Caesarea in book 3 of his Evangelical Demonstration, 2, and book 9, ch. 9, Athanasius on the saving advent of Christ, and in his Synopsis of Scripture, Augustine in book 16 against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 16; to whom, from among the Papists themselves, if Grotius prefers them, Cajetan in this place, Guilb. Estius in this place, and Joseph a Costa in book 3 on Christ revealed, assent, and explain the illustrious passage solely concerning Christ. Menochius, whom Grotius valued most highly, although he wishes the words of verse 15 to be able to be taken either concerning the Prophets to be sent from time to time or concerning Christ, nevertheless interpreted verse 18 solely concerning Christ. Leonhardus Marius also verse 15 understood primarily concerning Christ; Vatablus and Emanuel Sa contend that Joshua is understood in type and according to the letter, and Christ in truth and in the allegorical sense; Bonfrerius, conversely, takes it in the literal sense concerning Christ; indeed, he openly professes, though contrary to himself, that all things which are said here can be understood solely of Christ. Since, therefore, not even among the Papists are those found who agree with Grotius entirely, he seems to have followed the Jews, those blind leaders, who snatch this oracle away to all the Prophets of all ages, although some of the Jews themselves, who see that a certain one is designated μοναδικῶς, have had to confess that some Prophet like Moses was promised here, some indeed Joshua, others truly Jeremiah. Grotius therefore Judaizes here, and for the sake of the Jews pours darkness upon an illustrious prophecy, which whether it be Christian, let the very admirers of Grotius decide. Whom, however, he has not been consistent with himself even in that, as his Annotations on Matth. 17, 5, where he confesses that these things fit Christ more excellently, and his notes on the Acts of the Apostles teach. For thus on Acts 7, 37: ὁ εἰπὼν τοῖς ὑιοῖς Ἰσραὴλ: Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει κύριος. He commended Jesus to you, with words pertaining indeed to other Prophets TO SOME EXTENT, but pertaining preeminently to Jesus. But if those words pertain only TO SOME EXTENT to others, why then does he interpret them here in his explanation only concerning others, and does not make mention by any word of Jesus, to whom he confesses they pertain preeminently? Grotius provides similar things to these on Acts 3, 22, but burdened with another error: Generally, he says, this law of GOD (he makes a law out of an Evangelical promise) pertains to this, that whoever Prophet shall have arisen in the people of God, doing a miracle, or certainly predicting unknown future things, and not leading the people away to false Gods, he should be obeyed, EVEN IF HE SHOULD COMMAND SOMETHING AGAINST THE LAW. This is diametrically opposed to the divine law: For if anyone had commanded something against the law, he was not to be obeyed. Perhaps these things tend toward the end that he might insinuate that the Roman Pontiff, who not rarely exalts himself with miracles, is to be believed and obeyed, even if he should decree or command something against the law of God or Scripture. So that, indeed, he may be exalted ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα, above all that is called GOD, or that is worshipped, 2 Thess. 2, verse 2.

Latin:

Vers. 15. PROPHETAM DE GENTE TUA ET DE FRATRIBUS TUIS, SICUT ME, SVSCITABIT DEUS)

Sæpe scilicet, ubi magna necessitas aut evidens utilitas id exegerit: cum autem ait, sicut me, non loquitur de munere νομοθέτε, sed de Prophetico, & vox sicut communitatem quandam nominis atque autoritatis, non omnimodam æqua- litatem notat, ut apparet infra 34. v. 10.

IPSUM AVDIES] Ipsi per omnia pare, etiamsi quid contra legem jubeat. Potest enim Deus mutare legem qua vult parte, quo vult tempore. Et quia notæ omnes veri Prophetæ, de quibus agetur infra, in Jesum Nazarenum con- gruunt, ideo parendum ei fuit, etiamsi is Messias promissus non fuisset, Act. 3, 23.

Detestanda depravatio vaticinii illustris de Christo. Promittitur enim hîc SINGULARIS quidam Propheta: non vero de alio atque alio sub- inde excitando Propheta agitur. Ideo μοναδικῶς di- citur, PROPHETAM exsuscitabit DEUS. Et quidem insignis vel magnus Propheta, Mose non inferior. Particula enim SICUT vim integram re- tinere debet, neque à proprietate vocis istius est, quod discedamus, quum peculiariter talem, qualis Moses fuit, promittat Deus. Communitate enim nominis atque autoritate Prophetica omnes Pro- phetæ à Deo missi erant, sicut Moses: neque id singulare quid est, ut hoc in loco verba postulant sensu proprio accepta. Jam cum Deuter. 34, 10. ha- beatur, non surrexisse amplius Prophetam in Israel ut Mose, quem nosset Dominus à facie ad faciem, concludit hîc ipse Fagius in annotat. in Chaldaic. praraphr. etsi alias non omnino alienus ab illa Gro- tiana ψευδερμηνείᾳ, patere præsentem locum non pos- se de ullo alio Prophetarum, qui omnibus seculis in

Israel, omnesque Mose inferiores fuerint, proprie intelligi, quam de Christo Salvatore nostro, qui Mo- si non tantum par fuit, sed multis parasangis eum su- peravit. Imo Judæi ipsi, ut addit Fagius, testantur & habent in articulis fidei suæ, Mosen esse Patrem o- mnium Prophetarum præcedentium ipsum, sequenti- um, atque suo tempore existentium, ita quod nullus Prophetarum eo dignior aut præstantior fuerit. Et eximie observat Fagius, etsi partes nonnullas Moses cum aliis Prophetis communes habuerit: esse tamen partes muneris Mosaici, quas unus Christus adæqua- vit, imo superavit: utpote quod excitatus Moses fuit in Prophetam & ducem populi primum, qui superio- rem nullum agnosceret, qui neminem tanquam se ma- jorem ex Patribus observaret. Ideo juxta promissio- nes Patriarchis præstitas in fœdus & partim in terram promissam populum perduxit. Quam similitudinis rationem neque Ezra & Zorobabel ductores populi ex Babylone, neque judex Samuel & idem Propheta, neque adeo Propheta David assecutus est. Solus Chri- stus in his dotibus par est vel potius major Mose. Solus Christus hac parte, sicut Moses excitatus, magnus Propheta fuit & conciliator populi cum Deo, qui in exemplum aliud & in antecessum nul- lum respicit.

Porro si occasionem Prophetiæ respiciamus, pe- tierat à Domino populus, ut per mediatorem sibi loqueretur, sive quod territi voce legis, tacitè & in intimo cordis affectu desiderarint, præter Mo- sen, quem tunc internuncium cupiebant, tandem aliquando etiam mitti promissum illum Schiloh, & benedictum semen, in quo sperabant ἀνάπαυσιν, si- ve quod Deus ipsis ampliora, quæ est ejus Φιλαν- θρωπία, promiserit, quam ipsi expresse petere au- derent. Ut ita illud, UT PETIISTI à Domino Deo tuo, non tam intelligatur ex mente precantium, quam ex voluntate exaudientis Dei, atque in illis su- spirantis etiam Sancti Spiritus, qui suspiria nobis ἄῤῥητα in nobis format Rom. 8, 26. Non loquatur nobis Dominus, ne moriamur, inquiebant ipsi Exod. 20, 19. precantes scilicet, ne ita loquatur secum Do- minus, ut ipsis pereundum sit: Dominus vero hoc ita exaudiit, ut promiserit, se loquuturum ipsis ita, ut non moriantur, sed per verbum suum vitam conse- quantur. Subscribit iterum huic rationi, quæ vis & evidentia veritatis est, Fagius: Etsi ad omnium ætatum Prophetas hic locus nonnihil pertineat, TOTA tamen promissio (at tota spectari debet, non vero pars aliqua seorsim considerari) si causam conside- ras, in UNO Christo completur. Nam qui terrores de lege Domini conceptos animo eximat, sicut populus efflagitavit, nemo est, præter Christum. Antiqui quo- tiescunque petebant redemtionem; peccatorum remif- sionem, ruptique fœderis renovationem, semper occul- to modo petierunt Christum. Populus stans ad mon- tem Sinai verbum solatii per mediatorem à Domino petiit: deprecabantur enim verbum legis, quo in mor- tiferos terrores conjecti erant. Cum ergo populus in monte Horeb deprecaretur amplius audire vocem DEI (terribilem scil. illam & occidentem) sed peteret Mediatorem, respondit Dominus & dixit ad Mosen: Bene egerunt in hoc, quod locuti sunt: Prophe- tam suscitabo in eis: quasi dicat, Bene quidem po- pulus orat, sed ejus desideria non tu, verum alius, quem suscitabo, adimplebit. Atque is est Dominus noster Jesus Christus, verus Dei Filius, benedi- ctus in secula seculorum. Conf. B. Chemnit. cap. 46. Harmon. Evangelic. Et agnovit Grotius ipse ad Matth. 17, 5. hanc in Mosaico textu συνέχει- αν: Notanda, inquit, sunt quæ sequuntur apud Mosen: quasi dicatur: postulastis ipsi ne Deus vobis- cum signis illis ad terrorem facientibus ageret. Præstat

Deus quod voluistis. Verbum caro factum est, &c. His accedat nunc divinum illud mandatum universale: IPSUM AUDIES, quod simul tacitè involvit promissionem vitæ, ut ex collatione manifestum est: Populus dicebat, ultra non audiam vocem Domini Dei mei, ne moriar: Moses ex inspiratione Dei respondet: Prophetam suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus. Ipsum audies, subintellige & non morieris, imo vives. Similiter id elucet ex oppositione v. 19. Qui verba ejus, quæ loquetur in nomine meo audire noluerit, ego ultor existam. Ut enim inobedientibus ultio & pœna; ita obedientibus gratia & vita indicitur. Jam quis ille, qui ab omnibus audiendus unus est, nisi quem Deus ipse de Cœlo audiendum simili voce proclamavit, HUNC AUDITE, Matth. 17. quæ ex oraculo illo quasi desumta videri possit, aut ad hoc oraculum certe digitum intendit. Imo ut fatetur Grotius l. c. Sunt ipsa Mosis verba Deuter. 18, 15. אליו תשמען. Quis ille, cujus unius verbum si audiatur, vitam; si contemnatur, pœnam & mortem adferat, nisi qui testatur, verba, quæ ego loquor, Spiritus & vita sunt Joh. 6, 63. Qui verbum meum servabit, mortem in æternum non videbit Joh. 8, 51. Et rursus cap. 12, 47. Si quis audierit verba mea, & non custodierit, ego non judico eum. Qui spernit me & non accipit verba mea, habet, qui judicet eum. Neque insuper habenda B. Lutheri nostri observatio, quod hîc dicatur, ponam verba mea in ore ejus: quod non ablegemur tantum hîc à Mose ad Christum, cui Moses quasi lampada tradit, sed quod Propheta ille aliud verbum promulgaturus sit, quam fuit verbum legis, quod deinceps demum Deus in os ejus positurus sit. Aliud vero verbum ultra verbum Mosis non est, nisi verbum Evangelii. Vid. B. Luther. Tom. III. Germ. Jenens. fol. 126. qui merito ait, principem hunc esse locum totius Deuteronomii, imo totius Pentateuchi Mosaici ac plane expressam de Christo novo Doctore & Mediatore prophetiam.

Quæ clariora omnia evadunt, si N. T. interpretatio, ἀνυπεύθυνος certe, omnique exceptione superior accedat. Nam & Christus ipse haud obscure respicit hunc locum Joh. 5. vers. 16. Si credideritis Mosi, crederetis etiam Mihi; de me enim ille scripsit, & disertissime de Christo uno hoc oraculum explicavit cum Stephanus protomartyr Act. 7. v. 37. tum Apostolorum coryphæus Petrus Actor. 3. v. 21. 22. ut nulla Christianis dubitatio de eo superesse possit, nefas etiam sit, secus illud accipere: siquidem ita palam Spiritui S. contradicatur. Tum vero singula etiam verba oraculi dilucide Christo applicata leguntur in Nov. Test. qui Propheta ille promissus est Matth. 21. v. 11. Propheta magnus Luc. 7. v. 16. Propheta potens opere & sermone coram Deo & omni populo (uti Moses) Luc. 24. v. 19. Propheta, qui venturus erat Joh. 6. v. 14. quem excitavit DEUS, Actor. 3. v. 26. cap. 5. v. 30. cap. 13. v. 23. juxta promissionem Patribus factam vers. 32. 33. (voce ἀναστήσας utitur Petrus Actor. 3. & Paulus Actor. 13. quæ hîc penes LXX. Interpp. legitur.) Excitatus de gente Judaica, & de fratribus Rom. 1, 3. c. 9, 5. de medio fratrum Luc. 7, 16. Propheta magnus surrexit inter nos. Propheta ejusmodi sicut Moses fuit Ebr. 3. vers. 12. in cujus os Deus posuit verba sua, quiq; locutus est, in nomine Dei, Patris sui, omnia quæ præcepit illi. Conf. Joh. 7, 17. cap. 8, 27. 29. Sicut docuit me Pater, hæc loquor. v. 40. cap. 12, 49. Ego ex me ipso non sum loquutus, sed qui misit me Pater, ipse mandatum mihi dedit, quod dicam & quod loquar. vers. 50. Quæ ego loquor, sicut Pater dedit mihi, sic loquor. cap. 5. vers. 13. Ego vero in nomine Patris mei: Propheta ille, quem omnes audire tenentur, qui perire nolunt Matth. 17, 5. Quem qui non audit, eradicetur e populo, Deus ultor existit Joh. 12, 48. Luc. 3, 16. Joh. 3, 36.

Neque dubium hoc fuit apud antiquos Judæ- os, de Christo hic promissionem factam essn: quod non tantum ex locis istis, quibus hoc oraculum re- spexisse videntur Matth. 21, 11. Luc. 7, 16. Joh. 6, 14. apparet, sed imprimis e concione laudata Petri atque Stephani, qui tanquam ὁμολογουμένως certum, & ceu κυρίαν δόξαν, de qua nemo dubitarit, assumunt, at- que urgent Act. 3. & 7. In Midras Coheleth super Eccles. 1. hæc leguntur: Quid est, quod fuit ipsum, quod erit? Legitur R. Berachias in nomine Isaac di- xisse, sicut fuit redemtor primus, i. e. Moses, ita erit Red- emtor ultimus, i. e. Messias. Mahumetani ipsi Ma- gnum Prophetam esse Jesum agnoscunt & profiten- tur, oculatiores hac in parte Grotio Christiano; qui omnibus istis posthabitis sibi sapere vel potius Papi- stis suis gratificari maluit, & cum Lyrano, Tostato, O- leastro, Corn. a Lapide, Jacobo Bonfrerio, Tirino, ac Mario locum hunc de Prophetis in genere accipere.

Qui vero antiquitatis quum voluerit haberi observantissimus, audire potius debuerat Patres, o- raculum de Christo unice interpretantes, Justinum Martyrem in Dial. cum Tryph. Tertullianum lib. 4. adversus Marcion. Lactantium lib. 4. Institut. c. 17. Eusebium Cæsariensem l. 3. demonstr. Evangel. 2. & l. 9. c. 9. Athanasium de salutari adventu Christi, & in Synopsi Script. Augustin. lib. 16. contr. Faust. Manich. c. 16. quibus ex ipsis Papistis, si hos malit Grotius, Cajetanus in h. l. Guilb. Estius in h. l. Jose- phus a Costa l. 3. de Christ. revel. adstipulantur, ac de Christo unice locum illustrem explicant. Meno- chius, quem maximi fecit Grotius, etsi verba v. 15. vel de Prophetis subinde mittendis, vel de Christo accipi posse velit, ver sum tamen 18. unice de Christo interpre- tatus est. Leonhardus Marius versum etiam 15. pri- mario de Christo intellexit, Vatablus & Emanuel Saa Josuam in typo & secundum literam, Christum in ve- ritate & in sensu allegorico intelligi contendit; Bon- frerius vice versa sensu literali de Christo accipit, i- mo ea, quæ hic dicuntur omnia de SOLO Christo intelligi posse aperte, etsi sibi ipsi contrarius, profite- tur. Quum ergo nec inter Papistas reperiantur ex asse Grotio adstipulantes, Judæos maxime, Ducto- res illos cæcos, sequutus videtur, qui hoc oraculum ad omnes ætatum omnium Prophetas abripiunt, ta- metsi nonnulli ex ipsis Judæis, qui μοναδικῶς certum quendam designari vident, fateri debuerint, Pro- phetam aliquem Mosi similem hic promissum, alii quidem Josuam, alii vero Jeremiam. Judaizat ergo hic Grotius, & in Judæorum gratiam illustri vatici- nio tenebras affundit, quod an Christianum sit, ipsi- met Grotii admiratores decernant. Quem tamen in eo etiam sibi non constitisse, Annotata ad Matth. 17, 5. ubi excellentius hæc Christo quadrare, fatetur, & ad Acta Apostolica docent. Sic enim ad Act. 7, 37. ὁ εἰπὼν τοῖς ὑιοῖς Ἰσραὴλ: Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστή- σει κύριος. Ille vobis Jesum commendavit, verbis ad Prophetas quidem alios ALIQUATENUS, sed ad Jesum eximie pertinentibus. At si ad alios ALI- QUATENUS solum verba illa pertinent, cur er- go hic in explicatione solum de aliis eadem inter- pretatur, nec verbo ullo Jesu, ad quem eximie illa pertinere fatetur, mentionem facit. Gemina his tradit Grotius ad Act. 3, 22. sed alio errore stipata: Generaliter, inquit, hæc DEI lex (e promissione Evangelica legem facit) eo pertinet, ut quicunque Propheta in populo Dei surrexerit, miraculum faciens, aut futura incognita certo prædicens, nec abducens populum ad Deos falsos, ei pareatur, ETIAMSI QUID CONTRA LEGEM PRÆCIPIAT. E diametro adversum hoc est divinæ legi: Nam si quis contra legem quid præceperit, ei parendum non erat. Forte hæc eò tendunt, ut Romano Pontifici, qui miraculis sese non raro effert, credendum ac parendum innuat, etiamsi quid contra legem Dei aut Scripturam statuat vel præcipiat. Ut extollatur nempe illi ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα, supra omne, quod dicitur DEUS, aut quod colitur 2. Thess. 2. vers. 2.

## 18:21
Vers. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

## 18:22
HOC HABEBIS SIGNVM (THIS YOU SHALL HAVE AS A SIGN) The sign which he will now give pertains to the former point, where the Prophet says he was sent by the one God. For if he acts in the name of false Gods, he is to be killed immediately without waiting for any sign: indeed, even if he has given some specious signs: above 13, 1. For this is a temptation permitted by God, easy to overcome by those who believe that which both reason dictates and the many miracles of Moses, to 74, as the Hebrews say: namely, that God is one.

Verse 22.

THAT WHICH THE PROPHET SHALL HAVE PREDICTED IN THE NAME OF THE LORD AND IT SHALL NOT COME TO PASS) This is not to be referred to promises of good things to some or punishments denounced, for since both of these are suspended upon some condition that is in some measure potential, it can happen that, the matter being changed, it lacks the outcome, just as one may see in Jeremiah 18:1, 8, 9, 10; Jonah 2:4, 9; but it is to be referred to those things which cannot happen by nature, and which the Prophet predicted would be future, as Moses [predicted] that a rod would be turned into a serpent. For if such things are predicted in the name of God, God will not permit them to happen, lest He bring about an insuperable temptation. Moreover, someone can be convicted of being a false prophet also from a predicted success, if, while the same circumstances remain, that success does not come to pass, Jeremiah 28:9. But a Prophet cannot be known conversely from success alone corresponding to his words, unless he has added many circumstances to the success, which no human prudence could foresee. But here the comparison with the beginning of chapter 13 above shows that it is not a question of the prediction of such things, but of prodigies. It is to be noted also that no signs are required from him who only exhorts men to fulfill the commands of the law. For the signs were made for him long ago, when the law was given. The judgment concerning a true or false prophet belonged to the Sanhedrin, as we said before. One convicted of being a false prophet was punished with death at the Passover, at which time the gathering of the people was greatest, and that according to the law which is above in chapter 17:13, by an argument drawn from the lesser to the greater. For it is a greater thing to falsely invent divine commands than to stubbornly maintain a dogma from human opinion. Therefore, the LXX translate וְזָדוּ there as ὑπερηφανίαν (pride), but here as ἀσέβειαν (impiety).

Latin:

HOC HABEBIS SIGNVM) Signum quod jam dabit ad superiorem speciem pertinet, ubi Propheta dicit se ab unico Deo missum. Nam si agat nomine falsorum Deorum, nullo signo expectato illico interficiendus est: imo etiamsi signa quædam speciosa dederit: supra 13, 1. Est enim hæc tentatio a Deo permissa, facilis superatu ab iis, qui id credunt, quod & ratio dictat, & Mosis tot miracula, ad 74. ut ajunt Hebræi: nempe Deum unum esse.

Vers. 22.

QVOD IN NOMINE DOMINI PROPHETA ILLE PRÆDIXERIT ET NON EVENERIT) Hoc non referendum ad promissa aliquibus bona aut pœnas denunciatas, utrumque enim hoc cum suspensum sit ab aliqua conditione aliquatenus potestativa, fieri potest, ut re mutata eventu careat, quemadmodum videre est Jerem. 18, 1. 8. 9. 10. Jonæ 2, 4. 9. sed referendum ad ea quæ per naturam fieri non possunt, & quæ futura prædixit Propheta, ut Moses, virgam conversum iri in colubrum. Talia enim si prædicantur in Dei nomine, non permittet ea fieri Deus, ne tentationem inferat insuperabilem. Potest præterea falsi argui aliquis etiam ex successu prædicto, si rebus iisdem manentibus is successus non evenerit, Jerem. 28, 9. Non autem contra ex solo successu verbis respondente cognosci Propheta potest, nisi successu multas addiderit circumstantias, quas nulla humana prudentia prospicere possit. Verum hîc non de talium rerum, sed de prodigiorum prædictione agi ostendit collatio initii cap. 13. supra. Notandum & hoc, ab eo qui tantum hortatur homines ad implenda legis jussa, nulla signa requiri. Sunt enim pro illo signa olim facta, cum lex prodita fuit. Cognitio autem de vero aut falso propheta ad Synedrium pertinebat, ut ante diximus. Falsi convictus in Paschate supplicio afficiebatur, quo tempore maximus erat populi conventus, idque ex lege quæ supra est cap. 17, 13. argumento ducto a minore ad majus. Plus enim est falso fingere mandata divina, quam ex humana opinione dogma pertinaciter tueri. Itaque וְזָדוּ ibi quidem ὑπερηφανίαν, hîc vero ἀσέβειαν vertunt LXX.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

Concerning the six cities of refuge, true and false witnesses, and that boundaries are not to be moved.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

De sex urbibus refugii, veris falsisq; testibus, & terminis non transferendis.

## 19:3
Verse 3.

AND THOU SHALT DIVIDE THE WHOLE PROVINCE OF THY LAND INTO THREE EQUAL PARTS) In Hebrew: Thou shalt divide the boundary of thy land into three. In Greek: τριμεριεῖς τὰ ὅρια τῆς γῆς σου (thou shalt divide into three parts the borders of thy land). These towns were at the halfway point from the borders of the land to the center. But understand three [to be] in the land which was then theirs beyond the Jordan. For on this side of the Jordan there were likewise three others, although in a smaller space of land, as appears in Numbers 35:14. The Hebrews bring forward the reason that homicides were more frequent there because of the ferocity of the Gileadites. See Judges 10 and 11, and Hosea 6, verse 8.

Grotius does not touch upon the difficulty concerning the number of the cities of refuge. For although from Numbers 35:13, 14, Deuteronomy 4:41, 43, and Joshua 20:2, 3 it seems sufficiently manifest that only six cities were established, three on this side of the Jordan and the remaining three in Canaan beyond the Jordan; yet a not insignificant doubt arises from verse 8: 'When the Lord thy God shall enlarge thy borders, as He swore to thy fathers and shall give thee all the land which He promised them, thou shalt add three other cities.' Whence R. Solomon, Lyranus, Dionysius, Brentius, Osiander, and Drusius collect nine cities of refuge, which the text indeed clearly implies: because to those three beyond the Jordan to be added, concerning which [is] verse 2, three others are still added in verse 8. Which contradiction (ἐναντιοφανεία) is thus removed by granting that only those three were beyond the Jordan in the land of Canaan, which was occupied by the Israelites: just as three others were ordained on this side of the Jordan. But as for those three, of which mention is made in v. 8, they are defined with that condition, if God should enlarge the borders of Israel beyond the limits of the land of Canaan as far as the river Euphrates, provided that they themselves kept the commandments of the Lord. Which condition of obedience not being fulfilled, they did not obtain that promise of enlargement. And therefore they had no need of cities of refuge outside the borders of the land of Canaan. For although David and Solomon made the regions outside those borders tributary to themselves, yet the borders of Israel were not enlarged. And therefore there is no reason why we should agree with Rabbi Solomon, who asserts that three other cities of refuge were founded afterwards, but it must be established that there were no more than six of them in total. Moreover, before the cities of refuge were established, murderers used to flee to the altar of the tabernacle, etc. 21. From Ex. p. 14, it is clear, as the example of Joab teaches, that those who were cleansed from slaughter took refuge at the altar of the temple, 1 Kings 2:29. Paul Fagius, on Num. 31, relates many things from the Hebrews concerning those cities and the rites by which a fugitive murderer was received there. The reason for the granted refuge is given in the law itself, v. 6, where גאל הדם, the redeemer of blood, is the ἀγχιστεὺς, the kinsman of the slain, as the LXX, Josephus in Antiquities book 4, ch. 7, and Philo in his book on the special laws have it; for just as in the case of leased fields and vineyards a kinsman has the right of redemption, so he could also avenge a slain brother by the right of blood, even without a preceding ordinary investigation of the case, which violence God tolerated in a stiff-necked people rather than approved, as Osiander rightly says. If that had not been permitted, but there had always been a need for an investigation of the case, they could have done without cities of refuge: just as we now do without them in Christian republics, because a kinsman could not have pursued such involuntary murderers by the right of blood, but would have had to avenge the blood of the slain by an ordinary process. Here we have Grotius as our ὁμόψηφος in his annotations on v. 6. Meanwhile, it is certain that God wished to show by this constitution how much He detests homicides; whence even after the case was investigated, the involuntary murderer was ordered to live in exile in a city of refuge until the death of the High Priest, Num. 35:28, Jos. 20:6. Nor did God wish to deal with them where the High Priest resided, the reason for which matter Fagius explains from the Hebrews in the aforementioned place: The murderer shortens the days of man, but the High Priest prolongs them, whence it is not right that the shortener of life should dwell before the prolonger. Likewise, the murderer contaminates the land and removes the majesty of the divine presence, but the High Priest cleanses it, and is the occasion for the majesty of the divine presence to rest upon men on earth. This was a figure of Christ, who is called Goel, Gen. 48:16, Job 19:25, Isa. 59:20, ch. 63:9. For He became our kinsman by the assumption of human flesh, so that by the right of kinship He might free us from the power of Satan, and avenge our death in Himself. Nor is a return to our heavenly fatherland open to us, unless the death of the High Priest intervenes. Whence Jerome, book 5 against Pelagius, ch. 4: The murderer is ordered to go to the city of fugitives, and to be there until the High Priest dies, that is, until he who flees is redeemed by the blood of the Savior.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ET IN TRES ÆQVALITER PARTES TOTAM TERRÆ TVÆ PROVINCIAM DIVIDES) In Hebr. Tripartieris terminum terræ tuæ. Græce τριμεριεῖς τὰ ὅρια τῆς γῆς σου. Erant hæc oppida medio itinere a finibus terræ ad meditullium. Tres autem intellige, in terra quæ tunc ipsis erat trans Jordanem. Nam cis Jordanem aliæ tres itidem erant, quanquam in minore terræ spatio, ut apparet Num. 35, 14. Causam adferunt Hebræi, quod crebriora illic homicidia ob ferociam Galaaditarum. Vid. Jud. 10. & 11. & Oseam 6. vers. 8.

NOn tangit Grotius difficultatem de numero civitatum refugii. Quamvis enim e Num. 35, 13. 14. Deut. 4, 41. 43. Jos. 20, 23. satis manifestum videatur sex solum civitates constitutas esse, tres cis Jordanem, & reliquas tres in Cananæa trans Jordanem; Dubium tamen non leve oritur ev. 8. cum dilataberit Dominus Deus tuus terminos tuos, sicut juravit Patribus tuis & dederit tibi omnem terram, quam eis pollicitus est, addes tres alias civitates. Unde R. Salomo, Lyranus, Dionysius, Brentius, Osiander, Drusius, novem colligunt effugii urbes, quas utique aperte textus infert: quia tribus illis trans Jordanem addendis, de quo v. 2. tres aliæ adhuc adjunguntur v. 8. Quæ vero ἐναντιοφανεία sic tollen- da, quod tres solum illæ trans Jordanem fuerint in terra Canaan, quæ ab Israelitis occupata est: uti tres aliæ cis Jordanem ordinatæ erant. Quod vero ad tres istas, quarum v. 8. mentio fit, illæ cum conditione ista definiuntur, si Deus dilataverit terminos Israelis ex- tra fines terræ Canaan usq; ad flumen Euphratis, sinem- pe ipsi custodierint mandata Domini. Qua conditione obsequii non impleta, nec promissione illa dilata- tionis potiti sunt. Ideoq; nec urbibus refugii extra fines terræ Canaan opus habuere. Nam etsi Da- vid & Salomon regiones extra fines istos sibi tribu- tarias fecerint, non tamen fines Israelis dilatati sunt. Ideoq; non est, quod assurgamus R. Salomoni asse- renti, quod tres aliæ postmodum conditæ sint refu- gii urbes, sed statuendum est, non nisi sex earum in universum fuisse. Cæterum ante constitutas refu- gii urbes ad altare tabernaculi homicidas confugis- se e c. 21. Ex. p. 14. liquet, uti expiatos a cæde sese ad altare templi recepisse Joabi exemplum docet 1. Reg. 2, 29. De civitatibus illis, & quibus ritibus fugiti- vus homicida ibi receptus fuerit ex Ebræis multa tradit Paul Fagius ad Num. 31. Causæ refugii con- cessi redditur in ipsa lege v. 6. ubi גאל הדם re- demtor sanguinis est ἀγχιστεὺς cognatus occisi, ut LXX. & Joseph l. 4. antiqu. c. 7. & Philo lib. de spe- cial. leg. habent; ut enim in elocatis agris, & vineis propinquus jus habet redemtionis, ita ulcsci quoq; poterat fratrem occisum jure sanguinis, etiam non præcedente ordinaria causæ cognitione, quam vio- lentiam Deus in populo duræ cervicis toleravit verius, quam approbavit, ut recte Osiander. Si id non licu- isset, sed semper causæ cognitione opus fuisset, care- re civitatibus refugii potuissent: quemadmodum nunc in Christianis Rebuspubl. iisdem caremus, quia involuntarios ejusmodi homicidas persequi propinquus sanguinis jure non potuisset, sed ordi- nario processu vindicare sanguinem occisi neces- sum habuisset. Est hic nobis ὁμόψηφος Grotius annot. ad v. 6. Interea certum est Deum hac consti- tutione ostendere voluisse, quantopere detestetur homicidia; unde etiam post causam cognitam, invo- luntarius homicida in urbe refugii exulare jubeba- tur usque ad mortem summi Sacerdotis Num. 35. v. 28. Jos. 20, 8. nec voluit Deus cum illis agere, ubi summus Pontifex degebat, cujus rei causam ex E- bræis ita exponit Fagius l. c. Homicida abbreviat dies hominis, summus vero Pontifex prolongat, unde non est æquum, ut vitæ abbreviator versetur coram pro- longatore. Homicida item contaminat terram & re- movet majestatem divinæ præsentiæ, summus autem Pontifex mundat eam, & occasio est præsentiæ majesta- tis divinæ, ut quiescat super homines in terra. Figu- ra hic erat Christi, qui Goel vocatur Gen. 48, 16. Job. 19, 25. Es. 59, 20. c. 63, 9. Factum enim est propin- quus noster carnis humanæ assumtione, ut jure pro- pinquitatis nos ex potestate Satanæ liberaret, mor- temque nostram in ipso vindicaret. Neq; regres- sus nobis in patriam cœlestem patet, nisi interveni- ente morte summi Pontificis. Unde Hieron. l. 5. contr. Pelag. c. 4. Jubetur homicida pergere ad urbem fugitivorum, & tamdiu ibi esse, donec Sacerdos maxi- mus moriatur, id est, donec redimatur is qui fugit san- guine Salvatoris.

## 19:4
WHO YESTERDAY AND THE DAY BEFORE IS PROVEN TO HAVE HAD NO HATRED AGAINST HIM) The proconsul of Baetica, Taurinus Ignatius, uses this argument in a consultation sent to the Emperor Hadrian, so that a homicide might not be believed to have been committed with malice: it appeared there was no enmity that had existed with Evaristus. That consultation exists in the collation of Mosaic and Roman laws, which P. Pithou edited under title 1.

Latin:

QVI HERI ET NVDIVS TERTIVS NVLLVM CONTRA EVM ODIVM HABVISSE COMPROBA- TVR) Hoc argumento & Taurinus Ignatius Proconsul Bæ- ticæ in consultatione ad Hadrianum Imperatorem missa uti- tur, ne homicidium dolo commissum credatur: apparebat nulla inimicitia qua cum Ebaristo fuisset. Extat ea consulta- tio in Mosaicarum & Romanarum legum collatione, quam edidit P. Pithœus titulo 1.

Verse 5.

LEST PERCHANCE HIS KINSMAN, WHOSE BLOOD HAS BEEN SHED, STIMULATED BY GRIEF, SHOULD PURSUE HIM) Therefore, if the kinsman had caught the murderer on the road and killed him, he did so with impunity.

NE FORSITAN PROXIMVS EJVS, CVJVS EF- FVSVS EST SANGVIS, DOLORE STIMVLATVS PERSEQVATVR) Quare si in via homicidam deprehendis- set proximus, & occidisset, ferebat impune.

## 19:14
Verse 14.

YOU SHALL NOT TAKE AND MOVE THE BOUNDARIES OF YOUR NEIGHBOR) This was severely forbidden among peoples who consulted for the public peace. Job 24:2. Plato, Laws 8. The Digest, Title on the Moved Boundary: the old collation of Mosaic and Roman laws, title 13. Paul, Sententiae 1.16 and 5.22.2.

WHICH THE FOREFATHERS SET) He means to say 'have set'. For that was done by Joshua and Eleazar.

NON ASSVMES ET TRANSFERES TERMINOS PROXIMI TVI) Severe id vetutum apud quieti publicæ consulentes populos. Job. 24, 2. Plato 8. de Legibus. Di- gesta Titulo de Termino Moto: collatio vetus legum Mo- saicarum cum Romano titulo 13. Paulus sententiarum 1, 16. & 5. 22, 2.

QVOS FIXERVNT PRIORES) Fixerint vult dicere. Factum enim id per Josuam & Eleazarum.

## 19:15
Verse 15. WHATEVER THAT SIN AND CRIME MAY HAVE BEEN) In the Hebrew it is, עון & חטאת, the former of which is against God, the latter against man, in this particular place.

Latin:

Vers 15. QVICQVID ILLVD PECCATI ET FA- CINORIS FVERIT) In Hebræo est, עון & חטאת quorum illud est contra Deum, hoc contra hominem, hoc quidem loco.

## 19:16
Verse 16. IF A FALSE WITNESS STANDS UP) One witness is sufficient not for condemning, but for inquiring: and in pecuniary matters, for deferring the purgatory oath to the defendant. Maimonides. But in a loan, no one was condemned from a contract unless it was made in the presence of witnesses.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SI STETERIT TESTIS MENDAX) Vnus testis sufficit non ad damnandum, sed ad inquirendum: & in pecuniariis, ad deferendum reo jusjurandum purgatori- um. Maimonides. At in mutuo non damnabatur quis ex contractu, nisi coram testibus facto.

## 19:18
Verse 18.

IF THEY HAVE FOUND A FALSE WITNESS TO HAVE SPOKEN A LIE AGAINST HIS BROTHER) In a capital case and one where a sentence has followed because of it: thus usage has restricted the law.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

INVENERINT FALSVM TESTEM DIXIXISSE CONTRA FRATREM SVVM MENDACIVM) In causa capitali & secuta ob id sententia: ita usus restrinxit legem.

## 19:20
Verse 20. SO THAT THE OTHERS HEARING MAY HAVE FEAR) Note the end of public punishments, which Demosthenes expressed thus: ἵνα ἄλλοι πρόνοιαν ποιῶνται καὶ φοβῶνται. See book 2 of the Law of Peace and War, chapter 20, § 9.

Vers. 20. VT AVDIENTES CÆTERI TIMOREM HABEANT) Nota finem publicarum pœnarum, quam Demosthenes sic expressit: ἵνα ἄλλοι πρόνοιαν ποιῶνται καὶ φοβῶνται. Vide libro 2. de Jure Pacis & Belli cap. 20. §. 9.

Verse 21. YOU SHALL NOT PITY HIM) The law speaks to the judge.

Vers. 21. NON MISEREBERIS EJVS) Judici lex lo- quitur.

CAPUT XX. Leges Bellicæ.

Verse 2. THE PRIEST SHALL STAND BEFORE THE BATTLE LINE) A priest anointed for this purpose, who also sounded the trumpet.

Vers. 2. STABIT SACERDOS ANTE ACIEM) Sa- cerdos ad hoc unctus, qui & tuba canebat.

Verse 3. LET NOT YOUR HEART BE AFRAID) It was the custom to amputate the legs of those fleeing.

Vers. 3. NON PERTIMESCAT COR VESTRVM) Mos fuit crura amputare fugientibus.

## 20:5
Verse 5. AND HAS NOT DEDICATED IT) Has not lived in it for a year.

AND HAS NOT YET MADE IT COMMON) He has not yet freed it from sacred status, which was done in the fifth year.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET NON DEDICAVIT EAM) Non habita- vit per annum.

NEC DVM FECIT EAM ESSE COMMVNEM) Nondum eam a Sacris liberavit, quod fiebat sub annum quintum.

## 20:7
Verse 7. WHO IS THE MAN WHO HAS BETROTHED A WIFE AND HAS NOT TAKEN HER? LET HIM GO AND RETURN TO HIS HOUSE) See below 25, 5. ἵνα μὴ στρατεύοιτ᾽ ἀλλὰ βινοίη μένων, says Aristophanes in the Acharnians. But it is to be noted that these exemptions from service did not have a place in the wars of God, that is, against the seven nations, but in other wars, as Maimonides noted.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVIS EST HOMO, QVI DESPONDIT VXOREM ET NON ACCEPIT EAM? VADAT ET REVERTATVR IN DOMVM SVAM) Vide infra 25, 5. ἵνα μὴ στρατεύοιτ᾽ ἀλλὰ βινοίη μένων, ait Aristophanes in Acharnensibus. Sed notandum has ἀλειτουργησίας locum non habuisse in bellis Dei, id est, contra septem populos, sed in bellis aliis, ut notavit Maimonides.

## 20:8
Ver. 8. LET HIM GO AND RETURN TO HIS HOUSE, LEST HE MAKE THE HEARTS OF HIS BRETHREN TO FEAR) For this very reason Alexander sent back to Macedonia those who had no heart for military service. See Arrian, book 7; Curtius, book 10.

The Lord prescribed military laws to the people, that He might show that just wars are not to be imputed to Him, and might teach how they ought to conduct themselves in them. He made special mention of chariots, however, because they caused great slaughter and struck the most grievous terror. Ex. 14, 7. Jos. 17, 16. Jud. 4, 3. 1. Sam. 13, 6. Wherever scythed chariots passed, they wrought slaughter in the army. Regarding the address of the Priest to the people, Paul Fagius has these things from the Talmudic books and R. Moses Maimonides: First, to the promiscuous people, not yet separated into classes and troops, the Priest of war said: Whoever has built a house, etc.; soon men of that kind had the power of returning home, if the war was not commanded by law, but undertaken from elsewhere.
