Soon the multitude was separated into military troops under captains of thousands, centurions, captains of fifty, etc. And with the troops thus arranged, the anointed of war or the Priest addressed them with these words: Fear not, neither be ye faint-hearted, because the Lord your God is in the midst of you. Furthermore, when the battle line was just about to be drawn up, and the troops were now standing in order, from an elevated place the Priest of war said this: Hear, O Israel, etc.

up to [the point], that he might rescue you from danger, and he continued with an even and steady voice. These same things the priests who were not anointed explained in a clear voice through the individual troops, etc. Thus he.

However, that which is said about the high priest does not deserve approval. For there was no need for the high priest to go off to battles, nor to institute such exhortations to the people, which was not always done even then, when the ark was carried into battle. 1 Sam. 4:13; Num. 31:6.

But it was rightly observed by Grotius that the man who had built a new house had the privilege for a year of not going out to battle. Thus Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, ch. 8: 'Let those be exempt from military service who, having built a new house, have not yet used it for a full year.' But for those who had planted a new vineyard, a five-year period was granted. For the fruits of the vineyards were judged unclean for the first three years; whatever was born in the fourth year, all of that was offered to God as first-fruits; only in the fifth year was it permitted to the owner of the vineyard and others to eat of the fruit, and this was to make the vineyard common, v. 6. Those who had recently taken a wife enjoyed the same privilege in the first year after the nuptials, as Deut. 24:5 contains an explanation of this constitution. The reasons why this triple class of men did not have the necessity to go into battle, Dionysius

Carth. [Dionysius of Carthage] gives two: first, because it was especially miserable that after such efforts and such fervent affections toward things labored for and desired, they would not attain what they wished; second, because such men are accustomed to fear the danger imminent to them, the more intensely they are affected toward their objects. The moral gloss on this passage explains the moral significations thus: those who have recently taken wives are reputed unfit for spiritual warfare, by whom are signified the soft and effeminate; likewise those who have recently built houses for their own magnificence, by whom are signified men lifted up to pride. Likewise those who have recently planted vineyards, by whom are designated men too occupied with earthly greed: others understand the avaricious primarily by these. B. Luther, who applies this whole chapter allegorically to spiritual warfare in his Commentary on this passage, Vol. III, Jena, Lat. f. 130, has it thus concerning these: 'What he says here about dedicating a house, making a vineyard common, and bringing a bride home, signifies that a soldier of the word ought to be exercised by use, so that he may know the doctrine not by hearing alone, but also by experience.' For a house is dedicated in Hebrew when it is occupied by use and dwelling, and a vineyard is made common when one enjoys its use and fruit, and a bride is received when a custom of life is had with her.

But Grotius distinguishes wars in vain with Maimonides: as if those classes of men ought not to have enjoyed these privileges in all wars. In almost the same manner, the Rabbis are accustomed to observe that one thing is a war of license (הרשות), or a permitted one, and another is one of command or precept (המצוה). Asserting that in the former, not in the latter, was an exemption from military service granted to such men. Where the law does not distinguish, it is not for us to distinguish.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VADAT ET REVERTATVR IN DOMVM SVAM, NE PAVERE FACIAT CORDA FRATRVM SVORVM) Hac ipsa de causa eos, quibus militia cordi non erat in Macedoniam remisit Alexander. Vide Arianum lib. 7. Curtium libro 10.

LEges militares præscripsit populo Dominus, ut ostenderet, bella justa sibi non imputari, & quo- modo in illis se gerere debeant, doceret. Curruum autem mentionem peculiarem fecit, quia illi ma- gnam stragem faciebant, & terrorem gravissimum incutiebant. Ex. 14, 7. Jos. 17, 16. Jud. 4, 3. 1. Sam. 13, 6. Quaqua transibant falcati currus, stragem in exerci- tu edebant. De alloquio Sacerdotis ad populum hæc habet e libris Thalmudicis & R. Mose Maimon. Paul. Fagius: Primum populo promiscuo, & nondum in clas- ses ac turmas separato Sacerdos belli dicebat: Quis- quis domum ædificaverit &c. mox ejus generis homi- nes potestatem habuerunt redeundi domum, si bellum lege præceptum non erat, sed aliunde susceptum. Mox in turmas militares multitudo secernebatur sub Chiliar- chas, Centuriones, quinquagenarios &c. Et turmis ita dispositis, his verbis unctus belli vel Sacerdos alloqueba- tur: Ne timueritis, neq; trepidaveritis, quia Dominus Deus vester in medio vestri est. Porro cum acies jam- jam instruenda esset, & jam turmæ pariter consisterent, ex edito loco Sacerdos belli hoc dixit: Audi Israel &c.

usq́; ad, ut eruat vos de periculo, & differebat voce æ- quabili & constanti. Quæ eadem Sacerdotes non uncti exerta voce exposuerunt per singulas turmas, &c. Hæc ille.

Id tamen quod de Sacerdote summo dicitur, calculum non meretur. Neque enim opus erat, ut summus Sacerdos ad prælia abiret, ut ad populum ejusmodi adhortationes institueret, quod ne tum quidem semper factum, cum arca in prælium delata est 1. Sam. 4,13. Num. 31, 6.

Recte autem observatum a Grotio privilegium eum, qui novem domum extruxit, habuisse per an- num non exeundi in prælium. Sic Josephus l. 4. antiq. c. 8. Immunes sint a militia, qui ædificata do- mo nova nondum integrum annum illa sunt usi. Illi ve- ro, qui vineam plantaverat novam, quinquennium in- dultum fuit. Nam tribus primis annis fructus vi- nearum immundi judicabantur, quicquid quarto anno nascebatur, illud omne tanquam primitivum Deo offerebatur, quinto demum anno licebat Do- mino vineæ, & aliis de fructu comedere, & hoc erat vineam communem facere, v.6. Qui uxorem nuper du- xerant, itidem illo privilegio fruebantur primo post nuptias anno, ut Deut. 24, 5. hujus constitutionis ex- plicatio habet. Causas cur hoc triplex virorum ge- nus non necessum haberet ire in prælium, Dionyf.

Carth. duas reddit: primo quoniam specialiter erat miserabile, quod post tantos conatus, tamq́; ferventes affectus ad elaborata & concupita, non consequerentur optatum; secundo quoniam tales viri solent formidare de imminente sibi periculo, quanto intensius afficiuntur ad sua objecta. Glossa moralis ad h. l. significatio- nes morales ita explicat: ad bellum spirituale inepti reputantur, qui de novo duxerunt uxores, per quos si- gnificantur molles & effœminati, item illi, qui de novo domos ædificarunt ad sui magnificentiam, per quos si- gnificantur homines elati ad superbiam. Item illi, qui de novo plantarunt vineas, per quos designantur homi- nes nimis occupati circa cupiditatem terrenam: Avaros alii per hosce imprimis intelligunt. B. Lutherus, qui totum hoc caput allegorice applicat ad spiri- tualem militiam in Comm. ad h. l. T. III. Jen. Lat. f. 130. ita de hisce habet: Quod hic de domo dedican- da & vinea facienda communi, & sponsa domum ducen- da dicit, significat usu exercitatum esse debere militem verbi, ut non auditu solo, sed experientia quoq́; doctri- nam noverit. Domus enim Hebraice tunc dedicatur, quando usu & habitando occupatur, & vinea communis fit, quando quis usu & fructu ejus potitur, sponsa acci- pitur, quando consuetudo vitæ cum ea habetur.

Frustra autem distinguit Grotius cum Maimoni- de bella: quasi non omnibus bellis his privilegiis illa ho- minum genera gaudere debuerint. Ad eundem fere modum Rabbini solent observare, aliud esse bellum licentiæ הרשות, vel licitum, aliud המצוה jussio- nis vel præceptum. In istis solum, non in his vacatio- nem a militia talibus concessam fuisse, asserentes. Ubi lex non distinguit, nostrum non est distinguere.

## 20:9
Verse 9. HE SHALL PREPARE HIS BANDS FOR BATTLE]

In the Hebrew [it is] פקדו, which is 'they shall muster.' So indeed some explain it, but the sense is perplexed, and 'the princes of the orders shall muster the people at the head,' i.e., the princes and leaders of the orders shall muster their soldiers and shall arrange the people at the head. Thus the plural should have been used, 'at the heads,' as in 1 Sam. 11:11. More correctly B. Luther: 'They shall place the captains for the people at the head.' So also the LXX, 'at the foot' (κατὰ πόδα), you might render: 'Then' (thus 'vav' is taken sometimes as signifying order) 'they shall constitute' (or set before) 'the princes of the armies at the head' (or beginning) 'of the people.' Compare 2 Chron. 13:12, ch. 20, verse 27.

Latin:

Vers. 9. SUOS AD BELLANDUM CUNEOS PRÆPARAVIT]

In Hebræo פקדו, quod est recensebunt. Ita quidem exponunt nonnulli, sed sensus est perplexus, & recensebunt Principes ordinum in caput populum h. e. Principes & Ductores ordinum mi- lites suos recensebunt, ac disponent populum in caput. Sic plurale adhiberi debuisset in capita: ut 1. Sam. 11,11. Rectius B. Lutherus: Sie sollen die Haupt- leute für das Volck an die Spitze stellen. Sic etiam LXX. κατὰ πόδα reddas: Tunc (ita vav accipitur quandoque, ut significativum ordinis) constituent (vel præponent) principes exercituum in capite (vel principio) populi. Cons. 2. Par. 13. v. 12. cap. 20. versu 27.

## 20:10
Verse 10.

IF AT ANY TIME YOU SHALL APPROACH TO CONQUER A CITY) Naturally, as Terence says: 'It behooves a wise man to try everything before arms.' And Apollonius: 'Do not even thus try with strength before [trying] with words.' This also held true in the land of Canaan. Therefore, the law which is in Exod. 22:32-33 and in this book 7:12 is to be understood with a benign exception, unless some should obey at the first proclamation. Thus Maimonides and Moses of Coucy in the 15th commanding precept. See the reasons for this opinion in book 2 of 'On the Law of War and Peace,' ch. 13, § 4. Just causes of war among the Hebrews are considered to be: against a Hebrew city practicing idols; against a Hebrew city falling away from the law; on account of faith violated toward a King, 2 Kings 3; on account of rebellion, 2 Kings 20; on account of defending a guilty person, Judg. 20; on account of an injury brought upon a King or the Republic, 2 Sam. 10; if the Hebrews are reclaiming their own property; to repel an enemy; to forestall an enemy, Num. 21; against an ally of an enemy, 2 Kings. 1 Sam. 8. for rescuing a friend; Gen. 14. against tyranny: such wars were undertaken by decree of the Sanhedrin of 70 men.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

SI QVANDO ACCESSERIS AD EXPVGNANDAM CIVITATEM) Nimirum ut Terentius ait: Omnia prius experiri quam armis sapientem decet. Et Apollonius: Μηδ’ αὕτως ἀλκῇ πρὶν ἔπεσσί γε πειρηθῆναι. Valuit hoc etiam in terra Canaan. Itaque lex quæ est Exod. 22. v. 32. 33. & hoc libro 7. v. 12. intelligenda est, cum beni- gna exceptione, nisi siqui ad primam denuntiationem parue- rint. Ita Maimonides & Moses de Kotzi præcepto jubente 15. Vide rationes pro hac sententia libro 2. de jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 13. §. 4. Justæ autem belli causæ apud Hebræos censentur, in civitatem Hebræam colentem idola: in civita- tem Hebræam deficientem a lege: ob fidem Regi violatam 2. Reg. 3. ob rebellionem 2. Reg. 20. ob defensum nocentem Jud. 20. ob injuriam Regi aut Reipublicæ illatam 2. Sam. 10. si res suas repetant Hebræi: ad repellendum hostem: ad ho- stem præveniendum Num. 21. contra auxiliatorem hostis 2. Reg. Sam. 8. ad amicum hostibus eripiendum Gen. 14. ad- versus tyrannidem: talia bella sumebantur ex decreto Sy- nedrii LXX. virum.

## 20:11
Verse 11.

AND SHALL SERVE THEE UNDER TRIBUTE) See what was said in book 3 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 15, § 6. By tribute are understood also labors, as appears in 1 Kings 9, verse 15; 2 Chronicles 8, verse 7. At the same time these peoples had to subject themselves to the dominion of the Hebrews, and consequently also to embrace the precepts given to Noah.

Latin:

Vers 11.

ET SERVIET TIBI SUB TRIBUTO) Vide quæ di- cta libro 3. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 15. §. 6. Sub tributo intelliguntur & operæ, ut apparet 1. Reg. 9. vers. 15. 2. Para- lip. 8. versu 7. Simul debebant hi populi ditioni Hebræo- rum se subjicere, ac proinde & præcepta Noæ data amplecti.

## 20:13
Verse 13.

SMITING EVERY MALE THAT IS THEREIN) The punishment for great contumacy, below 16.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

PERCVTIENS OMNE QVOD IN EA GENE- RIS MASCULINI EST) Pœna magnæ contumaciæ in- fra 16.

## 20:14
EXCEPT THE WOMEN AND THE LITTLE ONES) Age excuses the boy, sex the woman. Seneca, book 3 of On Anger, chapter 24. Add the writers produced by us in book 3 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 11, § 9.

Latin:

ABSQVE MULIERIBUS ET INFANTIBUS) Puerum ætas excusat, fœminam sexus. Seneca libro 3. de ira cap. 24. Adde scriptores productos a nobis libro 3. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 11. §. 9.

## 20:19
Verse 19.

THOU SHALT NOT CUT DOWN THE TREES OF WHICH THOU MAYEST EAT) Pythagoras in Iamblichus: ἡμερὸν φυτὸν καὶ ἔγκαρπον μήτε βλάπτειν μήτε φθείρειν. The Talmudists extend this law by analogy to any thing that would perish without cause: Porphyry, book 2, περὶ ἀποχῆς, where he describes Jewish customs, extends it even to animals of the field serving for work. However, trees that stand in the way of the besiegers' missiles against the city are to be excepted. See what was said in book 3 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 12, § 2.

Verse of the same.

FOR THE TREE IS AND NOT MAN) He takes כי for הלא, which is clearer in the Greek: μὴ ἄνθρωπος τὸ ξύλον, does the wood have the strength of a man, so that it can resist you as you besiege it? Philo understood it no differently in On the Constitution of a Prince: τὶ γάρ φησι τοῖς ἀψύχοις μὲν, τὴν δὲ φύσιν ἡμέροις καὶ ἡμέρες καρπὸς ἀπογεννῶσι μνησικακεῖς. And in his book On Humanity: ἄδικον τὴν πρὸς ἀνθρώπως ὀργὴν ἀποσκήπτειν εἰς τὰ μηδενὸς αἴτια κακῶ. The same sense is also found in Josephus at this place.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

NON SUCCIDES ARBORES DE QVIBUS VE- SCI POTEST) Pythagoras apud Jamblichum: ἡμερὸν φυ- τὸν καὶ ἔγκαρπον μήτε βλάπτειν μήτε φθείρειν. Thalmu- dici extendunt a simili hanc legem ad rem quamvis sine cau- sa perituram: Porphyrius libro 2. περὶ ἀποχῆς, ubi mores Judaicos describit, producit eam etiam ad animantia ruris operi inservientia. Excipiendæ autem arbores, quæ telis obsidentium in urbem obstant. Vide quæ dicta lib. 3. de jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 12. §. 2.

Vers. eod.

QVONIAM LIGNUM EST ET NON HOMO) Sumit כי pro הלא quod manifestius in Græco: μὴ ἄν- θρωπος τὸ ξύλον, an vim habet hominis, ut tibi obsidenti re- sistere possit? Nec aliter accepit Philo de Principis consti- tutione: τὶ γάρ φησι τοῖς ἀψύχοις μὲν, τὴν δὲ φύσιν ἡμέροις καὶ ἡμέρες καρπὸς ἀπογεννῶσι μνησικακεῖς. Et libro de hu- manitate: ἄδικον τὴν πρὸς ἀνθρώπως ὀργὴν ἀποσκήπτειν εἰς τὰ μηδενὸς αἴτια κακῶ. Idem sensus & apud Josephum h. l.

## 20:20
Verse 20.

BUILDING THE BULWARK) In the Hebrew: מצור, which the Greeks rightly translate as χαράκωσιν, a military rampart, wooden towers, and the like.

In the same way also the Targum of Onkelos, and likewise B. Luther, so that the sense is: the fruit-bearing tree is useful to you, and it cannot besiege you nor be a hindrance to you, for it is not a man; but other trees, although they cannot be a hindrance, are unfruitful, they will serve you for constructing engines of war, as Abulensis explains. Others, however, because it is said THAT IT MAY COME FROM YOUR FACE, or that it may proceed BEFORE YOU, and not indeed against you as a bulwark, explain it thus: is it a man, that one should fear lest it flee from you to the enemy into the city, and become a bulwark for it? To which also the Grotian explanation tends: does it have the strength of a man, so that it can resist you as you besiege it? But if indeed it was necessary to withdraw from the siege, fruit-bearing trees were to be cut down, lest they be left for the use of the enemy, just as the Israelites did in the Moabite siege, and that by divine command 2 Kings 3:19. For although the remaining Moabite cities were occupied and devastated, they nevertheless released the metropolis of the region from the siege v. 27.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

INSTRUENS MACHINAS) In Hebræo: מצור, quod Græci bene vertunt χαράκωσιν, vallum castrense, turres li- gneas & similia.

Eodem modo & Targ. Onkelos, nec non B. Luther. ut sensus sit, lignum pomiferum tibi utile est, nec te obsidere tibiq́; obesse potest, non enim homo est; alia vero ligna licet obesse non possint, infrugifera sunt, servient tibi ad machinas bellicas instruendas, ut A- bulensis explicat. Alii tamen, quia dicitur UT VE- NIAT A FACIE TUA, vel ut procedat ANTE TE, non vero contra te ad propugnaculum, ita ex- plicant: num homo est ut metuendum sit, ne à te ad hostes in urbem confugiat, eiq; propugnaculum fiat. Quo etiam abit Grotiana explicatio: num vi- res hominis habet, ut tibi obsidenti resistere possit. Quod si vero ab obsessione recedendum fuit, arbores fru- giferæ cædendæ erant, ne relinquerentur hostibus in usum, quemadmodum Israelitæ fecerunt in ob- sidione Moabitica, idq; ex mandato divino 2. Reg. 3, 19. Licet enim reliquæ civitates Moabiticæ oc- cupatæ & devastatæ fuerint, metropolin tamen re- gionis obsidione solverunt v. 27.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAP. XXI. Concerning secret homicide: Of a son who is hateful and contumacious, hanged on a tree.

Latin:

CAP. XXI. De occulto homicidio: Filio odiosæ, & contuma- ce, suspenso in ligno.

## 21:2
Verse 2.

THY ELDERS AND THY JUDGES SHALL GO FORTH) The name of elders signifies sometimes age, sometimes dignity: therefore, ἐξηγητικῶς (by way of explanation), judges is added: who for this matter are taken in an odd number, three or five.

AND THEY SHALL MEASURE FROM THE PLACE OF THE CORPSE) This pertains to stimulating the diligence of the inquiry.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

EGREDIENTUR MAJORES NATU, ET JUDICES TUI) Senum nomen modo ætatem, modo dignitatem signifi- cat: ideo ἐξηγητικῶς additur judices: qui ad hanc rem sumti numero impare, tres aut quinque.

ET METIENTUR A LOCO CADAVERIS) Hoc pertinet ad excitandam inquirendi diligentiam.

## 21:2 Addition
On ch. 21, v. 2, at p. 592, a. AND THY JUDGES.

Episcopius notes (Instit. bk. 3, ch. 8, no. 10, p. 101) that this execution did not pertain to the 70 Elders, nor to the College of 13 Judges, or to the triumvirs, but to a special senate of five men, and that this precept was intended to indicate a serious detestation of homicide, and served to uncover and identify the author of the slaughter. Because that senate also used many ceremonies, an exact and curious investigation into the facts, and the solemn beheading of a heifer of that kind, it could hardly happen that many and frequent conversations would not be mixed among the people, and thus either the author of the slaughter would be detected, or he would be betrayed by someone who knew or through suspicions and conjectures, or he would be recognized from certain signs and proofs (τεκμηρίοις). Besides the fact that the lord of that land in which the corpse was found applied every effort and industry to detect the murderer before the heifer itself was beheaded; because that place in which it was beheaded was profaned forever, so that it could neither be cultivated nor sown; what fear of such great loss should we believe to have excited diligence in the mind of the lord of that place to detect the author of the slaughter? Episcopius also rightly disapproves, following Franc. Junius, of that custom received among many, by which the indication of a murderer is sought from the eruption of blood which happens at the presence or touch of a stabbed corpse, made by one of the bystanders, as not being worthy of imitation. For if that method were of a most certain judgment, God would without doubt have prescribed it here, and would not have instituted that laborious ceremony of the heifer to be beheaded. Not to mention now that this experiment is not only uncertain and based on no natural cause, but is also most fallacious: because it has not rarely been observed that blood has erupted from the corpse of the deceased at the presence of those whom he had held most dear and most closely joined to himself in his life; so that this flow of blood did not have as the cause of its presence an antipathy, but a sympathy.

Latin:

Ad cap. 21. vers. 2. ad p. 592. a. ET JUDICES TUI.

Pertinuisse hanc executionem non ad LXX. Seniores, nec ad Collegium XIII. Judicum, aut ad triumviros, sed ad peculiarem quinque virorum Se- natum, & præceptum hoc fuisse ad seriam homicidii detestationem indicandam, ac serviisse ad detegen- dum & agnoscendum cædis autorem notat Episcop. lib. 3. Instit. c. 8. n. 10. p. 101. Quia etiam senatus ille multis ceremoniis, exactaque & curiosa in fa- ctum inquisitione, solemnique vitulæ ejusmodi decervicatione, utebantur, fieri vix poterat, quin plurimi crebrique miscerentur in populo sermo- nes, atque ita vel cædis autor deprehenderetur, vel a conscio aut per suspiciones & conjecturas delato proderetur, vel ex signis quibusdam & τεκμηρίοις dignosceretur. Præterquam quod Dominus ter- ræ istius, in qua cadaver repertum erat, omnem operam atque industriam adhibebat, ut homici- dam deprehenderet, antequam vitula ipsa decer- vicabatur; quia locus iste, in quo ea decervicaba- tur, in æternum profanabatur, ut nec coli nec con- seri posset; damni tanti metus quam non diligen- tiam in animo Domini loci istius, ad auctorem cæ- dis deprehendendum excivisse credamus? Recte etiam improbat Episcopius ex hoc præcepto cum Franc. Junio, morem illum apud multos receptum, quo homicidæ indicium quæritur ex sanguinis eruptione, quæ contingat ad præsentiam vel con- tactum cadaveris confossi, ab aliquo circumstan- tium factum, non esse imitandum. Si enim ra- tio ista compertissimi esset judicii, Deus sine du- bio eam hic præscripsisset, & operosam istam vi- tulæ degutturandæ ceremoniam non instituisset. Ut jam non dicam, non incertum modo nullaque causa naturali nixum esse experimentum istud, sed & fallacissimum esse: quia non raro observatum est, sanguinem ex cadavere defuncti erupisse ad præsentiam eorum, quos in vita sua carissimos sibi habuerat, & conjunctissimos; ut fluxus iste sangui- nis non haberet causam sui præsentis ἀντιπάθειαν, sed συμπάθειαν.

## 21:3
Verse 3.

A HEIFER FROM THE HERD WHICH HATH NOT DRAWN THE YOKE, NOR HATH CUT THE EARTH WITH A PLOWSHARE) Chaeremon places those among the prohibited victims in Egypt: τὰ δεδαμασμένα ὡς ἤδη καθωσιωμένα τοῖς πόνοις (those broken in, as already consecrated to labors). In Euripides in the Phoenissae, the four-legged creature untamed by toil is praised as a drink offering. Seneca on the same matter: — A heifer which the plowshare had not bent, or the curved yokes of a slow wagon.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VITULAM DE ARMENTO QUÆ NON TRAXIT JUGVM, NEC TERRAM SCIDIT VOMERE) Chæ- remon inter victimas prohibitas in Ægypto ponit : τὰ δεδα- μασμένα ὡς ἤδη καθωσιωμένα τοῖς πόνοις. Euripidi in Phœ- nissis laudatur τετρασκελὴς μόχθῳ ἀδάμαςος πόσημα. Sene- ca de eadem re: — Vaccæ quam non flexerat Vomer, aut tardi juga curva plaustri.

## 21:5
EVERY MATTER, AND WHATEVER IS CLEAN OR UNCLEAN SHALL BE JUDGED) In the Hebrew it is: Every suit and every stroke. The universal word is to be understood from the subject matter concerning victims, offerings, and leprosy; for concerning these was the cognizance of the Priests. See concerning leprosy below 24. verse 8.

The Priests were present at this act, not as Judges, as Abulensis and Lyranus wish, but, as Bonfrer says, so that they might testify with others that they were immune from this crime; add that they might expiate the secret homicide with these rites. Therefore, the Papists wrongly infer from this that the parts of judging belong to the Pontiff. The Priests were never the sole judges, according to the testimony of the Hebrews in the book Sanhedrin. Procopius, Rabanus, and others note the type of the expiation of Christ in this heifer. See B. Gerhard on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 5. OMNE NEGOTIUM, ET QUICQVID MUNDUM VEL IMMVNDVM EST JUDICETVR) In Hebræo est : Lis omnis & plaga omnis. Vox universalis intelligenda ex subjecta materia de victimis, oblationibus & lepra; de his enim notio erat Sacerdotum. Vide de lepra infra 24. vers. 8.

SAcerdotes huic actui interfuere, non ut Judices, uti Abulensis, & Lyranus volunt, sed, ut Bonfrer. ut immunes se flagitii hujus cum aliis testarentur; ad- de ut ritibus hisce occultum homicidium expiarent. Male ergo Papistæ hinc colligunt, Pontifici judican- di partes convenire. Nunquam soli Sacerdotes fue- re judices, testibus Ebræis in libro Sanhedrin. Ty- pum expiationis Christi in hac vitula notant Proco- pius, Rabanus, alii. Vid. B. Gerhardus in h. l.

## 21:6
Verse 6.

TO THE SLAIN) To the place where the slaughter was committed, which after that could neither be cultivated nor counted.

AND THEY SHALL WASH THEIR HANDS) To testify to their innocence in this matter. See what [is written] at Matthew 27. v. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

AD INTERFECTUM) Ad locum ubi facta cædes, qui post id nec coli nec censeri poterat.

LAVABANTQVE MANVS SVAS) Ad testandam suam in hac re innocentiam. Vide quæ ad Matth. 27. v. 24.

## 21:7
Verse 7.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

## 21:8
BE PROPITIOUS TO THY PEOPLE) Thus also Draco had ordained, a homicide having been committed, the author of which was unknown, to purify the people on the same day. Demosthenes mentions it.

Latin:

PROPITIUS ESTO POPVLO TVO) Sic & Draco constituerat homicidio facto, cujus auctor ignoraretur, κα- θᾶραι τὸν δῆμον ἀυθήμερον. Meminit Demosthenes.

## 21:11
Vers. 11.

AND YOU SHALL HAVE LOVED HER) In Greek καὶ ἐνθυμηθῇς ἀυτῆς. The Hebrew חשק is to adhere, to be joined, which the Hebrews in the Talmud, Moses Gerundensis, Maimonides, and all others wish to be said modestly, for 'you shall have lain with her': which the word for humbling, which will follow, also confirms. Thus Homer says, ἐν φιλότητι μιγῆναι. This law is not to be understood concerning the women of the Canaanites and other nations who, after the proclamation is spurned, are ordered to be killed, but concerning other foreign women, whose marriage, if they were to accept the law, that is, and were baptized into it, was not forbidden to the Israelites, but to the Priests alone. Lest, however, this should happen often and rashly, the law applies many cautions. It indulges the first congress to military license and the right of victory, if by chance the Hebrew, sated with her, should abstain from her. It does not permit a second congress unless she has been solemnly made a wife: but before that is done, the law takes away from the woman all charms, pleasantries, and delights, through which a man could be enticed, so that such marriages may be rarer.

This invention of the Hebrews does not deserve approval. For the discourse is not about foul love, which is forbidden, but about chaste and connubial love, if you have loved her so that you have decided to take her as a wife; nor does God indulge congress with captive women, but prescribes laws by which it is permitted to take such women captured in war, and therefore there is no reason why they should be tortured along with the Hebrews, Tremellius, Piscator, Amama, Pelargus, and Grotius, [saying] that this rite was prescribed to render the woman deformed, when it should rather have been applied so that it might be taught, by this shaving of the hair, paring of the nails, and laying aside of the former garment, that they were bidding a final farewell to the superstition and perverse rites of the Gentiles: which is the opinion of most Christian interpreters, both ancient and modern, Cajetan, Vatablus, Pagninus, Leonhard Marius, Oleaster, and Corn. a Lapide, which, among the Jews also, R. Bechai, as Fagius testifies, has embraced; he says, she is ordered to shave her hair, so that by such a rite the religion of the household gods may be extirpated by the root. This agrees more with the Hebrew phrase, for 'to make her nails,' to be, to let grow, is an unusual locution, but 'to make the nails' for 'to prepare, to dispose the nails,' which is done by trimming their clippings, is similar to that in 2 Sam. 19:24. Mephibosheth had not 'made,' that is, had not cut his feet (the nails of his feet) nor had he 'made' his beard, that is, he had not trimmed it, as the Targum explains, whence also the LXX rendered it thus in this place, περιονυχήσεις ἀυτὴν, and Philo in his book on charity, περιελὼν ὄνυχας. The Vulgate and B. Luther, 'she shall pare her nails.' The Rabbis themselves explain it thus in the Talmud in Massechet Yebamoth, R. Eliezer; where the word עשׂתה is explained by הקוץ, 'she shall cut.' And what such great deformity is there, that if the nails are not cut for the space of one month, it should have to be sanctioned by a special law for the sake of deformity? But it is especially to be reproved what is assumed in this explanation, as if congress with a captive woman were first granted by this divine constitution, and afterwards, in a peculiar way, a restraint of love against the captive was attempted by her being deformed. For this is not to be attributed to God, that He granted base and dishonest things, such as that whoredom with captive women. Much sounder are the things which Philo reports about these rites: Moses, he says, ordered everything beautifully: For first, he did not loosen the reins to lust, but repressed it for thirty days. Secondly, he examines the love, whether it is merely furious and fastidious, or whether it has some reason mixed in. For reason was restraining concupiscence, so that it might not act too insolently; it will await the end of the month. Thirdly, because he pities the captive if she is a virgin, because her parents did not arrange the desired nuptials for her, or if she is a widow, because, having lost the one to whom the girl had been married, she is about to experience another, not so much a husband as a Master, even under the equitable law of marriage. In no way is it to be established, says this our B. Gerhard (even though leaning toward another opinion), that God granted to the Israelite people wandering copulations with captive women. Nor is the garment of captivity to be explained as the garment of liberty, nor is any other garment than that which she had to assume in its place the garment of captivity, [and] that which she lays aside [the garment] of liberty, as Grotius explains; and that Rabbinic tradition rashly supposes that Gentile women were adorned with most beautiful garments when battle was imminent, so that if by chance victory fell to the Israelites, they might find favor in their eyes. Finally, it is not necessary to interpret 'YOU HAVE HUMBLED' as referring to lust satisfied with her. For although they are sometimes said to be humbled in that sense, yet this also was a humiliation, that she had to submit herself to foreign customs, to shave her head, to put off her garment, to assume another, and not even to have freedom in the cutting of her nails, nay, even to leave her parents, and to mourn them as if they were not, and to testify openly by that monthly mourning that she would never visit her parents and relatives: all of which bring about some humiliation, and when that submission has been lightened by the hope of marriage, but he now does not want to lead into marriage her whom he had loved before, and now rejects her, is this not to be considered a humiliation? Wherefore there is no need that we should establish this humiliation as compression through copulation, either with Grotius, or with others believe that the captive was led into marriage and humbled in another way. For nowhere is joining someone to oneself in marriage expressed by the name of humiliation. We add the allegory of Jerome, who in Epistle 84 to Magnus the Roman Orator, rendering a reason why in his writings he puts many things from exotic literature, cites the Apostle's example, adding these things: He had read in Deuteronomy the command by the voice of the Lord, that the head of a captive woman should be shaved, her eyebrows, all the hairs and nails of her body should be cut off, and thus she should be held in marriage. What wonder then, if I also desire to make a secular wisdom an Israelite from a handmaid and captive because of the charm of her eloquence and the beauty of her limbs? And if, whatever in her is dead, of idolatry, of pleasure, of error, of lusts, I cut off and shave, and from that race I generate for the Lord of Sabaoth those born in the house mixed into a most pure body? My labor profits the family of Christ, fornication increases the number of fellow servants in another. Hosea took a wife of whoredom, Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, and there is born to him from the harlot a son Jezreel, who is called the seed of GOD Os. 1. Isaiah with a sharp razor shaves the beard and the legs of those sinning Is. 7. Ezekiel in the type of the whoring Jerusalem shears her hair, so that whatever in her is without sense and life may be taken away. And Ep. 26 to Pammachius it holds thus: If you have fallen in love with a captive woman, that is, secular wisdom, and have been captured by her beauty, shave her bald and cut off the allurements of her hair and the ornaments of words along with her dead nails; wash her with prophetic niter, and then resting with her say: His left hand under my head and his right hand will embrace me, and the captive will give you many offspring, and from a Moabitess she will be made an Israelite.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET ADAMAVERIS EAM) Græce καὶ ἐνθυμηθῇς ἀυ- τῆς. Hebræum חשק, est adhærere, conjungi, quod He- bræi in Thalmode, Moses Gerundensis & Maimonides alii- que omnes σεμνῶς dictum volunt, pro concubueris cum ea: quod & firmat vox humiliandi, quæ sequetur. Sic Homerus dicit, ἐν φιλότητι μιγῆναι. Lex hæc non de fœminis Cana- næorum aliarumque gentium quæ post denuntiationem spretam jubentur interfici, intelligenda est, sed de aliis fœ- minis alienigenis, quarum matrimonium si legem scilicet susciperent, & in id baptizarentur, interdictum Israëlitis non erat, sed Sacerdotibus solis. Ne tamen sæpe ac temere id fieret, lex multas adhibet cautiones. Primum congres- sum indulget licentiæ militari ac juri victoriæ, si forte ea sa- tiatus abstineat se ab ea Hebræus. Secundum congressum non permittit, nisi solenniter conjunx facta sit: sed antequam id fiat lex aufert fœminæ omnes veneres, amœnitates atque delicias, per quas vir posset allici, quo rariora sint conjugia talia.

Commentum hoc Ebræorum calculum non meretur. Non enim sermo est de spurco amore, qui vetitus est, sed de amore casto, & connubiali, si ad- amaveris eam ita, ut decreveris in conjugem ducere, neque Deus indulget congressum cum captis mu- lieribus, sed leges præscribit, quibus tales mulieres bello captas ducere liceat, ideoque non est quod torqueantur cum Ebræis, Tremellio, Piscatore, Ama- ma, Pelargo, Grotio ritus hic præscripti ad deformem reddendam mulierem, quum potius adhibendi fue- rint, ut doceretur, hac capillitii rasione, unguium bræcisione, vestis pristinæ depositione illas gentilium superstitioni ac perversis ritibus penitus valedicere : quæ est Christianorum plerorumque Interpp. sententia, cum veterum, tum recentiorum, Cajetani, Vatabli, Pagnini, Le- onhard. Marii, Oleastri, Corn. a Lapide, quam e Ju- dæis quoq; R. Bechai, teste Fagio amplexus est; ca- pillos, inquit, radere jubetur, ut tali ritu domesticorum deorum religio radicitus extirpetur. Congruit id ma- gis phrasi Ebrææ, nam facere ungues suos, esse, crescere sinere, inusitata est locutio, at facere ungues pro apta- re, disponere ungues, quod fit præsegmina eorum re- fecando, simile illi est 2. Sam. 19, 24. Mephiboseth non fecerat, id est, non præciderat pedes suos (ungues pedum suorum) nec fecerat barbam suam, id est, non totonderat, ut Targum explicat, unde etiam reddide- re ita LXX. h. l. περιονυχήσεις ἀυτὴν, & Philo lib. de caritate περιελὼν ὄνυχας. Vulgata & B. Lutherus, circumcidet ungues. Rabbini ipsi sic exponunt in Talmud in Massechet Jobamoth R. Eliezer; ubi ver- bum עשׂתה per הקוץ præcidet explicatur. Et quænam tanta inde deformitas, quod spatio unius mensis non præscindantur ungues, ut lege etiam pe- culiari id sanciendum fuerit deformitatis causa? Sed imprimis reprobandum, quod in hac explicatione assumitur, quasi concessus primum hac divina con- stitutione fuerit congressus cum muliere captiva, postea vero peculiari modo deformata tentata a- moris adversus captivam continentia. Non enim Deo hoc tribuendum, quod concesserit turpia & in- honesta, qualis illa scortatio cum captivis mulieri- bus. Multo saniora sunt, quæ de his ritibus Philo tradit: Moses, inquit, omnia pulchre ordinavit: Primo enim non laxavit frena libidini, sed per triginta dies eam repressit. Secundo amorem examinat, num mere furiosus fastidiosusq́ sit, an aliquid rationis admixtum habeat. Ratio enim cohibebat concupiscentiam, ne quid agat insolentius, expectabit mensis terminum. Tertio quod miseratur captivam si virgo est, quia paren- tes ei optatas nuptias non conciliarunt, sin vidua, quia amisso, cui puella nupserat, expertura est alium, non magis maritum, quam Dominum etiam sub æquabili jure conjugii. Nullo modo statuendum est, inquit hic B. Gerhardus noster, (etsi in aliam propendens sententiam) Deum vagos cum mulierculis captivis concubitus populo Israelitico concessisse. Neque vestimentum captivitatis vestimentum libertatis ex- ponendum, nec alia vestis, quam ejus loco assumere debebat, vestis captivitatis sit, illa, quam deponit, li- bertatis, uti exponit Grotius; temereq; supponit il- la Rabbinica traditio, Ethnicas mulieres imminen- te prælio pulcherrimis vestibus exornatas fuisse, ut si forte Israelitis victoria cederet, gratiam in oculis ipsorum invenirent. Denique necessum non est τὸ HUMILIASTI de expleta cum ea libidine inter- pretari. Etsi enim humiliatæ aliquando dicantur eo sensu, tamen etiam hæc erat humiliatio, quod se submittere alienis moribus debuerit, caput radere, vestem suam exuere, aliam assumere, ac ne libertatem quidem in præscindendis unguibus habere, imo & pa- rentes suos relinquere, eosq; quasi non essent, lugere, ac de parentibus ac cognatis nunquam adeundis lu- ctu illo menstruo palam testari: quæ omnia ταπέ- νωσιν aliquam inferunt, & quum submissio illo spe matrimonii levata fuerit, illam vero jam in matri- monium ducere nolit, quam adamaverat antea, jam reprobet, annon hæc humiliatio est censenda? Qua- propter non opus est, ut vel cum Grotio hanc humi- liationem compressionem per concubitum statuamus, vel cum aliis captivam in matrimonium ductam, ac a- liter hnmiliatam credamus. Nuspiam enim alí- quam matrimonio sibi jungere humiliationis nomi- ne exprimitur. Addimus allegoriam Hieronymi, qui in Epist. 84. ad Magnum Oratorem Romanum rationem reddens, cur in scriptis suis multa po- nat ex literatura exotica, Apostoli exemplum alle- gat, haec subjiciens: Legerat in Deuteronomio Domini voce praeceptum, mulieris captivae radendum caput, su- percilia, omnes pilos & ungues corporis amputandos, & sic eam habendam in conjugio. Quid ergo mirum, si & ego sapientiam secularem propter eloquii venustatem & membrorum pulchritudinem de ancilla atq; captiva Israelitidem facere cupio? & si, quicquid in ea mortuum est, idololatriae, voluptatis, erroris, libidinum, praecido & rado, & mixtos purissimo corpori vernaculos ex eo genero Domino Sabaoth? labor meus in familiam Chri- sti proficit, stuprum in alienam auget numerum conser- vorum. Osee accepit uxorem fornicariam, Gomer fi- liam Debelaim, & nascitur ei de meretrice filius Jozra- el, qui vocatur semen DEI Os. 1. Esaias novacula a- cuta barbam & crura radit peccantium Es. 7. Eze- chiel in typo fornicantis Jerusalem tondet caesariem suam, ut quicquid in ea absq; sensu & vita est aufera- tur. Et Ep. 26. ad Pammachium ita habet: Si adama- veris mulierem captivam, hoc est, sapientiam secula- rem, & ejus pulchritudine captus fueris, decalva eam & illecebras crinium atq; ornamenta verborum cum e- mortuis unguibus seca; lava eam Prophetali nitro, & tunc requiescens cum ea dicito: Sinistra ejus sub capite meo & dextra illius amplexabitur me, & multos tibi foetus captiva dabit, ac de Moabitide efficietur Israelitis.

## 21:12
Verse 12.

SHE SHALL SHAVE HER HEAD) She shall shave her hair, as is the custom for women in deep mourning. But there is a certain deformity in this: The hair, which is the only ornament of beauty, has fallen. Conversely, men were not shaved after the first seven days of mourning. AND SHE SHALL PARE HER NAILS) In the Hebrew, she shall make her nails, that is, she shall make them long, she shall let them grow, as Rabbi Akiba interprets. To pare the nails is a part of cleanliness, which was neglected in mourning, so that for the first seven days vile garments were worn, and they were not washed, nor was washing used except for the face and hands: nor any anointing.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

RADET CAESARIEM) Comas radet, ut in luctu gravi mos est feminis. Est autem in hoc deformitas quaedam: Quod solum formae decus est, cecidere capilli. Contra viri post septem primos luctus dies non radebantur. ET CIRCVMCIDET VNGVES) In Hebraeo, faciet un- gues suos, id est, faciet eos longos, crescere sinet, ut interpre- tatur Rabbi Akiba. Vngues praecidere est pars munditiae, quae in luctu negligebatur, ita ut septem diebus primis ve- stes viles sumerentur, neque eluerentur, nec lotio usurpare- tur nisi faciei & manuum: nec unctio ulla.

## 21:13
Verse 13.

SHE SHALL PUT OFF THE GARMENT IN WHICH SHE WAS CAPTURED) The garment of liberty, for which she shall take the garment of captivity and mourning, that is, a filthy one, if even by this reason love might be cooled. For it is most true what one too skilled in such things said: We are taken by adornment: all things are covered with gems and gold: the girl herself is the smallest part of herself. A MONTH) In the Hebrew: a moon of days, that is, until the moon returns to the same state. AFTERWARD THOU SHALT GO IN UNTO HER) Baptized and joined in marriage.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DEPONET VESTEM IN QVA CAPTA EST) Ve- stem libertatis, pro qua sumet vestem captivitatis & luctus, id est, sordidam, si vel hac ratione refrigerari amor possit. Verissimum enim est quod nimium peritus talium dixit: Auferimur cultu: gemmis auroque teguntur Omnia: pars minima est ipsa puella sui. VNO MENSE) In Hebraeo: luna dierum, id est donec luna in eundem statum redeat. POSTEA INTRABIS AD EAM) Baptizatam & jun- ctam conjugio.

## 21:14
Verse 14. BUT IF AFTERWARD SHE SHALL NOT PLEASE THY SOUL) Omit that 'afterward'. For this is what it means, if having seen that deformity of adornment you do not wish to marry her. The Greeks: ἐὰν μὴ θέλῃς αὐτήν. THOU SHALT LET HER GO FREE) Thus also the Greeks, ἐλευθέραν. In the Hebrew, of her soul, that is, so that she may be of her own will. AND THOU SHALT NOT OPPRESS HER BY POWER) Greek: ἐκ ἀθετήσεως. In the Hebrew: לא תתעמר that is, you shall not use her as a handmaid: this word is taken thus, and below 24, 7.

BECAUSE THOU HAST HUMBLED HER) Thus also the Greeks: διότι ἐταπείνωσας αὐτήν. More elegant Greeks would say, ὅτι ἐφύβρισας αὐτήν. In this meaning the word ענה is found below 22, 24 and 29. Likewise 2 Sam. 13 v. 12 concerning Tamar whom Absalom had mocked: in all which places the Greeks, as here, use the verb ταπεινοῦν. This is a penalty of sorts for satisfied lust, that the Lord by right of war having become the owner of the woman he had known could neither sell her, nor force her to servile works; but he had to either marry her, or send her free from his hand.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SI AVTEM POSTEA NON SEDERIT ANIMO TVO) Omitte illud postea. Hoc enim vult, si conspecta ista cultus deformitate ducere eam nolueris. Grae- ci: ἐὰν μὴ θέλῃς αὐτήν. DIMITTES EAM LIBERAM) Sic & Graeci, ἐλευθέραν. In Hebraeo, animae suae, id est, ut sui sit arbitrii. NEC OPPRIMERE PER POTENTIAM) Graece: ἐκ ἀθετήσεως. In Hebraeo: לא תתעמר id est, non uteris ea pro ancilla: ita sumitur haec vox, & infra 24, 7.

QVIA HVMILIASTI EAM) Sic & Graeci: διότι ἐτα- πείνωσας αὐτήν. Graeci elegantiores dicerent, ὅτι ἐφύβρισας αὐτήν. Hoc significatu vox ענה reperitur infra 22, 24. & 29. Item 2. Sam. 13. v. 12. de Thamare cui illuserat Absa- lom: quibus omnibus in locis Graeci, ut hic, verbum ταπει- νοῦν usurpant. Est haec qualiscunque expletae libidinis poe- na, quod Dominus belli jure factus foeminam cognitam nec vendere poterat, nec ad serviles operas adigere; sed aut du- cere eam debebat, aut liberam e manu emittere.

## 21:16
Verse 16. AND SHALL HAVE WILLED TO DIVIDE HIS SUBSTANCE AMONG HIS SONS) The father therefore had the right of assigning to each child his portions, by giving or by bequeathing: which were valid until the Jubilee, which the place of Sirach 33 v. 24 also teaches. See concerning the Law of War and Peace book 2, chapter 6, § 14. Formerly before the law even strangers could be left as heirs, Genesis 15 v. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 16. VOLVERITQVE SVBSTANTIAM INTER FILIOS SVOS DIVIDERE) Jus ergo pater habebat affi- gnandi cuique liberum suas portiones, donando sive testan- do: quae valebant usque ad Jubilaeum, quod & Sirachidae do- cet locus 33. v. 24. Vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. 2. cap. 6. §. 14. Olim ante legem etiam extranei haeredes relinqui poterant, Genes. 15. v. 3.

## 21:17
Verse 17.

OF THOSE THINGS WHICH HE SHALL HAVE) Which he shall have possessed in reality. For thus the word מצא is accustomed to be taken in law.

AND HE SHALL GIVE TO HIM) In the Hebrew: לו masculine, as also in Greek αὐτῷ. For a female is not capable of the birthright. AND TO THIS ONE THE FIRSTBORN RIGHTS ARE OWED) From the most ancient law before the law, which gave to the firstborn, namely the males, as we have already said, the leadership in the family, a double inheritance in the goods possessed by the father, and the priesthood of the family rites. The double inheritance had the use for making feasts and the expenses of the rites. Hence an inheritance of pure profit without rites in Plautus. This birthright the father could transfer to a later-born for grave reasons. But the law takes away that liberty from one having several wives at the same time, lest, captured by the allurements of one wife, he either feign false causes or grasp at light ones against the firstborn. The same reason is given in the Lombard law 2. 20, 3. A double portion of the inheritance is called the mouth of two, v. 17, by metaphor, as if the firstborn had two mouths, the remaining brothers single ones, by which portion of the paternal inheritance they are to be fed and filled. Thus Elisha, 2 Kings 2:9, asks for the mouth of two of the spirit of Elijah, that is, a double portion over the other fellow-disciples, not a greater power of the spirit than that of his own Master Elijah. Conf. Zech. 13:8. Therefore, a double portion was not given to the firstborn as if he received half of the entire inheritance, but because as much fell to him as to two sons and heirs. Which were figures of Christ, the true firstborn, to whom a double inheritance is due, of which he keeps one for himself, and communicates the other to us. However, the act of Jacob transferring the birthright of Reuben, born of Leah, to Joseph, born of the beloved Rachel, Gen. 49:3, ought not to be judged by this law. For that was done not out of some preposterous hatred, but out of a special instinct of God, to whom also must be attributed the transfer of the birthright of Esau to Jacob, Gen. 27:39, and of Manasseh to Ephraim. Although indeed God here disposes of children in polygamy, he by no means sanctioned or approved of polygamy itself. For he who disposes of the consequent does not immediately also will the antecedent. Thus God disposes of the hire of a harlot, Deut. 23:18, yet he does not approve of the harlot's gain. It is one thing to recount nakedly some act received by public custom, and to form a case from it, and another thing to approve of that act.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

DE HIS QVAE HABVERIT) Quae reipsa possederit. Ita enim vox מצא in jure sumi solet.

DABITQVE EI) In Hebræo : לו masculinum, ut & Græce αὐτῷ. Fœmina enim τῶν πρωτοτοκείων capax non est. ET HVIC DEBENTVR PRIMOGENITA) Ex jure antiquissimo ante legem, quod primogenitis, nempe mari- bus, ut jam diximus, dabat principatum in familia, duplam hæreditatem in bonis a patre possessis, & sacerdotium sa- crorum familiæ. Dupla hæreditas usum habebat ad facien- da convivia & sacrorum sumtus. Inde merum lucrum sine sacris hæreditas apud Plautum. Hæc πρωτοτοκεῖα pater gravibus de causis transferre ad post natum poterat. Verum eam libertatem lex adimit plures simul uxores habenti, ne uxoris unius delinimentis captus præter causas in primo na- tum aut fingat falsas, aut captet leves. Eadem ratio reddi- tur in lege Longobardica 2. 20, 3. Duplex hæreditatis portio dicitur os duorum v. 17. per metaphoram, ac si primogenitus duo habe- ret ora, reliqui fratres singula quæ portione hæ- reditatis paternæ pascenda & replenda sint. Ita Elisaus 2. Reg. 2,9. petit os duorum de spiritu Eliæ, hoc est duplicem portionem præ ceteris condiscipulis, non virtutem ampliorem spiritus præ ipso Magistro suo Elia. Conf. Zach. 13,8. Non ergo duplex portio pri- mogenito ita dabatur, quasi dimidiam partem to- tius hæreditatis acceperit, sed quod tantum ipsi ces- serit, quantum duobus filiis ac hæredibus. Quæ figu- ra erant Christi veri primogeniti, cui debeatur duplex hæreditas, quarum alteram sibi servat, alteram nobis communicat. Cæterum factum Jacobi primogeni- turam Rubenis ex Lea suscepti in Josephum ex di- lecta Rachele susceptum Gen. 49,3. transferentis ex hac lege judicari non debet. Id enim non ex odio quodam præpostero, sed ex peculiari Dei instinctu fa- ctum, cui etiam tribuenda est translatio primogenitu- ræ Esavi in Jacobum Gen. 27, 39. Manassis in Ephrai- mum. Quanquam vero Deus hic disponat de libe- ris in πολυγαμίᾳ, neutiquam tamen πολυγαμίαν ipsam sanxit aut approbavit. Non enim qui dispo- nit de consequente, ille statim etiam antecedens vult. Ita disponit Deus de mercede prostibuli Deut. 23, 18. nec tamen meretricis quæstum approbat. Aliud est fa- ctum aliquod publica consuetudine receptum nude recensere, & ex eo casum formare, aliud factum il- lud approbare.

## 21:18
Vers. 18.

IF A MAN SHALL HAVE BEGOTTEN A STUBBORN SON) And this law, because it is sufficiently harsh, has received a stricter interpretation. For because the law names a son, it is not extended to a daughter: and because it requires stubbornness, the first age, not yet capable of malice, is excluded. Excluded also is he who is of a fuller age, and manages his own affairs separately from his father. Regarding the quantity of food or drink, which needs to have been produced for there to be a place for the law, interpreters vary. They also wish it to be required that the father and mother be alive: because he who is bereft of father or mother generally has some goods, from which the damage given can be compensated.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

SI GENVERIT HOMO FILIVM CONTVMACEM) Et hæc lex, quia satis dura est, interpretationem accepit stri- ctiorem. Quia enim filium nominat lex, non producitur ad filiam: & quia contumaciam requirit, excluditur ætas prima malitiæ nondum capax. Excluditur & is qui plenio- ris est ætatis, & seorsim a patre res suas agit. De quantitate vero esculentorum vel poculentorum, quam opus sit proda- ctam esse, ut legi locus sit, variant interpretes. Requiri et- iam volunt ut pater & mater vivant: quia patre aut matre qui orbus est, plerumque bona habet aliqua, unde damnum datum sarciri possit.

## 21:20
Vers. 20.

AND THEY SHALL SAY TO THEM: OUR SON HIMSELF IS PROTERVOUS AND STUBBORN) Josephus expresses the rite in Antiquities 16: 'the ancestral law, which commanded that if the parents of those accused should place their hands upon the head, it was necessary for those standing around to cast stones and kill him in this manner.' Therefore, no authority of a judge was required here, as neither in certain other crimes. Sopater on the law which permits a father to kill his children: 'the law, knowing that the father would be an impartial judge, commanded this.' See what is in De Jure Belli ac Pacis, book 2, chapter 5, § 1 and 28. What is stubborn here, in Hebrew is סורר: what is protervous, there is מורה. The former word suits him who refuses to do what is commanded: the latter, him who does what is forbidden.

That distinction of these words is not solid or certain. More correctly to others, a protervous or perverse (intolerable) son, and סורר ומורה, a rebellious and stubborn one, so that to perversity is added notable stubbornness, which can by no means be curbed and restrained, such as the unruly, where all hope of amendment is lost, into public workhouses and houses of correction to- day are thrust out. Let him be led to the gate, because Eastern peoples exercised judgments at the gate (Gen. 34:20; Ex. 17:5), whence in every city of the Israelite people there was some gate which was called the gate of judgment (Neh. 3:20). But whether parents are commanded to lead such a disobedient son to the gate, or whether it is only prescribed what the people ought to do to him if the parents have led him there, the interpreters vary. The latter seems to us to be the case, so that all the preceding things in verses 18, 19, and 20 pertain to the formation of the case, as they say, and are to be rendered hypothetically: if anyone has a stubborn son, and thus the father and mother, having apprehended him, have brought him to the elders, saying, etc., and the imperative words or the decision follow in verse 21; whence the Hebrews note that this law never came into practice; they would more correctly say that such an example did not easily occur. For natural affection does not allow parents to believe that they are going to offer their son to death, unless the son has been extremely wicked, so that they are convinced his soul cannot otherwise be set free. It is not likely that parents were established as informers by a special law; nor would the matter have been free from the danger of either failing in natural affection or transgressing the divine law. Cf. Prov. 19:18. Piscator, however, gathers in vain from this law that stubborn sons are still to be subjected to capital punishment. That law was forensic, and therefore only what was moral in it—namely, that a stubborn son ought to be punished by the magistrate—now holds; but the determination of the penalty, that he should be overwhelmed with stones, was of the Jewish forum and does not bind us. Therefore, just as the capital punishment which is decreed for those who curse father or mother (Ex. 21:15, 16; Lev. 20:9) indeed had a place among the Jews, but not among Christians, nor will a Christian state be easily shown in which stubborn sons are subjected to capital punishment.

must be sold, lest the land be defiled. But it is not to be conceded to Zepper (Book 5, On the Mosaic Laws, ch. 7) that the divine law conflicts with the divine law regarding the punishment accepted among Christians, by which corpses are left on the gallows today; for that law was forensic, and therefore does not bind Christians, among whom that opinion also expires—that those who are hanged are specifically cursed—which pertained to the ceremonial law, as will now be said; I pass over the fact that Schickard, in his On Royal Law, shows that it was permitted for a king to leave a hanged man on the gallows longer than the law commands.

Same verse.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

DICENTQVE AD EOS: FILIVS NOSTER IPSE PROTERVVS ET CONTVMAX EST) Ritum exprimit Josephus Antiquæ historiæ 16. πάτριον νόμον, ὃς ἐκέλευσεν εἰ τὰ κατηγορηθέντων οἱ γονεῖς ἐπιδοῖεν τῇ κεφαλῇ τὰς χεῖ- ρας, ἐπάναγκες εἶναι τοῖς περιεστῶσι βάλλειν καὶ τοῦτον ἀπο- κτείνειν τὸν τρόπον. Nulla ergo hîc, ut nec in aliis quibus- dam criminibus, judicis requirebatur auctoritas. Sopater de lege quæ patri permittit liberos interficere: ὁ νόμος τῶ- το εἰδὼς ὡς εἰλικρινὴς γένοιτ' ἂν δικαστὴς ὁ πατὴρ, τοῦτο προσέ- ταξεν. Vide quæ de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 2. cap. 5. §. 1. & 28. quod hîc est contumax, in Hebr. est סורר: quod pro- tervus, ibi מורה. Illa vox ei convenit, qui imperata facere detrectat: hæc ei qui facit prohibita.

Illud discrimen harum vocum non est solidum aut certum. Rectius aliis filius protervus vel perver- sus (intolerabilis) & סורר ומורה rebellis atque contu- max, ut ad perversitatem insignis accedat contu- macia, quæ nullo pacto frenari, ac compesci possit, quales immorigeri, ubi omnis spes emendationis decollat, in ἐργαστήρια & παιδευτήρια publica ho- die detruduntur. Ad portam deducatur, quia orientales populi judicia in porta exercebant Gen. 34, 20. Ex. 17, 5. unde in qualibet urbe populi Israelitici erat porta aliqua, quæ dicebatur porta judicii Neh. 3, 20. Num autem jubeantur parentes filium ejusmodi immorigerum ad portam deducere, an vero solum præcipiatur, quid populus ei, si deduxerint ipsum eo parentes, facere debeant, Interpp. variant. Posterius nobis videtur, ut ita antecedentia omnia v. 18. 19. 20. ad casus formationem, ut loquuntur, pertineant, & hypothetice reddenda sint, si cui fuerit filius contumax, adeoque apprehendentes eum Pater & mater produxerint ad Seniores, dicentes &c. ac verba διατακτικὰ, vel decisio sequatur v. 21. unde Ebræi notant hanc legem nunquam in consuetudinem venisse; non facile exemplum tale accidisse rectius dixerint. Nam parentes, nisi extreme malus fuerit filius, ut aliter animam ejus liberari non posse persuasi sint, eum ad necem oblaturos esse ςοργὴ naturalis credere non permittit. Non est verisimile parentes delatores fuisse constitutos peculiari lege; nec periculo res vacasset seu prævaricandi in ςοργὴν naturalem, seu legem divinam transgrediendi. Conf. Prov. 19, 18. Nequicquam autem Piscator ex hac lege colligit, filios contumaces, etiamnum supplicio capitis afficiendos esse. Lex ea forensis erat, ideoque non nisi quod morale in ea fuit, nempe quod filius contumax a Magistratu puniri debeat, nunc obtinet; determinatio aut pœnæ, quod lapidibus obruendus sit, fori Judaici erat, nos non obligat. Proinde uti capitale supplicium, quod illi, qui Patri aut matri maledicunt, decernitur Ex. 21, 15. 16. Lev. 20, 9. apud Judæos quidem locum habebat, non autem apud Christianos, nec monstrabitur temere Resp. Christiana, in qua filii contumaces supplicio capitali afficiantur.

vendum sit, ne terra inquinetur. Non autem Zeppero concedendum l. 5. de leg. Mos. cap. 7. quasi divina pugnet cum lege divina supplicium penes Christianos receptum, quo cadavera hodie relinquuntur in patibulo; nam lex illa forensis erat, adeoque Christianos non obligat, penes quos etiam expirat illa sententia, quod suspensi peculiariter maledicti sint: quæ ad legem ceremonialem spectabat, ut jam dicetur; taceo, quod Schickardus de Jur. Reg. ostendat licuisse Regi suspensum diutius, quam lex jubet, in patibulo relinquere.

Vers. eod.

## 21:22
Vers. 22. ADJUDGED TO DEATH HE SHALL HAVE BEEN HUNG ON A GALLOWS) That was done for a display in the case of those who had been stoned for idolatry or blasphemy. For hanging was not the punishment. For the Hebrews used to strangle them while standing, not by hanging. Concerning burning, the sword, and stones, it is sufficiently apparent that these punishments were distinct from hanging.

The Hebrews altogether reckon hanging among punishments, indeed as the highest kind of capital punishment. R. Moses Nachman calls it suspension, because it was inflicted for contumely against God and undisguised idolatry. Although indeed they were usually first stoned among the Hebrews, and only afterwards hung on wood; yet that hanging is not therefore to be considered as not being a punishment; just as when someone is beheaded, and the head is fixed on a stake, both have the nature of a punishment, and it is considered a milder sentence when only beheading is adjudged. Add that for those who committed grave crimes, on account of which the wrath of God was provoked against an entire community, a punishment of that kind was dictated, so that their bodies were hung, Num. 25, 4, 2 Sam. 21, 6, and they were judged unworthy for that reason to touch the earth, and because they were held to be cursed in a peculiar way when they were hung, Joseph. l. 4. antiq. c. 8. He who has blasphemed GOD, let him be overwhelmed with stones and hang for the day, then let him be buried ignominiously and obscurely. For that burial was not commanded for the honor of burying the corpse, but because that corpse of the cursed man should quickly be removed from the surface of the earth that Christ underwent that [curse] which we were bound to undergo through the condemnation of the law, or we would not have been redeemed from that curse. Therefore, the Apostle says that Christ was made a curse (κατάραν) in the abstract, so that he might designate the curse κατ' ἀντονομασίαν (by antonomasia). And just as the Apostle demonstrates that Christ procured for us here not only a temporal, but primarily an eternal blessing and everlasting blessed life, so it is necessary that Christ liberated us from eternal curse and death, which was done while he was made a curse for us. For he was made subject to the same curse to which we were subject, and from which he liberated us. Which, through the punishment of the cross, was once typologically (τυπικῶς) foreshadowed, but in truth is completed in the cross of Christ. There, he was cursed by God, suspended on a tree, not indeed because he underwent an eternal curse, but because he merited it, and had to die by a death peculiarly execrable to God and ignominious by God's constitution; here, having been made a curse and suspended on the wood of the cross, because he truly undergoes for us the eternal curse, which not he, but we merited, and therefore he had to undergo the punishment which by divine law was peculiarly a curse. Concerning which, see St. Athanasius, On the Incarnation of the Word, Vol. 1 of his works, p. 77: 'If he had come for this reason, that he might bear our sins and our execration, in what other way would he have been a curse (κατάρα) and execration, unless he had received into himself an execrable death? And this is the cross itself: just as it is written: execrable is everyone who hangs on a tree.' Add to these the things which Athanasius had handed down a little earlier on p. 72. Since, therefore, the debt had to be paid for all, and it was owed that all should die—which was his most powerful reason for coming here—therefore, after the monuments of his divinity were published through his deeds, it now remained that he should offer a sacrifice for all, delivering his own temple to death for all, by which he might make all unliable and free from the ancient transgression, and declare himself the victor over death. For there was need of death, and it was necessary to endure death for all, so that what was owed by all might be paid. Certainly, with the common Savior of all having died for us, we no longer die by death, as once according to the threat of the law, as many of us as trust in Christ Jesus. For that very condemnation has been obliterated. Let us also hear Chrysostom on chapter 3 to the Galatians. Since, therefore, even he who hangs is execrable, it was not fitting that he who was about to take away that execration should become liable to the same execration (through transgression of the law), but for that one, another execration had to be undertaken, which he also undertook, and through it took that one away, doing just as if, when someone is adjudged to death, another innocent person should spontaneously and willingly snatch him away in place of that condemned man. So also Christ did: for when he was not liable to the execration of transgression, he received this into himself for all, so that he might liberate all from it: 'For sin,' he says, 'he did not commit, nor was guile found in his mouth.' Therefore, just as by dying he exempted those who were to die from death, so also by receiving the execration into himself, he liberated them from the execration. Consequently, the cross took away the execration and brought in righteousness, and righteousness indeed enticed the grace of the Spirit. I add also Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, p. 251. Just as, therefore, God ordered a sign to be made through the bronze serpent, and on that account is blameless: so indeed also in the law a curse is proposed against those men who are driven onto a cross, but not likewise is a curse established against Christ of God: through whom he saves all who have admitted into themselves things worthy of a curse. For the whole human race will be found liable to a curse according to the law of Moses: 'For cursed is everyone who does not remain in those things which are written in the book of the law, to do them,' and certainly no one has performed all things exactly; you will not dare to deny that even with a desire to oppose it. But there are those who have kept the commandments more and less than others. Therefore, God, the parent of all things, willed his Christ to take upon himself the curses of all from every kind of mortal, because he was about to raise him up crucified and dead. Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges this. Therefore, regarding this Mosaic passage, he says, 'Christ, suspended on the cross, is called a curse by the Apostle, because, as Rupertus says, God transferred the curses of the human race onto Christ, while Christ undertook for us the infamous and execrable death of the cross.' Which Menochius also repeats on the Apostolic passage Galatians 3:13.

In vain, therefore, does Grotius pervert the distinguished passage of the Apostle in the Socinian manner: by subaudition of the particle 'as' (ώς) in his annotations on the same: thinking that it is indicated only that Christ was treated by men as if he were a curse (κατάρατος) to God: for he was not only treated by men as if he were a curse to God, but was made entirely a curse (κατάρα) even to God, because he had to liberate us from the curse of God. Our Brentius, however, excellently weighs the emphasis of the passage: whose words are worthy to be read here in their entirety: 'This law,' he writes on the Mosaic passage, 'most of all looks to Christ our Lord. For the wicked who were driven onto a cross were judged so contemptible and abject that it was thought that the earth and air were infected by their presence, and therefore they were buried under the earth on the same day. The same happened to Christ; he was held among the extreme wicked, he was driven onto a cross, he was taken down from the cross on the same day, see, lest he infect the air and the earth.' This is the extreme curse, nor can a greater and more execrable one happen to anyone in these lands. What, therefore, was done? 'Christ,' says Paul, 'was made a curse for us, so that we might become a blessing.' For we, by our sins, have merited every curse, and indeed so great a one that we are unworthy even of the earth and air. Christ, however, having taken the curse upon himself, expiated our sins, so that we might become worthy not only of the earth, but also of heaven. These things must be thought upon by us in our abjection, so that we may conceive a hope of glory in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ADJVDICATVS MORTI SVSPENSVS FVERIT IN PATIBVLO) Fiebat id ostentui in iis, qui lapidati fuerant ob idololatriam vel blasphemiam. Non enim pœna erat suspensio. Strangulabantur enim stantes apud Hebræos, non suspendio. De ustione, gladio, lapidibus, satis apparet pœnas has remotas a suspendio.

Ebræi omnino pœnis accensent suspendium, imo summum supplicii genus. R. Moses Nachmanni suspensionem vocat, quod pro contumelia in Deum & idololatria non dissimulata illatum fuerit. Quamvis vero primum lapidari apud Ebræos solebant, ac postea demum in ligno suspendi; non tamen ideo suspendium illud pro pœna habendum non est; quemadmodum ubi decollatur quis, & caput palo infigitur, utrumque pœnæ rationem habet, ac mitior sententia censetur, cum solum decollatio adjudicatur. Adde quod illis, qui gravia crimina, ob quæ ira Dei contra totam aliquam communionem provocabatur, committebant, pœna ejusmodi dictata fuerit, ut corpora eorum suspenderentur, Num. 25, 4. 2. Sam. 21, 6. atque indigni judicati ea ratione sint, qui terram attingant, quodque maledicti habiti sint peculiariter, cum suspensi sunt, Joseph. l. 4. antiq. c. 8. Qui DEUM blasphemarit, lapidibus obrutus per diem pendeat, deinde ignominiose & obscure sepeliatur. Nec enim illa sepultura præcepta in honorem cadaveris sepeliendi, sed quod cadaver illud maledicti hominis cito a superficie terræ remo- fubiisse Christum, eam, quam per condemnationem legis nos subire tenebamur, aut nos redemti non e- rimus ab illa maledictione. Ideo Apostolus in ab- stracto κατάραν maledictionem factum Christum di- cit, ut maledictionem κατ' ἀντονομασίαν, designa- ret. Et quemadmodum non temporalem solum, sed æternam imprimis benedictionem & vitam bea- tam sempiternam hic nobis peperiisse Christum Apo- stolus demonstrat, ita oportet, liberarit nos Christus ab æterna maledictione, ac morte, quod factum, dum maledictio pro nobis factus est. Eidem enim maledictioni obnoxius factus est, cui nos eramus subjecti, & a qua nos liberavit. Quod per suppli- cium crucis maledictum τυπικῶς quondam adum- bratum, in veritate autem in cruce Christi completur. Ibi maledictus erat Deo, suspensus in ligno, non quidem, quod æternam maledictionem subierit, sed quod eam promeruerit, ac morte peculiariter Deo ex- ecrabili, & ignominiosa ex Dei constitutione mori debuerit; hic maledictum factus suspensus in ligno crucis, quod vere pro nobis maledictionem æter- nam subeat, quam non ipse, sed nos promeruimus, atque ideo supplicium, quod lege divina maledi- ctum peculiariter erat, subire debuit. Quo de S. Athanasius de incarnat. verbi T. 1. oper. p. 77. Si ideo venerat, ut nostra piacula execrationemque no- stram portaret, quomodo alia ratione κατάρα execra- tio fuisset, nisi execrabilem mortem in se recepisset? est autem hæc ipsa crux: sicut & scriptum est: execrabilis quicunque in ligno pendet. Adde his ea, quæ paulo an- te tradiderat Athanasius p. 72. Quandoquidem igitur debitum pro omnibus solvendum erat, debebatur autem ut omnes morerentur, quæ causa illi potissima fu- it huc proficiscendi, ideoque post edita factorum ope di- vinitatis suæ monumenta, reliquum jam erat, ut pro omnibus sacrificium offerret, pro omnibus templum suum morti tradens, quo omnes innobnoxios, & liberos a veteri prævaricatione efficeret, seque declararet mortis victorem. Morte enim opus fuit, & mortem pro omni- bus perferre necessum erat, ut quod ab omnibus debi- tum erat, lueretur. Certe communi omnium Salva- tore mortuo pro nobis, non jam ulterius, sicuti olim se- cundum legis comminationem, morte morimur, quot- quot in Christo Jesu confidimus. Obliterata enim est illa ipsa condemnatio. Audiamus & Chrysostomum in c. 3. ad Gal. Quoniam igitur, & qui pendet, execra- bilis est, non oportuit illum, qui execrationem illam erat sublaturus, obnoxium eidem fieri execrationi (per le- gis transgressionem) verum pro illa erat alia suscipi- enda execratio, quam & suscepit, ac per eam illam su- stulit, perinde faciens, ac si morti adjudicato quopiam, alius insons illius damnati vice sponte & volens eripiat illum. Sic & Christus fecit: quum enim non esset ob- noxius execrationi transgressionis, hanc in se recepit pro omnibus, ut omnes ab illa liberaret: Peccatum enim, inquit, non fecit, nec inventus est in ore illius dolus. Ita- que sicut mortuus eos, quibus erat moriendum, exemit a morte, ita & execratione in se recepta ab execratione li- beravit. Proinde crux sustulit execrationem, & inve- xit justitiam, justitia vero gratiam Spiritus allexit. Ad- do & Justinum Martyrem Dial. cum Tryph. p. 251. Quemadmodum ergo Deus signum fieri per æneum ser- pentem jussit, & eo nomine inculpabilis est: ita sane & in lege maledictio proposita est contra eos, qui in cru- cem aguntur homines, non itidem vero adversus Chri- stum Dei maledictio est statuta: per quem omnes salvat, qui maledictione digna in se admiserunt. Nam genus humanum omne maledictioni obnoxium esse invenietur juxta legem Mosis: Maledictus enim quisque dictus est, qui non permanet in eis, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea, nemo certe exacte omnia præstitit; id neque ipsi adver- sandi studio negare audebitis. Sed sunt, qui aliis plus & minus mandata servaverint. Itaque rerum uni- versarum parens Deus Christum suum ex omni mortali- um genere omnium maledictiones excipere voluit, quod eum crucifixum, & mortuum suscitaturus fuerit. A- gnoscit id Corn. a Lap. ideo ad hunc locum Mosai- cum, Christus, inquit, in cruce suspensus ab Apostolo vo- catur maledictum, quia, ut ait Rupertus, Deus maledi- ctiones humani generis in Christum transposuit, dum infamem & execrabilem mortem crucis pro nobis Chri- stus suscepit. Quæ repetit etiam Menochius in locum Apostolicum Gal. 3, 13.

Nequicquam ergo Grotius insignem Aposto- li locum more Sociniano pervertit: subaudiendo particulam ώς in annotat. ad eundem: id solum in- dicari censens, quod Christus ita tractatus sit ab ho- minibus, quasi esset Deo κατάρατος execrabilis: ne- que enim solum tractatus est ab hominibus, quasi κατάρατος Deo, sed factus omnino Deo etiam κατά- ρα, quia nos a maledictione Dei liberare debuit. Em- phasin vero loci eximie Brentius noster expendit: Cujus verba digna sunt, quæ hic legantur integra: Hæc lex, scribit in locum Mosaicum, maxime omni- um respicit Christum Dominum nostrum. Scelerati enim in crucem acti judicabantur tam comtemti & ab- jecti, ut putaretur, terram & aerem præsentia eorum infici, ideoque eadem die condebantur subter terram. Idem accidit Christo, habitus est inter extreme scelera- tos, actus est in crucem, eadem die sublatus est de cruce, vid. ne inficeret aerem & terram. Hæc est extrema maledictio, nec potest alicui in his terris major & exe- crabilior accidere. Quid ergo factum est? Christus, inquit Paulus, factus est pro nobis maledictio, ut nos fieremus benedictio. Nos enim peccatis nostris me- riti sumus omnem maledictionem, adeoque tantam, ut etiam terra & aere simus indigni. Christus autem su- scepta in se maledictione expiavit peccata nostra, ut non solum fiamus digni terra, sed etiam cælo. Hæc nobis in abjectione nostra cogitanda sunt, ut spem gloriæ in Christo concipiamus.

## 21:23
FOR HE WHO HANGS ON A TREE IS CURSED BY GOD) It is enough that he be exposed for a short time so that it may appear to the people that the law has been satisfied. Furthermore, his punishment is not to be prolonged, as he has already borne the punishment imposed by God before he was hanged. The word qelalah (curse) often has the meaning of punishment, just as eulogia (blessing) has the meaning of a benefit, with the meaning transferred from words to things. See Gen. 8:21, Jer. 4:23, Deut. 29:27, Psalm 109:16.

We do not deny that punishment is included under the name of curse. But not every punishment brings about such a curse as is designated here. Therefore, something special is held here in the punishment of hanging, while he who hangs on a tree is pronounced cursed by God. Some indeed render the Hebrew word as 'alleviation,' because the wrath of God is alleviated when the criminal is hanged. But the Septuagint more correctly explained it as 'cursed,' whom Paul followed in Gal. 3:13, just as the word qalal also denotes to curse, to execrate, to devote (Lev. 20:9, ch. 24:14), and qelalah denotes a curse (Gen. 27:12): 'I will bring a curse upon me and not a blessing.' It nowhere occurs for the alleviation of wrath, but for vilification, which does not fit here. But that curse was only temporal, and partly pertained to the ceremonial law: insofar as it prefigured Christ, who had to be made a curse for us; and partly to the forensic: because this kind of punishment was the most severe and most ignominious of all, and was accustomed to be inflicted upon those who had committed those crimes on account of which the wrath of God was kindled against the whole community (Num. 25:4, 2 Sam. 21:6). Seneca calls the cross an 'infamous stake' (Ep. 101); Livy (1.14) calls it the 'unlucky tree.' Criminals driven to the cross, as Brentius has in this place, were judged so abject and despised that it was thought the earth and air were defiled by their presence, and therefore they were buried under the earth on the same day. He who is hanged is judged, by that symbol of being lifted on high, as if unworthy to touch the earth with his feet, and so wicked that, if it were possible, men would thrust him out of the whole world. All of which Grotius conceals, in favor, as it seems, of the Papists: who explain Christ being made a curse too jejunely: inasmuch as they deny that he underwent divine malediction and infernal punishment. But since Christ took upon himself our guilt and our sins, Is. 53, 6, having been made sin for us, 2 Cor. 5, 21, and therefore drained the entire punishment of our sins, so that we might be redeemed equally from all punishment and guilt, Is. 53, 7, 10, 11, Rom. 8, 3. Certainly, either Christ drained the infernal punishment for us, or we shall not be redeemed from infernal punishment through Christ. Since Christ was substituted in our place, and gave himself in our stead as ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. 2, 4, it is necessary that he also underwent and bore our punishment, which, to wit, was the one we had to undergo, which certainly was chiefly infernal, in our stead. Since he was made for us κατάρα, a curse, as the Apostle testifies, Gal. 3, 13, so that he might redeem us from the curse, it is necessary that he underwent, IN OUR PLACE, the same curse to which we were liable.

Vers. eod. HE IS GIVEN TO REVELRY AND LUXURY, AND BANQUETS) In the Hebrew זולל וסבא. From that word סבא comes the Phrygian σαβάζειν. Many words of the Phrygians and Lydians are from the Syrians.

Latin:

QVIA MALEDICTVS A DEO EST QVI PENDET IN LIGNO) Satis est ad breve tempus exponi eum ut populo appareat satisfactum legi. Cæterum non protrahenda est ejus pœna, qui, antequam suspenderetur pœnam tulit a Deo impositam. קללה κατάρα sæpe pœnæ habet significationem, ut εὐλογία beneficii, significatione a verbis ad res translata. Vide Gen. 8, 21. Jerem. 4, 23. Devt. 29, 27. Psalm. 109, 16.

Pœnam comprehendi maledictionis nomine non imus inficias. Sed non omnis pœna maledictionem ejusmodi infert, qualis hic designatur. Peculiare ergo hic quidpiam habetur in pœna suspendii, dum maledictus a Deo pronunciatur, qui pendet in ligno. Reddunt quidem nonnulli vocem Ebræam alleviatio, quod allevetur ira Dei, quando reus suspenditur. Sed LXX. rectius exposuerunt κεκατηραμένος, quos sequutus est Paulus Gal. 3, 13. quemadmodum etiam verbum קלל maledicere, execrari, devovere notat Lev. 20, 9. c. 24, 14. & קללה maledictionem Gen. 27, 12. Adducam super me maledictionem & non benedictionem: pro alleviatione ire nuspiam occurrit, sed pro vilipendio, quod hic non congruit. Maledictio autem illa temporalis tantum erat, & partim ad legem ceremonialem pertinebat: siquidem præfiguravit Christum, qui pro nobis fieri debuit maledictum: partim ad forensem: quod hoc genus supplicii omnium fuerit gravissimum & ignominiosissimum: atque illis irrogari consueverit, qui crimina ea commiserant, ob quæ ira Dei adversus totam communionem exardebat: Num. 25, 4. 2. Sam. 21, 6. Seneca crucem infamem stipitem vocat Ep. 101. Livius 1. 14. infelix lignum.
