Scelerati in crucem acti, quod habet Brentius in h. l. judicabantur tam abjecti & contemti, ut putaretur, terram & aërem præsentia eorum infici, ideoque eadem die condebantur subter terram. Qui suspenditur, isto Symbolo sublationis in altum indignus quasi judicatur, qui terram attingat pedibus, ac tam nefarius, ut si fieri posset, homines toto mundo eum extruderent. Quæ omnia dissimulat Grotius, in gratiam, ut videtur, Pontificiorum: qui Christum maledictum factum jejune nimis explicant: utpote quem maledictionem divinam & pœnam infernalem subiisse negant: At quum Christus in se susceperit culpam, & peccata nostra Es. 53, 6. factus pro nobis peccatum 2. Cor. 5, 21. omnemque etiam peccatorum nostrorum pœnam ideo exantlarit, ut æque a pœna & culpa omni redimeremur Es. 53, 7. 10. 11. Rom. 8, 3. Certe, aut pœnam infernalem exantlavit Christus pro nobis, aut a pœna infernali per Christum redemti non erimus. Quum Christus surrogatus sit in nostri locum, & vice nostri se dederit ἀντίλυτρον 1. Tim. 2, 4. necessum est, ut pœnam etiam nostram, quæ sc. nobis subeunda erat, quæ certe præcipue erat infernalis, nostri vice subierit ac portarit. Quum factus sit pro nobis κατάρα maledictum, teste Apostolo Gal. 3, 13. ut nos a maledicto redimeret, oportet eandem maledictionem, cui nos obnoxii eramus, LOCO NOSTRI subiisse

Vers. eod. COMMESSATIONIBUS VACAT ET LVXVRIÆ, ATQVE CONVIVIIS) In Hebræo זולל וסבא. Ex illo verbo סבא, est Phrygium σαβάζειν. Multæ voces Phrygum & Lydorum a Syris.

## 21:23
Ver. 23. THOU SHALT NOT POLLUTE THE LAND) The land is polluted when a human body, once the dwelling of the divine image, wasting away, flows into the earth and is given to the cattle. To pluck the grass rising from our bones, as Lucan speaks. This law concerning burial pertains not only to those stoned, but also to all who have died by capital punishment. Such persons, however, were not buried in the sepulchers of their ancestors, but in public burial grounds.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NEQVAQVAM CONTAMINABIS TER- RAM) Contaminatur terra ubi corpus humanum, divinæ quondam imaginis domicilium, tabescens in terram defluit, daturque pecoribus. Vellere surgentem de nostris ossibus herbam. Vt Lucanus loquitur. Hæc lex de sepultura non ad lapida- tos tantum, sed & ad omnes supplicio capitali mortuos per- tinet. Sepeliebantur autem tales non in sepulchris majo- rum, sed in publicis sepulchretis.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. Concerning piety toward the property of a neighbor: concerning the garment of the other sex: concerning surrounding a roof: concerning not mixing things of a different kind: concerning fringes: concerning the signs of virginity, adultery, and fornication.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII. De pietate in rem proximi: de veste alterius se- xus: de tecto circumdando: de non com- miscendis rebus diversi generis: de fim- briis: de signis virginitatis, adulterio & scortatione.

## 22:2
Ver. 2. THEY SHALL BE WITH THEE UNTIL THY BROTHER SEEKS THEM AND RECEIVES THEM) See matters pertaining to this in Book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 10. The title of discovery has no place except in things ἀδεσπότοις (ownerless).

Latin:

Vers. 2. ERVNT APUD TE QVAMDIV QVÆRAT EA FRATER TVVS ET RECIPIAT) Vide ad hanc rem pertinentia l. 2. de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. 10. Inventionis ti- tulus locum non habet nisi in rebus ἀδεσπότοις.

## 22:5
Ver. 5. THE WOMAN SHALL NOT WEAR A MAN'S GARMENT, NEITHER SHALL A MAN USE A WOMAN'S GARMENT: FOR HE THAT DOES THESE THINGS IS ABOMINABLE TO GOD) A precept in itself honest and useful. Nevertheless, Maimonides says the occasion was given by idolaters, among whom it was the custom in honor of Mars for women to be clothed in arms, and men in women's garments in honor of Venus. He speaks the truth, and cites authors. This is the γενέσεως ἐναλλαγὴ (change of generation), which the son of Sirach (14:27) places among the rites of idolaters. Philochorus affirmed that Venus was the Moon, and that men sacrificed to her in women's clothing, and women in men's, because Venus was both male and female. The passage is in Macrobius, Saturnalia 3, ch. 12. So also Servius on Aeneid 2, in the Fulda manuscripts: The image of Venus in Cyprus is of female body and clothing, with a scepter and male nature, which they call ἀφρόδιτον (hermaphroditic): to whom men sacrifice in women's clothing, and women in men's clothing. Moreover, in Cyprus were those colonies of the Phoenicians, from whence that custom had come. Wherefore I also think the name ἀφροδίτης was corrupted by the Greeks from תַּפְעֹורִית, which is the feminine of the masculine פְעֹור, who is the God of the turpitudes of the Moabites. Num. 25,3.

It is also likely that the Israelites saw something of the sort among the Egyptians who were given to idolatry, just as Herodotus, book 2 of his Histories, derives the festival of the Bacchanalia from them. Therefore, that changing of garments is called an abomination: which, moreover, is a sign of levity, a beginning of luxury, and a lure for great fraudulence and lust. Nature herself, or rather the author of nature, distinguished the female and male sex, and distinct signs or garments are agreeable to nature 1 Cor. 11,4.14. There is also a moral [reason] underlying it, concerning which Cyril [writes] in book 5 on adoration. God abominates and considers it a most shameful spectacle when there is an opinion of fortitude in a soft life, or in a strong man the languor of a soft spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NON INDVETVR MVLIER VESTE VI- RILI, NEC VIR VTETVR VESTE FOEMINEA: ABOMINABILIS ENIM DEO EST, QVI FACIT HÆC) Præceptum per se honestum & utile. Attamen oc- casionem datam ait Maimonides ab idololatris, apud quos mos erat in honorem Martis fœminas armis indui, viros mu- liebribus vestibus in honorem Veneris. Verum dicit, & au- ctores citat. Hæc est γενέσεως ἐναλλαγὴ, quam inter idolola- trarum ritus ponit Sirachides 14, 27. Philochorus Venerem affirmabat esse Lunam, & ei sacrificium facere viros cum ve- ste muliebri: mulieres cum virili: ideo quod Venus & mas es- set & fœmina. Locus est apud Macrobium Saturnal. 3. c. 12. Sic & Servius ad 2. Æneid. in chartis Fuldenfibus: Veneris in Cypro simulacrum corpore & veste muliebri, cum sceptro & natura virili, quod ἀφρόδιτον vocant: cui viri in veste mulie- bri, mulieres in virili veste sacrificant. In Cypro autem mul- tæ coloniæ Phœnicum, unde is mos venerat. Quare & nomen ἀφροδίτης ego a Græcis corruptum arbitror ex תַּפְעֹורִית quod fœmininum fit masculini פְעֹור, qui Deus turpitudinum Moabitis. Num. 25,3.

Verisimile etiam est, quod Israëlitæ tale quid viderint inter Ægyptios Idololatriæ deditos, uti He- rodotus l. 2. Hist. festum Bachanaliorum ab iis de- ducit. Ideo abominatio dicitur illa vestium muta- tio: quæ præterea indicium est levitatis, initium lu- xuriæ, ac magnæ fraudulentiæ, libidinis illicium. Natura ipsa vel potius autor naturæ sexum fœmi- neum & virilem distinxit, ac signa vel vestimenta di- stincta naturæ consentanea sunt 1. Cor. 11,4.14. Mo- rale etiam subest, de quo Cyrillus l. 5. de adorat. Abominatur Deus ac turpissimum putat spectaculum tum fortitudinis opinionem in molli vita tum in forti viro mollis animi languorem.

## 22:6
Verse 6. THOU SHALT LET GO) Porphyry on Jewish Institutions: 'It was forbidden even if they were not suppliants, and even if they had not fled to the houses, to kill them.' But the law deals only with chicks that are being brooded, and indeed those found on the road, not birds that are raised at home, such as hens and doves.

Nay, it seems general: the reason for which was an instruction toward gentleness and mercy. See Tertullian, book 2 against Marcion, ch. 17; Theodoret, question 21 on Deuteronomy. Whence also that general rule: that affliction should not be added to the afflicted, Deut. 25, 18; Is. 42, 3; Zach. 1, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ABIRE PATIERIS) Porphyrius de Institutis Judaïcis: ἀπηγόρευτο δὲ κᾀν μὴ τὰ ἱκετεύοντα κᾀν ὥστε προσ- φύγοντα ταῖς οἰκίαις, ἀναιρεῖν. Sed agit lex tantum de pullis quibus incubatur, & quidem in via repertis, non avium, quæ domi aluntur, ut gallinarum & columbarum.

Imo videtur generalis: cujus ratio erat ad mansuetudinem & misericordiam informatio. Vid. Tertull. l. 2. contr. Marcion. c. 17. Theodoret. quæst. 21. in Devter. Unde etiam Regula illa generalis : quod afflicto non sit addenda afflictio Deut. 25, 18. Es. 42,3. Zach. 1, 15.

## 22:6 Addition
On ch. 22, v. 6, toward the end of the note on page 596, a.

This is a precept of clemency, says Episcopius (Instit. bk. 3, ch. 6, no. 3, p. 90), and of humanity. For it savors of cruelty when you have taken the young, to snatch away either liberty or life from the very one from whom you received the benefit. The precept about not slaughtering on one and the same day, from the animals, the father or mother and the son, that is, for example, a cow and its calf at the same time (Lev. 22:28), pertains to the same thing. But it can also be said that God wished that our cruelty should not place an impediment to generation. But the Hebrews rashly value this precept so highly, when taken according to the letter, that if anyone observes only this, even if he has transgressed the other precepts, by that very fact he deserves both the forgiveness of previous sins and the benefit of a longer life, because it is added, that it may be well with you and you may prolong your days: and therefore the sense of those words is negative, namely, that we should not contract a curse by voluntarily sinning against the divine law. I add, however, that by this reasoning the divine severity against the unmerciful is simultaneously hinted at (James 2:13).

Latin:

Ad cap. 22. vers. 6. sub finem notar. ad pag. 596. a.

Præceptum hoc est clementiæ, inquit Episco- pius lib. 3. Instit. cap. 6. num. 3. pag. 90. & humani- tatis. Crudelitatem enim sapit cum pullos acce- peris, illi ipsi, a quo beneficium accepisti, vel li- bertatem vel vitam eripere. Eodem pertinet præceptum de non mactando una eademque die, ex animalibus patrem sive matrem & filium, id est, ex. gr. vaccam simul ac vitulam ejus: Lev. 22. v. 28. Sed & dici potest, voluisse Deum, ut generationi im- pedimentum non poneret crudelitas nostra. Temere autem præceptum hoc tanti faciunt Ebræi, secun- dum literam acceptum, ut si quis istud tantum ob- servet, etiamsi cætera præcepta transgressus fuerit, eo ipso mereatur & præcedentium peccatorum ve- niam, & longioris vitæ beneficium, quia additur, ut bene sit tibi & prolonges dies tuos: ideoq; sensus il- lorum verborum est negativus, ne sc. voluntarie pec- cando contra divinam legem maledictionem con- i trahamus. Addo autem hac ratione innui simul divinam severitatem adversus immisericordes Ja- cob. 2. v. 13.

## 22:8
Verse 8. THOU SHALT MAKE A WALL) The Greeks [call it] στεφάνην; Philo, θωράκιον: See what [is said] on Matt. 4,4 and 28,2. Onkelos here has תֵיקֹור, which is from the Greek θήκη. Thus the Greeks call other things, and the circuit of a tomb, by this name. The height had to be at least three and a half feet.

THAT BLOOD BE NOT SHED IN THY HOUSE) Parity of reason forbids having broken stairs and biting dogs. Compare Exod. 21, 29.

Latin:

Vers. 8. FACIES MURUM) στεφάνην Græci : Philo θω- ράκιον : Vide quæ ad Matth. 4,4. & 28, 2. Onkelos hic ha- bet תֵיקֹור quod est ex Græco θήκη. Sic Græci & alia vocant & ambitum sepulchri. Altitudo esse debebat mini- mum ad tres pedes cum dimidio.

NE EFFUNDATVR SANGVIS IN DOMO TUA) Paritas rationis vetat habere scalas fractas & canes morda- ces. Conf. Exod. 21, 29.

## 22:9
Verse 9. THOU SHALT NOT SOW THY VINEYARD WITH DIVERS SEEDS. The Hebrew כִּלְאַיִם denotes a mixture of different species, Lev. 19,19, or it is the same as 'promiscuously'; therefore others render it 'with diverse seeds' or 'species of seeds,' along with the Chaldean, the LXX, and B. Luther, meaning that no one should mix oats with barley, or wheat with rye, in sowing; some wish it to be forbidden that a vineyard be fertilized with the seeds of crops at the same time. For since Palestine was hot and fertile, they were accustomed to sow something in the intervals between the vines, and therefore it is prohibited either that seeds be mixed in the sowing within the vineyard, just as the same was forbidden for fields in Lev. 19,19, or it is absolutely forbidden that anything be sown between the vines. Josephus, book 4 of Antiquities, ch. 8, seems to favor the former explanation, but Philo, in 'On the Creation of Principles,' handed down the latter, concerning not making a sowing between vines to obtain a double fruit.

Verse of the same. LEST BOTH THE SEED WHICH THOU HAST SOWN AND THE FRUIT OF THE VINEYARD BE SANCTIFIED TOGETHER. In Hebrew, 'lest perhaps the fullness be sanctified (or rather polluted),' (that is, the ripe fruit, which they wish to be so called either because it is full of ripeness, or because it ought to have filled the hands of the Priests, Ex. 22,29; Num. 18,17. Although in the former passage 'fullness' refers to dry fruits, such as wheat and barley, yet to liquid fruits, must, oil, etc., the term 'tear' is attributed, because they flow down from the press drop by drop like tears, to which, however, the word 'fullness' can also be referred, as the latter passage teaches) the seed which thou hast sown, and the produce of the vineyard. The name of seed seems to explain the word 'fullness,' and thus metonymically introduces the fruit of the seed. The sense of this reason, which the supreme legislator added, is the simplest: that the crops not be polluted by the neighboring grapes, because grapes were unclean for three years, or common, as were the fruits of trees, and an offering could not be made until the fourth year, Lev. 19, 23; Deut. 20, 6. But concerning other fruits of seeds, an offering could be made in the first year, which I also see handed down by Dionysius the Carthusian. Those who interpret the law concerning diverse seeds will be able to explain this reason thus: that it is commanded that pure grain be sown, so that pure grain may also be offered to God in sacrifices. The explanations of others—that I should not be compelled to offer them to Him; which Theodor, Junius, and Tremellius follow, or that you should not believe that crops and grapes are sanctified together, so that by paying tithes or firstfruits of one, the other is paid, as Abulensis explains—are incongruous and do not deserve consideration. Calvin's exposition, that it tends toward their cultivating cleanliness and simplicity, and not desiring mixtures through perverse curiosity, which might eventually lead to the worship of God, concerns only the moral [aspect] of the law, but does not interpret the reason for the law added by Moses. Different reasons for the law concerning moral matters can be given, for instance, about avoiding syncretism in religion, so that another seed is not sown where the wine of spiritual grace or heavenly doctrine ought to be produced, as Rabanus [says]; about fleeing hypocrisy and fraud, as well as polypragmosyne, and also avarice and the suppression of subjects, etc. But these do not exclude the literal sense of the law (just as Cajetan wrongly judged that these are only symbolic, and do not have the sense that the words present, but another mystical and hidden one, to which William of Paris also leans in his book 'On Faith and Laws,' drawing these to the prohibition of idolatry), nor do they contribute to the explanation of the law added by God Himself. Other causes for the law can also be brought forward: that different kinds, crops and trees, not be confused; that one species not be harmed by the other; that the field not be oppressed by goods, vexed by a most heavy burden, either by the work of those sowing and planting returning to the city, or by the doubled fertility of the fruits. For it is enough if the Lord demands one annual tribute from His estate, just as a King [does] from his domain: but he who attempts to impose more on his subjects does not perform the duty of a good Prince, but of an avaricious one, and one fighting against the laws of nature, which reasons Philo executes. But it is one thing to seek symbolic, moral, or physical reasons of any kind, and another to explain the reason handed down by God Himself, and there can be several causes for one thing: we therefore acquiesce to the sense of the divine reason previously handed down.

Latin:

vers. 9. NON SERES VINEAM TUAM AL- TERO SEMINE. Ebr. כִּלְאַיִם mixturam ex diversis speciebus no- tat, Lev. 19,19. aut idem est, quod promiscue, ideo alii reddunt diversis seminibus, vel speciebus seminum, cum Chald. LXX. B. Luthero, puta ne quis avenam cum hordeo, triticum cum filigine in satione com- misceat; nonnulli interdictum volunt, ne vinea fru- gum seminibus simul fœcundetur. Quum enim cali- da & fertilis fuerit Palæstina, ideo solebant inter vi- neas aliquid seminare in intervallis, ac proinde vel ne in satione semina commisceantur in vinea, prohi- betur, quemadmodum idem de agris interdictum fuit Lev. 19,19. vel etiam plane vetatur, ne quicquam inter vineas seminetur. Priori explicationi favere videtur Josephus l. 4. Antiq. c. 8. posteriorem vero Philo de creat. Princip. tradidit, de non facienda se- mente inter vineas ad reportandum fructum duplicem.

vers. eod. NE ET SEMENTIS QUAM SE- VISTI ET QUÆ NASCUNTUR EX VINEA, PARITER SANCTIFICENTUR. Ebr. ne forte sanctificetur (vel potius polluatur) plenitudo, (id est, fructus maturus, quem ita dictum volunt, vel quod plenus sit maturitate, vel quod im- plere debuerit Sacerdotum manus Ex. 22,29. Num. 18,17. Quanquam in priori loco plenitudo, ad fructus aridos, uti triticum, hordeum referatur, fructibus au- tem liquidis, musto, oleo, &c. lachryma tribuitur, quod guttatim lacrymarum instar e torculari deflu- ant, ad quos vero etiam vocem plenitudinis referri posse, locus posterior docet) semen quod seminaveris, & proventus vineæ. Nomen seminis explicare videtur vocem plenitudinis, adeoque metonymice fructum seminis infert. Senfus hujus rationis, quam summus legislator addidit, ille est simplicissim9, ne polluantur segetes a vicinis uvis, quia uvæ per triennium immundæ erant, aut communes, uti & fructus arborum, nec nisi quarto demum anno oblatio fieri poterat Lev. 19, 23. Deut. 20, 6. de fructibus vero aliis seminum oblatio fieri poterat primo anno, quem etiam video a Dio- nys. Carthus. traditum. Qui legem interpretan- tur de diversis seminibus, ita rationem hanc explica- re poterunt, ideo juberi, ut purum frumentum sera- tur, ut etiam purum frumentum Deo in sacrificiis possit offerri. Aliorum explicationes, ne cogami- ni mihi ea offerre; quo Theodor. Junius & Tremellius abeunt, vel ne credatis, quod fruges & uvæ simul san- ctificentur, ita ut solvendo decimas vel primitias de uno solutum sit de alio, ut Abulensis exponit, incon- cinnæ sunt, nec calculum merentur. Calvini expo- sitio, quod eo tendat, ut munditiem ac simplicitatem colant, nec mixturas appetant prava curiositate, quæ tandem perveniat ad cultum DEI, morale solum concernit legis, non vero rationem legis a Mose ad- ditam interpretatur. Possunt diversæ legis ratio- nes moralia concernentes reddi, utputa de vitando Syncretismo in religione, ne aliud semen seratur, ubi vi- num gratiæ spiritualis vel doctrinæ cælestis gigni debet, uti Rabanus, de fugienda hypocrisi ac fraude, ut & πο- λυπραγμοσύνη, nec non avaritia & suppressione sub- ditorum &c. Sed illæ sensum literalem legis non excludunt (quemadmodum Cajetanus perperam censuit, hæc solum Symbolica esse, ac sensum non ha- bere eum, quem verba præ se ferunt, sed alium my- sticum & occultum, quo etiam Guil. Parisienf. abit l. de fide & legib. hæc ad interdictum idololatriæ tra- hens,) neque ad explicationem legis a Deo ipso ad- ditæ faciunt. Causæ etiam aliæ legis adferri pos- sunt, ne confundantur diversa genera, segetes & arbu- sta, ne altera species lædatur ab altera, ne bonis ager pre- matur, onere gravissimo vexatus, vel serentium plantan- tiumque operis in urbem redeuntibus, vel duplicata fe- racitate fructuum. Satis enim est, si Dominus e suo prædio tributum unum exigat annuum, sicut Rex e sua ditione: qui vero plura conatur subditis imponere, non facit officium boni Principis, sed avari & pugnantis cum naturæ legibus, quas rationes exequitur Philo. Sed etiam est quærere rationes Symbolicas, morales, physicas quascunque, aliud explicare rationem a Deo ipso traditam, ac possunt unius rei plures esse causæ: Acquiescimus ergo sensui rationis divinæ antea tra- dito.

## 22:10
Verse 10.

YOU SHALL NOT PLOW WITH AN OX AND AN ASS TOGETHER

Calphurnius in declamation 29 is right: Not even cattle submit to the yoke unless they are matched. But an ox and an ass differ greatly. Plautus, Aulularia, Act 2: ...it comes to mind that you are an ox and I am a little ass. The mystical sense is in Paul, 2 Cor. 6:14. The foundation of the mystical sense is that the ox is a clean animal, the ass an unclean one. Furthermore, this law removes occasions, so that nothing may be done against the law, which is in Lev. 19:19.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

NON ARABIS IN BOVE SIMVL ET ASINO)

Bene Calphurnius declamatione 29. Ne pecora quidem jugum nisi paria succedunt. Plurimum autem distant bos & asinus. Plautus Aululariæ actu 2. - - in mentem venit Te bovem esse & me asellum. Sensus mysticus apud Paulum 2. Cor. 6, 14. Fundamentum sensus mystici, quod bos est animal mundum, asinus immun- dum. Præterea lex hæc occasiones tollit, ne quid fiat con- tra legem, quæ est Lev. 19, 19.

## 22:14
Verse 14. BRINGING AGAINST HER A MOST EVIL NAME) הוציא, to bring forth, signifies here and elsewhere to divulge. To divulge an evil name, in one word, is to defame. See Num. 14:36.

Latin:

Vers. 14. OBJICIENS EI NOMEN PESSIMUM) הוציא, Educere significat hic & alibi Vulgare. Vulgare au- tem nomen malum, uno verbo est diffamare. Vid. Num. 14, 36.

## 22:17
Verse 17. THEY SHALL SPREAD OUT THE GARMENT) Τὸ ἐκμαγεῖον. Isidore the Philosopher, citing Photius: The Alexandrians called the tokens of women's defilement (namely, in the first intercourse) φυλακτε͂α, and the marriage is not genuine unless the priest of the goddess has signed the marriage contracts with his own hand. Among the Hebrews, these were not kept by priests, but by the paranymphs, who are called by them שושבנים.

Concerning those paranymphs, see Fagius on this passage. Moreover, that law is to be understood concerning her who has committed fornication after betrothal, as noted by B. Gerhard and Cornel. a Lapide. For others were not punished with death, Exod. 22:16. Although B. Gerhard acknowledges that this sign of violated chastity was not sufficient in itself, according to Cypraeus de Spons. c. 3, (B. Sennertus l. 4. Medic. Pract. part. 2. Sect. 3. c. 1. q. 11. teaches that if that sign is present, it is certain that she is a virgin, if it is absent, it does not immediately indicate that she has been deflowered, since it can be absent for other causes) he observes that in the O.T. that proof could have had a place, both because the supreme Legislator could easily have prohibited that danger be created for any innocent person on account of it, and because the Israelites gave their daughters in marriage while still tender, in the twelfth year of their age.

Latin:

Vers. 17. EXPANDENT VESTIMENTUM) Τὸ ἐκμα- γεῖον. Isidorus Philosophus citante Photio: φυλακτε͂α οἱ Αλε- ξανδρεῖς ἐκάλεν τὰ ἐκμαγεῖα τῶν γυναικείων μολυσμῶν, (nem- pe in primo congressu) ἐκ ἧι δὲ γνήσιο ὁ γάμῷ εἰ μὴ ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ τῆς θεᾶ ἐν τοῖς γαμικοῖς συμβολαίοις ὑπεσημήνατο χειρὶ τῇ ἑαυτᾶ. Apud Hebræos non a Sacerdotibus hæc ser- vabantur, sed a paranymphis qui ipsis שושבנים.

De illis Paranymphis vid. Fagius ad h. l. Est autem lex illa intelligenda de ea, quæ post despon- sationem fornicata, notante B. Gerhardo & Cornel. a Lapide. Nam aliæ non puniebantur morte Exod. 22, 6. Etsi autem B. Gerhard. agnoscat, hoc fignum laesae pudicitiae non fuisse per se sufficiens, Cy- praeo de Spons. c. 3. teste, (B. Sennertus l. 4. Medic. Pract. part. 2. Sect. 3. c. 1. q. 11. fignum illud si adsit, certum esse virginis, si absit, non statim defloratam indi- care, quum ex aliis causis abesse possit, docet) observat tamen in V. T. probationem illam locum habere po- tuisse, tum quia summus Legislator facile prohibe- re potuit, ne cui innocenti ob id periculum creare- tur, tum quia Israëlitae filias suas adhuc teneras, anno aetatis duodecimo elocabant.

## 22:17 Addition
On ch. 22, v. 17, after our note on page 597, a.

There is no light doubt here as to how this evidence could serve to prove that a virgin allowed herself to be defiled after her betrothal, since she could have been corrupted beforehand: Whence the Hebrews deny that this law is to be understood according to the letter, and interpret it metaphorically thus; namely, that the parents of the defamed girl, when witnesses were produced by the accuser as if he were the husband, ought to have opposed other witnesses, through whom the former witnesses would be convicted of being so manifestly false, as if all the signs of virginity were in the open, and the assurance of preserved chastity had been made before the sun, and exposed like a cloth which is unfolded and spread out, and given to the eyes of those looking on to be inspected. But since one must not depart from the literal sense in such divine precepts, the sense of which cannot be established from elsewhere, this law does not seem to be restricted to those who have been defiled after betrothal (as Episcopius wishes with the cited authors, lib. 3. Instit. cap. 10. pagin. 117.) since from that evidence it could not be proven that the virgin was corrupted after betrothal. Moreover, the passage in Exodus 22, verse 16, concerns a special case, namely when a virgin is seduced by someone into intercourse. Which case is furthermore to be distinguished from that which is treated in the present chapter, verse 29, as Episcopius rightly warns in note 7, page 116. For there it concerns a virgin who, without force, by blandishments and specious persuasion, perhaps under the pretext of future marriage, was enticed and induced by the ravisher and defiler: whereas here it concerns her who, without the enticement of blandishments, suffered force and defilement. This is argued by 1. the different words. For in that place there is a word for enticing or alluring; here a word for seizing: whence there a persuasion, here an assault seems to have been made. 2. The different penalty. For in that place the defiler is not necessarily compelled to marry the girl in such a way that after he had married her he could never repudiate her; here he is compelled to marry her, so that he can never dismiss her or make a divorce from her. In that place, if the father of the virgin refused the marriage, the defiler was bound to give a dowry to the virgin; here he was not bound to give a dowry to the virgin, but 50 shekels of silver, on account of the injury brought upon the parent through the defilement of the daughter. For it is to be noted that those 50 shekels were assigned to the virgin not in place of a dowry, but for the injury to be repaired and as it were compensated to her parent. Thus far Episcopius, who nevertheless corrects himself afterwards, that he ought to have given a dowry here as well. Whether a dowry, he says, ought to have been established for this defiled virgin is uncertain: To me it is likely: lest the condition of a virgin violently oppressed seem to have been worse than that of a virgin to whom, consenting, the defilement had been offered, as can be seen in Exodus 22. Philo certainly asserts this expressly in his book on special laws. The Hebrews add many other things regarding the virgin's chastity, the passion, and the damage to be repaired, which ought to have been paid by the defiler at the discretion of the judges, and according to the quality and condition of the virgin: which, however, does not appear from the text. The proper penalty of such a defiler is said in the text to be that he was compelled, whether he liked it or not, to marry such a defiled virgin, without the exception of any blemish; that is, whether she were one-eyed, deformed, hunchbacked, or lame; or morose, refractory, litigious, or of inconvenient and rustic manners. What, you say, if she were beautiful, wealthy, and agreeable, but the defiler were one-eyed, deformed, a gambler, a debauchee, poor, and grim? etc. The text does not say that, nor does it seem likely to me, especially if the father were to refuse and the virgin were to object; because otherwise the condition of a seducer of that kind would not have been made worse by that punishment, but better through the obtaining of such a spouse, and an opportunity would have been given to the worst men to seek and commit such seductions, with the most certain hope of an excellent and most happy marriage, which they could not otherwise obtain, or it was necessary that they lose it. Wherefore I am persuaded that in such a case the consent of both the offended father and the defiled virgin ought to have been added. I believe it is only indicated in the text that, outside of such a case, that virgin ought to have been taken by the seducer whether she wanted it or not, and indeed that was his most appropriate punishment, without any hope of repudiation, or license to give a Guet or bill of divorce: which was without doubt a most severe punishment at that time, when divorces were lawful by divine concession. Thus far Episcopius. Junius and Malvenda agree with him on this, that a fine was imposed here on account of the dowry, as does Bonfrerius, following Philo on special laws. Furthermore, the same author observes that it is asserted by certain Rabbis in the Hebrew commentaries on the book of Judges, chapter 21, that there were three ways of testing or examining a virgin. The first by which they made them pass before the ark. The virgin who was such, the ark retained; the one who had suffered a blemish, or had known a man, the ark did not retain. The second by which they made them pass before a flower. The one who was diminished or deflowered, or had suffered a man, her face would turn pale or yellow. The third, by which they placed her over a cask of wine: the odor of one who had been subdued or defiled would spread; that of a virgin would not. But he adds concerning these: Let faith be with the authors.

betrothal: But that is not in the text, nor is it deduced from the word חָרַשׂ. It cannot be denied that that rite was customary among the people and prudently instituted, and Episcopius thinks it is not obscurely hinted at in Deuteronomy 20:7: however, he denies that this rite was prescribed in this or any other text, but since the Hebrews themselves admit that the common custom of taking a wife was through the taking or abduction of a consenting virgin into the house and mutual cohabitation without any other formula or ceremony, he thinks that the custom of betrothal, even if not commanded by God, was established by the Sages so that the religion of marriage might be holier, since it was not lawful to arrive at it except through solemn and preliminary ceremonies. He observes, however, that those betrothals were made either by money, or by a writing, or by intercourse, according to the opinion of the Hebrews: which last, however, he rightly denies is deservedly referred to among betrothals, because after intercourse she is not a betrothed woman but a wife. See book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 10, number 2, page 114.

Latin:

Ad cap. 22. v. 17. post notam nostram pag. 597. a.

Dubium hic non leve est, quomodo hoc in- dicium facere potuerit ad id probandum, quod post sponsalia vitiari se passa sit virgo, quum antea potuerit corrupta esse: Unde Ebræi legem hanc secundum literam intelligendam esse negant, & me- taphorice ita interpretantur; parentes nempe puellæ diffamatæ testibus ab accusatore quasi marito produ- ctis, testes alios opponere debuisse, per quos testes priores tam manifeste falsi convincerentur, ac si vir- ginitatis signa omnia in propatulo essent, & pudicitiæ servatæ fides coram sole facta esset, expositaque veluti pannus, qui explicatur & evolvitur, oculisque intuen- tium spectandus datur. Sed quum a sensu literali in talibus præceptis divinis discedendum non sit, quorum sensus aliunde constare non potest, non vi- detur restringenda hæc lex ad ea, quæ post spon- salia vitiatæ sunt (uti cum autoribus laudatis vult Episcopius lib. 3. Instit. cap. 10. pagin. 117.) siquidem ex illo indicio probari non poterat, virginem post desponsationem corruptam esse. Locus autem Exod. 22. vers. 16. specialem casum concernit, cum nempe virgo ab aliquo seducitur ad concubitum. Qui casus porro ab eo, de quo cap. præsenti vers. 29. agitur, distinguendus est, ut recte monet Epi- scopius not. 7. pag. 116. Ibi enim de virgine agitur, quæ sine vi, blanditiis & speciosa persua- sione, forte obtentu futurarum nuptiarum illecta & inducta est a compressore & stupratore: cum hic agatur de ea, quæ sine illicio blanditiarum vim & stuprum passa est. Id arguunt 1. verba diversa. Istic enim verbum pelliciendi aut alliciendi est; hic verbum prehendendi: unde illic persuasio, hic im- petus factus videtur. 2. Diversa pœna. Istic enim stuprator non adigitur necessario ad puellam sic du- cendam, ut postquam eam duxisset eam non posset unquam repudiare; hic cogitur eam ducere, ita ut nunquam eam dimittere aut ab ea divortium pos- sit facere. Istic si pater virginis renueret conju- gium, dotem dare virgini tenebatur stuprator; hic dotem dare non tenebatur virgini, sed 50. siclos ar- genti, propter injuriam parenti illatam per stuprum filiæ. Notandum enim est 50. siclos istos virgini non dotis vice, sed injuriæ reparandæ & quasi sarciendæ pa- renti ejus fuisse assignatos. Ita Episcopius hactenus, qui tamen se emendat deinde, quod & hic dare do- tem debuerit. An dos etiam, inquit, virgini huic vitiatæ constituenda fuerit, incertum est: Mihi veri- simile id est: ne conditio virginis violenter oppressæ deterior fuisse videatur, quam virginis, cui consen- tienti vitium oblatum fuerat, uti Exod. 22. videre est. Philo certe id diserte asserit libr. de specialibus legi- bus. Addunt Hebræi plura alia virginis pudicitiæ, passioni & damno reparando, a stupratore ad arbi- trium judicum, & pro qualitate ac conditione virgi- nis pendi debuisse: quod tamen ex textu non con- stat. Propria pœna hujusmodi stupratoris in textu esse dicitur, quod vitiatam ejusmodi virginem, vellet nollet, ducere cogebatur, absque ullius maculæ exce- ptione; id est, sive lusca, deformis, gibbosa aut clau- da esset; sive morosa, refractaria, litigiosa aut in- commodioribus rusticisque moribus. Quid, si in- quies, si formosa, opulenta, & commoda, stu- prator vero luscus, deformis aleator, ganeo, pauper & torvus esset? &c. Id textus non dicit, nec mihi verisimile sit, imprimis si renueret pa- ter & refragaretur virgo; quia alioquin stuprato- ris ejusmodi conditio non deterior facta fuisset per poenam istam, sed melior per conjugis ejus- modi impetrationem, & occasio data fuisset pessi- mis ad ambiendum & confectandum ejusmodi stu- pra, certissima spe optimi & felicissimi conjugii, qua alioqui potiri non possent, aut excidere eos necesse erat. Quare consensum tum patris offen- si, tum vitiatae virginis accedere debuisse mihi per- suadeo in tali casu. Tantum credo in textu in- dicari, extra talem casum virginem istam a stupra- tore duci debuisse volente nolente, & quidem qua propriissima ejus poena erat, sine ulla spe repu- dii, aut licentia dandi Guet sive libellum divortii: quae sine dubio gravissima tum temporis poena fuit, quo divortia ex divina concessione licita erant. Hactenus Episcopius. Cui in eo adstipulatur Ju- nius & Malvenda, quod propter dotem mulcta hic indicta sit, ut & Bonfrerius praeeunte Philone de le- gibus specialibus. Caeterum observat idem a Rabbinis quibusdam adseri in scholiis Ebraicis ad li- brum Judicum cap. 21. tres fuisse modos probandi sive explorandi virginem. Primum quo faciebant eas transire ante arcam. Quae virgo erat, eam arca retinebat: quae vitium passa erat, aut virum cogno- verat, eam arca non retinebat. Secundum quo transire eas faciebant coram flore. Quae immi- nuta aut deflorata erat, aut virum passa, ejus vultus pallebat, aut flavescebat. Tertium, quo colloca- bant eam super dolium vini: subactae aut vitiatae odor diffundebatur: virginis non idem. Sed ad- dit de illis: Fides esto penes auctores.

desponsatione: Sed id in textu non est, nec ex verbo חָרַשׂ deducitur. Ritum istum in populo usitatum fuisse & prudenter institutum non negandum, eum- que Deuteronom. 20, 7. non obscure innui, Episco- pius censet: negat autem ritum istum in textu hoc aliove praescriptum esse, sed quum fateantur ipsimet Ebraei, communem ducendi uxorem morem fuisse, per sumtionem sive abductionem virginis consen- tientis in domum mutuamque cohabitationem abs- que ulla alia formula, aut ceremonia, putat, morem desponsationis etsi non praeceptum divinitus, a Sa- pientibus constitutum esse, ut religio conjugii san- ctior esset, quippe ad quod non nisi per gradus solemnes- que & praevias ceremonias pervenire fas esset. Spon- salia autem illa facta esse observat, vel pecunia, vel Scriptura, vel congressu ex mente Ebraeorum: quod posterius tamen recte inter sponsalia referri merito negat, quia post congressum non sponsa est sed uxor. Vid. l. 3. Instit. c. 10. n. 2. p. 114.

## 22:19
Vers. 19. WITH A HUNDRED SHEKELS) Double the dowry. See below here 29.

AND HE SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO PUT HER AWAY) This is a penalty for him, not retaliation. For jealousy is pardoned, as Augustine notes here.

Therefore, the reason for the law of retaliation in Deut. 19, 18 is different, which was not heeded here for the reason noted by Augustine. Add that the rights of wives and husbands in the O.T. were not equal. For the latter could take several wives and give a bill of divorce. Which were not permitted to wives.

Latin:

Vers. 19. CENTUM SICLIS) In duplum dotis. Vide infra hic 29.

ET NON POTERIT DIMITTERE EAM) Haec illi poena est, non talio. Ignoscitur enim zelotypiae, ut hic notat Augustinus.

Alia ergo ratio est legis talionis Deut. 19, 18. quae hic ob rationem ab Augustino notatam non atten- debatur. Adde, quod jura uxorum & maritorum in V. T. non fuerint paria. Hi enim plures uxores ducere, ac libellum repudii dare poterant. Quae uxo- ribus non permittebantur.

## 22:21
Vers. 21. OUTSIDE THE DOORS OF HER FATHER'S HOUSE) In which girls were accustomed to live until marriage. Before that house, in which she had sinned, she was stoned.

BECAUSE SHE HAS WROUGHT FOLLY IN ISRAEL) In Hebrew, נבלה folly. The Greeks, ἀφροσύνην.

Latin:

Vers. 21. EXTRA FORES DOMUS PATRIS SUI) In qua vivere puellae ad nuptias usque folebant. Ante eam domum, in qua peccaverat, lapidabatur.

QVONIAM FECIT NEFAS IN ISRAEL) In Hebraeo, נבלה stultitiam. Graeci, ἀφροσύνην.

## 22:23
Vers. 23. AND HE SHALL HAVE LAIN WITH HER) The Hebrews do not understand lying with her except with one who is marriageable, that is, one who has completed her twelfth year.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET CONCVBVERIT CVM EA) Concubi- tum Hebraei non intelligunt nisi cum viripotente, id est, quae duodecimum annum impleverit.

## 22:24
Vers. 24. BECAUSE SHE DID NOT CRY OUT) For the understanding of this law, see the Annotations to book 2 of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter 1, §. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 24. QVIA NON CLAMAVIT) Ad intellectum hujus legis vide Annotata ad librum 2. de Jure Belli ac Pa- cis cap. 1. §. 12.

## 22:26
Vers. 26. AS A THIEF RISES) Chastity is equated to life. See book 2 of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter 1, §. 7. & 12. By this example, the law teaches that those who have sinned because they were compelled by force should be spared.

Latin:

Vers. 26. SICVT LATRO CONSVRGIT) Pudicitia vitae aequiparatur. Vide libr. 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 1. §. 7. & 12. Docet hoc exemplo lex parcendum iis qui vi adacti aliquid peccaverint.

## 22:29
Vers. 29. HE SHALL HAVE HER AS WIFE, BECAUSE HE HAS HUMBLED HER: HE SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO PUT HER AWAY ALL THE DAYS OF HIS LIFE) Force against a girl is punished more harshly than seduction. For what is more foul than to act against a citizen in the manner of an enemy? Therefore, the penalty for this is heavier. He who seduced, if he is permitted to take her as a wife, does not give a dowry, nor is he forbidden to put her away. See what is above at Exod. 22, 6. The defamer of a virgin is held equal to one who uses force.

Latin:

Vers. 29. HABEBIT EAM IN VXOREM, QVIA HVMILIAVIT ILLAM: NON POTERIT DIMITTE- RE EAM CVNCTIS DIEBVS VITAE SVAE) Vis in pu- ellam quam pellacia durius punitur. Quid enim foedius quam hostili more in civem agere? Itaque hujus poena gra- vior. Qui pellexit, fi eam permittitur uxorem ducere, non dat dotem, nec dimittere vetatur. Vide quae supra Exod. 22, 6. Diffamator virginis par habetur vim inferenti.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

Certain persons are excluded from public offices. Cleanliness of the camps: concerning servants, harlots, usury: concerning vows, concerning the vineyard and the grain of a neighbor.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

Excluduntur certae personae ab officiis publicis. Castrorum mundities: de servis, scortis, usu- ra: de votis, de vinea, & fegete proximi.

## 23:2
Vers. 2. A MAMZER, THAT IS, ONE BORN OF A HARLOT, SHALL NOT ENTER INTO THE CONGREGATION OF THE LORD. A Mamzer is one born from a union for which the penalty is death or כרת (excision). To enter בקהל, εἰς ἐκκλησίαν (into the congregation), as the LXX translate here and a little above, is to have the right of marriage among the people of God. Thus Maimonides here. That right was commonly given to proselytes, provided they were of free condition and accepted the law, and they were reckoned to the tribe from which they had taken a wife. Eunuchs, bastards, those born of bastards, and those born of certain ill-deserving nations are excepted, from which proselytes some were never admitted to the right of marriage, others only in the third generation. Eunuchs in Egypt were accustomed to take wives, so as not to be devoid of all pleasure in venery. Exod. 39, 1. But the holy law does not allow Hebrews to marry without hope of offspring. Handmaids and freedwomen adopted into the nation were excepted.

Vatablus, Cornel. a Lap. and others explain this and the following regarding exclusion from marriage, even with the Hebrews. Others, such as Theodoret, Dionys. Carthus., and Leonh. Marius, understand by entry into the Church an entry into the atrium. But it is established that no one is excluded from that (Ex. 12, 42; Lev. 22, 18; Num. 9, 14). More correctly, other Hebrews, Fagius, B. Luther, and B. Gerhard, wish the assembly of judges to be noted, which is called the congregation of God in Ps. 82, 1, so that the discourse is about persons who are not admitted to public offices, such as eunuchs, bastards, Ammonites, and Moabites. For if it is only a matter of the prohibition of marriage, what need was there to establish this law concerning eunuchs, who are unfit for marriage, says P. Fagius in this place. Cf. Neh. 13, 1; Syr. 38, 36, 37. Chytraeus explains it concerning eunuchs and bastards not being admitted to public functions, or government in the Church of God, or even to public and solemn assemblies and festive sermons, lest the offices themselves come into contempt because of the baseness and disgrace of the persons' origins. What ממזר is to the Hebrews, Aben-Ezra teaches thus: Our wise men explain it as one who comes from incestuous nuptials. Münster and Fagius recount from them three kinds of Mamzers: certain, uncertain, and those whom the scribes judge to be such. Thus you have nothing certain from them. Therefore, to others it seems that by the name Mamzer, anyone born outside of legitimate wedlock is understood here, from זר (stranger), a bastard. Thus Targ. Jonath., LXX, Hieronym., and B. Luther. The Talmudists wish it to be derived from מום זר, which sounds like 'strange blemish': and that name is usually taken more strictly for one who is born from a coitus that is to be punished by כרית (excision) or capital punishment. See. Selden, De success. ad leges Ebr., p. 23. The example of Jephthah was extraordinary (Jud. 11, 1). Achior, leader of the sons of Ammon, although he is read to have been admitted to the people of Israel, was not admitted to honors or assumed into the senate (Judith 14, 3).

Latin:

Vers. 2. NON INGRED IETVR MAMZER, HOC EST, DE SCORTO NATVS IN ECCLESIAM DO- MINI) Mamzer est natus ex congressu, cui poena mors vel כרת. Ingredi בקהל εἰς ἐκκλησίαν, ut hic & paulo supra vertunt LXX. est jus accipere connubii in populo Dei. Ita hic Maimonides. Id jus communiter proselytis, modo liberae essent conditionis, legem fufcipientibus dabatur, ac- censebanturque illi tribui, unde uxorem duxerant. Exci- piuntur spadones, spurii, ex spuriis, & ex quibusdam male meritis gentibus orti, e queis proselytis nati alii nunquam, alii tertio demum gradu ad jus connubii admittebantur. Spado- nes in Aegypto conjuges sumere solebant, ut non omnis volu- ptatis in venere expertes. Exod. 39, 1. Lex vero sancta He- braeas non sinit nubere sine spe prolis. Excipiebantur an- cillae, libertinae, in gentem adscitae.

DE exclusione a matrimonio haec & sequentia ex- plicant etiam cum Ebraeis Vatablus, Cornel. a Lap. Alii per ingressum in Ecclesiam ingressum atrii intelligunt, uti Theodoretus, Dionys. Carthus. Leonh. Marius. Sed ab eo nullum excludi constat Ex. 12, 42. Lev. 22, 18. Num. 9, 14. Rectius alii ex Ebraeis, Fa- gius, B. Lutherus, B. Gerhardus, confessum judicum no- tari volunt, qui congregatio Dei dicitur Pf. 82, 1. ut de personis sermo sit, quae non admittantur ad officia publica, quales sint Eunuchi, Spurii, Ammonitae, Moa- bitae. Quod fi enim tantum de matrimonii prohibitione agitur, quid opus fuit, hanc legem statuere de Eunuchis, qui ad matrimonium inepti, ait P. Fagius in h. l. Conf. Neh. 13, 1. Syr. 38, 36. 37. B. Chytraeus, de Eunuchis & Spu- riis ad publicas functiones, seu gubernationem in Ecclesia Dei, vel etiam ad publicos, & solemnes coe- tus, ac conciones festivas præcipue non admittendis explicat, ne officia ipsa propter personarum ortus vilitatem & probrum in contemtum veniant. Quid ממזר Ebræis sit, Aben-Ezra ita docet ; Sapientes nostri exponunt de eo, qui venit ex incestis nuptiis. Mün- sterus & Fagius ex illis triplicis generis Mamzeros recensent, certos, incertos, & quos scribæ tales judicant. Ita nihil certe ex illis habeas. Aliis ergo videtur Mamzeris nomine quemvis extra legitimum conjugi- um natum hic intelligi, a זר extraneus, spurius. Sic Targ. Jonath. LXX. Hieronym. & B. Luther. Tal- mudici a מום זר deduci volunt, quod maculam extraneam sonat: & accipitur id nomen plerumq; strictius de eo, qui ex coitu כרית excisione seu ul- timo supplicio afficiendo, natus est. Vid. Seldenus de success. ad leges Ebr. p. 23. Exemplum Jeph- thæ fuit extraordinarium Jud. 11, 1. Achior Dux filiorum Ammon, etsi ad populum Israel, non tamen ad honores admissus vel in senatum assumtus legi- tur. Judith. 14, 3.

## 23:3
Vers. 3. AN AMMONITE OR MOABITE SHALL NOT ENTER EVEN AFTER THE TENTH GENERATION) That is, never. This is because the Moabites, with the help of the neighboring Ammonites, as Nehemiah 13, 1 shows, had made the people sin: which is worse than lying in wait for their lives, which the Egyptians and Edomites had done. The law deals with males: for women from these peoples who were converted to God, like Ruth, could marry an Israelite. Thus Maimonides and Moses de Kotzi.

Latin:

Vers. 3. AMMONITES ET MOABITES ETIAM POST DECIMAM GENERATIONEM NON INTRA- BVNT ) Id est, nunquam. Hoc ideo quia Moabitæ ad- juvantibus, ut ostendit Nehemias 13, 1. vicinis Ammonitis, peccare populum fecerant : quod pejus est quam vitæ infi- dijari, quod fecerant Ægyptii & Idumæi. Agit lex de mari- bus : nam mulieres ex his populis ad Deum conversæ ut Ruth, nubere Israëlitæ poterant. Ita Maimonides & Moses de Kotzi.

## 23:6
Vers. 6. THOU SHALT NOT MAKE PEACE WITH THEM) In Hebrew: Thou shalt not seek their peace: thou shalt not ask for peace from them. See De J. B. & P., book 2, ch. 15, § 9.

Because it is added, 'and their good,' they are prohibited not only from entering into a covenant with them, but also from having commerce with them, and from consulting for their tranquility and happiness, to declare the gravity of the sin by which they had harmed the Israelites, and to prevent the seduction of the latter. The example of David is special and extraordinary, and concerns private friendship (2 Sam. 10, 2).

Latin:

Vers. 6. NON FACIES CVM EIS PACEM) In Hebr. Non quæres eorum pacem : non petas ab illis pacem. Vide de J. B. & P. l. 2. c. 15. §. 9.

Quia additur, & bonum eorum, non tantum fœdus cum illis inire prohibentur, sed etiam com- mercia cum illis habere, ac tranquillitati, & felicita- ti ipsorum consulere, ad declarandam peccati gra- vitatem, quo Israelitas læserant, & præcavendam ho- rum seductionem. Exemplum Davidis speciale & ex- traordinarium est, & amicitiam privatam concernit. 2. Sam. 10, 2.

## 23:8
Vers. 8. IN THE THIRD GENERATION) Grandchildren will have the right of marriage. Thus the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 8. TERTIA GENERATIONE) Nepoti bus jus erit connubii. Ita Hebræi.

## 23:10
Vers. 10. WHO IS POLLUTED BY A NOCTURNAL DREAM) Chaeremon on the Egyptian priests: 'And if ever it should happen that they have a dream, they immediately cleanse the body with a bath.'

Latin:

Vers. 10. QVI NOCTV RNO POLLVTVS SIT SO- MNIO) Chæremon de Ægypti sacerdotibus, εἴδέ ποτε συμ- βαίη κἀκ ὀνειρώττειν, παραχρῆμα ἐπεκαθήραι λκτρῷ τὸ σῶμα.

## 23:13
Vers. 13. UPON THY WEAPON) In the Hebrew it is אזן, from the Chaldean זינ, whence the Greek ζόνη, which the LXX have here.

AND WHEN THOU SHALT SIT DOWN, THOU SHALT DIG AROUND) Josephus on the Essenes, and Porphyry from him: 'Otherwise they sit, or having dug a pit a foot deep, and having covered themselves with their garment.'

Latin:

Vers. 13. IN BALTEO) In Hebræo est אזן, ex Chaldæo זינ, unde Græcum ζόνη, quod hic habent LXX.

CVMQVE SEDERIS, FODIES PER CIRCUITVM) De Essenis Josephus, & ex eo Porphyrius : ἄλλως ἤ θακέου- σιν ἤ βόθρον ὀρύξαντες εἰς βάθος ποδιαῖον, περικαλύψαντές τε θοιματίῳ.

## 23:14
Vers. 14. LET NOTHING OF FILTHINESS APPEAR IN THEM) In the Hebrew: shameful to speak of: that is, whoredoms, such as are everywhere in the camps of other nations. Thus Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed 3, 41.

By the name of filthiness are understood not only whoredoms, but in general any obscene thing, as the Targum, the LXX, Luther, an evil thing; as in v. 9, uncleanness, as much spiritual as corporal, whatever fights against piety and honesty, which for the most part are exiled from camps. Drusius on difficult passages of Deut. ch. 84 notes that there were three camps: (1) the camp of the Deity, the tabernacle and the courtyard around it, (2) the dwellings of the Levites around the courtyard, (3) the dwellings of the rest of the people: observing that those about to perform the work of nature ought to have gone out beyond those three camps, that lepers were cast out from all, those with issues from the first two, and those polluted by the touch of a dead body from the first only. The Targum applies the words concerning Jehovah walking in the midst of them to the Son of God: from which may his word be averted, so that he might not do good to you.

Latin:

Vers. 14. NIHIL IN EIS APPAREAT FOEDITATIS) In Hebræo : turpe dictu: id est scortationes, quales ubique in aliarum gentium castris. Ita Maimonides Duce Dubi- tantium 3, 41.

Nomine fœditatis non intelliguntur tantum scortationes, sed in genere quævis res obscœna, ut Tar- gum, LXX. Lutherus, res mala ; ut v. 9. immundities, tam spiritualis, quam corporalis, quicquid cum pieta- te & honestate, quæ plerunqve in castris exulant, pu- gnat. Drusius ad loca diff. Deut. c. 84. notat tria fu- isse castra : (1) castra Deitatis, tabernaculum & atri- um circa ipsum, (2) Levitarum habitationes circa a- trium, (3) Habitationes reliqui populi: opus naturæ fa- cturos extra tria illa castra egredi debuisse, leprosos ex omnibus, feminifluos e primis duobus, pollutos a tactu mortui e primis solum ejectos fuisse obser- vans. Targum verba de Jehovah ambulante in me- dio ipsorum applicat ad Filium Dei : unde avertatur verbum ejus, quo minus benefaciat tibi.

## 23:15
Vers. 15. TO HIS MASTER) To a foreigner. Thus the Israelite land may be an asylum. The laws of Moses greatly favor liberty: but a price was given publicly to the Master: and to the other of the Masters, if the other had freed the slave. See Moses of Coucy, commanding precept 180.

This is to be understood of a Gentile slave, who fled to the Israelite people, especially from the neighboring nations, the Canaanites; for these were devoted to destruction,

& all that they possessed, given to the Israelites. And it was better to be among the true worshippers of God, which the Hebrews give as the reason for the law.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DOMINO SVO) Extraneo. Sic terra Israë- litica asylum sit. Multum favent Mosis leges libertati : sed Domino dabatur publicitus pretium : & alteri Domino- rum, si alter servum liberasset. Vide Mosem de Kotzi præ- cepto jubente 180.

Intelligendum hoc de servo Ethnico, qui ad Israeliticum populum profugit, imprimis e genti- bus vicinis, Cananæis ; hæ enim exitio devotæ erant,

& omnia, quæ poffidebant, Israelitis data. Et præ stabat talem inter veros Dei cultores versari, quam legis causam reddunt Ebræi.

## 23:17
Verse 17. HARLOT) קדשׁה, concerning which word see Gen. 38, 21.

FORNICATOR) In the Hebrew: קדשׁ, a catamite. Greek πορνέυων in the same sense: for those who prostitute themselves are called πορνεύειν by the Greeks. Thus in Xiphilinus, πεπορνευκὼς, who is a spintria in Tranquillus. Abenesdra rightly translates it הנשׁכב. But what is added here in the LXX: ἐκ ἔσαι τελεσφόρος ἀπὸ θυγατέρων Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ ἐκ ἔσαι τελισκόμενος ἀπὸ ὑι̂ων Ἰσραὴλ, crept in from another version of those interpreters who took קדשׁ & קדשׁה in the sense of idolatrous initiation. And so Theodoret interprets τελεσφόρον as the one who initiates, and τελισκόμενον as the one who is initiated: which words, being poorly understood, certain Christians have dragged into the matter of the freedom of taxes.

Latin:

Vers. 17. MERETRIX) קדשׁה , de qua voce vid Gen. 38, 21.

SCORTATOR) In Hebræo: קדשׁ catamitus. Græc πορνέυων eodem sensu: nam πορνεύειν Græcis dicuntur qui s vulgant. Sic Xiphilino πεπορνευκὼς, qui spintria Tran- quillo. Abenesdra bene vertit הנשׁכב. Quod vero hic in LXX. additur: ἐκ ἔσαι τελεσφόρος ἀπὸ θυγατέρων Ἰσρα ὴλ, καὶ ἐκ ἔσαι τελισκόμενος ἀπὸ ὑι̂ων Ἰσραὴλ, ex alia versio- ne irrepsit eorum interpretum qui קדשׁ & קדשׁה su- mebant sensu initiationis idololatricæ. Itaque Theodore- tus τελεσφόρον interpretatur τὴν μυσαγωγόσαν, τελισκόμενον ve- ro τὸν μυσαγωγόμενον : quas voces male intellectas Chri- stiani quidam ad vectigalium libertatem traxere.

## 23:18
Verse 18. NOR THE PRICE OF A DOG) That animal was vile to the Hebrews 1 Sam. 17, 43. c. 24, 19. Ezek. 9, 4.

Others more correctly understand by the price of a dog the price that is given to a catamite, or a boy for hire, because a dog is joined with a harlot, and in Rev. 22, 15, shameless men are called dogs.

Latin:

Vers. 18. NEC PRETIUM CANIS) Vile id animal Hebræis 1. Sam. 17, 43. c. 24, 19. Ezech. 9, 4.

Alii rectius per pretium canis intelligunt pre- tium quod cinædo, seu puero meritorio datur, quia cum meretrice canis conjungitur, & Apoc. 22, 15. homines impudici canes vocantur.

## 23:19
Verse 19. BUT TO A STRANGER) whether living outside the borders, or within the borders, but not subject to the law.

These things are to be understood not of any alien or stranger, but of the Canaanites, inasmuch as their possessions were otherwise given to the Israelites, whence it was lawful to take interest from them, as B. Hunnius rightly observed in 2 Cor. 8. Compare Ex. 23, 29. 30. Interest against strangers was a political law, and had a peculiar reason in the land which God had given to the people, of which they were remaining as if mercenaries or feudatories for a time, until God should drive them out entirely, as Ant. Walaeus says in the cited places, p. 58. Furthermore, even in the O.T. interest was prohibited Ps. 15, 5. Ez. 18, 8. Yet this was not a precept, but only a bare permission, i.e., but to a stranger you may lend at interest. This permission of the Jews, says Luth. in Declam. on the 7th Commandment, Vol. 1, Lat. 5, f. 156, was only permitted so that they might the more willingly abstain from interest against Jews, the more freely they could against Gentiles.

But the Jews falsely collect from this that it is lawful for them to take interest from Christians, because the condition of Christians is one thing, and the condition of the Canaanites devoted to destruction is another. B. Luth. in his book against the Jews notes that there are two kinds of Jews. Some, he says, are the Jews of Moses, whom, to wit, God brought through Moses out of Egypt into the land of Canaan, and gave them the law to be kept in that land until the Messiah should come: but some are the Jews of Caesar, not of Moses, whose ancestors, to wit, said before Pilate: We have no King but Caesar; to them this law does not pertain, but if they wish to use and enjoy it, they must return to the land of Canaan. Wherefore Fagius rightly [notes] on the Chaldean Interpreter, ch. 1. The Magistrates do very badly who permit the Jews to take interest from Christians. For thus they strengthen them all the more in their errors and impieties: Effort should be devoted so that they might be treated in such a way that they would know they are under a yoke and servitude, so that they might be more humbled, acknowledge their sins, and meditate on repentance, etc. How greatly the Jews fleece Christians, the calculations of Jewish interest show: if indeed with one gold coin, within the space of twenty years, with the interest of individual weeks accumulated at two Frankfurt obols, they would lend more than 2500 gold coins, as B. Chytræus observes. Furthermore, they were forbidden to lend at interest to a brother of the nation, as in Lev. 19, 17. Num. 24, 18. Deut. 3, 18. A brother is called, i.e., a Hebrew, or one born of the Israelite people; they were forbidden to lend at interest of money, interest of food, and of every thing which is given for interest, that is, to demand back something beyond the principal for those things given as a loan. But when it is asked concerning interest, whether it be lawful or not? one must distinguish between interest properly so called, and what is improperly called interest. Interest properly so called is the profit which is demanded beyond the principal in money or a thing which can be estimated in money, for the sole service of lending, with manifest damage to the borrower. For the sole service of the loan, I say. For if it is for another reason, or because of emerging damage, or ceasing profit, it is not interest properly so called. Add that it happens with manifest damage to him from whom it is demanded, for if it brings him no damage, but rather a memorable benefit in his household affairs, it is not interest properly so called. That those kinds of interest, when something is demanded from a poor brother beyond the principal, are prohibited by every law, is certain. By Divine [law] Ex. 22. 5. Lev. 25. 35. 36. 37. Deut. 23, 19. Ex. 18, 8. Neh. 5, 2. Ps. 16. By Canon [law] C. Non licet. C. Sicut Dist. 46. C. Episcopus, C. Quoniam Dist. 47. C. cum fœneraveris with the following, caus. 14. q. 3. Ecclesiastico, as being things condemned in the first Council of Nicaea can. 18. and the Council of Elvira c. 15. By the law of nations, to which can be referred those words of Cicero in De Officiis 3: to take away from another and for a man to increase his own advantage by the disadvantage of another is more against nature than death; and what he himself relates about Cato, that for him to lend at interest was the same as to kill a man, and that Lycurgus expelled usurers from all of Sparta, and that Agis is said to have burned all the usurious ledgers at Athens, having built a fire in the middle of the forum. Whence the witty saying of Agesilaus: That he had never seen a brighter light in his life than this very fire, likewise that others have judged that a thief should be punished twofold, a usurer fourfold, etc. Usury is called by the Hebrews by the ill-omened name נֶשֶׁךְ from biting and gnawing, and it is such an increase and such an overabundance, which burdens, weighs down, oppresses, and consumes the giver, and as Rabbi Solomon says, it behaves like the bite of a serpent (for נֶשֶׁךְ by metathesis is שָׁנַךְ a serpent) which bites a small wound in someone's foot, but soon it creeps and spreads its poison, until it reaches his head; so also the increase of usury behaves, for it is not felt, nor is it known, until it is so increased that it exhausts someone's entire substance. Whence Baldus compares usury to the woodworm, which appears soft to the touch, but has very hard teeth, and gnaws the marrow of the wood so that the surface appears as if unharmed. Which Jerome condemns in Ezekiel book 6, chapter 18; Ambrose in the book On Tobias chapter 13; Chrysostom in chapter 5 of Matthew; Lactantius in Institutes book 16, chapter 18; B. Luther in the sermon on Usury, Vol. 1, German, Jena, fol. 188, and in the admonition to Pastors on Usury, Vol. 7. Jena, fol. 373, as being that which fights not only with divine law, but also with the duty of humanity, and with the nature of a loan, which ought to be gratuitous. Therefore, the opinion of Socinus in his Epistle, p. 503, is to be entirely rejected: That usuries are not forbidden in any way by themselves, whatever either Philosophers or Theologians may argue to the contrary.

Contracts that are just and equitable and permitted by the laws of the civil Magistrate, such as compensation, interest, or annual pensions, are sometimes improperly called by the name of usury. Where, however, the distinction of persons must necessarily be observed. For some are extremely poor, who cannot even return the principal, to whom a loan of alms is owed (Luke 6:35); some are needy, who have need of a sum of money for the sustenance of life, by which they do not desire to make a profit, but to provide for their necessity; to these an 'officious' loan, as they call it, is owed, in which a certain sum of money is given to a neighbor on the law and condition that at an appointed time he returns the same, and τὰ ἴσα (the equal amount), whence this indeed can be demanded back, for nothing beyond the principal should be exacted for the use of money (Lev. 25:35); others are wealthy, or at least seek our money in such a way, not that they may provide for necessity, but that they may trade with the same, make a profit, buy lands and estates, and their fortunes more and more increase, with whom it is lawful to enter into such a contract, that they pay something annually for the use of the money, while the principal remains unchanged, provided that those usuries, so called improperly, are moderate and the principle of Christian charity is not neglected, which jurists call compensatory, and distinguish from lucrative, admitting the former, but condemning the latter. Whence Christian Magistrates have approved contracts of this kind, by which, for example, one hundred florins are let out for an annual payment of five florins (which are also called by Persius the quincunx of returns), so that those who can trade with them are obligated not only to the restitution of the principal, but also to some compensation for our service. Which contracts are not prohibited by divine law 2, and concerns the needy and the poor, from whom nothing beyond the principal ought to be exacted for the sake of the service of a loan, and it conforms to natural equity according to the precept of Christ, Matthew 7:12: 'Everything that you want people to do to you, do also to them,' as well as the rule of charity, 2 Corinthians 8:13, that one should do good to others in such a way that it is not an ἄνεσις, a relaxation for them, but a θλίψις, an affliction for us, but ἐξ ἰσότητος, so that there may be equality. For since the creditor could likewise have traded with this money of his in the meantime and provided himself with conveniences, equity itself and gratitude, which is of natural law, demand that the debtor, to whom it was entirely possible by the benefit of the money lent to trade and seek his own conveniences, should deal with the creditor in the way he would wish to be dealt with in a similar case, and thus admit the creditor into some participation of the profit, and in compensation for that increase of his resources which he could have obtained by the use of the money and is forced to lack in the meantime, he should pay him something annually, so that there may not be such a relaxation for the debtor and an affliction for us, provided that we have lacked our money and have not been able to provide our own same conveniences, but that there may be some equality here. Which rule of the Apostle, although it is applied there to charitable beneficence, is nevertheless in itself and by itself general, and the foundation of all contracts and duties, which ought to be performed in such a way that equality is preserved, and we do not feel a loss while others feel mere profit. Because, therefore, a gratuitous loan, and one otherwise not owed, made to the wealthy, produces indeed an ἄνεσιν for them, but a θλίψιν for us, while they increase their property with our money, and in the meantime the opportunity of increasing our own property is taken away from us: anyone surely understands that it is consistent both with natural equity and with this Apostolic Aphorism if we desire to be admitted at the same time into a participation of the profit which the wealthy take from our money, and thus demand annual payments from them, so that in this way their περίσσευμα or abundance may yield εἰς τὸ ἡμῶν ὑσέρημα, for our supplement, or so that what is left over for them may supply what is lacking to us, and thus there may be and is made equality, as the blessed Meisner has it, Part 3, Phil. Sobr. p. 165. Add that we are not bound to a loan by rich men or merchants or entire Republics. or even to Princes themselves; from these, therefore, if anything is received beyond the principal, it is not usury, because it is not taken from the needy, nor for the sake of the service of the loan alone, but for their own convenience, and therefore we can expect something from their money in place of compensation on account of our money, which we had to lack in the meantime. Just as not simply every acceptance of gifts is prohibited, but that which is done against the innocent and by which justice is bent, so neither is that which is taken beyond the principal simply prohibited, but if it is Nesech, if it bites, afflicts, and strikes the needy brother. But if it is not foreign to the law to mortgage some field in place of a pledge for a certain sum of money lent, and to grant the fruits to the creditor in place of annual interest, as they call it, how will it be unjust to retain the field and the fruits, and in place of annual interest for the money let out, to pay some certain pension? How these, as well as the contracts of antichresis, the purchase of returns, and partnership, serve to confirm annual payments, the blessed Meisner teaches, p. 3, Ph. Sobr. Sect. 1. c. 6. p. 167. It cannot, therefore, be simply approved what Aristotle says, l. 1. Pol. c. 7, that usurious acquisition is most against nature. The reason is that money is not a sterile thing, or at least not fit πρὸς τὸ τοκεῖν, for bearing (whence they called usury τόκον, i.e., a certain birth), for how much money often bears, those who trade with it know. Also to be rejected is Wolff. The opinion of Musculus in his Commentary on Psalm 15, who absolutely reprobates usury, as also that of Benedict Aretius in the aforementioned places, Loc. CXXXI, who reprobates even simple terrestrial and nautical usury, not only from the besse with 8 florins per hundred, and the semissales, when 6 are paid annually for 10. These species, he says, col. 741, we all judge to be wicked, condemned by divine and human law: we have one lawful usury, by which men trade with the earth itself, the mother. For this is accustomed to return for the most part with greater interest what it receives; hence it is not badly called by the Germans Erdwucher. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and other pious men enjoyed this: today it is pushed back to miserable farmers, formerly it was in delight among Kings and Princes. Who brings forward the Practice of Ferrariensis, lib. CLXXVIII, as also the theses formerly published at Wittenberg, in which those are called usurers or money-lenders, whoever receive from money lent, even the smallest farthing or a drink of cold water by agreement beyond the principal, and it is inferred that those who receive by agreement five florins out of 100 lent, and pertinaciously adhere to such an opinion that five can be received from 100 lawfully and without sin beyond the penalties which they incur by positive law, sin and offend God most greatly, and are to be judged as robbers and heretics. Rivetus brings forward John Jewel, Lancelot, and Andrewes, Bishop of Winchester, all of whom disapprove of all usury. But annual payments and pensions are not condemned by the Orthodox Wittenberg Theologians. Megalander himself, although he wrote sharply against usury, was nevertheless more moderate in that cause in his later years, Tom. 6. Witteberg. He also determined that the elderly who are unfit for labor, widows, orphans, and ecclesiastical treasuries may receive a fixed pension in return for a certain sum of money for the honest sustenance of themselves and their own, and he advised that the magistrate should establish ἐπιείκειαν in such matters, and thus he approved of moderate annual pensions. The opinion of B. Hunnius on 2 Cor. ch. 8 can be seen as ὁμόψηφος to this explanation; likewise B. Gesner on Ps. 15, B. Balduinus in Cas. Consc. b. 4 & 3 ch. 4, B. Meisner Part. 3 Phil. Sobr. ch. 6, and B. Hülsemann in Brev., which other theologians of ours clearly support. See B. Brentius vom wucherl. Contract., B. Chemnitius p. 2 LL. CC., B. Jac. Andreæ in Concion. Ratisb. editis, Chytraeus & Pelargus in Comm. ad h. l., B. Herbrand & B. Schnepfius in Consil. Theol. Bidenbach. Dec. 1. Consil. 4. & Decad. 6. Consil. 8., and B. D. Hoë, Unterricht, ob ein Christ mit gutem Gewissen Geldzinsen nehmen könne. B. D. Gerhard T. 6. LL. CC. p. 911. B. Backmeister Disp. 9. in Decal. th. 38. B. Paul. Tarnov. l. 1. c. 2. de Minist. Consil. Dedekenn. Vol. 1. fol. 167. Of the Calvinists, most others depart from the opinion of Aretius. Polanus in Syntagm. l. 10. c. 63. Compensatory usury, which consists within the limit defined by public laws, is not forbidden and illicit for the following arguments: 1. Because it is not profit exacted above the principal for the service of lending, but the price or valuation of the use of the consumed principal along with the loss of the creditor. For the creditor could have sought legitimate profit in other things with his money and perceived some advantage, of which he is deprived because another has meanwhile used his money. 2. Because it is consistent with the duty of humanity, which commands one to help another in such a way that you keep yourself unharmed, 2 Cor. 8:13. 3. Because it is permitted by the constitutions of Christian Emperors. 4. Because common necessity and the utility of trade require it. 5. Because it compensates the loss of the creditor; which no reason prohibits. Voetius, in his Select Disputations on Law and Justice, Vol. 1, p. 400, teaches that commercial and maritime interest, for which the Magistrate has set a limit, is lawful, but not any other kind that is also biting and exacted from an impoverished brother. Andr. Riv. on Ex. 20, p. 277, laboriously teaches that the lending of money for business is lawful. Spanhem, p. 3, Dub. Evang. 127, p. 665, brings forward Calvin and Ames to this opinion, and confirms the same at length. Three things, he says, p. 669, I judge must be distinguished here: 1. Usury and interest. 2. Those who give money for interest. 3. Those who receive it. 1. As regards usury, I think one must distinguish between compensatory usury and predatory usury, helpful usury and gnawing or biting usury, likewise simple usury and compound usury, that is, ἀνατοκισμὸν, moderate and immoderate usury. 2. Those also who give money for interest must be distinguished, for they are either money-lenders and usurers by profession, and this is their only business, or they are not: Or they give a loan for interest only, or sometimes even gratuitously, or they deprive themselves of the ability to give something to the needy for nothing, or they reserve for themselves the means to provide that, and they actually provide it when the occasion is given: or they look only to their own advantage, or along with their own advantage, they also look to the advantage of him to whom they lend money: or such men can honestly trade with their own money, and increase their capital either by tilling a field, or by doing business, or by some other similar method, so that they have wherewith to live and honestly provide for their own: Or they are entirely occupied with public duties, whether sacred or political, so that they cannot themselves spend their money with profit, or are otherwise destitute of the strength or the suitability to provide that. 3. Those also who receive money for interest are either poor, or in circumstances that are at least wealthy or moderate: or they are in need of our money, or they are not: or they receive money on loan for necessary uses, or for their own advantages and profits: or they have the means to pay back both the principal and the profit without loss, or they do not have them. With these and other circumstances of this kind weighed, lawful usury can easily be distinguished from unlawful, permitted from prohibited. We judge those usuries to be unlawful, not which are compensatory, but which are predatory, which are gnawing and biting, and only נשׁך. Which Grotius supports in book 2 of The Law of War and Peace, ch. 12, n. 20. Nor did Ferrariensis simply disapprove of usury; indeed, in his Practice, p. 379, he taught that the world could hardly be sustained or governed without usury. And although most Scholastics after Thomas 2. 2. q. 78. art. 1, Dominicus a Soto in book 6 of Justice & Law q. 1. art. 1, and the Jesuits Greg. de Valentia Vol. 3, Disp. 5, q. 21, Lessius in book 2 of The Four Cardinal Virtues, ch. 20, dub. 4, and the moralists Azorius, Part 3, Inst. Mor. book 5, on Usury, ch. 2, Toletus, book 5, instr. ch. 20, contend that all usury is unlawful and a mortal sin, indeed Lessius with Toletus argues that it is heresy to teach that usury is not a sin, and that this was defined in the Council of Vienne, and is contained in Clem. unica tit. on usury §. last, yet the Papists do not remain consistent with themselves in this matter of conscience; and Toletus himself, in the aforementioned book, ch. 32 et seqq., lists the causes for which some profit beyond the principal can be justly demanded, such as delay of payment, damage arising, profit ceasing, etc., which can also be seen in Azorius, Lessius, and Soto, concerning which see B. Meisn. in the aforementioned book, p. 171. Furthermore, they commend the mount of piety approved by Pius II and received again in the Lateran Council under Leo X, as do Azorius, Lessius, Toletus, Valentinianus, Medina on usury q. 10, Navarrus in his treatise on Usury n. 59, which is a gathered heap of money for the use of the poor, so that it may be given to them as a loan, but under a pledge, and on the condition that if the loan is not paid within the designated time, the pledge is sold, and what is owed to it is given to the mount, and that every month some sum is paid by him to whom the loan is given; which mount, although Soto and Cajetan, Vol. 2, Opusc. 6, do not approve, the others nevertheless defend as having been approved by Leo X, and indeed they consider those who disagree to be heretics; they also commend other usurious mounts, the mount of faith, of flour, of taxes, of tithes, which Soto taxed on account of usury in book 6 of Justice & Law q. 1. art. 6, they finally contend that on account of profit ceasing, it is lawful to receive something beyond the principal, not only when we lend to the wealthy, but also when we lend to the needy, which opinion Azorius, Part 3, book 5, ch. 5, teaches is the common one, having brought forward many authors (even those who dissent), concerning which see at length B. Meisn. in the aforementioned book, whose reasons for an annual income he repeats and makes his own, as does Rivetus in the aforementioned book, with the addition also of his own warnings and cautions: 1. One must take care that nothing beyond the principal is demanded from him who is needy and receives a small sum on loan, by which he gains absolutely nothing but uses it only for his own sustenance, for then it is sufficient if he restores the principal. 2. If those who are wealthier and receive money on loan suffer, by some chance, without their own fault, some notable detriment in their family affairs, such as by fire, robbery, shipwreck, or by some other reason, so that they gain nothing, but even suffer a great loss, not only should an annual return not be demanded from them, but also some thanksgiving should be made to them regarding the restitution of the principal, until their affairs have come into a better state. 3. One must always distinguish between the needy and the wealthy; for with the former it is by no means lawful to make an agreement about an annual income, because a gratuitous loan is owed to them, as they do not trade with our money in any way. But those who give loans to the wealthier, if they do this for the sake of mere idleness and laziness, because they themselves do not wish to trade or exercise an honest function, they cannot be excused, because they propose to themselves an evil end contrary to the divine will. But those who, out of an inability to trade and by reason of necessity, such as widows, orphans, the elderly, the learned, and the like—who are otherwise not idle, but are devoted to other duties and are less suited for conducting business—do not sin in the least by making such an agreement, because since they themselves cannot trade, whatever they have in substance would be consumed in a short time if they lived off it and provided for their own needs, and did not lend it out to those who could profit from it by fair means, from which they might call them into a share of the annual return. 4. A pious man must also see to it that he does not lend out whatever he has to those who can pay annual returns in such a way that he is not afterwards fit to help the needy through a loan or the poor through alms, for since he has an express command of God concerning this, it ought not to be neglected for the sake of that which is permitted not absolutely, but with certain conditions established. Whence there is a complaint about the loan-offices of their Lombards (similar to the Jews), who publicly practice gnawing usury in Belgium and elsewhere: where also responses to the arguments of the Bishop of Winchester may be read.
