He adds on p. 285: If it could be proven that the acceptance of any surplus had been absolutely forbidden to the Jews, even with respect to a wealthy brother, it would not follow that annual rents are entirely illicit at this time; because in this law there could be something ceremonial and forensic mixed in, which would not bind other nations outside of Judea. For the Jews could not alienate their possessions in perpetuity through sale; but the buyer received only the usufruct until the jubilee year, at which time the immovable property had to be restored to the owner, Lev. 25, 10. 15. But if it had been permitted for an Israelite to take usury from a brother for a loan, the force of that law would have been eluded, because one would never have bought a possession from another, but rather would have accepted an annual rent without labor, since he would have known that the possession was to be restored to his neighbor at a certain time. There is another law about remitting debts to a brother every seventh year, Deut. 15, 1; if, however, it had been lawful to exact that increment from a brother, they would have devoted their efforts during the space of six years to their exactions, so that at the appointed time there would be nothing left which they might remit to their brother. These causes could have been forensic, why among the Israelites usury was more severely forbidden, which nevertheless was permitted regarding foreigners; just as it was not permitted to demand a debt from a brother after seven years, but it was permitted from a stranger. Regarding the passage Luke 6:35, he responds on page 276, it does not treat immediately of not hoping for usury, but of not hoping for the principal itself, when our neighbor, who has need of a loan, is established in extreme necessity, asks for a loan. The Lord therefore wishes that it be granted not only to him whom we know can and wishes to repay; but also to him whom we know cannot, even if he wishes; or of whom we justly doubt that it will happen that he cannot. Whence it is evident that this is not a universal precept, that we should always and to everyone give a loan without hope of restitution; for thus all contracts between men would be rescinded; in which, while a loan is given, a promise of repayment at a certain time is made, and the creditor stipulates that. The Lord wishes only this, although that may be done, and justly according to the reason of the circumstances, yet that it is not only owed by us to our neighbor, but also, where we hope for nothing of the sort, it must be given as a loan, namely to the poor, or to him who is established in the greatest necessity, so that although he may have the intention of repaying if he can, we perform this duty to him, with this consideration set aside.

This, therefore, the Lord intended; that sinful men, as he speaks, about to give money as a loan, provide diligently that they do not give a loan to those from whom the danger of the principal hangs, although they may be in the greatest need of that duty. A Christian, however, ought always to be prompt for this duty of a loan. But it does not follow from that that a loan must also be given to the rich without hope of restitution, but in those words that we give TO EVERYONE WHO ASKS, the universal particle is to be restricted to all those asking whom we are bound to help with alms, not to be taken indiscriminately.

Latin:

Vers. 19. SED ALIENO) sive extra fines habitanti, sive intra fines, sed legi non subdito.

Non de quovis alieno, vel extraneo, sed de Cananæis hæc intelligenda, utpote quarum possessiones alio- quin Israelitis datæ, unde usuras ab illis accipere lice- bat, ut recte observavit B. Hunnius in 2. Cor. 8. Conf. Ex. 23,29.30. Usura adversus extraneos fuit lex politi- ca, & habuit peculiarem rationem in terra, quam Deus populo dederat, cujus reliqui erant quasi mercenarii aut feudatarii ad tempus, donec eos Deus plane abigeret, ut ait Ant. Walæus in LL. CC. p. 58. De cætero etiam in V. T. prohibitæ fuere usuræ Ps. 15, 5. Ez. 18, 8. Non tamen hoc præceptum fuit, sed tantum permissio nu- da, q. d. sed alieno poteris mutuum dare cum usura. Hoc Judæorum permissum, inquit Luth. in Declam. de 7. Præcept. T. 1. Lat. 5. f. 156. tantum permissum fuit, ut eo libentius abstinerent ab usura in Judæos, quo licentius potuerunt in gentiles.

Falso autem Judæi hinc colligunt, sibi licere usuras accipere a Christia- nis, quia alia est Christianorum, alia Cananæorum exitio devotorum ratio. B. Luth. lib. contr. Judæos notat duo esse Judæorum genera. Quidam, inquit, sunt Judæi Mosis, quos sc. Deus per Mosen ex Ægypto in terram Canaan introduxit, ac legem illis dedit in terra ista servandam, donec veniret Messias: quidam vero sunt Judæi Cæsaris non Mosis, quorum sc. majores coram Pi- lato dixerunt: Non habemus Regem nisi Cæsarem, ad illos non pertinere hanc legem, sed si ea uti frui ve- lint, in terram Canaan ipsis esse redeundum. Qua- propter recte Fagius ad Interp. Chald. c. 1. Pessime faciunt Magistratus, qui Judæis permittunt, ut usuras a Christianis accipiant. Ita enim illos in suis errori- bus ac impietatibus magis corroborant: Opera danda esset, ut ita tractarentur, quo scirent, se esse sub jugo & servitute, quo magis humiliarentur, peccata sua agno- scerent, & pœnitentiam meditarentur &c. Quantope- re Judæi emungant Christianos, rationes usurarum Judaicarum subductæ docent: siquidem uno aureo, intra viginti annorum spacium accumulatis singula- rum hebdomadarum usuris duobus obolis Francof. amplius 2500. aureos fœnerentur, observante B. Chytræo. Cæterum fratri gentis ratione uti Lev. 19, 17. Num. 24, 18. Deut. 3, 18. Frater dicitur, h. e. E- bræo, vel ex populo Israelitico oriundo vetabantur fœnerari usura pecuniæ, usura cibi & omnis rei, quæ fœnori datur, id est, pro illis mutuo datis ultra sortem aliquid repetere. Cum autem de usuris quæritur, lici- tæ sint, nec ne? distinguendum inter usuras proprie dictas, & quæ improprie nominantur usuræ. Usura proprie dicta est lucrum, quod ultra sortem exigitur in pecunia aut re, quæ pecunia æstimari potest propter so- lum mutuationis officium, cum damno manifesto mutu- atarii. Propter folum mutui officium, inquam. Nam si aliam ob causam, aut propter damnum emergens, aut lucrum cessans, non usura est proprie sic dicta. Adde, quod cum manifesto damno ejus a quo exigitur fiat, si enim nullum ei affert damnum, sed potius memorabile commodum in re familiari, non est usura proprie dicta. Illas ergo usuras, cum ultra sortem aliquid a paupere fratre exigitur, omni jure prohibitas esse, certum est. Divino Ex. 22. 5. Lev. 25. 35. 36. 37. Deut. 23, 19. Ex. 18, 8. Neh. 5, 2. Ps. 16. Canonico C. Non licet. C. Sicut Dist. 46. C. Episcopus, C. Quoniam Dist. 47. C. cum fœneraveris cum seqq. caus. 14. q. 3. Ecclesiastico, utpote quæ damnata in Concilio Niceno primo can. 18. Elibertino c. 15. Jure gentium, quo referri possunt illa Ciceronis in Offic. 3. detrahere alteri & hominem hominis incommodo suum augere commodum magis est contra naturam, quam mors; & quod refert ipse de Catone, illi fœnerari idem fuisse, quod hominem occidere, & quod Lycurgus e tota Sparta usurarios expulit, quodq; Agis Athenis dicitur omnes tabulas usurarias concremasse, igni in medio foro extructo. Unde lepidum Agesilai dictum: Se nunquam aliud clarius lumen in vita vidisse, quam hunc ipsum ignem, item quod alii furem duplo, usurarium quadruplo puniendum censuerint &c. Usura Ebræis infausto nomine vocatur נֶשֶׁךְ a morsu ac arrosione, estq; tale incrementum ac talis superabundantia, quæ dantem gravat, onerat, opprimit & absumit, ac R. Salomone dicente, se habet instar morsus serpentis (nam נֶשֶׁךְ per metathesin est שָׁנַךְ serpens) qui mordet vulnus parvum in pede alicujus, mox autem serpit & diffundit se venenum, donec perveniat ad verticem ejus, sic quoq; incrementum usuræ se habet, non enim sentitur, neq; cognoscitur, donec ita augeatur, ut totam substantiam alicujus exhauriat. Unde Baldus usuram comparat vermiculo ligni, qui tactu lenis apparet, sed dentes habet durissimos, & medullam ligni sic arrodit, ut superficies quasi illæsa appareat. Quam damnant Hieron. in Ez. l. 6. c. 18. Ambros. l. de Tobia c. 13. Chrys. in c. 5. Matt. Lactantius l. 16. Inst. c. 18. B. Luth. serm. de Usur. T. 1. Germ. Jen. f. 188. & in admonit. ad Pastor. de Usuris T. 7. Jen. f. 373. utpote quæ non modo cum lege divina, sed etiam cum officio humanitatis, & cum natura mutui, quod debet esse gratuitum, pugnat. Itaq; reprobanda omnino Socini sententia in Epist. p. 503. Usuras per se non esse vetitas ullo modo, quicquid vel Philosophi vel Theologi contra disputent.

Improprie vocantur nonnunquam usuræ nomine contractus justi & æqui legibus civilis Magistratus permissi compensationis census, vel pensiones annuæ. Ubi vero necessario observandum est personarum discrimen. Quidam enim extreme pauperes sunt, qui ne sortem quidem reddere possunt, quibus debetur mutuum eleemosynarum Luc. 6 35. quidam indigentes sunt, quibus summa pecuniæ opus est ad vitæ sustentationem, qua non cupiunt lucrari, sed necessitati consulere; his mutuum officiosum, ut vocant, debetur, in quo certa pecuniæ summa proximo datur ea lege ac conditione, ut constituto tempore eandem, & τὰ ἴσα reddat, unde hoc quidem repeti potest, nihil enim ultra sortem ob usum pecuniæ exigendum Lev. 25, 35. alii sunt opulenti, vel certe ita pecuniam nostram petunt, non ut necessitati consulant, sed ut eadem negotientur, lucrentur, fundos, ac prædia emant, & suas fortunas magis, magisq; augeant, cum quib9 talem inire contractum, ut quotannis pro usu pecuniæ aliquid persolvant, salva interim sortis permutatione, licitum est, dummodo usuræ illæ improprie ita dictæ moderatæ sint & charitatis Christianæ ratio non negligatur, quas JCTI compensatorias vocant, & a lucratoriis distinguunt, illas admittentes, has vero damnantes. Unde contractus ejusmodi Magistratus Christiani legibus approbarunt, quibus v. g. centum floreni pro 5. florenorum pen- fione annua elocantur (quæ quincunces reditus Per- sio etiam vocantur) ut qui illis negotiari possunt, non solum ad sortis restitutionem, sed etiam ad offi- cii nostri aliquam compensationem obligentur. Qui contractus neque lege divina prohibiti sunt, hæc e- nim usuras mordaces ac corrodentes respicit Mich. 3. vers. 2. & egenos, ac pauperes concernit, a quibus ultra sortem propter mutui officium nihil exigen- dum, & naturali æquitati congruit ex præcepto Christi Matth. 7, 12. omne quod vultis, ut faciant vo- bis homines, etiam ipsis facite, ut & regulæ caritatis 2. Cor. 8, 13. quod aliis ita benefaciendum sit, non ut ipsis sit ἄνεσις relaxatio, nobis vero θλίψις affli- ctio, sed ἐξ ἰσότητος, ut sit æqualitas. Quum enim creditor itidem potuerit interea hac pecunia sua ne- gotiari, & commoda sibi parare, æquitas ipsa, ac gra- titudo, quæ juris est naturalis, postulat, ut debitor, cui beneficio pecuniæ mutuo datæ, integrum fuit, negotiari, ac commoda sua quærere, cum creditore eo modo agat, quomodo secum in simili casu actum velit, adeoque in participationem aliquam com- modi creditorem admittat & in compensationem augmenti illius facultatum suarum, quod pecu- niæ usu parare poterat atque interim eo carere co- gitur, quotannis aliquid ipsi expendat, ne debitori tantum inde relaxatio sit, nobis vero afflictio, siqui- dem ipsi pecunia nostra caruerimus, nec eadem commoda nostra parare potuerimus, sed ut aliqua hic sit æqualitas. Quæ regula Apostoli, licèt ibi ad beneficentiam eleemosynariam applicetur, in se ta- men ac per se generalis est, & fundamentum omnium contractuum atq; officiorum, quæ ita debent fieri, ut servetur æqualitas, nec nos sentiamus damnum, & alii merum commodum. Quia igitur mutuatio gra- tuita, & alias indebita opulentis facta, illis quidem ἄνεσιν, nobis autem θλίψιν parit, dum illa nostra pe- cunia rem suam augent, & nobis interim occasio au- gendi rem nostram adimitur: quivis sane intelligit, tum æquitati naturali, tum huic Aphorismo Aposto- lico consentaneum esse, si in participationem lucri, quod ex nostra pecunia opulenti capiunt, simul ad- mitti cupiamus, adeoque census annuos ab iis postu- lemus, quo sic ipsorum περίσσευμα vel abundantia cedat εἰς τὸ ἡμῶν ὑσέρημα, in nostrum supplementum, sive ut quod superest illis suppleat id quod deest nobis, atque ita sit & fiat æqualitas, ut habet B. Meis- nerus Part. 3, Phil. Sobr. p. 165. Adde quod diviti- bus aut mercatoribus aut integris Rebuspubl. vel etiam Principibus ipsis obstricti non simus ad mu- tuum; ab his ergo, si quid ultra sortem accipitur, non est usura, quia non accipitur ab egenis, nec pro- pter solum mutuationis officium, sed propter ipso- rum commodum, ideoq; compensationis loco de i- psorum pecunia aliquid expectare possumus ob no- stram pecuniam, qua nobis interea carendum fuit. Uti non simpliciter omnis munerum acceptio prohi- betur, sed ea quæ fit super innocentem, & qua jus in- flectitur, ita nec illud quod ultra sortem accipitur, simpliciter prohibitum est, sed si Nesech est, si morde- at, affligat, & cædat egenum fratrem. Quod si a jure alienum non est ob certam pecuniæ summam mu- tuo datam agrum aliquem hypothecæ loco mancipa- re, & fructus creditori loco annui interesse, ut vo- cant, concedere, quomodo injustum erit agrum & fructus retinere, & loco interesse annui ob pecuni- am elocatam certam aliquam pensionem solvere? Quæ ut & contractus antichreseos, emtionis redituum, ac societatis, quomodo ad census annuos confir- mandos faciant, docet B. Meisn. p. 3, Ph. Sobr. Sect. 1. c. 6. p. 167. Non ergo simpliciter probari potest, quod ait Aristot. l. 1. Pol. c. 7. usuraria acquisitio est maxime contra naturam. Ratio est, quod res sterilis haud sit pecunia, vel minime apta πρὸς τὸ τοκεῖν ad pariendum (unde τόκον usuram appellarunt, h. e. par- tum quendam) quantum enim pecunia pariat sæpe, norunt qui eadem negotiantur. Rejicienda etiam Wolff. Musculi in Comm. in Ps. 15. usuras absolute re- probantis sententia, ut & Bened. Aretii in LL. CC. Lo- co CXXXI. qui simplices etiam usuras terrestres ac nauticas, non solum ex besse cum 8. floreni pro cen- tum, & semissales, cum annuatim 6. pro 10. solvun- tur, reprobat. Has species, inquit col. 741. omnes judicamus improbas jure divino, & humano damna- tas: usuram licitam unam habemus, qua negotiantur homines cum ipsa terra matre. Solet enim hæc ple- runque majori cum fœnore reddere, quæ accipit, hinc non male dicitur Germanis Erdwucher. Hac ga- visi sunt Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, aliiq́; pii: hodie ad miseros colonos retrusa est, olim Regibus & Principibus in deliciis. Qui adducit Practicam Ferrariensis lib. CLXXVIII. ut & theses olim Wittebergæ excusas, in quibus usurarii seu fœneratores dicuntur, quicunque ex pecunia mutuo data, vel minimum etiam obulum vel haustum frigidæ aquæ ex conventione ultra sortem ac- cipiunt, atq; infertur, quod recipientes ex conventione quinq́; florenos de 100. mutuo datis, & pertinaciter ad- hærentes opinioni hujusmodi de 100. licite & sine pecca- to recipi posse quinq́; ultra pœnas, quas de jure positivo incurrant, peccent, & Deum maxime offendant, & tan- quam raptores & hæretici sint censendi. Rivetus ad- ducit Joannem Ivellum Lanselottum, Andrewes Epi- scopum Vintoniensem omnem usuram improbantes. Sed census & pensiones annuæ a Theologis Orthodo- xis Wittebergensibus non damnantur. Megalan- der ipse etsi acriter contra usuras scripsit, tamen mo- deratior in ea causa posterioribus annis fuit, Tom. 6. Witteberg. statuitq́, senes, qui ad labores inepti sunt, vi- duas, orphanos, fiscos Ecclesiasticos certam pensionem pro certa pecuniæ summa recipere posse in honestam suæ & suorum sustentationem, ac consuluit, ut Magistratus constituat ἐπιείκειαν in talibus, adeoq́; pensiones an- nuas moderatas approbavit. B. Hunnii sententia huic explicationi ὁμόψηφος videri potest in 2. ad Cor. c. 8. B. Gesneri in Ps. 15. B. Balduini in Cas. Consc. l. 4. & 3. c. 4. B. Meisn. Part. 3. Phil. Sobr. c. 6. B. Hülfem. in Brev. quibus plane suffragantur alii nostrates Theologi. Vid. B. Brentius vom wucherl. Con- tract. B. Chemnit. p. 2. LL. CC. B. Jac. Andreæ in Concion. Ratisb. editis, Chųtræus & Pelargus in Comm. ad h. l. B. Herbrand. & B. Schnepfius in Con- sil. Theol. Bidenbach. Dec. 1. Consil. 4. & Decad. 6. Consil. 8. B. D. Hoë Unterricht, ob ein Christ mit gu- tem Gewissen Geldzinsen nehmen könne. B. D. Ger- hard. T. 6. LL. CC. p. 911. B. Backmeister. Disp. 9. in De- cal. th. 38. B. Paul. Tarnov. l. 1. c. 2. de Minist. Consil. Dedekenn. Vol. 1. fol. 167. E Calvinianis recedunt ab Aretii sententia pleriq; alii. Polanus in Syntagm. l. 10. c. 63. Usura compensatoria, quæ intra modum publicis legibus definitum consistit, non est interdicta & illicita propter sequentia argumenta: 1. Quia non est lucrum supra sortem exactum propter officium mutuationis, sed pretium aut æstimatio usus sortis consumtæ cum damno creditoris. Potuisset enim creditor pecunia sua aliis in rebus lucrum legiti- mum quærere & commodum aliquod percipere, quo privatus est, propterea quod alius pecunia ipsi- us sit interea usus. 2. Quia est consentanea officio humanitatis, quæ jubet sic alium juvare, ut te serves indemnem, 2. Cor. 8, 13. 3. Quia Christianorum Im- peratorum constitutionibus est permissa. 4. Quia eam communis necessitas requirit & utilitas nego- tiationum. 5. Quia compensat damnum credito- ris; quod nulla ratio prohibet. Voetius de Jure & Just. Disp. Select. T. 1. p. 400. usuras mercatorias & nauti- cas, quibus Magistratus modum posuit, licitas esse docet, non autem quasvis alias etiam mordentes a fra- tre attenuato exactas. Andr. Riv. in Ex. 20. p. 277. mu- tuationem negotiationis licitam esse operose docet. Spanhem. p. 3. Dub. Evang. 127. p. 665. in eam sententi- am adducit Calvinum & Amesium, eandemq; prolixe confirmat. Tria, inquit, p. 669. hic distinguenda cen- seo, 1. Usuram & fœnus. 2. Illos, qui pecuniam dant fœ- ori. 3. Illos qui accipiunt. 1. Usuram quod attinet, di- stinguendum arbitror inter usuram compensatoriam, & usuram expilatoriam, usuram juvantem, & usuram ro- dentem vel mordentem, usuram item simplicem & usu- ram conjunctam, hoc est, ἀνατοκισμὸν, usuram modera- tam & immoderatam. 2. Illi etiam, qui pecuniam dant fœnori, distinguendi, vel enim danistæ & fœneratores sunt ex professo, & hoc unum agunt, vel non: Vel mutu- um fœneratitium tantum dant vel gratuitum etiam quandoq;, vel se privant facultate egenis gratis aliqua erogandi, vel reservant sibi unde id præstent, & id reve- ra præstant occasione data: vel suum tantum commo- dum respiciunt, vel cum suo commodo commodum etiam illius, cui mutuo dant pecuniam: vel ejusmodi homines propria pecunia honeste negotiari possunt, & vel agrum colendo, vel mercaturam faciendo, vel alia ratione simi- li censum augere, ut habeant unde vivant, & suis hone- ste prospiciant: Vel toti publicis muneribus distinentur sive sacris, sive politicis, ut non possint ipsi pecuniam su- am cum fructu expendere, vel cæteroquin sive viribus destituuntur, sive idoneitate id præstandi. 3. Illi etiam qui fœnore accipiunt pecuniam, vel pauperes sunt, vel in re sive lauta, sive mediocri saltem: vel indigent pecunia nostra, vel non: vel in usus necessarios pecuniam mutuo accipiunt, vel in commoda & lucra sua: vel habent unde exsolvant & sortem & lucrum sine dispendio, vel non habent. His & aliis id genus circumstantiis expensis usuræ licitæ facile possunt distingui ab illicitis, permissæ a prohibitis. Usuras illas illicitas censemus, non quæ compensatoriæ sunt, sed quæ sunt expilatoriæ, quæ sunt rodentes & mordentes, & נשׁך tantum. Quibus suffra- gatur Grotius l. 2. de Jur. bell. & pac. c. 12. n. 20. Neq; Ferrariensis improbavit simpliciter usuras, imo in pract. p. 379. docuit mundum vix sustineri posse aut re- gi sine usuris. Et quamvis pleriq; Scholastici post Tho- mam 2. 2. q. 78. art. 1. Dominicus a Soto l. 6. de Just. & Jure q. 1. art. 1. ac Jesuitæ Greg. de Valentia T. 3. Disp. 5. q. 21. Lessius l. 2. de quat. virt. card. c. 20. dub. 4. ac moralistæ Azorius p. 3. Inst. Mor. l. 5. de Usur. c. 2. To- letus l. 5. instr. c. 20. usuram omnem illicitam pecca- tum mortale esse contendant, imo Lessius cum Toleto hæresin esse disputat, docere, usuram non esse peccatum, atq; id definitum esse in Concilio Viennensi, & haberi Clem. unica tit. de usuris §. ult. non tamen in hac cau- sa conscientiam concernere sibi constant Papistæ; ac recenset Toletus ipse l. c. c. 32. seqq. causas, qui- bus lucrum aliquod ultra sortem juste exigi possit, ut- pote moram solutionis, damnum emergens, lucrum ces- sans &c. quæ etiam apud Azorium, Lessium, Sotum videri possunt, de quibus B. Meisn. l. c. p. 171. Com- mendant adhæc montem pietatis a Pio II. approba- tum & in Lateranensi Concilio sub Leone X. iterum receptum Azorius, Lessius, Toletus, Valentinianus, Medina de usuris q. 10. Navarrus tr. de Usur. n. 59. qui est cumulatus æris acervus in usum pauperum, ut mutuo illis detur, sed sub pignore, & ea lege, ut si intra tempus signatum non solvatur mutuum, pignus vendatur, & de- tur monti, quod ei debetur, & ut singulis mensibus ero- getur aliqua summa ab illo, cui mutuum datur; quem montem utut non probent Sotus & Cajetanus Tom. 2. Opusc. 6. cæteri tamen ceu approbatum a Leone X, tuentur, imo refragantes pro hæreticis habent; commendant & alios montes usurarios, montem fi- dei, farinæ, gabellarum, decimarum, quos ob usuram taxavit Sotus l. 6. de Just. & Jur. qv. 1. art. 6. conten- dunt deniq;, quod ratione lucri cessantis aliquid ul- tra sortem accipere liceat, non tantum cum opulen- tis mutuamus, sed etiam cum egenis, quam sententi- am communem esse adductis multis autoribus (etiam dissentientibus) Azorius part. 3. l. 5. c. 5. docet, de quibus prolixe videatur B. Meisn. l. c. cujus ratio- nes pro censu annuo repetit, suasque facit Rivetus l. c. additis etiam ejusdem monitis, & cautionibus : 1. Cavendum est, ne quid ultra sortem exigatur ab eo, qui egenus est, & exiguam summam mutuo accipit, qua nihil prorsus lucratur sed ad suam tantum sustentatio- nem utitur, tum enim sufficit, si restituat sortem. 2. Si, qui ditiores sunt, & pecuniam mutuo accipiunt, ali- quo casu, citra suam culpam, notabile aliquod detri- mentum in re familiari patiantur, ut per incendium, ra- pinas, naufragium, aut alia ratione, ita ut nihil lucren- tur, sed etiam grandem jacturam faciant, ab iis non so- lum exigendus non est annuus reditus; sed etiam de sor- tis restitutione facienda est eis aliqua gratia, donec res eorum in meliorem statum devenerint. 3. Distin- guendum semper inter egenos & opulentos; nam cum illis minime licet pacisci de censu annuo, quia iis de- betur gratuitum mutuum, qui de pecunia nostra nullo modo negotiantur. Qui autem opulentiori- bus mutuo dant, si solius otii causa & pigritiæ hoc fa- ciant, quia ipsi negotiari, vel honestam functionem exercere nolunt, illi non possunt excusari, quia fi- nem malum & divinæ voluntati contrarium sibi proponunt. At, qui ex impotentia negotiandi, & ne- cessitatis causa, ut viduæ, pupilli, senes, literati & simi- les, qui alioqui otiosi non sunt, sed aliis muneribus addicti, ad negotiationes exercendas minus sunt i- donei, ita paciscendo minime peccant, quia cum ipsi nequeant negotiari, quicquid habent in substantia, brevi tempore absumerentur, si ex illa viverent, & suis necessitatibus subvenirent, nec eam elocarent iis, qui justis rationibus ex ea lucrari possent, unde eos in partem reditus annui vocarent. 4. Videre et- iam debet vir pius, ne quæcunq; habet ita elocet iis, qui possunt reditus annuos pendere, ut aptus postea non sit ad juvandos egenos per mutuum, vel paupe- res per eleemosynam, cum enim de eo habeat ex- pressum Dei mandatum, nõ debet illud negligi, pro- pter id, quod non absolute, sed positis quibusdam certis conditionibus est permissum. Unde queritur de officinis suorum Danisticis Longobardorum nempe (Judæis similium) in Belgio, & alibi usuras rodentes publice exercentium: ubi etiam responsiones ad Vintonienf. argumenta legi poterunt. Addit p. 285. Si probari posset, Judæis absolute prohibitam fuisse omnis superabundantiæ acceptionem, etiam respectu fratris o- pulenti, non sequeretur hoc tempore census annuos esse plane illicitos; quia in hac lege posset aliquid ceremonia- le & forense immixtum esse, quod alias nationes, extra Judæam, non obligaret. Judæi enim non poterant posses- siones suas in perpetuum alienare per venditionem; sed emtor usumfructum tantum percipiebat, usq; ad annum jubilæum, quo bonum immobile restitui debuit possessori Lev. 25, 10. 15. At si licuisset Israëlitæ usuras a fratre pro mutuo accipere, elusa fuisset vis legis illius, quia nun- quam emisset unus ab alio possessionem, sed potius cen- sum annuum accepisset sine labore, cum scivisset proximo esse restituendam possessionem certo tempore. Est alia lex de debitis septimo quoq; anno fratri remittendis, Deut. 15, 1. si autem licitum fuisset a fratre exigere in- crementum illud, dedissent operam sex annorum spatio suis exactionibus, ut præstituto tempore nihil reliquum esset, quod fratri remitterent. Hæ causæ potuerunt esse forenses, cur apud Israëlitas severius prohibita fue- rint usura, quæ tamen circa extraneos licebant; quem- admodum non licebat post septennium à fratre de- bitum exigere, licebat autem à peregrino. Ad lo- cum Luc. 6, 35. respondet pag. 276. non agit imme- diate de non speranda usura, sed de non speranda ipsa sorte, cum proximus noster, qui opus habet mutuatione in extrema necessitate constitutus, mu- tuum petit. Vult ergo Dominus, ut non solum concedatur ei quem novimus posse & velle redde- re; Sed etiam ei, quem scimus non posse, etiam si ve- lit; aut de quo juste dubitemus futurum, ut non possit. Unde constat, non esse hic præceptum universale, ut semper, & omnibus mutuo demus sine spe restitutionis; sic enim omnes contractus inter homines rescinderentur; in quibus dum mutuum datur, fit promissio reddendi certo tempore, & id stipulatur creditor. Hoc tantum vult Dominus, quamvis id fiat, & juste pro ratione circumstantia- rum, tamen id non solum à nobis deberi proximo, sed etiam, ubi nihil tale speramus, mutuo dandum esse, nempe pauperi, aut ei qui in maxima necessi- tate constitutus est, ita ut quamvis animum habeat reddendi si possit, nos id officii ei præstemus, sepo- sita hac consideratione.

Hoc ergo voluit Dominus; homines pecca- tores, ut loquitur, pecuniam mutuo daturi sedulo provident, ne mutuum dent iis, à quibus fortis pe- riculum impendet, quamvis illo officio maxime in- digeant. Christianus autem ad hoc mutui offi- cium semper debet esse promptus. Non autem inde sequitur, mutuum etiam divitibus dandum es- se sine spe restitutionis, sed in illis verbis ut OMNI PETENTI demus, universalis particula restrin- genda ad omnes petentes, quos eleemosyna juvare te- nemur, non indiscriminatim accipienda.

## 23:21
Verse 21.

BUT WHEN YOU HAVE MADE A VOW) Namely, concerning a lawful matter, and which is in your power. See also above 31:3.

Grotius perhaps wished to say in Numbers 30:3. A vow is a religious promise made to God with a spontaneous mind concerning those things which are pleasing to God. We call the promise religious, so that it may be distinguished from other promises in which there is no act of religion, whence it can be made to God alone: as is indicated here; add Psalm 50:14, Psalm 76:12, Isaiah 19:12. The Papists also

They make vows to the saints: But they cannot explain how vows can be made to the saints, if indeed they acknowledge them to be acts of latria. Some say it is so that the vows are terminated toward God, others wish them to be terminated also toward the saints themselves. But they can in no way prove this from the Scriptures, and they admit that no vows made to the saints are found therein, which Bellarmine says is because they were not yet in use at that time, by which very thing he admits that this is a new ἐθελοθρησκείαν [will-worship], concerning which nothing is held in the scriptures, and no precept or example is read. Moreover, it is a spontaneous promise: because God neither commands a coerced promise, nor finds it pleasing. And therefore vows ought to be made concerning those things which are in our power, Numbers 30:5. God does not delight in exacted services, but requires spontaneous obedience Psalm 54:8, 110:5, Jeremiah 31:33. To which pertains that of Epiphanius, heresy 61. The worship of God is not by necessity, but by will. The teachers of the Hebrews acknowledge this, whence they posit these species of vows which do not bind: such as coerced vows, vows which are made through ignorance or error, vows made through the admonition of another, all of which they say are not free. Deservedly, therefore, are Monastic vows to be reprobated, which are made by those who, by reason of age or subjection to paternal power, cannot make a vow. Finally, a vow is a promise concerning those things which are pleasing to God: and therefore it ought to be made concerning lawful matters, and not those contrary to the word of God.

There are, however, things which fall under a vow, some necessary, others indifferent. Most Papists deny that things commanded by divine mandates are the subject matter of a vow. Hesselius of Louvain, however, in his Catechism admits that there are certain vows concerning those things which are necessary for salvation, as does Jacobus Bajus in his Inst. Relig. Christ. book 3, chapter 46. Furthermore, one necessary vow is common, such as the vow made in baptism, 1 Pet. 3:21; another is personal, of the kind that was the vow of Jacob, Gen. 28:20, and of Hannah consecrating her son to God, who as a Levite had to be entirely consecrated to God, 1 Chron. 7:28. Now as to indifferent things, although they may be the subject matter of a vow, yet a part of divine worship is not to be constituted in them per se: for this would be ἐθελοθρησκεία. They do indeed pertain to the worship of God, but accidentally, in that they are vowed, and formally; for when they are vowed, they thus far take on necessity, because they must be kept for God; they are not, however, materially and per se necessary, but indifferent. Vows, therefore, are either ceremonial or moral. The former pertain to the Old Testament, where men vowed either in time of peace, or of war, Num. 21:1, or with a condition, Gen. 28:22, or absolutely, as were the vows of the Nazarites, Num. 6:2, to exercise virtues, Jer. 35:6, Lam. 4:7, or to declare gratitude, Ps. 132:2. Moral vows are made concerning those things which are owed to God even without a vow, such as vows of faith, invocation, love, and obedience, to which the pious therefore bind themselves by a vow, so that the inconstancy of the human will may be more tightly constrained by this as it were bond. He hallucinates, however, Petrus Martyr, who against Smythaeus entirely rejects vows among Christians, unless perhaps he is to be explained more kindly as referring to ceremonial vows, which pertained to the Old Testament, and to Popish or Monastic ones, made under the opinion of worship and rash, namely of perpetual chastity, voluntary poverty, and Monastic obedience, which are deservedly to be rejected: which have no mandate in the Scriptures, no example, and in more than one way are contrary to the Scriptures, in that they cast a snare upon consciences regarding indifferent things, 1 Cor. 7:35, Gal. 5:1, and rely upon impious hypotheses concerning new Evangelical counsels, concerning the perfect fulfillment of the law, and works of supererogation, concerning merits and one's own satisfactions, etc.; furthermore, they are inept and vain: For the vow of perpetual continence is rash, Matt. 19:11. The vow of poverty is ridiculous: For who would not laugh at a poverty that is in need of nothing? the vow of Monastic obedience is stupid and blind; because it makes free men the servants of men, 1 Cor. 7:23, and demands blind obedience, contrary to the Apostolic rules, 1 Thess. 5:21, Rom. 14:5, and not rarely it is concerned with ludicrous, inept, preposterous, and sometimes even impious matters.

YOU SHALL NOT DELAY TO RENDER) So that, even if the promised thing has perished, because of the delay the valuation is owed: for the best reason: For after the delay, the destruction of the thing does not free the debtor, l. Nemo §. Si post. D. de Verb. obligat. l. Si homines certi. C. de usuris & fructibus legatorum.

Rightly, therefore, did David not keep his vow concerning the extermination of the family of Nabal, 1 Sam. 25:31, 34, because it fought against the love of one's neighbor, which does not permit that the innocent be afflicted with punishments. Vows must be kept, but pious, honest, lawful ones, and those which are in our power; If public, 22. q. 4. from the Council of Toledo. It is more tolerable to reject the vows of a foolish promise than to fill the horrible measure of crimes through the keeping of useless promises. C. in malis caus. & quæst. from the same Isidore. What you have vowed incautiously, do not do. C. si aliquid. from Bede: If by chance it happens that we swear something too incautiously, which if observed would turn to a worse outcome, we should know that it must be freely changed by wholesome counsel, etc. Therefore, the Papists cannot prove from this law the vow of continence, that those who have vowed cannot with a safe conscience contract marriage, even if they feel the burnings of passion. Bellarmine, book on matrimony, ch. 21. Because that vow of perpetual continence rests neither on a command, nor a promise, nor an approved example of Holy Scripture, nor is it a matter that is within your power; indeed, by reason of all the causes, it is illicit, concerning which see B. Gerhard on Marriage, § 505 ff. Grotius himself, although he otherwise offers a sop to the Papacy in most matters, and even proves himself its advocate in his annotations to Cassander's Consultations on Religion, chapter on Monks, page 199, had to admit that it is very dangerous and prone to many evils to admit men who are ignorant of their own strengths and by no means prepared for such a sublime vow to perpetual vows (of perpetual continence), and that one must take care that nothing is vowed which is contrary to divine law, or which might at some time be impossible, so that the rights of those in whose power we are may not be injured, so that vows are not made rashly and improvidently, and finally so that it is not believed that there is perfection in such vows. He also approved with his own vote what Cyprian said concerning virgins who have professed a purpose of virginity: if they do not wish to persevere, or cannot, it is better that they marry than fall into the fire by their own delights; and what Jerome said to Demetrias: to whom it must be openly said that they should either marry, if they cannot contain themselves, or contain themselves, if they do not wish to marry. Who does not see, he says, that the same could have been granted to many monks, the situation being changed? He also approved of Augustine's opinion: that marriages contracted after a vow ought not to be dissolved; which, although related in the Corpus of Gratian's Decretals, 27, question 1, chapter 'Nuptiarum', is not valid at this time in the Papacy, whence Claud Espencæus in his work on continence, book 10, chapter 1, sweats in vain over that passage of Augustine taken from the book on the Good of Widowhood, chapters 9 and 10, concerning which he himself is forced to profess that Augustine is so clear here that it is more easily denied than solved. Which he also confessed concerning the brilliant passage of Epiphanius against heresies. Apostolic, number 61, in the passage: It is better for one who has fallen from the course to take a wife openly for himself according to the law, etc.

The Papists also err most gravely when they claim for their pontiff the power of dispensing in lawful vows, and the Roman Pontiff sins against the law in this matter when he assumes that power for himself, in which part they Judaize; for the Rabbis also teach that vows can be dissolved if he who made the vow repents of the vow, and that through a wise and authentic man, whom they call ממוחא, whence B. Luther gravely warns in his Works on Psalm 15, Vol. II, Lat. Jena, fol. 160: Let everyone beware for himself of the insipid, indeed impious and heretical decretals, Title on vows and the redemption of vows, where the Roman Pontiff, or rather some most unlearned scribe of his, dares to establish that it is in his hand to dispense and change vows and oaths, or, as some speak more mildly, to declare what are and are not vows, saying against the express text of Deut. 23 that he is not a transgressor of a vow who has delayed to fulfill the commands of the Roman Pontiff. Not a Shepherd, but a destroyer of Christ's sheep, bringing forward as a cover for his impiety, or the foundation of his opinion, that it is written in Exod. 13 and 34 that the firstborn of an ass must be slaughtered, or redeemed with a sheep, not content that that scripture sounds nothing of an oath or a vow, and then that such a change was established not by the judgment of men but by the command of God, thus having depraved the words of God to establish his own Tyranny, but also boasting with a loud mouth that he has stopped the mouths of those speaking iniquities, showing himself in this as if he were God in the Temple of God, equally powerful, as he read that God could, indeed daring to dissolve what God has commanded. If, however, only a declaration is sought, not power, then knowledge has a place here, which discerns whether it is a vow or not; therefore some pious and learned man will declare it better than the omnipotent and omnivolent Apostolic See, which is for the most part unlearned and unskilled in the Holy Scriptures.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

CUM AUTEM VOTUM VOVERIS) Nempe de re licita, & quæ tuæ sit potestatis. Vide & supra 31, 3.

Dicere forte voluit Grotius Num. 30, 3. Vo- tum est promissio religiosa Deo facta animo sponta- neo de iis, quæ Deo grata sunt. Religiosam di- cimus promissionem, ut discernatur ab aliis pro- missionibus, in quibus nullus est actus religionis, unde soli Deo fieri potest: ut hic indicatur; adde Pfal. 50, 14. Psal. 76, 12. Es. 19, 12. Pontificii etiam

Sanctis vota nuncupant: Sed explicare non pos- sunt, quomodo Sanctis vota fieri queant, siquidem actus latrias esse agnoscant. Alii dicunt ita, ut ad Deum vota terminentur, alii terminari etiam ad ipsos sanctos illa, volunt. Sed nullo modo è Scri- pturis id probare possunt, & fatentur nulla illic re- periri vota sanctis nuncupata, quod inde esse ait Bellarminus: quia tum nondum fuerint in usu, quo ipso fatetur, novam esse hanc ἐθελοθρησκείαν, de qua nihil in scripturis habetur, nullumque vel præ- ceptum vel exemplum legitur. Est autem pro- missio spontanea: quia coactam promissionem Deus neque præcipit, neque gratam habet. Ideo- que vota fieri debent de illis, quæ in nostra sunt pote- state, Num. 30, 5. Deus non delectatur exactis ser- vitiis, sed spontaneam requirit obedientiam Psal. 54, 8. 110. 5. Jer. 31, 33. Quo pertinet illud E- piphanii hæres. 61. Cultus Dei non est ex necessita- te, sed ex voluntate. Agnoscunt id Ebræorum Ma- gistri, unde ponunt has votorum species, quæ non ligant: utpote vota coacta, vota quæ per ignoran- tiam vel errorem fiunt, vota per alterius admoniti- onem facta, quæ omnia dicunt non esse libera. Me- rito itaque reprobanda vota Monastica, quæ ab il- lis fiunt, qui per ætatem aut subjectionem Patriæ po- testatis vovere non possunt. Denique votum est promissio de iis, quæ Deo grata sunt: ideoque de rebus licitis, nec verbo Dei adversis fieri debet.

Sunt autem res, quæ sub votum cadunt, aliæ necessariæ, aliæ indifferentes. Pontificii plerique res præceptas divinis mandatis materiam voti esse negant. Hesselius tamen Lovaniensis in Catech. fatetur vota quædam esse de his, quæ necessaria sunt ad salutem, ut & Jacobus Bajus Inst. Relig. Christ. l. 3. c. 46. Porro votum necessarium aliud commu- ne est, quale votum in baptismo fit, 1. Petr. 3, 21. aliud personale, cujusmodi votum erat Jacobi, Gen. 28, 20. & Hannæ filium suum Deo consecrantis, qui ut Levita omnino consecrandus erat Deo. 1. Chron. 7, 28. Jam quod ad indifferentia, etsi materia voti sint, non tamen in illis pars cultus divini per se consti- tuenda: hoc enim foret ἐθελοθρησκεία. Pertinent quidem ad cultum Dei, sed per accidens, qua voven- tur, & formaliter; nam cum voventur, hactenus in- duunt necessitatem, quia Deo servanda sunt; non a. materialiter & per se necessaria sunt, sed indifferen- tia. Vota itaque vel ceremonialia sunt, vel mo- ralia. Illa ad V. T. pertinent, ubi vovebant ho- mines vel pacis tempore, vel belli Num. 21, 1. vel cum conditione, Gen. 28, 22. vel absolute, uti erant vota Nazaræorum Num. 6, 2. ad exercendas virtu- tes. Jer. 35, 6. Thren. 4, 7. vel ad declarandam grati- tudinem Ps. 132. 2. Moralia præstantur de iis, quæ etiam sine voto Deo debentur, qualia sunt vota fi- dei, invocationis, dilectionis, obedientiæ, ad quæ ideo se pii voto obligant, ut inconstantia humanæ vo- luntatis hoc veluti vinculo arctius constringatur. Hallucinatur a. Petrus Martyr, qui adversus Smyt- thæum vota inter Christianos prorsus reprobat, nisi benignius forsan explicandus sit de votis cere- monialibus, quæ ad V. T. pertinebant, & Papisti- cis vel Monasticis, opinione cultus factis & temera- riis, castitatis nempe perpetuæ, paupertatis sponta- neæ, & obedientiæ Monasticæ, quæ merito reproban- da: quæ nullum in Scripturis mandatum, nul- lum exemplum habent, nec uno modo Scripturæ adversantur, qua laqueum conscientiis de rebus me- diis injiciunt, 1. Cor. 7, 35, Gal. 5, 1. impiisque hypo- thesibus nituntur de novis consiliis Evangelicis, de per- facta legis impletione, & operibus supererogationis, de meritis & satisfactionibus propriis &c. adhæc inepta, & vana sunt: Votum enim continentiæ perpetuæ temerarium est, Matth. 19. 11. Votum paupertatis est ridiculum: Ecquis enim non rideat paupertatem nullius rei indigam? votum obedientiæ Monasti- cæ stolidum est, & cæcum; quia liberos homines facit servos hominum 1. Cor. 7, 23. cæcumque postu- lat obsequium, contra regulas Apostolicas 1. Thess. 5, 21. Rom. 14, 5. ac non raro versatur in rebus lu- dicris, ineptis, præposteris, quandoq; etiam impiis.

NON DIFFERES REDDERE) Ita, ut etiamfi res pro- missa perierit, propter moram debeatur æstimatio: optima ra- tione: Post moram enim rei interitus debitorem non liberat l. Nemo §. Si post. D. de Verb. obligat. l. Si homines certi. C. de usuris & fructibus legatorum.

Recte ergo David votum de extinguenda fa- milia Nabalis, quia pugnabat cum charitate proxi- mi, quæ non permittit, ut innocentes pœnis affici- antur, non servavit 1. Sam. 25, 31. 34. Servanda sunt vota, sed pia, honesta, licita, & quæ in nostra pote- state; Si publicis 22. q. 4. ex Concil. Tolet. Tolerabilius est stultæ promissionis vota rejicere, quam per inutilium promissorum custodiam exhorrendam criminum im- plere mensuram. C. in malis caus. & quæst. iisdem ex Isi- doro. Quod incaute vovisti, ne facias. C. si aliquid. ex Beda: Si aliquid forte nos incautius jurare contigerit, quod observatum in pejorem vergat exitum, libere illud salubri consilio mutandum noverimus &c. Non ergo ex hac lege probare possunt votum continen- tiæ Pontificii, eos qui voverunt non posse salva con- scientia matrimonium contrahere, etsi ustiones sen- tiant. Bellarm. l. de matrim. c. 21. Quia votum illud continentiæ perpetuæ nec mandato, nec promisso, nex exemplo probato S. literarum nititur, neq; est de re, quæ tuæ sit potestatis, imo ratione causarum omnium illicitum est, quo de vid. B. Gerh. de Conjug. §. 505. seqq. Grotius ipse, etsi in plerisque Papatui palpum alias obtrudat, ejusque advocatum etiam se probet in annot. ad Consult. Cassandr. de relig. cap. de Monach. pag. 199. fateri debuit, homines suarum virium ignaros minime ad tam sublime votum præparatos admitti ad vota perpetua (perpetuæ continentiæ) valde periculosum etiam & multis malis obnoxium & cavendum esse, ne quid voveatur, quod legi divinæ contrarium sit, aut aliquando etiam possit, ne lædantur jura eorum, quorum sumus in potestate, ne temere & improvide vota fiant, deinde ne credatur in votis talibus esse perfectio. Probavit etiam calculo suo, quod de virginibus virginitatis propositum professis dixit Cyprianus, si perseverare nolunt, vel non possunt, melius est nubant, quam in ignem deliciis suis cadant: & quod Hieroym. ad Demetriad. Quibus aperte dicendum est, ut aut nubant, si se non possunt continere, aut contineant, si nolint nubere. Idem, inquit, monachis multis mutato statu concedi potuisse, quis non videt? Probavit etiam Augustini sententiam; connubia post votum contracta non debere dirimi; quod vero, etsi relatum in Corpus Gratiani Decret. 27. quæst. 1. cap. Nuptiarum, hoc tempore in Papatu non valet, unde in loco illo Augustini desumto è libr. de Bono viduit. cap. 9, 10. frustra sudat Claud. Espensæus de continentia lib. 10. cap. 1. de quo profiteri ipse cogitur, Augustinum tam hic esse clarum, ut facilius negetur, quam solvatur. Quod etiam fassus est de luculento Epiphanii contra hæres. Apostolic. num. 61. loco: Melius esse à cursu lapsum palam sibi uxorem sumere juxta legem &c.

Errant etiam gravissime Pontificii, cum in votis licitis potestatem dispensandi pontifici suo vendicant, & peccat in hac legem Pontifex Rom. cum illam potestatem sibi sumit, qua in parte judaizant; nam & Rabbini docent vota dissolvi posse, si illum qui votum fecit, voti pœniteat, idque per sapientem & authenticum virum, quem ipsi vocant ממוחא unde B. Luther. graviter monet in Oper. in Ps. 15. Tom. II. Lat. Jen. fol. 160. Quisque sibi caveat ab infulsis imo impiis & hæreticis decretalibus. Tit. de vot. & vot. redemt. Ubi Romanus Pontifex vel potius scriba ejus aliquis indoctissimus audet statuere, in manu sua esse dispensare & mutare vota & juramenta, seu, ut quidam mitius loquuntur, declarare, quæ sint, & non sint vota, dicens contra expressum textum Deut. 23. eum voti transgressorem non esse, qui mandata Romani Pontificis implere distulerit. Non Pastor, sed perditor ovium Christi, adducens in operculum impietatis suæ, seu fundamentum sententiæ suæ, quod Exod. 13. & 34. scriptum sit, asini primogenitum mactandum, seu redimendum ove, non contentus, quod ea scriptura nihil de juramento aut voto sonet, deinde quæ mutatio non hominum arbitrio, sed Dei mandato statuta sit, sic depravatis verbis Dei in suam Tyrannidem stabiliendam, verum etiam magnum crepante bucca, se os obstruxisse loquentium iniqua, cum fiducia gloriatur, ostendens se in hoc, quasi sit Deus in Templo Dei, idem potens, quod Deum potuisse legit, imo solvere audens, quæ Deus præcepit. Si vero declaratio tantum quæritur, non potestas, sed scientia hic locum habet, quæ discernat, sit votum, nec ne, ideo melius declarabit pius aliquis & eruditus vir, quam omnipotens, & omnivolens Sedes Apostolica, plerumque inerudita, in sacris literis imperita.

## 23:24
EAT GRAPES AS MUCH AS PLEASES YOU, BUT DO NOT CARRY THEM OUT WITH YOU. Lest a fruit be gathered from another's into one's own basket, in the old law, Laurentius according to Festus.

This right was not given only to grape-gatherers and reapers, as R. Solomon thought with the Chaldean Paraphrase, but it is a general law for anyone who has entered a neighbor's vineyard or field. The region of the Canaanites was most fertile, its cultivation did not cost much labor, and God so blessed the vineyards and fields that they could enjoy their fruits without significant detriment to the owners. The disciples of Christ plucked ears of grain, Matt. 12, 1. Josephus observes, book 4, Antiquities, ch. 8, that the same was also permitted regarding fruits and other produce of gardens and meadows.

But that pertained to the Jewish polity. Yet the moral part still binds us even now, that the wealthier ought to share from the produce of their vineyards and fields with others as well.

Latin:

COMEDE UVAS QVANTUM TIBI PLACUERIT, FORAS AVTEM {NE EFFERAS TECUM) Ne pomum ex alieno legatur in armum, in veteri lege Laurentium apud Festum.

Non tantum vindemiatoribus & messoribus hoc jus datum, ut cum Chald. Paraph. R. Salomo opinatus est, sed generalis lex est, de quovis proximi vineam vel segetem ingresso. Fuit Cananæo- rum regio fertilissima, cultura ejus non magno constitit labore, & benedixit Deus ita vineis atque agris, ut absque insigni possessorum detrimento eorum fructibus potuerint frui. Discipuli Chri- sti spicas evellebant Matth. 12, 1. Josephus obser- vat. l. 4. Antiq. c. 8. idem etiam in pomis & aliis hortorum ac pratorum proventibus licuisse.

Sed id pertinebat ad politiam Judaicam. Morale tamen nos etiamnum obligat, quod ditiores ex proventi- bus vinearum & agrorum aliis etiam communica- re debeant.

## 23:25 Addition
To chapter 23, verse 28, to page 598, column a, after the note.

Therefore, most understand a male prostitute or a harlot: Junius, Piscator, Bonfrerius, Menochius, B. Gerhard. Because this fits best with the preceding verse: as in verse 17 a sodomite is joined with a harlot, so in verse 18 a dog is joined with a prostitute. And male prostitutes compete with dogs in impudence and obscenity, as a harlot is a secret prostitute: so a dog is a prostitute publicly plying his trade, according to Junius. This does not please Bochart in 'Hierozoicon' book 2, 59, page 690, because legislators are not accustomed to use tropes and metaphors; but to express edicts in proper words: so that no ambiguity may underlie them. He gives this reason why GOD prohibited this, because in Egypt, from where they had recently departed, the dog was intensely worshipped. Juvenal, Satire 15: 'Whole towns worship a dog, no one Diana.' Herodotus and Diodorus, book 1, page 52, expressly affirm this. And Anubis, one of the highest gods of Egypt, had a dog's head; Diodorus, page 54. Hence Lucian's Momus in the 'Council of the Gods' calls him dog-faced; and Virgil in Aeneid book 8 and Ovid in Metamorphoses book 9 call him the barking Anubis. The dog fell from these honors after he alone of all animals dared to violate with his bite the flesh of the Apis, which had been slaughtered and cast out by Cambyses; Plutarch in 'Isis'. Which opinion, because of the reason given about laws being taken in their proper sense, now also seems to be preferred.

Latin:

Ad cap. 23. v. 28. ad pag. 598. a. post notam.

Itaque plerique canem meritorium vel mere- tricem intelligunt Junius, Piscator, Bonfrerius, Me- nochius, B. Gerhardus. Quod hoc optime conve- niat cum antecedente versu: ut versu 17. cum mere- trice cynaedus, ita v. 18. cum scorto canis conjungitur. Et certant meritorii cum canibus impudentia & ob- scoenitate, ut prostibulum est meretrix occulta: ita canis scortum publice prostans, autore Junio. Non placet id Bochardo in Hieroz. l. 2. 59. p. 690. quia legislatores tropis & metaphoris uti non solent; sed edicta verbis propriis efferre: ne ulla subsit aequivocatio. Causam autem, cur DEUS hoc prohiberet, hanc reddit, quia in Aegypto, unde nu- per excesserant, canis impense colebatur. Juvenalis Satyr. 15. Oppida tota canem venerantur, nemo Dia- nam. Expresse hoc affirmant Herodotus & Dio- dorus, lib. 1. p. 52. Et Anubis, unus ex summis Ae- gypti diis, caninum habuit caput; Diodorus, pagin. 54. Inde κυνοπρόσωπον vocat Luciani Momus in Deorum concilio; & latrator Anubis Virgil. AEn. libr. 8. & Ovid. Metamorphos. libr. 9. Ab his honoribus canis excidit, postquam Apidis a Cam- byse mactati & projecti carnes solus omnium ani- malium morsu violare ausus esset; Plutarch. in Iside. Quae sententia ob rationem datam de legi- bus proprio sensu accipiendis nunc etiam praefe- renda videtur.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV. A bill of divorce. Mercy towards poor debtors. Wages not to be denied. Concerning the judgment of the stranger and the orphan. Concerning the gleanings of the harvest and the vintage.

Ver. 1. FOR SOME UNCLEANNESS

Suppose it is something supervening, or which he finally notices, not which he had previously detected in the woman. But a transgression is not noted, as the Targum has it, but any uncleanness, whether of mind, or of body, or in moral matters, such as stubbornness, disobedience, drunkenness, etc., or in natural matters, epilepsy, mania, sterility, and whatever could stir up hatred; yet a bill of divorce was not permitted for any cause whatsoever, as the Pharisees in Christ's time wished, Matt. 19:3, although Christ did not advise concerning the causes of divorce, but rather wished the whole matter to be recalled to the norm of the primeval institution, and referred that permission only to the Mosaic Polity, and the cause of the same to their σκληροκαρδίαν [hardness of heart]. Episcopius distinguishes here in lib. III. Instit. Theolog. Question 10, between repudiation and a bill of divorce or divorce, referring the former among things permitted, but the latter, that a bill of divorce should be given into the hands of the repudiated woman, among the precepts. The very reason of σκληροκαρδίας [hardness of heart], on account of which divorce was permitted, teaches that it was a bare permission and tolerance even regarding repudiation, and not a concession, dispensation, and indulgence, as is clear from the primeval institution of marriage. For it is not to be thought, with the Arminians in their Apology, that the law of the institution did not extend itself so far as to grant divorce for no other cause than adultery, as it is now to be accepted in the N.T. For it is false that divorce was granted in the moral law otherwise than it is now granted. As for the fact that a bill of divorce was permitted here in this forensic law, for which there is no longer a place under the N.T., what does this have to do with the imperfection of the moral law, such as the law of marriage was, under the O.T.? That primeval law of marriage was certainly not abolished by that permission: nor was a contrary command sanctioned: it was only a bare permission, without true approval, or certainly a certain remedy against inordinate desertions and repudiations, so that, namely, they might not be permitted without a previous bill of divorce, adapted to the state of the people: which indeed left inviolate the primeval moral law of marriage, as its perpetual divine rule; to which also all the holy ones conformed themselves, whence there was no need for the sanction of a new law, but only for the repetition of the primordial sanction, which those who did not know are accused of hardness of heart [σκληροκαρδίας], which was done by Christ: In the beginning it was not so, Matt. 19. 8. as we noted in Arminianismi considerat. c. 15. For the Jews were a σκληροτράχηλος [stiff-necked] people, Ex. 32, 9. cap. 33, 3. and they treated their wives, against whom they had conceived hatred, with such inhumanity and cruelty that wife-murder was to be feared; therefore divorce was indeed permitted to them, but restrained and repressed by conditions concerning a bill of divorcement, which they had contracted from the contagion of Egypt in an itch for license. For God, as Augustine notes, l. 16. contr. Faust. p. 26. interposed this delay, so that in the disagreement a headlong mind might be broken and desist by the writing of a bill, and might consider what an evil it was to dismiss a wife, especially because the scribes, whose task it was to write the letters, were as it were prudent men and dissuaders of the disagreement. For the bill could not be written except by them, who through this occasion and necessity coming in a certain way into their hands might cover it with good counsel, and by acting peacefully between husband and wife might persuade them to love and concord. It seems therefore that the process of the bill of divorcement can not inconveniently be compared with the process of malicious desertion, in such a way that here marriage is not granted to the deserted party unless the process of desertion intervenes: so in divorce another marriage was not granted except by the intervention of a bill of divorcement; and as the Christian Magistrate by no means approves of malicious desertion, even if he defines its process by certain laws, so Moses did not approve of divorce, even though he gave laws to be observed in the process of writing a bill of divorce, lest, for example, if a wife were dismissed from the husband's house with bare words, any woman could go out and say that she had been divorced, and when she committed whoredom, she and the adulterer could say that she was divorced, which cause for writing a bill of divorce Maimonides in More Nebuchim l. 3. c. 49. adduces, and lest a husband should dismiss a wife by private rashness without any probable cause or κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν [for every cause], but that public authority might intervene, and that license might be restrained by it. To restrain which this prohibition also contributes, by the force of which former husbands could not take back a wife who had been dismissed, so that, for example, they might be warned by that reason not to reject wives whose help they had felt to be good and convenient, since the right of taking them back, if another has married them, is taken away from them, and no place for repentance is then left: Therefore it was called: ספר כריתות a book of cutting off, or of extermination, because it leaves no power to the man to approach the woman thereafter, as Fagius notes in h. l. What of the fact that he ought to have received back a former wife unjustly dismissed, if she had not yet married another, by the dismissed woman being taken back, concerning which Jerome in c. 2. Mal. The Prophet rebukes the Jews, and provokes them to the divorce of new wives, so that they might receive back the wives whom they had dismissed. The bill of divorce was therefore granted, not as something in itself lawful before the Lord, but as a lesser evil, which is to be noted not only against the Scholastics, Thomas, Scotus, Durandus, and other Papists, Cajetan, Abulensis in Matt. 19, Bonfrerius, Bellarmin. de Matrim. c. 17, but also against Episcopius himself, for both sides conspire in this, that by that Jewish divorce the bond of matrimony was dissolved, and that the Jews could not only with impunity, but also lawfully, dismiss their wives, as Episcopius holds, as also Bonfrerius l. c. Which, however, openly contradicts the decision of Christ Matt. 5, 32. c. 19, 9. Mark 10, 11. Luke 16, 18. that both he who dismisses a wife, except for the cause of fornication, and he who marries the dismissed woman commit adultery. For how would adultery be committed if a wife were dismissed not only with impunity in the political forum, but also lawfully in the forum of conscience, and how does adultery have a place when the bond of matrimony is dissolved? Add that this is also contrary to the primordial institution of marriage, since from it Christ demonstrates that the bond of marriage is indissoluble outside the cause of fornication, and that he who dismisses or divorces a spouse outside that cause, and he who marries the dismissed woman (because of the indissoluble bond of marriage) commits adultery, and is held an adulterer in the divine forum, even if he were not treated as an adulterer by forensic constitution, but by the intervention of a bill of divorce both the divorce and the new marriage were with impunity, in which part the reason for malicious desertion and divorce is different, because in the former the innocent party can pass to other vows without adultery, and passes lawfully without sin. Add also this, that Christ teaches that it was permitted in the Jewish polity only because of the σκληροκαρδιαν [hardness of heart] of the Jews. He does indeed call it in Mark 10. ἐντολὴν [a commandment]; but he calls only the law prescribed concerning divorce so, not indeed the giving of a divorce, and it is manifest, both from the response of the Pharisees in Mark, and from the collation of Matthew, that the word of commandment is used generally for a certain political concession, which Matthew calls a permission. Whatever, however, is permitted only because of σκληροκαρδιαν, is not done lawfully without sin, but is at least tolerated in the polity to avoid greater evils. Nor can an ἐπιταγὴ [injunction] be shown from this Mosaic law. There is only here a συγχώρησις [concession] and permission, not indeed that wives are to be dismissed, but if anyone should stubbornly resolve to dismiss a wife, for a bill of divorce to be given to him to restrain the license and petulance of husbands, and to prevent the slaughter or perpetual butchery of wives, in the power of a thick and stiff-necked people; nor is a permission of divorce handed down here, but a limitation of the dismissal of a woman, so that she might not be dismissed secretly and without a bill of divorce, both so that time might be given to the husband to change his purpose, and so that the freedom of the woman might be established, and so that the infamy and levity of husbands might be either proscribed or inhibited; indeed, not even that, from the words of Moses, is above all doubt, that the permission of divorces is contained in them, inasmuch as they can be explained in such a way that they exhibit only a prohibition, namely, that if it should happen that a wife be dismissed by her husband, it would not be intact for him to return to his right, and to marry again a woman once cast out and married to another, so that in this way the Jews might be deterred and recalled from rash divorces. For what forbids the Mosaic text from being rendered thus: when someone has taken a wife, and has cohabited with her, and it has been, as if she does not find favor in his eyes, etc. that writing a bill of divorce he has dismissed her, and so having left his house she has married another man, then the latter husband hating her, by a written bill of divorce has dismissed her, or, if that latter husband should die, (as is held in v. 1, 2, 3) her former husband, who dismissed her, will not be able to marry her again v. 4, so that the first three verses dispose of nothing, but only propose a case, and the particle וְהָיָה 'if' in the first verse is referred also to the word וְכָתַב 'and he shall write' and to the following (and if he shall have written a bill of divorce, and if he shall have given it into her hand, etc.) and the decision of the case is considered to be handed down only in the fourth verse. Which sense is confirmed by the parallel passage Jer. 3, 1. If a man shall dismiss his wife, and she departing from him shall have married another man, shall he return to her again, shall not the land be polluted and contaminated because of the woman, namely, that one returning to her former husband? This explanation standing, there will be no need to establish with others that divorce was indeed an evil, but

That God could dispense regarding the law of marriage, which He freely instituted, and thus grant to the Jesuits Bonfrerius and others that divorce is not so contrary to the law of nature that it could not have been made lawful by God dispensing and dissolving the bond of the first marriage. For Chrysostom, Homily 63 on Matthew, rightly teaches that divorce is παρὰ φύσιν, καὶ παρὰ νόμον, contrary to nature and contrary to law. Contrary to nature indeed, because one flesh is cut, but contrary to law, because when God has joined and commanded not to separate, men dare the opposite. Add that most Papists, with Thomas, admit and acknowledge that divorce was not made lawful by dispensation, but merely permitted for the sake of avoiding a greater evil, which opinion Dionysius the Carthusian teaches in this place is the more common one from Thomas in Book IV of the Sentences, and Lyranus defends the same in his annotations on this place, with Burgensis impugning it in vain, as the author of the reply, Matthaeus Döring, acknowledged. See also Innocent, Chapter 'Gaudemus' on Divorces; Lombard, Bonaventure, Richard, Paludanus in Book IV of the Sentences; Dominicus à Soto; Azorius, Book VI of Moral Institutions, chapter 13, question 3; Covarruvias, Part II on marriage, chapter 7, section 4; Franciscus Haraeus in annotations on chapter 24 of Deuteronomy.

Nor can the passage in Mal. 2:16 be opposed. For the Prophet's words are spoken either in the person of the Priests who were approving the license of divorces, or in the person of God, but by mere irony, as is gathered from the threats that follow: 'Go to, if anyone hates his wife, let him dismiss her, but he shall cover iniquity with his garment,' i.e., he shall both sin gravely and bring a grave judgment upon himself, as Frid. Spanheim teaches from a similar example in Eccl. 11:9, Dubia Evangelica 120, Part III, page 604.

Episcopius urges the formula of the bill of divorce: 'Be dismissed by me, and permitted to any other.' But that is the point in question: was that lawful? Christ certainly demonstrated from the marriage law that it was illicit. He urges the words of the text, 'and when she has gone out and married another,' but these pertain to the case, and are not approved by the Lord, nor do they teach that those wives could be released from the bond not only with impunity but also lawfully. He urges that a repudiated woman who has married another husband is prohibited from returning to the former. But if that proves anything, it proves that the bond was not dissolved by the repudiation, but by the new marriage. He urges that priests are prohibited from marrying a repudiated woman (Lev. 21:7). But from that, it can only be concluded that others could marry a repudiated woman with impunity in the political forum, not that they were immune from guilt before the tribunal of God. Finally, he urges the response of Christ in Matt. 19:9. and 5:32, and thus he concludes: just as one who marries a fornicator does not commit adultery, nor does he make the fornicator commit adultery, likewise just as one who marries a dismissed fornicator does not commit adultery, so he who formerly dismissed and repudiated his wife and married another by the concession of the Mosaic law did not sin, did not commit adultery, nor did he make the repudiated woman commit adultery: likewise, he who married a repudiated woman did not commit adultery, if the bond had been dissolved. Response: The case of a fornicator and a repudiated woman is very different; for it is beyond doubt that fornication or adultery dissolves the bond of marriage: but that it is dissolved by repudiation is now controverted and is in question; nor can the consequence be confirmed in any way from the words of Christ, but it is most openly refuted by them; for He teaches that marriage is dissolved only by fornication, therefore not by other causes, not by repudiation for any cause whatsoever; indeed, Christ testifies with a loud voice that whoever dismisses or repudiates his wife (gives her a bill of divorce), except for the cause of whoredom, and marries another, commits adultery and makes her commit adultery; likewise, he who marries a dismissed woman commits adultery. But where the bond is dissolved, there is no adultery, which only has a place among bound persons, not among those who are released. You will say that this is indeed the opinion of Christ, but not of Moses, who permitted divorce. Response: Christ is not to be opposed to Moses. For from Moses He corrects the abuse of that forensic Mosaic constitution; that Moses permitted repudiation in the Jewish forum, but because of the hardness of heart: that He did not approve it as lawful, but tolerated it in that polity to avoid a greater evil: that He did not absolve from guilt in the forum of conscience and before God, but only from punishment in the political forum: for that it was not free from guilt, the institution of marriage brought forward from Moses, the norm of marriage, as interpreted by Christ, demonstrates, because those whom God has joined, man cannot separate. Therefore, Christ did not correct Moses by His own authority, but corrected the Pharisaic corruptions of Moses and recalled them to the primordial Mosaic law of Gen. 2, and thus restrained the levity and wandering lusts of the Jews, who turned the forensic impunity given to divorces into license and violation of the mutual bed, seduced by their Teachers, who by no means allowed the religion of the sixth commandment to intervene, provided that those who dismissed their wives did so with the intervention of a bill of divorce; against which wicked gloss Christ opposed Himself and strove to keep the integrity and holiness of the sixth commandment, as well as of marriage, safe and inviolate. Whence the Lord does not oppose His words 'But I say to you' to the words of Moses speaking about divorces, but to the perverse gloss of the Teachers among the Jews, who were depraving both the words and the sense of Moses. For they were stating both conditional clauses of Moses (if anyone dismisses a wife, etc. and writes her a bill of divorce) in this way: 'Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.' But it is one thing to speak hypothetically, another categorically and imperatively. Thus the words of Moses are restrictive: 'if a man, etc., finds some indecency in her, and writes her a bill of divorce, etc.' The words of the Scribes and Pharisees are far broader and indeed indefinite: 'Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce'; as if the dismissal of a wife, made for any cause whatsoever (Matt. 19:3), would by no means interfere with the law, provided that the dismissal was observed with the formula, and the husband, by a solemn bill, ordered the woman to keep her own things to herself and to manage her own affairs, as Spanheim rightly observed in the cited place against the Anabaptists and Samosatenians, p. 608, whose error they here make their own along with Episcopius. The Arminian, then the Papists previously brought forward. Moreover, all of them insist upon the footsteps of Faustus the Manichaean, against whom Augustine disputed in book 19, chapter 26. For with him they contend that the law was corrected by Christ, and they strive to show this from this law, as is manifest from Episcopius in the place cited. But most ineptly. For this Mosaic constitution pertains to forensic laws, from the correction of which the consequence to the correction of the moral law is not valid, unless someone should also wish to conclude the abrogation of the moral law from the abrogation of the forensic law.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV. Libellus repudii. Misericordia erga debito- res pauperes. Merces non neganda. De judicio advenæ, & pupilli. De reliquiis messis, & vindemiæ.

Vers. 1. PROPTER ALIQUAM FOEDITA- TEM.

PUta supervenientem, vel quam demum anim- advertat, non quam antea in muliere deprehen- derat. Non autem transgressio notatur, ut Tar- gum habet, sed fœditas quævis, seu animi, seu corporis seu in moralibus, ut est pertinacia, inobedientia, e- briositas &c. seu in naturalibus epilepsia, mania, sterilitas, & quicquid odium poterat concitare, non tamen quacunque ex causa libellus repudii per- missus, ut Pharisæi Christi tempore volebant Matth. 19, 3. etsi Christus de causis repudii non monuerit, sed rem universam ad primævæ institu- tionis normam potius revocatam voluerit, ac per- missionem illam solum ad Politiam Mosaicam, causamque ejusdem ad σκληροκαρδίαν ipsorum re- tulerit. Distinguit hic Episcopius lib. III. Instit. Theolog. Quæst. 10. inter repudium & libellum repudii vel divortii, illud inter permissa, hoc vero, ut repudiatæ in manus daretur libellus repudii, inter præcepta referens. Permissionem nudam, & tolerantiam fuisse etiam quoad repudium, non vero concessionem, dispensationem, & indulgentiam ipsa ratio σκληροκαρδίας, ob quam permissum fuit divortium docet, ut ex institutione primæva con- jugii luculentum est. Neque enim cum Armi- nianis in Apolog. existimandum, legem institutio- nis eo se non extendisse, ut ob nullam aliam causam quam ob adulterium divortium concesserit, prouti nunc accipienda in N. T. Falsum enim est in lege morali concessum fuisse divortium, secus quam nunc conceditur. Quod hic in lege hac forensi permissus repudii libellus, cui locus non amplius sub N. T. quid hoc ad legis moralis, qualis erat lex conjugii, imperfectionem sub V. T.? Illa certe permissione sublata non fuit primæva conjugii lex: nec contrarium mandatum sancitum: nuda solum erat permissio, sine approbatione vera, vel certe re- medium quoddam adversus inordinatas desertiones & repudia, ne sc. sine prævio libello repudii per- mitterentur, statui populi accommodatum: quod vero legem moralem conjugii primævam, ceu perpetuam ejusdem divinam regulam invio- latum relinquebat; ad quam etiam sese omnes san- cti conformarunt, unde non novæ legis sanctione, solum primævæ sanctionis repetitione, quam qui non sciverunt, σκληροκαρδίας arguuntur, opus fuit, quæ à Christo facta: In principio non erat sic, Matth. 19. 8. ut in Arminianismi considerat. c. 15. monuimus. Judæi enim populus erant σκληροτράχηλος, Ex. 32, 9. cap. 33, 3. & uxores suas, adversus quas odi- dium conceperant, tanta inhumanitate & trucu- lentia tractabant, ut metuendum esset uxoricidium, ideo quidem permissum ipsis fuit divortium, sed conditionibus de libello repudii coercitum, & re- pressum, quod ex contagio Ægypti contraxerant licentiæ prurigine. Deus enim, notante August. l. 16. contr. Faust. p. 26. interposuit hanc moram, ut in dissidium animus præceps libelli conscriptione refra- ctus absisteret, & quid mali esset, uxorem dimittere, cogitaret, præsertim quia scribæ, quorum erat literas scribere, quasi viri prudentes dissidii dissuasores essent. Non enim potuit scribi libellus nisi ab ipsis, qui per hanc occasionem & necessitatem venientem quo- dammodo in manus suas bono consilio tegerent, atque inter maritum & uxorem pacifice agendo dilectionem concordiamque suaderent. Vide- tur itaque processus libelli repudii non inconve- nienter cum processu malitiosæ desertionis in tantum conferri posse, uti hic desertæ non conceditur ma- trimonium nisi interveniente processu desertionis: ita non concedebatur in repudio aliud conjugium nisi interventu libelli repudii; & uti Magistratus Christianus minime approbat malitiosam desertio- nem, etsi legibus certis processum ejus definiat, ita non approbavit Moses repudium, utut leges de- derit in processu scribendi libellum repudii obser- vandas, ne sc. si nudis verbis è domo mariti dimitte- retur uxor, quævis mulier exire posset & dicere se re- pudiatam esse, & cum scortaretur, ipsa & adulter dicerent, quod sit repudiata, quam causam scriben- di libelli repudii Maimonides in MoreNebuchim l. 3. c. 49. adducit, neve maritus privata temeritate sine ulla probabili causa vel κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν u- xorem dimitteret, sed ut publica autoritas interve- ni ret, eaque licentia illa coërceretur. Ad quam compescendam hoc etiam interdictum facit, vi cu- jus mulierem dimissam iterum repetere priores mariti non poterant, ut sc. monerentur ea ratione, ne mulieres, quarum adjutorium bonum, ac com- modum senserant, reprobarent, siquidem repeten- di jus, si alius eas duxerit, ipsis ademptum, neque pœnitendi locus tum relictus sit: Ideo dicebatur: ספר כריתות liber excidii, vel exterminii, quod nihil facultatis viro relinquat mulierem posthac adeundi, notante Fagio in h. l. Quid quod uxorem priorem injuste dimissam, si nondum alii nupserit, vir reci- pere dimissa superinducta, debuerit, quo de Hiero- nym. in c. 2. Mal. Corripit Judæos Propheta, & ad repudium novarum conjugum provocat, ut uxo- res, quas dimiserant, reciperent. Concessus ergo fuit repudii libellus, non ut aliquid per se coram Domi- no licitum, sed ut minus malum, Quod non mo- do contra Scholasticos, Thomam, Scotum, Duran- dum, aliosque Pontificios, Cajetan. Abulensem in Matth. 19. Bonfrerium, Bellarmin. de Matrim. c. 17. notandum, sed etiam contra ipsummet Episco- pium, utrique enim in eo conspirant, quod repu- dio illo Judaico solutum fuerit matrimonii vincu- lum, quodque Judæi potuerint non impune tan- tum, sed & licite uxores suas dimittere, ut habet E- piscopius, ut & Bonfrerius l. c. Quod vero deci- sioni Christi palam refragatur Matth. 5, 32. c. 19, 9. Marc. 10, 11. Luc. 16, 18. quod & qui dimittit uxo- rem, excepta fornicationis causa, & qui dimissam ducit adulterium committant. Quomodo enim adulterium committeretur, si non modo in foro politico impune, sed etiam in foro conscientiæ licita dimitteretur uxor, & quomodo vinculo matrimo- nii soluto adulterium locum habet? Adde quod id etiam primævæ institutioni conjugii adversum sit, siquidem ex ea Christus demonstret insolubile esse matrimonii vinculum extra fornicationis causam, & qui dimittit vel repudiat extra illam causam con- jugem, & qui dimissam ducit (ob indissolubile matrimonii vinculum) adulterium committere, & in foro divino adulterum haberi, utut forensi con- stitutione non tractaretur ut adulter, sed interve- niente libello repudii impune fuerit tam repudium, quam novum conjugium, qua in parte diversa est ratio malitiosæ desertionis & repudii, quia in illa citra adulterium pars innocens ad alia vota transire potest, & licite absque peccato transit. Adde & hoc, quod Christus doceat, ob σκληροκαρδιαν Ju- dæorum solum id permissum fuisse in politia Judai- ca. Vocat quidem Marc. 10. ἐντολὴν præceptum; Sed ita vocat solum legem circa repudium præscri- ptam, non vero de dando repudio, & manifestum est, tum è responso Pharisæorum apud Marcum, tum è collatione Matthæi, vocem præcepti generaliter usurpari pro politica quadam concessione, quam Matthæus vocat permissionem. Quicquid autem ob σκληροκαρδιαν solum permittitur, absque pecca- to licite non fit, sed in politia saltem toleratur ob majora vitanda mala. Nec è lege hac Mosaica monstrari potest ἐπιταγὴ. Solum hic συγχώρησις & permissio est, non quidem dimittendas esse uxo- res, sed si quis uxorem dimittere præfracte insti- tueret, dandi ei libelli repudii ad coercendam licen- tiam & petulantiam maritorum, & cavendam u- xorum cædem aut carnicinam perpetuam, penes populum crassum & duræ cervicis; nec permissio- nem divortii hic tradi, sed limitationem dimissionis mulieris, ne illa dimitteretur clam & sine libello di- vortii, tum ut marito detur tempus mutandi pro- positum, tum, ut constaret de libertate mulieris, tum infamia & levitas maritorum sive proscri- beretur, sive inhiberetur, imo ne id quidem, è ver- bis Mosis, dubitatione omni superius est, divor- tiorum permissionem illis contineri, utpote quæ ita explicari possint, ut solum prohibitionem exhibe- ant, ne sc. si contingeret uxorem dimitti à marito, illi integrum esset ad jus suum redire, & mulierem semel ejectam alterique nuptam denuo ducere, ut ita à divortiis temerariis absterrerentur, & re- vocarentur Judæi. Quid enim vetat, quo minus ita textus Mosaicus reddatur, cum ducta quis uxo- re, ei cohabitaverit, fueritque, ut si non inveniat gratiam in oculis ejus &c. ut scribens libellum re- pudii dimiserit eam, itaque egressa domo ejus alteri nupserit viro, deinde eam odio habens vir posterior per scriptum ei repudii libellum, eam dimiserit, aut, si moriatur vir ille posterior, (ut habetur v. 1. 2. 3.) non poterit maritus ejus prior, qui dimiserit, eam, rursus ducere v. 4. ut sc. versus priores tres nihil disponant, sed casum tantum proponant, & particu- la וְהָיָה Si versu primo referatur etiam ad ver- bum וְכָתַב & ad sequentia (& si scripserit libellum repudii, & si dederit in manu illius &c.) referatur, ac versu demum quarto casus decisio tradita cen- seatur. Quem sensum firmat locus parallelus Jer. 3, 1. Si dimiserit vir uxorem suam, & illa recedens ab eo nupserit alteri viro, numquid revertetur ad eam ultra, numquid non polluta & contaminata erit terra ob mulierem, sc. illam ad virum priorem rede- untem? Qua explicatione stante, non opus erit cum aliis statuere divortium fuisse quidem malum, sed
