Deum dispensare potuisse circa legem matrimonii, quam libere instituit, adeoque Jesuitis Bonfrerio, & aliis concedere, divortium non ita esse contra jus naturæ, ut id non potuerit fieri licitum Deo dispensante, & matrimonii primi vinculum solvente. Recte enim. Chrys. hom. LXIII. in Matth. docet: divortium esse παρὰ φύσιν, καὶ παρὰ νόμον prater naturam & præter legem. Prater naturam quidem, quia una caro inciditur, contra legem vero, quia cum Deus conjunxerit, ac jusserit non separare, contrarium audent homines. Adde quod plerique Pontificii cum Thoma id fateantur & agnoscant, divortium non fuisse ex dispensatione factum licitum, sed duntaxat majoris mali vitandi causa permissum, quam sententiam communiorem esse ex Thoma in IV. sententiarum docet Dionyf. Carth. in h. l. eandemque in annot. ad h. l. tuetur Lyranus, nequicquam impugnante Burgenfi, ut autor replicæ Matth. Döring agnovit. Vid. etiam Innocentius C. gaudemus de Divortiis, Lombardus, Bonaventura, Richardus, Paludanus in IV. sentent. Dominicus à Soto, Azorius l. VI. Inst. moral. c. 13. q. 3. Covarruvias part. II. de matrim. c. 7. §. 4. Francisc. Haræus in annot. ad cap. 24. Deut.

Neque opponi potest locus Mal. 2, 16. Nam Prophetæ verba vel in persona Sacerdotum dicta licentiam divortiorum probantium, vel in persona Dei, sed per ironiam meram, ut ex minis subjectis colligitur: Agedum, si quis uxorem odio habeat, dimittat eam, operiet vero iniquitatem vestimento suo, h. e. & graviter peccabit, & grave judicium sibi accerset, ut è simili exemplo Eccl. 11, 9. docet Frid. Spanh. Dub. Evangel. 120. p. III. pag. 604.

Urget Episcopius formulam libelli repudii: Esto à me dimissa, & alteri cuique permissa. At id τὸ κρινόμενον est an illa licita fuerit? Christus certe illicitam fuisse, è lege matrimoniali demonstravit. Urget verba textus, cumque egressa alterum duxerit, verum hæc ad casum pertinent, non vero à Domino approbantur, neque docent vinculo uxores illas solvi non impune tantum sed & licite potuisse. Urget, quod prohibeatur mulieri repudiatæ alteri marito nuptæ ad priorem redire. Id vero si quid probat, non per repudium solutum fuisse vinculum probat, sed per novum matrimonium. Urget quod Sacerdotibus prohibeatur repudiatam ducere Lev. 21, 7. Sed ex eo id solum concludi potest, quod alii impune in foro politico potuerint repudiatam ducere, non vero, quod immunes fuerint à culpa coram tribunali Dei. Urget denique responsum Christi Matth. 19, 9. & c. 5, 32. atque ita colligit: uti fornicariam ducens non mœchatur, nec fornicariam adulterari facit, item uti fornicariam dimissam ducens jam non mœchatur, ita qui uxorem olim dimittebat & repudiabat, aliamque ducebat ex legis Mosaïcæ concessione non peccabat, non mœchabatur, nec mœchari repudiatam faciebat: item qui repudiatam ducebat, non mœchabatur, si vinculum solutum erat. Resp. disparrima est ratio fornicariæ, & repudiatæ; fornicationem enim vel adulterium solvere vinculum matrimonii, extra dubium est: at per repudium id solvi, jam controvertitur, & in quæstione est; Nec consequentia è verbis Christi ullatenus firmari potest, sed apertissime ex iisdem refellitur; nam per solam fornicationem solvi matrimonium docet, non ergo per alias causas, non per repudium ex quacunque causa, imo sonora voce testatur Christus, qui dimiserit, vel repudiarit uxorem, (libellum repudii ei dederit) nisi ob scortationem, & aliam duxerit, eum mœchari, & facere eam mœchari, item qui dimissam duxerit, eum mœchari. Ubi autem solutum vinculum est, ibi nullum est adulterium, quod solum penes ligatas personas locum habet, non penes solutas. Dices, hanc Christi quidem esse sententiam, non autem Mo- sis: qui divortium permittebat. Respond. Christus Mosi opponendus non est. E Mose enim corri- git forensis istius Mosaicæ constitutionis abusum; Mosen permisse in foro Judaico repudium, sed ob σκληροκαρδιαν: non approbasse id ut licitum, sed tu- lisse in illa politia,ob majus evitandum malum: non absolvisse à culpa in foro conscientiæ & divino, sed solum à pœna in foro politico: nam quod culpa non vacarit, institutio conjugii è Mose adducta, norma matrimonii,interprete Christo, demonstrat, quia quos Deus conjunxit, homo separare non potest. Non ergo Mosen sua autoritate, sed corruptelas Pharisaicas è Mose correxit Christus & ad legem primordialem Mosaicam Gen. II. eos revocavit, adeoque levitatem, & libidines vagas Judæorum coërcuit, qui impunitatem forensem divortiis da- tam, vertebant in licentiam, & violationem tori mutui, à Magistris seducti, haudquaquam reli- gioni sexti præcepti intercedere, qui dimitterent uxores, modo fieret interveniente libello repudii; cui nefariæ glossæ se opposuit Christus & præcepti sexti, æque ac conjugii integritatem, ac sanctitatem salvam illibatamque præstare sategit. Unde ver- ba sua ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, non opponit Dominus verbis Mosis loquentis de divortiis, sed perversæ glossæ Magistrorum è Judæis, qui hic & verba Mosis depravabant, & sensum. Mosis enim com- ma utrumque conditionatum (si quis uxorem &c. dimiserit & libellum discessionis ei scripserit) ita efferebant: Quisquis dimiserit uxorem suam δότω ἀυτῇ ἀποστάσιον, det illi libellum discessionis. Aliud vero est hypothetice loqui, aliud categorice & impe- rative. Sic Mosis verba restrictoria sunt, si vir &c.invenerit ערות דבר ἄσχημον πρᾶγμα turpi- tudinem aliquam in ea, & scripserit ei libellum repu- dii &c. Scribarum & Pharisæorum verba ampliora longe indefinata quippe: Quisquis dimiserit u- xorem suam, det ei libellum discessionis; quasi dimis- sio uxoris, κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀιτίαν Matth.19, 3. quacun- que de causa facta, haudquaquam intercederet le- gi, modo observaretur dimissio cum formula, & maritus solenni libello res suas sibi habere, & res suas sibi agere juberet mulierem, ut recte observa- vit l. c. contra Anabaptistas & Samosatenianos Span- hemius p. 608. quorum errorem hic suum faciunt cum Episcop. Arminianus, tum Pontificii antea adducti. Omnes autem in eo Fausti Manichæi, contra quem August. l. 19, c. 26. disputavit, vesti- giis insistunt. Nam cum eo legem à Christo cor- rectam esse contendunt, idque ex hac lege osten- dere satagunt, ut ex Episcopio l. c. manifestum. Sed perquam inepte. Hæc enim constitutio Mosaica ad leges forenses pertinet, ex quarum correctione ad correctionem legis moralis non va- let consequentia, nisi etiam è legis forensis abro- gatione quis moralis abrogationem concludere velit.

On chapter 24, verse 1.

ONLY.

TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS

TANTUM.

## 24:3
Vers. 3.

AND HE SHALL HAVE GIVEN HER A BILL OF DIVORCE) In the presence of עדה, that is, no fewer than ten witnesses, which witnesses were also employed for marriage and for circumcision. However, upon the giving of the bill of divorce, the restitution of the goods which the wife had brought into the marriage, and the possession and fruits of which had been with the husband while the marriage stood, was made to the woman just as if the husband were dead. The Hebrews call those goods כרוניא, just as those which the man gives to the wife כתבה. But if the husband received the wife's goods by valuation, he shall return the valuation upon which they agreed. A man, however, could repudiate his wife: not also, as among the Romans, the wife the husband: which Salome did first against the law, as Josephus notes.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

DEDERITQVE EI LIBELLVM REPVDII) Coram עדה, id est, testibus non minus decem, quos testes etiam ad matrimonium & ad circumcisionem adhibebantur. Dato autem divortii libello, bonorum,quæ uxor in matrimonium contulerat, quorumque possessio, & fructus stante matrimo- nio penes maritum fuerat, restitutio fiebat mulieri perinde ut marito mortuo. Ea bona Hebræi vocant כרוניא, sicut quæ vir dat uxori כתבה. Quod si maritus bona uxoris æstimato accepit, reddet æstimationem de qua convenit. Vir autem uxorem repudiare poterat: non etiam ut apud Roma- nos,uxor virum: quod prima contra legem fecit Salome,no- tante Josepho.

## 24:4
Verse 4.

FOR SHE IS POLLUTED) In Hebrew, after she is polluted: that is, made unclean to her former husband through intercourse with another husband: every thing prohibited to someone is called טמאה, as in Jud. 13, 7. So also the Greeks: κατὰ τὸ μιανθῆναι ἀυτήν. Before that has been done, he is not forbidden to take her back.

AND SHE HAS BECOME ABOMINABLE BEFORE THE LORD) Better in the Hebrew: Because that is an abomination before the Lord: that is, that matter displeases God: βδέλυγμά ἐσιν ἐναντίον κυρίε LXX. It displeases, however, because it has the appearance of a wife given to another for use: and all pandering could have been covered by that veil. Someone, wondering why adulteries were not heard of among the Lacedaemonians, said that the marriages themselves were adulteries, because of the custom of lending wives.

Latin:

Verf. 4.

QVIA POLLVTA EST) Hebraice, postquam est pollu- ta: id est, immunda facta priori marito per concubitum cum altero marito: omnis res alicui prohibita dicitur טמאה, ut Jud. 13, 7. Sic & Græci: κατὰ τὸ μιανθῆναι ἀυτήν. Ante- quam id factum sit, recipere eam non vetatur.

ET ABOMINABILIS FACTA EST CORAM DO- MINO) Melius in Hebræo: Quia abominatio ista est coram Domino: id est, res ista Deo displicet: βδέλυγμά ἐσιν ἐναν- τίον κυρίε LXX. Displicet autem ideo, quia speciem habet uxoris alteri in usum datæ: omniaque lenocinia eo velo obte- gi potuissent. Quidam miranti quod apud Lacedæmonios adulteria non audirentur, dixit ipsa matrimonia adulteria es- se, ob morem commodandarum uxorum.

## 24:6
Verse 6.

YOU SHALL NOT TAKE AS A PLEDGE THE LOWER AND UPPER MILLSTONE) Μύλον ἡ ἐπιμύλιον Philo: Paulus the Jurisconsult calls it the millstone and the hand-mill in l. Cum de Lanionis. §. Idem Consultus. D. De instructo vel instrumento legato. For the same reason, it was forbidden by the Romans to seize plow-oxen or plow-implements for the sake of a pledge.

Latin:

Verf. 6.

NON ACCIPIES LOCO PIGNORIS INFERIOREM ET SVPERIOREM MOLAM) Μύλον ἡ ἐπιμύλιον Philo: Molam & catillum vocat Paulus Jurisconsultus l. Cum de Lanionis. §. Idem Consultus. D. De instructo vel instrumen- to legato. Pari ratione à Romanis vetitum pignoris causa abstrahere boves aratorios, vel instrumentum aratorium.

## 24:7
Verse 7. HE SHALL BE PUT TO DEATH.

The kidnapper who has stolen a brother and sold him, by the evidence of the fact, or having been convicted in judgment, was to be put to death, he shall die the death Exod. 21, 16. The reason is, because if he had sold him to a Gentile, he was a chattel of death, since among most nations the master had the right of life and death over slaves bought for a price. If to a Jew, he will be considered to have likewise exposed him to death, since indeed a Jew could kill a slave with a rod or a staff without the law of retaliation Exod. 21, 21. In the Vulgate it is SOLICITING, a brother. Wrongly, for the original text does not speak of solicitation to apostasy, but of the theft of a brother, to which the Chaldean and the LXX agree, as Bonfrerius admits.

Latin:

Vers. 7. INTERFICIETUR.

Plagiarius qui fratrem furatus, eumque ven- diderit evidentia facti, vel in judicio convictus, in- terficiendus erat, morte morietur Exod. 21, 16. Causa est, quia si gentili eum vendiderat, erat mor- tis mancipium, quum apud plerasque gentes Do- minus in servos, pretio emtos jus vitæ & necis ha- bebat. Si Judæo, itidem morti eum objecisse cen- sebitur, siquidem Judæus servum virga vel baculo occidere poterat sine talionis lege Exod. 21, 21. In vulgata est SOLICITANS, fratrem. Male, non enim de solicitatione ad apostasiam, sed de furto fra- tris loquitur textus originalis, cui Chald. & LXX. consentiunt, fatente Bonfrerio.

## 24:8
Verse 8.

OBSERVE DILIGENTLY, LEST YOU INCUR THE PLAGUE OF LEPROSY, BUT YOU SHALL DO WHATEVER THE PRIESTS OF THE LEVITICAL LINE SHALL TEACH YOU) Who also devoted effort to medicine.

There is no discussion here about the observation of medical precepts, nor is it established that all priests devoted effort to medicine. In the Hebrew it is, you shall observe IN THE PLAGUE, or concerning the plague of leprosy. So also the Targum, and the LXX. The Vulgate seems to have understood it as if one must beware of sins through which the plague of leprosy is incurred: but the Lord commands what things ought to be observed in the plague of leprosy, which indeed the Levites shall have taught, just as the Lord commanded them. However, He had given them no medical precepts: nor had He ordered the priests to inculcate medical precepts concerning leprosy, or bound them to the study of physicians. These things refer to the judgment of the priests concerning leprosy, and the exclusion of lepers from human society, lest anyone stubbornly oppose them, because that had been entrusted to them by divine authority. Therefore the example of Miriam is brought forward, both because she had opposed herself to Moses, and because she herself, even though she was Moses' sister, had been shut away for a full seven days by divine command. Leprosy signifies the contagion of spiritual impiety, therefore it must be diligently avoided by the judgment and ministry of the Levites, says Luther in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

OBSERVA DILIGENTER, NE INCURRAS PLA- GAM LEPRÆ, SED FACIES QVÆCVNQVE DOCVE- RINT TE SACERDOTES LEVITICI GENERIS) Qui & medicinæ dabant operam.

Non hic de observatione præceptorum medi- corum sermo, neque constat, Sacerdotes omnes me- dicinæ dedisse operam. In Ebr. est, observabitis IN PLAGA, vel circa plagam lepræ. Sic etiam Tar- gum, & LXX. Vulgatus accepisse videtur, quasi ca- vendum sit à peccatis, per quæ incurritur plaga le- præ: sed jubet Dominus, quæ observari in plaga lepræ debeant, quæ nempe docuerint Levitæ, quemadmodum eis præcepit Dominus. Nulla autem præcepta medica ipsis dederat: nec Medica præcepta circa lepram inculcare jusserat Sacerdo- tes, aut ad studium Medicorum eos adstrinxerat. Respiciunt hæc judicium Sacerdotum de lepra, & exclusionem leprosorum à Societate humana, ne illi quis proterve se opponat, quia id divina auto- ritate ipsis demandatum erat. Ideo exemplum Miriam adducitur, tum quod ipsa se Mosi oppo- fuerat, tum quod & ipsa, utut Mosis Soror, per in- tegrum septiduum reclusa fuerat ex mandato di- vino. Lepra significat contagium spiritualis im- pietatis, ideo diligenter cavenda est judicio & mini- sterio Levitarum, inquit Luther. in h. l.

## 24:11
Verse 11.

AND HE SHALL BRING FORTH TO THEE WHAT HE SHALL HAVE) What he shall have, is not in the Hebrew. The sense is, let the debtor choose what pledge he wishes to give, not the creditor.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected. Moreover, the most wise lawgiver (νομοθέτης) wished it to be provided for in this way, lest the creditor, having entered the house, should shake out all the debtor's furniture, or even offer violence to him, and harshly and unmercifully extort from him the pledge that he might please. But what is added about returning the pledge to the poor man before the setting of the sun is not to be understood, with the Hebrews, as meaning that the creditor could demand the pledge back again every morning, but God rather wished to deter the creditor from seeking and demanding the pledge from the needy daily, as if to say: either take upon yourselves again and again that useless trouble of returning and demanding the pledge, or leave the pledge to the poor without hope of restitution.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET ILLE TIBI PROFERET QVOD HABVERIT) Quod habuerit, non est in Hebræo. Sensus est, debitor eli- gat quod pignus dare velit, non creditor.

Merito Vulgata corrigitur. Cæterum cau- tum ita voluit sapientissimus νομοθέτης, ne credi- tor domum ingressus, omnem debitoris suppelle- ctilem excutiat, aut vim etiam eidem inferat, ac duriter & inclementer pignus, quod libuerit, ei extorqueat. Quod autem additur de reddendo pauperi pignore ante occasum solis, non eo accipi- endum cum Ebræis, quod quolibet mane iterum repetere potuerit creditor pignus, sed absterrere Deus potius voluit creditorem à petendo & repe- tendo ab egeno quotidie pignore, q. d. aut inu- tilem istam reddendi & repetendi pignoris molestiam in vos suscipite iterum iterumque, aut pauperibus re- linquite pignus sine spe restitutionis.

## 24:13
Verse 13.

AND THOU SHALT HAVE JUSTICE BEFORE THE LORD THY GOD) In the Hebrew: And it shall be justice to thee before the Lord thy God, that is, God will account this as a great thing.

In vain, therefore, do the Papists gather justice and merits of works from this. For by the name of justice is understood a good and just work pleasing to God, but not meritorious. Our good works please God through faith and are affected by rewards from God, but they are by no means meritorious, because in many ways they are owed and imperfect. Luke 17:10.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ET HABEAS JVSTITIAM CORAM DOMINO DEO TVO) In Hebræo: Et erit tibi justitia coram Domino Deo tuo, id est, hoc pro re magna Deus ducet.

Frustra ergo justitiam, & merita operum hinc colligunt Pontificii. Nam justitiæ nomine opus bonum & justum Deo placens intelligitur, non autem meritorium. Opera nostra bona per fidem Deo placent & præmiis à Deo afficiuntur, nequa- quam autem meritoria sunt, quia multis modis de- bita & imperfecta sunt. Luc. 17, 10.

## 24:16
Verse 16.

NOR THE SONS FOR THE FATHERS.

The parallel passage is Ezek. 18:20. Nor is it contrary to Exod. 20:15, because there the discourse is about children following the wicked footsteps of their parents, but here about those who are immune from the guilt of their parents. Furthermore, one must distinguish in this place between human and divine judgment. For here a law is prescribed to Magistrates, not to punish innocent children for their parents: the reason for divine judgment is different, before whom no one is entirely innocent, Job 14:2, Ps. 143:2. Ordinary judgments must also be distinguished from extraordinary cases; and therefore when David, by divine command, killed the sons and grandsons of Saul on account of the parent's crime, 2 Sam. 21:1, 8, 9, he acted extraordinarily.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

NEC FILII PRO PATRIBUS.

Locus parallelus est Ezech. 18, 20. Nec con- trariatur Exod. 20, 15. quia ibi sermo de filiis pa- rentum vestigia prava sectantibus, hic vero de iis qui à culpa parentum immunes sunt. Distin- guendum præterea hoc loco inter judicium huma- num & divinum. Hic enim Magistratibus lex præscribitur, ne filios innoxios pro parentibus pu- niat: divini judicii alia est ratio, coram quo nemo plane est innoxius Job. 14, 2. Ps. 143, 2. Judicia etiam ordinaria à casibus extraordinariis distinguenda; ideoque cum David jussu divino filios & nepotes Saulis ob parentis delictum occidit 2. Sam. 21, 1. 8. 9. extraordinarium fecit.

## 24:19
Verse 19.

AND HAST FORGOTTEN A SHEAF AND SHALT HAVE LEFT IT) As much you as the reapers.

But what if those things which are left behind by the owners of the fields are gathered not by the needy, but by the wicked? Augustine answers in q. 44 on Deuteronomy. One must first consider that he performs an act of mercy who leaves these things with the intention that the needy may have what is left behind. Then, when these things are commanded to the people, those who are not in need are at the same time warned not to seek them. But if they do seek them, what else are they to be judged as doing than invading the property of others, and what is more serious, the property of the poor? Both, therefore, are admonished by these precepts: both those whose fields they are, that they may mercifully leave them, and those who are not needy, that they may abstain from them; since both are stated, both by whom they are to be left, and to whom they are to be left,

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ET OBLITUS MANIPVLVm RELIQVERIS) Tam tu quam messores.

Quod si vero quæ ab agrorum Dominis di- mittuntur, non egentes, sed improbi colligant? Respondet August. q. 44. in Deut. Consideran- dum primo misericordiam facere, qui hoc animo di- mittit, ut egentes habeant quod dimittitur. Dein- de cum hæc populo præcipiuntur, simul etiam admo- nentur ii, qui non indigent, ista non quærere. Quod si vero quæsierint, quid aliud quam res alienas, & quod gravius est, pauperum invadere judicandi sunt? Utrique ergo commonentur his præceptis, & quorum agri sunt, ut misericorditer ei relinquant; & qui indigentes non sunt, ut inde se abstineant; quan- do utrumque dicitur, & à quibus dimittenda sunt, & quibus dimittenda sunt,

## 24:21
Verse 21.

YOU SHALL NOT GATHER THE REMAINING GRAPES) After the vintage, the gleaning of grapes, says Tertullian in his Apology. It is the same as the gleaning of ears of corn in the harvest. The Septuagint here, ἐκ ἐπανατρυγήσεις, as also in Leviticus 19:10. Aquila, ἐκ ἐπιφυλλίσεις. This is τρυγητῶν κατάλειμμα in the Greek of Jeremiah 49:8, 9. Improperly καλάμη in Isaiah 17:6, and καλαμᾶσθαι for ἐπανατρυγᾷν in Jeremiah 6:9.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

NON COLLIGES REMANENTES RACEMOS) Post vindemiam racematio, ait Tertullianus Apologetico. Est idem quod in messe spicilegium. LXX. hic, ἐκ ἐπανατρυγήσεις, ut & Levit. 19, 10. Aquila ἐκ ἐπιφυλλίσεις. Hoc est, τρυ- γητῶν κατάλειμμα in Græco Jerem. 49, 8. 9. Improprie καλάμη Es. 17, 6. & καλαμᾶσθαι pro ἐπανατρυγᾷν Jerem. 6, 9.

## 25:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXV.

Rules prescribed primarily for judges. And concerning the destroying of the Amalekites.

Verse 1.

THEY SHALL JUDGE) Not one: but at least three. How many there were in number in smaller towns. From this it appears that what is said immediately after, שׁפְטוּ, is of the plural number, just as both the Greeks and the Latin have understood it.

THEY SHALL GIVE THE PALM OF JUSTICE] In the Hebrew, they shall justify, which is often significant not of an effect, but of an estimation or declaration: to which is opposed that which follows, הִרְשִׁיעַ, which signifies to declare someone wicked, to treat as wicked.

Latin:

CAPUT XXV.

Regulæ Judicibus imprimis præscriptæ. Et de Amaleticis delendis.

Vers. 1.

JUDICABUNT) Non unus: sed ad tres minimum. Quot numero erant in minoribus oppidis. Hinc apparet quod mox dicitur שׁפְטוּ esse numeri δυαναγῆν, quomodo & Græ- ci & Latinus accepere.

ILLI JUSTITIÆ PALMAM DABUNT] In Hebræo ju- stificabunt, quod sæpe est non effectionis, sed æstimationis aut declarationis significativum: cui opponitur id quod sequitur הִרְשִׁיעַ, quod significat improbum aliquem declarare, tra- ctare ut improbum.

## 25:2
Verse 2.

BUT IF THEY SEE THAT HE WHO HAS SINNED IS WORTHY OF STRIPES) This, however, happens wherever another penalty or fine is not expressed in the law, and the sin is against a prohibitive commandment, not in mind or word, but in deed. Even where there is כרת, that is, ἐξολόθρευσις, a penalty reserved for God, without the mention of death being added, the judges, if the matter comes to them and a warning has preceded, purge him with stripes. Those stripes, with the addition of confession, were believed to be effective for avoiding the θεήλατον penalty. He who relapsed into the same offenses three times in more serious cases, or four times in lesser ones, was fed with barley after fasting until death.

THEY SHALL CAST DOWN] In Hebrew: הפילו. LXX. καθιεῖς αὐτόν. You shall incline him to a low pillar.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SIN AVTEM EUM QVI PECCAVIT, DIGNUM VIDERINT PLAGIS) Hoc autem fit ubicunque alia pœna aut mulcta in lege expreffa non est, peccatumque est contra præceptum vetans, non mente, aut verbo, sed facto. Etiam ubi est כרת, id est, ἐξολόθρευσις pœna Deo reservata, mortis mentione non addita, judices, si ad ipsos res devenerit, & monitio præcesserit, verberibus eum expiant. Ea verbera, accedente confessione, credebantur valere ad evitandam pœnam θεήλατον, Qui in gravioribus ter, in minoribus quater ad eadem delicta relabebatur, post inediam pascebatur hordeo ad mortem usque.

PROSTERNENT] In Hebræo: הפילו. LXX. καθιεῖς αὐτόν. Inclinabis eum ad humilem columnam.

## 25:3
THAT THEY MAY NOT EXCEED THE NUMBER OF FORTY] Μας εἰς προφυλακὴν νόμο he subtracted one. See 2 Cor. 11:24. One of the judges recited the threats of the law: another counted the stripes: the third ordered the lictor to strike.

Verse 3.

LEST YOUR BROTHER BE FOULLY TORN BEFORE YOUR EYES] ἀσχημοσήσει in Greek: for this chastisement was as it were paternal, inflicting no infamy.

Verse 3.

THAT THEY MAY NOT EXCEED THE NUMBER OF FORTY.

That they inflicted 40 stripes minus one, as is evident from Josephus, Book IV of Antiquities, ch. 8, is not undeservedly attributed by others to hypocrisy, because they thus exhibited a show of mercy, not only for the προφυλακὴν νόμο. They call this stripe מלקות or מלקות ארבעים, the punishment of 40 stripes: And they inflict them upon violators (1.) Of an interdict which threatens extermination or excision of the soul, not death of the body, e.g., he who eats fat, blood, or leavened bread at Passover, who has lain with his sister, aunt, maternal aunt, sister-in-law, or brother's wife, etc. (2.) Of an interdict which is sanctioned by the threat of θεηλάτε death, which death, according to them, is lighter than כרת or extermination. For this penalty of extermination is paid after death. But that θεήλατος one removes the guilt with life, which some also call כרת; just as Grotius also called it here, e.g., when a foreigner performs sacred rites, or is polluted, or who is clothed in priestly vestments, or who has bathed on the same day, who ministers in the temple with unwashed hands and feet, who is drunk, with bare head, or in torn garments. 3. Of an interdict of work, e.g., concerning garments: not weaving wool and linen together, of which the Hebrews count 170. Which human traditions are deservedly rejected.

The punishment was carried out by stripes, which were not inflicted with a rod, a staff, nor a whip made of ropes or a lash, according to Josephus, but with an ox-hide thong: concerning the rite of which, see Buxtorf in his preface on Abbreviations. But they always required that witnesses of the crime be present, and that a prior warning had been given, which latter, in enormous crimes such as incest and the like, which are to be abhorred as nature and conscience itself dictate, rested on no equity; indeed, it loosened the buckle for crimes and provided a passage for the wicked to sin. However, they did not always inflict so many stripes, but according to the proportion of the debt, they either reduced the number, or because they were not allowed to exceed it, they cast the guilty party into prison and beat him again after a day or two. The law ordered that the measure of the stripes be defined according to the gravity of the sin. And that the beating might take place before the face of the judge, both because vengeance belongs to the Magistrate, his careful inspection, and because it contributed to the greater confusion of the guilty party, to be stripped and beaten with scourges in the presence of an honored person.

Latin:

VT QVADRAGENARIVM NVMERVM NON EXCEDANT] Μας εἰς προφυλακὴν νόμο unam detraxit. Vide 2. Cor. 11, 24. Judicum unus minas legis recitabat: alter numerabat plagas: tertius ferire lictorem jubebat.

Vers. 3.

NE FOEDE LACERATVS ANTE OCULOS TVOS ABEAT FRATER TVVS] ἀσχημοσήσει Græce: castigatio enim hæc erat velut paterna, nullam infamiam infligens.

Vers. 3.

UT QUADRAGENARIUM NUMERUM NON EXCEDANT.

Quod XL. plagas minus una infligebant, ut è Joseph. lib. IV. Antiq. c. 8. constat, ad hypocrisin etiam non immerito ab aliis refertur, quod ita speciem misericordiæ exhibuerint, non tantum ad προφυλακὴν νόμο. Vocant eam plagam מלקות vel מלקות ארבעים Supplicium 40. plagarum: Et infligunt violatoribus (1.) Interdicti, quod exterminium sive excisionem animæ comminatur, non mortem corporis, e. g. qui adipem, sanguinem, aut in paschate fermentatum edit, qui cum sorore, amita, matertera, sororia aut fratria concubuit &c. (2.) Interdicti, quod mortis θεηλάτε comminatione sancitur, quæ mors secundum ipsos levior est quam כרת sive exterminium. Hæc enim exterminii pœna post mortem luitur. Illa vero θεήλατος cum vita reatum aufert, quam etiam nonnulli כרת vocant; uti etiam hic Grotius vocavit, v. g. quando peregrinus sacra facit, aut pollutus, aut qui est indutus sacerdotali amictu, aut qui eodem die lotus est, qui illotis manibus, pedibusque, qui ebrius, nudo capite, laceris vestibus ministrat in templo. 3. Interdicti operis, v. g. de vestibus: lana linoque non texendis, qualia CLXX. numerant Ebræi. Quæ traditiones humanæ merito reprobantur.

Fiebat pœna per plagas, quæ non ferula, non baculo, nec flagello ex funibus vel scutica, teste Josepho, sed loro bubulo inferebatur: de cujus ritu Buxtorff. in præfat. de Abbreviat. Semper autem requirebant, ut testes facinoris adsint, & præmonitio præcesserit quod posterius in enormibus flagitiis, qualis est incestus & similia, quæ natura & conscientia ipsa dictitante, abominanda sunt, æquitate nulla nitebatur, imo fibulam laxabat sceleribus & sceleratis commeatum peccandi faciebat. Non autem semper tot plagas inferebant, sed pro ratione debiti, aut minuebant numerum, aut quia excedere eum non debebant, reum in carcerem detrusum, post unum atque alterum diem iterum cædebant. Id jussit lex pro peccati mensura definiretur plagarum modus. Et ut ad facies judicis percussio fieret, tum quia ad Magistratum pertinet vindicta, accurata ejus inspectio, tum quia id faciebat ad majorem rei confusionem, coram persona honorata nudari, & flagellis cædi.

## 25:4
Verse 4.

THOU SHALT NOT MUZZLE THE OX) Thou shalt not halter. For thus Pliny and Columella speak. The same is to be observed in other living creatures that provide labor for man. Moreover, mercy will be the more ready toward men if it has also shown itself toward other living creatures. Thus also the Pythagoreans made their

gentleness toward beasts a practice of humanity and mercy, as Porphyry speaks in the second book of On Abstinence.

The Jews were accustomed to thresh with oxen, as were other nations, the Romans, Greeks, etc. See Varro, book on agriculture, ch. 5, 2; Columella, book II on agriculture, ch. 21; whom they led through the grain scattered on the threshing floor, so that they might thresh out the kernels either with their feet and hooves (Micah 4:13) or with a wagon (Isa. 25:10, 28:27; Hos. 10:11; Amos 1:3). But where some were so greedy and unmerciful that they would pull back the mouths of the oxen with a certain wooden instrument placed on their necks, so that they might not snatch certain ears of grain. Wherefore it is forbidden by law, not only on account of the oxen and other living creatures serving us, but, as Grotius rightly observed, because it is much less fitting to deny mercy to men who are laboring. Not on account of the oxen, concerning which the Apostle denies that God has primary care here (1 Cor. 9:19), yet not placing them outside all care of God (Ps. 104:28, Ps. 127:9). But FOR OUR SAKE it is written entirely, because men are primarily the care of God. Therefore, a different sense is not to be invented than that which was handed down by the Apostle, as it seems to some (1 Cor. 9:9 and 1 Tim. 5:18). The Apostle uses this precept only for the confirmation of an argument of the law: and he teaches us to conclude that if the mouth of a threshing ox is not to be muzzled, much less are the necessities of life to be denied to the ministers of the word performing their duty. Wherefore it is much less to be granted that the Apostle brings forward another literal sense, which Abulensis wishes, but Cornelius refutes, nor with Cajetan that that sentence pertains only to the preachers of the word in a literal sense, because an ox literally signifies not a preacher of the word, but a brute animal, and it is so accepted by Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, ch. 24; Ambrose on 1 Cor. 9; Augustine, book VI against Faustus, ch. 9; Theodoret, q. 31 on Deut. Compare Prov. 20:10.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NON LIGABIS OS BOVIS) Non capistrabis. Ita enim Plinius loquitur & Columella. Idem observandum in animantibus cæteris operam homini præbentibus. Eo autem erit paratior in homines misericordia, si etiam in animantes alias se prætentaverit. Sic & Pythagorici τὴν πρὸς τὰ

θηρία πραότητα, μελέτην ἐποιήσαντο τῶ φιλανθρώπῳ καὶ φι- λοικτίρμονος, ut Porphyrius loquitur de abstinentia secundo.

Bobus triturare solebant Judæi, ut & aliæ gentes Romani, Græci &c. V. Varro libr. de re rust. c. 5, 2. Columella l. II. de re rust. c. 21. quos per frumentum in area dispersum ducebant, ut vel pedibus, & unguibus Mich. 4. 13. vel plaustro gra- na excuterent Es. 25, 10. c. 28, 27. Os. 10, 11. Am. 1, 3. Ubi vero tam avari & misericordes erant nonnulli, ut boum' ora instrumento quodam li- gneo collo injecto retraherent, ne spicas quasdam carperent. Quapropter lege id prohibetur, non so- lum propter boves, & alia animantia nobis inser- vientia, sed, ut recte observavit Grotius, quod mul- to minus conveniat hominibus laborantibus mi- sericordiam negare. Non propter boves, de qui- bus Deo hic curam primariam esse negat Aposto- lus 1. Cor. 9, 19. non tamen eos extra omnem Dei curam locans Pf. 104, 28. Pf. 127, 9. Sed δι᾿ ἡμᾶς PROPTER NOS πάντως OMNINO scriptum id est, quia homines imprimis Deo curæ sunt. Non ergo sensus diversus fingendus est, qui ab A- postolo traditus sit, uti nonnullis videtur 1. Cor. 9, 9. & 1. Tim. 5, 18. Adhibet solum Apostolus hoc præceptum ad confirmationem ob argumentum legis: & concludere nos docet, si bovi trituranti os obturandum non est, multo minus verbi ministris officium suum facientibus τὰ βιωτικὰ deneganda esse. Quapropter multo minus concedendum, Apostolum alium adferre sensum literalem, quod Abulensis vult, sed refellit Cornelius, nec cum Caje- tano sententiam illam tantum ad verbi præcones pertinere, sensu literali, quia bos literaliter signifi- cat non verbi præconem, sed brutum animal, atque i ta à Tertul. l. 4. contr. Marc. c. 24. Ambrosio in 1. Cor. 9. August. l. VI. contr. Faust. c. 9. Theodor. q. 31. in Deut. accipitur. Conf. Prov. 20, 10.

## 25:4 Addition
To chapter 25, verse 4.

YOU SHALL NOT MUZZLE THE MOUTH OF THE OX,

to the end of the note on page 606, column b.

There was a double method of threshing by the work of oxen: 1. By oxen pulling a sledge over the ears of corn. 2. The herd of oxen itself was led into the threshing floor, which would shake out the grain immediately with their feet and hooves. Varro in 'On Agriculture' book 1, chapter 52, and Columella in 'On Agriculture' book 1, chapter 21, indicate both methods, though he prefers horses to oxen for this use; but there was hardly any use of horses among the Hebrews. We have both in Scripture, most certainly by the sledge in Isaiah 25:10, 28:27, 41:15, and Amos 1:3; sometimes, however, by hooves and feet in Isaiah 28:28 and Micah 4:13. And this method of threshing is said to exist even now in some region of Spain, in the Canary Islands; and also in Asia. Olearius, an eyewitness and a most trustworthy witness, asserts in his book 4 of his Muscovite and Persian journey that the same is used by the Tartars around the mouths of the Volga, as Pole observed here from various sources.

Latin:

Ad cap. 25. v. 4.

NON LIGABIS OS BOVIS,

ad finem notae p. 606. b.

Duplex modus erat triturandi boum opera, 1. Bobus plaustrum trahentibus super spicas. 2. Grex ipse boum in aream inducebatur, qui pedibus imme- diate, & ungulis frumentum excuteret. Utrum- que modum indicat Varro de re Rustica l. 1. c. 52. & Columella de re rustica lib. 1. cap. 21. qui tamen ad hunc usum bobus equos praefert; verum equorum apud Ebraeos vix ullus erat usus. Utrumque ha- bemus in Scriptura maxime quidem per plaustrum Esa. 25, 10. & 28, 27. & 41, 15. & Amos. 1, 3. interdum tamen ungulis & pedibus Esa. 28, 28. & Mich. 4, 13. Et haec triturandi ratio etiamnum in aliqua Hispa- niae regione esse fertur, in Canariae insulis; nec non in Asia. Idem a Tartaris circa Volga ostia usur- pari asserit Olearius, testis ἀυτόπτης, idemque ἀξιοπισότατος, Moscovitici & Persici itineris l. 4. ut e diversis hic observavit Polus.

## 25:5
Verse 5.

WHEN BRETHREN DWELL TOGETHER] In the same land.

WITHOUT CHILDREN] Often among other nations also the masculine is taken for the common. But among the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and other Syrians, the scarcity of common nouns makes this especially necessary. Wherefore what is in Hebrew בֵּן (ben), the Greeks translate as seed, just as זֶרַע (zera) is taken in Gen. 38:8. The Latin here [translates it as] children, the interpreter of Matthew 22:24 [as] children. But the Latin Interpreter rightly used a legal term in this place when he said 'without children.' For he is not without children who has even one son or one daughter. For this statement, 'he has children,' 'he does not have children,' is always brought forth in the plural number, just as 'pugillares' (writing tablets) and 'codicilli' (codicils), says Gaius, L. Non est, D. de verborum signific. Therefore 'without children' is worth the same as in Luke 20:28, 'childless.' Where the deceased had left a daughter, there was no need to come to this law, since a grandson from a daughter could be adopted into the grandfather's family. Indeed, even offspring adopted from elsewhere caused it so that one did not need to come to this law.

It is rightly observed that the law did not have a place where the deceased had left a daughter, contrary to what Abulensis thought against the express text of Num. 27, 15, because if daughters were alone, they entered into the inheritance of their father, but so that they would not marry outside their tribe, Num. 36. Therefore, Matt. 22, 24, it is said, if anyone shall have died, not having τέκνα, neither son nor daughter. Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, ch. 34: If any brother shall have died childless, let him be supplied by his brother, that is, let seed be substituted for him. Therefore Abulensis amended his opinion in question 49 to chapter 4. Luther. Nor indeed was seed to be raised up only for the firstborn, as the same Abulensis as well as Junius and Tremellius wish, for the little word אֶחָד denotes one, and it is not to be restricted to the firstborn alone. The name of brother, however, is to be understood not generally of the nearest kinsman, as Calvin wishes, but properly of the brother of the deceased, because יָבָם denotes a brother-in-law, whence יִבֵּם to perform the levirate, that is, to take the widow of a brother as a wife, Gen. 38, 8. And this constitution makes express mention of BROTHERS living together, and thus understood Ruth 1:11. Naomi concerning brothers german: are there still sons in my womb for me, that they may be husbands to you? The same is confirmed by the case of the woman who had seven husbands, Matthew 22:25. Therefore Beza, book on the Republic, p. 76, Junius & Tremellius in this place, and most others acknowledge that brother here is understood as strictly so called. Yet they understand not only brothers, ὁμοπάτριοι, as Jansenius does, but also uterine or ὁμομήτριοι; for these also are properly called brothers.

But that Boaz married Ruth, who was not the brother of the deceased husband, but the nearest kinsman, is because that law in the absence of a brother had to be extended to the nearest kinsman, by argument of the law, even though the kinsman was not included in the law itself by the word brother (as Episcopius thought), which is also gathered from a similar statute, Numbers 27:11. Nor was this optional for the nearest kinsman, but by argument of this law, lest the name of the deceased be blotted out from Israel, he was bound to marry the wife of the deceased kinsman, which Cornelius indeed denies, but Bonfrerius confesses in this place.

But those born of concubines or secondary wives did not have an obligation or right to the marriage, because they did not succeed to the inheritance, Genesis 21:10, ch. 35:5 (Galatians 4:30), Judges 11:2, nor does the law deal with any wife or concubine to be married, but with the primary wife: but if there were several primary wives, a free option was left to the brother as to which one he wished to marry. Compare Episcopius, loc. cit., p.

116. Therefore, regarding the law of Leviticus 18:10, you shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife, to which this constitution openly opposes itself, it must be held that this is a special case and an exception to the general rule, as Augustine observes, q. 61 in Leviticus. For this law was clearly singular and merely forensic, restricted to the Hebrew polity, for a singular end, namely the preservation of the distinction of tribes and families, so that the family from which the Messiah was to be born could be known. Whence, he being exhibited and the Hebrew polity destroyed, it no longer obtains: nor can anyone marry his sister-in-law. But all are bound by the general prohibition of Leviticus 18, and the Jews themselves have guarded against this today with anathema, as Fagius testifies. But how could that exception be made if that constitution about not marrying is of the law of nature? May one not gather from that exception with Bellarmine, book I on matrimony, ch. 27, that those matrimonial constitutions of Leviticus 18 are not of the law of nature? Response: Bellarmine establishes a dispensation with the sons of Adam so that they might be joined with their sisters, yet he did not deny that it is of the law of nature that brothers should not be joined with sisters. Therefore, Philip's distinction between the eternal honorable and that which is not such makes for this; the latter is subject to change and dispensation, the former not at all. Nor is the law of nature spoken of in the same way; sometimes it is what is immediately inscribed in nature: such as that God is to be worshipped, parents honored, and no one harmed, and that to each his own must be given; sometimes it is so called because it redounds mediately from the law of nature, a certain condition being posited, such as the law of marriage; in these there is some dispensation from God, who freely and most wisely sanctioned these things of this kind through the matrimonial law for the good of man, so that two might be one flesh, so that incests might be avoided, and the nakedness of this or that person not be uncovered: which, however, are not merely positive laws, and that this constitution of the levirate flourished before the forensic law was given to the Jews, the example of Judah in Genesis 38 teaches.

Verse same. WIFE OF THE DECEASED] Sammai and the Samaritans wrongly interpret this only of one betrothed. Both other things and Genesis 38:6 stand in the way.

SHE SHALL NOT MARRY ANOTHER] In the Hebrew: She shall not marry outside to a stranger. The Greeks well: The wife of the deceased shall not be for an outside man who does not draw near. The stranger here is opposed to the brother, as in Roman law to the son. Custom indeed produced the same for other relatives, where brothers were not available, Ruth 4:7. But this is called גאל, to act as a kinsman, not יבם, to act as a brother-in-law. Between the death and the new nuptials of the widow, three months were interposed.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QVANDO HABITAVERINT FRATRES SIMVL] In terra eadem.

ABSQVE LIBERIS] Sæpe apud alias etiam gentes ma- sculinum pro communi sumitur. Apud Hebræos autem, Chaldæos, Syrosque alios maxime id necessarium facit vocum communium penuria. Quare quod in Hebræo est בֵּן bene Græci transferunt σπέρμα, quomodo זֶרַע sumitur Gen. 38, 8. Latinus hic liberos, τέκνα Matthæi interpres 22, 24. Recte autem Latinus Interpres hoc loco verbo juris usus est, cum absque liberis dixit. Non est enim sine liberis, cui vel unus filius unave filia est. Hæc enim enunciatio, habet liberos, non habet liberos, semper plurativo numero profertur, sicut & pugillares & codicilli, ait Cajus L. Non est D. de verborum signific. Valet ergo absque liberis idem quod apud Lucam 20, 28. ἄτεκνος. Vbi filiam reliquerat mortuus, non opus erat ad hanc legem veniri, cum ex filia nepos in avi familiam adopta- ri posset. Imo etiam aliunde adoptata proles faciebat, ne ad legem hanc veniretur.

Recte observatur, legem locum non habuisse, ubi defunctus filiam reliquerit, secus atque sensit Abulensis contra expressum textum Num. 27, 15. quia filiæ si solæ erant, hæreditatem Patris sui adi- bant, sed ut extra tribum suam non nuberent Num. 36. Ideo Matth. 22, 24. dicitur, si quis mortuus fue- rit, non habens τέκνα, nec filium, nec filiam. Tertul. l. 4. contra Marc. c. 34. Si quis frater illiberis deces- serit, à fratre ipsius supparetur, h. e. substituatur illi semen. Ideo Abulensis emendavit sententiam suam quæst. 49. ad c. 4. Luth. Nec vero soli pri- mogenito semen erat excitandum, ut idem Abulen- sis nec non Jun. & Tremell. volunt, nam vocula אֶחָד unum notat, nec ad solum primogenitum restrin- genda est. Intelligendum autem fratris nomen non generaliter de cognato proximo, ut Calvinus vult, sed proprie de fratre defuncti, quia יָבָם levirum notat, unde יִבֵּם leviritare, id est, viduam fratris in uxorem accipere, Gen. 38, 8. Et constitutio hæc mentionem expressam facit FRATRVM simul habitantium, atque ita intellexit Ruth. 1, 11. Nae- mi de fratribus germanis: nunquid ultra mihi filii in utero meo, ut sint vobis in viros? idemque confir- mat casus mulieris septemviræ Matth. 22, 25. Ideo agnoscunt Beza l. de rep. p. 76. Junius & Tremel- lius in h. l. & plerique alii fratrem hic intelligi pro- prie dictum. Nec tamen fratres solum, ὁμοπά- τριoι, ut Jansenio, sed etiam uterini vel ὁμομήτριοι intelligunt; nam & hi proprie fratres dicuntur.

Quod autem Boaz Rutham duxerit, qui non frater defuncti mariti, sed proximus cognatus fuit, inde est, quod lex illa in defecsu fratris ad proximum cognatum, argumento legis, extendi debuerit, utut voce fratris cognatus in lege ipsa (uti Episco- pius putavit) comprehensus non fuerit, quod etiam ex simili statuto Num. 27, 11. colligitur. Nec li- berum id erat proximo cognato, sed argumento legis hujus, ne deleretur nomen defuncti ex Israël, te- nebatur uxorem defuncti cognati ducere, quod negat quidem Cornelius, sed fatetur Bonfrerius in h. l.

Non autem obligationem, vel jus habebant ad matrimonium nati ex concubinis vel secundariis u- xoribus, quia illi non succedebant in hæreditatem Gen. 21. 10. c. 35, 5. (Gal. 4, 30.) Jud. 11, 2. neque de quavis uxore, aut de concubina ducenda lex a- git, sed de primaria uxore: Si autem plures prima- riæ uxores erant, libera optio relinquebatur fratris, quamnam ducere vellet. Conf. Episcopius l. c. p.

116. Quod ergo ad legem Levit. 18, 10. turpitu- dinem uxoris fratris tui non revelabis, cui hæc con- stitutio aperte refragatur, tenendum, quod hic ha- beatur casus specialis, & à regula generali exceptio, ut observat August. q. 61. in Levit. Fuit enim hæc lex plane singularis, ac mere forensis, ad Ebræo- rum politiam adstricta, ob finem singularem, distin- ctionem nempe tribuum ac familiarum conser- vandam, ut cognosci possit familia, ex qua nasci- turus erat Messias. Unde illo exhibito, destructaq; politia Ebræorum, amplius ea non obtinet: nec quisquam fratriam suam ducere potest. Sed in- terdicto generali Lev. 18. adstringuntur omnes, idque ipsi Judæi anathemate hodie caverunt, teste Fagio. Sed quomodo exceptio ista fieri potuit. si legis naturæ est constitutio illa de non ducenda? Annon ex illa exceptione colligere liceat cum Bel- larm. l. I. de matrim. c. 27. constitutiones illas ma- trimoniales Lev. 18. non esse legis naturæ? Resp. statuit Bellarm. dispensationem cum filiis Adæ ut sororibus jungerentur, nec tamen negavit legis naturæ esse, ne jungantur fratres sororibus. Facit ergo huc distinctio Philippi inter honestum æter- num & illud, quod non tale; Hoc mutationi & di- spensationi obnoxium, illud haudquaquam. Nec eodem modo lex naturæ dicitur; interdum quod naturæ immediate insculptum est: utpote quod Deus colendus, parentes honorandi, & nemo læden- dus, unicuique suum tribuendum sit; interdum ita dicitur, quod mediate è naturæ lege redundat, cer- ta posita conditione, qualis est lex matrimonii; in hisce aliqua dispensatio à Deo, qui hæc ejusmodi per legem matrimonialem libere at sapientissime sancivit in bonum hominis, ut duo essent in carne una, ut vitentur incestus, non detegatur hujus vel illius turpitudo: quæ tamen non sunt mere positivæ le- ges, & viguisse hanc leviratus constitutionem ante legem forensem, Judæis latam, exemplum Judæ Gen. 38. docet.

Vers. eod. VXOR DEFVNCTI] Male Sammai & Sama- ritani hoc de desponsata tantum interpretantur. Obstant tum alia tum Genes. 38, 6.

NON NVBET ALTERI] In Hebræo: Non nubet foras extraneo. Bene Græci: ὐκ ἔσαι ἡ γυνὴ τῦ τεθνηκότος ἔξω ἀνδρὶ μὴ ἐγγίζοντι. Extraneus hic fratri opponitur, ut in Romano jure filio. Mos vero idem produxit ad alios propinquos, ubi fratres non extabant, Ruth. 4, 7. Sed hoc גאל dicitur ἀγχισέυειν, non יבם ἐπιγαμβρέυειν. Inter mortem & novas nuptias viduæ tres menses interponebantur.

## 25:6
AND THE FIRSTBORN SON FROM HER) The Samaritan also rightly added this masculine word here.

HE SHALL CALL BY HIS NAME] Not by the proper name of the deceased, but he shall call him the son and heir of the deceased. Thus the one born from Ruth was not called Mahalon, but Obed the son of Mahalon. The name draws the inheritance with it: and therefore it is also put for inheritance, Numbers 27:4.

THAT THE NAME MAY NOT BE BLOTTED OUT FROM ISRAEL] This is what Demosthenes says to Macartatus: ἵνα μὴ ἐξερημωθῇ ὁ οἶκος. Otherwise, as Josephus speaks of the deceased, he will be ἀνώνυμος (nameless).

Latin:

ET PRIMOGENITUM EX EA FILIVM) Vocem hanc masculinam recte hic addidit etiam Samaritanus.

NOMINE ILLIUS APPELLABIT] Non nomine proprio defuncti, sed vocabit eum defuncti filium & hæredem. Sic natus ex Rutha non dicebatur Mahalon, sed Obed filius Mahalon. Nomen secum trahit hæreditatem: ideoque & pro hæreditate ponitur Num. 27, 4.

VT NON DELEATVR NOMEN EX ISRAEL] Hoc est, quod Demosthenes ait ad Macartatum: ἵνα μὴ ἐξερημωθῇ ὁ οἶκος. Alioqui, ut Josephus de defuncto loquitur, ἀνώνυμος ἔσαι.

## 25:9
Ver. 9.

BEFORE THE ELDERS] Before three judges. One orders the shoe to be removed, the other two proclaim, so shall it be done to the man, etc. The shoe is a sign of obligation: the removal of the shoe is a sign of liberation.

This contributed to the infamy of him who refused to marry the widow of his deceased brother; for which reason the law ordained these three things: 1. The woman took the shoe from his foot. For servants walked barefoot. Therefore, such a man was judged unworthy to wear a shoe and to associate among free men, as if to say: you are worthy of your brother, that you yourself should also be naked of feet, that is, without a family and subjects, as B. Luth. says. Since he abdicated the inheritance and family of his brother just as he did the widow of the same. The shoe was a sign of possession, but its removal was a sign of alienated and lost possession. (2. His name was called the house of the unshod in Israel, because he was publicly and solemnly despoiled of his shoe. (2.) The woman spat in his face, as the Chaldean and the LXX rendered it, or, as R. Solomon says, before him, on the ground, which was a sign of extreme contempt, Num. 12, 14. Matt. 24, 6. 7. c. 27, 30. But as for Ruth 4, 7. that the shoe was not removed by Ruth herself from the kinsman, nor did she spit in his face, it seems to have happened because she was not present, and had just causes for her absence, as in rites not pertaining to the substance of the matter, there has sometimes been variation. The removal of the shoe was indeed performed, and he was held to be an unshod man in Israel, even if it was not done by that woman.

WHO DOES NOT BUILD UP THE HOUSE OF HIS BROTHER] בנה whence בן, here it is to fill with offspring. See above Exod. 1, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

CORAM SENIORIBVS] Coram judicibus tribus. Vnus jubet calceamentum solvi, duo alii acclamant, sic fiet homini, &c. Calceamentum signum obligationis: excalceatio liberationis.

Faciebat hoc ad infamiam ejus, qui nolebat defuncti fratris viduam ducere; cujus ergo tria hæc sancivit lex: 1. Mulier tollebat calceamentum de pede ejus. Servi enim incedebant nudipedes. Talis ergo indignus judicatus, qui gestet calceum, & inter ingenuos versetur, q. d. fratrue dignus es, ut & ipse nudus sis pedibus, h. e. sine familia & subditis, ut B. Luth. Siquidem fratris hæreditate ac familia æque, uti vidua ejusdem, se abdicavit. Calceus possessionis signum erat, detractio vero alienatæ & amissæ possessionis. (2. Vocabatur nomen ejus domus discalceati in Israël, eo quod publice & solemniter spoliatus sit calceo. (2.) Vidua expuebat ei in faciem, ut Chald. & LXX. reddidere, vel, ut R. Salomo, coram eo, in terram, quod signum fuit extremi contemtus Num. 12, 14. Matth. 24, 6. 7. c. 27, 30. Quod vero Ruth. 4, 7. à Rutha ipsa calceus propinquo non fuerit detractus, nec ea in faciem ipsi expuerit, inde factum videtur, quod ipsa præsens non fuerit, justasque absentiæ causas habuerit, ut in ritibus ad substantiam rei non facientibus quandoque variatum sit. Fiebat utique discalceatio, & habebatur in Israële discalceatus, etsi à muliere illa non fieret.

QVI NON ÆDIFICAT DOMUM FRATRIS SVI] בנה unde בן hic est prole implere. Vide supra Exod. 1, 21.

## 25:11
Ver. 11.

AND SHALL TAKE HOLD OF HIS PRIVY PARTS] Of the adversary. Thus the Hebrews rightly: for it is the custom of wrestlers to twist the genitals. You will find that in the second life of the Emperor Claudius.

YOU SHALL CUT OFF HIS HAND] Not the woman's. But the sense is: it will be lawful for her to save her husband and to do this, and more, namely even to cut off the hand of the adversary: that is, let her attempt anything so that she may both rescue her husband from danger and, if it can be done, leave the life of the attacker. 'You shall cut off' is placed here impersonally, as often elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET APPREHENDERIT VERENDA EJVS] Adversarii. Ita Hebræi recte: nam contorquere genitalia mos luctantibus. Invenies id in vita Imperatoris Claudii secunda.

ABSCINDES MANVM ILLIVS] Non fœminæ. Sed sensus est: licebit illi ad maritum servandum & hoc facere, & amplius, nempe vel manum præscindere adversario: id est, quidvis tentet ut & maritum eximat periculo & aggessori, si modo id fieri potest, vitam relinquat. Abscindes positum hic impersonaliter, ut sæpe alibi.

## 25:12
AND YOU SHALL NOT BE MOVED BY ANY PITY TOWARD HER] 'Toward her' is not in the Hebrew. But 'Your eye shall not spare': that is, there is no reason why such a woman should be anxious about the safety of the attacker's limbs; she shall bear this care for her husband's safety with impunity.

The sense of the law is clearly perverted. For in the Hebrew there is a feminine suffix, "you shall cut off her (the woman's) hand," and the words, "your eye shall not spare," pertain to the judge, who is commanded to cut off the hand and not to spare the woman, for the reason that she laid hold of the man's private parts. All Christian interpreters follow this sense, as it is most evident in the text. Grotius did not examine the Hebrew text, and therefore, as often elsewhere, he allowed himself to be misled by the Jews, whose corruption in this law Episcopius noted in l. III. instit. Theol. c. 12, n. 16, as being so putrid that it is tiresome to recount anything of it: the penalty is dictated to the woman, it is not prescribed to her how she is to assist the man in a fight. The judge is informed by this law concerning the penal cutting off of the hand; the seizing of the private parts is not permitted to the woman. Therefore it is added, that your eye may not spare, so that the gravity of the crime may be expressed and the judge be constrained to the execution. Whence the opinion of R. Solomon has no place, as if this amputation of the hand could be redeemed by a pecuniary fine. Therefore other Hebrews note some law of retaliation in this χειροκοπίᾳ, because the woman has injured the body member of another with her hand, it is just that the hand should pay again, and she be mutilated in some body member in return. Since that matter is not only shameful, but the generative power can also easily be corrupted by that seizing, or the antagonist be rendered so feeble and weak that he is precipitated into danger of life, and thus the woman so contributes to the brawl and the slaughter, there was need of so grave a punishment. Some, however, of the Hebrews warn that if she could not free her husband from the slaughter in any other way, she was absolved from this ordinary punishment. Which does not seem alien to equity.

Latin:

NEC FLECTERIS SVPER EAM VLLA MISERICORDIA) Super eam non est in Hebræo. Sed Non parcet oculus tuus: id est, non est, quod talis fœmina de incolumitate membrorum aggressoris sit solicita, impune feret hanc pro mariti salute curam.

Pervertitur plane sensus legis. Nam in Ebræo habetur fœminium suffixum, abscindes manum illius (fœminæ) & verba, non parcet oculus tuus, ad judicem pertinent, qui manum abscindere jubetur, & non parcere mulieri, eo quod viri verenda apprehenderit. Quem sensum, utpote in textu luculentissimum, omnes sequuntur interpp. Christiani. Grotius Ebræum textum non inspexit, ideoque, ut sæpe alias seduci à Judæis se passus est, quorum corruptelam in hac lege notavit Epifcopius l. III. instit. Theol. c. 12, n. 16. tam putidam, ut pigeat quicquam de ea recensere: pœna dictatur mulieri, non præscribitur ei quomodo fuccurrere viro in pugna debeat. Judex hac lege de pœnali manus abscissione informatur, mulieri non conceditur pudendorum apprehensio. Ideo additur, ne par- cat oculus tuus, ut gravitas facinoris exprimatur & judex ad exequutionem adstringatur. Unde lo- cum non habet R. Salomonis opinio, quasi hæc ma- nus amputatio mulcta pecuniaria redimi potuerit. Ideo alii Ebræi aliquam talionis legem in hac χειροκοπίᾳ notant, quia mulier alteri corporis membrum manu læserit, æquum, ut manus iterum luat, & aliquo corporis membro ipsarursus muti- letur. Quum res illa non tantum pudenda sit, sed facile etiam vis generativa corrumpi ea apprehen- sione possit, aut antagonista ita imbellis, & debi- lis reddi, ut in periculum vitæ præcipitetur, adeo- que ita cooperetur mulier rixæ, ac cædi, tam gravi pœna opus erat. Nonnulli tamen ex Ebræis mo- nent, Si alio modo maritum à cæde liberare non potue- rit, ab hac pœna ordinaria ipsam absolutam fuisse. Quod ab æquitate alienum non videtur.

## 25:13
Verse 13.

YOU SHALL NOT HAVE IN YOUR BAG DIVERSE WEIGHTS, A GREATER AND A SMALLER.

This is to be observed against some Papists, who do not fear to defend such frauds in contracts. Toletus in Instruct. Sacerdot. on the seven sins, ch. 49, p. 744: 'There is someone who cannot sell wine at a just price, either because of the iniquity of the judge, or because of the malice of the buyers, who agree among themselves that few may buy to lower the price, or for another reasonable cause; then he can diminish the measure, or mix in a little water, and sell for a pure and complete measure, to exact a just price, provided he does not tell a lie. But if he does tell a lie, it will not be pernicious, nor mortal, nor obliging to restitution.' For Moses says, v. 16, 'The Lord your God abominates him who does these things, and detests all injustice.'

Mention is made specifically of the Ephah, because it was a most celebrated and frequent measure, and as it were the mode and exemplar of other measures, as Arias warns in his book on the Sato, but the remaining measures of either dry or liquid things are understood similarly. The Hebrews say that he who uses unjust measures and weights is the cause of five crimes and evils. First, he pollutes the land; second, he violates or profanes the name of God; third, he causes the majesty, glory, and presence of the divinity to recede; fourth, he causes Israel to fall by the sword; fifth, he causes them to be cast into exile from their land. In Canon Law, C. ut mensuræ & pondera justa fiant, Extra. de Emtion. & Vend., from the Council of Mainz, it is defined: 'If anyone shall have presumed to change just measures and just weights for the sake of gain, let him do penance for thirty days on bread and water.' In Civil Law, l. Hodie 32. §. 2. de lege Cornelia de falso. If a seller or buyer has corrupted the publicly approved measures of wine, grain, or any thing whatsoever, or has committed fraud with evil intent, he is condemned for double the value of that thing; and by the decree of the Divine Hadrian it was ordered that those who had falsified weights or measures be relegated to an island.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

NON HABEBIS IN SACCULO TUO DIVERSA PONDERA, MAJUS ET MI- NUS.

Observandum id contra Pontificios nonnul- los, qui fraudes ejusmodi in contractibus defen- dere non verentur. Toletus in instruct. Sacerdot. de sept. peccat. c. 49. p. 744. Est aliquis qui ju- sto pretio non potest vendere vinum, vel propter ini- quitatem judicis, vel propter emptorum malitiam, qui conveniunt inter se, ut pauci emant ad redden- dum pretium, vel propter aliam causam rationabi- lem, tunc iste potest minuere mensuram, aut parum aquæ miscere, & vendere pro pura ac completa men- sura, justum exigere pretium, dummodo non dicat mendacium. Quod si dicat, non erit perniciosum, nec mortale, nec obligans ad restitutionem. Abomi- natur enim, inquit Moses v. 16. Dominus Deus tuus eum, qui facit hæc, & aversatur omnem injustitiam.

Fit in specie Ephæ diversæ mentio, quia mensura erat maxime celebris & frequens, & cæterarum mensurarum veluti modus & exemplar, monente Aria l. de Sato, sed intelliguntur similiter reliquæ mensuræ seu aridorum seu liquidorum. Ebræi eum, qui injustis utitur mensuris & ponderibus, quinque scelerum & malorum causam esse dicunt. Primo polluit terram, secundo violat sive prophanat no- men Dei. Tertio facit recedere majestatem, glo- riam & præsentiam divinitatis. Quarto in gladium cadere facit Israël. Quinto efficit, ut in exilium ejiciatur ex terra ipsorum. In Jure Canonico C. ut mensuræ & pondera justa fiant Extra. de Emtion. & Vend. ex Concil. Mogunt. definitur; Si quis ju- stas mensuras & justa pondera causa lucri mutare presumpserit, triginta dies in pane & aqua pœniteat. In Civili Jure l. Hodie 32. §. 2. de lege Cornelia de falso. Si venditor mensuras publice probatas vini, frumenti, vel cujuslibet rei, aut emptor corruperit, dolove malo fraudem fecerit, quanti ea res est ejus dupli condemnatur; decretoque Divi Hadriani præceptum est, in Insulam eos relegari, qui ponde- ra aut mensuras falsassent.

## 25:18
Verse 18.

HOW HE MET YOU) Jarchi says the Hebrew word קָרְךָ is obscene; he wants it to be understood as 'he had carnal knowledge of you,' that is, of some of the Hebrews.

THE LAST OF YOUR ARMY WHO were weary and sitting down, he struck) Here also the Hebrew word יְזַנֵּב is taken by Bachai and others in a different sense, namely, they wish it to mean those cut off from the Israelites. But the Greek and Latin versions are supported by the passage in Joshua 10:19, where the word is the same. And the same expression is used among other nations as often as they say the rear guard was struck.

AND DID NOT FEAR GOD) By mocking the law of circumcision, as the Hebrews wish. The word קיר has nothing obscene in it; it means to come to meet; the word זנב, however, metaphorically denotes that the rear guard of an army has been struck. ALL THE WEAK BEHIND YOU is added. Chaldee: How did he kill in you all those who were following more slowly? Those are understood who, because of bodily languor or Levitical uncleanness, were bringing up the rear, to which also the unwarlike group of women and children belongs. This serves to exaggerate the guilt of the Amalekites, who did not hesitate, beyond all merit, to attack from the rear and by ambush those who, having been afflicted more than enough in Egypt by God, had been manifested as His people by notable miracles, and who cruelly killed the weary, who were unwarlike. Although God justly proposed this on account of the preceding murmurings and other sins of the Israelites, to shake off security and excite confidence, yet that deed of the Amalekites was unjust, and therefore God commanded that they be destroyed, as those of whom He knew no hope of conversion remained. But cruelty is abominable to God: to add affliction to the afflicted, to attack the innocent in war, to kill an unwarlike crowd from ambush. We add an elegant allegory of the ordinary gloss from Rabanus: The Amalekites are the demons who oppose us as we go out from spiritual Egypt through Baptism, and who strive to kill those who are weary in the final virtues and on the journey of this life by suggesting sin. When the Lord has given the opportunity, we must utterly overthrow them, and utterly cast out and destroy their suggestions, lest if we save any remnants, as Saul did, we ourselves be overthrown as disobedient along with them.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

QVOMODO OCCURRERIT TIBI) Vocem Hebræ- am קָרְךָ obscœnam esse ait Jarchi, vult intelligi perciderit te id est, aliquos Hebræorum.

EXTREMOS AGMINIS TUI QUI LASSI RESIDE- BANT CECIDERIT) Hic quoque vox Hebræa יְזַנֵּב Bachai aliisque in alium sensum sumitur, nempe penes ab- cissos Israëlitis volunt. Sed pro versione Græca & Latin facit locus Josue 10, 19. ubi verbum idem. Et locutio ea- dem apud gentes alias quoties extremum agmen cæsum dicunt.

ET NON TIMUERIT DEUM) Irridendo legem cir- cumcisionis, ut Hebræi volunt. Verbum קיר nihil obscœni habet, est ob- viam venire; vox a. זנב decaudavit metaphorice notat extremum exercitus agmen percussum esse. Ad- ditur OMNES DEBILES POST TE. Chald. Quomodo occiderit in te omnes eos, qui tardius se- quebantur? Intelliguntur illi, qui ob corporis languorem vel immunditiem Leviticam agmen claudebant, ad quod etiam grex imbellis mulie- rum, & parvulorum pertinet. Facit id ad exagge- randam culpam Amalekitarum, qui non dubita- runt illos, præter omne meritum, à tergo & insidiis aggredi, qui in Ægypto plus satis afflicti à Deo, ceu populus ejus insignibus prodigiis manifestati e- rant, ac lassos, qui imbelles, crudeliter interficie- bant. Quod etsi Deus juste ob antegressas mur- murationes, & alia peccata Israëllitarum proposuit, ad excutiendam securitatem, & excitandam fidu- ciam, injustum tamen fuit illud Amalekitarum fa- ctum, ideoque præcepit Deus, eosdem deleri, ut- pote de quibus nullam spem restare conversionis noverat. Abominabilis autem Deo est crudeli- tas, afflictis afflictionem addere, innoxios bello aggredi, im党员lem turbam ex insidiis interficere. Addimus elegantem allegoriam glossæ ordinariæ ex Rabano: Amalecita sunt Dæmones, qui nobis per Baptismum de spirituali Ægypto exeuntibus ad- versantur, & in virtutibus extremis, & in itinere hu- jus vitæ lassatos peccatum suggerendo, student occi- dere. Hos cum Dominus facultatem dederit, omni- no debemus subvertere, & suggestiones eorum omni- no ejicere atque delere, ne si aliquas reliquas, sicut Saul servaverimus, quasi inobedientes cum suis sub- vertamur.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI.

Firstfruits and tithes.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI.

Primitiæ, ac decimæ.

## 26:2
Ver. 2.

YOU SHALL TAKE FROM ALL YOUR FRUITS THE FIRSTFRUITS) Which for that reason were marked with a rush. IN A BASKET) A Greek word from the Greek version. You would rightly translate it as in a basket. See below XXVIII. 5. The Hebrews teach that seven fruits of the holy land are understood: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, dates. The firstfruits of the fruits: those which anyone first curiously searching and observing discovered to be ripening, he marked with a rush, by virtue of this law, so that he might distinguish them from the rest, and afterwards brought them when plucked to Jerusalem, and left them to the Priests. With an ox crowned with olives and its horns gilded, those deputed from all the cities would walk, singing the words of the gradual Psalm, rejoicing with those saying to me, we shall go into the house of the Lord. And what other ceremonies of theirs there are: concerning which see Episcopius l. c. p. 86 and Fagius in h. l. But this refers to the traditions of the Jews, commandments of men, as do infinite others. But Abulensis rightly observed that this constitution did not bind the Jews until after their entry into the land of Canaan and their habitation of the same, which the text openly implies, and therefore this was held to be a confirmation of the promise concerning the possession of the land of Canaan. Yet it was not to be done only once upon entry, but had to be repeated every year, as is manifest from a comparison of Lev. 2:14, c. 23:10, Num. 15:10, c. 18:12, c. 29:26, Deut. 18:4. One kind of firstfruits was offered on the second day of the Passover from the grain not yet threshed, another at the feast of Pentecost from the new loaves; a third at the feast of tabernacles, from all the fruits of the earth: concerning which the Hebrews understand this law. Luther and Brentius and the Cause of the offering of firstfruits.

they explain concerning the firstfruits of the feast of Pentecost. This was done, both that they might testify their gratitude to God, and that by this offering of firstfruits they might profess that the ownership of that land did not belong to them, but only the usufruct, just as an emphyteuta is accustomed by the payment of a canon to testify that he is only the tenant of that estate, because the owner does not pay the canon, and also that they might be drawn away from the idolatrous cults of the Gentiles, who attributed the fertility of the land to fictitious deities. It is to be observed that it is said: take of the firstfruits: for it does not seem to be a matter of all that which was otherwise to be offered in place of firstfruits, since all that could by no means be carried in a basket, but only of some part of them. Nor indeed were they bound to bring firstfruits only of certain fruits of the earth, but of all. And you shall take of the firstfruits of ALL THE FRUIT OF THE EARTH. Which universality, however, is accommodative, as they call it: because from Matt. 23, 23. Luke 11, 42. it appears that it was not necessary for tithes or firstfruits to be offered from absolutely all fruits, since it is attributed to the hypocrisy of the Pharisees that they tithed cumin and mint.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

TOLLES DE CUNCTIS FRUGIBUS TVIS PRIMI- TIAS) Quæ ob id junco fignabantur. IN CARTALLO) Vox Græca ex Græca versione. Recte verteris in cophino. Vide infra XXVIII. 5. Fructus terræ sanctæ septem intelligi docent Ebræi, triticum, hordeum, uvas, ficus, mala granata, olivas, dactylos, Primities fructuum: quos quis pri- mum curiose vestigans & observans deprehende- rit maturescere, filio signavit, vi hujus legis, ut à cæ- teris discerneret, ac decerptos postmodum Hiero- solymam adduxit, & Sacerdotibus reliquit. Cum bove olivis coronato, & cornibus inaurato omnium civitatuin deputati incedebant, cantantes verba Psalmi gradualis, exhilorar cum dicentibus mihi, in domum Domini ibimus. Et quæ aliæ sunt ipso- rum ceremoniæ: De quibus vid. Episcopius l. c. p. 86. & Fagius in h. l. Sed hoc ad traditiones Judæorum ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων, ut infinita alia spectant. Recte autem observavit Abulensis, non obligasse hanc constitutionem Judæos, nisi post ingressum in terram Canaan, & inhabitationem e- jusdem, quod textus aperte innuit, ideoque habe- batur hic promissionis de possidenda terra Ca- naan βεβαίωσις. Non tamen solum id sub ingres- sum semel fieri, sed quotannis repeti debuit, ut è collatione Lev. 2, 14, c. 23, 10. Num. 15, 10. c. 18, Tempus 12. c. 29, 26. Deut. 18, 4. manifestum est. Unum primitiarum genus offerebatur altero die Pascha- tos de frugibus nondum excussis, alterum in festo Pentecostes de novis panibus; tertium in festo taber- naculorum, de omnibus terræ fructibus: de quo hanc legem Ebræi intelligunt. Luther. ac Brentius & Causa ob- lat. primi- tiar.

de primitiis festi Pentecostes explicant. Factum id, tum ut Deo gratitudinem testarentur, tum ut isthac primitiarum oblatione profiterentur sibi non competere dominium illius terræ, sed tan- tum usumfructum, uti solet emphyteuta solutione canonis testari se tantum colonum est illius præ- dii, quod canonem non solvit proprietarius, tum ut ab idololatricis cultibus gentilium, qui fictitiis numinibus fertilitatem terræ tribuebant, abstra- herentur. Observandum, quod dicatur: accipite de primitiis: non enim videtur de omni illo, quod primitiarum loco offerendum alias erat, agi, quum id omne in canistro portari minime potuerit, sed tantum de aliqua parte earum. Nec vero tantum de quibusdam terræ frugibus afferre primitias de- buere, sed de omnibus. Et capies de primitiis OMNIS FRUCTUS TERRÆ. Quæ ta- men universalitas accommoda, ut vocant, est: quia è Matth. 23, 23. Luc. 11, 42. apparet, non ex omnibus omnino fructibus decimas, aut primitias offerri necessum fuisse, siquidem id Pharisæorum hypocrisi tribuatur, quod cuminum & mentham de- cimarint.

## 26:5
Verse 5.

SYRIAN WAS PERSECUTING MY FATHER] In the Hebrew: A Syrian was my wretched father. He calls him a Syrian because of his dwelling in Mesopotamian Syria. The Latins would say Syriensian as they say Hispaniansian. I have translated אבד as wretched. For the Greeks also translate it as τὸν ἐν λυπαῖς. Proverbs 31, 6. and the word from which this participle is made in Job 6, 18. is translated ἀπωλόμην, and is explained as ἄξοικος ἐγενόμην. His history shows that this eulogy fits Jacob very well.

What Grotius understands concerning Jacob, Blessed Luther understands concerning Abraham in Expl. Genes. Germ. T. IV. Jen. f. 44. Blessed Gerhard, with the Chaldean, understands it concerning Laban in this manner: Laban the Syrian (for they are called in Gen. 28. 5. ארמי Syrian) was a destroyer of my father, that is, he was seeking to destroy him, as the Targum has explained. But because אבד in Kal does not signify he destroyed, but he perished, therefore with Glassius he is of the same opinion in Gramm. S. p. 234. either that the conjugation Kal and Piel exchange signification here, or because the discourse is about a Syrian, the Syro-Chaldean word from the conjugation Aphet, in which for the Chaldeans אובד and for the Syrians אובר is a destroyer, is used after the example of the Syriac word נחתים, sent down, or descending, 2 Kings 6, 9, when the discourse was about the Syrians. But so that we may not have need to posit a permutation of conjugations regarding the meanings, or to admit a Chaldean word here, it is better with Vatablus, Tremellius, and the Belgian Interpreters to interpret with Grotius and others concerning Jacob (1.) Because the proper signification of the word demands it: A perishing or wretched Syrian was my father Jacob. The word אובד, says Fuller, l. III. miscell. c. 20. p. 383. since it is in Kal, cannot but be absolute or intransitive: For it is nowhere found used in a transitive sense, but always and everywhere in an absolute one. Therefore it cannot be attributed to Laban, but fits Jacob alone. For he was truly אובד, i.e., perishing, or already about to perish or to be destroyed and finished by Laban by most grievous and numberless (evils) had he not been always surrounded by the singular providence of the Deity, and finally liberated. Fagius in ann. ad Paraphr. Chald. In Hebrew it has it thus: A perishing Syrian, or one laboring in penury, was my father; of which words he thinks this is the sense: i.e., we did not receive these riches from our parents, from our father Jacob, but from our God: so that it may be shown that the sons of Israel did not receive the holy land by hereditary right, but by the gift of God. (2.) The discourse is about one person, who is called both wretched or lost, and, driven about by wandering, had descended into Egypt. For the pronoun אשר is not interposed: A Syrian was destroying my father, who descended, but the particle Vau is held:

A perishing Syrian was my father, and he descended into Egypt. Therefore, the one descending is the same as that אֹבֵד: these are not distinct persons. (3.) Jacob can be called a Syrian, not indeed by reason of his native soil, but because he served twenty years of servitude with his father-in-law in Syria, and born of a Syrian mother, he took Syrian wives, and begat all his children, except the youngest, in Syria, and there acquired for himself the greatest faculties. Others understand Laban by the Syrian, but in the same sense, rendering it thus: by a Syrian my father was perishing, or was being destroyed, as the Belgians note, and thus the Targum expressed the sense, not the words, as also Blessed Luther in his Biblical version: Die Syrer wolten meinen Vater umbringen. (4.) All agree in this, that the persecutions and afflictions of Jacob are meant; therefore they easily agree in the sense, however much they may differ in rendering the words, for among them those almost stand out which he sustained in Syria: although, if Jacob is described indefinitely as almost lost, other afflictions of his, before which he himself all but perished, can be comprehended at the same time. For in many ways, as Fuller says again, the most holy man seemed about to perish almost from his childhood, even to extreme old age. For example, by the hatred and machinations of Esau, then by his flight into exile in a tumult, by the deceit and perfidy of Laban, by the indignation and terror on account of the Shechemites being killed, by the premature death of his dearest wife, soon by the incest of another who survived, by the believed tearing to pieces of his sweetest son Joseph, by the dire famine subsequently encroaching, and finally by the Egyptian migration. Hence that sad and mournful voice of his burst forth before Pharaoh: Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life. Which Moses expressed very significantly by the word אֹבֵד, i.e., lost by grief and miseries, and therefore not only wretched, but also most wretched. Add (5.) that those things which he endured in Syria or Mesopotamia do not immediately cohere with the departure into Egypt, and that meanwhile, while he stayed in Canaan, having returned from Syria, and having been forced to change his dwelling several times, the wretched Jacob also suffered not a few things, until he descended into Egypt with a small number, and there grew into a great nation, so that thus his entire misery and perdition is described no less by the word אֹבֵד, than his increase, which the remaining parts exhibit, and furthermore the oppression of his sons in Egypt, as well as their glorious liberation, is commemorated, and so that for the liberation of both their wretched Father and the afflicted Israelites, and their introduction into the promised rest, thanks may be given. (6) It thus agrees with our passage what is held in Hos. 12. v. 12. where likewise the wretched condition of Jacob in Syria and the leading out of the people from Egypt is designated: Jacob fled into the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept. But by a Prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a Prophet he was kept.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

STRUS PERSEQVEBATUR PATREM MEUM] In Hebræo: Syrus miser pater meus. Syrum vocat ob habita- tionem in Syria Mesopotamiensi. Latini Syriensem dicerent ut Hispaniensem. אבד verti miserum. Nam & Græci vertunt τὸν ἐν λυπαῖς. Proverb. 31, 6. & verbum unde hoc participi- um factum est Jobi 6, 18. vertitur ἀπωλόμην, & explicatur ἄξοικος ἐγενόμην. Optime hoc elogium Jacobo convenire ostendit ejus historia.

Quod de Jacobo Grotius, B. Lutherus de Ab- rahamo intelligit in Expl. Genes. Germ. T. IV. Jen. f. 44. B. Gerhardus cum Chaldæo de Labano h. m. Laban Syrus (vocantur enim Gen. 28. 5. ארמי Syrus) perdens erat Patrem meum, id est, perdere quærebat, ut Targum exposuit. Quia vero אבד in Kal non significat perdidit, sed periit, ideo cum Glassio ejusdem est sententiæ Gramm.
