S. p. 234. vel conjugationem Kal, & Piel significationem hic permutare, vel quia de Syro sermo est, Syro- Chaldeam vocem è conjugatione Aphet, in qua Chaldæis אובד Syris אובר est perdens adhiberi ad exemplum vocis Syriacæ נחתים dimissi, seu descen- dentes 2. Reg. 6, 9. cum de Syris ageretur, usurpa- tæ. Sed ne opus habeamus statuere conjugationum permutationem, quoad significata, aut vocem Chaldæam hic admittere, præstat cum Vatabl. Tre- mellio, Belg. Interpp. Grotio, & aliis de Jacobo in- terpretari (1.) Quia id vocis propria significatio postulat: Syrus periens vel miser pater meus Ja- cob. Vox אובד, inquit, Fullerus l. III. miscell. c. 20. p. 383. quum sit in Kal, non potest non absoluta seu intransitiva esse: Nusquam enim sensu transiti- vo usurpata invenitur, sed semper & ubique absoluto. Itaque Labani attribui nequit, sed Jacobo duntaxat convenit. Is enim vere אובד h. e. periens, aut jam periturus vel perdendus & conficiendus erat à La- bano gravissimis & innumeris (malis) nisi singulari numinis providentia circumseptus semper, ac tan- dem liberatus fuisset. Fagius in ann. ad Paraphr. Chald. Hebraice sic habet: Syrus periens, sive pe- nuria laborans fuit Pater meus; Quorum verbo- rum hunc sensum esse putat: q. d. has divitias non accepimus à parentibus a patre nostro Jacob, sed à Deo nostro: ut ostendatur filios Israël non acce- pisse terram sanctam jure hæreditario, sed dono Dei. (2.) De una persona sermo est, quæ & mi- sera, vel perdita dicitur, & peregrinatione circuma- cta, in Ægyptum descenderat. Non enim inter- ponitur pronomen אשר: Syrus perdebat patrem meum, qui descendit, sed habetur particula Vau:

Syrus periens pater meus, & descendit in Ægyptum. Idem ergo est descendens cum illo אֹבֵד: non distin- ctæ hæ sunt personæ. (3.) Jacob Syrus dici potest, non quidem ratione natalis soli, sed quia viginti an- norum servitutem apud Socerum in Syria servivit, ac matre Syra natus, uxores Syras duxit, liberosque omnes, minimo natu excepto, in Syria procreavit, ibique maximas facultates sibi comparavit. Alii per Syrum Labanum quidem intelligunt, sed sen- su eodem, ita reddentes: à Syro peribat, vel perde- batur pater meus, uti notant Belgæ, atque ita sen- sum, non verba expresserit Targum, ut & B. Lu- therus in versione Biblica: Die Syrer wolten meinen Vater umbringen. (4.) Omnes conve- niunt in eo, quod Jacobi persequutiones, & affli- ctiones indigentur, in sensu ergo facile consen- tiunt, utut in vocibus reddendis differant, nam in- ter illas fere eminent, quas sustinuit in Syria: quam- vis, si indefinite Jacobus, ceu perditus propemo- dum describatur, simul aliæ ejus afflictiones, præ quibus ipse tantum non peribat, comprehendi possint. Multis quippe modis, ut iterum Fullerus, periturus prope à pueritia videbatur vir sanctissi- mus, ad extremam usque senectutem. Verbi gra- tia, odio & machinationibus Esavi, exilio dein fu- gave tumultuaria, dolo ac perfidia Labanis, indi- gnatione ac terrore ob Sichæmitas interemtos, morte præmatura carissimæ conjugis, mox alterius superstitis incestu, credita suavissimi filii Josephi dilaniatione, dira ingruente postmodum fame, & migratione demum Ægyptiaca. Hinc tristis illa & luctuosa ipsius vox coram Pharaone erupit: Pauci & mali fuerunt dies annorum vitæ meæ. Quod valde significanter expressit Moles vocabu- lo אֹבֵד q. d. mærore ac miseriis perditus, ideoque non miser tantum, sed etiam miserrimus. Adde (5.) quod non immediate cohæreant ea, quæ in Syria vel Mesopotamia sustinuit, cum profectione in Ægyptum, quodque interea, dum in Canaan hæsit, redux èSyria, ac aliquoties sedem suam mutare co- actus, non pauca etiam miser Jacob perpessus sit, do- nec exiguo numero in Ægyptum descenderet, ibi- que in gentem magnam excresceret, ut ita non mi- nus universa ejus miseria & perditio voce אֹבֵד, quam ejus incrementum, quod reliqua exhibent, describatur, ac porro filiorum ejus tum pressura in Ægypto, tum liberatio gloriosa commemoretur, adeoque pro liberatione tum miseri sui Patris, tum afflictorum Israëlitarum, atque introductione in quietem promissam gratiæ agantur. (6) Convenit ita loco nostro quod habetur Os. 12. v. 12. ubi pariter misera Jacobi conditio in Syria & populi eductio ex Ægyto designatur: Fugit Jacob in regionem Syriæ, & servivit Israël in uxorem, & in uxorem servavit. In Propheta autem eduxit Dominus Israël de Ægypto, & in Propheta servatus est.

## 26:11
Vers. 11. AND YOU SHALL FEAST.

That sacred and solemn banquet was instituted after the offering of the firstfruits had been made, not from those firstfruits, for these were to be left in the sight of the Lord, ver. 10, but from other foods: and when they had offered a peace offering at the same time, it was to be performed before the altar of burnt offering, in the court of the sanctuary; but if it were prepared from other things, which they had either brought with them with the firstfruits, or had procured for themselves in the place, it was in a private lodging, to which banquet, besides the household and friends, the Levites, widows, orphans, and strangers were to be invited, Deut. 12, 12. 18. 19. c. 14. v. 27. 29. c. 16, 11. 14. And therefore these banquets were testimonies of public joy, invitations to frequent acts of gratitude and devotion, symbols of mutual charity, and of beneficence toward the needy.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET EPULABERIS.

Sacrum illud, atque solemne convivium post oblationem de primitiis factam instituebatur, non è primitiis illis, hæ enim dimittendæ erant in conspe- ctu Domini vers. 10. sed de aliis cibis: & cum victi- mam pacificam simul obtulerant, peragendum id coram altari holocausti, in atrio sanctuarii; Si au- tem pararetur de aliis, quæ vel cum primitiis secum attulerant, vel in loco sibi compararant, in privato hospitio, ad quod convivium præter domesticos & amicos Levitæ, viduæ, pupilli, & advenæ invitandi erant Deut. 12, 12. 18. 19. c. 14. v. 27. 29. c. 16, 11. 14. Ideoque erant hæc convivia testimonia publicæ læti- tiæ, invitamenta ad frequentandum actus gratitudinis & devotionis, symbola caritatis mutuæ, ac beneficentiæ in egenos.

## 26:12
Verse 12. WHEN YOU HAVE FINISHED THE TENTH.

There is here a constitution concerning triennial tithes. For every third year they were bound to pay three tithes: one to the Levites, which was to be given every year; another for offerings at the three solemn feasts, from which the givers themselves also feasted. The third they gave only in the third year; this went for the use of the Levites, widows, orphans, and strangers, which were distributed within the city of each offerer, so that they might have something from which to be sustained; therefore, with two tithes paid, the third also had to be set aside this year; which for that reason is called by way of excellence the year of tithes, which are treated here. Compare Deut. 14, 28.

Latin:

Vers. 12. QUANDO COMPLEVERIS DECI- MAM.

Habetur hic constitutio de decimis trietericis. Tertio enim quoque anno tres decimas solvere te- nebantur, unam Levitis, quæ singulis annis danda erat, Alteram ad oblationes in tribus festis solemni- bus, de qua etiam ipsi dantes epulabantur. Ter- tiam tertio solum anno dabant; hæc in usum Le- vitarum, viduarum, pupillorum & advenarum ce- debat, quæ inter urbem cujusque offerentis di- stribuebantur, ut haberent, unde sustentarentur; Ideo solutis decimis duabus tertiæ etiam erant hoc anno separandæ; qui eo nomine ἐξοχικῶς dicitur annus decimarum, de quibus hic agitur. Conf. Deut. 14, 8.

## 26:13
Verse 13. I HAVE REMOVED WHAT IS SANCTIFIED FROM MY HOUSE) בער is often to abolish: but in this place to remove, as appears also below 14. The LXX here: I have cleared the holy things from my house. Thus they translated the same word by καθαρίζειν above 19, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ABSTULI QVOD SANCTIFICATVM DE DOMO MEA EST) בער sæpe est abolere: sed hoc loco remove- re, ut apparet & infra 14. LXX. hic ἐξεκάθαρα τὰ ἅγια ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας με. Sic eandem vocem per καθαρίζειν verterunt supra 19, 13.

## 26:14
Verse 14. I HAVE NOT EATEN OF THEM IN MY MOURNING, NOR HAVE I SET THEM APART IN ANY UNCLEANNESS, NOR HAVE I SPENT ANY OF THEM FOR A FUNERAL MATTER.

Some refer the first to the cheerfulness of the one asserting, the second to the cleanliness of the thing offered, the third to the exclusion of expense for a funeral matter, because he took nothing for that purpose to the detriment of the tithes. But most simply, all three seem to exclude the suspicion of a defect, that he took nothing away from them, either for his own necessity in his straits, I have not eaten in my sadness (on account of a narrow situation at home), or for uncleanness or profane, idolatrous, or voluptuous use: nor have I taken from it for uncleanness, or even for a funeral matter, or a funeral feast, such as was accustomed to be instituted among the Jews in the houses of the deceased, Jer. 16, 7. Ez. 24, 17. Hos. 9, 4. nor have I given from it for the dead, since not even for the burial of the dead was anything to be torn away from the tithes. For since God knew the character of the Jews, that they easily act not only sparingly but also fraudulently in these matters, Neh. 13, 10. Hagg. 1, 9. Mal. III, 8. He wished to guard against this as if by a solemn oath, so that in tithes and firstfruits one might act in good faith.

Latin:

Vers. 14. NON COMEDI EX EIS IN LUCTU MEO, NEC SEPARAVI EA IN QUA- LIBET IMMUNDITIA, NEC EXPENDI EX HIS QUIDQUAM IN RE FUNE- BRI.

Primum ad hilaritatem nonnulli referunt adserentis, alterum ad munditiem rei oblatæ, tertium ad exclusionem expensæ in rem funebrem, quod nihil eam in rem decerpserit in decimarum decrementum. Sed simplicissime videntur omnia tria excludere suspicionem defectus, quod nihil iis detraxerit, vel in propriam necessitatem in angu- stiis suis, non comedi in tristitia mea (ob rem angu- stam domi) vel in immunditiem aut usum pro- phanum idololatricum voluptuarium: nec abstuli ex ea in immunditiem, vel etiam in rem funebrem, vel convivium funebre, quale solebat institui apud Judæos in ædibus defuncti Jer. 16, 7. Ez. 24, 17. Os. 9, 14. neque dedi ex eo pro mortuo, quum ne in mortuorum quidem funerationem aliquid è decimis discerpendum fuerit. Quum enim De- uş Judæorum ingenium norit, quod facile in hisce non solum parce, sed & fraudulenter agant Neh. 13, 10. Hagg. 1, 9. Mal. III, 8. cavere hoc veluti Sa- cramento solemni voluit, ut in decimis & primitiis bona fide ageretur.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII. The law to be inscribed on stones. Mount Gerizim and Ebal.

Verse 1. BUT MOSES AND THE ELDERS OF ISRAEL COMMANDED THE PEOPLE] Moses to the Priests: the Priests to the elders: the elders to the people.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII. Lex lapidibus inscribenda. Mons Garizim, & Hebal.

Vers. 1. PRÆCEPIT AVTEM MOSES ET SENIORES ISRAEL POPVLO] Moses Sacerdotibus: Sacerdotes seni- bus: Senes populo.

## 27:2
Verse 2. YOU SHALL ERECT HUGE STONES AND SMOOTH THEM WITH LIME.

The stones must have been huge, because the law was to be inscribed upon them. They had to be joined or coated with lime, so that the law could be inscribed upon them clearly and brightly. However, it was not only the Decalogue that was to be inscribed, as Lyranus thinks, or only the sum of the Decalogue's precepts comprised of the love of God and neighbor, as Cajetan thinks, who for that reason also judges that two stones had to be erected on account of the two tables of the Decalogue, nor were only the blessings and curses recited on Mount Gerizim and Ebal to be inscribed, as it seemed to Josephus in book IV.

last chapter, book V, chapter 1 (see Andr. Masius on Josh. 8), as also to Jerome and Oleaster, nor only the law which was described in the preceding chapter 25, which the same Oleaster thought, but on these stones was to be written משנה תורה, a duplication or repetition of the law, Deuteronomy, as appears from the completion of John 8:32, whether it means the entire Deuteronomy, or that they inscribed on the stones the laws repeated from Deuteronomy (omitting the historical parts), which could easily be done if 12 huge stones were erected according to the number of the tribes, with each inscribed in a smaller character, or in three chapters if the entire book was to be inscribed, or in about two if the historical parts were omitted.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ERIGES INGENTES LAPIDES ET CALCE LEVIGABIS EOS.

INgentes esse debuere lapides, quia lex illis inscri- benda erat. Calce uniri vel incrustari debebant, ut plane & lucide illis inscribi lex possit. Non in- scribendus autem tantum decalogus erat, ut Lyra- nus, vel summa tantum Decalogi præceptis de dile- ctione Dei & proximi comprehensa, ut Cajetanus putat, qui ideo etiam duos lapides erigi debuisse censet ob duas decalogi tabulas, neque solum be- nedictiones, & maledictiones in monte Garizim, & Ebal recitatæ inscribendæ, uti Josepho visum l. IV.

cap. ult. lib. V. cap. 1. (vid. Andr. Masius in Jos. 8.) ut & Hieronymo, & Oleastro, neque solum lex, quæ cap. præced. 25. descripta, quod idem Olea- ster putavit, sed in lapides hosce scribenda משנה תורה duplicatio vel repetitio legis, Deuteronomi- on, ut ex complemento Joh. 8, 32. apparet, sive quod integrum Deuteronomium, sive quod è Deu- teronomio leges repetitas (historicis prætermissis) lapidibus inscripseriut, quod fieri facile potuit, si lapides 12. ingentes juxta numerum tribuum ere- cti fuere singulis inscriptis charactere minutiori sive tribus capitibus, si integer liber inscribendus, sive duobus circiter, si historica prætermissa.

## 27:5
Verse 5. AND YOU SHALL BUILD THERE AN ALTAR TO THE LORD YOUR GOD, OF STONES WHICH IRON HAS NOT TOUCHED.

Josephus seems to have understood these as the same stones as those mentioned just before. But these were different; those were erected only as a monument, these were built into an altar: those for the inscription of the law, these for the offering of sacrifices. Those were coated with lime, these remained unhewn and retained their natural roughness: because this altar had to be made only in a hurried manner, and for a single act after the entry into the land of Canaan; for this altar was clearly extraordinary, and therefore the altar of burnt offerings in the tabernacle and temple was to be adorned much more elegantly thereafter as a permanent one, Ex. 38:1, 1 Kings 7:12, 2 Chron. 4:1. Both, however, were to be erected on Mount Ebal, on which the curses were to be recited; so that the stones on which the law was inscribed might denote the law denouncing the curse; but the altar, on which sacrifices were offered, might denote Christ deriving the curse upon Himself and expiating it on the altar of the cross, and it was hinted that both were to be taught in the Church, both the law and the Gospel. Regarding this altar, Blessed Luther on this passage: This altar later resulted in a great scandal, when the people offered there and worshipped God, puffed up by the example of the Fathers who had sacrificed there on that occasion, and by the authority of Moses who had ordered it to be done. For the Samaritan woman also objected this to Christ, John 4. But they did not see that this temporary command was not to be drawn into a perpetual example, since they otherwise had an express command that whatever place the Lord had chosen, there they ought to offer, which Moses also repeats so often in this book. However, the place which He chose was always certain, namely wherever the ark of the covenant was, over which He had promised that He would remain among them, so that we may see that we ought to trust and rely not on the example of the Fathers nor on a past word of God, which has now ceased with the past deed, but only on the present word of God, concerning the present deed.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET ÆDIFICABIS IBI ALTARE DO- MINO DEO TUO, DE LAPIDIBUS QUOS FERRUM NON TETIGIT.

Eosdem Lapides, de quibus proxime, videtur Josephus intellexisse. Sed diversi hi erant; illi so- lum in monumentum erecti, bi in altare extructi: illi ad legis inscriptionem, bi ad sacrificiorum obla- tionem. Illi calce obducti erant, hi impoliti man- sere, ac nativam scabritiem retinuerunt: Quia al- tare hoc tantum tumultuarie fieri debuit, & ad u- nicum actum post ingressum in terram Canaan; erat enim plane extraordinarium hoc altare, ideo- que altare holocaustorum in tabernaculo & tem- plo longe politius deinde ornandum ceu perpetu- um Ex. 38, 1. 1. Reg. 7, 12. 2. Par. 4, 1. Utrique tamen in monte Ebal erigendi, in quo recitandæ maledictiones; ut ita lapides, quibus lex inscripta le- gem maledictionem denunciantem; altare vero, in quo oblata sacrificia, Christum maledictionem in se derivantem & expiantem in ara crucis deno- tarent, & utrumque in Ecclesia docendum esse, tum legem, tum Evangelium, innueretur. De hoc al- tari B. Luth. ad h. l. Hoc altare postea cessit in ma- gnum scandalum, cum populus ibidem offerret, & coleret Deum, inflatus exemplo Patrum, qui ibi hac vice immolassent, & autoritate Mosis, qui id fieri jussisset. Nam & mulier Samaritana id Christo quoque objecit Joh. 4. Sed non viderunt, quod tem- porale hoc mandatum non erat trahendum in exem- plum perpetuum, cum alias haberent expressum mandatum, quod quemcunque locum elegisset Domi- nus, illic offerre deberent, quod & toties in hoc libro repetit Moses. Locus autem, quem elegit, erat cer- tus semper, nempe ubicunque esset arca fœderis, super quam promiserat se mansurum inter eos, ut videa- mus, quod non exemplo Patrum nec verbo Dei præ- terito, quod jam defiit cum facto præterito, sed soli verbo Dei præsenti, de facto præsente, fidere & niti de- beamus.

## 27:12
Verse 12. THESE SHALL STAND TO BLESS THE PEOPLE)

The more important tribes born from the legitimate wives of the families, except for Reuben because of his fault, and Zebulun as the last from Leah: who were added to complete the number for the ministry of the descendants.

Regarding which Fagius says: The sons of the free women are employed for blessing, because an external and temporary blessing is held to be as it were the effect of that heavenly and interior one. However, this does not happen without the Spirit of the Lord. Then the sons of the bondwomen are added for the curse, because that is an argument of servitude and the absence of the Spirit according to the law of Leviticus 26, to bear the curse and adverse things. Now because only four were born from the bondwomen, Reuben the firstborn and Zebulun the last born of the sons of Leah are added. For the former was reduced as it were to servitude by the sin committed against his father, Gen. 49. The latter, however, because he is the last, is also considered the least in dignity.

Verse of the same. UPON MOUNT GERIZIM.

It was one and the same mountain, and that the highest in Samaria, but of two peaks, of which one was called Mount Gerizim, pleasant with springs and gardens, on which the blessing was given; the other Mount Ebal, arid, full of rocks and stones, on which the curse was given. Gerizim denotes cutters, because here the peak is as it were cut from the other; Ebal signifies the vinegar of antiquity or a flowing heap. The former word, however, sometimes denotes the whole mountain, as Jud. 9, 7, where Jotham is said to have stood on the peak of Mount Ebal of Gerizim, called so in its entirety. On this mountain a temple, in emulation of the Jerusalem one, by the concession

of Alexander the Great, Manasseh, brother of Jaddua the High Priest of the Jews, having been ejected from the Jerusalem priesthood because he had taken the daughter of Sanballat, Duke of Samaria, as his wife, built it with the help of his father-in-law. See Josephus, book 11, Antiquities, ch. 7, and book 13, ch. 4, book 18, 7, 12. And therefore the Samaritans held that mountain as sacred on account of the blessing performed there, worshipped on it, and offered sacrifices, John 4, 20. Yet this temple was destroyed two hundred years later by John Hyrcanus the Priest, and all worship was brought back to the Jerusalem temple. Andreas Masius locates Mount Gerizim near Hai; but others more correctly place it near Shechem, so named from Shechem, son of Hamor, who founded it, which later became a city of refuge, Jos. 20, was destroyed by Abimelech, Jud. 9, and restored by Jeroboam, 1 Kings 12. It is called in the N.T. Sychar, John 4, 5. Josephus teaches in book 4, ch. 8, that Moses ordered an altar to be erected not far from the city of Shechem between two mountains, the right one Gerizim, the left one Ebal. Serarius proves this with more detail in q. 14 on Jos. 8. Near this city of Shechem was a famous valley filled with oaks, to which Abram came when he had first crossed from Chaldea into Canaan, Gen. 12, 6, in which oak grove there was a place destined for sacred worship. It is called in Deut. 11, 30, the valley of Moreh, which is a proper name taken from its pleasantness, as Brocardus thinks, or rather from the appearances of God made to his Abraham. Compare regarding these blessings and curses Josephus, as also Paul Fagius on this passage. Cornelius à Lapide has this to say about them: This whole matter seems to have been performed in this order and manner. First, in the valley itself between the two mountains, namely Gerizim and Ebal, stood those priests who carried the ark of the covenant, as is evident from Joshua 8, 33. Then around these stood other priests and all the Levites: thirdly, around these stood the elders, leaders, and judges of the people: fourthly, all the tribes in order, namely so that six designated ones stood ascending towards Mount Gerizim, and six others towards Mount Ebal. Fifthly, Joshua, either by himself as a Prophet or through the priests, blessed the people, as is evident from Joshua 8, 34. Sixthly, some priests, who seemed the most vocal, recited the law. Seventhly, the same ascended the peak of Mount Gerizim, as Abulensis wishes, or rather, standing in the valley near the fortress, as the Hebrews, Masius, Serarius, and others teach; from a higher place, or from a platform, turning themselves towards Mount Gerizim they pronounced the blessings, then turning themselves to Mount Ebal, they pronounced the curses. Rabbi Solomon thinks that the priests, after individual blessings to which the six tribes responded 'Amen', turned themselves to Ebal and pronounced the contrary curse, to which the other six tribes responded 'Amen' in an alternating voice and chorus, as it were. For this seems more fitting and harmonious. Others, however, such as Andreas Masius and Abulensis, no less probably believe that the priests first pronounced all 12 blessings together towards Gerizim, with the six tribes responding 'Amen' to each one. Then after them they pronounced in order the 12 curses towards Ebal, with the other six tribes responding 'Amen'. Rabanus, following Origen on ch. 9 of Joshua, handed down the mystical meaning in this passage. Those who walk near Mount Gerizim to be blessed are those who, kindled not by fear of punishment but by hope and love of the heavenly promise and eternal blessing, tend towards salvation: others, who walk near Ebal, on which the curses were pronounced, are those who fulfill the law not for love of the promises, but for fear of punishments, so that they may be saved. But all these walk around the ark, because they do not depart from the bosom of the Church, although those are nobler than these. Joshua, however, set them near these mountains because Jesus calls and brings his elect to salvation either by hope of reward or fear of punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 12. HI STABUNT AD BENEDICENDUM POPULO)

Potiores tribus natæ ex justis matribus familias, excepto Ru- bene ob culpam, & Zabulone ut postremo ex Lea: qui ad implendum numerum adjecti posteris ministratum.

De quo Fagius: Liberarum filii ad benedi- cendum adhibentur, quod benedictio externa ac temporaria illius cœlestis ac interioris velut effe- ctus habeatur. Hæc autem non contingit sine spi- ritu Domini. Deinde servarum filii ad maledictio- nem adjunguntur, quod argumentum servi- tutis & absentiæ spiritus sit juxta legem Le- vit. 26. ferre maledictionem & res adversas. Jam quia ex servis quatuor tantum nati sunt, Ruben primogenitus & Zebulon postremus natu ex filiis Leæ adjiciuntur. Illum enim peccatum in Pa- trem admissum quasi in servitutem redegit Gen. 49. Hic autem quia ultimus, dignitate etiam mi- nimus censetur.

Vers. eod. SUPER MONTEM GARIZIM.

Unus erat idemque mons, isque altissimus in Samaria, sed duorum cacuminum, quorum unum vocabatur Mons Garizim, fontibus & hortis amœ- nus, in quo data benedictio, alterum mons Ebal, ari- dus, saxis & lapidibus plenus, in quo data fuit male- dictio. Garizim notat scissores, quia hic cacumen ab altero quasi scissum, Ebal acetum vetustatis vel acervum defluentem significat. Prior tamen vox quandoque totum montem notat, ut Jud. 9, 7. ubi in cacumine Ebal montis Garizim ὁλικῶς sic dicti stetisse dicitur Jotham. In hoc monte templum, ad æmulationem Hierosolymitani, concessione

Alexandri M. Menasses frater Jaddi Pontificis Ju- dæorum, sacerdotio Hierosolymitano, quod filiam Saneballat Samariæ Ducis in uxorem duxerat, eje- ctus, auxilio soceri sui extruxit. Vid. Joseph. l. 11. Antiq. c. 7. & l. 13. cap. 4. l. 18. 7. 12. Ideoque Sama- ritani montem illum ob benedictionem ibi fa- ctam pro sacro habebant, in eo adorabant, & sa- crificia offerebant Joh. 4, 20. Dirutum tamen ducentis post annis fuit hoc templum à Johanne Hircano Sacerdote, & cultus omnis ad templum Hierosolymitanum reductus fuit. Andr. Masius locat montem Garizim juxta Hai; sed rectius alii juxta Sichem eum constituunt ita appellatam à Sichemo, Hemoris, qui eam condidit, filio, quæ postea urbs refugii facta Jos. 20. ab Abimelecho destructa Jud. 9. à Jeroboamo instaurata 1. Reg. 12. Dicitur in N. T. Συχὰρ Joh. 4, 5. Non procul à Sichemis urbe aram erigi jussisse Mosen inter duos montes dextrum Garizæum, sinistrum Gebalem, Josephus docet lib. 4. c. 8. Quod pluribus pro- bat Serarius q. 14. in Jos. 8. Juxta hanc civitatem Sichem erat vallis celebris quercubes referta, ad quam venit Abram, cum ex Chaldæa in Canaan primum transiisset Gen. 12, 6. in quo querceto lo- cus fuit cultui sacro destinatus. Vocatur Deut. 11, 30. vallis מוֹרֶה quod nomen proprium est ab amœnitate petitum, ut Brocardus putat, vel potius ab appariti- onibus Dei suo Abrahamo factis. Conf. de his benedictionibus & maledictionibus Joseph. ut & Paul. Fagius in h. l. Cornel. à Lapide ita de illis habet: Tota hæc res hoc ordine & modo peracta videtur. Primo, in valle ipsa inter duos montes, Garizim. sc. & Hebal, stabant sacerdotes ii, qui ar- cam fœderis gestabant, ut patet Josuæ 8, 33. Dein- de circum hos stabant alii Sacerdotes, ac Levitæ omnes: circum hos tertio, stabant majores natu duces & judices populi: Quarto deinceps tribus omnes ita scil. ut sex designatæ starent ascendendo versus montem Garizim, sex aliæ versus montem Hebal. Quinto Josue vel per se, tanquam Pro- pheta, vel per Sacerdotes benedixit populum, uti patet Josue 8, 34. Sexto Sacerdotes aliqui, qui vocalissimi videbantur, legem recitarunt. Septimo iidem conscenderunt cacumen montis Garizim, ut vult Abulens. vel potius in valle, juxta arcem consistentes, ut docent Hebræi, Masius, Serarius, & alii; ex editiore loco, vel ex suggestu, vertentes se versus montem Garizim pronunciarunt bene- dictiones, deinde vertentes se ad montem Hebal, pronuntiarunt maledictiones. Putat R. Salomon, Sacerdotes post singulas benedictiones, quibus sex tribus respondebant, Amen, se convertisse ad He- bal, & contrariam maledictionem pronuntiasse, cui sex aliæ tribus, alterna quasi voce & choro re- spondebant, Amen. Hoc enim magis congruum & concinnum videtur. Alii vero, ut Andr. Ma- sius, & Abulens. non minus probabiliter censent, sacerdotes primo omnes 12. benedictiones simul pronuntiasse ad Garizim, sex tribubus responden- tibus ad singulas; Amen. Deinde post eas pronun- tiasse ordine 12. maledictiones ad Hebal, sex aliis tribubus respondentibus Amen. Significationem mysticam sic tradidit post Origenem in c. 9. Jos. Rabanus in h. l. Juxta montem Garizim incedunt ad benedicendum, qui non metu pænæ sed cælestis promissionis & benedictionis æternæ spe & amore suc- censi tendunt ad salutem: alii, qui juxta Hebal, in quo maledictiones prolatæ sunt, incedunt, sunt ii, qui non amore promissorum, sed timore suppliciorum im- plent legem, ut salventur. Omnes autem hi circa arcam incedunt, quia ab Ecclesiæ sinu non recedunt, licet nobiliores illi sint, quam hi. Josue autem con- stituit eos juxta hos montes : quia Jesus electos suos vel spe præmii vel timore pœnæ ad salutem vocat & producit.

## 27:15
V. 15. AND SHALL SAY AMEN.

Amen, as St. Jerome notes in Epistle 137 to Marcella, and at the end of his commentary on Galatians. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it πεπισωμένως, that is, faithfully or truly. The Septuagint translated it γένοιτο, that is, let it be. Therefore, Amen signifies truly, or also firmly: for the root אָמַן signifies to make firm, to establish, whence the noun אֱמֶת, that is, firmness, stability, truth. Amen, therefore, is not a particle of one swearing, as the common people think, but of one affirming and confirming; it is of one affirming when it is placed before a prayer, as 'Amen, amen, I say to you'; it is of one confirming when it is placed after a prayer. Again, when it is placed after, and signifies the consent of the hearer, it is sometimes of one asserting and conceding, sometimes of one wishing. It can be taken here in either way: for the people responding 'Amen' approve the blessing or the curse of the Levites, that is, of the Priests, and at the same time wished it to be so done, and this to the end that they might always remember themselves to be blessed by their blessing, and cursed by their execration, if they acted well or ill, says Cajetan.

Latin:

V. 15. ET DICET AMEN.

Amen, notante S. Hieronym. ad Marcell. Epist. 137. & in fine comment. ad Galat. Aquila, Symmach. & Theodot. verterunt πεπισωμένως, id est, fideliter vel vere. Septuag. verterunt γένοιτο, id est, fiat. Significat ergo Amen vere, vel etiam fir- miter: radix enim אָמַן significat firmare, stabilire, unde nomen אֱמֶת id est firmitas, stabilitas, veritas. Amen ergo non est particula jurantis, ut vulgus putat, sed affirmantis & confirmantis; affirmantis est, cum orationi præponitur, ut Amen amen dico vobis; confirmantis est, cum orationi postponitur. Rursum cum postponitur, & significat consensum audientis, nunc asserentis est, & concedentis, nunc optantis. Utrovis modo hic accipi potest: nam populus respondens Amen approbat benedictio- nem vel maledictionem Levitarum, id est, Sacer- dotum, & simul optabat ita fieri, idque ad hoc, ut sua benedictione benedictos, & execratione sua execratos, semper se meminissent, si bene vel male a- gerent, inquit Cajet.

## 27:16
Verse 16.

CURSED IS HE WHO DOES NOT HONOR HIS FATHER AND HIS MOTHER] In the Hebrew there is the positive word מַקְלֶה, in the Greek ἀτιμάζων, that is, treating with indignity. Understand this concerning him whose crime is unknown, otherwise he was punished with death, Leviticus 20:19. The same judgment applies to other crimes for which the law prescribes death.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

MALEDICTUS QVI NON HONORAT PATREM SUUM ET MATREM] In Hebræo est vox positiva מַקְלֶה, in Græco ἀτιμάζων, id est, indignitate afficiens. Intellige hoc de eo, cujus crimen ignotum est, alioqui morte plecte- batur Levit. 20, 19. Idem judicium de aliis criminibus, qui- bus lex mortem indicit.

## 27:17
V. 17.

WHO MOVES THE BOUNDARIES. Of the fields, so that indeed by that method he may enlarge his estates through deceit and injustice.

Latin:

V. 17.

QUI TRANSFERT TERMINOS. Agrorum, ut nempe ea ratione per dolum & injustitiam dilatet prædia sua.

## 27:18
Verse 18.

CURSED IS HE WHO MAKES THE BLIND TO WANDER IN THE WAY] Diphilus: ἀγνοεῖς ἐν ταῖς ἀραῖς Ὅτι ἐστὶν, εἴτις μὴ φράσαι ὀρθὴν ὁδὸν. To this head must be referred the fault of those who give wicked counsel.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

MALEDICTUS QVI ERRARE FACIT CÆCUM IN ITINERE] Diphilus: ἀγνοεῖς ἐν ταῖς ἀραῖς Ὅτι ἐστὶν, εἴτις μὴ φράσαι ὀρθὴν ὁδὸν. Ad hoc caput referenda culpa eorum, qui prava dant con- silia.

## 27:26
Verse 26.

IN THE WORDS OF THIS LAW] The Greeks add πᾶσι. The Samaritan, which we have today, follows the Greeks, as it usually does. So also Paul in Galatians 3:10. These things are said against those who, having been warned, act stubbornly, or with a high hand, against some special precept.

The universal particle, which the Greeks and the Apostle, as well as our blessed Luther, add for the sake of ἐξηγήσεως, is understood in the text. For it is manifest that a curse is pronounced upon whoever transgresses any commandment, or who does not remain in all those things which are written in the book of the law. But those things are said only against those who, having been warned, act obstinately or with a high hand against any commandment of GOD, is a gloss of Grotius, consistent neither with the text nor with the Apostle's citation. The text is general and indefinite; and therefore it deals with every transgression of the law, not only that which is committed with a high hand. And the Apostle proves from the same that WE ALL outside of Christ are under a curse, because it is written, cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. Gal. 3, 10. Therefore, he concludes all men, by the force of this sentence, under a curse; just as he also teaches in verse 22, that the Scripture has concluded τὰ πάντα all things under sin. But do all men sin against the commandments of God with a high hand? And for this reason, as D. Pelargus observes, that exclamation and affirmation by the confirmatory particle Amen was especially enjoined upon the whole people: so that they might confess individually, without exception, that because of the corruption of nature they were subject to these thunderbolts of the law, and might with true faith take refuge in the ἐυλογίαν (blessing) of the blessed seed, Christ, in whom alone is salvation and life, who redeemed us from the curse of the law, while he was made a curse for us. Grotius wished to favor those Socinians who laboriously contend that not all sins are to be condemned, but only those which are committed with a high hand. Or even the Papists, from whom Bellarmine, lib. I. de amiss. grat. & statu peccat. cap. 12, wishes this curse to concern only more serious sins. However, he could have been instructed more correctly by his Menochius: who, in the place of the Apostle, rightly observed the force of the Apostolic argument, which certainly no one will be able to refute. The argument, he says, upon which the Apostle relies, is of this kind: Whoever violates ANY LAW, is cursed by the law. But ALL who are under the law, excluded from the faith and grace of Christ, violate the law, not only those who sin with a high hand, or designate more serious sins, such as idolatry, incest, homicide (as Bellarmine wishes such only to be understood). Therefore, all who are under the law are cursed. Tirinus has similar things on this passage, and before them Chrysostom, Theophylact, and other ancients. For the force of the Apostolic proof cannot stand otherwise. Nor is Grotius sufficiently consistent with himself, when in his annotations on Gal. 3, 10, he wishes all the other commandments to be understood, which had not yet been named in that chapter (Deut. 27). For he had previously conceded, not obscurely, that not only those, but also those which were named there, were comprehended by this general clause. But that he corrupts the passage of the Apostle ὅσοι γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων νόμε εἰσὶν, ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσὶ: that is, they have no promises of eternal and heavenly life, that argues a man too rash, nay, brazen, who believes that anything is permitted to him in Scripture. For it is not the Apostle's purpose to prove that there are no promises of eternal life in the law: but to conclude under condemnation those who wish to be justified by the works of the law. He teaches in v. 12 that the law promises eternal life, but to those who observe the law perfectly. Here, however, because no one observes the law perfectly, and all transgress it, he concludes all under condemnation by the voice of the law, so that he may teach that no one is justified by the law.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

IN SERMONIBUS LEGIS HUJUS] Addunt Græci πᾶσι. Sequitur Græcos, ut plerumque, quem hodie habe- mus, Samaritanus. Sic & Paulus Gal. 3, 10. Dicta hæc ad- versus eos, qui moniti pertinaciter, sive elata manu agunt con- tra præceptum aliquod speciale.

Particula universalis, quam ἐξηγήσεως causa addunt Græci & Apostolus, ut & B. Lutherus no- ster, in textu subintelligitur. Manifestum enim est, maledictum pronunciari, quisquis aliquod mandatum transgreditur, vel qui non permanet in omnibus illis, quæ in libro legis scripta sunt. Dici autem illa tantum adversus eos, qui moniti pertinaciter sive elata manu agunt contra aliquod præceptum DEI, glossa est Grotii, neque textui, neque allegationi Apostoli congrua. Textus generalis est, & indefinitus; ideoque de omni trans- gressione legis, non ea solum, quæ elata sit manu, agit. Et Apostolus ex eodem probat, OMNES nos extra Christum esse sub execratione, quia scri- ptum est, maledictus omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea. Galat. 3, 10. Omnes ergo homines, vi hujus sententiæ, sub maledicto concludit; uti etiam vers. 22. docet, Scripturam τὰ πάντα omnia conclusisse sub peccatis. At num omnes homines elata manu peccant contra præcepta Dei? Et hanc ob cau- sam, observante D. Pelargo, potissimum univer- so populo injuncta fuit illa exclamatio, & assevera- tio per particulam βεβαιωτικὴν Amen: ut fate- rentur singuli, absque exceptione, ob naturæ cor- ruptionem subjectos sese esse legis his fulminibus, fideque vera confugerent ad ἐυλογίαν benedicti se- minis Christi, in quo uno salus & vita, qui redemit nos ab execratione legis, dum factus est pro nobis execratio. Favere voluit istis Grotius Socinia- nis, qui non omnia peccata damnare, sed quæ elata manu committuntur, operose contendunt. Aut Papistis etiam, è quibus Bellarm. lib. I. de amiss. grat. & statu peccat. cap. 12. vult, hoc maledictum tantum peccata concernere graviora. Edoceri autem rectius poterat à Menochio suo: qui in lo- cum Apostoli vim argumenti Apostolici probe observavit, quam certe elidere nemo poterit. Ar- gumentum, inquit, quo nititur Apostolus, est hujus- modi: Quicunque ALIQUAM LEGEM vio- lat, est maledictus à lege. Atqui OMNES, qui sub lege sunt, seclusi à fide & gratia Christi, non so- lum qui elata manu peccant, aut graviora peccata designant, idololatria, incestu, homicidio (uti Bellarminus tales solum intelligi vult) legem vio- lant. Ergo omnes, qui sub lege, sunt maledicti. Si- milia habet Tirinus ad h. l. & ante illos Chryso- stomus, Theophylactus, & alii veteres. Nec enim aliter constare vis probationis Apostolicæ potest. Neque sibi constat satis Grotius, cum in annotat. ad Gal. 3, 10. intelligi vult omnia præcepta cætera, quæ nondum eo capite (Deut. 27.) nominata fue- rant. Nam non solum illa, sed etiam quæ nomi- nata ibi erant, generali hac clausula comprehendi antea haut obscure concesserat. Quod autem locum Apostoli hic corrumpit ὅσοι γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων νόμε εἰσὶν, ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσὶ: id est, nulla habent illi promissa vitæ æternæ, atque cælestis, id hominem nimis emerarium, imo effrontem arguit, qui quid- vis sibi licere in Scriptura, crediderit. Apostolo enim non est propositum probare, in lege nulla promissa esse vitæ æternæ: sed eos, qui ex operibus legis justificari volunt, sub condemnatione con- cludere. Promittere legem vitam æternam v. 12. docet, sed iis, qui observant perfecte legem. Hic vero, quia nemo observat legem perfecte, omnes eam transgrediuntur, omnes sub condemnatione voce legis concludit, ut neminem per legem justifi- cari doceat.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII.

An enumeration of various blessings and curses.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII.

Enumeratio benedictionum & maledictionum variarum.

## 28:2
Ver. 2.

ALL THESE BLESSINGS) Which were read aloud to the people together with the curses at the entry into the land. Joshua 8, at the end.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

UNIVERSÆ BENEDICTIONES ISTÆ) Quæ simul cum maledictionibus prælectæ populo in terræ ingressu. Josue 8. in fine.

## 28:4
Ver. 4.

BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB) Eminently fulfilled in Mary, the mother of Christ.

An alien example, unless a Papistic hypothesis is assumed, that Mary obtained by her own merits or certainly by her innocence and holiness that she should be the mother of Christ. For these blessings are promised to the observance of the law. Nor is Christ the fruit of the womb blessed in the way that is promised here to mere men who keep the law. He is blessed because he is the fountain of all blessing; for in him are all the nations of the earth blessed. Or if he be said to be blessed also passively, he certainly did not obtain that blessing by his own merits, because he merited whatever he merited for us, not for himself, and he was blessed from the womb: Holy from birth, Luke 1, 35.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

BENEDICTUS FRUCTUS VENTRIS TUI) Eximie impletum in Maria, matre Christi.

EXemplum ἀλλότριον, nisi Papistica supponatur hypothesis, quod Maria meritis suis vel certe innocentia ac sanctitate obtinuerit, ut esset Christi mater. Nam hæ benedictiones promittuntur observationi legis. Neque ita Christus benedictus est ventris fructus, uti hic ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις legem servantibus promittitur. Benedictus est, quia fons est omnis benedictionis; in ipso enim benedicuntur omnes gentes terræ. Aut si passive etiam benedictus dicatur, non certe meritis suis eam obtinuit benedictionem, quia nobis meruit, quicquid meruit, non sibi, & benedictus erat ab utero: Sanctus inde à nativitate, Luc. 1, 35.

## 28:5
BLESSED BE THY BARNS) The Chaldean for טנא has placed סלא, which appears to be a basket or hamper from Gen. 40, 17. That the Jews used baskets much appears from Matt. 14, 20. 16, 9. Mark 8, 19. 6, 43. Luke 9, 17. John 6, 13. and from Juvenal. The LXX did not badly call this κάρταλλον above in this book 26, 2. 4. where in the Hebrew is טנא. With the same Greek word they render סל corresponding to that Chaldean סלא in Jer. 6, 9. But elsewhere κανῶν, as in the said place of Genesis, Exod. 29, 3. 23. Levit. 8, 2. 25. 31. Num. 6, 15. 17. 19. Jud. 6, 9. Ἀποθήκην which the LXX have here is a noun of general kind.

Latin:

BENEDICTA HORREA TUA) Chaldæus pro טנא posuit סלא, quod esse canistrum sive cophinum apparet ex Genes. 40, 17. Cophino multum usos Judæos apparet ex Matth. 14, 20. 16, 9. Marci 8, 19. 6, 43. Luc. 9, 17. Joh. 6, 13. & ex Juvenali. Id κάρταλλον non male dixere LXX. supra hoc libro 26, 2. 4. ubi in Hebræo טנא. Eadem voce Græca reddunt סל respondens illi Chaldæo סלא Jerem. 6, 9. At alibi κανῶν, ut dicto loco Genes. Exod. 29, 3. 23. Levit. 8, 2. 25. 31. Num. 6, 15. 17. 19. Jud. 6, 9. Ἀποθήκην quod hic habent LXX. nomen est generis.

## 28:20
v. 20. THE LORD SHALL SEND UPON THEE FAMINE AND HUNGER.

Cornelius rightly corrects the Vulgate here. In the Hebrew it is: he shall send upon thee a curse, and confusion, or a terrible noise. AND REBUKE, not verbal, but real. For God's saying is doing, to rebuke is to destroy: whence the LXX render it consumption.

Latin:

v. 20. MITTET DOMINUS SUPER TE FAMEM ET ESURIEM.

Recte hic vulgat. corrigit Cornel. In Ebr. est: mittet in te maledictionem, & conturbationem, vel strepitum terribilem. ET INCREPATIONEM, non verbalem, sed realem. Dei enim dicere est facere, increpare est destruere: unde LXX. reddunt consumptionem.

## 28:22
AND WITH COLD) So also the LXX ῥίγει. But the Hebrew sounds clearly the opposite: for it comes from the verb דלק, which is to burn: whence Kimchi interprets it here as fever. The Greek καύσων, which is a kind of fever, corresponds best to the Hebrew. But the preceding word קדחת coming from a verb of equal meaning, is here indeed πυρετὸς, and in Latin fever: but in Levit. 26, 18 it is translated ἴκτερος, where the Latin has placed the general name of heat.

Latin:

ET FRIGORE) Sic & LXX. ῥίγει. At Hebræum plane contrarium sonat: venit enim a verbo דלק, quod est incendere: unde febrim hic interpretatur Kimchi. Græcum καύσων, quod febris est genus, optime Hebræo respondet. At vox præcedens קדחת a verbo paris significatus veniens, hic quidem πυρετὸς, & Latino febris: at Levit. 26, 18. ἴκτερος vertitur, ubi generale nomen ardoris posuit Latinus.

## 28:33
Vers. 33. THE FRUIT OF THY LAND AND ALL THY LABOURS SHALL A PEOPLE EAT WHOM THOU KNOWEST NOT] The impious soldier shall have these cultivated fallows, the barbarian these crops. Virgil. Eclog. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 33. FRUCTUS TERRÆ ET OMNES LABORES TUOS COMEDAT POPULUS QVEM IGNORAS] Impius hæc tam culta novalia miles habebit, Barbarus has segetes. Virgil. Eclog. 1.

## 28:36
Vers. 36.

AND THY KING] See 2 Kings 25. Jer. 39. and 52.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ET REGEM TUUM] Vide 2. Reg. 25. Jerem. 39. & 52.

## 28:48
Vers. 48.

THOU SHALT SERVE THINE ENEMY IN HUNGER AND THIRST AND NAKEDNESS AND IN ALL WANT] That these things happened to them through the Chaldeans, and indeed as a punishment for idolatry, Jeremiah shows in 5, 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. and in the whole of Lamentations. The Hebrews note from the Prophets that there are certain punishments for certain sins as if proper to them: famine from drought, on account of tithes not being paid equally, and false testimonies: famine from tumult, where those who are full do not pay tithes: pestilence, where those who ought to be killed are not, or the poor are neglected: evil beasts on account of perjuries and blasphemies: exile and captivity on account of idolatry, illicit lust, the unjust shedding of blood, the violation of the Sabbatical year.

Latin:

Vers. 48.

SERVIES INIMICO TUO IN FAME ET SITI ET NUDITATE ET OMNI PENURIA] Hæc per Chaldæos eis contigisse, & quidem in pœnam idololatriæ, ostendit Jeremias 5, 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. & totis Threnis. Notant autem ex Prophetis Hebræi esse certas pœnas certis peccatis velut proprias, famem ex siccitate, ob decimas non æqualiter persolutas, & falsa testimonia: famem ex tumultu, ubi saturi decimas non solvunt: pestilentiam, ubi non interficiuntur, qui debent, aut negliguntur pauperes: malas bestias ob perjuria & blasphemias: exilium & captivitatem ob idololatriam, Venerem illicitam, effusionem injustam sanguinis, violationem anni Sabbatici.

## 28:57
Vers. 57. AND WITH THE FILTH OF THE AFTERBIRTH] The Greeks τὸ κόριον αὐτῆς. So also Rabbi Solomon בנים קטנים. The same view was held by the Chaldean.

FOR THEY SHALL EAT THEM] See the fulfillment in Lamentations 4, 10. and compare 2 Kings 6, 28. and those things which are in Josephus regarding the siege of Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 57. ET ILLUVIE SECUNDARUM] Græci τὸ κόριον αὐτῆς. Sic & Rabbi Salomo בנים קטנים. Idem visum Chaldæo.

COMEDENT ENIM EOS] Implementum vide Thren. 4, 10. & confer 2. Reg. 6, 28. & quæ apud Josephum in obsidione Hierosolymitana.

## 28:66
Vers. 66. THY LIFE SHALL BE AS IF HANGING] As if hanging by a thread, as the Latins say.

AND YOU SHALL NOT BELIEVE IN YOUR LIFE] You shall not be certain of your life, for thus can תאמין be best translated; this is what Paul called ἀστατεῖν in 1 Cor. 4:11, to be tossed about in continuous dangers and anxiety.

The Fathers with great consensus accept these things concerning Christ, as a prophecy about the cross of Christ, and our life being suspended on the cross, which explanation is that of Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 16; of Athanasius on the Incarnation, as also on the salutary advent of Christ, and in the questions to Antiochus; of Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 13, the illuminator; and of Procopius on this passage; and of Damascene, oration on the Holy Sabbath, and book 4, on the Orthodox Faith, chapter 12. And among the Latins, Tertullian, book on the Trinity; Jerome, or Rufinus on the Creed, which is also ascribed to Cyprian; Lactantius, book 4, Institutes, chapter 9; Rabanus, Bernard, etc.

Augustine, book 16 against Faustus, chapter 22. Leo, Sermon 8 on the Passion, as if it were said: Christ is your life, O Jew, who was seen by you hanging on the cross, and yet you did not believe in him. Tertullian, in the book against the Jews, chapter 11, reads: Your life will be hanging on the wood, before your eyes, and you will not believe in your life. If anyone denies that a prophecy about Christ is contained here, because these things are included among the curses: Augustine replies, among other things, that this will be the greatest curse of all, that the Jews were not going to believe in Christ crucified, that is, in their own life. For he has it thus in the aforementioned book. But indeed, among the other curses, this also is placed; is it therefore not a prophecy? Since the others, among which it is placed, are nothing other than a prophecy? Or is it therefore not a prophecy about Christ, because those things which follow in that reading, whether preceding or consequent, seem to have nothing to do with Christ? As if indeed there were anything worse among the curses that befell the Jews for the merit of their pride and impiety than to see their life, that is, the Son of God, hanging, and not to believe in their life. For curses, when they are spoken from prophecy, are not from the evil wish of one imprecating, but from the foreknowing Spirit denouncing. Pelargus, in his Commentary on Deuteronomy, in a special explanation of this aphorism on page 419, considers that this kind of execration concerning our life, Christ, suspended on the cross, is expressed among other curses for two main reasons: 1. Because that misery of our race from the condemnation and curse of the law was the προκαταρκτικὴ (preliminary cause) of the passion of Christ, on account of which it was absolutely necessary for Christ to suffer for us, since otherwise no mortal could have escaped the force and sense of that lightning bolt. 2. Because Christ was made a curse for us, according to that saying, accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. However, it seems that a simpler answer can be given, that the cause of these curses and punishments is being rendered here, which will happen to the people in the last time (of the Jewish polity), and why God is going to send upon them a fearful heart, failing eyes, and sorrow of soul: והיו BECAUSE YOUR LIVES WILL BE HANGING FOR YOU FROM THE REGION, so that here Vav may be αἰτιολογικὸν (etiological), or causal. And 'hanging for you' can be taken as if 'hanging by the Jews': since the crucifixion of Christ was the primary cause of the total destruction, blinding, and subsequent despair of the Jews. Nothing also prevents joining the rest in the sense of Tertullian, Leo the Great, and others, so that, for instance, it is added, and you will fear night and day (out of despair) ולא־תאמין BECAUSE you will not believe in your life: For this is the sole cause of the perpetual fear and despair of the Jews, because they do not believe in Christ crucified IN THE LIFE HANGING on the wood of the cross, or ἀπισίᾳ (unbelief). The whole sentence will perhaps flow most conveniently thus: The Lord will give you sorrow of soul: BECAUSE your life will be hanging FOR YOU for your sake, or for your good, and yet you will fear night and day, BECAUSE you will not believe in your life, although it is FOR YOU, for the sake of liberation from every execration, and YOUR SALVATION HANGING on the cross. Galatians 3:13. In that it is said FROM THE REGION, Pelargus notes that the place of Christ's cross outside the gates of the city of Jerusalem is designated (which we leave to its own place): comparing here also the disputation of Gregentius, a certain African Archbishop, with Herbanus the Jew, a Nomodidascalos (teacher of the law), which can be read there, and to the objection that in the Hebrew it is not read YOUR LIFE, but YOUR LIVES, from Galatinus, book 8, Cath. Ver., chapter 17, and Porchetus Victor, chapter 16, he replies: that Moses said LIVES in the plural for this reason, because just as the nature of the Messiah is twofold, so also is his life, namely GOD & soul: and these two lives, which were to be hung for us on the cross, are ours, because they are united for our salvation in Christ.

Which are also read in the Pugio Fidei, part 3, distinction 3, chapter 16, page 665, and are taken from there: where the author, Raimundus Martinus, says that the hanging of GOD and the Messiah is HAD QUITE EXPRESSLY in Deuteronomy 28:66. Compare John 14:6, 1 John 1:2, chapter 5:11, 12, 20. Saint Augustine observes that not even Faustus himself could have denied that these things could be understood of Christ, and to those who say that the same things can be explained otherwise, he replies in the aforementioned book: That these words can be understood otherwise, someone may say: but that they cannot be understood of Christ, not even Faustus dared to say: NOR WILL ANYONE AT ALL DARE, unless he denies either that Christ is the life, or that he was seen by the Jews hanging, or that they did not believe in him. Since, however, he himself says, I am the Life, and it is established that he hung before the eyes of the Jews who did not believe in him: I do not see why we should doubt that he also wrote about Christ, of whom Christ says: For he wrote about me. We add also the opinion of Leo the Great, Sermon 8 on the Passion of the Lord. With Christ exalted through the cross, let not only that appearance occur to the sight of the mind which was in the eyes of the impious, to whom it was said through Moses, your life will be hanging before your eyes, and you will fear day and night, and you will not believe in your life. For they could think of nothing in the crucified Lord except their own crime, having a fear not by which true faith is justified, but by which an iniquitous conscience is tormented. But let our intellect, which the Spirit of truth illuminates, receive the glory of the cross radiating to heaven and earth with a pure and free heart. Compare also Theophanes, oration on the elevation of the cross, Vol. 9, Bibliotheca Patrum, page 630. Does this opinion, thus exposed, deserve such a grave censure as Sixtinus Amama brought in his Anti-Barbarus? Bibl. p. 376. Let sensible readers now judge: He who can approach the sources, he says, even if he be a Crassus, cannot but LAUGH at such ABSURDITIES. But what is contrary to the sources here? What is absurd, what, I pray, is worthy of laughter in this interpretation of the Holy Fathers? Doubtless because Junius posits a proverbial expression here, taken from physical things which hang by a thin thread and are about to fall, for that reason the Holy Fathers were to be harassed by Amama and held up to ridicule, as if they were ignorant of the proverbial expression. But they were not ignorant that the words of Moses could be taken in such a way, but they denied that they ought to be so taken; nay, they felt that they must be understood entirely of Christ, as we showed from Augustine arguing against Faustus. And Pelargus, even before Amama was born, judged that the gloss of Tremellius (Junius) and the OBSTINACY of those like him could easily be refuted from the Fathers themselves. Athanasius certainly with a loud voice and very clearly judged the crucifixion to have been predicted here, and he cited that passage three times, in his oration on the incarnation, having it thus: Perhaps you ask, hearing the prophecies about the death of Christ, to learn what exactly was pre-signified concerning THE CROSS among the Prophets: For it was not passed over in silence concerning it also, but this very thing was OPENLY declared by the saints. For Moses first with A GREAT VOICE already before announced (προεπαγγέλλει) saying: ὄψεσθε τὴν ζωὴν ὑμῶν κρεμαμένην ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὑμῶν καὶ ὐ μὴ πισεύσητε: you shall see your life hanging before your eyes, and you shall not believe. Nor did St. Irenaeus doubt this sense, which he seems to have assumed as received in the early Church, and lying beyond all dispute: The Word, he says, was made flesh and hung upon the wood, that he might recapitulate all things in himself, and his own men did not receive him, just as he manifested all things: and your life shall be hanging before your eyes. Therefore those who did not receive him, did not receive life. The African Archbishop, whom we mentioned, to the Jew the same sense, from the context with Amama, Junius, & others, he did not fear to answer the one pressing, 'You heap up an UNEQUAL word upon a word.' For he says, 'You shall see LIFE HANGING.' But whatever hangs (the literal sense presses, from which one certainly should not rashly deflect to a proverbial expression) is either a body or some matter, which does not hang without that which holds it by force, because they cannot hang by themselves. There is therefore NO DOUBT that Moses said this concerning the humanity of the only-begotten Son of GOD, that it was to come to pass that He would hang in the flesh from the wood of the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 66. ERIT VITA TUA QVASI PENDENS] Quasi a filo pendens, ut Latini loquuntur.

ET NON CREDES VITÆ TUÆ] Non eris certus vitæ tuæ, ita enim optime verti potest תאמין; hoc est, quod ἀστατεῖν dixit Paulus 1. Cor. 4, 11. in continuis periculis & anxietate jactari.

Patres magno consensu hæc de Christo accipiunt, ceu prophetiam de cruce Christi, & vita nostra in cruce suspendenda, quæ explicatio est Irenei l. 5. c. 16. Athanasii de incarnat. ut & de salutari adventu Christi, nec non in quæstion. ad Antioch. Cyrilli Hieros. Catech. 13. illuminator.& Procopii in h. l. ac Damasc. orat. in S. Sabbat. & l. 4. de Orth. Fid. c. 12. Et è Latinis Tertull. lib. de Trinit. Hieron. vel Ruffini in Symbol. quod Cypriano etiam adscribitur. Lactant. l. 4. Inst. c. 9. Rabani, Bernh. &c.

Augustini lib. 16. contra Faustum cap. 22. Leon. Serm. 8. de passione, quasi dicatur: Christus est vita tua, o Judæe, qui a te visus est pendens in cruce & tamen tu illi non credidisti. Tertull. l. c. Jud. c. 11 legit: Erit vita tua pendens in ligno, ante oculos tuos, & non credes vitæ tuæ. Si quis neget hic prophe- tiam haberi de Christo, quia inter maledictiones hæc continentur: Respondet August. inter alia omnia maximam hanc maledictionem futuram, quod Judæi in Christum crucifixum, in vitam nem- pe suam non sint credituri. Ita enim habet l. c. At enim inter cætera maledicta & hoc positum est, num ideo non est Prophetia? cum & cætera, inter quæ po- situm est, nihil sint aliud quam Prophetia? aut ideo non est de Christo Prophetia, quia illa, quæ in ea lectio- ne vel præcedentia, vel consequentia consequuntur, ni- hil pertinere videntur ad Christum? Quasi vero quic- quam sit pejus inter maledicta, quæ Judæis pro merito superbiæ, impietatis acciderunt, quam videre vitam suam, hoc est, Filium Dei pendentem, & non credere vi- tæ suæ. Maledicta enim cum ex Prophetia dicuntur, non sunt de malo voto imprecantis, sed de præscio Spi- ritu denunciantis. Pelargus in Comm. in Deut. peculiari explicatione hujus aphorismi pag. 419. ob duplicem potissimum causam inter maledicta alia hanc quoque execrationis speciem de vita nostra, Christo, in cruce suspensa, exprimi censet: 1. Quia miseria illa generis nostri a condemnatione & maledi- ctione legis προκαταρκτικὴ fuit passionis Christi, propter quam necesse fuit omnino Christum pro nobis pati, cum alioqui nemo mortalium fulminis istius vim sensumque effugere potuisset. 2. Quia Christus pro no- bis factus est maledictio, juxta illud, execrabilis quis- quis pendet in ligno. Simplicius autem videtur re- sponderi posse, quod causa hic reddatur istarum maledictionum, & pœnarum, quæ tempore novis- simo (politias Judaicæ) populo evenient, & cur Deus pavidum cor, oculos deficientes & dolorem ani- mi, immissurus ipsi sit: והיו QUIA ERUNT VI- TÆ TUÆ SUSPENSÆ TIBI E REGIONE, ut hic Vav sit αἰτιολογικὸν, vel causale. Et sus- pensæ tibi accipi poterit, quasi a Judæis suspensæ: si- quidem crucifixio Christi causa fuerit præcipua totalis interitus, excæcationis, & consequutæ de- sperationis Judæorum. Nihil etiam vetat cætera sensu Tertulliani, Leonis M. & aliorum jungere, ut nempe addatur, & pavebis nocte & die (præ despe- ratione) ולא־תאמין QUIA non credes in vitam tuam: Nam hæc causa unica est pavoris perpetui, & de- sperationis Judæorum, quia non credunt in Chri- stum crucifixum IN VITAM SUSPENSAM in ligno crucis, seu ἀπισίᾳ. Tota oratio fic fortas- sis quam commodissime fluet: Dominus dabit ti- bi dolorem animi: QUIA vita tua erit suspensa TIBI pro te, vel tuo bono, & pavebis tamen nocte & die, QUIA non credes in vitam tuam, quamvis TIBI, ob liberationem ab omni execratione, & Salutem Tuam SUSPENSAM in cruce. Gal. 3, 13. In eo, quod dicitur E REGIONE Pelargus no- tat designari locum crucis Christi extra portas ur- bis Hierosol. (quod suo loco relinquimus:) conferens etiam hic disputationem Gregentii Archi-Episcopi cujusdam Africani cum Her- bano Judæo Nomodidascalo, quæ ibi legi po- terit, & ad objectionem, quod in Ebr. non le- gatur VITA TUA, sed VITÆ TUÆ e Gala- tino lib. 8. Cath. Ver. cap. 17. & Porcheto victor. cap. 16. respondet: quod propterea pluraliter di- xerit VITAS Moses, quia sicut duplex natura Messiæ, ita & ejus vita, DEUS sc. & anima: & hæ duæ vitæ, quæ pro nobis in cruce suspendendæ erant, nostræ sunt, quia unitæ ad salutem nostram in Christo.

Quae leguntur etiam in Pugione Fidei part. 3. dist. 3. c. 16. p. 665. atque inde petita sunt: ubi autor Raimund. Martin. de suspendio DEI ac Messiae, SATIS EXPRESSE haberi Deut. 28, 66. Conf. Joh. 14, 6. 1. Joh. 1, 2. cap. 5, 11. 12. 20. S. Augustinus observat, ne Faustum quidem ipsum negare potuis- se, haec de Christo intelligi posse, iisque qui aliter eadem explicari posse ajunt, respondet l. c. Quae verba & aliter posse intelligi, potest aliquis dicere: de Christo autem non posse intelligi, nec Faustus ausus est dicere: NEC QUISQUAM PROR- SUS AUDEBIT, nisi qui negaverit, aut Christum esse vitam aut Judaeis visum non esse pendentem, aut eos illi non credidisse. Cum vero & ipse dicat, Ego sum Vita, & eum pependisse constet ante ocu- los ei non credentium Judaeorum: non video cur dubitare debeamus, id etiam de Christo scripsisse illum, de quo Christus ait: Ille enim de me scripsit. Ad- dimus & Leonis M. sententiam Serm. 8. de Pas- sion. Dom. Exaltato per crucem Christo non illa tantum species aspectui mentis occurrat, quae fuit in oculis impiorum, quibus per Mosen dictum est, erit vita tua pendens ante oculos tuos, & timebis die, ac nocte, & non credes vitae tuae. Isti enim nihil in cru- cifixo Domino praeter facinus suum cogitare potue- runt, habentes timorem non quo fides vera justificatur, sed quo conscientia iniqua torquetur. Noster vero intellectus, quem Spiritus veritatis illuminat, gloriam crucis caelo, terraeque radiantem, puro ac libero corde suscipiat. Conf. & Theophan. orat. de elevat. cruc. T. 9. Biblioth. Patr. p. 630. Haec sententia ita expo- sita num tam gravem censuram mereatur, quam tu- lit Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barb. Bibl. p. 376. ju- dicent jam cordati lectores: Qui fontes, inquit, adire potest, si vel Crassus sit, non potest ad tales IN- EPTIAS non RIDERE. Quid vero hic fonti- bus adversum? Quid ineptum, quid obsecro, risu dignum in hac S. Patrum interpretatione? Nimirum quia Junius proverbialem hic loquu- tionem ponit, sumtam a rebus corporeis, quae a te- nui filo pendent jamjam ruitura, idcirco ab Ama- ma exagitandi erant S. Patres, nasoque suspendendi adunco, ac si ignorarint locutionem proverbia- lem. At non ignorarunt posse tali modo accipi ver- ba Mosis, sed negarunt accipi ita debere, imo sen- serunt de Christo ea omnino intelligenda esse, ut ex Augustino contra Faustum disputante ostendi- mus. Et Tremellii (Junii) glossema, ac similium PERTINACIAM ex ipsis Patribus facile argui pos- se, jam ante natum Amamam judicavit Pelargus. Athanasius certe μεγάλῃ φωνῇ καὶ λίαν τηλαυγῶς hic praedictam crucifixionem judicavit, eumque locum ternis vicibus adduxit, orat. de incarnat. ita habens: Fortasse auditis de morte Christi vaticiniis requiras discere, quidnam DE CRUCE apud Prophe- tas presignificatum fuerit: Nam de ea quoq́; tacitum non fuit, sed APERTE hoc ipsum a sanctis declaratum est. Primus enim Moses INGENTI VOCE jam an- tea denunciavit (προεπαγγέλλει) dicens: ὄψεσθε τὴν ζωὴν ὑμῶν κρεμαμένην ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὑμῶν καὶ ὐ μὴ πισεύσητε: vitam vestram suspensam ante oculos vestros videbitis, & non credetis. Neque dubitavit S. Ireneus de hoc sensu, quem ceu rece- ptum in Ecclesia prisca, & ἔξω πάσης τῆς συῤῥάξεως κείμενον supposuisse videtur: Caro, inquiens, factum est verbum & pependit super ligno, ut universa in se- metipso recapitularet, & sui proprii illum non recepe- runt homines, quemadmodum universa manifestavit: & erit vita tua pendens ante oculos. Qui igitur non receperunt illum, non acceperunt vitam. Ar- chi-Episcopus Africanus, quem diximus, Judaeo eundem sensum, e contextu cum Amama, Junio, & aliis, urgenti non veritus est respondere, IN- ÆQVALE verbum verbo congeris. Dicit enim VITAM PENDENTEM videbitis. Quic- quid autem pendet, (urget τὸ ῥητὸν, a quo utique te- mere ad proverbialem loquutionem deflecten- dum non est) vel corpus, vel materia aliqua est, quæ non pendet absque eo, quod per vim continet, quia a se ipfis pendere nequeunt. NON igitur DUBIUM est, quin de humanitate unigeniti DEI Filii hoc dixerit Moses, quod futurum erat, hunc carne pendere a li- gno crucis.

## 28:68
Vers. 68. GOD SHALL BRING YOU BACK IN SHIPS TO EGYPT] Under the successors of Alexander, a huge multitude of Jews immigrated to Alexandria. Hecataeus: 'And not a few (myriads) of Jews also moved into Egypt and Phoenicia at the death of Alexander because of the sedition in Syria.' Philo in Flaccum and Josephus in Antiquities 12, 2. 3. 13, 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 14, 17. 18, 10 also mention this.

Others more correctly say this was fulfilled under Titus from Josephus, book 7, Bell. Jud. chap. 16, where he teaches that Jews captured by the Romans under 17 years of age were sold into Egypt in such abundance that buyers could scarcely be found. B. Chytreus also explains verse 49, concerning a nation to be brought from afar upon the Jews, just as an eagle flies, as referring to the Romans, or to the Eagle of the Roman Empire and Vespasian, from a comparison of Matt. 24 and Luke 19. Moreover, because Moses names ships, it is clear that in his time there were already ships and vessels. Since, therefore, historians and poets make the first ships of the Gentiles those of Jason and the Argonauts, who were a little before the Trojan War, when Jephthah was judging or ruling the Hebrews, it is manifest how much older the history of Moses is than that of the Gentiles: since Moses in his own time spoke of ships and vessels as things known to the people.

OF WHICH I SAID TO YOU, THAT YOU SHOULD NOT SEE IT AGAIN.

A similar passage is chap. 17, 16. Jehovah said to you, 'You shall not add to return,' i.e., to Egypt. That is nowhere read. Yet it was said: because it is written here. Therefore, it is not an unwritten word because it is written: even if it is not written in the preceding parts. However, the word 'I SAID' can also be taken as referring to a decree: that the Lord had determined within Himself that they should not return to Egypt: which will of His He manifested in chap. 17, 16. But here He threatens concerning a penal reduction after the Jewish polity was destroyed: 'GOD shall bring you back.' As long as the people of God remained, they ought not to have returned to Egypt: but once the Jewish polity was overturned, by the just judgment of God they were sold and brought back to Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 68. REDUCET TE DEUS CLASSIBUS IN ÆGYPTUM] Sub successoribus Alexandri ingens Judæo- rum multitudo immigravit Alexandriam. Hecatæus: ὀὐκ ὀλί- γαι δὲ (μυριάδες) Ἰυδαίων καὶ κατὰ τὸν Ἀλεξάνδρε θάνατον εἰς Αἴγυπτον καὶ Φοινίκην μετέστησαν διὰ τὴν ἐν Συρίᾳ ςάσιν. Meminere & Philo in Flaccum, & Josephus Antiquæ Histo- riæ 12, 2. 3. 13, 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 14, 17. 18, 10.

Alii rectius sub Tito id impletum dicunt e Jo- sepho lib. 7. Bell. Jud. cap. 16. ubi docet Judæos a Romanis captos minores 17, annis in Ægyptum venditos tanta copia, ut vix invenirentur emto- res. B. Chytreus etiam vers. 49. de gente a longinquo adducenda super Judæos, quemadmodum volat aquila, de Romanis explicat, vel de Romani Imperii Aquila, & Vespasiano, e collatione Matth. 24. & Luc. 19. Cæterum quia classes nominat Mo- ses, liquet ipsius tempore jam classes & naves fuis- se. Quum ergo primas naves gentiles Histo- rici, & Poetæ faciant Jasonis & Argonautarum, qui paulo ante bellum Trojanum fuere, cum Jephta Ebræos judicaret, vel regeret, manifestum est, quanto antiquior sit Mosis historia, quam gentilium: quum Moses suo tempore de classibus & navibus, ceu notis populo loquutus sit.

DE QUA DIXI TIBI, UT EAM AM- PLIUS NON VIDERES.

Locus similis est cap. 17, 16. Jehovah dixit vo- bis, non addetis ad revertendum sc. in Ægyptum. Id nuspiam legitur. Dictum tamen fuit: quia hic Scriptum est. Non ergo, quia scriptum, verbum est ἄγραφον: etsi in anterioribus scriptum non sit. Potest tamen etiam verbum DIXI de decreto acci- pi: quod penes se id Dominus constituerit, ne re- vertantur in Ægyptum: quam voluntatem suam cap. 17, 16. manifestavit. Hic autem de reductione pœnali, post destructam Politiam Judaicam mina- tur: Reducet te DEUS. Quamdiu mansit po- pulus Dei, reverti non debuit in Ægyptum: ever- sa vero politia Judaica, justo Dei judicio venditi & reducti sunt in Ægyptum.

## 29:1 Argument
CHAP. XXIX. The covenant of the Israelites with GOD. vers. 1. BESIDES THE COVENANT.

This covenant, which is now being discussed, embraces both the manner of the law and its end, namely the Gospel of Christ, as Junius says in his Commentary on this passage, which Cocceius proves, who in chapter 29 and following prepared a learned work under the title THE LAST THINGS OF MOSES, in which he is altogether to be praised because he does not, like his Calvin, snatch away most of the oracles of the Old Testament from Christians, or render them ambiguous, but skillfully explains them concerning Christ, and in many places even seeks Christ with pious zeal, even if he does not find Him. He attributes much to himself, whence there are 'private interpretations' (ἰδίαι ἐπιλύσεις) throughout. Because of his remarkable knowledge of Hebraism and his scrutiny of new things in the old, the lucubrations of this man are worthy of reading, but they must be read with judgment, lest one be captured by a specious analysis before a more accurate discussion. Certainly, very many things in this explanation of the last things of Moses deserve just consideration and a prudent critical judgment (ἐπίκρισιν).

Latin:

CAP. XXIX. Fœdus Israelitarum cum DEO. vers. 1. PRÆTER FOEDUS.

HOc fœdus, de quo nunc agitur, & modum le- gis complectitur & finem ejus, nempe Evan- gelium Christi, dicente Junio in Comment. ad h. l. quod probat Coccejus, qui in cap. 29. & seqq. eruditum opus sub titulo ULTIMA MOSIS adornavit, in quo laudandus omnino est, quod pleraque oracula Vet. Test. non cum Calvino suo Christianis eripiat, aut ambigua reddat, sed dextre de Christo explicet, in multis etiam Chri- stum pio studio quærat, etsi non inveniat. Mul- tum tribuit sibi ipsi, unde passim ἰδίαι ἐπιλύσεις. Ob insignem Ebraïsmi notitiam, & scrutinium novorum in veteribus lectu dignæ hujus Viri lu- cubrationes, sed legendæ cum judicio, ne specio- sa analysi ante accuratiorem discussionem quis ca- piatur. Plurima certe in hac ultimorum Mosis explicatione justam merentur considerationem, ac prudentem ἐπίκρισιν.

## 29:4
THE LORD HAS NOT GIVEN YOU A HEART TO UNDERSTAND] That is, you have not received. Thus, 'given' in law is often understood as that which is also 'received.' Thus Maimonides interprets it here. Thus the word 'to give' is taken also in 2 Tim. 2:25. Thus 'Satan filled' (ἐπλήρωσεν ὁ Σατανᾶς) for 'you allowed yourself to be filled by Satan,' Acts 5:3. Thus many words are taken in that meaning which include not only the purpose and the power of effecting, but also the outcome, such as 'to reveal' in Isa. 53:1, 'to give' in John 6:39, 'to send' in Matt. 10:34.

Latin:

NON DEDIT VOBIS DOMINUS COR INTELLI- GENS] Id est, non accepistis. Sic datum in jure sæpe in- telligitur quod & acceptum est. Sic Maimonides hic inter- pretatur. Sic vox dandi sumitur & 2. Tim. 2,25. Sic ἐπλή- ρωσεν ὁ Σατανᾶς pro sivisti impleri a Satana. Actor. 5,3. Sic multa verba sumuntur eo fignificatu qui non propositum tantum & vim efficiendi, sed & eventum includant, ut reve- lare Esa. 53. 1. dare Joan. 6, 39. mittere Matth. 10, 34.

## 29:5
Verf. 5.

HE BROUGHT YOU) In the Hebrew it is, 'I brought you,' with the person changed. For it is understood, says the Lord, as in Isa. 53 and often elsewhere.

Latin:

Verf. 5.

ADDUXIT VOS) In Hebræo est, adduxi vos, mu- tata persona. Subauditur enim, ait Dominus, ut Ef. 53. & alibi sæpe.

## 29:15
Verse 15.

TO ALL PRESENT AND ABSENT ] That is, with those who are born and those who shall be born. For the covenant is one pertaining to the whole nation. Thus Kings say that they give fiefs to this man and his descendants, who are not yet born: yet they do not believe in the προϋπαρξιν (pre-existence) of souls with this man, which the Jews labor to construct from this passage.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

CUNCTIS PRÆSENTIBUS ET ABSENTIBUS ] Id est, cum iis qui nati sunt & qui nascentur. Fœdus enim est ad gentem totam pertinens. Sic dicunt Reges se dare feuda huic & posteris ejus, qui nondum nati sunt: neque tamen cum hoc agunt προϋπαρξιν credunt animarum, quam ex hoc loco adstruere laborant Judæi.

## 29:18
Verse 18.

BY THE LORD OUR GOD ] Faith in one God, the foundation of true piety and concord. Therefore Jacob was accustomed often to ask his family whether they believed with him in one God. Maimonides records this.

A ROOT BEARING GALL AND BITTERNESS ] ῥίζα ἄνω φύεσα ἐν χολῇ καὶ πικρίᾳ (a root springing up in gall and bitterness) say the Greeks: from whence the words were taken for Heb. 12:15. Instead of πολλὴν καὶ πικρίαν (much and bitterness), Luke said χολὴν πικρίας (gall of bitterness), Acts 8:23. For the one is an explanation of the other. The root is thought, as the Chaldean rightly says here. The gall-like bitterness, evil works.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

A DOMINO DEO NOSTRO] In unum Deum fides, fundamentum veræ pietatis & concordiæ. Ideo Jacobus so- litus sæpe interrogare familiam suam, an secum crederent unum Deum. Memorat Maimonides.

RADIX GERMINANS FEL ET AMARITUDI- NEM] ῥίζα ἄνω φύεσα ἐν χολῇ καὶ πικρίᾳ Græci: unde sumta verba ad Hebr. 12, 15. Pro πολλὴν καὶ πικρίαν dixit Lucas χολὴν πικρίας, Act. 8, 23. Est enim alterum alterius ἐξήγησις. Radix est cogitatio, ut hic recte Chaldæus. Ama- rities fellea, opera mala.

## 29:19
Verse 19.

AND THAT THE DRUNKEN MAY CONSUME THE THIRSTY ] In the Hebrew: that he may add the drunken to the thirsty, that is, that the drunken may draw the sober along with him to dance: by which are allegorically indicated the beginnings of evils, which must be avoided, however slight, lest they always creep further. Thus the Latins say: Vara vibiam. Certain Hebrews interpret the thirsty as the intellect poorly irrigated, but the drunken as the concupiscent part.

Regarding this interpretation, Cocceius, last Mof. §. 234. To interpret it thus is to dance out of the choir, nor does רוה signify drunken, nor is it about dancing or צמא, nor is the thirsty sober, nor if the drunken draws the sober, is the drunken added to the sober, but on the contrary the sober to the drunken. Cocceius cites 9 other explanations there, and rejects them. But he brings forth another new one, and as I believe, unheard of. I confess that I am unable to grasp its meaning, even though he is prolix in explaining it. He says the Church is called thirsty, which has the desire and expectation of those things which have been promised. But the satiated one is that to which the promise is represented. But what does this have to do with the matter? He wants it to be about a fault alien to the covenant, and he makes it twofold: (1.) an inclination of the heart toward idolatry. (2.) The adjunction of the irrigated to the thirsty. And that this was the fault of the Jews, who did not want to accept Christ abrogating the ceremonies of the law, but altogether wanted to combine the satiated with the thirsty in state and condition. But these things are alien, nay even twisted, which no one would rashly extract from these words except Cocceius. The Lord warns that they should beware lest there be among them a malignant root, lest profane men, having held the divine warning in contempt, walking in the hardness of their hearts, promise themselves peace and impunity, and add the drunken to the thirsty, which Blessed Luther rendered quite conveniently: Bisz daß die Trunckene mit den Durstigen dahin fahren (Until the drunken perish with the thirsty), lest the wealthy be destroyed with the thirsty. Compare Osiander's paraphrase. To which also the LXX go: ἵνα μὴ συναπολέσῃ ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς τὸν ἀναμάρτητον (that the sinner may not destroy the sinless). Thus also Cornel. correcting the common reading of the Vulgate: ET ABSUMAT (so it must be read with the Roman and Royal [editions], not assumat, as the Plantin [edition] has) EBRIA SITIENTEM. The Hebrew is, that the drunken may be added to the thirsty, namely in punishment as well as in fault: whence the LXX clearly translate, that the sinner for gives the innocent one at the same time. For the word NON, which the LXX add, saying 'let him not destroy,' is not in the Hebrew, and it was added only prohibitively, whence it is better and more plainly omitted. It seems, however, that at that time there was a proverb: 'the drunkard leads the thirsty or the sober,' or if it must be rendered entirely SATUR SITIENTEM (as with us 'the blind leads the blind'), that is, the impious and wicked man, sated with impiety, leads the simple and greedy—not so much for truth and wisdom, as Rabanus wishes, as for novelty and pleasure; for drunkenness and thirst are of the same thing—leads and seduces to his wicked pleasures and idolatries. Paul Fagius, at this place, having reviewed the expositions of the Hebrews and Steuchus, says: 'To me, however (saving the judgment of others), it seems to be a proverbial sentence: to add the drunkard to the thirsty or to be consumed, the drunkard with the thirsty (for it can be read in either way). For the Hebrew infinitive ספות can be derived either from the verb ספה, that is, 'he added, he joined,' or from the verb ספה, 'he consumed, he destroyed'; by which it is signified that it will come to pass that the innocent perishes with the guilty. It is implied, therefore, that if an impious idolater arises among them, who is tolerated and not immediately taken from their midst, it will eventually come to pass that this evil will also redound upon the good and the innocent.

Latin:

Verf. 19.

ET ABSUMAT EBRIA SITIENTEM] In Hebræo: ut addat ebriam sitienti, id est, ebria sobriam secum trahat ad saltandum: quo allegorice indicantur vitanda, quamvis levia malorum initia, ne semper longius serpant. Sic Latini dicunt: Vara vibiam. Hebræi quidam sitientem interpre- tantur intellectum male irrigatum, ebriam vero partem con- cupiscentem.

De hac interpretatione Coccejus, ult. Mof. §. 234. Sic interpretari est extra chorum saltare, nec רוה significat ebriam, neque de saltatione vel צמא, neque sitiens est sobria, neque si ebria trahat sobriam, ebria additur sobria, sed contra sobria ebriæ. Addu- cit ibi 9. alias explicationes Coccejus, easque rejicit. Sed aliam novam, & uti credo, inauditam profert. Cujus sensum, etsi prolixus in ea explicanda sit, fa- teor, me assequi non posse.
