Ecclesiam dicit sitien- tem vocatam, quæ habet desiderium & expecta- tionem eorum, quæ promissa sunt. Satiatam autem eam, cui repræsentatur promissio. Quid autem hæc ad rhombum? De culpa aliena a fœde- re agi vult, eamque duplicem facit: (1.) inclinatio- nem cordis ad idololatriam. (2.) Adjunctionem ir- rigui ad sitiens. Et hanc fuisse culpam Judæorum, qui noluerunt Christum accipere abrogantem ceremo- nias legis, sed omnino voluerunt, satiatam cum siti- culosa in statu & conditione combinare. Sed hæc aliena sunt, imo & contorta, quæ non temere quis præter Coccejum ex his verbis exsculpserit. Monet Dominus, caveant, ne sit inter illos radix ma- ligna, ne homines prophani susque deque habita divina monitione, in duritie cordis ambulantes, si- bi pacem & impunitatem promittant, & ebriam siti- enti addant, quod B. Lutherus satis commode red- didit: Bisz daß die Trunckene mit den Durstigen da- hin fahren, ne opulenti cum sitientibus perimantur. Confer Osiandr. paraphr. Quo abeunt etiam LXX. ἵνα μὴ συναπολέσῃ ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς τὸν ἀναμάρ- τητον. Sic etiam Cornel. corrigens Vulgatæ com- munem lectionem: ET ABSUMAT (ita legen- dum cum Rom. & Regiis, non assumat, ut habent Plantin.) EBRIA SITIENTEM. Hebr. est, ut addatur ebria sitienti, scil. in pœna æque ac in culpa: unde LXX. clare vertunt, ut peccator pro- dat fimul innocentem. Vox enim NON quam addunt LXX. dicentes non perdat, non est in Hebræo, & prohibitivè tantum addita est, unde melius & planius omittitur. Videtur autem illo tempore fuisse pro- verbium, ebrius sitientem aut sobriam ducit, aut fi reddendum omnino SATUR SITIENTEM (ut apud nos cæcus cæcum) id est, impius & scelera- tus, fatur impietate simplicem & avidum non tam veritatis & Sapientiæ, ut vult Rabanus, quam novi- tatis & voluptatis, ebrietas enim & sitis sunt ejus- dem rei, ducit, & seducit ad suas sceleratas volupta- tes, & idololatrias. Paul. Fagius ad h. l. recensitis Ebræorum, & Steuchi expositionibus, mihi, inquit, videtur (salvo tamen aliorum judicio) senten- tia proverbialis esse: addere ebriam sitienti vel con- sumi ebriam cum sitienti (utroque enim modo legi potest. Nam infinitivus Hebraicus ספות vel de- duci potest a verbo ספה, id est, addidit, adjecit, vel a verbo ספה consumsit, perdidit;) qua significatur, fu- turum ut innocens cum nocente pereat. Innuitur ergo, ut si exurgat inter eos impius idololatra, qui toleretur, & non statim e medio tollatur, fore tandem, ut hoc malum etiam redundet in bonos, & innoxios.

## 29:23
Verse 23. NOR SHALL ANY GREEN THING GERMINATE, AS AN EXAMPLE OF THE SUBVERSION OF SODOM AND GOMORRAH] Concerning which places Tacitus says: 'the land, scorched in appearance, has lost its fruit-bearing power.' See also what follows, and Solinus.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NEC VIRENS QVIPPIAM GERMINET IN EXEM- PLVM SVBVERSIONIS SODOMÆ ET GOMORRÆ] De quibus locis Tacitus: terram specie torridam vim frugi- feram perdidiss. Vide & quæ sequuntur, & Solinum.

## 29:28
Verse 28. AND HE CAST THEM OUT] He cast them out because of the violated covenant: just as a beast is cast out between which those who make a covenant walk in the middle. Gen. 15:10. See what is said at Matthew 26:28.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ET EJECIT EOS] Disjecit eos ob viola- tum fœdus: sicut pecus disjicitur inter quam medii ince- dunt qui fœdus faciunt. Gen. 15, 10. Vide quæ ad Matth. 26, 28.

## 29:29
Verse 29. THE HIDDEN THINGS ARE TO THE LORD OUR GOD, BUT THE MANIFEST THINGS ARE TO US AND TO OUR CHILDREN] A more apt sense in the Hebrew: 'The hidden things to the Lord our God, and the revealed things to us.' Those things which God had previously retained to Himself, He has laid open to us, so that we might have a norm by which to compose our life.

That opinion is not to be disapproved, provided it is not restricted to the law alone, as it seems to be restricted by Grotius when he calls it a 'norm of life' in his own sense. For the things that were hidden were primarily those which pertain to the Gospel, kept silent for eternal times (Rom. 16:26), which indeed were also revealed to the Israelites, inasmuch as the entire heavenly doctrine, Law and Gospel, was delivered to them. Nor is the explanation of those who take it in a disjunctive sense alien either to the text or to the analogy of faith: 'the secrets to God; the revealed to us'; and they warn that we should not curiously inquire into the hidden things, nor ungratefully disdain or neglect the open ones, according to the rule of the author of 'De vocatione gentium': 'What God willed to be hidden must not be scrutinized; but what He has made manifest must not be neglected, lest we be found illicitly curious in the former, and damnably ungrateful in the latter.'

to the Jews? For He has not done so for every nation. Therefore Moses speaks of the people, 'the things which are revealed to US and to our children forever, to do all the words of this law,' which are wrongly twisted toward the assumption of the Gentiles into the place of the Jews. Although these threats were indeed fulfilled in the Jews, Moses is not directly occupied here with prophecy, but threatens punishment to the transgressors of the covenant, which the Israelites experienced entirely after they violated the covenant of God.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ABSCONDITA DOMINO DEO NOSTRO MANIFESTA SVNT NOBIS, ET FILIIS NOSTRIS] Aptior sensus in Hebræo: Abscondita Domino Deo nostro, & revelata nobis. Quæ ante penes se retinuerat Deus, illa no- bis patefecit, ut haberemus normam, ad quam componere- mus vitam.

Non improbanda illa sententia, modo non ad solam legem restringatur, uti restringi videtur a Grotio, cùm normam vitæ suo sensu nominat. Nam abscondita imprimis fuere ea, quæ ad Evangelium pertinent, æternis temporibus tacita Rom. 16, 26. quæ vero Israelitis etiam patefacta sunt, utpote quibus universa doctrina cœlestis Lex & Evangelium tra- dita. Neq; aliena est sive a textu, sive a fidei analogia illorum explicatio, qui sensu disjuncto accipiunt: ar- cana Deo; revelata nobis: monentque, ut ne curiose inquiramus in abscondita, nec ingrati fastidiamus, aut negligamus aperta, juxta regulam autoris de vo- cat. gent. Quæ Deus occulta esse voluit, non sunt scru- tanda; quæ autem manifesta fecit, non sunt negligen- da, ne & in illis illicite curiosi, & in his damnabiliter inveniamur ingrati.

Judæis? Non enim fecit taliter omni nationi. Ideo Moses de populo, quæ revelata sunt NOBIS & filiis nostris usque in seculum, ad faciendum omnia verba le- gis hujus, quæ perperam detorquentur ad gentium assumptionem in locum Judæorum. Quanquam ve- ro hæ comminationes reapse impletæ in Judæis sint, non tamen hic in Prophetia occupatur directe Moses, sed fœderis transgressoribus pœnam mina- tur, quam experti Israelitæ omnino sunt, postquam fœdus Dei violarunt.

## 30:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXX.

An exhortation to repentance, with life and death proposed.

In this chapter, Coccejus notes first the signs of the approaching Christ. The first sign is the exhibition of blessings to him (v. 1), common to all Israel, such as the victories over the Canaanites and the kingdom of the tribe of Judah. The second sign is the curses, such as the abduction of the ten tribes, with the deletion of their name, and the Babylonian deportation, by which it is said that the scepter was taken away from Judah (Deut. 22:30; Ez. 19:14; c. 20:30; Am. 9:11), though not the lawgiver; but no one has yet been able to observe that anything was predicted in the preceding chapter (v. 20 seqq.) concerning the abduction of the ten tribes or the Babylonian captivity, just as nothing is openly held there concerning the victories over the Canaanites or the kingdom of the tribe of Judah, much less are those things designated there as signs of the coming of the Lord. He makes the third sign the illumination of the exiles in a foreign land, unto understanding, repentance, and obedience, of which he places the example in Daniel and his companions, and likewise in Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The fourth is the recollection and reduction into the land (v. 3, 4). The fifth is the beneficence toward the recollected people (v. 5). The sixth is the amplification beyond the fathers, which he places in the multiplication of the seed and the exaltation of the Republic through the subjugation of neighboring nations and the kingdom of priests. But in these, the returning Jews did not surpass the happiness of the fathers, the times of David and Solomon. And therefore one must not stop at these, if indeed that multiplication extends itself to the spiritual accession made in the New Testament. Although God promises the reduction here to the converted people, He does not constitute this as a sign of the approach of the Messiah, nor is the circumcision of the heart a benefit proper to the faithful in the time of the New Testament. Coccejus himself acknowledges that the fathers in the Old Testament had regeneration and consolation from the hope of eternal life through the expiation of Christ (which he wishes to be noted by the circumcision of the heart) (§ 339). He says the circumcision of the heart is promised here, and regeneration through the Spirit of adoption (§ 363). But did not that regeneration through the Spirit of adoption have a place in the Old Testament? The reduction and blessing which is promised here concerns the return from the Babylonian captivity, from which time the circumcision of the heart promised here cannot be excluded. Although that promise of multiplication beyond the ancestors was not fulfilled so much in the amplification of the Jewish polity itself and the number of citizens (for the Hebrew polity did not reach that amplitude after the captivity as it flourished under the Davidic and Solomonic rule) as in the amplification and diffusion of the Jewish Church through the accession of the Gentiles.

Junius expresses the sense correctly. This does not please Cocceji, Ult. Mos. §. 165. However true it may be that hidden things are to be left to God, and revealed things are revealed, so that I may do the law, yet I fear that what Aben-Ezra says, that he wishes to be said in this place, has neither head nor foot. He therefore wishes from v. 20 that the prophecy of the hard vision (Is. 21:2) be held concerning any part of the tribes of Israel (v. 21), certainly so great that their vengeance will cast the land itself into desolation (v. 22, 23, 28) and the nations will be adopted into the place of the defectors (v. 24, 25, 29). He therefore judges the words of the last verse to be of the nations, like the preceding ones, glorifying God because those things which were hidden from the ancients have been revealed to them for worshipping God. But we cannot agree with Cocceji. He changes words of mere threatening into a prophecy; what are attributed and left to God, he takes concerning the blind nations. For Moses does not say, what were once hidden from the nations, but what are hidden, are to be left to Jehovah our God, not to be searched out by human reason. Finally, he snatches away what was said about the Jews to the nations. For who else are they, to whom the words of this law were delivered, that they might do them, than

Latin:

CAPUT XXX.

Exhortatio ad pœnitentiam, proposita vita & morte.

IN hoc capite Coccejus signa primum appropin- quantis Christi notat. Primum signum ipsi sunt exhibitio benedictionum v. 1. toti Israeli commu- nium, uti sunt victoriæ de Canaanæis, regnum tribus Judæ. Secundum signum maledictiones, utpote ab- ductio X. tribuum, cum deletione nominis illa- rum, & deportatio Babylonica, qua ablatum esse dicit sceptrum de Juda (Deut. 22, 30. Ez. 19, 14. c. 20, 30. Am. 9, 11.) non tamen legislatorem: sed cap. præ- ced. v. 20. seqq. quicquam de abductione X. tri- buum, aut captivitate Babylon.prædictum esse nemo hactenus observare potuit, quemadmodum nec de victoriis de Cananæis, aut regno tribus Judæ ibi aper- te quid habetur, multo minus ista ceu signa adven- tus Domini illic designata. Tertium signum facit il- luminationem exulum in terra aliena, ad σύνεσιν, & μετάνοιαν & ὑπακοὴν, cujus exemplum ponit in Da- niele ejusque sociis, in Sorobabele item, Esdra, & Ne- hemia. Quartum recollectionem & reductionem in terram v. 3. 4. Quintum beneficentiam in populum recollectum v. 5. Sextum amplificationem præ patri- bus: quam in multiplicatione seminis & exaltatio- ne Reip. per subjugationem gentium vicinarum & regnum Sacerdotum collocat: Sed in his non su- perabant reduces Judæi Patrum felicitatem, tem- pora Davidis & Salomonis. Ideoque in illis non subsistendum, siquidem multiplicatio illa extendat sese ad spiritualem accessionem in Nov. Test. factam. Quanquam vero Deus reductionem hic pollicea- tur populo converso, non tamen signum appropin- quationis Messiæ hoc constituit, neque circumcisio cordis est beneficium fidelium tempore N. T. pro- prium. Agnoscit Coccejus ipse, regenerationem & consolationem de spe vitæ æternæ per expiationem Chri- sti, (quam vult per circumcisionem cordis notari) ha- buisse etiam Patres in V. T. §. 339. Dicit, circumcisio- nem cordis hic promissam, & regenerationem per Spi- ritum filiationis §. 363. Annon vero illa regeneratio per Spiritum filiationis in V. T. locum habuit? Redu- ctio & benedictio, quæ hic promittitur, concernit reditum e captivitate Babylonica, a quo tempore il- la cordis circumcisio hic promissa excludi non po- test. Quanquam promissio illa multiplicationis præ majoribus non tam impleta, in ipsa politiæ Ju- daicæ amplificatione, & civium numerositate, (ad eam enim amplitudinem non pervenit politia E- bræa post captivitatem, qua floruit sub Davidico & Salomoneo regimine) quam in Ecclesia Judaica per accessionem gentium ampliatione & diffusione.

Sensum recte exprimit Junius. Non placet is Coccejo ult.Mos.§.165. Utut verum sit abscondita Deo esse relinquenda, revelata esse revelata, ut faciam legem,tamen vereor, ne quod Aben-Esdra dicit, id hoc loco dici velle, nec caput nec pedem habent. Vult ergo a v. 20. Prophetiam visionis duræ(Es.21,2.)haberi de quo- tacunque parte tribuum Israelis (v.21.) certe tanta, ut ipsorum vindicta terram ipsam præcipitatura sit in de- solationem (v.22.23.28.) & gentes in defectorum locum adoptentur v. 24. 25. 29. Verba ergo ultimi versus gentium esse censet ut præcedentia, Deum glorifi- cantium, quod sibi ea, quæ veteribus abscondita, reve- lata fuerint ad colendum Deum. Sed adstipulari Coccejo non possumus. Verba comminationis meræ in Prophetiam mutat; quæ Deo tributa & reli- cta sunt, de gentibus cæcis accipit. Nam Moses non ait, quæ abscondita olim gentibus fuerunt, sed quæ ab- scondita, Jehovæ Deo nostro se, relinquenda sunt, non ratione humana rimanda. Denique quæ de Judæis dicta, ad gentes abripit. Quinam enim alii sunt, quibus verba legis hujus tradita, ut ea faciant, quam

## 30:6
Vers. 6. AND THE LORD THY GOD WILL CIRCUMCISE THINE HEART, TO LOVE THE LORD THY GOD] Namely, by the magnitude of incredible benefits, which also had its effect for some time in the time of Zerubbabel, and in the times following, which were rudiments to the Gospel: lest anyone with certain Jews think these pertain to the ages after the resurrection. Bachai refers it to the time of the Messiah.

It is a Pelagian and Socinian hypothesis, that the grace of God, by which we are spiritually circumcised and renewed, is situated in promises, and in the fulfillment of them. But Scripture describes this grace of God in a far different way, namely as an efficient, nay, a creative force, by which a new heart is created in us, by which God works according to the ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως ἀυτῒ, Eph. 1, 19. Augustine, book on the grace of Christ against Pelagius and Caelestius, ch. 24: Let them read therefore and understand, let them behold and confess, that God works in the hearts of men not by law and doctrine sounding from without, but by an internal and hidden, wonderful and ineffable power, not only true revelations, but also good wills. The magnitude of divine benefits does indeed contribute to the recognition of divine grace, but it is false that conversion or the circumcision of the heart arises from the mere consideration of them. And how many myriads are there to whom various benefits are shown, and yet they remain uncircumcised in heart. Nor is it less false that those ancient times were only rudiments for the Gospel, for Zerubbabel and the following believers. For the ancients also had the Gospel concerning the Messiah, both in promises and oracles, and in types and figures. But a Socinian deceit lies hidden here again: as if the promise of eternal life (thus they interpret the Gospel) was not in the Old Testament, but that in those last times of Zerubbabel and others there existed only certain rudiments for the Gospel. Meanwhile, Bechai does not wrongly refer this promise of spiritual circumcision to the times of the Messiah, which then ought to have been more illustriously fulfilled: other Jews do not wrongly refer it to the ages after the resurrection, because then at last a perfect circumcision and renewal is to be expected, which in this age is only imperfect. Augustine, book on the Spirit and the letter, ch. 22: when he shall appear, we shall be like him. This likeness now begins to be reformed, as long as the inner man is renewed day by day according to the image of him who created him. But to the perfection of that eminence, which is to be then, what is this, or how great is it?

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET CIRCVMCIDET DEVS COR TVVM, AD DILIGENDVM DOMINVM DEVM TVVM] Be- neficiorum scilicet incredibilium magnitudine, quod & ali- quandiu effectum suum habuit Zorobabelis tempore, & tem- poribus proximis, quæ rudimenta erant ad Evangelium: ne quis cum Judæis quibusdam hæc pertinere putet ad secula post resurrectionem. Bachai refert ad tempus Messiæ.

Pelagiana & Socinistica hypothesis est, gra- tiam Dei, qua circumcidimur spiritualiter & reno- vamur, in promissis sitam esse, eorumque præstatione. Scriptura vero longe aliter gratiam hanc Dei de- scribit, nempe ut effectricem, imo creatricem, qua nobis cor novum creatur, qua operatur Deus se- cundum ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως ἀυτῒ, Eph. 1, 19. Augustinus lib. de grat. Christ. contra Pelag. & Cœlest. c. 24. Legant ergo & intelligant, intuean- tur & fateantur, non lege atque doctrina insonante fo- rinsecus, sed interna atq; occulta, mirabili atq; ineffa- bili potestate operari Deum in cordibus hominum, non solum veras revelationes, sed etiam bonas voluntates. Beneficiorum divinorum magnitudo facit quidem ad agnoscendam divinam gratiam, sed e sola illo- rum consideratione oriri conversionem aut cordis circumcisionem, falsum est. Et quam multæ sunt myriades, quibus beneficia exhibentur varia, & corde tamen incircumcisi manent. Neq; minus fal- sum est, tempora illa antiqua rudimenta fuisse tantum ad Evangelium, Zorobabelis & sequentium fidelium. Habebant enim & veteres Evangelium de Messia, cum in promissionibus & oraculis, tum in typis & fi- guris. Latet autem hic ὕπουλον Socinianum iterum: quasi promissio de vita æterna (ita Evangelium in- terpretantur) in V. T. non fuerit, sed illis postremis fere temporibus Zorobabelis & aliorum solum rudi- menta quædam extiterint ad Evangelium. Interim non male hanc promissionem de spirituali circum- cisione Bechai ad tempora Messiæ refert, quod tum illustrius compleri debuerit: non male Judæi alii ad secula post resurrectionem, quod tum perfecta demum expectanda sit circumcisio, & renovatio, quæ in hoc seculo imperfecta solum est. Augusti- nus lib. de Spirit. & liter. c. 22. cum apparuerit, simi- les ei erimus. Hæc similitudo nunc incipit reformari, quamdiu homo interior renovatur de die in diem se- cundum imaginem ejus, qui creavit eum. Sed ad il- lius eminentiæ perfectionem, quæ tunc futura est, quid hoc est, aut quantum est?

## 30:11
Ver. 11. THIS COMMANDMENT, WHICH I COMMAND THEE THIS DAY &c. Moses speaks of the commandment of faith unto righteousness, Rom. 10, 6. 7. 8. which is not wonderful and far off after the revelation has been made, but outside of it, it surpasses all human intellect by a very long way. But the Apostle teaches, as Cocceius does here, that the law of faith could not have been announced unless by the Son of God descending: and that his descent was the incarnation, and that he was required to taste death for all, but that the return from transmarine and inaccessible places is the resurrection from the dead to preach righteousness and liberty to all who labor and are heavy laden. For the Apostle shows quite clearly that to say, who shall ascend into heaven for us? is to bring Christ down, or to deny his descent, and to say, who shall go beyond the sea and return, is to bring Christ up from the dead, or to require Christ's death and resurrection, that is, to deny that it has happened. From which it is clear in itself; That faith affirms Christ's descent from heaven and his death and resurrection, and that the commandment of faith presupposes all these things. And that the only reason for saying 'who shall ascend?' is Christ's descent, and for not saying 'who shall return from beyond the seas' is Christ's resurrection from the dead. The authority of St. Paul would be enough for us to defend this explanation, even if this enigma had been insoluble up until him, and such an exposition had come to no one's mind, so that it is truly monstrous that Hugo Grotius dares to diminish the words of Moses as if they signify nothing else than 'you do not need astronomy and travel to learn this commandment,' as if only the objection of difficulty were forbidden and not that of impossibility. But it is more, since God and Moses, by the mouth of the Prophets and by the very fact, have testified that the Gospel cannot be announced without the sacrifice of the Son of God, and thus his descent, death, and resurrection, who can doubt that Moses looked to that? Thus far Cocceius on the last of Moses, §. 468. seqq. Compare what we have handed down in the Apostolic Theology on Romans, loc. cit.

Latin:

Verf. 11. MANDATUM HOC, QUOD PRÆCIPIO TIBI HODIE &c. Moses loquitur de præcepto fidei ad justitiam Rom. 10, 6. 7. 8. quod mirabile & longinquum non est post factam revelationem, extra eam autem omnem humanum intellectum longissime superat. Docet autem Apostolus, ut hic Coccejus, non potuis- se annunciari legem fidei, nisi a Filio Dei descendente: illiusq; descensum esse incarnationem, & eum requiri ad gustandum pro omnibus mortem, reditum autem a transmarinis & inaccessis locis esse resurrectionem ex mortuis ad prædicandam justitiam & libertatem omnibus laborantibus & oneratis. Apostolus enim fa- tis clare ostendit, quod dicere, quis nobis ascendet in cœlum? sit Christum deducere, sive descensum ejus negare, & dicere, quis abibit ultra mare & redibit, sit Christum e mortuis reducere, sive Christi mor- tem & resurrectionem requirere, id est, eam factam negare. Ex quo per se liquet; Fidem affirmare Chri- sti descensum de cœlo & mortem & resurrectio- nem, & præceptum fidei præsupponere hæc omnia. Et solam rationem dicendi quis ascendet? esse Christi descensum, & non dicendi, quis redibit a transmarinis, esse Christi resurrectionem a mor- tuis. Satis nobis esset ad tuendam hanc explicationem autoritas S. Pauli, etsi usq; ad illum ænigma hoc fuisset insolubile, & nemini venisset in mentem ea expositio, ut plane portentofum sit, Hug. Grotium verba Mo- sis audere extenuare quasi nihil aliud significent, quam non egetis astronomia & peregrinatione ad di- scendum hoc præceptum, quasi vetetur tantum ob- jectio difficultatis & non impossibilitatis. Sed amplius est, quandoquidem Deus & Moses & Prophetarum ore & ipso facto testatus est, non posse absque sacrifi- cio Filii Dei, atque ita ipsius descensu, morte & re- surrectione Evangelium annunciari, quis potest du- bitare, quin eo Moses respexerit? Hactenus Cocce- jus in ult. Mos. §. 468. seqq. Conf. quæ in Theol. Apost. Rom. l. c. a nobis tradita.

## 30:12
Vers. 12. NEITHER IS IT IN HEAVEN) To attain this wisdom there is no need for Astrology, such as the Magi and Chaldeans required.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NEC IN COELO SITVM) Ad hanc sapien- tiam consequendam nihil opus est Astrologia, qualem requi rebant Magi & Chaldæi.

## 30:13
Vers. 13. NEITHER IS IT BEYOND THE SEA) There is no need to go to distant nations for the sake of acquiring it, as the Egyptians and Phoenicians were accustomed to do.

These things have nothing to do with Astrology: or with the commerce of distant nations: This Commentary is merely precarious. The word of God is taught not to be difficult, but in the heart and in the mouth of Israel: and thus the obvious perspicuity of the word is insinuated, which God willed to be the medium of repentance and spiritual circumcision. And indeed it is a discourse about the word of the Gospel, not only about the law, as the interpreter who is above all exception, the holy Apostle, explains in Rom. 10, 6. This, he says, is that word of faith which we preach. Which therefore does not require much solicitous and anxious investigation, as Moses teaches, so that it must be pulled down from heaven or recalled from the abyss, but that it is very near to the Israelites: so that it can be in his mouth by reason of external confession, and in his heart by reason of internal faith for all. The grace of Evangelical manifestation is proclaimed. What then would the ἄρσις of either Astrology or any other wisdom of distant Gentiles have to do with this? Rather, the Apostle fixes the mystery in the prophetic mode of speaking, that mention is made of ascent into heaven and crossing of the sea, or descent into the abyss, so that it may be hinted that to obtain the object of the Gospel, which is Christ, there is no need for our ascent or descent, so that we might bring Christ down from the heavens, or bring him back from the dead. That Christ himself for our sake descended from the heavens, so that he might join himself to us, and returned from the dead, so that he might manifest himself to us; and thus by his descent and return he merited for us all grace, and brought it about that the word of faith is near to us, and the salvation and life which comes to us through it. This, therefore, is what the Apostle wants, as we observed in the Apostolic Theology on Romans, orac. 74. p. 401. that it is not the case that we should strive either to fly into heaven or to cast ourselves into the abyss in order to seek salvation, but that the word of faith is near us, inasmuch as it is both in our mouth and in our heart through the proclamation of the Apostles, and thus the righteousness of faith is accessible to all, because the word has been preached to all. For faith is conferred by the proclamation and hearing of the word, but through faith righteousness is apprehended, and eternal salvation is obtained. Therefore, at least here, our merits and works and efforts are removed, and thus God's grace is established in our justification. What the Apostle had said above, that it is not of him who runs, nor of him who wills, but of GOD who shows mercy, he says here, that it is not of those who either fly into heaven or submerge themselves into the abyss to obtain righteousness, but that the grace of GOD and the word of faith are near to all, and that there is need of faith alone. Moreover, the Apostle employs those indubitable articles of faith concerning Christ's ascension into heaven and resurrection, because those who attempt to ascend to heaven by their own works and merits do nothing other than deny that Christ descended from heaven for the sake of our salvation, or ascended into heaven; indeed, they deny that Christ was raised from the dead, which, however, were both by far the most certain and most well-attested things. He therefore leads them to an absurdity, that they deny the first elements of Christianity, namely Christ's descent from heaven, his ascension, and his resurrection, that is, they render the whole faith void (1 Cor. 15:14), whoever attempts to establish the righteousness of works. For what need would there have been for Christ to descend for the sake of our redemption, to ascend into heaven to intercede for us, indeed, even to rise from the dead to seal our justification, if by our own righteousness we could ascend to heaven, or so fulfill the law that through it we might obtain eternal life. To this pertains the marginal gloss of B. Luther: He who does not believe that Christ has died and risen again to make us righteous from sins, righteous by works, and not by faith, even if they say so with their mouths, but not in their hearts. D. Balduinus in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans explains these things thus: The Apostle, he says, teaches two things from Moses: first, where the righteousness of faith is to be sought? Not above or below us, not in some hidden will of God, for this would be to drag Christ down from heaven as if he were a new interpreter of the divine will, or to call him back from the dead, as if he had not already sufficiently revealed all things to us before, but near us in the revealed word, which is preached among us and heard by us, and is therefore called the word of faith, because in it faith in Christ is communicated to us, and through it faith is conferred, and it is understood only by faith. Next, he teaches what the righteousness of faith comprises, namely, the confidence of the heart and the confession of the mouth. But these are matters for another place, to be weighed more exactly elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 13. NEQVE TRANS MARE POSITVM) Non opus est ejus adipiscendæ causa adire gentes longinquas, ut Ægyptii, & Phœnices facere solebant.

Nihil ista ad Astrologiam: aut ad gentium lon- ginquarum commercia: Mere precarius hic est Commentarius. Verbum Dei docetur non diffi- tum esse, sed in corde atq; ore Israel: adeog; verbi ob- via perspicuitas insinuatur, quod Deus medium esse voluit resipiscentiæ & circumcisionis spiritualis. Et quidem de verbo Evangelii sermo est, non solum de lege, ut explicat interpres omni exceptione ma- jor S. Apostolus Rom. 10, 6. Hoc est, inquit, verbum illud fidei, quod prædicamus. Quod proinde non multam requirere solicitam, atque anxiam indaga- tionem, Moses docet, ut vel de cœlo detrahendum sit, vel ex abysso revocandum, sed valde propin- quum Israelitis esse: ut in ore ipsius ratione externæ confessionis, & in corde ratione internæ fidei omni- bus esse possit. Deprædicatur gratia patefactionis Evangelicæ. Quid ergo huc faceret ἄρσις vel Astro- logiæ, vel sapientiæ cujusvis alterius Gentilium dissitarum? In modo potius loquendi Prophetico Apostolus mysterium figit, quod ascensus in cæ- lum & transsretationis maris mentio fiat, aut descen- sus in abyssum, ut innuatur ad objectum Evangelii, quod Christus est, obtinendum non nostro opus esse sive adscensu, sive descensu, ut Christum e cœ- lis deducamus, vel ex mortuis reducamus. Chri- stum ipsum nostri causa e cælis descendisse, ut nobis se jungeret, & ex mortuis rediisse, ut se patefaceret nobis; sicq; suo descensu & reditu nobis gratiam omnem pro- meruisse, atq; effecisse, ut verbum fidei prope sit nobis, & quæ per illud nobis obtingit, salus & vita. Hoc er- go vult Apostolus, ut in Theologia Apostolica Ro- mana orac. 74. p. 401. observavimus; non esse, quod vel in cœlum volitare contendamus, vel in abyssum nos præcipitemus, ut quæramus salutem, sed prope nobis esse verbum fidei, quippe quod & in ore & in corde nostro est per Apostolorum præconium, adeoque fidei justitiam omnibus esse obviam, quia omnibus verbum prædicatum. Everbi autem præconio & auditu fides confertur, per fidem vero apprehendi- tur justitia, & obtinetur salus æterna. Removentur ergo saltem hic merita & opera ac conatus nostri, & stabilitur ita Dei gratia in nostri justificatione. Quod supra dixerat Apostolus, non esse currentis, neq; volen- tis, sed miserentis DEI, id hic ait, non esse eorum, qui vel in cœlum volitent, vel in abyssum se submergant, ut justitiam obtineant, sed gratiam DEI verbumque fidei prope omnibus esse, solaq; fide opus esse. Adhibet autem Apostolus articulos illos fidei indubios de Christi adscensu in cœlum & resurrectione, quod illi qui co- nantur operibus & meritis suis cœlum conscendere, nihil aliud agant, quam quod negent, Christum sa- lutis nostræ causa de cælo descendisse, vel in cœlum adscendisse, imo inficientur, Christum a mortuis resu- scitatum esse, quod utrumq; tamen erat longe certissi- mum, testatissimumq;. Deducit ergo eos ad absurdum, quod negent prima Christianismi elementa, Christi tum defensionem e cælo tum ascensionem & resurre- Etionem quod, h. e. totam fidem irritam reddant 1. Cor. 15, 14. quicunq; operum justitiam stabilire conantur. Quid enim opus fuisset, ut Christus descenderet nostræ redemtionis gratia, adscenderet in cœlum ad interpel- landum pro nobis, imo ut resurgeret etiam a mortuis ad obsignandam justificationem nostram, si propria justitia nos cælum conscendere possemus, vel legem ita adimplere, ut per eandem vitam æternam consequa- mur. Quo facit glossa marginalis B. Lutheri: Wer nicht glåubet, daß Christus gestorben und auffgestan- den ist, uns von Sůnden gerecht zu machen, der spricht: Wer ist gen Himmel gefahren, und in die Tief- fe gefahren? Das thun aber die, so mit Wercken, und nicht mit Glauben wollen gerecht werden, ob sie wohl mit dem Munde auch also sagen, aber nicht im Her- zen. D. Balduinus in Comment. Epist. ad Rom. ita hæc explicat: Apostolus, inquit, ex Mose duos docet: primum ubi quærenda sit Justitia fidei? Non supra, vel infra nos, non in abscondita quadam voluntate Dei, hoc enim esset, Christum quasi novum voluntatis divi- næ interpretem de cælo detrahere, vel e mortuis revo- care, ac si non jam ante nobis omnia sufficienter reve- lasset, sed juxta nos in verbo revelato, quod inter nos prædicatur & a nobis auditur, & propterea verbum fidei vocatur, quia in eo fides in Christum nobis com- municatur, & per illud fides confertur, & non nisi fide intelligitur. Deinde docet, quidnam justitia fidei com- plectatur, nimirum fiduciam cordis & confessionem oris. Sed hæc alterius loci sunt, alibi exactius per- pendenda.

CHAPTER XXXI. The investiture of Joshua.

CAPUT XXXI. Josuæ investitura.

AND WHEN ALL THE PEOPLE WERE GATHERED TOGETHER) This is the institution of Synagogues. Vers. 16. RISING UP WILL GO WHORING AFTER STRANGE GODS) The Rabbis well note here a testimony of divine foreknowledge: in which there are many things not to be scrutinized except by the wise, says Maimonides.

Vers. 2. EGREDI ET INGREDI) Id est, fungi ducis munere. Vers. 6. CONFORTAMINI) Hebræum, roborate vos. Obedientia Dei auxilium impetrat. Vers. 9. TRADIDIT EAM SACERDOTIBVS FL LIVS LEVI) Vt convocarent populum, & legem doce- rent: Archetypum autem servarent in Sanctuario. infra 28. Josuæ 24, 26. PARS III. DEUTERONOMII προφητικὴ, Vaticinium Mosis novissi- mum, & benedictionem Propheti- cam continens.

## 31:17
vers. 17. I WILL HIDE MY FACE.

That the Israelite state after the death of Moses is described here, Cocceius notes on the last of Deuteronomy §. 657. (1.) In benefits. They are introduced into the land of Canaan. They eat, are satisfied, are fattened with all good things (which happened especially under Solomon, and again after the Babylonian captivity). They see God visiting them, and hear his covenant promulgated, as is evident from what follows. (2.) In sins. They look to other gods, and serve them, and reject God, and make his Testament void v. 20. The first of which was fulfilled as often as they neglected the study of knowing God, and in straits placed their confidence in the nations to help them, or worshipped God in high places; the second as often as they permitted idols to be built in the land, or even they themselves openly worshipped false gods. The third most properly in the visitation of God. He understands therefore the rejection of God manifested and addressing them with his own mouth. Fourth, in the rejection of the Gospel preached by the Apostles after the resurrection of Christ, announcing the New Testament according to the prophecies, and demanding faith and repentance for salvation. (But Cocceius ought to have proved, not merely asserted, that the time of the manifestation in the flesh and the proclamation of the Gospel by the Apostles is designated here. For was not the covenant of God made void by them before the economy of the incarnation? But let Cocceius proceed now.) (3.) In evils 1. It will be for devouring, i.e., he will be vexed by many enemies, and will be diminished. 2. They will find many evils besides that devouring of the sword to the diminution of men and goods, and besides straits, 3. Straits will find him. That this is said with emphasis is clear in itself. But such straits (stenochoriai) are primarily two, one in the Babylonian captivity, the other in the Roman War. (That they experienced the force of these threats in these straits, there is no doubt. But that the Babylonian captivity and the Roman war are predicted here by Moses, does not appear) (4.) In repentance partly true, partly not true, and the consequent giving and denial of help. Since mention is made of straits, both from the word itself and from a comparison of chapter 30, 2.3., it appears that the straits are of a distinct time, and that the former of both is both abundance and the desertion of the covenant. But from the former, recreation and restoration to integrity would be given through repentance, but in some other strait (which the event and the order of other prophecies prove to be the Roman one) he shows indeed v. 21 that the song will be for them as a witness, so that they are compelled, just as it is v. 17, to confess and acknowledge that their God is not in the midst of them, but v. 18 testifies nevertheless that their heart will look to other gods, and therefore God also will hide his face from them. For this will happen in the end of days v. 29. Thus Cocceius. But that there is a prophecy here of a double strait, and specifically of the Babylonian captivity and the Roman war, appears by no indication. As far as the words in the end of days are concerned, they do not always denote the final times of the Jewish polity, as is evident even from that passage which Cocceius cited, Deut. 4, 30, which he draws in vain to the final time of the world. Most understand the end of the time in which the punishment inflicted by God is completed, Gen. 4, 3, in the end of days is the same as after many days, as the Vulgate, B. Luth., and others render it: Whence in this place B. Luth. explained it, hernach [afterwards] indefinitely.

Latin:

vers. 17. ABSCONDAM FACIEM.

STatum Israeliticum post mortem Mosis hic descri- bi, notat Coccejus ult. Mos. §. 657. (1.) in be- neficiis. Introducuntur in terram Canaan. Edunt, fatiantur, impinguantur omnibus bonis (quod ma- xime sub Salomone factum, & iterum post captivit. Babylon.) Vident Deum ipsos visitantem, & fœdus ipsius promulgatum audiunt, ut ex sequentibus pa- tet. (2.) In peccatis. Respiciunt ad Deos alios, & serviunt illis, & rejiciunt Deum, & irritum faciunt Testam. ejus v. 20. Quorum primum impletum, quoties omiserunt studium cognoscendi Deum, & in angustiis fiduciam posuerunt in gentibus ad auxilian- dum ipsis, aut Deum coluerunt in celsis; alterum quo- ties permiserunt εἰδωλεῖα exstrui in terra, aut etiam ipsi falsos Deos aperte adorarunt. Tertium propriis- sime in visitatione Dei. Aspernationem ergo intelli- git Dei manifestati, & suo ore alloquentis ipsos. Quar- tum in rejectione Evangelii ab Apostolis post Christi re- surrectionem prædicati, Test. Novum secundum pro- phetias annuntiantis, & fidem, ac pœnitentiam ad sa- lutem exigentis. (Sed probare debebat Coccejus, non nude asserere, tempus Φανερώσεως in carne, & præconii Evangelii per Apostolos hic designari, Annon enim fœdus Dei irritum factum ab ipsis est ante οἰκονομίαν ἐνσαρκώσεως? Pergat autem jam Coccejus.) (3.) In malis 1. Erit ad comedendum, h. e. a multis hostibus vexabitur, & attenuabitur. 2. Inve- nient ipsum mala multa præter illam devorationem gladii ad imminutionem hominum, ac bonorum, & præter angustias, 3. Invenient eum angustiæ. Hoc in emphasi dici per se clarum est. Sunt autem tales an- gustiæ (ςενοχωρίαι) imprimis duæ, una in captivita- te Babylon. altera in Bello Romano. (In hisce angu- stiis vim comminationum istarum eos expertos esse, nullum est dubium. Sed captivitatem Babylo- nicam, bellumq́; Romanum hic prædici a Mose, non apparet) (4.) In pœnitentia partim vera, partim non vera, & consentanea opis datione, ac negatione. Quum angustiarum fiat mentio tum ex ipso vocabulo, tum ex collatione cap. 30, 2.3. apparet angustias esse distincti temporis, & utraq́; priorem esse tum abundantiam tum desertionem fœderis. Sed ex priori datum iri re- creationem & restitutionem in integrum per pœniten- tiam, sed in alia quadam ςενοχωρίᾳ (quam eventus & aliarum Prophetiarum ordo probat esse Romanam) ostendit quidem v. 21. canticum fore ipsis ceu testem, ut cogantur, quemadmodum est v. 17. confiteri & agno- scere, Deum suum non esse in medio ipsorum, at v. 18. testatur nihilominus cor ipsorum respecturum ad Deos alios, & proinde Deum quoq́; absconsurum faciem suam ab ipsis. Futurum enim hoc in fine dierum v. 29. Hæc Coccejus. Verum de gemina ςενοχωρίᾳ & in specie de captivitate Babylon. & bello Romano hic prophetiam haberi, nullo apparet indicio. Quod verba in fine dierum attinet, ea non semper novissi- ma politiæ Judaicæ tempora notant, ut vel ex illo o- co, quem adduxit Coccejus Deut. 4, 30. patet, quem nequicquam ad ultimum mundi tempus trahit. Fi- nem temporis, quo completur pœna inflicta a Deo, ple- rique intelligunt, Gen. 4, 3. in fine dierum est idem quod post multos dies, ut Vulgat. B. Luth. & alii red- dunt: Unde hoc in loco B. Luth. exposuit, hernach indefinite.

## 31:26
Vers. 26. IN THE SIDE OF THE ARK) Jonathan bequpsa that is, in a chest. For this word, like many others, came into Hebrew from the Latin language.

Abarbenel thinks that not only the tablets of the law, but the whole book of the law, ought to have been kept in the ark itself. But most other Hebrews more correctly understand the words מִצַּד הָאֲרוֹן (at the side of the ark) as meaning from the exterior side, because it is not said from the side of the testimony, or of the Tablets of the law, which were placed in the middle of the ark, but from the side of the ark, i.e., exteriorly at its side, just as this word is also taken in 1 Sam. 6:8. Therefore, not only does Jonathan understand a small chest to have been affixed or attached to the side of the ark, but it is also explained in this way in the Jerusalem Gemara, Schekalim chapter 6: Moses made for it (the ark) a γλωσσοκόμου (small chest), and within it was placed the book of the law, where the gloss on the word גלוסקום notes: A certain board protruded, made like a small chest. In the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Baba Bathra, fol. 14, R. Judah said: Where did the book of the law lie? A board protruded from the ark, and upon it lay the book of the law. Menasse Ben-Israel in Conciliat. calls it a shelf affixed to the ark. Which opinion concerning a chest outside the ark, or at the side of the ark, is proven (1) from the open passage 1 Kings 8: There was nothing inside the ark except the two stone tablets. (2) When the tablets were placed in the ark, it was closed with the lid along with the Cherubim. It is therefore not probable that, with the lid removed and the Cherubim uncovered, the book of the law was thrust into it. This is the argument of Aben-Ezra. (3) The ark of the covenant contained only two and a half cubits, both in length and in breadth, from which the whole volume of the law [could] scarcely [be contained]. together with the stone tablets, he was able to include. 4. For that purpose, the book of the law was kept in the sacred archives, so that if necessity demanded, if corruption occurred, one could have recourse to it, as R. Jannai, Abraham, Seba, Maimonides & Abarbenel confess. But who would have been permitted to have recourse to the holy of holies, or even to unlock the ark, as often as use required? For what some Hebrews think, that the high priest could have entered the holy of holies at another time than the day of atonements, that is repugnant to Holy Scripture, Heb. 9, and the common tradition of the Hebrews. Nor is it read anywhere that the high priest entered on the day of atonements to bring out the book of the law. Cf. Exod. 30, 10. & Levit. 16. chap.

if they have truly done penance. Cf. v. 21, 22, 30. For it is very manifest that these things pertain to that which is subjoined in the poem, v. 32. Coccejus, in his final notes on Moses §. 690, wishes this whole song of Moses to be a prophetic discourse, as if performing in the present matter the δικαίωσιν or justification of God revealed in the flesh before the people. The Jews think it is a rebuke of the Israelites, and a promise of their redemption from this present captivity through the plague of those who hold them in captivity. But just as the Jews rightly acknowledge that the rebuke and punishment which still presses upon them is proposed in this song of Moses, so they rashly promise themselves redemption from this, which they call, captivity or dispersion, when not liberation from it, but eternal rejection and dispersion has been predicted. I would not, however, say that only the δικαίωσιν of the Son of God before the people is exhibited in this whole song, nor all things are to be referred to God revealed in the flesh, or the Son of God, although it cannot be denied that some things are contained in this song concerning the final rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. The scope and status is not only the judicial justification of the judgment of God, but the Lord is entirely in it, so that by the commemoration of the benefits exhibited, he may recall the Jews to μετάνοιαν, as the wish subjoined in v. 29, 'O that they were wise and understood these things!', sufficiently testifies. 'I will celebrate the name of the Lord,' the proposition of verse 3, that is, interpreting with B. Luther, 'I will sing of invoking and worshipping one only God, against the idolaters who will be in my people.' 'Give greatness to our God,' that is, do not worship any other God, or attribute any majesty or power to anyone, except to our one God; to Him alone belongs majesty, greatness, power. All other gods are vain, lying, and nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 26. IN LATERE ARCÆ) Jonathan בְּקוּפְסָא id est, in capsa. Vox enim hæc, ut multæ aliæ ex latino ser- mone in Hebræum devenit.

Abarbenel in ipsa arca putat non solum tabulas legis, sed totum librum legis asservari debuisse. Sed rectius alii pleriq; omnes Ebræi verba מִצַּד הָאֲרוֹן a latere arcæ de latere exteriori intelligunt, quia non dicitur a latere testimonii, vel Tabularum legis, quæ in media arca repositæ, sed a latere arcæ, sc. exterius ad latus ejus, uti hæc vox etiam accipitur 1. Sam. 6, 8. ideo non tantum Jonathan capsulam ad latus arcæ affixam vel adjectam intelligit, sed etiam ita in Ge- mara Hierosolymitana explicatur Schekalim cap. 6. instar γλωσσοκόμου Scrinioli fecit ei (arcæ) Moses, & intra illud inditus fuit liber legis, ubi glossa ad vocem גלוסקום notat: Tabula quædam prominebat facta instar capsellæ. In Talmud Babylonico Tract. Barab. f. 14. R. Jehuda dicebat: Liber legis ubi jacebat? Tabu- la prominebat ex arca, & super ea jacebat liber legis. Menasse Ben-Israel in Conciliat. vocat pluteum arcæ affixum. Quæ sententia de capsa extra arcam, vel ad latus arcæ, probatur (1.) e loco aperto 1. Reg. 8. Nil erat intra arcam præter duas tabulas lapideas. (2.) Cum tabulæ in arca repositæ fuere, operculo ea cum Cherubinis clausa fuit. Non ergo probabile est remoto operculo, & Cherubinis eam reclusam, & librum legis in eam intrusum esse. Quod argumen- tum est Aben-Ezræ. (3.) Arca fœderis non contine- bat nisi duos cubitos cum semisse, tam in longitudine, quam in latitudine, unde vix totum volumen legis, una cum tabulis lapideis complecti potuit. 4. Ea fini asservatus fuit in archivis sacris liber legis, ut necessitate exigente, si depravatio contingeret, ad eum recurri posset, ut R. Jannai, Abraham, Seba, Maimonides & Abarbenel fatentur. Qui vero ad sancta sanctorum recurrere, vel etiam arcam rese- rare integrum fuisset, quoties usus posceret? Quod enim Ebræi nonnulli putant, alio etiam tempore, quam die expiationum summum Sacerdotem ingredi potuisse sanctum sanctorum, id Scripturæ S. cum- ptimis Ebr. 9. & communi Ebræorum traditioni repugnat. Neq; legitur uspiam, quod in die ex- piationum ingressus fuerit Sacerdos summus, ut legis librum expromeret. Conf. Exod. 30, 10. & Levit. 16. cap.

nie, si vere pœnitentiam egerint. Conf. v. 21. 22. 30. Hæc enim pertinere ad illud, quod v. 32. subjunctum est carmen, oppido manifestum est. Canticum hoc Mosis Coccejus ult. Mos. §. 690. totum vult esse ser- monem propheticum tanquam in re præsenti peragen- tem δικαίωσιν sive justificationem Dei in carne revela- ti apud populum. Judæi censent esse correptionem Israelitarum, & promissionem redemtionis ipsorum ex hac præsenti captivitate per plagam eorum, qui eos in captivitate retinent. Sed uti recte agnoscunt Judæi correptionem & pœnam, quæ eos etiamnum premat, in hoc Mosis cantico proponi, Sic temere redem- tionem ex hac, quam vocant, captivitate vel disper- sione sibi pollicentur, quum non liberatio ex eo, sed æterna abjectio & dispersio prædicta sit. Non tamen tantum δικαίωσιν Filii Dei apud populum in hoc toto cantico exhiberi dixerim, neq; omnia ad Deum in carne revelatum, vel Filium Dei referenda, etsi non negandum, quod de Judæorum finali rejectione, & gentium vocatione nonnulla in hoc cantico habean- tur. Scopus & status non est juredicialis solum justi- ficationis judicii Dei, sed in eo totus est Dominus, ut Judæos beneficiorum exhibitorum commemora- tione ad μετάνοιαν revocet, ut votum subjunctum v. 29. utinam saperent atq; intelligerent ista! satis testa- tur. Celebrabo nomen Domini, propositio vers. 3. hoc est, interprete B. Luthero, Cantabo de in- vocando & colendo uno solo Deo, contra idololatras fu- turos in populo meo. Date magnitudinem Deo no- stro, id est, nolite ullum alium Deum colere, aut ulli quicquam majestatis aut potestatis tribuere, nisi uni Deo nostro, hujus solius est majestas, magnitudo, pote- stas. Omnes alii dii vani, mendaces & nihil sunt.

## 32:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXII. The Song of Moses.

HEAR, O HEAVENS, WHAT I SPEAK, AND LET THE EARTH HEAR THE WORDS OF MY MOUTH) He calls upon witnesses who will always remain, and those through whom God was about to execute His judgments. See above 5, 26. 28, 12. 23. Aeneas in Virgil, book 12.

Be now the sun my witness, and this earth to me praying.

Then Latinus:

These same things, Aeneas, I swear by the earth, the sea, the stars.

That comparison of the most holy prayer of the divine spirit with profane things does not please. Nor can an oath made by creatures please any Christian, which was disapproved by Christ, Matt. 5, 34, 35. Therefore, let it be a matter of religion for us to compose such things with those which are by divine inspiration, and written for our instruction, Rom. 15, 4. Nor are heaven and earth invoked only as witnesses, or organs of the judgment of GOD, because of the things that are said: but because of the true greatness, which are altogether worthy, so that not only the earth, but also heaven should perceive them, the man of GOD uses this notable preface. Which is also observed in Isaiah c. 1, 2. For the greatest of the Prophets determined not only to explain the transgression of the people and to propose the judgments of God, but also to refresh the faithful with Evangelical promises, lest they should fail in spirit. Which is clear especially from verses 36, 39, 43. And although we do not reject the common opinion, by which earth and heavens are taken by prosopopoeia: yet not inconveniently, in our judgment, you may understand by the metonymy of the name of heavens the angels, and by the earth, men. For they are both witnesses of deeds, and ministers of the judgments of the Lord, and they are those who desire to look into (παρακύψαι) divine mysteries, 1 Tim. 3, 16. 1 Pet. 1, 12. Heb. 2, 2. And by that reason the dignity of the speech and of the things to be said is more exalted: to which not only all men, but even the angels themselves and archangels, and thrones, and dominions, and celestial powers ought deservedly to prick up their ears: because the Lord is speaking; these are not the words of Moses, but of the Lord speaking through Moses: nor of a common argument, but of a principal one, concerning future things, such as the Israelites are about to show themselves, and what things they are about to have: exhibiting not only sad threats or predictions, but also joyful Evangelical promises. Indeed, a magnificent pathetic speech also required a magnificent prologue, and with the Lord speaking such and so great things, the heavens and all the inhabitants of the earth deservedly attend with reverence and admiration. For how much God wanted this Song to be held is clear from the preceding chapter, v. 19: 'Now therefore write this Song for yourselves, and teach the children of Israel it (that they may hold it by memory) and sing it with their mouth, and let this song be for me as a witness among the children of Israel,' that is, interpreting with Osiander, a song, which contains a prophecy about the defection of my people, will testify that I paternally warned them, lest they should rush into idolatry, and will show that hope is not denied to any. The Hebrews distribute the song into VI. parts, to which they make a sign with the words הויז לך 'splendor to you,' which they wish to be as a consolation (παραμυθίαν) for the Jews sitting in darkness. Composing those words from the initial letters of v. 17, 19, 29, 40.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXII. Canticum Mosis.

Vers. 1. AVDITE COELI, QUÆ LOQVOR, AVDI- AT TERRA VERBA ORIS MEI) Testes advocat sem- per mansuros, & eos, per quos Deus judicia sua erat exequu- zurus. Vide supra 5, 26. 28, 12. 23. Æneas apud Virgilium libro 12.

Esto nunc sol testis, & hæc mihi terra precanti.

Deinde Latinus:

Hæc eadem, Ænea, terram, mare, sidera juro.

Non placet illa cum prophanis collatio sanctis- simæ orationis divini spiritus. Neque ulli Christiano placere potest juramentum per creatu- ras factum, quod improbatum a Christo Matth. 5, 34. 35. Talia ergo componere cum iis, quæ in- spiratione divina, & ad nostram scripta doctri- nam' sunt, Rom. 15, 4. religio nobis sit. Nec ut testes solum, aut organa judicii DEI advocan- tur cælum & terra, ob ea, quæ dicuntur: sed propter verum magnitudinem, quæ dignæ omnino, ut non modo terra, sed & cælum easdem perci- piant, hoc insigni præloquio utitur vir DEI. Quod etiam in Esaia c. 1, 2. observatur. Nam non tan- tum transgressionem populi explicare, ac judicia Dei proponere constituit Prophetarum maximus, sed etiam Evangelicis promissionibus fideles refocilla- re, ne animo deficerent. Quod e versu 36. 39. 43. imprimis liquet. Et quanquam non reprobemus communem sententiam, qua terra, & cæli per pro- sopopæiam accipiuntur: non incommode tamen, nostro judicio, per metonymiam cælorum nomine angelos, ac per terram homines intelligas. Illi enim & testes factorum, & administri judiciorum Domi- ni, & παρακύψαι mysteriorum divinorum sunt 1. Tim. 3, 16. 1. Petr. 1, 12. Ebr. 2, 2. Atq; ea ratione di- gnitas orationis & rerum dicendarum magis extol- litur: ad quas non homines tantum universi, sed ipsimet etiam angeli & archangeli, & throni, & do- minationes, & potestates cœlestes aures arrigere merito debeant: quia Dominus loquitur; non Mosis verba hæc sunt, sed Domini per Mosen loquentis: nec vulgaris argumenti, sed præcipui, de rebus fu- turis, quales præbituri sese Israelitæ, & quæ habitu- ri sata sint: non tristes tantum comminationes, aut prædictiones, sed lætas etiam Evangelicas promis- siones exhibentia. Nimirum magnificam oratio- nem patheticam magnificum etiam decebat προ- οίμιον, & loquente talia ac tanta Domino, merito cum reverentia & admiratione attendunt cœli, ter- ræq; incolæ universi. Quanti enim Canticum hoc Deus haberi voluerit, e capite præcedente v. 19. li- quet: Nunc igitur scribite vobis Canticum istud, & docete filios Israel illud (ut memoriter teneant) & ore decantent, & sit mihi carnem istud pro testimonio inter filios Israel, id est, interprete Osiandro, carmen, quod continet vaticinium de populi mei defectione, te- stabitur me paterne eos præmonuisse,ne in idololatriam ruerent, & ostendet non esse denegatam ullis spem ve- Ebræi canticum in VI. partes distribuunt, quibus signum faciunt voces הויז לך splendoris tibi, quam volunt esse tanquam παραμυθίαν Judæorur in te- nebris sedentium. Componentes illas voces ex li- teris initialibus v. 17. 19. 29. 40.

## 32:2
V. 2. CONCRESCAT VT PLVVIA) The Masoretes read יערף. But the Chaldean and the Greeks read יערב, let it be pleasing, προσδοκάσθω. Elsewhere they translate that word as ἐνδέχεσθαι, ἡδὺ γίνεσθαι, ἀρέσκειν.

This is not only the reading of the Masoretes, but the writing of the divine Moses as an amanuensis. Nor should a diverse reading be immediately concluded because the Chaldean and the Greeks translated it otherwise. They could have had other reasons for their translation than a diversity of reading in their codices, which it is permitted to observe in very many other places of the sacred codex, where no indication of a diverse reading, or trace of analogy, appears, nor will anyone be able to rashly guess the cause of the version by divining, especially among the LXX. And why could the Chaldean יבסמון ריתנא not be explained as, they shall drop sweet fatness, when in Ps. 65:12 it is so accepted, as noted by Buxtorf in Vind. Ver. Hebr. p. 724. Capellus, and Grotius, who was seduced by him, rashly invented diverse readings, both here and very frequently elsewhere, where he was not instructed by the authority of any Hebrew codex exhibiting a different reading. But more rashly and ignorantly, Brian Walton compiled those diverse Grotian readings from the whole codex, and thus exhibited a complete and quite long catalog of diverse readings, without any examination. He who ought to have listened to his Buxtorf, the defender of Hebrew truth, rather than follow without judgment those insane Bibliomastiges, Ludov. Capellus and Hug. Grotius. In this place, certainly, from the added declaration, he could have gathered that, for that reason, as the Hebrew codices have it, the words were conceived by the Holy Spirit in no other way: Let my doctrine drop (not, let it be pleasing) as the rain, let my speech flow, or rather, descend, as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass. For the Holy Spirit remains in the allegory. Moses indeed desires the fruit of his doctrine, so that it may render the minds of the hearers fruitful like rain and dew. Isa. 55, 10. 11. Cf. Mic. 5, 7. Isa. 32, 1. ch. 61, 3. Hos. 14, 6. Ps. 1, 3. Ps. 94, 17. 1 Cor. 3, 7. Phil. 1, 12. Because there is distinct mention of herbs and grass, which are irrigated by rain and dew so that they may grow, some think that by this allegory great and small, old and young are denoted. This is supported by the observation of Sebastian Münster on this passage, that according to Kimchi שׂעיר is a light rain, which is more beneficial to the sprouting herb than a downpour, just as רביבים is a stronger rain consisting of many drops, and that עשׂב is a somewhat large herb, which grows into a stalk, as is Hyssop, whereas דשא is a more tender herb. In any case, salutary increments are wished for all, as through this supreme and swan-like song, so through the entire doctrine which Moses has handed down hitherto, both legal and Evangelical. Which ought to be the prayer of all ministers of the word when they preach the τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ (oracles of God). Since the heavenly doctrine trickles like rain and descends like dew, like a downpour upon the herb and like drops upon the grass, and it is altogether pleasing and sweet, Psalm 19, 1. Ps. 119, 103. Psalm 34. 1 Pet. 2, 3. nor will it return empty, but brings forth fruits pleasing to God. Isa. 55. v. 11. 12. We add, moreover, the observation of B. Luther, from the succinct and learned explanation which is held in his Commentary on Deuteronomy published in the year 1524, and set forth a little more fully in the special ἐξηγήσει (exegesis) of this 32nd chapter, composed in the year 1529, Vol. V. Wittenberg, f. 248, and Vol. V. Altenburg. page 786, it is read: He opposes drops, rain, and dew to clouds without water, such as are human doctrines, which profit nothing: therefore He wishes His word to be rain, not an empty cloud, but He opposes the herb and grass to ferns, sands, and similar unfruitful things, upon which it rains in vain; even if the rain is salutary, i.e., He desires hearers in whom the word may bear fruit: for both are required, that the doctrine be salutary and the hearer teachable.

Latin:

V. 2. CONCRESCAT VT PLVVIA) Legit יערף ut Mosoretæ. At Chaldæus & Græci יערב, grata sit, προσδοκά- σθω. Alibi id verbum vertunt ἐνδέχεσθαι, ἡδὺ γίνεσθαι αρέσκειν.

Non Masoretarum hæc tantum lectio, sed ama- nuensis divini Mosis scriptura est. Neq; diversa actutum lectio concludenda, quod aliter transtu- lerint Chaldæus & Græci. Alias illi potuere habuisse translationis suæ causas, quam diversitatem lectio- nis in suis codicibus, quod in aliis bene multis ob- servare licet codicis sacri locis, ubi nullum vel di- versæ lectionis indicium, vel analogias vestigium apparet, nec quisquam divinando conjectare te- mere poterit causam versionis, imprimis apud τές ὁ. Et quidni Chaldaicum יבסמון ריתנא exponi queat, dulcem stillabunt pinguedinem, quum Ps. 65, 12. ita accipiatur, notante Buxtorff. in vind. ver. Hebr. p. 724. Temere Capellus, &, qui ab eo seductus est, Grotius, diversas commentus est lectiones, & hic & alibi frequentissime, ubi nulla codicis alicujus Ebræi autoritate instructus fuit, aliam lectionem exhibentis. Sed magis temere, & imperite Brianus Waltonus compilavit lectiones illas Grotianas di- versas e toto codice, atq; catalogum integrum ita exhibuit bene longum diversarum lectionum, sine ullo examine. Qui Buxtorfium suum audire potius debuisset, Ebraicæ veritatis vindicem, quam sine judicio sequi Bibliomastigas illos male sanos Lu- dov. Capellum & Hug. Grotium. Hoc certe loco ex addita declaratione colligere poterat, quod ea ra- tione, ut habent Ebræi codices, non aliter verba a Sp. S. concepta fuerint: Stillet (non, grata sit) ut plu- via doctrina mea, fluat, vel potius, descendat, ut ros, eloquium meum, quasi imber super herbam, & quasi stillæ super gramina. Manet enim Spir. S. in allego- ria. Optat nempe Moses fructum doctrinæ suæ, ut fœcundos reddat instar pluviæ & roris animos au- ditorum. Esa. 55, 10. 11. Conf. Mich. 5, 7. Esa. 32, 1. cap. 61, 3. Os. 14, 6. Ps. 1, 3. Psal. 94, 17. 1. Cor. 3, 7. Phil. 1, 12. Quia herbæ & graminis distincta sit men- tio, quæ per pluviam & rorem irrigantur, ut cre- scant, hac allegoria nonnulli magnos & parvos, se- nes & juvenes notari putant. Quibus favet observa- tio Sebast. Münsteri ad h. l. quod juxta Kimchium שׂעיר sit pluvia tenuis, quæ nascenti herbæ magis prodest, quam imber, ut רביבים sit pluvia fortior multis constans guttis, quodque עשׂב sit herba grandiuscula, quæ in stipitem crescit, ut est Isopus, דשא vero herba sit tenerior. Omnibus utique in- crementa optantur salutaria, ut per hanc supremam & cygneam cantionem, ita per universam doctri- nam, quam hactenus tradidit Moses, tum legalem tum Evangelicam. Quod omnium ministrorum verbi, cum τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ prædicant, votum esse debet. Cum ita stillat ut pluvia, & descendit, ut ros, doctrina cœlestis, ut imber super herbam, & ut stillæ super gramina, & grata, atque suavis omnino ea est Psalm. 19, 1. Ps. 119, 103. Psalm. 34. 1. Petr. 2, 3. nec inaninis revertetur, sed fructus Deo gratos fert. Esa. 55. v. 11. 12. Addimus autem B. Lutheri obser- vationem, e succincta, & erudita explicatione, quæ in Commentario ejus in Devteron. ann. 1524. edi- to habetur, & paulo fusius deducta in capitis hujus 32. peculiari ἐξηγήσει Ann. 1529. concinnata Tom. V. Witteberg. f. 248. & Tom. V. Altenburg. pag. 786. legitur: Stillas, pluviam, & rorem oppo- nit nubibus sine aqua, ut sunt doctrinæ humanæ, quæ nihil prosunt: ideo suum verbum vult plu- viam, non inanem nubem esse, herbam vero & gramen opponit filicibus, arenis, & similibus in- fructuosis, super quæ frustra pluit; etiamsi salu- bris sit pluvia, h. e. optat auditores, in quibus fructificet verbum: utrumque enim requiritur, ut & doctrina sit salutaris & auditor docilis.

## 32:3
Ver. 3. ASCRIBE GREATNESS TO OUR GOD.

Cocceius wishes the heavens to be addressed here, so that they may attribute greatness to the Son of God. But although at the beginning of the canticle, by prosopopoeia or metonymy, the heavens are stirred up to attention along with the earth, so that the people of the Lord may observe the most excellent canticle the more attentively and accurately, Moses does not, however, address the heavens and the earth in the proposition which is held in verse 3. And therefore Cocceius is in vain in investigating the heavens, as to which ones are to be understood as bearing witness to the greatness of the God of Israel visiting His people ἐνσάρκῳ (in the flesh): nor do so many diverse meanings fit this one word in one and the same place, as if (1) the heaven itself, the dwelling-place of God, (2) metonymically God Himself, (3) the angels of heaven, (4) analogically the order and, as it were, the chair of the leaders of the people of God, who are called πρεσβύτεροι (elders), were to be understood. It is certainly absurd for the same word, once placed, to be taken properly, and metonymically, and analogically, as he calls it, whence he also absurdly understands by the earth both the system of sea and dry land itself, and the place of death and the destruction of corpses at the same time, and for that reason calls upon the healing of diseases and the resuscitation of the dead brought about through Christ as witnesses here, which no one besides Cocceius would have rashly sought in these Mosaic words about the heavens and the earth, and then he also judges that by synecdochical metonymy the people of the 12 tribes living in the land of Israel, then further the whole world or the nations in the world, without distinction, and then finally by metaphor, the Church gathered and built, are designated by those same words. Indeed, the Reformed are so accustomed to tropes that they place such diverse meanings in the same word, and yet sometimes wish for it to be taken properly at the same time. Cocceius also refers verse 14 to the time of the advent of Christ. Butter of the herd and milk of the flock; with the fat of the kidneys of wheat, and you drink the blood of the grape, pure wine, because Moses had previously said in the past tense, He made him sit, etc., and now he changes the discourse into the present, saying: You drink. As if to say: And formerly Jacob perceived those things, and now you enjoy the same, so that the time may be noted when they are about to reject the rock of salvation, namely, obtaining the land in peace, abounding in all good things. But this is too thin a proof that these things sound of the time of the advent of Christ. The future is held here just the same as in the preceding verse, and by some it is rendered in the future, by others in the past because of the vav conversive, therefore it does not appear that the form of the order has been changed. And that it treats of the times before Christ, the following verse teaches: And Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked (you grew fat, I say, O Israel, you grew thick, you covered yourself with fat) and forsook God who made him, and treated the rock of his salvation as a wicked one. Thus Cocceius rendered it, serving a hypothesis, which Tremellius, Junius, and others exposed as 'he despised the rock of his salvation.' Cocceius himself refers most of these things to the preceding times, noting that three degrees of happiness are placed here, so that the first is to become rich from being lean, which fits the time of the judges. The second is to grow fat, corresponding to the time of the Kings. The third is to be covered with fat, fitting the time that followed the captivity: when, besides the παροικίας (sojournings) or colonies led into the whole world, they held the entire land of Palestine from Damascus to the desert, along with Idumea itself and the cities of the Philistines. But this distribution of times seems merely arbitrary, and the state after the return from Babylon is not to be compared, let alone preferred, to the happiness of the strong Jewish people under David and Solomon. Similarly, the explanation of the degrees of sin seems truly arbitrary, that they kicked under the judges in the institution of altars and images, forsook God the creator under the Kings, with the introduction of the worship of false gods, and treated the rock of salvation as a wicked one when they rejected Christ.

The principal foundation of this interpretation is the word נִבֵּל nibbel, which, whether it comes from נָבַל to wither, to die, and means to cause to die, or from נְבֵלָה Nebelah a corpse, and means to treat as a corpse or as something polluted, or from נָבָל Nabal a fool, corrupted in mind and spirit, and means to treat as a wicked person; to which Cocceius adds another from the name Jeshurun from שׁוּר to discern, to behold. For he wishes the cause of the name to be the vision of God, first in the desert, second in Christ, comparing Zephaniah 3:5, from which the abundance of seeing was made, and which was asserted for the persecuting city. But I fear that so great a matter, namely the prophecy concerning the passion of Christ, can be effectively asserted by such weak proofs. The rock of salvation is the name not only of the Son of God, but also of God the Father, and of the whole Holy Trinity. And it is the same God who had magnified Israel, whom he deserted, who is the rock of salvation, which Israel treats with contempt. Nor does the word נִבֵּל anywhere denote to treat as a wicked person, but to treat with contempt, to make vile, or to hold as vile. Nehemiah 3:6, Micah 7:6. The Chaldee renders it 'provoked'. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi says 'he affected with disgrace and despised', Kimchi 'he diminished', the Jerusalem Targum 'he denied'. Junius and Tremellius 'he treated with contempt': so also Blessed Luther. Sebastian Münster 'he held for nothing', with this note added: It is written in Hebrew נִבֵּל in Piel, and it signifies to make a fool. Gerundensis explains it as being ungrateful, and rendering evil for good. Aben-Ezra indeed thinks it should be taken as to blaspheme in heart and mouth. Vatablus: 'And he was ungrateful to the Rock of his salvation': likewise: 'and he depressed the dignity of the God of his salvation', that is, he attempted to depress God, who had saved him.

He did not translate the word Jeshurun, but retained it

Junius and Tremellius think that he is so called from uprightness, to which he was called, or, as others say, because he possesses the upright judgments of God. The Vulgate rendered it 'beloved'. The LXX, Deut. 33:5, 26, translated it in this passage as 'Jacob' and 'the beloved', from ישר, 'he was upright', 'he was pleasing'. To Grotius it is a diminutive, as we shall see at verse 15. Nor do they seem to admit that the things which follow in this song in verses 16 and 17 should be restricted to the time of the passion of Christ. They provoked God to jealousy through abominations; they themselves acted wickedly; they sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods whom they had not known, new ones who had come from nearby, whom your fathers had not feared—which Cocceius understands of the ancient Jews, although he thinks that in verse 18 the latest sin committed against Christ is compared with their sins, and that therefore changes of person occur: that in the third person it deals with the men of earlier times, but afterwards they are addressed as if present in the second person: 'You neglect the Rock that protected you, and you forget God the Almighty, your creator.' But these things are not uttered in the present, but in the future, nor is the alternation of the second and third person new in this song, even if it deals with the same subject, as is clear from verse 15. Although neither that distribution of times, or ages, or even degrees of sin according to different ages can prove itself to us, nor do we restrict the vilification and neglect of the Rock of salvation precisely to the time of the New Testament, there is nevertheless no doubt that the rejection of the Messiah pertains especially to that vilification and contempt of the Rock; since those things which Moses subsequently predicts in this song of his look primarily to the fates which were to befall the Israelites under the New Testament on account of their contempt for divine grace, namely: (1) the hiding of the divine face from the Jews until their end, verse 28; (2) their being moved to jealousy by those who are not a people; (3) their vexation by a foolish nation, i.e., one ignorant of God and His wisdom, given to foolish counsels and opinions, namely, primarily by the Romans and their successors in trampling upon the Jews, as Cocceius does not poorly [state] in § 1172. (4) the destruction of the land and the mountains with their fruits and foundations, verse 22; (5) all the arrows of the Lord to be sent against them, verse 23, which are enumerated here as plague, famine, beasts and serpents, the sword sparing neither age nor sex, domestic terror, and internal dissensions and movements. All of which refer to a universal and final excision. The man of God also sprinkles in the causes of this, namely that they are a distorted age, children in whom there is no faith, who act wickedly toward GOD with their vanities, and have provoked Him to jealousy through a non-God. Besides other things, that they placed their trust in Caesar and the Romans, in their own works, and in a Messiah who is not God, a mere man, a liberator from oppressors, and a worldly preserver of the temple and the land. For whoever is trusted for salvation who is a non-God, through him GOD is provoked to jealousy. Furthermore, just as the most sad fate of the Jews, and that the latest one, concerning which verse 29 is to be compared with Luke 19:42, so also the most gracious calling of the Gentiles into their place teaches that the times of the New Testament are being looked at, as we have from the infallible interpretation of the New Testament. For both their irritation at the 'non-people' is explained concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Romans 10:19, and the Mosaic 'shout' for solemn joys in verse 34 is declared in the same sense in Romans 15:10. Finally, what else does the conjunction of the song of Moses the servant of God and the song of the Lamb, which both are sung by the triumphant Church to proclaim the justice and truth and holiness of God (Rev. 15:3), testify, other than that this prophecy looks to the times of the New Testament? To which all the Gentiles are to come, and are to worship before the Lord on account of the judgments manifested against the enemies of God, just as it is held there in verse 4.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DATE MAGNITUDINEM DEO NOSTRO.

Cœlos hic compellari, ut Filio Dei magnitudi- nem tribuant, Coccejus vult. Sed quanquam in Ex- ordio cantici, per prosopopœiam, vel metonymiam, cœli ad attentionem cum terra excitentur, ut eo at- tentius, & accuratius canticum excellentissimum observet populus Domini, non tamen in propositio- ne, quæ vers. 3. habetur, cœlos & terram Moses compellat. Ideoque frustra est Coccejus in inda- gandis cœlis, quinam intelligantur, Dei Israelis ἐν- σάρκῳ populum suum visitantis magnitudini testi- monium perhibendi: neque conveniunt huic uni voci, in uno eodemq; loco, tot diversa significata, ac si (1) cœlum ipsum Dei κατοικητήριον, (2) metony- mice Deus ipse, (3) Angeli cœli, (4) analogice ordo, & quasi cathedra præsidum populi Dei, qui πρεσβύ- τεροι appellentur, intelligantur. Absurdum certe, eandem vocem semel positam & proprie, & metony- mice, & analogice, ut vocat, accipi, unde absurde quoque per terram, tum ipsum systema maris atque aridæ, tum locum mortis & destructionis cadave- rum simul intelligit, & ea ratione huc in testes vo- cat sanationem morborum, resuscitationem mortuo- rum per Christum factam, quæ nemo præter Cocce- jum in his verbis Mosaicis de cœlis & terra temere quæsierit, tum etiam per synecdochicam metony- miam populum 12. tribuum habitantem in terra Israe- lis, tum porro totum mundum seu gentes in mundo, sine discrimine, tum denique per metaphoram, Ec- clesiam collectam & ædificatam designari verbis iis- dem censet. Nimirum sic assueti sunt Reformati tropis, ut in eadem voce tam diversos locent, ac eandem tamen simul proprie acceptam quandoque velint. Ad tempus adventus Christi refert etiam Coccejus v. 14. Butyrum armenti & lac ovium; cum adipe renum, tritici, & sanguinem uvæ bibis merum, quia antea Moses in præterito dixerat, faciebat ipsum insidere &c. & nunc mutat orationem in præsenti dicens: Bibis. q. d. Et olim Jacob illa percepit, & nunc tu iisdem frueris ut notetur tempus, quando rupem salutis reprobaturi sint, nempe obtinentes terram in pace abundantes omnibus bonis. Sed hæc nimis tenuis est probatio, quod hæc de tempore adventus Christi sonent. Habetur hic itidem futurum, ut in antecedenti versu, & a nonnullis in futuro redditur, ab aliis ob vav conversivum in præterito, non ergo apparet mutatam esse ordinis formam. Et de temporibus ante Christum agi, versus sequens docet: Et impinguatus est Jeschurum, & recalcitravit (impinguatus es inquam, o Israel, incrassatus es, texisti te adipe) & omisit Deum, qui fecit ipsum, & pro scelerato tractavit rupem salutis suæ. Sic Coccejus reddidit ὐποθέσει δὐλεύων, quæ Tremellius, Junius, & alii, vilipendit rupem salutis suæ exposuere. Ad præcedentia tempora ista pleraq; refert ipse Coccejus, tres gradus felicitatis hic poni notans, ut primus sit opimum fieri ex macilento, qui conveniat in tempus judicum. Secundus ingrassari, congruens tempori Regum. Tertius cooperiri adipe conveniens in tempus secutum captivitatem: quum præter παροίκιας velut colonias in totum mundum deductas, totam terram Palæstinam a Damasco usq; ad desertum cum ipsa Idumea & Philistæorum urbibus tenuerunt. Sed hæc distributio temporum mere arbitraria videtur, neque status post reditum e Babylone comparandus, nedum præferendus felicitati fortis populi Judaici sub Davide & Salomone. Similiter vere arbitraria videtur graduum peccati explicatio, quod recalcitrarent sub judicibus in altarium & imaginum institutione, omiserint Deum factorem sub Regibus, invecto falsorum Deorum cultu, rupem salutis pro scelerato tractarint, cum Christum reprobarint.

Fundamentum præcipuum hujus interpretationis est verbo נִבֵּל nibbel, quod vel a נָבַל marcescere, emori, sit emori facere, vel a נְבֵלָה Nebelah cadaver, sit pro cadavere, aut polluto tractare, vel a נָבָל Nabal stultus, mente atq; animo corruptus, sit pro scelerato tractare; cui addit Coccejus alterum e nomine Jeschurum a שׁוּר cernere, intueri. Causam enim nominis vult esse visionem Dei primo in deserto, secundo in Christo, conferens Soph. 3. V a cui videndi copia facta, quæque asserta est urbi persecutrici. Sed vereor, ut res tanta, prophetia nempe de passione Christi, tam infirmis probationibus efficaciter adseri queat. Petra salutis non solum Filii Dei, sed etiam Dei Patris nomen est, ac totius S.S.
