Trinitatis. Et idem est Deus, qui magnifica verat Israelem, quem deseruit, qui petra salutis, quam vilipendit Israel. Neq; verbum נִבֵּל uspiam notat pro scelerato tractare, sed vilipendere, vilem facere, vel habere. Nehem. 3. v. 6. Mich. 7, 6. Chald. reddit irritavit. R. Salomo Jarchi dedecore affecit, & contempsit, Kimchi imminuit, Targ. Hierosolymit. abnegavit. Jun. & Tremell. vilipendit: Sic etiam B. Lutherus. Sebast. Münsterus pro nihilo habuit, addita hac nota: Scribitur in Ebr. נִבֵּל in Piel, & significat stultum facere. Gerundensis exponit ingratum esse, & malum pro bono reddere. Aben-Ezra vero putat, accipiendum pro blasphemare corde & ore. Vatablus: Et ingratus fuerit Petræ salutis suæ: item: & depressit dignitatem Dei salutis suæ, id est, deprimere conatus est Deum, qui servaverat eum.

Vocem Jeschurum non transtulit, sed retinuit

Junius, & Tremell. ac Israelem sic vocari censent a rectitudine, ad quam vocatus est, vel, ut alii, quod habeat recta Dei judicia. Vulg. reddidit dilectus. LXX. ἠγαπημέν@ Deut. 33, 5. 26. hoc loco & Ἰα- κὼβ & ὁ ἠγαπημέν@ interpretati sunt, a ישר rectus fuit, placuit. Grotio est diminutivum, ut ad verf. 15. visuri sumus. Neque admittere videntur ea, quæ sequuntur in hoc cantico v. 16. 17. ut hæc restrin- gantur ad tempus passionis Christi. Ad zelum provo- cabant Deum per abominationes, faciebant ipsi ægre, sacrificabant dæmonibus, non Deo, Diis quos non noverant, novis, qui e propinquo vene- rant, quos non formidaverant Patres vestri, quæ Coccejus de priscis Judæis intelligit, quamvis putet, cum illorum peccatis comparari v. 18. novissimum peccatum in Christum commissum, atque ideo mu- tationes fieri personarum: in tertia persona de ho- minibus superiorum temporum agi, postea vero eos quasi præsentes in secunda persona compellari: Rupem, quæ te protexit, negligis, & oblivisceris Deum omnipotentem formatorem tuum. Verum hæc non in præsenti efferuntur, sed in futuro, nec nova est alternatio personæ secundæ, & tertiæ in hoc canti- co, etsi de eodem subjecto agatur, ut e v. 15. liquet. Quanquam vero nec illa temporum, vel ætatum, aut etiam graduum peccati pro diversa ætate distribu- tio sese probare nobis possit, nec restringamus ru- pis salutis vilipendium & neglectum præcise ad tem- pus Nov. Test. nullum tamen dubium est, quin ad illud vilipendium, & ad contemtum rupis impri- mis etiam rejectio Messiæ pertineat; siquidem ea quæ deinceps prædicit Moses, in hoc cantico suo, respiciant imprimis fata, quæ Israelitis ob contem- tum divinæ gratiæ eventura erant sub Nov. Test. utpote (1) absconsio faciei divinæ a Judæis usque ad finem eorum: v. 28. (2) commotio eorum ad Zeloty- piam per eos, qui non sunt populus. (3) vexatio eo- rum per gentem stultam, h. e. Dei & sapientiæ ipsius ignaram, stultis consiliis & opinionibus deditam, nimirum imprimis per Romanos, eorumque suc- cessores in conculcandis Judæis, ut non male Coccejus §. 1172. (4) destructio terræ, & mon- tium cum fructibus & fundamentis v. 22. (5) Tela Domini universa ipsis immittenda v. 23. quæ hic re- censentur pestis, fames, bestiæ & serpentes, gladius nulli parcens vel ætati vel sexui, terror domesticus, & interiora dissidia & motus. Quæ omnia univer- salem & finalem excisionem referunt. Cujus etiam causas inspergit vir Dei, quod nempe ætas distorta sint, filii in quibus nulla est fides, qui ægre DEO fa- ciunt vanitatibus suis, & zelare eum fecerunt per non - Deum. Præter alia, quod fiduciam posuerunt in Cæsare, & Romanis, in operibus suis & in Messia non Deo, mero homine, liberatore ab oppressoribus, & templi ac terræ conservatore terreno. Cui enim ad salutem confiditur non - Deo, per eum DEUS ad zelum provocatur. Porro uti Judæorum fatum tristissimum, idque novissimum, de quo vers. 29. conferendus cum Luc. 19, 42. ita & gentium in eo- rum locum vocatio gratiosissima docet, tempora N. T. spectari, ut habemus ex infallibili Nov. Testam. interpretatione. Nam & irritatio eorum in non-po- pulo de gentium vocatione explicatur Rom. 10. v. 19. & κέλευσμα Mosaïcum ad solemnia gaudia vers. 34. eodem sensu declaratur Roman. 15. vers. 10. Denique quid aliud conjunctio cantici Moses servi Dei & can- tici agni, quod utrumque ad deprædicandam justi- tiam & veritatem ac sanctitatem Dei a triumphante Ecclesia decantatur Apoc. 15. v. 3. testatur, quam quod hoc vaticinium ad tempora Nov. Testam. spectet? quo gentes omnes venturæ, & coram Do- mino adoraturæ sint ob manifestata similia in ho- stes Dei judicia, quemadmodum ibidem habetur versu 4.

## 32:5
Verse 5. THEY HAVE SINNED) Ἡμάρτησαν. It is an explanation of the Hebrew, 'they have corrupted for themselves', supply 'their way'. This is said excellently concerning the worship of idols.

Nor, however, is idolatry alone noted: but all those crimes by which, as if with filth, they rendered themselves unworthy of being children of God any longer, as is added: 'not His children (degenerate children) have corrupted for themselves by their filth', to their great destruction, namely that which God had rightly established among them for their salvation through His word; therefore all those things by which they branded a stain upon themselves and in a way upon the divine covenant are designated. Cocceius rendered it thus: 'Corruption to Him? Not-His-children are their blemish, of a perverse and distorted age': with this commentary added, 'Do you think that there is truly any corruption in Him (the Messiah)? Not at all. They are His children who are their blemish and stain, that is, the least and most vile among the people are the children of the Lord. Of a perverse and corrupt age. Their blemish, who are a perverse generation.' But in truth, the Tiphcha accent in the poem is not of such importance that, having dismissed a simple interpretation, such as is primarily that of Blessed Luther, as well as the Vulgate, we should adopt this sufficiently twisted and perplexed one of Cocceius. He admits that all interpreters acknowledge that here is signified the perversity and tortuosity of some generation among the Israelites, which corrupts itself to its own ignominy, so that they are not His children. He also praises the exposition in Akedath Isaac: 'Did the Lord do corruption to Him? Not-His-children are their blemish.' It would have been stated too concisely if the meaning were this: that men who reject Christ judge that there is corruption in Him, and that they are refuted here. And the rest, which Cocceius here, hardly anyone else would have extracted from the words themselves. Our German version is favored by verse 20 when compared with this fourth one.

Capellus here again investigates a different reading, q. LXX. while they rendered ἡμάρτησαν ὀχ ἀυτῷ τέκνα μωμητὰ, they sinned not to him, blameworthy children, in a contrary sense, thus they may have read שחתו לא לו, but Grotius did not wish to follow him in this place. Let Buxtorf's Vindiciae veritatis Hebraicae, page 663, be seen concerning that translation of the LXX. The sense of the words of the Hebrew truth is in the open, provided a grammatical confusion not unusual is observed; for with the words reduced to order, the text stands thus: A perverse and crooked generation, who are not his children, to their own shame corrupts itself to him. Thus Vatablus and Paul Fagius, whom B. Glassius followed in Grammatica Sacra, book 4, tract 2, observation 25.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PECCAVERVNT) Ἡμάρτησαν. Explicatio est He- bræi, corruperunt sibi, supple viam suam. Id eximie de idolo- rum cultu dicitur.

Nec tamen idololatria sola notatur: sed omnia illa scelera, quibus ceu sordibus sese indignos red- didere, qui essent amplius filii Dei, ut additur: non filii ejus (filii degeneres) sordibus suis corruperunt sibi, magno suo exitio, id nempe, quod Deus saluti ipsorum per verbum suum recte inter ipsos insti- tuerat; omnia ergo illa, quibus & sibi, & fœderi quodammodo divino maculam inusserunt, desi- gnantur. Coccejus ita reddidit: Corruptio ipsi (est?) Non-filii ejus labes ipsorum, ætatis perverse & distor- tæ: hoc addito commentario, Putasne ipsi (Messlæ) revera aliquam corruptionem inesse? minime. Filii ejus sunt, qui labes & macula illorum sunt, hoc est, minimi & vilissimi in populo sunt filii Domini. Ætatis perverse & corruptæ. Labes illorum, qui sunt generatio perversa. Verum enim vero Accentus Tiphcha, in carmine, tanti non est, ut missa simpli- ci interpretatione, qualis imprimis B. Lutheri est, ut & Vulgata, hanc satis contortam & perplexam Cocceji assumamus. Omnes Interpretes agnoscere, fatetur, hic significari alicujus generationis inter Israe- litas perversitatem, & tortuositatem, quæ se cor- rumpat ipsa ad ignominiam suam, ut non sint filii ejus. Laudat etiam expositionem in Akedath Isaac: An Dominus fecit ipsi corruptionem? Non - filii ejus sunt labes sua. Nimis concise dictum foret, si hic sensus esset: homines qui Christum rejiciunt, judicare ipsi corruptionem inesse, eosque hic re- felli. Et reliqua, quæ hic Coccejus, vix ullus alius e verbis ipsis exsculpserit. Germanicæ nostræ ver- sioni favet v. 20. cum hoc quarto collatus.

Capellus hic iterum investigat diversam lectio- nem, q. LXX. dum reddidere ἡμάρτησαν ὀχ ἀυτῷ τέκνα μωμητὰ, peccarunt non ipsi filii vituperabiles, sensu contrario, sic legerint שחתו לא לו, sed noluit eum hoc loco sequi Grotius. Videatur autem de illa LXX. virili translatione Buxtorf. vind. verit. Ebr. pag. 663. Sensus verborum veritatis Ebraicæ in aprico est, modo σύγχυσις Grammatica non inconsueta observetur; verbis enim in ordinem re- dactis textus ita habet: Generatio prava, & perver- sa, qui non sunt filii ejus, in ignominiam suam corru- pit sese illi. Sic Vatablus, & Paul. Fagius, quos se- quutus est B. Glassius Gramm. S. l. 4. tr. 2. observ. 25.

## 32:8
Vers. 8. HE SET THE BOUNDS OF THE PEOPLES ACCORDING TO THE NUMBER OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL) He dispersed them so far that there were nowhere so many but that the Israelites could prevail over them. The LXX, with three letters omitted, read אל instead of ישראל, and from there Christians took material to discourse many uncertain things about the Angels, whom they thought were called the sons of God here.

That it may be possible to be certain about these things, one must look both at the text and at the sense of the words of Moses. The text למספר בני ישראל cannot be called into suspicion: nor is a different reading to be invented, even if the LXX translated otherwise. However, how they translated this seems doubtful. Grotius says that they rendered it, according to the number of the sons of God. But neither the Vatican nor the Basel edition of the year 1547 has it so. Both read κατ᾽ ἀριθμον ἀγγέλων Θεῦ. Lyranus, however, and Abulensis attribute that reading of the sons of God to the LXX Interpreters, to which Bonfrerius notes that someone had inscribed the name of the Angels in the margin, which then crept into the text of the LXX Interpreters. Cornelius a Lapide, however, judges that the LXX Interpreters did not read otherwise in the Hebrew, but through the sons

that Israel understood the sons of God, who is called in Hebrew Israel, that is, a strong ruler, and thus explained the sons of God as the Angels. But it is not likely that the LXX Interpreters understood God by Israel. Moreover, Origen seems to have noted yet another reading of the LXX, when in Homily 28 on Numbers he cites this passage thus: He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (or as we read in other copies) according to the number of the sons of Israel. However the version of the LXX Interpreters may be, the genuine reading is that which occurs in the Hebrew source. Since all copies have it so, and no diversity has been observed: and the Chaldean translated it in the same way, likewise Aquila, and Symmachus, and the Latin Vulgate in the same way, interpreting according to the number of the sons. And the other interpreters likewise. And Petavius observes that Origen himself in Homily 13 on Ezekiel prefers the Hebrew reading.

Therefore, as to the sense of these words, that interpretation of certain ancients is deservedly dismissed, bought not so much from the Greek translation as from the inventions of certain Jews, as well as Platonists and Poets, which those ignorant of the Hebrew truth, or occupied by a preconceived opinion, believed were strengthened here: as if, forsooth, this concerned the Angels who are the guardians of peoples and provinces, to which opinion Dionysius in Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 9, Origen in Homily 11 on Numbers, Justin Martyr in Dialogue with Trypho, Epiphanius in Adversus Alogos, and others have noted that the present passage is to be taken, and Becanus in On the Office of Angels, chapter 5, has attempted to defend it. Cornel. a Lapide attributes that explanation also to Rufinus in the Creed, to Chrysostom in Homily 3 on Colossians, to Procopius, and to Severus in the catena on the Canticles of Scripture edited by Caraffa. However, Cornelius a Lapide does not approve of this interpretation: It is certain that the LXX version here is not literal, nor genuine. For the sons of Israel are not literally the Angels of God. And Dionysius Petavius in book 2 on Angels, chapter 7, refutes their gloss. What do these words mean, that God set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the Angels of God? Are there not more angels than there are peoples or regions or provinces? Or, just as certain principal peoples are signified, are certain and principal angels also to be understood, to whom the peculiar care of them is committed? Or do more angels preside over individual peoples, and are they divided in troops according to the number of the peoples? There is nothing in this in which the mind can rest. We have said more against that invention, that guardian angels were given to individual peoples and nations, in Volume 4 of our System of Theology, On Angels, chapter 2, Question 6.

Origen, in the place cited, added another, but an even more absurd sense: At the beginning of the next age, God will again divide the sons of Adam, so that those who could not be so pure of heart as to see the holy Angels, will be according to the number of the Angels of God. But Cornel. a Lapide confesses that this sense is as rash and erroneous as it is new; noting a third explanation of others: God created as many men as He designated guardian Angels for them. But this does not concern individual men, but entire peoples and provinces, nor was any mention of Angels made in the authentic text. He also cites a fourth interpretation of Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels (which he also attributes to Rabanus): That heavenly city consists of men and Angels, to which as many (so many) men ascend, as many (how many) others of the Angels remained. But he asserts that this is uncertain, and that others say with equal probability that there will be as many men to be saved as there were Demons who fell. Neither can be proven from the Scriptures: nor does that have any connection with this passage.

Therefore, fifthly, Procopius and Lyranus, insisting on the Vulgate, explain it thus: When God dispersed the nations at Babel, He established as many nations as there were persons in the people of Israel who entered into Egypt with Jacob, according to the LXX. But that gloss is too clever: and Pererius and Cornel. a Lapide, on Genesis 10, verse 31, observed that there were not 70 nations in the dispersion of Babel, or 72, as Augustine, Jerome, Prosper, and Epiphanius count, but 55, because the names of the Patriarchs are to be subtracted, not added, who certainly did not make a different nation or family from their sons. If Canaan is added, there will be 56.

Now Grotius presents another and a sixth sense concerning the dispersion of the nations, so that they would not prevail over the Israelites: but how this can be elicited from the words or the context does not appear. The boundaries of the nations are said to be established according to the reason, or number, of the sons of Israel, but the nations were not scattered so sporadically, lest they be so many: because the Israelites prevailed over them. And the Israelites prevailed not so much by their own multitude and abundance, as by divine power and assistance.

Seventhly, Rupertus offers yet another sense: God established that the human race should endure until the limit and number of the elect is filled. But here the elect are not compared with the rest of men, but the Israelites are compared with the nations which they exterminated.

What then, finally, is the sense? Moses means this: even then, when in the dispersion and confusion of tongues at Babel the sons of men were scattered throughout the world, God had provided for the sons of Israel, and had established the distinct boundaries of certain peoples, just as He foresaw would be advantageous for them, so that the care and providence of God toward the Israelites might be celebrated. Therefore it is added in verse 9, BECAUSE the Lord's portion is His people: Jacob the cord of His inheritance: so that the cause of this providence might be rendered. For in the Hebrew there is a causal particle, and the Chaldean also rendered it thus. Paulus Fagius and Franc. Vatabl. render this sense: When the Most High divided the homelands and regions, and assigned them to all the nations, even then He had decreed to give to the sons of Israel the land of those seven peoples, whom He cast out of the land of Canaan upon the arrival of the Israelites themselves, or then He gave it to the seven nations, the Amorites, etc., the Hivites, etc. such a plain of the region, which would suffice for the number of the children of Israel. Thus also our blessed Lyserus explained in his Commentary on Genesis 10, page 397. Blessed Luther expressed the sentiment very well in the cited explanation: The first benefit is that, although He is GOD, and the God of all nations, as He divided them in Genesis 11 and distributed to them the orb of the earth, to each nation its own portion and boundary, as Paul in Acts 17, emulating this verse, teaches, yet He did not choose for Himself a people from all of them, whose true and legitimate God He would be, but He set limits, so that only where the children of Israel were, there would be His people. But where the limit of the children of Israel ended, there the people of God would cease, and the boundaries of the nations would begin. Because His people is the portion of the Lord, Jacob is the cord of His inheritance, i.e., His people does not extend more widely than Jacob or Israel. By these words, of course, it is described how peculiar this people of GOD is. The Vulgate is wrong, 'BUT the portion of the Lord.' Whence there is again no place for the glosses of Becanus, as if these things were said by way of antithesis in this manner: that since the other nations were committed to the guardianship of angels, the Jews alone, as a people beloved by GOD above others, have God as their guardian and protector. Oleaster, Cardinal Cajetan, and Cornelius a Lapide, from among the Papists, approve our sense; I transcribe his words: The sense, therefore, is, when God dispersed the nations at Babel, He set the boundaries of the regions and lands for them all, and for this purpose, namely that he might set apart and reserve for the sons of Israel, not yet born but about to be born, as much space of land as he knew was required and sufficient for their number and the convenient habitation of each; that is to say, from then on God designated and marked out the land of Canaan, so that it might not be occupied by others be destroyed and expelled by the Hebrews. Thus also Jacob Tirinus, who adds: He immediately subjoins the cause of such swift, such singular providence, because from then on Israel was beloved by God or designated as the portion, or the cord of God, that is, as His hereditary portion. So also Menochius and Bonfrerius in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 8. CONSTITVIT TERMINOS POPVLORVM JVXTA NVMERVM FILIORVM ISRAEL) Tam lon- ge eos dispersit, ut nusquam tam multi essent, quin Israëli- tæ illis possint prævalere. LXX. pro ישראל tribus li- teris omissis legere אל, & inde Christiani materiam sumpsere multa incerta differendi de Angelis, quos hic filios Dei dici arbitrabantur.

Ut de his constare queat, tum de textu, tum de sensu verborum Mosis videndum. Textus למספר בני ישראל in suspicionem vocari non potest: neque diversa lectio fingenda est, etiamsi se- cus verterint οἱ ὀ. Quomodo autem hi transtule- rint, dubium videtur. Grotius reddidisse eos, se- cundum numerum filiorum Dei, ait. Sed ita neque Vaticana, neque Basiliensis editio de anno 1547. ha- bet. Utraque legit κατ᾽ ἀριθμον ἀγγέλων Θεῦ. Ly- ranus tamen & Abulensis LXX. Interpp. tribuit il- lam lectionem filiorum Dei, cui ad marginem quempian nomen Angelorum adscripsisse notat Bonfrerius, quod deinde in textum LXX. Interpp. irrepserit. Cornelius vero a Lapide LXX. Interpp. non legisse aliter in Ebræo censet, sed per filios

Ifrael filios Dei intellexisse, qui dicatur Ebraice Israel, id est, dominator fortis, adeoque filios Dei explicasse de Angelis. Sed non est verisimile LXX. Interpp. per Israelem intellexisse Deum. Videtur autem adhuc aliam lectionem τǿν LXX. annotasse Origenes, quum hom. 28. in Num. ita hunc locum adducat: Statuit fines gentium secundum numerum angelorum Dei (vel ut in aliis Exemplaribus legi- mus) secundum numerum filiorum Israel. Quomo- docunque autem sese habeat LXX. Interpp. versio, genuina est lectio, quæ in fonte Ebræo occurrit. Siquidem omnia Exemplaria ita habeant, nec ulla observata sit diversitas: & eodem modo transtule- rit quoque Chaldæus, eodem modo Aquila, & Sym- machus, eodem modo Vulgatus Latinus, juxta nu- merum filiorum interpretantes. Nec aliter cæteri interpretes. Et Origenem ipsum Hom. 13. in Ez. Ebræam lectionem præferre, observat Petavius.

Quod itaque ad sensum horum verborum, merito dimittitur illa veterum quorundam inter- pretatio non tam e Græca translatione, quam e Judæorum quorundam, ut & Platonicorum, & Poe- tarum commentis emta, quæ roborari hic crede- bant Ebrææ veritatis ignari, aut præconcepta opi- nione occupati: quasi scilicet hic de Angelis præsi- dibus populorum & provinciarum agatur, in quam sententiam locum præsentem accipere Dionysium de Cœlest. Hierarch. cap. 9. Origenem Hom. 11. in Num. Justinum Martyr. Dial. cum Tryph. Epipha- nium in Alogian. & alios notavit, eamque propu- gnare conatus est Becanus de offic. Angel. cap. 5. Cornel. a Lapide eam explicationem tribuit quoque Ruffin. in Symb. Chrysostomo hom. 3. ad Coloss. Procopio, & Severo in catena Canticor. Script. a Ca- raffa edita. Non probat autem Cornelius a Lapide hanc interpretationem: Certum est, versionem LXX. hic non esse literalem, nec genuinam. Nec enim filii Israel ad literam sunt Angeli Dei. Et refellit illo- rum glossam Dionys. Petavius lib. 2. de Angel. c. 7. Quid sibi ista volunt, constituisse Deum terminos po- pulorum juxta numerum Angelorum Dei? An plures Angeli non sunt, quam populi vel regiones aut provin- ciæ? An, ut præcipui quidam populi significantur, sic etiam certi ac præcipui intelligendi sunt Angeli, qui- bus peculiaris illorum cura est commissa? An plures Angeli singulis populis præsident, & turmatim illi pro populorum numero partiti sunt? Nihil horum est, in quo animus acquiescat. Plura adversus commentum illud, quod singulis populis & gentibus angeli præ- sides dati sint, diximus Tom. 4. System. Theol. de Angel. c. 2. Quæst. 6.

Alium, sed adhuc magis absurdum sensum ad- junxit Origenes l. c. Initio seculi alterius rursus Deus dividet filios Adam, ut qui non potuerint ita mundi esse cordis, ut videant sanctos Angelos, & sint secun- dum numerum Angelorum Dei. Quem vero sen- sum uti novum, ita temerarium esse, & erroneum fatetur Cornel. a Lapide; Tertiam aliorum explica- tionem hanc observans: Deus creavit tot homines, quot eis designavit Angelos custodes. Sed hic non de hominibus singulis, sed integris populis, & pro- vinciis agitur, nec ulla facta est Angelorum in textu authentico mentio. Adducit & quartam interpre- tationem Gregorii M. hom. 34. in Evang. (quam etiam Rabano tribuit) Superna illa civitas ex homi- nibus & Angelis constat, ad quam tanti (tam multi) conscendunt hominum, quanti (quam multi) aliire- manserunt Angelorum. Sed id incertum esse, & æque probabiliter alios dicere, tot fore homines salvan- dos, quot ceciderunt Dæmones, asserit. Neutrum e Scripturis probari potest : nec illud quicquam cum hoc loco commercii habet.

Proinde quinto Procopius & Lyranus Vulgatæ insistentes, ita exponunt : Quando Deus in Babel dispersit gentes, tot gentes constituit, quot erant in po- pulo Israel personæ, quæ cum Jacobo in Ægyptum ingressæ sunt juxta LXX. Sed glossa illa arguta nimis est: neque 70. gentes in dispersione Babel fuisse, aut 72. uti Augustinus, Hieronymus, Prosper & Epiphanius numerant, sed 55. quia demenda, non annumeranda sunt nomina Patrum, qui certe di- versam a filiis gentem aut familiam non fecere, ob- servavit Pererius & Cornel. a Lapide, ad Gen. 10. v. 31. Si addatur Canaan, erunt 56.

Jam alium & sextum exhibet sensum Grotius de dispersione gentium, ne Israelitis prævalerent : qui vero quomodo e verbis aut contextu erui possit, non apparet. Pro ratione, vel numero filiorum Israel gentium termini constituti dicuntur, non vero ita σποραδικῶς gentes disseminatæ, ne adeo multæ essent: quia prævaluerunt iisdem Israëlitæ. Nec tam sua multitudine & copia, quam divina virtute & assistentia prævaluere Israëlitæ.

Septimo Rupertus alium adhuc sensum promit: Constituit Deus ut duret genus humanum, donec im- pleatur terminus & numerus electorum. Sed hic non electi cum reliquis hominibus, sed Israëlitæ cum gentibus, quas exterminarunt, conferuntur.

Quis ergo denique sensus? Hoc vult Moses; jam tum, quando in dispersione & γλωττοσυγχύσει Babelica filii hominum per orbem disseminati sunt, fi- liis Israel Deum prospexisse, & terminos distinctos cer- torum populorum constituisse, prout ipsis commo- dum fore prævidit, ut cura & providentia Dei erga Israëlitas celebretur. Ideo additur vers. 9. QVIA pars Domini populus ejus : Jacob funiculus hæredita- tis ejus : ut causa reddatur hujus providentiæ. In Ebræo enim est particula causalis, atque ita etiam reddidit Chaldæus. Paulus Fagius & Franc. Vatabl. sensum hunc reddunt: Quando altissimus divisit Patrias & regiones, & assignavit eas cunctis gentibus, jam tum decreverat dare filiis Israel terram septem eorum populorum, quos sub adventum ipsorum Israe- litarum ejecit e terra Chanaan, vel tunc dedit septem gentibus, Amorrhæis st. Hevæis &c. tantam regionis planitiem, quæ numero filiorum Israel sufficeret. Sic etiam exposuit B. Lyserus noster Commentar. in Gen. 10. pag. 397. Optime sententiam expressit B. Lutherus in explicatione laudata : Primum benefi- cium est, quod cum DEUS sit, & omnium gentium Deus, ut quas divisit Gen. 11. distribuit eis orbem terrarum, unicuique genti suam portionem & termi- num, ut Paulus Act. 17. hunc versum æmulatus do- cet, tamen non omnes elegit sibi populum, quorum peculiariter esset DEUS vero & legitimo cultu, sed posuit limites, ut solum ubi filii Israel essent, ibi esset populus ejus. Ubi vero finiretur limes filiorum Israel, ibi cessaret populus Dei, & inciperent termini gen- tium. Quia populus suus est portio Domini, Jacob est funiculus hæreditatis ejus, i. e. non latius patet populus ejus, quam est Jacob seu Israel. Istis scilicet verbis describitur, quam peculiaris sit iste populus DEI. Perperam Vulgata, pars AUTEM Domi- ni. Unde Becani glossæ iterum nullus locus, quasi hæc κατ᾿ ἀντίθεσιν hoc pacto dicantur : quod cum gentes cæteræ Angelorum tutelæ commissæ sint, soli Judæi, ceu populus præ aliis DEO dilectus Deum custodem atque protectorem habeant. Pro- bat sensum nostrum e Pontificiis Oleaster, Card. Cajetanus ac Cornel. a Lapide; cujus verba adscri- bo: Sensus ergo est, quando Deus in Babel gentes dis- persit, statuit terminos regionum & terrarum illis omnibus, idque ad hoc, ut scil. tantum terræ spacium filiis Israel, nec dum natis, sed nascituris ad habitan- dum secerneret & eximeret, quantum noverat ad nu- merum eorum atq; commodam singulorum habitatio- nem requiri & sufficere; q. d. Ex tunc Deus terram Chanaan designavit & terminavit, ne ab aliis oc- cuparetur, quam a Chananæis, qui delendi & ex- pellendi erant ab Hebræis. Sic etiam Jacob Ti- rinus, qui addit: Causam tam citæ, tam singularis providentiæ mox subnectit, quia ex tunc erat Israel a Deo dilectus seu designatus in partem, seu funiculum Dei, id est, in portionem Ejus hæreditariam. Ita quo- que Menochius & Bonfrerius in h. l.

## 32:10
Verse 10. HE FOUND HIM IN A DESERT LAND] Thus also Aquila and Theodotion: but the LXX [translate] he sufficed him, which is another interpretation of the word מצא, whence it is also translated by ἀρέσκω in Judges 21:14. The Chaldean rendered it, he gave him necessary things sufficiently, whence Paul Fagius on the Chaldean Paraphrase says: The Hebrew word signifies both to find and to suffice. The Chaldean paraphrast followed the latter reading; those who follow the former reading and take it for to find, explain it thus, that is to say, as if he claimed for himself by first occupying a thing pertaining to no one's power, which happened not in Egypt, but in the desert, where glory first began to appear to the multitude.

Latin:

Vers. 10. INVENIT EVM IN TERRA DESERTA] Sic & Aquila & Theodotio: at LXX. αὐτάρκησεν αὐτὸν, quæ altera est vocis מצא interpretatio, unde & per ἀρέσκω vertitur Jud. 21, 14. Chald. reddidit, sufficienter dedit ei necesfaria, unde Paul. Fagius ad Paraphras. Chald. Verbum Hebraicum inquit, & invenire & sufficere significat. Posteriorem lectionem secutus est paraphrastes Chal- dæus; qui priorem lectionem sequuntur & pro inve- nire accipiunt, sic exponunt q. d. veluti rem ad nul- lius potestatem attinentem primus occupando sibi vendicavit, quod non in Ægypto, sed in deserto evenit, ubi primum cœpit gloria multitudini ap- parere.

## 32:11
Verse 11. AS AN EAGLE STIRRING UP HER YOUNG TO FLY. In Hebrew, stirring up his nest, that is, his young, the container for the contained. He takes him up, namely the nest, that is, his young, as Vatablus rightly [notes]. When an eagle, says Münster, strives to transfer her young to another place, she stirs the nest, that is, the family of the young, and flutters around the nest until she has taken them all upon her shoulders. Thus the Lord in the desert carried his people as it were on his shoulders, nourished, watered, and defended them from enemies. HE CARRIED HIM, or made him ride to the high places of the earth, that is, to the land of Canaan, which is found to be higher than the other lands of those regions, so that, namely, he might eat the rich fruits of the fields: where שָׂדָי is written for שָׂדוֹת, as Münster [notes] here again.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SICUT AQVILA PROVOCANS AD VOLANDUM PULLOS SUOS. In Ebr. provocans nidum suum, id est, pullos suos, continens pro contento. Assumit illum, scil. ni- dum, id est, pullos suos, ut recte Vatablus. Cum aqui- „ la, inquit Münsterus, pullos suos in alium locum „ transferre contendit, excitat nidum, hoc est fami- „ liam pullorum & tamdiu circa nidum volitat, do- „ nec omnes super humeros suos susceperit. Sic Do- „ minus in deserto populum suum q. in humeris por- „ tavit, nutrivit, potavit & ab hostibus defendit eum. VEXIT EUM, sive equitare fecit eum ad loca terræ excelsa, id est, ad terram Canaan, quæ cæteris terris illarum regionum altior invenitur, ut scil. comederet uberes fructus agrorum: ubi שָׂדָי scribitur pro שָׂדוֹת, ut iterum hic Münsterus.

## 32:13
v. 13. THAT HE MIGHT SUCK HONEY OUT OF THE ROCK. He describes the fertility of the holy land. In the rocks are bees, and olives, and oil from the olives; that is to say, there is no place there unfruitful and empty of good and sweet things: for in the very rocks there are olives, and honey, according to the interpretation of Vatablus. In Hebrew it is and he suckled him with honey from the rock, and with oil from the flinty stone: And Scripture speaks in past verbs, although all these things were still to be, and by honey, oil, butter, milk, fat, wheat, and the like, the abundance of all things is signified: as Münster [notes] here. It follows concerning the rams of the sons of Bashan, and the goat with the fat of the kidneys or of the wheat, in Hebrew, which Vatablus explains thus, that is to say, He ate rams reared in Bashan, a most fertile region, and goats with the flour of the grains of wheat, which present the appearance of a kidney, and a little kidney: that is, with the best flour of wheat. AND THEY MIGHT DRINK THE BLOOD OF THE GRAPE most pure, that is, as Münster notes, the best and red wine. For they think, he says, that חמר signifies the same as ארום, that is, red, brought into Hebraism from Arabism. He calls the juice blood, because on account of its color it appears to be blood: because for them the wine was mostly red. But pure [wine] is placed by way of opposition, you drank pure wine.

Latin:

v. 13. UT SUGERET MEL DE PETRA. Fœcunditatem terræ sanctæ describit. In ru- pibus apes, & olivæ & oleum ex olivis; q. d. illic nullus locus est infœcundus & vacuus rebus bonis & suavibus: nam in rupibus ipsis sunt olivæ, & mel, interprete Vatablo. In Ebr. est & lactavit eum melle de petra, atque oleo de flicis saxo: Et loquitur Scriptu- ra per præterita verba, licet omnia ista adhuc essent futura, significaturque per mel, oleum, butyrum, lac, adipem, triticum & similia, omnium rerum abundantia: ut hic Münsterus. Sequitur de arieti- bus filiorum Basan, & hirco cum adipe renum seu testium tritici, in Ebræo, quæ Vatablus ita exponit, q. d. Comedit arietes educatos in Basan regione ferti- lissima, & hircos cum farina granorum tritici, quæ præ se ferunt speciem testis, & renunculi: h. e. cum fa- rina optima tritici. ET SANGUINEM UVÆ BIBERENT meracissimum, hoc est, notante Münstero, vinum optimum & rubeum. Putant enim, inquit חמר idem significare, quod ארום, id est, rubeum, ex Arabismo in Ebraïsmum inve- ctum. Succum autem vocat sanguinem, quod propter colorem videatur sanguis: quia illis vinum maxime fuit rubeum. Merum autem per oppositio- nem positum, merum vinum bibisti.

## 32:15
Verse 15. THE BELOVED GREW FAT] For beloved in Hebrew is ישׁרון, which is a diminutive shortened from ישׂראל, just as we are accustomed to address infants: thus also 33:5 and 26.

Such diminutives, with the shortening of the whole name, will not easily be found in the Hebrew language. And why the name should be deduced from the word ישראל does not appear: since it may be conveniently derived from ישר, he was upright, because he was chosen, so that he might follow uprightness. We have spoken before about the various interpretations of the word at verse 3.

Latin:

Vers. 15. INCRASSATVS EST DILECTVS] Pro dile- cto in Hebræo est ישׁרון, quod diminutivum est curtatum ex ישׂראל, quomodo infantes alloqui solemus: sic & 33, 5. & 26

Non facile invenientur talia diminutiva, cum decurtatione nominis integri, in lingua Ebræa. Et cur a voce ישראל deducendum nomen sit, haud apparet: quum a ישר rectus fuit, commode derivetur, quod electus sit, ut rectitudinem sequa- tur. De variis vocis interpretationibus antea dixi- mus ad vers. 3.

## 32:17
Verse 17. THEY SACRIFICED TO DEMONS] שדים are said to be water-demons to the Hebrews. Grotius has this again from Fagius, who says that Shedim are believed to be harmful spirits that come forth from the waters. But not only those, but generally Demons, whom the Israelites served, are noted, who are so called from devastating, because it is the nature of demons to devastate religion and all laws: indeed, whatever good there is in the world. And whom God understands by demons, Moses explains in the following words: they sacrificed to demons, and not to God, to gods whom they did not know. To new ones who came recently, whom your fathers did not worship. This is, according to the interpretation of Luther, field idols, namely in groves, valleys, mountains, about which nothing had been said to them in the law, nor had they heard anything about them, but itching in their ears, just as anyone brought in some new worship, so they flocked most of all, having abandoned God, whom they had learned from their fathers, or as Megalander [writes] more fully in T. V. Altenb. page 793. That is all kinds of idolatries of the heathens, such as Baal, Astaroth, Moloch, Chemosh, Camarin, etc., and they set up all kinds of divine service on the mountains and heights, in the woods and groves, about which nothing was commanded in the law, of which their fathers knew nothing, which they had invented and devised for themselves, when they followed their own darkness and thoughts, about which all the true prophets complain vehemently afterwards. Buxtorf has handed down in his Lexicon far different things than these from the Hebrews concerning שדים from the Talmudic writings. Rabbin. page 2339, even if still more fabulous: They have wings like Angels and fly from one end of the world to the other like Angels, they eat and drink like men, they beget and multiply like men, and they die like men.

Latin:

Vers. 17. IMMOLAVERUNT DÆMONIIS] שדים Hebræis esse dicuntur dæmones ě́νυδροι. Hoc iterum a Fagio habet Grotius, qui Sche- dim, inquit, creduntur esse noxii spiritus, qui ex aquis prodeant. At non illi tantum, sed γενικῶς Dæmones, quibus servierunt Israëlitæ, notantur, qui sic vo- cantur a vastando, quia Dæmonum est religionem, & omnia jura vastare: imo quicquid boni est in mundo. Et quosnam Deus per Dæmonia intelli- gat, verbis sequentibus explicat Moses: sacrifica- verunt dæmoniis, & non Deo, sed diis, quos nescierunt. Novis qui recens venerunt, quos non coluerunt Patres vestri. Hoc est, interprete Luthero, idolis campe- stribus, scilicet in lucis, vallibus, montibus, de quibus nihil erat eis dictum in lege, nec quicquam de eis audie- rant, sed prurientes auribus, ut quilibet novum ali- quem cultum advehebat, ita maxime affluebant, re- licto Deo, quem ex patribus didicerant, vel uti Mega- lander plenius T. V. Altenb. pag. 793. Das ist aller- ley Abgötteren der Heyden, als Baal, Astoroth, Moloch, Chamos, Camarin sc. und richten aller- ley Gottesdienst an, auf den Bergen und Höhen, in den Wäldern und Håynen, von welchen nichts im Gesetz geboten war, davon ihre Våter nichts ge- wust, die sie ihnen selbst erfunden und erdichtet hat- ten, da sie ihrem Dunckel und Gedancken folgeten, darüber hernach alle rechte Propheten hefftig klagen. Longe alia, quam hic, ex Ebræis de שדים tradidit e Talmudicis Buxtorfius in Lex. Rabbin. pag. 2339. etsi magis adhuc fabulosa: Alas habent sicut Angeli & volant ab una extremitate mundi ad alte- ram sicut Angeli, edunt & bibunt, sicut homines, gi- gnunt & multiplicantur sicut homines, & moriuntur sicut homines.

## 32:21
IN HIM WHO IS NOT A PEOPLE] A fellowship of law makes a people. By that name, a multitude is unworthy which has either no laws or bad ones. It is not a fellowship of any law whatsoever that is regarded, but a divine one in this designation of a People. For Grotius would not have said that all nations alien to the true God had no fellowship of law, and had only no laws or bad ones. Osiander correctly expresses the force of the divine sentence: just as they made me as it were jealous, while they worshipped foreign gods, when they ought to have adhered to me alone: just as it befits a virtuous wife to adhere to her husband alone: so I in turn will make them jealous. For having cast off the Jews, I will betroth to myself the nations through faith, whom I know to be extremely despised by the Jews as a foolish people, full of blindness and ignorance of God: and not even considered worthy of the name of a people. And I will do this if by chance some of the Jews, being incensed, may repent and believe the Gospel: so that they may become partakers of eternal salvation together with the nations. That this is the meaning of this passage, Paul clearly teaches in Rom. 10 and 11. And indeed the event responded to the prophecy; for some Jews were converted to Christ. But concerning the Jews who, even before Christ was born, having spurned the preachings of the Prophets, persisted in impiety: or after the Savior of the world was born, did not cease to persecute his Gospel, Moses speaks in the following words: A fire is kindled, says the Lord, in my fury, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 21. IN EO QUI NON EST POPULUS] Juris consociatio populum facit. Eo nomine indigna multitudo, quæ aut nullas, aut malas habet leges. Non respicitur cujuscunque juris consociatio, sed divini hac Populi ἐπωνυμίᾳ. Nec enim gentes universas a vero Deo alienas omni juris consocia- tione, nullasque aut malas solum habuisse leges, di- xiffet Grotius. Vim sententiæ divinæ recte expri- mit Osiander: sicut ipsi quasi zelotypum me fecerunt, dum coluerunt alienos Deos, cum mihi uni adhærere deberent: sicut probam uxorem marito suo soli adhæ- rere decet: ita ego vicissim zelotypos faciam. Abje- ctis enim Judæis, desponsabo mihi gentes per fidem, quas scio a Judæis extreme tanquam populum stultum, plenum cæcitate, & ignorantia Dei, contemni: ac ne populi quidem nomine dignum censeri. Idque faciam si forte aliqui ex Judæis accensi, pœnitentiam agant, & credant Evangelio: ut fiant salutis æternæ una cum gentibus participes. Hanc esse hujus loci sententiam, manifeste docet Paulus ad Rom. 10. & 11. Capp. Et sane eventus respondit vaticinio; nonnulli enim Judæi ad Christum conversi sunt. De Judæis ve- ro, qui vel ante natum Christum, spretis Prophe- tarum concionibus, in impietate perseverarunt: vel post natum Salvatorem mundi Evangelion ipsius persequi non destiterunt, loquitur Moyses in sequentibus verbis: Ignis succensus est, inquit Dominus, in furore meo, &c.

## 32:22
UNTO THE LOWEST HELL) The flame will burn not only buildings and the soil, but also the innermost parts of the earth. Taking the passage in a recondite sense, the Hebrews almost derive from here the name שאול, תחתית, by which they designate the region or state of the most grievous punishments after this life. Thus they also mystically interpret vengeance, the mention of which is below in verse 35, and the life opposed to it in verse 47. In a similar sense they say this song is the foundation and perfection of the law.

There is no need for a mystical sense to be admitted: for in the literal sense the fire of divine wrath, which, kindled, burns even to the LOWEST parts of hell, as is held in Hebrew, is designated: because the indignation and wrath of God, like his enemies, pursues them into hell, to the eternal flames and torments of hellfire, just as it also devours their land with its grass and burns the foundations of the mountains. Therefore, the kindled fire is to be understood not as material fire, but as the fire of divine wrath, which both destroys men eternally and burns the inner parts of the earth. Nor indeed does divine vengeance in verse 35, or even life in verse 47, imply eternal punishment or life only in a mystical sense; but since it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God, and divine vengeance and retribution, as regards the impenitent, extend themselves into all eternity, and since those devastations of the land—whether they happen by flame of fire, or by flood of waters, or by any other means—no less proceed from the fire of divine indignation and wrath, just as all other calamities, whether public or private, do, it is manifest that divine vengeance embraces all those things, when the Lord says, 'Vengeance is mine': just as, on the contrary, eternal life itself is also simultaneously embraced by the promises of the divine law; see what we have observed regarding verse 47. Thus there is no need to invent a hyperbole in the words regarding the lower hell, and to understand it, with some who follow Vatablus and Münster, as the barrenness of the deep places of the earth.

Not undeservedly, however, have the Rabbis called this Song the foundation and perfection of the law, even if the song is understood not in a mystical but in a literal sense: because in this very sense it gravely inculcates the law to be kept in perpetual memory, proclaims divine benefits, places the threatening of the most grievous judgments prophetically as it were before the eyes, and demonstrates the true use of the law. Paulus Fagius in the Targum and Pentateuch and Sebastian Münster in his Biblical commentaries, collected from the Rabbis, observe that the Hebrews call this song a summary of the whole law, because it makes mention of the magnificence of God, of the creation of the world, of worshipping one God, of the generation of the flood, of the division of languages and lands, of the election of the Israelite people, of the benefit shown to it in the desert, of the future resurrection of the dead, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 22. VSQUE AD INFERNI NOVISSIMA) Flamma non ædificia & solum tantum, sed & penetralia terræ peruret. Accepto loco in sensum reconditum sum- fere hinc Hebræi nomen שאול ,תחתית , quo gra- vissimarum post hanc vitam pœnarum regionem aut statum appellant. Sic etiam mystice interpretantur ultionem, cu- jus mentio infra 35. & oppositam ei vitam 47. Pari sensu di- cunt hoc canticum esse fundamentum, & perfectionem legis.

Non opus est, ut sensus mysticus admittatur: literali enim sensu ignis iræ divinæ, qui succensus ardet usq́; ad inferni INFIMA, ut in Ebr. habetur, designatur: quia Dei indignatio, & ira uti hostes ejus in infernum prosequitur, ad æternas flammas, & cruciatus infernalis ignis, sic etiam terram eo- rum devorat cum gramine suo, & montium combu- rit fundamenta. Ignis ergo succensus non de ma- teriali igne, sed de igne iræ divinæ intelligendus est, qui & homines æternum perdit, & penetralia ter- ræ perurit. Neque vero ultio divina vers. 35. vel etiam vita v. 47. sensu tantum mystico æternam pœnam, aut vitam subinfert, sed quum horrendum sit in manus Dei viventis incidere, & ultio, ac vindicta divina, quoad impœnitentes, in æternitatem omnem sese extendat, nec minus ab igne divinæ indignationis, & iræ illæ terræ vastationes, seu ignis flamma, seu aquarum diluvio, seu alia ratio- ne fiant, proficiscantur, ut & aliæ quæcunque cala- mitates, qua publicæ, qua privatæ, manifestum est, ultionem divinam ea omnia complecti, cum Do- minus ait, Mea est vindicta : quemadmodum ex adverso vita æterna ipsa legis divinæ promissioni- bus simul etiam comprehensa est, vid. quæ ad v. 47. observavimus. Ita non opus est hyperbolen in ver- bis ad infernum inferiorem fingere, & de sterilitate profundorum terræ locorum cum nonnullis, Va- tablum & Münsterum sequentibus intelligere.

Non immerito autem Rabbini Canticum hoc fundamentum dixere, ac perfectionem legis, etsi non mystico sed literali canticum intelligatur sen- su: quia hoc ipso sensu legem graviter inculcat, in perpetua servandam memoria, beneficia divina de- prædicat, comminationem gravissimorum judi- ciorum veluti πρὸς ὄμμα Prophetice collocat, & verum legis usum commonstrat. Paulus Fagius in Targum & Pentatevch. & Sebast. Münsterus in commentar. Bibl. e Rabbin. collectis, observant, Ebræos Canticum hocce dicere summarium totius legis, quia facit mentionem de magnificentia Dei, de creationi mundo, de uno Deo colendo, de generatione diluvii, de divisione linguarum, & terrarum, de ele- ctione populi Israelitici, de beneficio in deserto ei exhi- bito, de futura resurrectione mortuorum &c.

## 32:26
Verse 26. I SAID, WHERE ARE THEY] The Greeks more correctly [translate] διασπερῶ αὐτούς. Just as Aben-Ezra also interprets it. And hence the 'diasporas' of the Israelites in Babylonia, Media, Egypt, Greece, and elsewhere are so called. The word is derived from 'corner,' as if he were to say, I will scatter them into all corners.

Others prefer to render it, as Cocceius does, with Junius: I would have said: Sebastian Castellio: And indeed I had determined to destroy them. Similarly also Leo Judae, I had indeed determined; to whose translation Vatablus noted these things: I would have said, I will thrust them down, etc., that is, I had decided within myself in this manner: I will drive this Israelite nation from me into a corner of the world, and I will take away their memory from among men: had I not feared the enemy, angry and hostile to that people of mine, lest that enemy might not acknowledge that I had done it, or might pretend not to acknowledge who had done it. That is to say: I had already determined to destroy that nation entirely, had I not seen that the enemy would attribute this to himself, which ought to be attributed to me: that he had conquered his enemies the Israelites, whom I myself had destroyed. To be sure, according to that interpretation, God institutes here a consultation, as it were, as to whether he ought to destroy the entire memory of the Jews in that destruction, as they had fully deserved, or not? Which some accept as if God does not wish to destroy the Jewish nation entirely, since in the last time of the world a notable multitude of them is to be converted to the faith. Thus also Cocceius teaches that the Jews are to be reassumed at some time. Concerning which, in section 1490, he speaks thus: Certainly, that God preserves them as a separate nation, that is done without doubt to the end that in them divine grace and power may be singularly demonstrated, and the life of the nations and every heresy may at length be refuted by them. These things are from the comparison of verses 26 and 43, to which end he also brings forward these passages: Lev. 26:44, 45; Ps. 85:2, 3, 4, 9; Ps. 106:47; Is. 6:13, ch. 19:18, 19, 20, 21, 22, ch. 59:21; Jer. 3:21, ch. 31:39, 40; Ez. 39:25; Hos. 3:5; Mic. 4:6, 7, ch. 5:20. Luke 21:24; Rom. 11:11, 15, 25, 26, 31, 32. But just as all those things are weighed in their own place, so it is by no means clear that the preservation and a certain universal conversion of the Jews are promised here. For it is only hinted that God does not wish to cut off the Jews entirely from corner to corner, and to destroy their name from among men, just as the names of many nations have been destroyed with them, but that some posterity would be scattered through all nations, retaining its name and the character of its fathers in circumcision and the observation of the precepts of the law, as Cocceius explains in section 1298. Indeed, in Psalm 16:8, when he says, 'I will not take their names upon my lips,' God denies that he will acknowledge them as his own, or impart consolation to them, yet he does not deny that they will have a name among the nations of the world. Add that he is prophesying here about the Roman destruction: through which, however, they were not all immediately destroyed, nor was their memory entirely abolished. I would have said, he says, I will cut them off to the corners, and I will abolish their name from among men, unless. He did not say, he did not decree this, but the contrary. Therefore, what is held above in verse 21, 'I will make them jealous by a no-people,' when they are said here to be preserved for that end, was fulfilled in the successive conversion of some of them, but not therefore is a simultaneous conversion of such a huge and great multitude of them to be expected at last, so that a universal conversion might seem to be the case. Neither the Latin nor the Greeks sufficiently express the Hebrew word אַפְאֵיהֶם. Cocceius more correctly [renders it]: I will cut them off from the corner, for that is what its emphasis imports. It is not to be explained as a dispersion into all corners. For this has happened: but as an utter excision, because the deletion of the name is also added. Blessed Luther explains these things, however, not hypothetically but absolutely, not indeed concerning the total slaughter of all Jews, but concerning the excision of the people, not that no Jews will remain, but that they will have no certain place, kingdom, or priesthood, as all other peoples have, and he says that their memory being taken away means that nothing more is boasted of them: as before, that they are, or can do anything, in the manner of other peoples, and as they themselves had been previously. But as for what follows in v. 28, 'Unless I feared the wrath of the enemy,' Luther judges it to be spoken thus because God sometimes deferred His just wrath and delivered even the unworthy and undeserving, but He did this for the sake of His own name (so long, that is, as some memory of the divine name still flourished among the Jewish people) lest it be blasphemed by idolaters. Osiander, along with Brentius, follows this sense, and the Vulgate version indicates it: 'But I deferred because of the wrath of the enemies.'

Latin:

Vers. 26. DIXI UBINAM SUNT] Rectius Græci διασ- περῶ αὐτούς. Quomodo & Aben-Esdra interpretatur. Et hinc dictæ Israelitarum διασποραὶ in Babylonia, Media, Æ- gypto, Græcia & alibi, Verbum est deductum ab angulo, quasi dicat, in omnes angulos disjiciam.

Alii reddere malunt uti Coccejus, cum Junio: dixissem: Sebastianus Castellio: Et quidem statue- ram Eos profligare. Similiter quoque Leo Judæ, sta- tueram quidem; ad cujus translationem Vatablus hæc notavit, dixissem, Detrudam eos &c. id est, de- crevissem apud me in hunc modum: Abigam hanc gentem Israeliticam a me in angulum orbis, & exi- mam ex hominibus memoriam eorum: nisi ti- muissem inimicum, iratum & infensum illi popu- lo meo, ne non ille inimicus agnosceret me illud fecisse, aut simularet se non agnoscere, quis id fecisset. q. d. Jam decrevissem omnino perdere eam gentem, nisi vide- rem, quod inimicus hoc sibi tribueret, quod mihi tri- buendum est: se inimicos suos Israelitas vicisse, quos ego ipse delevissem. Scilicet juxta illam interpretationem instituit hic Deus velut consultationem de eo, utrum in excidio illo confestim omnem Judæorum me- moriam delere debeat, uti meriti omnino erant, nec ne? Quæ nonnulli eo accipiunt, ac si Deus no- lit plane delere Judæorum gentem, quandoquidem novissimo mundi tempore insignis eorum multitudo convertenda sit ad fidem. Ita etiam Coccejus Judæos olim reassumendos tradit. Quo de §. 1490. sic loquitur: Certe quod Deus illos conservat gentem separatam, id sine dubio fit eo fine, ut in ipsis singulariter divina gratia & potentia demonstretur, & vita gentium omnisq́; hæresis tandem per ipsos confutetur. Hæc e collatione v. 26. & 43. in quem finem etiam hæc adducit loca Lev. 26, 44. 45. Ps. 85. v. 2. 3. 4. 9. Psal. 106, 47. Es. 6, 13. cap. 19, 18. 19. 20. 21. 22. cap. 59, 21. Jer. 3, 21. c. 31, 39. 40. Ez. 39, 25. Hos. 3, 5. Mich. 4, 6. 7. c. 5, 20. Luc. 21, 24. Rom. 11, 11. 15. 25. 26. 31. 32. Sed ut illa omnia suo expenduntur loco, ita hic Judæorum conservationem & universalem conversionem quandam promitti, neutiquam liquet. Nam id solum innuitur, nolle Deum Judæos totos ab angulo ad angulum exscindere, & delere nomen ipsorum ex hominibus, quemadmodum multarum gentium nomina cum ipsis deleta sunt, sed & posteritatem aliquam sparsam fore, per omnes gentes, retinentem nomen suum & characterem Patrum suorum in circumcisione & observatione legis præceptorum, ut explicat Coccejus §. 1298. Sane Psalm. 16, 8. cum ait, non assumam nomina eorum in labia mea, negat Deus, eos se pro suis agniturum, aut consolationem ipsis imperturum, non tamen negat, eos habituros nomen inter gentes mundi. Adde, quod hic de excidio Romano vaticenetur: per quod vero non confestim omnes deleti, aut memoria ipsorum plane abolita est. Dixissem, inquit, angulotenus excindam illos, & abolebo nomen illorum ex hominibus, nisi. E. non dixit, non decrevit hoc, sed contrarium. Quod ergo supra habetur v. 21. faciam zelare per non populum, quum hic eo fine conservandi dicuntur, impletum est in successiva nonnullorum ex ipsis conversione, non vero demum ideo expectanda simultanea ingentis tantæque multitudinis eorum conversio, ut videri possit universalis conversio. Verbum Ebr. אַפְאֵיהֶם nec Latinus, nec Græci satis exprimunt. Rectius Coccejus ab angulo succidam eos, id enim importat emphasis ejus. Non de dispersione in omnes angulos explicandum. Hæc enim facta est: sed de excisione omnimoda, quia additur etiam nominis deletio. Quæ tamen non hypothetice, sed absolute, non quidem de totali Judæorum omnium internecione, sed de populi excisione, non quod nulli Judæi futuri sint reliqui, sed quod nullum locum certum, regnum, aut sacerdotium habituri sint, sicut omnes alii populi habent, explicat B. Lutherus, & memoriam eorum tolli, dicit esse nihil amplius de illis jactari: sicut antea, quod sint, aut possint aliquid, more aliorum populorum, & sicut prius ipsi fuerant. Quæ vero sequuntur v. 28. Nisi iram inimici vererer, ita dicta censet Lutherus, quia aliquando Deus distulit iram justam, & liberavit etiam indignos & immeritos, sed hoc fecit propter nomen suum (quamdiu sc. penes Judaicum populum adhuc nominis divini quædam vigebat memoria) ne blasphemaretur ab idolatris. Quem sensum etiam sequitur Osiander cum Brentio, indicatque vulgata versio: Sed propter iram inimicorum distuli.

## 32:27
Ver. 27. BUT I DEFERRED BECAUSE OF THE WRATH OF THE ENEMIES, LEST PERCHANCE THEIR FOES SHOULD BE PROUD.

In Hebrew: 'Unless I feared the insult of the enemy.' By the enemy we do not understand the Devil, as Cocceius wishes, but the enemies of the Jews, the ministers of the Devil, whom he himself in v. 27 thinks are called a lost nation. 'Unless I had feared the indignation or vexation from him,' which he was about to cause through a triple blasphemy: one, by which the Romans were going to attribute this to their false gods, in these words: Lest their enemies ALIENATE. Vulg. & others, lest their enemies should be proud. A second, by which some were going to boast as if exalted by their own hand. A third, by which certain ones were not going to attribute this work to Jehovah. This is Cocceius. But those predicates speak not of different, but of the same enemies, nor is there anything here about idols & false gods. The Hebrew word can be rendered thus with Avenarius, lest by chance their enemies judge, or if it be explained lest they alienate, the following words will provide an ἐξήγησιν, lest they say our hand was high, and Jehovah did not work these things. For this is to alienate, when it is not attributed to Jehovah. The words which follow, v. 28. A nation void of counsels up to v. 34. Cocceius thinks should be included in a parenthesis; at the very least it must be said that verse 31 is parenthetical, since these words: not as our rock is their rock, cannot be attributed to God, who in v. 26, 27 is undoubtedly speaking: but nothing stands in the way of our attributing that votive exclamation of v. 29 & what follows in v. 30, 31 to God, so that it is not a work of parenthesis, as will now be said.

Latin:

Vers. 27. SED PROPTER IRAM INIMICORUM DISTULI, NE FORTE SUPERBIRENT HOSTES EORUM.

In Ebr. Nisi insultationem hostis timerem. Per inimicum non Diabolum intelligimus, ut Coccejus vult, sed hostes Judæorum Diaboli ministros, quos ipse v. 27. gentem perditam dici putat. Nisi indignationem vel ægritudinem ab ipso timuissem, quam facturus erat per triplicem blasphemiam, unam, qua ascripturi hoc erant Romani falsis diis suis, his ver- bis: Ne ALIENENT hostes ipsorum. Vulg. & alii, ne superbirent hostes eorum. Alteram qua nonnulli ceu manu sua exaltati gloriaturi erant. Tertiam, qua quidam hoc opus Jehovæ non erant tributuri. Hæc Coccejus. Verum prædicata illa non de diver- sis, sed iisdem loquuntur hostibus, neque hic de idolis & falsis diis quicquam habetur. Ebræum ver- bum ita reddi potest cum Avenario, ne forte judi- cent hostes eorum, aut si exponatur ne alienent, da- bunt verba sequentia ἐξήγησιν, ne dicant excelsa ma- nus nostra fuit, nec Jehovah operatus est hæc. Hoc enim est alienare, cùm Jehovæ id non tribuitur. Verba quæ sequuntur, v. 28. Non gens perlens con- siliis usque ad v. 34. parenthesi includenda esse, putat Coccejus; ad minimum certe dicendum, vers. 31. esse parentheticum, quum hæc verba: non ut rupes no- stra rupes ipsorum, non possint Deo tribui, qui v. 26. 27. indubitato loquitur: sed nihil obstat, quo mi- nus exclamationem illam votivam v. 29. & quæ se- quuntur v. 30. 31. Deo tribuamus, ut opus paren- thesi non sit, quemadmodum jam dicetur.

## 32:28
v. 28. A NATION VOID OF COUNSEL, AND WITHOUT PRUDENCE.

Some understand this of the enemies of the Jews, Abulensis, Vatablus, Agellius, Leonh. Marius, Quiros, Magalanus, Sebast. Castellio, Vatablus, & others; which opinion Lorinus in his Commentary on this place judges not to lack probability, so that, namely, those blasphemers are said to lack both counsel and prudence, since they could easily perceive that the victories reported over the Hebrews happened with their God as their avenger. Thus also Cocceius §. 1273. But the more common exposition of Theodoret, or Cyril, according to him, Procopius, Euthymius, is that these things are to be taken again concerning the Jews themselves, of whom also verse 29 speaks: O that they were wise, and understood! because he speaks of the same nation, which the Lord had complained was without counsel and prudence: A nation is without counsel, and without intelligence, that is, according to Luther's paraphrase: it cares for nothing, neither wrath, nor grace, nor does it take heed, so that their affairs might be before me, they presumptuously imagine [God] to be propitious to them, when I am angry, therefore they do not think to take counsel for themselves, and correct themselves. O that they were wise and prudent in this, and understood their latter end? All this is said, because they are thoughtless, concerning their present state, and concerning their future punishment, or secure, because they are good, and hope for the best, when far contrary things are present, and impending. Junius, Piscator, Osiander, and others side with Luther. Indeed, as Lorinus admits, it declares a vehement desire that they might finally wish to be wise, and to understand what will happen in the future, what reward of wickedness awaits them, what grave punishment, which admonition openly demonstrates that God is compelled by a certain necessity to send calamities, and to chastise those desirous of the salvation of men. Whence Lorinus, with Cornel. a Lap., also acknowledges that the whole context favors it, along with the preceding and following [verses]: Thus also Christ deplores the destruction of the Jews in Luke 19, 24, if you had known even you, etc. Paul also wished to be anathema for them, Romans 9, 3, which Rupertus says is nothing else in this place than what is now wished in this very sentence, that the Jews might be wise to the evils foretold, and that we also ought to wish the same for them. Which Rabanus, the Glossa, Hugo, and others rightly apply to any other impious persons who are without the counsel of salvation. Our B. Joh. Schmidius presented several special sermons on this votive sentence of Moses. Counsel, says Hugo, is concerning present things, prudence concerning future things, the former in discerning, the latter in choosing & executing: it is to be wished that they might be wise by themselves, understand through Doctors, foresee the latter end, whether torments or rewards, in the present, and weigh the present, because now is the time of providing, then of receiving what was foreseen: likewise let them be wise to the present, understand the past, foresee the future, and according to the warning of Jeremiah, let them see their ways in the valley, let them know what they have done, explaining the ways are light runners: furthermore let men be wise as to what they are, because a vessel of dung, let them understand what they were, because stinking seed, let them foresee what they will be, because food for worms, let them think with Bernard, whence they came and blush, where they are and groan, whither they go and tremble.

Latin:

v. 28. GENS ABSQUE CONSILIO EST, ET SINE PRUDENTIA.

Hoc de hostibus Judæorum nonnulli intelli- gunt, Abulensis, Vatablus, Agellius, Leonh. Marius, Quiros, Magalanus, Sebast. Castellio, Vatablus, & alii; quam sententiam non carere probabilitate censet Lorinus in Comment. ad h. l. ut videl. dican- tur isti blasphemi & consilio, atque prudentia ca- rere, quum facile possint advertere victorias ex E- bræis reportatas, Deo ipsorum vindice, contigis- se. Sic & Coccejus §. 1273. Sed communior exposi- tio Theodoreti, seu Cyrilli, apud eum, Procopii, Eu- thymii de Judæis ipsis hæc iterum accipienda esse, de quibus etiam vers. 29. Utinam saperent, & intel- ligerent! quia loquitur de eadem gente, quam absq; consilio & prudentia esse questus erat Dominus: Gens absq; consilio est, & sine intelligentia, id est, juxta Lu- theri paraphrasin: nihil curat, neque iram, neque gratiam, neque advertit, ut habeat res eorum, co- ram me, præsumtuosi fingunt sibi propitium, cum sim iratus, ideo non cogitant, ut sibi consulant, & sese corrigant. Utinam saperent & prudentes essent in hoc, & novissima intelligerent? Hoc totum dici- tur, quod sint incogitantes, de præsenti eorum sta- tu, & de futura eorum pœna, seu securi, quod bo- ni sint, & optima sperent, cum longe contraria ad- sint, & impendeant. Cum Luthero faciunt Junius, Piscator, Osiander, alii. Nimirum, ut Lorinus fa- tetur, vehemens declarat desiderium, ut sapere tan- dem velit, ac intelligere, quid olim eventurum sit, quæ sceleris maneat illum merces, quam grave sup- plicium, quæ admonitio aperte demonstrat, neces- sitate quadam compulsum Deum calamitates im- mittere, & castigare cupidum salutis hominum. Unde huic posteriori sententiæ etiam accessit Lori- nus, cum Cornel. a Lap. eique totum contextum favere, cum præcedentibus, sequentibusque agno- scit: Sic etiam Christus deplorat Judæorum interi- tum Luc. 19, 24. si cognovisses & tu &c. Paulus etiam optabat anathema esse pro illis, Roman. 9, 3. quod nihil aliud esse Rupertus h. l. ait, quam quod nunc optatur istamet sententia, ut sapiant Judæi mala prænunciata, idque nos quoque iisdem optare de- bere. Quæ recte ad alios quosvis impios, qui sine consilio salutis sunt, applicat Rabanus, Glossa, Hugo, & alii. B. Joh. Schmidius noster plures peculiares conciones de hac sententia votiva Mosis exhibuit. Consilium, inquit Hugo, est de præsentibus, pru- dentia de futuris, illud in discernendo, hæc in eligendo & exequendo: optandum, ut sapiant per se, intelligant per Doctores, novissima vel tormenta, vel præmia pro- videant in præsenti, pensentque præsentia, quia nunc est tempus providendi, tunc accipiendi prævisa : item sapiant præsentia, intelligant præterita, provideant fu- tura, & juxta Jeremiæ monitum, videant vias suas in convalle, sciant quid fecerint explicantes vias sunt cursores leves : præterea sapiant homines quid sunt, quia vas stercoreum, intelligant quid fuerunt, quia sperma fœtidum, provideant quid erunt, quia esca vermium, cogitent cum Bernardo, unde venerint, & erubescant, ubi sint, & ingemiscant, quo vadant & contremiscant.

## 32:29
Vers. 29. O THAT THEY WERE WISE AND UNDERSTOOD! ] Properly: they would make to understand, supply themselves. Therefore Aquila translates, ὄφελον συνιετίθησαν, by which word also the LXX elsewhere express this Hebrew.

Vers. eod. AND WOULD FORESEE THEIR LATTER END. In Hebrew their latter end; O that they could or would foresee their destruction, so that they might prevent it by true repentance! For God does not delight in the destruction of the impious. Vatablus renders and interprets it thus: If they had been wise to that, they would have understood their end (also), i.e., if they had been prudent, they would have understood that it was done by divine power, not human, namely that I destroyed this people of mine, not they themselves: They would have understood furthermore, what end or exit awaits them: They would have understood that the same things would happen to them on account of their own sins, which happened to my people. Sebast. Castellio handed down this version: Who would that they were only so wise, that they understood this, and considered their end thus, could it happen, that one should pursue a thousand, and two put to flight ten thousand, unless their own deity delivered them, unless Jehovah consigned them? With this paraphrase added: for the enemies do not have so much reason & prudence, as to think that it could not happen that so many Israelites would be overcome by so few enemies (which nevertheless will happen then, when I shall take notice of the Israelites) unless they were not only deserted by me their GOD, but also subdued and broken. But this prudence is more rightly desired in the Jews. For Moses predicts their fault, both their ἄγνοιαν [ignorance] and their ἀπείθειαν [disobedience], and their punishment, so that he may provoke them to repentance.

Latin:

Vers. 29. UTINAM SAPERENT ET INTELLIGE- RENT? ] Proprie: intelligere facerent, supple sese. Ideo Aquila vertit, ὄφελον συνιετίθησαν, qua voce & LXX. alibi hoc Hebræum exprimunt.

Vers. eod. AC NOVISSIMA PROVIDE- RENT. In Ebr. novissima SUA; Utinam prævidere possent aut vellent exitium suum, ut id vera pœni- tentia præcaverent! Non enim delectatur Deus impiorum interitu. Vatablus ita reddit, & inter- pretatur: Si sapuissent istud, finem (quoque) suum intellexissent, i. e. si prudentes fuissent, intellexissent, vi divina factum esse, non humana, nempe quod ego gentem hanc meam perdiderim, non ipsi: In- tellexissent præterea, quis finis sive exitus eos ma- neat: Intellexissent eadem sibi eventura propter peccata propria, quæ ipsi meæ genti acciderunt. Sebast. Castellio hanc tradidit versionem: Qui utinam tantum saperent, ut hoc intelligerent, & eo- rum exitum sic considerarent, fierine posset, ut perse- queretur unus mille, & duo fugarent decem millia, nisi illos ipsorum numen dederet, nisi Jova addiceret? Ad- dita hac paraphrasi: neque enim tantum rationis & prudentiæ habent hostes, ut cogitent, fieri non posse, ut tot Israelitæ a tam paucis hostibus superentur (id quod tamen tum fiet, cum Israelitas animadvertam) nisi essent a me DEO suo non solum destituti, sed etiam subacti atque fracti. Verum rectius hæc desideratur in Judæis prudentia. Illorum enim culpam, illo- rum tum ἄγνοιαν, tum ἀπείθειαν, illorumque pœnam prædicit Moses, ut eos ad pœnitentiam provocet.

## 32:30
Ver. 30. HOW SHOULD ONE CHASE A THOUSAND AND TWO PUT TEN THOUSAND TO FLIGHT. Cornelius corrects the Vulgate from the Roman edition in this place. How SHOULD HE CHASE. But as to who those pursuers are, the interpreters disagree. Some make the pursuers the enemies of the Jews. Thus Osiander: But they will not be willing to avert their evils by true repentance: therefore they will be put to flight and struck down by their enemies: Therefore it will commonly be said then: How did one of the enemies chase a thousand Jews, and two (what is the cause, that) put ten thousand to flight? Whence this trepidation to the Jews, a nation which otherwise was accustomed to resist enemies bravely? And it will be answered: Is it not for this reason? Because their God, whom they basely deserted, with the Messiah rejected, sold them, delivered and subjected them to the nations, and the Lord shut them up as captives, so that they could not escape such great evils, which happened under the Emperor Vespasian. It was done by a Roman in the city of Jerusalem, when the city, filled with Jews at the feast of the Passover, was surrounded by a siege. Cornelius explains it thus, (not badly) i.e., Even from this indeed which I shall say, they ought to have been admonished of their impiety, and incited to be wise, and to learn and heed the Judgments of God, for how could it happen that one of the enemies should chase a thousand Israelites, and two put ten thousand of them to flight, unless because God delivered them, and as it were sold them to their enemies, and shut them up in their hands. But others say the pursuers are the Jews themselves. How should one chase a thousand, and two put a myriad to flight? If, namely, they were wise, which condition is to be understood from the preceding verse 29: or re- The discourse is to be tightened from the words immediately added: IF NOT, BECAUSE THEIR ROCK HAS GIVEN THEM UP. Junius posits an ellipsis: If one Israelite does not pursue a thousand, but on the contrary they are routed by enemies, this happens because their rock has given them up. Coccejus also understands the enemies of the Jews and the Church to be those who are to be put to flight, and says they are sold by their rock, that is, the Devil: but what rock is understood in v. 30, the appended epexegesis teaches: unless their rock has sold them, and Jehovah has delivered them up. Jehovah, therefore, is the rock of the Jews, because He ought to have been acknowledged as such by them. For these things are expressed synonymously, and explain each other: their rock has sold them. And: Jehovah has delivered them up. How, therefore, shall we understand the Devil by the rock?

Latin:

Vers. 30. QUOMODO PERSEQUEBATUR UNUS MILLE ET DUO FUGARENT DE- CEM MILLIA. Vulgatam e Romana editione corrigit Cor- nel. h. m. Quomodo PERSEQUATUR. Quinam autem sint illi persequentes, discrepant interpretes. Nonnulli persequentes faciunt hostes Judæorum. Ita Osiander: Sed nolent vera pœnitentia avertere mala sua: propterea ab hostibus fugabuntur & ster- nentur: Itaque vulgo tum dicetur : Quomodo perse- quebatur unus hostium mille Judæos, & duo (quid in causa est, ut) fugarent decem millia? unde hæc trepidatio Judæis, genti, quæ alias fortiter hostibus re- sistere solebat? Et respondebitur : Nonne ideo? quia Deus ipsorum, quem turpiter deseruerunt, Messia abjecto, vendidit eos, tradidit ac subjecit eos genti- bus, & Dominus conclusit illos tanquam captivos, ne tanta mala effugere possent, quod sub Vespas. Impe- rat. Romano factum est in urbe Jerosolyma, cum ibi in festo Paschatos civitas repleta Judæis obsidione cin- geretur. Cornelius ita explicat, (non male) q. d. Vel ex hoc sane quod dicam, admoneri debuissent suæ im- pietatis, & ad sapiendum incitari, ac discere & ad- vertere Judicia Dei, qui enim fieri posset, ut unus ho- stium persequatur mille Israelitas, & duo fugent eo- rum decem millia, nisi quia Deus eos tradidit, & quasi vendidit hostibus eorum, & conclusit eos in manibus illorum. Alii vero persequentes dicunt ipsos Ju- dæos. Quomodo persequeretur unus mille, & duo fugarent myriadem? si scilicet saperent, quæ con- ditio e versu præcedenti 29. subaudienda: vel re- stringenda oratio è verbis immediate additis: SI NON, QUIA RUPES EORUM DEDIDIT EOS. Ellipsin ponit Junius: Si unus Israelita non persequitur mille, sed contra funduntur ab hostibus, fit hoc quia rupes eorum dedidit eos. Coccejus etiam hostes Judæorum & Ecclesiæ fugandos intelligit, eos- que venditos à rupe sua, id est, Diabolo, dicit: sed quæ rupes v. 30. intelligatur, epexegesis subjuncta docet: nisi quia rupes ipsorum vendidit eos, & Jeho- vah tradidit ipsos. Jehovah ergo rupes Judæorum est, quia talis ab ipsis agnosci debebat. Nam hæc συνω- νύμως efferuntur, ac se mutuo explicant: rupes ipso- rum vendidit eos. Et: Jehovah tradidit eos. Quo- modo ergo per rupem intelligemus Diabolum?

## 32:31
Vers. 31. FOR OUR GOD IS NOT AS THEIR GODS. In Hebrew: For not as our Petra, or rock, is the rock of them (the enemies) which leaves the sins of its worshippers unpunished, and which is powerless to avenge itself and its own, and to do good or evil to anyone, of which thing our enemies themselves are witnesses, who have experienced the power, severity, and justice of God, in preference to their own idols, such as the Egyptians, Amalekites, Amorites, and other nations, so that the words may be those of Moses, or of the Church, to be read in a parenthesis: as it seemed to some interpreters, provided that the preceding and following words are of God. An apostrophe of Moses, says Junius, because he explains the cause of the surrender into servitude, that God brings aid to His own, and opposes deserters, neither of which ought to be ascribed to fictitious gods. Piscator also includes those things in a parenthesis. Castellio observes that there is a change of person here, since it is not God who speaks those things, but the people. That these are the words of the Church, Vatablus likewise hints in his notes on this passage, or of Moses himself. Coccejus objects: because they are said in one breath, as it were: Their rock had sold them: because their rock is not as our rock. If, therefore, their rock were the rock of the Jews, Jehovah Himself would be the rock of the Church, and how then would their rock be denied to be as the rock of the Church? Resp. In the former, their rock has sold them, there can be no doubt that Jehovah is understood as the rock of Israel, because of the infallible exegesis appended by the Holy Spirit. But in these words, which are said to be included in a parenthesis, and are claimed for Moses or the Church, not as our rock is their rock, an opposition is instituted between the rock of the Church and their rock: where by these 'themselves' some understand the enemies, of whom mention had been made before, and of whom mention is made again by the words immediately appended: others understand the Israelites sold into the power of the enemies, because they made for themselves a non-God as a rock, when they served foreign gods and rejected the true God, or as Osiander, because they committed idolatry by a cult not prescribed by God, and thus did not worship the true God, who does not allow His worshippers to be confounded, so that it is no wonder they succumb. But the former sense is simpler: because as the rock of the Church is not the rock of the nations, or of the enemies of the Church, by the very testimony of the enemies themselves. To which B. Luther's commentary tends: Because their Rock is not like our Rock, of which thing our enemies themselves are witnesses. Understand this to be said because other gods, and the worshippers of gods, confessed that the God of Israel is such that, if He did not deliver them up, they could never have stood, just as Balaam advises the king of Moab to induce the people to sin, and thus conquer them. This Balaam, therefore, is one of the witnesses of whom Moses speaks here, who said magnificent things about God. Witnesses also are the Egyptians, who said in Exod. 14: Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them. Witnesses also are the Philistines, 1 Kings 5, who were afraid of the ark of God. No gods, therefore, were so present to their peoples, so showed their power, etc. For there is no other nation so great, as above in chapter 3. That: And our enemies are judges, Sebastian interprets thus. Münster: although our enemies are now our judges, they do not have that from their gods, but from our God, who delivered us into their hands. Furthermore, since the continuous discourse is of GOD Himself, and it is not fitting to introduce a change of the speaking person where there is no trace in the text, as in this place not only in the preceding v. 26 and 27 God speaks, but also without any indication of another person the divine discourse is continued, and in the following v. 34, 35 it is beyond controversy that God Himself is speaking: are not these things stored up with me, and sealed in my treasuries? even if those words also must be attributed to God, Their Rock is not as our Rock, of which thing our enemies themselves are witnesses. For it is not right to fix and invent parentheses where the text suggests no indication.
