Unde hîc verbum fidei, & justitiam fidei proponi, docet Apostolus Rom. 10.

Non ergo recte hic se habet observatio Cocceji §. 1518. in Vet. Testam. terrenis promissionibus ita sub- jectos fuisse pios, ut cogerentur ordinarie metuere mor- tem tanquam contrariam promissioni, adeoque ut pœ- nam & execrationem aliquam: in Novo autem terre- nis promissionibus nos non subjici, quia etiam in afflicti- onibus gloriari possimus. Nam nec fidelibus in Vet. Testam. ulla fuit condemnatio metuenda Act. 15, 11. neque pii in Novo terrenis promissionibus desti- tuuntur 1. Tim. 4, 8. & gloriatos etiam Veteres fu- isse in afflictionibus, non Job solum testis est, & David, sed integrum catalogum talium fidelibus Ebræis sub Nov. Testam. in exemplum stitit ipse Spir. S. Ebr. 11. cap.

## 32:50
Vers. 50. WHICH ASCENDING YOU SHALL BE JOINED TO YOUR PEOPLE.

From this, Interpreters gather that Moses, on the same day that he sang this song, ascended the mountain, and from it viewed the holy land, and soon departed this life. Before that, however, he blessed Israel, and the individual tribes, and predicted to them what was to come. Concerning verses 49, 50, 51, we have also treated homiletically in Conc. 28, Memorial of the Just, Wittenberg, under the title: The Mountain of the Prospect of the Promised Land.

Latin:

Vers. 50. QUEM CONSCENDENS JUN- GERIS POPULIS TUIS.

Ex eo colligunt Interpp. Mosen eodem die, quo cecinit hoc canticum, montem conscendisse, ex eoque speculatum esse terram sanctam, & mox vita esse de- functum. Prius tamen benedixit Israel, & singulis tribubus, iisque ventura prædixit. De vers. 49. 50. 51. egimus etiam homiletice in Conc. 28. Me- mor. justor. Witteberg. sub titulo: Mons prospectûs terræ promissæ.

## 33:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIII. The Patriarchal Blessings and Predictions of Moses.

Vers. 1. THIS IS THE BLESSING WITH WHICH MOSES THE MAN OF GOD BLESSED THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL BEFORE HIS DEATH.

The Patriarchs were accustomed before their death, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, to predict future events to their descendants, and at the same time to speak well of them; these predictions and prayers were called blessings. For although the name of blessing signifies as much as a favorable prayer, it must nevertheless be held that Moses here does not pray in the common manner, as if he were a private man, as fathers are accustomed to conceive vows for their sons, but with a prophetic spirit, to bring forth the benefits which were to be hoped for from God. This, therefore, is the reason why he splendidly extols the dignity and honor of his rule, so that the twelve tribes of Israel may certainly determine that God is the author of blessings. For the same reason he calls him a man of God, lest the people should receive what he is about to say otherwise than if they had proceeded from God, whose undoubted minister he is. Nor does the circumstance of time lack weight, before death or in death, which adds to the force of the prophecy that of a testament.

Coccejus is here again singular, and makes the blessing of Moses only a prophecy concerning the state of Israel in the New Testament, for which purpose he imagines that under the name of the Patriarchs he signifies the faithful of whatever tribes in different conditions, on account of an allusion and analogy either of the name, or of the habitation and condition of the tribes, which they had in the land of Canaan. Which hypothesis rests on no foundation. Nor is it indeed right, having dismissed the literal meaning, to seek a hieroglyphic sense. As to what Coccejus says, that there are not a few things predicted which do not agree with the tribes in the letter, we shall examine that in the exegesis. He is, however, utterly mistaken when he asserts that if all the things predicted agreed with those tribes according to the letter, and according to the hieroglyphic meaning with the Church of Christ, both explanations should be joined; for a double sense to be applied in the same passage will be proven when the Holy Spirit shall be taught to have wished to play with ambiguities, that is, at the Greek Calends.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIII. Benedictiones & Predictiones Mosis Patriar- chales.

Vers. 1. HÆC EST BENEDICTIO QUA BENEDIXIT MOSES HOMO DEI FILIIS ISRAEL ANTE MORTEM SUAM.

Solebant Patriarchæ ante mortem suam ex Spir. S. revelatione posteris suis futura prædicere, simulque iis bene prædicari; prædictiones & preca- tiones vocabantur benedictiones. Etsi enim benedi- ctionis nomen tantundem valet ac fausta precatio: tenendum tamen est, Mosen hic non precari vul- gari modo, quasi privatum hominem, ut vota con- cipere solent Patres pro filiis: sed prophetico spiritu, quæ à Deo speranda erant beneficia in medium proferre. Hæc igitur ratio est, cur imperii sui di- gnitatem ac decus splendide extollat, ut certo sta- tuant duodecim tribus Israel, Deum esse benedicti- onum autorem. Eadem ratione virum Dei nomi- nat, ne quæ dicturus est, aliter accipiat populus, quam si profecta essent à Deo, cujus indubius est minister. Nec pondere caret temporis circumstan- tia, ante mortem vel in morte, quæ Prophetiæ vim quoque Testamenti adjungit.

Coccejus hic iterum singularis est, ac benedicti- onem Mosis prophetiam tantum facit de statu Isra- elis in Novo Testamento, quo fine fingit, eum sub nomine Patriarcharum significare fideles quarum- cunque tribuum in diversis conditionibus, propter allusionem & analogiam vel nominis, vel habitati- onis & conditionis tribuum, quam habuerunt in terra Canaan. Quæ hypothesis nullo fundamento nititur. Neque vero fas est, missa literali significa- tione hieroglyphicum sensum quærere. Quod ait Coccejus, non pauca esse prædicata, quæ tribubus in litera non conveniant, de eo in ἐξηγήσει dispiciemus. Fallitur autem oppido, dum asserit, si omnia præ- dicata convenirent in istas tribus, secundum lite- ram, & secundum hieroglyphicum significatum in Ecclesiam Christi, utramque explicationem con- jungendam; nam geminum sensum in eodem lo- co adhibendum, tum probabitur, cum Spir. S. lu- dere voluisse ambiguitatibus docebitur, h. e. ad Calendas Græcas.

## 33:2
Verse 2. THE LORD CAME FROM SINAI, AND ROSE UP FOR US FROM SEIR, HE APPEARED FROM MOUNT PHARAN.

Calvin wishes all these things to denote the same thing. Wrongly, he says, in my judgment, do some translate, God came in Sinai: because Moses rather understands that God went forth from there, where His brightness was seen: through Seir and Pharan he repeats the same thing for the sake of ornamentation. And since these three are synonyms, therefore to come, to go forth, and to rise, designate also one thing, namely, that manifestation of heavenly glory, which ought to have seized all minds in admiration of itself, as if he were saying that His blessings were to be received with the same veneration as that which God had acquired for His Law, while His face had shone conspicuously on Mount Sinai: which is almost the opinion of Cajetan, Bochard (book on Hebrew Pilgrimages, ch. 1), Marius, and also Lorinus. But neither are those proper names synonyms, nor do the words denote exactly the same thing. It is said of Sinai that He came to the people when He gave the law, Exod. 19, 20. He rose from Mount Seir when He helped many who were wounded by the bite of serpents; for this happened when they were circling Mount Seir. Cf. Num. 21. Deut. 1, 43. ch. 2, 27. He appeared from Mount Pharan when He gave quails and appointed the 70 judges, Numbers 11, in which most interpreters agree, Lyranus, Burgensis, Vatablus, Marzilla, Cornelius, Ribera, Osiander, etc. And Junius observes here a continuous metaphor, taken from the Sun, which at the beginning sends forth light, afterwards rises itself, and finally illuminates the lands; thus God gradually declared His presence among the people, wherever they made their journey, i.e., from the nearest border of Egypt, until they arrived at the Edomites bordering the promised land. Cf. Hab. 3, 1. Thus the blessed Luther: I understand this in such a way that it signifies the glorious and remarkable coming of God to the land of promise; He came there also, beginning from Mount Sinai, where He gave the covenant of the law: and He rose from Seir, that is, He passed through the land of Seir as far as Canaan, and thus He came as if a rising Sun about to illuminate that land with a new kingdom. It is the same as that He shone forth from Mount Pharan, because He passed through there in the borders of Edom.

Coccejus includes other things here as well, and renders it in this way: He came from Sinai, after He had appeared in it to Moses, namely, into Egypt, in order to deliver the people from servitude, likewise after the law was given from the mountain, and He took a place before the camp of Israel, and He rose from Mount Seir, as if meeting the people, and looking out from His land, so that He might lead them to Himself into the holy land promised to the Fathers, although the people did not obey then; and He shone forth from Mount Pharan, i.e., He appeared to them in every part of the desert, namely, when He led them around Idumea and Moab, so that having crossed the Jordan they might enter into the land of Paran, and between Mount Seir and Sinai, Gen. 14, 6. Num. 10, 12. ch. 13, 3. near Kadesh, Num. 13, 26, which is on the border of the Idumeans, Num. 20, 19. In Paran the murmuring of the Israelite people took place, and they sat near Kadesh for many days. Magalianus and Lorinus recount other explanations of the Rabbis, the Fathers, and others, and various mystical senses, for the most part wonderful, but they are unworthy to be cited.

Verse same. AND WITH HIM THOUSANDS OF SAINTS.

More correctly myriads, that is, innumerable holy angels. The blessed Luther understands the peoples of Israel, of whom there were indeed many thousands, although not every one was holy, yet the thousands were holy on account of the many saints among them, but it is gathered from Acts 7, 35 and Galatians 3, 19 that the myriads of angels, by whom the Lord was surrounded, are to be understood. The Rabbis talk nonsense, that the souls of the Prophets and Rabbis were there, and received their doctrine. AT HIS RIGHT HAND A FIERY LAW, or the fire of the law for them (which is added in Hebrew), understand: existed, or the law is established at his right hand, as Calvin notes, not only as a scepter or badge, but as power, or a method of governing: for He did not appear only as a king, but showed how He wished to rule. Moreover, the law is called fire, for the purpose of striking terror, and compelling all to humility. Although it does not displease me that Moses in this epithet alludes to the external symbols of fire and flame, of which he spoke in the twentieth chapter of Exodus. The blessed Luther: At his right hand a fiery law to them: whether you understand this truly of the law of Moses, by which He rules them at his right hand, so that it may burn in the spirit, and be loved, namely by the saints, or of the pillar of fire, by which He led them, not with a fist: although the former sense pleases more, because it was a remarkable benefit that the law, the oracles of God, should be entrusted to this people. The law is said to have been in the right hand of this Lord, but not carried by ministering angels, as Cajetan trifles, even though for the sake of Majesty He promulgated it surrounded by myriads of angels. The Protomartyr makes this the angel who appeared to Moses in the bush, and spoke to him here in the ἐκκλησίᾳ, Acts 7, 38. Who therefore cannot be understood as a ministering angel. For Moses calls Him Jehovah, and distinguishes Him from the myriads of angels, and testified that Jehovah Himself promulgated the law αὐτοπροσώπως (in person), Exod. 19, 21. Whence Coccejus rightly observes in §. 1559 that the Apostle, in Galatians 3, 19 (he also adds the passage Heb. 2, 1), and Stephen in Acts 7, 53, understand εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων (by the disposition of angels), that the law was given with angels as witnesses (in which sense the word διὰ is used in 2 Tim. 2, 1 and 1 Thess. 4, 1) and approvers, and as future avengers, which Moses also attests, and so they do not look to the angel himself who spoke to Moses, but to the myriads, from whom He who spoke is said to have come forth into the midst. The LXX have σὺν μυρίασι κάδης (with myriads of Kadesh). Where Marius understands the passage as meaning that He appeared in Kadesh, but Theodoret more correctly notes in question 44 that it is not the desert, but the interpretation of that name, that is, holy, which is understood from the Hebrew קדש. The law is called fiery, both because it was promulgated among lightnings and flashes, and because it announces the consuming fire of divine vengeance, and is in the conscience like a burning and consuming fire.

Latin:

Verf. 2. DOMINUS DE SINAI VENIT, ET DE SEIR ORTUS EST NOBIS, APPARUIT DE MONTE PHARAN.

Hæc omnia idem notare vult Calvinus. Perpe- ram, inquit, meo judicio, quidam vertunt, Deus in Sinai venit: quia potius intelligit Moses, Deum in- de prodiisse, ubi conspectus fuit ejus fulgor: per Seir & Pharan idem repetit ornatus causa. Et quando hæc tria synonyma sunt, ideo venire, egredi, & oriri, rem quoque unam designant, illam scil. gloriæ cœle- stis manifestationem, quæ in sui admirationem rapere debebat omnium mentes, ac si diceret, ea- dem veneratione accipiendas esse suas benedictiones, at- que illam, quam Legi suæ Deus acquisierat, dum in monte Sinai conspicua enituerat ejus facies: quæ fere Cajetani, Bochard. l. de Peregr. Hebr. c. 1. Marii, ut & Lorini est sententia. Sed nec nomina illa propria synonyma sunt, nec verba idem prorsus notant. De Sina dicitur ad populum venisse, cum legem dedit, Exod. 19, 20. de monte Seir exortus est, cum multis morsu serpentum vulneratis, erecto serpente æneo subvenit; hoc enim contigit cum montem Seir cir- cuirent. Conf. Num. 21. Deut. 1, 43. cap. 2, 27. De monte Pharan apparuit, cum coturnices dedit, & LXX. judices constituit Numer. 11. in quo plerique Interpp. conveniunt, Lyran. Burgens. Vatabl. Mar- zilla, Cornelius, Ribera, Osiander &c. Et metapho- ram hic perpetuam observat Junius, à Sole sumtam, qui initio lucem præmittit, postea oritur ipse, tan- dem terras illustrat; sic gradatim Deus præsentiam suam in populo declaravit, quacunque iter fece- runt, q. d. inde à termino proximo Ægypti,usque dum perventum est ad Edomæos finitimos terræ promissæ. Conf. Hab. 3, 1. Ita B. Lutherus: hoc sic intelligo, quod significet adventum Dei gloriosum & insignem, ad terram promissionis, illuc etiam venit incipiens à monte Sinai, ubi pactum legis dedit: & ortus est de Seir, id est, transivit terram Seir usque ad Canaan, & fic venit quasi oriens Sol novo regno illustraturus terram illam. Idem est, quod inclaruit à monte Pha- ran, quia illic transivit in finibus Edom.

Coccejus alia quoque hic complectitur, atque h. m. reddit: Venit ex Sinai, postquam in eo apparu- isset Mosi, sc. in Ægyptum, ut liberaret populum ex servitute, item post legem latam de monte, & ante castra Israelis locum cepit, & exortus est ex monte Seir, quasi obviam occurrens populo, & prospe- ctans ex terra sua, ut eum ad se deduceret in terram sanctam promissam Patribus, quanquam tum po- pulus non obedivit; & eluxit ex monte Pharan, h. e. in omni parte deserti ipsis apparuit, nominatim, quando illos circumduxit Idumæam & Moabiti- dem, ut transito Jordane intrarent in terram Paran, & inter montem Seir & Sinai Genes. 14, 6. Num. 10, 12. cap. 13, 3. prope Kadeschan Num. 13, 26. quæ est in limite Idumæorum Num. 20, 19. In Paran facta est murmuratio populi Israelitici, & prope Kades sederunt diebus multis. Alias explicationes Rab- binorum, Patrum & aliorum, & sensus varios my- sticos, magnam partem mirabiles, recenset Ma- galianus & Lorinus, sed indigni sunt, qui addu- cantur.

Verf. eod. ET CUM EO SANCTORUM MILLIA.

Rectius myriades, id est, innumerabiles sancti angeli. B. Lutherus populos Israel intelligit, quorum fuerunt quidem multa millia, licet non singuli sancti, tamen sancta fuerunt millia propter multos inter eos sanctos, sed angelorum myriades, quibus stipatus fuit Dominus, intelligi ex Actor. 7, 35. Galat. 3, 19. colligitur. Rabbini ineptiunt, quod animæ Pro- phetarum & Rabbinorum ibi fuerint, & doctrinam suam acceperint. IN DEXTRA EJUS IGNEA LEX, vel ignis legis ipsis (quod in Ebr. additur) subint. extitit, seu statuitur ad dextram ejus lex, no- tante Calvino, non modo tanquam sceptrum vel insigne, sed tanquam potestas, vel ratio gubernan- di: neque enim tanquam rex apparuit solum, sed ostendit, quomodo praeesse vellet. Lex autem ignis vocatur, ad injiciendum terrorem, & omnes ad humilitatem cogendos. Quanquam non displiceat, Mosen in hoc epitheto alludere ad externa ignis & flamme symbola, de quibus vicesimo capite Exodi loquutus est. B. Lutherus: A dextris ejus ignea lex ad eos: sive hoc vere de lege Mosis intelligas, qua re- git eos in dextera, ut spiritu ardeat, & ametur, nem- pe a sanctis, sive de columna ignis, qua duxit eos, non pugno: quamvis prior sensus magis placet, quia in- signe fuit beneficium, huic populo credi legem, eloquia Dei. In dextra hujus Domini lex dicitur fuisse, non vero portata ab angelis ministris, ut nuga- tur Cajetanus, etsi Majestatis causa stipatus ange- lorum myriadibus eam promulgarit. Hunc Pro- tomartyr facit angelum, qui Mosi apparuit in rubo, ei- que in ἐκκλησίᾳ hic loquutus sit Act. 7, 38. Qui pro- inde non potest intelligi angelus minister. Moses enim Jehovam eum nuncupat, & a myriadibus ange- lorum distinguit, ac Jehovam ipsum legem promul- gasse αὐτοπροσώπως testatus est Exod. 19, 21. unde recte Coccejus observat §. 1559. Apostolum legem da- tam δι' ἀγγέλων Galat. 3, 19. (addit etiam locum Ebr. 2, 1.) & Stephanum Act. 7, 53. εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγ- γέλων intelligere, angelis testibus (quem in sensum τὸ διὰ usurpetur 2. Tim. 2, 1. & 1. Thess. 4, 2.) & appro- batoribus, ac futuris vindicibus datam esse legem, quod etiam Moses attestatur, adeoque non respice- re ipsos ad angelum, qui Mosi loquutus est, sed ad myriades, a quibus in medium processisse dicitur is, qui loquutus est. LXX. habent σὺν μυρίασι κά- δης. Ubi Marius locum intelligit, quod in Cades ap- paruerit, at rectius Theod. notat qv. 44. non deser- tum, sed interpretationem ejus nominis, hoc est, sanctum intelligi ex Ebraeo קדש. Lex ignea dicitur, tum quia inter fulgura, & coruscationes promul- gata fuit, tum quia ignem consumentem vindictae divinae annunciat, & in conscientia est instar ignis ardentis, & consumentis.

## 33:3
Vers. 3. HE LOVED THE PEOPLES, ALL THE SAINTS ARE IN HIS HAND. More correctly, he loves the peoples: Which some understand of other peoples and nations, with the Jesuit Lorinus and Calvin not denying it: If one were free to take it of the nations, the sentence would have to be resolved thus: Although he loves all mortals, he nevertheless deems the saints worthy of peculiar favor, so that he may guard their salvation. Who nevertheless (Calvin) judges that it is more correctly explained of the sons of Abraham alone, whom he therefore calls peoples, because on account of the multitude, into which they had grown divided into tribes, they could be reckoned as so many nations. Thus also the tribes of Israel are called Jud. 5, 14. Conf. & Genes. 48, 19.

Coccejus, however, having left Calvin and Junius, prefers to understand the nations, rendering it thus: he also carried the peoples in his bosom, whose all saints are in thy hand. Vatablus translated it in this manner: And he vehemently loves the peoples, all his saints are in thy hands. Supplying: O Lord, as if to say: you protect them: by which form of address the distinction of the divine persons is insinuated: namely, the Lord, whose saints they are said to be, and the Lord whom he addresses, and in whose hand he says the saints of the Lord are. Coccejus observes that Moses says, even though he came with the fire of the law, Jehovah nevertheless carried the nations in his bosom, and all his saints were in his hand, and thus by the legislation nothing was prejudiced against the Testament. Jehovah having in his right hand the fire of the law, nevertheless he carried the peoples in his bosom, and all the saints were in his hand, i.e., the Son of God together with the Father and the Spirit (2 Cor. 3:12) promulgating the law which works wrath, did not lay aside the will and love of the suretyship Heb. 7:2, with which love he asked from eternity to give those who subdue as an inheritance, and for them he offered himself immaculate to the Father by an eternal spirit, nor did he wish to prejudice the sanctification which is in his blood and Spirit, or the power of preserving them, which he has by the grace of the Father and his own merit, for this is that eternal Testament, by which the Father assigned to the Son, who promised satisfaction for sins, a seed and an inheritance. So he. Although these things may be true, yet in this place to carry in the bosom is not that suretyship. For that work is common to the Holy Trinity, just as this is proper to the Son.

Verse of the same.

ALL THE SAINTS) Thus the Israelites are called, even in Daniel 7:25. See above Exod. 19:6, Num. 16:3.

Not only are the Israelites indicated, but all the faithful of whatever lineage they may be, even if the ordinary seat of the Church and the assembly of the saints was among the Israelites. For all the saints, everywhere in the world, are in his hand: he cherishes, preserves, and protects them all. Nor are the Israelites understood in Dan. 7:25. For the discourse is about the Anti-Christ who is to kill the saints and change the times.

AND THEY WHO APPROACH HIS FEET SHALL RECEIVE OF HIS DOCTRINE) In the Hebrew: they are joined to thy foot, that is, they are thy disciples. For it is the custom of disciples to sit between the feet of the master. Philo: νέοι ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις καθίζονται. Add Acts 12:3, the explanation follows: they shall receive of thy sayings.

Some Hebrews render it thus: They were struck at thy feet: as if they were subdued by rods, so that they might obey God. Grotius's explanation is more correct: so Junius and Tremellius. In turn, let them be brought into the midst at thy feet, let (each one) receive from thy words (saying) Moses commanded us the law, etc., that is, let them be made thy disciples, and be rendered obedient to thee, as disciples are to their teachers, at whose feet they sit, as is said of Paul in Acts 22:3. Thus also Calvin: They adhered to thy feet. The metaphor is drawn from disciples, who, by the received usage of the Hebrew language, are said to sit at the feet of the master, so that they may be more diligently attentive. And that is proved from the context. For the faithful are said to have joined themselves to the feet of God, so that they may receive from his sermons, that is, that they may progress in his doctrine. Similarly Vatablus. And they themselves inserted within thy feet shall receive from thy words, or they joined themselves to thy feet, and took from thy words, that is, they also followed thy footsteps, and committed to memory a good part of thy words. Nor do Osiander or others say otherwise. Lorinus in this place, p. 626: The multitude of the saints, as is written of the whole Hebrew people in the previous book, had once approached and drawn near to the feet of the Lord as if sitting on Mount Sinai, where he was giving the law, when standing in the valley of that mountain, it was receiving the law, and as if pressing and treading the footsteps of God, it was promising that it would follow them, as if by retaining in memory and keeping those things impressed in the precepts of the law, or when it was receiving the oracles and responses of God from the ark, above which God seemed to sit. Cocceius, however, loves to be singular here again; rendering it thus: And they themselves in the midst walked to thy foot, or, and thou didst walk them in the midst with thy foot. What is it to walk with his foot, if not to walk in assumed flesh? He urges that nothing compels us to depart from the literal sense, since we have already learned above that God wished to come in the flesh, indeed, having compared the passage Levit. 24:12, he adds too confidently: No one can reject this literal sense unless he has an obstinate mind not to believe that the Son of God came in the flesh. But neither above is there anything about the coming of the Son of

God in the flesh, nor is it clearly evident here that the discourse is about the person of the Son of God, and just as Cocceius did not insist on the literal sense in the name of bosom and hands, so neither is it necessary to take the name of feet literally; therefore that new and barbaric translation of Cocceius is vain: And they in the midst walked to thy foot, that is, thou didst walk them in the midst with thy foot. The word תכו brings in nothing more than that they were made or brought into the midst at the feet of the Lord, which we have already said how it should be understood. Finally, the comparison with the passage Levit. 24:12 is merely arbitrary, which he likewise interprets in a new way, having deserted the Apostle's sense in 2 Corinthians 6:16. And who would grant him that by words here is understood (1) The asking of the inheritance from the Father, with the offering of his body, or the suretyship or mediatorial intercession, which is a powerful word, which specifically sustained the Church from Heb. 1:3. Isa. 63:9, 10, he teaches very irrelevantly: (2) the instinct by which he moved the prophets to promulgate the counsel of God 1 Pet. 1:11. (3) the proper announcement, with a real demonstration of the truth. We add the interpretation of Castellio, who indeed understands the former part of v. 2 about the coming of the Son of God, but before the incarnation; but he wishes the latter part to be said to the Father: If here, he says, we remember that he who is called Jehovah here is the Christ the Son of God, just as we showed in Exod. 3, we shall understand this passage more easily. This, therefore, is the meaning: Jehovah, that is, the Son of God sent by God, who is one with God the Father: He came from Sinai: for there he appeared, and gave the law. He arose from Seir, where he also spoke to Moses, and ordered the bronze serpent to be made. He appeared from Mount Paran, where he promised quails to Moses: And he came for the sake of the sacred legions, that is, for the sake of the sacred people of the Israelites: Having for those legions the fire of discipline, that is, fiery discipline: At his right hand, that is, bringing to them his law with much fire: Truly a lover of men: for the love of him who did not disdain to dwell as God among men must be wonderful. Of whom all the saints, viz. the Israelites, who are in his faith and protection. They are in thy hand, O God his Father: and indeed they prostrate themselves at thy feet, they are simple to thee, and depend on thee: With him, thy son, taking from thy edicts: for what law he delivered to Moses, he received it from thee.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DILEXIT POPULOS, OMNES SANCTI IN MANU ILLIUS SUNT. Rectius, diligit populos: Quod nonnulli de aliis populis, & gentibus intelligunt, non abnuente Lo- rino Jesuita, & Calvino: Si de gentibus accipere li- beret, sic resolvenda erit oratio: Quamvis diligat cunctos mortales, peculiari tamen favore dignatur san- ctos, ut eorum salutem custodiat. Qui tamen (Calvi- nus) censet, rectius exponi de solis Abrahae filiis, quos ideo vocet populos, quia ob multitudinem, in quam excreverant in tribus divisi, poterant censeri totidem gentes. Sic etiam vocantur tribus Israelis Jud. 5, 14. Conf. & Genes. 48, 19.

Coccejus tamen, relicto Calvino & Junio, ma- vult gentes intelligere, ita reddens: etiam sinu gessit populos, cujus omnes sancti sunt in manu tua. Vata- blus transtulit h. m. Et vehementer diligit populos, omnes sancti ejus sunt in manibus tuis. Subint. Domi- ne, q. d. tutaris illos: qua compellatione discrimen personarum divinarum insinuatur: Dominus nem- pe, cujus illi sancti esse dicuntur, & Dominus quem compellat, & in cujus manu sanctos Domini esse dicit. Observat Coccejus, quod Moses dicat, etsi venerit cum igne legis, nihilominus & gentes sinu gestasse Jeho- vam, & omnes sanctos suos in manu ipsius fuisse, atque ita per legislationem Testamento nihil fuisse praeju- dicatum. Jehova habens in dextra ignem legis, nihilominus gessit in sinu populos, & omnes san- cti fuerunt in manu ipsius, h. e. Filius Dei una cum Patre & Spiritu (2. Cor. 3, 12.) promulgans legem quæ operatur iram, non deposuit voluntatem & a- morem sponsionis Ebr. 7, 2. quo amore ab æterno postulavit subigentes dare in hæreditatem, & pro eis æterno spiritu se obtulit immaculatum Patri, neque voluit præjudicare sanctificationi, quæ est in sanguine & Spiritu ejus, aut potestati conservandi ipsos, quam habet gratia Patris & suo merito, hoc enim est Testamentum illud æternum, quo Pater Fi- lio spondenti satisfactionem pro peccatis, semen & hæreditatem assignavit. Hæc ille. Quæ etsi vera sint, non tamen h. l. gerere in sinu est illa sponsio. Nam illud opus commune S. Trinit. uti hæc pro- pria est Filio.

Vers. eod.

OMNES SANCTI) Sic vocantur Israëlitæ, etiam in Da- niele 7, 25. Vide supra Exod. 19, 6. Num. 16, 3.

Non tantum Israëlitæ indigitantur, sed univer- si fideles cujuscunque sint prosapiæ, etsi penes Is- raelitas ordinaria sedes Ecclesiæ, & cœtus sancto- rum fuerit. Omnes enim sancti, ubique terrarum, in manu ejus: omnes fovet, conservat, protegit. Neque Dan. 7, 25. Israëlitæ intelliguntur. De An- ti-Christo enim sermo est sanctos occisuro, & tem- pora mutaturo.

ET QVI APPROPINQVANT PEDIBUS EJUS ACCI- PIENT DE DOCTRINA ILLIUS) In Hebræo: ipsi juncti sunt ad pedem tuum, id est, discipuli tui sunt. Mos enim di- scipulorum sedere inter pedes magistri. Philo: νέοι ὑπὸ πρεσ- βυτέροις καθίζονται. Adde Act. 12, 3. sequitur explicatio: accipient de eloquiis tuis.

Ebr. nonnulli sic reddunt: Percussi sunt ad pe- des tuos: quod quasi ferulis subacti sint, ut Deo pa- rerent. Rectius habet Grotii explicatio: ita Juni- us & Tremell. Vicissim ipsi medii inferantur pedibus tuis, suscipiat (quisque) è verbis tuis (dicens) legem præcepit nobis Mose &c. id est, efficiantur tui disci- puli, tibique morigeri reddantur, ut sunt discipuli præceptoribus, quorum pedibus assident, ut de Paulo dicitur Act. 22, 3. Sic & Calvinus: Ipsi adhæse- runt pedibus tuis. Ducta est metaphora à Discipu- lis, qui recepto linguæ Hebraicæ usu dicuntur se- dere ad pedes magistri, ut diligentius attenti sint. Idque probatur ex contextu. Dicuntur enim fide- les se adjunxisse pedibus Dei, ut accipiant è sermonibus ejus, hoc est, in ejus doctrina proficiant. Similiter Vatabl. Et ipsi inserti intra pedes tuos accipient ex verbis tuis, vel ipsi adjunxerunt se pedibus tuis, & sumserunt de verbis tuis, id est, ipsi quoque sectati sunt vestigia tua, & memoriæ mandaverunt bonam partem verborum tuorum. Nec aliter Osiander, aut alii. Lorinus in h. l. p. 626. Multitudo Sanctorum, ut de integro populo Hebræo scribitur, libro priore, acces- serat quondam & appropinquaverat pedibus Domini tanquam sedentis in monte Sinai, ubi legem dabat, quando in illius montis valle stans, legem excipiebat, ac tanquam vestigia Dei premens ac terens, illa se secta- turum promittebat, velut in præceptis legis impressa memoria retinendo ipsa atq; servanda, aut quando ex arca, super quam Deus sedere videbatur, Dei oracula responsag; accipiebat. Singularis autem iterum hic esse amat Coccejus; sic reddens: Et ipsi medii peram- bulati sunt pedi tuo, sive, & tu ipsos pede tuo medios perambulasti. Quid est pede suo perambulare, nisi in carne assumta perambulare? Urget, quod nihil co- gat nos à proprietate recedere, quum jam supra co- gnoverimus, Deum in carne venire voluisse, imo collato loco Levit. 24, 12. addit nimis confidenter: Non potest hanc proprietatem respuere, nisi qui ob- stinatum habet non credere, Filium Dei in carne venis- se. Sed neque supra quicquam de adventu Filii

Dei in carne, neque hic liquido constat, de per- sona Filii Dei sermonem esse, & quemadmodum in sinus ac manus nomine proprietati non inhæsit Coc- cejus, ita neque pedum nomen proprie necessum est accipere, vana proinde illa nova, & barbara translatio Cocceji; Et illi medii perambulati sunt pedi tuo, id est, tu ipsos pede tuo medios perambulasti. Verbum תכו nihil amplius infert, quam quod me- dii facti vel inferti sunt pedibus Domini, quod quo- modo accipiendum sit, jam diximus. Denique mere arbitraria est collatio cum loco Levit. 24, 12. quem itidem nova ratione interpretatur, deserto Apostoli sensu 2. Corinth. 6, 16. Et quis ei largie- tur, per loquelas hic intelligi (1.) Postulationem hæ- reditatis à Patre, cum oblatione corporis sui, sive sponsionem aut intercessionem mediatoriam, quod verbum esse potens, quod speciatim sustentavit Ecclesiam ex Ebr. 1, 3. Es. 63, 9. 10. valde ἀπροσδιο- νύσως docet: (2.) instinctum, quo Prophetas com- movit ad consilium Dei promulgandum 1. Petr. 1, 11. (3.) annunciationem propriam, cum reali de- monstratione veritatis. Castellionis addimus in- terpretationem, qui priora quidem v. 2. de adven- tu Filii Dei intelligit, sed ante ἐνσάρκωσιν; poste- riora vero ad Patrem dicta vult: Si hic, inquit, me- minerimus, qui hic Jova dicitur, eum esse Christum Dei Filium, quemadmodum in 3. Exod. ostendimus, hunc locum facilius intelligemus. Est igitur hæc sen- tentia: Jova, id est, missus à Deo Dei Filius, qui unum cum Patre Deo est: Venit de Sina: nam illic apparuit, & legem dedit. Ex Seire ortus est, ubi etiam Mosem allocutus est, jussitque serpentem æneum fieri. Patuit ex monte Pharone, ubi Mosi coturnices promisit: Venitque ob sacras legiones, id est, ob Israelitarum populum sacrum: Habens eis legionibus ignem disci- plinæ, hoc est, igneam disciplinam: Ad dexteram su- am, id est, eis afferens legem suam cum multo igne: Hominum sane amator: oportet enim mirum esse il- lius amorem, qui Deus inter homines versari non sit dedignatus. Cujus sancti omnes, scil. Israelitæ, qui sunt in ejus fide, & tutela. Sunt in manu tua, ô Deus ejus Pater: & quidem ad pedes tuos prosternuntur, tibi simplices sunt, & à te pendent: Eo, tuo filio, de tuis edictis sumente: quam enim legem Mosi tradi- dit, eam à te accepit.

## 33:4
Verse 4. MOSES COMMANDED US A LAW, AN INHERITANCE FOR THE MULTITUDE OF JACOB.

Junius thinks these words are more correctly those of the congregation or assembly of Jacob, of disciples sitting at the feet of the Lord, or of pious Israelites preparing themselves for obedience to the law. Others think Moses is speaking of himself in the third person, so that it may have more authority. For the interpreters generally refer the inheritance to the law, both because it had to pass to the descendants of Jacob as if by hereditary right, as Vatablus holds; and because it had to be held like the highest treasure and a most ample inheritance. Cf. Psalm 119, 11. Cocceius alone distinguishes the inheritance from the law, and in these words invents a twofold end for his twofold visitation, which he has devised here (namely, the σκηνώσεως in the pillar of cloud and fire, and the ἐνσαρκώσεως) §. 1574. Therefore Jehovah visited the people twice, (1.) so that Moses might receive from his words the doctrine which he commanded to Israel and to all future heirs. (2.) So that the assembly of Jacob, that is, of the firstborn from Jacob described in heaven, might receive the inheritance from his words, that is, from his intercession and name, or authority, and from this testimony sealed by faith, not indeed of the land of Canaan, but the communion and entry into the heavenly city, to which the Fathers also aspired Heb. 11, 13. 14. 15. and (3.) the kingdom among the nations Ps. 2. which is the inheritance of the world promised to Abraham Rom. 4, 12. It is wonderful with what art (perhaps Cabbalistic) Cocceius was able to carve these things out of those words. And how can his discourses signify at once the doctrine of Moses, and the intercession, and the name of Christ, and at the same time the inheritance and the communion of the heavenly city, and the kingdom among the nations? Add that the Silluq accent opposes the interpretation of Cocceius, so that it should read: from your words (here the verse ends) the law (which) Moses commanded us. It is not said that Moses received the law, but it is predicated here of Moses that he commanded the law. But of those who have been inserted into the middle of the foot of the Lord, or have approached him as disciples to a teacher, it is said that they have approached, so that (each one) might receive from his words.

Latin:

Vers. 4. LEGEM PRÆCEPIT NOBIS MO- SES HÆREDITATEM MULTITUDINIS JACOB.

Rectius congregationis seu cœtus Jacob. Verba hæc esse discipulorum sedentium ad pedes Domini, seu piorum Israelitarum ad legis obsequium se comparantium Junius putat. Alii Mosen de seipso in tertia persona loqui, ut eo plus habeat autorita- tis. Hæreditatem enim ad legem referunt communi- ter Interpp. tum, quia jure quasi hæreditario transire debebat ad posteros Jacob, ut Vatabl. habet; tum quia instar summi thesauri, & amplissimæ hæreditatis haberi debebat. Conf. Psalm. 119, 11. Solus Coccejus hæreditatem à lege distinguit, & geminum visitatio- nis suæ geminæ, quam hic commentus est (nempe σκηνώσεως in columna nubis & ignis, & ἐνσαρκώσε- ως) finem in his verbis fingit §. 1574. Ideo visitavit Je- hovah populum bis, (1.) ut à verbis ejus Moses accipe- ret doctrinam, quam præcepit Israeli & omnibus hæ- redibus futuris. (2.) Ut panegyris Jacobi, id est, pri- mogeniti ex Jacobo in cælo descripti, à sermonibus ejus, hoc est, ipsius intercessione & nomine, sive autoritate, & hoc testimonio per fidem obsignato acciperent hære- ditatem, non quidem terræ Canaan, sed communio- nem & ingressum civitatis cælestis, ad quam & Patres adspirarunt Hebr. 11, 13. 14. 15. & (3.) regnum inter gentes Ps. 2. quæ hæreditas mundi promissa Abraha- mo Rom. 4, 12. Mirum qua arte (Cabbalistica for- te) hæc è verbis istis exsculpere potuerit Coccejus. Et quomodo sermones ejus simul & doctrinam Mosis, & intercessionem, & nomen Christi, hæreditas simul & cælestis civitatis communionem, & regnum inter gen- tes significare possunt? Adde, quod accentus Syl- luck refragetur interpretationi Cocceji, ut acciperet à loquelis tuis (hic finit versus) legem (quam) præcepit nobis Moses. Non Moses dicitur accepisse legem, sed de Mose hic prædicatur, quod legem præceperit. De illis autem, qui inserti sunt medii pedi Domini, vel appropinquarunt ei, ceu præceptori discipuli, dicitur, quod accesserint, ut acciperet (unusquisque) de verbis ejus.

## 33:5
Verse 5.

IT WILL BE AMONG THE MOST UPRIGHT, THE KING HAVING BEEN GATHERED WITH THE PRINCES OF THE PEOPLE WITH THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL) The King governed the people not indeed in name and pomp, but by royal right. See what was said above 17, 9.

In Hebrew: And there was in Jeshurun (that is, in the Israelite people) a King when the heads of the people were gathered together (assembling) the tribes of Israel. Vatablus: And there was an equitable King, when the heads of the people gathered themselves, and at the same time the tribes of Israel. Item: Moreover, there was in Israel (as it were) a King, when they were gathered &c. subint. to him. Most understand this of Moses, who was like a King among the people, and who kept both the Princes of the people and the people themselves, as much as he could, in duty and concord and unity, which interpretation is easy and straightforward: Conf. Gen. 36, 31. & handed down by the Blessed Luther: he was in the place of a King, and was in the authority and stead of God among them, so that beyond the written law he might rule them by the oracle of the living voice from the mouth of God. Among the Papists, because of the Vulgate version, which has in the future ERIT (HE SHALL BE) King, some wish it to be a prophecy concerning Saul, and after him concerning David. Hugo, Lyran. Abulens. Marius, Cornel. à Lapid. & others explain it thus: Among Israel God shall be King, or rather: God ruling them through the law, as long as the Princes are of one mind with the people. R. Gerundensis explains it thus also concerning God: Lorinus; before Moses descends to the individual blessings, he still prophesies by blessing in a general way, that it will come to pass for the people, whom he surnames the most upright, if they maintain this epithet in reality, so that they may live most uprightly, & according to the prescription of the law received from God through Moses, the law itself may be in the place of a King, nor shall they need another king, but this shall rule them, or rather God through it, together with the princes and the tribes, by preserving them, with the greater and the lesser, in peace, security, and prosperity, which is, after piety and religion, the greatest happiness of a republic. Augustine, by reading (& there shall be a Prince in the beloved) understands it of Christ, qv. 56. when the princes of the peoples, that is, of the nations, are gathered together, along with the tribes of Israel; whom Rabanus follows. Rupert interprets this King as Christ, who was to sit at the right hand of the most righteous Lord forever. Coccejus, in his final commentary on Moses §. 1565, has it thus: Jehovah (coming from Sinai, and walking with His foot among the Israelites) became King in Jeshurun, that is, in Israel, which is partaker of the vision of God. This he distinguishes from the days of His flesh and says it was accomplished through His exaltation into the heavens. He asserts that the phrase of the Prophets concerning the kingdom of the exalted Christ owes its origin (perhaps solely) to this passage of Moses. He also criticizes the common interpretation concerning Moses as being Jewish and contrary to the text. The Jews, he says, who interpret these words, "And He became King in Jeshurun," as referring to Moses (which some of our own people incautiously follow), break the connection and thread of the text. For in order to be able to apply it to Moses, they explain the preceding verse wrongly by inferring something that is not in the text. For they read it almost thus: Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob. And yet there is no sign of the dative in the second clause as there is in the first, and thus the speech of the last clause in v. 3, "would receive from thy words," would remain imperfect. For who? what would it receive? These are the words of Cocceius, who rendered these verses thus: v. 3, "and would receive from thy words," v. 4, "the law (which) Moses commanded us, an inheritance of the assembly of Jacob." But by what right does he himself drag the two nominatives in v. 4, MOSES and ASSEMBLY, to the verb "would receive" in verse 3, and by what right does he insert the pronoun (WHICH) in v. 4? Do not all things flow more correctly when the verses remain distinct, as is proper, and the law commanded by Moses is called an inheritance for the congregation or given to the congregation of Jacob? For it is most well known that the Hebrews do not always add signs of the cases, which must often be elicited from the text. Not because of the authority of the Jews, but because of the evidence of the text, do the interpreters understand the passage as being about Moses. Christians, even the master of Cocceius, John Calvin, who states it thus: Moses prescribed the Law to us. What he discussed concerning the glory of God and the excellence of the Law, he now applies to his own person: because his purpose was (as I have said) to give assurance to his ministry. Therefore, so that his legation might be certain, he boasts that he was appointed by God as a teacher to the people, and not for a short time, but for all ages. For by the name of inheritance the perpetuity of the Law is denoted. He then claims for himself the authority of a king, not because he ruled in the royal manner, but so that the dignity of supreme authority might add weight to his words. He says, moreover, that the heads were gathered, and that they united into tribes, in respect of the miserable dissipation which was tending toward destruction: as if he were saying that by his leadership and effort the state of the people was renewed from the beginning. Similarly Junius and Tremellius. Moses commanded a law for us, an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob, that is, one to be observed by the present and future descendants of Jacob (see chap. 33:4). For he was King in Jeshurun, when the leaders of the people were gathered, together with the tribes of Israel (discharging the office of King, he governed the people: therefore he brought the law to them). This explanation is neither forced, and is exceedingly clear. Which the blessed Luther also delivered, although he rendered "inheritance" in the dative case, not in the accusative: "Moses commanded a law for the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob." Here Moses speaks of himself, as to what sort of person he was in his office. Whence not even the Jesuit Lorinus himself, although he makes God the King, along with others, has reproved that sense concerning Moses. With whom Vatablus and Em. Sa. also agree. These did not follow Aben-Ezra, who explains it concerning Moses, any more than Cocceius followed R. Moses Gerundensis, who understands it concerning God. They had an evident text, which favors Moses. No one has been able to find Cocceius's meaning from the words of Moses: concerning the walking of Christ's foot & concerning the Kingdom of Christ after his ascension into the heavens. Likewise, concerning Christ made King when the heads of the people, that is, the Apostles, were gathered. Likewise, when the tribes of Israel were gathered together, that is, when the collection of the tribes shall have been made in the land, which he makes a sign of that time in which the kingdom of God is to be manifested. §. 1599. sqq. Whence he concludes that the following blessings are to be applied to the people in the kingdom of Christ in the time of the N. Testament. But such as the premises are, such is the conclusion. Those are merely arbitrary and brought into the text. How therefore is this to be held as necessary and redundant from the text?

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ERIT APVD RECTISSIMUM REX CONGREGA- TIS PRINCIPIBUS POPULI CUM TRIBUS ISRAEL) Rex non quidem nomine & pompa, sed jure regio populum gubernavit. Vide quæ dicta supra 17, 9.

In Ebr. Et fuit in Jeschurum (id est, in populo Israelitico) Rex in colligendis capitibus populi in unum (congregandis) tribubus Israel. Vatablus: Et fuit æquabilis Rex, cum se congregarent capita populi, si- mulque tribus Israel. Item: Fuit autem in Israele (tanquam) Rex, quando congregatæ sunt &c. subint. ad eum. Plerique de Mose intelligunt, qui Regis in- star fuerit in populo, & tum Principes populi, tum ipsum populum, quantum potuit, in officio & con- cordia atque unitate continuit, quæ sententia facilis & expedita est: Conf. Genes. 36, 31. & à B. Luthe- ro tradita: fuit vice Regis, & autoritate & loco Dei erat inter illos, ut ultra legem scriptam & vivæ vocis oraculo eos regeret ex ore Dei. E Pontificiis ob vulga- tam versionem, quæ habet in futuro ERIT Rex, non- nulli de Saule, & post eum de Davide vaticinium esse volunt. Hugo, Lyran. Abulens. Marius, Cor- nel. à Lapid. & alii sic explicant: Apud Israelem Rex erit Deus, vel potius: Deus regens eos per legem, quamdiu Principes cum populo unanimes erunt. Sic etiam R. Gerundensis de Deo explicat: Lorinus; antequam descendat Moses ad singulas benedictio- nes, communiter adhuc benedicendo vaticinatur, fore ut ad populum, quem cognominat rectissimum, si hoc epitheton reipsa tueatur, ut rectissime vivat, & ex præscripto acceptæ legis à Deo per Mosen, lex ipsa Regis loco sit, nec alio egeant rege, sed hæc eam regat, Deusve potius per eam, una cum principibus atque tribubus, cum majoribus & minoribus illos in pace, securitate, prosperitate conservando, quæ est post pietatem, religionemque maxima reipu- blicæ felicitas. Augustinus, legendo (& erit in dilecto Princeps) de Christo intelligit qv. 56. congregatis au- tem principibus populorum, id est, gentium, simul cum tribubus Israel; quem sequitur Rabanus. Ruper- tus hunc Regem interpretatur Christum, qui sessurus erat à dextris Domini rectissimi in æternum. Coccejus ult. Mosis §. 1565. ita habet: Jehovah (veniens ex Si- nai, & pede suo perambulans Israelitas) factus est Rex in Jeschurum, h. e. Israele, visionis Dei compote. Quod distinguit à diebus carnis & factum dicit per evectio- nem in cælos. Huic loco Mosis (fortasse soli) phrasin Prophetarum de regno Christi exaltati originem debe- re, asserit. Traducit etiam communem interpreta- tionem de Mose, ceu Judaicam, & textui adversam. Judæi, inquit, qui hæc verba: Et factus est in Jeschu- rum Rex, de Mose interpretantur (quas nostri qui- dam incaute sequuntur) solvunt concatenationem & filum textus. Ut enim de Mose accipere possint, ver- sum præcedentem male explicant, inferendo aliquid, quod in textu non est. Sic enim fere legunt: Moses le- gem nobis præcepit hæreditatem congregationi Jacobi. Atqui nullum signum dativi est in colo se- cundo ut in primo, & sic oratio ultimi coli in v. 3. ac- ciperet à loquelis tuis, maneret imperfecta. Quis enim? quid acciperet? Hæc Coccejus, qui ita hos versus reddidit: v. 3. at acciperet à loquelis tuis v. 4. legem (quam) præcepit nobis Moses, hæreditatem pa- negyris Jacobi. Sed quo jure duos nominativos v. 4. MOSES, & PANEGYRIS ipse rapit ad verbum acciperet in vers. 3. quo jure inserit pronomen (QUAM) v. 4. Annon omnia fluunt rectius, cum versus distincti, ut par est, distincti manent, & lex à Mose præcepta hæreditas dicitur pro congregatione vel congregationi Jacobi data? Non enim semper si- gna casuum adjicere Ebræos, notissimum, quæ è textu sæpe eruenda. Non ob Judæorum autorita- tem, sed ob textus evidentiam, de Mose intelligunt locum Interpp. Christiani, etiam Cocceji Magi- ster Joh. Calvinus, qui ita habet: Legem præcepit nobis Moses. Quod de gloria Dei & legis præstantia disseruit, nunc ad suam personam accommodat: quia propositum erat (ut dixi) ministerio suo fidem asse- rere. Ergo, ut certa sit ejus legatio, divinitus se Docto- rem populo præfectum esse, gloriatur, neq; ad exiguum tempus, sed in omnes ætates. Nam hæreditatis nomi- ne Legis notatur perpetuitas. Vendicat deinde sibi Re- gis imperium, non quod regio more dominatus fuerit, sed ut summi imperii dignitas verbis ejus pondus addat. Collecta autem capita fuisse dicit, & tribus coaluisse, re- spectu miseræ dissipationis, quæ ad interitum tendebat: ac si diceret, suo ductu & opera de integro renovatum esse statum populi. Similiter Jun. & Tremell. Legem præcepit nobis Moses hæreditariam congregationi Ja- cobi, id est, observandam præsentibus & futuris Jaco- bi posteris supra cap. 29, 29.) Fuit enim Jehusscherun Rex, quum se congregarent primores populi, simul tri- bus Israelis (Regis munus obiens populum gubernabat: ideo legem eis tulit.) Quæ explicatio nec coacta, & oppido luculenta est. Quam etiam B. Lutherus tradidit, etsi hæreditati in casu Dativo reddiderit, non in accusativo: legem præcepit Mose hæreditati Ecclesiæ Jacob. Hic de se loquitur Mose, qualis fuerit officio. Unde nec ipse Jesuita Lorinus, etsi Deum, cum aliis, Regem faciat, sensum illum de Mo- se reprobavit. Cui consonat etiam Vatablus & Em. Sa. Non magis hi Aben-Ezram de Mose ex- plicantem, quam Coccejus R. Mosen Gerundensem de Deo intelligentem sequuti. Textum eviden- tem habuere, qui Mosi favet. Sensum Cocceji è verbis Mosis nemo invenire potuit: De pedis Chri- sti perambulatione & de Regno Christi post evectionem in cælos. Item, de Christo Rege facto congregatis ca- pitibus populi, hoc est, Apostolis. Item, congregatis una tribubus Israelis, id est, cum collectio tribuum fa- cta erit in terra, quam signum facit temporis illius, quo manifestandum erit regnum Dei. §. 1599. sqq. Unde concludit, sequentes benedictiones aptandas es- se populo in regno Christi tempore N. Test. Sed quales præmissæ, talis conclusio. Illæ mere arbitrariæ & textui illatæ. Quî ergo hæc pro necessaria & è tex- tu redundante habenda?

## 33:6
Vers. 6. LET RUBEN LIVE AND NOT DIE, AND LET HIM BE FEW) However much the multitude of his tribe may decrease, yet that tribe will never perish entirely.

In the Hebrew it is held: nor let his people be numerable, as Pagninus, or rather let there not be a number to his men, as Tremell. & Jun. rendered, as if the negative is to be repeated from the common, because this part also pertains to the blessing. So also Vatablus: and let his descendants be innumerable. By others the vulgate interpretation is not disapproved: since not only a blessing, but also a prophecy concerning the future state is held here, and it is of blessing and of grace that the tribe of Ruben is still to be preserved with the rest. Thus not only the Papists, but also from our own ranks B. Luther and Osiander, whose paraphrase is this: Although Reuben, on account of the incest committed with his stepmother, was worthy not only to lose the priesthood and the kingdom (which were otherwise owed to him by reason of primogeniture), but also deserved that his entire posterity should be blotted out: yet the Lord, in his clemency, does not wish this tribe to be abolished. But nevertheless, the rule was transferred from that tribe to the tribe of Judah: which will be far superior to the tribe of Reuben, not only in dignity but also in the multitude of its people: so that Reuben may be small in number, not having as copious a posterity as the tribe of Judah. And from the Reformed, Calvin himself: It seems more probable that what the order of primogeniture carried was taken away from the family of Reuben, and thus some remaining disgrace was sprinkled upon the promise of grace. And certainly not only the tribe of Judah, but also Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali excelled in the multitude of men. Thus, the exception will not fit badly, that Reuben is counted among the people of God, provided he does not recover his dignity in full. Which explanation, as being more consistent with the Jacobean discourse in Genesis 49:3 concerning Reuben and confirmed by the event, is also more approved by us.

Furthermore, all interpreters have hitherto accepted these words by way of a vow and blessing of Moses, as the aforementioned Mosaic title requires and the words themselves sound. But Cocceius transforms them into a discourse which Moses prescribed to those to whom he gave the law, as if Moses were leading the way with these words for certain Israelites of a future time, namely under the New Testament, or after the ascension of Christ into the heavens. All interpreters explain them concerning the tribe of Reuben, as the text has it; Cocceius alone snatches them away to the faithful under the New Testament, who do not pertain to the tribe of Reuben any more than to others. All interpreters consider the preceding discourse in verses 2, 3, 4, and 5 to be complete, and acknowledge that it contains a reward placed before the blessings, by which the Man of God wished to win authority and trust for his blessings, and to recall to the Israelites' memory former benefits. Cocceius wishes nothing to be exhibited to them all except a description of God invoked, and he takes the name Jehovah, v. 2, not in the nominative case, but in the vocative case §. 1545, and hence, according to his own whim, he inserted the pronoun 'Who' in v. 2 and 5: O Jehovah (who) came from Sinai, etc. And (who) was made King in Jeshurun, for which construction he brings forward examples Ps. 18:48, 49, 50, 51, Ps. 91:12, Hab. 2:15, 16, but they are dissimilar. However, he does not explain the discourse or petition for Reuben, that he may live and not die, concerning the tribe of Reuben, but concerning the whole people: Here by Reuben I understand the whole Israelite people in that condition in which it was when God occupied the kingdom, who had been made guilty of destruction through the rejection and infamous treatment of the rock of salvation. These could easily be compared to Reuben, both as the firstborn and as the violator of his father's marriage. The word Reuben can sound 'they saw the son,' or 'see the Son,' the Son who was given to the Church (Is. 9:6). But this is an open false interpretation, which will recur in this new interpreter one after another regarding individual tribes. Moses speaks distinctly about the tribe of Reuben, not about others: Cocceius, on the contrary, contends that not the tribe of Reuben separately or peculiarly, but the whole Israelite people is to be understood. Moses prophesied about the tribe of Reuben while it was still distinct from the others: Cocceius takes it concerning the Israelites after the final destruction and the confusion of the tribes: Moses predicts the preservation of the Reubenite tribe without destruction: Cocceius dreams of something concerning the Israelites after their total excision. Since these faults of interpretation, as we have said, recur in the remaining tribes, it may suffice to have indicated them here once.

The arguments for the new gloss or perversion of the text are extremely inept and slippery, namely that comparison and allusion of the name (for those things concerning the infamous treatment of Christ and the total destruction of the Jews seek only a beginning), upon which there is no need to dwell, for they fall of their own accord by their own futility. What, I ask, is the analogy of the incest of Reuben with the state of the Israelites after the Roman destruction? And why should that name be rendered 'they will see the Son' rather than as is commonly done 'Son of vision,' why should that be dragged to the people of God, or what reason is there why such an epithet of 'son of vision' should fall to Reuben rather than to Judah? And what is that petition for Reuben, that there may be at least a few men from him who may live? i.e., he wishes it to be petitioned that the whole of Israel, guilty of death and extreme deletion, may not die. That this is the blessing of a people guilty of death, that it would have through the grace of God a remnant who would not die, but would live and praise the name of the Lord, from Rom. 9:27, ch. 11:5. But whence is it established that these passages are parallel to this blessing? Why should it be petitioned for under the name of Reuben rather than Judah or Levi? What of the fact that the version of Cocceius seems to favor a multitude: 'And let his men be (men) of number,' for men of number are said to be not so much those who are few in number, as those whose number is great, which sense some of the Reformed, along with the LXX interpreters, embrace. But it is manifest that this in no way agrees with this interpretation concerning a few remnants of Israelites being preserved.

Latin:

Vers. 6. VIVAT RUBEN ET NON MORIATUR, ET SIT PARVUS) Utcunque decrescat ejus tribus multi- tudo, nunquam tamen ea tribus tota interibit.

In Ebræo habetur: nec sint populi ejus numera- biles, ut Pagninus, imo non sit hominibus ejus nume- rus, ut Tremell. & Jun. reddidere, quasi negativa ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetenda, quia hæc etiam pars ad bene- dictionem pertinet. Sic etiam Vatablus: sintque ne- potes ejus innumeri. Aliis vulgata interpretatio haud improbatur: siquidem non solum benedi- ctio, sed etiam prophetia de statu futuro hic habea- tur, & benedictionis sit atque gratiæ, quod adhuc conservanda sit tribus Ruben cum reliquis. Ita non solum Pontificii, sed etiam e nostris B. Luthe- rus & Osiander, cujus haec est Paraphrasis: Etsi Ru- ben propter incestum cum noverca commissum, dignus erat, ut non modo sacerdotium & regnum (quae ratione primogeniturae ipsi alias debeban- tur) amitteret: sed etiam meritus erat, ut ejus to- ta posteritas deleretur: tamen Dominus pro sua clementia non vult, ut haec tribus aboleatur. Sed nihilominus ab ea tribu imperium translatum est in tribum Juda: quae non dignitate modo, sed & po- puli multitudine tribu Ruben multo erit superior: ut sit Ruben parvus in numero: non tam copiosam habens posteritatem, quam tribus Juda. Et e Re- formatis Calvinus ipse: Magis probabile videtur, detrahi familiae Ruben quod ferebat ordo primo- geniturae, & ita promissioni gratiae aspergi aliquod dedecus residuum. Et certe non modo tribus Ju- da, sed etiam Simeon, Isaschar, Zabulon, Dan, & Nephtali multitudine hominum praecelluit. Ita non male quadrabit exceptio, censeri Ruben in populo Dei, modo ne suam dignitatem in solidum recuperet. Quae explicatio ceu orationi Jacobeae Genes. 49, 3. de Rubene magis consentanea & ab eventu com- probata magis etiam nobis probatur.

Porro verba haec per modum voti, & benedictio- nis Mosis hactenus accepere Interpp. omnes, ut praemissus titulus Mosaicus requirit, & verba ipsa sonant. Sed Coccejus transformat ea in orationem, quam Moses praescripserit iis, quibus dedit legem, quasi Moses his verbis praeeat Israelitis quibusdam futuri temporis, sub novo nempe Testamento, vel post evecti- onem Christi in coelos. Interpp. omnes de Rubenis tribu explicant, ut habet to ρητον, Coccejus solus ad fideles sub Nov. Test. abripit, qui non magis Rubenis tribum, quam alias attineant. Interpp. omnes ora- tionem praecedentem vers. 2. 3. 4. 5. pro completa habent, eamque praemium continere benedictioni- bus praemissum agnoscunt, quo autoritatem ac fi- dem benedictionibus suis conciliare, ac beneficia priora Israelitis in memoriam revocare voluerit Vir Dei. Coccejus illis omnibus non nisi Dei invocati de- scriptionem exhiberi vult, & nomen Jehovah, v. 2. non in casu nominandi, sed in casu vocandi acci- pit §. 1545. atque hinc pro lubitu suo pronomen Qui v. 2. & 5. inseruit, o Jehovah (qui) ex Sinai venit &c. Et (qui) factus est in Jesuchurum Rex, pro qua constructione exempla affert Ps. 18, 48. 49. 50. 51. Ps. 91, 12. Habac. 2, 15. 16. sed dissimilia. Orationem au- tem vel petitionem pro Rubene, ut vivat, & non mo- riatur, non explicat de Rubenis tribu, sed toto po- pulo: Hic per Rubenem intelligo totum populum Israe- liticum in ea conditione, qua fuit, quum Deus regnum occuparet, qui reus factus erat excidii per rejectionem & infamem tractationem rupis salutis. Hi Rubeni, tum ut primogenito & ut violatori conjugii Patris fa- cile contefferentur. Vox ראובן Reuben potest sonare, viderunt filium, vel videte Filium, Filium qui datus est Ecclesiae (Es. 9, 6.) viderunt. At haec aperta est Ψευδερμηνεία, quae penes singulas tribus in novo hoc interprete deinceps recurret. Moses distincte loquitur de tribu Ruben, non de aliis: Coccejus ex adverso contendit, non Rubenis tribum seorsim aut peculiariter, sed totum populum Israeliticum intelli- gendum esse. Moses de Rubenis tribu, cum adhuc distinctus erat a caeteris, vaticinatus: Coccejus de Is- raelitis post excidium novissimum & confusionem tri- buum accipit: Moses conservationem tribus Rube- niticae, sine excidio praedicit: Coccejus aliquid de Is- raelitis praedicit, post totalem eorum excisionem somniat. Quae interpretationis vitia quum, ut dixi- mus, in reliquis tribubus recurrant, hic semel indi- casse sufficiat.

Argumenta novae glossae vel perversionis textus perquam inepta & lubrica sunt, Contesseratio nem- pe illa, & allusio nominis, (nam ista de infami tracta- tione Christi & excidio totali Judaeorum principium solum petunt) quibus immorari opus minime est, nam futilitate sua ultro ruunt. Quaenam obsecro est analogia incestus Rubenis cum statu Israelita- rum post excidium Romanum? Et cur nomen il- lud reddendum potius videbunt Filium, quam ut vulgo solet Filius visionis, cur id ad populum Dei tra- hendum, aut quae ratio, cur Rubeni potius talis ἐπωνυμία visionis filii cesserit, quam Judae? & quae- nam illo petitio pro Rubene, ut sint saltem pauci ho- mines ex ipso, qui vivant? sc. peti vult, ne moriatur to- tus Israel, mortis reus & deletionis extremae. Hanc esse benedictionem populi rei mortis, quod habiturus sit per gratiam Dei reliquias, qui non morerentur, sed vive- rent, & laudarent nomen Domini è Rom. 9, 27. c. 11, 5. At unde haec loca huic benedictioni parallela esse constat? Cur magis sub Rubenis, quam Judae, aut Levi nomine id peteretur? Quid quod versio Coc- ceji numerositatipotuis favere videatur: Et sint ho- mines ejus (homines) numeri, nam homines numeri dicuntur, non tam qui pauci sunt numero, quam quorum magnus est numerus, quem sensum non- nulli è Reformatis cum LXX. Interpp. amplectun- tur. Quem vero huic interpretationi de paucis re- liquiis Israelitarum conservandis nullatenus con- venire manifestum est.

## 33:7
Vers. 7. THIS IS JUDAH'S. HEAR, O LORD, THE VOICE OF JUDAH, AND BRING HIM UNTO HIS PEOPLE. HIS HANDS SHALL FIGHT FOR HIM, AND HE SHALL BE HIS HELPER AGAINST HIS ADVERSARIES.

This is Judah's, to wit, blessing. The tribe of Simeon is passed over, even though that name has crept into the translation of the LXX, who draw the last part of the preceding prophecy to Simeon, and 'Simeon is many in number.' The Vulgate, however, agrees here with the Hebrew and Chaldean text, nor do Ambrose, Procopius, Apollinaris, Diodorus, Epiphanius, or Theodoret, who are accustomed to follow the LXX interpreters, have that name. Theodoret brings forward this cause for the omitted blessing of Simeon, that Simeon was the author of the snares which the brothers laid for Joseph. But in that way, Reuben also should have been omitted on account of incest. Abulensis, Pererius, and Cornelius à Lapide allege the fornication and idolatry of Baal-Peor, by which this tribe was contaminated. Num. 26:12. But in truth, it would have had all the more need of a blessing, so that it might be raised up by it. Others more correctly wish his blessing to be included in the blessing of Judah, because Simeon was reckoned to Judah and his possession was spread through the tribe of Judah, Jos. 19. 1. Chron. 4, 24. and from that it happened that expeditions were common between these tribes, Jud. 1, 3. 24. To which also Blessed Luther inclines: You see here the tribe of Simeon is omitted, and not blessed. For what reason, who knows? For as for the Hebrews claiming the sale of Joseph and the fornication in Baal as the cause, I do not care at all. Jerome thinks that Judas Iscariot, being about to come from this tribe, deserved this, but let fables be fables. It is certain, however, that Simeon did not have his own lot. Let him therefore be content with the general blessing. Osiander wishes it to be included under the tribe of Levi, since Jacob also joined these two tribes, and it is believed that most of the scribes were in the tribe of Simeon, they themselves also teaching the law among the people of God: So that for this reason these two tribes are also rightly joined by Moses on account of related duties. It also seemed to Vatablus that the blessing of the Levites pertains to the tribe of Simeon.

Lyranus takes the first part of the blessing of Judah concerning his introduction after death into limbo, so that he may be joined there to the holy Fathers & the people, but Cornelius himself disapproves of that. Nor does Scripture know of such a limbo. And these Prophecies sound forth concerning the state of the militant Church, and concern the whole tribes. Cornelius more correctly follows the Chaldean, who renders it thus: Hear O Lord the prayer of Judah, when he shall have gone forth to war, and bring him in unto his people, that is, give him strength against his enemies, that he may obtain his own portion of the holy land and a strong victor. But that does not yet exhaust the vow of Moses: for such a victory was common to him with the other tribes. He therefore has regard to his dignity, because it was his to go before the other tribes to expeditions, and when he had foreseen the happiness, concerning which Jacob had prophesied to this tribe, that it would not be lacking in many obstacles, nor were all things joyful to be hoped for there, nay rather various disasters would follow, by which the kingdom of David would be diminished, he turns himself to prayers, for the happiness of this tribe: that the Lord may constitute Judah the governor of the people and King, and may help him in adversities, that he may be brought in to govern his people, because it is necessary to struggle with many difficulties, before he should emerge and aspire to the government of the people, therefore he claims the Israelitic people as if to a King and governor.

Coccejus says that this predicate is such, that he does not see how it was literally fulfilled in the tribe of Judah before the kingdom of Christ, or who is the people of Judah, to whom he ought to have been led. But is it not sufficiently clear that the Israelitic people is indicated, who, as we have said, is claimed for Judah, as King and Governor as his own people? But it does not appear how the calling forth of the people of Israel or its remnants from their own people, and the leading of them to the nations, is contained in these words. For the discourse is not about the remnants of all Israel, but about the tribe of Judah, not about the leading of Judah to the nations, but to his own people. And since the preservation of the remnants was already designated in the preceding blessing according to Coccejus, so that they might not die, but live and praise the name of God, in that state they ought then to have been viewed as the people of the Lord: for no one lives spiritually, and praises the name of the Lord, unless he be in the people of the Lord. How therefore is it now at last vowed, that they may be led to the people of the Lord?

The rest in the Hebrew have it thus: Let his hands be many for him as help against his enemies, by which he vows to him strength and forces against enemies and divine παράστασιν, therefore the Chaldean and the LXX add: You shall be a helper to them O LORD: for him he had addressed in the beginning: Hear O Lord, Coccejus translates: Let his hands be patronizing to him, and may you become help from his assailant! Because of this dignity and principate Moses also preferred Judah to the tribe of Levi, although this one was the Elder of Judah. Osiander thinks that Moses is praying at the same time also that God the Father may send His Son, the true heavenly King of Israel (believing in the Gospel), to be incarnated or to assume flesh from the tribe of Judah: and may strengthen the same in overthrowing his and our enemies, death, the world, Satan, hell etc. Which can be comprehended under help against enemies, provided that Christ be sprung from the tribe of Judah, and help be vowed to this tribe against spiritual enemies no less than bodily ones. But how these things pertain directly to the help of the Church among the nations, so that by Judah the remnants of Israel surviving after the Jerusalemite destruction, and spiritually living through the grace of God are understood, and efficacy, through their speech, defense, through the ἔλεγχον of the Spirit and sustenance in persecutions primarily to be sustained from the Jews, then also from the nations and the Anti-Christ, are contained in these words immediately, and uniquely as to the literal sense, as Coccejus wishes, appears neither to us, nor I believe to others.

Latin:

Vers. 7. HAEC EST JUDAE. AUDI DOMI- NE VOCEM JUDAE, ET AD POPULUM TUUM INTRODUC EUM. MANUS EJUS PUGNABUNT PRO EO, ET ADJUTOR ILLIUS CONTRA ADVERSARIOS EJUS ERIT.

Haec est Judae scil. benedictio. Praetermittitur tribus Simeon, etsi in translationem LXX. id nomen irrepserit, qui postremam partem antecedentis va- ticinii ad Simeonem trahunt, & sit Simeon multus in numero. Vulgata autem consentit hic cum Ebraeo & Chaldaeo textu, nec id nomen habent Ambros. Pro- copius, Apollinar. Diodor. Epiph. Theodor. qui sequi solent LXX. Interpp. Omissae autem benedictionis Simeonis hanc adfert causam Theodoretus, quod Si- meon auctor fuerit insidiarum, quas fratres Josepho struxere. Sed ita omittendus etiam fuisset Ruben ob incestum. Abulens. Perer. Corn. à Lapid. fornica- tionem & idololatriam Beel Phegor allegant, qua haec tribus contaminata. Numer. 26, 12. Sic vero eo ma- gis benedictione opus habuisset, ut eadem erigere- tur. Rectius alii inclusam ejus benedictionem vo- lunt benedictioni Judae, quia Simeon accensitus est Ju- dae & possessio ejus per Judae tribum diffusa fuit Jos. 19. 1. Chron. 4, 24. atque inde factum, ut expeditiones inter has tribus communes essent Jud. 1, 3. 24. Quo etiam propendet B. Lutherus: Vides hic tribum Si- meon omitti, & non benedici. Qua causa, quis novit? Nam quod Ebraei venditionem Joseph & stuprum in Baal causantur, nihil moror. Hieron. arbitratur Judam Ischarioten de hac tribu futurum id meruisse, sed fabulae sint fabulae. Certum autem est, quod Si- meon propriam sortem non habuit. Sit ergo contentus generali benedictione. Osiander comprehendi eam vult sub tribu Levi, siquidem & Jacob has duas tri- bus conjunxerit, & credatur plerosque in tribu SI- MEON fuisse scribas, profitentes et ipsos legem in popu- lo Dei: Ita ut hac ratione etiam recte hae duae tribus à Mose propter cognata officia conjungantur. Bene- dictionem Levitarum etiam ad Simeonis tribum per- tinere visum quoque est Vatablo.

Prius membrum benedictionis Judae Lyranus de introductione ejus post mortem in limbum ac- cipit, ut ibi jungatur sanctis Patribus & populo, sed id improbat ipse Cornelius. Neque novit talem lim- bum Scriptura. Et de statu Ecclesiæ militantis hæ Prophetiæ sonant, totasque tribus concernunt. Re- ctius Cornelius Chaldeum sequitur, qui ita reddit: Suscipe Domine orationem Judæ, cum egressus fuerit ad bellum, & ad populum suum introduc eum, id est, robur contra hostes illi da, ut suam terræ sanctæ partem & fortem victor obtineat. Sed id nondum exhaurit votum Mosis: nam talis victoria ipsi communis erat cum aliis tribubus. Respicit ergo dignitatem ejus, quia ipsius erat præire cæteris tribubus ad ex- peditiones, & quum præviderit felicitatem, de qua tribui huic vaticinatus erat Jacob, non carituram multis obstaculis, nec omnia læta ibi speranda esse, imo varias sequuturas clades, quibus regnum Davi- dis imminuetur, ad preces se convertit, pro tribus hujus felicitate: ut Judam gubernatorem populi ac Regem constituat Dominus, eique in adversis opitule- tur, ut introducatur ad populum suum regendum, quia necessum sit cum multis difficultatibus luctari, an- tequam emergeret & ad regimen populi adspira- ret, ideo populum Israeliticum & tanquam Regi & gubernatori vindicat.

Coccejus tale hoc prædicatum esse dicit, ut non videat, quomodo literaliter in tribu Juda ante Christi regnum impletum fuerit, aut quis sit populus Judæ, ad quem deduci debuit. Sed annon satis luculentum est populum Israeliticum indicari, qui ut diximus, Ju- dæ vindicatur, ceu Regi & Gubernatori tanquam ipsius populus? Id autem non apparet, quomodo in his verbis contineatur evocatio populi Israelis seu reliquiarum ejus ex populo suo, & deductio eo- rum ad gentes. Non enim de reliquiis totius Israelis, sed de tribu Juda, non de deductione Judæ ad gentes, sed ad populum suum sermo est. Et cum reliquia- rum conservatio in præcedenti benedictione jux- ta Coccejum jam designata, quo non moriantur, sed viverent & nomen Dei laudent, in illo jam statu tum eos oportuit spectari ceu populum Domini: non enim vivit quis spiritualiter, & laudat nomen Do- mini, nisi in populo Domini sit. Quomodo ergo nunc demum vovetur, ut deducantur ad populum Domini?

Cætera in Ebræo ita habent: Manus ejus mul- tæ (sint) illi auxilium contra hostes suos, quibus vovet ei robur & vires contra hostes ac divinam παράστα- σιν, ideo Chald. & LXX. addunt: Adjutor eris illis DOMINE: hunc enim initio compellarat: Audi Domine, Coccejus vertit: Manus ejus patrocinans ipsi, & auxilium ab impugnatore ipsius fias! Ob hanc dignitatem & principatum Judam etiam præposuit Moses tribui Levi, etsi hic Senior Juda fuerit. Osi- ander existimat, orare simul etiam Mosen, ut Deus Pater mittat Filium suum, verum Israelis (credentis Evangelio) Regem cœlestem, incarnandum seu as- sumturum carnem è tribu Juda: atque eundem con- fortet in profligandis hostibus suis & nostris, mor- te, mundo, Satana, inferno &c. Quæ sub auxilio con- tra hostes comprehendi possunt, siquidem Christus de tribu Judæ oriundus sit, & adversus hostes spi- rituales non minus, quam corporales auxilium huic tribui voveatur. Quomodo autem ad adjutorium Ecclesiæ inter gentes hæc directè pertineant, ita ut per Judam reliquiæ Israelis superstites post excidium Hie- rosolymitanum, & per gratiam Dei spiritualiter vi- ventes intelligantur, atque efficacia, per ipsorum sermonem, defensio, per ἔλεγχον Spiritus & susten- tatio in persequutionibus imprimis à Judæis susti- nendis, tum etiam à gentibus & Anti-Christo, hisce verbis immediate, atque unice quoad literalem sen- sum, uti Coccejus vult, contineatur, nec nobis, nec credo aliis apparet.

## 33:8
Vers. 8. HE ALSO SAYS OF LEVI: THY PERFECTION AND THY DOCTRINE BE TO THY HOLY MAN WHOM THOU DIDST PROVE IN TEMPTATION, AND DIDST JUDGE AT THE WATERS OF CONTRADICTION.

You should translate more correctly, of Levi, than to Levi: because the discourse is directed to God. By the holy man of the Lord or the man of the clemency of the Lord, or the meek one of the Lord, Castalio understands Christ, whom Moses and Aaron provoked, but wrongly: Abulensis wishes Moses to be designated, springing from the tribe of Levi, to whom God gave the integrity of the law, that he might communicate the same to the people or especially to the Levites: but Moses speaks of another, not of himself: and therefore others more correctly commonly [understand] Aaron, who indeed sinned, when the Lord proved him, and judged him, that he should not enter into the land of promise Num. 20, 12. Yet he was the holy man of the Lord, not only as to the holiness of his office, but as to having been received into grace he truly strove for holiness. It is therefore vowed to the tribe of Levi, that perfection and doctrine Urim and Thumim, or what were referred to these, the illumination of doctrine, and the integrity of life may be with it, as one to whom the deposit of heavenly doctrine had been entrusted, which that it may be further granted to this lineage, so that it may shine with the splendor of truth, and the integrity of life, just as Urim and Thumim ought to shine in the breastplate of the priest, the man of God hopes and prays: May that dignity remain, I pray, in the progeny of Aaron, even though when you proved his faith, and constancy in Massa (the proper name is retained more correctly than when it is rendered in the vulgate in temptation) he fell from infirmity, when you made him contend at the waters of contention, when the Israelites with great and bitter contention raised against him demanded waters: for there he sinned by incredulity. Do not punish this fall in his posterity, nor take away the sacred office from them on that account. And there is no doubt, with the agreement of our Reverend Theological Faculty in the preface to the Witteberg Theological Consultations, how properly the Man of God understood the Urim and Thummim in the breastplate of the high priest to shadow forth the light of doctrine and the perfection of holiness in the breast of the true Pontiff of the New Testament, Christ, in whom all the treasures of knowledge are hidden Col. 2, 3, and who had the law of the Lord in his heart Ps. 40, 7; and that Moses sighed at the same time: O that thy Thummim and thy Urim may be with that holy one of thine! O that that true Pontiff and holy one of the Lord may arise, who will not carry these in shadow, but will exhibit them σωματικῶς!
