Not that it should be thought that this sense underlies those words, which speak only of the tribe of Levi, but that the Man of God had in his mind him whom Aaron shadowed forth with this ornament of his. Conf. Ezra 2, 63 and the passages cited there. To which pertains that which is from Josephus, book 4. Antiq. Castalio observes here: Of the gems which the Pontiffs carried on their shoulder (they were, however, sardonyxes), one was accustomed to shine whenever God was present for divine service, namely that which marked the right shoulder, with a splendor leaping forth and appearing from very far away, although it was not in the gem before. This is truly a wonder to those who have not exercised wisdom for the contempt of divine things; but I will say what is more wonderful. For by the twelve gems which the pontiff carries sewn to his breast, God signified victory to those about to fight in battle. For such splendor flashed from them, before the army had even moved, that it was known to the whole multitude that God was present to help. Whence the Greeks, who hold our customs in high regard, since they have nothing with which to contradict these, call the breastplate a rationale. Although both the breastplate and the sardonyx ceased to shine two hundred years before I composed this work, God being indignant on account of violated laws. These things Josephus. From which Castalio gathers that the splendor ceased about the time of Christ (who is the true light of the Levites). But these things are not to be understood literally concerning Christ, as Cocceius does: Urim & Thumim are yours for the man who is studious of you. He says that a priest with Urim & Thumim is in truth the same as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, that is, one who is eternal. But the priesthood with Urim &amp; Thumim, or the Aaronic priesthood, was one thing, and the Priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek is another, which is later than Christ: the former, however, only bore the shadow of Christ: Nor is the Seed of the woman, the Man the branch, understood by the man in this place, through the τὸν ὅσιον as the LXX. that ὁ ὅσιος κυρίε Ps. 16, 10. or absolutely ὅσιος Heb. 7, 26.: But he, whom the Lord tempted in Massah, with whom he contended in Meribah. Cocceius says that this is to be taken analogically, whom you tempted similarly as Moses in that place, nay and in truth: because Christ was tempted in Massah not only by the people, but by God himself, directing the temptation of the people against him. But in truth, neither does any particle of similarity or comparison occur here, but it is simply a matter of the temptation not of Moses, but of Aaron, nor is it true that Christ was then tempted by God, and is viewed here as tempted by God: for he who was tempted fell there. And what is this, that God risked the grace of Christ as a rock, whether it suffices to satisfy thirst, and thus he was tempted? These things are distorted, and insipid, not to say anything more severe. We pass over the rest that are truly enigmatic, nay ludicrous, fearing lest Scripture should in reality become a nose of wax, if we treat it in such a way, and convert it into any forms whatsoever at will. What is clearer than that Aaron in the desert is indicated here according to the letter, not Christ, that the temptation of Aaron in the desert is looked back upon, and not, as Cocceius contends, that of Christ, who underwent the contention of God demanding our sins, and answered and paid as a sponsor for them.

Latin:

Vers. 8. LEVI QUOQUE AIT: PERFE- CTIO TUA ET DOCTRINA TUA VIRO SANCTO TUO QUEM PROBASTI IN TEN- TATIONE, ET JUDICASTI AD AQUAS CONTRADICTIONIS.

Vertas rectius, de Levi, quam ad Levi: quia ad Deum directus est sermo. Per virum sanctum Do- mini vel virum clementiæ Domini, aut mansuetum Domini Castalio Christum intelligit, quem lacessi- verit Moses & Aaron, sed aliene: Mosen designari vult Abulensis, oriundum ex tribu Levi, cui dedit in- tegritatem legis Deus, ut eandem populo seu maxi- me Levitis comunicaret: sed de alio loquitur Mo- ses, non de semetipso: ideoque rectius alii com- muniter Aaronem, qui peccavit quidem, cum eum Dominus probavit, & judicavit, ne in terram pro- missionis ingrederetur Num. 20, 12. Vir tamen san- ctus Domini fuit, non solum qua officii sanctitatem, sed qua receptus in gratiam sanctitati vere studuit. Tribui ergo Levi vovetur, ut perfectio & doctrina Urim & Thumim, vel quæ istis referebantur, illu- minatio doctrinæ, & integritas vitæ penes eam sit, utpote cui depositum doctrinæ cœlestis commen- datum erat, quod ut porro ita huic stirpi conceda- tur, ut luceat fulgore veritatis, & integritate vitæ, quemadmodum in pectorali sacerdotis Urim & Thumim fulgere debent, optat & precatur vir Dei: Maneat, quæso, ea dignitas in prosapia Aaronis, tam- etsi cum probaris ejus fidem, & constantiam in Massa (rectius nomen proprium retinetur, quam cum vulgata redditur in tentatione) ex infirmitate lapsus sit, cum contendere fecisti eum ad aquas conten- tionis, cum Israëlitæ magna & acerba cum eo con- tentione excitata aquas flagitarent: ibi enim in- credulitate peccavit. Hunc lapsum ne in ipsius posteritate punias, nec ab illis sacrum ideo auferas munus. Et quam probe intellexerit Vir Dei Urim & Thumim in pectorali summi Sacerdotis, lumen do- ctrinæ & perfectionem sanctitatis in pectore veri Pon- tificis Nov. Testam. Christi, in quo omnes scientiæ the- sauri reconditi Col. 2, 3. quique legem Domini habuit in corde suo Ps. 40, 7. adumbrare, dubium nullum est, consentiente Rev. Facultate Nostra Theologi- ca in præfat. Consiliorum Theologicorum Wit- teberg. quin Moses suspirarit simul: utinam Thu- mim tui & Urim tui sint penes sanctum illum tuum! Utinam exsurgat verus ille Pontifex & sanctus Domi- ni, qui hæc non in umbra gestabit, sed σωματικῶς ex- hibebit! Non quod illis verbis hunc sensum subes- se censendum sit: quæ loquuntur solum de tribu Levi: sed quod in mente sua habuerit Vir Dei eum, quem Aaron cum hoc ornatu suo adumbravit. Conf. Esdr. 2, 63. & ibi dicta. Quo facit, quod è Jo- sepho lib. 4. Antiq. observat hic Castalio: Gemma- rum, quas in humero ferebant Pontifices (erant autem Sardonyches) altera, quandocunq; rei divinæ Deus ad- erat, lucere solebat, scilicet ea, quæ dextrum humerum insigniebat, absiliente splendore, & longissime apparen- te: cum tamen is antea non esset in gemma. Mirum sane hoc est eis, qui non sapientiam ad contemtum re- rum divinarum exercuerunt: sed dicam quod mira- bilius est. Nam per duodecim gemmas, quas ad pectus pontifex insutas effeni fert, victoriam prælio dimica- turis præsignificabat Deus. Tantus enim splendor ab eis rutilabat, nondum moto exercitu, ut toti multitudi- ni notum esset, Deum adesse in auxilium. Unde Græ- ci, qui nostros in pretio mores habent, quoniam nihil habent, quod his contradicant, effenem rationale vo- cant. Quanquam desiit & effen & sardonyx lu- cere annis ducentis, antequam ego hoc opus compo- sui, Deo ob leges violatas indignato. Hæc Jose- phus. Ex quibus colligit Castalio, splendorem illum sub Christi tempus (qui vera Levitarum lux est) desiisse. Non autem cum Coccejo hæc secundum literam de Christo intelligenda: Urim & Thumim tua sunt viro studioso tui. Dicit, sacerdotem cum Urim & Thumim in veritate esse idem, quod sacerdotem secun- dum ordinem Melchisedechi, hoc est, qui æternus sit. At aliud erat sacerdotium cum Urim & Thumim seu Aaronium, aliud vero est Sacerdotium secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech, quod posterius Christi est: prius vero tantum umbram Christi gessit: Nec per virum hoc loco Semen mulieris, Vir germen, per τὸν ὅσιον ut LXX. ille ὁ ὅσιος κυρίε Pf. 16, 10. vel ab- solute ὅσιος Ebr. 7, 26. intelligitur: Sed ille, quem tentavit Dominus in Massa, cum quo contendit in Meriba. Dicit Coccejus analogice id capiendum, quem similiter tentasti atque Mosen in eo loco, imo & revera: quia in Massa tentatus Christus non tan- tum à populo, sed ab ipso Deo, dirigente populi tenta- tionem in eum. Verum enim vero neque hic ulla si- militudinis particula, aut comparatio occurrit, sed simpliciter de tentatione non Mosis, sed Aaronis agi- tur, neque verum est, Christum tum à Deo tentatum esse, & hic ut à Deo tentatum spectari: nam is qui ten- tatus est, lapsus ibi est. Et quid hoc est, quod Deus periclitatus sit gratiam Christi ceu petræ, an illa suffici- at ad satiandam sitim, & ita ipsum tentarir? Distorta hæc sunt, & insipida, ne quid gravius dicam. Cæte- ra vere ænigmatica, imo ludicra mittimus, veren- dum ne Scriptura reapse nasus cereus fiat, si ita eam tractemus, & in quasvis formas convertamus pro arbitrio. Quid clarius, quam Aaronem in deserto hic secundum literam indicari, non Christum, tentatio- nem Aaronis in deserto respici, non vero ut contendit Coccejus, Christi, qui contentionem Dei exigentis peccata nostra subierit, & tanquam sponsor pro iis re- sponderit, & solverit.

## 33:9
Ver. 9. WHO SAID TO HIS FATHER AND TO HIS MOTHER, I KNOW YOU NOT) See the things pertaining to this matter in book II. of the Law of War and Peace, chap. 26. §. 3. and in the Annotations to that place.

Calvin understands this concerning Aaron and thinks that in his person an example is proposed to all Levites to imitate. But these things only present the subject, for the predicate follows then, what such men have to expect. Therefore they do not complete the entire proposition, as if the subject were to be repeated from the previous verse and comprehended at the same time by the word הַאֹמֵר. It is not described what kind of person Aaron was, but what kind of persons the Levites ought to be, and in part also were, having given a specimen in the punishment of the idolaters Ex. 32, 28. where they did not spare friends or kinsmen, that is, brothers or sons. For the words of Moses are not to be restricted to this act alone, even though it could look to the same, nor is it in the Hebrew: who SAID in the past tense, but who SAYS. Whence there is no reason why we should be anxious whether the Levites also killed their Parents in that execution, namely as Cornelius affirms against Abulensis. The discourse is not about the deed of the Levites, but about the duty, that namely for God's sake it must be said even to parents themselves, I know you not. Cf. Matt. 12, 49. c. 19, 29. Luke 14, 26. as also Matt. 10, 37. It signifies what kind of persons the ministers of the word ought to be, namely dead to the world, says Luther here.

Ver. same. THESE HAVE KEPT THY WORD. In Heb. Because they have kept thy word and reserved thy covenant: THEY SHALL TEACH (which the Vulgate omits) thy judgments, or statutes, O Lord, to the posterity of the Patriarch Jacob, and thy law to the people of Israel. The sense therefore of the whole sentence is this, which Osiander expressed: They who for the word of God (which they rightly profess, and strive to adorn with the probity of their life) renounce parents, relatives and children, and all things which they have: prepared even to pour out their life rather than yield a hair's breadth concerning the true religion, these are truly fit for the ministry of the word of God.

THEY SHALL PUT INCENSE IN THY WRATH.

The Hebrew text is more correctly translated: in thy nostrils, and burnt offerings upon thy altar. Vatablus translates in the past tense, they have put, and Cornelius wishes the sense to be, because of this zeal of the Levites you, O Lord, chose them as Priests, who namely have offered, offer, and will offer henceforth always incense, and burnt offerings: But in the source the word is of the future tense, and a Prophecy is held here, and a blessing for the future, not a history, or an eulogy of preceding deeds. They are therefore said to be about to perform this duty, and their sacrifices are to be acceptable in the nostrils of the Lord (by anthropopathy) moved to the mouth, and burnt offerings upon the altar of the Lord, to appease the Lord with victims, and incenses: although we do not deny that the zeal of the Levites pleased the Lord so much, that on account of it he deigned to confirm the calling of their ministry: in which, that they may be confirmed, and perform their office with divine εὐδοκίᾳ, the man of God prays.

Cocceius again takes these things concerning all Israelites and believers in the kingdom of God, although they were said concerning the tribe of Levi, nay the words of Moses, he says §. 1923. manifestly cry out, that he is not speaking of the Levitical Priest. But who indeed? For that was not the saying of all who observe the word of God and his covenant, and for that cause renounce their neighbors, but only of the sons of Aaron, who even if they were not such, yet were legitimately approached, that they might offer victims for the people. But here the Levites are specially bound to keep the word of the Lord and his covenant, who were to lead others by a good example, and to instill into them the word and covenant of the Lord, and although their office would not cease, if they were not such, they are nevertheless reminded, that they ought to be such, nay Moses vows and prays for this, and promises to the tribe, not only that that function is to be preserved with it, but that their sacrifices are to be acceptable to the Lord, if they have kept the covenant of the Lord. But that which is predicted, that it shall come to pass, that any of the faithful in the kingdom of God shall sacrifice and offer incense before the Lord, on an altar not human, but ἀχειροποιήτῳ or of God, Cocceius will certainly never prove from this passage, who has fallen into that error here also §. 1629. that in the O. T. the conscience of those approaching God was not perfected and purified, since a propitiatory sacrifice did not yet exist, and priests did not yet exist (Ps. 132, 16.) and that believers did not have access to God, to ask for those things which are of the sons, and of those having a perfected conscience. For although by external sacrifices the conscience was not purified, there is no doubt that it was purified by faith in Christ Acts 15, 10. nor was the power of the sacrifice of Christ lacking to them, which was valid both forward and backward. The adornment of the priests of the O. T. was indeed typical also with respect to the adornment of the faithful in the N. T. and the tabernacle with its closed inner sanctuary was a figure of things in the N. T. but neither the priests nor the other faithful of the O. T. lacked the garment of salvation, the robe of the righteousness of Christ, or the faculty of approaching God to ask for those things which are of the sons of God: just as they themselves were by no means excluded from the ἐξοσία of the sons of God, unless one wishes to err in the Socinian error.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVI DIXIT PATRI SUO ET MATRI SUÆ, NESCIO VOS) Vide ad hanc rem pertinentia libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 26. §. 3. & in Annotatis ad eum locum.

De Aarone hoc intelligit Calvinus & in ejus per- sona exemplar Levitis omnibus ad imitandum pro- poni censet. At hæc subjectum tantum sistunt, prædicatum enim sequitur deinde, quidnam tales expectare habeant. Non ergo integram propo- sitionem absolvunt, ac si subjectum è priori versu repetendum voce הַאֹמֵר simul comprehendatur. Non qualis Aaron fuerit, describitur, sed qualis Le- vitæ esse debeant, atque ex parte etiam fuerint, edi- to specimine in punitione idololatrarum Ex. 32, 28. ubi miserti non sunt amicorum aut consanguineo- rum, id est, fratrum aut filiorum. Non enim ad hunc actum solum restringenda verba Mosis, etsi eundem respicere potuerit, neque in Ebræo est: qui DIXIT in præterito, sed qui DICIT. Unde non est, quod soliciti simus utrum in illa exequutione etiam Paren- tes suos occiderint Levitæ, nempe ut affirmat contra Abulensem Cornelius. Non de facto Levitarum ser- mo est, sed de debito, quod nempe Dei causa paren- tibus etiam ipsis dicendum sit, nescio vos. Conf. Matth. 12, 49. c. 19, 29. Luc. 14, 26. ut & Matth. 10. 37. Significat, quales debeant esse verbi ministri, nimi- rum mortui mundo, inquit hic Lutherus.

Vers. eod. HI CUSTODIERUNT ELOQUI- UM TUUM. In Ebr. Quia custodierunt eloquium tuum & pa- ctum tuum reservarunt: DOCEBUNT (quod omittit Vulgata) judicia, seu statuta tua, Domine, posterita- tem Patriarchæ Jacob, & legem tuam populum Israel Sensus ergo integræ orationis hic est, quem ex presfit Osiander: Qui propter verbum Dei (quo jure profitentur, vitæque probitate ornare student) renunciant parentibus, cognatis & liberis, omnibus- que, quæ habent: parati etiam vitam potius pro- fundere, quam de vera religione latum unguem ce- dere, hi vere idonei sunt ad ministerium verbi Dei.

PONENT THYMIAMA IN FURORE TUO.

Rectius Ebræus textus vertitur: in naribus tuis, & holocausta super altare tuum. Vatabl. in præterito vertit, posuerunt, & sensum esse vult Cornelius, ob hunc Levitarum zelum tu Domine eos in Sacerdotes de- legisti, qui scil. tibi obtulerunt, offerunt, offerent deinceps semper thymiama, & holocausta: Sed in fonte verbum est futuri temporis, & habetur hic Prophetia, & benedictio in futurum, non historia, aut elogium factorum præcedentium. Functuri ergo di- cuntur hoc munere, & sacrificia eorum futura gra- ta in naribus Domini (κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν) ad ora mota, & holocausta super altare Domini, ad placan- dum Dominum victimis, & thymiamasi: etsi non ne- gemus zelum Levitarum Domino ita placuisse, ut ob eundem vocationem ministerii eorum confir- mare dignatus fuerit: in qua ut confirmentur, & officium suum cum εὐδοκίᾳ divina peragant, preca- tur vir Dei.

Coccejus de omnibus Israelitis & fidelibus in re- gno Dei hæc iterum accipit, etsi dicta sint de tribu Levi, imo verba Mosis, inquit §. 1923. manifeste cla- mant, eum non loqui de Sacerdote Levitico. Qui vero? Nam id non erat omnium observantium dictum Dei & fœdus ejus, & ex causa abnegantium proximos, sed solum filiorum Aaronis, qui etsi tales non essent, tamen legitime adibantur, ut victimas pro populo offerrent. At hic specialiter adstringuntur Levitæ ad custodi- endum eloquium Domini & pactum ejus, qui aliis bono exemplo præire, ipsisque eloquium & pactum Domini instillare debebant, & quamvis non desi- neret officium eorum, si tales non essent, commo- nesiunt tamen, ut tales sint, imo vovet id ac preca- tur Moses, & promittit tribui, non modo, quod conservanda sit penes ipsam illa functio, sed quod sacrificia ipsorum accepta futura sint Domino, si fœdus Domini custodierint. Quod autem prædi- catur, fore, ut fidelium quivis in regno Dei sacrificet & suffitum faciat coram Domino, in altari non huma- no, sed ἀχειροποιήτῳ sive Dei, ex hoc certe loco nun- quam probabit Coccejus, qui in illum etiam erro- rem hic lapsus est §. 1629. quod in V. T. accedentium ad Deum conscientia non fuerit consummata & purifi- cata, quippe cum nondum exstaret sacrificium propitia- torium, & sacerdotes nec dum exstarent (Ps. 132, 16.) quodque credentes non habuerint accessum ad Deum, ad petenda ea, quæ sunt filiorum, & consummatam conscientiam habentium. Quanquam enim per sa- crificia externa purificata non fuerit conscientia, fi- de tamen in Christum purificatam fuisse non est du- bium Actor. 15, 10. neque deerat ipsis sacrificii Chri- sti vis, quod valuit antrorsum, & retrorsum. Orna- tus sacerdotum V. T. fuit quidem typicus etiam re- spectu ornatus fidelium in N. T. & tabernaculum cum clauso intimo sacrario figura erat rerum in N. T. sed non çarebant vel sacerdotes vel alii fideles V. T. indumento salutis, veste justitiæ Christi, aut fa- cultate accedendi ad Deum ad petendum ea, quæ fi- liorum Dei sunt: quemadmodum etiam ipsi ab ἐξοσία filiorum Dei minime exclusi fuere, nisi quis Socinianum errorem errare velit.

## 33:11
Vers. 11. BLESS LORD HIS STRENGTH, AND ACCEPT THE WORKS OF HIS HANDS: SMITE THE LOINS OF HIS ENEMIES, AND LET NOT THOSE WHO HATE HIM RISE UP.

Abulensis thinks that this prophecy is about the Maccabees, who were descended from Levi, conceived in the form of a prayer, rendering it thus: Bless, O Lord, his army: nor is there any doubt that the power of this blessing reached even to them, but this prayer must be explained generally: because Moses prayed for success for the fortitude of the Levitical tribe at all times, so that they might be strong and courageous, and might happily execute the work of the Lord, but that on the contrary the loins and strength of the enemies might be broken, and the counsels of those who hate the Lord might not succeed. Calvin translates: THAT THEY MAY NOT RISE, because, he says, Moses did not wish to express the Levites by the troubles of wars, but only to promise victory: because God will destructively prostrate their enemies. Coccejus has not convinced by any proof that enemies under the N. T., and especially the Anti-Christ, are here specifically designated, nor will there be a reason why these things should be said specifically to the tribe of Levi, if they concern all Israelites, or how a different condition of the faithful is here proclaimed, which might not have a place in the preceding blessing, according to that enigmatic interpretation.

Latin:

Vers. 11. BENEDIC DOMINE FORTITU- DINI EJUS, ET OPERA MANUUM ILLI- US SUSCIPE: PERCUTE DORSA INIMI- CORUM EJUS, ET QUI ODERUNT EUM, NON CONSURGANT.

Prophetiam hanc esse de Maccabeis ex Levi prognatis per modum orationis conceptam Abu- lensis putat, ita reddens: Benedic Domine exercitui e- jus: neque dubium est ad eos etiam penetrasse vim istius benedictionis, sed generaliter hæc precatio ex- plicanda: quia omnibus temporibus fortitudini Le- viticæ tribus successum exoravit Moses, ut fortes at- que animosi sint, & feliciter opus Domini exequan- tur, ex adverso autem hostium lumbi ac vires fran- gantur, neque succedant consilia eorum, qui ode- runt Dominum. Calvinus vertit: NE RESUR- GANT, quia noluit, inquit, Moses Levitas molestiis pugnarum exprimere, sed tantum promittere victori- am: quia Deus hostes eorum exitialiter prosternet. Ho- stes sub N. T. & imprimis Anti-Christum hic peculia- riter designari, nullo documento convicit Coccejus, nec causa erit, cur hæc ad tribum Levi dicta sint spe- ciatim, si Israelites omnes concernunt, aut quomo- do hic diversa conditio fidelium prædicatur, quæ in præcedenti benedictione locum non habeat, juxta ænigmaticam istam ἐπίλυσιν.

## 33:12
Verf. 12. AND OF BENJAMIN HE SAID THE BELOVED OF THE LORD SHALL DWELL) Or rather, the most beloved by the Lord, ἠγαπημένος ὑπὸ κυρίου κατασκηνώσει πεποιθώς. The Greeks explain what follows, with the word God added. The firm dwelling of Benjamin is signified, namely in Jerusalem, and the Sanctuary in his portion. See Gen. 49, 27.

Therefore he blesses Benjamin after Levi, because the temple was to be built in his portion. The Hebrews also render it thus: THY BELOVED, (that is, the temple and the worship with which God is delighted, shall be), shall be exercised safely in this tribe, but it can be understood that Benjamin himself would dwell confidently in the Lord, because he had God with him in the temple and his dwelling place. Indeed, not only was the city itself situated in this tribe, Jos. 18, 27, but also the most important part of the sanctuary. The ancients are in doubt about the altar, as appears from Kimchi on that place. However, some part belonged to the tribe of Judah, Ps. 78, 68, and therefore the city is also reckoned to it, Jos. 15, last.

AS IN A CHAMBER HE SHALL DWELL ALL THE DAY: AND BETWEEN HIS SHOULDERS HE SHALL REST) He reads not חפף, but חפה. But the Greeks read, as the Masoretes: God covers over him all the days.

Another reading is not to be invented immediately where the interpretation is otherwise. Moreover, in the Hebrew there are verbs of the past tense: All the day he protected him, and between his shoulders he rested, yet they are rightly taken in the future, in the prophetic manner. Thus the former words, The beloved of the Lord shall dwell confidently in him, are in the form of a wish, the rest in the form of a prophecy and promise. Coccejus understands the beloved of the Lord to be the Son of God, Is. 5, 1. 2. and the words, let him dwell tranquilly upon him, and the rest, who all the day protected him, he takes as a periphrasis of him: and he wishes the sense to be, that he protected the faithful from the Jews and Gentiles at all times, and at length in some part or generation of the Church manifested his dwelling upon it with the terror of the enemies and their flight, and that Moses asks that he might wish to dwell further upon the Church with such majesty, and that that age of the Church is called Benjamin because of the analogy of the indwelling, which he refers to the inclusion of the Dragon into the abyss, Ap. 20, 3. But these latter things are the dreams of a man, not the prophecy of Moses; there is nothing here about the inclusion of the Dragon into the abyss, about which John speaks, nothing which even slightly persuades that the name of Benjamin is the name of an age of the Church, and that it refers to that time, nothing which convinces that the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles is indicated, or a dwelling in some part of that Church; although it were admitted that the Son of God is understood, and that it is wished that he dwell upon the tribe of Benjamin, just as in truth, in, or even upon that tribe (if the emphasis of the particle עַל be urged) the Son of God dwelt, when he deigned for the temple to be his dwelling place. It seemed far otherwise to Calvin, who makes Benjamin dwell upon God, and calls the explanation about God dwelling upon Benjamin violent: To dwell upon God: and between his shoulders, is worth as much as to recline upon him: by a likeness taken from Fathers, who carry their children while still small and tender. Others elicit the contrary sense, that God will dwell upon the shoulders of Benjamin: but too violently. It is also otherwise to Junius and Tremellius, who render it thus: The beloved of Jehovah (as Benjamin was singularly to his father, Gen. 44, 10) shall dwell securely with him (with Jehovah, as formerly with his Father) protecting him daily, and between his shoulders (in Jerusalem, the metropolis of his possession. A metaphor, by which the whole possession of Benjamin is compared with a body and its metropolis with a head placed upon its shoulders: Thus Eph. 8, 8.) dwelling, Gen. 49, 25. Osiander refers the former, concerning the beloved of the Lord, to Benjamin, or rather the temple of the Lord, the latter partly to the Lord: He will cover over him all the day (i. e. the Lord will always protect his temple) partly again to the temple, and between his (the Lord's) shoulders he shall rest, i. e. the Lord will sustain and as it were carry his Church on his shoulders, in which the legitimate worship of God will flourish. B. Luther similarly almost: the lovely one of the Lord shall dwell securely: At all times he will hold over him, and will dwell between his shoulders. In the Latin Commentary, Ann. 1524. Perhaps, he says, Moses says this, because the tribe of Benjamin dwelt between the tribe of Judah and Ephraim, both royal and powerful, and had the temple in its tribe.

Latin:

Verf. 12. ET BENJAMIN AIT AMANTISSIMUS DO- MINI HABITABIT) Imo dilectissimus Domino, ἠγαπημέ- νος ὑπὸ κυρίου κατασκηνώσει πεποιθώς. Quæ vero sequun- tur explicant Græci, addita voce θεός. Significatur Benjami- nis habitatio firma, Hierosolymis scilicet, & Sanctuarium in ejus parte. Vide Genes. 49, 27.

Ideo post Levi benedicit Benjamin, quia in ejus parte ædificandum erat templum. Ebræa etiam ita reddunt: DILECTUM TUUM, (id est, templum & cultum quo Deus delectatur, erit), exercebitur tu- to in hac tribu, sed intelligi potest, ipsam Benjamin confidenter in Domino habitaturum, quia Deum se- cum habebat in templo & habitaculo suo. Nimirum non modo urbs ipsa in hac tribu erat sita Jos. 18, 27. sed etiam potissima sanctuarii pars. De ara veteres dubitant, ut ex Kimchio ad illum locum apparet. Pertinebat autem pars aliqua ad tribum Juda Ps. 78, 68. atq; ideo etiam illi accensetur urbs Jos. 15, ult.

QVASI IN THALAMO TOTA DIE MORABI- TVR: ET INTER HVMEROS ILLIVS QVIESCET) Legit non חפף, sed חפה. At Græci legerunt, ut Maso- rethæ: ὁ θεὸς σκιάζει ἐπ' αὐτῷ πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας.

Non statim alia lectio fingenda est, ubi aliter se habet interpretatio. Cæterum in Ebræo sunt verba præteriti temporis: Omni die protexit ipsum, & inter scapulos ejus requievit, recte tamen, more propheti- co, in futuro accipiuntur. Ita priora verba Dilectus Domini habitet confidenter in eo, per modum voti se habent, reliqua per modum prophetiæ & promissio- nis. Coccejus dilectum Domini intelligit Filium Dei Es. 5, 1. 2. & verba, habitet super ipsum tranquille, & cætera, qui omni Die protexit ipsum, pro περιφράσει ejus habet: ac sensum esse vult, protexisse eum omni tempore fideles ex Judæis & gentibus, & tandem in a- liqua Ecclesiæ parte aut generatione habitationem su- per ea cum terrore hostium & fuga eorum manifestasse, Mosenque expetere, ut is cum tali majestate velit super Ecclesia porro habitare, eamq; Ecclesiæ æta- tem vocari Benjaminem propter inhabitationis analo- giam, quam refert ad Draconis inclusionem in abyssum Ap. 20, 3. Sed hæc posteriora somnia viri sunt, non vaticinium Mosis; nihil hic de Draconis inclu- sione in abyssum, de qua Johannes, nihil quod vel le- viter suadeat, Benjaminis nomen esse nomen ætatis Ecclesiæ, & illud tempus referre nihil, quod convin- cat Ecclesiam ex Judæis & gentibus collectam indicari, aut habitationem aliqua parte istius Ecclesiæ; quam- vis admitteretur Filium Dei intelligi, & voveri, ut is super Benjaminis tribu habitet, quemadmodum revera, in, vel etiam super tribu illa (si particulæ עַל emphasis urgeatur) habitavit Filius Dei, cum tem- plum habitaculum suum esse dignatus est. Longe aliud visum fuit Calvino, qui Benjamin super Deum habitantem facit, & explicationem de Deo super Benjamin habitantem violentam dicit: Habitare su- per Deum: & inter humeros ejus, tantundem valet, at- que in eum recumbere: similitudine a Patribus sumta, qui filios adhuc parvulos & teneros gestant. Alii contrarium sensum eliciunt, Deum habitaturum super humeros Benjamin: sed nimis violenter. Aliud etiam Junio ac Tremellio, qui sic reddunt: Dilectus Jehove (ut patri singulariter fuit Gen. 44, 10. Benjamin) ha- bitet secure cum eo (cum Jehovah, ut olim cum Patre) protegente eum quotidie, & inter humeros ejus (in Je- rusalem metropoli possessionis ejus. Metaphora, qua tota possessio Benjamin cum corpore confertur & me- tropolis ejus cum capite humeris ejus imposito: Sic Ef. 8, 8.) habitante Gen. 49, 25. Osiander prius, de dilecto Domini ad Benjaminem, vel potius templum Domini refert, posteriora partim ad Dominum: Opperiet su- per ipsum tota die (i. e. Dominus semper proteget templum suum) partim iterum ad templum, & inter humeros illius (Domini) requiescet, i. e. Dominus su- stentabit & quasi gestabit in humeris suis Ecclesiam suam, in qua vigebit legitimus Dei cultus. B. Luthe- rus similiter fere: das liebliche des HErrn wird sicher wohnen: Allezeit wird er über ihm halten, und wird zwischen seinen Schultern wohnen. In Commen- tario Latino Ann. 1524. Forte, inquit, hoc Mose di- cit, quod tribus Benjamin inter tribum Juda, & E- phraim utramque Regiam & potentem habitavit, & templum in sua tribu habuit.

## 33:13
Vers. 13. AND OF JOSEPH HE SAID OF THE BLESSING OF THE LORD HIS LAND, OF THE FRUITS OF HEAVEN, AND OF THE DEW AND OF THE DEEP THAT LIETH BENEATH.

Latin:

Vers. 13. JOSEPH QUOQUE AIT DE BENEDI- CTIONE DOMINI TERRA EJVS, DE POMIS COE- LI, ET RORE ATQVE ABYSSO SVBJACENTE.

## 33:14
Vers. 14. OF THE FRUITS OF THE PRODUCE OF THE SUN AND OF THE MOON) The principles of generation, the Sun by heat, the Moon by moisture.

Latin:

Vers. 14. DE POMIS FRVCTUVM SOLIS AC LU- NAE) Principia generationis, Sol calore, Luna madore.

## 33:15
Verse 15. CONCERNING THE SUMMIT OF THE ANCIENT MOUNTAINS.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DE VERTICE ANTIQVORVM MON TIVM.

## 33:16
Verse 16. CONCERNING THE FRUITS OF THE ETERNAL HILLS AND CONCERNING THE PRODUCE OF THE EARTH AND CONCERNING ITS FULLNESS.

In Hebrew: The blessing of the Lord (or blessed of Jehovah) be his land, from the best (or delicate) gifts (or produce) of heaven (or from the excellence of heaven), from the dew and from the deep that lies beneath, and from the best gifts (or produce) of the Sun and from the best gifts of the Moon (or of the months) and from the summit of the ancient mountains, and from the best gifts (or produce) of the hills of the world: from the (best) fruits of the earth and from its fullness, or whatever is had on earth for passing life comfortably. The Vulgate is very insufficient, and with it Cornelius a Lapide and others, in [interpreting it as] the fruits which are born by the influence of heaven, the Sun, and the Moon; the land of Joseph shall be blessed. By the deep that lies beneath, they understand fountains continually gushing from the earth like an abyss, just as it is blessed from above on account of the dew of heaven. Natural causes are joined together, which concern the production of fruits and produce, or temporal goods: heaven, dew, the deep of the fountains, the Sun, the Moon, and whatever can be expected from the summit of the mountains and from the delicate [gifts] of the hills, whatever can be expected from the fruits of the earth and from its fullness; the best and most excellent is vowed to him, and at the same time prophetically promised, and thus it is also taught that no part of the land, not even the mountains and hills excepted, will be sterile or uncultivated, but that they have reason to hope for the best produce from them as well. Cf. Gen. 49, 26. The opinion of B. Luther seems to be that all these things are said figuratively, so that he understands the kingdom of Israel to flourish, with heaven, and dew, and the deep, the sun, the moon, the ancient mountains, and the hills of the world favoring it, i.e., while God and men grant it everything, kings, princes, the great, the rich, the peoples, and the common folk. Namely, these diverse orders by these diverse names signifying. For concerning the fruits of the earth he says immediately: And of the fruits of the earth and its fullness, i.e., whatever the earth brings forth, and animals and men beget.

V. same verse. THE BLESSING OF HIM WHO APPEARED IN THE BUSH, SHALL COME UPON THE HEAD OF JOSEPH, AND UPON THE CROWN OF THE NAZARITE AMONG HIS BRETHREN.

The Hebrew, if account is taken of the Atnach accent, is to be rendered thus: And the good pleasure (or grace) of the dweller in the bush, let it come (that blessing of the Lord and good pleasure of the one dwelling in the bush) upon the head of Joseph, etc. That dweller in the bush is none other than the Son of GOD. For it was not a created angel who appeared to Moses in the bush, but Jehovah, who testified of Himself: I SHALL BE who I SHALL BE Ex. III, with whom Moses was in the ἐκκλησίᾳ and from whom he received living oracles Act. 7, 38. The Man of God, established on the boundary of death, had this especially in his heart; therefore, just as Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph in his name, The Angel who redeemed me from all evil, bless them Gen. 48, 16, so Moses also prayed for a blessing for the posterity of Joseph from this Angel; just as the Patriarch Jacob joined God, who fed him from his youth, God the Father and the angel Goel in the blessing, on equal terms, so likewise Moses joins the blessing of Jehovah, and the good pleasure of the habitation in the bush, of the angel of the Lord, who delivered the people from Egypt. An ἄγγελος λειτυργικὸς or ministering angel cannot be joined in this way with Jehovah, nor is it right to pray for grace from a ministering angel. Wherefore no other is to be understood than the angel of the covenant of the grace of God, from whom, and in whom, every blessing is obtained Gen. 12, 3. Joh. 1, 17. Eph. 1, 3.

Coccejus understands by the land of Joseph that place in the world which the Church of Christ, at a certain age after the cessation of persecutions, indeed, and the destruction of idolatry in the Roman Empire, is to possess, which abounds in every temporal blessing, and is the head, or the chief of the ancient mountains, or those which God founded from the beginning, and the most excellent of the earth or of the whole world and its fullness, i.e., of the cities and habitations with which the earth is filled, and it embraces the head or the chief, or ἀρχὴν and principality of the mountains and hills, and thus he judges this to be a picture of the Empire, such as it was under Constantine, and he calls that land the ἐυδοκίαν or benevolence of the one dwelling in the bush, that is, to experience his grace and placation. But these can be held as ingenious comments; no one will recognize them as a solid commentary. The matter is not about the Church under the Roman Empire, in the time of Constantine, but about the blessing of the tribes of the sons of Joseph, which they were to have while they existed, nor do these things exhibit a description of time or place, but an induction of manifold blessings, both corporal and spiritual, in the ἐυδοκίᾳ of the dweller in the bush.

Joseph is called a Nazarite, or separated among his brethren, not because he was separated from them by being sold into Egypt and shut up in prison, not because he grew his hair long in prison, not because a crown fell to him when Israel or the ten tribes were separated from the house of David, which reasons Cornelius alleges, but because he was glorified among his brethren, as the LXX rendered it, partly when he was exalted to the Principality in Egypt, and partly and primarily when he was raised to the kingdom of Israel in his grandsons, for Jeroboam was from the tribe of Ephraim, sprung from Joseph. For the Hebrew word denotes A CROWN, and it is thus rendered by Osiander, upon the crown of the head among his brethren, whose paraphrase here is elegant and clear: Whatever good is born from the good temperament of the sky or air, whatever comes forth either from the moistening of dew or from the inner marrow of the earth, whatever is concocted, vegetated, increased, and fostered on earth by the heat of the sun or the waxing and waning of the moon: whatever is born elegant on the summits of the most fertile mountains, whatever on the hills of the world, whatever finally the earth brings forth most excellent, and with whatever good the earth is filled (and it abounds in many most useful things), may all that be given to this tribe from the good pleasure of the Lord (who once appeared to Moses in the burning bush, being about to send him to deliver the Israelites), especially indeed to him who shall be adorned with the Royal crown τῷ imperio among the rest of the Israelites, his brethren. For the Israelite kings (after the kingdom was divided under Rehoboam) were many of them sprung from the tribe of Ephraim, which had descended from Joseph. Thus the Lord promised and provided the greatest corporal benefits to the Israelite kings, who nevertheless were almost all idolaters and the worst of men, not to approve of their impiety, but to invite them to repentance by so many and such great benefits. Joshua also, who drove the kings out of the land of Canaan, was from the tribe of Ephraim, and Midian, who defeated the Midianites, was from the tribe of Manasseh. Luther interpreted it not of the kingdom, but of the prophets, may the favor of Christ be upon them, that it may abound in Prophets, which also happened; for the kingdom of Israel had many Prophets: because the things that follow concern the kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DE POMIS COLLIVM AETERNORVM ET DE FRVGIBVS TERRAE ET DE PLENITVDINE EJVS.

In Ebr. Benedictio Domini (vel benedicta Je- hovae) terra ejus (sit) de optimis (vel delicatis) donis (aut proventibus) cœli (vel a praestantia cœli) de rore & de abysso, quae jacet infra & de optimis donis (seu proventibus) Solis & de optimis donis Lunae (vel mensium) & de vertice montium antiquorum, & de optimis donis (vel proventibus) collium mundi: de frugibus (optimis) terrae & de plenitudine ejus vel quicquid ad vitam commode transigendam habe- tur in terra. Valde insufficienter Vulgata, & cum ea Cornelius a Lapide & alii, in pomis, quae cœli, Solis & Lunae influxu nascuntur, erit benedicta terra Joseph. Per abyssum, quae jacet infra, intelligunt fontes e terra jugiter scaturientes instar abyssi, quemadmodum superne benedicta est ob rorem cœli. Conjungun- tur causae naturales, quae concernunt ad productio- nem frugum & proventuum, vel bonorum tempo- ralium, cœlum, ros, abyssus fontium, Sol, Luna, & quic- quid a vertice montium, & a delicatis collium, quicquid a frugibus terrae & e plenitudine ejus expectari potest, optimum & praestantissimum, id ipsi vovetur, ac pro- phetice simul promittitur, adeoque docetur etiam, nullam terrae partem, ne montibus & collibus qui- dem exceptis, sterilem fore, aut incultam, quin opti- mos proventus inde quoque sperare habeant. Conf. Gen. 49, 26. B. Lutheri sententia hec omnia figurate dici videntur, ut regnum Israel florere intelligat, favente cœlo, & rore, & abysso, sole, luna, montibus antiquis, collibus mundi, i. e. dum ei Deus & homines omnia tri- buant, reges principes, magni, divites, populi & vulgus. Scil. hos diversos ordines diversis his nominibus signi- ficans. Nam de fructibus terræ mox dicit: Et de fručti- bus terræ & plenitudinis ejus, i. e. quicquid terra pro- fert, & animalia & homines gignunt.

V. eod. BENEDICTIO ILLIUS, QUI APPA- RUIT IN RUBO, VENIAT SUPER CAPUT JOSEPH, ET SUPER VERTICEM NAZARÆI INTER FRATRES SUOS.

Ebræa, si ratio habeatur accentus Atnach, ita reddenda, Et beneplacitum (vel gratia) habitatoris rubi, veniat (illa benedictio Domini & beneplacitum habitantis rubum) in caput Josephi &c. Ille rubi ha- bitator nullus alius est, quam Filius DEI. Non enim angelus creatus apparuit Mosi in rubo, sed Jehovah, qui de se testatus est: ERO qui ERO Ex. III. cum quo Moses fuit in ἐκκλησίᾳ & a quo accepit oracula viva Act. 7,38. Hunc in mortis confinio constitutus maxi- me habuit in corde Vir Dei, ideo ut Jacobus bene- dixit filiis Josephi in ejus nomine, Angelus qui redemit me ab omni malo, benedicat ipsis Gen. 48, 16. ita Moses quoque posteritati Josephi ab hoc Angelo precatus est benedictionem; uti Jacob Patriarcha conjunxit Deum, qui pavit ipsum a juventute, Deum Patrem & angelum Goelem in benedictione, ex æquo, ita pariter conjungit Moses benedictionem Jehovæ, & beneplaci- tum habitationis in rubo, angeli Domini, qui libera- vit populum ex Ægypto. Non potest ita conjun- gi ἄγγελος λειτυργικὸς vel ministrans cum Jeho- vah, neque fas gratiam precari ab angelo ministro. Quapropter nullus alius intelligendus est, quam an- gelus fœderis gratiæ Dei, a quo, & in quo omnis ob- tingit benedictio Gen. 12,3. Joh. 1, 17. Eph. 1, 3.

Coccejus per terram Josephi locum eum in mun- do intelligit, quem Ecclesia Christi certa ætate post cessationem nimirum persecutionum, & destructionem idolatriæ in Rom. Imperio possessura sit, qui abundet omni benedictione temporali, & sit caput, seu præcipuus montium antiquorum, vel quos Deus ab initio condidit, & præstantissimus terræ sive mundi totius & plenitudi- nis ejus, h. e. urbium habitationumque, quibus impletur terra, & complectatur caput sive præcipuum, seu ἀρ- χὴν & principatum montium & collium, adeoque hæc censet esse picturam Imperii, quale erat id sub Con- stantino, eamque terram dicit ἐυδοκίαν vel benevo- lentiam habitantis rubum, id est, experiri ejus gratiam & placationem. Sed hæc pro ingeniosis commen- tis haberi possunt, pro solido commentario nemo a- gnoverit. Non de Ecclesia sub Romano imperio, tempo- re Constantini, sed de benedictione tribuum filiorum Josephi res est, quam dum erant illæ, habituræ erant, nec descriptionem ista exhibent temporis, aut loci, sed inductionem multiplicium benedictionum cum corporalium, tum spiritualium, in ἐυδοκίᾳ habita- toris rubi.

Dicitur autem Joseph Nazareus, vel separatus inter fratres suos, non quod per venditionem in Æ- gyptum ab illis separatus, & carceri inclusus fuerit, non quod in carcere intonsus comam aluerit, non quod corona eiobtigerit, quando Israel vel decem tribus separabantur a domo David, quas rationes al- legat Cornelius, sed quia glorificatus est in fratribus, ut LXX. reddidêre, partim ubi exaltatus fuit ad Principatum in Ægypto, partim & imprimis ubi in nepotibus ad regnum Israelis evectus, Jeroboam e- nim fuit ex tribu Ephraim ex Josepho oriundus. Vox enim Ebræa CORONAM notat, atque ita red- ditur ab Osiandro, super verticem coronæ inter fratres suos, cujus paraphrasis hîc elegans & dilucida: Quidquid boni nascitur ex bono temperamento cœli seu aëris, quicquid vel ex roris humectatio- ne vel e terræ intimis medullis provenit quicquid ex calore solis, vel lunae augmento & decre- mento in terris concoquitur, vegetatur, augetur at- que fovetur: quicquid in verticibus fertilissimorum montium, quicquid in collibus mundi elegans gigni- tur, quicquid denique terra praestantissimum pro- fert, & quocunque terra bono repleta est (abundat autem multis utilissimis rebus) id omne ex benepla- cito Domini (qui olim Mosi in rubo ardenti apparu- it, missurus eum ad liberandos Israelitas) donetur huic tribui, praesertim vero ei, qui Regia corona τῷ imperio erit ornatus inter reliquos Israelitas, fratres suos. Reges enim Israelitici (post divisum sub Ro- boamo Regnum) multi oriundi erant ex tribu E- phraim, quae a Josepho descenderat. Ita Dominus regibus Israeliticis, qui tamen fere omnes erant ido- lolatrae, & pessimi erant, maxima corporalia bene- ficia promisit, & praestitit, non ut impietatem eo- rum approbaret, sed ut tot tantisque beneficiis ad poe- nitentiam invitaret. Fuit & Josua, qui Reges ex terra Canaan expulit, e tribu Ephraim, & Midian, qui Midianitas cecidit ex tribu Manasse. B Luthe- rus non de regno, sed prophetis interpretatus est, favor Christi sit super eos, ut abundet Prophetis, quod & factum est; multos enim habuit regnum Israel Pro- phetas: quia quae sequuntur regnum concernunt.

## 33:17
Vers. 17. AS THE FIRSTBORN OF A BULL HIS BEAUTY, THE HORNS OF A RHINOCEROS HIS HORNS) But the Greeks κέρατα μονοκέρωτος τὰ κέρατα ἀυτῦ. And so the Greeks always translate. That the rhinoceros is one animal, and the monoceros (unicorn) another, has been shown by many. The horn of the monoceros rises from the middle of the forehead two cubits high. Plin. 8, 21. The bull is the emblem of Joseph Gen. 49, 6, but a bull so strong that each of its horns equals the horn of a monoceros. From the Syrians and Arabs ראם is a monoceros.

It is translated much more correctly as μονοκέρωτος, Unicorn. Moreover, both the glory and majesty (for thus the Hebrew word must be rendered, not beauty) of the Israelite kingdom are noted, as well as its force and power, because that kingdom would be magnificent and glorious and equipped with great power, both for repelling force and for inflicting it. For that is what wild beasts are accustomed to do with their horns. Alien are the things which Cornelius brings forward from Rupertus concerning the beauty of Joseph, by which his mistress was captivated, to whom he resisted bravely, just as wild beasts are accustomed to do with their horns, and the things which he himself, as well as Junius, bring forward concerning the name of a bull, that Joseph was compared to a bull, because he was to be worshipped on account of agriculture preserved in Egypt, and his tomb was to be adorned with the image of an ox. More fitting is what is brought forward from Diogenes: that the bull was a symbol of a King. Junius renders it, of the firstborn of the ox, that is his beauty, and by the word firstborn he wishes to refer to the fact that the right of the firstborn was transferred from Reuben to Joseph 1. 1 Chr. 5,1.

See the same. HE SHALL WINNOW THE NATIONS EVEN TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.

Namely, with his horns and his strength he will rout, and as it were scatter like chaff the hostile nations, even to the ends of his land, namely. And if neighboring peoples conspire against him, he will nevertheless drive them bravely outside the boundaries of his kingdom. Tertullian (Against the Jews, ch. 10), Ambrose (Book on the Blessing of the Patriarchs, ch. 11), and Augustine (q. 56) apply these things to Christ as a certain figure. Whose horns are the horns of the cross, who through faith winnows all nations, subjecting them to himself, and at the end of the world he will winnow all the unbelievers through judgment. Coccejus renders it: To the firstborn of the bull, his is the majesty, and he explains it thus: The firstborn of the bull is the first of the Princes. And he gives royal majesty and horns as of a unicorn, with which the people [shall push] the rams, likewise the ends of the earth by apposition, that is, those peoples who place themselves outside the land of Joseph, in whom the land and the people of the Church fail, understanding it of Constantine, who crushed opposing peoples everywhere and everywhere abolished idolatry. But what do these things have to do with Joseph the Nazirite (as Coccejus renders it) of his brothers? Doubtless this age of the Church

inheriting the land of enemies and idolatry, is best compared with Joseph ruling in the land of Egypt and there begetting children by the myriads and thousands. Before he arrived at this rule, he was in prison, and so was the Church, he for three years, she for 300 years. If one must play with such allusions in Scripture, and they are to be sold as the literal sense, what will become of Scripture, if not sport and jest?

Vers. same. THESE ARE THE MULTITUDES OF EPHRAIM, AND THESE THE THOUSANDS OF MANASSEH.

In Hebrew: These myriads of Ephraim. These things will happen in the most populous tribe of Ephraim, and partly also in the tribe of Manasseh, who was the brother of Ephraim: Therefore Manasseh will also share in the aforementioned happiness: although Ephraim holds the first place in dignity, strength, and multitude. Jacob confirms the opinion by which he had preferred Ephraim, the younger by birth, to the elder. Therefore he recounts only the thousands of Manasseh, but the myriads of Ephraim: a proof of which thing God had already published in the census, of which mention was made, in which the tribe of Ephraim was found to be more populous, as Calvin [notes] in this place. Of the Ephraimites, four myriads and 500 went out from Egypt; of the tribe of Manasseh, 32,300. Num. 1, 32. 34.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QVASI PRIMOGENITI TAVRI PVL- CHRITVDO EJVS, CORNVA RHINOCEROTIS CORNUA ILLIVS) At Graeci κέρατα μονοκέρωτος τὰ κέ- ρατα ἀυτῦ. Et ita semper vertunt Graeci. Aliud esse ani- mal Rhinocerota, aliud monocerota ostensum multis. Mono- ceroti cornu media fronte cubitorum duum eminet. Plin. 8, 21. Bos Josephi insigne Genes. 49, 6. sed bos ita validus, ut unumquodque ejus cornu aequet cornu monocerotis. Ex Syris & Arabibus ראם monoceros.

Rectius omnino vertitur μονοκέρωτος Uni- cornis. Notatur autem tum gloria & majestas (fic e- nim reddenda vox Ebraea, non pulchritudo) regni Israelitici, tum vis & potentia, quod regnum illud magnificum & gloriosum magnaq; potentia instru- ctum futurum sit, ad vim tum repellendam, tum infe- rendam. Id enim folent facere ferae cornibus suis. Aliena sunt quae de pulchritudine Josephi, qua capta fuit hera, cui fortiter restitit, veluti cornibus folent ferae, e Ruperto affert Cornelius, & quae ipse ut & Ju- nius de nomine tauri afferunt, Josephum tauro com- paratum, quia ipse ob agriculturam, in Aegypto ser- vatam, colendus, & sepulchrum ejus simulacro bo- vis exornandum fuit. Convenientius, quod e Diogene affertur: taurum symbolum Regis fuisse. Ju- nius reddit, primogeniti bovis, illius decor ei, & voce primogeniti respici vult, quod primogenitorum jus a Rubene in Josephum translatum 1. Chr. 5,1.

V. eod. VENTILABIT GENTES USQUE AD TERMINOS TERRAE.

Cornibus sc. & viribus suis profligabit, & quasi inventum disperget gentes hostiles, usq́; ad terminos terrae suae sc. Et si populi vicini adversus eum conspi- raverint, propellet tamen eos fortiter extra pomo- ria regni sui. Ad Christum haec ceu figuram aliquam applicant Tertul. c. Jud. c. 10. Ambros. l. de Benedict. Patr. c. 11. August. q. 56. Cujus cornua sunt cornua crucis, qui per fidem ventilat omnes gentes, eos sibi subjiciens, & in fine mundi omnes incredulos ven- tilabit per judicium. Coccejus reddit: Primoge- nito tauri, ejus est majestas, & ita explicat: Primoge- nitus tauri est primus Principum. Et dat majestatem re- giam & cornua ut monocerotis, quibus populus arietes, pariter terminos terrae per appositionem, h. e. eos popu- los, qui se ponunt extra terram Josephi, in quibus deficit terra & populus Ecclesiae, de Constantino intelligens, qui populos adversarios ubiq́; contudit & idololatriam ubiq́; distulit. Sed quid ista ad Josephum Nasiraeum (ut reddit Coccej9) fratrum suorum? Nimirum hac aetas Ecclesia-

hæreditans terram hostium & idololatriam, optimè comparatur cum Josepho dominante in terra Ægypti & ibi procreante liberos in myriades & chiliades. Antequam ad hoc imperium perveniret, fuit in carcere, ita & Ecclesia, ille per triennium, hæc per 300. annos. Si talibus allusionibus in Scriptura ludendum, eæque pro sensu venditandæ literali, quid e Scriptura fiet, nisi lusus & jocus?

Vers. eod. HÆC SUNT MULTITUDINES EPHRAIM, ET HÆC MILLIA MANASSE.

In Ebræo: Hæ myriades Ephraim. Fient hæc in tribu populosissima Ephraim, & partim etiam in tribu Manasse, qui fuit frater Ephraim: Participabit igitur & Manasse de prædicta felicitate: quanquam Ephraim dignitate, robore & multitudine primas partes teneat. Confirmat sententiam Jacob, qua Ephraim natu minorem prætulerat majori. Ideo chiliadas tantum Manasse recenset, Ephraim vero myriadas: cujus rei documentum iam ediderat Deus in censu, cujus facta fuit mentio, in quo tribus Ephraim reperta fuit populosior, ut Calvinus h. l. Ephraimitarum ex Ægypto exiverunt quatuor myriades & 500. tribus Manasse 32300. Num. 1, 32. 34.

## 33:18
vers. 18. AND ZEBULUN SAID, REJOICE ZEBULUN IN THY GOING OUT.

The interpreters understand this concerning the success of commerce. For since this tribe was to dwell near the seashore, by going out frequently on voyages to other provinces, it was to bring back great advantages from there by virtue of this prediction and Mosaic blessing: See Gen. 49, 13.

AND ISSACHAR IN THY TENTS.

For this tribe was to be occupied not with merchandise, but with agriculture in the quiet of its own home, Gen. 49, 14. 15. They are then joined together in the blessing.

Latin:

vers. 18. ET ZABULON AIT, LÆTARE ZABULON IN EXITU TUO.

Id de commerciorum successu intelligunt Interpp. Quum enim habitatura esset tribus hæc juxta littus maris, crebris navigationibus egrediendo ad alias provincias, magna inde reportatura erat commoda vi hujus prædictionis & benedictionis Mosaicæ: Vid. Gen. 49, 13.

ET ISASCHAR IN TABERNACULIS TUIS.

Hæc enim tribus non mercimoniis, sed agriculturæ domi suæ quiete erat vacatura Gen. 49, 14. 15. conjunguntur deinde in benedictione.

## 33:19
Vers. 19. THEY SHALL CALL THE PEOPLES UNTO THE MOUNTAIN THERE THEY SHALL OFFER SACRIFICES OF RIGHTEOUSNESS) By their own example they will lead the others, liberally bringing sacrifices to the temple.

THEY SHALL SUCK THE ABUNDANCE OF THE SEAS AS MILK) In Hebrew: they shall suck the abundance of the seas: that is, Zebulun and Issachar will grow rich from the abundance of the sea. The Greeks: they shall suck the wealth of the sea.

These things are not badly explained in this way, and the interpreters easily agree here. Moses subscribes, says Calvin, to the prophecy of Jacob, who said that Zebulun would dwell at the haven of the sea, so that he might sail for the sake of trade. But because Issachar will be more delighted with leisure, he will be sluggish and slothful, so that he will not refuse to pay tribute for the sake of buying peace. THEY SHALL CALL THE PEOPLES UNTO THE MOUNTAIN, because both Issachar and Zebulun were to invite other tribes to the temple on their mountain by word and example. For there were teachers among them, and although they were most remote from Mount Zion, they nevertheless flowed to it zealously according to the law, and by no means empty-handed, and they stirred up others by their example; And there THEY SHALL SACRIFICE, or they shall worship God with that worship with which He wishes to be worshipped, which will be acceptable to Him. THEY SHALL SACRIFICE SACRIFICES OF RIGHTEOUSNESS, legitimate and just sacrifices. Vatablus interprets it similarly. To Blessed Luther, this seems to pertain to the history of Deborah, where Barak, having collected an army on Mount Tabor, won the victory over Sisera. FOR THEY SHALL SUCK THE ABUNDANCE OF THE SEAS AS MILK (those who will be in the tribe of Zebulun will obtain goods and wealth imported by ships through the waves of the sea) AND THE TREASURES HIDDEN IN THE SAND. Onkelos: they shall eat the wealth of the peoples, and the treasures which are hidden in the sand will be revealed. This latter part can be understood concerning the tribe of Issachar, which was to devote effort to agriculture, because it would collect treasures from there, as if hidden in the sand. Others explain it concerning gems, which they explain as gold and other metals, which are mixed into the sands and are hidden like treasures to be transported by sea. Rupert and Cornelius a Lapide refer this to the teaching of Christ and the Apostles in the land of Zebulun, but because a double sense cannot be admitted in explaining Scripture, which has only one and the same certain and constant meaning, Osiander judges that this prophecy began to be fulfilled only when Christ taught in that region: because He taught there frequently, and performed many miracles, so that not a few were called there to the kingdom of God by the preaching of Christ and were converted to the true knowledge of GOD, Matt. 4.

Coccejus rejects the literal sense approved by the common calculation of interpreters, because the convenience of inviting the nations to the worship of God was equally great for all the tribes, because they all had neighboring nations, and because the mountain is rashly determined as the mountain of GOD. But however much the convenience of inviting others to worship was not lacking to others, here, nevertheless, because of commerce by sea and land due to the singular prosperity of these tribes in those things, a singular convenience of inviting the nations, and because of their piety at the same time, the invitation of other tribes of Israel is predicted as exemplary, and not rashly, but from the determination added by the Holy Spirit, the mountain of God is defined: because it concerns that mountain in which sacrifices were duly offered in the Old Testament, which is none other than Mount Zion. Thus Calvin: What follows, I think was added, as if Moses had said, that the distance of places would not be an obstacle to their ascending to Jerusalem together with others, to cultivate the exercises of piety. For the more remote they were from the temple, the zeal for legal worship could grow cold among them. Although, therefore, they dwell in the extreme borders, Moses says they will come nevertheless, so that they may sacrifice to God. Some understand by 'peoples' other tribes: which seems by no means consistent: others, however, understand foreign nations, to whom commerce gave access. I, however, interpret it simply: although the length of the journey might persuade them to rest at home, they would nevertheless mutually exhort one another, so that they might betake themselves to the temple in great crowds. Coccejus also raises a doubt about the treasures of those hidden, as he himself renders it, and the sand, because the shore is usually sterile. But that is resolved by the very exegesis provided above, so that there is no need to seize upon, with some of the Rabbis, ἄμμον ὑάλινον, sand which is melted into glass, according to Strabo and Pliny. Calvin clearly agrees with our interpretation: The end of the verse can be a rendering of the cause: as if it had been said, they will be the more attentive to the worship of God, because, having been enriched by Him, they will strive to render praise. And certainly it is a sign of foul ingratitude not to be stimulated by the benefits of God, so that the more liberally He deals with us, the more eagerly we strive to render thanksgiving. At the same time, Moses teaches that the expenses of the journey will by no means be burdensome to them, given their great wealth. For although the region was not so fertile, its location was nevertheless very convenient for enriching them. Thus here, where it is said: They shall suck the abundance of the sea, an antithesis is to be understood between the fruits of the fields and the manifold proceeds from trade; the hidden treasures of the sand point to the same thing. For as to what some explain, that they would have such great treasures that they would hide them in the sand: others, that the sands there would be productive of gold and silver: others, that they would collect what the sea vomits up, it is insipid. Since, therefore, others grew rich from their own lands, Moses says with a fitting figure that the sands in the land of Zebulun are filled with hidden treasures on account of adventitious gain. Coccejus imagines for himself that such a literal sense is indicated in this magnificent, as he calls it, enigma, namely the EXIT of the pious from the peoples and their separate dwelling in their tents: And that he will be for the peoples calling to the mountain, not to sacrifices of righteousness, but on that occasion the pious will offer sacrifices of righteousness, that is, they will endure various sufferings. The motives, however, for avoiding the sacrifice on the mountain, and for enduring sufferings, are both the taste of the gifts of God overflowing into the sea, that is, the whole world, and the taste of the goods which they have according to the Spirit, and which those founded in the earth in the sepulchers enjoy. Finally, that the Church is called, which goes out from the peoples of Zabulon, because this tribe extended to the north of the land and the sea, and that Church is extended to the north and the sea. A truly wonderful gloss, of a brain more ingenious than judicious. It is a discourse about the tribe of Zabulon and Issachar, not about Christians called from the nations, with the distinction of those tribes having been extinguished, and the very names themselves having been deleted. About a prosperous and joyful departure, because Zabulon and Issachar are bidden to rejoice. But that one must depart from the Roman Church is not a cause for joy, but for sadness, because it neither persists in the faith itself, but falls away from it, nor does it suffer the faithful worshipers of God. Furthermore, who will admit that being called to the mountain denotes, both literally one mountain or a mountainous place, Rome, and hieroglyphically and in an emblem, a worldly kingdom? And whence will it be proved that Rome is designated here by Moses, what business has it with the tribes of Issachar and Zabulon? Whence that the mountain which Moses notes, and the sacrifices of justice are opposed to one another, and are contrary, to call to the mountain and to the sacrifices of justice? Does not Moses testify with a resounding voice that sacrifices of justice were to be offered there on the mountain? Which Cocceius perverts to no purpose, as if the word 'there' were the same as 'therefore,' when the proper sense is local, and the reference to the mountain is evident. Whence will it be proven that the burnt offerings of sufferings are understood here by the sacrifices of justice? Whence, that by the seas the whole world, by the treasures of those founded in the sand, the goods of the souls of the departed are indicated, that to suck the abundance of the seas is to receive Christ, who was given to the world (or the seas) as Savior? That to suck the treasures of those founded in the sand is to have communion with those who are no longer in the body, but have been translated according to the Spirit into heaven? Whence, finally, that these things suit the Waldensians and the disciples of Wycliffe and Hus? If this is not a twisting of Scripture, I do not know what it could be.

Latin:

Vers. 19. POPVLOS JVDICABVNT AD MONTEM IBI IMMOLABVNT VICTIMAS JVSTITIÆ) Exemplo suo præibunt cæteris, victimas ad templum liberaliter adferendo.

INVNDATIONEM MARIS QVASI LAC SVGENT) In Hebræo: affluentiam marium sugent: id est, Zabulon & Isaschar ex maris copia ditescent. Græci πλῦτος θαλάσσης θηλάσουσι.

Non male hæc ita explicantur, & consentiunt facile hic Interpp. Subscribit Mose, inquit Calvinus, vaticinio Jacob, qui dixit Zabulon habitaturum in porta maris, ut naviget mercaturæ causa. Isaschar vero quia magis otio delectabitur, desidem fore & ignavum, ut redimendæ pacis causa tributum pendere non recuset. POPULOS VOCABUNT AD MONTEM, quia tum Isaschar, tum Zabulon verbo & exemplo suo invitatutæ erant alias tribus ad templum in monte suo. Erant enim ex eis Doctores, & quum remotissimi essent a monte Zion, studiose tamen ex lege, ac minime vacui eo profluentes, alios exemplo suo excitarunt; Ibique IMMOLABUNT, vel colent Deum eo cultu, quo vult coli, qui ipsi acceptus erit. SACRIFICABUNT VICTIMAS JUSTITIÆ, legitima & justa sacrificia. Similiter etiam interpretatur Vatabl. B. Luthero hoc ad historiam Deboræ pertinere videtur, ubi in monte Thabor collecto exercitu Barac victoriam de Sissera reportavit. QUIA INUNDATIONEM MARIS UT LAC SUGENT (qui in tribu erunt Zabulon, merces & opes per undas maris navibus importatas consequentur) ET THESAUROS ABSCONDITOS ARENARUM. Onkelos, facultatem populorum comedent, & thesauri, qui absconditi sunt, in arena revelabuntur. Hoc posterius de tribu Isaschar agriculturæ operam daturæ intelligi potest, quod inde thesauros, quasi in arena absconditos collectura sit. Alii de gemmis, quas auro & metallis aliis explicant, quæ arenis immi- scentur & occultantur quasi thesauri per mare ad- vehendi. Ad doctrinam Christi & Apostolorum in terra Zabulon refert Rupertus, Corn. a Lap. sed quia geminus sensus in explicanda Scriptura admitti ne- quit, cujus non est nisi una eademque certa & con- stans sententia, Osiander unice tum impleri cepisse hanc prophetiam censet, cum in ea regione docuit Chri- stus: quia frequenter ibi docuit, & plurima edidit miracula, ita ut non pauci ibidem prædicatione Christi ad regnum Dei vocati atque ad veram DEI agnitionem fuerint conversi Matth. 4.

Coccejus literalem sensum Interpp. communi calculo approbatum reprobat, quod commoditas gentes ad cultum Dei invitandi æque magna fuerit o- mnibus tribubus, quia gentes finitimas habuere omnes, quodque temere mons determinetur ad montem DEI. Sed utut commoditas aliis non defuerit alios ad cul- tum invitandi, hic tamen e commerciis mari terra- que ob tribuum harum in illis felicitatem singula- rem, singularis commoditas gentes invitandi, & ob earum pietatem simul aliarum Israelis tribuum in- vitatio exemplaris prædicitur, neque temere, sed e determinatione a Spir. S. adjecta mons Dei definitur: quia de eo monte agitur, in quo rite offerebantur in V. T. sacrificia, qui alius non est, quam mons Zi- on. Sic Calvinus: Quod sequitur, additum existi- mo, ac si dixisset Moses, locorum distantiam obstaculo non fore, quo minus una cum aliis Jerosolymam ascen- derent, ad colenda pietatis exercitia. Nam quo re- motiores erant a templo, frigere apud eos poterat lega- lis cultus studium. Quamvis ergo in extremis finibus habitent, dicit Moses venturos nihilominus, ut Deo sa- crificent. Per populos quidam intelligunt alias tri- bus: quod minime consentaneum videtur: alii vero exteras gentes, ad quas accessum dabant commer- cia. Ego vero simpliciter interpretor: quamvis itine- ris longitudo suadeat domi quiescere, se tamen mutuo cohortaturos, ut in magnis catervis ad templum se con- ferant. De thesauris etiam conditorum, uti reddit ipse, & sabulo dubium movet Coccejus, quia littus solet sterile esse. Sed id expeditum est ipsa ἐξηγήσει superius tradita, ut opus non sit cum Rabbinorum a- liquo arripere ἄμμον ὑάλινον arenam, quæ funditur in vitrum, juxta Strab. & Plin. Nostræ interpre- tationi plane consonat Calvinus: Finis versus potest esse causæ redditio: quasi dictum esset, eo magis atten- tos fore ad cultum Dei, quia ab ipso locupletati, stude- bunt laudem referre. Et certe fœdæ ingratitudinis si- gnum est, non stimulari Dei beneficiis, ut quo liberalius nobiscum agit, alacrius enitamur ad reddendam gra- tiarum actionem. Simul docet Moses minime illis graves fore itineris sumtus in magnis opibus. Quam- vis enim non adeo pinguis esset regio, situs tamen valde commodus erat ad ipsos locupletandos. Ita hic, ubi di- citur: Sugent maris affluentiam, subaudienda est an- tithesis inter fructus agrorum & multiplices proven- tus ex mercaturis, eodem spectant reconditi thesauri arenæ. Nam quod exponunt quidam, tantos illis fore thesauros, ut recondant in arena: alii vero, a- renas illic auri & argenti feraces fore: alii, collectu- ros, quæ mare evomet, insipidumes est. Quum ergo alii ex suis fundis ditescerent, concinna figura dicit Mo- ses, arenas in terra Zabulon refertas esse occultis the- sauris propter adventitium quæstum. Fingit Coc- cejus sibi ejusmodi sensum literalem in hoc magnifi- co, uti vocat, ænigmate, indicari nempe EXITUM pio- rum a populis & separatam mansionem in tentoriis suis: Illumque futurum populis ad montem, non ad sacrifi- cia justitiæ vocantibus, ea vero occasione pios sacrificia justitiæ oblaturos, hoc est, passiones varias exantla- turas. Motiva autem vitandi facrificationem in monte, ac sustinendi passiones esse tum gustum donorum Dei redundantium in mare, hoc est, totum mundum, tum gustum bonorum, quæ secundum Spiritum habent, & quibus fruuntur conditi in terra in sepulcris. Vo- cari denique Ecclesiam, quæ exit a populis Zabulon, quia hæc tribus extendebatur ad septentrionem terra & mare, & Ecclesia illa ad septentrionem & mare ex- tenditur. Glossa vere mirabilis, cerebri magis in- geniosi, quam judiciosi. De tribu Zabulon & Isa- schar sermo est, non de Christianis e gentibus vocatis, extincta tribuum istarum distinctione, deletisque ipsis etiam nominibus. De egressu prospero & læto, quia jubetur lætari Zabulon & Isaschar. At quod exeundum ab Ecclesia Romana, causa non est lætitiæ, sed tristitiæ, quod illa nec in fide persistat ipsa, sed ab ea deficiat, nec fideles Dei cultores patiatur. Por- ro ad montem vocari, tum literaliter unum montem, sive locum montosum Romam, tum Hieroglyphice & in emblemate regnum mundanum notare quis admit- tet? & unde probabitur Romam hic a Mose desi- gnari, quid illi cum tribubus Isaschar & Zabulon commercii? Unde quod mons ille, quem Moses no- tat, & sacrificia justitiæ sibi opponantur, & contraria sint, vocare ad montem & ad sacrificia justitiæ? An- non sonora voce testatur Moses ibi in monte oblatum iri sacrificia justitiæ? Quod nequicquam pervertit Coccejus, quasi vox ibi, idem sit, quod idcirco, cum sensus proprius sit localis, & respectus evidens ad mon- tem. Unde evincetur, quod passionum holocau- sta hic per sacrificia justitiæ intelligantur? Unde, quod per maria totus mundus, per thesauros condito- rum in fabulo bona animarum defunctarum indigi- tentur, quod abundantiam marium sugere, sit Chri- stum, qui donatus est mundo (vel maribus) in Servato- rem recipere? quod sugere thesauros conditorum in sabulo sit habere communionem cum iis, qui non am- plius sunt in corpore, sed secundum Spiritum translati sunt in cælum? Unde denique, quod hæc Waldenfi- bus & Wiclefi ac Hussi discipulis conveniant? Si hæc non sit στρεβλότης Scripturæ, quid tandem sit nescio?

## 33:20
Ver. 20. BLESSED IN LATITUDE GAD: AS A LION HE RESTED) See 1 Chronicles v. 18 and following.

In Hebrew: Blessed is he who enlarges (his borders) Gad: It will be well for this tribe: because it will possess a joyful and fertile region, this tribe will also be warlike: as a Lion, having seized prey, he rested (the past tense for the future, so that he may enjoy the prey, and he has seized, more correctly he will tear the arm and the crown, i.e., he will break the power of his enemies, and will overturn their empire, as Osiander here (Conf. Josh. 13, 24.) to whom he at the same time snatches the HEAD AND SHOULDERS. For a lion, as if with one blow, tore the head and shoulders from its prey. Vatablus: Blessed is he who enlarges Gad, or who has caused Gad to enlarge: that is, who has yielded to Gad himself; who has not resisted him. As a lion lingers, who tears the arm, with the crown; He will dwell like a lion: he will snatch the arm and the head: i.e., in his land he will be no different than a lion, whom the other animals fear: he will be formidable to all: therefore he will kill the Princes and Kings who will resist him. The word 'enlarges,' Osiander refers to Gad, enlarging his own borders; Vatablus to others yielding to Gad; Calvin seems to refer it to God himself. But Osiander's opinion is to be preferred in this. I am pleased to add what Calvin has: In the blessing of the tribe of Gad, mention is made only of the hereditary part which he had obtained outside the lot. Therefore he praises the benefit of God: because he granted the Gadites an ample habitation: for the word 'enlarging' is referred to the extent of the land. Moreover, since in that extremity beyond the Jordan they were neighbors to enemies, he pronounces that they would be warlike, and in this sense compares them to a lion, which snatches prey now from the head, now from the arm. Because, therefore, that seat was not as peaceful as some other region in the middle of the land of Canaan, he pronounces that they would be safe and sound from violence: Although, however, the condition is not very joyful, to be exercised by continuous wars: yet in that inconvenience the grace of God is not to be despised, to be formidable to enemies and [to take] prey. If anyone objects that the license of plundering is by no means becoming to the children of God, the solution is easy: it is not related here simply what is lawful, what is desirable, or what is worthy of praise, but the comfort of defense is proposed against the incursions and vexations of enemies. Furthermore, the desire for plundering is not permitted, but only military strength for overcoming enemies is praised.

Latin:

Vers. 20. BENEDICTVS IN LATITUDINE GAD: QUASI LEO REQVIEVIT) Vide Paralipom. 1. v. 18. & fequentibus.

In Ebr. Benedictus dilatans (terminos suos) Gad: Bene erit huic tribui: quia lætam & fœcun- dam regionem possidebit, erit & bellicosa hæc tri- bus: quasi Leo, capta præda, requievit (præteritum pro futuro, ut fruatur præda, cepitque, rectius dila- niabit brachium & verticem i. e. franget hostium suorum potentiam, & eorum evertet imperium, uti hic Osiander (Conf. Jos. 13, 24.) cui simul rapit CA- PUT ET HUMEROS. Leo enim uno quasi ictu ex præda sua abrupit caput & humeros. Va- tablus: Benedictus, qui dilatat Gad, vel dilatare fecerit Gad: id est, qui cesserit ipsi Gad; qui non re- stiterit ei. Ut Leo moratur, qui lacerat brachium, cum vertice; Similis leoni habitabit: rapiet brachi- um, & caput: h. e. in terra sua non erit aliter, atque leo, quem reliqua animalia timent: erit omnibus formidolosus: propterea interficietPrincipes &Re- ges, qui ei resistent. Verbum dilatat, refert Osian- der ad Gad, terminos suos dilatantem; Vatablus ad alios Gadi cedentes; Calvinus ad ipsum Deum re- ferre videtur. Sed præferenda in eo est Osiandr sententia. Adjicere, quæ habet Calvinus, lubet: In benedictione tribus Gad tantum fit mentio partis hæ- reditariæ, quam adeptus fuerat extra sortem. Dei er- go beneficium laudat: quia Gaditis amplam habita- tionem concesserit: verbum enim Dilatandi, ad terr amplitudinem refertur. Cæterum quoniam in illa ex- tremitate trans Jordanem hostibus vicini erant, bellico sos fore pronunciat, & hoc sensu comparat eos leoni, qui prædam rapit nunc a capite, nunc a brachio. Quia igitur non tam pacata erat illa sedes, quam aliqua alia regio in medio terræ Canaan, tutos & salvos fore pro- nuntiat a violentia: Etsi autem non admodum læta est conditio, exerceri continuis bellis: in illo tamen incom- modo non spernenda est Dei gratia, formidabiles esse ho- stibus & prædam. Si quis objiciat rapiendi licenti- am minime decere filios Dei, solutio facilis est, non hic simpliciter referri quid liceat, quid optabile sit, vel lau- de dignum, sed contra incursus & vexationes hostium proponi solatium defensionis. Adhæc non permitti prædandi cupiditatem, sed tantum laudari robur mi- litare ad vincendos hostes.

## 33:21
ver. 21. AND HE SAW HIS PRINCIPALITY, THAT IN HIS PART A LAWGIVER WAS REPOSITED.

They explain the former regarding the Principality as the land of Og and Sihon, which the Gadites occupied first before others, before the other tribes had crossed the Jordan, i.e., the tribe of Gad first chose for itself a lot and dominion in the land of the Amorite Kings Og and Sihon: Some declare the latter regarding the burial of Moses in the lot of Gad with the Chaldean, even Cornelius a Lapide, but that fits poorly, and does not pertain to the matter. In the edition of Vatablus, these things are rendered thus: he first looked out for himself, because there was the portion of the hidden Lawgiver, or also he saw the firstfruits, because there was the portion of the lawgiver hidden, with this commentary: He has already asked of me a portion and part of the land, which he might inhabit, namely the land of Sihon and Og, because he saw there many fortresses covered with precious material. For there were the palaces of the lawgiver, that is, of the princes. Calvin has it thus: And he saw the beginning, because there the portion of the lawgiver was hidden: It is added how they were provident in choosing a domicile there: namely because God suggested to them that it would be in the discretion of Moses that that part be distributed to them. For it is called the portion of the lawgiver, about which Moses could rightfully decide: just as he assigned it to the Gadites not rashly, nor otherwise than by the command of God. But the portion is called hidden, which God had not included in his promise. The sum is, although the will of God had not yet been revealed regarding that accession of land: yet they had obtained it by his hidden liberality. And thus Moses wishes his decree to be ratified, that the Gadites remain beyond the Jordan, otherwise a controversy could have been stirred up: because the promise of God had assigned the borders to the whole people on the nearer bank.

WHO WAS WITH THE PRINCES OF THE PEOPLE AND EXECUTED THE JUSTICES OF THE LORD AND HIS JUDGMENT WITH ISRAEL.

Vatablus says thus concerning these things: And he will come with the princes of the people and will execute the justice of the Lord and his judgments with Israel. He will not dwell there, however, before he comes together with the Princes to subjugate the land which the Lord promised to his Israelite brethren, so that he may execute the justice and judgment of God with them, i.e., that he should do just as the Lord had commanded him to do with his brethren. For the Lord had commanded him to accompany his brethren into the holy land and to help them in defeating the Canaanites, which he had undertaken to do. Therefore, to execute the justice and judgment of the Lord is to do what God has commanded, and as we have promised God that we would do.
