Calvin also says thus: who adds that justice is spoken of here not only because it was right to wage war with his brethren and to be helpers in acquiring the land, but because God had determined to execute his vengeance upon the profane and impious nations through all of Israel, and had chosen all the tribes in common as ministers of his judgment. Similarly Cornelius a Lapide: WHO WAS WITH THE PRINCES OF THE PEOPLE. I.e., with the princes of the nine tribes, when, namely, in the crossing of the Jordan the Gadites preceded the other tribes in battle to conquer the Canaanites, just as Moses had commanded, and they themselves had promised him: and so Gad did the righteousness of the Lord and his judgment with Israel, that is, Gad did that which by covenant and his duty he ought to have done toward God and toward his fellow tribesmen the Israelites. The final words can also be understood in this way, that the Gadites, although they were to have their domains in the land of Og and Sihon, were nevertheless to observe the laws and judgments just as the remaining tribes of Israel across the Jordan. Osiander gives this meaning to these and the preceding words: And he saw his principality, because in his part a Doctor was stored, in Hebrew covered, or hidden: that is, to this tribe shall be given an excellent Governor, (but a spiritual one) namely Elijah the Tishbite, from the citizens of Gilead: for Gilead was a part of that region which in the division of the land fell to the tribe of Gad, as Joshua ch. 13 testifies.) He shall be a Doctor, (of the true religion) but covered, or hidden, namely for a time as if lurking: when he had predicted the drought: and was compelled for almost three whole years to avoid the sight of King Ahab. He afterwards before King Ahab, having called together the nobles of the kingdom, and all the people, but especially having collected and gathered the Baalitic Priests, by a huge miracle calling down fire from heaven by his prayers, which consumed that man's burnt offering, restored among the elect the true knowledge of God, and religion in the Israelite people 2. Kings 17, 18. for this truly was to do the righteousness of the Lord, and his judgment with Israel: even if this restoration of the Church did not last very long. B. Luther refers the whole blessing concerning Gad to the times of Jehu: And Gad said, Blessed is the enlarger of Gad, because he dwells as a lion, and has torn the arm and the crown, (this seems to me to have been fulfilled by King Jehu, who made room for piety, having abolished the Baalites, and broke through like a lion bravely, having even slain two kings, as if the arm and the crown) and he saw his beginning, because there the portion of the Doctor was stored (this I think is said of the good Prophets, who under Jehu were secure in their kingdom, having been put to flight before under the Baalites, so that it is a singular for a plural: The portion of the Doctor, that is, the collection of Doctors.) And he came with the princes of the people, and did the righteousness of the Lord and his laws with Israel, because he brought back the princes and the people from those idolaters, whence he is also praised by God. These things B. Luther: which explanation is not inappropriate. And whether one wishes to embrace this of Luther, or the Osiandric one, he would do better, in our judgment, than by approving Vatablus's paraphrase; because Moses is not dealing with past things, but with future ones: nor was there any need to prophesy about the company of other tribes, since the lands around the Jordan were granted to this tribe on that condition.

Coccejus, after he had agitated against the Dutch version, because there it was in the part of the lawgiver, newly translated it thus, for there it is the portion of the encrusted lawgiver, which he so encrusted with the discovery of a new interpretation: By Gad, which signifies an army, the faithful of that age are to be understood, which follows the one described above, as the army of the lamb of God, at the time of the preaching of the eternal Gospel Rev. 14. verse 6. and the announced fall of Babylon verse 8. To bring the enlargement of Gad, because the Church had been in distress and small in number: he saw a beginning for himself, that is, small beginnings and first fruits; with whom the matter was with the heads of the people, in whom shall be the portion of the encrusted lawgiver, that is, with the Emperors, Kings, Princes, Magistrates of that people and society, with whom the Pseudo-Prophet, or Anti-Christ, had mixed himself, so that he might have his portion in the same people. AND THAT CHURCH, or the small assembly of the faithful, APPROACHED THE HEADS OF THE PEOPLE, i.e., came into the sight of the Princes and Kings in the assemblies, AND DID THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF JEHOVAH, it did that which belongs to Pastors, by professing the truth, by refuting falsehood. AND HIS JUDGMENTS ARE AMONG ISRAEL: for he propagated the judgments of God to Israel, i.e., he filled the earth with the knowledge of his name. He was enlarged, and he tore in the adversary's kingdom both the arm and the crown. These things he: which will be acknowledged as solid, when it is solidly proven that the subject is the faithful of the said age. For if any accommodation of preachers made in any way whatsoever suffices, more subjects could be substituted. This is a prophecy about the tribe of Gad, not about the faithful of the New Testament. Otherwise, that B. Luther attacked the Roman Anti-Christ with leonine fortitude and stood before the heads of the people in public assemblies, and did the righteousness of Jehovah (if Coccejus wishes this to be understood of him, and not of his Zwingli) is a most certain matter. But that here either the Anti-Christ is marked by the word of lawgiver, or B. Luther is shadowed forth by the image of a lion, with his faithful supporters, no one has been able to see thus far, nor do I believe anyone will easily see it, even if he uses the spectacles of Coccejus.

Latin:

vers. 21. ET VIDIT PRINCIPATUM SUUM, QUOD IN PARTE SUA DOCTOR ESSET REPOSITUS.

Prius de Principatu explicant de terra Og & Sihon, quam videlicet præ aliis primo occupant Gaditæ, priusquam aliæ tribus Jordanem transiis- sent, q. d. tribus Gad prima sibi sortem & ditionem elegit in terra Regum Amorrhæorum Og & Sihon: Alterum de sepultura Mosis in sorte Gad cum Chal- dæo nonnulli declarant, etiam Cornelius a Lapide, sed id parum convenit, nec ad rem facit. In edi- tione Vatabli sic ea redduntur: primum sibi prospe- xit, quod illic esset portio Legislatoris latentis, vel & vi- dit primitias, quia illic esset portio legislatoris tecta, cum hoc commentario: Jam petivit a me portionem & partem terræ, quam habitaret, nempe terram Sihon & Og, quod illic videret multas arces tectas materia pretiosa. Erant enim illic palatia legislatoris, id est, principum. Calvinus ita habet: Et vidit principium, quod illic portio legislatoris tecta: Additur, quomodo providi fuerint in eligendo illic domicilio: nempe quia Deus illis suggessit, in arbitrio Mosis fore, ut ipsis ea pars distribuatur. Portio enim legislatoris vocatur, de qua jure potuit Moses decernere: sicuti eam non te- mere, nec aliter, quam Dei mandato assignavit Ga- ditis. Portio autem dicitur abscondita, quam Deus in sua promissione complexus non fuerat. Summa est, quamvis nondum patefacta esset Dei voluntas, quoad illam terræ accessionem: tamen oc- culta ejus liberalitate potitos esse. Atq; ita ratum vult Moses esse suum decretum, ut Gaditæ trans Jor- danem maneant, alioqui moveri poterat contro- versia: quia Dei promissio fines toti populo assigna- verat in citeriori ripa.

QUI FUIT CUM PRINCIPIBUS POPULI ET FECIT JUSTITIAS DOMINI ET JUDI- CIUM SUUM CUM ISRAELE.

De his ita Vatablus: Et veniet & cum principi- bus populi & faciet justitiam Domini atque judicia ejus cum Israele. Non habitabit autem illic, antequam ve- niat una cum Principibus ad subjugandam terram, quam Dominus est pollicitus fratribus ejus Israeli- tis, ut faciat justitiam & judicium Dei cum ipsis, i. e. ut quemadmodum illi præceperat Dominus, ut face- ret cum fratribus, faceret. Præceperat autem illi Do- minus, ut comitaretur fratres suos in terram san- ctam, & juvaret eos in debellandis Cananæis, quod se facturum receperat. Facere igitur justitiam & judi- cium Domini, est facere quod Deus præcepit, & ut Deo promisimus nos facturos. Sic etiam Calvinus: qui addit, justitiam hic dici non tantum, quia æquum erat bellare cum fratribus, & adjutores esse ad terram acquirendam, sed quia de profanis & impiis gentibus vindictam suam exequi statuerat Deus per totum Israe- lem, & communiter omnes tribus elegerat judicii sui ministras. Similiter Cornel. a Lapide: QUI FUIT CUM PRINCIPIBUS POPULI. I. e. cum Princi- pibus novem tribuum, cum scilicet in transitu Jorda- nis Gaditæ præcesserunt cæteras tribus in acie ad ex- pugnandum Chananæos, sicuti jusserat Moses, ipsi que ei promiserant: itaque Gad fecit justitias Domi- ni & judicium suum cum Israel, id est, fecit Gad id quod ex pacto & officio suo erga Deum, & erga con- tribules suos Israelites facere debuit. Postrema ver- ba ita etiam intelligi poterunt, quod Gaditæ etsi in terra Og & Sehon suas habituri ditiones, tamen leges & judicia observaturi sint æque ac reliquæ tribus Is- raelis trans Jordanem. Osiander hunc tradit sen- sum horum & præcedentium verborum: Et vide- principatum suum, quod in parte sua Doctor esset repo- situs, in Ebr. opertus, seu absconditus: id est, Huic tri- bui dabitur excellens Gubernator, (sed spiritualis) nempe Elias Thesbites, de civibus Galaad: fuit e- nim Galaad pars ejus regionis, quæ in divisione ter- ræ cessit tribui Gad, teste Josua c. 13.) Is erit Doctor, (veræ religionis) sed opertus, seu absconditus, nempe ad tempus quasi latitans: cum prædixisset sterilita- tem: & cogeretur totum pene triennium conspe- ctum Regis Ahab declinare. Is postea coram Re- ge Ahab, convocatis proceribus regni, & toto po- pulo, imprimis vero collectis & congregatis Sacer- dotibus Baaliticis ingenti miraculo ignem precibus suis de cælo devocans, qui absumsit istius holocau- stum, restituit apud electos veram Dei agnitionem, & religionem in populo Israelitico 2. Reg. 17, 18. hoc enim vere fuit facere justitias Domini, & judicium suum cum Israel: etiamsi hæc Ecclesiæ restauratio non admodum diu duravit. B. Lutherus totam benedictionem de Gad ad tempora Jehu refert: Et Gad ait, Benedictus dilatator Gad, quia sicut leo habi- tat, rapuitque brachium & verticem, (hoc mihi rex Jehu videtur implesse, qui fecit pietati locum, abo- litis Baalitis, & perrupit quasi leo fortiter cæsis etiam duobus regibus, quasi brachio & vertice) & vidit principium suum, quod ibi portio Doctoris reposita es- set (hoc puto dici de bonis Prophetis, qui sub Jehú in suo regno securi erant, ante sub Baalitis fugati, ut sit singulare pro plurali: Portio Doctoris, id est, colle- ctio Doctorum.) Et venit cum principibus populi, & fe- cit justitias Domini & jura ejus cum Israel, quia redu- xit principes & populum ab idololatris illis, unde & laudatus est a Deo. Hæc B. Lutherus: quæ expli- catio non inconcinna est. Et seu hanc Lutheri, seu Osiandricam quis amplecti velit, rectius, nostro ju- dicio, fecerit, quam Vatabli paraphrasin approban- do; quia non de præteritis, sed de futuris agit Moses: nec opus erat de comitatu aliarum tribuum vatici- nari, quum ea conditione terræ circa Jordanem concessæ huic tribui fuerint.

Coccejus postquam exagitavit Belgarum ver- sionem, quia ibi in parte legislatoris erat, noviter ita transtulit, nam ibi est portio legislatoris incrustati, quod ἕυρημα novæ interpretationis ita incrustavit: Per Gad, quod exercitum significat, fideles ea ætate intelligi, quæ superius descriptam insequitur, ceu exercitus agni Dei, tempore prædicati æterni Evangelii Apoc. 14. vers. 6. & annunciati casus Babylonis vers. 8. Dilatationem Gadis inferre, quod Ecclesia fuerit in angustia & parvo numero: vidit principium sibi, id est, parva initia & primitias; cui res fuerit cum capi- tibus populi, in quo erit portio legislatoris incrustati, hoc est, cum Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principi- bus, Magistratibus ejus populi & societatis, cui se admiscuerat Pseudo-Propheta, vel Anti-Christus, ut in eodem populo haberet portionem suam. ET ACCESSIT Ecclesia illa, vel parvus fidelium cœtus CAPITA POPULI, h. e. venit in conspe- ce ctum Principum & Regum in comitiis, ET JU- STITIAM JEHOVÆ FECIT, id fecit, quod Pastorum est, veritatem profitendo, falsitatem con- futando. ET JUDICIA EJUS APUD ISR AE- LEM sunt: propagavit enim judicia Dei ad Israe- lem, h. e. implevit terram cognitione nominis sui. Dilatatus est, & laniavit in regno adversario & brachium & verticem. Hæc ille: quæ tum solida agnoscentur, cum solide probabitur subjectum es- se fideles dictæ ætatis. Nam si quælibet accommo- datio prædicatorum quomodocunque facta suffi- ciat, plura substitui poterunt subjecta. Hic de tribu Gad vaticinium est, non de fidelibus Nov. Test. A- lioquin B. Lutherum leonina fortitudine aggres- sum Anti-Christum Romanum ac stetisse coram capitibus populi in publicis comitiis, fecisse justi- tiam Jehovæ (si de eo, non de Zvvinglio suo hæc intellecta velit Coccejus) res certissima. Sed hic vel Anti-Christum voce legislatoris notatum esse, vel B. Lutherum imagine leonis adumbratum, cum parastatis suis fidelibus, nemo hactenus videre po- tuit, nec facile quisquam credo, videbit, etiamsi perspicillo Cocceji utatur.

## 33:22
V. 22. DAN IS A LION'S CUB HE SHALL FLOW LARGELY FROM BASHAN.

In Hebrew: he shall leap down, as the Septuagint, Vatablus, Cajetan render HE SHALL LEAP. Dan shall be like a lion's cub, by reason of magnanimity and fortitude, he shall leap down from Bashan, like the strongest lions, which are in the region of Bashan, he shall rush upon his enemies. Which is predicted generally about the fortitude of the tribe, as Vatablus noted. He shall be like a lion's cub, which leaps forth from Bashan. In Bashan were the strongest lions. For he says that Dan will be most strong, like the lions of Bashan, and most warlike: yet he could have looked to certain special specimens of fortitude; and thus Samson, who was born from the tribe of Dan, according to Osiander, fulfilled this prophecy. Cf. Gen. 49, 17. For with heroic and truly leonine fortitude he leaped down upon the Philistine enemies. Thus also the Danites rushed suddenly into Laish Jud. 18, 7. 27. Whence Luth. Dan is a Lion's cub, (because they fought bravely against Laish, f. Lesem) shall flow from Bashan, that is, they shall flourish from the city of Dan even unto Bashan. Corn. a Lap. with the Vulgate and the Chaldean, following Lyranus and Cajetan, interprets it thus in the latter part: that in Dan is the origin of the most famous river Jordan, which makes the whole of Bashan fertile, but this is cold. Abarbanel notes an ancient tradition that by the lion's whelp the Messiah is signified, whose father was to be from Judah, and his mother from the tribe of Dan. But this, in the judgment of Cocceius, is a fiction of Satan, by which he mocked Scripture. Cocceius understands it of the age of the Church, which, after the struggle with the Anti-Christ and its expansion, experienced chastisement, and he says it is compared to a lion's whelp because of its constancy and fortitude, a lion's whelp leaping forth from Bashan, which, having been expelled from its seats and camps, leaps forth into the fields subject to it on account of flight and exile from its own places. But this is a mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις.

Latin:

V. 22. DAN CATULUS LEONIS FLUET LARGITER DE BASAN.

In Ebræo: desiliet, uti Septuag. Vatabl. Cajeta- nus reddunt SALTABIT. Dan erit instar Catuli leonis, ratione magnanimitatis & fortitudinis, de- siliet de Basan, instar leonum fortissimorum, qui in re- gione Basan sunt, irruet in hostes suos. Quod ge- neraliter de fortitudine tribus prædictum, ut Vata- blus notavit. Erit sicut Catulus leonis, qui prosilit è Basan. In Basan erant fortissimi leones. Dicit enim Dan futurum fortissimum, ut leones Basan, & belli- cosissimum:respicere tamen potuit ad specialia quæ- dam simul fortitudinis specimina; atque ita hoc va- ticinium Simson oriundus ex tribu Dan,secundum Osiandrum,implevit. Conf. Gen. 49,17. Heroica enim & vere leonina fortitudine desiliit in hostes Philisthæos. Sic etiam irruerunt Danitæ subito in Lais Jud. 18,7. 27. Unde Luth. Dan Catulus Leonis, (quia fortiter pugnarunt contra Lais, f. Lesem) fluet de Basan, id est, florebunt ex civitate Dan usǫ in Ba- san. Corn. a Lap. cum Vulg. & Chald. præeunte Lyran. & Cajetan. ita in posteriori parte interpreta- tur: quod in Dan sit origo celeberrimi fluvii Jordanis fœcundantis totam Basanitidem, sed hoc frigidum est. Abarbenel notat vetustam traditionem per ca- tulum leonis notari Messiam, cujus Pater ex Juda,ma- ter ex tribu Dan futura sit. At hoc, Coccejo judice,Sa- tanæ est commentum, quo irrisit Scripturam. Coc- cejus de ætate Ecclesiæ, quæ post dimicationem cum An- ti-Christo, & dilatationem experta est castigationem, intelligit, eamque comparari catulo leonis ait, pro- pter constantiam & fortitudinem, catulo leonis prosi- lienti ex Basan, qui ex suis sedibus & castris expulsus in campos sibi subjectos prosilit ob fugam & exilium ex lo- cis suis. Sed hæc mera ἰδία ἐπίλυσις.

## 33:23
Vers. 23. NEPHTHALI SHALL ENJOY ABUNDANCE) Symmachus to the Hebrew more expressively πλησμονὴ ἐὐδοκίας. It is the same as that which follows, full of blessing. For the Hebrews love to display a copiousness of words in a language that is sufficiently needy.

These things are rightly said. In Hebrew, he shall enjoy an abundance of good pleasure, i. e., he shall abound in those things in which he will take delight. Oleaster, he shall be free, he shall do what he wishes, like a hind let loose, as Jacob says in Gen. 49, 21.) God will bless him with every kind of happiness. HE SHALL POSSESS THE SEA AND THE SOUTH, his region extends towards the west to the sea, and to the southern region, as Osiander holds. Others: merchandise and wealth will be brought to the Nephthalites from the south and from the west.

For the Naphtalites were bordering on the Phoenicians, that is, the Tyrians and Sidonians, whence they could easily obtain the merchandise of the whole world from them. If this explanation is accepted, the exception of Cocceius §. 1692 from Josh. 19:34 falls into a sponge, where it is said that the border of the land of Naphtali touched Zebulun to the south, and Asher from the west, and the Jordan from the east. How can he who possesses the northern boundary of the holy land, and has neighboring tribes to the east and west, where the sea is, be said to possess the west and the south? Yet Cocceius himself meets this exception against Calvin's explanation in this way: unless perhaps the learned interpreter meant this: It is hinted in the place of Joshua 19 that Naphtali possessed the Sea of Tiberias with other tribes, and through the convenience of the Jordan, he ought to have valued Judah and the sanctuary to the south as his inheritance. The Targum and R. Solomon refer it to the fact that the Sea of Tiberias fell into his portion, where they could fish in every direction, even to the south. B. Luther thus: he will possess the sea and the south: namely, the south of the Galilean sea. Cocceius renders: Naphtali satisfied with thanks, and full of the blessing of Jehovah, shall inherit the sea and the south. He says to note that he draws 'thanks' to the forgiveness of sins, or the removal of the cup of wrath, or the chastisement of the Church, and the fullness of blessing to his own age (he published these things in the year 1650). There is indeed, he says, a people in the world who, now that the disturbances are, as it seems, quieting down, are bound to acknowledge that a light has risen upon them, Isa. 61:2, and following, wonderfully vindicated, and wonderfully increased with the goods of the kingdom of God and temporal things, and with men, if things remain in the same state, and thus we can now say that God is moved with repentance over his servants, Deut. 32:36. The rest, 'inherit the sea and the south,' he takes as an exhortation, not a prophecy or blessing, and considers it to be like a commentary on Isa. ch. 60, after the trampling and liberation of the Church described in Isa. ch. 59. But as for the designation of the sea or the west, and the south, which regions, he says §. 1691, are given to the Church as the firstfruits of the inheritance, one must not guess; just look at Isa. 60:9, 'The ships of the ocean at the beginning.' Meanwhile, from the analogy of what follows, he deduces that an amplification of the Church is promised, either towards the west, or from the sea, or from the south, until it possesses the strongholds of the earth. There is need of an Oedipus or a Delian augur for the man's enigma to be understood. We do not wish to guess that. In Moses and the Prophets, he places I know not what Sibylline leaves and Oedipus's riddles. If Cocceius still survives, he will be able to explain what those last words of Moses and the fullness of Naphtali's blessing contribute to the movements of the nearest times in Belgium, and England, and other shores of the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NEPHTHALI ABVNDANTIA PERFRVE- TVR) Symmachus ad Hebræum expressius πλησμονὴ ἐὐδο- κίας. Idem est cum eo quod sequitur plenus benedictione. Amant enim Hebræi oftentare verborum copiam in lingua satis inope.

Recte hæc dicuntur. In Ebr. abundantia bene- placiti perfruetur, i. e. quibus rebus delectabitur, iis abundabit. Oleaster, liber erit, faciet, quod volet, quasi cerva emissa, ut ait Jacob Gen. 49, 21.) Deus omnis generis felicitate eum beabit. MARE ET MERIDIEM POSSIDEBIT, regio ipsius ad occa- sum versus mare, & ad meridianam plagam se ex- tendit, ut habet Osiand. Alii: ad Nephthalitas mer- ces & opes advehentur ex meridie, & ex occidente.

Nam Naphthalitæ erant conterminæ Phœnicibus, puta Tyriis, Sydoniis, unde ab iis totius orbis mer- ces facile habere poterant. Quæ explicatio si ac- cipiatur, in spongiam incumbit exceptio Cocceji §. 1692. e Jos. 19, 34. ubi dicitur quòd limes terræ Naphthali tetigerit Zabulonem ad meridiem, & Asse- rem ab occasu & Jordanem ab ortu. Quomodo is qui possidet terræ sanctæ terminum septentrionalem, & ab ortu atque occasu, ubi est mare, vicinas tribus habet, possit dici possidere occasum & meridiem? Cui tamen exceptioni adversus Calvini explicationem Cocce- jus ipse ita occurrit: nisi forte hoc voluit doctus inter- pres: Innui in loco Josuæ 19. quod Naphthali mare Ti- beriadis cum aliis tribubus possederit, & per opportuni- tatem Jordanis Judam & sanctuarium, ad meridiem, pro sua hæreditate æstimare debuerit. Targum & R. Salomo eo referunt, quod mare Tiberiadis ceciderit in parte ejus, ubi quaquaversum, etiam ad meridiem po- tuerint piscari. B. Luther. ita: mare & meridiem pos- sidebit: meridiem scilicet maris Galilæi. Coccejus reddit: Naphthali satur gratia, & plenus benedictio- ne Jehova, mare & meridiem hæreditabit. Gratiam, notare, ait, condonationem peccatorum, seu ablationem calicis iræ, vel castigationis Ecclesiæ, & plenitudinem benedictionis ad suam ætatem (edidit autem hæc an- no 1650.) trahit. Est sane, inquit, in mundo populus, qui jam consilescentibus, ut videtur, turbis, teneatur agnoscere, super se lucem exortam esse Es. 61, 2. seq. mi- rabiliter vindicatum, & bonis regni Dei & temporali- bus, & hominibus mirifice auctum, si maneant res in eodem statu, sicque jam possumus dicere, Deum pœni- tudine affici super servis suis Deut. 32, 36. Cætera, mare & meridiem hæredita, pro adhortatione, non vaticinio, aut benedictione habet, & commentarii in- star esse c. 60. Es. censet, post conculcationem & li- berationem Ecclesiæ c. 59. Esa. descriptam. Quod autem attinet designationem maris sive occidentis, & meridiei, quæ regiones, inquit §. 1691. ut primitiæ hære- ditatis dantur Ecclesiæ, non licet hariolari; tantum in- spice Es. 60, 9. Naves oceani initio. Interim ex a- nalogia subsequentium deducit, promitti Ecclesiæ amplificationem primo vel versus occasum, vel a mari, vel a meridie, donec possideat arces terræ. Oedi- po, vel Delio augure opus, ut ænigma viri intelliga- tur. Nos id ariolari nolumus. In Mose & Pro- phetis nescio quæ folia Sibyllæ & ænigmata Oedipi locat. Si adhuc superat Coccejus, quid ad proxi- morum temporum motus in Belgio, & Anglia, aliis- que Ecclesiæ oris conferant illa ultima Mosis, & ple- nitudo benedictionis Nephthali cæ, edisserere poterit.

## 33:24
Vers. 24.

BLESSED AMONG THE SONS OF ASHER. Calvin understands this concerning a blessing above the sons, as if there were a comparison between him and the remaining tribes. But it is more correctly explained concerning fertility, he will be enriched by the Lord with much offspring. HE SHALL BE, or rather he will be, PLEASING TO HIS BRETHREN. He will be in singular favor among the Israelites. AND HE SHALL DIP HIS FOOT IN OIL, he will abound in the fatness of the land itself: he will be fertile in grain and oil. He would sit in a real fat-pit. Oil will be most cheap in his country because of the abundance, so that he even washes his feet in it, as Vatablus has it. IRON AND BRASS HIS SHOE, i. e. fortified with iron and brass, he will bravely, where there is need, engage in battle with enemies, as Osiander has it. Simpler seems the explanation of Vatablus: Thy shoes, i. e. thy shoeing, an instrument for action, as if to say, whatever thou shalt tread with thy shoes, will be iron and brass. But it is a Hebraism

for in thy region there will be metals of iron and brass. Thus also Calvin and Junius wished to denote an abundance of richer things, of iron and of brass, because of the mines. Conf. Gen. 49:11, succinctly with Luther, Castellio: Asher rich in offspring, dear to his brethren, abounding in oil, iron, and brass.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

BENEDICTUS IN FILIIS ASER. Id de benedictione præ filiis, quasi compara- tio sit inter illam & reliquos tribus intelligit Calvi- nus. Sed rectius de πολυτεκνίᾳ explicatur, multa sobole a Domino ditabitur. SIT, vel potius erit PLACENS FRATRIBUS SUIS. Erit in singula- ri gratia apud Israelites. ET TINGET IN OLEO PEDEM SUUM, abundabit pinguedine terræ ipsius: erit ferax frumenti, & olei. Er würde in einer rechten Schmalz-Gruben sitzen. Erit oleum vilis- simum in patria ejus præ abundantia, ita ut etiam in eo lavet pedes, ut Vatablus habet. FERRUM ET ÆS CALCEAMENTUM EJUS, i. e. ferro & ære mu- nitus, fortiter, ubi opus erit, capesset pugnam cum ho- stibus, ut habet Osiander. Simplicior videtur Va- tabli explicatio: Calceamenta tua, i. e. calceatio tua, instrumentum pro actione, q. d. quicquid calcabis cal- ceamentis tuis, erit ferrum & æs. Est autem Hebraism9

pro in regione tua erunt metalla ferri, & æris. Sic et- iam Calvin. & Junius, copiam rerum pinguiorum, ferri, atque æris, ob fodinas denotari voluit. Conf. Gen. 49, 11. succincte cum Luthero, Castellio: Aser progenie dives, fratribus charus, oleo, ferro, ære abundans.

## 33:25
Vers. 25.

AS THE DAYS OF THY YOUTH, SO ALSO THY OLD AGE) He took indeed דבא for דוא from זוב, which is to flow. The days of flow are old age. The Greeks, 'as thy days, thy strength,' that is, the longer this tribe shall last, the more powerful it will become. This agrees with the Hebrew, which we have. Others read דבריך, thy fame. Others דבעך for צבעך, thy colors. The Greek interpretation is the best.

He invents distinct readings because Grotius found diverse interpretations. But it is viciously concluded from the diversity of interpretations to a variety of reading. For there can be various causes for a variety of interpretation. Most people explain the Vulgate thus with B. Luther: As the days of thy youth are peaceful, flourishing, and robust, so also thy old age will be peaceful, flourishing, and robust. Vatablus: Heb. 'and according to thy days will be thy strength': a Hebrew phrase; for, as long as thou shalt live, thou shalt be strong: thy strength will last as long as thou shalt live. Others apply it to the men in this tribe: Thy citizens will have firm bodies, even in old age no less than in youth. Junius renders: as long as thy days shall last, there will be talk about thee, that is, the praise of thy soil commends thy name forever. Castellio translated: Strength according to the proportion of age: that the same place of age which Asher held among his brethren, his descendants may obtain the same of strength among the tribes. That sense is to be preferred, which Grotius followed, concerning the increase of the citizens of the tribe in later ages. Cocceius §. 1694 thinks these things, which were predicted about Asher, concern the Church having a similar situation to Asher, which was also the last towards the north, with the tribe of Naphtali, and partly the colony of Dan, and half the tribe of Manasseh, so that Asher dwelt to the west, and on the shore of the great sea, Naphtali to the east of the Jordan on Mount Bashan. He thinks the Church of the last time restored to its former place, and the Nurse of peoples, is denoted. Which (1) is declared blessed above the sons, because it sees Christ in the kingdom, the victor of his enemies. (2) To whom he wishes the favor of the brethren with the abolition of their discord and aversion. (3) The abundance of the olive of earthly fruits, but more so of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. (4) The strength of the gates. Iron and bronze shall be your footwear. (5) The perpetuity of speech; so that your days may be your speech. Which exposition of the same verse is of a piece with the preceding ones, that is to say, equally precarious and merely arbitrary: not to say frivolous and rash. He refers these to the last times, or to the seventh period of the Church, as he himself calls it. For he reduces everything to seven periods, by a frivolous and utterly inept μεταμόρφοσις of the seven Asian Churches of the same time in which St. John lived, Apoc. ch. II & III, into seven periods of different times, from the beginning of the New Testament to the end of the age, which is the slippery, nay, false foundation that Cocceius has placed under his wonderful interpretation of the Mosaic blessings.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

SICVT DIES JVVENTVTIS TVÆ, ITA ET SE- NECTVS TVA) Sumsit nempe דבא pro דוא a זוב, quod est fluo. Dies fluxus sunt senectus. Græci, ὡς αἱ ἡμέραι σου ἡ ἰσχύς σου, id est, quo diutius durabit tribus ista, eo fiet va- lentior. Congruit hoc Hebræo, quod habemus. Alii le- gerunt דבריך fama tua. Alii דבעך pro צבעך colores tui. Optima est interpretatio Græca.

Distinctas lectiones fingit, quia diversas inter- pretationes invenit Grotius. Sed a diversitate in- terpretationum ad varietatem lectionis vitiose con- cluditur. Variæ enim causæ possunt esse varietati interpretationis. Vulgatam ita explicant cum B. Luthero plerique: Sicut dies juventutis tuæ placidi, floridi, & robusti sunt, ita & senectus tua erit placida, florida, & robusta. Vatablus: Hebr. & juxta dies tuos erit fortitudo tua: Hebraica phrasis; pro, quam- diu vixeris, eris fortis: vires tuæ tam diu durabunt, quamdiu vives. Alii hominibus applicant in hac tribu: Cives tui habebunt corpora firma, etiam in sene- Etute non minus, quam in juventute. Junius reddit: quamdiu durabunt dies tui, sermones habentur de te, id est, laus soli tui commendat nomen tuum in perpe- tuum. Castellio transtulit: Vires pro ætatis ratione: ut quem locum ætatis Aser inter fratres habuit, eun- dem ejus posteri fortitudinis obtineant in tribubus. Præferendus sensus ille, quem sequutus est Grotius, de incremento civium tribus, in posterioribus æta- tibus. Coccejus §. 1694. putat hæc, quæ de Ascher prædicta, concernere Ecclesiam parilem situm cum A- scher habentem, quæ & ultima fuerit ad septentrionem, cum tribu Naphthali, & partim colonia Dan, & dimi- dia tribu Manasse, ita ut Aschar ad occidentem, & in littore maris magni, Naphthali ad orientem Jordanis in monte Basan habitaverit. Ecclesiam autem ulti- mi temporis restitutam in pristinum locum, & Altri- cem populorum denotari putat. Quæ (1) benedicta prædicetur præ filiis, quod Christum videat in regno, victorem hostium suorum. (2) Cui optet gratiam fratrum cum abolitione dissidii & aversionis eorum. (3) Abundantiam oleæ fructuum terrenorum, magis au- tem charismatum S. S. (4) Fortitudinem portarum. Ferrum & æs calceamentum tuum. (5) Perpetui- tatem loquelæ; ut dies tui loqui tuum. Quæ expositio ejusdem commatis est cum superioribus, h. e. æque precaria ac mere arbitraria: ne dicam frivolam & temerariam. Ad ultima tempora hæc refert, vel ad Ecclesiæ septimam, quam vocat ipse, periodum. Omnia enim ad septem periodos revocat, e frivola, & perquam inepta μεταμορφόσει septem Asiatica- rum Ecclesiarum ejusdem temporis, quo S. Johan- nes vixit, Apoc. II. & III. capp. in septem periodos diversorum temporum, inde ab initio N. T. ad fi- nem seculi, quod lubricum, imo falsum fundamen- tum suo mirabili benedictionum Mosaicarum in- terpretamento supposuit Coccejus.

## 33:26
V. 26. THERE IS NO OTHER GOD, EXCEPT THE GOD OF THE MOST UPRIGHT.

Jeschurum, as above, which is the name of the Israelite people. Having finished the blessings, he celebrates God, the fountain of every blessing. THE RIDER, or rather the dweller of heaven, the Lord of heaven, whose seat is heaven, IS THY HELPER, or may He be, O Israel, HIS MAGNIFICENCE RIDES UPON THE CLOUDS. Heb. And in his magnificence are the clouds, i.e., his glory and majesty are seen in the clouds and tempests. Blessed Luther: who shows his majesty by his thunder. Cocceius wishes it to be understood of Christ sitting in the heavens after his ascension with his exaltation to bring help to the Church, but without solid reason. This explanation is Vatable's; and his magnificence rides the clouds: as if to say, there is no God like your God: for your God inhabits heaven, whence he brings you help. He ascends the clouds and sits there, that he may hasten to bring you help. But the former explanation is simpler.

Latin:

V. 26. NON EST DEUS ALIUS, NISI DEUS RECTISSIMI.

Jeschurum, ut supra, quod nomen populi est Israelitici. Absolutis benedictionibus celebrat Deum omnis benedictionis fontem. ASCEN- SOR, vel potius insessor cæli, Dominus cæli, cu- jus sedes est cælum, AUXILIATOR TUUS est, vel sit, o Israel, MAGNIFICENTIA EJUS SDICURRUNT NUBES. Ebr. Et in ma- gnificentiam ejus sunt nubes i, e. gloria & majestas e- jus conspicitur in nubibus & tempestatibus. B. Lu- therus: qui tonitru suo ostendit majestatem suam. De Christo in cœlis sedente post ascensionem cum elatione sua ad opem ferendam Ecclesiæ intelligi vult Coccejus, sed sine solida ratione. Vatabli hæc explicatio est; & magnificentia sua nubes subequitat: q. d. non est Deus similis Deo tuo: nam Deus tuus habitat cœlum, unde tibi fert opem. Nubes conscendit & illic in- sidet, ut properet ad opem tibi ferendam. Sed simplicior est prior explicatio.

## 33:27
Vers. 27. HIS DWELLING PLACE [IS] ABOVE) The true sense is: His refuge is the eternal God. מעונה σκεπάσον σε: the Greeks are right. For elsewhere they translate the noun, מעון, מעונ or מעונה, as refuge. אלהי קדם, not the beginning god, but the ancient God, as perhaps the LXX wrote. The word קדם is translated before the ages in Psalm 55:20 and elsewhere: for the Hebrews do not have a proper word by which to express eternity: therefore they use translation or circumlocution. Thus God is called עתיק יומין in Daniel 7, and there are many others of that form.

In Hebrew, it is a word that denotes an eye and a fountain. The Vulgate renders it eye. Osiander explains it thus: The eye of Jacob [shall be] upon a land of corn and wine (he will look back at, or will gaze upon it with pleasure, as being fertile in corn and wine. Similarly Castalio, let him see the fertile land, and let him possess it: for to see is put for to possess) and his heavens SHALL DROP down dew: the abundance of dew will aid and increase fertility. Vatable rendered it as fountain, with this explanation added: by apposition he calls Israel the fountain of Jacob and his offspring, as if to say, the Israelite people, who are as it were a stream drawn from Jacob, who is the fountain. But this is forced: however, the former interpretation flows best, which Luther also embraces: therefore Israel shall dwell secure, alone, and the eye of Jacob shall be upon a land of corn and must (that is, he will take delight in a fertile land) for his heaven shall drop down dew, so that it may make it fruitful. Cornelius also followed it.

Cocceius translated: And Israel dwells securely apart (at) the fountain of Jacob in a land of corn and must, and his heavens drop down dew. He joined the words dwelling at the fountain of Jacob, because the accent Zakeph katon with the preceding Paschta does not allow these words En Jaakob to be torn away from the preceding ones: he calls the fountain of Jacob the fountain of salvation in Isaiah 12:3. Although he also does not deny that by the fountain of Jacob his carnal seed is understood from Isaiah 51:1, in this way, Israel shall dwell at the fountain of Jacob, i.e., he will obtain and occupy the seed of Jacob, who had long been separated from the tribes of Israel: applying this to the reassumption of the Jews, and still expecting the fulfillment of these things: but after great distress. But by what right will these things be drawn to the last times, and the conversion of the Jews under the New Testament? If, however, they are to be understood spiritually, our people, with Osiander, do not deny that the dew of the Gospel is signified, moistening and refreshing the hearts of believers, whence from faith they bring forth abundant fruit of good works.

Some render the Hebrew text thus: The dwelling place of God is antiquity, that is, eternity, with Cajetan. Others [understand it] of the clouds and the ether: Which are the dwelling place of God from of old: as Blessed Luther: That is the dwelling of God from the beginning, Junius, Protection as the eternal God. The Grotian interpretation is not displeasing. Cocceius is almost similar: The dwelling and place of the Church's mansion is God before, or God, who is before all things. In the same sense he says God is called a rock in Psalm 90:1, 91:9, and 71:3, be to me a rock of habitation: and to the Hebrews מקום is a place. Thus also the other part agrees: AND UNDERNEATH ARE THE EVERLASTING ARMS. In Hebrew, And underneath the arms of the age, because the refuge of the Church is also underneath the eternal arms. Therefore, Cocceius notes not badly that the support is not only of power, but also the embrace of grace, and carrying in the bosom. Similarly Oleaster: God was your dwelling place from eternity, and he embraces you with eternal arms. Junius in almost the same way: underneath are the arms, or everlasting omnipotence, as if to say, above and below you have him as a protector: to which Vatable's explanation is twin, (that) God is the eternal dwelling place: and underneath are the everlasting arms, i.e., indefatigable, as if to say, the eternal God protects his people, just as a hut defends its inhabitants from the injury of the sky: underneath the Israelite people are indefatigable arms. From head to foot the Lord diligently guards the whole of Israel. In the latter member Osiander agrees, although he renders the former a little differently: God has always dwelt, dwells, and will dwell in his people, and with his arms he will kindly embrace, and will always defend. Blessed Luther explains it thus: Although he dwells in the heavens, yet his arms rule in the world, that he may deliver his own. Which is also the exposition of Castalio: Although he dwells in the heavens, he does not however so despise earthly things that he does not always lower his arms to the earth, that is, that he is not present to the Israelites, and having driven out their enemies, places them in safety. Cajetan's gloss is foreign and discordant: Underneath him are the arms and durations of each age, whether they be the powers of angels, or of celestial bodies, or of inferior ones. Under God, and the eternity of God, are the angels, or the heavens, which are as it were the everlasting arms of God.

Latin:

Vers. 27. HABITACVLVM EJVS SVRSVM) Verus sensus est: Refugium ejus Deus æternus. מעונה σκεπάσον σε: bene Græci. Nam & alibi nomen, מעון, מעונ sive מעונה vertunt καταφυγή. אלהי קדם, non θεο̄ ἀρχὴ, sed θεὸς ἀρχαῑος, quomodo forte scripserunt LXX. Vox קדם vertitur πρὸ αἰώνων Psal. 55,20. & alibi: nam Hebræi vocem propriam non habent, qua æternitatem exprimant: itaque translatione aut circumlocutione utuntur. Sic Deus dicitur עתיק יומין Dan. 7. multaque sunt alia ad eam formam.

In Ebr. Vox est, quæ oculum, & fontem notat. Vulgata oculum reddit. Quod sic explicat Osian- der: Oculus Jacob in terram frumenti & vini (respi- ciet, vel intuebitur eam cum voluptate, ceu feracem frumenti atque vini. Similitet Castallio, terra fe- racem videat, & ea potiatur: nam videre pro potiri ponitur) cœlique STILLABUNT rore: abundan- tia roris fertilitatem adjuvabit & augebit. Vata- blus per fontem reddidit, hac addita explicatione: per appositionem vocat Israelem fontem Jacob & pro- geniem, q. d. populus Israeliticus, qui est velut rivulus deductus a Jacob, qui est fons. Sed hoc coactum est: Optime autem fluit prior interpretatio, quam etiam amplectitur Lutherus: ideo habitabit Israel securus, solus, & oculus Jacob erit in terra frumenti & mu- sti (id est, delectabitur in terra fertili) cælum enim ejus stillabit rore, sic ut fœcundet eam. Eam sequu- tus etiam est Cornelius.

Coccejus transtulit: Et habitat Israel secure seor- sim (apud) fontem Jacobi in terra frumenti & musti, & cæli ejus stillant rore. Conjuncxit voces habitans fontem Jacobi, quia accentus Zakeph katon præcedente Paschta non patitur, ut verba hæc En Jaakob a præce- dentibus divellantur: Fontem Jacob dicit fontem sa- lutis Es. 12, 3. Quanquam etiam non abnuat, per fontem Jacobi semen ejus carnale intelligi ex Es. 51, 1. hoc modo, Israel habitabit fontem Jacobi, h. e. obti- nebit, & occupabit semen Jacobi, qui ab Israelis tri- bubus separati erant dudum: applicans hoc ad reas- sumtionem Judæorum, & complementum horum ad- huc expectans: sed post angustiam magnam. Sed quo jure hæc trahentur ad novissima tempora, & conversionem Judæorum sub N. Testamento? Si ta- men spiritualiter intelligenda, non abnuunt Nostri, cum Osiandro, significari rorem Evangelii,humectan- tis ac recreantis corda credentium, unde ex fide copio- sum fructum bonorum proferunt.

Ebræum textum nonnulli sic reddunt: Habi- taculum Dei est antiquitas, id est, æternitas, cum Ca- jetano. Alii de nubibus & æthere: Quæ sunt habi- taculum Dei ab antiquo: uti B. Lutherus: Das ist die Wohnung Gottes von Anfang, Junius, Prote- ctio ut Deus sempiternus. Non displicet interpre- tatio Grotiana. Similiter fere Coccejus: Habita- culum & locus mansionis Ecclesiæ est Deus ante, sive Deus, qui ante omnia est. Eodem sensu Deum pe- tram dici ait Ps. 90,1. 91,9. & 71, 3. esto mihi in petram mansionis: & Ebræis מקום locum. Sic etiam con- gruit alterum: ET SUBTER BRACHIA SEMPI- TERNA. In Ebr. Et subter brachia seculi, quod re- fugium Ecclesiæ etiam sit subter æterna brachia. Notari ergo non male notat Coccejus sustentationem non tantum potentiæ, sed etiam gratiæ amplexum, & gestationem in sinu. Similiter Oleaster: Deus fuit habitaculum tuum ab æterno, & æternis te complecti- tur brachiis. Junius fere eodem modo: inferne brachia, vel omnipotentia sempiterna, q. d. supra & infra habeas eum protectorem: cui gemina est Vatabli explicatio, (ut) habitaculum est Deus æternus: & subter brachia sempiterna, i. e. infatigabilia, q. d. Deus æternus protegit populum suum, velut tugurium de- fendit habitatores suos ab injuria cæli: sub populo Is- raelitico sunt brachia infatigabilia. A vertice ad caleem diligenter custodit totum Israelem Dominus. In posteriori membro consonat Osiander, etsi prius paulo aliter reddat: Deus semper habitavit, habitat, & habitabit in populo suo, & cum brachiis suis beni- gne complectetur, atque semper defendet. B. Luthe- rus sic exponit: Licet in cœlis habitet, tamen brachia ejus dominantur in mundo, ut sua liberet. Quæ etiam est ἔκθεσις Castellionis: Quamvis in cœlis habitet, non tamen ita terrena despicit, ut non in terram sua semper brachia demittat, id est, ut non Israelitis adsit, eorumque hostibus exactis eos in tuto collocet. Alie- na & absona est Cajetani glossa: Subter eum sunt bra- chia & durationes cujusque seculi, sive sint vires ange- lorum, sive corporum cælestium, sive inferiorum. Sub Deo, & Dei æternitate sunt angeli, vel cæli, qui quasi brachia Dei sunt sempiterna.

## 33:27
vers. eod. HE SHALL CAST OUT THE ENEMY FROM BEFORE THEE, AND SHALL SAY, DESTROY.

In Hebrew it is, crush. To which Cornelius wrongly prefers the Vulgate, even though the Chaldean and the LXX favor him. For these did not always render it word for word. The sense in the source is plain: Crush, destroy, or rout, O Israel, your enemies: for with God to speak is to act.

author. Concerning the sword of the Messiah Ps. 45, 4. Concerning the triumph in that glorious one Hos. 13, 4. 1. Cor. 15, 55.

Verse of the same.

Latin:

vers. eod. EJICIET A FACIE TUA INIMICUM, DI- CETQUE CONTERERE.

In Ebr. est, contere. Cui male præfert Cornelius Vulgatam, etsi Chald. & LXX. ei faveant. Hi enim katὰ πόδα non semper reddidere. Planus est in fonte sensus: Contere, perde, vel profliga o Israel ho- stes tuos: nam Dei loqui est facere.

autor. De gladio Messiæ Ps. 45, 4. De triumpho in ipso glorioso Hos. 13, 4. 1. Cor. 15, 55.

Vers. eod.

## 33:28
ISRAEL SHALL DWELL CONFIDENTLY AND ALONE.

With the enemies cast out and routed, he will not be mixed with other nations. Some understand this of the land of Canaan, from which those who could cause him trouble were to be cast out. But it is more correctly taken generally of any enemies whatsoever. Cocceius refers it to peace in the kingdom of Christ, and in his own way compares the passage in Isaiah 2:4.

V. 28. THE EYE OF JACOB [SHALL BE] UPON A LAND OF CORN AND WINE, AND HIS HEAVENS SHALL DROP DOWN DEW.

Latin:

HABITABIT ISRAEL CONFIDENTER ET SOLUS.

Ejectis & profligatis hostibus non admiscebi- tur aliis gentibus. Quod de terra Chanaan, e qua ejiciendi erant, qui ei molestiam exhibere poterant, nonnulli intelligunt. Sed rectius accipitur genera- liter de quibusvis hostibus. Ad pacem in regno Christi refert Coccejus, & suo modo locum Es. 2,4. confert.

V. 28. OCULUS JACOB IN TERRA FRU- MENTI, ET VINI, COELIQUE CALIGA- BUNT RORE.

## 33:29
V. 29. BLESSED ART THOU O ISRAEL, WHO IS LIKE UNTO THEE, O PEOPLE, WHO ART SAVED BY THE LORD? THE SHIELD OF THY HELP, AND THE SWORD OF THY EXCELLENCY.

Osiander rightly explains these things: Blessed are you, O Israel, who is like you in eternal and bodily goods? O people, who are saved in the Lord, whom the Lord will save forever, and in this life also will never forsake. These congratulations pertain to true Israelites, i.e., to those believing in Christ their God, the true Savior (who, namely, were found in those tribes of Israel, lest these things be believed to be said here literally and peculiarly of Christians of a certain time of the New Testament). Christ Himself is God, your Savior, He is the shield of your help, that is, your protector in all adversities: and the sword of your glory. He fights for you, and makes you a victor over death, sin, the devil, hell (and even the world) so that you may be able to triumph gloriously forever. For to be saved in the Lord is to be saved in the Messiah, Hos. 1, 7. He is also the shield and buckler of the faithful, Gen. 15, verse 1, and of our glorious triumph.

Latin:

V. 29. BEATUS ES TU ISRAEL, QUIS SI- MILIS TUI POPULE, QUI SALVARIS IN DOMINO? SCUTUM AUXILII TUI, ET GLADIUS GLORIÆ TUÆ.

Recte hæc explicat Osiander: Beatus es tu Is- rael, quis similis tui est in æternis & corporalibus bo- nis? Popule, qui salvaris in Domino, quem Dominus in æternum salvum faciet, & in hac etiam vita nun- quam deseret. Hæ gratulationes ad veros Israeli- tas, h. e. ad credentes in Christum Deum suum, verum Salvatorem, pertinent (qui scil. in tribubus illis Is- raelis reperti sunt, ne hæc de Christianis certi tempo- ris Novi Testamenti peculiariter ad literam hic di- cta credantur) Ipse Christus Deus est Salvator tuus, est scutum auxilii tui, id est, protector tuus in omnibus adversis: & gladius gloriæ tuæ. Is pro te pugnat, te- que facit victorem mortis, peccati, diaboli, inferni (etiam mundi) ut gloriose queas in æternum trium- phare. Salvari enim in Domino est salvari in Messia Hos. 1, 7. Hic etiam scutum & clypeus fidelium est Gen. 15. vers. 1. & gloriosi triumphi nostri

## 33:29
YOUR ENEMIES SHALL DENY YOU, AND YOU SHALL TRAMPLE UPON THEIR NECKS) In the Hebrew: they shall lie to you, that is, if the subjected peoples break faith, you will tame them.

Others, your enemies shall be deceived, that is, the outcomes will not correspond to their bloody counsels, but they will be divinely frustrated, and will fall void Ps. 2. Corn. a Lapide your enemies shall lie to you, that is, your enemies shall be altogether subjected to you, for this Hebraism signifies this Ps. 80, 16. Ps. 65, 3. Ps. 17, 46. For enemies, when defeated and captured, in order to obtain pardon and favor from the victor, are accustomed to lie much, and to say that they were not truly and from the heart his enemies, and that they did many other things for his favor, thus Cajetan, Vatablus, and others. Castellio, your enemies shall be subjected to you. The Hebrew word, he says, is יכחשו which can be well explained in Greek as σφάλλονται, let them be found succumbing. B. Luther, for thus your enemies shall be wearied: AND YOU SHALL TRAMPLE UPON THEIR HIGH PLACES, that is, you shall trample down all the lofty things in which your enemies place their hope. Vatablus understands by high places the Princes, as if to say you shall trample the neck of the kingdoms of your enemies. Coccejus in his own manner explains: They lie to you, i.e., having denied their hatred, they profess themselves friends of Christ and of the Church. Ps. 18, 45. Ps. 66, 3. Ps. 81. you trample their strongholds, that is, the Gospel is preached everywhere freely, and the Church has a place of free congregation in the land of its enemies Psal. 18, 34. Is. 58, 14. Mic. 1, 3. Am. 4, 13. Hab. 3, 18. But that the universal proclamation of the Gospel is indicated here does not appear. For it is not sound to proceed from the indefinite to the universal. And these things concerning the blessings of Moses. But do you, O Lord, cause us to be saved in you and we shall be blessed. Be the shield of our help, and the sword of our glory. Let your enemies be subjected to you. Cause, however, that you may trample their high places. Amen.

Latin:

NEGABVNT TE INIMICI TUI, ET TU EORUM COLLA CALCABIS) In Hebræo: mentientur tibi, id est, si populi subacti fidem fallant, edomabis eos.

Alii, fallentur inimici tui, id est, non responde- bunt cruentis ipsorum consiliis eventus, sed divini- tus eludentur, & irrita cadent Ps. 2. Corn. a Lapide mentientur tibi inimici tui, id est, omnino subjicientur tibi hostes tui, hoc enim significat, hic Ebraismus Ps. 80, 16. Ps. 65, 3. Ps. 17, 46. Hostes enim devicti & ca- pti, ut a victore veniam & gratiam impetrent, multa mentiri solent, ac dicere, se vere & ex animo ejus non fuisse inimicos, multaque alias in ejus gratiam fecisse, ita Cajetan. Vatabl. & alii. Castellio, tibi subjicientur hostes tui. Verbum Hebræum, inquit, est יכחשו quod Græce bene exponi potest σφάλ- λονται, succumbant inventi. B. Lutherus, sic enim lassabuntur inimici tui: ET TU EORUM EXCEL- SA CALCABIS, id est, sublimia quæq́;, in quibus ho- stes tui spem ponent, dejecta proculcabis. Vatablus per excelsa intelligit Principes, q. d. tu calcabis cervi- cem regnum inimicorum tuorum. Coccejus suo mo- re explicat: Mentiuntur tibi, i. e. abnegato odio suo profitentur se amicos Christi, & Ecclesiæ. Ps. 18, 45. Ps. 66, 3. Ps. 81. arces eorum calcas, id est, Evangelium prædicatur ubique libere, & Ecclesia habet locum li- beræ congregationis in terra hostium suorum Psal. 18, 34. Es. 58, 14. Mich. 1, 3. Am. 4, 13. Hab. 3, 18. Sed universale præconium Evangelii hic indicari non apparet. Non enim ab indefinito ad universale procedere integrum est. Atque hæc de benedi- ctionibus Mosis. Tu autem Domine, fac in te salve- mur & beati erimus. Sis scutum auxilii nostri, & gladius gloriæ nostræ. Subjiciantur tibi inimici tui. Fac autem conculces excelsa eorum. Amen.

## 34:1 Argument
PART IV. THE HISTORICAL [PART] OF DEUTERONOMY. CHAPTER XXXIV.

Moses dies and is mourned, and Joshua is substituted for him. The book is concluded with a divine funeral oration for Moses.

Latin:

PARS IV. DEVTERONOMII ΙΣΤΟΡΙΚΗ. CAPUT XXXIV.

Moritur & deploratur Moses, illique Josua substituitur. Divina Mosis parentatione concluditur liber.

## 34:5 Addition
On chapter 34, verse 5.

AND HE DIED, etc.

This was not written by Moses prophetically, as Jonathan and Philo [thought]; but either by Eleazar, as Ezra [was written by] Ezra: or by Ezra, as others wish, or rather by Joshua, which pleased Mercerus, Bonfrerius, and Menochius after Tostatus. Furthermore, what is added, BY THE COMMAND OF THE LORD, is foolishly snatched up by the Jews, as if, since it is in the Hebrew, AT THE MOUTH OF THE LORD, God by kissing Moses and exhaling his soul had torn it from his body, when the sense is clear, ACCORDING TO THE MOUTH, that is, according to that which God had said, or according to the word of the Lord, as similar phrases indicate, Genesis 43:6, Exodus 23:13 and 34:27, Numbers 9:20 and 13:4 and 27:21, Deuteronomy 17:6, 10, 11, 2 Samuel 13:32, Proverbs 22:6. It is just as foolish as when they invent that Moses buried himself. Concerning which a long fable can be read in Episcopius, book 3, Institutions, chapter 3, page 54. But his own particular error (to touch upon it in passing), that Moses did not clearly know the gracious will of God, nay, did not even apprehend God as the eternal rewarder of those who were to obey his laws, c. 2, l. c., p. 52, does not deserve a refutation.

Latin:

Ad cap. 34. vers. 5.

MORTUUSQUE EST &c.

Non hoc scriptum a Mose prophetice, ut Jo- nathan & Philo; sed vel ab Eleazaro, ut Esdras: vel ab Esdra, ut alii volunt, aut potius a Josua, quod Mercero, Bonfrerio & Menochio post Tostatum pla- cuit. Caeterum quod additur JUBENTE DO- MINO a Judaeis inepte eo abripitur, quasi, cum in Ebraeo sit, AD OS DOMINI, DEUS osculan- do Mosen animam ejus exhalando avulserit a corpore, quum sensus clarus sit, SECUNDUM OS, id est, secundum id, quod dixerat Deus, vel juxta verbum Domini, ut similes phrases indicant, Genes. 43, 6. Exod. 23. vers. 13. & 34. v. 27. Numer. 9. v. 20. & 13, 4. & 27, 21. Deuteronom. 17, 6. 10. 11. 2. Sam. 13.32. Proverb. 22. v. 6. AEque ineptum id est, ac cum fingunt Mosen semetipsum sepelivisse. De quo pro- lixam fabulam legere est apud Episcopium libr. 3. Instit. cap. 3. pag. 54. Cujus vero proprius error (ut obiter id tangam) quod Moses non clare cogno- verit voluntatem Dei gratiosam, imo ne apprehenderit quidem Deum remuneratorem aeternum eorum, qui le- gibus ejus parituri essent c. 2. l. c. p. 52. refuta- tionem non meretur.

## 34:6
Verse 6.

AND HE BURIED HIM) By the work of the Angels, whose Prince is Michael: and this so that the Jews might not at some time pay superstitious worship to the remains of so great a man.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET SEPELIVIT EUM) Opera Angelorum, quorum Princeps Michael: idque ne Judæi aliquando reliquiis tanti viri superstitiosum cultum deferrent.

## 34:7
Verse 7.

MOSES WAS OF ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS) See what was said above Gen. 6, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

MOSES CENTUM ET VIGINTI ANNORUM ERAT) Vide quæ dicta supra Gen. 6, 3.

## 34:8
Verse 8.

THIRTY DAYS) How many days, which Josephus relates were also spent in mourning for Aaron and Miriam. For mourning over people of common lot, seven days were sufficient. Sirach 22:13. Josephus at the end of the sixth book of Antiquities. Ammianus Marcellinus book 19.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

TRIGINTA DIEBUS) Quot dies etiam Aaronis & Ma- riammes luctui impensos narrat Josephus. In luctu super communis sortis hominibus sufficiebant dies septem. Sirach 22, 13. Josephus fine sexti Antiquæ historiæ. Ammianus Marcellinus libro 19.

## 34:8
DAYS OF MOURNING) Thirty, Josephus.

The text does not express how the burial was performed, and whether the work of angels or of Michael was employed? Grotius notes in his annotations on the Epistle of Jude that a Hebrew book, which is called דברי הימים של משה, relates that certain words of the devil to Moses before his death, and the ministries which the angels showed to Moses, are commemorated, but that book is undoubtedly fabulous. Jude in his Catholic Epistle, v. 9, asserts that there was an altercation with Michael about the body of Moses, but he does not express that an altercation took place concerning the burial. Epiphanius in his 9th heresy, Oecumenius in the Epistle of Jude, and others, however, believe that he was buried by the work of angels.

The reason for such a divine and hidden burial is also not defined in the Holy Scriptures. Philo gives it as that God deemed such a great man worthy of such an admirable tomb, which no man was ever worthy to behold. Augustine brings forward a twofold reason in book 1 of De mirabilibus Scripturae, ch. 35. For two reasons no one was aware of his death and tomb: so that no one might see that face, which had glowed with the fellowship of the Lord's speech, repressed by the sorrow of death: and so that the people of Israel, if they had known where his tomb was, might not worship it, from which source he also took away with him the rod with which he had performed signs, as very many think, so that it might not be worshipped, since the children of Israel afterwards worshipped the serpent which he had made. Nor is the observation of the Blessed Luther to be despised, who indeed does not deny that the tomb was hidden on account of the Jews, so that they would not make an idol of it: yet he judges that it is signified more that, with the coming of the light of the Gospel, the ministry of the law is so taken away that the Jews can neither find nor restore it ever.

We cannot but add here what Grotius left behind on Matthew 17 concerning the body of Moses: namely, that it was guarded by angelic ministry, so that it might not fall into the power of the devil, τῶ̃ ἔχοντο̇ τὸ κράτο̇ τῶ̃ διαβόλε, Heb. 2:14, who is called the angel of death by the Hebrews, by whose command the body is dissolved into dust: and thus it was preserved from putrefaction. Grotius says that Jude seems to indicate this in his Epistle, but he proves it with no evidence: this is proper to the body of Christ alone, not to see corruption, Ps. 16:10. The bodies of all other saints who have died have seen corruption. What is brought forward from the fables of the Jews concerning the angel of death dissolving bodies into dust, we do not envy the admirer of blind guides. That the body of Elijah was likewise preserved by God is diametrically opposed to the Scripture, which testifies that he was translated into heaven, and thus Elijah was carried over alive in soul and body. Therefore it did not need angelic preservation from putrefaction for so many centuries. Meanwhile, it is certain that Moses was also seen in his true body at the transfiguration of Christ; not in an alien one, as Thomas, Lyranus, Abulensis, Cornelius a Lapide, and others trifle (such as angels are accustomed to assume: for it does not befit a human soul to appear in an alien body, since it rejoices in its own body) but in his own and genuine one; not that Moses was translated in the same, which some attribute to Gregory of Nyssa, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, along with Suarez and Viega, whose opinion, however, seems doubtful to others: but because the body of Moses was truly buried, which was raised by God (since it was very easy for God to raise the body of Moses), and Christ wished to give assurance of his own future resurrection by the resuscitation of Moses. But these things are as it were παραφυαδικω̃ς: with which we conclude our Anti-Grotian observations on the Pentateuch; and we render thanks with a devoted heart to God, the author of all wisdom and Truth itself, praying ὁλοψύχως that He may further sanctify us in the truth; Thy Word, O Lord, is Truth! Amen.

I. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS’S ILLUSTRATED BIBLE OF THE OLD TESTAMENT, VOLUME I, PART II, EXHIBITING ANNOTATIONS ON THE HISTORICAL BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT: JOSHUA, JUDGES, RUTH, 2 SAMUEL, 2 KINGS, 2 CHRONICLES, EZRA, NEHEMIAH, AND ESTHER. With Prolegomena to the Prophets.

DEDICATORY PREFACE TO THE ANTI-GROTIAN ANNOTATIONS ON THE HISTORICAL BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT TO THE MOST EMINENT MAN, LORD BENEDICT CARPZOV, DOCTOR OF LAWS, MOST EXCELLENT PRIVY COUNCILLOR OF THE MOST SERENE ELECTOR OF SAXONY, HIS GREAT LORD AND PATRON, GREETINGS.

Magnificent, Most Noble Sir,

When I was deliberating in my mind to whom these Biblical exercises ought to be inscribed, it did not seem inappropriate to choose as Patron for the Refutations of a Great Man, a Royal Legate, a Doctor of Laws, and a Polymath deserving of high praise in the field of letters, a man likewise Great, the chief Councillor of the Most Serene Elector—under whose shadow, by divine gift, it has been permitted for more than nine years to adorn these and other works—a Doctor of Laws and a Polymath illustrious for his merits toward the Christian Republic. Therefore, I believed that that name, with which the learned world has long shone, would bring light to my small and obscure papers. Nor indeed did I have to fear that the work undertaken against such a great man and Doctor of Laws would be less than welcome. For I know that the glory of the divine Name, which is to be trembled at, is holier to you, the care of the true faith entrusted to us is holier, and the instruction of the Church of God is holier than any name in the world. Moreover, that remarkable skill in the Holy Scriptures and the monuments of the Theologians, joined with most dexterous judgment, nay, with a Theological mind and Spirit, in so great a Doctor of Laws, an outstanding ornament of our century, as writings worthy of Cedar attest, deeply provoked and animated me to this boldness, which I shall say without vanity. For those things are such that, after incredible diligence and study of deserving well of the public, Politicians, Doctors of Laws, and Theologians admire, cherish, and marvel at the heroic quality in them. Furthermore, the defense of the most holy Code, which is your Councillor or rather the law, soul, and supreme director of your holy counsels, as well as the defense of the precious faith—the custody and unblemished defense of which, along with the increase of the Republic (which divine kindness deigns to preserve for the sake of His Church and to adorn with His gifts), you constitute as the prow and stern of your counsels—and finally, the assertion of the divinely inspired Oracles concerning Christ, which are the nucleus, marrow, and Spirit of the Old Scripture, against exquisite and pernicious deceits, seemed to demand you above all as PATRON. I promise these to him entirely, provided that public cares allow him to glance at them with a fleeting eye. For I know well, Most Eminent Sir, that you will detest the itch of a Great Man for perverting the Code, which was written not by the hands of man but by the Spirit and hands of almighty God and entrusted to the Holy Church, as truly execrable: nay, in your own judgment, which will be sacred to me, you will easily confirm me in completing the Refutatory work. For although I do not deny that the Grotian Annotations shine with varied erudition, and in some places even bring some light to the text in historical and philological matters, yet those shadows by which the dogmas of faith and the divine oracles concerning them are obscured, and an eclipse is induced upon the original text itself, must be entirely dispelled, so that the divine light of Scripture may shine in the Church with its native purity and splendor, and we may not suffer the glory of the great light of the world and the Father of lights to be obscured. To me, indeed, this work seemed most useful, both to the universal Church and especially to the Academic youth entrusted to our faith, so that they might be led to the fountains of Scripture—without which any skirmishes, however much they may swell with Philosophy or Oratory, are of little use—and be instructed in the necessary defenses, especially in the classic sayings of Holy Scripture. Finally, if these Academic disputations should perhaps seem unworthy of the splendor of so great a name, they will be considered all the more in need of it: a declaration made at Dresden and by letter bids me be secure that this will not be denied to me, with the rays of favor and the benevolence that one ought to admire and venerate in such a height of dignity. A reciprocal gift of a grateful mind will be so far from unwelcome that I dare to promise myself from it an argument for further grace and benevolence: I shall pray to GOD that He may preserve you, Patron, for the Elector, the Church, the Republic, the Nestor of our century, for Nestorian years!

Wittenberg, February 24, in the year 1660.

A worshiper of your illustrious name, Abraham Calovius, D.

I. PROLEGOMENA ON PROPHETS

Concerning Prophets and Prophecies, first occurs Onomatology, then Pragmatology. In the former we examine the word:

(1.) As to Etymology: Which is of Greek origin and also in Latin use. Now it is called προφήτης from πρόφημι, I predict, I foretell, by the reason of which derivation you would call a Prophet a foreteller of future things. Among the Hebrews he is called נביא from נבא, which specially denotes to predict future things, Deut. 13, 1. yet this is not the reason for it, that it descends from בוא, as Cornelius wishes, for how could נבא be derived from בוא grammatically? Nor is that its only meaning: for it also denotes to interpret, Exod. 7, 1, cf. 4, 14. Hos. 12, 10. to pray 1. Kings 18, 29. to sing 2. Sam. 10, 5. 1. Chron. 25, 1. and generally, to act in a prophetic manner 1. Sam. 18, 9. Ezra 5, 1.

(2) Regarding Homonymy, the word Prophet is used either properly, where it denotes him who reveals secrets, and especially future things, by the inspiration of God, in which sense it is used both commonly of Prophets 1. Kings 22, 8. 2. Sam. 12, 7. Dan. 9, 24. Acts 26, 22. and ἐξαιρέτως of Christ, that great Prophet, Deut. 18, 25. Acts 3, 22. 23. John 1, 2. ch. 6, 54. or improperly, as (1) Metaphorically, when it denotes him who does something similar and conducts himself in a prophetic manner: and thus it occurs both of an interpreter of the divine will, or a Teacher, who delivers secrets about God, even if not by divine inspiration Gen. 20, 7. Ex. 7, 1. Matt. 10, 41. ch. 13, 57. Luke 1, 66. ch. 7, 28. 1. Cor. 14, 1. thus sons of the Prophets, that is, disciples of faithful Teachers, whom we call Students of Theology today 2. Kings 2, 3. Am. 7, 14. 1. Tim. 1, 12. and of him who invokes or celebrates God by singing, playing the psalms, etc. 1. Sam. 10, 5. ch. 19, 20. as 1. Chron. 25, 1. the sons of Asaph are said to have prophesied with harps; see also 1. Chron. 15, 22. 27. 1. Kings 19, 29. (2) Metonymically, when the name of Prophets is used for Prophetic writings Luke 16, 29. ch. 24, 27. Acts 24, 14. In which sense either generally the Prophets are called the Scriptures of the O.T. Eph. 2, 20. or specially, so that Prophetic writings are distinguished from the law or Mosaic books; and by them the remaining θεόπνευστα Scriptures of the O.T. are denoted Luke 16, 29. or also, as they are distinguished from the Law and Psalms, and with them complete the O.T. Codex Luke 24, 24. (3) Catachrestically of Saul 1. Sam. 18, 10. representing prophetic speech and gesture by the impulse of an evil spirit, and also of the prophets of the devil 1. Kings 18.

(3.) As to Synonymy, a Prophet is called ראה a seer, which name is the most ancient of all prophetic names 1. Sam. 9, 9. from the mode of revelation through a vision of the mind, whence prophetic visions are Is. 1, 5. ch. 21, 2. Ez. 1, 1. Dan. 10, 9. to which the name חֹזֶה seer is twin 2. Sam. 7, 17. 2. Chron. 9, 29. and also צֹפֶה Watchman, which name, however, they obtain not only from divine vision, but also from the vision and speculation which Prophets, as inspectors, had over those whom they were set over Ez. 3, 17. Jer. 6, 16. and for whom they kept watch themselves as if in a watchtower 2. Kings 9, 17. Next, he was called MAN OF GOD, a man of God, both from a peculiar intercourse with GOD, and from a divine office, or one committed by GOD 1. Sam. 2, 27. ch. 7, 6. 1. Kings 12, 22. ch. 17, 18. 24. ch. 20, 28. ch. 23, 1. 2. Kings 4, 7. 2. Pet. 1, 21. by which name the Jews note in Seder Olam Rabba f. 9 that only ten men of God are called from among the Prophets. The name man of God is taken more generally for any minister of the word 2. Tim. 3, 16. Prophets are also called specially servants of God 2. Kings 17, 23. Jer. 7, 25. But this is not a synonym, but is joined with the name of Prophets as an epithet, or a periphrasis taken from the office. Finally, a Prophet is called a dropper, from נטף to drop, Mic. 2, 6. Which also means to teach: because doctrine drops, indeed the saving Evangelical grace, but the legal [doctrine] with threats of wrath Deut. 32, 2. 2. Chr. 12, 4. whence there is a special meaning when it is taken concerning threats of divine wrath, of which the Prophets denounce first as it were small drops, but which a great storm is later to follow, unless they repent Job 18, 8. Ez. 20, 46. ch. 22, 24. For generally it denotes any doctrine by a metaphor taken from rain, because words follow one another just as one drop follows another, or rather, because speech flows like rain Deut. 32, 2.

In Pragmatology, first the causes must be examined, and among these (1) the efficient, and that (1) remote is the immediate calling of the Prophets, which is common to them with the Apostles. For the principal cause of the Prophets is the Holy Spirit, by whom the holy men of God spoke being moved φερόμενοι 2. Pet. 1, 21. Prophecy is the gift of Him, as the Apostle testifies 1. Cor. 12, 10. 11. And therefore, even if Satan also sometimes reveals secrets through his organs, these, however, are not prophecies. For the Spirit, however most perspicacious and by its agility most swift, does not know of itself those things which deeply transcend the supreme mind, but either from the revelation of God, or through an understanding observed by men agitated by the Spirit of God, which it suggests and manifests to its organs as if proceeding from itself, whence the presage concerning the death of Saul is not to be judged a certain Prophecy, but a denunciation of the execution upon Saul, which Satan had known was enjoined upon him by God, as the blessed Hulsemann rightly judged in Prolegom. in Jer. de natur. Prophet. (2) The near revelation of secrets exceeding human grasp. 1 Pet. 1, 11. which is viewed partly as it proceeds from God, partly as it is received by the Prophets.

The first requirement, therefore, of Prophetic knowledge is revelation itself, as it was made by God. God, however, revealed secrets to them in various ways, sometimes through visions, sometimes through dreams, sometimes through oracles; visions are called ὀπτασίας, dreams ὁράματα, oracles θεοπρέπεια. Through visions or species, forms, or images of things which were revealed, either external, as when He revealed secrets through certain symbols presented to the sight Dan. 5, 24, or internal, which He subjected to the fantasy or mind of those awake, either with ἐκςάσει, that is, excess, abstraction, or elevation of the mind from external or internal senses, but in such a way that the mind remained intact Act. 10, 11, or without it Jer. 1, 11. 13. Concerning which Epiph. adv. Cataphryg. Abraham was also in an ἐκςάσει, not of mind, but of fear. The Prophets were also, but not in an ἐκςάσει of thoughts and reason; they spoke with a sound mind in sober and chaste thoughts, and not in a consternation of madness. Dreams were images sent by God to those sleeping concerning divine matters, as in Daniel throughout: Oracles, however, were words by which God revealed secret things, whether external, both in person and through an angel: or internal or intellectual, by which He addressed the Prophets through imaginary voices.

Revelation is also distinguished in this way, that it is either symbolic or open; the former which was done both through images of things, in figure or idea, and through enigmas; in the former, the same things that were seen were signified, in the latter, other things than those which were seen were signified. The latter, however, was done by a clear and evident signification of the divine will, without symbols, figures, or enigmas.

Augustinus Steuchus establishes five kinds of prophetic revelations from Num. 12:6, 7. 1. בַּמַּרְאָה by vision, when the Prophets intuited the thing offered in visions. 2. בַּחֲלוֹם in a dream, which happened to those sleeping by internal visions being presented. 3. בְּחִידוֹת in enigmas, when one thing was seen and another was hinted at. 4. בִּתְמֻנָה in a figure or idea, when images of things were exhibited. 5. פֶּה אֶל־פֶּה from mouth to mouth, by which Moses is said to have conversed familiarly with God as a friend with a friend. But these modes are only extraordinary; the ordinary ones are both by the word and by Urim and Thummim. The word of God was both external and internal, made to the men of God through a sensible or even an imaginary representation, from which concepts were born, or through the infusion or irradiation of knowledge, which derived its origin neither from sense nor from imagination, but arose immediately through light poured into the intellect, through intellectual species newly imparted, or even pre-existing ones, but used or applied by divine power to form some conception of the mind. Regarding the manifestation through Urim and Thummim, some refer it to internal illumination, others to the perception of an external voice, others to a vision in the breastplate of the High Priest. Otherwise, most Papists, with Thomas 2, 2. quest. 1. art. 1, Suarez, Tannerus, Forerus, and Cornel., constitute seven species of prophecy; which can be compared here: (1) Ecstasy. (2) Visions. (3) Dream. (4) Revelation through a cloud. (5) A voice from heaven. (6) Parable. (7) Fulfillment through the Holy Spirit. Others assign those species or degrees of prophecy differently, concerning which B. Hülsemannus l. c., who distinguishes between the modes of conceiving prophecies, which are designated as either internal or external, or rather intellectual or sensual in Num. 12:6. The intellectual mode is that which occurs through the illustration of the mind without the mediation of a voice or the showing of some image. 2. Sam. 33:2. The sensual mode is that which occurs through the mediation of external senses, and that is either true or analogical. The true mediation of external senses is when God shadowed forth future events to the Prophets by some visible species, as Jeremiah saw a pot and a rod, ch. 1:13, or by an audible voice, either immediately, as to Moses in Num. 12:8, or through an angel, as to Zechariah, Luke 1. The analogical sensible mode is that which occurs through internal vision, Is. 29:11, or through ecstasy, Dan. 8:1, or through dreams, Num. 11:3, Jer. 23:25.

The second requirement of prophetic knowledge is judgment arising from the prophetic light, by which the intellect of the Prophets is elevated and illustrated, so that they may discern and judge what has been represented. For the mere representation of images did not make a prophet, as such were represented to Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and Belshazzar, but they did not understand what they saw, nor were they prophets. Although true prophets also did not always understand what the things seen signified, they nevertheless received their meaning successively, as is evident from the example of Daniel and Zechariah. See August. l. 2. de Gen. ad lit. c. 17. But it is otherwise with those who, as Augustine says, prophesied by chance, and as Basil speaks in Proœm. Es., economically. Whence Rupert in c. 11. Joh. compared Caiaphas to a tinkling cymbal, because just as it does not hear its own tinkling, so he did not notice nor understand the power of his own voice and speech. For in the words of Caiaphas, uttered in a pious and false sense, the Holy Spirit intended another divine and salutary sense. Isidorus Pelusiota l. 37. Ep. 15 says: What is more impure or wicked than Balaam, and yet God abused his tongue for blessings. What is more wicked than Caiaphas, and yet he prophesied. And indeed He chose his tongue, but not in that way his mind.

(2.) The ultimate end of the Prophet is the glory of God and the salvation of men, Prov. 29:8, 2 Pet. 1:19. The intermediate end is the denunciation of secrets revealed by God, when indeed they are viewed as Prophets, although as men they may also pronounce certain things not revealed by God, in which they themselves are mistaken, just as when Samuel conjectured that Eliab was the Lord's anointed, 1 Sam. 16:7. This denunciation is read to have been done either by words alone, or by images and actions without words, or by both. The former is done (1) either by proper speech, and that either simple and humble, which they call הטיפה, instillation, from Job 29:22, or elegant and sublime, which they call מליצה from the word מלץ, to grow sweet, from Ps. 119:103, or by parabolic and allegorical speech, the sense of which, however, was evident, the form of which is called משל, Ef. 17:2, or (3) by enigmatic speech, consisting of allegories and figures which are difficult and of recondite meaning: called by the Hebrews חדה from חדר, to sharpen, because it is not permitted to penetrate it except by the sharpness of the mind, such as was the chariot of Ezekiel ch. 1, and the visions of Zechariah ch. 1.

To the announcements of revelations are also referred the deeds of the Patriarchs and Prophets, who in their own person, life, and actions foreshadowed Christ and his Church. For examples of mixed announcements see 1 Kings 11, 13; Isaiah 20; Jeremiah 13, 27, etc., as the blessed Hopfner has executed these in his Prolegomena to Micah. Furthermore, men of God delivered prophecy either by living speech, as Isaiah 1, 10; likewise Abraham concerning his sons in Genesis 27; Jacob concerning the 12 tribes in Genesis 49; Joseph concerning the 7 years of fertility and sterility in Genesis 41; or by letters, Habakkuk 2, 2; Isaiah 8, 16; chapter 30, 8; Jeremiah 36, 2; which they were accustomed to hang from the doors, so that they might be open to any passerby, and afterwards those tablets were deposited by the Priests in the archives of the temple and preserved for the memory of posterity, as Cornelius notes in his Major Prophets, folio 21; Sanctius on Isaiah 34. Moreover, those announcements of the Prophets, like their duties, consisted of three things: (1) They were didactic, teaching both things to be believed and things to be done; by reason of which the Prophets were most eminent theologians taught by God.
