(2) Parenetic, situated in exhorting and dissuading, not without threatening toward the impenitent and consolation for the faithful and penitent, since their sayings and writings were most ardent and effective, like hammers crushing rocks, and they themselves were most fruitful and equally most effective heralds and preachers. (3) Prophetic specifically so called, or vaticinatory, by which they predicted future things and especially concerning the Messiah, who is the most important goal of the whole Scripture, as also of all the Prophets, Acts 10, 43; concerning whom Theodoret writes in his work on curing the affections of the Greeks. Just as other paths in villages and fields converge into the royal road, so the Prophets showed that this Christ is the way for believers. And concerning the Old and New Testaments, Augustine elegantly says in his book on catechizing, see chapter 4, that in the Old Testament there is the concealment of the new, and in the New Testament there is the manifestation of the old. Concerning the comparison of prophecy and the Gospel, it is deservedly said: that prophecy is the sealed Gospel, but the Gospel is the unsealed prophecy. Nor do the Prophets rarely pass from history or legal preaching to prophecy concerning Christ, and from Christ they return again to history and the affairs of their own time, which happens among other reasons so that it may appear to be prophecy, not an ordered narrative or history, whence in it, as in a variegated robe interwoven with gold, they often cut the thread of history so that they may attach and interweave Christ into the history;

See Jerome in Office ch. 1. The same Jerome, he says, in ch. 1 of Malachi, weave a prophecy of future things so as not to desert the present time, for they mix the discourse of both, and from the occasion of the latter they predict happiness. This happens especially when history was a type of Christ. For when some shadow of the Messiah shows itself, or something that can stir up his memory, the Prophets are stirred up, and are carried away into him with great affection, and they explain, salute, and propose to be recognized by all what lies hidden in that figure. Then, as if from stupor and ecstasy, they recover themselves and refer themselves to the instituted narrative. Thus lovers, having seen an image or thing that refreshes the memory of the beloved for them, are accustomed to think of him, speak to him, and pant for him. For this is the nature of love.

There now succeeds (3.) the Material Cause, to which belongs both the subject and the object. The subject is certain men, from whatever walk of life, status, and sex, since GOD, with whom there is no respect of persons (προσωποληψία), has called not only Isaiah from a royal family, Jeremiah and Ezekiel from a priestly family, but also Amos the herdsman, and has adorned the female sex itself in Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, etc., with the gift of prophecy, even if otherwise women are ordinarily not permitted to teach, 1 Cor. 14:34, 1 Tim. 2:12. For the office of the Prophets was extraordinary. The question is raised here about the Sibyls, whether they also were Prophetesses of GOD? This Cornelius à Lapide affirms without hesitation, while he wishes to maintain that the prediction of future things is a mark of the true Church alone. Although indeed Augustine, book 18 of The City of God, ch. 23, seems to refer the Erythraean Sibyl to the number of those who belong to the City of God, he does not speak there except hypothetically, and in book 2 of On Genesis Literally, ch. 19, he refers the Sibyls to the seers of the Gentiles, not to the prophetesses of God; but among the Jesuits, Sanctius on Eph. 8:2, 3, 9, asserts that the Sibyls prophesied by a Pythonic spirit, and Maldonatus on Daniel, p. 596, opposes the sudden frenzy of the Sibyls to the inflammation of the divine Spirit. What should be held concerning them, we have said in Isag. Theol. on Natural Theology, ch. 8. There are no Prophets or prophetesses of GOD except those persons who were called immediately by GOD to that end from the assembly of the faithful, and were moved by the Holy Spirit; and therefore the impious and infidels cannot be reckoned among the Prophets and men of God, even if some prophecies perhaps happened to them by way of passing, as Augustine speaks in book 3 of On the Miracles of Scripture, who in book 2 to Simplicianus So much, he says, does it differ between the prophecy of the Prophets, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and all the others were, and that transitory one which appeared in Saul, as much as it differs between human speech and the speech of Balaam's ass; for that beast received this for a time. Much less is it to be wondered at that prophecy was given to a reprobate man for a moment of time by a transitory affection, when He had given it who also made the ass speak when He willed. For if anyone has said something that pertains to wisdom, he is not immediately to be considered wise. So neither is anyone, if he has sometimes prophesied, among the Prophets. Whence Blessed Hülsemann, Prolegomena on Jeremiah, judges that divine Prophets are in the true Church also, either by faith or by profession: for as the other gifts of the Holy Spirit do not go beyond the boundaries of the Church, John 14:17, so the gift of prophecy is proper to the assembly of the called, 1 Cor. 12:10, Joel 2:28, Rev.

19:10. Nor does he judge that Balaam, before he fell away from the true worship of GOD on account of avarice, was perhaps outside the Church by profession and faith, although he fell away through avarice. But Caiaphas, who did not formally prophesy, even though his words, uttered by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, materially contained a prophecy in themselves, was in the Church of God by profession, John 11:51, 52.

The object is secret things removed from the knowledge of men, whether past, 2 Sam. 12:7, or of the present time, but absent by reason of place, or otherwise not known, 2 Kings 5:12, ch. 6:9, 1 Sam. 10:32, or future, which nevertheless pertain especially to prophecies; whether they are secret and remote from human knowledge because of their sublimity, as are divine mysteries, or for another reason, because they are still future contingencies, or otherwise lie hidden, as occult things and the thoughts of hearts. Therefore, Cornelius à Lapide, Prol. on Isaiah, does not correctly define the object of the Prophets from Thomas 2.2, q. 171, art. 3, as contingent things, that is, those depending on the free act of angel and man. For there is no doubt that prophecies about the Messiah, his mission, and death pertain to prophetic oracles, as also about the resurrection of the dead, the end of the world, etc., which indeed are not such contingencies: Therefore Thomas himself 2.2, q. 174, art. 1, makes one prophecy of predestination or of necessary things, another of foreknowledge, or of things indeed foreseen by GOD, but depending on the free will of angels and men.

(4.) The form from which Prophets or Prophecy are denominated is the θεόπνευστος knowledge of hidden things, because divine inspiration, both as the principle and as the efficient cause of revelation, can be considered as the act of God inspiring, and as the form of revelation, or of the revealed word, insofar as it formally constitutes the word of GOD in the being of the word of GOD, which is specified in Prophecy by that revelation and knowledge of hidden things. But since the Devil, as the ape of God, also has his own Prophets, feigning the appearance of divine revelation, or Pseudo-Prophets, and deludes them with the illusions of revelations, the question is asked, how can divine Prophetic revelations be distinguished from such diabolical illusions? For the sake of this matter, certain γνωρίσματα must be noted: which can be sought partly from the manner and circumstances of the revelation, partly from the matter, and partly also from the end of the revelations. As to the manner, divine revelations are not ambiguous or doubtful, such as the harmful and black Spirit renders them, but they have indubitable certainty; furthermore, they are attended by a certain singular majesty, or are confirmed by miracles, which can proceed from no other than the first cause, or they so effectively illuminate and strike the intellect, or convince it of their own divinity. As regards the matter, divine Prophetic revelations disclose only true, useful, and salutary things that are truly hidden, which can be known to GOD alone, and they prove their truth by the event. Pseudo-Prophets can only reveal those hidden things which have been perpetrated either by the demon himself and his minions, or are known by certain documents to have been so effected by others, and are hidden only in a qualified sense, namely with respect to the person to whom they are revealed: nor can they disclose future contingencies, or those things which lie in the recesses of the heart, unless they are revealed either by God himself when He wishes to use the ministry of Satan, or if Satan, the prince of them, steals from true Prophets those things which they have from divine revelation. Finally, true Prophecy is infallible and always true in all things, whether past, present, or future, whether necessary or contingent, and whether they occur for the most part, equally, or rarely—in all things, I say, it is infallible and always true: but false Prophecy can reveal things about the present, but not about merely future contingent things, or at least only by way of conjecture, and he always mixes in some falsehoods John 8:54. Whence we are commanded to distinguish false prophets by these criteria Deut. 18.

As to the end, divine revelation intends the information and salvation of men, whereas on the contrary diabolical illusions do not truly intend the information or salvation of man, but rather errors, blasphemies, crimes, superstitions, idolatries, etc., and also the destruction and ruin of man, partly temporal, and partly and especially eternal. Thus the prophecy of Tiresias promised victory to the Thebans, but with that intention and condition, that the son of Creon should be sacrificed. Calchas predicted the destruction of Troy and happy successes, but at the same time ordered that the daughter of Agamemnon be sacrificed, etc. Whence, even if Satan sometimes brings forth true and useful things, he does so not from a zeal for truth and for the benefit of man, but for his destruction.

As to the effects, true prophecy illuminates the mind of the prophet, so that he understands not only what he sees, but also what is represented by those visions. But false prophecy not only does not dispel natural darkness, but even increases it, as it arises from the prince of darkness, and indeed often strikes the mind of the prophets with madness.

Some gather these criteria of true prophets from the Old Testament: (1.) an unusual mode of revelation Num. 12:6, 7, 8. (2.) a peculiar and evident calling Exod. 3:21. (3.) the harmony of the event with the prophecy Deut. 18:22, 1 Kings 22:28, Jer. 28:8, 9. (4.) agreement with other undoubted divine revelations Deut. 13:1, Is. 8:20. (5.) the efficacy of the doctrine in moving the hearts of men Jer. 33:28. (6.) confirmation by true miracles Exod. 4:1, 2, ch. 8:48. Which things, however, as they served to generate the truth of prophecies, were nevertheless used freely, for not all prophets confirmed their prophecies with miracles, which is evident especially concerning the later prophets. For God willed that attention be paid rather to the doctrine of the prophets already sufficiently confirmed, and reserved miracles for the times of the Messiah Matt. 11:5. Certain characters of the prophets are also sought from things, such as notable and admirable visions, such as are Is. 6:1, Ezek. 1, Zach. 1, abstruse or sacred prophecies Is. 7:14, Zach. 9:9, or profane ones 1 Kings 23:3, Is. 45:1, Jer. 38:17, the majesty of the matters treated, the holiness of the precepts; and from words that are altogether singular Is. 2:22, ch. 27:1, etc., and either very vehement, striking by their gravity, Is. 1:2, or very mild and sweet Is. 25:6, ch. 41, seqq., etc.; and from gestures regarding the habit of the body 2 Kings 1:8, and manners in praying 1 Kings 18:42, Neh. 8:7, prophesying 2 Kings 13:16, Ez. 21:2, Am. 7:16, protesting Neh. 5:13, etc. False prophets are therefore called those who either invent false oracles by the instinct of a demon, or those who corrupt true ones with false interpretations, or as Jeremiah ch. 23:28 distinctly proposes them, those who either tell their own dreams, see 1. Kings 22:23, Jerem. 2:8, or teach the word of God, but not truly, and therefore they are said to steal words from their neighbor, to which latter class all false teachers belong Matt. 7:15, ch. 24:24.

The causes having been thus set forth, the second definition of a prophet emerges, that a prophet is a teacher or minister immediately raised up by God, who declares secret things exceeding human knowledge, but especially future things known and understood by divine revelation, for the glory of God and the salvation of men. Less adequate, and only some explanation of the name, is the description of Irenaeus lib. 4, cap. 37, that prophecy is the pre-signification of things that happen afterwards; for although we do not deny that prophecy is primarily called the prediction of future things, prophecies also concern present and past things. To most Papists, Lorinus, Forerius, Cornel. a Lap. Ribera approves the definition of Cassiodorus from the Proemium in Psalm., that prophecy is a divine inspiration foreknowing and foretelling with immovable truth and the greatest certainty things distant from us: but that is too narrow, because prophecy does not concern only future things, whence Chrysostom, Proem. in Psalm., more correctly says: Prophecy is the discovery of that which is hidden. Some of the Papists also require a perpetual and immanent habit for true prophecy. But this addition is not necessary, for the knowledge of prophecies and the correction of the prophets did not happen by way of a continuous habit, but of a transient motion: as Elisha 2 Kings 4:27 confesses that the Lord had hidden from him the death of the son of the Shunammite, and he excited the Spirit of prophecy by musical song 2 Kings 3:15, and therefore the Spirit is said to have rushed upon the prophets, and the word of God to have come to them. Which Lorinus also acknowledges in Act. fol. 591. Bellarm. lib. 1 de grat. cap. 10.

III. The number and chorus of the prophets is gathered here from the Scriptures: (1.) The Patriarch Enoch is called a prophet, whose prophecy is cited by St. Jude, verse 14. (2.) Abraham, Gen. 20:7, is so called by God himself, and some think all the patriarchs were prophets; to which perhaps may be referred that which is said in Jude v. 14, that Enoch the seventh from Adam prophesied concerning Adam's ἐκςάσει in Paradise, and the prophecy is found in Gen. 2:21, 23, 24. Noah's prediction concerning the flood is found in Gen. 6:13, and concerning the fates of his sons in Gen. 9:25. Likewise Abraham's concerning his sons in Gen. 27. Jacob's concerning the 12 tribes in Gen. 49. Joseph's concerning the seven years of fertility and sterility in Gen. 41. But because the name of patriarchs is more eminent, they are rather designated by that than called prophets, and thus they are usually distinguished from the prophets. (3.) Moses, than whom no similar prophet has arisen in Israel, Deut. 34:10; on account of which, because of his ἐξοχὴν and familiar conversation with God above the rest, his principal, nay, royal dignity, the frequency of most illustrious miracles, the publication of the law received from God and inspired, and many other ἀξιώματα both proper and peculiar, Moses is sometimes distinguished from the prophets and preferred before them, who was held worthy by God that He should compare Christ, that great prophet and Redeemer of the human race, to him, Deut. 18:15, 18. (4.) JOSHUA, successor of Moses, filled with the spirit of wisdom, Deut. 34:8, Num. 27:18, had many addresses from God and divine apparitions, and many sermons from the immediate instinct of the Holy Spirit; therefore he is called a prophet of the Lord by Sirach, chap. 46:1. (5.) SAMUEL, who is reckoned by Peter as the first among the prophets who arose after Moses, Acts 3:24, not that no other existed between Moses and Samuel, but that no other is read of in the Holy Scriptures mentioned by express name under this eulogy or title: Indeed, mention is made of a certain prophet sent by the Lord to the people, Judg. 6:8, but ἀνωνύμως; nor is any prophecy of his reported, but only an ἐπανορθωτικὴ sermon; therefore the name of prophet is used in the same place for a teacher sent extraordinarily, or an ordinary one generally can be understood, or if he was specifically called a Prophet, he could not however be cited by Peter, because no prophecy of his is read to have been consigned to the monuments of letters. There is also another Man of GOD but anonymous 1 Sam. 2, 21. seqq. who prophesied only concerning the abdication of Eli, and the substituting of Samuel. Samuel however is celebrated as a distinguished Prophet of the Lord 1 Sam. 9, 9. Acts 13, 20. and his prophecies and prophetic deeds were commended to letters by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. (7.) Saul having been sent away, and the whole band of prophets, who met Saul 1 Sam. 10, 10. DAVID, King and most eminent Prophet, comes into the census, a not insignificant part of whose most brilliant prophecies make up Holy Scripture, Acts 2, 30. There follows (7.) NATHAN 2 Sam. 7, 5. who flourished in the time of David, as also (8.) ASAPH, author of some Psalms. (9.) SOLOMON is nowhere explicitly named a Prophet, yet he is included under the number of the prophets, e.g., in that of Christ Luke 16, 39. They have Moses and the Prophets, under whom are also contained the writings of Solomon, and his illustrious prophecies are extant most especially in the Song of Songs. (10.) We dismiss again those who are commemorated in 1 Kings 13, namely the man of GOD from Judah, who first prophesied against the Altar of Bethel, v. 1. and the old prophet who lived in Bethel, verse 11. For these are anonymous. But AHIAS the Shilonite is named 1 Kings 11, v. 29. chap. 14, 12. who threatened extinction to Jeroboam. (11.) The history and prophecies of ELIJAH the Tishbite, a most famous prophet, 1 Kings 17 seqq., as also (12.) of ELISHA 1 Kings 19, 19 seqq. are described at some length. (13.) MICAIAH son of Imlah in the time of Jehoshaphat, 1 Kings 22, 2. 2 Chron. 13, 9. (14.) SHEMAIAH 2 Chron. 11, 20. (15.) IDDO, 2 Chron. 13, 22. (16.) JAHAZIEL, 2 Chron. 20, 14. (17.) HANANI seized by Asa 2 Chron. 16, 7. (18.) JEHU son of Hanani, 2 Chron. 19, 21. (19.) AZARIAH son of OBED 2 Chron. 15, 8. (20.) ELIEZER son of Dodavahu, originating from Mareshah, 2 Chron. 20, 37. (21.) ZECHARIAH under King Uzziah, 2 Chron. 26, 5. (22.) OBED in the time of Ahaz, 2 Chron. 29, 9. (23.) URIAH son of Shemaiah, of Kiriath-jearim, Jer. 26, 20. 23. (24.) To whom are to be added the Canonical writer Prophets, who come under the title of Major and Minor Prophets in the Biblical Codex.

From the female sex there flourished MIRIAM, sister of Moses, Prophetess, Ex. 15, 20. DEBORAH, Judg. 4, 4. HANNAH, 1 Sam. 2. HULDAH, 2 Chron. 30, 18. 22.

Some constitute 4 classes of prophets: The first is of the Patriarchs. The second, from Moses onwards, of the others who are commemorated in the Sacred writings besides the Canonical writers specifically so called, and who did not consign their own to letters. The third, of those Canonical writers, for instance the 4 Major and 12 Minor. The fourth, of the prophets of the N.T., such as Zechariah Luke 1, 67. Simeon the aged Luke 2, 34. John the Baptist, Luke 1, 76. Agabus Acts 11, 28. Acts 21, 11. Paul, who prophesied concerning the Anti-Christ: finally John the Evangelist and Apostle, whose Apocalypse is full of prophecies. And from the female sex ELIZABETH mother of John Luke 1, 41. MARY mother of the Lord Luke 1, 46. ANNA the Prophetess, Luke 2, 26. The 4 VIRGINS daughters of Philip the Evangelist, who was one of the seven Deacons Acts 21, 9.

But on account of the order of the Canonical books, the distinction of the Prophets of the O.T. into those who adorned the Canonical writings, and those who did not adorn such specific Canonical writings, such as were Elijah, Elisha, Micaiah son of Imlah etc., is especially relevant here. The former are called by other more illustrious names, as Moses is called Legislator, and his books are called the Law: David is called Psalmist and Hieropsaltes, and his prophecies are the Psalms: or they retain the name of Prophet, and are divided into former and latter. And thus are distinguished the Law and the Prophets Luke 16, 24. c. 24, 27. Acts 24, 14. not that Moses is not a Prophet, but because the name of Legislator is more worthy, and his writings contain the law most especially Matt. 5, 17. c. 22, 40. David however is a Prophet, because he was especially excellent in the Psalms, Israel 2 Sam. 23, 1. and his Canonical writing comes under the name of Psalms, it is distinguished from the Prophets by this special name, even though he was a most excellent Prophet: And under the name of Psalms are included at the same time the Solomonic [writings], on account of analogy, because the Song of Songs has the likeness of a Psalm, and his remaining books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes are more analogous to the Psalms than to the Prophecies in their manner of speaking Luke 24, 44.

Furthermore, those are called former prophets by some, who lived after Moses before the schism of Israel from Judah under Jeroboam the first, which could indeed be said of the authors of the book of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, as also of the books of Samuel, but not so of the author of the book of Kings of either [book]: for these were written after the times of Jeroboam, and long after the kingdom of Jeroboam I, in the time of JONAH, who was the most ancient of the latter Prophets, flourished, nearly one hundred and fifty years after that schism. Others therefore call those former, who lived before the times of Uzziah or Azariah son of Amaziah, to whom JEROBOAM the second son of Joash was contemporary in the Kingdom of Israel, and latter, those who lived in the times of Uzziah and thereafter. Because those prophets who are called latter, and are distributed into Major and Minor, are contained in the Canon, and flourished in the times of Uzziah and following. Although indeed the second book of Kings extends beyond the times of Uzziah, and up to the abduction of Zedekiah, and it is not certainly established concerning the author of the books of Kings, whom some think to have been Jeremiah from among the latter prophets, while others judge that different prophets consigned the histories of the same at distinct times: yet those books contain for the most part the former prophets and their histories, and therefore seem still to be related to the writings of the former prophets: although, if one must say what is the case, that commonly received distribution into former and latter prophets, which originated from the Jews, is very crude.

Nor can any other judgment be made concerning the distinction of the sacred books into נביאים Prophetic and כתובים ἁγιογράφως, likewise accepted by the Jews, if it be recalled to a more accurate examination. For since all those proceeded from the Prophets, these are wrongly distinguished from those in such a way that the name of Prophets is left to the latter alone, nor can a solid reason be found which might support this distinction. For the Hebrews, distributing the Code of the Old Testament into four sections, attach to the first, which they call תורה Law and חומש Pentateuch, in the place of an appendix, five volumes of festival books, namely שיר השירים the Song of Songs, רות Ruth, איכה the book of Lamentations, קהלת Ecclesiastes, and מגלּת אסתר the volume of Esther. Which, even if it be done by them for this reason, because the Song of Songs [is read] on the feast of Passover, the book of Ruth on the feast of Pentecost or of Weeks, [the book of] Lamentations on the 9th day of July, on which both temples were burned, Ecclesiastes on the feast of Tabernacles, and finally the volume of Esther on the 14th and 15th days of the month Adar, or of the lots

February in their Synagogues they have been accustomed to read publicly, yet they ought not to have had the Sacred volumes so torn apart, and thrown into disorder in their arrangement, on account of that series of their readings; since Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs ought to be referred to the Proverbs of Solomon, as being writings of the same author, and the Song is not to be preferred to the book of Ruth or the Lamentations to Ecclesiastes, nor are those to be torn away from the book of Jeremiah, nor the book of Ruth to be sequestered from the former Prophets, nor finally was the volume of Esther to be attached to those others of the Law, and to be placed before the Historical books of Joshua and Judges.

Furthermore, since in the second Section they constitute under the title נְבִיאִים רִאשׁוֹנִים [Former Prophets] the book of Joshua, Judges, the two of Samuel, and the two of Kings, in the third under the title נְבִיאִים אַחֲרֹנִים [Latter Prophets], Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and תְּרֵי עֲשַׂר or תְּרֵיסַר [Twelve] the Twelve Prophets, viz. the Minor [Prophets], in the fifth section finally they present the כְּתוּבִים [Writings] or Hagiographa, and they call them Psalms, Proverbs, the books of Job, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, as also דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים [words of the days], or the deeds of the times, or the books of Chronicles, they are not only, as we have said, less accurate in the distinction of the Former and Latter Prophets; but they also wrongly tear away from the former Prophets the books of Chronicles, which certainly belong to them by the same right by which the books of Kings are reckoned to them: nor do they conveniently tear the books of Chronicles away from the books of Kings, and assign them the last place in the Biblical codex, as being those to which most of the later Prophets are posterior in chronology and time. Violent certainly and plainly indecent are all those separations, by which they tear apart those things which are joined together in this distribution and ordering of theirs, as not only the book of Ruth from the History of Judges, and the books of Chronicles from the books of Kings; but also the book of Esther from Ezra, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs both from each other, and from the third book of Solomon, namely Proverbs, and finally the Lamentations from Jeremiah. But above all, however, the inept distinction of the Prophetic books and the Cethubim deserves castigation, and the unjust elimination of Daniel from the class of the Prophets. Some distinguish the books of the Cethubim from the Prophetic ones by this name, that they hand down doctrine and history rather than prophecies: But they cannot be distinguished in this way from the former Prophets: nor does Daniel hand down history more than Isaiah and Jeremiah, but he is likewise full of prophecies. Then on account of the poetry and melody they wish them to be distinguished ἐξόχως [excellently] and singularly from the Prophets, which cannot be said of the books of Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, nor even of the book of Daniel. For these do not contain poetry, whatever may be the case regarding the books of Job, David, and Solomon. Some with greater likelihood say those are called Prophets who performed the Prophetic office, which consisted in instructing and ruling the Church: such were those three whom they call the Major, and the 12 Minor Prophets, but the others, who were illuminated by the Holy Spirit, since they were not otherwise prophets by profession, were called holy writers: and such were David and Solomon the Kings, Daniel the purple-clad official of Nebuchadnezzar, Ezra the Scribe of the law, and Nehemiah, as also Job the Princes. But with that distinction posited, the book of Ruth and the Lamentations would have been no less to be reckoned among the Prophetic books than the book of Joshua and Judges, indeed these also together with the books of Samuel were all to be numbered among the Cethubim. R. David Kimchi says they are called Prophetic because they were dictated through Prophecy while the senses were at rest, or even in visions, but the Cethubim because they were dictated to those who were awake through the Holy Spirit. But such a distinction has no foundation. For not a few things were dictated to the Prophets also while they were awake, if not most things, and Daniel had visions no less than the other Prophets.

Moreover, of the Hagiographa, which Epiphanius calls γραφεĩα [writings], they constitute two orders, as can be seen in Hottinger in Thes. Phil. lib. 2. c. 1. In the first are placed the חֲמֵשׁ מְגִלּוֹת [five scrolls] so called κατ’ ἐξοχὴν [pre-eminently], and accustomed to be read throughout the year on feast days, the Song, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther: but in the second order six books are held, three Poetic, of Psalms, Proverbs and Job, one Prophetic of Daniel, and two Historical of Ezra (and Nehemiah) and the words of the days.

How, however, that trichotomy of the Biblical Codex of the Old Testament into the law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, with the festival books being recalled to the law, can be reduced to a sounder sense, we have shown in System. Theol., in what manner Jerome in the Prologus Galeatus retained the same, numbering the books in total 22, namely Five Mosaic: eight Prophetic: viz. the four former, Joshua, Judges with the annexed book of Ruth, Samuel and Kings: likewise four latter, Isaiah, Jeremiah with the annexed Lamentations, Ezekiel, and the twelve minor Prophets, who on account of the brevity of the volumes are reckoned as one, finally nine Hagiographa, as are Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Job, Daniel, Ezra, with the annexed Nehemiah, the history of Esther; finally the words of the days, as an Epitome of the old Instrument. The sacred books are ordered and proposed a little differently by Josephus in Eusebius lib. 3. Histor. Eccles. c. 9. in which besides the five Mosaic, he designated thirteen Prophetic and four hymns, and precepts of human life: so that these indeed are Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song, but those are Joshua, Judges and Ruth, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah with Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel and the minor Prophets. That Philo also handed down this division, Sixtus Senensis notes in Bibl. 4. p. 2. and Christ also seems to have retained the same, as being then customary, and adequately comprising all the canonical books, when he distributed the Scripture into the law, the Psalms, and the Prophets, Luke 24, 44.

Concerning the distinction of the Prophets, with regard to the time before the Babylonian captivity, about the same, and after it, because it concerns the Prophets whom they call the latter, we shall treat of it at the threshold of those books. Since a trichotomy instituted according to subject matter pleases most theologians—into Historical, which are comprised with the Mosaic Pentateuch, whom the Hebrews call by the name of the former Prophets, including however the book of Ruth, Esther, as also the history of Job: Poetic, which are the Solomonic books along with the Psalms: and Prophetic, which are completed by the books of the four Major and 12 Minor Prophets—we adhere to the same as being received and sufficiently convenient, nor do we tear away the Lamentations from Jeremiah with Grotius, so that the order approved in our Codices may remain intact. Here, however, because we are presenting the entire annotations of Grotius, we shall adhere to the Grotian order.

Latin:

DIES PLANCTUS) Triginta, Josephus.

Non exprimit textus, quomodo sepultura fa- cta sit, & an adhibita Angelorum, aut Michae- lis opera? Grotius annotat. in Ep. Judæ, librum E- braicum, qui vocetur דברי הימים של משה re- fert, in quo verba quædam diaboli ad Mosen ante mor- tem ejus, & ministeria, quæ Angeli Mosi exhibuere, com- memorantur, sed ille sine dubio fabulosus est. Al- tercatum cum Michaele de corpore Mosis fuisse diabolum Judas Ep. Cathol. v. 9. perhibet, sed circa sepulturam factam altercationem non exprimit. O- pera tamen Angelorum sepultum esse Epiphanius hæ- ref. 9. Oecumenius in Ep. Judæ & alii existimant.

Causa etiam sepulturæ divinæ tam occultæ, in S. literis definita non est. Philo eam reddit, quod dignatus tantum virum sepulcro tam admirando DEUS fuerit, quod nullus homo dignus fuerit ad- spicere unquam. Augustinus geminam causam ad- fert l. 1. de mirabil. Scr. c. 35. Duabus de causis mor- tis ejus & sepulchri nemo erat conscius: quatenus istam faciem, quæ consortio sermonis Domini rutilaverat, mortis mærore repressam nullus videret: & ne sepul- chrum ejus populus Israel, si cognovisset, ubi esset, ado- raret, unde & virgam, in qua signa fecerat, ut plurimi putant, ne adoraretur secum abstulerit, quoniam & ser- pentem, quem fecerat, filii Israel postmodum adora- bant. Neque contemnenda B. Lutheri observatio, qui non negat quidem, propter Judæos sepulchrum fuisse absconditum, ne idolum facerent: censet tamen magis significari, veniente luce Evangelii ministerium legis sic tolli, ut Judæi neǵ; invenire, neǵ; reparare un- quam possint.

Non possumus, quin adjungamus hîc, quæ de corpore Mosis Grotius ad Matth. 17. c. reliquit: Illud nempe custoditum Angelico fuisse ministerio, ne perveni- ret in potestatem diaboli τῶ̃ ἔχοντο̇ τὸ κράτο̇ τῶ̃ διαβόλε, Ebr. 2, 14. qui Angelus mortis Ebræis vocatur, cujus imperio corpus in pulverem dissolvatur: adeoque asservatum a putredine. Quod in Epistola sua indicare videri Judam ait quidem Grotius, sed nullo probat documento: Christi unius corpori proprium hoc est; non videre corruptionem Pf. 16, 10. Cætera Sancto- rum omnium, qui diem obiere, corruptionem vi- derunt. Quod de Angelo mortis, corpora in pulverem dissolvente, adfertur e Judæorum fabulis, non invi- demus admiratori cæcorum ductorum. Eliæ cor- pus pariter a Deo asservatum, Scripturæ e diametro repugnat, quæ id in cœlos translatum, eoque vivum anima & corpore traductum Eliam testatur. Non ergo Angelica preservatione a putredine per tot anno- rum secula indiguit. Interim certum est, etiam Mo- sen vero corpore in Christi transfiguratione conspectum fuisse; non alieno, uti nugantur Thomas, Lyranus, A- bulensis, Cornelius a Lapide, & alii (quale sc. Angeli assumere consuevere: Id enim animæ humanæ non convenit, in alieno apparere corpore, utpote quæ pro- prio corpore gaudet) sed proprio & genuino; non quod eodem etiam translatus fuerit Moses, quod nonnulli Gregorio Nysseno, Hieronymo, Ambrosio, Au- gustino tribuunt, cum Suaresio & Viega, quorum ta- men sententia dubia aliis videtur: sed quia vere se- pultum est corpus Mosis, quod a DEO excitatum, (quum facillimum Deo id fuerit, corpus Mosis ex- citare) ac Christus resuscitatione Mosis futuræ suæ resurrectioni fidem facere voluerit. Sed hæc vel- uti παραφυαδικω̃ς: quibus nostras in Pentatevchum observationes Anti-Grotianas concludimus; Deoque sapientiæ omnis auctori & veritati ipsi gratias devoto pectore persolvimus, ὁλοψύχως orantes, ut porro nos in veritate sanctificet, Verbum tuum, Domine, est Veritas! Amen.

I. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVII BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA VETERIS TESTAMENTI TOMI I. PARS II. EXHIBENS ANNOTATA AD LIBROS HISTORICOS VETERIS TESTAMENTI, JOSUÆ. JUDICUM. RUTH. SAMUELIS II. REGUM II. | PARALIPOMENΩN II. ESDRÆ. NEHEMIÆ, ET ESTHER. Cum Prolegomenis in Prophetas.

PRÆFATIO DEDICATORIA AD ANNOTATA ANTI-GROTIANA IN LIBROS HISTO- RICOS V. T. VIRO SUMMO DN. BENEDICTO CARPZOVIO, JCTO, SERENISSIMI ELECTORIS SAXONIÆ CONSILIARIO INTIMO EXCELLENTISSIMO, DOMINO ET PATRONO SUO MAGNO S. P.

Magnifice, Nobilissime Vir,

QUum apud animum meum delibe- rarem, cuinam hæc meletemata Biblica inscribenda essent, non in- conveniens videbatur Viri Magni, Legati Regii, J Cti & Polyhistoris de re literaria egregie meriti Elencticis Patro- num Virum itidem Magnum, Serenissimi Ele- ctoris sub cujus umbra, divino munere, ultra novennium hæc & alia adornare licuit, Confi- liarium præcipuum, JCtum & Polyhistora me- ritis in Rempublicam Christianam illustrem eligerem. Nomen ergo illud, quo jam pri- dem orbis literatus coruscat, exiguis & obscu- ris chartis lucem conciliaturum credebam. Neque vero mihi verendum erat, minus gra- tam fore operam adversus JCtum Tantumque virum susceptam. Novi enim sanctiorem Tibi tremendi Nominis divini gloriam, San- ctiorem veræ depositæ fidei curam, Sanctio- rem Ecclesiæ Dei informationem, quam ullum in orbe nomen. Insignis autem illa in Sacris li- teris & monumentis Theologorum peritia, cum judicio dexterrime, imo animo, Spiritu- que Theologico, in tanto JCto, egregio seculi nostri ornamento devincta, quam scripta Ce- dro digna referunt, me ad hanc audaciam, quod præfiscini dixero, provocabant penitus, atque animabant. Ea enim talia sunt, quæ post incredibilem diligentiam & studium de publico merendi Heroicum in iisdem suspici- unt, colunt, mirantur Politici, JCti, Theologi. Porro vindiciæ Codicis sanctissimi, qui Confi- liarius Tuus vel potius consiliorum Sanctio- rum lex, anima, & director summus, tum fidei pretiosæ, cujus custodiam, & propugnationem intemeratam, cum incremento Reipublicæ, ut- pote quam ob Ecclesiam suam conservare, do- nisque suis ornare dignatur divina benigni- tas, proram & puppim consiliorum constituis, defensio; denique Oraculorum de Christo di- vinitus inspiratorum, quæ nucleus, medulla, & Spiritus sunt Veteris Scripturæ, adversus ex- quisitas, & perniciosas Strophan assertio, Te cumprimis PATRONUM postulare videban- tur. Quem his omnino polliceor, modo pu- blicæ curæ ista fugitivo oculo lustrare permi- serint. Detestaberis enim sat scio, Vir Sum- me, Viri Magni Cacoëthes in Codice non ho- minis, sed omnipotentis Dei Spiritu & mani- bus exarato, ac Ecclesiæ Sanctæ credito, per- vertendo vere execrandum: imo judicio et- iam Tuo, quod mihi Sacrum erit, in opere Elenctico pertexendo facile me confirmabis. Quanquam enim non diffitear, varia eruditio- ne Annotata Grotiana fulgere, alicubi etiam lucis aliquid textui in Historicis, & Philologi- cis adferre, tenebræ tamen illæ, quibus dogma- ta fidei & oracula divina de iisdem obfuscan- tur, textuique ipsi originali eclipsis inducitur, discutiendæ omnino sunt, ut divina Scripturæ lux puritate ac splendore suo nativo fulgeat in Ecclesia, neque magnæ mundi lucis, Patrisque luminum gloriam obscurari patiamur. Mihi profecto hæc opera, cum Ecclesiæ universæ, tum imprimis Academicæ juventuti, fidei no- stræ creditæ, maxime utilis videbatur, ut ad fontes Scripturæ, sine qua velitationes quæ- cunque utut Philosophia aut Oratoria turge- ant, parum utiles sunt, deducatur, & in classi- cis cumprimis S. Scripturæ dictis necessarii vindiciis instruatur. Postremo si nominis tanti splendore hæ Academicæ disputationes indignæ fortassis videantur, indigæ tamen eo magis eodem censelbuntur: quem, cum favo- ris radiis, mihi non denegatum iri, benevolen- tiæ, ea humanitate, quam, in tanto apice digni- tatis, mirari ac venerari oportet, Dresdæ, ac per literas facta declaratio securum me esse jubet. Grati etiam animi qualecunque redhostimen- tum adeo non ingratum erit, ut ulterioris gra- tiæ ac benevolentiæ mihi, meisque inde polli- ceri ausim argumentum: DEUM adoraturus, ut TE, Patrone, Electori, Ecclesiæ, Reipublicæ, seculi nostri Nestorem, annis servet Nestoreis!

Wittebergæ, VI. Cal. Martii, Anno cIɔ Iɔc LX.

Illustris nominis Tui Cultor Abraham Calovius, D.

I. PROLEG IN PRO

DE Prophetis, & Prophetiis, occurrit primo Onomatologia, tum Pragmatologia. In illa vocem expendimus:

(1.) Quantum ad Etymologiam: Quæ origine Græca usu Latina etiam est. Dicitur autem προ- φήτης a πρόφημι, prædico, prænuncio, cujus derivatio- nis ratione Prophetam dixeris prænuncium rerum fu- turarum. Ebræis נביא dicitur a נבא, quod specia- liter notat futura prædicere Deut. 13, 1. non tamen e- jus ratio hæc est, quod a בוא venire, descendat, ut Cornelius vult, nam quomodo נבא derivari a בוא Grammatice poterit? neque illa tantum ejus est si- gnificatio: nam etiam notat interpretari, Exod. 7, 1, Conf. 4, 14. Hos. 12, 10. orare 1. Reg. 18, 29. cantare 2. Sam. 10, 5. 1. Par. 25, 1. & generaliter, more propheti- co agere 1. Sam. 18, 9. Esdr. 5, 1.

(2) Quoad Homonymiam Prophetæ vox usurpa- tur vel proprie, ubi notat eum qui arcana, & im- primis futura ex inspiratione Dei revelat, quo sensu tum communiter de Prophetis 1. Reg. 22, 8. 2. Sam. 12, 7. Dan. 9, 24. Act. 26, 22. tum ἐξαιρέτως de Christo ma- gno illo Propheta adhibetur, Deut. 18, 25. Act. 3, 22. 23. Joh. 1, 2. c. 6, 54. vel improprie, utpote (1) Meta- phorice, cum eum, qui simile quid agit, & more Pro- phetico se gerit, notat: & ita tum de interprete volun- tatis divinæ occurrit, aut Doctore, qui arcana de Deo, etsi non ex inspiratione divina tradit Gen. 20, 7. Ex. 7, 1. Matth. 10, 41. c. 13, 57. Luc. 1, 66. c. 7, 28. 1. Cor. 14, 1. ita filii Prophetarum, id est, discipuli Doctorum fideli- um, quos hodie Studiosos Theologiæ vocamus 2. Reg. 2, 3. Am. 7, 14. 1. Tim. 1, 12. tum de eo, qui Deum invo- cat aut celebrat canendo, psallendo, &c. 1. Sam. 10, 5. c. 19, 20. uti 1. Par. 25, 1. filii Assaph in cytharis prophe- tasse dicuntur; vid. etiam 1. Par. 15, 22. 27. 1. Reg. 19, 29. (2) Metonymice, cum Prophetarum nomen pro scri- ptis Propheticis usurpatur Luc. 16, 29. c. 24, 27. Act. 24, 14. Quo sensu vel generaliter Prophetæ dicuntur Scripta V. T. Eph. 2, 20. vel specialiter, ut scripta Prophetica a lege vel libris Mosaicis distinguantur; iisque reliqua V. T. θεόπνευστα Scripta notentur Luc. 16, 29. vel etiam, uti a Lege & Psalmis distinguuntur, & cum illis V. T. Codicem absolvunt Luc. 24, 24. (3) Catachrestice de Saule 1. Sam. 18, 10. impulsu Spiritus mali sermonem & gestum Propheticum repræsen- tante, nec non de vatibus diaboli 1. Reg. 18.

(3.) Qua Synonymiam, vocatur Propheta ראה videns, quod nomen Propheticum omnium anti- quissimum est 1. Sam. 9, 9. a modo revelationis per vi- sionem mentis, unde visiones Prophetiæ sunt Es. 1, 5. c. 21, 2. Ez. 1, 1. Dan. 10, 9. cui geminum est nomen חֹזֶה videns 2. Sam. 7, 17. 2. Chron. 9, 29. nec non צֹפֶה Spe- culator, quod tamen nomen non tantum a visione divina obtinent, sed etiam a visione, & speculatione, quam ceu inspectores Prophetæ in eos habebant, quibus præfecti erant Ez. 3, 17. Jer. 6, 16. & pro quibus excubabant ipsi velut in specula 2. Reg. 9, 17. Deinde dicebatur VIR DEI, homo DEI, tum e commercio peculiari cum DEO, tum ab officio divino, vel a DEO commisso 1. Sam. 2, 27. cap. 7, 6. 1. Reg. 12, 22. c. 17, 18. 24. c. 20, 28. c. 23, 1. 2. Reg. 4, 7. 2. Pet. 1, 21. quo nomine viri Dei tantum decem e Prophetis nuncupari notant Judæi in Seder Olam Rabba f. 9. Generalius accipitur nomen hominis Dei de quovis verbi ministro 2. Tim. 3, 16. vocantur & Prophetæ spe- cialiter servi Dei 2. Reg. 17, 23. Jer. 7, 25. Sed hoc non est synonymon, sed cum Prophetarum nomine ceu epit heton, vel περίφρασις ab officio sumta conjun- gitur. Deniq; vocatur Propheta stillans, a נטף stilla- re Mich. 2, 6. Quod etiam est docere: quia doctrina stillat, Evangelica quidem gratia salutifera, legalis au- tem comminationibus iræ Deut. 32, 2. 2. Chr. 12, 4. unde specialis est significatio, cum de comminatio- nibus iræ divinæ accipitur, cujus primum parvas veluti stillas denunciant Prophetæ, sed quas postea sequutura sit magna procella, nisi pœniteant Job. 18, 8. Ez. 20, 46. c. 22, 24. Nam generaliter quamvis doctrinam notat per metaphoram a pluvia desum- tam, quia verba se invicem sequuntur sicut gutta u- na aliam, vel potius, quia sermo fluit instar pluviæ Deut. 32, 2.

In Pragmatologia primum causæ expendendæ sunt, & in hisce (1) efficiens eaque (1) remota est imme- diata Prophetarum vocatio, quæ communis iisdem cum Apostolis. Nam Prophetarum causa principalis est Sp. S. quo φερόμενοι locuti sunt sancti Dei homi- nes 2. Pet. 1, 21. Hujus donum est prophetia, teste Apost. 1. Cor. 12, 10. 11. Ideoque etsi Satanas etiam per orga- na sua quandoq; arcana revelat, hæ tamen Prophe- tiæ non sunt. Neq; enim ex se novit Spiritus utut perspicacissimus, & agilitate sua velocissimus, ea, quæ summam mentem penitus transcendunt, sed vel ex revelatione Dei, vel per observatam ab ho- minibus Spiritu Dei agitatis intelligentiam, quæ or- ganis suis quasi ex se profecta suggerit & manifestat, unde præsagium de morte Saulis non censendum est Prophetia quædam, sed denunciatio exequutionis in Saulem, quam sibi a Deo injunctam Satanas nove- rat, ut recte B. Hulsemannus judicavit Prolegom. in Jer. de natur. Prophet. (2) Propinqua arcanorum captum humanum excedentium revelatio. 1. Pet. 1, 11. quæ spectatur partim ut a Deo proficiscitur, partim, ut a Prophetis recipitur.

Primum ergo requisitum cognitionis Prophe- ticæ est ipsa revelatio, prout a Deo facta. Deus autem variis modis arcana illis revelavit, modo per visio- nes, modo per somnia, modo per oracula; visiones ὀπτασίας, somnia ὁράματα, oracula θεοπρέπεια di- cuntur. Per visiones vel species formas, aut imagi- nes rerum, quæ revelata, sive externas, utpote cum per certa symbola visui objecta arcana revelavit Dan. 5, 24. sive internas, quæ vigilantium phantasiæ, aut menti, sive cum ἐκςάσει, h. e. excessu, abstractio- ne, seu elevatione mentis a sensibus externis vel inter- nis, sed ita ut mens integra manserit Act. 10, 11. sive sine ea subjecit Jer. 1, 11. 13. De quo Epiph. adv. Ca- taphryg. Fuit & Abraham in ἐκςάσει non mentis, sed timoris. Fuerunt & Prophetæ, sed non in ἐκςάσει co- gitationum & rationis, mente sana loquuti sunt in co- gitationibq sobriis & castis, & non in amenti consternati- one. Somnia imagines dormientibq a Deo de rebus di- vinis immissæ fuere, ut apud Danielem passim: Oracula vero verba, quibus Deus res arcanas revelavit, sive externa tum ἀὐτοπροσώπως, tum per angelum: sive interna vel intellectualia, quibus per voces imagina- rias Prophetas allocutus est.

Distinguitur etiam revelatio hoc pacto, quod vel Symbolica sit, vel aperta; illa quæ facta tum per rerum imagines, in figura seu idea, tum per ænigmata; ibi ea- dem, quæ videbantur, hic alia, quam videbantur, si- gnificata sunt. Hæc autem facta est, perspicua & e- videnti voluntatis divinæ significatione, sine Sym- bolis, figuris, vel ænigmatibus.

Augustinus Steuchus Propheticarum revelatio- num quinq. genera constituit e Num. 12, 6. 7. 1. בַּמַּרְאָה per visionem, cum rem in visionibus oblatam, intui- ti sunt Prophetæ, 2. בַּחֲלוֹם in somnio, quod contigit dormientibus objectis internis visionibus. 3. בְּחִידוֹת in ænigmatibus, cum aliud videbatur, aliud innuebatur. 4. בִּתְמֻנָה in figura, vel idea, cum rerum imagines exhibebantur. 5. פֶּה אֶל־פֶּה ab ore ad os, quo Moses veluti amicus cum amico familiariter cum Deo conversatus dicitur. Sed hi modi extra- ordinarii tantum sunt; ordinarii vero sunt tum per verbum, tum per Urim & Thummim. Verbum Dei erat tum externum, tum internum ad viros Dei fa- ctum per sensibilem, aut etiam imaginariam repræ- sentationem, ex qua conceptus nascebantur, aut per cognitionis infusionem, vel irradiationem, quæ neque a sensu, neque ab imaginatione originem ducebat, sed immediate oriebatur per lumen intellectui affusum, per species intellectuales de novo inditas, aut præe- xistentes etiam, sed divina virtute ad aliquam men- tis conceptionem formandam adhibitas, vel appli- catas. Manifestationem per Urim & Thumim, alii ad internam illuminationem referunt, alii ad vocis externæ perceptionem, alii ad visionem in pectorali Pontificis. Alioquin Pontificii plerique cum Tho- ma 2, 2. quæst. 1. art. 1. Suarez, Tannerus, Forerus, Cor- nel. septem species prophetiæ constituunt; qui con- ferri hic poterunt: (1) Ecstasin. (2) Visiones. (3) So- mnium. (4) Revelationem per nubem. (5) Vocem de cœ- lis. (6) parabolam. (7) Impletionem per S. S. Alii aliter illas sive species sive gradus prophetiæ assi- gnant, de quibus B. Hülsemannus l. c. qui distinguit inter modos concipiendi prophetias, qui vel interni, vel externi, aut potius intellectuales vel sensuales de- signati Num. 12, 6. intellectualis modus est, qui fit per illustrationem mentis sine mediatione vocis, aut i- maginis cujusdam ostensione, 2. Sam. 33, 2. sensualis, qui fit mediatione externorum sensuum eaque vel vera, vel analogica. Vera mediatio externorum sen- suum est, quando Prophetis Deus eventus futuros specie aliqua visibili adumbravit, uti Jer. ollam & virgam vidit, c. 1, 13. vel voce audibili, seu immedia- te, ut Mosi Num. 12, 8. seu per angelum, ut Zach. Luc. 1. Modus sensibilis analogicus est, qui fit per internam visionem Es. 29. 11. vel per ecstasin Dan. 8, 1. vel per so- mnia Num. 11, 3. Jer. 23, 25.

Alterum requisitum cognitionis Propheticæ est judicium ortum ex lumine Prophetico, quo elevatur & illustratur intellectus Prophetarum, ut dignoscant & dijudicent, quæ sunt repræsentata. Nam sola re- præsentatio imaginum non faciebat Prophetam, uti Pharaoni tales repræsentatæ sunt, Nebucadnezari, Baltasari, sed non intellexerunt, quæ viderunt, nec Prophetæ erant. Quanquam vero Prophetæ veri etiam non semper intellexerint, quid visa notarent, successive tamen eorum significationem accepe- runt, ut exemplo Dan. & Zach. constat. Vid. August. l. 2. de Gen. ad lit. c. 17. Secus autem se habet in iis, qui per transitum, dicente Augustino, & οἰκονομικῶς ut Basil. in Proœm. Es. loquitur, forte vaticinati sunt. Unde Rupert. in c. 11. Joh. Caipham comparavit cymbalo tinnienti, quia ut hoc tinnitum suum non au- dit, ita ille vocis ac loquelæ suæ virtutem non adver- tit, neq; intellexit. Nam in verbis Cajaphæ, sensu pio ac falso prolatis, Spiritus S. alium sensum divi- num & salutarem intendebat. Isidorus Pelusiota l. 37. Ep. 15. Quid Bileamo, inquit, impurius, aut scelestius, & tamen ipsius lingua ad benedictiones Deus abusus est. Quid Caipha sceleratius, & tamen vaticinatus est. Et gratia quidem linguam ipsius, sed non ita men- tem delegit.

(2.) Finis Prophetæ ultimus est gloria Dei, & sa- lus hominum Prov. 29, 8. 2. Pet. 1, 19. intermedius est denunciatio arcanorum divinitus revelatorum, cum nempe ipsi spectantur ut Prophetæ, tametsi idem ut homines etiam quædam pronunciare possint non re- velata divinitus, in quibus ipsi falluntur, utpote cum conjiciebat Samuel Eliabum esse unctum Domini, 1. Sam. 16, 7. Hæc autem denunciatio vel verbis so- lum, vel imaginibus & actionibus absque verbis, vel u- trisque facta legitur. Illa fit (1) vel oratione propria, eaque vel simplici, ac humili, quam vocant הטיפה in- stillationen ex Job. 29, 22. vel eleganti, & sublimi, quam appellant מליצה a verbo מלץ dulcescere e Ps. 119, 103. vel oratione parabolica & allegorica, cujus ta- men sensus erat evidens, cujus forma dicitur משל Ef. 17, 2. vel (3) oratione ænigmatica, & ex allegoriis atq; figuris, quæ sunt difficiles, & reconditæ significatio- nis, constante: Ebræis dicta חדה a חדר acuere, quod non nisi acie mentis penetrare liceat, qualis currus fuit Ezechielis c. 1. Zachariæ visiones c. 1.

Ad denuntiationes revelati onum per res & signa referuntur etiam gesta Patriarcharum & Propheta- rum, qui in persona sua, vita & factis Christum & ejus Ecclesiam adumbrabant. Denunciationum mixta- rum exempla vid. 1. Reg. 11, 13. Ef. 20. Jer. 13, 27. &c. uti hæc exequutus est B. Hopfner. Proleg. in Mich. Porro referebant Prophetiam viri Dei vel sermone vivo ut Ef. 1, 10. Abraham itidem de filiis suis Gen. 27. Jacob de 12. tribubus Gen. 49. Josephus de 7. annis fer- tilitatis & sterilitatis Gen. 41. vel per literas Heb. 2, 2. Ef. 8, 16. c. 30, 8. Jer. 36, 2. quas a valvis suspendere consueverant, ut cuivis prætereunti paterent, ac postmodum a Sacerdotibus tabulas illas in archiva templi depositas, ac memoriæ posterorum asserva- tas esse, notat Corn. in Proph. Major. f. 21. Sanctius in Ef. 34. Denunciationes autem illæ Prophetarum, uti munia eorum, in tribus versabantur (1) Erant didacti- cæ, docentes tum credenda, tum agenda; quarum ratio- ne Prophetæ Theologi erant θεοδιδακτοι eminentissi- mi (2) Paræneticæ in hortando & dehortando sitæ, non sine comminatione quoad impœnitentes, & conso- latione fidelium ac pœnitentium, quum dicta & scri- pta eorum conciones fuerint maxime ardentes, & efficaces, quasi mallei petras conterentes, & ipsi præ- cones fuerint ac concionatores fœcundissimi, æque ac ef- ficacissimi. (3) Propheticæ specialiter ita dictæ, seu va- ticinatoriæ, qua futura prædicebant & imprimis de Messia, qui est σκόπος σκοπιμώτατος ut universæ Scripturæ, ita etiam omnium Prophetarum Act. 10, 43. vaticinabantur: de quo Theodoret. de curand. Græcor. affect. Sicut in regiam viam reliqui calles in pagis agrisq́; conveniunt, ita Prophetæ hunc Christum viam esse credentibus ostenderunt. Et de V. ac N. T. ele- ganter Augustin. l. de catech. vid. c. 4. in V. T. esse occul- tationem novi, in N. T. esse manifestationem veteris. De prophetiæ & Evangelii comparatione merito dici- tur: Prophetiam esse Evangelium signatum, Evangelium vero esse Prophetiam resignatam. Nec raro Prophe- tæ ab historia aut concione legali transeunt ad Prophe- tiam de Christo, & a Christo rursus redeunt ad histo- riam & res sui temporis, quod inter alia ideo fit, ut videatur esse Prophetia, non ordinata narratio aut hi- storia, unde in ea quasi in cyclade variegata & auro intertexta præcidunt sæpe historiæ filum ut Christum historiæ attexant, & intertexant;

vid. Hieron.in Of. c. 1. Prophetæ, inquit idem Hie- ronym. in c. 1. Mal. futurorum texunt vaticinium, ut præsens tempus non deserant, nam utriusque miscent sermonem & ex occasione hujus felicitatem prædicunt. Quod maxime fit, cum historia typus Christi fuit. Nam cum aliqua umbra sese ostendit Messiæ, aut aliquid, quod ipsius memoriam excitare possit, ex- citantur Prophetæ, & affectu magno in eum rapi- untur, ac in figura illa latentem explicant, salutant, & omnibus agnoscendum proponunt. Deinde quasi de stupore, & ecstasi seipsos recipiunt, ac ad institutam narrationem sese referunt. Ita solent amantes visa imagine aut re, quæ amati memori- am eis refricat, mox de eo cogitare, loqui ad eum, anhelare. Hæc enim est natura amoris.

Succedit jam (3.) Causa materialis, ad quam tum subjectum pertinet, tum objectum. Subjectum sunt certi homines, è quocunque vitæ genere, sta- tu & sexu, siquidem DEUS, penes quem nulla est προσωποληψία, non tantum Esaiam ex Regio, Je- remiam & Ezechielem è sacerdotali familia, sed eti- am Amosum bubulum vocarit, ipsum quoque fœ- mineum sexum in Miriam, Debora, Hulda &c. dono Prophetiæ ornarit, etsi alias ordinarie mulie- ribus docere non permittatur 1. Cor. 14, 34. 1. Tim. 2, 12. Fuit enim Prophetarum munus extraordina- rium. Quæritur hic de Sibyllis, an illæ etiam DEI Prophetissæ fuerint? quod incunctanter affir- mat Cornel. à Lapide, dum futurorum prædictio- nem solius veræ Ecclesiæ notam esse tueri vult. Quam- vis vero Augustinus lib. 18. de Civ. Dei cap. 23. vi- deatur Sibyllam Erythræam, ad eorum nume- rum, qui pertinent ad Civitatem Dei referre, non tamen nisi hypothetice ibi loquitur, & lib. 2. de Gen. ad lit. cap. 19. refert Sibyllas ad gentilium vates, non ad Dei prophetissas, è Jesuitis vero Sanctius in Ef. 8, 2. 3. 9. Sibyllas Spiritu Pytbonico vaticinatas fuis- se, asserit, & Maldonatus in Daniel. p. 596. op- ponit subitum furorem Sibyllarum inflammationi divini Spiritus. Quid de illis habendum sit, di- ximus in Isag. Theol. de Natur. Theolog. cap. 8. Non sunt Prophetæ aut prophetislæ DEI, nisi il- læ personæ, quæ à DEO immediate ad id è cœtu fi- delium vocatæ, & à Spiritu S. agitatæ fuere, ideo- que impii & infideles non possunt Prophetis & vi- ris Dei accenseri, etiamsi aliqua ipsis forte obtigerint vaticinia per transitum nempe, uti Augustinus loqui- tur lib. 3. de mirabil. Script. qui lib. 2. ad Simpl. Tantum, inquit, distat inter Prophetarum prophe- tiam, sicut Esaias, Jeremias & cæteri omnes fuerunt, & inter istam transitoriam, quæ in Saul apparuit, quantum distat inter loquelam humanam, & loque- lam asinæ Bileami; accepit enim hoc ad tempus il- lud jumentum. Multo minus mirandum est homi- ni reprobo datam fuisse ad mementum temporis affe- ctu transitorio Prophetiam, quando ille dederat, qui & asinam, cum voluit, loqui fecit. Non enim si quispiam aliquid quod ad sapientiam pertinet, dixe- rit, continuo sapiens existimandus est. Ita nec quis- piam, si aliquando prophetarit, inter Prophetas est. Unde B. Hülsemann. Prolegom. in Jerem. Divi- nos Prophetas in vera etiam Ecclesia, vel fide, vel professione esse, censet: uti enim cætera Spir. S. mata pomœria Ecclesiæ non egrediuntur Joh. 14, 17. ita Prophetiæ donum cœtui vocato- rum proprium est 1. Corinth. 12, 10. Joel. 2. 28. Ap.

19, 10. Neque Bileamum, antequam à vero DEI cultu propter avaritiam deficeret, professione for- tassis & fide fuisse extra Ecclesiam judicat, quam- vis per avaritiam defecerit. Caiphas vero, qui formaliter non prophetavit, etsi verba ejus in- stinctu Spiritus S. prolata, materialiter Propheti- am in se continuerint, professione fuit in Ecclesia Dei, Joh. 11, 51. 52.

Objectum res arcanæ sunt ab hominum co- gnitione remotæ, sive præteritæ 2. Sam. 12, 7. sive præsentis temporis, sed ratione loci absentes, aut alioqui non notæ 2. Reg. 5, 12. c. 6, 9. 1. Sam. 10, 32. sive futuræ, quæ tamen imprimis ad Prophe- tias pertinent; seu arcanæ sint & remotæ ab huma- na cognitione ob sublimitatem, uti sunt mysteria di- vina, seu alio respectu, quod adhuc sint futura con- tingentia, vel alioquin lateant, ut occulta & cor- dium cogitata. Non ergo recte Cornel. à Lapide Prol. in Es. objectum Prophetarum è Thom. 2. 2. q. 171. art. 3. definit res contingentes, id est, ab actu libero angeli & hominis dependentes. Nullum enim dubium est, vaticinia de Messia, ejus missione, & morte ad Prophetica oracula pertinere, ut & de re- surrectione mortuorum, fine mundi &c. quæ vero non sunt talia contingentia: Ideo Thomas ipse 2. 2. q. 174. art. 1. Prophetiam aliam facit prædesti- nationis seu rerum necessariarum, aliam præscientiæ, seu rerum à DEO quidem prævisarum, sed à li- bera angelorum & hominum voluntate depen- dentium.

(4.) Forma, à qua denominantur Prophetæ vel Prophetia est θεόπνευστος rerum abditarum notitia, quia inspiratio divina, & ut principium & causa revelationis efficiens, qua est actus Dei inspirantis considerari potest, & ut forma revelationis, aut verbi revelati, siquidem formaliter verbum DEI in esse verbi DEI constituat, quæ specificatur in Prophetia per istam rerum abditarum revelatio- nem & notitiam. Quum vero Diabolus ceu simia Dei suos etiam Prohetas, mentientes speciem di- vinæ revelationis, vel Pseudo-Prophetas habeat, eosque revelationum Præstigiis ludificetur, quæri- tur, quomodo dignosci possint revelationes divinæ Pro- pheticæ à Diabolicis ejusmodi præstigiis? Ejus rei cau- sa γνωρίσματα aliqua notanda sunt: quæ partim à modo & circumstantiis revelationis, partim à mate- ria, partim etiam à fine revelationum peti possunt. Quod ad modum, divinæ revelationes non sunt ambiguæ, vel dubiæ, quales reddit noxius & ater Spiritus, sed certitudinem indubitatam habent, ad- hæc majestate quadam singulari stipatæ, aut mira- culis confirmatæ sunt, quæ non nisi à causa prima proficisci possunt, aut ita efficaciter irradiant & percellunt intellectum, vel de sui divinitate ipsum convincunt. Quod ad materiam attinet, divinæ revelationes Propheticæ non nisi vera, utilia, & salutaria vere abdita patefaciunt, quæ soli DEO constare possunt, & eventu veritatem comprobant. Pseudo-Prophetæ ea tantum abdita revelare pos- sunt, quæ vel ab ipso dæmone, ejusque mancipiis patrata sunt, vel ab aliis ita effecta per certa docu- menta innotescunt, & secundum quid solum ab- dita sunt, respectu nempe ejus, cui revelantur: nec futura contingentia, aut ea, quæ in recessibus cordis latent patefacere possunt, nisi vel ab ipso Deo quando Satanæ ministerio uti vult, revelentur, aut Prophetis veris illi, & princeps eorum Satanas ea quæ ex revelatione divina habent, suffuren- tur. Denique Prophetia vera in omnibus tam præteritis & præsentibus quam futuris, tum ne- cessariis tum contingentibus, iisque aut ut pluri- mum aut æqualiter, aut raro contingentibus, in omnibus, inquam, est infallibilis & semper vera: falsa autem Prophetia de præsentibus potest reve- lare, non autem de futuris mere contingentibus, aut certe tantum per modum conjecturæ, & sem- per miscet falsa aliqua Johan. 8, 54. Unde hisce κριτηρίοις dignoscere jubemur Pseudoprophetas Deut. 18.

Quod ad finem, divina revelatio intendit infor- mationem & salutem hominum, quum contra dia- bolicæ præstigiæ neque informationem, neque sa- lutem hominis vere intendant, sed tum errores, blasphemias, scelera, superstitiones, idololatrias &c. tum perniciem & interitum hominis partim temporalem, partim & præcipue æternam. Sic Ti- resiæ vaticinium promittebat Thebanis victoriam, sed ea intentione, & lege, ut Creontis filius ma- ctaretur. Calchas prædicebat excidium Trojæ & successus felices, sed jubebat simul Agamemno- nis filiam immolari &c. Unde, etsi vera proferat quandoque Satanas & utilia, non tamen studio ve- ritatis, & in utilitatem hominis, sed in perniciem ejusdem.

Quantum ad effecta, vera Prophetia mentem Prophetæ illuminat, ut intelligat non tantum quid videat, sed etiam quid per illa visa repræsentetur. At Pseudo-Prophetia naturales tenebras non mo- do non discutit, sed & auget, utpote à principe te- nebrarum orta, imo & furore mentem Propheta- rum sæpe percellit.

Nonnulli hæc κριτήρια verorum Propheta- rum è Vet. Testam. colligunt (1.) modum reve- lationis insolitum Num. 12, 6. 7. 8. (2.) peculia- rem & evidentem vocationem Exod. 3, 21. (3.) Har- moniam eventus cum vaticinio Deut. 18, 22. 1. Reg. 22, 28. Jer. 28, 8. 9. (4.) Consensum cum aliis indubitatis revelationibus divinis Deut. 13, 1. Es. 8, 20. (5.) Efficaciam doctrinæ in cordibus hominum commovendis Jer. 33, 28. (6.) Confir- mationem per vera miracula Exod. 4, 1. 2. cap. 8, 48. Quæ vero, uti faciebant ad generandam veritatem prophetiarum, ita libere tamen adhibita sunt, nam non omnes Prophetæ miraculis vaticinia sua con- firmarunt, quod de posterioribus imprimis Prophetis constat. Nam Deus voluit potius ad doctrinam Prophetarum jam satis confirmatam attendi, & reservavit miracula temporibus Messiæ Matth. 11, 5. Petuntur etiam certi Prophetarum Chara- cteres tum à rebus, visionibus puta insignibus & ad- mirandis, quales sunt Es. 6, 1. Ezech. 1. Zach. 1. va- ticiniis abstrusis sive sacris Es. 7, 14. Zach. 9, 9. sive prophanis 1. Reg. 23, 3. Es. 45, 1. Jer. 38, 17. majestate rerum tractatarum, sanctitate præceptorum; tum à verbis prorsus singularibus Es. 2, 22. c. 27. 1. &c. & vel admodum vehementibus, gravitate sua percellen- tibus, Es. 1, 2. vel admodum blandis & suavibus Es. 25, 6. c. 41. seqq. &c. tum à gestibus quoad habi- tum corporis 2. Reg. 1, 8. & mores in orando 1. Reg. 18, 42. Neh. 8, 7. vaticinando 2. Reg. 13, 16. Ez. 21, 2. Am. 7, 16. obtestando Neh. 5, 13. &c. Pseudo- Prophetæ ergo dicuntur tum qui falsa oracula in- stinctu Dæmonis fingunt, tum qui vera falsis in- terpretationibus depravant, vel ut Jerem. c. 23, 28. distincte eos proponit, qui vel somnia sua e- narrant, vid. 1. Reg. 22, 23. Jerem. 2, 8. vel ver- bum DEI docent, sed non vere, atque ideo di- cuntur verba furari à proximo, ad quam posterio- rem classem omnes falsi Doctores pertinent Matth. 7, 15. c. 24, 24.

Expositis ita causis, II. Definitio Prophetæ hæc emergit, quod Propheta sit Doctor, seu mi- nister à DEO immediate excitatus, qui res arcanas, humanam cognitionem excedentes, maxime autem futuras divina revelatione cognitas & intellectas denunciat, ad DEI gloriam & hominum salutem. Minus adæquata, nec nisi nominis aliqua expli- catio est descriptio Irenæi lib. 4. cap. 37. quod Prophetia sit eorum, quæ post fiunt, præsignificatio; etsi enim non diffiteamur primario Prophetiam dici futurorum prædictionem, versantur tamen Prophetiæ etiam circa res præsentes & præteritas. Pontificiis plerisque, Lorino, Forerio, Cornel. à Lap. Riberæ probatur Cassiodori definitio è Procem. in Psalm. quod Prophetia sit divina inspiratio re- rum à nobis distantium eventus immobili veritate & maxima cum certitudine prænoscens & prænun- cians: sed ea angustior est, quia Prophetia non versatur tantum circa futura, unde rectius Chry- sostom. Procœm. in Psalm. Prophetia est ejus, quod occultum est, inventio. Nonnulli è Pontifi- ciis ad veram Prophetiam requirunt etiam habi- tum perpetuum & immanentem. Sed hoc προσ- κείμενον non est necessarium, non enim cognitio Prophetiarum, & correptio Prophetarum per modum habitus continui, sed motus transeuntis fa- cta: uti Elisæus 2. Reg. 4, 27. fatetur, Dominum celasse sibi mortem filii Sunamitidis, & Spiri- tum Prophetiæ excitavit cantu musico 2. Reg. 3, 15. atque ideo irruisse dicitur Spiritus in Prophe- tas, factum esse verbum DEI ad eosdem. Quod agnoscit etiam Lorinus in Act. fol. 591. Bellarm. l. 1. de grat. c. 10.

III. Prophetarum numerus & Chorus hic è Sa- cris colligitur, (1.) Propheta dictus est Enoch Patriarcha, cujus Prophetia à S. Juda adducitur vers. 14. (2.) Abraham Gen. 20, 7. à DEO ipso ita vocatus, & censent nonnulli omnes Patriar- chas Prophetas fuisse; quo referri fortassis pote- rit, quod Jud. v. 14. Enoch septimus ab Adam prophetasse dicitur de Adami ἐκςάσει in Paradiso, & Prophetia habetur Gen. 2, 21. 23. 24. Noahi va- ticinium de diluvio habetur Gen. 6, 13. de fatis fi- liorum suorum Gen. 9, 25. Abrahami itidem de fi- liis suis Gen. 27. Jacobi de 12. tribubus Gen. 49. Josephi de septem annis fertilitatis & sterilitatis Gen. 41. Quia vero Patriarcharum nomen eminentius est, eo potius indigitari, quam Prophetæ vocari, adeoque ita à Prophetis distingui solent. (3.) Mo- ses, cui similis Propheta non surrexit in Israël Deut. 34, 10. ob quam ejus præ reliquis ἐξοχὴν & fami- liarem cum Deo conversationem, principalem, imo Regalem dignitatem, miraculorum illustrissimorum frequentiam, legis à Deo acceptæ, & inspiratæ publica- tionem, ac multa alia ἀξιώματα & propria, & pecu- liaria, Moses quandoque à Prophetis distinguitur, iisdemque præfertur, qui dignus habitus à Deo est, ut Christum, Prophetam illum magnum & Re- demtorem humani generis, eidem compararit, Deut. 18, 15. 18. (4.) JOSUA Successor Mosis repletus spiritu sapientiæ Deut. 34, 8. Num. 27, 18. multa habuit Dei alloquia, & apparitiones divi- nas, multas ex instinctu S. S. immediato conciones, ideo Propheta Domini dicitur à Siracid. cap. 46, 1. (5.) SAMUEL, qui inter Prophetas post Mosen exortos primus recensetur à Petro, Act. 3, 14. non quod alius inter Mosen & Samuelem nullus extiterit, sed quod alius expresso nomine in S. lite- ris commemoratus, sub hoc elogio, vel titulo non legatur: Fit quidem mentio Prophetæ alicujus à Domino ad populum missi Jud. 6, 9. sed ἀνωνύμως; nec ulla ejus Prophetia refertur, sed concio ἐπανορ- θωτικὴ solum; ideo Prophetæ nomen ibidem de Do- ctore extraordinarie misso, vel ordinario generali- ter accipi potest, aut si Propheta specialiter dictus fuit, allegari tamen a Petro non potuit, quia illius nullum vaticinium literarum monumentis consignatum legitur. Est & alius Vir DEI sed ἀνώνυμος 1. Sam. 2, 21. seqq. qui vaticinatus so- lum est de Eli abdicatione, & Samuele surrogan- do. Samuel autem ut insignis Propheta Domi- ni celebratur 1. Sam. 9, 9. Actor. 13, 20. ejusque vaticinia, & facta Prophetica instinctu S. S. literis commendata sunt. (7.) Misso Saule, & toto Prophetarum cuneo, qui Sauli obviam fa- ctus 1. Sam. 10, 10. DAVID, Rex, & Prophe- ta eminentissimus in censum venit, cujus Prophe- tiæ luculentissimæ non exiguam partem Scriptu- ræ S. faciunt, Act. 2, 30. Sequitur (7.) NA- THAN 2. Sam. 7, 5. qui tempore Davidis flo- ruit, ut & (8.) ASSAPH, autor aliquot Psalmorum. (9.) SALOMO nuspiam Pro- pheta exerte nominatur, sub Prophetarum ta- men numero comprehenditur, E. g. in illo Chri- sti Luc. 16, 39. Habent Mosen, & Prophetas, sub quibus etiam continentur Scripta Salomonis, & extant Prophetiæ ejus illustres maxime in Can- tico Canticorum. (10.) Mittimus denuo illos, qui 1. Reg. 13. commemorantur, utpote virum DEI de Juda, qui primus contra Altare Be- thel vaticinatus est, v. 1. & Prophetam senem, qui in Bethel habitavit vers. 11. Hi enim ἀνώνυμοι sunt. Nominatur autem AHIAS Silonites 1. Reg. 11. v. 29. cap. 14, 12. qui extinctionem Jeroboamo minatus est. (11.) ELIÆ Thesbitis maxime celebris Prophetæ, 1. Reg. 17. seqq. ut & (12.) ELISÆI 1. Reg. 19, 19. seqq. historia & vaticinia prolixiuscule describuntur. (13.) MICHA filius Jemla tempore Josaphati, 1. Reg. 22, 2. Paral. 13, 9. (14.) SEMAIAH 2. Paral. 11, 20. (15.) IDDO, 2. Paral. 13, 22. (16.) JEHASIEL, 2. Pa- ral. 20, 14. (17.) HANANI ab Asa captus 2. Pa- ral. 16, 7. (18.) JEHU filius Hanani. 2. Paral. 19, 21. (19.) ASARIAS filius OBED 2. Paral. 15, 8. (20.) ELIESER filius Dodan, oriundus de Ma- resa. 2. Par. 20, 37. (21.) ZACHARIAS sub rege Josia, 2. Par. 26, 5. (22.) OBED tempore Achaz. 2. Par. 29, 9. (23.) URIA filius Semaia, de Kiriath Jearim, Jer. 26, 20. 23. (24.) Quibus ad- dendi Prophetæ Scriptores Canonici, qui sub ti- tulo Majorum & Minorum Prophetarum veniunt in Codice Biblico.

E sexu fœmineno claruerunt MIRIAM, soror Mosis, Prophetissa, Ex. 15, 20. DEBORA, Jud. 4, 4. HANNA, 1. Sam. 2. HULDA, 2. Par. 30, 18. 22.

Nonnulli 4. classes constituunt Prophetarum: Prima est Patriarcharum. Secunda inde a Mose cæ- terorum, qui in Sacris commemorantur præter Ca- nonicos scriptores peculiariter ita nuncupatos, quique sua literis non consignarunt. Tertia Cano- nicorum istorum scriptorum, puta 4. Majorum, & 12. Minorum. Quarta Prophetarum N. T. qualis Zacharias Luc. 1, 67. Simeon grandævus Luc. 2, 34. Johannes Baptista, Luc. 1, 76. Agabus Act. 11, 28. Act. 21, 11. Paulus, qui de Anti-Christo vaticinatus est: denique Johannes Evangelista & Apostolus, cujus Apocalypsis plena est vaticiniis. Et e sexu fœmineo ELISABETHA mater Johannis Luc. 1, 41. MA- RIA mater Domini Luc. 1, 46. HANNA Pro- phetissa, Luc. 2, 26. VIRGINES 4. filiæ Philippi Evangelistæ, qui unus fuit e septem Diaconis Act. 21, 9.

Sed ob ordinem librorum Canonicorum im- primis huc facit distinctio Prophetarum V. T. in eos, qui Scripta Canonica adornarunt, & qui tal scripta peculiaria Canonica non adornarunt, qua- les fuere Elias, Elisæus, Micheas filius Jemlæ &c. Illi vel aliis illustrioribus appellantur nominibus, uti Moses vocatur Legislator, & ejus libri dicuntur Lex: David vocatur Psalmista & Hieropalstes, & Pro- phetiæ ejus Psalmi: vel Prophetæ nomen retinent, & dividuntur in priores & posteriores. Atque ita di- stinguuntur Lex, & Prophetæ Luc. 16, 24. c. 24, 27. Act. 24, 14. non quod Moses non sit Propheta, sed quia dignius est nomen Legislatoris, & scripta ejus legem continent maxime Matth. 5, 17. c. 22. 40. Da- vid vero Propheta, quia cumprimis excellens fuit in Psalmis, Israël 2. Sam. 23, 1. & Scriptum ejus Ca- nonicum Psalmorum nomine venit, à Prophetis di- stinguitur hoc speciali nomine, etsi Propheta fuerit excellentissimus: Et sub Psalmorum nomine com- prehenduntur simul Salomonea, ob analogiam, quia Canticum Canticorum instar Psalmi habet, & reliqui libri ejus Proverbiorum, & Ecclesiastes Psalmis ma- gis, quam Prophetiis analogi sunt dicendi genere Luc. 24, 44.

Porro Prophetæ priores nonnullis dicuntur, qui post Mosen ante discidium Israëlis à Juda sub Jero- boamo primo vixerunt, quod de autoribus libri Josuæ, Judicum, Ruth, ut & librorum Samuelis dici quidem posset, non item de autore libri Regum utriusque: nam hi scripti sunt post tempora Jeroboa- mi, & multo demum post Jeroboami I. regnum tem- pore JONAS, qui posteriorum Prophetarum an- tiquissimus fuit, floruit, annis centum fere & quin- quaginta discidio illo posterior. Alii ergo illos di- cunt priores, qui ante tempora Uziæ vel Azariæ filii Amasiæ, cui σύγχρονος in Regno Israëlis fuit JE- ROBOAM secundus filius Joas, vixere, posterio- res, qui Uzi temporibus, & deinde vixerunt. Quia Prophetæ illi, qui posteriores vocantur, & in Majo- res ac Minores distribuuntur, in Canone continen- tur, Usiæ temporibus, & sequentibus floruerunt. Etsi vero liber secundus Regum ultra tempora U- ziæ, & usque ad Zedeciæ abductionem sese porri- gat, neque de autore librorum Regum certo constet, quem nonnulli è posterioribus prophetis Jeremiam fuisse arbitrantur, alii vero diversos Prophetas hi- storias eorundem distinctis temporibus consignasse censent: libri tamen illi fere priores Prophetas, eo- rumque historias continent, ideoque adhuc ad scripta priorum Prophetarum relati videntur: quamvis, si dicendum quod res est, valde παχυ- λῶς sese habeat ista vulgo recepta, à Judæis profe- cta, in priores & posteriores Prophetas distributio.

Nec aliud judicium fieri potest de distinctione librorum sacrorum in נביאים Propheticos & כתובים ἁγιογράφως itidem à Judæis accepta, si ad accura- tius examen revocetur. Nam quum profecti omnes illi sint à Prophetis, perperam hi ab istis discrimi- nantur ita, ut istis solum relinquatur Prophetarum nomen, nec causa inveniri potest solida, quæ hanc distinctionem juvare queat. Nam Ebræi in quatuor Sectiones Codicem V. T. distribuentes priori, quam תורה Legem & חומש Pentateuchum vo- cant, appendicis loco quinque volumina libro- rum festivalium, utpote שיר השירים Canticum Canticorum, רות Ruth, איכה librum Thre- norum, קהלת Ecclesiastis & מגלּת אסתר volu- men Esther attexunt. Quod etsi ideo ab iis fiat, quia Canticum Canticorum in festo Paschatos, li- brum Ruth in festo Pentecostes seu Hebdoma- dum, Threnorum d. 9. Julii, quo templum u- trumque exustum, Ecclesiasten in festo taberna- culorum, volumen denique Esther in diebus Purim seu sortium 14. & 15. Mensis Adar, vel

Februarii in suis Synagogis publice ipsi legere consveverunt, non tamen ob illam lectionum sua- rum seriem debuerunt Sacra volumina ita discer- pi, & in ordine suo turbari; quum Ecclesiastes & Canticum Canticorum ad Proverbia Salomonis, ut- pote ejusdem autoris scripta, referenda, nec Can- ticum libro Ruth aut Threni Ecclesiasti præferendi, neque isti à libro Jeremiæ divellendi, neque liber Ruth à prioribus Prophetis sequestrandus, nec de- nique volumen Esther cum cæteris illis Legi atte- xendi, ac libris Historicis Josuæ, Judicum præpo- nendi fuerunt.

Porro cum in altera Sectione constituunt sub titulo נְבִיאִים רִאשׁוֹנִים Prophetarum prio- rum librum Josuæ, Judicum, duos Samuelis, & duos Regum, in tertia sub titulo נְבִיאִים אַחֲרֹנִים Prophe- tarum posteriorum, Esaiam, Jeremiam, Ezechielem, & תְּרֵי עֲשַׂר vel תְּרֵיסַר Duodecim Prophetas scil. Minores, in quinta denique sectione כְּתוּבִים vel Hagiographa sistunt, eaque vocitent תְּהִלִים Psal- mos מִשְׁלֵי Proverbia, Jobi, Danielis, Esdræ, Nehe- miæ libros, ut & דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים verba dierum, seu res gestas temporum, vel libros Chronicorum, non solum, uti diximus, minus accurati sunt in Prio- rum & Posteriorum Prophetarum distinctione; sed à prioribus Prophetis perperam etiam abri- piunt libros Chronicorum, qui parili utique jure ad eosdem pertinent, quo illis libri Regum ac- censentur: nec convenienter libros Chronicorum avellunt à Regum libris, illisque postremum lo- cum in codice Biblico assignant, utpote quibus plerique Prophetæ posteriores sunt Chronolo- gia, & tempore. Violentæ certe & plane inde- centes sunt omnes illæ separationes, quibus ea quæ conjuncta sunt, divellunt in ista sua distributio- ne, & ordinatione, utpote non tantum librum Ruth a Judicum Historia, & libros Chronicorum à libris Regum; sed etiam librum Esther ab Esra, Ecclesiasticis & Cantici Canticorum tum a se invicem, tum à tertio Salomonis libro nempe Proverbio- rum, Threnorum denique à Jeremia. Sed imprimis tamen castigationem meretur inepta librorum Propheticorum, & Cethubim distinctio, & iniqua Danielis e classe Prophetarum eliminatio. Distin- guunt nonnulli libros Cethubim à Propheticis hoc nomine, quod doctrinam potius, & historiam tradant, quam vaticinia: Sed ita distingui neque- unt à prioribus Prophetis: nec Daniel magis tradit historiam quam Esaias, & Jeremias, sed plenus iti- dem est vaticiniis. Deinde propter Poësin, ac Me- lodiam ἐξόχως & singulariter à Prophetis eos di- stingui volunt, quod de libris Chronicorum, Esdræ ac Nehemiæ dici nequit, nec etiam de libro Danie- lis. Hi enim Poësin non continent, quicquid sit, de libris Jobi, Davidis, & Salomonis. Nonnulli ma- jori verisimitudine Prophetas dictos ajunt, qui munus Propheticum obiere, quod in erudienda, & regenda Ecclesia consistebat: quales fuerunt illi tres, quos vocant Majores, & 12. Minores Pro- phetæ, cæteros autem, qui à Spiritu S. illuminati sunt, quum cæteroquin professione haud fuerint prophetæ, sanctos scriptores dictos: & tales fuisse Davidem ac Salomonem Reges, Danielem Nebu- cadnezaris purpuratum, Esdram Scribam legis, & Nehemiam, ut & Jobum Principes. Sed ista distin- ctione posita, liber Ruth, & Threnorum accen- sendi non minus fuissent Propheticis, quam liber Jo- suæ, & Judicum, imo hi etiam cum libris Samue- lis omnes Cethubim annumerandi erant. R. Da- vid Kimchi Propheticos dictos ait, quod per Pro- phetiam sensibus quiescentibus, vel etiam in visioni- bus, Cethubim autem, quod vigilantibus per Spiritum Sanctum dictati sint. Sed talis distinctio nullum fundamentum habet. Nam & Prophetis vigi- lantibus non pauca sunt dictata, si non pleraque, & visiones habuit Daniel non minus, quam alii Prophetæ.

Cæterum Hagiographorum, quæ Epiphanius γραφεĩα vocat, duos ordines constituunt, ut vi- dere est apud Hontinger. in Thes. Phil. lib. 2. c. 1. In primo ponuntur חֲמֵשׁ מְגִלּוֹת quinque libelli κατ’ ἐξοχὴν ita dicti, & per annum in festis legi so- liti, Canticum, Ruth, Threni, Ecclesiastes, & Esther: in secundo autem ordine sex libri habentur, tres Poëtici, Psalmorum, Proverbiorum & Jobi, unus Propheticus Danielis, & duo Historici Esdræ (& Nehemiæ) ac verba dierum.

Quomodo autem ad saniorem sensum illa trichotomia Codicis Biblici Vet. Test. in legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa, missa festivalium li- brorum ad legem revocatione, reduci queat, in System. Theol. ostendimus, quo pacto Hiero- nym. in prolog. Galeato eandem retinuit, libros numerans in universum 22. nempe Quinque Mo- saicos: Propheticorum octo: priorum scil. quatuor Josuæ, Judicum cum annexo libro Ruth, Samue- lis & Regum: posteriorum itidem quatuor Esaiæ, Je- remiæ cum annexis Threnis, Ezechielis, & duode- cim minorum Prophetarum, qui ob brevitatem vo- luminum pro uno censentur, Hagiographorum de- nique novem, ut sunt Psalmi, Proverbia, Ecclesi- astes, Canticum Canticorum, Jobus, Daniel, Esdras, cum annexo Nehemia, historia Esther; denique verba dierum, ceu veteris Instrumenti Epitome. Paulo aliter ordinantur & proponuntur libri sacri à Josepho apud Eusebium lib. 3. Histor. Eccles. c. 9. quo præter quinque Mosaicos, tredecim Prophe- ticos & quatuor Hymnos, ac præceptorum vitæ humanæ designavit: ut hi quidem sint Psalmi, Pro- verbia, Ecclesiastes & Canticum, illi vero Josua, Ju- dicum & Ruth, Samuelis, Regum, Paralipomenon, Esdræ, Esther, Jobi, Esaiæ, Jeremiæ cum Threnis, Ezechiel, Daniel & Prophetæ minores. Quam pe- riochen etiam Philonem tradidisse, notat Sixtus Senenfis Bibl. 4. p. 2. atque eandem etiam retinu- isse videtur Christus, utpote tum usitatam, o- mnesque libros canonicos adæquate complecten- tem, cum in legem, Psalmos, & Prophetas Scriptu- riam distribuit Luc. 24, 44.

De distinctione Prophetarum, intuitu tem- poris ante captivitatem Babylonicam, circa & post eandem, quia ea concernit Prophetas, quos vo- cant, posteriores, in earum limine acturi sumus.
