Quum plerisque Theologis placeat juxta mate- riam instituta τριχοτομία in Historicos, qui cum Mosaico Pentateucho comprehensi sunt, quos Prophetarum priorum nomine Ebræi vocant, in- cluso tamen libro Ruth, Esther, ut & Jobi histo- ria: Poeticos, qui cum Psalmis sunt libri Salo- monei: & Propheticos, qui absolvuntur quatuor Majorum & 12. Minorum Prophetarum libris, eidem ceu receptæ & satis convenienti inhæremus, neque Threnos à Jeremia cum Grotio divellimus, quo ordo maneat integer in Codicibus nostris pro- batus. Hic tamen, quia integras Grotii an- notationes exhibemus, ordini Grotiano inhærebimus.

Verse 9.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

# Joshua

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. Preface to Joshua

The book of Joshua takes its name partly from its ministerial author, Joshua the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chron. 8:29), whom many believe to have described his own deeds after the example of Moses among the Hebrews, and some even take the words of chapter 24:26 to mean this. He also wrote all these words in the volume of the law of the Lord: some refer only the diaries and annals, or the material, to Joshua, but attribute the order and form of the book either to Ezra with Masius, or to Samuel with Abulensis, or to Eleazar the High Priest; nor is there any doubt that at least those things which happened only after the death of Joshua, chapter 15 concerning Achsah, chapter 19:47 concerning the sons of Dan, with the very history of his death in chapter 24, were added by another, which seems to have been done by Samuel: compare what is said at Judges 18:7; partly from the subject matter, because it describes the deeds of Joshua and his death, which were accomplished by him after the departure of Moses, as his successor in the leadership, until the end of his life, in the occupation and distribution of Canaan, and also in the constitution and government of the Republic in the same land. Moreover, Joshua was not only the supreme Prince and Commander of Israel, in whom you may best find the idea of a perfect prince governing all things excellently both in war and in peace, but also a notable Prophet, and familiar with God, whose book holds the first place among the former Prophets after the law of Moses: compare Ecclesiasticus 46:1; and also a glorious victor and triumpher, who, having expelled the Canaanites, brought the Israelites into the land of Canaan. And therefore he bore an excellent type of Christ, by whose name he was also distinguished, having previously been called Hoshea (Num. 13:17), which both appellations, הוֹשֵׁעַ and יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, are of the same signification and denote a savior. Whence Jerome, in his Epistle to Paulinus: Jesus Nave presents a type of the Lord not only in his deeds but also in his name: he crosses the Jordan, subverts the kingdoms of enemies, divides the land to the victorious people, and assigns the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem to individual cities, villages, mountains, rivers, torrents, and borders.

Now the life of Joshua, since it relates to three states—the first of servitude in Egypt, where he was born for 53 years; the second in the pilgrimage in the desert for 40 years, in which he defeated Amalek (Ex. 17:10), and Og, and Sihon, and other enemies; the third in the leadership—this last one alone pertains to this history, concerning the years of which Serarius reviews various opinions, but the better view is that he presided for 17 years, as Venerable Bede, Genebrard, Salianus, Torniell, Adrichomius, Arias, Cornel. à Lap., Tirinus, Lucidus, B. Luther, Gerhard, Broughton, and most others think, and that he spent seven years in wars and ten years in peace and in ordering the Republic, since by living he completed 110 years (ch. 24:29), and after the seven years of war he was one hundred years old, when Caleb was 85 years old (ch. 14:10), than whom Joshua was 15 years older.

The chronology of the book of Joshua, therefore, will be this: Moses died in the fortieth year from the exodus of the Hebrews, which was the year of the world 2553, to whom Joshua succeeded and ruled for 17 years, that is, until the year 2570; and since it is believed that Eleazar survived Joshua by a decade, at whose death the book ends, it seems to have arisen from this that others have attributed 27 years to Joshua; which is true concerning the years of the book of Joshua (not of his leadership), therefore this history will extend until the year

M. 2580. In which way that opinion concerning the 27 years of Joshua, which pleased the Hebrews, Eusebius (lib. 10, Praep.), Clem. Alex. (lib. 1, Strom.), Augustine (lib. 18, de Civ. Dei, c. 21), Sulpitius Severus (lib. 1, Sacr. Hist.), and Masius (in Jos. 24), can be reconciled. The interpreters of Joshua, besides the general ones praised above, are Andr. Masius, Joh. Ferus, Nicolaus Serarius, Jacobus Bonfrerius, Arias-Montanus, and among our own B. Chytraeus, B. Balduinus (in his Sermons), as also among the Reformed, Lavatherus.

The book is conveniently distributed into the History of the deeds of Joshua: and a προσθήκην concerning his death, and the consequences up to the death of Eleazar. That History exhibits first the deeds performed at the time of war, and the subjugation of the Canaanites from chapter 1 to 11. Where the calling of Joshua and his confirmation and the first ordering of the same for the crossing of the Jordan Chapter 1, and the sending out of the scouts, who were received by Rahab, chapter 2, and also the crossing through the Jordan chapter 3, predicted and chapter 4, instituted, and the memorial signs of the same, pertain to the παρασκευὴν for the wars of Joshua, together with the circumcision of the people, and the celebration of the Passover, and the appearance of the Prince of the host of the Lord chapter 5. Furthermore, the victories of Joshua follow, both in the destruction of the walls of Jericho chapter 6, where the sacrilege of Achan intervenes chapter 7, and in the storming of Ai chapter 8, the consequence of which is the crafty submission of the Gibeonites chapter 9, and then with the five kings defeated while the Sun stood still in the sky, the excision of other cities, chapter 10, and then with Jabin and the confederate Kings overcome, the occupation of the remaining cities chapter 11. To which is subjoined an ἀνακεφαλάιωσις of the regions occupied on this side and beyond the Jordan chapter 12. Then the deeds performed under Joshua the Commander are handed down, in the time of peace, both regarding the distribution of the land, and regarding the remaining government. As for the former, it is repeated first chapter 13, the distribution to the tribe of Reuben and Gad, and to the half tribe of Manasseh made by Moses, afterwards preparation is made for describing the distribution chapter 14, and furthermore the casting of lots and the distribution by lot to the remaining tribes is subjoined up to chapter 19. Namely the tribe of Judah chapter 15. The children of Joseph and particularly the tribe of Ephraim chapter 16. The half tribe of Manasseh chapter 17, the tribe of Benjamin chapter 18, of the remaining tribes chapter 19. To the government of Joshua pertains the designation of the cities of refuge chapter 20, the assignment of the dwellings of the Levites chapter 21, the acts with those on this side of the Jordan chapter 22. The celebration of the assembly for the keeping of the law chapter 23, and after the final speech to all the tribes, the obligation of the whole people by a new covenant to worship one God chapter 24. Finally from chapter 24, 29, up to verse 33, and the last, it describes both the death and burial of Joshua, and the religion of the people after the fate of the same, and the burial of the bones of Joseph, and finally the death and burial of Eleazar.

Latin:

I. AD JO PRÆF

LIber Josuæ nomen habet partim ab autore ministeriali, Josua filio Nun, è tribu Ephraim 1. Chron. 8, 29. quem plerique res gestas proprias ad exemplum Mosis descripsisse credunt cum Ebræis, atque eo etiam quidam accipiunt verba cap. 24, 26. Scripsit quoque omnia verba hæc in volumine legis Domini: nonnulli solum diaria & annales, seu materiam ad Josuam referunt, ordinem autem & formam libri vel Esdræ cum Masio, vel Samueli cum Abulensi, vel Eleazaro Pontifici tribuunt; neque dubium est, saltem ea, quæ post mortem Josuæ demum contigerunt, cap. 15. de Achsa, c. 19, 47. de filii Dan, cum ipsa mortis historia cap. 24. ab alio adjecta, quod videtur à Samuele factum: Conf. quæ ad Jud. 18, 7. dicta; partim à materia, quia describit gesta Josuæ & mortem ejus, quæ sc. ab ipso post decessum Mosis, ceu successore in Principatu, usque ad finem vitæ expedita sunt, in Canaanææ occupatione, ac distributione, nec non in Reipubl. in eadem constitutione & gubernatione. Cæterum fuit Josua non tantum Princeps & Imperator Israëlissummus, in quo ideam perfecti principis optime omnia tam in bello, quam in pace gubernantis, eximiam invenias, sed & Propheta insignis, Deoque familiaris, cujus liber post legem Mosis inter Prophetas priores locum primum obtinet: Conf. Eccles. 46, 1. nec non victor & triumphator gloriosus, qui expulsis Canaanæis Israëlitas in terram Canaan introduxit. Ideoque typum Christi gessit egregium, cujus etiam nomine insignitus fuit, antea nuncupatus Osee Num. 13, 17. quæ utraque appellatio, הוֹשֵׁעַ & יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, ejusdem significationis est, & salvatorem notat. Unde Hieronymus Epist. ad Paulin: Jesus Nave typum Domini non tantum gestis, sed & nomine præfert: Jordanem transit, hostium regna subvertit, dividit terram victori populo, & per singulas urbes, viculos, montes, flumina, torrentes, atque confinia Ecclesiæ, cælestisque Jerusalem spiritualia regna adscribit.

Vita autem Josuæ, quum tres status referat, primum servitutis in Ægypto, ubi natus est per annos 53. alterum in peregrinatione in deserto per 40. annos, in quo Amalec Ex. 17, 10. & Og, ac Sihon aliosque hostes debellavit; tertium in Principatu, hic postremus solum ad hanc historiam pertinet, de cujus annis duodecim sententias recenset Serarius, sed potior est, quod per 17. annos præfuerit, ut Vener. Beda Genebrard. Salianus, Torniell. Adrichomius Arias, Cornel. à Lap. Tirinus, Lucidus B. Lutherus, Gerhardus, Brugthonus & alii plerique sentiunt, ac septennium in bellis, decennium in pace, & ordinanda Republ. exegerit, quum vivendo fecerit 110. annos c. 24, 29. & post septennium belli centum annorum fuerit, cum Caleb 85. annos habuit c. 14, 10. quo senior annis 15. fuit Josua.

Chronologia ergo libri Josuæ hæc erit: Moses ab exitu Ebræorum anno quadragesimo, qui fuit mundi 2553. mortuus est, cui successit Josua, ac 17. annis imperavit, hoc est, ad annum 2570. & quum Josuæ decennio supervixisse credatur Eleazar, in cujus obitu finitur liber, ortum inde videtur, quod Josuæ alii 27. annos tribuerint; quod verum est de annis libri Josuæ (non principatus ejus) ideo porriget sese hæc historia usque ad annum

M. 2580. quo pacto conciliari poterit sententia illa de 27. annis Josuæ, quæ Hebræis, Eusebio lib. 10. Præpp. Clem. Alex. lib. 1. Strom. August. lib. 18. de Civ. Dei c. 21. Sulpitio Severo lib. 1. Sacr. Hist. & Masio in Jos. 24. placuit. Interpp. Josuani præter generales supra laudatos sunt Andr. Masius, Joh. Ferus, Nicolaus Serarius, Jacobus Bonfrerius, Arias- Montanus, & è Nostris B. Chųtræus, B. Balduinus, (in Concionib.) ut & è Reformatis Lavatherus.

Distribuitur liber commode in Historiam re- rum gestarum Josuæ: & προσθήκην de morte ejus, ac consequentibus usq́, ad mortem Eleazari. Historia illa exhibet primo res gestas tempore belli, & subjuga- tionis Cananæorum à c. 1. ad 11. Ubi Josuæ vocatio & confirmatio ejusdemque prima ordinatio ob trans- itum Jordanis Cap. 1. & exploratorum emissio, qui à Rachab excepti, cap. 2. nec non transitus per Jordanem cap. 3. prædictus & cap. 4. institutus, ejusdemque signa memorialia, ad παρασκευὴν ad prælia Josuana pertinent, una cum populi circum- cisione, ac Paschatos celebratione, & Principis ex- ercitus Domini apparitione cap. 5. Sequuntur por- ro victoriæ Josuanæ, tum in murorum Jerichun- tis destructione cap. 6. ubi sacrilegium Achanis in- tervenit cap. 7. tum in Ai expugnatione cap. 8. cujus consequens Gibeonitarum astuta submissio cap. 9. tum devictis quinque regibus Sole in cœ- lo stante aliarum civitatum excisio, cap. 10. tum Jabino & confœderatis Regibus superatis reli- quarum civitatum occupatio cap. 11. Quibus sub- jungitur ἀνακεφαλάιωσις regionum occupatarum cis & trans Jordanem cap. 12. Deinde traduntur res gestæ sub Josua Imperatore, tempore pacis, tum qua terræ distributionem, tum qua reliquam gubernationem. Quod ad illam repetitur primum cap. 13. distributio tribui Ruben & Gad, ac dimi- diæ tuibui Manasse à Mose facta, postea præpara- tio fit ad distributionem describendam cap. 14. ac porro sortitio & distributio per sortem qua reli- quas tribus subjungitur usque ad cap. 19. Utpote tribus Juda cap. 15. Filiorum Joseph & peculiari- ter tribus Ephraim cap. 16. Dimidiá tribus Ma- nassis cap. 17. tribus Benjamin cap. 18. residua- rum tribuum c. 19. Ad gubernationem Josuæ per- tinet designatio urbium refugii cap. 20 assignatio habitationum Levitarum cap. 21. acta cum cis-Jor- danitis cap. 22. Comitiorum ob legis custodiam ce- lebratio cap. 23. & post orationem novissimam ad o- mnes tribus totius populi per novum fœdus ad colen- dum unum Deum obligatio c. 24. Tandem à c. 24, 29. usque ad v. 33. & ultimum, tum Josuæ mortem & sepulturam describit, tum religionem populi post e- jusdem fata, tum ossium Josephi contumulationem, tum denique Eleazaris obitum & sepulturam.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. THE WARLIKE DEEDS OF JOSHUA. SECTION I. ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΙΚΗ. CHAPTER I.

The confirmation of Joshua, and the preparation for the crossing of the Jordan. The duty of the Trans-Jordanic tribes.

Ver. 1. AFTER THE DEATH OF MOSES.

The 30 days of mourning having been completed Deut. 34, 18. and thus towards the third day of the month Nisan, on the tenth of which they crossed the Jordan chap. 4, 19. on the fourteenth they celebrated the Passover chap. 5, 10.

THAT THE LORD MIGHT SPEAK.

Some Papists say that this was done through an angel, especially Cornelius, whether by a spiritual locution or a corporal one in some assumed body: but these things are invented ἄτεργραφῆς. Intermediate persons are not to be introduced into divine apparitions and addresses where Scripture names none. Otherwise there will be no certainty whether GOD is speaking, or another in the place of GOD; nor will it be possible to be sure about the apparitions, whether they were made immediately or through an intermediary. Jehovah is said to have spoken these things, not an angel, verse 1. Moses was the servant of Jehovah, not of an angel, verse 2. Heb. 3, 5. Jehovah had promised this land through Moses, and was about to give it to Israel, not an Angel. Jehovah comforts Joshua with this promised assistance, not an angel, verse 5. Heb. 13, 5.

But because Jehovah speaks here about Jehovah, verse 9, 'Jehovah your God is with you in all things to which you shall go,' you will believe that God the Father rightly said these things about the Son, who is Immanuel, God with us, and chap. 5, 14, presented himself for assistance: who, being the same, had promised about the Son, the ὁμοοσίῳ, Exod. 23, 20. Which he does, because the Chaldean here translated it thus: 'As my word was a help to Moses, so will my word be a help to you.'

Same verse.

TO JOSHUA THE SON OF NUN, How the name יהושוע was changed in Greek into ἰησοῦς, see what we said on the first chapter of Matthew. The father's name ναυῆ seems to be a scribal error for ναῦ. Joshua was very fit for the command of war, clever in talent, brave in spirit, more severe than Moses. If anyone from other nations is to be compared to him, without prejudice to the distinction of piety and divine inspiration, I would take Cato the Elder.

It is pleasing to add what Grotius has learnedly commented there on this name, because the annotations on the Evangelical books are in few hands. That name which in the times of Moses was written יהושוע, after the Babylonian exile began to be written ישוע in place of ה and ו, which usage had worn away, produced under the vocal Jod. And thus we find it written in Ezra and Nehemiah, although Haggai and Zechariah retained the ancient writing. This had indeed come from the commerce of the Syrians, with whom it was accepted to omit letters of that kind. Wherefore the Syrian interpreter also writes this word in the same way. Thus from βαρἰωαννᾶ was made βαρἰωνᾶ. Thus the city צער is in Chaldean סגן, in Greek τάνις, and משיח Μεσσίας. To the Babylonians בבר, which to others is בער, thus שוחה is a pit for שוחת, and many other similar things among the Hebrews of later times, and among the Chaldean interpreters. But also the last letter of the word was at first lightly pronounced, as appears from the Latin word Josue and the Greek Ἀβίοσε, that is, ראבישוע 1 Chron. 8, 4. to which is similar ὠσηὲ from הושע, and in a similar letter נוכ vῶε gradually vanished from the letter itself, which ease of sound the Hellenist Jews followed and wrote ἰησοῦ with a circumflex on the last syllable, because almost all Hebrew names are written among the Greeks with an accent on the last syllable, as can be seen everywhere, which accent indeed, because of the syllable being long by nature, became here more produced, as also in μανασσῆ. But since such endings were unknown to the Greek language, and therefore did not suffer variation of cases, for the sake of easier construction two cases were fashioned in the Greek manner, the nominative with the addition of σ, and the accusative with the addition of ν. And so it is said ὁ μανασσῆς, τὸν μανασσὴν

(although we also read τὸ μανασσή above in verse 10) and ὁ Ιησῦς, τὸν Ιησῦν. Thus ἠσαυ̃ in the accusative case in Josephus. Thus Ἐλιᾶς from Ἐλιᾶ among the Greek interpreters. Otherwise these words remain indeclinable. For we say τἳ μανασσῆ, τῷ μανασσῆ, ὦ μανασσῆ, and τἳ Ιησἳ, τῷ Ιησἳ, ὦ Ιησἳ. And in this way that name is both written and declined, both among the LXX and among the son of Sirach, about which the writers of the New Testament changed nothing, distinguishing by no difference of Scripture this proper name of Christ from the name of him who, succeeding Moses and leading the people into the promised lands, foreshadowed Christ, the giver of eternal rest, not only by the sound of the name, but also by his deeds: as can be seen in Acts 7, 45 and Heb. 4, 8. Nor is any other meaning of this word to be invented than that which the Angel teaches us, ἀπὸ τἳ σώζειν, which manifestly agrees with the Hebrew origin. Jesus is therefore in Greek σωτὴρ: by which word Cicero says only that it is signified, so that it cannot be expressed by one Latin word. To me, it does not seem that a Latin word of the same origin and efficacy is lacking, but an older one, and one more accepted in sacred matters than in popular usage, namely sospitatoris. Moreover, that certain Christian writers, and indeed those not unskilled in the Hebrew language, derive this name from ἰᾶσθαι, in that they do not seem to me to have looked to another Hebrew word, but to have sought a Greek word which would cohere with the Hebrew ישע not only in meaning, but also in sound, in the manner of Philo, who loves to allude to Greek words in such a way that he departs as little as possible from the Hebrew notation. It is certain, however, that the Hebrew ישע sometimes means the same as the Greek ἰᾶσθαι, and sometimes, through a most accepted translation, the meaning of giving salvation is expressed by that word, just as in Latin one who frees another from trouble is said to heal the evils of another. Whence also ἰᾶσθαι is used, as in Matt. 13:15, Luke 4:18, and conversely σώζειν is used for ἰᾶσθαι, as in Matt. 9:21, Mark 6:56, Acts 4:9. Indeed, David Kimchi at Jer. 3:22 explains 'to heal' as 'to forgive sins.' And from this I think it happened that certain Jews living among the Greeks, and imbued with Greek literature, when they were called by this very Hebrew name, made for themselves the Greek name Jason, because that name of Greek custom would approach most closely to that Hebrew one both in the proximity of sound and in the meaning of its origin. Among whom was that Cyrenaean, the writer of the Maccabean history, of the same fate as Trogus Pompeius. But what is in Theodoret, ἰαῶ ἡ σωτηρία παρὰ τοῖς Εβραίοις λέγεται, seems to me faulty, and it should be written ἰασὼ so that it may be ישוע, for it is not unusual that ע be expressed in Greek by ω. These are the words of Grotius there.

Moreover, the name of SAVIOR is more emphatic, which is also more accepted among the Fathers. Because the name of Sospitator embraces the universal salvation which Christ provided by reason of goods both privative and positive, as they are called. But these are matters for another place. As for the etymology of the name, there is no reason why it should be derived from יהושוע, since it can be derived immediately from the verb ישע, just as the fowler יָקוּשׁ is derived from יָקַשׁ, or from the future יוֹשִׁיעַ 'he will save.' The Jesuits are accustomed to excuse their misspelling when they write the name IHESUS with an aspiration, on this pretext, that it descends from יהושוע. But the Syriac interpreter does not write the name of the savior in the New Testament with an ה, but without an aspiration, ישוע. Grotius derives that from the commerce of the Syrians. Irenaeus, in book 2, chapter 41, handed down a completely foreign etymology, which must be imputed to ignorance of the Hebrew language, but we do not wish to go further beyond the boundaries.

Latin:

PARS I. RES GESTÆ BELLICÆ JOSUANÆ. SECTIO I. ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΑΣΤΙΚΗ. CAPUT I.

Josuæ confirmatio, & ad transitum Jordanis præparatio. Trans-Jordanicarum tri- buum debitum.

Vers. 1. POST MORTEM MOSIS.

EXpletis 30. luctus diebus Deut. 34, 18. adeoque sub tertiam diem mensis Nisan, cujus decima Jordanem transierunt cap. 4, 19. decima quarta celebrarunt Pascha cap. 5, 10.

UT LOQUERETUR DOMI- NUS.

Per angelum id factum dicunt Pontificii nonnulli, imprimis Cornelius, sive spirituali lo- cutione, sive corporali in assumpto aliquo cor- pore: sed hæc finguntur ἄτεργραφῆς. Non inge- rendæ sunt personæ intermediæ in apparitioni- bus & compellationibus divinis, ubi nullas Scri- ptura nominat. Alias nulla certitudo erit, loqua- turne DEUS, an vice DEI alius? nec de appa- ritionibus constare poterit, factæne sint ἀμέσως, an mediante internuncio. Jehovah hæc dixisse fertur, non angelus vers. 1. Jehovæ servus fuit Moses, non angeli vers. 2. Ebr. 3, 5. Jehovah ter- ram hanc promiserat per Mosen, ac daturus erat Israëli, non Angelus. Jehovah parastasi hac pro- missa confortat Josuam, non angelus vers. 5. Ebr. 13, 5.

Quia vero loquitur hic Jehovah de Jeho- vah vers. 9. Jehovah Deus tuus tecum est in omnibus ad quæcunque perrexeris, Deum Patrem de Filio, qui est Immanuel Deus nobiscum & cap. 5, 14. sese stitit ad assistentiam, recte hæc dixisse, credideris: qui idem de Filio ὁμοοσίῳ promiserat Exod. 23, 20. Quod facit, quod Chaldæus hic ita transtulerit: Sic- ut verbum meum fuit auxilio Moysi, sic erit verbum meum auxilio tibi.

Vers. eod.

AD JOSUE FILIVM NVN, Quomodo nomen יהושוע Græce mutatum sit in ἰησοῦς, vide quæ ad primum caput Matthæi diximus. Patris nomen ναυῆ videtur scribatum esse vitium pro ναῦ. Fuit Josue ad belli imperium peridoneus, ingenio sollers, fortis animo, Mose severior. Huic si quis ex aliis gentibus comparandus sit, salvo pietatis & divini affla- tus discrimine, sumam Catonem majorem.

Adscribere placet, quæ ibi commentatus de hoc nomine erudite est Grotius, quia annotata in libros Evangelicos in paucorum sunt manibus. Nomen illud quod Mosis temporibus יהושוע scri- bebatur, post exilium Babylonicum cæpit scribi ישוע in locum ה & ו quæ usus detriperat producta sub Jod vocali. Atque ita scriptum reperimus apud Esdram & Nehemiam, quanquam Aggæus & Zacharias antiquam Scripturam retinuerunt. Nimirum ve- nerat hoc ex Syrorum commercio, quibus receptum literas ejus generis prætermittere. Quare & Sy rus interpres eodem modo scribit hanc vocem. Sic ex βαρἰωαννᾶ factum est βαρἰωνᾶ. Sic urbs צער Chaldæo est סגן, Græce τάνις, & משיח Μεσσίας. Babyloniis בבר qui aliis בער, sic שוחה fovea pro שוחת multaque alia similia apud Hebræos po- steriorum temporum, & apud Chaldæos interpretes. Sed & ultima vocis litera primum leviter pronuncia- ta, ut apparet ex Latina voce Josue & Græca Ἀβίοσε, id est, ראבישוע 1. Par. 8, 4. cui simile est ὠσηὲ ex הושע & in simili litera נוכ vῶε paulatim ex ipsa e- vanuit, quam soni facilitatem secuti Hellenistæ Judæi ἰησοῦ scripserunt circumflexa ultima, quia nomina He- bræa ferme omnia apud Græcos scribuntur cum ac- centu in Syllaba ultima, ut passim videre est, qui quidem accentus ob Syllabam natura longam factus est hic productior, ut & in μανασσῆ. Cum autem ta- les exitus ignoti essent Græco sermoni, ideoque casu- um variationem non paterentur, facilioris tamen constructionis gratia duo casus sunt effigiati in Græ- cum morem, rectus addito σ, & quartus casus ad- dito ν. Itaque dicitur ὁ μανασσῆς, τὸν μανασσὴν

(quanquam & τὸ μανασσή legimus supra commate (10.) & ὁ Ιησῦς, τὸν Ιησῦν. Sic ἠσαυ̃ quarto casu apud Josephum. Sic Ἐλιᾶς ab Ἐλιᾶ apud Græcos interpretes. Cæteroqui manent hæ voces ἄπλωτοι. Dicimus enim τἳ μανασσῆ, τῷ μανασσῆ, ὦ μανασσῆ, & τἳ Ιησἳ, τῷ Ιησἳ, ὦ Ιησἳ. Atque hoc modo no- men illud & scribitur & declinatur, tum apud LXX. tum apud Sirachidem, de quo nihil immuta- runt scriptores novi fœderis, nulla Scripturæ diffe- rentia distinguentes hoc Christi proprium nomen ab ejus nomine, qui Mosi succedens populumque ducens in terras promissas, Christum, æternæ quietis dato- rem, non tantum nominis sono, sed & rebus gestis adumbravit: ut videre est Actor. 7, 45. & Hebr. 4, 8. Neque alia significatio hujus vocis commini- scenda est ab ea, quam nos Angelus docet ἀπὸ τἳ σώζειν, quæ cum Hebræa origine manifeste consentit. Est ergo Jesus Græce σωτὴρ: qua voce tantum ait si- gnificari Cicero, ut id Latino uno verbo exprimi non possit. Mihi non videtur deesse vox Latina ejus- dem originis & efficaciæ, sed antiquior, & in sacris magis, quam in usu populari recepta, sospitatoris. Cæterum, quod Christiani quidam Scriptores & qui- dem Hebræi sermonis non imperiti nomen hoc ἀπὸ τἳ ἰᾶσθαι deducunt, in eo mihi non videntur ad ali- am vocem Hebræam respexisse, sed quæsivisse vocem Græcam, quæ Hebrææ ישע non sola significatione, sed sono insuper cohæreret, Philonis more, qui ita ad Græcas voces amat alludere, ut ab Hebræa nota- tione quam minimum recedat. Certum autem est Hebræum ישע modo idem valere quod Græcum ἰᾶσθαι, modo per receptissimam translationem salu- tis dandæ significationem ea voce exprimi, sicut & Latine mederi alterius malis dicitur, qui alterum ab incommodo liberat. Unde & ἰᾶσθαι ponitur, ut Matth. 13, 15. Luc. 4, 18. & vicissim σώζειν pro ἰᾶσθαι ponitur, ut Matth. 9, 21. Marc, 6, 56. Actor. 4, 9. Quin & David Kimchi apud Jerem. 3, 22. sanare explicat peccata condonare. Et hinc factum arbitror, ut Judæi quidam inter Græcos ver- santes, & Græcanica literatura imbuti cum hoc ipso nomine Hebræo vocarentur, Græce sibi nomen Ja- sonis fecerint, quod id nomen Græcæ consuetudinis ad Hebræum illud & soni vicinitate & originis si- gnificatu proxime accederet. Quos inter fuit Cy- renæus ille Maccabaicæ historiæ scriptor paris fa- ti cum Trojo Pompejo. Quod vero apud Theo- doretum est, ἰαῶ ἡ σωτηρία παρὰ τοῖς Εβραίοις λέγε- ται, mendosum mihi videtur, scribendumque ἰασὼ ut sit ישוע nam ut ע Græce per ω exprimatur, non est infolens. Hæc ibi Grotius.

Cæterum magis emphaticum est nomen SALVATORIS, quod etiam apud Patres rece- ptius est. Quia Sospitatoris nomen salutem uni- versam, quam ratione bonorum tum σερητικῶν, tum θετικῶν, uti vocantur, præstitit Christus, complectitur. Sed hæc alterius loci sunt. Quod autem ad ἔτυμον nominis attinet, non est, quod deducatur à יהושוע, quum immediate à verbo ישע derivari possit, ut à יָקַשׁ derivatur יָקוּשׁ au- ceps, vel à futuro יוֹשִׁיעַ salvabit. Jesuitæ excusare suam κακογραφίαν solent, dum nomen IHESUS per aspirationem scribunt, hoc prætextu, quod à יהושוע descendat. At Syrus interpres non per ה scribit nomen salvatoris in N. T. sed sine aspi- ratione ישוע. Illud autem ex Syrorum com- mercio deducit Grotius. Alienam prorsus ety- mologiam tradidit Irenæus lib. 2. c. 41. quæ igno- rantiæ linguæ Ebrææ imputanda, sed nolumus amplius extra metas.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. EVERY PLACE THAT THE SOLE OF YOUR FOOT SHALL TREAD UPON I WILL GIVE UNTO YOU) Just as in matters that belong to no one, possession gives right, so here, because those whom God has condemned to punishment are to be held as belonging to no one. See Deuteronomy 11, verse 24.

Latin:

Vers. 3. OMNEM LOCUM QUEM CALCAVERIT VESTIGIVM PEDIS VESTRI VOBIS TRADAM) Sic- ut in rebus quæ nullius sunt possessio jus dat, ita hic, quia pro nullis habendi quos Deus pœnæ damnavit. Vide Dev- teronom. 11. vers. 24.

## 1:4
Vers. 4. THE GREAT RIVER EUPHRATES) See what is said at Genesis 2, verse 14.

The boundaries of the promised land are defined by the regions of the world: Lebanon to the north, the river Euphrates toward the east, which is called the great river because it is most famous among other great rivers, and perhaps also the greatest in width after it has received the Tigris into itself: to the west the great sea, which is also called the western sea, namely the Mediterranean sea; the fourth boundary designates the desert lying between Egypt and the land of Canaan, toward the south: Compare Deut. 11, verse 24; Gen. 15, 18. Nor is the Jordan, but the Euphrates, established as the eastern boundary, which Cornelius rashly held to be the same as the northern boundary along with Lebanon; since these boundaries are openly distinguished in Moses and Joshua. Although indeed in Exod. 23, 31, the boundaries seem to be designated otherwise, in reality, however, four opposing boundaries are not noted there, but rather the length of the land from the desert to the river Euphrates, where, namely, it flows into the Persian Gulf, not to the parts of the northern river, is designated, as well as the width from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, or the entire maritime coast, which the Palestinians, under whom the Phoenicians, or Tyrians and Sidonians, are also included, inhabit along the great sea. Compare what is said at Deut. 11, verse 24.

Vers. same. ALL THE LAND OF THE HITTITES.

The Hittites are named specifically, as being the strongest, whom the Hebrews feared above the rest, among whom the descendants of the giants, the Anakim, remained, Num. 13, v. 34; yet under their name, synecdochically, the rest of the Canaanites are included, as in Gen. 27, v. last. Compare c. 82, v. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 4. FLUVIVM MAGNVM EVPHRATEM) Vi- de quæ ad Genesin 2. vers. 14.

Termini definiuntur promissæ terræ à mun- di plagis: Libanus ad septentrionem, fluvius Eu- phrates versus Orientem, qui dicitur fluvius ma- gnus, quia intra cætera flumina magna maxime ce- lebris, ac forte etiam latitudine maximus, post quam in se Tigrim recepit: ad Occidentem mare magnum, quod etiam mare Occidentale dicitur, ma- re scil. mediterraneum; quartum terminum desi- gnat desertum inter Ægyptum & terram Canaan in- terjacens, versus Meridiem: Conf. Deut. 11. vers. 24. Gen. 15, 18. neque Jordanis, sed Euphratis terminus Orientalis constituitur, quem cum Libano temere pro eodem termino septentrionali habuit Corne- lius: quum aperte distinguantur in Mose & Josua hi termini. Licet vero Exod. 23, 31. aliter videantur termini designati, revera tamen ibi non quatuor oppositi notantur termini, sed tum longitudo terræ à deserto usque ad flumen Euphratem, ubi scil. in sinum Persicum devolvitur, non ad partes fluminis borealis, designatur, tum latitudo à mari rubro us- que ad mare Pelistim, seu oram maritimam totam, quam Palæstini, sub quibus etiam Phœnices, seu Tirii & Sidonii includuntur, ad mare magnum ac- colunt. Conf. quæ ad Deut. 11. vers. 24.

Vers. eod. OMNIS TERRA HETHÆO- RUM.

Nominantur peculiariter Hethæi, utpote fortissimi, quos præ cæteris formidabant Ebræi, penes quos Enacim gigantum posteri supererant Num. 13. v. 34. sub eorum tamen nomine synecdo- chice cæteri Cananæi comprehenduntur, ut Gen. 27. v. ult. Conf. c. 82. v. 1.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. THERE SHALL NOT ANY MAN BE ABLE TO STAND BEFORE YOU.

If, that is, you persist in my commandments, and have not provoked vengeance by your transgression: for this promise is conditional, whence, because of the violated anathema, the Israelites were put to flight, and some were even slain, when they attacked the city of Ai. c. 7, verse 4.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NULLUS POTERIT VOBIS RE- SISTERE.

Si scilicet præceptis meis insistetis, nec trans- gressione vestra vindictam provocaveritis: hæc e- nim promissio conditionalis est, unde ob violatum anathema, salva eadem Israëlitæ fugati, nonnulli etiam cæsi sunt, cum urbem Hai aggrederentur. c. 7. versu 4.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. AND THAT THOU MAYEST OBSERVE TO DO ACCORDING TO ALL THE LAW, WHICH MOSES MY SERVANT COMMANDED THEE) Which law was to remain until the Great Jubilee, that is, until the times of the Messiah.

Concerning the law of Moses taken universally, this is false; nor can it be conceded by any reason concerning the moral law, which is the principal one, that it lasted only until the times of the Messiah, or that it ought to have remained so. The Messiah protests against this in Matthew 5, 17, 18, 19: Think not that I am come to destroy the Law, or the Prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the Law, till all be fulfilled. Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven. Christ pronounces anathema upon one who breaks the Law, and teaches the breaking of even the least commandment, so far is he from having broken it himself, or having taught or brought about its breaking or abrogation. There lies hidden a festering Socinianism concerning the imperfection of the Mosaic Law, which therefore ought to have remained only until Christ, so that a new and more perfect one might be sanctioned by him. The forensic law, which was proper to the Jewish Polity, not indeed immediately with the arrival of the Messiah, nor precisely because of the arrival of the Messiah; but with the destruction of the Mosaic Polity, which accidentally coheres with the exhibition of the Messiah, and because of the destruction of the same, finally in the most recent ruin

made at Jerusalem, has been abolished. Finally, the ceremonial law was brought to an end not so much by the arrival of the Messiah as by his death and the reformation that followed the removal of the Scepter from Zion and the ministry of the Apostles, in a due and decent order. For the Jewish Synagogue was to be buried with honor.

Verse same. DO NOT TURN ASIDE FROM IT TO THE RIGHT OR TO THE LEFT.

It can be taken as a proverbial expression taken from travelers, to whom it is usually said that they should proceed by the straight and royal road, nowhere turn aside to the side, and leave behind the paths occurring on the right and left, as Bonfrerius and Cornelius explain, or according to the interpretation of the Hebrews, that they should not turn aside to the right by adding something, or to the left by taking something away, or that they should not admit excess or defect, but observe the middle, which pleased Megalianus also among the Papists.

Verse same. SO THAT YOU MAY UNDERSTAND ALL THAT YOU DO.

The Rabbis explain it as 'that you may prosper,' with the Chaldean. But תַּשְׂכִּיל implies intelligence and prudence. Therefore rightly the LXX: ἵνα συνῆς. So also Pagninus, Masius, Serarius, and the Tigurines with the Vulgate. What is added, DO NOT LET THE BOOK OF THIS LAW DEPART FROM YOUR MOUTH, means nothing else than that the law is to be read frequently, as if this were the only study, to know what is consistent with the divine law, in which solid prudence consists.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET FACIAS OMNEM LEGEM QVAM PRÆCEPIT TIBI MOSES) Quæ lex manere debebat ad Magnum usque Jubilæum, id est, ad tempora Messiæ.

De lege Mosis universem accepta falsum hoc est; neque de lege morali, quæ præcipua est, conce- di potest ulla ratione, quod ad tempora Messiæ tantum duraverit, aut manere debuerit. Protesta- tur contra Messias Matth. 5, 17. 18. 19. nolite putare, quod venerim solvere Legem aut Prophetas. Non veni solvere, sed implere. Amen quippe dico vobis, donec transeat cælum & terra, jota unum aut apex unus non præteribit à Lege, donec omnia fiant. Qui ergo solverit unum de mandatis istis minimis, mini- mus vocabitur in Regno cælorum. Anathema dicit Christus solventi Legem, & docenti vel minimi mandati solutionem, tantum abest, ut ipse solverit, aut solutionem vel abrogationem ipsius docuerit vel attulerit. Latet ὕπουλον Socinistisum de Legis Mosaïcæ imperfectione, quæ proinde manere solum debuerit ad Christum usque, ut nova & perfectior ab illo sanciretur. Legem forensem, quæ Politiæ Ju- daicæ propria erat, non quidem illico cum adven- tu Messiæ nec propter adventum Messiæ præcise; sed cum destructione Politiæ Mosaïcæ, quæ per accidens cum exhibitione Messiæ cohæret, ac propter ejus- dem destructionem in excidio demum novissimo

Hierofolymitano factam, sublatam esse constat. Ceremoniali denique legi non tam adventus Messia, quam mors ejusdem & consecuta per emissionem Sceptri e Zion, & Apostolorum ministerium re- formatio, debito ac decenti ordine finem attulit. Erat enim Synagoga Judaica cum honore sepe- lienda.

Vers. eod. NE DECLINES AB EA AD DEXTERAM VEL AD SINISTRAM.

Accipi potest ut proverbialis loquutio a via- toribus sumta, quibus dici solet, ut recta & regia via procedant, nusquam ad latus deflectant, semi- tasque a dextris ac sinistris occurentes relin- quant, ut Bonfrerius & Cornelius explicant, vel juxta interpretationem Ebræorum, ne ad dextram declinent, aliquid addendo, aut sinistram aliquid de- mendo, vel ne excessum aut defectum admittant, sed medium observent, quod e Pontificiis etiam Megaliano placuit.

Vers. eod. UT INTELLIGAS CUNCTA QUÆ AGIS.

Rabbini explicant, ut prospereris cum Chal- dæo. Sed תשכיל intelligentiam & prudentiam infert. Ideo recte LXX. ἵνα συνῆς. Sic etiam Pa- gninus, Masius, Serarius, Tigurini cum Vulgata. Quæ adduntur, NON RECEDAT VOLU- MEN LEGIS HUJUS AB ORE TUO, ni- hil aliud volunt, quam frequenter legem esse le- gendam, ac si hoc unicum esset studium, scire quid divinæ legi sit consentaneum, in quo solida pru- dentia consistit.

## 1:9
Verse 9. BEHOLD I COMMAND YOU, BE STRONG, οἱ νόμοι ἀγορεύουσι περὶ πάντων, says Aristotle on Ethics, book 5, chapter 3. Also concerning Fortitude, τὰ τῇ ἀνδρείᾳ ἔργα ποιεῖν, ὅιτε μὴ λείπειν τὴν τάξιν, μηδὲ φεύγειν, μηδὲ ῥίπτειν τὰ ὅπλα, as the same adds.

For the third time this exhortation is repeated, BE STRONG, so that all fear may be driven away. Which fortitude is not to be estimated from natural things, nor learned from Aristotle, but implies a Heroic faith, which is obtained only in the school of the Holy Spirit. Which even the Jesuits acknowledge, who otherwise attribute much to nature. Cornelius says, there is need of huge and heavenly strength, so that we may overcome concupiscences, temptations, and all things opposing the law of God, and thus fulfill the whole law of God (which indeed the Apostle testifies is impossible for us after the fall, Rom. 8:3), for which reason God repeats here three times 'be strong' and 'be robust,' as is evident in verses 6, 7, 9, to indicate that he is in need of the threefold and supreme strength of the most holy Trinity.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ECCE PRÆCIPIO TIBI, CONFORTARE, ὁἱ νόμοι ἀγορεύουσι περὶ πάντων, ait Aristoteles de Moribus, 5. cap. 3. Etiam de Fortitudine, τὰ τῆ ἀνδρεία ἔργα ποιεῖν, ὅιτε μὴ λείπειν τὴν τάξιν, μηδὲ φεύγειν, μηδὲ ῥίπτειν τὰ ὅπλα, ut idem adjicit.

Tertia vice hæc adhortatio repetitur, CON- FORTARE, ut omnis timor pellatur. Quæ for- titudo non ex naturalibus æstimanda, nec ab Ari- stotele discenda, sed fidem Heroicam, quæ in sola Sp. S. schola obtineatur, infert. Quod etiam Je- suitæ agnoscunt, qui alias naturæ multum tribuunt. Cornelius ingenti, inquit, & cælesti robore opus est, ut concupiscentias, tentationes, omniaque legi Dei ad- versantia vincamus, itaque totam Dei legem exequa- mur (quod vero post lapsum impossibile nobis esse, testatur Apostolus Rom. 8, 3.) qua de causa ter repetit hic Deus τὸ confortare & esto robustus, ut patet v. 6. 7. 9. ut indicet eum trino, summoque robore sanctissimæ Trinitatis indigere.

## 1:11
Verse 11. PREPARE PROVISIONS FOR YOURSELVES.

Suppose from those things which remained from the spoil of the kingdoms of Og and Sihon, so that they might prepare stews and meats. Manna rained down from heaven daily; it was not to be prepared and kept for the following days. However, the Israelites were permitted to eat other foods besides manna, Deut. 2:6, 27, even if they had no bread other than that which rained from heaven, ch. 29:6.

Verse same. FOR AFTER THE THIRD DAY YOU SHALL CROSS THE JORDAN.

The command concerning preparation was not given before the sending of the spies, but after their return: from there, therefore, the three days are to be reckoned, even if here, by hysteron proteron, it is recounted after the divine apparition, which Jun. and Tremell. also note on ch. 2:1. For after Joshua undertook the leadership, strengthened by divine vocation and confirmation, he immediately sent out two spies from that place, Shittim, who, secretly sent away by Rahab, hid in the mountains for three days. When they had returned, he finally moved the camp from Shittim to the Jordan; and there for three days, he ordered provisions to be prepared, and other things necessary for the crossing of the Jordan, and on the following day, i.e., the tenth of the month of Nisan, he crosses the Jordan. Bonfrerius seeks other reconciliations, but ones by which he only aids the Vulgate version. To cross the Jordan for him is to go toward the Jordan with the intention of crossing it. But this is forced, and he himself finally slips into a hysteron proteron: the sending of the spies could have preceded those three days, even if it is narrated later. By no means, however, must one subscribe here to Augustine, q. 2 on Joshua, with some others: That Joshua, having fallen into error, ordered this to be proclaimed without consulting God, not from divine revelation, but from human hope, because he hoped, albeit rashly, that the crossing would happen after three days. This is by no means to be presumed of such a great leader, confirmed by the divine voice and performing everything at the divine nod.

V. same verse. TO POSSESS THE LAND. Some render the Hebrew word TO INHERIT, which would be an inheritance for them from Shem, to whom this land fell in the division according to the ancient tradition recounted by Augustine, Serm. 105 de Tempor., and by Serapion the Abbot in Cassian, Collat. 5, c. 24, and also by certain Syrians in Masius on Joshua, p. 11, which Dr. Walther approves in Harmon. on Joshua 1, 2, as being due; but because that tradition is uncertain, and the posterity of Abraham received the land of Canaan not by title of inheritance, but of donation, it is said to be obtained as an inheritance now in no other way than that it was so given by God that it might henceforth be possessed by hereditary right.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PRÆPARATE VOBIS CIBA- RIA.

Puta ex his, quæ ex præda regnorum Og & Sihon supererant, ut pulmenta & carnes parent. Manna cœlitus depluebat quotidie, præparari ac servari in dies sequentes non debebat. Permissi autem erant Israëlitæ cibis etiam aliis vesci præter manna Deut. 2, 6. 27. etsi panem alium quam illum cœlo deplutum non haberent c. 29, 6.

Vers. eod. QUONIAM POST DIEM TER- TIUM TRANSIBIT JORDANEM.

Non traditum præceptum de præparatione fuit ante missionem exploratorum, sed post re- ditum eorum: inde ergo inchoandum est triduum, etsi per hysteron proteron hic, post apparitionem divinam recenseatur, quod etiam notant Jun. & Tremell. ad c. 2, 1. Nam postquam suscepit divina vocatione ac confirmatione roboratus Principa- tum Josua, statim ex isto loco Setim exploratores duos emisit, qui a Rahab occulte dimissi per tridu- um in montanis delituere. Illis reversis demum e Setim ad Jordanem movit castra; ibique per tri- duum, parari jussit cibaria, & alia ad Jordanis tran- situm necessaria, ac postera die, h. e. decima Men- sis Nisan Jordanem transit. Bonfrerius alias quæ- rit conciliationes, sed quibus solum versionem Vulgatam juvet. Jordanem transire ipsi est versus Jordanem eo animo ire, ut transeant. Sed hoc coa- ctum est, & labitur ipse tandem ad ὑστερολογίαν: exploratorum missio tres illos dies præire potuit, etsi po- sterius narretur. Nullatenus vero cum nonnullis Augustino q. 2. in Jos. hic subscribendum: Quod errore lapsus Josua inconsulto Deo id edici præ- ceperit, non ex revelatione divina, sed spe huma- na, quod post triduum, licet temere, sperarit tran- situm futurum. Quod de tanto duce, divina vo- ce confirmato & ad divinum nutum omnia pera- gente, præsumendum minime est.

V. eod. AD POSSIDENDAM TERRAM. Ebræam vocem reddunt nonnulli AD HÆ- REDITANDUM, quod esset hæreditas ipsis in- de à Semo, cui hæc terra in divisione juxta tradi- tionem antiquam ab Augustino recensitam Serm. 105. de Tempor. & à Serapione Abbate apud Cas- sian. Collat. 5. c. 24. nec non à Syris quibusdam ap. Masium in Jos. p. 11. quam approbat D. Walther. in Harmon. ad Jos. 1, 2. obtigerit, debita; Sed quia traditio illa incerta, nec titulo hæreditatis, sed donationis terram Canaan Abrahæ posteritas acci- piebat, ad hæreditatem nunc eadem non aliter consequutura dicitur, quam quod ita data sit à Deo, ut deinceps jure hæreditario possideatur.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. TO THE RUBENITES ALSO AND TO THE GADITES AND TO THE HALF TRIBE OF MANASSEH HE SAID.

Although this could perhaps be demanded by right from all by the tenor of the obligation made in Num. 32, there was no need for all, nor were all required by Joshua, and it is certain that not even all the warriors from that region across the Jordan were employed; since only 40,000 are numbered in c. 4, 13, whereas the number of warriors among them was far greater, as appears from the census of Numbers 26; therefore, when ALL MIGHTY IN VALOR are required in v. 14, it is to be understood of all the robust ones who were more illustrious in strength and military skill: since it would not have been advisable to leave that whole region, just recently snatched from the Amorites, empty and destitute of all defenders. Therefore, that the wives and children and cattle are ordered to remain there; this is to be understood only of the wives, children, and cattle of those who were to be deputed to the fight as mighty in valor above the rest.

Latin:

Vers. 12. RUBENITIS QVOQVE ET GA- DITIS ET DIMIDIÆ TRIBUI MANASSIS AIT.

Utut hoc fortassis ab omnibus tenore obliga- tionis Num. 32. factæ jure postulari poterat, omni- bus tamen opus non erat, neque omnes etiam re- quirebantur à Josua, & ne omnes quidem bellatores, è regione illa trans Jordina adhibitos esse con- stat; cum 40000. tantum c. 4, 13. numerentur, bellatorum vero longe major inter illos numerus fuerit, ut è recensione Numer. 26. apparet; ideo cum OMNES FORTES MANU v. 14. requi- runtur, de robustis quibusque, qui fortitudine, & rei militaris peritia illustriores erant, id intelligen- dum: siquidem totam istam regionem Amorrhæis paulo ante ereptam propugnatoribus omnibus vacuam & destitutam relinquere consultum haud fuerit. Quod ergo uxores & filii ac jumenta re- manere illic jubentur; de illorum solum uxoribus, filiis, ac jumentis accipiendum, qui fortes manu præ cæteris ad pugnam deputandi erant.

## 1:14
Vers. 14. BUT YOU CROSS ARMED BEFORE YOUR BRETHREN) Among all citizens there is a partnership of arms just as there is of law. However, these words of Moses are not found elsewhere, but the sense is in Num. 32, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 14. VOS AVTEM TRANSITE ARMATI AN- TE FRATRES VESTROS) Inter cives omnes ut juris, ita & armorum est societas. Verba autem hæc Mosis non reperiun- tur alibi, sed sensus est Num. 32, 6.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. ONLY MAY THE LORD THY GOD BE WITH THEE) Do not be anxious about us, provided God favors you, all things will go well. This is the wish of those praying, not, as some think, of those stipulating. You will see what this expression, the Lord be with you, is worth in Judges 6, 12, Ruth 2, verse 4, Jerem. 1, 8, Malach. 28, at the end, Acts 8, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 17. TANTUM SIT DOMINVS DEVS TVVS TECUM) De nobis ne sis sollicitus, Deus modo tibi faveat, omnia se bene habebunt. Optantium hoc est, non ut qui- dam putant, restipulantium. Locutio hæc, Dominus sit tecum, quid valeat videbis Judicum 6, 12. Ruth. 2. vers. 4. Jerem. 1, 8. Malach. 28. in fine, Act. 8. 9.

## 1:18
Vers. 18. WHOEVER SHALL CONTRADICT THY MOUTH, AND SHALL NOT OBEY ALL THE WORDS WHICH THOU SHALT COMMAND HIM, LET HIM DIE) Shall contradict or shall not obey, namely contumaciously. This is the law of the King of the Hebrews: for the king was distinguished from a Prince among them, as we have said elsewhere, by pomp, retinue, and wealth, being otherwise equal in right. He who is condemned by this law is said among the Hebrews to be condemned for the cause of the kingdom, just as among the Romans for treason, and among the Greco-Romans for kathosioseos. In this one crime, goods were confiscated, as the goods of the posterity of Saul in the time of David, 2 Sam. 9, 7, and the judges used this pretext, although falsely, against Naboth, 1 Kings 21, 14, 15. It is truly a wonder that regarding this crime pertaining to the injury of kings, both kings by prevention, as they speak in the forum, and public judges have judged, as appears in 3 Kings 2, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34, and it is noted there by Levi

Bengerson, and David Kimchi. So great was the estimation of the Hebrews regarding the probity of their kings.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QVI CONTRADIXERIT ORI TUO, ET NON OBEDIERIT CUNCTIS SERMONIBUS, QVOS PRÆCEPERIS EI, MORIATVR) Contradixerit aut non obedierit, nempe contumaciter. Hæc est lex Regis He- bræorum: nam rex a Principe apud ipsos, ut alibi diximus, pompa, satellitio & opibus distinguebatur, pari de cætero ju- re. Qui ex hac lege damnatur, dicitur apud Hebræos da- mnari causa regni, sicut apud Romanos Majestatis, apud Græco-Romanos καθοσιώσεως. In hoc uno crimine bona confiscabantur, ut bona Saulis posterorum, Davidis tempore 2. Sam. 9,7. & hoc obtentu, quanquam falso, usi judices in Nabuthem 1. Reg. 21, 14. 15. Mirum vero de hoc crimine ad regum injuriam pertinente, tam reges per præventio- nem, ut in foro loquuntur, quam publicos judices judicasse, ut apparet 3. Reg. 2, 29. 30. 31. 33. 34. & ibi notatur a Levi

Bengerson, & Davide Kimchi. Tanta fuit Hebræorum de regum suorum probitate æstimatio.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. Spies of Jericho. Rahab.

Vers. 1. HE SENT THEREFORE) He had sent. Thus the passages are easily reconciled, above 11 and here below 22.

SPIES) Spying as here and Num. 13, the receiving of enemies as soon 4, the announcement of hostile counsels as 1 Samuel 17, 5, are odious things, and if they are detected, subject to grave punishments, yet they are not wicked against the enemies of God, or of him who has been anointed by God: for with such there is no communion of the law of nations. Therefore, the receiving which now follows is celebrated as an act of faith, Heb. 11, 31, of a mind, namely, renouncing polytheism because of the miracles heard. See soon 9, 10, 11.

HARLOT) That this way of life was considered at that time among those nations more vile than shameful, although the discipline of the Hebrews even before the law had been far different, Gen. 38, 24. You may not unfittingly compare Rahab to Aspasia, who from a harlot came to great power: and in later centuries to Theodora, married to Justinian. Rahab, however, seems to have lived in Jericho: but not to have been of the seven nations: because she was married to Salmon the Hebrew, as we have in Matthew, nay, and even to Joshua himself, as the Hebrews maintain.

Others, with the Chaldean and the Rabbis, render it as an innkeeper. But the LXX and the Apostle in Heb. 11, verse 30, explain it as a harlot, and Masius teaches from Talmudic tradition that she was a harlot, and Lyranus, Abulensis, Vatablus, Pagninus, Montanus, Jun. Tremell. etc., acknowledge it, along with Irenaeus, Origen, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Serarius argues at length on Tob. 6, q. 3, that in that age inns and public hostels were not in use. That argument, however, that she was married to Salmon the Hebrew, I do not know if it is solid enough to prove that she was not of the seven nations. For marriages with converts were not illicit: nor do they prejudice the law of Deut. 7, 3, and extraordinary examples, as is evident regarding Samson, that he did not take a Philistine woman without the direction of God, Jud. 16, 1. Therefore, just as she was preserved extraordinarily, so out of the ordinary she could also be taken into marriage, and that not without the counsel of God, so that in the Genealogy of Christ there might also be a Canaanite: as one who came for all nations, and had to become a victim for all. The marriage of Rahab with Joshua is rightly referred to among Jewish fables: which not a few interpreters, following Ignatius Epist. ad Philadelph., Jerome l. 1. centr. Jovin., and Chrysostom Serm. de martyr., maintain that he remained a celibate.

Of a similar kind is that Jewish tradition about these two spies, that they were Phinehas and Caleb. For who would admit that Phinehas the High Priest, already designated by God, and Caleb, very aged, were chosen for this very dangerous task, and when Scripture is silent about the persons, who would presume to name them? How ingenious and prompt the Jews are for any fictions can be evident even from another fable about these spies. For they trifle that only one of them, namely Caleb, was hidden by Rahab, not Phinehas: who said: I am a Priest: but Priests, being like angels, if they wish, are visible, if they do not wish, they cannot be seen. Furthermore, some rashly doubt about this mission of the spies, whether it was done by divine counsel? For Joshua would not have undertaken this without the nod of God, who had known the unhappy outcome of the previous expedition of spies, Num. 14. and in more serious matters he had been commanded to consult God through Eleazar the Priest, Num. 27, 21. And not only the mission made by Joshua, but also the reception of the sent ones is attributed by some to a divine precept, if indeed Rahab seems to have been taught about the whole future matter divinely, verse 9, by the force of which precept they pronounce her free from obligation toward her country.

One must certainly acknowledge the nod and direction of God, both that they betook themselves to the house of Rahab, and that they were received by her: nor is she with difficulty absolved from the sin of treason against her country, even on the ground that she knew that by the right of supreme Dominion that land had been handed over to the Israelites, and that for that reason the Canaanites had no longer any right in it, and that the destruction and ruin of her nation by the Israelites had been decreed by God: and that therefore she would try to prevent it in vain, nay, that she could not even lawfully do so, lest she oppose the decree of God. The Apostle, however, removes all doubt when he ascribes all this to faith: which, since it ought always to rely on the word of God, it is necessary that the holy woman was not destitute of the same: who in v. 9 confesses: I know that the Lord has handed over to you the land, that is, has decreed to hand it over, which it must be believed she knew not so much from the miracles which the Lord had performed while fighting for the Hebrew people, as from divine revelation. The Hebrews say that Rahab, by her faith and piety, merited that eight Prophets and Priests should be born from her lineage, namely, Jeremiah, Hilkiah, Seraiah, Maaseiah, Baruch, Hanameel, Shallum, Ezekiel, and Huldah. But these are fabrications. The Lord deemed her worthy of greater grace. Inasmuch as she was married to Solomon, a Prince of the tribe of Judah, and became the mother of David, Solomon, all the Kings of Judah, and the King of Kings, Christ, Matt. 1. Which, however, is to be attributed not to her own merits, but solely to divine mercy and grace.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Exploratores Jericho. Rahab.

Vers. 1. MISIT IGITUR) Miserat. Ita facile conci- liantur loca, supra 11. & hic infra 22.

EXPLORATORES) Exploratio ut hic & Num. 13. rece- ptatio hostium, ut mox 4. consiliorum hostilium nuntiatio, ut 1. Samuel. 17, 5. res sunt odiosæ, & si deprehendantur gra- vibus pœnis obnoxiæ, non improbæ tamen adversus hostes Dei, aut ejus, qui a Deo unctus est: cum talibus enim nulla est juris gentium communio. Itaque receptatio quæ jam sequitur celebratur ut actus fidei, Hebr. 11, 31. animi scilicet πολυθεΐαν abdicantis ob audita miracula. Vide mox 9. 10. 11.

MERETRICIS) Quod vitæ genus eo tempore apud illas gentes vile magis quam flagitiosum habebatur, cum longe alia fuisset Hebræorum etiam ante legem disciplina Genes. 38, 24. Rahabæ non male Aspasiam compares, quæ ex me- retrice ad magnam potentiam venit: posterioribus autem se- culis Theodoram, nuptam Justiniano. Videtur autem Ra- hab habitasse Jerichunte: sed non fuisse ex septem populis: quia nupta fuit Salmoni Hebræo, ut apud Matthæum habe- mus, imo & ante ipsi Josuæ, ut volunt Hebræi.

ALii cum Chaldæo & Rabinis reddunt caupona- riam. At LXX. & Apostolus Ebr. 11. vers. 30. meretricem explicant, ac meretricem fuisse è tradi- tione Talmudica docet Masius, atque agnoscunt Lyranus, Abulensis, Vatablus, Pagninus, Monta- nus, Jun. Tremell. &c. cum Iren. Origen. Ambros. Au- gust. Hieron. & contendit prolixe Serarius ad Tob. 6, q. 3. illo ævo non fuisse in usu cauponas, nec hospi- tia publica. Illa vero ratio, quod Salmoni Ebræo nupta fuerit, nescio, an satis solida sit, ut id evin- catur, eam non fuisse ex septem populis. Nam con- jugia cum conversis non erant illicita: neque præ- judicant legi Deut. 7, 3. & exempla extraordinaria, uti de Simsone constat, quod non sine Dei directio- ne Philistæam duxerit Jud. 16, 1. Proinde quem- admodum extraordinarie illa servabatur, ita extra ordinem etiam in matrimonium adscisci potuit, nec id absque consilio Dei, ut in Genealogia Chri- sti etiam Cananæa haberetur: utpote qui propter omnes gentes venit, & pro omnibus victima fieri debuit. Conjugium vero Rahabæ cum Josua inter fabulas Judaicas merito refertur: quem cœlibem mansisse Ignat. Epist. ad Philadelph. Hieronym. l. 1. centr. Jovin. & Chrysostom. Serm. de martyr. se- quuti non pauci interpp. statuunt.

Similis commatis est traditio ista Judaica de exploratoribus hisce duobus, quod fuerint Phinees & Caleb. Quis enim admittet Phineen Pontificem à Deo jam designatum, & Calebum valde grandæ- vum ad hoc munus admodum periculosum ele- ctos, & quum scriptura de personis taceat, ecquis eas nominare præsumet? Quam ingeniosi & prompti ad commenta quævis Judæi sint, vel ex alia de hisce exploratoribus fabula constare potest. Nugantur enim unum tantum eorum, Calebum nempe à Rahab absconditum, non Phineen: qui dixerit: Ego sum Sacerdos: Sacerdotes vero, quippe angelorum similes, si volunt, aspectabiles sunt, si nolunt, cerni nequeunt. Cæterum de missione hac explora- torum temere nonnulli ambigunt, an consilio divi- no ea facta? Non enim Josua hoc citra nutum Dei aggressurus fuisset, qui tam infelicem exitum prio- ris expeditionis exploratorum Num. 14. noverat. & in causis gravioribus Deum per Eleazarum Sa- cerdotem consulere jussus erat Num. 27, 21. Neque solum missio à Josua facta, sed etiam receptio misso- rum divino præcepto à nonnullis tribuitur, siqui- dem de re tota futura edocta divinitus videatur Rahab vers. 9. vi cujus præcepti eandem liberam ab obligatione adversus patriam pronunciant.

Nutum certe ac directionem Dei, & quod ad Rahabæ domum se receperint, & quod ab ipsa suscepti fuerint, agnoscere oportet: nec difficulter a peccato proditionis patriæ absolvitur vel ea ratione, quod sciverit ipsa jure summi Dominii eam terram Israëlitis traditam, ob idque nullum amplius in ea jus esse Cananæis, & decretam esse à Deo gentis suæ internecionem, & excidium per Israëlitas: adeoque frustra se id conaturam impedire, imo nec licite id facere posse, ne decreto Dei se opponat. Dubium autem omne tollit Apostolus, cum fidei totum hoc adscribit: quæ cum niti semper debeat verbo Dei, eodem destitutam non fuisse oportet sanctam mulierem: quæ v. 9. profitetur: Novi quod Dominus tradiderit vobis terram, id est tradere decreverit, quod non tam ex miraculis, quæ pro gente Ebræa pugnans, operatus erat Dominus, quam ex divina revelatione ipsam novisse credendum. Ebræi Rahabem fide ac pietate sua meruisse dicunt, ut octo Prophetæ, & Sacerdotes ex ejus stirpe procrearentur, scil. Jeremias, Helcius, Serajas, Maafias, Baruch, Hanameel, Sellum, Ezechiel & Hulda. Sed hæc commenta sunt. Majori dignatus est eam Dominus gratia. Siquidem Salomoni Principi tribus Juda nupta, Davidis, Salomonis, Regum omnium Juda, & Regis Regum Christi mater effecta sit, Matth. 1. quod vero non meritis ipsius, sed unice divinæ tribuendum est misericordiæ & gratiæ.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. AND THE WOMAN TAKING THE MAN HID HIM.

Vatablus renders the Hebrew text thus: But the woman had taken those two men, not only one as the Rabbis quibble, but each one of them separately, as Montanus rightly says, so that it is taken distributively, by a Hebrew idiom. The verb should be rendered in the pluperfect: because before the arrival of the King's messengers, when the neighbors were undoubtedly whispering about an investigation being instituted, she had hidden them.

Ver. same. I KNEW NOT WHENCE THEY WERE: AND WHEN THE GATE WAS SHUT IN THE DARK, AND THEY LIKEWISE WENT OUT) Before the Gospel, a lie beneficial to good men was not considered a fault. See what we have collected on the Law of War and Peace, book 3, ch. 1, § 16. And in the Annotations. This deed is praised, as being appropriate to that time, both in the cited passage to the Hebrews, and in James 2:25.

Lies were at no time lawful. Whatever is repugnant to the moral law today, has always been repugnant to it. As the Gospel did not abolish the Law, so neither did it bring new laws. For it is nothing else than the glad tidings of the remission of sins and the grace of God through Christ. Therefore it has no dealings with the law. Before the Gospel concerning Christ exhibited, or before the times of the New Testament, no lawlessness, and therefore no sin, was lawful, none was not considered a fault, just as it was under the New Testament. For in that, no diversity of these times can be fixed. But a lie is without doubt lawlessness, and therefore sin, 1 John 5, verse 4. Whatever God prohibits and condemns, that is, without controversy, sin. But He prohibited and condemned every lie even in the Old Testament, Lev. 19, v. 11. You shall not lie, nor shall each one deceive his neighbor. Ps. 5, v. 7. You shall destroy all who speak a lie. Prov. 6, 16. There are six things which the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests, haughty eyes, a lying tongue, ch. 12, 22. The Lord abominates lying lips, ch. 12, 45. The just man will detest a lying word. Wisd. 1, v. 11. The mouth that lies kills the soul. Eccl. 7, v. 14. Do not wish to lie any lie. There are no clearer prohibitions in the New Testament. Nor are they handed down there as new, but are conversely repeated and inculcated. And the Jesuits, who otherwise too much favor lying equivocations, acknowledge that a lie is by its nature a sin, not only by position, which Becanus proves in Tome 2, Opusc. 1, ch. 6, concluding thus among other things, from John 8:44. That of which the first Author and inventor is the Devil, cannot be anything but evil. Since, on the contrary, God is the Author of all good. But the Devil is the Author and inventor of a lie. Therefore, a lie cannot be anything but evil.

As for the example of Rahab, Junius indeed replies that it is not necessary that a lie be attributed to Rahab here. For others could have stayed with her as an innkeeper, about whom she answered, so that it was a work of divine providence that other guests were indicated from the truth and others were concealed by faith and charity: But setting aside that solution, if the exploration of enemies, otherwise liable to severe penalties, is not however wicked against the enemies of God, but the harboring is even deservedly celebrated as an act of faith, namely, of a mind renouncing polytheism because of the miracles heard, which Grotius thinks at v. 1, then the concealment made to the explorers, whether by words or by the deed itself, will not be wicked, who were sent against the enemies of God and by divine command. For one must obey God rather than men. Nor is the dissimulation of truth to be immediately considered a lie: and it is one thing not to tell the truth, another to lie, since in a lie there is deceit, which is not always present when someone does not tell the truth. Rahab certainly uttered whatever she uttered not out of evil intent, but out of reverence for the Divine; and not with a wicked intention, but a just one, of saving the legates of the supreme Lord, whose honor, glory, and authority piety dictates must be preferred far above all human ἐξουσία. And the common distinction of a lie is known from Lombard, lib. 3. Sent. Dist. 38, that it is either officious, or jocose, or pernicious. Which not a few defend in such a way that they acknowledge only the pernicious as a lie properly so called. An officious lie, when someone says or simulates something false, not rashly or out of some levity, or with the will to deceive or harm, but because the honor of God and the public safety, or that of one's neighbor, or even one's own, requires it, they by no means consider to be a lie in the true sense. Which things, however, we leave to their proper place. For since a lie is evil in itself, it is certain that it can in no case become good or licit. Nor can that which is formally and intrinsically vicious become licit from external circumstances, such as the end, time, place, or persons. For extrinsic circumstances cannot change the intrinsic nature of a thing. Whence the Apostle teaches in Rom. 3:8 that evils are not to be done so that goods may come; because what is evil in itself cannot become licit on account of the intention of a good end. Some indeed argue that when by lying we harm no one, but can benefit some, or promote a good, it is licit. Just as Plato with Socrates taught that magistrates, as physicians of the Republic, sometimes have need of a lie, lib. 3 de Republ., and the Sophists are observed to have handed down similar things in Clement of Alexandria, l. 2 Stromat.; and not only the Priscillianists, who taught that what is true must be kept in the heart, and to utter what is false to outsiders is no sin: in August. contra mendac. c. 2, and Origen defended that lies are licit in some case; but Chrysostom also, lib. de Sacerd. and in cap. 12 and 17 Genes., asserted that for the sake of duty a good man must sometimes lie, and also Cassian, collat. 17 v. 17, that a lie must be used as if it were hellebore, to ward off some great danger; indeed, Augustine indicates that this was an almost common opinion, Quæst. 68 in Levit.

It seems to almost EVERYONE that where no one is harmed, one must lie for the sake of safety. Abulensis even goes so far, q. 30 in Jos., as to say that Rahab was moved by GOD to a venial, officious lie, and that it is permissible to lie for the sake of some great good. But the Apostle's axiom in Rom. 3:8 contradicts this. The nature of a lie contradicts it, for it is evil in itself, falling upon undue matter; because words were instituted, as Durandus rightly says in lib. 3, Dist. 38, lib. 1, not so that men might deceive one another by them, but so that they might notify their thoughts to others. It is therefore an undue act when someone uses words to signify that which he does not have in his mind. Whence St. Augustine, Enchir. to Laurentius: Everyone who lies speaks against that which he feels in his mind with the will to deceive. And certainly words were instituted for this reason, not through which men might deceive one another, but through which each one might bring forth his thoughts into the knowledge of another. Therefore, to use words to deceive, not for what they were instituted, is a sin. Especially worthy of being read here are the things which Augustine wrote expressly on this matter; namely, his book On Lying, and his book Against Lying, of which a large part of the former is occupied with the discussion of the inquiry, while in the latter there is an open attack on lying throughout, as he himself noted in lib. 1, Retractat., last chapter. Also deserving of comparison are the things which Augustine wrote to Jerome on this matter in Epistol. 8 and 9, inasmuch as the latter had taught in his Epistle to Gal. 2, and had labored to defend it in an epistle written to Augustine, that Peter was only feignedly rebuked by Paul, and that Peter himself used simulation when he withdrew from the table upon the arrival of the Jews. Augustine brings forward arguments on both sides in his book On Lying to Consentius. scriptural passages, as to whether it is ever permissible, but he concludes in the last chapter: It is evident, therefore, all things having been discussed, that those testimonies warn a man of nothing else than that one must never lie at all. Whoever, however, thinks that there is some kind of lie that is not a sin, will deceive himself shamefully when he considers himself an honest deceiver of others. And in the book Against Lying, chapter 1, he teaches that it is not permissible to lie in order to convert heretics. How, therefore, shall I be able to rightly pursue lies with a lie? Or are robberies to be pursued with robbery, and sacrileges with sacrilege, and adulteries with adultery? But if the truth of God abounded in my lie, shall we also say, let us do evil that good may come, etc.? Therefore he warns in general in chapter 7. It matters indeed very much for what cause, for what end, and with what intention something is done, but those things which are established to be sins must not be done under any pretext of a good cause, no matter what good end, or what good intention. Likewise: if lies are just because they are done with this intention, that hidden heretics may be destroyed, then in this way, provided they are done with the same intention, adulteries could be chaste. Who is there who would say that we should sell false testimonies for the sake of vices? Who would say such things, unless he is one who tries to subvert human affairs and all customs and laws? For what most wicked crime, what most shameful disgrace, what most impious sacrilege would not be said to be able to be done rightly and justly, if we once concede that in all the evil works of men, one must seek not only what is done, but why it is done, so that whatever is found to have been done for good causes is not judged to be evil itself. Similar things to these are held in the Enchiridion, where in chapter 18 he asks whether it pertains to the duty of a just man to lie at some time? Which are finally resolved in chapter 22 as follows: Nor should any lie be thought not to be a sin because we can sometimes benefit someone by lying. For we can also benefit someone by stealing, if the poor man, to whom it is given openly, feels the advantage, and the rich man, from whom it is taken secretly, does not feel the disadvantage. Nor would anyone say that such a theft is not a sin. We can also benefit by committing adultery, if some woman, unless one consents to this for her, appears likely to die from love, and if she lives, is to be purified by repenting, nor will such adultery be denied to be a sin. If, however, chastity pleases us by merit, what, I ask, does truth offend, so that for the sake of another's utility the former is not violated by committing adultery, and the latter is violated by lying? A lie cannot be praised at any time just because we sometimes lie for the safety of certain people. Other Fathers follow the opinion of Augustine: Isidore, lib. 2, Sentent., cap. 31; Gregory the Great in lib. 18, Moral., cap. 14, etc. The Scholastics: Durandus, Bonaventura, Thomas II. 2, qu. 110, Art. 13. And most Papists: Sotus, Gregorius de Valentia, Becanus, and others. And Cornelius rightly and deservedly taxes Tostatus here: Those things, he says, (which were previously brought forward from Abulensis) are false and paradoxical. For God cannot be the author of any sin, since He is supreme purity, truth, and holiness. Again, it is not permissible to lie, even if the salvation of the whole world were to follow from it: For evil things must not be done so that good may come, nor is a lie necessary for saving another's life. But what he adds, that one can use amphibology in such a case, betrays a Jesuitical mind and one that is cauterized. For that deceit of equivocations is no less illicit than a lie, as we have shown elsewhere. Nor is Cornelius consistent with himself in this, that he now calls the woman a rude, pagan, and crafty person, and now a very sensible one in faith and piety.

Therefore, one must respond to the example of Rahab and other similar ones that the lie is not approved, nor was it permissible at that time, but other things are praised in Rahab, such as that she placed faith in the messengers of God, received them kindly through faith (Heb. 11:31), hid them, and sent them away by another way (Jas. 2:25). Augustine indeed uses another response along with the general one, that in the Old Testament not only words but also deeds are written down figuratively, because they were also done figuratively: In figures, however, that which is called a lie, when well understood, may be found to be true: lib. contr. mendac. cap. 12. Lib. de mendacio cap. 5. In the Old Testament, whatever was done can be taken figuratively, although it happened in reality. Whatever, however, is done and said figuratively is not a lie. For every statement must be referred to that which it states. Moreover, every deed, or word, or figure declares this, which it signifies to those for whom it was brought forth to be understood. Then specifically, that Rahab was not yet then fully converted, Chap. 12. And Rahab, indeed, having been liberated from Jericho, made a passage into the people of God, where, progressing, she could arrive at eternal and immortal gifts, which are to be sought by no lie. At that time, however, when she performed that good work, and one praiseworthy for the condition of her life, for the Israelite scouts, she was not yet such that it was required of her that there be in your mouth 'yes, yes' and 'no, no.' This is what Erasmus, or whoever added the marginalia to Augustine, interprets as meaning that they could more tolerably lie in the Old Law than in the New. But that this was not the mind of Augustine, who here considers only the state of Rahab, that she had not yet been fully converted at that time, is manifest from book 5 of 'On Lying,' since he proves from the Old Testament that one must never lie, not even for the salvation of a neighbor, since it is written in the Decalogue itself: 'Do not bear false witness,' by which kind, he says, every lie is encompassed. For whoever declares anything bears witness to his own mind. But lest anyone contend that not every lie should be called false witness, what will he say to that which is written (Wisdom 1): 'The mouth that lies kills the soul.' And lest anyone think that this can be understood of certain particular liars, let him read in another place (Ps. 5): You will destroy all who speak a lie. Moreover, because Rahab is commended for faith in the reception of the spies, and faith has no place except in the reborn and converted, the other response of St. Augustine, which he uses in the book Against Lying, ch. 17, holds itself more correctly. Therefore, Rahab in Jericho, because she received foreign men of God into hospitality, because she believed in their God, because she diligently hid them where she could, because she gave the most faithful counsel for returning by another way, is praised as one to be imitated even by the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. But that she lied, even if something prophetic is intelligently explained there, it is not, however, wisely proposed to be imitated; although God memorably honored those good deeds, He mercifully forgave this evil. What he explains in ch. 15, that it is written: that God did well with the Hebrew midwives, and with Rahab the harlot of Jericho, was not done because they lied, but because they were merciful toward the men of God. Therefore, it is not the deceit that is enumerated in them, but the benevolence; the kindness of the mind, not the iniquity of the one lying. For just as it would not be evil and absurd if God, on account of later good works, wished to forgive some evil works committed by them at an earlier time: so it is to be wondered at that at one time, in one cause, God, seeing both, that is, the deed done mercifully and the deed done deceitfully, both rewarded the good and, on account of this good, forgave that evil. It is therefore to be ascribed to infirmity that Rahab, placed in distress, when she knew not how otherwise to consult for the safety of the spies, judged that the legates of God were to be freed from most imminent danger by an officious lie, which was graciously forgiven her on account of her faith. Lorinus confesses this in his commentary on the Epistle of James 2, v. 25, and brings forward into that opinion against Joseph the Abbot, and likewise Chrysostom and Jerome, along with Augustine and Gregory the Great, Thomas and Innocent III. Tertullian, in his book On Modesty, places lying by necessity among the faults of daily incursion to which we are all exposed. Grotius, however, contradicts himself here: For while he here, before the Gospel, absolves from guilt only lies that are salutary to good men in his book On the Law of War and Peace, he asserts that the same guilt is absent in certain cases even under the Gospel: As one who would not take it ill, who knows of a lie, nay, who would even give thanks to someone on that account, because no injury is done to one who is willing. E.g., If someone consoles a sick friend with a persuasion that is not true, or in battle gives heart to one in danger by a false report, by which, being incited, he procures victory and safety for himself, and thus deceived is not captured: Likewise, as often as one who has eminent right over all the rights of another uses that right for the good of the other, whether his own or public: By which method he excludes Plato's opinion: Likewise, as often as the life of an innocent person or something equal cannot otherwise be saved for another and averted from the completion of a wicked crime: Finally, that it is permitted to use false speech against an enemy. He observes that this exception is added by Plato, Xenophon, Philo, and Chrysostom.
