In Ebr. quem apprehenderit Dominus. Rab- bini ita apprehensum dicunt, ut immotus stare coa- ctus sit. Alii per Urim & Thumim ostensum. Sed haec non conveniunt. Recte ergo de inventione per sortem explicat Vulgatus, cui consentit Jose- phus & R. Levi Ben-Gerson. Sic deprehensus forte dicitur Jonathan 1. Sam. 14, 42. quia forte directa a Domino, capitur & deprehenditur per sortem Prov. 6, ult. Et usus est Josua in distribu- tione terrae cap. 14. seqq. Unde liquet sortium usum simpliciter improbari non posse, nec solum in Vet. Testam. sortes adhibitae, sed etiam in Novo Actor. 1, 17. Non ergo subscribendum Chrysosto- mo, qui eam rationem inquirendi de rebus dubiis in Nov. Test. plane rejicit, & ad imperfectionem Veteris refert. Distinguendae autem sortes, qua- rum aliae divinae, aliae humanae, aliae Magicae & Dia- bolicae; divinae medium fuere extraordinarium, quae hodie non habent locum, cessante divina re- velatione. Magicae a Daemonibus ex pacto vel expresso vel tacito institutae, quin illicitae sint, nemo pius dubitat: ideo infame est fortiariorum nomen. Humanae aut politicae sunt, vel ludicrae, ut aleatoriae ac similes, in quibus vanitas vel temeritas. Politi- cae sua natura non sunt illicitae, quandoq; etiam necessariae, uti sunt divisoriae imprimis, quas vocant. Nam communiter, praeeunte Thoma 2. 2. quaest. 95. art. 8. distinguuntur in divisorias, qualis erat Joh. 19, 24. (ad quas etiam referunt nonnulli ele- ctiones personarum, quae per sortem fiunt) & con- fultorias, quando in rebus ambiguis, quid agen- dum sit, forte inquiritur: nec non divinatorias, cum quæritur veritas rei arcanæ, vel futuræ. Græ- ce alia fors dicitur διαιρετικὴ, alia βουλευτικὴ, alia μαντικὴ: Divisoriæ & Consultoriæ illicitæ non sunt, uti docet August. lib. 2. de doctr. Christi cap. 28. & Epist. 180. ad Honorat. & instituuntur de rebus arbitrio nostro subjectis, atq; nituntur autoritate legum, vel consensu sortientium, modo non im- misceat se fraus aut superstitio. At divinatoriæ su- perstitiosæ & illicitæ sunt, nisi Deo jubente insti- tuantur.

Quid vero de sortitione habendum per paginas Evangelii, quæ apud Christianos quondam inva- luit? Recte illam reprobat August. Epist. 119. ad Ja- nuar. cujus verba repetuntur Caus. 26. q. 2. cap. 3. istam sibi displicere ait consuetudinem, ad negotia secu- laria propter aliam vitam loquentia velle convertere divina oracula. Quæ enata videtur ex sortibus Virgilianis, quibus usi Ethnici, ex apertura ejus du- bia inquirentes. Quo pacto Mart. Delrio in Dis- quis. Magic. notat l. 4. c. 2. q. 7. apud Christianos huic vanitati gentilium successisse apertionem Vete- ris aut Novi Test. quam non sine impietate voca- runt sortes Apostolorum aut Sanctorum. Vid. B. D. Balduin. l. 3. Cas. Consc. c. 6. c. 9. Rivetus in ex- plic. Decal. p. 96. seqq.

## 8:14
Ver. 14. TOWARD THE DESERT.

In the Hebrew, which Bonfrerius also notes, [the phrase] at the appointed time is added, because once the Israelites were sighted, the King of Ai had proclaimed a certain hour at which all, equipped with arms, should be ready for a sortie, elated and secure on account of the preceding victory.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CONTRA DESERTUM.

In Ebræo, quod etiam monet Bonfrerius, ad- ditur ad tempus constitutum, quia conspectis Israe- litis Rex Hajensis certam horam indixerat, qua omnes armis instructi ad eruptionem parati essent, elatus ac securus ob præcedentem victoriam.

## 8:15
Verse 15. HE SHALL BE BURNED WITH FIRE) The men having been stoned first. Below v. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 15. COMBVRETVR IGNE) Hominibus prius la- pidatis. Infra v. 25.

## 8:17
Ver. 17.

AND NOT EVEN ONE REMAINED IN THE CITY OF AI AND BETHEL.

Naturally [this refers] to the fighting men, for verse 17 teaches that the non-combatant crowd remained. The men of Bethel are joined [with them], either because they were subject to the King of Ai, or because they were present having been called for assistance: since the men of Ai feared a siege.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ET NE UNUS QUIDEM IN URBE HAI ET BETHEL REMANSISSET.

Nimirum de viris bellatoribus, nam imbel- lem turbam remansisse vers. 74. docet. Junguntur Bethelei, sive quod Hajensi Regi subjecti, sive quod in subsidium vocati præsto fuerint: siquidem Hajenses obsidionem metuerint.

## 8:18
Verse 18.

TAKE UP THE SHIELD) Josephus here and Symmachus [use] ἀσπίδα. And certainly that seems to be the proper meaning of the word כידון from the passage 1 Sam. 17:6 and Jer. 6:23. Others, however, translate it as γαισὸν, and some explain it as an all-iron javelin or a spear.

Theodoret also understood it as Shield, and Pagninus and Arias rendered the Hebrew word that way elsewhere, as did the LXX, because in 1 Sam. 17:6, 45 they translated it as ἀσπίδα. The Tigurini, however, along with Pagninus and Montanus, more correctly have lance or spear here, just as the LXX have γαισὸν; Lyranus and Vatablus, along with the Rabbis, say it was an upright lance and a standard. The erection was made then as a sign of the army of Israel fighting under God and with God, who ordered it to be erected, and by that very act declared war, and also as a sign of rushing into the city for those who were in ambush: which reason not only Josephus, Theodoret, Abulensis, Lyranus, and the Rabbis give, but the text itself also indicates with the words subjoined. Although indeed nothing had been agreed upon beforehand concerning such a sign, and it was suggested here by Joshua on the spur of the moment (which Bonfrerius urges), they could nevertheless gather from it that the battle had already begun, and that it was therefore time to rush into the city: although, like Moses in the battle with the Amalekites, Joshua did not lower his hand until the entire slaughter of the people of Ai had been completed.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected. For the entire Deuteronomy was not inscribed on stones. But neither was the Decalogue alone, concerning which matter we have spoken more fully at Deut. 27, where the altar, the erection of which is described here, was also discussed.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

LEVA CLYPEUM) ἀσπίδα Josephus hic & Symma- chus. Et certe videtur ea esse propria vocis כידון significa- tio ex loco 1. Sam. 17, 6. & Jerem. 6, 23. Alii tamen vertunt γαισὸν, & explicant quidam ἐμβόλιον ὁλοσίδηρον aut κόντιον.

De Clypeo etiam intellexit Theodor. atque ita alibi vocem Ebræam reddidit Pagninus, & Arias, nec non LXX. quia 1. Sam. 17, 6. 45. ἀσπίδα ex- posuere. Rectius tamen lanceam vel hastam Ti- gurini cum Pagnin. & Montano hic habent, uti LXX. γαισὸν, Lyranus & Vatablus cum Rabbinis dicunt lanceam erectam fuisse & vexillum. Ere- ctio facta fuit tum in signum præliantis sub Deo & cum Deo, qui erigere jussit, & eo ipso præ- lium indixit, exercitus Israelitici, tum in signum in civitatem irruendi illis, qui erant in insidiis: quam causam non tantum Josephus, Theodoretus, Abulen- sis, Lyranus & Rabbini reddunt, sed etiam textus ipse verbis subjunctis indicat. Etiamsi vero de tali indicio antea nihil conventum, idq; hic ex tempo- re Josuæ suggestum fuerit ( quod Bonfrerius ur- get ) colligere tamen inde poterant initum jam esse prælium, atq; tempus proinde esse irruendi in urbem: quamvis instar Mosis in pugna cum Ama- lecitis manum non ante demiserit Josua, quam to- ta Hajensium strages peracta fuerit.

Recte corrigitur Vulgata. Non enim inte- grum Deuteronomium lapidibus inscriptum. Sed nec Decalogus solus, de qua re uberius diximus ad Deut. 27. ubi etiam de altari, cujus hic erectio describitur, actum.

## 8:23
Ver. 23. THEY CAPTURED HIM ALIVE AND BROUGHT HIM TO JOSHUA) It is the custom of peoples that a captured king yields to a king, or to the leader of an army, who pays the reward to the captors: indeed, even the goods of the defeated King yielded to the victor, as the Talmudists note under the title concerning the king. See what has been adduced on this matter in the book on the Law of War and Peace, book 3, chap. 6, § 24.

Latin:

Verf. 23. APPREHENDERVNT VIVENTEM ET OBTVLERVNT JOSVÆ) Mos populorum est, ut rex ca- ptus cedat regi, aut duci exercitus, qui præmium persolvit captoribus: imo & suppellex Regis victi victori cedebat, ut notant Thalmudistæ titulo de rege. Vide quæ ad hanc rem adducta de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 3. cap. 6. §. 24.

## 8:30
Verf. 13. AN ALTAR TO THE LORD) Then indeed for the use of sacrifice, but in the future for the sake of a monument, as below 22, 22. and following.

Verf. 32. AND HE WROTE UPON THE STONES A COPY OF THE LAW OF MOSES) Rather a copy of the law, in the way the term משנה תורת is taken in Deut. 17, 18. But understand the law here as that which is the chief part of the law, the Decalogue.

Latin:

Verf. 13. ALTARE DOMINO) Tunc quidem in Sacrificii usus, in posterum vero monumenti causa, ut infra 22, 22. & se- quentibus.

Verf. 32. ET SCRIPSIT SVPER LAPIDES DEVTERONO. MIVM LEGIS MOTSI) Imo exemplum legis, quomodo vox משנה תורת sumitur Deut. 17, 18. Legem ve- ro hic intellige id, quod legis præcipuum est, Decalogum.

## 8:33
Ver. 33. ELDERS AND LEADERS) זקנים Elders by birth or old men are the Senators of the LXX, γερυσία to Josephus: שטרים whom he translates here as leaders, the Greeks as scribes, are those who appeared before the senate: שפטים in this place are those who, being set over thousands and hundreds, judged lesser cases; to Josephus, sometimes phylarchs, sometimes authorities.

AND THEY BURNED IT.

That part which faced toward the North, so that the fire could be seen by Joshua and the people of Ai who had broken out of the city, for Joshua burned the rest of the city, ver. 24, and the Israelites had previously divided the spoils of the city among themselves.

NEAR MOUNT GERIZIM.

Concerning the mountains of Gerizim and Ebal, where they were situated, and concerning this whole ceremony of blessings and curses, see Deut. 11:29, chap. 27:11. Not near Jericho, as Eusebius, nor near Ai, as Masius wishes, but near Shechem, as Josephus handed down, Serarius teaches they were situated, h.l. q. 14. The matter is clear from Deut. 11:29, 30 and Gen. 12:6 compared with one another. Add Jud. 9:7. And the geographers agree, Brocardus, Breidenbach, Arias, Adrichomius, and most interpreters.

Latin:

Verf. 33. MAJORES NATV DVCESQVE) זקנים Majores natu sive senes sunt Senatores LXX. γερυσία Jose- pho: שטרים quos hic duces vertit, Græci γραμματει̃ς, sunt qui senatui apparebant: שפטים hoc loco illi qui millenis & centenis præfecti, minores causas dijudicabant: Josepho modo φίλαρχους modo ἀρχάς.

ET SUCCIDERUNT EAM.

Illa parte, quæ ad Septentrionem vergebat, ut incendium a Josua & Hajensibus, qui urbe erupe- rant, videri posset, nam reliquum urbis Josua suc- cendit verf. 24. atq; urbis spolia prius sibi divise- runt Israelitæ.

JUXTA MONTEM GARIZIM.

De montibus Garizim & Hebal ubinam siti fuerint & de tota hac ceremonia benedictionum & maledictionum vide Deut. 11, 29. cap. 27, 11. Non juxta Jericho, ut Euseb. nec juxta Hai, ut Ma- sius vult, sed juxta Sichem, ut Josephus tradidit, eos sitos fuisse Serar. h. l. q. 14. docet. Res lucu- lenta est e Deut. 11, 29. 30. & Gen. 12, 6. inter se collatis. Adde Jud. 9, 7. Et consentiunt Geo- graphi, Brocardus, Breidenbach. Arias, Adrichom. & Interpp. pleriq;.

## 8:34
Ver. 34. AND ALL THINGS THAT WERE WRITTEN IN THE VOLUME OF THE LAW.

FROM MAN EVEN TO WOMAN) That is not customary, except as a punishment for great impiety. Num. 31:15.

According to this interpretation, the whole law seems to have been read aloud, not only the blessings and curses recited. But that is not found in the Hebrew, nor among the LXX, as Bonfrerius rightly observes, thus amending the Vulgate; he reads all the words of the blessing and the curse according to all that is written in the book of the law.

It is therefore false what Josephus says, that the Hebrews captured and spared the children, women, and servants of the city of Ai; whether, however, the people of Bethel are also included under the number 12,000, or whether the people of Ai alone made up this number, may seem doubtful. Abulensis thinks none of them were killed. But that is not likely. For they were mixed with others in the battle. Masius includes them under the said number. It is more certain, however, that they are not counted here, because it is added in the text ALL OF THE CITY OF AI.

Latin:

Verf. 34. ET CUNCTA QUÆ ERANT SCRIPTA IN LEGIS VOLUMINE.

A VIRO VSQVE AD MVLIEREM) Non usitatum id, nisi in pœnam magnæ impietatis. Num. 31, 15.

Juxta hanc interpretationem videtur tota lex prælecta, non tantum benedictiones & maledi- ctiones recitatæ. Sed id non habetur in Ebræo, nec apud LXX. ut recte observat Bonfrerius, ita emendans Vulgatam, legit omnia verba benedictio- nis & maledictionis juxta omne, quod scriptum est in libro legis.

Falsum ergo est, quod ait Josephuss, Ebræos ce- pisse & servasse parvulos, fœminas & servos urbis Hai, utrum autem sub numero 12000. compre- hendantur etiam Bethelai, an vero soli Hajenses hunc numerum fecerint, dubium videri queat. A- bulensis nullos ex iis cæsos putat. Sed id verisimi- le non est. Fuerunt enim aliis permixti in prælio. Masius comprehendit eos sub dicto numero. Certius tamen est, eos hic non annumeratos esse, quia additur in textu OMNES URBIS HAI.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. The Gibeonites are spared.

ver. 1. WHO DWELT IN THE MOUNTAINS.

Ver. 28. HE MADE IT A MOUND) In the place where the city had been, he placed a heap of stones.

Mountains are found everywhere in Canaan, especially in the tribe of Judah Deut. 1, 24. Jud. 1, 19. Luke 1, 39.

He is said to have made an everlasting mound: or rather a heap, as is held in the following verse concerning the pile or heap of stones over the corpse of the King. Moreover, the word עולם does not signify eternity here, but a long duration of time, as it often does. For the city of Ai is mentioned in Ezra 2 & Neh. 7 & 11 after the return from the Babylonian captivity, and thus built about a thousand years after this destruction, as some think, although it may be considered as another city, even if it was erected in the same borders.

IN THE MARITIME REGIONS AND THE SHORE, OF THE GREAT SEA, THESE ALSO WHO DWELL NEAR LEBANON.

In Heb. And on all the shore of the great sea, over against Lebanon. Chald. which is in the region of Lebanon. The great sea is the Mediterranean, near which the Sidonians, Tyrians, and other Phoenicians dwelt, who were themselves also Canaanites by race; likewise the Philistines, who, although they were not Canaanites by race, were nevertheless to be cast out of their seats along with them, if the Israelites had remained in their duty and the divine law, just as their cities were also afterwards distributed among the Israelites. For the Philistines themselves had already expelled the Canaanites from those seats. Conf. Gen. 10, 14. Deut. 2.

Ver. 29. ALSO HIS KING HE HUNG ON A GALLOWS) Having first killed him. For hanging was not a punishment there, but bodies were exposed to public view in that manner, as was said at Deut. 21, 22. Interpret in this way also what is below 10, 26.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Gabaonitæ servantur.

verf. 1. QUI VERSABANTUR IN MON- TANIS.

Verf. 28. FECIT EAM TVMVLVM) In loco ubi urbs fuerat la- pidum congeriem posuit.

MOntes passim in Cananæa, maxime in Judai- ca tribu Deut. 1, 24. Jud. 1, 19. Luc. 1, 39.

Fecisse dicitur tumulum sempiternum: vel po- tius cumulum, ut in versu sequenti habetur de acer- vo vel cumulo lapidum super cadavere Regis. Vox autem עולם non æternitatem, sed tempus diutur- num, ut sæpe, hic sonat. Nam commemoratur ci- vitas Hai Esdr. 2. & Neh. 7. & 11. post reditum e captiv. Babyl. adeoq; mille circiter annis ab hac eversione extructa, ut nonnullis placet, quamvis ea pro alia urbe, utut in confiniis iisdem erecta, haberi possit.

IN MARITIMIS AC LITTORE, MA- GNI MARIS, HI QUOQUE QUI HABI- TANT JUXTA LIBANUM.

In Ebr. Et in omni litore maris magni, contra Libanum. Chald. quod e regione Libani. Mare magnum est mediterraneum, juxta quod Sidonii, Tyrii, Phœnices cæteri habitabant, qui & ipsi Cana- næi genere; item Palæstini, qui etsi non essent Ca- nanæi genere, erant tamen cum iis sede ejiciendi, si Israelitæ in officio & lege divina permansissent, uti etiam postmodum forte ipsorum civitates in- ter Israelitas distributæ. Nam & ipsi Palæstini Cananæos iis sedibus jam expulerant. Conf. Gen. 10, 14. Deut. 2.

Verf. 29. REGEM QVOQVE EJVS SVSPENDIT IN PATIBVLVM) Interfectum prius. Neque enim suspen- sio pœna ibi erat, sed corpora eum in modum oftentui ex- ponebantur, ut dictum ad Deut. 21, 22. Sic etiam inter- pretare, quæ infra 10, 26.

## 9:3
ver. 3. WHO DWELT IN GIBEON.

The text has nothing concerning any other kind of death than hanging, and for that reason, namely that life was taken from him by hanging, other interpreters also conclude, because nothing else is found in Scripture, even though in later times they were accustomed to first stone those who were to be hanged. See Joseph. b. 4. Antiq. c. 8. Concerning the passage Deut. 21, 22, we have spoken in the same place: by virtue of which the hanged man could not be left on the gallows longer than until sunset, even if he were an enemy. What is 'gallows' here in the Vulgate, the LXX have 'double wood' ξύλον δίδυμον, as if it were a cross, either joined or inserted; in the Hebrew text it is simply held as עץ wood.

A city named from the hills, situated on a mountain, whence 'Gibeon the high' is mentioned here and there; it is located on Mount Shiloh by Brocard and Adrichom. It fell afterwards to the tribe of Benjamin, Josh. 18, 25, and later became a Priestly city, ch. 21, 17. It was a great and Royal city of the Hebrews, ch. 10, 2, in which, under David and Solomon, the tabernacle of the covenant was, 1 Chron. 16, 39, ch. 21, 29, 2 Chron. 1, 3, 13. It had under it the cities of Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. It was 50 stadia distant from Jerusalem, according to Josephus, book 2, War, ch. 23; therefore it is not correctly said by Eusebius in his book on Hebrew places to be at the fourth milestone of Bethel, and indeed situated on the eastern side, when it was rather to the west of it, as Bonfrer teaches here. But if it were to the east of Bethel, how could the Gibeonites have arranged an embassy as if from afar? For Joshua was staying in the vicinity of Bethel, and indeed in its eastern part, namely in Gilgal, Jericho, and Ai.

Latin:

verf. 3. QUI HABITABANT IN GABAON.

Nihil de alio mortis genere, quam suspendii textus habet atq; ea ratione, nempe per suspensio- nem ipsi vitam ademtam esse, aliiq; interpp. sta- tuunt, quia aliud eScriptura non habetur, etsi poste- rioribus temporibus lapidibus primum obrui con- sueverint, qui suspendendi erant. Vid. Joseph. l. 4. Antiq. c. 8. De loco Deut. 21, 22. ibidem diximus: vi cujus non poterat suspensus diutius in patibulo re- linqui, quam usq. ad occasum Solis, etiamsi hostis esset. Quod in Vulgata hic est patibulum, LXX. ha- bent geminum lignum ξύλον δίδυμον, quasi crux fue- rit vel commissa, vel immissa, in Ebræo textu sim- pliciter habetur עץ lignum.

Urbs a collibus dicta in monte sita, unde ex- celsa Gabaon passim, in monte Silo locatur a Bro- card, & Adrichom. Cecidit deinde in tribum Benjamin Jos. 18, 25. ac postea facta urbs Sacerdo- talis cap. 21, 17. Fuit urbs magna ac Regia Ebræo- rum c. 10, 2. in qua sub Davide, ac Salomone ta- bernaculum fœderis fuit 1. Paral. 16, 39. cap. 21, 29. 2. Paral. 1, 3. 13. Habuit sub se civitates Caphira, Beroth & Cariathiarim. Hierosolyma aberat 50. stadiis, teste Josepho lib. 2. Bell. cap. 23. non er- go recte ab Eusebio l. de locis Hebr. in quarto miliario Bethelis, & quidem contra Orientalem pla- gam sita dicitur, quum potius occidentalis ei fue- rit, ut hic docet Bonfrer. Quod si Betheli ori- entalis esset, quomodo legationem quasi e lon- ginquo ordinare potuissent Gabeonitæ? Nam in Bethelis vicinia versabatur Josua, & quidem in ejus orientali parte, utpote in Galgalis, Jericho, & Hai.

## 9:4
Verse 4. AND DEALING CRAFTILY.

In Hebrew: they also acted in craftiness. This was a shrewd prudence for escaping destruction: yet from this that persuasion or opinion of Plato and Cassian cannot be proven, as was done by Cornelius, as if in a moment of such necessity it were lawful to lie: whence, because of the lies that intervened here, the Gibeonites were afterwards punished with servitude.

Latin:

Verf. 4. ET CALLIDE COGITANTES.

In Ebr. fecerunt etiam ipfi in calliditate. Astu- ta hæc erat prudentia excidium evadendi: non tamen inde probari potest illa persuasio, aut opi- nio Platonis & Cassiani, uti a Cornelio factum, quasi in articulo tantæ necessitatis licitum sit menti- ri: unde ob ea quæ hic intervenere mendacia Gibeonitæ postmodum servitute mulctati sunt.

## 9:7
Verse 7.

LEST PERCHANCE YOU DWELL IN THE LAND WHICH IS OWED TO US BY LOT) Fame had already reached far and wide that those lands of the seven peoples had been given by God to the Hebrews.

AND WE CANNOT MAKE A COVENANT WITH YOU) Namely, a social covenant, by which lands and full liberty would be left to them. See regarding this whole matter what we said in book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 13, section 4.

What is to be thought of the Grotian opinion, we have said at Deuteronomy 7, 1.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

NE FORTE IN TERRA QVÆ NOBIS SORTE DEBETVR HABITETIS) Fama jam longe pervenerat a Deo terras illas septem populorum Hebræis datas.

ET NON POSSVMVS FOEDVS INIRE VOBIS- CVM) Nempe fœdus sociale, quo terræ & plena libertas ipsis relinquerentur. Vide de tota hac re quæ diximus l. 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 13. §. 4.

Quod de Grotiana sententia habendum sit, diximus ad Deut. 7, 1.

## 9:11
Verse 11.

AND OUR ELDERS AND ALL THE INHABITANTS OF OUR COUNTRY SAID TO US) The consent of the people followed the senators, πρεσβέλοις. There were many democracies with aristocracies at that time.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

DIXERVNTQVE NOBIS SENIORES, ET OMNES HABITATORES TERRÆ NOSTRÆ) Senatoribus πρε- σβέλοις secutus populi consensus. Multæ erant eo tempore δημοκρατίαι μετ᾿ ἀριϛοκρατίας.

## 9:15
Verse 15.

HE PROMISED THAT THEY WOULD NOT BE KILLED) He accepted them into surrender, so that they would be subjects to the Israelites: which would have been lawful even if the truth of the matter had been known. Therefore, nothing was done here against the law. See 2 Samuel 21 and 1 Kings 9, 20.

But if that was simply permitted, why then are they reproved, because they did not first inquire of the mouth of the Lord? For that which is forbidden by no law, but is simply permitted, concerning that there was no need to inquire of the mouth of the Lord. Grotius supposes as certain that only those from among those peoples were devoted to destruction by the law of the Lord who, having been warned, did not immediately do what was commanded. Concerning which we have seen Deut. 7, 1. Nevertheless, Bonfrerius, and with him Cornelius, thinks that it was permitted to spare those seven peoples and to receive them into surrender, these two conditions having been posited: (1.) If they were prepared to embrace the Jewish religion. (2.) If they conceded their lands to the Israelites (inasmuch as they were to be distributed to them by lot) as regards the fruitful fields, vineyards, olive groves, orchards, so that movable goods, houses, and even unfruitful soil could be left to them. But concerning these, l. c. But how could the Israelites be deceived, when they were asked by the Gibeonites only that they would deign to spare their lives, from which they could easily suspect and conclude that they were of the Canaanites, for if they had lived outside the borders of Canaan, there was no reason why they should have feared the invasion of the Israelites? Resp. It is likely that the Israelites thought that these wished to look out for themselves, because they did not know how far the arms of the Israelites were to be carried, whether even outside Canaan, or whether they were to be contained within the borders of that land?

Latin:

Verf. 15.

POLLICITVS EST, QVOD NON OCCIDEREN- TVR) In deditionem eos accepit, ut subditi essent Israë- litis: quod licuisset etiam si veritas rei fuisset cognita. Ni- hil ergo factum hic contra legem. Vide 2. Sam. 21. & 1. Reg. 9, 20.

At si id simpliciter licuit, cur ergo redarguun- tur, quod non prius os Domini interrogarint? Quod enim nulla lege vetitum, sed simpliciter licitum, de eo opus non erat os Domini interrogare. Suppo- nit Grotius tanquam certum, eos solum ex illis po- pulis internecione per legem Domini devotos fuisse, qui moniti imperata statim non fecerint. De quo Deut. 7, 1. vidimus. Licitum tamen fuisse illos septem populos servare, ac in deditionem suscipere Bon- frerius, & cum eo Cornelius duabus hisce condi- tionibus positis censet. (1.) Si parati essent Judai- cam religionem suscipere. (2.) Si terras suas Israeli- tis concederent (utpote quæ illis sorte distribuen- dæ erant) quod ad agros frugiferos, vineta, oliveta, pomaria, ita ut iis relinqui potuerint bona mobilia, domus etiam ac solum infrugiferum. Sed de his l. c. Quomodo vero Israelitæ decipi potuere, quum a Gabeonitis tantum rogati fuerint, vitæ ipsorum parcere dignarentur, unde illi facile suspicari, ac col- ligere poterant, eosdem e Cananæis esse, si enim extra Cananææ fines habitassent, non erat, quod Israelitarum invasionem metuerint? Resp. veri- simile esse, Israelitas censuisse, hos sibi voluisse con- sulere, quod nescirent, quousq; Israelitarum arma essent proferenda, an etiam extra Cananaam, an ve- ro intra illius terræ fines continenda?

## 9:18
Vers. 18. BECAUSE THE PRINCES OF THE MULTITUDE HAD SWORN TO THEM) Eleazar, with the senate, as Josephus says here, with Joshua indeed as the author above 15, who alone had the right to bind the people in such matters. The Hebrews could have caviled here. But to use the words of Livy from the third book: This negligence of God which now holds the age had not yet come, nor was each one making oaths and laws suitable for himself by interpreting them, but was rather adapting his own morals to them.

The interpreters ask whether the oath was valid, and whether Joshua was bound to keep it. Augustine, quest. 13 in the book of Joshua, does not seem to acknowledge it as valid; Abulensis, Masius, Serarius, and Magalian also deny this, either because it was concerning an illicit matter, or because a condition intervened, if the Gibeonites were foreigners; yet they think that the Israelites thought themselves bound to keep it, and that upon a new pact being added they were entirely bound. But Ambrose in book 3 of his Offices, ch. 10, Lyranus, Hugo, Dionysius the Carthusian, Cajetan, Bonfrerius, and Cornelius a Lapide, with Gratian, 22, q. 4, c.

final. Thomas, Bonaventura, Richard, Suarez, lib. 2 de Juram. cap. 18, think that the oath was valid, because God permitted the Canaanites to be spared if they themselves sought peace, ceded their cities to the Hebrews, and embraced their religion, chap. 11, 19, and there was no deceit concerning the substance of the matter, but only concerning an accident, the proximity or distance of their habitation. Which they also seem to indicate in verse 19: we have sworn to them in the name of the Lord, and therefore we cannot touch them. They also add that God avenged the violation of the oath by the crucifixion of the descendants of Saul, 2 Reg. 21. Which opinion is more probable on this account, that GOD devoted the Canaanites to destruction only from the foreknowledge of their hardening, but not by any absolute decree; since therefore the Gibeonites submitted themselves of their own accord, and embraced the true religion, Joshua could not presume that they were of the peoples divinely devoted to destruction, whom he also believed to be further removed: although therefore he was deceived in this latter point concerning their habitation, yet not in the former, that his presumption was false, both the signs of submission and devotion testified, and the event itself confirmed, verse 24. Although it also seems likely to some that they were confirmed by a divine response given through Eleazar, that they should indeed spare the lives of the Gibeonites, yet that they should assign them to the servitude of wood-cutting and water-drawing. Thus both the religion of the oath was preserved, and the Gibeonites were punished for their deceit, even if it later resulted in an honorable lot and condition of serving the temple of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 18. EO QVOD JVRASSENT EIS PRINCIPES MVLTITVDINIS) Eleazarus, μετὰ γερουσίας, ut hic ait Josephus, auctore nempe Josue supra 15. qui vel solus jus ha- buerat in talibus populum obligandi. Cavillari hic aliqua potuissent Hebræi. Sed ut Livii ex libro tertio utar verbis: Nondum hæc quæ nunc tenet seculum negligentia Dei venerat, nec interpretando sibi quisque jusjurandum & leges aptas facie- bat, sed suos potius mores ad eos accommodabat.

Quærunt Interpp. an validum fuerit juramen- tum, & ad id servandum obligatus fuerit Josua. Non videtur id validum agnoscere August. quæst. 13. in libr. Jos. negant etiam hoc Abusensis, Ma- sius, Serarius, Magalian. sive quod fuerit de re illi- cita, sive quod conditio intervenerit, si sint extranei Gabaonitæ; putasse tamen censent Israelitas se obli- gari ad id servandum, atq; accedente nova pactione omnino obligatos fuisse. Ambrosius vero libro 3. offic. c. 10. Lyranus, Hugo, Dionys. Carthuf. Cajeta- nus, Bonfrerius, Corn. a Lap. cum Gratian. 22. q. 4. c.

final. Thoma, Bonavent. Richard. Suaretz. lib. 2. de Juram. cap. 18. censent, validum fuisse juramen- tum, quia Deus permiserit parci Cananæis, si ipsi pacem peterent, urbes suas Ebræis cederent, eorumque religionem capesserent cap. 11, 19. neque dolus fue- rit circa substantiam rei, sed circa accidens tantum proximitatem vel longinquitatem habitationis eorum. Quod etiam indicare videntur vers. 19. juravimus illis in nomine Domini, & idcirco non possumus eos contingere. Addunt etiam, Deum vio- lationem juramenti ultum esse crucifixione postero- rum Saulis 2. Reg. 21. Quæ sententia hoc nomi- ne magis probabilis est, quod DEUS Cananæos solum ex prævisione indurationis ipsorum, non au- tem per decretum aliquod absolutum exitio devo- verit; Quum ergo Gabaonitæ sese ultro submise- rint, & religionem veram amplexi sint, non pote- rat Josua præsumere, eosdem esse ex populis exi- tio divinitus devotis, quos etiam longius remo- tos credebat: Etsi ergo in hoc posteriori de ha- bitatione ipsorum deceptus fuerit, non tamen in priori falsam esse suam præsumtionem tum signa submissionis & devotionis testabantur, tum vero eventus ipse confirmabat vers. 24. Quanquam etiam verisimile nonnullis videatur, eos responso divino per Eleazarum reddito confirmatos fuisse, ut vitæ quidem Gabaonitarum parcerent, servitu- ti tamen lignationis & aquationis eosdem addi- cerent. Sic & juramenti religio servabatur, & ob dolum pœna afficiebantur Gabaonitæ, etsi ea postea cesserit in honestam sortem & conditio- nem serviendi templo Domini.

## 9:21
vers. 21. LET THEM BE RESERVED INDEED THAT THEY MAY LIVE.

In the Hebrew these are prefixed: And the Princes said to them, not in an inconvenient sense, as Bonfrerius judges, but so that either a continuation of the speech of the Princes of the people to the people, or a new proposal is indicated as proposed to the people, on what condition they wish to keep them alive: although neither Jerome nor the LXX in the Roman Codex have those words. But those words, as the Princes spoke (the Vulgate renders, while they were speaking these things Joshua called, which sense neither the punctuation allows, nor the particle Vav beginning a new sentence in the following verse) look not to this counsel concerning the servitude of wood-cutting and water-drawing, but only to that יִחְיוּ LET THEM LIVE. Because the Princes had promised them preservation in life by an oath.

THAT THEY MAY CUT WOOD AND CARRY WATER FOR THE USES OF THE WHOLE MULTITUDE.

In the Hebrew it is, and let them be wood-cutters, and water-drawers FOR ALL THE CONGREGATION, which is to be understood of the whole sacred or Ecclesiastical congregation, in the place of the congregation or the tabernacle of the Lord, not of the entire multitude in their private tents; for the Gibeonites could not suffice for these services for all. Therefore those ministries are expressly restricted to the house of the Lord, verse 23. And by this name the Gibeonites were afterwards called Nethinim, as if God-given, because they were given and dedicated to God or his temple. 1 Chron. 9, 2. and among Ezra and Nehemiah passim: Josephus book 11. Antiq. chap. 5. calls them sacred servants: because they served the temple and sacred things, by bringing water, with which victims or Priests were washed, and by cutting wood which was necessary for the altar of burnt offerings, and for other uses of the temple, which servitude, although perhaps it was not a little mitigated and diminished by the sheep pool, near the sheep gate at the roots of mount Moriah, and the fountain of perennial water, of which

Tacitus, Book 5 of the Histories, and Eupolemus in Eusebius, Book 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, as well as through the festival of Xylophoria in Josephus, Book 2 of the Jewish War, ch. 17. Serarius in this place, question 18, yet it did not cease entirely, because they were occupied in carrying water to the kitchens of the temple, and in carrying other wood, if those things which were brought on the said festival did not suffice, and also in carrying those things which had been brought into the inner court: since a great and almost incredible quantity of wood was needed for the many thousands of sacrifices which were performed at the altar of burnt offerings and the many kitchens. However, the Nethinim seem to have lived not in any one city (which could not have contained them) but, as Bonfrerius and some others think, in the Priestly and Levitical cities: which they gather from Ezra 2, last verse, Nehemiah 7, last verse, 1. Paragraph 22. Although not a few ministered in Jerusalem even outside the solemn festivals, they lived not far from the temple in the place called Ophel, Nehemiah 3:26, ch. 11:21.

Latin:

vers. 21. RESERVENTUR QUIDEM UT VIVANT.

In Ebr. hæc præmittuntur: Et dixerunt ad eos Principes, non incommodo sensu, uti judicat Bonfrerius, sed ut vel continuatio orationis Princi- pum populi ad populum, vel novum προβούλευμα indicetur populo propositum, qua conditione ipsos in vita servare velint: utut ea verba nec Hieronym. nec LXX. in Cod. Romano habeant. Illa autem quemadmodum loquuti sunt Principes (Vulg. red- dit, quibus hæc loquentibus vocavit Josue, quem sensum nec interpunctio patitur, nec particula Vav novam ordiens in vers. seqv. sententiam) re- spiciunt non hoc consilium de servitute lignatio- nis & aquationis, sed solum illud יִחְיוּ VIVANT. Quia juramento promiserant ipsis Principes con- servationem in vita.

UT IN USUS UNIVERSÆ MULTITU- DINIS LIGNA CÆDANT AQUASQUE COMPORTENT.

In Ebræo est, & sint ligna cædentes, & aquas haurientes OMNI CONVENTUI, quod de conventu omni sacro vel Ecclesiastico, in loco conventus vel tabernaculi Domini intelligen- dum, non de universa multitudine in privatis ten- toriis; nam pro omnibus sufficere non poterant Gabaonitæ ad hæc servitia. Ideo restringuntur illa ministeria diferte ad domum Domini vers. 23. Atque hoc nomine dicti deinde Gabaonitæ sunt Nathinæi, quasi Deo-dati, quod Deo vel tem- plo ejus donati & dedicati sint. 1. Par. 9, 2. & apud Esdram ac Nehemiam passim: Josephus lib. 11. An- tiqq. cap. 5. vocat eos servos sacros: quia templo rebusque sacris serviebant, aquis, quibus victimæ vel Sacerdotes abluerentur, comportandis, lignisque quæ holocaustorum altari, & ad alios templi usus necessaria erant cædendis, quæ servitus, etsi for- tassiss non parum mitigata & imminuta fuerit per probaticam piscinam, juxta portam gregis ad radi- ces montis Moria, & fontem perennis aquæ, de quo

Tacitus lib. 5. Hist. & Eupolemus apud Euseb. lib. 9. præpar. Evangel. nec non per festum Xylophoriæ apud Joseph. lib. 2. Bell. c. 17. Serar. in h. l. qv. 18. non tamen defiit omnino, quia aquæ ad culinas templi portandæ, & lignis aliis, si ea quæ festo di- cto advehebantur, non sufficerent, advehendis, nec non advectis in interius atrium deferendis occu- pati erant: siquidem magna lignorum copia & fere incredibili opus fuerit ob multa sacrificiorum millia, quæ peragebantur, ad altare holocausto- rum & culinas plurimas. Habitasse autem Natha- næi videntur non in una aliqua civitate (quæ ipsos capere non potuisset) sed ut Bonfrerius & alii non- nulli putant, in urbibus Sacerdotalibus, ac Leviticis: quod colligunt ex Esdr. 2. ult. Neh. 7. ult. 1. Par. 22. etsi Hierosolymis non pauci etiam extra festa so- lemnia ministrarint, non procul a templo in loco Ophel dicto habitarint Neh. 3, 26. c. 11, 21.

## 9:23
Verse 23. THERE SHALL NOT FAIL FROM YOUR LINE ONE WHO CUTS WOOD AND CARRIES WATER) The victor has the right to punish the surrendered, as those who have been made subjects. If deceit had been absent, they would have remained only subjects. Because of the deceit, they are assigned to servile work, as the Bruttii were once by the Romans, from whose likeness they were called Bruttiani, who performed servile duties for the Magistrates, because the Bruttii had surrendered themselves to Hannibal and had persisted with him until he withdrew from Italy. See Festus. To carry water is servile. Athenaeus: ὁ ἐπειὸς ὑδροφόρεῖ τοῖς Ατρείδαις ὡς καὶ Στησίχορός φησιν· ὤκτειρε γὰρ αὐτὸν ὕδωρ ἀεὶ φορέοντα Διὸς κόρᾳ βασιλεύσῃ.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NON DEFICIET DE STIRPE VESTRA LIGNA CÆDENS AQVASQVE COMPORTANS) De- ditos puniendi jus est victori, ut subditos factos. Si dolus abfuisset, subditi tantum mansissent. Ob dolum operis ser- vilibus addicuntur, ut olim a Romanis Bruttii, a quorum similitudine Bruttiani dicti, qui officia servilia Magistratibus præstabant, eo quod Bruttii Hannihali se tradidissent, & cum eo perseverassent usque dum recederet de Italia. Vide Festum. Aquam portare servile. Athenæus: ὁ ἐπειὸς ὑδρο- φόρεῖ τοῖς Ατρείδαις ὡς καὶ Στησίχορός φησιν· ὤκτειρε γὰρ αὐ- τὸν ὕδωρ ἀεὶ φορέοντα Διὸς κόρᾳ βασιλεύσῃ.

## 9:27
Verse 27. AND HE DECREED ON THAT DAY THAT THEY SHOULD BE IN THE MINISTRY.

In Hebrew ויתנם And Joshua gave them on that day as woodcutters, etc., whence the name נתינים Ezra 2:43, 50, ch. 8:20, Nehemiah 3:26, concerning which see verse 21. Compare Jerome, Hebrew Traditions in 1 Chronicles. Sigonius, Book 5 on the Hebrew Republic, ch. 7. Ribera, Book 3 on the Temple, ch. 4. Villalpando in Apparatus, part 1, book 2, ch. 7.

IN THE MINISTRY OF ALL THE PEOPLE, AND OF THE ALTAR OF THE LORD.

Some gather from this a twofold burden and duty of theirs. The first, to carry wood and water for the entire camp of the Hebrews. Then, to carry for the tabernacle and afterwards for the temple, to which, however, they acknowledge they were assigned almost solely after the division of the camps and tribes, and the possession of the promised land. But others more correctly take the particle AND exegetically, of all the people, that is, of the altar; but the matter is best and most simply explained from the Hebrew source, in which they are said to have ministered not to all the people, but to לעדה the congregation, or the tabernacle of the congregation, and the altar of the Lord: thus the customary force of the conjunction Vav is retained, and they are restricted only to sacred ministries. Nor in any other sense are they called by Josephus δημόσιοι public servants, than that they performed for the whole people those things which pertained to the tent of the congregation and the altar, to sacred things, just as ministers of the word are called ministers of the Church.

IN THE PLACE WHICH THE LORD HAD CHOSEN.

Where, namely, He willed the tabernacle to be placed, which was then at Gilgal, until, the seven-year wars being finished, it was moved to Shiloh, ch. 19:1, afterwards to Nob: and from there it was in Gibeon. Finally, the ark was moved into the temple.

Latin:

vers. 27. DECREVITQUE IN ILLO DIE EOS ESSE IN MINISTERIO.

In Ebr. ויתנם Et dedit eos Josua in illo die in li- gnorum cæsores &c. unde nomen נתינים Esdr. 2, 43. 50. c. 8, 20. Neh. 3, 26. de quo ad v. 21. Conf. Hie- ronym. Tradit. Hebr. in 1. Paral. Sigon. l. 5. de Rep. Hebr. c. 7. Riebera l. 3. de Templ. c. 4. Vilalp. in Ap- par. part. 1. l. 2. c. 7.

IN MINISTERIO CUNCTI POPULI, ET ALTARIS DOMINI.

Colligunt hinc nonnulli duplex onus & offi- cium eorum. Prius comportare ligna & aquam to- tis Ebræorum castris. Deinde comportare taberna- culo & postea templo, cui tamen soli pene post di- visionem castrorum & tribuum, terræque promissæ possessionem addictos fuisse agnoscunt. At rectius alii particulam ET exegetice accipiunt, cuncti po- puli, id est, altaris; optime autem ac simplicissi- me res expeditur e fonte Ebræo, in quo nihil de cuncto populo, sed לעדה conventui ministrasse di- cuntur, seu tabernaculo conventus, & altari Domini: sic vis usitata copulæ Vav retinetur, & adstringun- tur tantum ad sacra ministeria. Nec alio sensu Jo- sepho dicuntur δημόσιοι publici servi, quam quod ea, quæ ad tentorium conventus, & altare, ad sacra spectabant, pro universo populo expedierint, uti verbi ministri dicuntur ministri Ecclesiæ.

IN LOCO QUEM DOMINUS ELEGIS- SET.

Ubi sc. collocatum voluit tabernaculum, quod tum erat in Galgalis, donec bellis septennalibus fi- nitis in Silo translatum est c. 19, 1. post in Nobe: ac dehinc in Gaban fuit. Tandem arca translata est in templum.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. Five Kings defeated. The standing still of the sun. The slaughter of other Kings.

Verse 1. WHEN ADONIZEDEK KING OF JERUSALEM HAD HEARD THESE THINGS.

These things could easily reach him from Gibeon: because Jerusalem is only two leagues or hours from the aforementioned city. Which, therefore, King Adonizedek invaded, because it had crossed over to the Hebrews, and could easily open an approach to his own seat for them.

The name Adonizedeck is twin to the name Melchisedech, which was the proper name of the King of the same place 400 years before: the former denotes Lord, the latter King of righteousness, yet one may safely affirm with Masius and Bonfrerius that not all the Kings of that city derived their name from righteousness.

Melchisedech was a distinguished King, therefore it is no wonder he was distinguished by a similar name: however, that name of Melchisedech is celebrated as a proper, not a common name, Heb. 7. Nor is it likely that that city was first called צדק righteousness, which Melchisedech, the first righteous King, planted in it, as seemed good to Masius and Cornelius: for in the time of Melchisedech it was already called שלם from peace.

But afterwards it acquired the name Jerusalem, which is ineptly derived from ἱερῷ sacred or temple, as if it were so called on account of the temple, whether founded there by Melchisedech, as Josephus, book 7, Bell. ch. 8, and Hegesippus, book 3, ch. 9, or Solomonian, as Eusebius, book 9, Praepar. ch. 4, wish; for that name is neither Greek, but Hebrew, nor did Melchisedech and Solomon speak Greek but Hebrew, nor is anything certain about the temple of Melchisedech, and that name was given to the city long before the Solomonian temple. But most think it was so called from ראה, as if a vision of peace, which Masius refers to that of Abraham, Gen. 22:14, the Lord יראה, as if he taught from that word and the ancient name Salem; they derive it so that the doctrine of peace, which proceeded from there, may be noted. Christoph. a Castro on ch. 4 of Baruch, as also Pasor in his Lexicon of the N.T., wishes it to be so called by the Jebusite inhabitants, as if to say Jerusalem, that is, fear our city Salem. Hieron. on Hebrew places (or rather Eusebius) derives it from Jebus, as if Jebus Salem. Whence by antistoechon Jerusalem, for the sake of the pleasantness of the etymology, according to Chytr. in Onomast. Theol. But the first derivation from the vision of peace is most convenient: according to which it will have the same reason for its denomination as Mount Moriah, upon which it was in part built: and by the etymon of the name it will call to memory the illustrious vision made to Abraham, and will lead to the type of the Messiah and to the vision of peace obtained in the Church and in heaven through the Messiah. But whether it first received this name from David, which seemed good to B. Glassius in his Grammatica Sacra, p. 785, is doubtful even from the fact that it is so called here, nor is it likely that the author of the book of Joshua lived only in the time of David, or that names in a divinely inspired book were changed in subsequent times. It is sometimes written in the dual form, as Jer. 26:18, etc. which they not badly refer to the two parts of the city, the upper and the lower, of which one was in the lot of Judah, the other common to Benjamin with Judah, but the citadel belonged to Benjamin alone, as Junius notes on Judg. 1:7, concerning which Bonfrerius has this on Jos. 15:63: that the more southern part of the city, that is, Mount Sion, and a small part perhaps of the lower city, with the line drawn through the top of Mount Moriah, were in the tribe of Judah; the remaining part of the lower city towards the North, indeed almost the whole lower city (which Adri-chomius in his description of the city of Jerusalem observes was called the daughter of Sion, because it seemed to be born, as it were, from Mount Sion, Ps. 9 and 72, Zach. 9), belonged to the Benjaminites, and they had the larger part of the city with the temple, Deut. 33:12. Joseph. b. 5, ch. 1, 2. Conf. Jos. 18, last. Judg. 1:21. Yet the royal house and the seat of the kingdom on Mount Sion belonged to the tribe of Judah, which more elevated and fortified part the Jebusites retained until the times of David, by whom at last it was captured, 2 Sam. 5. If the citadel belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, certainly David, of the stock of Judah, with the rest of the kings of Judah, did not have their royal residence in the tribe of Judah, which I would by no means say.

Moreover, it was also called Jebus in ancient times Jud. 19, 10. 1. Par. 11, 4. 5. which name, however, some think was attributed to it only by the common people, and it seems to have been proper to the inhabitants rather than the city Jos. 18, 28. Zach. 9, 7. even though the city itself was sometimes commonly named so by the inhabitants.

Latin:

CAP. X. Quinque Reges devicti. Solis statio. Aliorum Regum occisio.

vers. 1. QUÆ CUM AUDISSET ADONISE- DEC REX JERUSALEM.

FAcile hæc de Gabaone ad ipsum penetrare po- terant: quia Jerusalem duabus leucis seu horis tantum ab urbe prædicta. Quam proinde Rex A- donisedeck invasit, quod ad Ebræos transierit, iis- que aditum ad sedem suam facile pandere possit

Nomen Adonisedeck geminum est nomini Mel-chisedech, quod Regis ibidem ante 400. annos fuit proprium: Illud Dominum, hoc Regem justitiaæ no-tat, non tamen Reges omnes istius urbis a justitia nomen habuisse, cum Masio & Bonfrerio certo af-firmare licet.

Insignis Rex fuit Melchisedech, ideo non mirum hunc simili nomine insignitum: illud ta-men Melchisedeci nomen ut proprium, non ut com-mune celebratur Ebr. 7. Neque verisimile est, urbem illam primum צדק justitiam appellatam, quam in ea primus justus Rex Melchisedech plantavit, uti cum Masio, Cornelio visum: nam Melchisedeci tempore jam vocata est שלם a pace.

Dehinc vero nomen Jerusalem adepta est, quod inepte deduci-tur ab ἱερῷ sacro vel templo, quasi ob templum, sive a Melchisedeco ibi conditum, ut Joseph. l. 7. Bell. c. 8. & Hegesipp. lib. 3. cap. 9. sive Salomonæum, ut Euseb. lib. 9. Præpar. cap. 4. volunt, ita dicta fue-rit, nam nec nomen illud Græcum est, sed Ebræ-um, nec Græce sed Ebraice loquuti sunt Melchi-sedech & Salomo, nec de templo Melchisedeci quicquam constat, & longe ante Salomonæum templum nomen illud urbi datum. At ראה ita vo-catam, quasi visionem pacis plerique existimant, quod refert Masius ad illud Abrahami Gen. 22, 14. Dominus יראה quasi e verbo isto & nomine anti-quo Salem docuit; deducunt, ut notetur doctrina pacis, quæ inde prodiit. Christoph. a Castro in c. 4. Bar. ut & Pasor in Lex. N. T. ita dictam vult a Je-busæis incolis q. d. Jerusalem, id est, timete urbem nostram Salem. Hieron. de locis Hebr. (vel po-tius Eusebius) a Jebus derivat, quasi Jebus Sa-lem. Unde per antistæchon Jerusalem ob ety-mi jucunditatem secundum Chytr. in Ono-mast. Theol. Sed prima derivatio a visione pacis convenientissima: juxta quam eandem denomi-nationis rationem habebit cum monte Morija, cui illa ex parte superstructa fuit: ac nominis Ety-mo in memoriam vocabit illustrem visionem Ab-rahæ factam, & typum Messiæ atque ad visionem pacis in Ecclesia, & cœlo per Messiam partam de-ducet. Num autem a Davide primum hoc no-men acceperit, quod B. Glassio in Gramm. Sacra p, 785. visum, dubium vel ex eo est, quod hic ita vo-cetur, neq; verisimile est autorem libri Josuæ Da-vidis demum tempore vixisse, aut nomina in libro θεοπνεύστῳ immutata esse subsequentibus tempo-ribus. In Duali forma quandoq; scribitur ut Jer. 26, 18. &c. quod non male referunt ad duas civita-tis partes superiorem & inferiorem, quarum altera in forte Jehuda fuit, altera Benjamini cum Juda communis, arx vero solius Benjaminis, notante Junio ad Judic. 1, 7. de quo vero ita habet Bonfre-rius ad Jos. 15, 63. partem urbis australiorem, hoc est, montem Sion, & urbis inferioris forte modicam par-tem ducto funiculo per verticem montis Moria in tribu Juda fuisse; reliquam inferioris urbis partem versus Aquilonem, imo totam fere inferiorem ur-bem (quam filiam Sion appellatam, quod e monte Sion veluti nasci videbatur Psal. 9. & 72. Zach. 9. observat in descriptione urbis Hierusalem Adri-chomius) Benjaminitarum fuisse, atque hos amplio-rem urbis partem cum templo habuisse Deut. 33, 12. Joseph. l. 5. c. 1. 2. Conf. Jos. 18. ult. Jud. 1, 21. regiam tamen domum & regni sedem in monte Sion ad tribum Juda pertinuisse, quam editiorem & mu-nitiorem partem Jebusæi usque ad tempora Davi-dis retinuerunt, a quo demum eadem expugnata est 2. Sam. 5. si ad Benjaminis tribum pertinuit arx, utique David de stirpe Juda cum reliquis regibus Juda regiam suam in tribu Juda non habuere, quod haud dixerim.

Vocatà autem etiam fuit Jebus antiquitus Jud. 19, 10. 1. Par. 11, 4. 5. quod tamen nomen a Vulgo illi nonnulli tributum solum putant, & incolarum potius, quam urbis proprium id fuisse videtur Jos. 18, 28. Zach. 9, 7. etsi ab incolis aliquando urbs etiam ipsa vulgo sic nominata sit.

## 10:3
Verse 3.

THEREFORE ADONIZEDEK KING OF JERUSALEM SENT TO OHAM KING OF HEBRON, AND TO PHIRAM KING OF JARMUTH, AND TO JAPHIA KING OF LACHISH, AND TO DEBIR KING OF EGLON) A common danger provides a cause for alliances. See below chapter 11, in the beginning, and the letter of Mithridates to King Arsaces in the fragments of the Histories of Sallust.

HEBRON, seven years older than Tanis or Zoan, the royal city of Egypt, Num. 13, 23. founded one hundred and seventy years after the flood according to the calculation of Bonfrère at the cited place, which is the most ancient of cities in the whole world after the flood, and the first expressed by name in Scripture, distant 6 ½ miles from Jerusalem, previously called Kiriath-arba, did not receive its name from Eber, for עבר and חברון, which is society, differ greatly, but as Serarius teaches at Jos. 14, q. 5, from the society which Abraham entered into with the principal men of that place Gen. 23, 2. And therefore Eusebius is mistaken in his work on Hebrew places, deriving the origin of that name from Hebron the son of Caleb. It was originally called Mamre, as Moses testifies Gen. 23, 19. c. 35, 27. It was a royal city and the metropolis of the Philistines, and the dwelling place of the Anakim, by whom, after being conquered by Caleb, it was made a city of refuge, and given to the Levites with a suburb of 2000 cubits; the remainder of the city, fields, and villages was given as a gift to the victor Caleb himself Jos. 15. Jud. 1. Afterwards it became the seat of the kingdom of David, who reigned in it for 7 ½ years 2. Sam. 2, 11. It was taken from the Edomites by Judas Maccabeus 1. Mac. 5, 55. Concerning another Hebron see Jos. 19, 8. Zacharias lived in it Luke 1, 39. and Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, built a temple: But now new Hebron is infamous for a mosque, or Saracen temple.

JARMUTH, a city, likewise had its own king by the name of Piram, distant four miles from Eleutheropolis near the valley of Eshtaol, as is held in the book on Hebrew places; it was attributed to the tribe of Judah Jos. 15, 35. Crellius in his Concordance translates it 'Altitudes' or 'Fear of death,' and says it is situated five miles from Jerusalem towards the west.

LACHISH is likewise in the tribe of Judah Jos. 15, 39. Neh. 11, 30. It is distant seven miles to the south for those traveling in Daroma from Eleutheropolis, as Eusebius testifies in his work on Hebrew places, and according to Crellius in his Concordance, 1 ½ German miles from Jerusalem. It was fortified afterwards by Rehoboam 2. Par. 11, 9. destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar Jer. 34, 3. rebuilt again Neh. 11, 30. It is explained as 'Valley of the walker,' it had Japhia as king here, for whom the LXX read Japhia.

EGLON is listed likewise among the cities of Judah, Jos. 15, 39, distant three miles from Jerusalem, 2 from Lachish, 4 from Hebron. Its King is called DEBIR, which name is also that of a city mentioned later in v. 38, situated not far from Hebron. Besides this, there was another of the same name, Dabir, situated across the Jordan, which belonged to the tribe of Gad, Jos. 13, 26. That one is located in the tribe of Simeon by Adrichomius, but more correctly in the tribe of Dan by Eusebius. See Jos. 15, 49, c. 21, 15, 1 Chron. 6, 58; it was a priestly city. It was called Dabir from speaking, because there was the Academy of Palestine and a Gymnasium of eloquence, whence it was also called Cariath Sepher, the city of letters, Jos. 15, 15. It was also called Cariath Senna, v. 39, in the same place. Perhaps this Debir, King of the city of Eglon, was also the lord of Debir.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

MISIT ERGO ADONISEDEC REX JERVSALEM AD OHAM REGEM HEBRON, ET AD PHARAM REGEM JERIMOTH, AD JAPHIA QVOQVE REGEM LACHIS, ET AD DABIR REGEM EGLON) Commune periculum causam dat foederibus. Vide infra cap. 11. in principio, & epistolam Mithridatis ad regem Arsacem in fragmentis Historiarum Sallustii.

CHEBRON annis septem Tani vel Zoan Ægypti Regia urbe antiquior Num. 13, 23. centum & septuaginta annis post diluvium juxta Bonfrerii calculum ad l. c. condita, quæ urbium post diluvium in toto orbe antiquissima, & prima in Scriptura nominatim expressa, 6 ½. miliaribus a Jerusalem distans, antea Ciriatharbe dicta, non ab Eber nomen accepit, maxime enim differunt עבר & חברון quod est societas, sed ut Serarius docet ad Jos. 14, q. 5. a societate, quam Abraham iniit cum ejus loci viris præcipuis Gen. 23, 2. Ideoque fallitur Euseb. in de locis Hebraic. ab Hebrone filio Caleb illius nominis originem deducens. Primitus vocata fuit Mamre, teste Mose Gen. 23, 19. c. 35, 27. Regia fuit & metropolis Philistinorum, & habitaculum Enakim, quibus a Caleb expugnatis, civitas refugii facta, & Levitis data cum suburbano 2000. cubitorum, reliquum urbis, agri, villæ dono datum est ipsi victori Caleb Jos. 15. Jud. 1. Postea sedes regni David, qui per 7 ½. annos in ea regnavit, facta est 2. Sam. 2, 11. Edomitis a Juda Maccabæo erepta 1. Mac. 5, 55. De alia Chebrone vid. Jos. 19, 8. In ea Zacharias habitavit Luc. 1, 39. & Helena mater Constant. M. templum exstruxit: Sed nunc nova Hebron Moschea, seu templo Saracenico infamis est.

JARIMUTH urbs proprium Regem itidem habuit nomine Pharam, quarto distans ab Eleutheropoli lapide juxta vallem Esthaol, ut l. de loc. Heb. habetur, attributa fuit tribui Judæ Jos. 15, 35. Crellius in Concord. vertit Altitudines vel Timorem mortis, & quinque miliar. a Jerusalem versus occasum dissitam ait.

LACHIS itidem in tribu Juda est Jos. 15, 39. Neh. 11, 30. Septem miliaribus ad Austrum pergentibus in Daroma ab Eleutheropoli distat teste Euseb. de loco Hebraic. & juxta Crellium in Concord. 1 ½. Germ. a Jerusalem. Munita fuit postea a Rehabeam 2. Par. 11, 9. destructa a Nebucadnezar Jer. 34, 3. denuo reædificata Neh. 11, 30. Exponitur Spatzier-Thal, Regem hic habuit Japhia, pro quo LXX. legunt Jephta.

EGLON recensetur pariter inter urbes Juda Jos. 15, 39. tribus miliaribus a Jerusalem distans 2. a Lachis, 4. ab Hebron, Rex ejus DEBIR vocatur, quod nomen etiam est urbis postea commemoratæ v. 38. non procul ab Hebrone sitæ. Præterquam alia fuit ejusdem nominis Dabir, trans Jordanem sita, quæ ad tribum Gad spectabat Jos. 13, 26. Illa in tribu Simeon ab Adrichomio, rectius autem in tribu Dan ab Eusebio locatur. Vid. Jos. 15, 49. c. 21, 15. 1. Par. 6, 58. fuit urbs sacerdotalis. Dicta est Dabir a loquendo, quod ibi esset Academia Palestinæ, & Gymnasium eloquentiæ, unde etiam vocata Cariath Sepher civitas literarum Jos. 15, 15. Appellata quoque est Cariath Senna v. 39. ibidem. Forte hic Debir Rex Eglon urbis etiam Debir dominus fuit.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. DO NOT WITHDRAW YOUR HANDS FROM THE HELP OF YOUR SERVANTS) Subjects are to be defended. Livy, book 7: It seemed that faith was at stake, that those who had surrendered should not be betrayed.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NE TRAHAS MANUS TUAS AB AUXILIO SERVORUM TVORUM) Subditi defendendi. Livius libro 7. Fides agi visa, deditos non prodi.

## 10:9
V. 9. JOSHUA THEREFORE CAME UPON THEM SUDDENLY, ASCENDING ALL NIGHT FROM GILGAL.

Having set out through the entire night, he arrived at Gibeon very early in the morning. Themistocles said that friends are to be overcome by patience, enemies by speed.

Latin:

V. 9. IRRUIT ITAQUE JOSUE SUPER EOS REPENTE, TOTA NOCTE ASCENDENS DE GALGALIS.

Per noctem integram profectus summo mane ad Gabaon pervenit. Amicos patientia, hostes celeritate superandos esse, dixit Themistocles.

## 10:10
Vers. 10.

AND HE SMOTE THEM WITH A GREAT SLAUGHTER IN GIBEON, AND PURSUED THEM BY THE WAY OF THE ASCENT OF BETH-HORON.

It is manifest that these things are said not of God, but of Joshua. Therefore, God is not said to have smitten them, or if that must still be referred to God, who threw them into confusion, the pursuit is nevertheless to be attributed to the Israelites, as was also done by the LXX. Therefore, Bonfrerius refers that to the more remote noun in v. 10, JOSHUA: but it can be referred to the closer one, namely to the noun Israel: that Israel smote the enemies, after the Lord had thrown them into confusion (by sending terror from heaven), with a great slaughter in the Gibeonite territory (because they had besieged Gibeon), and pursued them by the way by which one ascends to that place where later the city of Beth-horon was built by Sherah, the granddaughter of Ephraim, 1 Chron. 7, 24. For they are said to have fled from the face of Israel, v. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

CONTRIVITQUE PLAGA MAGNA IN GABAON, AC PERSECUTUS EST EOS PER VIAM ASCENSUS BETHORON.

Manifestum est, hæc non de Deo, sed Josua di- ci. Non ergo Deus contrivisse eos dicitur, vel si id adhuc ad Deum referri debeat, qui eos conturbavit, persecutio tamen Israelitis tribuenda, ut a LXX. etiam factum. Ideo ad nomen remotius v. 10. irruit JO- SUE, id refert Bonfrerius: Sed potest referri ad propinquius, nimirum ad nomen Israel: quod Israel hostes, postquam eos Dominus conturbarat (immisso cœlitus terrore) percussione magna in Gabaonitico agro (quia Gabaon obsederant) contriverit, & persequu- tus sit per viam, qua ascenditur in eum locum, ubi post- ea Bethoron urbs a Sera nepte Ephraim extructa 1. Par. 7, 24. Nam a facie Israel fugisse dicuntur v. 11.

## 10:11
Vers. 11.

THE LORD CAST UPON THEM GREAT STONES) It rained stones. Often in histories.

Josephus, Ant. book 5, ch. 2, reports thunders and lightnings; therefore, hailstones of unusual size were joined to them, such as the storm that had once been in Egypt, Ex. 9, 23. Concerning the thunderbolt legion, which under M. Antonius obtained similar help from heaven by prayers against the Marcomanni, and was so named by the emperor, see Tertullian in Apologeticus, ch. V, and Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book 5, ch. 5. Compare Sirach 46, 6. Nor is it to be doubted that the Canaanites were struck by the blow of these stones sent from heaven so certainly that hardly any stone was in vain. Meanwhile, the Israelites, whether pressing them from the rear or mingled with them, were unharmed and untouched, which increases the miraculous help of God.

AS FAR AS AZEKAH.

Previously in verse 10 it was said that Joshua pursued them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon, and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah. And so the ether, or rather the Lord of the ether, fought for them even as far as that, by sending hailstones upon the enemies, so that more perished by the stones of hail than by the swords of the Israelites. It is therefore likely that the Canaanites, whose flight was from Gibeon into lower Beth-horon (that was two miles distant from Jerusalem), that is, between the west and the north, terrified by the rain of stony hail, turned aside into another part more towards the South, so that from Gibeon, which was in the tribe of Benjamin, they came indeed then into the Ephraimite tribe, but on the side where the same was bordering on the tribe of Benjamin, and soon rushed into the tribe of Judah; for those two cities, Azekah and Makkedah, were situated in the tribe of Judah, Jos. 15, 35. 41. The former of which, עזקה, 'fenced about', was situated two miles from Jerusalem towards the South, not far from Socoh, between Beth-horon and Makkedah, near which the Philistines encamped when David cut off the head of Goliath 1 Sam. 17, 40, which was fortified by Rehoboam 2 Chron. 11, 6, and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar Jer. 34, 7.

The other, מקדה, 'a burning', Brandstadt, Brandenburg, not far distant from the former, was 1 1/2 miles from Bethlehem towards the west, and 1/2 a mile from Libnah towards the North, in whose cave the hostile kings hid themselves Jos. 10, 16. cf. c. 12, 16. c. 15, 41.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

DOMINUS MISIT SUPER EOS LAPIDES MA- GNOS) Lapides pluit. Sæpe in historiis.

Tonitrua & fulmina refert Josephus l. 5. Ant. cap. 2. grandinibus ergo inusitatæ magnitudinis ea juncta, qualis tempestas olim in Ægypto fuerat Ex. 9, 23. De legione κεραυνοβόλῳ fulminatrice, quæ sub M. Antonio adversus Marcomannos similia auxilia precibus de cœlo obtinuit, inde ita ab imperatore nominata, vid. Tertul. in Apologetic. c. V. Euseb. l. 5. Hist. Eccl. c. 5. Conf. Syrac. 46, 6. Neque du- bitandum ita certo horum lapidum de cœlo misso- rum ictu tactos Cananæos, ut non facile lapis ullus irritus fuerit. Israelitis interim, sive a tergo ipsos prementibus, sive iisdem immixtis, illæsis & intactis, quod auget miraculosum Dei auxilium.

USQUE AD AZECA.

Antea vers. 10. dicebatur Josua eos persecutos per viam ascensus Bethoron, & percussisse usq; ad A- zēka & Maceda. Itaque eo usque ipsi militavit etiam æther, vel potius Dominus ætheris, missis grandini- bus in hostes, ut plures grandinis lapidibus, quam gladiis Israelis perierint. Verisimile ergo est, Cha- nanæos, quorum fuga erat a Gabaone in Bethcho- ron inferiori (ea duobus miliaribus distabat a Jeru- salem) hoc est, inter occidentem & septentrionem, lapidosæ grandinis pluvia exterritos in partem alte- ram magis versus Austrum declinasse, ut a Gabaon, quæ erat in tribu Benjamin, venerint quidem dein- de in tribum Ephraimiticam, sed qua parte eadem erat contermina tribui Benjamin, at mox in tribum Juda se proripuerint; nam duæ illæ urbes Azeca & Maceda in tribu Judæ sitæ erant Jos. 15, 35. 41. qua- rum prior עזקה circumsepta, duobus miliaribus ab Hierosalem versus Austrum non procul a Socho, inter Bethoron & Makeda sita fuit, penes quam Phi- listæi castrametati sunt, cum David Goliatho caput amputavit 1. Sam. 17, 40. quæ a Rehabeamo munita 2. Par. 11, 6. a Nebucadnezare destructa Jer. 30, 4. 7.

Altera מקדה incendium, Brandstadt, Branden- burg non multum a priori dissita, 1 1/2 miliar. a Beth- lehem versus occasum, 1/2 mil. a Libna versus Septen- trionem distabat, in cujus spelunca Reges hostiles latuerunt Jos. 10, 16. conf. c. 12, 16. c. 15, 41.

## 10:12
V. 12. THEN JOSHUA SPOKE TO THE LORD.

The Chaldean understands the song of the Rabbi as being about praise, and Lyranus as being about thanksgiving: but because the battle was not yet finished, there was without doubt a silent vow or an express prayer joined with the thanksgiving, which Augustine acknowledges here in book 21 of The City of God, chapter 8. Thus the following words explain by way of exegesis what he said to the Lord, or if this prayer made to the Lord is distinct (which we prefer), having been strengthened in prayer in his confidence, with a truly heroic impetus, the Spirit of the Lord moving him, he commanded the Sun and Moon not to proceed in their motion, and he restrained the motion of the whole heaven by a divinely inspired command with great boldness, where the Sun was compelled to stay its step and, remaining motionless by a stupendous miracle, to serve him as he fought with its light, until all the enemies were overthrown and destroyed.

SUN, STAND THOU STILL OVER GIBEON, AND THOU, MOON, IN THE VALLEY OF AJALON.

It has been spoken of before regarding Gibeon. Adrichomius locates Ajalon (which they interpret as Oak, or strength, or stag) in the tribe of Dan. See Josh. 19:41, Judg. 1:35. It was a priestly city of refuge, Josh. 21:20, 24, distant 24 miles from Jerusalem, as Crellius notes, concerning which compare 1 Sam. 14:27, 45, 1 Chron. 9:13. There is also another of that name in the tribe of Zebulun, Judg. 12:12, and also yet another in the tribe of Ephraim, 1 Chron. 17:69, from all of which Crellius distinguishes the city of Ajalon in the tribe of Judah, 2 Chron. 11:5, 6, 10, which Bonfrerius concludes is the same as this one of ours, from the adjoining names of the cities, so that it was inhabited by the Benjaminites and the tribesmen of Judah, on whose border it was, and therefore he establishes that it was more to the west and perhaps also somewhat more to the south than Gibeon, inasmuch as the tribe of Dan was to the west and contiguous to the Philistines. Wherefore he thinks these words were spoken in the morning and forenoon time, because it could not be that the Sun could be seen in some city further to the east, or be looming over it, if it were inclining toward the west. But if the sun were 50 degrees above the horizon (at which time it ascends almost to their zenith at midday), it could have appeared toward the east above Gibeon, situated on a higher slope, at about the ninth hour in the month of July, so that the Moon was lower toward the west in Aquarius, in its waning phase. Which things may be read in Bonfrerius.

Latin:

V. 12. TUNC LOCUTUS EST JOSUE DO- MINO.

De cantico Rabbini, Chaldæus de laude, Lyra- nus de gratiarum actione intelligunt: sed quia non- dum finita pugna cum gratiarum actione conjun- ctum fuit sine dubio votum tacitum, aut precatio ex- pressa, quam agnoscit hic Augustinus l. 21. de civ. Dei c. 8. Sic verba sequentia κατ᾿ ἐπεξήγησιν expri- ment, quid Domino loquutus sit, vel si hæc oratio ad Dominum facta distincta sit, (quod malumus) confortatus in oratione in fiducia sua, cum impetu vere heroico, movente Spiritu Domini, Soli & Lu- næ imperavit, ne in motu pergerent, cælique totius motum imperio θεοπνεύστῳ μετὰ πολλῆς παῤῥησίας cohibuit, ubi Sol gradum sistere, ipsique pugnanti luce sua, miraculo stupendo immobilis persistens mnistrare coactus fuit, donec hostes universi pro- sternerentur, ac delerentur.

SOL CONTRA GABAON NE MOVEARIS ET LUNA CONTRA VALLEM AJALON.

De Gabaone ante dictum. Ajalon (quam in- terpretantur Quercum, vel fortitudinem vel cervum) Adrichomius in tribu Danitica locat. Vid. Jos, 19, 41. Jud. 1, 35. Fuit Sacerdotalis civitas refugii Jos. 21, 20. 24. miliari distans a Jerusalem, notante Crel- lio, de qua conf. 1, Sam. 14, 27. 45. 1. Par. 9, 13. Est & alia ejus nominis in tribu Sebulon Jud. 12, 12. nec non alia iterum in tribu Ephraim 1, Par. 17, 69. a quibus o- mnibus Crellius distinctam facit urbem Ajalon in tribu Juda 2. Par. 11, 5. 6. 10. quam vero eandem cum hac nostra esse, ex adjunctis urbium nominibus col- ligit Bonfrerius, ita ut a Benjaminitis & Judæ tribuli- bus, in quorum erat confinio, habitata fuerit, ideo- que Occidentaliorem & forte etiam nonnihil Austra- liorem eam fuisse, quam Gabaonem statuit, siquidem tribus Dan ad Occidentem erat, & Philistæis conti- gua. Quapropter tempore matutino & antemeri- diano hæc dicta putat, quod fieri non possit, ut cer- natur Sol in urbe aliqua Orientaliore, aut ei supra imminere, si ad occasum inclinaret. Si autem sol fuerit 50. grad. supra horizontem (quo tempore fe- re meridie ad eorum verticem afcendit) apparere potuisse versus Orientem supra Gabaonem in edi- tiore clivo sitam, hora circiter nona mense Julio, ut Luna versus Occidentem depressior in Aquario fue- rit, in sui decremento. Quæ penes Bonfrerium le- gantur.

## 10:13
Ver. 13. IS NOT THIS WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF THE JUST?) It seems to have been some triumphal poem, in which Israel was called by the contraction Jashar, as if excelling other nations in equity.

Some ineptly understand Genesis, others Exodus, others the Pentateuch: for how could this miracle be written down in them before it happened? And no less inconveniently do others think the book of the twelve Prophets, or the prophecy of Habakkuk, is noted because of chapter 4:11: because the author of the book of Joshua is without doubt older than these. There are those who, with Masius, wish the book of the annals of the people of the Jews to be noted, but one which was included in the sacred volumes, which Bonfrerius rightly rejects. That opinion is more correct regarding a metrical book, in which the deeds of heroes and men were sung, from which also the lamentations of David were taken, 2 Sam. 1:8, concerning which are Sanctius and Bonfrerius. Cornelius thinks that the book of annals was not canonical or a catalog of saints. But annals are not usually described in rhythms, such as these are held to be by many, even by Cornelius himself. Let Sixtus Senensis be compared, as well as B. Walther in Officina Biblica, p. 1186.

SO THE SUN STOOD STILL IN THE MIDST OF HEAVEN.

The midst of heaven is not to be understood mathematically, but morally, and it denotes not the middle of the whole hemisphere, but the middle of the quadrant from the horizon to the zenith. Nor do the words, AND HASTED NOT TO GO DOWN, imply that a solstice happened toward evening, when the sun was setting. But they note only the motionless station of the Sun. Therefore he ordered the Sun to stand, before the day grew hot, so that the Israelites would not fail in pursuing their enemies, and because he desired to finish that war completely on that day.

FOR THE SPACE OF ONE DAY) The Hebrews, as in a perfect day, that is, a summer one, such as that was then for them in those places. Thus Maimonides and the Hebrews, whom Masius cites, acknowledging no miracle here; but a poetic phrase, as if the Sun had waited until the slaughter of the enemies was complete, when rather the Israelites did not cease to press upon the enemies as long as either the Sun or the moon provided light, just as night often brings an end to pursuit in histories. The writer to the Hebrews, referring to the great rewards of faith in chapter 8, mentions the destruction of Jericho: he does not mention the changing of the celestial course, which would have been much greater. And now it will follow that God accommodated Himself to the voice of man, not indeed by stopping the Sun, but by fighting, i.e., by supplying strength to the combatants and an invincible spirit against labors, sending in addition stones instead of hail. These things can thus be said not implausibly, although it is not impossible for God to delay the course of the Sun or even, after the setting of the Sun, to show its appearance in a cloud standing above the horizon through reflection.

Although Grotius acknowledges that it is not impossible for God to delay the course of the sun, he nevertheless tries to evade the miracle here by a twofold invention so as not to admit it: The first is that of the Rabbis, Maimonides, and others, who posit a poetic phrase here, as if the sun had waited until the slaughter of the enemies was complete. Which does not seem improbable to him. The second is peculiar to him, that after the setting of the sun its appearance was shown by reflection in a cloud standing above the horizon, unless perhaps he borrowed this from the atheist Isaac La Peyrère, the father of the Pre-Adamites, who strives to weaken this most illustrious miracle with a similar fiction, as if this miracle did not proceed beyond the sensible horizon of Joshua and the Gibeonites, or that in the ethereal sphere or the region of vapors which hovered over the city of Gibeon in the middle of the sky and air, or from the reflection of an opposite mountain, the brightness of the sun without the sun itself remained for 12 hours or more in that tract alone. He could, however, have added a third from a certain Jewish philosopher named שם טוב, to whom it seems that God created a body of a new kind in the sky, which would represent the sun after it had set, and illuminate the world until the Israelites had finished fighting. Then a fourth also of R. David Kimchi and other Jews, that the moon as a substitute light was placed in the stead of the sun's light after it had set, so that they would not fight in the dark, like gladiators, which that monstrous Pre-Adamite also made his own, as if a splendor similar to the moon had succeeded the sun in the valley of Ajalon until the Hebrews had slaughtered all their enemies. But inventions of this kind have already been refuted by the most learned Masius, whom Grotius praises here, even though he follows his Rabbis more. And Grotius saw without a doubt that there was no place for the Kimchian fiction, because Joshua did not command that the moon as a substitute light should succeed the sun and illuminate the night, which happens ordinarily when the moon is full, but that the sun should not proceed in its ordinary motion: and so he ordered the sun to stand, which happened by a miracle. He also saw that the most brave commander did not wish for a new body to be created that would represent the sun, but that he addressed the sun, saying: Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon. But he also ought to have seen that the words of Joshua cannot be understood concerning the reflection of the sun in a cloud standing above the horizon, made after the sun had set: for he speaks expressly of the sun itself, not of an image of the sun: Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon. And he adds: So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day; and so that there might be no doubt that the discourse was about the sun itself standing and remaining above the horizon, he still adds for the exaggeration and celebration of such a great miracle: There was no day so long before or after, the Lord obeying the voice of a man. Therefore, it must be shown not what was possible for the Lord, but what was done, and what the scripture declares to have been done. Concerning which the son of Sirach also clearly testifies in ch. 46, 5. Was not the Sun hindered in his wrath, and one day made as if it were two? He says the Sun was hindered, not that a reflection of the Sun arose, which if it be posited, there would have been no need for any hindering of the Sun. He says one day was like two others, just as the Holy Spirit also testifies, the Sun did not hasten to set for the space of one day. Therefore, it is necessary that the Sun itself remained established above the horizon, and did not set, because its lingering above the horizon makes the day, its setting produces the night, and terminates the day. And how could the brightness of the Sun have survived without the Sun itself for an entire day or the space of twelve hours, or longer, in that region alone, or have remained above the Horizon while the Sun itself was hidden many degrees below the Horizon? Furthermore, unless Grotius had been blinded by the fascination of the Rabbis, he could have seen, and ought to have seen, that the text is too clear to be obscured by I know not what poetic license. For he also reports the very words of Joshua, uttered in the heat of battle with a great and heroic Spirit, Sun, stand thou still against Gibeon, and Moon against the valley of Ajalon; but who will suffer himself to be persuaded that in the heat of battle that renowned hero played with meters; or if you say his words were related poetically (although no trace of rhythm, let alone verse or poem, is found here in the sources), yet it is necessary that Joshua commanded a solstice, otherwise it ought not to have been inserted into a poem, much less would it have been confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who most clearly, and not just once, affirms that the Sun stood still, where there is no room for the evasion of a poetic phrase: And the Sun and Moon stood, he says, until the nation had avenged itself upon its enemies. And again: So the Sun stood in the midst of heaven, and did not hasten to set for the space of one day. Finally, how could the Holy Spirit have countered that figment about a Poetic Phrase more effectively than when, for the sake of illustrating the miracle, He added that there had not been such a long day before or after, and that the Lord obeyed the voice of a man? Therefore, that φρεξελότης of the Hebrews is not to be allowed, that the Sun only stood for a perfect day, that is, a summer one; because after that command of the Emperor Joshua, to which the Lord Himself is said to have obeyed, the sun is said in the Hebrew source to have stood still for an entire day, so that then the days were joined together. Therefore the son of Sirach says the Sun was hindered in its course, and one day was made like two. And Josephus, Antiq. book V, ch. 2, says the day was prolonged, lest the succeeding night should restrain the attack of the Hebrews. Ambros. book 1, offic. ch. 40. When Jesus Nave was rising against the Gibeonites, and feared that night would hinder the victory, with greatness of mind and faith he cried out, Stand, Sun, and it stood, until this victory was consummated. Chrys. hom. 27 on the Ep. to the Hebrews. Understand how great the righteous man is. Jesus Nave said: Stand, Sun, around Gibeon, and it was done. Let the whole world therefore come, or rather two or three, or ten, or twenty worlds, and let them say and do this, but they will not be able to. But the friend of God commanded his friendly creatures, or rather he petitioned his friend, and the servants obeyed: and he who was below, commanded the Superiors. And hence Dionysius the Areopagite, as he is commonly called, Epist. 7, warned that Apollophanes the Sophist ought to have been led by this change in the perpetual order of celestial things into admiration of the greatest, and in speech inexplicable, power of GOD, who created all things, and preserves them, and moderates them according to His own nod. Similarly, Nemesius observes in his work on the nature of man, ch. 38, that God for this reason once restrained by His command the course of the Sun and Moon, which is otherwise perpetual and always uniform by a certain necessity of nature, to show that He is held by no laws of necessity, but that He Himself is the Lord of all necessity, just as He is its maker.
