The blessed Isaiah also acknowledged the same from the Hebrews among others, whose words are these: And the Sun lingered and the Moon stood still, etc. Masius cites these in his most learned commentary on this passage, and judges it credible that the Moon was new at that time, and had not traveled far from the Sun, so that the lingering of both stars could be seen in the sky: but from the sacred words themselves, he says that no one but the most stupid would fail to understand that the Sun did not depart from our horizon until the battle was finished.

The things which Grotius brings forward against this are frivolous. For the fact that in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 11, there is no mention of the changed course of the heavens, can no more detract from this miracle than the omission of other miracles of Moses, or Joshua, or other men of God in that record of examples of faith detracts from them. For it was not the intention to recount some, but not all, proofs or effects of faith. For there is no mention made of the production of water from the rock, nor of the drying up of the Jordan, nor of very many other most illustrious miracles.

But as for what Grotius wishes, that God accommodated Himself to the voice of man not only by standing still, but by fighting, or by supplying strength and courage to the combatants, and by casting down stones like hail; in that he speaks against the truth itself. For the text is too clear, that God obeyed the voice of a man by making the day so long, such as never was before, nor will be hereafter, even if Joshua was also heard by the Lord in that, that He fought for him with hailstones, Sirach 46, 6. But how this day is said to be so long here, so that the miracle which happened in the time of Hezekiah is not detracted from, can be seen in Sixtinus ab Amama, Anti-Barbar. Bibl. book III, p. 381, seqq. Masius has this to say about it: the comparison does not concern the length of this day of ours. But it is preferred to any days whatsoever only in this, that God never produced any other day at the prayers of any man, for the sake of a falling enemy, by interrupting the course of the sun, as He produced this one. Which things easily suffice, so that there is no need here for curious questions, about which, however, Sixtinus can be consulted there.

Latin:

Vers. 13. NONNE SCRIPTUM EST HOC IN LIBRO JŪSTORVM?) Videtur poema aliquod fuisse ἐπινίκιον, in quo ישראל contracte ישר dicebatur, quasi cæteris genti- bus æquitate præstans.

Inepte nunnulli Genesin, alii Exodum, alii Pen- tateuchum intelligunt: quomodo enim in illis hoc miraculum perscribi potuit, antequam evenit? Nec minus inconvenienter alii librum duodecim Prophe- tarum, aut Prophetiam Habacuci, ob c. 4, 11. notari putant: quia autor libri Josuæ sine dubio his est an- tiquior. Sunt qui cum Masio librum annalium po- puli Judæorum notari volunt, sed qui relatus sit in sa- cra volumina, quod merito rejicit Bonfrerius. Re- ctius sese habet illa sententia de libro metrico, quo res gestæ Heroum & virorum decantatæ, e quo etiam planctus Davidis desumti sunt 2. Sam. 1, 8. de quo San- ctius & Bonfrerius. Cornelius putat, quod liber anna- lium non canonicus aut catalogus sanctorum fuerit Sed annales non solent rhythmis describi, quales h a plerisque etiam ab ipso Cornelio habentur. Con ferantur Sixtus Senensis, ut & B. Waltherus in officin Bibl. p. 1186.

STETITQUE ITAQUE SOL IN MEDIC COELI.

Medium cæli non mathematice, sed moralite intelligendum, & notatur non medietas totius he misphærii: sed medietas quadrantis ab horizonte a verticem. Neque verba, ET NON FESTINAVIT OCCUMBERE, inferunt Solstitium sub vesperam factum, cum Sol occumberet. Sed notant solum immobilem stationem Solis. Stare ergo Solem jussit, priusquam dies incalesceret, ne deficerent Israelitæ in persequendis hostibus, & quod bellum illud eo die plane conficere cuperet.

SPATIO UNIUS DIEI) Hebræi, ut in perfecta die, id est, æstiva, qualis tunc erat illa illis in locis. Ita Maimoni- des & Hebræi, quos citat Masius, nullum hîc miraculum agno- scentes; sed phrasin Poeticam, quasi Sol expectasset, donec occidio hostium perfecta foret, cum potius Israelitæ non de- stiterint insistere hostibus, quamdiu aut Sol, aut luna lumen præbeant, sicut sæpe in historiis insequendi finem nox adfert. Scriptor ad Hebræos fidei præmia ingentia referens c. 8. de- jectæ Hierichuntis meminit: mutati cœlestis cursus, quod multo majus fuerat, non meminit. Et jam sequetur, Deum voci hominis se accommodasse, non quidem Solem sistendo, sed pugnando, i. e. pugnantibus vires, & invictum contra la- bores animum subministrando, immittendo præterea lapides, pro grandine. Hæc ita non improbabiliter dici possunt, quamquam impossibile Deo non est, Solis cursum morari aut etiam post Solis occasum speciem ejus in nube supra horizon- tem exstanti per repercussum ostendere.

Quamvis impossibile Deo non esse Solis cursum morari, agnoscat Grotius, id tamen ne hîc admittat, gemino commento miraculum eludere conatur: Primum est Rabbinorum, Maimonidis, & aliorum, qui Phrasin Poeticam hic ponunt, quasi Sol expectasset, donec occidio hostium perfecta foret. Quod non im- probabile ipsi est. Alterum ipsi proprium est, quod post solis occasum species ejus in nube supra horizontem exstanti per repercussum ostensa fuerit, nisi forte id mutuo accepit ab homine Atheō Isaaco Peirerio Præ- Adamitarum Parente, qui simili figmento miracu- lum illustrissimum enervare satagit, quasi hoc mira- culi ultra Horizontem sensibilem Josuæ & Gabao- nitidis non processerit, aut in ætherea Sphæra aut regione vaporum illa, quæ civitati Gabaonicæ cœli & aeris medio incubabat, vel ex repercussione mon- tis oppositi fulgor Solis sine ipso Sole per 12. horas aut amplius in solo tractu superfuerit. Poterat au- tem addidisse etiam tertium è Philosopho quodam Judæo nomine שם טוב, cui videtur, Deum novi ge- neris corpus in cœlo condidisse, quod solem postquam ille occidisset, repræsentaret, & usque eo orbem terrarum illustraret, dum depugnatum ab Israelitis esset. Tum Quartum etiam R. Davidis Kimchi, & aliorum Ju- dæorum, Lunæ vicarium lumen solis lumini, postquam is occubuisset, fuisse suppositum, ne in tenebris, Andaba- tarum more scilicet, pugnaretur, quod suum etiam fe- cit monstrosus ille Præ-Adamita, quasi splendor Lunari similis in valle Ajalon Solari succefferit, do- nec inimicos suos omnes mactassent Ebræi. Sed commenta istiusmodi jam refutata apud doctissi- mum Masium sunt, quem hic laudat Grotius, etsi Rabbinos suos magis sequatur. Et vidit procul dubio Grotius, Kimchiano figmento locum non es- se, quia non ut Lunæ vicarium lumen succedat Soli, noctemque illuminaret, mandavit Josua, quod or- dinarie fit, cum Luna plena est, sed ut Sol in motu suo ordinario non pergeret: adeoque solem stare jussit, quod per miraculum contigit. Vidit etiam novum corpus condi, quod solem repræsentaret, non optasse fortissimum illum Imperatorem, sed Solem alloquutum esse, ut staret: Sol contra Gibeon ne mo- vearis. Sed videre etiam debuit, non posse de reper- cussione Solis in nube supra horizontem exstanti, post solem occasum facta, verba Josuæ intelligi: Qui diserte de Sole ipso, non de imagine Solis loquitur: Sol contra Gibeon ne movearis. Additque: Stetit itaque Sol in medio cœli, & non festinavit occumbere spa- tio unius diei; ac ne dubium ullum esset, de Sole ipso stante & consistente supra horizontem, sermonem esse, esse, (quamvis ista verba jam omne dubium exclu- dant) subjungit adhuc ad miraculi tanti exaggera- tionem & celebrationem: Non fuit antea, nec postea tam longa dies, obediente Domino voci hominis. Non quid ergo possibile fuerit Domino, sed quid factum sit, quidque scriptura factum esse perhibeat, osten- dendum. Quo de clare etiam testatur Syracides c. 46, 5. Annon in iracundia ejus impeditus est Sol, & una dies facta est quasi duo? Solem dicit impeditum, non repercussionem Solis exortam, quæ si ponatur, nulla solis impeditione opus fuerit. Unum diem dicit fuisse instar duorum aliorum, prouti etiam Spiritus sanctus testatur, non festinavit Sol occumbere spatio u- nius diei. Solem ergo ipsum supra horizontem constitutum mansisse, non vero occidisse oportet, quia ejusdem mora supra horizontem diem facit, occasus ejus noctem parit, diem terminat. Et quo- modo Solis fulgor sine Sole ipso per integrum diem vel duodecim horarum spatium, aut amplius in illo solo tractu superfuisset, aut Sole ipso multis gradi- bus sub Horizonte latente, supra Horizontem re- mansisset? Porro nisi Rabbinorum fascino excæca- tus fuisset Grotius, videre etiam poterat, & debebat, textum clariorem esse, quam ut per licentiam nescio quam Poeticam obscurari queat. Nam & verba ipsa Josuæ refert, in pugna fervente, magno & heroi- co Spiritu prolata, Sol contra Gibeon ne movearis, & Luna contra vallem Ajalon; Quis autem persuadere sibi patietur, in fervore pugnæ metris lusisse heroëm istum inclytum; aut si verba ejus poetice relata di- cas (quamvis nullum rythmi, nedum versus, aut car- minis vestigium hic in fontibus deprehendatur) Jo- suam tamen Solstitium imperasse oportet, alioquin id carmini inferi non debuisset, multo minus testi- monio Spiritus sancti comprobatum fuisset, qui lu- culentissime, nec semel tantum affirmat, Solem ste- tisse, ubi nullus effugio poeticæ phraseos locus: Ste- teruntque, inquit, Sol & Luna, donec ulcisceretur se gens de inimicis suis. Atque iterum: Stetit itaque Sol in medio cæli, & non festinavit occumbere spatio unius diei. Deniq; quomodo figmento isti de Phrasi Poe- tica efficacius occurrere poterat Spiritus Sanctus, quam cum miraculi illustrandi causa addidit, non fuisse antea nec postea tam longum diem, & quod obe- dierit Dominus voci hominis? Non ergo permitten- da ista Ebræorum φρεξελότης, quod Sol tantum stete- rit per diem perfectam, id est, æstivam; quia post illud Imperatoris Josuæ mandatum, cui Dominus ipse obediisse dicitur, adhuc per integram diem stetisse sol dicitur in Ebræo fonte, ut ibi tum dies conjuncti fuerint. Ideò Syracides Solem impeditum fuisse dicit in cursu suo, unamque diem factam instar dua- rum. Et Josephus l. Antiq. V. c. 2. diem productum esse ait, ne nox succedens Hebræorum impetum cohibe- ret. Ambros. l. 1. offic. c. 40. Jesus Nave cum adversum Gabaonitas surgeret prælium, & vereretur, ne nox impediret victoriam, magnitudine mentis & fi- dei clamavit, stet Sol, & stetit, dum hæc victoria con- summaretur. Chrys. hom. 27. ad Ep. ad Ebr. In- tellige quantus est justus. Dixit Jesus Nave: Stet Sol circa Gabaon & factum est. Veniat igitur omnis mundus, magis autem duo aut tres, aut decem, & vi- ginti mundi dicant & faciant hoc, sed non poterunt. Amicus vero Dei creaturis amicis suis imperabat, ma- gis autem amicum suum postulavit, & obedierunt ser- vi: & ille qui deorsum erat, Superioribus imperabat. Atque hinc Dionysius Areopagita, prout vulgo vo- catur, Epist. 7. monuit, Apollophanem Sophistam ista perpetui cælestium rerum ordinis mutatione in- duci debuisse in admirationem maximæ, atque ora- tione inexplicabilis potentiæ DEI, qui res omnes condidit, & conservat, proque suo nutu moderatur. Si- militer observat Nemesius de hominis natura cap. 38. Deum ideo semel suo imperio, perpetuum alioqui & quadam naturæ necessitate semper æquabilem Solis Lu- næque cursum cohibuisse, ut ostenderet, nullis se necessi- tatis legibus teneri, sed ipsum omnis necessitudinis ut o- pificem sic & Dominum esse. Idem agnovit quoque ex Ebræis inter alios B. Isaias, cujus hæc sunt: Et mo- ratus est Sol & Luna substitit &c. Citat hæc Ma- sius in comment. doctissimo ad h. l. ac credibile esse censet, Lunam illo tempore novam fuisse, neque procul ab Sole measse, ut utriusq; astri mora conspici in cælo po- tuerit: Ex ipsis vero sacris verbis neminem nisi stupi- dissimum non intelligere ait, Solem non ante confectam pugnam e nostro orbe finiente excessisse.

Frivola sunt, quæ contra affert Grotius. Nam quod in Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 11. nulla mentio fiat mutati cæli cursus, miraculo huic non magis deroga- re potest, quam aliis sive Mosis, sive Josuæ, sive alio- rum virorum Dei miraculis eorum in ista exemplo- rum fidei consignatione omissio derogat. Non- nulla enim, non vero omnia fidei specimina aut ef- fecta recensere propositum erat. Nam nec aquæ e petra productionis, nec Jordanis exsiccationis, nec aliorum plurimorum miraculorum perquam illustrium facta est mentio.

Quod vero Grotius vult, Deum voci hominis se accommodasse non solum sistendo, sed pugnando, seu pugnantibus vires & animum sufficiendo, ac lapides pro grandine immittendo; in eo soli ipsi veritatis ob- loquitur. Textus enim nimis luculentus est, obe- disse Deum voci hominis, tam longum efficiendo di- em, qualis nec antea fuit unquam, nec deinceps futura est, etsi in eo etiam exauditus fuerit Josua a Domi- no, quod pugnarit saxis grandinis pro eo, Syrac. 46, 6. Quomodo autem dies ista tam longe hic dicatur, ne miraculo, quod Ezechiæ tempore contigit, deroge- tur, videri poterit Sixtinus ab Amama Anti-Barbar. Bibl. l. III. p. 381. seqq. Masius ita de eo habet: de hu- jus nostri diei longitudine non agit comparatio. Sed is eo solum antefertur diebus quibusvis, quod nullum alium diem Deus ad ullius hominis preces, cadendi hostis gra- tia, interrupto solis cursu, sic produxit, ut hunc produ- xit. Quæ facile sufficiunt, ut curiosis hic opus non sit quæstionibus, de quibus tamen illic Sixtinus con- suli poterit.

## 10:14
V. 14. THERE WAS NOT BEFORE, NOR AFTER SO LONG A DAY.

Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho makes Joshua's day 36 hours long, as if 24 supernatural hours were added to the twelve ordinary and natural hours. But Cosmus Magalianus in this place more correctly understands it as an artificial day, inasmuch as it alone provides light. One day was made as two, says Sirach 46:5, that is, the day, which at that time in Judea was 14 hours long, was made 28 hours long. Furthermore, in the Hebrew there is nothing held regarding a comparison of length: the Vulgate Version, therefore, which has given birth to various disputes, is to be amended thus: There was not like that day before it and after it, that the Lord might obey the voice of a man. In vain, therefore, do Papist interpreters wear themselves out concerning the reconciliation of the maximum length of this day of Joshua with the length of the day of Isaiah, in the time of Hezekiah, which they observe from Dionysius to Polycarp to have been 32 hours. Some say that there had not been so long a day up to the time when Samuel, or someone else, wrote this: others judge that the day of Hezekiah, prolonged by Isaiah, was only 15 hours long, because five hours were added to the ten hours of the day, which is the solution of Cornelius. Bonfrerius also adds, and indeed Maresius too, that the comparison is made only with respect to the same region of Palestine: lest longer days in polar regions be objected. And what other responses of theirs might be noted.

Some also raise a doubt about the Solstice, namely that not only did Joshua make the sun stand still, but also the son of Sela, 1 Chron. 4:22, as Rabanus and the Glossa have it there. But that error is of the Vulgate version; in the Hebrew is the name Joakin, which the Vulgate rendered as 'he made to stand,' and the interpreter added 'the Sun' of his own accord. Other solstices of Abbot Mutius, as also under Charlemagne and under Charles V, were such only κατὰ δόκησιν (in appearance), when the sun was seen longer not in itself, but through reflected rays, concerning which see Cornelius on Eccl. 46:5.

We add the allegory of Theodoret in this place, q. 13. Just as the Sun stood still while Joshua was fighting, so while Christ dying on the cross was dissolving death by His death, the Sun held back its rays at midday and filled the earth with darkness. And that of Rabanus: JESUS acts so that the Sun of righteousness may never set for the faithful, but may always rise and infuse the hearts of believers with the light of truth.

Latin:

V. 14. NON FUIT ANTEA, NEC POSTEA TAM LONGA DIES.

Justinus Martyr Dial. cum Tryph. facit Josua- num diem 36. horarum, quasi 24. horæ supernatura- les accesserint duodecim ordinariis & naturalibus horis. Sed rectius Cosmus Magalian. in h. l. diem artificialem intelligit, utpote quæ sola lucem præbet. Una dies facta est quasi duo, ait Siracid. 46, 5. hoc est, dies, quæ isto tempore in Judæa erat 14. horarum, facta est 28. horarum. Cæterum in Ebræo nihil de comparatione longitudinis habetur: Versio ergo Vulgata, quæ varias peperit Disputationes, ita e- mendanda: Non fuit sicut dies illa ante eam & post eam, ut obediret Dominus voci viri. Frustra ergo se macerant Pontificii Interpp. de conciliatione longitu- dinis maximæ hujus Josuanæ diei cum Esaianæ diei longitudine, tempore Ezechiæ, quam e Dionysio ad Polycarp. 32. horarum fuisse observant. Non tam longam fuisse diem usque ad tempus illud, quo hæc scripsit Samuel, aut quis alius, nonnulli dicunt: alii diem Ezechiæ ab Esaia prolongatum XV. dun- taxat horarum fuisse censent, quod decem horis diei quinque adjectæ fuerint, quæ Cornelii est solu- tio. Addit & Bonfrerius, imo & Maresius compa- rationem fieri non nisi respectu ejusdem regionis Palæstinæ: ne objiciantur dies prolixiores in regio- nibus nibus polaribus. Et quæ aliæ notari posfent ipsorum responsiones.

Nonnulli dubium etiam movent de Solstitio quod nempe non Josua tantum solem stare fecerit, sed etiam filius Sela 1. Par, 4, 22. ut illic Rabanus & Glossa habent. Sed error ille est versionis Vulgatæ; in Hebræo est nomen Joakin, quod vulgata reddidit, qui stare fecit, & de suo addidit interpres Solem. Alia Solstitia Abbatis Mutii, ut & sub Carolo Magno & sub Carolo V. talia solum fuere κατὰ δόκησιν, quum Sol diutius visus non in se, sed per radios reflexos, de quibus Cornel. ad Eccl. 46, 5.

Addimus allegoriam Theodoreti in h. l. q. 13. Sicut Sol pugnante Josua stetit, ita dum Christus in cruce moriens morte sua mortem dissolveret, Sol in meridie continuit radios suos, & tenebris opplevit terram. Et Rabani: JEsus facit, ne unquam Sol justitiæ fidelibus occumbat, sed semper oriatur, & credentium corda lumine veritatis infundat.

## 10:15
V. 15. AND JOSHUA RETURNED WITH ALL ISRAEL.

He is said to have returned because he began to return and turned back his journey, as Vatablus says, and Joshua was preparing the return. Thus there is no need here to posit an anticipation of those things which were to be placed in the last verse, with Masius.

IN THE CAMP AT GILGAL) In the stationary camp. Ver. 17. FIVE KINGS HIDING IN A CAVE) Some to desert the villages and depart into pathless places, and to act as those who would hide themselves and their most precious things with them in caves. Tacitus, Annals 14, in the affairs of Armenia. See Judg. 6:2. TO THE MOUTH OF THE CAVE) Tacitus called them the mouths and exits of caves in the same place. Ver. 19. STRIKE THE REARMOST OF THE FUGITIVES) That is זנב to the Hebrews, to harass the rear guard to Tacitus and others. καταλαμβάνειν τὴν ὐραγίαν to the Greeks in this place. Ver. 21. WHERE THE CAMP THEN WAS) Stationary or temporary.

Others understand the military camp, or the stronger and more fortified portion of the army, which had been ordered to pitch camp there until one part of the army pursued and struck the fugitives. The ordinary and stationary camp was situated at Gilgal, see the last verse.

Latin:

V. 15. REVERSUSQUE EST JOSUA CUM OMNI ISRAEL.

Reversus dicitur, quod reverti inceperit, iterq; reflexerit, ut Vatabl. et Josue adornabat reditum. Ita non opus est hic anticipationem ponere eorum, quæ v. ultimo locanda erant, cum Masio.

IN CASTRA GALGALE) In stativa. Vers. 17. QVINQVE REGES LATENTES IN SPELVNCA) Quidam deserere vicos, & in avia digredi, ac fucere qui se speluncis, & carissima secum abderent. Tacitus Annalium 14. in rebus Armeniæ. Vid. Jud. 6, 2. AD OS SPELUNCÆ) Ora & exitus specuum dixit Tacitus eodem loco. Vers. 19. EXTREMOS QVOSQVE FUGIENTIVM CÆDITE) Id זנב Hebræis, carpere agmen Tacito & aliis. καταλαμβάνειν τὴν ὐραγίαν Græcis hoc loco. Vers. 21. VBI TVNC ERANT CASTRA) Stativa sive subitaria.

Alii castra intelligunt militaria, vel potiorem & munitiosem exercitus portionem, qui ibi jussus fuerit castra figere, donec pars una exercitus fugientes persequeretur & cæderet. Ordinaria & stativa castra in Galgalis sita erant v. ult.

## 10:24
V. 24. PUT YOUR FEET UPON THE NECKS OF THESE KINGS.

That was not of an insolent or haughty spirit in victory, but of prudence, because he wished to add confidence to his own men, that God would fulfill what He had promised. Deut. 30, last verse, you shall tread upon their necks, and he might draw them away from the unspeakable crimes of the Canaanites, who were suffering these things for those crimes by their own desert: but he would afflict the enemies of God and of God's people with just punishments. This was not cruelty, says Origen, homily 11. But humanity, signifying the Sacrament of Christ, which the Lord JESUS, having been previously foreshadowed by the son of Nun through individual cities, now completes in truth through the individual souls of believers, so that those things which were possessed by the worst Kings, according to the prince of this world, having been expelled and destroyed, He might deign to make them a dwelling place of faith and a temple of the Holy Spirit. Just as Joshua trod with his feet those five kings, the adversaries of the Israelite people, so JESUS trod upon the five enemies of the human race—sin, the devil, death, hell, the curse of the law—and freed us from their tyranny and power.

Latin:

V. 24. PONITE PEDES SUPER COLLA REGUM ISTORUM.

Non id insolentis, aut elati victoria animi fuit: sed prudentiæ, quia fiduciam suis addere voluit, quod impleat Deus, quæ promiserat. Deut. 30. ult. tu calcabis eorum colla, eosdemque ab infandis Cananæorum sceleribus, qui ob ea hæc patiebantur merito suo, abstraheret: hostes autem Dei, & populi Dei justis pœnis afficeret. Fuit hoc non crudelitas, ait Origenes homil. 11. Sed humanitas, Christi Sacramentum designans, quod Dominus JEsus adumbratum prius a filio Nave per singulas civitates, nunc in veritate per singulas animas credentium complet, ut quæ possidebantur a pessimis Regibus secundum Principem mundi hujus expulsis iis & peremtis facere eas dignetur habitaculum fidei, & sancti Spiritus templum. Ut Josua quinque illos reges, adversarios populi Israelitici pedibus calcavit, ita JEsus calcavit quinque hostes humani generis, peccatum, diabolum, mortem, infernum, legis maledictum, nosque ab eorum tyrannide ac potestate liberavit.

## 10:24
v. 24.

Latin:

v. 24.

## 10:27
Ver. 27. AND WHEN THE SUN WAS SETTING, HE COMMANDED HIS COMPANIONS TO TAKE THEM DOWN FROM THE GALLOWS.

The command was not given at the very time when the sun was setting, as if Joshua had remained there until that time; for he hastened to conquer the cities of Makkedah and Libnah. But when he commanded the hanging, he ordered at the same time that those who were left there, when the sun set, should take down those gallows-birds, the kings, from the gallows.

Latin:

Vers. 27. CUMQUE OCCUMBERET SOL, PRÆCEPIT SOCIIS UT DEPONERENT EOS DE PATIBULIS.

Præceptum non est datum demum, cum Sol occumberet, ac si eo usq; ibi mansisset Josua; properavit enim ad expugnandas urbes Macedam & Lebnam. Sed cum præcepit suspendium, jussit simul, ut qui ibi relinquebantur, cum Sol occumberet, Reges istos patibularios de patibulis deponerent.

## 10:28
V. 28. ON THE SAME DAY ALSO HE TOOK MAKKEDAH.

On that prolonged day, and not on the following one, as Masius and Serarius wish. For in the Hebrew it is: on that very day. And there would still remain five or six hours of the artificial day, or before the sun set, even if, victory having been won and the kings having been hanged, he began to move again from the place, by which that city of Makkedah, with its inhabitants greatly terrified and unable to resist, could easily be taken.

AND ALL THE INHABITERS THEREOF) In the Hebrew: Every soul that was in it. πᾶν ἐμπνέον the Greeks here. Compare above 6, 21.

Thus v. 32, 35, 37. But in v. 40 the Vulgate rendered it: He killed everything that could breathe. Most understand this of all men, and establish a different reason for Jericho in c. 6, 21, which was entirely anathema, Abulensis, Bonfrerius, Cornelius, and others, since they divided all the animals and domestic beasts among themselves as booty, which the Lord nowhere commanded to be killed throughout all the cities. Cf. Deut. 20, 16, 17. Jos. 11.

Latin:

V. 28. EODEM QUOQUE DIE MACEDAM CEPIT.

Die illo prolongato, non autem fequenti, ut Mafius & Serarius volunt. Nam in Ebræo est: in die ipsa. Et restabunt adhuc horæ quinque vel sex diei artificialis, vel antequam Sol occumberet, e- tiam si parta victoria, Regibusque suspensis moveri loco denuo ceperit, quibus urbs illa Macedam in- colis maxime territis, nec repugnare valentibus, fa- cile capi potuit.

ET OMNES HABITATORES EJUS) In Ebræo: Omnem animam, quæ in eo. πᾶν ἐμπνέον Græci hic. Con- ter supra 6, 21.

Sic v. 32. 35. 37. At v. 40. reddidit Vulgar. Omne quod fpirare poterat, interfecit. De omnibus hominibus plerique intelligunt, aliamque rationem in Jericho c. 6, 21. quæ tota anathema fuit, statuunt, Abulens. Bonfrer. Cornelius, alii, siquidem anima- lia omnia & jumenta domestica prædæ loco inter se diviserint, quæ nuspiam Dominus per omnes civi- tates occidi jusserit. Conf. Deut. 20, 16. 17. Jos. 11.

## 10:28
AND HE DID TO THE KING OF MAKKEDAH, AS HE HAD DONE TO THE KING OF JERICHO.

Whom it is likely was fastened to a gallows and killed by hanging: although this is not reported. For the others were hanged.

Latin:

FECITQUE REGI MACEDA, SICUT FE- CERAT REGI JERICHO.

Quem patibulo affixum, & suspendio neca- tum verisimile est: quamvis id non referatur. Cæ- teri enim suspensi sunt.

## 10:29
V. 29. IN LIBNAH.

Which city was in Judah in that part where that tribe extends to the west, and indeed a priestly city c. 21, 13. 1 Par. 6, 57. In the Crellian Concordance Libnah is rendered, moon, whiteness, incense, Mond, Wittenberg, Weyrauchsstadt, situated 2 1/2 miles from Jerusalem, 1 1/2 miles from Makkedah. It revolted in the time of Joram 2 Kings 8, 22. 2 Par. 21, 10. It was besieged by Sennacherib 2 Kings 19, 8. Is. 37, 8. There is also a homonymous Libnah, the 17th station of the Israelites in the desert Num. 33, 20.

Latin:

V. 29. IN LEBNA.

Quæ urbs in Juda erat ea parte, qua tribus il- la ad occasum excurrit, & quidem Sacerdotalis c. 21, 13. 1. Par. 6, 57. In Concord. Crellianis Libna reddi- tur, luna, albedo, thus, Mond, Wittenberg, Wey- rauchsstadt 2 1/2. mil. ab Hieros. dissita 1 1/2. mil. a Ma- keda. Defecit tempore Joram 2. Reg. 8, 22. 2. Par. 21, 10. A Sennacheribo obsessa fuit 2. Reg. 19, 8. Es. 37, 8. Est etiam Libna ὁμώνυμος, 17. statio Israe- litarum in deserto Num. 33, 20.

## 10:32
V. 32. THE NEXT DAY.

From the siege and assault of Lachish, and not on the day after the illustrious victory, as Bonfrerius wishes. For this verse refers to the preceding one, and there is no reason why we should compress those battles into such a narrow space of time without necessity. Lachish was distant from Libnah 2 1/2 miles. Nor does it appear from the text that Libnah was destroyed on that solemn and miraculous day, much less that Joshua had departed from there to Lachish, which Bonfrerius thinks.

Latin:

V. 32. DIE ALTERO.

Ab obsidione & oppugnatione Lachis, non vero altero die ab illustri victoria, ut vult Bonfrerius. Nam refert sese hic versus ad præcedentem, nec est, quod ista prælia in eam angustiam temporis compinga- mus citra necessitatem. Distabat Lachis a Libna 2 1/2. milliar. Neque e textu apparet die illo solemni & miraculoso Libna deletum, nedum inde adhuc La- chisum digressum fuisse Josuam, quod Bonfrerius putat.

## 10:35
V. 35. AT THAT TIME HORAM KING OF GEZER WENT UP.

Horam (their mountain) King in Gezer, intending to help the city of Lachish, is cut off. Gezer גזר Cut off, a city of division in the tribe of Ephraim, was a dwelling place of the Levites and a designated city of refuge, Jos. 16:10, ch. 21:21, Jud. 1:29, according to the Concordance of Crell. It was 7 miles distant from Jerusalem towards the North. The Israelites did not obtain it for a long time, the Canaanites remaining in it, Jos. 16:10, Jud. 1:29, until at length in the time of Solomon, Pharaoh King of Egypt captured it and gave it to Solomon as a dowry for his daughter, which Solomon fortified, 1 Kings 9:15. Mention is also made of it in 1 Chron. 14:16 under the name Gazera, because David struck the Philistines from Gibeon even to Gazera. Compare 2 Sam. 5:25.

Latin:

V. 35. EO TEMPORE ASCENDIT HORAM REX GAZER.

Horam (mons eorum) Rex in Gazer, urbi La- chis auxiliaturus exscinditur. Gazer גזר Abscissa, Theilungs-Stadt in tribu Ephraim Levitarum ha- bitaculum, & urbs refugii designata fuit Jos. 16, 10. c. 21, 21. Jud. 1, 29. juxta Concord. Crell. 7. miliar. Hierosolyma distabat versus Septentrionem. Eam ad multa tempora Israelitæ non obtinuere, rema- nentibus in ea Canaanæis Jos. 16, 10. Jud. 1, 29. donec tandem Salomonis tempore eam cepit Pharao Rex Ægypti, ac Salomoni in dotem filiæ suæ dedit, quam Salomon munivit 1. Reg. 9, 15. Ejus etiam mentio fit 1. Par. 14, 16. sub nomine Gazera, quia David Phi- listæos percussit a Gabaon usque Gazera. Confer. 2. Sam. 5, 25.

## 10:37
V. 37. ALSO ITS KING.

Because the King of Hebron, Hoham, is one of the five who were hanged, it seems another was suddenly created by the Hebronites, lest they be ἀκέφαλοι (headless) with enemies threatening: who is said here to have been killed along with them. For what others imagine, that this was another Hebron, neither agrees with Scripture nor is it in any way likely. That the same Hebron is being discussed as in v. 3, 36 is too manifest. The same must also be held concerning the King of Debir in v. 39, for both were likewise killed, and

The King or petty king of Hebron and Debir is mentioned, as is the petty king in Libnah, together with the souls that were in those cities. Therefore, those two Kings cannot be understood, whose necks were trodden upon v. 24.

Same verse. HE TOOK IT, AND SMOTE IT WITH THE EDGE OF THE SWORD.

But Hebron was finally occupied by Caleb, Josh. 15, 14. Judg. 1, 10. It seems, therefore, that it must be said that this city was recovered by other Canaanites and giants. For since Joshua had exterminated all the inhabitants and the sons of Anak there, ch. 11, 22, it must be that they were from other cities of the Philistines, who were slain there by Caleb, Judg. 1. The same must also be held regarding the city of Debir, which is said to have been occupied by Othniel in Josh. 15 and Judg. 1, because new inhabitants from the Canaanites, having ejected the Israelites, possessed it afterwards, and the city was snatched back from them by Othniel.

Latin:

V. 37. REGEM QUOQUE EJUS.

Quia Rex Hebron Oham unus est e quinque patibulariis, videtur alius subito ab Hebronitis creatus, ne essent ἀκέφαλοι, hostibus imminenti- bus: qui hic cum ipsis interfectus dicitur. Nam quod alii fingunt, aliam hanc fuisse Hebronem, nec Scripturæ convenit, nec ullo modo verisimi- le est. De eadem Hebrone v. 3. 36. agi nimis est manifestum. Idem etiam habendum de Re- ge Dabir v. 39. nam occisus similiter uterque, &

Hebronis & Dabir Rex vel Regulus dicitur, uti Re- gulus in Lebna, una cum animabus, quæ in illis ur- bibus erant. Non ergo isti duo Reges intelligi possunt, quorum colla calcata v. 24.

Vers. eod. CEPIT EAM, ET PERCUSSIT IN ORE GLADII.

At Hebron a Caleb demum occupata Jos. 15, 14. Jud. 1, 10. Dicendum ergo videtur, hanc ur- bem ab aliis Cananæis & gigantibus recuperatam. Quum enim incolas omnes filiosque Enakim ibi extirparit Josua c. 11, 22. ex aliis Philistinorum ur- bibus eos fuisse oportet, qui a Calebo illic cæsi sunt Jud 1. Idem etiam de urbe Dabir habendum, quæ Jos. 15. Jud. 1. ab Othoniele occupata dici- tur, quod novi incolæ e Cananæis ejectis Israelitis eam postmodum possederint, illisque ab Othonie- le urbs iterum erepta sit.

## 10:40
Verse 40. AND SO JOSHUA SMOTE ALL THE MOUNTAINOUS LAND, AND THE SOUTHERN, AND THE CHAMPAGNE, AND ASEDOTH.

Lest there be a need to commemorate individual things, it is indicated generally that that whole region to the west and south was occupied by Joshua, whether you look at mountainous places, or champagne lands and level tracts. Asedoth is opposed to the southern lands, just as the champagne is to the mountainous. The LXX and the Vulgate accept the word אשדות as a proper name of a place, concerning which Jerome in Hebrew Places: Asedoth, a city which Jesus [Joshua] stormed, its King having been killed. But he distinguishes from it Asedoth in the tribe of Reuben, which is called Asedoth Pisgah: which appellation occurs in Josh. 12, 3; ch. 13, 20; Deut. 3, 17; ch. 4, 49. Others, however, prefer to have Asedoth as an appellative: even Jerome. Deut. 3, 17; ch. 4, 49, rendering it 'at the roots of Mount Pisgah': where Pagninus and Cajetan interpreted it as 'under the effusions of the hill', the Tigurine as 'under the springs of the hill', Forster as 'underneath the inflows of Pisgah': Vatablus as 'under the effusions of the waters of Pisgah', the Chaldean as 'under the effusion or slope of the hill', B. Luther with the Vulgate 'Unten am Berge Pisga'. But he who rendered the word אשדות here as 'an den Bächen' [at the brooks], as also in Josh. 12, 3; ch. 13, 20. Which interpretation the Papists themselves approve, departing here from the Vulgate version. Bonfrerius wishes the word נגב, which is accustomed to denote the south, to designate a dry land scorched by the excessive heat of the Sun, but by the opposite word אשדות, that region which is irrigated by more frequent moisture, such as are in valleys and at the roots of mountains, from which abundant waters are accustomed to flow down from the mountains, or even the very outflows of waters. Thus also Masius and others accept this name as an appellative, and translate it 'effusions'. Jonathan likewise interprets it through משפך, an effusion. Tremellius and Junius [interpret it as] 'decursibus' [down-flowings], i.e., irrigated, thus explaining the Hebrew κατά πόδα, 'of the mountain and the south, and the plain and the down-flowings': the Belgian version has 'decursiones aquarum' [down-flowings of waters].

Latin:

Vers. 40. PERCUSSIT ITAQUE JOSUE O- MNEM TERRAM MONTANAM, ET ME- RIDIANAM, ATQUE CAMPESTREM ET ASEDOTH.

Ne opus sit singula commemorare, generaliter indicatur, totam illam regionem ad occidentem & Austrum a Josua occupatam esse, sive montana spectes loca, sive campestria tractusque æquabiles. Terræ meridianæ opponitur Asedoth, uti Montanæ campestria. Vocem אשדות LXX. & Vulgata ac- cipiunt tanquam nomen loci proprium, de quo Hieronym. in locis Hebraic. Asedoth civitas, quam expugnavit Jesus Rege ejus interfecto. Sed ab ea di- stinguit Asedoth in tribu Ruben, quæ vocatur Ase- doth Phasga: quæ appellatio occurrit Jos. 12,3. c. 13, 20. Deut. 3, 17. c. 4, 49. Alii tamen malunt Asedoth appellativum habere: etiam Hieronym. Deut. 3, 17. c. 4, 49. reddens ad radices montis Phasga: ubi Pa- gninus & Cajetanus interpretati sunt sub effusionibus collis, Tigurina sub scatebris collis, Forsterus subtus in- fluxibus Phasga: Vatablus sub effusionibus aquarum Phasga, Chaldæus sub effusione vel declivio collis, B. Luther. cum Vulg. Unten am Berge Pisga. Qui vero hic vocem אשדות reddidit an den Bächen, ut & Jos. 12, 3. c. 13. 20. Quam interpretationem pro- bant ipsimet Papistæ, discedentes hic a versione Vul- gata. Bonfrerius vocem נגב quæ meridiem notare solet, terram aridam & nimio Solis fervore exustam designari vult, voce autem opposita אשדות regio- nem eam, quæ frequentiori humore irrigatur, qua- les in vallibus, & ad radices montium sunt, quo co- piosæ e montib9 aquæ solent defluere, vel etiam ipsa aquarum defluvia. Sic etiam Masius, & alii acci- piunt hoc nomen ut appellativum, vertuntq; effusio- nes. Jonathan per משפך effusionem itidem interpre- tantur. Tremellius & Junius decursibus, sc. irriguam, Ebræa κατά πόδα ita exponentes, montis & austri, & planitiei & decursuum: Belg. versio habet decur- siones aquarum.

## 10:41
FROM KADESH-BARNEA EVEN UNTO GAZA.

Bonfrerius rightly notes that by these words is signified that part of Judea which verges toward the South and, in the southern region, mostly to the West. Because Kadesh-barnea was on the southern border of the promised land and the tribe of Judah, Num. 34, 4; Josh. 15, 3. But Gaza was a maritime city of the Philistines, and the same was the extreme [point] toward Egypt, not far from Rhinocolura and the river of Egypt, the extreme boundary of the whole Israelite land in almost the very corner of the south and west. It was assigned to the tribe of Judah, Josh. 15, 47, and stormed by it, Judg. 1, 28. But it was occupied again by the Philistines, ch. 3, v. 3. It was a very fortified and great city / a strong fortress, or Festenburg, 1/2 a mile from the Mediterranean sea, 2 miles from Jerusalem, the border of Canaan from the most ancient times, Gen. 10, 19, as also in the time of Solomon, 1 Kings 4, 24; 2 Kings 18, 6.

ALL THE LAND OF GOSHEN EVEN TO GIBEON.

This Goshen is different from that which is in Egypt, Jos. 11, 15, namely a city in the southern region of the tribe of Judah, c. 15, 51, whence the tract is described here from the South towards the North, which Gibeon was more northerly in comparison to the land of Goshen.

Latin:

A CADESBARNE USQUE GAZAM.

Recte notat Bonfrerius his verbis significari eam Judææ partem, quæ ad Austrum & in Australi regione maxime ad Occidentem vergit. Quia Cades- barne erat in Australi terræ promissæ & tribus Judæ limite Num. 34, 4. Jos. 15, 3. Gaza vero Philistinorum urbs erat maritima, eademque versus Ægyptum extrema non procul a Rhinocolura, ac rivo Ægy- pti extremo totius Israeliticæ terræ termino in ipso propemodum Austri & occidentis angulo. Tri- bui Judæ assignata est Jos. 15, 47. & ab ea expugnata Jud. 1, 28. Sed rursus a Philistis occupata c. 3. v. 3. Fuit valde munita, & magna civitas / fortis feste, vel Festenburg, 1/2. milliari a mari mediterraneo, 2. milliaria a Jerusalem, Cananææ limes ab antiquiffimis temporibus Gen. 10, 19. ut & tempore Salomonis 1. Reg. 4, 24. 2. Reg. 18, 6.

OMNEM TERRAM GOSEN USQUE GA- BAON.

Alia hæc Gosen ab ea, quæ in Ægypto Jos. 11, 15. urbs nempe in Australi regione tribus Judæ c. 15, 51. unde hic describitur tractus ab Austro versus se- ptentrionem, quæ Gabaon comparatione terræ Go- sen borealior erat.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. The conquest of King Jabin and others.

V. 1. JABIN KING OF HAZOR.

Jabin, the head of three other Kings, who seem to have been subject to him, v. 10. There is also another Jabin, a Canaanite King, Jud. 4, whence some make the name Jabin common to those Kings, as Pharaoh in Egypt.

HAZOR, the metropolis of the kingdoms of the Philistines, according to Jerome in the Hebrew places, or rather of the Canaanites, namely the northern ones. It fell to the lot of Naphtali, whence Hazor in Naphtali is wrongly cited as another in the Hebrew places. There is, however, still another Hazor in the tribe of Judah, and that a double one, Jos. 15, 23 and 25, which the latter is called New Hazor, where a third also seems to be added in the same tribe for the sake of distinction, also called by another name, Hezron. And again another in the tribe of Benjamin, Neh. 11, 33, and besides those, Hazor is read of moreover in Kedar or the Israelite region.

HE SENT TO JOBAB KING OF MADON, AND TO THE KING OF SHIMRON, AND TO THE KING OF ACHSHAPH.

Of the city of Madon, it is read nowhere else. But Shimron is located in the tribe of Zebulun, c. 19, 15, and is thus distinct from Simeron or Samaria in the tribe of Ephraim, which was built long after, 1 Kings 16. Achshaph was assigned to the tribe of Asher, Jos. 19, 35, situated 22 miles from Jerusalem towards the North.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Regis Jabin, & aliorum expugnatio.

V. 1. JABIN REX ASOR.

JAbin Caput aliorum trium Regum, qui ei viden- tur fuisse subditi v. 10. Est & alius Jabin Rex Ca- nanæus Jud. 4. unde nonnulli Jabin nomen commu- ne istorum Regum faciunt, ut in Ægypto Pharaonis.

ASOR metropolis regnorum Philistiim juxta Hier. in loc. Ebr. vel potius Cananæorum videlicet septen- trionalium. Cecidit in sortem Nephthaliin, unde perperam Asor in Nepthalim ceu alia in loc. Ebr. adducitur. Est tamen alia adhuc Asor in tribu Ju- da, eaque gemina Jos. 15, 23. & 25. quæ posterior A- sor nova vocatur, ubi etiam tertia addi videtur in eadem tribu distinctionis causa, alio item nomine Hesron vocata. Atque iterum alia in tribu Benja- min Neh. 11, 33. ac præter illas legitur insuper Asor in Cedar seu Israelitide regione.

MISIT AD JOBAB REGEM MADON, ET AD REGEM SEMERON, ATQUE AD RE- GEM ACHSAPH.

De urbe Madon nuspiam alias legitur. Semeron vero in tribu Zabulon collocatur c. 19, 15. adeoque a Simeron, vel Samaria in tribu Ephraim distincta est, quæ longe post ædificata 1 Reg. 16. Achsaph assi- gnata fuit tribui Aser Jos. 19, 35. ab Hierusalem 22. miliar. versus Septentrionem dissita.

## 11:2
V. 2. TO THE KINGS ALSO OF THE NORTH, WHO DWELL IN THE MOUNTAINOUS REGIONS.

In Mount Lebanon, which is the northern part of Canaan, the LXX wrongly (translate) as being near great Sidon.

AND IN THE PLAIN OVER AGAINST THE SOUTH OF CHINNEROTH.

Those who dwelt in that plain which is to the south of the Sea of Gennesaret. See Num. 34, 11.

Latin:

V. 2. AD REGES QUOQUE AQUILONIS, QUI HABITANT IN MONTANIS.

In Libano monte, qui Aquilonaris est Cana- nææ, LXX. perperam, qui juxta Sidonem magnam.

ET IN PLANITIE CONTRA MERIDIEM CINEROTH.

Qui habitabant in ea planitie, quæ mari Gene- sareth est ad meridiem. Vid. Num. 34, 11.

## 11:3
V. 3. THE CANAANITE ALSO FROM THE EAST AND WEST.

To be corrected from the Hebrew: The Canaanite from the East and West (is) the Amorite. For these are not different from the preceding ones.

Latin:

V. 3. CANANÆUM QUOQUE AB ORIEN- TE ET OCCIDENTE.

Corrigendum ex Ebræo: Cananæus ab Oriente & Occidente (est) Amorrhæus. Non enim hi diversi sunt a præcedentibus.

## 11:3
IN THE LAND OF MIZPAH,

We add the Tremellius-Junius note: In the region of Mitzpa: a watchtower: for the region is situated at the entrance of Lebanon above the Jordan, in which watchmen were stationed, so that by their guard the region might be kept secure. Moreover, that is not the Mitzpa which belongs to the tribe of Judah, infra 15, 38, nor of Benjamin, infra 18, 26, nor that Mitzpe of the Moabites, concerning which 1 Sam. 22, 3, but that which is joined to Gilead, concerning which Genesis 31, verse 49, and Judges 10, verse 3. Thus they seem to be named from their situation, because they were in the upper tract of the Israelites towards Tabor, where the King of Shimron-Meron held dominion, for which reason also the fields of Merom or the high places are named by Deborah, Jud. 5, verse 18.

Latin:

IN TERRA MASPHA,

Addimus notam Tremellio-Junianam: In regio- ne Mitzpa: specula: nam regio est sita in ingressu Libani super Jordanem, in quæ speculatores collo- cati erant, ut eorum custodia secura servaretur re- gio. Non est autem illa Mitzpa, quæ ad tribum Je- hudæ pertinet inf. 15, 38. neq; Benjaminis, inf. 18, 26. illa Mitzpe Moabitar. de qua 1. Schem. 22, 3. sed ea quæ est Gilhadi juncta, de qua Genes. 31. vers. 49. & Jud. 10. vers. 3. Sic videntur appellari a situ, quod in supero essent Israelitarum tractu Tha- borem versus, ubi Rex Schimronis Meronis impe- rium tenuit, quamobrem etiam Merome agri l. lo- ca edita a Debora nominantur. Jud. 5. ver- su 18.

## 11:4
V. 4. AS THE SAND THAT IS UPON THE SEA SHORE.

A great and innumerable multitude of men is indicated by hyperbole. Josephus, book 5, Antiquities, chapter 2, teaches that there were 30,000 foot soldiers and 2,000 chariots.

Latin:

V. 4. SICUT ARENA QUÆ EST IN LIT- TORE MARIS.

Indicatur magna & innumerabilis multitudo hominum per hyperbolen. Joseph. l. 5. Antiq. 1. 2. docet fuisse 30000. peditum, & 2000. currum.

## 11:5
AT THE WATERS OF MEROM.

It is a lake, by another name Samachonitis: See Josephus, book 4, Wars, chapter 1; Num. 34, 11, near which the metropolis of Hazor is situated.

Latin:

AD AQUAS MEROM.

Lacus est, alio nomine Samachonitis: Vid. Joseph. l. 4. Bell. c. 1. Num. 34, 11. ad quem metropolis A- shon sita.

## 11:6
V. 6. TO BE WOUNDED.

Others more correctly [translate it as] slain, B, Luther. erschlagen. That corresponds to the outcome. For in v. 8 all are said to have been struck down, so that no remnants remained. The LXX have τετροπωμένως, turned to flight: some codices have τετρωμένως, wounded. YOU SHALL HOUGH THEIR HORSES, AND BURN THEIR CHARIOTS WITH FIRE. God did not want [them] to rely on such external defenses of that kind, in which the nations placed all their confidence Deut. 17, 16. Ps. 19, 8. You shall hough, i.e., you shall cut the tendons of their legs, so that they may be useless for war and running thereafter.

Latin:

V. 6. VULNERANDOS.

Rectius alii occisos, B, Luther. erschlagen. Id respondet eventui. Nam v. 8. percussi dicuntur omnes, ut nullæ reliquiæ remanserint. LXX. habent τετροπωμένως in fugam versos : nonnulli Codd. τε- τρωμένως vulneratos. EQUOS EORUM SUBNERVABIS, ET CURRUS IGNE COMBURES. Nolebat Deus externis ejusmodi præsidiis ni- ti, in quibus gentes omnem fiduciam collocabant Deut. 17, 16. Ps. 19, 8. Subnervabis h. e. crurum nervos incides, ut imposterum ad bellum & cursum inutiles sint.

## 11:8
V. 8. AS FAR AS GREAT SIDON.

It is called so not in respect of another lesser Sidon, but because it was great in celebrity, both for its antiquity, because it was founded by Sidon the firstborn of Canaan, from whom it has its name, as Josephus testifies in book 1 of the Antiquities, ch. 6, whence it is also older than Tyre, as Strabo reports in book 16, Justin in book 18, Eusebius in the Chronicles, which is called the daughter of Sidon in Isaiah 23, 12, because it was built by the Sidonians; and also for its location, because it was built on a rock and adorned with an elegant harbor; and also for its status as an emporium, and for the sciences and arts which were cultivated in it, as Strabo and Pliny testify in book 5, ch. 19, and book 36, 26, above many others by way of excellence, in which astronomy, arithmetic, the glass-making art, the making of mirrors, weaving, and the extraction of purple flourished, and because this city did not easily obtain an equal in that region of Syria. It was situated on the mainland by the sea not far from Mount Anti-Lebanon, 29 miles from Jerusalem towards the north, 4 miles from Tyre. AND THE WATERS OF MISREPHOTH.

The name Misrephoth is more correctly taken as an appellative, burnings of waters. Vatablus, along with R. David, understands hot waters or thermal springs, as does B. Luther, and also the Tigurine. Others [understand] salt-works, because the water there is boiled by the rays of the sun and as it were hardened into salt, along with the Chaldean, R. Solomon, Lyranus, Adrichomius; Masius, with Bonfrerius not disagreeing, wishes it to denote glass furnaces: as if the sand, boiled and melted by the power of fire, from which glass is fashioned, were called water. Thus also Tremellius and Junius [translate] as far as the glass furnaces: with which that tract abounds, the material being taken from the Belus river, which the Cenderia marsh pours out within the roots of Mount Carmel, see Pliny in the cited book. Moreover, this is the western boundary, Sidon the northern.

Latin:

V. 8. USQUE AD SIDONEM MAGNAM.

Dicitur ita non respectu alterius minoris Sido- nis, sed quod magna fuerit celebritate, tum ob anti- quitatem, quia a Sidone Chanani primogenito con- dita, a quo nomen habet, teste Josepho l. 1. Antiqv. c. 6. unde etiam Tyro antiquior, ut tradit Strabo l. 16. Justinus l. 18. Eusebius in Chronic. quæ filia Sido- nis dicitur Esa. 23, 12. quia a Sidoniis constructa, tum ob situm, quia in rupe extructa & eleganti por- tu ornata, tum ob emporii, atque scientiarum ac arti- um, quæ in illa cultæ sunt, teste Strabone & Plinio l. 5. c. 19. lib. 36, 26. præ multis ἐξοχὴν, in qua Astrono- mia, Arithmetica, ars vitraria, conficiendorum speculo rum, texturæ, extrahendæ purpuræ floruere, quodque hæc urbs non facile in illa Syriæ regione parem ob- tinuerit. Sita fuit in continenti ad mare non pro- cul ab Anti-Libano monte, 29. milliar. a Jerusalem versus Septentrionem, 4. milliar. a Tyro. ET AQUAS MASEREPHOT.

Rectius nomen משׂרפות accipitur ut appel- lativum, commissiones aquarum. Vatablus cum R. David aquas calidas vel thermas intelligit, ut & B. Lutherus, nec non Tigur. Alii salinas, quod aqua ibi solis radiis cocta & quasi in salem induretur, cum Chald. R. Salom. Lyran. Adrichomio, Masius, non ab- nuente Bonfrerio fornaces vitrarias notari vult: qua- si arena vi ignis excocta, & liquata, ex qua vitrum conflatur, aqua vocetur. Ita & Tremell. Junius usque ad fornaces vitrarias : quibus abundat ille tractus, materia sumta ex Belo flumine, quod Cenderia pa- lus fundit intra montis Carmeli radices, vid. Plin. l. c. Est autem hic occidentalis terminus, septentrio- nalis Sidon.

## 11:10
Vers. 10.

AMONG ALL THESE KINGDOMS IT HELD THE PRINCIPALITY] Where kingdoms are small, one of the kings is usually chosen to have the leadership of the war, which histories testify also happens in Japan, Java, and other places of the Orient. Others more correctly judge that this king did not have the others merely as allies, but also as subjects, from v. 1, whose power is also gathered from Jud. IV.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

INTER OMNIA REGNA HÆC PRINCIPATUM TENEBAT] Ubi regna sunt exigua, solet unus regum deli- gi, qui belli ductum habeat, quod & in Japane, Java aliisque locis Orientis fieri testantur historiæ. Alii rectius regem hunc censent non habuisse cæteros tantum fœderatos, sed etiam sibi subditos e v. 1. cujus potentia etiam e Jud. IV. colligitur.

## 11:11
Verse 11.

HE LEFT NO SURVIVORS.

It seems to be indicated that no one was left alive who fell into the hands of the Israelites: yet some may have saved themselves by flight, or escaped beforehand, who after the death of Joshua regained their strength, and restored cities, and created new kings for themselves, as Jud. 4:1, 1. Jabin King of Hazor is said after 130 years to have dominated the Hebrews for 20 years. There is no reason why we should posit another Hazor with the Abulensis, see Joseph. b. 5, c. 6.

Latin:

Versus 11.

NON DIMISIT RELIQUIAS.

Indigitari videtur, neminem in vita relictum, qui in manus Israëlitarum venerit : potuere tamen nonnulli fuga se salvasse, vel antea evasisse, qui post mortem Josuæ vires receperint, ac urbes restaura- rint, novosque reges sibi crearint, ut Jud. 41, 1. Jabin Rex Aser post 130. annos dicitur per 20. annos E- braeis dominatus. Non est, quod cum Abulensi aliam Aser statuamus, vid. Joseph. l. 5. c. 6.

## 11:13
Verse 13.

EXCEPT FOR THE CITIES WHICH WERE SITUATED ON HILLS AND MOUNDS, ISRAEL BURNED THE REST) Because they could neither be held without a strong garrison, nor did we have such a force as could be divided for strengthening a garrison and undertaking war: Tacitus says in a similar case in Annals 13.

Those which were situated on the plain were burned, those on the hills were saved. Others say those which were fortified were saved, the rest were burned. In Hebrew it is, which stand upon their mound: which the LXX render τὰς πόλεις τὰς κεχωματισμένας, fortified with mounds: Theodotion: ὀχύρας, strong, the Chaldean, which stood upon their strength. Vatablus, which stood in their might. Junius & Tremellius are unique here, rendering it thus: nevertheless Israel did not burn any of those cities which remained with their mound, that is, which indeed awaited a siege, but surrendered before the mounds were thrown down according to the law of Deut. 20:10. But that sense is very laboriously extracted from the Hebrew truth, nor does it agree with what follows, except for Hazor, which Joshua alone burned. For did all the others surrender according to the law of Deut. 20:10? He consumed only one city (of those which were situated on a hill or were fortified), Hazor, with fire.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ABSQVE VRBIBVS QVÆ ERANT IN COLLIBVS ET TVMVLIS SITÆ, CÆTERAS SVCCENDIT ISRAEL) Quia nec teneri sine valido præsidio, nec id nobis Sirium erat, quod firmando præsidio, & capessendo bello divide- retur : ait in re simili Tacitus Annalium 13.

Illæ, quæ in planitie sitæ, succensæ, servatæ, quæ in collibus. Aliis, quæ munitæ fuere servatæ, cæteræ succensæ dicuntur. In Ebr. est, quæ stant supra tu- mulum suum: quod LXX. reddunt τὰς πόλεις τὰς κεχωματισμένας aggeribus munitas: Theodotion: ὀχύρας fortes, Chaldæus, quæ stabant super fortitu- dine sua. Vatablus, quæ stabant in robore suo. Ju- nius & Tremellius hic singulares sunt, ita reddendo: veruntamen nullam earum civitatum, quæ manserunt cum aggere suo combussit Israel, id est, quæ obsidionem quidem expectarunt, sed antequam aggeres vi de- jicerentur, se dediderunt ex lege Deut. 20, 10. Sed sensus ille ægerrime exsculpetur e veritate Ebræa, neque congruit quod sequitur, præter Chazorem, quam solam combussit Josua. Num enim omnes aliæ se dediderunt ex lege Deut. 20, 10. Unam tantum civitatem, (ex his quæ in colle sitæ, vel munitæ e- rant,) Azer incendio consumsit.

## 11:14
Verse 14.

THE SPOIL OF THESE CITIES AND THE CATTLE THEY DIVIDED] For the חרם anathema had not preceded.

AND THE MOUNTAIN OF ISRAEL.

It is not the mount Sion, in which the temple was, that is understood, nor, as Masius and Arias wish, the mount of Samaria, for neither of these was called the mount of Israel at that time. More probable is the conjecture of Cajetan and Salianus that the mount Gerizim or a similar one situated near Sichem in the field which Jacob (called Israel) had bought there, Gen. 33, 19, is to be understood. Most convenient, however, is the translation of B. Luther, und das Gebürge Israel: Junius and Tremellius, that is, the highlands of Israel, taking the vav exegetically. Osiander and the highlands of Israel, which later fell to the Israelites.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

PRÆDAM ISTARVM VRBIVM AC JVMENTA DIVISERVNT] Neque enim præcesserat חרם ἀνά- θεμα.

MONTEMQUE ISRAEL.

Non intelligitur mons Sion, in quo templum, nec ut Masius & Arias volunt, mons Samariæ, neuter enim isto tempore mons Israel dictus est. Probabi- lior est Cajetani & Saliani conjectura montem Gari- zim vel similem juxta Sichem in agro, quem Jacob (Israel dictus) ibi emerat Gen. 33, 19. situm intelligi. Commodissima tamen est B. Lutheri translatio, und das Gebürge Israel: Junius & Tremellius, id est, montana Israelis vav exegetice accipientes. Osian- der & montana Israelis, quæ postea cesserunt Israe- litis.

## 11:17
Verse 17. AND THE PART OF THE MOUNTAIN WHICH ASCENDS TO SEIR AS FAR AS BAAL GAD THROUGH THE PLAIN OF LEBANON.

In Hebrew, from the mountain which divides (the region) which is the ascent into Seir, and as far as Baalgad, which (city) is in the valley of Lebanon. Junius & Tremellius render: from the smooth mountain, which is entirely a bare place without trees: as Masius also rendered; and Symmachus translating λεῖον, smooth, polished, bare. But the former explanation is simpler, which is consonant with the translations of Osiander, Aquila, the Chaldean, and Vatablus, as well as B. Luther, concerning the mountain of division, which divides and separates Canaan from Idumea. The LXX retained the Hebrew name החלק as if it were a proper noun.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET PARTEM MONTIS QUÆ A- SCENDIT SEIR USQUE BAAL GAD PER PLANITIEM LIBANI.

In Ebr. a monte qui dividit (regionem) qua a- scensus est in Seir, & usque ad Baalgad, quæ (urbs) est in valle Libani. Junius & Tremellius reddunt: a monte glabro, qui totus est glabretum sine arboribus: uti Masius quoque reddidit; ac Symmachus vertens λεῖον, levem, politum, glabrum. Sed simplicior est prior explicatio, quæ Osiandri, Aquilæ, Chald. & Va- tabl. ut & B. Luther. translationibus consona de mon- te divisionis, qui Chananæam dividit & disterminat ab Idumæa. LXX. nomen Ebræum החלק reti- nuerunt quasi proprium.

## 11:18
Verse 18. FOR A LONG TIME JOSHUA FOUGHT AGAINST THESE KINGS.

For about seven years, as the Hebrews in Seder Olam, and Theodoret, Abulensis, Masius, Serarius, Torniellus, Cornelius a Lapide, Bonfrerius, Junius, and others. Cf. Josh. 14:7. Therefore Canaan was not subdued in five years, as Josephus wishes in book 5, chapter 2.

Latin:

Vers. 18. MULTO TEMPORE PUGNAVIT JOSUE CONTRA REGES ISTOS.

Septennio fere ut Ebræi in Seder Olam, ac Theo- doret. Abulens. Masius, Serarius, Torniellus, Cornel. a Lap. Bonfrerius, Junius & alii. Conf. Jos. 14, 7. Non ergo quinquennio subacta Cananæa, uti vult Jo- seph l. 5. c. 2.

## 11:20
Verse 20.

IT WAS THE SENTENCE OF THE LORD THAT THEIR HEARTS SHOULD BE HARDENED] God did not strike into them the kind of terror He could have; indeed, He also took away much of their prudence.

In the Hebrew it is indicated that they hardened themselves, as Masius and Cornelius rightly observe; it was from the Lord that they should harden their heart. From the Lord, namely, not by effecting it, but by permitting it; not impulsively, but objectively. For one must not believe with Calvin that God Himself hardened them and drove them into blind fury, so that they would not give place to mercy. Nor is this hardening explained here otherwise than that it was ordained in this, that they should resolve to oppose the Israelites, but not, like the Gibeonites, to implore mercy; which, if they had done, and had submitted themselves to the true worship of God, they would by no means have been cut off.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

DOMINI SENTENTIA ERAT VT INDVRAREN- TVR CORDA EORVM] Non immisit in eos Deus qua- lem potuit terrorem, imo & prudentiæ multum ademit.

In Ebræo indicatur, quod semetipsos indura- rint, ut recte Masius & Cornel. observant, a Domino erat, ut indurarent cor suum. A Domino, nempe non efficiendo, sed permittendo, non impulsive, sed objective. Non enim cum Calvino credendum, Deum ipsum eos indurasse, ac in cæcum furorem impulisse, ne locum darent misericordiæ. Neque induratio hæc aliter hic explicatur, quam quod in ea posita fuerit, ut decernerent se Israelitis oppone- re, non autem cum Gabonitis misericordiam exo- rare, quod si fecissent, ac vero Dei cultui se submi- sissent, minime excisi fuissent.

## 11:22
V. 22. HE LEFT NONE OF THE STOCK OF ENACIM IN THE LAND OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL EXCEPT THE CITIES OF GAZA AND GETH, AND AZOTUS, IN WHICH ALONE THEY WERE LEFT. He did not therefore occupy these cities of the Philistines by the sea, in which very many of the giants remained, to which also some from Canaan betook themselves. Nor were the Israelites ever able to utterly defeat them; nay, after the death of Joshua, having recovered their strength, they regained and occupied the seats of their ancestors, Hebron, Dabir, & Anab, until they were indeed cast out and destroyed from them by Caleb and Othoniel. Jos. 14, 12. Jud. 1, 10. 11. 12. Verf. 23. JOSHUA THEREFORE TOOK ALL THE LAND] He defeated. Understand of Canaan, and indeed not simply but almost all, or all which he attempted in war, and wished to approach. Jos. 1, 3. But he left the cities of the Philistines, as also those of the Phoenicians, and indeed some even in Canaan itself untouched, partly because there was not yet such a multitude of Israelites as could fill the whole land, and there was a fear that, with wild beasts multiplied and a lack of cultivation, the fertile land would grow wild, Ex. 23, 29; partly so that the Israelites would not become slothful through idleness; and partly so that the faith and constancy of their descendants might be tested by the custom of the Canaanites. Jud. 3, 2. 9.

Latin:

V. 22. NON RELIQUIT ULLUM DE STIR- PE ENACIM IN TERRA FILIORUM ISRAEL ABSQUE CIVITATIBUS GAZA ET GETH, ET AZOTO, IN QUIBUS SOLIS RELICTI SUNT. Has ergo urbes Philistiim ad mare non occu- pavit, in quibus plurimi ex gigantibus remanfe- runt, ad quas etiam exCananæa se recepēre nonnul- li. Nec unquam eas penitus debellare potuerunt If- raelitæ, imo post mortem Josuæ viribus refumtis ma- jorum suorum sedes Hebron, Dabir, & Anab recu- perarunt, & occuparunt, donec ex illis quidem eje- čti & deleti fuerint a Caleb & Othoniele Jof. 14, 12. Jud. 1, 10. 11. 12. Verf. 23. CEPIT ERGO JOSUE OMNEM TERRAM] Debellavit. Intellige Cananæ, & quidem omnem non ἁπλῶς sed pene omnem, vel omnem, quam bello tentavit, & adire voluit Jof. 1, 3. Philistinorum autem urbes, ut & Phœniciæ, nec non aliquas etiam in ipfa Cana- næa intactas reliquit, tum quod nec dum ea esset If- raelitarum multitudo, quæ posset totam terram im- plere, metusque foret, ne feris multiplicatis, cultu- ræque defectu terra fertilis silvesceretEx. 23, 29. tum ne otio ignavi fierent Israëlitæ, tum ut Cananæorum consuetudine probaretur fides ac constantia eorum Jud. 3, 2. 9.

## 12:1 Argument
SECTION III. OF PART I. Comprehensive. CHAPTER XII. An enumeration of the kings on this side and beyond the Jordan who were struck down.

Verf. 1. THESE ARE THE KINGS] A summary is gathered here of the kings whom Moses and Joshua had defeated on this side and beyond the Jordan. Kingdoms were bounded by each one's own country, says Justin regarding the most ancient times. Specifically, however, Strabo says of these peoples: τὸ παλαιὸν μὲν ἦν οἱ Ἀράδιοι καθ’ ἑυτὲς ἐβασιλεύοντο παραπλησίως, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἑκάστη πόλεων τῶν Φοινίκων.

FROM THE TORRENT ARNON UNTO MOUNT HERMON. This was the length of the region beyond the Jordan, the torrent Arnon being its boundary from the south, Mount Hermon from the north. Deut. 3, 8. c. 4, 48.

Latin:

SECTIO III. PARTIS I. συλληπτική. CAPUT XII. Regum 31. cis & ultra Jordanem percussorum enumeratio.

Verf. 1. HI SUNT REGES] Summa hic colligitur Regum quos Moses & Jofue cis & ultra Jordanem devicerant. Intra su- am cuique patriam regna finiebantur, ait de antiquissimis temporibus Justinus. Speciatim autem de his populis Stra- bo: τὸ παλαιὸν μὲν ἗ν οἱ Ἀράδιοι καθ’ ἑυτὲς ἐβασιλεύοντο παραπλησίως, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἑκάση πόλεων τῶν Φοινί- κων.

A TORRENTE ARNON USQUE AD MONTEM HERMON. LOngitudo hæc erat regionis trans Jordanicæ, torrens Arnon terminus ejus a meridie, mons Her- mon a Septentrione Deut. 3, 8. c. 4, 48.

## 12:2
V. 2. AND OF THE MIDDLE PART IN THE VALLEY. In the Hebrew it is, And in the middle of the torrent and in the middle part of Galaad, which is to say that King Sehon ruled from Aroer (which he had snatched from the Moabites) which was situated at the bank of the torrent (thence proceeding to the middle of the torrent) and in the middle part of Galaad: so that half of the river Arnon and the adjacent valley was his, but the other half part was the Moabites'. Deut. 3, 16. UNTO THE TORRENT JACOB. The length of his kingdom was from the torrent Arnon unto the torrent Jaboc. Num. 21, 24.

Latin:

V. 2. ET MEDIÆ PARTIS IN VALLE. In Ebr. est, Et in medio torrentis & in media parte Galaad, quod sc. rex Sehon dominatus sit ab Aroër (quam Moabitis eripuerat) quæ sita erat ad ripam torrentis (inde progrediendo ad medium torrentis) & in media parte Galaad: ita ut medietas fluvii Arnon & vallis adjacentis ipsius esset, altera vero dimidia pars esset Moabitarum. Deut. 3, 16. USQUE AD TORRENTEM JACOB. Longi- tudo regni ejus fuit a torrente Arnon, usque ad torren- tem Jaboc. Num. 21, 24.

## 12:4
V. 4. CONCERNING THE REMAINS OF THE REPHAIM. See what is said concerning the Rephaim at Gen. 14, 5. That OG, of the race of the giants, is said to have dwelt IN ASHTAROTH AND EDREI, which were his primary cities, Deut. 1, 4; Num. 21.

Latin:

V. 4. DE RELIQIIS RAPHAIM. Vide quæ de Raphaim ad Gen. 14, 5. OG ille de stirpe gigantum habitasse dicitur IN AST- HAROTH ET EDREI, quæ ejus urbes primariæ fuere Deut. 1, 4. Num. 21.

## 12:5
V. 5. UNTO THE BORDERS OF GESSUR AND MACHATI. There were two cities in the northern part of the region of Og towards Mount Hermon. The southern borders proceeded unto the middle part of Galaad or the borders of King Sehon.

Latin:

V. 5. USQUE AD TERMINOS GESSUR ET MACHATI. Erant duæ urbes in parte Aquilonari regionis Ogi versus montem Hermon. Australes termini procedebant usque ad dimidiam partem Galaad seu fines regis Sehon.

## 12:23
V. 23. THE KING OF THE GENTILES OF GALGAL. It is not Galgal, where Joshua had fixed his camp, nor Galilee as Masius and Cornelius wish (for the appellation 'Galilee of the Gentiles' did not yet exist then), but another city of this name, because those who are listed here were petty kings of cities defeated by Joshua, whose list is woven here; perhaps he is called King of the Gentiles because his subjects consisted of diverse peoples.

Latin:

V. 23. REX GENTIUM GALGAL. Non est Galgal, ubi castra fixerat Josua, nec Galilæa uti Masius & Cornelius volunt (nondum enim tum appellatio erat Galilæa gentium) sed alia civitas hujus nominis, quia qui hic recensentur ci- vitatum Reguli fuere a Josua devicti, quorum indi- culus texitur, forte Rex gentium dictus, quia e diver- sis gentibus subditi ejus constabant.

## 13:1 Argument
PART II. DEEDS DONE IN TIME OF PEACE. SECTION I. GEODETIC, concerning the distribution of the land. CHAPTER XIII. The division of the occupied land. The portion beyond the Jordan.

verf. 1.

THERE IS LEFT, WHICH HAS NOT YET BEEN DIVIDED BY LOT. In the Hebrew, no mention is made of the casting of lots: For the words are to be rendered thus, as Bonfrerius admits, And the land remained very much to possess it. The Chaldean also has it thus. Therefore, it is not indicated that any division of the land by lot has already been made.

Latin:

PARS II. RES GESTÆ TEMPORE PACIS. SECTIO I. GEODÆTICA, terræ distributionem concernens. CAPUT XIII. Terræ occupatæ divisio. Portio trans Jorda- nem.

verf. 1.

DERELICTA EST, QUÆ NEC DUM SOR- TE DIVISA EST. In Ebræo nulla de sortitione mentio facta : Verba enim ita reddenda, fatente Bonfrerio, Et ter- ra remansit multa valde ad possidendum eam. Sic ha- bet etiam Chaldæus. Non ergo indicatur aliquam jam factam terræ per sortem divisionem.

## 13:2
Verse 2. NAMELY ALL GALILEE OF THE PHILISTINES.

The LXX, Lyranus, Pagninus, Montanus, Forsterus, Masius, Bonfrerius, Tremellius & Junius, and others take the word גלילות as an appellative. Bonfrerius confirms that the Vulgate lies in error, both because Galilee had no commerce with the Philistines, and because Galilee had already been subdued in chapter 10, with the war at the waters of Merom finished along with the Galilean king, the instigator of the whole war. AND ALL GESHURI. Which was indeed assigned to the half-tribe of Manasseh in verse 11. But the Israelites did not wish to drive out the inhabitants of Geshur and Maacath in verse 13, whence even in the time of David, Geshur had its own king, whose daughter David took, from whom Absalom was born, 2 Sam. 3, 3. But what of the passage 1 Chron. 2, 23, where Jair the Gileadite is said to have taken Geshur; which was done before Joshua, Num. 32, 41, Deut. 3, 14. Answer. That Jair had occupied at least some part of the Geshurite region, and that the Canaanites left there had recovered even those places which had been taken from them, whence it is said here that all Geshur remained to be occupied.

Latin:

Vers. 2. OMNIS VIDELICET GALILÆA PHILISTIIM.

Vocem גלילות ceu appellativum accipiunt LXX. Lyranus, Pagnin. Montan. Forsterus, Masius, Bonfrerius, Tremellius & Junius aliique. In mendo ergo cubare Vulgatam Bonfrerius confirmat, tum quia nihil commercii Galilææ cum Philistiim, tum quia Galilæa jam subacta c. 10. bello ad aquas Meron cum Galilæo rege totius belli incensore confecto. ET UNIVERSA GESSURI. Quæ assignata quidem dimidiæ tribui Manaf- se v. 11. Sed Israëlitæ noluere habitatores Gessuri, & Machati dispellere v. 13. unde Davidis adhuc tempore Gessur regem suum habuit, cujus filiam David duxit, e qua natus est Absolom 2. Sam. 3, 3. At quid de loco 1. Par. 2, 23. ubi Sair Galaadites Gessur cepisse dicitur; quod ante Josuam factum Num. 32, 41. Deut. 3, 14. Resp. Jair aliquid saltim de Gessu- ræa regione occupasse, & Cananæos ibi relictos ea etiam loca, quæ sibi erepta erant, recuperasse, unde hic dicitur universa Gessurea occupanda reman- sisse.

## 13:3
FROM THE TURBID RIVER WHICH IRRIGATES EGYPT] In the Hebrew, from Shihor which is above Egypt. Shihor signifies any black, that is, turbid, river, not liquid. I would believe that the Sicoris in Spain was named by the Phoenicians from this. Jeremiah 2, 18 calls the Nile by this name. Dionysius Afer: Σῆρις ὑπ᾿ Αἰθιόπων κικλήσκεται· οἱ δὲ Συήνης Ενιάσται ςρεφθέντι μετ᾽ ὄνομα Νεῖλον ἔθεντο. And hence the name Sirius, because the Nile is moved by that star. But the Greeks seem to have read שׁוֹחֵן instead of שיחור. For they translate, from the uninhabited land which is before Egypt. B. Luther and Osiander retain the Hebrew Shihor, and think that the river is indicated which washes Egypt on that side where Egypt faces the land of Canaan, namely, that which flows from the Serbonian bog near the city of Asedec into the Mediterranean Sea. However, R. Solomon, Kimchi, Lyranus, Pagninus, Masius, Magalianus, Bonfrerius, and Cornelius [take it as] the Nile. The Tigurines understand [it as] that which is called שיחור, i.e., turbid, because its water is turbid and black with the silt which it carries, so that the Nile is called the Southern boundary, namely, of Palestine. But the Northern [boundary is] Accaron. For although the promised land did not extend as far as the Nile, but to a certain torrent coming from the desert, which is called the torrent of the desert, or even of Egypt, Gen 15, Am 6, last [verse], yet because that torrent is a stream of the Nile, and between that torrent as far as Rhinocolura, which city is the boundary of Judea toward the south, as Pliny testifies, b. 5, ch. 13, Strabo, b. 16, Augustine, b. 15, On the City of God, ch. 24, nothing is but solitude and uninhabited land; therefore, it is rightly said to extend as far as the Nile, where, namely, the land is cultivated and fertile near the Nile. Junius retains with Tremellius the name Sichor, and understands Rhinocolura with Epiphanius against the Manichaeans, rendering it thus: from Sichon, which (is) before Egypt. For in the Hebrew there is nothing about the irrigation of Egypt, as the Vulgate has, from which that interpretation concerning the Nile arose.

THE LAND OF CANAAN.

In the Hebrew, it is to be reckoned as of the Canaanites (as Masius rendered it), so that this predicate may refer to the preceding words from Sichor: which is before Egypt as far as the borders of Accaron to the north, it is to be reckoned as (the land) of the Canaanites. Rashly, therefore, does the Vulgate here begin a new clause: The land of Canaan, which is divided into the five lords of the Philistines. Which clearly does not fit. For was the land of Canaan divided into those five satrapies? Were not the Philistines distinct from the Canaanites, as being descended not from Canaan, but from Mesraim, the other son of Cham? More correctly, therefore, in the Junius-Tremellius translation, which follows the Hebrew sources, it is hinted that that region is to be reckoned as belonging to the five satrapies, and B. Luther most excellently joins these five satraps to them as being distinct from the Canaanites, which he also ought to have occupied those satrapies, even though they are Philistines, not Canaanites; because they were formerly possessed by the Canaanites, whom the Philistines had expelled. Deut. 2:22. Which, however, the Hebrews, on account of their sloth and wickedness, did not obtain, except for a short time under David and Solomon, and there were almost perpetual wars between them and the Hebrews, namely Gaza, Azotus, Ascalon, Geth, and Accaron.

Ver. 3. LORDS) Satraps, placed under Kings: such as were called elsewhere סרנים, as here, elsewhere נשאים, elsewhere נסיכים, as below v. 21.

More correctly, therefore, B. Luther rendered it Lords, and Jerome elsewhere interpreted the Hebrew word more conveniently, namely Princes or Satraps, and Bonfrerius notes that a different kind of government is indicated among the Philistines than among the Canaanites, because a monarchical one pleased the latter, but an aristocratic or democratic one the former, because the prefects governed not in their own name, but in the name of another, either a king or the people, called by the Persian word Satraps.

PHILISTINES) Lands are named sometimes by their most recent possessors, as here, sometimes by their more ancient ones, as below v. 22.

Latin:

A FLUVIO TURBIDO QUI IRRIGAT ÆGYPTUM] In Ebræo a Sichor qui supra Ægyptum est. Sichor fluvium quemvis nigrum, id est, turbidum, non liquidum significat. Crediderim inde a Pœnis dictum in Hispania Sicorim. Ni- lum hoc nomine vocat Jeremias 2, 18. Dionysius Aser: Σῆρις ὑπ᾿ Αἰθιόπων κικλήσκεται· οἱ δὲ Συήνης Ενιάσται ςρεφθέντι μετ᾽ ὄνομα Νεῖλον ἔθεντο. Et hinc Sirio nomen, quod eo sidere moveatur Nilus. At Græci pro שיחור videntur legisse שׁוֹחֵן. Vertunt enim, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀοικήτε τῆς κατὰ πρόσωπον Αἰγύπτε. Ebræum Sichor retinet cum B. Luthero Osian- der, putatque indicari fluvium, qui Ægyptum alluit ea parte, qua respicit Ægyptus terram Canaan, eum sc. qui ex Sirbonis palude prope urbem Asedec in mare mediterraneum influit. Nilum tamen R. Sa- lomo, Kimchi, Lyranus, Pagninus, Masius, Magalianus, Bonfrer. Cornel. Tigurini intelligunt, qui שיחור di- catur, h. e. turbidus, quia aqua ejus limo, quem ve- hit, est turbida & nigra, ut dicatur Nilus terminus Meridionalis sc. Palæstinæ. Aquilonaris vero Acca- ron. Etsi enim terra promissa sese non porrigebat usque ad Nilum; sed ad torrentem quendam de e- remo venientem, qui torrens deserti, vel etiam Ægypti dicitur Gen 15. Am. 6. ult. tamen quia tor- rens ille est rivus Nili, & inter torrentem illum usque ad Rinocoluram, quæ urbs terminus Ju- dæe est versus meridiem teste Plinio l. 5. c. 13. Stra- bone l. 16. August. l. 15. de Civ. Dei c. 24. ni l est nis solitudo & inhabitata terra, ideo usque ad Nilum, u- bi sc. terra culta & fertilis juxta Nilum est, sese porri- gere recte dicitur. Junius retinet cum Tremellio nomen Sichor, & Rhinocoluram cum Epiphanio con- tra Manichæos intelligit, ita reddens: a Sichone, quæ (est) ante Ægyptum. In Ebræo enim nihil de irri- gatione Ægypti, uti Vulgata habet, e qua illa de Ni- lo interpretatio orta.

TERRA CANAAN.

In Ebræo, Cananæorum censenda est, (ut Ma- sius reddidit) ut prædicatum hoc referatur ad ante- cedentia a Sichor: quæ est ante Ægyptum usq́; ad ter- minos Accaron ad Aquilonem Cananæorum (terra) censenda est. Temere ergo Vulgata hic novum co- lon orditur: Terra Canaan, quæ in quinque regulos Philistiim dividitur. Quod plane non congruit. Num enim terra Canaan in quinque Satrapias istas divisa fuit? Annon Philistiim distincti erant a Cha- nanæis, utpote non a Chanaan, sed a Mesraim altero filio Chami oriundi? Rectius ergo in Junio - Tre- mell. fontes Ebræos sequuta translatione regionem illam quinque Satrapiarum accensendam esse, in- nuitur, & B. Lutherus optime hosce quinque Satra- pas ceu a Chananæis distinctos illis adjungit, quod etiam Satrapias istas occupare debuerit, etsi Phili- stiim sint, non Cananæorum; quia olim a Cananæis possidebantur, quos Philistiim ejecerant. Deut. 2, 22. Quas tamen Ebræi ob ignaviam & scelera sua non adepti sunt, nisi exiguo tempore sub Davide ac Salomone & perpetua fere illis cum Ebræis fue- re bella, nimirum Gaza, Azoto, Ascalon, Geth, & Ac- caroni.

Vers. 3. REGULOS) Satrapas, sub Regibus positos: quales alibi סרנים, ut hic, alibi נשאים, alibi נסיכים vocaban- tur, ut infra v. 21.

Rectius ergo B. Lutherus Dominos reddidit & interpretatus est vocem Ebræam alibi convenien- tius Hieronymus, nempe Principes vel Satrapas, no- tatque Bonfrerius indicari aliud genus regiminis a- pud Philistinos, quam apud Chananæos, quod his Monarchicum placuerit, illis vero Aristocraticum vel democraticum, quia Præfecti non suo, sed alterius vel regis, vel populi nomine gubernarint, Persica voce Satrapæ dicti.

PHILISTIIM) Terræ modo a novissimis possessoribus ut hic, modo ab antiquioribus ut infra v. 22. nominantur.

## 13:4
Ver. 4. BUT TO THE SOUTH ARE THE HIVITES ALL THE LAND OF CANAAN) It well draws that והעוים to a new period, contrary to what the Hebrew punctuation has, which, having promised that it would count five, counts six.

Most poorly, against the Hebrew truth, does Grotius handle these things; although only five satrapies of the Philistines are counted, yet that name is not added rashly, but if the particle Vav is understood in an explanatory sense, the reason is given why those five satrapies of the Philistines are also to be granted to the Hebrews, because, namely, they were once the Hivites', Deut. 2:23. But if the copulative meaning is retained, whatever the Hivites still inhabit and defended from the violence of the Philistines will be added to the five satrapies: which pleases Junius and Osiander.

Latin:

Vers. 4. AD MERIDIEM VERO SVNT HEVÆI OMNIS TERRA CANAAN) Bene illud והעוים trahit ad novam periodum, contra quam habet Hebræa distinctio, quæ cum promisiffet, se quinque numeraturam, numerat sex.

Pessime contra Ebraicam veritatem hæc Gro- tius, etsi autem quinque Satrapiæ solum numeren- tur Philistæorum, non tamen temere nomen illud adjicitur, sed si particula Vav αἰτιολογικῶς intelliga- tur, causa redditur, cur concedendæ Ebræis etiam illæ Satrapiæ quinque Philistæorum, quia sc. Havæo- rum quondam fuere Deut. 2, 23. Si autem retinentur significatus copulandi, adjungetur quinq; Satrapiis quicquid adhuc Havæi incolunt, & defenderunt a vi Philistinorum : quod placet Junio & Osiandro.

## 13:5
Ver. 5. AND ITS BORDERS.

It is an oversight of the Vulgate, for הגבול is not had, i.e., the terminal land, but הגבלי, which Masius and Vatablus take as a proper noun, the land of the Gebalites. So also the LXX, the Chaldean, the Tigurines, B. Luther, as also Tremellius and Junius; the Giblite land also from the promontory of Gabale above Sidon, so called in Pliny. Cornelius, with Bonfrerius, notes that Byblus is a city in Phoenicia not far from Sidon. See Ps. 28:8, Ez. 27:9, 1 Kings 5, last verse.

Latin:

Vers. 5. EJUSQUE CONFINIA.

Est παρόραμα Vulgatæ, non enim הגבול ha- betur, i. e. terminalis terra, sed הגבלי quod Masius & Vatablus ut nomen proprium accipiunt, terra Ge- balenorum. Sic etiam LXX. Chald. Tigurini, B. Lu- therus ut & Tremell. ac Junius; Terra etiam Giblæa e Gabale promontorio supra Sidonem sic dicta a- pud Plin. Byblum urbem esse in Phœnicia non pro- cul a Sidone notat Cornelius cum Bonfrerio. vid. Ps. 28, 8. Ez. 27, 9. 1. Reg. 5, ult.

## 13:6
Ver. 6. AND ALL THE SIDONIANS] Sidon is the name of the nation before it is of the city. Gen. 10:15. Sidones in Curtius: Sidonis in Stephanus and others.

They were neighbors to the inhabitants of Lebanon, and to those dwelling near the West and the sea. The Israelites never possessed their land, the whole of Phoenicia, likewise Philistia, and Mount Lebanon, by right of inheritance and habitation. This promise, therefore, was not absolute, but conditional; if the people remained constant in the worship of God. And the sloth of the Jews is to blame for the fact that they did not occupy the places promised to them. Yet in the time of David and Solomon those regions were made tributary to the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 6. VNIVERSIQVE SIDONII] Sidon gentis no- men antequam urbis. Gen. 10, 15. Sidones Curtio : Sidonis Stephano aliisque.

Erant illi Libani incolis, & accolis ad Occi- dentem & mare finitimi. Horum terram, totam Phœniciam, Philistæam item, & montem Libanum nunquam possederunt Israelitæ hæreditatis & habi- tationis nomine.
