For this leading out and liberation is not ascribed to only one divine person, but to more than one אלהים 2 Sam. 7, 23. besides the Father it is attributed to the Angel, who calls himself Jehovah Exod. 3, ch. 23, 20. to the Son of God 1 Cor. 10, 9. as the Angel of the face of the Lord, the Angel Redeemer, as also to the Holy Spirit, who led them through Moses Isa. 63, 8. 9. etc. It is certain, therefore, that more than one person is understood by the name אלהים קדשים whom the Israelites were bound to serve, because they led them out and liberated them.

Socinus, fragm. Script. duor. pag. 46, objects: (1.) That regard is had here to the termination of the noun אלהים, which is of the plural number, and although the discourse is of one only, the noun also joined to it is of the plural number for the sake of greater honor. (2.) He shows that a noun of the singular number is joined to a plural adjective, by the example of Ef. 46, 6. (3.) The noun אלהים itself, when it is of an altogether singular signification, is joined with a plural adjective in Exod. 20, 3. I reply to (1.) Socinus presupposes a double false hypothesis, both that the noun Elohim is plural only in termination, but singular in signification, and that it is used in the plural concerning God for the sake of honor. But since it has been shown that the noun אלהים obtains a plural signification, certainly the added adjective also retains its force of plural signification. Regarding (2.) The case of the example in Isa. 46, 6 is different. For there, a plural adjective is not joined to a plural substantive with a singular signification: an example of which kind could not be produced until now: but the singular בֶּן־בָּקָר son of the ox: or calf is joined to the plural תְּמִימִם which, since it is not only an adjective, but is also sometimes used as a substantive, as noted by Schindler in the Pentaglot Lexicon, Lyranus explains those in the state of regimen as 'calf of the unblemished': But even if it is taken as an adjective, it can be established here that it is used as a plural through διαίρεσιν [distribution], so that, namely, each calf to be offered may be whole. If, finally, an enallage is conceded here, an enallage is not to be admitted in those places where a plural adjective is constructed with אֱלֹהִים, since in the cited example the substantive is singular in terms of both termination and signification; but the name אֱלֹהִים is plural both in termination and also in signification. Regarding (3.) the διαίρεσις [distribution] is manifest, customary to the Hebrews, and frequent in the sacred Code: לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים 'There shall not be to you other Elohim [Gods]', that is, any of the other gods before me. None of the other gods shall be to you, neither this one nor that one. Therefore, Elohim here is not of singular signification, nor is the added adjective, but both retain a plural signification, and a distribution is designated by a singular verb, as in Gen. 1, 14. ch. 49, 22. Exod. 17, 12. ch. 31, 14. 1 Sam. 16, 4. Prov. 14, 1. ch. 27, 1. Hos. 10, 14. Joel 1, 20. Zech. 9, 5. and elsewhere passim.

Latin:

Vers. 19. DIXITQVE JOSVÆ AD POPVLVM) Sti- pulatio.

DEUS ENIM SANCTUS.

In Ebr. Quia Elohim Kedoschim vel Sancti IPSE. Quo plurali numero cum pronomine sin- gulari pluralitas personarum in una essentia divina designatur. Argumentamur hic ita: Plures קדשים SANCTI, qui sint אלהים, plures sunt personæ, quia substantivum plurale cum adjectivo plurali rei significatæ veram infert pluralitatem, quod ex inductione locorum constat. In Jehova vel es- sentia divina plures sunt קדשים SANCTI, qui אלהים sunt & vocantur. E. Quod argumentum confirmatur (1.) è subjecto, quod hic est nomen Je- hovah, quod pluribus אלהים convenit, cum in Scripturis introducantur Jehovah mittens, & Je- hovah missus &c. (2.) è Substantivo nomine, cui ad- jungitur, quod nomen אלהים plures inferre in Deo personas supra ostendimus. Ideoque non est, quod hic admittamus enallagen, quin plures potius Elohim sanctos innui credendum: sed & corrobo- ratur id (3.) è rei significatæ distributione: Sanctitas enim divina inter personas plures distribuitur, vel potius communis est pluribus personis, quum non tantum Pater sit sanctus Deus, sed & Filius sanctus Deus sit (qui distincta à Patre est persona) ἅγιος ille Actor. 3, 14. 1. Joh. 2, 20. ὁ ἅγιος ἀληθινὸς Apoc. 3, 7. קדש קדשים Sanctus ille Sanctorum vel omni- um Sanctissimus Dan. 9, 24. Sanctus & Spiritus S. In- de trinis vicibus illud קדוש à Sanctis Angelis Deo acclamatur Esa. 6, 3. Adhæc (4.) è servitutis religiosæ objecto: quandoquidem serviendum sit non uni tan- tum personæ Patris, sed & Filio religioso cultu, ad- eoque personis pluribus: quum omnes honorare debeant Filium, ut Patrem Joh. 5, 23. (5.) Denique è servitutis religiosæ causa, quæ hic adducitur, quod Jehovah Elohim populum ex Ægypto eduxerit, & liberarịt. Hæc enim eductio & liberatio non ad- scribitur uni tantum personæ divinæ, sed pluribus אלהים 2. Sam. 7, 23. præter Patrem tribuitur Angelo, qui se Jehovam dicit Exod. 3. cap. 23, 20. Filio Dei 1. Cor. 10, 9. ceu Angelo faciei Domini, An- gelo Redemtori, ut & Spiritui Sancto, qui per Mosen eos deduxit Esa. 63, 8. 9. &c. Plures ergo personas nomine אלהים קדשים quibus Israelitæ servire debebant, quod eduxerint eosdem & liberarint, intelligi certum est.

Excipit Socinus, fragm. Script. duor. pag. 46. (1.) Habitam hic rationem terminationis nominis אלהים, quæ est numeri pluralis, & quamvis de uno tantum sit sermo, nomen quoque adjunctum esse pluralis numeri amplioris honoris gratia. (2.) No- men singularis numeri adjectivo plurali jungi, exem- plo Ef. 46, 6. ostendit. (3.) Ipsum nomen אלהים cum singularis omnino significationis est, cum adjectivo plu- rali conjungi Exod. 20, 3. Resp. ad (1.) præsupponit Socinus geminam falsam hypothesin, tum quod no- men Elohim terminatione solum plurale, significa- tione autem singulare sit, tum quod honoris gratia plurale adhibeatur de Deo. Quum vero ostensum sit, nomen אלהים pluralem significationem obti- nere, utique adjectum additum etiam vim suam pluralis fignificationis retinet. Ad (2.) Dispar est Exempli Esa. 46, 6. ratio. Non enim ibi plurale Adjectivum jungitur substantivo plurali significa- tione singulari: cujusmodi exemplum nullum ad- huc produci potuit: sed singulare בֶּן־בָּקָר filius bo- vis: seu vitulus jungitur plurali תְּמִימִם quod cum non tantum adjectivum sit, sed etiam quandoque ut substantivum adhibeatur, notante Schindlero in Lexico Pentaglotto, Lyranus illa in statu regiminis explicat vitulus immaculatorum: Sed etiamsi acci- piatur ut adjectivum, statui potest hic per διαίρεσιν pluralis adhibitum, ut scil. unusquisque offeren- dus vitulus integer sit. Si denique enallage hic con- cedatur, non tamen in locis illis, ubi cum אֱלֹהִים construitur plurale Adjectivum, enallage admit- tenda, quum in allato exemplo substantivum sin- gulare sit & terminationis & fignificationis ratio- ne; nomen vero אֱלֹהִים plurale sit tum termina- tione tum etiam fignificatione. Ad (3.) manifesta est διαίρεσις Ebræis usitata, & in sacro Codice fre- quentata לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים non ERIT tibi Dii Elohim alieni, id est, ullus ex Diis alienis co- ram me. Nullus Deorum alienorum erit tibi, neque hic neque iste. Non ergo Elohim hic fignificatio- nis singularis est, nec adjectivum additum, sed reti- net utrumque pluralem fignificationem, designa- turque per verbum singulare distributio, ut Gen. 1, 14. cap. 49, 22. Exod. 17, 12. cap. 31, 14. 1. Sam. 16, 4. Prov. 14, 1. cap. 27, 1. Hos. 10, 14. Joel. 1, 20. Zach. 9, 5. & alibi passim.

## 24:21
Verse 21. AND THE PEOPLE SAID TO JOSHUA) A pledge. Compare 2 Chron. 34, v. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 21. DIXITQUE POPVLVS AD JOSVE) Spon- sio. Confer. 2. Paral 34. v. 32.

## 24:23
Verse 23. TAKE AWAY THE STRANGE GODS FROM AMONG YOU.

But there do not seem to have been idols among them, which August. q. 24 gathers from v. 31, understanding by idols phantasms and thoughts alien to God and the majesty of God; but although there was no public idol at that time, some could nevertheless have had idols privately in their houses, which it is established from Am. 5, 25 and Acts 7, 43 were also worshipped by them privately in the desert. And these things concern not only the present Israelites, but also their descendants.

Latin:

Vers. 23. AUFERTE DEOS ALIENOS DE MEDIO VESTRI.

At nulla videntur fuisse inter ipsos idola, quod è v. 31. August. q. 24. colligit, per idola phantasma- ta & cogitationes à Deo Deique majestate alienas intelligens; verum quamvis nullum isto tempore idolum publicum fuerit, habere tamen potuere privatim nonnulli in ædibus suis idola, quæ etiam in deserto ipsis privatim culta fuisse, constat ex Am. 5, 25. Actor. 7, 43. Nec tantum præsentes Israelitas hæc concernunt, sed etiam posteros eorum.

## 24:26
Verse 26. JOSHUA ALSO WROTE ALL THESE THINGS IN THE BOOK OF THE LAW OF THE LORD) He ordered these promises to be inscribed in that codex, which was kept near the Ark (see Deut. 17, 18 and 31, 26).

UNDER THE OAK) That very one, the mention of which is in Gen. 35, 4 in the history of Jacob and Judg. 9, 6. That place was for a long time a temple in honor of Jacob: But the Samaritans were wrong, who, after the temple was established at Jerusalem by royal authority, made a schism under the pretext of an obliterated custom, which erupted into heresy.

Grotius has it from the Rabbis, not from Scripture, that that oak which is commemorated in Gen. 35, 4 is indicated, and they also want it to be the same one near which God first appeared to Abram in Gen. 12, v. 6. That it is also the same one designated in Judg. 9, 6, whence, I ask, is it established? And are we to believe that an oak remained for so many centuries? The Holy Scriptures also know nothing about that place being held as a temple in honor of Jacob, nor would such an ἐθελοθρησκεία [will-worship] have been approved by Joshua. Therefore, by the sanctuary is understood either that place in which the ark stood for a while, until the assembly was finished, in which or near which that oak was, to which that stone was placed as a monument to be for posterity, which Bonfrerius wants, or rather the tabernacle. For as to what Bonfrerius says, that an oak had no place in a tabernacle only ten cubits high, nor was it permitted by the law of Deut. 16, 21. Resp. That the preposition בְּ is sometimes the same as AD [at/near], and that the sense could be, not that the oak was in the sanctuary, but that it was near the sanctuary, as the Rabbis, Tirinus, and others explain, and that it is indeed forbidden by God in Deut. 16 to plant a grove near the altar, in the manner of the Gentiles, but not to erect a tabernacle near the ark. And Bonfrerius himself notes at v. 25 that the precept of Deut. 16 is to be understood as applying when the tabernacle was to be fixed to remain somewhere, but not when it was there incidentally and for a short time; otherwise, it would have had to be seen to in the desert that, in the place where it was to be located, all trees round about should be cut down. Although it is not a matter of trees planted, but of those to be planted by industry there: Thou shalt not make a grove of any tree.

Latin:

Vers. 26. SCRIPSIT QVOQVE OMNIA HÆC IN VOLVMEN LEGIS DOMINI) Codici isti, qui apud Ar- cam custodiebatur (vide Devter. 17, 18. & 31, 26.) hæc pro- missa adscribi jussit.

SVBTER QVERCVM) Illam ipsam, cujus mentio Gen. 35, 4. in historia Jacobi & Judæ 9, 6. Is locus in honorem Jaco- bi diu pro templo fuit: Male autem Samaritani, qui post con- stitutum auctoritate regia Hierosolymis templum moris ob- literati obtentu schisma fecerunt, quod in hæresin erupit.

Quercum illam, quæ Genes. 35, 4. commemo- ratur, indicari, à Rabbinis habet Grotius, non è Scriptura, qui & eandem volunt, juxta quam pri- mum Deus Abræ apparuit Genes. 12. v. 6. Eandem etiam Judic. 9, 6. designari, unde obsecro constat? Et num quercum tot seculis mansisse credemus? De loco etiam isto in honorem Jacobi pro templo habito nihil norunt S. literæ, neque ejusmodi ἐθελοθρησκεία probata fuisset Josuæ. Per sanctu- rium ergo vel locus ille intelligitur, in quo ar- ca tantisper, dum comitia absolverentur, stabat, in quo vel juxta quem quercus illa erat, cui lapis iste suppositus fuit posteris monumentum futurus, quod vult Bonfrerius, vel potius tabernaculum. Nam quod Bonfrerius dicit, in tabernaculo decem tantum cubitos alto quercum locum non habuisse, nec per legem Deut. 16, 21. concessum id fuisse. Resp. Præ- positionem בְּ quandoque idem esse quod AD, sen- sumque esse posse, non quod in sanctuario, sed quod vel juxta sanctuarium fuerit quercus, uti ex- ponunt Rabbini, Tirinus, alii, & vetari quidem à Deo Deuter. 16. plantari lucum juxta altare, more gentilium, non autem juxta arcam erigi taberna- culum. Et monet Bonfrerius ipse ad verf. 25. præ- ceptum Deuter. 16. intelligendum esse, cum alicu- bi mansurum figeretur tabernaculum, non autem cum obiter & ad breve tempus, alias curandum fuisset in deserto, ut in loco, quò locaretur, cir- cumcirca omnes arbores exscinderent. Quan- quam non de arboribus plantatis, sed de industria plantandis ibi agatur: Non facies lucum ex omni arbore.

## 24:27
Vers. 27. THAT IT HATH HEARD ALL THE WORDS OF THE LORD.

By prosopopoeia these things are attributed to the stone, as if to say: If you do not hear, this stone will be a mute witness that it has heard these covenants and that you have violated them. Compare Deut. 32, 1. Isa. 1, 2. Jer. 2, 12. But that the words were inscribed upon the stone, which Cornelius holds with the Chaldean, cannot be proven from Scripture.

Latin:

Vers. 27. QUOD AUDIERIT OMNIA VER- BA DOMINI.

Per prosopopœiam lapidi hæc tribuitur, q. d. Si vos non audieritis, lapis hic erit testis mutus hæc pacta audiisse & violasse. Conf. Deuter. 32, 1. Ef. 1, 2. Jerem. 2, 12. Quod autem lapidi inscripti fuerint verba, quod cum Chaldæo Cornel. habet, è Scri- ptura probari nequit.

## 24:29
Vers. 29. AND AFTER THESE THINGS JOSHUA THE SON OF NUN THE SERVANT OF THE LORD DIED, BEING A HUNDRED AND TEN YEARS OLD.

In what year of his leadership Joshua died, we have said in the Prolegomena. Salian and Torniellus teach at length that he spent 17 years, neither more nor fewer, in the leadership. Compare also Bonfrerius on this passage. Tirinus concurs, and from the Calendar of the Hebrews designates the day of his death as the 26th of Nisan, in which same month also died the true Joshua, our Lord Jesus Christ, in whose type also Joshua lived as a celibate, as witnessed by Ignatius in his Epistle to the Philadelphians, Jerome in Book 1, Chapter 1 of Against Jovinian, and Chrysostom in his Sermon on the Martyrs.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ET POSTHÆC MORTUUS EST JOSUE FILIUS NUN SERVUS DOMINI CENTUM ET DECEM ANNORUM.

Quoto anno principatus sui mortuus sit Josua, diximus in Prolegomenis. Annos 17. nec plures nec pauciores egisse in Principatu fuse docent Sa- lian. & Torniellus. Conf. & Bonfrer. in h. l. Tirinus suffragatur, & è Calendario Ebræorum diem obitus designat 26. Nisan, quo eodem mense & mortuus verus Josua Dn. noster Jesus Christus, in cujus ty- pum quoque Josua cælebs vixerit, teste Ignatio Epist. ad Philad. Hieroy. l. 1. c. Jovin. Chrysostom. Serm. de Martyr.

## 24:30
THAMNATHSARE) תמנת־סרח. But in Judges 2, 9, the same is called תמנת־חרס. In one of these two places the letters are transposed. The Latin in both places is Thamnathsare. The Greek Codices vary.

The Hebrews in Seder Olam, as well as Masius, Montanus, Cajetan, Megalian, Serarius, and Adrichomius, report that this metathesis was made not by error but by design, namely that it was called by the former name in Josh. 19, 50, and here [it is called by the latter] because of the aridity and uselessness of the place, as if to say: a flowing figure, and useless, or as others say, an image of superfluity or stench; but in the latter [it is called] an image of the Sun, concerning which see chapter 19, verse 50.

Latin:

Vers. 30. THAMNATHSARE) תמנת־סרח. At Ju- dicum 2, 9. idem dicitur תמנת־חרס. In altero horum lo- corum literæ sunt transpositæ. Latinus utrobique Tham- nathsare. Græci Codices variant.

Hanc metathesin non per sphalma, sed studio factam in Seder Olam tradunt Ebræi, ut & Ma- sius, Montan. Cajetan. Megalian. Serarius, Adri- chom. vocatum nempe priori nomine Jof. 19, 50. & hic ab ariditate & inutilitate loci, q. d. figura dif- fluens, & inutilis, vel ut alii, imago superfluitatis aut fœtoris, in posteriori vero imago Solis, de quo ad cap. 19. vers. 50.

## 24:31
ALL THE DAYS OF JOSHUA AND OF THE ELDERS WHO LIVED A LONG TIME AFTER JOSHUA) Namely, those who had been partners with Joshua in governing the people. For it will appear from the book of Judges that the people did not remain in obedience to God for long; where you have words opposite to these in 2, 8, 9, 10. So great is the value of the fresh memory of good deeds and the authority of men who have been observed. See a similar case in 2 Chronicles 24, v. 2, 16, 17, 18. It appears from this that this book was written some time after Joshua, as we noted above.

That the whole book was written after Joshua does not appear from this, but only that this clause was added, and we have previously observed that certain other things were inserted somewhere into this book after the death of Joshua. Therefore, the whole book is not to be judged as not being Joshua's.

WHO LIVED A LONG TIME AFTER JOSHUA.

In the Hebrew it is nothing other than 'who had prolonged or extended the days (of their life) after Joshua,' which can be understood as referring either to many or to fewer years.

Latin:

Vers. 31. CUNCTIS DIEBUS JOSVE ET SENIO- RVM QVI LONGO VIXERVNT TEMPORE POST JOSVE) Nempe eorum qui Josuæ participes fuerant in populo regendo. Neque enim diutius mansisse in Dei ob- fequio populum ex Judicum libro apparebit: ubi opposita his verbis verba habes 2, 8. 9. 10. Tantum valet benefacto- rum recens memoria, & virorum spectatorum auctoritas. Vi- de simile 2. Paralipom. 24. v. 2. 16. 17. 18. Apparet hinc post Josuam aliquando tempore scriptum hunc librum, ut supra monuimus.

Totum librum post Josuam scriptum esse, hinc non apparet, sed solum clausulam hanc additam es- se, & alia quædam inserta alicubi huic libro esse post fata Josuæ antea observavimus. Non ergo to- tus liber Josuæ abjudicandus.

QUI LONGO VIXERUNT TEMPORE POST JOSUE.

In Ebr. nihil aliud est, quam qui prolonga- verant vel prorogarant dies (vitæ suæ) post Josue, quod intelligi potest vel ad plures vel ad pauciores annos.

## 24:32
AND THE BONES OF JOSEPH WHICH THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL HAD BROUGHT UP OUT OF EGYPT THEY BURIED IN SHECHEM) According to the promise in Genesis 50, 24.

This Cornelius relates a story about the bones of Adam being religiously received into the ark of Noah, and distributed among the tribes, whence the skull fell to Shem. But these trifles do not deserve a review, much less a refutation.

THEY BURIED HIM IN SHECHEM.

In the suburban field of the city of Shechem, as the subjoined ἐξήγησις (exegesis) teaches. Bonfrerius does not render the verb badly by using the pluperfect, THEY HAD BURIED; it is not likely that the burial was delayed until this time, which could have taken place many years before, after the Israelites rested from their battles.

AND IT WAS INTO THE POSSESSION OF THE SONS OF JOSEPH.

Not by a lot cast by Joshua, but outside the lot, by the gift of the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. 48:22.

Latin:

Vers. 32. OSSA QUOQUE JOSEPH QUÆ TVLE- RANT FILII ISRAEL DE ÆGTPTO SEPELIERVNT IN SICHEM) Ex promisso Genes. 50, 24.

Refert hic Cornelius fabulam de Adami offi- bus in arcam Noæ religiose receptis, & inter tri- bus distributis, unde Semo cranium obtigerit. Sed hæ næniæ recensionem non merentur, nedum re- futationem.

SEPELIERUNT IN SICHEM.

In agro suburbano urbis Sichem, uti ἐξήγησις subjuncta docet. Non male per plusquamperfe- ctum reddit verbum Bonfrerius, SEPELIERANT, non est verisimile ad hoc usque tempus dilatam se- pulturam, quæ ante plures annos jam fieri poterat, postquam à præliis quievere Israëlitæ.

ET FUIT IN POSSESSIONEM FILIO- RUM JOSEPH.

Non sortitione à Josua facta, sed extra sortem, donatione Jacobi Patriarchæ Genes. 48, 22.

## 24:33
Vers. 33. WHICH WAS GIVEN TO HIM IN MOUNT EPHRAIM)

Namely, through his wife; for the Levites did not have private fields in their own name. See a similar case in 2 Chronicles 2, verses 21, 22, 23.

It is doubtful whether Gibeah was given to Eleazar or to Phinehas? Abulensis and Masius favor the former, but Vatablus desires the latter, with Jerome not denying it in Epit. Paul. Certainly Gibeah was called the city of Phinehas. Most think it was given out of the ordinary course, partly on account of his merits, and partly so that Eleazar or Phinehas might be a neighbor to the Prince Joshua, who was dwelling in the tribe of Ephraim, since most of the other cities assigned to the Levites were in the tribe of Judah or Benjamin.

Latin:

Vers. 33. QVÆ DATA EST EI IN MONTE EPHRAIM)

Nempe per uxorem; nam Levitæ suo nomine privatos agros non habebant. Vide simile 2. Paralip. 2. versu 21. 22.23.

Dubium est, an Gabaa data Eleazari an Phineæ? Illud Abulensis, & Masius, hoc vero Vatablus vult, non abnuente Hieron. in Epit. Paul. Dicta certe fuit Gabaa Phineæ. Plerique datam esse extra ordinem putant, partim ob merita, partim ut Eleazar sive Phineæ Principi Josuæ vicinus esset, habitanti in tri- bu Ephraim, quum alias civitates Levitis assignatæ pleræque in tribu Judæ, vel Benjamin fuerint.

# Judges

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. TO THE BOOK IN THE PRESS

The book is called שׁוֹפְטִים (Shophetim) by the Hebrews, κριτῶν (Kriton) by the Greeks, and JUDGES by the Latins, because it describes the history of most of the Judges, or their deeds, or what happened under their rule. I say 'most': for the deeds of the last two, namely Eli and Samuel, cohere with the history of the Kings; since the first King was appointed and inaugurated by Samuel, from whose deeds the history of Eli the Priest and Judge, as far as the events of his old age which are chiefly commemorated, could not be torn away. These, therefore, being reserved for the first book of Kings or Samuel, the histories of the preceding JUDGES are commemorated in this book, but primarily as regards the vicissitudes of the prosperous and adverse affairs of the People of God: because, as Augustine testifies in Book 16 of The City of God, chapter 43, in the times of the Judges, just as the sins of the people and the mercy of God stood, so did the prosperous and adverse events of wars alternate.

But if it be asked whence those who commanded after Joshua were specifically called JUDGES, Bonfrerius, à Lapide, and others indeed respond that they were so called because they vindicated the people from the hand of their enemies, which they make their primary office: but that reason for the denomination is not adequate. For although this was done by most, yet some Judges are not read to have waged wars with enemies, such as Thola and Jair in chapter 10, Abesan, Ahjalon, and Abdon in chapter 12, nor are Heli or Samuel reported to have led the army of the Israelites. And when those judges who were leaders of war (Josephus calls them ἡγεμόνας and στρατηγὲς Commanders, as also ὑποστρατήγες, under GOD, to wit, Commander) are said to have judged Israel for so many years, not only expeditions of war or times are designated, but also of peace: They were called Judges, therefore, as the name itself indicates, from JUDGING, or also from GOVERNING, because to judge for the Hebrews is sometimes to govern, because judgment is some part of rule, just as also to vindicate subjects from force,

It is therefore falsely located in the tribe of Benjamin in the book on Hebrew places. In the Roman edition of the LXX, as also in the Syriac text, and in Theodoret, there is a clause of this book which neither the authentic Hebrew text recognizes, nor the versions, Chaldean, LXX Complutensian or Royal, Latin, therefore it is deservedly rejected as spurious. It reads thus: On that day the children of Israel taking the ark of God, they surrounded it in themselves: and Phinees performed the Priesthood for Eleazar his Father, until he died, and was buried in Gabaa, which is his: But the children of Israel went each one to his place to his city. And the children of Israel had worshipped Astharte and Astharoth and the Gods of the nations which were in their circuit. And the Lord delivered them into the hands of Eglon king of Moab, and he ruled over them for eighteen years. There is no need for a lengthy refutation of it. It betrays itself by its own futility. We end here, and attribute glory to God through our true and heavenly Joshua CHRIST the Savior, in the Holy Spirit. May his name be blessed for ages. Amen.

N. 7. M OF JUDGES. OQUIUM.

and the dangers of enemies pertains to the parts of rule. See here especially chapter 4, 4. 5. But although Moses and Joshua also governed the people before Kings were given to them, they are not to be counted in the number of the JUDGES, unless that word is taken more generally, in which way Jerome under the name of Judges in Isaiah 1, 26 includes them: but by the force of this inscription, and the special use of the name in this book, the first of the Judges is to be established as Othniel. Since Moses and Joshua had a more ample dignity; the former indeed that of the Redeemer, who liberated the people from Egypt, as he is called by Stephen in Acts 7, 35, and of the Lawgiver; the latter truly that of the Commander of the army, who led the people into the promised land, occupied it with an armed hand, and divided it among the Israelite tribes. Add that those two set over the people did not yet have a fixed seat, but the other Judges were given to the same in the promised land, when the tribes of Israel were already enjoying their possessions.

Furthermore, although the excellence and eminence of the Judges was significant, this dignity of the Judges is nevertheless distinguished not a little from the august dignity of Kings: because the former administered the Republic according to laws prescribed by God in such a way that they did not have the power to establish new laws, nor were they themselves Lords of the people, as Kings were; for then the law was Lord, and GOD the author of the law was their King, whence when they asked for a King, they are considered to have rejected God, that he should not reign (any longer, to wit, in the way in which he reigned before) over them 1 Sam. 8, 7. Nor were they unaccountable, but in grave cases were bound to the decrees of the Sanhedrin: hence also they did not have the power of imposing tributes on the people like Kings. Therefore they were neither anointed in the manner of kings, nor did they use a diadem, which is the sign of absolute Lords, or Royal insignia, as the Kings of other nations 2 Sam. 12, nor were they surrounded by a bodyguard or a crowd of attendants like Kings, concerning which in the Royal law 1. Sam. 8.

As regards the form of government, however, Serarius on Judges 3, Salianus in his Annals, Bonfrerius, and à Lapide do not wrongly assign to the rule of the Judges a Monarchical form, although Feuardent on Ruth 1, along with Genebrard in his Chronology, Tostatus in his Commentary, and Sigonius in book 1 of De Republica Hebraeorum, prefer an Aristocratic form. For there were not many judges, nor did they preside over the government, but one, nor did they administer the state for a short time, but until the end of life. We admit meanwhile that the word Monarchy must be taken more loosely here (since it is not unknown that Aristotle otherwise makes every Monarchical government Royal) or that the monarchical form must be understood in this place κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν (by analogy), at least in this sense, that the government of the judges approached it more closely than it did an Aristocracy. But since Josephus in book 4, last chapter, and book 5, chapter 4, makes ἀριστοκρατείαν (aristocracy) the form of the Jewish Republic, having misused that name, he seems to have accepted aristocracy as a species of Monarchy, as Bonfrerius observes: since he divides this into βασιλείαν (kingship) and Ἀριστοκρατείαν (aristocracy). Nor is there any doubt that Josephus also looks to the fact that the judges had to hear the opinion of the supreme Sanhedrin in more difficult matters. By which name you might perhaps not inappropriately say that the Monarchy was mixed with aristocracy. But it is most true that it was a θεοκρατείαν (theocracy), as is clear from Judges 8:22 and 1 Samuel 8:7, 12.

And therefore the judges—if you except one, Abimelech, who was not a Judge but a tyrant, and who invaded the principate by force after all his brothers were killed, and was not appointed by God as the others were, who were established extraordinarily from whatever tribe—were holy, endowed with the Spirit of God, and on that account are celebrated particularly in the Catalogue of ancient saints in Sirach 44:14 and Hebrews 11:32 ff. Who also, as Saviors of Israel, stood as types of Christ the true Savior, as Jerome says in Epistle 103 to Paulinus: in the book of Judges, as many princes of the people as there are, so many are the figures.

As for the ministerial author of the book, the opinions of the Doctors vary. Some make Ezra, or some later Prophet, the author. Most attribute it to the Prophet Samuel. Hugo Cardinalis writes in his Prologue that each judge recorded the deeds of his own times into acts, but that finally either Ezra, or Jeremiah, or rather Hezekiah collected these into one volume. B. Gerhard thinks this conjecture about Hezekiah is confirmed in his Exegetica de Scriptura Sacra, § 126, because his scribes are said to have collected certain proverbs of Solomon into one, Proverbs 25:1. But in truth, just as it is not likely that that history remained ἄγραφον (unwritten), or left in diaries and annals by GOD, the supreme and principal author of the sacred canon, for so many centuries until Hezekiah, or even the prophets of later times: so it is established far more correctly that, since the other θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired) books were added to the Canon successively, this one also was written by divine inspiration and added to the Mosaic books and the history of Joshua before the Histories of Kings and Chronicles were compiled.

The argument of the book is a description of the state of the Polity and certain memorable events in it from the passing of Joshua until the times of Eli, and especially regarding the vicissitudes of the Israelites, how they often fell away from God and were afflicted with just punishments, and how in turn, pressed by enemies, they were converted to God and liberated by the hands of the judges through divine aid: concerning which St. Augustine says in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 13: In the times of the Judges, there alternated among the people of God both the humiliations of labors for their sins, and the prosperities of consolations through the mercy of the Lord. The book is conveniently distributed into two parts: In the first, those things are commemorated which pertain especially to the state of the promised land and the deeds performed under the judges, from chapter 1 to 16. In the other, in the five later chapters, those things which happened after the passing of Joshua and the Elders who remained surviving Joshua, under the ἀναρχίᾳ (anarchy), to the state

of the Republic and the Church are described. Which later part is as an appendix to the former: since it does not continue the history which had preceded, but only commemorates some ἀξιομνημόνευτα (things worthy of memory) which occurred before the raising up of the Judges: whence in the former only is a just chronotaxis found: the latter, however, neglects the same, nay, it regresses to the prior anarchic state, lest that be left entirely untouched, and the histories be neglected, which the Holy Scriptures judged it useful to have observed. Whence the character of those times is expressed sometimes, that they were those in which there was no King in Israel, but everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Jud. 17, 6. ch. 18, 1. ch. 19, 1. ch. 21, 25. that is, when there was no Magistrate endowed with supreme power, who might keep the people in the duty of piety and honesty, which times were those that followed the Elders after the death of Joshua, before they were reduced to servitude by Chushan: during which there was ἀναρχία, and the Israelites first fell away from the true worship of God in the land of Canaan, and defiled themselves with idolatry Jud. 2, 7. 14. concerning which those things are worthy which are observed at ch. 17, 1. in the Junius-Tremellius annotations, which are repeated here: Whatever things are narrated from this chapter until the end of the book pertain to those things which are written above at 2, v. 11. and following, so that it appears they were done not long after the death of Joshua: first, as far as the history of this and the following chapter pertains, because it is not likely that the tribe of Dan, which was numerous, could have lacked its own possession for long, as it is said to have lacked it below 18, 1. and is confirmed Josh. 19, 47. Then, because he whom the Danite tribe adopted as Priest was a young man and a great-grandson of Moses from Manasseh, as appears from 18, 30. Third, because the author shows below 20, 1. that this history was done before the following one concerning the Benjaminites. Similarly, as regards the following history of chapter 19. and following, it is proved that it happened about the same time, first from Phinehas, who at that time was performing the Priesthood, as appears from 20, v. 28. then from the fact that that part of the Jebusites (which was called Jebus) which pertained to Benjamin was still held by the Jebusites, as is taught below chapter 19, verse 12. See above chapter 1, verse 8. and 21. lastly from the words of Deborah Jud. 5, verse 14. The state of the Israelite Republic of this and the following chapters is therefore that it was most corrupt both in religion and in morals: because from small beginnings in a short time whole tribes rushed into idolatry and open crimes, which it was sufficient to have confirmed by a single example in each kind. The end, however, is that the justice of the judgments of God (which have been commemorated above from chapter 3 until here) may shine forth.

The prior part delivers certain particular expeditions in chapter 1. and executes them as far as they pertain to the state of the whole promised land: and this partly generally, explaining the occasion and cause of the vicissitudes of servitude or pressure, and of the rest of the land in chapter 1. for the rest from verse 22. as also chapter 2. chapter 3. to verse 2. partly specifically executing the same in order under the rule of the judges: whom we distinguish into the former, before Abimelech, who invaded the government through tyranny and was created king by the Shechemites, and is unworthy of the name of judge: and into the latter, who saved the Israelite people after the death of Abimelech. Three of the former Judges and Saviors of the people, namely Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar, are described as to the liberation provided to the people in chapter 3. from v. 8. Afterwards chapter 4. Deborah's rule and victory: and chapter 5. her Eucharistic song is exhibited: finally in the three following chapters the history of Gideon, namely chapter 6. by which his divine calling and confirmation, chapter 7. by which the victory and the liberation of the people, and chapter 8. by which sequence, the slaughter of the Succothites, the punishment of the remaining Midianite princes, and the rest of the Israelites in the time of Gideon. In the following chapter 9, the history of the tyranny of Abimelech and his end is described.

Thenceforth the later Judges are commemorated according to the series of the times of their rule, and according to the twofold new apostasy of the Israelites, and the consequent oppression and servitude, first under the Philistines and Ammonites, which is described as regards the preceding quiet government under Tola and the manifold idolatry and most grave punishment under Jair in chapter 10, as also as regards the divine liberation from enemies through Jephthah, whose victory against the Ammonites and vow in chapter 11, as well as the war against the seditious Ephraimites in chapter 12, is handed down: By which the following Judges also, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon, are succinctly described. Secondly under the Philistines: from whose power the Israelites were liberated by Samson. His birth is treated in chapter 13, his marriage in chapter 14, his delivery into the hands of the Philistines by the tribe of Judah and the slaughter of the enemies in chapter 15, the betrayal by Delilah and the oppression of the Philistines in his death in chapter 16.

And this is the first part of Judges: in the other is commemorated the history of the Idol of Micah, whose erection in the house of Micah in chapter 17, its seizure by the tribe of Dan, and the idolatry in that tribe in chapter 18 is set forth: then concerning the Benjamite war: the cause of which was the crime of the Benjaminites, the nefarious rape in chapter 19, and the battle itself of the Israelites against the tribe of Benjamin in chapter 20, and what followed that, how provision was made for the remaining Benjaminites for wives, by saving the virgins in Jabesh, and destroying the married women, as well as through the abduction of the maidens of Shiloh in chapter 21.

Concerning the chronology of the book there is a great discrepancy among authors: Some, with Josephus, make the interval from which the Judges presided just too long. For Josephus counts the time of the servitudes separately from the time of the judgeships, namely 8 years of Mesopotamian, 18 of Moabite, 20 of Canaanite, 7 of Midianite, 18 of Ammonite, 40 of Philistine servitude; and thus besides 40 years of Othniel, 80 of Ehud, 1 of Shamgar, 40 of Deborah, 40 of Gideon, 3 of Abimelech (23 years of Tola are omitted in Josephus: which is without doubt a blunder. See Judges 10, verses 1, 2) 22 of Jair, 6 of Jephthah, 7 of Ibzan, 10 of Elon, 8 of Abdon (although Josephus names him without mention of the number of years, which is a not obscure sign of a blunder), 20 of Samson. And thus also the numbers of Laur. Codoman have it, as also those of Wolther, and likewise of Nicolaus Reimers Ursus, except that Josephus attributes a year to Shamgar and 18 years. of anarchy before the Mesopotamian servitude he counts separately, Wolther 21, Codomannus 20 years of the rule of the elders he places before the same, which 20 years, however, Codomannus omits in the judgeship of Samson, including them in the years of the Philistine servitude. By which method, by the calculation of Josephus, 429 years are going to emerge, by Wolther's 431, by Codomannus's and Reimers's 410 from the death of Joshua to the passing of Samson: nor will it be possible in any way to save that great and famous number of 480 years from the exodus of the Israelites from the land of Egypt until the time of the beginning of the building of Solomon's temple, clearly designated in 1 Kings 6, verse 1. For to those undoubted 40 years of wandering in the desert must be added the years of the rule of Joshua, which 25 of the principate of Eli, which 40 of the judgeship of Samuel and Saul, which 50. Josephus assigned, (with whom the aforementioned authors agree in these matters, except that they assign only 40, and more correctly, to Samuel and Saul, Wolther constitutes 26 years of the principate of Joshua, Reimers only 7), with 40 years of the Davidic reign, and the three primordial years of Solomon, and thus the sum collected from there will exceed by an immense amount the number 480 designated by the Holy Scriptures. We are certainly not unaware that many, and not ignoble, writers add their calculation to this separate numbering of the years of servitudes and judgeships, although not all by one method: namely Jerome in Epistle 132 to Vitalis, Augustine in book 15 of The City of God, ch. 13, Sulpicius Severus, Nicephorus of Constantinople, Cedrenus in his Chronicle, Philastrius p. 3, heresy 63, Sigonius on Sulpicius, Serarius on 1 Kings 6, Canus book 1, on loci, argument 12. Likewise Codomannus, Petavius, Petrus Possinus, Nicolaus Abrami and others: But because that number of years intervenes from the exodus until the temple, it was certainly a matter of conscience for others to depart from the letter and clear words of the book of Kings: most therefore entered upon another calculation, with the Hebrews and Eusebius, comprehending the years of the servitudes under the years of the rule or principates: by which method Eusebius, through an error omitting the ten-year judgeship of Elon, counted 289 years from the passing of Joshua to the death of Samson: but most others, not omitting Elon, 299 years, namely 40 years of Othniel (Judges 3:11), 80 of Ehud (ch. 3:30), a few months of Shamgar, 40 of Deborah (ch. 5, last verse), 40 of Gideon (ch. 8:28), 3 of Abimelech (ch. 9:22), 23 of Tola (ch. 10:2), 22 of Jair (ch. 10:3), 6 of Jephthah (ch. 12:7), 7 of Ibzan (ch. 12:9), 10 of Elon (ch. 12:11), 8 of Abdon (ch. 12:14), 20 of Samson (ch. 15, last verse), which opinion most embrace: some, however, take the 18 years of the Ammonite servitude, of which Judges 10:8, separately, and add them to those 299 years, whence a sum of 370 years emerges. D. Johannes Behrm. thinks the 6 years of Jephthah should be counted among those 18 years of the Ammonite servitude. But more correctly the years of the Ammonite servitude (like the other years of the servitudes) are comprehended in the years of the judgeships of Jair, of whom we are about to speak at chapter 10 of Judges: and thus that great number in 1 Kings 6 will be perfectly consistent with itself. If indeed the 299 years with a few months are counted until the death of Samson: to which sum collected from the book of Judges, if the 40 previous years from the exodus from Egypt until the death of Joshua, and 17 of the rule of Joshua are added, and furthermore the 40 years of the judgeship of Eli (1 Sam. 4:18), and again 40 of the rule of Samuel and Saul (Acts 13, 21.) so that also the 40 years of the Davidic reign (1 Kings 2:11) and the first 4 of the Solomonic reign are added, the total sum thence to be produced will be 480 years, which namely are designated from the exodus up to the beginning of the construction of the Solomonic temple.

Which chronology seems most expeditious before others previously mentioned: but that which is especially objected to it by Canus, Codomannus, Petavius, and others, is that the years of servitude should not be confused with the years of the judgeships, since it would be absurd for the land to have been at rest and infested by war at the same time; to which difficulty the blessed D. Behmius responds: that there could also have been peace between the Israelites and their oppressors during the time of the servitude of the Israelites, since the years are called years of servitude, not indeed of war. In which manner, without an ἀντικείμενον ἐν προσκειμένῳ, by which Codomannus urges that opinion, the eight years of the Mesopotamian Israelite servitude (Judges 3:8) will be included in the 40 years of Othniel; the 18 years of the Moabite servitude (ch. 3:14) will be comprised in the 80 years of the judgeship of Ehud. Under the 40 years of the rule of Deborah will likewise be contained the 20 years of the Canaanite servitude (ch. 4:3) and furthermore the 7 years of the Midianite servitude will have to be included in the 40 years of the leadership of Gideon (ch. 6:1); and likewise the 18 years of the Ammonite servitude (ch. 10:7, 8) will have to be comprised under the 22 years of the prefecture of Jair; but under those of Samson and the years of the three preceding Judges (which together make 45) or, as others prefer, the first 20 years of the following judge Eli, are to conclude the 40 years of Philistine servitude, concerning which Jud. 13, 1. That servitude, therefore, is not necessarily to be understood in such a way that the prefecture of the Judges is excluded: which Grotius s had become tributary to those whom they are said to have served, such a servitude as could have taken place even if the Israelites had their own Judge, whom God, as the occasion arose, when the Israelites, oppressed or even vexed by other burdens of servitude, cried out to the Lord, raised up to liberate the people, so that there is no need to establish that he began to reign only then, when he was raised up by the Spirit of the Lord for liberation: since he could have already been in charge of the judgeship before. Concerning the times of the judgeship of Deborah, it is certain from Jud. 4, 3 that the Israelites served King Jabin for 20 years, even when Deborah was in charge of the judgeship: and Samson is said to have judged the Israelites for 20 years during the times of the Philistines, or under their oppression, ch. 15, 20. However, the most learned Archbishop of Ireland, James Ussher of Armagh, in his Sacred Chronology published at Oxford in the year 1660, part two, ch. 12, p. 197, has recently initiated a new, and perhaps not inconvenient, method in assigning the years of the Judges, who indeed acknowledged that the times of war and servitude must be separated from the times of peace and rest, but he established that by the notation of years applied to the rest of the land, the beginning of that rest is designated, but not the duration of the rest itself or of the prefecture of the Judges, so that thus that וַתִּשְׁקֹט, 'and it rested,' is 'it began to rest,' just as in Gen. 5, 32, ch. 11, 26, 'he begat' is next to it 'he began to beget,' 1. Reg. 6, verse 1, 'he built' is 'he began to build,' and when any King is said to have been of so many or so many years, בִּמְלֹכוֹ, that is, when he began to reign. Since, therefore, the reason for numbers in the notation of times is such that sometimes it indicates when some event happened, and sometimes how long it lasted, Ussher judges that in the years of the oppressed the latter is to be taken as explicit, but in the years of the rest of the land the former, so that under Othniel the land, Jud. 3, v. 11, is not to be understood as having rested for 40 years, but that 40 years elapsed from some preceding Epoch, for instance from the most famous rest of the land, which (after the Kings of Canaan were defeated, who with joined forces and all their troops rose up against the Israelites) was established by Joshua, and is mentioned as preceding the partition of the land, Jos. 11, verse 23, ch. 14, 15, or, which comes to the same thing, that the rest under Othniel began in the fortieth year from that Josuan rest, so that the cardinal number, according to the custom of the Hebrews, is said to be used for an ordinal. Therefore, after the Mesopotamians were overcome (who, after those Kings of Canaan were defeated, were the first of the foreigners to wage war against the WHOLE Israëlitic LAND), rest (40 years after the beginning of that former one) began to be restored, with Othniel thereafter as victor, administering the Republic and striving to keep the people in the true worship of God, which was the chief work of these Judges, ch. 2, 17, 18, 19. And Ussher judges that this enumeration by intervals of the rest of the land is handed down in the former part of the History of the Judges, after the series of oppressions and liberations has been summarized, Jud. 2, v. 14 to 19, with special notes of times added, in the six following chapters, but that in the latter part the calculation is instituted by the spaces of the prefecture of the Judges. According to this method of computing, it will be permissible to exhibit a sufficiently neat Chronotaxis of the book of Judges of this kind:

I. From the Josuan rest (Jos. 11, 23) to the oppression of Chushan, years - - - 32.

And from there to the liberation and the rest beginning to be restored under Othniel, years - - 8.

(These are the 40 years of Jud. 3, 11 up to the rest which began to be restored under the judgeship of Othniel: which was preceded by the eight-year Mesopotamian oppression, v. 33. To those 40 years, therefore, are to be referred the 10 years of the rule of Joshua, from that rest of the land under Joshua up to his death: 8 years (so that we may place them thus probably) of the rule of the elders who survived after Joshua (so that the most famous opinion concerning the 17 years of the Principate of Joshua may be reconciled with the tradition of Josephus, l. 5, Antiqu. c. 1, concerning the 25 years of the dominion of Joshua, with the eight-year period of the government of the Elders added, namely) and 18 years of anarchy (how many years the Israelites were without a Magistrate, Josephus, l. 6, Antiqu. c. 6, has handed down), as well as 8 years of Mesopotamian servitude (according to Josephus, l. 5, c. 3), the sum comes to 44 years. Perhaps it will be permissible to say that the 4 prior years of servitude are included in the 18 years of anarchy, because for about four years they had no Prince of their own kind, and because only in the fourth year was some Magistrate given to them from among themselves, or even Othniel was appointed Judge while the servitude still remained for four years, whom the Lord thereafter, because of the groans of Israel, raised up and clothed with His spirit to liberate Israel, and through whom rest was restored to the land, in the fortieth year from the Josuan rest, after Chushan, King of Mesopotamia, was defeated.)

II. From that time up to the Moabite servitude and oppression, years - 62. Of that oppression, years - - - 18. (Which added make 80 years, Jud. 3, 30, from the rest of the land restored under Othniel up to the rest through Ehud, when Eglon, King of the Moabites, was killed and the land was restored.)

III. From there to the oppression of Jabin (Jud. 4, 3), 20 years, which lasted up to the liberation of Deborah for years - - - - 20. (These 40 years are counted from the rest of the land restored through Ehud to the rest through Deborah and Barak, when Jabin was killed and the land was restored, Jud. 5, 3.)

IV. Thence to the Midianite oppression (concerning which Jud. 6, 1.) years - - - 33. From which that oppression lasted for 7 years. (And these 40 years are designated c. 8, 28. namely from the rest restored by Deborah until the rest restored by Gideon after the Midianites were defeated)

V. Thence to the beginning of the reign of Abimelech the son of Gideon - - - - - - 10. These ten years the Holy Scripture did not express, but they can be gathered by subtraction from the entire sum of 479 years until the construction of Solomon's temple: just as they gather by subtraction the 16 or 17 years of the prefecture of Joshua, who count the first years of rest from the death of Joshua, and terminate them at the departure of the following Judge.)

VI. Abimelech's years were (Jud. 9, 22.) - 3.

VII. Thola presided over the judgeship (Jud. 10, 2.) for years. - - - - - - 23.

IIX. Jair presided (c. 10, 3.) for years. - 22. (In which are included 18 years of the oppression of the Philistines, and of the Ammonites c. 10, 8.)

IX. Jephthah presided (c. 12, 7.) for years - 6.

X. Ibzan presided over the judgeship (c. 12, 9.) for years 7.

XI. Elon presided (c. 12, 11.) for years - 10.

XII. Abdon presided (c. 12, 14.) for years 8.

XIII. Samson presided (c. 15, 20. c. 16, 21.) for years - - - - - - 20. (Who judged Israel in the days of the Philistines or of their oppression, which lasted for 40 years chap. 13, 1.)

The sum of which years, 309 years, will be the entire interval from the Joshua-rest (which we consider to have been established a decade before the death of Joshua) until the death of Samson: and thus from the death of Joshua up to this point the years will have to be counted as 299, and perhaps some months: to which, as we have warned before, by adding the 57 years from the exodus to the death of Joshua and the 123 from the passing of Samson to the beginning of the construction of the temple, there emerges a sum of 479 years and some months. Ussher attributes to the interval from the rest restored to the land by Gideon until the beginning of the reign of Abimelech only 9 years and 2 months, and he establishes 6 years and 4 months from the crossing of the Jordan to the finished wars and the rest given by Joshua. But he makes the years of Samson, Eli, Samuel, and Saul 101, which, since we find only one hundred assigned, we preferred to count ten years from the Gideonic rest to the tyrannical occupation of the government by Abimelech. Ussher also distributes those years of the later judges and of Saul (the reasons for which, because he was prevented by death, he did not provide, having only produced the work up to the death of Abdon) differently than they are commonly distributed, with Scripture as a guide: for he assigns to the combined government of Eli and Samson 40 years: to Samuel 12, to Saul 40. But Scripture attributes to Samson 20 years (ch. 15, 20; 16, 21), to Eli 40 (1 Sam. 4, 18), and to the government of Samuel and Saul likewise 40 (Acts 13, 21). Ussher perhaps followed Dr. Behm regarding the years of Eli and Samson: who, including the 20 years of Samson as well as the 40 of Eli within the 40 years of Philistine servitude (Chronolog. Manuduct. Book 1, Tit. 3, c. 6, p. 50), concludes that both Samson and Eli judged the people jointly under Philistine servitude, from the fact that Samson is also said to have judged the people of the Lord in the days of the Philistines (Judg. 15, 20). and Eli still in those times, and even after his death, up to the times of Samuel, the Philistines were superior to the Jews (1 Sam. 5, 6, 7). Thinking it nothing absurd if it is said that the people of the Lord, in their liberation, chose one and another judge for themselves jointly, whose years are counted separately in the book of Judges; but with this hypothesis admitted, there will be no certainty about the years of the judges, whether those who ruled jointly are counted separately or not. And although we may easily admit that the 40 years of Philistine servitude are included under the judgeship of Samson, as well as under the earlier years of Eli, those 40 years do not, however, exhaust all the years of the government of both Samson and Eli, as they make up 60 years combined. Nor is it permissible to conclude from that, that the servitude and oppression of the Philistines lasted through the entire government of Eli, because they prevailed after the death of Eli, since the Philistines could have again become superior to the Israelites in the later 20 years of the government of Eli, whom they then also defeated after the capture of the Ark of the Lord, which news was the cause of the fall and death of Eli.

Clear evidence seems to favor this Chronotaxis of the book of Judges: inasmuch as the Holy Scripture uses a clearly distinct phrase in the first part of the history of the Judges up to the reign of Abimelech: For concerning Abimelech, 'And so Abimelech reigned,' it says, 'over Israel three years' (Judg. 9, 22). Concerning Tola (ch. 10, 2), 'And he judged Israel 23 years, and he died and was buried in Shamir.' Concerning Jair (v. 3), 'He judged Israel for twenty and two years' (v. 5), 'And Jair died, etc.' Concerning Jephthah (ch. 12, 7), 'And so Jephthah the Gileadite judged Israel 6 years, and he died and was buried in his city Gilead,' and v. 9 concerning Ibzan: 'Who judged Israel seven years, and he died and was buried in Bethlehem.' Similarly concerning Elon (ch. 12, 11), whom Abdon the Zebulonite succeeded, 'and he judged Israel ten years, and he died and was buried in Zebulon': and concerning Abdon (v. 13), 'After him Abdon judged Israel,' v. 14. He judged Israel eight years, and he died and was buried in Pirathon. Finally, concerning Samson (ch. 15, 20), 'He judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.' Which, just as they define most clearly the years of each of these Leaders and Judges, so they leave no doubt about them. But it does not speak in this way about the earlier judges; it makes no mention of the years of their judgeship, no mention of the immediate succession of others; it reduces everything to the rest of the land, when that began to be restored, and it adds not the succession of another judge, but a new prevarication and servitude, and the years of this, and finally defines the time of the rest restored again. Thus ch. 3, 11, 'And the land rested forty years (or in the fortieth year), and Othniel died,' and after the victory of Ehud (v. 30), 'and the land rested eighty years.' Concerning the death of this Judge, nothing is added. Similarly, after the described victory and the Eucharistic ode of Deborah, nothing else is held except that the land rested for 40 years (ch. 5, 32). After the humiliation of Midian, it is added (ch. 8, 28), 'the land rested for 40 years': where, however, it is added at the same time in the Vulgate, 'in which Gideon presided.' But the Hebrew text can be rendered, 'the land began to rest in the fortieth year (namely, from the previous restoration of rest made by Deborah) in the days of Gideon.' Since, therefore, the phrase varies everywhere, and nothing is handed down here about the time of the government begun or ended, but only about the rest of the land restored, it seems to be in the open that the intervals of the rest restored from time to time are presented, and not indeed the government of the Judges; (2) if the Holy Scripture wished to designate the time of the government of the Judges, how does it happen that there is no mention by a single word of Shamgar, or the course of his government, or his death? At least after Ehud, Shamgar is said to have been (namely, a judge) and also to have saved Israel (ch. 3, 31), but it is not defined how long he judged the people, or when he died. (3) Concerning Ehud, it might seem doubtful whether he began to judge the people in the very next year after the death of Othniel; for the text has nothing about it; indeed, it rather adds the prevarication of Israel, which followed the death of Othniel, and the excitation of Eglon, King of Moab, against the people, and the years of the Moabite servitude (ch. 3, 12 seqq.). Nor after the mentioned Shamgar is it added that Deborah succeeded him immediately after his death (about which nothing is held, as we have said), but rather that the children of Israel added to do evil in the sight of the Lord, and that the Lord delivered them into the hands of Jabin (v. 2), and that they cried out to the Lord (v. 3), and at that time (when the people cried out) Deborah judged the people. It does not therefore seem certain that he began to be judged immediately after Shamgar, or even after Ehud. (4.) Nor is it clearly expressed that the government of Gideon began immediately after the passing of Deborah. The contrary might rather seem to be the case from chapter 6, 1 et seqq., because it is added after the designation of 40 years (which they think should be attributed to the judgeship of Deborah) that the Israelites did evil further, that they were delivered into the hands of the Midianites for seven years, and being greatly humbled they finally cried out to the Lord, and from then on the raising up of Gideon is reported: so that it appears that it happened only after the years of Midianite servitude and the conversion and prayers of the Israelite people to the Lord. (5) Although in the latter part of the history of the Judges the servitudes and oppressions of the Israelites are likewise mentioned, yet they are subjected to the government of the Judges and are reduced to the years of the same: the matter stands otherwise in the former part: inasmuch as in it the time of the raising up of the saviors is recalled to the years of oppression, without the years of their judgeship being established, and account is taken not of the duration of the rule, but of the beginning of the restoration of peace. (6.) The number of 300 years designated by Samson from the death of Moses, or the defeat of the Amorites up to his own times, will thus easily agree, because to the rule of Samson thus 289 years will be counted from the rest of the land under Joshua: to which, if the seven years of Joshua's warfare from the death of Moses are added, 296 years will result.

However, no light doubt is raised against that double method of calculation—either the earlier Eusebian one according to the intervals of the judges' rule alone, or this later one already explained, by which the intervals of restored rest and the intervals of the time of rule are considered—from Acts 13, verse 20, because the Apostle seems to count 450 years from the distribution of the land made by Joshua and Eleazar to the Prophet Samuel. For if the 40 years of Eli are added to these 309 years from the rest under Joshua to the death of Samson, 349 years will result. How, therefore, are 450 years counted? Hence, those who wish the times of the servitudes and judgeships to be counted separately for all the Judges in this book, such as Codomannus and others, establish their opinion from this passage. And indeed, from that collection of the years of the servitudes and judgeships, 410 years result, to which, if the 40 years of the Judge Eli are added, the 450 years from the death of Joshua arise. 460 from the distribution of the land under Joshua. Since they did not know how to solve this knot, some have considered it a second one, asserting that in Paul's words the word 'tetrakosiois' is now read by mistake instead of the word 'triakosiois,' to which Dr. Behmius also gave his assent: But because it is a matter of conscience for us, as is right, to call into doubt the purity of the sources, or with Beroaldus (Chron. lib. 3, c. 4) to attribute to Paul that he followed the received opinion of the Jews, however erroneous, in a matter which is not of faith but of enumeration, the explanation of those who wish the beginning or the term from which of the 450 years to be fixed here not in the distribution of the land, but in the time of the birth of Isaac, is entirely to be preferred; and the term to which not the rule of Samuel, but the distribution of the land, because from the birth of Isaac to the Exodus there are 405 years (Gen. 15:13; Exod. 12:40), and from there to the distribution of the land 47 years intervened, so that the entire interval is 452. Hence Sanctius. Paul used the word 'hos' or 'as': The Greek text will therefore be thus: 'kai meta tauta hos etesi tetrakosiois kai pentekonta (genomenai) edoke kritas,' and after those things for 450 years (having passed) he gave judges: an ellipsis of such a participle is established in the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1, verse 11. Although there is no need for that ellipsis, according to the ancient Alexandrian codex, which is held in England written in large letters, as testified by Armachanus (l.c. p. 195), who reads thus: 'Kateklerodotesen autois ten gen auton hos etesi tetrakosiois kai pentekonta, kai meta tauta edoke kritas': which reading is also found among those various readings which Robertus Stephanus took care to have appended to the New Testament printed by himself in Greek at Paris in the year 1568; with the agreement also of a certain other Greek codex likewise published at Paris, produced by Beza in his annotations on this passage, and a manuscript copy of New College at Oxford. the other, as also in the Vulgate version: 'He distributed their land to them by lot, as it were after four hundred and fifty years: and after these things he gave judges.' And therefore those 450 years are to be referred not to the duration of the judges, but to the time of the partition of the land, so that the beginning of the calculation depends on the first words of the Apostle's speech in verse 17, 'The God of this people Israel chose our Fathers,' namely in Isaac, or from the time Isaac was born. Let those things which are at 1 Kings 6, verse 1 be compared. Grotius's calculation is foreign, as if the 450 years were counted from the exodus from Egypt up to that time when David cast out the Jebusites. Beda, Glossa, Hugo, Lyranus, Dionysius, Walterus, Junius, Usserius, Ludovicus de Dieu, Salianus, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, etc., agree with our explanation.

The sum of the years of the book of Judges according to the common computation is 299, i.e., 250.

Years of Othniel - - - 40.

Ehud - - - 80.

Barak - - - 40.

Gideon's - - - 40.

Abimelech's - - - 3.

Tola - - - 23.

Jair - - - 22.

Jephthah - - - 6.

Ibzan - - - 7.

Elon - - - 10.

Abdon - - - 8.

Samson - - - 20.

Years collected 299. from the death of Joshua to the death of Samson.

Thus, therefore, from the rest restored by Joshua, ten years before his death, as according to our calculation above, 309 years have passed; from the entry into the promised land 315 years and some months; from the departure out of Egypt 356 years are counted up to the death of Samson.

Interpreters of the Book of Judges, besides the Hebrews, Kimchi, R. Solomon, etc., and the ancient Christians Origen, Augustine, Theodoret, Procopius, Bede, Isidore; among the Papists the more important are Hugo the Cardinal, Dionysius the Carthusian, Tostatus, Cajetan, Joh. Ferus, Montanus, Cosmas, Magalianes, Nic. Serarius, Jac. Bonfrer, Cornelius à Lapide, Jac. Tirinus, Stephan Menochius, Eman. Saa, Estius; among our own after B. Luther, Brentius, Chytræus, D. Balduinus, D. Fabricius in his sermons, Osiander in his Paraphrase, as also the Weimar theologians, Walther in his Harmony; among the Reformed, Calvin, Bucer, Martyr, Lavater, Wolfius, Piscator, Junius, Drusius, Lud. de Dieu, etc.

FOLLOWS THE GROTIAN PREFACE.

Among the Hebrews, Tyrians, and Carthaginians, the שׁוֹפְטִים (Shophetim) were called κατ' ἐξοχὴν (for otherwise the word has a wider scope, as we have already often observed) the supreme Magistrates, whom the Greeks here call κριτὰς (judges), and Josephus in the affairs of the Tyrians calls δικαςὰς (judges). The Latins in Punic history, having preserved the Punic word, call them Suffetes. Josephus calls them αὐτοκράτορες (autocrats), ἡγεμόνες (leaders). See regarding these things what is at Deut. 17, 9. Add the passage below 5, 13. It seems, however, that in these times the creation of the Synedrion of LXXII was omitted through negligence. Just as also before the times of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 19, 5. And so, where God did not raise up such men outside the ordinary course, the body of the Republic was dissolved, and nothing was done for the common good. Individual tribes managed their own affairs at their own risk and advantage, unless some had made a treaty among themselves according to the needs of the times, below 3. Josephus: 'it happened that the aristocracy had already been corrupted.' and they did not appoint the councils of elders, nor any other magistracy of those previously established: likewise: 'the order of the state having been moved by anarchy, affairs were in a state of disease.' Such was the state of Greece when the Achaean League was dissolved by the arts of the Romans, and of Gaul before the times of Caesar: but of Germany and Britain, even much later.

Grotius had handed down thus concerning the judges at Deut. 17, verse 9. Such interreges also existed among the Tyrians by the same name שׁפטים, which name Josephus, translating the acts of the Tyrians into Greek in the first book against Apion, translates as δικαςάς (judges). For after the kings Ithobalus and Baalem, he says thus: 'After him, judges were appointed and they judged, Ecnibalus son of Baslach for two months, Chelbes son of Abdaeus for ten months, Abbarus the high priest for three months, Mungon and Gerastratus son of Abdelim for six years as judges.' The same name may come from the Tyrians to the Carthaginians, the descendants of the Tyrians, among whom the supreme magistrates were called suffetes, as Festus teaches us from Calidius. I have called it the supreme magistracy with Livy, who also elsewhere says their power was as it were consular. Suffetes for שׁופטים is either from a softer pronunciation, such as that of the Ephraimites, Judges 12, 6, or corrupted by Latin writers.

These, moreover, among the Hebrews שפטים were clearly similar to the Roman interreges, and later to the dictators, and they differed from the Hebrew kings in no respect, except that they did not have a bodyguard and royal pomp: and for that reason they demanded neither tributes nor taxes. Furthermore, they were, as Josephus speaks, ἡγεμόνες ἀυτοκράτορες (sovereign leaders). And so they are also called kings Jud. 9, 6. They made Abimelech king, that is, δικαστὴν (a judge) Jud. 18, 1. when Samson was dead: In those days there was no King in Israel: that is, a Judge. And just as kings without a Sanhedrin had the right of putting to death, as the Talmudic title concerning the king teaches, and 2 Sam. 1, 15, and other places, so also these judges, or interreges, as appears from the example of Gideon Jud. 8, 16, 17, and Jephthah Jud. 12, 6, which things are rightly noted by Abarbanel at the beginning of the book of Judges. These things there Grotius. With which may be compared those things which we have said about the judges in the preface. Nor is there any doubt that Abimelech assumed a greater dignity for himself than the other judges had, and so, just as he was called King, he usurped royal axioms, or at least affected them.

But what Grotius conjectures concerning the interrupted creation of the LXXII men of the Sanhedrin, and the dissolved body of the Republic, rests on no firm reason. For the fact that they consulted God as to who ought to lead the army against the Canaanites, came about because they were always bound, even with the Sanhedrin established, to undertake such things at the mouth of the Lord. The state of the Republic is certainly commended after the death of Joshua, as long as the elders who were contemporaries survived, Jos. 24, 31, and it is akin to the truth that the Sanhedrin did not fail within that short time. And what is to be held concerning the government and state among the Israelites during the time of the judges, we have warned before. That the body of the Republic was dissolved during those entire three centuries, unless by judges raised up out of the ordinary, is neither credible, nor will it be solidly taught by any evidence. And it is clear from history that judges succeeded one another in order after Abimelech, up to Samson. Finally, since the rest of the land is understood of the whole Israelite land, how can so dissolved a body of the Israelite Republic be posited? For peace or rest of the Republic is feigned in vain when the body of the Republic is dissolved.

Latin:

I. N AD LIBRUM PRÆLO

Dictus est liber שׁוֹפְטִים Ebræis, κρι- τῶν Græcis, JUDICUM Latinis, quia historiam plerorumque Judicum descri- bit, seu res gestas eorundem, aut quæ sub regimine ipsorum contigere. Plerorumque dico: nam postremorum duorum, Heli nempe, ac Samue- lis, res gestæ cum historia Regum cohærent: siqui- dem Rex primus à Samuele constitutus, & inaugu- ratus sit, à cujus gestis historia Heli Sacerdotis, ac Judicis, quantum ad casus senectutis, qui potissi- mum commemorantur, divelli non potuit. His ergo ad librum primum Regum, vel Samuelis refer- vatis, præcedentium JUDICUM historiæ hoc li- bro commemorantur, sed imprimis quantum ad vicissitudines rerum prosperarum & adversarum Populi Dei: quia Augustino lib. 16. de C. D. cap. 43. teste, temporibus Judicum sicut se habebant & peccata populi, & misericordia Dei, alternabant prospera, & adversa bellorum.

Unde autem illi, qui post Josuam imperarunt, peculiariter JUDICES dicti sint, si quæratur, re- spondent quidem Bonfrerius, à Lapide, alii, di- ctos ita esse, quod populum ab hostium manu vin- dicarint, quod primarium eorum officium faciunt: sed ea denominationis ratio non est adæquata. Nam etsi hoc à plerisque factum sit, nonnulli ta- men Judices bella cum hostibus gessisse haud le- guntur, utpote Thola, ac Jair cap. 10. Abesan, Ah- jalon, & Abdon cap. 12. neque Heli, aut Samuel Israe- litarum exercitum duxisse perhibentur. Et quum judices illi, qui belli fuere duces (Josephus vo- cat ἡγεμόνας & στρατηγὲς Imperatores, ut & ὑπο- στρατήγες, sub DEO scil. στρατηγῷ) Israelem ju- dicasse dicuntur tot vel tot annis, non belli tan- tum expeditiones, vel tempora, sed etiam pacis designantur: Vocati ergo Judices, quod nomen ipsum indicat, à JUDICANDO, vel etiam à GU- BERNANDO, quia judicare Ebræis quandoque est gubernare, quod judicium pars aliqua sit re- giminis, quemadmodum & vindicare subditos à vi,

Falso ergo in tribu Benjamin locatur in lib. de locis Hebraicis. In editione LXX. Romana, ut & Syriaco textu, & apud Theodoretum clausula habe- tur hujus libri, quam nec textus Ebræus authen- ticus agnoscit, neque versiones, Chaldæa, LXX. Complut. aut Regia, Latina, ideo merito tan- quam notha rejicitur. Ea ita habet: In illa die su- mentes filii Israel arcam Dei, circumdederunt in sei- pfis: & Phinees functus est Sacerdotio pro Eleazaro Patre suo, quoad usque mortuus est, & defossus in Gabaa, quæ ipsius: Filii autem Israel abierunt unus- quisque ad locum suum ad suam civitatem. Et colue- rant filii Israel Astharten & Astharoth & Deos genti- um, quæ in circuitu ipsorum. Et tradidit eos Domi- nus in manus Eglon regis Moab, & dominatus est eo- rum annos decem & octo. Non opus est prolixa ejus reprobatione. Sua futilitate se prodit. Nos hic finimus, Deoque gloriam tribuimus per verum, & cœlestem nostrum Josuam CHRISTUM Salva- torem, in Spir. S. Sit nomen ejus benedictum in se- cula. Amen.

N. 7. M JUDICUM. OQUIUM.

& periculis hostium ad partes regiminis pertinet. Videatur hic imprimis cap. 4, 4. 5. Etsi autem Moses, & Josua populum quoque gubernarint, antequam Reges ipsi dati, non tamen cum quibusdam JUDICUM numero accensendi sunt, nisi generalius vox ista capiatur, quo pacto Hieronymus sub Judicum nomine Esa. 1, 26. eosdem comprehendit: sed vi hujus ἐπιγραφῆς, & usus no- minis specialis in hoc libro, primus Judicum Oth- niel constituendus est. Siquidem Moses & Josua di- gnitatem ampliorem habuerint; Ille quidem Re- demptoris, qui ex Ægypto populum liberavit, uti à Stephano vocatur Act. 7, 35. & Legislatoris; hic vero Imperatoris exercitus, qui populum in terram pro- missam deduxit, eam armata manu occupavit, & in- ter Israeliticas tribus divisit. Adde, quod duo illi populo præfecti nondum certam sedem habue- rint, cæteri vero Judices eidem in terra promissa dati sint, quum jam tribus Israelis suis possessioni- bus gauderent.

Porro etsi insignis fuerit Judicum ἐξοχὴ, & emi- nentia, discriminatur tamen hoc Judicum ἀξίωμα ab augusta Regum dignitate non parum: quia isti se- cundum leges à Deo præscriptas ita Rempubl. ad- ministrabant, ut potestatem non haberent leges no- vas condendi, neque Domini ipsi fuerint populi, uti Reges; erat enim tum lex Domina, & DEUS legis autor Rex ipsorum, unde quum Regem poscerent, Deum rejecisse censentur, ne regnet (amplius, eo scil. modo, quo regnabat antea) super eos 1. Sam. 8, 7. Neque etiam ἀνυπεύθυνοι erant, sed in gravibus causis ad decreta Synedrii alligati: hinc etiam non habebant potestatem tributa imponendi populo instar Regum. Ideo nec ungebantur regum more, nec dia- demate, quod absoluti Domini signum, Regiisve in- signibus, ut aliarum gentium Reges 2. Sam. 12. ute- bantur, nec Satellitio, aut stipatorum turba instar Re- gum cingebantur, de quibus in jure Regio 1. Sam. 8.

Formam tamen regiminis quod attinet, non ma- le Serarius in Judic. 3. Salianus in Annalib. Bonfre- rius, à Lapide, hîc assignant gubernationi Judi- cum Monarchicam, etsi Fevardentius in Ruth. 1. cum Genebrardo in Chronol. Tostato in Comment. Sigonio l. 1. de Republ. Ebræor. Aristocraticam formam præferant. Neque enim plures erant judices, aut regimini præerant, sed unus, neque ad breve tempus Remp. administrabant, sed usque ad finem vitæ. Fatemur interim vocem Monarchias laxius hic accipiendam esse (quum non ignotum sit Aristotelem alias omne regimen Monarchicum facere Regium) aut κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν intelligendam hoc loco formam monarchicam, hoc saltim sensu, quod judicum regimen ad eam propius accesserit, quam ad Aristocratiam. Cum vero Josephus l. 4. c. ult. l. 5. c. 4. ἀριστοκρατείαν facit Reipubl. Judaicæ formam, nomine illo abusus, & aristocratiam pro specie Monarchiæ accepisse videtur, ut observat Bonfrerius: siquidem hanc dispescat in βασιλείαν & Ἀριστοκρατείαν. Neque dubium est, eo etiam respicere Josephum, quod judices in rebus difficilioribus supremi Synedrii sententiam audire debuerint. Quo nomine forte non incommode dixeris Monarchiam aristocratiæ mixtam fuisse. Verissime autem θεοκρατείαν extitisse e Jud. 8, 22. 1. Sam. 8, 7. 12. liquet.

Ideo autem judices, si unum excipias Abimelechum, qui non Judex, sed tyrannus fuit, & vi principatum, occisis fratribus omnibus, invasit, non à Deo, uti extra ordinem cæteri è quacunque tribu constituti sunt, præfectus, sancti fuerunt, Spiritu Dei induti, atque eo nomine peculiariter in Catalogo veterum sanctorum Syr. 44, 14. & Ebr. 11, 32. seqq. celebrantur. Qui etiam ceu Salvatores Israelis typi extiterunt Christi veri Salvatoris, uti Hieron. Epist. 103. ad Paul. in Judicum libro quot principes populi, tot figuræ sunt.

Quod ad autorem libri ministerialem, variant Doctorum sententiæ. Nonnulli Esdram, vel Prophetam aliquem posteriorem autorem faciunt. Plerique Samueli Prophetæ eum tribuunt. Hugo Cardinal. in Prolog. scribit, quemvis Judicum suorum temporum res gestas in acta retulisse, tandem autem vel Esdram, vel Jeremiam, vel Ezechiam potius in unum volumen isthæc collegisse. Quam conjecturam de Ezechia confirmari inde putat B. Gerhard. in Exeget. de Script. S. §. 126. quod amanuenses ejus quædam Salomonis proverbia in unum contulisse dicantur Prov. 25, 1. Verum enim vero uti verisimile haud est, historiam illam ἄγραφον mansisse, vel in diariis, & annalibus relictam à DEO, sacri canonis autore summo, & principali, per tot secula usque ad Ezechiam, vel etiam prophetas posteriorum temporum: ita longe rectius statuitur, quum cæteri libri θεόπνευστοι succesfive ad Canonem relati sint, hunc etiam divino afflatu conscriptum Mosaicis libris, & historiæ Josuæ adjectum fuisse, antequam Historiæ Regum & Chronicorum confignarentur.

Argumentum libri est descriptio status Politiæ & memorabilium quorundam in eadem ab excessu Josuæ usque ad tempora Heli, & imprimis quantum ad vicissitudines Israelitarum, quomodo sæpe à Deo defecerint, justisque suppliciis affecti fuerint, & quomodo vicissim ab hostibus pressi ad Deum conversi per manus Judicum divina ope liberati sint: de quo S. Augustin. lib. 18. de Civ. Dei c. 13. Temporibus Judicum alternaverunt apud populum Dei & humilitates laborum pro eorum peccatis, & prosperitates consolationum per miserationem Domini. Distribuitur liber commode in duas partes: In prima ea potissimum, quæ statum terræ promissæ, & res gestas sub judicibus attinent, commemorantur à cap. 1. ad 16. In altera quinque posterioribus capitibus ea, quæ post excessum Josuæ & Seniorum, qui Josuæ superstites manserunt, sub ἀναρχίᾳ acciderunt ad statum

Reip. & Ecclesiæ pertinentia describuntur.
