Quæ iterum non sunt angeli creati: Filio autem Dei apprime conveniunt; hujus enim vocem audire debebant. Ex. 23, 21. Quamobrem, pergit Angelus ille, nolui eos delere à facie vestra, ut habeatis, hostes, & Dii eo- rum sint vobis in ruinam. Quæ non esse ministri, sed Dei verba, quivis videt, & vers. 20. 21. manifestis- simum est. Angelus ergo Dominus intelligendus est, Filius nempe Dei, qui potestatem habet delendi hostes, imo unum est cum Deo Patre Joh. 10, 30. Huic etiam Domino ibi in Bochim sacrificia obtulit popu- lus vers. 5. Hujus denique proprium est, oves per- ditas quærere, & peccatores vocare ad pœniten- tiam, Matth. 9, 13. Luc. 15, 2. feqq. Quod hic fa- ctum est. Bonfrerius Jesuita cum pleraque ista ex- penderet, ridendos censebat Rabbinos, quod Phine- am Angelum hunc esse velint, quia non conveniat

Prophetæ talis Oratio. Sed non minus sefe riden- dum propinat Michaelem Angelum creatum intel- ligens. Num enim in Michaelem cadunt ista, Eduxi vos de Ægypto, & introduxi in Terram, pro qua juravi Patribus, & quæ porro sequuntur? Pas- sim enim hoc sibi Deus uni, verba sunt Bonfrerii ad hunc locum, in Scriptura tribuit, quod de Ægypto eos eduxerit, in Terramque promissam introduxerit, multo vero magis illud juramentum factum Patri- archis, uni Deo, non Angelis adscribendum. An- gelum autem creatum ex persona Dei ita loqui, è Scri- pturis hactenus doceri nullo exemplo potuit. Su- pereft ergo, ut Angelum increatum hic loqui ad- mittatur. Neque obstat illa de Galgalis profectio huic explicationi de Filio Dei: Imo firmat potius eandem: Revocatur enim ita Israelitis in memori- am apparitio, & promissio illic facta, paulo post Jordanis transitum Jos. 5. cum renovatione fœde- ris per circumcisionem ibidem institutam, & haud obscure docetur, eundem hic Angelum fuisse, qui Josuæ apparens, dixit, se esse Principem Exercitus Domini, quod etiam Bonfrerius post Theodoretum, & Serarium hic agnovit. Quem vero Filium Dei fuisse, illic ostendimus. Subscribunt huic senten- tiæ cum Vinarienses Paraphrastæ Bibliorum Ger- manicorum, tum auctores Notarum ad translatio- nem Belgicam, qui agnoscunt clare patere, Filium Dei, non Angelum creatum hic designari. Quod ob Calvinum, & plerosque alios in Schola ejus no- tandum. Illi enim solent tales apparitiones de alio potius, quam de Filio Dei accipere, & interpretari.

vers. eod. AD LOCUM FLENTIUM.

In Bochim. Est enim nomen proprium, etsi à fletu ibi instituto impositum vers. 5. Locum fuisse juxta Hierosolymam, sylvam, in qua David delituit 2. Sam. 5, 22. Josephus vult. l. 7. c. 4. ubi apparitio fa- cta, quod locus is in vicinia & prospectu Hieroso- lymæ esset, ubi aliquando templum extruendum erat. Non autem hæc gesta sunt, vivente adhuc Jo- sua, quemadmodum Abulensis, Torniellus, & Salia- nus putarunt: quia ejus tempore publice Ebræi non coluere idola, sed Deo vero fervierunt: post mortem autem ipsius, & seniorum συγχρόνων nova progenies è commerciis & conversatione cum vici- nis gentibus, Tyriis & Sidoniis idola Baalim, & Asta- roth colere ceperunt, v. 9. 10. Ideo post Josuæ mor- tem hæc accidisse Procopius, Cajetanus, Serarius, alii docent.

## 2:2
verse 2. THAT YOU SHOULD NOT STRIKE A COVENANT WITH THE INHABITANTS OF THIS LAND.

The same God had forbidden it, Exod. 29, 32. c. 34, 12. And therefore these covenants were entirely illicit: which nevertheless, if they had been entered into, were by no means void, but remained firm, especially those sanctioned by an oath. Indeed, from the covenants themselves arose the obligation to keep them. In which manner also matrimonial covenants entered into with Gentiles, although illicit, were to be kept, nor was the marriage of Samson, or of Solomon with foreign women considered as concubinage, but as those women are called their wives, so the marriage was firm, nor were such marriages dissolved Esdr. 9, 10. because they were null, but because for a just cause divorce was permitted, such as it was, if the foreign wife was unwilling to convert to the true worship of God, and there existed a fear of scandal, danger, or even seduction.

Latin:

vers. 2. UT NON FERIRETIS FOEDUS CUM HABITATORIBUS TERRÆ HUJUS.

Prohibuerat idem Exod. 29, 32. c. 34, 12. Deus: Ideoque illicita erant omnino hæc fœdera: quæ ta- men, si inita erant, minime fuere irrita, sed firma manebant imprimis juramento sancita. Quin ex fœderibus nata fuit obligatio eadem servandi. Quo pacto etiam fœdera matrimonialia cum gentilibus inita, etsi illicita, servanda erant, nec habebatur Samsonis conjugium, aut Salomonis cum fœminis alienigenis pro concubinatu, sed ut illæ uxores eo- rum vocantur, ita firmum erat matrimonium, neq; dirempta sunt talia matrimonia Esdr. 9, 10. ideo quod nulla essent, sed quod ex justa causa permis- sum esset repudium, qualis erat, si uxor alienigena ad verum Dei cultum converti nollet, ac scandali, pe- riculi, imo seductionis metus subesset.

## 2:3
Vers. 3. THAT THEIR GODS MAY BE A RUIN TO YOU.

The particle UT is to be taken not αἰτιολογικῶς (causally), but ἐκβατικῶς (consecutively). For God could not intend the idolatry or apostasy of the people, however much He may have permitted it to them as a punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 3. UT DII EORUM SINT VOBIS IN RUINAM.

Particula UT accipienda est non αἰτιολογικῶς, sed ἐκβατικῶς. Deus enim intendere non potuit idololatriam vel apostasiam populi, utut eam per- miserit iisdem in pœnam.

## 2:5
vers. 5. AND THEY SACRIFICED THERE.

Whence some think Bochim was Shiloh: Namely, it was not permitted to sacrifice except in the tabernacle: but although this ought ordinarily to have been done there, yet for grave causes, especially in divine apparitions, sacrifices are read to have been performed elsewhere also, because that was a holy place, and the temple of the special divine presence, where the Lord appeared; indeed, since the Son of God is the true altar, sacrifices were deservedly performed in the place of his very apparition. Conf. Jud. 6, 20. c. 13, 19. 1. Sam. 16, 4.

Latin:

vers. 5. IMMOLAVERUNTQUE IBI.

Unde existimant nonnulli Bochim fuisse Silo: Scilicet non licitum erat nisi in tabernaculo sacrifi- care: sed quamvis hoc ordinarie ibi fieri debuerit, ob graves tamen causas, maxime in apparitionibus divinis, sacrificia etiam alibi peracta leguntur, quia ibi sacer locus fuit, & templum specialis præsentiæ divinæ, ubi apparuit Dominus; imo quum Filius Dei verum altare sit, merito in loco apparitionis ipsius peragebantur Sacrificia. Conf. Jud. 6, 20. c. 13, 19. 1. Sam. 16, 4.

## 2:6
ver. 6. JOSHUA THEREFORE DISMISSED THE PEOPLE.

It is more correctly rendered 'for he had dismissed': so that there may be no hysterology, which the Pontifical interpreters posit here.

Latin:

vers. 6. DIMISIT ERGO JOSUA POPU- LUM.

Rectius redditur dimiserat enim: ut opus non sit hysterologia, quam hic ponunt Interpp. Pontificii.

## 2:9
ver. 9. IN THAMNATH-SERAH.

In Hebrew it is תמנת סרח: concerning which diversity of the word it has already been spoken in the notes to Joshua.

Latin:

vers. 9. IN THAMNATHSARE.

In Ebræo est תמנת סרח : de qua vocis diver- sitate jam dictum fuit in notis ad Josuam.

## 2:13
Ver. 13. AND THEY SERVED BAAL] Who is fully בעל שמין Beelsamēn, Lord of Heaven, the Sun, the highest of the gods to those nations, whence he is called the Assyrian Jupiter. See Macrobius c. 23. lib. 1. Saturnal.

The name בעל is common, nor is it said only of the Sun worshipped as God. Selden observes in 'De Diis Syris' Syntagm. 2. c. 1, that it first designated the supreme and ineffable creator of all things, because בעל is Lord, just as he is called אדן by the Hebrews, κύριος by the Greeks, and Abras by the Arabs, which sounds the same. Thence, therefore, the Sun, whom the Phoenicians thought to be μόνον ὐρανῶ Θεὸν, the only God in the heavens, as witnessed by Philo of Byblos, the interpreter of Sanchuniathon, was worshipped under this name, and afterwards that name was impiously derived to the images of either the stars or kings, whose memory was pleasing to posterity. Thus some made their own Assyrians, others Chaldeans, others Phoenicians, and worshipped Baalim, or Belus; for the word Bel was proper to the Chaldeans or Babylonians, with the dropping of the ע, which occurs in Is. 46, 1. Jer. 50, 2. c. 51, 44, just as it was בעל to the Hebrews, Phoenicians, and those adjacent. Thus, therefore, the Gentiles called those whom they held as gods Baalim, i.e. Lords, sometimes absolutely, sometimes with an addition, when they believed them to be lords of a certain thing, as Beelzebub, the God of Ekron, was called the Lord of flies, and Beelphegor the God of shame. Bonfrerius thinks that Baal absolutely was called nothing else among the Assyrians and Babylonians than that Belus, or Saturn, who is written to have reigned first among the Assyrians, and is called Nimrod in the sacred writings: nor among the Tyrians and Phoenicians anything other than Jupiter, and that he was called Beelsamin, that is, Lord of heaven in the Syrian language, who would be called בעל שמים in Hebrew, and that he is understood everywhere in Scripture when Baal is named without an addition, except in Daniel, who designates the Bel of the Chaldeans. Bonfrerius does not deserve assent when he says that no one was held by the Gentiles as Baal or Lord absolutely except Jupiter, and that he is always understood by this name in Scripture. For Jupiter was unknown to the Orientals and Asiatics: indeed, as Selden rightly observes, just as Joves were to the Europeans, so Baalim was a general name for gods to the Asiatics; just as there were three hundred Joves to them, according to Varro, so to the Syrians there were Baal Peor, Baalzebub, Baal Meloch, etc. He who derives the name of Jove from the tetragrammaton says that Jupiter is nothing else than Jovis pater, that is, ἰαὼ πατὴρ or ἰαὼ πατὴρ Jehovah Father, if indeed the tetragrammaton was written as Jao by the Greeks in Clem. Alexandr. V. Strom., Diodorus Siculus Biblioth. 2, Euseb. Apod. 4, and 1. Præpar. (from Philo of Byblos), Epiphanius, Irenæus, and Theodoret quæst. 15. in Exod. Although, therefore, by those who once committed the affairs of the Orient to Greek letters, Belus, both the Babylonian and the Phoenician Ζεὺς, has been mostly named, yet these testify only to a permutation of names, but not to an identity of idols or gods, just as Berosus the priest of Belus in

Eusebius's Belus, whom they interpret as Jupiter, and who was Baal to the Tyrians or Phoenicians, is called Zeus by Menander, who rendered their annals into Greek from the Phoenician language, and by Dio, a writer of the same matters: he was called Zeus of the Olympians in ancient times, as Josephus testifies in book 8, chapter 11, and indeed also by Philo of Byblos, who [wrote] from Taautus and Sanchuniathon: Ὁ ἐστι παρὰ Φοινίξι κύριος ὐρανῶ Ζεὺς δὲ παρ᾽ Ἕλλησι, which is, 'He who is among the Phoenicians the Lord of Heaven, but among the Greeks, Jupiter.'

But who Baal, whom they worshipped, properly is, seems ambiguous: Theophilus, Patriarch of Antioch, says that not even the worshippers themselves know it, in his work to Autolycus, book 3. Some attribute divine honors to Cronus and name him Belus and Bal: yet men who inhabit the eastern climates do this most of all; who does not know who Cronus is, and who Belus is? Damascius in the Life of Isidore [says]: Φοινίκες καὶ Σύροι τὸν Κρόνον Ἡλ καὶ Βὴλ καὶ Βολάθην ἐπονομάζουσι, 'The Phoenicians and Syrians name Saturn Hel, and Bel, and Bolathen.' Among the Assyrians, indeed, it is testified by Eusebius in his Chronicle that their first king was named Belus and worshipped as a god; in the 28th year of Thara, 'The first King of the Assyrians, Belus, died, whom the Assyrians named a god,' and others say Saturn. Concerning Thurus, successor of King Ninus, whom he writes was also called Mars, the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle [writes] according to Selden, book [1], chapter [?], thus: To this Mars the Assyrians erected the first statue, and worshipped him as a god, calling him Baal, which is interpreted as Mars, the deity of wars. Yet it is established that the Phoenicians worshipped the Sun as the greatest deity, whom they called μόνον ὀρανῶ Θεὸν ('the only God of heaven'), whose nod the planets and other stars would observe: just as also among the ancient Egyptians, the twelve signs of the zodiac were considered Θεοὶ βελαῖοι ('counselor gods'), but the planets were considered ῥαβδόφοροι ('rod-bearers'), that is, lictors who stand by the consistory of the ignited sun, as testified by the ancient scholiast on the Argonautica of Apollonius of Rhodes, book 4. Nor is it unknown how the most ancient philosophers attributed divinity primarily to the Sun. And for that reason, fire was also worshipped by the Chaldeans as a symbol of the Sun, the King of the heavens. Nevertheless, it seems likely to the same Selden that the deity Baal was also spoken of regarding Heaven and the host of Heaven, for whom Manasseh built an altar in the court, loc. cit., p. 200. He, after many things brought forward from sacred, ecclesiastical, and exotic writers, finally added these most true things on p. 229: 'But since Saturn, Jupiter, Heaven, and Uranus are so confused in fables that not even Phoebus himself can sufficiently distinguish them from one another, or himself from them, and that numerous crowd of gods is reduced by mythologists to the deity of Apollo or the Sun, one certainly should no longer hesitate so much, because from one Belus, Baal, or Jupiter (under which names, failing from the true worship of God, they worshipped the Sun primarily), invoked according to the ridiculous custom of the ancients, those countless titles were propagated. For by heaping up praises and piling up titles, they thought the Deity was captured, and that the greatest honor was thereby conferred: so that finally, those things which had been merely diverse names at the beginning of superstition, with error spreading, were held to be diverse deities.' These are the words of Selden. Thus, therefore, it must be held: First, indeed, the celestial bodies were worshipped without idols or images: But by images, the memory of the dead was honored: but this honor of theirs degenerated into idolatry, so that they were subsequently held to be gods themselves: the worship of demons also was added, which would force themselves into the images, or were taught by the hierophants to be present: whence demons began to be worshipped at those images under the names of the dead, and were even celebrated. Furthermore, also at the same statues, the Sun and other stars were accustomed to be worshipped, so that finally they were clearly confused among themselves, and they did not sufficiently distinguish the dead themselves from the demons, nor either of these from the celestial bodies, nor these from one another in their worship pers. Nor did it matter so much whether they worshipped the Symbol, or the Divinity himself, or the figure of the Symbol, so that from the number of idols, stars, and Symbols—no less than the names used in sacred rites—the multitude of Gods grew: just as the most learned Selden taught in Prolegomena, chapter 3.

And Astharoth (אשרות & אשרים) are groves, as in Exodus 34:13, Deuteronomy 7:5, 12:3, and in this book 3:7, where אשרות is joined with Bahalim: whence it is clear that עשתרות is another pronunciation signifying the same thing, wherefore also in 1 Samuel 7:4 the Greeks translate עשתרות as ἄλση. In such groves, however, the Earth was worshipped, which was thence called עשתרות, and by the Greeks expressing Syrian matters, Astarte. This custom passed under the name of Cybele to the Phrygians and other nations. Ovid in the seventh book of the Metamorphoses: 'The temples of the mother of the Gods, which once the famous Echion had made according to a vow, hidden in the woody forests.' Thus Tacitus teaches us that a chaste grove was dedicated to the Earth by the Germans. Elsewhere, however, mere groves were dedicated to the Earth, elsewhere images were added, such as the form of a sheep among the Moabites, according to the Rabbis. Others conjecture that Astarte is the moon, others Venus, others Juno, but what I have said is most credible. For then Venus is the mother of things, which suits the earth: and the Moon is the ἀντίχθων to the ancients: & Juno is the air, which is around the Earth.

Grotius distinguishes the name עשתרות, plural here and in 1 Samuel 7:4 (in the singular עשתרת in 1 Kings 11:5, 33), from the word אשרות which signifies groves: but it could appear that this name is also used as equivalent to the former, even if it otherwise signifies groves: and that it denotes some goddess: for just as here the Israelites are said to have served Baal and Astharoth, so in the following chapter, verse 7, they are said to have worshipped Baalim, ואת האשרות in the same sense, as it appears. And when Manasseh placed the image or carved figure האשרה in the house of the Lord, 2 Kings 21:7, how can it be understood that he placed an image of a grove, unless it is understood as an idol worshipped in a grove, as Luther translates 'Hayngötz'? For the grove itself, planted with trees, cannot be understood, since in 2 Kings 27:10 they are said to have erected statues and groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree; how could they consecrate groves or woods under a leafy tree, unless you understand by groves the Gods accustomed to be worshipped in groves, or their statues and wooden images? Which pleases Selden, book 2, Syntagma, chapter 2, thinking that false divinities were designated under the names of grove and oak, in reproach of a feigned divinity, and that wooden images dedicated to Astoreth were called Aslerim and Asseroth or groves, so that the name might also allude to the image, and the insult of the material might be reproached to such an unequal divinity by the very word. The passage Isaiah 57:5 seems to favor this: 'You who inflame yourselves with oaks under every leafy tree.' For it is not oaks under a leafy tree, but εἶδωλα, as the LXX render it, that are indicated as consecrated. In which manner Selden also interprets other passages in which groves are dealt with, when the worship of idols is designated: Judges 6:25, 28, 'he destroyed the altar, and burned the grove that was upon it,' 2 Chronicles 15:16, concerning Maacah, who had consecrated an idol לעשרה which he translates not as 'in a grove,' but τῇ Ἀσάρτῃ; also Exodus 33:13, Deuteronomy 7:5, 12:3. Although we do not deny that by that name idols or Gods were sometimes indicated, to whom worship was exhibited in groves, yet we doubt whether, where it is a matter of cutting down groves or the worship of groves, that meaning always holds: since the woods themselves, as places consecrated to idols, were also to be cut down, just as the high places were to be destroyed, in which idolatry was committed. Which, however, is only to be understood insofar as that profanation of places extended: so that, namely, nothing of profanation remained, that is, insofar as they are viewed under the formal aspect of idolatrous worship; for the places themselves, considered materially—groves, high places, and the like—were not demolished, but the idols, images, statues, and whatever pertained to idolatrous worship. And therefore, this word seems to have denoted now a Divinity or idol and image by metonymy, because it was worshipped in groves, and now the groves themselves.

Furthermore, I cannot agree with Grotius that the earth is denoted by Astharoth or Astarte in this passage; it was the Divinity of the Sidonians, as is evident from 1 Kings 11:5, 33, and of those bordering them. But from where will it be taught that the earth was worshipped by them as a Goddess? Lucian in his work 'On the Syrian Goddess' favors the Moon more: 'Αςάρτην δὲ εγὼ δοκέω σεληναίαν ἐμμεναι,' 'but I think Astarte is the Moon': and Phavorinus, 'ἡ Ἀσάρτη Θεὰ ἡ σελήνη τιμώμενη παρὰ Σιδωνίοις': or Astarte is the Goddess Moon, worshipped by the Sidonians: Cornelius à Lapide on this passage says, 'at first, the ancient gentiles, not knowing the true God, worshipped the Sun and Moon, from which all fertility flows into the earth, whence the Romans called them Jupiter and Juno, the Egyptians Osiris and Isis, the Syrians Baalim and Astharoth.' He also cites Philo of Byblos on this matter: 'Philo says, Astarte placed upon her own head the royal insignia, the head of a bull, to signify the horned Moon.' The same author, however, also distinguishes Astarte: There was one Astarte of the Babylonians, whom St. Epiphanius in heresy 19 calls Diana, another of the Carthaginians, whom St. Augustine here in q. 16 asserts was Juno, another of the Edessenes, whom Lucian says was the Moon. For this one multiplies the offspring of fish, birds, and sheep while she is full, and thus enriches men. But Cornelius also conjectures that the mother of Melchizedek was once worshipped under this name: Epiphanius writes in heresy 55 that the mother of Melchizedek was called Astaroth or Asteria. What if she was worshipped by posterity as a Goddess and thence the Goddesses were called Astaroth? Which conjecture, because it rests on no foundation, we dismiss.

Not a few testimonies support Venus: Suidas says: Ἀςάρτη, ἡ παρ᾽ ἕλλησιν ἀφροδίτη λεγο- μένη. Astarte is called Venus among the Greeks. Cicero, Book 3 de Nat. Deor.: the fourth Venus is Syrian, conceived in Tyre, who is called Astarte, who is handed down to have married Adonis. Also Philo of Byblos: τὴν Ἀςάρ- την Φοίνικες τὴν ἀφροδίτην εἶναι λέγ8σι: The Phoenicians say that Astarte is Venus. And Ptolemy, book 2 of the Tetrabiblos: Those who inhabit these regions generally venerate Venus as the mother of the gods, and designate her by various native names. Moreover, Theophilus and Phavorinus note that the image of Venus was Astarte, who was worshipped by the Sidonians in the figure of a star. The same opinion pleases Gyraldus in Syntagma 13, Floridus Sabinus in Lectiones Subcisivae 2, c. 7, Rhodiginus in book 23 of the Lectiones Antiquae, chapter 5, as well as Mercerus in his additions to Pagninus, Forsterus in his Dictionary, and Kircher in his Concordance. who the latter three think that the word עשתר, which denotes a flock of sheep, especially of females bearing turgid udders, was used because Astarte was an image of Venus πολυμάσθε (many-breasted), and was worshipped among the Sidonians for the fecundity of offspring. Scaliger, however, in his Conjectanea suspects she was named from the multitude of victims.

Augustine prefers Juno at this place, question 16: Juno without doubt is called Astarte (by the Carthaginians). And since those languages (Punic and Phoenician) do not differ much from each other, it is deservedly believed that Scripture says this about the children of Israel, that they served the Baals and the Astartes, because they served Jupiters and Junos. Nor should it disturb one that it did not say Astarte, that is, Juno, but as if there were many Junos, it placed this name in the plural. For he wished the meaning to be referred to the multitude of images, since every single image of Juno was called Juno, and through this he wished as many Junos to be understood as there are images. Plutarch in Crassus, citing Gyraldus, is doubtful whether Astarte is Venus or Juno.

Selden, Venus or Moon p. 249. The Assyrians called this celestial being, whether Venus or the Moon, Meglitta, the Arabs Abilat, the Persians Mitra, as Herodotus wrote. But what Selden had observed about Baal, he also rightly applies to Astarte on page 260. What we wrote in the previous chapter about the solemn multitude of deities pertains at the same time to this Goddess. And Silius Italicus elegantly called the deities of the Ennea a goddess, so that he might show that many things in the same, that is, the goddess Hecate, were hidden, which nevertheless constituted one Hecate. But no one is ignorant that this Hecate of ours is the Moon, for Apollo or the Sun was called ἕκατος, and the Moon ἑκάτη. See, if you please, Julian's Epistle to Serapion concerning Hecatos. And page 246: The names of Minerva, Juno, Venus, and the Moon are so confused when you look at the Asiatic Gods, that whoever says Minerva is Belesama, Juno is Belisama, or Venus or the Moon, has always said the same thing. He judges there that Belisama is Astarte herself. Hesychius: Βήλθης ἡ Ἥρα ἢ Ἀφροδίτη, that is, Belthes is Juno or Queen Moon.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET SERVIERUNT BAAL] Qui plene בעל שמין Βεελσαμὴν Dominus Cæli, Sol summus Deorum illis gentibus, unde Jupiter Assyrius dicitur. Vide Macrobius c. 23. lib. 1. Saturnal.

Nomen בעל commune est, nec de Sole tan- tum pro Deo culto dicitur. Eo primum summum, & ineffabilem omnium rerum creatorem designa- rum observat Seldenus de diis Syris Syntagm. 2. c. 1. quia בעל est Dominus, uti Ebræis אדן Græcis κύριος, Arabibus Abras dicitur, quod idem sonat. Inde ergo Solem, quem μόνον ὐρανῶ Θεὸν solum in cœlis Deum putarunt Phœnicii, teste Philone Bi- bliensi Sanchuniatonis interprete, sub hoc nomine cultum, post ad simulacra sive Astrorum, sive Regum, quorum memoria posteris grata erat, nomen illud impie derivatum esse. Ita alios Assyrios, alios Chal- dæos, alios Phœnicos suos fecisse, ac coluisse Baa- lim, vel Belos, Chaldæis enim seu Babyloniis pro- priam fuisse vocem Bel excidente ע, quæ occurrit Es. 46, 1. Jer. 50, 2. c. 51, 44. uti Ebræis, Phœniciis & adjacentibus בעל erat. Sic ergo Ethnici eos, quos pro diis habebant Baalim, h. e. Dominos voca- bant modo absolute, modo cum addito, cum certæ rei Dominos credebant, uti Beelzebub, Deus Aka- rim, Dominus muscarum, Beelphegor Deus turpitudi- nis vocabatur. Absolute Baal non alium apud Assy- rios, & Babylonios, quam Belum illum, vel Saturnum, qui primus apud Assyrios regnasse scribitur, & in sa- cris Nimrod vocatur, dictum censet Bonfrerius: nec apud Tyrios & Phœnices alium, quam Jovem, eumq; Beelsamin vocatum esse, hoc est, cæli Dominum lin- gua Syra, qui Ebræa בעל שמים diceretur, eum- que passim intelligi in Scriptura, cum Baal sine addi- to nominatur, præterquam apud Danielem, qui Chaldæorum Belum designat. Non meretur assensum Bonfrerius, cum neminem absolute Baal vel Domi- num habitum ab Ethnicis quam Jovem, indefinite dicit, eumque in Scriptura semper hoc nomine in- telligit. Jupiter enim Orientalibus & Asiaticis igno- tus fuit: imo uti Europæis Joves, ita Asiaticis Baalim generale Deorum nomen fuisse recte observat Sel- denus; uti illis trecenti Joves erant, apud Varronem, ita Syris Baal Beor, Baalzebub, Baal Meloch &c. Qui Jovis nomen è tetragrammato deducens, nihil ali- ud, inquit, Jupiter est, quam Jovis pater, id est, ἰαὼ πα- τὴρ seu ἰαὼ πατὴρ Jehovah Pater, siquidem tetra- grammaton à Græcis Jao exaratum fuerit apud Clem. Alexandr. V. Strom. Diodor. Siculus Biblioth. 2. Euseb. Apod. 4. Et 1. Præpar. (è Philone Bibliensi) Epiphan. Iren. & Theodor. quæst. 15. in Exod. Etsi ergo ab his, qui Græcis literis res Orientis olim man- darunt, Belus tam Babylonius, quam Phœnicum Ζεὺς plerumq; nominatus sit, tamen hæc nominum solum permutationem testantur, non autem idolorum, vel Deorum indentitatem, uti Berosus Beli Sacerdos apud

Eusebium βῆλον, ὃν δὲ Δία μεθερμηνεύουσιν, Belus quem Jovem interpretantur, & qui Tyriis seu Phœ- niciis Baal erat, Menandro, qui ex Phœnicum ser- mone annales eorum Græce reddidit, Ζεὺς appella- tur, & Dio earundem rerum Scriptor: prisco Ζεὺς ὀλύμπων, teste Josepho l. 8. c. 11. dictus est, imo & Phi- loni Bibliensi, qui ex Taauto, & Sanchuniatbone. Ὁ ἐστι παρὰ Φοινίξι κύριος ὐρανῶ Ζεὺς δὲ παρ᾽ Ἕλλησι, qui Phœniciis est cæli Dominus Græcis vero Jupiter.

Quisnam vero Baal proprie sit, quem coluere, ambiguum videtur: Theophilus Antiochenus Patri- archa nec ipsos cultores id scire ait, ad Autolycum l. 3. Quidam divinos honores Crono deferunt eumque Belum & Bal nominant: maxime tamen id factitant homines, qui orientalia climata inhabitant, nescit quis Cronus, & quis sit Belus? Damascius in vita Isidori Φοίνικες καὶ Σύροι τὸν Κρόνον Ἡλ καὶ Βὴλ καὶ Βολάθην ἐπονομάζουσι, Phœnices & Syri Saturnum Hel, & Bel & Bolathen nominant. Penes Assyrios sane regem ipforum primum Belum nominatum, & pro Deo cultum esse testatur Eusebius in Chronic. Thara anno 28. Assyriorum Rex primus Beli mortuus est, quem Assyrii Deum nominarunt, & alii dicunt Satur- num De Thuro, Nini Regis successore, quem Mar- tem etiam nuncupatum scribit Chronici Alexandr. autor apud Seldonuml. c. ita: Huic Marti primam statuam erexerunt Assyrii, & eum uti Deum adorarunt nuncupantes cum Baal, quod interpretatur Mars, bel- lorum numen. Phœnices tamen Solem ceu maximum numen coluisse constat, quem μόνον ὀρανῶ Θεὸν nuncuparunt, cujus nutum planetæ & cætera Syde- ra observarent: quemadmodum & Ægyptiis pri- scis Dodecatemoria signiferi Θεοὶ βελαῖοι seu Dii consiliarii, planetæ vero ῥαβδόφοροι, hoc est, lictores, qui accensi solis consistorio adstent, censebantur, teste vetere ad Apollonii Rhodii Argonauticon 4. Scholiasta. Nec ignotum est, quomodo Soli imprimis divinitatem tribuerint Philosophi vetu- stissimi. Atque ideo etiam Chaldæis ignis ut Symbo- lum solis cælorum Regis colebatur. Verisimile tamen eidem Seldeno videtur, numen Baal etiam de Cælo & exercitu Cæli, dictum, cui aram in atrio extruxit Manasses l. c. p. 200. Qui post multa è sa- cris, Ecclesiasticis & exoticis Scriptoribus addu- cta, hæc tandem verissima adjecit p. 229. Atqui cum Saturnus, Jupiter, Cælum: Uranus ita fabulis sint confusi, ut nec ipse Phœbus eos aut ab iis ipsum se queat satis distinguere, numerosaque illa divum turba ad Apollinis sive solis numen à Mythologis reducatur, haud amplius sane adeo hæsitandum est, quia ex uno Belo, Baale seu Jove (sub quibus vocibus à vero Dei cultu deficientes Solem imprimis adorabant) ad mo- rem priscorum ridiculum invocato, innumeri illi titu- li fuerint propagati Coacervatis enim elogiis, titu- isque congestis capi Numen putabant, maximoque affi- ci inde honor: ita ut tandem, quæ diversa folummodo nomina superstitionis primordio fuerant, grassante er- rore, diversa numina haberentur. Hæc Seldenus. Ita ergo habendum: Primum quidem corpora cæle- stia absque idolis vel simulacris colebantur: Simulacris vero memoria demortuorum honorata fuit: sed dege- neravit hic eorum honor in idololatriam, ut pro diis ipsi deinde haberentur: accessit etiam Dæmoniorum cultus, quæ sese simulacris ingerebant, aut adesse ab hierophantis docebantur: unde Dæmonia sub mortuorum nominibus ad illa simulacra coli ce- perunt, imo celebrabantur. Porro etiam simul ad easdem statuas Sol, & alia sydera coli consue- verunt, ut tandem inter se plane confunderen- tur, nec mortuos ipsos à Dæmoniis, nec ho- rum alterutra à cœlestibus corporibus, neque hæc satis ab invicem disterminarent eorum cul- tores. Neque ita intererat, an Symbolum, an Nu- minis ipsius, an Symboli figuram adorarent, ut ex idolorum, stellarum, & Symbolorum non minus quam nominum in sacris adhibitorum numero, Deorum multitudo creverit: quemadmodum do- ctissimus Seldenus Prolegom c. 3. docuit.

Et Astharoth (אשרות & אשרים) sunt luci, ut Exod. 34, 13. Deut. 7, 5. c. 12, 3. hoc libro 3, 7. ubi אשרות conjungitur cum Bahalim: unde liquet עשתרות esse aliam pronuntiationem idem significantem, quare & 1. Sam. 7, 4. עשתרות Græci vertunt ἄλση. In talibus autem lu- cis Terra colebatur, quæ inde dicta עשתרות, & Græcis res Syras exprimentibus Astarte. Is mos sub Cybeles no- mine ad Phrygas, gentesque alias transiit. Ovidius septimo Metamorphoseon: Templa Deum matri quæ quondam clarus Echion Fecerat ex voto nemorosis abdita silvis. Sic castum nemus Terræ dicatum a Germanis Tacitus nos do- cet. Alibi autem meri luci dicati Terræ, alibi addita simula- cra ut ovis specie apud Moabitas narrantibus Rabinis. Alii Astarten lunam esse, alii Venerem, alii Junonem conjectant, sed quod dixi maxime credibile est. Tum vero Venus re- rum genetrix, quod terræ convenit: & Luna ἀντίχθων ve- teribus: & Juno aer, qui circa Terram.

Nomen עשתרות plurale hic & 1. Sam. 7. 4. (in singulari עשתרת 1. Reg. 11, 5. 33.) à voce אשרות quæ lucos significat, distinguit Grotius: sed videri possit hoc nomen ceu æquivalens prioris etiam adhiberi, utut alias lucos significet: & deam aliquam notare: nam uti hic Israëlitæ dicuntur ser- viisse Baali, & Astharoth, ita cap. sequ. v. 7. colu- isse dicuntur Baalim, ואת האשרות sensu, ut apparet, eodem. Et quum Manasse in domo Do- mini simulacrum vel sculptile האשרה posuit 2. Reg. 21, 7. quomodo intelligi potest simulacrum luci posuisse, nisi intelligatur de idolo in luco culto, ut Lutherus vertit Hayngötz. Lucus enim ipse arbo- ribus consitus intelligi nequit, cum 2. Reg. 27, 10. statuas & lucos erexisse perhibentur in omni colle excelso & super omnem arborem frondosam; quomo- do sub arbore frondosa lucos vel nemora sacra- runt, nisi intelligas per lucos Deos in lucis coli solitos, aut statuas eorum, & simulacra lignea? Quod Seldeno l. 2. Synt. cap. 2. placet, existiman- ti designata esse falsa numina sub luci & quercus vo- cabulis, in fictæ divinitatis opprobrium, & simu- lacra lignea τῇ Astoreth dicata Aslerim & Asseroth seu lucos dicta esse, ut & ad nomen simul alludere- tur, & tam impari divinitati materiæ contumelia ipso vocabulo exprobraretur. Favere videtur locus Es. 57, 5. Calefacitis vos apud quercus sub omni arbore frondosa. Non enim quercus sub arbore frondosa, sed εἶδωλα, uti reddunt LXX, sacrata in- digitantur. Quo pacto etiam interpretatur Sel- denus cætera loca, in quibus de lucis agitur, cum cultus idolorum designatur: Jud. 6, 25. 28. destruxit altare, & succendit lucum, qui super illud, 2. Par. 15, 16. de Maacha, quæ idolum sacrarat לעשרה quod vertit non in luco, sed τῇ Ἀσάρτῃ; etiam Ex. 33, 13. Deut. 7, 5. c. 12, 3. Quanquam vero non abnua- mus, per id nominis idola vel Deos quandoque in- digitari, quibus in lucis cultus exhibebatur, num ta- men ubi de lucis excindendis agitur, aut de cultu lu- corum, semper ea significatio locum habeat, ambi- gimus: siquidem & nemora ipsa, ceu loca idolis sa- crata exscindenda fuerint, uti excelsa destruenda, in quibus idololatria committebatur. Quod eatenus tamen solum intelligendum, qua se illa locorum profanatio extendebat: ut nempe nihil reliquum profanationis remaneret, hoc est, qua sub formali cultus idololatrici spectantur; loca enim ipsa ma- terialiter considerata, luci, excelsa, & similia non diruebantur, sed idola, simulacra, statuæ, & quic- quid ad cultum spectabat idololatricum. Ideo- que modo Numen aut idolum & simulacrum ista vox per metonymiam, quia in lucis colebatur modo lucos ipsos denotasse videtur.

Porro neque terram per Astharoth vel Astar- ten hoc loco notari, Grotio suffragari possum, Numen erat Sidoniorum, ut è 1. Reg. 11, 5. 33. con- stat, & conterminorum. At ab illis terram cul- tam esse pro Dea, unde docebitur? Lunæ magis favent Lucianus in opusc. de Syria Dea Αςάρτην δὲ ἐγὼ δοκέω σεληναίαν ἔμμεναι, Astartem vero ego opinor Lunam esse: & Phavorinus, ἡ Ἀσάρτη Θεὰ ἡ σελήνη τιμώμενη παρὰ Σιδωνίοις: aut Astarte Dea Luna est, culta à Sidoniis: Cornelius à Lap. in h. l. primitus, inquit, prisci gentiles ignorantes Deum ve- rum adorabant Solem & Lunam, à quibus omnis in terram fertilitas manat, unde eos Romani vocabant Jovem & Junonem, Ægyptii Osiridem & Isidem, Syri Baalim & Astharoth. Laudat quoque eam in rem Philonem Bibliensem: Philo, Astarte, ait, impo- suit proprio capiti regni insigne caput tauri, ut corni- culatam Lunam significaret. Idem tamen Astartem etiam distinguit: Erat Astarte alia Babyloniorum, quam S. Epiphanius hæresi 19. Dianam vocat, alia Car- taginensium, quam S. Augustinus hic q. 16. asserit fu- isse Junonem, alia Edessinorum, quam Lucianus ait fu- isse Lunam. Hæc enim fœtus piscium, avium, ovium, dum plena est, multiplicat, itaque homines ditat. Sed & conjicit Cornelius matrem Melchisedech hoc nomine cultam olim fuisse: scribit Epiphanius hæ- resi 55. matrem Melchisedech dictam Astaroth sive Asteriam. Quid si hæc à posteris culta fuerit ut Dea indeque Deæ dictæ sint Astaroth? Quam vero conjecturam, quia nullo nititur fundamento, mis- sam facimus.

Pro Venere faciunt non pauca testimonia: Sui- das: Ἀςάρτη, inquit, ἡ παρ᾽ ἕλλησιν ἀφροδίτη λεγο- μένη. Astarte apud Græcos Venus appellata. Cicero Lib. 3. de Nat. Deor. quarta Venus Syria, Tyroque concepta, quæ Astarte vocatur, quam Adonidi nupsis- se traditum est. Etiam Philo Bibliensis: τὴν Ἀςάρ- την Φοίνικες τὴν ἀφροδίτην εἶναι λέγ8σι: Astartem Phœnices Venerem esse dicunt. Et Ptolomæus l. 2. Tetrabibli: Qui has incolunt regiones plerumque Ve- nerem ut matrem Deum venerantur, & variis pa- triisque nominibusque indigitant. Simulacrum insu- per Veneris Astarten fuisse, quæ à Sidoniis astri figu- ra culta fuerit, Theophilus ut & Phavorin. notant. Eadem sententia placet Gyraldo Syntagm. 13. Flo- rido Sabino lect. subcisiv. 2. c. 7. Rhodigino l. 23. le- ction. antiqu. cap. 5. ut & Mercero in additioni- bus ad Pagnin. Forstero in Diction. Kirchero in Concordant. qui posteriores tres vocem עשתר, quæ ovium gregem maxime fœmellarum turgidas mammas ferentium notat, adhibitam putant, ideo quod Astarte simulacrum esset Veneris πολυμάσθε multimammeæ, & ad prolium fœcunditatem apud Sidonios coleretur. Scaliger tamen in conjecta- neis suspicatur dictam eam à victimarum multitu- dine.

Junonem mavult Augustinus ad h. l. quæst. 16. Juno sine dubitatione (à Pœnis) Astarte vo- catur. Et quoniam istæ linguæ (Punica & Phœ- nicia,) non multum inter se differunt, merito cre- ditur de filiis Israel hoc dicere Scripturam, quod Baali servierint, & Astartibus, quia Jovi & Ju- nonibus. Nec movere debet, quod non dixit Astar- ti, id est, Junoni, sed tanquam multæ sint Junones, pluraliter hoc nomen posuit. Ad simulacrorum enim multitudinem referri voluit intellectum, quo- niam unumquodque Junonis simulacrum Juno voca- batur, ac per hoc tot Junones, quot sunt simulacra, intelligi voluit. Plutarchus in Crasso, citante Gyraldo dubius est, Venusne an Juno sit Astarte?

Seldenus, Venusne an Luna p. 249. Cœlestem hanc sive Venerem sive Lunam vocabant Assyrii Meglittam, Arabes Abilat, Persæ Mitram, ut scri- psit Herodotus. Sed quod de Baale observarat Seldenus, recte etiam Astartæ applicat pag. 260. Quæ de numinum multitudine solemni scripsimus capite superiore, ad hanc Deam simul pertinent. Et Enneæ Numina divæ eleganter dixit Silius Itali- cus, ut plura in eadem, id est, Hecate Dea, Nu- mina, quæ tamen unam constituerent Hecatem, la- tete ostenderet. Hecaten autem hanc nostram, id est, Lunam esse nemo nescit, Apollo enim seu Sol ἕκατος, Luna ἑκάτη dicebatur. Vide de He- cato, si placet, Juliani Epistolam ad Serapionem. Et pag. 246. Minervæ autem Junonis, Veneris, Lu- næ nomina sunt ita, cum ad Asiaticos Deos respexe- ris, confusa, ut qui Minervam Belesamam, Juno- nem Belisamam, Venerem aut Lunam dixerit, sem- per idem dixerit. Belisamam autem esse ipsam Astartem ibi judicat. Hesychius: Βήλθης ἡ Ἥρα ἢ Ἀφροδίτη, id est, Belthes Juno aut Luna Regina.

## 2:14
verse 14. AND THEY SOLD TO ENEMIES.

In the Hebrew: And (God) sold to enemies. Therefore, it is falsely referred in the Vulgate to the plunderers: for these were the very enemies to whom the Israelites were sold: The LXX agree with the Hebrew.

Latin:

vers. 14. ET VENDIDERUNT HOSTI- BUS.

In Ebr. Et vendidit (Deus) hostibus. Falso ergo id refertur in Vulgata ad diripientes: hi enim fuere ipsi hostes: quibus venditi sunt Israëlitæ: LXX. consonant Ebræo.

## 2:21
Verse 21. AND I WILL NOT DESTROY THE NATIONS) Quickly, that is.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET EGO NON DELEBO GENTES) Cito scilicet.

## 2:22
verse 22. THAT IN THEM I MAY TRY ISRAEL.

The Hebrew לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת means 'that I may test'. Therefore, GOD did not wish to experience something, but He tested the Israelites through the enemies, and proved them, whether they themselves keep, that is, wish to keep the way of the Lord, and thus He taught them to serve not idols, but Himself. The Vulgate renders that word in chapter 3, 1, as 'that he might instruct Israel in them,' and might test their virtue and constancy, whether they were going to obey the divine commands and destroy the Canaanites and destroy the idols, or not.

Latin:

vers. 22. UT IN IPSIS EXPERIAM ISRAEL.

Ebr. לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת est tentem. Non ergo aliquid experiri voluit DEUS, sed tentavit per hostes Israëlitas, eosdemque probavit, utrum ipsi custo- diant, hoc est, custodire velint viam Domini, ita- que docuit eos non idolis, sed sibi servire. Vocem illam cap. 3, 1. ita reddit Vulg. ut erudiret in eis Israëlem, ac periclitaretur eorum virtutem ac constantiam, num divinis mandatis parituri & Cananæos deleturi, & idola destructuri essent, nec ne?

## 2:23
verse 23. THE LORD THEREFORE LEFT ALL THESE NATIONS.

It must be translated: For the Lord had left all these nations: for the discourse is about things past under Joshua.

SECTION II.

SPECIAL [HISTORY] OF THE EARLIER JUDGES.

Latin:

vers. 23. DIMIST ERGO DOMINUS OMNES NATIONES HAS.

Vertendum est: Dimiserat enim Dominus omnes has nationes: nam de rebus præteritis sub Josua sermo est.

SECTIO II.

SPECIALIS JVDI- CUM PRIORUM.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

The people, associated with the nations, are afflicted. Three times delivered through Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Populus gentibus sociatus affligitur. Ter libe- ratus per Othoniel, Aod, Samgar.

## 3:2
verse 2. THAT AFTERWARDS THEIR CHILDREN MIGHT LEARN TO FIGHT AGAINST ENEMIES.

Three reasons are found why GOD wished the remnants of the Canaanites to remain among the Israelites, even before they deserved it by their sins. The first, so they would not be infested by wild beasts, Ex. 23, 29. Deut. 7, 22. The second, so they might be tested in faith, Jud. 2, 22. chap. 3, v. 4. The third, so they might be trained for battles, which is handed down here. Whence it is established that the use of arms is lawful among the people of God.

Latin:

vers. 2. UT POSTEA DISCERENT FI- LII EORUM CERTARE CUM HOSTI- BUS.

CAusæ tres reperiuntur, cur DEUS re- liquias Chananæorum inter Israëlitas su- peresse voluerit, etiam antequam peccatis id me- ruerunt. Prima ne à feris infestarentur Ex. 23, 29. Deut. 7, 22. Altera ut in fide probarentur Jud. 2, 22. cap. 3, l. 4. Tertia ut ad prælia instruerentur, quæ hic traditur. Unde constat licitum esse ar- morum usum in populo Dei.

## 3:3
Verse 3. FIVE SATRAPS) See Joshua 13, 3. Those five cities, Ashkelon, Ekron, Ashdod, Gath, and Gaza, each with its own towns and villages, constituted Satrapies or Prefectures, over which as many Satraps presided. Judah had indeed captured, chap. 1, 18, Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron; but soon the Philistines recovered them again. Therefore, it is said that God left these Satrapies for the testing of the Israelites. AND ALL THE CANAANITE. The Phoenicians are to be understood, as those who, being descended from Canaan, are also called Canaanites. See Prov. 30, 24. Matt. 15, 22. For Sidon was the capital of Phoenicia. Verse 4. THAT HE MIGHT TEST ISRAEL BY THEM) Since the Israelites had not immediately destroyed them, as they ought to have, God, using this occasion, judged that they should be preserved for a long time, so that if the Israelites did not imitate their customs, the integrity of the Israelites would appear: if they did imitate them, their wickedness. Furthermore, God wished to use those peoples as ministers to punish the Israelites, if they should sin for a long time or gravely.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QVINQVE SATRAPAS) Vide Josue 13, 3. Urbes illæ quinque Ascalon, Accaron, Azoth, Geth, & Gaza singulæ cum suis quæque vicis & pa- gis constituebant Satrapias vel Præfecturas, qui- bus totidem Satrapæ præfuerunt. Ceperat qui- dem Juda cap. 1, 18. Gazam, Ascalonem, & Ac- caron; sed mox Philistini easdem iterum recu- perarunt. Ideo reliquisse Deus has Satrapias ad experimentum Israëlitarum dicitur. OMNEMQUE CHANANÆAM. Intelligendi sunt Phœnices, utpote qui ex Cha- naan oriundi etiam Chananæi dicuntur. Vid. Prov. 30, 24. Matth. 15, 22. Sidon enim erat caput Phœniciæ. Vers. 4. UT IN IPSIS EXPERIRETUR ISRAELEM) Cum eos non statim delessent Israëlitæ, ut debuerant, Deus hac usus occasione, servandos eos diu censuit, ut si eorum mores non imitarentur Israëlitæ, probitas Israëlitarum ap- pareret : si imitarentur, improbitas. Præterea Deus illis po- pulis ministris uti voluit ad puniendos Israëlitas, si diu aut gravia delinquerent.

## 3:7
Verse 7. AND ASHTAROTH.

In Hebrew it is אשרות and so also the LXX have it. Which word denotes groves or woods dedicated to gods, in which they erected altars to sacrifice to them, and here it is taken metonymically for the idols which were worshipped in the groves, as we said at verse 13 of the preceding chapter. Junius, Piscator, the Geneva translation in the marginal note, Sixtinus Amama, Cornelius à Lapide, and Bonfrer agree.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET ASTHAROTH.

In Ebr. est אשרות atque ita etiam habent LXX. Quæ vox lucos vel sylvas diis dicatas, in qui- bus aras erexerunt ad sacrificandum iisdem, notat, & hic metonymice pro idolis accipitur, quæ cole- bantur in lucis, uti diximus ad vers. 13. cap. præce- dentis. Consentiunt Junius, Piscator, Genev. trans- latio in nota marginali, Sixtin. Amama, Cornel. à Lapide, Bonfrer.

## 3:8
Verse 8. HE DELIVERED THEM INTO THE HANDS OF CHUSHAN-RISHATHAIM KING OF MESOPOTAMIA.

Delivered, in Hebrew: Sold: delivery follows sale as an effect, and so to sell is used metonymically for to deliver. This was the first servitude in the land of Canaan: when it began is not indicated, only the time of its duration is expressed: that it lasted for eight years. King of Mesopotamia, later v. 10, of Syria of the two rivers, Naharaim, or of the two rivers by which it is intercepted, namely the Tigris and the Euphrates: called Chushan-Rishathaim. Pagninus interprets it as Ethiopian of two impieties, because he despoiled both the body of liberty and the soul of religion.

Verse of the same. AND THEY SERVED HIM EIGHT YEARS) That is, they were forced to redeem peace with heavy tributes, yet not so that they received garrisons from that king. Similar to soon 12, 13, 14, and so it was easy for them, having resumed their courage, to cast off such a burden, as the following shows.

According to this explanation of the servitude, it will perhaps be more easily reconciled what is said in verse 11 about the rest of the land for 40 years, than if the King of Mesopotamia had burdened them with military garrisons.

Latin:

Vers. 8. TRADIDIT EOS IN MANUS CHU- SAN RASATHAIM REGIS MESOPOTA- MIÆ.

Tradidit, in Ebr. Vendidit: traditio vendi- tionem sequitur tanquam effectus, itaque vendere metonymice ponitur pro tradere. Prima hæc servi- tus fuit in terra Chanaan: quæ quando ceperit, non indigitatur, solum tempus durationis ejus exprimitur: quod per octo annos durarit. Rex Mesopotamiæ, postea v. 10. Syriæ interamnis Na- haraim, vel duorum fluminum, quibus interce- pta, Tigris scil. & Euphratis: dictus Cusan Rasatha- im. Pagn. interpretatur Æthiops duarum impie- tatum, quod & corpus libertate & animum religio- ne spoliarit.

Vers. eod. SERVIERUNTQUE EI OCTO ANNIS) Id est, coacti sunt pacem gravibus tributis redimere, non ta- men ut præsidia ab eo rege acciperent. Simile mox 12. 13. 14. itaque facile illis fuit resumto animo onus tale exuere, ut se- quentia ostendunt.

Juxta hanc explicationem servitutis forte fa- cilius conciliabitur, quod vers. 11. dicitur de quiete terræ per 40. annos, quam si Rex Mesopotamiæ ipsos præsidiis militaribus onerasfet.

## 3:9
verse 9. WHO RAISED UP A SAVIOR FOR THEM.

Although the name of Savior belongs by way of excellence to Christ, who is the Savior not so much of the body as of the soul, and who preserves us primarily from spiritual evils unto eternal salvation, it is nevertheless also attributed to other bodily preservers, through whom the Lord has delivered His people from certain temporal evils; indeed, even those through whom He Himself leads us to eternal salvation are called Saviors in a diaconal and ministerial sense. It should be noted, says Augustine in question 18 on this passage, that a man through whom God makes people safe is also called a Savior. Thus, the Judges and others through whom He delivered the people from their enemies are called Saviors to the Israelites. Cf. v. 15, 2 Kings 13:5, Neh. 9:27. Ministers of the word, through whom He regenerates, converts, and leads us to eternal salvation, and who are the ministerial cause of salvation, are also called Saviors. Obad. 5:21, 1 Tim. 4:16. Cf. John 20:21, Luke 10:16, 1 Thess. 2:13, 1 Cor. 9:22. There is, therefore, no reason for Bonfrerius to accuse us of astonishment when we refuse to bestow the name of Savior upon the Virgin Mother and the saints in Heaven, as if we denied that anyone could be called a Savior in a secondary sense, for we readily admit this secondary meaning of the word yet that Mary and the saints in heaven, after Christ, bring eternal salvation to us by their own aid, as the Jesuit says, is ἄγραφον [unwritten], and ἀντίγραφον [a copy], nay even ἀντίλογον [contradictory]: For those who are ignorant of us, which is certain concerning the saints in heaven, Is. 64:16, and do not specifically understand our needs, how can they bring aid to us or provide salvation? Moreover, the name of Mediator in the cause of salvation is proper to Christ alone, so that no one should be acknowledged as mediator between God and men except the one Christ Jesus, 1 Tim. 2:5. Which, therefore, Bonfrerius attributes to the Virgin Mary and the saints in heaven, not without the ἀτιμίᾳ [dishonor] of our one Mediator, nor does Cornelius sufficiently piously honor himself and others by the name of the Society of Jesus, the impious followers of Loyola, because they contend that as associates of Jesus they save everyone. For he acknowledges no Jesus as an associate in the SALVIFIC office, Isa. 63:3, ch. 45:22, Acts 4:12, even though he has ministers through whom he dispenses salvation. For it is one thing to be an ASSOCIATE of JESUS in saving, another to be his minister and a ministerial cause of salvation: just as associate causes are greatly distinguished where there is coordination, and principal, instrumental, and ministerial cause where subordination only, not coordination, has a place.

Latin:

vers. 9. QVI SUSCITAVIT EIS SALVA- TOREM.

Salvatoris nomen etsi ἐξοχικῶς Christo, qui non tam corporis, quam animæ Salvator est, nosque imprimis a Spiritualibus malis sospitat, ad æter- nam salutem, conveniat, aliis tamen etiam tri- buitur corporalibus servatoribus, per quos à tem- poralibus quibusdam malis liberavit Dominus populum suum, imo etiam Salvatores διακονικῶς & ministerialiter dicuntur, per quos ipse nos ad salutem æternam perducit. Advertendum, inquit Augustinus quæst. 18. in h. l. Salvato- rem etiam dici hominem, per quem Deus salvos fa- ciat. Ita salvatores Israëlitis dicuntur Judices & alii, per quos populum ab hostibus suis liberavit. Conf. v. 15. 2. Reg. 13, 5. Neh. 9, 27. Salvatores etiam dicuntur Ministri verbi, per quos ad salutem æter- nam nos regenerat, convertit & perducit, qui cau- sa salutis ministerialis sunt Obad. 5, 21. 1. Tim. 4, 16. Conf. Joh. 20, 21. Luc. 10, 16. 1. Thess. 2, 13. 1. Cor. 9, 22. Non ergo est, quod stuporis nos arguat Bonfrerius, cum nomen Salvatoris Virgini Matri, sanctisque in Cælo deferri renuimus, quasi negemus secun- dario quemquam Salvatorem dici posse, nam hanc secundariam vocis significationem ultro admitti- mus: Mariam tamen & sanctos in cœlis post Chri- stum sua ope salutem æternam nobis adferre, ut Jesuita ait, ἄγραφον, & ἀντίγραφον, imo etiam ἀν- τίλογον est: Qui enim nos ignorant, quod de san- ctis in cœlo certum, Es. 64, 16. neque necessitates nostras speciatim intelligunt, quomodo opem nobis adferre, aut salutem præstare possint Me- diatoris autem nomen in causa salutis soli Christo proprium est, adeo ut non agnosci debeat inter Deum & homines mediator nisi unus Christus Jesus 1. Tim. 2, 5. quod proinde Bonfrerius Mariæ virgini, sanctisque in cœlo, non sine uniusMediato- ris nostri ἀτιμίᾳ tribuit, neque satis pieCornelius a se & alios impii Lojolæ sectatores societatis Jesu nomine honorat, quod quasi socii Jesu salvare o- mnes contendant. Nullum enim agnoscit Jesum socium in SALVATORIO munere Esa. 63, 3. cap. 45, 22. Actor. 4, 12. etsi ministros habeat, per quos dispensat salutem. Aliud enim est JESU SOCIUM esse in salvando, aliud ejusdem esse mi- nistrum, & causam ministerialem salutis: quemad- modum maximopere distinguuntur causæ sociæ, ubi coordinatio, & causa principalis, instrumentalis & ministerialis, ubi subordinatio solum, non coordi- natio locum habet.

## 3:10
verse 10. AND ISRAEL JUDGED.

Cornel. à Lap. explains: He vindicated, and liberated from oppression. But we taught in the introduction that the word of judging implies something more. The liberation has already been treated before: and the following words speak of the battle and victory.

Latin:

vers. 10. ET JUDICAVIT ISRAEL.

Cornel. à Lap. explicat: Vindicavit, & ab oppressione liberavit. Sed verbum judicandi am- plius quid inferre in procœmio docuimus. De li- beratione jam antea actum: & de pugna ac victo- ria verba sequentia loquuntur.

## 3:11
verse 11. AND THE LAND RESTED FORTY YEARS, AND OTHNIEL DIED.

It was said before that under 40 years the eight-year period of servitude is included, nay even the earlier years of rule before they were reduced to servitude, and the whole period from the departure of Joshua. The difficulty is how the land is said to have rested for 40 years, if indeed the Israelites served for eight years, which Melchior Canus, Loc. Theol. 11. c. 5, Laur. Codomannus, lib. 12. quæst. 16, Dionysius Petavius, de doctr. tempor. l. 9. cap. 23, Possin. Diallact. general c. 19, Nic. Abrahamus in Pharo Vet. Test. lib. 10. cap. 5 urge. But to that difficulty Bonfrerius responds (1.) that the word of resting is placed absolutely, it is not said that it rested from battles or from calamity, but that it is to be taken in such a way that it rested from sins and new idolatry; But the word of resting has a relation to the preceding, where there was talk of servitude and battles, nor is a sense to be brought into the text, but to be brought out of the text, nor can the land be said to have rested from sins in those years, because by their sins within the course of those years they had provoked the Lord to sell them to the King of Syria. Therefore, the second response of Bonfrerius seems more convenient, that it is not new in Scripture for something to be ascribed to a whole number which belongs only to a part, especially when the part to which it belongs is greater, so that in a way it absorbs the remaining number, which is smaller: whence it is not a wonder if Scripture includes within 40 years, of which 32 were of rest, which partly preceded the servitude under the Elders and then in the time of idolatry, and partly followed, after the King of Mesopotamia was defeated, the eight intermediate years of servitude. But the best explanation is that which we indicated in the Chronotaxis: And the land rested 40 years, not that it had peace and rest for so many years after Othniel's victory, but that it began to rest in the fortieth year, with the counting done from the Josuan rest: and therefore the following words of verse 11. & 12. are to be rendered thus: And Othniel the son of Kenaz died, and again the children of Israel did evil: as can be seen in similar places ch. 2:19 and ch. 4:1, not that Othniel died precisely in that fortieth year, but that it is indicated that after his departure the Israelites again defected from GOD, and were delivered into the hands of Eglon, King of the Moabites. For the year of Othniel's death is not expressed. But the year of the rest of the land restored by Othniel, which after the death of Othniel a new transgression having arisen, another oppression followed, under Eglon, of 18 years, Jud. 3:12, 13, 14, just as neither the time of the death of Ehud nor of Shamgar is expressed in verses 30, 31.

Latin:

vers. 11. QUIEVITQUE TERRA QUA- DRAGINTA ANNIS, ET MORTUUS EST OTHONIEL.

Dictum est antea sub 40. annis & octennium servitutis comprehendi, imo etiam priores annos regiminis antequam redigerentur in servitutem, ac totam periodum inde à Josuæ excessu. Difficultas est, quomodo dicatur terra quievisse 40. annos, si- quidem per octo annos servierint Israelitæ, quam urgent Melchior Canus Loc. Theol. 11. c. 5. Laur. Codomannus lib. 12. quæst. 16. Dionysius Petavius ductu tempor. l. 9. cap. 23. doctr. ib. Possin. Diallact. general c. 19. Nic. Abrahamus in Pharo Vet. Test. lib. 10. cap. 5. Ad eam vero difficultatem Bonfre- rius respondet (1.) verbum quiescendi absolute poni, non dici, quod quieverit à præliis vel à calami- tate, sed ita id accipiendum esse, quod quieverit à peccatis, & nova idololatria; Sed verbum quie- scendi relationem habet ad præcedentia, ubi de servitute & præliis sermo fuit, nec in textum infe- rendus est sensus, sed è textu efferendus, neque quievisse à peccatis dici potest terra istis annis, quia peccatis suis intra istorum annorum decursum Do- minum provocarat, ut eos Regi Syriæ venderet. Altera ergo responsio Bonfrerii convenientior videtur, quod novum in Scriptura non sit, ut ali- quando toti alicui numero adscribatur, quod parti tantum competit, præsertim cum pars, cui illud convenit, major est, ut quodammodo reliquum numerum, qui minor est, absorbeat: unde mi- rum non sit, si Scriptura intra 40. annos, quo- rum 32. fuerunt quietis, qui partim servitutem an- tecesserunt sub Senioribus & deinde idololatriæ tempore, partim sequuti sint, devicto Rege Me- sopotamiæ, octo anni intermedii servitutis in- cludantur. Sed optima explicatio est, quam inChro- notaxi indicavimus: Et quievit terra 40. annis, non quod post Otthonielis victoriam tot annis pacem & quietem habuerit, sed quod quadra- gesimo anno quiescere cœperit, numeratione facta inde à Josuana quiete: ideoque verba sequentia vers. 11. & 12. ita reddenda: Et mortuus est Otho- niel Kenaci filius, atque iterum fecerunt malum filii Israel: ut in similibus locis cap. 2, 19. & cap. 4, 1. videre est, non quod anno illo quadragesimo de- cesserit præcise Otthoniel, sed ut indicetur, quod post excessum ejus iterum à DEO defecerint Israëlitæ, traditique sint in manus Eglonis Regis Moabitarum. Annus enim mortis Otthonielis expressus non est. Sed annus quietis terræ per Otthonielem redditæ, quam post fata Ottho- nielis nova exorta prævaricatione altera excepit oppressio, sub Eglone, annorum 18. Jud. 3, 12. 13. 14. quemadmodum nec Aodi, nec Samgaris tem- pus mortis vers. 30. 31. expressum est.

## 3:15
Verse 15. HE RAISED UP A SAVIOR FOR THEM BY THE NAME OF EHUD)

The command of God, which is also expressed below in 28, ensures that this cannot be drawn into an example, where such a command of God does not exist: no more than what Abraham was commanded to do concerning his son, and what the Israelites took away from the Egyptians. Brutus, who killed Caesar, seems to have been of a similar spirit, but he lacked both the divine command and the success.

The command of God pertains only to the liberation of the people, not to the simulation and deceit through whose intervention Ehud carried it out. But that he helped his people, and went to vindicate them into liberty, I do not see why it should not be drawn into an example, or compared with that Abrahamic immolation of his own son, and the Israelitic carrying away of Egyptian things: for to liberate a people from the oppression of enemies is nowhere forbidden; but because a heroic spirit was needed for that work, God is said to have raised up and instructed Ehud with that fortitude out of the ordinary, as with other vindicators of the people; not that a peculiar dispensation or precept was needed, but because without divine virtue so great a matter, even if lawful, could not have been expedited.

Latin:

Vers. 15. SVSCITAVIT EIS SALVATOREM VOCABULO AOD)

Dei jussus, qui & infra exprimitur 28. efficit, ne in exemplum hoc trahi possit, ubi talis Dei jussus non est: non magis quam quod Abraham de filio jussus est facere, & quod Israëlitæ res Ægyptiorum abstulere. Brutus qui Cæsarem oc- cidit, paris videtur fuisse animi, sed ei ut divinum imperi- um, ita & successus defuit.

Jussus Dei ad liberationem populi tantum per- tinet, non ad simulationem, & dolum, cujus in- terventu eandem exequutus est Aod. Quod autem opitulatus est a populo suo, eumque in li- bertatem vindicatum ivit, non video, cur non in exemplum trahendum, aut cum illa filii proprii immolatione Abrahamica, & rerum Ægyptiaca- rum ablatione Israëlítica id componendum sit: nam ab oppressióne hostium liberare populum nuspiam interdictum est; quia vero heroico ad id opus erat animo, suscitasse DEUS & instru- xisse ea fortitudine Aodum dicitur extra ordinem, uti alios populi vindices; non quod peculiari di- spensatione, aut præcepto opus fuerit, sed quod sine virtute divina res tanta, etsi licita, expediri nequiverit.

## 3:18
Vers. 18. WHO USED BOTH HANDS FOR THE RIGHT.

Vatablus, Arias, Pagninus, and Cajetan render the Hebrew more correctly as 'shut' or 'captured' in the right hand, who, namely, had a right hand that was maimed or contracted and useless, whence he was bound to use his left hand, as is held below in verse 21, and is described by Josephus, that he was better with his left hand and had all his strength from it. Cornelius ineptly excuses the Vulgate, that one who is 'shut in the right' can be called ambidextrous, because using both hands for the right, he is surrounded and protected as it were on all sides from either flank. Who would wring 'ambidextrous' out of 'shut' or 'captured in the right,' or by divination conjecture that it is to be understood in such a way?

Latin:

Vers. 18. QUI UTRAQUE MANU PRO DEX- TRA UTEBATUR.

Rectius Ebræum reddunt Vatablus, Arias, Pagninus, Cajetanus, clausum sive captum manu dextra, qui sc. manum dextram mancam vel con- tractam, & inutilem habuerit, unde uti tene- batur manu sinistra, ut infra habetur vers. 21. & à Josepho describitur, quod manu sinistra melior fuerit, & ab eo omnem virtutem habuerit. Inepte excusat Cornelius Vulgatam, quod ambidexter dici possit clausus dextra, quia utraque manu pro dextra utens undique ab utroque latere cingitur quasi & protegitur. Ecquis ex claúso vel capto dextra, ambidextrum extorquebit, vel divinatione conjectabit ita intelligendum esse?

## 3:19
Vers. 91. I HAVE A SECRET WORD FOR THEE.

Because Ehud lied here, Cornelius observes from the opinion of philosophers and theologians that it is lawful to lie in such a case, but he does not himself disapprove of it; or with Augustine he thinks it should be excused from being a lie, because by 'word' he understood 'deed' in the Hebrew phrase, i.e., 'I have that which I shall say to you,' that is, 'I shall do,' namely, that I may kill you, and thus he spoke so that the King might think an oracle of his idols was being brought to him from Gilgal: and thus he also explains verse 20: 'I have a word of God for thee,' that is, 'God commands me to kill you, the oppressor of Israel.' Which things approach the art of Jesuitical equivocations. But it is not right to approve of any lie, nor of such equivocations: even if some invent a certain 'good deceit,' which according to Ulpian, ff. de dol. c. 1, is said to be not only that which is harmless, or brings utility to the deceived, but also skill against enemies and robbers: and that it is permitted to use it sometimes against public enemies, declared by God Himself or the Magistrate, unless an oath has been interposed, or if the other party has first violated faith, they think, yet here not only is skill used against the enemy, but such a lie, by which he who spoke peace with his mouth, had snares in his heart, which is altogether condemned by the Holy Spirit Jer. 9, 8. nor are evils to be done, or lies to be designed, so that good may come about by the removal of the enemy of the Republic Rom. 3, 8. having put away lying speak the truth EVERYONE with his neighbor, the Apostle admonishes Ephes. 4, 5. And what else is a lie, than the voluntary enunciation of a falsehood, for the sake of deceiving, as Augustine defines in the book on Lying to Consentius c. 4. Therefore that opinion of the Philosophers, especially of Plato and Socrates, that Magistrates must sometimes use lies, as physicians do for the Republic, to which is akin the saying in Cassian's Conferences 17, c. 17: That a lie must be used as hellebore to ward off some great danger; the opinion of Chrysostom in the book on the Priesthood and in chapters 12 and 17 of Genesis, that for the sake of duty a good man must sometimes lie, deserves no approval: against which stand those things which St. Augustine argued in a special book against lying. Nor indeed is equivocation any better: which, if the intention to deceive underlies it, the Jesuits themselves acknowledge to be equally a lie: Therefore Bonfrerius does not deny that a lie is here imputed to Ehud, but he judges it to be an officious and venial one, or at least materially a lie: which the saints thought it was permitted for them to do from time to time to achieve some great good. But that this was the opinion of the saints, he falsely assumes, nor if it had been the opinion of any of the saints, would it therefore be holy or consistent with the word of God, rather since every lie is prohibited by GOD, it is not permitted to lie even for the sake of some great good: as Augustine warned in c. 22 of the Enchiridion, that no lie is to be thought not a sin, because we can sometimes benefit someone by lying. Certainly, from the end, that which is evil by its nature cannot be made good. Nor is any sin venial by its nature: which the Jesuit again rashly assumes. Finally, it was not only materially a sin, because Ehud asserted that which was not: I have a secret word for you O King, but also formally, because by this false assertion of his he intended to imprint a false opinion in the mind of the listener; as if he were truly bringing an oracle, and for that purpose, so that the king, by the object of religion, namely about to receive the words of GOD, would rise, and by that reason the way would be open for the wound to be inflicted secretly and without noise, which intention of his Bonfrerius himself acknowledges. Wherefore Ehud can by no means be absolved from sin, even though he had a good end proposed; nor are the examples of the saints, but divine commands, the rule and norm of good and evil or sin. Even if therefore by divine instinct he killed the tyrant stirred up by GOD to liberate the people; yet certain things intervene in this act, in which he himself, using the prudence of the children of this world, carried out the matter, and suffered something human. For does GOD need our lie? Job 13, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 91. VERBUM SECRETUM HABEO AD TE.

Quia hic mentitus est Aod, tali casu mentiri licitum esse observat Cornelius ex sententia Philoso- phorum & Theologorum, sed quam non improbat ipse; aut cum Augustino excusandum censet à mendacio, quod per verbum intellexerit factum Ebræa phrasi, q. d. Habeo, quod tibi dicam, hoc est, faciam, sc. ut te occidam, atque ita loquutus sit, ut Rex sibi ex Galgalis idolorum suorum oracu- lum afferri putet: atque ita etiam vers. 20. explicat: Verbum Dei habeo ad te, hoc est, jubet me Deus, ut te Israëlís oppressorem occidam. Quæ ad artem æqui- vocationum Jesuiticarum accedunt. Sed neque mendacium ullum, neque æquivocationes ejusmo- di probare fas est: etiamsi enim nonnulli bonum quendam dolum fingant, qui secundum Ulpianum ff. de dol. c. 1. dicatur non solum, qui innoxius est, aut decepto utilitatem adferat, verum etiam contra hostes & latrones solertia: eoque uti licere inter- dum adversus hostes publicos, à Deo ipso vel Ma- gistratu declaratos, nisi juramentum interpositum fuerit, aut si altera pars prior fidem violaverit, exi- stiment, hic tamen non solertia tantum est contra hostem adhibita, sed mendacium tale, quo qui pacem loquutus est ore, in corde habuit insidias, quod omnino damnatur à Spiritu S. Jer. 9, 8. nec facien- da mala sunt, aut designanda mendacia, ut bonum sublato Reip. hoste eveniat Rom. 3, 8. deposito men- dacio loquimini veritatem QVISQVE cum proximo suo, monet Apostolus Ephes. 4, 5. Et quid aliud est mendacium, quam voluntaria falsi enunciatio, fallen- di causa, definiente Augustino l. de Mendac. ad Con- sent. c. 4. sententia ergo illa Philosophorum, Plato- nis imprimis, & Socratis, quod Magistratibus inter- dum utendum sit mendaciis, ut Reip. Medicis, cui af- fine est Cassiani collat. 17. c. 17. dictum: Menda- cio utendum esse quasi belleboro ad discrimen aliquod magnum propulsandum; Chrysostomi opinio lib. de Sacerdot. & in cap. 12. & 17. Gen.officii causa aliquan- do viro bono mentiendum esse, nullum meretur cal- culum: adversus quam faciunt, quæ peculiari libro contra mendacium disputavit S. Augustinus. Neq; verò melius se habet æquivocatio: quam utique si fallendi intentio subsit, æque esse mendacium agno- scunt ipsimet Jesuitæ: Ideo Bonfrerius non abnuit, hic Aodo mendacium impingi, sed id officiosum, & veniale, vel saltem materialiter mendacium esse censet: quod putarint sancti, sibi licitum esse sub- inde mentiri ad magnum aliquod bonum. Verum eam fuisse sanctis sententiam,falso assumit,neque si alicui fuisset sanctorum, ideo sancta aut verbo Dei consentanea fuerit, imo cum omne mendacium à DEO prohibitum sit, ne quidem ob magnum ali- quod bonum mentiri concessum est: ut monuit Au- gustinus c. 22. Enchir. non ideo ullum mendaci- um putandum esse non peccatum, quia possumus aliquando prodesse alicui mentiendo. Ex fine certe non potest fieri bonum, quod natura sua ma- lum est. Nec ullum peccatum est natura sua ve- niale: quod temere iterum assumit Jesuita. De- nique non tantum materialiter id peccatum fuit, quia asserebat id Aod quod non erat: Verbum se- cretum habeo ad te o Rex,sed etiam formaliter, quia hoc suo falso asserto intendebat falsam opinionem in mente audientis imprimere; quasi revera oracu- lum adferret, idque eo fine, ut rex religionis obje- ctu, nimirum verba DEI accepturus, assurgeret, eaque ratione vulneri clanculum & sine strepitu in- ferendo via pateret, quam intentionem ejus agno- scit ipse Bonfrerius. Quapropter à peccato absolvi Ahod neutiquam potest, utut bonum finem pro- positum habuerit; neque sanctorum exempla, sed mandata divina regula & norma boni & mali vel peccati sunt. Etiamsi ergo instinctu divino tyran- num excitatus à DEO ad liberandum populum in- terfecerit; quædam tamen in hoc facto interveni- unt, in quibus ipse prudentia filiorum seculi usus rem exsequutus, & humani quid passus est. Num- quid enim DEUS indiget mendacio nostro? Job. 13,7.

## 3:21
Verse 21. HE ROSE FROM THE THRONE) As having honor for a Prophet.

Latin:

Vers. 21. SVRREXIT DE THRONO) Tanquam Pro- phietæ honorem habens.

## 3:30
Verse 30. AND THE LAND RESTED FOR EIGHTY YEARS.

It must be rendered again, in the eightieth year, namely from the rest restored by Othniel verse 11. For it is not likely that Ehud, or Ehud, presided over the judgeship for so many years, nor is any word about him in this

History held. It is only hinted that, Eglon the King of the Moabites having been killed by Ehud, to whom the Israelites had served for 18 years, the land began to rest again in the eightieth year after the previous peace restored to it by Othniel.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ET QVIEVIT TERRA OCTUAGIN- TA ANNIS.

Iterum reddendum est, anno octuagesimo scil. à quiete per Othonielem reddita vers. 11.Non enim ve- risimile est,quod Aod, vel Ehud per tot annos ju- dicatui præfuerit,neq; verbum nullum de eo in hac

Historia habetur. Id solum innuitur, quod oc- ciso per Ehudem Eglone Moabitarum Rege, cui per 18. annos Israelitæ servierant, quiescere cepe- rit iterum terra anno octogesimo post priorem pacem ab Othoniele illi restitutam.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. Sisera defeated by Deborah and Barak, killed by Jael.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. Sissera à Debora & Barack devictus, à Jabele occisus.

## 4:2
Verse 2. HE REIGNED IN HAZOR.

ALTHOUGH Joshua burned Hazor Jos. 12, 12. yet it was restored by the Canaanites, and Jabin had his seat in it. HE HIMSELF HOWEVER DWELT IN HAROSHETH) Namely Sisera. Verse 4. DEBORAH WAS ALSO A PROPHETESS) A woman leader of the deed. Thus the cowardice of men is reproached below 19. Verse 6. THE LORD THY GOD COMMANDED THEE) In Hebrew: Did He not command: which locution the Hebrews use, so that they strongly affirm even that which the other did not know before. Thus also below 14. Verse 11. HEBER THE KENITE HAD DEPARTED FORMERLY FROM THE REST OF THE KENITES HIS BRETHREN) He had made himself neutral in this war, not daring to claim for himself a part of the land won by war. See below 17. Verse 17. THERE WAS PEACE BETWEEN JABIN THE KING OF HAZOR, AND THE HOUSE OF HEBER THE KENITE. The Kenites had not indeed entered into a covenant with Jabin, nor is it likely that a peace confirmed by oath existed, but they were friends, so that the one expected nothing hostile from the other, whether Heber had redeemed peace and security with tribute, or whether without tribute he had obtained the same by divine providence, so that King Jabin, while harassing the Hebrews, allowed the Kenites to live in peace, because they abstained from wars and political affairs, devoted themselves to piety and tranquility, and were held in love and honor even by the tyrant. Therefore, Jael did not violate a sworn peace or act as a covenant-breaker when she killed Jabin; not to mention that it was done by a special instinct of GOD, to liberate the people from tyranny, for which reason she is celebrated for this deed in chapter 5, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 2. REGNAVIT IN ASOR.

ETsi Josua Asor succenderit Jos. 12, 12. restau- rata tamen ea fuit à Cananæis, & in ea sedem habuit Jabin. IPSE AUTEM HABITABAT IN HAROSETH) Nem- pe Sisara. Vers. 4. ERAT AVTEM DEBORA PROPHETIS) Dux fœmina facti. Ita viris exprobrata ignavia infra 19. Vers. 6. PRÆCEPIT TIBI DOMINVS DEVS TVVS) In Hebræo: Nonne præcepit: qua locutione utuntur Hebræi, ut valde affirment etiam quod alter ante nesciebat. Sic & infra 14. Vers. 11. HEBER AUTEM CINÆVS RECESSERAT QVONDAM A CÆTERIS CINÆIS FRATRIBUS SV- IS) Medium se in hoc bello fecerat, non ausus sibi partem de terra bello parta vindicare. Vide infra 17. Vers. 17. ERAT PAX INTER JABIN REGEM AZUR, ET DOMUM HABER CINÆI. Non quidem fœdus inierant cum Jabin Cinæi, neque pacem juramento firmatam viguisse verisi- mile est, sed amici erant, ita ut alter ab altero nihil hostile expectaret, sive tributo pacem securita- temque redemerit Haber, seu citra tributum divina providentia eandem obtinuerit, ut Rex Jabin E- bræos vexans, siverit Cinæos in pace vivere, quod ipsi à bellis rebusque politicis abstinuerint, pietati & tranquillitati vacarint, & amore ac honore eti- am apud tyrannum essent. Non ergo pacem ju- ratam violavit aut fœdifraga fuit Jabel, quando Jabin occidit; ne dicamus, quod speciali DEI in- stinctu id factum fuerit, ad populum à tyrannide liberandum, unde ob hoc facinus celebratur cap.5, 24.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. TURN IN TO ME MY LORD, TURN IN FEAR NOT.

Regarding this invitation, there is a doubt whether it was made with a deceitful mind and joined with a lie and sin, since Jael killed the one invited after she had lured him to her with flattering words and promised him security with the explicit words: fear not? Bonfrerius acknowledges that some Roman Catholics do not excuse her from a lie and deceitful simulation, even if they praise the deed itself; he himself, however, absolves her, with this argument among others, that there is nothing here of an open lie, since she affirms nothing, nor of simulation, which cannot be licit under certain circumstances, because she could have allowed Sisera to be deceived by her words, even if she herself understood them in another sense; and although he admits that the simulation of friendship and security made with the intention that someone be deceived seems to have the appearance of a lie, he nevertheless thinks it is not, if that simulation can have a true sense from the intention of the one acting or speaking; such as it could have been here; turn in, fear not, for no one is at home from whom you might deservedly fear: since neither was she herself at home or in the tent, nor should a leader of war have deservedly feared a woman. Therefore, she did nothing against a given pledge or promised security, since she had not promised it except by the false persuasion of Sisera. Cornelius attempts to absolve her with a similar equivocation: Fear not, i.e., there are no armed men here, no enemies, whose swords you might fear. She does not lie, because this was true. But if she had in mind at that time to kill Sisera, that person cannot be absolved from fraud and lying by this equivocation of words, do not fear: for she warned him not only not to fear from armed men, or not to fear from those who might be in an inner room or tent, but she testified absolutely and simply to complete security with these clear words, "Come in, my Lord, come in, do not fear": so that he had no need to fear either from her, or from any servant, or from anyone else present with her. This would therefore be an open lie, since she affirms that there is no need for fear at all; it would be a simulation, most illicit and fraudulent, since she fosters friendship and hostility in her mind at the same time: nor is any sense to be looked for here other than that which the words themselves make manifest, not one which might perhaps lie hidden under the words through some equivocation. Concerning which St. Augustine warns in Enchiridion to Laurentius, ch. 22. Words were certainly instituted for this purpose, not so that men might deceive one another, but so that each might bring forth his thoughts into the knowledge of another: Therefore, to use words for deceit, and not for what they were instituted, is a sin. But if the Jesuits defend themselves with their customary escape, that such assertions are not false, because there is only one proposition, which is partly expressed, namely, you will not be in danger with me, and partly not expressed, but conceived in the mind, to wit, from armed enemies, I reply: by that very fact a lie is committed, because the truth is retained in the mind, that there is no danger from such enemies, and a falsehood is uttered with the mouth, that there is no cause for fear, no danger present with her: for although the true and the false can be considered in the internal concept of the mind, a lie properly so called regards the external declaration of the mind through the signs of words; and therefore that hypothesis is most false, even though approved by other Jesuits also, Valentianus, Toletus, Sanchez, Suarez, Lessius, that it is not a lie when a statement can have some true sense in the mind of the speaker, even if the words are not ambiguous by their own signification, nor does ambiguity appear from the circumstance or otherwise outwardly in any way, but it is added only by the mind of the one equivocating, which might serve for their verification: which hypothesis of Jesuitical equivocation is solidly refuted by Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, in his treatise on the abuse of mental restriction, ch. 8, and he teaches that there is no outwardly uttered speech which can be verified, when it is otherwise false, by the sole addition or mental restriction, unless something else has been added. The virtue, he says, of truthfulness forbids the falsehood of an utterance to be corrected by the poultice of mental restriction by any such outwardly signified meaning as is then understood by the restricting mind.
