For what does it profit you to speak truthfully, when by a statement mixed from thought and speech you bring forth a true proposition for yourself, which you mutilate for your neighbor in such a way that you bring forth nothing but a falsehood? This is not to speak the truth with one's neighbor, but to lie, with the lie cooked up again in the mind. He lies who says he has not seen, when he has seen (that one must not fear, when one must fear) if, acknowledging this lie, he says, I saw, but not in Rome, when he saw in Capua (or you must fear, but not from armed enemies, but from me myself) what else is he doing than confirming his lie in his mind by saying in his mind I saw (or you must fear at all) when he has uttered to his neighbor that he did not see (that he must not fear). By adding but not in Rome (but not from enemies) he does not correct the lie, because if he were to correct it, he would only correct it for himself, but he does not correct it for himself, because no one properly lies to himself. Let Paulus Laymannus also be compared, book 4, Moral Theology, treatise 3, ch. 13, n. 5, f. 616, seqq. & especially Joseph Barnes, the English Benedictine, who in a long treatise demolished that art of equivocation, and with it approved by the Parisian School, and taught that equivocation is the principle of Babylonian confusion, a curse upon the Christian people, that it pertains to the doctrines of demons, is repugnant to justice, paves the way to atheism, etc.

What, therefore, is to be thought of that invitation of Jael? Not only Lavater and others from the Reformed, but also Lyranus and other Papists judge that it cannot be absolved from sin, deceit, and lying, even though for the heroic deed itself she is celebrated by Deborah, ch. 5:24, Blessed above women be Jael; which eulogy pertains only to those things which are praised there, v. 24, 25, and is not to be extended to this invitation made under the guise of friendship with a promise of security. For however much the heroic deeds of the Saints may proceed from the Spirit of God, yet the organs of the Holy Spirit, carrying His power in earthen vessels, 2 Cor. 4:7, are by no means immune from lapses and sins, which are also wont to creep into them sometimes in the execution of those very divine things. But since such a fraudulent invitation can not undeservedly seem too abominable; for lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, Proverbs 12:22, especially of those who with a gracious voice hide a hostile mind, ch. 26:25, Ps. 55:21, the Lord detests a double-tongued mouth, Prov. 8:13, who are of a double heart, Ps. 12, Sir. 2:14. Therefore, I would not rashly impute such a crime to the holy heroine. Wherefore I judge thus, that Jael, when she invited Sisera, did not yet have in mind that deed of killing the tyrant, but spoke thus with a simple heart (not a double one), Come in to me, my Lord, come in, do not fear: she even covered him with a mantle, with a good heart, in her tent, v. 18, and indeed even offered milk to Sisera, and brought butter, which is added in ch. 5:25 (although it can also be understood of the first and thick milk) in a bowl of PRINCES or a noble and excellent one, which befits Princes, so that she might refresh him; because there was peace for her with Jabin: (that she mixed in opium or mandrake is Cornelius's frivolous conjecture) but when he, weary from the slaughter and flight, and perhaps also buried in sleep, or rather a stupor divinely sent, by the vapors and humors excited by the generous drink of milk, had been aroused and impelled by the secret instinct of God to this deed, so that the people might be liberated from tyranny. Such an outcome did Deborah predict in chapter 5, verse 9: Sisera is delivered into the hands of a woman. Concerning which Ambrose says in his book on widows: Deborah prophesied the outcome of the battle; the righteous Barak led forth the army, Jael took the triumph. Therefore, there is no deceit here, no lie; nor did Jael wickedly violate the security she had promised, but piously obeyed a divine impulse, and she avenged her people. This decision I see is not disapproved of even by Bonfrerius, when he says that it is not certain whether Jael had already thought of the killing (when she invited Sisera to her) or whether that plan occurred to her afterwards. Yet she ought by no means to have carried it out against the faith she had pledged, had she not been moved by God, whose promptings and commands are deservedly preferred to all our promises, nor are there any bonds or rights so tight that they should not be dissolved for the sake of divine ones.

Latin:

Vers. 18. INTRA AD ME DOMINE MI, IN- TRA NE TIMEAS.

De hac invitatione dubium est, annon ea ani- mo doloso facta, & cum mendacio ac peccato con- juncta sit, quum Jaël invitatum interfecerit, post- quam blandis verbis eundem ad se allexit, eique securitatem promisit, verbis disertis: ne timeas? A mendacio, & dolosa simulatione non excusare eandem, etsi facinus ipsum laudent, Romano-Ca- tholicos nonnullos agnoscit Bonfrerius, ipse ta- men absolvit eandem, hoc inter alia argumento, quod nihil hic vel aperti mendacii sit, quum nihil ipsa affirmet, vel simulationis, quæ non certis cir- cumstantiis possit esse licita, quia potuerit permit- tere ipsa, ut è verbis suis deciperetur Sissera, licet ipsa alio sensu ea acciperet; & quanquam fateatur simulationem amicitiæ & securitatis eo animo fa- ctam, ut quis decipiatur, videri mendacii speciem, non esse tamen putat, si ista simulatio verum sensum ex operantis vel loquentis intentione habere possit; qualis hic esse potuerit; intra, ne timeas, nemo enim domi est, à quo merito tibi timere possis: quando- quidem nec ipsa jam domi vel in tabernaculo esset, neque à fœmina belli dux merito timere debuerit. Ni- hil ergo ipsam contra datam fidem, vel securita- tem promissam fecisse, quum ipsa ea non pro- misisset nisi falsa perfuasione Sisseræ. Simili æqui- vocatione absolvere conatur eandem Cornelius: Ne timeas, q.d. nulli hic sunt armati, nulli ho- stes, stes, quorum gladios extimescas. Non menti- tur, quia hoc erat verum. Sed si hoc habuit tum in mente Siseram interficere, a fraudulentia ac men- dacio absolvi non potest ista æquivocatione ver- borum, ne timeas: non enim tantum ne timeat ab armatis, aut ne timeat ab iis, qui sint in inte- riori conclavi, vel tabernaculo monuit, sed te- stata est absolute & simpliciter omnimodam secu- ritatem verbis hisce luculentis, intra AD ME Domine mi, intra, ne timeas: quod neque ab ipsa, vel a domestico aliquo aut alio quocunque sibi præsente timere opus habeat. Foret ergo hoc apertum mendacium, quum omnino affirmet, nullo opus esse timore; foret simulatio, maxime illicita & fraudulenta, quum amicitiam simul & hostilitatem animo foveat: nec sensus hic spe- ctandus alius, quam quem verba ipsa manifesta reddunt, non qui forte subesse per aliquam æ- quivocationem verbis possit. Quo de monet S. Augustin. Enchir. ad Laurent. c. 22. Utique verba propterea sunt instituta, non per quæ invi- cem homines fallant, sed per quæ in alterius quisque notitiam cogitationes suas proferat: Ver- bis igitur uti ad fallaciam, non ad quod instituta sunt, peccatum est. Quod si se tueantur Jesuitæ consueto effugio, tales assertiones falsas non esse, quia unica est tantum propositio, quæ partim expri- mitur, nempe non periclitaberis apud me, partim non exprimitur, sed mente concipitur, sc. ab ho- stibus armatis, Resp. eo ipso mendacium com- mittitur, quod verum animo retineatur, non esse periculum a talibus hostibus, falsum ore pro- feratur, quod nulla timoris causa, nullum peri- culum penes ipsam sit: quamvis enim verum & falsum in mentis conceptu interno considerari possint, mendacium tamen proprie dictum respi- cit externam mentis declarationem per signa ver- borum; ideoque falsissima est illa hypothesis, etsi aliis etiam Jesuitis Valentiano, Toleto, Sanchez, Suarezio, Lessio probata, quod mendacium non sit, quum aliquem verum sensum in mente lo- quentis oratio habere potest, etiamsi verba ex sua significatione ambigua non sint, neque ex circum- stantia, aut aliter exterius ulla ratione ambiguitas appareat, sed sola mente æquivocantis addatur, quod ad eorum verificationem facere possit: quam hypothesin æquivocationis Jesuiticæ solide re- fellit Malderus Antwerpiensis Episcopus tract. de abusu restrict. Mental. cap. 8. docetq; nullum esse exterius prolatum sermonem, qui verificari possit, cum alius falsus sit, sola additione, vel restri- ctione mentali, nisi aliud accesserit. Virtus, in- quit, veracitatis prohibet restrictionis mentalis ma- lagmate corrigi falsitatem enuntiationis ullo tali exterius significato, quale per mentem restrin- gens tum subintelligitur. Quid enim prodest ti- bi veraciter loqui, quando oratione mixta ex co- gitatione & eloquio veram propositionem tibi effers, quam mutilas proximo sic, ut non nisi falsum effe- ras? Hoc non est loqui veritatem cum proximo, sed mentiri, recocto in mente mendacio. Mentitur qui se dicit non vidisse, cum viderit (non metuendum esse, cum timendum sit) si recognoscens hoc men- dacium dicit, vidi, sed non Romæ, cum Capuæ vi- derit (vel metuendum est tibi, sed non ab ho- stibus armatis, verum a me ipsa) quid aliud agit, quam quod mendacium suum mente confirmet di- cendo in mente vidi (vel omnino metuendum est tibi) cum effatus sit proximo se non vidisse (ipsi metuendum non esse) Addendo sed non Romæ (sed non ab hostibus) non corrigit mendacium, quia si corrigeret, sibi tantum corrigeret, sibi autem non corrigit, quia sibi nemo proprie mentitur. Conferatur etiam Paulus Laymannus l. 4. Theol. Moral. tract. 3. c. 13. n. 5. f. 616. seqq. & imprimis Josephus Bar- nesius Benedictinus Anglus, qui prolixo tractatu artem illam æquivocationis profligavit, eoque ap- probato a Schola Parisiensi, & docuit, æquivoca- tionem esse principium confusionis Babylonicæ, ma- ledictionem populi Christiani, pertinere ad doctrinas dæmoniorum, justitiæ repugnare, atheismo viam sternere &c.

Quid ergo de illa Jabelis invitatione haben- dum? Non Lavaterus tantum, aliique e Reformatis sed etiam Lyranus aliique Pontificii eandem a pec- cato, dolo, & mendacio minime absolvi posse cen- sent, etsi ob factum ipsum heroicum a Debora cele- bretur c. 5, 24. Benedicta præ mulieribus Jabel; quod elogium ad ea tantum pertinet, quæ illic laudantur, v. 24. 25. non vero extendendum ad hanc invita- tionem sub amicitiæ specie factam cum securitatis promissione. Utut enim facta Heroica Sancto- rum a Spiritu Dei proficiscantur, organa tamen S. S. virtutem ejus in vasis testaceis portantia 2. Cor. 4, 7. a lapsibus & peccatis immunia minime sunt, quæ in ipsorum divinorum exequutione iisdem etiam obrepere quandoque solent. Sed quum nimis abominabilis talis fraudulenta invitatio vi- deri haud immerito possit; labia enim mendacia abominatio Domini sunt, Proverb. 12, 22. eorum maxime qui voce gratiosa occultant hostilem animum cap. 26, 55. Psal. 55, 24. os bilingue de- testatur Dominus Prov. 8, 13. qui duplici sunt corde Psal. 12, Sir. 2, 14. Idcirco non temere tantum crimen sanctæ Heroinæ impegerim. Qua- propter ita censeo, Jaelem cum invitavit Sise- ram, facinus istud tyrannum interficiendi nondum habuisse in animo, sed ita loquutam esse simplici corde (non duplici) intra ad me, Domine mi, intra ne timeas: texisse etiam ipsum pallio, bono animo, in tabernaculo suo vers. 18. imo & lac præbuisse Sisseræ, ac butyrum attulisse, quod cap. 5, 25. additur (quamvis de lacte primo & spisso etiam accipi possit) in Phiala PRINCIPUM vel præclara ac præstante, quæ Principes decet, ut reficeret eundem; quia pax erat ipsi cum Ja- bin: (quod opium aut mandragoram admiscue- rit, frivola est Cornelii conjectura) sed ubi ille fessus a strage, & fuga, forte etiam lactis potu largiori vapores, & humores excitante, somno, aut potius sopore divinitus immisso sepultus es- set, instinctu Dei arcano ad hoc facinus exci- tatam fuisse, atque impulsam, quo populus a ty- rannide liberaretur. Qualem eventum prædixit Debora cap. 5. vers. 9. In manus mulieris trade- tur Sisara. De quo Ambrosius libr. de viduis: Debora prælii prophetavit eventum; Barac ju- stus produxit exercitum, Jabel cepit triumphum. Nullus ergo hic dolus, nullum mendacium: neque improbe securitatem promissam violavit Jahel, sed pie divino impulsu obtemperavit: populumque suum vindicavit. Quam decisio- nem video etiam a Bonfrerio non improbari: cum ait, non constare, an Jahel jam tum de nece cogitarit, (cum Siseram ad se invitavit) an vero postea istud ei consilium inciderit. Quod tamen contra fidem datam exequi minime debuisset, nisi a Deo excitata fuisset, cujus instinctus & mandata omnibus nostris promissis merito præferuntur, nec ulla tam arcta sunt vincula aut jura, quæ non solvenda sint propter divina.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. The Song of Deborah.

Latin:

CAPUT V. Epinicion Deboræ.

## 5:2
Verse 2. YOU WHO OFFERED YOURSELVES WILLINGLY FROM ISRAEL TO THE DANGER.

In the Hebrew it is, as Pagninus, Arias Montanus, and Cajetan translate, while he avenges the revenges in Israel, while the people offer themselves willingly, BLESS THE LORD.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUI SPONTE OBTULISTIS DE ISRAEL ANIMAS VESTRAS AD PERI- CULUM.

IN Ebr. est, ut Pagninus, Ariasmontanus, Cajetanus vertunt, dum ulciscitur ultiones in Israel, dum sponte se offert populus, BENEDICITE DOMINO.

## 5:4
Verse 4. WHEN YOU WENT FORTH FROM SEIR.

Lord, when you led your people through the borders of Seir in the region of the Edomites, the earth shook, and the heavens and the clouds distilled water, the mountains flowed from the face of the Lord Christ. Sinai from the face of the Lord God of Israel; which is added exegetically, because at Mount Sinai then lightning, thunder, rain, and earthquakes were seen; as Lyranus, Cajetan, Arias Montanus, and others rightly state. So that there is no need to posit with Tostatus that these things happened so literally: or to understand Kings and Princes metaphorically through the mountains, because they were moved during the transit through the regions of Edom; for nothing of the sort is read in Scripture, and the Israelites passed peacefully through the extreme borders of the Idumeans, Deut. 2. And if Deborah's discourse had been about the insolent disturbance of the nations; one should rather have been silent about the Idumeans, and spoken of the Moabites, Midianites, and Amorites, as Bonfrerius observes. But it is said to have begun from Seir, because when the Israelites were stationed at Mount Sinai from that side where Idumea was, and Mount Seir towards the east, the divine splendor first seemed to appear and arise from the fiery cloud, so that it seemed to come clearly from that region. Indeed, former benefits are recalled, so that the Israelites might still proclaim with a grateful mind that the Lord continues his grace. Cf. Ps. 69, 1. Deut. 33, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 4. CUM EXIRES DE SEIR.

Domine, cum populum tuum infiinibus Seir re- gione Edomitarum traduseres, terra mota est, cæliq; ac nubes destillarunt aquam, montes fluxerunt a fa- cie Domini Christi. Sinai a facie Domini Dei Israel; quod exegetice additur, quia in monte Sina tum visa fulgetra, tonitrua, pluviæ, terræ motus; ut re- cte Lyranus, Cajetanus, Ariasmontanus, & alii. Ut opus non sit cum Tostato statuere, quod hæc ita pro- prie contigerint: vel Reges & Principes metapho- rice intelligere per montes, quod commoti sint in transitu per regiones Edom; nihil enim tale legitur in Scriptura, & pacifice transiere Israelitæ per Idu- mæorum extremos fines Deut. 2. ac si de insolenti perturbatione gentium Deboræ sermo fuisset; de Idumæis silendum potius erat, & de Moabitis, Mi- dianitis, & Amorrhæis dicendum, ut observat Bon- frerius. De Seiro autem cepisse dicitur, quod Israe- litis ad montem Sinai consistentibus ab ea parte, ubi erat Idumæa, & mons Seir versus orientem pri- mum divinus splendor e nube ignea apparere & exoriri visus sit, ut plane ex ea regione venire vide- retur. Nimirum revocantur in memoriam pristina beneficia, ut adhuc continuare Dominus suam gratiam mente grata Israelitæ deprædicent. Cons. Pf. 69, 1. Deut. 33, 2.

## 5:6
Verse 6. THE PATHS CEASED) You would translate more correctly: public roads: these being deserted, the Israelites followed byways, as follows. It signifies that commerce was broken off. In the Hebrew, the paths ceased, which is to be understood not so much of public roads being worn out and commerce broken off, as of the corrupt state of the Church and the Republic, so that Osiander's paraphrase is to be preferred here entirely: The face of the Church and Republic was most miserable at that time. For although Shamgar slaughtered six hundred Philistines (Judg. III.), yet a true reformation of the Church did not follow that victory; nor was solid liberty recovered in the Republic. For both in matters of religion the people did not walk in the ways or commandments of the Lord: and in civil cases there were none who governed the Republic according to justice and equity.

Latin:

Vers. 6. QVIEVERVNT SEMITÆ) Rectius vertas itinera publica: iis desertis Israelitæ devia sectabantur, ut se- quitur. Significat commercia abrupta. In Ebræo, cessaverunt semitæ, quod non tam de itineribus publicis intritis, & abruptis commer- ciis, quam de corrupto Ecclesiæ & Reipubl. statu ac- cipiendum, ut præferenda hic omnino sit Osiandri paraphrasis: Miserrima erat facies Ecclesiæ & Rei- publicæ eo tempore. Etsi enim Samgar trucidavit sexcentos Philistæos (Judic. III.) tamen non est eam victoriam sequuta vera reformatio Ecclesiæ; nec recuperata est solida libertas in Republica. Nam & ratione religionis populus non incedebat in viis seu mandatis Domini: & in causis civilibus non erant, qui juxta justitiam & æquitatem guber- narent Rempublicam.

## 5:7
Verse 7. THE STRONG CEASED) In the Hebrew: פרזון that is, villages. And the towns and fields lay deserted on account of the plunderings of the Canaanites. Bonfrerius admits that all those skilled in Hebrew, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Cajetan with his Rabbi, Forster, Mercer, Vatablus, and the Tigurines translate it as villages, and that this interpretation is not rejected by the passages Esth. 9, 19. Ez. 38, 11. Zach. 2, 4. as also Deut. 3, 5. 1 Kings 6, 18. and that the sense is convenient, and yet he tries to defend the unusual meaning of the word, which the Vulgate and the LXX Interpreters rendered, with a clever comment, namely, that the strong are those who trust to dwell in an unwalled town; but the Vulgate is rightly corrected by Pagninus, Arias, and others, and here by Grotius; and Cornelius adopts that amendment; the villages ceased, namely, of the rustics, deserted on account of the incursions of the enemies. For the villagers themselves are noted metonymically, who ceased under the most grievous tyranny, and could not cultivate the field. Sixtin. Amama explains it as empty villages, destitute of inhabitants: so that the difficulties were greatest, not less in the Economy than in the Church and Republic, until Deborah arose, a mother in Israel, who, maternally affected towards the people, showed the Israelites again the paths of the word of God, in which they were to walk, and began to judge for this people, and exhorted her leader Barak, so that with a brave spirit he might vindicate and restore it to liberty.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CESSAVERUNT FORTES) In Hebræo: פרזון id est, pagi. Et villæ & agri deserti jacebant ob rapinas Ca- nanæorum. Omnes Ebraice peritos, Pagninum, Ariammon- tan. Cajetanum cum suo Rabbino, Forsterum, Mer- cerum, Vatablum, Tigurinos villas reddere, nec reji- ci eam interpretationem locis Esth. 9, 19. Ez. 38, 11. Zach. 2, 4. ut & Deut. 3, 5. 1. Reg. 6, 18. & quod sensus commodus sit, fatetur Bonfrerius, & tamen si- gnificationem vocis inusitatam, quam reddidit Vulgatus, & LXX. Interpp. tueri conatur lepido scil. commento, quod fortes sint, qui in oppido non murato habitare confidunt; sed recte corrigitur Vulgata a Pagnino, Aria & aliis, atque hic a Gro- tio; & assumit eam emendationem Cornelius; Ces- saverunt villæ scil. rusticorum ob grassationem ho- stium desertæ. Metonymice enim notantur ipsi vil- liçani, qui cessarunt sub gravissima tyrannide, nec agnum colere potuere. Sixtin. Amama de pagis va- cuis, destitutis habitatoribus explicat: ut ita diffi- cultates maximæ fuerint, non in Oeconomia mi- nus, quam in Ecclesia & Republ. donec surgeret Debora mater in Israel, quæ materné erga populum affecta ostendit iterum Israelitis semitas verbi Dei, in quibus ambulandum, tcepitq; jus dicere huic po- pulo, & Ducem suum Barac adhortata est, ut forti animo eum in libertatem vindicaret ac restitueret.

## 5:8
V. 8. THE LORD CHOSE NEW WARS. In the Hebrew, wars are not found. But what is new, which he chose, the added words explain: he himself overturned the gates of the enemies: A shield and spear (i.e., appeared) among forty thousand of Israel, that is, among many thousands (a certain number for an uncertain) there was almost no one who carried a shield or spear into the expedition against Sisera, so that the victory must be attributed solely to divine power. For the Israelites fought almost with mattocks, stakes, and other rustic instruments, especially at that time. Cf. 1 Sam. 13, 19. The LXX, Theodoret, Augustine, and Cajetan are different: Israel chose new gods, therefore he was delivered by God. Adelg. Pistat. Angl. Jun. Ital. Gen. Amam. with when Israel chose new gods, then they had enemies in the gates, which sense Bonfrerius does not disapprove. but here it is already a matter of those things which happened under mother Deborah, not of preceding times: nor is the interpretation alien to the Hebrew text, but it fits properly: Elohim chose new things, then war in the gates, i.e., of the enemies, which Jerome added for the sake of the sense, so that there is no need here to invent a change of points, as Bonfrerius himself admits: and so also B. Luther: God has chosen a new thing, he has fought the gates, whether the gates of the enemies themselves or the princes are understood by the name of gates: but that the gates are understood is persuaded by the text itself and confirmed by the comparison of verse 11: then the people of the Lord descended to the gates. The LXX also have the contrary sense about the spears: which the Hebrew text implies were lacking, although the copies of that version vary, about which Bonfrerius should be seen.

Latin:

V. 8. NOVA BELLA ELEGIT DOMINUS. In Ebr. bella non habentur. Quid autem novi sit, quod elegerit, addita verba explicant: portas hostium ipse subvertit: Clypeus & hasta (sc. apparuerunt) in quadraginta millibus Israel, hoc est, inter multa millia (numerus certus pro incerto) nemo fere fuit, qui clypeum aut hastam in expeditionem con- tra Siseram ferret, ut unice divinæ virtuti tribuen- da sit victoria. Pugnabant enim Israelitæ fere ligo- nibus, sudibus, & aliis instrumentis rusticis eo præ- sertim tempore Conf. 1. Sam. 13, 19. Aliene v. LXX. Theodor. August. Cajetanus: novos Deos elegit Israel, ideo traditus a Deo. Adelg. Pistat. Angl. Jun. Ital. Gen. Amam. cum novos Deos elegit Israel, tunc hostes in portis habuisse, quem sensum non im- probat Bonfrer. sed hic de iis, quæ sub matre Debora contigere, jam agitur, non de præcedentibus tem- poribus: neq; a textu Ebræo aliena est interpreta- tio, sed probe convenit: Elegit Elohim nova, tunc bellum in portis sc. hostium, quod sensus causa adje- cit Hieronymus, ut nullam hic opus sit fingere pun- ctorum mutationem, fatente ipso Bonfrerio: atq; ita etiam B. Luther: Ein neues hat GOtt erwählet, er hat die Thor bestritten, sive portæ ipsæ hostium sive principes nomine portarum intelligantur: sed in- telligi portas & τὸ ῥητὸν suadet & collatio v. 11. confirmat: tunc descendit ad portas populus Domini. Contrarium etiam sensum LXX. habent de hastis: quas defuisse Ebræus textus innuit, quanquam ver- sionis istius exemplaria varient, de quo Bonfrerius videatur.

## 5:9
Verse 9. BY THEIR OWN WILL) With a ready mind for obedience to God, as above 2.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PROPRIA VOLUNTATE) Animo promto in Dei obsequium, ut supra 2.

## 5:10
Ver. 10.

YOU WHO RIDE UPON SHINING DONKEYS) See below 10, 4. 12, 14. That was done because of the scarcity of horses in those lands, about which we spoke at Deut. 17, 16.

In the opinion of some, magistrates and subjects are joined together, those who sit in judgment, and those who walk in the life prescribed by the laws of their superiors, or also as Osiander says, You subjects, who do not ride horses, but go on foot. Junius understands those traveling as merchants. In sum, all are invited, those riding, those sitting in judgment, those walking on the way.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

QVI ASCENDITIS SVPER NITENTES ASINOS) Vide infra 10, 4. 12, 14. id factum ob equorum in illis terris penuriam, de qua diximus ad Deut. 17, 16.

Conjunguntur nonnullorum sententia Magi- stratus & subditi, qui sedent in judicio, & qui am- bulant in vita præscripta legibus superiorum, vel etiam ut Osiander, Vos subditi, qui non equitatis, sed pedibus ingredimini. Junius commeantes mercatores intelligit. Summa omnes invitantur equitantes, se- dentes in judicio, ambulantes in via.

## 5:11
V. 11. WHERE CHARIOTS WERE DASHED TOGETHER AND THE ARMY OF THE ENEMIES SUFFOCATED, THERE LET THE RIGHTEOUSNESSES OF THE LORD BE TOLD, AND THE CLEMENCY OF THE STRONG ONE IN ISRAEL. The Hebrew is conveniently rendered and explained by Osiander: from the voice of the archers among those drawing (water) there the righteousnesses of the Lord were given, the righteousnesses of the villagers in Israel. Then the people of the Lord descended to the gates, that is, at the torrent of Kishon, where water is drawn, the cries and groans of the dying were heard, whom the Israelites slaughtered: There God administered justice to His peasants, and severely punished the impious enemies and tyrants, of which justice the Israelites were the executors: then the Israelites, having obtained victory, also approached to occupy the cities of the enemies: so that the object is expressed, not the place for singing of righteousness: concerning the righteousness shown to the villages or villagers, Aldegond, Jun., Pisc., Engl. Amama notes that the Italian also explains it, rashly correcting the Belgian (Luther's) version, which easily already agrees with the Hebrew. The Tigurines, Piscator, and the Genevans also rendered it from the voice of the archers among the dying. And from this Osiandrine Paraphrase it is evident that the Hebrew text is un- deservedly accused of obscurity by Bonfrerius and Cornelius: from which Arias Montanus, Cajetan, Vatablus, and others more correctly correct the Vulgate, or at least explain it, whose interpretations Bonfrerius himself confesses to be excellent. Junius interpolates the text according to his custom (as does the English version), adding the word (liberated) from the noise of the archers among the drawing places, there they shall recount the righteous acts of Jehovah, that is, the boys and girls who, for the sake of drawing water, were undergoing the danger of life from the arrows of the enemies, meeting in the same place, shall proclaim the divine liberation: righteous acts (towards) their pagans in Israel (from) which the people of Jehovah descend to the gates, they meet at the chariot and the hearth, or go out from the towns for convenience, necessity, pleasure, or for any other cause whatsoever. If it is permissible to add words to the text, what certainty will there finally be? It is not about danger or being liberated from danger, nor about the place of the Lord's celebration, but about victory, which Jerome also observed in his version, and his passage is designated. Cornelius reconciles it thus with the Hebrew, from the word of the archers among those drawing water; when, namely, the Sisarian archers, having been precipitated into the waters of Kishon, drew them, and were drawn by them and suffocated, and to that opinion he praises Arias, Cajetan, and Vatablus. Then the people of the Lord descended to the gates and obtained the principality (which later things Jerome added for the sake of exegesis), that is, when Sisera was killed, Israel obtained the gates and the cities of the enemies.

NARRENTUR) The word here is Chaldean from תנה to narrate.

Latin:

V. 11. UBI COLLISI SUNT CURRUS ET HOSTIUM SUFFOCATUS EXERCITUS, IBI NARRENTUR JUSTITIÆ DOMINI, ET CLEMENTIÆ FORTIS IN ISRAEL. Ebræa ab Osiandro commode redduntur & expli- cantur: a voce Sagittariorum inter haurientes (aquas) ibi datæ sunt justitiæ Domini, justitiæ villicanorum in Israel. Tunc descendit ad portas populus Domini, id est, apud torrentem Cison, ubi hauritur aqua, au- diti sunt clamores & gemitus morientium, quos Israelitæ trucidarunt: Ibi Deus justitiam admini- stravit rusticis suis, & graviter animadvertit in im- pios hostes & tyrannos, cujus justitiæ executores fuerunt Israelitæ: tunc Israelitæ parta victoria ac- cesserunt etiam ad occupandas hostium urbes: ut objectum exprimatur non locus decantandæ jnsti- tiæ: de justitia exhibita pagis vel villicanis Aldegond. Jun. Pisc. Angl. Ital. etiam explicare notat Amame, temere corrigens Belgicam (Lutheri) versionem, quæ facile Ebræo jam consonat. A voce jaculatorum inter morientes etiam Tigurini, Piscator, Genevenses reddi- dere. Atq; ex hac Osiandrina Paraphrasi patet imme- rito Ebræum textum obfcuritatis argui a Bonfrerio & Cornelio : ex quo Ariasmontanus, Cajetanus, Va- tablus, & alii rectius corrigunt Vulgatam, aut cer- te explicant, quorum interpretationes optimas ef- se fatetur ipse Bonfrerius. Junius interpolat pro more suo textum (ut & Anglic. versio) addens vo- cem (liberati) a strepitu Sagittariorum inter haustus ibi confabulentur de justis operibus Jehovæ, id est, pueri & puellæ, qui ad hauriendum aquam discri- men vitæ subibant ab hostium Sagittis eodem loco convenientes divinam liberationem prædicent: justis operibus (erga) paganos suos in Israele (ex) quo descendant ad portas populus Jehove, conve- niunt ad currum & focum, aut ex oppidis exeunt commodi, necessitatis, voluptatis, aut alia qua- cunque de causa. Si integrum sit voces addere tex- tui, quæ tandem erit certitudo? Non de periculo aut liberatis e periculo, neq; de loco celebrationis Domini, sed de victoria agitur, quod observavit etiam in versione sua Hieronymus, ejusq; locus de- signatur. Quam ita cum Ebræo conciliat Cor- nelius, a voce sagittantium inter haurientes aquas; Cum sc. Sifariani Sagittarii præcipitati in aquas Ki- son eas hauserunt, & ab eis hausti suffocatiq; sunt, & in eam sententiam laudat Ariam, Cajetan. & Vatablum. Tunc descendit populus Domini ad portas & obtinuit principatum (quæ posteriora ἐξηγήσεως causa addidit Hieronymus) id est, quando occisus est Sisara, Israel obtinuit portas, & urbes hostium.

NARRENTUR) Vox hic est Chaldaica a תנה narrare.

## 5:12
Vers. 12. APPREHENDE CAPTIVOS TUOS. In Hebrew: Take those who take you captive.

Latin:

Vers. 12. APPREHENDE CAPTIVOS TUOS. In Ebræo: Cape captivantes te.

## 5:13
Vers. 13. SALVATÆ SUNT RELIQUIÆ POPULI, DOMINUS IN FORTIBUS DIMICAVIT. Cornelius here rightly prefers the Hebrew text: which holds thus: Then the remnants of the people dominated the excellent, that is, those who were previously oppressed and reduced to a small number, have now become masters of the proud Canaanites: The Lord dominated for me among the mighty, i.e., the Lord dominated for my good against the powerful enemies, and was subjecting them to me.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SALVATÆ SUNT RELIQUIÆ POPULI, DOMINUS IN FORTIBUS DIMI- CAVIT. Præfert hic merito Ebræum textum Corne- lius: qui ita habet: Tunc dominabantur reliquiæ præ- stantibus populi, id est, qui prius oppressi & ad pau- citatem redacti, jam facti sunt Domini superbi Ca- nanæorum: Dominus dominabatur mihi in forti- bus, i. e. Dominus meo bono dominabatur contra potentes hostes, eosque subjiciebat mihi.

## 5:14
Vers. 14. EX EPHRAIM DELEVIT EOS IN AMALEC. In Hebrew: From Ephraim their root against Amalek, that is, Joshua, who was as it were the root from which the victories arose, and from the tribe of Ephraim. Cf. Ex. 17, 13. There is therefore no reason for Cornelius to argue against the Hebrew text, as if it had no sense, and to correct its points so that the word eradicated might emerge; but he ought rather to have corrected his Vulgate's delevit and the τὸ ἐξέῥῥίζωσεν of the LXX interpreters.

Vers. eod. ET POST EUM EX BENJAMIN IN POPULOS TUOS O AMALEC. In Hebrew there is nothing about Amalek, which word the Vulgate added of its own accord, and it remains nonetheless in that version, as Cornelius confesses, a sense difficult and obscure: but the LXX in the edition of Rome amended have it as it is read in the Hebrew: after you Benjamin in your peoples, which Cornelius notes that the Chaldean, the Rabbis, Hugh of St. Victor, Abulensis, Lyranus, Dionysius the Carthusian, Arias, Vatablus, and others understand of Saul, who was born of Benjamin and who was about to strike down the Amalekites after Joshua, but Cornelius rejects it: and he understands it of the Amalekites bringing reinforcements to Sisera, slaughtered by the Ephraimites and Benjaminites, about which see in this history there is deep silence. And the interpretation of the Papists relies primarily on the Vulgate version; since, however, there is no mention of Amalek here in the Hebrew, the words are more correctly rendered: after you (Joshua)

Benjamin in your peoples, i.e., stood out: because Ehud was a distinguished leader of the people from the tribe of Benjamin, who killed Eglon and restored liberty to Israel, so that the land rested for 80 years.

From Machir came down the princes, and from Zabulon, they that lead the army to battle.

In the Hebrew in the latter member, Leaders with the rod of the scribe: Osiander understands the former of Shamgar, who slaughtered six hundred Philistines, the latter of Deborah, who was of the tribe of Zabulon: and governed the people, not so much by arms as by laws; for she herself did not handle arms, because she was a Prophetess, and thus she seemed to have administered the Republic with the pen of a scribe rather than with a scepter or sword. Aldegond, the English, Drusius, the Genevan, and Amama render it, from Zabulon who handle writing pens. And they are commended below v. 18, the Zabulonites for the assistance rendered, from which some think the scribes and doctors exchanged their pens and styli for arms, and descended into battle: but others more correctly think it is implied that they aspired to primary dignities through pens or administered the government with them, because that was especially proper to the Zabulonites. Simplicius therefore here understands the princes from Machir, or the tribe of Manasseh, whose son Machir was, and the leaders from Zabulon to have been present, so that the praise of assisting may be attributed to them, just as afterwards Zabulon and Naphtali, from which tribe Barak himself was, are specially celebrated, because they exposed their souls to danger in the region of Merone. The Junian Paraphrase relies on mere interpolations in v. 13, 14, 15, and does not even deserve discussion here.

Latin:

Vers. 14. EX EPHRAIM DELEVIT EOS IN AMALEC. In Ebr. De Ephraim Radix eorum contra A- malek, id est, Josua, qui fuit veluti radix, ex qua exortæ victoriæ sunt, & ex tribu Ephraim. Conf. Ex. 17, 13. Non ergo est, quod arguat textum E- bræum Cornelius, quasi nullum habeat sensum, ejusque puncta corrigat, ut prodeat verbum era- dicavit; sed vulgatæ suæ delevit, & τὸ ἐξέῥῥίζωσεν LXX. Interpp. corrigere potius debuit.

Vers. eod. ET POST EUM EX BENJA- MIN IN POPULOS TUOS O AMALEC. In Ebræo nihil de Amalec, quam vocem de suo addidit Vulgatus, & manet nihilominus in ea versione, fatente Cornelio, sensus difficilis & ob- scurus: sed LXX. in editione Romæ emendata ha- bent, uti in Ebræo legitur: post te Benjamin in popu- lis tuis, quod de Saule e Benjamin oriundo, qui post Josuam Amalecitas prostravurus erat, Chaldæum, Rabbinos, Hugonem de S. Victore, Abulensem, Ly- ranum, Dionyf. Carthuf. Ariam, Vatablum & alios intelligere notat, sed reprobat Cornelius: & de Amalecitis suppetias Sisaræ ferentibus ab Ephrai- mitis & Benjaminatis trucidatis intelligit, de quo v. in hac historia altum est silentium. Et nititur in- terpretatio Pontificiorum imprimis vulgata ver- sione; quum v. in Ebræo hic nulla Amalek mentio habeatur, rectius verba redduntur: post te (Josua)

Benjamin in populis tuis, sc. eminuit: quia Ehud in- signis Dux populi e tribu Benjamin fuit, qui Eglo- nem interfecit, & Israeli libertatem restituit, ut terra 80. annis quiesceret.

DE MAGHIR PRINCIPES DESCENDE- RUNT ET DE ZABULON, QUI EXERCI- TUM DUCERENT AD BELLANDUM.

In Hebræo in posteriori membro, Duces in virga scribæ: Prius de Samgar intelligit Osiander, qui sex- centos trucidavit Philistæos, posterius de Debora, quæ fuerit de tribu Zabulon: & populum guber- narit, non tam armis quam legibus; ipsa enim arma non tractavit, quia Prophetissa fuit, adeog; visa est stylo scribæ potius quam sceptro aut gladio admi- nistrasse Remp. Aldegond. Angli, Drus. Genev. & Amama reddunt, e Zabulon qui calamos scriptorios tractant. Et commendantur infra v. 18. Zabuloni- tæ ob præstitam παράστασιν, e quibus nonnulli scri- bas & doctores putant calamos & stylos suos in ar- mos commutasse, & in prælium descendisse: rectius v. alii per calamos ad dignitates primarias eos ad- spirasse aut iisdem gubernationem administrasse innui censent, quod Zabulonitis imprimis proprium id fuerit. Simplicius ergo hic principes de Machir, vel Manassis tribu, cujus filius Machir fuit, & Du- ces de Zabulon adfuisse intelliguntur, ut illis laus assistentis tribuatur, quemadmodum postea spe- cialiter Zabulon, & Naphthali, e qua tribu ipse Ba- rack fuit celebrantur, quod animas suas periculo in regione Merone exposuerint. Juniana Paraphrasis meris fere interpolationibus nititur v. 13. 14. 15. ac ne discussionem quidem hic meretur.

## 5:15
Vers. 15. DIVISO CONTRA SE RUBEN, MAGNANIMORUM REPERTA EST CONTENTIO.

Which words are afterwards repeated v. 16. Serarius accepts them as spoken in praise of the Reubenites. Most others believe they are rebuked: some indeed, because the Reubenites were of different opinions concerning bringing aid: those who attend to the Hebrew text, in which nothing is held concerning those contentions, wish the division of the Reubenites from the Israelites to be rebuked, which provided a great occasion for Barak's associates to speak about that matter, with different people opining different things and searching for the causes of such a great division, as Bonfrerius explains: Vatablus and Piscator render it, concerning the divisions of Reuben, that is, concerning the Reubenites separated by the Jordan from the others, as he explains; I wonder vehemently that they did not come to bring aid to their brothers: For the heart was debating within itself, why they had not come to the battle. Aldeg. and the English thus: in the separation of Reuben arise great thoughts of the heart: Junius indeed with the Italian version, great are the purposes of the mind in the parts of Reuben, whose gloss should be seen. Which version Amama adapts here to the context by the form of a question, you great-minded ones of the parts of Reuben? why did you sit between two sheepfolds? &c. But it should have been said in the plural thus, why did you sit? The Osiandrian paraphrase is simpler: in the divisions of Reuben there are great thoughts of the heart, that is, Reuben withdrew himself from us in this public danger, despising our small number, and thinking proudly of himself, and afterwards of the following verse, for the divisions of Reuben there are great searchings of the heart, that is, from this separation of yours your heart can easily be known toward your brothers. For while the Church is in danger, the thoughts of many hearts are revealed Luke 2. What would it matter, that the judgments and contentions of others be referred to in the Song concerning the separation of the Reubenites, when their own pride was rather rebuked? Thus Musculus thinks their swelling and pride are being censured, as if they were unwilling to follow the commands and auspices of the woman Deborah. He who for divisions renders streams in streams, or rivulets, calls the places of the Reubenites streams, for they had obtained fertile pastures by the river Jordan: he indeed attributes to them prudence and greatness, but accuses them on this account, that they cared only for their own affairs.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DIVISO CONTRA SE RUBEN, MAGNANIMORUM REPERTA EST CON- TENTIO.

Quæ verba postea repetuntur v. 16. Serarius ut in laudem Rubenitarum dicta accipit. Alii ple- riq; omnes eos reprehendi credunt: nonnulli qui- dem, quod diversis sententiis fuerint Rubenitæ de ferendis suppetiis: qui v. textui Hebræo attendunt, in quo de istis contentionibus nihil habetur, divisio- nem Rubenitarum ab Israelitis reprehendi volunt, quæ magnam occasionem Barac sociis ea de re lo- quendi præbuerit, diversa diversis opinantibus & causas tantæ divisionis scrutantibus, ut Bonfrerius explicat: Vatablus & Piscator reddunt, de divisioni- bus Ruben, id est, de Rubenitis Jordane separatis ab aliis, ut ille exponit; vehementer miror, quod non venerint, ut opem ferrent fratribus suis: Cor enim disceptabat apud se, cur illi non venissent ad præ- lium. Aldeg. & Angl. ita: in separatione Rubenis ori- untur magnæ cogitationes cordis: Junius vero cum Ital. versione, magni institutis animi in partibus Ru- benis, cujus glossa videatur. Quam versionem contextui hic aptat Amama per interrogationis formam, vos magnanimi de partibus Rubenis? cur sedisti inter duas caulas? &c. Sed ita pluraliter dicen- dum fuisset, cur sedistis? Simplicior Osiandrina est paraphrasis: in divisionibus Ruben magnæ sunt co- gitationes cordis, id est, Ruben sese in hoc publico periculo a nobis subtraxit, aspernata paucitatem nostram, & superbe de seipsa sentiens, & postea versus sequentis ad divisiones Ruben magnæ sunt in- vestigationes cordis, id est ex hac separatione tua fa- cile cor tuum erga fratres agnosci potest. Dum enim Ecclesia periclitatur, revelantur multorum cordium cogitationes Luc. 2. Quid attineret, in Cantico aliorum judicia & contentiones referri de separatione Rubenitarum, quum reprehensa ipsorummet potius fuerit superbia? Ita Musculus eorum tumorem & superbiam perstringi censet, q. mulieris Deboræ jussa & auspicia sequi nolue- rint: Qui pro divisionibus reddit rivos in rivis, vel rivulis; loca Rubenitarum vocat rivos, nam ad flu- men Jordanem felicia pascua sortiti erant: tribuit quidem eis prudentiam, & magnitudinem, sed eo nomine accusat, quod sua tantum curarint.

## 5:16
Ver. 16. WHY DO YOU DWELL BETWEEN TWO BOUNDARIES?

Some explain it thus with Bonfrerius, why do you sit between two hedges, or sheepfolds? others, why do you remain idle in your land situated between the two boundaries of Moab and Canaan? But since this word also signifies a battle line, it is more correctly rendered in this place with the Chaldean, why do you dwell between two battle lines? do you show yourself neutral between the army of Sisera and the battle line of the people of God? awaiting the outcome of the battle: so that you may hear the hissings, or rather the bleating of the flocks, i.e., that you may meanwhile attend to your own livestock business? Some, allegorically, as Musculus notes, think that the lamentations and complaints of the flock of Israel, i.e., the people of God, are indicated as being neglected. Cornelius also approves of our sense: as if to say, you prefer to feed your flocks and hear their bleatings and the hissings of the shepherds, rather than the sound of my trumpet; you prefer the quiet of an estate to the labor and danger of battle.

Latin:

Vers. 16. QUARE HABITAS INTER DUOS TERMINOS?

Nonnulli sic exponunt cum Bonfrerio, cur in- ter duas sepes, vel septa ovium sedes? alii cur in terra tua inter duos terminos Moab & Canaan sita desides? Sed quum hæc vox etiam aciem significet, rectius cum Chaldæo redditur hoc loco, quare inter duas acies habitas? inter Sisaræ exercitum & populi Dei aciem te neutralem præbes? eventum pugnæ ex- pectans: ut audias sibilos, vel potius balatum gre- gum, i.e. rem tuam pecuariam interea cures? Non- nulli allegorice, notante Musculo gregis Israel, h. e. populi Dei lamentationes & querimonias negle- ctas indicari putant. Sensum nostrum probat etiam Cornelius: q.d. mavis greges tuos pascere eorumq; balatus, & pastorum sibilos audire, quam buccinæ meæ sonitum, mavis quietem prædii, quam labo- rem, & discrimen prælii.

## 5:17
Ver. 17. GILEAD REMAINED BEYOND THE JORDAN AND DAN WAS OCCUPIED WITH SHIPS. ASHER DWELT ON THE SEASHORES.

Just as Junius thinks that by the former apostrophe to Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, those tribes are called to the obedience of Deborah, so he also takes these words concerning Gilead, Dan, and Asher in the same way. But it is manifest that all those who are reproved are not called to perform homage: although Musculus thinks otherwise concerning Gilead and establishes an ἀντωποφορὰν here; You indeed, Reuben, dwell by the banks of the Jordan, and Gilead dwelt in the same place, who nevertheless betook himself to the war, but he acknowledges concerning Dan and Asher that they are taxed here. The same doubt arises, how is Dan said to have been occupied with ships, when his lot did not fall by the sea? Therefore they understand it of the ships of the Jordan, not as if Dan had been situated entirely at the Jordan, but that this tribe, having seen the armies, was struck with terror and threw itself into ships, in order to cross over to the Reubenites. But Bonfrerius rightly observes that the tribe of Dan was contiguous to the Palestinians by the Mediterranean Sea, and that in this tribe there was a port called Joppa; concerning which see Adrichom. Asher was also by the sea, but more northerly than the tribe of Dan, bordered on the East by the Naphtalites and Zebulonites: into whose lot Tyre and Sidon, equipped with convenient ports, had fallen as trading centers, which, although the Asherites never possessed, they nevertheless had other ports of less renown.

Latin:

Vers. 17. GALAAD TRANS JORDANEM QUIESCEBAT ET DAN VACABAT NA- VIBUS. ASER HABITABAT IN LITTORI- BUS MARIS.

Junius ut per Apostrophen priorem ad Rube- nem, Gad, & Manassen, tribus illas ad obsequium Deboræ vocari putat, ita etiam hæc, de Galaad, Dan & Ascher eo accipit. At reprehendi omnes il- los manifestum est, non ad Homagium præstan- dum vocari: etsi Musculus de Galaad secus sentiat, & ἀντωποφορὰν hic statuat; Tu quidem Ruben habitas ad ripas Jordanis, & ibidem Gilead habitavit, qui ta- men ad bellum se contulit, qui vero de Dan & Aser agnoscit, quod hic taxentur. Dubium idem movet, quomodo Dan dicatur vacasse navibus, cum sors ejus juxta mare non obtigerit? ideo de navibus Jor- danis intelligunt, non quasi Dan ad Jordanem penitꝫ situs fuerit, sed quod hæc tribus visis exercitibus pa- vore percussa in naves se conjecerit, quo ad Rube- nitas transmitteret. Sed recte observat Bonfrerius, quod tribus Dan Palæstinis contigua ad mare me- diterraneum, & in hac tribu portus fuerit Joppe ap- pellatus; de quo vide Adrichom. Erat & Aser ad mare, sed Borealior tribu Dan, ab Oriente Neph- thalitis & Zabulonitis contermina: in cujus sor- tem Tyrus & Sidon portibus commodis instructa emporia ceciderant, quibus etsi nunquam Aseritæ potiti sunt, alios tamen minoris nominis portus habuere.

## 5:18
Ver. 18. In THE REGION OF MEROM.

In the Hebrew: in the height of the field: because those soldiers had been led up onto Mount Tabor: from which place they could survey the entire army of the adversaries with their eyes: but they were by no means so terrified by that sight that they desisted from their undertaking.

Latin:

Vers. 18. In REGIONE MEROME.

In Ebræo: in sublimitate campi: quod ii mili- tes in montem Thabor educti fuerint: ex quo loco universum exercitum adversariorum oculis lustra- re poterant: sed eo conspectu nequaquam ita per- territi sunt, ut ab incepto desisterent.

## 5:20
Ver. 20. THE STARS REMAINING IN THEIR ORDER AND COURSE FOUGHT AGAINST SISERA) i.e., the Angels fought against them as if from a higher place. Cf. 2 Macc. 10, 29. 11, 8. מסלות are high places. Angels are called by the name of stars because of their celestial nature and splendor.

We easily admit that Angels are called Stars because of their celestial nature and splendor, I add because of their beauty, purity, incorruptibility, and constancy. For they are called Morning Stars, Job 38, 7. To whom also the name of Star is attributed in Rev. 12. It seems to Fr. Spanheim, part 2, dub. Evang. 33, p. 352, from a comparison of verses 4 and 9. Although Grotius is mistaken in that he attributes a celestial nature to Angels in such a way that he makes them most subtle bodies according to Ps. 104, 4, which is repugnant to their spiritual essence. But we shall weigh that in that place §. θ. Here, however, it does not appear that Angels ought to be understood by the stars. For the added description teaches that the discourse is about stars placed in the firmament: While the stars are said to have fought remaining in their order and course. Which agrees with the heavenly bodies observing their course and order in the sky, which happened differently than in the time of Joshua, not with Angels. For these, when they fight for the faithful on earth, stand by them. Just as can be seen in the cited passages from the second book of Maccabees. Whence most take it concerning the influence of the Stars upon the air to excite various Meteors, thunders, lightnings, winds, and hail, from which Sisera suffered a notable defeat, as Josephus testifies, book 5, Antiq. c. 6, who says that in the very battle a great rain, and much water, and hail supervened, and that the storm drove into the faces of the opposing Canaanites, knocked the shields from their arms, and by this means threw their weapons, battle line, and ranks into confusion; and on the contrary gave courage to the Israelites, and a sense of the help of God. Similar things are read under Samuel, 1 Sam. 7, and Emperor Theodosius against the tyrants Eugenius and Maximus, as Eusebius testifies. Which explanation has approved itself to Cajetan, Tostatus, Lyranus, Delrio, Menochius, Tirinus, and others. To this point serves what the Rabbis say in the tractate Berachot, that all things, both those in the heavens and those on the earth, fought against Sisera for the Jews.

Some seek an argument from this for the astrologers: but that is futile: because the discussion here is not about the natural influence of the stars, but about a supernatural direction; not about an ordinary action, but an extraordinary one; not about an influence upon the wills and counsels of men, but for producing meteors: nor can it be supposed that all who fell here were born and brought forth under the same position of the stars. Those explain it most simply who say that the stars are said to have fought in a poetic phrase, because the victory happened from heaven, and all things favored the Jews just as if the stars themselves had fought for them, as Osiander's paraphrase has it, explaining it thus: God himself fought against our enemies, by sending such terror upon them that they could not withstand our attack, and (as there is also a proverb among the Germans) no star wished to shine for them. No star wished to shine for them, all the elements were against them, or the very machinery of this world was opposed to them. The authors of the notes to the Belgian version also incline toward this.

Latin:

Vers. 20. STELLÆ MANENTES IN ORDINE ET CVRSV SVO ADVERSVS SISERAM PVGNAVERVNT) i. e. Angeli velut de loco superiore in eos pugnaverunt. Conf. 2. Macc. 10, 29. 11, 8. מסלות sunt loca celsa. An- geli stellarum nomine appellantur ob naturam cœlestem, & splendorem.

Angelos Stellas nominari ob naturam cœle- stem & splendorem, addo ob pulchritudinem, puri- tatem, incorruptibilitatem & constantiam facile ad- mittimus. Vocantur enim Stellæ matutinæ Job. 38, 7. Quibus etiam nomen Stellæ tribui Apoc. 12. Fr. Spanhemio part. 2. dub. Evang. 33. p. 352. videtur ex collatione v. 4. & 9. Quanquam in eo fallatur Gro- tius, quod naturam cœlestem Angelis ita tribuat, ut corpora subtilissima eos faciat ad Ps. 104, 4. quod spi- t rituali eorum effentiæ repugnat. Sed id isto loco ex- pendemus §. θ. Hic vero per stellas intelligi debere Angelos, non apparet. De stellis enim in firmamen- to positis sermonem esse descriptio addita docet: Dum Stellæ pugnasse dicuntur manentes in ordine & cursu suo. Quæ syderibus in cœlo cursum & ordi- nem suum observantibus, secus atq; Josuæ tempore accidit, convenit, non Angelis. Hi enim cum pu- gnant pro fidelibus in terris, adsistunt iisdem. Quemadmodum in allegatis e secundo Maccabæorum videre est. Unde de influxu Syderum in aerem ad excitanda Meteora varia, tonitrua, fulmina, ven- tos, grandinem pleriq; accipiunt, a quibus Sissera cladem insignem passus est, teste Josepho l. 5. Antiq. c.6. qui ait, in ipsa pugna supervenisse ὄμβρον μέγαν, καὶ ὕδωρ πολὺ, καὶ χάλαζαν, & eventum illam tem- pestatem in vultus adversos Chananæorum impegisse, scu- ta armis excussisse, & hac ratione tela, aciem & ordines illorum turbasse; Israëlitis contra dedisse animum, & ἐννοίαν τῆς βοηθείας τῦ Θεῦ. Similia leguntur sub Sa- muele 1. Sam. 7. & Imper. Theodosio contra Eugenium & Maximum Tyrannos, teste Eusebio. Quæ explica- tio Cajetano, Tostato, Lyrano, Delrio, Menochio, Ti- rino, aliis sese probavit. Huc facit, quod Rabbini in tractatu Berachot ajunt, omnia & quæ in cælis & quæ in terris, pugnasse contra Sisseram pro Judæis.

Nonnulli pro Genethliacis inde Argumentum petunt: Sed id futile est: quia non de influxu Syde- rum naturali, sed directione supernaturali hic ser- mo est, non de actione ordinaria, sed extraordinaria, non de influxu in voluntates & consilia hominum, sed ad Meteora producenda: neque censeri potest omnes, qui hic ceciderunt, eodem Syderum positu in lucem editos ac prognatos esse. Simplicissime explicant, qui dicunt Phrasi poetica sidera pugnasse dici, quod cælitus obtigerit victoria, omniaq; ita Ju- dæis faverint, ac si Stellæ etiam ipsæ pro iisdem decer- tarint, uti paraphrasis Osiandri habet, sic explicans: Deus ipse pugnavit contra hostes nostros, immittendo illis tantum terroris; ut impressionem nostram non sustinerent, & (ut Germanis etiam proverbium est) nulla stella illis lucere voluerit. Es hat ihnen kein Stern leuchten wollen, alle Element seyn wider sie gewesen, seu ipsa hujus mundi machina adversata est illis. Eo etiam propendent auctores notarum ad versionem Belgicam.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. TORRENT CADUMIM.

Others [translate it as] of antiquities, Vatablus of the number of the ancients: Musculus notes that some translate it as of the ancients, that is to say, of counsels, because God himself from the foundations of the world destined him for this, that he might devote his effort to Him in this victory. It is more correctly held as a synonym for the torrent Kishon: because of the repetition customary among the Hebrews, especially in poetry. Concerning which Jerome in the Hebrew Places: Cadumim is a torrent, near which Deborah waged war: Adrichomius notes that a certain stream proceeding from the torrent Kishon is called Cadumim.

Latin:

Vers. 21. TORRENS CADUMIM.

Alii antiquitatum, Vatabl. de numero priscorum: Musculus notat quosdam vertere antiquorum, ni- mirum consiliorum, quod ipse Deus a jactis mundi fundamentis illum ad id destinavit, ut in hac victo- ria sibi operam navaret. Rectius habetur pro Syno- nymo torrentis Cison: ob repetitionem Ebræis, imprimis in poesi usitatam. Quo de Hieronymus in Locis Hebr. Cadumim torrens, juxta quem Debora bellum gessit: Adrichomius notat, rivulum quendam ex torrente Cison procedentem Cadumim vocari.

## 5:23
Vers. 23. CURSED BE THE LAND OF MEROZ) Let them be infamous. The crime of ἀποταξία, i.e., refusing military service, was serious at Athens, as we learn from Demosthenes, his scholiast Ulpian, and Harpocration. Much more justly are those to be held infamous who had been absent from a war commanded by God.

Pagninus wishes it to be the land of Merom: concerning which [see] Josh. 11:7. which is cursed, so that it becomes the land of Merotz, i.e., lean and sterile, instead of Merom, which word denotes height. It is cursed above others, who did not bring aid, because those [others] might be worthy of pardon due to the distance of places or other causes, in comparison, whereas these lacked only the spirit to help, not the ability, nor the opportunity.

Latin:

Vers. 23. MALEDICTE TERRÆ MEROZ) Infames sint. Grave erat Athenis ἀποταξία, i. e. detrectatæ militiæ crimen, ut ex Demosthene, Scholiaste ejus Ulpiano & Har- pocratione discimus. Multo justius infames habendi qui bello defuerant imperato divinitus.

Terram Merom esse vult Pagninus: de qua Jos. 11, 7. cui maledicitur, ut fiat terra Merotz, i. e. macilenta, & sterilis, pro Merom, quæ vox celsitudinem notat. Ma- ledicitur ei præ aliis, qui suppetias non tulerunt, quod illi ob distantiam locorum aliasve causas digni venia, in comparatione, essent, his a. solus defuerit animus succurrendi, non facultas, nec commoditas.

## 5:25
Vers. 25. AND IN A BOWL OF PRINCES SHE OFFERED BUTTER) In the Hebrew here and below 6:39 is ספל, whence the name of the simpulum came to the Lydians, from the Lydians to the Etruscans, and thence to the Romans. Varro interprets it as a cyathus in book 4, and Festus and the Greco-Latin glossaries do not interpret it otherwise. Pliny also mentions it in book 35, chapter 12.

The 'bowl of the princes' is the prince, or the chief; the Hebrew word denotes anything illustrious and chief in its kind: by butter most understand the cream and fatness of milk. R. D. Kimchi, however, takes it properly of butter, which provided not only drink, but also food: whence by the name of bowl a kind of vessel is to be understood, in which food is also accustomed to be served.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ET IN PHIALA PRINCIPUM OBTULIT BUTTRUM) In Hebræo hic & infra 6, 39. est ספל, unde simpuli nomen ad Lydos, a Lydis ad Etruscos, inde ad Ro- manos venit. Cyathum interpretatur Varro l. 4. nec aliter Festus & Glossæ Græcolatinæ. Meminit & Plinius l. 35. c. 12.

Phiala Principum est princeps, vel præcipua; vox Ebræa notat quodvis illustre & præcipuum in suo genere: per butyrum lactis cremorem & pinguedinem plerique intelligunt. R. D. Kimchi vero de butyro proprie accipit, quod non tantum potum, sed etiam cibum dederit: unde phialæ nomine genus vasis intelligendum, in quo & cibus apponi soleat.

## 5:28
Ver. 28.

LOOKING OUT THROUGH THE WINDOW) This one passage shows that those nations had very poetic thoughts.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

PER FENESTRAM RESPICIENS) Ostendit vel hic unus locus illis gentibus ἐννοίας valde poeticas fuisse.

## 5:31
Ver. 31. BUT THEY THAT LOVE THEE, AS THE SUN SHINETH IN HIS RISING, SO LET THEM SHINE.

In Hebrew: in his virility, in his strength. LXX. ἐν δυναμίᾳ αὐτῶ̃. They shall shine in this and the future age: Compare Eccl. 27, 12. Wisd. 3, 7. Matt. 13, 43.

Latin:

Vers. 31. QUI AUTEM DILIGUNT TE, SICUT SOL IN ORTU SUO SPLENDET, ITA RUTILENT.

In Ebræo: in virilitate, in fortitudine sua. LXX. ἐν δυναμίᾳ αὐτῶ̃. Splendebunt in hoc & futuro seculo: Confer. Eccl. 27, 12. Sap. 3, 7. Matth. 13, 43.

## 5:31
Ver. 32. AND THE LAND HAD REST FORTY YEARS.

It must be rendered, in the fortieth year after the rest previously restored to the land by Ehud: within which space the time of Shamgar is also to be included, who after Ehud delivered Israel, having struck 600 Philistines with an ox goad c. 3, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 32. QUIEVITQUE TERRA PER QUADRAGINTA ANNOS.

Reddendum est, anno quadragesimo post priorem quietem ab Ehude terræ redditam: intra quod spatium etiam Samgari tempus concludendum, qui post Ehudem Israelem vindicavit, percussis 600. Philistæis stimulo bovis c. 3, 21.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. Gideon's calling, and sign.

Ver. 1. INTO THE HAND OF MIDIAN.

It was different from the Midian into which Moses fled near the Red Sea to the east Ex. 2. This Midian was neighboring to the Moabites, whose inhabitants were cut off Num. 31, 2: some, however, having then fled, returned and inhabited that region with certain neighbors.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. Gideonis vocatio, & signum.

Vers. 1. IN MANU MADIAN.

ALia fuit a Madian, in quam fugit Moses juxta mare rubrum ad orientem Ex. 2. hæc Madian Moabitis vicina, cujus incolæ Num. 31, 2. excisi: nonnulli tamen tum profugi reversi cum vicinis quibusdam eam regionem inhabitarunt.

## 6:3
Ver. 3. AND THE REST OF THE NATIONS OF THE EAST.

Heb. Children of the East, begotten of Abraham by Keturah Gen. 25, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CÆTERIQUE ORIENTALIUM NATIONUM.

Ebr. Filii Orientis, Abraham e Cethura progeniti Gen. 25, 6.

## 6:4
Ver. 4. AND PITCHING TENTS AMONG THEM, AS THEY WERE IN THE HERBAGE, THEY WASTED EVERYTHING)

Clarius in the Hebrew: They pitched camps against them, and wasted the fruits of the earth: that is to say, every year at the empty time before the new sowing, they returned about the time of harvest: see below 33. Herodotus in Clio relates a clearly similar stratagem of Alyattes against the Milesians: he waged war on the Milesians, having received the war from his father; for he besieged Miletus in the following manner, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET APVD EOS FIGENTES TENTORIA SICVT ERANT IN HERBIS CVNCTA VASTABANT)

Clarius in Hebræo: Castra ponebant adversus eos, & vastabant fruges terræ: quotannis scilicet dato tempore vacuo ad novam sementem, sub messis tempus revertebantur: vide infra 33. Plane simile artificium Alyattæ contra Milesios narrat Herodotus Clio: ἐπολέμησε Μιλησίοισι παραδεξάμενος τὸν πόλεμον παρὰ τ̃υ πατρὸς· ἐπελάνων γὰρ, ἐπολιόρκησε τὴν Μίλητον τρόπῳ τοιῷδε. &c.

## 6:12
Ver. 12. THE ANGEL OF THE LORD APPEARED] Maimonides thinks this happened in a dream.

Latin:

Vers. 12. APPARVIT ANGELVS DOMINI] In somnio hoc factum putat Maimonides.

## 6:14
Ver. 14. AND THE LORD LOOKED UPON HIM]

יהוה is thus called the Angel, because he acted in the place and with the power of God, as has already been noted often.

The Angel is nowhere in the Scriptures called Jehovah in the nominative case for the reason that he acted in the place and with the power of God. Nor do Angels act in the place of God, nor does God, who is everywhere present, need such a vicar: much less is it fitting that the essential and incommunicable name of God be attributed to an Angelic minister: which will not be taught by any example either; We have treated of this at length, and expressly, against Socinus and those who agree with him in Natural and Revealed Theology, p. 326 seqq., and we have proved that the name Jehovah is not, and cannot be, attributed to Angels as Legates, who in some way sustain the person of God. If Angels sustain the person of God in such a way that they have his authority at the same time, and do not act or speak otherwise than if God himself were present, they would certainly have to be treated with the honor proper to God alone, with the worship of religious adoration and invocation, and confusion could not but arise in the Sacred history of the Theophany and Angelophany. But here, not some created Angel—which Grotius, along with the Socinians, Bucer, as also Arias Montanus, Tostatus, Vatablus, Serarius, and other Papists, maintains—but the Son of God, the uncreated Angel, appeared; that not an angelophany, but a theophany is described, we have confirmed with many arguments in the cited book, p. 422. Not only from the attribution of the name Jehovah; because if it is asked who that was, no more certain answer will be had than from the Holy Spirit himself, who asserts in v. 14 that he was Jehovah himself: But also from the divine mission of Gideon in verse 14, if indeed he sent him in such a way that by the power of this calling he could miraculously rescue and save the people, 'Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of Midian, have not I sent thee?' i.e., do you still doubt that you will rescue and save the people, when I myself, the Lord of all things, have sent you? Then from Gideon's address: for he calls him who appeared to him here Adonai, with Kamez, which name does not befit any Angel or creature, but is proper to God alone: 'I beseech thee,' he says, 'Adonai, my Lord.' Furthermore, from the promise of gracious assistance also. For he who so promises his presence and assistance that by his benefit victory is undoubtedly to be obtained, and that a miraculous one, he is truly God himself, the author of all victory and miracles. But here the Angel thus promises his presence in v. 16: 'Because I will be with thee, thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man.' Moreover, from the request for a miracle. Because for that purpose Gideon sought a miracle, that he might be certain that this Angel was Jehovah himself, verse 17: 'If I have found grace in thy sight, then thou shalt show me a sign that thou art he that talketh with me,' i.e., that you yourself have deigned to speak with me in person. He desires, therefore, the grace of divine favor, as that phrase is understood in Gen. 6:18, c. 19:19, Exod. 33:12, 13, 16, c. 34:9, Num. 11:11, 15, 2 Sam. 15:21, Jer. 31:2. Further, from the offering of a Sacrifice. Since, having recognized the divine presence from the conversation itself, he wished to offer a sacrifice to him who was speaking with him. For sacrifices are not to be offered except to the one God. Moreover, from the designation of the miracle. For that Angel miraculously drew fire from the Rock by the divine power, by the mere touch of the tip of his staff, with which fire the flesh and unleavened flour were consumed; and Jehovah (thus the Angel is called) said to Gideon: 'Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die.' Add that the Angel himself offered the sacrifice here, as Theodoret observes. Which certainly does not befit a created Angel. For no created Angel undertakes the office of a Priest. But it befits the Son of God, as the eternal High Priest, to offer sacrifice. Therefore, the Son of God was seen here, not an Angelic minister. To which, finally, is added what is held in verse 23 from the Junian translation: 'And Gideon built there an altar unto Jehovah, when he had proclaimed peace to him himself,' that is, when he had confirmed him both concerning the common salvation of the Israelites and concerning his own particular one (For he was trembling from the sight of Jehovah, and was despairing of his own life). The Weimar Theologians, as well as the authors of the Belgian Notes from the Reformed, agree with us here, along with most others of our own. Compare the dissertation of our Dr. Dorscheus on the name Jehovah, § 26.

Latin:

Vers. 14. RESPEXITQVE AD EVM DOMINVS]

יהוה sic vocatur Angelus, quia Dei vice & potestatem gerebat, ut jam sæpe annotatum est.

Angelus nuspiam in Scripturis in casu recto vocatur Jehovah ideo, quod Dei vices ac potestatem gesserit. Neque Angeli aut Dei vicem gerunt, aut tali vicario Deus ubique præsens indiget: multo minus convenit, ut Angelo ministro nomen Dei essentiale, & incommunicabile tribuatur: quod nullo etiam exemplo docebitur; Egimus de eo prolixe, & ex professo adversus Socinum, & qui ei adstipulantur in Theologia naturali & revelata p. 326. seqq. ac probavimus, nomen Jehovah neǵ, tribui, neǵ, tribui posse Angelis ut Legatis, personam Dei aliquaratione sustinentibus. Si Angeli Dei personam ita sustinent, ut ejus auctoritatem simul habeant, nec aliter se gerant ac loquantur, quam si Deus ipse adesset, utique honore soli Deo proprio, cultu religiosæ adorationis & invocationis prosequendi fuerint, nec poterit non oriri confusio in historia Sacra τῆς Θεοφανείας & ἀγγελοψίας. Hic vero non Angelum aliquem creatum; quod cum Socinianis, Bucero, ut & Ariamontano, Tostato, Vatablo, Serario, aliisque Papistis vult Grotius, sed Fi- lium Dei Angelum increatum apparuisse, non ἀγγελοφίαν, sed θεοφανείαν describi, multis Argu- mentis libro citato firmavimus p. 422. Non tan- tum e nominis Jehovah attributione; quia si quæra- tur, quisnam ille fuerit, non habebitur certior re- sponsio, quam ab ipsomet Spiritu Sancto, qui Je- hovam ipsum fuisse v. 14. asserit: Sed etiam e divina Gideonis missione vers. 14. siquidem ita illum mi- serit, ut virtute hujus vocationis miraculose popu- lum eripere, & servare potuerit, vade in hac forti- tudine tua, & salvum facies Israel de manu Mi- diam, nonne misi te? q. d. adhuc dubitas te ereptu- rum & salvaturum populum, quum ego ipse rerum omnium Dominus te miserim? Tum e Gideonis compellatione: vocat enim eum, qui hic ipsi visus Adonai, cum Kamez, quod nomen Angelo aut creaturæ nulli convenit, sed soli Deo proprium est: Obsecro, inquit, Adonai Domine. Porro e gra- tiosæ etiam assistentiæ pollicitatione. Qui enim ita præsentiam & assistentiam suam pollicetur, ut ejusdem beneficio indubitato sit obtinenda victo- ria, eaque miraculosa, is profecto est Deus ipse, omnis victoriæ & miraculorum autor. At hic An- gelus ita pollicitis παράστασιν suam v. 16. Quia ero tecum, percuties Midiam tanquam virum unum. Adhæc e miraculi postulatione. Quia eo fine expe- tiit Gideon miraculum, ut certus esset, hunc An- gelum ipsum esse Jehovam vers. 17. Si inveni gra- tiam in oculis tuis, facies mihi signum, quod tu sis, qui loqueris ad me, h. e. quod tu ipse mecum in præsentia colloqui dignatus es. Gratiam ergo desiderat divini favoris, uti phrasis illa accipitur Gen. 6, 18. c. 19, 19. Exod. 33, 12. 13. 16. c. 34, 9. Num. 11, 11. 15. 2. Sam. 15, 21. Jer. 31, 2. Ulterius e Sacrificii oblatione. Siqui- dem cognita ex ipso colloquio præsentia divina sa- crificium offerre voluerit ei, qui cum ipso collo- quebatur. Sacrificia enim offerenda non sunt nisi uni Deo. Insuper e miraculi designatione. Ange- lus enim ille virtute divina miraculose ignem eli- cuit e Petra, solo summitatis baculi contactu, quo igne caro & farina infermentata absumpta fuit; dixitq; Gideoni Jehovah (sic Angelus vocatur) Pax tibi, ne timeas, non morieris. Adde, quod sacrificium hic obtulerit ipse Angelus, uti observat Theodoretius. Quod certe non convenit Angelo creato. Nullus enim creatus Angelus Sacerdotis munus subit. Fi- lio autem Dei, utpote æterno Pontifici apprime convenit, sacrificium offerre. Proinde Filius Dei hic visus est, non Angelus minister. Quibus denique accedit, quod vers. 23. habetur e translatione Ju- niana: Exstruxit autem ibi Gideon altare Jehove, quum proclamasset ipsi Jehovah pacem, id est, quum eum & de communi Israelitarum salute, & de par- ticulari ipsius (Nam ex conspectu Jehovah trepi- debat, suæque vitæ diffidebat) confirmasset. Ad- stipulantur hic nobis, cum plerisque aliis nostrati- bus, Theologi Vinarienses, nec non Belgicarum No- tarum autores e Reformatis. Conf. Dn. D. Dor- schei nostri dissert. de nomine Jehovah §. 26.

## 6:15
I AM THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE) Where God wishes to manifest His power, He uses despised men. You may compare Gideon to Cincinnatus, a Dictator from the plow, seeking not power but to show his virtue.

Latin:

EGO MINIMVS IN DOMO PATRIS MEI) Deus ubi vim suam vult apparere, hominibus utitur contemtis. Ge- deoni comparare possis Cincinnatum, ab aratro Dictatorem, virtutis ostendendæ non imperii appetentem.

## 6:17
Ver. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

## 6:19
Ver. 19.

HE OFFERED TO HIM) That he might eat, below 13, 16. The Angel showed himself to be an Angel, not a man, in that he did not need food.

The Vulgate interpretation, which is authentic to Grotius, expressly teaches that it was a sacrifice, not indeed a feast, in verse 18, rendering it thus: And depart not hence, until I return to thee, bringing a sacrifice and offering it to thee. And concerning the sacrifice, with Theodoret and Augustine, most

The interpreters understand. Although, however, sacrifices ought ordinarily to have been made in the tabernacle or the place of the ark of the covenant and by the priests, they were nevertheless sometimes offered extraordinarily by a special command of God, or where God attested to His presence. See Jud. ch. 13, 19. 1 Kings 15, 22. 2 Sam. 24, 25. And in this chapter v. 25. Nor did Gideon offer his Mincha here, unless the will had been explored first and permission asked, v. 18. And therefore the consent of the Lord protects him, which Augustine observes in the questions on the book of Judges. See more on that in Theol. Natur. & revel. p. 246. seqq. And Grotius prunes his own vines here at verse 20. Place upon that rock, noting thus; which for you at this time, God so permitting, will serve as an altar. For thus he confesses that not a feast, but a sacrifice was performed here. And at verse 21. Fire ascended from the rock, which was sent from heaven, as below XIII, 20. See what was said on Genesis 4, v. 4. But those things in both places concern a sacrifice, not a feast.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

OBTVLIT EI) Vt ederet infra 13, 16. Ostendit An- gelus se Angelum esse, non hominem, eo quod cibo non egeret.

Vulgata interpretatio, quæ Grotio avthen- tica est, sacrificium, non vero epulum fuisse diserte docet vers. 18. ita reddens: Nec recedas hinc, donec revertar ad te sacrificium portans & offerens tibi. Et de sacrificio cum Theodoreto, & Augustino plerique

Interpp. intelligunt. Quanquam autem ordinarie Sacrificia in tabernaculo, vel loco arcæ fœderis, & a Sacerdotibus fieri debuerint, extraordinarie ta- men quandoque e peculiari Dei mandato, aut ubi Deus præsentiam suam contestabatur, offereban- tur. Vide Jud. c. 13, 19. 1. Reg. 15, 22. 2. Sam. 24, 25. Et in hoc capite v. 25. Neque hic offerebat Mincha suum Gedeon, nisi explorata prius voluntate, ro- gataque facultate v. 18. Ideoque tuetur eum con- sensus Domini, quod observat August. in qq. ad lib. Judic. Vide de illo plura Theol. Natur. & revel. p. 246. seqq. Et cædit hic propria vineta Grotius ad vers. 20. Pone super petram illam, ita annotans; quæ tibi hoc tempore, Deo sic permittente, erit pro al- tari. Sic enim fatetur non epulum, sed sacrificium hic peractum esse. Et ad vers. 21. Ascendit ignis de Petra, qui immissus cœlitus, ut infra XIII, 20. Vide quæ dicta ad Genesin 4. v. 4. At illa utrobique con- cernunt Sacrificium, non epulum.

## 6:20
Verse 20.

PLACE UPON THAT ROCK) Which for you at this time, God so permitting, will serve as an altar. See below 13, 16. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

PONE SUPER PETRAM ILLAM) Quæ tibi hoc tempore, Deo sic permittente, erit pro altari. Vide infra 13, 16. 19.

## 6:21
Verse 21.

FIRE ASCENDED FROM THE ROCK) Sent from heaven, as below 13, 20. See what was said on Genesis 4, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ASCENDIT IGNIS DE PETRA) Immissus cœlitus, ut infra 13, 20. Vide quæ dicta ad Genesin 4, 4.

## 6:23
Verse 23.

YOU SHALL NOT DIE) This is a very ancient fear of men, that they might be afflicted with death or some grave evil upon seeing any of the heavenly ones, because they believed themselves unworthy of such a spectacle. See below 13, 22. Callimachus: For these are the laws of Cronus, that whoever sees any of the immortals, unless the god himself chooses it, shall see him at a great price.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

NON MORIERIS) Vetustissimus hic hominum metus ne morte aut malo aliquo gravi afficerentur conspecto cœli- tum aliquo, quod indignos se tali spectaculo crederent. Vide infra 13, 22. Callimachus: κρόνιοι δ' ὧδε πέγοντι νόμοι Ὅς κέ τιν' ἀθανάτων, ὅκα μὴ θεὸς αὐτὸς ἕληται, Ἀθρήσῃ, μισθῷ τῦτον ἰδεῖν μεγάλῳ.

## 6:25
Verse 25.

THE LORD SAID TO HIM) In this sacrifice there are many things against the law: but the command of God defends Gideon, as it does Elijah 1 Kings 18:36.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

DIXIT DOMINVS AD EUM) In hoc sacrificio multa sunt contra legem: sed mandatum Dei Gedeonem defendit, ut Eliam 1. Reg. 8, 36.

## 6:25
Verse 25. TAKE THE BULL.

The bull, namely that notable one of your father, which is destined for the Baalitic sacrifice, take and remove from sight, or slaughter it, so that it may no longer be offered to Baal: and take another bull of seven years from the herd, so that it may be offered to the true God.

Latin:

Vers. 25. TOLLE TAURUM.

Taurum sc. illum insignem Patris tui, qui sa- crificio Baalitico destinatus est, tolle ac remove ex oculis, vel macta eum, ut nequeat amplius Baal of- ferri: & alterum taurum annorum septem de ar- mento accipe, ut offeratur vero Deo.

## 6:40
Verse 40. AND THERE WAS DRYNESS ON THE FLEECE ONLY AND DEW ON ALL THE EARTH.

Namely, the rest: It was signified that Christ was first to be revealed to the Jews, who inhabited a small corner of the world at that time with respect to the whole globe, but that He would later recreate the whole globe with His Gospel as if with dew. Thus Origen, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Procopius, Ambrose, book 1 on the Holy Spirit & book on Widows. Augustine, sermon 108 on the Season & book on the unity of the Church, ch. 5, where he says, I do not see what else is figured and foretold here, unless we understand the threshing floor as the globe of the earth; the place of the fleece, the people of Israel. But this gift was with that people in the fleece, that is, in a covering, and as it were in a cloud of secrecy, because it had not yet been revealed. But now we see the globe of the earth already being nourished by the revealed dew through the Gospel of our Lord, which was then figured in that covering; but that nation, having lost the priesthood which it had, because it does not understand Christ in the Scriptures, has remained as if in a dry fleece. The Fathers are also accustomed to apply this sign to the conception of Christ from a virgin. Ambrose, Sermon 9. Bernard, Sermon on the Nativity of Mary & sermon 1 on the Annunciation. Just as it was a notable miracle and above the laws of nature that the fleece alone was moistened with dew: So the Son of God was born of a pure virgin above the order of nature. The heavenly shower poured itself with a gentle fall into the virgin fleece, and the whole wave of divinity hid itself in the absorbent fleece of our flesh, says Chrysologus. When the whole human race lay dry because of the heat of divine wrath, the Son of God, clothed in human flesh, derived the dew of grace into us. Conf. Ps. 72, 6. Is. 9, 4. And what Blessed Gerhard, Sacred Homilies part I, p. 468.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ET FUIT SICCITAS IN SOLO VELLE- RE ET ROS IN OMNI TERRA.

Scil. reliqua: Significatum fuit Christum pri- mum revelandum Judæis, qui exiguum tum mundi angulum respectu totius orbis terrarum incolue- runt, sed eundem postea recreaturum Evangelio suo ceu rore universum terrarum orbem. Ita Ori- genes, Chrysostom. Theodor. Procopius, Ambros. l. 1. de S. S. & l. de Viduis. August. serm. 108. de Tem- pore & libr. de unitat. Eccl. c. 5. ubi, non video, inquit, quid hic aliud figuratum & prenunciatum sit, nisi ut aream intelligamus orbem terrarum; locum velleris, populum Israel. Erat autem apud illum popu- lum hoc munus in vellere, hoc est, in velamine, & quasi in nube secreti, quia nondum fuerat revelatum. Nunc autem videmus orbem terrarum jam revelato rore saginari per Evangelium Domini nostri, quod tunc in illo tegmine figurabatur; illam vero gentem amisso Sacerdotio, quod habebat, quia in Scripturis non intelligit Christum, tanquam in sicco vellere re- mansisse. Applicare etiam hoc signum solent Patres conceptioni Christi ex virgine. Ambros. Serm. 9. Bernh. Serm. in Nativ. Mar. & serm. 1. super Mis- sus est. Petr. Chrysol. serm. 3. de annunc. sicut insi- gne miraculum & supra naturæ leges fuit, quod so- lum vellus rore humectatum fuit: Sic filius Dei su- pra naturæ seriem ex pura virgine natus est.
