Cæle- stis imber virgineum in vellus placido se fudit lapsu, & tota divinitatis unda bibulo carnis nostræ sese ce- lavit in vellere, ait Chrysologus. Cum totum ge- nus humanum aridum jaceret ob æstum iræ di- vinæ, Filius Dei humana carne indutus rorem gra- tiæ in nos derivavit. Conf. Pf. 72, 6. Es. 9, 4. Et quæ B. Gerhard. Homil. sacr. part. I. p. 468.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. The selection of soldiers & the stratagem of Gideon.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. Selectus militum & strategema Gedeonis.

## 7:1
Verse 1. OF THE HIGH HILL.

IN Hebrew, from the hill of Moreh: The Midianite camp looked toward the hill of Moreh: Piscator and the English version also take it as a proper name.

Verse 30.

BRING OUT YOUR SON) Hand him over to us as a guilty man. Regarding the demanded surrender, see what is said in book II of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 21, § 4.

Latin:

Vers. 1. COLLIS EXCELSI.

IN Ebr. a colle More: Respiciebant castra Madia- nitica collem More: pro nomine proprio habent etiam Piscator, & Anglic. versio.

Vers. 30.

PRODUC FILIUM TUUM) Dede eum nobis ut son- tem. De postulata deditione vide quæ dicta l. II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 21. §. 4.

## 7:3
Verse 3. WHO IS FEARFUL AND TIMID, LET HIM RETURN] See Deut. 20:8.

Verse same. FROM MOUNT GILEAD.

Adrichom and Serarius think that Mount Gilboa is so called, where Gideon had his camp. There is another Mount Gilead, but it is across the Jordan, about which Gen. 31:48.

Ver. 31. WHO IS HIS ADVERSARY.

Luther more correctly: Wer um ihn hadert. Whoever undertakes to plead his cause, let him die. But if Baal has need of another's patronage, how fine a god is he?

Latin:

Vers. 3. QVI FORMIDOLOSVS ET TIMIDVS EST REVERTATVR] Vid. Deut. 20, 8.

Vers. eod. DE MONTE GALAAD.

Montem Gilboë ita dictum esse Adrichom. & Serarius putant, ubi castra habuit Gideon. Alius mons Galaad, sed trans Jordanem est, de quo Gen. 31, 48.

Vers. 31. QUI ADVERSARIUS EST EJUS.

Rectius Lutherus: Wer um ihn hadert. Quisquis causam ejus agendam susceperit, moria- tur. Quod si opus habet alieno patrocinio Baal, quam bellus est Deus?

## 7:5
Ver. 5.

AS DOGS ARE WONT TO LICK] It is an Egyptian proverb: The dog drinks and runs. Macrobius mentions it in Saturnalia 2, 2. What is said here could be drawn to the sense of haste rather than of fear. But Josephus clearly had in mind the proverb I mentioned here. For he says: ὅσοι δ' ἂν ἐσπευσμένως καὶ μετὰ θορύβου πίνοντες τύχοιεν τέτ τες νομίζων ὑπὸ δειλίας τῦτο πάσχειν κὰι καταπεπληγότας τὺς πολεμίυς. And he says that this command was given by God, so that they might believe that victory was owed not to their own might, but entirely to God. Thus God wished not only to reduce the number to a third part, and then this third to a thirtieth part, but at the same time to take to Himself those of whose might there was the least hope. And these three hundred, not like the cohort of Leonidas, but men fearful by nature, scattered 135,000 men.

Ver. same.

IF HE IS A GOD LET HIM AVENGE HIMSELF ON HIM] Thus Tertullian, Apology. All your gods were worshipped by all, when the Senones occupied the Capitol itself. And well, because if any adversity still happens to cities, the same destruction of temples occurred as of walls, so that I may now prove that it does not come from the gods, because it happens to them as well. Many of his sentiments are found among other Christian writers.

In Hebrew: Let Baal plead for himself, i.e., against him who destroyed his altar, as if to say: We acknowledge Gideon as a great man, who dared to abolish the worship of Baal, which he himself could not defend. Thus God can easily reconcile the wills of men to us, provided we strenuously perform our duty.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

SICVT SOLENT CANES LAMBERE] Proverbium est Ægyptium: Canis bibit & fugit. Meminit Macrobius Saturnalium 2, 2. Poterat ad festinationis magis, quam ad formidinis sensum trahi quod hic dicitur. Sed Josephus pla- ne id quod dixi Proverbium in animo hic habuit. Ait enim: ὅσοι δ' ἂν ἐσπευσμένως καὶ μετὰ θορύβου πίνοντες τύχοιεν τέτ τες νομίζων ὑπὸ δειλίας τῦτο πάσχειν κὰι καταπεπληγότας τὺς πολεμίυς. Et ait id præceptum a Deo datum, ut crederent non suæ virtuti, sed Dei ex solido victoriam deberi. Ita non numerum tantum ad tertiam primum partem, deinde hanc tertiam ad minus parte tricesima, redigere voluerit Deus, sed simul eos sibi assumere, de quorum virtute minima spes erat. Et hi trecenti, non quasi cohors Leonidæ, sed homines inge- nio trepidi 135. hominum millia disjecerunt.

Vers. eod.

SI DEUS EST VINDICET SE DE EO] Sic Tertul. Apoloc. Omnes dii vestri ab omnibus colebantur, cum ipsum Capitolium Senones occupaverunt. Et bene, quod si quid adhuc adversi urbibus accidit, eadem clades templorum, quæ & mœnium fuerunt, ut jam bos revincam non a Deis eveni- re, quia & ipsis evenit. Multa ejus sensus apud alios scripto- res Christianos.

In Ebr. Litiget pro se ipso Baal, sc. contra eum, qui destruxit aram ejus q. d. Nos agnoscimus Ge- deonem pro magno viro, qui ausus fuit cultum Baal abolere, quem ipse tueri non potuit. Ita facile Deus hominum voluntates conciliare nobis potest, mo- do nos officium nostrum strenue faciamus.

## 7:8
Ver. 8. AND WITH TRUMPETS) Namely, with the trumpets also of those who had departed, so that each one had a trumpet, below 18. Similar arts, simulating by sight and noise forces greater than they were, you have everywhere in histories.

One must fight with cunning. A lighter praise in a leader, the right hand. says Silius Italicus.

Ver. 35.

AND HE SENT MESSENGERS THROUGHOUT ALL MANASSEH] It shows the supreme authority of the right to summon the people.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET TUBIS) Nempe tubis etiam eorum qui abie- rant, ita ut singuli tubam haberent, infra 18. Similes artes, ma- jores quam erant copias visu ac strepitu simulantium, passim in historiis habes.

Bellandum est astu. Levior laus in duce, dextra. ait Silius Italicus.

Vers. 35.

MISITQUE NVNTIOS IN UNIVERSVM MA- MASSEM] Jus populi convocandi summum imperium oftendit.

## 7:11
Ver. 11. INTO THE PART OF THE CAMP] In the Hebrew: To the edge of the armed men. See the remarks on Exodus 13, 18.

Ver. 37.

IF THE DEW ON THE FLEECE ALONE &c.) Not as an unbeliever, but as one doubting somewhat concerning that either portent or dream, he seeks to be confirmed, much like the Apostles in their early stages, Mark 9:24. Consider also what follows here.

Latin:

Vers. 11. IN PARTEM CASTRORVM] In Hebræo: Ad extremum quintatorum. Vide dicta ad Exodi 13, 18.

Vers. 37.

SI ROS IN SOLO VELLERE &c.) Non ut incredu- lus, sed ut nonnihil de isto sive ostento sive somno dubitans confirmari expetit, ferme ut in suis rudimentis Apostoli Marc. 9, 24. Considera & quæ hic sequuntur.

## 7:13
Ver. 13. I SAW A DREAM) God sends terror into his enemies even through dreams. See Cassius of Parma the dream [signified] that the Israelites, under the force of the Midianites, were badly and as if fed on barley, [and] would break forth like a flame into the sudden destruction of the Midianites.

Latin:

Vers. 13. VIDI SOMNIUM) Pavorem Deus hosti- bus suis etiam per somnia immittit. Vide Casii Parmensis somnium Israelitas sub vi Madianitarum male ac velut hor- deo pastos, erupturos flammæ modo in subitam pernitiem Madianitarum.

## 7:18
Verse 18. SHOUT FOR THE LORD AND GIDEON) Supply, successfully, ἀλαλαγμός. See Josh. 6, 5.

From a comparison of v. 20, Junius, Piscator, the English, the Genevan, and Sixtus Amama render [it] The sword of the Lord and of Gideon; but there is no reason why we should reject the Vulgate version, or the translation of B. Luther: The Lord and Gideon here. For they could have shouted both the Lord with Gideon, and that the sword of the Lord was the sword of Gideon: whether some shouted this way, others that way, or even if all varied in the exclamation in such a manner. Thus the letter of the text is retained in both cases.

Latin:

Vers. 18. CONCLAMATE DOMINO ET GIDEO- NI) Supple, feliciter, ἀλαλαγμός Vid. Jos. 6, 5.

E collatione v. 20. Junius, Pisc. Angl. Genev. & Sixt. Amama reddunt Gladius Domini & Gideo- nis; Sed non est cur reprobemus vulgatam versio- nem, aut B. Lutheri translationem: Hic Dominus & Gideon. Nam & Dominum cum Gideone, & gladium Domini Gideonis gladium esse, clamare potuére: seu alii hoc, alii isto modo exclamarint aut etiam omnes in exclamatione ita variarint. Sic re- tinetur utrobique litera textus.

## 7:19
Verse 19. AND THE THREE HUNDRED MEN.

The Vulgate is to be corrected: for in the Hebrew text there are only one hundred.

AT THE BEGINNING OF THE MIDDLE NIGHT WATCH.

It seems not badly rendered by the Vulgate: with which the Helvetic, Piscator, English, and Italian versions agree (although Osiander here amends the Vulgate to 'at the first watchmen, who were stationed there'), but as for what it adds about the guards being awakened, in the Hebrew it is, 'when they had set the guards': as Junius and Tremellius [have it], they were only just then setting the guards, that is, around midnight, when guards and watchmen are accustomed to be changed.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ET TRECENTI VIRI.

Corrigenda Vulgata est: In Ebræo enim textu tantum habentur centum.

INCIPIENTIBUS VIGILIIS NOCTIS ME- DIÆ.

Non male a Vulgata reddi videntur: cui con- sonat Helvet. Piscat. Angl. Ital. Versio (etsi hic Vulgatam emendet Osiander h. m. ad primos vigi- les, qui ibi dispositi erant) at quot addit de custodi- bus suscitatis, in Ebr. est, cum custodes constituissent: uti Junius & Tremellius, tantummodo demum sta- tuebant custodes, id est, sub mediam noctem, quum custodes & vigiles mutari solent.

## 7:20
Verse 20. THEY HELD IN THEIR LEFT HANDS THE LAMPS] The Falisci and Tarquinienses disturbed the Roman battle line with many of their men carrying torches and snakes in a frenzied manner. The Veientes and Fidenates did the same, having snatched up torches. Frontinus notes this in book 2, chapter 4.

Latin:

Vers. 20. TENVERVNT SINISTRIS MANIBVS LAMPADAS] Falisci & Tarquinienses compluribus suorum faces & angues furiali habitu præferentibus aciem Romano- rum turbaverunt. Idem Vejentes & Fidenates facibus arreptis fecerunt. Notat Frontinus lib. 2. cap. 4.

## 7:22
Verse 22. AND THEY CUT EACH OTHER DOWN IN MUTUAL SLAUGHTER] Suspecting treachery among themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET MVTVA SE CÆDE TRVNCABANT] Proditionem inter se suspicantes.

## 7:24
Verse 24. SEIZE THE WATERS) To snatch rivers away from enemies is of great use. See Frontinus book 3, ch. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 24. OCCVPATE AQVAS) Flumina hostibus eripere magni usus. Vide Frontinum lib. 3. c. 7.

## 7:25
Verse 25. HE SLEW OREB) There were no customs of war that forbade captives from being killed. See [Grotius,] On the Law of War and Peace, book III, ch. 4, § 10. See also below 8, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 25. INTERFECIT OREB) Nulla erant Belli com- mercia quæ captivos vetarent interfici. Vide Juris Belli ac Pa- cis l. III. c. 4. §. 10. Vide & infra 8, 18.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

The Ephraimites appeased. After Zebee and Salmana were defeated, the men of Succoth and Phanuel were destroyed. The ephod of Gideon. After his death, the Israelites played the harlot with the Baalim.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

Ephraimita sedati. Devicto Zebee, & Salma- na viri Succot, & Phanuel perditi. Ephod Gedeonis. Post mortem ejus cum Baalim fornicati Israelita.

## 8:2
Ver. 2. WHAT HAVE I BEEN ABLE TO DO LIKE THIS) Strong minds are appeased by the concession of glory.

Ver. same. IS NOT THE GLEANING OF EPHRAIM BETTER THAN THE VINTAGES OF ABIEZER.

A few persons killed by Ephraim, namely the princes Oreb and Zeb, are to be valued more highly than all the Midianites killed by the Manassites; or, the metaphor being preserved, this gleaning of yours is more excellent than my vintage: Abiezer was the great-grandson of Manasseh. Strong minds are appeased by the concession of glory, says Grotius.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QVID ENIM TALE FACERE POTVI) For- tes animi placantur concessione gloriæ.

Vers. eod. NONNE MELIOR EST RACE- MUS EPHRAIM VINDEMIIS ABIEZER.

PAucæ personæ ab Ephraim cæsæ, Principes sc. Oreb & Zeb, pluris æstimandæ, quam omnes Midianitæ a Manassensibus interfecti; vel Meta- phora servata, hæc vestra racematio præstantior est mea vindemia: Abiezer erat pronepos Menasse. Fortes animi placantur concessione gloriæ, ait Grotius.

## 8:5
Ver. 5. GIVE I BESEECH YOU BREAD TO THE PEOPLE, WHO ARE WITH ME) Those who are in the same parts ought not to deny food to a soldier in a time of necessity: otherwise they are punished. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DATE OBSECRO PANES POVLO, QVI MECUM EST) Qui in iisdem sunt partibus alimenta militi in necessa- rio tempore negare non debent: alioqui puniuntur. 16.

## 8:10
Ver. 10. ZEBE AND SALMANA WERE RESTING.

In the Hebrew: They were in Carcor, as Luther rendered it with the Chaldean and the LXX, which Jerome says is a castle in that place, in the Hebrew by the name of Carraria, distant one day's journey from Petra (a city of Arabia, which is called Petraea from that in the Moabite region, to which the tribe of Reuben was adjacent).

Latin:

Vers. 10. ZEBE ET SALMANA REQUI- ESCEBANT.

In Ebr. Erant in Carror, ut Lutherus reddidit cum Chald. & LXX. quod castellum dicit Hier. in loc. Ebr. cognomento Carraria, unius diei itine- re a Petra (civitate Arabiæ, quæ inde Petræa dicta in Moabitica regione, cui confinis erat tribus Ru- ben) distans.

## 8:11
Ver. 11. WHO DWELT IN TENTS.

That is, of the Arabs, who are therefore called Scenitae. For Gideon did not invade the camp of Zebe and Salmana by a direct path, but from the rear through the Arabs.

Latin:

Vers. 11. QUI IN TABERNACULIS MO- RABANTUR.

Hoc est, Arabum, qui inde Scenitæ vocantur. Non enim recta via, sed a tergo per Arabes invasit castra Zebe & Salmane Gideon.

## 8:16
Ver. 16. HE TOOK THEREFORE THE ELDERS OF THE CITY) Senators. It is mild to punish the leaders who are the authors of evil, and to pardon the multitude. Book III of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 11, § 5.

HE THRESHED. In the Hebrew: he made them know, namely by scourges and blows, as a teacher punishing his disciples, and thus he taught them how dangerous it is to insult a magistrate raised up by God.

Latin:

Vers. 16. TVLIT ERGO SENIORES CIVITATIS) Senatores. Mite est principes auctores mali punire, multitudini ignosce- re. Libro III. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 11. §. 5.

CONTRIVIT. In Ebr. scire fecit, sc. per flagella, & verbera, ut præceptor discipulos castigans, adeoque docuit eos, quam periculosum sit insultare Magistratui divinitus excitato.

## 8:18
Vers. 18. ONE OF THEM AS THE SON OF A KING. One more excellent in form than the rest from the whole habit of his body, as if he were the son of a King or of some Prince, and it appeared sufficiently that he was not a plebeian man, as Osiander here. Some, however, explain it thus with the LXX. One, that is, any one of them was of such elegant form that he seemed to be the son of a King, and B. Luther rendered it thus.

Latin:

Vers. 18. UNUS EX EIS QUASI FILIUS REGIS. Unus forma ex toto corporis habitu reliquis excellentior quasi esset filius Regis aut Principis cujusdam, satisque apparebat, non esse hominem plebejum, ut hic Osiander. Nonnulli tamen ita ex- plicant cum LXX. Unus, id est, quilibet ex eis erat forma tam eleganti, ut videretur esse filius Regis, atque ita reddidit B. Lutherus.

## 8:21
Vers. 21. YOU ARISE AND FALL UPON US) There is some consolation. You fall by the right hand of great Aeneas. See shortly 9, 54. HE TOOK THE ORNAMENTS AND THE BULLAE) He stripped off the spoils. In the Hebrew it is little moons, the badge of the Israelites, a part of which the Saracens transmitted to the customs of the Turks.

Latin:

Vers. 21. TV SVRGE ET IRRVE IN NOS) Aliqua est consolatio. Æneæ magni dextra cadis. Vid. mox 9, 54. TVLIT ORNAMENTA ET BVLLAS) Exuvias de- traxit. In Hebræo est lunulas, insigne Israëlitarum, quorum pars Sarraceni ad Turcas mores transmifere.

## 8:22
Vers. 22. RULE OVER US YOU, AND YOUR SON, AND THE SON OF YOUR SON,) That is, they conferred the hereditary principate upon him on account of his virtue and merits.

Latin:

Vers. 22. DOMINARE NOSTRI TU, ET FILIUS TVUS, ET FILIVS FILII TVI,) Id est, hæreditarium ei principatum detulere ob virtutem & merita.

## 8:23
Vers. 23. THE LORD SHALL RULE OVER YOU] He will designate princes for you, which, as long as God was doing it, it was not fitting for the people to make a king by their own judgment. 1 Sam. 8, 7. and much less to subject themselves to one family.

Latin:

Vers. 23. DOMINABITVR VOBIS DOMINVS] Is vobis prin- cipes designabit, quod quamdiu faciebat Deus, regem popu- lus suopte arbitratu facere non decebat. 1. Sam. 8, 7. multo- que minus uni se familiæ subjicere.

## 8:24
Vers. 24. GIVE ME THE EARRINGS FROM YOUR SPOIL) For it was customary for something to be given to leaders as a choice gift. Book III of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 7, § 17.

Latin:

Vers. 24. DATE MIHI INAVRES EX PRÆDA VE- STRA) Solebat enim ducibus aliquid dari ἐξαίρετον. l. III. de Jure Belli & Pacis c. 7. §. 17.

## 8:26
Vers. 26. ONE THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED SHEKELS OF GOLD. Which make almost 70 pounds of gold. For a shekel is a half-ounce. Therefore, this whole amount of gold was not spent on the Ephod alone; for who could have carried that? but also on other ornaments. A similar passage is 1 Par. 20, 2. 2 Reg. 12, 30. For no one is able to carry a talent of gold on his head. Therefore, August. q. 41, Theodor. q. 16, and others think that Gideon made a Pontifical Ephod and the remaining vestments of the Pontiff, which are understood under the primary one, just as the LXX render Ephod in Os. 3, 4 by ἱερατείαν, priesthood, and every priestly instrument.

Latin:

Vers. 26. MILLE SEPTINGENTI AURI SICLI. Qui faciunt libras auri fere 70. Siclus enim est semiuncia. Non ergo in solum Ephod impen- sum totum hoc aurum; quis enim id ferre potuis- set? sed etiam in alia ornamenta. Similis locus est 1. Par. 20, 2. 2. Reg. 12, 30. Nemo enim talentum auri in capite gestare valet. Ideo August. q. 41. Theodor. q. 16. & alii existimant, Gedeonem fe- cisse Ephod Pontificiale ac reliquas vestes Ponti- ficis, quæ sub primaria intelliguntur, uti LXX. Ephod Os. 3, 4. per ἱερατείαν sacerdotium, omneque instrumentum sacerdotale reddunt.

## 8:27
Vers. 27. HE PUT THE EPHOD IN HIS CITY OF EPHRA, AND ALL ISRAEL COMMITTED FORNICATION IN IT) A prolepsis. For only after the death of Gideon was that which had been a monument of victory turned to the use of idolatry. Below 33.

Cajetan and Airas also explain it as a monument of victory, as do Junius and Tremellius, and others. Most, however, with August. and Theodor. understand it as the Pontifical one, because in Ex. 28, 6 it is taken for the Pontifical Ephod, which, even if it was not to be worn by Gideon himself, but by the Pontiff living in Silo not far from the city of Ephra: just as Gideon himself did not offer sacrifice on the altar in ch. 6, 27, which Serarius contends, but some priest: yet it is not free from sin, because the Lord had not ordered the altar to be built for that end, that sacrifices might be made on it frequently, but that a single sacrifice might be offered there, and He had commanded that sacrifices should be made to Him in no other place than in the tabernacle of the covenant. Whence, without a special command of God, it was not lawful elsewhere: and that act is expressly called fornication in this place: all Israel committed fornication in it there. And therefore B. Chytreus, Osiander, as also B. Gerhard in De Bon. Operib. §, rightly state that Gideon sinned out of will-worship. 93. rightly state. Whence ruin was brought upon not only the house of Gideon, but also upon Gideon himself through it, v. 23. Therefore, the Papists excuse this deed in vain, so that they may favor their own will-worships. Abulensis, Serarius, Benedictus Justinianeus, Corn. a Lapide, Salianus, Bonfrerius. And Cornel. himself praises the opinion of August. q. 41, that God bore that deed of Gideon patiently, although it was a deed which He Himself had forbidden, and he excuses him from mortal sin only. and idolatry: but since all sins are mortal by their nature, this certainly was neither light, nor can it be freed from idolatry, which is committed not only by reason of the object, when that is worshipped as God which is not God, but also by reason of the mode, when the true God is worshipped not as the true God commanded and willed to be worshipped, not according to the commandment or worship instituted by Himself, but invented by men beyond the word of God Deut. 12, 33. Matth. 15. And Lyranus and Estius admit that Gideon sinned in this, that he instituted a tabernacle, sacrifices, and the whole apparatus of sacrifices to be built at his own house, where he sacrificed either himself or through others against the decrees of the divine law. Nor does it stand in the way that Gideon is numbered among the Saints Heb. 11, because Aaron also, even though he was a saint, sinned by μοσχολατρείᾳ: nor is there any doubt that Gideon did penance, and having acknowledged his fall, was reconciled to God through true faith and received into grace again, if indeed he is said to have died in a good old age, which Bonfrerius notes is said of no one in Scripture except of him who died a holy death: and after his death the Israelites turned away from God v. 33, by whose piety and authority they were preserved in the worship of the true God while he was among the living. But what is said, that this was done for the ruin of Gideon and all his house, by which Bonfrerius wishes to note that what was done with a good intention happened beyond the intention into scandal, ruin, and destruction, does not make for the absolution of the deed. Because it does not suffice for a deed to be good that it be done with a good intention, but it is required that it be done well and in conformity with the Law of God. But such worship was not conformable to the law, and therefore it was ἀνομία, and ἁμαρτία in the true sense 1. Joh. 3, 4. Yet Bonfrerius's opinion is more tolerable, by which he, with Theodor., maintains that the Ephod was made only so that he might consult God through it, without the need of summoning the Priest from the vicinity when there was need. For if it was permitted to seek oracles outside the place of the tabernacle, he could also have used the Ephod for the matter outside the tabernacle. And therefore some take the Vav in those words: it became to Gideon AND all his house for a ruin, exegetically, to Gideon, that is, to all his house, and they understand the fornication IN IT as the abuse of the Ephod for the sacrilegious worship of the Israelites, not, as they say, of Gideon.

Latin:

Vers. 27. EPHOD POSVIT IN CIVITATE SVA EPHRA, FORNICATVSQVE EST OMNIS ISRAEL IN EO) πρόληψις. Nam post mortem demum Gedeonis id quod monumentum victoriæ fuerat, versum est in usum idololatriæ. Infra 33.

De monumento victoriæ etiam Cajetanus & Airas explicant, ut & Junius & Tremellius, & alii. Plerique tamen cum August. & Theodor. Pontificiale intelligunt, quia Ex. 28, 6. de Pontificali Ephod accipitur, quod etsi non ipsi Gideoni, sed Pontifi- ci in Silo non procul ab urbe Ephra habitanti por- tandum: uti non ipse Gideon in altari sacrificium obtulit c. 6, 27. quod Serarius contendit, sed sa- cerdos aliquis: peccato tamen non vacat, quia aram non eo fine jusserat Dominus exstrui, ut sæ- pius in illo sacra fierent, sed ut unicum ibi offer- retur sacrificium, & mandaverat, ut nullo alio loco, quam in tabernaculo fœderis ipsi sacra fierent. Un- de citra speciale Dei mandatum id alibi non erat li- citum: & vocatur diferte actus ille fornicatio hoc loco: fornicatus est omnis Israel in eo ibi. Ideoq; ex ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ peccasse Gideonem B. Chytreus, Osiander ut & B. Gerhard. de Bon. Operib. §. 93. recte statuunt. Unde non tantum domui Gideo- nis, sed etiam ipsi Gideoni ruina per id accersita v. 23. Nequicquam ergo excusant hoc factum Papistæ, ut suis ἐλελοθρησκείαις velificentur. Abu- lens. Serarius, Benedictus Iustinianeus, Corn. a La- pide, Salianus, Bonfrerius. Et laudat ipse Cornel. sententiam August. q. 41. quod Deus illud factum Gedeonis patienter tulerit, licet factum quod ipse prohibuerat, eumque excusat a mortali tantum cul- pa & idololatria : sed cum omnia peccata natura sua mortalia sint, hoc certe nec leve erat, nec ab idololatria liberari potest, quæ committitur non tantum ratione objecti, cum ut Deus colitur, quod Deus non est, sed etiam ratione modi, cum Deus verus colitur non ut Deus verus jussit ac voluit co- li, non juxta mandatum vel cultum a se institutum, sed humanitus præter verbum Dei inventum Deut. 12, 33. Matth. 15. Fatenturque Lyranus & Estius, peccasse in eo Gideonem, quod domi suæ extrui ta- bernaculum, sacrificia & totum sacrificiorum ap- paratum instituerit, ubi vel ipse vel per alios con- tra divinæ legis decreta sacrificarit. Nec obstat, quod Sanctis annumeretur Gedeon Ebr. 11. quia & Aaron, etsi sanctus fuerit, μοσχολατρείᾳ peccavit: neque dubium est Gideonem egisse pœnitentiam, lapsuque suo agnito, per veram fidem Deo reconci- liatum in gratiam iterum receptum esse, siquidem mortuus dicatur in senectute bona, quod de nemine in Scriptura dici, nisi de eo, qui sancta morte obie- rit, Bonfrerius notat: & post mortem ejus aversi a Deo sint Israelitæ v. 33. cujus pietate & autoritate dum in vivis erat ipsi in veri Dei cultu conservati sunt. Quod vero dicitur factum hoc esse in ruinam Gideoni & omni domui ejus, quo notari Bonfrerius vult, id quod bona intentione factum est, præter inten- tionem evenisse in scandalum, ruinam & exitium, non facit ad facti absolutionem. Quia non sufficit ad id, ut bonum sit factum, ut bona intentione fiat, sed ut bene ac Legi Dei conformiter fiat, requiritur. Non autem legi conformis erat talis cultus, ideoque ἀνομία erat, & veri nominis ἁμαρτία 1. Joh. 3, 4. To- lerabilior tamen est Bonfrerii sententia, qua cum Theodor. statuit solum ideo factum esse Ephod, ut per illum Deum consuleret opera Pontificis e vici- nia accersendi, cum opus erat. Si enim captare ora- cula extra tabernaculi locum licuit, potuit & extra tabernaculum Ephodis ad rem usus esse. Ideoque Vav in illis verbis: factum est Gedeoni ET omni do- mui ejus in ruinam, accipiunt nonnulli exegetice, Gedeoni, id est, omni domui ejus, & fornicatio- nem IN EO intelligunt de abusu Ephodis ad cul- tus sacrilegos Israelitarum, non v. Gideonis.

## 8:28
Vers. 28. THE LAND RESTED FOR FORTY YEARS. In the fortieth year after the previous rest restored by Deborah and Barak Jud. 5, 31. For then at last the land of Israel began to rest again, namely in the days of Gideon, the Midianite oppression having ended.

Latin:

Vers. 28. QUIEVIT TERRA PER QUA- DRAGINTA ANNOS. Anno quadragesimo post quietem priorem a Debora & Barac restitutam Jud. 5, 31. Tum enim demum iterum quiescere cepit, in diebus nempe Gedeonis, terra Israelis, finita oppressione Madia- nitica.

## 8:30
Vers. 30. BECAUSE HE HAD MANY WIVES) The reason why many wives were permitted to men at one time was the hope of more abundant offspring.

Latin:

Vers. 30. EO QVOD PLVRES HABERET VXORES) Causa cur concessæ fuerint viris plures uno tempore uxores, spes fuit uberioris sobolis.

## 8:31
Vers. 31. BUT HIS CONCUBINE] Concubinage was not forbidden at that time, nor did a concubine differ from a matron except in dignity. They were usually taken from handmaids or from humbler women.

We have refuted this Socinian error in Socin. Profl. Sect. 5. subs. 2. contr. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 31. CONCVBINA AVTEM ILLIVS] Non erat vetitus eo tempore concubinatus, neque concubina a ma- trona nisi dignitate distabat. Solebant autem sumi de an- cillis, aut de humilioribus fœminis.

Errorem hunc Socinian. confutavimus Socin. Profl. Sect. 5. subs. 2. contr. 7.

## 8:35
Vers. 35. NEITHER DID THEY SHOW MERCY TO THE HOUSE OF JERUBBAAL GIDEON, ACCORDING TO ALL THE GOOD WHICH HE HAD DONE TO ISRAEL) Sophocles: Φεῦ τοῦ θανόντος, ὡς ταχεῖα τοῖς βροτοῖς Χάρις διαῤῥεῖ κᾀν προδοῦσ᾽ ἁλίσκεται; See a similar passage Exod. 1, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 35. NEC FECERVNT MISERICORDIAM CVM DOMO JEROBAAL GEDEON, JVXTA OMNIA BO- NA QVÆ FECERAT ISRAEL) Sophocles: Φεῦ τοῦ θανόντος, ὡς ταχεῖα τοῖς βροτοῖς Χάρις διαῤῥεῖ κᾀν προδοῦσ᾽ ἁλίσκεται; Simile vide Exod. 1, 8.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. The tyranny and destruction of Abimelech.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Abimelechi tyrannis, & interitus.

## 9:2
Vers. 2. THAT THEY MAY RULE OVER YOU SEVENTY MEN] As princes of the city, πρωτοπολῖται.

OR THAT ONE MAN MAY RULE] Here indeed he did not only sin in what we just said 8, 23. But also because he was drawing a part of the people away from the people. Idolatry of no common sort was added. Below 46. Josephus well says of this time: πάντα τὰ τῶν ἐβραίων εἰς ἀκοσμίαν καὶ ὕβριν τῶν νόμων ἐφέρετο. Vers. HE IS OUR BROTHER) Carnal affection, from which Moses was far removed.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VT DOMINENTVR VESTRI LXX. VIRI] Tanquam principes civitatis, πρωτοπολῖται.

AN VT DOMINETVR VNVS VIR] Hic vero non id duntaxat peccabat quod modo diximus 8, 23. Verum etiam quod partem populi a populo abstrahebat. Accesfit Idololatria non vulgaris. Infra 46. Bene Josephus hoc tempore : πάντα τὰ τῶν ἐβραίων εἰς ἀκοσμίαν καὶ ὕβριν τῶν νόμων ἐφέρετο. Vers. FRATER NOSTER EST) Carnalis affectus, a quo Moses multum abfuit.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. AND THEY GAVE HIM SEVENTY PIECES OF SILVER.

In the Hebrew there is only seventy of silver, which Vatablus and others take to mean shekels. But the fact that the Rabbis and Montanus observe that by silver pieces in the Pentateuch shekels are indeed meant; in the prophetic books, however, to which this also belongs, pounds; and in the Hagiographa talents, lacks foundation. Such an equivocation is not to be rashly admitted in Holy Scripture, as we have said elsewhere.

WHO HIRED FOR HIMSELF FROM IT NEEDY AND VAGRANT MEN) The dregs of their cities, as Curtius speaks. Thus Pisistratus fortified with a bodyguard the dominion which he had obtained by deceiving the people. Herodotus book I. Diodorus Siculus book 13. Plutarch in Solon. Justin book II. Valerius Maximus book III. VIII. 9. Aelian VIII. 16. Χρῆσθαι ξενικοῖς μᾶλλον ἢ πολιτικοῖς τυραννικόν: Aristotle book 5 of the Politics, chapter 11. Concerning the Germans in the age of Nero, Tacitus: In whom the prince trusted as foreigners.

Latin:

Vers. 4. DEDERUNTQUE ILLI SEPTUA- GINTA PONDO ARGENTI.

IN Ebr. tantum habetur septuaginta argenti, quod de siclis Vatablus & alii accipiunt. Quod vero ob- servent Rabbini & Montanus per argenteos in Penta- tevcho quidem siclos; in propheticis autem libris, ad quos etiam hic pertinet, libras, in Hagiographis ta- lenta intelligi, fundamento caret. Non est talis æquivocatio in Script. S. temere admittenda, ut alias diximus.

QVI CONDVXIT SIBI EX EO VIROS INOPES ET VAGOS) Purgamenta urbium suarum, ut Curtius loqui- tur. Sic Pisistratus quem decepto populo obtinuerat do- minatum, satellitio munivit. Herodotus libro I. Diodorus Siculus libro 13. Plutarchus Solone. Justinus libro II. Va- lerius Maximus l. III. VIII. 9. Ælianus VIII. 16. Χρῆσθαι ξενικοῖς μᾶλλον ἢ πολιτικοῖς τυραννικόν: Aristoteles libro 5. Polit. cap. 11. De Germanis Neronis ævo Tacitus: Qui- bus princeps fidebat ut externis.

## 9:5
Verse 5. HE SLEW HIS BRETHREN) As the Turks do now.

Verse of the same. SEVENTY MEN.

The total sons of Gideon were that many in number: wherefore 68 were slain, since Jotham escaped: and Abimelech slew his brothers. Therefore they are called seventy by rounding of the number. By the slaughter of these and other things which are related here concerning Abimelech, the family of Gideon was punished for idolatry, as chapter 8, 27 indicates.

Latin:

Vers. 5. OCCIDIT FRATRES SUOS) Ut nunc Turcæ.

Vers. eod. SEPTUAGINTA VIROS.

Universi filii Gideonis tot erant numero: qua- re 68. occisi sunt, quum effugerit Jotham: & Abi- melech fratres occiderit. Ergo septuaginta dicun- tur numeri rotundatione. Horum occisione & aliis, quæ de Abimelecho hic referuntur, punita est fa- milia Gideonis ob idololatriam, ut c. 8, 27. indi- catum.

## 9:6
Verse 6. ALL THE FAMILIES OF THE CITY OF MELLO.

From 2 Samuel 5, 1 Kings 9, 2 Chronicles 32, some gather that Mello was a fortified place contiguous to the city of Jerusalem: whose inhabitants joined themselves with the Shechemites in this conspiracy to Abimelech: But this Mello was different from that chasm which was between Zion and Jerusalem. For it was situated near Shechem, and was as it were its colony and municipality.

THEY MADE HIM KING) They made him reign, in the Hebrew: namely, above the laws.

BY THE OAK THAT STOOD IN SHECHEM.

In that field near Shechem, where Joshua is read to have erected a great stone under the oak, Joshua 24, 26. See Junius here.

Latin:

Vers. 6. UNIVERSÆ FAMILIÆ URBIS MELLO.

E 2. Sam. 5. 1. Reg. 9. 2. Par. 32. colligunt non- nulli Mello fuisse locum munitum contiguum urbi Hierusalem: cujus incolæ cum Sichemitis in hac conspiratione sese junxere Abimelecho: Sed hæc Mello diversa fuit ab illa voragine, quæ erat inter Sion & Jerusalem. Erat enim juxta Sichem sita, ejusque velut colonia, & municipium.

CONSTITVERVNT REGEM) Regnare fecerunt, in He- bræo: nempe supra leges.

JUXTA QVERCUM QUÆ STABAT IN SICHEM.

In campo illo prope Sichemum, ubi Josua ma- gnum lapidem erexisse legitur sub quercu Jos. 24, 26. Vid. hic Junius.

## 9:7
Verse 7. ON THE TOP OF MOUNT GERIZIM.

That he might be heard, and be secure there: he brings forth an execration in the form of an apologue: that it might more penetrate the minds.

Latin:

Vers. 7. IN VERTICE MONTIS GA- RIZIM.

Ut exaudiri posset, ac securus ibi esset: Exe- crationem in forma apologi profert: ut magis pe- netret animos.

## 9:8
Vers. 8. THE TREES WENT TO ANOINT A KING OVER THEM) Hesiod called this kind of teaching an αἶνον, later writers called it an Apologue. See a similar one in 2 Chron. 25:18.

Latin:

Vers. 8. IERVNT LIGNA VT VNGERENT SV- PER SE REGEM) Hoc genus docendi Hesiodus αἶνον, po- steriores Apologum dixere. Similem vide 2. Par. 25,18.

## 9:20
Vers. 20. BUT IF NOT, LET FIRE COME OUT FROM IT AND DEVOUR THE INHABITANTS OF SHECHEM) God is accustomed to fulfill the imprecations of those who are oppressed by force. See below 57.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SIN AVTEM EGREDIATVR IGNIS EX EO ET CONSVMAT HABITATORES SICHEM) So- let Deus implere imprecationes eorum, qui per vim oppri- muntur. Vide infra 57.

## 9:21
Vers. 21. AND WHEN HE HAD SAID THESE THINGS HE FLED) The flight of leading men follows tyranny. Below 41. For Tyrants are accustomed to make war upon the notable and to destroy them secretly and openly and to banish them as rivals and obstacles to their rule: says Aristotle in the place just mentioned.

Latin:

Vers. 21. QVÆ CVM DIXISSET FVGIT) Tyranni- dem sequitur virorum principum fuga. Infra 41. Solent enim Tyranni πολεμεῖν τοῖς γνωρίμοις καὶ διαφθείρειν λάθρα καὶ φανερῶς καὶ φυγαδεύειν ὡς ἀντιτέχνες καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐμποδίως : ait Aristoteles loco modo dicto.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. SHOULD I LEAVE MY WINE WHICH CHEERETH GOD AND MAN) Pliny, book 14, ch. 22. There are two liquids most pleasing to human bodies, wine within, oil without, both the most excellent of the tree kind.

Latin:

Vers. 23. NVMQVID POSSVM DESERERE VINVM MEVM QVOD LÆTIFICAT DEVM ET HOMINES) Plinius l. 14. c. 22. Duo sunt liquores corporibus humanis gratissimi, intus vini, foris olei, arborum e genere ambo præ- cipui.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. AND THE LORD SENT AN EVIL SPIRIT BETWEEN ABIMELECH AND THE INHABITANTS OF SHECHEM.

The nobles of Shechem: He sent the Spirit permissively, that is, He permitted that Satan, as a punishment for their crimes, should exacerbate their minds against one another; and objectively: by casting in a scruple concerning the parricides of Abimelech, on account of which they began to detest him. God was the positive cause of that scruple, but he merely permitted the sin and the hatred that followed from it, as Cornelius rightly says with Abul.

WHO BEGAN TO DETEST HIM) Nothing is more unstable than the popular breeze gathered by evil arts: then indeed, even crimes are hated by those who profit from them.

Latin:

Vers. 23. MISITQUE DOMINUS SPIRI- TUM PESSIMUM INTER ABIMELECH ET HABITATORES SICHEM.

Optimates Sichem: immisit Spiritum συγχω- ρητικῶς, id est, permisit, ut Satanas in pœnam scele- rum animos eorum invicem exacerbaret; & λικῶς objective: injiciendo scrupulum de parricidiis Abi- melechi, ob quæ eum detestari ceperunt. Scrupuli istius causa fuit Deus positive, peccatum vero & odium inde sequutum permisit duntaxat, ut recte cum Abul. Cornelius.

QVI CEPERVNT EVM DETESTARI) Nihil insta- bilius populari aura malis artibus collecta: tum vero scelera etiam quibus prosunt invisa.

## 9:25
Verse 25. THEY PRACTICED ROBBERY) As the beginnings of civil wars are wont to be savage.

Latin:

Vers. 25. EXERCEBANT LATROCINIA) Vt solent sæva esse bellorum civilium initia.

## 9:27
Verse 27. LAYING WASTE THE VINEYARDS. In the Hebrew: They gathered the grapes of their vineyards; And with choirs of singers made they were exulting, as is wont to happen in the vintage, now secure in the presence of Gaal, when previously they had not dared to leave the city on account of Abimelech, against whom the ambush had been revealed. And having entered the temple of their god Baal Berith and offered victims on account of the leader Gaal having been stirred up, they were giving thanks as if the matter were already accomplished, and with the sacrifices completed, they were holding banquets there according to custom.

Latin:

Vers. 27. VASTANTES VINEAS. In Ebræo: Collegerunt uvas vinearum suarum; Et factis cantantium choris exultabant, ut in vindemia fieri solet,securi jam præsentia Gaal,quum prius ur- bem ob Abimelechum, cui detectæ insidiæ erant, egredi ausi non essent. Et ingressi fanum Dei sui Baal Berith & oblatis victimis ob excitatum Ducem Gaal, quasi re jam confecta gratias agebant, ac sacrificiis peractis pro more convivia ibidem agitabant.

## 9:28
Verse 28. GAAL THE SON OF OBED CRYING OUT) By frequently bringing forward complaints and ambiguous remarks about Galba, and other such disturbances of the common people: Tacitus, Histories 1. HE APPOINTED ZEBUL AS PRINCE. In the Hebrew: And Zebul is his prefect; Serve (rather) the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem, that is, I am surprised that you have brought your minds to serve Abimelech, who did not derive his origin from the royal stock of this city, nor does he rule you so much as his servant does: entrust rather the government of the Republic to the primates of this city, who derive their origin from the most noble stock of Hamor, the Prince of this city, whose son is Shechem. Gaal said these things grandly; but the insane man did not remember that the true Shechemites were slaughtered by the sons of Jacob, Gen. 34. Thus the sense is plain in the Hebrew text, which Cornelius rashly argues against, because it has been changed by the Masoretes and hardly has an open meaning.

Latin:

Vers. 28. CLAMANTE GAAL FILIO OBED) Inferen- do sæpius querelas & ambiguos de Galba sermones, quæque alia turbamenta vulgi: Tacitus Historiarum 1. CONSTITUIT PRINCIPEM ZEBUL. In Ebr. Et Zebul est præfectus ejus; Servite (potius) viris Hemor, patris Sichem, id est, miror vos induxisse in animum servire Abimelecho, qui non duxit originem a regia stirpe urbis hujus, nec tam ipse vobis imperat, quam servus ejus: commit- tite potius Reip. gubernationem primatibus hujus urbis, qui a nobilissima stirpe Hemor Principis hujus urbis originem ducunt, cujus filius Sichem. Hæc splendide dicebat Gaal; at insanus homo non meminerat veros Sichemitas trucidatos a filiis Ja- cobi Gen. 34. Ita sensus planus est in Ebræo textu, quem temere arguit Cornelius, quod mutatus sit a Masoretis & vix apertum habeat sensum.

## 9:34
Verse 34. IN FOUR PLACES) In the Hebrew: four heads. The Greeks, τέτρασιν ἀρχαῖς. Thus, in Tacitus, Histories 5, the civil [war] attacks the Roman garrisons with four columns.

Latin:

Vers. 34. IN QVATVOR LOCIS) In Hebræo: quatuor capita. Græci,τέτρασιν ἀρχαῖς. Sic civilis quatuor agminibus Romana præsidia aggreditur apud Tacitum Histor. 5.

## 9:45
Verse 45. SO THAT HE SCATTERED SALT UPON IT) The cause of this custom is in Pliny, book 31, 7. Every place in which salt is found is sterile, and produces nothing. Tostatus notes that it was an ancient custom to punish cities by scattering salt in them for the crime of high treason. Cf. Deut. 26, 22. 23. Ps. 106, 31. 34. Jer. 17, 6. Soph. 2, 9. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say with Cornelius: that it was customary for this to be done in fields, to the end that they might not be sown, not in a city, which is not cultivated or sown, but inhabited: because it was not to be inhabited any longer as a city, nor cultivated, or even sown, like a field, according to the judgment of Abimelech.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ITA VT SAL IN EA DISPERGERET) Cau- sa hujus moris apud Plinium l. 31, 7. Omnis locus in quo reperi- tur sal, sterilis est, nihilque gignit. Tostatus notat veterem illum morem fuisse puniendi urbes per aspersum in iis sal in crimine læ- sæ majestatis. Conf. Deut. 26, 22. 23. Ps. 106, 31. 34. Jer. 17, 6. Soph. 2, 9. Nec est, quod dicat quis cum Cornelio: in agris id fieri consuevisse, eo fine, ne seran- tur, non in urbe, quæ non colitur, nec seritur, sed incoli- tur: quia nec incoli amplius ut urbs,nec coli, aut se- ri etiam, instar agri debebat, Abimelechi sententia.

## 9:49
Verse 49. SO THAT BY SMOKE AND FIRE A THOUSAND MEN WERE KILLED) Places situated on a plain and not defended by a rampart are most easily attacked by bringing up fires. See below 52.

Latin:

Vers. 49. VT FVMO ET IGNE MILLE HOMINES NECARENTVR) Loca in plano sita, neque vallo defensa facillime oppugnantur admotis ignibus. Vide infra 52.

## 9:53
Verse 53. CASTING A PIECE OF A MILLSTONE FROM ABOVE, HE STRUCK THE HEAD OF ABIMELECH) A similar end almost for Pyrrhus, a tile thrown by a woman, which broke his head. Plutarch in his life. Joab, a man excellent in war, gave a lesson to kings from this case of Abimelech, not to take part in sieges. 2 Sam. 11, 21. That same Plutarch in the life of Sulla says that for this reason wall-fighting was disapproved of by the Spartans, because in them even a most brave man could be killed by a woman.

Latin:

Vers. 53. FRAGMEN MOLÆ DESVPER JACIENS ILLISIT CAPITI ABIMELECH) Similis ferme Pyrrho finis, tegula a muliere jacta, quæ caput ei confregit. Plutar- chus in ejus vita Joab vir bello egregius ex hoc casu Abimele- chi documentum dedit regibus, ne oppugnationibus interes- sent. 2. Sam. 11, 21. Idem ille Plutarchus in Sullæ vita ideo τε- χομαχίας ait Spartanis improbatas, quod in illis vel a mulie- re interficeretur vir fortissimus.

## 9:54
Verse 54. LEST PERCHANCE IT BE SAID THAT I WAS KILLED BY A WOMAN) Seneca in Hercules Oetaeus: O shameful fate! A woman shall be called the author of the Herculean death.

Latin:

Vers. 54. NE FORTE DICAR QVOD A FEMINA INTERFECTVS SVM) Seneca Oetæo: O turpe fatum! femina Herculeæ necis Auctor feretur.

## 10:1 Argument
SECTION III. OF THE LATER JUDGES. CHAPTER X. Tola and Jair judges. The idolatry, punishment, and repentance of the Israelites.

Vers. 1. ABIMELECH'S UNCLE. In Hebrew: Son of Dodo. Thus, along with the Rabbis, also Pagninus, Arias, Vatablus, Cajetan, and B. Luther. The Vulgate must therefore be corrected here. Gideon, the father of Abimelech, was of the tribe of Manasseh; Phua, v. 1, of the tribe of Issachar.

Latin:

SECTIO III. JUDICUM POSTERIORUM. CAPUT X. Thola & Jair judices. Israelitarum Idololatria, pœna & pœnitentia.

Vers. 1. PATRUI ABIMELECH. IN Ebr. Filii Dodo. Sic cum Rabbinis etiam Pa- gninus, Arias, Vatabl. Cajetan. B. Lutherus. Cor- rigenda ergo hic Vulgata. Gedeon Pater Abime- lech fuit de tribu Manasse,Phua v. de tribu Isaschar.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. AND HE JUDGED ISRAEL TWENTY AND THREE YEARS. Thola, after the three-year reign of Abimelech, presided for so many years over the government or judgeship of Israel. He was succeeded by Jair the Gileadite, who judged for 22 years: in which years are included the 18 years of Philistine and Ammonite oppression, concerning which see ch. 10, 28, from which Jephthah the Gileadite delivered them. For God was repeating the punishment for the idolatry of the Israelites, begun under Abimelech after the death of Gideon, by which they worshipped Baal Berith under Jair, by sending the Philistines and Ammonites upon them, even though the death of Jair is mentioned by prolepsis in ch. 10, 5, 6, 7, before this oppression. Therefore the words of ch. 10, 6, are to be rendered in the pluperfect: THEY HAD DONE EVIL, already from the time of the death of Gideon, so that the beginning of this oppression is to be referred to the fifth year of Jair; but those things which are held in 10, 8, and which in ch. 11, 4, pertain to the earlier times of Jephthah's leadership, should look to the 22nd and final year. Whence those things which Eusebius has in his Chronicle do not deserve calculation: After Jair, the Ammonites reduce the Hebrews into servitude for 18 years; for under Jephthah, who followed Jair in the judgeship, the Ammonites were humbled, they did not prevail.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET JUDICAVIT ISRAELEM VI- GINTI ET TRIBUS ANNIS. Thola post triennale regnum Abimelechi tot an- nis præfuit regimini, vel Judicatui Israelis. Cui suc- cessit Jair Galaadites, qui per 22. annos judicavit: in quibus v. annis comprehensi sunt 18. anni oppres- sionis Philistinae, & Ammoniticae, de qua c. 10, 28. unde eos liberavit Jephtha Galaadites. Repetebat enim Deus idololatriae Israelitarum sub Abimele- cho post fata Gideonis ceptae qua cultum Baal Be- rith sub Jairo poenas, immissis in eos Philistaeis & Ammonitis, utut ante horum oppressionem mors Jairis c. 10, 5. 6. 7. per prolepsin commemoretur. Ideo verba c. 10, 6. in Plusquamperfecto reddenda FECE- RANT MALUM, jam inde a morte Gideonis, ut ita ad annum Jairis quintum oppressionis hujus ini- tium referendum sit; ad 22. vero & ultimum spectent quae 10, 8. habentur, & quae c. 11, 4. ad priora princi- patus Jephthae tempora pertineant. Unde calculum non merentur, quae habet Eusebius in Chronico: Post Jair Hebraeos redigunt in servitutem 18. annis Ammo- nitae, sub Jephtha enim qui Jairi sequutus est judica- tum, humiliati sunt Ammonitae, non praevaluerunt.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. JAIR] This is not the one who is discussed in Num. 32, 41. But another, the son of Segub, also indicated in 1 Chron. 2, 22.

He is certainly different from that one in Num. 32, as being much more recent. But he is not indicated in 1 Chron. 2, 22. For in the Chronicles, the older one is listed, and that same Jair whom Moses named there; whom we observed at the passage in Numbers to have been the son of Segub, and this younger Jair seems to be called Bedan for the sake of distinction from the older one, 1 Sam. 12, 11, and 1 Chron. 7, 17. Grotius, however, is not consistent with himself: because in the note immediately following at v. 4, he confuses this younger one with the elder Jair.

Latin:

Vers. 3. JAIR] Non hic ille est, de quo agitur Num. 32, 41. Sed alius Segubi filius indicatus etiam 1. Par. 2, 22.

Diversus sane ab illo Num. 32. hic est, utpote re- centior multo. Sed non indicatus 1. Par. 2, 22. Nam in Chronicis antiquior, & idem ille Jair recensetur, quem ibi Moses nominavit; quem Segubi filium fuisse ad locum Numer. observavimus, & videtur ju- nior hic Jair ad differentiam Antiquioris etiam Be- dan vocatus 1. Sam. 12, 11. & 1. Chr. 7, 17. Grotius au- tem sibi non constat: quia nota proxime sequente ad v. 4. juniorem hunc cum Seniore Jairo confundit.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. PRINCES OF THIRTY CITIES) There were seven from Hesron the grandfather, twenty-three from the daughter of Machir the grandmother. Thus it seems to be gathered from Num. 32, 40, Deut. 3, 14, 1 Chron. 2, 22.

Vers. 4. UPON THIRTY DONKEY COLTS. Thus their dignity is indicated: because that was customary for men of princely rank.

OPPIDA JAIR (TOWNS OF JAIR). Those towns had already been named long ago by the older Jair in Num. 32, 41, which name was confirmed for them by this Jair.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PRINCIPES TRIGINTA CIVITATUM) Se- ptem erant ab Hesrone avo, viginti tres ab avia Machiris filia. Ita colligi videtur ex Num. 32, 40. Deut. 3, 14. 1. Par. 2, 22.

Vers. 4. SUPER TRIGINTA PULLOS ASI- NARUM. Ita indigitatur dignitas eorum: quia id Principibus viris usitatum erat.

OPPIDA JAIR. Nuncupata jam olim oppi- da illa fuere ab antiquiore Jair Num. 32, 41. quod nomen illis ab hoc Jair confirmatum.

## 10:7
Vers. 7. HE DELIVERED THEM INTO THE HANDS OF THE PHILISTINES AND THE CHILDREN OF AMMON) To be vexed, namely, with many evils, not that they should serve them completely. For this is an introduction to those things which will be said about Jephthah and Samson.

Latin:

Vers. 7. TRADIDIT EOS IN MANUS PHILISTIIM ET FILIORUM AMMON) Vexandos scilicet multis ma- lis, non ut plane eis servirent. Est enim haec introductio ad ea quae de Jephthe & Samsone dicentur.

## 10:10
Vers. 10. WE HAVE FORSAKEN OUR GOD) against the precepts of תעשה (thou shalt do), AND WE HAVE SERVED BAALIM) against the chief of the precepts of לא תעשה (thou shalt not do).

Latin:

Vers. 10. DERELIQVIMVS DEUM NOSTRUM) contra praecepta תעשה ET SERVIVIMUS BAALIM) contra praecipuum praeceptorum לא תעשה.

## 10:12
Vers. 12. AND CANAAN.

In Hebrew: Inhabitants of the place Maon: concerning which Jerome in Hebrew places. Maon is a region of the Moabites according to Jeremiah ch. 48, 23. The Vulgate must therefore be corrected here along with the LXX.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET CANAAN.

In Ebr. Habitatores loci Maon: de quo Hier. in loc. Hebr. Maon regio Moabitarum juxta Jerem. c. 48, 23. Corrigenda ergo hic Vulgata cum LXX.

## 10:14
Verse 14. GO AND CALL UPON THE GODS WHICH YOU HAVE CHOSEN) spoken emphatically. Those whom you preferred to me, who am known to you by no benefits, the author of so many good things for you. God does not immediately forgive those who confess their sins, but [delays] his punishment with the patience of some time, while they approve [of their sins] and produce contrary deeds, as appears here in 10, and below in 15, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ITE ET INVOCATE DEOS QVOS ELE- GISTIS) ἐμφατικῶς dictum. Illos quos nullis beneficiis cogni- tos mihi, tot bonorum vobis auctori, praetulistis. Deus non statim confitentibus peccata remittit, sed poenam suam ali- cujus temporis patientia, approbantibus, & facta edentibus contraria, ut apparet hic 10. & infra 15. 16.

## 10:16
Verse 16. WHO GRIEVED OVER THEIR MISERIES) The Greeks are closest to the Hebrew: ὠλιγώθη ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ ἐν κόπῳ Ἰσραήλ. Jonathan omitted this as sounding bad. But the sense is, as Maimonides notes, God ceased to afflict them, and he wishes for this to be placed for מ, as in Leviticus 8, 32; 25, 52.

In Hebrew: ἐμφατικώτερος, divine compassion is expressed, his soul was narrowed in the labor of Israel. Thus also the LXX: ὠλιγώθη ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ. Compare Jeremiah 31, 20.

Latin:

Vers. 16. QUI DOLUIT SVPER MISERIIS EORVM) Graeci proxime ad Hebraeum: ὠλιγώθη ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ ἐν κό- πῳ Ἰσραήλ. Hoc ut male sonans omisit Jonathan. At sensus est, ut notat Maimonides, cessavit Deus eos affligere, vult- que hic poni pro מ, ut Levit. 8, 32. 25, 52.

In Ebr. ἐμφατικώτερος exprimitur miseratio divi- na, angustata est anima ejus in labore Israelis. Sic & LXX. ὠλιγώθη ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ. Conf. Jer. 31, 20.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. Jephthah's victory and vow.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Jephthae victoria & votum.

## 11:11
Verse 11. SON OF A HARLOT WOMAN.

God granted a dispensation regarding the law of Deuteronomy 23, 2, because Jephthah abolished that stain by virtue and holiness: he is listed in the catalog of the faithful in Hebrews 11. Grotius, however, prefers 'foreign woman' instead of 'adulteress,' following Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 11. FILIUS MULIERIS MERETRICIS.

DIspensavit Deus de lege Deut. 23, 2. quia ma- culam illam abolevit Jephthe virtute & san- ctitate: in Catalogo fidelium relatus Ebr. 11. Grotius tamen extraneam pro adultera mavult e Josepho.

## 12:2
Verse 2. BECAUSE HE WAS BORN OF AN ADULTEROUS MOTHER. 'Foreign woman' as here [in] Josephus. Among some nations, those born of a mother who was not a citizen were called νόθοι, as we showed from Aristophanes in book 2 of The Law of War and Peace, ch. 5, § 15. Among the Hebrews, however, a mother who had subjected herself to the law did not stain the birth, nor did it stand in the way of taking up an inheritance. Wherefore Jephthah rightly complains of this injury below in 7.

VIRI INOPES) ריקים in Hebrew & Chaldean, ἄνδρες κενοὶ in Greek. In those times, oppressed innocence sometimes resorted to such safeguards. See 1 Sam. 22, 2. ET LATROCINANTES) By private counsel, yet against public enemies, the Ammonites. You might not unfairly compare Jephthah to Viriatus. Cornelius rightly corrects the Vulgate here, because in the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek, the word for 'latrocinantes' (raiders) is not found. Vers. 9. EGO ERO VESTER PRINCEPS) Do you acknowledge me as a judge given by God to the people? Vers. 11. CORAM DOMINO. Either by invoking the Lord as a witness to the pact, as Tostatus says, or before the altar which they had erected there, so that they might sanctify this covenant holily. Vers. 15. HÆC DICIT JEPHTHE) He anxiously clears himself of the infamy of an unjust war, as befitted a good prince. NON TULIT ISRAEL TERRAM MOAB. Which, namely, the Moabites were actually possessing, for that had been forbidden in Num. 21, Deut. 2, & 3. But the land which Sihon, King of the Amorites, had occupied by war, the Israelites had occupied by God's command: even though Sihon the Amorite had previously taken Hebron and its entire region from Vaheb, King of the Moabites, from the Amorites, Num. 21, 14, 26, 28; but once the Amorite was struck down, Moses occupied all his land by right of war, which he had not brought upon himself, but had repelled. Vers. 21. POSSEDIT OMNEM TERRAM AMOR- RHÆI HABITATORIS REGIONIS ILLIUS ET UNI- VERSOS FINES EJUS) Even those things which the Amorite had snatched from others by force of war became the property of those who had defeated the Amorite by the law of nations, which is indicated here and in 1 Sam. 30, 20. And we have shown that the Greeks and Romans thought no differently in our book on the Law of War and Peace, chap. 6, § 7, and in the Annotations to that place. Vers. 24. QUÆ POSSIDET CHAMOS. Which he occupies, according to human understanding. By claiming your regions by right, you certainly could not have said anything more splendid than that they were given to you by your god Chamos. But I similarly assert that our God gave that land to us through victory. Vers. 25. NISI FORTE MELIOR ES BALAC. When the Hebrews occupied the regions of Sihon after he was killed, Balac was then King of Moab, and he was wise and powerful: he did not claim any territories for himself, not even by a single word, because the Amorite had long ago disturbed him from his possession by right of war. Vers. 26. JUXTA JORDANEM. In the Hebrew it is, 'By the Arnon.' PER TRECENTOS ANNOS. And so, by a very long prescription of time, we possess these lands without contradiction. Not 300 full years had elapsed, but as Ussher calculates in his Annals, p. 34, 264 years. For in the year of the World 2553, Sihon the Amorite was defeated, in which year the leadership of Joshua also began, but this embassy of Jephthah falls in the year of the World 2817. And so he said 300 years as a round number. From the beginning of Joshua's rule until the rest of the land under Joshua, six years flowed by: from there to the rest under Othniel, 48. Jud. 3, 11; from there to the rest under Ehud, 80, v. 30; from there to the rest restored to the land through Deborah, 40, chap. 5, 3; from there to the rest under Gideon, 40, c. 8, 28; from there to Abimelech, 10 years are to be counted, who ruled for 3 years, c. 9, 22; Thola ruled 23, Jud. 10, 2; Jair for 22 years, chap. 10, 3; all of which, when added together, make 264 years. For those who are defending their possessions against adversaries by prescription of time are accustomed to amplify it rather than diminish it, and that perfect number approached 300 years more than 200. Vers. eod. QUARE TANTO TEMPORE NIHIL SUPER HAC REPETITIONE TENTASTIS) For three hundred years, as he has already said: that is, approximately. For, as the most learned believe, some years are missing. But this way of expressing numbers is frequent in the Scriptures, as can be seen in Num. 1, 46 & 2, 32 & 11, 21. And often elsewhere. τὰς κτήσεις καὶ τὰς ἰδίας, καὶ τὰς κοινὰς ἢν ἐπι- γένηται πολὺς χρόνος, κυρίας καὶ πατρώας ἅπαντες εἶναι νο- μίζουσι, say the Lacedaemonians to Archidamus in Isocrates. Indeed, just as civil laws establish that there is some time by which actions are excluded for the sake of the public good, so among nations, but over a longer span of time, the same holds true, by a received law, about which we treated in the second book on the Law of War, chap. 4.

Vers. 27. LET THE LORD THE JUDGE JUDGE THIS DAY BETWEEN THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL AND THE CHILDREN OF AMMON) Josephus, book 15: μεθ' ὧν τὸ δίκαιόν ἐστι, μετ' ἐκείνων ὁ θεός. Totilas in Procopius: ὀ γάρ ἐστιν οὐκ ἔστι τὸν ἀδικοῦντα καὶ βιαζόμενον ἐν τοῖς ἀγῶσιν εὐδοκιμεῖν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν βίον ἑκάστῳ ἡ τῆς πολέμῳ πρυτανεύεται τύχη. See more on this matter in the Prolegomena to the Law of War and Peace.

Vers. 29. SPIRITVS DOMINI) Who would give him strength and success beyond human measure.

These things are rendered by the Vulgate in such a way that Jephthah's rash vow seems to be attributed to the Spirit of the Lord: 'The Spirit of the Lord therefore came upon Jephthah, and circling Gilead, etc., he made a vow,' as if all these things had proceeded from the same Spirit, whereas in the Hebrew they are distinguished, and the narrative of Jephthah's vow begins a new sentence, as Cajetan rightly observes. Furthermore, v. 31, the Vulgate interprets: 'Whoever shall have come out first, etc., I will offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord.' In the Hebrew we read thus: 'and it shall be the one coming out, that which shall have come out, etc., and it shall be to the Lord, and I will offer it as a burnt offering,' as Pagninus rendered it. The Vulgate therefore translated it carelessly, both because it seems to restrict the vow to a human being alone, which rather extended to beasts, and because it contracts the text and omits the words, 'it shall be to the Lord.'

Vref. 30. VOTVM VOVIT DOMINO DICENS: SI TRADIDERIS FILIOS AMMON IN MANUS MEAS, QVICVNQVE PRIMVS FVERIT EGRESSVS DE FO- RIBVS DOMUS MEÆ, MIHIQVE OCCVBRERIT REVERTENTI CVM PACE A FILIIS AMMON, EUM HOLOCAVSTUM OFFERAM DOMINO] Something similar is told about Idomeneus. Servius on the 3rd Aeneid: 'Idomeneus, born of the seed of Deucalion, King of the Cretans; when he was returning after the destruction of Troy, during a storm, he vowed to the gods that he would sacrifice from the thing that first met him. It happened that his son met him first: whom, when he had sacrificed—or as others say, had wished to sacrifice—and a plague had subsequently arisen, he was driven from the kingdom by the citizens.' The same on book 11: 'Idomeneus was King of the Cretans, who, when he was struggling in a storm, vowed that he would sacrifice to Neptune from the thing that first met him.' By chance, when his son first met him, and, as others say, he sacrificed him, or as others say, he wished to sacrifice him, he was driven from the kingdom by the citizens on account of his cruelty. Many Hebrews and Christians have also believed that the daughter was sacrificed by Jephthah. But that this is credible concerning a man whose faith is proclaimed in Heb. 11:32 does not seem so to me. Wherefore it is to be noted that here in the masculine is placed 'whosoever', which in Hebrew is אֲשֶׁר, which is of every gender, and is best translated here by the neuter: just as Josephus translates it, πᾶν ὅ τι καὶ πρῶτον αὐτῷ συντύχῃ. Furthermore, it is common for the Hebrews that a conjunctive particle has the sense of a disjunctive, as we have noted elsewhere: and that וְהָיָה לַיהוָה וְהַעֲלִיתִיהוּ עוֹלָה is thus best translated: It shall be to the Lord, or I will cause it to ascend as a burnt offering: namely, if that animal is capable of being a burnt offering. For burnt offerings by the law could not be made except from oxen, birds, goats, turtledoves, or pigeons. What if an ass or a dog had met him, ought it to have been made a burnt offering? Certainly not. Therefore, neither anything of the human race: but it was to be dedicated to those ministries which men perform for God, for instance in the sanctuary, if it were a male: if a female, to prayers, abstinence from wine, and a solitary life. For in a human being, 'it shall be to the Lord' has a sense equal to that in 1 Sam. 1:28, 'I have lent him to the Lord.' You have an example of celibacy enjoined upon women, and that under custody, also in 2 Sam. 20:3.

Grotius is therefore compelled to abandon the Vulgate, which he nevertheless holds as authentic. For thus it rendered the vow of Jephthah: 'If thou shalt deliver the children of Ammon into my hands, whosoever shall first come forth out of the doors of my house, and shall meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I will offer him a burnt offering to the Lord.' He also abandons the Hebrews, whom he is accustomed to esteem highly; he abandons most of the Fathers, whose consonant interpretation he otherwise holds as a rule.

end? Namely, to gratify the monastic life; but who, I ask, will believe the Papists and Grotius, who is sailing with them here, that Jephthah had in mind his daughter when he made or fulfilled the vow? They who extol the monastic life to heaven and bind free consciences with vows, even if rash, wicked, and pernicious, have hitherto produced no example of such a vow of celibacy, no rule, and not even any counsel from the Old Testament. Nor is any species of vow held in 2 Sam. 20:3, let alone celibacy: for those women were not celibates, but widows, who were shut up against their will, not indeed by a vow. For that ought to be free. Therefore, that IT SHALL BE THE LORD'S, to be explained as a woman to be consecrated to God for the monastic life, neither the force of that phrase, nor any parallel passage, or even custom, or the Law of those times, such as none can be produced, implies; and its reason is far different from what is held in 1 Sam. 1:28, I have lent him to the Lord. For there it is clearly explained in what manner Hannah consecrated her son to the Lord, a kind of thing which does not occur here regarding celibacy. And that phrase AND IT SHALL BE THE LORD'S is sacrificial by the solemn usage of Scripture, and therefore when AND I WILL OFFER IT UP AS A BURNT OFFERING is added, it is manifest that it was added by way of explanation, and not in a disjunctive sense. And hence also Jephthah grieved so much when his daughter met him: Alas for me, my daughter! That a holy man so lamented the lost hope of posterity from his daughter, that he held this in a higher place than a vow about a virgin to be consecrated to God for life, and its fulfillment, will not be easily said by those who so greatly extol and proclaim the holiness and excellence of these vows; for he was vehemently terrified, and tore his garments and lamented his daughter. But then the ordinary gathering at that place of the virgins, that they might lament the daughter of Jephthah, confirms her immolation, and does not favor the vow of celibacy. For perpetual virginity is such a good thing, according to the Pontificians, that it ought not to be lamented and mourned, but extolled with praises and greatly celebrated. These causes move our theologians, so that most of them, with Luther (if you except Chytræus, Brentius, and Franz), believe that an immolation was made, but not the perpetual virginity sanctioned by a vow of the daughter of Jephthah, whom Philo calls Seila by her own name. And in this they follow the Chaldean Targum, Josephus, Antiquities book 5, chapter 12, the most ancient Rabbis, and the almost common consensus of the Fathers: along with the Greeks Justin Martyr, question 99, Chrysostom, homily on Jephthah and homily at Antioch, Nazianzen, oration on the praises of the Maccabees, likewise Origen, Theodoret, Epiphanius, Procopius, Anastasius of Nicaea, and others. Then of the Latins, Tertullian, book 2 against Marcion, chapter 4; Ambrose, book 1 of Duties, last chapter, book 3, chapter 12; Jerome, Epistle 34 to Julian, Vol. 1 of his works, as also in chapter 7 of Jeremiah; Augustine, question 49 on the book of Judges and book 1 of The City of God, chapter 21; the author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament among the works of Augustine, chapter 43; Sulpicius Severus, book 1 of Sacred History; Bede, book of questions on Judges; Anselm. To these add Rupert on this passage, Hugh of St. Victor on this passage, Thomas Aquinas, book 12, question 88, Article 2. Nor do most of the Calvinists themselves, nor the more recent and modern Pontificians, deny this; Abulensis, Dionysius, Cajetan, the Carthusian, Victoria, Azorius, Schvarez, Justinianus, Torniellus, Salianus, Ribera, Lessius, Serrarius, Jac. Bonfrerius, Menochius, Tirinus, etc. But few of the Papists themselves stand on the side of Grotius, or rather of Rabbi David Kimchi and Levi Ben-Gerson (for he followed these as guides), such as Lyranus, Vatablus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Mariana, Estius, and whoever else: to whom from the Calvinists, Pelec., Broughton, Perkins, Junius and Tremellius, Piscator, de Dieu, Amama, the Belgian translators, and some others accede. Nor without merit does Bonfrerius here ask from the opposing side, where they have read elsewhere of an example of such a vow or separation from the company of men? And why not rather, just as when an unclean animal was vowed to God, it was redeemed by a price, according to that which is held in the last chapter of Leviticus, that this daughter of Jephthah was not also redeemed by a price? And indeed (these are also the words of Bonfrerius) what if Jephthah's first wife had met him, or some servant bound by marriage, would it have had to be concluded in the same way according to Jephthah's intention that she lead a celibate life? All of which (concludes Bonfrerius), since they sufficiently refute this opinion by themselves, I do not see how rightly some, having abandoned the common sense of the ancient Fathers and the whole Church, and the opinion of our Vulgate version, deflect to the figments of unskilled Hebrews. And hence seems to be the fable of the poets about Iphigenia or Jephthigenia, and that the inhabitants in Sisimis were accustomed to make a sacrifice in the name of a girl, as testified by Epiphanius, heresy 78, whom he thinks was the daughter of Jephthah once offered in sacrifice. Nor is there any reason for Grotius to object about an ass or a dog, if the one or the other had met him. For those on the opposite side deny that other animals were included in that vow, and thus they wish it to have been conceived only of humans, as the Vulgate interpreter rendered it, primarily because Jephthah added in his vow: And it shall meet me when I return, since it is the property of a human alone to meet another, to applaud, and to congratulate one on his return, whence Augustine, question 49: He did not by any means vow some beast with these words, which he could offer as a burnt offering according to the law. For it is not or was not the custom that beasts should meet leaders returning from war with victory.

The scruple which moved Grotius, that the offering of a daughter does not befit a man whose faith is proclaimed in Scripture, does not move others. Tirinus, certainly a Jesuit, attributes this vow to the instinct of the Holy Spirit, and with Anselm, Serarius, and Salianus, judges that Jephthah did not sin when he vowed in this way that he would immolate as a burnt offering to God whoever should first meet him to congratulate him upon his return home as victor, even if it were the most beloved of his household, even if it were his wife, even if it were his only daughter. And indeed, that a victory so illustrious was granted from heaven in view of this vow is an indication that this vow was singularly pleasing to God; nay, that its fulfillment is praised in Hebrews 11, and that God, as the author and Lord of the life of all, even in the more fragile sex, wished there to exist in a most difficult matter an example of full obedience, and to set forth a type in which the tolerance of the willing mind of the Messiah might be shadowed forth. They also bring forward the example of Samson, who brought death upon himself: but if they say that this was done by the instinct of the Spirit, why might not this deed of the one vowing or immolating his daughter also be approved, as having been carried out by the impulse of the same Spirit? To which view Augustine also seems to be favorable in book 1 of The City of God, chapter 21. And it is deservedly asked: whether that which Jephthah did, when he killed his daughter who met him, since he had vowed that he would immolate to God whatever should first meet him returning as victor from battle, is to be held as a command of God? And likewise Jerome in his Epistle to Julian, when he says: That Jephthah offered his virgin daughter, and for that reason was placed by the Apostle in the enumeration of the saints. Others, although they disapprove of this vow, to which view Augustine also inclines in Question 49, saying: 'This man, however, even with God neither commanding nor requesting it, and contrary to His legitimate precept, vowed a human sacrifice beyond what was required'; yet they excuse Jephthah on account of ignorance and erroneous conscience, of which the words of the same man seem to bear witness:

I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I shall not be able to do otherwise. For who could believe that he, to whom there was only one daughter, and for that reason uniquely dear, because he had grieved so much over that event of the meeting of his daughter, would have sacrificed her, unless he had been persuaded that he was bound by a vow to do so? But if Jephthah offered his virgin daughter to God, says Jerome in chapter VII of Leviticus, it was not the sacrifice that pleased, but the spirit of the one offering. But because that error is too gross, and that deed is not only most explicitly prohibited by divine law in Deut. 12:30 ff., but is also contrary to the very law of nature, as being parricidal, and no other victims are to be sacrificed to God except those over whom we have the right of life and death, such as a pious head of a household can by no means imagine for himself regarding his children, wife, or servants, Jephthah certainly cannot be absolved of guilt; but there is no doubt that he obtained salvation through the repentance he performed, and for that reason is numbered among the Saints in Heb. 11: In which catalogue, indeed, not a few are contained whose sins were quite serious and even noted in the Sacred Code, but which were forgiven them through faith. Jephthah certainly cannot be cleared of his lapse and guilt, even if it is said with Grotius that he devoted his daughter to a monastic life: since in vowing the virginity of a daughter, her own consent is absolutely required, and it is not lawful for parents to consecrate their children to perpetual virginity without their consent. Consult on this vow the Spicilegium of Ludovicus Capellus and the Spicilegium Scholasticum Sacrificiorum of Johannes Cloppenburg, p. 216.

Verse of the same.

ONLY-BEGOTTEN) Monogenes in the LXX here and Josephus. Aquila, pothete (beloved). Thus yachid is translated elsewhere as agapetos (beloved) and agapomenos (loved). See on Matt. 3:17.

Verse 34.

WITH TIMBREL AND DANCES) Similar to 1 Kings 6:6. But because their priests played the flute and timbrel. Tacitus on the Jews.

Verse 35.

WOE IS ME, MY DAUGHTER) He laments the lost hope of posterity from his daughter.

Rather, Jephthah laments the death of his daughter, not her virginity. For because of this, the daughter who submitted herself with a ready spirit to her father's vow would not have been so much to be lamented; nor indeed is it likely that that distinguished hero, having won such a glorious victory, was of such a dejected and dismayed spirit that, terrified, he tore his garments and lamented for the reason that his daughter was to be dedicated to God for prayers, abstinence from wine, and a monastic life. What is more, it was never accepted among the Jews that women should foster perpetual virginity, for whom barrenness was a disgrace, as is gathered from 1 Sam. 1:10, Luke 1:25: nor is there any example available of women among the people of God having taken a vow of Naziriteship, although it is clear from the example of Samson and Samuel that not even Nazirites abstained from marriage perpetually, Jud. 14:5, 1 Sam. 8:1. But that Jephthah's daughter laments her virginity is not surprising, since she saw that she had to die a virgin, with no offspring left to raise up the people of God, which condition made her death all the more bitter to her, because she was deprived of the effect of the divine promise made in Ex. 23:26.

Verse 37.

AND I WILL BEWAIL MY VIRGINITY) For she could not serve God alone, if she had been subject to a husband. For he had a right over his wife. Thus among the Greeks, animals dedicated to the gods are called ἄφετα, because they served no one, but were kept in honor of the gods. It is otherwise with men, who although [...] dedicated to the Temple could have wives, from whose embrace, however, they abstained during the time of their ministry. For men remain their own masters.

Ver. 40.

AND LET THEM BEWAIL THE DAUGHTER OF JEPHTHAH) Others, Let them console the daughter of Jephthah: But it is more true that it is the Chaldean word תנא which signifies to recount, and that the ק which follows is put for ד, as is often the case. The sense is, in memory of the victory, and of the faith kept to God, virgins came to that place four times a year, and celebrated the matter by conversation, or even by songs; which Epiphanius narrates was done in the same place by the Samaritans even in his own times.

Since Grotius here again departs from the Vulgate version, how will he defend its authority with the Tridentine Fathers? But he wished to serve his own hypothesis that the daughter of Jephthah was not killed, but alive and consecrated to God. The Vulgate, however, can cite in its favor the Chaldean, and the LXX Interpreters, as well as R. Solomon: whom B. Luther and the French version also follow, for which interpretation some repeat the force of the Hebrew word from the noun תנין Dragons, whose wailing is wont to be great, Job 30, Micah 1, Malachi 1. But Amama refutes these in his Antibarbarus. Bibl. libr. III. p. 390, that לתנות cannot be a gerund from the reduplicating verbs: rather it must necessarily be ascribed to the quiescent Lamed He and be a Gerund in Piel, and thus its theme is תנה, which word he says is more Chaldean than Hebrew, and explains it from Jud. 5:11, there יתנו let them recount the righteousnesses of the Lord, in this sense: to recount, or that the daughters of Jephthah might recount the things done, or new things, so as to alleviate the tedium of solitude: or to converse with the daughter of Jephthah; to which Junius and the Tigurine also incline; to converse with her. But because that assembly was instituted even long after the times of Jephthah, which appears from the text, and as Grotius observed from Epiphanius, it cannot be understood as a conversation instituted with the living daughter of Jephthah; and therefore Grotius more correctly explains it as to converse about her. However, the observation of Ludovicus de Dieu in his animadversion on this passage pleases more, that the meaning is to be sought from Arabism: where from the Hebrew שנו to repeat, whence is שנים two, with the change of ש into ת according to custom, it becomes the verb תנ, which in the Second Conjugation, that is, the same which occurs here, namely Piel, signifies to celebrate, to praise, to give thanks, because the first one gave a benefit, he bound the recipient to the second parts, which are acts of thanksgiving. Thence therefore de Dieu translates the passage Jud. 5:11 thus, there let them praise the righteousnesses of the Lord: And in this place: To praise the daughter of Jephthah. For the memory of the daughter of Jephthah was celebrated there, on account of her unusual obedience and patience. That this memory was celebrated annually, however, is clear from the Hebrew text, from days to days, that is, from year to year, as Drusius observed the force of the phrase in his commentary on difficult places in this passage. Grotius therefore ought not to have left the passage to the fiction of the Rabbis, that virgins gathered at that place four times a year; of which there is no trace in the sacred text.

The LXX, Jonathan, the Syriac, the Arabic, Montanus, Cajetan, B. Luther, Osiander, and the English render it 'to lament,' a sense which Piscator rejects for the sole reason that the preposition ל is used, and not the article ה; but that seems to us of so little importance that one should not depart from the explanation of so many interpreters, if perhaps room is not to be left for Dievius's new interpretation. Our Mr. Pfeiffer recently replied to Sixtinus Amama in his Disputation on whether Jephthah sacrificed his daughter, that it is not unusual for imperfect verbs of different classes to sustain the same meaning, nor is it for grammarians to prescribe to the Holy Spirit the mode and manner of establishing [language]: and that ספד, which is likewise 'to lament' in 1 Kings 14:13, is similarly constructed with ל, even though in Zechariah 12:10 it is constructed with על with the same meaning. But those who explain it as 'to converse' or 'to narrate' about her, just as in Judges 5:11 the meaning of 'to narrate' prevails, are helped by a comparison of passages where תנה is the same as 'about,' Gen. 26:13, Ps. 91:11, as also Gen. 26:7, Ps. 3:3, Ps. 45:2, Exod. 14:3, 2 Sam. 11:7. Nor, however, does he reject the explanation of Dievius or even Forster for 'to give,' i.e., praise to Jephthah's daughter, provided that the consecration of the living daughter to celibacy is not thereby carved out; to which that annual statute in Israel, which lasted among the Samaritans even in the time of Epiphanius, Haer. 55 & 78, in no way corresponds.

arising from the similarity of the numerals H and K. Since it is said of this one, and of the preceding judges Abesan and Elon, that they judged Israel, the opinion of Nicolaus Abramus in Phar. V. T. lib. 10, c. 22, that they presided only over the Gileadites and the tribes beyond the Jordan liberated by Jephthah from the servitude of the Ammonites, while Eli the High Priest meanwhile administered justice to the other tribes still pressed by the yoke of the Philistines, does not deserve consideration. For although Jephthah, having defeated the Ammonites, obtained only the Gileadite prefecture by the pact entered into with his own people, c. 11:9, 10, yet after the slaughter of 42,000 Ephraimites, c. 12:6, 7, he is said to have judged Israel, which is likewise reported of these also, that they judged ISRAEL, just as it was said of Thola and Jair in c. 10:2, 3. Nor indeed does any reason appear why, after Jephthah, the Gileadites should have subjected themselves not to some of their own tribesmen, but to others from the tribe of Judah, Zebulun, and Ephraim.

Latin:
