Vers. 2. QVIA DE ADVLTERA MATRE NATVS EST Extranea ut hic Josephus. Apud gentes aliquas matre non ci- ve nati νόθοι dicebantur, ut ex Aristophane ostendimus l. 2. de Jure Belli & Pacis c. 5. §. 15. Apud Hebraeos vero mater quae legi se subjecerat non maculabat natales, neque ad haere- ditatem capessendam obstabat. Quare merito Jephthes de hac injuria queritur infra 7.

VIRI INOPES) ריקים in Hebræo & Chaldæo, ἄνδρες κενοὶ in Græco. Illis temporibus interdum oppressa inno- centia ad talia præsidia decurrebat. Vide 1. Sam. 22, 2. ET LATROCINANTES) Privato consilio, adversus hostes tamen publicos Ammonitas. Jephtæ Viriatum non male compares. Merito hic Vulgatum corrigit Cornelius, quod in Ebr. Chald. & Græco τὸ latrocinantes non ha- beatur. Vers. 9. EGO ERO VESTER PRINCEPS) Agnosce- tis me ut judicem a Deo populo datum? Vers. 11. CORAM DOMINO. Sive invocando Dominum in testem pacti, ut Tostatus, seu coram altari, quod ibi extruxerant, ut sancte hoc fœdus sancirent. Vers. 15. HÆC DICIT JEPHTHE) Sollicite a se infa- miam belli injusti amolitur, ut decebat bonum principem. NON TULIT ISRAEL TERRAM MOAB. Quam scil. actu possidebant Moabitæ, id enim vetitum fuerat Num. 21. Deut. 2. & 3. Sed quam bel- lo occuparat Sehon rex Amorrhæorum, eam Dei jussu occuparant Israëlitæ : etsi Sihon Amorrhæus prius a Vahebo Rege Moabitarum Hebronem & totam ejus regionem Amorrhæis ademerit Numer. 21, 14. 26. 28. percusso vero Amorrhæo terram ejus omnem jure belli occupavit Moses, quod ipsi non intulerat, sed repulerat. Vers. 21. POSSEDIT OMNEM TERRAM AMOR- RHÆI HABITATORIS REGIONIS ILLIUS ET UNI- VERSOS FINES EJUS) Etiam quæ Amorrhæus per vim bellicam aliis eripuerat, facta sunt eorum, qui Amorrhæum devicerant jure gentium, quod & hic indicatur & 1. Sam. 30, 20. Nec aliter sensisse Græcos & Romanos ostendimus li- bro de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. 6. §. 7. & in Annotatis ad eum locum. Vers. 24. QUÆ POSSIDET CHAMOS. Quæ occupavit, κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον. Edicto jure obtinens regiones tuas sane nihil splendidius dixe- ris, quam quod datæ tibi sint a Deo tuo Chamos. At ego similiter assero Deum nostrum terram illam nobis per victoriam dedisse. Vers. 25. NISI FORTE MELIOR ES BALAC. Cum Ebræi cæso Sihon occuparunt ejus regio- nes, tunc Balac erat Rex Moab, isque sapiens & po- tens : qui ne verbulo quidem ditiones ullas sibi vin- dicavit, eo quod jure belli Amorrhæus eum olim sua possessione deturbarit. Vers. 26. JUXTA JORDANEM. In Ebræo est, Juxta Arnon. PER TRECENTOS ANNOS. Adeog; longissima temporis præscriptione ci- tra contradictionem has terras possidemus. Elapsi erant non integri 300, sed ut Usserius in Annalibus p. 34. computat, 264. anni. Nam anno Mundi 2553. devictus est Sihon Amorrhæus, quo anno cepit etiam Josuæ principatus, Jephthæ vero hæc legatio in annum Mundi 2817. incidit. Adeoque numero rotundo 300. annos dixit. A Josuani regiminis ini- tio usq; ad quietem terræ sub Josua sex anni efflu- xerunt: inde ad quietem sub Othoniele 48. Jud. 3, 11. inde ad quietem sub Ehud 80. v. 30. inde ad quietem per Deboram terræ redditam 40. cap. 5, 3. inde ad quietem sub Gideone 40. c. 8, 28. inde ad Abimelechum 10. anni numerandi, qui 3. annis præfuit c. 9, 22. Thola præfuit 23. Jud. 10, 2. Jair 22. annis cap. 10, 3. qui omnes in summam redacti effi- ciunt 264. annos. Solent enim, qui temporis præ- scriptione in possessionibus suis contra adversarios tuendis, amplificare potius eam, quam minuere, ac perfectus ille numerus magis ad trecentos, quam ducentos accedebat annos. Vers. eod. QUARE TANTO TEMPORE NIHIL SUPER HAC REPETITIONE TENTASTIS) Per annos, ut jam dixit, trecentos: id est, circiter. Nam, ut doctissimi sentiunt, de- ficiunt aliquot anni. Sed hîc modus exprimendi numeros frequens Scripturis, ut videre est Num. 1, 46. & 2. 32. & 11, 21. Et alibi sæpe. τὰς κτήσεις καὶ τὰς ἰδίας, καὶ τὰς κοινὰς ἢν ἐπι- γένηται πολὺς χρόνος, κυρίας καὶ πατρώας ἅπαντες εἶναι νο- μίζουσι. ajunt Lacones apud Isocratem Archidamo. Nimirum sicut esse aliquod tempus, quo actiones excluderentur publici boni causa statuunt civiles leges, ita inter gentes, sed longio- re temporum spatio, idem valet, recepto jure, de quo egimus libro secundo de Jure Belli cap. 4.

Vers. 27. JVDICET DOMINVS ARBITER HVJUS DIEI INTER ISRAEL ET INTER FILIOS AMMON) Joseph. lib. 15. μεθ' ὧν τὸ δίκαιόν ἐστι, μετ' ἐκείνων ὁ θεός. Totilas apud Procopium: ὀ γάρ ἐστιν οὐκ ἔστι τὸν ἀδικοῦντα καὶ βιαζόμενον ἐν τοῖς ἀγῶσιν εὐδοκιμεῖν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν βί- ον ἑκάστῳ ἡ τῆς πολέμῳ πρυτανεύεται τύχη. Vide plura ad hanc rem in Prolegomenis de Jure Belli ac Pacis.

Vers. 29. SPIRITVS DOMINI) Qui supra humanum modum fortitudinem ei ac successus daret.

Hæc ita redduntur a Vulgato, ut Spiritui Do- mini tribui videatur temerarium Jephtæ votum: Factus est ergo Spiritus Domini super Jephthe, & cir- cuiens Galaad &c. votum vovit, quasi hæc omnia ab eodem Spiritu profecta essent, quum in Ebræo distinguantur, & narratio voti Jephthæi novam in- choet sententiam, ut recte observat Cajetanus. Porro v. 31. Vulgat. interpretatur: Quicunque pri- mus fuerit egressus, &c. eum holocaustum offeram Domino. In Ebr. sic legimus: & erit egrediens, quod egressum fuerit &c. & erit Domino, & offeram illud in holocaustum, ut reddidit Pagninus. Incurio- se itaq; transtulit Vulgatus, tum quod ad solum ho- minem videatur restringere votum, quod potius se ad bestias extendebat, tum quod textum contrahat & omittat verba, erit Domino.

Vref. 30. VOTVM VOVIT DOMINO DICENS: SI TRADIDERIS FILIOS AMMON IN MANUS MEAS, QVICVNQVE PRIMVS FVERIT EGRESSVS DE FO- RIBVS DOMUS MEÆ, MIHIQVE OCCVBRERIT REVERTENTI CVM PACE A FILIIS AMMON, EUM HOLOCAVSTUM OFFERAM DOMINO] Simile ali- quid de Idomeneo narratur. Servius ad 3. Æneid. Idome- neus de semine Deucalionis natus Cretensium Rex; cum post eversam Trojam reverteretur in tempestate, devovit diis sacrifi- caturum se de re, quæ primum occurrisset. Contigit ut filius ejus primum occurreret: quem cum immolasset, ut alii vero, im- molare voluisset, & post orta esset pestilentia, a civibus pulsus est regno. Idem ad librum 11. Idomeneus Rex Cretensium fu- it, qui tum tempestate laboraret, vovit se sacrificaturum Ne- ptuno de re, quæ primum ei occurrisset. Casu cum ei primum filius occurrisset, eumque, ut alii dicunt, immolasset, ut alii im- molare voluisset, ob crudelitatem regno a civibus pulsus est. Immolatam etiam ab Jephthe filiam multi credidere Hebræo- rum Christianorumque. Sed id de homine, cujus fides præ- dicatur Hebr. 11, 32. mihi credibile non fit. Quare notan- dum, quod hic in masculino ponitur quicunque in Hebræo esse אֲשֶׁר, quod est omnis generis, & optime hic per neu- trum verti: Sicut Josephus vertit, πᾶν ὅ τι καὶ πρῶτον αὐτῷ συντύχῃ. Deinde vero frequens esse Hebræis, ut conjunctiva particulæ disjunctivæ sensum habeat, ut & alibi notavimus: & illa וְהָיָה לַיהוָה וְהַעֲלִיתִיהוּ עוֹלָה sic optime trans- ferri: Erit Domino, aut ascendere faciam holocaustum: nem- pe si id animal holocausti sit capax. Holocausta enim per legem fieri non poterant, nisi ex bobus, avibus, capris, turtu- re, columba. Quid si asinus aut canis occurrisset, debuitne holocaustum fieri? non sane. Ergo nec humani generis quicquam: sed dedicandum id ad ea ministeria, quæ homines Deo exhibent, puta in sanctuario, si mas esset: si femina ad preces, vini abstinentiam & vitam μονάζουσαν. Nam in ho- mine, erit Domino, sensum habet parem illi 1. Sam. 1, 28. Feci eum Domino. Cœlibatus feminis indicti, idque sub custodia, exemplum habes & 2. Sam. 20, 3.

Deserere ergo cogitur Grotius vulgatam, quam tamen pro avthentica habet. Ita enim illa vo- tum Jephthæ reddidit: Si tradideris filios Ammon in manus meas, quicunq; primus fuerit egressus de fori- bus domus meæ, mihiq; occurrerit revertenti cum pa- ce, a filiis Ammon, eum holocaustum offeram Domi- no. Deserit etiam Ebræos, quos magnifacere solet; deserit plerosq; Patrum, quorum interpretationem consonam pro regula alioquin habet.

fini? Ut nempe gratificetur vitæ monasticæ; quam vero de filiâ in animo habuisse, cum votum fecit, aut exequutus est Jephthæ, quis obsecro, Papistis & Grotio illis hic velificanti credet? Nullum talis cælibatus voti exemplum, nullam regulam ac ne confilium quidem ullum e V. T. hactenus protule- re, qui vitam μονάζουσαν in cælum extollunt, & vo- tis, licet temerariis, iniquis, ac perniciosis con- scientias liberas constringunt. Neq; ulla voti spe- cies 2. Sam. 20, 3. habetur, nedum cælibatus: Fue- rant enim illæ non cælibes, sed viduæ, quæ præter voluntatem suam includebantur, non vero ex vo- to. Id enim liberum esse debet. Illud ergo ERIT DOMINO, de fæmina in vitam μονάζουσαν con- secranda Deo explicari, neque vis phraseos istius, nec parallelus locus ullus, aut consuetudo etiam, vel Lex temporum istorum, qualis nulla proferri potest, importat; ac longe dispar ejus ratio est, quod 1. Sam. 1, 28. habetur, feci eum Domino. Ibi enim qua ratione filium Domino consecrarit Han- na, luculenter expositum est, quale quid de cælibatu hic non occurrit. Et phrasis illa והיה ליהוה ET ERIT DOMINO ex usu scripturæ solenni sacrificialis est, ideoque cum addatur והעליתיהו עולה Et ascendere faciam illud holocaustum, κατ᾽ ἐπεξήγησιν id additum esse, non autem sensu dis- junctivo, manifestum est. Atque hinc etiam tan- topere doluit Jephtha, cum occurreret ipsi Filia: Heu me filia mea! Deplorasse adeo virum sanctum amissam spem posteritatis ex Filia, ut hanc potiori habuerit loco, quam votum de virgine per vitam Deo consecranda, ejusque exequutionem, non fa- cile dicent, qui sanctitatem & præstantiam horum votorum tantopere extollunt & deprædicant; ve- hementer enim perterrefactus fuit, & vestimenta sua laceravit ac deploravit filiam suam. Tum vero conventus ad locum illum ordinarius virginum, ut plangerent filiam Jephtha, immolationem ejusdem confirmat, non vero voto cælibatus favet. Perpe- tua enim virginitas tantum bonum est, secundum Pontificios, quod non plangi ac lugeri, sed laudi- bus efferri, ac maximopere celebrari debeat. Quæ causæ nostros movent Theologos, ut pleriq; cum Luthero (si Chytreum, Brentium & Franzium ex- cipias) immolationem factam credant, non au- tem virginitatem perpetuam voto sancitam filiæ Jephthæ, quam Seilam nomine suo Philo appellat. Et sequuntur in eo Targum Chaldaicum, Jose- phum Antiquit. l. 5. c. 12. Rabbinos antiquissimos, & communem fere Patrum consensum: cum Græ- corum Justini Martyr. quæst. XCIX. Chrysost. ho- mil. de Jephthæ & hom. Antioch. Nazianz. orat. de laudibus Maccab. Origenis item Theod. Epi- phanii, Procopii, Anastasii Niceni, & aliorum. Tum Latinorum Tertulliani lib. 2. contra Mar- cion. cap. 4. Ambrosii lib. 1. offic. cap. ult. lib. III. cap. 12. Hieronymi Ep. 34. ad Julian. Tom. I. oper. ut & in cap. 7. Jerem. Augustini q. 49. in libr. Judic. & libr. 1. de C. D. Cap. 21. Auctoris Quæst. Vet. & Nov. Test. apud August. c. 43. Seve- ri Sulpitii lib. 1. Sac. Historiar. Bedæ libr. quæst. in Judic. Anshelmi. Quibus adde Rupertum h. l. Hugonem de S. Vict. in h. l. Thomam de Aquino lib. 12. quæst. 88. Art. 2. Neq; abnuunt ipsis tum Calviniani plerique, tum Pontificii recentiores & moderni; Abulensis, Dionys. Cajetanus, Carthru- sianus, Victoria, Asorius, Schvarez, Justinia- neus, Torniellus, Salianus, Ribera, Lessius, Sera- rius, Jac. Bonfrerius, Menochius, Tirinus, &c. Pauci vero ex ipsis Papistis hic a Grotii vel potius a Rabbi Davidis Kimchii & Levi Ben - Gersonis (hos enim duces sequutus est) stant partibus, ut- pote Lyranus, Vatablus, Pagninus, Ariasmonta- nus, Mariana, Estius & si qui alii : quibus e Cal- vin. Pelec. Brugton. Perkins. Junius & Tremel. Piscator, de Dieu, Amama, translatores Belgici, & alii nonnulli accedunt. Nec immerito hic Bonfre- rius ab adversa parte petit, ubi Exemplum talis vo- ti vel separationis ab hominum convictu alibi lege- rint? Et cur non potius, quemadmodum cum Deo vovebatur immundum animal, illud pretio redime- batur, juxta id quod habetur Levit. ult. non & hæc Jephthæ filia pretio redemta fuerit? Et vero (Bon- frerii etiam hæc sunt) quid si Jephthæ uxor prima occurrisset, vel servus aliquis conjugio illigatus, an eodem modo ad cælibem vitam ducendam ex Jeph- thæ intentione concludi debuisset? Quæ omnia (con- cludit Bonfrerius) cum per se satis hanc sententiam refellant, non video, quam recte nonnulli relicto an- tiquorum Patrum totiusq; Ecclesiæ communi sensu, nostræq; vulgatæ versionis sententia ad imperitorum Ebræorum figmenta deflectant. Atq; hinc videtur esse fabula Poetarum de Iphigenia vel Jephthigenia, & quod in Sisimis incolæ sacrificium facere consue- verint in nomen puellæ, teste Epiphanio hæres. LXXIIX. quam existimat fuisse filiam Jephthæ olim in sacrificium oblatam. Neque est quod asi- num objiciat aut canem Grotius, si ille vel hic oc- currisset. Negant enim οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας, animalia alia voto illo comprehensa fuisse, adeoque volunt de solis hominibus id conceptum, uti vulgatus inter- pres id reddidit, imprimis, quia in voto suo addidit Jephthe: Mihiq; occurrerit revertenti, siquidem so- lius hominis sit alteri occurrere, applaudere, & de reditu gratulari, unde Augustinus quæst. 49. Non utiq; his verbis pecus aliquod vovit, quod secun- dum legem holocaustoma posset offerre. Neq; enim est aut fuit consuetudinis, ut redeuntibus cum victo- ria de bello Ducibus pecora occurrerent.

Scrupulus, qui movit Grotium, quod homini, cujus fides prædicatur in Scriptura, non conveniat filiæ oblatio, alios non movet. Tirinus certe Je- suita votum hoc instinctui Spiritus S. tribuit, & cum Anshelmo, Serario, & Saliano censet, non peccasse Jephthæ cum ita vovit, se in holocaustum im- molaturum Deo, quicunq; victori domum reduci primus gratulabandus occurreret, etsi foret domesti- corum gratissimus, etsi foret uxor, etsi filia unigenita. Et vero victoriam tam illustrem intuitu hujus voti cœlitus concessam, indicio esse, votum istud Deo sin- gulariter placuisse, imo laudari ejus expletionem Ebr. 11. ac voluisse Deum auctorem & Dominum vitæ omnium, etiam in sexu fragiliore, in re difficilli- ma extare plenæ obedientiæ exemplum, typumq; siste- re, in quo ultroneæ mentis Messiæ tolerantia adum- braretur. Adducunt etiam isti exemplum Simso- nis, qui sibi mortem conscivit: Quod si ajunt, in- stinctu Spiritus id factum, quidni probari etiam pos- sit factum hoc voventis vel immolantis filiam, ceu impulsu ejusdem Spiritus expeditum? Quibus fa- vere videtur etiam Augustinus libr. 1. de C. D. cap. 21. Et merito quæritur? utrum pro jussu Dei sit habendum, quod Jephthæ filiam, quæ Patri occur- rit, occidit, cum se immolaturum Deo vovisset, quod ei redeunti de prælio victori primitus occurrisset? nec non Hieronymus Epist. ad Julian. cum ait: Obtulisse Jephthem virginem Filiam, & idcirco in sanctorum enumeratione ab Apostolo positum esse. Alii etsi improbent votum istud, quo etiam August. quæst. 49. inclinat; Iste vero, inquiens, & Deo non jubente, neq; poscente, & contra legitimum ejus præ- ceptum ultra sacrificium vovit humanum; Excu- sant tamen Jephtham, ob ignorantiam, & erroneam conscientiam, de qua testari videntur verba ejusdem:

Aperui os meum ad Dominum, & aliud facere non potero. Ecquis enim credat eum, cui unica tan- tum filia, ob idque unice cara, quia de eventu illo occursus Filiæ suæ tantopere indoluerat, eam fuisse immolaturum, nisi se ad id voto te- neri persuasus fuisset? Quod si Jephte obtulit Fi- liam suam virginem Deo, inquit Hieron. in cap. VII. Lev. non sacrificium placuit, sed animus offe- rentis. Sed quia error ille nimium crassus, fa- ctumque illud non tantum lege divina dissertissi- me prohibitum Deut. 12, 30. seqq. sed ipsi etiam naturæ legi contrarium, utpote parricidiale, ne- que aliæ victimæ immolandæ Deo sunt, nisi in quas jus vitæ & necis habemus, quale in libe- ros, uxorem, aut servos nequaquam sibi fin- gere potest pius Paterfamilias, a culpa profecto absolvi non potest Jephtha; Sed eundem acta pœnitentia salutem consecutum esse, ob idque Sanctorum numero Ebr. XI. accenseri, dubium nullum est: In quo utique Catalogo non pauci continentur, quorum peccata satis gravia etiam notata sunt in Sacro Codice, sed quæ ipsis per fi- dem condonata sunt. Non potest sane a lapsu & culpa expediri Jephthe, etsi cum Grotio di- catur filiam vitæ monasticæ devovisse: Siquidem in vovenda virginitate filiæ consensus ejusdem omnino requiritur, neque parentibus integrum sit, absque liberorum consensu perpetuæ virgini- tati eosdem consecrare. Confer de hoc voto Spicileg. Lud. Capell. & Spicil. Schol. Sacrif. Joh. Cloppenb. p. 216.

Vers. eod.

VNIGENITA) Μονογενὴς LXX. hic & Josephus. Aquila ποθητὴ. Sic יחיד alibi vertitur ἀγαπητὸς & ἀγαπώμενος. Vi- de ad Matth. 3, 17.

Vers. 34.

CVM TTMPANIS ET CHORIS) Simile 1. Reg. 6, 6. Sed quia Sacerdotes eorum tibia tympanique concinebant. Tacitus de Judæis.

Vers. 35.

HEU ME FILIA MEA) Deplorat amissam spem po- steritatis ex Filia.

Imo deplorat Jephthe mortem Filiæ, non virginitatem ejusdem. Ob hanc enim, qui ala- cri animo sese voto paterno submittebat filia, plangendum adeo non fuisset; neque vero affi- ne est, heroem istum insignem tam præclara par- ta victoria, animi tantopere abjecti, & conster- nati fuisse, ut perterritus vestimenta dilacerarit, & lamentatus ideo fuerit, quod Deo dicanda fi- lia ad preces, vini abstinentiam, & vitam μο- νάζουσαν. Quid, quod nunquam apud Judæos receptum fuerit, ut mulieres perpetuam virgini- tatem foverent, quibus probrosa erat tum sterilitas, uti e 1. Sam. 1, 10. Luc. 1, 25. colligitur: neque ullum exemplum suppetit, fœminas in populo Dei votum Nazaræatus nuncupasse, quanquam ne Nazaræos quidem perpetuo a conjugio absti- nuisse, Samsonis & Samuelis exemplo constet Jud. 14, 5. 1. Sam. 8, 1. Quod vero Jephte Fi- lia virginitatem suam deplorat, mirum non est, siquidem sibi moriendum esse virgini videbat, nulla quæ populum Dei erigeret relicta prola, quæ conditio ipsi omnino mortem reddebat acerbio- rem, quia promissionis divinæ Ex. 23, 26. factæ, ef- fectu privabatur.

Vers. 37.

ET PLANGAM VIRGINITATEM MEAM) Deo enim servire soli, si marito subjecta fuisset, non poterat. Ei enim jus in uxorem. Sic apud Græcos diis dicata ani- malia vocantur ἄφετα, quod nemini servirent, sed in Deo- rum honorem servarentur. Aliud in viris, qui quamvis [...] Templo dicati uxores habere poterant, a quarum tamen con- gressu ministerii tempore abstinebant. Viri enim sui juris manent.

Vers. 40.

ET PLANGANT FILIAM JEPHTHÆ) Alii, Conso- lentur filiam Jepthha: Sed verius Chaldæam esse vocem תנא quæ differere significat, & ק quod sequitur pro de po- situm, ut sæpe. Sensus est, in memoriam victoriæ, servatæ- que Deo fidei quater anno ad eum locum venisse virgines, & colloquio, aut etiam carminibus rem celebraffe; quod ad sua quoque tempora a Samariiis eodem in loco factum narrat Epiphanius.

Quum hic iterum abeat a vulgata versio- ne Grotius, quomodo cum Tridentinis Patri- bus ejusdem ἀυθεντίαν tuebitur? Sed voluit suæ ὑποθέσει δουλέυειν de filia Jephthæ non occisa, sed viva Deo consecrata. Vulgatus tamen pro se Chaldæum, & LXX. Interpr. nec non R. Salo- monem laudare potest: quem etiam sequuntur B. Lutherus, & versio Gallica, pro qua interpre- tatione repetunt nonnulli vim verbi Ebræi e no- mine תנין Dracones, quorum ingens esse planctus solet Job. 30. Mich. 1. Mal. 1. Sed hos refellit Amama Antibarb. Bibl. libr. III. pag. 390, quod לתנות non possit esse gerundium ex dupli- cantibus: imo necessario quiescentibus Lamed He ad- scribi debeat ac Gerundium sit in Piel, adeoque the- ma ejus sit תנה, quam vocem magis Chaldæam quam Hebream dicit, & e Jud. 5, 11. exponit, ibi יתנו narrent justitias Domini, hoc sensu: ad narrandum, vel ut narrarent Filiæ Jephthe res la- tas, vel novas, quo sic levarend solitudinis tædium: vel ad alloquendum filiam Jephthe; quo etiam Junius & Tigur. abeunt; ad differendum cum ea. Verum quia conventus ille institutus etiam lon- ge post Jephtæ tempora, quod e textu appa- ret, atque ex Epiphanio observavit Grotius, non potest intelligi colloquium cum Jephthe filia viva institutum; Ideoque Grotius rectius exponit ad differendum de illa. Magis tamen arridet ob- servatio Ludovici de Dieu in animadversione ad h. l. significationem ex Arabismo petendam esse: ubi ab Ebræo שנו iterare, unde est שנים duo, mutato pro more ש in ת fit תנ verbum, quod in Secunda Conjugatione, id est, eadem, quæ hic occurrit, nempe Piel, significat celebrare, laudare, gratias agere, quia primus dedit beneficium, ob- strinxit accipientem ad secundas partes, quæ sunt gratiarum actionis. Inde ergo locum Jud. 5, 11. ita vertit de Dieu, ibi laudent justitias Domini: Et hoc loco: Ad laudandum filiam Jephte. Celebrata enim illic memoria filiæ Jephte, ob inusitatam cum obedientiam, tum patientiam. Annuatim autem celebratam illam memoriam fuisse, ex Ebræo textu patet, a diebus in dies, id est, ab anno in annum, uti vim phraseos ob- servavit Drusius comment. ad diffic. loca in b. l. Non ergo locum relinquere debuit Grotius commen- to Rabbinorum, quod quater anno convenerint ad locum illum virgines; cujus in textu sacro nullum est vestigium.

Ad lamentandum reddunt LXX. Jonath. Syr. Arabs, Montanus, Cajet. B. Luther. Osiand. Angl. quem sen- sum ex ea solum causa rejicit Piscator, quod præpo- sitio ל, non vero articulus ה adhibeatur; sed ea nobis minime tanti videtur, ut a tot interpp. ex- plicatione recedatur, si Dievii novellæ interpreta- tioni locus forte relinquendus non sit. Sixtino A- mama respondit nuper Dn. Pfeifferus noster Dispu- tat. an Jepththa filiam suam immolarit, non insolens esse, ut verba imperfecta diversarum classium ean- dem sustineant significationem, nec Grammatici es- se præscribere Spiritui S. modum & rationem con- stituendi: atque ספד quod itidem est plangere 1. Reg. 14, 13. pariter cum ל construi, etsi Zach. 12, 10. cum על construatur eadem significatione. Illos au- tem qui exponunt ad confabulandum vel narrandum de ea, uti Jud. 5, 11. narrandi significatio obtinet, juvat collatione locorum, ubi תנה idem est quod de, Gen. 26, 13. Ps. 91, 11. ut & Gen. 26, 7. Ps. 3, 3. Pf. 45, 2. Exod. 14, 3. 2. Sam. 11, 7. Neque tamen explicationi Dievii vel etiam Forsteri ad donandum sc. laudem filiæ Jeph- thæ abnuit, modo ne consecratio filiæ vivæ ad caliba- tu hinc exsculpetur; cui nullatenus convenit illud sta- tutum anniversarium in Israele, quod apud Samari- tanos adhuc tempore Epiphanii duravit Hær. 55. & 78.

numeralium H. & K. similitudine orto. Quum & de hoc, & de præcedentibus judicibus Abesan, & Elone dicatur, quod judicarint Israelem, calculum non meretur Nicolai Abrami in Phar. V. T. lib. 10. c. 22. sententia, quod præfuerint tantum Galaaditis, & tribubus transmananis per Jephtham ab Ammonita- rum servitute liberatis: Eli interim Pontifice aliis tribu- bus Philistæorum jugo adhuc pressis, jus dicente. Quam- vis enim Jephthe devictis Ammonitis ex pacto cum suis inito Galaaditicam solum præfecturam adeptus sit, c. 11. 9. 10. cæsis tamen postea Ephraimitis 42000. c. 12, 6. 7. Israelem judicasse dicitur, quod de his pa- riter quoque perhibetur, quod ISRAELEM judi- carint, perinde uti de Thola, & Jaire id dictum est c. 10, 2. 3. Neque sane ratio apparet, cur post Jephtham Galaaditæ, non tribulium suorum quibusdam, sed aliis ex tribu Juda, Zabulon, & Ephraim sese subje- cerint.

## 12:4
Verse 4.

HE FOUGHT AGAINST EPHRAIM) Naturally because they would not allow themselves to be satisfied with kind words, as in the time of Gideon of old, 8:2, Jephthah was forced to use the right of a prince against them.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

PVGNABAT CONTRA EPHRAIM) Nimirum quia benignis verbis, ut olim Gedeonis tempore 8, 2. satisfieri sibi non patiebantur, jure principis in eos uti coactus fuit Jephthes.

## 12:7
Verse 7.

IN HIS CITY GALAAD.

In the Hebrew it is 'in the city of Galaad' or of that region, for he was not buried in a city whose name was Galaad, but in Mispha, which was a city of the Galaadite region, as Serarius and Cornelius acknowledge.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

IN CIVITATE SUA GALAAD.

In Ebr. est in civitate Galaadis seu regionis istius, non enim in civitate, cui nomen Galaad, sed in Mis- pha, quæ civitas erat Galaaditis regionis, sepultus est, ut agnoscit Serarius & Cornelius.

## 12:8
verse 8.

ABESAN OF BETHLEHEM.

Latin:

verf. 8.

ABESAN DE BETHLEHEM.

## 12:11
verse 11.

TO WHOM AHJALON SUCCEEDED.

Eusebius omitted that Elon, who presided for 10 years, in his Chronicle, because he did not find him among the LXX, as did Bede in his book on times. Whom, however, Anianus, the Alexandrian, and Menochius read among the LXX, as did the most ancient writer Theophilus of Antioch in book 1 to Autolycus; indeed, Eusebius himself in book 10 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 14.

Latin:

verf. 11.

CUI SUCCESSIT AHJALON.

Elonem illum, qui per 10. annos præfuit, omisit Eusebius in Chronico, quod non invenerit apud LXX. ut & Beda l. de temporib. Quem tamen apud LXX. legit Anianus, Alexandrinus, Menochius, ut & antiquissimus scriptor Theophilus Antiochenus l. 1. ad Autol. imo Eusebius ipse l. 10. de Præpar. Evang. c. 14.

## 12:15
verse 15.

AND HE DIED AND WAS BURIED IN PHARATHON.

For he was an Ephraimite, the son of Hillel the Pharathonite: whose burial Josephus narrates to have been splendid, in the mountain called Amalekite, because it had once belonged to the Amalekites. Others wish it to be said that the Amalekites still inhabited the same in part, whom Saul finally drove out from there, 1 Sam. 15. In the eastern tract of the Ephraimites, as Junius has it: Which, when someone from the Roman Catholics also approved, Bonfrerius disapproved, and not without cause: because the Amalekites neither lived among the Ephraimites, nor are they said to have been driven out from there by Saul, 1 Sam. 15, on which Bonfrerius himself may be seen in this place. Ussher in his Annals, p. 46, makes Eli the High Priest the successor to this Abdon, who judged Israel for 40 years, 1 Sam. 4:18. and he judges that Samson was conceived only after the death of Abdon, whom he establishes as the defender of the Israelites under the judgeship of Eli, when the Philistines were dominating the Israelites, with Eli performing the office of judge in forensic matters under their very domination. But because, just as with the preceding judges, Thola, Jair, Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon, it is also said of Samson that he judged Israel for 20 years, Judg. 15:20, c. 16:31, which phrase Ussher understands as the government of all Israel regarding those judges, there is no reason to doubt that Samson similarly presided over the government of the people, and therefore that Eli the High Priest did not perform the office of judge.

CHAPTER XII. The slaughter of the Ephraimites, Abesan, Ajalon, and Abdon judges.

Latin:

verf. 15.

MORTUUSQUE EST AC SEPULTUS IN PHARATHON.

Fuit enim Ephraimita, Hillelis Pharathonitæ filius: cujus sepulturam splendidam fuisse narrat Josephus lib. 13. Antiqv. in monte Amalecita dicto, quod ad Amalecitas olim pertinuerit. Alii ita di- ci volunt, quod eundem ex parte adhuc Amalecitæ incolerent, quos inde demum Saul ejecit 1. Sam. 15. In orientali Ephraimitarum tractu, ut habet Junius: Quæ cum probaret etiam aliquis eRomano-Catho- licis, improbavit Bonfrerius, nec immerito: quia Amalecitæ nec inter Ephraimitas habitarunt, neque a Saule inde ejecti dicuntur 1. Sam. 15. quo de Bonfre- rius ipse videatur h. l. Huic Abdoni successorem fa- cit Eli Pontificem Ufferius in Annalibus p. 46. qui annis 40. judicavit Israelem 1. Sam. 4, 18. & post fata Abdonis conceptum demum fuisse Simsonem cen- set, quem vindicem Israelitarum sub judicatu Eli constituit, cum Philistæi dominarentur Israelitis, Eli judicis officium in rebus forensibus sub ipsorum dominatu exequente. Sed quia æque ut de ante- cedentibus Judicibus, Thola, Jaire, Jepththa, Ibsane, Elone, Abdone, de Simsone etiam dicitur, quod judi- carit Israelem per 20. annos Jud. 15, 20. c. 16, 31. quam phrasin de gubernatione totius Israelis, quoad istos Judices, intelligit Usserius, dubitandum non est; Samsonem similiter gubernationi populi præfuisse, adeoque non Eli summum Sacerdotem judicis fun- ctum esse officio.

CAPUT XII. Ephræeorum strages, Abesan, Ajalon, & Abdon judices.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

The idolatrous Israelites oppressed by the Philistines. The conception and birth of Samson.

V. 1. HE DELIVERED THEM INTO THE HANDS OF THE PHILISTINES FOR FORTY YEARS.

Bethlehem is not in the tribe of Zabulon, as Maldonatus in Matt. 2:1 wishes, but in the tribe of Judah. By the Rabbis, Abesan is believed here to have been Boaz, the husband of Ruth, but without solid evidence.

Ussher wishes these 40 years of servitude to have begun only after the death of Abdon, about 20 years before Samson undertook the office of judge, ending them at the death of Eli. Eusebius in his Chronicle, Lyranus, Abulensis, and the Genevan [commentators] begin them with the leadership of Samson, so that they lasted throughout his entire rule for 20 years, and subsequently under Eli for another 40 years. Junius begins them in the 14th year of Jair, but terminates them at the wedding of Samson. Others say that they indeed began 20 years before Samson presided over the government, but ceased with the death of Samson: and thus the years of Samson's judgeship are included in the years of the oppression of the Israelites: because, however often Samson struck the Philistines, he nevertheless did not entirely remove their yoke from the Hebrews,

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

Israelitæ idololatræ a Philistæis pressi. Simsonis conceptio, & nativitas.

V. 1. TRADIDIT EOS IN MANUS PHILI- STINORUM QUADRAGINTA ANNIS.

Bethlehem non in tribu Zabulon, ut Maldona- tus in Matth. 2, 1. vult, sed in tribu Juda. Rabbinis Abesan hic creditur fuisse Boaz maritus Ruth, sed si- ne solido documento.

Hos 40. annos servitutis post mortem Abdonis demum cœpisse vult Ufferius, annis 20. circiter antequam Simson vindicis officium subiret, finiens eosdem in morte Eli. Eusebius in Chron. Lyran. A- bulens. & Genev. ordiuntur eosdem cum Principatu Simsonis, ut durarint toto ejus regimine per 20. an- nos, ac deinceps sub Eli per 40. itidem annos. Junius inchoat eos anno 14. Jairis, terminat vero in nuptiis Simsonis. Alii eos cœpisse ajunt quidem 20. annis, antequam præesset gubernationi Simson, sed desiif- se cum obitu Simsonis: adeoque includi annos ju- dicatus Simsonis annis oppressionis Israelitarum: quia utut sæpius Simson Philistæos ceciderit, jugum tamen eorum ab Ebræis prorsus non abstulit,

## 13:5
Vers. 5. FOR HE SHALL BE A NAZARITE OF GOD) Consecrated to God after the manner of the Nazarites. He was bound, however, to those things which are expressed here: not to all the things of the Nazarites: but here perpetually, they for a time. See what was said at Num. 6. HE SHALL NOT TOUCH HIS HEAD WITH A RAZOR) The promised hair is a sign of a votive obligation, as we said at the mentioned place in Numbers.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ERIT ENIM NAZARÆVS DEI) Deo sacer ad modum Nazaræorum. Tenebatur autem ad ea quæ hic ex- pressa sunt: non ad omnia Nazaræorum : sed hic perpetuo, illi ad tempus. Vide quæ dicta ad Num. 6. NON TANGET CAPUT NOVACULA) Promissus capillus votivæ obligationis nota, ut ad dictum locum Num. diximus.

## 13:6
Verse 6.

SHIBBOLETH WHICH IS INTERPRETED AS AN EAR OF CORN) The Latin added this regarding the interpretation, but the Hebrews note that it was the name of a river in those regions.

The Ephraimites could not pronounce it with an aspiration, but said Sibboleth. The Vulgate interprets the word as 'ear of corn': but Pagninus and Vatablus more correctly render it as the flow of a river, a channel, or an inundation, which fits the location: because that examination of the Ephraimites took place at the fords and the flow of the Jordan. It is taken in this way in Ps. 69:3, Jos. 17:12. Whence the Hebrews perhaps made that the name of the river.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

SCHIBBOLETH QVOD INTERPRETATVR SPI- CA) Hoc de interpretatione Latinus addidit, sed notant He- bræi nomen amnis fuisse in illis regionibus.

Ephraimitæ ita pronunciare non poterant a- spiraret, sed dicebant Sibboleth. Vulg. vocem in- terpretatur Spica: sed rectius fluminis fluxum, alve- um vel inundationem reddunt Pagninus, & Vatablus, quod loco congruit: quia examen illud Ephratæo- rum ad vada & fluxum Jordanis fiebat. Ita acci- pitur Ps. 69, 3. Jos. 17, 12. Unde Ebræi nomen id fluvii fortassis fecerunt.

## 13:13
V. 13. AFTER HIM ABDON JUDGED ISRAEL.

He presided for 8 years. Julius Africanus attributes 20 years to him by an error, as it seems, from the Greeks except in death, when their Princes perished with him in the ruin of the house: and therefore it is said c. 15, 20. that he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines. They place the beginning, therefore, of these days, or years of oppression, in the 6th year of Abesan; and they judge that Samson was born in the following seventh, because the Lord willed him to be born after the servitude had begun, or rather because of the servitude that had begun. Which opinion seems more consistent with the truth. And therefore, since that oppression began two years before the deeds of Abesan, and lasted through the decade of Elon and the octennium of Abdon, Samson began to judge and deliver the Israelites at twenty years of age. Thus also Bonfrerius in h. l. p. 345, with Torniellus and Salianus: But Torniellus, he says, and Salianus, to whom I subscribe, relegate twenty years of this servitude to the preceding years of the Judges, and the twenty later years to the years of Samson, who is said to have judged Israel for twenty years, so that this servitude ceased at the death of Samson. And indeed they prove this, because it is entirely likely that the strength of the Philistines was completely weakened and cut down when all the princes of the Philistines were killed by Samson in his death, and for that reason the Israelites were free from the domination of the Philistines for many years in the time of Eli, until, that is, his final times, when the Philistines again began to afflict the Israelites with wars. This being established, it is necessary to take twenty years before the leadership of Samson, so that these forty years may be completed, namely that this servitude began in the sixth year of Abesan, but the idolatry of the Israelites preceded the servitude by a year or two; so that not long after the death of Jephthah there was a return by the Israelites to idolatry. Furthermore, about the same time that this servitude began, or rather a little after, occurred that which follows, the apparition of the Angel, and the foretelling of the birth of Samson; since those words in v. 5 clearly indicate that the servitude of the Philistines had already begun before: He shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines. From which Eusebius and others are clearly refuted, who relegate the later years of this servitude to the times of Eli. Furthermore, the birth of Samson is relegated to the following year, that is, the seventh and last of Abesan. From which it can again be gathered that Samson was 39 years old at his death. The Usserian Chronotaxis is easily reconciled by the reason of the years of the world, because it judges that Eli the priest fell with a broken neck shortly after the death of Samson, so that the end of the oppression of the Philistines falls into almost the same year according to his opinion and ours.

Latin:

V. 13. POST HUNC JUDICAVIT ISRAEL ABDON.

Per annos 8. præfuit. Julius Africanus tri- buit ei annos 20. errore, ut videtur, ex Græcorum nisi in morte, cum Principes eorum secum ruina domus occidit : atque ideo dici c. 15, 20. quod judi- carit Israel in diebus Philistinorum. Initium ergo ho- rum dierum, vel annorum oppressionis in 6. anno Abesan ponunt; ac sequenti septimo Simsonem na- tum censent, quia post ceptam, imo propter ceptam servitutem eum nasci voluit Dominus. Quæ sen- tentia veritati magis consentanea videtur. Ideo- que quum biennio ante facta Absanis ea oppressio ce- perit, per decennium Elonıs, & octennium Abdonis durarit, Simson viginti annos natus Israelitas & judi- dicare & vindicare cepit. Sic etiam Bonfrerius in h. l. p. 345. cum Torniello & Saliano: At Torniellus, inquit, & Salianus, quibus ego subscribo, viginti annos hujus servitutis ad antecedentes Judicum annos rejici- unt, viginti posteriores ad Samsonis annos, qui annis vi- ginti dicitur judicasse Israelem, ita ut in Samsonis mor- te ea servitus desierit. Et vero id ipsi probant, quod plane verisimile sit omnino debilitatas & accisas Phi- listinorum vires occisis a Samsone in morte omni- bus Philistinorum principibus, ob idque a Philistæo- rum dominatu Heli tempore Israelitas liberos mul- tis annis fuisse, usque ad ipsius videlicet extrema tempora, quo rursum ceperunt Philistæi Israelitas bellis affligere. Quo constituto necesse est viginti annos ante Samsonis principatum sumere, ut hi an- ni quadraginta compleantur, videlicet ut anno sex- to Abesan cœpta sit hæc servitus, idolatolatria autem Israelitarum uno alterove anno servitutem ante- cesserit; ita ut non diu post mortem Jephthe redi- tum sit rursum ab Israelitis ad idololatriam. Porro sub idem tempus, quo cœpta hæc servitus, vel potis paulo post contigit ea, quæ sequitur, Angeli appa- ritio, & de ortu Samsonis prænunciatio; siquidem jam ante cœptam fuisse Philistæorum servitutem manifeste indicant ista verba v. 5. Ipse incipiet libera- re Israel de manu Philistæorum. Ex quo manifeste refellitur Eusebius & cæteri; qui ad Heli tempora posteriores hujus servitutis annos rejiciunt. Porro Samsonis nativitas in annum sequentem, hoc est, se- ptimum & ultimum Abesan rejicitur. Ex quo rursum colligi potest Samsonem in morte annorum 39. fuisse. Facile autem ratione annorum mundi conciliatur Usseriana Chronotaxis, quia paulo post Samsonis mortem Eli sacerdotem cervice fracto oc- cubuisse censet, ut in eundem ferme annum termi- nus oppressionis Philistinorum juxta ipsius & no- stram sententiam incidat.

## 13:18
V. 18. AND HE PLACED IT UPON THE ROCK OFFERING TO THE LORD, WHO DOES WONDROUS THINGS. In Hebrew: And he (the angel) sacrificed upon the rock to the Lord and did wondrously, either because he prepared everything wondrously, or because he even added a miracle by bringing forth fire from the Rock.

Latin:

V. 18. ET POSUIT SUPER PETRAM OF- FERENS DOMINO, QUI FACIT MIRABILIA. In Ebræo: Et sacrificavit (angelus) supra pe- tram Domino & mirabiliter fecit, seu quod præpa- rarit omnia mirabiliter, seu quod addiderit etiam miraculum ignem de Petra educens.

## 13:20
Vers. 20. THE ANGEL OF THE LORD LIKEWISE ASCENDED IN THE FLAME) Through the smoke as if it were a chariot, Josephus. Vers. 22. WE SHALL DIE THE DEATH) See regarding these and the preceding things a similar history above in 6. and what was said there. WE HAVE SEEN GOD) Through the Angel revealing himself to us.

This is a manifest σχεθλότης. The parents of Samson say that it was God who appeared to them, we have seen God: Grotius on the contrary says that it was not God who was seen, but an Angel alone sustaining the role and power of GOD, or sent by God. They shudder because they saw God himself, we shall die the death, because we have seen God; He, on the contrary, contends with the Rabbis that they did not see God himself, but an Angel, through whom God revealed himself. Since, therefore, he who appeared is called both the Angel of the Lord and GOD, no other should be understood than the Son of GOD, who is also the Angel of the Lord, because he was sent by the Father Is. 63, 8. Mal. 3, 1. and GOD blessed forever Rom. 9, 5. because he is one with the Father, GOD in essence John 10, 30. 1 John 5, 7. It is added that the Angel says his name is wonderful Jud. 13, 18. which is the name of the Son of GOD himself Is. 9, 6. as it is a name that no one knows, except himself Rev. 19, 12. Finally, when the wife of Manoah says that the Lord had accepted a holocaust from her hand, she speaks of that Lord from whom they feared for themselves, because they had seen him; for she consoles her husband, that there is nothing to be feared from him: since he not only showed himself to be seen by them, but also accepted Sacrifices from their hand, which is a sign of divine favor. And thus also the Vinarie Paraphrasts understand it, as well as Junius from the Reformed and the Belgian Interpreters, who added notes to the recent translation: namely, concerning the Son of God, the uncreated Angel. And Corn. a Lap. admits at v. 19 that this Angel sacrificed, which, since it befits no created Angel, one must understand the Son of God, who alone is called Priest and Angel at the same time. Compare what was said at c. 6, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ANGELUS DOMINI PARITER IN FLAMMA ASCENDIT) Διὰ καπνẽ ὥσπερ ὀχήματος, Josephus. Vers. 22. MORTE MORIEMUR) Vide ad hæc & quæ præcedunt similem historiam supra 6. & ibi dicta. VIDIMUS DEUM) Per Angelum se nobis patefaci- entem.

Manifesta hæc est σχεθλότης. Parentes Sim- sonis ajunt, Deum fuisse, qui ipsis apparuit, vidi- mus Deum: Grotius ex adverso non Deum fuisse visum, sed Angelum solum vicem & potestatem DEI sustinentem, vel a Deo missum. Illi exhorrescunt, quod Deum ipsum viderint, morte moriemur, quia vidimus Deum; Hic e contrario non Deum ipsum eos vidisse, sed Angelum, per quem se Deus patefe- cit, cum Rabbinis contendit. Quum ergo hic qui apparuit, & Angelus Domini dicatur, & DEUS, nul- lus alius intelligi debet, quam Filius DEI, qui & An- gelus Domini est, quia missus a Patre Es. 63, 8. Mal. 3, 1. & DEUS benedictus in secula Rom. 9, 5. quia u- nus est cum Patre, essentia DEUS Joh. 10, 30. 1. Joh. 5, 7. Accedit, quod Angelus nomen suum dicat esse mirabile Jud. 13, 18. quod est nomen ipsius Filii DEI Es. 9, 6. utpote, quod nemo novit, nisi ipse Ap. 19, 12. Denique quum uxor Manoah Dominum susce- pisse holocaustum de manu sua dicat, de eo loquitur Domino, a quo sibi metuebant, eo quod ipsum vi- derint; Solatur enim maritum, non esse ab ipso me- tuendum: Siquidem non visendum solum ipsis se præbuerit, sed etiam Sacrificia de manu ipsorum acceperit, quod gratiæ divinæ signum est. Atque ita etiam intelligunt Vinarienses Paraphrastæ, nec non e Reformatis Junius & Belgici Interpretes, qui no- tas translationi nuperæ addidere: de Filio nempe Dei, Angelo increato. Et fatetur Corn. a Lap. ad v. 19. Angelum hunc sacrificasse, quod cum nulli Angelo creato conveniat, Filium Dei, qui solus Sa- cerdos & Angelus simul dicitur, intelligere oportet. Conf. quæ ad c, 6, 14. dicta.

## 13:25
V. 25. AND THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD BEGAN TO BE WITH HIM. In Hebrew: to stir him, so that he produced some heroic specimens against the Philistines: this is not, however, to be dragged toward a latent fire of love with Junius. IN THE CAMP OF DAN BETWEEN SARA AND ESTHAOL) The possession of the Danites was insinuating itself in this place within the borders of Judah. See 1 Paralip. 2, 54.

Latin:

V. 25. CEPITQUE SPIRITUS DOMINI ES- SE CUM EO. In Ebr. agitare eum, ut nonnulla ediderit he- roica specimina contra Philistinos: non vero hoc ad latentem amoris ignem cum Junio trahendum. IN CASTRIS DAN INTER SARAA ET ESTHA- OL) Danitarum possessio hoc loco se insinuabat intra fines Judæ. Vide 1. Paralip. 2, 54.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. The marriage of Samson: The lion torn apart, and the riddle.

V. 1. AND SEEING A WOMAN THERE. She is nowhere called a virgin or a girl, but only a woman: by which the Holy Spirit, in the judgment of Osiander, seems to hint that she had been defiled by another before. Which we leave to its proper place.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. Simsonis conjugium: Leo discerptus, & æni- gma.

V. 1. VIDENSQUE IBI MULIEREM. Nuspiam vocatur ea virgo, aut puella, sed tan- tum mulier: quo videtur Spiritus S. judicio Osiandri, innuere, quod ab alio ante vitiata fuerit. Quod suo loco relinquimus.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. THEY KNEW NOT THAT THE THING WAS OF THE LORD) They did not know that he had a special command to take a Philistine woman against the law. See a similar case in Hosea 1, according to some.

Marriages with infidels were otherwise forbidden by divine law: Ex. 34. Lev. 12, 3. Deut. 22, 12. but here there was a peculiar impulse of God in Samson, or a certain divine revelation: Conf. Ambrose, book 3, Ep. 24. Bonfrerius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NESCIEBANT QVOD RES A DOMINO FIERET) Nesciebant illum speciale habere mandatum du- cendi Philistinam contra legem. Simile vide Oseæ 1. secun- dum quosdam.

Conjugia cum infidelibus alias interdicta erant divina lege: Ex. 34. Lev. 12, 3. Deut. 22, 12. sed hic peculiaris Dei impulsus in Simsone fuit, aut revela- tio quædam divina: Conf. Ambros. l. 3. Ep. 24. Bon- frerius in h. l.

## 14:6
Vers. 6. HE RENT THE LION) Thereby making an omen for himself for greater things, as David did, 1 Sam. 17, 34.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DILACERAVIT LEONEM) Inde sibi ad majora au- spicium faciens, ut David 1. Sam. 17, 34.

## 14:8
V. 8. A SWARM OF BEES IN THE MOUTH OF THE LION. Bees do not frequent the bones of corpses when the flesh has been eaten away or dried up.

Latin:

V. 8. EXAMEN APUM IN ORE LEONIS. Apes cadaverum ossa carnibus exesis vel ex- siccatis non afficiunt.

## 14:11
Vers. 11. THIRTY COMPANIONS) For the sake of honor, as was accustomed to be done for new husbands: (see below 20, and what was said at John 3, 29.) in reality so that they might guard him.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SODALES TRIGINTA) Honoris causa, ut fieri novis maritis solebat: (vide infra 20. & quæ dicta ad Joan. 3, 29.) revera ut eum custodirent.

## 14:12
Vers. 12. I WILL PROPOSE A RIDDLE TO YOU) An ancient custom of excellent men to compete with one another regarding their wit by proposing riddles. See the passages from the history of Dii and Menander concerning the riddles exchanged between Solomon and Hiram in Josephus, Against Apion, book one. Add 1 Kings 10:1. You have examples also in Herodotus: and in the writer of the Banquet of the Seven Sages among the works of Plutarch, and among those who have written about the life of Aesop.

IF YOU SOLVE FOR ME WITHIN SEVEN DAYS OF THE FEAST, I WILL GIVE YOU THIRTY LINEN GARMENTS AND AS MANY TUNICS) For such wagers about riddles were accustomed to be made, as appears in the cited passages of Dio and Menander. A similar one is in the third Eclogue of Virgil. Moreover, it was the custom for wedding feasts to be celebrated for seven days. Some doubled this number of days. Tob. 8:22.

TUNICS. In the Hebrew, change-garments, or garments of changes, which can be honorably changed on festive days.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PROPONAM VOBIS PROBLEMA) Mos vetus viro- rum Excellentium de ingenio inter se certandi proposi- tis ænigmatibus. Vide loca ex historia Dii & Menandri de ænigmatis inter Salomonem Iromumque mutatis apud Josephum contra Appionem libro priore. Adde 1. Reg. 10, 1. Habes & apud Herodotum exempla: & apud Scriptorem convivii septem sapientum inter opera Plutarchi, & apud eos qui de Æsopi vita scripsere.

SI SOLVERITIS MIHI INTRA SEPTEM DIES CONVIVII, DABO VOBIS TRIGINTA SINDONES ET TOTIDEM TVNICAS) Solebant enim sponsiones tales de ænigmatibus fieri, ut apparet dictis Dii & Menandri locis. Simile in tertia Virgilii Ecloga. Mos autem per septem dies convivia nuptialia celebrari. Quidam duplicabant hunc dierum numerum. Tob. 8, 22.

TVNICAS. In Ebr. Vestes mutatorias, vel mutationum, quæ commutari diebus festivis honeste possunt.

## 14:15
Verse 15.

COAX YOUR HUSBAND) Women's coaxing is often stronger than the command of parents. You may not badly compare the Theban Hercules to Samson in the immense strength of body and mind, addicted to women. See also below 16:15 and 16.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

BLANDIRE VIRO TVO) Muliebres blanditiæ parentum imperio sæpe validiores. Herculem Thebanum Samsoni non male compares ingenti robore corporis animique, mulieribus addictum. Vide & infra 16, 15. & 16.

## 14:17
Verse 17. SHE WEPT BEFORE HIM) Naturally, 'That she might teach her eyes to weep.' The master of such things says, 'These words, by Hercules, one false little tear, which she might have barely squeezed out by rubbing her eyes miserably, will extinguish.' Parmeno says this in the Eunuchus of Terence.

Latin:

Vers. 17. FLEBAT ANTE EUM) Nimirum Vt flerens oculos erudire suos. Ait talium magister Hæc verba, mehercule, una falsa lacrymula, Quam oculos terendo misere vix vi expresserit, Restinguet. Ait in Eunucho Terentiana Parmeno.

## 14:18
Verse 18. ON THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE SETTING OF THE SUN) Let that which is done on the seventh day be within seven days. See 1. 'If anyone shall have said thus,' D. on the significations of words, and what was said in book three of The Law of War and Peace, chapter 21, § 4, and in the Annotations to that place. The setting of the sun is the end of the νυχθημέρꙋ among the Hebrews and neighboring nations.

IF YOU HAD NOT PLOWED WITH MY HEIFER. Junius correctly explains this proverb: unless you had searched out by the work of my bride the things that lay hidden in my mind, just as rustics uncover by plowing the works of youth that lay hidden under the earth, you would not have found them. Thus he touches upon the perfidy of the bride and their own fraud.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DIE SEPTIMO ANTE SOLIS OCCVBITVM) Intra dies septem sit quod die fit septimo. Vide 1. Si quis sic dixerit. D. de verborum significationibus, & quæ dicta libro tertio de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. 21. §. 4. & in Annotatis ad eum locum. Solis occasus finis νυχθημέρꙋ apud Hebræos, vicinasque gentes.

SI NON ARASSETIS IN VITULA MEA. Recte hoc proverbium Junius explicat, nisi ut rustici juventæ opera arando, quæ sub terra latebant, retegunt, vos sponsæ meæ opera, quæ in animo meo latebant, scrutati fuissetis, non invenissetis. Ita sponsæ perfidiam & ipsorum fraudem perstringit.

## 14:19
Verse 19. ASHKELON) Which is a city of the Philistines, 2 Sam. 1:20.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ASCALONEM) Quæ urbs Philistinorum, 2. Sam. 1, 20.

## 14:20
Verse 20. BUT HIS WIFE) Without waiting for a divorce, below 15:2.

Verse 21.

ONE OF HIS FRIENDS, AND OF HIS GROOMSMEN. The Hebrew text has his companion, whom he had taken to himself as a companion, namely, from those thirty whom he had as companions at the wedding, Samson's wife married one. The LXX call him νυμφαγωγόν.

Latin:

Vers. 20. VXOR AVTEM EJVS) Non exspectato repudio infra 15, 2.

Vers. 21.

UNUM DE AMICIS EJUS, ET DE PRONUBIS EJUS. Sodalem ejus, Ebræus textus habet, quem sibi in sodalem asciverat, de iis sc. triginta, quos sodales in nuptiis habebat, uni nupsit uxor Simsonis. LXX. vocant νυμφαγωγόν.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. The little foxes, and the strength of Samson.

Verse 1.

HE BROUGHT HIM A KID OF THE GOATS) It is added 'of the goats' because the Hebrew word גדי also includes lambs, as D. Kimchi has noted. This was a gift not to be despised among those riches, as Virgil testifies: 'Besides, two kids found for me in a safe valley, both with their skins still dappled, twice a day they drain the ewes' udders, which I am keeping for you.'

Latin:

CAPUT XV. Vulpeculæ, & fortitudo Simsonis.

Vers. 1.

ATTVLIT EI HOEDVM DE CAPRIS) De capris ideo additur, quia גדי vox Hebræa etiam agnos comprehendit, ut notavit D. Kimchi. Erat hoc illis opibus munus non spernendum, Virgilio teste: Præterea duo nec tuta mihi valle reperti Capreoli, sparsis etiam nunc pellibus ambo, Bina die siccant ovis ubera, quos tibi servo.

## 15:3
Verse 3.

FROM THIS DAY THERE SHALL BE NO BLAME IN ME AGAINST THE PHILISTINES: FOR I WILL DO YOU HARM) See also below 2. and 6, 28. Among Thucydides, the Plataeans say: 'We rightly took vengeance according to the law established for all, that it is holy to defend oneself against an attacking enemy.' Civilis in Tacitus: 'Sought for punishment, I demand retribution by the law of nations.' See on the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 20, § 8. Neither the law of nature nor the law of nations forbids one from avenging oneself, but because the measure was exceeded, and then also lest quarrels arise from any cause whatsoever, the civil law prohibited it—such as is also the law given to the Hebrews, indeed by God, but very much after the manner of human laws, by which law no one is forbidden to avenge himself regarding foreigners: regarding citizens, it is not forbidden, except in minor and daily matters. The reason for the discourse sanctioned by the cross is different, in which, just as there is an open promise of eternal things, so also a contempt for perishable things, from which vengeance arises, is required. Many confuse these things badly, being less harmful if they [confuse them] with the Law

The heroes among Homer and other Greeks, as noted by the Scholiasts, were given to loves, given to anger. The Light of the Gospel has given us other heroes, of which I shall speak with the Terence-like Seneca: 'Now this day brings another life, demands other morals.'

These things smell of the lamp of Socinus, to whom Grotius was addicted more than is sufficient. But one must distinguish between private and public vengeance. For public vengeance, which is done through the Magistrate, is prohibited by no law. But vengeance, or private retribution, although corrupt nature is too prone to it, according to that of the Poet: 'Vengeance is a good more pleasant than life itself;'

It is not, however, of the law of nature, nor of the law of nations, insofar as this is built from the law of nature, whatever may be the case regarding the corrupt customs of certain nations, which proceeded from corrupt nature, not from the remnants of the divine image, which reflect the law of nature. Although even small sparks of the same among the Gentiles convinced them of the lawlessness (ἀνομίᾳ) of private vengeance, for in the judgment of Seneca, book 2 of 'On Anger', chapter 32, 'Vengeance is an inhuman word, and does not differ from an insult, except only in order. He who returns pain sins only more excusably.' According to Dio in Plutarch, 'Vengeance and injury, if nature is considered, are born from the same disease of the soul.' According to Musonius, 'It is the mark of a beast, not a man, to think how one may bite back the one who bites, and harm the one who harms.' Indeed, according to Maximus of Tyre, 'the one who takes vengeance is more unjust (ὁ τιμωρῶν τᾶ προϋπάρξαντος ἀδικώτερος) than the one who first did the harm.' Nor does civil law prohibit only the excess of private vengeance, or vengeance for any cause whatsoever, but any private vengeance at all. Whence King Theodoric in Cassiodorus, book 4, Ep. 10: 'Hence it is that the sacred reverence of the laws is open, so that nothing should be done by hand, nothing by one's own impulse.' Also the Emperors, Honorius and Theodosius, L. Nulli C. de Judaeis: 'For this reason the vigor of the courts and the protection of public law were established in the midst, so that no one might be able to permit vengeance to himself.' The Mosaic divine law also simply prohibits private vengeance, which, as far as these interdicts of vengeance are concerned, does not look to the Hebrews alone, but insofar as they are of the moral law, it obligates all men of all times. For it was enacted and given to all. But as to where Grotius gets the idea that a certain peculiar civil law was given to the Hebrews concerning revenge, under that distinction that private vengeance was permitted against foreigners, but not against citizens, or even against citizens, but only in greater matters, not in lesser and daily ones, unless perhaps from the impure cisterns of the Jews? In the clear fountains of Israel such things are certainly not found. Furthermore, that there is another reason for the Sermon sanctioned by the cross, or the Evangelical Law, as it is wont to be called by Grotius, that indeed should not have been asserted nakedly with the Socinians and Pelagians, but ought to have been demonstrated from the sacred scriptures. The sermon of the cross is accustomed to be called, not some new law instructing life or directing morals, but the sermon of the Gospel concerning the saving cross, or concerning salvation to be obtained through the cross of Christ. Compare 1 Cor. 1, 17. & 18. 21. 23. chap. 2, 2. The whole of Scripture is ignorant that a new law was either enacted by Christ or sanctioned by the cross, teaching on the contrary that the Law was indeed given through Moses, but grace and truth, or true grace, by which the Law is performed and fulfilled, came through Christ, John 1, 17. Therefore, a new Legislator is not to be feigned from Christ, who redeemed us from the curse of the Law and fulfilled the law for us, along with the Socinians and Pelagians, lest the redemption and satisfaction of Christ be denied, and much less is it to be admitted that Christ enacted more rigid laws and far more difficult to observe, which they desire, making, if I may say so, the most Mosaic thing out of Moses himself. Private vengeance is as strictly forbidden in the books of the New Testament by Christ and the Apostles, as it was never granted to anyone in the Old Testament, but was equally prohibited. For that passage in Matt. 5:43, 'You have heard that it was said, You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,' was certainly not said in the Law; for nowhere in the Law are they commanded to hate an enemy, nor was the neighbor, whom they were bound to love according to the Law, to be understood only as fellow citizens, but also as foreigners, just as Christ convinced the lawyer concerning this in Luke 10. Indeed, that one must do good even to enemies, the Apostle proves from the Old Testament in Rom. 12:20, citing the Solomonic passage in Prov. 25:21; and that all private vengeance is forbidden by the Mosaic Law, he demonstrates from Deut. 32:35, in the same place at Rom. 12:19. What then remains, but that we say, as the thing itself also cries out, that this was said about hating enemies, beyond, or rather against, the written Law, by those who had corrupted the Law with their traditions, against whose corruptions the Lord here vindicates the Law, as Malachi had predicted concerning this in chapter 3:3. Therefore, those who say that all private vengeance is prohibited by the Mosaic Law do not attribute more than is sufficient to it, but in this they follow the Apostle, who attributes the same thing to it in Rom. 12:19: 'Do not avenge yourselves, but give place to wrath. For it is written (in the Law, Deut. 32:35), Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.' But Grotius attributes less than is proper to it, wrongly confusing the errors of the nations with the divine law in verse 9. That civil [expression] in Tacitus: 'sought for punishment, I demand retribution by the law of nations'; and asserting even worse that the divine law was given by God himself in the likeness of human laws, and indeed of such highly corrupt ones, not without reproach to the divine law. If Gentile heroes were given to wrath, given to loves, what is this to the illustrious heroes among the people of God? For if Grotius was ignorant of how greatly the law of nature was obscured and depraved among them, he could have learned it from Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, in Rom. ch. 1. But are the renowned heroes of the Patriarchs and of the faithful in that people, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. 3:2), to be measured by their standard? Concerning whom the sacred psalmist says in Ps. 147:19-20: 'He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and his judgments to Israel. He has not dealt so with any nation, and his judgments he has not made known to them.' Are not the faith, patience, and mighty works of the ancients set before us everywhere as an example in the New Testament? Is not an entire cloud of witnesses from ancient times proposed by Paul to the Hebrews converted to the faith of Christ, before the illustrious light of the Gospel arose, so that by their example we and they may learn to lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily besets us, under which wrath, hatred, the desire for revenge and vengeance, quarrels, and contentions are also contained, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us (Heb. 12:1)? That the people of God under the Old Testament were entirely devoid of the light of the Gospel is a Socinian fiction. Although it shone more illustriously under the New Testament, when the Dayspring from on high visited us (Luke 1:78), it was nevertheless not entirely lacking to the ancients, because the Prophetic Scripture was a light to them, and a lamp shining in a dark place, as Peter testifies in 2 Epistle 1, verse 19, until the day should dawn; and the ancients had the same Jesus Christ, the Messiah, who is the true light, yesterday, whom we have today (John 1:9; Heb. 13:8). They believed that they would be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as we also believe (Acts 15:11). Nor were the ancients lacking a sufficiently clear promise of eternal things, by which they raised themselves up, as is shown by the example of Job ch. 19:25, David in Psalm 17, last verse, Isaiah ch. 35:10 (cf. ch. 65,

17), Daniel ch. 12:1, etc. Otherwise than Grotius dreams with the ancient and recent Pelagians, as if the ancients were sustained only by the acorns of perishable and earthly goods; whose faith is adorned with most eminent praises in Heb. ch. 11, whence also the contempt of perishable things is everywhere required in the books of the Old Testament, so that the faithful might not cling to them or set their hearts upon them. Whoever does not see this in the Davidic Psalms and the Solomonic Ecclesiastes, must be too occupied with, or rather blinded by, Pelagian errors. But to return to those things which properly belong to this place, Grotius must be heard here from book 2 of 'De Jure Belli ac Pacis', ch. 20, § 8, to which place he referred us, as to how he says and proves that vengeance is not prohibited by the law of nature and nations: namely, if it is undertaken for this end, that he who has been injured may not suffer such a thing hereafter, either from him against whom he takes vengeance, or from others. For if private vengeance also is directed to these ends and within the bounds of equity, he judges it not to be illicit by the law of nature, whether it is done by the one who was injured or by another. And thus he says that Samson defended himself here by natural law against the Philistines, when he testified that he would be innocent if he did evil in return to the Philistines who had done evil to him. He also observes that Ambrose in 'De Officiis', book 1, ch. 40, praises the Maccabees because they avenged the slaughter of their innocent brothers even on the Sabbath. But neither was Samson a private person, being a Judge among the people of the Lord, nor were the Maccabees. And the things he cites from Thucydides concerning the Plataeans, and from Sallust concerning the Roman people and others, concern public vengeance, not private. But he ought to have taught that this [private vengeance] is lawful by the law of nature, not that [public vengeance]. On the other hand, when he praises that saying of Quintilian, that compensation for injury is not only hostile to the LAW, but to peace: For what is law, a forum, a judge, unless for one who is ashamed to be avenged by law; And that of Demosthenes in the Canon; It has been decided to exercise judgment concerning all these injuries by the laws, and not by the impulse or whim of any individual; and what we have previously said that the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, and also King Theodoric, sanctioned to that effect; does he not openly admit that private vengeance is by no means lawful, but is HOSTILE TO THE LAW. For as to that law which he opposes to the old natural liberty, which granted revenge to everyone, in that he at least begs the question. It had to be proven that nature grants this liberty or license of revenge to us and to any private individual. For this is certainly not to be attributed to nature, but to the way in which it is corrupted by sin. The unskilled and the foolish, says Lactantius, if they ever receive an injury, are led by a blind and irrational fury, and attempt to return the favor to those who harm them. And Juvenal agrees; for revenge is always the pleasure of a small and weak mind, and a petty one. Which Grotius himself acknowledged in §. 5. It conflicts, he says, with the nature of a man acting upon a man by means of another's pain, by which pain one is satisfied, and therefore the less a man is capable of the use of reason, the more prone he is to vengeance. He had given a reason, which deserves to be ascribed; because such an appetite, viewed in itself, does not befit the rational part, whose duty it is to command the affections, and therefore neither does it befit the law of nature, because that is the dictate of a rational and social nature, as such. But reason dictates to man that nothing should be done by which another man is harmed, unless it has some good as its purpose. But in the mere pain of an enemy, viewed so nakedly, there is no good, except a false and imaginary one. But what he says, that in revenge he does not look only at the enemy's pain, but at the utility of the one who has been harmed, so that he may not suffer such a thing hereafter, that utility strengthens public punishment, not private vengeance. For further harm can be prevented by a penalty inflicted by the Magistrate: just as he says the law for the Hebrews permitted taking revenge, not by hand, but by approaching a judge: indeed, he admits that through laws the power of avenging the injured was given to judges alone, where judges have been established; since in our own affairs and those of our kin we are corrupted by affection. But that constitution of judgments is consistent with the law of nature, and it does not take away anything from the law of nature, or from that which nature has indulged. Such vengeance through judges, because it is consistent with the law of nature, was not taken away by Christ, nor could it be taken away.

Grotius does indeed here oppose the words of Christ in Matthew 5, verse 38: 'You have heard that it was said, an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say to you, do not resist evil, but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.' But those things are not opposed to the Law of Moses, but to that perverse interpretation of the law, as if private vengeance had been sanctioned there, or even as if the law of retaliation had been precisely instituted by Moses in Exod. 12:24 [sic], Deut. 19:21, since on the contrary, the administration of justice is enjoined there not upon the injured party, but upon the judge; nor do the words of Christ tend to anything other than to commend patience to his own: for he is not instructing those established in office, or Magistrates and judges, but Christians. That it is better to endure evil patiently than to repay with evil, ἐκ ἀδίκꝫ τῆς δι- καίας ἀμύνης ὔσης, ἀλλὰ κρείττονꝰ τῆς ἀνεξικα- κίας [not because just vengeance is unjust, but because patience is better than it], not because just vengeance is unjust, but because patience is better than it, which Grotius himself praises from the constitutions of Clement, book 7, ch. 23. Which, however, was also true in the Old Testament. Let Tertullian be heard, praised by Grotius himself, against Marcion, 4: 'And so this must be immediately declared, whether the discipline of patience is preached by the Creator (in the Old Testament: for he demonstrates its harmony with the New against Marcion:). Thus he commands through Zechariah that no one should remember the malice of his brother, nor even of his neighbor (Zech. 5:11). For again: Let no one, he says, recall the malice of his neighbor (Zech. 8). Much more did he enjoin patience toward injury, who enjoined oblivion. But also when he said: (Deut. 32.) 'Vengeance is mine, and I will repay'; therefore he teaches patience. Insofar, then, as he does not desire that the same person should appear to demand a tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye in return for an injury—he who prohibits not only the return, but even the vengeance, even the record and recall of the injury—to that extent it is revealed to us how he judged 'an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth,' not to permit a second injury of retaliation, which he had prohibited by forbidding vengeance; but to restrain the first, which he had prohibited by the opposing retaliation, so that everyone, looking at the license of a second injury, might restrain himself from the first. For he knows that force is more easily compressed by the representation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance. Both, however, had to be established, according to the nature and faith of men, so that he who believed in God would expect vengeance from God; he who believed less would fear the laws of retaliation. This will of the law, laboring under [mis]understanding, Christ, the Lord both of the Sabbath and of the Law and of all paternal dispositions, both revealed and made capable, commanding the offering of the other cheek as well, so that he might the more extinguish the return of injury, which the Law also had wished to prevent through retaliation, certainly which Prophecy had manifestly restrained, both by prohibiting the memory of injury and by relegating vengeance to God; thus, if Christ added anything, it was not as an adversary, but as a helper of the precept, he did not destroy the disciplines of the Creator. All these things are Tertullian's, which are entirely adverse to Grotius. For Tertullian clearly proves the opposite of what Grotius defends: that there is no diversity between the Old and New Testaments, which Grotius asserts along with the heretic Marcion: I add, and with Faustus the Manichaean. For the latter contends that Christ is contrary to Moses in that he abolished the law of retaliation. See August. book 22, against Faustus, ch. 76. What of the fact that Grotius admits that not even among the Hebrews, as witnessed by Josephus and other of their Doctors, was retaliation in use, but he who had been injured was accustomed, beyond the expenses incurred by him, to receive a pecuniary fine in place of retaliation? Therefore, the Jews did not accept the Law of retaliation in such a way that it permitted a second injury to the injured, as Tertullian speaks; rather, they understood it to have been given so that it might restrain the first injury. Since even in the Law itself it was prescribed that injuries should be tolerated rather than repaid; 'You shall not take vengeance, nor shall you reserve (hatred or anger) against the children of your people,' the Lord commanded in Leviticus 19:18. 'Do not say, as he has done to me, so I will do to him, I will repay this man according to his work,' Prov. 24:29. 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him, if he is thirsty, give him water to drink; you will heap coals upon his head, and the Lord will repay you,' Prov. 24:21, 22. What else is this than what the Apostle advises, 'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good,' which he proves from that Solomonic passage in Rom. 12:20, 21, or what Christ commands: 'I say to you, do not resist evil'? Nor is anything new commanded when we are ordered to offer the other cheek to one who strikes one; by that figurative manner of speaking it is only hinted that Christians ought to be prepared to bear a second injury rather than to return the former, but the office of the Magistrate, who repays in return or punishes by the right of retaliation, is by no means hindered. For it is not a matter of the office or right of the Magistrate, but of the office and charity of the Christian man in private life.

Marcellinus had raised scruples with Augustine concerning these precepts, as if they were not suitable for the customs of the Republic, but Augustine replied excellently in Epistle 5: That the Republic is preserved most of all by the bond of concord; these precepts, however, are of concord: For this is done, so that the evil man may be overcome by good, or rather that evil may be overcome by good in the evil man, and the man may be freed from evil, not an exterior and foreign one, but an intimate and his own, by which he is ravaged more gravely and perniciously than by the savagery of any enemy from without. Therefore, he says, a just and pious man ought to be prepared to endure patiently the malice of those whom he seeks to become good, so that the number of the good may rather grow, not that he himself should add to the number of the evil with equal malice. Finally, he says that these precepts pertain more to the preparation of the heart, which is within, than to the work which is done in the open, so that patience with benevolence may be held in the secret of the mind, but in the manifest that which seems able to profit those to whom we ought to wish well may be done. This he illustrates with the example of Christ in Luke 22 and of the Apostle in Acts 23, and thus concludes: Therefore these precepts of patience are always to be retained in the preparation of the heart, and that very benevolence, lest evil be returned for evil, is always to be fulfilled in the will. Many things, however, must be done even with the unwilling, who are to be bent with a kindly harshness, and whose utility is to be consulted rather than their will. For in correcting a son, however harshly, paternal love is surely never lost. Yet that is done which he does not want, and he who even against his will is seen to be in need of healing through pain, suffers. And by this, if the earthly Republic keeps Christian precepts, even wars themselves will not be waged without benevolence, so that a peaceful society of piety and justice may be more easily provided for the conquered. For he from whom the license of iniquity is snatched away is usefully conquered. Since there is nothing more unhappy than the happiness of sinners, by which penal impunity is nourished, and an evil will, like an interior enemy, is strengthened. These are the words of Augustine.

THREE HUNDRED FOXES, AND JOINED THEIR TAILS TO TAILS, AND TIED TORCHES IN

Latin:

Vers. 3.

AB HAC DIE NON ERIT CVLPA IN ME CONTRA PHILISTÆOS: FACIAM ENIM VOBIS MALA) Vide & infra 2. & 6, 28. Apud Thucydidem Platæenses, ὀρθῶς ἐτιμωρησάμεθα κατὰ τὸν πᾶσι νόμον καθεστῶτα τὸν ἐπιόντα πολέμιον ὅσιον εἶναι ἀμύνεσθαι. Civilis apud Tacitum: ad supplicium petitus jure gentium pœnas reposco. Vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 2. cap. 20. §. 8. Neque jus naturæ neque jus gentium prohibet se ulcisci, sed quia modus excedebatur, deinde etiam ne ex quavis causa rixæ orirentur, prohibuit id jus civile, quale est etiam jus Hebræis a Deo quidem, sed valde ad modum legum humanarum, datum, quo jure de extraneis ulcisci se nemo prohibetur: De civibus non prohibetur, nisi in rebus minoribus & quotidianis. Alia est ratio sermonis per crucem sanciti, in quo sicut rerum æternarum aperta est sponsio, ita & rerum caducarum, ex quibus ultio oritur, contemtus exigitur. Male hæc confundunt multi, minus nocentes, si Legi

Hebrææ plusquam fatis est, tribuant: magis vero si ex istis temporibus ad nostra Dei indulgentiam extendant. Heroas apud Homerum & Græcos alios, ut notatum Scholiastis, de- diti amoribus, dediti iræ. Alios Heroas nobis dedit Ev- angelii Lux, de qua dicam cum Sene Terentiano: Nunc hic dies aliam vitam adfert, alios mores postulat.

Lucernam Socini hæc olent, cui plus quam satis est, addictus fuit Grotius. Distinguendum ve- ro inter vindictam privatam & publicam. Vindicta enim publica, quæ per Magistratum sit, nullo jure prohibita est. Ultio autem, vel vindicta privata, etsi ad eam natura corrupta nimis quam proclivis sit, juxta illud Poetæ: Est vindicta bonum vita jucundius ipsa;

Non tamen est juris naturæ, neque juris gentium, quatenus hoc e naturæ jure exstructum est, quic- quid sit de corruptis gentium quarundam moribus, e natura corrupta profectis, non e reliquiis imagi- nis divinæ, quæ jus naturæ referunt. Quanquam etiam scintillulæ ejusdem apud gentiles reliquæ ipsos convicerint, de ultionis privatæ ἀνομίᾳ, Sene- ca enim l. 2. de ira c. 32. judice, inhumanum verbum est ultio, & a contumelia non differt, nisi tantum ordi- ne. Qui dolorem regerit, tantum excusatius peccat. Secundum Dionem apud Plutarchum, ultio & inju- ria, si natura spectetur, ex eodem animi morbo na- scitur: Secundum Musonium feræ est, non hominis, id cogitare, quomodo remordeat quis mordentem, & no- centi noceat? Imo secundum Maximum Tyrium, ὁ τιμωρῶν τᾶ προϋπάρξαντος ἀδικώτερος iniqui- or est, qui se ulciscitur eo qui prior nocuit. Neque ex- cessum tantum ultionis privatæ, aut vindictam ob cau- sam quamlibet, sed quamcunque ultionem privatam jus civile prohibet. Unde Theodoricus Rex apud Cassiodorum l. 4. Ep. 10. Hinc est, quod legum a- perta est sacra reverentia, ut nihil manu, nihil proprio ageretur impulsu: Nec non Imperatores, Honorius & Theodosius L. Nulli C. de Judæis; idcirco judiciorum vigor jurisque publici tutela in medio constituta, ne quisquam sibi ipsi permittere valeat ultionem. Sim- pliciter etiam vindictam privatam prohibet jus di- vinum Mosaicum, quod, quantum ad hæc interdicta vindictæ, non ad Ebræos solos spectat, sed qua illa legis moralis sunt, omnes homines omnium tempo- rum obligat. Ea enim lata & data est omnibus. Quod autem peculiare quoddam jus civile Ebræis da- tum sit, de ultione, sub illo discrimine, quod adversus extraneos privata vindicta licita sit, non adversus ci- ves, vel adversus cives etiam, sed in rebus tantum majoribus, non in minoribus & quotidianis, unde, ob- secro, habet Grotius, nisi forte ex lacunis Judæorum impuris? In fontibus certe limpidis Israelis talia non reperiuntur. Porro aliam rationem esse Ser- monis per crucem sanciti, vel Legis Evangelicæ, uti vo- cari solet a Grotio, id vero non nude afferendum cum Socinianis, ac Pelagianis erat, sed e sacris literis demonstrari debebat. Sermo crucis dici consue- vit, non lex aliqua nova vitam instruens, aut mo- res dirigens, sed sermo Evangelii de cruce saluti- fera, vel de salute per crucem Christi obtinenda. Confer. 1. Cor. 1, 17. & 18. 21. 23. cap. 2, 2. Le- gem novam a Christo vel latam, vel cruce sancitam esse, tota ignorat Scriptura, ex adverso docens, Legem per Mosen quidem datam, gratiam vero & veritatem, vel veram gratiam, qua Lex præstatur & impletur, per Christum factam Joh. 1, 17. Non er- go ex Christo, qui nos redemit a Legis maledicto, legemque pro nobis implevit, novus Legislator fin- gendus est, cum Socinianis & Pelagianis, ne abnege- tur Christi redemtio & satisfactio, multo vero minus admittendum, Christum rigidiores leges tulisse, atq; observatu longe difficiliores, quod illi volunt, ex ipso Mosen, ut ita dicam, Mosissimum facientes. Vindicta privata uti in Novi Instrumenti libris a Christo & Apostolis prohibita est gravissime, ita nunquam nec ulli in Veteri Instrumento concessa, sed æque interdicta est. Illud enim Matth. 5, 43. Audistis, quod dictum sit, Proximum tuum diliges & inimicum odio habebis, non utiq; in lege dictum, nuspiam enim in lege jubentur odio habere inimicum, nec proximus, quem diligere secundum legem debebant, de civibus tantum intelligendus erat, sed etiam de extraneis, quemadmodum Legisperitum de eo convicit Christus Luc. 10. imo inimicis etiam benefaciendum esse, e veteri Instrumento probat Apostolus Rom. 12, 20. adducto Salomoneo loco Prov. 15, 21. vindictam autem privatam omnem interdictam esse e Lege Mosaica Deut. 23, 35. demonstrat, eodem ad Rom. 12. c. v. 19. Quid ergo restat, quam ut dicamus, quod res etiam ipsa clamat, dictum id esse de odio habendis inimicis, præter, imo contra Legem scriptam, ab iis, qui traditionibus suis corruperant legem, adversus quorum corruptelas legem istic vindicat Dominus, uti de eo prædixerat Malachias c. 3, 3. Non ergo legi Mosaicæ plus quam satis est tribuunt, qui omnẽ vindictam privatam eadem prohibitam dicunt, sed sequuntur in eo Apostolum idem ipsi tribuentem Rom. 12, 19.
