Non vosmet ipsos usciscentes, sed locum date iræ. Scriptum est enim (in lege Deut. 23, 25.) Mihi vindicta, ego retribuam, dicit Dominus. Minus autem, quam par est, ei tribuit Grotius, male cum lege divina confundens errores gentium v. 9. Civilis illud apud Tacitum: ad supplicium petitus jure gentium pœnas reposco; & pejus adhuc legem divinam a Deo ipso ad humanarum, & quidem talium admodum corruptarum legum instar datam, non absque probro divinæ legis asserens. Si Heroes Gentiles dediti iræ, dediti amoribus, quid hoc ad Heroas illustres, sub populo Dei? penes illos enim Lex naturae quantopere obscurata & depravata fuerit, si ignoravit Grotius, e Paulo, gentium Apostolo, Rom. 1. cap. discere potuit. Sed num illorum modulo metiendi erunt Heroes incluti Patriarcharum, & fidelium in isto populo, cui credita τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ Rom. 3, 4. de quo Hieropsaltes Ps. 147, 19, 20. Annunciat verbum suum Jacob, justitias & judicia sua Israel. Non fecit taliter omni nationi, & judicia sua non manifestavit eis. Annon fides, patientia, & virtutes veterum nobis passim in exemplum sistuntur in Novo Testamento? Annon nubes integra testium ex antiquis temporibus ante exortam Evangelii illustrem lucem a Paulo proponitur Ebræis ad fidem Christi conversis, ut eorum exemplo deponere illi, & nos discamus omne pondus & circumstans nos peccatum, sub quo ira, odium, ultionis, & vindictæ cupiditas, rixæ, contentiones etiam continentur, & per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen Ebr. 12, 1. Sub Veteri Testamento populum Dei expertem lucis Evangelii plane fuisse ἄρτημα Socinianum est: Quæ etsi illustrius sub Novo Testamento effulserit, cum oriens ex alto nos visitavit Luc. 1, 78. antiquis tamen non defuit omnino, quia Scriptura Prophetica ipsis Lux fuit, & lucerna, in caliginoso loco lucens, teste Petro 2. Epist. 1. versu 19. donec dies illucesceret; & habuerunt antiqui heri eundem Jesum Christum, Messiam, qui lux vera est, Joh. 1, 9. quem hodie nos habemus Ebr. 13, 8. crediderunt per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi se servatum iri, quemadmodum & nos credimus Act. 5, 10. Neque antiquis defuit rerum æternarum sponsio satis aperta, qua sese erexerunt, ut exemplo est Hiob cap. 19, 25. David Psalm. 17, versu ult, Esaias cap. 35, 10. (Conf. cap. 65,

| 17.) Daniel c. 12,1. &c. Secus atque Grotius cum Pe- lagianis antiquis & recentioribus somniat , quasi tantum glandibus caducorum & terrenorum bonorum sustentati fuerint antiqui; quorum fides eminentis- simis elogiis ornatur Ebr. 11. cap. unde & rerum ca- ducarum comtemtus passim exigitur in libris Veteris Testamenti, ne illis adhærescant, vel cor appendant fideles, quod in Psalmis Davidicis, & Ecclesiaste Salomoneo qui non videt, eum erroribus Pelagia- nis nimis occupatum, vel excæcatum potius esse o- portet. Sed ut ea revertamur, quæ hujus proprie loci sunt, audiendus hic erit Grotius e libr. 2. de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. 20. §. 8. ad quem locum nos remi- sit, quomodo jure naturæ ac gentium haud prohibitam ultionem dicat, ac probet : nempe, si eo fine suscipia- tur, ne qui læsus est, posthac tale quid patiatur, aut ab eo, adversus quem se ulciscitur, aut ab aliis. Ad hos enim fines & intra æqui terminos si dirigatur vindica- tio etiam privata, jure naturæ non esse illicitam autu- mat, sive ab ipso fiat, qui læsus est, sive ab alio. Atq; sic naturali jure se hic defendisse Samsonem ait ad- versus Palæstinos, cum insontem se fore testatus est, si Palæstinos qui malo se affecerant, malo vicissim affe- cerit. Maccabæos etiam laudari Ambrosium de of- fic. libr. 1. cap. 40. observat, quod etiam Sabbatho ulti sint innocentium necem fratrum suorum. Sed neque Simson privatus erat, utpote Judex in popu- lo Domini, neque Maccabæi. Et quæ e Thucydide de Platæensibus, e Salustio de populo Romano & aliis adducit, vindictam publicam, non privatam concer- nunt. Hanc autem licitam esse jure naturæ, doce- re debebat, non illam. Ex adverso cum Quinti- liani illud laudat, injuriæ compensatio non solum JU- RI inimica, sed paci : Est enim lex, forum, judex, nisi quem vindicari jure pudet; Et Demosthenis in Cano- nem; Placuit de omnibus his injuriis legibus judicium exercere, non autem ex cujusque impetu aut arbitrio; & quæ eam in sententiam sancivisse Honorium, & Theodosium Imperatorem, nec non Regem Theodori- cum antea diximus; annon fatetur palam privatam vindictam haudquaquam licitam, sed JURI INI- MICAM esse. Quod enim jus illud veteri natura- li libertati opponit, quæ cuique ultionem concesserit, in eo principium saltem petit. Naturam hanc no- bis & privato cuivis libertatem vel licentiam ultio- nis concedere probandum erat. Non enim natu- ræ hoc sane, sed qua per peccatum corrupta est, tri- buendum. Imperiti & insipientes, ait Lactantius, si quando accipiunt injuriam, cæco & irrationabili fu- rore ducuntur, & iis qui sibi nocent, vicem retribuere conantur. Et concinit Juvenalis; quippe minuti, semper & infirmi est animi, exiguique voluptas, ultio. Quod Grotius ipse agnovit §. 5. Pugnat ergo, in- quit, cum natura hominis in hominem agentis alieno dolore, qua dolor est satiari, atque adeo quo hominum quisque minus valet rationis usu, eo ad vindictam est pronior. Rationem dederat, quæ ut adscribatur, meretur; quia talis appetitus in se spectatus non conve- nit parti rationali, cujus est imperare affectibus, ac proinde nec juri naturæ, quia id dictatum naturæ ra- tionalis ac socialis, qua talis est. Dictat autem ra- tio homini nihil agendum, quo noceatur homini alteri, nisi id bonum aliquod habeat propositum. In solo autem inimici dolore ita nude spectato, nullum est bo- num, nisi falsum & imaginarium. Quod autem di- cit, se in ultione non respicere solum inimici dolorem, sed utilitatem ejus, qui læsus est, ne posthac tale quid patiatur, ea utilitas publicam firmat ultionem, non vindictam privatam. Potest enim præcaveri per pœnam a Magistratu illatam ulterior læsio : quem- admodum legem Ebræis graviores injurias, ait, permisisse ulcisci, non manu, sed adito judice: imo per leges judicibus solis datam potestatem vindicandi læsos, ubi judices constituti sunt, fatetur; siquidem in rebus nostris & nostrorum affectu corrumpamur. At judi- ciorum illa constitutio, legi naturæ consentanea est, nec vero adimit quicquam juri naturæ, aut ei, quod natura indulsit. Cujusmodi vindicta per judices, quia juri naturæ consentanea est, a Christo sublata non est, neque tolli potuit.

Opponit quidem hic Grotius verba Christi Matth. 5. versu 38. Audistis, quia dictum est oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente: Ego autem dico vobis, non resistere malo, sed si quis percusserit te in dexteram maxillam tuam, præbe illi & alteram. Sed ea Legi Moylis opposita non sunt, sed perversæ illi legis in- terpretationi, ac si vindicta privata ibi sancita esset, aut præcise etiam jus talionis a Mose institutum Exod. 12, 24. Deut. 19, 21. quum ex adverso ibi non læso vindicta, sed judici justitiæ administratio injungatur; Nec alio tendunt verba Christi, quam ut patientiam commendent suis: non enim in offi- cio constitutos, aut Magistratus & judices, sed Chri- stianos instruit. Quod præstet malum patienter sustinere, quam malo rependere, ἐκ ἀδίκꝫ τῆς δι- καίας ἀμύνης ὔσης, ἀλλὰ κρείττονꝰ τῆς ἀνεξικα- κίας, non quod iniqua sit justa ultio, sed quod ei præstet patientia, quod e constitutionibus Clementis lib. 7. c. 23. laudat ipse Grotius. Quod vero in Veteri quo- que Testamento verum fuit. Audiatur Tertullia- nus ipsi Grotio laudatus advers. Marcion. 4. At- que adeo hoc statim renunciandum est, an disciplina patientiæ prædicatur penes creatorem (in Veteri Te- stamento: hujus enim consonantiam cum Novo de- monstrat contra Marcionem: ) Sic per Zachariam præcipit, ne unusquisque malitiam fratris sui memi- nerit, sed nec proximi, (Zach. 5, 11.) Nam & rursus: Malitiam, inquit, proximi sui unusquisque ne reco- gitet (Zach. 8. Multo magis patientiam indixit in- juriæ, qui indixit oblivionem. Sed & quum dixit: (Deut. 32.) mihi vindicta, & ego vindicabo; Proin- de patientiam docet. In quantum ergo non cupit, ut idem videatur & dentem pro dente, oculum pro oculo in vicem injuriæ exigere, qui non modo vicem, sed etiam ultionem, etiam recordationem & recogitationem in- juriæ prohibet, in tantum aperitur nobis, quomodo oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente censuerit, non ad secundam injuriam talionis permittendam, quam prohibuerat interdicta ultione; Sed ad primam coer- cendam, quam prohibuerat talione opposita, ut u- nusquisque respiciens licentiam secundæ injuriæ, a prima semetipsum contineret. Facilius enim vim comprimi scit, repræsentatione talionis, quam repromis- sione ultionis. Utrumque autem constituendum fuit, pro natura & fide hominum, ut qui Deo crederet, ultio- nem a Deo expectaret; qui minus fideret, leges talio- nis timeret. Hanc legis voluntatem de intellectu la- borantem Dominus & Sabbathi & Legis & omnium paternarum dispositionum Christus & revelavit, & compotem fecit, mandans alterius quoque maxillæ oblationem, ut tanto magis vicem injuriæ extingueret, quam & Lex per talionem voluerat impedisse, certe quam Prophetia manifeste coercuerat, & memoriam injuriæ prohibens, & ultionem ad Deum relegans, ita si quid Christus intulit, non adversario, sed adjutore præcepto, non destruxit disciplinas Creatoris. Hæc o- mnia Tertullianus, quæ Grotio prorsus adversa sunt. Plane enim contrarium probat Tertullianus ejus, quod defendit Grotius: Nullam esse Vet. & Nov. Test. diversitatem, evincens, quam cum Marcione hæ- retico adserit Grotius: Addo & cum Fausto Ma- nichæo. Hic enim contendit Christum contrarium Mofi in eo esse, quod legem talionis aboleverit. Vi- de August. l. 22. contr. Faust. c. 76. Quid quod fa- teatur Grotius, quod ne apud Ebræos quidem, teste Jofepho, & aliis eorum Doctoribus, in usu fuerit talio, sed solitus fuerit, qui læsus erat, ultra impendia a se fa- cta, pro talione pecuniariam mulctam accipere. Non ergo ita Legem talionis accepere Judæi, ut quæ læsis secundam injuriam, uti loquitur Tertullianus, per- mitteret; quam datam esse potius intelligebant, ut primam injuriam refrenaret. Siquidem etiam in Lege ipsa præscriptum fuerit, injurias potius tole- randas, quam reddendas esse; Non ulcisceris te, neq; reservabis (odium vel iram) contra filios populi, præ- cepit Dominus Levit. 19, 18. Ne dicito, quemadmo- dum fecit mihi, ita faciam ei, reddam isti viro secundum opus ipsius Prov. 24, 29. Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum, si sitiverit, da ei aquam bibere; brunas ei congre- gabis super caput ejus, & Dominus reddet tibi Prov. 24, 21. 22. Quod quid aliud est, quam quod monet A- postolus, noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum, qui hoc e loco illo Salomonæo probat Rom. 12, 20. 21. aut quod præcipit Christus: Ego dico vobis, non resi- stere malo. Nec novi quidquam præcipitur, cum percutienti maxillam unam, alteram præbere jube- mur; solum figurata illa loquendi ratione innuitur, paratos esse debere Christianos ad ferendam potius se- cundam injuriam, quam ad regerendam priorem, neu- tiquam autem officium Magistratus vicem reddentis, vel talionis jure punientis sufflaminatur. Non enim de officio vel jure Magistratus, sed de officio & cha- ritate hominis Christiani in vita privata agitur.

Moverat de his præceptis Augustino scrupu- los Marcellinus, quasi Reipublicæ moribus non conveni- rent, sed respondit præclare Augustinus Epist. 5. Rempublicam vinculo concordiæ maxime conservari; hæc vero præcepta esse concordiæ: Hoc quippe fieri, ut vincatur bono malus, imo in homine malo vincatur bono malum, & homo liberetur a malo, non exteriore & alie- no, sed intimo ac suo, quo gravius & perniciosius, quam cujusvis hostis extrinsecus immanitate vastatur. Pa- ratus itaque, inquit, debet homo esse justus & pius, pa- tienter eorum malitiam sustinere, quos fieri bonos quæ- rit, ut numerus potius crescat bonorum, non ut pari ma- litia se quoque numero addat malorum. Deniq; ista præcepta magis ad præparationem cordis, quæ intus est, pertinere ait, quam ad opus, quod in aperto fit, ut tenea- tur in secreto animi patientia cum benevolentia, in ma- nifesto autem id fiat, quod eis videtur prodesse posse, quibus bene velle debemus. Quod illustrat exem- plo Christi Luc. 22. & Apostoli Act. 23. atque ita concludit: Sunt ergo ista præcepta patientiæ semper in cordis præparatione retinenda, ipsaque benevolentia, ne reddatur malum pro malo, semper in voluntate com- plenda est. Agenda sunt autem multa etiam cum in- vitis, benigna asperitate flectendis, quorum potius uti- litati consulendum est, quam voluntati. Nam in corripiendo filio quamlibet aspere, nunquam profecto amor paternus amittitur. Fit tamen, quod nolit, & doleat, qui etiam invitus videtur dolore sanandus. Ac per hoc si terrena Respublica præcepta Christiana custo- diat, & ipsa bella sine benevolentia non gerentur, ut ad pietatis justitiæque pacatam societatem victis facilius consulatur. Nam cui licentia iniquitatis eripitur, u- tiliter vincitur. Quoniam nihil est infelicius felicita- te peccantium, qua pænalis nutritur impunitas, & mala voluntas, velut hostis interior roboratur. Hæc Au- gustinus.

## 15:4
MEDIO) You have a clearly similar Carseolan story, concerning foxes and torches, and the harvest burned by means of them, in Ovid, Fasti 4.

Latin:

MEDIO) Plane similem historiam Carseolanam, de vulpi- bus & facibus, ac per eas incensa messe habes apud Ovidium Fastorum 4.

## 15:6
Verse 6.

AND THEY BURNED BOTH THE WOMAN AND HER FATHER) Immense cruelty toward those who had only given the occasion for the evil, and not foreseeing it.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET COMBUSSERVNT TAM MVLIEREM QVAM PATREM EJVS) Ingens crudelitas in eos qui malo occa- sionem tantum, nec id providentes dederant.

## 15:8
Verse 8. HE SMOTE THEM WITH A GREAT SLAUGHTER, SO THAT THEY IN STUPOR PUT LEG UPON THIGH.

In Hebrew, from shoulder to thigh, according to Osiander's interpretation, because he hewed them down from the upper to the lower parts of the body: or rather, from shoulder to thigh, from the upper to the lower, he struck the highest and the lowest. The Targum of Jonathan understands horsemen and footmen. Junius rendered it: and he struck them with a brandished leg upon their thighs with a great slaughter, that is, attacking them with no other weapons than his foot, as if they were cowardly soldiers.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PERCUSSIT EOS INGENTI PLA- GA, ITA UT STUPENTES SURAM FEMORI IMPONERENT.

In Ebr. ab armo ad femur, interprete Osiandro, quod egregie eos a superioribus ad inferiores par- tes corporis dedolarit: vel potius, ab armo ad fe- mur, a superioribus ad inferiores, summos & imos percusserit. Targum Jonath. equites, & pedites in- telligit. Junius reddidit: percussitque eos crure vi- brato in femora eorum plaga magna, id est, non aliis armis eos petens, quam pede velut ignavos milites.

## 15:11
Verse 11. THEY RULE OVER US) Hebrew: let them have dominion over us, that is, let them prevail over us. See what is above 10, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 11. IMPERENT NOBIS) Hebræum: dominentur in nos, id est, prævaleant nobis. Vide quæ supra 10, 7.

## 15:15
Verse 15. JAWBONE THAT IS MANDIBLE.

In Hebrew, a moist jawbone, and therefore fresh, not yet dry.

Latin:

Vers. 15. MAXILLAM ID EST MANDIBU- LAM.

In Ebr. Maxillam humidam, adeoque recen- tem, nondum aridam.

## 15:19
Verse 19.

A MOLAR TOOTH IN THE JAWBONE OF AN ASS) The Greeks [say] the pit, others the wound. It is credible that it signifies the gap which that tooth, knocked out with such force, had made in the jawbone when it was thrown. Luther: Then God splits a molar tooth in the jawbone, so that water came out of it. Whence Osiander: a fountain began to gush from the molar tooth. Junius, Piscator, the Tigurine, the Italian, and the English versions take the word Lechi as a proper name from verse 17, that in that place, which had been called Lehi, God had made a gap and an opening. To which B. Chytreus also seems to incline. Although the word מכתש in two other places, Prov. 27:22, Zeph. 1:11, denotes a mortar, nothing prevents it from designating a molar tooth here by analogy: because food is crushed by a molar tooth, as Avenarius and Forster explain. For a mortar has no place here. Whence the Italian version understands a concave rock, the Chaldean interpreted it as a Rock (but here he places it in the jawbone), Junius rendered it a certain hollow because of the similarity to a mortar on account of the cavity: in which way Ussher also accepted it, Annal. p. 47, he produced a fountain in Lehi from a certain cleft in the earth. We have no reason to depart from the Vulgate version and that of B. Luther: which the Ancients approve. Ambrose, Ep. 70: When he had thrown the jawbone, the mercy of God opened its fissure, and a fountain erupted from it. Jerome, in Ep. Paul: He produced a fountain from the molar tooth of the jawbone. Prudentius, in Enchir.: the jawbone of an ass vomits a fountain of its own accord; so also Chrysostom, Ephrem, and others. Corn. a Lap. and Hier. and Glycas, part 2 of the annals, teach that that fountain is still to be seen today in the suburb of Eleutheropolis, and is called the fountain of the jawbone: which Serarius says still pours forth waters even now.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

MOLAREM DENTEM IN MAXILLA ASINI) Græci τὸν λάκκον, alii τὸ τραῦμα. Credibile est significari hiatum, quem in maxilla projecta fecerat dens ea vi excussus. Lutherus: Da spaltet GOtt einen Backenzahn in die Kinbacken, daß Wasser daraus gieng. Unde Osiander: cœpit fons ex dente molari scaturire. Ju- nius, Piscator, Tigur. Ital. Anglic. accipiunt vocem Lechi ceu nomen proprium e v. 17. quod in illo lo- co, qui si: dictus erat, hiatum & aperturam fecerit Deus. Quo etiam B. Chytreus inclinare videtur. Quamvis vero vox מכתש duobus aliis locis Prov. 27, 22. Zeph. 1, 11. mortarium notet, nihil tamen ob- stat, quo minus hic dentem molarem ob analogiam designet: quia molari dente cibus contunditur, ut Avenarius, & Forsterus explicant. Nam neque hic locum habet mortarium. Unde Italica versio concavum saxum intelligis, Chaldæus interpretatus est Petram (sed hic eam in maxilla constituit) Junius cavum quoddam reddidit ob similitudinem cum mortario propter cavitatem: quo pacto & Usserius accepit Annal. p. 47. fisso cavo quodam terræ in levi fontem produxit. Non habemus causam disceden- di a versione Vulgata, & B. Lutheri: quam appro- bant Veteres. Ambrosius Ep. LXX. Dei misericor- dia cum projecisset ille maxillam, aperuit scissuram e- jus, & fons erupit ex ea. Hieronym. in Ep. Paul. Fon- tem de molari maxillæ dente produxit. Prudent. in Enchir. maxilla asini fontem vomit ultro, sic etiam Chrysostomus, Ephrem & alii. Corn. a Lap. & Hier. & Glyca parte 2. annal. fontem illum adhuc hodie in suburbio Eleutheropolis conspici, & fontem ma- xillæ nuncupari docet: quem etiamnum aquas fun- dere Serarius ait.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. Samson carried the gates of Gaza to the mountain. Shorn by Delilah, he is mocked, and dying, he destroys his enemies.

Verse 1.

A HARLOT WOMAN) The Law forbids Israelite women to be harlots. It does not forbid using those of foreign nations who profess such a life. It is otherwise in the Evangelical law, which ignores the distinctions of nations. See what is said at Deut. 23:17 and 21:11.

It is evident that it is forbidden for there to be a harlot among the daughters of Israel, nor a whoremonger among the sons of Israel, Deut. 23:17, but where is it written that it is permitted to use foreign women who profess a harlot's life? The passage Deut. 21:11 does not deal with a harlot, or one who professes such a life, but with a beautiful woman among the captives, whom someone might desire and wish to have as his wife, which is granted to him. Grotius indeed, in his annotations to that place, wants the Hebrew word דבק to mean to adhere, to be joined, spoken modestly for having lain with her, following the Talmud, Moses Gerundensis, and Maimonides; but that interpretation can neither be confirmed from the text, nor, if it were confirmed, should such a foreign woman, who, having been brought under the power of a Jewish man, had to lie with him, be counted among those who profess a harlot's life, since she is considered to be restored to her honor through marriage. But as for such a captive being taken if she has been so desired, the Law indeed permits it, but it does not therefore permit that she be so desired; it does not permit fornication, which Grotius thinks: since that is forbidden to them by the Sixth Commandment of the Decalogue. When something is permitted under a hypothesis, it is not permitted to act, nor is the hypothesis itself approved. Nor is there any other reason here under the New Testament, or anything new decreed, which has been added to the Mosaic moral Law. Which neither any of the Socinians, nor Grotius, has been able to prove thus far. The Evangelical Law in the sense of Grotius and the Socinians is an iron-wood: for Law and Gospel are opposites. Moreover, as the Gospel ignores the distinctions of nations, because whoever believes, of whatever race or nation he may be, shall be saved, according to the sentiment of the Gospel: so also the moral Law, inasmuch as it prescribes obedience to all, and threatens punishment to all if they do not obey, indeed is inscribed in the minds of all by nature, even if, because of the obscuration caused by sin, it was solemnly repeated to the Israelite people and promulgated on Mount Sinai: yet we do not deny that the forensic laws were proper to this people. But the prohibition of fornication does not pertain to the forensic laws, but to the Decalogue or the moral law.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. Simson portas Gazæ in montem tulit. A Da- lila detonfus illuditur, & hostes moriens interimit.

Vers. 1.

MVLIEREM MERETRICEM) Lex vetat Israëlitidas esse meretrices. Extraneis talem vitam profitentibus uti non vetat. Alud est in Evangelica lege, quæ gentium discri- mina ignorat. Vide quæ dicta ad Deut. 23, 17. & 21, 11.

INterdictum, ne meretrix sit de filiabus Israel, nec scortator de filiis Israel Deut. 23, 17. evidens est, sed meretriciam vitam profitentibus extraneis uti licere, ubinam scriptum legitur? Locus Deut. 21, 11. non de meretrice, vel quæ talem vitam profitetur, agit, sed de muliere pulchra in numero captivorum, quam quis adamaverit, sibique uxorem habere voluerit, quod eidem conceditur. Vult quidem Grotius annot. ad istum locum Ebræum דבק adhærere, conjungi, σεμνῶς dictum pro concubueris cum ea, sequutus Thalmudem, Mosen Gerundensem, & Maimonidem, sed neque e textu firmari ea interpretatio potest, neque si firmaretur maxime, talis extranea, quæ sub potestatem redacta viri Judæi, concumbere cum eo necessum habuit, meretriciam vitam profitentibus accenseri debet, ubi matrimonio deinceps jungitur: siquidem honori suo per matrimonium restitui censeatur. Ut autem, si ita adamata fuerit, talis captiva ducatur, permittit quidem Lex, non autem ideo permittit, ut ita adametur, non permittit fornicationem, quod putat Grotius: Siquidem illi interdictum sit Sexto Decalogi præcepto. Cum quid sub hypothesi permittitur, non permittitur acturum, aut probatur ipsa hypothesis. Neque hic alia est sub Nov. Test. ratio, aut novi quid sancitum, quod Legi morali Mosaicæ additum sit. Quod hactenus neque Socinianorum quisquam, neque Grotius probare potuit. Lex Evangelica sensu Grotii & Sociniano σιδηρόξυλον est: Lex enim & Evangelium opposita sunt. Cæterum ut Evangelium gentium discrimina ignorat, quia quicunque crediderit, cujuscunque gentis aut nationis sit, salvus erit, juxta sententiam Evangelii: sic etiam Lex moralis, utpote quæ omnibus præscribit obedientiam, omnibus, si non obediverint, minatur pœnam, imo omnium mentibus τῇ φύσει insculpta est, etsi propter obscurationem per peccatum factam populo Israëlitico solenniter repetita, & promulgata fuerit in Monte Sinai: Leges tamen forenses populi hujus proprias fuisse, non diffitemur. Sed fornicationis interdictum non ad leges forenses pertinet, sed ad Decalogum vel legem moralem.

## 16:2
verse 2. TO THE TOP OF THE MOUNTAIN THAT LOOKS TOWARD HEBRON. Hebron, according to Adrichomius, was fourteen hourly miles distant from Gaza. It is therefore altogether wonderful that he could tear up such strong gates with their posts, and carry them for such a journey, and transfer them to the mountain; from which it is gathered how great a strength was divinely infused into this hero. For in the Hebrew it is not 'that looks toward Hebron,' but 'that is above the face of Hebron' or 'over against it,' and therefore it was not far distant from Hebron: so that Adrichomius is mistaken, thinking that that mountain was near to Gaza.

Latin:

verf. 2. AD VERTICEM MONTIS QUI RESPICIT HEBRON. Hebron, juxta Adrichomium, quatuordecim milliaribus horariis Gaza distabat. Mirum ergo omnino, quod tam validas portas cum postibus evellere, & per tantum iter portare, ac in montem transferre potuerit; unde quanta fortitudo divinitus indita huic Heroi fuerit, colligitur. In Ebræo enim est, non qui respicit Hebron, sed qui est super faciem Hebron vel e regione, ideoque non longe distabat ab Hebron: ut fallatur Adrichomius, putans, montem illum Gazæ vicinum fuisse.

## 16:4
verse 4. WHO DWELT IN THE VALLEY OF SOREK. Jerome, in the 'Hebrew Places,' locates it on the northern side of Eleutheropolis, where in his time a village still existed, by the name of Caphar Sorek near the town of Saran, where Samson was born. Chrysostom, Ephrem, and Prosper make Delilah Samson's wife; Josephus and Ambrose and Suidas judge that she was his harlot, to whom most interpreters accede, because the Satraps of the Philistines deal with her so confidently with money offered, which declares a harlot's love rather than a wife's.

Latin:

verf. 4. QUÆ HABITABAT IN VALLE SOREC. Eam Hieron. in Loc. Hebr. locat ad Septentrionalem plagam Elevtheropoleos, ubi suo tempore adhuc vicus extabat, nomine Caphar Sorec juxta villam Saran, ubi natus fuit Simson. Delilam Chrysost. Ephrem, ac Prosper Simsonis uxorem faciunt, Josephus & Ambrosius ac Suida meretricem ejus fuisse censent, quibus plerique interpretes accedunt, quod Satrapæ Philistinorum cum ea tam fidenter agant oblata pecunia, quod potius meretricium, quam uxorium amorem declarat.

## 16:5
Verse 5. PRINCIPES OF THE PHILISTINES) Satraps as above. See also below 27.

WE WILL GIVE THEE EVERY MAN OF US ELEVEN HUNDRED PIECES OF SILVER.

To Osiander it seems that the silver piece was of no less value than a Thaler, and so, since there were five Satraps of the Philistines, 5500 thalers were offered to the harlot for the betrayal of Samson: But if the Shekels are estimated according to the usage of Scripture, 2750 thalers will be produced; but if pounds are understood, 1100 pounds will make 132000 shekels, that is 66000 thalers. Compare what is at ch. 9, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PRINCIPES PHILISTHINORVM) Satrapæ ut supra. Vide & infra 27.

DABIMUS TIBI SINGULI MILLE ET CENTUM ARGENTEOS.

Osiandro videtur argenteus non minoris fuisse pretii quam Thalerus, adeoq; quum quinq; Satrapæ Philistinorum fuerint, 5500. thaleros scorto pro Simsonis proditione oblatos esse: At si Sicli ex usu Scripturæ æstimentur, 2750. thaleri prodi- bunt, si v. libræ intelligantur, 1100. libræ efficient 132000. Siclos, h. e. 66000. thaleros. Conf. quæ ad c. 9, 4.

## 16:7
Verse 7. TO WHOM SAMSON REPLIES) Eluding an unjust demand with a lie, as is wont to happen among lovers.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CVI RESPONDET SAMSON) Iniquum po- stulatum mendacio eludens, ut inter amantes fieri solet.

## 16:17
Verse 17. IF MY HEAD SHALL BE SHAVEN, MY STRENGTH WILL DEPART FROM ME) For the covenant was violated which he had with God, who was the donor of such immense power. It is not unlike what not only the poets, but also Pausanias, relate about the fate of Nisus, king of the Megarians: For from the king's head, wonderful to tell, a white lock of hair flourished, and a rosy hair shone in the middle of the crown: had its nature been preserved for long, the Fates, in harmonious power, would have confirmed Nisus's country and kingdom safe forever.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SI RASVM FVERIT A ME CAPVT ME- VM, RECEDET A ME FORTITVDO MEA) Quippe federe violato, quod ei cum Deo intercedebat, qui roboris tam immensi donator erat. Non dissimile est quod de fato Nisi Megarensium regis narrant non Poetæ tantum, sed & Pausanias: Nam capite a summo regis mirabile dictu, Candida Cæsaries, florebant tempora lauro, Et roseus medio fulgebat vertice crinis: Cujusquam servata diu natura fuisset, Tam patriam incolumem Nisi, regnumque futurum Concordes stabili firmarunt numine Parcæ.

## 16:19
Verse 19. IMMEDIATELY HIS STRENGTH DEPARTED FROM HIM.

Not that it was situated in the hair, but because that non-shaving of hair was the moral cause or condition without which this Nazarite's strength could not exist: to which, by reason of the pact and promise, the preservation of his powers was annexed.

Latin:

Vers. 19. STATIM AB EO FORTITUDO DISCESSIT.

Non quod in capillis ea sita fuerit, sed quia causa moralis vel conditio sine qua non erat fortitudi- nis hujus Nazaræi illa non-rasura capillorum : cui ratione pacti & promissi divina annexa virium con- servatio.

## 16:21
Verse 21. AND THEY MADE HIM GRIND IN THE PRISON) He calls the mill a prison here too, as in Exodus 12, verse 29. Moreover, it was customary for the eyes of those condemned to the mill to be put out, so that dizziness would not hinder their work; for which reason Herodotus in Melpomene relates that the eyes of slaves turning the milk-churns, and those running around the vessel in which the milk was, were put out.

Others understand a workhouse, in which they formerly ground grain with hand-mills: such as were accustomed to be turned by beasts of burden or slaves. Some, however, think that there were mills in prisons, both so that the captivity might be rendered more burdensome, and so that the captives would not consume food in vain.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET CLAVSVM IN CARCERE MOLERE FECERVNT) Pistrinum & hic carcerem vocat, ut Exod. 12. vers. 29. Oculi autem adimi in pistrinum damnatis solebant, ne vertigo labori obstaret; qua de causa & servis lac versanti- bus, & vas in quo lac erat circumcursantibus, ademtos ocu- los narrat Herodotus Melpomene.

Alii ergastulum intelligunt, in quo frumentum olim commolebant, trusatilibus molis : quales ju- mentis vel mancipiis circumagi solebant. Nonnul- li tamen molas in carceribus olim fuisse putant, cum ut captivitas molestior redderetur, tum ut captivi non frustra alimenta absumerent,

## 16:22
V. 22. AND NOW HIS HAIR BEGAN TO GROW AGAIN.

In Hebrew: And his hair began to sprout: which was such as it was when it was being shaved: as the 70 interpreters also imply. Nor is there any doubt that Samson had repented, who had brought these evils upon himself by his fornication, and had thus obtained his former strength from God through prayers, as the Author of the Miracles of Holy Scripture observes, book 2, ch. 6.

Latin:

V. 22. JAMQUE CAPILLI RENASCI CEPE- RUNT.

In Ebr. Et cœpit capillus ejus germinare : quod talis fuerit qualis cum raderetur erat: ut LXX. inter- pretes etiam innuunt. Neque dubium est pœniten- tiam egisse Samsonem, qui fornicatione sua hæc ma- la attraxerat & precibus a Deo ita impetrasse forti- tudinem pristinam, ut observat Autor mirabilium S. Script. l. 2. c. 6.

## 16:23
Verse 23. TO DAGON HIS GOD) They are fish bearing a human form above, whence the nations made them deities, which the Greeks called Tritons, the Phoenicians Dagon from דג which is fish, not from דגן which is grain, as Philo Byblius thought, deceived by the ambiguity of the word. Such in the female sex are Nereids and Sirens: of which species was the goddess of the Phoenicians, Derceto or Dercetis, by others Atargatis. Lucian mentions her in 'On the Syrian Goddess': Diodorus Siculus says she was worshipped near Ascalon. Pliny and the Greek and Latin scholiasts of Aratus also mention her. I think the Greeks interposed the letter R: but that her Phoenician name was דגתו Dageto, female fish.

Similarly others, with Lyranus and certain Hebrews in vain inverting the form, observe that he had the image of a fish below, but a human form above, as the ancients fashioned Tritons and Nereids: and that from this it is that in 1 Samuel 5, 4, mention is made of Dagon's hands; but none of his feet, Bonfrerius warns: who discourses at length about this idol. Compare 1 Chronicles 10, 10; 1 Maccabees 10, 83. Selden, 'On the Syrian Gods', Syntagma 2, chapter 3, notes that those names Aturgatis, Adergatis, Atergata, Derceto, Derce, Astargidis, Atargatis, which are all found for this goddess, are corrupted words from Addir-daga, that is In Hebrew אדיר דג that is, magnificent fish, and it is, in his judgment, that fish worshipped in Azotus, Oannes, about whom Berosus, Apollodorus, and Polyhistor write, whose figure was likewise mixed from human and marine, from whom, having emerged from the sea, men learned arts, letters, and agriculture, according to Berosus; whom Helladius calls Oes, testifying about the same that he was entirely a man, but that he was reported as a fish because he was clothed in a cetacean skin, as Photius reports from him in Codex 279. Selden does not deny, however, that Dagon is Venus: which Bonfrerius also proves with Serarius. Others say that Derceto is the daughter of Venus, who is also called Dagon, following Diodorus Siculus, book 3. There is no doubt that there were androgynous, or both-sexed, gods among the heathens.

Latin:

Vers. 23. DAGON DEO SVO) Sunt pisces superne ho- minem præferentes, unde gentes numina fecere, quæ Trito- nes Græcis, Dagon Phœnicibus a דג quod est piscis, non a דגן quod est frumentum, ut putavit Philo Byblius ambiguo vocis deceptus. Tales in fœminino sexu Nereides & Sire- nes : qua specie Dea Phœnicum erat Derceto vel Dercetis, aliis Atargatis. Meminit Lucianus de Dea Syria : Diodo- rus Siculus apud Ascalonem cultam ait. Meminere & Plinius & Arati Scholiastæ Græci & Latini. Puto Græcos literam R interposuisse : nomen autem ejus Phœnicium fuisse דגתו Dageto, piscis fœmina.

Similiter alii, Lyrano cum Ebræis quibusdam formam nequicquam invertente, ei inferne piscis imaginem, superne vero formæ humanæ fuisse ob- servant, ut Tritonas & Nereidas antiqui finxere : at- que inde esse, quod 1. Sam. 5, 4. manuum Dagonis mentio fiat; nulla autem pedum, Bonfrerius monet: qui prolixe de hoc idolo differit. Conf. 1. Par. 10, 10. 1. Macc. 10, 83. Seldenus de Diis Syris Synt. 2. cap. 3. nomina illa Aturgatis, Adergatis, Atergata, Derce- to, Derce, Astargidis, Atargatis, quæ omnia pro hac Dea reperiantur, corrupta vocabula esse ab Addir- daga h. e. Ebraice אדיר דג id est, piscis magnificus, estque illius judicio, piscis ille cultus in Azoto, Σιάν- νης, de quo Berosus, Apollodorus, & Polyhistor, cujus figura itidem ex humana & marina mixta, e quo ex mari emerso homines, artes, literas, agriculturam didicerint Beroso autore ; quem ὀτὴν appellet Helladius, testatus de eodem, quod omnino homo fuerit, piscem autem retulerit, quod cetaceo pelle indueretur, ut ex eo refert Pho- tius Codic. 279. Non abnuit autem Selde- nus Dagon Venerem esse: quod etiam Bonfrerius cum Serario probat. Alii filiam Veneris esse Der- ceto, quæ etiam Dagon dicatur, ajunt, Diodor. Sicu- lum sequuti l. 3. Androginos q. vel utriusque sexus Deos apud Ethnicos fuisse, nullum est dubium.

## 16:27
V. 27. THE HOUSE WAS FULL OF MEN AND WOMEN.

Ambrose, Isidore, Suidas, and most interpreters think that it was the temple of Dagon itself, because in verse 23 the Princes of the Philistines are said to have gathered to offer a sacrifice to Dagon their god: and once these were offered, they instituted a sacred feast, as was the custom among the Gentiles to celebrate in temples: which, however, Bonfrerius calls into doubt with a not-frivolous argument, that it is nowhere read that there was an image or temple of Dagon in Gaza, but in Ashdod.

Latin:

V. 27. DOMUS PLENA ERAT VIRORUM ET MULIERUM.

Fanum ipsum Dagonis fuisse Ambrosius, Isido- rus, Suidas, & plerique interpp. putant, quia vers. 23. convenisse Principes Philistinorum dicuntur, ut ho- stiam immolarent Dagon Deo suo: quibus oblatis epulum sacrum apud Ethnicos in fanis celebrari so- litum instituerunt: quod tamen in dubium vocat Bonfrerius argumento non futili, quod nuspiam legatur Gazæ fuisse Dagonis simulacrum vel fanum fuisse, sed Azoti.

## 16:30
Vers. 30.

LET MY SOUL DIE WITH THE PHILISTINES

That passed into a proverb among the Hebrews, equal to that Latin one: Let friends perish so long as enemies perish together. But the Hebrews, not being taught laws of patience as great as Christians, deemed that there were causes grave enough for bringing death upon oneself, as has been demonstrated by many in the second book on the Law of War and Peace, chapter 9, § 5.

It is false that the Hebrews were not taught laws of patience as great as those Christians are taught. For the precepts of patience were commended to the Jews just as to the Christians, and were held holy by them: Isa. 30:15. Prov. 3:11, ch. 14:25, ch. 16:32, ch. 19:11. Lam. 3:31. Sir. 2:4, 5, ch. 34:9. See also Job 1:21. Jer. 10:24. Tob. 2:12. 2 Mac. 6:19. Indeed, Christians are exhorted to patience by the example of the Hebrews at length in Heb. 11 and 12:1, as also by the example of Job in James 5:11. However, I find no causes for αὐτοφω- νίας [self-slaughter] sufficiently grave in the cited passage, nor any that the faithful Hebrews (of whose number Samson was) would have believed to be sufficiently grave. The Rabbis, blind leaders of the blind, are little to be heeded: whose opinions on this question, however, Grotius himself observed to have varied, l. c. in the annotations to book II of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 19, § 5. And what can those causes be, so grave that one should bring death upon oneself? Grotius said in the cited § that the Hebrews allow only one cause (not several, as here) for the law of not killing oneself, namely, if one sees that he will henceforth live to the disgrace of God himself. For because they establish that the right to our life belongs not to us, but to God, they think that the presumed will of God is the only thing that justifies the decision to anticipate death. And to this (Grotius continues) they refer the example of Samson, who saw that the true religion was being mocked in his own body, and of Saul, who fell upon his sword so that he would not be mocked by God's enemies and his own. The third is the example of Razis, a Senator of Jerusalem, in the Maccabean History. But who can certainly foresee this, whether he will live to the disgrace of God or not? And does God not have a thousand ways of revealing the glory of His name and vindicating it from reproach? Therefore, evils are not to be done so that good may come, Rom. 3:8. But our life, and its direction toward the glory of His name, must be committed to God. Nor were the Hebrews taught otherwise; God certainly nowhere allows this cause. Nor do the examples prove it. For the one taken from the Apocryphal book of Razis, even if it is approved there, has no weight: since that book proceeded from a human spirit, not a divine one. See the Gloss to C. Canones dist. 16. What wonder is it, says Augustine concerning Razis, Ep. 61 to Dulcitius, if, as happens to a man, a proud elation crept in, so that he preferred to be destroyed by his own hand rather than to endure, after that, unworthy cruelty at the hands of his enemies in the sight of his own people. Such things are wont to be praised in the writings of the Gentiles; God said, do not kill the innocent and the just; if, therefore, this man was not innocent and just, why is he proposed as one to be imitated, but if he was innocent and just, why then should the slayer of the innocent and just, that is, of Razias himself, be thought worthy of praise? Conf. lib. II. contra Gauderit. Epist. As regards Saul, he was impious, not faithful, and he laid hands upon himself out of desperation, not for the glory of the divine name. That he repented after his death was predicted to him by a specter is a fable of the Rabbis. He received from David praise for martial bravery, not for repentance, 2 Sam. 1. And it is known that the wrath of the Lord could not be appeased in David's time except by the hanging of seven men from the house of Saul, 2 Sam. 21:6. Finally, the example of Samson is entirely singular, of which more later. Grotius does indeed bring forward similar examples from Christian history of those who brought death upon themselves lest, driven by torments, they should abjure the religion of Christ: and of virgins who, lest they lose their chastity, threw themselves into a river. But what reasons does he pretend for Christians, whom he surely believes to have been taught laws of patience far holier than the Hebrews? Ignorance of those laws, therefore, could not excuse them, by which he wished the Hebrews to be excused.

And because he judges it worth the effort to see what Augustine thinks about these matters, why does he not agree with him rather than with the Jews? Thus Augustine, l. c.: 'Because everyone who kills a man without any authority of legitimate power is a murderer, whoever kills himself is a murderer, if he is a man.' We have said all these things in many ways in our many other sermons and letters. Origen agrees with him in book 2 on Job: 'Those who kill themselves will never have rest, nor will they find refreshment, but their souls, as soon as they have departed from the body, will be led into darkness.' Chrysostom on those at Gal. 4:4: 'But now,' he says, 'God punishes them more severely than murderers, and we all detest them, and that rightly and deservedly: for if it is not lawful to kill others, it is much more unlawful to kill oneself.' Council of Orleans. III. decrees thus: 'We judge that the offerings of the dead who were killed while in some crime ought to be received, if, however, they are not proven to have brought death upon themselves with their own hands.' Although indeed Augustine, book 1 of The City of God, ch. 26, regarding the holy women who, during the time of persecution, threw themselves into a river that would seize and kill them so as to avoid the violators of their chastity, because their martyrdoms are celebrated with the greatest veneration in the Catholic Church, dares not judge rashly whether they did this not deceived by human impulse but commanded by God, neither erring nor disobedient, just as he judges that it is not lawful for us to believe otherwise about Samson, he nevertheless concludes this disputation with this memorable sentence: 'We say this, we assert this, we approve this in all ways: that no one ought to bring spontaneous death upon himself, as if by fleeing temporal troubles, lest he fall into eternal ones.' No one on account of the sins of others, lest by this very act he begin to have a most grave sin of his own, which the sin of another did not pollute. No one on account of his own past sins, for which there is more need of this life, so that they may be healed by repenting: No one as if from a desire for a better life, which is hoped for after death: because a better life after death does not receive those guilty of their own death. In the following chapter he inquires specifically: whether spontaneous death should be sought for the sake of avoiding sin? 'There remains,' he says, 'one cause, of which I had begun to speak, for which it is thought useful that if anyone kills himself, he does so lest he fall into sin, either by alluring pleasure or by raging pain.' If we were to admit this cause, it will progress so far that men should be exhorted to kill themselves rather when, having been offered to the bath of holy regeneration, they have received the remission of all their sins. For then is the time for avoiding all future sins, when all past ones have been wiped away. But if this is done rightly by spontaneous death, why is it not done then most of all?

Or does such a foolish perversity overturn the heart and turn it away from the consideration of truth: that if anyone ought to kill himself, lest he fall into sin through the tyranny of captivity, he thinks he must live to endure the world itself, full of temptations at every hour, and such as is feared under one master, and countless others, without which this life is not led? He concludes finally thus: 'Therefore, O faithful of Christ, let not your life be a weariness to you, if your chastity was a mockery to your enemies. You have a great and true consolation; if you retain a faithful conscience, that you did not consent to the sins of those who were permitted to sin against you.' But that case of self-murder, which is brought about for the sake of chastity, is decided openly at James 2:10-11: 'For whoever shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, he is guilty of all. For he who said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill.' But if you do not commit adultery, but you do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law. For since it is certainly not permitted for anyone to kill a man by private authority, even a guilty one, says Augustine in Book 1 of The City of God, ch. 17, for whose killing no law grants permission, surely even he who kills himself is a murderer: And he is the more guilty when he kills himself, the more innocent he was in that cause for which he thought he should be killed.

Therefore, regarding the example of Samson, about which it still remains to speak, setting aside for now the responses of others, we shall set forth that which comes to our mind as we think about him. This, however, is the point: that if we wish to weigh the matter more accurately, it does not seem that it should be conceded that Samson killed himself. The reason is this: because those were not his own powers, by which he might overthrow the columns upon which the house was leaning by grasping one with his right hand and the other with his left, by the fall of which he perished. He did not do this himself, but the Spirit of the Lord, who was in him. For such a shaking of the columns is above human strength, and was not done except by divine power. God, therefore, brought about this ruin of the house and this slaughter of the Philistines through him, even though He used this instrument. Just as, therefore, it was not human but divine power that shook the house and made it collapse, so it is evident that that entire multitude, along with whom Samson was also struck down, was struck down by the divine hand: he himself only grasped the columns and wished, if it pleased God so and was not destructive to his own salvation, that his soul might die with the Philistines rather than that the Philistines should triumph over the defeated Prince of God's people against the true God of Israel. But it was God who caused the columns to be shaken and overthrown through that grasping, and the house to fall upon all the Princes and the rest of the multitude that had been gathered there, and also upon Samson himself. For Samson had invoked Him: Lord God, remember me, and restore to me now my former strength, O God, that I may avenge myself upon my enemies: (concerning which prayers see Chytræus on this passage.) Who also heard him, and because such a work could not be accomplished by human strength, He equipped him with divine power, so that the Palestinians ought to be considered as having been struck down by God rather than by Samson, even though it was done through the intervention of Samson's grasping of the columns. He did not kill himself, says Augustine in book 1 of The City of God, chapter 21, he who owes service to the one commanding, just as the sword is a tool to the one using it. Therefore, if we wish to be precise, this is not strictly suicide, but Samson fell by the divine hand: he wished for himself a glorious death with his enemies, but he did not lay hands upon himself. For God could have, with the columns demolished and the house falling upon the Philistines, if He had so willed, still preserved Samson safe and unharmed in a miraculous way, just as the Israelites were kept safe in the midst of the same waves while the Egyptians perished in the Red Sea. But It pleased divine wisdom and goodness in his death, the conqueror of enemies, to exhibit the victory of Christ's death over our enemies, and to transfer Samson, now deprived of his eyes, gloriously to a better life. St. Augustine judges that Samson was divinely commanded, not humanly deceived, and that he did not perish, but acted in obedience to what he did here; and he asserts that it is not right for us to believe otherwise about him, lib. 1. de Civ. Dei cap. 26, which we observed above, and he teaches that this killing is to be excepted from the crime of homicide c. 21. Nor, he says, is Samson otherwise excused, that he crushed himself with his enemies by the ruin of the house: except that the Spirit had secretly commanded this, who was performing miracles through him. These therefore being excepted, whom either a just Law generally, or God himself, the fountain of justice, specially commands to be killed, whoever kills a man, whether himself or anyone else, is bound by the crime of homicide. This deed is certainly attributed not obscurely to faith by the Holy Spirit himself, when Samson is numbered among those who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises Heb. 11. 31. 33. Cornelius a Lapide says that he did not properly and physically kill himself, but only permitted himself to the common ruin, nor did he even kill himself by moral imputation, because he directly intended to kill the Philistines. Cajetan compares him to a prince of an army, about to strike down enemies, who does not refuse his own death accompanying it: in which opinion Cornelius also praises Lyranus, Franciscus Victoria, Dominicus Soto, and Lessius. Osiander likewise compares him to a brave warrior fighting for the people of God against the Turks, rushing into the thickest of the enemies, even if he himself must die. Similarly B. Chytreus h. l. p. 238.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

MORIATVR ANIMA MEA CVM PHILISTIIM)

Id apud Hebræos abiit in proverbium, par isti Latino: Pereant amici dum una inimici interibunt. Hebræi autem non tantas edocti patientiæ Leges, quantas Christiani, aliquas esse mortis sibimet consciscendæ causas satis graves existimarunt, ut multis demonstratum est libro secundo de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 9. §. 5.

Falsum est, Ebræos non edoctos fuisse tantas pa- tientiæ leges quantas Christiani edocti sunt. Nam æ- que Judæis ut Christianis patientiæ præcepta com- mendata, sancteque ab illis habita sunt: Esa. 30, 15. Prov. 3, 11. c. 14, 25. c. 16, 32. c. 19, 11. Thr. 3, 31. Sir. 2, 4. 5. c. 34, 9. vide & Job. 1, 21. Jer. 10, 24. Tob. 2, 12. 2. Mac. 6, 19. Iino Christiani Ebræorum exemplo ad pa- tientiam excitantur prolixe Ebr. 11. & 12, 1. uti & exemplo Jobi Jac. 5, 11. Nullas autem causas αὐτο- φωνίας satis graves invenio loco laudato, nec quas Ebræi fideles (e quorum numero Simson fuit) satis graves crediderint. Rabbini cæcorum Duces cæci parum attendendi sunt: quorum tamen super hac quæstione sententias variasse, Grotius ipse l. c. in an- not. ad l. II. de Jure bell. ac pacis c. 19. §. 5. observa- vit. Et quænam illæ tam graves causæ esse possunt, ut quis sibi mortem ipse consciscat? Unam tantum de Lege se non interficiendi causam (non ut hic plures) Hebræos excipere §. citata dixit Grotius, si nempe quis videat se deinceps victurum in probrum ipsius Dei. Nam quia non nobis, sed Deo in vitam nostram jus esse statu- unt, existimant, præsumtam Dei voluntatem solam esse, quæ mortis anticipandæ consilium absolvat. Atque huc referunt (pergit Grotius) Samsonis exemplum, qui in suo corpore veram religionem videbat esse deri- sui, & Saulis, qui gladio incubuit, ne a Dei suisque hosti- bus illuderetur. Tertium est exemplum Razes Hiero- solymitani Senatoris, in Historia Maccabeica. Sed quis certo hoc prævidere potest, num in probrum Dei victurus sit, nec ne? Et annon Deus mille vias habet gloriam nominis sui patefaciendi, & ab op- probrio vindicandi? Non ergo facienda mala, ut eve- niant bona Rom. 3, 8. Sed Deo vita nostra, ejusque in gloriam nominis sui directio committenda. Ne- que aliter edocti Ebræi, nuspiam certe Deus hanc causam excipit. Nec exempla id probant. Raziæ enim e libro Apocrypho depromptum, etsi illic pro- betur, nihil momenti habet: Siquidem ab humano Spiritu, non divino profectus liber ille sit. Vide Gloss. ad C. Canones dist. 16. Quid mirum est, in- quit Augustinus de Raze, Ep. 61. ad Dulcit. si tan- quam homini elatio superba surrepsit, ut mallet manu propria perimi, quam post illam in suorum aspe- Etibus celsitudinem sustinere indignam in hostium ma- nibus sævitatem. Solent in literis gentilium ista lau- dari, Deus dixit, innocentem & justum ne occidas, si ergo iste innocens & justus non fuit, cur propo- nitur imitandus, si autem innocens & justus fuit, quare interfector innocentis & justi, id est, ipsius Razii insuper putetur esse laudandus? Conf. lib. II. contra Gauderit. Epist. Saulem quod attinet, impius fuit, non fidelis, & ex desperatione manus sibi intulit, non ob gloriam nominis divini. Resipuisse ipsum, postquam ei mors prædicta a spectro, fabula est Rabbi- norum. A Davide laudem fortitudinis bellicæ, non resipiscentiæ retulit, 2. Sam. 1. Et notum est, quod ira Domini Davidis tempore expiari non po- tuerit, nisi suspendio mulctatis septem viris e Saulis domo 2. Sam. 21, 6. Samsonis deniq;, exemplum pror- sus singulare est, de quo deinde. Adfert quidem Grotius etiam exempla e Christiana Historia simi- lia, eorum, qui sibi mortem intulerunt, ne tormentis ad- acti Christi religionem ejurarent: & virginum, quæ ne pudicitiam amitterent, in flumen se præcipitarunt. Sed quas Christianis causas prætexet, quos utique cre- dit longe sanctiores patientiæ Leges edoctos, quam E- bræos? Ignorantia ergo legum istarum ipsos excusa- re non potuit, per quam Ebræos excusatos voluit.

Et quia operæ pretium judicat, videre, quid de his sentiat Augustinus, cur non illi potius, quam Judæis astipulatur? Sic Augustinus l. c. Quia omnis, qui sine ulla legitime potestatis autoritate hominem occi- dit, homicida est, quisquis seipsum occidit, non sit homicida, si non homo est. Hæc omnia multis modis in aliis plurimis nostris sermonibus, & li- teris diximus. Cui adstipulatur Origenes libr. 2. in Job. Qui seipsos interficiunt, nunquam requiem habebunt, nec invenient refrigerium, sed animæ eorum mox ut corpore exierint, in tenebras deducentur. Chrysostomus de illis ad Gal. 4, 4. Nunc vero, in- quit, Deus illos acrius punit, quam homicidas, & nos eos omnes detestamur, atque id jure meritoque: Nam si alios occidere fas non est, multo magis nefas est sei- psum occidere. Concilium Aurelianens. III. ita de- cernit: Oblationes defunctorum, qui in aliquo crimine fuerunt interemti, recipi debere censemus, si tamen non ipsi sibi mortem probentur propriis manibus intulisse. Quanquam vero Augustinus libr. 1. de Civit. Dei c. 26. de sanctis fœminis, quæ persecutionis tempore, ut sectatores suæ pudicitiæ devitarent, in rapturum atque necaturum se flumen projecerunt, quia martyria ea- rum in Ecclesia Catholica veneratione celeberrima fre- quentantur, nihil temere judicare ausit, utrum hoc fecerint non humanitus deceptæ, sed divinitus jussæ, nec errantes, sed obedientes, sicut de Samsone aliud nobis fas non esse credere censet, concludit tamen hanc di- sputationem ista memorabili sententia: Hoc dicimus, hoc asserimus, hoc modis omnibus approbamus, nemi- nem spontaneam mortem sibi inferre debere, velut fu- giendo molestias temporales, ne incidat in perpetuas. Neminem propter aliena peccata, ne hoc ipso incipiat habere gravissimum proprium, quem non polluebat alie- num. Neminem propter sua peccata præterita, pro- pter quæ magis hac vita opus est, ut possint pœni- tendo sanari: Neminem velut desiderio vitæ me- lioris, quæ post mortem speratur: quia reos suæ mor- tis melior post mortem vita non suscipit. Sequen- ti capite peculiariter disquirit: an propter decli- nationem peccati mors spontanea appetenda sit? Re- stat, inquit, una causa, de qua dicere ceperam, qua utile putatur, ut si quisquam occidat se, ne in pecca- tum irruat, vel blandiente voluptate, vel dolore sæ- viente. Quam causam si voluerimus admittere, eo usq; progressa perveniet, ut hortandi sint homines, tunc se potius interimere, cum lavacro sanctæ regenerationis oblati universorum remissionem acceperint peccato- rum. Tunc enim tempus est cavendi omnia futura peccata, cum omnia sunt deleta præterita. Quod si morte spontanea recte fit, cur non tunc potissimum fit?

An vero tam insulsa perversitas cor evertit, & a consi- deratione veritatis avertit: ut si se quisquam interime- re debeat, ne minus captivitatis dominatu corruat in peccatum, vivendum sibi existimet, ut ipsum perferat mundum, per omnes horas tentationibus plenum, & ta- libus, qualis sub uno domino formidatur, & innumera- bilibus cæteris, sine quibus hæc vita non ducitur? Con- cludit denique ita: Non itaque vobis, o fideles Chri- sti, sit tædio vita vestra, si ludibrio fuit hostibus castitas vestra. Habetis magnam veramque consolationem; si fidam conscientiam retinetis, non vos consensisse pec- catis eorum, qui in vos peccare permissi sunt. Sed ca- sus ille de αὐτοχειρίᾳ, quæ pudicitiæ causa infertur, decisus aperte est Jac. 2, 10. 11. Quia qui totam le- gem servaverit, offendit autem in uno, factus est omni- um reus. Qui enim dixit, non mœchaberis, dixit e- tiam, non occides. Quod si non mœchaberis, occides autem, factus es transgressor legis. Nam utique se non licet privata potestate alicui hominem occidere, vel nocentem, ait Augustinus Libr. 1. de civit. DEI c. 17. cujus occidendi licentiam Lex nulla concedit, profecto etiam qui seipsum occidit, homicida est: Et tanto nocen- tior cum se occidit, quanto innocentior in ea causa fuit, qua se occidendum putavit.

Quod ergo ad Samsonis exemplum, de quo adhuc dicendum restat, missis nunc aliorum responsionibus, id, quod nobis de eo cogitantibus in mentem venit, exponemus. Hoc autem est, quod nempe, si rem accuratius expende- re velimus, concedendum haud videatur, Samsonem semetipsum interfecisse. Causa hæc est; quia ipsius non erant istæ vires, ut columnas, quibus inniteba- tur domus, unam dextra, alteram sinistra apprehen- dendo, prosterneret, quarum casu periit. Non ipse id fecit, sed Spiritus Domini, qui in ipso erat. Supra humanam enim fortitudinem est tanta columna- rum concussio, nec nisi divina virtute facta. Deus ergo per ipsum hanc ruinam domus, & hanc stra- gem Philistinorum fecit, utut hoc instrumento usus sit. Ut itaque domum concussit & corruere fecit, non humana sed divina virtus, ita universam illam multitudinem etiam divina manu prostratam esse, cum qua prostratus simul Simson est, constat: Ipse tantum apprehendit columnas, & optavit, si Deo ita placuerit, suæque saluti perniciosum non fuerit, anima sua moriatur cum Philistæis potius, quam ut Philistæi de devicto populi Dei Principe adversus verum Israelis Deum triumphent. Deus autem fuit, qui fecit, ut per apprehensionem illam columnæ concuteren- tur, & prosternerentur, domusque caderet super omnes Principes, & cæteram multitudinem, quæ ibi congregata fuerat, etiam super ipsum Simso- nem. Hunc enim invocarat Simson: Domine Deus memento mei, & redde mihi nunc fortitudinem pri- stinam Deus, ut ulciscar me de hostibus meis: (de qui- bus precibus vid. Chytræus in h. l.) Qui eundem etiam exaudivit, & quia humana fortitudine tan- tum opus effici non poterat, divina virtute eun- dem instruxit, ut a Deo potius prostrati Palæstini censeri debeant, quam a Simsone, etsi interventu apprehensionis columnarum Simsonis id factum. Non ipse occidit, ait Augustinus libr. 1. de Civit. Dei, cap. 21. qui ministerium debet jubenti, sicut admini- culum gladius est utenti. Non ergo, si ἀκριβολογεῖν velimus, hæc proprie ἀυτοχειρία est, sed divina ma- nu cecidit Simson: mortem sibi optavit gloriosam cum hostibus, sed ipse sibi manus non intulit. Po- tuisset enim Deus columnis dirutis, domoque in Philistæos cadente, si voluisset, Samsonem adhuc mirabili ratione salvum & incolumem præstare, uti pereuntibus in mari rubro Ægyptiis salvi con- servati sunt Israelitæ, in mediis ejusdem undis. Sed placuit divinæ sapientiæ & Bonitati in morte ejus, hostium victirce, victoriam mortis Christi de hostibus nostris exhibere, Samsonemque oculis jam orbatum ad meliorem vitam gloriose transferre. S. Augustinus Samsonem divinitus jussum, non humanitus deceptum, nec pereuntem, sed obedientem fecisse, quod hic fecit, censet; neque aliud fas esse nobis de ipso credere lib. 1. de Civ. Dei cap. 26. quod supra observavimus, asserit, eamque interfectionem ab homicidii crimine excipiendam docet c. 21. Nec Samson, inquit, aliter excusatur, quod seipsum cum hostibus ruina domus compressit: nisi quia Spiritus latenter hoc jusserat, qui per illum miracula faciebat. His igitur exceptis, quos vel Lex justa generaliter, vel ipse fons justitiæ Deus specialiter occidi jubet, quisquis hominem vel seipsum vel quemlibet occiderit, homicidii crimine innectitur. Fidei utique hoc factum haud obscure tribuitur ab ipso Spiritu Sancto, cum Samson illis accensetur, qui per fidem vicerunt regna, operati sunt justitiam, adepti sunt remissiones Ebr. 11. 31. 33. Cornel. a Lapide proprie & Physice seipsum non occidisse, sed permisisse tantum se communi ruinæ, nec etiam morali imputatione se interfecisse, ait, quia directe intendebat Philistæos occidere. Cajetanus confert eum cum Principe exercitus, hostes prostraturo, qui mortem propriam concomitante non respuit: in quam sententiam Cornelius etiam laudat Lyran. Francisc. Victor. Domin. Soto & Lessium. Osiander pariter eum componit cum forti bellatore pro populo Dei contra Turcas pugnante in consertissimos hostes irruente, etsi moriendum sibi etiam sit. Similiter B. Chytreus h. l. p. 238.

## 17:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE BOOK OF JUDGES ACTS UNDER ANARCHY. CHAPTER XVII. The idolatry of Micah, and the anarchy of the people.

verse 1.

AND THERE WAS AT THAT TIME A CERTAIN MAN FROM MOUNT EPHRAIM.

In the Hebrew those words are not present, At that time: which therefore, being rashly inserted, provided an occasion for error, as if these things happened after the death of Samson, which opinion Serarius defends q. 14. nor is Osiander alien to it. But those histories concerning the idolatry of Micah and its translation into the tribe of Dan are of earlier times, which we have in hand in the present chapter 17 and the following 18: because it is in no way likely that the tribe of Dan lacked its own possession for 300 years after the entry into the land of Canaan, as it is said to have lacked it in chapter 18, verse 1, nor could the great-grandson of Moses, Menasse, be a youth at that time, as he was such a one, whom the Danite tribe adopted as a priest c. 18, 30. Add that also those things which are related in the three last chapters, concerning the rape in the tribe of Benjamin and its destruction, and the restoration of the city of Laish, which was afterwards called Dan, are posterior to the conquest, as is manifest from c. 20, 1, which indeed it is certain happened long before Samson. Since Phinehas performed the priesthood at the time of the war instituted with the Benjaminites c. 20, 27, who was almost contemporary with Joshua. Conf. Bonfrer. and Junius on this passage. But as to the time when these things happened, opinions vary: Some of the Rabbis judge that these things happened while Joshua was still alive, but languishing from old age and not resisting the idolaters, but others refer them to the times of Caleb or those elders who lived after Joshua, to whom Junius agrees with Lyranus, Tostatus, Masius, and Ribera: but in those times the Israelites are said to have served God Jos. 24, 31. Jud. 2, 1. nor is it likely that Joshua, Caleb, or those elders would have tolerated such idolatry. The argument, which is urged, that Jerusalem is called the city of the Jebusites Jud. 19, 11, which however Caleb already conquered in chapter 18, does not hold: because even if it was conquered by him, yet a little later the Jebusites occupied it again; they certainly held the citadel; whence an overnight stay seemed less safe there. Raschi and the author of the book Seder Olam refer these things to the judgeship of Othniel, others to that of Ehud: but neither would those judges have permitted public idolatry: and therefore it is more likely that these things happened in the time of anarchy, after the death of the elders, when the Israelites acted securely: which is indicated in chapter 17, 6, in those days there was no King in Israel (there was no supreme Magistrate) but everyone did what seemed right to himself. Which opinion Ussher, Bonfrerius, and Cornelius a Lapide approve with their vote: and B. Chytreus says it is the common opinion, otherwise not denying if anyone refers it to the times of Eli, during which the Israelites were destitute of a certain Ruler. Which we judge the reasons brought forward do not permit at all: Whence the Papists cannot help their Vulgate with that interpretation, which they borrow from Lyranus, Dionysius, Carthusianus, Abulensis, and Salianus: AT THAT TIME, that is, according to the interpretation of Cornelius, when those things were done which are contained in this book of Judges. For these histories preceded the times of the Judges, which would be a tautology: or as Bonfrerius, at some time under those judges; which contradicts his own hypothesis: because he establishes that these things happened before Othniel the first Judge, indeed before the servitude under the king of Mesopotamia. The cause of which servitude he makes the idolatry introduced here among the Israelites. Which hypothesis he himself proves from Josephus, who in book 5 of Antiquities c. 2, after the death of Joshua, after the wars waged by Caleb, and the peace established by other tribes with the Canaanites, recounts this Danite expedition, and then in c. 3 describes that servitude under Chusan, king of Mesopotamia.

Latin:

PARS II. LIBRI JUDICUM ACTA SUB ANAPXIA. CAPUT XVII. Idololatria Michæ, & anarchia populi.

vers. 1.

FUITQUE EO TEMPORE VIR QUIDAM DE MONTE EPHRAIM.

IN Ebræo illa non habentur, Eo tempore: quæ proinde temere injecta errandi occasionem præbuerunt, quasi hæc post Samsonis mortem contigerint, quam sententiam propugnat Serarius q. 14. neque alienus ab ea est Osiander. Sed historiæ illæ de idololatria Michæ ejusque in tribum Dan translatione, occasione Daniticæ expeditionis anteriorum sunt temporum: quas præsenti cap. 17. & sequenti 18. præ manibus habemus: quia post Samsonis tempora adhuc caruisse possessione propria tribus Dan per 300. annos post ingressum terræ Canaan nullo modo verisimile est, ut caruisse dicitur cap. 18. versu 1. neque eo tempore pronepos Mosis Menasse juvenis esse potuit, uti talis fuit, quem tribus Danitica in Sacerdotem adoptavit c. 18, 30. Adde quod & ea, quæ tribus capp. postremis referuntur, de stupro in tribu Benjamin hujusque excidio, & restauratione urbis Lais, quæ postea Dan vocata, expugnatione posteriora esse, e cap. 20, 1. manifestum sit, quæ vero longe ante Samsonem contigisse constat. Quum functus sit tempore belli cum Benjaminatis instituti, Sacerdotio Pinehas c. 20, 27. qui fere Josuæ coævus fuit. Conf. Bonfrer. & Junius ad h. l. Quo autem tempore hæc acciderint, variant sententiæ: E Rabbinis nonnulli Josua adhuc vivente, sed præ senio languente nec idololatris obsistente hæc contigisse censent, alii autem ad Calebi aut Seniorum illorum tempora ea refe- fere runt, qui post Josuam vixerunt, quibus annuit Junius cum Lyrano, Tostato, Masio & Ribera: sed istis tem- poribus Israelitæ Deo serviisse dicuntur Jos. 24, 31. Jud. 2,1. neque verisimile est, Josuam, Calebum aut Seniores illos talem idololatriam toleraturos. Ar- gumentum, quod urget, quod Hierosolyma Jebu- sæorum dicatur Jud. 19, 11. quam vero Calebus jam expugnavit cap. 18. non stringit: quia etsi ab eo ex- pugnata sit, tamen paulo post eandem iterum occu- parunt Jebusæi; arcem certe tenuere; unde minus tuta illic videbatur pernoctatio. Raschi & autor libri Seder Olam referunt hæc ad Othonielis, alii ad E- hudi judicatum: sed nec illi judices permisissent ido- lolatriam publicam: ideoque magis verisimile est, hæc contigisse tempore ἀναρχίας, post mortem Se- niorum, quum secure agerent Israelitæ: quod indi- catur cap. 17, 6. in diebus illis non erat Rex in Israel (nullus erat Magistratus summus) sed unusquisque quod sibi rectum videbatur, hoc faciebat. Quam o- pinionem calculo suo probant Usserius, Bonfrerius, Cornelius a Lapide: eamque communem sententiam esse dicit B. Chytræus, cæteroquin non abnuens, si quis referat ad Eli tempora, quibus Israelitæ certo Rectore destituti fuere. Quod vero rationes alla- tas non permittere omnino censemus: Unde Ponti- ficii juvare non possunt Vulgatam suam, isto inter- pretamento, quod a Lyrano, Dionysio, Carthuf. Abu- lensi & Saliano mutuantur: EO TEMPORE, id est, interprete Cornelio, quo gesta sunt ea, quæ hoc li- bro Judicum continentur. Hæ enim historiæ an- tegressæ sunt Judicum tempora, quod esset ταυτο- λογικὸν: vel ut Bonfrerius, quodam sub judicibus illis tempore; quod repugnat ipsiusmet propriæ hypo- thesi: quia ante Othonielem primum Judicem, imo ante servitutem sub rege Mesopotamiæ hæc conti- gisse statuit. Cujus servitutis causam facit idolo- latriam hic inter Israelitas introductam. Quam hypothesin ipse e Josepho probat, qui l. 5. Antiqu. c. 2. post mortem Josuæ, post bella a Calebo gesta, pa- cemque ab aliis tribubus cum Cananæis firmatam, Daniticam hanc expeditionem recenseat, ac deinde c. 3. servitutem illam sub Chusan Mesopotamiæ re- ge describat.

## 17:2
V. 2. ELEVEN HUNDRED SILVER PIECES.

If, as they report is observed in the Prophetic books (see what is at ch. 9, 4), those silver pieces are understood as shekels, each of which consisted of 24, that is, about 12 Joachimics, the sum that would result is 13,200 thalers, which they call Joachimics. Certainly no small sum of silver was required for this preparation of sacred objects: for those things which were to be cast from silver, as well as for the graven images, only two hundred silver pieces were spent. The remaining sum of 900 silver pieces was applied to the priestly garment, the Ephod, and the Teraphim. That those things were not of small or meager value is apparent from the fact that a special shrine was built for it, and that by an entire tribe, in the city of Dan, and it was subsequently worshipped.

verse same. WHICH YOU HAD SET APART FOR YOURSELF.

In Hebrew: which were taken away for you, (by theft, that is) AND CONCERNING WHICH YOU HAD SWORN IN MY HEARING. In Hebrew: And you adjured (or cursed the thief) and you also spoke in my ears, that is, you cursed with imprecations in my hearing him who had stolen them; because perhaps you suspect that I took those silver pieces: I confess, my mother: BEHOLD I HAVE THEM, THEY ARE WITH ME, In Hebrew: I took them (and I now signify this to you), not that he wished to retain, but that he wished to return them to you. Thus Osiander corrects the Vulgate: and I indicated, not that the Vulgate indicated that the mother had separated this money for herself. But that most interpreters, not only the Tigurines, but also the Papists, Cajetan, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Eman. Saa, as well as the LXX Elders in the Basel and Royal Codices, acknowledge that it was taken from him by theft, but Bonfrerius disapproves of it only on the grounds that the sense of the Hebrew text is preferred to the Vulgate. But that adjuration of the mother, which Bonfrerius himself here establishes as joined with an execration, does not concern the separation or consecration of the money, which he thinks she only later revealed to her son in verse 3 as her intention for consecration, but the removal of the money, which he attributes to the son, or about which he suspects the same person knows something, and therefore he adjures him to indicate it to him or restore it. Junius and Piscator also go along with this, along with the English, Genevan, and Italian versions, with the approval of Sixtinus Amama in the Biblical Conferences. Which sense the interpreters of the New Belgian version also retain. But that אֲשֶׁר לֻקַּח־לָךְ can be conveniently rendered as 'which (silver) was received,' so that they are not implied to have been taken by theft, but specifically received from the mother and set aside; and the word אָלִית may be explained as 'you vowed with an oath or execration,' just as B. Luther correctly expressed the sense: 'which you took for yourself, and swore, and said before my ears.' For what prevents referring this to a vow and execration made in the hearing of the son, from whom, therefore, the mother not objecting, the money could have been kept for this purpose, who now reminds the mother of that vow: whence the mother blesses him on that account. For that observation does not seem rash, that the word לָקַח, whenever there is talk of a third party who takes or steals something from another, is never accustomed to be constructed with ל, but with מִן, as can be seen in Gen. 2:22, 23, Deut. 3:4, 2 Kings 2:9, 10, Is. 49:24, Jer. 29:22. And that conversely, when someone is said to take something for himself or for his own benefit, that word is always constructed with ל, never otherwise. See Gen. 6:2 & 7:20, ch. 12:19, etc. The son therefore testifies that he still has those silver pieces which he had received from his mother to be kept: 'The silver pieces which were received for you (separated or set aside), behold, they are with me, for I myself received them, in case you have forgotten that you handed them over to me to be kept, or your vow has slipped your memory.' There is therefore no reason for us to add our calculation to Grotius, who explains it thus:

UPON WHICH YOU HAD SWORN IN MY HEARING) and you cursed. The Greeks, i.e., you had devoted with curses him who had that money.

BLESSED BE MY SON BY THE LORD.

The word יהוה is wrongly understood here as an idol or a fictitious God by Corn. a Lap. and Bonfrerius, for whom that statue and silver image was being prepared: because this name is attributed to no one but the true GOD; nor was this worship exhibited by Micah to any other fictitious God, of which there is no trace in the sacred texts, or even by the tribe of Dan, to which it was transferred, but to the Lord himself, whose ministers the Levites were, and from whom Micah hoped for a blessing, v. 18. But it was idolatrous in that respect, because God was not worshipped in the divine manner prescribed by God, but by elective worship through an idol, just as the Israelites worshipping God through the golden calf are accused of idolatry, with the Papists denying it in vain, lest the idolatry of the Roman Church shine through.

Latin:

V. 2. MILLE ET CENTUM ARGENTEOS.

Si, quod in libris Propheticis observari tra- dunt, (vid. quæ ad c. 9, 4.) illi argentei intelligantur de libris, quarum quælibet 24. Siclis, hoc est, 12. Joa- chimicis circiter constabat, summa proditura 13200. thalerorum, quos Joachimicos vocant. Non utiq; parva requirebatur summa argenti ad hunc appa- ratum Sacrorum: ad ea, quæ ex argento fundenda erant, ut & ad sculptilia ducenti argentei solum sunt imspensi. Reliqua summa 900. argenteorum ad vestem Sacerdotalem Ephod & Teraphim adhibita. Non exigui aut exilis pretii fuisse illa, inde apparet, quod peculiare ei fanum sit constructum idq; a tri- bu integra, in civitate Dan, cultum deinde fuerit.

vers. eod. QUOS SEPARAVERAT TIBI.

In Ebræo: qui ablati sunt tibi, (furto sc.) ET SUPER QUIBUS ME AUDIENTE JURAVE- RAS. In Ebr. Et tu adjurasti (seu execrata es furem) & loquuta es etiam in auribus meis, id est, me audien- te diris devovisti eum, qui surripuisset; quod forte susspicaris, me abstulisse eos argenteos: fateor mea mater: ECCE EGO HABEO, APUD ME SUNT, In Ebr. Ego abstuli eos (idq; nunc tibi significo,) non quod retinere, sed quod reddere eos tibi cupiam Ita Osiander Vulgatam corrigit: & significavi, non quod vulgata, indicavit, quod mater separarit sib banc pecuniam. Sed quod furto ipsi ablata fuerit plerosque interpp. velle,non Tigurinos solum, sea etiam Pontificios, Cajetanum, Pagninum, Ariamon tanum, Eman. Saa, ut & LXX. Seniores in Codice Basiliensi, & Regio agnoscit Bonfrerius, sed eo solum nomine improbat, quod præferatur sensus textus Ebræi Vulgatæ. At adjuratio illa matris quam cum execratione conjunctam hic statuit ipse Bonfrerius, non respicit separationem, aut consecra- tionem pecuniæ, quam consecrationis intentionem suam deinceps demum aperuisse filio versu 3. pu- tat, sed ablationem pecuniæ, quam filio tribuit, aut de qua eidem aliquid constare suspicatur, ideoque adjurat ipsum, ut sibi indicet, vel restituat. Quo abit etiam Junius, Piscator cum Anglicana, Genevens & Italica versione, approbante Sixtin. Amama in Biblic. Confer. Quem sensum retinere quoque Interpp. Novi Belgici. Sed illud אֲשֶׁר לֻקַּח־לָךְ commode reddi potest qui (argentei) accepti,ut non ablati per furtum innuantur, sed peculiariter acce- pti a matre,ac sepositi,& verbum אָלִית explicare licet, vovisti cum juramento, vel execratione, uti sen- sum recte expressit B. Lutherus, die du zu dir genom- men hast,und geschworen, und gesagt für meinen Oh- ren. Quid enim vetat referre hoc ad votum & ex- ecrationem factam, filio audiente, a quo proinde, matre non abnuente, in hanc rem pecunia asservari potuit, qui nunc matrem de voto isto commonefa- cit: unde ipsi eo nomine benedicit mater. Non enim temeraria videtur illa observatio, quod ver- bum לָקַח quoties sermo est de tertio quopiam,qui alteri rem aufert, vel furatur, nunquam cum construi soleat, sed cum מִן ut videre est Gen. 2, 22. 23. Deut.3,4. 2.Reg.2,9. 10. Es. 49, 24. Jer. 29, 22. & quod vice versa, cum aliquid sibi vel in suam utili- tatem quispiam accipere dicitur, semper illud ver- bum cum ל construatur,nunquam aliter. Vid. Gen. 6,2. & 7,20. c. 12,19 &c. Testatur ergo filius se ha- bere adhuc illos argenteos, quos acceperat a matre asservandos: Argenteos, qui accepti tibi sunt (separa- ti vel sepositi) ecce apud me sunt, accepi enim eos ipse, si forte oblita es, quod mihi tradideris asservandos, aut excidit memoria votum tuum. Non ergo est, quod calculum adjiciamus Grotio ita explicanti:

SVPER QVIBVS ME AVDIENTE JVRAVERAS) καὶ υε ἠράσω. Græci,i. e. diris devoveras eum, qui pecuniam il- lam haberet.

BENEDICTUS FILIUS MEUS DOMINO.

Perperam per vocem יהוה hic idolum vel fictitius Deus intelligitur a Corn. a Lap. & Bonfrer. cui statua illa & simulacrum argenteum parabatur: quia nomen hoc nulli nisi vero DEO tribuitur; ne- que cultus hic alii fictitio Deo a Micha exhibitus est, de quo nullum vestigium est in sacris, aut etiam a tribu Dan, ad quam is translatus est, sed ipsi Do- mino,cujus ministri Levitæ erant, & a quo benedi- ctiouem sperabat Mich. v. 18. qui vero idololatricus eo nomine erat, quod Deus non coleretur divino modo a Deo præscripto, sed cultu electitio per ido- lum,quemadmodum in vitulo aureo IsraelitæDeum colentes idololatriæ arguuntur, nequicquam id in- ficiantibus Papistis, ne transpareat Idololatria Ec- clesiæ Romanæ.

## 17:3
Ver. 3. HE THEREFORE RETURNED THEM TO HIS MOTHER.

Who had devoted them with an execration to sacred worship, so that she might fulfill her vow: as is added, what she had promised in his hearing: WHICH SHE HAD SAID TO HIM (the pluperfect is correctly used) 'I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord, so that my son may receive it from my hand and make a graven and a molten image: and now I hand it over to you': so that you may keep it for that purpose.
