Thus she had said before in his hearing. Therefore it is added again, so that the sense might be clearer, v. 4. HE THEREFORE RETURNED THEM TO HIS MOTHER. Sc. just as she had given them to him to be kept. Pope Sixtus had omitted that sentence, 'He therefore returned them to his mother, who had said to him, I have consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord,' which Clement therefore deservedly restored from the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek, according to the Louvain edition.

Latin:

Vers. 3. REDDIDIT ERGO EOS MATRI SUÆ.

Quæ cum execratione eos devoverat cultui sacro, ut votum suum exolvat: uti additur, quod se audiente ipsa promiserat: QUÆ DIXERAT EI (recte adhibitum est plusquamperfectum) consecra- vi & vovi hoc argentum Domino, ut de manu mea susci- piat filius meus & faciat sculptile, atque conflatile: & nunc trado illud tibi: ut nempe in eum finem asserves. Ita illa ipso audiente antea dixerat. Ideo additur denuo, ut sensus luculentior esset, v. 4. REDDIDIT ERGO EOS MATRI SUÆ. Sc. quemadmodum ipsi asservandos dederat eosdem. Sixtus Pontifex omiserat sententiam illam, Reddidit ergo eos matri suæ, quæ dixerat ei consecravi & vovi hoc argentum Domino, quam proinde merito Clemens ex Ebr. Chald. & Græc. secundum Lovan. edit. restituit.

## 17:4
V. 4. SO THAT HE MIGHT MAKE FROM THEM A GRAVEN AND A MOLTEN IMAGE.

That these two were different, both the words themselves teach, פסל a graven image and ומסכה a molten image: and especially it is clear from ch. 12:17, where these are openly distinguished with the others interposed, which were prepared for the idolatry itself, 'and they took the graven image and the Ephod and the Teraphim and the molten image.' Therefore Abulensis did not correctly consider them as one and the same idol. For the fact that it is said in the singular, that it was in the house of Micah, proves nothing; because various things were used for the same worship: although the Hebrew יורו can also be taken distributively, and 'each of them was in the house of Micah.' Therefore Serarius, Bonfrerius, Cornelius, and others make these different; for a molten image is one thing, which is made by the founder's work, and a graven image is another, which is made by chisel and incision. Grotius understands by graven and molten images altars, a candlestick, and other things of that kind, which pertained to private worship by imitation of those things which were prepared in the tabernacle: and he thinks the idol was designated only by the word Teraphim, as will appear in v. 5.

Latin:

V. 4. UT FACERET EX EIS SCULPTILE, ATQUE CONFLATILE.

Duo hæc diversa fuisse cum verba ipsa docent פסל sculptile & ומסכה conflatile: tum impri- mis e c. 12, 17. luculentum est, ubi hæc aperte distin- guuntur interpositis reliquis, quæ ad idololatriam ipsam parata erant, & ceperunt sculptile & Ephod & Teraphim & conflatile. Non ergo recte Abulensis illa pro uno & eodem idolo habuit. Quod enim in singulari dicitur, quod fuit in domo Michæ, nihil pro- bat; quia ad eundem cultum varia adhibita sunt: quamvis etiam Ebræum יורו distributive accipi pos- sit, & fuit unumquodque eorum in domo Michæ. Ideo Serarius, Bonfrerius, Cornelius, aliique hæc di- versa faciunt; aliud enim est conflatile, quod sufo- rio opere fit, aliud sculptile, quod cælo & incisione fit. Grotius per sculptilia & fictilia intelligit altaria, Can- delabrum & alia ejusmodi, quæ ad privatum cultum per imitationem eorum, quæ in tabernaculo parata erant, spectarint: & idolum voce Teraphim solum designatum censet, ut v. 5. apparebit.

## 17:5
V. 5. AND HE MADE AN EPHOD.

Concerning the Priestly Ephod, this word is first taken as the Pontifical Ephod described in Ex. 28, 6, and that Micah wished to imitate it, that worship which he instituted out of ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ (will-worship), sufficiently teaches.

AND TERAPHIM) μορφώματα (images), which Jerome considers to have had the form of Cherubim in his letter to Marcella and 1 Sam. 22, and 2 Sam. 6, 14, how it also seems to be understood in Hosea 3, v. 4. For it is a neutral word pertaining to both good and bad images. If we follow this interpretation, we shall say that these Teraphim are called below אלהים, that is, angels, because they signified angels. But the graven and molten images were altars, a candlestick, and other small things of that kind, in place of the great ones which were in the sanctuary, just as Torquatus built elegant baths of Parian marble, and Otacilius made a cooking pot.

Thus Grotius understands Teraphim only as idols: but graven and molten images as other things pertaining to the apparatus of worship: whence 13,200 thalers could easily be spent on them: from which sum perhaps something was also spent on the small shrine or the construction of the temple: just as B. Chytreus thinks 900 silver pieces were spent not only on the building of the small shrine, and on sacred furniture, priestly vestments and ornaments, but also on the foundation of a benefice or the annual stipend of a priest. Nor does that interpretation seem inappropriate, since the Ephod is also distinctly mentioned: but because in the following chapter, verses 30 and 31, a graven image is spoken of as an idol, even with the demonstrative He, it cannot be denied that an idol is also indicated here by that word, or at least included, since that word and idol, graven image, and whatever else was prepared for that worship by the sculptor's art in this place can be embraced generally. As for the Teraphim, they are translated as idols for the most part by Jerome in Gen. 31, verses 19, 34, 35; Ezek. 21, verse 21; or as images in Zech. 10, verse 2; or as figures of idols in 2 Kings 23, 24, etc. Just as Jerome has his own conjecture about the Cherubic form of them, so others report that they had the image of a human form. Elias in Thisbi notes that Teraphim were accustomed to be made by the slaughter of a firstborn man, whose head they would sever and preserve with salt and aromatics, placing under it a golden plate upon which the name of an unclean spirit was inscribed, which, placing it on a wall, they would light candles before it and worship before it, and that Laban spoke with such things in Gen. 31, 19, such as are likewise read in the Chaldean paraphrase of Ben Uziel. But those are undoubtedly fabulous. They are rightly called μορφώματα [forms]: by Josephus τύποι τῶν θεῶν [types of the gods], by Onkelos צלמנייא [images] figures or effigies: which Aben Ezra also says were made in human form, so that they might be capable of celestial influence, which form is gathered from 1 Sam. 19, when Michal, his wife, placed the Teraphim in the bed in place of David. Grotius observes on Gen. 31, 19 that those images were adorned for a certain position of the stars with the figures of the stars according to the ancient superstition of the Syrians and Arabs. With which agree those things which Selden, Syntagm. 1. de Dis Syris [on the Syrian Gods] chap. 2, page 103, has, that both the στοιχεῖα [elements], as they called them, and the Teraphim were accustomed to be formed according to certain positions of the stars, and according to figures believed to be in the heavens, of which the former were used for warding off evils, as ἀλεξήτηριοι [averting] or Averrunci Gods, the latter for predicting future events, as oracles: and what R. Moses the Egyptian handed down in More Nebuch. book 3, c. 30: They built palaces, and placed images in them and said that the splendor of the powers of the stars was diffused over those images and they spoke with men and announced useful things to them. Concerning which it is helpful to add these things also from Selden: Closer, he says on page 107, to the nature of the Teraphim approach images which were thought not only to be from the position of the stars, but also ἀπὸ τῶν προσεγγίσεων [from the approaches] of demons, both to render oracles and to ward off evils. But demons are said to make Προσ- εγγίσεις [approaches] to Michael Psellus, when, having been invoked, they enter images dedicated to themselves. To which opinion he brought forward some things from Hermes Trismegistus in the Asclepius, that the gods made from the likeness of a human face were animated statues, full of sense and spirit, i.e., a demon, or angel, prescient of future things, causing weaknesses to men and curing them: and from Iamblichus, against whom John Philoponus wrote a book about the same, that they were ἀγάλματα θείας μετουσίας ἀνάπλεα [statues full of divine participation], images full of divine fellowship or of demons, whom they called by name with sacred rites duly performed for that purpose. The same is the Talisman, or Talismath of the Arabs, which are the στοιχεῖα [elements], the same Selden observes in the same place, p. 116, and treats at length of the Talfemis, and Hottinger proves this, Hist. Orient. book 1, c. 8, p. 196, that the Tilsema of the Arabs or Sabaeans, which indeed were for the most part Averrunci Gods, to which however they also attributed the office of χρηματισμῶν [oracles] or oracles, are the Teraphim of the Hebrews, observing from Maimonides that the heresy of the Sabaeans was most prevalent in the time of Abraham, whom he reports from Keffaeus to boast of the religion and books of Seth, Enoch, and Noah, and even the book of Adam, and assigns this as their chief article of faith, that the stars are gods, but the sun is the greatest God. But it is not probable that such impiety clung to Laban the Syrian, although an idolater, with whom St. Jacob stayed for 20 years; much less is such a thing to be presumed about Micah, who wished to serve Jehovah the one GOD in these images: which Grotius acknowledges in this place at v. 5: and therefore we do not deny his opinion, that the word Teraphim was a middle term, pertaining to both good and bad images, which the passage Hos. 3, 4 seems to confirm, where the LXX. interpreters translate that word by Δήλες [manifestations]. By which word Urim is also called by them in 1 Sam. 28, which they translated by δήλωσιν [manifestation] in the same sense in Exod. 28. Aquila sometimes translates this word Teraphim by Φωτισμὺς [illuminations]. Whence it is very credible that Micah wished to imitate or shadow forth the Urim and Thummim by the making of the Teraphim, and to construct those images, whatever form they had, which might have a similar use, namely of predicting hidden things, and be in the place of oracles, for which use they are also taught to have been employed in the Danite expedition, c. 18, v. 6. Compare Zech. 10, 2; Ez. 21, 21. Whence also the most learned Selden warns on page 97, who however does not deserve assent in this, that he judges Micah to have mixed the worship of the true God and of idols or Demons here: so that he consecrated the Ephod and the Levite to the true God, and the molten and graven image to the demons: and that Micah established that the graven and molten image were gods, to which he consecrated the Teraphim, which however, because of their excellent use in divination, were themselves also held as gods. Micah committed idolatry entirely, but by reason of the mode, not the object: he did not believe that either the graven or molten image was God, nor did he hold the Teraphim for God, but in the graven and molten image he worshipped and adored God through forbidden idolatry, and through the Teraphim he consulted God, not otherwise than he was consulted through the Urim and Thummim by divine institution. Which will-worship of his was true idolatry. Among the Jews themselves there was a controversy about it, as R. Simeon Ben Jochai reports in the book Zohar, whether they were accustomed to worship them as gods, or whether they held them only as instruments of divination? And although it may easily be granted concerning Laban the Syrian, and other idolatrous nations, that they held their Teraphim even as gods, Gen. 31, 19; Ezek. 21, 21; 1 Sam. 15, 23; 2 Sam. 23, 24, yet this is not to be asserted of Micah, or the Israelites, who, for the sake of oracles, used them only in place of Urim and Thummim, in which, however, it is certain that they sinned, and committed idolatry, by reason of the mode of worshipping God and of eliciting divine responses, since even the true God is not to be worshipped otherwise than as He has prescribed in His word. That no idol is understood by the name Teraphim in Hos. 3, 4. But Chytraeus on Judges 17:5 asserts that the oracles and responses, which were sought through Urim and Thummim, are so called καταχρηστικῶς (improperly); and he thinks it is manifest from that, that the Teraphim are referred to oracles and responses.

Nor indeed are angels to be understood by אלהים in chapter 18:5, whom the Danites did not wish to consult at that time, and from whom they themselves did not seek a response; but just as they desired to be made certain by God himself concerning the success of the expedition, so they hoped that through the Levite, by the benefit of the Teraphim adorned like an oracle in the likeness of Urim and Thummim, they would obtain the mind and response of GOD. Therefore, what Grotius says is not to be admitted, that the Teraphim are called Elohim, that is, angels, because they signified angels, but that through the Teraphim they were inquiring of Elohim, that is, the true God. And how did the Teraphim signify angels? Was it because angels were present to them in the mind of the Danites, or of Micah, as if to return a response concerning those things which were being sought: or because they represented the angelic images of the Cherubim? Grotius seems to intend the former here, but he is inconsistent with himself. For to those words, 'and he became his priest,' [he argues that he] worshipped the true God (not angels), and maintains that the answer was given there by God (not by angels).

AND HE FILLED THE HAND OF ONE OF HIS SONS.

He consecrated one of his sons as priest: a phrase which, according to some, arose from the fact that the hands of the Aaronic priests were accustomed to be anointed and filled with oil: but such as this consecration is, such also is the priest, that is to say, clearly ἄνομος.

Verse same. AND HE BECAME A PRIEST TO HIM) Doubtless because the priests were not publicly performing their office, through fault or because the places were infested with robbers, Micah thought that God should be worshipped by him with a private religion, and therefore when he had wished his first son to be a priest for him, he soon preferred the Levite he had found to him, so that he might approach as closely as possible to the statutes of the law. For he was worshipping the true God יהוה, here 3, and 13. 18, 5. And God answers the one consulting Him with true things. Below 18.

Latin:

V. 5. ET FECIT EPHOD.

De Sacerdotali Ephod πρώτως hæc vox acci- pitur & Ephodem Pontificalem Ex. 28, 6. descri- ptum imitari voluisse Micham, cultus ille, quem ex ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ instituit, satis docet.

ET TERAPHIM) μορφώματα, quæ Cherubinorum ha- buisse formam censet Hieronymus ad Marcellam & 1. Sam. 22, & 2. Sam, 6, 14. quomodo accipiendum etiam videtur Oseæ 3. v. 4. Est enim vox media ad bonas malasque ima- gines pertinens. Hanc interpretationem si sequimur, hæc Teraphim dicemus infra vocari אלהים id est angelos, quia Angelos significabant. Sculptilia autem & fictilia erant altaria, candelabrum, aliaque ejusmodi minuta, vice magnorum quæ erant in sanctuario, sicut Torquatus nitidas Pario de marmore thermas Exstruxit, cucumam fecit Otacilius.

Sic Teraphim tantum de Idolis intelligit Gro- tius: Scuptilia vero & futilia de aliis ad cultus appa- ratum spectantibus: unde facile 13200. thaleri im- pendi ad ea potuere: e qua summa forsan etiam ad ædicula vel fani exstructionem aliquid impensum: quemadmodum B. Chytreus 900. argenteos non ad ædificationem tantum ædiculæ, & ad supellectilem sacram, vestes & ornamenta Sacerdotalia, sed etiam ad fundationem beneficii seu stipendium sacrificuli annuum impensos existimat. Neque inconcin- na videtur illa interpretatio, quum & Ephod di- stincte commemoretur: sed quia cap. seq. vers. 30. & 31. sculptile de Idolo dicitur, etiam cum He de- monstrativo, non negandum, ea voce etiam ido- lum hic indigitari, aut certe simul comprehendi, quum vox ea & idolum, sculptile, & quæ præterea ad cultum illum arte sculptoria parata sunt hoc loco generaliter complecti possit. Quod ad Teraphim, idola vertuntur plerumque ab Hieronymo Gen. 31. versu 19. 34. 35. Ezech. 21. versu 21. aut simulacra Zach. 10. vers. 2. aut figuræ idolorum 2. Reg. 23, 24. &c. Uti de forma Cherubina eorum Hieronymus suam conjecturam habet : ita humanæ formæ imaginem habuisse eosdem, alii referunt. Elias in Thisbi Teraphim fieri consuevisse notat, mactatione ho- minis primigeniti, cujus caput discerpserint & sale ac aromatibus condierint, lamina aurea, cui inscri- ptum nomen Spiritus immundi, eidem supposita, quod in pariete ponentes incenderint coram eo candelas & adorarint coram eo, & cum istiusmodi Labanum lo- quutum fuisse Gen. 31, 19. qualia in paraphr. Chald. Ben Uziel itidem leguntur. Sed illa fabulosa sine dubio sunt. Recte μορφώματα dicuntur : Jose- pho τύποι τῶν θεῶν, Onkeloso צלמנייא figuræ vel effigies : quas etiam Aben Ezra humana forma factas ait, ut cœlestis influentiæ capaces essent, qua- lis forma colligitur e 1. Sam. 19. quum Teraphim loco Davidis in lecto posuerit Michal, uxor ejus- dem. Imagines illas ad certum stellarum posi- tum cum stellarum figuris ex veteri Syrorum & Arabum superstitione adornatas observat Grotius ad Gen. 31, 19. Quibus congruunt ea, quæ Selde- nus Syntagm. 1. de Dis Syris cap. 2. pag. 103. habet, quod & στοιχεῖα, quæ vocarunt, & Teraphim forma- ri consueverint ad certos Syderum positus, & secun- dum figuras in cœlo creditas, quorum illa malis ar- cendis, ceu ἀλεξήτηριοι vel Averrunci Dii, hæc fu- turis prædicendis, ceu oracula adhibita: & quæ R. Moses Ægyptius in More Nebuch. lib. 3. c. 30. tradi- dit: Ædificarunt palatia, & posuerunt in eis imagi- nes & dixerunt, quod splendor potentiarum stellarum diffundebatur super illas imagines & loquebantur cum hominibus & annunciabant eis utilia. De quibus etiam hæc e Seldeno addere juvat : Propius, inquit pag. 107: ad τῶν Teraphim naturam accedunt ima- gines, quæ non solum a Syderum positura, verum eti- am ἀπὸ τῶν προσεγγίσεων dæmoniorum, & oracula reddere, & mala depellere simul putabantur. Προσ- εγγίσεις vero ποιήσασθαι dicuntur dæmones Mi- chaeli Pselli, cum invocati simulacra sibi dicata ingre- diantur. In quam sententiam nonnulla ex Her- mete Trismegisto in Asclepio adduxit, quod Dii fa- cti ex humani vultus similitudine statuæ fuerint ani- matæ, sensu & spiritu plenæ, h. e. dæmone, sive angelo, futurorum præscie, imbecillitates hominibus facientes, easque curantes : & e Jamblicho, contra quem de iis- dem librum conscripsit Joh. Philoponus, quod fue- rint ἀγάλματα θείας μετουσίας ἀνάπλεα, simula- cra plena consortio divino vel dæmonum, quos nomine ciebant sacris ad eam rem rite peractis. Eadem esse Ta- lisman, vel Talismath Arabum, quæ στοιχεῖα, observat idem Seldenus l. c. p. 116. & prolixe de Talfemis a- git, idque probat Hottingerus, Hist. Orient. l. 1. c. 8. p. 196. quod Tilsemæ Arabum vel Sabæorum, quæ ut plurimum quidem Dii Averrunci fuerint, quibus tamen etiam χρηματισμῶν vel oraculorum officium tribue- rint, Ebræorum Teraphim sint, Sabæorum hæresin Ab- rahami tempore maxime invaluisse ex Maimonide ob- servans, quos Sethi, Enoch, & Noachi religionem & libros, imo etiam codicem Adami jactitare ex Keffæo refert, eorumque hoc præcipuum fidei caput assignat, quod stellæ Dii sint, sol autem Deus maximus. Sed eam impietatem Labani Syro, etsi idololatræ, cui per 20. annos adfuit S. Jacob hæsisse non est verisi- mile ; multo minus tale quid de Micha præsumen- dum, qui Jehovæ uni DEO in his imaginibus servire voluit : quod hoc loco ad v. 5. agnoscit Grotius : ideoque non abnuimus ejusdem senten- tiæ, quod vox Teraphim media fuerit, ad bonas ma- lasque imagines pertinens, quam locus Of. 3, 4. con- firmare videtur, ubi LXX. Interpp. per Δήλες eam vocem interpretantur. Quo vocabulo Urim e- tiam ab illis appellatur 1. Sam. 28. quod per δήλωσιν fenfu eodem Exod. 28. transtulerunt. Aquila vo- cem hanc Teraphim per Φωτισμὺς interdum in- terpretatur. Unde credibile admodum, quod Mi- cha τῶν Teraphim fabricatione Urim ac Thummim imitari vel adumbrare voluerit, easque imagines quamcunque formam habuerint, construere, quæ similem usum habeant, prædicendi nempe occulta, & oraculorum vice essent, in quem usum etiam in Danitica expeditione easdem adhibitas esse c. 18. v. 6. docetur. Conf. Zach. 10, 2. Ez. 21, 21. Unde etiam ipsos Teraphim pro Diis habitos monet doctiss. Sel- denus pag. 97. qui tamen in eo assensum non me- retur, quod cultum Dei veri & idolorum seu Dæ- moniorum hic Micham miscuisse censet: ita ut E- phod & Levitam Deo vero & conflatile & sculptile dæ- moniis sacrarit: quodque sculptile & conflatile Deos fuisse Micha statuit, queis Teraphim sacraverit, qui ta- men ob egregium in divinatione usum etiam ipsi, ut Dii habiti sint. Idololatriam omnino commisit Mi- cha, sed ratione modi, non objecti: non credidit, seu sculptile seu conflatile Deum esse, neque Te- raphim pro Deo habuit, sed in sculptili, & confla- tili Deum per idololatriam prohibitam, coluit & adoravit, & per Teraphim Deum consuluit, non secus atque per Urim & Thummim consulebatur ex institutione divina. Quæ ἐθελοθρησκεία ipsius vera erat idololatria. Inter Judæos ipsos de eo controversia fuit, referente R. Simeone Ben Jo- chai in libro Zohar, utrum ut Deos colere consueve- rint, an vero tantum pro divinationis instrumentis habuerint? Et quanquam de Labane Syro, aliisque idololatris gentibus id facile dari possit, quod illi Teraphim suos pro Diis etiam habuerint Gen. 31, 19. Ezech. 21, 21. 1. Sam. 15, 23. 2. Sam. 23, 24. non tamen de Micha, aut Israelitis id afferendum, qui, oraculorum causa, loco Urim & Thummim eosdem solum adhibuere, in quo tamen eosdem peccasse, & idololatriam, ratione modi colendi Deum, & divi- na suscitandi responsa commisisse, certum est, quum verus etiam Deus aliter colendus non sit, quam prout in verbo suo id præscripsit. Non intelligi idolum aliquod nomine Teraphim Hos. 3, 4. Sed oracula & responsa, quæ per Urim & Thummim ca- ptabantur, καταχρηστικῶς ita dici Chytraus ad Jud. 17, 5. asserit: atque inde manifestum esse putat The- raphim ad oracula & responsa referri.

Nec vero per אלהים cap. 18, 5. angeli in- telligendi sunt, quos tum interrogare nolebant Danitæ, a quibus etiam ipsi responsum non expe- tebant; sed ut a Deo ipso certiores reddi deside- rabant de successu expeditionis, ita per Levitam beneficio τῶν Teraphim ceu oraculi ad instar U- rim & Thummim adornati se mentem, & respon- sum DEI adepturos sperabant. Non ergo ad- mittendum est, quod dicit Grotius, Teraphim vocari Elohim, id est, angelos, quia angelos signifi- cabant, sed per Teraphim sciscitabantur Elohim, hoc est, verum Deum. Et quomodo Teraphim significabant angelos? an quod adessent ipsis angeli ex mente Danitarum, aut Michæ, velu- ti responsum reddituri de his, quæ quære- bantur: an quod angelicas imagines τῶν Che- rubim referebant? prius hic utique intende- re videtur Grotius, sed sibi ipsi adversus est. Nam ad verba illa, & factus est ei Sacer- dos, verum Deum (non angelos) coluisse, & a Deo (non Angelis) responsum ibi redditum esse statuit.

IMPLEVITQUE UNIUS FILIORUM SUO- RUM MANUM.

Consecravit unum ex filiis suis in sacerdotem: quae phrasis inde juxta quosdam orta, quod solerent sacerdotum Aaronicorum manus inungi, & oleo im- pleri: sed qualis haec consecratio, talis etiam sacer- dos, hoc est plane ἄνομος.

Vers. eod. ET FACTUS EST EI SACERDOS) Nimirum quia publice Sacerdotes officio non fungebantur, per culpam aut loca infesta latrociniis, existimavit Michas vel privata reli- gione Deum sibi colendum, ideoque cum primum filium su- um voluisset sibi esse sacerdotem, mox repertum Levitam ei praetulit, ut quam proxime ad legis constituta accederet. Co- lebat enim verum Deum יהוה, hic 3, & 13. 18, 5. Et Deus consulenti vera respondet. Infra 18.

## 17:6
Verse 6. IN THOSE DAYS THERE WAS NO KING IN ISRAEL) After the death of Samson. The word king is taken here more broadly so as to include also a Judge or Dictator, as in Gen. 33, 5. and below at the end of this book.

Which is also repeated in ch. 18, 1. and at the end. The name of King, however, is taken here more generally, so that the times of the Judges might also be included: Compare Gen. 36, 31. Deut. 33, 35. Grotius thinks these things happened after the death of Samson; but we have advised what is to be thought about that at verse 1.

Latin:

Vers. 6. IN DIEBUS ILLIS NON ERAT REX IN ISRAEL) Post Samsonis mortem. Vox regis hic latius sumta ut & Judicem sive Dictatorem comprehendat, ut Gen. 33, 5. & infra fine hujus libri.

Quod etiam repetitur c. 18, 1. & ult. Nomen Regis autem generalius hic accipitur, ut Judicum e- tiam tempora comprehendantur: Conf. Gen. 36, 31. Deut. 33. 35. Post Samsonis mortem haec contigisse Grotius putat; sed quid de eo habendum ad v. 1. monuimus.

## 17:7
Verse 7. OF HIS KIN) In the Hebrew: of the family of Judah, which can be referred to the designation of Bethlehem: for there was also another town by that name.

It is so: It pertains to the periphrasis of the city, not of the person, as is clear from verse 9. For this person was of the tribe of Levi. But that (Bethlehem) belonged to the family of Judah, and is described in such a way that it may be distinguished from the Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun, Jos. 19, 15. Therefore the Vulgate version is to be corrected here: as also in the following word: AND HE DWELT THERE, for in the authentic text it is, and he had sojourned there. It appears, however, from the text that this Levite, compelled by hunger, had sought another place of dwelling: if the tithes had been lawfully given, he would have had no reason why he should change his seat.

Latin:

Vers. 7. EX COGNATIONE EJUS) In Hebraeo: de familia Juda, quod referri potest ad denotationem Bethle- hem: nam erat & aliud oppidum eo nomine.

Ita est: Ad urbis περίφρασιν pertinet, non per- sonae, ut e v. 9. liquet. Haec enim de tribu Levi e- rat. Illa autem (Bethlehem) ad familiam Judae per- tinebat, & ita describitur, ut a Bethlehem in tribu Sebulon Jos. 19, 15. distinguatur. Emendanda ergo hic Vulgata versio: ut & in verbo sequenti: ET HA- BITABAT IBI, in textu enim authentico est, & peregrinatus fuerat ibi. Apparet autem e textu hunc Levitam fame compulsum quaesivisse alium habitandi locum: si decimae legitime fuissent datae, nullam habuisset causam, cur sedem mutaret.

## 17:10
Verse 10. AND I WILL GIVE THEE BY THE YEAR TEN SILVER PIECES.

If a silver pound is understood, it will be an annual salary of 120 thalers: but ten shekels make only five thalers, which would have been too meager a stipend.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DABOQUE TIBI PER SINGULOS ANNOS DECEM ARGENTEOS.

Si libra argentea intelligatur, 120. thalerorum annuum salarium erit: Decem autem sicli non nisi quinque thaleros efficiunt, quod nimis exiguum fu- isset stipendium.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

The tribe of Dan seeks a possession for itself. It takes away the idol of Micah. It occupies the city of Laish.

Ver. 1. AND THE TRIBE OF DAN WAS SEEKING POSSESSIONS FOR ITSELF) It had not been able to snatch from the Canaanite the lot which Joshua had assigned to it. Joshua 19, 40.

The matter stands entirely thus: It had indeed been assigned to it, Jos. 19, 40, but on account of the Philistines and Amorites they had not been able to occupy it fully until now. Conf. 6. 1, 34.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

Tribus Dan quaerit sibi possessionem. Aufert Michae idolum. Urbem Lais occupat.

Vers. 1. ET TRIBUS DAN QUAEREBAT POSSES- SIONES SIBI) Non potuerat eripere Cananaeo sortem, quam Josua ipsi assignaverat. Josue 19, 40.

Ita omnino res habet: Assignata quidem ei e- rat Jos. 19, 40. sed ob Philistaeos & Amorrhaeos hacte- nus eam plene occupare non poterant. Conf. 6. 1, 34.

## 18:6
Ver. 6. GO IN PEACE, THE LORD LOOKS UPON YOUR WAY.

This response was given through the priest Micah: For since this man was a Levite, had an Ephod, and was giving responses through Teraphim, as if they were Urim and Thummim, they believed they were duly inquiring of the Lord. Although the outcome indeed corresponded to this response, it was by no means to be considered a divine oracle. For Satan also sometimes foresees future events according to his own sagacity, and thus confirms men in their superstition and idolatry.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ITE IN PACE, DOMINUS RESPI- CIT VIAM VESTRAM.

Per sacerdotem Micham reddita est haec re- sponsio: Quum enim hic Levita esset, Ephod ha- beret, ac per Teraphim, quasi Urim & Thumim re- sponsa redderet, Dominum se rite interrogare cre- debant. Quanquam vero responsio huic eventus respondit, minime tamen fuit pro oraculo divino id habendum. Nam & Satanas quandoque futura pro sagacitate sua praevidet, hominesque ita in sua su- perstitione, & idololatria confirmat.

## 18:7
Ver. 7. THEY CAME TO LAISH) It seems to have been a colony of the Sidonians: But far removed from Sidon, joined by treaty to none of its neighbors, wonderfully secure, and rich, all of which are incentives to enemies.

Which history is also related in Jos. 19, 47: but by anticipation: because it was done a long time after Joshua: whence it seems likely that the history of Joshua was recorded not by Joshua, but by a more recent author, and as is believed, by Samuel. For that city is called Leshem there: afterwards named Dan, Jud. 18, 29: but called Caesarea Philippi by Philip the Tetrarch: where Jeroboam placed his golden calves just as in Bethel: because it was the boundary of the land of Israel towards the north at the roots almost of Mount Lebanon, between the two streams Jor and Dan: just as Beersheba was to the south, c. 20, 1. In that city also Christ healed the woman with the issue of blood, Matt. 9, 20. Peter made his confession concerning Christ.

AND OF GREAT WEALTH) In the Hebrew: possessing treasures.

AND FAR FROM SIDON.

It seems to have been a colony of Sidon, but because it was too far removed, namely a journey of one day, as Josephus teaches, it could not be immediately helped, and otherwise this city was secure and the citizens unarmed.

Latin:

Vers. 7. VENERUNT LAIS) Colonia videtur fuisse Sidoniorum: Sed a Sidone longe absita, nulli vicinorum juncta foedere, mire secura, ac dives, quae omnia incitamenta hostibus.

Quae historia etiam Jos. 19, 47. refertur: sed per anticipationem: quia longo post Josuam tempore gesta: unde non a Josua, sed recentiore, & ut creditur Samuele Historiam Josuae consignatam esse, verisi- mile videtur. Vocatur enim ibi civitas haec Lesem: postea Dan nuncupata Jud. 18, 29. a Philippo vero Tetrarcha Caesarea Philippi appellata: ubi Jerobeam aeque ac in Bethel vitulos suos aureos collocavit: quia terminus erat terrae Israel versus septentrionem ad radices fere montis Libani, inter duos rivos Jor & Dan: sicut Bersebe ad Austrum c. 20, 1, In illa urbe etiam haemorrhoüsam Christus sanavit Matth. 9, 20. Petrus confessionem de Christo edidit.

MAGNARVMQVE OPVM) In Hebraeo: possidens the- sauros.

ET PROCUL A SIDONE.

Videtur colonia fuisse Sidoniae, sed quia nimis dissita, itinere sc.unius diei, ut Josephus docet, ipsi extemplo succurri non potuit, & secura erat alio- quin haec civitas ac cives inermes.

## 18:19
Ver. 19. THAT WE MAY HAVE THEE AS A FATHER) Thus priests were accustomed to be addressed for the sake of honor, above 17, 10. Thus it was made from a private sacred thing into a tribal one.

Latin:

Vers. 19. VT HABEAMVS TE PATREM) Ita hono- ris causa appellari solebant Sacerdotes supra 17, 10. Sic ex sa- cro privato tribule factum est.

## 18:26
Ver. 26. BUT MICAH SEEING THAT THEY WERE STRONGER THAN HE, RETURNED TO HIS HOUSE) Very wisely: Ἄφρων δ' ὃς κ' ἐθέλοι πρὸς κρείσσονας ἀντιφερίζειν.

Latin:

Vers. 26. VIDENS AVTEM MICHAS QVOD FOR- TIORES SE ESSENT, REVERSUS EST DOMVM SVAM) Bene sane: Ἄφρων δ' ὃς κ' ἐθέλοι πρὸς κρείσσονας ἀντιφερίζειν.

## 18:28
Vers. 28. IN THE REGION OF ROHOB) בֵּית רְחוֹב which it took as a common noun in Hebrew, just as the Greeks also did ἐν κοιλάδι τῶ ὄικε ῥαάϐ. Others think it is part of a proper name, so that the region was called Betrahab.

Latin:

Vers. 28. IN REGIONE ROHOB) בֵּית רְחוֹב quod in Hebraeo est pro communi nomine sumsit, ut & Graeci ἐν κοιλάδι τῶ ὄικε ῥαάϐ. Alii nominis proprii partem censent, ut regio dicta fuerit Betrahab.

## 18:29
Vers. 29. WHICH WAS FORMERLY CALLED LAIS) אוּלָם it took as an affirmative adverb. But the LXX took it as a noun, so that the city was called אוּלָם לַיִשׁ, that is, the portico of Lais. We had a similar case in Gen. 28, 19, where see.

Latin:

Vers. 29. QVAE PRIVS LAIS DICEBATVR) אוּלָם sumsit pro adverbio affirmantis. At LXX. pro nomine, ut dicta sit urbs אוּלָם לַיִשׁ , id est, porticus Laischi. Simile habuimus Gen. 28, 19. ubi vide.

## 18:30
Vers. 30. SON OF GERSAM) That is, from the descendants of Gersam. SON OF MOTSI) The interpreter read מֹשֶׁה not מְנַשֶׁה, as the Hebrew codices have, but the more corrected ones, with a suspended Nun, by which the Masoretes indicated that this letter is an insertion. Gersam was the son of Moses, Ex. 18, 2; 1 Chron. 26, 24.

Not only does the Hebrew text have Menasse, but also the Chaldean and the LXX interpreters, whence it does not appear why Moses should be read here: nor is Jonathan ever recounted among the sons of Gerson, the son of Moses. To B. Glasfius, however, it seemed that the suspended letter נ was an indication that both Menasse and Moses could be read, whether the letter Nun was retained or neglected: because he was the son of Menasse by study and imitation, and the son of Moses by lineage and generation: such suspended letters also occur in Ps. 80, 14; Job 38, 13, 15. See Phil. S. p. 1, p. 394. The Danites certainly did not care much for the law of God, which required priests from the tribe of Levi: and therefore Osiander observes that Jonathan was ordained against the law.

UNTIL THE DAY OF THEIR CAPTIVITY) In Hebrew: until the land was captured: that is, a great part of the land: by the Philistines, namely, 1 Sam. 4, 10. For then the ark ceased to be in Silo, as follows here. See also Ps. 78, 60.

Most understand this of the captivity under Heli the Priest, by which many even from the tribe of Dan were carried away, the cause of which was then, among other things, idolatry. Cajetan could not prove from Scripture another peculiar captivity of the tribe of Dan. But that this idolatry flourished in that tribe until the Assyrian captivity, as is explained in Seder Olam and as Raschi wished, is not likely, since the worship of the calves instituted by Jeroboam prevailed in the kingdom of Israel, and it is not to be believed that David in his time would have tolerated this idolatry in any way, not to speak of Samuel. For the cause of that idolatry is given as this, that there was no King in Israel, who, namely, might remove it by his authority: therefore, under the rule of David, a most pious King, it would by no means have been permitted. And an explicit explanation is added here: And the idol of Micha remained among them all the time that the house of God was in Silo: which was there until Heli and Samuel.

Latin:

Vers. 30. FILIUM GERSAM) Id est, e posteris Gersami. FILII MOTSI) Legit interpres מֹשֶׁה non מְנַשֶׁה , ut Hebraei codices habent, sed emendatiores, Nun suspenso, quo Masoretae indicarunt hanc literam esse παρένθετον. Ger- samus Mosis filius Ex. 18, 2. 1. Paral. 26, 24.

Non tantum Ebraeus textus habet Menasse, sed & Chaldaeus, & LXX. Interpp. unde non apparet causa cur hic Moses legendus sit: nec inter filios Gersonis filii Mosis recensetur uspiam Jonathan. B. Glasfio ta- men visum literam נ suspensam indicio esse & Me- nasse & Mosi legi posse, seu retenta seu neglecta lite- ra Nun: quod Menassis fuerit filius studio & imitatio- ne, Mosis prosapia, & generatione: quales suspensae etiam literae occurrunt Ps. 80, 14. Job. 38, 13. 15. Vid. Phil. S. p. 1. p. 394. Danitae certe non adeo curabant legem Dei, quae ex tribu Levi & Sacerdotes require- bat: ideoque contra legem Jonathanem ordinatum esse observat Osiander.

VSQVE AD DIEM CAPTIVITATIS SVAE) In He- braeo: usque dum caperetur terra: id est magna pars terrae: a Philistinis, nempe 1. Sam. 4, 10. Nam tunc arca desiit esse in Silo, ut hic sequitur. Vide & Psal. 78, 60.

De captivitate sub Heli Pontifice plerique intel- ligunt, qua multi etiam ex tribu Dan abducti, cujus causa tum inter alia fuit idololatria. Aliam pecu- liarem captivitatem tribus Dan Cajetanus e Scriptu- ra probare non potuit. Ad Assyriacam autem ut in Seder Olam explicatur & Raschi voluit hanc idolo- latriam in ista tribu viguisse, non est verisimile, cum vitulorum cultus a Jeroboamo institutus in regno Is- rael obtinuerit, neque suo tempore Davidem hanc idololatriam toleraturum fuisse ullo modo creden- dum sit, ne de Samuele dicamus. Causa enim idolo- latriae illius haec redditur, quod non fuerit Rex in Is- rael, qui sc. eandem autoritate sua tolleret: sub re- gimine ergo Davidis Regis pientissimi illa minime permissa fuisset. Et additur hic explicatio diserta: Mansitque apud eos idolum Micha omni tempore, quo fuit domus Dei in Silo: quae usque ad Heli & Samue- lem ibi fuit.

## 18:31
V. 31. THAT THE HOUSE OF GOD WAS IN SILO.

In Shiloh the house of God remained from the sixth year of Joshua until the last year of Eli for 328 years. Ussher in his Annals p. 41 wishes Shiloh to be Salem, partly from the meaning of the name, because as שלם denotes peaceful & tranquil Gen 34, 21. Nah. 1, 12. so also does שלם Dan. 4, 1; then from the location of the place, because the palace of Melchizedek was shown to Jerome in the city of Salem, near which John was baptizing, Epist. 126 to Evagrius, which in Gen. 33, 18 is called the city of the Shechemites from the field of Shechem, in which Shiloh was also situated. Compare Jos. 24, 25. 26. with 29, 1. Gen. 35, 4. Jud. 9, 6. c. 21, 19. The passage of Jerome. Vol. 3, p. 40, has it thus: 'Salem, however, is not, as Josephus and all our people think, Jerusalem, a name composed from Greek and Hebrew: which the mixture of a foreign language shows to be absurd: but a town near Scythopolis, which is called Salem to this day, and the palace of Melchizedek is shown there, demonstrating the magnificence of ancient work by the size of its ruins: concerning which it is also written in the latter part of Genesis: Jacob came to Succoth, that is, to tabernacles, and made for himself houses and tents there, and passed into Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan.' It must also be considered that when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies, whom he pursued as far as Dan, which is today called Paneas, he was not on the road to Jerusalem, but on the road from the town of the metropolis of Shechem. Concerning which we also read in the Gospel: 'John was also baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there.' He professes to have learned these things from the most learned of the Jewish nation. In his Hebrew Places he reviews various places called by this name: 'Salem,' says Jerome, 'the city of the Shechemites, which is Shechem: but also another village is shown to the present day near the linden tree on the western side by this name: also at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis in the field a village is called Salumias.' Josephus, however, affirms that Salem is the place where Melchizedek reigned, which was later called Solyma, and at last received the name Hierosolyma. Adrichomius agrees with Jerome regarding Salem on p. 74, which was in the tribe of Manasseh: but he places Shiloh in the tribe of Ephraim at the tenth milestone from Neapolis or Shechem in the Acrabatene region, and observes that it is now named Saint Samuel, as is Ramah, p. 30.

Latin:

V. 31. QUO FUIT DOMUS DEI IN SILO.

In Silo domus Dei mansit a sexto Josuae anno usque ad ultimum Heli per annos 328. Silo Usserius Salem esse vult in Annalibus p. 41. partim ex nominis significatione, quia ut שלם pacificum & tranquillum Gen 34, 21. Nah. 1, 12. ita & שלם Dan. 4, 1. notat; tum ex loci situ, quia Melchisedeci palatium in urbe Salem, prope quam Johannes baptizabat, Hieronymo ostensum Epist. 126. ad Evagr. quae Gen. 33, 18. urbs Sichmorum appellatur ab agro Sichemitano, in quo etiam Silo posita. Conf. Jos. 24, 25. 26. cum 29, 1. Gen. 35, 4. Jud. 9, 6. c. 21, 19. Locus Hieron. T. 3. p. 40. ita habet: Salem autem non ut Josephus & nostri omnes arbitrantur esse Hierusalem, nomen ex Graeco Hebraicoque compositum: quod absurdum esse, peregrinae linguae mixtura demonstrat: sed oppidum juxta Scythopolim, quod usq; hodie appellatur Salem, & ostenditur ibi palatium Melchisedec, ex magnitudine ruinarum, veteris operis ostendens magnificentiam: de quo in posteriore quoq; parte Geneseos scriptum est: Venit Jacob in Socoth, id est, in tabernacula, & fecit sibi ibi domos atque tentoria & transivit in Salem civitatem regionis Sichem, quae est in terra Canaan. Considerandum quoque est, quod Abrahae a caede hostium revertenti, quos persecutus est usq; Dan, quae hodie Paneas appellatur, non de via Hierusalem, sed de oppido Metropoleos Sichem in itinere fuerit. De quo in Evangelio quoque legimus: Erat autem Johannes baptizans in Ennon juxta Salim, quia aquae erant multae ibi. Haec ab eruditissimis gentis Judaicae se didicisse profitetur. In locis Ebr. varia loca hoc nomine appellata recenset: Salem, inquit Hieronymus, Civitas Socimorum, quae est Sichem: Sed & alia villa ostenditur usq; in praesentem diem juxta tiliam contra occidentalem plagam hoc nomine: in octavo quoq; lapide a Scythopoli in campo vicus Salumias appellatur. Josephus vero Salem esse affirmat, in qua regnavit Melchisedec, quae postea dicta est Solyma, & ad extremum Hierosolyma nomen accepit. Consentit de Salem Hieronymo Adrichomius p. 74. quod in tribu Manasse fuit: at Sila in tribu Ephraim decimo milliario Neapoleos vel Sichimae in Regione Acrabatana collocat, & nunc ad Sanctum Samuelem ut & Rama nominari observat p. 30.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

The unspeakable crime of the Gibeonites against the wife of the Levite.

Verse 1. HE TOOK A WIFE) In the Hebrew: a female concubine: for the name פילגש is more honorable than the Greek παλλακὴ, and the Latin pellex, which nevertheless came from it. A pellex is of one who has a wife: a concubine can be unmarried: nor was such a union against the law or good morals in those times.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

Infandum Gabaonitarum scelus adversus uxorem Levitae.

Vers. 1. ACCEPIT VXOREM) In Hebraeo: feminam concubinam: nam nomen פילגש honestius est quam Graecum παλλακὴ, & Latinum pellex, quae tamen inde venerunt. Pellex est uxorem habentis: concubina potest esse coelebis: neque talis conjunctio contra legem aut bonos mores erat illis temporibus.

## 19:2
Verse 2. WHO LEFT HIM) Thus the LXX: ἐπορεύθη ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ. In the Hebrew it is ותזנה עליו: But those interpreters seem to have read תזנח. Yet after זנה, which properly signifies to commit fornication, it signifies metaphorically an alienation of mind: in which sense some Greek Codices have ὠργίσθη αὐτῷ: Jerome in Micah chapter 5: 'And his concubine was angry with him.'

NOT another (certainly it was not a good one) reading of the LXX interpreters, but a slip: nor is there need for that translated meaning. For it follows later that she left. Josephus wishes this to have been done because of jealousy, others because of quarrels, disputes, and wrangling with her husband, because in v. 3 she wished to be reconciled to him. But in the authentic text the cause is expressed, which the Vulgate rashly omits: She committed fornication, and left him, whether she was treated more harshly for that reason, or feared it, as she had deserved. Yet the pious husband wished to be reconciled to her, although she was worthy of death according to the law of Moses, and thus he preferred to recall her to repentance by his humanity, rather than expose her to punishment, or to the snares of Satan, and the danger of public prostitution. The laws of the Emperors Severus and Alexander are harsher, which decree that a husband who has retained a wife caught in adultery or has taken her back after she was dismissed, incurs the crime of pimping: and therefore it is permitted by Ecclesiastical laws to take back an adulteress who is doing penance, just as GOD always receives the Church, his bride, even if she has often committed fornication, when she does penance. Cf. 1 Cor. 7. Augustine to Pollentius: 'Do you think her polluted, whom baptism and penance have purged? She whom God has cleansed ought not to seem polluted to you.'

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUAE RELIQUIT EUM) Sic LXX. ἐπορεύθη ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ. In Hebraeo est ותזנה עליו: Sed videntur תזנח legisfe isti interpretes. Post tamen & זנה quod proprie scortari significat, translate significare abalienationem animi: quo sensu quidam Graeci Codices habent ὠργίσθη αὐτῷ: Hieronym. in Michaeam cap. 5. Et irata est ei concubina sua.

NON alia (certe non proba fuit illa) Interpp. LXX. lectio, sed παρόραμα: neq; opus est illa translata significatione. Sequitur enim postea derelictione. Quam ob zelotypiam factam Josephus vult, alii ob simultates, lites & jurgia cum marito, quia v. 3. reconciliari eidem voluit. Sed in textu authentico causa expressa est, quam temere omittit vulgata: Scortata est, & reliquit eum, sive ideo tractata fuerit durius, seu id metuerit, uti meruerat. Reconciliari tamen ei vir pius voluit, quum digna fuerit juxta legem Mosis morte adeoque humanitate sua eam ad poenitentiam revocare, quam vel supplicio, vel Satanae insidiis, & publicae scortationis periculo exponere maluit. Duriores sunt Severi, & Alexandri Imper. leges, quae maritum si deprehen- sam in adulterio uxorem retinuerit vel dimissam reduxerit, lenocinii crimen contrahere decernunt: ideoque per leges Ecclesiasticas adulteram pœniten- tiam agentem reducere licet, uti DEUS Ecclesiam sponsam, etiamsi sæpius fornicata sit, semper reci- pit cum pœnitentiam agit. Of. 1. 1. Cor. 7. Augustin. ad Pollent. An tu pollutam existimas, quam bapti- smus & pœnitentia purgavit? Quam Deus emun- davit, ea non debet tibi videri polluta.

## 19:12
Verse 12. A TOWN OF A FOREIGN NATION. Although Caleb occupied Jerusalem Jud. 1, 8, yet the Jebusites later recovered it again; or at least still holding the fortress of Zion they dominated the city, in which the Jebusites lived mixed with the Jewish Benjaminites, so that the Levite might easily have believed that he could fall into danger or commerce with idolaters, and therefore did not wish to stay there overnight.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OPPIDUM GENTIS ALIENÆ. Etsi Jerusalem occuparit Caleb Jud. 1, 8. ta- men postea eam recuperarunt iterum Jebusæi; aut saltim arcem Sion adhuc tenentes urbi domina- bantur, in qua admixti Judæis Benjaminitis Jebu- sæi habitabant, ut facile in periculum aut commer- cium cum idololatris se incidere posse crediderit Levita, ideoque illic pernoctare noluerit.

## 19:15
Verse 15. LODGING) There were no inns open to everyone in those places at that time. The wondrous savagery of men is described here, with the character having turned from the hospitality of Abraham to the customs of the citizens of Sodom.

Latin:

Vers. 15. HOSPITIO) Non erant eo tempore illis in locis diversoria omnibus patentia. Mira hominum feritas hîc de- scribitur ab Abrahami τῆ ξενοδόχῳ moribus, ad Sodomi civi- um mores deflexo ingenio.

## 19:16
Verse 16. TWIN SONS. That is, by aphaeresis, Benjamin.

Latin:

Vers. 16. FILII GEMINI. Id est, per aphæresin, Benjamin.

## 19:18
Verse 18. TO THE HOUSE OF GOD. In Shiloh, for there was the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant, chapter 18, verse 31.

Latin:

Vers. 18. AD DOMUM DEI. In Silo, ibi enim erat tabernaculum & arca fœ- deris cap. 18. vers. 31.

## 19:21
Verse 21. AFTER THEY HAD WASHED THEIR FEET) Which is the custom before supper. See John 13:5.

Latin:

Vers. 21. POSTQVAM LAVERUNT PEDES SUOS) Qui mos ante cœnam. Vid. Joh. 13, 5.

## 19:24
Verse 24. I HAVE A VIRGIN DAUGHTER, AND THIS MAN HAS A CONCUBINE, I WILL BRING THEM OUT TO YOU) See a similar case in Gen. 19:8.

Interpreters here ask: Did this host sin by offering his daughter, and the Levite by bringing out and handing over his concubine to be abused by men of lust? Most Papists judge that he did not sin, because they might lawfully offer their own to redeem a greater injury; such as was the unspeakable Sodomy. Thus Cornelius thinks that it is lawfully advised to one wishing to commit adultery to commit fornication with a harlot instead. Which the Papists contend for without doubt, so that they may excuse their public brothels. For thus they say that a lesser evil is advised not absolutely, but under this condition: If you are clearly going to commit a greater sin, commit the lesser one instead: for which opinion Cornelius also cites Gregory the Great, book 32 of Morals, chapter 20; Cajetan here; Barthol. Fumus in his summary of Cases under the word Tyrant; Dom. Soto, book 6 on justice, question 1, article 5; Adrian, Quodlibet 1, question 1; Thomas, question on Evil; Navarrus, chapter 14, number 40. He also cites the ancient Fathers: Chrysostom, homily 27 to the people of Antioch, and homily 43 on Genesis; Ambrose, book 1 on Abraham; Augustine, book 2 on adulterous marriages, chapter 15; but neither that host nor the Levite can be absolved from guilt, because it is not lawful to advise a sin in order to avoid another sin, nor do a parent or husband have the right under any pretext to prostitute the body of their daughters or wife, even if she is a secondary one; and Cornelius himself admits with Lyranus, Abulensis, Dionysius, and Pererius on chapter 19, verse 5 of Genesis, that the host acted against piety, which dictates that a parent should consult for the modesty and good of his daughter rather than that of an external guest, and against justice, if he offered her to be violated while she was unwilling and resisting, and against charity if there was a danger of consent in her to the venereal act. But as for what he judges, that if this danger of consent was not in the daughter and she herself submitted to her father of her own accord, or offered herself to avoid such a great wickedness, there was no sin at all on the part of the parent, in that he errs. For how can he be absolved from all sin and guilt who morally concurs in a sin by prostituting the modesty of his daughter, even if she agrees to it? Even if it is imagined that she would not consent to the venereal pleasure, nevertheless a parent cannot, with a safe conscience, offer or submit her himself, or agree to her offering herself: it is one thing when she is snatched away to it by force, another when she voluntarily submits to avoid a greater crime: there he is passive; here, however, he actively concurs in the sin, so that another sin may be avoided, or the parent herself even commits a fault, by transgressing against the Decalogue, so that another may not be snatched away into a graver sin: where St. Augustine, in his book against Lying, ch. 9, opportunely warns that if we open this path to sins, that we commit lesser ones so that others may not commit greater ones, with a wide limit, or rather with no limit but with all boundaries torn down and removed, all sins will enter and reign in an infinite space. But others in vain turn to the providence of God, who could avert such disgrace and shame: since God is not to be tempted: and the same thing entirely should have been presumed or hoped for here concerning the providence of God, that God would not have permitted that injury to be inflicted upon the guest, the Levite, a pious man. For it is not permitted to make an experiment of divine grace or power at our own pleasure. And finally, Cornelius himself acknowledges the fault here, when he says that perturbation of mind, thoughtlessness, and lack of counsel greatly diminish the fault: which, while they serve to some extent as an excuse, yet it still remains that a fault, and not a light one, was designated in the offering of the daughter and the prostitution of the Levite's concubine. Nor can the cloud of Popish Moralists move us, nor can the authority of Chrysostom or Ambrose prejudice the Apostolic definition in Romans 3:8: evils are not to be done so that good may come. We have already received the mind of Augustine, to which those things which Cornelius cites must be recalled. That Cornelian hypothesis, that it is not advised absolutely, but under this condition, if you wish to commit a greater sin, commit a lesser one instead, cannot excuse the Jesuit; because we ought not to cooperate with the evil of a fault, either absolutely or hypothetically, whether physically or morally, and we are bound to suffer every violence rather than consent to any fault, unless GOD averts it: for by suffering evil we do not sin; but by advising or promoting sin in any way, we commit a wrong entirely. Nor does he only sin against the sixth commandment who defiles his body with lusts, but also he who is the author of lusts to another, or provides the means; meanwhile, we do not doubt that sudden perturbation and lack of counsel provide some excuse. Nor is there any reason for Bonfrerius to except that offering made not for fornication, but to avert his own injury, as when someone offers or permits his sword, otherwise about to be killed if he did not do so, even if he sees that another might perhaps be killed by that sword: because thus, not being able to escape death otherwise unless the sword is handed over, the very handing over of the sword is not immediately the cause of the other's killing; just as he who hands over his daughters or wife so that they may be humiliated, in the Hebrew phrase, is the cause of the fornication or adultery which is brought about by that phrase; he does not merely provide an instrument here, but suggests a plan for satisfying lust, which cannot be absolved from sin: and therefore the other example of Bonfrerius is also irrelevant, when someone is given into the hands of a tyrant who would otherwise destroy the city, not so that he may be killed, but so that the destruction of the city may be averted. Concerning the gravity of the crime of the Gibeathites, see Hosea 9:9.

Verse same. THAT YOU MAY HUMILIATE THEM] Concerning the meaning of this word, see what is said at Deuteronomy 21:14.

Latin:

Vers 24. HABEO FILIAM VIRGINEM, ET HIC HOMO HABET CONCUBINAM, EDUCAM EAS AD VOS) Simile vide Gen. 19, 8.

Quærunt hic interpp. Anne peccarit hic ho- spes offerendo filiam suam, & Levita educendo & tradendo libidinois hominibus illudendam con- cubinam suam? Non peccasse pleriq; Pontificii cen- sent, quia ad minorem injuriam licite obtulerint suos ad redimendam graviorem; qualis erat Sodomia ne- fanda. Sic volenti committere adulterium licite suaderi putat Cornelius fornicationem cum mere- trice. Quod ideo contendunt Papistæ sine dubio, ut exculpent sua lupanaria publica. Sic enim suaderi dicunt minus malum non absolute, sed sub condi- tione hac: Si vis plane committere majus peccatum, committe potius minus: in quam sententiam allegat etiam Cornelius Gregorium M. l. 32. Moral. c. 20. Cajetanum hic, Barthol. Fumum in summula Casuum verbo Tyrannus. Dom. Soto l. 6. de justit. quæst. 1. art. 5. Adrian. Quodlibet 1. q. 1. Thomam quæst. de Malo: Navarrum c. 14. n. 40. Adducit quoque Pa- tres antiquos Chrysost. hom. 27. ad pop. Antioch. & homil. 43. in Genes. Ambros. l. 1. de Abrah. August. l. 2. de adult. Conjug. c. 15. sed a culpa absolvi nec ho- spes ille, nec Levita potest, quia non licet peccatum suadere, ad declinandum peccatum aliud, neque parens vel maritus jus habent quovis prætextu filiarum aut uxoris, etsi secundariæ, corpus prosti- tuendi; & fatetur Cornelius ipse cum Lyrano, Abu- lensi, Dionysio, & Pererio in c. Gen. 19, 5. & contra pietatem egisse hospitem, quæ dictat, ut parens filiæ suæ pudori & bono consulat potius, quam hospitis externi, & contra justitiam, si ea invita & repugnan- te violandam obtulit, & contra charitatem si in ea periculum consensus fuit in rem veneream. Quod vero censet, si hoc periculum consensus non fuit in filia ipsaq; sponte Patri se submiserit, aut ad tantum etiam nefas evitandum obtulerit, nullum omnino fuisse Pa- rentis peccatum, in eo errat. Quomodo enim a pec- cato & culpa omni absolvi potest, qui moraliter concurrit ad peccatum, filiæ suæ pudicitiam, etsi illa annuente, prostituendo; quæ si maxime fingatur in delectationem veneream non consensura, tamen se ipsam offerre vel submittere illa aut offerenti an- nuere parens non potest salva conscientia: aliud est, cum coacta eo abripitur, aliud cum se ad majus scelus declinandum sponte submittit: ibi passive se habet; hic vero active concurrit ad peccatum, ut aliud evitetur peccatum ipsa aut pa- rens etiam culpam committit, contra Decalogum prævaricando, ut ne alius ad peccatum gravius ab- ripiatur: ubi S. August. l. contra Mendac. c. 9. opor- tune monet, si hanc peccatis aperimus viam, ut com- mittamus minora, ne alii majora committant, lato li- mite, imo nullo limite sed convulsis & remotis omnibus terminis infinito spatio cuncta intrabunt & regna- bunt peccata. Nequicquam autem alii Dei obver- tunt providentiam, qui tale dedecus & probrum avertere posset: siquidem Deus tentandus non sit: atque idem omnino de providentia Dei hic præsu- mendum, vel sperandum fuisset, Deum non permis- surum, ut hospiti Levitæ viro pio ea inferatur inju- ria. Non enim licet pro nostro lubitu experimen- tum facere divinæ gratiæ, vel potentiæ. Et agnoscit denique Cornelius ipse hic culpam, cum animi per- turbationem, incogitantiam, & inopiam consilii cul- pam valde imminuere, ait: quæ uti ad excusationem quadantenus faciunt, ita manet tamen adhuc, quod culpa, eaque non levis designata sit in oblatione fi- liæ, & prostitutione concubinæ Levitæ. Neque Pontificiorum Moralistarum nubes nos movere, nec Chrysostomi aut Ambrosii autoritas præjudicare potest definitioni Apostolicæ Rom. 3, 4. non sunt fa- cienda mala ut eveniant bona. Augustini vero men- tem jam accepimus, ad quam ea, quæ citat Corne- lius, revocanda sunt. Illa hypothesis Corneliana, quod non suadeatur absolute, sed sub hac conditione, si vis committere majus peccatum, committe potius minus, non excusare potest Jesuitam; quia nec ab- solute, nec hypothetice ad malum culpæ cooperari debemus, seu physice seu moraliter, & pati potius omnem violentiam nisi avertat DEUS, tenemur, quam in ullam consentire culpam: patiendo enim malum non peccamus; suadendo autem vel promo- vendo ulla ratione peccatum, omnino delinquimus. Nec is tantum peccat contra sextum præceptum, qui corpus libidinibus polluit, sed etiam qui alteri ad libidines autor est, aut adminicula subministrat; interim subitam perturbationem & consilii ino- piam ad excusationem aliquam facere, non ambigi- mus. Nec est, quod Bonfrerius excipiat oblationem illam factam non ad stuprum, sed ad arcendam suam injuriam, ut cum gladium suum quis offert vel per- mittit, alias occidendus, ni faceret, etiamsi videat, eo gladio alterum forte occidendum: quia sic ali- ter mortem effugere non valens, nisi gladius trada- tur, ipsa gladii traditione non statim causa est occi- sionis alterius; quemadmodum qui filias vel uxo- rem tradit, ut humilientur, phrasi Ebræa, causa est stupri vel adulterii, quod ea phrasi infertur; non præbet tantum hic instrumentum, sed suggerit sup- plendi libidinem consilium, quod a peccato absolvi non potest: ideoque etiam alterum Bonfrerii exem- plum ἀλλότριον est, cum in manus quis deditur ty- ranni alias civitatem deleturi, non ut occidatur, sed ut exitium urbis avertatur. De gravitate autem sce- leris Gabaitarum vid. Os. 9, 9.

Vers. eod. VT HVMILIETIS EAS] De hujus vocis significatu vide quæ Dicta ad Devteronom. 21, 14.

## 19:26
Verse 26. AND THERE SHE FELL] We have examples of those raped even unto death in the histories of the Muscovites and the Turks.

Dead. By which foul kind of death God avenged her previous lust.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET IBI CORRVIT] Stupratarum ad mortem usque exempla etiam in Moscovitarum & Turcarum historiis habemus.

Mortua. Quo fœdo mortis genere Deus priorem ipsius libidinem ultus est.

## 19:29
Verse 29. CUTTING HER INTO TWELVE PARTS AND PIECES.

Not for the dishonoring of the wife's body, but rather for the honor to be restored to her through the vengeance of such a great crime, it was done thus, as Tostatus rightly observes: and therefore it is praised by Athanasius in his Epistle to the Orthodox. Concerning which Grotius says: The atrocity of the deed compelled him to atrocious remedies. Nor was he false in his hope, for this sight caused all the tribes to consult in common, which had not been done for a long time.

Latin:

Vers. 29. IN DUODECIM PARTES AC FRUSTA CONCIDENS.

Non ad dehonestacionem corporis uxoris, sed potius ad honorem illi restituendum per vindi- ctam tanti flagitii sic factum, ut recte Tostatus ob- servat: ideoque id laudatur ab Athan. Epist. ad Orthod. Quo de ita Grotius: Atrocitas facti ad atrocia remedia eum compulit. Nec falsus spei fuit, nam hic conspectus fecit, ut omnes tribus in commune consulerent, quod pridem factum non fuerat.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX. The slaughter of the Benjaminites.

Verse 1. THEN ALL THE PEOPLE WENT OUT FROM DAN EVEN TO BEERSHEBA. THAT is, all the Israelites on this side of the Jordan, except the Benjaminites, who, namely, could conveniently be away from home and go out, from Dan, which was previously called Laish, towards the North and Lebanon, as far as Beersheba towards the South and the desert.

IN MIZPAH. Namely, that which was situated on the border of the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. For this was near both the city of Shiloh and Gibeah. Compare 1 Samuel 7:10, Jeremiah 40:1. Those things which are treated in the solemn assemblies of kingdoms are also said to be done before the Lord, Psalm 82:1.

Latin:

CAPUT XX. Clades Benjaminitarum.

Vers. 1. EGRESSI ITAQVE SUNT OMNES DE DAN USQVE BERSEBE. HOC est, omnes Israelitæ cis Jordanem exceptis Benjaminitis, qui scil. commode domo abesse egredique poterant, de Dan, quæ prius Lais dicta versus Aquilonem & Libanum usque Bersabe ver- sus austrum & desertum.

IN MASPHA. Eam scilicet, quæ in confinio tribus Judæ & Benjamin sita fuit. Hæc enim & urbi Silo vicina & Gabææ erat. Conf. 1. Reg. 7, 10. Jer. 40, 1. coram Do- mino agi dicuntur etiam, quæ in solemnibus regno- rum conventibus tractantur Psalm. 82, 1.

## 20:2
Verse 2. ALL THE CORNERS ALSO OF THE PEOPLES. That is, the Princes; they are so called because they hold the people together, just as corners bind and hold together the whole house, and support the polity, just as cornerstones sustain a building. Cf. 1 Sam. 14:38, Ps. 118:22, Is. 19:5, Zeph. 3:6, Zech. 10:4.

INTO THE CHURCH OF GOD] קהל, the Hebrew and Greek ἐκκλησία, here signifies the same as the Greek σύνοδος, the Latin conventus or assembly. Caesar uses this word regarding Gaul, Tacitus regarding Germany.

Verse of the same. FORTY THOUSAND FIGHTING MEN. In the Hebrew, four hundred thousand are read; therefore the patrons of the Vulgate wonder in vain why no more warriors were found, since this error is manifest in the Vulgate version, and only those on this side of the Jordan were numbered, with the tribe of Benjamin also excepted. In some copies of the Vulgate, however, at verse 17 below, this error is corrected, and four hundred thousand are read.

Latin:

Vers. 2. OMNES QVOQVE ANGULI PO- PULORUM. Id est, Principes; sic dicuntur, quia populum continent, sicut anguli stringunt continentque totam domum, & politiam fulciunt, quemadmo- dum angulares lapides ædificium sustentat. Conf. 1. Sam. 14, 38. Pf. 118, 22. Es. 19, 5. Zeph. 3, 6. Zach. 10. vers. 4.

IN ECCLESIAM DEI] קהל, Hebræum & Græ- cum ἐκκλησία, idem hic valet quod Græcum σύνοδος, Lati- num conventus aut auxilium. Hanc vocem de Gallia usurpat Cæsar, Tacitus de Germania.

Vers. eod. QUADRAGINTA MILLIA PE- DITUM PUGNATORUM. In Ebræo leguntur quadringenta millia, ideo frustra Vulgatæ Patroni mirantur, quod non plures inventi sint bellatores, cum error hic apertus sit in versione vulgata, & numerati sint tantum cis-Jorda- nini, excepta quoque tribu Benjamin. In nonnullis tamen exemplaribus Vulgatæ v. 17. infra emenda- tus hic error est, ac leguntur quadringenta millia.

## 20:10
Verse 10. AND TO RENDER TO HIM FOR THE WICKEDNESS WHICH HE DESERVES] Repeat what was said above on Joshua 22:11.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET REDDERE EI PRO SCELERE QVOD MERETVR] Repete quæ dicta supra Josuæ 22, 11.

## 20:12
Verse 12. THEY SENT MESSENGERS] See what was said on Joshua 22:16.

Latin:

Vers. 12. MISERVNT NVNTIOS] Vide quæ dicta Josuæ 22. v. 16.

## 20:13
Verse 13. DELIVER UP THE MEN OF GIBEAH] Give them up to punishment, that you may be freed. See what was said on the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 21, sections 4 and 5.

Latin:

Vers. 13. TRADITE HOMINES DE GABAA] Dedite illos noxæ, ut vos liberemini. Vide quæ dicta de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 2. cap. 21. §. 4. 5.

## 20:15
Verse 15. TWENTY-FIVE THOUSAND. In the Hebrew, twenty-six thousand are held. The Papists rashly argue here that the Hebrew text is corrupt based on the Vulgate and the LXX version; whereas those versions should rather be corrected from the Hebrew, with which the Chaldean agrees. But as to why at verse 35 only 25,000 of the slain are numbered (to which, however, a hundred more are added), the reason is that in the two previous battles some hundreds of the Benjaminites were also slain, since among the Israelites 22,000 were killed in the first and 18,000 in the second, a thousand Benjaminites easily succumbed, as Grotius rightly notes on verse 35.

Latin:

Vers. 15. VIGINTI QVINQVE MILLIA. In Ebræo Viginti & sex millia habentur. Te- mere hic Papistæ e vulgata & LXX. versione E- bræum textum corruptionis arguunt; quum ex Ebræo potius, cui Chaldæus consentit, illæ versiones emendandæ sint. Quod autem v. 35. numerentur tantum 25000. cæsorum, (quibus tamen addun- tur adhuc centum) inde sit, quod in prioribus duo- bus præliis etiam aliquot centeni e Benjaminitis cæsi sint, quum ex Israelitis in priori 22000. in poste- riori 18000. interfectis facile mille Benjaminitæ suc- cubuerint, ut recte Grotio adv. 35.

## 20:18
Verse 18. AND THEY CONSULTED GOD] They ought to have consulted God first as to whether war should be undertaken against Benjamin. For it was chiefly for that matter that the Urim and Thummim were given. See verse 26, where this fault is corrected.

It is asked, since they did not act without the counsel of God, why such a great sum of them was slain here, 22,000, and subsequently in another conflict again 18,000. The cause is that they did not inquire about waging war, but concluded the war without the Lord and only consulted the Lord in it as to who should be the leader of the army, verse 18. Furthermore, because in their own strength and number they placed their trust v. 23. even then when they wept before the Lord: so that repentance was by no means a holiday, which requires true humility and trust in the grace of God alone. Thirdly, the Israelites had deserved this slaughter on account of the idolatry established in Dan. For it is clear that this history is later than ch. 20 v. 1: for they are said to be gathered from Dan even to Beersheba. And so even then Laish had been conquered and had yielded to the Danite tribe, which was thence called Dan, which reason the Hebrews, Lyranus, and Tostatus hand down. Fourthly, it could happen that the sins of those who are blind, or of others among the people, deserved this slaughter: and that this slaughter was brought about for the sake of exercising the example, humiliation, conversion, patience, and faith and piety of others.

Latin:

Vers. 18. CONSVLVERVNTQVE DEVM] Prius con- sulere Deum debuerant, an bellum suscipiendum esset in Benjaminem. Ejus enim rei causa præcipue datum erat Vrim & Thumim. Vide 26. ubi hæc culpa corrigitur.

Quæritur, cum non sine consilio Dei egerint, cur hic tanta summa ex ipsis cæsa sit 22000. & post- modum altero conflictu iterum 18000. Causa est, quod non de bello gerendo quæsierint, sed sine Do- mino bellum concluserint & solum in eo con- suluerint Dominum, quis militiæ Dux esse debeat? vers. 18. Deinde quod in fortitudine sua & numero fiduciam collocarint v. 23. etiam tum ubi coram Domino fleverunt: ut poenitentia adeo non fuerit feria, quae veram humilitatem & fiduciam in solam Dei gratiam requirit. Tertio promeriti hanc cladem erant Israelitae ob idololatriam in Dan constitutam. Nam quod haec historia posterior sit e c. 20. v. 1. liquet: congregati enim dicuntur de Dan usque ad Bersabee. Adeoque jam tum Lais expugnata erat & Daniticae tribui cesserat, quae inde Dan nuncupata est, quam rationem Ebraei, Lyranus, & Tostatus tradunt. Quarto fieri potuit, ut peccata eorum, qui caeci sunt, vel aliorum in populo hanc cladem meruerint: & ad aliorum exemplum, humiliationem, conversionem, patientiam & fidem ac pietatem exercendam ea clades facta sit.

## 20:23
Vers. 23. AND THEY WEPT) Very piously, which Christians have followed in excommunications. And thus the ancients interpret that 1 Cor. 5, 2. ἐπενθήσατε.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET FLERENT) Pie admodum, quod in excommunicationibus secuti Christiani. Ac sic veteres interpretantur illud 1. Cor. 5, 2. ἐπενθήσατε.

## 20:26
vers. 26. UNTIL EVENING. From this it appears that the fasts of the Jews were accustomed to be prolonged until the setting of the sun and until evening 1 Sam. 6, 7.

AND THEY OFFERED TO HIM BURNT OFFERINGS AND PEACE OFFERINGS) By public decree they restored the public worship which had been interrupted on account of the negligence not of Phinehas, but of other priests, or on account of unsafe places. See above 17, 5.

Latin:

vers. 26. USQUE AD VESPERAM. Inde apparet Judaeorum jejunia produci solita usque ad occasum solis & ad vesperam 1. Sam. 6, 7.

ET OBTVLERVNT EI HOLOCAVSTA ATQVE PACIFICAS VICTIMAS) Restituerunt decreto publico cultum publicum intermissum ob negligentiam non Phineae, sed aliorum sacerdotum aut ob loca non tuta. Vide supra 17, 5.

## 20:28
Vers. 28. GO UP: FOR TOMORROW I WILL DELIVER THEM INTO YOUR HANDS) God promised and granted victory on that day, yet not before He had purged the very corrupt people by the destruction of the worst: which itself was also a kind of benefit.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ASCENDITE: CRAS ENIM TRADAM EOS IN MANVS VESTRAS) Victoriam eo die promisit Deus & praestitit, non ante tamen quam populum valde corruptum pessimorum interitu purgasset: quod & ipsum beneficii erat genus.

## 20:29
Vers. 29. AND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SET AMBUSHES) See Joshua 8, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 29. POSVERVNTQVE FILII ISRAEL INSIDIAS) Vide Josue 8, 2.

## 20:31
vers. 31. THE OTHER TO GIBEAH. That path, or road paved with stones, led to Gibeah, or rather, as it is held in the Hebrew and among the LXX, that road tended toward the field of the city of Gibeah, even though the Israelites were fleeing from Gibeah, and were striving to draw the Benjaminites, who had gone out from Gibeah and were pursuing, further away from the city of Gibeah.

vers. 31. THEREFORE ALL THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL. These things are intricate in the Vulgate version: but easier according to the Hebrew truth: Therefore as the (remaining) children of Israel, who were not in that battle line which had begun the fight, in order to draw the enemies away from the city, rising from their seats, or their tents, stretched themselves out, drew up the battle line in the place which is called Baal-tamar, the ambushes also, which were around the city, began to open themselves little by little, and to proceed from the western part of the city: in the Heb. And the ambushes of the Israelites went out from their place, from the cave of Gibeah (from a place suitable for hiding a large number of soldiers: and this was the third battle line) but also another ten thousand men from all Israel were provoking the inhabitants of the city to combat; in the Heb. And they came to (the city) Gibeah, namely ten thousand chosen (most valiant) men from all Israel. These therefore hastened to occupy the city, and once captured, they immediately set it on fire by throwing in torches. Therefore these 10,000 were not different from the ambushes, but that army lying in ambush consisted of 10,000 most valiant men: but by the smoke ascending, the Israelites perceived that the city was already taken, and the way for the Benjaminites to flee into the city was cut off, and so, stopping their feigned flight, they made a most valiant attack upon the Benjaminites: and the war was pressed against the children of Benjamin, and they did not immediately understand that destruction was threatening them (more correctly, themselves) from every side. (and so for some time they fought bravely, but in vain) And the Lord struck them etc. Which things, handed down in summary, are explained more fully. But the children of Benjamin, when they had seen that they were inferior, began to flee. Seeing which, the children of Israel gave them room to flee, in

Hebrew: For the children of Benjamin saw that (Israel) was being struck (the Israelites gave room to Benjamin himself) so that they might come to the prepared ambushes, which they had placed near the city. Who, when they had suddenly risen from their hiding places, and Benjamin was turning his back to those striking, they entered the city, and struck it with the edge of the sword. Which things must be entirely corrected from the Hebrew as follows: Because (the Israelites) relied on the ambushes which they had placed against Gibeah: and the ambushes hastened, and had made an attack against Gibeah: and the ambushers had drawn out and struck the whole city with the edge of the sword.

Latin:

vers. 31. ALTERA IN GABAAN. Semita illa, seu via lapidibus strata ferebatur in Gabea, vel potius, ut in Ebraeo habetur & apud LXX. via illa tendebat ad agrum urbis Gabeae, etsi Israelitae a Gabea refugerent, & Benjaminitas Gabea egressos & insequentes longius a civitate Gabaa abducere niterentur.

vers. 31. OMNES ITAQUE FILII ISRAEL. Intricata haec sunt in Vulgata versione: sed faciliora juxta Ebraicam veritatem: Ut itaq; (reliqui) filii Israel, qui non erant in illa acie, quae praelium inceperat, ut hostes a civitate avellerent, surgentes de sedibus, seu tabernaculis suis tetenderunt se, instruxerunt aciem in loco, qui vocatur Balthamar, insidiae quoque, quae circa urbem erant, paulatim se aperire ceperunt, & ab occidentali parte urbis procedere: in Ebr. Et insidiae Israelitarum egressae sunt de loco suo, de spelunca Gabaa (ex loco idoneo ad occultandum magnum militum numerum: & haec erat tertia acies) sed & alia decem millia virorum de universo Israel habitatores urbis ad certamina provocabant; in Ebr. Et venerunt ad (urbem) Gabaa nempe decem millia virorum electorum (fortissimorum) ex omni Israel. Hi ergo festinarunt ad urbem occupandam, & captam statim injectis facibus succenderunt. Non itaque alii erant hi 10000. ab insidiis, sed exercitus ille in insidiis latens constabat 10000. virorum fortissimorum: fumo autem adscendente animadverterunt Israelitae, urbem jam raptam, & interclusam Benjaminitis viam in urbem refugiendi, adeoque fuga simulata sistentes fortissime in Benjaminitas impressionem fecerunt: ingravatumque est bellum contra filios Benjamin, & non statim intellexerunt, quod ex omni parte illis (rectius sibi) instaret interitus. (itaque aliquandiu fortiter pugnarunt, sed frustra) Percussitque eos Dominus &c. Quae summatim ita tradita copiosius explicantur. Filii autem Benjamin cum se inferiores esse vidissent, ceperunt fugere. Quod cernentes filii Israel dederunt eis ad fugiendum locum, in

Ebræo: Nam viderunt filii Benjamin, quod (Israel) percuteretur (dederunt Israelitæ locum ipsi Benja- min) ut præparatas insidias devenirent, quas juxta urbem posuerunt. Qui cum repente de lati- bulis suis surrexissent, & Benjamin terga cædenti- bus daret, ingressi sunt civitatem, & percusserunt eum in ore gladii. Quæ ex Ebræo emendanda omnino sunt h.m. Quia (Israelitæ) freti sunt insidiis, quas posuerant contra Gabeas: & insidiæ festinarent, & impetum fecerant contra Gibea: & pertraxerant & percusserant insidiatores totam urbem ad os gladii.

## 20:35
Vers. 35. ON THAT DAY TWENTY-FIVE THOUSAND AND ONE HUNDRED MEN) Well, on that day: for even in the previous battles, although the Benjaminites were superior, they had lost almost a thousand of their own. See above 15.

Latin:

Vers. 35. IN ILLO DIE VIGINTI QVINQVE MIL- LIA ET CENTVM VIROS) Bene in illo die: nam & prio- ribus præliis quanquam superiores Benjaminitæ, suorum ami- serant ferme mille. Vide supra 15.

## 20:42
vers. 42. BUT ALSO THESE, WHO HAD SET THE CITY ON FIRE, MET THEM.

From the Hebrew these can be rendered thus: And those who were from the cities (the remaining Benjaminites in Gibeah) these they destroyed in the midst of it, as rightly B. Luther & Osiander: They surrounded (and so on every side) Benjamin. It is added in the Hebrew: And they pursued them (even unto) Menuchah, they trampled, or they prostrated them even unto the sight of the city of Gibeah from the rising of the sun: toward the eastern region of the city they pursued them, and in the sight of the city they slaughtered them, so that wandering here and there, whithersoever they turned, they were cut down. But in the Latin Vulgate those things also have it otherwise: AND THERE WAS NO REST OF THE DYING: which Bonfrerius rashly attempts to carve out from the Hebrew, suspecting that it ought to be read מנוח from rest, that is, without rest. Which are forced. Nor is there any cause for suspicion of a corrupt text, and the Chaldean, Jerome, and the LXX accepted the word as a proper noun, and rendered it ἀπὸ νόα. For one may not presume about the corruption of the text from the Vulgate version.

Latin:

vers. 42. SED ET HI, QUI URBEM SUC- CENDERANT, OCCURRERUNT.

Ex Ebr. hæc ita reddi possunt: Et eos qui de civi- tatibus (reliquis Benjaminitarum in Gabaa erant) hos delebant in medio ejus, ut recte B. Lutherus & O- siander: Circumdederunt (itaque undiquaq;) Benja- min. Additur in Ebr. Et persequuti sunt eos (usq; in) Menoa conculcarunt, vel prostraverunt eos etiam usque in conspectum urbis Gabaæ ab ortu solis: versus orientalem plagam urbis consectati sunt, atque in conspectu urbis trucidarunt eos, ita ut passim pa- lantes, quocunque se verterent, cæderentur. Sed in Latina Vulgata aliter etiam illa habent: NEC ERAT ULLA REQUIES MORIENTIUM: quæ temere ex Ebræo exsculpere conatur Bonfrerius, suspicans, legi debere מנוח a requie, id est, absque requie. Quæ coasta sunt. Neq; ulla est causa suspi- cionis corrupti textus, & acceperunt vocem Chal- dæus, Hieronymus, & LXX. ceu nomen proprium, ac reddidere ἀπὸ νόα. Non enim e versione Vulga- ta præsumere licet de textus corruptela.

## 20:44
Vers. 44. BUT THERE WERE THOSE WHO WERE SLAIN IN THE SAME PLACE EIGHTEEN THOUSAND MEN) In the very heat of the battle. For it is an ἐπάνοδος, therefore you may rightly translate it, they were slain.

Latin:

Vers. 44. FVERVNT AVTEM QVI EODEM LOCO INTERFECTI SVNT DECEM ET OCTO MILLIA VIRORVM) In ipso pugnæ æstu. Est enim ἐπάνοδος, ita- que recte vertas fuerant interfecti.

## 20:45
vers. 45. REMNON.

It is called elsewhere the hill of Remnon, here the Rock of Remnon, and it is established to the south of Jerusalem, Zech. 4, 10, in the tribe of Judah, or Simeon, where also the city of Remnan was situated, Josh. 15, 19, 1 Chron. 4, Neh. 11.

THEY KILLED.
