In the Hebrew it is they gleaned, just like grapes remaining from the vintage. LXX. ἐκαλημήσαντο, they gathered the remaining ears of corn, or also metaphorically the remaining clusters. See Jer. 6, 9.

THEY PURSUED THEM.

In the Hebrew and among the LXX the place is added even unto Gideom: which B. Luther and other translations rightly retained, the Vulgate wrongly omitted.

v. 45. ALL THE REMAINDERS OF THE CITY. Of Gibeah: which perhaps in the first destruction had hidden themselves having sought hiding places.

Latin:

vers. 45. REMNON.

Dicitur alias collis Remnon, hic Petra Remnon, & constituitur ad austrum Jerusalem Zach. 4, 10. in tribu Juda, vel Simeonis, ubi etiam Remnan urbs sita erat Jos. 15, 19. 1. Par. 4. Neh. 11.

OCCIDERUNT.

In Ebr. est racemārunt, veluti residuos a vindemia acinos. LXX. ἐκαλημήσαντο, residuas spicas collegerunt, aut etiam per metaphoram racemos residuos. Vid. Jer. 6, 9.

PERSECUTI SUNT EOS.

In Ebr. & apud LXX. additur locus usq; in Gi- deom: quem recte B. Lutherus & aliæ translationes retinuerunt, perperam omisit Vulgatus.

v. 45. OMNES RELIQUIAS CIVITATIS. Gabeæ: quæ forte in excidio primo latebris quæsitis se occultarant.

## 20:46
Vers. 46. TWENTY FIVE THOUSAND] And what exceeds. See above 35. It is common for all nations to express larger numbers, and to pass over smaller ones, where they contribute little to the sum.

Latin:

Vers. 46. VIGINTI QVINQVE MILLIA] Et quod ex- cedit. Vide supra 35. Commune gentibus omnibus majores numeros exprimere, reticere minores, ubi parum ad summam conferunt.

## 20:48
FROM MEN EVEN UNTO BEASTS.

It is wrongly omitted in the Vulgate, which is added in the Hebrew, even unto everything that was found: because it is indicated that the city was destroyed in the manner of an anathema, Deut. 13. All the remaining cities also were consumed by fire, with everything that was found in them, which was a horrible example of divine wrath: because it was done not by the rash impulse of the Israelites, or unjust vengeance, as it seemed to Tostatus, Cajetan, and Suarez, but by the counsel of GOD, and even if divine responses are not to be extended to special cases, yet these deeds do not seem to have occurred without special divine direction, therefore the Israelites grieved so much on account of the tribe being destroyed, chap. 21, vers. 2. For in such public and universal calamities not even the innocent (comparatively) or the little ones or the adults are spared, because no one is simply and absolutely innocent before God; and God wished to establish so horrible an example, that the whole world might understand how vehemently God detests and punishes impurities, adulteries, and abominable lusts of this kind; and to warn, lest anyone by defending crimes, as was done by the Benjaminites, render himself guilty of them and at the same time liable to divine judgment. Rightly B. Chytraeus h. l. p. 255. Since even in the pious and obedient, or the true Church, many dregs of sins, darkness and doubts, and many depraved inclinations toward security, self-admiration, and other vicious affections remain, God first chastises the children whom He loves, so that they may recognize and amend this interior uncleanness, which the world neglects and does not even think to be a sin: and that repentance, faith, invocation, and other virtues may grow and increase in them. Furthermore, even if God had promised victory to the Israelites, which, however, He did not grant on the first two occasions: yet He would not have the manner and time of the victory prescribed to Himself. For generally God exhibits promises at a far different time and manner than human reason imagines. He had promised the Apostles the preservation and propagation of the Gospel and the Church until the end of the world, and yet He allows them and their disciples to be killed, and nevertheless propagates the Gospel and the Church throughout the whole world. Thus in this place He finally grants victory to the Israelites, even if they receive some slaughters beforehand, etc.

Latin:

A VIRIS USQVE AD JUMENTA.

Omissum perperam est in Vulgato, quod in Ebr. additur usque ad omne quod inveniebatur: quia indicatur anathematis in morem urbem excisam esse Deuteron. 13. Omnes etiam urbes reliquæ igne absumtæ, cum omnibus, quæ inventa in iisdem sint, quod horribile iræ divinæ ex- emplum fuit: quia non temerario Israelis impe- tu, aut injusta vindicta, uti Tostato, Cajet. Sua- rez visum, sed consulto DEO id factum, ac si ad specialia extendenda non sint responsa di- vina, non tamen gesta hæc videntur sine speciali directione divina, ideo tantopere doluerunt Israe- litæ, ob tribum excisam cap. 21. vers. 2. Nam in talibus publicis & universalibus calamitati- bus nec innocentibus (comparate) seu parvulis seu adultis parcitur, quia nemo simpliciter & abso- lute coram Deo innocens est; & statuere voluit Deus tam horrendum exemplum, ut totus orbis intelligat, quam vehementer Deus impuritates, adulteria, ac nefandas ejusmodi libidines deteste- tur, atque puniat; ac monere, ne quis defendendo scelera, uti a Benjaminitis factum, se reum eorum & judicio divino simul obnoxium reddat. Recte B. Chytraeus h. l. p. 255. Cum in piis etiam & obe- dientibus seu vera Ecclesia, multae sordes peccatorum, caligo & dubitationes, & multae pravae inclinationes ad securitatem, admirationem sui, & alios affectus vitiosos reliquae maneant, Deus filios, quos diligit, pri- mum castigat, ut hanc interiorem immundiciem, quam mundus negligit, ac ne quidem cogitat esse pec- catum, agnoscant & emendent: & poenitentia, fides, invocatio & caeterae virtutes in eis crescant & augean- tur. Deinde etiamsi promisisset Deus victoriam Israelitis, quam tamen duabus primis vicibus non addixit: tamen modum & tempus victoriae sibi praescribi noluisset. Plerumque enim longe alio tempore & modo Deus promissa exhibet quam ratio humana imaginatur. Apostolis pollicitus erat conservationem & propagationem Evangelii & Ecclesiae usque ad finem mundi, & tamen ipsos ac eorum Discipulos interfici sinit, ac nihilominus Evangelion & Ecclesiam toto orbe terrarum pro- pagat. Ita hoc loco Israelitis victoriam tandem tri- buit, etiamsi prius clades aliquot accipiunt, &c.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. Virgins in the slaughter of Jabesh reserved for the remnants of the tribe of Benjamin, stolen in Shiloh.

vers. 1. THEY SWORE.

It must be rendered in the pluperfect: they had sworn, i.e., before they entered into war, because it was done in Mizpah, where they had gathered before the war, c. 20, 1. Tostatus not undeservedly judges that this oath was illicit, but committed out of ignorance: because it was concerning an illicit matter, tending against charity, either to the destruction of the tribe, or to intermarriage with the Gentiles. Bonfrerius denies that it was rash: because he thinks these things happened by accident: since with the Benjaminitic women slaughtered, it is simply necessary, if wives are denied from other tribes, that that tribe perish, unless either whoredoms or intermarriages with the Gentiles are admitted. The oath was therefore preposterous and clearly illicit, which Cornelius acknowledges, and thus denies that it was obligatory in such a case: but that they thought through simplicity that they were bound by this oath. Which latter is not to be approved: For it is not likely that all in the whole people were so rude and simple, nay, from the counsel which they took, their religious prudence appears afterwards: for lest they should seem to gratify the affections or conveniences of others with the disgrace of the divine name, or to save the tribe among the people, but violate the faith given to GOD, and invite others by their example to violation, they found that method by which both the oath and the tribe of Benjamin might be saved; when by punishing the citizens of the town of Jabesh in Gilead, who refused the military service ordered by public authority, they joined the daughters of the slain to the surviving Benjaminites and thus restored the tribe.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. Virgines in caede Iabes reservatae pro reliquiis tribus Benjamin in Silo raptae.

vers. 1. JURAVERUNT.

IN plusquamperfecto reddendum: juraverant, sc. antequam bellum inirent, quia id in Mispha, ubi ante bellum convenerant, factum c. 20, 1. Illi- citum autem id juramentum fuisse Tostatus non immerito censet, sed ex ignorantia commissum: quia super re illicita, contra charitatem vergente, vel ad interitum tribus, vel ad commixtionem cum gentilibus. Negat id temere Bonfrerius: quod existimet haec per accidens evenisse: quum excisis mulieribus Benjaminiticis simpliciter necessarium sit, si e tribubus aliis denegentur uxores, tribum illam interire, nisi vel scortationes, vel commixtio- nes cum gentilibus admittantur. Praeposterum er- go & illicitum plane erat juramentum, quod agno- scit Cornelius, adeoq; negat, obligatorium id fuisse in tali casu: per simplicitatem autem eos putasse se hoc juramento teneri. Quod posterius non pro- bandum: Non enim verisimile omnes adeo rudes atq; simplices fuisse in toto populo, imo e consilio quod ceperunt, postea religiosa prudentia eorum apparet: nam ne cum contumelia nominis divini aliorum affectibus aut commodis gratificari, vel tri- bum servare in populo, DEO autem datam fidem violare viderentur, aliosque suo exemplo ad vio- lationem invitare, eam invenerunt rationem, qua & juramentum & tribus Benjamin servaretur; cum puniendo cives oppidi Jabes in Galaad, qui mili- tiam publico imperio indictam detrectabant, fi- lias interfectorum Benjaminitis superstitibus jun- xerunt atque ita tribum restaurarunt.

## 21:2
Vers. 2. AND WITH A GREAT WAILING THEY BEGAN TO WEEP] Vengeance having been completed, pity follows.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET MAGNO ULULATU COEPERUNT FLE- RE] Expleta ultione subit miseratio.

## 21:4
vers. 4. ALTAR.

This does not seem to have been built without God's dispensation, response, or instinct, as 2 Sam. 7,

11. 16. c. 24. 1 Kings 18. otherwise they would have designated the crime of will-worship.

Latin:

vers. 4. ALTARE.

Non videtur hoc citra Dei dispensationem, re- sponsum aut instinctum extructum, ut 2. Sam. 7,

11. 16. c. 24. 1. Reg. 18. alias ἐθελοθρησκείας crimen defignassent.

## 21:6
AND LED BY REPENTANCE.

It was not properly repentance, because they did not sin by killing the Benjaminites, but grief on account of an almost entire tribe being extinguished in Israel.

Latin:

DUCTIQUE POENITENTIA.

Non proprie pœnitentia fuit, quia non peccarunt occidendo Benjaminitas, sed dolor ob exstinctam integram pene tribum in Israel.

## 21:7
Vers. 7. ONE TRIBE HAS BEEN TAKEN AWAY FROM ISRAEL]

Latin:

Vers. 7. ABLATA EST TRIBUS UNA DE ISRAEL]

## 21:10
vers. 10. TEN THOUSAND.

In the Hebrew, Chaldean, Septuagint, and in Josephus, book 5 of Antiquities, chapter 2, twelve thousand are held, whence not undeservedly the version of the Vulgate is suspected by Bonfrerius, which the Reverend Fathers ought to have corrected.

STRIKE THE INHABITANTS OF JABESH GILEAD]

This was a just vengeance of the Magistrate or of the common tribes: since in a public cause of the Republic and a common battle brought about by public decree they withdrew themselves: and thus the sentence of death was justly sanctioned for them. However, they exceeded the measure of vengeance, because they killed little ones and innocent women. Naturally, as Seneca says, arms do not observe a measure. Jabesh Gilead is mentioned for the sake of distinction from Jabesh in Judah, 1 Chron. 2:55, which is written יעבץ. But יבש in Gilead was a village across the Jordan, in the half-tribe of Manasseh, at the sixth milestone of the city of Pella, above the mountain for those going to Gerasa, as Jerome has it in his Hebrew Places, which Saul liberated from the siege of the Ammonites, 1 Sam. 11, and for that reason gratitude was shown to him after his death by those inhabitants, 1 Sam. 31.

Latin:

vers. 10. DECEM MILLIA.

In Ebr. Chald. LXX. & apud Joseph. l. 5. antiq. c. 2. duodecim millia habentur, unde non immerito suspecta est Bonfrerio Vulgatæ versio, quam emen- dare debuissent R. R. P. P.

PERCUTITE HABITATORES JABES GALAAD]

Justa hæc vindicta Magistratus seu commu- nium tribuum fuit : quum in publica causa Reip. & prælio communi ex decreto publico inducto sese subdu- xerint : adeoque mortis sententia ipsis juste sancita. Modum tamen excesserunt vindictæ, quod parvu- los & mulieres innocentes occiderunt. Nimirum, ut Seneca ait, arma non servant modum. Dicitur Ja- bes Galaad ad differentiam Jabes in Juda 1. Par. 2, 55. quæ יעבץ scribitur. At יבש in Galaad fuit vicus trans Jordanem, in dimidia tribu Manasse, in sexto milliari civitatis Pellæ, super montem euntibus Gera- sam, ut habet Hier. in loc. Ebr. quam ab Ammoni- tarum obsidione Saul liberavit 1. Sam. 11. eoque nomine ipsi gratitudo post mortem exhibita ab eis incolis est, 1. Sam. 31.

## 21:19
vers. 19. BEHOLD, THE SOLEMNITY OF THE LORD IS IN SHILOH.

Of the feast, as it seems, of tabernacles: which was celebrated in September: Compare v. 20. Shiloh is said to be situated to the north of the city of Bethel, in the tribe of Ephraim, as observed by Jerome in his Hebrew Places. Bethel, however, was on the border of the tribe of Ephraim and Benjamin, whence whatever is to the north of Bethel is included within the lot of the Ephraimites, just as here Shiloh is called northern to Bethel. The text adds: AND TO THE EASTERN SIDE OF THE WAY, WHICH GOES FROM BETHEL TO SHECHEM. Now Shechem or Neapolis was situated in the tribe of Ephraim towards its northern borders at the tenth milestone from Shiloh, as noted by Jerome.

AND TO THE SOUTH OF THE TOWN OF LEBONAH.

Lebonah, according to Adrichomius, was a beautiful fortress in the tribe of Ephraim, distant four leagues from Shechem, which is here placed to the north of the city of Shiloh.

Latin:

vers. 19. ECCE SOLEMNITAS DOMINI EST IN SILO.

Festi, ut videtur, tabernaculorum : quod in Se- ptembri celebrabatur : Conf. v. 20. Silo ad Septen- trionem urbis Bethel sita dicitur, in tribu Ephraim, uti ab Hieronymo in locis Ebr. observatum. Be- thel autem fuit in confinio tribus Ephraim & Ben- jamin, unde quicquid ad Aquilonem est Betheli in- tra Ephraimitarum sortem concluditur, quemad- modum hic Betheli Silo Aquilonaris dicitur. Ad- dit textus : ET AD ORIENTALEM PLA- GAM VIÆ, QUÆ DE BETHEL TENDIT AD SICHIMAM. Erat autem Sichem seu Nea- polis sita in tribu Ephraim versus fines ejus Aquilona- res in decimo milliario ab Silo, notante Hieronymo.

ET AD MERIDIEM OPPIDI LEBONA.

Lebona, Adrichomio autore, castrum pulcrum fuit in tribu Ephraim, quatuor leucis Schima distans, quod hic urbi Silo ad Aquilonem statuitur.

## 21:21
Vers. 21. SEIZE FOR YOURSELVES EACH ONE WIVES) Thus Romulus, and those who were with him, seized the Sabine women at the Great Games. Ambrose defends or excuses this deed of the Benjaminites in the place we cited in book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 13, § 5. Seneca in the excerpts: The law holds him who helps an exile, not him who suffers him to be helped. Symmachus: He attempts to strike an empty fear into your divine mind, whoever asserts that you have the conscience of those providing, unless you undergo the odium of those taking away. Certainly those were innocent who had not given the counsel of seizing: which deed itself would not have happened if a prince with authority had been among the people. See the end of this chapter.

It is not properly called a rape prohibited by laws, because it is commanded by the common authority of those to whom the care of the people pertains, and for the common good by the law of necessity, because it had to be provided that an oath should not be violated, and yet the restoration of the tribe by wives should be consulted: nor was it done against the will of the daughters to any great extent, nor even of the parents, except for the danger of perjury: which however as far as they themselves were concerned was none, because they were not privy to the counsel of the rape, nor did they give their daughters, as they had promised by oath they would not give, indeed they refused those asking, whence these were snatched from them, not given by them; lest anyone should accuse those who gave the counsel of the rape of perjury, this intervenes, that they had only sworn individually and in part that they would not give their own daughters to the Benjaminites, but they did not receive them, they would not give the daughters of others by common decree. Therefore Lyranus, Cajetanus, Arias, Cornelius, Bonfrerius, as also our B. Chytræus, rightly deny that the sin of abduction intervened. Moreover, most severe penalties were established for the crime of abduction even by Roman laws, so that abductors and their companions were punished with death, and those caught in that crime ἐπαυτοφώρῳ were killed with impunity by the parents, kinsmen, guardians, or masters of the abducted women, and all the goods of the abductor and his associates were confiscated to the treasury if the abducted woman did not marry the abductor, but if she did marry, they were to be adjudicated: Constitut. Novell. 143. 150. which severity of civil laws, however, by Canons 36. q. 1. and 28. q. 2. has been mitigated, and in our Consistories the abductor, if the girl has consented willingly to the abduction and the will of the parents has been added, having performed public penance, is not prohibited from marrying and keeping the abducted woman; but if anyone abducts a woman betrothed or married to another against her will, she is restored to those in whose power she was. The abductor, however, as guilty of a double crime, of abduction and adultery, is punished most severely by the Magistrate or certainly by God himself, as is evident from the example of the abduction of Dinah.

Latin:

Vers. 21. RAPITE EX EIS SINGULI UXORES) Sic Romulus, & qui cum eo erant Magnis Circensibus Sabinas rapuere. Defendit aut excusat hoc factum Benjaminitarum Ambrosius loco quem protulimus libro 2. de Jure Belli & Fa- cis c. 13. §. 5. Seneca in excerptis : Lex eum tenet, qui juvat exu- lem, non qui patitur juvari. Symmachus : Inanem metum divi- no animo vestro tentat incutere, si quis asserit conscientiam vos habere præbentium, nisi detrahentium subieritis invidiam. Cer- te illi innocentes erant, qui consilium rapiendi non dederant : quod ipsum factum non fuisset, si princeps cum imperio fuis- set in populo. Vide finem hujus Capitis.

Non est proprie dictus raptus legibus prohibi- tus, quia communi eorum autoritate mandatur, ad quos cura populi spectat, & communi bono ex ne- cessitatis lege, quia providendum erat, ne violaretur juramentum, & consuleretur tamen tribus restau- rationi uxoribus : neque admodum invitis filiabus factus, ac ne parentibus quidem, nisi ob periculum perjurii : quod tamen quoad ipsos nullum erat, quia ipsi consilii raptus non erant conscii, nec dederunt filias suas, uti juramento receperant, se non datu- ros, imo petentibus negarunt, unde hæ illis abre- ptæ sunt, non ab illis datæ ; Ne quis vero eos, qui consilium raptus dederunt perjurii arguat, interce- dit hoc, quod singuli tantum particulatim jurave- rint, se non daturos Benjaminitis proprias filias, non autem receperint non daturos aliorum filias communi decreto. Ideo Lyranus, Cajetanus, Arias, Cornelius, Bonfrerius, ut & B. Chytræus noster peccatum raptus intervenisse, merito negant. Cæterum in raptus crimen gravissimæ pœnæ constitutæ sunt etiam Romanis legibus, ut raptores eorumq; comites capite plectantur, ἐπαυτοφώρῳ vero in illo crimine deprehensi a parentibus, consanguineis, tutoribus, aut Dominis raptarum, impune interficiebantur, & bona raptoris, ac sociorum omnia raptæ, si raptori non nupserit, fisco, fin nupserit, dijudicentur : Constitut. Novell. 143. 150. quæ severitas tamen legum civilium per Canones 36. q. 1. & 28. q. 2. mitigata est, & in nostris Consistoriis raptor, si puella volens in raptum consenserit, & voluntas parentum accesserit, acta publice pœnitentia, ducere ac retinere raptam non prohibetur, si vero quis alteri desponsatam vel nuptam invitam rapit, rapta iis, quorum in potestate erat, restituitur. Raptor vero ut duplicis criminis rapinæ & adulterii reus, gravissime a Magistratu vel certe a Deo ipso, ut raptus Dinæ exemplo constat, punitur.

## 21:22
vers. 22. HAVE COMPASSION ON THEM: FOR THEY DID NOT TAKE THEM BY THE RIGHT OF WARRIORS AND VICTORS.

Others render the Hebrew: Have compassion on us for them: or for their sake, because we did not take a wife for each man in the war, which they explain concerning the war waged against Jabesh, in which so many had not taken virgins as would suffice for the surviving Benjaminites, as Piscator, Junius, the English Version, and the recent Dutch versions render and explain, with Sixtinus Amama approving and Bonfrerius not denying it. Our German version, however, follows the Vulgate, send ihnen gnädig, denn wir haben sie nicht gewonnen mit Streit: nor is this foreign to the sources; indeed, it approaches them more closely if that paragogic nun is in the verb וכנו as Pagninus, Forsterus, the Tigurines, and others also believed. For the sense can be this: Have compassion on them, i.e., the abductors, because אותם is masculine. Nor is there need for an enallage of gender to be posited with Amama. For they had not taken them in war by force and injury, as happens in wars unjustly undertaken: where victors are accustomed to treat those they have captured insultingly as slaves: but by our authority and public sentence: because you did not give them to those who asked, or refused to give them, and you are therefore in fault or the cause why your daughters had to be abducted from you by such a process, not that it is truly a sin, since they were restrained by the religion of an oath, but that this matter, if considered in itself, setting aside the oath, would have a certain appearance of unmercifulness, inhumanity, and cruelty, as Bonfrerius explains, or also: Die Schuld ist euer, that is, you will sin if you demand them back with matters thus situated. In the Hebrew it is, because you did not give to them, according to the time, or as the times now indeed have it, you will be delinquent: For this time (according to the state of affairs) you are altogether delinquent if you wish to demand back those whom they themselves abducted in this necessity; you will act against what is fair and good.

Latin:

vers. 22. MISEREMINI EORUM : NON ENIM RAPUERUNT EAS JURE BELLANTIUM AC VICTORUM.

Ebræum alii reddunt: Miseremini nostri illorum: vel pro illis, quia non accepimus unicuique uxorem suam in bello, quod explicant de Bello contra Jabes gesto, in quo tot non acceperant virgines, quotBenjaministis superstitibus sufficerent,uti Piscator, Junius, Angl. Versio & Belgici nuperi reddunt, & explicant, approbante Sixtino Amama nec abnuente Bonfrerio. Vulgatam tamen sequitur Germanica nostra versio, send ihnen gnädig, denn wir haben sie nicht gewonnen mit Streit: neque aliena hæc a fontibus est, imo propius accedit iisdem, si illud נו paragogicum sit in verbo וכנו ut Pagninus, Forsterus, Tigurini & alii etiam credidere. Sensus enim hic esse potest : Miseremini illorum sc. raptorum, quia אותם masculinum est. Neque opus ut enallage generis cum Amama statuatur. Non enim rapuerant eas in bello per vim & injuriam, ut in bellis injuste susceptis fit : ubi victores contumeliose tanquam servas tractare solent, quas cepere : sed nostra autoritate, publicaque sententia: quia rogantibus illis non dedistis, vel dare recusastis, & vos in culpa ergo vel causa estis, cur tali processu rapiendæ vobis filiæ vestræ fuerint, non quod revera peccatum sit, cum prohiberentur juramenti religione, sed quod ea res, si secundum se consideretur, seposito juramento, speciem quandam immisericordiæ, inhumanitatis, & crudelitatis haberet, uti Bonfrerius explicat, vel etiam : Die Schuld ist euer, id est, peccabitis si repetetis rebus ita comparatis. In Ebr. est, quoniam non vos dedistis eis, juxta tempus, vel ut nunc quidem tempora habent, der linquetis : Pro hoc tempore (pro ratione status) omnino delinquitis, si eas, quas ipsi rapuerunt hac necessitate, repetere volueritis, contra æquum & bonum agetis.

## 21:24
vers. 24. IN THOSE DAYS THERE WAS NO KING.

Nor a Leader in Israel, who would keep the people in their duty according to the law of GOD: which is not to be drawn, as seems to have been done by Grotius, to the whole time which is called the Judges, but is to be taken concerning the time when these things were done, while, namely, anarchy prevailed after the passing of Joshua and the Elders. Therefore everyone is said to have done then what seemed right to himself or pleased himself, a state which could by no means have persisted throughout the whole time of the History of the Judges, even though it might have been corrected by Judges occasionally raised up extraordinarily. For how great the evils that followed from that short time of anarchy is sufficiently clear from these final chapters. Whence God is to be prayed to, that He may give, rule, and protect pious Magistrates who promote true religion and preserve honest discipline, for the sake of the grace of His name and the salvation of the Church. Amen!

Latin:

vers. 24. IN DIEBUS ILLIS NON ERAT REX.

Neque Dux in Israel, qui juxta legem DEI populum in officio contineret: quod non trahendum, uti a Grotio factum videtur, ad totum tempus, quod dicitur Judicum, sed de tempore, quo hæc gesta, accipiendum, dum nempe ἀναρχία vigeret post excessum Josuæ & Seniorum. Ideo unusquisque, quod sibi rectum videbatur vel sibi placebat, tum fecisse dicitur, qualis status per totum tempus Historiæ Judicum consistere minime potuisset, utut extraordinarie quandoque excitatis Judicibus idem emendatus fuisset. Quanta enim mala e tempore illo exiguo τῆς ἀναρχίας sequuta sint, ex hisce postremis capitibus satis liquet. Unde orandus Deus, ut Magistratus pios, qui religionem veram promoveant, & honestam disciplinam conservent, donet, regat ac tueatur ob nominis sui gratiam, & Ecclesiæ salutem. Amen!

# Ruth

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOK OF RUTH. PREFACE.

This book weaves the Genealogy of Judah from Perez down to David, so that the birth of Christ from the tribe of Judah may be shown, Gen. 49, 10, among whose ancestors Ruth, a Moabitess, is numbered, so that it may be taught, as Jerome notes, that He who had come to blot out the sins of all did not disdain to be born from sinners, and so that the calling and election of the Gentiles, to be made by Christ with the Jews excluded, might be foreshadowed in Ruth, a Gentile and great-grandmother of Christ.

The author of the book is believed by Hezekiah to be Peter Comestor, by some to be Ezra according to Serarius, but more correctly by Isidore, Eugubinus, Tostatus, Serarius, Bonfrerius, Drusius, and the Rabbis to be Samuel, who seems to have lived around this time, and to have written the first book which is called Samuel.

His interpreters are Serarius, Bonfrerius, Sanctius, Gabriel a Costa, Fevardentius, Leo Judae, Lavatherus, Wolfius, Drusius.

It consists of two parts.

The sadder lot of Naomi and Ruth in chapter 1.

The happier lot of Ruth in chapters 2, 3, and 4 it exhibits.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD LIBRUM RUTH. PRÆFATIO.

TExit hic liber Genealogiam Judæ a Phares usque ad Davidem, ut ortus Christi e tribu Juda ostendatur, Genes. 49, 10. in cujus majoribus Ruth, Moabitis, numeratur, ut doceatur, Hieronymo notante, non dedignatam ex peccatoribus nasci, qui venerat, ut omnium peccata deleret, utque gentium vocatio & electio Judæis exclusis a Christo facienda in Ruth gentili, & avia Christi præsignificaretur.

Autor libri creditur Ezechias Petro Comestori, Esdras cuidam apud Serarium, rectius autem Isidoro, Eugubino, Tostato, Serario, Bonfrerio, Drusio, & Rabbinis Samuel, qui videtur sub hoc tempus vixisse, & librum I. qui Samuelis dicitur, conscripsisse.

Interpretes ejus sunt Serarius, Bonfrerius, Sanctius, Gabriel a Costa, Fevardentius, Leo Judæ, Lavatherus, Wolfius, Drusius.

Duabus constat partibus.

Sortem Noemi & Ruthis tristiorem cap. 1.

Sortem Ruth feliciorem capp. 2. 3. & 4. exhibet.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. Elimelech, on account of famine, travels with Naomi and his sons into Moab. The others having died, Naomi returns to Bethlehem with her daughter-in-law Ruth.

Verse 1. IN THE DAYS OF ONE JUDGE) Under Eli the Priest and Judge. Josephus.

The Rabbis and Lyranus say this judge was Ibzan, and they make him Boaz. Cornelius refutes this from the calculation of time. Junius gathers from Matthew 1:5 that the history happened in the time of Deborah. Salianus and Cornelius refer it to the times of Abimelech: yet with Josephus, the Master of Scholastic History and Zonaras refer it to the times of Eli: Augustine, however, in De doctrina Christiana, book 2, chapter 8, refers it to the beginning of the Kings: those who recall this history to the times of Samuel agree with him. But it could seem to be even later, if indeed it ends with David; but it seems to B. Walther that that part about David was added later: perhaps Ezra added it: to whom some attribute the whole book. Bonfrerius warns that the opinion of Josephus is hindered by the fact that the times of the generations are too much compressed. That all things here are uncertain appears from the Synopsis Critica of Matthew Poole.

THERE WAS A FAMINE) By whose ministry God often accomplishes great things.

Latin:

CAPUT I. Elimelech ob famem cum Noemi & filiis peregrinatur in Moab. Defunctis reliquis Noem cum Nuru sua Ruth Bethlehemum redit.

Vers. 1. IN DIEBVS VNIVS JVDICIS) Sub Heli Sacerdote ac Judice. Josephus.

RAbbini, & Lyranus judicem hunc dicunt Abisan, eumque Boos faciunt. Quod e temporis ratione refellit Cornelius. Deboræ tempore storiæ contigisse Junius e Matth. 1, 5. colligit. Salianus & Cornelius ad tempora Abimelechi: cum Josepho tamen Magister Historiæ Scholasticæ, & Zonaras ad tempora Heli: Ad principium vero Regum August. 1, 2. de doctr. Christ. c. 2. refert: cui consonant, qui ad Samuelis tempora hanc historiam revocant. Posterior autem adhuc videri posset, siquidem in Davide finiatur; sed dicendum B. Walthero videtur, illud de Davide postea fuisse adjectum : forte id Esdras addidit: cui nonnulli totum tribuunt librum. Josephi sententiæ obstare, quod generationum tempora nimis coarctentur, Bonfrerius monet. Incerta hic omnia esse e Synopsi Critica Matth. Poli apparet.

FACTA EST FAMES) Cujus ministerio Deus sæpe ma- gna efficit.

## 1:4
BUT THE OTHER RUTH) The great-granddaughter of Balac from Eglon, as the Gemara hands down. I am accustomed to compare this woman to Ocrisia of Corniculum: both were foreigners. Ocrisia bore a king to the city of Rome: Ruth, the progenitor of David, the greatest of the Hebrew kings. Matthew rightly placed Rahab and Ruth in the genealogy of the Messiah, as preludes to the calling of the Gentiles, which was to be accomplished through the Messiah.

That tradition about the lineage of Ruth is as certain as the other one of the Rabbis about Naomi, that she was the granddaughter of Nahasson, who was Prince of the tribe of Judah: or even the third, that Orpah was the mother of the giant Goliath. None of them has a foundation. Harapha was also not the mother of Goliath, but the Father from the Philistines: whose name is also very different.

Ver. 4. THEY TOOK MOABITISH WIVES.

Against the law of Deut. 7:3. Cf. Ezra 9:11. Whence Jonathan explained: They transgressed the statute of the word of the Lord by taking foreign wives from the daughters of Moab: who also adds, therefore their days were shortened. The Rabbis, Fevardentius, and Bonfrerius agree with him in this, that they cannot be excused from sin. For neither does the necessity which Cornelius pretends, that they did not find Israelites in Moab, because they could easily have found them in Canaan, or a divine instinct on the part of Naomi, which must not be rashly invented against the divine law, excuse them: nor can it be said with the same Cornelius that Orpah and Ruth were proselytes, since verse 15 and 16 stand in the way, as Bonfrerius well observed.

Latin:

ALTERA VERO RUTH) Proneptis Balaci ex Eglone, ut tradit Gemara. Hanc ego feminam conferre soleo Ocrisiæ Corniculanæ: peregrina utraque. Ocrisia regem urbi Romæ genuit: Ruth Hebræorum regum maximi Davidis progenito- rem. Merito autem Rahabam & Ruthem in Genealogia Messiaæ posuit Matthæus, tanquam præludia vocationis gen- tium, quæ per Messiam facienda erat.

Tam certa est traditio illa de Ruthis prosapia, quam altera Rabbinorum de Noemi, quod Neptis fuerit Nahassonis, qui Princeps fuit tribus Juda: aut etiam tertia, quod Orpha Goliathi gigantis mater fuerit. Nulla eorum fundamentum habet. Harapha etiam Goliathi non mater, sed Pater e Philistæis fuit: cujus nomen adhæc multum di- versum est.

Vers. 4. ACCEPERUNT UXORES MOA- BITIDAS.

Contra legem Deut. 7, 3. Conf. Esdr. 9, 11. unde Jonathan exposuit: Transgressi sunt statutum verbi Domini, ducendo uxores peregrinas e filiabus Moab: qui etiam addit, ideo decurtati sunt dies eorum. Cui consonant in eo, quod a peccato excusari non pos- sint, Rabbini, Fevardentius, Bonfrerius. Neque enim necessitas, quam prætexit Cornelius, quod in Moab non invenerint Israelitas, quia in Canaan invenire facile eas poterant, aut instinctus divinus ex parte Naemi, qui temere fingendus non est, contra legem divinam, eos excusat: nec cum eodem Cornelio dici potest, quod Orpha, & Ruth proselytæ fuerint, quum obstet v. 15. 16. ut bene observavit Bonfrerius.

## 1:8
Ver. 8.

AS YOU HAVE DONE WITH THE DEAD] An improper expression, but easy to understand: that is, with your husbands, who are now dead.

Therefore, Cornelius a Lapide wrongly gathers from this that mercy toward the deceased, that one ought to pray and sacrifice for their souls. Which relies on no command, example, or promise of Holy Scripture: and therefore it is preposterous.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

SICUT FECISTIS CUM MORTUIS] Improptia lo- cutio, sed intellectu facilis: id est, maritis vestris, qui nunc sunt mortui.

Male ergo hinc Corn. a Lap. misericordiam illam ergo defunctos colligit, quod pro animabus eorum orandum & sacrificandum sit. Quæ nullo Scripturæ S. mandato, exemplo, aut promisso niti- tur: ideoque præpostera est.

## 1:13
Ver. 13.

IF YOU WISH TO WAIT FOR THEM UNTIL THEY GROW UP) Not that those not yet born are obligated by the law which exists in Deut. 25:3, but that they seemed to deserve this also. Thus the Hebrews.

Therefore, some gather in vain from this passage that it was also in use among the Gentiles that seed should be raised up for a deceased brother.

The word תֵּעָגֵנָה you will wait, from עָגַן, an anchor holding a ship, concerning which let Drusius and Bonfrerius be seen: the LXX render it αὐτοῖς καθεσχεθήσεσθε, will you be detained by them? Ar. and Syr. And will you be prohibited from marrying?

Latin:

Vers. 13.

SI EOS EXSPECTARE VELITIS DONEC CRE- SCANT) Non quod lege, quæ exstat Deut. 25, 3. obligentur nondum nati, sed quod hoc quoque meritæ videbantur. Sic Hebræi.

Frustra itaque ex hoc loco colligunt nonnulli in usu etiam apud gentiles fuisse, ut fratri defuncto semen suscitaretur.

Vox תֵּעָגֵנָה præstolabimini ab עָגַן anchora navem detinente, de qua Drusius & Bonfrer. videa- tur: LXX. reddunt αὐτοῖς καθεσχεθήσεσθε, ipsis detinebimini? Ar. & Syr. Et prohibebimini nubere?

## 1:16
Verse 16.

YOUR GOD, MY GOD] It was a great thing in a time of such widely reigning idolatry to believe in one God, see below 12, 12. Some friendship can exist even between people of different worship, see above 8. But that friendship is finally firm and indivisible which has the bond of true religion.

She permitted [her] to return to her gods, i.e., to that place in which the ancestral gods of her own are worshipped, according to the interpretation of Drusius, or to idolatry, both because she knew she would do this if she returned to her own people, and no one is to be forced into religion, and also to test the constant and sincere mind of Ruth, as Tostatus and Cornelius note.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

DEUS TUUS, DEUS MEUS] Multum erat tempore tam late regnantis idololatriæ unum Deum credere, infra 12, 12. Amicitia aliqua esse potest etiam inter diversi cultus homi- nes, supra 8. At ea demum firma atque individua est, quæ ve- ræ religionis habet vinculum.

Permisit, ut ad deos suos, i. e. ad eum locum, in quo coluntur dii Patrii ipsius, interprete Drusio, vel ad idololatriam redeat, cum quia facturam id sciebat, si reverteretur ad suos, neque cogendus quis est ad religionem, tum ut exploraret Ruthæ constantem & sincerum animum, ut Tostat. & Cornel. notant.

## 1:17
Verse 17.

MAY THE LORD DO THIS TO ME, AND ADD THIS] She expressed the evils themselves, such as poverty, hunger, plague, or other diseases, which it was not necessary to express for one writing this history.

Rather, she leaves those things unsaid through a euphemism for the sake of a good omen, so that, namely, the things she imprecates upon herself might not actually come to pass.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

HÆC MIHI FACIAT DOMINUS, ET HÆC AD- DAT] Mala ipsa expressit, puta egestatem, famem, pestem, aut alios morbos, quæ exprimere historiam hanc scribenti ni- hil fuit necesse.

Per Euphemismum potius illa subticet bona ominis causa, ne scilicet quæ sibi imprecatur, revera eveniant.

## 1:22
Verse 22. WHEN THE BARLEY WAS FIRST REAPED.

Viz., at the Passover. For the barley harvest began on the second day of unleavened bread, the 16th of Nisan, and it lasted for 49 days.

Ruth, gathering ears of grain in the field of Boaz, kindly received by Naomi, understands that Boaz is a kinsman to her.

Latin:

Vers. 22. QUANDO PRIMUM HORDEA METEBANTUR.

Scil. in Paschate. Nam secunda azymorum 16. Nisan messis hordeacea inchoabatur, durabat au- tem 49. dies.

Ruth in agro Boas spicas colligens, benigne exce- pta a Noemi, intelligit, Booz sibi affinem esse.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

THE LORD BE WITH YOU] It was the custom to pray well for those doing work, Ps. 126, 5. 6. 128, 7. 8. Concerning the formula itself, see what is at Luke 1, 28.

This formula is first found here: then repeated more often in the Code. To which corresponds the response in the greeting: MAY THE LORD BLESS YOU. These excellent formulas of greeting and returning a greeting are to be properly observed.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

DOMINUS VOBISCUM] Mos erat bene precari opus facientibus Ps. 126, 5. 6. 128, 7. 8. De formula ipsa, vide quæ ad Luc. 1, 28.

HÆc formula primum hic invenitur: Deinde sæpius in Codice repetita. Cui respondet ἀμοιβὴ in salutatione: BENEDICAT TIBI DO- MINUS. Quæ egregiæ salutandi & resalutandi formulæ probe observandæ.

## 2:7
Ver. 7. AND NOT EVEN FOR A MOMENT DID SHE RETURN HOME.

In the Hebrew, therefore she sits at home a little: or this is her dwelling, at home a little (is, or she sits) as Drusius in this place. It is foreign, what Ludov. de Dieu understands as the house belonging to the estate of Boaz. Junius, Tremellius, Piscator, and Luther agree as to the sense; and Pagninus, now her sitting, or her dwelling in the house is a little. Thus it seems Boaz did not find her on the very first day of gleaning.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET NE AD MOMENTUM QUI- DEM DOMUM REVERSA EST.

In Ebræo, ideo sedet domi paululum: vel his mansio ipsius, domi parum (est, vel sedet) ut Drusius b. l. Alienum est, quod Ludov. de Dieu domum ad prædium Boozi pertinentem intelligit. Consonat Jun. Trem. Pisc. Luther. quod ad sensum; & Pagnin. jam sessio, vel mansio ejus in domo paululum (est) Ita videtur non primo statim spicilegii die eam in- venisse Boas.

## 2:10
Ver. 10. WORSHIPPING UPON THE GROUND] Than which no greater honor could be shown. See at Matt. 2, 11. 8, 2.

Ver. eod. AND THAT YOU SHOULD DEIGN TO KNOW ME.

To know here is, whom you know to love, or to esteem. Words of knowledge imply affection among the Hebrews. Ps. 14 last [verse] & below v. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ADORANS SUPER TERRAM] Quo major honor non poterat exhiberi. Vide ad Matth. 2, 11. 8, 2.

Vers. eod. ET NOSSE ME DIGNARERIS.

Nosse hic est, quem noveris amare, vel æstimare. Verba notitiæ affectum inferunt apud Ebræos. Ps. 14 ult. & infra v. 19.

## 2:12
Ver. 12.

FROM THE LORD GOD OF ISRAEL, TO WHOM YOU HAVE COME] The great piety of Boaz appears, who both admires the piety of a foreign woman and liberally rewards it. Such a man of royal spirit was worthy, from whom a king should be born. Such was Cimon at Athens, who tore down the walls of his fields, so that those who wished might use the things born there.

It is added UNDER WHOSE WINGS YOU HAVE TAKEN REFUGE, for just as chicks are protected under the wings of a hen, so the faithful under the wings of God, Ps. 17, 8. 90, 4. Matt. 23, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

A DOMINO DEO ISRAEL, AD QUEM VENISTI] Magna Boozi pietas apparet, qui feminæ extraneæ pietatem & miratur, & liberaliter repensat. Tam regalis animi vir di- gnus erat, ex quo rex nasceretur. Talis Cimon Athenis, qui ma- cerias agrorum suorum diruit, ut qui vellent rebus ibi natis uterentur.

Additur SUB CUJUS CONFUGISTI ALAS, ut enim pulli sub alis gallinæ proteguntur, ita fide- les sub alis Dei, Ps. 17, 8. 90, 4. Matth. 23, 37.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. IN VINEGAR] Or in lora (a drink made from grape skins): concerning which see Varro on agriculture, book 1, 54. Columella 12, 40.

The frugality of that age is rightly noted here by the interpreters. Vinegar cools those laboring in the heat, constricts the nerves, strengthens the powers, and removes putrefaction. Pliny, book 23, chapter 1. Therefore they made a morsel, dipping bread in vinegar.

Vers. eod. AND SHE HEAPED UP PARCHED GRAIN FOR HIM.

In Hebrew: And he reached out to her (some one of the reapers; or impersonally, it was reached out to her) parched grain, an ear of corn roasted by fire, or roasted wheat; Jonathan: roasted flour, the Arab: pearl barley.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IN ACETO] Aut in lora: de qua vide Varro- nem de re rustica l. 54. Columellam 12, 40.

Frugalitas ævi istius recte hic notata ab Inter- pretibus. Acetum in æstu laborantes refrigerat, ner- vos astringit, vires corroborat, putredinem tollit. Plin. l. 23. c. 1. Offam ergo faciebant, panem intin- gentes aceto.

Vers. eod. ET CONGESSIT POLENTAM SIBI.

In Ebr. Et porrexit ei (messorum quispiam; vel impersonaliter, porrecta est ei) polentam, spicam igne tostam, vel tostum triticum; Jonath. farinam tostam, Arabs ptisanam.

## 2:15
Ver. 15. EVEN IF SHE WISHES TO REMAIN WITH YOU, DO NOT FORBID HER) He performs much more than what the law commands, Lev. 19, 10. 23, 22. Deut. 24, 19. Doubtless those special precepts of the law were only the rudiments of those virtues toward which illustrious souls are carried.

Although by that special law, concerning leaving gleanings for the poor, whatever Boaz performed more, he is not to be judged to have performed more than the Mosaic Law commands concerning the love of one's neighbor. For we ought to love him, by the tenor of the Law, as ourselves, which, since it is the first degree of love that can be directed toward a neighbor, there are in the Mosaic Law indeed not only the rudiments of the virtues of illustrious souls, but the most perfect norm of supreme perfection, and indeed of such a kind as now after the fall falls to no mortal, as the Apostle testifies Rom. 8, 3. This is the rule of love, says St. Augustine, book 1, on true religion, ch. 46, that whatever good things a man wishes to happen to himself, he should also wish for his neighbor, and whatever evil things he does not wish to happen to himself, he should not wish for him. But no one would say that Boaz here transcended this rule by his kindness toward Ruth. We could have passed over these things lightly; but it is known what Grotius disputes elsewhere concerning the observation of the law, on behalf of the Papists, and with them. Concerning which, more fully in its own place.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ETIAMSI VOBISCUM MANERE VOLUE- RIT, NE PROHIBETE EAM) Multo plus præstat, quam quod jubet lex, Levit. 19, 10. 23, 22. Deut. 24, 19. Nimirum præcepta illa specialia legis rudimenta tantum erant earum virtutum, ad quas feruntur illustres animæ.

Licet lege illa speciali, de spicilegio relinquendo pauperibus, quid præstiterit amplius Booz, non ta- men plus præstitisse censendus est, quam jubet Lex Mosaica, de dilectione proximi. Hunc enim diligere debemus, tenore Legis, sicut nosmet ipsos, qui cum primus sit dilectionis, quæ adversus proximum fer- ri potest, gradus, in Lege utique Mosaica non rudi- menta solum habentur virtutum illustrium anima- rum, sed perfectissima norma supremæ perfectionis, & tantæ quidem, quanta nunc post lapsum in nullum cadit mortalium, teste Apostolo Rom. 8, 3. Hæc est regula dilectionis, inquit S. August. l. 1. de ver. relig. c. 46. ut quæ homo sibi vult bona provenire, & proximo velit, ac quæ accidere sibi mala non vult, & illi nolit. Hanc vero regulam Boozum hic transcendisse be- nignitate sua erga Rutham, nemo dixerit. Præterire poteramus ista sicco pede; sed notum est, quid de observatione legis, pro Pontificiis, & cum iisdem alias disputet Grot. Quo de suo loco plenius.

## 2:18
Ver. 18. AND HE GAVE HER OF THE REMAINDER OF HIS FOOD ] Concerning the gifts given to guests to take home.

What he had left over from his lunch, from which she had been satisfied. As Vatablus has it.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ET DEDIT EI DE RELIQVIIS CIBI SUI ] De Apo- phoretis.

Quod de prandio suo reliquum fecerat, ex quo saturata fuerat. Ut Vatabl. habet.

## 2:20
Ver. 20. HE HATH KEPT AND TO THE DEAD] It seems that a kindness is done to the dead when it is well with those whom they held dear for their sake. Claudian, On the Praises of Stilicho, 2: Love is not bound to the living, nor does it cease to remember the buried: the kindness of fathers passes over to their offspring. By this you honored Theodosius while he held the scepter: by this you honor him even after his death: nor do you care more for your own children than for those whom he gave to you to be instructed and protected.

Michael of Ephesus on the 5th book of the Nicomachean Ethics: For what the wife or the children or the relatives received for the murdered man, is in a way given to him. A man about to die in Procopius, first book of the Persian Wars: by benefiting the children you will benefit me. Thus, when Valentinian was dead, Theodosius returned the kindness in his son, as Zosimus testifies.

In the Hebrew, word for word: Who hath not left his mercy, or his kindness, with the living, nor with the dead, as the LXX, Montanus, and Piscator with the Chaldean. Toward the living, that is, toward us: and toward the dead, our husbands.

Ver. same. OUR KINSMAN IS] In the Hebrew is added מנאלנו, he is of those who are our kinsmen. See Leviticus 25:25. Boaz is thought to have been the uncle of Mahlon, but not the eldest of the uncles.

Kinsman in Hebrew is גאל, redeemer: because the kinsman was the redeemer of the wife's field and inheritance, and also of her reputation and injury, whose duty it also was to avenge the death of a kinsman.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SERVAVIT ET MORTUIS] Mortuis videtur benefieri, cum eorum causa bene sit iis, quos illi caros habue- re. Claudianus de laudibus Stiliconis 2. Non vivis annexus amor, meminisse sepultos Desinit: in prolem transcurrit gratia patrum Hac tu Theodosium, tenuit dum sceptra, colebas: Hac etiam post fata colis: nec pignora curas Plus tua, quam natos dederas quos ille monendos Tutandosque tibi.

Michaël Ephesius ad 5. Nicomachiorum: ὁ γὰρ ἡ γυνὴ ἢ οἱ παῖδες ἢ οἱ συγγενεῖς τῶ φονευθέντι ἔλαβον, τρόπον τινὰ ἐκείνῳ δέδοται. Moriturus apud Procopium primo Persico- rum: τὰ παιδία ὠφελῶν ὠφελήσεις ἐμέ. Sic Valentiniano mortuo gratiam in filio ejus reddidit Theodosius, teste Zosimo.

In Ebr. ad verbum: Qui non reliquit mise- ricordiam, vel benignitatem suam cum viventibus, nec cum mortuis, ut LXX. Montan. Piscat. cum Chald. Erga vivos, id est, erga nos: & erga mortuos, mari- tos nostros.

Vers. eod. PROPINQVUS EST NOSTER] In Hebræo additur מנאלנו, ἐκ τῶν ἀγχιστευόντων ἡμῖν ἐστι. Vide Levitici 25, 25. Putatur Booz patruus fuisse Machlonis, sed non maxi- mus natu patruorum.

Propinquus in Ebr. גאל redemtor: quia propinquus redemtor erat agri uxoris & hæreditatis, nec non famæ & injuriæ, cujus erat etiam necem propinqui vindicare.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. Ruth seeks the marriage of Boaz.

Ver. 1. I WILL SEEK REST FOR THEE] A safe life under the protection of a husband.

According to the Hebrews, Vatablus, and Drusius, she calls marriage rest: whence Aben-Ezra says, For a woman, there is no rest until she has married. He understands rest in a general sense, as being freed from hardships, from poverty, from the bereavement of children, and other cares which made the mind restless. Marriage was the means of rest.

Latin:

CAPUT III. Ruth matrimonium Booz postulat.

Vers. 1. QVÆRAM TIBI REQVIEM] Vitam tutam sub ma- riti præsidio.

SEcundum Ebræos, Vatabl. & Drusium requiem vocat nuptias: unde Aben-Ezra, Mulieri, in- quit, nulla requies donec nupserit. Requiem in- telligit in genere ab ærumnis, ab egestate, ab orbita- te liberorum, & aliis curis, quæ animum redde- bant inquietum. Medium requiei erant nuptiæ.

## 3:3
Ver. 3. WASH THYSELF THEREFORE, AND ANOINT] Aids to appearance. See on Matthew 6:17.

Indeed, even the poor were anointed for brightness and joy, but with simple oil, not with stibium or white lead. Do not understand it with Fevardentius as a fragrant ointment: for the scent of this would have betrayed her, wishing to remain hidden: but simple oil: for that was better, and suited both her poverty and the deed, as Bonfrer notes here. But why that cultivation of the body, when everything was done in the dark? Answer: in case it should happen that she was seen, whether by a lamp being brought, or by the light of day glimmering more dimly, or by the arrival of light in the expected morning. And that she was seen in some way is taught by the fact that he measured out to her six measures of barley.

Latin:

Vers. 3. LAVARE IGITUR, ET UNGERE] Formæ adminicu- la. Vide ad Matth. 6, 17.

Nimirum ungebantur ad nitorem & lætitiam etiam pauperes, sed oleo simplici, non vero stibio, aut cerussa. Ne intelligas cum Fevardentio odo- riferum unguentum: hujus enim odor delitesce- re cupientem detexisset: Sed simplex oleum: id enim melius, & paupertati ejus, & facto con- gruebat, ut hic Bonfrer. Quorsum autem ille cor- poris cultus, cum omnia in tenebris gesta? Resp. si forte contingeret, ut conspiceretur sive accersita lucerna, sive diei luce obscurius intermicante, sive expectato mane lucis adventu. Et visam aliquo modo id docet, quod ei sex hordei mensuras ad- mensus est.

## 3:9
Vers. 9. SPREAD THY MANTLE OVER THINE HANDMAID] Receive me as a husband under your protection. See Jer. 4, 1. Euripides to the virgin in Pelias: Ὅταν δ' ὑπ' ἀνδρὸς χλαῖναν εὐγενὺς πέσῃς.

But the protection, which is signified by the wing, does not of itself signify marital protection any more than any other. The word כנף & πτερύγιον among the LXX does not signify the wing of a man metaphorically, but the hem of a mantle or covering, i.e., spread your covering, that it may cover me, and you may receive me into the same bed with you, as Bonfrer says. Or the sense is simpler: Contract marriage with me

& betroth me to yourself, not abruptly at this very hour, but as and when it shall please you, as the added explanatory words teach: Cover me, I pray. See Isa. 4, 1. Since the Jews, as Serarius notes, when the bridegroom gives his pledge to the bride, are in the habit of having the bridegroom place a part of his garment upon the bride, signifying by this gesture that he receives her into partnership and conjugal protection. i.e., Spread your garment, or only the hem of your garment, in the manner of those who were betrothing a wife, as Vatablus with Lyra & Serarius, Cornel. a Lap. & others: Which sense is held from the ratification of Boaz, verse 11, whatever you shall say to me, I will do for you.

Latin:

Vers. 9. EXPANDE PALLIUM TVUM SUPER FAMVLAM TVAM] Sub tutelam tuam ut maritus me recipe. Vide Je- rem. 4, 1. Euripides Peliasi ad virginem: Ὅταν δ' ὑπ' ἀνδρὸς χλαῖναν εὐγενὺς πέσῃς.

At protectio, quæ per alam significatur, per se non magis significat protectionem maritalem, quam aliam quamlibet. Vox כנף & πτερύγιον apud LXX. non significat alam hominis meta- phorice, sed oram pallii seu straguli q. d. extende stragulum tuum, ut me tegat, & intra eundem thorum tecum me recipias, ut Bonfrer. vel sim- plicius sensus est: Contrahe matrimonium mecum

& desponde me tibi, non ἀποτόμως hac ipsa ho- ra, sed prout, & quando libuerit, ut ἐξηγητικῶς addita docent: Obnubito quæso me. Vid. Esa. 4, 1. siquidem Judæi notante Serario, cum fidem Spon- sus dat Sponsæ, in usu habeant, ut sponsus partem vestimenti sui imponat sponsæ, significans hoc gestu, se eam in consortium, & tutelam conjuga- lem recipere. q. d. Expande vestem, vel oram tan- tum vestis tuæ, more eorum, qui despondebant uxo- rem, ut Vatabl. cum Lyr. & Serar. Cornel. a Lap. & alii: Qui sensus habetur ex ratihabitione Boas, vers. 11. quicquid dixeris mihi, efficiam tibi.

## 3:10
Vers. 10.

BECAUSE THOU HAST NOT FOLLOWED YOUNG MEN] It is rare in young women to prefer elderly gravity to youthful charms: that makes the counsel honest, which otherwise would seem base.

It was done by the inspiration of GOD, says the Author of the Imperfect Work on Matthew 1, but without foundation. Ambrose, book 3 on faith, chapter 3, disapproves of it as not sufficiently honest. She could certainly have requested marriage in another way. And Cornelius himself acknowledges this with Abulensis, Salianus, & Serarius, excusing it against Lyranus, that this act is not to be imitated, because it is dangerous and enticing to fornication. Osiander explains the imprudence of this counsel: which, however, GOD in his goodness turned to good. And Ruth conducted herself modestly, using no blandishments of words or actions, and placing herself crosswise at his feet, not at the side of the sleeper, as those in Genesis 19. She lay quiet all night, nor did she solicit the sleeper; when he was awakened, she asked for marriage, and indeed in a modest and very honest way of speaking, as Serarius says here: nor was she naked, but clothed: and she arranged it in such a way that she avoided the offense of her neighbor by the circumstances of place and time, for the rest, trusting in the age and piety of Boaz, and not doing it of her own accord but commanded and instructed by her mother-in-law. Although the manner was unusual and dangerous, for a woman adorned to approach secretly through the darkness alone to him alone while he was lying down and exhilarated by an evening meal, as Bonfrer acknowledges, guessing in vain that this was commanded by God.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

QVIA NON ES SECVTA JUVENES] Rarum in ju- venculis senilem gravitatem juvenilibus amœnitatem ante- habere: id honestum facit consilium, quod alioqui turpe videretur.

Ex inspiratione DEI factum, ait Autor imperfect. Oper. in Matth. 1. sed citra fundamentum. Ambrosius lib. 3. de fid. cap. 3. improbat quasi parum honestum. Alia certe ratione postulare poterat matrimonium. Et agnoscit ipse Cornelius id cum Abulensi, Saliano & Serario adversus Lyranum excusans, factum hoc imitandum non esse, quia periculosum, & ad forni- cationem illiciens. Imprudentia hujus consilii explicat Osiander: quod tamen DEUS pro bonita- te sua in bonum convertit. Et modeste se gessit Ruth nullis verborum aut factionum blanditiis usa ac pedes se transversum collocans, non ad dor- mientis latus, ut illæ Genes. 19. Tota nocte quie- ta jacuit, nec dormientem solicitavit, ab eo ex- citato matrimonium petiit, & quidem verecun- do, ac perhonesto loquendi modo, ut hic Sera- rius: nec nuda, sed vestita fuit: idque ita insti- tuit, ut offensionem proximi circumstantiis loci & temporis vitarit, de cætero, Boazi senio & pie- tati confisa, nec id sponte sua sed jussa & instru- cta a socru sua. Quanquam modus insolens & periculosus fuerit, mulierem ornatam, clam per tenebras solam ad solum eumque cubantem, & ve- spertina cœna exhilaratum accedere, ut agnoscit Bonfrer. nequicquam conjectans, hoc a Deo impe- ratum fuisse.

## 3:12
THERE IS ANOTHER KINSMAN NEARER THAN I] Not in degree, but prior in the order of birth.

Indeed, the Hebrews according to Drusius observe that this man was the brother of Elimelech: Boaz only the son of a brother.

Latin:

EST ALIUS ME PROPINQVIOR] Non gradu, sed na- scendi ordine prior.

Imo Ebræi apud Drusium observant istum fuisse fratrem Elimelechi: Booz tantum filium fratris.

## 3:15
vers. 15. SIX MEASURES OF BARLEY.

The Vulgate must be corrected. For how could Ruth have carried so many bushels? In the Hebrew it is six of barley; some understand an ephah, others seahs, others a homer. The homer was a common measure, and the tenth part of an ephah: therefore she easily carried six homers, and could contain them in a woman's apron.

Latin:

vers. 15. SEX MODIOS HORDEI.

Corrigenda est Vulgata. Quomodo enim Ruth tot modios portare potuisset? In Ebr. est, sex hordeorum, alii epha, alii sata, alii gomor subintel- ligunt. Gomor familiaris mensura erat, & decima pars ephæ: Sex ergo Gomor facile portabat, & suc- cintorio muliebri continere poterat.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. The kinsman ceding his right, Boaz marries Ruth, begetting of her Obed, the father of David.

Ver. 1. CALLING HIM BY HIS NAME.

In Hebrew it is פלוני אלמוני Ploni Almoni: ὁ δεῖνα, as Jun. Piscat. Drus. 'You whoever you are,' Tigur. For thus the Hebrews call one whom they do not wish to name, as if they signify that that name is hidden and kept silent, as Bonfrer and Serarius warn; because פלה is 'he hid,' and אלם is 'mute'.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. Propinquo jure suo cedente, Booz Ruthæ ducit, ex ea Obedum patrem David procreans.

Vers. 1. VOCANS EUM NOMINE SUO.

In Ebr. est פלוני אלמוני Ploni Almoni : ὁ δεῖνα, ut Jun. Piscat. Drus. Tu quisquis es, Tigur. Ita enim Ebræi vocant, quem nominare nolunt, quasi significent, nomen illud abscondi, & sileri, ut Bonfrer. & Serarius monent; quia פלה est oc- cultavit, & אלם est mutus.

## 4:2
Vers. 11.

BUT BOAZ TAKING TEN MEN] Which is עוד עד, accustomed to be employed for legitimate acts, such as marriage, divorce, emancipation, and cession in law.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

TOLLENS AUTEM BOOZ DECEM VI- ROS] Quod est עוד עד, adhibere solita ad actus legi- timos, ut matrimonii, divortii, mancipationis, cessionis in jure.

## 4:5
Verse 5.

RUTH ALSO THE MOABITESS, WHO WAS THE WIFE OF THE DECEASED YOU OUGHT TO TAKE] Naturally by the Law which is in Deut. 25:5 and following, with the custom having been extended by the author from brothers to other kinsmen, as we have said at that place. The Hebrews, however, say that here it is only a matter of the field, which had been given by the husband of Ruth. But what connection is there then: if you wish to have the field, you must also have the widow. And is not the taking off of the shoe here clearly as in Deuteronomy? Then indeed Josephus, not ignorant of the ancestral laws, explains this passage just as we have said.

Sixtinus Amama therefore wrongly corrects the Vulgate and Luther's version; and prefers the Genevan, Junian, Piscator's, the English, and the Italian translation, which has it thus: 'You must also from RUTH, that is, on account of Ruth, and in the name of Ruth, buy.' That the discourse is about marrying the widow, Grotius rightly proves. Not only the Vulgate agrees, but also the Chaldean, as well as the LXX Interpreters. And thus the Tigurines also rendered it, taking the word מאת for the simple את, which interpretation Drusius also says he prefers. Ludov. de Dieu interprets the Qere, which he wishes to be read קנית, not at all inconveniently: 'And Boaz said, on the day you acquire the field from the hand of Naomi, and from Ruth the Moabitess, you shall acquire the wife of the deceased, to raise up the name of the deceased upon the inheritance,' that is, by that very fact, that you will purchase this field for yourself not only from Naomi, but from the wife of the deceased, know that you are making her yours as well. But because the Kethiv has קניתי, he translates it thus: 'And Boaz said, on the day you acquire the field from the hand of Naomi, I would also acquire from Ruth the Moabitess the wife of the deceased, to raise up the name of the deceased, etc.' or, 'and from Ruth the Moabitess I would acquire the wife of the deceased, to etc.' that is, 'since you are acquiring the field of the deceased, if I were who I am, or if you ask me what I myself would do in that matter, I would also take the wife of the deceased.' And he accepts the explanation of Aben-Ezra in that sense.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

RUTH QVOQVE MOABITIDEM, QVÆ UXOR DEFUNCTI FUIT DEBES ACCIPERE] Nimirum Lege quæ est Deuteron. 25, 5. & sequentibus, auctore consuetudine a fratribus producta ad propinquos alios, ut ad eum locum diximus. Hebræi tamen hîc de agro tantum agi ajunt, qui à marito Ruthæ donatus fuerit. At quæ igitur connexio: si agrum habere vis, debes & viduam habere. Et excalceatio nonne hic plane, ut in Deuteronomio ? Tum vero Josephus legum patriarum non ignarus, ita ut nos diximus explicat hunc locum.

Male ergo corrigit Sixtinus Amama vul- gatam, & Lutheri versionem; ac præfert Gene- vensem, Junianam, Piscatoris, Anglicanam, & Italicam translationem, quæ ita habet: Debes & a RUTHA, id est, propter Rutham, & no- mine Ruthæ emere. De ducenda vidua sermo- nem esse, recte probat Grotius. Consonat non Vulgatus tantum, sed etiam Chaldæus, ut & LXX. Interpp. Atque ita reddidere quoque Tigurini, vo- cem מאת accipientes pro simplici את quam interpretationem & Drusius se præoptare dicit. Ludov. de Dieu ita קרי, quod legi vult קנית interpretatur, non sane incommode : Et dixit Boas, quo die acquisieris agrum e manu Naomi, & a Rutha Moabitide, uxorem defuncti acqui- sieris, ad suscitandum nomen defuncti super hæredi- tatem, id est, eo ipso, quod non tantum a Naomi, sed ab uxore defuncti hunc agrum tibi comparabis, scito te & ipsam tuam facere. Quia vero כתיב habet קניתי id ita vertit : Et dixit Booz, quo die acquiris agrum e manu Naomi, etiam a Rutha Moabitide uxore defuncti acquirerem, ad susti- tandum nomen defuncti &c. vel, & a Rutha Moa- bitide uxorem defuncti acquirerem, ad &c. id est, quin acquiris defuncti agrum, si essem qui es, aut si ex me quæras quid in ea re egomet facturus es- sem, uxorem quoque defuncti ducerem. Eoque sensu accipit Aben-Ezræ explicationem.

## 4:6
Verse 6.

FOR I OUGHT NOT TO DESTROY THE POSTERITY OF MY FAMILY] In the Hebrew: 'lest perhaps I corrupt my inheritance.' As if he were saying, I prefer to take another wife, so that there may be heirs for me, not for the dead man. But Josephus thinks, as we have seen, that this man had a wife and children: therefore, I think, he understood these words thus: I do not wish to bring another wife upon myself, and bring other children into the house, lest I disturb the peace of my family, and intent on foreign matters, I neglect my own.

In verse 7.

THE MAN LOOSED HIS SHOE AND GAVE IT TO HIS NEIGHBOR.

By the handing over of the shoe he designated the cession of the right, as if to say: 'Behold, I hand over to you the shoe with which I have hitherto trodden, or could have trodden, the field, so that you may tread it.' Cf.

Deut. 33, last verse. Psalm 107, verse 10. See Bonfrer and Piscator.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NEQVE ENIM POSTERITATEM FAMILIÆ MEÆ DELERE DEBEO] In Hebræo: ne forte corrumpam hæ- reditatem meam. Quasi dicat, malo aliam uxorem duce- re, ut mihi, non mortuo, hæredes sint. At Josephus putat, ut vidimus, huic homini fuisse uxorem & liberos: itaque hæc verba, puto, sic intellexit: nolo mihi aliam uxorem su- peraccersere, & alios in domum liberos adducere, ne pa- cem turbem familiæ meæ, & alienis rebus intentus meas ne- gligam.

Versu 7.

SOLVEBAT HOMO CALCEAMENTUM SUUM ET DABAT PROXIMO SUO.

Calcei traditione juris cessionem designabat q. d. En trado tibi calceum quo hactenus calcavi, vel calcare potui agrum, ut tu eam calces. Conf.

Deut. 33. vers. ult. Psalm. 107. vers. 10. Vid. Bonfrer. & Piscator.

## 4:11
Verse 11.

MAY THE LORD MAKE THIS WOMAN WHO ENTERS YOUR HOUSE LIKE RACHEL AND LEAH] A formula of auspicious wishing at weddings, now also used by the Jews.

For from Rachel and Leah were the most illustrious tribes: Ephraim, Benjamin, Judah, and Levi. From Leah were the Bethlehemite; and Rachel had an illustrious tomb in a place in the suburb of Bethlehem. And verse 12. LIKE THE HOUSE OF PHAREZ. Who was the progenitor of the Bethlehemite, and whose family stood out as the chief among the five families of Judah.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

FACIAT DOMINUS HANC MULIEREM QUÆ IN- GREDITUR DOMUM TUAM SICUT RACHEL ET LIAM] Formula faustæ apprecationis in nuptiis, nunc etiam Judæis usitata.

A Rahele enim & Lia erant tribus maxi- me illustres Ephraim, Benjamin, Juda, & Levi. A Lia erant Bethlehemitæ; & Rahel habebat il- lustre sepulcrum in suburbano Bethlehem loco. Et vers. 12. SICUT DOMUS PHAREZ. Qui progenitor Bethlehemitarum erat, & cujus familia ex quinque Judæ familiis præcipua exi- stebat.

## 4:13
Vers. 13.

BOAZ TOOK RUTH. For she had already been converted, and therefore, even though a foreigner, she could be married.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

TULIT BOOZ RUTH. Jam enim conversa erat, ideoque etsi aliegena duci poterat.

## 4:15
vers. 15.

FOR YOUR DAUGHTER-IN-LAW HAS BORN HIM, WHO LOVES YOU. Capellus rashly suspects that יוֹלֶדֶתְּ should be read instead of יוֹלַדְתְּ, i.e., because your daughter-in-law who loves you has born, and not יוֹלֶדֶתּ. For the infant is being looked at, as the Vulgate, i.e., Your daughter-in-law, who has led you, has born him (the infant). As the LXX also, Jonathan, the Syrian, Pagninus, Junius, and Tremellius explain. See Buxtorf in Vind. page 987.

Latin:

vers. 15.

DE NVRU ENIM TUA NATUS EST, QUÆ TE DILIGIT. Temere suspicatur Capell. legendum esse יוֹלֶדֶתְּ pro יוֹלַדְתְּ h. m. quia peperit nurus tua, quæ te amat, non vero יוֹלֶדֶתּ Nam infans re- spicitur, ut Vulg. h. m. Peperit eum (infantem) nu- rus tua, quæ duxit te. Ut LXX. etiam, Jonath. Syrus, Pagn. Jun. Tremell. exponunt. Vid. Buxtorf. in Vind. pag. 987.

## 4:17
vers. 17.

SALMON BEGAT BOAZ. Salmon was the husband of Rahab, Jos. 2. From the entry of the Hebrews into Canaan in the time of Rahab, 440 years have passed until the 4th year of Solomon, 1 Kings 6, 2. In so many years, therefore, there were only five generations: Salmon begat Boaz, from him Obed, from him Jesse begat David, whose son was Solomon, so that the first four, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse, begat children when they were nearly one hundred years old. Nor is this surprising: because Jacob also begat Benjamin in his 107th year, as can be seen in Gen. 35: and Caleb in the 84th year of his age was firm and clearly vigorous; indeed, in our own age, men 90 years old have still procreated children in these regions. Thomas Pavennas, ch. 5 of his book on prolonging human life beyond 120 years, affirms that two men from Lacedaemon and two others in the Aegean Sea were seen who were 130 years old. But as for Rahab, if she was twenty years old at the entry of Israel into Canaan, and had born Boaz after 42 years, she would not have exceeded the 62nd year of her age: but she would have brought forth Boaz in her 55th year, if she received the spies in her 15th year: and Boaz was 117 years old when he fathered Obed by Ruth. Compare here the Chronologists and Poole on this passage. This genealogy is deduced down to David, which is repeated in Matthew 1 on account of the ancestors of Christ, so that the truth of the divine promises concerning the Messiah might be established, as one who had to arise from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David, according to the flesh, GOD blessed forever over all. Amen.

Latin:

vers. 17.

SALMON GENUIT BOOZ. Salmon maritus fuit Rahab, Jos. 2. Ab in- gressu autem Ebræorum in Canaan tempore Ra- hab anni 440. præterlapsi sunt usque ad 4. an- num Salomonis 1. Reg. 6, 2. In tot ergo annis quinque tantum fuere generationes : Salmon ge- nuit Booz, hic Obed, ab hoc Jesse genitus Da- videm genuit, cujus filius Salomo fuit, ut priores quatuor Salmon, Booz, Obed, & Jesse fere cen- tum annos nati genuerint. Neque hoc mirum : quia & Jacob 107. anno Benjamin, ut videre est Gen. 35. genuit: & Caleb anno ætatis 84. firmus, & plane vegetus fuit; imo nostra ætate 90. annos nati adhuc liberos in his oris procrearunt. Tho- mas Pavennas, c. 5. libri de vita hominis ultra 120. annos protrahenda, duos viros ex Lacedæmone, & duos alios in Ægeo mari singulos 130. anno- rum visos fuisse affirmat. Quod vero ad Raha- bam, si vicenaria sub ingressum Israel in Canaan fuit, & post 42. annos Boozum peperisset, an- num ætatis 62. non excessisset: sed 55. anno edidisset Boozum, si 15. anno exploratores exce- pit: & Booz 117. annorum fuit, cum e Rutha Obedum suscepit. Conf. hic Chronologi & Po- lus in h. l. Deducitur autem hic genealogia usque ad Davidem, quæ Matth. 1. ob majores Christi repetita est, ut constaret de promissionum di- vinarum de Messia veritate, utpote qui ex tribu Juda, & semine Davidis oriri debebat, secundum carnem, DEUS benedictus in secula super omnia. Amen.

# 1 Samuel

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
TO THE FIRST BOOK AMONG

Latin:

AD LIBRUM PRI APUD H QVI APUD PRIMUS

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius's Preface
GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

The four books which now follow are called βασιλειῶν by the Greeks: and thus they are also called by certain ancient Latins by the Greek name: that is, of Kingdoms, because they say it is first about the kingdom of the XII tribes: then about the kingdom of Judah and Israel now divided among themselves. The Latins preferred to call them of Kings. And indeed they contain a sufficiently extensive history of the deeds performed by the kings, with only the history of Samuel prefixed, which itself was very necessary for knowing the origin of the institution of the kingdom. Later Hebrews, however, name the four books of Kings: but the two former, of Samuel; which may seem strange, since only the former, and indeed only a part of it, contains the affairs of Samuel. Nor, however, was there lacking to them a reason to follow. For the end of Saul shows that the things which Samuel had predicted to Saul were true: and the things which the other book narrates about the affairs of David, the prophecies of the same Samuel made to David confirm. Added to this is that Samuel anointed both, and instructed them with counsels; which, when spurned by Saul, God avenged, and gave to David, who obeyed the same, very prosperous and magnificent things. If anyone wishes to compare some of the foreigners to these, he will find Samuel always tenacious of the just and the right, a contemner of wealth, like Aristides. Saul, mixed of virtues and vices, and in both inconstant, like Alcibiades. David, from a private citizen a Prince, brave, ingenious, fortunate in war, renowned for victories, a subduer of nations, very clement, but woman-loving, like Caesar the Dictator. The writer of these four books is believed by the most learned of the Hebrews to be Jeremiah. The form of speech does not differ: see what we shall say at 1 Kings 6, 2. It is credible that he used those commentaries of Nathan and Gad the Prophets, of whom mention is made in 1 Chronicles 29, 29. And the Council of Frankfurt cites these books under the name of Jeremiah.

Others make Samuel himself the author of the first book of Samuel up to chapter 25, but Nathan with Gad, or some one of the disciples of Samuel, the continuator, who also wrote the later book. But it is hardly permitted to determine anything certain about these, except that in 1 Chronicles 29, verse 29, the deeds of David are said to be described in the words of SAMUEL the seer, namely, as far as the beginning: since the continuation of them was necessarily done by others. Interpreters on the books of Kings are celebrated by Sixtus Senensis, from the ancients Diodorus of Tarsus around the year 360, Eucherius of Lyon, and Isidore the Elder, Bishop of Cordoba, in the year of the Lord 430, and around the year 500, Procopius of Gaza. Hippolytus, Methodius, Theodotus, Anastasius, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and Bernard explained certain particles from the History of Kings. Sixtus also praises Angelomus the Monk, who [wrote] the 4th book of Stromata on the books of Kings in the year 830. And Andrew the Gaul, who wrote a Scholastic Postil on the same before Lyranus. Of the more recent ones, Victorinus Strigelius, Sanctius, and Serarius have commented on the books of Samuel and Kings; but Jerome Weller, as well as Peter Martyr, wrote separately on the books of Samuel. On the books of Kings, the same Martyr, and Mendoza, who also published certain things on book 1 of Samuel. The chronology of the first book of Samuel is of 40 years: namely, how long Samuel and Saul presided, Acts 13, 20 seqq. There are three parts: 1. The History of Samuel, up to chapter 9. 2. The History of King Saul up to his rejection, to chapter 16. 3. The rest of his history, and about the persecutions of David up to the death of Saul, chapter 31.

OF SAMUEL [TO THE] HEBREWS, [TO THE] LATINS [OF] KINGS.

or according to the dichotomy 1. The History of Samuel, 2. The History of Saul. Of the former, first the Nativity is described in chapter 1, and because of it the Eucharistic-Prophetic hymn of his mother Hannah. Furthermore, the rudiments of the ministry of Samuel, and the impiety of the sons of Eli as the cause of their rejection, and the occasion of the assumption of Samuel, chapter 2. Thirdly, the calling of Samuel and the prediction of the punishment of Eli, through which great authority is gained for Samuel in the Prophetic office, chapter 3, are exhibited: with the completion of the prophecy, the Israelites being defeated, and the ark of the Lord captured, Eli miserably perishing, chapter 4, and the consequent striking of Dagon and the Philistines, done by the ark of the Lord, chapter 5, and its dismissal with golden gifts to the Bethshemites, and the punishment of these for their irreverence, chapter 6. Fourthly, the ark having been transferred to Kiriath-jearim, Samuel recalls the people to repentance, and having abdicated idols, intercedes for them before God, judge of the people in Mizpah, and avenger against the Philistines struck and humiliated by a miraculous thunder, ruling the people in Ramah, and instituting ecclesiastical visitations, in peace, chapter 7. Fifthly, when the sons of Samuel degenerated, the people demanded a King, whose rights Samuel proposed to them, chapter 8.

The history of Saul is distributed into two sections: The first is of Saul elected and approved. The other of him rejected and reprobated. In the former, first occurs the calling of Saul, chapter 9, then his anointing, prophecy, and confirmation as King, chapter 10, and furthermore the deeds performed in his reign are described up to his rejection: namely (1.) Victory against the Ammonites, with a subsequent new confirmation, chapter 11, and the exhortation of Samuel to the fear and worship of God, chapter 12. (2.) Victory against the Philistines, with the consequent sacrifice of Saul, and the rejection denounced to him for that reason, chapter 13. (3.) The victory of Jonathan against the Philistines, which Saul followed up and bravely routed the enemies. (4.) The remaining victories of Saul, chapter 14, and especially against the Amalekites, by sparing whose cattle and King, Saul is rejected from the kingdom for the second time, chapter 15.

In the latter Section, those things which were done after Saul was rejected are set forth, namely 1. The election of David, chap. 16. 2. The striking down of Goliath, chap. 17. 3. The various persecution by Saul, (1.) Attempted by the demand of 200 Philistine foreskins, chap. 18. (2.) By piercing with a spear, and when he escaped by the help of Michal, by the sending out of attendants, chap. 19. (3.) And furthermore, when, having been sent away by Jonathan with the prior sign of arrows, he betook himself to flight, chap. 20. and having received a sword from Ahimelech, he went to Achish King of Gath, chap. 21. and from there betook himself into the cave of Adullam, and having collected some band, returned into Judea, by the continuous pursuit of David, then before the covenant entered into with David: with Ahimelech and other priests killed and their city destroyed, chap. 22. The intended capture of David in Keilah, and his apprehension in the wilderness of Maon, chap. 23. as also in the wilderness of Engedi, where Saul acknowledged the faithfulness of David and struck a covenant with him, chap. 24. then also after that covenant was entered into: where after the death of Samuel, and the ignominy brought upon David by Nabal, chap. 25. a new persecution befell David among the Ziphites, but Saul, shut up into the hands of David, whom he did not wish to be killed, acknowledged his guilt, having promised security to David, chap. 26. 4. David's dwelling with the King of Gath in Ziklag, and the striking of the neighboring nations, chap. 27. 5. The expedition of the Philistine war: in the description of which are related (1.) the destruction announced to Saul, struck with fear, consulting a Pythoness, chap. 28. (2.) The happy conflict of David, dismissed from the war, chap. 29. with the Amalekite plunderers of Ziklag, chap. 30. (3.) The miserable end of the life of the defeated Saul, chap. 31.

ONE OF THE DAUGHTERS OF BELIAL) Thy servant, thy handmaid, are words of honor among the Hebrews, as Gen. 33, 5. c. 42, 10. Ruth 3, 9. Men בליעל, that is, without a yoke, as Jerome interprets, are called those who have no law of living: therefore the Greeks sometimes translate them παράνομοι, sometimes λοιμοί, sometimes ἄσεβεις, sometimes ἄφρονες. And in this place the LXX have, εἰς θυγατίρα λοιμήν: Theodotion, ὡς μίαν τῶν ἀπαιδεύτων.

Vers. 17. MAY THE GOD OF ISRAEL GRANT THEE THY PETITION) God often directs the words of a priest. See John 11, 51.

Vers. 18. AND HER COUNTENANCE WAS NO MORE CHANGED) She was so full of good hope.

PART I. OF THE FIRST BOOK OF SAMUEL. THE HISTORY OF SAMUEL.

Latin:

GROTII PRÆFATIO.

LIBRI qui jam sequuntur quatuor, βασιλειῶν dicuntur Græcis : & sic a Latinis etiam quibusdam veteribus, Græco nomine appellantur : id est, Regnorum, quia primum de XII. tribuum regno ajunt: deinde de regno Judæ & Israëlis jam inter se divisis. Latini Regum dicere maluerunt. Et sane historiam satis fusam continent rerum gestarum a regibus, præposita tantum Samuelis historia, quæ ipsa ad noscendam originem instituti regni erat pernecessaria. He- bræi tamen posteriores ex quatuor nominant Regum libros : priores autem duos Samuelis; quod mirum videri potest, cum prior tantum, & quidem parte sui Samuelis res conti- neat. Neque tamen defuit illis quam sequerentur ratio. Nam Saulis exitus ostendit vera fuisse quæ Sauli Samuel prædixerat : & quæ liber alter de Davidis rebus narrat, Sa- muelis ejusdem vaticinia Davidi facta comprobant. Acce- dit quod unxit utrumque Samuel, & consiliis instruxit; quæ spreta a Saule vindicavit Deus, Davidi iisdem parenti res dedit valde prosperas atque magnificas. Si quis externorum aliquos his velit comparare,inveniet Samuelem justi ac recti semper tenacem, opum comtemtorem, qualis Aristides.
