Nec vero affine est, cum populus Regem postularet, Deum illi responde- re voluisse de consuetudine non Regum, sed Ty- rannorum, aut annuendo postulatis de Rege con- stituendo, solum abusum regiæ dignitatis indicasse, de usu autem ejusdem & potestate legitima, ac jure Regis proprio & vero nihil plane significasse. Por- ro si illa omnia, quæ ibi recensentur in illo משפט attendantur, nihil iisdem iniqui inest, tantum abest ut ipsum משפט iniquum censeri debeat. Quid enim in eo iniqui, si Rex, urgente aut status sui conditione & majestate, aut ipsa Reipublicæ necessitate, tollat ali- quos subditorum, & ponat in curribus suis, faciat- que sibi equites, & præcursores quadrigarum; si constituat sibi Tribunos, & Centuriones & arato- res agrorum suorum, & Messores segetum, & fabros armorum, & curruum suorum: Si filias etiam eo- rum faciat sibi unguentarias & focarias, & panificas. Quid iniqui, si agros & vineas, & oliveta optima subditorum in casu necessitatis tollat, & servis suis pro salute Reipubl. excubantibus destinet? Mul- tis utique hominibus indiget Rex, qui alienis ocu- lis videt, alienis manibus laborat, alienis pedibus currit; Et qui hic designantur, Regibus omnes ne- cessarii sunt: Utpote Satellites, seu corporis custo- des, qui domi ad præsidium præsto sint, & foris pu- blicæ dignatis causa eum comitentur. Ministri aulici, qui partim in cubiculo, partim ad mensam serviant, in quem finem optimos juvenes selectos ob- servat Maimonides, qui à corporis & mentis deco- re fuerint commendatissimi. Porro requiruntur & panifici ac coqui ob vitæ sustentationem: fabri item atque artifices, si quid ædificare necessum sit; & agricolæ ac vinitores, & pastores, ad œconomiam; Requiruntur securitatis publicæ causa Capitanei, Centuriones &c. Neque enim de acceptione hoc intelligendum, quæ per vim aut spolium, aut frau- dem & dolum fit: siquidem accipi possint bona sub- ditorum cum consensu, & compensationis con- ditione. Ministerio liberorum usus est Rex, si qui voluerint ob mercedem, aut spe gratiæ operam impen- dere, accedente parentum aut eorum, quorum inter- est, consensu, teste Maimonide; atque id hic ei so- lum concessum. Nec de ea acceptione agitur, quæ proprii solum commodi, augendi peculii, vel fisci sui causa fit, sed quæ in usum & necessitatem reipubli- cæ cedat. Decimarum etiam acceptio non magis iniqua censeri debet, quam tributorum exactio, quam jure divino sibi vendicat Magistratus Rom. 13, 2. Ac ne dubium supersit, jus verum Regium hic sanciri, non significatur modo hoc loco, submisisse se populum in hanc formam regiminis, cum isto etiam onere vers. 19. & 20. Deumque illam submissionem acceptasse: & sub hac conditione cum eodem contraxisse, ac Regem ea Lege ipsi præfecisse vers. 22. Sed jus etiam illud Regium ibi publicatum consignari debuit divino jussu, & in archivis instar sancti alicujus depositi, conservari: cap. 10, 25. non ad terrorem modo, sed etiam ad notitiam obligationis subditorum perpetuam conservandam.

Neque quicquam huic משפט contrarium inest juri Deut. 17. descripto. Nimia ibi equorum multiplicatio ea fini facta, ut reducat Rex populum in Ægyptum numero equitatus sublevatus, prohibetur; tum ne in immensum argenti, & auri ponderibus inhiet, per avaritiam, ac rapacitatem; & ne super fratres elevetur per superbiam: quæ hic minime indulta sunt. Et disparata esse illa loca nemo non videt: in Mose enim traditur officium Regis; hic autem subditorum; ibi modus imperandi, hic necessitas parendi describitur; Proinde si maxime hic recenserentur quædam, quæ Regi non licerent (quod vero non concedimus) subditis tamen non licere illis resistere, sed parendum esse, docetur.

Quod autem vers. 18. hujus nostri loci habetur de clamore ad Dominum, non præcise respicit injurias Regum futurorum, sed deteriorem solum populi statum, utpote talibus minime assueti, & qui sub Θεοκρατείᾳ libertate longe sereniori frui poterat; ac si maxime injurias etiam respiceret, non tamen illæ, vi hujus משפט, inferuntur, sed ex abusu potestatis & juris Regii, adeoque de facto. Proinde geminum dehortationis argumentum adhiberi à Domino, dici potest; alterum à jure Regio, quod ipsis inconsuetum, adeoque durum comparate, respectu aureæ istius libertatis, qua fruebantur, futurum sit; Alterum ab abusu juris istius, quod ne tum quidem sint audiendi, si Reges etiam ipsos præter fas oppresserint, & iniquiores futuri sint, quia semel, rejecto Deo, ejusque regimine, Regem alium petierunt, ac Domino etiam σκολιῷ obtemperandum, in cujus imperium quis redactus, nedum quem ipse expetiit, aut in quem sciens prudens consensit, 1. Petr. 2, 18. Sed non mirum Grotium hic משפט de jure usurpativo interpretari, ac de more Tyrannico, siquidem id maximopere extendat; Dominatus hic Regius, inquit in annotat. ad h. l. secum ferebat, ut pro arbitrio Reges delectus facerent, capitationes & operas hominibus, tributa agris, mercibus vectigalia imponerent, contradicente nemine. Illud enim ibi locum habebat: Rex sum, nil ultra quæro plebejus. Et impune quidvis facere, id est Regem esse. Hæc Grotius. Sed illa omnia in hoc jure Regio ex mente Dei, conditionem proponentis, aut populi suscipientis contineri, unde probabitur? Non arbitrio & libidini privatæ Regum ista prorsus permittuntur, sed necessitati & saluti Reipublicæ indulgentur, à qua iisdem modus & determinatio constitui debet: Neque excessus, vel extensio tanta potestatis modum legitimi Regiminis egrediens, conceditur; Sed potestas intra justitiæ & æquitatis terminos coercetur, ut in timore Domini regimen geratur, omniaque ad gloriam Dei & salutem Reipublicæ, quæ supremæ leges sunt, dirigantur. Quis admittet Deum indulgere Regi sive hic, sive alibi, facere quidvis & quodcunque libuerit animo ejus, & in authentica hac, qua in throno Regio constituent- di erant Israelitiei Reges, quæque ideo in archi- vis asservanda erat, Regem sic definiisse, impune quidvis facere, id est Regem esse. Solide atque accu- rate jus hoc post B. Gerhardum nostrum adseruit ve- nerandus Dn. Socer meus D. Hülsemannus Extensio- ne Breviar. Theolog. cap. 20. §. 12. ut & Dn. D. Wandelinus Archi - Episcopus jam Danæ, Ami- cus singulariter colendus, libris eruditis de Jure Regio editis. Nullam certe videmus causam, cur cum Judæis R. Jehuda & Levi Gerson, Calvinianis, Pezelio, Zeppero, Tossano, Calvino ipso, & Papistis, Becano, Adamo à Conzen, & aliis hic facere, ac de jure usurpato locum interpretari debeamus. Quæ enim Wilhelm Schickardus de jure Regio prolixe disputat, ex his, quæ diximus sine negotio expedi- ri posse existimamus. Nimis facile Ebræi nostri Rabbinis fimbrias suas undique extendentibus fi- dem adhibent, hinc non mirum eruditos cætera Viros à genuino sensu scripturæ abduci.

Præcipuum videri potest illud adversæ partis argumentum, quod decimæ ex instituto divino per- sonarum sacrarum fuerint : à quibus tamen non exclusas omnino fuisse personas politicas, R. Mo- ses Maimonides asserit. Etsi autem alias Regis de- cimæ non commemorentur, nunquam tamen ab istis Reges exclusi leguntur, & necessum non est, ut vox decimarum hic ἀποτόμως de parte decima ac- cipiatur, quum species tributi pro genere posita intel- ligi queat.

## 8:18
Vers. 18.

THE LORD WILL NOT HEAR YOU IN THAT DAY, BECAUSE YOU ASKED FOR A KING FOR YOURSELVES) Many things are of will at the beginning, then of necessity. You must eat what you have baked.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

NON EXAVDIET VOS DOMINVS IN DIE ILLA, QVIA PETISTIS VOBIS REGEM) Multa ab initio sunt voluntatis, deinde necesitatis. Exedendum est quod intristi.

## 8:19
Verse 19.

BUT THE PEOPLE REFUSED TO HEAR THE VOICE OF SAMUEL) The common people are captivated by empty things, and love changes. It seemed beautiful to them to behold a man gilded and jeweled, living and feasting splendidly, proceeding with a huge retinue, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

NOLVIT AVTEM POPVLVS AVDIRE VOCEM SAMVELIS) Vulgus capitur inanibus, & mutationes amat. Pulchrum iis videbatur conspicere hominem aura- tum & gemmatum, splendide habitantem & epulantem, procedentem cum ingenti satellitio, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς φαν- τασίας.

## 9:1 Argument
PART II. THE HISTORY OF SAUL. SECTION I. OF SAUL ELECTED AND PROSPEROUS UNTIL HIS REJECTION. CHAPTER IX. The designation of Saul to the Kingdom.

Latin:

PARS II. HISTORIA SAULIS. SECTIO I. SAULIS ELECTI ET FELICIS USQUE AD REJECTIONEM EJUS. DEM. CAPUT IX. Destinatio Saulis ad Regnum.

## 9:2
Verse 2.

ELECT AND GOOD) בחור elsewhere means excellent, here it signifies rather a young man, as often elsewhere. The Greeks here have εὐμεγέθης. Do not refer that 'good' to the mind. For it signifies here 'beautiful'. And so Jonathan here translates שפיר, David Kimchi explains טוב בתאר ובמראה. Thus we have the opposite רע for deformed in Gen. 41, 3.

FROM THE SHOULDER AND UPWARD HE WAS TALLER THAN ALL THE PEOPLE] Thus Diana in Virgil: And walking she towers above all the goddesses; for which Homer: Πασάων δ' ὕπερ ἤγε κάρη ἔχει, ἠδὲ μέτωπα. See below 10, 23. 24. The peoples of the East also loved this in their kings, so that Aristotle, Polit. 4, 4, said that among the Ethiopians honors were assigned based on the size of the body. And at Sparta a king was fined because, having taken a wife of small stature, it was said he would produce diminutive kings. Nor does Euripides despise it: Εἶδος ἄξιον τυραννίδος.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ELECTVS ET BONVS) בחור alibi eximium, hic po- tius juvenem significat, ut sæpe alibi. Græci hic habent εὐ- μεγέθης. Illud bonus noli ad animum referre. Signifi cat enim hic pulchrum. Itaque Jonathan hic vertit שפיר, Da- vid Kimchi explicatטוב בתאר ובמראה. Sic opposi- tum רע pro deformi habemus Gen. 41, 3.

AB HVMERO ET SVRSVM EMINEBAT SVPER OMNEM POPVLVM] Sic Diana apud Virgilium: Gradiensque Deas supereminet omnes; pro quo Homerus: Πασάων δ' ὕπερ ἤγε κάρη ἔχει, ἠδὲ μέτωπα. vide infra 10, 23. 24. Amabant etiam hoc in regibus suis Ori- entis populi, ita ut apud Æthiopes honores mandatos ex cor- poris magnitudine dixerit Aristoteles, Polit. 4, 4. & Spartæ mulctatus rex, quod exigui corporis uxore ducta reges mi- nutos daturus diceretur. Nec spernit Euripides : Εἶδος ἄξιον τυραννίδος.

## 9:3
Verse 3.

GO AND SEEK THE DONKEYS) This story can be turned into an excellent proverb. He sought donkeys, and found a kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VADE ET QVÆRE ASINAS) Potest hæc historia in egregium proverbium verti. Quæsivit asinas, & invenit regnum.

## 9:7
Verse 7.

WHAT SHALL WE BRING TO THE MAN OF GOD? The prophets, like the philosophers, used to take things from what was known for their needs, as Origen says against Celsus. See 1 Kings 13:9 and what was said on Matthew 10:8.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVID FEREMVS AD VIRVM DEI? Prophetæ, ut Philosophi ἀπὸ τῶν γνωρίμων ἐλάμβανον τὰ πρὸς τὰς χρείας, ut ait contra Celsum Origenes. Vide 1. Reg. 13, 9. & quæ di- cta ad Matth. 10, 8.

## 9:9
Verse 9.

GOING TO CONSULT GOD) You have this expression in Genesis 25:22.

FOR HE WHO IS CALLED A PROPHET TODAY, WAS FORMERLY CALLED A SEER) It appears that the book was written long after those times, by which the conjecture placed at the beginning of this book is confirmed. Also, among the Greeks προορᾷν, and among the Latins to foresee, is said of seers. Compare Numbers 24:4.

He had proposed this conjecture thus: The author of these four books (of Samuel and Kings) is believed by the most learned of the Hebrews to be Jeremiah. The style of the language does not differ: see what we shall say on 1 Kings 6:2. But it is credible that he used those commentaries of Nathan and Gad the prophets, of whom mention is made in 1 Chronicles 29:29. These things Grotius there. On the book of 3 Kings 6:1, regarding the name of the month Zio, he annotated these things: This name of the month, as also Bul below 38, is Chaldean: And by this it is convinced that this book was written late, and perhaps by Jeremiah.

However, it is not necessary that we establish the same author for the books of Samuel and Kings. And concerning these, indeed, R. Moses Kimchi, as also Procopius Isidorus, and also Abulensis and Dionysius, judge that they were written by Jeremiah, since the last chapter of Jeremiah is the same as the last chapter of the fourth book of Kings. But Sanchietz, in his commentary on the book of Kings, observes that if this reasoning holds, it should rather be said that the books of Kings were arranged in order by Isaiah, since the three chapters of the 4th book of Kings, 18, 19, and 20, were written in almost the same way as four from the prophecy of Isaiah, namely chapters 36, 37, 38, 39, and Isaiah is said to have written the deeds of Uzziah in 2 Chronicles 26. & of Hezekiah in the same place, verses 20, 32; whence Sanctius says he would rather attribute these books to Isaiah up to the reign of Manasseh: Although in that uncertainty of conjectures he also thinks that he would not wander far from the truth who attributed these books to King Hezekiah, or to those to whom he delegated that task, which he notes in the Historia Scholastica are attributed to the same person along with the book of Judges. But that conjecture of Sanctius deserves the least approval of all. To our Mr. D. Walther in the Officina Biblica, it is more probable that the history of the two books of Kings was originally written by various prophets or even priests, who were then the public registrars of all the temples, and was afterwards reduced to order by one person, but that the collector was Jeremiah. Which others attribute to Isaiah. That whole matter is uncertain, concerning the third and fourth books of Kings, as they are called in the Vulgate version. However, that these books were written late is not incorrectly inferred, among other things, also from those Chaldean names of the months: So that we easily accede to the opinion of the Hebrews concerning Jeremiah as the author. But as for the first book of Kings or Samuel, R. Moses Kimchi, citing Sixtus Senensis in Bibliotheca, book 2, under the title of Samuel, says it was written by Samuel himself, along with the book of Judges and Ruth, up to chapter 25, where his death is described: But its continuation is commonly attributed to the prophets Nathan and Gad. Which is also the mind of the ancient Church Fathers, Theodoret, Procopius, Gregory the Great, Eucherius, and also of the Papists, Hugo, Lyranus, Cajetan, Vatablus, Serarius, Cornelius à Lapide, and others, regarding the book of 1 Samuel. And those things which are read at the end of the book of 1 Chronicles favor this opinion. Now the first and last deeds of King David are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the volume of Gad the seer, and of all his reign, and of his might, and of the times that passed over him, either in Israel, or in all the kingdoms of the lands.

Nor do the words of the present passage in 1 Sam. 9:9 stand in the way of this opinion; for it does not appear so clearly from them, as it indeed seems to Grotius, that that book of Samuel was written long after the times of Samuel, as that the fact that a prophet was once called a seer may refer to earlier times, such as the Mosaic, in which the name of seer may have been more customary than the name of prophet, Num. 24, or it may even be said that that paragraph was inserted by Ezra in the revision of the sacred books.

And the second book of Samuel is also to be attributed to those authors, Nathan and Gad: which is likewise gathered from the cited clause in 1 Chronicles: Nor is there any reason for anyone to say with Grotius that that passage refers only to the commentaries or diaries of Nathan and Gad, which Jeremiah might have used: For divinely inspired Scriptures are not collected from diaries or commentaries, but are written by θεοπνευσίαν and at the dictation of the Holy Spirit, and how could Nathan and Gad have recorded in diaries those things which are read in the 3rd and 4th books of Kings, when they did not live to see those times: and indeed Nathan did not describe the work of Solomon alone, or with Gad, but with Ahijah the Shilonite and Iddo the seer, as is held in 2 Chronicles 9:29. Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Thus concerning the acts of Rehoboam 2. 2 Chron. 12:15, it is read that those things were written in the book of Shemaiah the prophet, and of Iddo the seer. Concerning the works of Abijah, it is held in 2 Chron. 12 that they were written in the book of Iddo the prophet: concerning the works of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20:34, it stands that they were written in the words of Jehu the son of Hanani, which he INSERTED into the books of the Kings of Israel. Thus, concerning the deeds of Uzziah, it is reported in 2 Chron. 26:22 that Isaiah the son of Amoz the prophet wrote them. Concerning Manasseh, however, it is said that Hozai wrote them, ch. 33:19. If it be said that Jeremiah collected, arranged, and inserted all these commentaries, not by a human spirit, but by the direction of the Holy Spirit ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος, we shall not object. Nor yet, perhaps, is it to be denied that there were also other journals, or words of days, such as 1 Kings 14:19, ch. 15:7. & more often in these books of Kings are cited those which were merely Chronological and Political, but not Sacred writings, nor did they ever belong to the Canon: which also are sometimes called the books of the Kings of Israel or Judah, and by the common consent of writers are something different from the four books of Kings, as Sanctius maintains. And indeed, that there was still some other book of Kings, non-canonical and distinct from the Canonical ones, Sixtus Senensis proves in lib. 2. Biblioth. under the word Regum liber, from 2 Chron. 24. Furthermore, The sons of Joash, and the sum of the money which had been collected under him, and the restoration of the house of God are written more diligently in the book of Kings; since these things cannot be referred to the History of the Kings inserted into the Canonical Scriptures, in which these things are not narrated at greater length, but for the most part are clearly omitted. Although it may appear in most places that the words of the days are to be understood as the books of Chronicles, if one attends to a comparison of parallel passages: so that it is probable that paragraphs of such a kind, in which those references to the words of the days are made, were inserted into the books of Kings by Jeremiah, or rather by Ezra, but by the divine Spirit. The Hebrews, Lyranus, Abulensis, Driedo, and Sixtus Senensis are of the opinion that the books of Chronicles were also written by him, to which Cornelius à Lapide adds his support, both because the end of Chronicles and the beginning of Ezra are the same, and because when the same history is narrated in the book of Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra, the narrative of Chronicles agrees with Ezra, and also because in the end of Chronicles are narrated the deeds of Cyrus, which Jeremiah, who lived before Cyrus, could not narrate, but Ezra, who lived after Cyrus, could. Add that the genealogy both of the Kings and of the leaders of the Israelites in 1 Chron. 13 extends beyond the return from the Babylonian captivity, and the captivity is commemorated in chapter 10 as having already been endured long ago.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

VADENS CONSVLERE DEVM) Habes hanc locu- tionem Gen. 25, 22.

QVI ENIM PROPHETA DICITVR HODIE, AP- PELLABATVR OLIM VIDENS) Apparet multo post ista tempora scriptum librum, quo firmatur conjectura posita hujus libri initio. Etiam Græcis προορᾷν, Latinis prævidere, de Vatibus dicitur. Conf. Num. 24, 4.

Conjecturam hanc ita proposuerat: Scriptor horum librorum quatuor (Samuelis & Regum) He- bræorum eruditissimis creditur esse Jeremias. Sermo- nis forma non discrepat: vide quæ dicemus ad 1. Reg. 6, 2. Eum vero credibile est usum commentariis illis Nathanis & Gadis Prophetarum, quorum mentio 1. Paral. 29, 29. Hæc ibi Grotius. Ad librum 3. Reg. 6, 1. de nomine Mensis Zio hæc annotavit: Nomen hoc Mensis, ut & Bul infra 38. Chaldaicum est: Eoque convincitur, sero scriptum hunc librum, ac forte ab Jeremia.

Non necessum autem est, ut eundem Autorem statuamus librorum Samuelis & Regum. Et de his quidem R. Moses Kimchi, ut & Procopius Isidorus, nec non Abulensis & Dionysius censent, quod à Je- remia scripti sint, siquidem caput ultimum Jere- miæ idem sit cum capite ultimo libri quarti Regum. Sed Sanchietz comm. in libr. Regum observat, si hæc ratio valeat, dicendum potius ab Esaia libros Re- gum in ordinem redactos, siquidem eodem pene mo- do scripta sint tria capita lib. 4. Regum 18. 19. & 20. quo quatuor ex Esaiæ vaticinio, nempe 36. 37. 38. 39. cap. ac Esaias scripsisse dicatur gesta Oziæ 2. Par. 26. & Ezechiæ ibidem vers. 20. 32. unde se libros hos potius Esaiæ usque ad Regnum Menasse tributurum dicit Sanctius: Quanquam in ista conjecturarum incertitudine etiam putet, illum à vero non procul aberraturum, qui Ezechiæ Regi, aut quibus ille id negotii demandavit, tribuerit hos libros, quos cum li- bro Judicum eidem in Historia Scholastica tribui no- tat. Sed ea conjectura Sanctii minime omnium calculum meretur. Dn. D. Walthero nostro in Of- fic. Bibl. probabilius est, Historiam librorum duo- rum Regum, à diversis Prophetis aut etiam Sacerdo- tibus, qui tum publici omnium templorum fuerint a- ctuarii, originaliter fuisse conscriptam, & postea ab uno in ordinem redactam, Collectorem vero fuisse Je- remiam. Quod alii Esaiæ tribuunt. Tota res illa incerta est, de tertio & quarto Regum libro, quos ita vocant in vulgata versione. Sero tamen scriptos esse libros istos, inter alia etiam ex istis Chaldaicis Mensium nominibus non inrecte colligitur: Ut facile opinioni Ebræorum de Jeremia auctore acce- damus. Sed quod ad primum Regum vel Samuelis li- brum, eum R. Moses Kimchi, citante Sixto Senensi in Biblioth. lib. 2. titulo Samuelis, à Samuele ipso conscriptum dicit, una cum libro Judicum, & Ruth, usque ad cap. 25. quo mors ejus describitur: Conti- nuatio vero ejusdem Prophetis Nathan & Gad com- muniter tribuitur. Quæ etiam de libro 1. Samuelis est mens veterum Ecclesiæ Dd. Theodoreti, Procopii, Gregorii M. Eucherii, nec non Pontificiorum, Hu- gonis, Lyrani, Cajetani, Vatabli, Serarii, Cornelii à Lapide & aliorum. Et huic sententiæ favent, quæ leguntur in fine libr. 1. Paral. Gesta autem David Re- gis priora & novissima scripta sunt in libro Samuelis videntis, & in libro Nathan Prophetæ, atque in volu- mine Gad videntis, universique regni ejus, & fortitu- dinis & temporum, quæ transierunt sub eo, sive in Is- rael, sive in cunctis regnis terrarum.

Neque obstant huic sententiæ verba præsentis loci 1. Sam. 9, 9. nam ex illis non apparet adeo luculenter, uti Grotio quidem videtur, multo post tempora Samuelis librum illum Samuelis scriptum esse, quam illud, quod olim Propheta videns dictus sit, anteriora tempora, utpote Mosaica respicere possit, quibus nomen videntis Prophetæ nomine usitatius fuerit Numer. 24. aut dici etiam queat, illum paragraphum in revisione librorum sacrorum ab Esdra insertum esse.

Atque istis etiam Autoribus Nathani, & Gad secundus liber Samuelis tribuendus est: quod pariter ex adducta clausula 1. Paralip. colligitur: Nec est, quod dicat quis cum Grotio, loco isto tantum respici commentaria vel Diaria Nathanis, & Gadis, quibus usus fuerit Jeremias: Nam Scripturæ divinitus inspiratæ non sunt è Diariis vel commentariis collectæ, sed per θεοπνευσίαν, & dictante Spiritu Sancto conscriptæ, & quomodo potuere Nathan & Gad ea in Diaria referre, quæ lib. 3. & 4. Regum leguntur, quum ista tempora vivendo non attigerint: ac ne Salomonis quidem opere Nathan solus descripserit, aut cum Gado, sed cum Asia Silonita & Addo vidente, uti habetur 2. Paral. 9, 29. Reliqua autem operum Salomonis priorum & novissimorum scripta sunt in verbis Nathan Prophetæ, & in libris Asiæ Silonitæ, in visione quoque Addo videntis contra Jeroboam filium Nabat. Sic de Roboami operibus 2. Paral. 12, 15. legitur; quod illa scripta sint in libro Semajæ Prophetæ, & Addo videntis. De operibus Abiæ habetur 2. Paralip. 12. quod scripta sint in libro Addo Prophetæ: De operibus Josaphat 2. Paralip. 20, 34. extat, quod ea scripta sint in verbis Jehu filii Hanani, quæ DIGESSIT in libros Regum Israel. Ita de Oziæ rebus gestis refertur 2. Paral. 26, 23. quod scripserit easdem Esaias filius Amos Prophetæ. De Manasse vero scripsisse dicitur Hozai cap. 33, 19. Quæ commentaria omnia collegisse, ordinasse, ac digessisse si dicatur Jeremias, non humano Spiritu, sed directione Spiritus Sancti ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος, non repugnabimus. Neque tamen fortassis negandum, fuisse etiam alia diaria, vel verba dierum, qualia 1. Reg. 14, 19. c. 15, 7. & sæpius in hisce libris Regum citantur, quæ fuerint merè Chronologica, & Politica, non vero Sacra scripta, nec ad Canonem unquam pertinuerint: quæ etiam aliquando dici libros Regum Israel sive Judæ, & communi scriptorum consensu aliquid esse diversum à quatuor libris Regum, Sanctius vult. Et sane librum adhuc aliquem Regum fuisse non canonicum à Canonicis diversum, probat Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Biblioth. verbo Regum liber, è 2. Paral. 24. Porro Filii Joas, & summa pecuniæ, quæ adunata fuerat sub eo, & instauratio domus Dei scripta sunt diligentius in libro Regum; Siquidem ista ad Historiam Regum Canonicis Scripturis insertam referri nequeant, in qua ista non narrantur fusius, sed pleraque plane prætermissa sunt. Quanquam videri possit in plerisque locis verba dierum de libris Paralipomenon intelligi, si attendatur collatio locorum parallelorum: Ut ita paragraphos ejusmodi, in quibus illæ remissiones ad verba dierum fiunt, libris Regum à Jeremia, vel potius ab Esdra, sed divino Spiritu, insertos esse, verisimile sit. A quo etiam conscriptos esse libros Chronicorum, Ebræi, Lyranus, Abulensis, Driedo, & Sixtus Senensis opinantur, quibus calculum addit Cornelius à Lapide, tum quia idem est finis Paralipomenon & initium Esdræ, tum quia cum eadem Historia narratur in libro Regum, Paralipomenon & Esrdæ, narratio Paralipomenon consentit cum Esdra, tum quia in fine Paralipomenon narrantur gesta Cyri, quæ nar- rare non potuit Jeremias, qui ante Cyrum, sed Es- dra, qui post Cyrum vixit. Adde quòd Genealo- gia cum Regum, tum Ducum Israëliticorum 1. Pa- ral. 13. ultrà reditum ex captivitate Babylonica ex- tendatur, & captivitas cap. 10. ceu jam pridem ex- antlata, commemoretur.

## 9:11
Ver. 11.

GOING OUT TO DRAW WATER] See Gen. 24, 11. 15. 43. 45. Exod. 2, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

EGREDIENTES AD HAURIENDAM AQVAM] Vi- de Gen. 24, 11. 15. 43. 45. Exod. 2, 16.

## 9:13
Ver. 13.

HE HIMSELF BLESSES THE SACRIFICE] For at that time, because of frequent migrations, there was no fixed place for sacrifice. See what is said in Deut. 12, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

IPSE BENEDICIT HOSTIÆ] Eo enim tempore ob crebras migrationes nullus erat certus ad sacrificium locus. Vide quæ dicta Deut. 12, 8.

## 9:15
Ver. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

## 9:16
LEADER OVER MY PEOPLE] In ancient times the king was ἡγεμὼν τῶν πρὸς τὸν πόλεμον (the leader of those things pertaining to war). Arist. Polit. 3. 14. Homer: Ἀμφότερον βασιλεύς τ' ἀγαθὸς κρατερός τ' αἰχμητής (Both a good king and a mighty spearman). And Tacitus: The rest may be dissembled in some way: but that it is the virtue of a good leader to be a commander (add, or a king).

Ver. 16.

HE SHALL SAVE THE PEOPLE FROM THE HAND OF THE PHILISTINES) God knows how to elicit good even from evil counsels.

Latin:

DVCEM SUPER POPULVM MEUM] Antiquitus rex erat ἡγεμὼν τῶν πρὸς τὸν πόλεμον. Arist. Polit. 3. 14. Homerus: Ἀμφότερον βασιλεύς τ' ἀγαθὸς κρατερός τ' αἰχμητής. Et Tacitus: Cætera utcunque dissimulari: sed boni ducis im- peratoriam (adde, aut regiam) esse virtutem.

Vers. 16.

SALVABIT POPULUM DE MANV PHILISTHI- NORVM) Novit Deus etiam ex malis consiliis bonum eli- cere.

## 9:21
Ver. 21. OF THE SMALLEST TRIBE OF ISRAEL AND MY KINDRED THE LEAST AMONG ALL THE FAMILIES OF THE TRIBE OF BENJAMIN) The first king was to be in a lesser position so that there would be less envy.

Latin:

Vers. 21. DE MINIMA TRIBV ISRAEL ET CO- GNATIO MEA NOVISSIMA INTER OMNES FAMI- LIAS DE TRIBV BENJAMIN) Eo in minore futurus erat invidia rex primus.

## 9:24
Ver. 24.

BUT THE COOK LIFTED THE SHOULDER) The left one. For the right one belonged to the Priest, Lev. 7, 32. This shoulder, therefore, was the portion of him who was of the highest dignity at the banquet, and consequently of the king, when he was present: Whence Josephus calls this part μερίδα βασιλικὴν (a royal portion).

Latin:

Vers. 24.

LEVAVIT AVTEM COQVVS ARMVM) Sini- strum. Nam dexter erat Sacerdotis Lev. 7, 32. Hic ergo ar- mus portio erat ejus, qui in convivio præcipuæ esset dignita- tis, ac proinde regis, ubi is aderat: Vnde hanc partem μερίδα βασιλικὴν vocat Josephus.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. The inauguration of Saul.

Ver. 1.

HE KISSED HIM) For the sake of reverence, as of a future king, he kissed his hand. See Gen. 41, 40; Psal. 2, 12.

BEHOLD THE LORD HATH ANOINTED THEE) By the example of the priests, Hebrew kings were also anointed, not indeed as priests, but as having much that was priestly: a seat, and the right of speaking in the sanctuary, inspection of sacred things, the right of electing and deposing the High Priest and other priests, and other things of that kind: yet in a different way: priests on the forehead in the form of a cross; kings on the crown of the head in the manner of a crown with the oil poured on. God is said to have anointed Saul here, and below in 24 to have chosen him: namely κατὰ τὸ θέλημα ἑπόμενον, not τὸ προηγούμενον. For so the ancients distinguish.

Latin:

CAPUT X. Saulis inauguratio.

Vers. 1.

DEOSCVLATVS EST EVM) Reverentiæ causa, ut fu- turi regis, manum osculatus est. Vide Gen. 41, 40 Psal. 2, 12.

ECCE VNXIT TE DOMINVS) Sacerdotum exemplo uncti sunt & reges Hebræi, non sacerdotes quidem, sed mul- tum habentes sacerdotale, sedem, & jus loquendi in sanctua- rio, inspectionem in sacra, jus eligendi, & destituendi Ponti- ficis Maximi, aliorumque Sacerdotum, & alia ejusmodi: alio tamen modo: Sacerdotes in fronte decussatim: reges in ver- tice ad coronæ modum illito oleo. Deus unxisse Saulem hic & infra 24. eum elegisse dicitur: nempe κατὰ τὸ θέλημα ἑπόμενον, non τὸ προηγούμενον. Ita enim distinguunt ve- teres.

## 10:2
Ver. 2. BY THE SEPULCHRE OF RACHEL) Gen. 35, 19. God, accommodating Himself somewhat to the disposition of His people, often gave them true omens, such as superstitious people vainly sought after. See Gen. 24, 14 and following.

God does not favor superstition, nor does He promote it: and therefore it must by no means be said that omens sought from vain superstition were approved by Him, and that God the Best and Greatest strengthened them by their fulfillment. For what else would this have been than to confirm vain men in vain superstition? The omen which Eleazar requested must be judged to have been requested not out of superstition, but out of faith, and therefore he was also heard by God, Jam. 1, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 2. JVXTA SEPVLCHRVM RACHEL) Gen. 35, 19. Deus se nonnihil accommodans populi sui ingenio sæ- pe suis vera dabat omina, qualia superstitiosi inaniter capta- bant. Vide Gen. 24, 14. & sequentibus.

DEus non favet superstitioni, nec eandem pro- movet: ideoque è superstitione inani captata omina ipsi probata esse, eaque complemento De- um optimum Maximum roborasse, neutiquam di- cendum. Quid enim hoc aliud fuisset, quam con- firmare vanos homines in superstitione inani? O- men, quod postulabat Eleazar, non ex superstitio- ne, sed ex fide postulasse censendus est, ideoque eti- am exauditus est à Deo, Jac. 1, 6.

## 10:5
Ver. 5.

WHERE IS THE GARRISON OF THE PHILISTINES) The Philistines were better than many Christians are now. For they spared those places in which men devoted to divine studies were living. See what we have said about the Law of War and Peace, book three, chap. 11, § 10.

A COMPANY OF THE PROPHETS) The prophets were accustomed to separate themselves from the crowd, and there to instruct the youth in piety.

AND BEFORE THEM A PSALTERY AND A TABRET AND A PIPE AND A HARP) Which it was the custom to use when thanks were given to God for some benefit. See what was said at Jud. 11, 34. Furthermore, such is the power of certain sounds that they calm an agitated mind, below 16, 16. Others rouse a sluggish one and prepare it for great things. 2 Kings 3, 15. Thus Pythagoras softened ferocious minds, Asclepiades checked ignited seditions, Damon brought back drunken and petulant youths to modesty, Xenocrates freed the frantic from their disease. Concerning whom see Capella, Satirae, book 10.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

VBI EST STATIO PHILISTHINORVM) Meliores erant Philisthini, quam nunc multi Christianorum. Parce- bant enim iis locis, in quibus degebant viri studiis divinis dediti. Vide quæ diximus de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro tertio cap. 11. §. 10.

GREGEM PROPHETARVM) Solebant Prophetæ à tur- ba se segregare, & ibi juventutem ad pietatem instituere.

ET ANTE EOS PSALTERIVM ET TTMPANVM ET TIBIAM ET CITHARAM) Quibus mos erat uti, ubi Deo gratiæ de beneficio aliquo agebantur. Vide quæ dicta Jud. 11, 34. Præterea ea vis est quorundam sonorum, ut ani- mum concitatum tranquillent, infra 16, 16. Alii torpentem excitant, & rebus magnis præparant. 2. Reg. 3, 15. Sic fero- cientes animos mollivit Pythagoras, seditiones accensas inhi- buit Asclepiades, Damon ebrios ac petulantes juvenes ad mo- destiam reduxit, lymphaticos morbo liberavit Xenocrates. De quibus vide Capellam Saturæ libr. 10.

## 10:9
Ver. 9. GOD CHANGED HIS HEART INTO ANOTHER) He made him stronger and wiser than usual, and, lest he should doubt that he was destined for the kingdom, God also conferred upon him a momentary gift of prophecy 11. Similar below 19, 20. But that spirit, suitable for administering the kingdom, God later took away from him as a punishment for his sins. Below 16, 14. Compare Psal. 51, 14.

Latin:

Verf. 9. IMMVTAVIT ILLI DEVS COR ALIVD] Fecit eum solito fortiorem ac prudentiorem, &, ne dubitaret se regno destinatum, etiam momentaneum Prophetiæ donum ei Deus contulit 11. Simile infra 19, 20. Spiritum autem illum re- gno administrando idoneum postea in pœnam peccatorum ei abstulit Deus. Infra 16, 14. Confer Psal. 51, 14.

## 10:12
Ver. 12. IS SAUL ALSO AMONG THE PROPHETS] The memory of this proverb is repeated below 19, 24, from a similar fact, as if they were saying: who would have hoped for this in a military man? But indeed Πολλάκι κὰι κηπωρός ἄνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἰ̃πε. And the Spirit blows where He wills. John 3, 8.

Latin:

Verf. 12. NVM ET SAVL INTER PROPHETAS] Ex facto pari repetita hujus Proverbii memoria infra 19, 24. quasi di- cerent: quis hoc sperasset in homine militari? At nimirum Πολλάκι κὰι κηπωρός ἄνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἰ̃πε. Et Spiritus ubi vult spirat. Joan. 3, 8.

## 10:16
Ver. 16. BUT OF THE MATTER OF THE KINGDOM HE TOLD HIM NOT, WHEREOF SAMUEL HAD SPOKEN UNTO HIM] He prudently lets the matter mature, lest by ambition he should make himself suspected.

Latin:

Verf. 16. DE SERMONE AVTEM REGNI NON INDICA- VIT EI, QVEM LOCVTUS FUERAT EI SAMUEL] Prudenter rem sinit maturescere, ne ambitus suspectum se fa- ceret.

## 10:19
Ver. 19. AND YE HAVE SAID NAY] It appears that this interpreter read לא instead of לו, just as both the LXX and Abenesdra read. A different reading is not immediately inferred from that. And the Hebrew text is correct: And ye have said to him, namely to the Lord: Set a king over us,

Latin:

Verf. 19. ET DIXISTIS NEQVAQVAM] Apparet hunc interpretem pro לו legisse לא, quomodo legerunt & LXX. & Abenesdra. Non statim diversa lectio inde colligitur. Et re- cte se habet Ebræus textus: Et dixistis ei, scilicet Domino: Regem constitue,

## 10:20
Ver. 20. AND THE LOT FELL ON THE TRIBE OF BENJAMIN] Aristotle in book 6 of the Politics, chapter 2, says that it is a popular institution, τὸ κλη- ρωτὰς εἰ̃ναι τὰς ἀρχάς. The ancient custom of certain nations also received this in priesthoods. Virgil, book 2 of the Aeneid: Laocoon, chosen by lot, priest of Neptune. See Acts 1, 26.

Latin:

Verf. 20. ET CECIDIT SORS TRIBUS BENJAMIN] Aristote- les libro 6. Polit. cap. 2. ait populare esse institutum, τὸ κλη- ρωτὰς εἰ̃ναι τὰς ἀρχάς. Id mos quarundam gentium vetus etiam in sacerdotiis recepit. Virgilius libr. 2. Æneidos: Laocoon lectus Neptuni forte sacerdos. Vide Act. 1, 26.

## 10:24
Ver. 24. GOD SAVE THE KING] To live here and elsewhere is to prosper.

Latin:

Verf. 24. VIVAT REX] Vivere hîc & alibi est prospere agere.

## 10:25
Ver. 25. THEN SAMUEL TOLD THE PEOPLE THE MANNER OF THE KINGDOM, AND WROTE IT IN A BOOK] Heb. משפט המלכה. In Greek, δικαίωμα τῦ βασιλέως, which Josephus interprets as the evils that would happen from the license customary to kings. See above 2, 13. Others prefer that it was precepts for reigning well, ὐποθήκας, such as Isocrates and Stobaeus have excellent ones. It was a building constructed upon foundations, which are in Deut. 17, 16, and following. There is no reason why we should not admit that the Royal Law, indicated by the same name משפט above in chapter 8, 11, is designated here as having been committed to writing.

Latin:

Verf. 25. LOCVTVS EST AVTEM SAMVEL AD POPVLVM LEGEM REGNI, ET SCRIPSIT IN LI- BRO] Hebr. משפט המלכה. Græce, δικαίωμα τῦ βασιλέως, quod Josephus interpretatur, mala eventura ex sueta regibus licentia. Vide supra 2, 13. Alii malunt fuisse bene regnan- di præcepta, ὐποθήκας, quales habet egregias Isocrates & Sto- bæus. Fuit ædificium exstructum super fundamentis, quæ sunt Deut. 17, 16. & sequentibus. Nulla est causa, cur non admittamus, Jus Re- gium eodem nomine משפט supra cap. 8, 11. indi- gitatum hîc designari literis consignatum.

## 10:26
Ver. 26. WHOSE HEARTS GOD HAD TOUCHED] Whose authority the Prophet Samuel had moved.

Latin:

Verf. 26. QVORVM DEVS TETIGERAT CORDA] Quos Samuelis Prophetæ moverat auctoritas.

## 10:27
Ver. 27. BUT THE CHILDREN OF BELIAL] Men impatient of any yoke. See above 1, 16. BROUGHT HIM NO PRESENTS] Without which it was not customary to approach the kings of the East. See Matt. 2, 10. BUT HE HELD HIS PEACE] Namely, because the reputation for clemency is useful to those beginning a new empire: as Tacitus says, Histories 4. See also 11, 13.

Latin:

Verf. 27. FILII VERO BELIAL] Homines omnis jugi im- patientes. Vide supra 1, 16. NON ATTVLERVNT EI MVNERA] Sine quibus reges Orientis adiri non solebant Vide Matth. 2, 10. DISSIMVLABAT SE AVDIRE] Nempe quia novum imperium inchoantibus utilis clementiæ fama: ut Tacitus ait Histor. 4. aide & 11, 13.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. Nahash defeated by Saul. He is confirmed in the kingdom.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Nahas à Saule profligatus. Hic in regno con- firmatus.

## 11:2
Ver. 2. THAT I MAY THRUST OUT ALL YOUR RIGHT EYES] Namely, to make them useless for war: for the left eye was accustomed to hide under the shield. Indeed, also for the reproach of the nation, which cause Nahash added immediately. But he had no right to the land of Israel, as Jephthah taught in Jud. 11, the King of the Ammonites.

Latin:

Verf. 2. VT ERVAM OMNIVM VESTRVM OCV- LOS DEXTROS] Nempe ut inutiles eos bello faceret: nam sinister oculos sub scuto latere solebat. Imo etiam in opprobrium gentis, quam causam statim addidit Nahas. Nullum autem jus habuit in terra Israel. Ammonitarum Rex, ut Jephthe Jud. 11. docuit.

## 11:3
Ver. 3. GIVE US SEVEN DAYS] We have placed certain examples of such surrenders made for a day under condition in the Annotations to the third book on the Law of War and Peace, chapter 24, §. 14.

Latin:

Verf. 3. CONCEDE NOBIS DIES SEPTEM] Talium deditionum factarum in diem sub conditione exempla quæ- dam posuimus in Annotatis ad librum tertium de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 24. §. 14.

## 11:7
Ver. 7. SO SHALL IT BE DONE UNTO HIS OXEN] A punishment for failure to serve in the army. See Jud. 21, 10.

Latin:

Verf. 7. SIC FIET BOBUS EJUS] Pœna ἀστρατείας. Vide Jud. 21, 10.

## 11:10
Verf. 10. AND THEY SAID] Supply the Ammonites. WE WILL COME OUT TO YOU IN THE MORNING, AND YOU SHALL DO TO US EVERYTHING THAT PLEASES YOU. Namely, if you are able. These things were said with παρ̀ρησία̜, not mendaciously, even though they concealed the fact that help was prepared. For they were thinking of coming out, but with their King, not into the hands of the enemy, but to slaughter, as Gregory the Great speaks, who nevertheless says that they promised one thing and believed another: which there is no need to say here.

Latin:

Verf. 10. ET DIXERVNT] Supple Ammonitis. MANE EXIBIMUS AD VOS, ET FA- CIETIS NOBIS OMNE, QUOD PLACUE- RIT VOBIS. Scil. si poteritis. Ex παρ̀ρησία̜ hæc dicta, non men- daciter, etsi auxilium paratum dissimularent. Exire enim, sed cum Rege suo cogitabant non ad hostium ma- nus, sed ad interfectionem, ut Gregorius M. loquitur, qui tamen aliud promisisse, aliud credidisse eosdem ait: quod hic opus non est dicere.

## 11:11
Verse 11.

HE ENTERED INTO THE MIDDLE OF THE CAMP) Which it is credible was not well fortified in the part that was turned away from the city, because the Ammonites feared nothing so sudden from that direction.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

INGRESSVS EST IN MEDIA CASTRA) Quæ cre- dibile est in parte, quæ ab urbe aversa erat, non bene fuisse munita, quod Ammonitæ inde nihil tam repentinum me- tuerent.

## 11:13
Verse 13. NO ONE SHALL BE PUT TO DEATH ON THIS DAY) It was permitted for the king to pardon only those things which pertained to his own injury: which philosophers also praise. Seneca in the first book of De Clementia, chapter 20, speaking of a prince: Let him be far more exorable in his own injuries than in those of others: for just as he is not of a great mind who is liberal with another's property, but he who takes from himself what he gives to another, so I will call him clement, not who is easy in another's pain, but he who, when he is agitated by his own goads, does not leap forth: who understands that it is of a great mind to suffer injuries in supreme power, and that no one is more glorious than a prince who is harmed with impunity. Livia to Augustus: τοὺς ἄρχοντας νομίζουσιν οἱ πολλοὶ τοὺς μὲν τὸ κοινὸν ἀδικεῖτας ἐπεξιέναι χρῆναι, τοὺς δ᾽ ἰδίᾳ τι εἰς αὐτοὺς πλημμελεῖν δοκοῦντας φέρειν. We have brought forward the examples of Antoninus and Theodosius in the second book of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter 24, § 3. However, the fault in question had some excuse in men unaccustomed to a kingdom. Saul well seizes the occasion for mercy from the day of the victory won. What day is free from punishment, when among sacred rites and vows, at which time it was the custom to abstain even from profane words, chains and the noose are brought in? say the fathers complaining about the cruelty of Tiberius in Tacitus, Annals 4. We shall have a clearly similar deed of David in 2 Sam. 19:22.

Latin:

Vers. 13. NON OCCIDETUR QVISQVAM IN DIE HAC) Regi condonare ea tantum licebat, quæ ad suam injuriam pertinebant: quod & Philosophi laudant. Seneca libro primo de Clementia cap. 20. de Principe loquens: Longe sit in suis quam in alienis exorabilior injuriis: nam quem- admodum non est magni animi, qui de alieno liberalis est, sed ille qui quod alteri donat, sibi detrahit, ita clementem vocabo, non in alieno dolore facilem, sed eum qui cum suis stimulis agi- tatur, non prosilit: qui intelligit magni animi esse, injurias in summa potentia pati, nec quisquam gloriosius esse Principe im- pune læso. Livia ad Augustum: τοὺς ἄρχοντας νομίζουσιν οἱ πολ- λοὶ τοὺς μὲν τὸ κοινὸν ἀδικεῖτας ἐπεξιέναι χρῆναι, τοὺς δ᾽ ἰδίᾳ τι εἰς αὐτοὺς πλημμελεῖν δοκοῦντας φέρειν. Exempla Antonini & Theodosii attulimus libro secundo de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 24. §. 3. Habebat autem culpa, de qua agitur, excusatio- nis aliquid in hominibus regno insuetis. Bene autem Saul oc- casionem misericordiæ arripit ex die partæ victoriæ. Quem diem vacuum pœna, ubi inter sacra & vota, quo tempore verbis etiam profanis abstineri mos esset, vincula & laqueus inducun- tur? ajunt patres de Tiberii sævitia querentes apud Tacitum Annalium 4. Simile plane factum Davidis habebimus 2. Sam. 19, 22.

## 11:15
Verse 15.

THEY MADE SAUL KING THERE) By common consent they declared him king. See a similar case in 2 Sam. 5:1, 2, 3, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

FECERUNT IBI REGEM SAUL) Communi consensu regem eum declararunt. Simile vide 2. Sam. 5, 1. 2. 3. 4.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. The integrity of Samuel, the ingratitude of the people. A sign from heaven. Prayer for the people.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. Samuelis integritas, populi ingratitudo. Signum de cælo. Oratio pro populo.

## 12:2
Verse 2.

BEHOLD I AM PRESENT: SPEAK OF ME) Departing from the magistracy, he voluntarily submits himself to a censure which he was not bound to undergo, and with the confidence of an excellent conscience challenges his accusers. With equal confidence Pericles of himself: ὅς οὐδενὸς ἥσσων οἴομαι εἶναι γνῶναί τε τὰ δέοντα καὶ ἑρμηνεῦσαι ταῦτα, Φιλόπολις τε καὶ χρημάτων κρείσσων.

MY SONS ARE WITH YOU.

Whose service you will be able to use, if you have need of them in any matter.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ECCE PRÆSTO SVM: LOQVIMINI DE ME) De magistratu abiens, censuræ quam ferre non tenebatur, ultro se subjicit, & optimæ conscientiæ fiducia accusatores provocat. Pari fiducia Pericles de sese: ὅς οὐδενὸς ἥσσων οἴομαι εἶναι γνῶ- ναί τε τὰ δέοντα καὶ ἑρμηνεῦσαι ταῦτα, Φιλόπολις τε καὶ χρη- μάτων κρείσσων.

FILII MEI VOBISCUM SUNT.

Quorum ministerio uti poteritis, si qua in re vo- bis opus erit.

## 12:11
Verse 11. AND BADAN.

Samson is so called according to the Chaldean and Jerome, as if בְּדָן, dwelling in Dan.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET BADAN.

Simson ita vocatur juxta Chald. & Hieronym. quasi בְּדָן in Dan habitans.

## 12:17
Verse 17.

IS IT NOT WHEAT HARVEST TODAY?) A clear day such as reapers might wish for.

Jerome teaches at Amos 4:7 that this was a miracle, because in that place, under a clear sky, Samuel suddenly elicited these thunders and rains: which the author of the book on miracles, lib. 2, cap. 9, reports he soon stopped for the penitent people.

VOICES) Or rather sounds, whence also the word for thundering among the Latins. Varro in the Eumenides: 'For you the drums, not with empty sound, for you we thunder.' That is, we sound, says Nonius.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

NVMQVID NON MESSIS TRITICI EST HODIE?) Dies serenus qualem messores optent.

Miraculum hoc fuisse Hieronym, docet ad Am. 4, 7. quod cælo sereno illic loci subito hæc toni- trua & pluvias Samuel elicuit: quas mox stitisse po- pulo pœnitenti Autor mirabil. script. lib. 2. cap. 9. tradit.

VOCES) Aut sonos potius, unde & tonandi vox Latinis. Varro Eumenidibus: Tibi tympana non inani sonitu tibi tonimus. Id est, sonamus, ait Nonius.

## 12:19
Verse 19.

FOR WE HAVE ADDED TO ALL OUR SINS EVIL, THAT WE MIGHT ASK FOR A KING FOR OURSELVES) Namely, to remove the Prophet from authority, the same man being most innocent.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ADDIDIMVS ENIM VNIVERSIS PECCATIS NO- STRIS MALVM, VT PETEREMVS NOBIS REGEM) Nempe ad demovendum ab imperio Prophetam, eundemque virum innocentissimum.

## 12:21
Verse 21.

WHICH ARE VAIN) Maimonides thinks it treats of magical things, which are rightly called περίεργα in Acts 19:19, things of no profit. Jeremiah 16:19. For even if no other evil is present, time, a thing so precious, perishes uselessly in them.

Others more correctly [think it treats] of idols, which are most vain and most lying.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

QVÆ VANA SVNT) De Magicis agi putat Maimoni- des, quæ περίεργα recte dicuntur Act. 19, 19. res nullius pro- fectus. Jerem. 16, 19. Nam ut non aliud adsit mali, tempus, res tam pretiosa, in illis inutiliter perit.

De Idolis rectius alii, quæ vanissima sunt, & mendacissima.

## 12:25
Verse 25. BOTH YOU AND YOUR KING LIKEWISE SHALL PERISH) By slaughter or captivity. We have examples of both.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ET VOS ET REX VESTER PARITER PER- IBITIS) Occidione aut captivitate. Vtriusque habemus exempla.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. The fortitude of Jonathan. The sacrifice of Saul, and his rejection.

Verse 1.

SAUL WAS A SON OF ONE YEAR WHEN HE BEGAN TO REIGN) That is, when those things were done which have already been narrated, Saul had spent almost a year in his reign.

AND HE REIGNED TWO YEARS OVER ISRAEL) These things are to be connected with what follows, so that it may be understood that only after the two years of his reign had passed, he gathered those military forces.

We approve this opinion, which R. Lev. Ben Gerson, B. Luther, Flacius, and B. Glassius [approve] as the simplest, noted in the Chronicles against the bold emendation of the text by Scaliger; where the expositions of others are also discussed.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. Jonathanis fortitudo. Saulis sacrificium, & re- jectio.

Vers. 1.

FILIVS VNIVS ANNI ERAT SAVL CVM REGNA- RE COEPISSET) Id est, cum ista acta sunt, quæ jam narra- ta sunt, annum ferme in regno egerat Saul.

DVOBVS AVTEM ANNIS REGNAVIT SVPER ISRAEL) Hæc connectenda cum sequentibus, ut intelligatur biennio demum regni exacto, contraxisse copias illas mili- tares.

HAnc sententiam, quæ R. Lev. Ben Gerson, B. Lutheri, Flacii, & B. Glassii, ceu simplicissi- mam probamus in Chronic. notata audaci Scalige- ri textus emendatione; ubi etiam de aliorum ex- positionibus actum.

## 13:4
Verse 4.

SAUL SMOTE THE GARRISON OF THE PHILISTINES) The Greeks think it is a proper name, νασίβ. But Aquila, whom this Latin interpreter follows here, [renders it] ὑπόσημα. Thus elsewhere a station is ὑπόστασις.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

PERCVSSIT SAUL STATIONEM PHILISTHINO- RUM) Græci nomen proprium putant νασίβ. At Aquila quem sequitur hic Latinus interpres, ὑπόσημα. Sic alibi statio ὑπόστασις.

## 13:5
Verse 5. THIRTY THOUSAND CHARIOTS] This is too many compared to the number of horsemen that follows. Therefore, there are those who think the last two letters should be cast away, so that there are three thousand, שְׁלֹשׁ אֶלֶף.

Very badly. For the sacred text is not to be changed by our own judgment, with which the Vulgate here agrees, along with the LXX, the Chaldean, and all ancient interpreters. Moreover, the Tyrian chariots were joined to the Philistines, Ecclesiasticus 46:20. Although chariots can also be taken for soldiers fighting from chariots, according to Lyranus. Compare Buxtorf, Vindiciae veritatis Hebraicae, p. 1001, refuting Capellus, whom Grotius followed here.

Latin:

Vers. 5. TRIGINTA MILLIA CURRUUM] Nimium hoc præ numero equitum qui sequitur. Itaque sunt, qui po- stremas duas litteras abjiciendas censent, ut sint tria millia, שְׁלֹשׁ אֶלֶף.

Pessime. Non enim ex nostro arbitrio mutan- dus est textus sacer, cui Vulgata hic consentit, cum LXX. Chald. omnibusque Interpp. antiquis. Juncti autem Philistinis fuere Tyrii currus, Eccles. 46, 20. Quanquam & currus pro militibus ex curribus pu- gnantibus cum Lyrano accipi possint. Conf. Bux- torf. Vind. ver. Hebr. p. 1001. Capellum, quem hîc sequutus est Grotius, refellens.

## 13:8
Verse 8. AND HE WAITED SEVEN DAYS ACCORDING TO THE APPOINTMENT OF SAMUEL) The sense is: Samuel had wanted the meeting and the sacrifice to be deferred until he himself had arrived. But Saul, when he had waited for him after seven days, did not want to wait any longer for the Prophet, the indicator of the divine will, which was imputed to him as a grave sin.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET EXSPECTAVIT SEPTEM DIEBVS JV- XTA PLACITUM SAMUELIS) Sensus est: Voluerat Sa- muel conventui & sacrificio supersederi, donec ipse advenis- set. Saul vero cum post septem dies eum exspectasset, ultra exspectare Prophetam divinæ voluntatis indicem noluit, quod ei pro peccato gravi imputatum est.

## 13:13
Verse 13. FOREVER) that is, as long as the posterity of Saul should live.

Latin:

Vers. 13. IN SEMPITERNUM) id est, quamdiu Saulis posteritas viveret.

## 13:19
Verse 19. FOR THE PHILISTINES HAD TAKEN CARE, LEST PERCHANCE THE HEBREWS SHOULD MAKE A SWORD OR A SPEAR) By an extorted treaty, not unlike the law which Porsena imposed in a treaty with the Romans, that they should not use iron except in agriculture. Historians are silent about this, as it was shameful to a people who later became the conqueror of nations. But Pliny ingenuously confesses it in book 34, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 19. CAVERANT ENIM PHILISTHIIM, NE FORTE FACERENT HEBRÆI GLADIUM AUT LAN- CEAM) Extorto fœdere, cui non dissimilis lex, quam Porse- na in fœdere cum Romanis posuit, ne ferro nisi in agricultura uterentur. Tacent id Historici, ut pudendum victori postea gentium populo. At Plinius ingenue fatetur lib. 34, 14.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. Jonathan the victor, because of the honey tasted, is with difficulty snatched from death.

Vers. 1. JONATHAS) He was brave, courteous, and not at all ambitious: much like Germanicus:

HIS ARMOR-BEARER) See below v. 14, c. 16, 22. Such was Automedon to Achilles: Achates to Aeneas. The common people call him a shield-bearer.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. Jonathan victor, ob mel degustatum ægre mor- ti eripitur.

Vers. 1. JONATHAS) Fuit is fortis, comis, minime am- bitiosus: Talis ferme Germanicus:

ARMIGERVM SVVM) Vide infra v. 14. c. 16, 22. Ta- lis Automedon Achilli: Æneæ Achates. Vulgus scutarium vocat.

## 14:6
Vers. 6. IT IS NOT DIFFICULT FOR THE LORD TO SAVE BY MANY OR BY FEW) A sentiment in use among the Hebrews. It appears in 2 Chronicles 14:11, and 1 Maccabees 3:18, 2 Maccabees 15:27. See examples in Judges 7:4, below 17:47, 2 Chronicles 25:8. A similar sentiment is in Psalm 147:10.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NON EST DOMINO DIFFICILE, SERVA- RE IN MULTIS, VEL IN PAUCIS) Sententia in usu apud Hebræos. Apparet 2. Paralip. 14, 11. & 1. Macc. 3, 18. 2. Macc. 15, 27. Exempla vide Jud. 7, 4. infra 17, 47. 2. Paral. 25, 8. Similis sententia Psal. 147, 10.

## 14:19
Vers. 19. AND SAUL SAID TO THE PRIEST: WITHDRAW THY HAND] Much like Capaneus in the third book of Papinius's Thebaid to Amphiaraus: -- but when the first trumpet sounds, and we drink the hostile Ismenus and Dirce with our helmets, I warn you not to try to stand in my way when I wish to go to arms, or to postpone the day of battle because of winds or the sight of a bird. Far from you shall be this soft fillet, and the madness of the terrifying Phoebus. There I am the augur, and with me whoever is prepared to be mad with the sword. He means to say: cease seeking an oracle. For there is no need, nor does the time allow, that while intent on sacred rites, we lose the opportunity of destroying the enemy, as Osiander rightly observes in Saul, noting the danger of hypocrites: who are religious in times of danger, but when those dangers seem to be absent, they no longer seek or care for God.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ET AIT SAUL AD SACERDOTEM: CON- TRAHE MANVM TVAM] Ita ferme Capaneus Thebai- dos Papinianæ tertio ad Amphiaraum: - - sed prima ad classica cum jam Hostilem Ismenon galeis Dircenque bibemus, Ne mihi tunc moneo lituos atque arma volenti Obvius ire pares, ventisque aut alite visa Bellorum proferre diem. Procul hæc tibi mollis Infula, terrificique aberit dementia Phœbi. Illic augur ego & mecum quicunque parati Insanire manu. Id vult dicere: desine oraculum quærere. Neque enim opus est, neque tempus fert, ut intenti sacris, occasionem delendi hostis amittamus, ut recte O- siander in Saule observans hypocritarum pericu- lum: qui in periculis religiosi, cum abesse ea viden- tur, Deum non amplius quærunt, aut curant.

## 14:21
Vers. 21.

THEY RETURNED, THAT THEY MIGHT BE WITH ISRAEL) It often happened that while the battle was raging, captives would desert to their own side.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

REVERSI SUNT, VT ESSENT CUM ISRAEL) Sæpe factum, ut calente prælio captivi ad suos transfugerent.

## 14:24
Vers. 24. CURSED BE THE MAN THAT EATETH BREAD) לֶחֶם here and elsewhere signifies not bread specifically, but any food whatsoever, as appears below v. 43, 44. This edict of Saul, a man both imperious and προπετοῦς (rash), argues his imprudence. For those fighting for a long time need to be refreshed with food, and the penalty is too severe for such an offense. Furthermore, those who are ignorant ought to be excepted.

Latin:

Vers. 24. MALEDICTVS VIR, QVI COMEDERIT PANEM) לֶחֶם hic & alibi non panem speciatim, sed quemvis cibum significat, ut apparet infra v. 43. 44. Edictum hoc Saulis hominis & imperiofi & προπετοῦς imprudentiam arguit. Nam & diu pugnantibus opus cibo refici, & pœna gravior tali delicto. Præterea excipi debent ignorantes.

## 14:27
Verf. 27. AND HIS EYES WERE ENLIGHTENED] For darkness arises from fasting, as Plautus says in the Curculio.

AMONG WOMEN THY MOTHER] The law of Rhadamanthus. See On the Law of War and Peace, book 1, chapter 2, section 5.

AND SAMUEL CUT HIM IN PIECES] When kings failed in their duty, God often executed the sanctions of His law through the Prophets. 1 Kings 18:40.

Latin:

Verf. 27. ET ILLUMINATI SUNT OCULI EJUS] Nam ex ine- dia tenebræ oboriuntur, ut Plautus ait Curculione.

INTER MULIERES MATER TUA] Jus Rhadamanthi. Vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 1. c. 2. §. 5.

ET IN FRUSTA CONCIDIT EUM SAMUEL] Ces- fantibus in officio regibus, sæpe per Prophetas Deus legis suæ sanctiones exsequebatur. 1. Reg. 18, 40.

## 14:33
Verf. 33. EVEN NOW] He has interpreted the Hebrew הַיּוֹם very well, because יוֹם among them often signifies time. Psalm 32:2, Numbers 3:13, Isaiah 30:26 show that the following events were already at night.

SECTION II. THE HISTORY OF THE REJECTED AND UNHAPPY SAUL UP TO HIS DEATH.

Latin:

Verf. 33. JAM NUNC] Valde bene interpretatus est Hebræum הַיּוֹם, quia יוֹם apud eos sæpe tempus significat. Pfal. 32, 2. Num. 3, 13. Efaiæ 30, 26. oftendunt sequentia jam no- ctem fuisse.

SECTIO II. SAULIS REJECTI ET INFELICIS HISTO- RIA USQUE AD MORTEM EJUS.

## 14:34
Verf. 34. AND YOU SHALL NOT SIN AGAINST THE LORD BY EATING WITH THE BLOOD] He who wishes his divine laws to be observed rigidly, wishes them to be bent according to the times. Among the laws of God, it is forbidden to eat before the blood, i.e., with the blood of the animal not removed or covered: Lev. 7:13, 19:26. Josephus well says here: συμβαίνει μὴ κρατεῖν λογισμῷ τοὺς ἐντυχόντας.

Latin:

Verf. 34. ET NON PECCABITIS DOMINO COMEDENTES CUM SANGVINE] Qui suas leges rigide vult observari di- vinas, pro temporibus flecti vult. Inter lege Dei vetita est ede- re coram sanguine, i. e. non amoto aut obtecto pecudis san- guine: Lev. 7, 13. 19, 26. Bene hic Josephus: συμβαίνει μὴ κρατεῖν λογισμῷ τοὺς ἐντυχόντας.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. Saul, sparing King Agag, is deprived of the kingdom, whom Samuel killed, mourning the fall of Saul.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. Saul Agag Regi parcens regno privatur, quem Samuel interfecit, lugens casum Saulis.

## 15:5
Verse 5. DEPART AND GO DOWN FROM AMALEK] Those who wish to be considered neutral ought to separate themselves from enemies: and show themselves fair to both sides. See what was said in Book III of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 17.

Latin:

Verf. 5. RECEDITE ATQVE DESCENDITE AB AMALEC] Qui medii haberi volunt, segregare se ab hostibus debent: & æquos se præstare utrisque. Vide quæ dicta lib. III. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 17.

## 15:12
Verse 12. BEAUTIFUL IN APPEARANCE] A beautiful soul is also accustomed to appear in the countenance. See Plato's Symposium.

Latin:

Verf. 12. PULCHER ASPECTU] Solet pulcher animus etiam in vultu apparere. Vide Platonis convivium.

## 15:13
Verse 13. HE ANOINTED HIM] This anointing did not give David the kingdom, but destined him for the kingdom, and gave him the right to preserve himself by whatever means he could until the time of obtaining the kingdom.

Latin:

Verf. 13. VNXIT EUM] Hæc unctio Davidi non re- gnum dedit, sed regno eum destinavit, jusque ei dedit semet conservandi quibus posset modis ad tempus usque adipiscen- di regni.

## 15:23
IT IS LIKE THE SIN OF DIVINATION TO REBEL] The Latin calls it ariolation, which some Greeks call διώνισμα, others μαντείαν, which is opposed to prophecy (τῇ προφητεία), as idols are to God. See Lev. 19:26, 31; 20:6, 27; Deuteronomy 18:10, 11. Well said by the ancients: ἐκ ὀλίγου τὸ παῦ ὀλίγυ.

IT IS LIKE THE CRIME OF IDOLATRY TO REFUSE TO SUBMIT] In the Hebrew: The vanity of Teraphim, where the word Teraphim, which is neutral, as we have said elsewhere, is shown by the adjunct of vanity to be taken in a bad sense. Symmachus translates it well: ἀτομία τῶν ἰδώλων τὸ ἀπειθές.

Osiander correctly expresses the meaning: If anyone, neglecting the command of GOD (even with the best intention), undertakes to act, he sins no less than if he were practicing magical arts, or if he were contaminating himself with the horrendous crime of Idolatry.

Latin:

QUASI PECCATUM ARIOLANDI EST REPUGNA- RE] Ariolationem Latinus vocat, quam Græci alii διώνισμα, alii μαντείαν, quæ opponitur τῇ προφητεία, ut idola Deo. Vi- de Lev. 19, 26. 31. 20, 6. 27. Deuteronomii 18, 10.11. Bene di- ctum ab antiquis ἐκ ὀλίγου τὸ παῦ ὀλίγυ.

QUASI SCELUS IDOLOLATRIÆ NOLLE ACQVIE- SCERE] In Hebræo: Vanitas Teraphim, ubi vox Tera- phim, quæ media est, ut alibi diximus, per adjunctum vani- tatis oftenditur sumi in malam partem. Bene vertit Symma- chus, ἀτομία τῶν ἰδώλων τὸ ἀπειθές.

Sensum recte exprimit Ofiander: Si quis negle- cto DEI mandato (licet optima intentione) agen- dum suscipit, non minus peccat, quam si magicas artes exerceret, aut si horrendo Idololatriæ sce- lere se contaminaret.

## 15:23
Verse 23. AND SOMETIMES THE EVIL SPIRIT OF THE LORD SEIZED SAUL) For such evils are accustomed to have their intervals. See what is at Matt. 4, 24. and 17. v. 15.

Latin:

Verf. 23. QVANDOQVE SPIRITVS DOMINI MALVS AR- RIPIEBAT SAVL) Solent enim talibus malis esse sua inter- valla. Vide quæ ad Matth. 4, 24. & 17. v. 15.

## 15:25
Ver. 25. PARDON I PRAY THEE MY SIN] In Hebrew: שא that is, take away, namely by praying to God.

Latin:

Verf. 25. PORTA QVÆSO PECCATUM MEUM] In Hebræo: שא id est, aufer, nempe apud Deum deprecando.

## 15:33
Ver. 33. AS THY SWORD HATH MADE WOMEN CHILDLESS, SO SHALL IT BE CHILDLESS to the Holy rite, to the author of Holiness. And verse 23 it is said that an evil spirit seized Saul: which could be established as being of a Demon or Devil, or from the places which Grotius compares here, Matt. 4, 24. chap. 17, 15. Nor was the gift of reigning returned in turn through the singing of the Psalms; but the evil spirit was driven away, so that the good and Holy Spirit of God might succeed, who takes delight in the Psalms.

Latin:

Verf. 33. SICUT FECIT ABSQVE LIBERIS MVLIE- RES GLADIVS TVVS, SIC ABSQVE LIBERIS ERIT ritui Sancto autori Sanctitatis. Et verf. 23. dicitur Spiritus malus corripuisse Saul: quod Dæmonis vel Diaboli esse, vel ex locis, quæ hic confert Grotius, Matth. 4, 24. cap. 17, 15. constare poterat. Neque per Pfalmorum cantum donum regnandi vicissim reddebatur; sed Spiritus malus pellebatur, ut succe- deret bonus & Sanctus Dei Spiritus, qui Pfalmis delectatur.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. David anointed as King: the lyre drives away Saul's evil spirit.

Verf. 35. AND SAUL BUILT AN ALTAR TO THE LORD: AND THEN HE FIRST BEGAN TO BUILD AN ALTAR TO THE LORD] It is better to take these latter words exegetically: Saul built an altar to the Lord, that is, he began to build; he laid the first stone for building the altar.

Verf. 1. HOW LONG DO YOU MOURN FOR SAUL, SINCE I HAVE REJECTED HIM] It is permitted to pray for sinners before God's defined decree against them has become known.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. David in Regem unctus: Cythara malum Sau- lis spiritum abigit.

Verf. 35. ÆDIFICAVIT AVTEM SAUL ALTARE DOMINO: TUNCQVE PRIMUM COEPIT ÆDIFICARE ALTARE DOMINO] Melius est hæc posteriora sumere ἐξηγητικῶς, Ædificavit Saul altare Domino, id est, cæpit ædificare: primus lapidem jecit ad ædificandum altare.

Verf. 1. USQUE QUO TU LUGES SAUL, CUM EGO PROJECERIM EUM) Orare pro peccatoribus licet, ante- quam definitum in eos decretum Dei innotuit.

## 16:2
FOR SAUL WILL HEAR AND WILL KILL ME] And deservedly so, had the divine command not been present.

Verf. 2. TO SACRIFICE TO THE LORD] The authority of the Prophet causes the sacrifice to be duly performed wherever he is present and commands. For ritual laws are subject to the authority of the Prophets, as the Hebrews admit.

Verf. 45. THE PEOPLE THEREFORE DELIVERED JONATHAN] Not by command but by entreaty, in the way the Roman people delivered Fabius Rutilianus before the Dictator Papirius, which history is in Livy, book VIII. Nor should Saul's oath have stood in the way here, as it contained an unjust atrocity within itself. See what was said in book II of On the Law of War and Peace, chapter 13, section 6. Nevertheless, Saul sinned by swearing rashly (προπετῶς ὀμύων), and the curses pronounced by him eventually fell back upon himself.

That a Prophet, as one borne along by the Holy Spirit (ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενον), could indeed command by divine authority and extraordinarily delegate a sacrifice to another, and even offer sacrifices himself, there is no doubt, if God so willed: it is also credible to some that Samuel was often accustomed to sacrifice for the safety of the Republic, as it is to Peter Martyr and others: but Cloppenburg, in his Spicileg. Schol. sacrif. p. 198, wishes that Samuel did not sacrifice only out of the ordinary, like Elijah, but that he was called as High Priest from the sons of Korah by divine dispensation outside the line of Aaron, appointed to the ordinary priesthood by an extraordinary vocation. But where are such things written? What is read here in the sources proves nothing. For there is no mention of immolation in them. Junius and Tremellius translate it as 'come to celebrate the feast of Jehovah,' because here the same word is taken for a feast, as above in chapter 9, 12, 13, and below in this chapter. But that which is added, 'Jehovah,' they say is not to be referred to sacrifices, appears even from the fact that it is celebrated within the domestic walls of Jesse; since no public or private sacrifices could be offered according to the law anywhere other than in the place designated by GOD, and before the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle, or in corrupt times, anywhere other than in the High Places: but 'JEHOVAH' is added so that it may be understood that it was instituted by the command of Jehovah for some divine matter.

Verse 52. WHOMSOEVER SAUL SAW A MIGHTY MAN AND FIT FOR BATTLE, HE JOINED HIM TO HIMSELF] In times of war, mighty men are valued at their own price.

Latin:

AUDIET ENIM SAUL ET INTERFICIET ME] Et merito, nisi divinum mandatum adfuisset.

Verf. 2. AD IMMOLANDUM DOMINO] Auctori- tas Prophetæ facit, ut sacrificium, ubicunque is adest & impe- rat, rite fiat. Subsunt enim Prophetæ imperio leges rituales, fatentibus Hebræis.

Verf. 45. LIBERAVIT ERGO POPULUS JONATHAN) Non imperio sed deprecando, quomodo populus Romanus Fabi- um Rutilianum apud Papirium Dictatorem, quæ historia apud Livium est libro VIII. Neque hic obstare debebat jusju- randum Saulis, ut quod injustam atrocitatem in se contineret. Vide quæ dicta libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 13. §. 6. At- tamen peccavit Saul προπετῶς ὀμύων, & diræ ab ipso pronun- tiæ tandem in ipsum reciderunt.

Posse quidem Prophetam ceu ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενον imperare, auctoritate divina, & ex- traordinarie sacrificium alteri demandare, adeoque etiam ipsummet sacrificia offerre dubium nullum est, si Deus ita vellet: nonnullis etiam credibile est, Samuelem sæpe solitum sacrificare pro salute Reipubl. utpote Petro Martyri, & aliis: Cloppenburgius vero vult, non extra ordinem tantum sacrificasse Samue- lem, ut Eliam, sed dispensatione divina extra lineam Aaronis ex filiis Korachi vocatum fuisse summum sa- cerdotem, vocatione extraordinaria præfectum sacer- dotio ordinario, in spicileg. Schol. sacrif. p. 198. sed ubi talia scripta? Quod hic legitur in fontibus, ni- hil probat. Immolationis enim in illis nulla men- tio. Junius & Tremell. reddunt ad celebrandum con- pivium Jehœvæ veni, quia hic eadem vox accipitur pro convivio supr. cap. 9, 12. 13. & infra hoc cap. Quod autem additur Jehœvah, ad sacrificia, inqui- unt, referendum non esse, vel inde apparet, quod in- tra domesticos Isai parietes celebratur; quum nulla publica aut privata sacrificia ex lege alibi quam in loco à DEO designato, & coram arca fœderis ac taberna- culo, vel temporibus corruptis, alibi quam in Excelsis offerri possent: sed ideo additur JEHOVÆH, ut intel- ligatur ex mandato Jehœvæ ad rem aliquam divinam institutum esse.

Verf. 52. QUEMCUNQVE VIDERAT SAUL VIRUM FOR- TEM ET APTUM AD PRÆLIUM, SOCIABAT EUM SIBI] Belli temporibus viri fortes suo pretio æstimantur.

## 16:7
Verse 6. NOW BEFORE THE LORD IS HIS ANOINTED] It happens outside the time of revelation that Prophets err. 2 Sam. 7:3.

BUT THE LORD LOOKS AT THE HEART] Those to whom the right of choosing a king falls ought to do the same, as imitators of God. See what Aristotle says on this matter in Politics 3, ch. 13.

Latin:

Verf. 6. NUNC CORAM DOMINO EST CHRI- STUS EJUS] Extra revelationis tempus accidit ut errent Prophetæ 2. Sam. 7, 3.

DOMINUS AUTEM INTUETUR COR] Idem facere debent,ut Dei imitatores,ii quibus eligendi regis jus contigit. Vide quæ hac de re Aristot. Polit. 3. c. 13.

## 16:14
Ver. 14. THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD DEPARTED FROM SAUL] That Royal Spirit: see above 10, 9.

AND AN EVIL SPIRIT TROUBLED HIM] Showing outwardly what lay hidden within. Josephus called this in this place Δαιμονίων ταραχὴν, πονηρὸν πνεῦμα, δαιμόνια ἐγκατεζόμενα.

It concerns the Holy Spirit, which is also called the principal Spirit in Psalm 51, 14, and not merely a virtue or gift by which someone is rendered fit for administering a Kingdom. For by the Spirit of the Lord in the Scriptures, the Holy Spirit is usually understood when that name is taken properly. But there is no reason why we should depart from the propriety of the word here. Furthermore, an evil Spirit is opposed to it in v. 17, but an evil Spirit is not opposed to the gift of commanding: But to the Spirit

Latin:

Verf. 14. SPIRITUS DOMINI RECESSIT A SAUL] Spi- ritus ille Regius: vide supra 10, 9.

ET EXAGITABAT EUM SPIRITUS NEQVAM) Ex- terius oftendens, quod intus latebat. Δαιμονίων ταραχὴν, πονηρὸν πνεῦμα, δαιμόνια ἐγκατεζόμενα, dixit hoc loco Josephus.

De Spiritu Sancto agitur, qui Spiritus etiam principalis dicitur Pfalm. 51, 14. non autem tantum de virtute vel dono, quo quis Regno administran- do idoneus redditur. Nam per Spiritum Domini in Scripturis intelligi solet Spiritus Sanctus, quum pro- prie accipitur id nomen. A proprietate autem vo- cis hic cur recedamus, nulla est ratio. Adhæc op- ponitur ei Spiritus nequam v. 17. dono autem im- perandi Spiritus malignus non opponitur: Sed Spi- ritui

## 16:17
Verse 17. SOMEONE PLAYING WELL] See what was said above on this Book 10, 5. Marinus on Proclus: παρεκέλευε ἓν ἑκάςοτε ὕμνος λόγειν καὶ λεγομένων τῶν ὕμνων, πᾶσα εἰρήνη τῶν παθῶν ἐγίγνετο καὶ ἀταραξία. Apollonius on Wonders: ἰᾶται ἡ καταύλησις τῆς διανοίας ἐκςάσεις. Where also other things on this matter. It was the custom of the Pythagoreans, says Quintilian in book 9, 4, when they sought sleep, to soothe their minds first with the lyre, or to compose whatever turbulent thoughts there might have been.

Latin:

Verf. 17. ALIQVEM BENE PSALLENTEM] Vide quæ dicta supra ad hunc Librum 10, 5. Marinus de Proclo: παρεκέλευε ἓν ἑκάςοτε ὕμνος λόγειν καὶ λεγομένων τῶν ὕμνων, πᾶσα εἰρήνη τῶν παθῶν ἐγίγνετο καὶ ἀταραξία. Apollonius de Miris: ἰᾶται ἡ καταύλησις τῆς διανοίας ἐκςάσεις. Vbi & alia ad hanc rem. Pythagoreis moris fuit ait Quintilianus libro 9, 4. cum somnum peterent, ad lyram prius lenire mentes, aut si quid fuisset turbidarum cogitationum componerent.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII. Goliath defeated by David, who cut off his head. Saul pursues the fleeing Philistines.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII. Goliath à Davide devictus, qui ei caput ampu- tavit. Philistæos profugos Saul persequitur.

## 17:4
Verse 4. AND THERE WENT OUT A SPURIOUS MAN) There are various interpretations of the word הַבַּנַיִם which appears in the Hebrew in this place. But here the interpreter took it as if it were said this man is one of the sons, that is, conceived σποράδην without a father. The LXX, as if it were said excellent among the sons, namely of the Philistines: for they translate it δυνατός. Others, from בֵּין, which is between, think it is understood that he went out εἰς τὰ μεταίχμια, as both Homer and Euripides speak. Thus that Gaul, the Challenger, whom Manlius Torquatus killed, as Livy narrates in book 7, went out into the middle between the camps to the bridge. The first interpretation is most approved by me, with the addition, which some of the Hebrews also noted, that this is a surname of the giants who, being despisers of all laws and of marriage, were for that reason born of an uncertain father.

The interpretation of the word בנים as between two battle lines, i.e., an intermediary, a sequester, a duel, is to be preferred entirely, which the Rabbis, Pagnini, Marin, Vatabl. [hold].

Latin:

Verf. 4. ET EGRESSVS EST VIR SPVRIVS) Variæ sunt interpretationes vocis הַבַּנַיִם quæ hoc loco in Hebræo apparet. At hîc interpres sumsit quasi diceretur hic homo unus filiorum, id est, sine patre σποράδην conceptus. LXX. quasi diceretur excellens inter filios nempe Philisthinorum: vertunt enim δυνατός. Alii a בֵּין, quod est inter, putant in- telligi processisse eum εἰς τὰ μεταίχμια, ut & Homerus & Euripides loquuntur. Sic in medium inter castra pontem pró- cessit Gallus ille Provocator quem interfecit Manlius Tor- quatus, narrante Livio libro 7. Prima interpretatio maxime mihi probatur, addito, quod & Hebræorum nonnulli nota- runt, cognomen hoc esse gigantum qui legum omnium & ma- trimonii comtemtores ob id incerto patre nascebantur.

Præferenda omnino Interpretatio vocis בנים inter duas acies q. d. intermedius, sequester, duel- lio, quæ Rabbini, Pagnini, Marin. Vatabl.

## 17:9
Verse 9. IF HE SHALL BE ABLE TO FIGHT WITH ME AND SHALL STRIKE ME, WE SHALL BE YOUR SERVANTS] Such responses were frequent in those ages, as between the Lacedaemonians and the Argives in the time of Othryades, [and] between the Romans and the Albans, when the Horatii and Curiatii fought.

Latin:

Verf. 9. SI QVIVERIT PVGNARE MECVM ET PERCVSSERIT ME, ERIMVS VOBIS SERVI] Frequen- tes responsiones tales illis sæculis, ut inter Lacedæmonios & Argivos Othryadis tempore, inter Romanos & Albanos, cum Horatii & Curiatii decertarunt.

## 17:12
Verse 12. AND AN AGED MAN AMONG MEN) Not only an old man but also of a very advanced age among old men. For בַּאֲנָשִׁים some books have בַּשָׁנִים which does not fit badly in the place.

Latin:

Verf. 12. ET GRANDÆVVS INTER VIROS) Non senex tantum sed & inter senes maxime provectæ ætatis. Pro בַּאֲנָשִׁים libri quidam habent בַּשָׁנִים quod non male loco convenit.

## 17:25
Verse 25. AND HE WILL GIVE HIS DAUGHTER TO HIM) As Creon promised Jocasta his sister to him who would overcome the Sphinx, a woman who, from ambushes, which they called riddles, brought many evils upon the Thebans, the citadel being defended. This is the truth of that fable, which the Attics understood very well in the poem to Demetrius, which is in Athenaeus.

Verse 25. AND HE WILL MAKE HIS FATHER'S HOUSE WITHOUT TRIBUTE IN ISRAEL) Among the rights of the king it was, just as to impose tributes, so to free from tributes whomsoever he wished for the sake of virtue. The Greeks call this ἀτέλειαν, the Latins immunity, the barbarians Francisia.

Latin:

Verf. 25. ET FILIAM SVAM DABIT EI) Vt Creon Jocasten sororem suam pollicitus est ei qui Spinghem supera- ret, feminam quæ ex insidiis, quæ ænigmata vocabant, multa mala inferebat Thebanis, arce defensa. Hæc est ejus fabulæ ve- ritas, quam optime intellexerunt. Attici in carmine ad De- metrium, quod est apud Athenæum.

Verf. 25. ET DOMVM PATRIS EJVS FACIET ABS- QVE TRIBVTO IN ISRAEL) Inter jura regis erat sicut tributa imponere, ita a tributis, quem vellet virtutis ergo, li- berare. Græci hoc ἀτέλειαν vocant, Latini immunitatem, bar- bari Francisiam.

## 17:28
Verse 28. WHY HAVE YOU LEFT THOSE FEW SHEEP IN THE DESERT? And yet once - - The Gods also cultivated the Woods. That is, the sons of kings.

I KNOW THY PRIDE) It is frequent that some name of a related vice is given to a virtue. But we invert the virtues themselves, and we desire to encrust the sincere vessel. Who lives with us as an honest man? etc. Horace Satyr. 3. lib. 1.

Latin:

Verf. 28. QVARE DERELIQVISTI PAUCULAS IL- LAS OVES IN DESERTO? Atqui olim - - Coluerunt Dii quoque Silvas Id est, regum filii.

EGO NOVI SVPERBIAM TVAM) Frequens est ut virtuti nomen aliquod detur affinis vitii. At nos virtutes ipsas invertimus, atque Sincerum cupimus vas incrustare. Probus quis Nobiscum vivit? &c. Horatius Satyr. 3. lib. 1.

## 17:36
Vers. 36. AND I SLEW BOTH THE LION AND THE BEAR. Hunting excellently prepares men for war.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ET LEONEM ET URSVM INTERFECI Venatus egregie homines bello parat.

## 17:40
Vers. 40. AND HE TOOK HIS STAFF) Not unlike the history in Strabo, book 8.

AND HE TOOK THE SLING IN HIS HAND) No one is ignorant that slingers fought in all the battles of the ancients. Vegetius, book one of military affairs, chapter 6, where there is also much else in praise of slings.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ET TVLIT BACVLVM SUUM) Histori non dissimilis & apud Strabonem lib. 8.

ET FVNDAM MANU TULIT) In omnibus autem ve terum præliis funditores militasse nullus ignorat. Veget. li bro primo de re militari cap. 6. ubi & multa alia ad lauden fundarum.

## 17:43
Vers. 43. AM I A DOG?) The name of a dog has a signification of vileness. See below 24, 15. 2 Sam 3, 8. 9, 8. 16, 9. 2 Kings 8, 13. Thus Helen in Homer:

Δᾶερ ἐμεῖο κυνός.

Latin:

Vers. 43. NVMQVID EGO CANIS SVM?) Canis no men vilitatis habet significationem. Vide infra 24, 15. 2. Sam 3, 8. 9, 8. 16, 9. 2. Reg. 8, 13. Sic apud Homerum Helena:

Δᾶερ ἐμεῖο κυνός.

## 17:47
Vers. 47. FOR THE BATTLE IS HIS) Those wars are called the wars of God which are waged against those peoples condemned by God. Other wars are called of the kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 47. IPSIVS ENIM EST BELLVM) Bella Dei di- cuntur ea quæ geruntur in populos illos a Deo damnatos. Cæ- tera bella regni vocantur.

## 17:54
Vers. 54. BUT HE PUT HIS ARMOR IN HIS TENT) A trophy.

Latin:

Vers. 54. ARMA VERO EJVS POSVIT IN TABER- NACVLO) Trophæum.

## 17:55
Vers. 55. OF WHAT STOCK DOES THIS YOUTH DESCEND?) In the Hebrew: Whose son is this youth? To which question the answer follows below 58. Saul had already seen him and heard of his lineage before, above 16, 20. But forgetfulness of such things easily comes to kings in such great affairs, in such a multitude of those approaching them, especially if illnesses also occur.

Latin:

Vers. 55. DE QVA STIRPE DESCENDIT HIC ADO- LESCENS?) In Hebræo: Cujus filius iste adolescens? Ad quam interrogationem responsum sequitur infra 58. Viderat eum, & genus ejus audierat Saul jam ante supra 16, 20. Sed facile talium oblivio subit reges in tantis negotiis, in tanta eos adeuntium multitudine, præsertim si & morbi accedant.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII.

Saul pursues David because of the people's song of victory, intending to brandish his spear, and exposing the same to the danger of the Philistines.

Vers. 1. THE SOUL OF JONATHAN WAS KNIT WITH THE SOUL OF DAVID) An excellent description of friendship. Aristotle noted in Nicomachean Ethics 9, 8, that friends are thus called μίαν ψυχὴν. The Latin word for concord signifies the same, as does the Greek ὁμονοίας. Papinius said that hearts are bound. Add what is below 20, 17.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII.

Davidem ob epinicion populi persequitur Saul lancea vibraturus, & periculo Philistæorum exponens eundem.
