Vers. 1. ANIMA JONATHÆ CONGLVTINATA EST ANIMÆ DAVID) Egregia amicitiæ descriptio. Ita amicos μίαν ψυχὴν dici notavit Aristoteles Nicomacheorum 9, 8. Significat idem Latine concordiæ vox, & Græca ὁμονοίας. Ligari pectora dixit Papinius. Adde quod infra 20, 17.

## 18:3
Vers. 3. AND DAVID AND JONATHAN MADE A COVENANT) That is, they mutually promised perpetual friendship. See below 20, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 3. INIERVNT AVTEM DAVID ET JONA- THAS FEDVS) Id est, perpetuam amicitiam mutuo pro- misere. Vide infra 20, 3.

## 18:5
Ver. 5. AND MOSTLY IN THE SIGHT OF THE SERVANTS OF SAUL) Except for a few whom his glory burned.

Latin:

Vers. 5. MAXIMEQVE IN CONSPECTV FAMVLO- RVM SAVL) Exceptis paucis quos gloria ejus urebat.

## 18:6
Ver. 6. AND LEADING DANCES) As in public rejoicing. See what [is said] at Matt. 11, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 6. CHOROSQVE DVCENTES) Vt in publico gaudio. Vide quæ ad Matth. 11, 17.

## 18:8
Ver. 8. BUT SAUL WAS VERY ANGRY) As Nero was to Corbulo, Domitian to Agricola. See Tacitus.

Latin:

Vers. 8. IRATVS AVTEM EST SAVL NIMIS) Vt Nero Corbuloni, Domitianus Agricolæ. Vide Tacitum.

## 18:10
Ver. 10. AND HE PROPHESIED IN THE MIDST OF HIS HOUSE) The Chaldean translates it as 'and he was acting madly.' Kimchi: he was speaking words of madness, so that there is a metaphor in the word ויתנבא such as is often found in the word 'limfari' [to be frantic] among the Latins.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET PROPHETABAT IN MEDIO DOMVS SVÆ) Chaldæus, & insaniebat vertit. Kimchi: loquebatur verba insaniæ, ut sit metaphora in voce ויתנבא qualis sæpe in voce limfari apud Latinos.

## 18:17
Ver. 17. LET THE HAND OF THE PHILISTINES BE UPON HIM) With a similar spirit Eurystheus exposed Hercules to dangers.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SIT SVPER EVM MANVS PHILISTHINORVM) Pari animo Eurysteus Herculem objecit periculis.

## 18:25
Ver. 25. THE KING DOES NOT NEED DOWRY) That is, the dowry which husbands used to give to new brides, as we have said elsewhere.

EXCEPT ONLY A HUNDRED FORESKINS. He sought these rather than the heads of the Philistines; lest David offer the heads of Hebrews, pretending they were those of Philistines: for the Hebrews laid aside foreskins in circumcision, as Theodoret and Procopius [note].

Latin:

Vers. 25. NON HABET REX SPONSALIA NECESSE) Id est, dote quam mariti novis nuptis dabant, ut alibi diximus.

NISI TANTUM CENTUM PRÆ- PUTIA. Hæc potius, quam capita petiit Philistinorum; ne David offerret Hebræorum capita, fingens illa Philistinorum esse: nam præputia Ebræi in circum- cisione deposuerunt, ut Theodor. & Procopius.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

Jonathan reconciles David to Saul, whose blow David avoids again, as also captivity through the prudence of Michal. Saul among the Prophets.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

Jonathan Davidem Sauli reconciliat, cujus ictum iterum declinat David, ut & capti- vitatem prudentia Michol. Saul inter Pro- phetas.

## 19:12
Ver. 12. AND HE FLED) Against the anger of a king, nothing is safer than flight.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET AVFVGIT) Contra regis iram nihil tutius fuga.

## 19:23
Ver. 23. AND HE PROPHESIED) For God sometimes grants this gift even to the wicked, as to Balaam. See Matt. 7, ver. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET PROPHETABAT) Donum enim hoc inter- dum etiam impiis concedit Deus, ut Balaamo. Vide Matth. 7. vers. 22.

## 19:24
Ver. 24. HE FELL) That is, he departed from his state of mind. Num. 24, ver. 4.

Why do we not understand it properly with others, that he fell as one destitute of strength, as Aben-Ezra, Abulensis, and Vatablus explain? Because it seems to have been done by divine providence, so that David might have sufficient time to escape.

Naked) In an undergarment, as Isaiah 20:2. See concerning this manner of speaking at John 21:7.

Latin:

Vers. 24. CECIDIT) Id est, de mentis statu excessit. Num. 24. vers. 4.

Cur non proprie cum aliis intelligamus, ceci- dit utpote viribus destitutus, uti Aben - Esdra, A- bulensis, Vatabl. exponunt? quia divina providen- tia id factum videtur, ut tempus effugiendi suffi- ciens haberet David.

NVDVS) In interula, ut Esaias 20, 2. Vide de hoc loquen- di genere ad Joan. 21, 7.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

Jonathan, having been consulted by David, manifests his father's hatred to him through arrows, and dismisses him with tears.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

Jonathan à Davide consultus odium Patris per sagittas ei manifestat, & cum lachrymis eum dimittit.

## 20:3
Verse 3. BY ONLY, SO TO SPEAK, A SINGLE STEP) Pace. Symmachus: as many steps as there are between me and death. Two thousand such steps in a Sabbath day's journey.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VNO TANTVM VT ITA DICAM GRA- DV) Passu. Symmachus : ὅσων βῆμα ἀναμεταξὺ ἐμὲ καὶ θα- νάτε. Tales passus bis mille in sabbati itinere.

## 20:6
Verse 6.

SOLEMN VICTIMS) Understand the feast which relatives held among themselves after a sacrifice for their own well-being. A similar solemn feast among the Romans was called charistia, at which no one was admitted except blood relatives and relatives by marriage: as Valerius Maximus speaks in book 2, chapter 1. Ovid, Fasti II: The dear relatives called the next feast charistia, and the related crowd came to the friendly gods.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

VICTIMÆ SOLENNES) Intellige convivium quod in- ter se habebant cognati post sacrificium pro ipsorum salute. Simile convivium solenne apud Romanos charistia dictum, cui præter agnatos & affines nemo interponebatur : ut loqui- tur Valerius Maximus libro 2. c. 1. Ovidius Fastorum II. Proxima cognati dixere charistia cari, Et venit ad socios turba propinqua deos.

## 20:9
FOR IT CANNOT BE THAT, IF I CERTAINLY KNOW THAT THE MALICE OF MY FATHER IS COMPLETE AGAINST YOU, I SHALL NOT ANNOUNCE IT TO YOU] Sons ought not to obey fathers in all things: a subject we have treated widely in the second book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 26, § 3. It was to David's advantage in Jonathan's mind, both his own innocence and the promises of God not unknown to Jonathan. That is clear below 23, 17.

WE WILL GO OUT INTO THE FIELD] For they were accustomed to swear in the open air.

Latin:

NEQVE ENIM FIERI POTEST, VT SI CERTE COGNOVERO COMPLETAM ESSE PATRIS MEI MALITIAM CONTRA TE, NON ANNUNTIEM TIBI] Non in omnia filii patribus parere debent : quam materiam late tractavimus libro secundo de Jure Belli ac Pa- cis cap. 26. §. 3. Davidi apud Jonathanis animum proderat, & innocentia ipsius, & Dei promissa Jonathani non incogni- ta. Id clarum infra 23, 17.

EGREDIEMUR FORAS IN AGRUM] Jurare enim sub dio solebant.

## 20:20
AS IF EXERCISING ME AT A MARK) Which the Greeks call σκοπόν: which word Symmachus and Aquila used here: in which way this noun is taken in book 16, 12, and Lam. 3, 12. But the LXX [use] εἰς τὴν ἁμαρταγί, as if it were the proper name of a place.

Latin:

QVASI EXERCENS ME AD SIGNVM) Quem σκο- πόν Græci vocant : qua voce hic usi Symmachus & Aquila : quomodo hoc nomen sumitur libro 16, 12. & Lam. 3, 12. At LXX. εἰς τὴν ἁμαρταγί, quasi proprium esset loci nomen.

## 20:21
Verse 21.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

## 20:23
Verse 23.

MAY THE LORD BE BETWEEN ME AND YOU) As witness, and if anyone deceives, as avenger, which is tacitly inherent in every oath, as we said in book II of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 13, § 10.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

SIT DOMINUS INTER ME ET TE) Testis, & si quis fallat, vindex, quod omni jurijurando tacite inest, ut diximus libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 13. §. 10.

## 20:24
Verse 24.

AND IF I LIVE, YOU SHALL SHOW ME THE MERCY OF THE LORD] He stipulates this because of the evil customs of neighboring kings, who used to kill the children and relatives of preceding kings, so that they might see nothing suspicious around them. Saul's request below 24, 22 looks to the same thing.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ET SI VIXERO, FACIES MIHI MISERICORDIAM DOMINI] Hoc stipulatur ob mores malos vicinorum re- gum, qui regum antecedentium liberos & propinquos interfi- ciebant, ne quid suspectum circa se viderent. Eodem respi- cit Saulis postulatio infra 24, 22.

## 20:26
Verse 26.

THAT WHICH BY CHANCE HAD HAPPENED TO HIM, SO THAT HE WAS NOT CLEAN) The word מקרה which is here in the Hebrew properly pertains to that species of which we treated in Leviticus 15, 16. NOR PURIFIED] Which was done by washing and the arrival of evening.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

QVOD FORTE EVENISSET EI, UT NON ES- SET MVNDVS) Vox מקרה quæ hic in Hebræo est proprie ad eam speciem pertinet, de qua egimus Levit. 15, 16. NEC PVRIFICATVS] Quod fiebat lotione & adventu vesperæ.

## 20:30
Verse 30.

SONS OF A WOMAN WHO VOLUNTARILY SEIZES A MAN) The sense of the Hebrew words seems to be: Sons of a depraved woman, even to the highest degree of contumacy. Sons are accustomed to be like their parents. Saul, who does not wish to accuse himself, casts the blame of his harsh disposition upon his mother.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

FILII MULIERIS VIRUM VLTRO RAPIENTIS) Videtur sensus Hebræarum vocum esse. Fili mulieris pravæ ad summam usque contumaciam. Solent filii parentibus es- se similes. Saul qui se accusare non vult, culpam duri inge- nii in matrem rejicit.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. David, fleeing, receives the showbread and the sword of Goliath; he feigns madness before Achish.

Verse 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. David fugiens panes propositionis, & gladi- um Goliath accipit: insaniam penes Achis simulat.

Vers. 1.

## 21:3
THE KING HAS COMMANDED ME A MATTER) Doubtless feeling the same as Euripides: Ὅτῳ δ᾽ ὄλεθρον δεινὸν ἡ ἀλήθη ἄγει, Συγγνωστὸν εἰπεῖν ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ μὴ καλόν. And with Diphilus: Ὑπολαμβάνω τὸ ψεῦδος ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ Λεγόμενον οὐδὲν περιποιεῖσθαι δυσχερές. Something must be pardoned to those times, with eternal life lying much in the dark.

An error concerning eternal life lying much in the dark in the time of the Old Testament, and that it was then lawful to lie. The former has often been noted already. And concerning the latter, we spoke at Joshua 2, 4. David cannot be absolved from the lie, even if he did not invent these things to deceive the priest, nor to create danger for him, but rather to consult for his safety, so that he might be helped by him with provisions without danger.

Latin:

REX PRÆCEPIT MIHI SERMONEM) Nimirum pa- tia sentiens cum Euripide : Ὅτῳ δ᾽ ὄλεθρον δεινὸν ἡ ἀλήθη ἄγει, Συγγνωστὸν εἰπεῖν ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ μὴ καλόν. Et cum Diphilo : Ὑπολαμβάνω τὸ ψεῦδος ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ Λεγόμενον οὐδὲν περιποιεῖσθαι δυσχερές. Condonandum aliquid illis temporibus, latente multum vita æterna.

Error de multum latente vita æterna tempore Vet. Testam. & quod licitum tum fuerit mentiri. Prior sæpe jam notatus. Et de posteriore ad Jos. 2, 4. diximus. Non absolvi potest David à men- dacio, etsi hæc non ut sacerdotem falleret, nec ut ei periculum crearet, sed potius ut incolumitati ejus consuleret, quod absque periculo commeatu ab ipso juvari posset, confinxerit.

## 21:5
Verse 4.

ONLY HOLY BREAD] Ritual laws easily allow themselves to be overcome by some necessity or great utility. See what was said at Matthew 12, 4.

IF THE YOUNG MEN ARE CLEAN, ESPECIALLY FROM WOMEN) Which was accustomed to be required in sacred matters. See Tibullus book 3, Propertius 2, 21, Ovid's Amores 1, 8, 3, and 9, Metamorphoses 10. See what was said at Exodus 19, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

TANTVM PANEM SANCTVM] Leges rituales facile ab aliqua necessitate aut utilitate magna vinci se patiuntur. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. 12, 4.

SI MVNDI SVNT PVERI MAXIME A MVLIE- RIBVS] Quod in sacris exigi solebat. Vide Tibullum l. 3. Propertium 2, 21. Ovidium Amorum. I, 8. III. & 9. Metam 10. Vide quæ dicta ad Exodum 19, 15.

## 21:10
Verse 9.

BEHOLD, HERE IS THE SWORD OF GOLIATH THE PHILISTINE] Seneca in the Controversiae: For the sake of the republic, temples are often stripped. See also other things brought forward in the third book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 5, § 2, and in the Annotations. Add § 'sacra res', Institutes, on the division of things, and what was said by us in that same book, chapter 20, § 23. Iolaus in the Heraclidae of Euripides, taking arms from the temple: Ἔστ᾽ ἐν δόμοισιν ἔνδον αἰχμάλωτ᾽ ὅπλα, Τοῖς δ᾽ ὅισι χρησόμεσθα κ᾿ αποδώσομεν Ζῶντες. θανόντας δ᾽ ἐκ ἀπαιτήσει θεός.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ECCE HIC GLADIVS GOLIATH PHILISTHÆI] Seneca in controversiis: Pro republica plerumque templa nu- dantur. Vide & alia allata libro tertio de Jure Belli ac Pa- cis cap. 5. §. 2. & in Annotatis. Adde §. sacra res. Instit. de rerum divis. & quæ nobis dicta eodem illo libro cap. 20. §. 23. Jolaus in Heraclidis Euripidis, arma de templo sumens: Ἔστ᾽ ἐν δόμοισιν ἔνδον αἰχμάλωτ᾽ ὅπλα, Τοῖς δ᾽ ὅισι χρησόμεσθα κ᾿ αποδώσομεν Ζῶντες. θανόντας δ᾽ ἐκ ἀπαιτήσει θεός.

## 21:11
Verse 10.

HE CAME TO ACHISH THE KING OF GATH] ἀνεπίφθονον δὲ ὅσοι ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑπὸ τῶν Αθηναίων ἐπιβυλευόμεθα, μὴ ἕλληνας μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ βαρβάρους προσλαβόντας διασωθῆ- ναι say certain Greeks in Thucydides.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

VENIT AD ACHIS REGEM GETH] ἀνεπίφθονον δὲ ὅσοι ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑπὸ τῶν Αθηναίων ἐπιβυλευόμεθα, μὴ ἕλληνας μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ βαρβάρους προσλαβόντας διασωθῆ- ναι ajunt Græcorum quidam apud Thucydiden.

## 21:12
Verse 11.

KING OF THE LAND] That is, leader. For this word is sometimes taken improperly, as in Deut. 33:5.

It can also be taken properly, as Osiander: Is this not the King of the land, who is believed among the Israelites to be already destined for the kingdom, on account of so many heroic deeds?

Latin:

Vers. 11.

REX TERRÆ] Id est, dux. Vox enim hæc impropriæ interdum sumitur, ut Deut. 33, 5.

Potest etiam proprie accipi, uti Osiander: Nun- quid non iste est Rex terræ, qui apud Israelitas creditur jam regno destinatus, propter tot heroi- ca facta?

## 21:14
Verse 13.

AND HE CHANGED HIS BEHAVIOR BEFORE THEM) In Hebrew את טעמו, that is here his gesture. The same words in this very matter are in the inscription of Psalm 34.

AND HE SLIPPED BETWEEN THEIR HANDS) In the Hebrew: he feigned madness in their hands, that is, surrounded by them. Thus Ulysses among the Greeks: He feigned madness. See Cicero, De Officiis, book three.

Some absolve David here from lying and sin: because he acted thus compelled by necessity; but unless he had behaved himself so moved by GOD, which seems to some, since he immediately composed the Psalm by divine inspiration, which is the 34th, from whose inscription and words full of confidence and exultation that opinion is entirely proven to us, that trusting in GOD suggesting this counsel he now rejoices in the happy outcome and celebrates God, he could not be absolved from sin.

AND HE BEAT UPON THE DOORS OF THE GATE) He painted. Thus Rabbi Solomon תוו is γράφειν, as much to paint as to write.

Thus also Vatablus: he painted, or wrote on the doors of the gate, as fools are wont to paint with their fingers, and describe various lines. Avenarius: and he marked (by beating) the doors of the gate: he marked by scratching with his nails on the leaves of the gates.

AND HIS SPITTLE RAN DOWN UPON HIS BEARD) See Mark 9:18, 20. Luke 9, verse 39, and what is said in the same place.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ET IMMVTAVIT OS SVVM CORAM EIS) He- braice את טעמו, id hic est gestum suum. Eadem ver- ba in hac ipsa re in inscriptione Ps. 34.

ET COLLABEBATVR INTER MANVS EORVM) In Hebræo: finxit se furere in manibus eorum, id est, circum- datus ab ipsis. Sic Ulysses apud Græcos: Furere assimulavit. Vide Ciceronem de officiis tertio.

Absolvunt nonnulli Davidem hic à menda- cio & peccato : quia coactus necessitate ita egit; sed nisi motus à DEO talem se gessisset, quod qui- busdam videtur, quum Psalmum inspiratione di- vina statim composuerit, qui est 34. è cujus inscri- ptione & verbis fiducia & exultatione plenis nobis omnino probatur ea sententia, quod DEO sugge- renti hoc consilium confisus jam de eventu felici lætetur Deumque celebret, à peccato absolvi non posset.

ET IMPINGEBAT IN OSTIA PORTÆ) Pingebat. Ita Rabbi Salomo תוו est γράφειν tam pingere quam scribere.

Sic etiam Vatabl. pingebat, sive scribebat in ostiis portæ, sicut fatui solent digitis suis pingere, & va- rias lineas describere. Avenarius, & signavit (im- pingendo) ostia portæ : signavit exarando unguibus in valvis portarum.

DEFLVEBANTQVE SALIVÆ EJVS IN BARBAM) Vide Marc. 9, 18. 20. Luc. 9. vers. 39. & quæ ibidem dicta.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII.

David flees into a cave. Achimelech, having been betrayed by Doeg, is killed along with the remaining priests.

Ver. 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII.

David in speluncam fugit. Achimelech à Doeg proditus cum reliquis sacerdotibus occiditur.

Vers. 1.

## 22:3
AND THOSE OPPRESSED BY DEBT) See what we have said at Jud. 11, 3.

The cave of Odollam in the rock was a place protected by nature. See Adrichom. David here is a type of Christ Luc. 15. ver. 2.

Latin:

ET OPPRESSI ÆRE ALIENO) Vide quæ diximus ad Jud. 11, 3.

Odolla spelunca in petra fuit locus natura tu- tus. Vid. Adrichom. David hic typus Christi Luc. 15. vers. 2.

## 22:6
Ver. 5.

DEPART AND GO INTO THE LAND OF JUDAH) Θεῦ θέλοντος κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέης; God shows great care for David, instructing him now through Prophets, now through Urim and Thummim.

HE CAME INTO THE FOREST OF HARETH. Which place was desert, inaccessible and uncultivated, bristling with nothing but briars and thorns: but by divine power made abundant in fruits, and animals, and irrigated springs, if faith is to be placed in R. Solomon.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

PROFICISCERE ET VADE IN TERRAM JVDÆ) Θεῦ θέλοντος κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέης· Magnam pro Davide curam ostendit Deus, nunc per Prophe- tas, nunc per Vrim & Thumim eum instruens.

VENIT IN SALTUM HARETH. Qui lo- cus desertus erat, invius & incultus non nisi senti- bus & vepribus perhorrescens: sed divina virtute factus abundans fructibus, & animalibus & irriguis fontibus, si fides habenda R. Salomoni.

## 22:10
Ver. 9.

DOEG THE IDUMEAN) Informers are a race of men discovered for the public ruin, says Tacitus, Histories IV. See the description of Doeg in Ps. 52.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

DOEG IDUMÆVS) Delatores genus hominum publi- co exitio repertum, ait Tacitus Histor. IV. Descriptionem Doegi vide Ps. 52.

## 22:15
Ver. 14.

AND WHO AMONG ALL THY SERVANTS, AS DAVID, FAITHFUL, AND SON-IN-LAW OF THE KING, AND GOING TO THY COMMAND, AND GLORIOUS IN THY HOUSE) A similar purgation of M. Terentius in Tacitus, Annals VI. I will confess both that I was a friend to Sejanus, and that I sought to be, and after I had attained it, I rejoiced. I had seen the colleague of his father, ruling the praetorian cohorts: soon performing the duties of the city and the military at the same time. His relatives and kinsmen were increased with honors: as anyone was intimate with Sejanus, so was he powerful for the friendship of Caesar. On the contrary, those to whom he was hostile were afflicted with fear and squalor. Nor do I take anyone as an example. I shall defend all of us who were devoid of the latest counsel by the peril of myself alone. For we were not cultivating Sejanus the Vulsinian, but a part of the house of Claudius and Julia, which he had occupied by affinity, your son-in-law, Caesar, the partner of your consulship, performing your duties in the republic. It is not for us to estimate whom you exalt above others and for what reasons. The gods have given you the supreme judgment of affairs: to us the glory of obedience is left.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ET QVIS IN OMNIBVS SERVIS TVIS, SICVT DAVID, FIDELIS, ET GENER REGIS, ET PERGENS AD IMPERIVM TVVM, ET GLORIOSVS IN DOMO TVA) Similis purgatio M. Terentii apud Tacitum Annal. VI. Fatebor & fuisse me Sejano amicum, & ut essem expetiisse, & postquam adeptus eram lætatum. Videram collegam patris, regendis prætoriis cohortibus: mox urbis & militiæ munia simul obeuntem. Illius propinqui & affines honoribus auge- bantur: ut quisque Sejano intimus, ita ad Cæsaris amicitiam validus. Contra quibus infensus esset, metu ac sordibus con- flictabantur. Nec quemquam exemplo assumo. Cunctos qui novissimi consilii expertes fuimus, meo unius discrimine defen- dam. Non enim Sejanum Vulsiniensem, sed Claudiæ & Iu- liæ domus partem, quas affinitate occupaverat, tuum Cæsar generum, tui consulatus socium, tua officia in republica capes- sentem colebamus. Non est nostrum æstimare quem supra cæ- teros & quibus de causis extollas. Tibi summum rerum judi- cium dii dederunt: nobis obsequii gloria relicta est.

## 22:18
Ver. 17.

KNOWING THAT HE HAD FLED, AND DID NOT TELL ME) Evil kings are suspicious, and that is often fatal to the most innocent.

BUT THE SERVANTS OF THE KING WOULD NOT EXTEND THEIR HANDS AGAINST THE PRIESTS OF THE LORD) They revered both the innocence and the sanctity of the order. What we said before about parents must be repeated about kings, that cruel and impious commands are sometimes piously refused: for it was not Zeus who proclaimed these things to me, said Apollonius against the edict of Nero. Which Tertullian said, that we ought to be subject to princes within the limits of discipline. See concerning the Law of War and Peace, book II, chapter 26, § 3.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

SCIENTES QVOD FVGISSET, ET NON INDICA- VERVNT MIHI) Mali reges suspicaces, idque sæpe inno- centissimis exitiale.

NOLVERVNT AVTEM SERVI REGIS EXTEN- DERE MANVS SVAS IN SACERDOTES DOMINI) Reveriti & innocentiam & ordinis sanctimoniam. Quod de parentibus ante diximus, de regibus repetendum, pie inter- dum detrectari imperia sæva atque impia: ὃ γὰρ τί μοι Ζεὺς ἦν ὁ κηρύξας τάδε. Ajebat Apollonius contra Neronis edictum. Quod Ter- tullianus dixit subditos nos esse debere principibus intra limites disciplinæ. Vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro II. cap. 26. §. 3.

## 22:19
Ver. 18.

TURN THOU ALSO, AND FALL UPON THE PRIESTS OF THE LORD) Such things commanded for a cause were included in the power of kings. See 2 Kings 1:14, but that also should have been considered: Kings are to be feared for their own flocks: over the kings themselves is the power of Jove.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

CONVERTERE ET TV, ET IRRVE IN SACER- DOTES DOMINI) Talia ex causa imperare in potestate regum erat comprehensum. Vide 2. Reg. 1, 14. verum cogitan- dum & illud fuerat: Regum timendorum in proprios greges: Reges in ipsos imperium est Iovis.

## 22:21
HE FLED TO DAVID) It is a prolepsis, as appears in 23, 6.

Latin:

FVGIT AD DAVID) Est πρόληψις, ut apparet 23, 6.

## 22:22
Ver. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

## 22:23
Ver. 22. I AM GUILTY.

He was not the cause, but only the occasion of this slaughter, and indeed beyond his intention and without his fault: therefore he was guilty not formally, but materially, because he provided the matter and the occasion. Some believe the wicked sons of Eli were punished in these grandsons of his, 1 Sam. 2, 33. Which Cornelius assumes and yet makes these men priests; which things are inconsistent.

Latin:

Vers. 22. EGO SUM REUS.

Non causa fuit, sed occasio tantum cædis hu- jus, & quidem præter intentionem & citra culpam suam: Reus itaque fuit non formaliter, sed materia- liter, quia materiam & occasionem dedit. Credunt nonnulli filios sceleratos Eli in his suis nepotibus punitos 1. Sam. 2, 33. Quod assumit Cornelius & Martyres tamen hos sacerdotes facit; quæ ἀσύστα- τα sunt.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

David delivered Keilah from the Philistines. But being about to be handed over to Saul by the Keilites, he hid himself in the wilderness of Ziph; being betrayed, he betook himself to the wilderness of Maon. Where, when Saul wished to capture him, he was recalled from his pursuit by an incursion of the Philistines.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

David Ceilam à Philistæis liberavit. Sed tra- dendus Sauli à Ceilanis in deserto Ziph se oc- cultavit, proditus in desertum Maon se con- fert. Ubi cum capere eum vellet Saul, per in- cursionem Philistæorum à persecutione ejus revocatus est.

## 23:3
Ver. 2.

SHALL I GO AND SMITE THESE PHILISTINES?) Great is the love of country in David, who, though judged a rebel by the king, not only does not harm his country, but even benefits it, while living in enemy territory.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

NVM VADAM ET PERCVTIAM PHILISTHÆOS ISTOS?) Magnus amor patriæ in Davide, qui a rege per- duellis judicatus, patriæ tamen non modo non nocet, sed & prodest, de hostico vivens.

## 23:9
Ver. 8.

SAUL COMMANDED ALL THE PEOPLE TO GO DOWN TO BATTLE) This was among the royal rights.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

PRÆCEPIT SAVL OMNI POPVLO VT IN PV- GNAM DESCENDERET) Erat hoc inter jura regia.

## 23:13
Ver. 12.

AND THE LORD SAID, THEY WILL DELIVER UP) Ungrateful men, who wished to withdraw themselves from danger by the surrender of a man who had deserved so well. How much better the Athenians, who refused to surrender Demosthenes and other orators, even when Alexander demanded it?

From this answer, however, it appears that God knows even conditional future events, namely that David would be delivered up by the Keilites if he remained there, concerning which see Vol. II of the System of Theology, p. 522.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET DIXIT DOMINVS, TRADENT) Ingrati ho- mines qui viri tam præclare meriti deditione periculo se sub- ducere volebant. Quanto melius Athenienses, qui Demo- sthenem & Oratores alios dedere noluerunt, idque poscenti Alexandro?

Ex hoc autem responso apparet Deum futura etiam conditionata cognoscere, utpote traditum à Ceilitis iri Davidem, si illic permanserit, quo de vid. Tom. II. Syst. Theol. p. 522.

## 23:16
Vers. 15. IN THE DESERT OF ZIPH. Near the city so named in a woody, bushy desert, accessible to wild beasts and ibexes, full of caves and dens, and very cavernous, as Brocard and Adrichom [state].

Latin:

Vers. 15. IN DESERTO ZIPH. Juxta civitatem ita dictam in deserto nemoroso, saltuoso, feris, & ibicibus pervio, antris & spelun- cis pleno, & plurimum cavernoso, ut Brocard. & Adrichom.

## 23:23
Vers. 22. FOR HE RECONSIDERS THAT I CRAFTILY LIE IN WAIT FOR HIM) David, being strong in intellect, easily conjectured his plans from Saul's known disposition toward him. Above 15. Furthermore, he used frequent scouts, as provident leaders are accustomed to do. Below 25.

Latin:

Vers. 22. RECOGITAT ENIM DE ME QVOD CALLIDE INSIDIER EI) David, ut ingenio valens, ex noto in se Saulis animo facile ejus consilia conjectabat. Supra 15. præ- terea crebris exploratoribus utebatur, ut solent duces provi- di. Infra 25.

## 23:26
Vers. 25. IN THE DESERT OF MAON. Concerning this, Jerome and Adrichom [write]. Maon was a city in the tribe of Judah, situated in the plains to the right of Jeshimon toward the sunrise of the South: near the city was a woody desert full of caves: it is adjacent to the desert of Carmel and Paran.

Latin:

Vers. 25. IN DESERTO MAON. De hoc Hieronym. & Adrichom. Maon erat civitas in tribu Juda, sita in campestribus ad dex- tram Jesimon contra Solis ortum Daromæ: juxta urbem erat desertum nemorosum & cavernis ple- num: Confine est deserto Carmeli & Pharan.

## 23:27
Vers. 26. HE DESPAIRED THAT HE COULD ESCAPE. By his own virtue, that is, and wisdom. But he did not despair of divine providence, since he had been anointed by God as King to succeed Saul.

Latin:

Vers. 26. DESPERABAT SE POSSE EVA- DERE. Sua scil. virtute, & sapientia. Non autem despe- rabat de divina providentia, quum à Deo unctus fue- rit in Regem, ut Sauli succederet.

## 23:28
Vers. 27. THE PHILISTINES INVADED THE LAND) Thus, an external enemy often brings some respite to civil troubles. There are many examples in Livy.

Latin:

Vers. 27. INFVDERVNT SE PHILISTIIM SVPER TER- RAM) Ita sæpe hostis externus malis civilibus adfert spira- menti aliquid. Exempla apud Livium multa.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV.

David in the cave of Engedi cuts off the hem of the cloak of Saul who is pursuing him, and being acknowledged as innocent, is reconciled to Saul by a prior oath.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV.

David in spelunca Engaddi oram Chlamydis Saul persequentis abscidit, & innoxius agni- tus prævio juramento Sauli reconciliatur.

## 24:4
Vers. 4. TO PURGE HIS BELLY. In the Hebrew, to cover his feet. See Judges 3:24. Because the Hebrews did not use breeches as we do, nor did the Romans, but tunics, by which the feet of those resting were covered. Which my son Abraham noted here.

DAVID AND HIS MEN WERE HIDING IN THE INNER PART OF THE CAVE) In a similar way, Masinissa once hid in a cave. See Appian's Punic Wars.

Latin:

Vers. 4. UT PURGARET VENTREM. In Ebr. ad tegendum pedes suos. Vid. Jud. 3, 24. quia non ut nos, braccis utebantur Hebræi, uti nec Romani, sed tunicis, quibus quiescentium pedes tegebantur. Quod hic annotavit B. Filius meus Abrahamus.

DAVID ET VIRI EJUS IN INTERIORE PARTE SPELUNCÆ LATEBANT) Simili modo in spelunca latuit aliquando Masinissa. Vide Appiani Punica.

## 24:7
Vers. 7. BECAUSE HE IS THE LORD'S ANOINTED) The person of kings ought to be sacred to all, 26:9, 11. For God is their Judge. 13:16. See what is said in the book on the Law of War and Peace, Book 1, chapter 4, § 6.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVIA CHRISTUS DOMINI EST) Regum persona omnibus sancta esse debet 26, 9. 11. Deus enim eorum Judex. 13, 16. Vide quæ dicta libro de Jure Belli ac Pacis 1. cap. 4. §. 6.

## 24:11
Vers. 11. AND I THOUGHT TO KILL THEE. The Vulgate is wrong here: whence Cornelius [says]: that David had indeed thought of it, but had not resolved or decreed it; that it was a simple thought and an inclination of the sensitive appetite. But in the Hebrew it is, and he (someone) said to me to kill: and so the Chaldean. And others said. For it had not come into David's mind: as is evident from v. 7, nor should any inclination of it be imputed to him.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET COGITAVI UT OCCIDE- REM TE. Perperam ita Vulgata: unde Cornelius: Cogitas- se quidem id Davidem, non autem statuisse, vel decre- visse; simplicem fuisse cogitationem & inclinationem appetitus sensitivi. Sed in Ebr. est, & dixit mihi (ali- quis) ut occiderem: atque ita Chald. Et dixerunt alii. Non enim id in mentem venerat Davidi: ut è v. 7. constat, nec ulla ejus inclinatio ei imputanda.

## 24:12
Vers. 12. MY FATHER) Thus sons-in-law are accustomed to call their fathers-in-law. And a king ought to be the father of the people.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PATER MI) Sic soceros vocare generi solent. Et rex pa- ter populi esse debet.

## 24:14
Ver. 14. IT IS SAID IN AN ANCIENT PROVERB: WICKEDNESS SHALL GO FORTH FROM THE WICKED) Similar to that of the Greeks: κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν. Actions are usually as the quality of the mind is.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IN PROVERBIO ANTIQVO DICITVR: AB IM- PIIS EGREDIETVR IMPIETAS) Simile Græcorum il- lud: κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν. Solent actiones esse prout est animi qualitas.

## 24:15
Ver. 15. WHOM DO YOU PURSUE, O KING OF ISRAEL: WHOM DO YOU PURSUE? DO YOU PURSUE A DEAD DOG) A highly pathetic speech and an index of David's utmost modesty, concerning which see Psalm 131.

see that she was not repudiated. Wherefore, as if no divorce had been made, David received her back 2 Sam. 3, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QVEM PERSEQVERIS, REX ISRAEL: QVEM PERSEQVERIS? CANEM MORTVVM PER- SEQVERIS) Valde παθητικὴ oratio & index summæ Da- vidis modestiæ, de qua vide Psal. 131.

vide non repudiatam. Quare, velut non facto divortio, re- cepit eam David 2. Reg. 3, 14.

## 24:18
Ver. 18. YOU ARE MORE RIGHTEOUS THAN I) A confession extorted from an unwilling person, with the mind not at all amended. See also below 26, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 18. JUSTIOR TV ES QVAM EGO) Confessio extorta in- vito, animo nihil emendato. Vide & infra 26, 21.

## 25:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXV.

The death of Samuel. The avarice and destruction of Nabal, whose widow Abigail David married.

Latin:

CAPUT XXV.

Mors Samuelis. Nabalis avaritia, & interitus, cujus viduam Abigail duxit David.

## 25:3
Ver. 3. AND THAT WOMAN WAS MOST PRUDENT) Such as Tanaquil.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ERATQVE MVLIER ILLA PRVDENTISSIMA) Qualis Tanaquil.

## 25:6
Ver. 6. LET THERE BE PEACE TO MY BRETHREN AND TO THEE) This interpreter reads לאחי: but our Hebrew has לחי. which the Greeks translate εἰς ὥρας, that is, may there be long prosperity to you.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SIT FRATRIBVS MEIS ET TIBI PAX) Legit hic in- terpres לאחי: at nostrum Hebræum habet לחי. quod Græ- ci vertunt εἰς ὥρας, id est, longa tibi sit prosperitas.

## 25:22
Ver. 22. MAY GOD DO THIS TO THE ENEMIES OF DAVID) David said: May God do this to me: but by κατ’ εὐφημισμὸν the expression has been changed. See Ruth 1, 17. Great injuries sometimes even expel the highest gentleness.

THAT I SHOULD NOT DWELL IN THE INHERITANCE OF THE LORD, SAYING: GO, SERVE OTHER GODS) A wise saying, for first he derives the blame from the king to Doeg and his like-minded counselors, as prudent men do. Then he shows that if it is partly to take away a leader, to take away a soldier from the king, certainly any Israelite from the common people ought not to have been cast into those straits, by which many, even not Idumeans, being pressed, were about to depart from God and the law. For those fruitful times of martyrs had not yet come.

Latin:

Vers. 22. HÆC FACIAT DEVS INIMICIS DAVID) Dixit Da- vid: Hæc faciat Deus mihi: sed κατ’ εὐφημισμὸν immutata est locutio. Vide Ruth 1, 17. Magnæ injuriæ interdum et- tam summam mansuetudinem expellunt.

UT NON HABITEM IN HEREDITATE DOMINI, DICENTES: VADE, SERVI DIIS ALIENIS) Cordate dictum, nam primum culpam a rege ad Doegum, & ejus simi- les consiliarios derivat, ut faciunt prudentes. Deinde often- dit si partim sit auferre ducem, auferre militem regi, certe quemvis de plebe Israëlitam non debuisse conjici in eas an- gustias, quibus pressi multi, etiam non Idumæi, a Deo & le- ge essent receffuri. Illa enim fœcunda martyrum tempora nondum venerant.

## 25:24
Ver. 24. UPON ME BE, O LORD, THIS INIQUITY) Impute this crime to me. Similar is that of Cato in Lucan II. - - let this fall satisfy Whatever the Roman morals have deserved to pay.

Latin:

Vers. 24. IN ME SIT, DOMINE, HÆC INIQVITAS) Mihi hoc crimen imputa. Simile illud Catonis apud Lucanum II. - - hac cade luatur Quicquid Romani meruerunt pendere mores.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI.

David, having entered the camp secretly, takes the spear and the cup from Saul's head: and is again acknowledged innocent.

Ver. 1. THEY BURIED HIM IN HIS HOUSE) Burials were accustomed to be private at that time. See Gen. 23, 9. 50. ver. 5. Matt. 27, 60. Samuel died, after he had presided over the people for 38 years; he governed alone indeed for 30 years: but eight years under Saul.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI.

David clam castra ingressus hastam & scy- phum a Saulis capite aufert: & iterum agno- scitur innocens.

Vers. 1. SEPELIERVNT IN DOMO SVA) Solebant privatæ esse sepulturæ eo tempore. Vide Gen. 23, 9. 50. vers. 5. Matth. 27, 60. Mortuus Samuel, postquam præfuisset populo 38. annis, solus quidem gubernavit 30. annis: octen- nium autem sub Saule.

## 26:5
Ver. 5. AND WHEN HE HAD SEEN THE PLACE) It is the mark of an excellent leader to explore the sites of places, from which often come great moments of affairs. SLEEPING IN THE TENTS] LXX. ἐν λαμπήνῃ. Thus the royal chariot was called, according to Pollux. Very well: for kings are accustomed, where there are no houses, to sleep in chariots: and the word עגלו, from the same origin, signifies a chariot in very many places: and among the Arabs the same word retains the same meaning. Others render it: within the rampart, which consisted of chariots.

Latin:

Vers. 5. CVMQVE VIDISSET LOCUM) Est hoc egregii du- cis, explorare locorum situs, unde magna sæpe momenta rerum. DORMIENTEM IN TENTORIIS] LXX. ἐν λαμπή- νῃ. Ita vocabatur currus regius, teste Polluce. Optime: nam reges solent, ubi domus non sunt, dormire in curribus: & vox עגלו, ab eadem origine currum significat plurimis in lo- cis: & apud Arabas eadem vox eundem significatum retinet. Alii reddunt: intra vallum, quod ex quadrigis constabat.

## 26:8
Ver. 8. WHATSOEVER THY HAND SHALL FIND GIVE TO THY SERVANTS) David prefers to ask for what is necessary for himself, and consequently also for himself, as the king destined by God, as being owed, rather than to seize it. What thy hand shall find, that is, what you will be able to give easily from such great abundance. See this manner of speaking Lev. 12, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8. QVODCVNQVE INVENERIT MANVS TVA DA SERVIS TVIS) Mavult David quæ sibi sunt neceffaria, ac proinde & ipsi, ut a Deo destinato regi, debita, petere quam rapere. Quod invenerit manus tua, id est, quod facile dare poteris ex tanta copia. Vide hoc loquendi genus Lev. 12, 8.

## 26:9
Ver. 9. AND THEY WERE SILENT) In the Hebrew: and they rested: that is, they spoke nothing more than what was commanded to them.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ET SILVERVNT) In Hebræo: & quieverunt: id est, nihil locuti sunt amplius quam mandatum ipsis erat.

## 26:11
Ver. 11. THE LORD BE MERCIFUL TO ME THAT I MAY NOT EXTEND MY HAND. In the Heb. May the Lord forbid that I should extend &c. Chald. It is a sin for me &c.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PROPITIUS MIHI EST DOMINUS NE EXTENDAM MANUM MEAM. In Ebr. Prohibeat Dominus, ne extendam &c. Chald. Nefas mihi &c.

## 26:12
Ver. 12. THE SLEEP OF THE LORD HAD FALLEN UPON THEM] God by His own power had both made the sleep deeper and had prolonged it: which physicians also sometimes do.

Latin:

Vers. 12. SOPOR DOMINI IRRUERAT SUPER EOS] Deus sua vi somnum & profundiorem fecerat & continuaverat: quod interdum & medici faciunt.

## 26:16
Ver. 16. YOU ARE SONS OF DEATH) He who has deserted the watch of the palace is punished with death, l. Qui excubias. D. de re militari.

Ver. 16. THEY WERE A WALL UNTO US) Against the Philistines.

Latin:

Vers. 16. FILII MORTIS ESTIS VOS) Qui excubias palatii dese- ruerit, capite punitur, l. Qui excubias. D. de re militari.

Vers. 16. PRO MVRO ERANT NOBIS) Contra Philistinos.

## 26:17
Ver. 17. IS THIS THY VOICE, MY SON DAVID) Extraordinary gentleness either makes friends out of enemies, or, if there is excessive hardness, it makes them condemn themselves inwardly: often they also betray this in words. See above 24, 18. and here below 21.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NUMQVID VOX TVA HÆC, FILI MI DAVID) Lenitas eximia aut ex inimicis amicos facit, aut, si durities est nimia, facit ut ipsi se intus damnent: sæpe & verbis id pro- dant. Vide supra 24, 18. & hic infra 21.

## 26:19
Ver. 19. FIVE MEASURES OF PARCHED CORN. A measure contained 26 pounds and 320 ounces. But it ought to be rendered for parched corn, grains of wheat collected from ears toasted by fire.

Ver. 19. IF THE LORD STIRRETH THEE UP AGAINST ME, LET HIM ACCEPT AN OFFERING) If this anger is just, I do not deprecate that it be expiated by my death, as if by a victim.

Latin:

Vers. 19. QUINQUE SATA POLENTÆ. Satum Libras 26. uncias 320. continebat. Red- di autem debet pro polentæ, granorum frumenti ex spicis igne tostis collecti.

Vers. 19. SI DOMINUS INCITAT TE ADVERSUM ME, ODORETUR SACRIFICIUM) Si justa est hæc ira, non de- precor quin morte mea, velut victimæ, expietur.

## 26:20
Ver. 20. LET NOT MY BLOOD BE SHED UPON THE EARTH BEFORE THE LORD) God watching and being the future avenger. 2 Chron. 24, 22. Thus the word before is often taken in these books.

AS THE PARTRIDGE PURSUES. A solecism of the Vulgate: 'persequitur' [is used] passively for 'suffers persecution'.

Latin:

Vers. 20. NON EFFUNDATUR SANGVIS MEUS IN TER- RAM CORAM DOMINO) Deo inspectante & vindice futuro. 2. Par. 24, 22. Sic vox coram sæpe in his libris sumitur.

SICUT PERSEQUITUR PERDIX. Solecismus vulgatæ: persequitur passive pro persecutionem patitur.

## 26:25
Ver. 25. HE IS A FOOL) Euripides. Δεινόν γε, τοῖς πλεῦσι τῦτο δ’ ἔμφυτον And Menander: Σκαιοῖσιν ὧνευ. - - - ὁ δὲ πλῦτος τυφλόν. Τυφλοὺς δ’ ἐς αὐτὸν ἐμβλέποντας δεικνύει Who would believe that the speech of David has been changed by a divinely inspired Historian? Nor yet is this imprecation ridiculous, as Cornelius thinks, which Osiander correctly explains; May God badly destroy all my enemies, many of whom, however, I wish to be saved. But David sinned gravely: because first he ought to have heard Nabal, and not to have arrogated to himself vengeance in a private cause, much less such a one, by which even the innocent are involved.

Latin:

Vers. 25. STVLTVS EST) Euripides. Δεινόν γε, τοῖς πλεῦσι τῦτο δ’ ἔμφυτον Et Menander: Σκαιοῖσιν ὧνευ. - - - ὁ δὲ πλῦτος τυφλόν. Τυφλοὺς δ’ ἐς αὐτὸν ἐμβλέποντας δεικνύει Quis credat immutatam ab Historico θεοπνεύ- στῳ esse Davidis loquutionem? Neque tamen ridi- cula est hæc imprecatio, uti putat Cornelius, quam recte explicat Osiander; Deus male perdat omnes hostes meos, quorum tamen multos salvos cupio. Peccavit autem David graviter: quia primum Na- balem audire debuisset, nec in causa privata vindi- ctam sibi arrogare, nedum talem, qua innocentes etiam involvantur.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII.

David obtained the city of Ziklag from the King of Gath, from whence he made incursions against the enemies of Israel.

Ver. 1. I SHALL THEREFORE FLEE FROM HIS HAND) See what was said above [at] 19, 12. 21, 10.

Ver. 26. WHO HATH FORBIDDEN THEE THAT THOU SHOULDST NOT COME INTO BLOOD) It was permitted for David, not yet having attained the kingdom, to defend himself, but not to avenge himself in the manner of a king. [See] below [at] 39.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII.

David à Rege Geth urbem Sicelec obtinuit, un- de in hostes Israelis excurrit.

Vers. 1. FVGIAM ERGO MANVS EJVS) Vide quæ supra dicta 19, 12. 21, 10.

Vers. 26. QVI PROHIBVIT TE NE VENIRES IN SANGVI- NEM) Davidi nondum regnum adepto licebat se tueri, non etiam se regio more ulcisci. infra 39.

## 27:6
Ver. 6. AND ACHISH GAVE HIM ZIKLAG ON THAT DAY] Great must have been the fame and expectation concerning David, that a city on foreign soil was granted to him for his security. FOR WHICH CAUSE ZIKLAG IS MADE [THE CITY] OF THE KINGS OF JUDA] Namely, after a war had subsequently arisen. 31, 1. For those things which are found among us at such a time become ours. 1. Transfugae. §. 1. D. de Acq. rerum dominio. L. In bello D. de Capt. & Postlim. reversis.

Ver. 28. FOR THE WARS OF THE LORD, MY LORD, THOU FIGHTEST) The wars of the Lord are, as we have said elsewhere, those which are waged against the Philistines and other peoples of like condition. David was harming these, while sparing his fellow citizens.

Ver. 38. AND HE DIED) From fear, which many have reported to have been the cause of death for Marius, seven times consul.

Ver. 42. FIVE DAMSELS) Free-born handmaids. See what was said [at] Gen. 30, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DEDIT ITAQVE EI ACHIS IN DIE ILLA SICE- LEG] Magna oportet fuerit fama & exspectatio de Davide, quod ei ad securitatem urbs in peregrino solo concessa est. PROPTER QVAM CAVSAM FACTA EST SICE- LEG REGVM JUDA) Bello scilicet postea suborto. 31, 1. nam quæ tali tempore apud nos deprehenduntur, nostra fiunt. 1. Transfugæ. §. 1. D. de Acq. rerum dominio. L. In bello D. de Capt. & Postlim. reversis.

Vers. 28. QVIA PRÆLIA DOMINI, DOMINE MI, TV PRÆ- LIARIS) Prælia Domini sunt, ut diximus alibi, quæ in Philistinos parisque conditionis gentes alias geruntur. His nocebat David, civibus parcens.

Vers. 38. ET MORTVVS EST) Præ metu, quam & Mario se- pties consuli causam fuisse mortis multi prodiderunt.

Vers. 42. QVINQVE PVELLÆ) Ministræ ingenuæ. Vide quæ dicta Gen. 30, 3.

## 27:8
Ver. 8. AND THEY MADE PREY OF GESSURI, AND OF GERZI, AND OF THE AMALEKITES) The Geshurites were the remnants of the Canaanites. Jos. 12, 5. The Gerzites, however, with the letters transposed, are the same as the Gezrites, who themselves were also a portion of the Canaanites, Jos. 16, 3. Therefore David harmed neither his hosts nor his own countrymen. See what was said above [at] 23, 2.

Ver. 44. BUT SAUL GAVE MICHAL HIS DAUGHTER, THE WIFE OF DAVID, TO PHALTI THE SON OF LAIS) Wrongly by Da-

There is therefore no need for us to imagine with Cornelius that David, as a leader of the war of the Israelites authorized by Saul, had the right and public authority to do these things, from the law of Deut. 20, 17. 25. For he was living there not as a leader of Israel, but as a guest of the King of Gath.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET AGEBANT PRÆDAS DE GESSURI, ET DE GERZI, ET DE AMALECITIS) Geffuritæ erant re- liquiæ Chananæorum. Jos. 12,5. Gerzitæ autem transpositis li- teris iidem qui Gezritæ, qui & ipsi portio Chananæorum Jos. 16, 3. Ergo nec hospitibus suis nocuit David, nec populari- bus. Vide quæ supra 23, 2.

Vers. 44. SAVL AUTEM DEDIT MICHOL FILIAM SUAM, VXOREM DAVID, PHALTI FILIO LAIS) Male a Da-

Non ergo opus est, ut fingamus cum Corne- lio Davidem ceu belli Israelis Ducem a Saule au- ctoratum jus & publicam auctoritatem habuisse haec faciendi, e lege Deuter. 20, 17. 25. vivebat enim ibi non ut Dux Israelis, sed ut hospes Regis Ge- thæi.

## 27:9
Verse 9.

AND HE LEFT NEITHER MAN NOR WOMAN ALIVE] Namely, so that he would not be betrayed by them, and come into danger among his hosts because of hatred of his religion. Fear often makes men who are otherwise mild more savage. See examples in On the Law of War and Peace, book 3, chapter 4, sections 9 and 10.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

NEC RELINQVEBAT VIVENTEM VI- RUM AUT MULIEREM] Nempe ne ab ipsis proderetur, & religionis odio apud hospites in periculum veniret. Metus homines alioqui mites saepe saeviores facit. Vide exempla de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 3. c. 4. §. 9. & 10.

## 27:10
Verse 10.

TOWARD THE SOUTH OF JUDAH, AND TOWARD THE SOUTH OF THE JERAHMEELITES] Jerahmeel is a part of Judah, 1 Chron. 2, 9. 26. The Kenites, however, from the house of Jethro, were neighbors of Judah and for the most part allies. David spoke ambiguously here, so that Achish would indeed believe that he had inflicted losses upon the Judeans and their allies: but he himself would know that he had invaded their neighbors. See what is above at 21, 2, and in On the Law of War and Peace, book 3, chapter 1, section 10.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

CONTRA MERIDIEM JUDÆ, ET CONTRA ME- RIDIFM JERAMEEL] Jerameel pars Judæ 1.Par. 2, 9. 26. Cenei autem ex Jethronis domo vicini Judæ & plerumque fe- derati. Perplexe locutus hic David, ut Achis quidem cre- deret eum Judæis eorumque sociis damna intulisse: ipse au- tem sentiret se invasisse finitimos eorum. Vide quæ supra 21, 2. & de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 3. c. 1. §. 10.

## 27:12
Verse 12.

SO ACHISH BELIEVED DAVID] As the Babylonians did Zopyrus: as witnessed by Herodotus in book three, Plutarch in the Apophthegms of Kings, and Justin, and the son of Tarquin at Gabii, concerning whom Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Florus may be consulted.

God directed these things in such a way that Achish knew nothing: otherwise it could not have happened but that the report of so many slaughters of the Philistines would have reached his ears.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

CREDIDIT ERGO ACHIS DAVID] Vt Babylonii Zopyro: teste Herodoto libro tertio, Plutarcho in Apo- phthegmatis regum, & Justino, & Gabii filio Tarquinii, de quo videri possunt Livius, Dionysius Halicarnasseus, & Florus.

Deus hæc ita direxit, ut nil resciret Achis: alias fieri non potuisset, quin ex tot cladibus Philistino- rum fama ad aures ejus pervenisset.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII.

Saul first consults God, then a necromancer, and receives his own death.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII.

Saul primum Deum, deinde Pythonissam con- sulit, ac cadem suam percipit.

## 28:2
Verse 2.

NOW YOU SHALL KNOW WHAT YOUR SERVANT WILL DO] You will experience my excellent service against the Hebrews. He promises this ἑκὼν ἀἑκοντί γε θυμῷ, as Themistocles once did to the Persians.

Paul of Burgos, in order to excuse David from sin, observes that David did not determine that he would go to war against the Israelites, but only said indeterminately: you shall know what your servant will do. However, Matth. Thoringius replies that David did determine those indeterminate words when, in chapter 29, 8, he said, after he had been removed by King Achish, what have you found in me that I should not fight against the enemies of my lord? Therefore, either he wanted to fight against the Israelites, which, although Becanus in part 2, Tom. 2, Theol. Schol. chapter 25, praises, Lyranus, Burgensis, and Thoringius avoid; or he wanted to deceive King Achish, which ought not to have been done. Whence that replicator Thoringius finally confesses: I do not think it is an error to concede that David sinned. In vain, therefore, does Becanus urge the example of David to argue that in a just war it is lawful to provide aid to infidels against the faithful by the example of David, who wanted to assist Achish against the people of Israel, 1 Sam. 28. & 29. But although David consented to set out for war with Achish, he does not seem to have had it in mind to fight against the Israelites, as appears from chapter 27, where Lyranus observes that David had lied to King Achish: who tries to excuse the fact that he had promised his service to King Achish against the Israelites, on the grounds that since David had been anointed King of Israel, he could have acquired it by the power of arms, with the opportunity concurring: to which, however, Paul of Burgos replies that David did not have the right in the kingdom to the execution of royal power over the people of Israel until the people had consented, and he proves this by many reasons, specifically from this, that after that anointing Saul always acknowledged him as his King, whom it would not be right to violate.

Although David may seem to have determined the indeterminate words of chapter 29, 8, in reality, however, he did not determine them. For he affirms nothing: but only inquires, in order to explore the judgment and opinion of the King concerning himself; nor does he therefore offer himself to fight against the Israelites: but he only protests that he has committed nothing by which faith should not be kept with him, and for which he should be excluded from this battle: even though he did not have it in mind to fight against the Israelites, since he knew well that the satraps of the Philistines would not admit him to the battle. And without a doubt David prayed most ardently in his heart, as soon as he was solicited by King Achish to provide allied service in the battle, that God would place some impediment in the way, so that he would not have to fight against his brothers the Israelites, and with that confidence he testified, now you shall know what your servant will do, if, that is to say, God does not prevent it: not to mention what he could have done to protect the life of the King and avoid slaughter, even if he did not attack the Israelites, if he had fought defensively, not offensively; and that he was in the greatest consternation and anguish when the King demanded his service. Cf. Sanctius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

NUNC SCIES QUÆ FACTURUS EST SERVUS TU- US] Egregiam meam operam contra Hebræos experieris. Promittit hoc ἑκὼν ἀἑκοντί γε θυμῷ, ut olim Themistocles Persis.

PAul. Burgensis ut Davidem à peccato excuset, observat Davidem non determinavisse, se ad bellum contra Israelitas iturum, sed tantum inde- terminate dixisse: scies quid facturus sit servus tuus. Respondet autem Matth. Thoringius Davidem de- terminasse illa verba indeterminata, cum cap. 29, 8. dixit, postquam amotus fuisset per regem Achis, quid invenisti in me ut non pugnem contra inimicos Domini mei? vel ergo pugnare voluit contra Is- raelitas, quod etsi Becanus part. 2. Tom. 2. Theol. Schol. cap. 25. laudet, Lyranus, Burgensis & Thorin- gius refugiunt: vel fallere voluit Regem Achis, quod fieri non debuit. Unde replicator ille Tho- ringius fatetur tandem: non puto errorem esse con- cedere David peccasse. Frustra ergo exemplum Davidis urget Becanus, ut adstruat quod in justo bel- lo licitum sit præbere auxilium infidelibus contra fide- les exemplo Davidis, qui Achi contra populum Is- rael adsistere voluit 1. Sam. 28. & 29. sed quamvis David consenserit ad bellum proficisci cum Achis, non tamen videtur id in animo habuisse contra Isra- elitas pugnare, ut ex cap. 27. id apparet, ubi Lyranus observat, mentitum fuisse David apud Regem A- chis: qui id excusare conatur, quod operam suam condixerit Regi Achis contra Israelitas, hac ratio- ne, quod cum David unctus esset in Regem Israelis potuerit id acquirere virtute armorum, facultat concurrente: cui vero respondet Paulus Burgen sis, Davidem non habuisse jus in regno ad executio nem regiæ potestatis in populum Israel, donec populu consensisset, idque multis rationibus probat, ex e nominatim, quod post unctionem illam Sauler semper agnoverit pro suo Rege, quem violare ne fas esset.

Quanquam vero determinasse verba indeterm nata cap. 29, 8. videatur David, revera tamen no determinavit. Nihil enim affirmat: Sed sciscitat tantum, ut exploret judicium & sententiam Reg de sese; nec offert ergo se ad pugnandum contra Is- raelitas: sed protestatur solum se nihil commisis- se, quo minus sibi fides habeatur, & ob quod à præ- lio hoc excludatur: utut in animo non haberet contra Israelitas pugnare, siquidem probe nosset sa- trapas Philistæorum se non admissuros ad prælium. Et procul ambiguo oravit David in corde suo ar- dentissime, cum primum à Rege Achis solicitare- tur ad præstandam operam sociam in prælio, ut Deus aliquod impedimentum objiceret, ne neces- se haberet contra fratres suos Israelitas pugnare, ea- que fiducia testatus est, nunc scies quæ facturus est servus tuus, si scil. Deus non impedierit: ut taceam, quod pro vita Regis tuenda & strage declinanda facere quid potuisset, etiamsi Israelitas non oppu- gnaret, si defensive, non offensive pugnasset; quod- que in summa tum consternatione fuerit & angu- stia, cum operam ejus Rex postularet. Conf. San- ctius in h. l.

## 28:3
Verse 3. NOW SAMUEL WAS DEAD] It was better, and so the following. For the writer repeats what had been said above at 25, 1, because of the connection of the following history.

AND SAUL HAD REMOVED THE WIZARDS AND SOOTHSAYERS FROM THE LAND] And here understand he had removed. He had done this, however, according to the law of Lev. 19, 31; 20, 6, 27; Deut. 18, 11.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SAMUEL AUTEM MORTUUS EST] Melius erat, & ita sequentia. Repetit enim scriptor quod supra di- ctum erat 25, 1. ob connexionem historiæ sequentis.

ET SAUL ABSTULIT MAGOS ET HARIOLOS DE TERRA] Et hîc intellige abstulerat. Fecerat hoc autem secundum legem Lev. 19, 31. 20, 6. 27. Deuter. 18, 11.

## 28:5
Verse 5. HIS HEART TREMBLED GREATLY] He was conscious of many evil deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 5. EXPAVIT COR EJUS NIMIS] Multorum ma- lorum facinorum erat sibi conscius.

## 28:6
Verse 6. AND HE DID NOT ANSWER HIM] Despising a profane man and one polluted by the blood of so many priests.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET NON RESPONDIT EI] Contemnens ho- minem profanum & tot sacerdotum sanguine pollutum.

## 28:7
A WOMAN HAVING A FAMILIAR SPIRIT] The Greeks [call her] Ἐγγαστρίμυθον, from the Hebrew. Such, however, were those among the Greeks who were called Pythiae from Pytho, which is the name of the city of Delphi.

Latin:

MULIEREM HABENTEM PYTHONEM] Græci Ἐγ- γαστρίμυθον, ex Hebræo. Tales autem erant apud Græcos quæ Pythiæ dicebantur a Pytho, quod nomen urbi Delphorum.

## 28:11
Verse 11. BRING UP SAMUEL FOR ME] A necromancy most ancient of all divinations, and a sign of the believed survival of souls. We learn that this was frequently done in the East from Aeschylus, the Persians, and Herodotus. Although, however, everywhere that which appears here is called Samuel, even in Josephus, both Samuel called from Hades and the soul of Samuel; it is more credible, however, that it was a deceitful spirit, of that kind about which Porphyry writes in the second book On Abstinence from Animal Food: a race of a deceitful nature, multiform and versatile, feigning both gods and demons and the souls of the dead. And the woman herself seems to signify this sufficiently when she says אלהים gods ascended from the earth, thus calling those spirits, one of whom had assumed the figure of Samuel, while the others were as it were his companions. See Tertullian, On the Soul, near the end.

In vain, therefore, do the Papists fashion a true Samuel out of a masked one, so that they may provide some destination for the limbo of the Fathers and the apparitions of souls. That it was a diabolical illusion is evident from verses 6, 19, and 1 Chronicles 10:13-14. See Justin, Q. 52; Tertullian, On the Soul, ch. 57; Chrysostom, Homily 29 on Matthew; Augustine, Book 2 to Simplicianus, Q. 3 and 27; and the Canon Law, C. Nec mirum, 26, q. 5; Thomas, Part 1, Q. 89, art. 8; from which it is also firmly concluded that the book of Sirach, in which chapter 46:20 this is attributed to the true Samuel, is outside the canon.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SAMVELEM MIHI SUSCITA] Νεκυία o- mnium divinationum antiquissima, & fignum creditæ τῆς τῶν ψυχῶν διαμονῆς. Frequenter id factitatum in Oriente discimus ex Æschylo, Persis & Herodoto. Qanquam autem ubique id quod hic apparet vocatur Samuel, etiam apud Jo- sephum, tum Samuel ἐξ ἅδε vocatus, tum Samuelis ψυχὴ; credibilius tamen est, fallacem spiritum fuisse, ejus generis, de quo Porphyrius secundo de Abstinentia animantium: γέ- νος ἀπατηλῆς φύσεως παντόμορφόν τε κὶ πολύτροπον, ὑπο- κρινόμενον κὶ θεοὺς κὶ δαίμονας κὶ ψυχὰς τεθνηκότων. Vi- deturque id ipsa mulier satis significare, cum dicit אלהים deos ascendisse de terra, ita appellans spiritus illos, quorum unus Samuelis figuram induerat, cæteri ei velut comites erant. Vide Tertull. de Anima circa finem.

Frustra ergo Papistæ è personato Samuele verum efformant, ut limbo Patrum, & apparationibus ani- marum destinam aliquam parent. Illusionem fu- isse Diabolicam è vers. 6. 19. & 1. Paral. 11, 13. 14. con- stat. V. Justin. q. LII. Tertull. l. de anim. c. 57. Chry- sost. hom. 29. in Matth. August. l. 2. ad Simplic. q. 3. & 27. & jus Canon. C. Nec mirum. 26. q. 5. Tho- mas p. 1. q. 89. art. 8. unde etiam firmiter concludi- tur, quod liber Syracid. in quo cap. 45, 23. vero Sa- mueli hoc tribuitur, extra canonem sit.

## 28:17
Verse 17. HE SHALL TEAR THE KINGDOM FROM YOUR HAND] God often compels even evil spirits to speak the truth. See Matthew 8:29. Tertullian in his Apology: 'Thus, seized by the contact and the breath of our power, and by the contemplation and representation of that fire, they even depart from bodies at our command, unwilling and grieving, and blushing in your presence. Believe them when they speak the truth about themselves, you who believe them when they lie.'

Latin:

Vers. 17. SCINDET REGNUM TUUM DE MANU TUA] Etiam malos Spiritus Deus sæpe cogit verum dicere. Vide Matth, 8, 29. Tertullianus Apologetico: Ita de contactu deque afflatu nostro contemplatione & repræsentatione ignis illius correpti, etiam de corporibus nostro imperio excedunt invi- ti & dolentes, & vobis præsentibus erubescentes. Credite illis cum verum de se loquuntur, qui mentientibus creditis.

## 29:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIX.

Achish dismisses David from the battle.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIX.

Achis Davidem à prælio dimittit.

## 29:3
Verse 3. DO YOU NOT KNOW DAVID] As the Persian king said: I have Themistocles.

And yet David was with him for only four months, chapter 27:7. Therefore, either Achish spoke hyperbolically to convince the Philistines, or he simultaneously looked back to David's first stay six years earlier.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NUM IGNORATIS DAVID] Vt rex Persa: Themistoclem habeo.

Atqui quatuor tantum mensibus apud eum fuit David cap. 27, 7. vel ergo hyperbolicē loquutus est Achis ad fidem faciendam Philistæis, vel simul respexit ad primam commorationem Davidis ante 6. annos.

## 29:4
Verse 4. AND THEY SAID TO HIM: LET THIS MAN RETURN] Wonderfully does God, through the enemies themselves, ensure that David does not defile himself with Hebrew blood, and thus make himself less fit for the kingdom.

LEST HE BECOME AN ADVERSARY TO US WHEN WE HAVE BEGUN TO FIGHT] Tacitus, Histories 4, concerning the wing of the Batavians: which had long since been corrupted and feigned loyalty, so that by betraying the Romans in the very battle line, it might flee for a greater price. Verse 8. AND DAVID SAID TO ACHISH: FOR WHAT HAVE I DONE?] David acts out the play he had begun well. Verse 9 BUT THE PRINCES OF THE PHILISTINES SAID: HE SHALL NOT GO UP WITH US TO BATTLE] Kings are often compelled in wars to adapt themselves to the desires of those whose services they need.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET DIXERUNT EI: REVERTATUR VIR ISTE] Mire Deus per hostes ipsos efficit, ne David Hebræo sanguine se contaminet, ac fic se minus idoneum regno faciat.

NE FIAT NOBIS ADVERSARIUS CUM PRÆ- LIARI COEPERIMUS] Tacitus Histor. 4. de ala Batavo- tum. Quæ jam pridem corrupta fidem simulabat, ut proditis in ipsa acie Romanis, majore pretio fugeret. Vers. 8. DIXITQVE DAVID AD ACHIS: QVID ENIM FECI?] Bene agit David quam cœperat fabulam. Vers. 9 SED PRINCIPES PHILISTINORVM DIXERUNT: NON ASCENDIT NOBISCUM IN PRÆLIUM] Coguntur sæpe in bellis reges aptare se eorum desideriis, quorum opera indigent.

## 30:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXX. David smites the Amalekites who were driving off spoils, and plunders them.

Latin:

CAPUT XXX. David Amalekitas prædas abigentes cædit, & spoliat.

## 30:2
Verse 2. AND THEY HAD KILLED NO ONE) By the wonderful arrangement of God, who willed that nothing should perish for David, nor for others on account of David. Verse 6. FOR THE PEOPLE WANTED TO STONE HIM) Sedition often follows a defeat received. As Tacitus says in Histories 2, those who were ready to compete in obedience during prosperous times, equally rejected his adverse fortune. Verse 7. BRING THE EPHOD TO ME) Turn the breastplate toward me, that I may understand the will of God from the brightness of the letters. AND THE LORD SAID TO HIM: PURSUE) These three letters shone forth רדף, for instance in the names Issachar, Dan, Naphtali: the rest are added exegetically. Grotius decides these things about the manner of the oracle as if he had been taught by the oracle itself. Concerning which, not even the Jews themselves have anything certain ascertained. However, as far as it appears, he wants David to have applied the Ephod to himself; which opinion Cunaeus boldly defends in book 1 of the Republic of the Hebrews, ch. 14, to such an extent that the Interpreters explaining this passage otherwise, he pronounces that he perverted it and was asleep here or did something else. But the Hebrew words הגישה לי can be rendered: Apply for me, or on my behalf, for my sake. Which sense the matter itself demands: Because it was not fitting for David to wear the Ephod, but this was proper to the high priest. Nor is it to be admitted that David usurped this for himself through the eminence of Royal Majesty: because the divine law, Num. 27, 21, is repugnant to it, from which the Hebrews conclude that the King himself ought to have stood before the high priest who was fulfilling the Urim and Thummim, as Maimonides notes, and therefore the Hebrews one and all, as well as most Christians, affirm that this was done by David in the ordinary and customary way through the high priest, as Buxtorff observed against Cunaeus in the History of Urim and Thummim, ch. 3. Verse 15. AND DAVID SWORE TO HIM) Informers are rewarded with impunity, as Tacitus speaks in Annals 15. Verse 16. BEHOLD THEY WERE LYING DOWN UPON THE FACE OF ALL THE LAND, EATING AND DRINKING) They invade the secure enemy, who was acting more sluggishly due to the success of affairs; the guards were slain, the camp broken through. Tacitus, Histories 2, who also elsewhere in the same book describes those loosened into luxury by too much indulgence of fortune. Livy says in book 26, favorable circumstances almost always create negligence. Titus Martius, a Roman knight, having attacked an enemy unorganized through confidence in victory, did not even leave messengers of the slaughter. Frontinus tells this in book 2, ch. 10. Verse 20. FLOCKS AND HERDS) In which the right of postliminy did not exist, which had a place in the case of free persons. See on the Law of War and Peace, book three, ch. 9, §. 5. 14. Verse 24. FOR THE SHARE SHALL BE EQUAL OF HIM GOING DOWN TO BATTLE AND OF HIM REMAINING WITH THE BAGGAGE) A prudent constitution, so that those who guarded the camp would not be found with difficulty. The Pisidians used to give a part of the booty to those who guarded the homes. Chalcocondylas mentions this in book 5. However, this law is to be understood concerning half the booty: for the other half was the King's. There are those who say that all these things have come down from the times of Abraham. For they assert that Eshcol and Mamre remained with the baggage, but that Abraham remitted his right. Lands captured in war were entirely at the disposal of the King. Verse 26. RECEIVE A BLESSING FROM THE SPOILS OF THE ENEMIES OF THE LORD] Seneca on Benefits 3, 33. It is most honorable for military men to make some rich man wealthy with the spoils of enemies.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET NON INTERFECERANT QVENQVAM) Miro Dei dispositu, qui neque Davidi quicquam perire voluit, neque aliis propter Davidem. Vers. 6. VOLEBAT ENIM EUM POPULUS LAPIDARE) Cladem acceptam sæpe seditio sequitur. Prosperis rebus certaturi ad obsequium, adversam ejus fortunam ex æquo detrectabant, ait Tacitus Hist. 2. Vers. 7. APPLICA AD ME EPHOD) Obverte mihi pectorale, ut ex fulgore literarum Dei voluntatem intelligam. DIXITQVE EI DOMINVS: PERSEQVERE) Hæ tres literæ effulserunt רדף, puta in nominibus Isaschar, Dan, Nephthali: cætera ἐξηγητικῶς adduntur. Hæc ita de oraculi modo decernit Grotius, tanquam ab oraculo edoctus. De quibus nec ipsis Judæis certi aliquid exploratum est. Quantum autem apparet, vult Davidem ipsum Ephod sibi applicasse; quam sententiam audacter propugnat Cunæus libr. 1. de Rep. Hebr. c. 14. adeo ut Interpp. secus hunc locum explicantes eum pervertisse & dormitasse hic aut aliud egisse pronunciet. Sed verba Ebræa הגישה לי reddi possunt: Applica pro me, vel propter me, in mei gratiam. Quem sensum postulat res ipsa: Quia Davidi non conveniebat, Ephod gestare, sed erat hoc proprium summi sacerdotis. Neque admittendum, quod David per Majestatis Regiæ eminentiam id sibi usurparit: quia repugnat lex divina, Num. 27, 21. è qua Ebræi concludunt, ipsum Regem per Sacerdotem summum complentem Urim & Thumim coram eo stare debuisse notante Maimonide, ideoque Ebræi ad unum omnes, nec non Christiani plerique à Davide modo ordinario, & consueto per Sacerdotem summum hoc factum esse affirmant, ut adversus Cunæum observavit Buxtorff. in Hist. Urim & Thum. c. 3. Vers. 15. ET JURAVIT EI DAVID) Indicia impunitate remunerantur, ut Tacitus loquitur Annal. 15. Vers. 16. ECCE ILLI DISCUMBEBANT SVPER FACIEM VNIVERSÆ TERRÆ, COMEDENTES ET BIBENTES) Securum hostem ac successu rerum socordius agentem invadunt, cæsi vigiles, perrupta castra. Tacitus Hist. 2. qui & alibi eodem libro nimia fortunæ indulgentia solutos in luxum describit. Ferme res secundæ negligentiam creant, ait Livius libro 26. Titus Martius eques Romanus hostem victoriæ fiducia incompositum aggressus, ne nuntios quidem cladis reliquit. Frontinus id narrat libro 2. c. 10. Vers. 20. GREGES ET ARMENTA) In quibus postliminii jus non erat, quod locum habebat in capitibus liberis. Vide de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro tertio c. 9. §. 5. 14. Vers. 24. ÆQVA ENIM PARS ERIT DESCENDENTIS AD PRÆLIVM ET REMANENTIS AD SARCINAS) Prudens constitutio, ne ægre reperirentur qui castra custodirent. Pisidæ partem prædæ dabant his qui domos servabant. Meminit Chalcocondylas libro 5. Intelligenda autem hæc lex de parte dimidia prædæ: nam altera dimidia Regis erat. Sunt qui omnia hæc venisse ajunt ab Abrahami temporibus. Asserunt enim Escolam & Mambrem mansisse ad impedimenta, Abrahamum autem jus suum remisisse. Terræ bello captæ totæ erant in Regis arbitrio. Vers. 26. ACCIPITE BENEDICTIONEM DE PRÆDA HOSTIVM DOMINI] Seneca de Beneficiis 3, 33. Militaribus viris speciosissimum est divitem aliquem spoliis hostilibus facere.

## 31:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXI. The Hebrews having been slain, Saul kills himself, whose body the men of Jabesh bury.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXI. Ebræis cæsis, Saul seipsum occidit, cujus corpus Jabesitæ sepeliunt.

## 31:3
AND HE WAS WOUNDED HEAVILY BY THE ARCHERS) This word המורים seems here not inconveniently to be repeated from the word a little before preceding, which signifies archers or throwers. Furthermore, we are forced to believe that the Greeks read otherwise here, whose LXX translate here εἰς τὰ ὑποχόνδρια. Theodotion, εἰς τὸ μέρος ἐγγὺς τῶ ἥπατος. How they may have read, let us inquire.

Latin:

ET VULNERATUS EST VEHEMENTER A SA- GITTARIIS) Dictio hæc המורים videtur hic non in- commode repeti ex voce paulo ante præcedente, quæ sagitta- rios aut jaculatores significet. Cæterum cogimur credere aliter hic legisse Græcos, quorum LXX. vertunt hic εἰς τὰ ὑποχόνδρια. Theodotio, εἰς τὸ μέρος ἐγγὺς τῶ ἥπατος. Quo- modo legerint, quæramus.

## 31:4
Verse 4.

LEST PERCHANCE THESE UNCIRCUMCISED COME AND KILL ME) What the Hebrew Doctors judged concerning this matter, we have said in the book on the Law of War and Peace, second book, Ch. 19, §. 5, which, however, by Christians, who are debtors of greater patience and who have before their eyes the examples of the Apostles and Apostolic men, should not be drawn into an example.

The judgment of the Hebrews concerning Saul, who fell upon his own sword: when others refused to kill him, lest he be mocked by God and His enemies, that he is to be excused, and did not sin against the Law of God, which Grotius praises in the same place, is frivolous, and rests upon no authority of Scripture, nor any solid reason. For what he says, that the Hebrews except this cause from the Law of not killing oneself, as a reasonable departure if one sees that he will live henceforth to the reproach of God Himself, who I pray gave them this power, of excepting this cause? And where does God except this cause, without whose authority we ought to have a religious fear of restricting His law, and excepting anything from His law? But truly, no one can certainly foresee that he will live henceforth to the reproach of God, since it is very easy for God, in ways unknown to us, which no one could even foresee, to avert his own reproach; and if anyone were to foresee this for certain, it should not or cannot be presumed from this that it is the will of God which would resolve upon a plan of anticipating death. Nor is it right to transgress one divine commandment concerning not killing, so that the violation of another, concerning not profaning the name of God, may be averted: for whoever shall have kept the whole Law, yet offends in one point, has become guilty of all. For He who said, you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, also said, you shall not kill: But if you have not taken or allowed to be taken in vain the name of the Lord, but have killed, you have become a transgressor of the Law, as St. James teaches us to argue in a similar case, ch. 2, 10. et seqq. Furthermore, if it is not permitted to violate the commandment concerning not killing, or to kill yourself, so that you yourself do not profane or bring reproach upon the name of God, it will be much less right to kill yourself so that the name of God is not brought into reproach by others. Which is to precipitate oneself into a most grave and destructive sin, so that a sin may not be committed by others, and to commit such a crime, where no place for repentance is left, so that others may not commit a sin which, by repenting, could be healed again in them. And what is this other than despair of God, as if He could not vindicate the glory of His name unless we inflict violence and death upon ourselves, and by that despair bring the name of the Lord into the highest reproach, so that the enemies of God may boast that the worshippers of the true God must finally despair of His help and power, in which manner the adversaries were able to boast of the death of Saul, which he took upon himself; whence David complains of this matter in the bow, which he calls, 2. Sam. 1, 20. What else is this than to devote oneself to the eternal blasphemy of the divine name, which is committed by the damned in hell against God, so that the name of the Lord may not perhaps be rendered liable to temporal reproach among others, to join oneself to the number of those blaspheming extremely, so that the presumed blasphemies of others may be prevented? For what is more certain than that by that despair they precipitate themselves into the abyss of eternal destruction, in which blasphemies against God by the devils, and his reprobate companions and damned spirits Is there no end? Woe to those who are faint-hearted, who do not believe in God, therefore they will not be protected by him, Sirach 2:14. The portion of the fearful and unbelieving will be in the lake burning with fire and brimstone, Revelation 21:8. And just is their condemnation, as the Apostle decrees, who say, let us do evil that good may come, Romans 3:8. But the Hebrews say that Saul repented after the shade of Samuel had predicted to him his death, which, knowing it to be imminent if he were to fight, he did not decline the battle for his country and the Law of God, earning eternal praise from it, even by the proclamation of David, from whom also those who buried Saul with honor received a testimony of a deed well done. Grotius praises this from the Hebrews in the cited passage. But in truth, it is certain that the Diabolical Specter was not the shade of Samuel, even though it feigned the form of Samuel, because it had predicted death to Saul, by believing which Saul sinned no less than by consulting the Pythoness: for in both ways he turned himself away from the Lord God of Israel to the Devil, and having deserted the true God, he venerated and adored the same out of mere desperation. It was not a matter of piety or repentance that he entered the battle: which he could by no means decline because of the enemies looming over him, nor did he undergo it out of zeal for the Law of God and piety for his country, but since he believed that Specter and gave it credence, he joined battle out of desperation with the enemy, from whom he did not doubt that his destruction was imminent. And what else do those things savor of but desperation, which he enjoined upon his armor-bearer regarding his killing: Draw your sword and strike me, lest perhaps these uncircumcised come and kill me, mocking me? Was it not mere desperation that, when the armor-bearer was unwilling to lay hands upon him, even though ordered, Saul himself seized the sword and fell upon it? Is not the cause of that desperation manifest, that he believed the Specter pronouncing to him: tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. 1 Samuel 29:19. For unless he had given it credence, he would not have been so certainly persuaded that he would be killed by the uncircumcised if he were not killed by his armor-bearer or did not bring death upon himself, whereas by truly performing repentance, trusting in the Lord, he could have believed that He could easily snatch him from the hands of his enemies through His infinite power, if indeed it were glorious to His divine name and salutary for Saul himself. And what is more clear than that Saul did not migrate to the blessed seats, but to the Society of the Devil and his angels, if that announcement 'tomorrow you and your sons will be with me' was true? For he who announced that was not Samuel, but the Devil himself, having feigned the form and habit of Samuel. Therefore, it must be believed that he was with this one, not with Samuel and the spirits of the perfect just. The proclamation he received from David after he had finished his fate was not reported because of the final battle, much less because he wished to subject himself in it to the death certainly looming over him for the law and country, but because he excelled in military fortitude, because he was swifter than eagles and stronger than lions with Jonathan. It is no wonder, however, that those who buried Saul received a testimony of a deed well done from David, since Saul was the Lord's anointed, the first King in Israel among the people of God, and the father-in-law of David himself, whose body, snatched from the hands of the enemies and the uncircumcised and committed to the earth, David praised, so that he might testify his loyalty to the deceased, even though he was his mortal enemy, to the Gileadites, the worshippers of Saul, and by this courtesy and gentleness of his, might win their benevolence for himself, 2 Samuel 2:5, 6. But what is gathered from that, that Saul, who had laid hands upon himself, had performed repentance, or what sign or trace of performed repentance can remain there, when someone kills himself with his own sword, and thus perishes immediately in desperation, homicide, and impenitence? Finally, did not the wrath of the Lord burn against Saul and his family even after the death of Saul, indeed long after his suicide, so that it could not be expiated except by the hanging of seven men from his house and devoted to the curse before the Lord? 2 Samuel 21:6. Let what we said about Samson at Judges 16:30 be compared, where also the Socinian error of Grotius regarding Christians being debtors of greater patience is chastised. If it ought not or cannot be drawn as an example from them that Saul killed himself so that God would not be affected by disgrace, why does Grotius himself praise the examples of Christians who killed themselves to avoid the disgrace of rape? For Grotius excuses such Christians just as he does the Hebrew Saul, and absolves both for the same cause.

Verse of the same.

AND HIS ARMOR-BEARER WOULD NOT] Fearing to lay a hand upon the King, even though he was willing: for he feared the shepherd of the people, as it is in Homer. See in the book immediately following 1:14. Not foolishly does Homer say: 'A terrible thing it is to kill a royal race.' For as we shall soon see, whoever succeeds is an avenger, as Tacitus teaches us in Histories 1.

Latin:

Verf. 4.

NE FORTE VENIANT INCIRCUMCISI ISTI ET INTERFICIANT ME) De hac re quid judicarint Docto- res Ebræi, diximus libro de Jure Belli & Pacis secundo Cap. 19. §. 5. quæ tamen a Christianis majoris patientiæ debito- ribus, & in conspectu habentibus exempla Apostolorum & Apostolicorum virorum, in exemplum trahi non debent.

Judicium Ebræorum de Saule, qui gladio incu- buit ipse: cum alii eundem interficere recusarent, ne à Dei suisque hostibus illuderetur, quod excu- sandus sit, nec contra Legem Dei peccarit, quod ibi- dem laudat Grotius, frivolum est, nullaque sive Scripturæ auctoritate, sive ratione solida nititur. Quod enim ait, Ebræos de Lege se non interficiendi, causam hanc excipere, tanquam εὔλογον ἐξαγωγὴν si quis videat deinceps se in probrum ipsius Dei victu- rum, ecquis obsecro ipsis hanc potestatem dedit, hanc causam excipiendi? Et ubiDeus hanc excipit causam, sine cujus autoritate legem ejus restringe- re, & quicquam de Lege ejus excipere, nobis reli- gio esse debet? Tum vero in probrum Dei se vi- cturum deinceps, nemo certo prævidere potest, si- quidem Deo perquam facile sit, modis nobis inco- gnitis, quos nemo etiam prævidere queat, probrum suum avertere; ac si omnino quis certo id prævide- ret, non hinc præsumi debet, aut potest voluntas Dei, quæ mortis anticipandæ consilium absolvat. Neque fas est, unum transgredi præceptum divi- num de non occidendo, ut alterius violatio, de non prophanando nomine Dei, avertatur: quicunq́; enim totam Legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, fa- ctus est omnium reus. Qui enim dixit, non assu- mes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum, dixit &, non occides: Quod si non assumseris vel permiseris af- sumi in vanum nomen Domini, occideris autem, factus es transgressor Legis, ut in simili argumen- tari nos docet S. Jacobus c. 2, 10. seqq. Porro si non liceat præceptum de non occidendo migrare, aut te- ipsum interficere, ne ipse prophanes, aut probris affi- cias nomen Dei, multo minus fas erit te interficere, ne ab aliis probro nomen Dei afficiatur.
