Quod est semetipsum in peccatum gravissimum & excitiaie præcipitare, ne ab aliis peccatum committatur, & tale patrare facinus, ubi locus pœnitentiæ non re- linquitur, ne alii peccatum committant, quod pœ- nitendo in ipsis sanari rursus queat. Et quid hoc aliud est, quam desperatio de Deo, quasi non possit nominis sui gloriam vindicare, nisi nobismet ipsis vim ac mortem inferamus, ac desperatione illa summo probro nomen Domini afficere, ut hostes Dei glorientur, cultoribus veri Dei de auxilio ac potentia ejusdem desperandum tandem esse, quo pacto de morte Saulis gloriari potuere adversa- rii, quam sibi adscivit ipse; unde queritur hoc no- mine David in arcu, quem vocat, 2. Sam. 1, 20. Quid aliud hoc est, quam se ad æternam nominis divini blasphemiam, quæ à damnatis in inferno adversus Deum committitur, devovere, ne forte nomen Domini temporali probro penes alios obnoxium reddatur, se jungere extreme blasphemantium nu- mero, ut aliorum præsumptæ blasphemiæ præcave- antur? Quid enim certius, quam quod despera- tione illa ipsi se præcipitent in barathrum æterni exitii, in quo blasphemiarum adversus Deum à Dia- bolis, ejusque sociis reprobis & damnatis Spiritibus nullus est finis? Væ dissolutis corde, qui non credunt Deo, ideo non protegentur ab eo, Syr. 2, 14. Timidis & incredulis pars erit in stagno ardente igne & sulphure Apoc. 21, 8. Et justa est, decernente Apostolo, eorum condemnatio, qui dicunt, faciamus mala, ut eveniant bona Rom. 3, 8. Sed dicunt Ebræi, resipuisse Saulem, postquam umbra Samuelis mortem ipsi prædixerat, quam gnarus sibi imminere, si pugnaturus, prælium pro patria & Lege Dei non detrectaret, æternam inde laudem meritus, Davidis etiam præconio, à quo & ii, qui Saulem cum honore sepelierunt, recte facti testi- monium retulerunt. Laudat hæc ex Ebræis Gro- tius citato loco. Verum enim vero certum est, Diabolicum Spectrum, non Samuelis umbram fuis- se, etsi illud formam Samuelis mentiretur, quod mortem Sauli prædixerat, cui fidem adhibendo non minus peccavit Saul, quam quod Pythonissam consuluerit: Utroque enim modo à Domino Deo Israelis ad Diabolum se avertit, eundemque deserto vero Deo, ex mera desperatione veneratus est, & adoravit. Non erat id pietatis, aut resipiscentiæ quod prælium inierit: quod propter hostes sibi imminentes nullatenus detrectare potuit, nec è zelo pro Lege Dei, ac pietate pro patria id subiit, sed cum Spectro illi crediderit, ac fidem adhibue- rit, ex desperatione cum hoste manus conseruit, à quo sibi exitium imminere non dubitavit. Et quid aliud illa, quam desperationem sapiunt, quibus Ar- migero suo injungebat interfectionem: Evagina glaudium tuum, & percute me, ne forte veniant incir- cumcisi isti & interficiant me illudentes mihi? An- non mera desperatio erat, quod cum Armiger ma- nus inferre ipsi, etsi jussus, nollet, Saul ipse gladium arripuerit, & irruerit super eum? Annon despera- tionis istius causa manifesta est, quod crediderit Spectro pronuntianti ipsi: cras tu & filii tui me- cum eritis. 1. Sam. 29, 19. Nisi enim fidem illi adhibu- isset, se ab incircumsis, nisi ab armigero suo occide- retur, aut sibi ipsi mortem conscisceret, interfe- ctum iri, non tam certo persuasus fuisset, quin vera acta pœnitentia, Domino confidens, credere po- tuisset, ipsum se è manibus hostium, per infinitam suam potentiam facile eripere posse, si quidem no- mini suo divino gloriosum, ipsique Sauli salutare fuerit. Et quid luculentius est, quam quod Saul non ad beatas sedes migrarit, sed ad Societatem Diaboli, & Angelorum ejus, si vera fuit illa prænun- ciatio cras tu, & Filii tui mecum eritis? Non enim qui id prænunciabat, Samuel erat, sed Diabolus ipse, formam & habitum Samuelis mentitus. Cum hoc ergo Saulem esse credendum erit, non cum Samuele ac Spiritibus justorum perfectorum. Præ- conium quod fatis functus à Davide retulit, non ob novissimum prælium, nedum quod in eodem pro lege & patria morti inde sibi certo eminenti se subjicere voluit, reportavit, sed quod excelluerit militari fortitudine, quod Aquilis velocior, Leonibus fortior cum Jonathane fuerit. Non mirum autem, quod illi, qui Saulem sepeliere, à Davide recte facti testimonium retulerint, siquidem Saul unctus Domi- ni primus Rex in Israel populo Dei, & Socer ipsius Davidis fuerit, cujus corpus è manibus hostium & incircumcisorum ereptum, terræque mandatum laudabat David, ut fidem defuncto, etsi hosti suo capitali, testaretur Gileaditis, Saulis cultoribus, suaque hoc comitate ac mansuetudine ipsorum be- nevolentiam sibi conciliaret 2. Sam. 2, 5, 6. Sed qui inde colligitur, Saulem, qui sibi manus intulerat, pœnitentiam egisse, aut quodnam ibi actæ pœni- tentiæ superesse indicium vel vestigium potest, cum quis gladio suo se interficit, atque ita in desperatio- ne, homicidio & impœnitentia actutum perit? De- nique annon post fata etiam Saulis, imo multo post eijus αὐτοχειρίαν adhuc exarsit ira Domini adversus Saulem, ejusque familiam, ut expiari quoque non potuerit, nisi suspensis septem viris è domo e- jus & anathemate devotis coram Domino? 2. Sam. 21, 6. Conferantur quæ de Samsone ad Jud. 16, 30. diximus, ubi etiam error Socinianus Grotii de Christianis majoris patientiæ debitoribus castiga- tus est. A quibus si in exemplum trahi non debet aut potest, quod Saul, ne probro afficeretur Deus, se interfecerit, cur Grotius ipse exempla Christiano- rum laudat, qui se interfecere, ut stupri probrum declinarent? Æque enim tales Christianos ac Sau- lem Ebræum excusat Grotius, & ex eadem causa utrosque absolvit.

Vers. eod.

ET NOLUIT ARMIGER EJUS] Veritus Regi ma- num inferre, quamvis volenti: περὶ γὰρ δίε ποιμένι λαῶν, ut est apud Homerum. Vide libro mox sequente 1, 14. Non stulte Homerus: Δεινὸν δὲ γένος βασιλήϊόν ἐςι. Κτείνειν. Nam ut mox videbimus, ultor est quisquis successit, ut nos docet Tacitus Histor. 1.

Verse 7.

THEY ABANDONED THEIR CITIES) See how much they needed a King.

Vers. 7.

RELIQVERUNT CIVITATES SUAS) Vide quam il- lis opus fuerit Rege.

## 31:9
IN THE TEMPLE OF IDOLS) Properly in the Hebrew: Of terrors. Lucilius: The terrors, the Lamiae, the Fauns, which the Numa Pompiliuses instituted.

Latin:

IN TEMPLO IDOLORUM) Proprie in Hebræo: Ter- ricularum. Lucilius: Terriculas Lamias, Fauni, quas Pompiliique Instituere Numæ.

## 31:10
Verse 10.

IN THE TEMPLE OF ASHTAROTH) The LXX rightly [translate] εἰς τὸ Ἀτάρτειον. For thus the Greeks speak, [as in] Heraion, Poseidonion. Arms captured from enemies were placed in sacred places. See above 21, 9. Virgil, Aeneid 1: And many arms besides on sacred doorposts, captive chariots hang, and curved axes, and crests of heads, and huge bolts of crests, and spears, and shields, and beaks snatched from ships.

BUT THEY HUNG HIS BODY ON THE WALL OF BETH-SHAN) Thus Tacitus, Annals 1, says that bodies cast out beyond the rampart were for a spectacle. That such mockeries of bodies were not infrequent in those times and places is apparent from the history of Joshua 8, 29; 10, 26.

## 31:13
Verse 13.

THEY FASTED SEVEN DAYS) As was accustomed to be done in public mourning: in the following book 1, 12.

But although (as Osiander [notes] here) the citizens in Jabesh-Gilead did not disapprove of the just judgment of God against Saul, yet they acted rightly in not approving the cruelty of the impious Philistines. And by their example they taught that when the governors of the Republic are lost, one must mourn seriously. But the most sad fall of so great a King warns us that we should truly fear God and walk in his commandments, so that we may not fall into despair, but, however it may go with our bodily life and fortunes, we may nevertheless obtain eternal life through faith in Christ. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

JEJUNAVERUNT SEPTEM DIEBUS) Ut in luctu publico fieri solebat: libro sequente 1, 12.

Etsi autem (ut hic Osiander) cives in Jabes Galaad non improbarunt judicium Dei justum adversus Saulem, tamen recte fecerunt, non appro- bantes crudelitatem Philistinorum impiorum. Et suo exemplo ducuerunt, amissis Reip. gubernato- ribus serio lugendum. Nos vero tristissimus ca- sus tanti Regis admonet, ut Deum vere timeamus & in præceptis ejus ambulemus, ne in desperatio- nem ruamus, sed, utcunque agatur de corporali vi- ta & fortunis nostris, per fidem tamen in Chri- stum, vitam consequamur æter- nam. Amen.

# 2 Samuel

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. ON THE BOOK OF SAMUEL IN THE HEBREW TEXT, WHICH IS ACCORDING TO THE SECOND PRINTING.

Just as the first book of Samuel exhibited the history of Saul, so the second proposes the deeds of David the KING. For the setting of Saul was the rising of David, who soon succeeded Saul in the kingdom of Judah, and later also in the kingdom of the other tribes. The authors appear to be the seers Gad and Nathan, 1 Chron. last, near the end. The chronology is of 40 years, namely from the death of Saul to the end of the Davidic reign, 2 Sam. 5, 5. There are three parts: I. Concerning the anointing and happy success of David up to chapter 11. II. Concerning his sins and punishments, up to chapter 22. III. Concerning his preparation for death, chapters 22, 23, and 24.

The first part then presents the confirmation of David the King, where after the news of the death of Saul and the mournful song of David concerning the death of Saul and Jonathan, chapter 1, is related the anointing of David as King of Judah, with Ishbosheth having been elected King by the Israelites, chapter 2, and having been killed by Joab, Abner, chapter 3, and by the ministers of Ishbosheth, chapter 4; there followed the anointing of David as King of Israel, and with the Jebusites defeated, the occupation of the metropolis Jerusalem, chapter 5; then it exhibits a description of the deeds performed: first, those which are Ecclesiastical: namely, the bringing back of the ark of the covenant, chapter 6, and the building of the house of the Lord, which David having meditated upon, receives an oracle concerning Christ, chapter 7. Then those which are military, the subjugation of the Philistines, Moabites, and others, as well as those which are political, or the administration of the government, chapter 8, as also those which are Economic, namely the provision made for Mephibosheth, chapter 9; finally, those which are external bonds of friendship, to which pertained the embassy made to the King of Ammon, but treated ignominiously, whence the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, which was successfully concluded by David, chapter 10.

In the second part, the more unhappy fates of David are commemorated: where then the cause of them, adultery with Bathsheba, and the murder of Uriah, chapter 11, whose consequent rebuke by Nathan, and the repentance of David, chapter 12; then the evils that followed in the house and kingdom of David: namely (1) the incest of Amnon, (2) the fratricide and flight of Absalom, chapter 13, and his reconciliation by the art and effort of Joab, chapter 14; (3) the sedition stirred up by Absalom driving David into exile, chapter 15; (4) the curses of Shimei cast upon David, (5) the concubines of David defiled by Absalom, chapter 16, and the counsel of Ahithophel rejected by Absalom according to the persuasion of Hushai, chapter 17; (6) the battle waged between Absalom and David, with Absalom miserably killed, tragically lamented by his parent, chapter 18, the consequences of which are recounted in chapter 19; (7) the new sedition of Sheba, soon however quelled, chapter 20. To which evils of the House and government of David is subjoined a public evil, a famine in Israel, and with its expiation made, a cessation, along with the battles concluded with the Philistines, chapter 21.

The third part contains 1. The Eucharistic hymn of David, chapter 22, 2. The Last Prophetic words, to which is subjoined a catalog of his Heroes, and the desire for the Bethlehemite drink, chapter 23, and a comparison, after

Latin:

I. N AD LIBRUM P SAMU APUD HE QVI APUD SECUNDV PRÆLO

SIcut primus liber Samuelis, & Saulis historiam exhibuit; ita secundus pro- ponit gesta Davidis REGIS. Siqui- dem occasus Saul, ortus fuerit Davidis, qui mox Sauli in regno Judæ, post et- iam in regno cæterarum tribuum successit. Auto- res videntur esse videntes Gad & Nathan, 1. Par. ult. sub fin. Chronologia est 40 annorum, à morte nempe Saulis ad finem regni Davidici 2. Sam. 5, 5. Partes tres sunt: I. De unctione & felici successu Davi- dis usque ad cap. 11. II. De peccatis ejus, & suppli- ciis, usque ad c. 22. III. de præparatione ejus ad mor- tem c. 22. 23 & 24.

Pars prima tum Davidis Regis confirmatio- nem sistit, ubi post nuncium obitus Saulis & carmen lugubre Davidis de morte Saulis & Janathan c. 1. refertur unctio Davidis in Regem Judæ, Isbosetho ab Israelitis in Regem electo, c. 2. & interfecto à Joabo Abnero c. 3. atque à ministris Isbosetho c. 4. sequuta Davidis in Regem Israelis unctio, & devictis Jebusæis metropoleos Hierusalem occupatio cap. 5. tum rerum gestarum descriptionem exhibet: primum qua Ecclesiastica: arcæ nempe fœderis reductionem c. 6. & domus Domini ædificationem, quam me- ditatus David oraculum de Christo accipit cap. 7. Deinde qua militaria, subjugationem Philistæorum, Moabitarum & aliorum, nec non qua politica, vel re- giminis administrationem c. 8. ut & qua Oeconomi- ca, provisionem nempe Mephibosetho factam, c. 9. denique qua externa amicitiæ vincula, quo perti- nebat legatio ad Regem Ammon facta, sed igno- miniofe habita, unde bellum cum Ammonitis & Syris, quod à Davide feliciter confectum c. 10.

In Secunda parte infeliciora Davidis comme- morantur fata: ubi tum causa eorum, adulterium cum Bathseba, & homicidium Uriæ c. 11. cujus con- sequens reprehensio Nathanis, & pœnitentia Davidis c. 12. tum mala sequuta in domo & regno Davidis: utpote (1.) Ammonis incestus (2) Absolonis fratrici- um ac fuga c. 13. eoque arte & studio Joabi recon- ciliato c. 14. (3.) Seditio ab Absalom mota Davidem in exilium agens cap. 15. (4.) Simei maledicta in Da- videm jactata (5.) concubinæ Davidis ab Absolomo vitiatæ c. 16. & Achitopheli co consilio ab Absolo- mo posthabito juxta Husai suasum c. 17. (6.) Prælium inter Absolomum & Davidem gestum, misere per- emto Absolomo, tragice à parente deplorato cap. 18. cujus consequentia c. 19. recensentur. (7.) Nova se- ditio Sebæ, mox tamen sedata c. 20. Quibus malis Domus & regiminis Davidis subjungitur publicum malum fames in Israel, ejusque expiatione facta ces- satio cum præliis cum Philistæis confectis c. 21.

Pars tertia continet 1. Hymnum Davidis Ev- charisticum c. 22, 2. Verba Novissima Prophetica, qui- bus subjungitur catalogus Heroum ejus, & deside- rium potus Bethlehemitici c. 23. & comparatio, post

## 1:16
Verse 16.

FOR YOUR MOUTH HAS SPOKEN AGAINST YOU) Tacitus, Histories 1, after narrating the slaughter of Galba: Vitellius later found more than 120 petitions from those demanding rewards for some notable service on that day, and he ordered them all to be sought out and killed, not out of honor for Galba, but according to the custom handed down to princes, as a protection for the present and vengeance for the future. Oedipus in Sophocles, speaking of the murder of Laius: 'For whoever killed him might perhaps wish to punish me also with such a hand. By helping him, I benefit myself.' Seneca in a tragedy on the same subject: 'The safety of a King is most of all to be protected by a King.' Not unlike this is what is said of Gaius Julius Caesar, that by restoring the statues of Pompey, he established his own. Ambrose on this deed of David: because he preferred honesty to utility, utility followed honesty.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

OS ENIM TVVM LOCVTVM EST ADVERSVM TE) Tacitus Histor. 1. post narratam cædem Galbæ: plu- res quam CXX. libellos præmia exposcentium ob aliquam no- tabilem illo die operam Vitellius postea invenit, omnesque con- quiri & interfici jussit, non honore Galbæ, sed tradito principi- bus more, munimentum ad præsens, in posterum ultionem. Oedipus apud Sophoclem de Laii cæde agens: Ὃς τις γὰρ ἦν ἐκεῖνον ὁ κτανὼν τάχ' ἂν Κἄμ ἂν τοιαύτῃ χειρὶ τιμωρεῖν θέλοι. Κείνῳ προσαρκῶν ἐν ἐμαυτὸν ὠφελῶ. Seneca in ejusdem argumenti tragœdia: Regi tuenda maxime est Regis salus. Non dissimile quod C. Julius Cæsar statuas Pompeji repo- nens suas stabilijsse dictus est. Ambrosius de hoc facto Davidis: quia honestatem prætulit utilitati, utilitas honestatem secuta est.

## 1:18
Verse 18.

AND HE COMMANDED THAT THEY SHOULD TEACH THE CHILDREN OF JUDAH THE BOW) He took care that these verses should be sung during military exercises. This shows that poetic figures flourished no less among those nations than among the Greeks or Latins.

Whence is it evident to Grotius that this epinikion, concerning the bow which is appended, ought to have been sung among the military exercises of David? He would certainly have done this not so much to rouse them to martial virtue as to cast down their spirits, since heroes, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions, had perished in such a miserable slaughter. Others more correctly say that this poem was inscribed 'the bow,' because in it the bow and the martial fortitude of Saul and Jonathan are praised, just as the pipe and shield in Theocritus, celebrating the deeds of Harmodius, is inscribed 'Harmodius' among the Greeks. Cf. 2 Chron. 35:25; Jer. 9:20. They depart entirely from the mark who, following the Chaldean, wish the children of Judah to have been taught to shoot the bow, along with Bede, Lyranus, Tostatus, Vatablus, and Salianus. For thus there would be no continuity in the text.

Verse of the same.

AS IT IS WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF THE JUST] See what we said at Jos. 10. v. 13. There I had noted these things regarding the words: IS NOT THIS WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF THE JUST? It seems to have been some victory poem, in which Israel was called by contraction Jashar, as if excelling other nations in equity. Setting aside the trifles of the Rabbis, R. Radacki, who understands the Pentateuch, and the author of Bereshith Rabba, who understands the book of Genesis in both places, as also the conjecture of Sanctius the Jesuit, who opines that some book of Canticles, or even with Arias Montanus some ritual book, is designated: most of our people, with Masius and Junius, wish for a particular book or one of forensic annals to be signified here, whoever that may finally have been, whom they nevertheless judge to have been by no means inspired or canonical: such as B. Bugenhagius, Balduinus, Osiander, Mr. D. Waltherus, and others. It is merely precarious that Grotius says Israel is called Jashar by contraction, without an example from Scripture. And since in this passage the victory poem seems to be distinguished from the book of the just (for this is recounted subsequently), it does not appear how these things ought to be accepted concerning that poem.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ET PRÆCEPIT VT DOCERENT FILIOS JVDÆ ARCVM) Curavit ut intra exercitamenta militaria ver- sus hi cantarentur. Ostendit hoc carmen figuras poëticas non minus apud illas gentes, quam apud Græcos aut Lati- nos floruisse.

Undenam constat Grotio, quod ἐπινίκιον hoc, De arcu quod subjungitur, inter exercitamenta militaria Davidis cantari debuerit? Fecisset hoc utique non tam ad erigendos ad virtutem bellicam, quam ad proster- nendos animos, siquidem Heroes, aquilis velocio- res, Leonibus fortiores tam miserabili clade perie- rint. Rectius alii arcum inscriptum fuisse hocce carmen dicunt, quia in eo laudatur arcus & fortitu- do bellica Saulis & Jonathæ, ut fistula & scutum a- pud Theocritum Harmodium, facta Harmodii cele- brans, apud Græcos inscribitur. Conf. 2. Par. 35, 25. Jer. 9, 20. A scopo plane abscedunt, qui præeunte Chaldæo, Filios Judæ ad arcum jaciendum edoctos, cum Beda, Lyrano, Tostato, Vatablo & Saliano volunt. Ita enim nulla esset in textu συνέχεια

Vers. eod.

SICVT SCRIPTVM EST IN LIBRO JVSTORVM] Vide quæ diximus Jos. 10. v. 13. Ibi hæc notarat ad verba: NONNE SCRI- PTUM EST HOC IN LIBRO JUSTO- RUM? Videtur poëma aliquod fuisse ἐπινίκιον, in quo ישראל contracte ישר dicebatur, quasi cæteris gen- tibus æquitate præstans. Missis Rabbinorum nugis R. Radacki, qui Pen- tateuchum, & auctoris Bereschith Rabba, qui librum Geneseos utrobiq; intelligunt, ut & conjectura San- ctii Jesuitæ, qui librum quendam Canticorum, vel et- iam cum Ariamontano librum aliquem ritualem designari opinatur: Nostrates plerique librum pecu- liarem seu annalium forensium cum Masio & Junio, vel quicunque tandem is fuerit, quem tamen mini- me θεόπνευστον aut Canonicum fuisse censent, hic significari volunt: Utpote B. Bugenhagius, Bal- duinus, Osiander, Dn. D. Waltherus & alii. Mere precarium est, quod Grotius ישראל contracte ישר dici ait, sine exemplo Scripturæ. Et quum hic loci à libro justorum poëma ἐπινίκιον distingui vi- deatur, (hoc enim deinceps recensetur) non appa- ret, quomodo hæc de poëmate illo accipi debeant.

## 1:19

THE RENOWNED) The beauty. But the Greeks read the beauty from to set: for the LXX translate it, set up. Aquila, make firm. A different reading regarding the consonants cannot be certainly gathered here. For they could have read the beauty, because to set is to establish, to erect a monument, whence a sepulchral monument. For they rendered it, set up a monument over those who died for you. See Buxtorff in the vindication of Hebrew truth, p. 777 and following.

INCLYTI) הצבי decor. At Græci legere הצב à יצב: vertunt enim LXX. στήλωσον. Aquila ἀκρίβασον. Non hic potest certo colligi diversa lectio quoad consonantes. Nam potuere legisse הצבי quia הציב est statuere, erigere monumentum, unde מצבה monumentum sepulcrale. Reddidere enim στήλωσον ὑπὲρ τῶν τεθνικότων σε, erige monu- mentum super mortuos tuos. Vid. Buxtorff. in vin- dic. verit. Hebr. p. 777. & seq.

Verse 4.

AND THE MEN OF JUDAH CAME, AND ANOINTED DAVID THERE) A single tribe, though an excellent one, makes a King by a pernicious example, unless the known will of God should break through every law. BLESSED BE YE OF THE LORD, THAT YE HAVE SHEWED THIS KINDNESS UNTO YOUR LORD SAUL) Therefore not all who died by their own hand were left unburied among the Hebrews. AND HE REIGNED TWO YEARS) Peacefully, that is, before David brought arms against him. ## 2:13

JOAB THE SON OF ZERUIAH) A brave man and good at warfare, but ambitious, irascible, and desirous of vengeance beyond measure, not unlike Achilles, who, in Horace, denies that laws were made for him and claims everything for his arms.

But he surpassed Achilles in the foresight of useful things: he was not unlike Mucianus in this respect, and also in arrogance, who handed over the empire to Vespasian, just as this man did to David.

Forsan au- tem Grotius Eglam in mente habuit v. 5. quam Ebraei Michol fuisse dicunt, sed falso: quia Michol sterilis fuit & de illa reducta agitur v. 14. cap. 6. v. 23. Egla vero v. 5. foecunda.

## 3:9
Verse 9. UNLESS AS THE LORD SWORE TO DAVID, SO WILL I DO WITH HIM) This ought to have been thought of before the civil war was undertaken.

Latin:

Vers. 9. NISI QVOMODO JVRAVIT DOMINVS DAVIDI, SIC FACIAM CUM EO) Hoc ante cogitatum oportuit, quam bellum civile susciperetur.

## 3:11
Verse 11. BECAUSE HE FEARED HIM) And David feared Joab, 3:39. Thus Otho did not yet have the authority to prevent the crime; says Tacitus, Histories 1, where he describes the beginnings of the Othonian principate.

Latin:

Vers. 11. QVIA METVEBAT ILLVM) Et David Joa- bum 3, 39. Sic Othoni nondum auctoritas inerat ad prohi- bendum scelus; ait Tacitus Histor. 1. ubi principatus Otho- niani initia describit.

## 3:14
Verse 14. RESTORE MY WIFE MICHAL) For there are even in war certain things which Tacitus, after Virgil, calls dealings, Homer calls συνημοσύνας.

Latin:

Vers. 14. REDDE VXOREM MEAM MICHOL) Sunt enim etiam in bello quaedam, quae Tacitus, post Virgilium commercia vocat, Homerus συνημοσύνας.

## 3:16
Verse 16. AND HER HUSBAND FOLLOWED HER WEEPING) As Achilles when Briseis was taken away. Homer, Iliad 1. The Hebrews say that Michal remained untouched by Phaltiel due to David's fear.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SEQVEBATVRQVE EAM VIR SVVS PLO- RANS) Vt Achilles abducta Briseide. Homerus Iliad. ά. Metu Davidis intactam a Phaltiele mansisse Micholem ajunt Hebraei.

## 3:21
Verse 21. THAT I MAY GATHER TO THEE MY LORD THE KING ALL ISRAEL) One man often counts for much among a huge multitude: that is less surprising in a leader, when two common soldiers undertook to transfer the empire of the Roman people, and did transfer it, as Tacitus speaks in Histories 1.

Latin:

Vers. 21. VT CONGREGEM AD TE DOMINVM MEVM REGEM OMNEM ISRAEL) Multum saepe u- nus homo apud ingentem multitudinem valet: minus id mirum in Duce, cum duo manipulares susceperint imperium populi Romani transferendum, & transtulerint, ut Tacitus loquitur Histor. 1.

## 3:24
Verse 24. WHY DIDST THOU LET HIM GO?) A peer and rival in military glory burned him. Tacitus observes such emulation and envy among the Vitellian leaders in the second book of his Histories.

Latin:

Vers. 24. QVARE DIMISISTI EVM?) Vrebat eum gloria militari par & aemulus. Talem aemulationem & in- vidiam inter duces Vitellianos Tacit. observat Hist. secundo.

## 3:27
Verse 27. THAT HE MIGHT SPEAK TO HIM IN DECEIT) Treacherously, as Livy speaks in a similar deed in book 38. See what we have said in our third book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 24, section 3.

Latin:

Vers. 27. VT LOQVERETVR EI IN DOLO) Perfide, ut Livius in facto simili loquitur libro 38. Vide quae dicta no- bis libro tertio de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 24. §. 3.

## 3:28
Ver. 28. I AM CLEAN) Prudently David avoids the authority, and purges himself against the suspicions of his conscience of that crime, which, on account of the newness of the kingdom and the remnants of civil war, he could not punish. See below 37.

Latin:

Vers. 28. MVNDVS EGO SVM) Prudenter David au- ctoritatem defugit, & adversus conscientiae suspiciones se purgat de eo crimine, quod ob regni novitatem, & belli civilis reliquias punire non poterat. Vide infra 37.

## 3:29
Ver. 29. NOR LET THERE FAIL FROM THE HOUSE OF JOAB ONE THAT HOLDETH THE FLUX AND IS A LEPER) It was their custom to curse a criminal along with his posterity. See Ps. 109, 10. 12. It is more correctly considered that David as a Prophet foretold these things to Jacob, which also happened in Ps. 109. For the man of God would not have followed an evil custom. Others say that these words sound not so much like a curse as the merit of Joab, namely, that he deserves to be afflicted with these punishments. AND HOLDING A SPINDLE) Nay, a staff. The Greeks κρατῶν σκυτάλης. Aquila explains it as blind.

Latin:

Vers. 29. NEC DEFICIAT DE DOMO JOAB FLV- XVM SVSTINENS ET LEPROSVS) Diris defigere faci- norosum posteros mos erat illorum. Vide Pf. 109, 10. 12. Rectius hæc David censetur ceu Propheta Jacobo prædixisse, quod & Pf. 109. factum. Non enim morem improbum vir Dei sectatus esset. Alii verba hæc non tam maledictionem, quam meritum Joab sonare, ajunt, eum sc. mereri, ut his pœnis afficiatur. ET TENENS FVSVM) Imo scipionem. Græci κρα- τῶν σκυτάλης. Aquila cæcum explicat.

## 3:30
Verse 30.

JOAB AND ABISHAI HIS BROTHER KILLED ABNER] Joab by his hand, Abishai by consent and assistance.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

JOAB ET ABISAI FRATER EJVS INTERFECE- RVNT ABNER ] Joab manu, Abisai consensu & auxilio.

## 3:31
Verse 31. KING DAVID FOLLOWED THE BIER) For women used to go before the bier. But kings were not accustomed to attend a funeral. But David wished to attend contrary to custom, so that he might the further remove suspicion from himself.

Latin:

Vers. 31. REX DAVID SEQVEBATVR FERETRVM) Nam ante feretrum ibant mulieres. Reges autem non solebant funeri interesse. Sed David præter morem interesse voluit, quo longius suspicionem a se amoliretur.

## 3:34
Verse 34. YOUR HANDS ARE NOT BOUND) You were not the kind of person who would lend your hands to another without discernment of matters. Thus the Hebrews, who refer this to the constancy of Abner, when he refused to kill the priests at the command of Saul.

Latin:

Vers. 34. MANVS TVÆ LIGATÆ NON SVNT) Non is tu eras, qui sine delectu rerum manus tuas alteri commoda- res. Ita Hebræi, qui id referunt ad constantiam Abneri, cum ad imperium Saulis Sacerdotes occidere noluit.

## 3:39
Verse 39. BUT I AM DELICATE AND ANOINTED KING) He notes two things, that his kingdom was recent (for that is what the word רך means) and that he was not born a King. For those who come to the kingdom by inheritance, or at least whose power has been established for a long time, rule more strictly. He is free from blame who knows, but cannot prevent. See what is said in the second book on the Law of War and Peace, ch. 32, §. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 39. EGO AVTEM DELICATVS ET VNCTVS REX) Duo notat, quod recens esset regnum suum (id enim vult vox רך) & quod non natus esset Rex. Adductius enim imperant qui hæreditate ad regnum veniunt, aut certe quo- rum potentia longo tempore firmata est. Culpa vacat qui scit, sed prohibere non potest. Vide quæ dicta libro secundo de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. 32. §. 2.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Ishbosheth killed, his killers hanged.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Isboseth occisus, occisores ejus suspensi.

## 4:2
Verse 2. CAPTAIN OF BANDITS) Better the Greeks, ἡγούμενοι συστρεμμάτων, leaders of cohorts.

FOR BEEROTH ALSO WAS RECKONED TO BENJAMIN) By right it belonged to the Benjaminites, although it was held by force by the Philistines 1 Sam. 31, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 2. PRINCEPS LATRONVM) Melius Græci, ἡγύ- μενοι συστρεμμάτων, cohortium duces.

SIQVIDEM ET BERETH REPVTATA EST IN BENJAMIN) Jure ad Benjaminitas pertinebat, quanquam vi a Philistinis tenebatur 1. Sam. 31, 7.

## 4:4
Verse 4. A SON WEAK IN HIS FEET) Not in vain is that mentioned in this place. For it made the assassins bolder, because he to whom the blood vengeance of Ishbosheth pertained was not in control of his limbs.

The Holy Scripture wished to signify primarily that from the stock of Saul no male remained fit for the kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 4. FILIVS DEBILIS PEDIBVS) Non frustra hoc loco istud refertur. Fecit enim percussores audaciores, quod is ad quem vindicta sanguinis Isbosethi spectabat, membro- rum suorum compos non erat.

Significare id imprimis volebat S. S. ex stirpe Saulis nullam superesse masculum regno idoneum.

## 4:7
Verse 7.

THEY KILLED HIM) Such things happen frequently in civil wars, in the hope of pardon and rewards.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

INTERFECERVNT EVM) Frequenter talia accidunt in bellis civilibus, spe veniæ ac præmiorum.

## 4:11
Verse 11.

AN INNOCENT MAN) He does not say King: for he had not been made King by right, but a man who had done them no harm, and therefore expected nothing of the sort from them.

By the judgment of charity he considers him innocent: because perhaps he believed that the kingdom belonged to himself, the son of the deceased King Saul, and he did not know for certain that David had been anointed by Samuel as King of all the tribes.

IN HIS HOUSE) Upon his bed.

Verse 22.

THEY KILLED THEM) Even when committed against our enemies, if they have the atrocity of a crime, they are punished by us with praise, as the crime of Bessus was by Alexander. Thus also the Romans did not allow the treachery of the Faliscan schoolmaster to go unpunished.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

VIRVM INNOXIVM) Non dicit Regem: neque enim jure factus Rex erat, sed hominem qui ipsis nihil nocuerat, & propterea nihil tale ab ipsis expectabat.

Judicio charitatis innoxium censet: quia credidit forte, ad se, filium Regis defuncti Saulis regnum pertinere, nec certo scivit Davidem a Sa- muele in Regem omnium tribuum unctum esse.

IN DOMO SVA) Super lectum suum.

Vers. 22.

INTERFECERVNT EOS) Etiam in hostes nostros ad- missa, si atrocitatem facinoris habeant, cum laude a nobis pu- niuntur, ut Bessi scelus ab Alexandro. Sic & Romani impuni- tatem non sivere perfidiam ludimagistri Falisci.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

David is anointed by the 11 tribes, he wrests the citadel of Zion from the Jebusites, in which the house of David is built.

Verse 1.

AND ALL THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL CAME) Conquered not by arms, but by what is a more beautiful victory, the justice and piety of David.

BEHOLD WE ARE THY BONE AND THY FLESH) We shall not sin against the law of Deut. 17, 15 if we take a King from among our countrymen.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

David ungitur ab XI. tribubus, Jebusæis extor- quet arcem Sion, in qua domus Davidis ædi- ficatur.

Vers. 1.

ET VENERVNT VNIVERSÆ TRIBVS ISRAEL) Victæ non armis, sed quæ pulchrior victoria, justitia ac pie- tate Davidis.

ECCE OS TVVM ET CARO TVA SVMVS) Non peccabimus in legem Deut. 17, 15. si Regem sumamus ex po- pularibus.

## 5:2
Vers. 2.

BUT THE LORD SAID TO THEE: THOU SHALT FEED MY PEOPLE) We have believed that the empire was destined for Vespasian and his children by a hidden law of fate and by omens and oracles, after the event. Tacitus says in Hist. I.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DIXIT AVTEM DOMINUS AD TE: TU PASCES POPULUM MEUM) Occulta lege fati & ostentis ac respon- sis destinatum Vespasiano liberisque ejus imperium, post fortu- nam credidimus. Ait Tacitus Hist. I.

## 5:3
Vers. 3.

THE ELDERS ALSO CAME) The senators of the great Sanhedrin.

AND KING DAVID MADE A COVENANT WITH THEM) Every agreement is called ברית by the Hebrews, such as this one was, by which David promised them indulgence for past deeds, and they in turn promised obedience to the King.

HE REIGNED FORTY YEARS) Full years, omitting the months, of which mention will follow.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VENERVNT QVOQVE ET SENIORES) Senatores magni Synedrii.

ET PERCVSSIT CUM EIS REX DAVID FOEDUS) Omnis conventio Hebræis ברית vocatur, qualis hæc fu- it, qua David illis indulgentiam ante actorum promisit, ipsi vero Regi obedientiam.

QVADRAGINTA ANNOS REGNAVIT) Solidos, omissis mensibus, quorum sequetur mentio.

## 5:6
Vers. 6.

THOU SHALT NOT COME IN HITHER UNLESS THOU TAKE AWAY THE BLIND AND THE LAME, SAYING: DAVID SHALL NOT COME IN HITHER) The meaning is, the Jebusites, trusting in the location, said in mockery that blind and lame men would suffice to repel the assault.

Abulensis explains it indeed in this way, and Serarius and Cornelius à Lapide, appealing to Josephus, Procopius, and Theodoret: But B. Luther, Osiander, and the Weimar theologians more correctly understand the idols, which the Jebusites had placed on the walls as tutelary gods, with Burgensis, which they call by that name because they were considered by David and the Israelites as blind and lame, Ps. 115, 5 seqq., and although they are considered to be in that place, they would nevertheless repel David and his men. Because it is added: whom the soul of David hateth (and not as it is held in the Vulgate, those who hate the soul of David) and from there the saying and statute arose: the blind and the lame shall not enter into the house: that is, let no one place such idolatrous images in his house, because there is nothing in them, neither help nor protection.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NON INGREDIERIS HVC NISI ABSTVLERIS CÆCOS ET CLAVDOS, DICENTES: NON INGRE- DIETVR DAVID HVC) Sensus est, Jebusæi fidentes lo- co per irrisum dixere, homines cæcos & claudos suffecturos repellendæ oppugnationi.

Ita quidem explicat Abulensis, & Serarius ac Cornelius à Lapide ad Josephum, Procopium, & Theodoretum provocans: Sed rectius B. Lutherus, Osiander, Vinarienses Idola, quæ Jebusæi, quasi De- os tutelares in muris collocarant, cum Burgenfi in- telligunt, quæ ita vocent, quod à Davide, ac Israe- litis pro cæcis, & claudis haberentur, Ps. 115,5.seqq. ac licet eo loco censeantur, repulsura tamen sint Davidem cum suis. Quia additur: quos odit ani- ma Davidis (non vero ut in vulgata habetur, odien- tes animam Davidis) & inde dictum & statutum ortum: non ingredietur cæcus & claudus in domum: h. e. nemo idololatricas ejusmodi imagines in do- mo sua collocet, quia nihil in eis est, neque auxi- lii neque præsidii.

## 5:8
Vers. 8.

FOR DAVID HAD PROPOSED IN THAT DAY A REWARD) He has well supplied what is understood in the Hebrew.

But that reward is defined in 1 Chron. 11, 6, which Joab obtained.

AND HAD TOUCHED THE WATER PIPES) He took the citadel with corrupted waters. See similar examples in Frontinus, book three, chapter 7.

Others, and had touched the canal: that is, he who had first scaled the wall: He who climbed the walls first.

THE BLIND AND THE LAME SHALL NOT ENTER THE TEMPLE) In the Hebrew: Into this house: That is, into the citadel of Zion. David ordained that no blind or lame person should enter there, in memory of the aforementioned history.

We have already said that another meaning underlies this.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

PROPOSVERAT ENIM DAVID IN DIE ILLA PRÆMIVM) Bene supplevit quod subauditur in Hebræo.

Præmium autem illud definitum est 1. Par. 11, 6. quod reportavit Joab.

ET TETIGISSET DOMUUM FISTULAS) Aquis corruptis cepit arcem. Similia exempla vide apud Fronti- num libro tertio c. 7.

Alii, & attigisset canalem: id est, qui primus murum transcendisset: Der die Mauren erstiege.

CÆCUS ET CLAUDUS NON INTRABUNT IN TEMPLVM) In Hebræo: In domum hanc: Id est, in ar- cem Sionis. Constituit David ne eo quis ingrederetur cæ- cus aut claudus in ante dictæ historiæ memoriam.

Alium subesse sensum jam diximus.

## 5:11
Verse 11.

HIRAM ALSO KING OF TYRE SENT MESSENGERS TO DAVID) The letters of these kings to one another were extant in the archives of the Tyrians in the time of Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

MISIT QVOQVE HIRAM REX TYRI NVNTIOS AD DAVID) Exstabant horum Regum inter se epistolæ in Tyriorum archivis Josephi tempore.

## 5:13
Verse 13. CONCUBINES) See what is above at Judges 8, 31.

Latin:

Vers. 13. CONCVBINAS) Vide quæ supra Jud. 8, 31.

## 5:21
Verse 21.

WHICH DAVID TOOK) He took them away by fire, 1 Chron. 14, 12, according to the law in Deut. 7, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

QUÆ TVLIT DAVID) Abstulit incendio, 1. Paral. 14, 12. ex lege Deut. 7, 5.

## 5:23
Verse 23.

CIRCLE BEHIND THEM) From where you would least be thought to come: a stratagem.

OVER AGAINST THE PYRI) It is the name of trees: and the Chaldean had enough to express that. Many interpret it as mulberries. But others take it as drops falling in the manner of tears, so that there is an א for a ה, for בכה is to weep. The Greeks here: of weeping. Hesychius: bacchus, the Phoenicians: weeping. Is it from this that we get bacchants?

What is the point here of rendering the received reading doubtful, when the words as they stand render a sense consistent with the text, and Grotius himself does not deny it.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

GYRA POST TERGVM EORVM) Vnde minime venturus puteris: stratagema.

EX ADVERSO PYRORVM) Arborum nomen est: id- que satis habuit exprimere Chaldæus. Plures, moros interpre- tantur. At alii stillas accipiunt cadentes lacrymarum more, ut sit א pro ה, nam בכה flere. Græci hic: τοῦ κλαυθμῶνος. Hesychius βάκχον, κλαυθμὸν Φοίνικες. An hinc βάκχοι;

Quid hic attinet dubium reddere receptam lectionem, quum verba uti habent, sensum textui congruum reddere nec ipse Grotius negat.

## 6:1 Argument
SECTION II. DESCRIPTION OF THE DEEDS OF DAVID. CHAPTER VI.

The ark of the covenant is transferred into the house of Obed-Edom, and from there into Zion. Michal mocks David as he dances, and is severely rebuked for it.

Ver. 1. THIRTY THOUSAND) The Greeks set down seventy thousand. The true reading seems to be 300 thousand, to which chapter 12, along with the beginning of the following chapter of 1 Chronicles, draws us.

There is no cause for correcting the Sacred text; for it is said here that there were 30,000 CHOSEN men from all Israel; and in 1 Chron. 13:5 they are likewise said to be gathered from all Israel, who were to bring the ark. But as for the fact that in v. 6 David is said to have gone up with all Israel, it is because those men had been chosen from all Israel and represented all Israel, since that matter had been deliberated and concluded in the assembly of all Israel.

Latin:

SECTIO II. RERUM GESTARUM DAVIDIS DESCRIPTIO. CAPUT VI.

Arca fœderis in domum Obed Edom, inde in Sion transfertur. Saltantem Davidem irri- det Michal, ob id graviter reprehensa.

Vers. 1. TRIGINTA MILLIA) Græci septuaginta mil- lia ponunt. Vera lectio videtur esse 300. millia, quo nos trahit caput 12. cum initio capitis sequentis Paral. 1.

Nulla est causa corrigendi textum Sacrum; dicuntur enim hic fuisse XXX. millia DELECTO- RUM quorumque ex Israele; & 1. Par. 13, 5. pariter congregati dicuntur ex toto Israele, qui adducerent arcam. Quod autem v. 6. cum toto Israele David ascendisse dicitur, sit, quia illi ex toto Israele de- lecti fuerant & totum Israel repræsentabant, fiqui- dem in comitiis totius Israelis res illa deliberata & conclusa fuerat.

## 6:2
Ver. 2.

OF THE MEN OF JUDA) Concerning Baalah of Juda. It is the name of a place, 1 Chron. 13, 6. to which place there is another name, Cariathiarim, and in the same place in the Chronicles, and Josh. 15, 9. 60. Moreover, the Ark was in that place at this time. 2 Sam. 6, 21. 7, 1.

The Vulgate is deservedly corrected. Therefore it is not ἀνυπεύθυνος (unaccountable).

UPON WHICH THE NAME OF THE LORD OF HOSTS HAS BEEN CALLED) That is, the ark, which the Hebrews figuratively called the Lord of hosts. See Ps. 24. Here in the Hebrew there is the word שם twice, but in the former place it may perhaps have been שם.

A double error. The first, when the incommunicable name, which R. Moses Maimonides calls שם המיוחד, שם המפורש, which is proper to God alone, because it explains the essence of God, or because it is most widely separated from creatures, שם הגדול, the great name, as the Rabbis call it, is attributed to the ark, as if it were called יהוה or even יהוה צבאות, Lord of Hosts. Which figment of the Hebrews, Socinians, Remonstrants, and Calvinists, as well as some Papists, we have refuted elsewhere, Theol. natural. & revel. chap. 2. p. 262. seqq. The words of the Hebrew truth can be rendered thus in this place: The ark of God (they will cause to ascend) whose (ark's) name has been called: The name (or even the glory) of Jehovah Zebaoth, dwelling in the Cherubim, (who are) upon it. Thus the ark is not called by the name Jehovah, but it has the appellation from thence, because the name or glory of God dwells upon it, nor is there any need for a figurative or metonymical explanation. And thus our blessed Luther rendered it. Others posit an ellipsis of the preposition אל, and explain it thus: Upon which the name has been called, the name of the Lord Zebaoth, dwelling in the Cherubim upon it; which is the interpretation of Piscator and Junius. Others take the word אשר adverbially, and say that it is so taken in Jud. 17, 8. 2 Kings 16, 5., in this sense: where the name of the Lord has been called. Others explain it causally, as in Ps. 31. and 1 Kings 15, 13., because the name of the God Jehovah Zebaoth sitting upon the cherubim has been called upon it. But it can be explained most simply in this way: the ark of that God, whose (God's) name has been called (or even invoked), the name of Jehovah Zebaoth sitting upon the Cherubim upon it, just as it is held in the parallel passage 1 Chron. 13, 6.: the ark of God Jehovah sitting upon the Cherubim, whose name has been called, or upon which the name has been called. But the Grotian interpretation is inept: That the name Jehovah Zebaoth is attributed to the ark, and indeed Jehovah Zebaoth sitting upon the Cherubim upon the ark. If the ark comes by the name Jehovah Zebaoth, who is said to sit upon the ark? Concerning Ps. 24, it will be spoken of in its own place.

The other error is that Grotius corrects the Hebrew text, and divines that שם might perhaps have been in the place of שם. For what we have already said teaches that there is no need for this correction and divination. All the adduced expositions hold themselves more correctly, even if the modern Hebrew reading is retained, other than which another is vainly feigned.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DE VIRIS JUDA) De Bahala Iuda. Nomen est loci 1. Paral. 13, 6. cui loco nomen aliud Cariathiarim & ibidem in Paralipomenis, & Jos. 15, 9.60. In eo autem loco ad hoc tem- pus fuit Arca. 2. Sam. 6, 21. 7, 1.

Merito corrigitur Vulgata. Non ergo est ἀνυπεύθυνος.

SUPER QUAM INVOCATVM EST NOMEN DO- MINI ETERCITUUM) Id est arcam, quam Ebræi appella- bant figurate Dominum exercituum. Vid. Psal. 24. Bis hic in Hebræo est שם, sed priori loco forte fuerit שם.

Geminum ἁμάρτημα. Primum, cum nomen ἀκοινώνητον, quod R. Moses Maim. vocat שם המיוחד, שם המפורש, quod soli Deo proprium id sit, quod exponat Dei essentiam, vel quod longissime se- paratum sit à creaturis, שם הגדול nomen ma- gnum, uti Rabbini vocant, tribuitur arcæ, quasi vo- cata fuerit יהוה vel etiam יהוה צבאות Domi- nus Exercituum. Quod Ebræorum, Socinianorum, Re- monstrantium, & Calvinianorum, ut & Pontificiorum nonnullorum commentum, alibi profligavimus, Theol. natural. & revel. cap. 2. p. 262. seqq. Verba ve- ritatis Ebraicæ ita reddi possunt hoc loco: Arcam Dei (ascendere facient) cujus (arcæ) vocatum est no- men: Nomen (vel etiam gloria) Jehovab Zebaoth, habitat in Cherubim, (qui sunt) super eam. Ita non arca vocatur nomine Jehovah, sed inde appellatio- nem habet, quod nomen vel gloria Dei super eam habitet, nec ulla opus est figurata vel metonymica explicatione. Atque ita reddidit B. Lutherus no- ster. Alii ellipsin præpositionis אל statuunt, at- que ita exponunt: Ad quam invocatum est nomen, nomen Domini Zebaoth, habitantis in Cherubim su- per ea; quæ Piscatoris & Junii est interpretatio. Alii vocem אשר adverbialiter accipiunt, atque ita eandem Jud. 17, 8. 2. Reg. 16, 5. accipi, ajunt, hoc sensu: ubi invocatum est nomen Domini. Alii eam explicant causaliter, ut Psal. 31. & 1. Reg. 15, 13. quia nomen Dei Jehovah Zebaoth insidentis cherubim in- vocatum est super eam. Sed explicari potest simpli- cissime hoc pacto: arcam Dei illius, cujus (Dei) vocatum (vel etiam invocatum) est nomen, no- men Jehovah Zebaoth insidentis Cherubim super eam, quemadmodum in loco parallelo 1. Par. 13, 6. habetur: arcam Dei Jehovah insidentis Cherubim, cujus invocatum est nomen, vel super quam invoca- tum est nomen. Inepta autem est Grotiana inter- pretatio: Arcæ nomen tributum esse Jehovah Ze- baoth, & quidem Jehovah Zebaoth insidens Cheru- bim super arcam. Si arco nomine Jehovah Zebaoth venit, qui arca super arcam sedere dicitur? De Psal. 24. suo loco dicetur.

Alterum ἁμάρτημα est, quod corrigat Gro- tius Ebræum textum, & שם forte fuisse loco שם divinet. Hac enim correctura ac divinatione opus non esse, ea, quæ jam diximus, docent. Expositio- nes adductæ omnes se rectius habent, etiamsi mo- derna lectio Ebræa retineatur, præter quam alia frustra fingitur.

## 6:3
Ver. 3.

UPON A NEW CART) Erroneously. For it was to be carried on the shoulders. Numb. 4, 15. here below 13. 1 Chron. 15, 15.

## 6:6
Verse 6.

UZZAH STRETCHED OUT HIS HAND TO THE ARK OF GOD) And this was against the law. For this was the duty of the Levites from the family of Kohath. See the cited place in Numbers.

Abrabanel observes that four transgressions concur in this action. (1.) Because by the prescription of the law, the carrying of the ark was enjoined upon the Levites alone, so that they should carry it on their shoulder; therefore a most grave sin was committed because they placed the ark on a new cart. For although the Philistines did the same, they were foreigners and did not have knowledge of the law. (2.) Because it was not permitted even for the Levites to touch the ark of God with their body, but they carried it with poles. (3.) The transgression of Uzzah was personal, who was not a Levite, nor did he have the authority to touch the ark (Num. 17, last verse; 1 Chron. 15:2). (4.) According to the opinion of the Rabbis, he sinned by ὀλιγοπισίᾳ [little faith], thinking that the ark would fall, as if it could not subsist by itself without a bearer. Which fourth reason, however, we shall leave to its authors. Rabbenu Jeschajah says he was punished with death on account of the error which he committed by stretching out his hand to the ark, not thinking that the ark would direct the cows into the right path by itself, without a guide or leader. The Rabbis also deny, along with Joshua ch. 4, that when the ark crossed the Jordan, it was raised above the waters, and that it was so far from being carried on the shoulders of the priests that it rather carried the priests itself. To the first reason, which Jerome reports in the Hebrew traditions on 1 Chronicles 2, and which Theodoret (q. 20), Procopius, and Lyra approve, Sanctius opposes this: that just as many consented to that work and plan, that the ark should be carried by a cart, so also many should have perished by the same or a similar punishment, or at the very least, Uzzah's brother, Ahio. He does not indeed deny that there was sin in it, but they deny that Uzzah was punished with sudden death on account of that sin. He says, however, that the opinion which seeks reverence in Uzzah is more literal, because he flew hastily and inconsiderately to support the ark, when the necessity of the matter did not demand it, because the tilting of the cart was only slight. That rashness in touching it, therefore, seems to have been punished. Which is also the opinion of Gregory the Great, Morals, book 5, ch. 10, and of Abulensis. To the third opinion, however, which is Grotius's, others object that Uzzah was a Levite: just as Jerome (Ep. 49) and Thomas (dist. 19, q. 1) thought, who hold that Uzzah sinned in this, that it was not for the Levites, but for the Priests, to touch the ark. But they are hallucinating in this; because it is expressly evident from Num. 4 and 1 Chron. 15 that this duty was enjoined not upon the Priests, but upon the Levites; and therefore Sanctius correctly locates the sin in this, that Uzzah was not a Levite, or if he was a Levite (which he himself asserted from Josephus on 1 Sam. 7:1: Although he attributed the contrary opinion to Josephus in his Commentary on 2 Sam. 6:7) he was not of the family of Kohath, to which these duties belonged, as indicated in Num. 4. He proves by this reasoning that he was not a Levite, nor a Priest, because the Priests and Levites had their own cities, destined by Joshua among the other tribes for their own uses and dwelling, and they could not and ought not to dwell in others. Since, therefore, Kiriath-jearim is not among the cities assigned to the Levitical order, as is evident from Josh. 21, it is likely that Abinadab and his sons Uzzah and Ahio were not of the number of the Levitical rank. That he was not a Levite is agreed upon by the Jews, as we have seen, Abarbenel, as also R. David Kimchi on 2 Sam. 6. Consult Buxtorff in the history of the ark of the covenant, ch. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

EXTENDIT OZA MANUM AD ARCAM DEI) Et hoc contra legem. Erat enim hoc Levitarum ex Cehathi fa- milia. Vid. dicto loco Numerorum.

Abrabanel quatuor prævaricationes in actione hac concurrere observat. (1.) Quia ex præscripto legis gestatio arcæ solis Levitis injuncta erat, ut illi humero portarent eam, ideo peccatum gravissimum commissum, quod arcam imposuerint plaustro novo. Nam quamvis Philistei idem fece- rint, illi extranei erant, nec legis habebant notiti- am. (2.) Quia ne quidem Levitis permissum fuit arcam Dei attingere corpore, sed vectibus eam ge- starunt. (3.) prævaricatio Usæ fuit propria, qui non fuit Levita, neque facultatem habuit tangendi ar- cam Num. 17, ult. 1. Chron. 15, 2. (4.) Ex sententia Rabbinorum peccavit ὀλιγοπισίᾳ, existimans ar- cam prolapsuram, quasi per se non possit subsistere sine bajulo. Quam tamen quartam rationem suis autoribus relinquemus. Rabbenu Jeschajah morte, inquit, mulctatus fuit, propter errorem, quem com- misit, extendendo manum ad arcam, non cogitans, ar- cam per seipsam vaccas in rectam viam directuram, sine rectore vel ductore. Negantur etiam Rabbini cum Jos. c. 4. arca trajiceret Jordanem, elevatam fuisse super aquas, & adeo non esse portatam Sacer- dotum humeris, ut ipsa potius Sacerdotes portave- rit. Primæ rationi, quam refert Hieronymus, tradi- tionibus Hebraicis ad 1. Par. 2. probatque Theodore- tus q. 20. Procopius, & Lyra, Sanctius hoc opponit, quod ut multi in opus illud, atque consilium, ut ar- ca plaustro vectaretur consensere, sic etiam multis eodem aut simili supplicio pereundum fuisse, aut ad minimum fratri etiam Usæ, Ahiò. Non negat quidem peccatum in eo fuisse, sed Usam ob illud peccatum repentina morte mulctatum fuisse, ne- gant. Illam vero sententiam magis ad literam esse di- cit, quæ in Usa desiderat reverentiam, quod festina- te & inconsiderate advolarit ad arcam sustentan- dam, cum rei necessitas non exigeret, quia levis so- lum erat plaustri inclinatio, Illam ergo in tangendo temeritatem punitam videri. Quæ etiam Gregor. M. Moral. lib. 5. c. 10. & Abulensis est sententia. Ter- tiæ vero, quæ Grotii est, alii opponunt, quod Usa Levita fuerit: quemadmodum Hieronymus Ep. 49. & Thomas dist. 19. q. 1. sensere, qui in eo peccasse Usam volunt, quod non Levitarum, sed Sacerdo- tum fuerit arcam tangere. Sed hallucinantur in eo; quia non Sacerdotibus, sed Levitis istud munus in- junctum fuisse ex Num. 4. & 1. Paral. 15. expresse constat; ideoque Sanctius in eo peccatum recte col- locat, quod Usa Levita non fuerit, aut si Levita fuit (quod ipse è Josepho ad 1. Sam. 7, 1. asseruit: Licet Josepho in Comment. ad 2. Sam. 6, 7. contrariam tribuerit sententiam) non fuerit è familia Caath, ad quam spectabant hæc officia, ut Num. 4. indica- tum. Non autem fuisse Levitam, neque Sacerdo- tem hac ratione probat, quia Sacerdotes ac Levitæ suas habuere civitates, inter alias tribus à Josua pro ipsorum usibus ac domicilio destinatas, neque in aliis habitare aut poterant aut debebant. Cum ergo Kiriathjarim non sit ex civitatibus assignatis ordini Levitico, ut constat Jos. 21. verisimile esse Abinadab, filiosque ejus Osam, & Ahio non fuisse ex numero Levitici gradus. Non fuisse Levitam an- nuit è Judæis, uti vidimus, Abarbenel, ut & R. David Kimchi ad 2. Sam. 6. Cons. Buxtorff. in histor. arc. fœder. c. 18.

## 7:2
Verse 2.

TO NATHAN THE PROPHET) This man was prudent, gentle, and what Josephus adds, ἀσεῖον, that is, tempering gravity with a certain sweetness, and one who also knew how to live with kings. Such was Manius Lepidus in Tacitus, Annals 4: I find, he says, that this Lepidus was a grave and wise man in those times. For he turned most things from the savage flatteries of others for the better, nor yet did he lack moderation, since he flourished with Tiberius with balanced authority and favor. Whence I am compelled to doubt whether, by fate and the chance of birth, as with other things, the inclination of princes toward some and offense toward others is determined: or whether there is something in our own counsels, and it is permitted to proceed on a path free from ambition and dangers between abrupt contumacy and shameful obsequiousness. Such also in book 6, Annals 50, is Piso the Pontiff: Not the author of any servile opinion of his own accord, and as often as necessity pressed, wisely moderating. Indeed, that saying of Eprius Marcellus is not entirely false, which the same Tacitus has in Histories 4: Just as the worst emperors like endless domination, so even the most excellent like a limit to liberty. And so Agricola is praised by the same: He did not provoke fame and fate by contumacy, nor by a vain boasting of liberty.

DO YOU SEE THAT I DWELL IN A HOUSE OF CEDAR) Such also was the palace of Cadmus in Euripides' Phoenissae: Cross the ancient cedar staircase with your foot.

AND THE ARK OF GOD IS PLACED IN THE MIDST OF SKINS) This purpose of David, to build a magnificent temple for God, although it lacked the event itself, did not lack its reward: for therefore God promises that He will build a house for him below in verse 11, as if repaying the favor.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

AD NATHAN PROPHETAM) Vir hic fuit prudens, lenis, & quod Josephus addit ἀσεῖον, id est, suavitate quadam gravitatem temperans, & qui etiam cum Regibus nosset vi- vere. Talis apud Tacitum Annal. 4. Manius Lepidus: Hunc ego Lepidum, ait, temporibus illis gravem ac sapientem vi- rum fuisse comperio. Nam pleraque ab sævis adulationibus aliorum in melius flexit, neque tamen temperamenti egebat, cum æquabili auctoritate, & gratia apud Tiberium viguerit. Vnde dubitare cogor, fato & forte nascendi, ut cætera, ita principum inclinatio in hos, offensio in illos: an sit aliquid in nostris consiliis, liceatque inter abruptam contumaciam & deforme obsequium, pergere iter ambitione ac periculis vacuum. Talis & libro 6. Annal. 50. Piso Pontifex: Nullius servilis sententiæ sponte au- ctor, & quoties necessitas ingrueret, sapienter moderans. Nimi- rum non omnino falsum illud Eprii Marcelli, quod idem Ta- citus habet Histor. 4. Quomodo pessimis imperatoribus sine fine dominationem, ita quamvis egregiis modum libertatis pla- cere. Itaque laudatus eidem Agricola: Non contumacia, neque inani jactatione libertatis famam fatumque provocabat.

VIDESNE, QVOD EGO HABITEM IN DO- MO CEDRINA) Talis & Cadmi regia apud Euripidem Phœnissis: Κέδρο παλαίαν κλίμακ᾽ ἐκπέρα ποδί.

ET ARCA DEI POSITA SIT IN MEDIO PELLI- VM) Propositum hoc Davidis, Deo templum magnificum struendi, quanquam eventu ipso caruit, non caruit mercede: ideo enim Deus promittit se ipsi domum ædificaturum infra 11. velut vicem rependens.

## 7:13
HE SHALL BUILD A HOUSE FOR MY NAME) Peace is more suitable for sacred things. 1 Chron. 22:8.

AND I WILL ESTABLISH THE THRONE OF HIS KINGDOM FOR EVER) עד־עולם among the Hebrews signifies time not infinite, but, according to the subject matter being discussed, a sufficiently long time. And so, in private possessions it extends to 50 years, in kingdoms longer. Now the kingdom in the posterity of David lasted for more than five hundred years through a series of more than twenty successors: which is rare enough.

I do not find in the Scriptures that to raise up seed from the womb is to place on the throne; and not even where it says to raise up seed? This is indeed most well known to be commonly understood of the procreation or conception of offspring, and when that phrase from thy womb is added, it is rendered so much the more manifest that the promise is given not concerning placement on the throne, but concerning the excitation of seed from the loins of David, or from his bowels, as Montanus interprets the Hebrew word. But as for that phrase from thy womb, why must it be rendered from thy wife? Why should it not be understood of David himself, as it sounds? Is a husband's wife his own womb, and where is it so indicated in the Holy Scriptures? For Grotius finds no similar passage. Or why should not room be left for Tertullian's explanation? Which, from a comparison with Psalm 131, investigates the virginity of the Mother of the Messiah in this phrase, book 3, chapter 20 against Marcion. And yet from this you ought the more to understand Christ, who was reckoned from David by carnal descent on account of the census of the virgin Mary. For concerning this promise it is sworn in the Psalm to David: From the fruit of thy belly I will set upon thy throne. Who is this belly? David's own? Certainly not. For David was not about to give birth. But neither his wife's. For he would not have said, from the fruit of thy belly, but rather from the fruit of thy wife's belly. By saying his own belly, therefore, it remains that he pointed to someone of his lineage, of whose belly the flesh of Christ would be the fruit, which blossomed from the womb of Mary. And therefore he also named only the fruit of the belly, as properly of the belly, as if of the belly alone, and not also of the man: And he referred the belly itself to David, to the prince of the lineage and father of the family. For because he could not attribute it to the man, he attributed the virgin's belly to the father. And so in Christ a new arrangement is found today: This was what the creator was promising then, calling those things religious and faithful of David, which were Christ's, because Christ is from David: indeed it will be his very flesh, religious and faithful of David, so holy in religion, and faithful from the resurrection. For Nathan the Prophet also, in the second book of Kings, makes a declaration to David: Thy seed, he says, which shall be from thy belly. If you explain this simply as Solomon, you will provoke my laughter, for it will seem that David gave birth to Solomon. Is Christ also signified here, the seed of David from that belly, who would be from David, that is, from Mary? But this gloss pleased Grotius, so that the divine oracle might not be understood of the Messiah, seeing that he cannot be considered the seed of Bathsheba, David's wife. For he twists the whole promise with the Jews to Solomon. Which, however, contains a most illustrious prophecy concerning the Messiah. (1.) Because it is a question here of seed being raised up from the womb, or loins, as Scripture speaks elsewhere, after the times of David. Therefore not of Solomon, who was not born after David had finished his fate, nor indeed was he placed on his throne after his fate, but while he was still living and commanding. Nor did he sit on the throne of David after him, but before his face and in his place, as is held in 1 Kings 1:30 et seqq. Nor (2.) was the throne of his kingdom established for Solomon for ever: But for the Messiah. Because the kingdom of Solomon cannot be said to have lasted for ever, as far as Solomon himself is concerned, and not even as regards his sons: because the kingdom of Israel was soon so torn apart in his son that not half the kingdom, nor a third part of it, nor even a fourth remained to him. Solomon left his son as king of a sixth part, says Grotius in the preface to the 3rd book of Kings. In the bipartite kingdom you will see all the Kings of Israel were evil, the Kings of Judah some evil, many mediocre enough; and as for the good ones, there were as many as could easily be inscribed upon a ring. Then indeed, that duration of עד עולם cannot be fixed upon the Davidic kingdom of posterity. For it is not so very rare a thing for the kingdom of some family to last for five hundred years, which was the period of many families: but here it is certain, and beyond doubt among all, that something altogether singular and excellent is promised. Furthermore, the matter here does not concern the whole posterity of David, but the monadic seed: not of seeds as of many, but of seed as of one, which the Apostle taught us to distinguish accurately in such oracles in Galatians 3:16. It concerns one person, as especially from the subjoined words is evident, HE shall build a house for my name. For these words designate an individual, not the whole family. To that person, therefore, the throne of the kingdom is promised to be established even unto eternity, and not indeed to the entire family. That pronoun הוּא used of the seed of David refers us not obscurely to that הוּא of the Proto-Evangelium in Gen. 3:15, concerning the seed of Eve promised there: so that we may now understand that which was restricted by this oracle to the family of David, which before, through the promises given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob concerning their very seed, had been restricted to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and through the Jacobite oracle in Gen. 49:10 to the tribe of Judah. And therefore the force of the words עַד־עוֹלָם even unto eternity remains intact, so that eternity properly so-called is designated, from the most proper meaning of the words, and not merely a long time; since not once, but again and again, the promise concerning the establishing of the kingdom is made in v. 12, 13, 16. & concerning the eternal duration of the same, let it be repeated three times v. 13 & 16, as also 1 Chron. 18, 12. 14, nay, let God protest that He does not wish to take His mercy away from him 2 Sam. 7, 15. Add that David himself sang concerning this kingdom and throne, that it ought to endure for all eternity Ps. 45, 7. Ps. 72, 7. 17. Ps. 89, 30. 37. and Isaiah testifies that his kingdom is truly eternal, and that there shall be no end to it chap. 9, 6. His empire shall be multiplied, and of peace there shall be no end: he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to strengthen it, and to establish it in judgment, and in justice from henceforth, and even forever. Which is also the explanation of the Angel Gabriel Luke 1, 32. The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the House of Jacob forever, and of his Kingdom there shall be no end. These interpretations of the oracle concerning the seed, or son of David, and his eternal Kingdom, being above all exception, ought certainly to have been preferred to Rabbinic inventions and dreams.

Furthermore (3), that this Son of David is said to be about to build a house for the name of the Lord is not to be understood of the material Solomonic temple, even though it was said on the occasion of the intended construction of the temple, but of the spiritual House, the Church of God, which is the house of the living God, 1 Tim. 3:15. Because the house to be built for the name of God had to endure no less eternally than the Kingdom of this seed, by whom it was to be built. For an eternal kingdom is promised to him, not because he was to build a house that would again be devastated and perish by fire, but because he was to build an eternal house for the name of the Lord. Which cannot be understood of any other than the Messiah. The words of 2 Sam. 7:16 must also be accurately compared here with 1 Chron. 17:14. What is said there: "Your house and your kingdom shall be faithful or firm forever before your face, and your throne shall be firm continually," is expressed here thus: "I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom, and his throne shall be most firm forever." Therefore, the house of the Lord and the kingdom of the Lord, and the house of David and his kingdom, are interchanged. The house of David is firm, and his seed shall be established in the house of the Lord; the kingdom of David is firm, and his seed shall be established in the kingdom of the Lord; they explain one another. It is not, therefore, a question of the Davidic house and family being established forever, but of the spiritual house and kingdom of David, which is the Church, the house of the Lord and His kingdom. In which house the Messiah reigns; therefore that house is most firm. Certainly, in a material house, the Solomonic temple, the seed of David was not to be established, nor was that house firm, nor was that the kingdom of the Lord itself.

That passage, which Grotius compares as a parallel in 1 Chron. 22:9, is not a parallel here: a fact which our blessed Luther long ago solidly demonstrated in Vol. 8 of the Jena German edition, fol. 69 et seqq., and acknowledges.

Cajetan and Sanctius. He treats of a clearly different apparition: in which God, because of much blood shed, did not grant David the building of His house, and promised the birth of a peaceful son, Solomon, who would enjoy peace and tranquility throughout his whole life, and would build a temple to the divine name: concerning which nothing at all is contained in this response of God made to David through Nathan. But the αὐτοψία teaches that far different things are handed down in this manifestation: in which God protests that He never requested the building of a house of cedar, and promises David that He wishes to build his house, and that his house will be firm, and his throne will endure forever. The former is a promise of grace, and made without condition concerning the Messiah, 2 Sam. 7. The latter is a legal promise, with the condition of Solomon’s integrity. For it is not of Solomon in the former, but of the seed of David to be raised up to him after his death, i.e. The Messiah is treated, and of his throne and everlasting kingdom.

(4) Although this has been abundantly shown thus far, it can be further confirmed by that most splendid promise: I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son. For this is so great that Paul teaches it was said to no mortal, nor indeed to any of the Angels: inasmuch as it expresses the Son of God as ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, Heb. 1, 6. Which the Apostle joined with that Davidic passage, Ps. 2, 7, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee, to demonstrate the eternal Deity of the Son of God, among the Hebrews themselves, inasmuch as among them that could not be denied, just as every disputation ought to proceed from conceded and common principles. What of the fact that David himself most clearly explained this promise concerning the Messiah in Psalm 89: concerning the eternal grace of God about to arise v. 3, concerning the (spiritual) eternal seed of David, and concerning his perpetual throne v. 5, concerning his hand being placed in the sea and his right hand in the rivers v. 25, concerning the same being exalted as the firstborn above all the kings of the earth v. 28, concerning an eternal seed being given to him, and concerning his throne being preserved as long as the days of heaven, as long as the Sun and Moon shall be, nay, unto eternity v. 30, 37, 38, concerning that ANOINTED ONE, without whom, if he were not, all men would have been created in vain, whose footsteps are a reproach to the enemies of the Church v. 48, 51, 52. Which cannot be explained otherwise than of the Messiah. For unless there were one Son of man who is the substance of Israel, says Augustine in book 17 of the City of God, chapter 11, through which Son of man many sons of men might be set free, all the sons of men would surely have been created in vain.

Nor must the response of David be passed over here, 2 Sam. 7, 20. 21. & 1 Chron. 17, 17. 18. which teaches not obscurely that the promise concerning the Messiah was made here. Because David esteems it so highly, that he judges all other things, and the fact that he himself was so greatly exalted from a humble house, to be held in little account, if they are compared with those things which God had spoken to him here concerning his House. (To which words Junius confesses that it is treated here of the seed, Christ, who was to come in the future, and that they cannot be referred solely to Solomon.) And he teaches that that promise looked למרחוק, into the far distance, or into the ages long after to come, being instructed by the Spirit of Christ searching into the times of the N. T., as Peter testifies in his 1st Epistle, ch. 1: and on that account he adds: this is the Law of the man, who is the Lord God: designating Christ the Θεάνθρωπον; whom he calls both the word of the Lord and the servant of the Lord, so that he may express both his divine and his human nature, as will be evident from what follows.

Furthermore (6) since it cannot be denied that in other oracles of Scripture reference is made to the promise of the Messiah made to David, Ps. 2, 7. Ps. 72, 7. seqq. Ps. 89, 50. Is. 9, 6. 7. Jer. 23, 5. ch. 33, 15. 16. Whence also Ps. 89, 50. the mercies of David are commemorated, (or to David promised) faithful & constant Is. 55, 3. (which passage treats openly of the Messiah, Conf. v. 1. 2. 4. 5. Acts 13, 34.) one must absolutely admit that the promise was made to him here! since no other oracle can be found which designates these places. To this contributes the fact that in Acts 2, 31 it is hinted that David, by virtue of this promise, prophesied openly concerning the resurrection of the Messiah in Ps. 16. Since he was a Prophet, therefore, and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that of the fruit of his loins he would sit upon his throne, (which if it was not done here, where at last was it done?) foreseeing, he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that he was neither left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption. Which is also the force and power of Paul's argument, concluding from the faithful holy things (promised to David) concerning the eternal kingdom of the Messiah, that the Messiah ought not to have remained in death, but to have risen again Acts 13, 34. But that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he said thus; Because I will give you the holy faithful things of David, Is. 55. 2. Sam. 7. promised. And therefore he also says elsewhere: You will not give your Holy One to see corruption.

We add to these finally (7) the suffrages and consent of the Interpreters. Among Christians Tertull. l. c. Lactantius book 4. c. 13. Augustine, Eucherius likewise, Rupert in this place, Lyranus, Burgensis, Abulensis, Angelomus, Catharinus, Sanctius, Cornelius a Lapide, Estius, and other Papists: Also from our own B. Luther, Hunnius, Gerhard, Cramer, Helvicus, Walther, Müller, Glassius, the Vinariean Theologians, and all the rest, finally even most of the Calvinists, Junius, Piscator, Pareus, the Authors of the Belgian Notes, &c. Then also of the ancient Hebrews, who also acknowledged that in this oracle the promise concerning the Messiah is exhibited, from all of whom Grotius separates himself here for the sake of some recent Jews, twisting the whole oracle to Solomon, nay even to his Successors. The Jews indeed confess that the promise was made to David concerning the Messiah. But if it was not made here to the same, what other place from Davidic History will they designate where it was made? Therefore the Lusitanian Rabbi in the Mittelburg colloquy confessed that the Messiah was promised to David here. Concerning the Jews, August. observes in book 17 de C. D. c. 8. that they also understand that the very son promised here was not Solomon. So that Grotius is more blind here than those Jews. It is pleasing only to transcribe the passage of Tertullian from book 3 against Marc. c. 20. who proves by various arguments that the discourse here is about Christ. The first from the womb of David was brought forward in its entirety on the occasion above. Now follow others, which he adds in the same place; Because also the house of God, he says, Christ would be more likely to build, to wit, a holy man, in whom the Spirit of God would inhabit as a more powerful temple, Christ should be held more as the son of God than Solomon the Son of David. Finally, both the Throne forever, and the kingdom forever, pertains more to Christ than to Solomon, a temporal King. But the mercy of God did not depart from Christ. But to Solomon, the anger of God also came after his luxury and Idolatry. For he raised up for him Satan, that is, an Idumean enemy. Since therefore none of these things pertain to Solomon, but to Christ, the reason for our interpretations will be certain, the very outcome of events also proving it, which it appears were predicted of Christ, and thus in this will be the holy and faithful things of David. God set this man as a testimony to the nations, not David as a Prince and ruler over the nations, not David, who ruled only over Israel. Today the Nations, who did not know him, call upon Christ, and peoples today flee to Christ, whom they previously ignored. It cannot be called future, which you see happening.

It must not indeed be concealed that some Interpreters explain the present passage also concerning Solomon, because as regards some predicates it ought to be taken concerning him according to the letter, but it seems otherwise to others, who with us interpret the whole passage concerning Christ, as far as the literal sense is concerned, such as the author of the Gloss, Angelomus, B. Luther, &c. Coccejus in the last of Moses §. 989. has this concerning this prophecy: There is promised to David a seed 1. all sinners partakers of the grace of God. 2. An heir of the kingdom according to the carnal mode, who might build the temple, and whose kingdom might last for all the time of the legal Pedagogy under the condition of observance. 3. A seed which might have in truth an eternal kingdom, and which might build a spiritual house for God, and always stand before God in his house, which is heaven, and be King in the kingdom of God. But the third explanation alone fits; the former two are alien, nor can a triple sense obtain in one and the same place at the same time. If the seed promised to David here is Christ, it cannot be Solomon, not all sinners partakers of the grace of God. If the house to be built is a spiritual house, it cannot be understood by it as a material temple. Furthermore, if you depart from the rebellious Jews of the Messiah, it will not be found easily who, with Grotius, accepts this oracle concerning Solomon alone, who here was entirely silent about the Messiah, and left him no place in the same. Most acknowledge that some predicates only must be explained of Christ by necessity; nor can they be understood otherwise according to the letter. Cornelius a Lapide, among the Papists, says it is a matter of faith that the passage is understood of Christ. Junius, not the least interpreter in the School of Calvin, concerning that, Your throne will be stable UNTIL THE AGE v. 16. says this; and all the consequences can properly pertain to none but Christ. So also the Belgian Interpreters, we ought to understand these things properly concerning the eternal spiritual kingdom of Christ. Others think that the whole passage can indeed be explained concerning Solomon in its own way, but since some things do not fully and entirely agree except with Christ, as the power of the oracle infers, some things are said concerning Solomon in himself, but some, as he was a Type of Christ, with Augustine book 17 de Civ. Dei c. 8. & 9. or they interpret concerning Solomon according to the literal sense, yet so that the Holy Spirit also intended a mystical sense, nay, especially here looked to Christ, of whom Solomon was a type. This so great a promise, says August., he who thinks it was completed in Solomon, errs much. For he attends to what was said: He shall build me a house: Since Solomon built that noble temple: and he does not attend to, his house shall be faithful forever before me. There was indeed some image of a future thing even in Solomon, in that he built the temple, and had peace according to his name, and was wonderfully praiseworthy in the beginnings of his reign; but that same person of his, which announced a future shadow, also himself exhibited Christ our Lord. Whence certain things are written about him, as if they were predicted about him, while Holy Scripture, prophesying also by deeds, in a certain way delineates in him a figure of things to come.

The principal things which are opposed to our opinion, that not everything here can be explained concerning the Messiah, seem to be these. First, that the divine response undoubtedly concerns the building of that temple, which was discussed in David's counsel. Which consequence, however, is to be conceded only in part. We confess that the response of God concerns the construction of a material temple, but κατ̓ ἄγσιν or ἄρνησιν. Shall you build me a House to dwell in? God brings forward the reasons for his negative response: both that he had not dwelt in a House since the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt, and that he had never requested this, or said: Why have you not built me a house of cedar? Nor indeed does God dwell in a material temple, which was acknowledged by Solomon himself, in the very inauguration of the temple 1 Kings 8, 27. Let Isaiah 66, 1 be compared. But as for the positive and affirmative answer, God in His promise inverts the proposal of David, in this Oracle indeed, not that David should build a house for Him, but vice versa, that He Himself would build a house for David: The Lord foretells to you (v. 11) that the Lord will make a house for you. But how?
