Siba Davidi cibos offert: Simei maledicit eidem, Absolom concubinas Patris violat.

## 16:3
Ver. 3. AND ZIBA ANSWERS THE KING: HE HAS REMAINED IN JERUSALEM, SAYING: TODAY THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL WILL RESTORE TO ME THE KINGDOM OF MY FATHER) A huge calumny: as appears below 19, 26. There are some calumnies so plausible that they can deceive even a most prudent King. Yet the memory of Jonathan alone, and the weakness of Mephibosheth, ought to have restrained David from believing anything rashly. An old saying, especially useful for Princes, νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν (be sober and remember to be skeptical). No less effective is the saying of Mardonius in Herodotus' Polymnia: 'For slander is a most terrible thing; in it there are two who do wrong, and one who is wronged: the slanderer does wrong, accusing one who is not present; the one who is wronged does wrong by being persuaded before he has learned the truth; and the one who is absent is wronged in this matter by the others, being slandered by the one and thought to be evil by the other.'

Latin:

Vers. 3. RESPONDETQVE SIBA REGI: REMANSIT IN JERUSALEM DICENS: HODIE RESTITUET MIHI DOMUS ISRAEL REGNVM PATRIS MEI) Ingens calumnia: ut apparet infra 19, 26. Sunt quædam ita speciosæ calumniæ, ut etiam prudentissimo Regi possint imponere. Attamen vel sola Jonathanis memoria, & debilitas Miphibosethi retinere Davidem debuerant, ne quid temere crederet. Vetus dictum, Principibus inprimis utile, νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. Nec minus efficax dictum Mardonii in Polymnia Herodoti: Διαβολή γάρ ἐσι δεινότατον' ἐν τῇ δύο μὲν εἰσι οἱ ἀδικέοντες, εἷς δὲ ὁ ἀδικεόμενος' ὁ μὲν γὰρ διαβάλλων ἀδικέει, ὐ παρεόντων κατηγορέων. ὁ δὲ ἀδικέει ἀναπειθόμενος πρὶν ἀτρεκέως ἐκμάθῃ' ὁ δὲ δὴ' ἀπεὼν τῶ λόγῳ τάδε ἐν αὐτοῖσι ἀδικέεται, διαβληθείς τε ὑπὸ τῶ ἑτέρε, καὶ νομισθεὶς πρὸς τῶ ἑτέρε κακὸς εἶναι.

## 16:4
Ver. 4. ALL THINGS THAT WERE MEPHIBOSHETH'S ARE THINE) Namely, by confiscation on account of the crime of high treason: meanwhile Kings, especially in war, give away things with eyes closed, as is in Seneca, De Beneficiis, book 4, 37. Thus informers, a race of men discovered for the public ruin, and never sufficiently restrained by punishments, were enticed by rewards. Tacitus, Annals 4.

Latin:

Vers. 4. TUA SINT OMNIA QUÆ FVERUNT MIPHIBOSETH) Nempe ex confiscatione ob crimen perduellionis: multa interim Reges, in bello præsertim, opertis oculis donant, ut apud Senecam est de Beneficio libro 4, 37. Sic delatores, genus hominum publico exitio repertum, & pœnis quidem nunquam satis coercitum, per præmia eliciebantur. Tacitus Annal. 4.

## 16:5
Ver. 5. SHIMEI THE SON OF GERA) An impudent man, and one who would have easily surpassed the Cynics in cursing.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SEMEL FILIUS GFRA) Homo impudens, & qui Cynicos maledicentia facile vicisset.

## 16:10
Ver. 10. FOR THE LORD HATH COMMANDED HIM TO CURSE DAVID: AND WHO IS HE THAT SHALL DARE SAY WHY HATH HE DONE SO) The 'ki' which is here in the Hebrew is better translated by 'if', as also in other places, so that the sense may be: if by chance he has a command from God to punish me with curses, who will have the right to prevent it? David, touched by the consciousness of true crimes, if the matter is with God, knows he has deserved great reproaches. But Shimei, since he had no command from God, sinned most gravely here against the law of Exod. 22, 28, so that he could be put to death on that account: below 19, 20. 21. 1 Kings 2, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DOMINUS ENIM PRÆCEPIT EI UT MALEDICAT DAVID: ET QVIS EST QVI AUDEAT DICERE QVARE SIC FECERIT) Melius כי quod hic in Hebræo est per si vertitur, ut & aliis in locis, ut sensus sit: si forte præceptum a Deo habet me maledictis puniendi, quis jus habebit ut id impediat? David verorum criminum conscientia tactus, si cum Deo res sit, scit magna probra se meritum. Semei autem cum nullum haberet a Deo præceptum, gravissime hic peccavit contra legem Exod. 22, 28. ita ut morte affici eo nomine posset: infra 19,20.21. 1. Reg. 2, 9.

## 16:12
Ver. 12. IF PERCHANCE THE LORD WILL LOOK UPON MY AFFLICTION) He reads 'be'onii', as also the LXX. Other books have 'be'einii', that is, upon my eye. But the Hebrews note that it was once 'be'ono', so that it is said, If perchance the Lord will look upon his eye, that is, return to himself. This was changed because it seemed to sound harsher.

IF Shimei sinned most gravely against the divine law, as Grotius acknowledges, David could not posit this hypothetical: IF PERCHANCE THE LORD COMMANDED HIM. For what is a sin by its own nature, GOD cannot command or order: inasmuch as He does not will iniquity, nor can He deny Himself, or be contrary to Himself. Wherefore that 'commanded' must be understood of permission; or of an occasion divinely permitted, which Shimei seized, so that he might overwhelm David with curses and injuries; and because Satan, after obtaining power from GOD, chose that occasion and inspired Shimei with the insolence to curse David, God is said to have commanded: just as GOD is said to have taken away from Job what Satan, after obtaining power from God, had taken away through the Sabeans and Chaldeans instigated by him. Furthermore, when God saw that malice and perverse lust in Shimei, He directed the same to the punishment of David; which David acknowledges with a humble spirit, not excusing the guilt of Shimei (which he wanted to be avenged), much less imputing it to GOD: But accepting the direction of the malice for his own chastisement, not undeserved in more than one way, with penitent and humble submission: concerning which Chrysostom on Ps. 38, 2: 'When Shimei assailed me with curses, I recalled to memory the sin I had committed, considering that on account of it I am attacked with curses, and punished, and expelled from the kingdom, and forced by flight to consult for my safety': i.e., I acknowledge that this man, obsessed by Satan, is sent by God to curse me. For although I have not committed those crimes which he charges against me: yet I confess that I have deserved such things, and even more atrocious reproaches, for my great and many sins: therefore I accept them as a punishment for sin, imposed and proceeding from God, as Osiander rightly paraphrases with Brentius. Thus the word 'commanded' is taken for an ordination, whether by ordering or by permitting it to happen, Matt. 19, 7. 1 Sam. 13, 14. 1 Kings 17, 4. Whence Ambrose, Apol. Dav. c. 6: 'He does not accuse the Lord as if He were the author of the injury, but rather praises Him, because He suffers us to endure lesser things, and we obtain pardon for greater sins'; and Augustine, De grat. et liber. arbitr. cap. 20: 'God inclined the will of Shimei, EVIL BY HIS OWN VICE, into this sin of cursing David: i.e., He directed it, so that it would not exert itself against another. God said to Shimei to curse David, that is, He sent, or let go, his evil heart.'

Latin:

Vers. 12. SI FORTE RESPICIAT DOMINVS AFFLICTIONEM MEAM) Legit בעוני, ut & LXX. Libri alii habent בעיני, id est, in oculum meum. Sed notant Hebræi fuisse olim בעונו, ut dicatur, Si forte respiciat Dominus in oculum suum, id est, ad se redeat. Mutatum hoc, quia videbatur sonare durius.

SI gravissimè peccavit Simei contra legem divinam, ut agnoscit Grotius, non potuit David hanc hypotheticam ponere: SI FORTE PRÆCEPIT id EI DOMINUS. Nam quod natura sua peccatum est, DEUS præcipere, aut jubere non potest: utpote qui iniquitatem non vult, nec semetipsum abnegare, aut sibi ipsi contrarius esse potest. Quapropter illud præcepit de permissione intelligendum; vel de occasione divinitus permissa, quam arripuit Simei, ut maledictis & injuriis Davidem obrueret; & quia Satan post impetratam à DEO potestatem elegit istam occasionem, & inspiravit Simei petulantiam maledicendi Davidi, Deus præcepisse dicitur: sicut abstulisse dicitur DEUS Jobo, quæ post impetratam à Deo potestatem Satanas per instigatos à se Sabæos, & Chaldæos abstulerat. Porro quum malitiam ac libidinem istam perversam Deus viderit in Simei, direxit eandem in pœnam Davidis; quod humili animo agnoscit David, non culpam Simei excusans, (quam vindicatam volebat) nedum DEO imputans: Sed directionem malitiæ ad sui castigationem, non uno modo promeritam, pœnitenti & humili submissio ne acceptans: de quo Chrysost. in Ps. 38, 2. Cum maledictis me incesseret Simei, peccatum à me commissum revocavi in memoriam, considerans, quod propter ipsum maledictis appetor, & punior, & regia expulsus, fuga cogor meæ saluti consulere: q. d. agnosco hunc hominem à Satana obsessum immitti i me divinitus, ut mihi maledicat. Etsi enim ea scelera, quæ mihi impingit, non admisi: tamen fateor me peccatis meis magnis & multis talia, & atrociora etiam convitia meritum: itaque ea suspicio tan- quam pœnam peccati, impositam & profectam à Deo, ut recte παραφράζει cum Brentio Osiander. Ita verbum præcepit accipitur pro ordinatione sive jubendo, sive permittendo ea fiat, Matth. 19, 7. 1. Sam. 13, 14. 1. Reg. 17, 4. Unde Ambrosius Apol. Dav. c. 6. Non accusat Dominum quasi auctorem injuriæ, sed magis laudat, quod patiatur nos minora perpeti, & majorum veniam peccatorum adipiscamur; & Augustinus de grat. & liber. arbitr. cap. 20. Deus voluntatem Simei VITIO SUO MALAM in hoc peccatum maledicendi Davidi inclinavit: h. e. direxit, ne in alium se exereret. Dixit Deus Simei, ut malediceret Davidi, id est, cor ejus malum misit, vel dimisit.

## 16:18
Ver. 18. FOR I WILL BE HIS WHOM THE LORD HATH CHOSEN) Hushai, in order to find faith for himself with Absalom, frees himself from suspicion regarding David in two ways: first, that the voice of the people is the voice of God, and therefore Absalom reigns by right: then, because, even if this were not so, he would not sin against the King, who instructs the King's son with good counsels.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QVIA ILLIVS ERO QVEM ELEGIT DOMINVS) Husai ut fidem sibi inveniat apud Absalomum liberat se a suspicione in Davidem duobus modis: primo quod vox populi sit vox Dei, & ideo jure regnet Absalomus: deinde quia, etiamsi hoc non esset, nihil peccet in Regem, qui filium Regis bonis consiliis instruat.

## 16:20
Ver. 20. GO IN TO THE CONCUBINES OF THY FATHER) A crafty man knows that those who follow Princes of royal blood in a faction fear nothing more than that those Princes might be reconciled with the King, and thus the King, having regained control of the kingdom, might seek opportunities to avenge himself. And so those who are in such a party are accustomed to act in such a way that matters are brought to a breaking point, and admit of no healing. But he who violates his father's bed is clearly believed to leave himself no retreat to his favor. Thus Artabanes the Persarmenian killed many Persians, so that by crossing over to the Romans he might find faith with them, as Procopius narrates, Goth. 4. But how great is the grief to a father from a concubine violated by his son can be understood from Jacob's animadversion on Reuben: and no less from this narration of Phoenix concerning his own sin in the Iliad 9: 'Just as when I first left Hellas, the land of fair women, fleeing the quarrels of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus.' Who was angry with me on account of the fair-haired concubine, whom he himself loved, but dishonored my mother, his wife; and she was always beseeching me by my knees to have intercourse with the concubine, so that she might hate the old man. I obeyed her and did it; but my father, immediately suspecting, cursed me much and called upon the hateful Erinyes.

Latin:

Vers. 20. INGREDERE AD CONCVBINAS PATRIS TVI) Homo vafer scit nihil magis timere eos, qui Principes sanguinis Regii in factione sequuntur, quam ne ii Principes reconcilientur cum Rege, & sic Rex compos iterum regni factus, occasiones semet vindicandi quærat. Itaque solent hoc agere, qui in tali parte sunt, ut res perducantur ad abrupta, nullamque sanationem recipientia. Thorum autem patris qui violat, is plane creditur nullum sibi receptum ad gratiam ejus relinquere. Sic Artabanes Persarmenius multos Persarum occidit, ut ad Romanos transiens fidem apud eos inveniret, ut narrat Procopius Gotth. 4. Quantus autem sit dolor patri ex stuprata per filium concubina, ex Jacobi animadversione in Rubenem intelligi potest: nec minus ex Phœnicis hac de suo peccato narratione Idiados I. Οἶον ὅτε πρῶτον λίπον Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα, Φεύγων νείκεα πατρὸς Ἀμύντορος Ὀρμενίδαο. Ὄς μοι παλλακίδος πέρι χώσατο καλλικόμοιο, Τὴν αὐτὸς φιλέεσκεν, ἀτιμάζεσκε δ᾽ ἄκοιτιν Μητέρ᾽ ἐμήνἡ δ᾽ αἰὲν ἐμὲ λισσέσκετο γούνων Παλλακίδι προμιγῆναι, ἵν᾽ ἐχθήρειε γέροντα. Τῇ πιθόμην καὶ ἔρεξα• πατὴρ δ᾽ ἐμὸς αὐτίκ᾽ ὀϊσθεὶς Πολλὰ κατηρᾶτο συγερὰς δ᾽ ἐπεκέκλετ᾽ Ἐριννῦς.

## 16:23
Verse 23. BUT THE COUNSEL OF ACHITOPHEL WHICH HE GAVE IN THOSE DAYS WAS AS IF ONE SHOULD CONSULT GOD) It could be said to Achitophel what Hecuba says to Ulysses in Euripides: 'Your reputation, even if you speak badly, will persuade. For a speech coming from the disreputable and from those of high standing does not have the same power,' which Ennius translates thus: 'Even if you say these things perversely, you will easily sway the Achaeans: For when the wealthy speak, just as the ignoble, the same words and the same speech do not have equal value.'

Latin:

Vers. 23. CONSILIVM AVTEM ACHITOPHEL QVOD DABAT IN DIEBVS ILLIS QVASI SI QVIS CONSVLERET DEVM) Poterat dici Achitopheli quod Vlyssi dicit Hecuba apud Euripidem: Τὸ δ᾽ ἀξίωμα κἂν κακῶς λέγῃ τὸ σὸν, Πείσει. λόγος γὰρ ἔκ τ᾽ ἀδοξόντων ἰὼν Κἀκ τῶν δοκόντων αὐτὸς ἐ ταυτὸν σθένει, quæ Ennius ita vertit: Hæc etsi tu perverse dices, facile Achivos flexeris: Nam quum opulenti loquuntur pariter atque ignobiles, Eadem dicta eademque oratio æqua non æque valet.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII.

Achitophel, when his counsel was disregarded, ended his life by hanging.

Verse 1. AND ARISING I WILL PURSUE DAVID THIS NIGHT) Frequently in all wars, but especially in civil ones, that deliberation occurs, whether it is better to hasten or to prolong the war and await greater forces: such was the excellent consultation among the Othonian leaders in Tacitus, Histories 2. But at this time of which we are now speaking, the day was undoubtedly for the legitimate king. First, the flight from the city had brought great fear upon those pursuing him, while which was fresh he could easily have been crushed: then that which the same Tacitus has in Histories 1 had a place here: 'it would give space for the repentance of the wicked, for the consensus of the good: crimes gain strength by impulse, good counsels by delay.' Livy says that there will never be lacking those who wish to seek favor for the better side for the public good.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII.

Achitophel, cum consilium suum posthaberetur, suspendio vitam finivit.

Vers. 1. ET CONSVRGENS PERSFQVAR DAVID HAC NOCTE) Frequenter in bellis omnibus, maxime vero in civilibus, incidit illa deliberatio, festinare rectius sit, an bellum ducere & majores copias opperiri: qualis consultatio egregia inter Othonianos duces Taciti Histor. 2. At in hoc tempore de quo nunc agimus, haud dubie dies pro legitimo rege erat. Primum fuga ex urbe magnum pavorem in sectantes ipsum intulerat, quo recente facile opprimi ille potuit: deinde locum hîc habebat illud quod idem ille Tacitus habet Histor. 1. daret malorum pœnitentiæ, daret bonorum consensui spatium: scelera impetu, bona consilia mora valescere. Livius nunquam defuturos ait, qui gratiam melioris partis bono publico velint quæsitam.

## 17:3
Verse 3. FOR YOU SEEK ONE MAN) Civil war is often settled by the blood of one man, as in the case of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius. With Piso killed, Otho's mind was relieved of all anxiety. But this especially has a place where the next in succession to the kingdom does not allow the kingdom to be held by the old age of the father. For such a person is absolved by the very crime for which he ought to be condemned.

Success makes certain crimes honorable. It once seemed a wonderful thing that King Antigonus allowed his son Demetrius to approach him with a weapon: For just as geometers, as Plutarch says in that history, have certain postulates, so it is a postulate of Kings that for the sake of their own security it is permitted for them to kill anyone: but the King of Kings laughs at the impious thoughts of men.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VNUM ENIM VIRVM TU QVÆRIS) Bellum civile sæpe unius hominis sanguine transigitur, ut in Galba, Othone, Vitellio. Pisone occiso, levata Othoni omni solicitudine mens. Præcipue vero id locum habet ubi proximus ad regni successionem regnum senecta patris detineri non patitur. Talis enim ipso crimine, unde damnandus estet absolvitur.

Honesta quædam scelera successus facit. Mira olim res visa, quod Rex Antigonus filium Demetrium cum telo ad se passus esset accedere: Nam sicut geometræ, ut ait in ea historia Plutarchus, αἰτήματα quædam habent, sic Regum αἴτημα est, ut suæ securitatis causa quemvis sibi liceat occidere: sed ridet impia hominum cogitata Rex Regum.

## 17:8
Vers. 8. AS IF A BEAR WHOSE CUBS HAVE BEEN STOLEN RAGES IN THE WOODS) Poets often describe anger with the simile of a lioness or tigress raging because of stolen cubs. Nor would you more safely provoke the smoking nose of a living bear.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VELVT SI VRSA RAPTIS CATVLIS IN SAL- TV SÆVIAT) Sæpe poetæ iram describunt similitudine leæ- næ aut tigridis furentis ob raptos catulos. Nec magis tuto Fumantem vivi nasum tentaveris ursi.

## 17:9
Vers. 9. PERHAPS NOW HE LIES HIDDEN IN PITS) For David was, like Lysander, diversifying his wars for the most part with ἀπάταις (deceptions).

AND WHEN ANY ONE SHALL FALL IN THE BEGINNING, WHOSOEVER HEARETH IT SHALL HEAR AND SHALL SAY: A SLAUGHTER HATH HAPPENED AMONG THE PEOPLE THAT FOLLOWED ABSALOM) He meant what Tacitus said in Hist. 2: that as the beginnings of the war proceeded, the reputation would extend to the rest.

LET ALL ISRAEL BE GATHERED UNTO THEE) Thus they said to Otho: Let him prolong the war; in a few days the fourteenth legion, itself of great reputation, would be there with the Moesian forces; if a battle were decided upon, they would fight with increased strength.

Latin:

Vers. 9. FORSITAN NVNC LATET IN FOVEIS) Erat enim David, ut Lysander, ἀπάταις τὰ πολλὰ διαποικίλ- λων τά πολέμε.

ET CUM CECIDERIT UNUS QVILIBET IN PRINCIPIO, AUDIET QVICUNQVE AUDIERIT ET DICET: FACTA EST PLAGA IN POPULO QVI SEQVEBATVR ABSALOM) Hoc volebat quod Tacitus dixit Hist. 2. uti initia belli provesissent, famam in cætera fore.

CONGREGETUR AD TE UNIVERSUS ISRAEL) Sic illi apud Othonem: Duceret bellum: paucis diebus quar- tam decimam legionem magna ipsam fama, cum Masiacis co- piis affore: si prælium placuisset, auctis viribus certaturos.

## 17:12
Vers. 12. WE SHALL COVER HIM AS DEW IS WONT TO FALL UPON THE EARTH) Thus Claudius Marcellus in his declamation for the three hundred at Thermopylae: They will not conquer us, but overwhelm us. Seneca, De Benef. 6, 31, concerning those who flattered Xerxes: One said that the messenger of war would not be endured, and that they would turn their backs at the first rumor of his arrival; another said there was no doubt that by that evil Greece would not only be conquered, but overwhelmed.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OPERIEMUS EUM SICVT CADERE SO- LET ROS SUPER TERRAM) Sic Claudius Marcellus in declamatione pro trecentis ad Thermopylas: Non vincent nos sed obruent. Seneca de Benef. 6, 31. de his qui Xerxi adu- labantur: Alius ajebat non laturos nuntium belli, & ad pri- mum adventus famam terga versuros: alius nihil esse dubii quin illo malo non vinci solum Græcia, sed obrui posset.

## 17:13
Vers. 13. ALL ISRAEL SHALL SURROUND THAT CITY WITH ROPES) The bonds and tackle of siege engines, Tacitus, Histor. 3.

WE SHALL DRAG THEM INTO THE TORRENT) We shall carry all the remains of the ruins or ashes into the river with the easy labor of so many hands, so that they may be carried into the sea, never to be seen again.

Latin:

Vers. 13. CIRCUMDABIT OMNIS ISRAEL CIVI- TATI ISTI FUNES) Vincula ac libramenta tormentorum Tacitus Histor. 3.

TRAHEMVS EAS IN TORRENTEM) Omnes rui- næ reliquias aut cineres in amnem deportabimus tot ma- nuum facili labore, ut ita in mare ferantur nunquam con- spiciendæ amplius.

## 17:14
Vers. 14. BUT BY THE WILL OF THE LORD THE USEFUL COUNSEL OF ACHITOPHEL WAS DISSIPATED) Ammianus, book 14, well says: When the fates cast their hand, the senses of men are dulled and blunted. Thus Homer: Τῷ δὲ φρένας ἐξέλετο ζεύς (And Zeus took away his wits).

Latin:

Vers. 14. DOMINI AUTEM NUTU DISSIPATUM EST CONSILIVM ACHITOPHEL VTILE) Bene Am- mianus libro 14. Manum injicientibus fatis, hebetari sensus hominum & obtundi. Sic Homerus: Τῷ δὲ φρένας ἐξέλετο ζεύς.

## 17:16
Vers. 16. SEND QUICKLY AND TELL DAVID) David's stratagem, which we had above at 15, 35-36, succeeded well.

Latin:

Vers. 16. MITTITE CITO ET NVNTIATE DA- VID) Bene successit Davidi commentum suum, quod habui- mus supra 15, 35. 36.

## 17:19
Vers. 19. PTISANAS (BARLEY-GROATS)) הרפות, which word the LXX left here as obscure.

Latin:

Vers. 19. PTISANAS) הרפות, quam vocem ut ob- scuram LXX. hîc reliquerunt.

## 17:20
Vers. 20. THEY PASSED HASTILY HAVING TASTED A LITTLE WATER) The Interpreter here read מאכל. But the Greeks read מיכל. For what we now have in the Hebrew as מיכל for a brook appears nowhere else.

It is falsely imagined that he read otherwise, whether the Latin or the Greek Interpreters, than what is now held in the Hebrew, because they everywhere explain it as water. But that the Hebrew תון מיכל signifies a brook no less than תון מיכל is known from the Chapters of Concordances of R. Mordechai Nathan. For it is observed there regarding both words that this name signifies the same as פלגי, a brook of waters. And how could the Latin have read מאכל, when this signifies not a brook or water, but food? The good Grotius seems to have been dozing when he wrote these things, or at least he was drunk with too great a zeal for criticizing the Hebrew sources.

Latin:

Vers. 20. TRANSIERVNT FESTINANTER GV- STATA PAVLVLVM AQVA) Legit hic Interpres מאכל At Græci מיכל. Nam quod nunc in Hebræo ha- bemus מיכל pro rivo nusquam alibi comparet.

Frustra fingitur secus legisse, sive Latinum, sive Græcos Interpretes, quam nunc habetur in Ebræo, quia ubique exponunt de aqua. At Ebræum תון מיכל non minus significare rivum, quam תון מיכל è R. Mar- dochai Nathan Capitulis concordantiar. notum est. Idem enim significare hoc nomen, quod פלגי rivus aquarum, ibi observatum de utraque voce. Et quo- modo legisset Latinus מאכל, quùm hoc non rivum aut aquam, sed escam significet? Dormitasse vide- tur bonus Grotius cum hæc scriberet, aut certe ni- mio Ebræos fontes carpendi studio ebrius fuit.

## 17:21
Vers. 21. CROSS THE STREAM QUICKLY) It is useful for the weaker party to interpose a river between themselves and the enemy.

Latin:

Vers. 21. TRANSITE CITO ELVVIVM) Infirmiori- bus utile est amnem inter se & hostes interponere.

## 17:23
Vers. 23. HE DIED BY HANGING) The word חנק, which signifies hanging, also signifies indignation: and the Arabs use it in this way. Regarding the Greek word ἀπήγξατο, see what we have said at Matthew 27:5.

Latin:

Vers. 23. SVSPENDIO INTERIIT) Vox חנק quæ suspendium, eadem & indignationem significat: & sic Arabes usurpant. De voce Græca ἀπήγξατο vide quæ diximus Matth. 27, 5.

## 17:24
Vers. 24. HE CAME INTO THE CAMP) The Greeks think it is the name of a place, Manaim.

Latin:

Vers. 24. VENIT IN CASTRA) Græci putant nomen esse loci Mavαήν.

## 17:25
Vers. 25. JETHRO THE ISRAELITE) With one letter changed, it seems that ישמעלי was once placed here, as in the Hebrew, Greek, and other interpreters. 2 Par. 2:17.

Sanctius indeed uses that divination: but he soon corrects that conjecture; and thus he believes that he had two names, and was in reality an Ishmaelite by birth, and an Israelite by religion, which is the opinion of Vatablus, Cornelius, Junius, and the Belgian interpreters. Namely, that he was a proselyte who, when he married an Israelite wife, changed his name: or that he was called an Israelite not by name, but by surname, because he had at some time stayed among the Ishmaelites: just as those 600 men, the bodyguards of David, in chapter 15:18, were called Gittites because they had been for some time in Gath, which is the explanation of Rabbi Solomon, R. Kimchi, Marinus, Tirinus, the Vinarienses, Luther, and others. And it is certainly better to subscribe to these than to suspect a corruption of the Sacred text, for which there is no necessity here by the total consensus of the codices, namely, of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Greeks, and Latins. Another explanation is still found among the Hebrews, as reported by St. Jerome, that Jether is called an Ishmaelite because his son Amasa, imitating the deeds of Ishmael, did not accompany David as he was fleeing. Which, however, Cornelius rightly considers only as symbolic fictions. But Grotius, who otherwise gladly rabbinizes, strove especially to teach that the Hebrew codices are corrupt, and therefore he alone wished to be wise here.

Vers. same. TO ABIGAIL THE DAUGHTER OF NAAS) A different person from her who is mentioned in 1 Par. 2:16.

Latin:

Vers. 25. JETHRO DE JESRAELI) Vna litera mutata videtur hic olim fuisse positum ישמעלי, ut in Hebræo, Græco & aliis Interpp. Par. 2, 17.

Utitur quidem illa divinatione etiam Sanctius: Sed corrigit tamen mox istam conjecturam: adeo- que credit ipsum habuisse duo nomina, & revera fuisse Ismaelitam genere, & Israelitam religione, quæ Vatabli, Cornelii, Junii est sententia, & Belgicorum Interpretum. Fuisse scil. proselytum, qui cum uxorem duxit Israeliticam, mutavit nomen: vel Israelitam appellatum fuisse non nomine, sed cognomento, quia aliquando inter Ismaelitas commoratus est: uti 600. illi viri parastatæ Davidis cap. 15, 18. Gethæi appel- lati sunt, quia aliquandiu fuerunt in Geth, quæ & Rabbi Salomonis, R. Kimchi, Marini, Tirini, Vina- riensium, Lutheri & aliorum est explicatio. Ac præ- stat utique his subscribere, quam corruptelam tex- tus Sacri suspicari, cujus hic nulla in Codd. summa consensu est necessitas, Hebræorum nempe, Chaldæorum, Græcorum & Latinorum. Alia adhuc reperitur apud Ebræos, referente S. Hieronymo explicatio, Jether dici Ismaelitam, eo quod ejus Filius Amasi opera Ismaelis imitatus Davidem fugientem comitatus non est. Quæ tamen recte pro Symbolicis figmentis tantum habet Cornelius. Grotius vero qui alias lubenter Rabbinizat, id maxime egit, ut Ebræos Codices corruptos esse doceat, ideoque solus hic sapere voluit.

Vers. eod. AD ABIGAIL FILIAM NAAS) Aliam ab illa cujus mentio 1. Par. 2,16.

## 17:29
Vers. 29. THEY OFFERED HIM BEDDING AND TAPESTRIES AND EARTHEN VESSELS, WHEAT AND BARLEY) Many things come under the name of a benefit because of the time in which they are given. How much do you value hospitality in the wilderness, shelter in the rain, a bath or fire in the cold? says Seneca in De Beneficiis 6:15. Darius to Syloson in Herodotus' Thalia: 'O most noble of men, you are the one who gave me a gift when I had no power, even if it was small, yet the thanks for it is equal, just as if I were to receive something great from you now.' This Barzillai was generous to David and his soldiers according to his means, just as Pythius was to Xerxes and his soldiers. But Barzillai found a more grateful guest: it profited Barzillai to have given his son to David; it harmed Pythius not to have given his. See below 19:38.

Latin:

Vers. 29. OBTULERUNT EI STRATORIA ET TAPETIA ET VASA FICTILIA, FRUMENTUM ET HORDEUM) Multa in beneficii nomen veniunt ob tempus quo dantur. Quanti æstimas in solitudine hospitium, in imbre tectum, in frigore balneum aut ignem? ait Seneca de Beneficiis 6, 15. Darius Sylofonti in Thalia Herodoti; ὦ γενναιότατ' ἀνδρῶν, σὺ κείνῶ- εἶ ὅς ἐδεμίαν ἔχοντί μοι δύναμιν ἔδωκας εἰ καὶ σμικρὰ, ἀλλ' ὦν ἴση γε ἡ χάρις ὁμοίως, ὡς εἰ νῦν κόθεν τι μέγα λάβοιμι. Fuit hic Berzillajus pro sua copia liberalis in Davidem & ejus milites, ut Pythius in Xerxem & milites ejus. Sed Barzillajus gratiorem invenit hospitem : Barzillajo profuit filium dedisse Davidi, Pythio nocuit non dedisse. Vide infra 19, 38.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII. Absalom is defeated in battle and pierced through, whom David mourns bitterly.

Vers. 1. THEREFORE DAVID HAVING REVIEWED HIS PEOPLE) So also the Greeks: 'And David reviewed the people who were with him.' These respond perfectly to the Hebrew יפקד, that is, when he saw that his forces were not inferior to the enemy's.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII. Absolom prœlio victus, & transfossus, quem deflet amare David.

Vers. 1. IGITUR CONSIDERATO DAVID POPULO SUO) Sic & Græci : καὶ ἐπεσκέψατο Δαβὶδ τὸν λαὸν τὸν μετ' αὐτῶ. Respondent hæc optime Hebræo יפקד, id est, cum videret copias suas non minores hostilibus.

## 18:3
Vers. 3. YOU SHALL NOT GO OUT) Thus it was fixed for Tiberius neither to expose himself nor the Republic to risk, Tacitus, Annals 1. Yet there is need here for a distinction, which the same writer dictates to us in the words of Mucianus at the end of Histories 4. If the state of the empire or the safety of Gaul were in jeopardy, Caesar ought to have stood in the battle line: the Caninefates and Batavians should have been delegated to lesser commanders. Therefore, in Histories 2, when he had narrated that it was debated whether it was in the interest of the battle for the Emperor Otho to be present, or if it would be better for him to be set aside, and he was finally persuaded to withdraw to Brixellum, and, removed from the uncertainties of battles, to reserve himself for the highest matters of the empire, he adds: 'That first day afflicted the Othonian party.' It matters so much at what time or place anything is done. David had provisions, cities, and strategies for drawing out the war.

YOU ALONE ARE COUNTED FOR TEN THOUSAND) It is very rare, and not granted except by reason of discipline, to place more reliance in a leader than in an army, says Tacitus, where he praises the Chatti. Virgil on bees: 'With the king safe, all have one mind; when he is lost, they have broken their faith.'

Latin:

Vers. 3. NON EXIBIS) Sic Tiberio fixum neque se neque Rempublicam in casum dare, Taciti Annal. 1. Distinctione tamen hic opus, quam idem scriptor nobis dictat Muciani verbis fine Histor. 4. Si status imperii aut salus Galliarum in discrimen verteretur, debuisse Cæsarem in acie stare : Caninefates Batavosque minoribus ducibus delegandos. Ideo Hist. 2. cum narrasset, dubitatum interesse pugnæ Imperatorem Othonem, an seponi melius foret, perpulsumque tandem ut Brixellum concederet, ac dubiis præliorum exemtus, summæ rerum & imperii seipsum reservaret, addit : Is primus dies Othonianas partes afflixit. Tantum refert, quo tempore aut loco quidque fiat. Davidi erant commeatus, urbes & trahendi artes.

TU UNUS PRO DECEM MILLIBUS COMPVTARIS) Rarissimum nec nisi ratione disciplinæ concessum plus reponere in duce, quam in exercitu, ait Tacitus, ubi Cattos laudat. Virgilius de Apibus: - - rege incolumi mens omnibus una, Amisso rupere fidem.

## 18:4
Ver. 4. WHAT SEEMS RIGHT TO YOU I WILL DO] Thus Claudius said that he alone was unequal to the citizens and their consensus, Tacitus, Annals 12. But especially in civil wars more is permitted to soldiers than to leaders, as it is in Histories 2.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVOD VOBIS VIDETVR RECTVM HOC FACIAM] Sic Claudius unum se civium & consensui imparem dicebat, Annalium Taciti 12. Præcipue vero civilibus bellis plus militibus quam ducibus licet, ut est Hist. 2.

## 18:5
Ver. 5. SAVE FOR ME THE BOY ABSALOM) Too indulgently, and with public ruin. And yet for the ancient Romans not only the safety of the people, but also the discipline of the camps was more ancient than the affection for children, L. Postliminium §. Filius. D. de captivis. Cicero, in the first book of De Finibus, dealing with Manlius Torquatus, says that he preferred the right of majesty and command to nature itself and to paternal love.

Absalom could have been saved, and the account of public safety maintained. And David was bound to be solicitous about Absalom for the sake of his eternal salvation: whom he wished to be recalled to repentance: and for that end he desired him to be saved: which is also the reason why he wept for him so bitterly, namely, that he himself had suffered the loss of eternal salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SERVATE MIHI PVERVM ABSALOM) Nimis indulgenter, & cum publica pernicie. Atqui Romanis antiquis non populi tantum salus, sed & disciplina castrorum antiquior fuit, quam caritas liberorum L. Postliminium §. Filius. D. de captivis. Cicero de finibus primo de Manlio Torquato agens, ait eum ipsi naturæ patrioque amori prætulisse jus majestatis atque imperii.

Poterat & Absalom servari, & salutis publicæ ratio haberi. Et tenebatur David solicitus esse de Absolomo ob æternam ejus salutem : quem ad pœnitentiam revocatum optabat : eaque fini servari cupiebat : quæ etiam causa est, quod tam acerbe ipsum defleverit, quod nempe ipse jacturam æternæ salutis fecerit.

## 18:7
Ver. 7. IN THE FOREST OF EPHRAIM) Where the Ephraimites were once slain, Judges 7.

Latin:

Vers. 7. IN SALTV EPHRAIM) Vbi cæsi olim Ephraimitæ Jud. 7.

## 18:8
Ver. 8. THERE WERE MANY MORE WHOM THE FOREST HAD CONSUMED OF THE PEOPLE) Who were killed in hiding places like cattle.

THAN THOSE WHOM THE SWORD HAD DEVOURED) That is, the battle line.

Latin:

Vers. 8. MVLTO PLVRES ERANT QVOS SALTVSC ONSVMSERAT DE POPVLO) Qui in latebris interfecti sunt pecorum ritu.

QVAM HI QVOS VORAVERAT GLADIVS) Id est, acies.

## 18:13
Ver. 13. AND THE STRIKERS KILLED HIM] As often as the future heir to the kingdom takes up arms against the King, it is in the interest of all good men that he perish, lest they pay for as a crime what they did out of duty, because No hand in war is clean when the judge is changed.

Joab, however, looked not to what David had commanded, but to what he ought to have commanded, and thought there was less danger in this agreement than if he had been forced to suffer Absalom as King at some point.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET PERCVTIENTES INTERFECERVNT EVM] Quoties hæres futurus regni in Regem arma sumit, illum interire bonorum omnium interest, ne quod ex officio fecerunt, luant pro crimine, quia Nulla manus belli mutato judice pura est.

Joabus autem non quid præcepisset David, sed quid præci- pere debuisset spectavit, putavitque minus in hoc pacto esse periculi, quam si Absolomum Regem pati aliquando coactus esset.

## 18:16
HE RESTRAINED THE PEOPLE FROM PURSUING FLEEING ISRAEL) Well. See above 2, 26. And add this from Cicero, book 4, Epist. 7 to his friends: A wise and good citizen undertakes the beginnings of a civil war unwillingly, and does not pursue its final stages gladly.

Latin:

RETINVIT POPVLVM NE PERSEQVERETVR FVGIENTEM ISRAEL) Bene. Vide supra 2, 26. & adde hoc Ciceronis 4. libro Epist. 7. ad familiares: Sapientem & bonum civem initia belli civilis invitum suscipere, extrema non libenter persequi.

## 18:17
Ver. 17. AND THEY HEAPED UP OVER HIM A VERY GREAT PILE OF STONES) That was used as a trophy in those times.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET COMPORTAVERUNT SVPER EVM ACERVVM LAPIDVM MAGNVM NIMIS) Id illis tem- poribus pro trophæo erat.

## 18:18
Ver. 18. FOR HE HAD SAID: I HAVE NO SON) He had had one: see above 14, 27, but while he was alive they were as dead. Thus the Chaldean here, and others.

ABSALOM'S HAND) Or rather a place, as in Deut. 23, 12, and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DIXERAT ENIM: NON HABEO FILIVM) Habuerat: supra 14, 27. sed eo vivente erant mortui. Ita hic Chaldæus, & alii.

MANVS ABSALOM) Aut potius locus, ut Deut. 23, 12. & alibi.

## 18:21
Ver. 21. AND JOAB SAID: CUSHI, GO AND TELL THE KING WHAT YOU HAVE SEEN: To a certain Ethiopian, for whom he considered it a light loss even if something sad were to happen to him from the King.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET AIT JOAB: CHVSI VADE ET NVN- TIA REGI QVID VIDISTI: Æthiopi cuidam, cui et- iam si quid triste accidisset a Rege, leve damnum existimabat.

## 18:24
Ver. 24. BUT THE WATCHMAN WHO WAS ON THE TOP OF THE GATE] It is the custom for watchmen to be stationed in high places, 2 Kings 9, 17; Ezek. 35, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 24. SPECVLATOR VERO QVI ERAT IN FASTIGIO, PORTÆ] Speculatores collocari in locis excelsis mos est 2. Reg. 9, 17. Ezech. 35, 2.

## 18:32
Ver. 32. MAY THE ENEMIES OF MY LORD THE KING BE AS THE YOUNG MAN, AND ALL WHO RISE UP AGAINST HIM FOR EVIL) Οὕτως πᾶς ἀπόλοιτο ὅ, τις τοιαῦτά γε ῥ᾽έζοι.

Latin:

Vers. 32. FIANT SICVT PVER INIMICI DOMINI REGIS, ET VNIVERSI QVI CONSVRGVNT ADVERSVS EVM IN MALVM) Οὕτως πᾶς ἀπόλοιτο ὅ, τις τοιαῦτά γε ῥ᾽έζοι.

## 18:33
Ver. 33. MY SON ABSALOM) David is excessively emotional. Grotius does not weigh the cause of such great lamentation, which we brought forward at v. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 33. FILI MI ABSALOM) Nimis περιπαθὴς David. Causam tantæ lamentationis non expendit Gro- tius, quam ad v. 5. adduximus.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. David is brought back into the kingdom, Mephibosheth clears himself. Emulation between the tribes.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. David in regnum reducitur, Mephiboseth se pur- gat. Æmulatio inter tribus.

## 19:5
Ver. 5. YOU HAVE SHAMED THIS DAY THE FACES OF ALL YOUR SERVANTS WHO HAVE SAVED YOUR LIFE) Joab, such as Silius in Tacitus, Annals 4, and Antonius in Histories 3 and 4, is unbridled in tongue, insolent in obedience, and excessive in recounting what he has deserved. Benefits boasted of so immoderately invite hatred instead of thanks. And no one likes to be in debt for their life.

Latin:

Vers. 5. CONFUDISTI HODIE VULTVS GMNIVM SER- VORVM TVORVM QVI SALVAM FECERVNT ANIMAM TUAM) Joab, qualis in Tacito Annalium 4. C. Silius Hist. 3. & 4. Primus Antonius, immodicus lingua, ob- sequii insolens, nimius commemorandis quæ meruisset. Be- neficia tam immodice jactata pro gratia odium accersunt. Et vitam nemo libenter debet.

## 19:7
Ver. 7. NOT ONE WILL REMAIN WITH YOU THIS NIGHT) As those who, seeing that the King's displeasure has been incurred through so many dangers, will seek another to whom they may impute these things.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NE VNVS QVIDEM REMANSVRVS SIT TECVM NOCTE HAC) Vt qui visuri sibi tot periculis offensam Regis partam, alium quærent cui ista imputent.

## 19:11
Ver. 11. WHY HAVE YOU COME LAST TO BRING BACK THE KING TO HIS HOUSE? He prudently gives assurance not only of pardon, but also of restored benevolence. The noble ends of wars are as often as they are settled by granting pardon, says Tacitus, Annals 12. Furthermore, by emulation he kindles the zeal of the tribes toward himself.

Latin:

Vers. 11. CVR VENISTIS NOVISSIMI AD REDVCENDVM REGEM IN DOMVM SVAM) Prudenter fidem facit non veniæ tantum, sed & redditæ benevolentiæ. Bellorum egregii fines, quoties ignoscendo transigitur ait Tacitus 12. Annalium. Præterea æmulatu tribuum studia in se accendit.

## 19:13
Ver. 13. IF YOU SHALL NOT BE COMMANDER OF THE ARMY BEFORE ME ALL THE TIME INSTEAD OF JOAB) Joab indeed retained his legion, 20, 7, but the command of the war was entrusted to Amasa, 20, 11, which, upon his death, Joab recovered more by fear than by the favor of David. 20, 23. 24, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SI NON MAGISTER MILITIÆ FVERIS CORAM ME OMNI TEMPORE PRO JOAB) Mansit quidem Joabo sua legio 20, 7. sed summa belli Amasæ con- credita est 20, 11. quam eo mortuo Joab metu magis quam favore Davidis recuperavit. 20, 23. 24, 3.

## 19:19
Ver. 19. DO NOT IMPUTE TO ME, MY LORD, INIQUITY) LXX. μὴ δὴ λογισάσθω ὁ κύριός με ἀνομίαν. In this sense, λογίζεσθαι is the opposite of ἀφιέναι, Rom. 4, 7. The same word elsewhere means to hold, to seek punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NE REPVTES MIHI, DOMINE, INIQVITATEM) LXX. μὴ δὴ λογισάσθω ὁ κύριός με ἀνομίαν. Est in hoc sensu λογίζεσθαι, contrarium τῷ ἀφιέναι Rom. 4, 7. Idem alibi κρατεῖν pœnam expetere.

## 19:22
Ver. 22. AGAINST SATAN) See Matt. 16, 23. SHALL THEREFORE A MAN BE PUT TO DEATH THIS DAY IN ISRAEL? A joyful day, because of the recovered kingdom, calls for examples of clemency rather than severity.

Latin:

Vers. 22. IN SATAN) Vid. Matth. 16, 23. ERGONE HODIE INTERFICIETVR VIR IN ISRAEL) Dies lætus ob recuperatum regnum clementiæ potius quam severitatis exempla poscit.

## 19:23
AND HE SWORE TO HIM) An oath, where no other cause underlies it, does not go beyond the person of the one swearing, nor does it bind an heir. See book 2 of The Law of War and Peace, ch. 13, § 17, and 1 Kings 2, 8 and 49.

Latin:

IVRAVITQVE EI) Juramentum ubi alia causa non subest personam jurantis non egreditur, neque hæredem ob- ligat. Vid. libr. 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 13. §. 17. & 1, Reg. 2, 8. & 49.

## 19:24
WITH UNWASHED FEET AND UNTRIMMED BEARD. AND HE HAD NOT WASHED HIS CLOTHES) As in public mourning.

Latin:

ILLOTIS PEDIBVS ET INTONSA BARBA. VESTESQVE SVAS NON LAVERAT) Vt in publico luctu.

## 19:28
Ver. 28. FOR MY FATHER'S HOUSE WAS NOTHING BUT SUBJECT TO DEATH BEFORE MY LORD THE KING) From that extreme rigor by which all who are among the enemy are considered enemies.

Latin:

Vers. 28. NEQVE ENIM FVIT DOMVS PATRIS MEI NISI MORTI OBNOXIA DOMINO MEO RE- GI) Ex summo illo rigore, quo omnes qui apud hostes sunt pro hostibus habentur.

## 19:29
Ver. 29. YOU AND ZIBA DIVIDE THE POSSESSIONS) Some think that the colonial right, of which above 9, 10, was restored to Ziba. But the Hebrews judge that David sinned here, either because he did not wish to rescind in every part his previous decree, which he had made while circumvented, above 16, 4, lest his own error be too manifest, or because he suspected that Mephibosheth had his eyes on excessive wealth. And they say that God looked to this sin also when He divided the kingdom of Rehoboam. Another cause for this division is given in 1 Kings ch. 11, namely, the idolatry of Solomon, and it seems probable what Abulensis, quest. 30, suspects, that David compensated Mephibosheth for the loss with another gift or benefit.

Latin:

Vers. 29. TV ET SIBA DIVIDITE POSSESSIONES) Quidam putant Sibæ restitutum jus illud colonarium, de quo supra 9,10. At Hebræi peccasse hic Davidem arbitrantur, sive quod prius decretum suum quod circumventus fecerat, su- pra 16, 4. noluit ex omni parte rescindere, ne nimis apertus esset ipsius error, sive quod nimias Mephibosethi opes su- spicaretur spectas habuit. Ajuntque Deum ad hoc quoque peccatum respexisse, cum Roboami regnum bipertivit. Alia causa hujus divisionis redditur 1. Reg. cap. 11. nimir. Idololatria Salomonis, & probabile vide- tur, quod Abulens. quæst. 30. suspicatur Davidem alia donatione vel beneficio damnum Mephibo- setho compensasse.

## 19:41
Ver. 41. WHY HAVE OUR BRETHREN THE MEN OF JUDA STOLEN YOU AWAY) An honest contest, and one arising from the hope of David, which nevertheless, kindled by the bitterness of words, provided an occasion for those wishing to revolutionize things. Honest indeed, but from which the worst things will arise, says Tacitus at the end of Annals 1.

Latin:

Vers. 41. QVARE TE FVRATI SVNT FRATRES NOSTRI JVDA) Honestum certamen & ex spe Davidis, quod tamen accensum acerbitate verborum occasionem præbuit res no- vare volentibus. Honesta quidem, sed ex quibus deterrima orientur, ait Tacitus fine Annal. 1.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX. The sedition of Sheba, and his destruction.

Latin:

CAPUT XX. Sebæ Seditio, & interitus.

## 20:2
Ver. 2. AND ALL ISRAEL WAS SEPARATED FROM DAVID, AND FOLLOWED SHEBA THE SON OF BOCHRI) Ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ ὁ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET SEPARATVS EST OMNIS ISRAEL A DAVID, SECVTVSQVE EST SEBEA FILIVM BOCHÆ) Ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ ὁ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς.

## 20:3
Ver. 3. THEY WERE SHUT UP UNTIL THE DAY OF THEIR DEATH, LIVING IN WIDOWHOOD) He indeed forgave the fear, but he himself wished neither to touch those who had been touched by his son, as being impure to him, nor to have them touched by others, being as they were the royal concubines.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ERANT CLAVSÆ VSQVE IN DIEM MORTIS SVÆ IN VIDUITATE VIVENTES] Ignovit quidem timori, sed a filio tactas neque tangere ipse voluit ut sibi im- puras, neque tangi ab aliis, quippe regias concubinas.

## 20:6
Ver. 6. PURSUE HIM LEST PERCHANCE HE FIND FORTIFIED CITIES, AND ESCAPE US) One must hasten before the weak conspiracy of a few grew. Tacitus, Histories 1.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PERSEQVERE EVM NE FORTE INVENIAT CI- VITATES MVNITAS, ET EFFVGIAT NOS) Festi- nandum antequam cresceret invalida adhuc conjuratio pauco- rum. Tacitus Histor. 1.

## 20:8
Ver. 8. WHO HAVING BEEN MADE WITH A LIGHT MOTION) The Greeks more correctly: καὶ ἡ μάχαιρα ἐξῆλθε καὶ ἀυτὴ ἐξῆλθε καὶ ἔπεσε. The sword hung in the scabbard in such a way that it could easily fall out of the scabbard, which happened with Joab also lightly assisting, so that Amasa believed the sword had fallen to the ground and was being picked up by him so that he might replace it in the scabbard.

Latin:

Vers. 8. QVI FABRICATVS LEVI MOTV ECREDI POTERAT ET PERCVTERE) Rectius Græci: καὶ ἡ μά- χαιρα ἐξῆλθε καὶ ἀυτὴ ἐξῆλθε καὶ ἔπεσε. Ita pendebat in vagina gladius, ut facile de vagina excideret, quod & Joabo leviter adjuvante, evenit, ita ut Amasa crederet delapsum humi gladium ab eo tolli, ut eum in vaginam reponeret.

## 20:9
Ver. 9. MY BROTHER) That is, colleague. Joab could not endure a rival.

Latin:

Vers. 9. MI FRATER) Id est, collega. Æmulum ferre Joab non poterat.

## 20:10
Ver. 10. WHO STRUCK HIM IN THE SIDE) Joab, seeing that everything was turning out for him with impunity, dares more. There is, however, atrocious treachery in this deed. A similar deed of Mithridates, who was the son of Ariobarzanes, against Datames, you have in Probus, who adds this: thus that man, who had captured many by counsel, none by treachery, was captured by feigned friendship. The end of Eumenes is not much different.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QVI PERCVSSIT EVM IN LATERE) Joab omnia videns impune sibi cedere, plura audet. Est autem in hoc fa- cto atrox perfidia. Simile factum Mithridatis, qui Ariobar- zanis filius, in Datamem, habes apud Probum, qui hoc addit: ita ille vir, qui multos consilio, neminem perfidia ceperat, simu- lata captus est amicitia. Eumenis haud multum dissimilis exitus.

## 20:12
Ver. 12. LEST THOSE PASSING BY SHOULD STOP BECAUSE OF HIM) And that spectacle would stir up the hatred of all against Joab more vehemently. THEY SURROUNDED THE CITY WITH FORTIFICATIONS) LXX: ἐξέχεαν πρόσχωμα πρὸς τὴν πόλιν: that is, they leveled the trench. AND THE CITY WAS BESIEGED) In the Hebrew: and it stood in the rampart, namely the city: ἕστη ἐν τῷ προτειχίσματι.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NE SVBSISTERENT TRANSEVNTES PROPTER EVM) Idque spectaculum odia omnium in Joabum vehementius concitaret. CIRCYMDEDERVNT MVNITIONIBVS CIVITA- TEM) LXX. ἐξέχεαν πρόσχωμα πρὸς τὴν πόλιν: id est, complanarunt fossam. ET OBSESSA EST VRBS) In Hebræo: & stetit in propugnaculo, nempe civitas: ἕστη ἐν τῷ προτειχίσματι.

## 20:16
Ver. 16. HE WAS ENDEAVORING TO DESTROY THE WALLS) That is, ὑπορύσσειν, as Josephus here, to undermine, namely with axes and mattocks, as Tacitus teaches us in Histories 2. WHO ASK, LET THEM ASK IN ABEL, AND SO THEY FINISHED) Some do not poorly judge that it is referred by the woman to what the townspeople had said among themselves from the beginning: They will send to us the besiegers, and will inquire whether we wish for peace: and thus the business will be finished in a short time. Thus generally Vatablus with the Hebrews from Deut. 20:10. Nor does the sense seem inconvenient. However, the Belgian censor Amama does not here criticize the Vulgate: whose sense Cornelius renders thus: Why do you dare to attack this city, which is an oracle of wisdom. So also Abulensis, Cajetanus, Osiander, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 16. MOLIEBATVR DESTRVERE MVROS) Id est, ὑπορύσσειν, ut hic Josephus, subruere, securibus nempe & dolabris, ut Histor. 2. Tacitus nos docet. QVI INTERROGANT, INTERROGENT IN ABE- LE, ET SIC PERFICIEBANT) Non male quidam cen- sent referri a muliere quod ab initio inter se dixerant oppi- dani: Mittent ad nos obsessores, & percunctabuntur an pacem velimus: & sic brevi confiet negotium. Sic fere Vatablus cum Ebræis è Deut. 20, 10. Nec sensus videtur incommodus. Vulgatam tamen hic non reprehendit censor Belgicus Amama: cujus sensum hunc Cornelius reddit: Cur tu audes oppu- gnare hanc urbem, quæ est oraculum sapientiæ. Sic & Abulensis, Cajetanus, Osiander, alii.

WITH ZEAL AS IF FOR THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL AND JUDAH] Having a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, as Paul speaks in Romans 10:2. For by no pretext ought the public faith to have been violated. Concerning which see Joshua 9.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

VOLVIT SAVL PERCVTERE EOS) Et percussit quos- dam, ut jamjam sequitur, & narrat Josephus.

## 21:6
Verse 6.

THAT WE MAY CRUCIFY THEM TO THE LORD) ἐξηλιάσωμεν αὐτούς, LXX here: that is, let us hang them openly under the sky from a tree, namely, having first killed them, which is tacitly understood, as in Numbers 25:4.

AND THE KING SAID, I WILL GIVE] Having consulted the prophets, which Josephus here expressly adds, and the divinely-sent famine demanded. And certainly if it were otherwise, David would not only have sinned against the law sufficiently clear in Deuteronomy 24:16, always observed by good kings in 2 Kings 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 25:4, and against another law in Deuteronomy 21:23. But he would also have burdened himself with suspicion among all prudent men, as one who was seeking pretexts to free himself and his descendants from the descendants of Saul, with only one, and that a weak one, being spared: See what is said on this argument in the second book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 22, number 14.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

VT CRVCIFIGAMVS EOS DOMINO) ἐξηλιάσωμεν αὐτούς, LXX. hîc: id est, sub dio palam eos de ligno suspen- damus, nempe prius interfectos, quod tacite intelligitur, ut Num. 25, 4.

ET AIT REX, EGO DABO] Consultis prophetis quod hic diserte adjicit Josephus, & fames θεήλατῶ exige- bat. Et certe aliter si esset, non tantum peccafset David in legem satis apertam Deut. 24, 16. semper observatam a bonis Regibus 2. Reg. 14, 6. 2. Paral. 25, 4. & in legem alteram Deut. 21, 23. Verum etiam apud omnes prudentes suspicione se one- rasset, quasi qui prætextus quæreret ut se & posteros suos li- beraret a posteris Saulis, uno tantum eoque debili servato: Vide quæ de hoc argumento dicta libro secundo de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 22. num. 14.

## 21:8
Verse 8.

AND THE FIVE SONS OF MICHAL THE DAUGHTER OF SAUL) And yet Michal had no sons, above 6:23. Certain Hebrews and the Chaldean interpreter here judge that the sons of Michal are spoken of improperly, whom she raised, having been born of Merab her sister, which kind of way of speaking appears in Numbers 2:1, 2; Ruth 4:17; 1 Chronicles 4:18. Others, however, think it not incredible that the scribe of the book, from whom many copies flowed, wrote Michal instead of Merab. Concerning Merab see 1 Samuel 14:49, 18:17, et seqq.

This, indeed, is by no means probable. For the Hebrew Codices agree here; nor has any different one been observed. Nor is any corruption of the sacred text to be admitted. For otherwise it would be easy to imagine or suspect the sources to be corrupted everywhere. For what has happened to any of the places of Scripture could happen to any. Which is to take away all certainty of the Scriptures entirely. This very Jesuit Cornelius absolves the Hebrew Codices from error; Cajetan, he says, thinks there is an error, and that Merob should be substituted for Michal, but all the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Codices have Michol and Merob. So also the Jesuit Sanctius: There is no reason why we should think a fault has crept in, when all the codices without exception agree. He also refutes the reasoning of Cajetan, that, namely, it is added, whom she had borne to Hadriel. For even the sons, he says, are called Michol by a figurative expression, where the form of similitude is understood, as, as if, as elsewhere a thousand times, because they were not sons, but as it were sons by love and care; so also by that same figure they can be called born of her, that is, as it were born, because they were not otherwise received and treated by her than if they had been conceived and brought into the light by her. Abulensis, quest. 29, thinks that GENUIT should be referred to Merob, which the Glossa ordinaria and Historia Scholastica likewise do. That, indeed, as I have said, is not necessary. Thus Sanctius. Tirinus and Menochius, likewise Jesuits, agree. Moreover, they follow Lyranus and Tostatus here from their own side: from the Rabbis, Aben-Ezra: from our own, the Weimar Paraphrasts likewise subscribe to this opinion, as does also Mr. Dr. Walther in Harm. Bibl. on 2 Sam. 6:27 and 1 Samuel 18:19. Another and easier, as it appears, solution of the doubt is that which Junius, Piscator, and the Belgian Interpreters have, understanding the name of the sister in this way; and the five sons of the sister of Michal, daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Hadriel, so that there is an ellipsis of the name signifying the relationship, such as Junius also posits in verse 19: He struck Elchanan the son of Jchare, a Bethlehemite by origin, of Goliath the Gittite (the brother), because, namely, it is so expressly written in 1 Chron. 20:5. Where, however, to interject this in passing, that ellipsis does not seem to have a place, because in the Hebrew the sign of the accusative case is held, he struck Goliath the Gittite: therefore it is better to say that that Giant is called a Gittite by similitude, because he was as it were another Goliath, and from there that name clung to him, and for that reason he is called the brother of Goliath in 1 Paralip. 20:5. Both those opinions can be joined regarding this present passage, so that, namely, the name sister may be understood, which the word bore seems to demand, but she herself is believed to be mentioned for the reason that Merob adopted those sons, or at least educated them. Other responses are also found: Emanuel Saa thinks Merob was also called Michal. Others say there were two Adrieles, just as two Mephibosheths are mentioned in 2 Samuel 21:7, 8, and that the latter called Michal the second-born of Saul, before she was joined in marriage to Phaltiel the son of Lais, Hadriel having died, from whom David reclaimed her, 2 Samuel 3:15. But the first two opinions are to be preferred. For these are destitute of any foundation. But it pleased our Hugo to choose the worst: which is injurious to the sources of Hebrew truth, and cannot be approved by the Papists themselves, if you except a few, such as Cajetan, Canus, and Salianus.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET QVINQVE FILIOS MICHOL FILIÆ SAVL) Atqui Michol Filios non habuit, supra 6, 23. Hebræi qui- dam & Chaldæus hic Interpres censent Micholis filios impro- prie dici, quos ex Merobe sorore natos ipsa educavit, quale loquendi genus apparet Num. 2, 1. 2. Ruth. 4, 17. 1. Chron. 4, 18. Alii vero non incredibile putant scribam libri, unde multa exemplaria fluxere, scripsisse מיכל pro מרב. De Merobe vid. 1. Sam. 14, 49. 18, 17. seqq.

ID vero neutiquam probabile est. Conspirant enim hic Codices Hebræi; nec ullus diversus est observatus. Neque admittenda ulla est corruptio sacri textus. Alias enim proclive esset, nusquam non corruptos fingere, aut suspicari fontes. Quod enim cuiquam locorum scripturæ contigit, cui- vis contingere potuit. Quod est omnem plane certitudinem Scripturarum tollere. Absolvit hic ipse Cornelius Jesuita Ebræos Codices à mendo; Ca- jetanus, inquit, putat esse mendum, & pro Michal substituendum Merob, verum omnes Codices Ebræi, Græci, Latini habent Michol & Merob. Sic etiam Sanctius Jesuita: Non est cur irrepsisse vitium exi- stimemus, quando omnes omnino codices consentiunt. Refellit etiam rationem Cajetani, quod scil. adda- tur, quos genuerat Hadrieli. Nam etiam filii, in- quit, dicuntur Michol figurata locutione, ubi sub- auditur similitudinis forma, sicut, quasi, ut alibi millies, quia Filii non erant, sed quasi filii amore ac cura; sic etiam ab illa eadem figura vocari possunt geniti, id est, quasi geniti, quia non aliter ab illa su- scepti sint atque tractati, quasi ab illa concepti forent, & in lucem editi. Abulensis quæst. 29. illud GENUIT ad Merob putat esse referendum, quod item facit Glossa ordinaria & Historia Scholastica. Id sane ut dixi, necessarium non est. Hæc Sanctius. Adstipu- lantur Tirinus & Menochius, itidem Jesuitæ. Se- quuntur autem hic illi Lyranum & Tostatum è suis: è Rabbinis Aben-Ezra: è nostris Vinarienses Para- phrastæ huic pariter subscribunt sententiæ, ut & Dn. D. Waltherus in Harm. Bibl. ad 2. Sam. 6, 27. & 1. Samuel. 18, 19. Alia & facilior, ut apparet, dubii solutio est, quam habent Junius, Piscator, & Interpp. Belgic. Nomen Sororis subaudientes hoc pacto; & quinque Filios sororis Michal, filiæ Sau- lis, quos pepererat Hadrieli, ut ellipsis sit nominis cognationem significantis, qualem etiam vers. 19. ponit Junius: Percussit Elchanam filius Jchare ori- gine Bethlehemita Goliathi Gattæi (fratrem) quia scil. sic expresse scribitur 1. Chron. 20, 5. Ubi tamen, ut obiter id inferamus, ellipsis ista non videtur lo- cum habere, quia in Ebræo nota accusativi casus habetur, percussit Goliathum Gethæum: proinde præstat dicere Goliathum vocari Gethæum illum Gigantem per similitudinem, quod velut alter Go- liathus fuerit, atque inde nomen illud ei hæserit, eaque de causa frater Goliathi dicitur 1. Paralip. 20, 5. Conjungi potest utraque illa sententia, de hoc præsenti loco, ut nempe nomen soror subintelli- gatur, quod postulare videtur verbum genuit, ipsa vero ideo commemorari credatur, quia Merob fi- lios illos adoptavit, aut certe educavit. Reperiuntur & aliæ responsiones: Emanuel Saa purat Merob eti- am Michal appellatam fuisse. Alii dicunt duos fu- iffe Adrieles, uti duo memorantur Mephiboseth 2. Samuel. 21, 7. 8. & posteriorem dixisse Michol se- cundogenitam Saulis, priusquam matrimonio jun- geretur Pfalti filio Lais, Hadriele demortuo, à quo David eam repetiit, 2. Samuel. 3, 15. Sed priores duæ sententiæ præferendæ. Hæ enim fundamen- to omni destituuntur. Hugoni autem nostro pla- cuit pessimam eligere: quæ & in fontes Ebraicæ veritatis injuriosa est, nec Papistis ipsis, si paucos excipias, Cajetanum puta, Canum & Salianum, probari potest.

UNTIL WATER DRIPPED UPON THEM FROM HEAVEN) And thus it would appear that God was appeased; for the famine had come through the drought. Josephus on this passage: And God began to rain immediately, and to call back the earth to the production of fruits, having removed the previous drought.

AND DID NOT ALLOW THE BIRDS TO TEAR THEM BY DAY, NOR THE BEASTS BY NIGHT) Piously. Ambrose in his book on Tobias: Nothing is more excellent than this duty: to bestow upon one who can no longer repay you: to defend from the birds, to defend from the beasts, a companion of nature.

DONEC STILLARET AQVA SVPER EOS DE COELO) Et sic appareret Deum esse placatum; nam fames per ficcitatem evenerat. Josephus hoc loco: ἤρξατο δὲ ὕειν παραχρῆμα ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ τὴν γῆν πρὸς γονὴν καρπῶν ἀνακαλῶν ἀποχούσῃ τῇ πρότερον ἀυχμῷ.

ET NON DIMISIT AVES LACERARE EOS PER DIEM, NEQVE BESTIAS PER NOCTEM) Pie. Am- brosius libro de Tobia: Nihil hoc officio præstantius: ei con- ferre, qui jam tibi non potest reddere: vindicare a volatilibus, vindicare a bestiis consortem naturæ.

WHO HAD SIX FINGERS ON HIS HANDS AND FEET) Pliny, Natural History, book 11, chapter 43. Some have six fingers on their hands. PART III. DAVID'S PREPARATION FOR DEATH. CHAPTER XXII. David's Eucharistic Hymn. Ver. 2.

PARS III. PRÆPARATIO DAVIDIS AD MORTEM. CAPUT XXII. Hymnus Davidis Eucharisticus. Vers. 2.

THE LORD IS MY ROCK) This hymn agrees in many respects with Psalm 18.

## 22:11
Ver. 11.

HE ASCENDED UPON THE CHERUBIM AND FLEW) In the Hebrew: He ascended upon a Cherub and flew: that is, he arrived most swiftly as if on a winged animal. Thus elsewhere he is said to be carried on a very light cloud, Isaiah 19, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ASCENDIT SVPER CHERVBIM ET VOLAVIT) In Hebræo: Ascendit super Cherub & volavit: id est velocis- sime advenit veluti in alato animali. Sic alibi nube levisfi- ma vectari dicitur Esaiæ 19, 1.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII. The last words of David, and his Heroes. Ver. 1.

NOW THESE ARE THE LAST WORDS OF DAVID) Namely, words of prophecy: for many other things not prophetic after that spoke, as will appear in the following chapter and the following book.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII. Verba novissima Davidis, & Heroes ejus. Vers. 1.

HÆC AVTEM SVNT VERBA DAVID NOVIS- SIMA) Nempe verba Prophetiæ: nam alia multa non pro- phetica post id locutus est, ut capite sequenti, & libro sequen- ti apparebit.

## 23:3
Verse 3. THE GOD OF ISRAEL HAS SPOKEN TO ME) Through Nathan: See above 7.

There is no reason why this should be restricted specifically to that revelation: although there is no doubt that it is also looked to here. For things that are said generally are not to be restricted according to our own judgment. But that these things were said generally, the things which are added show not obscurely.

Verse same. THE STRONG ONE OF ISRAEL, THE RULER OF MEN, A JUST RULER IN THE FEAR OF GOD.

The Strong One of Israel is the Son of GOD: who is joined to the Spirit of the Lord, who spoke through David, and whose word was made through his tongue: and to the GOD of Israel, by which name GOD the Father is designated, so that here a notable testimony of the Holy Trinity may be had. Blessed Meisner in his logologia or Disputation on John 1 understands by the Sermon of the Lord the hypostatic word: But Blessed Luther more correctly takes it concerning the spoken word: and notes that the God of Israel is called GOD the Father: who gave the promises to David, but he judges the Rock or crag and the strong one of Israel, the just ruler among men, to be called the Son of GOD: who is brought forward here, as dwelling among men, and likewise speaking, and bringing promises: and therefore he concludes thus in his book on the last words of David, Tom. 3. Lat. Witeb. f. 95. There are therefore Three Persons speaking, and yet one and the same God speaks, the same is the promiser, the same is the promise, just as one God, blessed forever. Coccejus supports this in the commentary added to the Psalms: Not ineptly here, if we attend to the propriety, shall we judge that three persons are distinguished. The Spirit of Jehovah verse 2. The God of Israel, who adjured Israel, that he should believe in Him, that He would be God to him, whom, namely, he could name, to whom he could swear, in whom he could glory. The Rock of Israel, he to whom Israel flees, as in the second Psalm verse 12, who carries Israel by his powerful word Isaiah 63, 9, nay, by his merit, as savior. Concerning which salvation is verse 5. This cannot seem inept, or not necessary, to one who has considered that the word which David commemorates here is the word of the Testament, and of the covenant, concerning faith unto righteousness, the foundation of which is the revelation of God in the flesh, for the performing of εὐδοκίαν. It is by no means inept that God should be denominated the author of the word from these things. Nay, it would be morose, and full of ἀπειθείας, to be unwilling to understand in the words that which can be understood in them, with attention to their emphasis. Finally, it is not to be thought that those words were multiplied without cause. Moreover, scripture attributes the name of Rock to Christ peculiarly Psalm 118, 22, Canticles 2, 13, Isaiah 8, 14, chapter 28, 16, Matthew 16, 18, 1 Corinthians 10, 4, because he is the most solid foundation of the Church, as of the building of GOD 1 Corinthians 3, 9, 11, Matthew 16, 19.

Verse same. RULER OF MEN, A JUST RULER IN THE FEAR OF GOD.

These now pertain to the argument of the Prophecy, but are not rightly drawn to the preceding things: which the distinctive accent Atnach indicates. Yet they sound concerning the Son of GOD: whose mention, therefore, when the persons of the Trinity were being recounted, was reserved for the last place, because more was to be said about him, as in Revelation 1, 4. Scripture is accustomed to call this one the Ruler in Israel Micah 5, 2, Jeremiah 30, 21. This is that one and only just ruler, whom the Holy Scriptures celebrate thus Jeremiah 23, 5, Zechariah 9, 9, Isaiah 11, 4, 5. That therefore is what is prophesied concerning the Rock of Israel: He shall be a ruler of men, a just ruler in the fear of GOD, either because he himself will most greatly inculcate and propagate the fear of GOD, without which there would have been no place for the fear of the Lord, and in the fear of the Lord his entire dominion will be instituted, Isaiah 11, 3, 5, or because he himself rules specially over those who serve GOD in fear Psalm 2, 11, so that it is to be held as an adjunct or epithet of the kingdom, or of the king, or of the subjects. Blessed Luther interprets it in the former way: A ruler effecting the fear of GOD. David by his government did not make even one man just and fearing GOD, nay, not even himself, and not even Moses himself, the institutor of the law and the polity, but whoever were ever just and fearing GOD, they were justified through this Lord, and led to the true fear of GOD. Sanctius, Cornel. explains it in the latter way, & Tirinus, because He is the Ruler of those who fear God. Cocceius rightly observes here: that those words already pertain to the argument of revelation: but he does not appropriately apply them to David: who in his final words prophesies not of himself and his own dominion, which he was about to lay down along with his life, but of the Messiah. That commentary is therefore foreign to this point: It is not only a prediction about David, but a promise that he would rule in the fear of the Lord. The Chaldean expounded it more correctly, who, as Cocceius himself notes, takes those words as spoken of Christ: For thus he παραφράζει: David said, The GOD of Israel has spoken of me, who has power over the sons of men, judging in truth, He says He will appoint a King for me, namely the Messiah in the future, who will arise and rule in the fear of the Lord. And Cocceius acknowledges the immediately following verse 4, which continues this discourse or promise through the copulative Vav, (which by the Interpreters (which by some is rashly neglected.) And as the morning light (or, as the light of the morning) the sun shall rise: to treat of Christ and his kingdom: and that in this the Interpreters AGREE, that it treats there of the Messiah: even the Jews. Why therefore does he draw the immediate coherence, and the things referring to the same subject, not to the Messiah, but to David? Although it is not simply true even of the Jews, who interpret these things of the Messiah only in a mystical sense, nor of all other Interpreters. Since both the Papists, Cornel. à Lapid. and others, and some Calvinists follow the Jews in that part: some even explain it simply of David with Ludov. de Dieu, or of those who enjoy great prosperity, as Ravanell. in Bibliothec. under the word Light &c. As for what Coccejus says: that they do not seem to connect well, because they think it is predicated copulatively of מושל the ruler, that it is like the morning light, and thus it does not appear how well τὸ וזרח it shall arise coheres, this is easily resolved: For it can be predicated copulatively by reason of the sense, so that the subject is the same, a ruler existing among men, and that sun arising, even if by reason of the words these are not coupled into one proposition, but form distinct propositions. The former is this: There shall be a ruler among men, a just ruler in the fear of GOD: The latter is this: And with the morning light the sun of righteousness shall arise: For Coccejus admits that this sun is being discussed. And he proves it thus on page 591. For there is no reason why we should here urge the literal sense, and think that a discourse is being held about the proper rising of the sun and the dawn, and the rain and the grass, which the oxen eat. But there is a great reason why we should think there is another meaning, and that these words are allegorized, and signify what they can and are accustomed to signify spiritually. For David, who gives thanks here to God for the greatest benefits, and in the enumeration of them he rises up; when he speaks of εὐδοκία πάσῃ and his σωτηρία, he cannot have forgotten his Son, the sun of righteousness. And afterwards: I do not think it is fitting for David, and for his modesty, that he should compare his kingdom to a pure sun, without clouds, and one that is increasingly proficient. not the sun, he did not shine as the sun, he did not bring joy as the sun. He left the people in their servitude and in their desire. He himself sinned, and by his sins he saddened and troubled Israel; and his kingdom suffered an eclipse: and the splendor of his house was diminished. We shall soon hear him saying something else. Cocceius is very correct in this. The words וּכְאוֹר בֹּקֶר can have a double meaning: first, of comparison: And, as, the light of the morning, or as the light of the morning, the sun shall rise: secondly, of time; And, when the morning shall shine, the sun shall rise. Neither is unsuitable regarding the sun of righteousness. Cocceius approves the former in this manner. When the light came into the world, it became day, and as it were morning. For the glory of him was seen as of the only-begotten from the Father. To those who saw and knew him, it was a clear day, like the morning. Yet he does not reject the latter as foreign, even if he considers it simpler: The time, he says, of the Old Testament is a time of shadows and of night. After that night there will be a morning in the παρουσίᾳ of Christ in the flesh. Soon the sun will rise, with Christ rising from the dead, and ascending into heaven, that he may shine in majesty and glory. Which does not seem to us inappropriate. And what prevents taking the morning in such a way that the time of the resurrection is designated, when the sun of righteousness began to rise, when Christ through death entered into his glory; or if you prefer, that at least that word is used here, as it loves to be done in prophecies, in similitudes, to allude to, and that time is tacitly insinuated? For that sun of righteousness rose in a peculiar way, when very early in the morning Christ came forth from the sepulcher: Soon it began to illuminate the hearts of the women, of Mary Magdalene, and of those who ran to the sepulcher: and of Simon Peter: and afterwards, the Apostles being illuminated, it began to unfold the rays of its majesty with full brightness through the whole world. Thus the words subjoined will have this meaning: In that morning there will be no clouds (of ignorance, and misery, or of sadness, and grief, inasmuch as the sun of righteousness will dispel them by its rising) from the splendor, from the rain there will be a sprout from the earth. The splendor of that sun, with the rain of the Spirit, will be the causes of spiritual fertility, so that spiritual sprouts will come forth from the earth, i.e., believers, in great number and yield: Cocceius explains the sense adversatively, in this way: Even if in that morning there will be no clouds, yet from the brightness and from the rain, grass will be born from the whole earth, i.e., even if in the παρουσίᾳ of Christ there will not be a great appearance of rain or of the blessing of the seed cast into the earth by Christ, i.e., of the word preached by him: nevertheless, with the heavenly brightness, rain will also fall, namely, the Holy Spirit poured out copiously, which will cause sprouts to be born from the whole world. By the word from the earth is noted, according to Cocceius, a great multitude. Immediately at the first Pentecost several thousand believed from every tribe and from every place; even proselytes. And that light does not cease to shine thereafter, and rain with light falls upon the earth, through which the whole world becomes fruitful. David expressed that abundance elsewhere by the similitude of dew copiously covering the earth, as in Psalm 110:3.

Others in these similitudes, which are used in this place in verse 4 in the latest words, rest so nakedly; that they interpret these things only concerning the sun, and clouds, taken physically, and also concerning the splendor, and rain, by which they promote the fertility of the earthly and material sprout, as if there were no mystery underlying them; in which way Lud. de Dieu wishes these to be brought forward: as those in which there is no constancy, or stability, nothing ordered everywhere and firmly kept in its order. For as far as the sun is concerned, it rises with the light of the morning, but the same sets again in the evening. Then as far as the serenity of the dawn is concerned, it is indeed accustomed at the first rising of splendor to dispel the clouds, but when the sun has already ascended for some time above the horizon, the clouds return, or others succeed, which darken and sadden the sky. Thirdly, as far as the tender herb is concerned, which sprouts from the earth through rain, it is joyful, and useful, but one which nevertheless suddenly withers. So that it is thus subjoined by way of contrast: Not so is my house before GOD, it has an eternal covenant, which is everywhere rightly ordered, and is kept in that order. But those similitudes are not used in a worse sense, nor is anything indicated about the inconstancy, or instability of either the splendor of the sun, or the serenity of the dawn, or the sprouting of herbs (which would have had to be expressed in other words); rather, those things are celebrated as pleasant, joyful, and useful, the rising of the sun, the golden serenity, the fertility of the earth from the splendor and rain: as the very tenor of the words teaches. And what was more stable and eternal in the house of David, what was more rightly ordered, and firm, than in the sun, whose rising and setting is established by a certain law, and being most ordered suffers no exorbitance? But what Diepius observes, that even if the house of David underwent many adversities, and various changes, that which had been entered into in the covenant of GOD with him nevertheless always remained, is a document that whatever is held here concerning stability, and an ordered and firm constitution, does not pertain to the family, or house of David, but to the promise concerning the Messiah, and his kingdom, by which the covenant was properly sanctioned; indeed, the sonorous words of the text testify that that certainty and stability is removed from the house of David itself: For not so (or right or stable, because interpreters observe that that word כֵּן can be rendered in either way) is my house with GOD: but he has placed for me an everlasting covenant, exposed among all, and kept: which is all my salvation, and all my good pleasure; which my house will not sprout; as Cocceius interprets.

Others think more fittingly that in those words concerning the sun, the dawn, the splendor, the rain, and the copious growth of grass, only the πρότασις (protasis) of the comparison is contained, but the ἀπόδοσις (apodosis) is tacitly insinuated at the same time, namely that their application ought to be made, not to the house and family of David, but to the Messiah and his kingdom, so that by the rising of the sun of righteousness, and the serenity when he arises, free from clouds, and by his splendor, and the rain sent down by him (which they understand either as doctrine irrigating man so that he may work righteousness, with the author of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew, hom. 20, from Deut. 32:2, Isa. 55:10-11, or as the rain of the Holy Spirit from Ps. 68:10), the spiritual fecundity of the earth is insinuated through those comparisons. This was the interpretation of the blessed Luther, who furthermore referred the πρότασις specifically to the springtime by comparing it with Cant. 2:11-12, Tom. 8 Germ. Jen. Von den letzten Worten Davids fol. 168. He compares the dominion or the kingdom of the Messiah, who is to bring back and establish righteousness and the fear of God, to the beautiful, lovely nature of springtime, when toward summer the dear sun approaches us again; then the earth opens up, turns green, blooms, everything smells beautiful, everything becomes new, and the world becomes alive and joyful again: Thus the dominion and the kingdom of grace is also a joyful joyful time, in which the Messiah makes us righteous and God-fearing, so that we grow green, bloom, smell sweet, grow, and become fruitful, for He is the Sun of Righteousness, wherefore He also wished to rise from the dead in the spring, or April, in the joyful time, and begin His dominion. And afterwards: In the times of the Messiah (says David,) when the Ruler of Israel Himself shall rule, to make us righteous and blessed with grace, it will be as lovely as the best time in the spring, when before day there has been a lovely warm rain, (that is, the comforting Gospel has been preached,) and immediately thereafter the Sun Christ rises in our hearts, through true faith, without the clouds, thunder, and lightning of Moses, there everything grows, greens, and blooms thereafter, and the day is full of joy and peace, such as the whole year does not have; for here it is called winter, clouds, thunder, sin, death, and all terror overcome, and a beautiful, joyful Easter day held until eternity; see, that is what David calls his son the Messiah's dominion, being like a day in the spring, when it has rained early, upon which the sun rises in the loveliest way, and makes everything green, blooming, smelling sweet, and alive and joyful; ask yourself therefore, if it is not the best and most joyful time of the year? By the same reasoning Luke. Osiander in his most beautiful paraphrase, after he rendered the Hebrew text thus: as the morning light, when the sun rises in the morning without clouds from the splendor (&) from the rain the grass of the earth springs forth; that is: Just as in spring, when after rain the sun rises most clearly in the morning, the earth is not only illuminated by the splendor of the sun, but also warmed, and produces herbs and flowers, so that everything is most pleasant at that time: so when after the fruitful rain of the Gospel Christ, the sun of righteousness, arises in the hearts of believers, everything becomes pleasant and delightful: so that a man, whose conscience has been pacified by the Gospel of Christ, seems to himself to have entered from the darkness of hell into the most delightful light, from a sad prison into Paradise, finally from death into life. Therefore my son Christ, says David, will restore the heavenly Paradise to believers in this world.

Therefore, as for the words which follow concerning the house of David, they, as we have said, do not proclaim the stability of David's kingdom positively, but are more correctly explained by most interpreters negatively, or that by them the Prophet testifies by negation that he is no longer dealing with his own house, but with the covenant confirmed for him concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, as Coccejus explained, or that he confesses that his house is not of such value that it is worthy of that grace, namely that from it the eternal King Christ is to come forth: which sense Osiander embraces, following B. Luther, from the comparison of 1 Chronicles 17. Nor is my house so great before GOD, that He should enter into an eternal covenant with me. Oh what am I? what is my house before GOD? It is indeed not such a house that it is worthy of such unspeakable honors before GOD, from which the Messiah, the Ruler of Israel, God's Son, the righteous Ruler among men, is to be born.
