Vers. 42. ET ORAVERIT IN HOC LOCO) In loco piis in- circumcisis seposito, qui ab Israelitarum locis lorica interpo- sita distinguebatur. Meminere ejus Josephus & Rabbini.

## 8:66
Ver. 66. AND ON THE EIGHTH DAY HE SENT AWAY THE PEOPLE) That is, he bade them farewell. But because that day was עצרת, they departed the next day. 2 Chron. 7, 9. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 66. ET IN DIE OCTAVA DIMISIT POPU- LOS) Id est, eis valedixit. Sed quia is dies erat עצרת profecti sunt postridie. 2. Paralip. 7, 9. 10.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

God appears to Solomon. King Hiram returns 20 cities to him. The Canaanites are made tributary. A fleet from Ophir brings gold.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

Apparet Deus Salomoni. Rex Hiram 20. civi- tates ei reddit. Cananæi redduntur tri- butarii. Classis ex Ophir advehit aurum.

## 9:3
Verse 3. AND MY EYES AND MY HEART SHALL BE THERE ALL DAYS) Namely, if this temple is piously worshipped. Thus here the Chaldean.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET ERUNT OCULI MEI ET COR MEUM IBI CVNCTIS DIEBVS) Nempe si hoc templum pie colatur. Ita hîc Chaldæus.

## 9:11
Verse 11. THEN SOLOMON GAVE HIRAM TWENTY TOWNS IN THE LAND OF GALILEE) Towns captured in war, such as we have shown by many examples are accustomed to be given as gifts by Kings in the first book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 3, § 12, and in the Annotations to that place. Add what is below 9, 16.

That passage of Grotius holds thus: King Solomon gave to Hiram, King of the Phoenicians (thus Philo of Byblos, who translated the history of Sanchuniathon, calls him in Greek), 20 cities, not from the cities of the Hebrew people; for Cabul, which name was given to those cities, is placed outside the borders of the Hebrews, Jos. 19, 27, but from the cities which the conquered enemies of the Hebrews had retained until that day, and which partly the King of Egypt, Solomon's father-in-law, had conquered and given to Solomon as a dowry, and partly Solomon himself had subdued. For that they were not inhabited by the Israelites at that time is evidenced by the fact that after Hiram returned them, only then did Solomon lead colonies of Hebrews there. The observation of Junius and Tremellius on this passage does not disagree with this opinion. who think that those cities were situated at the limit of the region of Asher bordering toward the north, but outside the possession defined by God by law, from which it was not permitted to give anything, not even for usufruct (as Solomon was doing here), to be possessed by others: For that Cabul did not at all belong to Asher is shown both from this passage and from the very number of the cities of Asher, which is held in Jos. 19 from verse 24 up to 30, and finally from the latter Chronicles 8, where it is read that Solomon led colonies of Israelites there. Which opinion Joh. Piscator in his Schol. on this passage and Joh. Diodati in his notes on this passage have also embraced, nor is there any reason why we should disapprove of it. Whence there is no need for that dispute, with which the Papist interpreters weary themselves concerning this passage, whether Solomon could alienate cities from the holy land for all time, since every possession returned in the Jubilee year to the original owners? Lev. 25. Could he have given holy peoples and the land of divine inheritance to a Gentile King? And since the transfer of possessions from one tribe to another was prohibited, how could he have devolved possessions to the Gentiles themselves? Where Torniellus, at the year M. 3033, following Abulensis, Vatablus, and Pineda, resorts to an exchange, that the said towns were not given as a gift, but given in place of other cities. Cajetan and Sanctius think that the ownership of those cities was not given, but the use, namely that he should receive their fruits for as long as he was satisfied for the expenses made in the construction of the temple and the royal house, which also pleased Salianus, Serarius, and Hottomannus; others think those towns were first King Hiram's, which, when he himself despised them, he handed over to Solomon to be built up and furnished with citizens, and once built and inhabited, Solomon returned them to the King, which is also Cajetan's conjecture. Some, with Dionysius, judge it probable that this Tyrian King was converted to the faith through long-standing friendship with David and Solomon: But since none of those opinions satisfy the proposed doubts, and neither could cities of Israel be ceded to a foreign nation for usufruct, nor is there a reason why Hiram should have rejected them if they sufficed for repaying expenses by being collected for a certain time (there was no need for them to please his eyes, which he was not to possess forever), the opinion of Grotius is to be preferred here, or rather that of Junius, from whom Grotius has it. Meanwhile, because some, with Cajetan, observe here that if a case of necessity had intervened, Solomon could have been excused, and thus they suppose that in a case of necessity or of averting a greater evil, or promoting a greater good, an alienation could have been made, our B. Dorscheus, in the dedicatory preface of his Theological Prodromus Anticriseos, not undeservedly opposes this judgment to the palliated Ernestus de Eusebiis, and to the anonymous vehicular author attacking the Peace of Osnabrück with the pretext of illicit alienation, especially because that cause of necessity, as they call it, was so frequently usurped in the Israelite Republic that examples are everywhere obvious where the claims and possessions of ecclesiastical persons, though indeed owed by law, nevertheless yielded to the public good and the unexpected cases of public affairs.

Latin:

Vers. 11. TVNC DEDIT SALOMON HIRAM VI- GINTI OPPIDA IN TERRA GALILÆÆ) Oppida bel- lo capta, qualia donari à Regibus solere multis exemplis ostendimus libro primo de Jure Belli ac Pacis capite 3. §. 12. & in Annotatis ad eum locum. Adde quod infra 9, 16.

L Ocus ille Grotianus ita habet: Rex Salomo Regi Phœnicum Hiromo (ita eum Græce vocat Philo Bi- blius, qui Sanchuniatonis historiam vertit) dedit urbes 20. non ex urbibus populi Hebræi; nam Chabul, quod nomen illis urbibus datum est, ponitur extra fines He- bræorum Jos. 19, 27. sed ex urbibus, quas populi devicti hostes Hebræorum ad eum diem retinuerant, quasque partim Rex Ægypti Salomonis socer vicerat, & Salomo- ni dotales dederat, partim subegerat ipse Salomo. Nam eo tempore ab Israelitis non habitatas argumento est, quod postquam Hiromus eas reddidit, tum demum Sa- lomo eo deduxit Hebræorum colonias. Non abnuit huic sententiæ observatio Junii & Tremellii ad h. l. qui civitates illas sitas fuisse putant ad regionis limi- tem Ascheri conterminum versus septentrionem, sed extra possessionem a Deo lege definitam, ex qua non licebat quicquam ne in usumfructum quidem (ut hic faciebat Salomo) cæteris possidendum dare: Nam Cabulem minime ad Ascherem pertinuisse tum ex h. l. ostenditur, tum ex ipso civitatum Asche- ris numero, qui habetur Jos. 19. a v. 24. usque ad 30. denique ex poster. Chronic. 8. ubi Salomon Israeli- tarum colonias eo deduxisse legitur. Quam sen- tentiam amplexus etiam est Joh. Piscator in Schol. ad h.l. & Joh. Deodatus in not. h.l. neque est cur eam improbemus. Unde non opus illa disputatione, qua se fatigant interpp. Pontificii circa h. l. anne potuerit Salomo civitates de terra sancta alienare ad omne tempus, quum redierit quælibet possessio in anno Jobelæo ad possessores pristinos? Lev. 25. an Regi Ethnico populos sanctos, & terram divinæ hære- ditatis dare potuerit? & quum transitus possessio- num de una tribu in aliam prohibitus fuerit, quo- modo ad ipsos gentiles possessiones devolvere po- tuerit? Ubi Torniellus ad ann. M. 3033. præeunte Abulensi, Vatablo, Pineda, ad permutationem, quod dicta oppida non donata, sed pro aliis civitatibus data sint, confugit. Cajetanus & Sanctius, non da- tum civitatum illarum mancipium, sed usum, ut nempe illarum fructum tamdiu perciperet, quam- diu de impensis in templi, regiæque domus con- structione factis sibi satis fieret, existimant, quod Sa- liano, Serario, Hottomanno etiam placuit; alii cen- sent oppida illa primum Regis Hiram fuisse, quæ cum ipse despiceret, Salomoni exædificanda, & ci- vibus instruenda tradiderit, & ædificata jam & inha- bitata Salomo iterum Regi reddiderit, quæ etiam Cajetani est conjectura. Nonnulli cum Dionysio probabile judicant, hunc Regem Tyrium ad fi- dem per diuturnam cum Davide, & Salomone a- micitiam conversum fuisse: Sed quum nulla ea- rum sententiarum satisfaciat dubiis propositis, nec ad usumfructum peregrinæ genti civitates Israel cedi potuerint, neque ratio sit, cur Hiramus illas repudiarit, si suffecerunt expensis rependendis ad certum tempus exinde percipiendis (non opus e- rat, ut placerent oculis ejus, quas in perpetuum possidere non debebat) præferenda hic Grotii sen- tentia, vel Junii potius, à quo illam habet Grotius. Interim quia nonnulli cum Cajetano hic observant, si casus necessitatis intervenisset, excusari potuisse Sa- lomonem, adeoque supponunt, in casu necessitatis vel majoris mali avertendi, aut majoris boni pro- movendi alienationem fieri potuisse, B. Dorscheus noster in præfat. dedic. prodromi anticriseos suæ Theologicæ non immerito judicium hoc opponit palliato Ernesto de Eusebiis, & Anonymo vehiculario PACEM Osnabrugensem prætensione illicitæ alie- nationis impugnanti maxime, quia ea necessitatis, quam vocant causa, in Republ. Israelitica tam fre- quenter usurpata fuit, ut ubique exempla sint ob- via, ubi prætensiones possessionesque Ecclesiasti- carum personarum jure quidem debitæ, cesserunt tamen bono publico, & negotiorum publicorum inopinis casibus.

## 9:13
Verse 13.

LAND OF CHABUL] Josephus teaches that this signifies 'displeasing' in the language of the Phoenicians. To the Arabs, حبل is to disturb. Moreover, we learn from 2 Chronicles 8:2 that these towns were returned by Hiram to Solomon. See Joshua 19:22.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

TERRAM CHABUL] Id Phœnicum lingua significare displicentem docet Josephus. Arabibus حبل est perturbare. Reddito autem ab Hiromo Solomoni hæc op- pida discimus 2. Paralip. 8, 2. Vide Josuam 19, 22.

## 9:16
Verse 16.

HE GAVE IT AS A DOWRY TO HIS DAUGHTER] Thus, in Homer, Agamemnon promises that he will give towns as a dowry to his daughter.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

DEDIT EAM IN DOTEM FILIÆ SUÆ] Sic apud Homerum Agamemnon oppida in dotem filiæ suæ daturum se pollicetur.

## 9:18
Verse 18.

PALMYRA IN THE LAND OF THE WILDERNESS) The Palmyrene wildernesses are named in Pliny, book V, chapters 24 and 26. Josephus also teaches us that what is Palmyra to the Greeks is called Thadamora by the Syrians.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

PALMYRAM IN TERRA SOLITUDINIS) Palmy- renæ solitudines apud Plinium nominantur libro V. cap. 24. & 26. Thadamoram autem a Syris vocari quæ Græcis sit Palmyra, etiam Josephus nos docet.

## 9:19
TO BUILD IN JERUSALEM) Which is the most famous of the cities of the East to Pliny: a most famous city to Tacitus.

Latin:

UT ÆDIFICARET IN JERUSALEM) Quæ clarissi- ma urbium Orientis Plinio: urbs famosissima Tacito.

## 9:21
Verse 21.

SOLOMON MADE TRIBUTARIES) He spared them: namely because they had not resisted, but had surrendered themselves to Solomon. See what is said at Deuteronomy 20:10 and in 'De Jure Belli ac Pacis', book 2, chapter 13, § 4. He ordered them, however, ἐντίνειν αὐτῷ καὶ οἰκετικὰς χρείας ἐκτελεῖν, as Josephus says here.

From them Solomon, besides a monetary tribute, also exacted perpetual servitude, whence even after the Babylonian captivity they retained the name of servants of Solomon, Ezra 2:55, Nehemiah 7:60.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

FECIT SALOMON TRIBUTARIOS) Servavit eos: nempe quia non repugnaverant, sed se Salomoni dediderant. Vide quæ ad Deuteron. 20, 10. & de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 2. c. 13. §. 4. Jussit autem eos ἐντίνειν αὐτῷ καὶ οἰκετικὰς χρείας ἐκτελεῖν, ut hic Josephus.

Ab illis Salomo præter pecuniarium tribu- tum servitutem etiam exegit in perpetuum, unde e- tiam post captivitatem Babyl. nomen servorum Sa- lomonis retinuerunt Esdr. 2, 55. Nehem. 7, 60.

## 9:22
Verse 22.

BUT OF THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL DID SOLOMON MAKE NO MAN SERVANTS) He did not assign them to base works.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

DE FILIIS AUTEM ISRAEL NON CONSTITV- IT SALOMON SERVIRE QVENQVAM) Operis vili- bus eos non addixit.

## 9:23
Verse 23.

OVER ALL THE WORKS OF SOLOMON WERE FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY) Namely Israelites, under whom were other ἐργοδιῶκται (taskmasters), three hundred foreigners, as we gather from 2 Chronicles 8:10 and ibid. 2:18, if you compare the passage of this book, verse 16.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

SUPER OMNIA OPERA SALOMONIS PRÆPOSI- TI QVINGENTI QVINQVAGINTA) Nempe Israeli- tæ, sub quibus erant alii ἐργοδιῶκται, peregrini trecenti ut colligimus ex 2. Paralip. 8, 10. & ibid. 2, 18. si conferas lo- cum hujus libri V. 16.

## 9:24
Verse 24.

THEN HE BUILT MILLO) A house joined to the walls of Jerusalem, into which they gathered for the sake of counsel. Thus David Kimchi.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

TVNC ÆDIFICAVIT MELLO) Domum conjun- ctam mœnibus Hierosolymorum, in quam consilii causa coi- batur. Sic David Kimchi.

## 9:26
Verse 26.

IN EZION-GEBER) Which was later called Berenice, according to Josephus.

BESIDE ELATH ON THE SHORE OF THE RED SEA) κόλπος Αἰλὰ (Gulf of Aila) according to Stephanus; the Elanitic Gulf according to Pliny. The city Αειλὰν (Ailan) according to Strabo, the gulf Ελανίτης (Elanites). Philostorgius says Αειλὰ (Aila) is the ancient name of the city in that part of the Red Sea which approaches Palestine. It is written Αἴλα (Aila) in the Notitia Imperii. Αἰλα (Aila) according to Procopius in his Persian Wars I.

IN THE LAND OF EDOM) From this we see that the borders of the Edomites extended as far as the Red Sea. And from the name of Edom turned into Greek, that sea was called Erythraean. Which the Latins wrongly translated as Red, since Strabo, Arrian, Ctesias in Photius, Solinus, Curtius, and Stephanus rightly note that Erythras is the name of an ancient king. When David completely subdued Edom, this maritime town also came to him. But from where did the Tyrians sail? From the island of Tyre in the Arabian Gulf, a colony of the Tyrians, concerning which see Strabo in book XVI and Stephanus. Nor do the manuscript books of Ptolemy write the name of this island otherwise. Others, however, call it Tyle, as Stephanus also warned, due to a corrupted pronunciation over time. But Strabo says openly that it is a colony of the Tyrians. Some place this island in the Persian Gulf: Theophrastus in the Arabian: Pliny sometimes in the Persian, sometimes in the Arabian, unless there were several islands of the same name.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

IN ASIONGABER) Quæ Berenice dicta postea Jose- pho teste.

JUXTA AILATH IN LITTORE MARIS RUBRI) κόλπος Αἰλὰ apud Stephanum : Ælanniticus sinus Plinio. Urbs Αειλὰν Straboni, sinus Ελανίτης. Philostorgius Ἀειλὰ dicit antiqui nominis esse urbem in ea parte Maris Rubri, quæ ad Palæstinam accedit. Αἴλα scribitur in Notitia Imperii. Αἰλα apud Procopium Persicorum I.

IN TERRA IDUMÆÆ) Hinc videmus ad mare rubrum usque pertinuisse Idumæos fines. Et ex nomine Edomi in Græcum verso mare illud Erythræum dictum est. Quod ma- le Latini Rubrum vertere, cum Erythram regis antiqui esse nomen recte notent Strabo, Arrianus, Ctesias apud Photi- um, Solinus, Curtius, Stephanus. Cum Idumæam omnem perdomuit David, etiam hoc oppidum maritimum ad eum devenit. At unde Tyrii navigarunt ? A Tyro insula in sinu Arabico Tyriorum colonia, de qua videndus Strabo libro XVI. & Stephanus. Nec aliter nomen hujus Insulæ scri- bunt Manuscripti libri Ptolemæi. Alii vero Tylen vocant, ut & Stephanus monuit, per tempora corrupta pronuntiatio- ne. Sed coloniam Tyriorum esse aperte dicit Strabo. Qui- dam hanc insulam in Persico ponunt Sinu: Theophrastus in Arabico: Plinius modo in Persico, modo in Arabico, nisi plu- res insulæ fuere ejusdem nominis.

## 9:28
Verse 28.

IN OPHIR) For אופיר, the LXX and Josephus read סופיר here and wherever the same name occurs in the following. But where shall we say this land was, whether to the right of those exiting the Red Sea, that is, in Africa; or to the left, that is, in Asia? Both Josephus and Jerome lead us to Asia, and indeed to that part of India which is called golden. The most learned of the Portuguese, to whom that coast became very well known, say that all the marks which we have here and below in 10, 11, and 22 correspond to that part of India which is beyond the Ganges and is now called the kingdom of Pegu. For there is a great abundance of gold and silver there, the best gems, elephants, apes, peacocks, and besides, most beautiful woods from which lyres are made. And perhaps the name Sapphiri comes from that land, and the city of Sambra in Ptolemy. Let us consider, however, whether perhaps the Phoenician and Jewish ships did not go as far as India, but to a town situated on the Arabian Gulf, where it looks toward the Ocean, which Arrian calls Aphar, Pliny Saphar, Ptolemy Sappara, Stephanus Sapphirina, so that the Indians indeed brought their goods here, but from there sought to go further away from India.

The fleet is said to have been made in Asion Gaber, עשה אניות, ναὺν ἐποίησεν. Josephus rendered it aptly with one word in book 8, chapter 2, ἐναυπηγήσατο, Solomon built ships, or caused them to be built. Asiongaber was therefore a place established for building, or assembling, adorning, and equipping Solomon's ships: it was called Essia in the time of Jerome, who says in his 'On Hebrew Places': It is the city Esan, which they think is now called Essia near the Red Sea and Aila. Here, moreover, was the port of Eloth for the Solomonic fleet, ἐλάνα or ἐλλάνα in Ptolemy, ἄλανα or ἄιλανα in Diodorus Siculus. Pliny, book 6, chapter 28, calls it Aelana. Naturally, after the promontory, as Strabo notes in Geography book 16, which extends as far as the rock of the Arabs who are called Nabataeans, and into Palestine (which is named Pharan by Ptolemy), there follows the Elamitic Gulf, which Diodorus, in book 3 of his History, says is inhabited by many villages of the Nabataean Arabs. The chief of which is Elana, from which the whole gulf took its name, called a city by Strabo because of its size: which is also called by one name, the white village or hamlet, by

Fuller notes Diodorus in book 4 of his Miscellanies, chapter 20. Concerning whom Strabo says: From the White Village to Petra, and from Petra to Rhinocolura, which is in Phoenicia itself near Egypt, Indian and Arabian goods used to be carried, and from here to other places: Now the greatest part is carried through the Nile to Alexandria: in which testimony of Strabo, Fuller observes that clear traces of the Indian trade first instituted by Solomon are detected: For as long as the Edomites were under the dominion of the Kings of Judah, Indian merchants were accustomed to seek Petra from the city of Elana or the White Village; and from there to transport goods to Jerusalem and Tyre. But after they created a king for themselves, the Edomites revolted from the Jews (which happened while the impious Joram, son of the pious Jehoshaphat, was reigning), the ancient custom was changed somewhat. For the merchants carried their goods from Elana, in the usual manner, to Petra: but from there they proceeded no further, for the Idumean King, having forbidden them the trade of the Jews, they began to divert to Rhinocolura by a new route. Which custom indeed seems to have remained for a very long time; until the Ptolemies, Kings of the Egyptians, flourishing in wealth and power, strove with the greatest effort to draw the Indian and Arabian trade to Alexandria. Noting the error of Josephus, who confused Ethion-Geber, situated to the east in Nabataea, with the Egyptian port of Berenice to the east, Fuller cites Arrian: To the left of Berenice, at a distance of two or three days' sailing from the port of the Sea, to one crossing the adjacent gulf towards the east, another port and garrison occurs, which is called the White Village. From which one goes to Petra to Malichus, king of the Nabataeans. That garrison itself also serves as an emporium for smaller vessels, which put in there from Arabia. Wherefore, for the sake of caution and custody, it is also customary to send there one who may exact the fourth part of the goods that are imported, and a Centurion with an army. From which words of Arrian, he judges it to be clear that, while the Egyptian or Alexandrian market was still in its greatest celebrity, the Edomite emporium was not entirely reduced to solitude, nor had it ceased to be frequented at all, but had preserved the remains of its ancient trade sufficiently illustrious and conspicuous, and that therefore that emporium, which posterity called by the recent name λευκὴν κώμην (White Village), is held to be, and in truth is, the ancient Elana: Comparing especially the place of Jerome on the Hebrew places: Ailat in the extreme borders of Palestine, joined to the southern solitude and the Red Sea. Whence one sails from Egypt to India and from there to Egypt. But a Roman legion, by the name of the Tenth, is stationed there. And formerly indeed it was called Ailat by the ancients, but now it is called Aila. To which also pertains the observation of Fuller concerning the Phoenician town founded not so far from Elana on the Arabian shore, named Astarte after the most ancient goddess of the Sidonians, of which Ptolemy makes mention in book 6, chapter 7. Compare what will be said on the next chapter, verse 22.

Moreover, since that shipyard of Ezion-geber is established near Ailoth, which is said to have been situated on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, it is manifest from this that the fleet likewise made by Jehoshaphat in Ezion-geber, which was to go to Tarshish, as is held in 2 Chron. 20:36, did not set sail in any port of the Mediterranean Sea, but rather in the port of the Red Sea, Ailoth, because it is said in this place that that fleet was equipped in Ezion-geber near Ailoth, or in the vicinity of the same; so that it could be dispatched from the nearby port of Ailoth in the Arabian Gulf. For if it had been necessary to set sail from the port of Joppa or another in the Mediterranean Sea (which some wish to be indicated by the name Tarshish), or to be dispatched to Tartessus in Spain, through the internal or Mediterranean sea, just as Grotius and some others understand Tarshish as Tartessus, the ships of either Solomon or Jehoshaphat, which were situated at the Red Sea, would by no means have been built in such an inconvenient place as Ezion-geber. For from the Erythraean or Red Sea, the navigation to the Mediterranean Sea is very long and dangerous, which therefore would have been inconvenient and entirely useless. Compare what is said on chapter 10 concerning Tarshish.

Verse 28. AND THEY TOOK FROM THENCE GOLD OF FOUR HUNDRED AND TWENTY TALENTS] Of purified gold: for the mass had been 350 talents, 2 Chron. 8:18.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

IN OPHIR) Pro אופיר & LXX. & Josephus legerunt סופיר hic & ubi in sequentibus idem nomen occurrit. Vbi vero dicemus hanc fuisse terram, an ad dextram egredienti- bus mare rubrum, id est, in Africa; an ad sinistram, id est in Asia ? In Asiam & quidem in partem Indiæ, quæ aurea dici- tur, nos ducunt & Josephus & Hieronymus. Lusitanorum, quibus ea ora maxime pernotuit, eruditissimi ajunt, in eam partem Indiæ, quæ ultra Gangem est & regnum Pegusiæ nunc dicitur, congruere omnes quas hic & infra 10. 11. & 22. habe- mus notas. Esse enim ibi auri & argenti magnam copiam, gemmas optimas, Elephantos, simias, pavones, præterea li- gna pulcherrima, unde citharæ funt. Et forte Sapphiri no- men habent ab ea terra, & Sambra urbs apud Ptolomæum. Cogitemus tamen an forte non in Indiam usque iverint naves Phœnissæ & Judaicæ, sed ad oppidum adfitum Arabico sinui, qua is ad Oceanum spectat, quod Aphar vocat Arrianus, Pli- nius Saphar, Ptolomæus Sappara, Stephanus Sapphirinam, ut Indi nempe suas res huc tulerint, inde autem petierint longius ab India absiri.

Classis facta dicitur in Asion Gaber עשה אניות ναὺν ἐποίησεν. Josephus uno verbo apposite reddi- dit l. 8. c. 2. ἐναυπηγήσατο naves fabricatus est, sive fabricandas curavit Salomo. Erat ergo Asionga- ber locus ædificandis vel compingendis, adornan- dis, instruendis navibus Salomonis constitutus: Essia nuncupabatur tempore Hieronymi; qui de lo- cis Hebraic. Est civitas, inquit, Esan,quam nunc Es- siam nuncupari putant juxta mare rubrum, & Ai- lam. Hic autem Elothis portus erat classis Salomo- neæ, ἐλάνα vel ἐλλάνα Ptolemæo, ἄλανα vel ἄιλανα Diodor. Sicul. Plin. lib. 6. c. 28. Aelana dicitur. Nimirum post promontorium, notante Strabone Geogr. lib. 16. quod usq; ad petram Arabum, qui Nabatæi dicuntur, & in Palæstinam pertendit (quod Pharan nominatur à Ptolemæo) succedit Elamiti- cus sinus, quem multis pagis Arabum Nabatæorum cir- cumhabitantium dicit Diodor. l. 3. Hist. Quorum præ- cipuus Elana, à qua totus sinus nomen traxit, Stra- boni πόλις ob magnitudinem vocatur: quam etiam album pagum, vel vicum uno nomine appellari à

Diodoro notat Fullers l. 4. Miscell. c. 20. De quo Strabo: Albo pago in petram, ex Petra Rhinocolu- ram, quæ in ipsa Phœnicia est apud Ægyptum, merces Indicæ Arabicæq́; solebant portari, atque hinc in alia loca: Nunc pars maxima per Nilum Alexandriam vehitur: in quo Strabonis testimonio negotiatio- nis Indicæ mari à Salomone primum institutæ ve- stigia non obscura deprehendi observat Fullerus: Donec enim Edomæi in ditione Regum Judæ erant, solebant mercatores Indici ex urbe Elana sive Albo pago Petram petere: atq́; inde Hierosolymam Tyrumq́; merces pervehere. At postquam creato sibi rege, dese- cerunt à Judæis Edomæi, (quod Joramo impio pii Jo- saphati filio regnante accidit) immutatus est aliquan- tum mos antiquus. Siquidem deportarunt Elana ne- gotiatores merces suas, more solito, Petram: inde au- tem nequaquam ulterius progressi, interdicente videlicet eis Rege Idumæo Judæorum commercio, novo jam itinere Rhinocoluram divertere cœperunt. Qui mos sane perquam diu mansisse videtur: usq́; dum Pto- lemæi, Ægyptiorum Reges, opibus & potentia floren- tes, Indicam & Arabicam quoq́; negotiationem Ale- xandriam pertrahere summo conatu studuerunt. Notato errore Josephi, qui Ethionem Geberis ad o- rientem in Nabatæa situm cum portu Ægyptiaco Be- renicis ad orientem confudit, Arrianum adducit Ful- lerus: Ad sinistram Berenices, bidui aut tridui à Maris portu navigatione, adjacentem sinum ortum versus transmittenti, occurrit portus alius & præsi- dium, quod Albus pagus dicitur. Ex quo Petram itur ad Mali Mam Nabatæorum regem. Est & ipsum il- lud præsidium Emporii loco minoribus navigiis, quæ ex Arabia illuc appellantur. Quocirca cautionis et- iam & custodiæ causa eodem mitti solet, qui quartam partem mercium, quæ importantur, exigat, & Centu- rio cum exercitu. Equibus Arriani verbis lique- re censet, vigente etiamnum mercatus Ægyptii, si- ve Alexandrini, maxima celebritate, Emporium Edomæum non prorsus ad solitudinem redactum, nec omnino frequentari desitum, sed antiquæ ne- gotiationis reliquias satis illustres & conspicuas us- que servasse, atque adeo Emporium illud, quod λευ- κὴν κώμην Album pagum nomine nupero vocarunt posteri, vetusto & suo Elanam perhiberi ac revera esse: Conferens imprimis Hieronym. locum de loc. Hebr. Ailat in extremis finibus Palæstinæ, jun- cta meridianæ solitudini & mari rubro. Unde ex Æ- gypto Indiam & inde ad Ægyptum navigatur. Sedet autem ibi legio Romana cognomento decima. Et olim quidem Ailat à veteribus dicebatur, nunc vero appellatur Aila. Quo etiam facit observatio Fulleri de Phœnicum oppido non ita procul Elana in littore Arabico condito Astarte à Sidoniorum Dea antiquissima nuncupato, cujus Ptolem. l. 6. 7. mentionem fecit. Conf. quæ ad cap. proximum 10. v. 22. dicentur.

Cæterum cum juxta Ailoth, quæ in littore ma- ris rubri in terra Edom sita fuisse dicitur, constitua- tur ναυπήγιον illud Aesiongeber, manifestum inde oppido est, classem in Asiongaber similiter factam à Josaphato, quæ in Tharsis iret, ut habetur 2. Par. 20, 36. neutiquam solvisse in portu aliquo maris mediterranei, sed potius in portu maris rubri, Ai- loth, quia ideo dicitur hoc loco juxta Ailoth, vel in vicinia ejusdem classem illam instructam esse in Asiongaber; ut è portu Ailoth propinquo in sinu Arabico expediri posset. Quum si è portu Joppen vel alio in mari mediterraneo (quod nomine Tarsis nonnulli indicari volunt) solvere debuisset, vel Tartessum in Hispaniam expediri, per mare inter- num seu mediterraneum, quemadmodum Grotius & alii nonnulli per Tarsin Tartessum intelligunt, nequaquam in tam diffito loco Asiongaber extru- ctæ fuissent naves sive Salomonis seu Josaphati, qui ad mare rubrum situs fuit. Nam ex mari Ery- thræo vel rubro longa admodum ac periculosa est ad mare mediterraneum navigatio, quæ proinde importuna, & inutilis omnino fuisset. Conf. quæ ad c. 10. de Tarsis.

Vers. 28. SVMTVMINDE AVRVM QVADRIN- GENTORVM VIGINTI TALENTORVM] Auri depu- rati: nam massa fuerat CCCL. talentorum 2. Par. 8, 18.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

The Queen of Sheba admires Solomon's wisdom. His riches, and magnificence with the Royal throne.

Verse 1.

QUEEN OF SHEBA) Of Meroe as it seems, in which for many centuries women ruled, having assumed the name Candace, as Strabo teaches us in books 16 and 17. Pliny however, 6.29. Under her reign were also the Sabritae, according to Strabo, which name does not differ much from Sheba.

They also make her the Queen of Ethiopia, along with Josephus, Ant. 8. c. 2, Rabanus, Nauclerus, Tostatus, Hugo, Dionysius, Toletus, Maldonatus, Jansenius, Barradius, Franciscus Lucas on Matthew 12, Genebrardus, Cornel. à Lapide here, likewise Junius and Tremellius, Sixtin. Amama, Spanhemius on Matthew 2, dub. Evangel., Ortelius, and others: and Erasmus Schmidius also fights for that opinion on Matthew 20 with this argument (which others have rather used against the same) that שבא with Schin denotes Ethiopia, not Arabia, and he thinks that is demonstrative. Others urge that Ethiopia is to the south of Judea, since this Queen is called the Queen of the South in Matthew 12:42, and that it is very far distant from Judea, as that Queen is said to have come from the ends of the earth in Matthew 12: and also that it abounds in gold more than Arabia, that it is incense-bearing and aromatic, and that women have been accustomed to rule there, which is Grotius's only argument here, and that there is a constant and continuous tradition among the Ethiopians or Abyssinians that their emperors trace their origin from Solomon, from whom the Queen conceived offspring, who acquired the name of David: whence Prester John, the Abyssinian Emperor, boasts of this David, son of David, son of Solomon, in his title, according to Ortelius in his Theatre, table 68. They also appeal to the authority of Gregory of Nyssa, hom. 7 on Canticles, Nazianzen, Orat. 40, Augustine, serm. 142 de Temp., as also Anastasius Sinaita, Euthymius, Anselm, Origen, likewise hom. 2 on Canticles, nay even Jerome on Isaiah 43.

But others more correctly maintain that this Queen was of Arabia, not Ethiopia: because שבא does not denote Ethiopia, but Arabia Felix, which is most clear from various places in Scripture, nay from the very origin of the naming, Gen. 10, where in verse 7, the son of Cush, called סבא, provided the name and family to the Sabeans of Ethiopia, as Josephus himself holds, and Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges, as does Pelargus, but not, as Schmidius wishes, to the inhabitants of Arabia Felix, nor, as Junius and Tremellius think, to those of Arabia Deserta. But the grandson of Cush from his son Raamah, called שבא, is celebrated as the Father of the inhabitants of Arabia Felix, as Jerome observes in his Hebrew Traditions, whom Tremellius and Junius, as well as Schmidius, vainly judge to be the progenitor of the Ethiopians. For Jerome deserves credit here above others, especially: whose observation is as follows: The sons of Raamah, Sheba and Dedan: This שבא is written with the letter Schin, but above (when the son of Cush is named) it is written with the letter Samech, from whom we said the Sabaeans were named. But now שבא is interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we have Kings of the Arabs and Saba shall offer gifts, it is written in Hebrew Kings שבא, the first name with Schin, the second with Samech. Cornelius à Lapide agrees with Jerome on Is. 60, 6. Saba (Arabia Felix) is said with Schin from Saba the son of Raamah the son of Cush: Just as Ethiopia is said to be Saba with Samech from Saba. From this name שבא Sabai Job 1, 15. the inhabitants in Arabia are called, who were given to plunder, as Pliny testifies l. 6. c. 28. Strabo l. 16. Diodorus l. 3. c. 12. where the interpreters understand the Arabs ὁμοθυμαδὸν, not the Ethiopians. Which name is also had in Job 6, 19. Teman is joined with שבא, and thus Arabia is denoted by this word. Ps. 72, 10. as has already been observed by Jerome, the Kings of שבא are the Kings of the Arabs; to whom the Kings of סבא of Saba are joined in bringing gifts: which the latter is commonly thought by interpreters to signify Ethiopia there, and the Jesuit Cornelius acknowledges it on Is. 60, 6. This name also occurs in Is. 60, 6. All from Sheba שבא shall come bringing gold and incense: In which place John Pineda on Job 1, 15. acknowledged that Jerome understands Arabia Felix, and Cornelius adds his support to him, although the Jesuit wishes for Ethiopia also to be included by that word, confusing the words which the Holy Scriptures clearly distinguished in Ps. 72, 10. The same name is also observed in Jer. 6, 20. why to me incense from Saba שבא bringing, and sweet-smelling cane from a far country? To which place Cornelius: For incense is produced in Sabaean Arabia. So also Jerome: That incenses come from Saba, no one doubts. Nor does anyone there, as far as is known, understand Ethiopia. The same must be held concerning the passage Ez. 27, 20. The sellers of שבא Saba and Raamah are your own merchants: where it is strange that Jerome complains that he could read רעמה from סבא and find in no other place of the Scriptures what it signifies. Since there is had in Gen. 10, 7. a son of Cush of that name, from whom the province in Arabia Felix obtained its name: just as Junius and Tremellius acknowledge that Raamah was the author of the peoples of Arabia Felix, and they prove it from Ez. 27, 22; and they observe that Ptolemy called it Regama. Whence rightly Corn. à Lap. on Ez. 27. Saba are the Arabians, the Sabaeans. Raamah is a city of Arabia Felix. Finally, Joel 3, 8. the name Saba is found again: They will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation. In which place Jerome understands neither Arabia nor Ethiopia, but a more distant nation, these things which are read in his commentary teach: so that the Jews might sell them not to the Persians, and Ethiopians, and the rest of the nations which are neighbors (for the Arabs are nearer to the Ethiopians) but to the Sabaeans, a most distant nation, which he previously called a nation beyond India, and he thinks Isaiah speaks of it in c. 45, 14. where, however, not שבא, but סבא with Samech is had, and Sabaea is rightly understood as Ethiopia, as also in Is. 43, 3. But although he himself warned in his Hebrew Traditions on Gen. c. 10. that these words are distinct, he nevertheless confuses them sometimes, as if they did not designate distinct provinces, which it is clear from Gen. 10, 7. and Ps. 72, 10. must be distinguished entirely. To this distant nation situated beyond India, the same Jerome, in the cited passage of Joel, places the Queen of Saba, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon: Whence he also says that incense comes: whose true native soil Jerome seems elsewhere to have designated as the Sabaea of Arabia. Who handed down these things concerning the Queen of Saba in his Commentary on Is. 60: Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, fertile in camels, and the whole province is called Saba, whence also the Queen of Saba, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and she herself bringing gold and incense etc. Some, however, reconcile Jerome in this way, that here he

placed Saba, simply so named, and did not draw the same from the tract and name of Arabia of widest extent; but only from that part of Arabia which enjoys only the name of Arabia, and is nearer to Arabia Deserta or Petraea; and thus they also bring light to the passage of Jerome on Joel 3. Sabaea is called a nation beyond India, from which was the Queen of Saba, whence also incense is said to come, Virgil saying, and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense. Although some suspect those to be the Arabians: where by the Arabs whom others suspect, they understand those very ones who are more rustic and predatory; but they think that by the Sabaean region beyond India, the lower Arabs toward the South and India and the Indian Sea in Arabia Felix are designated. Rightly, therefore, on that passage of Joel, Cornelius à Lapide observes a double Sabaea, both of them distant, although he hesitates as to which one he ought to understand, because he does not notice that in the Hebrew text שבא is read with Schin, which name he himself does not doubt is the Saba of Arabia. The Sabaeans, he says, are either Ethiopians or Arabs of Arabia Felix, of whom the poet says: And a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense. For Saba is twofold: One in Ethiopia, the other in Arabia, both distant and far removed from Judea. Thus, therefore, from the induction of the passages where the name שבא occurs, it is established that Arabia Felix has always been designated, but never Ethiopia, which is called by the distinct name סבא in 10, 7. Ps. 72, 10. Is. 43, 3. c. 45, 14. Whence Cornelius, when in this place 1 Kings 10, 1. would prefer to understand Ethiopia, he used this desperate exception, that the Rabbis had wrongly placed the dot on the right horn here, and thus had made a Schin, when it should have been placed on the left, and read as Sin, not noticing that the diversity of the names is not in the placement of the dot alone, but in the letters themselves, since one is written with Schin, the other with Samech, which difference, although he esteems it little, has nevertheless already been shown to be accurately observed in the Scriptures.

This opinion concerning Arabia Felix is further confirmed by the circumstances which are reported concerning the Queen of Solomonic wisdom: namely, that she heard of the fame of Solomon, which could have been carried to her by the commerce of navigation, which took place in the Red Sea, and from Ezion-geber into Arabia, as well as from the abundance of camels, in which Arabia Deserta especially abounds, on account of the breadth of the pastures of the wilderness and the temperateness of the air, in which this animal delights, as Jerome testifies at Ezekiel 27. (Adrichomius also establishes troops of camels and elephants in Arabia Felix in his description of the Holy Land under the title Manasseh, p. 77.) and also from the quality and quantity of the gifts which the Queen brought, which suit no region so well as Arabia, namely gold, spices, and gems: concerning which Adrichomius is prolix in the place cited. Moreover, it is called εὐδαίμων, Felix, on account of the abundance of incense and spices, as Jerome testifies at the Hebrew Places of the Acts of the Apostles, letter A. which Pliny calls odoriferous and rich, and famous by the surname of blessed, book 5, chapter 11; furthermore, others call it λι- βανόφορον and ἀρωματόφορον, that is, incense-bearing and spice-bearing. For frankincense is proper to this Arabia, nor is it produced elsewhere. It also abounds so much in veins and clods of gold and silver that almost all the furniture of this nation shines, some with gold, some with silver, and gold is sold to neighbors at triple the price of bronze, and silver at double: finally, it is very productive of the most precious gems and pearls. Compare Pliny, book 12, chapter 28; Diodorus Siculus, book 3, chapter 12; and the verses of Dionysius, who lived in that part of Arabia, concerning the excellence of this kingdom, in Hottinger, Oriental History, p. 240. Strabo, book 15, says: Such an abundance of spices overflows that they use cinnamon, cassia, and other such things instead of brushwood and useful timber. These (the Sabaeans) and the Gerrhaeans are the wealthiest of all on account of their exceptional resources joined, endowed with various equipment, with vessels of gold and silver, etc. On account of which fertility and pleasantness, ancient historians commemorate that Alexander the Great, after his return from India into Arabia, decided to found his royal seat. Whence also in the Scriptures it is celebrated for incense and gold Ps. 72, 10. Is. 60, 6. Jer. 6, 20. as well as for aromatics and gems Ez. 27, 20.

Furthermore, there occurs the description which Christ provided, Matt. 12, 42, when he called her the Queen of the South, who came from the ends of the earth. For that Arabia is to the south of Jerusalem is beyond doubt, and Schmidius acknowledges this: because Arabia Felix has almost the same meridian as Jerusalem, so that Judea and Jerusalem are more northerly, and Arabia Felix and its Saba are more southerly. Herodotus also places Arabia to the south in book 8, and Diodorus in the cited book. Moreover, she who came from Arabia is rightly said to have come from the ends of the earth. For it is distant 606 French leagues from Jerusalem, as Adrichomius notes. And therefore it is called a far country, Jer. 6, 20. And it is that region at the extreme part toward the Indian or Arabian Sea, of which Nicephorus speaks in book 8, 35: the Sabaeans of India were called first, then also the Homeritae. That nation born from Abraham and Keturah: that region which the Greeks say is Great and Happy Arabia, and whose borders reach the extreme Ocean, of which the metropolis and primary city is Saba. Herodotus in book 3 has it thus: To the south, the last of the inhabited regions is Arabia, in which ALONE all things are born: incense, myrrh, cassia, cinnamon, etc. Finally, they raise a doubt about the rule of women, which was more customary in Ethiopia than in Arabia; but Pineda observes in book 5 on the affairs of Solomon, chapter 14, § 6, that the same also prevailed in Arabia, although not always and by perpetual custom, but by time and chance.

And to this opinion concerning Arabia Felix, Cajetanus, Eugubinus, Gagneius, Lippomannus, Sanctius, Joh. Benedict. Christian. Adrichomius, Georg. Venet. Pererius, Schvarez, Baronius, and others among the Papists add their vote, as does Pineda, who in his Commentary on Job at chapter 1, 16, had contended that this queen was of Ethiopia, but afterwards, having weighed the matter more accurately with various documents in book 5 on the affairs of Solomon, he made her a queen of Arabia, to which our B. Luther and most others agree: and among the Fathers, not only Jerome, Eucherius, and Isidore in book 14 of the Etymologies, and Nicephorus in the cited book, favor this opinion, but also those whom the patrons of Ethiopia allege for themselves. For although they name Ethiopia, it must be observed, however, that they do not speak of African Ethiopia, which is across Egypt, but of Asiatic, which Theodoret calls Indian Ethiopia: which certainly is not African. For to question 32 in 1. Kings in the works of M. T. 1, p. 550, 'What is Sabaea?' he answers, 'Ethiopian': here, however, he says they are situated in the Indian Sea. They call them, however, the Homeritae. They are, moreover, from the region of the Axamitae. Between these and those, however, is the middle sea. Their Queen was that admirable woman, whose zeal he praised in the Gospel. So also Procopius of Gaza has it in Ecclesiastes: 'Queen of Saba: it is an Ethiopian nation, they say it is situated by the Indian Sea. They call them, however, the Homeritae, they are opposite the Axamitae, and the middle sea is between them.' For not only Nicephorus in the cited book, but also Ptolemy make the Homeritae a people of Arabia, and Nicephorus hands down that they were called Sabaeans, and Pliny also joins them in book 6, c. 28, the Homeritae with the Sabaeans, in Arabia. Cyril of Alexandria in book 5 on Isaiah c. 6, says: 'Saba is a region beyond the land of the Arabs and near the Red Sea, from which Saba the Queen of the Ethiopians came to Jerusalem in the times of Solomon.' That region is most fertile in incense, gold, and Indian stones. This explanation is also favored by Tirinus on Numbers 12, 1, observing that there is a double Ethiopia: one Western in Africa, extended further beyond Egypt, and subject to the Torrid Zone: over which Prester John now rules: the other Eastern, which is otherwise called Arabia, is certainly a part of Arabia, and includes the Midianites and other peoples who incline toward the Arabian Gulf toward the South. Thus Herodotus book 7, Pliny book 5, c. 8, Augustine, Theodoret, and others.

But not much is to be attributed to the tradition and boasting of the Ethiopians, who are known to be immoderate trumpeters of their own affairs, and that fable about Solomon and the impregnation of the Queen and the origin of the Abyssinian Kings is more like a tradition than history, and to it must be opposed the tradition of others concerning the Queen of Arabia, which Nicephorus also exhibits in the cited book, when he says that the FAME obtains that the Queen of the South came to Solomon from Arabia Felix. Sanctius also reports on 1 Kings 10 that Peter Paez, sent into that Indian Ethiopia, announced that a city was shown to him by the natives at the Arabian Gulf, in which the Queen of Saba is believed to have been born. Which the Arabs claim as their own just as much as the Ethiopians. Concerning whose trifles and more vain Sicilian tales in this matter, more can be read in Sanctius in the cited place. Grotius himself refuted the fabrication and boasting of the Abyssinians in this place. The Abyssinians falsely claim this woman for themselves, being also injurious to her reputation, when they say she came to Solomon with the same intention as Thalestris to Alexander. Nor does the fable of the Ethiopians agree with the narrative of Josephus: he says this queen was called Nicaula: they, however, call her Maqueda: some say she was a Sibyl, etc. Let Pineda be compared in the cited place, and our B. Walther, who presents the sum of the matter in this case from the same in the newest edition of his Harmony on 1 Kings 8, 1.

As for the demonstration of Schmidius for Ethiopia, reasoning thus: Of those lands which are south of Jerusalem, only that which once had the name of Sheba, the Queen of the South came to Solomon. But only Ethiopian Meroe had the name of Sheba, with historians and philologists agreeing as witnesses: Therefore, from Ethiopian Meroe alone came the Queen of the South to Solomon: this, with the major proposition admitted and Sheba of Arabia Felix substituted in place of the minor, will be invincible for our opinion, but for the opposing one it has no strength, because its minor cannot be proven. For who are those historians, who are those philologists, who assert with this consenting vote that Ethiopian Meroe, and it alone, was called by the name of Sheba? Genebrardus indeed, and the interpretation of Hebrew names which circulates at the end of the Bibles, as noted by Pineda on Job 1:15, say that שבא with Schin signifies Ethiopia, but סבא with Samech signifies Arabia Felix, and the Junius-Tremellius notes on Gen. 10:7 support this thus far, because Ethiopia draws its origin from שבא the son of Raamah, but they do not make סבא the son of Cush the planter of the inhabitants of Arabia Felix, as Schmidius does, but of Arabia Deserta; Josephus, however, makes the Sabeans in Ethiopia; and since the same notes constitute Raamah the author of the peoples of Arabia Felix from Ezek. 27:22, whose son שבא was, they do not sufficiently agree with themselves, since they place this Sheba in Ethiopia, which pertains to Africa, if indeed Arabia is situated in Asia. D. Chytræus also derives from סבא the son of Cush the Sabeans, peoples of Arabia Felix, whose metropolis Ptolemy made Saba, at the Arabian Gulf, of whom Ps. 72:10, Is. 43:3, and 45:14. and from שבא the son of Raamah, grandson of Cush, he derives other inhabitants of the same Arabia. For both, he says in the Onomasticon Sacrum, placed their seats in Arabia Felix, fertile in incense, gold, and myrrh, as Pliny says in book VI: 'The Sabeans, a people of the Arabs, most famous for their incense,' with nations stretched out to both seas, Jer. 6, 20. Ef. 60, 6. This was the homeland of the Queen of Sheba, who came to Solomon. He reports that another Sebah, son of Jectan, grandson of Heber, Gen. 10, 28, who is written with the same letters, is the stock of the Sabaeans in India; and besides that one, he brings forward another still called Sebah, who likewise had another parent, Jectan, grandson of Abraham, Gen. 25, 2, with no mention made of whose progenitor he was. Tremellius and Junius place the regions of those descendants of Abraham in the deserts of Arabia at Gen. 10, 7. Paulus Crellius in Concord. at סבא Gen. 10, 7. Deducing the inhabitants of Mauritania, he observes from that, that India is called Seba, in Ethiopia, whose Lord is commonly Prestegean, or Presbyter John, from שבא grandson of Chus, and likewise that a city in Meroe of Ethiopia has the name Schaba, and that the metropolis in Arabia was named from the son of Jaksan, son of Abraham, also called שבא, since the sons of Abraham by Keturah obtained the whole of Arabia toward the East. Furthermore, whatever may be the case regarding those proper names of men, when the name שבא is attributed to a region, what land it designates is learned not more correctly from elsewhere than from a comparison of Scripture, which an induction of passages shows to attribute it perpetually to Arabia Felix. Which suffices for us here. And therefore Bonfrerius in Onomast. urb. & locor. S. Script. at the name SABA rightly distinguishes the Saba of Arabia Felix, from which the Queen of the South came, and the Saba of African Ethiopia, because the former is written in Hebrew with ש, but the latter with ס. Compare what is at Num. 12, 1.

Verse of the same.

IN THE NAME OF THE LORD) The LXX here took the ל for a copula, so that the sense might be:—the fame of Solomon and of God, whom he worshipped, having been heard.

So also Junius and Tremellius; the fame of Solomon and of the name of Jehovah. Pagninus, however, with the Vulgate, has in the name of the Lord. B. Luther is more correct, Vom Namen des HERRN, with which the Tigurines easily agree: from the name of the Lord, and the Genevans, because of the name of the Lord, with R. Levi. For Solomon was celebrated because of the name of the Lord and for the sake of the name of the Lord, who had built a temple to the name of the Lord most celebrated in the whole world. Ludov. de Dieu's interpretation, into the glory of God, is more alien, because it is not the end of the celebrated fame of Solomon that is designated, but rather the efficient cause of that celebrity: nor is there any need to depart from the proper meaning of the word שם. Even more inconvenient is the other interpretation of Dievius, by which he wishes the word יהוה to introduce an intensive, just as in Ps. 104, 16, trees of the Lord are called great and tall trees, so that the sense might be: and the Queen of Sheba hearing the rumor of Solomon to the great name, or of the great name. For why should the proper meaning of the name Jehovah not be retained? Sanctius understands that she came in the name of the Lord thus: That she came with the Lord kindly helping, or rather with God inspiring and under his auspices, and secretly directing it, so that she might acknowledge the true God from Solomon, and imbue the nation subject to her with the studies of true religion, which divine direction, although we judge it must be acknowledged entirely, is not however introduced by the word לשם, which does not pertain to the latter colon, nor does it cohere with the verb came, as this Vulgate connects them, neglecting the distinctive accent Athnach, but it must be referred to the former colon concerning fame because of the name of the Lord; since Sanctius acknowledges that the particle ל often signifies Because of.

Verse of the same. TO TEST HIM WITH RIDDLES) A game of Kings at that time. See Judges 14, 12. The Abyssinians falsely claim this woman for themselves, also being injurious to her fame, when they say she came to Solomon with the same intention with which Thalestris came to Alexander.

Baronius in Annal. at the year 1, thinks she came because she believed Solomon was the Messiah from Balaam's prophecy, with the same zeal as the Magi in Matthew 2, but the case of the Magi is different, for whom a star shone forth and the light of the Messiah's birth beamed; nor is there anything here about that end of her arrival; but other causes by far are rendered, the fame of the Wisdom of Solomon and of the name of the Lord, or the worship of the same through the celebrity of the Solomonic temple publicly sung everywhere; so that she might both test the Wisdom of Solomon through riddles, and inquire into the name and worship of the God of Israel. Therefore in Matthew 12, 42, the Queen of the South is said to be about to condemn in the last judgment those who had Christ himself present, as the hypostatic wisdom of God, and refused to listen. It was customary in that age among Kings and illustrious persons to exercise themselves through riddles or obscure questions, such as the riddle Samson proposed to his guests, Jud. 14. and that he also transmitted riddle-like questions to Solomon, the Tyrian King, is attested by Josephus, who solved them all: book 8, Antiq. c. 2.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Regina Saba admiratur Salomonis sapien- tiam. Ejus divitiæ, & magnificentia cum throno Regio.

Vers. 1.

REGINA SABA) Meroes ut videtur, in qua multis sæ- culis fœminæ imperarunt assumto Candaces nomine, ut Strabo nos docet libro 16. & 17. Plinius autem 6, 29. sub hujus regno erant & Sabritæ, teste Strabone, quod nomen a Saba non longe abit.

Æthiopiæ Reginam etiam faciunt cum Jose- pho l. 8. c. 2. Rabanus, Nauclerus, Tostatus, Hugo, Dionysius, Toletus, Maldonatus, Jansenius, Barra- dius, Franciscus Lucas in Matth. 12. Genebrardus, Cornel. à Lapide hic, Junius item & Tremellius, Six- tin. Amama, Spanhemius ad Matth. 2. dub. Evan- gel. Ortelius, & alii: & pro ea sententia pugnat quoq; Erasm. Schmidius ad Matth. 20. eo argumen- to (quod alii potius contra eandem adhibuere) quod שבא cum Schin Æthiopiam notet, non Ara- biam, idque Apodicticum putat. Alii urgent, quod Æthiopia ad Austrum sit Judææ, siquidem hæc Re- gina Austri dicatur Matth. 12, 42. quodque longissi- me distet à Judæa, uti à finibus terræ venisse Regina illa Matth. 12. dicitur: nec non quod præ Arabia abundet auro, quod thurifera, & aromatica sit, & quod in ea fœminæ dominari consveverint, quod hic unicum Grotii argumentum est, & traditio sit penes Æthiopes, vel Abyssinos constans, & conti- nua, quod eorum imperatores à Salomone origi- nem ducant, ex quo prolem susceperit Regina, quæ Davidis nomen adepta sit: Unde Preto-Johannes Abyssinus Imperator in titulo suo jactat hunc Da- videm, filium Davidis, filium Salomonis apud Orte- lium in Theatro tab. 68. Provocant etiam ad au- toritatem Gregorii Nyssenii hom. 7. in Cant. Na- zianz. Orat. 40. August. serm. 142. de Temp. ut & Anastas. Sin. Euthym. Anshelm. Origen. item hom. 2. in Cantic. imo & Hieronym. in Es. 43.

Sed Reginam hanc Arabiæ fuisse, non Æthio- piæ, alii rectius statuunt: quia שבא non Æthiopi- am denotat, sed Arabiam felicem, quod è variis Scripturæ locis luculentissimum est, imo ex ipsa nuncupationis origine, Gen. 10. ubi vers. 7. filius Chus סבא dictus Sabæis Æthiopiæ nomen & fami- liam præbuit, ut Josephus ipse habet, & agnoscit Cor- nel. à Lapide, ut & Pelargus, non vero quemadmo- dum Schmidius vult, Arabiæ felicis, neque ut Junius & Tremellius putant, Arabiæ desertæ incolis. Nepos vero Chusi è filio Ragema, שבא vocatus, Arabiæ felicis incolarum Pater celebratur, observante Hie- ronymo in tradit. Hebraic. quem Tremellius, & Ju- nius, ut & Schmidius frustra censent Æthiopum Progenitorem. Fidem enim imprimis hic me- retur præ aliis Hieronymus: cujus observatio ita habet: Filii Rhegma, Saba & Dadan: Hic שבא per Schin literam scribitur, supra vero (cum filiusChus nominatur) per ס Samech, à quo diximus appellatos Sabæos. Interpretatur vero nunc שבא Ara- bia. Nam in septuagesimo primo Psalmo, ubi nos ha- bemus Reges Arabum & Saba munera offerent, in Hebreo scriptum est Reges שבא primum nomen per Schin,secundum per Samech. Consonat Hierony- mo Cornelius à Lapide ad Es. 60, 6. Dicta est Saba (Arabia felix) per Schin à Saba filio Regma filii Chus: Sicut Æthiopia dicta est Saba per Samech à Saba. Ab hoc nomine שבא Sabai Job.1,15. dicuntur in- colæ in Arabia, quirapinis dediti fuere, teste Plinio l. 6. c. 28. Strabone l. 16. Diodoro l. 3. c. 12. ubi Ara- bes intelligunt interpp. ὁμοθυμαδὸν, non v. Æthio- pes. Quod nomen habetur quoque Job.6,19. The- man cum שבא jungitur, adeoque Arabia hac voce notatur. Ps. 72,10. uti jam observatum Hieronymo, Reges שבא Arabum Reges sunt; quibus Reges סבא Sabe in donis adducendis junguntur: quod posterius Æthiopiam ibi significare, communiter censent Interpp. & ad Es.60,6. agnoscit Jesuita Cor- nelius. Occurrit etiam hoc nomen Es. 60, 6. Omnes de Scheba שבא venient aurum & thus deferentes: Quo loco Hieronymum Arabiam felicem intellige- re Joh. Pineda ad Job. 1, 15. agnovit,eique calculum addit Cornelius, etsi Æthiopiam quoque ea voce comprehendi Jesuita velit,confundens voces,quas S. S. aperte distinxit Ps.72, 10. Observatur idem no- men quoque Jer. 6, 20. ut quid mihi thus de Saba שבא afferenies, & calamum suaveolentem de terra longinqua? Ad quem locum Cornelius: Thus enim gignitur in Arabia Sabæa. Sic etiam Hieronymus: Quod thura de Saba veniant,nemo dubitat. Nec quis- quam ibi, quod constet, Æthiopiam intelligit. Similiter habendum de loco Ez. 27, 20. Venditores שבא Saba & Raema ipsi negotiatores tui: ubi mi- rum, Hieronymum legisse רעמה de סבא conqueri se nullo alio Scripturarum loco invenire potuisse, quid significet. Quum habeatur Gen. 10,7. filius Chus ejus nominis, à quo provincia in Arabia felici appellationem fortita est: quemadmodum Junius & Tremellius agnoscunt Rahemam Auctorem po- pulorum felicis Arabiæ fuisse, idque ex Ez. 27, 22. probant; & pro eo Regamam Ptolemæum dixisse ob- servant. Unde recte Corn. à Lap. ad Ez. 27. Saba Arabes Sabæi. Ræma urbs est Arabiæ felicis. Deni- que Joel.3,13. iterum reperitur nomenSaba: Venun- dabunt eos Sabæis genti longinquæ. Quo loco Hiero- nymum nec Arabiam, nec Æthiopiam, sed longin- quiorem gentem intelligere hæc, quæ in commenta- rio ejus leguntur, docent: ut vendant eos Judæi non Persis, & Æthiopibus, & cæteris nationibus, quæ vi- cinæ sunt (Arabes a. viciniores sunt Æthiopibus) sed Sabæis genti longissimæ, quam antea dixit gentem trans Indiam, & de ea Esaiam loqui censet c. 45, 14. ubi tn. non שבא,sed סבא cum Samech habetur, & Sabæa Æthiopiæ recte intelligitur,uti & Es. 43,3.Sed quanquam has voces distinctas esse ipse in tradit. Hebraic. ad Gen. c. 10. monuerit, confundit tn. eas- dem interdum,ac si non designarent distinctas pro- vincias, quæ omnino distinguenda esse è Gen. 10, 7. & Ps.72, 10. liquet. Genti huic longinquæ trans In- diam sitæ præficit idem Hieronymus, loco Joelis laudato, Reginam Sabæ, quæ venit Sapientiam au- direSalomonis: Unde & thus venire ait: cujus vero proprium natale solum alias Sabæam Arabiæ desi- gnasse videtur Hieronymus. Qui de Regina Sabæ in Comment, ad Es. 60. hæc tradidit: Madian & Epha regiones sunt trans Arabiam, fertiles Camelo- rum,omnisque provincia appellatur Saba, unde & Sa- ba Regina, quæ venit sapientiam audire Salomonis, & ipsa deferens aurum & thus &c. Conciliant tn. nonnulli Hieronymum hoc pacto, quod hic trans

Arabiam simpliciter ita nuncupatam Sabam collo- carit, non v. ex Arabiæ tractu & appellatione latis- simi ambitus, eandem traxerit; sed ex illa solum Arabiæ parte, quæ tantum Arabiæ nomine gaudet, & Arabiæ desertæ, aut Petrææ est proximior; atq; ita etiam lucem inferunt loco Hieronymi ad Joël. 3. Sabæam gens trans Indiam dicitur, de qua fuit Regina Saba, unde & thus venire perhibetur dicente Virgilio, centumque Sabæo Thure calent aræ. Licet qui- dam Sabæos Arabes illos suspicentur: ubi per Arabes quos alii suspicantur, intelligere ipsum agrestiores illos, & prædatores: sed per regionem Sabæam trans Indiam Arabes inferiores ad Meridiem & Indiam ac Mare Indicum in Felice Arabia designari, cen- sent. Recte ergo ad locum illum Joëlis Cornelius à Lapide geminam Sabæam observat, utramq; longin- quam, licet ambigat, quamnam intelligere debeat, quia non advertit, in Ebræo textu שבא cum Schin legi, quod nomen esse Sabæ Arabiæ ipse non dubi- tat. Sabæi, inquit, sunt vel Æthiopes, vel Arabes A- rabiæ Felicis, de quibus Poëta: Centumque Sabæo Thure calent aræ. Duplex enim est Saba: Una in Æthiopia, altera in Arabia, utraque longinqua longeƣ distans à Judæa. Sic ergo ex inductione locorum, ubi nomen שבא occurrit, constitit, semper desi- gnatam esse Arabiam felicem, nunquam autem Æ- thiopiam, quæ סבא distincto nomine nuncupata est 10, 7. Ps. 72, 10. Es. 43, 3. c. 45, 14. Unde Cornelius, quum hoc loco 1. Reg. 10, 1. Æthiopiam mallet in- telligere, hac desperata usus est exceptione, Rabbi- nos male hic posuisse punctum in dextro cornu, itaque fecisse Schin, cum ponendum esset in sinistro, legen- dumƣ Sin, non animadvertens, non in solius puncti collocatione, sed in literis ipsis diversitatem nomi- num esse, quum aliud per Schin scribatur, aliud per Samech, quam differentiam, etsi parvi æstimet, in Scripturis tn. accurate observari jam ostensum est.

Confirmatur autem ulterius hæc de Arabia fe- lice sententia è circumstantiis, quæ de Regina sa- pientiæ Salomonææ avida referuntur: utpote quod famam Salomonis audiverit, quæ ad eandem navi- gationis commercio deferri potuit, quæ fiebat in mari rubro, & ex Asiongaber in Arabiam, tum ex copia Camelorum, quibus abundat maxime Ara- bia deserta, ob pascuarum eremi latitudinem, aërjsq; temperiem, quibus hoc animal delectatur, teste Hieronymo ad Ez. 27. (etiam in Felici Arabia turmas camelorum, ac Elephantorum constituit Adricho- mius in descript. terræ sanctæ sub tit. Manass. p. 77.) nec non ex donorum, quæ attulit Regina, qualitate, ac quantitate, quæ nulli regioni sic conveniunt, au- ri nempe, aromatum, & gemmarum, ut Arabiæ: de quibus Adrichomius l. c. prolixe. Cæterum εὐδαί- μων Felix dicitur ob thuris & aromatum copiam, teste Hieronym. ad Loca Ebr. Actor. Apostol. lit. A. quam Plinius Odoriferam & divitem, & beatæ cognomine inclytam appellat, l. 5. c. 11. alii porro λι- βανόφορον & ἀρωματόφορον i.e. thuriferam, & aro- matiferam nuncupant. Thus enim huic Arabiæ pro- prium est, nec alibi gignitur. Auri quoq; & argenti venis, ac glebis usq; adeo scatet, ut omnis pene hu- jus gentis suppellex alia auro, alia argento splen- deat, aurumq; finitimis triplo æris pretio, argen- tum duplo vendatur: quæ deniq; pretiosissimarum gemmarum & margaritarum admodum ferax est. Conf. Plin. l. 12. c. 28. Diodor. Sicul. l. 3. c. 12. & Diony- sii, qui in ea Arabiæ parte vixit, versus de præstan- tia hujus regni, apud Hotting. Hist. Oriental. p. 240. Strabo l. 15. Tanta inquit aromatum copia redun- dat, ut pro sarmentis lignisque utilibus cinnamomo, ca- sia & reliquis talibus utantur. Isti (Judæi) simul & Geræi ob eximias facultates cunctorum locupletissimi junt, vario præditi apparatu, vasis aureis & argen- teis &c. ob quam feracitatem & amœnitatem pri- sci Historici Alex. M. post reditum ex India in Arabiam, regiam suam condere decrevisse, com- memorant. Unde & in Scripturis à thure & auro Ps. 72, 10. Es. 60, 6. Jer. 6, 20. nec non aromatibus, & gemmis Ez. 27, 20. celebratur.

Accidit porro descriptio, quam Christus tradidit, Matth. 12, 42. cum Reginam Austri eam dixit, quæ à finibus terræ accesserit. Nam Arabiam esse Australem Hierosolymæ extra dubium est, idque agnoscit Schmidius: quod Arabia Felix ferè eundem habeat Meridianum cum Hierosolyma, ita ut Judæa & Hierosolyma sit septentrionalior, Arabia felix & Saba ejusdem sit Australior. Etiam ita ad Meri- diem Arabiam constituit Herodotus l. 8. & Diodorus l. c. E finibus autem terræ accessisse etiam recte dici- tur, quæ ex Arabia accessit. Distat enim 606. leucis Gallicis ab Hierosolyma, notante Adrichomio. Ideoque terra longinqua vocatur Jer. 6, 20. Estque ea illa parte extrema regio ad Mare Indicum sive A- rabicum, de qua Nicephorus l. 8, 35. Indi Sabæi pri- mum, deinde etiam Homeritæ sunt appellati. Natio- nem eam ex Abraham & Ketura prognatam: Re- gionem eam, quam Græci magnam & felicem Arabi- am esse, extremumque Oceanum fines ejus pertingere dicunt, cujus metropolis & primaria urbs est Saba. Herodotus l. 3. ita habet: Ad meridiem ultima è re- gionibus, quæ habitantur, Arabia est, in qua SOLA omnia nascuntur thus, myrrha, casia, cinnamo- mum &c. Denique de dominatu fœminarum dubium movent, qui in Æthiopia potius, quam Arabia ufi- tatus fuit; Sed observat Pineda l. 5. de rebus Salom. cap. 14. §. 6. [eundem etiam in Arabia invaluisse, quamvis non semper & ex more perpetuo, sed tempore, & casu.

Atque huic sententiæ de Arabia Felici calcu- lum adjiciunt Cajetanus, Eugubinus, Gagneius, Lip- pomannus, Sanctius, Joh. Benedict. Christian. Adri- chomius, Georg. Venet. Pererius, Schvarez. Baro- nius, & alii è Pontificiis, etiam Pineda, qui in Com- ment. Job. ad c. 1, 16. reginam hanc Æthiopiæ fu- isse contenderat, sed postea accuratius re pensitata variis documentis l. 5. de reb. Salom. eandem Ara- biæ reginam fecit, quibus è nostris B. Lutherus, & plerique alii adstipulantur: E. Patribus v. huic sen- tentiæ favent non tantum Hieronymus, Eucherius & Isidor. l. 14. Etym. ac Nicephorus l. c. Sed illi etiam, quos pro sese Æthiopiæ patroni allegant. Nam etsi illi Æthiopiam nominent, observandum tamen, non de Æthiopia Africana eos loqui, quæ trans Ægy- ptum est, sed de Asiatica, quam Theodoretius Æthio- piam Indicam vocat: quæ certe Africana non est. Ad quæstionem enim 32. in 1. Reg. in operibus m. T. 1. p. 550. quænam est Sabæa? respondet, Æthiopi- ca: Hic a. eos esse sitos dicit in mari Indico. Nominant autem eos Homeritas. Sunt autem è regione Axami- tarum. Inter hos autem & illos medium est mare. Eo- rum Regina fuit admirabilis illa mulier, cujus stu- dium laudavit in Evangelio. Sic etiam habet Proco- pius Gazæus in Eccl. Regina Saba: Gens est Æthio- pica, sitam esse ajunt ad mare Indicum. Vocant autem Homeritas, sunt ex adverso Axamitarum, medium autem inter illos mare est. Homeritas enim non Nice- phorus tantum l. c. sed etiam Ptolemæus Arabiæ populos faciunt, eosque vocatos esse Sabæos Nice- phorus tradit, ac conjungit quoq; Plinius l. 6, c. 28. Homeritas cum Sabæis, in Arabia. Cyrillus Alex. l. 5. in Es. c. 6. Saba, inquit, regio est ultra terram Arabum & prope mare rubrum, ex qua Saba Æ- thiopum Regina temporibus Salomonis accessit Jeru- salem. Fertilissima est illa regio thure, auro, & lapidi- bus Indicis. Cui explicationi favet quoque Tirinus ad Num. 12, 1. observans, duplicem esse Æthiopiam: Occidentalem unam in Africa remotius ultra Egy- ptum porrectam, Zonæq́; Torridæ subjectam: cui nunc imperat Presto Johannes: Alteram Orientalem, quæ alias Arabia dicitur, certe Arabiæ pars est, complecti- turque Madianitas, aliosq́; populos, qui ad Arabicum sinum vergunt versus Austrum. Ita Herodotus l. 7. Plinius l. 5. c. 8. Augustinus, Theodoretius & alii.

Traditioni vero & jactantiæ Æthiopum non multum tribuendum, quos constat, rerum suarum buccinatores immodicos esse, ac fabellæ illa de Sa- lomone à Reginæ impregnatione, ac origine Abys- sinorum Regum traditio similior est, quam Historiæ, eiq; opponenda aliorum de Regina Arabiæ tradi- tio, quam etiam exhibet Nicephorus l. c. cum, FA- MAM obtinere, ait, Reginam Austri ex Arabia Felice ad Salomonem advenisse. Refert etiam San- ctius ad 1. Reg. 10. Petrum Paez in illam Æthio- piam Indicam missum nunciasse, illi ad Sinum Ara- bicum civitatem ab indigenis ostendi, in qua nata credatur Regina Sabæ. Quam Arabes æque suam ja- ctitant, ac Æthiopes. De quorum fabellis gerris Si- culis vanioribus in hac causa pluribus Sanctius l. c. legi! poterit. Grotius ipse commentum Abyssinio- rum, & jactantiam retudit h. l. Hanc fœminam Abys- sini falso sibi vindicant, in famam quoque ejus inju- riosi, cum venisse eam dicunt ad Salomonem eo ani- mo, quo Talestris ad Alexandrum. Neque consonat Josephi narrationi Æthiopum fabula: Ille reginam hanc Nicaulam dictam ait: hi vero vocant eandem Maquodam: nonnulli Sybillam fuisse ajunt, &c. Conferatur Pineda l. c. & qui summam rei in hac causa ex eodem sistit B. Waltherus noster in Har- mon. novissim. editione ad 1. Reg. 8, 1.

Quod ad apodixin Schmidii pro Æthiopia sic ratiocinantis: Ex earum terrarum, quæ à Jerosoly- ma sunt Australes sola illa, quæ habuit olim nomen Schebæ, venit regina Austri ad Salomonem. Atqui sola Meroe Æthiopica habuit nomen Schebæ, testibus Historicic & Philologis consentientibus: E. ex sola Meroe Æthiopica venit Regina Austri ad Salomo- nem: ea, admissa Majori propositione ac Minoris loco substituta Scheba felicis Arabiæ, pro nostra sententia invicta erit, pro adversa vero ideo nul- lum robur habet, quod Minor illius probari ne- queat. Quinam enim illi Historici, quinam Philolo- gi, qui hoc consentienti suffragio asserant, Meroen Æthiopicam, eamque solam nomine Schebæ appella- tam esse? Genebrardus equidem, & interpretatio no- minum Hebr. quæ in fine Bibliorum circumfertur, notante Pineda ad Job. 1, 15. ajunt, שבא cum Schin Æthiopiam significare, סבא vero cum Samech Arabi- am felicem, & suffragantur hactenus Junio-Tremel- lianæ notæ ad Gen. 10, 7. quod à שבא filio Ragema Æthiopia originem trahat, ast filium Chus סבא non faciunt incolarum Arabiæ felicis satorem, uti Schmie- dius, sed Arabiæ desertæ, Josephus vero Sabæorum in Æthiopia; & quum eædem notæ Regema auto- rem constituant populorum Felicis Arabiæ ex E- zech. 27, 22. cujus Filius שבא fuit, non satis sibi consonant, cum hunc Scheba in Æthiopia collo- cant, quæ ad Africam pertinet, siquidem Arabia in Asia sita sit. B. Chytræus & à סבא filio Chus Sabæos Arabiæ felicis populos, quorum Sabam metropolin Ptolemæus fecit, ad sinum Arabicum deducit, de quibus Ps. 72, 10. Es. 43. 3. & 45, 14. & à שבא filio Regma nepote Chus alios ejusdem Arabiæ in- colas derivat. Uterque enim, ait in Onomast. Sacro, in Arabia Felice thuris, auri & myrrhæ ferace sedes posuit, ut Plinius l. VI. inquit. Sa- bæos Arabum populos propter thura clarissimos ad utraque mari porrectis gentibus habitare, Jer. 6, 20. Ef. 60, 6. Haec patria fuit Reginae Sabae, quae ad Salomonem venit. Alium Sebah filium Jectan, nepotem Heberi Gen. 10, 28. qui iisdem literis scribitur, Sabaeorum in India stirpem esse, refert; ac praeter istum alium adhuc Sebah nuncupatum, qui itidem Jectan alium parentem habuit, nepotem Abrahae, Gen. 25, 2. adducit, nulla mentione facta, quorum ille fuerit progenitor. Tremellius v. & Junius regiones illorum Abrahae posterorum in Arabiae deserta collocat ad Gen. 10, 7. Paulus Crellius in Concord. à סבא Gen. 10, 7. Mauritaniae incolas deducens, inde observat, Indiam Seba nuncupatam, in Aethiopia, cujus Dominus Prestegean vulgo Presbyter Johannes, à שבא nepote Chusi, itidem civitatem in Aethiopiae Meroa Schaba nomen habere, à filio vero Jaksan filii Abrahae שבא pariter dicto Metropolin in Arabia denominatam esse, quum filii Abrahae Kethuraei totam Arabiam versus Orientem adepti sint. Caeterum quicquid de nominibus illis virorum propriis sit, nomen שבא cum regioni tribuitur, quamnam designet terram non aliunde rectius, quam à collatione Scripturae, discitur, quam illud perpetuo Arabiae Felici tribuere inductio locorum docet. Quod hic nobis sufficit. Ideoque recte Bonfrerius in Onomast. urb. & locor. S. Script. ad nomen SABA, distinguit Sabam Arabiae Felicis, è qua Regina Austri venit & Sabam Aethiopiae Africanae, quod illa in Ebraeo per ש, haec autem per ס scribatur. Conf. quae ad Num. 12, 1.

Vers. eod.

IN NOMINE DOMINI) LXX. hic ל pro copula sumsere, ut sensus sit :- audita fama Salomonis & Dei, quem is colebat.

Sic etiam Junius & Tremellius; famam Salomonis & nominis Jehovah. Pagninus v, cum Vulgato habet in nomine Domini. Rectius B. Lutherus, Vom Namen des HERRN, cui facile consonant Tigurini: ex nomine Domini, & Genevenses, propter nomen Domini, cum R. Levi. Nam de nomine Domini & propter nomen Domini celebrabatur fama Salomo, qui aedificarat nomini Domini templum toto orbe celebratissimum. Alienior est Ludov. de Dieu interpretatio in gloriam Dei, quia non finis celebratae famae Salomoneae, sed causa potius efficiens celebritatis istius designatur: neque opus est à vocis שם propria significatione discedere. Magis adhuc inconveniens est altera Dievii interpretatio, qua vocem יהוה vult ἐπίτασιν inferre, uti Ps. 104, 16. arbores Domini dicuntur arbores magnae & procerae, ut sensus sit: & Regina Sabae audiens rumorem Salomonis ad nomen magnum, vel nominis magni. Cur enim non retineatur nominis propria Jehova significatio? Sanctius in nomine Domini venisse sic intelligit: Quod Domino bene juvante venerit, vel potius Deo inspirante, atque auspice, idque occulte dirigente, ut à Salomone verum Deum agnosceret, & gentem sibi subditam studiis verae religionis imbueret, quam directionem divinam etsi omnino agnoscendam censeamus, non tamen voce לשם eadem infertur, quae non pertinet ad posterius colon, nec cohaeret cum verbo venit, ut vulgata haec connectit, neglecto accentu distinctivo Athnach, sed ad prius colon referenda de fama ob nomen Domini; quum particulam ל saepe significare Propter agnoscat Sanctius.

Vers. eod. TENTARE EUM IN AENIGMATIBUS) Ludus Regum eo tempore. Vide Judicum 14, 12. Hanc feminam Abysfini falso sibi vindicant, in famam quoque ejus injuriosi, cum venisse eam dicunt ad Salomonem eo animo, quo Thalestris ad Alexandrum.

Baronius in Annal. ad ann. 1. venisse eam putat, quod crediderit, Salomonem esse Messiam ex Bileami vaticinio, eodem quo Magi Matth. 2. studio, sed Magorum alia est ratio, quibus præluxit stella, & affulsit lux de Messiæ ortu: neque hic quicquam de illo adventus fine; sed aliæ longe causæ reddun- tur, fama de Sapientia Salomonis & de nomine Domini, vel cultu ejusdem per celebritatem templi Salomo- nei publice passim decantato; ut & Sapientiam Sa- lomonis per ænigmata tentaret, & nomen, cultumque Dei Israelis indagaret. Ideo Matth. 12, 42. conde- mnatura dicitur Regina Austri in judicio novissi- mo eos, qui Christum ipsummet præsentem ha- bebant, ceu sapientiam Dei hypostaticam, & au- dire renuebant. Usitatum ista ætate erat penes Re- ges, & illustres personas, ut exercerent se per ænig- mata, vel obscuras quæstiones, quale ænigma Sim- son hospitibus suis proposuit, Jud. 14. & ad Salo- monem Tyrium etiam Regem quæstiones ænigmati- cas transmisisse, autor est Josephus, qui omnes solve- rit: lib. 8. Antiq. c. 2.

For the temperate man himself is truly happy, and happy are those who hear these words from the mouth of the one who is temperate.
