Vers. 8. BEATI VIRI TUI ET BEATI SERVI TUI QVI STANT CORAM TE SEMPER, ET AUDIUNT SAPIENTIAM TUAM) Plutarchus Numa: Μία κακῶν παῦλα καὶ λύσις ἀνθρώποις ἐστὶν ἔκ τινος τύχης θείας εἰς ταυτὸ διανοίᾳ φιλοσόφῳ βασιλικὴν συμπεσοῦσαν δύναμιν ἐγκρα- τῆ καὶ ὑπὲρ δέξιον τῆς κακίας τὴν ἀρετὴν καταστῆσαι. μακά- ριος μὲν γὰρ αὐτὸς ὁ σώφρων ὡς ἀληθῶς, μακάριοι δὲ οἱ συν- ήκοοι τῶν ἐκ τοῦ σωφρονοῦντος στόματος τούτων λόγων.

## 10:9
Verse 9. HE SET THEE KING TO DO JUDGMENT AND JUSTICE) A kingdom is to speak right holily and to benefit as many as possible. Of this Hesiod: For therefore wise kings, for the sake of peoples being harmed in the assembly, accomplish changes in deeds. Of this Homer: As of some blameless king, who, god-fearing, ruling over many and mighty men, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CONSTITUIT TE REGEM UT FACERES JUDICIUM ET JUSTITIAM) Regnum est jus sancte dicere & prodesse quamplurimis. De illo Hesiodus: Τὄνεκα γὰρ βασιλῆες ἐχέφρονες ἕνεκα λαοῖς Βλαπτομένοις ἀγόρηφι μετατροπα ἔργα τελεῦσι. De hoc Homerus: Ὡσέ τευ ἢ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος, ὅςτε θεουδὴς Ἀνδράσιν ἐν πολλοῖσι καὶ ἰφθίμοισιν ἀνάσσων, &c.

## 10:10
Ver. 10. HE GAVE THEREFORE TO THE KING ONE HUNDRED TWENTY TALENTS.

Pineda begins their calculation, since each cost 1200 drachmas, which would be a sum of one million and four hundred thousand Spanish crowns. We calculate it thus: We showed at Exod. 38, 24 that a talent contains 3000 shekels, which in silver amount to 1500 Joachim thalers; since the proportion of silver to gold is twelvefold, a talent of gold will be worth 18000 imperial thalers: and thus 120 talents will be worth 2,160,000 Joachim thalers, that is, 2,468,571 Meissen florins, or two million and 4 1/2 tons of gold, and besides that 18,571 florins: if to these are added the precious gems, along with that countless abundance of spices, it will be possible to estimate how great this δῶρον βασιλικὸν (royal gift) was. For the divine Historian teaches that not more spices than these were brought, although very many spices were brought more often in Solomon's fleet, whence it is firmly concluded that the Queen came from Arabia the Rich and Happy, who gave such a quantity of gold, gems, and spices to Solomon.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DEDIT ERGO REGI CEN- TUM VIGINTI TALENTA.

Calculum eorum init Pineda, quum singula drachmis constiterint 1200. quod unius millionis & quadringentorum millium Hispanicorum coronato- rum summa fuerit. Nos ita computamus: Talen- tum 3000. siclos continere ad Exod. 38, 24. osten- dimus, qui in argento efficiunt 1500. Joachimicos, cum v. proportio argenti ad aurum duodecupla sit, talentum auri valebit 18000. thaleris imperialibus: adeoque 120. talenta valebunt 2160000. Joachi- micis, hoc est, 2468571. florenis Misnicis, vel duo- bus millionibus, & 4 1/2. tonnis auri, ac præterea 18571. florenis: quibus si addantur gemmæ pre- tiosæ, cum innumera illa aromatum copia, quan- tum hoc δῶρον βασιλικὸν fuerit, æstimare licebit. Non enim allata esse ultra aromata tam multa di- vinus Historicus docet, etsi sæpius in Salomonis classe plurima aromata adducta sint, unde firmiter colligitur, ex Arabia divite ac Felice venisse Regi- nam, quæ tantam vim auri, gemmarum & aroma- tum Salomoni donavit.

## 10:11
V. 11. HIRAM'S FLEET.

The fleet was not Hiram's alone: because Solomon's servants set out with his servants and brought these things, 2 Chron. 9, 10. Sanctius derives thyine wood from the Greek θύω, which means to offer incense, understanding it in a general sense as fragrant; not those which Lebanon produces, for there was no need to bring these from elsewhere, such as cedars were, but others, and indeed of such a kind as had not been seen there before, as v. 12, 2 Chron. 9, 14 indicate, whatever they may have been. Vatablus rendered it Brazil wood, others ebony: the LXX generally [rendered it] πελεκητὰ, that is, hewn, the Chaldean [rendered it] coral wood: the Vulgate, with the LXX in the parallel passage 2 Chron. 9, translates it as pine. Others more correctly wish to refer to the thyia tree, about which Pliny, book 3, chapter 16, reports from Theophrastus that great honor was shown to that tree, because the ceilings of ancient temples were made from it, attributing also a certain immortality to it. Theophrastus, book 5, chapter 5, makes it similar to the wild cypress.

Latin:

V. 11. CLASSIS HIRAM.

Non fuit solius Hiram classis: quia Servi Sa- lomonis cum ejus servis profecti hæc attulere 2. Pa- ral. 9, 10. Ligna thyina à Gr. θύω deducit Sanctius, quod suffire significat, in genere intelligens odora- ta; non ea, quæ Libanus gignit, hæc enim aliunde afferre opus non erat, quales cedri erant, sed alia, & quidem ejusmodi, quæ antea illic non visa v. 12. 2. Par. 9, 14. designant, quæcunque tandem ea fue- rint. Vatablus reddidit lignum Brasilicum, alii ebe- num: LXX. generaliter πελεκητὰ, id est, dolata, Chaldæus ligna Coralinorum: Vulgatus cum LXX. in loco parallelo 2. Par. 9. pinea vertit. Alii rectius respici volunt arborem thyiam, de qua Plin. l. 3, c. 16. è Theophrasto refert, magnum ei arbori exhibitum fuisse honorem, quod inde templorum veterum con- tignationes factæ, tribuens etiam eidem quandam immortalitatem. Theophr. l. 5. c. 5. Cupresso Syl- vestri similem facit.

was considered of any value; For why would he have mentioned silver, which had been brought from Tarshish just as much as gold, if it had been applied to no use in the vessels and furniture of Solomon?

alicujus pretii putabatur; Ad quid enim comme- morasset argentum, quod ex Tharsis allatum æ- que fuerit, ac aurum, si in vasibus & suppellectile Salomonis nullum adhibitum fuisset?

## 10:14
Verse 14. EVERY YEAR SIX HUNDRED SIXTY-SIX TALENTS OF GOLD] That is, the tributes were worth that much to him.

Villalpandus and Pineda observe that Solomon sent a triple fleet, of which each would return in about three years; that by the first fleet 420 talents of gold were brought, 1 Kings 9:28; by the second fleet 450, 1 Sam. 8:2; but by the third fleet, with the increasing industry of men and the multitude of diggers and the desire for gold, 660. Which make 11,880,000 Joachim florins; or 13,578,135 Misnian florins; that is, 13½ millions of gold with 78,135 florins.

Latin:

Verf. 14. PER ANNOS SINGULOS SEXCENTORUM SEXA- GINTA SEX TALENTORUM AURI] Id est, tantum valebant ei tributa.

Vilalpandus, & Pineda observant Salomonem triplicem Classem misisse, quarum singulæ tribus annis circiter redirent, prima classe 420. talenta auri allata esse 1. Reg. 9, 28. classe secunda 450. 1. Sam. 8, 2. tertia autem classe, crescente hominum industria, & fossorum multitudine aurique cupi- ditate 660. Quæ efficiunt 11880000. Joachamicos; florenos v. Misnicos 13578135. hoc est, milliones auri 13½ cum 78135. florenis.

## 10:16
Verse 16. SIX HUNDRED SHEKELS OF GOLD HE GAVE FOR THE PLATING OF ONE SHIELD.

The shields and bucklers, which are mentioned in the following verse, were not used for fighting; because six hundred shekels make 25 pounds, since one shekel is a half-ounce: but they were stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon for the sake of magnificence. For who would have carried such a weight?

Latin:

Verf. 16. SEXCENTOS AURI SICLOS DEDIT IN LAMINAS SCUTI UNIUS.

Non inserviebant scuta, neque peltæ, quarum sequenti versu mentio sit ad bellandum; quia sex- centi sicli 25. libras faciunt, quum lunus siclus sit se- miuncia: sed reponebantur in domo saltus Libani magnificentiæ gratia. Ecquis enim tantum pon- dus portasset?

## 10:17
Verse 17. THREE HUNDRED MINAS OF GOLD CLAD ONE BUCKLER.

The Vulgate must be corrected, because only three minas are mentioned in the source, since a mina contains 50 shekels, or 25 ounces, that is, 2 pounds and one ounce: three hundred minas would make 625 pounds; who would believe that so many were applied to one buckler? But three minas make 6¼ pounds, which certainly sufficed for one buckler. For a buckler is a shorter shield having the shape of a horned moon, just as a shield is a large buckler, covering almost the whole man. Concerning the reconciliation of this passage with 2 Chron. 9:16, see the treatise on coins, chapter 10.

Latin:

Verf. 17. TRECENTÆ MINÆ AURI UNAM PELTAM VESTIEBANT.

Emendanda vulgata est, quia tres minæ folum in fonte commemorantur, quum mina contineat 50. siclos, vel 25. uncias, h. e. 2. libras & unciam u- nam: trecentæ minæ 625. libras facient, quot uni Peltæ adhibitas ecquis credet? Tres autem minæ 6¼ libras efficiunt, quæ utique uni Peltæ sufficie- bant. Pelta enim est clypeus brevior habens formam lunæ corniculatæ, ut scutum clypeus magnus est, totum pene hominem tegens. De loci hujus cum 2. Chron. 9, 16. conciliatione vid. tract. de nummis cap. 10.

## 10:21
Verse 21. THERE WAS NO SILVER) In those drinking and eating vessels.

Others more correctly: it was not in estimation; since the following words are explanatory of the preceding, and it is not certain. Furthermore, since those authors who say that America was frequented by the ships of Solomon think that they have found the Ophir of Solomon itself in America, along with Christopher Columbus—namely Genebrardus, Robert Stephanus, and Franciscus Vatablus on 1 Kings 10 in Hispaniola, but Benedictus Arias Montanus, Marcus Alstedius, and Valerius Schindler in his Lexicon Pentaglotton, Franz and Erasmus Schmid in Peru: who will believe that Solomon, having left the nearer, better-known, and much more fertile Eastern India, instituted a voyage by an immense circuit into the American and Peruvian region, especially since he could have arrived there from Joppa through the Strait of Gibraltar by a much shorter voyage? What is more, in Peru, besides gold and pearls, the goods of Solomon are not found—no gems, no ivory, no peacocks, or monkeys. Therefore, we are content with that single expedition to Ophir, which was made from the Arabian Gulf, and we shall seek Ophir, with other men of great name, in Asia—not indeed with Grotius in the kingdom of Ormus in Persia, as if it were Aphar, as it pleased Georg Horn to observe in his notes on Sulpicius Severus, book 1 of History, p. 196, appealing to Grotius (Pliny calls a town situated on the Arabian Gulf Saphar), since the ships of Solomon traveled much further, but in Eastern India beyond the Ganges, since the two sons of Joktan (Gen. 10:28) divided India between themselves, so that Ophir occupied India beyond the Ganges, and Havilah occupied India within the Ganges, as Arias Montanus admits in his book Phaleg, ch. 9, and voyages through the Arabian Gulf into India from Egypt had already been famous for many centuries, as witnessed by Diodorus Siculus, book 15 of his Library, Strabo, book 11, Arrian, and others: and in India all the goods of Solomon are found, which Pliny (book 6, ch. 19, 20), Pomponius Mela (book 3, ch. 7), Solinus (ch. 55), Pliny (book 33, ch. 1; book 37, ch. 13), and Dioscorides and Diodorus Siculus, along with Pliny, testify to be rich in gems; in which the Golden Chersonese is so called from the abundance of gold; the gem-bearing rivers are the Acesinus and the Ganges, and India is truly the greatest of all lands. They carry gold into the rivers of India; the royal palace has columns entirely gilded, and the bodies of beasts are entirely covered with gold (Curtius, book 8). India, says Isidore (book 14, ch. 3), has Taprobane, filled with gems and elephants, and Chryse and Argyre, rich in gold and silver. It produces huge elephants, ebony wood, and cinnamon, etc., and sends ivory, and also precious stones: beryls, chrysoprases, diamonds, carbuncles, lychnites, pearls, and union pearls. In Curtius (book 5), a grove is mentioned that is frequent with a multitude of wild peacocks. Indians hunt monkeys that are white all over their bodies, according to Pliny (book 7, ch. 21). And therefore Josephus (book 8, ch. 2) places Ophir in Eastern India, calling it the Golden Chersonese: "The sailors," he says, "sailed to the region of India, now called the Golden Land." Eusebius and Jerome agree with this, in his work on Hebrew places and Epistle 140 to Principia, and Theodoret, question 31 on this passage. "There is a certain region of Asia," he says, "which geographers call the Golden." The same author (q. 35) and Procopius on this passage hold that a certain Indian region is called Tarshish. Nicetas Catena on Job, ch. 28, Rabanus Maurus, the Glossa Ordinaria, Lyranus, Abulensis, Emanuel Saa on this passage, Reuchlin in his exposition of Hebrew words, Adrichomius in his Theater of the Holy Land, p. 118, Joseph Acosta in his work on the navigation of the New World, ch. 13, Bunting in his Itinerary, Mercerus, Brentius, Forsterus, and many others of our own. Therefore, Bonfrerius correctly refutes Arias Montanus on Gen. ch. 10. Regarding Havilah, he says, he feels the same as we do, that it is the Gangetic region, but he makes Ophir to be Peru in America, which Goropius Becanus also felt in his Hispanicis, and our Pineda does not entirely reject in his previous work on Solomon, book 4, ch. 16. But I am entirely persuaded that it was in Eastern India, both from the location and the port from which the ships of Solomon set sail, which sailed to Ophir, which was Ezion-geber in the Arabian Gulf, and from the fact that at that time the method of navigating the high seas was unknown, nor was the mariner's compass known, without which the high seas cannot be navigated. Johannes Petrus Maffeius, in books 10 and 17 of his Indian History, says Ophir is India beyond the Ganges, and indeed Pegu, where there is the greatest abundance of gold and silver, about which Bonfrerius also reported that the people of Pegu trace their origin to Jewish exiles, who, having been condemned by Solomon to the gold mines, first held those places. Philipp Cluverius in his Introduction to Geography, among the various kinds of nations that were found in India, also lists the Hebrews (book 5, ch. 8) and says it is so rich in gold and silver that the ancients believed its very soil was golden and silver. Samuel Bochart praises Ceylon or Taprobane, in which is the port of Hipporus, which the Phoenicians and Greeks called Ophir. Although others prefer that an entire province be called by this name, these authors agree that it is situated in Eastern India. Add to these also the ancients and moderns alike, who judge that the river Pishon, which encompasses the land of Havilah, is the Ganges, which is not in Western but in Eastern India: where Havilah, the brother of Ophir, son of Joktan, great-grandson of Noah, lived (Gen. 10:29). Cassianus Varrerius, in his book on Ophir, specifically determines that all that coast which is contained by the people of Pegu, Malacca, and Sumatra is Ophir, and Cornelius à Lapide subscribes to him on Jer. 10:9, nor does Nicolaus Fullerus deny it (book 4, Miscellanies, ch. 11, which should be compared here. See what is said on 1 Kings 9:26.

Regarding the name Tarshish, the opinion of those pleases me who, even though they judge that this word specifically clung to the regions of the Mediterranean Sea from Tarshish, the son of Javan (Gen. 10), which look from Cyprus toward the rising sun and the northern region, and especially those which are near the shores of Asia, where in Cilicia the not ignoble coastal city of Tarshish is situated (see Josephus, book 1 of Antiquities, ch. 12; Jerome, question 61 on Genesis; Judith 2; and 2 Maccabees ch. 4), nevertheless think that that region, in which the islands and ports were more known to the Hebrews, is used for the whole sea, so that the ocean and Tarshish sometimes come under the name, especially because the dominion of Cilicia spreads itself far, and Cilicia, as Solinus says (ch. 41), previously extended as far as Pelusium in Egypt. On which see Sanctius on this passage and on Isaiah ch. 11. To me, he says, it is highly probable that Tharsis is not a certain city, as many wish, for instance Tarsus of Cilicia, or Tartessus in Spain, or Carthage, but the sea so called from its azure color, just as the poets for the same reason call it azure. Virg. 3. Aen. They strive and churn the foam and sweep the azure. Certainly the LXX do not translate it otherwise, which our interpreter also sometimes does, Isaiah ch. 23. Howl, ye ships of the sea, and Ezek. ch. 1. The vision of the sea, in Hebrew Tharsis. Nor do I see why ships of Tharsis should so often be called otherwise in Holy Scripture. It could certainly have happened that because the sea of Cilicia is nearest to the Hebrews and very well known, where Tharsis was a noble city, any other sea, not only the Mediterranean, but also the Ocean, is called Tharsis, which is not infrequent in other matters. For from that which is to us either first or most known, we often attribute the name to those things which are of the same kind. As for what is held in v. 14 concerning the gold brought to Solomon every year, in that the Vulgate departs from the Hebrew source. For not every year was a weight of 660 talents of gold brought (who could believe that in every year precisely the same weight was obtained, since revenues vary; nor is it indicated in this passage, v. 22, that the naval fleet of Solomon returned every year, but only every three years) but in one that so much gold was brought in one year is indicated as something special, for the sake of commemorating the richer yield of that year; so that there is no need to invent different fleets (contrary to the text and history), one that returned every year, another that returned every three years. Grotius rightly corrects the Vulgate at v. 22, that the fleet did not return every three years, but every third year.

those traveling into Syria had to pass through the straits between the Syrian and the Red Sea, which Solomon held. The Hittite kings were situated to the East, 1 Kings 10:29 [Ef. 1, 4 is likely a typo for 1 Kings 10:29], the Syrians to the North. The Vulgate here deviates from the Hebrew truth, which Grotius therefore deservedly abandons here at v. 28, 29, and 30, annotating these things which now follow, concerning which a judgment can be made from those things which we have said.

Vers. 21. NON ERAT ARGENTUM) In illis potoriis escariisque vasis.

Rectius alii: non erat in æstimatione; quum verba sequentia ἐξηγητικὰ sint præcedentium, nec certum sit. Porro, quum autores illi, qui Americam navibus Salomonis frequentatam dicunt, ipsam O- phir Salomonis se in America invenisse arbitren- tur, cum Christoph. Columbo, Genebrardus nempe Robert. Stephanus & Francisc. Vatablus ad 1. Reg. 10. in Hispaniola, Benedictus Arias montanus vero Marc. Marinus, Possevinus, Delrio, Postellus, ut & Petr. Martyr. Alstedius, Val. Schindlerus in Lex. Pentagl. Franz. & Erasm. Schmidius in Peru: ec- quis credet, Salomonem ex mari rubro, relicta In- dia Orientali viciniori, notiori, multoque rerum pretio non parum fertiliori, immenso circuitu na- vigationem in regionem Americanam & Perua- nam instituisse, imprimis cum ex Joppen per fretum Gaditanum, multo breviori navigatione eo perve- nire potuerit? Quid, quod in Peru præter aurum & margaritas, merces Salomoneæ non invenian- tur, non gemmæ, non ebur, non pavones, aut Si- miæ. Quapropter unica illa expeditione in Ophir contenti sumus, quæ e sinu Arabico facta, & Ophir quæremus cum aliis magni nominis viris in Asia, non quidem cum Grotio in regno Ormus in Persia, quasi sit Aphar, uti placuit Georg. Hornio observat. Sulpit. Sever. l. 1. Hist. S. p. 196. ad Grotium pro- vocanti (Plinius Saphar, dictum oppidum sinui Arabico adsitum, appellat) quum longe amplius excurrerint Salomoneæ naves, sed in India Orien- tali extra Gangem, quum duo Jactanis filii Gen. 10, 28. partiti sibi Indiam sint, ut Indiam extra Gan- gem Ophir, intra Gangem Chavila occuparit fa- tente Ariamontano l. Phaleg. c. 9. & navigationes per Arabicum sinum in Indiam ex Ægypto jam a multis seculis celebres fuerint, teste Diodoro Siculo l. 15. Bibl. Strabone, l. 11. Arriano & aliis: atque in India merces Salomoneæ omnes inveniantur, quam auro & argento abundare Plin. l. 6. c. 19. 20. Pompon. Mela l. 3. c. 7. Solin. c. 55. Gemmis Plin. l. 33, c. 1. l. 37. c. 13. Ebeno, Dioscorid. & Diodor. Sicul. cum Plinio testantur, in qua Chersonesus au- rea est ab auri copia ita dicta; gemmiferi amnes sunt Acesinus & Ganges, terrarum vero omnium maxima India. Aurum in Indiæ flumina vehunt, re- gia auratas columnas habet totas, belluarum corpo- ra tota teguntur auro. Curt. l. 8. India, inquit Isido- rus lib. 14. c. 3. Taprobanam habet, gemmis & Ele- phantis refertam, Chrysen & Argyren auro argen- toq, fæcundas. Gignit Elephantos ingentes, ebenum li- gnum, & cinnamomum &c. mittit & ebur, lapides quoque pretiosos, beryllos, Chrysopasios, ada- mantem, carbunculos, lychnites, margaritas, & u- niones. Curtio l. 5. nemus memoratur agrestium pa- vonum multitudine frequens. Indi simias toto corpore candentes venantur apud Plin. l. 7, c. 21. Ideoque Ophir in India Orientali constituunt Joseph. lib. 8. c. 2. vocans eam Chersonesum auream: Nautæ, in- quit, in regionem Indiæ nunc auream terram nomi- natam navigarunt. Cui annuunt Eusebius, & Hie- ronymus, de loc. Hebraic. & Epist. 140. ad Prin- cip. Theodor. quæst. 31. in h. l. Est quædam, inquit, regio Asiæ, quam Geographi nominant auream. Idem q. 35. & Procop. in h. l. regionem quandam Indicam Tharsis dictam volunt. Niceta Caten. in Job. c. 28. Raban. Maur. Gloss. Ordin. Lyran. Abulens. Emanuel Saa in h. l. Reuchlin. in expos. voc. Ebr. Adrichom. in Theatr. Terræ Sanct. p. 118. Joseph a Cost. in Nav. nov. orb. c. 13. Bunting. in Itinerar Mercer. Brentius, Forsterus aliique e nostris pluri mi. Ideo recte Bonfrerius ad c. 10. Gen. refellit A riæ-Montan. De Hevila, inquit, idem sentit nobis cum, esse Gangeticam regionem, sed Ophir facit Per in America, quod etiam sensit Goropius Becanus i Hispanicis, nec omnino rejicit Pineda noster in Salo mone prævio l. 4. c. 16. Sed eam in Orientali fuisse India mihi omnino persuadeo, tum è loco & portu, unde solvebant naves Salomonis, quæ navigabant in Ophir, qui fuit Asiongaber in sinu Arabico, tum ex eo, quod tunc incognita esset ratio navigandi per altum mare, nec nota pyxis nautica, sine qua altum mare na- vigari non potest. Joh. Petr. Maffæus l. 10. & 17. hi- stor. Indic. Ophir Indiam dicit extra Gangem, & quidem Pegu, ubi copia auri & argenti maxima, de qua Bonfrerius etiam retulit, quod Pegusii originem ducant a Judæis exulibus, qui à Salomone ad officinas aurifodinarum damnati ea loca primum tenuerint. Phil. Cluverus in Introduct. Geogr. inter varia nationum genera, quæ in India reperta, etiam He- bræos recenset l. 5. c. 8. eamque auro, argentoque adeo fœcundam dicit, ut solum ejus aureum argenteumque esse veteres crediderint. Samuel Bocardus Zeilam sive Taprobanam laudat, in qua portus Hipporus, quem Phœnices, & Græci Ophir vocarint. Etsi au- tem alii malint integram provinciam hoc nomine nuncupatam esse, in Orientali tamen India eandem sitam hi autores consentiunt. Adde his etiam vete- res pariter & recentiores, qui fluvium Phison terram Hevilæ circumeuntem Gangem esse censent, qui non in Occidentali, sed Orientali India est: ubi Hevila, frater Ophir, filius Jectan, abnepos Noæ habita- rit, Gen. 10, 29. Omnem illam oram, quæ Pegusiis, Malaca, & Somatra continetur, Ophir esse Cass. Varrerius l. de Ophir peculiari statuit, eique sub- scribit Corn. à Lap. ad Jer. 10, 9. nec abnuit Nic. Fullerus l. 4. Misc. c. 11. qui hic conferendus. Vid. quæ dicta ad 1. Reg. 9, 26.

De appellatione Tharsis placet illorum sen- tentia, qui etsi eam vocem specialiter à Tharsis fi- lio Javan Gen. 10. hæsisse regionibus Maris medi- terranei, quæ à Cypro ad Orientem Solem, & Aqui- lonarem plagam spectant, & maxime quæ vicinæ sunt Asiæ littoribus, censeant, ubi in Cilicia Tharsis civitas littoralis non ignobilis sita est (vid. Joseph. l. 1. Antiq. c. 12. Hier. quæst. 61. in Gen. Judith. 2. & 2. Macc. c. 4. existimant tamen, regionem illam, in qua Insulæ erant & portus, Ebræis magis noti pro toto mari usurpari, ut Oceanus & Tharsis nomine quandoque veniat, maxime quia Cilicium domina- tus longe se diffundit, & Cilicia dicente Solino c. 41. antea usque ad Pelusium Ægypti pertinuit. Quo de Sanctius in h. l. & ad Es. c. 11. Mihi, inquit, valde probabile est, Tharsis non esse civitatem quandam, ut multi volunt, puta Tharsum Ciliciæ, aut Tartessum in Hispania, aut Carthaginem, sed mare sic appellatum à colore cæruleo, sicut Poëtæ eandem ob causam cæru- leum vocant. Virg. 3. Æn. Adnixi torquent spumas & cœrula verrunt. Certe non aliter vertunt LXX. quod etiam aliquan- do facit noster interpres Isai cap. 23. Ululate na- ves maris, & Ezech. c. 1. Visio maris, Hebr. Thar- sis. Neque video cur aliter tam sæpe in Scriptura Sa- cra naves Tharsis appellari debeant. Fieri sane po- tuit, ut quia mare Ciliciæ proximum est Hebræis & valde notum, ubi Tharsis erat nobilis civitas, quod- cunque aliud mare, non solum mediterraneum, sed etiam Oceanus dicatur Tharsis, id quod in aliis rebus non infrequens. Nam ab eo quod nobis aut primum aut maxime notum est, nomen sæpe tribuimus eis, quæ ejusdem generis sunt. Quod v. 14. de auro per sin- gulos annos allato Salomoni habetur, in eo Vulgata discedit à fonte Ebræo. Non enim singulis annis pondus 660. talentorum auri allatum fuit (ecquis credat, quovis anno præcise idem pondus obten- tum fuisse, quum proventus varient; neq; singulis annis, sed quovis demum triennio navalem Salo- monis classem rediisse h. l. indicatur v. 22.) sed uno anno tantum auri adductum fuisse, ceu peculiare quid, ditioris proventus istius anni commemorandi gratia, indicatur; ut opus non sit diversas classes (contra textum, & historiam) fingere, aliam quæ quotannis, aliam quæ quovis triennio reversa sit. Recte emendat Grotius vulgatam ad v. 22. quod non per tres annos, sed tertio quoque anno classis reversa sit.

nere in Syriam proficiscentibus per angustias transeundum erat inter Syriacum, & rubrum mare, quas obtinebat Salomo. Reges Chittæi ab Oriente Ef. 1, 4. Syri ab Aquilone siti. Vulgatus hic aberrat à veritate Ebræâ, quem proinde merito hic defert Grotius ad v. 28. 29. & 30. hæc annotans, quæ jam sequuntur, de quibus ex iis quæ diximus, judicium fieri poterit.

## 10:22
Verse 22. FOR THE KING'S FLEET WENT TO TARSHISH) in Hebrew: ship of Tarshish. That, however, is an oceanic ship: for the Hebrews call the ocean thus from the most ancient city Tartessus, frequented long ago by the commerce of the Phoenicians, who called the same city, as some wish, or as others say a neighboring one, Gadir, that is, a hedge, as Pliny says, a place enclosed on all sides, as Avienus interprets גדר.

Therefore Cornelius à Lapide wrongly counts her among the 700 queens whom Solomon had, to whom, he says, if this one is added, what harm will there be? For he could have taken her as a wife like the others, so that through her, and her royal descendants, he might introduce and strengthen the faith and worship of the one true God among the Ethiopians, for through a bastard son that could not be done rightly and effectively. But since she returned home, how was she admitted among the queens? And who does not know that the consequence from possibility to actuality is not valid? Nor indeed was there any need for that fornication, or for a new marriage, for the propagation of the true religion, about which there is also no word in the sacred history. For could not the Queen have propagated the true worship of God without that in her own empire, according to the fullness of her power?

EVERY THREE YEARS) Others better, every third year. LXX. μία διὰ τριῶν ἐτῶν. That seemed sufficient, since in this way also a sufficiently large abundance of all things was brought.

This fleet seems to Cornel. à Lap. to be distinct from that which is said in verse 11 to have sailed to Ophir, which brought gold and thyine wood: But the present fleet, which went to Tarshish, brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks: the former went yearly to Ophir v. 14, this is said to have gone once in three years to Tarshish; The former set sail from Ezion-geber, situated in the gulf of Arabia, on the shore of the Red Sea 2 Chron. 8:17, this from Joppa, situated on the Mediterranean Sea, which they understand by Tarshish. But others more correctly establish that it was one and the same fleet, which went to Ophir, and that Solomon did not set that fleet sail from Joppa, but from Ezion-geber, but that it went to Tarshish, i.e., the sea: which they judge to be signified by that name: so that Ophir is the name of the region, and the terminus of Solomon's navigation, and Tarshish, i.e., the sea, is that in which the ships went. Certainly if it were established that there were different fleets, some of which were dispatched from the Arabian gulf to Ophir, others of which set sail from Joppa or another port of the Mediterranean Sea, so that the former returned yearly, the latter every three years, both of those more famous opinions about the Solomonic fleets, which are found among authors of primary name, could stand together, not indeed so that Ophir is sought in Asia and in America at the same time (which are inconsistent) but so that gold and other precious things were brought to Solomon partly by one fleet from Asia, viz. from Ophir, and partly by another fleet from America; If indeed they could have penetrated into America and the Peruvian dominion, where most gold is found, from Joppa, or another port of the Mediterranean Sea, through the strait of Gades. But that absurd voyage is not to be attributed to the Solomonic fleet, as Genebrard does for the year 3150, that they set sail from the Red Sea, and having traversed some part of the East Indies, then sailed straight to the Island of St. Lawrence, from which they proceeded to the Cape of Good Hope, thence to Brazil, thence to Cuba and the Island of St. Domingo. For why would Solomon have prepared that fleet in the Arabian gulf, to sail around all of Africa, when he could have more conveniently sailed the Herculean strait in the Mediterranean Sea? Whence Anastas. Sinait. lib. VII. Hexaëm. Forer. on Is. 23. Pineda lib. 4. de reb. Salom. c. 14. Riebera on Jon. 1. Gorop. Becanus l. 1. establish Tarshish as the terminus to which, to which either some private fleet of Solomon set sail from Joppa in the Mediterranean Sea, or the same one which went to Ophir also reached the Spanish Baetica. To whom also Tarshish is the Spanish Tartessus. But in truth, since from 1. 2 Chron. 20:36. Let it be clear that ships going to Tarshish went through the Red Sea, and that it is nowhere else said that an expedition was made from Joppa or another port of the Mediterranean Sea, but that Solomon only sent out his ships from Ezion-geber or Elath in the Arabian Gulf, and that those Solomonic goods which the ships going to Tarshish brought are not all found in Spain; Spain cannot be understood here as Tartessus, even though the Phoenicians had long since penetrated into Spain by sailing from Tyre through the internal or Mediterranean Sea,

Latin:

Verf. 22. QUIA CLASSIS REGIS IBAT IN THAR- SIS) in Hebræo: navis Tharsisch. Id autem est navis Ocea- nica: nam Oceanum sic vocant Hebræi ab urbe antiquissima Tartesso ad Oceanum frequentata jam olim Phœnicum com- mercio, qui eandem, ut quidam volunt, urbem, ut alii vici- nam, Gadir dixere, id est sepem, ut Plinius, locum undique se- ptum, ut Avienus interpretatur גדר.

Male ergo Cornelius à Lapide eandem nume- rat inter 700. Reginas, quas Salomo habuit, qui- bus, inquit, si una hæc inferatur, quid erit incommo- di? Potuit enim eam uti cæteras uxorem ducere, ut per eam, ejusque regios posteros fidem cultumq; unius veri Dei apud Æthiopes induceret, & firmaret, per filium enim spurium id rite & efficaciter fieri non potuit. Sed quum reversa illa domum sit, quo- modo inter reginas adscita? Et quis nescit à posse ad esse non valere consequentiam? Neque vero opus fuit seu fornicatione illa, seu novo conjugio ad ve- ræ religionis propagationem, de quo etiam nul- lum verbum in historia sacra. Annon enim Re- gina verum Dei cultum citra idem in imperio suo propagare potuit, pro potestatis suæ plenitu- dine?

PER TRES ANNOS) Melius alii, tertio quoque anno. LXX. μία διὰ τριῶν ἐτῶν. Satis id visum, quum sic quoque afferretur satis magna rerum omnium copia.

Distincta hæc videtur Cornel. à Lap. classis ab ea, quæ vers. 11. in Ophir navigasse dicitur, quæ aurum & ligna thyina afferebat: Præsens autem classis, quæ in Tharsis ivit, aurum, argentum, Ebur, simias & pavos attulit: illa quotannis ibat in Ophir v. 14. hæc semel in triennio in Tharsis ivisse dicitur; Illa solvebat ex Aziongaber, sita in sinu Arabiæ, ad oram rubri maris 2. Par. 8, 17. hæc ex Joppe sita ad mare mediterraneum, quod per Tharsis intelli- gunt. Sed rectius alii unam eandemque classem fuisse, quæ in Ophir ivit, neque ex Joppe, sed Asion- gaber solum Salomon eam classem solvisse statu- unt, ivisse autem in Tharsis, h. e. mari: quod eo no- mine significari censent: ut Ophir sit nomen regio- nis, & termini navigationis Salomonis, Tharsis v. mare sit, in quo naves ibant. Sane si id constaret, quod diversæ classes fuerint, quarum aliæ è sinu Ara- bico in Ophir expeditæ, aliæ ex Joppe vel alio por- tu maris mediterranei solverint, ita ut illæ quotan- nis, he quovis triennio redierint, utraque illa cele- brior sententia de classibus Salomoneis, quæ apud præcipui nominis autores reperitur, simul consiste- re posset, non quidem ut Ophir in Asia & in Ameri- ca simul quæratur (quæ ἀσύσατα) sed qua aurum & alia pretiosa partim una classe ex Asia advecta Salomoni ex Ophir sc. partim v. alia classe ex Ame- rica allata sint; Siquidem in Americam & Perua- nam ditionem, ubi plurimum auri reperitur, ex Joppe, aut alio maris mediterranei portu per fre- tum Gaditanum penetrare potuerint. Sed ita non cum Genebrardo ad ann. 3150. ineptus ille cursus, ut solverint ex mari rubro, & aliqua India Orienta- lis parte perlustrata, recta deinde contenderint ad In- sulam S. Laurentii, ex qua ad caput bonæ spei, inde ad Brasiliam, inde in Cubam & Insulam S. Dominici profečti sint, affingendus Salomoneæ classi erit. Cur enim apparavisset Salomon classem illam in sinu Arabiæ, ut circa totam Africam navigaret, quum commodius in mari mediterraneo fretum Hercu- leum navigare potuisset? Unde Anastas. Sinait. lib. VII. Hexaëm. Forer. ad Es. 23. Pineda lib. 4. de reb. Salom. c. 14. Riebera in Jon. I. Gorop. Becanus l. 1. Tharsis terminum ad quem constituunt, quo vel propria aliqua classis Salomonis ex Joppen in ma- ri mediterraneo solverit, vel eadem quæ in Ophir, etiam in Bæticam Hispanicam tetenderit. Quibus etiam Tharsis est Tartessis Hispanica. Verum enim vero quum è 1. Paral. 20, 36. luculentum sit, naves in Tharsis euntes per mare rubrum ivisse, nec u- spiam alibi dicatur expeditio facta è Joppe, vel alio portu maris mediterranei, sed Salomo tantum ex Asiongaber vel Ailah in sinu Arabico naves suas ex- pedierit, neq; merces illæ Salomoneæ in Hispania omnes reperiantur, quas naves in Tharsis euntes attulere, Hispania Tartissis hic intelligi nequit, etsi Phœnices jam pridem in Hispaniam à Tyro mare in- ternum vel mediterraneum navigantes penetrasse,

## 10:22
AND APES] In Hebrew קופים, a kind of ape, which Agatharchides and Diodorus Siculus call by the same word κῆπος. But if we believe Strabo, κῆποι were not apes, but wild beasts similar in appearance to a lion, with the body of a panther, and the size of a fallow deer. For thus he writes in book XVI, who nevertheless in book XVII gives us another form of κῆπος, the face of a Satyr (that does not differ much from an ape), the rest between a dog and a bear, so that the name seems to have been a general one for monster-bearing animals.

Latin:

ET SIMIAS] In Hebræo קופים, simiæ genus, quod eadem voce κῆπος vocant Agatharchides & Diodorus Siculus. At Straboni si credimus, κῆποι non simiæ fuerint, sed feræ leoni similes aspectu, corpore pantheræ, damæ magnitudine. Ita enim ille libro XVI. qui tamen libro XVII. aliam nobis dat κῆπω formam, faciem Satyri, (ea a simia non longe abit) cætera inter canem & ursum, ita ut nomen videatur fuisse generale monstriferorum animantium.

## 10:26
Verse 26. AND SOLOMON GATHERED CHARIOTS AND HORSEMEN, AND THERE WERE TO HIM ONE THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED CHARIOTS, AND TWELVE THOUSAND HORSEMEN) Behold another transgression of the Law, Deut. 17:18. Through excessive confidence in his own prudence, he thought he did not need those cautions of the law. Thus he stumbled first into those, then into the principal parts of the law.

Latin:

Vers. 26. CONGREGAVITQVE SALOMON CURRUS ET EQVITES, ET FACTI EI SUNT MILLE ET QUADRINGENTI CURRUS, ET DUODECIM MILLIA EQVITUM) Ecce alia prætergressio Legis Deut. 17, 18. Nimia prudentiæ suæ fiducia putabat se illis cautionibus legis non egere. Ita in illas primum, deinde in præcipua legis impegit.

## 10:28
Verse 28.

AND FROM COA] Such threads as were most well-known to the Greeks and Latins as Coan. But מקוה, or as it is read in Chronicles מקוא, others interpret as that which the Persians call a caravan, and they refer all these things to horses.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ET DE COA] Fila talia, qualia erant Coa Græcis & Latinis notissima. Sed מקוה, aut ut in Paralipomenis legitur מקוא, alii interpretantur id quod Persæ Caravannam vocant, & hæc omnia ad equos referunt.

## 10:28
THEY BROUGHT THEM AT A FIXED PRICE] that is, horses coming from Egypt, when they passed through Judea into Syria or to the Hittites, paid a large toll to Solomon for the transit, just as a toll was given for the transit of incense, as we noted in De Jure Belli ac Pacis, book II, ch. 2, § 14.

Verse 30.

STATUTO PRETIO PERDUCEBANT] id est, equi ex Ægypto venientes cum transirent per Judæam in Syriam aut ad Hethæos, vectigal pro transitu magnum pendebant Solomoni, sicut pro turis transitu dabatur vectigal, ut notavimus de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. II. c. 2. §. 14.

Vers. 30.

## 10:29
Verse 29.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

## 10:29
AND IN THIS MANNER ALL THE KINGS OF THE HITTITES AND OF SYRIA SOLD HORSES] Rather, they brought them out through them, as it is in the Hebrew. The LXX expressed the sense well: καὶ ὕτως πᾶσι τοῖς βασιλεῦσι Χεττὶν καὶ βασιλεῦσι Συρίας κατὰ θάλασσαν ἐξεπορεύοντο. Namely, those merchants who paid the toll to Solomon for the transit.

Latin:

ATQVE IN HUNC MODUM CUNCTI REGES HETHÆORUM ET STRIÆ EQVOS VENUMDABANT] Imo per eos educebant, ut in Hebræo est. Sensum bene expresserunt LXX. καὶ ὕτως πᾶσι τοῖς βασιλεῦσι Χεττὶν καὶ βασιλεῦσι Συρίας κατὰ θάλασσαν ἐξεπορεύοντο. Nempe illi mercatores qui, pro transitu Solomoni vectigal pendebant.

## 10:29
Verse 3.

Verse 29. AND IT CAME OUT OF EGYPT.

Here it is not a matter of the purchase of horses, but of merchandise exported by means of horse-drawn chariots and the tax paid for spun and finished goods; such as fine linen and others that were prepared there. See Proverbs 7:16, Ezekiel 27:7. Dievius renders the Hebrew text not inappropriately: 'And for the exit of horses, which was Solomon's from Egypt, and as for the spun yarn, the King's merchants received the spun yarn. And a chariot went up and came out of Egypt for six hundred silver pieces, and a horse for one hundred and fifty.' And thus they led them out to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Syria through them. By מקוה he understands spun yarn, as R. Levi does, meaning fine linen garments; and judging that this is implied: that with the taxes weighed out, such merchandise led out of Egypt to the Kings of the Hittites and Syria was not traded except through the King's merchants. Similarly, Junius and Tremellius: 'And the tax of the horses from Egypt, which was Solomon's, i.e.' the King's merchants of spun yarn (by whom, however, they understand the publicans, the redeemers of taxes) received the spun yarn for the price, etc. For from Egypt by land travel—AS SEVEN HUNDRED QUEENS] That is, matrons. He increased the number of both these and concubines after the song was written, where see chapter 6 and 7.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Vers. 29. EGREDIEBATUR AUTEM EX ÆGYPTO.

Hic non de equorum emtione, sed mercimonitis per equorum quadrigas exportatis agitur & vectigali soluto mercium netarum & confectarum causa; utpote byssi, & aliarum quæ ibi parabantur. Vid. Prov. 7, 16. Ez. 27, 7. Non incommode reddit Ebræum textum Dievius: & ad exitum equorum, qui Salomonis (erat) ex Ægypto & netum quod attinet, mercatores Regis accipiebant netum. Et ascendebat, exibata currus ex Ægypto sexcentis argenteis & equus quinquaginta & centum. Atque ita ad omnes reges Hitheorum & ad reges Syriæ per eos educebant. Per מקוה netum intelligit, ut R. Levi, vestes byssinas; idque innui censens: Quod pensitatis vectigalibus merces ejusmodi ex Ægypto eductæ ad Reges Hittæorum & Syriæ non nisi per mercatores Regios traductæ. Similiter fere Jun. & Tremellius: Et vectigal equorum ex Ægypto, quod erat Salomonis, i. e. neti mercatores Regis (per quos vero publicanos vectigalium redemtores intelligunt) accipiebant netum pro pretio &c. Nam ex Ægypto terrestri iti- QVASI REGINÆ SEPTINGENTÆ] Id est, matronæ. Auxit numerum & harum & concubinarum, post scriptum canticum, ubi vide cap. 6. 7.

## 11:1 Argument
SECTION III. THE UNHAPPY FATES OF SOLOMON. CHAPTER XI. Solomon's polygamy and idolatry, and the adversaries raised up against him: Hadad, Rezon, and Jeroboam, to whom the kingdom of Israel was promised through Abijah. The death of Solomon, and the succession of Rehoboam.

Regarding the transgression of the law, others here more correctly absolve Solomon, and thus observe that certain things were granted to the kingdom of Solomon which otherwise could not have been admitted. For the divine Majesty once wished to make known to all nations how greatly He could, if He so willed, adorn and endow His own with splendor, glory, abundance of all things, and with as much magnificence as could ever fall to anyone. That this was promised divinely to Solomon is evident from 1 Kings 3:13. Then, He also wished that that kingdom, from which the Messiah was to arise, should once be most abundant in every blessing, so that the glory and supreme Majesty of the Messiah might be foreshadowed in it. Cf. Matthew 12:21.

Verse 1. HE LOVED MANY FOREIGN WOMEN) A double crime: first, that he had many, in a huge number, in the barbaric manner, against the prohibition of Deuteronomy 17:17. Then, that they were Sidonians, that is, Canaanites and Hittites, against the prohibition of Deuteronomy 7:3. This was the source of the greatest evils for the descendants of Solomon and the Hebrew people, wisely foreseen by Moses.

From that flowed and, having slipped backward, returned the hope of Solomon: broken strength, the averted mind of God.

However, a certain contradiction seems to occur here with the passage in 1 Kings 4:26, where Solomon is said to have had forty thousand stalls of chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen; which the Junius-Tremellius notes reconcile not unsuccessfully: namely, Solomon had 40,000 horses, distributed by 4,000 decuries in such a way that each held ten, 2 Chronicles 9:25. He had besides four thousand chariots, as is reported in the aforementioned place; from which he chose one thousand four hundred, which he distributed here and there throughout the entire region and used for the journeys of himself and his own, so that both chariots and fresh horses would be available everywhere, 1 Kings 10:26. He distributed the cavalry, however, in such a way that he fitted 16,000 to the chariots, and handed over the remaining 12,000 to the horsemen, assigning two to each.

Latin:

SECTIO III. INFFLICIA SALOMONIS FATA. CAPUT XI. Salomonis Polygamia, & idololatria, eique suscitati adversarii Adad, Razon, & Jeroboam, cui promissum per Abiam regnum Israel. Mors Salomonis, & successio Roboami.

A legis prætergressione hic alii rectius absolvunt Salomonem, adeoque observant, regno Salomonis quædam fuisse concessa, quæ cæteroquin admitti non potuerint. Siquidem semel divina Majestas voluerit omnibus gentibus innotescere, quantopere splendore, gloria, omnium rerum copia, & quanta quidem ulli obvenire potuit, magnificentia, suos, si vellet, ornare & dotare posset. Quam promissam divinitus Salomoni fuisse, è 1. Reg. 3, 13. constat. Tum regnum quoque illud, ex quo Messias oriundus erat, semel esse voluit omni benedictione abundantissimum, ut gloria & Majestas summa Messiæ in eo adumbraretur. Conf. Matth, 12, 21.

Vers. 1. ADAMAVIT MULIERES ALIENIGENAS MULTAS) Duplex crimen : primum quod multas, ingenti numero, barbarico more, contra interdictum Deuteron. 17,17. Deinde quod Sidonias, id est, Cananæas & Hethæas contra interdictum Deut. 7, 3. Hic fons maximorum malorum fuit Salomonis posteris populoque Hebræo, sapienter prævisus Mosi.

Ex illo fluere ac retro sublapsa referri Spes Solymum: fractæ vires, aversa Dei mens.

Pugna autem hic quædam occurrere videtur, cum loco 1. Reg. 4, 26. Ubi Salomo habuisse dicitur quadraginta millia præsepia equorum currilium, & duodecim millia equestrium: quam non infeliciter conciliant notæ Junio-Tremellianæ: Fuerunt nempe Salomoni 40000. equi, per 4000. decurias ita distributi, ut singulæ denos caperent, 2. Par. 9, 25. Habuit præterea quatuor mille currus, uti loco jam dicto refertur: ex quibus mille quadringentos elegit, quos hinc inde distributos per universam regionem suis suorumque itineribus adhibuit, ut tam currus, quam'equi recentes ubivis essent obvii 1, Reg. 10, 26. Equitatum vero ita distribuit, ut curribus aptaret 16000. reliquos autem 12000. è quitibus traderet, singulisque binos assignaret.

## 11:2
Verse 2. CONCERNING WHOM THE LORD SAID) Refer this to the Sidonians, as I said, and the Hittites: it is apparent in the law itself. The other women are mentioned in passing, so that it may be understood from where Solomon acquired such a multitude of women for himself, and how he was an appetent of various forms, truly φιλογυνής (a lover of women), as the LXX have it here, although it was not permitted to marry women from other nations either, unless they were subject to the law, Nehemiah 13:23. But from the seven nations, not even such as these, lest the hidden evil break out.

The words of the text sufficiently teach that the law of the Lord in Deuteronomy 7:3 is to be referred not only to the Sidonians and Hittites, but also to the Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites, whom the daughter of Pharaoh joined to Solomon. Nor does anything else appear from the law itself than that women from the seven nations were prohibited for this reason, lest anyone be seduced to their idolatry. The example of Solomon himself confirms that this reason also applies to other foreigners. However, it was lawful to marry those subject to the law or converted from any peoples, even from the Canaanites, such as the Ashdodite women were, who are mentioned in the place cited by Grotius himself, Nehemiah 13:23. For it is clear from Joshua 13:3 that these belonged to the Canaanites. See what is said regarding the aforementioned Law and above at chapter 3:1.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SUPER QVIBUS DIXIT DOMINUS) Hoc refer ad Sidonias ut dixi & Hethæas : apparet id in ipsa lege. Cæteræ fœminæ obiter nominantur, ut intelligatur, unde istam multitudinem fœminarum sibi Solomon comparaverit, & quam variarum formarum fuerit appetens, vere φιλογυνής, ut hic habent LXX. quanquam & aliis gentibus fœminas ducere non licuit, nisi legi subjectas Nehem. 13, 23. Ex septem autem populis ne tales quidem, ne latens malum erumperet.

Verba textus satis docent, non ad Sidonias & Hethæas tantum, sed ad Moabitidas & Ammonitidas, Idumæasque legem Domini Deut. 7, 3. referendam esse, quas Filia Pharaonis adjunxit Salomoni. Nec è lege ipsa aliud apparet, quam quod ideo fœminæ è septem populis prohibitæ, ne quis ad idololatriam earum seduceretur. Quam rationem in cæteris alienigenis etiam militare exemplum ipsum Salomonis confirmat. Legi autem subjectas vel conversas è quibusvis populis ducere, integrum fuit, etiam è Cananæis, quales etiam Asdodica fuere, quarum in loco ab ipso Grotio laudato mentio fit Neh. 13, 23. Has enim pertinuisse ad Cananæas è Jos. 13, 3. liquet. Vide quæ ad dictam Legem & supra ad c. 3, 1.

## 11:4
AND WHEN HE WAS NOW OLD) It could be said to him: 'You began better than you end: the last things differ from the first.' And that which is in Tacitus: 'The beginnings are better for most, but the end declines, and many change into arrogance through length of time.'

THAT HE MIGHT FOLLOW STRANGE GODS) First, in secret he permitted those women to use their ancestral rites: Then, corrupted by their example, he himself did the same openly.

Latin:

CUMQVE JAM ESSET SENEX) Poterat ei dici: Cœpisti melius quam desinis: ultima primis Distant. Et quod apud Tacitum: Initia plerisque meliora, sed finis inclinat, & multi diuturnitate in superbiam mutant.

- VT SEQVERETVR DEOS ALIENOS) Primum in occulto permisit feminis illis uti avitis ritibus: Deinde ex- emplo earum & ipse corruptus palam idem fecit.

## 11:5
Verse 5. MOLOCH) Saturn, as we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 5. MOLOCH) Saturnum, ut alibi diximus.

## 11:9
Verse 9. WHO HAD APPEARED TO HIM TWICE) A graver fault because of such great favor from God. See above III. 5. IX. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVI APPARVERAT EI SECVNDO) Gravi- or culpa ob tantum Dei favorem. Vide supra III. 5. IX. 2.

## 11:11
Verse 11. THEREFORE THE LORD SAID TO SOLOMON) Through Ahijah the Shilonite, for He did not appear to him further. See below 29.

I WILL TEAR THY KINGDOM AND WILL GIVE IT TO THY SERVANT) That, that is, the greater part: servant, that is, subject.

Latin:

Vers. 11. DIXIT ITAQVE DOMINVS SALOMONI) Per Ahi- am Silonitam, non enim ultra ei apparuit. Vide infra 29.

SCINDAM REGNVM TVVM ET DABO ILLVD SERVO TVO) Illud, id est, majorem partem: servo, id est, subdito.

## 11:13
Verse 13. I WILL GIVE ONE TRIBE TO THY SON) Of Judah, clearly. For the tribe of Benjamin was not entirely Rehoboam's.

Latin:

Vers. 13. TRIBVM VNAM DABO FILIQ TVO) Ju- dæ scilicet. Nam Benjaminis tribus non integra fuit Ro- boami.

## 11:14
Verse 14. HADAD) He is Ader according to both Josephus and the LXX.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ADAD) Is Ader & Josepho & LXX.

## 11:27
Verse 27. AND THIS IS THE CAUSE) Rather, the beginning. When Solomon enclosed the city on all sides with walls, blocking everything that had been gaping open under David, he imposed a tribute on the people for that work: he placed Jeroboam over that tribute. Not rarely does evil come to kings from those who handle royal funds. Such was Philetaerus, from whom the Attalid kings arose, as Strabo records in book 13.

Sanctius, following the lead of others, gives this as the cause of the rebellion begun by Jacob. Tirinus on ch. 9, 24. This was a public area in Jerusalem, and a deeper part of the very wide valley of Millo subject to Mount Zion, which, because it was inhabited by a frequent multitude of men, was called Millo, which word indicates a multitude. This area Solomon, in order to serve the convenience and delights of his wife, the daughter of Pharaoh, took away from the public, and having constructed various buildings, added it to the palace of his wife nearby. Which was the occasion for the people, and especially for Jeroboam, first of murmuring, then also of rebellion. Because, namely, Solomon had filled the chasm of Millo with the help of Jeroboam with rubble, and had leveled it with the rest of the valley and the lower city, and had taken away from public use what was very convenient for the public because of the ascent into the temple, and had converted it into the private delights of his Egyptian wife. Which Jeroboam, along with the people, took ill. For Josephus, book 8, ch. 2, indicates that Solomon employed him for the construction of the walls when he was enlarging Jerusalem with walls, whence also that chasm was filled by him, in which area the people could gather and conveniently wait for the time of sacrifice. Sanctius handed this down by conjecture in an obscure matter, and did not dare to assert it: but Tirinus asserted it in this place. Others more simply [say] that the breach of the city of David, which David had made by conquering the Jebusites, 2 Sam. 5, 6, was obstructed when Solomon was building the fortification, and that Jeroboam was the prefect not only of this work, but also of the entire burden and tribute of Joseph, to whom, therefore, the complaints of the people were brought regarding the excessive tributes and taxes, which the uxorious King, caring more for womanly than public matters, was imposing or allowing to be imposed, whence from common grief he conceived indignation against Solomon and meditated something. Although those causes can be joined, as was also done by Sanctius. For to adorn and feed magnificently seven hundred Queens and three hundred concubines, immense wealth was needed, whence the subjects were exhausted by tributes. But the Rabbis' invention that Jeroboam was the son of Shimei, who sought vengeance against Solomon for his slain father, is foolish: because the father of Jeroboam was Nebat, not Shimei; an Ephrathite, not a Benjaminite.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ET HÆC EST CAVSA) Initium potius. Cum Salomon undique urbem mœnibus clausit, omnia quæ sub Davide hiæverant obstruens, tributum ad id opus indixit po- pulo: ei tributo imposuit Jeroboamum. Non raro malum regibus ab iis qui pecunias regias tractant. Talis fuit Phile- tærus, unde orti reges Attalici, memorante Strabone libro 13.

Causam Sanctio præeunte hanc reddit cæptæ rebellionis Jacob. Tirinus ad c. 9, 24. Erat hæc pu- blica Jerosolymis area, & pars profundior vallis la- tissimæ Mello monti Sion subjecta, quæ quod frequen- ti hominum multitudine incoleretur, dicta fuit Mello, quæ vox multitudinem indicat. Hanc aream Salo- mon, ut uxoris suæ, filiæ Pharaonis commodo deli- ciisque subserviret, publico ereptam, & ædificiis variis constructam vicino uxoris palatio adjecit. Quæ po- pulo, & imprimis Jeroboamo, murmuris primum, dein & rebellionis occasio fuit. Quia sc. Salomon vo- raginem Mello ope Jeroboami ruderibus imple- tam, & reliquæ valli, atque inferiori civitati coæ- quatam, & publico propter ascensum in templum valde oportunam eripuerat usibus publicis, & in u- xoris suæ Ægyptiæ privatas delicias converterat. Quod moleste tulit Jeroboam cum populo. Illum enim fabricæ murorum, quando Hierosolymam mœnibus augebat, adhibuisse Salomonem Joseph. l. 8. c. 2. indicat, unde etiam vorago ista ab illo im- pleta, in qua area populus convenire, ibique com- mode tempus sacrificii expectare poterat. Quæ ita per conjecturam tradidit Sanctius in re obscura, asserere ausus non fuit: asseruit autem Tirinus in h. l. Simplicius alii rupturam civitatis Davidis, quam Jebusæos expugnando David fecerat, 2. Sam. 5, 6. cum munitionem ædificaret Salomo, obstructam esse, ac præfectum non tantum operi huic, sed etiam uni- verso oneri, & tributo Josephi fuisse Jeroboamum, ad quem proinde querelæ populi de tributis, & vectiga- libus nimiis, quæ Rex uxorius nimis, res muliebres potius quam publicas curans imponebat, aut imponi patiebatur, delatæ fuere, unde ex communi dolore concepta indignatione contra Salomonem aliquid meditatus est. Quanquam causæ illæ conjungi pos- sint, ut à Sanctio etiam factum. Ad septingentas e- nim Reginas, & trecentas concubinas ornandas, & alendas magnifice, immensis opibus erat opus, un- de tributis exhausti subditi. Ineptum vero est Rab- binorum commentum Jeroboamum esse Simei Fi- lium, qui vindictam quæsiverit contra Salomonem ob interfectum Patrem: quia Pater Jeroboami Na- bath fuit, non Simei, Ephratæus, non Benjaminita.

## 11:30
Verse 30. HE RENT IT INTO TWELVE PARTS) Virgil, Aeneid 8. And Discord goes rejoicing in her rent cloak.

Latin:

Vers. 30. SCIDIT IN DVODECIM PARTES) Virgi- lius Æneid. 8. Et scissagaudens vadit Discordia palla.

## 11:31
Vers. 31. I WILL GIVE THEE TEN TRIBES) I will not only permit, but I will also confer the right upon thee. This appears below 37. 12, 24. 14, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 31. DABO TIBI DECEM TRIBVS) Non per- mittam tantum, sed & jus in te conferam. Apparet id infra 37. 12, 24. 14, 8.

## 11:32
Vers. 32. BUT ONE TRIBE SHALL REMAIN FOR HIM) Judah entire, with a part of Benjamin. See below 12, 21. A similar locution 2 Kings 17, 18.

Vers. I WILL AFFLICT THE HOUSE OF DAVID FOR THIS, YET NOT FOR ALL DAYS) This seems to be referred to the Messiah, who was to be the King of all the Israelite tribes and the nations.

It is rightly referred to the Messiah, because God does not wish to afflict the House of David eternally, but in turn to graciously raise it up entire, as regards all the tribes, which has not been fulfilled otherwise than in the Messiah. Therefore, it does not seem to be referred to him only, but it must be referred to him entirely. But Grotius, although he found no other interpretation, and thus clearly saw that it could not be referred to anything else than the Messiah, nevertheless wished to insert his VIDETVR [it seems] here, so that, namely, he might render the express oracle at least doubtful, or sell it as probable, not as undoubtedly certain, that it was promised concerning the Messiah. Perhaps for the sake of the Jews, who in Seder Olam c. 15 refer this to the Kingdom of King Asa of Judah, who greatly exalted the kingdom of Judah. However, prophecies are read everywhere concerning the raising up of the entire kingdom of David through the Messiah, explaining this oracle more clearly. To which opinion St. James in the Council of Jerusalem also brought the prophecy of Amos c. 9, 11. as is to be read in Acts 15, 16. Let the illustrious passage of Isaiah 49, 16 be seen in particular, and in the N.T. let Luke 1, 32.54 and Acts 1, 6 be compared.

PART II. HISTORY OF THE SUCCESSORS OF SOLOMON. SECTION I. HISTORY OF REHOBOAM.

Latin:

Vers. 32. PORRO VNA TRIBVS REMANEBIT EI) Judæ integra, cum parte Benjaminis. Vide infra 12, 21. Simi- lis locutio 2. Reg. 17, 18.

Vers. AFFLIGAM DOMVM DAVID SVPER HOC, VERVNTAMEN NON CVNCTIS DIEBVS) Videtur referendum hoc ad Messiam, qui Rex futurus erat omnium tribuum Israëliticarum & gentium.

Recte ad Messiam refertur, quia non æternum affligere, sed vicissim gratiose erigere Domum Da- vidis integram, quoad omnes tribus, vult Deus, quod aliter impletum non est, quam in Messia. Ad eum ergo referendum non videtur solum, sed o- mnino referendum est. Sed Grotius, etsi aliam in- terpretationem non invenerit, adeoq; probe vide- rit, alio referri non posse, quam ad Messiam, suum tamen VIDETVR hic ingerere voluit, ut sc. ex- pressum oraculum faltim dubium redderet, aut ceu verisimile, non indubitato certum de Messia promif- sum venditaret. Forte in Judæorum gratiam, qui in Seder Olam c. 15. hoc ad Regnum Assa regis Juda referunt, qui valde regnum Juda evexit. De eri- gendo autem per Messiam regno Davidis integro passim vaticinia, hoc oraculum clarius explicantia, leguntur. In quam sententiam S. Jacobus in Conci- lio Hierosolymitano etiam adduxit Amosi vatici- nium c. 9, 11. uti legere est Act. 15, 16. Videatur imprimis locus illustris Es. 49, 16. & in N. T. con- feratur Luc. 1, 32.54. Act. 1, 6.

PARS II. HISTORIA SVCCESSORUM PRIORUM SALOMONIS. SECTIO I. ROBOAMI HISTORIA.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

Division of the Kingdom. The calves of Jeroboam.

Vers. 1. TO MAKE HIM KING) As the firstborn of Solomon. For that law prevailed in Judah always after these times.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

Divisio Regni. Vituli Jeroboami.

Vers. 1. AD CONSTITVENDVM EVM REGEM) Vt primogenitum Salomonis. Ea enim lex in Juda post hæc tempora semper valuit.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. HIS FATHER MADE OUR YOKE VERY HARD) Heavy tributes.

LIGHTEN A LITTLE) They seek a relief of tribute, as Tacitus speaks in the first of his Histories.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PATER EJVS DVRISSIMVM JVGVL IM- POSVIT NOBIS) Tributa gravia.

IMMINVE PAVLVLVM) Tributi levamentum, ut Tacitus Historiarum primo loquitur, petunt.

## 12:6
Vers. 6. KING REHOBOAM TOOK COUNSEL WITH THE OLD MEN WHO STOOD BEFORE SOLOMON HIS FATHER WHILE HE YET LIVED) Both long age, and the perpetual use of affairs, and the company of so wise a king had made them fit for giving counsel. Ovid: — — — non omnia senior ætas Quæ fugiamus habet; longis venit usus ab annis. Euripides in the Erechtheus: Ομιλίας τε τᾶς γεραιτέρας θέλε. And in the Phoenissae: — — — οὐχ ἅπαντα τῷ γήρᾳ κακὰ, Ετεοκλέες, πρόσεστιν αἰδ' ἡ 'μπειρία Εχει τι δεῖξαι τῶν νέων σοφώτερον· Antiphanes: Σοφόν γετοί τι πρὸς τὸ βυλεύειν ἔχει Τὸ γῆρας ὡς δὴ πολλ' ἰδόν τε κὰι μαθόν· Then, as Cicero says in 2 de Oratore: The chief thing for giving counsel about the Republic is to know the Republic.

Latin:

Vers. 6. INIIT CONSILIVM REX ROBOAM CVM SENIORIBVS QVI ASSISTEBANT CVM SALOMO- NE PATRE EJVS DVM ADHVC VIVERET) Hos & longa ætas, & perpetuus usus negotiorum, & regis tam sapi- entis consuetudo idoneos dandis consiliis fecerant. Ovidius: — — — non omnia ferior ætas Quæ fugiamus habet; longis venit usus ab annis. Euripides Erechtheo: Ομιλίας τε τᾶς γεραιτέρας θέλε. Et in Phœnissis: — — — οὐχ ἅπαντα τῷ γήρᾳ κακὰ, Ετεοκλέες, πρόσεστιν αἰδ' ἡ 'μπειρία Εχει τι δεῖξαι τῶν νέων σοφώτερον· Antiphanes: Σοφόν γετοί τι πρὸς τὸ βυλεύειν ἔχει Τὸ γῆρας ὡς δὴ πολλ' ἰδόν τε κὰι μαθόν· Deinde ut Cicero ait 2. de Oratore: Ad consilium de Repu- blica dandum, caput est nosse Rempublicam.

## 12:7
Vers. 7. IF TODAY YOU WILL OBEY THIS PEOPLE AND SERVE THEM, AND YIELD TO THEIR PETITION, AND HAVE SPOKEN TO THEM GENTLE WORDS, THEY WILL BE YOUR SERVANTS FOR ALL DAYS) The beginnings of principalities are most difficult: and changes of affairs are opportune for disturbances, which appeared in the Pannonian and Germanic sedition at the beginning of the principate of Tiberius. So that I do not wonder that Vespasian, prudent and old, is described by Marcellus in Tacitus, Histories 4, as being in suspense at a new principate, and observing the countenances and speeches of everyone around him. Therefore, it is the counsel of the prudent, in those tender beginnings, to yield somewhat to consensus, and if we admit of ὑπερβολὴν, to do everything servilely for the sake of dominion. Time is needed for the authority of a prince to grow. Then, indeed, even the sadness of affairs must be softened by gentle words.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SI HODIE OBEDIERIS POPVLO HVIC ET SERVIERIS, ET PETITIONI EORVM CESSERIS, LOCVTVSQVE FVERIS AD EOS VERBA LENIA, ERVNT TIBI SERVI CVNCTIS DIEBVS) Initia princi- patuum difficillima: & opportuni motibus transitus rerum, quod apparuit seditione Pannonica & Germanica initio principatus Tiberii. Ita ut non mirer Vespafianum pruden- tem & senem describi a Marcello apud Tacitum Histor. 4. novo principatu suspensum, & vultus quoque ac sermones omnium circumspectantem. Ideo consilia sunt prudentum, in illis teneris printipiis, cedere nonnihil consenfui, & si ὑπερβολὴν admittimus, serviliter facere omnia pro domina- tione. Tempore opus est ut adolescat principis auctoritas. Tum vero etiam rerum tristitia verbis lenienda est.

## 12:8
Vers. 8. HE CALLED THE YOUNG MEN WHO HAD BEEN BROUGHT UP WITH HIM) It is frequent for new Kings to call to their councils their own intimates rather than those whose services their fathers used. The causes for this are that they wish to show their power by changing everything, and to repay as soon as possible those old obsequies, often not honorable, at the public expense, often to the grave harm of both themselves and their country. The similarity of morals also has something of an ἐλκυσικόν τι. But those words of Euripides in the Suppliants are true: — — — they destroyed the city, led astray by young men who rejoice in being honored, etc.

Similarly, we learn from the fragments of Diodorus Siculus that Hiero, the Syracusan prince, used the counsels of young men to his own great harm.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ADHIBVIT ADOLESCENTES QVI NV- TRITI FVERANT CVM EO) Frequens id novis Regi- bus, ut consiliis adhibeant potius familiares suos, quam eos, quorum opera patres sunt usi. Causæ hæc, quod ostendere potentiam suam volunt omnia mutando, & vetera illa obse- quia, sæpe non honesta, de publico quamprimum repensare, gravi sæpe, & suo & patriæ malo. Morum quoque similitudo habet ἐλκυσικόν τι. At vera sunt ista Euripidis in Supplicibus: — — — ἀπώλεσαν πόλιν Νέοις παραχθέντες οἵτινες τιμώμενοι Χαίρεσι, &c.

Similiter Juvenum consiliis magno suo malo usum Hiero- nymum Syracusanum principem, discimus ex fragmentis Diodori Siculi.

## 12:11
Verse 11. BUT I WILL CHASTISE YOU WITH SCORPIONS) That is, with scourges barbed after the manner of scorpions. These things those young men said, accommodated to the king's disposition, as flatterers are wont to do. Now the disposition of Rehoboam among the Hebrews was such as that of Appius Claudius among the Romans, whom Livy says was of a vehement and savage disposition, and therefore could never be persuaded to soften or lower his speech in any way from his accustomed harshness before the people. Of his are these: 'License is only the incitement of disturbances: and the common people are more prone to wantonness than to rage.' And also this: 'The prison is the home of the Roman plebs.' To such men, those words of Sophocles in the Antigone should often be whispered: Ἀλλ' ἄνδρα κἂν τις ᾖ σοφὸς, τὸ μανθάνειν. Πολλ' αἰσχρὸν οὐδὲν, καὶ τὸ μὴ τείνειν ἄγαν &c.

Latin:

Vers. 11. EGO AUTEM CÆDAM VOS SCORPIO- NIBVS) Id est, flagellis aculeatis ad modum scorpionum. Hæc juvenes illi dicebant accommodate ad regis ingenium, ut adulantes solent. Fuit autem ingenium Roboami apud Hebræos, quale apud Romanos Appii Claudii, quem vehe- menti trucique ingenio fuisse ait Livius, ideoque perpelli nunquam quîsse, ut apud populum ex consueta asperitate ora- tionis aliquid leniret atque submitteret. Hujus sunt illa: Licentia tantum concitum turbarum: & lascivire magis ple- bem quam sævire. Ejus & illud: carcerem esse plebis Romanæ domicilium. Talibus hominibus sæpe insusurranda Sopho- clis ista in Antigone: Ἀλλ' ἄνδρα κἂν τις ᾖ σοφὸς, τὸ μανθά- νειν. Πολλ' αἰσχρὸν οὐδὲν, καὶ τὸ μὴ τείνειν ἄγαν &c.

## 12:18
Verse 18. AND ALL ISRAEL STONED HIM) The most frequent cause of seditions is the severity of taxes: because this matter pertains to all, whereas the severity of punishments is wont to reach only a few. But the primary material of popular anger are those masters and ministers of royal avarice. All histories, ancient and recent, are full of examples.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ET LAPIDAVIT EVM OMNIS ISRAEL) Frequentissima seditionum causa tributorum gravitas: quia hæc res ad omnes pertinet, cum pœnarum sævitia ad paucos soleat pertingere. Materia autem prima popularis iræ sunt illi avaritiæ regalis magistri & ministri. Plenæ exemplorum omnes historiæ veteres & recentes.

## 12:26
V. 26. NOW THE KINGDOM SHALL RETURN TO THE HOUSE OF DAVID, IF &c.) Philo: αἴτιον τῆς ὁμονοίας τὸ ἀνώτατον καὶ μέγισον ἡ περὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς θεοῦ δόξα, ἀφ' ἧς οἷα πηγῆς ἑνωτικὴ καὶ ἀδίαλυτος φιλία κέχρηται πρὸς ἀλλήλους. But then the cause of the one possessing the Temple seemed stronger, and its king could bind to himself in many ways those coming to him on the occasion of religion.

Latin:

V. 26. NVNC REVERTITVR REGNVM AD DOMVM DAVID, SI &c.) Philo: αἴτιον τῆς ὁμονοίας τὸ ἀνώτατον καὶ μέ- γισον ἡ περὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς θεοῦ δόξα, ἀφ' ἧς οἷα πηγῆς ἑνωτικὴ καὶ ἀδίαλυτος φιλία κέχρηται πρὸς ἀλλήλους. Tum vero potior videbatur causa Templum possidentis, & rex ejus portionis venientes ad se ex religionis occasione alios multis modis devincire poterat.

## 12:28
Verse 28.

GOLDEN CALVES) Δαμάλεις χρυσᾶς ἐπωνύμως Θεῷ. Josephus. He wanted God to be worshipped in that figure which had once been dedicated to Joseph, the minister of God, from whom Jeroboam had sprung, and which formed a principal part in the Cherubim: so that even by that sight the people might be retained in the veneration of the posterity of Joseph, and might more easily believe that the kingdom was owed to those who had sprung from him, whose benefits to all the Israelites had been the greatest. Thus the Julian house wished the praises of Aeneas to be sung by all the poets, so that the people might the more mildly bear that empire as if it were given by the fates. Thus princes are wont to twist even sacred things to their own advantages. But Jeroboam ought not to have resorted to such trifles: but to trust in God, who was the author of his reigning, and to do what was his duty. But he, not content to sin in that he had erected a standing image against the law, and that he had performed sacred rites before it, made more temples instead of one, and priests not from that family which God had chosen.

Those conjectures are merely precarious: to which Grotius gave no credit, nor could he. But it is more likely, and approved by most other authors, that something still clung to that people from Egyptian idolatry, who were very prone to idolatrous worships, and were confirmed by Aaron himself in Egyptian idolatry with golden calves. For human dispositions are wont to return to their former customs, and are more easily entangled again by the seducing Devil in those things which once pleased them, however detestable they may be. But, these things being dismissed, those things which Grotius brings up a little later are worthy of more serious consideration. 'But he,' he says of Jeroboam, 'not content to sin in that he had erected a standing image against the law, and that he had performed sacred rites before it, made more temples instead of one, and priests not from that family which God had chosen.' For thus the sin of Jeroboam is less correctly defined: Nor is it so much exaggerated as it is extenuated. It was not prohibited to erect a standing image, therefore there was no sin in that, nor does that distinction between standing and non-standing images rest on any foundation. For even if the word פסל were to properly signify standing images, which in truth signifies no more to carve than to dig out, which is also clear from the tables of the law, which had letters not standing out, but hollowed, yet the Law is not to be restricted to those alone. For under one species in the Decalogue, others are contained by Synecdoche. And the rest, which are added concerning any likeness of animals, are referred by Philo and the LXX Interpreters to paintings, as Grotius admits; whence that Law was understood by the Jews not only of standing, but also of painted and excavated likenesses. Although indeed among the Jews existing and entire images, especially of human form, were held to be more dangerous (which is also the opinion of the modern Greeks), nevertheless they all believed ὁμοθυμαδὸν that figures of any things whatsoever in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, for the purpose of WORSHIP, whether sculpted, cast, or painted images, were prohibited by divine law; indeed, even that the use of images for direct worship was forbidden to the descendants of Noah before the law, Selden proved from Hebrew monuments in his book 2, On the Law of Nature and Nations according to the Doctrine of the Hebrews, ch. 5. Therefore, however true it may be that Jeroboam ought not to have erected more temples for one, and appointed other priests than those who were chosen by God, because this was forbidden by divine law, a more serious offense nevertheless occurs in this worship of Jeroboam, contrary to the first table of the law, and true idolatry; which Grotius conceals, without doubt for the sake of the Papists, whom he knows to be liable to a similar crime. For how can it be denied that Jeroboam made himself guilty of idolatry by the erection of the calves, when he is expressly accused of idolatry under that name in 1 Kings 14:9, and is declared there to be subject to the most severe punishment for the same? 'But you have done evil ABOVE ALL who were before you, and have made for yourself ALIEN GODS, and molten ones, to provoke me to anger, and me you have CAST behind your back,' etc. He is not chastised there for multiplied temples, or a different priesthood, but FOR ALIEN GODS, which he had made for himself by the erection of the golden calves. Although indeed Jeroboam was not so alienated from all religion, and of such madness, as to believe that those calves which he himself had made were the true God himself, he is nevertheless deservedly accused of idolatry because he worshipped God in them and before those calves, no differently than the Papists, who claim that they worship the true God in images. Grotius tried in vain to absolve them from idolatry, as witnessed by the writings exchanged in the Augustan Confession with Rivet. And that it is indeed forbidden to bow down before images in divine law, Grotius acknowledges in Discuss. p. 112, contending that those words, 'you shall not bow down to them,' signify 'at them' or 'before them': but he asserts, for the sake of his Papists, that this precept was given only as a positive law to the Jews, and does not bind Christians. But if to adore God before and in images is idolatry, how will that prohibition not bind Christians? Will idolatry be permitted to them? We have indeed proved that by the example of Jeroboam; to which is the twin example of Aaron, in the golden calves, and adoring the God of Israel before them: indeed, Grotius himself acknowledges this, while he attributes idolatry to Jeroboam for that reason, although contradicting himself, at chapter 13:24.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

VITVLOS AVREOS) Δαμάλεις χρυσᾶς ἐπωνύμως Θεῷ. Josephus. Volebat Deum coli in ea figura, quæ Josepho Dei ministro, unde ortus erat Jeroboamus, dicata olim fuerat, & quæ in Cherubinis partem faciebat præcipuam: ut vel illo aspectu populus retineretur in veneratione posteritatis Jose- phi, faciliusque crederet eis regnum deberi, qui orti essent ab eo, cujus maxima in omnes Israelitas fuerant beneficia. Sic Julia domus Æneæ laudes per omnes poetas cani voluit, ut eo lenius ferret populus imperium illud veluti, fatis datum. Sic solent principes etiam sacra ad suas utilitates torquere. Non debuerat autem Jeroboamus decurrere ad ejusmodi va- stramenta: sed Deo, qui regnandi ipsi auctor erat, confidere, & facere quod sui erat officii. At ille non in eo contentus peccare, quod exstantem imaginem erexisset contra legem, quodque apud eam sacra fecisset, plura pro uno fecit templa, & Sacerdotes non ex ea familia, quam Deus elegerat.

Mere precariæ sunt illæ conjecturæ: quibus fi- dem nullam fecit aut facere potuit Grotius. Verisi- mile autem magis est, aliisve autoribus plerisque probatum, hæsisse illi populo aliquid adhuc ex Æ- gyptiaca Idolatria, qui pronus admodum erat ad cultus idolatolatricos, & ab Aarone ipso vitulis aureis in Ægyptica idololatria confirmatus fuit. Redire e- nim solent ad pristinos mores humana ingenia, & facilius à Diabolo seductore illis vicissim implican- tur, quæ semel placuere, utut detestanda sint. Sed, istis missis, graviori animadversione digna sunt, quæ paulo post adducit Grotius. At ille, inquit de Jero- boamo, non in eo contentus peccare, quod exstantem imaginem erexisset contra legem, quodque apud eam sacra fecisset, plura pro uno fecit templa, & Sacerdo- tes non ex ea familia, quam Deus elegerat. Ita enim peccatum Jeroboam minus recte definitur: Nec tam exaggeratur, quam extenuatur. Non prohibi- tum erat, exstantem imaginem erigere, ideo in eo peccatum non fuit, neque ullo fundamento nititur illa inter imagines exstantes, & non exstantes distin- ctio. Nam etiamsi verbum פסל exstantes imagines proprie significaret, quod vero non magis sculpere, quam effodere significat, quod etiam ex tabulis le- gis, quæ literas habebant non extantes, sed cavatas, liquet, non tamen Lex ad illas solas restringenda. Sub una enim specie in Decalogo aliæ per Synecdo- chen continentur. Et referuntur cætera, quæ de quavis similitudine animalium addita sunt, à Philo- ne & LXX. Interpp. adpicturas, fatente Grotio; un- de à Judæis non de extantibus tantum, sed de pictis etiam & excavatis similitudinibus Lex illa intelle- cta. Quamvis vero apud Judæos extantes & inte- gras imagines, præsertim forma humana, periculo- siores habitæ sint, (quæ Græcorum etiam moderno- rum est sententia) nihilominus omnes figuras rerum quarumvis in cælo, terra & mari AD CULTUM sive sculptarum sive fusarum, sive pictarum imagi- num lege divina prohibitas esse ὁμοθυμαδὸν credi- derunt, imo etiam imaginum usum ad cultum dire- ctum posteris Noachi ante legem interdictam, credi- tum fuisse, ex Ebræorum monumentis Seldenus l. 2. de jure naturæ, & gentium secundum Doďtrinam E- bræorum c. 5. probavit. Utut ergo verum sit, quod Je- roboam non debuerit plura pro uno templa erigere, aliosq́ Sacerdotes, quam qui electi à Deo, constituere quia lege divina hoc interdictum, gravius tamen delictum in hoc Jeroboami cultu occurrit, tabulæ primæ legis contrarium, ac vera idololatria; quam dissimulat Grotius, sine dubio in Papistarum gra- tiam, quos parili crimini obnoxios novit. Quomo- do enim negari potest, Jeroboamum idololatrias reum se fecisse, vitulorum erectione, quum eo no- mine expresse idololatria arguatur 1. Reg. 14, 9. ac gravissimo ob eandem supplicio afficiendus ibi- dem prædicatur? Sed operatus es mala SUPER O- MNES qui fuerunt ante te, & fecisti tibi DEOS A- LIENOS, & conflatiles, ut me ad iracundiam provo- cares, me autem PROJECISTI post corpus tuum & c. Non ibi castigatur ob templa multiplicata, aut Sa- cerdotium diversum, sed OB DEOS ALIENOS, quos sibi fecerat, vitulorum aureorum erectione. Quamvis vero adeo ab omni religione alienus, tantæque dementiæ non fuerit Jeroboam, ut cre- deret, vitulos illos, quos ipse fecerat, esse ipsummet verum Deum, Idololatriæ tamen merito postula- tur, quod in illis, & coram illis vitulis Deum cole- ret, non secus atque Papistæ, qui in imaginibus De- um verum se colere, perhibent. Quos nequicquam ab Idololatria absolvere conatus est Grotius: te- stibus scriptis in August. Conf. amœbeis cum Riveto commutatis. Et vetitum quidem esse coram imagi- nibus se incurvare, in lege divina, Grotius in Discuss. p. 112. agnoscit, verba illa, non incurvabis te eis, id si- gnificare contendens, apud ea, vel coram eis: Sed hoc præceptum solum positivum esse Judæis datum, nec Christianos obligare, in gratiam Papistarum suo- rum asserit. At si coram, & in imaginibus Deum ado- rare idololatria est, quomodo interdictum illud non obligabit Christianos, num illis idololatria concessa erit? Illud vero probavimus exemplo Jero- boami; cui geminum Aaronis est, in vitulis aureis, & coram eis Deum Israelis adorántis: imo agno- scit id Grotius ipse, dum Jeroboamo ideo, quamvis sibi ipsi contradicens, idololatriam tribuit, ad capi- tis 13, 24.
