## 5:16
NON ACCIPIAM) Not that this was not often permitted and in use, as we have already noted more than once, but that not all things are suitable at all times. One had to take care lest a mind tender in piety should conceive such a thing regarding the Prophets of God as that which Creon objects to Tiresias in Sophocles: Τὸ μαντικὸν γὰρ πᾶν φιλάργυρον γένος. Compare a similar act of Abraham, Gen. 14, 22. 23. Furthermore, see what we have said regarding this matter at Matt. 10, 8.

Latin:

NON ACCIPIAM) Non quod hoc non sæpe liceret, & in usu esset, ut jam plus semel notavimus, sed quod non omnia omnibus temporibus conveniant. Cavendum erat ne tener in pietate animus de Prophetis Dei tale aliquid conciperet, quale est quod apud Sophoclem Creon Tiresiæ objicit: Τὸ μαντικὸν γὰρ πᾶν φιλάργυρον γένος. Confer simile factum Abrahami Genes. 14, 22. 23. præterea vi- de quæ ad hanc rem diximus ad Matth. 10, 8.

## 5:17
Verf. 17.

ONUS DUORUM BURDONUM) Of mules in the Hebrew, ἡμιόνων in the Greek: But Isidore distinguishes them thus, saying that a mule is from a mare and an ass, a burdo from a horse and a she-ass.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

ONUS DUORUM BURDONUM) Mulorum in Hebræo, ἡμιόνων in Græco: Verum Isidorus ita distinguit, ut mulum esse dicat ex equa & asino, burdonem ex equo & asina.

## 5:18
TEMPLUM REMMON) He seems to be Saturn, whose worship was widely spread in the East. The name comes from the fact that he is, as Tacitus speaks, in the highest sphere. The Greeks here [write] ῥεμμὰν, with the vowels changed. And perhaps Luke, Acts 7, 43, wrote ῥομμὰν, where now ῥεμφὰν is read. For in the place in Amos which he refers to, there is כִּיּוּן instead of כֵּיוָן, which Abenesdra taught us is how Saturn is called by the Persians and Arabs.

SI ADORAVERO] There is here in the Hebrew וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוִיתִי, a verbal noun of Chaldean form. It is, however, a certain extension of the hands and feet. To exhibit such a gesture before any idol was forbidden to the Israelites by law, without any exception of mind or interpretation. But foreigners were not bound by that law. Since, however, this Syrian never entered the idol-temple except for the sake of the king, and he himself professed that he was a worshipper of the most high God, and had even brought Israelite soil with him for sacrifices in His honor, the bystanders easily understood that this Syrian was performing that bowing of the body to the king, not to Saturn or his idol: See what we have said pertaining to this matter at Luke 4, 27.

UT IGNOSCAT MIHI DOMINUS) The Greeks [have] ἱλάσεται δὴ κύριος τῷ δούλῳ σου: that is, that God may not be offended by that matter, but rather take it in good and fair part.

Latin:

Verf. 18. TEMPLUM REMMON) Is videtur esse Sa- turnus, cujus in Oriente sparsus late cultus. Nomen inde quod sit, ut Tacitus loquitur, altissimo orbe. Græci hic ῥεμ- μὰν, mutatis ut sit vocalibus. Et forte Lucas Act. 7, 43. scri- pserit ῥομμὰν, ubi nunc ῥεμφὰν legitur. Nam in Amos. loco quem respicit, est כִּיּוּן pro כֵּיוָן quomodo & Persis & Ara- bibus vocari Saturnum nos docuit Abenesdra.

Verf. eod. SI ADORAVERO] Est hic in Hebræo וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוִיתִי, nomen verbale forma Chaldæa. Est autem extensio quædam manuum ac pedum. Talem gestum co- ram simulacro ullo exhibere Israelitis lege erat vetitum, sine ulla exceptione animi aut interpretationis. At alienigenæ lege ista non tenebantur. Cum vero hic Syrus nunquam in- grederetur idolium, nisi regis causa, ipse vero profiteretur se cultorem Dei summi, & in ejus honorem etiam humum Israe- liticam ad sacrificia sibi attulisset, facile intelligebant adstan- tes, Syrum hunc flexionem illam corporis regi præstare, non Saturno aut simulacro ejus: Vide quæ ad hanc rem perti- nentia diximus ad Luc. 4, 27.

UT IGNOSCAT MIHI DOMINUS) Græci ἱλάσεται δὴ κύριος τῷ δούλῳ σε : id est, ut Deus ea re non offendatur, verum eam boni & æqui consulat.

## 5:19
VADE IN PACE) Be secure in this regard. You will not be sinning against the law, which was not spoken to you.

Acts and gestures of religious adoration before idolatrous simulacra are prohibited in the law, not only to Israelites, but to all men whatsoever. For the Decalogue pertains to all. Grotius acknowledges that this is a part of it. Nor is that Law concerning not worshipping simulacra, or that no one should bow himself to alien Gods, or before them, merely positive, but it is a moral Law: Therefore, God exercised judgments upon the nations on account of the making of images for worship, because it is prohibited to all men to erect statues or images for worship, or to exhibit worship to them.

Moreover, as regards this request of Naaman, the interpretation of those who say that he is not asking about future, but past things, is best, so that God may be propitious to him because he had previously bowed himself in the temple of Rimmon in the company of the King: since he had subsequently determined no longer to serve idols, or to show them honor. Which sense the Weimar Paraphrasts also approve. That Grotius says Naaman brought Israelite soil for himself for the sake of sacrifices to the highest God, proceeded from a false interpretation of the text: that would have been superstition, lacking a divine command. The text is as follows: And there shall not be given now to thy servant (the Vulgate wrongly inserts the pronoun TO ME of its own, hence that common interpretation of the Papists, which pleased Grotius. But the servant of Elisha, Gehazi, is understood, not indeed Naaman) a burden of a pair of mules of earth? Thus is called the gift, which Naaman has only for a portion of earth, for the sake of extenuation. Concerning which he wished at least to give something to the servant of the Prophet, since the Prophet himself refused. That he might carry Israelite earth with him, he had no need to seek by prayers from the Prophet, nor was it of greater value, or efficacy in sacrifices. For where is such a thing found in the Holy Scriptures? In vain, therefore, does Cornelius gather from this the cult of the relics of the Saints. Many indeed, and commonly the Interpreters, explain the request of Naaman concerning the future, not the past; just as all versions (as far as is known) have rendered it in the future, even the Dutch one itself, although the authors in the added Notes warn that the Hebrew text can be explained otherwise, and propose another version, taking that request as concerning the past. R. Aben-Ezra on Exod. ch. 20, thinks that Naaman wished to worship the idol Rimmon alongside the true God, after the manner of the Samaritans 2 Kings 17, 33. But that this impiety is diametrically opposed to the law of God Exod. 20, 3. Josh. 24, v. 15. Matt. 6, 24. and is a limping between two sides 1 Kings 18, 21. and that Naaman intended to be converted, there is no doubt that it openly contradicts his most holy protestation v. 17. thy servant will no longer make burnt offering or sacrifice to strange Gods, but to the Lord: nor would Elisha have ratified it by tacit approval, who is indicated not obscurely to have assented to the request of the Syrian, v. 19.

However, the explanation of Adrian VI in IV Sententiar. tract. de Bapt. quaest. 1. art. 1. does not depart much from that opinion of Aben-Ezra, that here it is only a matter of external simulation of the adoration of Rimmon, which kind of simulation is not intrinsically evil, so that it can in no way be made honorable. Which also seems to have been the opinion of a certain person in B. D. Walther's Centur. Miscell. Theol. p. 102, suggesting to his son departing for Italy this kind of counsel by this example of Naaman, namely that he could with a safe conscience attend Mass, and use the same ceremonies as the Italians (Papists). But this is a species of idolatry, and Symbolization, and conformity, or communication with idolaters, an interpretative unequal yoking, and agreement and participation condemned by the Apostle, who admits no participation, no communion, no concord, no agreement, no portion of a believer with an unbeliever: and thus not even in external sacred rites, 2 Cor. 6, 14. seqq. This is simulation in religion, and a tacit denial of the true faith, for which true confessors have preferred to undergo death both in the Old and under the New Testament, as is evident from the example of Eleazar 2 Macc. 6, 21. seqq., the companions of Daniel, and the martyrs under the persecutions of the Gentiles and the Arians. Whence some, although they judge that Naaman sought to indulge himself in such simulation, yet say that the Prophet by no means assented to the same, since it is altogether illicit, and had the appearance of idolatry, nay, was by that very fact held by Naaman himself to be an illicit thing and a sin, in their own judgment, because he sought its pardon and forgiveness. To which view incline from the Reformed, Martyr in h. l., Aretius in L. C. col. 729; from the Papists, Gregorius Valentianus tr. de fid. profess. p. 107, and others. But if Naaman acknowledged this to be illicit, and truly a sin, with what appearance of piety could he ask of the Prophet either that he might indulge him in it, or that he might ask the Lord for him, if he were to admit such a thing, when he could have omitted it altogether? And was it not more correct for the Prophet to instruct Naaman and dissuade him from such a purpose, rather than to dismiss him in peace while he was still clinging to it, and to promise his prayers for a voluntary and deliberate intention of sinning, which they do not affirm of the Prophet with sufficient piety? Since Grotius saw this well in his Commentary on Luke 4, he attempted to resolve it thus: What is said concerning the bowing down of the body in the temple of Rimmon seems to me to be understood in such a way that it is not a deprecation of a sin not yet committed (which no wise man would admit), but rather an interpretation of an ambiguous act. For since that prostration of the body among the Syrians was as much a sign of ϑρησκείας as of that veneration which was shown to Kings, Naaman wished to testify that, as often as he was to accompany the King into the temple and was to bow down there, he was prepared to profess openly before the King and others that this was done not in honor of Rimmon, but of the Royal Majesty: he prayed that God would not so much forgive this, as take it in good part. that it is commended by Theodor Hackspan as excellent in his notes on this passage. For the very words of Naaman, which Hackspan himself rendered word for word, openly teach that Naaman is not interpreting an ambiguous act, but is begging for the forgiveness of a fault which he acknowledged: PARDON I PRAY THE LORD thy servant in this matter. The LXX render the word סלח as ἰλάσκεσθαι, which certainly implies propitiation. But Grotius objects in vain that the word סלח does not reject that sense of his, having adduced the passage in Numbers 30, verse 6, where יסלח means he will hold her innocent: For there also propitiation and the forgiveness of a vow made by a daughter, when the parent in whose power she is does not wish to ratify it, is insinuated by that word, nor is it anywhere merely the same as to take in good part: whence Osiander rightly interpreted that passage: The Lord will be propitious to her, that is, He will not be angry with her because she does not keep the vow, for the reason that she did not depart from the vow of her own accord, but her Father contradicted it: whose authority (the divine law commanding) she ought not to have despised. For the word סלח is he was propitious, he has been propitiated, he spared: having a contrary meaning to the word חסל he devastated without sparing, as Avenarius notes, whence by the conversion of the root ἰλάσκω I appease, ἱλάσκομαι I am propitious: See Exodus 34, verse 9. Numbers 14, verses 19, 20; chapter 30, verses 9, 13; Deuteronomy 29, verse 19; 2 Samuel 24, 4; 1 Kings 8, verse 30; Psalm 103; Jeremiah 31, verse 34; Daniel 9, verse 20; nor does it occur anywhere with another meaning.

Wherefore neither can that explanation of Grotius, which Georgius Abbatius, Archbishop of Canterbury, defends in his 6th lecture, illustrated question 4, along with most interpreters, that Naaman's request intends a dispensation regarding future duties to be performed for the King upon entering an idolatrous temple, have any place. For in that external political duty there was no fault in itself, and therefore it did not need forgiveness or propitiation. Nor indeed can that explanation be helped by the exception of Lyranus, and those who followed him, Abulensis, Estius, and Azorius in his Moral Institutions, book 8, chapter 37, page 836, Johannes Malderus on Theological Truth, question 3, page 107, and others, that Elisha did not indeed grant a dispensation in this, but only declared to him that what he feared was illicit was not illicit, as timid consciences are wont to do. For here an ambiguous and scrupulous conscience, as to whether that thing is illicit or not, does not appear. But since it was certain to this convert that the action of which he speaks was not free from sin, he seeks forgiveness for it, not a dispensation, and by those words, Go in peace, he receives absolution, which do not contain any declaration, nor are they ever taken in that way, but if they are used only for the sake of dismissal and leave-taking, they imply absolution: indeed, according to Tossanus, they imply displeasure and a denial of consent, and are explained by Junius and Tremellius thus, i.e., be of a quiet mind: and do not be anxious about those things which do nothing for the peace of your conscience, but would rather disturb it and provoke God against you. Thus 1 Samuel 1, 17, and above 4, 23, and 26. Strigelius indeed in his Commentary on this passage also goes so far as to say that Naaman anxiously asked whether he could with a good conscience accompany his master entering into an idolatrous temple? (which also seemed to be the case to Dr. Thummius in his Explanation of the Decalogue, page 88.) But it is manifest from the text that no question or case of conscience is proposed in a doubtful matter, but that here we have a most humble deprecation of a sin and an action which he acknowledged without doubt to be illicit. Whence he was a suppliant seeking its forgiveness, which the blessed Quistorpius acknowledges in his annotations on this passage, even though he also interprets this genuflection as done not in honor of the idol, but of the King: which we also observe in Hackspan, page 749. To Stephanus Menochius, who says that by the words Go in peace, it was granted by the Prophet that he could bow himself while the King was worshiping idols, because it was not done for the worship of the idol, but by reason of his ministry, I reply: But it is not to be granted even that far, and Cajetan argues far more correctly that in the words, Go in peace, no concession lies hidden, because the words are very common, and therefore by the force of the speech they affirm nothing. Add that it seems to some that even that genuflection, which was made of necessity by the minister upon whom the King leaned, while the King was bowing before the idol, even if not in honor of the idol, but on account of the performance of the duty owed to the King, cannot be absolved from symbolization and communication with idolatry: which opinion, however, of Gisbertus Voetius we set forth only humanly to other Reformed; because even if he seems to bow the knee with the same mind (which Voetius urges, part 3, Select Disputations, on indirect and participated idolatry, page 297), manner, and end as the idolatrous Lord, that does not yet infer participated idolatry, but only an appearance of such evil, unless it is in the open that it is truly not done with that mind, manner, and end, but only on account of the performance of a common and civil duty, for then the appearance of evil vanishes: nor is scandal given by him who performs only a due duty. Whence for that reason, not only the Pontificians Thomas a Jesu, book 10, on the conversion of the gentiles, chapter 3, and Caspar Santhius in his commentary, [do not] leave it to lax Casuists. to this place, but Voetius also rashly adds his Abbot in the same place, chapter 4, because they maintain that such bowing is lawful for handmaids or waiting-women, provided they speak of merely civil duties, and Voetius himself admits in the same place that it is lawful to be present, or rather to attend or stand by at idolatrous rites, not indeed willingly, but out of necessity, for those who are BOUND to be present in order to perform civil and common duties, yet in such a way that by a protestation and declaration of their intention they consult the conscience of the weaker and their own reputation. But what difference is there in the fact that someone is present by standing at the rites, and when he is present, by bowing down, when he is equally bound to perform this out of the necessity of his ministry, so that the Lord may lean upon him, and he performs it no otherwise than for the sake of a political duty, and with the protestation and declaration already mentioned? The position of standing, or lying down, certainly does not make or remove idolatry: since both are notoriously a merely political duty.

But this is what is especially missing in this example of Naaman, which is assumed by many as if it were undoubted, namely that only a civil duty is described here. For in the text two things are designated, of which the one is only a civil duty, namely that the King was accustomed to lean upon the hand of Naaman when he worshipped in the house of Rimmon, but the other introduces a religious act, not only of participated idolatry, but of direct idolatry, namely that then also Naaman himself worshipped in the house of Rimmon with his worship in the house of Rimmon (which is a Hebraism, he worshipped by worshipping, that is, he himself worshipped entirely). Where clearly the same verb, the same expression is in the Hebrew text, nor is anything else about the idolatrous King held to be worshipping, than what Naaman professes concerning himself, regarding this latter act: the object of the adoration is not added, but it is simply said, that he may worship there (the King) in the temple, namely Rimmon, and Naaman speaks similarly concerning himself: and I shall have worshipped in the temple of Rimmon. Some, neglecting that Hebraism, prefer that Naaman, when he leaned upon his hand, prayed for the adoration made with the King, and for his own adoration, since he sought not only that he be forgiven insofar as he worships together with the King, but, as they themselves distinguish the text, that he went to entreat pardon for his own adoration in the house of Rimmon, and thus for his own idolatry. There is added that observation, that the verb השתחוה when it is joined with a word that denotes an idol or an idolatrous temple, never signifies anything but religious worship: which observation Hackspan could not refute with any contrary example; nay, he concedes that religious worship is then especially denoted by this word, if mention is made of an idol, or of an idolatrous temple, nor can it be denied that in this very place this word is so understood concerning the King of Syria; which, however, is not used otherwise here concerning Naaman, but with the same determination, by reason of the place, the temple of Rimmon. At least he replies that it cannot be so understood here concerning Naaman, since his express protestation stands in the way, that he does not wish to serve strange gods any longer, and that he brings forward his duty. But this is to beg the question: for he assumes it as if he were speaking of the future, not of the past, and of a civil duty, not indeed of a religious act. The reason which is urged, that the petition was already formed beforehand concerning a future matter, namely, the building of an altar, and therefore the holy earth to be brought, which would serve for this matter, is nothing: because even if he had dealt beforehand concerning a future matter, why could he not now deal concerning a past one, and ask again and again for pardon for the sin committed? Nor is it admittedly certain that it was dealt with beforehand concerning a future matter, namely the building of an altar, because it cannot be proven by any document that that persuasion or will-worship concerning sacrificing on an altar built from holy earth had clung to this convert. Furthermore, as to Hackspan's appeal to the order of nature, that contrition should precede the change of worship, and that pardon should not finally follow where religion has already been changed, that in part does not prejudice our opinion: because we acknowledge that contrition preceded and pardon was obtained, even if here, with his conscience still urging, he solicitously asks for deprecation, which can also be done by those who have already obtained the remission of sins: but in part it must not be admitted; since pardon and the forgiveness of committed sins follow only after the change of religion, that is, the acknowledgment of the true GOD and faith in the one true God: because we do not obtain the remission of sins except through faith, Acts 10, verse 43, Romans 3, verse 25; but without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. 11, 6.

Nor indeed does the argument stand on its own foundation, upon which the most distinguished man seems to rely primarily, having followed Buxtorf, as appears from page 734, cited on page 752; if Naaman had sought the dismissal of the idolatry committed long ago, he ought to have alleged his own impiety, which he performed not as a servant of the King, but as a sectarian, who, even long before he was bound to the service of the King, was addicted to idolatrous religion or superstition, without a doubt so taught by his parents; nay, he ought to have alleged that idolatry in which he was educated, which he practiced willingly, and not at all forced, not without zeal when he was outside the King's office: and he ought to have detested not that alone, but his whole past life from the idolatry committed. For it can be answered that Naaman prayed especially against public idolatry, because in the very temple of Rimmon he worshipped the worst idol while others, and the King himself, were worshipping, because his conscience was most afflicted by the anguish of this; concerning which he teaches in no word that he was forced by any necessity, since he could have performed his duty without the adoration of the idol, nor was he driven to this by any force. Therefore, what was pressing most upon his conscience was this; not that he was educated in idolatry from his youth, not that he practiced it privately, but that, being established in eminence, when he could easily have had knowledge of the true GOD, having spurned it, he had seduced others by his example in the public worship of the idol Rimmon, or confirmed them in idolatry; that a man of such authority and prudence had openly worshipped that detestable idol with great devotion. Therefore he instituted a most humble deprecation of his crime repeatedly: Let Jehovah forgive thy servant, let Jehovah forgive, I pray, thy servant concerning this matter, not as if doubtful of the grace of God and the plenary forgiveness of sin, but that he might obtain the support and intercession of so great a Prophet, and through them might obtain more and more confirmation against any temptations of conscience, which even the most holy have need of, Psalm 32, verse 6. For this is especially to be observed (which we judge to appear from the whole history) that Naaman, before he met Elisha, had already acknowledged the GOD of Israel, and worshipped Him with his house, whether taught from the information of the Israelite girl captured in war, or otherwise taught concerning the God of Israel: but that he had also worshipped the idol Rimmon alongside the God of Israel, just as the Israelites not rarely worshipped idols along with the true GOD, and afterwards it was customary among the Samaritans, 2 Kings 17. For that he had worshipped the true God Himself, we are not allowed to doubt, both by his confidence concerning his deliverance from leprosy, on account of which he sets out to the Prophet of the Lord: and by his profession concerning calling upon the name of the God of Israel, verse 11; and by his obedience rendered to the admonition of his servants to Elisha, with the hope of purification from leprosy, verse 13. Nor does that confession after the miraculous restoration teach anything else: Behold I see that there is no GOD in all the lands, except in Israel, by which he testifies that although he had previously believed in other Gods along with the GOD of Israel, he now acknowledges that He alone is the true GOD, verse 15. Whence in verse 17 he protested that he would henceforth offer sacrifices to no other GOD except the Lord, and he prays for forgiveness for that sin, that he had previously served another GOD also, namely the idol Rimmon, thinking at that time that he could properly worship both the GOD of Israel and the GOD Rimmon, which idolatry he now openly detests, and prays that pardon for it be granted to him. If this had been accurately observed, as was proper, most interpreters would hardly have gone in entirely different directions here.

Add, however, here the grammatical argument, which Mr. Saubertus especially executed, by which he supported this explanation—that Naaman's petition is to be taken not as referring to the future, but to the past, as handed down in a German writing in a letter to a certain distinguished man, cited by Dr. Walther in the place cited, page 102—that this Vav in this place is copulative, not conversive, and [I read] 'and I worshipped,' or 'I bowed myself,' since in the first person of the past the accent holds the penultimate syllable, that is, Paschta, and in the word it is doubled in Millel: concerning which one may read there. They also urge this rule: The gerund must be understood as referring to the past: Regarding which, since Hackspan discusses it at length on both sides, we leave the judgment to the sons of the Grammarians. That, however, must not be rashly neglected which arises for us from a comparison of verses 18 and 19: For since 'Go in peace' is submitted to the deprecation of guilt, it is manifest that it is not a bare valedictory formula, bringing only a wish, but rather it brings about the remission of the guilt which one has deprecated: For this is what that mutual relation demands, the deprecation of guilt and the remission; this is also what usage demands. See Mark 5, verse 34; Luke 5, verse 24; chapter 7, verse 50; chapter 8, verse 48; chapter 17, verse 19; chapter 18, verses 13, 14. Compare 2 Kings 22, verses 19, 20.

Mr. Hackspan objects that a reason is supplied from the text why the formula is valedictory, bringing forward or involving nothing other than a wish: For he says that Naaman had asked for two things, in verse 17: 1. A portion of earth that would be enough for building an altar in Syria, and thus outside the holy land. For the proselyte, not being sufficiently instructed, thought that no one could aspire to the worship of the true GOD unless he also offered sacrifices, which could not be done without an altar. Therefore he asks for holy earth, and judged that which was in Syria to be profane, or certainly profaned, and thus unfit for building an altar to the true GOD. For this is how the Rabbis understand it. 2. He had asked for pardon for bowing down in the temple of Rimmon. But the Prophet replies to neither request anything other than לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם. Therefore, either by the words 'Go in peace' he granted both, or Elisha replies to both, or to neither. Not to both: for it is not permitted to the Prophets to innovate anything in worship, except in case of the necessity of the hour, that is, if the highest necessity so demands, which here there was none. Therefore the Prophet grants nothing by this formula, but dismisses him as he is leaving.

Reply. (1.) That this was the opinion of the neophyte concerning the necessity of sacrifices and an altar for the worship of GOD, and this intention of offering sacrifices on a small portion of earth to be brought from Judea, is less solidly proven from the mere persuasion of the Rabbis, because they understand it thus, namely that in that verse it is said concerning the earth to be presented לַעֲשׂוֹת מִזְבֵּחַ 'to make an altar'; since nothing of that is held in the text, nor can any solid reason for that opinion be brought forward. How much weight should be given to the Rabbis in such matters is obscure to no one. (2.) If Naaman had remained in that error and that superstition, without doubt the Prophet would have removed it from him, and would not have dismissed him with it. For he would have had to be fully informed how gross that opinion is concerning the necessity for the true worship of GOD outside the land of Israel, both of sacrifices and of an altar: how vain that superstition is, and the ἐθελοθρησκεία (will-worship) concerning building an altar from some small portion of Israelite earth, so that offerings might be made on it that are pleasing to GOD. (3.) Since the words of the text bear a far different sense, as we said before, there is no need to say that the reply 'Go in peace' was made to that institution, or that Naaman was simply dismissed. But as for the burden of two mules of that earth, there was no need for a further reply: because he had already simply refused that gift: and thus both that sworn assertion, 'The Lord lives, before whom I stand, that I will not accept,' and the refusal, when Naaman wanted to almost force him to accept the gift, was a sufficient reply in verse 16. (5.) What is brought forward from the Rabbis concerning innovation in worship being lawful for Prophets in a case of necessity (to touch upon it briefly) must be taken with a grain of salt. Namely, Prophets are viewed either as Prophets, or as they do something by the instinct and impulse of the Spirit, or by themselves. Therefore, that innovation could not be undertaken even by the Prophets, even in a case of necessity (for no necessity is to be feigned against the precepts of God regarding His worship), unless according to the divine dictate or the Spirit of God, by which the Prophets were moved as such.

Furthermore, Mr. Hackspan objects to some things against the explanation approved in the Weimar Bibles, that by משׂא צמד are to be understood the treasures which Naaman had carried with him, which he wanted to give to Elisha's servant, when Elisha himself refused to accept them; which he called by that name out of contempt or disparagement, which it would have been worth the effort to examine.

1. If that treasure is called so out of contempt, could he have honored the Prophet with a thing to be despised and of no value? Reply. Although that hero calls them so by way of disparagement, just as gifts are wont not so much to be praised by the offerer as to be disparaged, and in truth such gifts are only earth dug from the earth, and finally of altogether cheaper price or value, if they are compared with health, or rather with the salvation of the soul: yet they were not for that reason things to be despised and of no value simply. What is said κατά τι (in a certain respect) and συγκριτικῶς (comparatively) is not to be taken ἁπλῶς (simply).

2. He, he says, is understood by the servant, who denies that he wishes to worship foreign gods any longer. But that man was Naaman, not the servant of Elisha. I respond: the solid proof of that consequence is lacking: for why could Naaman not profess of himself, 'your servant,' and of Gehazi, 'your servant'? He named himself so out of veneration for the Prophet, but Gehazi because of the service by which he served the Prophet. For since the Prophet himself had sworn to refuse the acceptance of gifts, so that he might allow only his servant to be affected by some gift, the illustrious man entreats, so that, namely, he might not seem to have brought these gifts with him in vain, and so that he might declare his gratitude at least in that way to the minister of the Prophet.

3. The burden of two mules would not have been some cheap treasure, which ought to be distributed among servants; but it would have been a most distinguished gift. I respond: In what sense this gift is called cheap, has already been said. From such a great Satrap, who had brought such huge treasures for the sake of remuneration, what is the wonder that it is called cheap, and is offered to the minister of such a great Prophet, whom he venerated as a Lord?

4. The causal particle כי is repugnant. For what is this coherence: I do not wish to worship foreign gods any longer. Therefore, concede that I may give this treasure, which you refuse, to your servant? I respond: The connection is sound. Allow that the prophetic minister may accept the gift which I offer: because henceforth I will have no commerce with foreign gods, and their ministers; I will worship only the God of Israel, and I will hold his ministers of whatever order in reverence: Let this gift be a certain testimony of that thing, and as it were a pledge, and a certain earnest: for all my things will be consecrated to the glory of the one God.

5. Finally, Mr. Hackspan demands that a passage be brought forward where משׂא צמד is taken in this sense. I respond: No necessity demands that: provided only that it is understood conveniently here in this way, whether by metonymy, because those gifts are from the earth, or metaphorically, because he esteems them as so cheap with respect to the grace conferred upon him as the earth, which is trodden by the feet,

to be estimated with respect to heaven, of which he had already become a partner and citizen. Nor does he call the earth absolutely so: but he speaks of the present burden of two mules. But the mules certainly were not carrying a portion of earth: indeed, it is not to be understood as only a treasure of gold: for he had brought gifts of a different kind on the mules: just as is evident from verse 5 concerning the garments and talents of silver given to Gehazi. Why, therefore, is a passage demanded where earth is precisely taken for treasure? And these things are concerning the present passage, which, along with us, in the past, concerning the idolatry committed, B. Saubertus understands, who prolixly asserted this sense, B. Dorschæus T. I. Theol. Zachar. p. 83, urging the force of the word סלח. B. Dannhauer, Theol. conscient. Tom. I. pag. 652, comparing for the preterite signification 'that I have entered' Psalm 51, verse 1, Genesis 48, verse 7, Numbers 7, verse 87, B. D. Walther, Cent. 1. Miscell. pag. 102. and B. D. Mehlführerus, as well as ὁ δεῖνα, who had first contradicted Lord Saubertus, but finally adopted the same opinion, the votes of both of whom were adduced there by B. Walther on page 107. The blessed D. Glassius in Hackspan, page 233. Likewise the Weimar Paraphrasts, and the Dutch and English Annotators, as well as Gisbert Voet, in the place cited. Which opinion also Matthæus Radecius did not fear to point out as handed down by most in a letter to F. Socinus: nor did Socinus doubt that by the force of the words themselves it could have a place, even if he did not add his vote to it, Epist. 4 to Radec. in Epist. ad amicos page 175.

Latin:

VADE IN PACE) Securus hac parte esto. Non delin- ques in legem, quæ tibi dicta non est.

REligiosæ adorationis actus & gestus coram simu- lacris idololatricis non Israeliticis tantum, sed quibusvis hominibus prohibiti sunt in lege. Deca- logus enim ad omnes pertinet. Cujus hanc partem aliquam esse, agnoscit Grotius. Neque Lex illa de simulacris non colendis, vel ne quis incurvet se Diis alienis, aut coram iis, positiva tantum est, sed Lex moralis : Ideo propter imaginum ad cultum fabri- cationem Judicia Deus in gentes exeruit, quod omnibus hominibus id prohibitum sit, statuas vel imagines ad cultum erigere, vel cultum iis exhibere.

Cæterum quod ad hanc deprecationem Naamanis attinet, optima est eorum interpretatio, qui non futura, sed præterita ipsum deprecari dicunt, ut propitius ei Deus sit, quod antea in æde Rimmon in co- mitatu Regis se incurvaverit : Siquidem deinceps constituerit non amplius Idolis servire, aut hono- rem exhibere. Quem sensum etiam Vinarienses Pa- raphrastæ probant. Quod in honorem Dei summi hu- mum Israeliticam ad Sacrificia sibi attulisse Naama- nem dicit Grotius, e ψευδερμηνείᾳ textus profe- ctum est: Superstitio illa fuisset, mandato divino carens. Textus ita habet: Et non dabitur nunc servo tuo (Vulgatus de suo perperam ingerit prono- men MIHI, inde illa Papistarum communis inter- pretatio, quæ Grotio placuit. Intelligitur autem servus Elisæi, Gehasi, non vero Naaman) onus pa- ris mulorum terræ? Sic vocatur munus, quod pro terræ portione aliqua tantum habet Naaman, exte- nuationis gratia. De quo aliquid volebat saltem servo Prophetæ donare, cum Propheta ipse renue- ret. Ut terram Israeliticam secum referret, non opus habebat precibus expetere a Propheta, nec illa majoris pretii erat, aut efficaciæ in Sacrificiis. Ubi enim tale quid in Sacris literis habetur? Ne- quicquam ergo hinc cultum reliquiarum Sanctorum colligit Cornelius. Explicant quidem postula- tum Naamanni plerique,& vulgo Interpp. de futu- ro, non de præterito; quemadmodum versiones omnes (quantum constat) in futuro reddidere, etiam ipsa Belgica, tametsi autores in Notis adje- ctis moneant, textum Ebræum aliter exponi posse, ac versionem aliam, de præterito postulatum illud accipientem, proponant. R. Aben-Ezra ad Exod. cap. 20. existimat, Naamanem juxta cum vero Deo etiam idolum Rimmon colere voluisse, Sama- ritanorum more 2.Reg. 17, 33. Sed hanc impietatem καδδιάμετρον legi Dei adversam Exod. 20, 3. Jos. 24. v. 15. Matth. 6, 24. & claudicationem in utramque partem 1. Reg. 18, 21. Naamanem conversum in- tendisse, protestationi ejus sanctissimæ v. 17. non faciet ultra servus tuus holocaustum aut victimam Diis alienis, nisi Domino, aperte repugnare dubium non est: neque ratam eam habuisset approbatione tacita Elisæus, quem vero postulato Syri annuisse, v. 19. haud obscure indicatur.

Non multum tamen abit ab illa Aben-Esdrae sententia Adriani VI. in IV. sententiar. tract. de Bapt. quæst. 1. art. 1. explicatio, quod hic solum de externa simulatione adorationis Rimmon agatur, cu- jusmodi simulatio intrinsece mala non sit, adeo, ut nulla ratione honestari possit. Quod sensisse etiam videtur ὁ δεῖνα apud B. D. Waltherum in Centur. Mifcell. Theol. p. 102. filio in Italiam abiturienti hoc Naamanis exemplo istiusmodi suggerens con- silium, quod nempe salva conscientia Missæ inter- esse, & easdem cum Italis (Pontificiis) ceremonias usurpare possit. Sed hæc idololatriæ species est, & Symbolizatio, ac conformatio, vel communicatio cum idololatris, ἑτεροζυγία interpretativa, & συγκα- τάθεσις καὶ μετοχή ad Apostolo damnata, qui nul- lam μετοχὴν, nullam κοινωνίαν, nullam συμφώνησιν, nullam συγκατάθεσιν, nullam μερίδα πιστ͂ μετὰ ἀπίστ: adeoque ne in externis quidem sacris ad- mittit, 2. Cor. 6, 14. seqq. Simulatio hæc est in reli- gione, & tacita veræ fidei abnegatio, præ qua mor- tem subire maluere veri confessores cum in Vete- ri, tum sub Novo Testamento, ut exemplo Elea- zari 2. Macc. 6, 21. seqq. sociorum Danielis, & mar- tyrum sub persequutionibus gentilium, & Ariano- rum, constat. Unde nonnulli, etsi Naamanum si- mulationem ejusmodi sibi indulgere petiisse cen- seant, Prophetam tamen minime eidem annuisse ajunt, siquidem ea omnino illicita sit, ac speciem idololatriæ habuerit, imo eo ipso a Naamano pro re illicita & peccato, ipsorummet judicio, habita fue- rit, quod ejusdem veniam & condonationem pe- tierit. Quo abeunt e Reformatis Martyr in h. l. Aretius in L. C. col. 729. e Pontificiis Gregorius Valentianus tr. de fid. profess. p. 107. aliique. At si agnovit hoc Naaman illicitum, vereque peccatum esse, qua pietatis specie potuit a Propheta petere, vel ut sibi id indulgeret, vel ut pro se rogaret Do- minum, si tale quid admitteret, quum id intermit- tere omnino potuerit? Et annon Prophetæ erat rectius informare Naamanem, & dehortari a tali proposito, non vero eidem inhærentem in pace dimittere, ac intentioni voluntariæ & deliberate peccandi preces suas polliceri, quod illi de Prophe- ta non satis pie affirmant. Quod quum probe viderit Grotius Commentar. ad Luc. 4. ita expe- dire conatus est: Quod de corporis procubitu in templo Rimmonis dicitur, intelligendum ita mihi videtur, ut sit non peccati nec dum perpetrati de- precatio (quam nemo sapiens admiserit) sed potius interpretatio facti ambigui. Nam cum corporis ista dejectio apud Syros tam ϑρησκείας esset signum, quam ejus venerationis, quæ Regibus exhibebatur, teftatum volebat Naaman, se quoties Regem in tem- plum comitatus ibidem esset procubiturus, factum id non in honorem Rimmonis, sed Regiæ Majestatis, pa- ratus suit, id ipsum coram Rege atq; aliis palam profi- teri: non tam ut hoc condonaret, quam ut æqui confu- leret Deus, precabatur. Quam vero explicatio- nem nemo facile probaverit: ut mirari adeo ha- beat eam a Theodor. Hackspan. ceu egregiam in not. ad h. l. commendatam. Nam non interpretari Naaman, factum ambiguum, sed culpam, quam agnoscebat, deprecari, verba ipsa Naamani palam docent, quæ Hackspanius ipse κατὰ πόδα reddidit: IGNOSCAT QVÆSO DOMINUS servo tuo hac in re. Verbum סלח LXX. reddunt ἰλάσκεσθαι, quod utique propitiationem infert. Frustra autem Grotius obvertit verbum סלח sensum illum suum non respuere, adducto loco Numer. 30. vers. 6. ubi יסלח sit innocentem habebit: Nam ibi etiam propi- tiatio, & condonatio voti a filia emissi, cum id ra- tum habere non vult parens, in cujus potestate ipsa est, verbo illo insinuatur, nec uspiam illud tan- tum idem est, quod æqui bonique consulere: unde recte Osiander locum istum interpretatus est: Do- minus propitius erit ei, id est, non irascetur ei, quod votum non servet, eo quod non sua sponte a voto disces- serit, sed contradixerit Pater ejus: cujus autoritatem (lege divina jubente) contemnere non debuit. Ver- bum enim סלח est propitius fuit, propitiatus est, pe- percit: contrariam significationem habens verbo חסל vastavit absq; parcendo, notante Avenario, unde per conversionem radicis ἰλάσκω placo, ἱλά- σκομαι propitius sum: Vid. Exod. 34. vers. 9. Numer. 14. vers. 19. 20. cap. 30. vers. 9. 13. Deut. 29. vers. 19. 2. Sam. 24, 4. 1. Reg. 8. vers. 30. Psalm. 103. Jerem. 31. vers. 34. Dan. 9. vers. 20. nec uspiam alia significa- tione occurrit.

Quapropter nec explicatio illa Grotii quam Georg. Abbatius Archi-Episcop. Cantuar. in præ- lect. 6. illustr. quæst. q. 4. cum plerisque interpp. tuetur, quod postulatum Naamani dispensationem super futuris officiis Regi in aditu ad idololatricum templum præstandis intendat, locum habere potest. Qui in illo externo officio politico per se nulla culpa erat, ideoque nec condonatione, aut propi- tiatione id indigebat. Neque vero juvare eam ex- plicationem potest Lyrani, & qui eum sequuti sunt Abulensis, Estii, & Azorii in instit. moral. lib. 8. cap. 37. pag. 836. Johan. Malderi de Veritat. Theol. quæst. 3, p. 107. & aliorum exceptio, quod Elisæus quidem non in eo dispensaverit, sed solum ipsi de- claravit, illud non esse illicitum, quod timebat esse illicitum, sicut solent facere conscientiæ timorosæ. Non enim hic conscientia ambigua & scrupulosa, utrum res illa illicita sit, nec ne? apparet. Sed quum cer- tum huic converso esset, actionem illam, de qua loquitur, peccato non vacare, condonationem ejus- dem petit, non dispensationem, & verbis illis, Vade in pace, absolutionem accipit, quæ non declara- tionem aliquam continent, nec uspiam ita accipi- untur, sed sinon dimissionis solum & valedictionis ergo adhibentur, absolutionem inferunt: imo se- cundum Tossanum displicentiam & consensus dene- gationem important, & a Junio & Tremellio sic ex- ponuntur, q. d. quieto animo esto: & ne sis sollicitus de istis rebus, quæ nihil ad pacem conscientiæ tuæ fa- ciunt, sed potius illam turbaturæ essent, & Deum in te provocaturæ. Sic 1. Schem. 1, 17. & supra 4, 23. & 26. Strigelius sane in Comm. ad h. l. etiam eo abit, quod Naaman solicite quæsiverit, an possit bona conscientia comitari dominum ingredientem in tem- pium idololatricum? (quod etiam visum fuit Dn. D. Thummio in explic. Decalog. pag. 88.) Sed e textu manifestum est, non quæstionem, vel casum conscien- tiæ proponi, in re dubia, sed humillimam hic ha- beri deprecationem peccati, & actionis, quam indu- bitato agnoscebat illicitam. Unde ejus condona- tionem supplex petebat, quod agnoscit B. Quistor- pius in ann. ad h. l. etsi etiam hæc de genuflexione non in honorem idoli, sed Regis facta interpretetur: quod etiam in Hackspanio observamus pag. 749. Stephano Menochio, dicenti, per verba Vade in pace, concessum fuisse a Propheta, ut se incurvare posset, Rege idola colente, eo quod non fieret in cultum idoli, sed ratione ministerii, reponenti: At nec eo us- que concedendum est, ac longe rectius disputat Ca- jetanus in verbis, Vade in pace, nullam concessionem latere, quia verba sunt valde communia, & pro- pterea ex vi sermonis nihil affirment. Adde, quod nonnullis videatur, nec illam genuflexionem, quæ ex necessitate a ministro, cui Rex innitebatur, Rege coram idolo procumbente, fiebat, etiamfi non in honorem idoli, sed ob officii Regi debiti præ- stationem, a symbolizatione & communicatione cum idololatria absolvi posse: quam tamen sententiam Gisberti Voetii nar' ἄνθρωπον solum reponimus aliis Reformatis; quia etsi videatur eodem animo, (quod urget Voetius part. 3. Disp. select. de idololatria indi- recta & participata pag. 297.) modo, & fine genu flectere, quo Dominus idololatra, id tamen non- dum infert participatam idololatriam, sed speciem solum mali ejusmodi, nisi tamen in aprico sit revera eo animo, modo & fine id minime fieri, sed solum ob præstationem communis, & civilis officii, tum enim species mali evanescit: nec scandalum datur ab eo, qui debitum solum præstat officium. Unde ea quidem de causa laxis Casuistis non solum Pon- tificios Thomam a Jesu lib. 10. de convers. gent. cap. 3. Caspar. Santhium in comment. ad h. l. sed etiam Abbatum suum l. c. c. 4. temere accenset Voe- tius, quod licitam ejusmodi incurvationem esse ancillis, seu pedissequis statuant, siquidem de officiis mere civilibus loquantur, ipseque Voetius fateatur l. c. licitum esse interesse aut potius adesse aut adstare sa- cris idololatricis, non quidem sponte, sed ex necessita- te, illis, qui propter civilia & communia officia præ- standa adesse TENENTUR, sic tamen, ut prote- statione & declaratione consilii sui conscientiæ infir- miorum & famæ suæ consulant. Quæ autem diffe- rentia est in eo, quod quis adest, adstando sacris, & cum adest, procumbendo, cum hoc ex necessi- tate ministerii æque tenetur præstare, ut Domi- nus ipsi inniti possit, nec aliter præstat, quam offi- cii Politici causa, & cum protestatione & declara- tione jam dicta? Situs utique stationis, vel cubatio- nis non facit, vel tollit idololatriam: cum utrum- que notorie officium est mere politicum.

Id vero in hoc exemplo Naamani impri- mis desideratur, quod a multis velut indubium as- sumitur, quod nempe hic officium tantum civile describatur. Nam in textu duo designantur, quorum alterum civile tantum officium est, quod nempe inniti Rex consueverit super manum Naa- manis, cum in domo Rimmon adoravit, alte- rum vero actum religiosum infert, non idololatriæ participatæ tantum, sed directæ, quod nempe tum etiam adorarit Naaman ipse in domo Rimmon adoratione sua in domo Rimmon (qui Ebraismus est, adorando adoravit, id est, omnino adoravit ipse) Ubi plane idem verbum, eadem locutio est in E- bræo textu, nec quicquam aliud de Rege idololatra adorante habetur, quam quod de sese profitetur Naaman, quoad hunc posteriorem actum: non ad- ditur objectum adorationis, sed simpliciter dici- tur, ut adoret ibi (Rex) in templo, nempe Rim- mon, ac de se similiter loquitur Naaman: & ado- raverim in templo Rimmon. Nonnulli neglecto illo Ebraismo malunt Naamanum & adorationem cum Rege, cum inniteretur manui suae, factam de- precatum esse, & adorationem propriam, cum non tantum sibi ignosci petierit, quatenus una cum Rege adoret, sed ut ipsi textum distinguunt, suae etiam ipsiusmet adorationis in domo Rim- mon, adeoque idololatriae propriae veniam exora- tum eat. Accedit observatio illa, quod verbum השתחוה quando conjungitur cum voce, quae ido- lum aut templum idololatricum notat, nunquam signi- ficet nisi cultum religiosum: quam observationem nullo contrario exemplo elidere potuit Hackspa- nius, imo concedit, religiosum cultum tum hac voce maxime notari, si idoli fiat mentio, aut templi idololatrici, neque negari licere, hoc ipso in loco de Rege Syriae verbum hoc ita accipi; quod tamen non aliter de Naamane hic adhibetur, sed cum ea- dem, ratione loci, templi Rimmon, determinatio- ne. Saltim reponit, de Naamane hic ita ideo ac- cipi non posse, siquidem obstet diserta ejus protesta- tio, quod nolit amplius servire diis alienis, & quod adducit officium suum. Sed hoc est petere τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ: nam ita assumit, quasi de futuro loquatur, non de praeterito, deque officio civili, non vero actu religioso. Ratio quae urgetur, quod de re futura petitionem jam antea informarir, de aedificando scil. altari, adeoǵ, conferenda terra sancta, quae huic rei serviret, nulla est: quia etiamsi antea de re futura egisset, quidni jam de praeterita agere posset, ac peccati commissi veniam iterum iterumque postu- lare? neque ὁμολογουμένως certum est, de re futura, aedificatione puta altaris ante actum esse, quia illam persuasionem vel ἐθελοθρησκείαν de sacrificando in altari e sancta terra exstructo haesisse huic con- verso, nullo documento probari potest. Quod porro ad ordinem naturae provocat Hackspanius, quod contritio mutationem cultus praecedat, nec de- mum sequatur venia, ubi Religio mutata jam est, id partim non praejudicat nostrae sententiae: quia contritionem praecessisse, veniamque obtentam esse agnoscimus, etsi hic adhuc urgente conscientia, deprecationem solicite postulet, quod ab iis quo- que fieri potest, qui remissionem adepti sunt pec- catorum: partim vero admittendum non est; quum omnino religionis mutationem, hoc est, veri DEI agnitionem ac fidem in unum verum Deum sequatur demum venia, ac peccatorum commis- sorum condonatio: quia non nisi per fidem remis- sionem peccatorum consequimur, Actor. 10. vers. 43. Roman. 3. vers. 25. sine fide vero impossibile est Deo placere Ebr. 11, 6.

Neque vero suo consistit talo argumentum, quo praecipue niti videtur Vir clarissimus, Buxtor- fium, ut e pag. 734. apparet, sequutus pag. 752. ad- ductum; Si Naaman commissa olim idololatriae di- missionem petiisset, allegare debuisset suam ipsius im- pietatem, quam peregit non tanquam servus Regis, sed ut sectarius, qui multo etiam antequam Regis ser- vitio esset mancipatus religioni vel superstitioni ido- lolatricae erat addictus, dubio procul ita edoctus a pa- rentibus, quin imo eam allegare debuit idololatriam in qua educatus, quam non sine zelo extra officium Regis constitutus lubens, minimeque coactus exercue- rit: nec illam solam, sed totam detestari vitam ante- actam debuit ex idololatria commissa. Responde- ri enim potest, publicam idololatriam imprimis deprecatum esse Naamanum, quod in ipso Rim- monis templo prae aliis, & Rege ipso adorando ado- ravit idolum pessimum, quia hujus angore maxi- me conscientia afficiebatur; ad quam se aliqua ne- cessitate coactum nullo verbo edocet, quum po- tuerit suo defungi munere, citra adorationem ido- li, neque ad hanc vi quadam adactus fuerit. Quod ergo maxime premebat conscientiam, hoc erat; non quod in idololatria a teneris educatus, non quod eam privatim exercuerit, sed quod in eminentia constitutus, quum veri DEI noti- tiam facile habere potuerit, eadem spreta, publi- co Idoli Rimmon cultu alios exemplo suo sedu- xerit, vel in idololatria confirmarit; quod vir tan- tae autoritatis, ac prudentiae detestandum illud ido- lum palam magna devotione coluerit. Ideo ejus sceleris humillimam deprecationem iterato insti- tuit: Ignoscat Jehovah servo tuo, ignoscat quaeso Jehovah servo tuo super hac re, non quasi dubius de gratia Dei & condonatione plenaria peccati, sed ut suffragia & intercessionem tanti Prophetae obtineret, iisque magis magisque confirmationem adversus quasvis conscientiae tentationes, qua etiam sanctissimi opus habent, consequeretur Psalm. 32. vers. 6. Id enim imprimis observandum (quod e tota historia apparere censemus) Naamanum an- tequam Elisaeum conveniret, jam DEUM Israe- lis agnovisse, ac coluisse cum domo sua, sive ex informatione puellae Israeliticae bello captae, sive aliunde de Deo Israelis edoctum: sed juxta cum Deo Israelis etiam Idolum Rimmon adorasse, uti Israelitae non raro cum vero DEO idola colue- runt, & postea penes Samaritanos id solemne fuit, 2. Reg. 17. Nam verum Deum ipsum vene- ratum fuisse, non sinit nos dubitare tum fiducia de liberatione a lepra, ob quam ad Prophetam Domini proficiscitur: tum professio ejus de invo- cando nomine Dei Israelis vers. 11. tum obedien- tia ad monitum servorum suorum praestita Eli- saeo, cum spe purgationis a lepra vers. 13. Neque aliud docet illa post miraculosam restitutionem confessio: Ecce video, quod nullus DEUS in omnibus terris sit, nisi in Israel, qua id testatur, se etsi an- tea cum DEO Israelis etiam alios Deos credide- rit, jam agnoscere, ipsummet solum esse verum DEUM, vers. 15. unde vers. 17. protestatus est, se nulli alii DEO sacrificia deinceps oblaturum praeterquam Domino, & deprecatur peccatum illud, quod alii etiam DEO antea servierit, idolo nempe Rimmon, ratus tum temporis, se probe & DEUM Israelis colere posse, & DEUM Rim- mon, quam vero Idololatriam nunc palam detesta- tur, ejusque condonationem sibi postulari preca- tur. Quod si accurate, prout par erat, observa- tum fuisset, plerique Interpp. vix in alia omnia hic ivissent.

Adde autem hic argumentum Grammaticum, quod exequutus imprimis est Dn. Saubertus, quo hanc explicationem, Naamani petitionem non de futuro, sed de praeterito accipiendam esse, scri- pto Germanico traditam in Epistola ad virum quendam insignem a Dn. D. Walthero adducta l. c. pag. 102. adstruxit, quod Vav hoc in loco copu- lativum sit, non conversivum, & adoravi, vel in- curvavi me, siquidem in prima persona praeteriti accentus teneat Syllabam penultimam, id est, Paschta, in dictione Millel geminetur: de qua illic legi poterit. Urgent etiam hanc regulam: Gerundium debet accipi de præterito: De quibus quæ prolixe in utramque partem ventilat Hackspanius, censuram relinquimus Grammaticorum filiis. Id vero negligendum temere non est, quod e collatione vers. 18. 19. nobis enascitur argumentum: Quum enim ad deprecationem culpæ subjiciatur, vade in pace, manifestum est, non nudam esse formulam valedictoriam, votum solum inferentem, sed potius remissionem culpæ, quam quis deprecatus est, infert: Hoc enim postulat mutua illa relatio, Culpæ deprecatio, & remissio; hoc postulat item usus. Vid. Marc. 5. vers. 34. Luc. 5. vers. 24. cap. 7. vers. 50. cap. 8. vers. 48. cap. 17. vers. 19. cap. 18. vers. 13. 14. Cons. 2. Reg. 22. vers. 19. 20.

Excipit Dn. Hackspan. suppetere e textu rationem, cur formula sit valedictoria, nihil adferens, aut involvens aliud nisi votum: Duo enim, inquit, petierat Naaman, 1. versu 17. portionem terræ, quæ satis esset extruendo in Syria altari, adeoque extra terram sanctam. Arbitrabatur enim proselytus non satis recte instructus, ad veri DEI cultum neminem adspirare posse, nisi idem sacrificia offerat, quod ipsum sine altari non poterat fieri. Terram proinde sanctam postulat, ac profanam judicabat eam, quæ erat in Syria, certe profanatam, adeoque ineptam ad altare vero DEO extruendum. Sic accipiunt enim Rabbini. 2. Petierat veniam incurvationis in templo Rimmon. Propheta autem ad utrumque petitum nihil regerit aliud quam לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם. Vel itaq́; verbis Vade in pace utrumque concessit, vel ad utrumque respondet Elisæus, vel ad neutrum. Non ad utrumque: neque enim Prophetæ concessum est innovare aliquid in cultu, nisi ad necessitatem horæ, hoc est, si summa necessitas ita postulet, quæ hic nulla erat. Nihil itaque concedit hac formula Propheta, sed abiturientem dimittit.

Resp. (1.) Hanc Neophyti sententiam fuisse de necessitate sacrificiorum, & altaris ad cultum DEI, & hanc intentionem sacrificiis in portiuncula terræ e Judæa adducendæ offerendis, e sola Rabbinorum persuasione minus solide probatur, quod illi sic accipiant, quod nempe versu illo dictum est de terra exhibenda לַעֲשׂוֹת מִזְבֵּחַ ad faciendum altare; siquidem de eo nihil in textu habeatur, nec ulla adferri possit ejus opinionis solida ratio. Quantum etiam tribuendum in talibus sit Rabbinis, nemini obscurum est. (2.) Si in eo errore eaque superstitione hæsisset Naaman, sine dubio exemiffet ei eandem Propheta, non vero cum ea illum dimisisset. Informandus enim omnino fuisset, quam crassa sit illa sententia de necessitate ad verum cultum DEI extra terram Israelis, tum sacrificiorum, tum altaris: quam vana illa superstitio sit, & ἐθελοθρησκεία de altari e portiuncula aliqua terræ Israeliticæ extruendo, ut gratæ DEO in eodem fiant oblationes. (3.) Quum alium longe sensum ferant Verba textus, ut antea diximus, non opus est, ut dicatur, responsum fuisse his verbis Vade in pace ad illud institutum, aut simpliciter tantum dimissum esse Naamanum. (4.) Neque necessitas ulla est, ut dicatur ad utrumque, quod præcessit, hisce verbis responsum fuisse, aut ad neutrum. Datur enim tertium: aut ad alterutrum: Nimirum respondit Propheta ad postulatam veniam incurvationis. Quod vero ad onus duorum burdonum de terra ista, ulteriori responso opus non erat: quia munus illud jam simpliciter detrectarat: adeoque tum illa juratoria asseveratio, Vivit Dominus, ante quem sto, quia non accipiam, tum recusatio, cum ipsum ad acceptandum munus quasi cogere vellet Naamanus, satis responsum erat vers. 16. (5.) Quod de innovatione in cultu Prophetis in casu necessitatis licita adfertur e Rabbinis (ut obiter id tangam) cum grano salis accipiendum est. Scilicet Prophetæ spectantur vel qua Prophetæ, seu qua instinctu & impulsu Spiritus quid agunt, vel per se. Innovatio ergo illa ne a Prophetis quidem suscipi poterat etiam in casu necessitatis, (nulla enim fingenda est necessitas contra præcepta Dei quantum ad cultum ejus) nisi juxta dictamen divinum vel Spiritus Dei, quo agebantur Prophetæ, qua tales.

Cæterum regerit nonnulla Dominus Hackspanius adversus explicationem in Bibliis Vinariensibus approbatam, quod per משׂא צמד thesauros, quos secum vexerat Naaman, intelligendi sint, quos Elisæi servo donare voluerit, cum suscipere eos Elisæus ipse recusaret; quos per contemtum, vel extenuationem isto nomine appellarit, quæ operæ pretium fuerit expendere.

1. Si per contemtum ita vocatur thesaurus ille, poteratne honore afficere Prophetam re spernenda, & nauci? Respond. Etsi per extenuationem sic vocitet Heros ille, uti munera ab offerente non tam deprædicari, quam extenuari solent, ac revera terra tantum sunt munera talia e terra eruta, denique vilioris omnino pretii, vel æstimii, si cum sanitate imo cum salute animæ componantur: non tamen ideo res spernendæ, & nauci simpliciter erant. Quæ κατά τι, & συγκριτικῶς dicuntur, non accipienda ἁπλῶς.

2. Is, inquit, intelligitur per servum, qui negat se ulterius colere velle Deos alienos. Is vero Naaman erat, non servus Elisæi. Resp. consequentiæ illius solidam desiderari probationem: quidni enim Naaman & de se profiteri poterat, servus tuus, & de Gehasi, servus tuus. Se nominabat ita ob venerationem Prophetæ, Gehasi vero ob famulitium quo serviebat Prophetæ. Quum enim juratorie recusarit Propheta ipse susceptionem munerum, ut pateretur solum servum suum affici aliquo munere, solicitat vir illustris, ne scilic. frustra munera hæc secum adduxisse videretur, & ut gratitudinem suam eo pacto saltim ministro Prophetæ declararet.

3. Onus duorum mulorum non fuisset thesaurus aliquis vilis, qui in servos distribui deberet; sed fuisset donum quam maxime insigne. Respond. Quo sensu vile dicatur hoc munus, jam dictum. A tanto Satrapa, qui adeo ingentes thesauros adduxerat remunerationis gratia, vile nuncupari, & ministro Prophetæ tanti, quem ceu Dominum venerabatur, offerri quid mirum?

4. Repugnat particula causalis כי Quæ enim hæc est cohæsio: nolo amplius colere Deos alienos. E. concede ut thesaurum hunc, quem respuis, dem famulo tuo? Respons. Proba est συνέχεια. Patiaris, ut suscipiat tantum minister Propheticus munus, quod offero: quia posthac nihil commercii mihi erit cum alienis diis, eorumque ministris; solum Deum Israelis colam, ejusque ministros cujuscunque ordinis reverenter habiturus sum: Sit hoc munus ejus rei quoddam testimonium, & veluti pignus, & arrha quædam: omnia enim mea gloriæ unius Dei consecrata erunt.

5. Tandem postulat Dn. Hackspan. ut locus adducatur, ubi משׂא צמד hoc sensu accipiatur. Respond. Nulla id postulat necessitas: dum solum hic convenienter ita intelligatur, sive per metonymiam, quod munera illa de terra sint, seu metaphorice, quod tam vilia respectu gratiæ sibi collatæ æstimet uti terra, quæ pedibus calcatur,

respectu cœli, cujus jam consors & civis factus erat, æstimanda. Nec terram absolute ita vocat: sed loquitur de onere præsenti duorum mulorum. Muli autem certe non portabant terræ portio- nem: imo nec de auri tantum id accipiendum thesauro: nam mulis apportarat diversi generis munera: quemadmodum e versu 5. de vestimen- tis & talentis argenti Gehasi donatis constat. Cur ergo locus postulatur, ubi terra præcise pro the- fauro accipiatur? Atque hæc de loco præsenti, quem nobiscum in præterito de idololatria commissa in- telligunt B. Saubertus, qui prolixe hunc sensum asseruit, B. Dorschæus T. I. Theol. Zachar. p. 83. urgens vim vocis סלח. B. Dannhauer. Theol. con- scient. Tom. I. pag. 652. conferens pro significa- tione præteritiva quod ingressus fuerim Psalm. 51. vers. 1. Genes. 48. vers. 7. Num. 7. vers. 87. B. D. Walther. Cent. 1. Miscell. pag. 102. & B. D. Mehl- führerus, nec non ὁ δεῖνα, qui primum Domino Sauberto contradixerat, sed tandem eandem sen- tentiam induit, cujus utriusque suffragia illic a B. Walthero adducta pag. 107. Beat. D. Glassius apud Hackspan. pag. 233. Paraphrastæ item Vinarienses, & Annotatores Belgici & Anglicani, nec non Gisbert. Voet. l. c. Quam etiam sententiam Matthæus Ra- decius a plerisque traditam in literis ad F. Socin. indigitare veritus non est: neque dubitavit Socinus, quin ex vi ipsorum verborum ea locum habere possit, etsi calculum eidem non adjecerit Epist. 4. ad Radec. in Epist. ad amicos pag. 175.

## 5:23
Vers. 23.

IT IS BETTER THAT YOU TAKE TWO TALENTS] As if it were not fitting for such a Satrap to give less.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

MELIUS EST, UT ACCIPIAS DUO TALENTA] Quasi non deceret tantum Satrapam minus dare.

## 5:26
Vers. 26.

WAS NOT MY HEART PRESENT) I saw those things within in my mind. A similar way of speaking 1 Cor. 5, 3. 4.

NOW THEREFORE YOU HAVE RECEIVED) In Hebrew: was it the time for receiving? Many things are made good and bad not so much by the things themselves as by the times. And it must be understood, as Ulpian says, L. solent D. de officio Proconsulis, neither all things, nor always, nor from all people.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

NONNE COR MEUM IN PRÆSENTI ERAT) Vide- bam ista intus in animo. Simile loquendi genus 1. Cor. 5, 3. 4.

NUNC IGITUR ACCEPISTI) In Hebræo: an tempus erat accipiendi? multa non tam rebus quam temporibus fiunt bona & mala. Et accipiendum est, ut ait Ulpianus L. solent D. de officio Proconsulis, ὔτε πάντα, ὔτε πάντοτε, ὔτε πα- ρὰ πάντων.

## 5:27
Vers. 27.

THE LEPROSY OF NAAMAN SHALL CLING TO YOU) This punishment was not only for untimely bribery, but most especially for lying. For he who wishes to circumvent a Prophet concerning those things which pertain to his office is said to lie to the Holy Spirit, whose instruments the Prophets are. See Acts 5, verse 3. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

LEPRA NAAMAN ADHÆREBIT TIBI) Pœna hæc fuit non modo intempestivæ δωροδοκίας, sed vel maxime mendacii. Nam qui Prophetam circa ea quæ ad munus ipsius pertinent circumvenire vult, mentiri dicitur Spiritui Sancto cujus instrumenta sunt Prophetæ. Vide Act. 5. vers. 3. 5.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

The iron swimming. The secrets of the King of Syria revealed to the king of Israel. Dothan liberated, the Syrians about to seize Elisha blinded, and led into Samaria, yet not struck, but refreshed. Samaria besieged, pressed by famine.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Ferrum natans. Secreta Regis Syriæ regi Israel revelata. Dothan liberata, Syri Elisæum apprehensuri excæcati, & in Samariam ducti, non percussi tamen, sed refecti. Sa- maria obsessa, fame pressa.

## 6:2
THAT WE MAY BUILD A PLACE FOR OURSELVES THERE) A tabernacle. For this word, as also tabernae, comes from tabulae, as Festus teaches us. And many nations dwell in such buildings.

Latin:

UT ÆDIFICEMUS NOBIS IBI LOCUM) Taberna- culum. Nam hæc vox ut & tabernæ a tabulis venit, ut Fe- stus nos docet. Et multæ gentes in talibus ædificiis ha- bitant.

Vers. 5.

## 6:5
AND I HAD BORROWED THIS VERY THING) He spoke improperly: for he meant to say 'lent for use'. Moreover, whoever this is, he rightly grieves over the lost item lent for use. For one must religiously take care that no one suffers loss from his own kindness.

Latin:

ET HOC IPSUM MUTUO ACCEPERAM) Impro- prie locutus est: dicere enim voluit commodo. Merito autem dolet hic quisquis est de amissa re commodata. Re- ligiose enim cavendum est, ne quis ex beneficio suo damnum sentiat.

Verse 9.

BECAUSE THERE ARE MEN IN AMBUSH] Prophecy does not only reveal future things, but also those of this time which are hidden. See what was said in Matthew 26:68.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QVIA IBI STRI IN INSIDIIS SUNT] Prophetia non res futuras tantum aperit, sed & hujus temporis eas quæ la- tent. Vide quæ dicta Matth. 26, 68.
