Vers. 18. PERCUTE OBSECRO GENTEM HANC CÆCI- TATE) Scotomate, ut Gen. 19, 11.

## 6:19
Verse 19. THIS IS NOT THE WAY, NEITHER IS THIS THE CITY) Deceit against an enemy was considered lawful at that time. See 'On the Law of War and Peace', book 3, chapter 1, § 17.

In the said place it holds thus: The wise men generally establish that it is lawful to use false speech against an enemy. Thus Plato adds an exception to the rules about not lying, except against enemies; Xenophon, Philo among the Jews, and among the Christians, Chrysostom. To which you might perhaps not wrongly refer what exists in the Holy Scriptures, the lie of the Jabeshites in the siege, and a deed not dissimilar by the prophet Elisha, 1 Kings 6:18 ff. In the notes he adds: Another similar deed of the same Elisha is 2 Kings 8, verse 10, as the Masoretes read it, that is, according to the Qere, which the Latin Vulgate version follows. But how was deceit against an enemy lawful in the time of the Old Testament, which is not lawful under the New Testament? Certainly, lying, fraud, and deceit are no less prohibited in the Old Testament than in the books of the New Testament. Nor can any difference be imagined in that regard between the New or Old Covenant. And since he cites Chrysostom as an authority for that opinion, namely that it is permitted to use false speech against an enemy, does he not also indicate that this is permitted under the New Testament? For Chrysostom wrote under the New Testament; although it is not found in the passage cited by him, in his book On the Priesthood, he says: If you examine the most noble of leaders, you will find that most of their trophies are the works of fraud, and that such men are praised more than those who won by acting openly. He says that military stratagems are praised: he himself does not praise lies. What the Gentiles, Plato and Xenophon, thought does not teach what was permitted among the people of God. Nor is the opinion of Philo that of all the Jews, nor does it make us certain about what is held to be permitted in the writings of the Old Testament. As for the example of the Jabeshites in 1 Sam. 11, verse 11, that which is related there is neither praised, nor is it necessary to say that the Jabeshites lied there. They said, in the morning we will come out, and you shall do to us all that pleases you. But they wished for that to be understood with the condition which they had previously proposed to the Ammonites; if there is no one in the meantime to defend us, we will come out to you. For the seventh and final day of the truce was then impending. Gregory the Great indeed thinks, and with him Cornelius a Lapide and others, that they mocked the enemy. Gregory says, they are already secure about nearby help, how much hope they grant to the enemies whom they mock by promising; they simulate weakness with their voice, but keep the strength of the promised help within, promising one thing with their tongue, another with their heart. Osiander from among our own supports this, and adds in his Paraphrase: It is permitted to deceive enemies whom it is also permitted to kill. But just as it is permitted to repel force with force, so to commit deceit or fraud or a lie cannot be free from fault. Because this is evil in itself: but that can be done without sin. And although wars against enemies are legitimate, it is not therefore permitted to use deceits, frauds, and lies against them: But legitimate wars must also be waged legitimately, so that justice and truth may be preserved in wars as well. Nor is there any need for this deceit to be invented; because the Jabeshites only indicate that they will persist in the agreed terms, and thus they promise that they will come out to the enemies unless help arrives on that final day, which condition they had accepted. Although in the meantime they concealed the promised help, so that the enemies might be found unprepared: which they were not bound to reveal to them.

As for the present example of Elisha, no falsehood is found in it, even if those to whom it was said could have understood what was being said otherwise than what the Prophet had in his mind. He said to his enemies, who were seeking him, but had been struck with blindness by the Lord at his prayer, so that they might not see him: This is not the way, nor is this the city, namely, in which you will find Elisha: for in that way, and in that city, they were never to find, nor could they find, the same man, being as they were struck with blindness by the Lord: Therefore, he was leading them to another way, to another city: Samaria, for instance; in which they were finally to find, with eyes opened, the one whom they were seeking: For they were seeking and wishing to find him in such a way that they might see and recognize him, so that they might be able to apprehend him. Therefore, what Elisha was saying to them was true, not false; because they were to find him only in Samaria, not in Dothan. Follow me, he said, and I will show you the man whom you seek: in which matter he said nothing false: for when they follow him, in Samaria he shows them that man whom they were seeking, i.e., himself. Namely, when at the prayer of the Prophet the Lord opened their eyes, so that they might see where they were and recognize the Prophet. That was, therefore, only a prudent concealment of the truth for a time, under some dissimulation, as Augustine speaks. It was not a lie: indeed, the Prophet said what was the case: for Elisha could not or ought not to have been found in that way and city, because even if he was present to them in the way and in the city, he had not, however, been so present to them that he could be found, or that he could appear and be seen by them. Since their eyes were not yet to be opened there, by the divine will, of which the Prophet was certain, he could say thus: This is not the way, nor is this the city (in which you will find him whom you seek), follow me, and I will show (there, where the Lord wills him to be found and shown) him whom you seek. Nor did this ambiguity of speech, even if those who were being led understood it in another sense, pertain to their harm, but rather to their instruction, so that from it they might learn the power of the true God, and desist from their evil purpose of harming the Prophet of God: and it made for the exercise of beneficence toward his enemies. For he wished to lead them to the King, and there to refresh them for their evil deed with a good deed, and to receive them with a banquet: and although he could have killed them entirely, because he had his enemies, who were lying in wait for his life, in his power as they were struck with blindness, he had decided to send them away safe, for the greater glory of the GOD of Israel. Concerning which the Author of the Homily on Elisha in Chrysostom elegantly says: The most holy Prophet then becomes glorious among his own, more glorious among strangers. He shows signs of mighty works to his own, and here he shows causes of glory to others. The former taught that enemies should be cherished, he was the first to teach that enemies should be spared, he taught that for a punishment, banquets should be provided for adversaries. Likewise: They marvel and are astonished that for death, sustenance; for destruction, food; for punishment, a banquet is prepared for them. Elisha sends these armies away to their own: He sends away, I say, as many preachers as he had enemies; as many reporters of his mighty works as there were men of the enemy. With this response observed, there is no need for Abulensis, who thinks Elisha lied officiously, to rise up, or for us to excuse it with Lyranus by saying that he spoke of Samaria, where he had a house and had fixed his seat: because here the Prophet did not respond to the questions of the Syrians, since they were asking nothing, but to their intention: which was to seek him until they found him; where, therefore, he could be found, he answers: not where he had fixed his seat. We add the typical adumbration, which the aforementioned Author fixes here: O Lord Christ, both in the old the new, and in the new examples the old is figured! The most holy Elisha closes sight, and opens it: he makes them blind, and illuminates them: he takes away sight, and grants it: he makes strangers blind, and makes those enclosed in the city see. Those who had come to capture the Prophet are blinded, and those who had already been captured are given sight. The truth of both of these is fulfilled, so that both the figure of Christ and the example of the future people might be shown, so that those who were strangers might now become his own, enemies friends, and foes his own. And these things concerning the present passage.

We are about to speak of the third example from 2 Kings 8, verse 10, regarding that passage. In the notes, Grotius also brought forward the example of the Egyptian midwives in Exodus 1, verse 17, et seqq. But in the response of these women, it is possible to observe that they did not deny that they were saving the Israelite males, they only mentioned that the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, that they have the knowledge of midwifery and give birth before the Egyptian midwives come to them. Which, stated indefinitely, could be said of the truth, concerning some women: for they do not affirm it of all, however much Pharaoh may have understood it of all. For it is probable that God, touched by the compassion for His people, had endowed the Hebrew women with peculiar strength and vigor, both so that they might help one another, and so that some might be able to give birth without the help of midwives. Thus, therefore, this will not be a lie, but only a concealment of the truth, which is lawful, and sometimes necessary. They reported some truth, concerning certain women not needing Egyptian midwives: they prudently kept silent about the rest, so that they would neither lie to the King, nor expose themselves and the Hebrews to danger. It is one thing to lie, another to conceal the truth, says Augustine in Psalm 5, which is repeated in Causa 23, q. 2, which he also answered concerning Abraham in Genesis 20, question 20, in Genesis, he wished to conceal the truth, not to speak it. I add also Chrysostom, book 1, On the Priesthood: There is indeed great power in fraud, provided it is not done with a fraudulent mind; which I would not even call fraud, but rather a certain economy and wisdom, and an art, by which you can escape from the midst of, and from those impassable straits of desperate affairs, and from difficulties that have been corrected and vices of the mind that have been amended. Therefore, it must be denied, not only with Tostatus, that there was sin on the part of the midwives, but not even a lie is to be conceded, unless it is spoken ἀxύρως. Finally, if a true lie were to be conceded (which is not truly necessary), it would not thereby be shown to be approved by GOD: for GOD built houses for the midwives, that is, He blessed their houses and propagated their family, because they feared God and obeyed Him more than men, when they preserved the Hebrew males, Exod. 1, 17. 21. Therefore, God approved their deed here, not the palliation of that deed. To Augustine, indeed, in Questions on Exodus, book 2, question 1, it is uncertain whether He forgave the lie out of mercy, or whether He judged the lie itself worthy of a reward? For, he says, the midwives were doing one thing by keeping the infants alive, and another by lying to Pharaoh. For in the keeping of them alive there was a work of mercy, but they used that lie in itself so that Pharaoh would not harm them. But there is no need, as we have said, for us to attribute a lie to them: And Augustine praises the midwives elsewhere in Against Lying, to Consentius, chapter 15. Let him who wishes compare Thomas 2. 2. question 110. Article 4. ad 4.

Therefore, Grotius will gain nothing from these examples, by which he makes deceits and lies lawful under the Old Testament, or in any way defends deceits and lies properly so called. By which not even according to his own hypotheses, if he is to be consistent with himself, will he be able to succeed. In order for this to be understood, and for the matter to be more fully illustrated, those things which Grotius himself discusses concerning deceits in § 6 et seqq. must be repeated. For what was said by Homer, that an enemy must be harmed ἢ δόλῳ ἠὲ βίῃ, ἢ μαφαδὸν ἠὲ κρυφηδὸν, that is, by deceit or by manifest force, secretly or openly: What by Pindar; that in doing anything at all, the enemy's strength must be destroyed. What by Virgil, who would ask whether it be deceit or valor in an enemy? What by Silius regarding the affairs of Fabius Maximus: Then deceit pleased valor. What in Homer, where Ulysses, an example of a wise man, is introduced, full everywhere of deceits against the enemy. That Lucian professed those who deceive an enemy to be worthy of praise, and Xenophon, that nothing is more useful in war than deceits, and in Plutarch, Agesilaus, that it is both just and lawful to deceive enemies; that Plutarch praised deceit in war, as did Ammianus: and even the Roman jurists in D. l. 1. de dolo, designated a good deceit, if one plots against an enemy, and l. nihil de captivis, that it makes no difference whether one has escaped the power of enemies by force or by trickery: these things, and others of this kind, Grotius saw clearly, could not be accepted in the sense that deceits are simply approved, but that for their explanation there is need; that the ambiguity of the word deceit be unfolded, and that it be understood to be accepted so broadly that it extends even to those things which consist in a negative act: with the authority of Labeo, who refers to deceit, but not evil deceit, where one through dissimulation protects his own or another's property. He observes, therefore, that one kind of deceit consists in a negative act, another in a positive one; the former, where one dissimulates certain things; which he says is not an evil deceit: but properly it is not deceit: concerning which Augustine, in the book against Lying, ch. 10. It is permitted to hide the truth prudently under some dissimulation: an example of which Jeremiah provides in chapter 38, verse 15, when asked by the King about the outcome of the siege, he prudently hid this very thing according to the King's request, meanwhile bringing forward another cause for the conversation, yet not a false one: and Abraham in Genesis 20, calling Sarah his sister, that is, according to the common way of speaking then, a relative, a kinswoman, and dissimulating the marriage. He says that deceit which consists in a positive act, if it is in things, is called simulation, if in speech, a lie. For words, and nods, and signs were discovered for signification, with mutual obligation, but things are not. Hence he notes it happens that it is permitted to use OTHER things, even if we foresee that it will happen that another may conceive a false opinion from them, or that no harm will follow from them, or when the harm itself, with the consideration of deceit set aside, is lawful. An example of the former is in Christ, who among the companions at Emmaus προσεποιεῖτο to go further, that is, he presented the appearance of intending to go further, unless we prefer to think that he also truly wished to go further, yet under the condition that he not be held back by great effort, just as God is also said to will many things which do not happen, and in Mark 6, 48, Christ himself is said to have wished to pass by the Apostles who were sailing, namely, unless he were earnestly asked to board the ship. An example of the latter is in feigned flight, such as Joshua commands his men for the conquering of Ai, and other leaders often. For here the harm that follows is posited as being lawful from the justice of war, but the flight itself by design signifies nothing, although the enemy accepts it as a sign of fear, which the other is not bound to prevent, using his liberty to go here or there, and more or less quickly, and with this or that gesture or appearance. He refers to the same category the acts of those who are read everywhere to have used the arms, signs, clothes, and sails of enemies. Since all these things are of such a kind that they can be used by anyone at will even against custom, because custom itself was introduced by the will of individuals, not as if by common consent, which kind of custom binds no one. To the former class he also refers the example of Paul circumcising Timothy, Acts 16, 3. The deed of Michal, 1 Sam. 19, v. 16, and the feigned madness of David. But concerning such things he rightly observes in the Annotations to § 8, l. 3. of the Law of War and Peace, ch. 1, that we ought not to call these things, as Chrysostom warns in his book on the Priesthood, ἀπάτην, that is, fraud, but ὀικονομίαν. Who in 1 Corinthians 4, verse 6, also has this to say about the matter: ἦν δὲ ταῦτα ὐκ ὑπόκρισις, ἀλλὰ συγκατάβασις, καὶ ὀικονομία. This was not fraud here, but a certain condescension and dispensation: Thus, therefore, Chrysostom did not admit deceits or frauds, but the ὀικονομίαν and συγκατάβασιν of holy men there, just as he did other military stratagems, which are not properly deceit: he conceded some simulation and dissimulation, but did not approve of any lie: Nor did he make a distinction between the Old and New Testaments in these matters: Augustine himself, than whom no one wrote more vehemently against lying, in the book against lying, ch. 10, says: It is permitted, he says, to hide the truth prudently under some dissimulation, which was also warned before.

Grotius, the patron of lies, could not disapprove of the crude opinions of certain Gentiles concerning lying—of Socrates, Plato, Xenophon, and the Stoics, who, as Plutarch and Quintilian note, place lying among the wise gifts, where and how it is fitting—or the contrary axioms of others, Homer, Sophocles, Cleobulus, and Aristotle, of whom the former says, whoever is wise at heart hates a lie: the latter, that a lie is in itself base and blameworthy, truth beautiful and praiseworthy, without seeking a reconciliation from a broader or stricter acceptance of a lie: Even though he might admit that among both, a lie is taken not insofar as it escapes an imprudent person, in which way speaking a lie and lying are distinguished in Gellius: But because it is knowingly brought forth with a meaning that disagrees with the concept of the mind, whether in understanding or in willing: if indeed he does not lie who says a false thing which he thinks is true, but he who says a thing that is indeed true, but which he thinks is false, should rather be considered to lie; and thus the falsity of the signification is alone required for the common nature of a lie. Grotius, however, distinguishes thus: that when some word or complex of speech is πολύσημος, then if the concept of the mind corresponds to one meaning, a lie is not admitted, even if it is thought that the one who hears will accept it in another sense: such a mode of speech, although he does not think it should be rashly approved, he nevertheless judges can be rendered honest by certain accompanying causes, if, namely, it pertains to instructing someone, as examples occur in Job 11:11, chapter 2, verse 20, etc., or to avoiding an iniquitous interrogation; an example of which he provides from Vitellius. He rightly warns, however, that it is wicked to use such a manner of speaking when the honor of God, or the love owed to one's neighbor, or reverence toward a superior, or the nature of the matter being handled, requires that what is thought in the mind be fully revealed. Grotius removes here this loose acceptance of a lie, which includes even obscure speech: Wherefore Grotius could not defend lies properly and strictly so called, when what is said, written, noted, or hinted cannot be understood otherwise than in a sense that differs from the mind of the speaker, but he had to disapprove of them, even in the Old Testament; because no difference between the two can be found in this matter. Although he brings forward various limitations, he nevertheless confesses that a lie is illicit because of its repugnance to the existing and remaining right of the one to whom the speech or note is directed, that is, with the freedom of judgment which men conversing are understood to owe to one another by a kind of tacit agreement. Therefore, he excepts from the guilt of lying, first, when something is said which has a false meaning, in the presence of an infant or a madman, because they lack freedom, and therefore no injury can be done regarding it. Next, as often as speech is directed to one who is not deceived, even if a third party draws a false persuasion from it, because one is not dealing with him, and therefore there is no obligation toward him. Third, as often as it is certain that the one to whom the speech is addressed would not equally bear a lesion of his freedom in judging, but rather would give thanks for some advantage that follows from it, then he judges that a lie strictly so-called is not committed, just as he does not commit theft who, from the presumed will of the owner, consumes a small thing of his in order to prepare a great utility for him from it; for which opinion he praises Maximus of Tyre. And the physician deceives the sick man, and the Emperor the army, and the pilot the sailors, and there is nothing of evil in this: To which pertains that of Andronicus of Rhodes, concerning a physician lying to a sick man: he deceives indeed, but the one deceived is not, for he does not have it as his purpose to deceive, but to save the sick man. Fourth, as often as one who has preeminent right over all the rights of another uses that right for the good of the other, whether private or public: in which case he again thinks the guilt of a lie is absent. He places an example of such blameless false-speaking in Joseph, ruling in the king's stead, fictitiously accusing his brothers as if they were spies and as if they were thieves, and in Solomon, before the women litigating about the birth, uttering words which would signify a will to cut the infant, even though his mind was very far from such a will. Fifth, he absolves from the crime of lying, as often as the life of an innocent person or some equal thing cannot otherwise be saved, and another cannot otherwise be averted from the completion of a wicked deed: To which he adds finally this, that it is permitted to use false speech before an enemy, without the guilt of a lie. Whether all these exceptions ought to be approved, I vehemently doubt: For it is not permitted to do evil that good may come, nor does it appear how one can be absolved from a lie by false-speaking before an enemy: since false-speaking is nowhere conceded. But we have spoken more copiously about this matter at Jos. 2. Here only these things had to be repeated, so that it might be permitted to judge more rightly concerning the mind of Grotius, and whether it is sufficiently consistent and constant with itself. For to cut all such things to the quick here is not our intention, lest we transgress the limits of the annotations entirely; which if it should perhaps seem to anyone to have already been done, I would wish that he ascribe it to the gravity of the matter. For this question about a lie, which the Bishop St. Augustine, a man of great judgment, confesses is a dark treatment, and a disputation alternating even among the learned.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NON EST HÆC VIA, NEQVE EST ISTA CIVI- TAS) Dolus in Hostem licitus habebatur isto tempore. Vid. de Jure Belli ac Pacis lib. 3. cap. 1. §. 17.

DIcto loco ita habet: Passim statuunt Sapien- tes, apud hostem falso sermone uti licere. Sic regulæ de non mentiendo exceptionem, nisi adversus hostes, addit Plato, Xenophon, Philo inter Judæos, inter Christianos Chrysostomus. Quo forte non ma- le referas, quod in sacris Literis extat, Jabesitarum in obsidione mendacium, & factum non dissimile Pro- phetæ Elisæi 1. Reg. 6, 18. seqq. In Notis addit: Ejusdem Elisæi alterum simile est 2. Reg. 8. vers. 10. ita ut legunt Masoretæ, id est, secundum קרי, quod sequitur Latina vulgata versio. Sed quomodo do- lus in hostem licitus fuerit Vet. Testam. tempore, qui licitus sub Novo Testamento non sit? Non minus certe mendacium, non minus fraus & dolus prohibetur in Veteri Testamento quam in libris Nov. Testam. Neque ulla in ea fœderis Novi aut Veteris fingi potest diversitas. Et quum Chry- sostomum auctorem laudet in eam sententiam, quod nempe apud hostem falso sermone uti liceat, nonne etiam sub Nov. Testam. id licere indigitat? Scripsit enim sub Nov. Testam. Chrysostomus; Quamvis penes ipsum loco adducto id non repe- riatur, lib. de Sacerd. Si, inquit, nobilissimos Du- cum ad examen voces, pleraque eorum trophæa repe- ries fraudum esse opera, magisque tales laudari, quam qui aperte agendo vicerunt. Laudari Stratagema- ta, ait, militaria: non laudat ipse mendacia. Quod gentiles, Plato & Xenophon sensere, non docet, quid in populo Dei licitum fuerit. Nec Philonis opinio vel Judæorum omnium est, vel de eo, quid in Veteri Testamento scriptis licitum habeatur, nos certos reddit. Jabesitarum exemplum 1. Sam. 11. vers. 11. quod attinet, neque laudatur illud, quod ibi refertur: neque necessum est, ut dicetur men- titos ibi esse Jabesitas. Dixerunt, mane exibimus, & facietis nobis omne, quod placuerit vobis. Sed id cum conditione intellectum voluere, quam prius proposuerant Ammonitis; si non fuerit interim, qui defendat nos, egrediemur ad te. Imminebat enim tum septimus, & postremus induciarum dies. Pu- tat quidem Gregorius Magn. & cum eo Cornelius a Lapide, atque alii, quod illuserint hosti. Qui, in- quit Gregorius, jam de vicino auxilio securi sunt, quantam spem hostibus tribuunt, quos promittendo illudunt, voce quidem debilitatem simulant, sed for- titudinem promissi auxilii intus servant, aliud lin- gua promittunt, aliud corde. Suffragatur e No- stris Osiander, & addit in Paraphrasi: Fallere lici- tum esse hostes, quos interficere etiam lititum est. Sed ut vim vi repellere liceat, ita dolum vel fraudem aut mendacium committere, culpa vacare non potest. Quia hoc per se malum: illud vero sine peccato fieri potest. Et quamvis bella adversus hostes sint le- gitima, non tamen dolis, fraudibus & mendaciis adversus eosdem ideo uti licet: Sed legitima bella legitime etiam geri debent, ut in bellis quoque Justitia ac veritas servetur. Neque opus est, ut hic dolus fingatur; quia in legibus condictis se persistit- re solum indicant Jabesitæ, adeoque se ad hostes egressuros promittunt, nisi postremo isto die suppe- tiæ advenerint, quam conditionem receperant. Quamvis interea suppetias promissas dissimularint, ut hostes imparati reperirentur: quas manifestare ipsis non tenebantur.

Quod ad præsens Elissæi exemplum, in eo non reperitur falsiloquium, etsi aliter id quod diceba- tur, accipere poterant, quibus id dicebatur, quam quod mente habebat Propheta. Dixit ad hostes suos, qui ipsum quærebant, sed cæcitate à Domi- no ad preces ejusdem percussi erant, ne viderent ipsum: Non est hæc via, neque ista est civitas, scil. in qua Elisæum invenietis: in ea enim via, & in ea ci- vitate nunquam invenire debebant, aut poterant eundem, utpote cæcitate percussi à Domino: In aliam ergo viam, ad aliam eos deducebat civita- tem: Samariam puta; in qua inventuri demum, oculis apertis, erant, quem quærebant: Ita enim quærebant, & invenire volebant, ut viderent & agnoscerent eum, quo apprehendere possint. Ve- rum ergo erat, quod dicebat ipsis Elisæus, non falsum; quia in Samaria demum, non in Dothan ipsum invenire debebant. Sequimini me, dicebat, & ostendam vobis virum, quem quæritis: qua in re nihil falsi dixit: nam quum sequuntur eum, in Sa- maria virum illum ostendit ipsis, quem quærebant, h. e. seipsum. Quum nempe ad preces Prophetæ Dominus ipsis oculos aperiret, ut viderent, ubi essent, & agnoscerent Prophetam. Fuit ergo illa solum prudens veritatis occultatio ad tempus, sub ali- qua dissimulatione, uti Augustinus loquitur. Non fuit mendacium: imo id dixit Propheta, quod res erat: non enim in ista via, & civitate inveniri po- terat Elisæus aut debebat, quia etsi in via ipsis & in civitate præsto erat, non tamen ipsis ita præsto fuerat, ut inveniri posset, aut ut appareret, ac con- spici ab ipsis posset. Siquidem ibi oculi ipsorum nondum aperiri debuerint, divina voluntate, de qua Propheta certus, ita dicere poterat: Non est hæc via, neque ista est civitas (in qua ipsum inve- nietis, quem quæritis,) sequimini me, & ostendam (illic, ubi Dominus eum inveniri & ostendi vult) eum, quem quæritis. Neque hæc πολυσημασία orationis, etsi qui ducebantur, in aliam partem acciperent, ad nocumentum ipsorum, sed docu- mentum potius pertinebat, ut inde veri Dei vir- tutem discerent, atque à malo proposito Prophe- tæ Dei nocendi desisterent: & ad beneficientiam exercendam adversus hostes faciebat. Volebat enim eos ad Regem deducere, atque ibidem pro maleficio beneficio recreare, atque convivio ex- cipere: ac quum posset omnino ipsos, quia cæ- citate percussos in potestate sua hostes, animæ suæ insidiantes, habebat, interficere, salvos dimittere constituerat, ad majorem DEI Israelis gloriam. Quo de eleganter Autor Homil. de Elisæo apud Chrysost. Fit tunc Propheta Sanctissimus gloriosus in suis, gloriosior in alienis. Exhibet suis signa vir- tutum, & aliis hîc causas exhibet gloriarum. Do- cuit prior inimicos foveri, docuit primus debere ho- stibus parci, docuit adversariis pro pœna epulas ex- hiberi. Item: Mirantur & stupent, sibi pro morte victum, pro interitu cibum, convivium pro pœna parari. Dimittit Elisæus exercitus istos ad suos: Dimittit, inquam, tot prædicatores, quot ha- buit hostes; Tot relatores virtutum, quot homines hostium. Qua responsione observata, non opus est Abulensi, qui Elisæum officiofe mentitum pu- tat, assurgamus, vel cum Lyrano ita excusemus, quod locutus sit de Samaria, ubi habebat domum, & fixerat sedem: quia enim hîc non ad quæsita Syro- rum, utpote qui nihil interrogabant, sed ad men- tem eorum respondit Propheta: quæ erat, ipsum quærere, donec invenirent; Ubi ergo invenire po- terat, respondet: non ubi sedem fixerat. Addimus typicam adumbrationem, quam hic figit Autor prædictus: O Dominum Christum, & in veteribus no- vum, & in novis exemplis veterem figuratum! Eli- sæus sanctissimus clausit visum, & referat: cæcos effi- cit, & illuminat: aspectum adimit, & condonat: cæ- cos efficit alienos, & videntes efficit in civitate in- clusos. Qui captivare Prophetam venerant, excæ- cantur, & qui capti jam fuerant, oculantur. Hujus utriusque veritas completur, ut & figura Christi & exemplum futuri populi monstraretur, ut jam fie- rent ex alienis proprii, ex inimicis amici, & ex hosti- bus sui. Atque hæc de præsente loco.

De Tertio exemplo è 2. Reg. 8. vers. 10. ad istum locum dicturi sumus. In notis adduxit etiam Grotius exemplum Obstetricum Ægyptiacarum Exod. 1. vers. 17. seqq. Sed in responso harum mu- lierum observare licet, quod non negarint se ser- vare masculos Israelitas, solum commemorarint, quod Ebrææ non sint sicut Ægyptiæ mulieres, quod ipsæ obstetricandi habeant scientiam & priusquam Ægyptiæ Obstetrices ad eas veniant, pariant. Quod indefinite prolatum ex vero dici potuit, de non- nullis mulieribus: de omnibus enim id non affir- mant, utut de omnibus intellexerit Pharao. Pro- babile enim est, Deum populi sui commiseratione tactum peculiari virtute ac robore instruxisse mu- lieres Ebræas, cum ut sibi succurrerent mutuo, tum ut sine obstetricum ope nonnullæ parere potue- rint. Ita ergo hic non mendacium erit, sed tan- tum veritatis celatio, quæ licita est, & quandoque necessaria. Aliquid veritatis retulerunt, de qui- busdam mulieribus obstetricibus Ægyptiacis non indigentibus: aliquid de cæteris prudenter subti- cuerunt, ut neque mentirentur Regi, neque se, ac Ebræos periculo exponerent. Aliud est mentiri, aliud est verum occultare, ait August. in Psalm. 5. quod repetitur Causa 23. q. 2. quod etiam de Ab- rahamo ad Gen. 20. quæst. 20. in Genes. respondit, veritatem voluit celare, non dici. Addo & Chryso- stomum lib. 1. de Sacerdot. Fraudis quidem magna vis, modo ne fraudulento ea animo fiat; quam ipsam tum ne fraudem quidem nominandam putaverim, verum œconomiam quandam potius ac sapientiam, artemque, qua possis è mediis, iisque imperviis despe- ratarum rerum angustiis, difficultatibusque correctis, emendatisque animi vitiis, evadere. Ideo non tan- tum cum Tostato negandum, peccatum esse ab ob- stetricibus, sed ne mendacium quidem conceden- dum, nisi ἀxύρως dictum. Denique si concedatur mendacium verum (quod vero necessum non est) non tamen id DEO probatum ostendetur: nam ædificavit obstetricibus DEUS domos, hoc est, be- nedixit domibus, & propagavit familiam earum, ideo, quia timebant Deum, & magis obediebant ipsi, quam hominibus, cum conservarent masculos E- bræos Exod. 1, 17. 21. Factum ergo hic earundem, non facti istius palliationem Deus probavit. Au- gustino sane Quæst. super Exod. lib. 2. q. 1. incer- tum est, utrum promisericordia ignoverit mendacio, an & ipsum mendacium dignum præmio judicarit? Aliud enim, inquit, faciebant Obstetrices vivifican- do infantes, aliud Pharaoni mentiendo. Nam in illis vivificandis opus misericordiæ fuit, mendacio vero illo per se utebantur, ne noceret illis Pharao. Sed non opus est, uti diximus, ut mendacium illis tribua- mus: Et laudat alibi Obstetrices Augustinus contr. mendac. ad Consent. cap. 15. Conferat qui velit Thomam 2. 2. quæst. 110. Art. 4. ad 4.

Non ergo ab his exemplis lucrabitur quid- quam Grotius, quod dolos ac mendacia sub Vet. Testamento licita faciat, aut proprie ita dictis do- lis atque mendaciis ullatenus patrocinetur. Quibus ne quidem secundum proprias suas hypotheses, si sibi constare debeat, velificari poterit. Hoc ut in- telligatur, atque uberius ea res illustretur, repe- tenda ea, quae Grotius ipse de dolis disputat §. 6. seqq. Quod enim ab Homero dictum, hosti nocen- dum ἢ δόλῳ ἠὲ βίῃ, ἢ μαφαδὸν ἠὲ κρυφηδὸν sive dolo, seu vi manifesta, clamve palamve : Quod à Pindaro; Quidvis agendo, scilicet hostica delenda vis est. Quod à Virgilio, dolus an virtus quis in hoste requirat ? Quod à Silio in rebus Fabii Maximi : Exin virtuti placuit dolus. Quod apud Homerum Ulysses, viri sapientis exemplum introducatur, plenus ubiq; frau- dum in hostem. Quod Lucianus dignos laude profes- sus, qui hostem fallunt, & Xenophon, nihil in bello u- tilius dolis, & apud Plutarchum Agesilaus, hostes de- cipere & justum & licitum esse ; quod Plutarchus in bello dolum laudarit, ut & Ammianus : ac Juriscon- sulti etiam Romani D. l. 1. de dolo, bonum dolum in- digitarint, si adversus hostem quis machinetur, & 1. nihil de captivis, nihil interesse vi quis, an fallacia potestatem hostium evaserit : haec, & hujus generis alia probe vidit Grotius, non posse illam in sen- tentiam accipi, ut doli simpliciter probentur, sed pro eorum explicatione opus esse; ut vocis doli ambigui- tas evolvatur, eademque tam ample accipi intelli- gatur, ut ad ea etiam, quae in actu negativo consistunt, extendatur : Auctore Labeone, qui ad dolum, sed non malum refert, ubi quis per dissimulationem tuetur sua vel aliena. Observat ergo, dolum alium consistere in actu negativo, alium in positivo ; Illum, ubi quis dissimulat quaedam ; quem dolum non ma- lum dicit : Proprie autem dolus non est : quo de August. libr. contr. Mendac. c. 10. Licet veritatem occultare prudenter sub aliqua dissimulatione : cujus exemplum praebet Jeremias cap. 38. versu 15. à Re- ge interrogatus de obsidionis eventu, apud proce- res ex Regis postulato, hoc ipsum prudenter oc- cultavit, aliam interim causam, nec falsam tamen colloquii adferens : & Abraham Genes. 20. Saram Sororem, id est, ex usitato tum loquendi more, propinquam, consanguineam vocans, & matrimo- nium dissimulans. Dolum, qui in actu positivo con- sistit, si in rebus, simulationem, si in sermone, men- dacium vocari, ait. Voces enim & nutus, & notae repertae sunt ad significationem, cum mutua obligatio- ne, res alienon item. Hinc fieri notat, ut rebus A- LIIS uti liceat, etiamsi provideamus futurum, ut al- ter inde falsam concipiat opinionem, seu nullum inde sequatur incommodum, sive cum nocumentum ipsum seposita doli consideratione, licitum est. Prioris exem- plum est in Christo, qui apud Comites Emaunti- nos προσεποιεῖτο ire longius, id est, speciem praetulit ituri longius, nisi malimus vere quoque voluisse eum ire longius, sub conditione tamen, nisi magno nisu retineretur, quomodo & Deus multa velle dici- tur, quae non fiunt, & Marc. 6, 48. Christus ipse dicitur praeterire voluisse Apostolos navigantes, nempe nisi impense rogaretur, navem afcendere. Po- sterioris exemplum est in fuga ficta, qualem Josua suis praecipit ad Hajum expugnandum, & alii Du- ces saepe. Nam hic quod sequitur nocumentum, licitum esse ponitur ex belli justitia, ipsa autem fuga ex instituto nihil significat, quamquam hostis eam accipit ut signum pavoris, quod alter cavere non tenetur, utens sua libertate', hac vel illuc eundi, & magis minusque celeriter, & hoc vel illo gestu ha- bituve. Eodem refert etiam eorum actus, qui ho- stium armis, signis, vestibus, velis usi passim leguntur. Siquidem haec omnia ejus sint generis, ut à quo- vis pro arbitrio etiam contra consuetudinem usur- pari possint, quia consuetudo ipsa singulorum ar- bitrio, non quasi communi consensu, introducta est, qualis consuetudo neminem obligat. Ad prius genus refert etiam Grotius exemplum Pauli Timotheum circumcidentis Act. 16, 3. Factum Michalis 1. Sam. 19. v. 16. & simulatum Davidis furorem. Sed de talibus recte observat in Annotatis ad §. 8, l. 3. de jure Belli & pacis cap. 1. quod ea, monente Chrysostomo libr. de Sacerdot. non ἀπάτην, id est, fraudem vocare debeamus, sed ὀικονομίαν. Qui in 1. Corinth. 4. vers. 6. ita etiam hac de re habet ἧν δὲ ταῦτα ὐκ ὑπόκρισις, ἀλλὰ συγκατάβασις, καὶ ὀικονομία. Non hic fraus fuit, sed condescensio quædam, & dispensatio: Sic ergo Chrysostomus non dolos aut fraudes, sed ὀικονομίαν & συγκατάβασιν sanctorum virorum illic, uti alias stratagemata militaria, quæ proprie dolus non sunt, admisit: Simulationem & dissimulationem aliquam concessit, non autem probavit ullum mendacium: Nec in istis discrimen Veteris & Novi Testamenti fecit: Ipse utique Augustinus, quo nemo vehementius adversus mendacium scripsit, libro contra mendacium cap. 10. Licet, inquit, veritatem occultare prudenter sub aliqua dissimulatione, quod antea quoque monitum.

De mendacio etiam crudas gentilium quorundam sententias, Socratis, Platonis, Xenophontis & Stoicorum, qui notante Plutarcho, & Quintiliano inter sapientes dotes ponunt mentiri, ubi, & quomodo oportet, approbare, aut aliorum contraria axiomata Homeri, Sophoclis, Cleobuli, & Aristotelis, quorum ille, mendacium, inquit, odit, quisquis animitus sapit: hic per se mendacium turpe atque vituperabile, veritas pulchra ac laudabilis, reprobare haud potuit mendaciorum patronus Grotius, quin ex largiori aut strictiori mendacii acceptione conciliationem quæreret: Utut fateretur, penes utrosque mendacium sumi non quatenus imprudenti excidit, quomodo mendacium dicere, & mentiri apud Gellium discernuntur: Sed quod scienter profertur cum significatione, quæ mentis conceptui, sive in intelligendo, sive in volendo, disconveniat: siquidem non mentiatur, qui dicit rem falsam, quam veram existimat, sed qui dicit rem veram quidem, sed quam falsam putet, mentiri potius censeatur; adeoque significationis falsitas solum ad communem mendacii naturam requiratur. Distinguit autem Grotius ita: quod cum vox aliqua aut sermonis complexio πολύσημος est, tunc si animi conceptus uni significato congruat, non admittitur mendacium, etiamsi putetur is qui audit in aliam partem id accepturus: qualem locutionem etsi temere probandam non putet, ex causis tamen quibusdam accedentibus honestari posse, censet, si scil. id pertineat ad erudiendum aliquem, uti exempla occurrunt Job. 11, 11. cap. 2. vers. 20. &c. aut ad evitandam iniquam interrogationem; cujus exemplum è Vitellio præbet. Recte autem monet, tali loquendi genere uti improbum esse, cum Dei honor aut amor proximo debitus, aut reverentia adversus superiorem, aut rei, quæ agitur, natura exigunt, ut quod animo cogitatur, omnio patefiat. Laxam hanc mendacii acceptionem, quæ obscuram etiam locutionem includit, hic removet Grotius: Quapropter mendaciis proprie & stricte ita dictis, cum quod dicitur, scribitur, notatur, innuitur, aliter intelligi nequit, quam in eum sensum, qui à mente proferentis discrepet, patrocinari non potuit Grotius, sed improbare ea debuit, etiam in V. Testamento; quia nullam utriusque differentiam hac in re invenire est. Quamvis autem varias limitationes adferat, illicitum tamen mendacium esse, fatetur ob repugnantiam cum jure existente ac manente ejus ad quem sermo, aut nota dirigitur, h. e. cum judicandi libertate, quam homines colloquentes sibi quasi pacto quodam tacito debere intelliguntur. Ideo excipit à culpa mendacii, primo cum quid di- citur, quod falsam habet significationem, apud in- fantem aut dementem, quia illis deest libertas, ideo circa eam injuria fieri non potest. Deinde quoties sermo dirigitur ad eum, qui non decipitur, etiamsi tertius inde falsam hauriat persuasionem, quia cum eo non agitur, ideoque nulla est ad eum obligatio. Tertio quoties certum est, eum ad quem sermo est, libertatis suae in judicando laesionem non aeque laturum, imo gratias habiturum ob commodum aliquod, quod inde sequitur, tunc mendacium stricte di- ctum non committi censet, sicut furtum non per- petrat, qui ex praesumta Domini voluntate rem ipsius exiguam consumit, ut inde magnam eidem utilitatem paret; in quam sententiam laudat Maximum Ty- rium. Et medicus aegrotum, & Imperator exercitum, & gubernator nautas decipit, nec quicquam in hoc mali est: Quo facit illud Andronici Rhodii, de medi- co apud aegrotum mentiente: decipit quidem, at dece- ptus non est, non enim propositum sibi habet decipere, sed servare aegrotum. Quarto quoties qui habet jus superminens in omnia jura alterius, eo jure bono ipsius, sive proprio, sive publico utitur: quo in ca- su iterum mendacii culpam abesse putat. Qualis in- culpatae falsiloquentiae exemplum ponit in Josepho re- gia vice imperante, fratres quasi exploratores, & quasi fures ficte accusante, & in Salomone apud mulieres de partu litigantes voces eas proferente, quae voluntatem scindendi infantis significarent, etsi animus ei longissime à tali voluntate abesset. Quinto à crimine mendacii absolvit, quoties vita innocentis aut par aliquod aliter servari, & alter ab improbi facinoris perfectione aliter averti non potest: Quibus addit denique hoc, quod apud hostem falso sermone uti liceat, citra culpam mendacii. Quae ex- ceptiones omnes an probari debeant, vehementer ambigo: Nam neque facere licet malum, ut eveniat bonum, nec apparet, qui falsiloquentia apud hostem à mendacio absolvi queat: quum nuspiam conces- sum sit falsiloquium. Sed de hac materia diximus copiosius ad Jos. 2. Hic solum ista repetenda erant, ut de mente Grotii, & an ea sibi satis consona, & constans sit, rectius judicare liceret. Omnia enim talia ad vivum resecare hic nostri instituti non est, ne limites annotationum penitus transgrediamur; quod si forte jam factum alicui videatur, materiae gravitati id adscribat, velim. Magna enim haec de mendacio, quod fatetur magni judicii Episcopus S. Augustinus, quaestio, latebrosa tractatio, & alter- nans etiam inter doctos disputatio.

## 6:21
Vers. 21. MY FATHER] Thus also Christian Emperors have often addressed Bishops.

Latin:

Vers. 21. PATER MI] Sic etiam Episcopos saepe compel- larunt Christiani Imperatores.

## 6:22
Vers. 22. FOR YOU DID NOT TAKE THEM WITH YOUR SWORD AND YOUR BOW, THAT YOU MIGHT STRIKE] In the Hebrew it is: Would you kill those whom you had taken with your sword and your bow? Enemies who are a little more lenient are accustomed to spare captives. In the Heraclidae of Euripides, when the messenger had said: What is this? Is it noble to kill enemies? The chorus replies: Not those whom they take alive in battle. And in the Troades of Seneca, to Pyrrhus saying: No law spares the captive or hinders punishment, Agamemnon replies: What the law does not forbid, shame forbids to be done. Nature, fair and good, commands us to spare even captives, says Seneca in De Clementia I, 18. But it is an argument from the greater. You would spare your captives, how much more those whom the kindness of God has given into your hands.

Latin:

Vers. 22. NEQVE ENIM CEPISTI EOS GLADIO ET ARCV TVO, VT PERCVTIAS] In Hebraeo est: An quos cepisses gladio & arcu tuo eos interficeres? Hostium qui paulo leniores sunt captivis solent parcere. In Heraclidis Euripidis cum dixisset nuntius: Τί δὴ τόδ’; ἐχθροὺς τοῖσι δ’ Ὀ καλὸν κτανεῖν; respondet chorus: Οὐχ ὅντιν’ ἂν γε ζῶνθ’ ἕλωσιν ἐν μάχῃ. Et in Troadibus Senecae dicenti Pyrrho: Lex nulla capto parcit aut poenam impedit, Agamemnon respondet: Quod non vetat lex, hoc vetat fieri pudor. AEqui bonique natura parcere etiam captivis jubet, ait Seneca de clementia I, 18. Est autem argumentum à majori. Par- ceres tuis captivis, quanto magis iis quos Dei benignitas tibi in manus dedit.

## 6:23
Vers. 23. AND THE ROBBERS OF SYRIA CAME NO MORE INTO THE LAND OF ISRAEL) He calls the raiders robbers גדודי. Josephus: he no longer dared to invade the land of the Israelites secretly. Therefore a just army was needed, as follows.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET VLTRA NON VENERVNT LATRO- NES STRIAE IN TERRAM ISRAEL) Latrones vocat ex- cursores גדודי. Josephus κρύφα μὲν ὐκέτι διέγνω τῇ Ἰσραη- λιτῶν ἐπιχωρεῖν βασιλεῦ. Ergo justo exercitu opus fuit, ut sequitur.

## 6:25
Vers. 25. AND THERE WAS A GREAT FAMINE) The besieged lacked accustomed and unaccustomed foods, says Tacitus, Hist. 4, concerning those who were besieged in the Veterans.

THE HEAD OF AN ASS FOR EIGHTY PIECES OF SILVER) For also in Casilinum, besieged by Hannibal, they testify that a mouse sold for two hundred denarii, Pliny 7, 57. Valerius Maximus 8, cap. 6. Frontinus says for one hundred denarii.

AND THE FOURTH PART OF A CAB OF DOVES' DUNG FOR FIVE PIECES OF SILVER) From the Greek. In the Hebrew text here it is חרייונים, but because that word had become too filthy by long usage, דביונים is read for it here, and in Is. 36, verse 12, צואתהם, such a change made for similar reasons elsewhere too. But that men compelled by famine to [eat] the excrement of doves is the less to be wondered at, because both that passage of Isaiah and other histories teach us that human excrement was used in such necessity.

That doves' dung signifies a kind of food is most certain to the most learned Bochart in Hierozoicon, book 2, 7, 42: Doubtless the Arabs distinguish by this epithet Kali, which is chickpea, or a species of chickpea, just as also קלי 2 Sam. 17, 28 is rendered by Jerome as parched chickpea: of which Aristophanes also makes mention in the play Peace. Plautus in Bacchides. Horace in the Art of Poetry. Because they teach that the chickpea is most well-known in Judea, 2 Sam. 17, 28, as also the Talmud, and Bellonius, singular. 2, 53, 59, and a Cab is a measure of both legumes and grains, and that chickpea food is still cheaper than an ass's head; Aristophanes and Horace teach that nothing is cheaper than a chickpea, as also Martial, Epigram 1, 24, 104, and Persius, Satire 5. Add that nothing remains in excrements that can be digested, especially in doves' dung, which Varro in De Re Rustica 1, 38, Palladius 2, 33, Quintilius book 2 of the Geoponica, and Avicenna book 2 on Excrements teach is most fertile. Compare Matthew. Polus in Syn. Critic. & Interpp. ad h. l. Although this opinion does not seem new, it is not to be despised if the most ancient Hebrews also have advised it. Bochart says that it is pigeon dung from which salt is elicited (because Theophrastus, Cato, Columella, and Pliny acknowledge the saltiness of chick-peas), which was taken in bad faith by Josephus, who wrote that it was instead of salt. Meanwhile, one must rather adhere to the literal meaning, which most interpreters retain, because famine compels one even to such things, for which reason it is called obscene famine by Virgil, and the words of Rabshakeh, even if spoken boastfully in 2 Kings 18:27, sufficiently confirm the force of famine compelling one to obscene feasts, and Eutychius, Sanctius, and Cornelius note that pigeon dung was used when famine compelled it, both because it is from grains and other purer foods, and because it is more moist, and because there is something remaining in it which pigeons do not digest, yet human nature does not reject it.

Latin:

Vers. 25. FACTAQVE EST FAMES MAGNA) Cur- re- stiantibus solita insolitaque alimenta deerant, ait Tacitus Hi- stor. 4. de iis qui in Veteribus erant obsessi.

CAPVT ASINI OCTOGINTA ARGENTEIS) Nam & in Casilino ab Annibale obsesso murem ducentis denariis venisse testantur Plinius 7, 57. Valerius Maximus 8. cap. 6. centum denariis ait Frontinus.

ET QVARTA PARS CABI STERCoRIS COLVM- BARVM QVINQVE ARGENTEIS) Ex Græco. In Hebreo textu hic est חרייונים, sed quia ea vox longo usu facta erat spurcior, legitur pro ea hic דביונים, ac Ef. 36. vers. 12. צואתהם, qualis mutatio paribus de ausis & alibi facta. Fame autem compulsos homines ad ejectamenta co- lumbarum eo minus mirandum est, quod & humana alvi eje- ctamenta tali necessitate usurpata & Esaiæ ille locus & histo- riæ aliæ nos doceant.

Stercus columbarum cibi genus significare Doctissimo Bocharto in Hieroz. l. 2. 7. 42. certissi- mum est: Nimirum Arabes hoc Epithero insigni- re Kali, quod est Cicer, vel ciceris species, uti etiam קלי 2. Sam. 17, 28. ab Hieronymo redditur frixum Cicer: cujus meminerunt quoque Aristoph. fabula Pace. Plautus in Bachidib. Horatius in arte. Quia Cicer in Judæa notissimum esse docent 2. Sam. 17, 28. ut & Thalmud. & Bellonius singular. 2, 53. 59. & Cabus tam leguminum, quam frugum, mensura est, & vilior adhuc cibus ille Ciceris, quam capitis asini; Nihil cicere vilius esse docet Aristoph. & Horat. ut & Martial. Epigram. I. 24. 104. & Persius Satyr. 5. Adde quod nihil in excrementis supersit, quod concoquatur, maxime in columbarum stercore, quod fertilissimum esse docet Varro de Re rustica I, 38. Palladius 2, 33. Quintilius l. 2. Geopon. & A- vicenna l. 2. de Stercor. Confer. Matth. Polus in Syn. Critic. & Interpp. ad h. l. Quæ sententia etsi nova non videtur contemnenda, si & Ebræor. ve- tustissimi monuerint. Borchart. ait, stercus co- lumbarum esse unde elicitur Sal (quia salsedinem Ciceris agnoscunt Theophrast. Cato, Columella, Plin.) quod mala manu acceptum à Josepho, qui scripsit id pro Sale fuisse. Interim proprietati literæ, quam plerique Interpp. retinent, potius inhæren- dum, quia fames etiam ad talia compellit, ob id obscœna fames Virgilio dicta, & Rabsacis verba etsi thrasonice dicta Ef. 26, 13. vim famis ad obscœnas epulas cogentis satis confirmant, ac stercus co- lumbarum ea compellente adhibitum Eutych. Sanct. Cornel. notant, tum quia sit ex granis, ali- isque cibis purioribus, tum quia humidius est, tum quia in eo aliquid est reliquum, quod columbæ non concoquunt, hominum tamen natura non re- spuit.

## 6:27
Verse 27.

MAY THE LORD NOT SAVE YOU) In the Hebrew: May the Lord not make you safe: just as also the LXX: μή σε σώσαι κύριος. The sense is well expressed by Josephus: ὀργισθεὶς ἐπηράσατο αὐτῇ τὸν Θεόν. Doubtless, just as grievous evils tame some, so they embitter others. Thus Oedipus in the Phoenissae of Euripides: - πρὸς δὲ τῆς τύχης νοσῶν Ἀρὰς ἀρᾶται παισὶν ἀνοσιωτάτας.

Nimirum gravia mala ut edomant quosdam, ita efferant alios. Sic Oedipus in Phœnissis Euripidis: - πρὸς δὲ τῆς τύχης νοσῶν Ἀρὰς ἀρᾶται παισὶν ἀνοσιωτάτας.

Quintilian in the declamation 'Fed on corpses': The father hungers for his children and the mother, oppressed in the tenth month, gives birth to herself: the mangled infant returns into the womb.

Quintilianus in declamatione Pasti cadaveribus: Pater liberos esurit & op- pressa decimo mense mater sibi parit: redit in uterum lacera- tus infans.

Verse 4.

not well Latin, so that the force of the Hebrew expression might be more closely conveyed.

Vers. 4.

## 8:6
Verse 6. RESTORE TO HER ALL THAT IS HERS, AND ALL THE REVENUES OF THE FIELDS FROM THE DAY THAT SHE LEFT THE LAND UNTIL THE PRESENT) Those laws which impose heavy penalties for the sake of some public utility have great need of ἐπιεικείας (equity), so that persons, causes, and times may be distinguished. In these, often the highest law is the highest cross, the highest injustice. But this King is to be praised, because when he restored the goods to the woman, who had changed her residence only because of poverty, he also restored the fruits, so that he himself might not profit from that woman's calamity. To restore is to make one the possessor, and to return the fruits, says Gaius in L. Plus est. D. de verborum significationibus, to which can be added the statement of Paul in L. Restituere under the same title.

Latin:

Vers. 6. RESTITVITE EI OMNIA QVÆ SVA SVNT, ET VNIVERSOS REDITVS AGRORVM A DIE QVA RELIQVIT TERRAM VSQVE IN PRÆ- SENS) Leges istæ, quæ pœnas graves inferunt publicæ alicujus utilitatis causâ, multum egent ἐπιεικείας, ut discernantur personæ, causæ, tempora. In his sæpe summum jus, summa crux, summa injuria. Laudandus autem hic Rex, quod cum bona redderet fœminæ, quæ ob paupertatem solum mutaverat, simul & fructus reddidit, ne quid ipse ex ejus fœminæ calamitate lucraretur. Restituere est possessorem facere, fructusque reddere ait Cajus L. Plus est. D. de verborum significationibus, cui addi potest Pauli dictum in L. Restituere titulo eodem.

## 8:10
Verse 10. SAY TO HIM, YOU SHALL RECOVER: YET THE LORD HAS SHOWN ME THAT HE SHALL SURELY DIE) He reads לו as the Hebrew critics note in the margin, not לא as it is in the text. So also the LXX: ζωῇ ζήσῃ: Josephus: τὸν μὲν Ἀζάηλον ἐκέλευσε μηδὲν ἀπαγγέλειν τῷ βασιλεῖ κακόν: with which agrees what follows below in 17. If we follow this reading, this would not be mere dissimulation, such as Josephus posits, but something more, which at that time was considered permissible against foreigners and idolaters.

He wishes to say a lie. But who will admit that it was considered permissible by men of God against foreigners and idolaters? Since it is a sin in itself, it can never be judged permissible against anyone. Nor, however, is the correction of the Rabbis necessary: which the consensus of the Chaldeans, the LXX, and the Latin codices does not easily admit. Some, however, respond that these things were said ironically: Namely, you shall recover; just as it was done by Micaiah in 1 Kings 22, 15. Others think the nature of the minister is being considered: i.e., You will indeed go, O Hazael, and tell the King that he is going to recover, but the Lord has shown me something else: or Even if you say to him, you shall recover, the Lord has nevertheless shown me that he shall surely die. Most explain it thus: you shall be healed, as far as the part of the disease is concerned, it will not be lethal to you: For he did not die from that disease, but by a violent death, which is hinted at in verse 15, and explained by Josephus, that Benhadad was suffocated and strangled by Hazael, who was occupying the kingdom, on the following day with a wet net thrown over him. In this way Cajetan, Serarius, Salianus, Sanctius, Cornelius à Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus, and others explain it.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DIC EI, SANABERIS : PORRO OSTENDIT MIHI DOMINVS : QVA MORTE MORIETVR) Legit לו ut Critici Hebræi notant in margine, non לא ut est in textu. Sic & LXX. ζωῇ ζήσῃ: Josephus τὸν μὲν Ἀζάηλον ἐκέλευσε μηδὲν ἀπαγγέλειν τῷ βασιλεῖ κακόν: quicum convenit quod infra sequitur 17. Si hanc lectionem sequimur, fuerit hic non dissimulatio sola, qualem ponit Josephus, sed plus aliquid, quod tunc adversus extraneos & idololatras habebatur pro licito.

MEndacium dicere vult. Quod vero pro licito habitum fuisse à viris Dei adversus extraneos & idololatras, ecquis admittet? Quum in se peccatum sit, nunquam & adversus nullum licitum censeri potest. Neque tamen correctione Rabbinorum opus est: Quam consensus Chaldæorum, LXX. & Latinorum Codicum non facile admittit. Respondent autem nonnulli Ironice hæc dicta : Scilicet sanaberis; uti 1. Reg. 22, 15. à Michea factum: Alii ingenium respici ministri censent: q. d. Tu vades quidem ô Hasael, & dices Regi, quod convaliturus sit, sed aliud ostendit mihi Dominus: vel Etiamsi tu ei dicas, sanaberis, ostendit tamen mihi Dominus, quia morte morietur. Plerique ita exponunt, sanaberis, quantum est ex parte morbi, non erit is tibi letalis: Nam ex illo morbo mortuus non est, sed morte violenta, quæ vers. 15. innuitur, & à Josepho explicatur, quod ab Hazaele regnum occupante die sequenti reti uvido in eum injecto suffocatus & strangulatus fuerit Benhadad. Quo pacto exponunt Cajetanus, Serarius, Salianus, Sanctius, Cornelius à Lapide Menochius, Tirinus, & alii.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. FOR I KNOW WHAT EVILS YOU WILL DO TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL) And it was the duty of the Prophet to say what he had been commanded, and the duty of a good citizen to be moved by the evils of his countrymen. Elisha performed both duties well.

AND YOU SHALL RIP UP THE PREGNANT) You shall rip up, ἀναῥῥήξεις, the LXX, just as Josephus also does. Thus Homer: - - - nor let any whom a mother carries in her womb, being a male, escape, nor let him escape sheer destruction. This atrocity has been practiced both elsewhere and in the Sicilian Vespers.

Latin:

Vers. 12. QVIA SCIO QVÆ FACTVRVS SIS FILIIS ISRAEL MALA) Et Prophetæ erat quæ mandata habebat dicere, & boni civis moveri malis popularium. Vtroque officio bene perfunctus est Elisæus.

ET PRÆGNANTES DIVIDES) Findes ἀναῥῥήξεις LXX. quomodo & Josephus. Sic Homerus: - - - μήδ᾽ ὅντινα γαστέρι μήτηρ Κῦρον ἐόντα Φέροι, μηδ᾽ ὅς Φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον. Exercita hæc atrocitas tum alibi, tum in Vesperis Siculis.

## 8:13
Vers. 13. YOUR SERVANT IS A DOG) A submissive manner of speaking. See 1 Sam. 24:15.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SERVVS TVVS CANIS) Submissum loquendi genus. Vide 1. Sam. 24, 15.

## 8:15
Vers. 15 HE TOOK A COVERLET) In Hebrew, מַכְבֵּר: which word the LXX have retained here. Other interpreters whom Theodoret used, στρῶμα, Josephus δίκτυον διάβροχον. Tacitus on the death of Tiberius: Macro, undaunted, orders the old man to be smothered by throwing a large quantity of clothing over him, and for everyone to leave the threshold: thus Tiberius ended. Suetonius says a pillow was thrown over him in the same history. Hazael was too hasty for the outcome of the prophecy.

Latin:

Vers. 15 TVLIT STRAGVLVM) In Hebræo, מַכְבֵּר : quam vocem hîc retinuere LXX. Alii interpretes quibus usus est Theodoretus, στρῶμα, Josephus δίκτυον διάβροχον. Tacitus in exitu Tiberii: Macro intrepidus opprimi senem injectu multæ vestis jubet, discedique ab limine: sic Tiberius finivit. Pulvinum injectum dicit in eadem historia Suetonius. Nimis festinavit Azael ad vaticinii exitum.

## 8:16
Vers. 16. IN THE FIFTH YEAR OF JORAM.

The beginning of the reign of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, is connected with the fifth year of Joram of Israel. But in 2 Kings 1, verse 17, Joram of Israel is said to have begun to reign in the second year of Joram of Judah, who was made King in Israel in the 18th year of Jehoshaphat, 2 Kings 3:1, from which it follows that the second year of Joram of Judah was the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, and therefore the first year of Joram of Judah will be the 17th of Jehoshaphat, and the fifth of Joram

The twenty-second of the Israelite [king] will be that of Jehoshaphat. Furthermore, the same Judean Joram, succeeding his father Jehoshaphat after his death, who reigned for 25 years, is finally said to have reigned in 1 Kings 22, verse 51; 2 Chronicles 20, verse 31; 21, verse 1. These different beginnings of his reign cannot be reconciled more correctly than by saying that Joram was first appointed vicar by his father Jehoshaphat in his 17th year when he went out to war against the Syrians; and was finally admitted into the partnership of the kingdom in the 22nd year, and after his father died in the 25th year, he reigned alone.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ANNO QVINTO JORAM.

Initium regni Jorami filii Josaphati colligatur cum quinto Jorami Israëlitici. At 2. Reg. 1. versu 17. Joram Israeliticus dicitur regnare cepisse anno secundo Jorami Judæi, qui in Israel anno 18. Josaphati Rex factus est, 2. Reg. 3, 1. unde sequitur secundum annum Joram Judæi fuisse decimum octavum Josaphati annum, adeoque primus Jorami Judæi erit 17. Josaphati, & quintus Jorami

Israelitici erit vigesimus secundus Josaphati. Porro idem Joramns Judæus Patri suo Josaphato succedens, post mortem ejus qui 25. annos re- gnando fecit, demum regnasse dicitur 1. Reg. 22. vers. 51. 2. Chron. 20. vers. 31. 21. v. 1. Quæ di- versa regnandi initia rectius conciliari nequeunt, quam si dicatur Joramum a Patre Josaphato vica- rium constitutum esse primum patris 17. cum in bellum procederet adversus Syros; in societatem re- gni adscitum demum anno 22. defuncto a. anno 25. Patre solum regnasse.

## 8:18
Verse 18. BUT THE DAUGHTER OF AHAB WAS HIS WIFE) Add what is below in 27. Well said in the Antiope of Euripides: — πᾶσι δ' ἀγγέλω βροτοῖς Ἐσθλῶν ἀπ' ἀνδρῶν εὐγενῆ σπείρειν τέκνα.

Latin:

Vers. 18. FILIA AVTEM ACHAB ERAT VXOR EJVS) Adde quod infra 27. Bene in Antiope Euripidis: — πᾶσι δ' ἀγγέλω βροτοῖς Ἐσθλῶν ἀπ' ἀνδρῶν εὐγενῆ σπείρειν τέκνα.

## 8:20
Verse 20. EDOM REVOLTED FROM UNDER JUDAH) It defected according to the prophecy, Genesis 27:40.

Vers. 20. RECESSIT EDOM NE ESSET SVB JVDA) Defecit juxta vaticinium, Genes. 27, 40.

## 8:22
THEN LIBNAH ALSO REVOLTED AT THAT TIME] It is not proven that this was done, but the divine vengeance is shown, which even uses actions that are not upright against the wicked. Compare 2 Chronicles 21:10.

TVNC RECESSIT ET LOBNA ILLO TEMPORE] Non factum probatur, sed ostenditur divina ultio, quæ et- iam actionibus non probis adversus improbos utitur. Conf. 2. Paralip. 21, 10.

Verse 25. IN THE TWELFTH YEAR OF JORAM) Not completed. See below 9:29.

Vers. 25. ANNO DVODECIMO JORAM) Non im- pleto. Vide infra 9, 29.

Elisæi discipulus ungit Jehu, qui occidit Joram Israel, & Ochoziam, ac Jesabelem præci- pitari jubet à canibus devoratam.

Verse 2. JEHU) Concerning whom see above 1 Kings 19:15.

Verse 3. AND YOU SHALL FLEE] See 1 Kings 19:3.

Vers. 3. ET FVGIES] Vide 1. Reg. 19, 3.

## 9:11
Verse 11. THIS MADMAN) Thus Capaneus objects madness to Amphiaraus in the third book of the Thebaid.

YOU KNOW THE MAN AND WHAT HE SAID) You guessed well that the man is mad. Thus Josephus.

Vers. 11. INSANVS ISTE) Sic furorem Amphiarao obji- cit Capaneus Thebaïdos tertio.

NOSTIS HOMINEM ET QVID LOCVTVS SIT) Bene conjectastis insanire hominem. Sic Josephus.

## 9:13
Ver. 13. EVERY ONE TAKING UP HIS GARMENT PUT IT UNDER HIS FEET) Concerning which custom we have spoken at Matt. 21, 7.

IN THE LIKENESS OF A TRIBUNAL) In the Hebrew: at the mouth or bones of the steps: At the very top of the steps. The LXX preserved the Hebrew word: ἐπὶ τὸ γαρὲμ τῶ ἀναβαθμῶν. Some think that גרם was a stone placed on high to indicate the time of day. Others, from the Arabic, interpret it as the body of the steps, that is, the steps themselves.

THEY BLEW THE TRUMPET AND SAID, JEHU REIGNETH) Cf. above 1 Kings 1, 40. Reigneth, that is, has been made King.

Latin:

Vers. 13. VNVSQVISQVE TOLLENS PALLIVM SV- VM POSVERVNT SVB PEDIBVS EJVS) De quo more diximus ad Matth. 21, 7.

IN SIMILITVDINEM TRIBVNALIS) In Hebræo: ad os sive ossa graduum: In ipso graduum fastigio. Hebræam vocem servarunt LXX. ἐπὶ τὸ γαρὲμ τῶ ἀναβαθμῶν. גרם quidam putant fuisse lapidem in sublimi positum ad diei tem- pus indicandum. Alii ex Arabico corpus graduum, id est, gra- dus ipsos interpretantur.

CECINERUNT TVBA ATQVE DIXERVNT, RE- GNAVIT JEHV) Conf. supra 1. Reg. 1, 40. Regnavit, id est, Rex factus est.

Ver. 17. WATCHMAN) See 2 Sam. 18, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SPECVLATOR) Vide 2. Sam. 18, 24.

Ver. 20. BUT THE DRIVING IS LIKE THE DRIVING OF JEHU THE SON OF NIMSHI: FOR HE DRIVETH FURIOUSLY) His gait was equal to his agitated spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 20. EST AVTEM INCESSVS QVASI INCES- SVS JEHV FILII NAMSI: PRÆCEPS ENIM GRADI- TVR) Animo ejus concitato par erat gressus.

## 9:25
Ver. 25. CAST HIM INTO THE FIELD OF NABOTH THE JEZREELITE) Thus Caesar was stabbed at the statue of Pompey.

THAT THE LORD HATH LAID THIS BURDEN UPON HIM) Hath imposed this burden upon him. The Prophets call heavy predictions burdens.

Latin:

Vers. 25. PROJICE EVM IN AGRO NABOTH JEZ- RAHELITÆ) Sic Cæsar ad statuam Pompeji confossus est.

QVOD DOMINVS ONVS HOC LEVAVERIT SV- PER EVM) Imposuerit ei hoc onus. Onera vocant Pro- phetæ lævas prædictiones.

## 9:26
Ver. 26. AND FOR THE BLOOD OF HIS SONS) That is, as a punishment on account of the sons of Naboth unjustly reduced to poverty: for all punishment is דם to the Hebrews. Lev. 17, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET PRO SANGVINE FILIORVM EJVS) Id est, in pœnam ob filios Nabuthis injuste in paupertatem re- dactos: nam omnis pœna דם Hebræis. Lev. 17, 4.

## 9:27
Ver. 27. SMITE HIM ALSO) So that those who were equal in guilt might be equal also in punishment. See above 8, 26. However, it seems that in this matter Jehu exceeded the measure: for he had no command to kill this King.

And yet Ahaziah also belonged to the house of Ahab, and was his grandson, and was imitating his crimes and idolatry. Although he is said to have fled on this occasion, and to have hidden in Samaria, he was nevertheless caught there afterwards and brought to Jehu in Gaber, and having been struck in Megiddo, he died while fleeing 2 Chron. 22, 9. Cf. Lyranus here.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ETIAM NVNC PERCVTITE) Vt qui in culpa pares essent, pares essent & in pœna. Vide supra 8, 26. Videtur autem hac in re Jehu modum excessisse: nam de hoc Rege occidendo mandatum non habebat.

Atqui pertinebat Ochozias etiam ad do- mum Achab, ejusque nepos erat, & scelera, & idololatriam ejus imitabatur. Quanquam vero fugisse hac vice dicatur, & latuisse in Samaria, ibi tamen deprehensus postea ac deductus ad Jehu in Gaber, & percussus in Mageddo fugiens mortuus est 2. Par. 22, 9. Conf. hic Lyranus.

## 9:30
Ver. 30. SHE PAINTED HER EYES WITH STIBIUM) κοσμησαμένη ἡ Ἰεζαβέλα, says Josephus. The LXX: ἐσιμμίσατο τὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῆς. In Jeremiah 3, 30: ἐὰν ἐγχρίσῃς σίβι τὺς ὀφθαλμύς σα. Where other versions have εἰς τιμὴν, but erroneously, for

to which simmi: for simmis, or simmi is stibium also according to Dioscorides. Ion also in the tragedy Omphale: καὶ τὴν μέλαιναν σίμμι ὀμματογράφον. Where you see the use of stibium in procuring the blackness for the eyes which was considered beautiful. Hesychius: ὑπογράμματα, σιμμίσματα τ' ὀ- φθαλμῶν. And David Kimchi in the Book of Roots explains פוך as הכחול השחר. Strabo concerning the Troglodytes: σιβίζονται δ' ἐπιμελῶς αἱ γυναῖκες. Nicolaus Damascenus concerning the effeminate King: καθυπεσιβισμένον τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ. Apollonius against the prophet according to the Phrygians, tell me, is a prophet painted, is a prophet painted with stibium, is a prophet fond of adornment? Cyprian on the discipline and habit of Virgins: They paint their eyes with a surrounding blackness: on works and alms: Anoint your eyes not with the stibium of the devil, but with the eye-salve of Christ. But besides blackness, there is another use of stibium for dilating the eyes. Pliny dealing with it 33,6. Therefore also many have called it platyophthalmon, since in the beautiful eyelids of women it dilates the eyes. To this point those lines of Varro in Nonius: Oculi suppetuli, nigellis pupulis Quandam hilaritatem significantes animitus, Quos calliblepharo naturali palpebræ Tinctæ vallatos mobili septo tenent. Hence Tertullian: They extend their eyes with soot. Likewise: that very black powder by which the beginnings of the eyes are produced. And Cyprian on the lapsed: you who paint the outlines of your eyes with the application of black powder. Doubtless the women praised by many nations were μεγαλόφθαλμοι: whence Juno is ox-eyed in Homer. Therefore, as Pliny mentions, medicines were invented for gluing and folding back the eyelids. In these is the chief power of stibium, because as Galen says in his book 9 on Simples, σίμμι πρὸς τῇ δυνάμει τῇ ξη- ραντικῇ καὶ στύψει ἔχει. By this power, therefore, it contracts the eyelids and folds them back upon themselves, especially the lower one, whence he whom we just cited, Hesychius and Pollux, said ὑπογράμματα, and ὑπογράφειν ὀφθαλμοὺς in this matter is found in Athenaeus concerning Sardanapalus, in Lucian, Pollux, Herodian, and Chrysostom. Also, astringents like copper are beneficial to the health of the eyes, as the writer of the Mirabilia notes, whether he is Aristotle or another, and likewise Macrobius at the end of the Saturnalia.

Latin:

Vers. 30. DEPINXIT OCVLOS SVOS STIBIO) κοσμησα- μένη ἡ Ἰεζαβέλα, ait Josephus LXX. ἐσιμμίσατο τὺς ὀφθαλ- μοὺς αὐτῆς. In Jeremia 3, 30. ἐὰν ἐγχρίσῃς σίβι τὺς ὀφθαλ- μύς σα. Vbi aliæ versiones εἰς τιμὴν, sed mendose, pro

οἷς σίμμι: nam σίμμιs, sive σίμμι stibium etiam Dioscoridæ. Jon quoque in Tragœdia Omphale: καὶ τὴν μέλαιναν σίμμι ὀμματογράφον. Ubi stibii usum vides in conciliando oculis nigrore qui pul- cher habebatur. Hesychius: ὑπογράμματα, σιμμίσματα τ' ὀ- φθαλμῶν. Et David Kimchi in libro Radicum פוך explicat הכחול השחר. Strabo de Troglodytis: σιβίζονται δ' ἐπιμελῶς αἱ γυναῖκες. Nicolaus Damascenus de Rege effœ- minato: καθυπεσιβισμένον τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ. Appollonius ad- versus κατὰ Φρύγας προφήτης, εἰπέ μοι, βάπτεται, προφήτης σιβίζεται, προφήτης φιλοκοσμεῖ; Cyprianus de disciplina & habitu Virginum: Oculos circumducto nigrore fucant: de ope- re & eleemosynis: Inunge oculos tuos non stibio diaboli, sed col- lyrio Christi. Verum præter nigrorem alius quoque usus sti- bii ad dilatandos oculos. Plinius de eo agens 33,6. Ideo et- iam plerique platyophthalmon id appellavere, quoniam in cal- liblepharis mulierum dilatat oculos. Huc spectant illa Var- ronis apud Nonium: Oculi suppetuli, nigellis pupulis Quandam hilaritatem significantes animitus, Quos calliblepharo naturali palpebræ Tinctæ vallatos mobili septo tenent. Hinc Tertullianus: Oculos fuligine porrigunt. Item: illum ipsum nigrum pulverem quo oculorum exordia producuntur. Et Cyprianus de lapsis: qui nigri pulveris ductu oculorum li- neamenta depingis. Nimirum laudatæ multis gentibus mu- lieres μεγαλόφθαλμοι: unde Juno βοῶπις Homero. Ideo inventa, ut Plinius meminit, medicamina glutinandis repli- candisque palpebris. In his præcipua vis stibii, quia ut Ga- lenus ait de Simplicibus libro 9. σίμμι πρὸς τῇ δυνάμει τῇ ξη- ραντικῇ καὶ στύψει ἔχει. Hac ergo vi palpebras contrahit & in se replicat, inferiorem maxime, unde ὑπογράμματα dixit is quem modo citavimus Hesychius & Pollux, ὑπογράφειν ὀφθαλμοὺς in hac re est apud Athenæum de Sardanapalo, apud Lucianum, Pollucem, Herodianum, Chrysostomum. Et- iam sanitati oculorum prosunt τὰ συκτικὰ ut æs, notante Mi- rabilium scriptore, sive is Aristoteles est, sive alius, item Ma- crobio in Saturnaliurn fine.

## 9:31
Verse 31.

IS THERE PEACE?) In the Hebrew: Is there peace? that is, is everything according to your wish? ZAMBRI] Another Zambri. See above 1 Kings 16:10. Such is that: And now that Paris. from Aeneas.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

NVMQVID PAX POTEST ESSE) In Hebræo: Num pax? id est, an omnia ex voto? ZAMBRI] Alter Zambri. Vide supra 1. Reg. 16,10. Ta- le illud: Et nunc ille Paris. de Ænea.

## 9:32
Verse 32.

WHO IS THIS?) The Greeks: τίς εἶ σύ. They read מי את. But we have in the Hebrew מי אתי who is with me? That is, is there no one there of my party? The following words support this.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

QVÆ EST ISTA?) Græci: τίς εἶ σύ. Legerunt מי את. At nos in Hebræo habemus מי אתי quis mecum? Id est, nemone ibi est mearum partium? Favent sequentia.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

Jehu killed the 70 sons of Ahab, and the 42 brothers of Ahaziah, and all the worshippers of Baal, and obtains the progeny in the kingdom to the fourth generation. But because he worshipped the golden calves, his house was finally cut off.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Jehu 70. filios Achab, & 42. fratres Ochoziæ, omnesque cultores Baal occidit, & pro- geniem in regno consequitur in quartam generationem. Sed quia vitulos aureos co- luit, excisa tandem est domus ejus.

## 10:3
Verse 3.

CHOOSE THE BETTER ONE AND THE ONE WHO SHALL PLEASE YOU FROM THE SONS OF YOUR MASTER, AND FIGHT FOR THE HOUSE OF YOUR MASTER) He declares war on them with mockery, as if secure about the outcome.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ELIGITE MELIOREM ET EUM QVI VOBIS PLA- CVERIT DE FILIIS DOMINI VESTRI, ET PVGNATE PRO DOMO DOMINI VESTRI) Bellum eis indicit cum irrisu, tanquam de eventu securus.

## 10:7
Verse 7.

AND THEY PUT THEIR HEADS IN BASKETS, AND SENT THEM TO HIM IN JEZREEL) With this gift they purchased peace. Similar 2 Sam. 20, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET POSVERVNT CAPITA EORVM IN COPHI- NIS, ET MISERVNT AD EVM IN JEZRAEL) Hoc dono pacem redemerunt. Simile 2. Sam. 20,21.

## 10:9
Verse 9.

IF I HAVE CONSPIRED AGAINST MY MASTER, AND KILLED HIM) I will grant that these things are true which Jezebel reproached me with: above 9, 31. WHO STRUCK ALL THESE) Such a wonderful outcome shows that these things are ordered not by human means but by divine.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

SI EGO CONJVRAVI CONTRA DOMINVM ME- VM, ET INTERFECI EVM) Concedam hæc esse vera quæ mihi exprobravit Jezabel: supra 9, 31. QVIS PERCVSSIT OMNES HOS) Tam mirabilis eventus ostendit, hæc non humanitus sed divinitus disponi.

## 10:11
Verse 11.

AND ALL HIS GREAT MEN, AND HIS FAMILIAR FRIENDS AND PRIESTS?) From the bald to the bald, as the saying goes.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET VNIVERSOS OPTIMATES EJVS, ET NOTOS ET SACERDOTES?) A calvo ad calvum, ut dici solet.

## 10:12
Verse 12.

AT THE SHEARING HOUSE) The Seventy retained the Hebrew word ἐν Βαιθακὰν, as they are accustomed to do when they are stuck. Those words signify a place of binding, namely, as the Hebrews think, because sheep to be shorn were bound there by the feet.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

AD CAMERAM PASTORVM) Hebræam vocem retinuere LXX. ἐν Βαιθακὰν, ut facere solent, ubi hærent. Significant eæ voces locum ligationis, nempe, ut Hebræi existimant, quod ibi oves tondendæ pedibus liga- bantur.

## 10:14
IN THE CISTERN) For at the cistern. Jehu did this also without a command: Δεινὸς ἀνὴρ τάχα κεν καὶ ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IN CISTERNA) Pro ad cisternam. Hoc quo- que fecit Jehu sine mandato: Δεινὸς ἀνὴρ τάχα κεν καὶ ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο.

## 10:15
HE FOUND JONADAB.

This is he who is praised in Jeremiah 35, v. 6: whom some say was a disciple of Elisha, through whom Jehu was winning for himself authority and a reputation for piety.

Latin:

Vers. 15. INVENIT JONADAB.

HIc ille est, qui Jerem. 35, v. 6. laudatur : quem Elisæi discipulum nonnulli fuisse dicunt, per quem auctoritatem & opinionem pietatis sibi con- ciliabat Jehu.

## 10:19
HE DID THIS INSIDIOUSLY) He notes that he used not less the fox-like than the lion-like, a man who is ἀμφιδέξιος.

Cornelius à Lapide excuses this lie, but against the will, as he admits, of Thomas, and the better men of his own order, Valentianus and Schvarez, and indeed of Augustine himself in book against lying, ch. 2, because he did not say it seriously, and the simulation lasted for a short time. But not only must the intention be good, but the action itself as well, and actions are not to be judged only from the end, but from their internal form: nor does the brevity of time absolve any sin, so that it is any the less a sin.

Latin:

Vers. 19. FACIEBAT HOC INSIDIOSE) Notat vulpi- na non minus quam leonina uti, homo ἀμφιδέξιος.

Mendacium hoc excusat Cornelius à Lapide, sed invito, uti fatetur, Thoma, & sui ordinis me- lioribus, Valentiano & Schvarezio, imo ipso Au- gustino l. contr. mendac. c. 2. quia non serio dixe- rit, & simulatio brevi durarit. Ast non inten- tio tantum bona esse debet, sed ipsa etiam actio, nec ex fine æstimandæ solum actiones, sed ex in- terna forma: neque brevitas temporis absolvit ul- lum peccatum, quo minus peccatum sit.

## 10:20
A SOLEMN DAY) In Hebrew, עֲצָרָה, in which way the last day, most festive, of the Tabernacles was called, Leviticus 23, 36.

Latin:

Vers. 20. DIEM SOLENNEM) In Hebræo, עֲצָרָה quomodo vocabatur dies ultimus maxime festus Tabernacu- lorum Levit. 23, 36.

## 10:24
Vers. 24.

HIS LIFE SHALL BE FOR HIS LIFE) The same manner of speaking in a not dissimilar matter, 1 Kings 20, verse 39.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ANIMA EJUS ERIT PRO ANIMA ILLIUS) Idem loquendi genus in re non dispari 1. Reg. 20. vers. 39.

## 10:26
Vers. 26.

AND THEY BROUGHT OUT THE STATUE FROM THE TEMPLE OF BAAL, AND THEY BURNED AND CRUSHED IT) From the law of Deuteronomy 7, 25 and 12, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ET PROTULERUNT STATUAM DE FANO BAAL, ET COMBUSSERUNT ET COMMINVERUNT EAM) Ex lege Deuteronomii 7, 25. & 12, 3.

## 10:27
Vers. 27.

THEY ALSO DESTROYED THE TEMPLE OF BAAL] And this from the law of Deuteronomy 7, 5; 12, 2.

AND THEY MADE FOR IT LATRINES] As a perpetual monument of contempt. Similar to Ezra 6, verse 11.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

DESTRUXERUNT QUOQUE ÆDEM BAAL] Et hoc ex lege Deuteronomii 7, 5. 12, 2.

ET FECERUNT PRO EA LATRINAS] In perpetu- um contemtus monumentum. Simile Esdræ 6. vers. 11.

## 10:30
Ver. 30.

YOU DID WHAT WAS RIGHT) Namely in part, as appears both above and in the following. Therefore his kingdom is given to his descendants, but it is not long-lasting.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

EGISTI QVOD RECTUM ERAT) Nempe ex parte, ut apparet & supra & in sequentibus. Ideo regnum ejus po- steris datur, sed non diuturnum.

## 10:31
Ver. 31.

FOR HE DID NOT DEPART FROM THE SINS OF JEROBOAM) He did not worship Baal, but God: yet he worshipped in the calves, which is a fault, but a lighter one.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

NON ENIM RECESSIT A PECCATIS JEROBOAM) Coluit non Baalem, sed Deum: verum coluit in vitulis, quæ culpa, sed levior.

## 10:34
Ver. 34.

HIS MIGHT) His mighty deeds: τὰς συνάψεις ἃς συνῆψεν. LXX.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

FORTITUDO EJUS) Facta ejus fortia: τὰς συνάψεις ἃς συνῆψεν. LXX.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. Athalia, having extinguished the royal seed, reigns, killed by Jehoiada the High Priest, who established Joash, son of Ahaziah, as King.

Ver. 1.

BUT ATHALIA THE MOTHER OF AHAZIAH) In the LXX and Josephus, Gotholia: for the ע is sometimes omitted, sometimes rendered by γ. A violent woman, and desirous of domination, such as Tacitus describes to us Agrippina, the mother of Nero.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. Athalia extincto semine regio regnat, occisa a Jojada Pontifice, qui Joas Ochaziæ fi- lium Regem constituit.

Vers. 1.

ATHALIA VERO MATER OCHOSIÆ) LXX. & Jo- sepho Γοθολία: nam ע interdum omitti, interdum per γ reddi solet. Fœmina violenta, & dominationis cupida, qua- lem nobis Agrippinam Neronis matrem describit Tacitus.

## 11:2
Ver. 2.

SHE STOLE HIM) Thus Electra [stole] her brother Orestes: See Seneca in Agamemnon. Thus the House of David was saved in one boy, as once the house of Gideon. Judg. 9.

CONCERNING THE DINING ROOM) In the Hebrew it is not 'of' but 'in'. Josephus: βαστάσασα μετ' αὐτῆς εἰς τὸ ταμεῖον. LXX: 'she stole him from the midst of the king's sons who were being put to death, him and his nurse in the bedchamber.' Therefore, he was first hidden in the women's bedchamber, then in the temple, a place of asylum.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

FURATA EST EVM) Sic Electra fratrem Orestem: Vi- de Senecam Agamemnone. Sic Domus Davidis servata in uno puero, ut olim Gedeonis domus. Jud. 9.
