## 17:31
Ver. 31. BUT THESE WHO WERE OF SEPHARVAIM BURNED THEIR CHILDREN IN THE FIRE, ADRAMMELECH AND ANAMMELECH THE GODS OF SEPHARVAIM) Adrammelech seems to be the same as Melech, Moloch, Melcham, namely Saturn, with the title of the powerful אדיר added. Anammelech, however, is the star of Jupiter, because it was a cloud, that is, a protection, against Moloch, a benign star opposed to a malignant one. Ver. 32. AND THEY MADE FOR THEMSELVES FROM THE LOWEST) In the Hebrew: And some of them made for themselves. AND THEY PLACED THEM IN THE HIGH SHRINES) In the Hebrew: And they were making for them in the house of the high places: that is, those priests were performing sacred rites for the sake of those men, and that in the shrines of the hills.

Latin:

Vers. 31. HI AVTEM QVI ERANT DE SEPHAR- VAIM COMBVREBANT FILIOS SVOS IGNI, ADRA- MELECH ET ANAMELECH DIIS SEPHARVAIM) Adramelech videtur esse idem qui Melech, Moloch, Mel- cham, Saturnus scilicet, addito titulo potentis אדיר. Ana- melech vero Jovis stella, quod esset nubes, id est, protectio, contra Molochum, benignum sidus maligno oppositum. Vers. 32. FECERVNT AVTEM SIBI DE NOVISSI MIS) In Hebræo: Et fecerunt sibi quidam eorum. ET PONEBANT EOS IN FANIS SVBLIMIBVS) In Hebræo: Et fuerunt facientes eis in domo excelsorum: id est, Sacerdotes illi sacra faciebant in illorum hominum gratiam, idque in collium fanis.

## 17:34
Ver. 34. NOR DO THEY KEEP HIS CEREMONIES) That 'nor' is not from the Hebrew, which now reads אינם. But it appears the LXX read אותם in the Chaldean manner: that is, 'Themselves.' Then they translated חקתם well, not 'His ceremonies,' but their own, ancestral and hereditary ones. And the sense certainly coheres more correctly with the previous ones in this way. They were observing, he says, both their own ancient rites and those holy rites which God had prescribed to the Israelites, which were by no means to be mixed with other rites; see also what is below at 41. They would have done better if they had worshipped the one true God without Hebrew rites. The sense according to the Hebrew text coheres perfectly: And therefore, to this day they (the discourse is about the ten tribes) follow the ancient custom, they do not fear the Lord, nor do they keep their own ceremonies and judgments, that is, the law and the commandment which the Lord had commanded the sons of Jacob. For they ought to have been diligent in observing those alone. But how could the one God of Israel be worshipped then without the rites which He prescribed to them, and which He wished to be observed at that time? This is a new Samaritanism, which the Syncretist Grotius could have suggested if he had lived in that age. But God wished to be worshipped then according to the law and the precepts which He Himself had prescribed; nor was worship to be devised by one's own judgment. Therefore, even the Gentiles were invited to the Jerusalem temple itself, and a special courtyard was destined for them. Thus, they themselves ought not to have neglected the Hebrew rites: nor, however, was it permissible to mix them with the ceremonies of the Gentiles, but to perform the worship of God solely according to the tenor of the divine laws. Ver. 40. BUT THEY DID NOT LISTEN] They of the ten tribes had not obeyed, and thus they had given a very bad example to those coming into places where the traces of a corrupted religion were fresh.

PART II. EXHIBITS THE HISTORY OF THE KINGDOM OF JUDAH AFTER THE KINGDOM OF ISRAEL WAS REMOVED.

Latin:

Vers. 34. NEQVE CVSTODIVNT CEREMONIAS EJVS) Il- lud neque est ex Hebræo, quod nunc legitur אינם. Sed apparet LXX. legisse אותם Chaldaico more: id est, Ipsi. Deinde bene verterunt חקתם, non ceremonias Ejus, sed suas, patrias & avitas. Et sensus sane cum prioribus rectius sic cohæret. Observabant, ait, & ritus suos veteres, & illos san- ctos ritus, quos Deus Israëlitis præscripserat, cum aliis riti- bus minime miscendos; vide & quæ infra 41. Rectius fecis- sent, si unum verum Deum coluissent, sine ritibus Hebraicis. Sensus juxta Ebræum textum cohæret opti- me: Ideoque, in præsentem diem isti (de decem tribubus sermo est,) morem sequuntur antiquum, non timent Dominum, neque custodiunt ceremonias suas, & judi- cia, hoc est, legem & mandatum, quod præceperat Do- minus filiis Jacob. Illis enim solis observandis stude- re debuissent. Quomodo autem unus Deus Israë- lis tum coli potuit sine ritibus, quos eis præscri- psit, atque isto tempore observari voluit? Novus hic Samaritanismus est, quem suggerere potuisset Syncretista Grotius, si ista ætate vixisset. Atqui Deus coli tum volebat secundum legem, & præce- pta, quæ ipse præscripserat; Neque proprio arbi- trio cultus excogitandus erat. Ideo ad templum ipsum Hierosolymitanum gentiles etiam invita- bantur, iisque atrium peculiare destinatum erat. Sic ipsi ritus Ebraicos negligere non debebant: ne- que tamen integrum erat, eosdem cum gentilium ceremoniis commiscere, sed secundum tenorem legum divinarum cultum Dei unice peragere. Vers. 40. ILLI VERO NON AVDIERVNT] Non obedierant illi de decem tribubus, & ita pessimum exemplum dederant venturis in loca, ubi recentia erant corruptæ religio- nis vestigia.

PARS II. REGNI JUDÆ HISTORIAM POST SUBLATUM ISRAELIS RE- GNUM EXHIBET.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII. Hezekiah overthrows the idols, defects from King Sennacherib, who devastates Judea, and, with Hezekiah sending gifts in vain, moving his camps toward Jerusalem, blasphemes God through Rabshakeh and insults Hezekiah.

Ver. 1. HEZEKIAH REIGNED] A good man indeed, but of a rather timid nature, such as that Fabius among the Romans, called by some the delayer, by others a little sheep, to whom Plutarch compares Pericles among the Greeks. Ver. 2. HE WAS TWENTY-FIVE YEARS OLD) He was entering his twenty-fifth year. See above 16, 2. Because he was 25 years old when he succeeded his father, who lived only 36 years, 2 Kings 16, 2, Chronologists conclude that Ahaz begat Hezekiah in his eleventh year: but Abulensis, Petavius, Bailius, and others more correctly refer the begetting of children to the 13th or 14th year of Ahaz, since not all years are counted precisely, but with some months having passed, and thus incomplete years are sometimes passed over in Scripture. He was, says Tostatus, when he began to reign, 20 years old, namely, completed, and one incomplete, which Scripture does not count.

Again he reigned for sixteen years, that is to say, completed, and in addition the seventeenth incomplete: wherefore he died in the thirty-eighth year of his age; Hezekiah also was only 24 completed years old when he began to reign, but he had begun his 25th year. The opinion of Calvisius, that Hezekiah was not the natural son of Ahaz, but legal or a stepson or brother, has no place, because it openly contradicts this passage, in which both his father and his mother are expressly named.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII. Hiskias idola subvertit, deficit à Rege Sennache- rib, qui devastat Judæam, & nequicquam mittente munera Hiskia Hierosolymam ver- sus castra sua movens, Deum per Rabsacem blasphemat & Hiskiæ insultat.

Vers. 1. REGNAVIT EZECHIAS] Vir sane bonus, sed ingenio timidiore, qualis apud Romanos Fabius ille, aliis cun- ctator, aliis ovicula dictus, cui de Græcis Periclem confert Plutarchus. Vers. 2. VIGINTI QVINQVE ANNORVM ERAT) Inibat annum vigesimum quintum. Vide supra 16,2. Quia 25. annorum fuit, cum succederet Patri, qui tantum 36. annis vixit 2. Reg. 16, 2. colligunt Chro- nologi Achazum undecimo anno genuisse Ezechi- am: sed Abulensis, Petavius, Bailius, & alii rectius ad annum ætatis 13. vel 14. Achazi παιδογονίαν re- ferunt, quum non omnes anni præcise, sed præteritis aliquot mensibus numerentur, adeo- que taceantur quandoque in Script. anni incom- pleti. Erat, inquit Tostatus cum regnare cœ- pit Achaz 20. annorum scil. completorum, & unius incompleti, quem Scriptura non numerat.

Rursum sedecim annis regnavit sc. completis, in- super decimo septimo incompleto: quare mor- tuus est anno ætatis trigesimo octavo, Ezechias quoque erat tantum 24. annorum completorum cum regnare cepit, sed inchoarat annum 25. Cal- visii sententia, quod Hiskias Ahazi non fuerit na- turalis filius, sed legalis vel privignus aut frater, lo- cum non habet, quia repugnat palam huic loco, in quo & Pater, & mater ejus diserte nominantur.

## 18:4
Verse 4. HE REMOVED THE HIGH PLACES) He did a great thing: but the punishment of the ten tribes before his eyes had made the tribe of Judah more obedient to the law than before.

AND HE BROKE IN PIECES THE BRASS SERPENT THAT MOSES HAD MADE] Note, that Moses had made. An excellent lesson for Kings, that although things are well instituted, but not necessary, where for the most part they are wrongly misused, they should be removed from sight, lest they place a stumbling block for the blind.

AND BURNED INCENSE TO IT) Which was among those things that, reserved for the honor of God alone, it was not lawful to use outside the Temple, Exod. 30. v. 38.

AND HE CALLED ITS NAME NEHUSHTAN) The more eagerly it was worshipped, the more he thought it should be depreciated, as if he were saying: It is brass, and nothing more.

Latin:

Vers. 4. IPSE DISSIPAVIT EXCELSA) Rem ma- gnam fecit: sed pœna decem tribuum ante oculos, Judæ tri- bum magis quam ante morigeram legi fecerat.

CONFREGITQVE SERPENTEM ÆNEUM QVEM FECERAT MOSES] Nota, quem fecerat Moses. Egregi- um documentum Regibus, ut quamvis bene instituta, sed non necessaria, ubi ἐπιτοπολὺ male usurpantur, è conspectu tol- lant, ne ponant offendiculum cæcis.

ADOLEBANT EI INCENSUM) Quod inter illa erat, quæ Dei solius honori reservata extra Templum usurpare non licebat, Exod. 30. v. 38.

VOCAVITQVE NOMEN EJUS NOHESTAN) Quo impensius id colebatur, eo magis depretiandum putavit, quasi diceret: Æs est, præterea nihil.

## 18:5
Verse 5. HE TRUSTED IN THE LORD GOD OF ISRAEL) A huge testimony, and one which contains all virtues by its own power. For it is not easy to trust in God alone without any addition, because of the kinship with the mortal to which we are joined, which persuades us to trust in wealth, and glory, and power, and friends, and health, and strength of body, and many other things. But to wash oneself clean of each of these and to disbelieve in creation, which is in all things untrustworthy of itself, and to trust only in God, who is also in truth the only trustworthy one, is the work of a great and Olympian mind, no longer enticed by any of the things among us. Which are the words of Philo in the book, Who is the heir of divine things.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IN DOMINO DEO ISRAEL SPERAVIT) Ingens testimonium, & quod omnes virtutes vi sua continet. Nam μόνῳ Θεῷ χωρὶς προσπαραλήψεως ἐ ῥᾴδιον πιστεῦσαι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ θνητὸν, ᾧ συνεζεύγμεθα, συγγένειαν, ὅπερ ἡμᾶς καὶ χρήμασι καὶ δόξῃ καὶ ἀρχῇ καὶ φίλοις, ὑγείᾳ τε καὶ ῥώμῃ σώματος, καὶ ἄλλοις πολλοῖς ἀναπείθει πεπιστευκέναι. Τὸ δὲ ἐκνίψασθαι τούτων ἕκαστον καὶ ἀπιστῆσαι τῇ γενέσει, τῇ πάντα ἐξ ἑαυτῆς ἀπίστῳ, μόνῳ δὲ πιστεῦσαι Θεῷ, τῷ καὶ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν μόνῳ πιστῷ, μεγάλης καὶ ὀλυμπίου διανοίας ἔργον ἐστὶ, πρὸς οὐδε- νὸς ἔτι δελεαζομένης τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν. Quæ Philonis verba libro, quis rerum divinarum hæres.

FROM THE TOWER OF THE WATCHMEN TO THE FENCED CITY) See above 17, 9.

## 18:13
Verse 13.

IN THE FOURTEENTH YEAR OF KING HEZEKIAH SENNACHERIB KING OF ASSYRIA CAME UP)

Josephus testifies that Berosus makes mention of this King of the Assyrians, in which those words must be deleted: saying thus: for what follows after that is manifest not to be of Berosus, but of Josephus. Herodotus also mentions Sennacherib in Euterpe. But I wonder that Herodotus is noted for error by Josephus, because he said Sennacherib was not King of the Assyrians, as Berosus and the sacred scriptures do, but King of the Arabians; since the codices of Herodotus, which we use, have: Sennacherib king of the Arabians and Assyrians. Also those words in Josephus: as this king came against the king of the Egyptians who was a priest of Hephaestus, do not cohere with the preceding, and have crept into the text from some marginal annotation. This whole history is in almost the same words in Isaiah 36.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ANNO QVARTO DECIMO REGIS EZE- CHIÆ ASCENDIT SENNACHERIB REX ASST- RIORVM)

Hujus Assyriorum Regis meminisse Berosum te- statur Josephus, in quo delenda illa: λέγων ὕτως: nam quæ post id sequuntur manifestum non Berosi esse, sed Josephi. Meminit Sennacheribi & Herodotus Euterpe. Miror autem ab Josepho erroris notari Herodotum, quod Senacheribum dixerit non Assyriorum, ut Berosus & sacræ literæ, sed Ara- bum Regem; cum Herodoti codices, quibus utimur, habeant: Σαναχάριβον βασιλέα Ἀραβίων τε καὶ Ἀσσυρίων. Etiam illa verba apud Josephum: ὡς ὗτος ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν Αἰ- γυπτίων βασιλέα ἦλθεν ἱερέα ὄντα τῶ Ἡφαίστ, cum superio- ribus non cohærent, & ex marginali annotatione aliqua in textum irrepsere. Tota hæc historia iisdem prope verbis est apud Esaiam 36.

## 18:14
Verse 14.

THREE HUNDRED TALENTS OF SILVER AND THIRTY TALENTS OF GOLD.

300 talents of silver make 450,000 Joachimici: but thirty talents of gold 540,000. The total sum is 990,000. That is, nine tons of gold, and ninety thousand Joachimici: to produce which it was necessary to exhaust the treasures of the temple and of the royal palace. See what is said at 1 Chron. 22, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

TRECENTA TALENTA ARGEN- TI ET TRIGINTA TALENTA AURI.

Talenta argenti 300. efficiunt 450000. Joachimicos: triginta vero talenta auri 540000. summa tota est 990000. hoc est, novem tonna- rum auri, & nonaginta millium Joachimico- rum: ad quam conficiendam opus erat exhau- riri thesauros templi, & Regii palatii. Vide quæ ad 1. Par. 22, 14.

Verse 15.

AND HEZEKIAH GAVE ALL THE SILVER) The good cause passed to Hezekiah in such a way, as we noted in Book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, chapter 1, § 18. Thus, when God wishes to liberate His own, He even provides them with an honorable cause.

Vers. 15.

DEDITQVE EZECHIAS OMNE ARGENTUM) Ita bona causa ad Ezechiam transiit, ut notavimus 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis capite 1. §. 18. Sic Deus ubi suos liberare vult, causam etiam honestam ipsis præstat.

Verse 25.

WITHOUT THE WILL OF THE LORD) יהוה, that is, of your God: for thus Rabshakeh esteemed him, as Shalmaneser 17, 27.

Verse 27.

TO THE MEN WHO SIT UPON THE WALL) Those who besiege cities, if they wish to offer any terms, devote every effort so that knowledge of them may reach not only the leaders, but also the people, who are usually more easily moved by such things.

THAT THEY MAY EAT THEIR OWN DUNG) See what was said above 6, 25.

AND DRINK THEIR OWN URINE) Which has happened in many places, when water was lacking.

UT COMEDANT STERCORA SVA) Vide quæ dicta supra 6, 25.

Verse 34.

DEUS EMATH) Above 17, 24.

AND APHRAD) It is joined with Emath in Jeremiah 41. The same name with a letter changed; with almost the same sound ארוד Genesis 10, 16, where the Latin correctly placed Aradios.

ANA) Perhaps Ange, situated in Arabia Felix according to Ptolemy. For it appears to be the name of a city below 19, 13, so that I wonder that Symmachus interpreted Ana and Ava as if they were words, not proper names. But we also had the name of Ava above 17, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

DEUS EMATH) Supra 17, 24.

ET APHRAD] Conjungitur cum Emath Jeremiæ 41. Idem nomen litera mutata; sono pene eodem ארוד Gen. 10, 16. ubi Latinus Aradios posuit, recte.

ANA) Forte Ange, in Arabia Felice posita Ptolemæo. Nam urbis esse nomen apparet infra 19, 13. ut mirer Symma- chum Ana & Ava quasi verba essent, non propria nomina, interpretatum. At Avæ nomen etiam supra habuimus 17, 24.

## 19:1 Argument
v. 1. which was not accustomed to be done, unless whenever such words had been pronounced by one of the Israelites.

Latin:

v. 1. quod fieri non solebat, nisi quoties talia verba ab Israeli- tarum aliquo pronuntiata fuerant.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

To the prayers of Hezekiah, Isaiah promises divine help. As the Assyrian repeats his blasphemous threats, Hezekiah prays fervently, and is confirmed concerning his deliverance by a sign through Isaiah. The Assyrian army is struck down by an Angel, Sennacherib by his own sons.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

Ad Hiskiæ preces Esaias divinum promittit auxilium. Repetente Assyrio minas blasphemas ardenter orat Hiskias, & de liberatione signo confirmatur per Esaiam. Assyriacus exercitus ab Angelo, Senna- cherib à propriis filiis percutitur.

## 19:2
Verse 2.

TO ISAIAH THE PROPHET THE SON OF AMOS) I compare him to the Demosthenes of the Greeks: the purity of Hebraism in Isaiah, of Atticisms in Demosthenes: a magnificent character of speaking for both: frequent figures of speech, but especially that which Quintilian says Demosthenes excelled in, δείνωσις, adding force to unworthy, harsh, and odious matters. But the dignity of his birth and royal affinity also adorned Isaiah.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

AD ESAIAM PROPHETAM FILIUM AMOS) Huic ego Græcorum Demosthenem comparo: puritas Hebraismi in Esaia, Atticifmi in Demosthene: magnificus utrique di- cendi character: frequentia schemata, maxime vero illa, qua Demosthenem excelluisse ait Quintilianus, δείνωσις, rebus in- dignis, asperis, invidiosis vim addens. Sed Esaiam etiam na- talium dignitas & regia affinitas ornabant.

## 19:3

THE CHILDREN HAVE COME EVEN TO THE BIRTH, AND SHE WHO IS BRINGING FORTH HAD NO STRENGTH) A not dissimilar comparison in Homer, Iliad Λ. Ὡς δ’ ὅταν ὠδίνουσαν ἔχῃ βέλος ὀξὺ γυναῖκα Δριμὺ, τό, τε προϊεῖσι μογοστόκοι εἰλείθυιαι Ἥρης θυγατέρες πικρὰς ὠδῖνας ἔχουσαι· Ὣς ὀξεῖ’ ὀδύναι δῦνον μένος Ἀτρείδαο.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VENERUNT FILII USQVE AD PARTUM, ET VI- RES NON HABEBAT PARTURIENS) Non dissimilis comparatio apud Homerum Iliados Λʹ. Ὡς δ’ ὅταν ὠδίνουσαν ἔχῃ βέλος ὀξὺ γυναῖκα Δριμὺ, τό, τε προϊεῖσι μογοστόκοι εἰλείθυιαι Ἥρης θυγατέρες πικρὰς ὠδῖνας ἔχουσαι· Ὣς ὀξεῖ’ ὀδύναι δῦνον μένος Ἀτρείδαο.

FOR THE REMNANT) For one tribe and parts of two tribes, which alone remain of such a copious posterity of Jacob.

Ver. 9. OF TIRHAKAH) Who is Thearchon to Strabo. GOZAN) See above 17, 6. HARAN) חרן Carrhae of Assyria. AND RESEPH) Resapha in Palmyrene according to Ptolemy. AND THE CHILDREN OF EDEN) Of Mesopotamia. See Gen. 2. WHICH WERE IN TELASSAR) Contracted to Thelda in Ptolemy, Thilutha in Ammianus.

## 19:24
Ver. 24. AND THE FRUITFUL FIELD OF HIS CARMEL) Carmel is not a proper name here, but signifies fruitful places. For thus Isaiah uses it in 10:18, 16:10, 19:23. AND I HAVE DRUNK STRANGE WATERS) Concerning Sesostris, Lucan says: "Yet before Sesostris drank the Rhone and the Po, he drank the Nile from its source." AND I HAVE DRIED UP WITH THE SOLES OF MY FEET ALL THE SHUT-UP WATERS] I crossed rivers fortified with great embankments, the waters having been driven away, of course. The LXX have ποταμὸς περιοχῆς here. See similar examples in Frontinus, book 3, chapter 7. Add what we have brought forward concerning Cyrus from Herodotus in book 3 of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET SALTUM CARMELI EJUS) Non est hîc Carmel nomen proprium, sed loca frugifera significat. Ita enim utitur Esaias 10, 18. 16, 10. 19, 23. ET BIBI AQVAS ALIENAS) De Sesostri Lucanus: Ante tamen Sestros amnes Rhodanumque Padumque Quam Nilum de fonte bibit. ET SICCAVI VESTIGIIS PEDUM MEORUM OMNES AQVAS CLAUSAS] Transii flumina magnis ag- geribus munita, aquis nimirum abactis. ποταμὸς περιοχῆς habent hîc LXX. Exempla similia vide apud Frontinum li- bro 3. cap. 7. Adde, quæ de Cyro attulimus ex Herodoto ad librum 3. pro Veritate Religionis Christianæ.

## 19:25
Ver. 25. HAST THOU NOT HEARD, WHAT I HAVE DONE FROM THE BEGINNING) In Hebrew: Have you not heard long ago that I have done it. Namely, when I led the Israelites through the Arabian gulf. FROM ANCIENT DAYS I HAVE FORMED IT) I did this by my own power, without the help of nature or human art: for thus the verb יצר is excellently used in Gen. 2, 8. and elsewhere. AND NOW I HAVE BROUGHT IT) Now also you would not have done it, unless it had pleased me to permit it. AND THE FENCED CITIES WERE FOR THE RUIN OF FIGHTING HILLS) In the Hebrew: This was to lay waste fenced cities into heaps of ruins. That is, for this reason I permitted this, that I might punish with destruction the cities hateful to me: for this reason I leveled the way for you.

Latin:

Vers. 25. NUNQVID NON AUDISTI, QUID AB INITIO FECERIM) In Hebr. Nonne audisti jam olim me id fecisse. Nempe cum Israelitas deduxi per Arabicum sinum. EX DIEBUS ANTIQVIS PLASMAVI ILLUD) Feci hoc vi mea, sine naturæ aut humanæ artis ope: ita enim exi- mie usurpatur verbum יצר Gen. 2, 8. & alibi. ET NUNC ADDVXI] Nunc quoque tu id non fecisses, nisi mihi libuisset permittere. ERANTQVE IN RVINAM COLLIUM PUGNAN- TIVM CIVITATES MUNITÆ) In Hebræo: Hoc erat ad sertendum civitates munitas in cumulos ruinarum. Id est, ideo hoc permisi, ut civitates mihi exosas punirem excidio: ideo tibi complanavi viam.

AND A BRIDLE IN THY LIPS) As is wont to be done to horses and mules. Psal. 32, 9. AND I WILL BRING THEE BACK BY THE WAY, BY WHICH THOU CAMEST) I will drive you back.

FROM MY HAND] He reads מידי, as the books of the Eastern Jews have, not מידו, as ours and those which the LXX used.

V. 29. EAT THIS YEAR, WHAT THOU SHALT FIND) In the Hebrew: ספיח: which both here and elsewhere the LXX translate as τὰ αὐτόματα. BUT IN THE SECOND YEAR, WHAT GROWS OF ITSELF) It is in the Hebrew: שחיש, or שחיש, which the LXX translate as ἀνατέλοντα. PORRO IN TERTIO ANNO SEMINATE ET ME- TITE) Vt in alta pace, longe remoto non hoste tantum, sed & hostis metu.

AND WHATEVER REMAINS OF THE HOUSE OF JUDA, SHALL SEND ROOT DOWNWARD, AND SHALL BEAR FRUIT UPWARD] It will have firm foundations, and will produce offspring. A metaphor taken from plants.

FOR OUT OF JERUSALEM SHALL GO FORTH A REMNANT) The sense is the same as in those lines of Virgil: Therefore all Teucria frees itself from long grief: the gates are opened: it is a pleasure to go and see the Dorian camps and the deserted places.

Latin:

Vers. 31. DE JERUSALEM QVIPPE EGREDIENTVR RELIQVIÆ) Idem est sensus, qui in illis Virgilii: Ergo omnis longo solvit se Teucria luctu: Panduntur portæ: juvat ire, & Dorica castra Desertosque videre locos.

NOR SHALL HE SHOOT AN ARROW INTO IT) To cast down the defenders. NOR SHALL A SHIELD COME BEFORE IT) That is: he shall not attack it by forming a tortoise, which is the συνασπισμὸς to the Greeks. NOR SHALL HE CAST A BANK AGAINST IT) The Hebrews interpret סללה as a ballista. He shall not pour forth ballista stones against it.

Vers. 32. NEC MITTET IN EAM SAGITTAM) Ad dejiciendos defensores. NEC OCCVPABIT EAM CLTPEVS) Id est: non ag- gredietur eam facta testudine, qui συνασπισμὸς Græcis. NEC CIRCVMDABIT EAM MVNITIO) Hebræi סללה interpretantur ballistam. Non effundet in eam saxa ballistaria.

THE ANGEL OF THE LORD CAME, AND SMOTE IN THE CAMP OF THE ASSYRIANS A HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-FIVE THOUSAND) Mention of this history is in Tobias 1, 21. Ecclesiasticus 48, 24. 1 Maccabees 7, 41.

Latin:

Verf. 35. VENIT ANGELUS DOMINI, ET PER- CVSSIT IN CASTRIS ASSYRIORUM CENTUM OCTOGINTA QVINQVE MILLIA) Mentio hujus hi- storiæ Tobiæ 1, 21. Ecclefiastici 48, 24. 1. Macc. 7, 41.

## 19:37
AND AS HE WAS WORSHIPPING IN THE TEMPLE OF NESROCH HIS GOD] The LXX: μεσερά. But Josephus: in his own temple called Araske.

ADRAMELECH AND SARASAR HIS SONS) The eldest, who are said to have been driven to this crime because the father, when he was in danger, had bound himself by a vow to sacrifice them.

AND THEY FLED INTO THE LAND OF THE ARMENIANS) To the Cordyaeans. See Gen. 8, 4. And thus they were cut off from the succession of the kingdom, as Josephus notes here.

AND ASAR-HADDON HIS SON REIGNED IN HIS STEAD) By Ptolemy, Asaradinus.

That Asarhaddon is not Sardanapalus, as Genebrard, Arias, and Serarius maintain: because according to Eusebius, Sardanapalus must be placed earlier, namely under Azarias King of Juda: to whom Cornelius thinks Jonas announced the destruction of Nineveh: but Codomannus more correctly refers that to Phul, his successor, at the Year of the World 3321.

Latin:

Verf. 37. CUMQVE ADORARET IN TEMPLO NESROTH DEUM SUUM] LXX. μεσερά. At Jofephus: τῷ ἰδίῳ ναῷ Ἀράσκη λεγομένῳ.

ADRAMELECH ET SARASAR FILII EJUS) Maxi- mi natu, qui ad hoc facinus impulsi dicuntur, quod pater cum in periculo esset, voto se obstrinxisset illos immolandi.

FUGERUNTQUE IN TERRAM ARMENIORUM) Ad Cordiæos. Vide Gen. 8, 4. Atque ita exciderunt successi- one regni, ut hic notat Josephus.

ET REGNAVIT ASAR-HADDON FILIUS EJUS PRO EO) Ptolemæo Ἀσσαραδίνο.

Asarhaddon ille non est Sardanapalus, ut Gene- brard, Arias & Serarius volunt: quia secundum Eusebium anterius collocandus Sardanapalus, ni- mirum sub Azaria Rege Juda: cui Ninives excidi- um Jonam indixisse Cornelius putat: sed id rectius ad Phulem ejus successorem refert Codomannus ad Ann. Mundi 3321.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

To Ezechias, who is sick and praying, health is promised with a sign on the sundial: who showed his treasures to the legates of Merodach, and therefore it is announced to him that all of them will be plundered by the Babylonians.

Ver. 1.

SET THINE HOUSE IN ORDER) Give your final instructions. Plutarch on the Poetry of Homer: 'The poet was not unaware that it is a custom among all people for those going out to war, or placed in danger, to instruct their kin in something; for Andromache, shaking Hector, says: "For you did not stretch out your hand to me from the bed as you were dying, nor did you speak to me a wise word, which I might always remember, shedding tears night and day." And Penelope remembers the instructions of Odysseus, who said when he was departing: "Therefore I do not know whether God will bring me back, or whether I shall be taken there in Troy. But let all things be a care to you here: remember my father and mother in the halls, as now, or even more, when I am far away. But when you see our son with a beard, marry whom you wish, leaving your own house." You have an excellent example of such instructions in Stobaeus under the title On Prudence, from the Erechtheus of Euripides.'

FOR THOU SHALT DIE, AND SHALT NOT LIVE) In this announcement lay a certain tacit condition, as in Jonah 3:4.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

Ezechia ægrotanti et oranti sanitas dato in horo- logio figno promittitur: qui Merodachi lega- tis thesauros suos ostendit, ideoq; indicitur ei omnes illos à Babyloniis direptum iri.

Verf. 1.

PRÆCIPE DOMUI TUÆ) Da suprema mandata. Plu- tarchus de Homeri Poesi: τὸ δὲ τὰς ἐξιόντας ἐπὶ πόλεμον, ἢ ἐν κινδύνῳ καθεστῶτας ἐντέλλεσθαί τι τοῖς οἰκείοις εἰθισμένον παρὰ πᾶσιν, οὐκ ἠγνόησεν ὁ ποιητής• ἡ μὲν γὰρ Ἀνδρομάχη σείοσα τὸν Ἔκτορα φησίν Οὐ γάρ μοι θνήσκων λεχέων ἐκ χεῖρας ὄρεξας Οὐ δέ τί μοι εἶπας πυκινὸν ἔπος, ὅ τεκεν αἰεὶ Μεμνήμην νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα δακρυχέουσα. ἡ δὲ Πηνελόπη ῷ τῷ Ὀδυσσέως ἐντολῶν μιμνήσκεται, φήσαντος ὁπότε ἐξῄει• Τῷ οὐκ οἶδ' ἤκεν μ' ἀνέση θεὸς, ἤκεν ἁλώω Αὐτῷ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ. σοὶ δ' ἐνθάδε πάντα μελόντων, Μεμνῆσθαι πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος ἐν μεγάροισιν, Ὡς νῦν, ἢ ἔτι μᾶλλον, ἐμεῦ ἀπονόσφιν ἐόντος. Αὐτὰρ ἐπειδὰν παῖδα γενειήσαντα ἴδηαι, Γήμασθαι ὧκ' ἐθέλησθα τεὸν κατὰ δῶμα λιπῦσα. Exemplum talium mandatorum egregium habes apud Stobæ- um titulo de Prudentia ex Erechtheo Euripidis.

MORIERIS ENIM TU, ET NON VIVES) In hac denuntiatione latebat tacita quædam conditio, ut Jonæ 3, 4.

## 20:3
Verse 3.

REMEMBER NOW, I BESEECH THEE, HOW I HAVE WALKED BEFORE THEE IN TRUTH, AND WITH A PERFECT HEART) They proclaimed their works to God with a certain noble confidence of conscience, as Nehemiah 13:14. In the New Testament we do not see this done in the same way, because both the power of grace is much greater, and a greater progress is required day by day, so that it may be said of a Christian: 'And thinking nothing done, while anything remained to be done.' Socinian hypotheses recurring here and there in Grotius. The grace of God is indeed declared more clearly in the N.T. But the power of grace ought not therefore to be considered much greater. For by the same grace of our Lord Jesus Christ the ancients were saved, by which we also are saved. Acts 15:11. And Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13:8. Furthermore, just as now a greater progress day by day is required of Christians, so there can be no doubt that the same was required repeatedly in the time of the O. Testament. The path of the just is as the shining light, and it grows until the perfect day, says Solomon, Prov. 4:18. But that we do not read that the faithful in the N.T. celebrated their own righteousness with the same confidence of conscience, is not surprising: because the prayers of the faithful are not described and presented there in the same way as in the O. Testament. Nor, however, were Paul and Timothy afraid to boast of their sincerity, 2 Cor. 1:12: 'For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, and not with fleshly wisdom,' but we have conducted ourselves in the grace of God in this world, but more abundantly toward you. Such things also occur elsewhere. But thus are Zechariah and Elizabeth also celebrated in Luke 1. Both were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord without complaint. And those proclamations of the works of the saints in the Old Testament are to be rightly understood. For they do not speak of the perfect fulfillment of the law. But the righteousness of the person being presupposed, which is obtained solely through faith, since by the obedience of one many are made righteous, Rom. 5:19, that is, whoever are ever justified, they proclaim the righteousness of their deeds to this extent, that they have studied to obey the precepts of God ἀνυποκρίτως, and sincerely (which is called in the Hebrew a perfect heart, just as the Hebrews speak of a heart and a heart, when hypocrisy underlies it, Ps. 12:3, 2 Chron. 12:13. and have subsequently striven more and more toward true perfection: How Augustine speaks excellently of the precept of love in De Spiritu et Littera, ch. 36. That precept of love (you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart) will be completed in that life, when we shall see face to face; but for this reason it is also commanded to us now, that we might be admonished what to ask for by faith, why to set hope before us, and by forgetting those things which are behind, we ought to extend ourselves to those things which are before.

Hezekiah therefore wept with a great weeping) With the hope of eternal life less clearly revealed, death was also feared more.

That death is feared is natural. But that the hope of eternal life was less clearly revealed, the Socinian hypothesis, nay the Pelagian hypothesis of Grotius, has already been refuted quite often.

Latin:

Verf. 3.

MEMENTO QVÆSO, QVOMODO AMBVLAVE- RIM CORAM TE IN VERITATE, ET IN CORDE PERFECTO) Prædicabant illi, generosa quadam conscien- tiæ fiducia, Deo opera sua, ut Nehemias 13, 14. In Novo fœ- dere non æque id videmus fieri, quia & vis gratiæ multo ma- jor est, & profectus indies major requiritur, ut de Christiano dici possit: Nihilque putans actum, dum quid superesset agendum. Socinianæ hypotheses passim recurrentes in Grotio. Luculentius quidem declarata est gratia Dei in N. T. Sed vis gratiæ ideo multo major cen- seri non debet. Per eandem enim gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi salvati sunt veteres, per quam & nos salvamur. Actor. 15, 11. Et Jesus Christus heri, ho- die, idem & in secula Ebr. 13, 8. Porro quemadmo- dum nunc profectus indies major requiritur à Christianis, ita & V. Testamenti tempore eundem subinde majorem requisitum fuisse, nullum esse potest dubium. Justorum semita quasi lux splendens procedit, & crescit usque in perfectam diem, ait Salo- mo Prov. 4, 18. Quod vero conscientiæ fiducia ju- stitiam suam non æque in N. T. celebrasse fideles le- gamus, mirum non est: quia precationes fidelium ibi non æque, uti in V. Test. descriptæ exhibentur. Neque tamen veriti sunt Paulus & Timotheus 2. Cor. 1, 12. de sinceritate sua gloriari: Gloria nostra hæc est testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, quod in simplicitate cordis & sinceritate Dei, & non in sapientia carnali, sed in gratia Dei conversati simus in hoc mundo, abun- dantius autem ad vos. Qualia etiam alibi occurrunt. At ita celebrantur etiam Zacharias & Elisabetha Lu- cæ 1. Erant justi ambo ante Deum incedentes in omni- bus mandatis, & justificationibus Domini sine querela. Et recte intelligenda sunt illa præconia operum san- ctorum in V. Test. Non enim loquuntur de perfecta legis impletione. Sed præsupposita personæ justitia, quæ per fidem unice obtinetur, siquidem per unius obedientiam justi constituantur multi, Rom. 5, 19. h. e. quicunque unquam justificantur, justitiam facto- rum hactenus prædicant, quod & ἀνυποκρίτως, ac sincere studuerint præceptis Dei obedire, (quod E- bræis dicitur in corde perfecto, uti ex adverfo corde & corde Ebræi dicunt, cum hypocrisis subest Psal. 12, 3. 2. Paralip. 12, 13. & ad veram perfectionem subinde magis magisque contenderint: Quomodo de præ- cepto dilectionis præclare Augustin. de Spir. & Liter. cap. 36. Præceptum illud dilectionis (diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde) in illa vita complebitur, cum videbimus à facie ad faciem; sed ideo etiam nobis hoc nunc præceptum est, ut admoneremur, quid fide exposcere, cur spem præmittere, & obliviscendo, quæ retro sunt, ad anteriora nos extendere debeamus.

Flevit igitvr Ezechias fletv magno) Minus clare revelata spe æternæ vitæ mors etiam magis time- batur.

Mortem timeri naturale est. Minus clare autem revelatam fuisse spem vitæ æternæ, hypothesis Soci- niana, imo Pelagiana Grotii profligata est jam sæ- pius.

## 20:6
Verse 6. I will add to your days 15 years) To those years which you would have lived according to the order established in nature.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Addam diebus tuis xv. annos) Iis an- nis, quos vixisses secundum constitutum in natura ordinem.

## 20:7
Verse 7. Bring a lump of figs) Not that there was power in the figs to heal a hopeless disease, but it was a sign of divine efficacy. See a similar thing in John 9:6.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Afferte massam ficorvm) Non quod in ficubus vis esset medendi morbo deplorato, sed signum di- vinæ efficaciæ. Simile vide Joh. 9, 6.

## 20:11
Verse 11. Which had already descended on the sundial of Ahaz) The gnomon was constant, as Eliahon Chomer says, made from a semicircle, in the hollow of which was a globe, into which the falling shadow corresponded to the notches made in the semicircle to the number, as they say, of 28. These notches are here called מעלות, i.e., degrees. By ten of them the shadow was moved back. Isaiah 38:8 calls that shadow the sun, because it was accustomed to be made by the sun. But there was no need for the course of the universe to be changed, only for the sake of the sign. By a similar figure, windows are called by the name of the sun, Jer. 15:9.

The shadow could not be moved back without the sun being moved back, from which the shadow is made. Which is undoubted from sundials and astronomical science. And by the Holy Spirit both are said, both that the shadow was moved back, and that the sun returned, as is explicitly held in Isaiah 38:8. And the sun returned ten lines by the degrees which it had descended. Which is likewise proclaimed in Ecclesiasticus 48:26, in his days the sun went backward, and he added life to the King. Which are in vain elided by metonymical interpretation; so that we might believe the shadow to be called the sun, because it is accustomed to be made by the sun. For one must not depart from the literal sense without necessity, especially where divine miracles are historically recounted: for otherwise all miracles could be elided, without trouble, if it be permitted to understand by the sun the shadow, or the image of the sun, as Grotius invented concerning the passage in Josh. ch. 10, by cause the effect, by subject the adjunct, and so on, as one pleases: which is to change not only squares into rounds, but heaven with earth, substance and body with shadow, and to play with the words of the Holy Scriptures as if they were dice. But where is the shadow called the sun in the Holy Scriptures? Jer. 15:9. It does not appear that windows are indicated by the name of the sun. The sun has set for her, while it was yet day, says the Prophet, where interpreters understand by the sun setting a declining happiness. Certainly the miracles of God are not to be diminished for the sake of our own ingenuity: But it is necessary to believe that God is able to perform more than we can understand. Nor has it been easily doubted hitherto in the Church concerning the sun itself having been moved back, and not even among the Jews, who even give reasons why the day was increased by ten hours, but as they are accustomed to do, fabulously: namely, that ten hours had been subtracted from that day on which Ahaz the impious King was committed to the earth, so that he might not be buried with sufficient royal honor, which they claim were restored when his son Hezekiah was sick. There were indeed some more recent ones who thought only the shadow had moved back; namely Vatablus, Burgensis, Arias Montanus, Sanctius; but with the ancients and most modern interpreters contradicting them. Recently, however, Peirerius, the author of the fable of the Pre-Adamites, dared to call into doubt the miracle of the sun moved back. To whom Grotius here joins himself, a supporter of monstrous novelty: which we have not rarely observed in him himself. But in truth, if that prodigy had happened only in the sundial of Ahaz, how would the King of Babylon have sent his envoys to inquire about the portent which HAD HAPPENED UPON THE EARTH, 2 Chron. 32:31. Doubtless the Babylonians saw the day longer than usual, and when they had heard by report that the miracle was done for the sake of Hezekiah, they thought it necessary to inquire about it, so that they might investigate the cause of such a great miracle. Let Sam. Mares. be compared in Refutat. Fabulae Prae-Adamit. Quest. 7, p. 630, seqq. I pass over the fact that it could naturally happen sometimes that the shadow alone moves back on a sundial, if the sundials are erected in such a way; whence Petrus Nonius, eliding this miracle, contends that it was a natural return of the shadow: which, however, the Jesuit Clavius, a most learned mathematician, refutes. Nor do I urge that point, that the poets took their own from there concerning the sun's course moved back, just as he sings: While we were guiding the horses against the sun. Concerning which see Corn. à Lap. on Isaiah ch. 38.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Qvibus jam descenderat in horo- logio Achaz) Erat gnomon constans, ut ait Eliahon Chomer, ex semicirculo, in cujus cavo erat globus, in quem cadens umbra respondebat cæsuris factis in semicirculo ad nu- merum, ut ajunt 28. Eæ cæsuræ hic vocantur מעלות i. e. gradus. Per eorum decem retroacta est umbra. Eam umbram solem vocat Es. 38, 8. quia à Sole fieri solebat. Nihil autem opus erat universi cursum immutari, tantum figni causa. Si- mili figura fenestræ Solis nomine appellantur Jer. 15, 9.

Umbra retroagi non potuit, quin Sol retroagere- tur, à quo fit umbra. Quod ex Sciatericis & Astrono- micis indubitatum est. Et à Spiritu S. utrumque di- citur, tum quod retroacta fuerit umbra, tum quod Sol regressus sit, uti deferte habetur Es. 38, 8. Et Re- gressus est sol decem lineis per gradus, quos descenderat. Quod pariter prædicatur Eccles. 48, 26. in diebus ipsius retro rediit Sol, & addidit Regi vitam. Quæ nequicquam eliduntur, per metonymicam in- terpretationem; ut umbram Solem vocari creda- mus, quia à Sole fieri solet. Non enim recedendum est à proprietate citra necessitatem, maxime ubi hi- storice recensentur divina miracula: alias enim mi- racula omnia elidi possint, citra negotium, si per So- lem umbram, aut Solis imaginem, uti de loco Jos. c. 10. comentus est Grotius, per caussam effectum, per sub- jectum adjunctum, & ita porro, prout libuerit, intel- ligere liceat: quod est mutare non quadrata rotun- dis solum, sed cælum cum terra, substantiam & cor- pus cum umbra, ac S. S. verbis, veluti taxillis, lude- re. Ubi vero umbra vocatur Sol in S. Literis? Jerem. 15, 9. Solis nomine fenestras indigitari non apparet. Occidit ei Sol, cum adhuc esset dies, inquit Propheta, ubi per Solem occasum felicitatem vergentem In- terpretes intelligunt. Miracula certe Dei extenuan- da pro nostro ingenio non sunt: Sed credere opor- tet, Deum plura præstare posse, quam nos intelli- gere. Neque dubitatum hactenus facile in Ecclesia fuit, de Sole ipso retroacto, & ne apud Judæos quidem, qui causas etiam reddunt, cur decem horis aucta dies fuerit, sed uti solent fabulose : decem nempe horas subtractas fuisse diei illi, quo Achaz impius Rex terræ mandatus erat, ne regie satis sepeliretur, quas restitu- tas agunt, cum filius ejus Ezechias ægrotaret. Fuere quidem nonnulli recentiores, qui solum umbram retrocessisse putarunt; Vatablus nempe, Burgensis, Ariasmontanus, Sanctius; sed Veteribus & plerisque etiam modernis Interpp. contradicentibus. Nuper tamen Peirerius fabulæ Præ-Adamitarum autor, au- sus est in dubium vocare miraculum de retroacto Sole. Cui hic se jungit Grotius Novitatis portento- sæ fautor: Quod non raro in ipso observavimus. Verum enim vero si in Achazi Sciaterico tantum prodigium id contigisset, quomodo misisset legatos suos Rex Babyloniæ ad inquirendum de portento, quod ACCIDERAT SUPER TERRAM 2. Par. 32, 31. Nimirum viderunt Babylonii diem solito pro- lixiorem, & quum fama percepissent in gratiam E- zechiæ factum miraculum, de illo inquirendum duxerunt, ut causam tanti miraculi indagarent. Conferatur Sam. Mares. in Refutat. Fabulæ Præ-A- damit. Quæst. 7. p. 630. seqq. Taceo, quod naturali- ter id fieri quandoque possit, ut sola umbra in ho- rologio retroëat, si ita erigantur Scioterica; unde Petr. Nonius miraculum hoc elidens, naturalem fu- isse regressum umbræ contendit: quem vero refellit Jesuita Clavius, Mathematicus doctissimus. Nec il- lud urgeo, quod Poëtæ sua inde sumserint de solis cur- su retroacto, sicut ille canit: Adversos Solis dum rege- remus equos. De quibus vide Corn. à Lap. ad Es. c. 38.

All that is in your house shall be taken away) Fulfilled below 24, 13.

AVFERENTVR OMNIA, QVÆ SVNT IN DOMO TVA) Impletum infra 24, 13.

## 20:19
Ver. 19. The word of the Lord is good, which you have spoken. Let there be peace and truth in my days) When I am dead, let the earth be mingled with fire.

Latin:

Vers. 19. BONVS SERMO DOMINI, QVEM LOCV- TVS ES. SIT PAX ET VERITAS IN DIEBVS MEIS) Ἐμοῦ θανόντος γαῖα μιχθήτω πυρὶ.

## 20:20
Ver. 20. Pool) Concerning which see Nehemiah 3, 16.

And he brought water into the city) By secret channels, so that he might both intercept it from the enemies and that water would not be lacking to the city. 2 Chron. 32, 3. 4. 30. Tacitus, where he describes Jerusalem: A perennial fountain of water, mountains hollowed out beneath the ground; and pools and cisterns for preserving rainwater. The founders had provided for frequent wars due to the diversity of customs: hence everything was prepared for a long siege. You have an excellent example of secret water conduits in Procopius, book 4 of the Gothic War, during the siege of Petra of the Lazi.

Ver. same. Are not these things written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?) In the daily records, from which Ezra excerpted many things into the Chronicles, though not omitting the most important matters which are in these Annals. Tacitus noted this distinction well in Annals 13: In the consulship of Nero for the second time and Lucius Piso, few things worthy of memory occurred: unless it pleases one to fill volumes by praising the foundations and beams with which Caesar had constructed the mass of the amphitheater in the Campus Martius: since it has been found consistent with the dignity of the Roman people to commit illustrious deeds to the annals, and such things to the daily records of the city. He names the daily writings of the acts elsewhere, the daily records of the Roman people, as does Vopiscus regarding Probus. There is mention of the daily records of Alexander the Great in Plutarch.

By the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, others understand the books of the Chronicles, or Paralipomenon, in which more things are written about Hezekiah in book 2, ch. 29, 30, 31, 32. That Ezra, moved by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, drew his material from daily records written by the human spirit, is by no means likely. For the Holy Spirit, who is without doubt the author of the Canonical books, does not take from human writings those things which He wishes to be consigned to the monuments of literature. The sacred writers are merely amanuenses of the Holy Spirit and pens, which David confesses of himself in Psalm 45, 3. The same must also be held regarding the note of Grotius on ch. 21, 17. For those things which are there in the book of the chronicles of days are said to be handed down concerning Manasseh, in the 2nd book of Chronicles, chapter 35, as far as appears they are read as recorded: So that there is no need to have recourse to daily records, or a non-sacred book, or to impute it to Ezra, that he plundered the archives of others, who wrote ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενοι 2. Pet. 1, 21. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, for all Canonical Scripture is divinely inspired, as the Apostle testifies 2. Tim. 3, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PISCINA) De qua vide Nehem. 3, 16.

ET INTRODVXERIT AQVAS IN CIVITATEM) Arcanis viis, ut & hostibus eas interciperet, & urbi aquæ non deeffent. 2. Paral. 32, 3. 4. 30. Tacitus ubi Hierosolyma de- scribit: Fons perennis aquæ, cabati sub terra montes; & piscinæ cisternæq́; servandis imbribus. Providerant conditores ex diversi- tate morum crebra bella: inde cuncta quamvis adversus longum obsidium. Arcani aquæ ductus egregium specimen habes apud Procopium 4. Gothicorum in obsidione Petræ Lazorum.

Vers. eod. NONNE HÆC SCRIPTA SVNT IN LIBRO SERMONVM DIERVM REGVM JVDA?) In diurnis, unde multa excerpsit Esdras in Paralipomena, non omissis tamen potissimis rebus, quæ in his sunt Annalibus. Id discri- men bene notavit Tacitus Annal. 13. Nerone secundum, L. Pi- sone Consulibus pauca memoria digna evenere: nisi cui libeat, laudandis fundamentis, & trabibus, queis molem amphithea- tri apud Campum Martis Cæsar adstruxerat, volumina implere: cum ex dignitate populi Romani repertum sit, res illustres anna- libus, talia diurnis urbis actis mandare. Nominat alibi diurna actorum scripta, diurna populi Romani, ut & Vopiscus Pro- bo. Diurnorum Alexandri M. mentio est apud Plutarchum.

Per librum sermonum dierum Regum Juda alii Chro- nicorum libros, vel Paralipomenon intelligunt, in quibus plura de Hiskia perscripta sunt lib. 2. c. 29. 30. 31. 32. Esdram afflatu Spiritus S. immediato actum è diurnis humano Spiritu scriptis sua depromsis- se, neutiquam sit verisimile. Nec enim è scriptis humanis Spir. S. qui sine dubio auctor est librorum Canonicorum, desumit ea, quæ literarum monu- mentis consignari vult. Scriptores vero sacri ama- nuenses solum sunt Spir. S. & calami, quod de se pro- fitetur David Pf. 45, 3. Idem etiam de nota Grotii ad c. 21, 17. habendum. Quæ enim illic in lib. sermonum dierum dicuntur de Manasse tradita, in libr. Paral. 2. cap. 35. quantum apparet leguntur consignata : Ut non opus sit ad diurna, vel librum non sacrum re- currere, aut Esdræ id imputare, quod scrinia alio- rum expilarit, qui scripsit ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενοι 2. Petr. 1, 21. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, omnis enim Scriptura Canonica divinitus inspirata est, teste Apostolo 2. Tim. 3, 16.

Manasses idololatra, templum prophanans, Pro- phetas pœnam minantes interficit. Ei Ammon filius succedit, à servis interfectus : cui succe- dit Josias.

ET DELENS VERTAM, ET DVCAM CREBRIVS SVPER FACIEM EJUS) In Hebræo : & vertit super faciem suam. LXX. κὰι κατασρέφεται ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἀυτῶ. Solent alabastra aut scutellæ bene abstersæ ore deorsum verso reponi.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII.

Josiah reigns piously, causes the law to be read, and is informed by Huldah concerning the punishments that will happen after his death.

Ver. 1. JOSIAH WAS EIGHT YEARS OLD] "Excellent by nature and well-born toward virtue," says Josephus. Aristotle says there are certain improperly called virtues, innate in some, "natural virtues." Philo thinks Isaac was endowed with such. Among the Greeks, Epaminondas seems to me to have been such a one especially, yet he too was no less unhappy than Josiah, more by the deserts of the people than his own.

These things smell of the Pelagian lamp: That anyone is endowed with virtues by nature. This is the doctrine of the Catholic Church: that there is nothing good in us by nature, for we are all defiled by sin, and begotten with corrupt concupiscence; for the Holy Scripture testifies, with a clear voice (Gen. 6, c. 8; Ps. 51, 6), that not virtues, whether properly or improperly so called, are born in us, but sin, and that we are not naturally inclined to good, but only prone to evil all our days from our infancy. Nor is it to be heard here what Joseph, what Philo, what Aristotle says, but what the Holy Spirit says. And therefore it must be believed that the virtues which were in Josiah were stirred up by the Holy Spirit, not innate by nature. For to do what pleases the Lord, and not to turn aside from the ways of the Lord, either to the right hand or to the left, is not of natural powers, but of divine grace. That gloss is colder than ice, HE DID NOT TURN ASIDE EITHER TO THE RIGHT HAND, OR TO THE LEFT, i.e., he performed everything that could be hoped for from a man: For to walk in the ways of the Lord, and not to turn aside from them, cannot be hoped for from a man left to himself, or viewed in pure naturals. For that, the grace and direction of the Holy Spirit is needed, as the whole Scripture testifies: There is need of regeneration and renewal, the creation of a new heart, and the gift of a new Spirit. Whence it is only wrongly that Epaminondas is compared to Josiah, a Gentile man to a faithful King, and the virtues of the Gentiles, so called homonymously, are compared with the virtues of the Saints: For of Josiah it is truly said, Sirach ch. 49, 3: He was directed divinely into the repentance of the nation, and he took away the abominations of impiety: and he directed his heart toward the Lord, and in the days of sinners he strengthened piety. Which of these would any pious person call "natural virtues"? Who would deny that they are to be ascribed to the Holy Spirit? But this is clearly a habit for Grotius, to hold in equal place the saints and the Gentiles, works performed by the power of the Holy Spirit, and those done without the Holy Spirit. He seems similar in this part to Julian, against whom Bede the Priest writes in lib. 1 in Cant. "What Julian says, that many of the Philosophers have patience, chastity, modesty, and other virtues from the good of nature, it is certain that whoever of the Philosophers did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, these could have no true virtue, nor any true wisdom." Let Augustine be heard here concerning the Palestinian acts, ch. 14: "However much the works of infidels may be praised, we know the true sentence of the Apostle: everything that is not of faith is sin"; And Prosper from Augustine, Sentent. ch. 6: "The whole life of infidels is sin"; And "nothing is good without the highest good." Where the recognition of eternal and unchangeable truth is lacking, there is false virtue, even in the best of morals. Let Hieronymus himself be heard in Galat. 5. For just as according to the Apostle James faith without works is dead, so without faith, although works may be good, they are reckoned as dead. Those, therefore, who do not believe in Christ, and are of upright morals, what else do they have more than the works of virtues? I add finally the writer of the books on the calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 7. Although there was one who by natural intellect attempted to struggle against vices, he only adorned the life of this time fruitlessly; but he did not advance to true virtues and eternal happiness. And hence it is that August. lib. 4. contr. Julian. c. 3. judged thus concerning the better Gentiles: Fabricius will be punished less than Catilina, not because he himself is GOOD, but because the other is more evil, and Fabricius is less impious than Catilina, not by having TRUE VIRTUES, but by not deviating very much from true virtues. And Leo M. Serm. 2. on the Pentecost Fast, comparing the fasting of Christians and Pagans: One thing, he says, reason does under truth, another thing deception does under falsehood. Among us, faith justifies even the one eating; among them, infidelity pollutes even the one fasting: Whence, because outside the Catholic Church nothing is whole, nothing is chaste, as the Apostle says, everything that is not of faith is sin, since we are compared by no likeness to those divided from the unity of the body of Christ, and we are mingled by no communion. For to the virtue of continence nothing pertains more primarily than to abstain from errors, because then at last one walks well, when one proceeds along the way of truth. And this is the Faith of the Catholic Church concerning good works: which if Grotius had taken into account, he would not have drifted so far toward the borders of the Pelagians and Socinians. But let it suffice to have warned of this once. For such emblems occur here and there in these commentaries of Grotius.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII.

Josias pie regnat, legem prælegi curat, & ab Hul- da informatur de suppliciis post fata ejus eventuris.

Vers. 1. OCTO ANNORVM ERAT JOSIAS] φύσιν ἄριστος κὰι πρὸς ἀρετὴν εὖ γεγονὼς, ait Josephus. Aristoteles dicit esse quasdam improprie dictas virtutes, agnatas aliqui- bus, φυσικὰς ἀρετάς. Talibus instructum fuisse Isaacum putat Philo. In Græcis talis præcipue mihi videtur fuisse Epa- minondas, infelix tamen & ipse non minus, quam Josias, po- puli magis meritis, quam suis.

Pelagianam hæc olent lucernam : Natura quem- quam virtutibus instructum esse. Catholicæ Ec- clesiæ hæc est doctrina : natura nihil boni nobis in- esse, omnes enim inquinati sumus peccato, & cum prava concupiscentia procreati ; Scriptura quippe sacra non virtutes, seu proprie dictas, seu impro- prie, nobis adnasci, sed peccatum, non ad bonum nos natura propensos, sed tantum ad malum pronos esse omnibus diebus inde ab infantia nostra, λευκάδι φω- νῇ testatur Genes. 6. c. 8. Psal. 51, 6. Neque hic quid Jo- seph, quid Philo, quid Aristoteles dicat audiendum, sed quid Spiritus S. Ideoque virtutes, quæ in Josia fuere, a Spiritu S. excitatas esse, non a natura inge- nitas, credendum est. Facere enim quod Domino placeat, nec a viis Domini declinare, sive ad dex- tram, sive ad sinistram, non est virium naturalium, sed gratiae divinae. Glossa illa glacie frigidior est, NON DECLINAVIT sive AD DEXTRAM, SI- VE AD SINISTRAM, i. e. praestitit omnia, quae ab homine sperari poterant: Nam in viis Domini am- bulare, nec ab illis declinare, ab homine sperari non potest, sibi relicto, vel in puris naturalibus specta- to. Ad id enim opus est Spir. S. gratia & directione, teste tota Scriptura: Opus est regeneratione & re- novatione, cordis novi creatione, & Spiritus novi do- natione. Unde nonnisi perperam Josiae compara- tur Epaminondas, Regi fideli homo gentilis, vir- tutesque gentilium ὁμονύμως ita dictae componun- tur cum virtutibus Sanctorum: De Josia enim ve- re Syrac. cap. 49, 3. Ipse est directus divinitus in pae- nitentiam gentis, & tulit abominationes impietatis: & gubernavit ad Dominum cor ipsius, & in diebus pec- catorum corroboravit pietatem. Quas φυσικὰς ἀρε- τὰς quis pius dixerit? Quis Spiritui S. adscribendas negarit? Sed Grotio hoc solenne plane est, sanctos & gentiles, opera Spiritus S. virtute patrata, & quae sine Spir. S. facta, parili habere loco. Similis hac in parte videtur Juliano, adversus quem Beda Presby- ter lib. 1. in Cant. Quod Julianus dicit, multos Phi- losophorum patientiam, castitatem, modestiam, ali- asque de naturae bono habere virtutes, constat, quia quicunque Philosophorum Christum Dei virtutem & Dei sapientiam nescierunt, hi nullam veram virtu- tem, nec ullam veram sapientiam habere potuerunt. Audiatur hic Augustinus de gestis Palaestinis cap. 14. Quantumlibet opera infidelium praedicentur, A- postoli sententiam veram novimus: omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est; Et Prosper ex Augustin. Sen- tent. cap. 6. omnis infidelium vita peccatum est; Et nihil est bonum sine summo bono. Ubi deest agnitio aeternae & incommutabilis veritatis, falsa virtus est, etiam in optimis moribus. Audiatur ipse etiam Hie- ron. in Galat. 5. Quomodo enim juxta Apostolum Ja- cobum fides absque operibus mortua est, sic absque fide, quamvis bona opera sint, mortua computantur. Qui igitur in Christo non credunt, & sunt probis moribus, aliud quid magis habent, quam opera virtutum? Ad- do denique Scriptorem librorum de vocatione genti- um lib. 1. c. 7. Etsi fuit, qui naturali intellectu conatus sit vitiis reluctari, hujus tantum temporis vitam steri- liter ornavit; Ad veras autem virtutes, aeternamq; bea- titudinem non profecit. Atque hinc est, quod August. lib. 4. contr. Julian. c. 3. de gentilibus melioribus ita judicavit: Minus Fabricius quam Catilina punietur, non quia ipse BONUS, sed quia ille magis malus, & minus impius, quam Catilina Fabricius, non VERAS VIRTUTES habendo, sed a veris virtutibus non plu- rimum desviando. Et Leo M. Serm. 2. de Jejun. Pen- tecost. comparans Christianorum & Paganorum je- junium: Aliud, inquit, agit sub veritate ratio, aliud sub falsitate deceptio. Apud nos fides justificat etiam manducantem, apud illos infidelitas polluit etiam je- junantem: Unde quia extra Ecclesiam Catholicam ni- hil est integrum, nihil castum, dicente Apostolo, omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est, cum divisis ab uni- tate corporis Christi nulla similitudine comparamur, nulla communione miscemur. Ad virtutem enim con- tinentiae nihil prius pertinet, quam ab erroribus absti- nere, quia tum demum bene ambulatur, cum per viam veritatis inceditur. Atque haec est Fides Ecclesiae Catholicae de operibus bonis: quam si pensi habu- isset Grotius, non ita ad confinia Pelagianorum & Socinistarum declinasset. Sed hoc semel monuisse sufficiat. Occurrunt enim passim talia Emblema- ta in commentis hisce Grotianis.

## 22:14
Ver. 14. WHO DWELT IN JERUSALEM IN THE SECOND) The Greeks, having retained the Hebrew word, [say] ἐν τῇ μασενᾷ. I think the Chaldean correctly interprets it בית אח אלפנא as ἐν τῷ διδασκαλείῳ. For משנה to the Hebrews is the tradition of the interpreter of the law.

Jerome understands the second part of the city near the middle gate, which is called the fish gate, through which one went into the temple: whence through it the Chaldeans invaded Jerusalem and the temple. See also Villalpando, Adrichomius, Ribera, Serarius, Salianus.

Latin:

Vers. 14. QVÆ HABITABAT IN JERVSALEM IN SECVNDA) Græci retenta Hebræo voce ἐν τῇ μασενᾷ. Chal- dæum puto recte interpretari בית אח אלפנא ἐν τῷ διδα- σκαλείῳ. Nam משנה Hebræis est traditio legis interpres.

Hieronym. secundam urbis partem juxta por- tam mediam, quæ vocatur piscium, per quam iba- tur in templum, intelligit: unde per eam Chaldæi invaserunt Jerusalem & templum. Vid. & Vilal- pand. Adrichomius, Ribera, Serarius, Salianus.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

Josiah, having ratified the covenant with God, abolishes idols, shrines, etc., and celebrates the solemn Passover: he is killed in battle with Pharaoh Necho: who [takes] his son Jehoahaz, and having led him away, substitutes King Jehoiakim.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

Josias sancito fœdere cum Deo abolet idola, fa- na, &c. ac solemne Pascha celebrat: in præ- lio cum Pharaone Necho interficitur: qui fi- lium ejus Joahas, eog abducto Jojakimum Regem substituit.

## 23:4
Verse 4.

TO THE PRIESTS OF THE SECOND ORDER) To the vicar of the high priest, and to the captain of the temple.

Others understand the second class: because the priests were distributed into classes by David.

ALL THE VESSELS, WHICH HAD BEEN MADE FOR BAAL] From the law of Deut. 7, 25.

AND HE TOOK THE DUST OF THEM TO BETHEL] That he might render that place entirely profane, and drive far from it those who wished to worship God. Moreover, Bethel was in the jurisdiction of the kings of Judah from the times of Abijah, 2 Chron. 13, 19.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SACERDOTIBUS SECUNDI ORDINIS) Vicario summi Pontificis, & τῷ στρατηγῷ τοῦ ἱεροῦ.

Alii secundam classem intelligunt: quia Sacer- dotes in classes distributi erant à Davide.

OMNIA VASA, QVÆ FACTA FUERANT BA- AL] Ex lege Deut. 7, 25.

ET TULIT PULVEREM EORUM IN BETHEL] Ut illum locum omnino profanum redderet, & inde longe arce- ret eos, qui Deum colere vellent. Erat autem Bethel in ditio- ne regum Judæ jam ab Abiæ temporibus 2. Paral. 13, 19.

## 23:5
Ver. 5. AND HE PUT DOWN THE IDOLATROUS PRIESTS] In Hebrew הכמרים, Camilli. So also in Zephaniah 1, 4. Camilli are ministers of the gods. Servius on Aeneid 11: and before him Varro on the Latin language, book 6. Festus also, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Plutarch.

BAAL AND TO THE SUN] More correctly in the Hebrew, Baal to the Sun. For it is the same.

TO THE TWELVE SIGNS] In the Hebrew: למזלות, which seems to be derived from מזל and to signify the influences of the stars, for which, with the n changed to l, as we just noted in the word כמר and Camilli, Job has מזרות 38, 31, and changes the gender to מזרים 37, 8. Some understand Jupiter, others Venus, others all the planets except the Sun and the Moon. The LXX, as they are accustomed to do in cases of uncertain meaning, left the Hebrew word.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET DELEVIT ARUSPICES] In Hebr הכמרים Camillos. Sic & Sophoniæ 1, 4. Camilli Deo- rum ministri. Servius ad 11. Æneidos: & ante eum Varro de lingua Latina libro 6. Festus quoque ac Dionysius Hali carnassensis & Plutarchus.

BAAL ET SOLI] Rectius in Hebræo Baal Soli. Ef enim idem.

DUODECIM SIGNIS] In Hebræo: למזלות quod à מזל videtur deduci & significare influxus siderum pro quo, נ mutato in ל, ut modo in voce כמר & Ca milli notavimus, Job habet מזרות 38, 31. & מזרים mutat genere 37, 8. Alii Jovem, alii Venerem, alii planetas omn præter Solem & Lunam intelligunt. LXX. ut solent in incert significatione vocem Hebræam reliquerunt.

Simile apud Ezechielem 44, 10. & sequentibus. Aliae culpae, poenitentia sequente, non amovebant reos a functione sacerdotii: idololatria & cultus in loco illicito, amovebant.

## 23:15
Ver. 15. THE ALTAR THAT WAS IN BETHEL.

Cornelius thinks that after the Israelites were led away, the land of Israel returned to its original master, to the family of David: And because God had promised 300 years before that Josiah would do this in Bethel, by that very fact He had given Josiah the right and power to do it, nay, had ordained and commanded that he should do it, 1 Kings 13:2. Furthermore, as Osiander rightly warns here, those who disturb images with tumult following Josiah's example, indeed imitate the external act, but they do not imitate the sincerity of religion: for they are fanatics. And if they think themselves bound by the laws of the Old Testament in demolishing statues, they will also think themselves obligated to slaughter those who embrace a religion different from theirs.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ALTARE QVOD ERAT IN BE- THEL.

Israelitis abductis terram Israel ad pristinum Dominum, ad Davidis familiam rediisse putat Cor- nelius: Et quia Deus id Josiam in Bethel facturum ante 300. annos promiserat, eo ipso jus & potesta- tem id faciendi Josiae dederat, imo ordinaverat, atque jusserat, ut id faceret 1. Reg. 13, 2. Caeterum quod recte hic monet Osiander, qui Josiae exemplo imagines cum tumultu deturbant, factum quidem externum imitantur, sed non imitantur sincerita- tem religionis: sunt enim phanatici. Et si V. Test. legibus teneri se putant, in demoliendis statuis, ex- istimabunt etiam se obligari, ut eos, qui diversam ab illis religionem amplectuntur, trucident.

Vers. 24.

Vers. 26. BECAUSE OF THE PROVOCATIONS WITH WHICH MANASSEH HAD PROVOKED HIM) Because he had added the immense cruelty of idolatry, with a great part of the people approving: below 24, 3. And many followed Josiah himself more out of fear than from a truly corrected purpose of mind, Ezek. 4, 6.

## 23:29
Vers. 29. NECHO KING OF EGYPT) Necoes in Herodotus, as we said at 3, on the Truth of the Christian Religion.

HE WAS SLAIN IN MEGIDDO) Ἐν Μαγδόλῳ: Herodotus, with the pronunciation somewhat corrupted. See Jud. 1, 27. The same place, because it is situated on a mountain, Ἀρμαγεδὼν. Thus Garizim is Ἀγγαρίζιν in Eusebius and others. And another place in Pliny and Tacitus is Arsamofata הר שמשת, that is, the mountain of the sun. The Hebrews say this evil happened to Josiah because he had not consulted Jeremiah.

Necho was marching with an army through the borders of Josiah's kingdom (without harm, however) to the river Euphrates. But Josiah did not want to grant him passage, and that for the sake of the King of Assyria, with whom he was on good terms at that time, and he went out with a levied army to meet him to prevent the passage, in vain, King Necho asking that he desist from his undertaking, for he had a just war not with Josiah, but with the Assyrian King, 2 Chron. 35. He sinned, therefore, by rashness and imprudence, meeting him with whom he had no business. Moreover, although Megiddo was in the lot of Manasseh and Israel, not in Judah, over which Josiah presided, yet Josiah, for the reason brought forward at v. 15, held that land also subject to himself. Add that the Israelites remaining from the captivity of Shalmaneser joined themselves to the kingdom of Judah, and accepted Josiah as their King, so that they might more easily resist the Syrians, Egyptians, and others.

WHEN HE HAD SEEN HIM) Αὐτότης, that is, he had fought with him: as 1 Kings 14, 8.

AGAINST THE KING OF THE ASSYRIANS) The Babylonian, who then also held Assyria. Thus Josephus here.

Latin:

Vers. 29. NECHAO REX ÆGYPTI) Necoës Herodoto, ut diximus ad 3. de Veritate Religionis Christianæ.

OCCISVS EST IN MAGEDDO) Ἐν Μαγδόλῳ: Hero- dotus, corrupta nonnihil pronunciatione. Vide Jud. 1, 27. Idem locus, quia in monte positus Ἀρμαγεδὼν. Sic Garizin Ἀγγαρίζιν apud Eusebium & alios. Et alius locus Plinio & Tacito Arsamofata הר שמשת, id est, mons solis. Ajunt Hebræi hoc malum evenisse Josiæ, ideo quod Jeremiam non consuluisset.

Tendebat Necho cum exercitu per fines regni Josiæ (sine maleficio tamen) ad flumen Euphratem. Noluit autem Josias ei transitum præbere, idque in gratiam Regis Assyrii, cum quo illi tum bene con- veniebat, & abiit conscripto exercitu in occursum ejus prohibiturus transitum, nequicquam Rege Necho rogante, ut ab incepto desisteret, sibi enim non cum Josia, sed cum Rege Assyriaco bellum ju- stumesse 2. Par. 35. Peccavit ergo temeritate & im- prudentia, ei occurrens, cum quo ipsi nihil erat ne- gotii. Cæterum etsi Mageddo in forte Manasse & Israel esset, non in Juda, cui Josias præerat, tamen Josias ob causam ad v. 15. adductam illam quoque terram sibi subjectam habuit. Adde, quod Israeli- tæ reliqui à captivitate Salmanassar regno Judæ se junxerint, ac Josiam pro Rege suo acceptarint, ut facilius Syris, Ægyptiis aliisque resisterent.

CVM VIDISSET EVM) Αὐτότης, id est, pugnasset cum eo: ut 1. Reg. 14, 8.

CONTRA REGEM ASSYRIORVM) Babylonium, qui tunc & Assyriam tenebat. Ita hic Josephus.

## 23:30
Vers. 30. JEHOAHAZ) Who is also Shallum in Jeremiah 22, 11.

Latin:

## 23:33

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV.

Jehoiakim becomes a tributary of the King of Babylon, but rebelled again; therefore an army was sent in, and the Word of the Lord was fulfilled, that He would remove the people of Judah from before Him. Jehoiachin was substituted for him: who, being surrounded by a siege by Nebuchadnezzar, surrendered himself and his people into his power, and was led away by him, after the temple and the palace had been plundered, with Zedekiah appointed King of Judah.

Vers. 1. IN HIS DAYS NEBUCHADNEZZAR CAME UP] Ναβυχοδονόσορ in Berosus, and in the Acts of the Tyrians. Ναβυκοδρόσορ in Abydenus. Ναυοκοδρόσορ in Strabo from Megasthenes, as we noted in the third book on the Truth of the Christian Religion. He came up, however, after he had defeated the Egyptian in battle. Jerem. 46, 1.

JEHOIAKIM BECAME HIS SERVANT) He gave himself into his protection.

This is said to have happened according to the word of the Lord against Judah, that He might remove them from before Him; or rather from Himself. This, therefore, is the beginning of that rejection, and in this fourth year of Jehoiakim those 70 years of Babylonian servitude begin: and Daniel, with other nobles, was carried off to Babylon, even though he left the King, who was promising tribute, in Jerusalem. Which abduction took place in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, from which the 70 years flowed to the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus. Compare Jerem. 25, 1. seqq. Dan. 1, 1. seqq. 2. Chron. 36, 31. Ezra 1, 1.

AND HE REBELLED AGAIN AGAINST HIM] It is credible that this was done when Egypt had begun to recover from its misfortune, which, however, did not last long, as appears shortly at 7.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV.

Joachim sit tributarius Regis Babylonici, sed rursus rebellavit; ideo immissus exercitus, & impletum Verbum Domini, fore ut auferret populum Juda à se. Surrogatus ei Jehojachin: qui obsidione à Nebucadnezare cinctus se & suos in potestatem ejus tradidit, ab ipso, spo- liato templo, & Regia, abductus, constituto Sedecia Rege Judæ.

Vers. 1. IN DIEBVS EJVS ASCENDIT NABVCHODONO- SOR] Ναβυχοδονόσορ Beroso, & in Actis Tyriorum. Ναβυκοδρόσορ Abydeno. Ναυοκοδρόσορ Straboni ex Megastene, ut ad tertium librum de Veritate Religionis Christianæ annotavimus. Ascendit autem, postquam Ægy- ptium prælio vicerat. Jerem. 46, 1.

FACTUS EST EI JOAKIM SERVUS) Se in fidem ejus dedit.

FActum hoc dicitur juxta verbum Domini con- tra Judam, ut auferret eum coram se; vel potius à se. Hic ergo initium est illius abjectionis, & inci- piunt hoc quarto anno Joachimi LXX. illi anni ser- vitutis Babylonicæ : & Daniel cum aliis nobilibus in Babylonem translatus est, etsi Regem tributum promittentem Hierosolymis reliquerit. Quæ ab- ductio facta est anno Nebucadnezaris primo, unde ad primum Monarchiæ Cyri fluxere LXX. anni. Conf. Jerem. 25, 1. seqq. Dan. 1, 1. seqq. 2. Par. 36, 31. Esdr. 1, 1.

ET RURSUM REBELLAVIT CONTRA EUM] Cre- dibile id factum, cum Ægyptus à suo malo respirare cœpisset, quod tamen non diu duravit, ut apparet mox 7.

Verse 14.

AND HE CARRIED AWAY ALL JERUSALEM) That is, the most powerful, as appears 25, 18. Among these was Ezekiel. Berosus called them the captives of the Jews. Hecataeus mentions this deportation and the following one in Josephus, and Demetrius in Clement of Alexandria.

AND ALL THE MIGHTY MEN OF THE ARMY TEN THOUSAND) Seven thousand from the tribe of Benjamin, of whom below 16. Three thousand, and what exceeds that, from the tribe of Judah, Jer. 52, 28.

Grotius confuses different deportations; for that which is commemorated in Jerem. 52:28 took place in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, while Jehoiakim was still surviving; but this one, concerning which we read in this place, verses 14 and 16, occurred in the time of Jeconiah, when the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar was nearly complete. See Jac. Ussher’s Chronolog. sacr. page 36, and our own Chronic. sacr. There, 3023 Jews are said to have been led away; here, the number of Jerusalemites, including all the commanders and all the men of valor, amounts in total to 10,000, besides the smiths and carpenters; indeed, 7000 of the best men and 1000 smiths and carpenters (from the remaining cities) are added, so that the number of those led away increased to over eighteen thousand. Among these captives was also Ezekiel, who for this reason derives his epoch from this deportation, Ezek. 1:2–3, which he therefore also calls his own deportation, Ezek. 40:1.

AND EVERY CRAFTSMAN AND CLOSER) Thus also Jer. 24, 1. The Greeks [say] πάντα τέκτονα καὶ συγκλείοντα. חרש. Deut. 27, 15. is a sculptor, as also Is. 40, 18. Jer. 10, 3. Hos. 8, 6. 13, 2.
