# 1 Chronicles

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the name of Jesus. To the Books of Chronicles. To the former. Grotius's Preface.

It has always been a constant tradition among the Hebrews that these two books were written by Ezra: who call these books the words of the days: that is, as we have said elsewhere, excerpts from the daily records of the Kings. Now, the purpose of Ezra was to narrate the affairs of David and his descendants up to a certain shadow of the kingdom restored in Zerubbabel, who himself was also of the descendants of David: but in order that it might be better understood, he judged that certain things must be said beforehand, namely, a review to be made of the authors of the human race, then of the ancestors of David and those descending from him, then of all the tribes: with these things laid as a foundation, so that he might arrive at the kingdom of David, he commemorates the final events of Saul, just as Tacitus does for Augustus, when about to narrate the affairs of Tiberius. And because the affairs of those who reigned in the ten tribes, through wars, treaties, and affinities, cohere with the affairs of the Kings born from David, those also ought not to have been omitted. But since it is the custom of daily records to narrate many things more λεπτομερέστερον (in greater detail) than the method of Annals allows, it has come about that we owe not a few things to these books which are not found in the Annals, which the Hebrews call the books of Samuel and Kings, for reasons produced by us elsewhere: and that very fact was the reason why the Greeks called these books by the name Paralipomenon, namely, from the most necessary part, since otherwise many things here are the same as those in the Annals, with the change of words being sometimes none, sometimes slight. The same Ezra attached to these books the history of his own affairs, that is, of the restored city of Jerusalem, which he wrote himself, and another history of the restored temple and sacrifices, which Nehemiah wrote, while Ezra was still living: He added besides the history of Esther, which had happened in the middle time of those things which are narrated in those two latter books, written, as the Hebrews hand down, and the book itself seems to testify, by Mordecai, a most illustrious man. And here end the histories which are in the Hebrew Canon, naturally because those which reach up to this point were either written by Prophets, or approved by Prophets, as those latter books were by Zechariah, Malachi, and Haggai, who were contemporaries of Ezra and helpers in his counsel. After that time, however, prophecy ceased among the Hebrews until the times of Christ.

Latin:

I. N. J. AD LIBROS PARALIPOMENON. AD PRIOREM. GROTII PRÆFATIO.

AB Esdra scriptos hos duos libros, constans semper fuit apud Hebræos fama: qui hos libros vocant verba dierum: id est, ut alibi diximus, excerpta ex Regum diurnis. Propositum autem Esdræ fuit res narrare Davidis, posterumque ejus usque ad umbram quandam regni restitutam in Zorobabele, qui & ipse ex Davidis fuit posteris: sed ut melius intelligeretur, quædam anteloquenda sibi censuit, nempe recensionem faciendam auctorum humani generis, deinde majorum Davidis, & ex ipso descendentium, deinde tribuum omnium: quibus præstructis, ut ad Davidis regnum perveniat, Saulis extrema commemorat, plane ut Augusti Tacitus, res Tiberii narraturus. Et quia res eorum, qui in decem tribus regnarunt, per bella, fœdera, affinitates cum rebus Regum ex Davide genitorum cohærent, eæ quoque omitti non debuerunt. Cum vero diurnorum mos sit multa λεπτομερέστερον narrare, quam ferat Annalium ratio, eo factum est, ut his non pauca debeamus, quæ in Annalibus, quos Hebræi Samuelis & Regum libros, ob causas alibi à nobis proditas, vocant, non in- veniuntur: eaque ipsa causa fuit, cur hos libros Græci appellaverint Paralipomenon nomihe, ex parte scilicet maxime necessaria, cum alioqui multa hic sint eadem, quæ in Annalibus, verborum mutatione modo nulla, modo exigua. Idem Esdras his libris attexuit suarum ipse rerum, id est, Hierosolymorum urbis instauratæ historiam, quam scripsit ipse, & alteram historiam repositi templi ac Sacrificiorum, quam scripsit Nehemias, Esdra etiam tunc vivente: Addidit præterea historiam Estheris, quæ medio tempore eorum, quæ duobus illis libris postremis narrantur, contigerat, scriptam, ut Hebræi tradunt, & ipse liber testari videtur, à Mardochæo viro perillustri. Et hic desinunt historiæ, quæ in Canone sunt Hebræo, nimirum quia quæ hucusque pertingunt eæ aut scriptæ sunt à Prophetis, aut probatæ à Prophetis, ut postremi illi libri à Zacharia, Malachia, Aggæo, qui Esdræ σύγχρονοι & consilio adjutores fuere. Post id autem tempus desiit apud Hebræos prophetia usque ad Christi tempora.

## 1:1 Introduction: Critical Appraisal of Grotius's Preface
CRITICAL APPRAISAL OF GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

That Grotius thought very meanly of the books of Chronicles is not obscure. He renders the Hebrew name VERBA DIERUM as EXCERPTS FROM THE DAILY RECORDS OF THE KINGS. Just as if it were necessary for the author to consult the daily records of the Kings in order to extract these things, and he wrote or patched these together by a human Spirit, as Ludovicus Capellus, a colleague of Grotius, does not fear to speak: which, if Grotius believed it entirely, as it appears, it will be all over with the Canonical authority of these books. For the Holy Spirit does not extract His own material from human writings in order to patch together books. And from where will Grotius provide proof for his assertion that these were extracted by Ezra from the daily records of the Kings? The name does not teach that. For דברי הימים are called the deeds of the times, as it is known that the word דבר יומי is used everywhere for time. Whence the books of Chronicles are most correctly rendered: which name the Blessed Luther also retained. Furthermore, regarding the scope of the book, while he says the Author's purpose is to note the affairs of David, and those of his descendants up to a certain shadow of the kingdom restored in Zerubbabel, who was himself also among the descendants of David, he has not attained the primary end, which is to exhibit the family of our Savior, whom all the θεόπνευσοι (God-breathed) writers of Holy Scripture primarily regarded as the σκοπον σκοπιμώτατον (most important goal). Which the Holy Spirit also did not neglect in the Chronological and Genealogical accounts, so that it might be the more openly established concerning the family and blood-relatives of the Messiah. Nor is there any doubt that these books of Chronicles were composed for the sake of sacred Chronology, which is much aided by them. Therefore, the author did not believe that those things were to be prefaced to the books only because of the history of David, which pertain to the review of the authors of the human race, and the ancestors of David, and those descending from him, as well as all the tribes, but especially because of the tribe, and lineage, and family of the Messiah, and because that would contribute to the fullness of the sacred Chronicles. Nor did he deal with the ten tribes only because of a certain coherence of affairs concerning the Kings, but because it had been decided to describe both, namely the Kings of Judah and the Kings of Israel, and their deeds, especially regarding τὰ παραλειπόμενα (the things left out), whence the book obtains its name among the Greeks, as also among the Latins, that is, the things omitted or remaining in the books of Kings. Therefore, he explains somewhat those things which were either omitted or not fully described there, or commemorates them further regarding certain περίστασεις (circumstances), and adds them to the others summarized. Therefore, that it pleased Grotius to call the books of Samuel and Kings Annals with the Hebrews, so that the books of Paralipomenon might be like daily records, although that distinction is not entirely convenient, we could easily pass over dry-shod, provided he did not hold these books to be excerpts from the daily records of the Kings, which were written only by human authority. For even if he adds later that they were approved by the later Prophets, that nevertheless in no way suffices for the Canonical authority of any book, since a Canonical book must also be divine and θεόπνευστος (God-breathed) by reason of its origin, dictated by the Holy Spirit and by a sacred amanuensis, such as the Prophets were in the Old Testament, and because of that divine origin be held worthy of approval and believed to be received into the Canon. For no books were admitted into the Canon of the Hebrews in the Old Testament unless they were written by Prophets, with the Holy Spirit suggesting them. Therefore, by Christ and the Apostles, all the books of the Old Testament are designated by the name of the Prophets, or are distributed into the writings of Moses, who was a great Prophet, or legal writings, and into the Prophetic writings of the remaining Prophets. There is, therefore, no reason why, with Grotius, some should be considered written by Prophets and others only approved by Prophets. For the rest, it can be conceded that Ezra was the author of these books, but Φερόμενον ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε (borne along by the Holy Spirit) 2 Pet. 1:21, because the review of the Genealogy extends beyond the return from the Babylonian captivity 1 Par. 13, and there is mention of the same as having been long since completed, etc. 10:45, the conclusion was made for almost the same reason concerning the return to the holy land as those are reviewed under the beginning of the book of Ezra. And thus R. Moses Kimchi, Solomon, Lyranus, Sixtus Senensis, Driedo, Cornelius à Lapide, and others attribute these books to Ezra, even if some ascribe them to Jeremiah. They are called by some an Epitome of the Kings of Judah, even though they also insert some things about the Kings of Israel. Jerome, in his Epistle to Paulinus, calls them an Epitome of the Old Testament, and says that this (twin) book of Chronicles is such and so great that if anyone wishes to arrogate to himself the knowledge of the Scriptures without it, he mocks himself. For through individual names and the connections of words, both the histories omitted in the books of Kings are touched upon, and innumerable questions of the Gospel are explained. The primary scope is to place before the eyes the Genealogy of Christ and the History of his ancestors, as well as the state of his Church. These are the more important interpreters of the Chronicles: Sarcerius, Victor, Strigelius, Peter Martyr, Lavatherus, Sanctius, Serarius, and Fevardentius.

The first book is completed in two parts. In the first, the patriarchs from the beginning of the world and the families of the XII Tribes of Israel are presented in IX Chapters, namely the children of the Patriarchs, as also of Esau ch. I, of Judah ch. II, and particularly of David and the rest from Judah ch. III, of Simeon ch. IV, of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh ch. V, of Levi ch. VI, of the remaining tribes ch. VII, reserved however ch. VIII, of the tribe of Benjamin because of Saul, as also of the inhabitants of Jerusalem of various tribes ch. IX. In the other, after some things are premised concerning Saul, the History of David is described in the remaining XX chapters, namely I. The anointing of David ch. XI and XII. II. Ecclesiastical care, where then the assemblies concerning the bringing of the ark ch. XIII, and after the Philistines were humbled ch. XIV, its bringing into the place of the solemn tabernacle ch. XV, with sacrifices and Eucharistic hymns ch. XVI, then the counsel concerning the building of the temple ch. XVII. III. Victories against the Philistines, Moabites, Syrians, Edomites ch. XIIX. The Ammonites, violators of the ambassadors, ch. XIX. whose crown was taken, ch. XX. IV. The arrangement of those things which pertained to the house of the Lord (1.) by which the place, the occasion of which was the sin of the numbering of the people, and its expiation and sacrifices on the threshing floor of Araunah, ch. XXI. (2.) by which Solomon as ἐργοδιώκτην [taskmaster], and the treasure collected for him for that reason, ch. XXII. (3.) by which the ministry of the Levites, ch. XXIII. (4.) the priestly orders, ch. XXIV. (5.) the classes of musicians, ch. XXV. (6.) the gatekeepers and inspectors, ch. XXVI. V. The military order, ch. XXVII. VI. The assembly on account of the contribution for the structure of the temple, ch. XXIX. with the contribution that followed, David leading the way with his own example, ch. XXIX.

The first book presents a chronology of 2990 years, in which year of the world David put off mortality.

Latin:

EPICRISIS AD GROTIANAM PRÆFATIONEM.

DE libris Chronicorum valde abjecte sensisse Grotium, haud obscurum est. Ebræum no- men VERBA DIERUM, reddit, EXCER- PTA EX DIURNIS REGUM. Non secus, ac si autor diurna Regum consulere necessum habue- rit, ut hæc excerperet, & humano Spiritu hæc conscripserit, vel consarcinarit, ut Ludovicus Capel- lus Grotii Socius loqui non veretur: quod si omni- no, ut apparet, credidit Grotius, actum erit de Ca- nonica librorum horum auctoritate. Spir. S. enim non excerpit è scriptis humanis sua, ut libros con- sarcinet. Et unde fidem faciet assertioni suæ Gro- tius, hæc ab Esra excerpta fuisse de Regum diurnis? Nomen id non docet. Nam דברי הימים dicun- tur res gestæ temporum, uti notum est vocem דבר יומי de tempore passim usurpari. Unde rectissime libri Chronicorum redduntur: quod nomen etiam B. Lutherus retinuit. Porro quod ad scopum libri attinet, dum pro- positum Autoris dicit, res Davidis notare, posterum- que ejus usq; ad umbram quandam regni restitutam in Zorobabele, qui & ipse ex Davidis fuit posteris, præcipuum finem assequutus non est, qui est fa- miliam Salvatoris nostri exhibere, quem tanquam σκοπον σκοπιμώτατον S. Scripturæ omnes θεό- πνευσοι Scriptores primario respexere. Quem eti- am non neglexit Spiritus S. in Chronologicis & Ge- nealogicis, quo tanto apertius de familia & consan- guineis Messiæ constaret. Neque dubium est Chro- nologiæ sacræ causa hos Chronicorum libros con- textos esse, quæ multum iisdem juvatur. Non er- go tantum ob Davidis historiam anteloquenda libris illa credidit autor, quæ ad recensionem auctorum gene- ris humani, & majorum Davidis, & ex ipso descen- dentium, ut & tribuum omnium spectant, sed cum- primis ob tribum, & stirpem & familiam Messiæ, & quod ad plenitudinem Chronicorum sacrorum illa faceret. Neque solum ob cohærentiam quandam rerum de Regibus decem tribuum egit, sed quia utrosque puta tum Reges Juda, tum Reges Israelis, & eorum res gestas, maxime quoad τὰ παραλειπό- μενα, unde liber apud Græcos, ut & Latinos nomen obtinet, hoc est, prætermissa, vel residua in libris Re- gum, describere constitutum fuerit. Idcirco ea, quæ aut omissa, aut non plene descripta ibi fuerunt, nonnihil explicat, vel quoad quosdam περίστασεις ulterius commemorat, ac cæteris summatim recen- sitis addit. Quod ergo cum Ebræis Samuelis & Regum libros Annales vocare libuit Grotio, ut diurnorum instar sint libri Paralipomenon, quamvis ea distinctio non omnino commoda sit, facile sicco pede præterire poteramus, modo non haberet hosce libros pro excerptis ex Regum diurnis, quæ humana autori- tate tantum conscripta erant. Nam utut deinde addat, eosdem à Prophetis postremis approbatos fuis- se, id tamen neutiquam sufficit ad auctoritatem Ca- nonicam libri alicujus, quum liber Canonicus Ori- ginis etiam ratione divinus ac θεόπνευστος esse de- beat, à Spiritu S. inspiratus, & amanuensi sacro, qua- les in Vet. Testam. erant Prophetæ, dictatus, & ob il- lam divinam originem approbatione dignus habe- atur, atque in Canonem receptus credatur. Nulli enim libri in Vet. Testam. in Canonem Ebræorum admissi sunt, nisi qui à Prophetis, Spiritu S. sugge- rente, conscripti sint. Idcirco à Christo & Aposto- lis omnes libri Vet. Testam. Prophetarum nomine designantur vel in scripta Mosis, qui magnus Pro- pheta fuit, seu legalia, & in scripta Prophetica, reli- quorum Prophetarum distribuuntur. Non ergo est, quod cum Grotio alii à Prophetis scripti, alii approbati solum à Prophetis censeantur. De cæ- tero autorem horum librorum Esdram fuisse con- cedi potest, sed Φερόμενον ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε 2.Pet. 1, 21. quia extenditur recensio Genealogiæ ul- tra reditum è captivitate Babylonica 1. Par. 13. ejus- demque ceu jam pridem exantlatæ mentio sit & c. 10, 45. conclusio eadem pene ratione facta est de reditu in terram sanctam, qua sub initium libri Es- dræ illæ recensetur. Atque ita Esdræ tribuunt hos libros R. Moses Kimchi, Salomo, Lyranus, Sixtus Se- nens. Dried. Cornel. à Lapide, & alii, etsi nonnulli eos Jeremiæ adscribant. Vocantur à quibusdam Epitome Regum Juda, utut etiam de Regibus Israel nonnulla inserant. Hieronymus Epistol. ad Paul. vocat eos Epitomen instrumenti veteris, librumque hunc (geminum) Chronicorum tantum ac talem es- se ait, ut absque illo si quis scripturarum scientiam sibi voluerit arrogare se ipsum irrideat. Per singula quip- pe nomina juncturasque verborum, & prætermissæ in Regum libris tanguntur Historiæ, & innumerabiles ex- plicantur Evangelii quæstiones. Scopus præcipuus est Christi Genealogiam & majorum ejus Historiam, nec non Ecclesiæ ejus statum ob oculos ponere. In- terpp. Chronicorum hi potiores sunt, Sarcerius, Vi- ctor. Strigelius, Petr. Martyr, Lavatherus, Sanctius, Serarius, & Fevardentius.

Liber primus duabus partibus absolvitur. In prima patriarchæ ab initio mundi, & familiæ XII. Tribuum Israelis sistuntur IX. Capp. utpote Patri- archarum liberi, ut & Esavi cap. I. Judæ c. II. & pe- culiariter Davidis & reliquorum è Juda c. III. Si- meonis c. IV. Ruben, Gad & Manassis c. V. Levi c. VI. reliquarum tribuum c. VII. reservata tamen c. VIII. Benjaminis tribu ob Saulem, ut & incolis Hierosolymæ diversarum tribuum c. IX. in altera præmissis nonnullis de Saule Historia Davidis reli- quis XX. capitibus describitur, Utpote I. Davidis unctio c. XI. & XII. II. Cura Ecclesiastica, ubi tum Comitia de arcæ adductione c. XIII. ejusque post humiliatos Philistæos c. XIV. adductio in locum ta- bernaculi solemnis c. XV. cum sacrificiis, & hymnis Eucharisticis c. XVI. tum consilium de templi ædi- ficatione c. XVII. III. Victoriæ adversus Phili- stæos, Moabitas, Syros, Edomæos c. XIIX. Am- monitas legatorum violatores c. XIX. quorum co- rona capta c. XX. IV. Ordinatio eorum, quæ ad domum Domini faciebant (1.) qua locum, cujus occasio peccatum numerationis populi, ejusque expiatio & sacrificia in area Aravnæ c. XXI. (2.) qua ἐργοδιώκτην Salomonem, & thesaurum ideo ipsi collectum, c. XXII. (3.) qua Levitarum mini- sterium c. XXIII. (4.) Sacerdotum ordines hie- raticos c. XXIV. (5.) Musicorum classes, c. XXV. (6.) Janitores & inspectores c. XXVI. V. Mili- tarem ordinem c. XXVII. VI. comitia ob con- tributionem ad templi structuram c. XXIX. cum contributione sequuta, exemplo suo præeunte Da- vide c. XXIX.

Chronologiam exhibet primus Liber annorum 2990. quo mundi anno David mortalitatem exuit.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

The descendants of Adam, as also of Abraham, and likewise of Isaac, the sons of Esau, are commemorated.

Ver. 1. ADAM, SETH &c.

The word 'begat' is to be inserted in this way: Adam begat Seth, Seth begat Enos &c. But ver. 4. Noah begat Shem, Ham, Japheth. In the rest the verb is added, or even a noun, as for instance v. 5. these are the sons of Japheth. v. 10. Cush begat Nimrod etc.

Same verse.

ADAM, SETH, ENOS) Genealogy is made in two ways, either by descending as here, or by ascending, as in Luke.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Adami posteri, ut & Abrahami, nec non Isaci, filii Esavi, commemorantur.

Vers. 1. ADAM, SETH &c.

Inferenda est vox genuit hoc modo: Adam ge- nuit Seth, Seth genuit Enos &c. Sed vers. 4. Noah genuit Sem, Ham, Japhet. In reliquis verbum addi- tur, vel etiam nomen, utpote v. 5. filii Japheth hi sunt. v. 10. Chus genuit Nimrod &c.

Vers. eod.

ADAM, SETH, ENOS) Duobus modis fit Genealogia, aut descendendo ut hic, aut ascendendo, ut apud Lucam.

## 1:7
Verse 7.

DODANIM] The LXX, both here and in Genesis, read רוֹדָנִים. For they translate it Ῥόδιοι quite probably. But the Latin, both here and in Genesis, has דּוֹדָנִים. Just as the Jerusalem Interpreter also reads. We have said elsewhere that these letters are accustomed to be interchanged not only in writing, but also in pronouncing. To me, the Greek reading here, which is the same in the Hebrew in this place, is more approved.

He rightly prefers the Hebrew text, as being authentic. If the Latin and the Jerusalem Interpreter read otherwise, it must be believed that they read it wrongly. Yet a variation of the Hebrew Codex is not to be invented for that reason, since the interpreters could have erred in the permutation of similar letters. Although we do not deny the particular error of one or another of the codices. Since scribes could err in writing just as interpreters could in reading. But how Grotius wishes to prove that those letters ד and ר, of a different kind and organ, were accustomed to be interchanged both in writing and in pronouncing, does not appear. Nor have I observed that in him thus far.

Otherwise, he himself is wont to rush too rashly into the temerity of his Cappel; who, when he was endeavoring to invent various readings without the testimony of Hebrew codices, patched together many things from the different pronunciation and writing of proper names, which if you call them specimens of an idle, vain, or even profane wit, you will not stray far from the truth. Thus, when in this chapter, to note one or two by way of example, v. 22. עֵיבָל is named, who in Gen. 10, 28 is called עוֹבָל, when v. 34 is called צְפִי who in Gen. 36, 2 is called צְפוֹ, when v. 38 שׁוּפִי who in Gen. 36, 23 שׁוֹפִי, when v. 39 עוֹמָם who in Gen. 36, 22 הֵימָם, when v. 49 פָּעִי who in Gen. 36, 39 is called פָּעוּ, that critic, without judgment, immediately judges one or the other place to be corrupt: As if the same proper name could not be expressed and pronounced in different ways, or even changed somewhat in the progress of time by reason of the pronunciation of vowels, where the Hebrews used the commerce of the Chaldeans, so that Moses followed that manner of uttering which was in use in his times, and Ezra that which was in use in his own age. Truly this is to seek a knot in a bulrush, so that by any means the sincerity, and therefore the very authority of the original text, may be disturbed. But because Grotius saw that these things were too inept for such a matter, he did not wish to follow his Cappel in them.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

DODANIM] LXX. & hic & in Genesi legerunt רוֹדָנִים. Vertunt enim Ῥόδιοι satis probabiliter. At Latinus & hic & in Genesi דּוֹדָנִים. Quomodo & Hierosolymitanus Inter- pres legit. Diximus alibi has literas non in scribendo tan- tum, sed & in pronuntiando permutari solere. Mihi hic Græ- ca lectio, quæ eadem in Hebræo hoc loco, magis probatur.

Merito præfert Ebræum textum, utpote authen- ticum. Si Latinus & Hierosolymitanus Interpres aliter legerunt, male eos legisse credendum est. Neque tamen fingenda ideo variatio Ebræi Codi- cis, quum errare in permutatione literarum affini- um Interpp. potuerint. Quanquam particularem Codicum unius vel alterius exerrationem etiam non negemus. Quum æque scribendo librarii, ut legendo Interpp. potuerint errare. Quomodo vero probare velit Grotius literas istas ד & ר diver- si generis & organi, tum in scribendo, tum in pro- nunciando, permutari consuevisse, non apparet. Neque id hactenus penes ipsum observavi.

Nimis alias προπετῶς ipse in Capelli sui temeri- tatem ruere solet; qui cum moliretur varias lectio- nes adinvenire, sine Codicum Ebræorum testimo- nio, multà è nominum propriorum diversa pro- nunciatione ac scriptione consarcinavit, quæ si oti- osi, vani, imo prophani ingenii specimina dixeris, à vero haud aberrabis. Ita cum in hoc capite, ut exempli causa unum atque alterum notemus, v. 22. עֵיבָל nominatur, qui Genes. 10, 28. dictus est עוֹבָל, cum v. 34. vocatur צְפִי qui Gen. 36, 2. צְפוֹ dictus est, cum v. 38. שׁוּפִי qui Gen. 36, 23. שׁוֹפִי cum v. 39. עוֹמָם qui Genes. 36, 22. הֵימָם, cum v. 49. פָּעִי qui Genes. 36, 39. פָּעוּ appellatur, Criticus ille, sine κρίσει, actu- tum locum alterutrum corruptum judicat: Quasi non potuerit idem nomen proprium diverfimode exprimi & pronunciari, vel etiam progressu tem- poris nonnihil, ratione vocalium proferendo imu- tari, ubi Ebræi Chaldæorum commercio usi sunt, ut Moses sequutus sit eam efferendi rationem, quæ suis temporibus Esdras eam, quæ sua itidem ætate fuerit usitata. Vere hoc est nodum in scyrpo quære- re, ut quacunque ratione solicitetur sinceritas, ad- eoque etiam ipsa autoritas textus originarii. Quia vero hæc ad rem tantam nimis inepta esse vidit Grotius, in iis Capellum suum sequi noluit.

## 1:52
Vers. 52.

AND THE SONS OF SOBAL THE FATHER OF KIRIATH-JEARIM WERE: HE WHO SAW HALF OF THE RESTING-PLACES.

B. Luther: And Sobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, had sons, he who saw half of the Manuhoth; with a marginal gloss added: The prophets are called seers or beholders in the Scripture, and to see means to teach or preach. Thus, this Sobal was a prophet or preacher in half of Manuhoth, which is the name of a small land that is perhaps situated quietly and well, which is why it is called Manuhoth, that is, rest. Junius and Piscator make Haroeh a proper name of the son of Sobal, who in chapter 4:2 is called Reaiah, and they understand the word 'father' to be implied, i.e., Haroeh (father of the inhabitants), father or half of Menuhoth, a city named in chapter 8:6. The Spanish and French versions interpose the conjunction AND, and couple two words into one, as if the proper name of the sons were Father Haroeh and Chezi Hammenuoth. But in the Hebrew there is no conjunction, nor are those words joined into one, and it is certain that Manuhoth is the proper name of a place from chapter 8:6, and therefore it must undoubtedly be rendered as HALF OF MANNOTH, so that the Vulgate must be entirely amended here. But it is rightly doubted whether that הָרֹאֶה is a proper name. That He seems rather to be demonstrative. Whence Santes Pagninus and Arias Montanus, with the Vulgate, render it HE WHO SAW. Nor do we have cause to depart from the opinion of B. Luther, which is sufficiently probable. We allow everyone, however, to abound in their own sense here. There are some things in such onomastic and genealogical lists that one can scarcely define with certainty. Jerome, however, favors the Vulgate here in his Hebrew Traditions, explaining it thus: Sobal the father of Kiriath-jearim saw half of the resting-places because of the proximity of the sepulcher of the Patriarchs. By resting-place, the sepulcher is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 52.

FUERUNT AUTEM FILII SOBAL PA- TRIS KIRIATHIARIM, QUI VIDEBAT DI- MIDIUM REQUIETIONUM.

B. Lutherus: Und Sobal, der Vater Kiriathjea- rim hatte Söhne, der sahe die helffte Manuhoth; ad- dita glossa marginali: Die Propheten heissen Seher oder Schauer in der Schrifft, und sehen heisset Leh- ren oder Predigen. Also ist der Sobal ein Prophet oder Prediger gewesen in dem halben Manuhoth, das ist ein Nahme eines Ländleins, das vielleicht still und wohl gelegen ist, darum es Manuhoth, das ist, Ruhe heisset. Junius & Piscator Haroëh nomen pro- prium filii Sobal faciunt, qui cap. 4, 2. dicatur Rea- jah, & subintelligunt vocem patris h. m. Haroeh (pater incolarum) patris vel dimidii Menuhoth, ci- vitatis cap. 8, 6. nominatæ. Hispanica & Gallica ver- sio interponunt copulam ET, ac duas voces in u- nam copulant, quasi nomen proprium filiorum sit pater Haroeh & Chezi Hammenuoth. Sed in Ebræo nulla est copula: neque conjunguntur voces illæ in unam, ac certum est, Manuhoth nomen proprium loci esse è cap. 8, 6. ideoque sine dubio reddi de- bet per MEDIUM MANNOTH, ut emendanda hic omnino sit vulgata. Sed de illo הָרֹאֶה jure dubitatur an sit nomen proprium. Illud He potius demonstrativum videtur. Unde Santes Pagninus, & Ariamontanus cum vulgata reddunt QUI VIDE- BAT. Nec habemus causam a B. Lutheri senten- tia discedendi, quæ satis probabilis. Permittimus tamen hic quemvis suo abundare sensu. Sunt in ta- libus onomasticis & genealogicis nonnulla, quæ vix certo definias. Vulgatæ tamen favet hic Hie- ronymus in tradit. Hebraic. ita explicans: Sobal pa- ter Kiriathjarim videbat dimidium requietionum pro- pter viciniam sepulcri Patriarcharum. Requietio se- pulcrum intelligitur.

## 2:7
Verse 32. AND TIMNAH AND AMALEK.

For the sake of Cappel we add this, because this scruple occurs. For the sons of Eliphaz are listed, and among them Timnah, who was the concubine of Eliphaz, from whom he begat Amalek, Gen. 36, 12, whence the critic concludes that this place is defective. But because all copies agree here, who would believe that all were corrupted by the error of one scribe, and what would that blindness of all the interpreters have been, that no one observed that error? Therefore some Hebrews, R. Moses Gerundensis and Chaskuni, think that Eliphaz also had a son named Timnah, who is commemorated here; others say that Timnah was both the daughter and the concubine of Eliphaz: Tremellius and Junius place an ellipsis in the Hebrew words, or an abbreviation, of which R. Kimchi also warned here, and thus they explain those words וְתִמְנַע וַעֲמָלֵק, and Timnah (the son) namely Amalek. It can also be explained in the same sense, with an ellipsis of the preposition מִן, and from Timnah. To which the interpretation of Osiander and the Vinarienses returns. But no one has yet accused the Hebrew Codex of corruption.

From the sons of Jacob, the descendants of Judah are listed, up to Jesse the father of David, and especially those who came forth from Hebron.

SONS OF CHARMI ACHAR.

He is called throughout the whole book of Joshua עָכָן, but here, as R. Kimchi and R. Solomon note, he is called עָכָר for the sake of reproach because he troubled Israel, which description of him is also added below, עֹכֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל, whether because he was commonly called so thereafter from this crime of his, or because it pleased the Holy Spirit to call him so from the same. There is no reason, therefore, for Capellus to invent that that name in the book of Joshua is corrupted, in which he is constantly called Achan, so that no suspicion of corruption can underlie it. One may refer this example to the Rule which Jerome hands down in his Hebrew Traditions on Paralipomenon, Vol. III of his works, p. 254, and illustrates with certain examples: Certain names are indeed changed for their own reasons; in Genesis is written Jemuel: Jemuel, day of God. In Paralipomenon Namuel: Namuel speaking with God. Another, however, is called Ohad in Genesis, in Paralipomenon Jarib. Ohad is interpreted as praise, Jarib as litigating, because from his progeny came Zambri, who, sinning with a Midianite harlot, was slain by Phinehas. Jachin in Genesis, which is interpreted as preparation, in Paralipomenon Zara, which is interpreted as rising. But Saul, whom he commemorates by the same name in both books, here is silent about the son of the Canaanite woman, and by the proximity of the brothers of the name, adorns him from Zara, who is interpreted as rising. Jerome had said before about Achan: Achan son of Charmi in Joshua Achan, that is, a lurking serpent, in Paralipomenon Achar, that is, a troubler.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ET TIMNAH ET AMALECK.

In gratiam Capelli hoc addimus, quod scrupu- lus hic occurrat. Recensentur enim filii Eliphas, & inter eos Timnah, quæ Eliphasi pellex fuit, ex qua suscepit Amaleck Genes. 36, 12. unde locum hunc mancum esse concludit Criticus. Sed quia omnia exemplaria hic consentiunt, quis credat, unius scri- bæ errore corrupta fuisse omnia, & quænam illa fu- isset Interpp. omnium cæcitas, ut nemo errorem illum observarit? Ideo Ebræi nonnulli, R. Moses Gerundens. & Chaskuni putant Eliphaso etiam filjum fuisse Thimna dictum, qui hic commemoretur; alii Thimna & filiam & concubinam Eliphasi fuisse di- cunt: Tremellius & Junius in verbis Ebræis ellipsin ponunt, vel abbreviationem, de qua etiam R. Kim- chi hic monuit, & ita illa וְתִמְנַע וַעֲמָלֵק expo- nunt, & Thimna (filium) nempe Amalek. Potest etiam sic exponi eodem sensu, cum ellipsi præposi- tionis מִן & ex Thimna. Quo redit Osiandri & Vi- nariensium interpretatio. Nemo vero accusavit ha- ctenus Ebræum Codicem corruptionis.

E filiis Jacobi Judæ posteri recensentur, usq; ad Isai Patris Davidis, & imprimis qui ex He- bron prodiere.

FILII CHARMI ACHAR.

Vocatur is per totum librum Josuæ עָכָן, sed hic notante R. Kimchio & R. Salomone probri cau- sa vocatur עָכָר quia turbavit Israelem, quæ ejus de- scriptio etiam subjungitur, עֹכֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל, sive quod ita deinceps vulgo ab hoc crimine suo voca- tus fuerit, sive quod ita ab eodem appellare placue- rit Spiritui S. Non ergo est, quod comminiscatur Capellus nomen illud in libro Josuæ corruptum esse, in quo constanter appellatur Achan, ut nulla corru- ptionis suspicio subesse queat. Referre hoc exem- plum licet ad Regulam, quam tradit Hieronymus in tradit. Ebraic. ad Paral. Tom. III. oper. p. 254. & exemplis quibusdam illustrat: Mutantur vero nomi- na quædam suis rationibus, in Genesi scribitur Jemuel: Jemuel, mare Dei. In Paralipomenon Namuel: Na- muel loquens cum Deo. Alius vero in Genesi vocatur Ohad, in Paralipomenon Jarib. Ohad interpretatur laudatio, Jarib litigans, quia de ejus progenie exivit Zambri, qui cum scorto Madianitide peccans, à Phi- nees peremtus est. Jachin in Genesi, quod interpre- tatur preparatio, in Paralipomenon Zara, quod in- terpretatur ortus. Saul vero, quem eodem nomine in utroq; libro commemorat, hic filium Cananitidis ta- cet, & vicinitate fratrum nominis, ex Zara, qui inter- pretatur ortus, decorat. De Achan dixerat ante Hieronymus: Achan filius Charmi in Josuæ Achan, id est, coluber insidians, in Paralipomenon Achar, id est, turbator.

## 2:15
Ver. 15. THE SEVENTH DAVID] There had been eight sons of Jesse, but one of them was dead before David came to the Kingdom 1 Sam. 16, 10.

JETHER THE ISHMAELITE] It seems that the Scripture at 2 Sam. 17, 25 ought to be corrected from this.

We have observed that this correction of Scripture to that passage is vain and rash. There is no reason for us to do what has already been done.

Latin:

Vers. 15. SEPTIMUM DAVID] Octo fuerant filii Isai, sed eorum unus erat mortuus, priusquam David ad Regnum perveniret 1. Sam. 16, 10.

JETHER ISMAHELITES] Videtur hinc corrigi debere Scriptura 2. Sam. 17, 25.

Vanam & temerariam hanc esse Scripturæ cor- rectionem ad locum istum observavimus. Non est, quod actum agamus.

## 2:18
Ver. 18. BUT CALEB THE SON OF HEZRON TOOK A WIFE NAMED AZUBAH OF WHOM HE BEGAT JERIOTH: AND HER SONS WERE JASER, AND SOBAB AND ARDON.

The Latin version is to be corrected here. For Jerioth is not said to have been begotten by Azubah, much less can she be considered a son of Azubah, as it seemed to Jerome in his Hebrew Traditions. The text holds thus: And Caleb the son of Hezron begat אֶת־עֲזוּבָה אִשָּׁה וְאֶת־יְרִיעוֹת, where the particle אֵת cannot be a sign of the accusative case, because Azubah was the wife of Caleb; therefore he did not beget her, but he begat with her (children, which noun is to be understood here) AND WITH JERIOTH he likewise begat children. Who therefore was not his daughter, but his concubine: whose sons are listed here: And her sons were Jaser &c. just as the sons of Azubah, or those whom Caleb begat with Azubah, are enumerated in v. 42. And the sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel, Mesha his firstborn &c. And v. 46. The concubines of Caleb the son are listed. And v. 48. His concubines Maachah. And v. 50. the sons and grandsons whom he begat with Ephrath after the death of Azubah taken as wife, where our Luther rightly rendered: These were the children of Caleb, Hur the first son of Ephrath, Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim. Junius preferred to render it thus: These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur the firstborn of Ephrath: Shobal the father of the Kiriath-jearimites: with whom the Spanish, English, French, Italian, Zurich, Piscator, and Sixtine versions agree. Amama, and Junius thinks that in this 50th verse the sons of the second Caleb are enumerated. But that there was another Caleb, and whence he was, is not reported; indeed, it is certain from verse 19 that Hur was the firstborn son of Caleb from Ephrath. Since, therefore, he wishes to recount other sons and grandsons from Ephrath alongside this firstborn (as they had not yet been brought forward), he presents them here. The Holy Scriptures do not affirm that Hur, the son of Caleb, begat another Caleb, but makes him the son of Hur, namely Uri, v. 20. Andreas Masius in Josh. 14:6 has it thus: Let us see how Caleb can be called the son of Jephunneh, when in Chronicles he is mentioned as born to Hezron. It is certain that Hezron was among those who had descended into Egypt with Jacob, about two hundred and sixteen years before Caleb, at the age of forty, was sent by Moses to spy out Canaan. And it is also attested in the Holy Scriptures that Caleb ought to be reckoned among those sons of Hezron whom he begat from his former wife, and not from the daughter of Machir, whom he finally took as a wife when he was sixty. It is clearly concluded from these things, therefore, that Caleb is indeed called the son of Hezron, but is certainly a grandson by his former wife. For otherwise he would have been more than three times forty years old when he was sent as a spy from Kadesh-barnea. Nor is it unusual for grandsons to be numbered among sons, especially if they are famous for the glory of their deeds. He is therefore rightly called the son of Jephunneh, since he had Hezron not as a father, but as a grandfather, or perhaps a great-grandfather, or a great-great-grandfather. Wherefore the invention of those who imagine that Hezron also had the name Jephunneh is foolish and proceeds from an ignorance of history. Even more inept are the Hebrew Doctors, who, when they treat of offerings in sacrifice not being interchangeable, say: that Caleb was called the son of Jephunneh, not because he was born of any parent who had that name, but because he himself was circumspect when he refused to join the society of the wicked conspiracy of the spies. For the meaning of the word צפה is well known. But that which they babble in the Sanhedrin, chapter eight, is not only inept but more than childish: that there were men who begat children at the age of eight. Cf. Buxtorff, Histor. arc. foeder. c. 2, p. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 18. CALEB VERO FILIUS HESRON ACCE- PIT UXOREM NOMINE AZUBA DE QUA GENUIT JERIOTH: FUERUNTQUE FILII EJUS JASER, ET SOBAB ET ARDON.

Corrigenda hic Latina versio. Nam Jerioth non dicitur genita ab Azuba, multo minus pro filio Azu- bæ haberi potest, uti visum Hieronymo in tradit. Ebraic. Ita habet textus: Et Chaleb filius Chefron genuit אֶת־עֲזוּבָה אִשָּׁה וְאֶת־יְרִיעוֹת, ubi par- ticula אֵת nequit esse nota accusativi casus, quia A- zuba fuit uxor Chalebi; non ergo eam genuit, sed genuit cum ea (liberos, quod nomen hic subintelli- gendum) ET CUM JERIOTH pariter liberos ge- nuit. Quæ proinde non filia ejus, sed concubina fuit: cujus filii hic recensentur: Et fuerunt filii ejus Jaser &c. quemadmodum filii Azubæ, vel quos cum Azu- ba genuit Chaleb, enumerantur v. 42. Et filii Chaleb fratris Jerachmeel, Mefa primogenitus ejus &c. Et v. 46. Hephæ concubinæ Chaleb filii recensentur. Et v. 48. Concubinæ ejus Maachab. Et v. 50. filii ac nepo- tes quos genuit cum Ephrata post fata Azabæ in u- xorem ducta, ubi Lutherus noster recte reddidit: Diß waren die Kinder Caleb, Hur der erste Sohn von Ephrata, Sobal der Vater Kiriathiarim. Ju- nius ita maluit reddere: Isti fuerunt filii Calebi filii Churis primogeniti Ephratæ: Schobal pater Kiriath- jeharaimorum: cum quo faciunt Hispan. Angl. Gallic. Ital. Tigur. Piscat. & Sixtin. Amama, pu- tatque Junius hoc 50. vers. recitari filios Calebi secun- di. Sed Calebum alterum fuisse, & unde ille fuerit, non refertur, imo Calebi filium Hur ex Ephrata pri- mogenitum fuisse certum est è vers. 19. Quum ergo alios etiam filios & nepotes ex Ephrata juxta cum hoc primogenito recensere velit (utpote hactenus nondum adductos) hic eosdem sistit. Hur Calebi filium alium Calebum genuisse non affirmat S. S. sed filium Huri facit τὸν Uri, v. 20. Andreas Masius in Jos. 14, 6. ita habet: Videamus, quì possit Calebus Jephone filius dici, cum in Paralipomenis Hesrone na- tus memoretur. Certum est, Hesronem inter eos fu- isse, qui cum Jacobo in Ægyptum descenderant, an- nis circiter ducentis & sedecim ante, quam Caleb quadragenarius mitteretur à Mose speculatum Cha- nanæam. Estq; etiam illud testatum sacris literis, Ca- lebum inter eos Hesronis filios recenseri debere, quos ille ex priori conjuge procreavit: non autem ex Ma- chiris filia; quam demum sexagenarius duxit uxorem. Plane ergo ex his confectum est, Calebum Hesronis quidem filium dici, at certe nepotem ex priore uxore esse. Alioqui enim plus quam ter quadraginta an- norum fuisset, cum è Cadesbarnea mitteretur specu- lator. Neque vero insolens est, ut nepotes inter filios adnumerentur; præsertim si sunt rerum gestarum gloria clari. Recte ergo Filius Jephona dicitur, cum Hesronem, non patrem, sed avum, aut fortasse pro- avum, vel abavum habuerit. Quare insulsum est eorum commentum & ab historiæ ignoratione profe- ctum, qui fingunt Hesroni etiam Jephona fuisse no- men. Ineptius etiam Doctores Ebræi, qui ubi tra- ctant de hostiis in sacrificio non permutandis, dicunt: Calebum Jephonæ filium esse appellatum, non quia parente aliquo, cui id nominis fuerit, natus esset, sed quia fuit ipse circumspectus, cum ad sceleratæ specu- latorum conspirationis societatem se nollet adjungere. Nota est enim verbi צפה significatio. Sed illud eo- rundem non ineptum modo, verum plus quam puerile est, quod ἐν τῷ συνεδρίῳ capite octavo effutiunt; fuisse homines qui anno ætatis octavo liberos procrearint. Conf. Buxtorff. Histor. arc. fœder. c. 2. p. 26.

Vers. 22.

AND HE POSSESSED TWENTY-THREE CITIES IN THE LAND OF GILEAD) See what we said at Judg. 10:4.

Vers. 51. SALMA THE FATHER OF BETHLEHEM) For villages and towns are named after families. See Aristotle at the beginning of the Politics.

Vers. 51. SALMA PATER BETHLEHEM) Nam ex fa- miliis vici & oppida. Vide Aristotelem initio Politicorum.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. The generations of David, the Kings of Judah with their sons and daughters.

Latin:

CAPUT III. Generationes Davidis, Reges Juda cum filiis, & filiabus.

## 3:5
Verse 5. AND SOLOMON] He names this last one of the children of Bathsheba, because the discourse is about to return to him.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET SALOMON] Hunc postremum nominat è Bethsabeæ liberis, quia ad eum rediturus est sermo.

## 3:6
Verse 6. ELISHAMA AND ELIPHALET) These two names were given to boys who died in early childhood. Afterwards the same were given to others born later. Those who died in early childhood are omitted in 2 Sam. 5:14.

NOGAH] Who is also Elishua in the mentioned passage of Samuel.

Thirteen sons of David are listed here, while the book of Samuel has only eleven. That reconciliation of Grotius is not to be disapproved. Kimchi thinks slightly otherwise; that Eliphelet and Nogah are omitted in Samuel because they died without memory, having done nothing illustrious, and having left no children. Moreover, that the former Elishama is called Elishua in Samuel. But Capellus here accuses the Codices of Chronicles of error, because Nogah and Eliphelet are repeated twice here, while in 2 Sam. 5 they are named only once. The critic saw poorly. For Nogah is placed here only once, and in the Codex of Samuel this name is not found at all. And how can he suspect an error here, when in 1 Chron. 14 those nine sons of David are listed again, and in this place it is expressly added besides, Four from Bathsheba, and nine from other wives, namely: whence it is clearly evident that nothing was added by the scribes, otherwise the number nine would not be consistent. Therefore Grotius deservedly abandoned his critic here, whom Simon de Muis chastised in his Varia Sacra, and Buxtorf in his Vindiciae, page 391.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ELISAMA ET ELIPHALET) Hæc duo no- mina imposita fuere pueris, quin prima ætate sunt mortui. Deinde eadem data aliis post natis. Illi in prima ætate mortui omittuntur 2. Sam. 5,14.

NOGE] Qui & Elisua dicto Samuelis loco.

Recensentur hic tredecim Davidis filii, quum liber Samuelis undecim tantum habeat. Conci- liatio illa Grotii non improbanda. Paulo aliter Kimchius; Elipheleth & Noge apud Samuelem omit- ti, quod absq; memoria, nulla re præclare gesta, nullis liberis relictis obierint. Priorem autem Elisama a- pud Samuelem vocari Elisua. Sed Capellus hic vitii accusat Codices Chronicorum, quod Nogeh & Eli- pholeth bis hic repetantur, 2. Sam. 5. semel tantum nominentur. Male vidit Criticus. Nam Nogeh hic semel tantum ponitur, in Codice vero Samue- lis plane hoc nomen non habetur. Et quomodo errorem suspicari hic potest, quum 1. Chron. 14. de- nuo novem illi Davidis filii recenseantur, & hoc in loco præterea expresse addatur, Quatuor de Beth- seba, & novem ex aliis scil. uxoribus: unde liquido patet, nihil esse a librariis additum, alias numerus novenarius non constaret. Merito itaque Grotius deseruit hic Criticum suum, quem castigavit Si- mon de Muis in variis sacris, & Buxtorff. in vindic. pag. 391.

## 3:15
Verse 15. AND THE SONS OF JOSIAH WERE THE FIRSTBORN JOHANAN, THE SECOND JOAKIM, THE THIRD ZEDEKIAH, THE FOURTH SHALLUM.

Because of the various and inextricable difficulties which occur among the interpreters, it is to be observed: that the sacred texts can be best reconciled and explained; if it is said that Johanan the firstborn died before his father or with his father in battle, and therefore Jehoahaz, who is said to have succeeded his father in 2 Kings 23:30, is the one who is called Shallum here and in Jeremiah 22:11 by another name; for the periphrasis fits him that he was led away and was destined to die in a foreign land; and that he reigned before Jehoiakim and Jeconiah. He is named in the fourth place, even though Zedekiah was younger than him, not with regard to age, but to dignity, because he reigned for only three months and was immediately led away by the King of Egypt. But while Tremellius and Junius wish him to be called not only Jehoahaz, but also Johanan, they certainly confuse two different persons, and instead of four distinctly numbered sons, they leave only three.

Latin:

Vers. 15. FILII AUTEM JOSIÆ FUERUNT PRI- MOGENITUS JOHANAN, SECUNDUS JO- AKIM, TERTIUS SEDEKIAS, QUARTUS SELLUM.

Ob varias & inextricabiles difficultates, quæ penes Interpp. occurrunt observandum: optime conciliari & expediri posse textus sacros; si dica- tur, Johanan primogenitum ante Patrem vel cum patre in prælio obiisse, adeoque Joachazum, qui pa- tri successisse dicitur 2. Reg. 23, 2. esse illum qui hic, & Jerem. 22, 11. Sallum dicitur alio nomine; nam ei convenit περίφρασις quod abductus sit, & in terra peregrina mori debuerit; quodque ante Jojaki- mum & Jechoniam præfuerit. Nominatur autem quarto loco, etsi junior eo fuerit Sedekias, non æta- tis habita ratione, sed dignitatis, quia per tres men- ses tantum regnavit, & a Rege Ægypti statim abdu- ctus est. Quem vero dum Tremell. & Junius non so- lum Joachazum, sed & Johannam dictum volunt, confundunt utique duas diversas personas, & loco quatuor distincte numeratorum filiorum tres tan- tum relinqunt.

## 3:16
Verse 16. OF JOAKIM WAS BORN JECONIAH AND ZEDEKIAH] In Hebrew: The sons of Jehoiachin, Jeconiah his son [namely of Joachim], Zedekiah his son [namely of Jeconiah], in which latter place son is taken for heir. See what we have said at Luke 3. Moreover, that plural of son is for the singular: perhaps it was placed thus, so that if anyone should find more, he might add them. Thus below 16. sons of Elah, Kercura.

Heirs are not listed here, but because the genealogy is woven through sons. Therefore, Zedekiah here is different from the Zedekiah in the preceding verse, the son of Josiah. That one was heir to the paternal kingdom: this one, however, was only a private person: nor was he the son of Jeconiah; for he is not found among those eight listed in verses 17 and 18: but another son of Jehoiakim, as the Vulgate rightly says: which Grotius undeservedly corrects.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DE JOAKIM NATUS EST JECHONIAS ET SEDECIAS] In Hebr. Filii Jehojachin, Iechonia filius ejus [nempe Joachimi) Sedecias filius ejus (nempe Jechoniæ) quo loco posteriore filius sumitur pro heres. Vide quæ dicta nobis ad III. Lucæ. Illud autem filii plurale est pro singulari: forte ideo sic positum, ut si quis plures reperiret eos adjunge- ret. Sic infra 16. filii Elah, Kercura.

Non hic hæredes recensentur, sed quia ge- nealogia pertexitur filii. Proinde Sedekias hic alius est à Sidekia vers. præced. filio Josiæ. Ille hæ- res fuit regni paterni: hic vero privatus tantum fuit: neque Jechoniæ filius; nam non reperitur in- ter octo illos v. 17. & 18. recensitos: sed Jojakimi alter filius, ut recte Vulgata: quam immerito cor- rigit Grotius.

## 3:17
Verse 17.

THE SONS OF JECONIAH WERE ASSIR, SALATHIEL) And here in the Hebrew it is otherwise: namely, sons of Jeconiah, (that is, son) Assir, Salathiel his son, that is, heir again: for he was the son of Neri, as we said at the mentioned place.

The Vulgate is again less correctly castigated. Nor does he suspect with sufficient reverence that the plural noun sons was placed for the singular so that, if anyone should find more, he might add them. For the Holy Spirit leaves to no one this power of adding anything to a Canonical writing; or did Grotius perhaps not consider this writing to be Canonical and divine? However, there are altogether more sons of Jeconiah listed here: For even if Assir were not considered a proper name, as it is by B. Luther and Frid. Spanheim (Dub. Evang. part 1, 12, p. 57), it is an appellative denoting bound or captive, and an epithet of Jeconiah, who may have begotten those sons while bound or after the act of transportation, yet not only one son, Salathiel, is assigned to him here, but also those who follow in verse 18: For lest anyone should understand in verse 18 the name of son, i.e., sons of. Salathiel, Melchiram and Pedaiah, the prefixed Vav stands in the way, AND MELCHIRAM, coupling this one as a brother with Salathiel: so that in this way seven sons of Jeconiah are left altogether. Nor indeed was Salathiel the heir of Josiah, but a private person, from which Salathiel listed in Matthew ch. 1, the Salathiel son of Neri, listed in Luke 3, is different, as we shall observe at Luke 3.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

FILII JECHONIÆ FUERUNT ASIR, SALATHIEL) Et hic in Hebræo aliter: nempe filii Iechoniæ, (id est filius) Assir, Salatiel filius ejus, id est, hæres rursum: nam filius erat Neri, ut ad dictum locum diximus.

Minus recte iterum castigatur vulgata. Neque satis reverenter ille suspicatur, nomen plurale filii pro singulari positum esse ideo, ut si quis plures re- periret, eos adjungeret. Hanc enim potestatem Ca- nonico scripto aliquid adjiciendi nemini relinquit Spiritus Sanctus; aut num forte non habuit scri- ptum hoc Grotius pro Canonico ac divino? Sunt autem hic omnino plures Jechoniæ filii recensiti: Nam si maxime Asir non haberetur pro nomine proprio, uti à B. Luthero & Frid. Spanhemio אסיר part. 1. Dub. Evang. 12. p. 57. appellativum est no- tans vinctum vel captivum, & Epitheton Jechoniæ, qui vinctus, vel post actum transportationis filios illos genuerit, non tamen unus solum assignatur hic ei filius Salatiel, sed etiam qui v. 18. sequuntur: Nam ne quis subintelligat in v. 18. nomen filii h. m. filii scil. Salatielis Melchiram & Phadaja, obstat Vav præfixum, ET MELCHIRAM, hunc ceu fratrem cum Salatiele copulans: ut ita omnino septem re- linquantur Jechoniæ filii. Neque vero Salatiel hæ- res fuit Josiæ, sed privata persona, à quo Salatiele Matth. recensito c. 1. diversus est Salatiel Neri filius, recensitus Luc. 3. ut ad Luc. 3. observabimus.

## 3:19
Verse 19.

MESHULLAM) That Jew also had this name, the mocker of auguries, whose mention is from Hecataeus in Josephus.

Vers. 19.

MOSALLAM) Hoc nomen & ille Judæus habuit, auguri- orum irrisor, cujus mentio ex Hecatæo apud Josephum.

## 4:10
Verse 10.

IF YOU WILL INDEED BLESS ME) It was a conditional vow: but what was promised in that vow is passed over in silence.

AND BORE MERIAM) Jalon, as it seems.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

SI BENEDICENS BENEDIXERIS MIHI) Votum fu- it conditionale: quid vero promissum sit eo voto, reticetur.

GENUITQUE MERIAM) Jalon, ut videtur.

## 4:18
Verse 18.

THESE HOWEVER ARE THE SONS OF BETHIAH THE DAUGHTER OF PHARAOH, WHOM MERED TOOK) It seems the name of Mered is missing from the sons or son of Bethiah. And so the writer left a space empty as if he were going to inquire further. But the Hebrews understand Caleb by Mered, because he opposed the spies, and they take the word והיהודיה, which preceded, as a gentilic name, and they say that Jochebed is understood, who bore the aforementioned sons, whom the daughter of Pharaoh raised as her own. To me these things seem rather forced.

The writer, being θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired), had no need for such an inquiry. Nor could the Holy Spirit have been ignorant of the sons of Mered by Bethiah. Therefore, no gap is to be imagined here in the sacred scripture. Indeed, those sons born of Bethiah have already been listed in the preceding verse, just as in this verse the sons born of Judah or of a Jewish woman are enumerated, which Piscator and Junius observed in their notes on this passage, as well as the authors of the notes added to the Belgian version, and others. Grotius judges the authors of the Holy Scriptures no differently than he does profane writers and mere men. Furthermore, the Hebrews hand down strange things about Ezer and his sons in verse 17 and 18, whom they wish to be Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron, understanding Aaron by Jether and Moses by Mered, which absurdities Jerome recounts at length in his Hebrew Traditions.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

HI AUTEM FILII BETHIÆ FILIÆ PHARAONIS, QVAM ACCEPIT MERED) Videtur vacare nomen Me- redi ex Bechia filiorum aut filii. Itaque velut amplius in- quisiturus scriptor spatium reliquit vacuum. At Hebræi per Mered Calebum intelligunt, quod exploratoribus obstiterit, & והיהודיה, quod præcessit, sumunt pro gentilitio, & ajunt Jo- chebedam intelligi quæ peperit filios ante dictos, quos edu- caverit pro suis filia Pharaonis. Mihi hæc duriora videntur.

Scriptor utpote θεόπνευστος, tali inquisitione opus non habuit. Nec ignorare potuit Spiritus S. Meredi ex Bechia filios. Ideo hîc nulla fingen- da in scriptura sacra lacuna. Imo recensiti jam sunt filii isti versu præcedente è Bechia progeniti, uti hoc versu filii ex Jehuda, vel muliere Judæa progna- ti enumerati sunt, quod observarunt Piscator & Junius in notis ad h. l. & auctores notarum versio- ni Belgicæ additarum, aliiqne. Grotius de auto- ribus S. literarum non aliter judicat, quam de pro- phanis scriptoribus, merisque hominibus. Cæte- rum de Efra, & filiis ejus vers. 17. 18. mira tradunt Ebræi, quem volunt esse Amram, patrem Mosi & Aaron, per Jether Aaronem, per Mared Mosen intelligentes, quas ineptias prolixe recenset Hie- ronymus in Tradit. Hebraic.

## 4:22
Verse 22.

AND WHO MADE THE SUN STAND STILL] These and the following are proper names.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected. Such a false translation gave occasion for the fable of the Hebrews concerning the miraculous standing still of the Sun, which Elimelech obtained from God by his prayers, concerning which Jerome writes in his Hebrew Traditions, the Ordinary Gloss, the Carthusian, Hugo, Lyranus, Tostatus, as also Torniellus in Annales M. 2300, Fevardentius on Ruth 1, and Barradius on Matthew 1. Which, however, Cornelius à Lapide refutes in this passage, acknowledging that names are listed here. Which Vatablus also noted, and Pagninus, and Menochius admits in this passage. Nor did the Septuagint interpreters take them as anything other than proper names. But here we have Grotius agreeing. Capellus suspects that the last words of this verse are corrupt, because the Septuagint read them differently. But the editions of the Septuagint vary here. For some have it exactly as it is read in the Hebrew: οἱ δὲ λόγοι πάλαιοί εἰσιν (and the words are ancient). Others retain the Hebrew words, but somewhat changed, and these editions also vary, and they give only a sound without meaning. But to wish to prove the corruption of the Hebrew text from corrupt copies of the Septuagint, is that not most absurd?

WHO WERE PRINCES IN MOAB) They ruled over the land of Moab.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET QVI STARE FECIT SOLEM] Hæc & quæ se- quuntur nomina sunt propria.

Merito corrigitur Vulgata. Talis ψευδερμη- νεία occasionem fabulæ dedit Ebræorum, de mira- culosa Solis statione, quam Elimelech precibus suis obtinuerit à Deo, de qua Hieronymus in Trad. Ebr. Glossa ordinaria, Carthusianus, Hugo, Lyranus, To- status, ut & Torniellus ad Ann. M. 2300. Fevardent. in Ruth. 1. Barrad. in Matth. 1. Quam vero refel- lit Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l. agnoscens, quod nomi- na hic recenseantur. Quod etiam Vatablus nota- vit, & Pagninus, ac fatetur Menochius in h. l. Nec aliter quam ut nomina propria accepere LXX. In- terpp. sed habemus hic Grotium consentientem. Capellus verba ultima hujus versus corrupta esse su- spicatur, quod aliter legerint LXX. Sed variant hic editiones τῶν ὁ Nonnullæ enim prorsus ita habent, ut in Hebræo legitur οἱ δὲ λόγοι πάλαιοί εἰσιν. A- liæ verba Ebræa, sed immutata nonnihil, retinent, quæ editiones etiam variant, ac tantum dant sine mente sonum. E corruptis autem τῶν ὁ exemplari- bus corruptionem Ebræi textus probare velle, an- non ineptissimum est?

QVI PRINCIPES FVERVNT IN MOAB) Terræ Mo- abiticæ dominati sunt.

## 5:26
Verse 26.

AND IN LAHEL AND IN HABOR] In the Hebrew: In Hala and in Habor, as in 2 Kings 17:6, where see what we have said concerning these places.

AND ARA) Some, from the passage in 2 Kings 17:6, think that the mountainous regions of Media are meant, because the Syriac word admits that interpretation. It appears, however, that the same places of exile for the Hebrews are attributed here to the action of Tiglath-Pileser, which in the aforementioned passage of Kings are attributed to the action of Shalmaneser; I believe that both transferred the peoples conquered by them into those regions which were most vacant of men. Media, moreover, had many mountainous areas, as both Strabo and Ptolemy testify: and what Berosus narrates, that the wife of Nebuchadnezzar was greatly delighted by the sight of mountains, because she had been raised in the regions of Media.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ET IN LAHELE ET IN HABOR] In Hebræo: In Hala & in Habor, ut 2. Reg. 17,6. ubi vide quæ de his locis diximus.

Apparet autem hic eadem loca exilii He- bræorum attribui facto Teglathphalasari, quæ dicto loco Regum tribuuntur facto Salmanasari; credo quod ambo vi- ctos à se populos in eas transtulerint regiones, quæ ab homi- nibus vacabant maxime. Mediæ autem plurima erant mon- tana, ut & Strabo & Ptolemæus testantur: & quod Berosus narrat Nabuchodonosori uxorem montium aspectu delecta- tam plurimum, quod in Mediæ locis educata esset.

## 6:28
Ver. 28.

THE SONS OF SAMUEL: THE FIRSTBORN VASSENI AND ABIA] Vasseni is a strange name among the Hebrews; it is credible that it was written ושני אביה, so that the sense might be: The sons of Samuel were, his firstborn (namely Joel) Samuel. 8:2. whose name, because he was less famous, is passed over here: and the second Abia: which agrees with the stated place of Samuel.

The LXX Interpreters understood it thus: καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Σαμουὴλ ὁ πρωτότοκος αὐτῶ Ἰωὴλ καὶ δεύτερος Ἀβιά. Ludovicus Capellus likewise carves out a different reading from there, because the LXX had another copy before their eyes, whose reading he judges to be far better even in this place. It is certain here that the sons of Samuel were Joel and Abia, not only from 1 Sam. 8:2, but also from this 6th Chapter of 1 Chron. v. 33, where Heman is called the son of Joel, the son of Samuel. And although the name of the firstborn is passed over here (which the LXX Interpreters are to be considered to have added from their own source from the Codex of Samuel, as often happens in translation, for who will allow himself to be persuaded in such a great consensus of Hebrew Codices that their copies had the name Joel in this place?); at any rate, the Grotian explanation could have a place, nor would there be need for that suspicion, as if the conjunction Vav were redundant now in the Hebrew text. Since it can be explained thus: his firstborn, and the second, namely Abia. For the prefix is taken in various ways, but Kimchi has already observed that other things stand in the way of the Grotian interpretation, and with him Buxtorf against Capellus, inasmuch as שני in this meaning is nowhere read pointed with a Scheva, and because the Vav should have been marked not with a Patach, but with a Scheva. Whence he judges that וַשְׁנִי is a proper name, and that Vasseni and Joel are the same person: just as Jerome also believes in the Hebrew Traditions.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

FILII SAMVEL PRIMOGENITVS VASSENI ET ABIA) Mirum nomen apud Hebræos Vasseni; credibile est scriptum fuisse ושני אביה, ut sensus sit: Filii Samuel fuere, primogenitus ejus (nempe Joel) Samuel. 8, 2. cujus no- men, quia minus clarus fuit, hic reticetur: & secundus Abia: quod convenit cum dicto Samuelis loco.

Sic & intellexerunt LXX. Interpp. καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Σα- μουὴλ ὁ πρωτότοκος αὐτῶ Ἰωὴλ καὶ δεύτερος Ἀβιά. Lud. Capellus pariter exsculpit inde diversam lectio- nem, quod aliud exemplum οἱ LXX. præ oculis ha- buerint, quorum lectionem etiam hoc loco longe meliorem esse judicat. Certum hic est, filios Samue- lis Joel, & Abia fuisse, non tantum ex 1. Sam. 8, 2. sed etiam ex hoc 6. Capite 1. Chron. v. 33. ubi Heman dicitur filius Joel, filii Samuelis. Et quamvis hîc nomen primogeniti reticeretur (quod LXX. In- terpret. ex Codice Samuelis de suo addidisse cen- sendi sunt, ut sæpe in interpretatione fit, nam exem- plaria ipsorum hoc in loco nomen Joel habuisse quis in tanto consensu Codd. Ebræorum sibi per- suaderi patietur? utique Grotiana explicatio locum habere posset, nec suspicione illa opus esset, quasi copula Vav abundet nunc in Ebræo textu. Quum ita exponi possit: primogenitus ejus, & secundus, nempe Abia. Varie enim accipitur præfixum, sed obstare alia interpretationi Grotianæ, jam observavit Kim- chius, & cum eo Buxtorfius contra Capell. utpote quod שני in hac significatione nuspiam legatur pun- ctatum cum Scheva, & quod Vav non cum Patach, sed cum Scheva notandum fuisset. Unde censet, וַשְׁנִי no- men proprium esse, & eundem esse Vasseni & Joel: quemadmodum etiam Hieronymus in Tradit. Ebræ- is credit.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. The descendants of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, & Asher.

Verse 1.

JASUB) Thus he is named also in Num. 26, 23. Whence the conjecture that it was omitted through carelessness ש in Gen. 46, 13.

That conjecture is nothing. For even if it be true that elsewhere ישוב is read, yet it does not follow from that that the common reading in Gen. 46, 13 is corrupt, as Drusius rightly says in Epistles, Epist. 65 to Edward Lively. For he could have been διώνυμος (of two names). Such as are Ahaz & Achan, Araunah & Ornan, Aram &

Ram, Abimelech & Ahimelech, Jethro & Reuel, & not a few others. This is Drusius. And not only the Latin Interpreter reads עו in Genesis, but also the Chaldean Paraphrast; nor is there any reason for suspecting a corruption of the Hebrew source, since all copies agree. If because of parallel passages and different names a change is to be immediately presumed in the Hebrew text, what at last will remain certain? How much more religiously did the Jews themselves judge concerning the sacred text? Aben-Ezra in the book Tzahut handed down this Rule: There are sometimes two words from two equal (parallel) places that are different: with this caution being highly necessary, which Grotius, a strenuous follower of the Jews, ought deservedly to have had before his eyes: Beware and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou believe the words of a Grammarian or Critic, who brings forward hundreds of such places, saying that they ought to be corrected. Far be it, far be it! For this is not even right in profane writings, much less in the words of the living God! And his book is worthy to be burned.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. Posteri Isaschar, Benjamin, Naphthali, Manas- se, Ephraim, & Aser.

Vers. 1.

JASVB) Sic nominatur & Num. 26, 23. Unde conjectura omissum per incuriam ש Genes. 46, 13.

Nulla est illa conjectura. Nam ut verum sit, alibi legi ישוב, tamen ex eo non sequitur vulgatam il- lam scripturam Genes. 46, 13. corruptam esse, ut recte Drusius in Epistolis Epist. 65. ad Edovard. Live- leum. Potuit enim διώνυμος esse. Qualia sunt Achaz & Achan, Aravnah & Orna, Aram &

Ram, Abimelech & Achimelech, Jethro & Raguel, & alia non pauca. Hæc Drusius. Neque solum lati- nus Interpres legit in Genesi עו, sed etiam Chal- dæus Paraphrastes; neque ratio ulla est suspicandi de corruptela fontis Ebræi, quum exemplaria omnia consonent. Si ob loca parallela ac diversa nomina mutatio statim in Ebræo textu præsumen- da, quid tandem certi remanebit? quanto religio- sius judicarunt ipsimet Judæi de textu sacro? Aben- Ezra in libro צחות hanc tradidit Regulam: Sunt quandoque duæ dictiones ex duobus locis æqualibus (parallelis) diversæ: cum hæc cautela summe necessa- ria, quam Grotius Judæorum sectator strenuus me- rito ante oculos habuisse debebat: Cave & custodi animam tuam valde, ne credas verbis Grammatici vel Critici, qui centena hujusmodi loca adducit, dicens, illa corrigenda esse. Absit, absit hoc! Hoc enim ne quidem in scriptis prophanis rectum est, quando minus in verbis Dei viventis! Et dignus est liber ejus, qui comburatur.

## 7:24
Ver. 24.

WHICH HE BUILT BETH-HORON] He restored the city on the old site, which the Israelites had destroyed after snatching it from the Canaanites.

The matter regarding the Ephraimites stands thus: impatient of delay and swelling with the glory of the birthright granted by Jacob, they attempted a departure from Egypt with grand designs, and having collected an army, while their father Ephraim was still living, they advanced from Egypt to the borders of the land of Canaan. For which reason Asaph accuses them in Psalm 78, because they dared to invade the promised land without waiting for the proper time, trusting in their forces and their skill in warfare, and he adds that by the just judgment of God they paid the penalty for their rashness, turned their backs, and perished miserably in flight. They invaded, however, specifically the Philistines, living in Gath, but the matter turned out in such a way that great mourning was brought upon their father Ephraim thereby. For the men of the city of Gath, the natives of the land of Palestine, killed them, as the Holy Spirit says in 1 Chronicles 7:21, because the sons and grandsons of Ephraim had descended to invade their possessions. Ephraim their father therefore mourned for many days, not only because he had lost so many dearest sons and grandsons, but because it seemed that his entire posterity was finished. Tirinus in Chronicles, chapter 17, from Abulensis on 1 Chronicles, chapter 7, and Nicolaus Serarius at the beginning of his Commentary on Joshua, says that the Philistines, the Hittites, plundered the tribe of Ephraim and destroyed almost the whole of it in the year next after the death of Joseph. But the Sacred Psalmist transfers the blame for that slaughter to the rashness of the Ephraimites themselves, which must indeed have been remarkable, because Ephraim their father mourned for many days or years, and his brothers had need to console him and raise him up, so that, having put aside his mourning, he might give his effort to propagating his family, and he imposed a name from this affliction upon the son whom he later begot, 1 Chronicles 7:22.

For do not believe that this was that Phinehas who was contemporary with Moses.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

QVÆ ÆDIFICAVIT BETHARON] Repo- suit urbem in veteri solo, quam Cananæis ereptam Israelitæ destruxerant.

De Ephraimitis res ita habet: mora impatien- tes & gloria primogenituræ à Jacobo concessæ tu- mentes tentarunt magnis consiliis eductionem ex Ægypto, adeoque progressi sunt, collecto exer- citu, vivente adhuc patre, Ephraimo, ex Ægypto ad fines terræ Canaan. Quo nomine accusat eos Asaph Psalm. 78. quod non expectato justo tem- pore terram promissam invadere ausi fuerint fidu- cia copiarum & peritia sua in re bellica, additque quod justo Dei judicio temeritatis suæ pœnas de- derint, terga verterint, inque fuga misere perierint. Invaserunt autem speciatim Philistinos, habitantes in Gad, sed res ita cessit, ut luctus ingens Patri Ephraimo inde conciliatus fuerit. Occiderunt enim eos, dicente Spiritu S. 1. Paralip. 7, 11. viri civi- tatis Chet, indigenæ terræ Palestinæ, quia descende- rant filii & nepotes Ephraim, ut invaderent possessio- nes eorum. Luxit igitur Ephraim Pater eorum multis diebus, non modo quod charissimos filios & nepotes tot amisisset, sed quod de tota sua po- steritate actum videretur. Tirin. in Chronic. cap. 17. ex Abulensi ad 1. Paralipom. cap. 7. & Nicolao Serario in initio Comment. in Josuam, Philistæos Chetitas deprædatos dicit esse tribum Ephraim, eamque pene totam excidisse anno a morte Josephi proximo. Sed Hieropsaltes culpam istius cladis in ipsorum Ephraimitarum temeritatem trans- fert, quam sane insignem fuisse oportet, quia plurimis diebus vel annis Ephraim pater luxit, & fratres ejus opus habuere ipsum consolari, atque erigere, ut misso luctu, propagandæ familiæ operam daret, nomenque ab hac afflictione fi- lio, quem postea genuit, imposuit, 1. Paralip. 7, 22.

qua. Noli enim credere hunc illum fuisse Phineen Mosi cœvum.

## 7:35
Verse 35.

AND THE NAME OF HIS WIFE MAACHAH) So also the Greeks: καὶ ὄνομα γυναικὸς αὐτῶ Μωχά. They read therefore not אחתו, as the published Hebrew codices now have, but אשתו. Nor are there lacking Hebrew books which have it thus, so that it should not be doubted that there are many discrepant readings, even those not annotated by the Masoretes.

That diverse readings, which later times introduced, are still found after the Masoretes, is ambiguous to no one; yet diverse readings of the Hebrew text are not to be presumed immediately from versions; much less is the Hebrew text to be amended according to these. And therefore new editions ought to be amended here not from the translation of the LXX Interpreters, but from the faith of the ancient Hebrew codices. For older Hebrew copies read אשתו and thus the first Venetian editions have it; thus also Tremellius testifies that he read in an ancient manuscript; thus the author of the Hebrew Concordances reads; thus the Latin Vulgate, Pagninus, Luther, and others have rendered it.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

ET NOMEN VXORIS EJVS MAACHA) Sic & Græ- ci: καὶ ὄνομα γυναικὸς αὐτῶ Μωχά. Legerunt ergo non אחתו, ut nunc habent editi Codd. Hebræi, sed אשתו. Nec defunt libri Hebræi, qui sic habeant, ut dubitari non de- beat, quin multæ sint lectiones discrepantes, etiam non an- notatæ à Masoretis.

Diversas lectiones, quas sequiora tempora in- vexere, post Masoretas adhuc reperiri, nemini ambiguum est; Non tamen præsumendæ statim diversæ lectiones Ebraici textus è versionibus; multo minus textus Ebræus ad hasce emendan- dus est. Ideoque non ex LXX. Interpp. transla- tione, sed ex veterum Ebræorum Codd. fide hîc emendari debent novæ editiones. Antiquiora enim exemplaria Ebræa legunt אשתו atque ita ha- bent primæ editiones Venetæ, ita etiam se legisse in antiquo manuscripto testatur Tremellius, ita legit autor Concordantiarum Ebraicarum, sic reddidere Vulgatus Latinus, Pagninus, Lutherus, & alii.

Now Manahath was indeed in the lot of Judah and Benjamin, but in a part not yet inhabited. This opinion is favored by what is above, where the descendants of Judah are treated, הראה חצי המנחור, if you translate it with some, 'to him who looked after the half part of Manahath'; that is, he took care that that part should not be vacant.

Erat autem Manaheth in forte quidem Judæ & Benjaminis, sed ex parte nondum habitata. Huic sententiæ favet quod supra est, ubi de Judæ posteris agi- tur, הראה חצי המנחור, si cum quibusdam ver- tas, ei qui prospexit dimidiæ parti Manahoth; id est, curavit ne ea pars vacaret.

## 11:25
Verse 10.

THESE ARE THE CHIEFS OF THE MIGHTY MEN OF DAVID, WHO HELPED HIM TO BE MADE KING OVER ISRAEL) Great affairs require great helpers, as Velleius said. Add what is below 12, 23.

Verse 20.

AND PHINEHAS THE SON OF ELEAZAR WAS THEIR LEADER) Both father and son had ancient names

Verse 25.

BUT DAVID SET HIM OVER HIS EAR-PIECE) That function is not at all suitable for a man born for wars. The Greeks read otherwise: καὶ κατέσησεν αὐτὸν Δαβὶδ ἐπὶ τὴν πατριαν αὐτῦ, namely משפחתו. Very learned men think that by changing two letters it was written משמרתו over his guard: he set him over his own bodyguards.

But who are those very learned men, if you depart from Ludovicus Capellus the Pseudo-Critic? That change is certainly vain and rash. Because all Hebrew codices agree here, and the Masora confirms our reading, nor is it read otherwise in the parallel passage 2 Samuel 23:23, where the LXX themselves rendered it πρὸς τὰς ἀκοὰς αὐτῦ: the Vulgate explained it: And David made him his ear-piece, or privy councillor. Others interpret it here as he set him to his hearing, that is, President of his secret council: or also he set him to his council. B. Luther: David made him his secret councillor: Kimchi explains it by ellipsis, he set him over the men of his obedience, the Cherethites and Pelethites from 2 Samuel 20:23. Which sense Vatablus also rendered. Junius and Tremellius translate it a little differently, but with the same sense, he set him over his bodyguard. Hebrew of his listening, i.e., his attendant soldiers, who were always ready at his command. Thus that sense, which Grotius approves, emerges, without prejudice to the integrity of the Authentic text, which we must be scrupulous about changing. For even the Jews considered that a most grave crime; as is evident from R. Moses Nachmanides in his Novellae on the Talmud chapter יש בוהלין fol. 91. The correction of books (sacred, in one's opinion or conjecture) is an absolute transgression, and for it one deserves to be excommunicated.

Vers. 10.

Vers. 20.

PHINEES AVTEM FILIVS ELEAZARI ERAT DVX EORVM) Et pater & filius nomina habebant anti-

Vers. 25.

POSVIT AVTEM EVM DAVID AD AVRICV- LAM) Minime convenit ea functio homini ad bella nato. Aliter legerunt Græci: καὶ κατέσησεν αὐτὸν Δαβὶδ ἐπὶ τὴν πατριαν αὐτῦ, nempe משפחתו. Viri pereruditi putant scriptum duabus literis mutatis משמרתו super custodiam suam: præfecit eum corporis suis custodibus.

Quinám vero illi viri pereruditi, si a Ludo- vico Capello Pseudo-Critico abeas? Vana utique & temeraria est ista mutatio. Quia consentiunt hic omnes Ebræi Codices, & confirmat lectionem nostram Masora, nec aliter legitur in loco pa- rallelo 2. Samuel XXIII, 23. ubi ipsimet LXX. red- didere πρὸς τὰς ἀκοὰς αὐτῦ: vulgatus exposuit: Fecitque eum David sibi auricularium, vel a secre- tis. Alii interpretantur hic posuit eum ad au- dientiam suam, hoc est, Præsidem consilii sui secre- tioris: vel etiam posuit eum ad consilium suum. B. Lutherus: David macht ihn zum heimlichen Rath: Kimchius explicat per ellipsin, præfecit eum viris obedientiæ suæ Crethi & Plethi e 2. Samuel. 20. vers. 23. Quem sensum reddidit etiam Vata- blus. Paulo aliter, sed eodem sensu transferunt Junius & Tremellius, præposuit eum satellitio suo. Hebr. auscultationis suæ, h. e. militibus stipatoribus suis, qui semper præsto erant ad imperium ipsius. Ita sensus ille, quem Grotius probat, emergit, salva integritate textus Authentici, quem immu- tare religio nobis esse debet. Nam & Judæi id pro crimine habebant gravissimo; ut e R. Mose Nachmanid. in Novellis in caput Talmud יש בוהלין fol. 91. constat. Correctio librorum (sa- crorum ex opinione, vel conjectura, est absoluta transgressio, & propter eam meretur quis, ut excom- municetur.

## 13:9
Verse 9.

AT THE THRESHING FLOOR OF CHIDON] It seems that here כידון is written for נכון, which is in 2 Sam. 6:6. This word is absent here in the Greek versions.

But what is the reason that it should seem so? No Hebrew copy, no ancient translation, no authority teaches this. Nor are the letters similar, but rather quite different. The parallel passage, even if it presents a different name, does not teach that it should also be read here, since nothing is clearer than that many in the sacred scriptures are διώνυμοι (having two names), and thus it appears from that comparison that the same person who was called Nachon was also called Chidon.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

AD AREAM CHIDON] Videtur hic כידון scri- ptum pro נכון, quod est 2. Sam. 6, 6. Abest hæc vox hic Græcis.

Quænam vero causa est, quod ita videatur? Nullum exemplar Ebræum, nulla translatio vetus, nulla authoritas id docet. Neque literæ similes, sed non parum diversæ sunt. Locus parallelus, etsi aliud nomen exhibeat, non docet hic illud etiam legi debere, quum nihil luculentius sit, quam quod multi in sacris sint διώνυμοι, adeoque e collatione ista appareat, eundem, qui Nachon, etiam Chidon nuncupatum fuisse.

## 14:1 Argument
Verse 1.

David, however, took counsel with the tribunes and centurions and all

the princes, and said to the whole assembly of Israel: If it pleases you] where the King is about to establish something concerning sacred matters, he will do rightly if he calls together a council not only of the priests, but also of the people, and obtains their consent as well, which is not difficult for a King who advises rightly. For there is hardly any religion where it is not voluntary. Concerning this kind of law, you may rightly say that which is in Tertullian: No law owes the consciousness of its justice to itself alone, but to those from whom it expects obedience.

Latin:

Vers. 1.

INIIT AVTEM CONSILIVM DAVID CVM TRIBVNIS ET CENTVRIONIBVS ET VNIVERSIS

PRINCIPIBUS, ET AIT AD VNIVERSVM COETVM ISRAEL: SI PLACET VOBIS] ubi de sacris aliquid con- stituturus est Rex, recte faciet si non sacerdotum tantum, sed & populi concilium advocet eorumque etiam consensum obtineat, quod Regi recte monenti non est difficile. Reli- gio enim vix ulla est, ubi non est voluntaria. De hoc le- gum genere recte dixeris illud quod apud Tertullianum est: Nulla lex sibi soli conscientiam justitiæ suæ debet, sed eis à quibus obsequium expectat.

Verse 2.

CHAPTER XV.
