Scaliger, and those who follow him (and Grotius is accustomed to follow him), think that the first year of Cyrus is mentioned in the Scriptures, which was the first from the release of the captivity. Concerning which, Sethus Calvisius, Isag. Chronol. ch. 31, p. 173. The first year of Cyrus is not understood as the beginning of Cyrus, when he conquered Astyages or captured Babylon: but it is understood only as the first year of the captivity released by Cyrus, and this era was instituted by the Jews for the sake of thanksgiving, by which they attempted to preserve the eternal memory of this benefit among their descendants; they would undoubtedly have used this era in the following centuries, even if Cyrus had long since departed from the living, had not the liberation of the Israelites and the restoration of the Jewish polity been hindered for many years by the succeeding Kings in Persia, both while Cyrus was still living and after he was dead. But this opinion cannot be proven: First, because it is not the beginning of the liberation of the Jews that is named here, but the beginning or the first year of Cyrus. For the empire of Cyrus is one thing, the liberation of the people is another, which, even if they concur in one year, should not be confused. Second, it is absurd to say that the captivity lasted until the first year of Cyrus, i.e., until the first year of the released captivity. Thus the term of the released captivity would not be explained. But the same would be explained by the same. Therefore, the first year of the released captivity is not meant, but a certain character is attributed to the year of the released captivity, from a certain illustrious Epoch, the beginning of which is connected by the Holy Scriptures with the year of the liberation of the people. Third, it is too manifest that the beginning of the Persian Monarchy is noted, since in verse 20 it is said that the Jews were carried off to Babylon and made servants until the Kingdom of the Persians should rule, namely in Babylon. And it is added in v. 22. In the first year of Cyrus King of Persia (when he began to reign in Babylon) that the prophecy of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, God stirred up the spirit of Cyrus. That the era was not instituted by the Jews, but that the era of the Persians is referred to, the letters of Tatnai and Shethar-boznai sent to Darius sufficiently teach, Ezra 5:13. But in the first year of Cyrus the King in Babel, that King Cyrus commanded that the house of God should be built. Which could be inquired into in the archives. Who will believe that the first year of the released captivity was either indicated here by those prefects, or understood by Darius and his counselors? Fifth, these things were found in the archives of Achmetha, as Ezra testifies in chapter 6:3. In the first year of King Cyrus, King Cyrus commanded that the temple of God should be built. But that a computation or era instituted by the Jews prevailed in the Kingdom and Chancery of Cyrus, and that the first year of the Monarchy was called not from the years of the Monarchy, but from the years of the dismissal of the Jewish captives, is in no way made likely. Add sixth, that this passage refers itself to the prophecy of Jeremiah, which is said to be fulfilled here. Since therefore in Jer. ch. 25:12 the end of the Babylonian captivity is connected with the end of that Monarchy, it is indicated in this place that at the very same time that an end was put to the Kingdom of Babylon by the empire of the Persians, the people were liberated, so that the prophecy of Jeremiah might be fulfilled completely. Compare what we said regarding Jer. 29:10. Whence I am surprised that the blessed D. Behm, when he had already abandoned the opinion of Scaliger and Calvisius concerning the beginning of the Babylonian captivity, still wrote a dissertation on the first year of Cyrus against Pererius at Königsberg in the year 1642; that the first year of Cyrus in the Bible was a singular epoch then used by the Jews in honor and memory of their magnificent liberation performed by Cyrus, provided that this is introduced by Ezra not as an era used by the Jews, but as a Persian or Babylonian era, as has already been shown.

Furthermore (2) Funccius, and those who follow his side in great number, refer the release of the captivity to the first year of the Persian reign of Cyrus: which was also done by the Jesuit Pererius in book 11 on Daniel. Who is wonderfully pleased with himself in this first year of Cyrus, and thinks that by the benefit of this first year he can concatenate exotic history with Biblical years, and construct an entire Chronological System, page 534. For it is, he says, as it were a most firm bond, by which external and profane chronographia can be best connected and bound together with the history and chronology which is contained in the Holy Scriptures. He institutes this concatenation, however, in this way: he places as a foundation that the FIRST of Cyrus corresponds with the 1st of the 55th Olympiad, or the 217th of Iphitus, about which it is easy to agree among chronologists. Thence he counts back 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, the beginning of which was in the eleventh of Zedekiah, or the year of the extermination of the Solomonic temple, as Thus the second year of the 37th Olympiad is reconciled with the 11th of Zedekiah. The years of the city, according to Pererius, began in the 1st year of the 7th Olympiad, whence the 11th year of Zedekiah corresponds with the 117th of the city. From here Pererius proceeds by ascending to the earlier times through the mutual connection of the Kings of Judah: Zedekiah reigned for 11 years (2 Kings 24:18; 2 Chron. 36); Jehoiakim the same (2 Kings 23:36; 2 Chron. 36:5); Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin 6 months (2 Kings 23:31; ch. 24:8; 2 Chron. 36:1 & 9); Josiah for 31 years (2 Kings 22:1; 2 Chron. 34:1); Amon for 2 years (2 Kings 21:19; 2 Chron. 33:21); Manasseh for 55 years (2 Kings 21:1; 2 Chron. 33:1); Hezekiah for 29 years (2 Kings 18:2; 2 Chron. 29:1). From the first of Hezekiah, therefore, to the 11th of Zedekiah, 139 years and 6 months elapsed in Biblical History: whence Pererius concludes that the beginning of the Olympiads must be placed in the eighth year of Ahaz, who reigned for 16 years (2 Kings 16:2; 2 Chron. 28:1). Yet in such a way that the two last are to be included in the first and second of Hezekiah: but the first year of the city is to be placed in the 16th of Hezekiah. And the Trojan destruction occurred at the beginning of Eli the High Priest and Judge of the Hebrews. For Pererius names four times celebrated among the profane: the Olympiadic epoch, that of the years of the city, of the Trojan destruction, and of the deluge of Ogyges. But this last epoch is not historical but mythical. The most noble Nabonassarean epoch, however, is omitted, which is most exact, being hung upon the motions of the heavens. For the rest, both the foundation and the entire chronological structure of Pererius are easily refuted. For first, the first year of Cyrus in the Sacred Scriptures is his first in the Babylonian kingdom, inasmuch as he, having occupied Babylon, relaxed the captivity for the Jews. But in the first year of the Persian Kingdom, Cyrus was not King of the Babylonian Kingdom, as universal history attests. Therefore, the first year of Cyrus in the sacred records is not his first year of the Persian Kingdom. Furthermore, in the first Biblical year of Cyrus, Cyrus wrote thus in the royal decree: 'The Lord has delivered all the kingdoms of the earth to me.' But in the first year of the Persian Kingdom he could by no means write this about himself, for at this time he was scarcely king of all Persia, and the Medes were ruling widely, while he had not even set foot in Babylonia; whence Scaliger, in his notes on the fragments, p. 16, not without reason says: 'Those who end the time of the captivity in this year profess nothing other than their own ignorance, who make him king of all Asia, who scarcely held on to the rugged and rough Persia.' Thirdly, the Ptolemaic canon, after the Babylonian kings are enumerated, assigns to Cyrus only nine years, as a Babylonian king. Since, therefore, by the confession of all, Cyrus presided over the Persian kingdom for 30 years, it is necessary that he occupied the Babylonian kingdom not when he began the Persian kingdom, but when he had already presided over it for 21 years: provided that during those 21 years of his Persian rule, Belshazzar and Darius or Nabonidus the Mede reigned in Babylon. Fourthly, the Pererian concatenation does not agree with the sacred history of Hezekiah, for in his 14th year Sennacherib, King of the Assyrians, besieged Jerusalem, whose army having been slain by an Angel, Merodach, King of Babylon, congratulated Hezekiah through envoys (2 Kings 18, 19; Isa. 37, 38, 39). Everyone says this Merodach is the Mardokempad of Ptolemy, whose first year, according to Ptolemy's calculation, confirmed by eclipses, agrees with the 27th Nabonassarean year. It is necessary, therefore, that the Nabonassarean epoch began before Hezekiah, in the time of Jotham, King of Judah, the grandfather of Hezekiah. But if you follow Pererius, who places the first year of the city in the 16th of Hezekiah, whence the first Nabonassarean year (which, from the demonstration of the chronologists, agrees with the 7th Varronian year of the city) must necessarily be cast back into the 22nd of Hezekiah, this absurdity emerges: that the 27th Nabonassarean year, or the first of Merodach, concurs with the 19th of Manasseh, which is truly absurd. Fifthly, he stumbles

into the history of Zedekiah. For if the first Nabonassarean year agrees with the 22nd of Hezekiah, then the last of Zedekiah will certainly be the 118th Nabonassarean year, because so many years are counted from the 22nd of Hezekiah to the last of Zedekiah: namely, 8 of Hezekiah, 57 of Manasseh and Amon, 31 of Josiah, and 22 years and 6 months of the four last kings. But the 118th Nabonassarean year does not fall into the years of Nebuchadnezzar, by whom Zedekiah was carried away, but into the years of his grandfather Chyniladanus, as the canon of Ptolemy testifies: indeed, the years of Nabopolassar, the father of Nebuchadnezzar, began in the 123rd Nabonassarean year, provided that the fifth of this, noted by a celestial character, an eclipse of the moon, was the 127th Nabonassarean year, as Ptolemy demonstrates from the motion of the heavens. Sixthly, he makes the interval from the destruction of Solomon's temple to the first year of Cyrus 70 years, introducing a prochronism of 40 years. Eusebius, as well as Africanus and other most ancient ecclesiastical and historical writers, assign an interval of 30 solid years from the year of the destruction, or the last of Zedekiah, to the first of Cyrus. Similarly, it was necessary for the Funccians also to depart from this Eusebian interval. For since Eusebius in his chronicle linked the year of the total destruction of the temple with the 2nd year of the 47th Olympiad or the 186th Iphitean, as did Clement of Alexandria in Book 1 of the Stromata, and Cyrus began his reign in the 1st year of the 55th Olympiad, or the 217th Olympiadic year, only 31 years are left as the interval from the extermination of the temple to the reign of Cyrus. Now, since Cyrus reigned for 30 years, from the destruction of the temple to the death of Cyrus there will be only 61 years. Did Cyrus, therefore, grant the Jews a free return to their homeland nine years after his own death? Since, therefore, that Funccian opinion can in no way stand with the connections of the ancients, and there is no solid reason why we should depart from the mind of the ancients, the modern discovery of Funccius—by which he converts the son Nebuchadnezzar into the father Nabopolassar, and Nabonassar into Shalmaneser—should rather be abandoned than the unanimous suffrage of the Fathers and the more ancient chronologists.

Third, the simplest opinion is that the first year of Cyrus denotes the first year of his Monarchy or Empire; First, because the words imply this. For when the years of a King are numbered, the years of his Reign are usually noted. Which is certain from an induction of similar passages. (2) The term of the Persian Monarchy is expressly defined in v. 21, until the Persian empire should reign. (3) The first year of Cyrus is not named simply, but is circumscribed, so that it is most evident that his Monarchy is being designated. For the Lord, he himself says, hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth v. 23. (4) The same first year is called the first of Cyrus, not as King of the Persians, but as King in Babel. Ezra 5, 3. Who also caused the vessels from the temple of Babel to be restored to the Jews v. 14. (5) That first year is also called in the Babylonian Archives themselves, the first, namely, of King Cores Ezra 6, 3. (6) Thus we are rendered more certain concerning the year of the completed captivity, and the beginning of the Persian Monarchy is connected with the liberation of the people. (7) Thus also the passage in Jer. 20, 1 will be more correctly consistent, as we shall show in the annotations to the same. (8) Finally, since it is manifest that the first year of the Persian reign of Cyrus cannot be understood otherwise, what other year could be the first of Cyrus than the first year of the Babylonian Empire or of that same Monarchy? Therefore, the Holy Scripture bestowed such favor upon that distinguished Monarchy, and upon the first Monarch in it, whom it had appointed as the liberator of its people, that it expressly designated its beginning in the sacred annals: and thus it ennobled even the very auspices of the rule of that Monarchy with this most illustrious ἀξιώματι of the liberation of the Lord’s people, and of the public proclamation of the Name of the Lord throughout all its kingdoms and the whole Monarchy: He is the God who dwells in Jerusalem, Ezra 1, 3. To whom be praise and glory for ever and ever, Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ANNO AVTEM PRIMO CYRI REGIS PER- SARVM) Hæc verba ad finem usque eadem sunt, unde suo- rum temporum historiam Esdras incepit. Is mos libros con- tinuandi est antiquus, quem & Procopius sequitur fine Van- dalicorum & Gothicorum initio.

De hoc anno primo Cyri variant sententiæ Chronologorum. Scaliger, & qui eum sequun- tur, (sequi autem solet Grotius) primum annum Cyri in scripturis putant dici, qui primus a solutio- ne captivitatis fuit. De quo Sethus Calvisius Isag. Chronol. cap. 31. p. m. 173. Primus annus Cyri non intelligitur de initio Cyri, quando Astyagem vicit, vel Babylonem expugnavit: sed tantum intelligitur primus annus solutæ captivitatis a Cyro, & gratitu- dinis ergo a Judæis hæc æra instituta fuit, qua sempi- ternam hujus beneficii memoriam apud posteros con- servare conabantur; usi etiam procul dubio hac æra sequentibus seculis fuissent, etiamsi Cyrus dudum e vivis excessisset, nisi statim & vivente Cyro, & eo defuncto, multis annis per successores in Persia Re- ges, liberatio Israëlitarum & instauratio politiæ Ju- daicæ impedita fuisset. Sed hæc sententia non po- test probari: Primo quia non initium hic nomina- tur liberationis Judæorum, sed initium vel primus annus Cyri. Aliud autem est, imperium Cyri, aliud liberatio populi, quæ etsi in unum annum con- currant, non tamen confundi debent. Secundo ineptum est dicere durasse captivitatem usque ad primum annum Cyri h. e. usque ad primum annum solutæ captivitatis. Ita non explicaretur terminus solutæ captivitatis. Sed idem per idem exponere- tur. Non ergo annus primus solutæ captivitatis intelligitur, sed anno solutæ captivitatis character certus tribuitur, ab Epocha quadam illustri, cujus initium cum anno liberationis populi colligatur a S.S. Tertio nimis manifestum est, initium Persicæ Monarchiæ notari, cum versu 20. dicuntur abdu- cti esse in Babyloniam Judæi & servi facti usque dum Regnum Persarum regnaret sc. in Babylonia. Et addi- tur v. 22. Anno primo Cyri Regis Persiæ (ubi is regna- re in Babylonia cœpit) ut impleretur Prophetia Jeremiæ, excitasse Deum Spiritum Cores. Quarto non institutam a Judæis æram respici, sed æram Persa- rum literæ Thatnai & Starbosnai ad Darium datæ satis docent, Esdr. 5, 13. Sed in primo anno Cyri Regis in Babel mandavit Rex ille Cores, ut domus Dei ædi- ficaretur. Quod inquiri in Archivis potuit. Quis hic annum primum solutæ captivitatis vel indica- tum a præfectis istis, vel intellectum a Dario ejusque consiliariis credet? Quinto in Archivis Ahmeticis hæc reperiebantur, teste Esdra c. 6, 3. Anno primo Regis Cores mandavit Rex Cores ut templum Dei ædi- ficaretur. At in Regno & Cancellaria Cyri com- putum vel æram invaluisse a Judæis institutam, & annum primum Monarchiæ vocatum esse non ab annis Monarchiæ, sed ab annis dimissionis captivo- rum Judæorum nullo modo fit verisimile. Adde Sexto, quod referat hic locus sese ad vaticinium Jere- miæ, quod hic impletum dicitur. Quum ergo in Jer. c. 25, 12. connectatur finis captivitatis Babylonicæ cum fine Monarchiæ istius, indicatur hoc loco eo- dem ipso tempore, quo Babyloniæ Regno per Per- sarum imperium finis impositus est, liberatum esse populum, ut prophetia Jeremiæ ex asse impleretur. Conf. quæ ad Jer. 29, 10. diximus. Unde miror, B. D. Behmium, cum jam deseruisset Scaligeri & Calvisii sententiam de initio captivitatis Babylonicæ adhuc scripsisse Diss. de primo anno Cyri contra Pererium Regiomonti Anno 1642. institutam; annum primum Cyri in Bibliis Epocham singularem fuisse Judæis tum usitatam in honorem & memoriam magnificæ eorum liberationis per Cyrum præstitæ, siquidem non ut æra Judæis usitata, sed ut æra Persica, vel Babylonica hæc introducatur ab Esdra, uti jam ostensum.

Porro (2) Funccius, & qui partes ejus se- quuntur magno numero, ad primum annum Per- sici Regni Cyri solutionem captivitatis referunt: quod etiam factum a Pererio Jesuita libr. 11. in Daniel. Qui mirifice sibi placet in hoc primo Cyri anno, & opinatur beneficio hujus primi anni exoticam historiam cum annis Biblicis se congrue concatenare, totumque Systema Chro- nologicum conficere posse pag. 534. Est enim, inquit, hic quasi vinculum firmissimum, quo ex- terna & prophana Chronographia cum historia & Chronologia, quæ continetur in Sacris literis optime connecti & colligari potest. Hanc autem conca- tenationem ita instituit: Fundamenti loco ponit PRIMUM Cyri convenire cum I. Olym. 55. vel Iphiti CCXVII. de quo penes Chronologos facile convenit. Inde retro numerat LXX. annos captivi- tatis Babylonicæ, quorum initium fuit in Zedekiæ undecimo, vel anno exterminii templi Salomonici, ut ita annus secundus Olympiadis 37. concilietur cum 11. Zedekiae. Anni vero urbis secundum Pererium inceperunt anno 1. Olympiadis 7. unde 11. annus Zedekiae conveniat cum 117. urbis. Hinc pergit Pe- rerius per ascensum ad anteriora per mutuam con- nexionem Regum Judae: Zedekias regnavit per an- nos 11. 2. Reg. 24, 18. 2. Chron. 36. Jojakim totidem 2. Reg. 23, 36. 2. Chron. 36, 5. Joahas & Jechonia 6. menses 2. Reg. 23, 31. c. 24, 8. 2. Chr. 36, 1. & 9. Josia per annos 31. 2. Reg. 22, 1.2. Chr. 34, 1. Ammon per 2. annos 2. Reg. 21, 29. 2. Chr. 33, 21. Manasses per an- nos 55. 2. Reg. 22, 1. 2. Chron. 33, 1. Ezechias per an- nos 29. 2. Reg. 18, 2. 2. Chron. 29, 1. A primo ergo Ezechiae ad 11. Zedekiae in Biblica Historia effluxe- re anni 139. 6. menses: unde concludit Pererius, ini- tium Olympiadum conjiciendum esse in octavum Achasi, qui 16. annos regnavit 2. Reg. 16, 2. 2. Chr. 28, 12. Ita tamen, ut duo postremi includendi sint primo, & secundo Ezechiae: Primum vero annum urbis conjiciendum esse in 16. Ezechiae. Trojanum vero excidium contigisse in principio Heli Pontifi- cis, & Judicis Ebraeorum. Quatuor enim Pererius nominat tempora apud prophanos celebrior Epocham olympiadicam, annorum urbis, Excidii Trojani, & diluvii Ogygis. Sed haec postrema Epo- cha non historica sed μυθική est: Omittitur autem nobilissima Epocha Nabonazarea, quae ad coeli mo- tus appensa exactissima est. De caetero facile refelli- tur tum fundamentum, ut tota structura chronologica Pererii. Nam primo annus Cyri primus in Sacris est primus ejus in Babylonico regno, utpote qui oc- cupata Babylone Judaeis captivitatem laxavit. At anno primo Persici Regni Cyrus non fuit Rex Ba- bylonici Regni, attestante universa historia. Annus ergo primus Cyri in sacris non est annus ejusdem primus Persici Regni. Porro anno primo Cyri Bibli- co Cyrus ita in regio Diplomate scripsit: Omnia Regna terrae tradidit mihi Dominus. At anno primo Regni Persici ita de se scribere minime potuit, hoc enim tempore vix Persidos totius rex erat & Medi late imperitabant, in Babyloniam vero ne pedem quidem intulerat, unde Scaliger notis in fragmenta p.16. non immerito, Qui hoc anno, inquit, finiunt tem- pus captivitatis, nihil aliud quam imperitiam suam profitentur, qui Regem totius Asiae faciunt, qui vix mor- dicus Persidem λεπρὰν καὶ τραχεῖαν retinebat. Ter- tio Ptolemei canon post Reges Babylonicos enume- ratos Cyro assignat tantum novem annos, tanquam Regi Babylonico. Quum ergo Cyrus omnium con- fessione 30. annis regno Persico praefuerit, oportet ipsum Regnum Babylonicum occupasse non cum Regnum Persicum iniit, sed cum 21. annos praefuis- set eidem: siquidem illis 21. annis regiminis ipsius Persici Belschasar & Darius vel Nabonidus Medus Babylone regnaverit. Quarto non convenit Pere- riana concatenatio cum historia sacra Ezechiae, hu- jus enim anno 14. Senacherib Rex Assyriorum ob- sidione cinxit Hierosolymam, cujus exercitu per Angelum caeso Merodach Rex Babyloniae per lega- tos Ezechiae gratulatus est 2. Reg. 18, 19. Es. 37, 38. 39. Quem Merodachum omnes dicunt esse Marko- Kempadum Ptolemei, cujus annus primus, cum 27. Nabonazaraeo juxta calculum Ptolemaei, Ecclipsi- bus firmatum, congruit. Oportet ergo Epocham Nabonazaraeam coepisse, ante Ezechiam, tempore Jothami Regis Juda, avi Ezechiae. At si Pererium se- quaris, primum urbis conjicientem in 16. Ezechiae, unde primus Nabonazaraeus (qui ex demonstratio- ne Chronologorum convenit cum anno 7. urbis Varroniano) rejiciendus necessario erit in 22. Eze- chiae, absurdum hoc emergit, vigesimum septimum Nabonazaraeum, seu primum Merodaci concurrere cum 19. Manassis, quod vere ἄτοπον. Quinto impin- 1

git Pererius in historiam Zedekiæ. Si enim primus Nabonazaræus convenit cum 22. Ezechiæ, utique ultimus Zedekiæ erit 118. Nabonazaræus, quia tot anni numerantur a 22. Ezechiæ ad ultimum Zede- kiæ: nempe 8. Ezechiæ, Manassis & Ammonis 57. Josiæ 31. ultimorumRegum quatuor 22. anni cum 6. mensibus. At annus Nabonassaræus 118. non incidit in annos Nebucadnezaris, a quo Zedekias abductus est, sed in annos avi ejus Chyniladani, teste canone Ptolomæi : imo anni Nabopalassaris parentis Ne- bucadnezaris inierunt Anno 123. Nabonassaræo, si- quidem quintus hujus cœlesti charactere, Lunæ de- liquio notatus, fuerit centesimus vigesimus septi- mus Nabonassaræus, Ptolomæo e motu cœli de- monstrante. Sexto intervallum ab excidio templi Salomonæi ad annum primum Cyri LXX. annorum facit: προχρονισμὸν introducens 40. annorum. As- signant Eusebius, ut & Affricanus, & alii antiquissi- mi scriptores Ecclesiastici & Historici ab anno ex- cidii, seu ultimo Zedekiæ ad primum Cyri interval- lum 30. annorum solidorum. Similiter discedendum etiam Funccianis fuit ab hoc Eusebiano intervallo. Quum enim Eusebius in chronico annum πανολε- θρίας templi cum anno 2. Olympiades 47. vel Iphi- teo 186. colligarit, ut & Clemens Alexandrinus in l. 1. Stromat. Cyrus autem Regnum inierit anno 1. Olympiadis 55. sive anno Olympiadico 217. interval- lum ab exterminio templi ad Regnum Cyri solum relinquitur 31. annorum. Jam cum Cyrus per 30. an- nos regnarit, a destructione templi ad mortem Cyri erunt tantum 61. anni. Num ergo Cyrus novennio post mortem suam Judæis liberum in patriam redi- tum concessit? Cum itaque nullatenus cum veterum colligations Funcciana illa sententia consistere pos- sit, solida autem causa non sit, cur a veterum mente discedamus, relinquendum potius neotericum εὕ- ρημα Funccii, quo Nabuchodonosorem filium in Na- bopalassarem patrem, & Nabonazarem in Salmanassa- rem convertit, quam Patrum & Chronologorum antiquiorum unanime suffragium.

Tertio simplicissima sententia est annum primum Cyri indigitari primum Monarchiæ vel Imperii ejus; Primo quia id verba inferunt. Cum enim Regis anni numerantur, anni Regni ejus solent notari. Quod ex inductione similium locorum certum est. (2) Expres- se definitur terminus Monarchiæ Persicæ v. 21. donec imperium Persicum regnaret. (3) Primus annus Cyri non simpliciter nominatur, sed circumscribitur, ita ut Monarchiam ejus designari luculentissimum sit. Dominus enim, inquit ipse, dedit mihi omnia Regna terræ v. 23. (4) Idem primus annus dicitur primus Cyri, non ut Persarum Regis, sed ut Regis in Babel. Esdr. 5, 3. Qui & vasa ex templo Babel restitui Judæis curavit v. 14. (5) Vocatur etiam ille annus primus in ipsis Archivis Babylonicis, primus nempe Regis Cores Esdr. 6, 3. (6) Ita de anno solutæ captivitatis certio- res reddimur & connectitur cum liberatione popu- li initium Monarchiæ Persicæ. (7) Sic etiam locus Jer. 20, 1. sibi rectius constabit, ut in annotatis ad eun- dem docebimus. (8) Denique quum manifestum sit, annum primum Persici Cyri regni intelligi non pos- se, quis alius annus Cyri primus esse poterit, quam annus primus Imperii Babylonici vel Monarchiæ ejusdem? Ea ergo dignatione affecit S. S. Monar- chiam illam insignem, & primum in ea Monarcham, quem liberatorem populi sui constituerat, ut ini- tium ejus in annalibus sacris ῥητῶς designarit: atque ita nobilitavit etiam ipsa auspicia imperii istius Mo- narchiæ hoc tam illustri ἀξιώματι liberationis po- puli Domini, & proclamationis publicæ Nominis Domini per omnia ejus regna, totamque Monar- chiam : Ipse est Deus, qui in Jerusalem habitat Esdr. 1, 3. Cui laus & gloria in secula seculorum, Amen.

# Ezra

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOK OF EZRA.

It is apparent both from this writing and from the reputation received among the Hebrews that Ezra was a man both highly learned and wonderfully φιλοπάτριδα (patriotic), to whom perhaps that Sempronius, called σοφός (wise) by the Romans, could be compared.

Setting aside that useless comparison, let us rather observe the argument of this book: which is occupied with exhibiting the truth and fulfillment of the divine promises concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, the return to Judea and the repair of the temple, and the restoration of all states and hierarchies. And therefore it is completed in three parts: first, it describes the liberty granted by Cyrus the most glorious Monarch, and usurped, in the first three chapters: then indeed in chapter 4 it commemorates the impediments cast in the way of the begun structure of the temple: thirdly, it sets forth the success of the work in the remaining six chapters: how, the difficulty raised by Tatnai the governor of Judea having been cleared and the mandate of Cyrus having been searched out, Darius granted a new diploma, and the temple was built and inaugurated, chapters 5 and 6; how likewise under the empire of Artaxerxes, and by his favor, Ezra set out into Judea for the repair of the ecclesiastical and political state, chapters 7 and 8. Who also dissolved marriages with foreigners in chapters 9 and 10, and thus restored the economic state to its entirety. Interpreters of the following book of Nehemiah are especially celebrated: Cassiodorus, Sanctius, and Johannes Wolffius. The chronology of this book from the liberty granted by Cyrus up to Ezra's arrival in Judea, namely the seventh year of Artaxerxes, or Artaxerxes Longimanus, comprises 78 years, namely 17 from the promulgation of Cyrus to the edict of Darius Hystaspis, obtained in his second year, and 61 years from the second year of Darius to the edict of Artaxerxes, which he handed to Ezra in the seventh year for the favor of the Jewish people. For Cyrus presided over the Monarchy for 7 years; Cambyses, who is called Ahasuerus in Ezra 4, presided for 7 years and 5 months; Smerdis, who took the name Artaxerxes for himself in Ezra 4, reigned for seven months; Darius Hystaspis held the empire for 36 years; Xerxes reigned for 21 years. To which if you add the six completed years of the reign of Artaxerxes μακρόχειρος (Longimanus), because he granted the edict in the seventh, there result 78 years, from which it will be taught in its proper place that the mystical 70 weeks of Daniel began to flow. Ezra therefore begins at the end of the 70 years of captivity, and ends at the beginning of the 70 weeks of Daniel. Whence it becomes manifest how great the utility of this sacred book is, as well as its necessity for demonstrating the truth of the Prophetic oracles.

The High Priests also can be collected without difficulty, who presided within the epoch of the captivity up to this term of the book. For Saraias, son of Azariah, is commemorated as having been killed by Nebuchadnezzar, 2 Kings 25:18, 21. His successor was Josedec, his son, who held the High Priesthood around the end of the captivity, 1 Chronicles 6:15. To him succeeded Joshua the son of Josedec, who with Zerubbabel led the Jews back from Babylon, Ezra 3:2. Thence Joachim the son of Joshua held the High Priesthood under Darius Hystaspis and Xerxes, Nehemiah 12:10; and further his son Eliasib under Artaxerxes Longimanus, Nehemiah 3:1, chapter 13:4, 7, whose successor under Darius Nothus was his son Jojada, Nehemiah 12:10; but Jonathan the son of Jojada presided over the High Priesthood under Artaxerxes Mnemon, Nehemiah

12:11, and this Jonathan's son Jaddo, likewise commemorated in Nehemiah 12:11, is that High Priest who met Alexander the Great and reconciled him when he was offended at the Jews, as Josephus records in Antiquities 11 near the end; whose brother Manasseh was the first High Priest of the Samaritans on Mount Gerizim, by the same testimony of Josephus.

Moreover, Ezra was also the son of Saraias, Ezra 7:1, 2 Chronicles 6:12, the brother of Josedec, as is evident from that place in Chronicles, a Prophet and scribe, or Doctor of the law of great authority, who by divine instinct and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit wrote not only this book, but as is commonly believed, the books of Chronicles also, and the last chapters of Deuteronomy and Joshua, indeed even Genesis chapter 36, supplying those things which seemed to be missing in the sacred books; from whom also that clause, as often as it occurs in the Old Testament, UNTO THIS PRESENT DAY, seems to have been added by the judgment of Bede, Salianus, and Cornelius a Lapide: whence it is likely that the Fathers, while they say the sacred books were restored by Ezra, had regard for this, that he arranged them in order and enriched them by divine authority and heavenly inspiration and θεοπνευσίᾳ (divine inspiration). Compare System of Theology, Vol. 1, p. 724.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD LIBRUM ESDRÆ.

APparet & ex hoc scripto & ex fama apud Hebræos rece- pta, Esdram virum fuisse & valde eruditum, & mire φι- λοπάτριδα, cui comparari forte possit Sempronius ille, Roma- nis dictus σοφός.

MIssa illa comparatione inutili, libri hujus argumentum potius observa- mus: qui in eo occupatur, ut ve- ritatem & complementum pro- missionum divinarum de libera- tione e captivitate Babylonica, reductione in Judæam & reparatione templi, ac restauratione statuum & Hierarchiarum omnium, exhibeat. Ideoque tribus absolvitur partibus: primum libertatem a Cyro Mo- narcha gloriosissimo concessam, & usurpatam de- scribit tribus prioribus capitibus: tum vero cap. 4. impedimenta cœptæ templi structuræ injecta com- memorat: tertio successum operis reliquis sex capp. exponit: quomodo difficultate a Thatnai præside Judææ mota expedita & mandato Cyri indagato, novum diploma Darius concesserit, ac templum ædificatum, & inauguratum sit capp. 5. 6. quomodo item sub Artachsastæ imperio, ejusque gratia Esdra profectus in Judæam sit ad reparationem status Ec- clesiastici & politici capp. 7. 8. Qui etiam matrimonia cum alienigenis dissolvit cap. 9. & 10. adeoque sta- tum Oeconomicum ita in integrum restituit. In- terpp. in hunc sequentem Nehemiæ librum impri- mis celebrantur Cass. Sanctius & Johannes Wolf- fius. Chronologia libri hujus a concessa per Cy- rum libertate usque ad Esdræ adventum in Judæam annum nempe septimum Artachsastæ, vel Artaxer- xis Longimani complectitur annos 78. nimirum 17. a Cyri promulgatione ad edictum Darii Hysta- spidis, anno ejus secundo impetratum, & 61. anni a Darii secundo ad edictum Artaxerxis, quod anno septimo in gratiam populi Judaici Esdræ tradidit. Cyrus enim præfuit Monarchiæ annis 7. Camby- ses, qui Esdr. 4. Ahasverus vocatur, 5. mensibus & 7. annis præfuit: Smerdis, qui Artachsastæ nomen sibi sumsit Esdr. 4. septem mensibus regnavit, Da- rius Hystaspis annis 36. functus est imperio: Xerxes imperavit annis 21. Quibus si Artaxerxis μακρό- χειρος completos sex regiminis annos adjeceris, quia septimo edictum concessit, prodeunt anni 78. ex quo fluere cepisse LXX. hebdomadas Danielis mysticas suo loco docebitur. Incipit ergo Esdras in termino LXX. annorum captivitatis, & desinit in initio LXX. hebdomadum Danielis. Unde quanta hujus libri sacri tum utilitas sit, tum necessitas ad veritatem oraculorum Propheticorum demonstrandam ma- nifestum evadit.

Pontifices etiam colligi possunt haud difficul- ter, qui intra Epocham captivitatis ad hunc termi- num libri præfuerunt. Nam Sarajas, filius Azariæ, a Nebucadnezare interfectus 2. Reg. 25, 18. 21. com- memoratur. Cujus successor fuit Josedec, filius ejus, Pontificatu functus circa finem captivitatis 1. Par. 6, 15. Huic successit Josua filius Josedec, qui cum Zorababele Judæos reduxit e Babylone Esdr. 3, 2. Dehinc Joachim Josuæ filius Pontificatum gessit sub Dario Hystaspis & Xerxe; Neh. 12, 10. ac porro filius ejus Eliasib sub Artaxerxe Longimano Neh. 3, 1. c. 13, 4. 7. cujus successor sub Dario Notho filius Jojada fuit Neh. 12, 10. Jonathan vero filius Jojadæ præfuit Pontificatui sub Artaxerxe Memoriofo, Neh.

12, 11. atque hujus Jonathanis filius Jaddo Neh. 12, 11. itidem commemoratus, est ille Pontifex, qui Alexan- dro Magno occurrit eumque Judæis offensum re- conciliavit, memorante Josepho 11. Antiq. sub finem: cujus frater Manasses primus Samaritanorum Pon- tifex fuit in monte Garizim eodem Josepho teste.

Cæterum Esdras Sarajæ etiam filius fuit Esdr. 7, 1. 2. Par. 6, 12. Josedeci frater, ut ex isto Chronicorum loco constat, Propheta, & scriba, seu legis Doctor magnæ autoritatis, qui instinctu divino & inspira- tione S. S. non hunc tantum librum, sed ut commu- niter creditur, libros etiam Paralipomenon, & Deut. ac Josuæ capita ultima, imo Gen. quoque c. 36. scri- psit, supplens ea, quæ in libris sacris desiderari vide- bantur, a quo etiam addita judicio Bedæ, Saliani & Cornelii a Lapide videtur clausula illa, quoties oc- currit in V. T. VSQVE IN PRÆSENTEM DIEM: unde verisimile est, Patres, dum ab Esdra restauratos dicunt sacros libros, id respexisse ple- rosque, quod in ordinem eos digesserit, & locuple- tarit divina autoritate, ac cœlesti afflatu, & Θεο- πνευσίᾳ. Conf. System. Theol. T. 1. p. 724.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. LIBERTY GRANTED BY CYRUS. CHAPTER I.

Cyrus, acknowledging the God of Israel, grants the Jews liberty and a return to their homeland, commands the prefects to assist them in rebuilding the temple, and restores to them the vessels taken away by the Chaldeans, which are listed here, brought by Sassabasar with those who went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

Latin:

PARS I. LIBERTAS A CYRO CONCESSA. CAPUT I.

Cyrus Deum Israelis agnoscens, Judais liberta- tem reditumque in Patriam concedit, Præfectis mandat, ut in reædificando templo eos juvent, ac vasa a Chaldæis ablata iisdem restituit, quæ hic recensentur, adducta a Sassabare, cum illis qui ascenderunt e Babylone in Jerusalem.

## 1:1
ALSO BY SCRIPTURE) For the better sense, and that in writing.

HE CAUSED THE VOICE TO PASS THROUGHOUT ALL HIS KINGDOM] He caused it to be published throughout all his kingdoms.

Latin:

ETIAM PER SCRIPTURAM) Ad sensum melius, id- que scripto.

TRADUXIT VOCEM IN OMNI REGNO SUO] Publicari fecit per omnia regna sua.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. FROM THE MOUTH OF JEREMIAH) Chap. 25. 29. 45. THE LORD STIRRED UP THE SPIRIT OF CYRUS KING OF PERSIA) The benevolence of kings is one of the best instruments of God through which He does good to the pious.

Brissonius, in book 1 on the Persian kingdom, along with Plutarch and Ctesias, maintains that the Persian name Cyrus signifies the sun; his origin, glory, and deeds were predicted by Holy Scripture two hundred years before in Isaiah 44:28, ch. 45:1, especially that he would lay the foundation of the temple: 'Who say to Cyrus: My shepherd and you shall fulfill all my will: because it shall be said to Jerusalem: You shall be built, and to the temple: You shall be founded.' Josephus (book 11, ch. 1), Theodoret (on Daniel 1), and others believe that these prophecies, shown to Cyrus by Daniel and others, contributed much to his conversion.

Latin:

Vers. 2. EX ORE JEREMIÆ) Cap. 25. 29. 45. SUSCITAVIT DOMINUS SPIRITUM CYRI REGIS PERSARUM) Regum benevolentia unum ex instrumentis Dei optimis per quæ piis bene facit.

CYRI nomen Persicum solem significare Briffo- nus l. 1. de regn. Persar. cum Plutarcho, & Ctesia statuit; cujus ortum, gloriam, & facta prædixit S. S. ducentis ante annis Es. 44, 28. c. 45, 1. imprimis etiam quod templum fundaturus sit: Qui dico Cyro: Pastor meus & voluntatem meam complebis: quia dicetur Jerusalem: Ædificaberis, & templo: funda- beris: Quas Prophetias a Daniele aliisque Cyro ostensas, ad ejusdem conversionem multum fecisse Joseph. l. 11. c. 1. Theodor. in Dan. 1. aliique censent.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. THE LORD GOD OF HEAVEN HAS GIVEN ME ALL THE KINGDOMS OF THE EARTH) Truly great empires: the Persian, by right of birth from the Median and Chaldean, and by right of victory. Yet such is the evidence of this truth, that there is one God, the architect of this supreme power, that even those kings and princes who, not so much by consent of mind as because they dared not go against received errors, worshipped a multitude of gods, were nevertheless often driven by the force of conscience to the confession of that one true God. We have an illustrious example in Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2:47, 3:43, 4:31, 32, 33, 34). And Cyrus and Darius wished to be prayed for in the Jerusalem Temple, as Josephus notes; Alexander the Great offered sacrifices to the God of the Jews, as the same author testifies. Ptolemy Philadelphus did the same, as did Augustus and Tiberius, and Vitellius in the time of Gaius, as we learn from the same Josephus and Philo. Very many kings gave gifts to the Temple, even Sosius gave a golden crown. Nor did the Jews in the Temple offer prayers with sacrifices only for their own countrymen, but for all human kind, as Philo notes, specifically for the Lacedaemonians and Romans. Their wise men were therefore not ἄμικτοι, ἀσύμφυλοι, as they were considered, partly through the bad interpretation of outsiders, partly because of the fault of the rude common people. See what we have said in book 2 of the Law of War and Peace 15. §. 8. 9.

Although it is evident by the light of nature that there is one God, yet that the God of Israel, Jehovah, is that true one God did not become known through the light of nature, but through divine revelation. Namely, so that it would not be unknown who that one true God is: God, proceeding from his secret Majesty, deigned to reveal himself to his own people, which knowledge also reached Cyrus: Not that there is such evidence of this truth that one is compelled to the confession of the true God by force of conscience: But that through the Prophetic oracles, especially of Isaiah, and also through the information of Daniel, that light arose for Cyrus, by the singular grace of God. For that confession which he issued concerning the true God, and his established constitution, are such that it is not obscure that he had been converted to the true God of Israel. He acknowledges Jehovah as the God of Heaven, from whom he received all his kingdoms and their power: He venerates his command, and in his honor, at the order of the Lord himself, he commands the temple to be built, and prays for grace and success for the Lord's people from the Lord: He also restores the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple, and consecrates them to the Lord. Josephus, book 11 of Antiquities, chapter 1, and Theodoret, chapter 1 of Daniel, observe that Daniel, who was an intimate, indeed a dinner companion to Cyrus, led him through the prophecy of Isaiah chapters 44 and 45 to acknowledge and worship the God of Israel: Since Isaiah had prophesied about him two hundred years before: from whose prophecy arguments for the conversion of Cyrus may likewise be sought, if anyone presumes to call it into doubt.

Regarding Nebuchadnezzar also, the matter is manifest, that he not only had a general knowledge of one God, but acknowledged the true God of Israel, for he confesses after the faithful of the Lord, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, were freed from the furnace, that there is no other God who can save in such a way, and he commands that one God to be worshipped and adored, and strictly forbids anyone to worship any other than that one true God, Dan. 3, 28. 29. And then, after the recovery of the use of his reason, he celebrates him as the supreme and eternal God, whose power is eternal, and whose kingdom lasts for ages: beside whom all the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing, who does according to his will both in the mighty works of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and there is no one who can resist his hand, and say to him, why have you done this? whose works are all true, and his ways justice, C. 31. 32. 34.

Nor can there be any doubt about Darius, that he arrived at the knowledge of the true God of Israel, inasmuch as he even sanctioned by public edict that the God of Daniel should be worshipped and feared throughout the entire empire, as the living and eternal God, whose kingdom is incorruptible, and whose power has no end, who is a deliverer and Savior, doing signs and wonders. Dan. 6, 26. 27. It cannot be said, as Grotius says at this place of Daniel, that the confession of the true God was wrung from the idolater Darius: for who in his right mind would believe that such edicts and commands could proceed from an idolatrous King? What of the fact that before the miracle of Daniel being freed from the Lions, Darius believed that the God of Daniel himself could snatch him away and deliver him, and religiously prayed for it: Your God, whom you serve always, he himself will deliver you. Grotius believes that the King conceived this hope from the liberation of the three youths. But from that he could not only conceive that hope, but also faith in the true God, which these vows and edicts of Darius proclaim with a clear voice.

Latin:

Vers. 2. OMNIA REGNA TERRÆ DEDIT MIHI DOMINUS DEUS COELI) Magna sane imperia: Persa- rum, jure nascendi e Medorum & Chaldæorum, jure victo- riæ. Tanta autem est evidentia hujus veritatis, unum esse Deum summæ hujus artificem, ut etiam ii Reges ac princi- pes, qui non tam animi consensu, quam quod receptis erro- ribus non auderent contra ire, multitudinem deorum cole- bant, sæpe tamen ad veri illius Dei confessionem conscien- tiæ vi adigerentur. Exemplum illustre habemus in Nabu- chodonosoro Dan. 2, 47. 3, 43. 4, 31. 32. 33. 34. Et Cyrus & Darius pro se orari in Templo Hierosolymitano voluere, ut notat Josephus, Alexander Magnus Deo Judæorum victimas obtulit, teste eodem. Fecere idem Ptolemæus Philadel- phus, Augustus quoque & Tiberius, & Caji tempore Vitelli- us, ut ex eodem Josepho & Philone discimus. Reges plurimi dona Templo dedere, etiam Sosfius coronam auream. Ne- que vero Judæi in Templo cum sacrificiis preces pro fuis tantum popularibus obtulere, sed pro omni humano genere, ut notat Philo, speciatim pro Lacedaemoniis & Roma- nis. Non erant ergo eorum sapientes ἄμικτοι, ἀσύμφυλοι, quales habebantur, partim mala extraneorum interpretatione, partim ob culpam vulgi rudis. Vide quae diximus libro 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis 15. §. 8. 9.

Etsi unum esse Deum naturae lumine pateat, Deum tamen Israelis Jehovam esse verum illum unum Deum neutiquam per lumen naturae, sed per revelationem divinam innotuit. Nempe ut quis- nam ille unus verus Deus sit, non ignoraretur: Deus ex arcana Majestate prodiens semetipsum re- velare dignatus est populo suo, quae notitia etiam ad Cyrum penetravit: Non quod tanta hujus verita- tis sit evidentia, ut ad veri Dei confessionem quis vi conscientiae adigatur: Sed quod per oracula Pro- phetica, Esaiae imprimis, nec non per Danielis in- formationem ea lux exorta fuerit Cyro, singulari Dei gratia. Ita enim confessio illa, quam de vero Deo edidit, & constitutio ejus comparata est, ut eundem ad verum Deum Israelis conversum fuisse, haud obscurum sit. Agnoscit Jehovam Deum Caeli, abs quo omnia regna sua eorumque potestatem acce- perit: Veneratur ejus mandatum, & in honorem ejus, ad praeceptum ipsius Domini, jubet templum aedificari, populoque Domini gratiam & successum a Domino precatur: Vasa etiam, quae abstulerat e templo Nebuchodonosor, iterum dicat, ac conse- crat Domino. Josephus lib. 11. antiquit. cap. 1. & Theodor. cap. 1. Dan. observant, Danielem, qui fa- miliaris, imo conviva fuit Cyro, per Prophetiam Esaiae cap. 44. & 45. ad Deum Israelis agnoscendum colendumque perduxisse: Siquidem de ipso ante du- centos annos vaticinatus fuit Esaias: e cujus Pro- phetia pariter de Cyri conversione argumenta peti queant, si quis eam in dubium praesumat vocare.

De Nebuchodonosore quoque res manifesta est, quod non tantum generalem de uno Deo notitiam ha- buerit, sed verum Israelis Deum agnoverit, fatetur enim post liberatos e fornace fideles Domini, Sa- drach, Mesach & Abednego, non esse alium Deum, qui possit ita salvare, Deumque illum unum colere jubet, atque adorare, ac severe praecipit, ne quis alium colat, quam illum unum verum Deum Dan. 3, 28. 29. ac deinde post recuperatum rationis usum celebrat eum, ceu summum & aeternum Deum, cujus potestas aeterna est, & regnum durat in secula: juxta quem omnes habitatores terrae pro nihilo repu- tati sunt, qui juxta voluntatem suam facit tam in virtutibus caeli, quam in habitatoribus terrae, & non est, qui resistat manui ejus, & dicat ei, quare fecisti? cujus omnia opera vera, & viae justitiae C. 31. 32. 34.

Neque de Dario dubium esse potest, quin ad veri Dei Israelis notitiam pervenerit, utpote qui publi- co edicto etiam sancivit, ut in universo imperio Deus Danielis coleretur ac timeretur, ceu vivus & aeternus Deus, cujus regnum incorruptibile, & pote- stas finem nullum habet, qui liberator ac Salvator est, faciens signa atque mirabilia. Dan. 6, 26. 27. Non dici potest, quod dicit ad locum istum Danielis Grotius, a Dario idololatra veri Dei confessionem expressam: quia talia edicta & mandata a Rege ido- lolatra proficisci ecquis sanus credat? Quid quod ante miraculum liberati a Leonibus Danielis, ic crediderit Darius, Deum Danielis ipsum eripere atque liberare posse, ac religiose id precatus sit Deus tuus, quem colis semper, ipse liberabit te. Quam spem Regem concepisse ex trium juvenum liberatione credit Grotius. At ex illa non tantum spem illam concipere potuit, sed etiam fidem in verum Deum quam etiam animo ejus inditam fuisse haec vota & edicta Darii λευκάδι φωνῇ proclamant.

## 1:3
WHO IS AMONG YOU OF ALL HIS PEOPLE? MAY HIS GOD BE WITH HIM) An effective expression: who is there of the Israelites who values God so much that he returns there? May God be propitious to him. Nothing will be desired by me.

Latin:

QVIS EST IN VOBIS DE VNIVERSO POPVLO EJUS? SIT DEUS ILLIUS CUM IPSO) Efficax locutio: quis est Israelitarum, qui tanti Deum facit, ut isthuc redeat? Deus ei sit propitius. A me nihil desiderabitur.

## 1:4
Ver. 4.

EXCEPT THAT THEY SHALL VOLUNTARILY OFFER] In the Hebrew it is עם, which here is not exceptive, but declarative. The Greeks translate it as with the others who were offered according to vows. Since by established law it was not permitted to take collections without the King's permission, the King here permits that those of the Jews who did not wish to return to their homeland (for he imposed necessity on no one) should contribute to the restoration of the temple of God, as much as they wished, of silver, gold, of movable goods (for that is what רכוש is) and of other things which it is right and lawful to offer to God. These things are to be interpreted from the passage in Exod. 35. Cyrus imposes no necessity on anyone to contribute, but gives permission to contribute: such as the Macedonian Kings and the Romans later gave. See what we have said at Matt. 17, 24.

Vatablus, Pagninus, and others seem to explain it more correctly as WITH A VOLUNTARY GIFT, that is to say, with an offering which they offer to the temple of their own accord; they shall also give other things for travel expenses: so that it may be commanded here also that the Jews remaining in Babylon should contribute something to those returning to Jerusalem, especially also for the building of the temple.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

EXCEPTO QVOD VOLUNTARIE OFFERENT] In Hebræo est עם, quod hîc non exceptivum est, sed declara- tivum. Græci vertunt σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς κατ’ εὐχὰς προσε- νεχθεῖσι. Cum jure recepto non liceret collectas facere im- permissu Regis, permittit hîc Rex, ut qui Judæorum redire in patriam nollent (neque enim ulli imponebat necessitatem) contribuerent ad reponendum templum Dei, quantum vel- lent, de argento, auro, de rebus mobilibus (id enim est רכוש) deque aliis rebus quæ Deo offerri jus fasque est. Interpretan- da hæc ex loco Exod. 35. Nullam cuiquam contribuendi ne- cessitatem Cyrus imponit, sed contribuendi dat licentiam: qualem & Macedones Reges postea & Romani dedere. Vide quæ diximus Matth. 17, 24.

Rectius videntur Vatabl. Pagninus & alii ex- ponere cum MUNERE SPONTANEO q. d. cum oblatione, quam sponte offerunt templo, da- bunt etiam alia pro viatico: ut hîc demandatum etiam id sit, ut aliquid Judæi in Babylone rema- nentes contribuant in Jerusalem redeuntibus, im- primis etiam ad templi ædificationem.

## 1:5
Verse 5.

AND EVERY ONE WHOSE SPIRIT GOD HAS STIRRED UP] The same expression as that in Livy 6: The gods will forbid these things, you say: but they will never descend from heaven on your account: they must give you the mind to forbid them. For such words indeed signify a divine benefit, but one that is well received.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ET OMNIS CUI DEUS SUSCITAVIT SPIRITUM] Eadem locutio cum illa apud Livium 6. Dii prohibebunt hæc, inquies: sed nunquam propter te de cælo descendent: tibi dent mentem oportet, ut prohibeas. Verba enim talia divinum quidem beneficium significant, sed bene acceptum.

## 1:7
Verse 7.

KING CYRUS ALSO BROUGHT FORTH THE VESSELS OF THE HOUSE OF THE LORD, WHICH NEBUCHADNEZZAR HAD BROUGHT FROM JERUSALEM, AND HAD PLACED THEM IN THE HOUSE OF HIS GOD] This is a great thing in the Persian King, that he dared to prefer the God who is the maker of the world to his ancestral gods, that is, to the inventions of men.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

REX QVOQVE CYRUS PROTULIT VASA TEM- PLI DOMINI, QVÆ TULERAT NABUCHODONO- SOR DE JERUSALEM, ET POSUERAT EA IN TEM- PLO DEI SUI] Multum hoc in Rege Persa quod Deum mundi opificem diis patriis, id est, hominum commentis, præ- ferre ausus est.

## 1:8
Verse 8.

MITHRIDATES] A name frequent among the Persians from the god Mithra.

In the Vulgate it is 'son of Gazabar', but the Hebrew text does not know the word 'son', nor do the LXX interpreters have it. And the other word is an appellative, not a proper name, which Vatablus, Pagninus, and Marinus with Cajetan, and also the Jesuit Cornelius, explain as 'by the hand of Mithridates the Treasurer'. Cf. ch. 7, 21. Josephus calls him the prefect of the royal treasury.

HE NUMBERED THEM TO SASSABASAR THE PRINCE OF JUDAH] προστάτῃ τῆς Ιεδαίας. Whence some think this is the same person who is later called Zorobabel 3, 2. 8. 4, 1. For many of the Jewish leaders, while they lived under the dominion of the Chaldeans, had one native or domestic name, and another Chaldean or courtly one. See Daniel 1, 7. See also what we shall say very soon about Nehemiah's other name. ששבצר is a name of good omen for riches, composed of 'byssus' and 'gold'. But זרבבל signifies the misery of the Israelite people at that time living in exile in Babylon. Thus, pious men, amidst the honors of the court (for Zorobabel was a guard of the royal body, σωματοφύλαξ, as Josephus speaks 11, 4), were admonished not to cast off sympathy for their own countrymen.

Regarding Schassabazar, see ch. 2, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

MITHRIDATIS] Nomen frequens apud Persas à Deo Mithra.

In vulgata est filii Gazabar, sed vocem filii ignorat textus Ebræus, neque habent LXX. Interpp. & altera vox est appellativum, non proprium no- men, unde Vatabl. Pagninus, Marinus cum Cajeta- no, Jesuita etiam Cornelius exponunt, per manum Mithridatis Thesaurarii. Conf. c. 7, 21. Josephus vocat, ærarii Regii præfectum.

ANNUMERAVIT EA SASSABASAR PRINCIPI JU- DÆ] προστάτῃ τῆς Ιεδαίας. Vnde nonnulli hunc eundem existimant, qui postea Zorobabel dicitur 3, 2. 8. 4, 1. Nam plurimi primores Judæi dum sub Chaldæorum agebant domi- natu, nomen habebant aliud patrium sive domesticum, ali- ud Chaldaicum sive aulicum. Vide Danielem 1, 7. Vide & quæ de Nehemiæ altero nomine jam mox dicemus. ששבצר no- men boni ad divitias ominis ex bysso & auro compositum. At זרבבל significat miseriam populi Israelitici eo tempore exulantis in Babylone. Ita viri pii inter aulæ honores (nam Zorobabel regii corporis custos fuit σωματοφύλαξ, ut Jose- phus loquitur 11, 4.) admonebantur, ne exuerent συμπάθειαν adversus suos populares.

De Schassabazare ad c. 2, 1.

## 1:9
Verse 9.

GOLDEN BOWLS] σπονδεῖα here in the Greek interpreter. See what we have said at Genesis 44, 2. Josephus translates it as ψυκτῆρας (wine-coolers).

THIRTY GOLDEN BOWLS] In Hebrew: כפורי, which certain Greeks have retained. See 1 Chron. 18:17.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

PHIALÆ AUREÆ] σπονδεῖα hîc Græcus interpres. Vide quæ diximus ad Genes. 44, 2. Josephus ψυκτῆρας vertit.

SCYPHI AUREI TRIGINTA] In Hebræo: כפורי, quod retinuere Græci quidam. Vide 1. Paral. 18, 17.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

FIVE THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED.

But when the specific numbers of the vessels are collected into a sum, only 2499 appear. I answer that only the principal ones were specifically enumerated; the others of lower value were not 1000 unnamed ones, but were counted by thousands, 'by the thousands,' as we are accustomed to speak, as Junius and Piscator rendered verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

QUINQUE MILLIA QUADRIN- GENTA.

At numeris specialibus vasorum in summam collectis prodeunt tantum 2499. Resp. præcipua tantum specifice recensita esse; cætera vilioris pre- tii ἀνώνυμα non fuisse 1000. sed numerata esse per millia bey tausenden, uti loqui solemus, ut v. 10. red- didit Junius & Piscator.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. A review of those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, and the number of gifts offered for the construction of the temple and the priestly vestments.

Ver. 1. NOW THESE ARE THE CHILDREN OF THE PROVINCE]

That is, men who were Jews by race, but born in the regions of the Chaldeans. This review often differs in numbers from that which is in Neh. 7, and in certain Greek copies it is missing here, as is the following chapter. Perhaps this review was transferred here from the book of Nehemiah by copyists, as well as what follows up to verse 68. For he who is named below as Tirshatha is Nehemiah himself, as appears in Nehemiah 8, 9; and what is written here as having been said, happened only on the second journey, when the city was being built after the temple, as can be known from Nehemiah 7, 70. Furthermore, Mordecai, whose name appears here, was in the company of the later journey, not the former, as the Hebrews agree.

No solid reason can be brought forward why we should believe that copyists inserted certain things here. The variation of the review arises from the fact that the review was made twice, once in Babylon, which Ezra describes; and again in Judea, which is described by Nehemiah; and because among those who had already given their names to the catalog of those to be transported, some remained in Babylon, and some even died on the way, whence sometimes the number is smaller in Nehemiah than in Ezra; and conversely, some who had not given their names at the beginning, returning to a sounder mind and led by love of country, nevertheless undertook the journey afterward and made the catalog of Nehemiah larger than Ezra's review was. Thus, the descendants of Arach are numbered here in v. 5 as seven hundred and seventy-five, who, namely, had given their names in Babylon, but six hundred and fifty-two arrived in Judea, Neh. 7, 10. On the other hand, to the descendants of Pahath-Moab in verse 6, six were added to the one thousand two hundred and fifty-four registered in Babylon, counted in the review made in Judea. As for the Tirshatha, of whom mention is made in Ezra 2, 62, it does not seem necessary to others to understand the same Nehemiah, even if Nehemiah is also called Tirshatha in Neh. 8, 9; nor do they admit that the same thing is reported of him here, which he said only on the second journey when the city was being built, Neh. 7, 65. For the name Tirshatha is common, denoting a legate or commissioner of the King in the Persian language. Junius thinks that Sheshbazzar is understood here in chapter 1, 8, who, although most people think he is Zerubbabel, Junius observes at that passage that he was nevertheless another and different person from him; nor is there any need for the same prohibition to be understood here in verse 62. and Nehem. 7, 65, since similar edicts could have been sanctioned by different commissioners of the King, or if it is the same prohibition, some judge that the verb in the place of Nehemiah can be rendered in the pluperfect, i.e., For the King's legate had commanded them not to eat of the most holy thing. Nor is it sufficiently certain who that Mordecai is whose name is reviewed here: nor are the opinions of recent Hebrews to be much heeded. There is certainly no reason why we should admit that the sacred text is corrupted because of such things. But we shall see about these at that place.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Recensio eorum, qui cum Zorobabele in Jerusalem reversi sunt, & numerus munerum ad templi fabricam, & vestes Sacerdotales oblatorum.

Vers. 1. HI SVNT AVTEM PROVINCIAE FILII]

Id est, ho- mines Judæi gente, sed nati in Chaldæis partibus. Recensio hæc sæpe numeris differt ab ea, quæ est Neh. 7. & in quibus- dam Græcis exemplaribus hic deest, ut & caput sequens. For- te ex Nehemiæ libro huc translata est à descriptoribus ista re- censio, & quæ sequuntur ad comma 68. Nam & qui infra nominatur Atherfata est ipse Nehemias, ut apparet Nehemiæ 8, 9. & quod scribitur hic dixisse, id secundo demum itinere, cum post templum urbs ædificaretur, evenit, ut cognoscere est Nehemiæ 7, 70. Præterea Mardochæus, cujus hic nomen exstat, fuit in comitatu posterioris itineris, non prioris, ut Hebræi consentiunt.

Nulla ratio adferri solida potest, cur credamus descriptores hic quædam inseruisse. Varia- tio recensionis inde est, quod bis facta sit recen- sio, semel in Babylonia, quam Esdras describit: At- que iterum in Judæa, quæ describitur a Nehemia, quodque inter illos etiam, qui jam nomina sua de- derant Catalogo transportandorum, remanserint nonnulli in Babylonia, nonnulli etiam in via obie- rint, unde quandoque numerus minor est apud Nehemiam, quam Esdram; ac vice versa quidam qui initio nomina sua non dederant, ad saniorem mentem redeuntes, amore patriæ ducti, deinceps nihilo secius profectionem susceperint, ac Cata- logum Nehemiæ auctiorem fecerint, quam fuit Esdræ recensio. Ita posteri Arachi hic v. 5. nu- merantur septingenti septuaginta quinque, qui sc. nomina sua dederint in Babylonia, pervenerunt autem in Judæam fexcenti quinquaginta duo Neh. 7, 10. Contra posteris Pachat-Moabi vers. 6. mille ducentis quinquaginta quatuor in Babylonia con- signatis sex accesserant, annumerati in recensio- ne in Judæa facta. Quod ad Athersatam, cujus Esdr. 2, 62. mentio sit, non necessum videtur aliis, per eundem Nehemiam intelligere, etsi Nehemias etiam Atherfates dicatur Neh. 8, 9. neque admit- tunt, idem de ipso hic perhiberi, quod in secundo demum itinere, cum urbs ædificaretur, dixit Neb. 7, 65. Nomen enim Atherfata commune esse, le- gatum vel commissarium Regis Persica lingua de- notans. Hic autem Scheschbazarum intelligi Ju- nius putat cap. 1, 8. designatum, quem etsi plerique Zorobabelem esse existiment, alium tamen & di- versum ab eo fuisse Junius ad locum istum obser- vat: nec opus esse, ut idem interdictum ejusdem intelligatur hic vers. 62. & Nehem. 7, 65. quum pa- ria edicta a diversis Regis commissariis sanciri po- tuerint, aut si ejusdem sit interdictum, in loco Ne- hemiæ verbum in plusquamperfecto reddi posse cen- sent nonnulli, h. m. Edixerat enim legatus Regis eis, ut non comederent de re sancta sanctorum. Neque quis Mardochæus ille sit, cujus nomen hic recense- tur, satis constat: Nec Ebræorum nuperorum opi- niones multum attendendæ sunt. Causa certe nulla est, cur ob talia textum sacrum corruptum esse ad- mittamus. Sed de his ad illum locum videbimus.

## 2:55
Ver. 55. THE CHILDREN OF SOLOMON'S SERVANTS.

Concerning them see 1 Kings 9, 21, who are now reviewed in order by reason of their families, such as the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, etc., and with the Nethinim, i.e., the surrendered ones, the Gibeonites, Josh. 9, 21, 27, they are brought into one sum in verse 58.

Latin:

Vers. 55. FILII SERVORUM SALOMONIS.

De illis vide 1. Reg. 9, 21. qui jam ordine ratio- ne familiarum recensentur, utpote filii Sothai, filii Sophereth &c. & cum Nethinim, h. e. dedititiis, Gi- beonitis, Jos. 9, 21. 27. in unam summam rediguntur vers. 58.

## 2:59
Ver. 59. AND THESE ARE THEY WHICH WENT UP FROM

TEL-MELAH, TEL-HARSA, CHERUB, AND ADDAN, AND IMMER.

These are accepted as names of families in the Weimar Paraphrase in this place, but in the 7th chapter of Nehemiah they are more correctly held in the same to be names of towns of Babylonia, from which also very many joined themselves to those returning to Judea, whose number is not expressed here, and concerning whom it was not certain whether they were of the Israelites. Osiander thinks that their families and number are expressed in verse 60: but in truth it is more likely that their number is not designated here, just as the children of the priests, or rather of those who passed themselves off as priests, in verse 61 are not defined as to number, and therefore it must be believed that those expressed in verse 60 are different from those who are said to have set out from the listed cities of Babylon: since these could not even indicate the houses or families of their parents: whereas the families of the former are listed in verse 60: namely, that they were the Children of Delaiah, the Children of Tobiah, and the Children of Nekoda: be it so, even if there was doubt about these, whether they belonged to the Israelites or not. And this seems to be the reason why the total number collected in verse 67 does not agree with the partials reduced to a sum, but is greater by many thousands, because, namely, the number of those with uncertain families and doubtful origin from the cities of Babylon, and of the sons of the priests not found in the genealogy, not being distinctly expressed, was gathered by Ezra into that total sum and included in it. If, however, one should choose to make the sons of Delaiah, and Tobiah, and Nekoda the same as the former, it must be said that those 12,542, by which the number collected from the partial sums is exceeded by this larger sum of 42,360 (since only 29,818 appear), were from the ten tribes, who indeed returned to Jerusalem with the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, but were not listed here. Moreover, it may seem strange how the total number in Neh. 7:66 in the other census agrees exactly with this total number, even though the partial sums vary not a little in both catalogs, for the reason indicated at Ezra 2:1, and with the partial sums collected, a number far different and smaller by several thousands results: for which matter no other reason occurs to us than that when Ezra was beginning the count in Babylon, not only from those who could indicate their families and certainly belonged to the Israelites, but also from the anonymous or unknown families who were joining the others from the cities of Babylon, many more associated themselves after the catalog was already completed, whence in the census made anew in Judea (which Nehemiah found in chapter 7), which seemed necessary on account of that accession, and on account of the μετάνοιαν [change of mind] of some who had declared their names in Babylon (who, namely, preferred to remain there afterwards rather than return to their homeland), and also the death of some on the journey, the number is found to be increased, on account of the influx of those ἀγενεαλογήτων [those without genealogy] that occurred after the first census, who joined together with the other Israelites and began the journey: and a wonderful divine providence is to be acknowledged here rather than a corruption of the scripture to be admitted: that while the undoubted Israelites remained, others from the doubtful ones were added as reinforcements, and that while even entire families changed their minds (as appears concerning the men from Magbish in Ezra 2:30, that they remained in Babylon, since they are not found in the other census in Neh. 7), from other families far more than had initially declared their names (as can be gathered concerning the Asgadites from a comparison of Ezra 2:12 and Neh. 7:17, that 1,100 more had joined, not to mention others now), and indeed even from those families from which none are found in the first census, some joined themselves afterwards (namely, from the sons of Bezai 324, from the sons of

Hariph. 112. Neh. 7, 23. 24.) so that by their addition the original number might be restored, and exactly as many, as far as the complete number is concerned, might come into Judea as had been registered in Babylon.

Latin:

Vers. 59. ET HI QUI ASCENDERUNT DE

THELMALA, THELHARSA, CHERUB, ET ADON, ET EMER.

Hæc accipiuntur ut nomina familiarum in Paraphrasi Vinariensi, hoc in loco, at Nehem. 7. cap. rectius in eadem habentur pro nominibus op- pidorum Babyloniæ, e quibus etiam plurimi sese redeuntibus in Judæam jungebant, quorum nume- rus hic non expressus est, de quibus non constabat, num ex Israelitis essent. Quorum familias, & nu- merum exprimi vers. 60. censet Osiander: sed ve- ro similius est, illorum numerum designatum hic non esse, quemadmodum neque sacerdotum vel potius eorum, qui se pro sacerdotibus vendita- bant, liberi v. 61. quantum ad numerum definiti sunt, adeoque credendum, 652. illos v. 60. expres- sos alios esse ab iis, qui de oppidis recensitis Ba- byloniæ profecti dicuntur: siquidem hi ne paren- tum quidem domus vel familias indicare poterant: illorum vero familiæ v. 60. recenseantur: quod Fi- lii Delaja, Filii Tobiæ, & Filii Nekoda fuerint: esto, quod etiam de his dubium fuerit, utrum ad Israelitas pertinerent, necne? Atque hæc videtur causa, cur numerus totalis v. 67. collectus cum par- tialibus in summam redactis non congruat, sed multis millibus major sit, quia sc. illorum incertæ familiæ, & dubiæ originis, e civitatibus Babylo- niæ, & sacerdotum in genealogia non invento- rum filiorum numerus distincte non expressus, ab Esdra in summam illam totalem simul conflatus est, eaque comprehensus. Si tamen lubeat filios Delaja, & Tobiæ, & Nekoda eosdem facere cum prioribus, dicendum erit, 12542. illos, quibus nu- merus e partialibus summis collectus ab hac majo- ri summa 42360. exceditur (quum prodeant solum 29818.) e decem tribubus fuisse, qui nempe cum tribu Juda, & Benjamin redierint in Jerusalem, sed hic recensiti non sint. Mirum autem videri pos- sit, qui numerus totalis Neh. 7, 66. in altera recen- sione exacte cum hoc numero totali conveniat, etiamsi partiales summæ non paucæ varient in utroque catalogo, ob causam ad Esdr. 2, 1. indica- tam, & partialibus summis collectis numerus lon- ge alius, ac aliquot millibus minor proveniat: cu- jus rei nulla alia nobis succurrit causa, quam quod Esdra in Babylonia numerum ineunte non solum ex iis, qui familias indicare poterant, & certo ad Israelitas pertinebant, sed etiam ex anonymis vel incognitis familiis, qui e civitatibus Babyloniæ cæteris accedebant, plures catalogo jam confecto sese associarint, unde in recensione in Judæa denuo facta (quam invenit Nehemias cap. 7.) quæ neces- saria ob eam accessionem, & ob nonnullorum, qui nomina sua professi erant in Babylone, μετάνοιαν, (qui sc. remanere deinde illic maluerunt, quam patriam repetere) quorundam etiam in itinere obitum, visa fuit, numerus auctior reperitur, ob ἀγενεαλογήτων illorum confluxum post primam recensionem factum, qui simul cum aliis Israelitis juncti iter ingressi sunt: & mirabilis hic potius agnoscenda divina providentia quam scripturæ de- pravatio admittenda: quod Israelitis indubiis re- manentibus alii e dubiis succenturiati sint, quod- que integris etiam familiis animum mutantibus, (ut de viris e Magbis Esdr. 2, 30. apparet, quod Ba- bylone remanserint, quum non reperiantur in al- tera recensione Neh. 7.) ex aliis familiis longe plu- res, quam initio nomen professi erant (uti de Asga- ditis colligere est e collatione Esdr. 2, 12. Neb. 7, 17. quod mille & centum adhuc accesserint, ne alios jam commemoremus) imo etiam ex iis familiis, e qui- bus nulli in prima recensione inveniuntur, nonnulli postea se junxerint (utpote e filiis Bezai 324. e filiis

Hariph. 112. Neh. 7, 23. 24.) ut eorum accesfione ita numerus pristinus redintegraretur, ac totidem omnino, quoad integrum numerum, in Judæam venirent, quot in Babylonia recensiti erant.

## 2:68
Verse 68. WHEN THEY ENTERED THE TEMPLE.

That is, the place in which the temple had stood (for this had been burned down) where, as in a sacred place, they soon erected an altar, and on it offered sacrifices. Chap. 3, 2. Jer. 41, 5. Bar. 1, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 68. CUM INGREDERENTUR TEMPLUM.

Id est, locum in quo steterat templum (hoc enim exustum erat) ubi ceu in loco sacro mox al- tare erexerunt, in eoque sacrificia obtulerunt. Cap. 3, 2. Jer. 41, 5. Bar. 1, 10.

## 2:69
Verse 69. GOLD SOLIDI] In the Hebrew is the Greek word דרכמונים, that is, drachmas, as also in Nehemiah 7, 70. This is not surprising, since, as we have said elsewhere, many Greek words had already penetrated into the Chaldean language from the times of Daniel: on the other hand, the words mina and hinis came into Greece from the Syriac language.

If a silver drachma, as it is usually valued, was worth three Meissen silver groschen, a gold drachma is gathered to have been worth 36 groschen, that is, 1½ Joachimthalers; and thus 1000 gold drachmas made 1500 Joachimthalers or Imperials: and 61,000 gold drachmas made 91,500 thalers or Joachimthalers. A pound of silver is 25 Joachimthalers, therefore 5000 pounds are 125,000 Joachimthalers.

Latin:

Vers. 69. AURI SOLIDOS] In Hebræo Græca vox דרכמונים, id est, drachmas, ut & Nehem. 7, 70. Non id mirum, cüm, ut alibi diximus, jam à Danielis temporibus multæ Græcæ voces in Chaldæum sermonem penetrassent: contra minæ vox & hinis ex Syriaco sermone in Græciam venere.

Si drachma argenti uti æstimari solet, tribus grossis argenteis Misnicis valuit, auri drachma 36. grossis, h. e. 1½. Joachimicos valuisse colligitur adeo- que mille drachmæ auri effecere 1500. Joachimi- cos, vel Imperiales: & 61000. drachmæ auri effece- runt 91500. thaleros, vel Joachimicos. Pondo argenti est 25. Joachimicorum, igitur 5000. pondo sunt 125000. Joachimici.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

Joshua and Zerubbabel, having built an altar, offer sacrifices, and celebrate the feast of Tabernacles, and lay the foundations of the new temple amidst trumpets and tears.

Verse 1. THE SEVENTH MONTH. Called Tisri by the Hebrews, Thot by the Chaldeans and Egyptians, corresponding partly to our September, partly to October; whence they seem to have departed from Babylon at the beginning of spring, so that they completed the journey in the space of four months: just as Ezra also departed from Babylon on the first day of the first month in the seventh year of Artaxerxes. c. 7, 1.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Josua & Zorobabel extructo altari sacrificant, & festum Tabernaculorum celebrant, ac fun- damenta templi novi inter tubas, & lachry- mas jaciunt.

Vers. 1. MENSIS SEPTIMUS. EBræis dictus Tisri, Chaldæis, & Ægyptiis Thot, respondens nostro partim Septembri, partim Octobri; unde videntur Babylone disces- fisse initio veris, ut quatuor mensium spatio iter absolverint: quemadmodum & Esdras septimo anno Artaxerxis primo die mensis primi Babylone discessit. c. 7, 1.

## 3:2
Verse 2. JOSHUA THE SON OF JOZADAK. The grandson of Jozadak by his brother, according to Ezra, who had succeeded his deceased father in the High Priesthood.

AND ZERUBBABEL THE SON OF SHEALTIEL.

Josephus, Lyranus, Dionysius, Vatablus, Mariana, Torniellus, Salianus, Cornel. à Lapide, and others make him the son of Jeconiah. But that Shealtiel, the son of Jeconiah in 1 Chron. 3, does not seem to be the father of Zerubbabel the Ethnarch: since it was predicted of Jeconiah in Jer. 22, 30 that no one of his sons would occupy the throne of David: whence that Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, listed in the line of Solomon in Matthew chapter 1, are entirely different from this Zerubbabel the Ethnarch and his parent Shealtiel: and Zerubbabel the Ethnarch, along with his parent Shealtiel, are rather to be sought in the line of Nathan in Luke chapter 3, as we teach more fully regarding the genealogy described by Luke.

Verse 2. THEY BUILT AN ALTAR] Namely, not wishing to be without sacrifices while the Temple was being built.

Latin:

Vers. 2. JOSVA FILIUS JOSEDEC. Esdra ex fratre Josedec nepos, qui patri de- functo in Pontificatu successerat.

ET ZOROBABEL FILIUS SALA- THIEL.

Hunc Jechoniæ filium faciunt Josephus, Ly- ranus, Dionysius, Vatablus, Mariana, Torniellus, Salianus, Cornel. à Lapide, & alii. Sed Sealthiel ille Jechoniæ filius 1. Par. 3. non videtur esse Pater Zo- robabelis Ethnarchæ: siquidem Jer. 22, 30. Jecho- niæ prædictum sit, quod nemo de filiis ejus thro- num Davidis occupaturus sit: unde Salathiel ille, & Zorobabel in linea Salomonis apud Matthæum cap. 1. recensiti, diversi omnino sunt ab hoc Zoro- babele Ethnarcha, & Parente ipsius Salathiele: ac Zorobabel Ethnarcha, cum Parente Salathiele quærendi potius sunt in Nathanis linea apud Lu- cam Cap. 3. ut ad genealogiam à Luca descriptam docemus uberius.

Vers. 2. ÆDIFICARUNT ALTARE] Nolentes scilicet, dum Templum struitur, à sacrificiis vacare.

## 3:7
Ver. 7. THAT THEY MIGHT BRING CEDAR WOOD FROM LIBANUS TO THE SEA OF JOPPE] Compare 2 Chron. 2:16.

Latin:

Vers. 7. UT DEFERRENT LIGNA CEDRINA DE LIBANO AD MARE JOPPE] Confer. 2. Paral. 2, 16.

## 3:11
Ver. 11. THEY SANG TOGETHER IN HYMNS AND CONFESSION TO THE LORD: FOR HE IS GOOD: FOR HIS MERCY IS FOR EVER UPON ISRAEL] See 2 Chron. 5:13 and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 11. CONCINEBANT IN HYMNIS ET CON- FESSIONE DOMINO: QUONIAM BONUS: QUO- NIAM IN ÆTERNUM MISERICORDIA EJUS SU- PER ISRAEL] Vide 2. Paral. 5, 13. & ibi dicta.

## 3:12
WHO HAD SEEN THE FORMER TEMPLE WHEN IT WAS FOUNDED, AND THIS TEMPLE IN THEIR EYES] Distinguish thus: Who had seen the former Temple, when it was founded, and this Temple in their eyes. In the Hebrew there is no need for anything except to shift the accent. This Temple did not correspond to the magnitude of that which Solomon had built. Hag. 2:3. Furthermore, the Urim and Thummim were missing, Neh. 7:65 in the Hebrew.

Latin:

QUI VIDERANT TEMPLUM PRIUS CUM FUN- DATUM ESSET, ET HOC TEMPLUM IN OCULIS EORUM] Distingue sic: Qui viderant Templum prius, cum fundatum esset & hoc Templum in oculis eorum. In Hebræo nihil opus nisi accentum trajicere. Non respondebat hoc Templum magnitudini ejus quod Salomon struxerat. Agg. 2, 2. Aberat præterea Urim & Thurim, Nehem. 7, 65. in Hebræo.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. The structure of the temple hindered until the reign of Darius, namely under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes.

Ver. 1.

NOW THEY HEARD) The first six verses of this chapter are also missing in the Greek. THE ENEMIES OF JUDA AND BENJAMIN) Especially the Cuthites, enemies from within, but sometimes feigning friendship, as Josephus teaches us.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. Structura templi præpedita usque ad Regnum Darii sub Ahasvero nempe & Artachsasta.

Vers. 1.

AUDIERUNT AUTEM) Etiam hujus capitis commata sex prima in Græcis desunt. HOSTES JUDÆ ET BENJAMINIS) Chutæi maxime, intus inimici, sed amicitiam simulantes interdum, ut Josephus nos docet.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

BEHOLD WE HAVE SACRIFICED VICTIMS) To your God, that is. 2 Kings 17:31. FROM THE DAYS OF ASAR-HADDON) He is the same who is named 2 Kings 19:37.

Latin:

ECCE NOS IMMOLAVIMUS VICTIMAS) Deo ve- stro scilicet. 2. Reg. 7, 31. A DIEBUS ASOR HADAN) Idem est qui nominatur 2. Reg. 19, 37.

Ver. 3.

WE OURSELVES ALONE WILL BUILD) For those Cuthites worshipped God in such a way that they also worshipped fictitious gods: and therefore they could not be admitted to the communion of the Temple.

NOS IPSI SOLI ÆDIFICABIMUS) Nam illi Chutæi ita Deum colebant, ut fictitios etiam Deos colerent: ideoque ad communionem Templi admitti non possent.

Ver. 5.

THEY HIRED COUNSELLORS AGAINST THEM) A frequent evil in courts: powerful freedmen asserted that all things were for sale: Tacitus says in his Histories, book 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

## 4:6
Verse 6.

BUT IN THE REIGN OF AHASUERUS) Certain Latin editions add here: he is Artaxerxes. Thus in the book of Esther, which is אחשורוש to the Hebrews, to the Greek interpreters and Josephus it is Ἀρταξέρξης, although Josephus says that he was also called Cyrus. It seems that after that Cyrus the Great, the gentile name for the Kings of the Persians was ξέρξης and Ἀρταξέρξης, besides the name they had before their reign. Diodorus Siculus in book 15 says that all Kings after him were called Artaxerxes the Memorian. Even Darius, defeated by Alexander, is called Artaxerxes by Jacchiades on Daniel 7:5. I shall say whence that is. The letter ש was accustomed to be turned by the Greeks into ξ, as שושן into Ἄξυμα: for the sound of both letters is almost the same, but transposed, just as the Dorians say συρίσδω instead of συρίζω, and the aspiration from the middle of the word Abraham was transferred by the Greeks to the beginning. Then indeed the gutturals are often omitted, as we have shown by many examples annotated to the first book on the Truth of the Christian Religion, where we deal with Ammon. Therefore אחשורוש, with the gutturals omitted, is xwerx: and because W is harder in the middle of a word, especially after a consonant that is hard by itself, for that reason it too was omitted by the Greeks, and it became Xerx, and with a Greek termination Xerxes. But Art is a certain honorific addition, like sa among the later Persians. It signifies great, according to Herodotus in book 6. A hero, according to Hesychius.
