Grotius did not dare to argue against the sources here: nor yet will I say he wrote of the Vulgate. But are different readings to be invented here too? No one would say that rashly, because all Hebrew codices agree. It remains, therefore, to say that that passage is an interpolation: however much it may be analogous to Scripture Lam. 3, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 21. NUDUS REVERTAR ILLUC.

Non in matris uterum, sed in terræ commu- nis matris finum, & gremium Sir. 40, 1. Eccl. 12, 7. quam hæc dicens Job digito monstraffe videtur.

Vers. eod. SICUT DOMINO PLACUIT ITA FACTUM EST. Vulgata hæc e LXX. Interpretibus habet. In Ebræo textu pericopa ista non reperitur. Non ausus hic est Grotius fontes arguere: neque tamen dicam scripsit vulgatæ. Num vero etiam hic diversæ lectiones fingendæ? nemo id temere dixerit, quia consonant Ebræi codices universi. Restat ergo, ut dicatur pericopam illam ἐμβολιμαῖον esse: utut Scripturæ analoga sit Thren. 3, 37.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. Upon Satan's repeated accusation, Job is struck with ulcers, he rebukes his insulting wife, he feels the sympathy of his friends.

Verse 1. AND SATAN HAD ALSO COME) Naturally, not invited.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Ad iteratam Satanæ accusationem Job ulceribus percutitur, uxorem insultantem reprehendit, amicorum συμπάθειαν sentit.

Vers. 1. VENISSET QUOQVE SATAN) Nimirum non vocatus.

## 2:2
Verse 2. HE WENT AROUND THE EARTH) For in heaven, where all things are pure, he has no right.

Latin:

Vers. 2. CIRCUIVIT TERRAM) Nam in cœlum ubi pura omnia nihil ei juris.

## 2:4
Verse 4. SKIN FOR SKIN.

This, according to the more common exposition, is indicated, that Job could easily suffer the skin of animals, servants, and children to be given up for his own: provided he saves only his own: as the Greeks in the Catena of Gregory the Great and Origen interpret. Skin for skin, i.e., every skin, all his faculties, as is immediately added by way of explanation. See Glass. Gram. S. p. 529.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PELLEM PRO PELLE.

ID secundum communiorem expositionem indicatur, Jobum facile pati potuisse, pellem animalium, servorum & filiorum pro sua ipsius tradi: dum solum suam servet: ut Græci in Caten. Greg. M. & Origenes interpretantur. Pellem pro pelle, i. e. omnem pellem, omnes facultates suas, ut statim κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν additur. Vid. Glass. Gram. S. p. 529.

## 2:6
Verse 6. SAVE HIS SOUL) I do not want you to take his life away: thus God circumscribes the boundaries of license for the evil Spirit. Matt. 8, 31. Rev. 20, 20. But Maimonides understands by soul the mind, which God does not want to be troubled in Job.

Maimonides, as also Ralbag, wish it to mean that the soul is not delivered into the hands of the Devil. Which is true of the pious soul, not the impious. But here, without doubt, soul is more correctly taken for life: which is the common opinion of the Interpreters. To save is to leave unharmed; just as he is said to give life in Hebrew, who does not take away life.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ANIMAM ILLIUS SERVA) Nolo vitam ei eripias: ita Deus malo Spiritui circumscribit licentiæ cancellos. Matth. 8, 31. Apoc. 20, 20. At Maimonides per animam mentem intelligit, quam Jobo turbari nolit Deus.

Maimonides ut & Ralbag id volunt, animam in manus Diaboli non tradi. Quod verum est de anima pia, non impia. Rectius autem hic sine dubio anima pro vita accipitur: quæ communis est Interpp. sententia. Servare est illæsam relinquere; uti vivificare dicitur Ebræis, qui vitam non adimit.

## 2:9
Verse 9. BUT HIS WIFE SAID TO HIM. Rabbis, the Chaldean, Philo, and others think this was Dinah. The LXX and Jerome derive Job's wife from the race of the Arabs. Others reconcile these two opinions by saying that after the death of Dinah he married an Arabian woman, who here was not a comforter of her husband, but a helper of the Devil: as Augustine says in Ps. 55.

BLESS GOD, AND DIE.

Which words are commonly understood as a curse: just as this word is used euphemistically in ch. 1, 11. ch. 2, 5. But Beza and Sixtus ab Amama in Anti-Barb. interpret them in a better sense. But Job's wife is excused in vain: for both her speech is directed toward impiety and despair: do you still persist in your simplicity, or in your sincerity: do you still cling to God? rather curse God, so that you may be freed by death from those most grievous pains of yours, which are more cruel than death; and Job's response sufficiently teaches that her counsel was not pious, as if, for instance, having done penance, he should bless God, nor did she meditate on anything other than euthanasia: for he vehemently rebukes her: you have spoken as one of the foolish women: and Beza himself acknowledges that the word Nabal is accustomed to denote a foolish and impious person, and that this fits this woman perfectly, if she urged her husband to curse God himself; Therefore, against the opinion of all interpreters and the very emphasis of the word, he tries to soften that word, as if it only concerned an imprudent application of counsel, against a husband who was the least of all such as he falsely gathered him to be from the magnitude of so many calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 9. DIXIT AUTEM ILLI UXOR SUA. Hanc Dinam fuisse Rabbini, Chald. Philo & alii putant. LXX. & Hieronym. Jobi uxorem ex Arabum gente deducunt. Quas duas sententias alii ita conciliant, quod post obitum Dinæ Arabicam fœminam duxerit, quæ hic non Mariti consolatrix, sed Diaboli adjutrix fuit: dicente August. in Ps. 55.

BENEDIC DEO, ET MORERE.

Quæ verba communiter de maledictione intelliguntur: uti verbum hoc κατ' εὐφημισμὸν c. 1, 11. c. 2, 5. adhibetur. Ast Beza, & Sixt. ab Amama in Anti-Barb. in meliorem partem interpretantur. Sed nequicquam excusatur uxor Jobæa: nam & oratio ejus ad impietatem, & desperationem directa est: adhuc tamen permanes in simplicitate, vel in sinceritate tua: adhuc adhæres Deo? imo maledic Deo, ut morte libereris a gravissimis illis doloribus tuis, qui morte diriores sunt; & responsio Jobi satis docet, consilium ejus non fuisse pium, ut nempe pœnitentia acta Deo benedicat, nec aliud quam εὐθανασίαν meditetur: nam vehementer redarguit eam: quasi una de stultis mulieribus loquuta es: & agnoscit ipse Beza voce Nabal stultam & impiam notari solere, idque optime huic mulieri convenire, si maritum ad Deum ipsum execrandum hortata fuit; ideo contra omnium interpretum sententiam, & ipsam vocis emphasin, emollire conatur vocem illam, ac si solum respiceret imprudentem consilii applicationem, adversus maritum minime omnium talem, qualem illum esse falso ex tot calamitatum magnitudine colligebat.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. THE THREE FRIENDS OF JOB HEARING ALL THE EVIL) Namely, as it is in the Iphigenia in Tauris of Euripides: for all those who have had some experience know the sufferings of kings.

ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE) That part of Arabia always had most excellent philosophers. Jerem. 49, 7. Baruch 3, 22. The Alcoran also mentions it.

It was agreed among the three friends of Job to visit him. Elihu, however, seems to have arrived only afterwards; or if he was present at the beginning, he visited Job of his own accord, not by agreement. Moreover, they were not only philosophers but theologians, and even prophets, as it seems to some; although no one would say that everything they said here was uttered by a prophetic spirit: because not everything can be approved in the sense in which it was uttered, and they were disapproved by God himself. For prophets are not moved by the Spirit of God in everything they say, but only in what they speak as prophets and as θεόπνευστοι (God-inspired).

Latin:

Vers. 11. AUDIENTES TRES AMICI JOB OMNE MALUM) Nempe prout est in Iphigenia Taurica Euripidis: τὰ γάρ τοι βασιλέων παθήματα Ἴσασι πάντες ὧν ἐπιστροφή τις ἦν.

ELIPHAZ THEMANITES) Habuit ea pars Arabiæ semper Philosophos præstantissimos. Jerem. 49, 7. Baruch. 3, 22. Meminit & Alcoranus.

Convenit inter tres amicos Jobi, ut ipsum invi- ferent. Elihu autem videtur deinceps demum su- pervenisse; aut si principio adfuit, proprio motu, non ex conventione Jobum visitasse. Non autem Philosophi tantum fuerunt sed Theologi imo etiam Prophetæ: ut nonnullis videtur; etsi omnia, quæ hic dixere spiritu Prophetico esse prolata nemo di- xerit: quia non probari possunt omnia eo, quo prolata sunt sensu, & a Deo ipso improbata sunt. Non enim Prophetæ in omnibus, quæcunque lo- quuntur, Spiritu Dei aguntur, sed quæ loquuntur ut Prophetæ, & θεόπνευστοι.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. Job curses the day of his birth because of his pain, and complains of the miseries of life.

Vers. 1. LET THE DAY PERISH IN WHICH I WAS BORN) Let my birthday be held among the black days. Ovid, Elegy 13, book 3: Behold, the superfluous birthday (for what was it useful to be born?) is here for its own time. Harsh one, why did you come to the years of a miserable exile? See also what follows.

This curse should neither be considered as blasphemy among the Jews, lest one judge that the Devil obtained what he wanted and that God's excuse should be neglected (c. 42, 8), nor is it to be entirely absolved from sin, since he himself acknowledges that he poured out certain things from infirmity and impatience (c. 42, 3). And there is in it a poetic amplification. For here begins the poetic manner of speaking, not that he spoke in this way at that time, but that it pleased him to express his pain in this manner when these things were committed to writing. Conf. Jerem. 20, 15, 16, 17. Coccejus says that Job looks solely to this: if a man were born for this, that in this life he should have either prosperity as a reward or evils as a punishment, it would have been better for him never to have been, and nature ought to have shuddered at such a birth. But the Jobic discourse introduces something more, and it is not merely hypothetical, like that of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 15, 19; therefore, it cannot be absolved from sin. Nor does it befit the faith of Job to believe that it would have been better never to have existed: for he believed in the resurrection of the dead and the blessed life: how then could he believe that it was better never to have existed.

Although Job is commended for patience and is set before us as an example (James 5, 11), which also shone forth in him during those greatest afflictions, he could nevertheless have his paroxysms, and have had that patience, and it could have been joined with a vehement struggle; indeed, that impatience could have arisen even in the most patient of mortals from the infirmity of the flesh and the gravity of the pain, as this curse of his birthday and other things in this book testify, even if the temptation, which was divine grace, was finally crowned with good. For he was not τελικῶς (finally) left in such a grave sin: by which he did not indeed blaspheme God directly, but cursed the day of his birth, not feeling as if it would have been better for him if he had never been, but if he had been extinguished even in his mother's womb (saving, however, his eternal salvation). Mercerus does not poorly explain the word הֹרָה as birth, to which Piscator and Coccejus agree: even if perhaps elsewhere it might always denote conception and not birth: because it is clear from the preceding verse that it is a matter of the day of birth. Truly, he desires that which is ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων (from the impossible), namely, that the day already past might perish or not be: at least that he might indicate what he would want, or what should have been wished for the embryo enclosed in the mother's womb, if that could be done or could have been accomplished by wishes. Conf. v. 10 and 11, which openly teach that he wished out of impatience that he had never been born: because he curses the night, because it did not close the doors of his womb, and complains why he did not die from the womb, which things pertain to birth, not to conception.

Latin:

CAPUT III. Job præ dolore diei nativitatis suæ maledicit, & de miseriis vitæ queritur.

Vers. 1. PEREAT DIES IN QVA NATVS SVM) Na- talis meus inter dies atros habeatur. Ovidius Elegia 13. libri 3. Ecce supervacuus (quid enim fuit utile nasci?) Ad sua natalis tempora noster adest. Dure, quid ad miseros veniebas exsulıs annos? Vide & quæ sequuntur.

MAledictio hæc neque cum Judæis blasphemiæ loco habenda, ne Diabolum, quod voluit, obtinuisse, Deique excusationem posthabendam esse, c. 42, 8. quis censeat, neque a peccato absolven- da omnino est, siquidem agnoscat ipse, se ex infir- mitate & impatientia quædam effudisse c. 42, 3. Estque in eadem amplificatio Poetica. Incipit enim hic Poeticum loquendi genus, non quod ita tum loquutus sit, sed quod libuerit dolorem suum hac ratione exprimere, cum ista scriptis commenda- rentur. Conf. Jerem. 20, 15. 16. 17. Coccejus hoc spectare Jobum unice ait, si homo ad hoc natus esset, ut in hac vita vel prospera pro præmio habeat, vel mala pro pœna, melius ipsi futurum nunquam fuisse, & debuisse naturam ad talem nativitatem cohor- rescere. Sed aliquid amplius oratio Jobica infert, nec hypothetica tantum est, qualis illa Apostoli 1. Cor. 15, 19. ideo absolvi a peccato non potest. Ne- que fidei Jobi convenit credere, melius fuisse nun- quam se extitisse : credidit enim resurrectionem mortuorum, & vitam beatam : quomodo ergo cre- dere potuit, melius esse nunquam extitisse.

Quanquam vero Jobus a patientia commende- tur, & in exemplum nobis sistatur Jac. 5, 11. quæ in maximis illis afflictionibus etiam eluxit in ipso, ha- bere tamen potuit suos paroxismos, & habuisse illam patientiam, ac cum lucta vehementi conjunctam fuisse, imo ex infirmitate carnis, & gravitate doloris impatientiam etiam subortam esse mortalium pa- tientissimo, hæc maledictio diei nativitatis, & alia in hoc libro testantur, etiamsi, quæ divina erat gra- tia, sine bono coronata tandem sit tentatio. Non enim τελικῶς relictus in peccato tam gravi fuit: quo non quidem Deum blasphemavit directe, sed diem nativitatis execratus est, non sentiens, quasi melius secum actum foret, si nunquam fuisset, sed si vel in utero matris, (salva tamen æterna salute sua) extin- ctus fuisset. Non male Mercerus verbum הֹרָה de partu explicat, cui Piscator & Coccejus annuit: etiam- si forte alibi non partum sed conceptionem notaret semper: quia ex antecedenti commate liquet de die nativitatis agi. Nimirum optat id quod ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων est, ut nempe dies jam præterita pereat, vel non sit: Saltim ut indicet, quid vellet, aut quid optandum sibi in utero matris concluso embryoni fuisset, si fieri id posset, aut votis confici potuisset. Conf. v. 10. & 11. qui aperte docent, id optasse præ impatientia ut natus nunquam esset: quia nocti ma- ledicit, quod non concluserit ostia ventris sui, & que- ritur, quare non ab utero mortuus sit, quæ ad nativita- tem pertinent, non ad conceptionem.

## 3:5
Verf. 5. AND LET IT BE WRAPPED IN BITTERNESS) Certain learned men think that כמרירי is put here with the Resch repeated for כמרי, so that the sense may be, let the priests of the day, i. e. those who distinguish the fates of days, make this terrible, i. e. mark it as terrible.

Why should the reading of the Hebrew Codices not be retained: Ter- reant eum כמרירי יום, the blacknesses of the day, that is, black days, from כמך, which signifies to be blackened or clad in mourning? As Tremellius, Piscator, Coccejus, and B. Luther explain: The Vulgate rendered it, let it be wrapped in bitterness, not because it read כמרי יום with a כ, as if from the root מרר to be bitter, as Lud. Capellus wishes in his Critica, but because it pleased it to express the sense, not to render word for word. Mr. D. Schmidius renders it, let them terrify him, as the bitternesses of the day, who would more truly be called the bitternesses of the day than days. Nor is there any cause why we should here admit the new ἕυρημα of either Grotius or Capellus in place of the ancient reading, since the customary reading is perfectly consistent with itself.

Latin:

Verf. 5. ET INVOLVATUR AMARITUDINE) Eruditi quidam putant כמרירי hic poni Resch repetita pro כמרי, ut sensus sit, Sa- cerdotes diei, i. e. qui dierum fata distinguunt, hunc terrificent, i. e. an- notent tanquam terribilem.

Quidni retineri possit lectio Ebræorum Codicum: Ter- reant eum כמרירי יום atrores diei, h.e. dies atri, a כמך quod atratum, pullatum esse significat? uti Tremellius, Pisca- tor, Coccejus, B. Luther, exponunt: Vulgatus reddidit, invol- vatur amaritudine, non quod legerit כמרי יום per כ, quasi a radice מרר amarum esse, uti vult Lud. Capellus in Critic. sed quod sensum exprimere placuerit, non verbum verbo reddere. Dn. D. Schmidius reddit, terreant eum, tanquam amaritudines diei, qui verius amaritudines diei, quam dies appelletur. Nec ulle causa est, cur hic vel Grotii vel Capelli novum ἕυρημα pro antiqua lectione admittamus, quum optime sibi constet usitata lectio.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. MALEDICANT EI) It may be they pierce him, from נקב, that is, ὀβολίζωσι.

WHO ARE PREPARED TO RAISE UP) That is, those who raise up monsters with magical incantations. It is a metaphor. Thus רפאים signifies both shades and sea monsters.

They would more rightly rouse the whale, that is, go fishing in the deep where whales are wont to encroach: or they would face danger. Conf. c. 41, 1. He who is to fight with beasts in the morning surely wishes the night to be twice or thrice as long: But, he says, this night is not pleasant and agreeable to them either, but rather hateful and execrable. Thus Coccejus. But the blessed Scultetus rendered the whole verse most excellently thus: Let the illuminators of the days (i. e., lightnings) pierce or transfix it (the night), and those who are prepared to rouse the whale (i. e., winds and whirlwinds, which by violently agitating the sea rouse the whales within it). Thus the preceding and following parts agree properly. However, that impiety is not to be imputed to Job with Dievius, as if he were compelling Satan to incite those prepared to curse more by his fury: LET THE CURSERS OF THE DAY CURSE IT, THOSE WHO ARE PREPARED TO ROUSE LEVIATHAN, or the Demon.

Latin:

Vers. 8. MALEDICANT EI) Potest esse perfodiant, a נקב, id est, ὀβολίζωσι.

QVI PARATI SVNT SVSCITARE) Id est, qui magicis canti- bus monstra suscitant. Est Metaphora. Sic רפאים, & manes si- gnificat, & monstra marina.

Rectius excitaturi balænam, hoc est, piscatum ituri in alto, ubi balænæ ingruere solent: vel discrimen adituri. Conf. c. 41, 1. Qui cum bestiis mane decertaturus sit, profecto optat, noctem duplo vel triplo esse longiorem: At nec illis, inquit, grata & jucunda sit hæc nox, sed odiosa potius & exe- crabilis. Ita Coccejus. Optime autem B. Scultetus versum totum sic reddidit: Perfodiant s. configant eam (noctem) illuminatores dierum, i. e. fulgura) & qui parati sunt excitare cætum, (i. e. venti & turbines, qui vehementer commoven do mare & balænas in eo suscitant) Sic antetedentia & con- sequentia probe conveniunt. Non autem Jobo cum Dievio ea affricanda est impietas, quasi Satanam compeller, ut pa- ratos ad execrandum magis furore suo excitet: MALEDI- CANT EI EXECRATORES DIEI, EOS QVI PARA- TI SUNT EXCITA LEVIATHAN, vel Dæmon.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. DORMIENS SILEREM) Death is called the sleep of the body by the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 13. DORMIENS SILEREM) Mors, somnus corporis He- bræis dicitur.

## 3:14
Vers. 14. WHO BUILD FOR THEMSELVES SOLITUDES) The LXX [render it] ἃ ἀγαυριῶντο ἐπὶ ξίφεσιν. For חרבות also signifies swords. Thus Ps. 9, 7. חרבות: others translate it solitudes: where the LXX [have] αἱ ῥομφαῖαι.

It is more correct to speak of the zeal for building sepulchres, which were erected in mountains and solitudes, or the desolate places of the earth which have never been inhabited, so that they might be furnished with buildings or palaces: which latter explanation is favored by the periphrasis of the Princes, v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 14. QVI ÆDIFICANT SIBI SOLITVDINES) LXX. ἅ ἀγαυριῶντο ἐπὶ ξίφεσιν. Nam חרבות etiam gladios significat. Sic Pf. 9, 7. חרבות: alii vertunt solitudines: ubi LXX. αἱ ῥομφαῖαι.

Rectius de studio ædificandi sepulcra, quæ in montibus & solitudinibq extruebantur, vel desolata terræ (loca) quæ nun- quam habitata sunt, ut ædificiis, aut palatiis instruantur: cui postremæ explicationi περίφρασις Principum v. 15. favet.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Eliphaz accuses Job of impatience and hypocrisy, claiming that he is being scourged on account of his sins.

Vers. 1. RESPONDENS AUTEM ELIPHAZ) The sentiment which Euripides expresses thus: Ἐν τοῖς κακοῖσι συγγένει᾽ ὅταν παρῇ Τραχεῖα κ᾽ ὀξύθυμῷ, ἀμαθίαν ἔχει, little occurred to his mind. In Aeschylus, when Oceanus says: Οὔκει Προμηθεῦ τοῦτο γινώσκεις, ὅτι Ὀργῆς νοσέσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι; Prometheus replies: Ἐάν τις ἐν καιρῷ γε μαλθάσσῃ κέαρ Καὶ μὴ σφριγῶντα θυμὸν ἰσχναίνῃ βίᾳ.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Eliphaz Jobum arguit impatientiæ, & hypocriseos, qui propter peccata sua flagelletur.

Vers. 1. RESPONDENS AUTEM ELIPHAZ) Parum ei in men- tem venit sententia, quam sic effert Euripides: Ἐν τοῖς κακοῖσι συγγένει᾽ ὅταν παρῇ Τραχεῖα κ᾽ ὀξύθυμῷ, ἀμαθίαν ἔχει. Apud Æschylum dicenti Oceano: Οὔκει Προμηθεῦ τοῦτο γινώσκεις, ὅτι Ὀργῆς νοσέσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι; Respondet Prometheus: Ἐάν τις ἐν καιρῷ γε μαλθάσσῃ κέαρ Καὶ μὴ σφριγῶντα θυμὸν ἰσχναίνῃ βίᾳ.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. WHERE IS THY FEAR, &c.

Ludovicus de Dieu correctly renders κατὰ πόδα; Is not your fear (your piety) your confidence, your hope (it was: so that it is an asyndeton) & the integrity of your ways? where I would prefer to repeat the predicate ἀπὸ κοινῶ, rather than to arrange the transposition thus; is not your piety, & the integrity of your ways, your confidence, your hope? although the sense comes to the same thing, to decide with Dievius. It is doubtless from this that you are now so dismayed (Eliphaz wishes to say) because in your piety was your confidence & your hope, & the integrity of your ways (which you imagine for yourself) was your confidence, & your hope. (i.e., because you attributed too much to your piety & the integrity of your ways, & placed your confidence in it: or also to explain it thus, Is not your piety, (which you yourself did not hesitate to presume about yourself) so much your confidence & hope, that you believed all your ways to be mere integrity, and were thus persuaded that you could deservedly place your confidence in it.

Latin:

Vers. 6. UBI EST TIMOR TUUS, &c.

Recte Ludovicus de Dieu reddit κατὰ πόδα; Annon timor tuus (pietas tua) fiducia tua, spes tua (erat: ut asyndeton sit) & integritas viarum tuarum? ubi ἀπὸ κοινῶ prædicatum re- petere malim, quam trajectionem ita ordinandam; annon pietas tua, & integritas viarum tuarum, fiducia tua, spes tua erat? licet eodem redeat sensus, cum Dievio statuere. Ni- mirum inde est, quod adeo jam consternaris (vult Eliphaz dicere) quia in pietate tua fiducia tua & spes tua fuit, & inte- gritas viarum tuarum (quam tibi imaginaris) fiducia tua, & spes tua fuit. (h.e. quia nimium quantum pietati & integri- tati viarum tuarum tribuisti, & in ea fiduciam habuisti: vel etiam h. m. explicare, Annon pietas tua, (quam ipse de te præsumere non dubitasti)ita fiducia & spes tua fuit, ut omnes vias tuas meram integritatem esse credideris, adeoque fidu- ciam te merito in ea locare posse perfuasus fueris.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. THE ROARING OF THE LION AND THE VOICE OF THE LIONESS AND THE TEETH OF THE YOUNG LIONS) By these similarities, wicked and rapacious men are usually denoted. Ps. 34, 10. 58, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 10. RUGITUS LEONIS ET VOX LEÆNÆ ET DENTES CATULORUM) His similibus denotari solent homines improbi ac rapaces. Ps. 34, 10. 58, 6.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. AND ALL MY BONES. In Hebrew AND THE MULTITUDE OF MY BONES YOU TERRIFY, as Mercerus rendered it. Yet by the multitude of bones, all bones can be understood, because bones are many, so that there is no need for that emendation of Dievius: Most of my bones.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ET OMNIA OSSA MEA. In Ebr. ET MULTITUDINEM OSSIUM MEORUM PERTERREFACIS, ut Mercerus reddi- dit. Per multitudinem tamen ossium omnia ossa intelligi possunt, quia ossa multa sunt, ut non opus sit, illa emen- datione Dievii: Pleraque ossa mea.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. AND I HEARD A VOICE AS OF A GENTLE BREEZE) That is the בת קול, through which God in those times often revealed His will to pious men. See 1 Kings 14, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ET VOCEM QVASI AVRÆ LENTIS AUDIVI) Ea est בת קול, per quam Deus illis temporibus sæpe voluntatem suam piis hominibus patefaciebat. Vid. 1. Reg. 14, 12.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

Eliphaz teaches that God punishes only the impious and the wicked, and shows grace to the miserable and the suffering.

Vers. 1. AND TO ANY OF THE SAINTS) LXX. if you shall see any of the holy angels. Angels are usually understood by the name of Saints Dan. 8, 13. Zach. 14, 5. Eliphaz boasts of heavenly visions above 4, 16. And see, he says, whether anything similar is going to happen to you, as if to say, you are unworthy.

This interpretation is certainly better than the forced explanation of the Papists: who try to carve out the invocation of Saints from this. Which has been done by Thomas, Lyranus, Jodocus Coccius, Alphonsus de Castro, Bellarmine, Jacobus Tirinus, & others, whence it is a wonder that Grotius, who is otherwise willingly Papist-leaning, did not gratify his Papists here. But perhaps he observed how invalid that argument is, since those words are Eliphaz's, and not Job's, or the sacred writer's: and in the Hebrew they are proposed not as a command, but interrogatively, to whom of the Saints will you look? which interrogation has the force of a negation; as the Chaldean correctly expressed, call, do not invoke, if there is anyone who will answer you? (no one will answer) & to whom of the saints will you look? (you will be able to look to none of the Saints) which are opposed to the invocation of Saints, and do not prove it. Whence Olympiodorus in the Catena, according to the Latin interpretation of the Jesuit Paulus Comitolus, explains it thus; Why do you speak beyond your dignity? and that too, being a man, for in this man is inferior to God, that not only can you neither see Him nor comprehend Him, but also, that even if called upon a thousand times by you, He will not answer. Why do I speak of God, since not even His angels can be affected by our emotion. Which is also the explanation of Mercerus and Vatablus, Call upon any of the angels, and cry out to him, will even the least of them answer you, will he deign to honor you with his speech and address? You will certainly find no one, you see how far you are from God: since not even the angels, who are far inferior to God, will speak to you, if you cry out to them, because of the distance that is between you and them. Therefore not without merit does Mercerus say it is mere delirium that they have applied this passage to the invocation of Saints, since everyone sees that this is irony, and however you understand it, it cannot be applied to that. From which explanation of Olympiodorus, Mercerus, and Vatablus, the Grotian one does not depart much, likewise taking it as referring to the angels.

Although it is not necessary to take it as referring to deceased Saints, nor to angels. Indeed, from the context, both from the end of the preceding chapter and from the antithesis added here, it appears sufficiently that the discourse is about saints acting on earth: namely, that no one of them can be named who has been punished in this way, but that such punishments await only the wicked. Therefore, the blessed Scultetus, our formerly honorable friend, rendered it best in Analys. typic. Conc. 32. Name I pray (someone who was pious and yet was so afflicted by God) is there anyone who will answer you, (or attest, or who is like you) & to whom of the saints will you look? (whose example will you be able to produce?) Which sense is also that of the blessed Luther in his marginal gloss, and among the Papists, Guil. Estius, the learned interpreter, approves of it: look around, he says in his golden notes, whether any Saint & just man is scourged by God as you are, and when you have found no one, understand from these blows that you are not just; which sense he says is most manifest from the preceding and following verses. Others explain it as referring to saints on earth, but in another sense, namely that Job cannot call any of them to the patronage of his cause, as Junius, Piscator, and also the Belgian interpreters in their annotations to this place, or that no one of the Saints can be named who has murmured against God in the cross in such a way, as R. Aben-Ezra, R. Solomon Jarchi, and Nachman interpret. Coccejus understands this of the saints, both angels and men on earth: but a little differently: To which of the saints will you turn: so that, namely, you may escape the judgment and wrath of God. He will reject you, who has been unwilling to flee to Him, but to his Creator and Sanctifier. But why do we linger in recounting these and the opinions of others, when it is now in the open that Grotius, who wished to be unique, has by no means attained the true sense, and that most others (if you except the Papists, patrons of angel-worship or saint-worship) have explained it more conveniently. Moreover, against the Papists, blessed Gerhard may be compared here in his Loci Communes on death, § 452.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

Eliphaz Deum impios & iniquos solum punire, mi- seris, & patientibus gratiam exhibere docet.

Vers. 1. ET AD ALIQVEM SANCTORVM) LXX. ἕι τινα ἀγ- γέλων ἁγίων ὄψῃ. Solent nomine Sanctorum intelligi Angeli Dan. 8, 13. Zach. 14, 5. Jactat se Eliphaz ob visa cœlestia supra 4, 16. Et vide, ait, an quid tibi simile sit eventurum quasi dicat, indignus es.

Melior est sane hæc interpretatio Pontificiorum confi- sta explicatione: qui hinc Sanctorum invocationem ex- sculpere conantur. Quod a Thoma, Lyrano, Jodoco Coc- cio, Alphonso de Castro, Bellarmino, Jacobo Tirino, & aliis factum, unde mirum, quod Grotius, libenter alias Papi- zans, hic Papistis suis gratificatus non fuerit. Sed obser- vavit fortassis, quam invalidum illud Argumentum sit, si- quidem verba illa Eliphazi sint, non autem Jobi, vel Scri- ptoris libri sacri: & in Ebræo non imperandi modo, sed in- terrogative proponantur, ad quem de Sanctis respicies? quæ interrogatio vim negandi habet; uti Chaldæus recte expressit, voca, non invoca, si quis est, qui tibi respondeat? (nullus respondebit) & ad quem de sanctis respicies? (ad nullum Sanctorum respicere poteris) quæ invocationi Sanctorum adversantur, non autem eam probant. Unde Olympiodorus in Catena, secundum interpretationem Latinam Pauli Comitoli Jesuitæ, ita explicat; Quid præter dignitatem loqueris? idque homo cum sis, in eo enim est ho- mo inferior Deo, ut non solum nec videre illum nec compre- bendere queas, sed etiam, ut nec millies a te inclamatus re- sponsurus sit. Quid loquor Deum, quandoquidem nec ejus Angelinostrum possunt affectum incurrere. Quæ etiam re- dit Merceri, & Vatabli explicatio, Voca Angelorum ali- quem, & eum inclama, an vero vel minimus eorum tibi re- spondebit, te suo sermone & alloquio dignabitur? Nullum sane reperies, vides quantum a Deo distes: cum ne Angeli quidem Deo longe inferiores te allocuturi sint, si ad eos cla- mes ob distantiam, quæ est inter te & illos. Ideo non im- merito Mercerus merum delirium esse dicit, quod hunc locum ad Sanctorum invocationem adhibuerint, cum nemo non videat hic ironiam esse, & quoquo modo intelli- gas, eo applicari non posse. A qua Olympiodori, Merceri & Vatabli explicatione non multum abit Grotiana, iti- dem de Angelis ea accipiens.

Quanquam nec de defunctis Sanctis, nec de Angelis ea accipere necessum sit. Imo ex contextu, cum capitis præcedentis fine, tum subjuncta hic ἀντιθέσει appareat satis, de sanctis in terra agentibus sermonem esse: quod nempe nemo eorum nominari possit, qui ste punitus fuerit, sed pœna ejusmodi solum improbos maneant. Ideo optime reddidit B. Scultetus, amicus quondam noster honorandus Analys. typic. Conc. 32. Nomina quæso (aliquem qui pius fuerit & tamen ita a Deo afflictus sit) num sit qui respondeat tibi, (vel attestetur, vel qui similis sit tibi) & ad quem san- ctorum respicies? (cujus exemplum producere poteris?) Qui sensus etiam B. Lutheri est in glossa marginali, ac e Papistis Guil. Estio erudito interpreti sese probat: circum- spice, inquit in notis aureis, an aliquis Sanctus & justus ita a Deo flagelletur, sicut tu, & cum neminem inveneris,intelli- ge ex his plagis, te non esse justum; quem sensum manife- stissimum esse, ait, ex præcedentibus & consequentibus. Alii de sanctis in terra, sed alio sensu, explicant, quod nempe nullum eorum in patrocinium sententiæ suæ advo- care possit Job, uti Junius, Piscator, etiam Belgici in- terpretes in annotat. ad h. l. vel quod nemo nominari possit Sanctorum, qui ita in cruce Deo obmurmuraverit, ut R. Aben - Esra, R. Salomo Jarchi, & Nachman. in terpretantur. Coccejus de Sanctis cum Angelis, tum hominibus in terra intelligit : Sed paulo aliter : Ad quem sanctorum respicies : ut scil. evadas Dei ju- dicium & iram. Rejiciet ille te, qui noluerit ad se con- fugi, sed ad creatorem & Sanctificatorem suum. Sed quid his aliorumque opinionibus recensendis im- moramur, quum in aprico jam sit, Grotium, qui singularis esse voluit, neutiquam verum assequu- tum esse sensum, ac cæteros plerosque (si à Papi- stis abeas, Angelolatriæ, vel Hagiolatriæ Patronis) convenientius explicasse. Conferri autem adver- sus Pontificios hic poterit B. Gerhardus LL. CC. de morte §. 452.

Verse 3.

I HAVE SEEN THE FOOL TAKING ROOT) The sense is the same as in Psalm 37. AND I CURSED HIS BEAUTY IMMEDIATELY) That is, I wished him ill.

EGO VIDI STULTUM FIRMA RADICE) Sensus idem qui in Psalm. 37. ET MALEDIXI PULCHRITUDINI EJUS STATIM) Id est, male ei ominatus sum.

Verse 4.

THEY SHALL BE CRUSHED IN THE GATE) They shall lose their case in judgment. Psalm 109:7.
