Vers. 4.

CONTERENTUR IN PORTA) Causa cadent in Judi- cio. Psal. 109, 7.

## 5:7
Verse 7. AND THE BIRD TO FLY.

Ludovicus de Dieu: AND SPARKS WOULD MAKE HIM FLY ON HIGH. That is, such is his lightness and vanity that even a single spark can carry him away with it. But this sense is confused: nor is the pronoun HIM held in the text, and the common interpretation, from which he rashly departs, agrees perfectly. For as birds tire themselves by flying, so does man by labor. I do not see why it cannot be rendered: AND THE SONS OF BIRDS FLY ON HIGH. See Schindler on the word רֶשֶׁף.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET AVIS AD VOLATUM.

Ludovicus de Dieu : ET SCINTILLÆ EUM IN ALTUM EVOLARE FACERENT. Id est, tanta est levitatis & vanitatis, ut vel sola scintilla eum secum abripere queant. Sed hic sensus perplexus est : nec pronomen EUM in textu habetur, & com- munis interpretatio, à qua temere abit, optime congruit. Nam ut aves volando se fatigant, ita ho- mo labore. Non video cur non reddi possit: ET FILII AVIUM SUBLIME VOLANT. Vide Schindler. in voce רֶשֶׁף.

## 5:9
Verse 9.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

## 5:10
WHO GIVES RAIN UPON THE FACE OF THE EARTH) A sign of divine favor.

Mr. Dr. Schmied has rendered the sense not unaptly from the preceding and following context: that GOD refreshes men fixed to the earth and afflicted, lying in the streets, with the rain of His blessing, so that He also sets the humble on high, and those who mourn are exalted with salvation.

Latin:

QVI DAT PLUVIAM SUPER FACIEM TERRÆ) Signum divini favoris.

Sensum non inconcinne ex antecedentibus, & consequentibus reddidit Dn. D. Schmied : quod DEUS homines terræ affixos, & afflictos in plateis ja- centes pluvia suæ benedictionis recreet, ita ut ponat eti- am humiles in alto, & atrati exaltentur salute.

## 5:12
Verse 12. WHAT THEY HAD BEGUN.

In Hebrew it is תּוּשִׁיָּה, Junius renders it ANYTHING. R. Levi interprets it as ordination and disposition. Pagninus as what they had decreed. Dievius seeks the sense from the Ethiopian: AND THEIR HANDS SHALL NOT PERFORM WISDOM, they shall be able to effect nothing wisely with their hands. But Coccejus rightly rendered it ANYTHING of a thing. תּוּשִׁיָּה as יֵשׁ from אֵוּן from אִין. Aben-Ezra also refers it to the root יש and so others commonly. They shall not perform anything according to their vow, or what they plot or have meditated; their counsels and efforts shall be void and vain.

Latin:

Vers. 12. QUOD CEPERANT.

In Ebræo est תּוּשִׁיָּה, Junius reddit QUIC- QUAM. R. Levi interpretatur ordinationem & dispositionem. Pagninus quod decreverant. Die- vius ex Æthiopia sensum petit: ET NON FA- CIENT MANUS EORUM SAPIENTIAM, nihil manibus suis sapienter efficere poterunt. Sed recte Coccejus reddidit QUICQUAM Rei. תּוּשִׁיָּה ut יֵשׁ à אֵוּן ab אִין. Aben-Ezra etiam re- fert ad Radicem יש & ita alii communiter. Non facient quicquam ex voto, vel quod machinantur, aut meditati sunt : irrita & evanida erunt eorum consilia, & molimina.

## 5:13
Ver. 13. WHO TAKES THE WISE IN THEIR CRAFTINESS) He catches them in their own nets. The Greeks here: ὁ καταλαμβάνων σοφοὺς ἐν τῇ φρονήσει. Paul 1 Cor. 3, 19: ὁ δρασσόμενος τοὺς Σοφοὺς ἐν τῇ πανεργίᾳ ἀυτῶν.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QVI APPREHENDIT SAPIENTES IN ASTUTIA EORUM) Suis eos retibus capit. Græci hic : ὁ καταλαμβάνων σοφοὺς ἐν τῇ φρονήσει. Paulus 1. Cor. 3, 19. ὁ δρασσόμενος τοὺς Σοφοὺς ἐν τῇ πανεργίᾳ ἀυτῶν.

## 5:16
Ver. 16. BUT INIQUITY SHALL STOP ITS MOUTH) The same words in Psalm 107, 43.

Latin:

Vers. 16. INIQVITAS AUTEM CONTRAHET OS SUUM) Eadem verba in Psalm. 107, 43.

## 5:17
Ver. 17. BLESSED IS THE MAN WHOM GOD CORRECTS)

A similar passage is in James 1, 12, but there the discourse is more about the adversities through which the pious are tested, here about those through which the wicked are corrected.

Latin:

Vers. 17. BEATUS HOMO QVI CORRIPITUR A DEO)

Simile apud Jacobum 1, 12. sed ibi magis de adversis per quæ pii explorantur, hic de iis per quæ pravi corrigun- tur, sermo est.

## 5:21
Ver. 21. FROM THE SCOURGE OF THE TONGUE)

Better, when the tongue was raging: that is, calumny: thus it follows concerning the waster, when he shall come.

Latin:

Vers. 21. A FLAGELLO LINGVÆ)

Melius, cum gras- sabatur lingua: id est, calumnia : ita sequitur de vastatore, cum venerit.

## 5:23
Ver. 23. WITH THE STONES OF THE FIELDS SHALL BE THY COVENANT)

The stones of the field will not hurt you even if you walk with bare feet. Others more correctly interpret it concerning the fertility of the fields: the stony field will yield abundant fruits as if by a covenant, Deut. 22, 13; Job 29, 6; or concerning the security of the fields: your fields and their produce will be safe from injury, as if fortified by stones, their boundaries will not be moved, nor will anyone stone them, 2 Kings 3, 25; because it is added: and the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you, that is, they will not devastate your fields.

Latin:

Vers. 23. CVM LAPIDIBVS REGIONUM PACTVM TVVM)

Lapides agri te quamvis nudis pedibus inceden- tem non lædent. Rectius de agrorum fertilitate alii : ager lapi- dosus quasi ex fœdere uberes fructus feret, Deut. 22, 13. Job. 29, 6. vel de agrorum securitate : agri tui eo- rumque proventus ab injuria turi erunt, quasi lapi- dibus muniti, limites eorum non movebuntur, nec quisquam eos lapidabit, 2. Reg. 3, 25. quia additur: & bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt tibi, id est, agros tuos non devastabunt.

## 5:24
Ver. 24. THOU SHALT NOT SIN.

So also Junius, IF THOU SHALT NOT SIN. Dievius and Coccejus, you shall not be frustrated, you shall not find yourself destitute of necessities: because Dievius thinks that חטא properly denotes a defect and lack from the Ethiopic language: But there is no reason why we should descend from the commonly accepted meaning of the word among the Hebrews to an Ethiopic one unused in Hebraism.

Latin:

Vers. 24. NON PECCABIS.

Ita etiam Junius, SI NON PECCABIS. Die- vius, & Coccejus, non frustraberis, non invenies te de- stitutum necessariis: quia חטא proprie defectum & carentiam notare ex lingua Æthiopica putat Die- vius: Sed non est causa cur a vulgata significatione vocis apud Ebræos recepta ad Æthiopicam in E- braismo inusitatam descendamus.

## 5:26
Ver. 26. THOU SHALT ENTER INTO THE GRAVE IN ABUNDANCE.

More correctly in OLD AGE. Dievius, from the Ethiopic language, with A CRY, with the applause and acclamation of others. He denies that the word occurs for OLD AGE. But the Talmudists so accept כלח and Rabbi Solomon, and most others explain it thus from Job 30, 2. Nachmanides' interpretation from כ and לח ὡς χλωρὸς as green and juicy is not to be approved. For it is not read כְּלַח but כֶּלַח.

Latin:

Vers. 26. INGREDIERIS IN ABUNDANTIA SE- PULCHRUM.

Rectius in SENIO. Dievius ex Æthiopica lingua, cum CLAMORE, cum plausu & acclamatione alio- rum. Negat vocem pro SENIO occurrere. Sed Talmudici sic accipiunt כלח & Rabbi Salomo, & plerique alii sic explicant e Job. 30, 2. Nachmani- dis interpretatio e כ & לח ὡς χλωρὸς tanquam vi- ridis & succosus non probanda est. Non enim כְּלַח sed כֶּלַח legitur.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

Job, describing the gravity of the misery on account of which he desires death, reproves his friends.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Job gravitatem miseriæ, ob quam mortem optat, describens, amicos suos redarguit.

## 6:2
Ver. 2. AND CALAMITY) In Hebrew הַוָּתִי: which word exists neither in the Law nor in the older Prophets. And therefore it can contribute to the indications of the time when this book was written.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET CALAMITAS) In Hebræo הַוָּתִי: quæ vox neque in lege exstat, neque in vetustioribus Prophetis. Ideo- que potest accedere ad indicia temporis quo scriptus hic liber.

## 6:5
Ver. 5. DOTH THE WILD ASS BRAY WHEN HE HATH GRASS: OR LOWETH THE OX WHEN HE HATH STOOD BEFORE A FULL MANGER?

Vatablus and Mercerus, along with Rambam, Ralbag, R. Solomon, and Abraham Perizol, correctly express the sense: do you think that I complain without cause, when not even brute animals complain when they have what they desire? The explanation of Piscator and Tremellius can be joined to this: if you were comforting me as would be fitting, I would not complain, just as the wild ass and the ox do not cry out when fodder is given to them. For if Job had what he desired—health and fortune that was at least tolerable, or even in this his pain some refreshment, or at least solid consolation—he would not complain, just as the wild ass does not bray in the pastures, and the ox does not low at the manger.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NUNQUID RUGIET ONAGER CUM HABUERIT HERBAM: AUT MU- GIET BOS CUM ANTE PRÆSEPE PLE- NUM STETERIT?

Sensus recte exprimit Vatabl. & Mercerus cum Rambam, Ralbag. R. Salom. Abraham Perizolid. putasne me sine causa conqueri, quum ne bruta qui- dem conquerantur, quum habent, quod optant. Con- jungi potest Piscat. & Tremellii explicatio, si vos me, ut conveniens esset, consolaremini, non con- quererer, sicut onager, & bos non clamant, quan- do ipsis datur pabulum. Nam si haberet quod optabat Job valetudinem & fortunam utcunque tolerabilem, vel etiam in hoc suo dolore refocilla- tionem, aut saltem solidam consolationem, non quereretur, uti onager in pascuis, bos ad præsepe non rugit, aut mugit.

## 6:6
Ver. 6. OR CAN THAT WHICH IS UNSAVORY BE EATEN.

These words specifically refer to the insipid consolation of his friends: Is that which is tasteless eaten without salt? Is there any flavor in the white of an egg? The Hebrews, with the agreement of Pagninus, Tremellius, Piscator, Mercerus, Cocceius, Luther, and Schmidius, interpret חלמות from the Talmudic language as the yolk of an egg; however, the Vulgate ineptly renders the latter clause, 'or can anyone taste that which when tasted brings death.'

Latin:

Vers. 6. AUT POTERIT COMEDI INSULSUM.

Hæc insulsam amicorum consolationem pecu- liariter respiciunt: Num comeditur insipidum sine sale? num est sapor in albumine vitelli? חלמות ex lingua Talmudica interpretantur E- bræi de vitello ovi annuente Pagnin. Tremell. Pi- scat. Mercer. Coccejo, Luthero, Schmidio, inepte vero Vulgat. posterius comma reddit, aut po- test aliquis gustare quod gustatum adfert mor- tem.

## 6:7
Ver. 7. THE THINGS WHICH BEFORE MY SOUL REFUSED TO TOUCH, NOW FOR ANGUISH ARE MY MEAT)

He translates כִּדְוֵי as 'for anguish,' from the Hebrew דָּוֶה, which signifies infirmity. Others prefer it to be a Chaldean word which can be rendered as 'in place of': so that the sense may be, 'the things which I formerly would not have tolerated, these are now set before me in place of food,' that is, for consolation.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVÆ PRIUS NOLEBAT TANGERE ANIMA MEA, NUNC PRÆ ANGUSTIA CIBI MEI SVNT)

כִּדְוֵי ver- tit præ angustia, ex Hebræo דָּוֶה, quod infirmitatem signi- ficat. Alii malunt Chaldaicam esse vocem quæ per vice reddi possit: ut sensus sit: quæ olim non eram toleraturus, ea nunc mihi apponuntur vice cibi, id est, pro solatio.

## 6:10
Ver. 10. THAT HE WHO AFFLICTS ME WITH PAIN MAY NOT SPARE: NOR WILL I CONTRADICT THE WORDS OF THE HOLY ONE.

The sense is: And let my consolation be this, that I may grow stiff in pain (the rigor of death) and that He may not spare: because or rather although I have not hidden the words of the Holy One, I have not suppressed them within my heart. Cf. Schmied.

Latin:

Vers. 10. UT AFFLIGENS ME DOLORE NON PARCAT: NEC CONTRADICAM SERMO- NIBUS SANCTI.

Sensus est: Et fiat adhuc consolatio mea, ut obri- gescam in dolore (rigore mortis) nec parcat: quia vel quamvis potius non celavi verba sancti, non sup- pressi intra cor meum. Conf. Schmied.

## 6:13
AND MY KINSMEN ALSO HAVE WITHDRAWN FROM ME) תושׁיה which he translates here as kinsmen, seems rather to denote the power of subsistence. Therefore the sense is: BUT NOT MY HELP IN ME, AND SUBSTANCE IS TAKEN AWAY, that everything by which he could be helped is lacking to him, even substance itself almost fails. Ludov. de Dieu, even counsel is driven away from me: but the Hebrew word imports something more.

Latin:

Verf. 13. ET NECESSARII QVOQVE MEI RECES- SERUNT A ME) תושׁיה quod hic neceffarios vertit, vim subsistendi potius videtur denotare. Ideo sensus est: SED NON AUXILIUM MEUM IN ME, & SUBSTANTIA SUBLA- TA EST, quod omne, quo juvari poterat, ipsi defit, etiam ipsa substantia deficiat pene. Ludov. de Dieu, etiam confilium expulsum est à me: sed Ebr. vox aliquid amplius importat.

## 6:14
HE WHO TAKES AWAY MERCY FROM HIS FRIEND, FORSAKES THE FEAR OF THE LORD) In the Hebrew: he will forsake. The sense is: those who treat an unhappy friend so cruelly will easily also shake off all reverence for God. Grotius rightly adheres to the Vulgate. Dievius is singular after his own fashion, but without cause. There is no reason why the things he notes should be brought forward.

Latin:

Verf. 14. QVI TOLLIT AB AMICO SVO MISERI- CORDIAM, TIMOREM DOMINI DERELINQVIT) In Hebræo: derelinquet. Sensus est: qui amicum infelicem tam crudeliter tractant, facile etiam Dei omnem reveren- tiam excutient. Recte vulgatæ inhæret Grotius. Singularis est pro more suo, sed citra causam Dievius. Non est, quod adducantur, quæ notat.

## 6:16
Ver. 16.

WHO FEAR THE FROST, THE SNOW SHALL FALL UPON THEM) The sense in the Hebrew is more convenient: He had called his friends like torrents which flow turbid for a long time because of the ice and snow melted into them: But (as the following verse intends) when summer has come they fail completely. An excellent simile pertaining to those who do not show themselves as friends in adverse circumstances. The words thus, with Mercer and Amama in Anti-Barb. and Biblica preceding, compare. B. Scultetus rendered it word for word: Which (torrents) grow black (or are darkened covered) with ice, upon which the snow hides itself (they are covered with snow) or spreads itself. At which time it grows warm, they are extinguished in their place, the paths of their journey turn aside (from their channel) they go up into the desert (cf. Job 12:24) and shall perish. Travelers from Tema (setting out from Tema, traveling in hot regions) see and expect them (but) are confounded (they come) to that (place or torrent) they were ashamed (when they see themselves deceived,) etc. Compare also Junius, Piscator, the English and Genevan, as also the Spanish and Tigurine and Italian version, which easily agree here. These wish the protasis of the simile to be handed down here: B. Luther and Mr. Dr. Schmidius refer those things to the apodosis concerning the friends of Job. Who are blackened by frost, do they sustain the snow? i.e., you do not sustain such light things, who therefore would trust you in heavier ones? In the time when they melt because of the heat they are cut off: when it (the snow or frost) grows warm they are extinguished in their place, (so that they are no longer in their place. When they are tested by fire, they appear cut off, and when they scarcely grow warm, they are extinguished.) The paths of their way are led around, the ways of treachery are twisted and entangled, so that they suffer loss, as many as enter them, or trust in them. (Who) looked at the ways of Tema. (And who in) the ways of Sheba hoped for themselves. What have I, a miserable man, done? The same ways led into Sheba and Tema (whence Eliphaz was). They were put to shame because they trusted; they came to it, and were ashamed. See Mr. Dr. Schmidius unfolding this sense.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

QVI TIMENT PRUINAM IRRVET SVPER EOS NIX) Sensus in Hebræo commodior: Dixerat amicos simi- les torrentibus qui diu turbidi incedunt præ glacie ac nive in ipsos resoluta: Sed (quod versus sequens vult) ubi æstas vene- rit plane deficiunt. Egregia similitudo ad eos pertinens qui in rebus adversis amicos se non oftendunt. Verba sic præeunte Mercero & Amama in An- ti-Barb. & Biblica confer. B. Scultetus κατὰ πό- δα reddidit: Qui (torrentes) nigrescunt (vel ob- fuscantur tecti) glacie, super quos nix se occultat (nive teguntur) vel insternit. Quo tempore incale- scit, extinguuntur in loco suo, declinant semita itine- ris eorum (à canali suo) ascendunt in desertum (V. Job. 12, 24.) & peribunt. Viatores de Thema (pro- ficiscentes de Thema in calidis regionibus iter agentes) vident & expectant eos (sed) confundun- tur (veniunt) ad illum (locum seu torrentem) erubuerunt (cum vident se deceptos,) &c. Con- fer. & Junius, Piscator, Anglica & Genev. ut & Hispan. ac Tigur. & Ital. versio, quæ facile hîc con- sentiunt. Hi πρότασιν similitudinis hic tradi vo- lunt: ad ἀπόδοσιν de amicis Jobi illa referunt B. Luther. & Dn. D. Schmidius. Qui denigrantur prui- na, num hi sustineant nivem? q. d. tam levia non su- stinetis, quis ergo vobis confidat in gravioribus? In tempore, quo præ calore diffluunt exciduntur: cum incalescit illa (nix, vel pruina) extinguuntur in loco suo, (ut non amplius sint in loco suo. Cum igne probantur, excisi apparent, & quando vix incalescunt, extinguuntur.) Circumducuntur se- mitæ viæ eorum, viæ perfidiæ contorquentur & in- tricantur, ut damnum patiantur, quotquot eas ingrediuntur, vel illis confidunt. (Qui) specta- runt vias Themæ. (Et qui in) viis Scheba sperarunt sibi. Quid ego miser feci? Eædem viæ in Sabam, & Themam (unde Eliphaz erat) deducebant. Pudefacti sunt, quod confisi sunt; venerunt ad eam, & erubuerunt. Vid. Dn. D. Schmid. hunc sen- sum enucleans.

## 6:25
Ver. 25.

WHY HAVE YOU DETRACTED FROM THE WORDS OF TRUTH) In the Hebrew: how firm are the words of the upright. The opposition follows: but what power of teaching have those things which you have brought?

Latin:

Verf. 25.

QVARE DETRAXISTIS SERMONIBUS VE- RITATIS) In Hebræo: quam firma sunt eloquia recti. Oppositio sequitur: quam vero vim docendi habent quæ vos attulistis?

## 6:30
Ver. 30.

NOR SHALL FOLLY SOUND IN MY THROAT) In the Hebrew: Certainly my palate will judge well those things which are corrupt: That is, I will weigh with right judgment no less those things which are said wrongly than those which are said rightly.

Latin:

Verf. 30.

NEC IN FAUCIBUS MEIS STVLTITIA PERSO- NABIT) In Hebræo: Certe palatum meum bene dijudicabi- ea quæ corrupta sunt: Id est, recto judicio expendam non mi- nus quæ prave quam quæ recte dicuntur.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

Job, exploring the calamities of life, seeks to be freed from miseries.

Verse 1.

THE LIFE OF MAN UPON EARTH IS A WARFARE Hierocles: that our life is in danger of being a long and many-yeared war. Arrian in the Discourses of Epictetus 3, 24. what is

life to each one. Maximus Tyrius in Sermon 3. God as the general, and life as the army. Marcus Antoninus 2. on life: but life is a war and a sojourn in a strange land. Seneca said we are born without discharge. From the miseries of human life Job wishes to show that death is not sought by him in vain.

Without cause does Sixtinus amend this version, which is also that of the blessed Luther and the Dutch, praising Calvin, Mercer, the English, and Cyprian de Valera, who render it thus: is there not a set time for man on earth? For he himself acknowledges that צבא denotes an army and warfare, and that life is here excellently compared to warfare: but no special word for a defined time of warfare occurs here, nor can it be signified by the same word, as he, along with Diodati, Junius, and the Genevans, wrongly thinks, both warfare and a defined time: because one word has only one sense: nor does it anywhere denote a defined time of warfare; and the days of a hireling simply imply servitude here, not indeed the determination and period of the servitude itself: therefore the new Dutch version has interpreted the word as warfare. Cocceius, however, was also pleased to render the word, a period is for man on earth. But the reasons adduced restrain assent. But in the explanation of servitude, I know not what ὕπωλον Cocceius fosters, which he should have feared, that he was under wrath, because he was not of the seed of Abraham, and others were excluded from salvation, and could have no πληροφορίαν; whereas, on the contrary, the line of the Messiah was indeed restricted to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but not the efficacy of his office, nor the spiritual blessing, which was opened and promised to all the nations of the earth in the seed of Abraham.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

Job calamitates vitæ explorans liberari à mise- riis expetit.

Vers. 1.

MILITIA EST VITA HOMINIS SVPER TERRAM Hierocles: ὡς βίον ἡμῖν κινδυνεύῃ μακρός τις εἶναι καὶ πολυε- τὴς πόλεμον. Arrianus in Epicteteis 3, 24. ςρατεία τί

ἔστιν ὁ βίος ἑκάστῳ. Maximus Tyrius Sermone 3. στρατηγὸν μὲν τὸν Θεὸν, στρατιὰν δὲ τὴν ζωήν. Marcus Antoninus 2. de vita: ὁ δὲ βίος πόλεμος καὶ ξένης ἀποδημία. Seneca dixit sine mis- sione nascimur. Ex miseriis vitæ humanæ vult ostendere Jo- bus non frustra abs se mortem optari.

SIne causa versionem hanc, quæ etiam B. Lu- theri, & Belgarum est, emendat Sixtinus, Calvinum, Mercerum, Anglos, & Cyprianum de Valera laudans, ita reddentes: annon præfinitum tempus est homini in terra? Nam צבא exerci- tum & militiam notare, & hic egregie militiæ com- parari vitam ipse agnoscit: de definito autem mi- litiæ tempore verbum peculiare nullum hîc occur- rit, nec eodem verbo, ut ipse cum Deodato, Ju- nio & Genevens. perperam putat, & militia signi- ficari potest, & tempus definitum: quia unius vo- cis unus tantum est sensus: nec uspiam ea notat definitum militiæ tempus; & dies mercenarii simpli- citer hic servitutem, non vero ipsam determinatio- nem & periodum servitutis insinuant: ideo nova Belgica versio vocem per militiam interpretata est. Coccejo tamen etiam placuit reddere vocem, perio- dus est homini in terra. Sed rationes adductæ cohi- bent assensum. In explicatione autem servitu- tis, nescio quid ὕπωλον foveat Coccejus, quod metuere debuerit se esse sub ira, quia non fuit de se- mine Abrahæ, & exclusi fuerint alii à salute, nul- lamque πληροφορίαν habere potuerint: quum ex adverso linea Mesiæ ad Abrahamum quidem, Ifaacum, Jacobum restricta fuerit, non vero of- ficii ejus efficacia, non spiritualis benedictio, quæ in semine Abrahæ omnibus gentibus terræ patuit, & promissa est.

## 7:3
Verse 3.

I HAVE HAD EMPTY MONTHS) The months were so sterile of good things for me, as winter months are wont to be.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

HABUI MENSES VACUOS) Menses mihi fuere ita ste- riles bonarum rerum, ut solent esse hyberni.

## 7:6
Verse 6.

AND THEY ARE CONSUMED WITHOUT ANY HOPE) The simile taken from a loom seems to be continued, and תקוה to signify a ball of thread, and אפס its defect.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET CONSUMPTI SVNT ABSQVE VLLA SPE) Vi- detur continuari similitudo à tela sumta, & תקוה signi- ficare glomum, & אפס ejus defectum.

## 7:12
Verse 12.

OR A WHALE BECAUSE THOU HAST SURROUNDED ME WITH A PRISON) תנין is a sufficiently general word, which signifies not only marine beasts, but also terrestrial ones, as appears in Jer. 9, 11, where it concerns Jerusalem, a city sufficiently remote from the sea: and in the same Prophet 51, 37, where there is discourse about Babylon. And certainly bars are suitable for terrestrial beasts, not marine ones.

Why not also for marine ones? Since the mention of the sea precedes, a whale which is in the sea is more rightly understood. As far as the sense is concerned, Mercer, Diodati, the Genevans, and Vatablus take it of immense pains, for the bearing of which one might not be equal: others, such as Piscator, the Dutch, Cocceius, as also the blessed Scultetus, take it of ferocity, am I a sea, am I a whale, that I must be restrained by these punishments as if by barriers, lest I rage against others? More rightly, Mr. Dr. Schmid explains it generally of any sins of contumacy, am I such a malicious and contumacious sinner, who will not suffer myself to be contained by the terms of the law, so that I must be restrained by the custody of thy punishments beyond the law, like an untamed sea and a whale, which is not ruled by laws, but must be curbed by force? Compare Isa. 57, 20. 21. Jer. 5, 22. Job 38, 8. What kind and how great this custody is, Job explains in verse 13 and following.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

AVT CETVS QVIA CIRCUMDEDISTI ME CAR- CERE) תנין vox est satis generalis, quæ feras non marinas tantum, sed & terrestres significat, ut apparet Jerem. 9, 11. ubi de Hierosolymis agitur, urbe à mari satis remota: & in eo- dem Propheta 51, 37. ubi de Babylone sermo. Et certe feris terrestribus conveniunt repagula, non marinis.

Quidni etiam marinis? Cum maris mentio antecedat, rectius balæna quæ in mari est, intelli- gitur. Quod ad sensum attinet, Mercerus, Deo- datus, Genevens. Vatablus de immanibus dolori- bus accipiunt, quibus perferendis par non sit: alii utpote Piscator, Belgæ, Coccejus, ut & B. Scul- tetus de ferocia, num mare, num cetus ego sum, ut coercendus hisce pœnis quasi claustris sim, ne sæviam adversus alios? Rectius Dn. D. Schmid. generaliter de quibusvis contumaciæ peccatis ex- plicat, num ego tam malitiosus & contumax pec- cator, qui terminis legis me contineri non patiar, ut præter legem custodia pœnarum tuarum coer- cendus sim, ut indomitum mare & balæna, quæ non legibus regitur, sed vi compescenda est? Con- fer. Esa. 57, 20. 21. Jerem. 5, 22. Job. 38, 8. Qualis vero & quanta hæc sit custodia vers. 13. & seqq. ex- plicat Job.

## 7:16
Verse 16.

I have despaired, I shall by no means live any longer) You may better translate from the Hebrew: I am weary, I shall not live any longer.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected. You may render the Hebrew κατὰ πόδα thus: I loathe life, namely this miserable one:

I shall not live forever. Since I must die altogether, why do I not die at once? as Vatablus and Mercerus explain: and B. Luther not much differently. SPARE ME) Better from the Hebrew: abstain from me: supply Thy Spirit, as Ps. 104, 29. below 34, 29. Life is from God, who also takes it away without natural causes when He wills. Thus below: how long wilt Thou not depart from me? That is, how long wilt Thou let me live? The Vulgate is corrected in vain. What need is there for that supplement? In the cited places another word and another sense is held: and regarding the latter, Job 34, 29, Grotius himself did not explain it concerning the taking away of life, but concerning turning away. The Vulgate rendered the sense correctly, spare me. For in Hebrew it is cease from me, desist from afflicting me. Thus also below verse 19. How long wilt Thou not depart from me? it is not a matter of the prolongation of life, but of affliction.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

DESPERAVI, NEQVAQVAM VLTRA JAM VIVAM) Melius vertas ex Hebræo tædet me, ne diutius vivam.

Recte corrigitur Vulgata. Ebræa κατὰ πό- δα ita reddas: aversor vitam scil. hanc miserabilem:

non in seculum vivam. Quum omnino morien- dum mihi sit, cur non statim morior? ut Vatablus & Mercerus exponunt: neque multum aliter B. Lu- therus. PARCE MIHI) Melius ex Hebræo: abstine a me: sup- ple Spiritum tuum, ut Pf. 104, 29. infra 34, 29. A Deo est vita, qui etiam sine causis naturalibus aufert eam ubi vult. Sic infra: quousque non recedes a me? Id est, quousque me fines vivere? Nequicquam corrigitur Vulgata. Quid opus est illo supplemento? In locis allegatis aliud ver- bum, aliusque sensus habetur: & posteriori Job. 34, 29. non de vitæ ablatione exposuit ipse Grotius, sed de aversatione. Sensum recte reddidit Vulga- tus, parce mihi. Nam in Ebr. est cessa a me, desine a me affligendo. Sic etiam infra verf. 19. Quousque non recedis a me? non de vitæ, sed de afflictionis prorogatione agitur.

## 7:17
Vers. 17. WHAT IS MAN, THAT THOU DOST MAGNIFY HIM. He marvels at the economy of divine providence: that He should make much of man, who is miserable and vanity, and heap him with spiritual and corporal benefits, nay, even set His heart upon him, above other creatures; and nevertheless visit him every morning with His chastisements Psalm 73, 14, and test him every moment, and that He should so greatly chastise him whom He had received into favor and so exalted and cared for: Which he himself had experienced most of all: whence he sighs, why then do You not at long last depart from me, do You not desist from me: until I swallow my spittle, or even a little, so that I may breathe, and by swallowing saliva may moisten my parched throat. Dn. D. Schmied: Before You afflict me to the very extreme. For by the swallowing of spittle he thinks the greatest afflictions are denoted, because those who are sick and already destitute of all strength do not even have the ability to eject their spittle. But perhaps this description of his state, by which he comes to the extremes, is more obscure, and the other interpretation seems simpler, which the Vulgate favors, and which Mercerus, Coccejus, and B. Sculterus have followed, and it can be considered that Job is adding a limitation to his petition, so that if God does not wish to free him from these evils, He might deign to grant at least some respite, so that they may not be too intolerable: just as the ancients were accustomed to pray, either free, or mitigate, or save.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QUID EST HOMO, QUIA MA- GNIFICAS EUM. Miratur ὀικονομίαν divinæ providentiæ: quod hominem, qui miser est, & vanitas, magni faciat, beneficiis spiritualibus & corporalibus ipsum cu- mulet, imo cor suum prorsus apponat ad eum, præ aliis creaturis; & nihilo secius ipsum singulis ma- ne visitet castigationibus suis Psalm. 73, 14. singulis- que momentis eum probet, & quem in gratiam re- ceptum ita exaltavit, & curavit, tantopere castiget: Quod expertus ipse vel maxime erat: unde suspi- rat, cur ergo non tandem aliquando recedis a me, non desistis a me: donec deglutiam spiritum meum, vel tantillum, ut respirare, & saliva deglutita aridas fauces rigare possim. Dn. D. Schmied: Priusquam ad extremum usque me affligas. Per deglutitionem enim sputi summas afflictiones denotari putat, quia ægrotantes, & omnibus viribus jam destituti non tantum amplius habent facultatis, ut sputum suum ejiciant. Sed obscurior forte hæc status illius, quo ad extrema devenitur, est descriptio, & simplicior vi- detur altera interpretatio, cui vulgata favet, quam- que Mercerus, Coccejus, B. Sculterus sequuti sunt, & petitionis suæ Jobus limitationem addere censeri potest, ut si non ab his malis liberare velit Deus, sal- tim aliquam respirationem concedere dignetur, ne nimis sint intolerabilia: uti veteres precari consue- verunt, aut libera, aut mitiga, aut salva.

## 7:20
Vers. 20. I HAVE SINNED, WHAT SHALL I DO UNTO THEE, O THOU PRESERVER OF MEN? Almost all the Hebrews, as noted by Mercerus, who agrees with them, explain it thus: Granted, I have sinned, as my companions say these things happen because of my crimes, what do You want me to do? so that I may appease You and expiate my guilt. Others make this a confession of Job: I have sinned, I confess, if You wish to judge me according to the rigor of the law. But there is no hypothetical particle added here, nor is there a need for us to add it, as the Hebrews do, beyond the text: IF I HAVE SINNED. It is rather a simple acknowledgment of sin: and a readiness to perform that by which sin might be expiated, by doing penance, by offering sacrifices with refuge to divine mercy, i.e., I acknowledge that I have sinned, but since I can do nothing else than repent and betake myself to Your kindness and grace, O preserver of men, which I certainly do, why have You set and do You still set me as an object of opposition to Yourself, or one against whom You might rush, (Conf. chap. 16. vers. 12.) so that I have become a burden to myself, why do You not take away my sin, and why do You not remove my iniquity according to Your accustomed mercy?

Vers. same. AND I HAVE BECOME A BURDEN TO MYSELF)

That this reading is not the most ancient, even the Masoretes admit. For the most ancient writing was not עלי but עליך: Whence the Greeks: and I am a burden upon Thee. The sense is: Why am I a burden to You? since You hold me in hatred, take me away. But to the masters this seemed cacophonous. And so they changed it: as if there were not many of the same character in the sacred scriptures.

This reading is entirely the most ancient. For thus also the Chaldean reads עלי as the old Vulgate: which B. Luther has followed. And the sense is plain: I have become a most heavy burden to myself: since You do not provide me with strength. Nor did the Masoretes deny this: much less did they change the Scripture: For the Tikkun Sopherim is not a change of Scripture, but a kind of interpretation; see what is in Dissert. Præl. §. 4. and in Critico sacro p. 187.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PECCAVI, QUID FACIAM TIBI O CU- STOS HOMINUM? Ebræi pene omnes, notante Mercero, qui eis accedit, ita exponunt: Esto, peccarim, sicut socii mei dicunt hæc accidere ob scelera mea, quid tibi vis faciam? ut te placem, & culpam meam expiem. A- lii Confessionem hanc Jobi faciunt: Peccavi fa- teor, si me judicare velis juxta legis rigorem. At nulla hic est hypothetica particula addita, nec opus est, ut cum Ebræis eam addamus, præter textum: Si PECCAVI. Agnitio potius simplex est pecca- ti: & promtitudo præstandi id, quo expiari pos- sit peccatum, agendo pœnitentiam, offerendo sa- crificia cum refugio ad divinam misericordiam, q. d. agnosco me peccasse, sed quum aliud non possim, quam pœnitere, & ad tuam me recipe- re, ô custos hominum, benignitatem, & grati- am, quod utique facio, cur posuisti & ponis ad- huc me tibi in contrarium, vel in quem incurras, (Conf. cap. 16. vers. 12.) adeo ut mihi ipsi factus sim oneri, cur non tollis peccatum meum, & quare non aufers pro solita tua misericordia iniquitatem meam?

Vers. eod. ET FACTVS SVM MIHIMETIPSI GRAVIS)

Hanc Scripturam non esse illam antiquissimam etiam Maso- retæ fatentur. Vetustissima enim scriptio fuit non עלי sed עליך : Vnde Græci : εἰμὶ δὲ ἐπὶ σοὶ φορτίον. Sensus est : Cur tibi gravis sum? quando me invisum habes, tolle me. At magistris hoc visum est κακόφωνον. Itaque mutarunt : quasi non multa sint ejusdem κόμματος in sacris literis.

Est omnino hæc Scriptura antiquissima. Ita enim etiam Chaldæus legit עלי ut vetus Vulgata : quam sequutus B. Lutherus est. Et sensus est planus : factus mihi ipsi sum sarcina gravissima : te vires mihi non sufficiente. Nec id negarunt Masoretæ : nedum immutarunt Scripturam : Nam תקון סופרים non est mutatio Scripturæ, sed genus interpretationis; vid. quæ in Dissert. Præl. §. 4. & in Critico sacro p. 187.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. Bildad, arguing that Job is suffering because of these sins, exhorts him to repentance, depicting the vain hope of hypocrites.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. Bildad Jobum ob peccata hæc pati arguens, eum ad pœnitentiam hortatur, vanam spem hy- pocritarum depingens.

## 8:12
Vers. 12.

WHILE IT IS YET IN ITS FLOWER] Better, in its greenness. For the name of the month Abib is derived from this, when the ears of corn are green, according to the interpretation of Jerome.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

CVM ADHVC SIT IN FLORE] Melius, in virore. Nam & nomen inde mensi אביב, cum virent spicæ, inter- prete Hieronymo.

## 8:14
Vers. 14.

AS THE SPIDER'S WEB IS HIS TRUST) Proverbial, as in Isaiah 56, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

SICVT TELA ARANEARVM FIDVCIA EJVS) Proverbiale, ut Esaïæ 56, 15.

## 8:17
Vers. 17.

AND HE SHALL DWELL AMONG THE STONES) That is, even if he has grown to such a height that he looks down upon the highest houses (for so it is in the Hebrew), yet he shall shortly disappear.

Others, although his roots reach to a stony place; so that it may be a continuation of the Author's Metaphor. Osiander, we do not cite the version. Mr. Dr. Schmiedius prefers the present verse, which he renders thus: his roots are entangled over a heap, he shall see a house of stones, interpreting the word גל with the Chaldean, Aben-Ezra, Rambam, LXX, Vulg, Tremellius, and Cocceius as a heap of stones, understanding it of the nature of hypocrites, that they flourish before the sunrise, or for some time, and extend their branches also over the garden in which they stand, but their roots are entangled in a heap of stones, and they experience a stony place, and have no sap except on the surface, and therefore cannot endure (Matt. 13, Luke 8), but some heat of misfortune soon dries them up. We, with the blessed Luther, take the word גל as a fountain or spring. As it is used in Canticles 4, 12, his roots are dense near the springs (Cf. Jerem. 17, 8, Psalm 1, vers. 3.) as Pagninus, Mercer, the Belgian, Diodati, Geneva, Piscator, the blessed D. Sculter, as also Ralbag and Perizolides have understood it. Moreover, we believe the word בית, as it sometimes does elsewhere, signifies a place or space: although they see a stony place, that is, reach or experience it: for hypocrites are accustomed to break through all obstacles and to spread their glory far and wide.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ET INTER LAPIDES COMMORABITVR) Id est, etiamsi eousque excreverit, ut altissimas domos despiciat, (ita enim est in Hebræo) tamen brevi disparebit.

ALii, licet ad locum lapidosum radices ejus con- tingant; ut continuatio Metaphoræ Auto- ris sit. Osiander, versionem non adducimus. Dn. D. Schmiedius mavult versum præsentem, quem ita reddit, super acervum radices ejus implican- tur, domum lapidum videbit, vocem גל cum Chald. Aben-Ezr. Rambam, LXX. Vulg. Tremell. & Coccejo de acervo lapidum exponens, intelligere de hypocritarum indole, quod vireant ante solis or- tum, vel aliquandiu, & ramos quoque super hor- tum, in quo stant, extendant, sed radices eo- rum implicentur acervo lapidum, & experiantur locum lapidosum, nec succum habeant nisi in superficie, adeoque durare non possint (Matth. 13. Luc. 8.) sed mox arefaciat eos aliquis infortu- nii æstus. Nos cum B. Luther. vocem גל de fonte, vel scaturigine accipimus. Uti Cantic. 4, 12. adhibita est, radices ejus densæ sunt juxta scatu- rigines (Conf. Jerem. 17, 8. Psalm. 1. vers. 3.) quem- admodum accepere Pagninus, Mercer. Belg. Dio- dat. Genev. Piscat. B. D. Sculter. ut & Ralbag. & Pe- rizolides. Vocem autem בית uti alias quando- que, locum, seu spatium significare arbitramur : licet locum lapidosum videant, hoc est, attingant vel experiantur : omnia enim impedimenta perrum- pere, & longe lateque gloriam suam diffundere so- lent hypocritæ.

## 8:18
Vers. 18.

HE SHALL DENY HIM) Namely, the place in which he was seen. An elegant personification.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

NEGABIT EVM) Nempe locus in quo conspiciebatur. Elegans προσωποποιΐα.

## 8:21
Vers. 21.

TILL THY MOUTH BE FILLED WITH LAUGHTER) The discourse is changed and becomes an apostrophe to some impious person, as is not rare in the Psalms.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

DONEC IMPLEATVR RISV OS TVVM) Mutatur sermo & fit ἀποστροφὴ ad impium aliquem, ut non raro in Psalmis.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. Job, having posited the justice of GOD, yet warning that His absolute power is not to be denied, complains of the severity of GOD, and acknowledging his sins, seeks a mitigation of the cross.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. Job posita DEI justitia, ἀυτεξοσίαν tamen ejus non negandam monens, de DEI severita- te queritur, & peccata sua agnoscens miti- gationem crucis petit.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. WHO HAS RESISTED AND HAD PEACE) For 'resisted him', in the Hebrew it is: 'He hardened himself against him.' These are those who 'speak hard things against God.' Jude 15.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVIS RESTITIT ET PACEM HABVIT) Pro restitit ei, in Hebræo est: Induravit se contra eum. Hi sunt τὰ σκληρὰ λαλῶντες κατὰ Θεῦ. Judæ 15.

## 9:9
Vers. 9. AND THE INNER PARTS OF THE SOUTH) Those stars which incline toward the South Pole, and are visible to the Arabs, but not to those situated further north from the Equinoctial. See Pliny 2, 72.

He seems here to comprehend the whole circuit of the heaven and the year. Arcturus in the north in autumn, Orion around winter, the Hyades in spring (by rising and setting). The southern stars in summer stir up the air: as our B. Scultetus does here.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ET INTERIORA AVSTRI) Sidera illa quæ ad polum Austrinum vergunt, & Arabibus sunt conspicua, non etiam longius in septentrionem ab Æquinoctiali sitis. Vide Plinium 2, 72.

VIdetur hîc comprehendere totum cæli & anni ambitum. Arcturus septentrionalis in autu- mno, Orion circa Hyemem, Hyades in vere (ab ortu & occasu.) Australes stellæ in æstate aërem commovent: ut hîc B. Scultetus noster.

## 9:13
Vers. 13. UNDER WHOM THEY BOW WHO CARRY BURDENS.

Philippus and Bede inappropriately interpret this as the pious, who sustain the world with prayers; Gregory the Great, Thomas, and Lyranus more ineptly as the angels; Cajetan and Mr. Dr. Schmiedius as the demons; Rabbi Abraham as those who hold the rudder of the Republic: to which opinion Gregory the Great also leans; because 'basileus' is said as if it were the basis and foundation of the people (which word Pineda foolishly derives here from 'bainein' and 'hileos', because he mercifully ascends, which things provoke laughter among grammarians). But in the Hebrew it is: HELPERS OF PRIDE, who foster pride, when they promise help to others with arrogance and pride, as Vatablus and others have rendered it, because even the powerful, who are persuaded by pride and the haughtiness of their mind that they are able to succor others, are bowed down by God, and are held to subject themselves to Him.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SUB QUO CURVANTUR QUI PORTANT ONERA.

Inconvenienter Philippus, & Beda de piis, pre- cibus orbem sustentintibus, ineptius Gregorius M. Thomas, & Lyran. de angelis, Cajetanus & Dn. D. Schmiedius, de dæmonibus accipiunt: Rabbi Abra- ham de iis, qui clavum Reipublicæ tenent: in quam sententiam etiam Gregorius M. propendet: quod βασιλεὺς dicatur quasi Basis & fundamentum popu- li (quam vocem infulse hîc Pineda à βαίνεν & ἵλεως, quod misericorditer ascendat, deducit, quæ risum cient Grammaticis.) Sed in Ebræo est: ADJU- TORES SUPERBIÆ, qui superbiam fovent, cum arrogantia & superbia aliis auxilium pollicentur, ut Vatablus, & alii reddidere, quod etiam potentes, qui se aliis succurrere posse, ex superbia & fastu ani- mi persuasi sunt, Deo curventur, eique se subjicere teneantur.

## 9:15
Vers. 15. IF I HAVE ANY JUST THING) In the Hebrew: if I shall be just.

BUT I WILL ENTREAT MY JUDGE) That is, I would deal with him suppliantly, as the winged ones of Isaiah 6:2 do.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QVI ETIAM SI HABVERO QVIPPIAM JVSTVM) In Hebræo: qui si justus fuero.

SED MEVM JVDICEM DEPRECABOR) Id est, sup- pliciter cum eo agerem, ut faciunt aneli Esaiæ. 6, 2.

## 9:20
Vers. 20. HE WILL PROVE ME PERVERSE) In the Hebrew: He will make me perverse. That is, I will appear perverse to you in this boasting.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PRAVVM ME COMPROBABIT) In Hebr. Prabum me faciet. Id est, pravus vobis videbor in hac ja- ctatione.

## 9:21
Vers. 21. EVEN IF I WERE SIMPLE, MY SOUL WILL IGNORE THIS VERY THING) Even if I were conscious to myself of absolutely no evil deed done, yet I would not assume judgment of myself. 1 Cor. 4:3, 4.

This interpretation is to be noted: which, as it stands on its own footing, being highly suitable to the preceding and following context, so it is to be opposed to the Papists, who attempt to prove the uncertainty of divine grace from this passage. But that it excludes only the confidence of one's own righteousness, and not the certainty of divine grace, is too manifest. Whence our author could not help the Pontificians Alphonsus de Castro, Costerus, Bellarmine, Raibingus, and others here. Indeed, not even the Jesuit Vasquez, who concedes in Tom. 2, in 1. Secund. Disput. CC. cap. 5, that only the confidence of one's own righteousness is reprobated. Which the preceding verse 20 especially teaches clearly: 'If my mouth should wish to justify me, it will condemn me; if I should show myself innocent, it will prove me perverse.' Coccejus renders this passage thus: 'I am upright, I will not acknowledge my soul, I will despise my life.' Even if I were to perfect righteousness and prove my integrity to GOD, which is impossible, I would nevertheless promote nothing by which life might be sweetened for me; I am an unprofitable servant: there is no cause why I should love and magnify this life, but rather there are causes why, having disregarded natural inclination and the appetite of my soul, I should despise this life and choose death over it. Others thus: I do not acknowledge my soul, that is, myself; I am not in my right mind in such terrors, so that I can revolve in my mind those things which make for my defense.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ETIAMSI SIMPLEX FVERO, HOC IPSVM IGNORABIT ANIMA) Etiamsi plane nullius malæ actæ rei mihi conscius fuero, tamen de memetipso mihi judicium non assumam. 1. Cor. 4 3. 4.

Observanda hæc interpretatio: quæ uti suo stat talo, antecedentibus & consequentibus appri- me conveniens, ita Papistis opponenda est, ex hoc loco incertitudinem gratiæ divinæ probare co- nantibus. Quem vero solum fiduciam propriæ ju- stitie, non autem certitudinem divinæ gratiæ exclu- dere, nimis manifestum. Unde hic Pontificios Alphonsum de Castro, Costerum, Bellarminum Raibin- gum & alios juvare non potuit noster. Imo ne Vas- quez quidem Jesuita, qui concedit Tom. 2. in 1. Se- cund. Disput. CC. cap. 5. reprobari solum fiduciam pro- priæ justitiæ. Quod cumprimis vers. 20. præcedens luculenter docet: si voluerit me justificare os meum, condemnabit me, si innocentem ostendero, pravum me comprobabit. Coccejus ita reddit hunc locum: integer sum, non agnoscam animam meam, spernam vitam meam. Etiamsi perficerem justitiam & inte- gritatem probarem DEO, quod impossibile est, nihil tamen promoverem, quo vita mihi edulcetur, inutilis servus sum: causa nulla est, cur diligam & magni- faciam vitam hanc, sed potius causæ sunt, cur insuper habita naturali inclinatione, & appetitu animæ meæ, hanc vitam sperniam, ac mortem eligam præ illa. Alii ita: non agnosco animam meam, id est, meipsum, non sum apud me in tantis terroribus, ut possim ea men- te revolvere, quæ ad meam defensionem faciunt.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. IF HE SCOURGES, HE WILL KILL AT ONCE AND WILL NOT LAUGH AT THE PUNISHMENTS OF THE INNOCENT) This is said 'kata physin', that is, let him not act in such a way as if he delighted in the punishments of the good.

Latin:

Vers. 23. SI FLAGELLAT, OCCIDAT SEMEL ET NON DE POENIS INNOCENTIVM RIDEAT) Dictum hoc κα- τὰ φύσιν, id est, ne ita agat, quasi pœnis bonorum de- lectetur.

## 9:24
Vers. 24. HE COVERS THE FACE OF THE JUDGES) Namely, the corrupter with gifts. Exod. 23, 8. Deuteron. 16, 19. he covers it so that he may not see the truth.

IF THEN IT IS NOT HE, WHO THEN IS IT?) In the Hebrew: If not, where, who is he himself? That is, if anyone denies that I am speaking the truth, let him show where he is, namely, the prince acting justly. See what is below at 24.

Others more correctly: If anyone says that this is not (so), I ask, who is he?

Latin:

Vers. 24. VVLTUM JVDICVM EJVS OPERIT) Nempe cor- ruptor donis. Exod. 23, 8. Deuteron. 16, 19. operit ne ve- rum videat.

QVOD SI NON ILLE EST, QVIS ERGO EST?) In Hebræo: Sinon, ubi, quis ipse? Id est, si quis neget ve- rum me dicere, ostendat ubi ille sit, nempe princeps juste agens. Vide quæ infra 24.

Rectius alii: Si quis dicat hoc non (ita se habere) quæso, quis ille est?

## 9:27
Vers. 27. IF I SAY, I WILL NOT SPEAK THUS. I WILL CHANGE MY FACE, AND BE TORMENTED WITH PAIN) In the Hebrew: if I say, I will forget my meditation, I will put aside my countenance, supply: sad, and I will be refreshed.

Latin:

Vers. 27. CVM DIXERO, NEQVAQVAM ITA LO- QVAR. COMMVTO FACIEM MEAM, ET DO- LORE TORQVEOR) In Hebræo: si dixero, obliviscar meditationis meæ, deponam vultum, supple tristem, ac re- creabor.

## 9:28
Vers. 28. I FEARED ALL MY WORKS. From this, the Papists wish to carve out a doubt concerning the grace of GOD. Bellarm. lib. 5. de just. cap. 5. But in the source it is held thus: I feared all my pains: which do not allow me to be quiet, and to omit my complaint: What have these to do with a doubt concerning the grace of GOD? Pineda acknowledges that it is correctly explained by the Chaldean and the LXX as concerning pains, and he renders this sense: wherever I turn myself, I must fear from the most laborious works, the most bitter pains, by which I am consumed. The things which follow: For I know that thou wilt not make me innocent, or wilt not acquit me, are consistent with Nah. 1, 3. and Exod. 34, 7: nor do they argue anything but the fear of temporal punishments, and not indeed of eternal ones, or a doubt concerning salvation. Conf. cap. 10. v. 13. cap. 13. v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 28. VEREBAR OMNIA OPERA MEA. Inde Papistæ dubitationem de gratia DEI ex- sculpere volunt. Bellarm. lib. 5. de just. cap. 5. Sed in fonte ita habetur: Timebam omnes dolores meos: qui me non sinunt quietum esse, & querelam omit- tere: Quid hæc ad dubitationem de DEI gratia? Pineda agnoscit recte à Chald. & LXX. exponi de doloribus, & hunc sensum reddit: quocunque me converto, timendum mihi est à laboriosissimis operibus, doloribus acerbissimis, quibus conficior. Quæ sequun- tur: Scio enim, quod non sic innocentem me facturus, vel dimissurus, è Nab. 1, 3. & Exod. 34, 7. constant: nec nisi metum temporalium suppliciorum, non vero infernalium, aut dubitationem de salute ar- guunt. Conf. cap. 10. v. 13. cap. 13. v. 15.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. Job's complaint and expostulation, with a remembrance of the benefits concerning his creation and formation, raising himself up again, and seeking death and refreshment.

Latin:

CAPUT X. Jobi querela, & expostulatio, recordatione be- neficiorum qua creationem & formationem se iterum erigentis, ac mortem & refocil- lationem expetentis.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. AND DOST THOU FAVOR THE COUNSEL OF THE WICKED) In the Hebrew: Shine upon: that is, may you make it glorious with success. The Greeks: and you have regarded the counsel of the ungodly.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET CONSILIVM IMPIORUM ADJUVES) In Hebræo: Illustres: id est, successu gloriosum id facias. Græci: βυλῇ δὲ ἀσεβῶν προσέσχες.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. HAST THOU EYES OF FLESH. The sense of these and the following is: Even if you do not inquire into my iniquity with eyes of flesh, but with divine and eternal ones, and thus know that I have done nothing wicked, yet you afflict me as if I were most wicked, so that there is no one who can snatch me from your hand, I say, the work of your hands.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NUMQUID OCULI CARNEI. Sensus horum & seqq. est: Etiamsi oculis non carneis, sed divinis & æternis inquiras meam iniqui- tatem, adeoque scias quod nihil impium fecerim, ita tamen me affligis, ac si summe impius essem, ut nemo sit, qui de manu sua eripere possit, me, in- quam, opus manuum tuarum.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. THY HANDS HAVE MADE ME) Those things which happen through nature, namely, that which was instituted by Him, are also ascribed to God. Compare Psalm 139, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 8. MANUS TUÆ FECFRUNT ME) Deo ad- scribuntur ea etiam, quæ per naturam fiunt, ab ipso scilicet institutam. Confer Psalmum 139, 4.

## 10:10
Vers. 10. HAST THOU CURDLED ME) Very properly. Pliny 7. cap. 15, dealing with menstrual blood: When this is the material for generating a human being, with the seed from the males curdling in the manner of a coagulum, gathering itself into this: which then in time itself is animated and embodied.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ME COAGVLASTI) Proprie admodum. Pli- nius 7. cap. 15. agens de sanguine menstruo: Quando hæc est generando homini materia semine è maribus coaguli modo hoc in sese glomerante: quod deinde tempore ipso animatur, corporaturque.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. THOU HAST CLOTHED ME WITH SKIN AND FLESH: THOU HAST JOINED ME TOGETHER WITH BONES AND SINEWS) This is the order in generation. First there is the skin, then flesh upon it: harder things are added little by little. The Hebrews say that the contrary order will be in the resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PELLE ET CARNIBVS VESTISTI ME: OSSIBVS ET NERVIS COMPEGISTI ME) Hic ordo est in genitura. Primum pellicula sit, deinde in ea caro: du- riora paulatim accedunt. Contrarium ordinem in resurre- ctione futurum ajunt Hebræi.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. ALTHOUGH THOU HIDEST THESE THINGS IN THY HEART. The sense is, although in temptation you show yourself so harsh to me, as if you did not know that I am your workmanship, yet I know and believe with firm faith that THIS IS WITH THEE, that you are mindful of this, and in reality you are going to demonstrate that you graciously regard and preserve your work.

Latin:

Vers. 13. LICET HÆC CELES IN COR- DE TUO. Sensus est, licet in tentatione tam durum te mihi præbeas, quasi nescias, quod tuum sim opificium, ta- men scio & firma fide credo, quod HOC APUD TE SIT, quod probe hujus recorderis, & reipsa demon- straturus sis, te gratiose opus tuum respicere & conservare.

## 10:15
Vers. 15. SATURATED WITH AFFLICTION AND MISERY] In the Hebrew: behold the misery: but it can be read with a changed vowel point, seeing the misery: looking at nothing else around me but the greatest evils. What need is there for the point to be changed? If such license is admitted, we shall have nothing certain in the fountains of Hebrew truth and in the Sacred Codex. The obvious sense is, without the change of a point, that he may point out his affliction demonstratively, which he may deign to look upon, O God. Mr. D. Schmiedius says it is an infinitive, and repeats the word SATUR from the common usage in this manner, and saturated by seeing my affliction.

Latin:

Vers. 15. SATVRATVS AFFLICTIONE ET MISE- RIA] In Hebræo: en miseriam: sed potest puncto mutato legi, videns miseriam: nihil aliud circum me aspiciens, quam mala maxima. Quid opus est, ut punctum mutetur? Quæ li- centia si admittatur, nihil certi in fontibus verita- tis Ebraicæ, & in Codice Sacro habebimus. Sen- sus obvius est, absque puncti mutatione, ut δεικτι- κῶς monstret afflictionem suam, quam respicere dignetur Deus. Dn. D. Schmiedius infinitivum esse dicit, & vocem SATUR ἀπὸ κοινἳ repetit h. m. & satur videndo afflictionem meam.

## 10:16
Verse 16.

AND BECAUSE OF PRIDE AS A LIONESS YOU WILL CATCH ME) שחל, which Jerome translates here and elsewhere as lioness, others prefer to be a panther. Word for word: if it exalts itself, namely my head, you will hunt me, as a panther, that is to say, the same.

The word ויגאה is more correctly referred to affliction: and although my affliction grows, yet like a lion you still hunt me; thus Mercer, the Belgian, the Genevan, Piscator, the Hebrew.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ET PROPTER SVPERBIAM QVASI LEÆNAM CAPIES ME) שחל, quod hic & alibi leænam vertit Hieronymus, alii pantheram esse malunt. Ad verbum: si extollat se, nempe caput meum, veneris me, quasi panthera, eamdem scilicet.

Rectius verbum ויגאה refertur ad afflictio- nem : & quamvis afflictio mea crescat, tamen tan- quam leo adhuc venaris me; sic Mercer. Belgic. Ge- nevens. Piscat. Ebrai.

## 10:20
Verse 20.

ARE NOT THE FEWNESS OF MY DAYS TO BE FINISHED SHORTLY) See Psalm 139, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

NVNQVID NON PAVCITAS DIERVM MEO- RVM FINIETVR BREVI) Vide Psalmum 139, 4.

## 10:22
BUT EVERLASTING HORROR DWELLS) In the Hebrew: where it shone, it is like darkness: that is, night is perpetual there, as the poets say.

Latin:

SED SEMPITERNVS HORROR INHABI- TAT) In Hebræo: ubi illuxit, est sicut caligo: id est, nox ibi perpetua est, ut loquuntur Poetæ.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

Zophar rebukes Job as one boasting of innocence in vain, teaches that God is incomprehensible, and promises all manner of happiness to him who repents.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Zophar Jobum ceu frustra innocentiam jactan- tem objurgat, Deum incomprehensibilem esse docet, & resipiscenti felicissima quæ- que promittit.

## 11:3
Verse 3.

SHALL MEN BE SILENT TO YOU ALONE) He reads בריך: but our Hebrew text has בדיך. Your trifles will impose silence upon men. The Greeks read ברוך, for they translate it blessed.

Trifles. A variety of interpretation does not immediately argue a variety of reading.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

TIBI SOLI TACEBANT HOMINES) Legit בריך: at noster textus Hebræus habet בדיך. Nugæ tuæ hominibus silentium imponent. Græci legere ברוך, ver- tunt enim ευλογημέν@.

NUgæ. Varietas interpretationis non statim ar- guit varietatem lectionis.

## 11:4
Verse 4.

FOR YOU HAVE SAID MY SPEECH IS PURE) In Hebrew: my doctrine: which was called לקח, which might be received by the hands, just as קבלה is said from handing down.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

DIXISTI ENIM PVRVS EST SERMO MEVS) In Hebræo: doctrina mea: quæ vocabatur לקח, quod per ma- nus acciperetur, sicut à tradendo dicitur קבלה.

## 11:6
Verse 6.

AND THAT HIS LAW MIGHT BE MULTIPLE) Understand the law given to Noah. Others understand the page of reasons.

Grotius is again delighted by Rabbinical inventions concerning the Law given to Noah. Gregory interprets it concerning the perfection of the moral law: This law is called multiple because by studious solicitude charity is dilated to all deeds of virtues, which indeed begins from two precepts, but extends itself to innumerable ones. Others explain the Hebrew words: that it is twofold in essence, or in reality, that you would scarcely understand half of it, and in reality it has many reasons for punishing. Which sense B. Luther followed in his version: as also B. Scultetus in his Analysis. Osiander: that there exist twice as many things which deserve punishment in you. Cocceius renders it: For it is another thing in truth, and understands it thus: so far is it from the case that Job spoke rightly, that he has not attained half of that which is, or has not even touched half of the known and certain truth, concerning תושיה that is, concerning that which is the thing. Ludov. de Dieu explains it thus: And he would indicate to you the hidden things of Wisdom: because there are twofold things of Wisdom (to him) taking תושיה for Wisdom, as in chapter 4, 13, chapter 12, 16, Proverbs 2, 7, chapter 3, 21, so that a reason may be rendered for the hidden things of the wisdom of GOD, because, to wit, double the wisdom is with him. Or as Mercerus interprets, because that essence has a double (to wit, of wisdom). B. Luther's version pleases: which is, however, here a paraphrase rather than a metaphrase: which the consequences confirm: Therefore know that God remits to you some of your depravity, he does not avenge it all, as it deserves.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET QVOD MVLTIPLEX ESSET LEX EJVS) In- tellige legem Noæ datam. Alii intelligunt rationum pa- ginam.

De Lege Noæ data commentis Rabbinicis ite- rum delectatur Grotius. Gregorius de perfectio- ne legis moralis interpretatur: Lex hæc multiplex dicitur, quia studiosa solicitudine charitas ad cuncta virtutum facta dilatatur, quæ à duobus, quidem præ- ceptis incipit, sed se ad innumera extendit. Alii ex- ponunt verba Ebræa: quod duplex sit in essentia, vel reipsa, quod vix dimidium ejus intelligas, & re- ipsa plures puniendi rationes habeat. Quem sensum B. Lutherus in versione sua sequutus: ut & B. Sculte- tus in Analysi. Osiand. quod duplo plura existant, quæ merentur in te pœnam. Coccejus reddit: Nam alterum est in veritate, & intelligit ita: tantum abesse ut Iob recte locutus sit, ut ne dimidium ejus, quod est, assecutus sit, vel ne dimidium quidem cognitæ, certæque veritatis at- tigerit, de תושיה hoc est de eo quod res est. Ludov. de Dieu sic exponit: Et indicaret tibi occulta Sapientiæ: quia duplicia Sapientiæ (sunt ei) תושיה pro Sapien- tia accipiens, uti cap. 4,13. cap. 12, 16. Prov. 2, 7. cap. 3. 21. ut causa reddatur de occultis sapientiæ DEI, quia sc. penes eum duplum sapientiæ est. Vel ut Mercerus inter- pretatur, quia duplum (scil. sapientiæ) habet ista es- sentia. Placet B. Lutheri versio: quæ tamen hîc paraphrasis potius, quàm metaphrasis est: quam consequentia firmant: Ergo scias quod Deus remit- tat tibi de tua pravitate, non totam, prout meretur, vindicet.

## 11:12
Verse 12.

A VAIN MAN IS LIFTED UP INTO PRIDE, AND THINKS HIMSELF BORN FREE LIKE A WILD ASS'S COLT) The sense here seems to be: A vain man will become wise, although man is born like a wild ass's colt. That is, without the knowledge of things actualized, as Maimonides explains.

B. Scultetus refutes this explanation: because the antecedents show that it is a matter of man's audacity, that he dares to oppose himself to the wisdom and judgments of GOD: A vain man takes heart or confidence: (so that he may audaciously contradict GOD) and man is born a wild ass's colt: he is similar in nature to it because of his asinine stupidity

and intractable, and untamed impulse Job 39, 5. Of. 8, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

VIR VANVS IN SVPERBIAM ERIGITVR, ET TANQVAM PVLLVM ONAGRI SE LIBERVM NA- TVM PVTAT) Videtur hic esse sensus: Vir inanis fiet cor- datus, quanquam homo nascitur ut pullus onagri. Id est, sine actuati scientia, ut explicat Maimonides.

Refellit hanc explicationem B Scultetus: quia antecedentia ostendunt de hominis audacia agi, quod sapientiæ & judiciis DEI se ausit oppo- nere: Vir vanus cor seu confidentiam sumit: (ut audacter DEO contradicat) & pullus onagri homo nascitur: similis est natura ei ob stuporem asininum

& intractabilem, & indomitum impetum Job. 39, 5. Of. 8, 9.

## 11:18
Verse 18. AND DUG IN YOU SHALL SLEEP SECURE) Rather, where you are dug in. For the Arabs used to dig wells, and place tents by them Gen. 26, 15. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ET DEFOSSVS SECVRVS DORMIES) Imo ubi foderis. Nam Arabes fodiebant puteos, & ad eos pone- bant tentoria Gen. 26, 15. 18.

## 11:19
Verse 19. MANY SHALL ENTREAT YOUR FACE) Many will flatter you, they will seek your friendship, as those of Abraham and Isaac Gen. 21, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 19. DEPRECABVNTVR FACIEM TVAM PLV- RIMI) Multi tibi blandientur, tuam amicitiam expetent, ut Abrahami & Isaaci Gen. 21, 26.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

Job, rebuking the rashness of his friends, teaches that it is not always well with the good and ill with the bad, and sets forth the power and wisdom of God acting most freely.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

Job temeritatem amicorum redarguens non semper bonis bene, malis male esse docet, ac DEI liberrime agentis potentiam ac sapien- tiam sistit.

## 12:4
Ver. 4.

WHO IS MOCKED BY HIS FRIEND) In the Hebrew: to mock a friend: the sense is: this which you are doing is mocking a friend. You say: call upon God, that God may answer you. (See above 11, 5.) This, indeed, I say, is mocking.

Dievius renders it thus: I AM A DERISION TO MY FRIEND, WHO CALLS UPON GOD, AND HE HEARS HIM, THE JUST AND UPRIGHT MAN IS A DERISION. I would prefer to interpret the former with the Vulgate: WHO IS A LAUGHINGSTOCK TO HIS FRIEND AS I AM, so that a particle of comparison may be understood, HE WILL CALL UPON GOD, for he speaks of himself and those like him.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QVI DERIDETVR AB AMICO) In Hebræo: ridere amicum: sensus est: hoc quod vos agitis, est ridere amicum. Dicitis: clama ad Deum, ut Deus respondeat tibi. (Vide su- pra 11, 5.) Hoc vero inquam, ridere est.

Dievius ita reddit: DERISIONI EST CUI AMICUS SUM, QUI INVOCAT DEUM, ET EXAUDIT EUM, DERISIONI EST JU- STUS INTEGER. Malim priora interpretari cum Vulgato: QUI RISUI EST AMICO SUO SICUT EGO, ut subintelligatur particula simili- tudinis, INVOCABIT DEUM, de se enim, & sui similibus loquitur.

## 12:5
Ver. 5.

A DESPISED LAMP) The two preceding words seem to pertain to this sentiment in this sense. A just and upright man is indeed a lamp, but one which the minds of those who have prosperous affairs despise, and it is easily overturned by them.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

LAMPAS CONTEMTA) Videntur præcedentia duo verba ad hanc sententiam pertinere hoc sensu. Homo justus & integer lucerna quidem est, sed quam contemnunt eorum animi quibus res sunt fecundæ, ac facile ab his evertitur.

## 12:11
Ver. 11.

DOES NOT THE EAR JUDGE WORDS, AND THE PALATE THE TASTE OF THE EATER? By this double translation, the critical power of human understanding is signified.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

NONNE AURIS VERBA DIJVDICAT, ET FAV- CES COMEDENTIS SAPOREM? Hac gemina trans- latione significatur intellectus humani vis κριτική.

## 12:19
Ver. 19.

HE WILL LEAD PRIESTS WITHOUT GLORY) כהנים, and they are called priests as ministers of God, and ministers of kings, in the way the Chaldean and Rabbi Levi have taken it here. For they translate it שרים.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

DVCET SACERDOTES INGLORIOS) כהנים, & Sacerdotes dicuntur tanquam Dei ministri, & ministri re- gum, quomodo hic sumpsere Chaldæus & Rabi Levi. Ver- tunt enim שרים.

## 12:20
Ver. 20.

CHANGING THE LIP OF THE TRUTHFUL) נאמנים seem to be called here not so much truthful, as men endowed with great authority.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

COMMVTANS LABIVM VERACIVM) נאמנים videntur hîc dici non tam veraces, quam homines auctoritate magna præditi.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

Job argues against the imprudence and iniquity of his friends, and threatens them with punishment, and prays against his own punishments.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

Job amicorum imprudentiam & iniquitatem arguit, iisque pœnam minatur, suasque pœ- nas deprecatur.

## 13:4
Ver. 4.

CULTIVATORS OF PERVERSE DOGMAS) In Hebrew: You are all useless physicians. Which you will rightly interpret from the verses of Aeschylus, which [I cited] at chapter 4.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

CULTORES PERVERSORUM DOGMATUM) In Hebræo: Medici inutiles vos omnes. Quod recte interpre- taberis ex versibus Æschyli, quos ad caput 4.

## 13:8
Ver. 8.

WILL YOU ACCEPT HIS PERSON) Do you wish to gratify God by oppressing me, as you are accustomed to do with princes? The Greeks: ὑποσελεῖσθε in this place. So also above 6, 7. For the Lord of all will accept a person.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

NUMQVID FACIEM EJUS ACCIPITIS) Vultisne Deo Gratificari me opprimendo, ut soletis facere apud prin- cipes? Græci: ὑποσελεῖσθε hoc loco. Sic & supra 6, 7. ὁ γὰρ ὑποστέλεται πρόσωπον ὁ πάντων δεσπότης.

## 13:10
Ver. 10. SINCE IN SECRET YOU ACCEPT HIS PERSON) He reads פניו: nor did the Chaldean, Symmachus, or Theodotion read otherwise.

There is no need for the pronoun: which they added of their own accord, not from a different reading; because they wished to render the sense clearer: which indeed is sufficiently evident from the Hebrew פנים. Nor is it necessary that it be referred to GOD, as if it regarded the person of GOD in secret. It is understood more conveniently with the Tigurines as the person of anyone. The LXX did not read otherwise than the Hebrew text has. My B. Scultetus refers it most excellently to GOD and to Job at the same time: He himself will argue you, since in secret you accept a person: indeed openly you hold up another veil for your judgment, hypocrisy and crimes, which you cast upon me without proof, but in your heart nothing other than the contemplation of divine majesty and my misery moves you.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QVONIAM IN ABSCONDITO FACIEM EJVS ACCIPITIS) Legit פניו: nec aliter Chaldæus, Sym- machus, Theodotion.

NOn opus est pronomine: quod de suo illi addidere, non è diversa lectione; quia cla- riorem reddere sensum voluere: qui vero satis constat ex Ebræo פנים. Nec ad DEUM neces- sum est ut referatur, quasi in abscondito perso- nam DEI respiciat. Commodius cum Tigurinis de cujusvis persona intelligitur. Non aliter lege- runt LXX. quam habet Ebræus textus. B. Sculte- tus meus optime ad DEUM & ad Jobum simul re- fert: Ipse vos arguet, quoniam in abscondito faciem accipitis: palam quidem aliud vestro judicio velum obtenditis, hypocrisin & scelera, quæ mihi sine probatione impingitis, sed in corde vestro nihil aliud, quam contemplatio divinæ majestatis & meæ miseriæ vos movet.

## 13:12
Ver. 12. YOUR NECKS SHALL BE REDUCED TO MUD) Better: your strongholds shall be as heaps of mud.

Latin:

Vers. 12. REDIGENTVR IN LVTVM CERVICES VESTRÆ) Melius: arces vestræ erunt ut lutei cumuli.

## 13:14
Verse 14. WHY DO I TEAR MY FLESH WITH MY TEETH) Why am I consumed by grief? Thus concerning Bellerophon in Cicero: Eating his own heart, avoiding the footsteps of men. And the precept of Pythagoras pertains to this, do not eat the heart.

AND I CARRY MY SOUL IN MY HANDS) That is, I am involved in the most serious dangers. You have this manner of speaking in Judges 12:3, 1 Samuel 19:5, chapter 28:21, Psalm 119:109.

Latin:

Verf. 14. QVARE LACERO CARNES MEAS DEN- TIBVS MEIS) Cur præ mœrore maceror? Sic de Belle- rophonte apud Ciceronem: Ipfe suum cor edens, hominum vestigia vitans. Et huc pertinet Pythagoræ præceptum, καρδίαν μὴ ἐσθίειν.

ET ANIMAM MEAM PORTO IN MANIBVS MEIS) Id est, in gravissimis periculis versor. Habes hoc loquendi genus Judicum 12, 3. 1. Sam, 19, 5. cap. 28, 21. Pfal. 119, 109.

## 13:15
Verse 15. EVEN IF HE SHOULD SLAY ME, IN HIM I WILL HOPE) He reads לו, although the Hebrew codices have לא in this sense: Even if God should wish to slay me, so that there would be no hope for me in life, I would still ask this, that I might be heard.

Thus Grotius, having followed the Chaldean. It has often been warned that a different reading should not immediately be invented in the Hebrew when the paraphrases interpret otherwise than the current Hebrew codices have: infinite varieties of Hebrew readings could otherwise be imagined. Although in this place the Masoretes note that for לא one should read לו, and all the Hebrews follow that reading, as well as the Genevans, Piscator, Diodati, the Spaniards, and the English: if he should slay me, yet I would hope in him. But even with the negative particle לא retained, the Vulgate can easily be reconciled with the Hebrew text, and has been reconciled by others: namely, so that the words are taken interrogatively: Behold, he slays me, shall I not hope? Even if I were to see death before my eyes now, shall I therefore cast away my hope in God? Do you think that because I desire to die, I despair? But even if God should slay me, I will not cease to trust in him even in death itself. Others, however, explain it differently: B. Luther and the old Dutch version thus: Behold, he slays me, I cannot wait, that is, there is nothing for me to expect or hope for better in this life: for he will slay me right now. Compare chapter 17:13. Or, I know indeed that he is going to slay me in these sicknesses: but I cannot wait for the end of them, because of their severity. Similar things to which are held above in chapter 6:12. This is Cocceius's interpretation: Behold, let him slay me, I shall not hope any longer: yet I will demonstrate my ways before his face, i.e., that he will not cease to examine and lay open his conscience, even if imminent death cuts off all hope. For then it is most important to think about coming to God and seeing his face. But the first interpretation concerning Job's trust and hope in the face of the final things is better. Although he adds: yet I will demonstrate my ways in his sight, acknowledging, that is, the wholesome counsel of repentance and the examination of his own conscience, but with trust in God preserved: He, he says, will be for my salvation: The elect, says Gregory the Great, book 11 of the Morals, chapter 19, never know how to spare their own faults, so that they may find the Judge of faults appeased. It has been observed by others that לא is not rarely taken for הלא, chapter 2:10, chapter 3:20, chapter 4:18, chapter 21:4, 29, chapter 22:5, chapter 30:24, chapter 20:20. Avenarius observes many other places in which the interrogative ה is missing. It is a very well-known Hebraism by which such an interrogation affirms most vehemently. Compare here Tarnovius on Malachi 2:15, and in Exercit. Bibl. p. 156 and p. 541. Glassius in Philol. S. part 1 and 2, Grammat. Sacr. p. 606. Franciscus Junius and Tremellius, as well as Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barbar., as also the most recent Dutch version.

Latin:

Verf. 15. ETIAMSI OCCIDERIT ME, IN IPSO SPERABO) Legit לו, cum Ebræi codices habeant לא hoc sensu: Etiamsi Deus me vellet interficere, ita ut vita mihi nulla esset spes, hoc tamen peterem, ut audirer.

Ita Grotius Chaldæum sequutus. Sæpe monitum, non fingendam statim in Ebræo diversam lectio- nem, cum aliter interpretantur paraphrases, quam hodierni Codices Ebræi habent: Infinitæ alias ex- cogitari possent varietates lectionum Ebraica- rum. Quanquam hoc in loco Masorethæ annotent, pro לא legendum לו & lectionem illam sequan- tur omnes Ebræi, nec non Genevenses, Piscator, Deo- datus, Hispani, Angli, si occiderit me, tamen in illum sperarem. Sed retenta etiam negandi particula לא, Vulgata conciliari facile potest cum Ebræo textu, & ab aliis conciliata est: Ita nempe, ut verba inter- rogative accipiantur: Ecce occidit me, non sperabo? Etiamsi mortem præ oculis jam viderem, num spem meam ideo in Deum abjiciam? Putatis me, quia mori cupio, desperare? sed etiamsi occiderit me Deus, non tamen desinam etiam in ipsa morte ipsi confidere. Aliter tamen alii explicant: B. Lu- therus & versio Belgica vetus ita: Ecce occidit me, non possum expectare, hoc est, non est quod meliora in hac vita expectem aut sperem: jamjam enim me occi- det. Conf. c. 17, 13. vel scio sane, quod me in his ægritu- dinibus occisurus sit: sed non possum expectare finem earum, præ gravitate earundem. Quibus gemina ha- bentur supra c. 6, 12. Cocceji hæc est interpretatio: Ecce occidat me, non sperem amplius: tamen vias meas coram facie ejus demonstr协作rem, q. d. se non intermis- surum excutere ac patefacere conscientiam suam, eti- amsi mors imminens omnem spem intercidat. Tum enim potissimum cogitandum est, ut ad Deum venias & fa- ciem ejus videas. Sed præstat prima Interpretatio de fiducia & spe Jobi πρὸς τὰ ἔσχατα. Quamvis subji- ciat: veruntamen vias meas in conspectu ejus demon- strabo, agnoscens scil. salutare consilium pœniten- tiæ, & excussionis conscientiæ suæ, sed salva in De- um fiducia: Ipse, inquit, erit mihi in salutem: Electi, ait Gregorius M. lib. 11. Moral. c. 19. culpis suis nun- quam sciunt parcere, ut possint culparum Judicem pla- catum invenire. Non raro לא pro הלא accipi, aliis observatum cap. 2, 10. cap. 3, 20. cap. 4, 18. cap. 21, 4. 29. cap. 22, 5. cap. 30, 24. cap. 20, 20. Plura alia lo- ca, in quibus ה interrogativum deficiat, observat Avenarius. Ebraismus notissimus est, quo talis inter- rogatio vehementissime affirmat. Confer. hic Tar- nov. in Malach. 2, 15. & in Exercit. Bibl. p. 156. & p. 541. Glassius in Philol. S. part. 1. & 2. Grammat. Sacr. p. 606. Francisc. Junius & Tremell. nec non Sixtin. Amama in Anti-Barbar. ut & Versio Belgica no- vissima.

## 13:16
Verse 16. SINCE NO HYPOCRITE SHALL COME INTO HIS SIGHT) חנף, who is called a hypocrite here, is in the Chaldean both here and below 17:8, רלטור, with the Latin word delator (informer). Before God, false informers are not heard. No one bringing false crimes against him will prevail.

That meaning is foreign. For the discourse is about hypocrites: from whom Job distinguishes himself, with his conscience as a witness, and thus concludes that he will not be excluded from the sight of the Lord.

Latin:

Verf. 16. QVVM IN EJVS CONSPECTVM NVL- LVS HYPOCRITA VENIAT) חנף, qui hic hypocrita dicitur, Chaldæo & hic & infra 17, 8. est רלטור Latina voce delator. Apud Deum falsi delatores non audiuntur. Ne- mo illi falsa crimina adferens imponet.

Aliena est illa significatio. De hypocritis enim sermo est: à quibus se distinguit Job, conscien- tia teste, adeoque colligit se non exclusum iri à conspectu Domini.

## 13:28
AND AS A GARMENT WHICH IS EATEN BY A MOTH) In the Hebrew: As a garment the moth will eat this: when he says this, he points to his body. Thus Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:53: this corruptible: which passage Tertullian explaining in Against Marcion V: For it is necessary for this corruptible, certainly holding his own flesh, the Apostle was saying. Compare what is below 19:25.

The whole verse is thus: And this (my body) will grow old like rottenness (a rotten thing), and like a garment which a moth eats.

Latin:

ET QVASI VESTIMENTVM QVOD COMEDI- TVR A TINEA) In Hebræo: Ut vestimentum comedet hoc tinea: hoc cum dicit, corpus suum monstrat. Sic Pau- lus 1. Cor. 15, 53. τὸ φθαρτὸν τῦτο: quem locum explicans Tertullianus adversus Marcionem V. Oportet enim corrupti- vum hoc, tenens utique carnem suam dicebat Apostolus. Con- fer quod infra 19, 25.

Versus integer ita habet: Et hoc (corpus me- um) sicut putredo (res putrida) veterascet, & sicut vestis, quam comedit tinea.

## 14:3
Verse 3.

AND BRING HIM INTO JUDGMENT WITH THEE) He reads תבא where we have תביא, in this sense: Would you wish to deal with me with the highest right and most rigidly? Psalm 143, 2.

He does not read it differently because he translates it differently. Could it not have been a slip of the eye? Then if he reads as he translates, how easily a scribe could have erred by writing a Vav in place of a Jod. But the errors of any particular codex are not to be immediately sold as accepted variant readings.

NOn ideo aliter legit, quia aliter vertit. An- non potuit esse παρόραμα? Tum si legit, ut vertit, quam facile labi potuit scriba loco Jod scri- bendo Vav. Quæ vero particularis alicujus Co- dicis errata non statim pro receptis diversis lectio- nibus venditanda sunt.
