## 14:4
WHO CAN MAKE CLEAN THAT WHICH IS CONCEIVED OF AN UNCLEAN SEED) In the Hebrew: Who shall give a clean thing from an unclean? In order to escape too severe judgments, he objects the common infirmity of human nature, concerning which we have brought forward some things in the second book of De Jure Belli & Pac. 20, 19.

The passage is an illustrious one concerning original sin. Grotius takes it too jejunely concerning the infirmity of human nature: nor does he understand it to be innate to man to sin in the cited book otherwise than as Sopater, Hierocles, and Seneca have set forth among the philosophers, who knew nothing of original sin; nay, he says it can be doubted whether sins of infirmity, which cannot be avoided, are rightly and properly called sins; whence he will much less hold original sin to be sin properly so called. Thus Pelagianism has revived in Grotius. Which also shines through from the annotations to Consult: Cassandr. Art. 2. August. Confess. But these things are covered in vain in the Grotian discussion of the Apologetic of Rivetus by the opinions of the philosophers concerning the corruption of human nature and its cause, who, according to the mind of Mornay in De veritate religionis Christianae, are on our side. For although the corruption of human nature was not unknown to the Gentiles, which everyone experiences sufficiently in himself, yet what that is, of what kind, and how great it is, and whence it has its origin, they could not penetrate, but this doctrine is proper to Scripture and the Church: If anything analogous to this occurs in the writings of the Gentiles, it is to be believed that it proceeded from the reading of certain sacred books, or from primeval tradition and report. Which is rightly used from the Gentiles against the Gentiles at least according to man, not that a true knowledge of these things is to be ascribed to them. Therefore, to return to our passage, Job does not merely object the common infirmity of human nature, but opens and shows the very fountain of all evils: namely, that we are conceived from an unclean seed, and therefore no one can make clean one so conceived and brought forth. Although indeed mention of that conception is not made ῥητῶς in the Hebrew text: yet κατὰ διάνοιαν the same is contained therein: Who shall bring a clean thing out of an unclean? For if everyone is begotten from an unclean thing, and from the very propagation is unclean, it must be that no one can be brought forth clean from an unclean thing, nor can anyone be begotten clean from an unclean thing. Of which no other cause is, other than that through the very procreation and propagation uncleanness is attracted, or as the common version has it, that we are conceived from unclean seed. To which that of Christ in John 3, verse 5 is entirely akin: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh: teaching that through the very birth or carnal propagation we are subject to carnal concupiscence, or sin; just as whatever is from the unclean is unclean, because it is conceived from unclean seed. One may compare, as far as the phrase is concerned, the passage in Genesis 17, 16: I will give you a son from her, i.e., I will cause a son to be born to you from her: so here, who will give the clean from the unclean, who will bring it about that the clean is born from the unclean? And so also the Chaldean: who will give the clean from a man contaminated by sins? Which the LXX Elders also expressed, here neglected by Grotius, though otherwise held in the highest regard, because, forsooth, they openly slaughter the Pelagian error, rendering it thus: Τίς γὰρ καθαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥύπου, ἀλλ' οὐδεὶς, ἐὰν καὶ μία ἡμέρα ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. For who will be pure from filth? But no one, not even if his life were of only one day on earth. Augustine cites that interpretation thus: no one is clean from filth, not even an infant, whose life is one day upon the earth. It is manifest that Job is speaking entirely of uncleanness and impurity, not of the body, but of the soul; not personal, but common; not particular, but universal; not temporal, but perpetually adhering and inevitable; not actual, but original, derived into us from our parents, to which we are subject. For since he has dealt with actual sins, both daily and youthful, he now deals with man as born of a woman, and subject to various miseries from birth, and to death itself, and expresses the cause of it. And Cocceius rightly observes here, when man is called טמא unclean, it is not to be understood lightly: because when Scripture wishes to indicate that one is subject to the curse and wrath of God, it is content to have called him unclean, and it says this of the most wicked men: just as the Greek words ἀκάθαρτος, βδελυγός, στυγητὸς, μυαρὸς and the like have a harsh meaning: And Paul used the word ἀκάθαρτος regarding hereditary impurity in 1 Cor. 7, verse 14. Thus Cocceius. Furthermore, man is called unclean in such a way that it cannot be understood that any part, faculty, or act of his is clean. Which is further confirmed, while he denies that anything clean can be elicited from the unclean. And hence R. Levi teaches that even all thoughts and actions are unclean. Who will elicit pure thoughts and actions from the foul? Clear and pure water from an unclean and putrid and poisonous well? implying that man is nothing other than a latrine full of filth. The already praised Cocceius indeed explains this passage a little differently, but he presupposes the sense already handed down: I will transcribe his interpretation: Job understands, and it is true, that God can demonstrate His justice even in one out of many guilty persons, if He wishes: Or out of many guilty persons, punish whom He wills. But he meets this thought thus: It would be without fruit with respect to the other guilty persons, if he himself were chosen for this. Through the equally guilty it cannot come to pass that the pure are made from the impure, or that those who are from impure parents, with their guilt removed, are considered pure: since there is not even one who is uncontaminated, whose punishment could satisfy God worthily, and illustrate His glory, nay, who could sustain that punishment. You see, he says, that we thus join both senses, and that the first (in which מן EX is of origin), which most interpreters follow, is built upon the second (in which מן EX is of change), so that they cannot be torn from each other. For the second exposition builds upon the fact that man is unclean, and absolutely every one, without exception, and that because he is born of a woman, and indicates that it cannot come to pass that the pure is made from the impure through the satisfaction of any other man. Thus Cocceius, who furthermore wishes those words לא אחד to be read interrogatively; Is there not one? and understands the one Christ, designated by God, who gives the clean from the unclean. But the common interpretation is simpler and more consistent with the text: therefore the present passage has been held as a notable testimony of original sin by the Doctors of antiquity: Origen in Leviticus, Ambrose on the Ark of Noah ch. 22, Augustine in The City of God book 20, ch. 26. Gregory the Great on this passage, who says: man, living in corruptible flesh, has the uncleannesses of temptations impressed upon himself, because he undoubtedly drew them from his origin. Hence it is that he is for the most part tempted even against his will. Hence it is that he suffers certain unclean things in his mind, although he resists them by his judgment, because, conceived from uncleanness, while he tends toward cleanliness, he attempts to overcome that which he is. But even the Jews themselves saw what Grotius did not wish to see. R. Aben-Ezra explained the passage from Psalm 51, 7. The sense here is like his: I was born in iniquities, because man is made from an unclean thing. R. Josephus Jahia interpreted it thus: Who could give or make something that would be pure in every part, like the Angels, when he is unclean by himself and material? Not even one. This is to say, you will not find one from the human race who is like an Angel of God, and who does not sin by error or of his own accord. Therefore, by himself and insofar as he has arisen from material seed—corrupt, namely, through sin—and unclean, he asserts by the force of this saying that man is unclean and prone and inclined to sin. The same also is the explanation of R. Moses Gerundensis: that from seed, a thing so unclean (spiritual impurity is understood, not carnal, as the consequence teaches), there cannot come forth even one who is entirely clean, namely, from spiritual uncleanness. Nor is the paraphrase of R. Abraham Peritsol dissimilar: You know, Lord, the structure of man: You know it is impossible to attain this perfection, because of the matter which makes him sin: (unclean seed, or as Christ says: because he is flesh born of flesh, whence he cannot but sin, he is always prone to sin) And why do You always afflict him? Can anyone come forth pure, or clean from any unclean thing? Certainly there is no one from this class, since there is no just man who does not sin. Similar things are read in R. Obadiah Sforno in Mispat Zedek, and in R. Meir Arama in Mehir Hiob, that it is impossible to find anyone born of a woman's womb who does not stumble into uncleanness. All of whom are cited by R. Manasseh Ben Israel in his book on human frailty, p. 5. This paraphrase of R. Nachmanides is praised by Cocceius in this place: Who can think a man who comes from an unclean place to be pure? There is not even one who is pure. The confession of the righteous concerning their sin: such as that: Behold I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sins my mother conceived me. But all those, as is manifest, interpreted the words of the Hebrew text: Who will bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one, just as the LXX Interpreters and the Vulgate version, and understood them, as Christian interpreters commonly understand them, namely concerning sin, as it is called in the Church, original. Which R. Aben-Ezra in Ps. 51 calls concupiscence innate to the human heart, and an evil figment implanted in our heart from birth. Let there be compared also here Gen. 6, 5. chap. 8, 21. concerning the evil figment of the human heart every day, from his childhood. Which R. Solomon Jarchi explains thus: as soon as he is shaken out, in coming forth from the bowels of his mother, the evil figment is placed in him. (Which explanation is read also in Midrash Koheleth on Eccles. ch. 4, 13. and in Midrash Tillim on Ps. 9.) and R. Menasse in the cited book p. 129. the evil appetite of man is from his childhood, that is, from that time in which he comes forth from his mother's womb. For as soon as he sucks the breasts, he follows his concupiscence, and even as an infant he is occupied by anger, envy, hatred, and other vices, by which tender age is liable; which he calls man's natural inclination toward evil, in the preface of the book, and he gives this as its cause: this depravity, having proceeded from the crime of our first parents, has by contagion invaded both faculties of the rational soul, the mind, by which we apprehend, and the will, by which we desire. cause back to the first sin: Behold, thy first father hath sinned: and he is the first Adam. For sin is fixed in the nature of man: because the imagination of his heart is evil from infancy. What of the fact that the same is also handed down in the Talmud in Sanhedrin ch. 11, where the Emperor Antoninus asks R. Jehuda Hakkadosch: from what time does concupiscence rule over man, whether from the moment of complete formation, or from birth? and receives the answer: from formation: Thus the Jews explained this article of our faith and religion more correctly than the Christian Grotius.

Latin:

QVIS POTEST FACERE MVNDVM DE IMMVN- DO CONCEPTVM SEMINE) In Hebræo: Quis dabit immundum de immundo? ut severa nimis judicia effugiat, objicit communem naturæ humanæ infirmitatem, de qua nonnulla adduximus libro secundo de Jur. Belli & Pac. 20, 19.

Locus illustris est de peccato originali. Gro- tius jejune nimis de infirmitate humanæ naturæ ac- cipit: nec aliter libro citato homini cognatum esse peccare intelligit, quam prout inter Philosophos Sopater, Hierocles, Seneca prodiderunt, qui de pec- cato originali nihil sciverunt; imo dubitari posse ait, an peccata infirmitatis, quæ evitari non possunt, recte & proprie peccata dicantur? unde multo mi- nus originale peccatum pro peccato proprie di- cto habebit. Ita revixit in Grotio Pelagianismus. Qui etiam ex annotatis ad Consult: Cassandr. Art. 2. August. Confess. pellucet. Nequicquam vero in discussione Apologetici Riveti Grotiana hæc teguntur sententiis Philosophorum, de naturæ humanæ cor- ruptione, ejusque causa, ex mente Mornei de veritat. relig. Christ. nobiscum facientium. Nam quamvis Ethnicis humanæ naturæ corruptio non ignota fuerit, quam quisque in se satis experitur, quæ tamen, qualis, & quanta illa sit, & unde originem habeat, ipsi penetrare non potuere, sed propria est hæc doctrina Scripturæ & Ecclesiæ: Si quid analogi huic in Scriptis gentilium occurrat, è lectione Sa- crorum quorundam librorum, vel traditione pri- mæva, ac fama id profectum esse credendum est. Quod è gentilibus contra gentiles recte adhibetur saltim κατ' ἄνθρωπον, non quod ipsis vera rerum istarum notitia adscribenda. Non ergo, ut ad locum nostrum redeamus, communem tantum naturæ humanæ infirmitatem obvertit Job, sed fontem ipsum malorum omnium aperit, atque osten- dit: quod nempe ex immundo concipiamur semine, ideoque nemo mundum facere queat ita conceptum atque editum. Quanquam vero conceptionis istius ῥητῶς in Ebræo textu mentio non fiat: κατὰ διάνοι- αν tamen eadem illic comprehensa est: Quis dabit mundum ex immundo? Nam si ex immundo quisque procreatur, inde ab ipsa propagatione immundus sit, oportet, ut mundus dari ex immundo, mundus ab immundo procreari possit nullus. Cujus nulla alia causa est, quam quod per ipsam procreationem & propagationem immundities attrahatur, vel prout vulgata habet, quod ex immundo concipiamur se- mine. Cui prorsus geminum est illud Christi Johann. 3. vers. 5. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est: per ipsam nativitatem vel propagationem carnalem nos carnali concupiscentiae, vel peccato obnoxios esse docens; quemadmodum quicquid ex immundo est, immundum est, quia ex immundo conceptum se- mine. Conferri potest, quantum ad phrasin, locus Genes. 17, 16. dabo ex illa tibi filium, h. e. faciam ut ex illa tibi filius nascatur: ita hic, quis dabit mundum ex immundo, quis efficiet, ut mundus nascatur ex im- mundo? Atque ita etiam Chaldaeus, quis dabit mun- dum ex homine contaminato peccatis? Quod ex- presserunt quoque LXX. Seniores, hic neglecti a Grotio, alias maximi habiti, quia scil. Pelagianum errorem palam jugulant, ita reddentes: Τίς γὰρ κα- θαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥύπου, ἀλλ' οὐδεὶς, ἐὰν καὶ μία ἡμέρα ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Quis enim purus erit a sor- dibus? Sed nullus, ne quidem, si unius tantum diei vita ejus esset in terra. Augustinus ita illam interpreta- tionem citat, nemo mundus a sorde, nec infans, cujus est vita unius diei super terram. Manifestum est, Jo- qui totum de immunditie & impuritate non corporis, sed animae, non personali, sed communi, non particu- lari, sed universali, non temporali, sed perpetuo ad- haerente & inevitabili, non actuali, sed originali, a parentibus in nos derivata, cui obnoxii sumus. Quum enim de peccatis actualibus tum quotidianis, tum juvenilibus egerit, nunc de homine ut nato ex muliere, & variis a nativitate miseriis, ipsique mor- ti obnoxio agit, ejusque causam exprimit. Et recte observat Coccejus hic, cum homo dicitur טמא im- purus, tenuiter id non esse intelligendum: quia cum maledictioni iraeque Dei obnoxium indicare Scriptura vult, impurum contenta est appellasse, atque hoc de sce- leratissimis hominibus dicit: uti Graeca etiam ἀκά- θαρτος, βδελυγός, στυγητὸς, μυαρὸς & similia atro- cem habent significationem: Et Paulus vocem ἀκα- θαρτος usurpavit de haereditaria impuritate 1. Cor. 7. vers. 14. Haec Coccejus. Praeterea sic dicitur homo impurus ut intelligi non possit, ullam partem, fa- cultatem aut actum ipsius esse mundum. Quod ma- gis confirmatur, dum negat, quicquam purum ab impuro elici posse. Atque hinc R. Levi impuras etiam cogitationes atque actiones universas esse docet. Quis eliciet puras cogitationes & actiones ex foedo? Limpi- dam & puram aquam ex impuro & putrido ac vene- nato puteo? Hominem nihil aliud esse innuens, quam latrinam sordibus plenam. Explicat quidem locum hunc paulo aliter jam laudatus Coccejus, sed sen- sum jam traditum praesupponit: Adscribam ejus in- terpretamentum: Intelligit Job, & verum est, posse Deum etiam in uno ex multis reis justitiam suam de- monstrare, si velit: Sive ex multis reis punire, quem vult. Sed huic cogitationi sic occurrit: Fore sine fru- ctu respectu caeterorum reorum, si ipse ad hoc deligatur. Per aeque reum non posse fieri, ut ex impuris fiant puri, aut ut qui sunt ex parentibus impuris, sublato ipsorum reatu, puri censeantur: siquidem nec unus sit, qui sit incontaminatus, cujus poena satisfacere Deo condi- gne, & ipsius gloriam illustrare, imo qui poenam illam sustinere possit. Vides, inquit, ita nos utrumque sensum conjungere, & primum (quo מן EX est originis) quem sequuntur plerique Interpretes, alteri (in quo מן EX est mutationis) praestructum esse, adeo ut divelli ab se in- vicem non possint. Praestruit enim altera expositio, ho- minem impurum esse, & absolute omnem, citra ex- ceptionem, idque quia ex muliere genitus est, & indicat, non posse fieri ex impuro purum per ullius hominis alte- rius satisfactionem. Haec Coccejus, qui porro verba illa לא אחד interrogativè legi vult; Annon unus? & unum Christum intelligit, à Deo designatum, qui dat purum ex impuro. Sed simplicior, textuique con- venientior est communis interpretatio: ideo lo- cus præsens insigne habitus est testimonium origi- nalis peccati ab antiquitatis Doctoribus: Origene in Levit. Ambrosio de arc. Noæ c. 22. Augustino de Civit. Dei lib. 20. c. 26. Gregorio M. ad h. l. qui ho- mo, inquit, in corruptibili carne vivens habet tenta- tionum immunditias impressas in semetipso, quia ni- mirum eas traxit ab origine. Hinc est quod plerumque tentatur & nolens. Hinc est, quod immunda quædam in mente patitur, quamvis ex judicio reluctetur, quia conceptus de immunditia, dum ad munditiem tendit, hoc conatur vincere, quod est. Sed & Judæi ipsi vide- runt, quod videre noluit Grotius. R. Aben-Ezra explicavit locum è Psalm. 51, 7. Sensus est hic, uti ejus, in iniquitatibus genitus sum, quia homo fit ex re im- munda. R. Josephus Jahia ita interpretatus est: Quis posset dare aut facere aliquid, quod esset ab omni parte purum, velut Angeli, cum sit impurus per se & materialis? Ne quidem unus. Hoc est dicere, non in- venies unum ex genere humano, qui sit velut Angelus Dei, & qui non peccet per errorem aut sponte. Per se ergo & qua ex materiali semine corrupto nempe per peccatum & impuro ortus est homo, impurum esse & ad peccatum pronum ac proclivem, vi hujus dicti asserit. Eadem etiam est explicatio R. Mosis Ge- rund. quod ex semine, re adeo impura (impuritas Spiritualis, non carnalis intelligitur, ut consequens docet) non possit prodire, ne unus quidem, qui totus sit mundus, spirituali nempe immunditie. Nec absi- milis paraphrasis est R. Abraham Peritsol. Nosti Do- mine structuram hominis: scis impossibile esse, hanc perfectionem consequi, ob materiam, quæ ipsum pec- care facit: (semen immundum, vel ut Christus ait: quia caro est ex carne natus, unde non potest non peccare, semper propensus est ad peccatum) Et quare hunc semper affligis? Potestne aliquis prodire purus, aut mundus ex re aliqua immunda? Certe non est ex hac classe aliquis, quoniam non est homo justus, qui non peccet. Similia leguntur apud R. Hobadia Sphorno in Mispat Zedek, & apud R. Mehir Ara- ma in Mehir Hiob, impossibile esse invenire aliquem natum de ventre mulieris, qui non impingat in im- munditiem. Qui omnes à R. Manasse Ben Israel lib. de Fragil. human. p. 5. adducti sunt. R. Nachmani- dis hæc laudatur à Coccejo in h. l. paraphrasis: Homi- nem qui venit ex loco immundo, quis putet eum pu- rum? Non est vel unus, qui sit purus. Confessio justo- rum super peccato suo: quale istud: Ecce in pravitate editus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Omnes autem illi, uti manifestum est, verba textus Hebræi: Quis dabit mundum ex immundo? ne unus quidem, ita interpretati sunt, ut LXX. Interpre- tes, & vulgata versio, ac intellexere, uti Christiani Interpretes communiter intelligunt, de peccato nempe, ut in Ecclesia vocatur, originali. Quod R. Aben-Ezra in Ps. 51. vocat concupiscentiam humano cordi innatam, & figmentum malum à nativitate cor- di nostro implantatum. Conferatur etiam hìc Gen. 6, 5. cap. 8, 21. de figmento cordis humani malo omni die, inde à pueritia ejus. Quod ita explicat R. Sa- lomo Jarchi: statim ac excussus est, egrediendo ex vi- sceribus matris suæ, positum in eo est figmentum malum. (Quæ explicatio legitur etiam in Midrasch Kohe- leth ad Eccles. c. 4, 13. & in Midrasch Tillim ad Ps. 9.) & R. Menasse libr. cit. p. 129. appetitus hominis ma- lus est à pueritia sua, h. e. ab eo tempore, quo prodit è ventre suæ matris. Nam simul ac ubera sugit, concu- piscentiam suam sequitur, & adhuc infans occupatur ab ira, invidia, odio, ac cæteris vitiis, quibus tenera illa ætas est obnoxia; quam dicit naturalem hominis in malum proclivitatem, in præfatione libri, cau- samque ejus hanc reddit: hæc vitiositas ex primorum parentum profecta crimine, contagioque invasit utram- que animæ rationalis facultatem, mentem, qua appre- hendimus, & voluntatem, qua appetimus. R. David Kimchi in Ef. 43, 26. idem malum describit, ejus- que causam repetit à primo peccato: Ecce Pater tuus primus peccavit: & is est primus Adam. Nam ho- minis naturæ infixum est peccatum: eo quod figmen- tum cordis ejus malum est ab infantia. Quid quod idem etiam in Talmude traditum sit in Sanhedrin cap. 11. ubi quærit Antoninus Imperator ex R. Jehu- da Hakkadosch: concupiscentia ex quo tempore domi- natur homini, utrum à momento absolutæ formatio- nis, an à nativitate? & responsum accipit: à forma- tione: Ita rectius articulum hunc fidei & religio- nis nostræ explicarunt Judæi, quam Grotius Chri- stianus.

## 14:5
Verse 5.

THOU HAST APPOINTED HIS BOUNDS) You have forbidden him to prolong his life for many ages, as in times past. Ps. 39, v. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

CONSTITVISTI TERMINOS EJVS) Vetuisti eum in plura sæcula, ut olim, vitam producere. Pf. 39. v. 4.

## 14:8
Verse 8. TURN FROM HIM A LITTLE, THAT HE MAY REST, TILL HE SHALL ACCOMPLISH, AS AN HIRELING, HIS DAY) The sense is: it is a small thing that you let him spend his life without torments. Old age will soon come, which will make death desirable to him.

Latin:

Vers. 8. RECEDE PAVLVLVM AB EO, VT QVIE- SCAT, DONEC OPTATA VENIAT, SICVT MER- CENARII, DIES EJVS) Sensus est: parum est ut eum fine cruciatibus finas ætatem agere. Jam veniet Senectus, quæ mortem ei faciet desiderabilem.

## 14:9
Verse 9. AS IF WATERS DEPART FROM THE SEA) Understand by sea a lake, just as the seven seas are said to be at the Po by the Latins. Livy book 5 tells of the Alban Lake being drained in the time of Camillus. Suetonius tells of the Fucine Lake under Claudius. Augustus drained the Pomptine marshes. Horace mentions it in his Art [of Poetry] and the scholiast on him.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVOMODO SI RECEDANT AQVÆ DE MARI) Mare intellige lacum, quomodo septem maria ad Padum dicta Latinis. De lacu Albano emisso Camilli tem- pore narrat Livius lib. 5. De Fucino Lacu Suetonius Clau- dio. Pomptinas paludes siccavit Augustus. Meminit in ar- re Horatius & ad eum Scholiastes.

## 14:14
Verse 14. ALL THE DAYS OF MY APPOINTED TIME WILL I WAIT, TILL MY CHANGE COME) The sense is: if another life were given to be spent on this earth, I would soothe present evils with the hope of a better state at some time. A similar thought is in Euripides in the Suppliants: Alas, why is this not granted to mortals, to be young twice and old again? But in our houses, if anything is not well, we correct it with later judgments. But it is not possible for a lifetime. If we were young twice, and old, if anyone had erred, having obtained a double life, we would correct it.

These are more correctly taken categorically: because he has already abandoned that hope here and in the preceding verses: And therefore B. Scultetus seems to interpret it not inappropriately concerning the resurrection, rendering it thus: All the days in which I now serve as a soldier, I will wait until my change comes, as if he were saying: this is my hope and expectation in this so hard warfare Job 7:1, that I shall at some time be changed for the better, in the future resurrection, Job 19:25. THOU SHALT CALL ME AND I WILL ANSWER THEE, with your omnipotent voice you will call me forth from the sepulcher, and I will obey you (John 11, verse 31.) THOU WILT HAVE A DESIRE TO THE WORK OF THINE HANDS, you will bring back and restore the body which you first created, and you will show your benevolence to it.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CVNCTIS DIEBVS QVIBVS NVNC MI- LITO EXPECTO DONEC VENIAT IMMVTATIO MEA) Sensus est: si alia vita in his terris agenda daretur, solarer præsentia mala spe status aliquando melioris. Simi- lis cogitatio apud Euripidem est in Supplicibus: Οἴμοι τί δὴ βροτοῖσιν ἐκ ἔστι τόδε, Νέους δὶς εἶναι καὶ γέροντας ἄν πάλιν; Ἀλλ' ἐν δόμοις μὲν ἤν τι μὴ καλῶς ἔχῃ, Γνώμαισιν ὑστέραισιν ἐξορθούμεθα. Αἰῶνα δ' ἐκ ἔξεστιν. εἰ δ' ἦμεν νέοι Δὶς, καὶ γέροντες εἴ τις ἐξημάρτανεν, Διπλᾶ βίε λαχόντες, ἐξορθώμεθ' ἄν.

Rectius Categorice hæc accipiuntur: quia il- lam spem hic & in superioribus jam abjecit: Ideo- que de resurrectione non incommode exponere videtur B. Scultetus, sic reddens: Cunctis diebus, quibus nunc milito, expectabo donec veniat immuta- tio mea, quasi dicat: hæc est spes & expectatio mea in hac tam dura militia Job. 7, 1. aliquando in me- lius me mutandum, in futura resurrectione, Job. 19, 25. VOCABIS ME ET RESPONDEBO TIBI, omnipotenti tua voce me è sepulcro evo- cabis, & ego tibi obediam (Joh. 11. vers. 31.) OPUS MANUUM TUARUM EXPETES, corpus quod primum creasti, reduces & restitues, ipsique benevolentiam tuam exhibebis.

## 14:17
Verse 17. BUT THOU HAST SEALED UP MINE INIQUITY) In the Hebrew: and you sew something onto my iniquity: In the balance you add some weight to my sins, if there are any.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SED CVRASTI INIQVITATEM MEAM) In Hebræo: & adsuis aliquid iniquitati meæ: In examine pondus aliquod adjicis culpis, si quæ sunt, meis.

## 14:19
Verse 19. THE WATERS WEAR THE STONES] A drop hollows out a stone, Ovid.

AND BY THE FLOOD THOU DESTROYEST THE THINGS WHICH GROW OUT OF THE DUST OF THE EARTH) More correctly from the Hebrew: the dust will inundate the growths of the earth. That is, shifting sands overwhelm herbs and trees.

Latin:

Vers. 19. LAPIDES EXCAVANT AQVÆ] Gutta cavat lapidem, Ovidius.

ET ALLVVIONE PAVLATI M TERRA CONSV- MITVR) Rectius ex Hebræo: inundabit germina terræ pulvis. Id est, Syrtes obruunt herbas & arbores.

## 14:20
Verse 20.

YOU HAVE STRENGTHENED HIM A LITTLE SO THAT HE MIGHT PASS INTO ETERNITY, YOU WILL CHANGE HIS FACE AND SEND HIM AWAY) The sense seems to be: you have given man some strength to spend this life, which being spent, nothing remains for him but that, with his whole face and habit of body changed, he should depart from this light. But Maimonides thinks these things are said of Adam, who, after he had changed his purpose, was expelled by God.

B. Luther expressed the sense more correctly here, or rather rendered it word for word.

Eliphaz accuses Job of boasting, impatience, and blasphemy; he asserts that no one is righteous before God, and describes the character and punishment of the wicked and tyrants.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ROBORASTI EVM PAVLVLVM VT IN PERPE- TVVM TRANSIRET, IMMVTABIS FACIEM EJVS ET EMITTES EVM) Sensus videtur esse: aliquid homini dedisti virium ad vitam hanc exigendam, qua exacta nihil ei restat, nisi ut tota facie habituque corporis immutato, abeat ex hac luce. At Maimonides putat de Adamo hæc dici, qui postquam propositum suum mutaverat, à Deo expul- sus est.

Rectius hic sensum expressit B. Lutherus imo κατὰ πόδα reddidit.

Eliphaz Jobum arguit jactantiæ, impatientiæ, & blasphemiæ, neminem coram Deo justum esse adserit, iniquorum ac tyrannorum in- dolem & pœnam describit.

## 15:4
Verse 4.

AS MUCH AS IN YOU LIES, YOU HAVE EMPTIED OUT FEAR) That is, you have destroyed religion with your words.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QUANTUM IN TE EST, EVACVASTI TIMO- REM) Id est destruxisti religionem verbis tuis.

## 15:20
Verse 20.

THE WICKED MAN IS PROUD ALL HIS DAYS) The Greeks express this sentiment, which Eliphaz had received from his ancestors, better: πᾶς ὁ βίος ἀσεβοῦς ἐν φροντίδι. Word for word from the Hebrew: The whole life of the wicked man is ἑαυτοντιμωρούμενος. AND THE NUMBER OF THE YEARS OF HIS TYRANNY IS UNCERTAIN) From the Hebrew you might perhaps translate more correctly thus: And as long as the number of his years lasts, he hides himself in fear. See Isaiah 48, verse 22; 57, 20. Add also what is in Deuteronomy 28, v. 65.

The sense is clear from the preceding verse: THE WICKED MAN ALL HIS DAYS TORMENTS HIMSELF (as if in labor) THE NUMBER OF YEARS WHICH IS HIDDEN FROM THE TYRANT (namely, torments himself.) He does not know how long he is to live, and he perpetually fears the end of life, THE SOUND OF TERROR IS IN HIS EARS, any sound, even the rustling of leaves, terrifies him, Leviticus 26, 36. Wisdom 17, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

CVNCTIS DIEBUS IMPIUS SVPERBIT) Melius Græci hanc sententiam, quam Eliphaz à majoribus accepe- rat, enunciant: πᾶς ὁ βίος ἀσεβοῦς ἐν φροντίδι. Ad verbum ex Hebræo: Tota vita impius est ἑαυτοντιμωρούμενος. ET NVMERVS ANNORVM INCERTVS EST TY- RANNIDIS EJVS) Ex Hebræo sic forte rectius vertas: Et quamdiu durat numerus annorum ejus, abscondit se timen- do. Vide Esaiam 48. vers. 22. 57, 20. Adde & quæ Devter. 28. v. 65.

SEnsus è præcedenti apertus est commate: IM- PIUS CUNCTIS DIEBUS CRUCIAT SEI- PSUM (veluti parturiens) NUMERUS AN- NORUM QUI ABSCONDITUS EST TY- RANNO (scil. cruciat se.) Nescit quam diu victu- rus sit, & perpetuo vitæ finem metuit, SONITUS TERRORIS IN AURIBUS EJUS, quivis sonus, etiam folis strepitus ipsum terret, Levit. 22, 36. Sa- pient. 17, 10.

## 15:22
Verse 22.

LOOKING AROUND EVERYWHERE FOR THE SWORD) An excellent description of a tyrant. Note the history of Dionysius and Damocles, to which Horace alludes, III, 1: For him over whose impious neck a drawn sword hangs, Sicilian feasts will not produce a sweet flavor: nor will the songs of birds and lyres bring back sleep.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

CIRCUMSPECTANS UNDIQUE GLADIUM) Opti- ma descriptio Tyranni. Nota Dionysii & Damoclis histo- ria, ad quam alludit Horatius III, 1. Destrictus ensis cui super impia Cervice pendet, non Siculæ dapes Dulcem elaborabunt saporem: Non avium citharæque cantus Somnum reducent.

## 15:23
Verse 23.

WHEN HE MOVES HIMSELF TO SEEK BREAD) In the Hebrew: He will wander for bread, where is it? He will wander as an exile, uncertain of life, like Oedipus in Sophocles: Who will receive the wandering Oedipus day by day with the gifts he now lacks? HE KNOWS THAT THE DAY OF DARKNESS IS PREPARED IN HIS HAND) In his hand, that is, very near him. He feels inevitable miseries approaching him.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

CUM SE MOVERIT AD QVÆRENDUM PANEM) In Hebræo: Vagabitur ad panem, ubinam? Errabit exsul, incertus vitæ ut Oedipus apud Sophoclem: Τίς τὸν πλανήτην Οἰδίπυν καθ’ ἡμέραν Τὴν νῦν σπανιστοῖς δέξεται δωρήμασι; NOVIT QVOD PARATUS SIT IN MANV EJVS TENEBRARVM DIES) In manu ejus, id est, proxime se. Sentit advenire sibi miserias inevitabiles.

## 15:24
Vers. 24.

AND ANGUISH SHALL BESET HIM, AS A KING WHO IS PREPARED FOR BATTLE) There are two Chaldean words here, תתקפהו & עתיד. The latter is usually explained by the Greek word received into Chaldaism, אסימוס, that is ἕτοιμος. However, it seems better that כמלך be translated as a king, rather than as a king. For he acts as if concerning a petty Satrap, whom a great king encounters. But כידור seems to be a drawn-up battle line. For also to the Arabs كيدورة is a tumult.

AS A KING PREPARED FOR BATTLE, who besieges a city, and surrounds his enemy with a crown, or troop of soldiers on every side. That word implies a globe or sphere, and a round ball. Isa. 22. vers. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ET ANGUSTIA VALLABIT EVM, SICUT REGEM QVI PRÆPARATVR AD PRÆLIVM) Duæ hîc sunt vo- ces Chaldaicæ, תתקפהו & עתיד. Posterius hoc exponi solet voce Græca in Chaldaismum recepta, אסימוס, id est ἕτοιμος. Videtur autem melius כמלך verti ut rex, quam ut regem. Agit enim quasi de minuto Satrapa, cui rex magnus occurrit. כידור autem videtur esse acies con- rerta. Nam & Arabibus كيدورة est tumultus.

UT REX PARATUS AD PRÆLIUM, qui urbem obsidet, hostemque suum corona, sive turma militum undique circumdat, Vox illa globum vel sphæram, & pilam rotundam infert. Esa. 22. vers. 18.

## 15:25
Vers. 25.

FOR HE STRETCHED OUT HIS HAND AGAINST GOD) He threatened God. The same expression is in Isa. 58. vers. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

TETENDIT ENIM ADVERSUS DEVM MANVM SVAM) Minatus est Deo. Locutio eadem Esa. 58. vers. 9.

## 15:26
Vers. 26.

HE RAN AGAINST HIM WITH AN ERECT NECK) In the Hebrew: he runs at him into the neck: namely God, or misfortune sent by God.

The following and preceding parts alike teach that these things are to be understood not of God, but of the Tyrant, with an uplifted neck, with a stubborn and fierce mind, and with all his defenses (which are understood by the shields) resisting God. For in Hebrew it is: HE RAN AGAINST HIM (with an erect) NECK, AND WITH THE THICKNESS OF THE BACK OF HIS SHIELDS. And therefore the gloss of Grotius, which now follows, is not to be approved.

AND HE IS ARMED WITH A FAT NECK) In Hebrew, into the thickened bosses of his shields: that is, it will profit him nothing to carry σάκη ἑπταβόεια (seven-fold ox-hide shields). Verse 27. AND FROM HIS SIDES HE HANGS DOWN FROM RUIN) פימה, which is here, the Chaldean translates רוטבא, that is, fatness. A similar kind of speaking is below, chapter 21, verse 23; Psalm 17, verse 10; 73, verse 7. Add also what is in Deuteronomy 32, verse 15. You may render the Hebrew thus: HE COVERED HIS FACE WITH FATNESS, AND MADE A WRINKLE AROUND HIS FLANKS. Just as fat and fatted oxen are more ferocious, so the Tyrant is depicted like a fat ox, to whom fatness has surrounded both face and sides, so that in the bending of the body it might create wrinkles. Compare Psalm 17, 10; Psalm 73, 5, 7, 10; Psalm 22, 13; Amos 4, 1. A fat neck is opulent pride, says Gregory the Great, book 12, chapter 22. Verse 28. HE DWELT IN DESOLATED CITIES) For where tyrants have made a solitude, they call it peace, as Tacitus speaks. Verse 30. [2] HE SHALL NOT DEPART FROM DARKNESS) He shall not be removed from evils. AND THE SPIRIT OF HIS MOUTH SHALL BE TAKEN AWAY) Of his mouth, namely God's: concerning whom it was treated above. God shall blow him away. Verse 31. HE SHALL NOT BELIEVE IN VAIN, DECEIVED BY ERROR, THAT HE IS TO BE REDEEMED BY ANY PRICE) More correctly from the Hebrew: Let him not believe in vanity who is deceived: for vanity shall be his reward. Verse 34. HE SHALL DEVOUR THE TABERNACLES OF THOSE WHO WILLINGLY RECEIVE GIFTS) δωροδεκτῶν, as the Greeks here. In the Hebrew: The tabernacles of gifts: that is, built from ill-gotten gains. Verse 35. HE CONCEIVED PAIN AND BROUGHT FORTH INIQUITY) In the Hebrew: he brought forth vanity: as also in Psalm 7, 14, and Isaiah 59, 4. The sense is: with great effort he accomplishes nothing. AND HIS WOMB PREPARES DECEITS) However often the matter may have turned out badly, yet he does not cease to plot new frauds in his mind.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

CVCVRRIT ADVERSVS EVM ERECTO COLLO) In Hebræo: incurrit ei in collum: nempe Deus, aut infortu- nium à Deo immissum.

Sequentia pariter & antecedentia docent hæc non de Deo, sed Tyranno accipienda esse, cervi- ce elata, pertinaci & feroci animo & omnibus præ- sidiis suis (quæ per clypeos intelliguntur) Deo re- luctanti. In Ebræo enim est: CUCURRIT AD- VERSUS EUM (erecto) COLLO, ET CRASSITIE DORSI CLYPEORUM SUO- RUM. Ideoque non probanda glossa Grotii, quæ jam sequitur.

ET PINGVI CERVICE ARMATVS EST) In Hebr. in densatos umbones scutorum ejus: id est, nihil ei proderit ferre σάκη ἑπταβόεια. Vers. 27. ET DE LATERIBVS EJVS A RVINA DE- PENDET) פימה, quod hic est, Chaldæus vertit רוטבא, id est, pinguedinem. Simile loquendi genus infra 21. vers. 23. Psalm. 17. vers. 10. 73. v. 7. Adde & quæ Deu- teronom. 32. v. 15. Ebræa ita reddas: OPERUIT FACIEM E- JUS CRASSITUDO, ET RUGAM FECIT CIRCA ILIA. Sicut boves pingues & saginati ferociores sunt, ita depingitur Tyrannus instar bo- vis pinguis, cui & faciem pinguedo circumdedit & latera, ut in flexione corporis rugas efficiat. Confer Psalm. 17, 10. Psalm. 73, 5. 7. 10. Psalm. 22, 13. Amos. 4, 1. Pinguis cervix est opulenta superbia, ait Greg. M. lib. 12. cap. 22. Vers. 28. HABITAVIT IN CIVITATIBVS DESOLA- TIS) Tyranni enim ubi solitudinem fecerunt, pacem vo- cant, ut loquitur Tacitus. Vers. 30. NON RECEDET DE TENEBRIS) Non amo- vebitur à malis. ET AVFERETVR SPIRITVS ORIS SVI) Oris ejus, nempe Dei: de quo actum supra. Deus eum difflabit. Vers. 31. NON CREDET FRVSTRA ERRORE DE- CEPTVS, QVOD ALIQVO PRETIO REDIMENDVS SIT) Rectius ex Hebræo: Ne credat vanitati qui decipitur: nam vanitas erit merces ejus. Vers. 34. DEVORABIT TABERNACVLA EORVM QVI MVNERA LIBENTER ACCIPIVNT) δωροδεκτῶν ut hic Græci. In Hebræo: Tabernacula munerum: id est, ex male partis exstructa. Vers. 35. CONCEPIT DOLOREM ET PEPERIT INI- QVITATEM) In Hebræo: peperit vanitatem: ut & in Psalm. 7, 14. & Esaiæ 59, 4. Sensus est: magno conatu nihil efficit. ET VTERVS EJVS PRÆPARAT DOLOS) Vtcunque sæpe male res cesserit, tamen non desinit animo novas fraudes moliri.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. Job complains about the austerity of his friends, the gravity of his calamity, and the severity of God, and purges himself of iniquity.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. Job de amicorum austeritate, calamitatis suæ gravitate, Deique severitate queritur, & se ab iniquitate purgat.

## 16:4
Verse 4. AND WOULD THAT YOUR SOUL WERE FOR MY SOUL) That לו, which is here translated by 'would that', would be more correctly translated by 'if', as in Judges 13, 23. The sense is: if you were in my place, I could say similar things to you. Thus in the Andria, Terence: We all, when we are well, easily give right counsels to the sick. You, if you were here, would feel otherwise. Verse 6. AND I WOULD MOVE MY LIPS AS IF SPARING YOU) In the Hebrew: the motion of my lips would restrain: namely, your pains. The simile seems taken from those who charm away poisons. Concerning the Psyllus, Lucan, book 9: Then he rolls many charms with foaming tongue / In continuous murmur, nor does the course of the wound give sighs, nor do the fates suffer it to be silent in the least. Verse 7. BUT NOW MY PAIN HAS OPPRESSED ME) In the Hebrew: Long since he has made me wretched. God, namely: although he soon changes the person: which is frequent in these writings. Or, my pain has made me weary, as Chrysostom and Olympiodorus in the context. Verse 8. [5] MY WRINKLES BEAR WITNESS AGAINST ME) קמט, which is translated by some here as 'to wrinkle', is a judicial word, which signifies to seize someone, and to drag them into court as if by a twisted neck. It exists in the Chaldean interpreters, as Proverbs 4, 4 and 5, 22, and in the Gemara; nor did the Greeks understand it otherwise, ἐπελάβο με. It can be rendered thus: κατὰ πόδα (at the foot): AND HE HAS WRINKLED (pain) HAS BECOME A WITNESS: he provides testimony against me. Verse 9. AND THE FALSE-SPEAKER IS RAISED UP AGAINST MY FACE, CONTRADICTING ME) He continues in the judicial simile. כחש, which some translate as 'leanness', is better translated as 'lying against me'. Symmachus best: ἀνέστη μοι καταψευδόμενος κατὰ πρόσωπόν με ἀντιλέγων μοι. Thus also B. Luther, 'my adversary', and the Vulgate, 'false-speaker'. The Hebrew word denotes both: he has lied, he has contradicted. He has the predicate thus: HE RISES UP AGAINST ME, TO MY FACE HE ANSWERS ME: [6] He contradicts me, and as a witness against me in judgment he accuses me. Verse 11. GOD HAS SHUT ME UP WITH THE UNJUST) God has handed me over, bound, to the unjust. He persists in the simile of judgments. Verse 13. HE HAS SURROUNDED ME WITH HIS LANCES) The word רבים signifies archers, Jeremiah 50, 29. Another comparison taken from war. HE HAS POURED OUT MY BOWELS ON THE GROUND) מרוה here and below 20, 14 seems to signify that which is contained by the intestines. Verse 15. UPON MY SKIN) גלד, which is translated here as 'skin', we learn from the Mishna is a word of the Scenitae (Tent-dwellers). The Arabs use it even now, and write جلد. I HAVE COVERED MY FLESH WITH ASH) In the Hebrew: my horn: that is, my glory is cast down. The Greeks: 'and my horn is extinguished in the earth'. Verse 18. THESE THINGS I HAVE SUFFERED WITHOUT THE INIQUITY OF MY HANDS) In the Hebrew: Not therefore is there rapine in my hands. Verse 19. [7] EARTH, DO NOT COVER MY BLOOD) If I have committed such a thing as these men think, then let dogs lick my blood. See 1 Kings 21, 23. NOR LET MY CRY FIND A PLACE OF HIDING IN THEE) In the Hebrew: Let there be no place for my cry. Let no one care for these complaints of mine. Verse 20. MY WITNESS IS IN THE HEIGHTS) שהד signifies a witness in the Syriac idiom, as appears in Genesis 31, 47. The Arabs even now say ساهد. Verse 22. FOR BEHOLD, THE SHORT YEARS SHALL PASS) In the Hebrew: The years of number shall come: that is, very few, as appears from the contrary in Genesis 41, verse 49. The word יאתיון, 'they shall come', is Chaldean, frequent in Daniel and Ezra.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ATQVE VTINAM ESSET ANIMA VESTRA PRO ANIMA MEA) Illud לו, quod hic per utinam vertitur, re- ctius verteretur per si, ut Jud. 13, 23. Sensus est: si vos meo essetis loco, possem vobis similia dicere. Sic in Andria Terentius: Facile omnes cum valemus recta consilia ægrotis damus. Tu, si hic sis, aliter sentias. Vers. 6. ET MOVEREM LABIA MEA QVASI PAR- CENS VOBIS) In Hebræo: motus labiorum meorum cohi- beret: nempe dolores vestros. Similitudo sumta videtur ab his qui venena excantant. De Psyllo Lucan. lib. 9. Plurima tum volvit spumanti carmina lingua Murmure continuo, nec dat suspiria cursus Vulneris, aut minimum patiuntur fata tacere. Vers. 7. NVNC AVTEM OPPRESSIT ME DOLOR MEVS) In Hebræo: Jampridem ærumnabilem me fecit. Deus scilicet: quanquam mox mutat personam: quod fre- quens his scriptis. Vel dolor meus, lassum me fecit, ut Chrysostomus & Olympiodorus vi contextus. Vers. 8. RVGÆ MEÆ TESTIMONIVM DICVNT CONTRA ME) קמט, quod hic per rugare à nonnullis vertitur, est vox judicialis, quæ significat prehendere aliquem, & in jus velut obtorto collo trahere. Exstat in Chaldæis in- terpretibus, ut Prov. 4, 4. & 5, 22. & in Gemara; nec aliter intellexere Græci, ἐπελάβο με. Reddi sic potest κατὰ πόδα: ET CORRU- GAVIT (dolor) TESTIS FACTUS EST: præ- bet testimonium contra me. Vers. 9. ET SVSCITATVR FALSILOQVVS | AD- VERSVS FACIEM MEAM, CONTRADICENS MIHI) Pergit in similitudine judiciali. כחש quod maciem ver- tunt quidam, melius vertitur mentiens in me. Symmachus optime: ἀνέστη μοι καταψευδόμενος κατὰ πρόσωπόν με ἀντι- λέγων μοι. Sic etiam B. Lutherus, mein Widersacher, & vulgatus, falsiloquus. Ebræa vox utrumque notat, mentitus est, contradixit. Prædicatum ita habet: INSVRGIT CONTRA ME, IN FACIEM RESPONDET MIHI: Contradicit mihi, & tan- quam testis contra me in judicio me criminatur. Vers. 11. CONCLVSIT ME DEVS APVD INI- QVVM) Vinctum me Deus iniquo tradidit. Perseverat in judiciorum similitudine. Vers. 13. CIRCVMDEDIT ME LANCEIS SVIS) Vox רבים sagittarios significat Jerem. 50, 29. Alia comparatio à bello sumta. EFFVDIT IN TERRA VISCERA MEA) מרוה hîc & infra 20, 14. videtur significare id quod intestinis con- tinetur. Vers. 15. SVPER CVTEM MEAM) גלד, quod hîc cu- tis vertitur, vocem esse Scenitarum, discimus ex Mischna. Vtuntur ea & nunc Arabes, & scribunt جلـو. OPERVI CINERE CARNEM MEAM) In Hebræo: cornu meum: id est, gloria mea dejecta est. Græci: τὸ δὲ κέρας με ἐν γῇ ἐσβέσθη. Vers. 18. HÆC PASSVS SVM ABSQVE INIQVITA- TE MANVS MEÆ) In Hebræo: Non ideo rapina in ma- nibus meis. Vers. 19. TERRA NE OPERIAS SANGVINEM ME- VM) Si tale quid patravi quale hi existimant, tum sangui- nem meum lingant canes. Vide 1. Reg. 21, 23. NEQVE INVENIAT IN TE LOCVM LATENDI CLAMOR MEVS) In Hebræo: Ne sit locus clamori meo. Querelas has meas nemo curet. Vers. 20. CONSCIVS MEVS IN EXCELSIS( שהד testem significat Syriaco idiomate, ut apparet Genes. 31, 47. Arabes etiam nunc ساهد dicunt. Vers. 22. ECCE ENIM BREVES ANNI TRANS- EVNT) In Hebræo: Anni numeri venient: id est pauci ad- modum, ut apparet ex contrario Gen. 41. vers. 49. Vox יאתיון venient, est Chaldaica, frequens apud Danielem & Esdram.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII.

Job renews his complaint, and consoles himself with the future manifestation of his innocence; he despairs of restitution in this life.

Latin:

CAPUT. XVII.

Job querelam redintegrat, & innocentiæ suæ futura manifestatione se solatur, de resti- tutione in hac vita desperat.

## 17:1
Ver. 1. MY DAYS SHALL BE SHORTENED) They shall be extinguished, נועכו for נרעכו as the Chaldean and Rabbi Solomon have it here; דעך for I extinguish, is found several times in this writer, and in Isaiah, and in Proverbs, and in the Psalms.

Latin:

Vers. 1. DIES MEI BREVIABVNTVR) Exstinguentur נועכו pro נרעכו ut hic habet Chaldæus & Rabbi Salomo דעך pro exstinguo, aliquoties est apud hunc scriptorem, & in Esaia, & in Proverbiis & in Psalmis.

## 17:2
Verse 2. I HAVE NOT SINNED.

THUS also B. Luther: In the Hebrew it is: IF NOT ILLUSIONS ARE WITH ME. Am I not mocked by my friends? The Vulgate neglected the particle אם. Therefore it had to be corrected here by Grotius. There is added

Verse of the same. AND IN THE BITTERNESSES OF THEM MY EYE DWELLS or passes the night: I am perpetually harassed by those bitter sarcasms, so that my eyes cannot take sleep even at night. Cocceius took אם as a particle of swearing: Unless mockeries (are) with me, even in their exacerbation my eye passes the night. But the former sense is simpler. There follows

Latin:

Vers. 2. NON PECCAVI.

SIC etiam B. Lutherus: In Ebræo est: SI NON ILLUSIONES MECUM. Annon ab amicis illudor? neglexit vulgata particulam אם. Ideo hîc emendanda erat à Grotio. Additur

Vers. eod. ET IN AMARITUDINIBUS E- ARUM MORATUR vel pernoctat OCULUS MEUS: amaris illis sarcasmis perpetuo exagitor, ut nec noctu oculi somnum capere possint. Coc- cejus אם ceu voculam jurandi accepit: Nisi ludi- bria apud me (sunt) etiam in exacerbatione eo- rum pernoctet oculus meus. Sed prior sensus sim- plicior est. Sequitur

## 17:3
Ver. 3. PONE QUÆSO (put, I pray, [thy hand, as in Exod. 23, v. 1, or thyself, station thyself.]) Fide jube pro me (he challenges to the judgment of God by asking that He be his Surety) QUIS MANUI MEÆ COMPLODET (hand?) in pledges the joining of hands takes place. The meaning is, as Cocceius notes, that there is not in his friends that πληροφορίαν of the cause, which could effect παῤῥησίαν before GOD, so that they might dare to undergo His judgment with the risk of paying a penalty, as it were, if they should lose their case. Mr. D. Schmiedius, observing that that rite of the joining of hands in judgments is not found in the O. T., renders it: for who (besides thee) is there, who for my hand would fix himself, i. e., would obligate himself by pledging for me, and he notes here Job’s faith concerning the Messiah as Surety: Which I would προθύμως accept, if here where God the Father is addressed, that interpretation concerning stationing another surety had a place: Station him, who might stand surety for me; or the Piscatorian: Stop to stand surety for me. But because the passage must be understood of him who presents himself as a surety for another, I do not sufficiently grasp how Christ is designated here as a surety.

Latin:

Vers. 3. PONE QUÆSO (manum, ut Exod. 23, v. 1. vel teipsum, siste te.) Fide jube pro me (ad Dei judicium provocat petendo ut Fidejussor sit) QUIS MANUI MEÆ COMPLODET (manum?) in sponsionibus manus fit consertio. Mens est, no- tante Coccejo, non esse in amicis suis illam causæ πληροφορίαν, quæ coram DEO παῤῥησίαν efficere possit, ut ipsius judicium subire audeant cum peri- culo luendæ quasi mulctæ, si causa cadant. Dn. D. Schmiedius ritum illum consertionis manuum in ju- diciis in V. T. haud inveniri observans, reddit: nam quis (præter te) est, qui pro manu mea figat se, h. e. obliget se spondendo pro me, & fidem Jobi hîc notat de Messia Sponsore: Quod προθύμως acciperem, si hîc ubi compellatur Deus Pater, interpretatio illa de altero sistendo sponsore locum haberet: Siste eum, qui spondeat pro me; vel Piscatoriana: Siste ad spo dendum pro me. Sed quia de eo, qui seipsum spon rem pro alio sistit, accipiendus est locus, non satis c pio, quomodo Christus sponsor hîc designetur.

## 17:5
Ver. 5. HE PROMISES PREY TO HIS COMPANIONS. Here too the Vulgate must be amended. For in the Hebrew it is held thus: BY FLATTERY HE INDICATES (impersonally, namely, each of the hypocrites) HIS THOUGHTS: (he knows how to adorn the cause of his own with flattering words) BUT THE EYES OF HIS CHILDREN SHALL WASTE AWAY: the punishment of such flatterers will redound even to their descendants. Thus the blessed Scultetus, Conf., and Cocceius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PRÆDAM POLLICETUR SOCII Etiam hîc vulgata emendanda. In Ebræo eni ita habetur: PER BLANDIMENTUM IND CAT (impersonaliter, hypocritarum scil. quisque COGITATIONES SUAS: (novit causam suar blandis verbis ornare) SED OCULI FILIORUM EJUS TABESCENT: pœna adulatorum taliur etiam ad posteros redundabit. Ita Beat. Scultetus Conf. & Coccejus in hunc locum.

## 17:6
Ver. 6. AND I AM A BYWORD BEFORE THEM) The Hebrews: I am a drum to them: thus I am deafened by curses, so that תפת becomes the same as תוף and with the Arabs تفت, the name being derived from the imitation of sound.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET EXEMPLVM SVM CORAM EIS) He bræi: Tympanum ipsis sum: ita maledictis obtundor, ut תפת fit idem quod תוף & Arabibus تفت ex foni imitatione ducto nomine.

## 17:12
Ver. 12. THEY HAVE TURNED NIGHT INTO DAY, AND AGAIN AFTER DARKNESS I HOPE FOR LIGHT) From the Hebrew it may be permitted to interpret thus: They make the night as the day (namely, my thoughts which grant me no rest) and the dawn near to darkness: that is, dark on account of calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NOCTEM VERTERVNT IN DIEM, ET RVRSVM POST TENEBRAS SPERO LVCEM) Ex Hebræo sic liceat interpretari: Noctem efficiunt velut diem (nempe cogitationes meæ quæ nullam mihi requiem indul- gent) & auroram propinquam tenebris: id est, tenebricosam ob calamitates.

## 17:16
Ver. 16. ALL MY THINGS SHALL DESCEND INTO THE DEEPEST HELL, DO YOU THINK THERE AT LEAST WILL BE REST FOR ME?] You might translate more closely from the Hebrew thus: They shall descend with burial garments: namely, those hopes which you propose to me: If, however, there will be rest for me, or even then when I shall be mingled with the dust.

Latin:

Vers. 16. IN PROFVNDISSIMVM INFERNVM DE- SCENDENT OMNIA MEA, PVTASNE IBI SALTEM ERIT REQVIES MIHI?] Propius ex Hebræo sic vertas: Vestibus sepulchralibus descendent: nempe spes istæ quas mihi proponitis: Si tamen quies erit mihi, vel tunc cum pulveri mi- scebor.

CHAPTER XVIII. Bildad, rebuking Job for his arrogance, recounts the curses of the wicked.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII. Bildad ob arrogantiam Jobum redarguens im- piorum maledictiones recenset.

## 18:4
Ver. 4. YOU WHO DESTROY YOUR SOUL IN YOUR FURY] In the Hebrew: Tearing his soul in his fury: that is, Listen, you who tear yourself apart with anger.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVI PERDIS ANIMAM TVAM IN FV- RORE TVO] In Hebræo: Rapiens animam suam in furore suo: id est, Audi tu qui temetipsum dilaceras iracundia.

## 18:7
Ver. 7. THE STEPS OF HIS STRENGTH SHALL BE STRAITENED) That is, of his power. This interpreter reads here just as we have it in the Hebrew. But the Greeks for יצרו read יצרו ἐλάχιστοι, and for צעדי they read צערי which they translate as least, less conveniently.

A different reading is not immediately present where there is one interpretation after another. For a misinterpretation could have arisen from elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ARCTABVNTVR GRESSVS VIRTVTIS EJVS) Id est, potentiæ ejus. Legit hic interpres ita ut nos in Hebræo habemus. At Græci pro יצרו legerunt יצרו dy- gv́svsav, & pro צעדי legerunt צערי quod vertunt ἐλάχι- soi, minus commode.

Non diversa statim lectio ubi alia atque alia est in- terpretatio. Aliunde enim oriri potuit παρερμηνεία.

## 18:12
Ver. 12. HIS STRENGTH SHALL BE WASTED BY HUNGER) That is, his seed, his posterity, as in Gen. 49:3.

Thus indeed the Targum and the Hebrews: But because it treats of children below, Mercer, Diodati, Piscator, Cocceius, and others explain these things more correctly as the strength of the body.

AND LET FAMINE INVADE HIS RIBS) In Hebrew: Let destruction be ready for his rib: that is, for his wife.

Some Hebrews, with the former Targum, explain it thus. But the proper sense concerning the side is to be retained, according to the second Targum, Aben-Ezra, and our own scholars.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ATTENVETVR FAME ROBVR EJVS) Id est, semen, posteritas, ut Gen. 49, 3.

Ita quidem Targum & Ebræi: Sed quia infra de filiis agitur, rectius de robore corporis hæc expli- cat Mercer. Diodat. Piscat. Coccejus & alii.

ET INEDIA INVADAT COSTAS ILLIVS) In He- bræo: Exitium paratum sit costæ ejus: id est, mulieri.

Ebræi nonnulli cum Targ. priori sic explicant. Sed retinendus proprius sensus de latere, juxta Targ. secundum Aben-Ezr. & Nostros,

## 18:13
Vers. 13. LET IT DEVOUR THE BEAUTY OF HIS SKIN, AND LET THE FIRSTBORN OF DEATH CONSUME HIS ARMS) In Hebrew: Let it devour the branches of his skin, let the firstborn of death devour the branches. The branches of the skin are the arms, as the Latin Interpreter rightly [translates] here in the latter place. The firstborn of death is putrefaction.

To others, it is better that the Firstborn of death is a bitter, horrendous, and cruel death. 'Firstborn' in Hebrew is that which is primary. Dr. Schmied understands it as the greatest disease, or the most atrocious among diseases born from death.

Vers. 13. HE SHALL TREAD UPON HIM AS A KING OF TERROR] In Hebrew: And he shall bring him (supply that which I said) to the king of terrors. The king of terrors seems to be the angel of death, of whom there is much mention in Baba Bathra, in the work of Rabbi Jacob in Caphthor. ὁ κράτος ἔχων θανάτε. Heb. 2, 14. Aquila and Symmachus translate that בלהות as ἀνυπαρξίαν.

There is no need for the commentary of the Hebrews concerning the angel of death: the simplest sense is: he will cast him into the greatest terror and despair, so that he may die in terror and despair, whence Cocceius: The king of mists or darknesses is the densest darkness. However, the highest darkness denotes sadness and despair here.

Latin:

Vers. 13. DEVORET PVLCHRITVDINEM CVTIS EJVS, ET CONSVMAT BRACHIA ILLIVS PRIMO. GENITA MORS) In Hebræo: Voret ramos cutis ipsius, vo- ret ramos primogenitus mortis. Rami cutis sunt brachia, ut recte hic posteriore loco Latinus Interpres. Primogenitus mortis est putredo.

Aliis melius Primogenitus mortis est mors acer- ba, horrenda, truculenta. Primogenitum in Ebræo est quod primarium est. Maximum morbum intelli- git Dn. D. Schmied. seu atrocissimum inter morbos è morte genitos.

Vers. 13. CALCET SVPER EVM QVASI REX IN. TERITVS] In Hebræo: Adducetque eum (supple id quod dixi) ad regem terrorum. Rex terrorum videtur esse ange- lus mortis, de quo multa mentio in Bababathra, apud Jaco- bum Rabinum in Caphthor. ὁ κράτος ἔχων θανάτε. Hebr. 2, 14. illud בלהות Aquila & Symmachus vertunt ἀν- παρξίαν.

Non opus commento Ebræorum de Angelo mortis: sensus simplicissimus est: conjiciet eum in maximum terrorem & desperationem, ita ut in terrore & desperatione moriatur, unde Coccejus: Rex nebularum seu caliginum sunt densissimæ te- nebræ. Tenebræ summæ autem tristitiam & de- sperationem hîc notant.

## 18:15
Vers. 15. LET HIS COMPANIONS DWELL IN HIS TABERNACLE WHO IS NOT) Better: let him dwell in his tabernacle who does not belong to him. A stranger. Others: let him dwell in the tabernacle, because it is not his, that is, the house. I prefer the former.

Others, let want dwell in his tabernacle. Word for word, NOTHING TO HIM, as B. Luther also rendered it. Dr. Schmied repeats the word of terror from verse 14, explaining it thus: (Terror) shall dwell in his tabernacle, because there will be no one who is his, all his household having been cast out either by terror or by death.

LET BRIMSTONE BE SCATTERED IN HIS TABERNACLE) Is there an allusion to the punishment of the Sodomites: concerning which see Gen. 19, 24, and what is said there: or is lightning understood by the word brimstone? Pliny, book 35, ch. 15: Lightning and thunderbolts also have the smell of brimstone, and their very light is sulphurous.

Latin:

Vers. 15. HABITENT IN TABERNACVLO ILLIVS SOCII EJVS QVI NON EST) Melius: habitet in taber- naculo ejus qui nihil ad eum pertinet. Homo extraneus. Alii: habitet in tabernaculo, quia non ei, est domus scilicet. Prius il- lud præfero.

Alii, habitet in tabernaculo ejus inopia. Ad verbum NIHIL IPSI, uti & B. Lutherus reddidit. Dn. D. Schmied. repetit è versu 14. vocem terro- ris h. m. exponens: Habitabit (terror) in taberna- culo ejus, eo quod non futurus, qui illius sit, ejectis vel terrore vel morte omnibus domesticis ejus.

ASPERGATVR IN TABERNACVLO EJVS SVL- FVR) An ad Sodomitarum pœnam alluditur: de qua vide Gen. 19, 24. & ibi dicta: an sulfuris voce fulmen intelligitur? Plinius lib. 35. c. 15. Fulmina & fulgura quoque sulfuris odo- rem habent, ac lux ipsa eorum sulfurea est.

Vers. 20. IN HIS DAY THE LAST ONES SHALL BE ASTONISHED) The younger ones.

AND HORROR SHALL INVADE THE FIRST) He understands contemporaries. For קדמון also signifies the present.

Vers. 20. IN DIE EJVS STVPEBVNT NOVISSIMI) Juniores.

ET PRIMOS INVADET HORROR) Coævos intelli- git. Nam קדמון etiam præsentem significat.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

Job, complaining of the inhumanity and injury of his friends, and of the hostile invasion of God, consoles himself with the hope of a blessed resurrection.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

Job querens de amicorum inhumanitate & in- juria, & hostili Dei invasione solatur sese spe beatæ resurrectionis.

## 19:7
Vers. 7. BEHOLD I WILL CRY OUT SUFFERING VIOLENCE) In Hebrew: If I shall cry out violence: for it indicates the very voice of the one crying out. This passage and the one that follows agrees plainly with the Lamentations of Jeremiah 3, 8 9.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ECCE CLAMABO VIM PATIENS) In Hebr. Si clamavéro vim: indicat enim ipsam clamantis vocem. Hic locus & qui sequitur plane convenit cum Threno Jer. 3, 8 9.

## 19:10
Vers. 10. HE HAS DESTROYED ME ON EVERY SIDE) He has plucked me up by the roots. For the similitude is taken from a tree, and נתץ and נתק are related.

AS IF FROM A PLUCKED-UP TREE HE HAS TAKEN AWAY MY HOPE) A Latin poet from Homer: As a scepter which has been cut from a tree, will now be able to flourish with no leaf.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DESTRVXIT ME VNDIQVE) Radicitus evul- sit me. Est enim ab arbore sumta similitudo & vicina sunt נתץ & נתק.

QVASI AVVLSÆ ARBORI ABSTVLIT SPEM ME- AM) Latinus Poeta ex Homero: Ut sceptrum quod ab arbore est recisum Nulla jam poterit virere fronde.

Vers. 12. HIS TROOPS CAME TOGETHER) His armies. The similitude is drawn from a besieged city. Μονόζωνοι to Theodotion, λόχοι to Symmachus.

Latin:

Vers. 12. SIMVL VENERVNT LATRONES EJVS) Exercitus ejus. Similitudo est ducta ab urbe obsessa. Mo- νόζωνοι Theodotioni, Symmacho λόχοι.

## 19:15
Vers. 15. AND MY MAIDSERVANTS) The Chaldean ולחנתי my concubines. So also 17. the children of my womb. The Greeks interpret it as υἱοὺς παλλακίδων με.

Niceta also understands it concerning those born from concubines with the LXX. These were raised outside the house, and the Devil, because he saw they were wicked, left them to Job, not for consolation, but for reproach. Lyra and others explain it as concerning grandchildren. The version of Junius and Piscator is foreign to the phrase and tenor of the other sentences in this context. Coccejus, however, agrees with them, explaining it thus: my breath is loathsome to my wife, even when I lament our common children, or even (if) I pity the children of my womb, because וחנותי is TO PITY, not TO SUPPLICATE. But the Chaldean translates ואתחנן as and I supplicated, and Schindler in his Pentaglot Lexicon notes that with ל it is to find favor, to be eager with prayers, that is, to supplicate: And he proves that in Niphal and Hithpael that meaning of praying and supplicating or imploring mercy is sufficiently accepted. If, however, the meaning of pitying is to be admitted, he renders it thus: And those whom I pitied, those whom I loved, namely my children, my breath has become strange. The explanation of Mr. D. Schmid pleases me above others: because the verb חנן in the Kal conjugation nowhere has the meaning of deprecating, and ל denoting 'on account of' is not infrequent: My spirit is strange, it loathes itself, on account of my wife, and her words and morose and quarrelsome gestures: and pitying, I mourn the children of my womb killed in a sad ruin.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ET ANCILLÆ MEÆ) Chaldæus ולחנתי concubinæ meæ. Sic & 17. filios uteri mei. Græci interpre- tantur υἱοὺς παλλακίδων με.

NIceta etiam de genitis è concubinis cum LXX. intelligit. Hi extra domum educabantur, & Diabolus, quia vidit malos esse, reliquit Jobo illos, non in solatium, sed in opprobrium. Lyra & alii de Nepotibus explicant. Junii & Piscat. versio à phra- si & tenore aliarum sententiarum in hoc contextu aliena est. Coccejus tamen annuit eis, sic exponens: fœtet uxori anima mea, etiam ubi communes libe- ros deploro, vel & (si) miseror filios ventris mei, quia וחנותי sit MISERER non SVPPLICEM. At Chaldæus vertit ואתחנן & supplicem, ac Schindle- rus in Lexico Pentaglotto notat cum ל esse gratiam inire, studuit precibus, id est, supplicavit: Et in Ni- phal & Hithpael eam significationem orandi & sup- plicandi vel misericordiam implorandi satis rece- ptam esse probat. Si tamen significatio miserendi admittenda, ita reddit: Et quorum misertus sum, quos dilexi, liberis meis scilicet, anhelitus meus fa- ctus est alienus. Placet præ aliis Dn. D. Schmidii ex- plicatio: quia verbum חנן in coujugatione Kal nu- spiam deprecandi significationem habet, ac ל pro- pter notare non infrequens: Spiritus meus alienus est, fastidit seipsum, propter uxorem meam, verba- que ejus atque gestus morosos & rixosos: & mise- rans lugeo filios ventris mei tristi ruina occisos.

Vers. 23. AND A PLATE OF LEAD) Jarchi says that it was customary for incisions to be made in marble, and for them to be filled with lead in the form of letters. There follows in the Hebrew לעד, which others translate as 'forever'. The Greeks better: εἰς μαρτύριον.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET PLVMBI LAMINA) Ait Jarchi in mar- more solitas fieri incisuras, & eas plumbo in formam litera- rum repleri. Sequitur in Hebræo לעד, quod alii vertunt in perpetuum. Græci melius: εἰς μαρτύριον.

## 19:24
OR BE ENGRAVED WITH A CHISEL IN FLINT) Celte, γλυφίω.

Latin:

VEL CELTE SCVLPANTVR IN SILICE) Celte, γλυφίω.

## 19:25
Verse 25. I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVES, AND AT THE LAST DAY I SHALL RISE FROM THE EARTH

The Jews never applied these words, and those which follow, to the resurrection, although they search for everything that can in any way be drawn toward that appearance. Not a few Christians have used it to prove the faith of the resurrection, but to do so they were forced in their versions to depart much from the Hebrew, as noted by Mercer and others. The Hebrew sounds thus: I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he will stand last in the field. Even if they should consume not only my skin, but also this (namely the fat which is under the skin), (i.e., the diseases), yet in my flesh I shall see God: (that is, I shall experience him as propitious:) I, I say, with these my eyes; I, and not another for me. God is called Redeemer because he delivers the pious from many evils, Ps. 77:35, Is. 41:14, ch. 43:14, 44:6, 47:4, 48:17, 49:7. To stand last in the field is the mark of a victor. Thus he says that God will be the victor over his adversaries. Nor indeed was it impossible for him to restore his body, nearly consumed by rot, to its former shape, which God also did. We spoke of this word above at 13:28.

The Jews were not to be listened to here in preference to the Christians, whom Grotius admits are not few in number in using this passage to prove the resurrection. What wonder is it that the blind guides of the Jews search for the resurrection in those places of Scripture which have nothing to say about it, but are blind in those which teach it? They lack the Spirit of Christ, and in divine judgment they hallucinate in the clearest matters. Nor have they understood the whole case of Job, who do not understand the Gospel. And therefore it is no wonder that they have strayed from the sense of the argument. Most also doubt the resurrection of the flesh, or at least the state of the pious from the Gentiles in the resurrection. Some pretend that Job himself denied the resurrection of the dead, concerning which see Menasse Ben Israel, book 1, on the resurrection of the dead, ch. 16, § 125. For this reason the ancients say that Job denied the resurrection of the dead, which Menasse thinks was done by him out of the vehemence of his grief, p. 132. But that Rabbi Moses explains those passages Job 7:9, ch. 15:12, in another way, in his Epistle on the Resurrection of the Dead, the same Menasse observes, namely that they are to be understood as the matter stands according to the order of nature: since naturally the dead do not rise. What sound judgment can you expect from those in this matter who attribute such a profane opinion to a holy man of God? The LXX, however, the seventy interpreters, were also Jews, who indeed seem to have accepted this passage concerning the resurrection of the dead: ἐπὶ γῆς ἀναστῆσαι τὸ δέρμα μὲ τὸ ἀνθλῶν ταῦτα: that he may raise up on the earth my skin, which endures these things. We shall note others later who interpret it likewise concerning the resurrection.

Nor indeed is there any need to depart much from the Hebrew text so that the meaning stands as an oracle concerning his resurrection, whatever Mercer or even Grotius may pretend: whose duty it was to defend the Vulgate translation, since he otherwise held the authority of the Council of Trent in high regard, or at least attempted to defend its decrees. Not a few Christians, most learned in Hebrew, have shown that the Hebrew words agree perfectly with the common interpretation. What? If we weigh everything accurately, it will be clear that this statement must be explained in no other way than as a resuscitation. Job desires that these words of his be written, nay, cut into rock: Who will grant me that my words may be written, who will grant me that they may be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus and a lead plate, or at least be sculpted in flint: לעד. The Greeks say εἰς μαρτύριον, others for eternity. Although some take these things concerning the deeds and words of Job in general, there is no doubt, since these things are placed before those which we are now treating, that he desired them most of all to be written and transmitted to posterity as an eternal testimony. Therefore, those things which he begins here with such an earnest vow, and which the most holy man vehemently desired to be inscribed for everlasting memory, whether on marble with the incisions filled with lead to the shape of letters, as Grotius explains from Sal. Jarchi, or inscribed by any other means of endurance, must be significant, not vulgar: and they must pertain not only to himself, but also to other believers, to whose common knowledge he wished them to be brought. Furthermore, he does not speak here of such a deliverance as could still be doubtful, but of that which was certain and indubitable to him, which he believed and expected with full confidence of heart in the midst of that desperate sickness of his body. But from where could he be so certain that it would come to pass that he would be delivered from that bodily affliction, that he would dare to profess that he KNEW it? I know, he says, that my Redeemer lives. Pineda teaches from Gen. 48:49, Psalm 138:2, Gen. 22:12, that the word ידע of knowing excludes all doubt and brings a certain and firm adhesion of the mind to a matter sufficiently and more than sufficiently explored. For he had no special promise concerning temporal and bodily deliverance: and therefore he speaks without doubt of that deliverance of which he was certain through faith, which, namely, will be obtained in the other life. How much hope remained for him in this life he had already often testified, ch. 7:7, ch. 10:20, 21, ch. 16:22, ch. 17:11 ff., ch. 19:10. How then could he profess here that he knew this, that he was to be delivered from those such great evils while still in this life? And those things which Grotius joins here are inconsistent; Even if they should consume not only my skin, but also this (namely the fat which is under the skin), yet in my flesh I shall see God. For what of the flesh will remain, with the skin and the fat which is under it completely consumed? And how could he have thus seen God with his eyes? Nor is seeing God to be understood only as meaning that he would experience him as propitious: But because he adds: I, I say, with these my eyes, and I, not others for me, it is manifest that the discourse is about the eyes of the body, and that seeing must be understood properly, not metaphorically concerning the sense of grace: because also otherwise it is not right to depart from the propriety of a word to figurative expositions, unless necessity compels it.

Then indeed he does not commonly designate as redeemer only him who frees from many evils, but with discernment he uses that word which denotes a Redeemer by right of kinship, or on account of a bond and communion of blood that frees, and redeeming by means of a λύτρον or price interposed. For this is the proper force of the word גואל, which it holds in the divine law, from which there is no reason here why we should depart, see Lev. 25, 25. Ruth 3, 13. Num. 35, 12. Therefore the Messiah is peculiarly designated, who is our kinsman, and brother, who is a partaker of our flesh and blood, and is not ashamed on that account to call us brothers Heb. 2, 14. 15. and who by that right of kinship redeems us, and not without a price Matt. 20, 28. Mark 10, 45. 1 Cor. 6, 20. 1 Tim. 2, 5. 1 Pet. 1, 18. whence Theodoret here translates it ὁ ἀγχιστεύς μου, my kinsman. Although indeed the word גואל is also used concerning a redeemer and redemption in general, yet this redemption, which was made through the blood of Christ, always takes precedence over the same, and by the power of the same every other liberation is promised: inasmuch as it is the cause and foundation of all redemption: whence Christ is peculiarly called Goel by it, even where bodily liberation is set forth, as having been done by this Redeemer. The reason is: because he performs the same by the power of the redemption made through his blood, outside of which there would be no redemption, and also no hope of any liberation: which is either connoted, or prepared and supposed in those places also which have been adduced by Grotius, it is certainly not excluded, nor can it be excluded anywhere. All of which things are also rightly accepted concerning Christ the Redeemer. Pineda on this passage is excellent: Christ Jesus is bone of our bones and flesh of our flesh by right of consanguinity and proximity, he redeemed us with his own blood, and most truly and most properly is he the Redeemer. I understand this person when I read the name of Redeemer or redemption in the sacred writings: not in some common, vulgar, and simple sense as the Rabbis and other Hebraizers do, as an assertor or deliverer, but, I say, as Redeemer by right of blood, by right of consanguinity. He proposes these laws of Redemption: 1. The Redeemer must be a kinsman. 2. He must redeem by right of consanguinity. 3. He must snatch the prey from the unjust possessor. 4. He must pay no price to him. 5. He must offer the price of redemption to the Lord. These things agree exactly with Christ the Redeemer, who is therefore called Goel in a peculiar way by Jacob in Genesis 48, verse 16, and by the Israelites in Isaiah 63, verse 9. The word גאל denotes him who, by right of proximity, vindicates either the alienated goods of a kinsman, or the kinsman himself from servitude, or the blood of the slain from the slayer. Thus Christ is the Goel, as our kinsman, who asserts for us anew the right to eternal life, which had been lost, and who finally delivered us from the servitude of sin, death, and the Devil, and also vindicated our blood in the slayer, Satan (Hebrews 2:14). If it should seem doubtful whether in Job's time the Mosaic גאל (vindicator) already existed, there is nevertheless no doubt from Job's confession and blessing that Christ was believed to be such a redeemer, who delivers us from all evil (Genesis 48:15), whence he is called Redeemer absolutely, as one who delivers even from sin, and the punishment of sin, and death itself.

Job calls him his vindicator and Redeemer; as the one through whom he hopes he will be redeemed, through whom he hopes he will be vindicated from death to life, from the dust to see God.

The pronoun MY is an argument of the confidence by which Job applies to himself the redemption of the Messiah, and believes that by the virtue of that ἀπολυτρώσεως (redemption) he also will be delivered.

Nor should it be overlooked that he calls his Redeemer LIVING: for he opposes this not obscurely to death, through which the ἀπολύτρωσις (redemption) was accomplished. As if to say: Although my redeemer is about to undergo death, I know and believe, however, that he is about to return to life, and is about to live forever, and therefore that he is about to recall me also, who have been delivered unto death, into life: just as Christ himself professes concerning himself in Revelation 1:18: I am the first and the last, and he who lives, and was dead, and behold I live for evermore, and I have the keys of death and of hell. Thus Jerome, Epistle to Pammachius: The Lord was not yet dead, and the Athlete of the Church saw his redeemer rising from the dead. And Gregory, book 14, chapter 16: I believe with certain faith, and profess with free voice, that my Redeemer lives, who died between the hands of the impious. If, however, you prefer to understand חי (living) as the endless divine life, because it is placed absolutely, as it is elsewhere concerning GOD when he is called living, this will be a description of the divine nature of Christ, which pleases Dr. Schmid, who, however, most correctly observes that life must at the same time be understood as working for the redemption of men: For it concerns a living REDEEMER: who not only lives himself by divine life, but also quickens us through his life, and works our life.

He adds that the Redeemer will finally stand, not in the field, as Grotius renders it, but על עפר UPON THE DUST; by which words he does not simply profess victory against his enemies, but also designates the manner of the victory, and more specially expresses the victory of his Redeemer: Who stands upon the dust, both because by rising from death he conquers and vindicates us to himself, and because he stands above the dust and the corruption of our bodies as an enemy prostrated at his feet, and stands against the dust, which that phrase also implies in Isaiah 31, verse 2, because he reclaims us and our flesh by the right of dust and death having been abolished, and asserts us to himself, and exerts his powers toward the dust, that is, toward bodies reduced to dust: whence the Vulgate, expressing the meaning, not the words: And in the last day I shall rise from the earth. Grotius understands that the consumed body is to be restored to its former shape: but because Job indicates a body not merely consumed, but thoroughly consumed, it is manifest that this concerns a restitution, not which happens here, but which is expected after the total consumption of the body on the last day. And what other action upon the dust is given than resurrection from the dust, into which we are reduced by the force of the divine sentence because of sin (Genesis 3:18)? But if he intended solely the restitution of goods in this life, what would it matter to make words about the Redeemer standing upon the dust? The word אחרון (last) also indicates the same: He will stand because of victory, because he is to be the survivor of all enemies, and therefore also of death, which is the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26). and because of the assistance, that our Redeemer will be present with us, and will not desert us until the final liberation, and that when death has already occupied all things, he alone will exert dominion over death and dust on the last day. THE LAST ONE will stand upon the dust. He, with all enemies already prostrated, nay even with all other men already reduced under the laws of death, will stand as a glorious victor, and will exhibit himself glorious, acting upon the dust in such a way that he will rouse the dust into which men have been reduced; see Johannes Cocceius and Dr. Christoph Scultetus on this passage. The Genevans explain it thus: I know that the last one will stand erect upon the dust; Diodati, that in the end he will raise himself above the dust, because he will ascend the tribunal or judge of men resolved into dust, and by his power already resurrected. Whom the Belgian interpreters follow. The Tigurines, at the last (time) he will apply his power to the dust. The English, at the last (day) on the earth (will stand). Let the interpretation of Junius be seen in his notes. B. Luther takes יקום transitively, as in Amos 7:2, and rendered it: at the last he will raise me up from the earth. Dr. Schmid translates it thus, and the last (new) that he will stand upon the dust: He takes 'the last' or 'the posterior one' as an epithet of Christ, who was to come in the last times, and is called ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδάμ, 1 Corinthians 15:45, so that it may be a confession of the incarnation: and that which he will rise upon the dust, he interprets concerning the resurrection of Christ: because dust occurs most frequently for earth in Scripture, as it is taken here by Ralbag and Luther, and יקום denotes not only to stand, but also to rise: so that it is a concise expression, in which the antecedent is to be gathered and supplied from the consequent, because he rises upon the earth who previously lay in the earth; so that thus the latter hemistich may cohere with the former: because, to wit, Job's Redeemer is living and is divine life itself: Therefore, by this life of his, insuperable by death, he will rise again upon the dust. A restoration of health certainly cannot be understood here; because Job points out such a thing that was to happen in the last time. To which are added those things which are said concerning the corrosion of the flesh.
