For death itself is designated, and total corruption by those words: after the worms, to wit, the corroders, which are understood in the word נקפו to corrode, have corroded. The Hebrew words are variously expounded. Zanchius renders: And after they have corroded my skin, this, that is, this very skin, or this very body will rise again. Others render it in Niphal: And after my skin shall be pierced, this will rise again. But the pronoun זאת coheres with the verb נקפו, therefore Pagninus, Tremellius, Junius, Piscator, and Vatablus rendered, and although after the worms have worn away my skin, this, or this, that miserable flesh of mine, yet from that flesh of mine I shall see God. Diodati's version also returns to this. Similar is

Grotius's translation, who by the pronoun זאת understands the skin; but why could not the flesh itself be understood deictically, since mention is made of it afterwards, or my body, which Mercerus understands, and the English version. But contrition, which the word נקף denotes, brings about total destruction, Isa. 29, 1. ch. 10, last, ch. 17, 6, ch. 24, 12. Which may be in ruin and death, or corruption: Thus therefore the flesh must be broken and crushed and subjected to corruption, so that we may see GOD again in the flesh, there is need for the resurrection of the flesh. Coccejus explains it thus: After they shall have destroyed my body this, or the whole skin, as regards this particle this of the skin, which, to wit, is the remainder, comparing verse 20, so that by the destruction of the remains of the skin, that is, as it were, the flaying of himself, death is noted, to which he says most interpretations look. Pineda notes, if the Hebrew word is explained as a striking or contrition, which denotes that which is joined with unfolding and a circle, and surrounds a man, and consumes him on every side, proving it from Isa. 3, 24. Some derive the word which occurs here from the verb נקף in Niphal נקפו to be surrounded, and they understand עצמי my bones, or my members: So that the sense may be: And after my skin these have been surrounded: which agrees with the Chaldee Paraphrase: After my skin shall have been inflated or surrounded, this shall be; in my flesh I shall see God: as well as the Vulgate version, B. Luther's, and the old Dutch. And again I shall be surrounded by my skin. Conf. Ezech. 37, 9. The Tigurines render, but after they shall have surrounded this with my skin (the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit shall have surrounded this, to wit, my body) but Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barb. judges the former passive translation to be more tolerable. nor does he desire anything in it, except that that word in Niphal occurs nowhere else: Which, however, is of very little moment, because there are not a few hapax legomena. Cajetan praises a certain Hebrew explaining it thus: And afterwards these limbs of mine are surrounded by my skin. Jerome, Ep. 41, renders: And after my skin they shall make this follow, that from my flesh I shall see God: on account of the Chaldaism, in which נקף is to follow, to adhere, since more Chaldaisms occur in this book, explaining it thus, i.e., after this skin of mine shall have been gnawed away, my Redeemer and his ministers shall cause this to follow, that from my flesh I am about to see God; or thus: after my skin shall have been consumed, this shall happen, they shall cause this to follow, that, to wit, my last Redeemer shall stand upon the earth, and from my flesh (then) I shall see God; also snatching the Chaldee text to that: who interprets it thus: After my skin shall have been taken away (shall have been made to cease), this shall happen. Schindler interprets the word עורי as my skin or hide: in this way: after my skin, i.e., after the putrefaction of my skin, these shall be cut down, consumed, crushed, that is, all visible things. To our blessed Gerhard, that interpretation seems the simplest, by which the word עורי is derived from עור he was awakened, he was aroused, and is verbally explained in this way: And after my awakening, or after I shall have been awakened from the dead by that Redeemer of mine, this shall be cut down deictically, this whole thing which I behold with my eyes in the world, so that the customary enallage of the past tense for the future in the verb, and of the singular number in the pronoun for the plural, may be established. To which opinion we easily add our vote; because it seems to agree with the words of the sacred text, nor is it alien to the subject matter of Job's confession. ואחר עורי נקפו זאת and after my awakening, these shall be cut down: so that he may intimate both his own resurrection and the consummation of the age, and finally subjoin the eternal vision of God, and in my flesh I shall see GOD. For these are the most efficacious foundations of consolation: because the faithful can easily despise all things in this world, and devour all afflictions, if indeed they contemplate the glorious resurrection, the consummation of all things, and the blessed vision of God. But the explanation of Dn. D. Schmiedius seems most simple, easily agreeing with the version of B. Luther: and after my skin these shall be surrounded: that is, after my skin shall have ceased to be, (as if to say, after I have died, and my skin shall have rotted away even to nothing) each of these, or this flesh of mine, to wit, and my bones, shall be surrounded, that, or by my skin, which relative or noun with the preposition מ can be supplied from what precedes; which, as regards the sense, B. Luther rightly rendered, Und werde hernach mit dieser meiner Haut umbgeben werden. However, whichever of these versions is chosen, it is certain that it does not look here to the temporal restoration of Job, but to his resurrection to another life: for the emphasis of the words does not suit the former: but that either the words themselves, or at least the entire sentence, import this, we judge to be sufficiently clear. Now if we weigh those words, and from or in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself am about to see, and my eyes are about to behold, and not another, what is more certain than that they speak not of the vision of God in this life, but of the future vision of another life, because the discourse is about the vision IN THE FLESH, as the particle מ is used in Psalm 68, 30, Ps. 72, 16, Jerem. 3, 20, Ezech. 48, and FROM THE FLESH, as in Gen. 15, 4. Mic. 5, 1, is used: in that flesh so crushed and corrupted: consequently to be resurrected one day: about the most singular vision of God, which he therefore describes so emphatically: which is the very most blessed vision of another life: about a vision which happens with bodily eyes; Therefore he adds, I myself am about to see: and my eyes are about to behold: About a vision which Job himself, who was suffering so many evils in his flesh, expects in his flesh with these very eyes, by which he believed that he himself would see God in his flesh and in his body, not another or in another body, but in that same body which here endured such great evils, so that the resurrection of the same body in number is intimated, and the same one who is afflicted here promises himself that glory, whence Nicetas: we are taught in this place an ecclesiastical dogma: the body itself, which received the attacks and tortures, is to be resurrected with the soul as a companion, so that it may enjoy it together with her. Gregory the Great: If, he says, I shall rise again in an aerial or in another body, I shall no longer be the one who rises. Mr. D. Schmied. prefers to take this particle concerning special faith, that is, that by which a man applies the promises to himself, and does not believe generally or indefinitely, as if to say, Job, I do not believe only in general in some resurrection, in which those who rise to life are to see with their own eyes Christ God and Redeemer: I do not believe, I say, only concerning others, but specially and definitely concerning myself: lest, namely, he should seem to doubt or despair concerning himself, although he believed concerning others. Although that NOT ANOTHER can also be taken concerning a stranger, that Job the faithful, not another, one alien from that faith, is one day to see God. Finally, this confession of Job's faith is also confirmed if its occasion is considered, since Bildad and Zophar, holding Job for an impious man, were denying him the hope of a blessed resurrection Job 18, 5. 13. 14. (conf. chap. 20, 9.) to whom he therefore opposes his confession and the certainty of his faith concerning his Redeemer, and a blessed resurrection, and the vision of GOD. For the sake of which he also adds in the conclusion of the same: this hope is laid up in my bosom. For concerning a temporal restitution he could have no certain hope. And he says that the root of the word was found in him: because this confession was well rooted. In Hebrew it is: the root of the word is found in me, that is, my cause has good foundations; as Grotius himself interprets, taking word for cause. Conf. Job 7, 15. By all of which having weighed that Jewish and Socinian gloss concerning restoration in this life, which Enjedini the Neo-Photinian wished to defend here with arguments, we conclude not undeservedly that it is to be rejected, and we add our vote to the common explanation of Christian interpreters concerning resurrection to the other life: which Clemens Romanus (or whoever the author is) Constit. L. 5. c. 5, Justin. orat. ad Annotat., Tertullian. de resurrect. carn. cap. 29, Cyprian. lib. 3. testimon. cap. 58, Ruffinus in exposit. Symbol., Gregorius Nazianzen. orat. 21, which is in praise of Hero, Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catech. 18, Augustin. lib. 22. de Civ. Dei c. 29, Nicetas Heracl. Caten. aur. Job. 14, Gregor. M. l. 14. moral. c. 28, Cassiodor. lib. 1. divin. lect. c. 5, and others, both ancient and more recent doctors, approve by common suffrage. Hieronym. ad Pammach. No one, he says, speaks so openly after Christ, as Job speaks before Christ concerning the resurrection. Nor do the Pontifical or Reformed interpreters deny this, if you perhaps except Mercerus. Coccejus brings forward these arguments for that opinion: 1. The simplicity of the interpretation, persuades this explanation. 2. The consistency of the argument and scope. 3. The truth of the matter. 4. The majesty of the words, which is not to be diminished by interpreting. 5. The affection which Job displays, namely, the proportion of joy and hope. 6. The unity of the Spirit in the Fathers and Apostles and all the faithful. Which compels one to understand the phrase of this passage as it is understood in the Gospel. 7. The practice of the Apostles in interpreting the Scriptures of the Old Testament from the event. See also Pineda, Diodatus, Genev. Belgic., Junius, Piscator, B. Lutherus, Osiander, Paraph. Vinariens., B. Gerhard, B. Meisner, B. Scultetus, Dn. D. Schmiedius, our Socinianism refuted, etc. From the Jews also, there can be brought into this opinion: 1. The LXX Interpreters, who seem to understand Christ through the Goel, and thus render it: οἶδα ὅτι ἀέναός εςιν ὁ ἐκλύειν με μέλλων, ἐπὶ γῆς ἀναςήσεται τὸ δέρμα με. I know that he is eternal who is to redeem me, and upon the earth he will raise up my skin. August. explains it thus: For I know that he is eternal who is about to resolve me, in the earth my skin shall rise again, exhausting these, etc. Add that in the Greek text of the last chapter of Job these things are read: Job died old and full of days. But it is written that he himself is to rise again (namely, c. 19) with those with whom the Lord rises, which words Pineda observes are read in the Sixtine Vatican edition and in Theodoret, and are brought forward by Origen in his Epistle to Africanus and by Clement of Rome, l. 5. constit. cap. 6: Suidas also brings them forward from that appendix. Although it is indeed missing in the Hebrew text, it appears nevertheless from that of the LXX Interpreters and the addition of Theodotion, that they accepted the present oracle in that sense, that Job is to rise again with the Savior before the universal resurrection, as judged by B. Gerhard the Elder in his Exegesis on Holy Scripture, §. 139. 2. The Chaldean paraphrase has it thus: And I know דפריק that my redeemer (which word is accustomed to be used concerning Christ the redeemer) remains, and after that his liberation (פורקניד) will stand upon the dust (in which the dead are buried), and after my skin has been inflated, this will be (which some interpret as said demonstratively, this will be my body, namely) and from my flesh I shall see הוב AGAIN God. It concerns a new vision of God after the skin itself has been inflated or surrounded, which, namely, will take place in the other life. 3. R. Hakkadosch interprets it likewise concerning Christ, even if he understands that God will be seen in assumed flesh, and does not accept this concerning the flesh of Job, as Galatinus brings forward his passage in lib. 3. de arc. Cath. verit. c. 19. Because the Messiah is to be God and man, his name was called Emanuel, which is interpreted as God with us in our body or flesh, just as Job testifies in chapter 19, saying: and from my flesh I shall see God. He refers it therefore to the incarnation. Which was also done by Augustine in Sermon II on the Nativity of the Lord. Job, he says, an eminent prophet, proclaims: in my flesh I shall see God: which he prophesied concerning that time when the Deity of Christ was clothed in the habit of our flesh. Pineda notes that that exposition, IN MY FLESH, that is, similar to mine, mortal and wretched, can also be referred to this: I shall see God made man, I sustain myself with this comfort, that I shall one day have him as a companion also of my punishments and sorrows: which exposition, however, although pious and not inelegant, Pineda acknowledges to be harsher, and by no means convenient with the preceding and following, or with the end of this passage. And Augustine himself admits that these things are to be explained concerning the resurrection of the flesh, l. 22. de Civit. Dei cap. 24: That which Job says, in my flesh I shall see God, he WITHOUT DOUBT prophesied the resurrection of the flesh. Furthermore, Galatinus proves in l. 1. c. 27 that this is also explained in the commentaries of the Jews concerning the resurrection of the flesh from Bereschit Ketanna cap. 18. Genesis. Pineda praises R. Samuel Marrochianus, who in his Epistle on the coming of the Messiah to Isaac the Israelite, c. 2, interprets this confession of Job concerning the resurrection, and proves from those words concerning the vision of the eyes that the Messiah is God and man, because, namely, bodily eyes do not see God as far as the divine essence itself is concerned. (5.) Pineda also refers to v. 26 a certain Hebrew Rabbi, who first in Constantinople, afterwards in Venice, and finally in Rome, taught the Jews, but who, having been converted to the faith of Christ at the age of sixty, had indeed explained that passage concerning the hope of recovering health, but when he had been more correctly informed by him, he had given his assent to the interpretation of the Catholics, and had ingenuously confessed that light was dawning upon him. R. Simeon Ben Jochai, while treating that passage, 'These are the generations of Noah': 'And from my flesh,' he says, 'I shall see God.' What does he mean by 'from my flesh'? For it was more fitting to say 'from my substance,' yet he said 'from my own flesh.' But this is what is written: 'And the flesh of holiness shall pass over you,' and furthermore: 'And my covenant shall be in your flesh.' For as often as a man shall be marked with this sign, which proceeds from Him, he shall see God Himself, and his soul shall become one with Him. But if you keep that sign, the divinity shall by no means depart from you, and in time you shall be bound to holiness and shall ascend into the prepared place. The same man a little later in the same place: 'From my flesh,' that is to say, 'from this very flesh of mine.' They shall be well-deserving both in this world and in the world to come. All of which things teach that it is in vain for Grotius, along with Enjedinus, to oppose the Jews to us here, as if the Hebrews never referred these things to Christ or to the resurrection. For the contrary is already clear from these things which we have brought forward. We conclude this oracle with the words of Pineda of the Society of Jesus, to whom Grotius attributed much while he lived: 'If we allow such a most clear testimony for the resurrection to be broken or weakened, what will there be so illustrious and so firm that some obscure and spurious little exposition could not obscure and debilitate? For by this saying, WITHOUT DOUBT, Job prophesied the resurrection of the flesh,' Augustine, book 22 of The City of God, ch. 29. 'EVIDENTLY he predicted it,' Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed not undeservedly asserted: 'Job,' he says, 'is entirely redundant with mystical utterances; he evidently predicts the resurrection of the dead.' Aurelius Cassiodorus professed that nothing is more manifest than this testimony, book 1 of Divine Readings, ch. 5. 'He prophesies,' he says, 'the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that no one seems to have written anything about it either more manifestly or more cautiously. I know,' he says, 'that my redeemer lives.' And Jerome to Pammachius, 'What,' he says, more clearly than this prophecy? No one speaks as openly after Christ, as this man does before Christ concerning the resurrection; he hopes for the resurrection, nay, he knows and has seen it. Our blessed Meisner wrote a special and learned dissertation on this testimony, under the title The Faith of Job, in which he prolixly established this illustrious confession concerning resuscitation. Whoever pleases may also compare our fifth Sermon in Memor. Justor. Witteberg. on the faith of Job.

Latin:

Vers. 25. SCIO QVOD REDEMTOR MEVS VIVIT, ET NO- VISSIMO DIE DE TERRA SVRRECTVRVS SVM)

Hæc verba, & quæ sequuntur Judæi nunquam ad resurrectionem retulere, cum tamen omnia rimentur, quæ aliquam in speciem eo trahi possunt. Christiani non pauci eo usi sunt ad probandam resurrectionis fidem, sed ut id facerent coacti sunt in versionibus suis multum ab Hebræo discedere, ut notatum Mercero, aliisque. Hebræa sic sonant: Scio ego Redemtorem meum vivere, & illum postremo staturum in campo. Etiamsi non pellem tantum meam, sed & hoc (nempe aruinam, quæ sub pelle est) consumerent, (morbi sc.) in carne tamen mea Deum videbo: (id est, propitium experiar:) Ego, inquam, hisce meis oculis; ego, non autem alius pro me. Deus redemptor dicitur, quia pios ex multis malis liberat Ps. 77, 35. Es. 41, 14. cap. 43, 14. 44, 6. 47, 4. 48, 17. 49, 7. Postremum in campo stare est victoris. Sic Deum dicit victorem fore adversariorum suorum. Neque vero ei esse impossibile, corpus ejus putredine prope exesum restituere in priorem formam, quod & fecit Deus. De voce hac supra diximus 13, 28.

Judæi hic audiendi non erant præ Christianis, quos non paucos ex hoc loco resurrectionem probare, fatetur Grotius. Quid mirum Judæorum cæcos ductores in illis Scripturæ locis resurrectionem rimari, quæ de illa nihil habent, in iis autem quæ eam tradunt, cæcutire? Carent Christi Spiritu, & divino judicio, in clarissimis hallucinantur. Nec intellexerunt totam causam Jobi, qui non intelligunt Evangelium. Ideoque haud mirum eos à sensu argumenti aberrasse. Plerique & de carnis resurrectione dubitant, vel certe de statu piorum ex gentibus in resurrectione. Nonnulli Jobum ipsum resurrectionem mortuorum negasse fingunt, de quo Menasse Ben Israel lib. 1. de resurr. mortuor. c. 16. §. 125. Idcirco dicunt antiqui, Jobus negavit resurrectionem mortuorum, quod ex vehementia doloris ab ipso factum putat Menasse p. 132. R. Mosen autem loca illa Job. 7, 9. cap. 15, 12. alia expedire via, Epist. de Resurrect. mortuorum, idem observat Menasse, nimirum quod intelligenda sint, prout se res habet secundum naturæ ordinem: siquidem naturaliter mortui non resurgunt. Quid ab illis sani expectes, in hac causa, qui tam prophanam Sancto Dei viro affingunt opinionem? LXX. tamen Seniores Interpp. fuere etiam Judæi, qui vero locum hunc de resurrectione mortuorum accepisse videntur; ἐπὶ γῆς ἀναστῆσαι τὸ δέρμα μὲ τὸ ἀνθλῶν ταῦτα: ut in terra resuscitet pellem meam, quæ hæc exantlat. Alios deinde notabimus, de resurrectione itidem interpretantes.

Neque vero opus est, ut ab Ebræo textu multum discedatur, ut oraculo de resurrectione sua constat sententia, quicquid Mercerus, quicquid etiam Grotius prætexat: cujus erat, vulgatam translationem tueri, siquidem Concilii Tridentini auctoritatem alias magni fecerit, aut decreta certe ejusdem defendere conatus fuerit. Optime congruere Ebræa verba communi interpretationi, Christianorum non pauci ostenderunt, Ebraice doctissimi. Quid? si accurate expendamus omnia, non aliter quam de resuscitatione explicare debere hanc sententiam, constabit. Exoptat Hiob sermones hos suos scribi, imo petræ incidi: Quis mihi tribuat, ut scribantur sermones mei, quis mihi det, ut exarentur in libro stylo ferreo, & plumbi lamina, vel certe sculpantur in silice: לעד. Græci εἰς μαρτύριον, alii in perpetuum. Quæ etsi nonnulli de rebus gestis, & sermonibus Jobi in genere accipiant, nullum tamen dubium est, quum hæc præmittantur illis, quæ nunc tractamus, quin ea maxime scribi & in perpetuum testimonium ad posteros transmitti optarrit. Ea ergo quæ voto tam enixo hic exorditur, & in perennem memoriam sive incidi marmori ad literarum formam plumbo repletis incisuris, uti è Sal. Jarchi explicat Grotius, sive quacunque alia duratu- ratione exarari, vehementer exoptavit vir San- ctissimus, insignia esse oportet, non vulgaria: nec ad ipsum tantum pertinere, sed ad alios etiam fide- les, ad quorum communem notitiam ea deferri voluit. Porro non loquitur hic de tali liberatio- ne, quæ adhuc dubia esse poterat, sed de ea, quæ penes ipsum certa erat, atque indubia, quam ple- na cordis fiducia credebat & expectabat in media, eaque desperata corporis sui ægritudine. Unde autem poterat tam certus esse, fore, ut ex illa cor- porali afflictione liberetur, ut SCIRE id sese profi- teri auderet? Scio, inquit, quod Redemptor meus vi- vat. Verbum ידע sciendi omnem dubitationem exclu- dere, & afferre certam atque firmam mentis adhæsio- nem ad rem satis superque exploratam, Pineda do- cet è Genes. 48, 49. Psalm. 138, 2. Gen. 22, 12. De tem- porali enim & corporali liberatione nullam habe- bat peculiarem promissionem: ideoque sine dubio de ea liberatione loquitur, de qua per fidem certus erat, quæ scil. in altera vita obtinget. In hac vita quam nihil spei sibi reliquum fuerit, jam sæpe te- status erat cap. 7, 7. cap. 10, 20. 21. cap. 16, 22. cap. 17, 11. seqq. cap. 19, 10. Quî ergo hic profiteri poterat se hoc scire, quod adhuc in hac vita ab istis tantis malis liberandus sit? Et ἀσύςατα sunt illa, quæ hic conjungit Grotius; Etsiamsi non pellem tantum me- am, sed & hoc (nempe arvinam quæ sub pelle est) consumeret, in carne tamen mea Deum videbo. Quid enim carnis reliquum erit, pelle & arvina, quæ sub ea est, prorsus consumpta? Et quomodo ita oculis suis videre potuisset Deum? Nec vero videre De- um tantum ita intelligendum, quod propitium ita experturus sit ipsum: Sed quia addit: Ego, inquam, hisce meis oculis, ego autem, non alii pro me, mani- festum est, de oculis corporis sermonem esse, at- que videre illud proprie intelligi debere, non meta- phorice de sensu gratiæ: quia etiam alias integrum non est, à proprietate vocis discedere ad figuratas expositiones, nisi cogat necessitas.

Tum vero redemptorem non indigitat com- muniter illum tantum, qui ex multis malis liberat, sed cum delectu ea voce utitur, quæ Redemptorem notat jure propinquitatis, vel ob nexum & commu- nionem sanguinis liberantem, ac λύτρῳ vel pretio in- terposito redimentem. Hæc enim vis est propria vo- cis גואל, quam in lege divina obtinet, à qua hic nulla causa est cur discedamus, vid. Lev. 25, 25. Ruth. 3, 13. Numer. 35, 12. Proinde peculiariter Messias indigitatur, qui propinquus noster est, & frater, qui carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps est, nec erube- scit nos ideo fratres appellare Ebr. 2, 14. 15. qui- que jure propinquitatis istius nos redimit, nec sine pretio Matth. 20, 20. Marc. 10, 45. 1. Corinth. 6, 20. 1. Timoth. 2, 5. 1. Petr. 1, 18. unde Theodoree. hic vertit ὁ ἀγχιστεύς με proximus meus. Quanquam vero verbum גואל de redemptore & redemptione in genere etiam adhibeatur, hæc tamen redemptio, quæ per sanguinem Christi facta est, eidem semper præ- fruitur, ac vi ejusdem omnis alia liberatio pro- mittitur: utpote quæ causa & fundamentum est omnis redemptionis: unde ab illa peculiariter Chri- stus Goel dicitur, etiam ubi liberatio corporalis exponitur, ab hoc Redemptore facta. Ratio est: quia præstat eandem virtute redemptionis per san- guinem ejus factæ, extra quam nulla redemptio, nulla etiam spes foret ullius liberationis: Quæ in illis etiam locis, quæ à Grotio adducta sunt, aut connotatur, aut præstruitur & supponitur, non ex- cluditur certe, nec excludi uspiam potest. Quæ etiam omnia de Christo Redemptore recte accipi- untur. Optime Pineda in h. l. Christus Jesus os de ossibus nostris & caro de carne nostra jure consan- guinitatis & propinquitatis suo nos sanguine redemit, & verissime, ac propriissime Redemptor est. Hunc intelligo, cum Redemptoris, aut redemptionis nomen in sacris lego: non cum Rabbinis atque aliis Hebraizantibus communi aliqua ratione & vulgari, & simplici Assertorem, aut liberatorem, sed Redemptorem, inquam, jure sanguinis, jure consanguinitatis. Leges Redemptionis has proponit: Redemptor 1. propinquus esto. 2. Consanguinitatis jure redimito. 3. Injusto possessori prædam eripito. 4. Huic pretium nullum solvito, 5. redemptionis pretium vero Domino offerto. Quæ exacte Christo redemptori conveniunt, qui peculiariter proinde Goel vocatur à Jacobo Genes. 48. vers. 16. & ab Israëlitis Es. 63. vers. 9. Notat vox גאל illum qui jure propinquitatis, vel alienata bona propinqui, vel ipsummet propinquum à servitute, vel sanguinem occisi in percussore, vindicat. Ita Christus Joel est, ut consanguineus noster, qui vitæ æternæ jus nobis denuo asserit, quod amissum erat, nosque à servitute peccati, mortis, & Diaboli denique liberavit, ac sanguinem etiam nostrum in percussore Sathana vindicavit Ebr. 2, 14. Si dubium videatur, num Jobi tempore גאל vindex Mosaïcus jam fuerit, dubium tamen non est è confessione, & benedictione Jobea Christum talem redemptorem creditum, qui ab omni malo liberat nos Gen. 48, 15. unde hic absolute Redemptor dicitur, utpote qui à peccato etiam, ac pœna peccati, & morte ipsa liberat.

Vocat eum Job vindicem & Redemptorem suum; utpote per quem redemptum se iri, per quem à morte ad vitam, à pulvere ad videndum Deum se vindicandum sperat.

Pronomen MEUS est argumentum fiduciæ, qua applicat sibi Job redemptionem Messiæ, ac virtute ἀπολυτρώσεως istius se etiam liberandum credit.

Nec prætermittendum quod Redemptorem suum VIVENTEM dicit: Nam hoc non obscure opponit morti, per quam facta est ἀπολύτρωσις. q. d. Etsi mortem subiturus est redemtor meus, scio tamen atque credo, quod iterum in vitam rediturus, in æternum victurus sit, ideoque me in mortem traditum etiam in vitam revocaturus: quemadmodum Christus ipse de se profitetur Apoc. 1, 18. Ego sum primus & ultimus, & is qui vivit, qui factus sum mortuus, & ecce vivo in secula seculorum, & habeo claves mortis & inferni. Ita Hieron. Epistol. ad Pammach. Nec dum mortuus erat Dominus, & Athleta Ecclesiæ redemptorem suum videbat ab inferis resurgentem. Et Gregor. lib. 14. c. 16. Ego illum post mortem vivere certa fide credo, libera voce profiteor, quod Redemptor meus vivit, qui inter impiorum manus occubuit. Si tamen חי intelligere malis de vita interminabili divina, quia absolute ponitur, uti alias de DEO, cum vivus dicitur, descriptio hæc erit naturæ Christi divinæ, quod placet Dn. D. Schmid. qui vero simul vitam intelligendam esse pro redemtione hominum operantem observat rectissime: Nam de REDEMPTORE vivo agitur: qui non tantum ipse vita divina vivit, sed per vitam suam etiam nos vivificat, & vitam nostram operatur.

Addit Redemptorem postremo staturum non in campo, uti reddit Grotius, sed על עפר SUPER PULVEREM; quibus verbis non simpliciter victoriam adversus hostes suos profitetur, sed modum etiam victoriæ designat, ac specialius victoriam exprimit Redemptoris sui: Qui super pulverem stat, tum quia resurgendo à morte vincit, nosque sibi vindicat, tum quia stat supra pulverem, & corruptionem corporum nostrorum ceu hostem ad pedes prostratum, & contra pulverem stat, quod phrasis etiam illa infert Esa. 31. vers. 2. quia nos & carnem nostram jure pulveris & mortis abolito repetit, sibique asserit, & vires suas erga pul- verem, hoc est, erga corpora in pulverem redacta exerit: unde vulgatus sententiam, non verba ex- primens: Et novissimo die de terra resurrecturus sum. Corpus exesum in priorem formam restitutum iri in- telligit Grotius: quia vero corpus non propemo- dum, sed penitus exesum Job indigitat, manifestum est de restitutione hic agi, non quæ hic fit, sed quæ post consumtionem totalem corporis in novissimo die expectatur. Et quæ alia in pulverem actio datur, quam resuscitatio ex pulvere, in quem redigimur vi sententiæ divinæ propter peccatum Genes. 3, 18? Quod si bonorum in hac vita restitutionem unice intenderet, quid attinebit de Redemptore super pulverem stante verba facere? Idem indicat etiam vox אחרון Novissimus stabit ob victoriam, quod superstes sit futurus omnibus hostibus, adeoque etiam morti, quæ hostis est novissimus. 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 26. & ob assistentiam, quod nobis ut Re- demtor noster affuturus sit, neque deserturus nos usque ad finalem liberationem, & quod cum omnia mors jam occupaverit, ipse solus dominium in mortem & pulverem exerturus sit in novissimo die. POSTREMUS super pulverem stabit. Ipse omnibus hostibus jam prostratis, imo etiam omnibus aliis hominibus jam sub mortis jura redactis, tanquam gloriosus victor stabit, & se gloriosum exhibebit, in pulverem ita agens, ut pulverem, in quem homines sunt redacti excitet; vide Joh. Coccejum & Dn. D. Christoph. Scultetum in h. l. Genevenses ita expli- cant: Scio quod postremus staturus sit erectus super pulvere; Deodatus, quod in extremo se elevabit su- pra pulverem, quia conscendet tribunal seu judex hominum resolutorum in pulverem, & ejus jam po- tentia resuscitatorum. Quem sequuntur Belgici in- terpp. Tigurini, novissimo (tempore) adhibebit vim suam pulveri. Angli, novissimo (die) in terra (sta- bit) Junii interpretatio videatur in notis ejus. B. Lutherus יקום transitive accipit, uti Amos. 7. v. 2, & reddidit: novissime ex terra resuscitabit me. Dn. D. Schmidius ita vertit, & postremum (novi) quod super pulverem staturus sit: Postremum vel posterio- rem habet pro Epithetō Christi, qui postremis tem- poribus venire debuit, & ὁ ἔσχατῶ Ἀδάμ vocatur, 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 45. ut sit confessio incarnationis: & illa quod super pulverem surget, de resurrectione Christi interpretatur: quia pulvis pro terra fre- quentissime in Script. occurrit, uti hic à Ralbago & Luthero accipitur, & יקום non tantum stare no- tat, sed etiam surgere: ut concisa locutio sit, in qua ex consequenti antecedens colligendum sit & supplendum, quia surgit super terram, qui prius in terra jacuit; ut ita posterius hemistichium cum priori cohæreat: quia scil. Redemtor Jobi vivus & vita ipsa divina est: Ideo eundem per hanc vi- tam suam à morte insuperabilem super pulverem resurrecturum esse. Restitutio certe sanitatis hic intelligi nequit; quia tale quid indigitat Job, quod novissimo tempore futurum erat. Quibus accedunt quæ de corrosione carnis adduntur. Designatur enim mors ipsa, & corruptio totalis verbis illis: postquam corroserint vermes scil. corrosores, qui in verbo נקפו corrodere subaudiuntur. Verba Ebræa varie exponuntur. Zanchius reddit: Et postquam pellem meam corroserunt, hoc, id est, hæc ipsa cutis, vel hoc ipsum corpus resurget. Alii in Niphal red- dunt: Et postquam cutis mea confodietur, hæc iterum surget. Sed pronomen זאת cohæret cum verbo נקפו, ideo Pagninus, Tremellius, Junius, Pisca- tor & Vatablus reddiderunt, & quamvis post pellem meam contriverunt vermes hanc, vel hoc, miseram illam carnem, tamen ex illa carne mea videbo De- um. Huc etiam Deodati versio redit. Similis est

Grotii translatio, qui per זאת pronomen arvi- nam intelligit; sed quidni caro ipsa δεικτικῶς subin- telligi queat, cum ejus postea mentio fiat, vel corpus meum, quod Mercerus subaudit, & Anglicana versio. At contritio, quam verbum נקף notat, totalem con- cisionem infert Esa. 29, 1. cap. 10. ult. cap. 17, 6, cap. 24, 12. Quæ in interitu & morte, vel corruptione sit: Sic ergo caro concidenda & conterenda ac corruptio- ni subjicienda, ut in carne iterum DEUM videa- mus, resuscitatione carnis opus est. Coccejus ita exponit: Postquam corpus meum destruxerint hoc, vel totam cutem, quoad hanc particulam hoc cutis, quod scil. reliquum est, conferens vers. 20. ut per reliquiarum pellis destructionem hoc est veluti exco- riationem sui mors notetur, quo plerasque interpre- tationes spectare ait. Pineda notat, si Ebræa vox de excussione vel contritione exponatur, quod eam notet, quæ cum evolutione & circulo conjuncta est, & hominem cingit, & undiquaque consumit ex Esa. 3, 24. id probans. Nonnulli a verbo נקף in Ni- phal נקפו circumdari deducunt vocem, quæ hic oc- currit, & subaudiunt עצמי ossa mea, aut membra mea: Ut sensus sit: Et postquam pelle mea circumdata sunt hæc: quod Paraphrasi Chaldaicæ congruit: Postquam inflata vel circumdata fuerit pellis mea, erit hoc; in carne mea videbo Deum: nec non versioni vulgatæ B. Lutheri & Belgicæ veteri. Et rursum circumdabor pelle mea. Conf. Ezech. 37, 9. Ti- gurini reddunt, postquam vero circumdederint hoc pelle mea (circumdederint Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus hoc scil. corpus meum) sed priorem passivam translationem tolerabiliorem judicat Sixtinus A- mama in Anti-Barb. nec in ea quicquam desiderat, nisi quod verbum illud in Niphal nuspiam alias oc- currat: Quod vero perexigui momenti est, quia non pauca dantur ἅπαξ λεγόμενα. Cajetanus E- bræum quendam laudat ita explicantem: Et post- ea pelle mea circumdati sunt isti artus. Hieronymus Ep. 41. reddit: Et post cutem meam facient sequi hoc, quod ex carne mea videbo Deum: propter Chaldai- smum, in quo נקף est sequi, adhærere, quum plu- res in hoc libro Chaldaismi occurrant, sic expli- cans, q. d. postquam hæc mea cutis corrofa fuerit, fa- cient Redemtor meus, ejusque ministri, ut hoc se- quatur, quod ex carne mea visurus sum Deum; vel ita: postquam cutis mea consumta fuerit, hoc fiet, hoc fa- cient sequi, quod nempe redemtor meus postremus perstiturus sit super terram, & ex carne mea (tunc) videbo Deum; Chaldaicum textum eo etiam abri- piens: qui ita interpretatur: Postquam ademta erit (cessare facta erit) cutis mea, fiet hoc. Schindlerus vocem עורי interpretatur pellem vel cutem meam: hoc modo: post cutem meam, h. e. post putrefactio- nem cutis meæ excindentur, abfumentur, conte- rentur hæc, hoc est, omnia visibilia. B. Gerhardo nostro simplicissima videtur ea interpretatio, qua vocabulum עורי deducitur ab עור excitatus est, ex- perrectus est, ac verbaliter exponitur hoc modo: Et post excitari meum, vel postquam ex mortuis per illum redemtorem meum excitatus fuero, excinde- tur hoc δεικτικῶς hoc omne, quod oculis in mundo in- tueor, ut usitata enallage temporis præteriti pro futuro in verbo, & numeri singularis in pronomine, pro plurali statuatur. Cui sententiæ facile calculum adjicimus; quia verbis textus sacri congruere vi- detur, nec a materia confessionis Jobææ aliena est. ואחר עורי נקפו זאת & post excitari meum, ex- cindentur ista: ut tum resurrectionem suam, tum seculi consummationem innuat, ac denique æter- nam Dei visionem subjungat, & in carne mea videbo DEUM. Hæc enim efficacissima sunt consola- tionis fundamenta: quia facile fideles omnia con- temnere possunt in hoc mundo, omnesque devora- re afflictiones, siquidem cogitent gloriosam resur- rectionem, rerum omnium consummationem, & beatam Dei visionem. Simplicissima autem vide- tur Dn. D. Schmiedii explicatio, facile versioni B. Lutheri consentiens: & post cutem meam circumda- buntur hæc: h. e. postquam cutis mea esse desierit, (q. d. postquam ego mortuus, & cutis mea usque ad nihilum putrefacta fuerit) circumdabuntur quod- que horum seu hæc caro mea scil. & ossa mea, illa, vel cute mea, quod relativum vel nomen cum præ- positione מ suppleri ex antegressis potest; quæ quoad sensum recte B. Lutherus reddidit, Und werde hernach mit dieser meiner Haut umbgeben werden. Quæcunque tamen ex his eligatur ver- sio, non restitutionem Jobi temporalem, sed resuscita- tionem ejusdem ad alteram vitam hic respici certum est: non enim illi verborum emphasis convenit: hanc autem vel ipsa verba, vel certe integram sen- tentiam importare, satis luculentum esse arbitra- mur. Jam si verba illa expendamus, & ex vel in carne mea videbo Deum, quem visurus sum ego ipse, & oculi mei conspecturi sunt, & non alius, quid certius quam quod loquantur non de visione Dei in hac vita, sed de futura alterius vitæ visione, quia de visione IN CARNE, uti particula מ Psalm. 68, 30. Psal. 72, 16. Jerem. 3, 20. Ezech. 48, & EX CARNE, uti Gen. 15, 4. Mich. 5, 1. usurpatur, sermo est: in carne illa sic contrita & corrupta: proinde olim resuscitanda: de visione Dei maxime singulari, quam ideo tam em- phatice describit: quæ est ipsa beatissima visio alte- rius vitæ: de visione, quæ oculis fit corporeis; Ideo addit, ego visurus sum ipse: & oculi mei conspecturi sunt: De visione, quam his ipsis oculis Jobus ipse, qui tot mala in carne sua patiebatur, in carne sua expectat, qua Deum ipsum se visurum in carne sua & in corpore suo credebat, non alium vel alio cor- pore, sed eodem illo corpore, quod hic tanta mala exantlavit, ut ita ejusdem numero corporis resuscita- tio innuatur, idemque qui hic affligitur, sibi gloriam illam polliceatur, unde Nicetas: docemur hoc loco Ecclesiasticum dogma: corpus ipsum, quod impetus & cruciatus excepit, anima comite resuscitandum es- se, ut cum illa una fruatur. Gregor. M. Si in aë- reo, inquit, aut in alio corpore resurrexero, jam ego non ero, qui resurgo. Dn. D. Schmied. mavult par- ticulam hanc accipere de fide speciali h. e. ea, qua sibi homo applicat promissiones, & non generali- ter aut indefinite credit, q. d. Jobus, non credo tan- tum in genere aliquam resurrectionem, in qua qui ad vitam resurgent visuri sunt oculis suis Christum Deum & Redemtorem: non credo, inquam, de aliis tantum, sed specialiter & definite de me ipso: ne scil. videretur de seipso vel dubitare, vel despe- rare, licet de aliis crederet. Quanquam illud NON ALIUS de peregrino etiam accipi possit, quod Job fidelis, non alius, a fide illa alienus visurus olim Deum sit. Denique confirmatur etiam hæc Jobæa fidei confessio, si occasio ejus respiciatur, siqui- dem Bildad & Zophar Jobum pro impio habentes, resurrectionis beatæ spem ipsi denegabant Job. 18, 5. 13. 14. (conf. cap. 20, 9.) quibus proinde confessio- nem, & fidei suæ certitudinem de Redemtore suo, & beata resurrectione, ac visione DEI opponit. Cujus gratia etiam in conclusione ejusdem addit: reposita est hæc spes in sinu meo. De restitutione enim temporali nullam spem certam habere poterat. Et radicem verbi in se inventam dicit: quia bene radi- cata erat hæc confessio. In Ebræo est: verbi radix inventa est in me, h. e. causa mea habet bona funda- menta; uti Grotius ipse interpretatur, verbum pro causa accipiens. Conf. Job. 7, 15. Quibus omnibus pensi habitis glossam istam Judaicam, & Socinianam de restitutione in hac vita, quam Enjedini Neo-Pho- tiniani argumentis hic tueri voluit Grotius, repro- bandam esse non immerito concludimus, ac com- muni Christianorum Interpp. explicationi de re- fuscitatione ad alteram vitam calculum adjicimus: quam Clemens Roman. (vel quisquis autor est) Constit. L. 5. c. 5. Justin. orat. ad Annotat. Tertullian. de resurrect. carn. cap. 29. Cyprian. lib. 3. testimon. cap. 58. Ruffinus in exposit. Symbol. Gregorius Na- zianzen. orat. 21. quæ est in laudem Heronis. Cyril- lus Hierofolymitanus Catech. 18. Augustin. lib. 22. de Civ. Dei c. 29. Nicetas Heracl. Caten. aur. Job. 14. Gregor. M. l. 14. moral. c. 28. Cassiodor. lib. 1. divin. lect. c. 5. & alii cum veteres, tum recentiores Dd. communi suffragio approbant. Hieronym. ad Pam- mach. Nullum, ait, tam aperte post Christum, quam Jobum ante Christum de resurrectione loqui. Ne- que abnuunt Pontificii, aut Reformati Intêrpp. si Mercerum forte excipias. Coccejus hæc pro ea sententia adducit argumenta: Suadet hanc explica- tionem 1. Interpretationis simplicitas. 2. Argu- menti, & Scopi concinnitas. 3. Rei veritas. 4. Verborum, non minuenda interpretando, majestas. 5. Affectus quem Job præ se fert, scil. gaudii, spei proportio. 6. Spiritus in Patribus & Apostolis, ac fidelibus omnibus unitas. Quæ compellit phra- sin hujus loci ita intelligere, ut in Evangelio intelli- gitur. 7. Praxis Apostolorum in Scripturis V. T. interpretandis ex eventu. Vid. etiam Pineda, Dio- datus, Genev. Belgic. Junius, Piscator, B. Lutherus, Osiander, Paraph. Vinariens. B. Gerhard. B. Meisner. B. Scultetus, Dn. D. Schmiedius, Socinismus noster profligatus &c. E Judæis etiam adduci in hanc sen- tentiam possunt, 1. LXX. Interpp. qui per Goel Christum intelligere videntur, atque ita reddunt: οἶδα ὅτι ἀέναός εςιν ὁ ἐκλύειν με μέλλων, ἐπὶ γῆς ἀναςήσεται τὸ δέρμα με. Scio ego, quod æternus est, qui me solvere debet, & super terram suscitabit pel- lem meam. August. ita explicat: Scio enim, quod æternus est qui me resoluturus est, in terra refurget pellis mea, exantlans hæc &c. Adde quod in Græ- co textu cap. ult. Jobi hæc legantur: Mortuus est Job senior & plenus dierum. Scriptum est autem ipsum resurrecturum (scil. c. 19.) cum illis, cum quibus resurgit Dominus, quæ verba in editione Sixti Vati- cana, & apud Theodor. legi atque ab Origene Epist. ad African. & Clementem Rom. l. 5. constit. cap. 6. adduci observat Pineda: Adducit ea & Suidas ex il- la appendice. Quamvis vero deficit ea in Ebræo textu, apparet tamen ex illo LXX Interpp. & Theo- dotionis additamento, quod oraculum præsens eo sensu acceperint, quod Hiob cum Salvatore ante universalem resurrectionem sit resurrecturus, ju- dice B. Gerhardo Seniore in Exegesi de Scriptura Sacr. §. 139. 2. Chaldaica paraphrasis ita habet: Et ego novi דפריק quod redemtor meus, (quod ver- bum de Christo redemtore adhiberi consuevit) manet, & post illa liberatio ejus (פורקניד) super pulvere (in quo conduntur mortui) extabit, & post- quam inflata fuerit pellis mea, erit hoc (quod inter- pretantur nonnulli, ut δεικτικῶς dictum, erit hoc corpus scilic. meum) & ex carne mea videbo הוב RUR- SUM Deum. De nova visione Dei postquam in- flata vel circumdata fuerit ipsa pellis, agitur, quæ sc. in altera vita fiet. 3. R. Hakkadosch interpretatur iti- dem de Christo, etsi intelligat Deum in carne assumta visum iri, non vero de carne Jobi hoc accipiat, uti locum ejus adducit Galatinus lib. 3. de arc. Cath. ve- rit. c. 19. Quia Messias Deus & homo futurus est, vocatum est nomen ejus Emanuel, quod interpretatur nobiscum Deus in corpore, vel carne nostra, quemad- modum Job. testatur cap. 19. dicens : & e carne mea videbo Deum. Refert ergo ad ἐνσάρκωσιν. Quod ab Augustino quoque factum Serm. II. de Nativitat. Domini. Job, inquit, prædicat, eximius Prophetarum: in carne mea videbo Deum: quod de illo tempore prophetavit, quando Christi Deitas habitu nostræ carnis induta est. Quo referri etiam posse expositio- nem istam IN CARNE MEA, id est, meæ simili, mortali & ærumnosa, Pineda notat: Videbo Deum hominem factum, hoc me solatio sustento, quod illum olim habiturus sim socium quoque pœnarum atque dolorum: quam tamen expositionem, etsi piam & non inelegantem, Pineda duriorem agnoscit, minime- que cum antecedentibus & consequentibus, aut cum fine hujus loci convenientem. Et de carnis resuscitatione explicanda hæc esse fatetur ipse Augustin. l. 22. de Civit. Dei cap. 24. Illud quod ait Job, in carne mea videbo Deum, resurrectionem carnis SINE DUBIO prophetavit. Porro in Judæorum quoque commentariis de resurrectione carnis hoc explicari e Bereschit Ketanna cap. 18. Genes. probat Galat. l. 1. c. 27. Pineda laudat R. Samuelem Marrochianum, qui in Epist. de adventu Messiæ ad Isaacum Israelitam c. 2. confessionem hanc Jobi de resurrectione interpretatur, atque ex verbis illis de visione oculorum probat, Messiam Deum esse atque hominem, quia scil. oculi corporei Deum non vident, quoad ipsam divinam essentiam. (5.) Refert etiam Pineda ad v. 26. Ebræum quendam Rabbinum, qui primum Constantinopoli, postea Venetiis, denique Romæ Judæos docuerit, Sexagenarius vero ad fidem Christi conversus fuerit, locum istum quidem de spe recuperandæ sanitatis exposuisse, sed ubi abs se rectius informatus fuisset, Catholicorum interpretationi assensum præbuisse, sibique lucem exoriri ingenue confessum esse. R. Simeon Ben Jochai dum tractat illud, hæ sunt generationes Noæ: Et de carne mea, inquit, videbo Deum: Quidnam sibi vult de carne mea? conveniens enim magis erat dicere, de substântia mea, tamen dixit, de carne mea propria. Hoc autem est, quod scriptum est: Et caro sanctitatis transibit super te: & insuper: Et erit fœdus meum in carne vestra. Quotiescunque vero signatus erit homo hoc signo, quod procedit ab illo, videbit Deum ipsum, & anima ejus fiet unum cum illo. Quod si custodies illud signum, divinitas nequaquam a te recedet, & in tempore colligaberis sanctitati & ascendes in præparatum locum. Idem paulo post ibidem: De carne mea q. d. de hac ipsa mea carne propria. Bene meriti erunt tum in mundo hoc, tum in mundo futuro. Quæ omnia docent, frustra Grotium cum Enjedino Judæos nobis hic opponere, quasi nunquam Ebræi hæc ad Christum aut ad resurrectionem retulerint. Contrarium enim ex his quæ adduximus, jam liquet. Concludimus oraculum hoc verbis Pinedæ e Societate Jesu, cui multum tribuit, dum vixit, Grotius: Si hujusmodi clarissimum pro resurrectione testimonium infringi, aut enervari patiamur, quodnam erit tam illustre, tamque firmum, quod expositiuncula quæpiam obscura & notha obscurare, & debilitare non possit? Hoc enim dicto SINE DUBIO prophetasse Jobum resurrectionem carnis August. l. 22. de Civ. Dei c. 29. EVIDENTER eam prædixisse Ruffin. in Symb. exposit. non immerito asseruit: Job, inquit, mysticis redundat totus eloquiis, evidenter resurrectionem mortuorum prædicit. Hoc testimonio nihil manifestius esse Aurelius Cassiodorus professus est libr. 1. Div. lect. c. 5. Resurrectionem, inquit, carnis sic prophetat, ut nullus de ea vel manifestius, vel cautius aliquid scripsisse videatur. Scio, ait, quod redemtor meus vivit. Et Hieronymus ad Pammachium, Quid, inquit, hac prophetia manifestius? Nullus tam aperte post Christum, quam iste ante Christum de resurrectione loquitur; sperat resurrectionem, imo novit & vidit. Peculiarem & eruditam disputationem de hoc testimonio conscripsit B. Meisnerus noster, sub titulo Fides Jobi, qua prolixe hanc de resuscitatione confessionem illustrem adstruxit. Conferre etiam cui placuerit, poterit Concionem nostram V. in Memor. Justor. Witteberg. de fide Jobi.

## 19:27
Vers. 27. THIS HOPE OF MINE IS LAID UP IN MY BOSOM] In Hebrew: My reins have failed in my bosom: that is, my inward parts are consumed out of indignation because of your curses. See the following. Beyond reason it again departs here from the Vulgate version, which agrees very well with the Hebrew text. For the word כלו does not only signify to fail, to finish, to consume: but also to wait, to desire, as R. Mardochai Nathan teaches, and other lexicographers, and when desire is attributed to the reins, they are called כליות from that, because they are also accustomed to be used for desire and inward affection. See Ps. 25, 6. Ps. 62, 2. Prov. 23, 16. Therefore the sense is, my reins have desired, or my desires, the thoughts and affections of my inmost soul in my bosom, or if you prefer, have been consumed in my bosom. Thus the Vulgate did not indeed express the words, yet it expressed the sense; This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom. For desire proceeding from faith brings forth hope, or is joined with hope. And desires are said to be consumed when vows are fulfilled. Therefore their hope can be said to be laid up in the bosom, because of certainty, because something is stored in a safe bosom: And we embrace a hope that is not vain in our bosom, certain that we shall never lose hope before we obtain what is desired, and that that hope, having been turned into reality, is received into our bosom. And because the bosom embraces the dearest things, and also all secrets, therefore Job says that he cherishes this mystical secret, and one far dearest to himself, in his bosom, and with inmost desire desires and awaits the completion of this his faith, as if to say: because of the vehement desire of seeing my God I almost fail, I have this uniquely in my inmost desires: I cherish this consumed desire and the sum of my vows as if in my bosom, as a most dear thing, I repeat it with constant memory, and as those things which are in the bosom are placed before the eyes, I hold them most certainly and firmly, as if I had them in my bosom. For we believe we hold nothing more certainly than what we hold in our bosom, says Gregory, lib. 14. Mor. cap. 33. But if the version of blessed Luther is retained, these things will cohere with the former ones in this way: Even if death and pain consume all the interior parts of the soul, indicated by synecdoche by the reins, yet I sustain myself with this hope of resurrection, and I know that I shall see God in my flesh. Conf. Pineda, and our Lord Dr. Scultetus on this passage. The gloss of Grotius is singular, and merely precarious, not so much because of the curses of the antagonists, as because of the diseases and torments the reins were failing and the interior parts of Job were being consumed: Against the vehemence of which he especially rises here. Whence Nicetas from the Hebrew interprets it thus, both the reins and all my inward parts had wasted away; Vatablus rendered it thus: because of affliction all my intestines have failed. But Pineda observes not beside the point: that the reins are not taken properly but metaphorically here is clearly indicated by what is added, in the bosom: because true and natural reins are not in the bosom, nor in the chest, or the embrace of the arms.

Latin:

Vers. 27. REPOSITA EST HÆC SPES MEA IN SINU MEO] In Hebr. Desecerunt renes mei in sinu meo: id est, intima mea vorantur ex indignatione ob maledicta vestra. Vide sequentia. Præter causam iterum a vulgata hic recedit versione, quæ optime Ebraico textui congruit. Nam verbum כלו non significat tantum deficere, perficere, consumere: sed etiam expectare, desiderare, ut R. Mardochai Nathan docet, aliique Lexicographi, ac quum renibus tribuatur concupiscentia, inde illi dicuntur כליות, quia pro desiderio ac intimo affectu etiam adhiberi solent. Vid. Ps. 25, 6. Ps. 62, 2. Prov. 23, 16. Job. 38, 36. Ideo sensus est, desideraverunt renes mei, vel desideria mea, intimæ animæ meæ cogitationes & affectiones in sinu meo, vel si maris, consummatæ sunt in sinu meo. Ita non verba quidem, sensum tamen vulgatus expressit; Reposita est hæc spes in sinu meo. Nam desiderium ex fide profectum spem infert, aut cum spe conjunctum est. Et consummata dicuntur desideria, cum vota complentur. Spes ergo eorum in sinu reposita dici potest, ob certitudinem, quia sinu tuto aliquid reconditur: Et spem non vanam in sinu complectimur, certi nunquam nos prius amissuros spem, quam desideratis potiamur, eaque spe in rem conversa sinu nostro excipiatur. Et quia sinus res charissimas, nec non arcana quæque complectitur, ideo mysticum hoc arcanum, sibique longe charissimum sinu suo se fovere ait Jobus, intimoque desiderio desiderare & expectare hujus suæ fidei complementum q. d. præ vehementi desiderio videndi Deum meum fere deficio, hoc unice in intimis desideriis habeo: hoc consummatum desiderium & summam votorum meorum quasi in sinu foveo, ut rem charissimam, jugi memoria repeto, & ut illa quæ in sinu sunt, ante oculos posita sunt, certissime & firmiter teneo, quasi in sinu habeam. Nil enim nos certius habere credimus, quam quod in sinu tenemus, inquit Gregor. lib. 14. Mor. cap. 33. Si vero B. Lutheri versio retineatur, ita hæc cohærebunt cum prioribus: Etiamsi omnia interiora animi per renes synecdochice indicata, morsus & dolor consumat, tamen hac spe resurrectionis me sustento, & scio me Deum visurum in carne mea. Conf. Pineda, & Dn. D. Scultetus noster in h. l. Glossa Grotii singularis est, & mere precaria, non tam ob maledicta Antagonistarum, quam ob morbos & tormenta deficiebant renes & consummabantur interiora Jobi: Adversus quorum vehementiam se potissimum hic erigit. Unde Nicetas ex Ebræo ita interpretatur, tum renes, tum cuncta mea præcordia contabuerant; Vatablus ita reddidit: præ afflictione defecerunt omnia intestina mea. Sed non præter rem observat Pineda: renes non proprie sed metaphorice hic accipi plane indicare, quod additur, in sinu: quia veri & naturales renes non sunt in sinu, neque in pectore, aut complexu brachiorum.

## 19:28
Vers. 28. WHY THEN NOW DO YOU SAY LET US PERSECUTE HIM) Better you might say, supply sometimes: why have we persecuted him? AND THE ROOT OF THE WORD BE FOUND AGAINST HIM] In the Hebrew: the root of the word is found in me. You will say this because my cause has good foundations. Word for cause John 7, 15. Others render it thus: For you say: How shall we pursue him? and the root of the matter be found in me, as if to say: Despairing of human comfort, I deservedly confer all my hope into eternity, while you and my friends, having held councils, think how to persecute me, a miserable man, and how you might find in me some foundation of just reproach. But with the interpretation of Grotius retained, these things are best joined to the preceding confession: Why, you might say sometimes, having known the full assurance of my faith, why have we persecuted him? because the root of the word, the foundation of faith with solid hope, is found in me. Behold, I have now set forth to you my faith in God, and firm hope, contempt of the present life, and desire for the future; this is the root of the word, hence I will not yield to evils, hence I will persist in that confidence.

Latin:

Vers. 28. QVARE ERGO NVNC DICITIS PERSEQVAMUR EUM) Melius dicatis, supple aliquando: cur persecuti eum sumus? ET RADICEM VERBI INVENIAMUS CONTRA EUM] In Hebræo: verbi radix inventa est in me. Hoc ideo dicetis, quia causa mea bona habet fundamenta. Verbum pro causa Joh. 7, 15. Alii ita reddunt: Nam vos dicitis: Quomodo prosequemur illum? & radix sermonis inveniatur in me, q. d. Merito desperans de solatio humano spem omnem in æternitatem confero, cum vos & amici mei collatis consiliis cogitetis, quomodo me miserum perse- qui, & in me fundamentum aliquod justæ reprehensio- nis invenire queatis. Retenta autem Grotii inter- pretatione hæc optimè confessoni præcedenti sub- junguntur : Quare, dicatis aliquando cognita fidei meæ πληροφορίᾳ, cur persecuti eum sumus? quia verbi radix fundamentum fidei cum spe solida in me in- venitur. Ecce jam meam de Deo fidem, & firmam spem, præsentis vitæ contemtum, & desiderium futuræ vobis jam exposui; hæc radix verbi, hinc non cedam malis, hinc persistam in illa fiducia.

## 19:29
Vers. 29.

FLEE THEREFORE FROM THE FACE OF THE SWORD) Fear the sword, with which God is accustomed to avenge wicked men, as follows.

THAT YOU MAY KNOW THAT THERE IS JUDGMENT) God will severely punish you, so that you may learn by experience that not all things happen by chance.

Job recalls to memory the final judgment. Fear for yourselves from the face of the sword: because burning wrath is upon the iniquities of the sword, that is, which deserve vengeance and death, such as the affliction and persecution of the just, or bloody iniquities, as Junius explains them: that you may know that there is judgment; since God is going to punish the same most severely on the last day with the most severe judgment. Thus he comforts himself with the future glory of resurrection and life, he terrifies his persecutors with the final judgment, and eternal punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

FVGITE ERGO A FACIE GLADII) Timete gladium, quo Deus ulcisci solet homines iniquos, ut sequitur.

VT SCIATIS QVOD JVDICIVM) Deus in vos severe animadvertet, ut experimento discatis non omnia casu fieri.

Revocat Job in memoriam judicium novissi- mum. Metuite vobis a facie gladii: quia ardens ira est super iniquitates gladii, hoc est, quæ vindictam & mortem mereantur, qualis est justorum afflictio, & persequutio, vel iniquitates cruentas, ut Junius eas exponit: ut sciatis, quod judicium sit; siquidem Deus easdem maxime in novissimo die severissimo judicio pu- niturus sit. Sic se solatur futura resurrectionis & vitæ gloria, persequutores suos terret novissimo ju- dicio, & pœna æterna.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

Zophar depicts the inconstant fortune of the wicked and hypocrites, the unhappy outcomes of sin, and the most grievous punishments.

Vers. 1.

THEN ZOPHAR THE NAAMATHITE ANSWERED AND SAID) Many things in these words are taken from the Psalms.

Although certain analogous things occur here with the sayings or sentiments of David, it is not to be believed that the same were taken from the Psalms. Many parallel things occur in the Scriptures, which the sacred writers did not in fact borrow from one another, but because they were moved by one Spirit, it is no wonder that similar things were brought forth by the same [Spirit] through different organs.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

Zophar impiorum & hypocritarum inconstan- tem fortunam & exitus peccati infelices, & pœnas gravissimas depingit.

Vers. 1.

RESPONDENS AVTEM SOPHAR NAAMATHITES DIXIT) Multa in hujus verbis de Psalmis desumta.

ETsi analoga quædam hic occurrant cum Davi- dis dictis vel sententiis, non tamen e Psalmis ea- dem desumta credendum est. Multa in Scripturis parallela occurrunt, quæ vero non abs se invicem mutuo petiere Scriptores sacri, sed quia uno Spiritu agitati sunt, non mirum per diversa organa similia ab eodem prolata esse.

## 20:5
Vers. 5.

THAT THE TRIUMPHING OF THE WICKED IS SHORT) In the Hebrew: from near, as torrents born from near do not last long. Rivers rush from on high and from afar. Jer. 18. vers. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QVOD LAUS IMPIORVM BREVIS SIT) In He- bræo: de propinquo, ut torrentes ex propinquo nati non diu durant. Flumina ab alto & longinquo ruunt. Jer. 18. vers. 14.

## 20:6
Vers. 6.

THOUGH HIS EXCELLENCY MOUNT UP TO THE HEAVENS) His loftiness: the similitude is taken from a tree.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

SI ASCENDERIT USQVE AD COELUM SUPER- BIA EJUS) Sublimitas ejus: sumta similitudo ab arbore.

## 20:15
Vers. 15.

GOD SHALL CAST THEM OUT) ἄγγελος, the Greeks. God by the ministry of an angel.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

EXTRAHET EAS DEUS) ἄγγελος, Græci. Deus angeli ministerio.

## 20:18
Vers. 18.

HE SHALL RESTORE THAT WHICH HE LABOURED FOR) From the Hebrew: He shall restore the withheld reward of labor (that is, in judgment he shall be compelled to restore it) so that he cannot enjoy it: he shall compensate for all things according to his ability (the damages given), so that he may not rejoice in theft: יגיע or יגע, is the reward of labor Gen. 31, 40. Psalm. 128, 2.

B. Scultetus rendered and explained it thus: HE SHALL RENDER THE LABOR AND SHALL NOT DEVOUR IT, ACCORDING TO THE ABUNDANCE OF HIS EXCHANGE HE SHALL NOT EXULT. Even if he has labored much, and has gathered things acquired by his own and others' labors, he shall not transfer them to his uses, but according to his ability he shall be compelled to render them, so that he shall derive no joy from them.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

LUET QVÆ FECIT OMNIA) Ex Hebræo: Restituet retentam mercedem laboris (id est, in judicio cogetur resti- tuere) ne ea frui possit: pro facultate compensabit omnia, (da- mna data) ne furto lætetur: יגיע vel יגע, est merces laboris Genes. 31, 40. Psalm. 128, 2.

B. Scultetus ita reddidit & exposuit: RED- DET LABOREM ET NON DEVORABIT, JUXTA COPIAM PERMUTATIONIS SUÆ NON EXULTABIT. Etiamsi plurimum labo- rayerit, & suis & alienis laboribus parta congrega- verit, illa tamen non transferet ad usus, sed pro fa- cultate sua reddere ea cogetur, ut nullum inde ca- pturus sit gaudium.

## 20:19
Verse 19.

HE HAS SEIZED A HOUSE AND HAS NOT BUILT IT) Compare Psalm 127, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

DOMUM RAPUIT ET NON ÆDIFICAVIT) Confer. Psalm. 127, 1.

## 20:20
Verse 20.

HE SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO POSSESS) He shall not be satisfied. Thus the Chaldean here. He shall not be content with what has been obtained.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

POSSIDERE NON POTERIT) Non satiabitur. Ita hic Chaldæus. Non erit contentus obtentis.

## 20:21
Verse 21.

Vers. 21. THERE REMAINED NOTHING OF HIS FOOD) He left nothing of his feasts for the use of the poor, as good men were accustomed to do. Thus Jarchi here. See Matt. 14, 20. Luke 9, 19. John 6. v. 12. 13.

Others explain it thus: nothing will remain with which he himself may satisfy his hunger. THEREFORE HIS GOOD DOES NOT REMAIN, because he will be reduced to poverty, his prosperous days also will cease.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Vers. 21. NON REMANSIT DE CIBO EJVS) Nihil de suis epulis reliquum fecit in usus pauperum, ut solebant facere viri boni. Ita hic Jarchi. Vide Matth. 14, 20. Luc. 9, 19. Joh. 6. v. 12. 13.

Alii sic explicant: nihil supererit, quo ipse famem satiet. IDEO NON PERMANET BO- NUM EJUS, quia ad paupertatem redigetur, etiam dies boni ejus cessabunt.

## 20:22
Vers. 22. WHEN HE SHALL BE SATIATED, HE SHALL BE STRAITENED, HE SHALL BE IN DISTRESS) Better: When he shall have filled himself to satiety, he shall covet. For the Hebrews say יצר for concupiscence Gen. 8. v. 21. Is. 26, 3.

AND EVERY PAIN SHALL RUSH UPON HIM) In the Hebrew: Every hand of the laborer shall invade him: he shall be weary as if he had labored much.

Others more conveniently: EVERY HAND OF PAIN SHALL RUSH UPON HIM, calamities of every kind shall invade him.

Latin:

Vers. 22. CVM SATIATVS FVERIT, ARCTABITVR, ESTVABIT) Melius: Cum se impleverit ad satietatem, con- cupiscet. Nam יצר Hebræi dicunt pro concupiscentia Gen. 8. v. 21. Es. 26, 3.

ET OMNIS DOLOR IRRVET SVPER EVM) In Hebræo: Omnis manus laborantis invadet eum: fessus erit quasi multum laborasset.

Commodius alii : OMNIS MANUS DO- LORIS IRRUET SUPER EUM, omnis generis calamitates ipsum invadent.

## 20:23
Vers. 23. WOULD THAT HIS BELLY BE FILLED THAT HE MAY SEND FORTH UPON HIM) More correctly: let him fill his belly as much as he wishes: and God will send forth the heat of His anger, and will rain upon him, that is, his flesh: לחם which the Arabs write لحم is flesh. And thus also victims are called in the law. You could also translate it to devour him.

B. Luther, with the Vulgate, derives the word from נלחם he waged war, so that the sense may be: he will copiously pour out his punishments upon him. Psalm 11, 6. 2 Chron. 12. vers. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 23. VTINAM IMPLEATVR VENTER EJVS VT EMITTAT IN EVM) Rectius: impleat ventrem quan- tum velit: & immittet Deus fervorem iræ suæ, & depluet su- per ipsum, id est, carnem ejus: לחם quod Arabes scribunt لحم est caro. Et sic etiam victimæ vocantur in lege. Pos- ses etiam vertere ad devorandum ipsum.

B. Lutherus cum vulgata vocem a נלחם bel- lum gessit deducunt, ut sensus sit: copiose effundet poenas suas super ipsum. Psalm. 11, 6. 2. Paral. 12. vers. 7.

## 20:24
Vers. 24. HE SHALL FLEE FROM IRON WEAPONS, AND SHALL RUSH INTO A BRAZEN BOW) In Latin you would say: He falls into Scylla, desiring to avoid Charybdis.

Latin:

Vers. 24. FVGIET ARMA FERREA, ET IRRVET IN ARCVM ÆREVM) Latine diceres: Incidet in Scyllam, cupiens vitare Charybdim.

## 20:25
Vers. 25. DRAWN AND COMING OUT OF HIS SHEATH) For sheath the Chaldean placed the Greek word θήκην: The sense seems to be: someone will draw an arrow, and it will come out of his body gleaming from the filth of his intestines. If he escapes, terror will perpetually accompany him. Concerning the word מורור see above 16, 13. concerning the sword stained from the bowels see Jud. 3. vers. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 25. EDVCTVS ET EGREDIENS DE VAGINA SVA) Pro vagina Chaldæus vocem Græcam θήκην posuit: Sen- sus videtur esse: educet aliquis sagittam, & ea e corpore ejus exibit coruscans de fæcibus intestinorum ejus. Si evaserit, perpetuo eum comitabitur terror. De voce מורור vide supra 16, 13. de gladio tincto e visceribus vide Jud. 3. vers. 22.

## 20:26
Vers. 26. ALL DARKNESS IS HIDDEN IN HIS SECRET PLACES) Adversities will await him, even where he thinks himself most safe.

A FIRE WHICH IS NOT KINDLED SHALL DEVOUR HIM) Pestilence.

Others explain it concerning lightning: Rabbi Solomon understands fire, such as was in the destruction of Sodom. The Chaldean, Origen, and Gregory refer it to hellfire. We, with B. Luther, judge that the burning fire of divine anger is generally designated, which is not kindled by man, but by God Himself.

HE WHO IS LEFT IN HIS TABERNACLE IS AFFLICTED) In his tabernacle. Whoever of his house shall remain, shall be consumed by the same pestilence.

Latin:

Vers. 26. OMNES TENEBRÆ ABSCONDITÆ SVNT IN OCCVLTIS EJVS) Adversa eum exspectabunt, etiam ubi maxime tutum se putabit.

DEVORABIT EVM IGNIS QVI NON SVCCEN- DITVR) Pestilentia.

Alii de fulmine exponunt : Rabbi Salomo ignem intelligit, qualis in excidio Sodomæ fuit. Chald. Origen. & Greg. ad ignem infernalem refe- runt. Nos cum B. Luthero generaliter ardentem iræ diviæ ignem designari censemus, qui non ab homine, sed ab ipso Deo succenditur.

AFFLIGITVR RELICTVS IN TABERNACVLO SVO) In tabernaculo ejus. Quicunque de ejus domo super- erit, eadem pestilentia absumetur.

## 20:28
Vers. 28. THE OFFSPRING OF HIS HOUSE SHALL BE REVEALED, IT SHALL BE DRAWN AWAY IN THE DAY OF THE WRATH OF GOD) More correctly thus: the produce of his house shall depart like flowing waters in the time of divine wrath.

Latin:

Vers. 28. APERTVM ERIT GERMEN DOMVS IL- LIVS, DETRAHETVR IN DIE FVRORIS DEI) Rectius fic: proventus domus ejus migrabit ut fluentes aquæ in tem- pore divinæ iræ.

## 20:29
Vers. 29. AND THE HERITAGE OF HIS WORDS) The Hebrews include even actions under words. We said something on Luke 2:34.

FROM GOD) The Greeks: παρὰ τῶ ἐπισκόπῳ. Did they understand God as the one who inspects all things, or the magistrate who acts in the place of God when he punishes crimes?

A just reward is pointed out as being rendered by God, which he shall obtain like an inheritance on account of his impious words and works.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ET HÆREDITAS VERBORVM EJVS) He- bræi sub verbis etiam actiones comprehendunt. Diximus aliquid Lucæ 2, 34.

A DEO) Græci: παρὰ τῶ ἐπισκόπῳ. An Deum intel- lexerunt omnia inspicientem, an magistratum qui Dei vice fungitur ubi punit crimina?

Justa merces indigitatur a Deo reddenda, quam hæreditatis instar obtinebit propter verba & opera impia.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI.

Job, asking why it is well with the wicked and ill with the good, teaches that it is not always so, that the misfortunes of the wicked are reserved for their descendants, that God has his own reasons, that all become equal in death, and that the wicked are kept for the day of destruction.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI.

Job quærens cur malis bene, bonis male sit? non perenne ita esse, reservari posteris impio- rum infortunia, Deum suas habere cau- sas, omnes in morte æquales fieri, malos ad diem perditionis servari docet.

## 21:4
Vers. 4. IS MY DISPUTATION AGAINST MAN, THAT I SHOULD NOT RIGHTLY BE SORROWFUL?) In the Hebrew: do I speak to man? which if I do, (supply: my conversation is with God) why should not my spirit be shortened? that is, why does God not immediately take away my life, if indeed, as you say, neither does evil happen without fault, nor does any fault remain unpunished? The same manner of speaking is in Psalm 89:46.

Others take the aposiopesis thus: But if I were complaining primarily to men, why should not my spirit be shortened? Who will blame me for being sorrowful and indignant? For this is what the shortening of the spirit signifies, Ex. 6:9, Num. 21:5. Cocceius: If my complaint were with man, why should I not be indignant that a man should so prevaricate and make light out of night? If with God, who will blame me if, with judgment denied to me, I lose heart and express my complaints more painfully?

Latin:

Vers. 4. NVMQVID CONTRA HOMINEM DISPV- TATIO MEA EST, VT MERITO NON DEBEAM CONTRISTARI?) In Hebræo: an hominem ego alloquor? quod si, (supple cum Deo mihi sermo est) cur non breviabitur Spiritus meus? id est, cur Deus non statim vitam mihi adimit, si nempe ita ut vos dicitis, nec malum evenit sine culpa, nec culpa ulla manet impunita? loquendi genus idem Psal. 89, 46.

Aposiopêsin alii ita accipiunt : Si autem ma- xime ad homines quererur, cur non abbreviaretur Spiritus meus? quis vitio mihi vertet, quod contri- stor & indignor ? Hoc enim fignificat abbreviatio Spiritus Ex. 6, 9. Num. 21, 5. Coccejus : Si cum ho- mine mihi questus, cur non indigner hominem ita prævaricari, & ex nocte lucem facere? fi cum Deo, quis vitio mihi vertet, fi denegato mihi judicio, ani- mo concidam & questus meos dolentius expri- mam?

## 21:5
Vers. 5. LAY YOUR FINGER UPON YOUR MOUTH) Like the Latins: Restrain your lip with your finger. You have this manner of speaking in Micah 7:16, Prov. 30:32.

Latin:

Vers. 5. SUPERPONITE DIGITUM ORI VESTRO) Ut Latini : Digito compesce labellum. Habes hoc loquendi genus Michææ 7, 16. Prov. 30, 32.

## 21:12
Vers. 12. AT THE SOUND OF THE ORGAN] The Chaldean here has אבובא, whence we have noted elsewhere the so-called Ambubajae. The Greeks translate עגב variously: cithara, psalms, psaltery, organ.

Compare Gen. 4:21 and what we said there.

Latin:

Vers. 12. AD SONITUM ORGANI] Chaldæus hîc אבובא, unde dictas Ambubajas notavimus alibi. Græci עגב varie vertunt, κιθάραν, ψαλμούς, ψαλτήριον, ὄργανον.

Cons. Gen. 4, 21. & quæ ibi diximus.

## 21:13
Vers. 13. THEY SPEND THEIR DAYS IN PROSPERITY AND IN A MOMENT GO DOWN TO THE GRAVE) This is that εὐθανασία which Augustus desired. Suetonius c. 99.

Latin:

Vers. 13. DUCUNT IN BONO DIES SUOS ET IN PUNCTO AD INFERNA DESCENDUNT) Hæc est illa εὐθανασία quam optabat Augustus. Suetonius c. 99.

## 21:17
Vers. 17. HOW OFTEN IS THE LAMP OF THE WICKED EXTINGUISHED) The כמה here is not 'how often' but 'how easily'.

Latin:

Vers. 17. QVOTIES LUCERNA IMPIORUM EX- STINGVETUR) כמה hîc est non quoties sed quam facile.

## 21:24
Vers. 24. HIS INTESTINES ARE FULL OF FAT) Thus also the Greeks: τὰ ἔγκατα ἀυτῦ πλήρη σέατος. The Hebrews, just as they signify fat by the name of milk, so they signify the innermost recesses of the body by the name of milk-pails.

HIS MILK-PAILS ARE FULL OF MILK.

By synecdoche it is noted that he abounds in goods of every kind.

Latin:

Vers. 24. VISCERA EJUS PLENA SUNT ADIPE) Sic & Græci : τὰ ἔγκατα ἀυτῦ πλήρη σέατος. Hebræi sicut lactis nomine adipem fignificant, ita mulctralium nomine intimos corporis recessus.

MULCTRALIA EJUS PLENA SUNT LACTE.

Per Synecdochen omnis generis bonis abun- dare notatur.

## 21:26
Vers. 26. AND YET THEY SHALL LIE DOWN TOGETHER IN THE DUST) As rich as poor: For pale death knocks with equal foot at the taverns of the poor and the towers of kings.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET TAMEN SIMUL IN PULVERE DOR- MIENT) Tam dives quam pauper : Nam Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas Regumque turres.

## 21:30
Vers. 30. THE WICKED IS RESERVED TO THE DAY OF DESTRUCTION) Rather, on the day of destruction. Many wicked men are withdrawn from common ruin. Therefore, not every judgment is carried out here.

Latin:

Vers. 30. IN DIEM PERDITIONIS SERVATUR MA- LUS) Imo in die perditionis. Multi mali subducuntur com- muni exitio. Non ergo omne judicium hîc peragitur.

## 21:31
Vers. 31. HE SHALL WATCH IN THE HEAP OF THE DEAD) He shall remain assiduously, as one who is agitated by vigils.

More correctly: AND HE SHALL WATCH OVER THE TOMB (a watchman, that is). His sepulcher is guarded by watchmen. Some explain it thus: he remains in the tomb, he is not cast out; indeed, his corpse is so preserved by medicinal embalming that he can be seen as if he were watching, or living.

Latin:

Vers. 31. IN CONGERIE MORTUORUM VIGILA- BIT) Manebit assidue, ut qui per vigilias agitant.

Rectius : ET SUPER TUMULUM VIGI- LABIT (vigil scilicet) Sepulchrum ejus per vigi- les custoditur. Nonnulli sic explicant : in tumu- lo permanet, non ejicitur, imo conditura medica- trici sic conservatur cadaver ejus, ut quasi vigila- ret, vel viveret, aspici possit.

## 21:33
HE WAS SWEET TO THE GRAVEL OF COCYTUS) In the Hebrew: The clods of the valley are sweet to him. Sepulchers were accustomed to be in valleys. There he rests, composed in placid peace.

Therefore, not as you wish, does the wicked man here always perish in the worst way.

AND HE DRAWS EVERY MAN AFTER HIM) All shall follow him in their own order. Antiphanes: -- - - - - τὴν ἀυτὴν ὁδὸν Ην πᾶσιν ἐλθεῖν ἐσ' ἀναγκαίως ἔχον, Προεληλύθασιν· εἶτα χ' ἡμεῖς ὕςερον Εἰς ταυτὸ καταγώγιον ἀυτοῖς ἥξομεν Κοινῇ τὸν ἄλλον συνδιατρίψοντες χρόνον.

Latin:

DULCIS FUIT GLAREIS COCYTI) In Hebræo: Dulcescunt ei cespites vallis. In vallibus esse sepulchra sole- bant. Ibi placida compostus pace quiescit.

Non ergo, ut vos vultis, impius hic pessime semper perit.

ET POST SE OMNEM HOMINEM TRAHIT) Omnes eum suo ordine sequentur. Antiphanes : -- - - - - τὴν ἀυτὴν ὁδὸν Ην πᾶσιν ἐλθεῖν ἐσ' ἀναγκαίως ἔχον, Προεληλύθασιν· εἶτα χ' ἡμεῖς ὕςερον Εἰς ταυτὸ καταγώγιον ἀυτοῖς ἥξομεν Κοινῇ τὸν ἄλλον συνδιατρίψοντες χρόνον.

## 21:34
Ver. 34. WHEN YOUR ANSWER HAS BEEN SHOWN TO CONTRADICT THE TRUTH) In the Hebrew: When malice is present in your answers. Very well.

In your answers there remains the rest of the prevarication. When everything has been examined, there remains the unjust prevarication of the cause, by which you not only desert me as a friend, but afflict me with injury.

Latin:

Vers. 34. CUM RESPONSIO VESTRA REPUGNARE OSTENSA SIT VERITATI) In Hebræo : Cum responsio- nibus vestris insit malitia. Optime.

In responsionibus vestris reliqua manet præ- varicatio. Omnibus examinatis superest injusta causæ prævaricatio, qua me amicum non tantum deseritis, sed injuria afficitis.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. Eliphaz accuses Job of lack of mercy and of questioning divine providence, promising many good things to the penitent.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII. Eliphaz Jobum immisericordiæ & solicitatæ di- vinæ providentiæ arguit, pœnitenti bona multa promittens.

## 22:2
Ver. 2. CAN A MAN BE COMPARED TO GOD) In the Hebrew: Does a man acting wisely profit God for that reason? Psalm 16:2, below 35:2, Rom. 11:35.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NUMQVID DEO POTEST COMPARARI HOMO) In Hebræo : An homo sapienter se gerens Deo ob id prodest? Psalm. 16, 2. infra 35, 2. Rom. 11, 35.

## 22:3
Ver. 3. WHAT DOES IT PROFIT GOD IF YOU ARE JUST) In the Hebrew: Does the Almighty desire that you be just? Namely, for the sake of his own utility, or as if something were added to him from that.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QVID PRODEST DEO SI JUSTUS FUERIS) In Hebræo : An cupit omnipotens ut justus sis? nempe suæ uti- litatis causa, aut quasi inde aliquid sibi accedat.

## 22:6
Ver. 6. YOU HAVE STRIPPED THE NAKED OF THEIR CLOTHES) Understand by naked those thinly clad, as we have explained elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NVDOS SPOLIASTI VESTIBVS) Nudos in- tellige tenuiter vestitos, ut explicavimus alibi.

## 22:9
Ver. 9. YOU HAVE SENT WIDOWS AWAY EMPTY) See similar complaints in Ps. 94:6. Serious, if they had been true.

Latin:

Verf. 9. VIDUAS DIMISISTI VACUAS) Similes querelas vide Pf. 94, 6. Graves, fi veræ fuiffent.

## 22:16
Ver. 16. WHO WERE SNATCHED AWAY BEFORE THEIR TIME] The Greeks here elegantly: συνελήφθησαν ἄωροι. Thus Virgil said 'before the day'.

Latin:

Verf. 16. QVI SUBLATI SUNT ANTE TEMPUS SVVM] Græci hic eleganter: συνελήφθησαν ἄωροι. Sic ante diem dixit Virgilius.

## 22:19
Ver. 19. THE RIGHTEOUS SHALL SEE AND REJOICE] It is the same in Psalm 107:42.

Latin:

Verf. 19. VIDEBUNT JUSTI ET LÆTABUNTUR] Idem eft in Pfalmo 107, 42.

## 22:20
Ver. 20. HAS NOT THEIR ERECTION BEEN CUT DOWN] In the Hebrew: because our substance has not been cut down. The Greeks translate קִים as substance. Eliphaz wishes to prove the justice of God from this, that the descendants of Esau always remained in their own lands.

He speaks thus because he wishes to include himself in the number of the pious, or he introduces the words of the rejoicing righteous by way of imitation. Cocceius also says this.

AND FIRE HAS CONSUMED THEIR REMAINS) He says 'of them', pointing to the region in which the impious Sodomites had lived.

Mr. Dr. Schmid presents the voice of the righteous thus: Has he not been cut down who stood against us? And has not the fire also consumed their remnant?

Latin:

Verf. 20. NONNE SUCCISA EST ERECTIO EORVM] In He- bræo: quia non excisa est substantia nostra. קִים ὑπόστασιν vertunt Græci. Justitiam Dei inde probare vult Eliphaz, quod posteri Esavi semper in suis sedibus manserint.

Loquitur ita, quia se piorum numero inclu- di vult, vel per mimesin verba lætantium justorum introducit. Sic etiam Coccejus.

ET RELIQVIAS EORUM DEVORAVIT IGNIS) Illorum dicit, monstrans regionem in qua impii Sodomitæ vi- xerant.

Vocem justorum ita exhibet Dn. D. Schmid. Annon excisus est, qui stetit contra nos? & annon etiam residuum eorum comedit ignis?

## 22:21
Ver. 21. ACQUIESCE THEREFORE TO HIM) Join yourself to him, namely to the good man, of such as were discussed above: Χρηστῷ μὲν παρὰ χρηστὰ μαθήσεαι.

Latin:

Verf. 21. ACQVIESCE IGITUR EI] Adjunge te illi, nempe vi- ro bono, de qualibus actum supra: Χρηστῷ μὲν παρὰ χρηστὰ μαθήσεαι.

## 22:24
Ver. 24. HE WILL GIVE FLINT FOR EARTH) David Kimchi quite rightly says both here and in the following verse that בצר is gold. The sense is: Do not value your gold more than dust, and gold from Ophir no more than the stones of the torrent: thus God will be to you both gold and strongest silver. For Ophir the Greeks also have σωφίρ here. See what was said at 1 Kings 9:28.

Some indeed explain it thus, like a command: others, however, more correctly take it as a promise: If you have repented, of which he had warned before, you will in turn be enriched; you will abound in such a quantity of gold that you will value it no more than dust and the stones of the rock. Cf. 1 Kings 10:21; 2 Chron. 1:15. Now you sit in the dust, but in its place you will have gold: now you sit on the hard rock, but in its place the best gold will be spread out under you. To which also the interpretation of Mr. Dr. Schmid tends.

Latin:

Verf. 24. DABIT PRO TERRA SILICEM) Recte admodum David Kimchi & hic & in sequenti versu בצר ait esse au- rum. Sensus est: Aurum tuum ne pluris fac quam pulverem, & aurum ex Ophir ne pluris quam lapides torrentis: ita Deus tibi erit & aurum & argentum fortissimum. Pro Ophir etiam hic Græci habent σωφίρ. Vide quæ dicta ad 1. Reg. 9, 28.

Ita sane explicant nonnulli, instar mandati: alii tamen rectius promissionis loco habent: Si pœ- nitentiam egeris, quo de antea monuerat, vicissim ditaberis; tanta copia auri abundabis, ut illud non plus æstimes, quam pulverem, & lapides petræ. Cons. 1. Reg. 10, 21. 2. Par. 1, 15. Jam sedes in pul- vere, sed illius loco habebis aurum: jam sedes in du- ra petra, sed illius loco optimum aurum tibi sub- sternetur. Quo etiam abit Dn. D. Schmidii inter- pretatio.

## 22:30
