Ver. 30. THE INNOCENT SHALL BE SAVED) In the Hebrew ימלט אי־נקי. Some explain that אי as an island, others take it for a negative, so that it is, not the innocent, but it is true that אי is an Arabic word which signifies 'whoever'.

It is certain that the particle of negation is אי by apocope for אין from Prov. 13:1; 1 Sam. 4:21: And thus the sense is, nay rather (God) will deliver the not-innocent: but he will be delivered on account of the purity of your hands: because you have lifted up pure hands for him in prayers, 1 Tim. 2:8, so that it is an exaggeration of the hearing and efficacy of prayers. See other senses in Cocceius and Mr. Dr. Schmid. But that which we have brought forward is without doubt the most suitable.

Latin:

Verf. 30. SALVABITUR INNOCENS) In Hebr. ימלט אי־נקי. Illud אי quidam insulam exponunt, alii fumunt pro negativa, ut sit, non innocens, sed verum est אי esse Arabicam vocem quæ significat quivis.

Particulam negandi esse אי per apocopen pro אין e Prov. 13, 1. 1. Sam. 4, 21. constat: Atque ita sensus est, quin imo eripiet (Deus) non innocentem: eripietur autem propter puritatem manuum tuarum: quia tu pro illo in precibus puras sustulisti manus, 1. Tim. 2, 8. ut sit exaggeratio exauditionis & effica- ciæ precum. Alios sensus vid. apud Coccejum, & Dn. D. Schmidium. Sed ille quem adduximus, fine dubio maxime conveniens est.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

Job testifies to his innocence.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

Job innocentiam fuam teftatur.

## 23:2
Ver. 2. IN BITTERNESS IS MY SPEECH) מרי שחי, that is, from an Arabism: my complaint seems most alien: But the Greeks for מרי read מירי ἐκ χειρός μ8.

Why should the sense of the Vulgate not be retained? Even this day my speech is bitter. I have been able to draw little consolation from your speeches, whence my mind, full of sadness, is still compelled to meditate upon and pour out a bitter complaint. If, however, it is urged that the word מרי cannot be derived from מרר, he was bitter, (although Avenarius, deriving that word from מרר, teaches that it signifies bitterness, and only by metaphor rebellion) and one prefers to translate it here as rebellion, as it is taken in 1 Samuel 15, verses 22, 23.

Ezek. 2, 8. with Rabbi Solomon it can be rendered: My complaint is stubborn, it persists, for you bring no consolation, it does not obey, it does not yield to your consolations: or also in this way: Even this day, in which my hand is heavy, or when the afflicting hand presses me, I am held for stubborn because of my complaint: so that my hand is a hand pressing and striking me, just as my weapon is the blow of a weapon cast into me, chap. 31, 6. or it is heavy upon my groaning. Thus Cocceius and Scultetus: Is my complaint still considered rebellion this day, when I have endured pains for so long, as if I were opposing myself to God (or even after my many excuses) when nevertheless my hand, which strikes me, is heavy upon my groaning, that is, greater than I can explain with groans.

THE HAND OF MY STROKE IS HEAVY UPON MY GROANING] That is, the more I complain, the more I am beaten by you. But for ידי the Greeks read ידו.

Those conjectures about different readings are empty. What if we say they are παροράματα, or that that interpretation arose from elsewhere?

Latin:

Vers. 2. IN AMARITUDINE EST SERMO MEUS) מרי שחי, id est, ex Arabismo: alienissima videtur querela mea: At Græci pro מרי legerunt מירי ἐκ χειρός μ8.

Cur non retineatur sensus vulgatæ? Etiam hoc die amarus est sermo meus. Parum folatii e ve- stris sermonibus haurire potui, unde animus mœsti- tia plenus adhuc amaram meditari & effundere co- gitur querelam. Si tamen urgeatur, vocem מרי a מרר amarus fuit, haud deduci posse, (quanquam vocem illam a מרר deducens Avenarius ama- ritudinem fignificare doceat, & per metaphoram solum rebellionem) & malit quis hic rebellionem vertere, uti accipitur 1. Samuelis 15. versu 22. 23.

Ezech. 2, 8. cum Rabbi Salomone reddi poterit: Contumax est quæstus meus, perstat, nihil enim solatii affertis, non paret, non cedit solatiis vestris: vel etiam hoc modo: Etiam hoc die, quo manus mea gravis est, vel quum manus affligens urget me, habeor pro contumace propter quæstum meum: ut manus mea sit manus premens & percutiens me, sicut telum meum est plaga teli in me injecti, cap. 31, 6. aut gravis est super gemitum meum. Sic Coccejus, & Scultetus: An etiam hoc die, cum tam diu tolerem dolores, rebellio querimonia mea habetur, quasi me Deo opponam (vel etiam post tot excusationes meas) cum tamen manus mea, quæ me percutit, gravis sit super gemitum meum, hoc est, major quam gemitibus explicare possim.

MANUS PLAGÆ MEÆ AGGRAVATA EST SUPER GEMITUM MEUM] Id est, quo magis queror, eo à vobis magis vapulo. Sed pro ידי Græci legerunt ידו.

Conjecturæ illæ de diversis lectionibus inanes sunt. Quid si dicamus esse παροράματα, aut aliunde ortam illam interpretationem?

## 23:3
Ver. 3.

EVEN TO HIS THRONE] Thus Symmachus and Jarchi also translate תכונתו.

He speaks of GOD ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, as if of an earthly judge. Would that I knew how I might find God, and arrive there, where he has a seat prepared for judgment Psalm 9, 8. For men judge only external things, and indeed sinisterly.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

USQUE AD SOLIUM EJUS] Sic תכונתו vertunt etiam Symmachus & Jarchi.

Loquitur de DEO ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, tanquam de judice terreno. Utinam scirem, quomodo Deum possem invenire, & pervenire eo, ubi sedem paratam habet ad judicium Psalm. 9, 8. Homines enim tantum externa judicant, & quidem sinistre.

## 23:7
Ver. 7.

LET HIM SET FORTH EQUITY AGAINST ME] In the Hebrew: There, disputing with him, I would appear upright, to be sure. The Greeks read these and other things far differently.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

PROPONAT ÆQVITATEM CONTRA ME] In Hebræo: Ibi cum eo disputans, rectus, scilicet apparerem. Longe aliter hæc & alia legere Græci.

## 23:8
Vers. 8.

IF TO THE WEST] By the Hebrews the west is called אחור because it is at the back when one is turned toward the east. By a similar reason the north is called the left, and the south the right.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

SI AD OCCIDENTEM] Hebræis occidens dicitur אחור quod à tergo sit in orientem obverso. Simili ratione Septentrio dicitur sinistra, & auster dextra.

## 23:10
Vers. 10.

HE HAS TESTED ME LIKE GOLD] 1 Pet. 1, vers. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

PROBAVIT ME QVASI AURUM] 1. Petr. 1. vers. 7.

## 23:12
Vers. 12.

AND IN MY BOSOM I HAVE HIDDEN THE WORDS OF HIS MOUTH] In the Hebrew: More than my measure I have kept the words of his mouth.

More than my daily bread I have kept and desired, as Mercerus explains. Cf. John 4, 34. Nor does Pineda speak badly: More than my statute or my custom I have kept the words of the mouth of the Lord, or the law of God. I preferred them to my customs and inveterate habits. The version of B. Luther: I keep the speech of his mouth more than I am bound to, to be understood according to the opinion of men.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET IN SINU MEO ABSCONDI VERBA ORIS EJUS] In Hebræo: Plusquam dimensum meum asservavi verba oris ejus.

Plus quam panem quotidianum servavi & appetii, ut Mercerus explicat. Conf. Joh. 4, 34. Nec male Pineda: Plusquam statutum meum aut consuetudinem meam servavi verba oris Domini, vel legem Dei. Prætuli meis consuetudinibus & moribus inveteratis. B. Lutheri versio: Ich bewahre die Rede seines Mundes mehr, denn ich schuldig bin, intelligenda quoad opinionem hominum.

## 23:14
Vers. 14. FOR HE HIMSELF IS ALONE] Better from the Hebrew: he himself in one: that is, he persists in his purpose.

He remains one in Essence and will, immutable. HIS SOUL HAS WILLED, HE HAS DONE: whatever he wills he does.

AND MANY OTHER SIMILAR THINGS ARE AT HAND FOR HIM] He does many other things according to his own will, the reasons for which are unknown to us.

Latin:

Vers. 14. IPSE ENIM SOLUS EST) Melius ex Hebr. ipse in uno: id est, in proposito suo perstat.

Manet in Essentia & voluntate unus, immutabilis. ANIMA EJUS VOLUIT, FECIT: quicquid vult facit.

ET ALIA MULTA SIMILIA PRÆSTO SUNT EI) Multa alia facit pro suo arbitrio, quorum rationes nobis sunt incognitæ.

## 23:16
Vers. 16. GOD HAS SOFTENED MY HEART] He has broken my spirit, which the following things also show.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DEUS MOLLIVIT COR MEUM) Infregit mihi animum, quod & sequentia ostendunt.

## 23:17
Vers. 17.

FOR I HAVE NOT PERISHED BECAUSE OF THE IMMINENT DARKNESS] Through so many hardships surrounding me.

NOR HAS HE COVERED MY FACE) More correctly from the Hebrew: And from my face he covers the darkness: that is, God begrudges me death.

Nay, the negative is more correctly repeated, as was done in the version of Blessed Luther: for the former clause had already dealt with the denied death: therefore the sense is: that God neither removes him from life, wrapped as he is in the darkness of so many calamities, nor hides that darkness of evils from himself, and removes and ends it. Cocceius's explanation comes to almost the same thing: God covers himself with darkness from my face, hides himself more and more from me, deserts me.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

NON ENIM PERII PROPTER IMMINENTES TENEBRAS] Per tot ærumnas me circumstantes.

NEC FACIEM MEAM OPERVIT) Rectius ex Hebræo: Et à facie mea operit caliginem: id est, Deus mihi mortem invidet.

Imo rectius negativa repetitur, ut in B. Lutheri versione factum: nam de negata morte prius membrum jam egerat: ideo sensus est: quod nec e vita se tollat Deus tot calamitatum tenebris involutum, nec caliginem illam malorum a se abscondat, eaque tollat ac finiat. Eodem fere redit Cocceji explicatio: a facie mea operit se caligine Deus, magis magisque abscondit se a me, deserit me.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV.

Job, teaching that the various crimes of the wicked are often committed with impunity, nevertheless asserts that punishments will follow.

Ver. 1.

TIMES ARE NOT HIDDEN FROM THE ALMIGHTY.

IN Heb. WHY ARE TIMES NOT HIDDEN FROM THE ALMIGHTY? Why are they not hidden from men by God? Since even the faithful do not see the judgments of God?

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV.

Job impiorum scelera varia sæpe impune desi- gnari docens, pœnas tamen sequituras asserit.

Vers. 1.

AB OMNIPOTENTE NON SUNT AB- SCONDITA TEMPORA.

IN Ebr. QUARE AB OMNIPOTENTE NON SINT ABSCONDITA TEMPORA? Cur non a Deo sint occulta hominibus? quum etiam fideles non videant Dei judicia?

## 24:4
Ver. 4.

THEY HAVE SUBVERTED THE WAY OF THE POOR] They ordered them to depart from the way for them. In a declamation in Seneca, a poor man against a rich man: By day we are forbidden the public way. Then, it is not permitted for me to walk at my own discretion. Again: An unworthy crime has been committed: the rich and the poor walk in the same footsteps.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SVBVERTERVNT PAVPERVM VIAM] Jusserunt eos sibi de via decedere. In declamatione apud Senecam pau- per adversus divitem: Interdiu publico nobis interdicitur. De- inde, ambulare mihi meo arbitrio non licet. Iterum: Facinus indignum commissum est: dives & pauper per eadem vestigia incedunt.

## 24:5
Ver. 5.

OTHERS AS WILD ASSES IN THE DESERT GO FORTH TO THEIR WORK] He well added that 'as', which is also found in many other places. He beautifully compares robbers to wild asses. For they hide themselves in solitary places.

WATCHING FOR PREY] In the Hebrew: rising early. Horace: That they may murder men, robbers rise by night. See what follows in 14.

THEY PREPARE BREAD FOR THEIR CHILDREN] In the Hebrew: Solitude is food for his children. But both the LXX and Symmachus read other words for ערבו. For they translate it as sweet and to be sweetened.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ALII QVASI ONAGRI IN DESERTO EGREDI- VNTVR AD OPVS SVVM] Bene addidit illud quasi, quod & aliis in locis multis reperitur. Prædones onagris pulchre comparat. Delitescunt enim in locis solitariis.

VIGILANTES AD PRÆDAM] In Hebræo: mane sur- gentes. Horatius: Ut jugulent homines, surgunt de nocte la- trones. Vide quod sequitur 14.

PRÆPARANT PANEM LIBERIS] In Hebræo: Soli- tudo ei alimentum liberis. Sed & LXX. & Symmachus aliis vocabulis legerunt ערבו. Vertunt enim ἠδὺς & ἡδυνθῆ.

## 24:6
Ver. 6.

THEY REAP A FIELD NOT THEIR OWN] For בלילו which is translated as his fodder, he reads with divided words בלי לו. Nor does the Chaldean, or the LXX, read otherwise, so that I do not think there is any reason to doubt that this reading is the truer one.

But I very much doubt that it is true; nay, I think it is not true, because according to the received reading of the Hebrew Codices the sense is clear: and the Chaldean, the LXX, and the Vulgate Latin agree with it, even if they do not explain the words according to the letter. For he who reaps another's fodder, or whatever grows in the field, and claims it for himself, certainly reaps what is not his own. That phrase בלי לו for 'not his own' is not in use, or let suitable examples of it be given. But what is more frequent than that interpreters should render the sense rather than explain the words word for word?

Latin:

Vers. 6.

AGRVM NON SVVM DEMETVNT] Pro בלילו quod vertitur pabulum ejus, legit divisis vocibus בלי לו. Nec aliter Chaldæus, & LXX. ita ut de hac le- ctione, quin sit verior, dubitandum non arbitrer.

Ego vero maxime illam veram esse dubito, imo non veram esse arbitror, quia juxta lectionem receptam Codicum Ebræorum sensus expeditus est: eique consonant Chaldæus, LXX. & vulgata Latina, etsi non quoad literam verba explicent. Qui enim pabulum alienum demetit, vel quicquid in agro crescit, sibi vendicat, utique non suum demetit. Phrasis illa בלי לו pro non suum usitata non est, aut dentur ejus exempla commoda. Quid vero frequentius, quam quod Interpp. magis sensum reddant, quam κατὰ πόδα verba exponant?

## 24:10
Ver. 10.

NAKED AND WALKING WITHOUT CLOTHING AND HUNGRY THEY CARRIED THE EARS OF CORN] In the Hebrew: they made the naked (that is, very thinly clothed as above 22, 6) to walk without clothing (that is, an undergarment) and those who carry the sheaf to be hungry: that is, they gave the reapers nothing for their labor.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

NVDIS ET INCEDENTIBVS ABSQVE VESTITV ET ESVRIENTIBVS TVLERVNT SPICAS] In Hebræo: nudum (id est, tenuissime vestitum ut supra 22, 6.) ambulare fecerunt sine veste (id est, interula) & famelicos esse eos qui por- tant manipulum: id est, messoribus nihil dederunt pro labore.

## 24:12
Ver. 12.

AND GOD DOES NOT ALLOW TO GO UNPUNISHED] In the Hebrew: And God does not place a prohibition.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET DEVS INVLTVM ABIRE NON PATITVR] In Hebræo: Et Deus non ponit prohibitionem.

## 24:13
Ver. 13.

THEY WERE REBELLIOUS TO THE LIGHT] Those who flee the light. The force of the phrase is different: to rebel against the light. Nor did he note that the wicked act secretly, but violently in the open light. Therefore it should rather be understood of God who is light, 1 John 1, 5 (or of his word.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

IPSI FVERVNT REBELLES LVMINI] Lucifugæ. Alia est phraseos vis: rebellare luci. Neque impios occulte, sed luce aperta violenter agere no- tarat. Ideo potius de Deo qui lux est, 1. Joh. 1, 5. (vel verbo ejus accipiendum.

## 24:15
Ver. 15. HE WILL COVER HIS FACE] He walks with his head wrapped.

HE PUTS A COVERING ON HIS FACE, Thus desiring to lie hidden from men: or foolishly thinking that he is hidden even from GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 15. OPERIET VVLTUM SVVM] Capite invo- luto incedit.

TEGMEN FACIEI SUÆ IMPONIT, Sic homines latere cupiens: vel se DEUM etiam latere stulte existimans.

## 24:18
Ver. 18. HE IS SWIFT UPON THE FACE OF THE WATER] The pirate is carried very swiftly in his light vessels.

Most wish the discourse to be continued still concerning the adulterer. Cf. Gen. 49, 4. But Mercerus refers these things to a robber or a thief.

LET HIS PORTION BE CURSED IN THE LAND] Nay, it is, that is, he is feared by all the land.

Others more correctly: His substance and wealth shall not be increased by blessing, but shall be diminished on account of the curse, Deut. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 18. LEVIS EST SVPER FACIEM AQVÆ] Pirata Myoparonibus celerrime vectatur.

De adultero adhuc continuari sermonem plerique volunt. Conf. Gen. 49, 4. Ad latro- nem vero vel furem hæc refert Mercerus.

MALEDICTA SIT PARS EJVS IN TERRA] Imo est, id est, ab omni terra timetur.

Rectius alii: Substantia & opes ejus non auge- buntur benedictione, sed propter maledictionem minuentur, Deut. 28.

## 24:19
Ver. 19.

LET HIM PASS TO EXCESSIVE HEAT FROM THE WATERS OF SNOW, AND EVEN TO THE NETHER WORLD HIS SIN) You will translate more correctly from the Hebrew thus: As the parched land

and heat consume the snow waters, so does death those who have sinned. That is, although they have done such atrocious things, they nevertheless depart by an easy death, not a violent one. See Psalm 73, ver. 4, above 21, ver. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

AD NIMIUM CALOREM TRANSEAT AB AQVIS NIVIUM, ET USQVE AD INFEROS PECCATUM IL- LIUS) Rectius ex Hebræo sic vertes: Ut terra torrida

& calor absumunt aquas nivales, ita mors eos qui peccarunt. Id est, cum tam atrocia egerint, morte tamen defunguntur fa- cili, non violenta. Vide Psalm. 73. v. 4. supra 21. v. 13.

## 24:20
Ver. 20.

LET MERCY FORGET HIM] More correctly, the merciful one (that is, God) forgets him; as if he had done nothing evil.

Nay, because he did nothing good, not even God, who is mercy itself, will have mercy on him.

HIS SWEETNESS IS WORMS] That is, he is sweet food for worms, like others.

BUT LET HIM BE BROKEN LIKE A FRUITLESS TREE] In the Hebrew: iniquity is broken, like a tree. That is, just as there is no memory of a tree cut into pieces, so neither is there of his crimes.

His works shall perish like a useless tree, his deeds shall be annihilated, as being unjust.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

OBLIVISCATVR EJVS MISERICORDIA] Rectius misericors (id est Deus) ejus obliviscitur; quasi nihil male fe- cisset.

Imo quia nihil boni fecit, nec Deus quidem, qui ipsa misericordia est, ejus miserebitur.

DVLCEDO EJUS VERMES] Id est, vermibus esca dul- cis est, ut cæteri.

SED CONTERATUR QVASI LIGNUM INFRU- CTUOSUM] In Hebræo: confringitur, velut arbor, iniqui- tas. Id est, sicut arboris in particulas dissectæ nulla est me- moria, ita nec scelerum ipsius.

Opera ejus tanquam arbor inutilis peribunt, acta ejus annihilabuntur, ut injusta.

## 24:21
Ver. 21.

BREAKING THE BARREN SO THAT SHE MIGHT NOT BEAR] Rabbi Solomon explains this concerning those who gave to one of their two wives medicines preventing conception, so that they might enjoy her beauty longer.

The Rabbinic gloss being dismissed, the sense is: HE FEEDETH THE BARREN THAT BEARETH NOT, that is: the childless woman, who is without the consolation of children, as Augustine explains.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

FRANGENS STERILEM NE PARERET] Explicat Rabbi Salomo de iis qui uxorum duarum alteri dabant me- dicamenta conceptum impedientia, quo diutius ejus forma fruerentur.

Missa glossa Rabbinica sensus est: DEPASCIT STERILEM QUÆ NON PARIT, hoc est: or- bam, quæ sine consolatione filiorum est, ut Augu- stinus explicat.

## 24:22
Ver. 22.

HE SHALL NOT BELIEVE IN HIS LIFE) Here in the text is בחיין with a ן at the end instead of a ם in the Chaldean manner, as above 12, 11. Such a form you may find both in Lamentations and in Daniel. This can be added to the conjectures of the time when this book was written.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

NON CREDET VITÆ SUÆ) Hic est in textu בחיין cum ן in fine pro ם more Chaldaico, ut supra 12, 11. qualem formam & in Threnis & in Daniele reperias. Potest id adjici ad conjecturas temporis quo scriptus hic liber.

## 25:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXV.

Bildad treats of the power of God and the impurity of man.

Latin:

CAPUT XXV.

Bildad de Dei potestate hominisque impuritate agit.

## 25:2
WHO MAKETH PEACE IN HIS HIGH PLACES.

Understand this of the angels, from whom war is entirely banished.

Latin:

QUI FACIT CONCORDIAM IN SUBLI- MIBUS SUIS.

DE angelis intellige, a quibus bellum plane exu- lat.

## 25:4
Ver. 4.

CAN MAN BE JUSTIFIED COMPARED WITH GOD?] He translates that well as with God. To be justified, that is, to be praised as just.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NUMQVID JUSTIFICARI POTEST HOMO COM- PARATUS DEO?] Bene vertit illud cum Deo. Justificari, id est, laudari ut justus.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI.

Job, showing that Bildad's speech is preposterous, establishes the divine power from those things which happen under the water, on the earth, in the clouds, and from the waves of the Sea, and from the tempests.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI.

Hiob præposteram Bildadi orationem esse osten- dens potentiam divinam ex iis, quæ sub aqua, in terra, in nubibus fiunt, & e fluctibus Ma- ris, & tempestatibus adstruit.

## 26:5
Verse 5.

BEHOLD THE GIANTS GROAN BENEATH THE WATERS) He seems to indicate Tritons. For groan, in the Hebrew it is are formed.

Whales rather seem to be indicated by our opinion and that of B. Luther, which are among the fish in the water, as giants are among men on the earth.

AND THEY THAT DWELL WITH THEM] Huge whales, like herds of Tritons.

AND THE INHABITANTS (others) OF THE WATERS, other fish, of which there is an innumerable multitude.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ECCE GIGANTES GEMUNT SUB AQVIS) Tritones videtur indicare. Pro gemunt, in Hebræo est formantur.

BAlenæ potius notari nostra & B. Lutheri senten- tia videntur, quæ inter pisces sunt in aqua, quod gigantes inter homines in terra.

ET QVI HABITANT CUM EIS] Ingentia cete, velut armenta Tritonum.

ET INHABITATORES (alii) AQUA- RUM, pisces alii, quorum innumerabilis est multi- tudo.

## 26:6
Verse 6.

AND THERE IS NO COVERING FOR DESTRUCTION] The bosom of the earth which hides all dead living creatures.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET NULLUM OPERIMENTUM PERDITIONI] Gremio terræ quod cuncta animantia mortua abscondit.

## 26:7
HE WHO STRETCHETH OUT THE NORTH OVER THE VOID] He seems to signify the whole axis by the Arctic pole as being more well-known. It sustains the universe. But it itself is sustained by nothing known to us.

AND HANGETH THE EARTH UPON NOTHING] Ovid, Fasti 6: The earth, like a ball, rests on no support.

Latin:

QVI EXTENDIT AQVILONEM SUPER VACUUM] Ex polo Arctico ut notiore totum axem significare videtur. Is universum sustinet. Ipse vero à nulla re nobis nota su- stinetur.

ET APPENDIT TERRAM SUPER NIHILUM] Ovi- dius 6. Fastorum: Terra pilæ similis nullo fulcimine nixa.

## 26:8
Verse 8. HE WHO BINDETH UP THE WATERS IN HIS CLOUDS, THAT THEY MAY NOT BURST FORTH TOGETHER DOWNWARD] He holds the waters hanging in the clouds for a long time. If all these things did not appear daily, they would be reckoned among miracles.

Latin:

Vers. 8. QVI LIGAT AQVAS IN NUBIBUS SUIS, VT NON ERUMPANT PARITER DEORSUM] Aquas in nubibus pendulas diu detinet. Omnia hæc nisi quotidie apparerent miraculis accenserentur.

## 26:9
Verse 9. HE WHO HOLDETH THE FACE OF HIS THRONE] For holdeth, in the Hebrew it is constraineth. The throne of God is heaven, Isaiah 66:1. Its face turned toward us is the air. God holds it stretched out as if by ropes: we spoke of this at Genesis 1.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVI TENET VULTUM SOLII SUI] Pro te- net, in Hebræo est constringit. Solium Dei cœlum Esaiaæ 66, 1. Ejus facies obversa nobis, aer. Eum Deus velut funibus ten- sum continet: diximus ad 1. Geneseos.

## 26:10
Verse 10.

HE HAS SET A BOUNDARY TO THE WATERS) He enclosed the sea with shores: In the Hebrew more poetically: he has circumscribed a boundary for the waters, as if with a compass.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

TERMINVM CIRCVMDEDIT AQVIS) Mare inclu- fit littoribus: In Hebræo magis Poetice: metam aquis cir- cumfcripfit, velut circino.

## 26:11
Verse 11.

THE PILLARS OF HEAVEN TREMBLE) Poetically he calls the highest mountains the pillars of heaven, which seem as if they support the heaven; whence the fable about Atlas.

Simplicius says the pillars of heaven tremble, because heaven, however firm, like a house that trembles when its columns are shaken, seems to be shaken at the wrath of GOD. Nicetas illustrates this with a paraphrase: the very firmaments of heaven, and properly the bases and foundations, shudder and tremble when He has commanded them. Pineda understands this trembling of heaven as concerning the end of the world, and compares the passage in Matthew 24:29 [19] regarding the powers being shaken to this sentiment here. That phrase about the mountains, the pillars of heaven, is too poetic, even if it does not please every interpreter; I do not know if it should be established here. Certainly, mountains are nowhere called the pillars of heaven in the Scriptures. Cocceius understands the air by the pillars of heaven, which takes the place of columns in position, not in function, unless it is for continuing and connecting the parts of the universe, and is shaken by the blasts of winds or the violence of thunder; or if mountains are understood, he thinks the air is included under the name of heaven.

Verse the same.

AND THEY ARE AFRAID AT HIS NOD] In the Hebrew: at his rebuke. Thus the Hebrews call thunder.

Verse the same.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

COLVMNÆ COELI CONTREMISCVNT) Poetice columnas cœli dicit montes altissimos, qui cœlum quasi susti- nere videntur; unde de Atlante fabula.

Simplicius columnæ cœli contremiscere dicun- tur, quod cœlum utut firmissimum, instar domus quæ concussis columnis contremiscit, ad iram DEI concuti videatur. Nicetas hac paraphrasi illustrat: ipsa cœli firmamenta, ac propriè bases ac fundamenta horrent, ac contremiscunt, cum iis imperarit. Quem tremorem cœli Pineda de mundi fine intelligit, lo- cumque Matth. 25, 19. de commovendis virtutibus, eam in sententiam hic confert. Phrasis ista de mon- tibus, columnis cœli, nimis Poetica, etsi non uni in- terpreti placeat, nescio an hic statuenda sit. Nu- spiam certe montes cœli columnæ in Scripturis di- cuntur. Coccejos per columnas cœli aerem intelligit, qui columnarum vice situ, non officio, nisi continuandi conferendique universi partes, & ventorum flabris aut tonitruum violentia concutitur, aut si montes intelli- gantur, aerem cœli comprehendi nomine, censet.

Vers. eod.

ET PAVENT AD NVTVM EJVS] In Hebræo ad in- crepationem ejus. Sic Hebræi vocant tonitru.

Vers. eod.

## 26:12
BY HIS STRENGTH HE SUDDENLY GATHERED THE SEAS] In the Hebrew: by his power he split the sea: namely the Red Sea, so that the Hebrews might cross.

BY HIS PRUDENCE HE SMOTE THE PROUD] Pharaoh. In the Hebrew רהב: but שׂיא is understood, as often.

It points rather to the proud sea, as blessed Luther also explained it concerning the sea raised up and as it were raging. Cf. Job 38:11, Jer. 12:5, Ch. 49:19.

Latin:

IN FORTITVDINE EJVS REPENTE MARIA CON- GREGATA SVNT] In Hebræo: vi sua scidit mare: nempe Erythræum, ut Hebræi transirent.

PRVDENTIA EJVS PERCVSSIT SVPERBVM] Pha- raonem. In Hebræo רהב: sed subintelligitur שׂיא, ut sæpe.

Mare superbum potius indigitat, uti etiam B. Lutherus de mari elevato, & veluti ferocienti ex- posuit. Conf. Job. 38, 11. Jer. 12, 5. C. 49, 9.

## 26:13
Verse 13.

His Spirit has adorned the heavens. By His Spirit He has adorned the heaven, and His hand has brought forth the straight serpent.

Coccejus notes here the mystery of the Trinity, as does also Mr. Dr. Schmidius. Because mention is made of GOD, and of His HAND, the Son of GOD, and of the SPIRIT: who exerted His power equally in the depths of the sea as in the heights (heaven). The blessed Gerhard also explained it concerning the Holy Spirit in his Exegesis of the Confession and our System, Vol. 3.

Verse 13.

BY HIS HAND THE TORTUOUS SERPENT HAS BEEN BROUGHT FORTH] The most learned of the Hebrews understand the Galaxy, which is spread out ambitiously in the manner of a serpent. This could be referred to the Dragon, which is between the Bears, if those constellations which we now use were as ancient.

Coccejus translates it as a bar-serpent, which is opposed to the tortuous one in Isaiah 27:1, because a bar is called בריח and tortuous עקלתון, and he understands here the whale, as in chapters 3, 40, and 41, a notable work of divine power in the depths. Those who understand the constellation of the Dragon in the heaven can say that the constellations which we now use are introduced elsewhere in this book, just as Grotius himself at chapter 28, 31, 32 interprets כימה as the Pleiades, and כסיל as Orion, and עי as Arcturus. Osiander explains it concerning the Galaxy. Others concerning lightning, which seems to fall from heaven like a serpent, and is depicted as such, and yet strikes directly what God intends. Wisdom 5:22.

Latin:

Versus 13.

SPIRITUS EJUS ORNAVIT COELOS. IN SPIRITU SUO ORNAVIT COELUM, ET MANUS EJUS PEPERIT SERPENTEM RE- CTUM.

Notat hic mysterium Trinitatis Coccejus, ut & Dn. D. Schmidius. Quia DEI, ejusque MA- NUS Filii DEI, & SPIRITUS mentio fit: qui æque in imo in mari, ut in summo (cœlo) potentiam suam exeruit. De Spiritu S. etiam exposuit B. Gerhard. in Exeg. Conf. & System. nostri T. 3.

Vers. 13.

MANV EJVS EDVCTVS EST COLVBER TOR- TVOSVS] Eruditissimi Hebræorum intelligunt Galaxiam, qui serpentis more ambitiosus funditur. Posset hoc ad Draco- nem, qui inter Arctos est, referri, si tam veteres essent ii, qui- bus nunc utimur ἀσερισμοὶ.

Coccejus serpentem vectem vertit, qui tortuoso opponitur Es. 27, 1. quia vectis dicitur בריח tortuo- sus עקלתון, & intelligit hic balenam, ut cap. 3, 40. & 41. insigne in imis opus divinæ potentiæ. Qui Draconis constellationem in cœlo intelligunt, asteri- smos, quibus nunc utimur, & alibi in hoc libro in- troduci, dicere possunt, uti Grotius ipse ad c. 28, 31. 32. כימה interpretatur Plejadas, & כסיל orio- nem & עי Arcturum. De Galaxia explicat O- siander. Alii de fulmine, quod instar serpentis de cœlo cadere videtur, & pingitur, & tamen di- recte ferit, quod Deus intendit. Sap. 5, 22.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII.

Job, appealing to conscience and protesting about his further good purpose, says that his antagonists are wicked and hypocrites, and he delivers the punishments of such, which [affect] their children and their fortunes.

IN Hebrew: IF MY LIPS SPEAK iniquity: אם is a formula of imprecation: through aposiopesis and a form of solemnity, the evil is left unsaid which the one swearing, if he should perjure himself, imprecates upon himself.

Latin:

CAP. XXVII.

Job ad conscientiam provocans, & de ulterio- ri bono proposito protestatus antagoni- stas suos iniquos & hypocritas esse ait, ac talium pœnas tradit, quæ liberos & fortu- nas eorum.

IN Ebræo: SI LOQUENTUR labia mea iniqui- tatem: אם formula imprecationis est: per apo- siopesin & speciem σεμνότητος reticetur malum, quod jurans, si pejeret, sibi imprecatur.

## 27:15
Verse 15.

HIS WIDOWS SHALL NOT WEEP) Among many nations, it was forbidden to mourn for those infamous for great crimes. Law of the Free, Digest, concerning those who are marked with infamy. Suetonius, Tiberius 61. It was forbidden for relatives to mourn those condemned to death.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

VIDVÆ ILLIVS NON PLORABVNT) Infames ma- gnorum criminum lugere vetitum apud multas gentes. L. Libercrum. D. de his qui notantur infamia. Suetonius Tiberio 61. Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lu- gerent.

## 27:18
Verse 18.

HE SHALL BUILD HIS HOUSE LIKE A MOTH) The house which he shall build will perish as easily as the dwelling of a moth, which it itself gnaws away.

AND AS A KEEPER HATH MADE A BOOTH] His house shall not be more durable than a booth, which for a short time the ὀπωροφύλαξ makes for himself. See Jon. 4, 5. and the following.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ÆDIFICABIT QVASI TINEA DOMVM SVAM) Domus quam ædificabit ita facile peribit, quam tineæ domi- cilium, quod ipsa corrodit.

ET SICVT CVSTOS FECIT VMBRACVLVM] Non durabilior erit domus ejus quam pergula, quam ad tempus breve sibi facit ὀπωροφύλαξ. Vide Jon. 4, 5. & sequen- tibus.

## 27:19
Ver. 19.

THE RICH MAN, WHEN HE SHALL SLEEP, SHALL CARRY NOTHING AWAY WITH HIM) In the Greek: πλούσιος κοιμηθήσεται καὶ οὐ προσθήσει. But it seems it should be read προτεθήσεται. For the Greek προσίθεσθαι, and the Hebrew אסף are said of those who are buried with honor in the monuments of their ancestors 2. Kings 22. v. 20. Jerem. 8. v. 2. Ezech. 22, v. 5.

HE SHALL OPEN HIS EYES AND SHALL FIND NOTHING] Often even while he lives he shall be deserted by his own people on account of diseases to be feared for their contagiousness.

Others refer it better to the person of the rich man himself, which the Hebrew איננו implies. AND NOT TO HIM, as if in the twinkling of an eye and suddenly he is to be taken from life.

Latin:

Verf. 19.

DIVES, CVM DORMIERIT NIHIL SECVM AVFE- RET) In Græco: πλούσιος κοιμηθήσεται καὶ ἐ προσθήσει. Sed legendum videtur προτεθήσεται. Nam προσίθεσθαι Græ- cum, & אסף Hebræum dicitur de iis qui cum honore in mo- numentis majorum sepeliuntur 2. Reg. 22. v. 20. Jerem. 8. v. 2. Ezech. 22, v. 5.

APERIET OCVLOS SVOS ET NIHIL INVENIET] Sæpe etiam dum vivit a suis deseretur ob morbos contagio formidandos.

Alii melius ad ipsam divitis personam, quam innuit Ebr. איננו referunt. ET NON IPSI, quasi in ictu oculi & repente tollendus sit de vita.

## 27:21
Ver. 21.

THE EAST WIND SHALL CARRY HIM AWAY) A pestilential blast. See Exod. 10. v. 13. above 15. v. 2. Jonah 4. v. 8.

Latin:

Verf. 21.

TOLLET EVM EVRVS) Pestilens aura. Vide Exod. 10. v. 13. supra 15. v. 2. Jonæ 4. v. 8.

## 27:22
Ver. 22.

FLEEING HE SHALL FLEE OUT OF HIS HAND] He will attempt everything, in order to escape.

But in vain: for he shall be ensnared on every side.

Latin:

Verf. 22.

DE MANV EJVS FVGIENS FVGIET] Omnia mo- lietur, ut effugiat.

Sed frustra: undique enim irretitus erit.

## 27:23
Ver. 23.

HE SHALL CLAP HIS HANDS AT HIM] Whoever is present will applaud for joy.

HE SHALL HISS OVER HIM, LOOKING AT HIS PLACE] The name of the dead man shall be hissed at.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

STRINGET SVPER EVM MANVS SVAS] Quisquis aderit plaudet præ gaudio.

SIBILLABIT SVPER EVM, INTVENS LOCVM EJVS] Exsibilabitur mortui nomen.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII.

The hidden wisdom of God is confirmed from metals and gems and other things, and its origin is taught.

Ver. 1.

SILVER HATH THE BEGINNINGS OF ITS VEINS.

Job enters into oryctology, either because he concludes from all things in nature and the passages of the earth disposed in order that human affairs are much more directed by divine counsel, as Chrysostom noted: or because he intimates that human industry can indeed to a certain extent search out the hidden things of the earth, but not likewise the hidden judgments of God, as Niceta advised: or as others, since the wicked here have their goods dug out of the earth, the pious man has eternal wisdom, which is not found in earthly things: and why the wicked do not find the true way of blessedness, because they do not seek it in wisdom, which is hidden with GOD: to which opinion Mr. Dr. Schmidt seems to accede, in this place p. 1082, delivering this reason for the connection and explanation, that a cause is rendered why he abstains from impiety: because piety alone is true wisdom and prudence, nor is it permitted to find true wisdom anywhere except in piety, since otherwise silver has its own outcome.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII.

Sapientia Dei abscondita, e Metallis & gemmis aliisque confirmatur, ejusque origo doce- tur.

Vers. 1.

HABET ARGENTUM VENARUM SUA- RUM PRINCIPIA.

Ingreditur Job oryctologiam, sive quod ex omnibus in natura & terræ meatibus ordine dispo- sitis concludat, multo magis humana divino dirigi confilio, ut Chrysostomus notavit: seu quod huma- nam industriam quidem quadantenus abdita terræ scrutari posse innuat, non item judicia Dei abscondi- ta, ut Niceta monuit: seu ut alii, cum impii hic ha- beant sua bona ex terra eruta, pium habere sapien- tiam æternam, quæ in terrenis non invenitur: & cur non inveniant impii veram beatitudinis viam, quia non quærunt eam in sapientia, quæ apud DEUM abscondita est: cui sententiæ videtur accedere Dn. D. Schmitdius, h.l. p. 1082. hanc rationem συνεχείας, & explicationem tradens, quod causa reddatur, cur ab impietate abstineat: quia sola pietas vera est sa- pientia, & prudentia, nec veram sapientiam uspiam invenire liceat, nisi in pietate, cum alioqui argento suus sit exitus.

## 28:3
Ver. 3.

HE HATH SET A TIME FOR DARKNESS] In Greek better: τάξιν ἔθετο σκότει. Even in the very bowels of the earth, which are deservedly named both gloom and the shadow of death, He has disposed the order of things.

AND HE HIMSELF CONSIDERS THE END OF ALL THINGS) He knows how far these or those metals and other subterranean things extend. THE STONE OF DARKNESS) Gems deeply hidden.

Latin:

Verf. 3.

TEMPVS POSVIT TENEBRIS] Græce melius: τάξιν ἔθετο σκότει. Etiam in ipsis terræ visceribus, quæ & caligo & mortis umbra merito nominantur, ordinem rerum di- sposuit.

ET VNIVERSORVM FINEM IPSE CONSIDERAT) Scit quousque hæc vel illa metalla & subterranea alia pertin- gant. LAPIDEM CALIGINIS) Gemmas abstrusas penitus.

## 28:5
Verse 5.

THE EARTH FROM WHICH BREAD WAS PRODUCED IS OVERTURNED IN ITS PLACE AS IF BY FIRE) The most fertile place of paradise is besieged by flame. Bread, that is, לחם, everything that is eaten. There is nothing here about the land of Paradise προς επω. It is concerned rather with subterranean fire. It is to be wondered at that, although the earth provides food, it nevertheless also contains fire; which consumes all things: which it contains indeed not only virtually in flint and sulphur; but also actually, since fire often breaks out in mines, and mountains are found to be ignited, such as Etna, Vesuvius, etc. although the particle כמו, not poorly observed by Pagninus, Piscator, and others, is converted, so that it becomes as if fire, implying that not only the fire itself but anything fiery, or that which becomes as if fire, is being looked at. I see now that Mr. Dr. Schmiedius also favors this interpretation, because it is not only converted into true fire, but also into other things, into which it is the same to be converted as to be converted into fire, as if it is converted into fire, into lime, and the like: whence he notes that it can be rendered thus: and that which is turned under it in such a way that it becomes something fiery: and that wonder is placed in it, that the same earth nourishes, by bringing forth bread from above, and consumes by generating something fiery, which are completely contrary, and yet are found in one earth.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

TERRA DE QVA ORIEBATVR PANIS IN LOCO SVO IGNI SVBVERSA EST) Locus paradisi fertilissimus flamma obsidetur. Panis, id est, לחם omne quod editur. Nihil hic de terra Paradisi προς επω. Agi- tur potius de igne subterraneo. Mirandum est, cum terra præbeat cibum, tamen ignem etiam ea contineri; qui omnia consumit : quem vero continet non so- lum virtualiter in filice & sulphure; sed etiam actua- liter, cum sæpe ignis in fodinis erumpat, & montes reperiantur igniti, ut Ætna, Vesuvius, &c. quamvis particula כמו non male observata a Pagnino, Pisca- tore, & aliis, convertitur, ut fiat velut ignis, non ignem tantum ipsum sed quodvis igneum, seu quod fit veluti ignis respici innuat. Video jam etiam huic interpretationi favere Dn. D. Schmiedium, quod non tantum convertatur in verum ignem, sed etiam in alias res, in quas converti perinde sit, ac con- verti in ignem, ut si convertitur in ignem, in calcem, & similia : unde ita reddi posse notat : & quod sub ea vertitur ita, ut fiat igneum quid : mirumque illud in eo positum sit, quod eadem terra nutriat, superne panem proferendo, & consumat igneum quid gene- rando, quæ sunt prorsus contraria, & tamen in una terra reperiuntur.

## 28:7
Verse 7.

NOR HAS THE EYE OF THE VULTURE LOOKED UPON IT) So also the Greeks. Others wish it to be a magpie, others a jackdaw, others a crow.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

NEC INTVITVS EST EAM OCVLVS VVLTVRIS) Sic & Græci. Alii picam esse volunt, alii graculum, alii cor- nicem.

## 28:8
Verse 8.

THE CHILDREN OF THE MERCHANTS HAVE NOT TRODDEN IT) In the Hebrew: children of pride: and in Greek: υἱοὶ ἀλαζόνων. Thus the Chaldean Paraphrast in the Psalms calls lions.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

NON CALCAVERVNT EAM FILII INSTITO- RVM) In Hebræo : filii superbiæ: & Græce : υἱοὶ ἀλαζόνων. Ita Chaldæus Paraphrastes in Psalmis appellat leones.

## 28:14
Verse 14.

THE ABYSS HAS SAID IT IS NOT IN ME: AND THE SEA SPEAKS IT IS NOT WITH ME) Wisdom is not accustomed to dwell among sailors. Thus indeed Rabbi Solomon explains the abyss as referring to miners, and the sea to sailors, which kinds of men care little for wisdom: But it is also a Prosopopoeia: if the abyss could speak, it would deny that wisdom was found within it, even if gems and gold are dug out of it: The Sea would also deny it; even if precious things, and things wonderful to behold, are sought from its depths.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ABYSSVS DIXIT NON EST IN ME: ET MARE LOQVITVR NON EST MECVM) Apud nautas non so- let habitare sapientia. Ita sane explicat Rabbi Salomo abyssum de me- tallicis, & mare de nautis, quales homines parum cu- rant sapientiam: Sed & Prosopopœia : si abyssus lo- qui posset, quæsita apud se esse negaret sapientiam, eti- amsi ex illa gemmæ & aurum effodiantur : Negaret & Mare; etiamsi ex illius fundo pretiosa, & mira visu petantur.

## 28:17
Verse 17. GOLD OR GLASS SHALL NOT BE EQUAL TO IT) So also the Greeks and Chaldeans. Other Greeks put κρύσταλλον. These names are often accustomed to be mixed up because of their similarity. Glass was found not far from Arabia in Judea. Tacitus Histor. 5, 7. Pliny 36, 26. Pagninus, Deodatus, Scultetus and others understand it rather as Diamond. Coccejus does not deny it, nor does Mr. Dr. Schmiedius. NOR SHALL VESSELS OF GOLD BE EXCHANGED WITH IT) He expressed the sense very well. In the Hebrew the negative is understood ἐκ κοινᾶ.

Latin:

Vers. 17. NON ADÆQVABITVR EI AVRVM VEL VITRVM) Sic & Græci & Chaldæi. Alii Græci ponunt κρύ- σταλλον. Solent ob similitudinem sæpe misceri ista nomina. Vitrum non longe ab Arabia in Judæa repertum. Tacitus Histor. 5, 7. Plinius 36, 26. Pagninus, Deodatus, Scultetus aliique Ada- mantem potius intelligunt. Nec abnuit Coccejus, neque Dn. D. Schmiedius. NEC COMMVTABVNTVR CVM EO VASA AV- RI) Sensum optime expressit. In Hebræo negativa ἐκ κοινᾶ intelligitur.

## 28:18
Verse 18. HIGH AND EMINENT THINGS SHALL NOT BE MENTIONED IN COMPARISON WITH IT] The first word in Hebrew is ראמות: Kimchi and others of the Hebrews interpret it as coral. The Greeks retained the other word γαβὶς. It is without doubt the very thing which the Arabs write as حسبا, and it signifies a carbuncle or pyropus. In an old Latin saying it is: Probity is a carbuncle. BUT WISDOM IS DRAWN FROM HIDDEN THINGS) In the Hebrew: The attraction of wisdom for pearls: that is, wisdom hangs down: which the Greeks call ἄγη.

Latin:

Vers. 18. EXCELSA ET EMINENTIA NON ME- MORABVNTVR COMPARATIONE EJVS] Vox pri- ma in Hebræo est ראמות : eam coralia interpretatur Kimchi & Hebræorum alii. Alteram vocem γαβὶς retinue- re Græci. Est haud dubie id ipsum quod Arabes scribunt حسبا, & carbunculum sive pyropum significat. In vetere dicto Latino est : Probitas est carbunculus. TRAHITVR AVTEM SAPIENTIA DE OCCVLTIS) In Hebræo : Attractio sapientiæ pro margaritis: id est, sapi- entia propendet : quod Græci dicunt ἄγη.

## 28:19
Verse 19. THE TOPAZ FROM ETHIOPIA SHALL NOT BE COMPARED TO IT) So also the Greeks. It seems that by the name of Ethiopia here is understood either an island of the Red Sea, or India, from where Pliny teaches us the Topaz comes.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NON ADÆQVABITVR EI TOPAZIVS DE ÆTHIOPIA) Sic & Græci. Videtur hic Æthiopiæ nomine intelligi aut insula maris rubri, aut India, unde Topazios Pli- nius nos esse docet.

## 28:22
Verse 22. DESTRUCTION AND DEATH HAVE SAID: WITH OUR EARS WE HAVE HEARD THE FAME OF IT) That all composite things return to their principles is a huge testimony of divine wisdom.

The preceding parts teach that there is a continuation: namely, that perfect wisdom cannot be sought either among demons marked by destruction, or among the dead. The sum of what is said is: that this wisdom is found nowhere in sublunary things, not in the highest air, not in the middle space above the earth, not in the lowest place under the earth, so much so that the dead under the earth, although they may have lived long and had great experience, and demons in hell, although they may wish and be able to speak the truth, would say that they indeed have heard something about it in obscure speech, but that solid wisdom is not found among them. Therefore, it is to be sought in God alone. Coccejus teaches that he is speaking of Hypostatic wisdom, which is in God and with God.

Latin:

Vers. 22. PERDITIO ET MORS DIXERVNT: AV- RIBVS NOSTRIS AVDIVIMVS FAMAM EJVS) Quod omnes res compositæ in sua principia redeunt, ingens est sa- pientiæ divinæ testimonium.

Antecedentia docent, continuationem esse : quod nempé nec inter dæmones perditione notatos, nec mortuos, perfecta sapientia quæri possit. Summa dictorum est : nullibi in rebus sublunaribus hanc sa- pientiam inveniri, non in summo aere, non in medio spatio super terram, non in infimo loco sub terra, adeo ut mortui sub terra, licet diu vixerint & expe- rientiam magnam habuerint, & dæmones in inferno licet subtilissimi & astutissimi verum dicere velint & possint, dicturi sint se quidem aliquid obscuro sermone de ea audivisse, solidam autem sapientiam apud se non inveniri. In Deo ergo solo quærenda est. Loqui eum de sapientia Hypostatica, quæ in Deo & apud Deum est, Coccejus docet.

## 28:25
Verse 25. WHO MADE A WEIGHT FOR THE WINDS AND WEIGHED THE WATERS BY MEASURE) He established the masses of things in a certain proportion. Compare Proverbs 8, 27-28.

Latin:

Vers. 25. QVI FECIT VENTIS PONDUS ET AQVAS APPENDIT IN MENSVRA) Rerum massas in certa proportione constituit. Confer. Proverb. 8, 27-28.

## 28:28
Verse 28. AND HE SAID TO MAN: BEHOLD THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAT IS WISDOM, AND TO DEPART FROM EVIL IS UNDERSTANDING) Having spoken of the wisdom of God, he shows what is the highest part of human wisdom. Compare Prov. 1, 7. 9, 10. Eccl. 12, 13. Jerem. 9, 23. 24.

Therefore, you would seek that infinite and archetypal wisdom of GOD outside of GOD in vain: but this Ectypal wisdom, communicated to us according to our measure, which consists in the fear of GOD, He does not deny to man.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ET DIXIT HOMINI: ECCE TIMOR DO- MINI IPSA EST SAPIENTIA, ET RECEDERE A MALO INTELLIGENTIA) De Dei sapientia locutus, ostendit quæ sit pars summa humanæ sapientiæ. Confer. Prov. 1 7. 9, 10. Eccl. 12, 13. Jerem. 9, 23. 24.

Illam ergo sapientiam DEI infinitam & arche- typam frustra extra DEUM quæras: hanc vero E- ctypam & nobis pro modulo communicatam, quæ in timore DEI consistit, homini non denegat.

## 29:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIX. Job commemorates his former authority, and the just administration of his office, as well as his domestic happiness.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIX. Job autoritatem pristinam, & officii sui admi- nistrationem justam, nec non felicitatem œconomicam commemorat.

## 29:2
Verse 2. OH THAT I WERE AS IN MONTHS PAST) He desires that a hearing be granted to him, as he once flourished with authority.

Nay, he desires that he might be able to be restored to his former state.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QVIS MIHI TRIBVAT VT SIM JVXTA MENSES PRISTINOS) Optat audientiam sibi præberi, ut olim cum autoritate floreret.

IMo optat se posse restitui in pristinum sta- tum.

## 29:4
Verse 4. AS I WAS IN THE DAYS OF MY YOUTH) So also Symmachus, a diligent interpreter. Moreover, חרף in this meaning is a Syriac word.

Latin:

Vers 4. SICVT FVI IN DIEBVS ADOLESCENTIÆ MEÆ) Sic & Symmachus diligens Interpres. Est autem חרף in hoc significatu vox Syriaca.

## 29:5
Verse 5. WHEN THE SECRET OF GOD WAS IN MY TABERNACLE] Better, when the secret (that is, the oracle) of God was in my tent: that is, when my responses were held as oracles.

It is more correctly explained: when God dealt graciously with me as with a familiar friend. Psalm 25, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QVANDO SECRETO DEVS ERAT IN TABER- NACVLO MEO] Melius, cum arcanum Dei (id est, oracu- lum) esset in tentorio meo : id est, cum mea responsa pro ora- culis haberentur.

Rectius exponitur : quando Deus gratiose mecum quasi cum familiari agebat. Psalm. 25, 15.

## 29:6
Ver. 6. AND THE ROCK POURED OUT RIVERS OF OIL FOR ME ) Olives also grow in the rocky places of Syria and Arabia. Deut. 32, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET PETRA FVNDEBAT MIHI RIVOS OLEI ) Olea etiam in saxosis locis Syriæ & Arabiæ prove- nit. Deuter. 32, 13.

## 29:7
Ver. 7. WHEN I WENT FORTH TO THE GATE OF THE CITY ) To the court.

AND IN THE STREET THEY PREPARED A SEAT FOR ME ) In the forum.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVANDO PROCEDEBAM AD PORTAM CIVITATIS ) In Curiam.

ET IN PLATEA PARABANT CATHEDRAM MI- HI) In foro.

## 29:8
Ver. 8. THE AGED AROSE AND STOOD ) A sign of reverence. Juvenal: If a youth had not risen for an elder.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SENES ASSVRGENTES STABANT ) Si- gnum reverentiæ. Juvenalis : Si juvenis setulo non assurxe- xerat.

## 29:9
Ver. 9. THE PRINCES CEASED TO SPEAK, AND LAID THEIR FINGER UPON THEIR MOUTH ) As in Virgil when Aeneas began to speak: They all fell silent and held their mouths intent.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PRINCIPES CESSABANT LOQVI, ET DI- GITVM SVPERPONEBANT ORI SVO) Vt apud Vir- gilium Ænea loqui orso : Conticuere omnes intentique ora tenebant.

## 29:13
Ver. 13. THE BLESSING OF HIM THAT WAS PERISHING ) The word אובד signifies a poor or miserable person, Prov. 31, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 13. BENEDICTIO PERITVRI) Vox אובד pauperem sive miserum significat Prov. 31, 6.

## 29:15
Ver. 15. I WAS AN EYE TO THE BLIND AND A FOOT TO THE LAME ) A similar way of speaking in an epigram about a blind man and a lame man: Ανέρα τις λιπόγυον ὑπὲρ νώτοιο λιπαυγὴς Ηγε, πόδας χρήσας, ὄμματα χρησάμενος.

Latin:

Vers. 15. OCVLVS FVI COECO ET PES CLAVDO) Simile loquendi genus in Epigrammate de cœco & claudo : Ανέρα τις λιπόγυον ὑπὲρ νώτοιο λιπαυγὴς Ηγε, πόδας χρήσας, ὄμματα χρησάμενος.

## 29:16
Ver. 16. THE CAUSE WHICH I KNEW NOT I SEARCHED OUT MOST DILIGENTLY ) Cf. Prov. 29, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 16. CAVSAM QVAM NESCIEBAM DILIGEN- TISSIME INVESTIGABAM ) Conf. Prov. 29, 6.

## 29:18
Ver. 18. AS THE PALM TREE I SHALL MULTIPLY MY DAYS ) From the Greek: ὥσπερ στέλεχος Φοίνικος. But many Hebrews understand the phoenix here, not the tree, but the bird which is otherwise called by them ארשניר, of wonderful longevity, but which the fables of the poets have exaggerated.

Thus also Tertullian on the Resurrection, ch. 13. But חול signifies sand. Therefore it ought to be rendered: and as the sand I shall multiply my days. Cf. Gen. 22, 17. Jud. 7, 12. Cocceius: as the sand I shall multiply my days: who explains the former, I shall expire with my nest in the nest among those children and unharmed: which others render, I shall expire in my nest: But according to Mercer, he calls his house a nest, and his country, family, and the abundance of goods which he enjoyed.

Latin:

Vers. 18. SICVT PALMA MVLTIPLICABO DIES MEOS ) Ex Græco: ὥσπερ στέλεχος Φοίνικος. At Hebræi multi φοίνικα hic intelligunt, non arborem, sed avem quæ ali- ter ארשניר ,ipfis dicitur miræ vivacitatis, sed quam au- xerunt Poetarum fabulæ.

Sic etiam Tertullianus de Resurrectione c. 13. Sed חול significat arenam. Ideo reddi debet: & sicut arenam multiplicabo dies meos. Conf. Gen. 22,27. Jud. 7, 12. Coccejus : ut fabulum multipli- cabo dies : qui priora, cum nido expirabo, explicat apud nidum inter liberos illos & incolumes: quæ alii reddunt, in nido meo expirabo: Nidum autem juxta Mercerum vocat domum suam, & patriam, familiam & bonorum affluentiam, qua fruebatur.

## 29:20
Verse 20.

MY BOW) That is, my strength, μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically).

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ARCUS MEUS) Id est, robur meum, μεταφορικῶς.

## 29:23
Verse 23.

AS FOR THE LATTER RAIN] Understand 'serotinum' (latter) as being late in the time of the year, ὄψιμον (late) to Theophrastus and others. James 5:7 distinguishes ὑετὸν πρωϊμὸν καὶ ὄψιμον (early and latter rain). The early rain מורה (moreh) in Joel 2:23 is in the autumn, when the natural year begins: the latter rain, at the end of the same year, מלקוש (malqosh).

Latin:

Vers. 23.

QUASI AD IMBREM SEROTINUM] Serotinum in- tellige sero anni tempore, ὄψιμον Theophrasto & aliis. Ja- cobus 5, 7. distinguit ὑετὸν πρωϊμὸν καὶ ὄψιμον maturum & serotinum. Maturus imber מורה Joel. 2. v. 23. est in au- tumno, cum incipit annus naturalis: serotinus, fine ejusdem anni מלקוש.

## 29:24
Verse 24.

IF I LAUGHED AT THEM, THEY DID NOT BELIEVE] They even thought my jokes concealed something serious. AND THE LIGHT OF MY COUNTENANCE DID NOT FALL TO THE GROUND] In the Hebrew: And they did not make the light of my countenance fall: my authority remained firm among them.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

SI QUANDO RIDEBAM AD EOS, NON CREDE- BANT] Etiam joca mea putabant aliquid occultare serii. ET LUX VULTUS MEI NON CADEBAT IN TER- RAM] In Hebræo: Et lucem vultus mei non faciebant cade- re: autoritas mihi mea apud ipsos constabat.

## 29:25
Verse 25.

AND WHEN I SAT AS A KING WITH AN ARMY STANDING AROUND, I WAS YET A COMFORTER OF THOSE WHO MOURN) When I looked upon myself as a king, I nevertheless adapted myself even to the least: I was συμπαθὴς (sympathetic), συγκαταβα- τικὸς (condescending). That word בגדוד (ba-gedud), the Greeks translate as ἐν μονοζώνοις (among the light-armed). We have had this word several times already: Hesychius interprets it as κατασκόπους ἢ μαχίμους (scouts or warriors): Suidas as ἀσυντάκτες καὶ ὡσανεὶ λῃστὰς (disorderly and as it were robbers): Isidore as στρατιωτικὰ τάγματα (military ranks): Jerome sometimes as latrunculos (little robbers). I think they are velites (skirmishers).

Latin:

Vers. 25.

CUMQUE SEDEREM QUASI REX CIRCUM- STANTE EXERCITU, ERAM TAMEN MOEREN- TIUM CONSOLATOR) Cum respicerem quasi rex, apta- bam me tamen etiam minimis: eram συμπαθὴς, συγκαταβα- τικὸς. Illud בגדוד, Græci vertunt ἐν μονοζώνοις. Habui- mus hanc vocem jam aliquoties: κατασκόπους ἢ μαχίμους in- terpretatur Hesychius: ἀσυντάκτες καὶ ὡσανεὶ λῃστὰς, Sui- das: στρατιωτικὰ τάγματα, Isidorus: latrunculos interdum Hieronymus. Puto esse velites.

## 30:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXX. Job complains about his present state, contempt, reproaches, and unhappiness.

Verse 1.

WHOSE FATHERS I WOULD NOT DEIGN TO SET WITH THE DOGS OF MY FLOCK) A similar expression is found in Martial: 'May I perish if you are worthy to offer scraps to Pylades, or to feed the pigs of Pirithous.'

Latin:

CAPUT XXX. Job de moderno statu, comtemtu, opprobriis & infelicitate queritur.

Vers. 1.

QUORUM NON DIGNABAR PATRES PONERE CUM CANIBUS GREGIS MEI) Similis locutio apud Martialem: Dispeream si tu Pyladi præbere macellam Dignus es, aut porcos pascere Pirithoi.

## 30:3
Verse 3.

STERILE FROM WANT AND FAMINE WHO WERE SITTING IN SOLITUDE] More closely thus: Who were desolate from want and famine, and were fleeing into desert places: namely, that they might hide their want there. And the word כפש which here signifies famine, and ערק which signifies to flee, are Syriac. SQUALID WITH CALAMITY AND MISERY] In the Hebrew it is: Who yesterday were in devastation and squalor. אמש properly signifies the night which has now passed.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

EGESTATE ET FAME STERILES QUI SEDE- BANT IN SOLITUDINE] Propius sic: Qui inopia & fa- me erant desolati, ac fugiebant in loca deserta: nempe ut ob- tegerent ibi inopiam suam. Et vox כפש quæ hic famem signi- ficat, & ערק quæ fugere, Syriacæ sunt. SQVALLENTES CALAMITATE ET MISERIA] In Hebræo est: Qui heri erant in vastitate & squallore. אמש proprie noctem quæ jam exacta est significat.

## 30:4
Verse 4.

AND THEY ATE HERBS] מלוח seems to signify salt-marsh herbs and those of unpleasant taste, which no one would eat unless very hungry.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ET MANDEBANT HERBAS] מלוח videtur signifi- care herbas salsuginosas & sapore ingratas, quas nemo nisi valde esuriens comederit.

## 30:8
Verse 8.

SONS OF FOOLS] בני נבל here seems to signify vile rather than foolish on account of what follows. Sons of vile men, that is, vile men. A locution used by Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Arabs. AS IF IN THE LAND UTTERLY NOT OBEYING] נכאו which he translates as not obeying, properly signifies they were crushed, as in Psalm 35:15.

IN the Hebrew it is: sons without a name cast out from the land: that is, infamous, as Cocceius and Scultetus.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

FILII STULTORUM] בני נבל hic potius vilem quam stultum significare videtur ob sequentia. Filii vilium, id est, homines viles. Locutio Hebræis, Chaldæis & Arabibus usitata. VT IN TERRA PENITUS NON PARENTES] נכאו quod hic vertit non parentes, proprie significat contriti erant, ut Psalm. 35, 15.

IN Ebræo est: filii sine nomine ejecti e terra: hoc est, infames, ut Coccejus & Scultetus.

## 30:11
Verse 11.

AND HE PUT A BRIDLE IN MY MOUTH] In the Hebrew: they let loose the bridle in my presence: that is, with unbridled license they inveighed against me.

They cast off, or despised, my authority, by which I ruled them as with a bridle.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET FRÆNUM POSVIT IN OS MEUM] In Hebræo: frænum dimiserunt me præsente: id est, effræni licentia in me invecti sunt.

Auctoritatem meam, qua ut freno eos rege- bam, abjecerunt, vel contemserunt.

## 30:12
Verse 12.

AT THE RIGHT HAND OF THE EAST MY CALAMITIES IMMEDIATELY AROSE] In the Hebrew: At the right hand youths arise, like false witnesses in judgment.

For פרחוח denotes a flower, i.e., of the young. They rise up against me in a hostile manner. MY FEET THEY HAVE SUBVERTED) They have overthrown me as wrestlers are wont to do. AND THEY HAVE OPPRESSED ME AS IF WITH WAVES IN THEIR PATHS) They have built destructive ways against me, namely, as besiegers are wont to do.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

AD DEXTRAM ORIENTIS CALAMITATES MEÆ ILLICO SURREXERVNT) In Hebræo: Ad dextram ado- lescentes insurgunt, ut falsi testes in judicio.

Nam פרחוח florem notat, adolescentium sc. Insurgunt contra me hostiliter. PEDES MEOS SUBVERTERUNT) Everterunt me ut luctatores solent. ET OPPRESSERVNT QUASI FLUCTIBUS SEMI- TIS SUIS) Struxerunt contra me vias exitiosas, nempe ut so- lent obsessores.

## 30:13
Verse 13.

THEY HAVE DISSIPATED MY WAYS) They have obstructed every approach of friends to me. This also is taken from sieges.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DISSIPAVERUNT ITINERA MEA) Omnem amicis ad me aditum obstruxerunt. Hoc quoque de obsidionibus sumtum.

## 30:14
Verse 14. AS IF WITH A BROKEN WALL] This is now drawn from the storming of cities. That which follows, an open gate, is not in the Hebrew. AND UNTO MY MISERIES THEY HAVE DEVOLVED) They have rushed in a dense troop to my destruction. Verse 17. AND THEY WHO EAT ME DO NOT SLEEP) Otherwise in the Hebrew: My arteries do not rest. The pulse is turbulent. ערק is an Arabic word عروق, but it signifies either a vein or an artery. Here it should be taken as arteries. Thus Mercerus, as if he complains that by the force of disease all rest is snatched from him. Others: THEY WHO PERSECUTE ME DO NOT SLEEP, and thus they also snatch everything from me.

Latin:

Vers. 14. QVASI RUPTO MURO] Hoc jam ab urbi- um oppugnationibus trahitur. Illud quod sequitur aperta janua, non est in Hebræo. ET AD MEAS MISERIAS DEVOLUTI SUNT) Ir- ruerunt globato agmine in perniciem meam. Vers. 17. ET QUI ME COMEDUNT NON DOR- MIUNT) Aliter in Hebræo: Arteriæ meæ non conquiescunt. Pulsus est turbidus. ערק est vox Arabica عروق significat autem aut venam aut arteriam. Hic de arteriis su- menda. Ita Mercerus, quasi morbi vi omnem sibi quietem eripi queratur. Alii: QUI ME PERSE- QUUNTUR NON DORMIUNT, & sic mihi quoque omnia eripiunt.

## 30:18
Verse 18.

IN THE MULTITUDE OF THEM MY GARMENT IS CONSUMED. Coccejus thus: WITH GREAT FORCE MY GARMENT IS STRIPPED OFF, glued to the body because of the pus, AS THE COLLAR OF MY SHIRT GIRDETH ME. Which version also pleased our blessed Lord Dr. Scultetus, so that he preferred it to his own. Coccejus explains the latter part thus: It seems to tighten and press me and as it were θλίβειν [to crush] even with a winding robe.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

IN MULTITUDINE EORUM CONSU- MITUR VESTIMENTUM MEUM. Coccejus ita: CUM MAXIMA VI EXUI- TUR VESTIS MEA agglutinata præ sanie cor- pori, UT OS INDUSII MEI CINGIT ME. Quæ versio placuit etiam B. Dn. D. Sculteto nostro, ut eam suæ prætulerit. Posteriora sic exponit Coccejus: Videtur me stringere & premere ac quasi θλίβειν etiam sinuosa toga.

## 30:24
Verse 24.

HOWEVER, THOU WILT NOT SEND THY HAND UNTO THEIR CONSUMPTION: AND IF THEY SHALL HAVE FALLEN, HE HIMSELF SHALL SAVE. In the Hebrew it is held thus: HOWEVER, UNTO THE TUMULUS HE SHALL NOT SEND HIS HAND: IF (or WHETHER) IN HIS DESTRUCTION THERE IS A CRY FOR THEM. Mercerus explains it thus: Even if men cry out here in the destruction of God, yet not in death: Others, such as Piscator and Diodati, in almost the same sense as the blessed Luther: Although I must die, yet death will be the end of evils: for the hand of God will not press me in the tumulus. Do the dead also cry out there because of the affliction sent by God? To which sense Pineda tries to recall the Vulgate; but in vain: because it rendered it 'consumption,' not 'tumulus': And 'salvation,' not 'cry': How then can this sentiment be chiseled out of it: He will not extend his hand to the tumulus, where he allows us to rest, no longer grieving or crying out when we have fallen. However, Pineda rightly rejects as foreign the interpretation of the Latins—Philippus Presbyter, Thomas, Dionysius, Titelmannus—that men are not to be reduced to perpetual consumption, but are eventually to be recalled from the underworld. Lord Dr. Schmiedius provides another sense, which coheres with what follows: However, let (God) send his hand (upon me) without prayer, if in his destruction there was a cry for them (against me). For he derives בע with R. Levi and Perizolides from בעה [to ask], and notes the opposition between בע [petition] and שוע [cry]; if I caused the afflicted to seek vengeance from me, GOD will not give place to my prayer. Which explanation you might perhaps not undeservedly prefer to others.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

VERUNTAMEN NON AD CONSUM- TIONEM EORUM EMITTIS MANUM TU- AM: ET SI CORRUERINT IPSE SALVABIS. In Ebræo ita habetur: VERUNTAMEN NON AD TUMULUM EMITTET MANUM: AN (vel SI) IN CONTRITIONE EJUS ILLIS CLAMOR. Mercerus id ita explicat: Etiamsi hic in contri- tione Dei homines clament, non tamen in morte: Alii utpote Piscator, & Deodatus sensu pene eodem cum B. Luthero: Quamvis moriendum mihi sit, tamen finis erit malorum mors: non enim manus Dei me in tumulo premet. An etiam ibi mortui clament præ afflictione a Deo immissa? Ad quem sensum revo- care conatur etiam Pineda vulgatam; sed frustra: quia illa consumtionem reddidit, non tumulum: Et salvationem, non clamorem: Qui ergo exsculpetur ex illa hæc sententia: Non extendet manum ad tumu- lum, ubi quiescere nos sinit, non amplius dolentes vel clamantes cum corruerimus. Latinorum autem in- terpretationem Philippi Presbyteri, Thomæ, Diony- sii, Titelmanni, homines non in perpetuam consumtio- nem redigendos, sed aliquando ab inferis revocandos, merito ceu alienam rejicit Pineda. Sensum alium reddit Dn. D. Schmiedius, qui cum consequentibus cohæreat: Veruntamen sine deprecatione mittat (Deus) manum (in me) si in exitio ejus illis clamor (contra me fuit) Nam בע deducit cum R. Levi, & Perizolide a בעה petiit, & oppositionem no- tat inter בע petitionem & שוע clamorem, si ego fe- ci ut afflicti peterent de me vindictam, DEUS non det locum meæ deprecationi. Quam explicatio- nem forte non immerito aliis præferas.

## 30:25
Verse 25.

I WEPT FORMERLY FOR HIM WHO WAS AFFLICTED. In the Hebrew: FOR THE HARD DAY; this Luther and others take concerning hard times, or public calamities: most take it concerning him who is in a hard day, or for whom the day is hard.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

FLEBAM QUONDAM SUPER EO QUI AFFLICTUS ERAT. In Ebræo: SUPER DURO DIE, id Lutherus & alii de duris temporibus, vel publicis calamitati- bus: plerique de eo accipiunt, qui est duro die, vel cui durus dies.

## 30:26
Verse 26.

EXPECTABAM. In Hebrew, BECAUSE I WAS EXPECTING. It refers back to verse 23, I know that thou wilt deliver me to death. -- Because I was expecting good things, and evil things came to me; or it can also be referred to verse 28, because evil things have come, I go mourning, &c.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

EXPECTABAM. In Ebr. QUIA EXPECTABAM. Respicit vers. 23. Scio quia morti trades me. -- Quia ex- spectabam bona, & venerunt mihi mala; vel referri etiam potest ad vers. 28. quia venerunt mala, niger incedo, &c.

## 30:28
Verse 28.

I went mourning without the sun. In the Hebrew it is: I go BLACK or darkened WITHOUT THE SUN. My skin is not blackened by external heat, but by the internal burning of my vitals.

Latin:

Verf. 28.

MOERENS INCEDEBAM SINE PUDORE. In Hebræo est: NIGER vel atratus INCEDO SINE SOLE. Non est denigrata cutis mea æstu externo, sed interno viscerum incendio.

## 30:29
Verse 29.

I HAVE BEEN A BROTHER TO DRAGONS) Dragons emit a hissing sound when they are crushed by elephants. Therefore, both here and in Micah 1:8, dragons are joined together with owls because of their mournful sound.

Latin:

Verf. 29.

FRATER FVI DRACONVM) Sibilum edunt Dracones ubi ab elephantis opprimuntur. Ideo & hic & Micheæ 1, 8. pariter junguntur Dracones cum ululis ob sonum lugubrem.

## 31:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXI.

Job, in order to purge himself of the slanders of his friends, removes from himself the graver crimes of unchastity, fraud, adultery, injustice, unmercifulness, idolatry, avarice, ἐπιχαιρεκακίας (rejoicing in evil), hypocrisy, and iniquity.

Verse 1.

I MADE A COVENANT WITH MY EYES) For as the poet says: The eyes are the leaders in love. In Pirke Aboth we read: The look of the eye is the beginning of crime. See Matthew 5:28, 29. THAT I SHOULD NOT EVEN THINK ABOUT A VIRGIN) Much less about a married woman. AND MY HEART FOLLOWED MY EYES) For the eye and the heart are the procurers of sin, as it is in the old Hebrew proverb.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXI.

Job ut de amicorum calumniis purget se, gravio- ra a se amolitur crimina impudicitiæ, fraudis, adulterii, injustitiæ, immisericordiæ, idolola- triæ, avaritiæ, ἐπιχαιρεκακίας, hypocrisœos, iniquitatis.

Verf. 1.

FEDVS PEPIGI CVM OCULIS MEIS) Nam ut Poeta: Oculi sunt in amore duces. In Pirke Aboth legimus: Aspe- ctus oculi, initium criminis. Vide Matth. 5. v. 28. 29. VT NE COGITAREM QVIDEM DE VIRGINE) Multo minus de nupta. ET SECVTVM EST OCVLOS COR MEVM) Nam oculus & cor sunt proxenetæ peccati, ut est in Hebræo vetere proverbio.

## 31:7
Verse 7.

AND IF ANY STAIN HAS CLUNG TO MY HANDS) In the Hebrew: And if anything has clung to my hands: If I have allowed myself to be corrupted by gifts.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

ET SI MANIBVS MEIS ADHÆSIT MACVLA) In Hebræo: Et si manibus meis quidquam adhæsit: Si donis cor- rumpi me sum passus.

## 31:10
Verse 10.

LET MY WIFE GRIND FOR ANOTHER) It seems to mean 'grind', which in Hebrew is to have taken in an obscene sense, in the way that Greeks and Latins use that word regarding men, but not regarding women. But that expression is not the custom of the Hebrew, and you would interpret it much more correctly as 'let my wife grind for another': that is, let her be a servant of the most menial labor. See Exodus 11:5, Isaiah 47:2. As for what follows, it states a shameful act in an honorable way. The Chaldean, Vatablus, and Cocceius also explain it thus: Compare Judges 16:13, Matthew 24:41. But there is no reason why the Vulgate should be abandoned here, which the LXX favor. 'Let my wife also be pleasing to another': Nicetas, who says this was said out of a desire for equality, so that he might receive the equivalent of what he had done. The Tigurina version: 'let another grind my wife': as also B. Luther, Dr. Schmid, Cajetan, Pineda, and others. The following clause also demands that sense: AND LET OTHERS BOW DOWN UPON HER. For Scripture is accustomed to signify an honorable action with many honorable words. See Pineda here on the σεμνότητι of holy speech. But is it permitted to compensate adultery with adultery, and to wish for that? By no means: nor does Job approve of this, but he indicates that he does not pray against this most grave punishment and ignominy being justly inflicted upon himself, if he had been such. Just as the adultery of David was punished in his own concubines with his ignominy and grief.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

SCORTVM ALTERIVS SIT VXOR MEA) Videtur molat, quod in Hebræo est sumfisse in sensu obscœno, quomo- do de viris, non autem de fœminis eam vocem usurpant Græci & Latini. Sed ea locutio non est moris Hebræi, multoque rectius interpreteris, molat alteri uxor mea: id est, ancilla sit vilissimi ministerii. Vide Exod. 11. v. 5. Esaiæ 47. v. 2. Quod autem sequitur, rem turpem honeste enunciat. Sic exponit etiam Chaldæus, Vatablus & Coccejus: Conf. Judic. 16, 13. Matth. 24, 41. At non est cur hic deseratur Vulgata, cui favent LXX. Pla- ceat quoque uxor mea alteri: Nicetas, qui hoc dictum ait æqualitatis studio, ut iis, quæ gesserat, paria accipe- ret. Tigurina, permolet uxorem meam alius: ut & B. Lutherus, Dn. D. Schmidius, Cajetanus, Pineda & alii. Sequens etiam colon eum sensum postulat: ET SUPER ILLAM INCURVENT SE ALII. Solet enim actionem honestam Scriptura multis honestis verbis significare. Vid. Pineda hic de σεμνότητι Sermonis sancti. Sed licetne adulterium adulterio compensare, illudque optare? minime: nec probat hoc Jobus, sed in detestationem & conscien- tiæ purgationem hanc gravissimam pœnam & igno- miniam juste sibi infligendam, si talis fuisset, se non deprecari indicat. Quemadmodum adulterium Davidis in ipsius pellicibus cum ejus ignominia & dolore punitum est.

## 31:11
Ver. 11.

GREATEST INIQUITY) In the Hebrew: iniquity of the judges: that is, which is accustomed to be brought before public judges. For it is their duty in well-ordered nations to punish not only adulteries, but also rapes.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

INIQVITAS MAXIMA) In Hebræo: iniquitas iudi- cum: id est, quæ ad judices publicos perduci solet. Eorum enim est in bene moratis populis, non adulteria tantum, sed & stupra punire.

## 31:18
Ver. 18.

FOR FROM MY INFANCY COMPASSION GREW WITH ME) He took that כאב well, not as two words, but as one, which signifies grief from another's evil, which they more frequently call חסד. But I would prefer to translate גדלני as 'he educated me' rather than 'he grew with me'. AND FROM MY MOTHER'S WOMB IT CAME FORTH WITH ME) Better, 'from my mother's womb I led it', that is, I had it as a companion. 'From my mother's womb' is a hyperbole for 'from the first age that is capable of good or evil'. There are, however, even in earliest infancy certain seeds of goodness, such as Plutarch observed in his little daughter. In the Hebrew, the noun COMPASSION is not held. Which Grotius tries in vain to elicit from the word כאב: for כאב 'grief' is not held: but כאב 'AS A FATHER'. The sense is, FOR FROM MY INFANCY (the orphan from v. 17) GREW WITH ME AS WITH A FATHER (or 'he grew up with me, as a Father'; there is an ellipsis of the preposition עַד as in Psalm 5:5) AND FROM MY MOTHER'S WOMB I LED IT (the widow from v. 16) as a son.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

QVIA AB INFANTIA MEA CREVIT MECVM MISERATIO) Illud כאב bene sumsit, non ut voces du- as, sed ut unam, quæ dolorem significat ex malo alieno, quod frequentius חסד dicunt. Sed גדלני malim vertere educa- vit me, quam crevit mecum. ET DE VTERO MATRIS MEÆ EGRESSA EST MECVM) Melius, ab utero matris meæ deduxi eam, id est, comitem habui. Ab utero matris ὑπερβολὴ pro à prima æta- te quæ boni aut mali capax est. Sunt tamen & in prima in- fantia bonitatis quædam semina, qualem in sua filiola obser- vavit Plutarchus. In Ebræo non habetur nomen MISERATIO- NIS. Quod nequicquam Grotius e voce כאב elicere vult: nam non habetur כאב dolor: sed כאב SICUT PATER. Sensus est, QUIA AB INFANTIA MEA CREVIT MECUM (pu pillus e v. 17.) UT CUM PATRE (vel adolevit apud me, tanquam Patrem; est Ellipsis præposit. עַד ut Psal. 5, 5. ) ET AB UTERO MATRIS MEÆ DUXI EAM (viduam e v. 16. ) tanquam filius.

## 31:21
Ver. 21.

IF I HAVE LIFTED MY HAND AGAINST THE ORPHAN] If I have inflicted blows upon him. See Isaiah 10:32, Zechariah 2:9.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

SI LEVAVI SUPER PVPILLVM MANVM MEAM] Si verbera ei intuli. Vide Esaia 10, 32. Zach. 2, 9.

## 31:26
Ver. 26.

IF I HAVE SEEN THE SUN WHEN IT SHINED] He rightly translated אוֹר as sun. For among the Egyptians the sun was called רֵע: as Macrobius teaches us in Saturnalia, Book 1, chapter 21.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

SI VIDI SOLEM CUM FVLGERET] Bene אוֹר ver- tit solem. Nam Ægyptiis sol רֵע vocabatur: ut nos docet Macrobius Saturnal. 1. cap. 21.

## 31:27
Ver. 27.

AND MY HEART HAS REJOICED IN SECRET] In the Hebrew: And my heart has seduced itself in secret: that is, this opinion crept upon me, that I should believe the sun or the moon to be the highest gods and the arbiters of all things, contrary to what Abraham had taught his descendants, and among them Esau: the Chaldean follows the same sense here. AND I HAVE KISSED MY HAND WITH MY MOUTH) Namely, with the intention that was mentioned. To kiss someone's hand is a sign of reverence. Since it was not permitted to kiss another's hand, they would kiss their own instead of another's with the same meaning. This is to throw kisses, to adore.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

ET LÆTATVM EST IN ABSCONDITO COR MEVM] In Hebræo: Et seduxit se in abscondito cor meum: id est subrepsit mihi hæc opinio, ut solem aut lunam summos deos rerumque omnium arbitros crederem, contra quam Abrahamus posteros suos & in his Esavum docuerat: eundem sensum hic sequitur Chaldæus. ET QSCVLATVS SVM MANVM MEAM ORE MEO) Nempe eo quo dictum est animo. Manum alicu- jus osculari signum reverentiæ. Cum manum alterius oscu- lari non liceret, suam pro aliena eodem significatu osculaban- tur. Hoc est basia jacere, adorare.

## 31:28
Ver. 28.

DENIAL AGAINST THE MOST HIGH) Because that which is not God is held in the place of God, nay rather that which was given by God for the use of men especially, and is endowed with motion, not with understanding.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

NEGATIO CONTRA ALTISSIMVM) Quia Dei loco habetur id quod Deus non est, imo quod à Deo datum in usum præcipue hominum, & motu præditum est, non intel- lectu.

## 31:29
Verse 29.

THAT EVIL HAD FOUND HIM) For as the mime says: Whom chance often passes by, it sometimes finds. This is great goodness, not to rejoice in the evil of an enemy. Prov. 24, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

QVOD INVENISSET EVM MALVM) Nam ut Mimus ait: Quem sæpe transit casus, aliquando invenit. Magna hæc est bonitas, non lætari inimici malo. Prov. 24, 17.

## 31:31
Verse 31.

IF THE MEN OF MY TABERNACLE HAVE NOT SAID, WHO WILL GIVE OF HIS FLESH THAT WE MAY BE FILLED. In the Hebrew they have the latter part, we shall not be filled. Most understand this of the flesh of Job. Gregory, Philip, Hugo, Vatablus, Clarius, Cajetan, Benedictus, Eugubinus, Pererius on Gen. ch. 24, Saa and others: but this cruelty is not to be presumed of the family of Job. It is more correctly explained by others, including Pineda, Scultetus, Cocceius, etc., as referring to the flesh of the enemy, of whom he spoke before; that when his own household wished to tear the enemy to pieces, and could not be satisfied because of their anger against them, he himself appeased them. Cf. 2 Sam. 16, 10. 11. Luke 9, 54. 55.

Latin:

Versus 31.

SI NON DIXERUNT VIRI TABERNA- CULI MEI, QUIS DABIT DE CARNIBUS E- JUS UT SATUREMUR. In Ebræo posteriora habent, non satiabimur. De carne Jobi plerique intelligunt. Gregor. Philipp. Hugo, Vatablus, Clarius, Cajetan. Benedictus, Eugu- binus, Pererius in Gen. c. 24. Saa & alii: sed hæc tru- culentia de familia Jobi non præsumenda. Rectius de carnibus hostis, de quo antea, explicatur ab aliis, etiam Pineda, Sculteto, Coccejo &c. quod quum fami- liares ejus hostes ipsius discerpere vellent, nec sa- tiari possent ob iram adversus eosdem, ipse eos pla- carit. Conf. 2. Sam. 16, 10. 11. Luc. 9, 54. 55.

## 31:35
Verse 35.

MAY THE ALMIGHTY HEAR MY DESIRE.

In the Hebrew the latter part is as follows: BEHOLD MY DESCRIPTION! MAY THE ALMIGHTY ANSWER ME. The sense is: would that I had a just judge. Behold, I have now written down my articles of defense; would that the Almighty himself might answer me concerning these, and judge me!

Verse 35.

AND MAY HE HIMSELF WHO JUDGES WRITE A BOOK) Better in the Hebrew: Let the man of my lawsuit write a book: that is, let my adversary hand over a written accusation. THAT I MAY CARRY THAT BOOK UPON MY SHOULDER) I will not hide that book, but I will show it to everyone.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

DESIDERIUM MEUM AUDIAT OMNI- POTENS.

In Ebræo posteriora ita habent: ECCE DE- SCRIPTIO MEA! OMNIPOTENS RESPON- DEAT MIHI. Sensus est: utinam justum judi- cem haberem. Ecce jam articulos defensionales conscripsi, utinam omnipotens ipse de his mihi re- spondeat, & me judicet!

Vers. 35.

ET LIBRVM SCRIBAT IPSE QVI JVDICAT) Me- lius in Hebræo: Librum scribat, vir litis mea: id est, scriptam accusationem tradat adversarius meus. VT IN HVMERO MEO PORTEM LIBRVM IL- LVM) Non abscondam illum librum, sed omnibus eum ostentabo.

## 31:40
Verse 40.

INSTEAD OF BARLEY A THORN) בׇּאְשָׁה is a plant harmful to crops, such as goatgrass is to barley, which is also called festuca by Pliny.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

PRO HORDEO SPINA) בׇּאְשָׁה est herba frugibus nocens, qualis hordeo ægilops, quæ & festuca Plinio.

## 32:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXII. Elihu accuses Job and his companions of folly, and having excused his silence, promises more solid things.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXII. Elihu Jobum & Socios insipientiæ arguit, & ex- cusato silentio suo solidiora promittit.

## 32:2
Ver. 2.

OF THE KINDRED OF RAM) That is, a Syrian by origin. For Buz was the son of Nahor the Syrian: Ram and Aram are interchanged with one another. We have spoken of him at Luke 3:33.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DE COGNATIONE RAM) Id est, Syrus origine. Nam Buzus Nachoris Syri filius: Ram & Aram inter se commutan- tur. Diximus de eo ad Lucam 3, 33.

## 32:3
Ver. 3.

BUT ONLY THEY HAD CONDEMNED JOB) Thus the experts in the law amended it, and placed אֶת אִיּוֹב where formerly it was read יהוה. We have spoken of the Tikkun Sopherim at chapter 7:20. And they condemned both God and Job. Compare Cocceius here.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SED TANTVMMODO CONDEMNASSENT JOB) Sic emendarunt legis periti, posueruntque אֶת אִיּוֹב cum olim legeretur יהוה. DE Tikkun Sopherim ad cap. 7, 20. diximus. Et Deum & Jobum condemnarunt. Confer, hic Coccejus.

## 32:6
Verf. 6. THEREFORE WITH BOWED HEAD I HAVE FEARED] In the text, I was terrified and afraid. In Chaldean דחל is to fear. Moreover, the letters ז and ד are related, and are easily interchanged with one another. The Arabic זحل, which signifies to retreat, does not go far from this.

Latin:

Verf. 6. IDCIRCO DEMISSO CAPITE VERITUS SUM] In textu, expavi & timui. In Chaldæo דחל est timere. Literæ autem ז & ד sunt affines, facileque inter se commutantur. Non longe abit Arabicum زحل, quod retrocedere significat.

## 32:8
verf. 8. THERE IS A SPIRIT IN MEN, AND THE INSPIRATION OF THE ALMIGHTY GIVES UNDERSTANDING. This is said of the Holy Spirit, who is the breath of the Almighty and the author of understanding, ch. 33, 4. Isa. 11, 2.

Latin:

verf. 8. SPIRITUS EST IN HOMINIBUS, ET IN- SPIRATIO OMNIPOTENTIS DAT INTEL- LIGENTIAM. De Spiritu S. hoc dictum, qui est spiraculum omnipotentis & autor intelligentiæ, c. 33, 4. Efa. 11, 2.

## 32:21
Verf. 21. I WILL NOT EQUATE GOD TO MAN] In the Hebrew: I will not give a surname to man. Thus also in the following verse. The sense is: I will not attribute magnificent epithets to him. I will not say, most excellent man, most wise man, admirable man. אל here is a preposition.

Latin:

Verf. 21. DEUM HOMINI NON ÆQVABO] In Hebræo: Ho- minem non agnominabo. Sic & commate sequente. Sensus est: non tribuam illi magnifica ἐπίθετα. Non dicam, vir optime, vir sapientissime, vir admirande. אל hîc præpositio est.

## 33:1 Argument
