## 34:33
Ver. 33.

SHALL GOD REQUIRE IT OF YOU, BECAUSE IT DISPLEASED YOU? FOR YOU BEGAN TO SPEAK, AND NOT I) This exposition seems to be the easiest: Or indeed from you? supply, has such a speech proceeded, as I have spoken: He will repay you, because you have rejected him. You made this choice, not I.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

NUMQVID A TE DEUS EXPETIT EAM, QVIA DISPLICVIT TIBI? TV ENIM COEPISTI LOQVI, ET NON EGO) Videtur facillima fore hæc expositio: An vero abs te? supple profecta est talis oratio, qualem dixi: Vicem tibi reddet, quod eum abjecisti. Tu hanc fecisti optio- nem, non ego.

## 34:36
MY FATHER) I would rather that אָבִי signifies I would or would that.

Nowhere does the word אָבִי denote would that or I would, but as it is rendered by almost everyone, My Father. The Chaldean alone seized upon the word אֶבָה will for it, and rendered it אֶבוֹוֹן I will.

Latin:

PATER MI) Potius illud אָבִי significat velim vel utinam.

Nuspiam vox אָבִי notat utinam vel velim, sed uti fere ab omnibus redditur, Pater mi. Solus Chaldæus pro ea arripuit vocem אֶבָה voluntas, & reddidit אֶבוֹוֹן volo ego.

## 35:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXV.

Elihu discourses concerning the justice of God, towards the powerful and the afflicted, asserting that piety profits and impiety harms not God but man.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXV.

Elihu disserit de Dei justitia, erga potentes & afflictos, non Deo sed homini & pietatem prodesse & impietatem obesse afferens.

## 35:3
Ver. 3.

FOR YOU HAVE SAID: IT DOES NOT PLEASE YOU WHAT IS RIGHT, OR WHAT WILL IT PROFIT YOU, IF I HAVE SINNED) Better thus: As if you were to say, what will it either profit you, or what utility shall I receive by expiating sin? חַטָּאת is often metonymically, the expiation of sin.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

DIXISTI ENIM: NON TIBI PLACET QVOD RECTVM EST, VEL QVOD TIBI PRODERIT, SI EGO PECCAVERO) Melius sic: Quasi dicas, quid aut tibi proderit, aut quid ego utilitatis accipiam expiando pecca- tum? חַטָּאת sæpe est μετωνυμικῶς, peccati expiatio.

## 35:9
Ver. 9.

BECAUSE OF THE VIOLENCE OF THE ARM OF TYRANTS רַבִּים, that is, of the powerful.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

PROPTER VIM BRACHII TYRANNORUM רַבִּים, id est, potentum.

## 35:10
Ver. 10.

WHO GAVE SONGS IN THE NIGHT) He who in the midst of calamities suddenly gave matter for rejoicing.

To be observed in the Hebrew text is the mystical construction: where there is אֱלוֹהַ עֹשָׂי God, who made you, giving songs in the night. For the plural verb constructed with a singular noun hints at a mystery: that in the singular divine essence a plurality of persons is given. Concerning which see Gen. 1, 1. and to Is. 44, 2. chap. 54, 5. Ps. 149, 2. which are similar passages, and refer the same plural verb to God. Therefore the singular noun is to be understood under distribution, so that each one who is אֶלוֹהַ our maker may be designated; just as in Genesis 1, 26, mention is openly made of several who created us. Of that creator of ours אֶלוֹהַ it is said here, that he instructs us, that it is his to hear us, that he is omnipotent: which things are common to the Son of God with the Father, inasmuch as he instructs us as hypostatic Wisdom, Proverbs 8, 22, Luke 11, 49. he hears our prayers, and by that name is to be invoked, and is truly omnipotent, Rev. 1, 8. as also the Holy Spirit, who is said to instruct and teach us, Neh. 9, 20. 1 Cor. 2, 13. 1 John 2, 27. is to be invoked by us, Matt. 28, 19. Rev. 1, 4. and possesses divine power, Eph. 1, 19. 2 Tim. 1, 7. etc.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

QVI DEDIT CARMINA IN NOCTE) Qui in me- diis calamitatibus subito dedit lætandi materiam.

OBservanda in textu Ebræo constructio mysti- ca: ubi est אֱלוֹהַ עֹשָׂי Deus, qui fecerunt te, dans cantica in nocte. Verbum enim plurale singu- lari nomini constructum mysterium innuit: quod in singulari divina essentia pluralitas detur persona- rum. De quo ad Gen. 1, 1. & ad Es. 44, 2. cap. 54, 5. Psal. 149, 2. quæ loca similia sunt, idemque verbum plurale ad Deo efferunt. Sub distributione ergo intelligendum nomen singulare, ut unusquisque qui est אֶלוֹהַ factor noster esse designetur; quemadmo- dum Genes. 1, 26. aperte plurium, qui nos crearunt, mentio facta est. De illo creatore nostro אֶלוֹהַ di- citur hic, quod erudiat nos, quod ejus sit exaudire nos, quod omnipotens sit: quæ cum Patre commu- nia sunt Filio Dei, utpote qui erudit nos ceu Sapien- tia hypostatica Proverb. 8, 22, Luc. 11, 49. exaudit preces nostras, eoque nomine invocandus est, & ve- re omnipotens est, Apoc. 1, 8. ut & Spiritui Sancto, qui nos erudire, ac docere, Nehem. 9, 20. 1. Cor. 2, 13. 1. Job. 2, 27. dicitur, a nobis invocandus est, Matth. 28, 19. Apoc. 1, 4. & divina potentia pollet, Ef. 11, 1. 2, Tim. 1, 7. &c.

## 35:11
Verse 11.

WHO TEACHES US) Thus also Origen: διδάσκων ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ τὰ κτήνη τῆς γῆς. Doubtless so that the letter N after D is omitted by a shorthand of writing. God gave us a mind capable of all sciences and arts, and by that he has preferred us greatly to other living creatures.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

QVI DOCET NOS) Sic & Origenes: διδάσκων ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ τὰ κτήνη τῆς γῆς. Nimirum ut omissa sit per compen- dium scribendi litera N post D. Dedit nobis Deus ani- mum scientiarum artiumque omnium capacem, eoque nos animantibus cæteris plurimum prætulit.

## 35:12
THERE THEY WILL CRY OUT) Placed in calamities.

Latin:

IBI CLAMABVNT) In calamitatibus positi.

## 35:13
Verse 13.

GOD WILL NOT THEREFORE HEAR IN VAIN) In the Hebrew: A man of lies (that is, a man of falsehood) God does not hear. The sense is the same as that which is in John in the Gospel ch. 9, 31.

Others more correctly: CERTAINLY VANITY, (vain prayers, such as are poured out without repentance) GOD WILL NOT HEAR. In the Hebrew that word MAN is not there.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

NON ERGO FRVSTRA AVDIET DEVS) In He- bræo: Virum mendaciorum (id est virum mendacii) non au- dit Deus. Sensus eodem qui est apud Johannem in Evange- lio c. 9, 31.

Rectius alii: CERTE VANITATEM, (preces vanas, quales sunt sine pœnitentia effusæ) NON AUDIET DEUS. In Ebræo non est vox illa VIRUM.

## 35:14
Verse 14.

EVEN WHEN YOU SHALL SAY: HE DOES NOT CONSIDER) Above 23.

EVEN WHEN YOU SHALL SAY, THAT YOU DO NOT SEE HIM.

You have complained that you cannot find him, so that he may judge your case, chap. 23, 8. 9. THERE IS JUDGMENT BEFORE HIM, WAIT FOR HIM. Know that he will judge in his own time. It is your part to wait for him patiently.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ETIAM CVM DIXERIS: NON CONSIDERAT) Supra 23.

ETIAM CUM DIXERIS, QUOD NON VIDEAS EUM.

Conquestus es, quod non possis eum invenire, ut tuam causam judicet, cap. 23, 8. 9. EST JUDI- CIUM CORAM IPSO, EXPECTA EUM. Scias suo tempore illum judicaturum. Tuum est patienter illum expectare.

## 35:16
Ver. 16.

AND WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE HE MULTIPLIES WORDS) He heaps them up. For that is what כבד often signifies.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ET ABSQVE SCIENTIA VERBA MVLTIPLICAT) Coacervat. Id enim sæpe significat כבר.

## 36:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVI.

Elihu defends the equity of divine judgment, exhorts to repentance, and teaches the divine greatness from the tempests.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVI.

Elihu æquitatem divini judicii tuetur, hortatur ad pœnitentiam & divinam magnitudinem e tempestatibus docet.

## 36:2
Ver. 2.

WAIT FOR ME A LITTLE, AND I WILL SHOW THEE) Both the word כתר and the word חוה, which appear here, are Chaldean.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SVSTINE ME PAVLVM, ET INDICABO TIBI) Tam vox כתר quam vox חוה, quæ hic exstant, Chal- daicæ sunt.

## 36:7
Ver. 7.

HE WILL NOT TAKE HIS EYES FROM THE JUST, AND HE PLACES KINGS ON THE THRONE) Better, with kings. For the following verses hint that it is about Joseph, even though they were in chains. The Greeks here: μετὰ βασιλέων εἰς θρόνον. A change of number is frequent, where from one example similar ones are to be understood.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

NON AVFERET A JVSTO OCVLOS SVOS, ET RE- GES IN SOLIO COLLOCAT) Melius, cum regibus. Nam de Josepho agi innuunt & sequentia, etsi fuerint in catenis. Græci hic: μετὰ βασιλέων εἰς θρόνον. Numeri mutatio fre- quens, ubi ex uno exemplo intelligenda & similia.

## 36:10
Ver. 10.

HE WILL ALSO OPEN THEIR EAR, TO CORRECT) The Latins would say for the same, he would open the ear.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

REVELABIT QVOQVE AVREM EORVM, VT CORRIPIAT) Latini pro eodem dicerent, vellet aurem.

## 36:11
Ver. 11.

IF THEY HEAR AND OBSERVE, THEY SHALL COMPLETE THEIR DAYS IN GOOD) Thus also the Greeks: συντελέσουσι τὰς ἡμέρας αὐτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοῖς. They read, as we do, יכלו not badly, although other codices had יבלו, that is, their days shall grow old.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

SI AVDIERINT ET OBSERVAVERINT, COMPLE- BVNT DIES SVOS IN BONO) Sic & Græci: συντελέ- σουσι τὰς ἡμέρας αὐτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοῖς. Legerunt, ut nos, יכלו non male, quanquam alii codices habuere יבלו, id est, betusti- fient dies eorum.

## 36:13
HYPOCRITES AND THE CUNNING PROVOKE THE WRATH OF GOD) In the Hebrew: The false of heart shall lay up wrath: where to lay up is the very thing which the Apostle called θησαυρίζειν in Rom. 2, 5.

NOR SHALL THEY CRY OUT WHEN THEY HAVE BEEN BOUND) Time will not be given to them to perform penance: so suddenly shall they be oppressed.

Latin:

SIMVLATORES ET CALLIDI PROVOCANT IRAM DEI) In Hebræo: Falsi corde ponent iram: ubi ponere est id ipsum, quod θησαυρίζειν dixit Apostolus Rom. 2, 5.

NEQVE CLAMABVNT CVM VINCTI FVERINT) Non dabitur illis tempus ad agendam pœnitentiam: ita subi- to opprimentur.

## 36:14
THEIR LIFE AMONG THE EFFEMINATE) Thus their life shall be cut off, just as the life of the Sodomites was cut off.

Latin:

VITA EORVM INTER EFFEMINATOS) Sic inter- cipietur eorum vita, quomodo Sodomitis intercepta fuit.

## 36:16
Verse 16.

THEREFORE HE WILL SAVE THEE FROM THE NARROW MOUTH MOST BROADLY, AND NOT HAVING A FOUNDATION UNDER IT, BUT THE REST OF THY TABLE SHALL BE FULL OF FATNESS] More conveniently thus: God would have removed thee far from the mouth of distress, near to breadth, under which there is no distress, and what is placed upon thy table would have been full of fatness. Namely, if thou hadst acted as I have already said. He shows, however, in the following, that he thinks otherwise concerning Job.

We add the explanation of the blessed Scultetus: AND ALSO HE WILL TURN THEE (thus the word הסית is understood in 2 Chron. 18:31, where it is also constructed with מ, which is not the case when it signifies to seduce to evil one who is ignorant) FROM THE MOUTH OF DISTRESS TO A BROAD PLACE (Rabbi Solomon and Jerome explain it as the mouth of a pit that is wide below and narrow above) which has NO FIRM (thus the word מוצק is understood in ch. 11 v. 15, ch. 38 v. 38, ch. 41 v. 15, 16) UNDER IT. If thou also usest thy calamity for a salutary end, and hast implored God, GOD will snatch thee from thy calamity, which is as it were a deep cage, which has no firm and solid foundation, but is marshy, which has a mouth wide for devouring, but narrow for emitting. The metaphor could also be taken from a rapacious animal, which catches prey with a gaping mouth, and holds it caught when it is tight and closed: unless perhaps the interpretation of Mr. Dr. Schmied is to be held as simpler: And he will remove thee from the mouth of distress: a breadth not narrowed (that is, most broad) shall be to thee in place of that (distress). AND THE REST OF THY TABLE SHALL BE FULL OF FATNESS. Thou shalt sit quietly at thy table, and shalt eat most delicate foods.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

IGITVR SALVABIT TE DE ORE ANGUSTO LA- TISSIME, ET NON HABENTE FVNDAMENTVM SVPTER SE, REQVIES AVTEM MENSÆ TVÆ ERIT PLENA PINGVEDINE] Commodius sic: Longe te amovis- set Deus ab ore angustiæ, prope latitudinem, sub qua nulla an- gustia, & quod imponitur mensæ tuæ plenum fuisset pinguedine. Nempe si ita egisses, ut jam dixi. Ostendit autem sequentibus, se aliter de Jobo opinari.

Addimus B. Sculteti explicationem: ATQUE ETIAM AVERTET TE (sic verbum הסית accipitur 2. Chron. 18, 31. ubi etiam cum מ construi- tur, quod non sit, quando seducere ad malum igno- rantem significat) AB ORE ANGUSTIÆ LA- TO (R. Salomo, & Hieronym. de ore foveæ infra latæ angusto explicant) quod NON FIRMUM (sic accipitur vox מוצק c. 11. v. 15. c. 38, 38. c. 41, 15. 16.) SUB SE habet. Si etiam ad salutarem finem ute- ris tua calamitate, Deumque imploraveris, eripiet te DEUS ex calamitate tua, quæ est quasi cavea profunda, quæ non habet firmum, & solidum fun- damentum, sed paludosum, quæ habet os latum ad devorandum, sed angustum ad emittendum. Posset etiam Metaphora ab animali rapace, quod ore hi- ante prædam captat, captamque stricto & clauso te- net, desumi: nisi forte simplicior habenda Dn. D. Schmiedii interpretatio: Et removebit te ex ore an- gustiæ: latitudo non arctata (id est, latissima) erit tibi loco (angustiæ) illius. ET REQUIES MEN- SÆ TUÆ ERIT PLENA PINGUEDINE. Quiete ad mensam tuam sedebis, & comedes escas delicatissimas.

## 36:17
Verse 17.

THY CAUSE AS THAT OF THE WICKED HAS BEEN JUDGED, THOU SHALT RECEIVE CAUSE AND JUDGMENT] Better: although thou indeed hast fulfilled the judgment for the wicked, that is, thou hast given such as he desired: nevertheless the cause and the judgment shall hold together, namely before God.

The blessed Luther understood the cause of the wicked confirmed in this way: Thou dost conduct thy cause as if thou wouldst wickedly confirm justice. Others, thou hast conducted thy cause in the manner of the wicked, by murmuring impatiently against God, and accusing him as if thou wouldst fill up the measure of impiety, Matt. 23:23, and become like the wicked. Therefore judgment and justice hold thee, hence judgment and punishment constrain thee, nor does justice permit thee to be freed. The translation of Mr. Dr. Schmied, insisting closely on the words, is especially pleasing: And thou shalt be filled with the judgment of the wicked (by which the wicked shall be judged). Judgment and justice shall sustain thee: If, however, one should prefer to understand the judgment of the wicked actively, this sense will emerge, not inconvenient, if perhaps thou shalt be filled with the judgment of the wicked (passed against thee), yet judgment and justice, or just judgment, shall sustain thee.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

CAVSA TVA QVASI IMPII JVDICATA EST, CAVSAM JVDICIVMQVE RECIPIES] Melius: etsi tu quidem improbo judicium implevisti, id est, quale optabat dedisti: attamen causa & judicium cohærebunt, nempe apud Deum.

B. Lutherus de causa impiorum confirmata hoc modo intellexit: Sic agis tuam causam, quasi jus improbe velles confirmare. Alii, tu more impio- rum causam tuam egisti, impatienter contra Deum murmurando, eumque accusando quasi mensuram impietatis implere Matth. 23, 23. & impiis similis fieri velis. Ideo judicium & jus tenent te, hinc judi- cium & pœna te constringunt, nec justitia permit- tit te liberari. Placet imprimis Dn. D. Schmiedii translatio verbis presse insistens: Et judicio impii (quo judicabitur impius) impleberis. Judicium & jus sustentabunt te: Si vero active quis malit intel- ligere judicium impii, hic emerget sensus, non in- conveniens, si forte judicio impii (adversus te lato) repleberis, judicium tamen & jus, vel judicium ju- stum te sustentabit.

## 36:18
Verse 18.

THEREFORE LET NOT WRATH OVERCOME THEE, SO THAT THOU OPPRESS ANYONE: NOR LET THE MULTITUDE OF GIFTS INCLINE THEE) Better thus: Wherefore see that wrath be not incited in thee more than is sufficient, so that thou canst not escape it even with the greatest price offered.

There is not here a sufficient cause why one should depart from the vulgate, which the blessed Luther also followed. For thus the words are conveniently rendered: BECAUSE THERE IS HEAT LEST PERCHANCE IT SHOULD SEDUCE THEE IN SUFFICIENCY, OR THE MULTITUDE OF PROPITIATION SHOULD NOT BEND THEE. Because it is vehement, see that this vehemence, when thou wert living in abundance, has not seduced thee from the path of right, or the multitude of gifts has not driven thee aside, so that thou shouldst deflect from justice.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

NON TE ERGO SVPERET IRA, VT ALI- QVEM OPPRIMAS: NEC MVLTITVDO DONO- RVM INCLINET TE) Melius sic: Quare ira vide ne in te plus satis incitetur, ita ut eam ne maximo quidem oblato pretio possis effugere.

Non hic est sufficiens causa, cur a vulgata disce- datur, quam sequutus etiam B. Lutherus est. Sic enim commode verba redduntur: QUIA ÆSTUS EST NE FORTE SEDUXERIT TE IN SUF- FICIENTIA, AUT MULTITUDO PRO- PITIATIONIS NON TE INFLEXERIT. Quia vehemens, vide ne te hæc vehementia, cum in abundantia viveres, à tramite recti seduxerit, aut multitudo donorum te in transversum egerit, ut à justitia deflecteres.

## 36:19
LAY DOWN THY MAGNITUDE WITHOUT TRIBULATION, AND ALL THE ROBUST IN STRENGTH) Better thus: Would he value thy riches? not even gold and all the force of power.

Latin:

DEPONE MAGNITVDINEM TVAM ABSQVE TRIBVLATIONE, ET OMNES ROBVSTOS FORTI- TVDINE) Melius sic: An ille æstimaret opes tuas? ne au- rum quidem & omnem potentiæ vim.

## 36:20
Verse 20.

DO NOT PROLONG THE NIGHT SO THAT THE PEOPLES MAY ASCEND FOR THEM) More correctly thus: Do not meditate by night on how peoples may be driven from their places. For at night, when the mind is most free for thoughts, men are accustomed to seek reasons for fulfilling those things which they most desire.

Elihu does not seem to have attributed that ferocity to Job: and therefore it is better to take it in this sense, that you do not meditate by night on the judgments of God with bitterness, but rather wonder at and praise them, even if He takes away whole peoples.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

NE PROTRAHAS NOCTEM VT ASCENDANT POPVLI PRO EIS) Rectius sic: Ne nocte id mediteris, quomodo populi exturbentur de locis suis. Nam nocte cum maxime vacat cogitationibus animus, solent homines ratio- nes quærere ad ea implenda, quæ maxime desiderant.

Non videtur Elihu eam ferociam tribuisse Jobo: ideoque præstat hoc sensu accipere, ne no- cte mediteris acrimeris judicia Dei, sed mireris potius ac laudes, etiamsi integros tollat populos.

## 36:22
Ver. 22.

AND NO ONE IS LIKE HIM AMONG LAWGIVERS) The Greeks not badly [translate] τίς γάρ ἐστι κατ᾽ ἀυτὸν δυνάστης; For מורד signifies a lord to the Chaldeans. From the same root מרד signifies a kingdom, according to Rabbi Solomon.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET NVLLVS EI SIMILIS IN LEGISLATORIBVS) Græci non male τίς γάρ ἐστι κατ᾽ ἀυτὸν δυνάστης; Nam מורד Chaldæis dominum significat. Ab eadem radice מרד regnum significat, teste Rabbino Solomone.

## 36:29
Ver. 29.

IF HE SHALL WISH TO EXTEND THE CLOUDS AS HIS TENT) Better thus: or will he understand (namely, man, from that which preceded above in 24) the expansions of the cloud (how waters hang in the sky) and the rumbling of His tent: that is, the thunder, for the clouds themselves are the tent of God, Psalm 18:12.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

SI VOLVERIT EXTENDERE NVBES QVASE TENTORIVM SVVM) Melius sic: an intelliget (nempe homo ex eo, quod præcessit supra 24.) expansiones nubis (quomodo aquæ in cœlo pendeant) & fremitum tentorii ipsius: id est, tonitru, nam tentorium Dei sunt ipsæ nubes Psalm. 18, 12.

## 36:31
Ver. 31.

FOR BY THESE HE JUDGES THE PEOPLES] That is, He punishes.

AND GIVES FOOD TO MANY MORTALS) He nourishes men. For rains from the clouds are sometimes destructive, sometimes salutary.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

PER HÆC ENIM JVDICAT POPVLOS] Id est, punit.

ET DAT ESCAS MVLTIS MORTALIBVS) Nu- trit homines. Nam imbres ex nubibus alias exitiosi sunt, alias salutares.

## 36:32
Ver. 32.

IN HIS HANDS HE HIDES THE LIGHT) He covers it as if with a hand.

AND COMMANDS IT THAT IT MAY RETURN) That it may meet [Him] in the Hebrew. The sense is well expressed.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

IN MANIBVS ABSCONDIT LVCEM) Obtegit eam velut manu.

ET PRÆCIPIT EI VT RVRSVS ADVENIAT) Ut oc- currat in Hebræo. Sensus bene expressus est.

## 36:33
Verse 33.

HE WILL ANNOUNCE CONCERNING IT TO HIS FRIEND) Nay, his companion will announce concerning it, that is, Lucifer, the forerunner of the day.

THAT IT IS HIS POSSESSION, AND THAT HE MAY ASCEND TO IT) More correctly, to the cattle and the produce of the land. Which, to be sure, rejoice at the arrival of light. Seneca in Hercules Furens depicts the time before dawn thus: The shepherd, with the flock dismissed, crops the fodder in the cold, white frost. The young bullock, its brow not yet broken, plays free in the open meadow. The empty mothers replenish their udders. The wanton kid wanders with uncertain gait in the soft grass.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

ANNVNCIABIT DE EA AMICO SVO) Imo annun- ciabit de ea sodalis ejus, id est, Lucifer diei prævius.

QVOD POSSESSIO EJVS SIT, ET AD EAM POS- SIT ASCENDERE) Rectius, pecori & proventui terræ. Quæ scilicet lucis adventu gaudent. Seneca in Hercule fu- rente antelucanum tempus sic depingit: Pastor gelida cana pruina Grege dimisso pabula carpit. Ludit prato liber aperto Nondum rupta fronte juvencus. Vacuæ reparant ubera matres. Errat cursu levis incerto Molli petulans hædus in herba.

## 37:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVII. The divine greatness is shown from thunder, lightning, snow, winds, and clouds, so that everyone may submit himself to the divine will.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVII. Ostenditur divina magnitudo e tonitru, fulmi- ne, nive, ventis, ac nubibus, ut quisque se nu- tui divino subjiciat.

## 37:7
Verse 7.

WHO SEALS IN THE HAND OF ALL MEN) More correctly: He will shut up all men in the hand: that is, by the pouring out of rain (for he continues the preceding discourse) he will cut them off from all work of the field.

THAT ALL INDIVIDUALS MAY KNOW THEIR WORKS) Better: that all men may know the work (namely, rustic) to be his: that is, in his judgment and power. See Ps. 128, 1.

They are foolish who have sought from this passage a defense of palmistry. The word חתם is often to restrain, to inhibit, Job 9, 7. Dan. 9, 24. Cant. 4, 12. Therefore, the explanation of Grotius does not seem to be disapproved: which Junius, and Tremellius, Piscator, and Sixtinus ab Amama embrace, and which B. Tarnovius especially supports in his Biblical Exercises.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVI IN MANV OMNIVM HOMINVM SIGNAT) Rectius: In manu omnes homines recludet: id est, imbre effuso (continuat enim præcedentem sermonem) ab omni ruris ope- re eos intercludet.

VT NOVERINT SINGVLI OPERA SVA) Melius: ut noverint omnes homines opus (nempe rusticum) esse ipsius: id est, in ipsius arbitrio ac potestate. Vide Pf. 128, 1.

INepti sunt, qui ex hoc loco patrocinium Chiro- mantiæ quæsivere. Verbum חתם sæpe est cohibe- re, inhibere, Job. 9, 7. Dan. 9, 24. Cant. 4, 12. Non improbanda ergo videtur explicatio Grotiana: quam Junius, & Tremellius, Piscator, Sixtinus ab Amama amplectuntur, & cumprimis adstruit B. Tar- novius in Exercit. Biblicis.

## 37:8
Verse 8.

Verse 8.

THE BEAST SHALL ENTER INTO ITS COVERT, AND SHALL REMAIN IN ITS DEN] Ps. 104, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Verf. 8.

INGREDIETUR BESTIA LATIBULUM, ET IN ANTRO SUO MORABITUR] Pf. 104, 18.

## 37:9
Verse 9.

OUT OF THE INNER CHAMBERS COMETH THE STORM] From the inner parts, that is, from the southern pole, which is invisible to us. This interpretation is confirmed by the passage which is above 9, 9. Auster (the South wind) is called imbricitor by Ennius, imbricus by Plautus, and imbrifer by others.

OUT OF THE NORTH COMETH COLD] I think the interpreter wrote 'from the north' (ab arcto). For that part is directly opposed to the South. Because of various interpretations, certain Greeks retained the word itself, μαζὲς, and below 38, 38, μαζουρὼ. Poets also call the north 'icy'. Aristotle notes in Meteor. 2, chapter 4, that most winds blow from the North or from the South.

Latin:

Verf. 9.

AB INTERIORIBUS EGREDIETUR TEMPE- STAS] A penetralibus, id est, ab austrino polo, qui nobis inconspicuus. Confirmatur hæc interpretatio ex loco, qui supra 9, 9. Auster imbricitor Ennio, imbricus Plauto, im- brifer aliis.

AB ARCTURO FRIGUS] Ab arcto puto scripsisse in- terpretem. Ea enim pars Austro directe opponitur. Ob varias interpretationes Græci quidam ipsam vocem μαζὲς, & infra 38, 38. μαζουρὼ retinuere. Arctos gelidas etiam Poe- tæ vocant. Notat Aristoteles Meteor. 2. cap. 4. plerosque ventos ab Arcto aut ab Austro flare.

## 37:11
Verse 11.

CORN DESIRETH THE CLOUDS] From the Hebrew you may translate best: Also serenity presseth the cloud, namely so that it may emit dew, which flows on serene nights.

It makes for the version of B. Luther that טרח among the Arabs is 'he prostrated, cast down, threw': B. Scultetus renders it: ALSO IN IRRIGATION GOD SHALL WEARY THE CLOUD, he also gives the clouds the business of irrigating the earth.

AND THE CLOUDS DISPERSE THEIR LIGHT] They make a rainbow with varied light.

Thomas understands it concerning the reddish color of the clouds, others concerning lightning. B. Luther: Through the mist shines his light. Because ענן properly signifies mist.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

FRUMENTUM DESIDERAT NUBES] Ex Hebræo optime vertas: Etiam serenitas premit nubem, nempe ut ro- rem emittat, qui serenis noctibus manat.

Pro B. Lutheri versione facit, quod טרח Arabi- bus est prostravit, elifit, projecit: B. Scultetus reddit: ETIAM IN IRRIGATIONE FATIGABIT NUBEM DEUS, etiam nubibus dat negotium ir- rigandi terram.

ET NUBES SPARGUNT LUMEN SUUM] Iridem faciunt lumine vario.

Thomas de colore nubium rubicundo, alii de Fulgure accipiunt. B. Lutherus: Durch den Nebel leucht sein Licht. Quia ענן proprie nebulam si- gnificat.

## 37:13
Ver. 13.

OR IN ONE TRIBE) For it often rains in one city: in another quite near it does not rain. Amos 4, 7.

OR IN HIS LAND] He calls the undivided land God's, which has not yet fallen to any man as property. Thus elsewhere the sea is said to be God's, by comparison made to the land.

The Vulgate adds: OR IN ANY PLACE OF HIS MERCY. Cajetan, Vatablus, Pagninus render the word שבט as rod, so that the sense may be, whether for a scourge or punishment, viz. for the impious. Or in his land among the faithful and the people of the Lord, or FOR FAVOR: so that the twofold use of rain is destined both as a punishment for the impious, and as a favor for the pious. While we admit this, because there is express mention of a benefit, and indeed under a disjunctive, whence it must tacitly be included at the very least that the other member of the disjunctive is about the penal use of rains: so the word שבט here seems entirely to be taken as tribe, in which sense James has already used the same in Gen. 49, 10, or as one family, just as R. Moses Nachmanides, the Vulgate, and our B. Luther rendered it, because the added disjunctive demands it, whether in one tribe or family, or in his (GOD'S) whole land, or the people of God, or commonly, as B. Luther: Uber ein land: for punishment, namely: for it is added further OR FOR FAVOR, so that the opportune rain may make the land fruitful, so that God may do good to it, Amos 4, 7.

Latin:

Verf. 13.

SIVE IN UNA TRIBU) Sæpe enim pluit in urbe una: in altera satis vicina non pluit. Amos 4, 7.

SIVE IN TERRA SUA] Terram Dei vocat indivisam, quæ nulli adhuc hominum in proprietatem obvenit. Sic alibi mare Dei esse dicitur, comparatione facta ad terram.

Vulgata addit: SIVE IN QUOCUNQUE LOCO MISERICORDIÆ SUÆ. Cajetan. Va- tablus, Pagninus vocem שבט per virgam reddunt, ut sensus sit, sive in flagellum vel pœnam, scil. impiis. Sive in terra sua penes fideles & populum Domini, vel IN GRATIAM: ut geminus pluviæ usus tum in pœnam impiis, tum piis in gratiam destinetur. Quod uti admittimus, quia beneficii expresse sit mentio, & quidem sub disjunctiva, unde tacite in- cludi ad minimum oportet alterum disjunctivæ membrum, de pœnali usu pluviarum: ita videtur vox שבט hic omnino accipienda de tribu, quo sen- su eadem usus jam est Jacobus Gen. 49, 10. vel de fa- milia una, quemadmodum R. Moses Nachmani- des, Vulgatus, nosterque B. Luther. reddidere, quia id disjunctiva addita postulat, sive in tribu seu fami- lia una, seu in terra sua (DEI) universa, vel popu- li Dei, vel communiter, ut B. Luther. Uber ein land: in pœnam nempe: additur enim porro SIVE IN GRATIAM, ut pluvia oportuna terra fœcunde- tur, ut Deus ei benefaciat Amos 4, 7.

## 37:15
Ver. 15.

DOST THOU KNOW WHEN GOD COMMANDED THE RAINS, THAT THEY SHOULD SHOW THE LIGHT OF HIS CLOUDS?] That is, can you predict when the rainbow will be? See what is above 11.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

NUMQVID SCIS, QVANDO PRÆCEPERIT DEUS PLUVIIS, UT OSTENDERENT LUCEM NUBIUM EJUS?] Id est,potesne tu prædicere, quando futura sit Iris? Vide quæ supra 11.

## 37:18
Ver. 18.

PERCHANCE HAST THOU WITH HIM MADE THE HEAVENS, WHICH ARE MOST SOLID AS IF CAST OF BRASS] In the word which is here לשחקים the particle ל has a use rare enough for אל. The word itself sometimes signifies aerial regions, sometimes ethereal, as also שמים. For it, as if they were cast from brass, the Chaldean has as if mirrors, from glass, namely. But how do חזקים strong, suit these? A certain very learned man thought it had been written חלקים, that is, smooth. Let those who have the means consult the old books.

Is it because the Chaldean translation is not sufficiently consistent with itself that something must be changed in the Hebrew source, even if in this all things agree perfectly? What if mirrors were accustomed to be made from metals, which are indeed firm and solid.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

TU FORSITAN CUM EO FABRICATUS ES COE- LOS, QVI SOLIDISSIMI QVASI ÆRE FUSI SINT] In voce quæ hic est לשחקים particula ל usum habet satis rarum pro אל. Ipsa vox modo aereas regiones,mo- do æthereas significat, ut & שמים. Pro eo,quasi ex ære fusa sint, Chaldæus habet quasi specularia, è vitro scilicet. At quomodo his convenit חזקים fortes? vir quidam pere- ruditus putabat scriptum fuisse חלקים, id est, læves. Con- sulant libros veteres ii, quibus copia est.

Num quia satis non constat sibi translatio Chaldæa, aliquid mutandum in fonte Ebræo, etsi in, hoc omnia apprime conveniant? quid quod specula è metallis fieri consveverunt, quæ utique firma & solida sunt.

## 37:21
Verse 21.

WHICH ILLUMINATE ROUND ABOUT) The clouds wander here and there. Here before מסבות the particle כ is missing, as is often the case.

WHITHERSOEVER THE WILL OF THE GOVERNOR SHALL LEAD IT) I should think it translated more correctly: it rolls itself upon its mountains. For جبل in Arabic is mountain. Moreover, clouds have the appearance of mountains.

The interpretation of B. Scultetus & Cocceius is simpler: AND HE (God) TURNS THE CIRCUITS OF THE CLOUDS BY HIS HELMS. Moreover, the Hebrew word is taken from nautical matters, and God is compared to a shipmaster, his providence to a rudder, etc.

Latin:

Verf. 21.

QVÆ ILLUSTRANT PER CIRCUITUM) Huc illuc vagantur nubes. Hic ante מסבות deficit particula כ, ut sæpe.

QVOCUNQVE SE VOLUNTAS GUBERNANTIS DUXERIT) Rectius verti putem: volvit se montibus suis. Nam جبل Arabice mons est. Habent autem nubes montium speciem.

Simplicior est interpretatio B. Sculteti & Coc- ceji: ET IPSE (Deus) CIRCUITUS NUBI- UM CONVERTIT GUBERNACULIS SUIS. Vox autem Ebræa è re nautica petita est, & confer- tur Deus nauclero, providentia ejus calvo, &c.

## 37:21
Verse 21.

BUT NOW THEY DO NOT SEE THE LIGHT, SUDDENLY THE AIR IS GATHERED INTO CLOUDS, AND HE WILL PURIFY THEM] More correctly thus: Behold now they do not see the sun shining in the ethereal regions. Suddenly comes a wind, which will join them: namely, and make the sun to be seen again. We said above 30, 25 that אור is the sun. That בהיר is the Arabic بهير.

Mercerus explains it thus: Men now cannot behold the sun shining clearly, the ether being purged by the winds, because their vision is dull: much less, therefore, will they dare to behold God, who is brighter than the sun, or be able to attain to his counsels.

Latin:

Verf. 21.

AT NUNC NON VIDENT LUCEM, SUBITO AER COGETUR IN NUBES, ET PURIFICABIT EAS] Rectius sic: En nunc non vident solem splendentem in æthe- reis regionibus. Subito venit ventus, qui eas junget: nempe & solem rursus conspici faciat. אור effe solem diximus supra 30, 25. illud בהיר est Arabicum بهير.

Mercerus ita exponit: Homines jam solem cla- re lucentem, æthere a ventis purgato non valent aspi- cere visu hebescente: multo minus ergo Deum so- le clariorem audebunt aspicere, aut consilia ejus at- tingere valebunt.

## 37:22
Verse 22.

FROM THE NORTH GOLD WILL COME) Serene: for βορέας αἰθρηγενέτης (Boreas, the bringer of clear sky).

AND UNTO GOD IS TERRIBLE PRAISE] The sense is: And for that reason, praise to that venerable God. All the Greeks not badly: ἐπὶ τύτοις μεγάλῃ ἡ δόξα καὶ τιμὴ τῷ παντοκράτορι. ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ μεγάλῃ ἡ δόξα. Another: Περὶ δὲ θε̃ φοβερὸς αἶνος.

Others have rendered the sense of this verse thus: That affliction (denoted by the north) brings great benefit (which gold designates) and therefore God is to be praised. Others explain it thus: FROM THE NORTH GOLD (golden serenity) COMES, WITH GOD IS TREMENDOUS MAJESTY. Just as the North wind brings serenity, so the majesty of God brings incomprehensible terror. Others commonly explain this in this way: From the North gold (golden serenity, as in Zech. 4, 12, oil is called most splendid and purest gold) comes, so that upon God there may be glorious majesty or to God the terrible there is glory, as Piscator, Diodati, Cocceius with Mercer and B. Luther and the Vulgate, whose sense Grotius therefore expressed not inconveniently. Compare the marginal gloss of B. Luther. I do not see why one should depart from that more accepted explanation: And the more subtle senses of others can be considered more clever than solid.

Latin:

Verf. 22.

AB AQVILONE AURUM VENIET) Serenum: nam βορέας αἰθρηγενέτης.

ET AD DEUM FORMIDOLOSA LAUDATIO] Sensus est: Et Deo illi venerando ob id laus. Græci omnes non male: ἐπὶ τύτοις μεγάλῃ ἡ δόξα καὶ τιμὴ τῷ παντο- κράτορι. ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ μεγάλῃ ἡ δόξα. Alius: Περὶ δὲ θε̃ φοβερὸς αἶνος.

Sensum hujus commatis alii sic reddiderunt: Afflictionem (per aquilonem notatam) magnum afferre commodum (quod designat aurum) & pro- pterea Deum laudandum. Alii ita exponunt: AB AQUILONE AURUM (aurea serenitas) VE- NIT, APUD DEUM TREMENDA MAJE- STAS. Sicut ventus Boreas serenitatem adfert, sic majestas Dei incomprehensibilis terrorem. Alii communiter explicant h. m. à Septentrione aurum (aurea serenitas, uti Zach. 4, 12. oleum splendi- dissimum, & purissimum aurum vocatur) venit, ut super Deo majestas sit gloriosa vel Deo tremendo sit gloria, ut Piscator, Diodatus, Coccejus cum Mer- cero & B. Luthero ac vulgata, cujus sensum proin- de non incommode expressit Grotius. Conf. glossa margin. B. Lutheri. Non video cur a re- ceptiori illa explicatione discedendum sit: Et ar- gutiores aliorum sensus censeri possunt, quam so- lidiores.

## 37:23
Verse 23.

WE CANNOT WORTHILY FIND HIM] More correctly, The Almighty is incomprehensible. ἀκατάληπτος.

GREAT IN STRENGTH AND JUDGMENT AND JUSTICE, AND HE CANNOT BE DECLARED] You would translate these last words more correctly: And he will not answer: that is, he will render accounts of his actions to no one. Consider the following.

Latin:

Verf. 23.

DIGNE EUM INVENIRE NON POSSUMUS] Re- ctius, Omnipotens est incomprehensibilis. ἀκατάληπτος.

MAGNUS FORTITUDINE ET JUDICIO ET JU- STITIA, ET ENARRARI NON POTEST] Hæc ulti- ma rectius vertas: Et non respondebit: id est, nemini ratio- nes reddet suarum actionum. Confidera sequentia.

## 37:24
Verse 24.

AND THEY SHALL NOT DARE TO CONTEMPLATE, ALL WHO SEEM TO THEMSELVES TO BE WISE] In the Hebrew it is: He does not care at all for those who are wise in their own opinion. Very aptly to the sentiment of Elihu.

Latin:

Verf. 24.

ET NON AUDEBUNT CONTEMPLARI OMNES, QVI SIBI VIDENTUR ESSE SAPIENTES] In Hebræo est: Minime curat eos, qui sua opinione sapientes sunt. Valde apposite ad sententiam Eliu.

## 38:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXVIII. God himself intervenes in the dispute, and warns that no one can comprehend his works: the foundation of the earth, the creation of the angels, the containment of the waters, the path of light, the measure and end of man, and the condition of meteors and stars.

Verse 1.

BUT THE LORD ANSWERING JOB OUT OF THE WHIRLWIND SAID] Job had indeed rightly said that he was not being punished for crimes, nor was he in any respect worse than those who, on the occasion of his calamities, were treating him most bitterly. Yet, because of an impatience that sometimes boiled over, certain things had escaped him which stood in need of correction. And so Job acknowledges these as pertaining to himself in chapter 42. The Lord, that is, the Angel of the Lord in his name. Out of the whirlwind, that is, out of some cloud formed beyond the order of nature.

Why not immediately and αὐτοπροσώπως [in person] the Lord? It is not for us to substitute an Angel in the place of the Lord, where Scripture names the Lord, but makes no mention of an Angel. Furthermore, why does God propose natural things to Job in his response? These reasons are given: 1. The inscrutable divine wisdom, which, since it shines forth in natural things, what wonder if we cannot penetrate the hidden counsels and judgments of God? 2. The divine majesty, so that we may learn to deal with God modestly and humbly, and not oppose ourselves to so great a Lord. 3. The divine goodness, so that since God cares for all things, and created and preserves them for the sake of man, we may believe that he does not neglect man, but deals well with him. 4. The admirable οἰκονομία [economy] of divine governance, so that we may humbly revere him in the macrocosm and the microcosm, and devotedly submit ourselves to him.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXVIII. Deus ipse disputationi se interponit, & opera sua funditationem terræ, creationem angelorum, aquarum conclusionem, lucis viam, hominis metrum & finem, meteororum & syderum conditionem neminem comprehendere posse monet.

Vers. 1.

RESPONDENS AVTEM DOMINVS JOB DE TVRBINE DIXIT] Job recte quidem se non ob scelera puniri dixerat, neque se ulla ex parte pejorem esse iis qui oc- casione calamitatum ejus acerbissime eum tractabant. At- tamen præ impatientia interdum ebulliente, quædam ei exci- derant, quæ castigationis egebant. Itaque & Job hæc tan- quam ad se pertinentia agnoscit capite 42. Dominus, id est, Angelus Domini nomine. De turbine, id est, de nube aliqua præter naturæ ordinem facta.

Cur non immediate & αὐτοπροσώπως Domi- nus? Nostrum non est Domini loco substituere Angelum, ubi Scriptura nominat Dominum, An- geli autem nullam facit mentionem. Cæterum cur in responso suo Deus Jobo res naturales proponat, hæ causæ redduntur: 1. Imperscrutabilis divinæ sapientiæ, quæ cum eluceat in naturalibus, quid mirum si non possimus abdita Dei consilia & judi- cia penetrare? 2. Divina majestas, ut modeste & humiliter cum Deo agere discamus, nec nos tanto Domino opponamus. 3. Divina bonitas, ut quum omnia curet Deus, & in hominis gratiam crearit, ac conservet, non negligere hominem, sed bene cum ipso agere credamus. 4. Gubernatio- nis divinæ admiranda οἰκονομία, ut eum in macro- cosmo, & microcosmo humiliter veneremur, eique nos devote submittamus.

## 38:5
Verse 5.

WHO STRETCHED THE LINE UPON IT] A plumb line. A similitude taken from architects, as we said in 2 Kings 21:13.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QVIS TETENDIT SVPER EAM LINE- AM] Amussim. Similitudo ab architectis sumta, ut diximus 2. Reg. 21, 13.

## 38:6
Verse 6.

UPON WHAT ARE ITS BASES FASTENED] He persists in the similitude of a building. It seems, however, to signify obscurely the center, which is the foundation for the earth.

OR WHO LAID ITS CORNERSTONE] The poles of the earth seem to be obscurely designated.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

SVPER QVO BASIS ILLIVS SOLIDATÆ SVNT] Perseverat in similitudine ædificii. Videtur autem obscure significari centrum, quod terræ pro fundamento est.

AVT QVIS DEMISIT LAPIDEM ANGULAREM EJVS] Videntur obscure designari poli terræ.

## 38:7
Verse 7.

WHEN THE MORNING STARS PRAISED ME TOGETHER] The most luminous stars. For בקר is often the same as אור. Aben-Ezra understands the planets, which are כוכבי אור Psalm 149:4.

AND ALL THE SONS OF GOD SHOUTED FOR JOY] That is, the Angels, as the Greek version has it here, which is confirmed by that which is above in 1:6.

Morning stars, by the common calculation of most interpreters, are said here to be those who are indicated by the subjoined clause as Sons of God, that is, Angels, as the Greek version has it, which Grotius acknowledges is confirmed by the fact that it is above in v. 6. For the latter words are explanatory of the former: when the morning stars praised me together, and all the Sons of God shouted for joy. And this appellation clearly suits the Angels, who are called stars because of their ethereal nature, light, splendor, purity, simplicity, beauty, firmness; morning [stars], because they were created before other things, in the highest, if we may so say, morning, before the primogenial light, which was the very matter of the sun, from whose rising the day was to be founded, as we showed in System. locor. commun. Theol. Tom. 3. Art. 5. c. 2. Q. 1., or because they announce the light, God James 1, 13. 1. John 1, 6. as others explain, the planets did not yet exist when the foundations of the earth were being laid, having been created only on the fourth day. Therefore they cannot be understood here. From light and ardor, Angels are also called שרפים and are compared to light, 2 Kings 2, 15. Is. 6, 2. Ezek. 1, 13. Dan. 7, 10. Heb. 1, 7. Nor is it necessary, nor does it agree with Cocceius, that we repeat that 'where were you?' in this way: where were you when the morning stars praised me: as if the angels were created only after the earth was founded. For we taught in our Syst. Theol. that these were created at the very beginning of creation and thus immediately on the first day, before all visible things. In the judgment of our blessed Scultetus, a simile seems to be taken here from magnates who employed music and votive acclamations at the foundations of buildings, Zech. 4, 7. Ezra 3, 10. But that Job is warned to admire and praise the works of God by the example of the Angels, not to murmur.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

CVM ME LAVDARENT SIMVL ASTRA MATV- TINA] Astra lucidissima. Nam בקר sæpe idem quod אור. Intelligit Aben-Esra planetas, qui כוכבי אור Pf. 149, 4.

ET JVBILARENT OMNES FILII DEI] Id est, An- geli, ut hic habet Græca versio, quæ confirmatur ex eo quod supra est 1, 6.

Astra matutina, communi Interpp. plerorum- que calculo, dicuntur hic, qui Filii Dei subjuncto commate indigitantur, id est, Angeli, ut habet Græ- ca versio, quam confirmari ex eo, quod supra est 1. v. 6. agnoscit Grotius. Sunt enim verba posteriora ἐξηγητικὰ priorum: cum me laudarent simul astra matutina, & jubilarent omnes Filii Dei. Et plane convenit appellatio hæc Angelis, qui astra nuncu- pantur ob naturam ætheream, lucem, splendorem, pu- ritatem, simplicitatem, pulchritudinem, firmitudi- nem; matutina, quia ante res cæteras creati sunt, summo, ut ita dicamus, mane, antequam lux primi- genia, quæ solis ipsius materia fuit, a cujus ortu dies conderetur, ut in System. locor. commun. Theol. Tom. 3. Art. 5. c. 2. Q. 1. ostendimus, vel quia nun- ciant lucem, Deum Jacob. 1, 13. 1. Joh. 1, 6. ut alii ex- plicant, Planetæ tunc cum fundamenta terræ con- debantur, nondum erant, quarto demum die con- diti. Non ergo hic intelligi possunt. A luce & ardore Angeli etiam שרפים dicuntur, luciq; compa- rantur, 2. Reg. 2, 15. Es. 6, 2. Ezech. 1, 13. Dan. 7, 10. Ebr. 1, 7. Neque vero necessum est, aut conveni- ut cum Coccejo repetamus illud ubi fuisti? hoc mo- do: ubi fuisti cum me laudarent astra matutina: qua- fi post terram conditam demum creati sint angeli. Hos enim sub primum initium creationis adeoque primo statim die, ante visibilia omnia, conditos effe in Syst. Theol. docuimus. B. Sculteto nostro ju- dice, videtur hic simile petitum à magnatibus, qui in ædificiorum fundamentis Musicam, & acclamatio- nes votivas adhibuere, Zach. 4, 7. Esdr. 3, 10. Mo- neri autem Jobum, ut exemplo Angelorum Dei opera miretur, & laudet, non fugillet.

## 38:8
Ver. 8.

WHO SHUT UP THE SEA WITH DOORS?] Who protected the sea in valves? סכך is often to protect, who was for the sea as a midwife? For the whole simile is taken from childbirth. דלתים are valves, τὰ χείλη of the womb.

The sea can be understood as the universal waters, as they were created on the first day: to which signification the blessed Scultetus thinks the following metaphor better agrees.

Latin:

Verf. 8.

QVIS CONCLUSIT OSTIIS MARE?] Quis protexit in valvis mare? סכך fæpe est protegere, quis mari pro ob- stetrice fuit? Nam tota similitudo à partu sumitur. דלתים valvæ sunt τὰ χείλη uteri.

Mare intelligi potest de aquis universis, ut pri- ma die conditæ sunt: Cui fignificationi sequentem Metaphoram melius convenire censet B. Scul- tetus.

## 38:9
Ver. 9.

WHEN I MADE THE CLOUD ITS GARMENT] For the air hangs over the sea. AND WRAPPED IT IN DARKNESS AS WITH SWADDLING BANDS FOR INFANCY] The Greeks very well: ὁ μίχλη δὲ αὐτὴν ἐσπαργάνωσα. For many mists are accustomed to arise above the sea.

Some refer to the first creation Gen. 1, 2. as an infant is covered with a cloth and linen: so God at the beginning covered the sea with a cloud and dark air. But perhaps these things will be more correctly accepted concerning the supercelestial waters, of which the cloud is as it were a covering, and the darkness as a swaddling band: just as it treats of the waters gathered into the sea, and concluded within their own boundaries v. 10 and 11.

Latin:

Verf. 9.

CUM PONEREM NUBEM VESTIMENTUM EJUS] Aer enim mari impendet. ET CALIGINE ILLUD QVASI PANNIS INFAN- TIÆ OBVOLVEREM] Græci optime: ὁ μίχλη δὲ αὐτὴν ἐσπαργάνωσα. Multæ enim nebulæ folent oriri supra mare.

Nonnulli respiciunt ad primam creationem Gen. 1, 2. ut infans tegitur panno & linteo: ita nube & aëre tenebroso Deus initio mare texit. Se de aquis supracoelestibus hæc fortassis rectius accipi- entur, quarum velut operimentum nubes, & caligo quasi pannus est: quemadmodum de aquis in ma- re congregatis, terminisque fuis conclusis v. 10. & 11, agitur.

## 38:10
Ver. 10.

I HAVE SURROUNDED IT WITH MY BOUNDARIES] The same expression Prov. 8, 29. AND SET A BAR AND DOORS] Namely the shores, as the passage of Jeremiah 5, 22 shows.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

CIRCUMDEDI ILLUD TERMINIS MEIS] Eadem locutio Prov. 8, 29. ET POSVI VECTEM ET OSTIA] Nempe littora, ut ostendit locus Jeremiæ 5, 22.

## 38:11
Ver. 11.

AND I SAID, THOU SHALT COME HITHER] The Hebrews use פה for a boundary, as appears in Ezek. 41:15. Therefore, they rightly translate עד פה as 'hitherto'.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

ET DIXI, VSQVE HVC VENIES] Hebræi פה pro termino ponunt ut apparet Ezech. 41, 15. Ideo recte עד פה vertit hucusque.

## 38:13
Ver. 13.

AND HAST TAKEN HOLD OF THE ENDS OF THE EARTH] More correctly, that it may obtain the extreme parts of the earth: that it may suddenly spread itself into all parts of the earth: the dawn, namely, of which it preceded. AND HAST SHAKEN THE WICKED OUT OF IT] This is because judgments were exercised in the morning.

Latin:

Verf. 13.

ET TENVISTI CONCVTIENS EXTREMA TER- RÆ] Rectius ut obtineat extremas partes terræ: ut subito se in omnes terræ partes diffundat: aurora scilicet, de qua præcessit. ET EXCVSSISTI IMPIOS EX EA] Id ideo quia ma- ne judicia exercebantur.

## 38:14
Ver. 14.

IT IS TURNED AS CLAY TO THE SEAL] In the Hebrew: it turns itself like sealing clay.

Doubtless every one of the wicked: For thus he understands it: and not badly.

AND SHALL STAND AS A GARMENT] It will not be more consistent than a variegated garment. Things are accustomed to change their appearance and color suddenly.

Latin:

Verf. 14.

RESTITVETVR VT LVTVM SIGNACVLVM] In Hebræo: vertit se ut argilla fignatoria.

Nimirum impiorum quisque: Sic enim in- telligit: nec male.

ET STABIT SICVT VESTIMENTVM] Non magis fibi constabit quam vestis versicolor. Rei solent subinde mutare vultum & colorem.

## 38:15
Ver. 15.

AND FROM THE WICKED THEIR LIGHT IS WITHHOLDEN, AND THE HIGH ARM SHALL BE BROKEN] He shall be condemned to death, and indeed a torturous one, such as breaking on the wheel.

THE HIGH ARM SHALL BE BROKEN is better understood as the power of the wicked being cast down and laid prostrate.

Verf. 15.

BRACHIUM EXCELSVM CONFRIN- GETUR melius de impii potentia dejicienda, eaque prosternenda intelligitur.

Vers. 21.

DID YOU KNOW THEN THAT YOU WERE TO BE BORN) You were so ignorant of these works of God, that you did not even know that you would ever exist. Certain of the Hebrews twist this toward the pre-existence of souls.

Vers. 21.

SCIEBAS TVNC QVOD NASCITVRUS ESSES) Adeo ista Dei opera nesciebas, ut ne quidem scires te un- quam exstiturum. Hoc ad προϋπαρξιν animarum detor- quent Hebræorum quidam.

Vers. 23.

## 38:25
Vers. 25.

WHO HAS GIVEN A COURSE TO THE MOST VIOLENT RAIN) In the Hebrew: Who has distributed channels for the inundation? Thus he calls those parts of the sky through which the rain breaks forth.

Others: WHO HAS DISTRIBUTED A CHANNEL (or AQUEDUCT) TO THE MOST VIOLENT RAIN (or INUNDATION). Men make their own aqueducts through the earth: But God distributes through the air and the cloud (where no force or human prudence could find a way for it) how, when, and in what quantity it ought to descend.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

QVIS DEDIT VEHEMENTISSIMO IMBRI CVR- SVM) In Hebræo: Quis distribuit inundationi elices? sic vocat eas partes cæli, per quas imber erumpit.

Alii QUIS DISTRIBUIT IMBRI VEHE- MENTISSIMO (vel EXUNDATIONI) RI- VUM, canalem vel aquæductum. Homines suos aquæductus per terram efficiunt: Sed Deus per aërem & nubem (ubi viam illi nulla vis vel pruden- tia humana invenire posset) distribuit, quomodo, quando, qua copia descendere debeat.

## 38:30
Vers. 30.

AND THE SURFACE OF THE DEEP IS CONGEALED) The sea freezes in some parts.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

ET SVPERFICIES ABTSSI CONSTRINGITVR) Ma- re in nonnullis partibus gelasceit.

## 38:31
Vers. 31.

CAN YOU BIND THE SHINING STARS OF THE PLEIADES) كمة in Arabic signifies a heap. Whence those seem to have conjectured well who interpret כימה as the Pleiades, a certain gathering of bright stars. The sense is: can you hinder the spring flowers of the Pleiades.

The words do not sound as if they are about binding them, or the restriction of their powers, but about joining them together. Because God alone has so joined the Pleiades, or directs their powers, so that being divinely coupled they may work more strongly in unison.

OR CAN YOU DISSIPATE THE CIRCUIT OF ARCTURUS? The Greeks: καὶ φραγμὸν Ὡρίωνος ἤνοιξας. Thus also כסיל, which Jerome above at 9, 9 translates as Orion, a winter constellation hindering labors. كسل to the Arabs is idleness. The sense is: will you be able to give the farmers the ability to work, when Orion hinders labors?

Nothing is held here concerning the hindered labors of farmers. OR WILL YOU LOOSE THE BANDS OF ORION? Orion is opposed to the Pleiades, and by its heliacal rising indicates autumn; its bands are the operations by which it draws in storms as if with ropes, and binds the earth with cold.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

NVNQVID CONJVNGERE VALEBIS MICANTES STELLAS PLEIADAS) كمة Arabice acervum signifi- cat. Vnde videntur bene conjecisse qui כימה interpretan- tu Plejades, ἀγροισμὸς quendam clarorum siderum. Sensus est: potesne impedire flores vernos virgiliarum.

Non de constringendis illis, vel restrictione virium ipsarum, sed de conjungendis verba sonant. Quod solus Deus Plejades ita conjunxerit, vel vires earum intendat, ut unitim fortius operentur divi- nitus copulatæ.

AVT GYRVM ARCTVRI POTERIS DISSIPARE) Græci καὶ φραγμὸν Ὡρίωνος ἤνοιξας. Sic etiam כסיל Hieronymus supra 9, 9. vertit Orionem, Hybernum sidus la- bores impediens. كسل Arabibus otium. Sensus est: poterisne tu rusticis facultatem da re laborandi, ubi labores Orion inhibet?

Nil hic habetur de rusticorum laboribus impeditis. AUT FUNES ORIONIS RESOL- VES? Orion opponitur Plejadibus, & ortu suo Heliaco autumnum indicat; funes ejus sunt opera- tiones, quibus tempestates quasi funibus attrahit, & frigore constringit terram.

## 38:32
Verse 32.

CAN YOU BRING FORTH THE MORNING STAR IN ITS TIME? The Bear, as above at 37, 9, in its time, namely at night.

Some notable star is indicated, or a constellation toward the south: yet in such a way that it could be seen in the region of Job. B. Scultetus understands it as Sirius. Suidas also held this opinion.

AND MAKE THE EVENING STAR RISE OVER THE SONS OF THE EARTH? Above, עש, which is the same as עיש, he rendered as Arcturus at 9, 9. عياث in Arabic is strength. For that 'over the sons of the earth,' the Hebrew has 'with its sons.' That is, with the other northern signs which are around Arcturus.

Others also understand the Great Bear with its sons, the smaller stars surrounding it: so that thus, through those four constellations of the Pleiades, Orion, Sirius, and the Bear or Arcturus, all the constellations toward the East, West, South, and North are comprehended at once.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

NVMQVID PRODVCIS LVCIFERVM IN TEMPORE SVO) Arctum ut supra 37, 9. suo tempore, no- cte scilicet.

Indicatur stella aliqua insignis, vel sydus ver- sus meridiem: ita tamen ut in regione Jobi videri potuerit. Sirium intelligit B. Scultetus. Ita etiam Suidas censuit.

ET VESPERVM SVPER FILIOS TFRRÆ CON- SVRGERE FACIS) Supra עש quod idem est cum עיש Arcturum reddidit 9, 9. عياث Arabice robur. Pro illo super filios terræ, Hebræum habet cum filiis suis. Id est, cum aliis signis septentrionalibus, quæ circa Arcturum sunt.

Ursam majorem cum filiis suis stellis minori- bus illam circumstantibus etiam alii intelligunt: ut ita per quatuor illa Sydera Plejadum, Orionis, Syrii, & Ursæ vel Arcturi omnia Sydera versus Orientem, Occidentem, Austrum & Septentrionem simul com- prehendantur.

## 39:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIX.

God sets before Job his wonderful works in lions, the feeding of ravens, wild goats, the wild ass, the rhinoceros, the ostrich, the horse, and the eagle, arguing that he dared to contend with Him; moved by which, Job acknowledges that he spoke rashly.

Verse 1.

DO YOU KNOW THE TIME OF THE IBEXES' BIRTH) This is because they give birth on inaccessible rocks.

OR HAVE YOU OBSERVED THE HINDES GIVING BIRTH) Can you act as midwife to the female deer: for their births are difficult. Pliny 8, 32.

The time also cannot be determined; since, living in perpetual motion and fear, they often anticipate the time.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIX.

Deus Jobo proponit mirabilia sua opera in leoni- bus, corvorum nutritione, ibicibus, onagro, rhinocerote, struthione, equo, & aquila, ar- guens eum, quod cum ipso contendere ausus sit? quibus commotus Job agnoscit se teme- re locutum.

Vers. 1.

NUMQVID NOSTI TEMPUS PARTUS IBICUM) Id ideo quia in rupibus inaccesfis pariunt.

VEL PARTURIENTES CERVAS OBSERVASTI) An obstetricari potes cervis feminis: sunt enim earum partus difficiles. Plinius 8, 32.

Tempus etiam determinari nequit; si quidem in perpetuo motu & metu viventes sæpe tempus antevertant.

## 39:5
Ver. 5.

WHO LOOSES ITS BONDS?) So also the Greeks. However, in the Hebrew, פרא precedes and ערוד follows, which therefore seems to be a different animal from the wild ass, though not differing much.

To others these seem rather to be synonyms: For the description fits the wild ass entirely. Its bonds are said to be loosed, not because it was previously in bonds, but because nature willed it to be without bonds. It lives in solitude and in arid and uncultivated places, which are called salt-marshes. In the solitudes of Arabia there was a great multitude of them, according to Xenophon, book II of the Expedition of Cyrus.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

VINCULA EJUS QVIS SOLVIT?) Sic & Græci. Attamen in Hebræo præcessit פרא sequitur ערוד.quod proinde aliud videtur animal ab onagro, non tamen multum differens.

Aliis hæc potius videntur synonyma: Nam descriptio Onagro convenit tota. Vincula ejus solu- ta dicuntur, non quod antea in vinculis fuerit, sed quod natura eum fine vinculis esse voluerit. Vi- vit in solitudine & in locis aridis & incultis, quæ salsuginosa dicuntur. In solitudinibus Arabiæ magna eorum fuit multitudo teste Xenophonte l. II. de expedit. Cyri.

## 39:7
Ver. 7.

WILL THE RHINOCEROS BE WILLING TO SERVE YOU) רים is the unicorn to the Syrians, and so the Greek interpreters are accustomed to translate, as we said in Deut. 33, 17.

So most interpreters, and this interpretation is more convenient than the Vulgate: which is deservedly abandoned here by Grotius. Compare Pliny, book 8, 12. Aelian, book 7, ch. 3. Gessner, History of animals, book 1, p. 689. Aldrovandi on Solid-hoofed animals, ch. 5. Bartholin on the unicorn.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

NUMQVID VOLET RHINOCEROS SERVIRE TI- BI) רים Syris est monoceros, & sic solent vertere Græci interpretes, ut diximus Deut. 33, 17.

Ita plerique Interpp. & commodior est hæc interpretatio quam vulgatæ: quæ merito hic à Gro- tio deseritur. Conf. Plin. l. 8, 12. Ælian. l. 7. c. 3. Gessner. Hist. animal. l. 1. p. 689. Aldrovando de So- liped. c. 5. Barthol. de unicornu.

## 39:13
Ver. 13.

THE WING OF THE OSTRICH IS LIKE THE WINGS OF THE HERON, AND THE HAWK) The Greeks have left these words as they are in the Hebrew. Other interpreters vary greatly. The most probable version is this: The wing exulting (you could supply 'you might give', as below in 18.) to the Peacock, or the wing of the stork or the ostrich? That רננים are Peacocks is the opinion both of R. Abraham and of others. החסידה [the stork] is the ciconia because of its piety: and thus certain Greeks have translated it, although others say it is an Indian bird. But that רננים [ostrich] is the ostrich, the following things, which are properly suitable to that animal, prove.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

PENNA STRUTHIONIS SIMILIS EST PENNIS HERODII, ET ACCIPITRIS) Græci has voces reliquere, ut in Hebræo sunt. Alii interpretes multum variant. Ma- xime probabilis versio hæc est: Alamne exsultabundam (sup- ple tu dare posses, ut infra 18.) Pavoni, aut pennam ciconiæ aut struthocamelo? רננים Pavones esse sentit, & R. Abra- ham & alii. החסידה ciconia ob spietatem: & sic Græci quidam verterunt, quanquam alii avem dicunt esse Indicam. רננים autem esse struthocamelum evincunt sequentia ei animali proprie convenientia.

## 39:14
Verse 14.

WHEN IT HAS LEFT ITS EGGS IN ITS LAND, WILL YOU PERHAPS WARM THEM IN THE DUST) From the Hebrew, the Greeks are better: ὅτι ἀφήσει εἰς γῆν τὰ ὠὰ αὐτῆς καὶ ἐπὶ χοῦν ϑάλψει. But כי is for אשר: who leaves its eggs on the ground, and warms them in the dust.

While other birds prepare their nests with great diligence, lay their eggs in them, and persistently incubate them, this one deposits them on the bare earth and sand, so that they may be hatched by the heat of the sun, where they can easily be trampled.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

QVANDO DERELIQVIT OVA IN SVA TERRA, TV FORSITAN IN PVLVERE CALEFACIES EA) Ex Hebræo melius Græci: ὅτι ἀφήσει εἰς γῆν τὰ ὠὰ αὐτῆς καὶ ἐπὶ χοῦν ϑάλψει. Sed כי est pro אשר : qui humi relinquit ova sua, & in pulvere ea calefacit.

Cum aliæ aves magna cum diligentia nidos parent, in eos ova ponant, & illis pertinaciter in- cubent, hæc in nuda terra & arena ea deponit, ut calore solis excludantur, ubi facile conculcari pos- sunt.

## 39:15
Verse 15.

IT FORGETS THAT A FOOT MAY TRAMPLE THEM OR A BEAST OF THE FIELD MAY CRUSH THEM) Ostriches lay very many eggs, as Pliny 10, 52 teaches us. Therefore it easily happens that some are trampled by wild beasts, which would not happen if they chose solitary places for incubation. The following words mean the same thing, which you may translate best thus: it treats its chicks harshly (ἀσοργεῖ). Its labor will vanish through carelessness.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

OBLIVISCITVR QVOD PES CONCVLCET EA AVT BESTIA AGRI CONTERAT) Plurima ova pariunt struthiocameli, ut docet nos Plinius 10, 52.Itaque facile fit ut aliqua à feris conculcentur, quod non fieret, si loca solitaria ad incubationem sibi deligerent. Idem volunt sequentia, quæ sic optime vertas: dure habet (ἀσοργεῖ) pullos suos. Labor ejus evanescet per incuriam.

## 39:17
Verse 17.

GOD HAS DEPRIVED IT OF WISDOM, NOR HAS HE GIVEN IT UNDERSTANDING) Set it, that is, the ostrich: about which Pliny 11. A wonderful nature: but no less stupidity, in such great height of the rest of the body, when they think they are hidden if they have concealed their necks in a bush.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

PRIVAVIT EAM DEVS SAPIENTIA, NEC DEDIT ILLI INTELLIGENTIAM) Pone eum, id est struthocame- lum: de quo Plinius 11. Mira natura: sed non minus stoliditas in tanta reliqui corporis altitudine cum colla frutice occultaue- rint latere se existimantium.

## 39:18
Verse 18.

WHEN THE TIME COMES, IT RAISES ITS WINGS ON HIGH: IT MOCKS THE HORSE AND ITS RIDER) This is the very thing that Pliny says: The nature of birds follows, of which the ostriches are the largest and almost of the class of beasts. Those of Africa or Ethiopia exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse, and surpass them in speed.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

CVM TEMPVS FVERIT IN ALTVM ALAS ERI- GIT: DERIDET EQVVM ET ASCENSOREM EJVS) Hoc ipsum est quod dicit Plinius: Sequitur natura avium, quarum grandissimi & pene bestiarum generis struthiocameli. Africi vel Æthiopici altitudinem equitis insidentis equo exce- dunt, celeritate vincunt.

## 39:19
Verse 19.

WILL YOU CLOTHE ITS NECK WITH A NEIGHING?) He has well expressed what is placed in the Hebrew metaphorically, thunder.

Others, however, prefer to take it thus: A horse's neck is accustomed to be adorned with trappings and bells, but its best ornament is a clear neighing, an index of its nobility.

CIRCVMDABIS COLLO EJVS HINNITVM) Bene expresfit quod in Hebræo positum est μεταφορικῶς, tonitru.

Alii tamen ita malunt accipere: Solet collum equi phaleris & nolis ornari, sed optimus ejus orna- tus est clarus hinnitus, generositatis ejus index.

GLORIA NARIVM EJVS TERROR) Virgilius: Collectumque premens volvit sub naribus ignem.

Pergit Deus majestatis suæ demonstrationem in Behemoth.

SHALL HE WHO CONTENDS WITH GOD REST SO EASILY?) Better thus: are there enough arguments on God's part? Supply, it has been brought forward.

NVMQVID QVI CONTENDIT CVM DEO TAM FACILE CONQVIESCIT?) Melius sic: satisne à parte Dei argumentorum? Supple, allatum est.

## 40:4
Ver. 34.

I WHO HAVE SPOKEN LIGHTLY, WHAT CAN I ANSWER] Better: Behold I am vile, what shall I answer? I would prefer: Behold I have been light, not indeed out of stubbornness or a desire to contradict, but out of human infirmity and impatience: what shall I answer? I find nothing to reply. He adds: I HAVE SPOKEN ONCE, AND I WILL NOT ANSWER, AND TWICE, AND I WILL ADD NOTHING. I have uttered one thing and another thoughtlessly, now being more cautious I will silently humble myself.

Latin:

QVI LEVITER LOCVTVS SVM, RESPONDERE QVID POSSVM] Melius: Ecce vilis sum, quid respondeam? Malim: Ecce levis fui, non quidem ex per- tinacia aut contradicendi studio, sed humana infir- mitate & impatientia: quid respondebo? nihil in- venio quod referam. Addit: VNVMLOCV- TVS SVM, ET NON RESPONDEBO, ET DUO, ET NON ADDAM. Unum atque alte- rum incogitanter protuli, nunc cautior humiliter silebo.

Verse 7.

CRUSH THE WICKED IN THEIR PLACE] Wherever they dwell.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

CONTERE IMPIOS IN LOCO SUO] Ubicunque ha- bitant.

## 40:13
Verse 8.

AND SUBMERGE THEIR FACES IN THE PIT] By burial he wishes death to be understood.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET FACIES EORVM DEMERGE IN FOVEAM] Ex sepultura mortem vult intelligi.

## 40:14
Verse 9.

AND I WILL CONFESS THAT YOUR RIGHT HAND CAN SAVE YOU] If you can do these things, I will acknowledge that you do not need my help.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ET EGO CONFITEBOR QVOD SALVARE TE POSSIT DEXTRA TUA) Si ista potes, agnoscam te mei auxilii non egere.

## 40:15
Verse 10.

BEHOLD BEHEMOTH WHICH I MADE WITH THEE] בהמות for בהמת בהמור, that is, a most excellent beast. All the Hebrews understand the elephant: I made with thee, that is, I made him such that, however wild, he can be tamed and serve man. HE EATETH GRASS AS AN OX) More correctly, herb, since he is so great and so strong, yet he does not live by plunder, as many animals do, but from the fruits of the earth, as beasts of burden.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ECCE BEHEMOTH QVEM FECI TECUM] בהמות pro בהמת בהמור, id est, fera excellen- tissima. Elephantem intelligunt omnes Hebræi: Feci tecum, id est, talem feci, ut quantumvis ferus mansuescere, & homini inservire possit. FOENUM QVASI BOS COMEDIT) Rectius, herbam, cum tantus sit tamque validus, non tamen rapto vivit, ut mul- ta animantia, sed ex terræ fructibus, ut jumenta.

## 40:16
Verse 11.

HIS STRENGTH IS IN HIS LOINS) He understands the back. Pliny: The back is the hardest part of the hide. AND HIS FORCE IS IN THE NAVEL OF HIS BELLY) The word זרות is more correctly understood here as pain than as strength, and it is established that it is often taken thus. The bellies of elephants are soft, as Pliny teaches. Therefore they are very easily wounded. Furthermore, elephants do not suffer from flux of the belly, nor other kinds of diseases, by the same witness.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

FORTITUDO EJUS IN LUMBIS EJUS) Dorsum in- telligit. Plinius: Durissimum dorso tergum. ET VIRTUS ILLIUS IN UMBILICO VENTRIS EJUS) Vox זרות rectius hic de dolore quam de virtute in- telligetur, & sæpe sic sumi constat. Ventres molles ele- phanto, docente Plinio. Ideo facillime vulnerantur. Præ- tereà elephanti alvi profluvium, nec alia morborum genera sentiunt, eodem teste.

## 40:17
Verse 12.

HE MOVETH HIS TAIL LIKE A CEDAR) Understand the proboscis. For stringit in Hebrew is יחפץ, namely with a polished צ, as often, for ז: Moreover, חפז is to move; this is what Aristotle said in History of Animals 2, 16, as ἐλίσσει. THE SINEWS OF HIS STONES ARE WRAPPED TOGETHER) They are intertwined. For he has his testicles hidden within. Aristotle on the generation of animals, book 12.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

STRINGIT CAUDAM SUAM QVASI CEDRUM) Proboscidem intellige. Pro stringit in Hebr. est יחפץ, nimirum צ polito, ut sæpe, pro ז: Est autem חפז movere; hoc est quod ἐλίσσει, dixit Aristoteles de historia Animalium 2, 16. NERVI TESTICULORUM EJUS PERPLEXI) Intri- cati sunt. Nam testiculos intus absconditos habet. Aristo- teles de generatione animalium lib. 12.

## 40:18
Verse 13.

HIS BONES ARE AS STRONG PIECES OF BRASS) By bones understand what some call horns, others teeth. See Pliny 8, 3. HIS BONES ARE LIKE BARS OF IRON) Also the word which is here in the Hebrew, גרמיו, signifies his bones. Therefore, understand the teeth again.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

OSSA EJVS VELVT FISTULÆ ÆRIS) Per ossa intel- lige quæ aliis cornua, aliis dentes vocantur. Vide Plinium 8, 3. CARTILAGO ILLIVS QVASI LAMINÆ FERREÆ) Etiam quæ hic in Hebræo est vox גרמיו ossa ejus significat. Rursus ergo dentes intellige.

## 40:20
Verse 15.

SURELY THE MOUNTAINS BRING HIM FORTH FOOD) He eats nine Macedonian modii in one feeding. Aristotle, History of Animals 8, c. 9.

ALL THE BEASTS OF THE FIELD SHALL PLAY THERE ] Such is the clemency of the elephant. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 1, book 9, chapter 46.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

HVIC MONTES HERBAS FERVNT) Edit uno pastu modios Macedonicos novem. Aristoteles historiæ animan- tium 8. c. 9.

OMNES BESTIÆ AGRI LVDENT IBI ] Tanta est ele- phanti clementia. Aristoteles Histor. Animal. l. 1. l. 9. cap. 46.

## 40:21
Verse 16.

AND IN MOIST PLACES) Aristotle on the elephant in the aforementioned place, 9, chapter 46: ἔστι καὶ τὸ ζῶον παραποτάμιον: and 2, 16: ἑλῶδες ζῶον. Pliny, 8, chapter 10: They rejoice in all things most of all, and they wander about rivers. Aelian reported the same.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ET IN LOCIS HVMENTIBVS) Aristoteles de ele- phante dicto loco 9. cap. 46. ἔστι καὶ τὸ ζῶον παραποτάμιον: & 2, 16. ἑλῶδες ζῶον. Plinius 8. c. 10. Gaudent omnibus ma- xime, & circa fluvios vagantur. Idem prodidit Ælianus.

## 40:22
Verse 17.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

## 40:23
BEHOLD HE WILL DRINK UP A RIVER ] That similar expression: - - - and rivers drunk up by the Mede at dinner. Furthermore, that the thirst of elephants is immense, Polybius also reported in Histories, 3. Aristotle, in the aforementioned place 8, 6, says that fourteen Macedonian measures of amphorae were drunk by one elephant at a single draught.

Latin:

ECCE ABSORBEBIT FLVVIVM ] Simile illud: - - - epotaque flumina Medo Prandente. Cæterum ingentem esse elephantis sitim etiam Polybius Hi- storiar. 3. prodidit. Aristoteles dicto loco 8, 6. Amphoras mensuræ Macedonicæ quatuordecim ab elephante uno potu dicit haustas.

## 40:24
Verse 19.

IN HIS EYES AS IF A MAN WILL TAKE HIM ] More correctly thus: Shall anyone in his eyes: that is, openly and without snares, take him: as if he were to say, by no means. Elephants are accustomed to be taken only by snares: concerning which see Pliny, 8, chapter 8.

Others interpret this as referring to Dragons, which nature has prepared as enemies to the Elephant, which fly upon him unexpectedly while he is drinking at the river, and either gouge out his eyes, or wrap their coils like nooses around his trunk, so that they may either strangle him or suck out his blood.

AND WILL YOU PIERCE HIS NOSTRILS WITH STAKES) With a hook, as is accustomed to be done with small fish, as below in 21.

It can be rendered: AND HE WILL PIERCE HIS NOSTRILS WITH NOOSES, in the sense which we have mentioned.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

IN OCVLIS EJUS QVASI HOMO CAPIET EUM ] Rectius sic: An quis in oculis ejus: id est, palam & sine insi- diis, eum capiat: quasi dicat, minime vero. Elephantes tan- tum insidiis capi solent: de quibus vide Plinium 8. cap. 8.

De Draconibus alii accipiunt, quos natura hostes Elephanto paravit, qui ad fluvium bibentem ex im- proviso involant, eique vel oculos effodiunt, vel suis spiris quasi laqueis proboscidem involvunt, ut vel strangulent, vel sanguinem ejus exsugere possint.

ET IN SUDIBUS PERFORABIS NARES EJUS) Unco, quod minutis piscibus fieri solet, ut infra 21.

Reddi potest : ET LAQUEIS PERFO- RABIT NARES, eo quo diximus sensu.

## 41:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLI.

The majesty of God is shown in the Leviathan and the whale.

Vers. 1.

NO ONE IS SO CRUEL THAT I WILL STIR HIM UP] It is a continuation of the previous discourse, poorly divided into chapters. The true sense of this passage is: No one is so bold as to dare to stir him up (namely, while sleeping), much less to show himself to him while he is awake.

There is no reason why the original text should be blamed, as if the speech in it were poorly divided. For in the previous chapter the ferocity of the indomitable whale is described, that he cannot be caught, humbled, or divided as prey, nor immediately attacked. In this chapter, however, before passing on to other things, an application is made to God, that much less can anyone oppose himself to God, who created whales as a testimony of His power. Then a progression is instituted to the magnitude of the whale's members, and the skin, mouth and teeth, scales, fiery eyes and nostrils, neck, flesh, and heart are explained; as well as his strength, which shines forth from his horrible movement, immutable hardness, terrible effect, and lack of an equal. Moreover, an application to God was premised to these at the beginning of the chapter, so that we may understand that these things also are brought forward because of the incomprehensible magnitude and strength of God.

FOR WHO CAN RESIST MY FACE? The particle ו is more correctly translated as 'therefore' than as 'for'. If Leviathan is so terrible, who is there who can resist me, his creator.

Latin:

CAPUT XLI.

Majestas Dei in Leviathan & ceto ostenditur.

Vers. 1.

NON QVASI CRVDELIS SVSCITABO EVM] Continuatio est prioris sermonis male discerpta capitibus. Verus sensus est hujus loci: Nemo ita est audax, ut eum (dormientem scilicet) suscitare audeat, nedum ut vigili ei se ostendat.

Non est, quod arguatur textus originalis, quasi male discerpta in eo sit oratio. Nam in priori capite ferocia ceti indomabilis descripta est, quod non possit capi, humiliari, aut ut præda dividi, neque protinus oppugnari. Hoc autem capite, priusquam ad alia transeatur, applicatio sit ad Deum, quod multo minus Deo, qui cetos in potentiæ suæ testimonium creavit, quis se opponere possit. Dehinc progressus instituitur ad membrorum ceti magnitudinem, & explicantur cutis, os & dentes, squama, igniti oculi & nares, cervix, carnes & cor ejus; nec non ad fortitudinem, quæ elusescit ex motu horribili, duritie immutabili, effectu terribili & negato pari. Præmissa autem fuit hisce sub initium capitis applicatio ad Deum, ut intelligamus etiam hæc ob magnitudinem & fortitudinem Dei incomprehensibilem afferri.

QVIS ENIM RESISTERE POTEST VVLTVI MEO) Particula ו rectius per ergo quam per enim vertetur. Si Leviathan adeo est terribilis, quis est, qui mihi opifici ejus possit resistere.

## 41:1
Verse 20.

CAN YOU DRAW OUT LEVIATHAN WITH A HOOK?] He passes from terrestrial to maritime things. There are many huge beasts in the Indian Ocean, some of four iugera. See Pliny, 9, chapter 3. However, those things which are said here about Leviathan seem to agree best with that which is named Musar. Tyrants, who eat those smaller than their own kind, are accustomed to be compared to Leviathan. Isaiah 27:1, where the discourse is about the king of Egypt: Psalm 74:14. The Greeks translate this word sometimes as κῆτος, sometimes from a similarity as δράκοντα. However, God here recounts all the ways by which fish are accustomed to be caught, in order to show that this marine animal is immensely greater, so that it cannot be caught by any of such methods.

AND WILL YOU BIND HIS TONGUE WITH A CORD] A hook hanging from a line catches now the tongue of a fish, now the nose, now another part. See what follows.

Other fish are caught by a hook, the hook penetrating their tongue, and thus they are pulled out with cords, but in that way you will not be able to catch a whale. It has a large and strong tongue, so much so that Olaus Magnus, in his History of the Northern Peoples, book 21, chapter 9, reports it to be 21 feet long.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

AN EXTRAHERE POTERIS LEVIATHAN HA- MO?] A terrestribus ad maritima transit. Multæ sunt in Oceano Indico ingentes belluæ, quædam quaternum juge- rum. Vide Plinium 9. cap. 3. Videntur autem quæ hic de Leviathane dicuntur optime convenire in eam, cui nomen Musar. Leviathani autem comparari solent tyranni, qui mi- nutiores sui generis comedunt. Es. 27, 1. ubi de rege Ægypti sermo: Ps. 74, 14. Vocem hanc Græci modo κῆτος vertunt, modo ex simili δράκοντα. Refert autem hic Deus omnes modos, quibus pisces capi solent, ut ostendat marinum hoc animal immenso esse majus, ut nequeat ullo talium modo- rum capi.

ET FUNE LIGABIS LINGVAM EJUS ] Hamus à li- nea pendens modo linguam piscis, modo nasum, modo aliam partem apprehendit. Vide sequentia.

Alii pisces hamo capiuntur penetrante hamo linguam eorum, & sic funibus extrahuntur, sed eo modo non poteris cetum capere. Linguam habet ille magnam & validam, adeo ut 21. pedes longam referat Olaus M. de gent. Sept. l. 21. c. 9.

## 41:2
Verse 21.

WILL YOU PUT A RING IN HIS NOSTRILS?] How caught fish are accustomed to be kept. Some Greeks here [call it] κρίκον.

OR WILL YOU PIERCE HIS JAW WITH A BRACELET] What is here called a bracelet and ψέλλιον by the Greeks seems to be the same thing as the ring just mentioned.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

NUMQVID PONES CIRCULUM IN NARIBUS EJUS?] Quomodo capti pisces retineri solent. κρίκον hic Græci quidam.

AUT ARMILLA PERFORABIS MAXILLAM EJUS] Quod hic armilla dicitur & ψέλλιον Græcis, idem esse vide- tur, quod modo circulus.

## 41:3
Verse 22.

WILL HE MULTIPLY PRAYERS TO YOU] These and the following [words] are drawn from weak peoples who, when a great army approaches, act with prayers so that they may attempt a surrender, like the Gibeonites.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

NUMQVID MULTIPLICABIT AD TE PRECES] Hæc & quæ sequuntur ducta sunt à populis infirmis, qui ad- ventante magno exercitu precibus agunt, ut deditionem mo- liantur, ut Gabaonitæ.

## 41:5
Verse 24.

HE IS THE CHIEF OF THE WAYS OF GOD) He calls works the ways of God. The beginning, that which is the chief. Thus ראשית is taken in Amos 6, 1; Numbers 24, 20. Thus ἀρχὴ in Ecclesiasticus 11, 3. HE HATH MADE HIS SWORD TO APPROACH) The elephant is accustomed to be pierced by the horn of the rhinoceros. Pliny 8, c. 20. Others, because חרבו does not imply force or hostility, prefer to understand it of the proboscis and teeth, with which God armed him as with weapons or a sword.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

IPSE EST PRINCIPIVM VIARVM DEI) Vias Dei vocat opera. Principium, id quod præcipuum est. Sic ראשית sumitur Amos 6, 1. Num. 24, 20. Sic ἀρχὴ Eccle- siastici 11, 3. APPLICAVIT GLADIVM EJVS) Cornu Rhinocero- tis perfodi elephas solet. Plinius 8, c. 20. Alii, quia חרבו non infert vim vel hostilitatem, malunt de proboscide & dentibus, quibus tanquam armis aut gladio Deus eum armavit, intelligere.

## 41:5
Verse 24.

WILL YOU MOCK HIM AS A BIRD, OR BIND HIM FOR YOUR MAIDENS?] Better from the Hebrew: for your girls. Girls are accustomed to be delighted with sparrows, like Lesbia, or with doves, like Violantilla.

The elephant also plays with man: but the whale in no way.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

NUMQVID ILLUDES EI QVASI AVI, AUT LIGA- BIS EUM ANCILLIS TUIS ?) Melius ex Hebræo: puellis tuis. Solent puellæ delectari passeribus, ut Lesbia, aut co- lumbis ut Violantilla.

Ludit & Elephas cum homine: sed cetus nul- lo modo.

## 41:6
Verse 25.

WILL FRIENDS CUT HIM UP, WILL MERCHANTS DIVIDE HIM] The first part in the Hebrew has: will companions feast because of him? Will a feast of sale be celebrated on his account? So also the Chaldean and the Greeks. That [word] merchants in the Hebrew is Canaanites, Φοινίκων ἔθνη to the Greeks here, namely synecdochically, the species for the genus. The Phoenicians were most well-known for trade.

Because he cannot be caught, therefore neither can a feast be celebrated on his account, nor can he himself be divided among merchants.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

CONCIDENT EUM AMICI, DIVIDENT ILLUM NEGOTIATORES] Prior pars in Hebræo habet: cœnabunt propter eum socii. An cœna venditionalis propter ipsum cele- brabitur? Sic Chaldæus quoque & Græci. Illud negotiatores in Hebræo est Cananæi, Φοινίκων ἔθνη Græcis hic, nempe συνεκ- δοχικῶς species pro genere. Phœnices mercatu notissimi.

Quia capi non potest, ideo nec cœna propter ipsum celebrari, nec dividi inter negotiatores ipse potest.

## 41:7
Vers. 26. WILL YOU FILL HIS SKIN WITH BARBED IRONS, AND HIS HEAD WITH FISH SPEARS?] If we believe Rabbi Levi, and שכות, which he here translates as barbed irons, and צלצל, which he translates as fish spears, are instruments with which fish are accustomed to be pierced, as if you were to say: Will you fill his skin with tridents, or his head with a fishing knife? Fish are accustomed to be struck first with tridents, as Aristotle also teaches in History of Animals 4, ch. 10, and afterwards opened with knives.

Latin:

Vers. 26. NUMQVID IMPLEBIS SAGENAS PEL- LE EJUS, ET GURGUSTIUM PISCIUM CAPITE ILLIUS?] Si Rabbino Levi credimus, & שכות, quod hic vertit sagenas, & צלצל, quod gurgustium, instrument sunt, quibus confodi pisces solent, quasi dicas: An implebis fuscinis pellem ejus, aut cultro piscatorio caput illius? Solent fuscinis primum pisces feriri, ut & Aristoteles docet de Histor. Animal. 4. c. 10. & postea cultris aperiri.

## 41:8
Vers. 27.

LAY YOUR HAND UPON HIM: REMEMBER THE BATTLE, AND DO NOT ADD TO SPEAK ANY MORE) Better thus from the Hebrew: Lay your hand upon him, do not remember the battle any more: That is, when you are not able to catch him by force, see if you can by guile, by soothing him and feigning friendship.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

PONE SVPER EVM MANVM TVAM: MEMENTO BELLI, NEC VLTRA ADDAS LOQVI) Melius sic ex Hebræo: Pone super eum manum tuam, belli ne ultra memineris: Id est, quando vi eum capere non vales, vide an dolo possis, cum demulcendo, & amicitiam simulando.

## 41:9
Vers. 28.
