BEHOLD HIS HOPE WILL FRUSTRATE HIM] In the Hebrew: Behold his hope (i.e., concerning him) has lied. That is, even this hope of catching him by guile will not succeed.

AND AT THE SIGHT OF HIM HE WILL BE CAST DOWN) More correctly: at his appearance he will collapse. Supply: anyone. No one would dare to approach so near to him as to attempt guile.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ECCE SPES EJVS FRVSTRABITVR EVM] In Hebræo: Ecce spes ejus (i. e. de eo) mentita est. Id est, etiam hæc spes dolo eum capiendi non succedet.

ET VIDENTIBVS CVNCTIS PRÆCIPITABITVR) Rectius: ad aspectum ejus concidet. Supple quilibet. Nemo ausurus sit tam prope ad eum accedere, ut dolos tentet.

## 41:11
Verse 2.

WHO HAS GIVEN TO ME BEFOREHAND THAT I MAY REPAY HIM? Who has anticipated me with a favor? Paul looked to this passage in Rom. 11:35, τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ καὶ ἀνταποδοθήσεται αὐτῷ. This statement, however, is as it were parenthetical. For it returns immediately to the previous discourse.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

QVIS ANTE DEDIT MIHI VT REDDAM EI?) Quis me beneficio prævenit? Hunc locum respexit Paulus Rom. 11, 35. τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ καὶ ἀνταποδοθήσεται αὐτῷ. Hoc vero dictum velut παρενθετικῶς. Reditur enim statim ad priorem sermonem.

## 41:12
I WILL NOT SPARE HIM AND WITH POWERFUL WORDS AND WORDS COMPOSED FOR ENTREATY) More correctly thus from the Hebrew: I will not be silent about his branches (the tubes on his forehead) and the matter of all his strength and the elegance of his proportion (thus Vitruvius calls συμμετρίαν, which Gellius calls 'competentia'). There is here דין for דין, because Jod was anciently written also for Tsere.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NON PARCAM EI ET VERBIS POTENTIBVS ET AD DEPRECANDVM COMPOSITIS) Rectius sic ex Hebræo: Non silebo ramos ejus (fistulas in fronte) & rem omnium virium ejus & concinnitatem commensus (ita Vitruvius vocat συμμετρίαν, quam Gellius competentiam, ipsius. Est hîc דין pro דין, quia Jod antiquitus etiam pro Tsere scribebatur.

## 41:13
Verse 4.

WHO HAS UNCOVERED THE FACE OF HIS GARMENT?) A simile taken from a horse: who shall strip off his blankets or saddles?

Others explain it concerning the skin: Who would dare to flay him, as other animals, and strip off the skin with which he is clothed as with a garment?

AND INTO THE MIDST OF HIS MOUTH WHO SHALL ENTER?] In the Hebrew: with his bit who shall come? Who will come to cast a bit into him? That kind of bridle is most harsh, therefore it is called a double bridle by the Hebrews.

Others interpret it in this way: INTO THE DOUBLE OF HIS BRIDLE WHO SHALL COME? Who would dare to insert a hand, arm, or body into both parts of the mouth or the upper and lower jaw, as is accustomed to be done to a horse and other animals, as Samson even dared in the lion, Jud. 14:6. But the horrible maw of the whale deters everyone. Olaus Magnus testifies that one was seen whose maw was 13 feet, and whose jaws were three feet wide and 23 feet long.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QVIS REVELAVIT FACIEM INDVMENTI EJVS?) Simile ab equo sumtum: quis ei detrahet stragulas aut ephippia?

Alii de cute explicant: Quis audeat illum excoriare, ut alia animalia, eique cutem detrahere, qua ut veste indutus est?

ET IN MEDIVM ORIS EJVS QVIS INTRABIT?] In Hebræo: cum lupato ejus quis adveniet? quis veniet ut lupatum ei injiciat. Id fræni genus asperrimum est, ideo duplicitas fræni dicitur Hebræis.

Alii hoc modo interpretantur: IN DUPLICITATEM FRENI EJUS QUIS VENIET? Quis manum, brachium aut corpus utrique oris parti vel maxillæ superiori & inferiori audeat inferere, ut equo & aliis animalibus fieri solet, Simson etiam in leone ausus est, Jud. 14. 6. Sed ceti rictus horribilis omnes deterret. Olaus M. testatur visum, cujus rictus 13. pedes, maxillæ tres latæ, 23. longæ essent.

## 41:14
Verse 5.

WHO WILL OPEN THE DOORS OF HIS FACE?] Jaws for inserting a bit.

ROUND ABOUT HIS TEETH IS TERROR] The very rows of his teeth are formidable.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

PORTAS VVLTVSEJVS QVIS APERIET?] Ma- xillas ad inferendum lupatum.

PER GTRVM DENTIVM EJVS FORMIDO] Ipsi ordines dentium ejus formidabiles sunt.

## 41:15
Verse 6.

HIS BODY IS LIKE MOLTEN SHIELDS] Aquila also translates his body. For molten shields you might more correctly put the strength of shields, that is συνασπισμὸς, a tortoise formation, to which that connection of scales is very similar, which the following words also explain.

Because the whale lacks scales, they think the density of its skin is described metaphorically, because it is so great, as if it were clothed in a breastplate, or they take it as referring to the scales of the head, or those bony shields which surround the bone like scales. Arrian, however, in his Indika, book 8, reports that a whale was seen in India of 50 cubits, with a scaly hide, so thick that it equaled a cubit, with oysters and seaweed growing on it.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

CORPVS EJVS QVASI SCVTA FVSILIA] Corpus ejus vertit & Aquila. Pro scuta fusilia rectius ponas fortitudi- nes scutorum, id est συνασπισμὸς, testudo, cui simillimus squammarum ille connexus, quem & sequentia explicant.

Quia balæna squammis caret, metaphorice densitatem cutis ejus describi putant, quod tanta sit, quasi lorica indutus esset, vel de squamis capitis, vel osseis illis scutls, quæ instar squammarum os cin- gunt, accipiunt. Arianus tamen in Indicis l. 8. re- fert, inIndia cetum visum 50. cubitis, corio squamo- so, tam crasso, ut cubitum æquaret, innatis ei ostreis & algis.

## 41:18
Verse 9.

HIS SNEEZING IS THE SPLENDOR OF FIRE] By his breath the dashed waters catch fire. The following words explain the same thing with more words and poetic abundance.

It is added: HIS EYES ARE LIKE THE EYELIDS OF THE DAWN, as the sun appears red and fiery at dawn. Olaus Magnus, book 20, chapter 1, reports concerning Norwegian whales that their eyes shine like huge flames, so that when seen from afar by fishermen they appear to be huge fires.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

STERNVTATIO EJVS SPLENDOR IGNIS] Flatu ejus collisæ æquæ ignescunt. Idem pluribus verbis ac poetica ubertate explicant quæ sequuntur.

Additur: OCULI EJUS UT PALPE- BRÆ AURORÆ, ut Sol in aurora apparet ru- beus & igneus. Olaus M. l. 20. c. 1. de cetis Norve- gianis refert oculos eorum ingentium flammarum modo lucere, ut procul visi piscatoribus ingentes ignes esse videantur.

## 41:22
Verse 13.

IN HIS NECK WILL DWELL STRENGTH] Alacrity.

AND BEFORE HIS FACE GOES WANT] And sorrow will be turned into joy for him: he will rejoice at the fear of sailors, whose ships he often overturns. See below 15.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

IN COLLO EJVS MORABITVR FORTITVDO] Alacritas.

ET FACIEM EJVS PRÆCEDIT EGESTAS] Et ei vertetur in lætitiam dolor : gaudebit metu nautarum, quorum sæpe naves evertit. Vide infra 15.

## 41:23
Verse 14.

THE MEMBERS OF HIS FLESH JOINED TOGETHER] The flesh.

HE WILL SEND LIGHTNINGS TO HIM, AND THEY SHALL NOT BE CARRIED TO ANOTHER PLACE] In the Hebrew: They are solid, and therefore they are not moved.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

MEMBRA CARNIVM EJVS COHÆRENTIA SIBI] Pulpæ.

MITTET AD EVM FVLMINA, ET IN LOCVM ALIVM NON FERENTVR] In Hebræo: Solide sunt, ideoque non commoventur.

## 41:24
Verse 15.

AND IT SHALL BE HARDENED AS THE ANVIL OF A HAMMER-SMITH) It is hard as an anvil, as the Greeks have it here, or, as others translate, the lower millstone.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ET STRINGETVR QVASI MALLEATORIS IN- CVS) Durum est ut incus, ut hic habent Græci, aut, ut alii vertunt, molæ meta.

## 41:25
Verse 16. WHEN HE SHALL BE LIFTED UP THE ANGELS SHALL FEAR] When he shall raise himself above the waters, even the most mighty shall fear. אילים is translated as rulers and leaders, Exod. 15, 15. Ezech. 31, 11. 17, 13.

AND BEING TERRIFIED THEY SHALL BE PURGED] Through contraction (that is, through fear of shipwreck) they shall purge themselves, that is, their bowels shall be loosened. Thus Rabbi Levi.

Schindler renders it: THEY SHALL DEFLECT, they shall snatch themselves away, because יחטאו also signifies to deflect.

Latin:

Vers. 16. CVM SVBLATVS FVERIT TIMEBVNT ANGELI] Cum se super aquas extulerit, timebunt etiam fortissimi. אילים vertitur ἄρχοντες & ἡγεμένοι Exod. 15, 15. Ezech. 31, 11. 17, 13.

ET TERRITI PVRGABVNTVR] Præ contractione (id est, præ metu naufragii) se purgabunt, id est, solvetur eis alvus. Sic Rabbi Levi.

Schindlerus reddit: DEFLECTENT, pro- ripient se, quia יחטאו etiam significat deflectere.

## 41:29
Verse 20.

HE SHALL ESTEEM THE HAMMER AS STRAW) Others better, I think, as a catapult, by which missiles are thrown, so that it may agree with the following member.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

QVASI STIPVLAM ÆSTIMABIT MALLEUM) Alii melius, ut puto, catapultam, qua tela ejiciuntur, ut conveniat cum sequenti membro.

## 41:30
Verse 21.

UNDER HIM SHALL BE THE RAYS OF THE SUN, AND HE SHALL STREW GOLD FOR HIMSELF) Better thus: with him shall be (those spears of the catapult thrown, of which he had treated) as fragments of potsherds, (thus they shall rebound from the hard skin) and he shall cast down the sharp (iron, indeed) into the mud, that is, into the bottom of the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

SVB IPSO ERVNT RADII SOLIS, ET STERNET SIBI AVRVM) Melius sic: apud ipsum erunt (hastæ illæ catapultæ ejectæ, de quibus egerat) ut testarum fragmina, (ita à dura cute resilient) & acutum (ferrum nempe) ille dejiciet in lutum, id est, in fundum maris.

## 41:31
Verse 22.

HE WILL MAKE IT BOIL LIKE A POT, THE DEEP SEA) He will stir up such great foam. Pliny, book 9, chapter 3: They turn the seas from the bottom; chapter 6: The waves, indeed, are such as no storms roll, in response to his breathing and striking.

HE WILL SET IT AS WHEN OINTMENTS BOIL) He will make it like a perfumer's cauldron: which the LXX call ἐξάλειπτρον, and Aquila and Symmachus call μυρεψητήριον. Olympiodorus interprets it as a vessel of ointment.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

FERVESCERE FACIET QVASI OLLAM PRO- FVNDVM MARE) Spumas tantas excitabit. Plinius 9. cap. 3. Ab imo vertunt maria, cap. 6. Fluctus vero ad anhelitus ictusque quanti nulli turbines volvunt.

PONET QVASI CVM VNGVENTA EBVLLI- VNT) Faciet eam ut ahenum pigmentarii: quod ἐξάλει- πτρον LXX. Aquilæ & Symmacho μυρεψητήριον. Olym- piodorus interpretatur τραλλίον μύρο.

## 41:32
Verse 23.

AFTER HIM A PATH WILL SHINE, HE WILL DEEM THE ABYSS AS GROWING OLD) The meaning is: he will leave a whitening path behind him, so that he (namely, the one who sees it) thinks the sea is turning gray.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

POST EVM LVCEBIT SEMITA, ÆSTIMABIT ABYSSVM QVASI SENESCENTEM) Sensus est : post se albicantem relinquet semitam, ita ut putet (nempe qui vi- det) pelagus canescere.

## 41:34
Verse 25.

HE SEES EVERYTHING HIGH) That is, he looks down upon it.

HE IS KING OVER ALL THE SONS OF PRIDE) The LXX: 'He is also king of all that are in the waters.' The word שחץ, which is written here in the Hebrew as שחץ, signifies 'to emerge' to the Arabs. He holds dominion over all things that emerge from the sea.

He explains everything concerning the whale. The ancients in the literal sense of chapter 40 explain it as the Devil, which can be seen in Ambrose, book 1, On Repentance, chapter 13; Jerome on this passage; Augustine, book 2, On Genesis according to the letter, chapter 20; Gregory the Great, book 32, chapter 10 and following; while others apply it to the Devil only allegorically, judging that it speaks properly of the Elephant. Similarly, the ancients explain chapter 41 according to the letter as the Devil: but it treats in the proper and literal sense of the whale, as the most excellent testimony of divine power in the waters: yet those who weave some allegory here concerning the Devil do not deserve reproach: as in Isaiah 28:1, Leviathan designates the Devil. Just as the world is to the sea, so that Lord of the world is compared to the greatest monster of the sea, because of his ferocity, because he cannot be caught, or bound, or forced into servitude, or attacked with impunity, and also because of his unbroken strength and power, which is figured in the horrible movement of the whale, his inviolable hardness, his terrible effect, and his lack of an equal: Then because of the members of the Devil (spiritual ones), namely the skin, which is not easily pierced, as hypocrisy and lies; the gaping mouth, or the desire to destroy; the horrible teeth (temptations); the scales (the concatenated multitude of the reprobate); the fiery eyes and nostrils (false teachers); the stiff neck (pertinacity); and the hard heart (lack of mercy), concerning which see B. Scultetus. We note here only the interpretation of Cocceius, who thinks that by these words is described the limitation of the power of Leviathan, and the ease of his coercion by God, so that the meaning is: He has no power over the land, although he is most robust in the sea; yet on dry land he has no power, since the earth was given to man, so that he might not fear these monsters on it. God sees everything high; He is King over all the sons of ferocity, not only this one, but He can coerce all the ferocious and powerful ones. But the common and vulgar interpretation is simpler. Nor is the word 'God' in the text. Therefore, it is rashly inserted. Cocceius brings forward many new expositions here and there, which might seem congruent: But not rarely they are foreign, and by their very novelty are not undeservedly held in suspicion.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

OMNE SVBLIME VIDET) Id est despicit.

IPSE EST REX SVPER VNIVERSOS FILIOS SV- PERBIÆ) LXX. ἀυτὸς κὰι βασιλεὺς πάντων ἳ ἐν τοῖς ὕδασιν Vox شخيط quæ hic in Hebræo שחץ scribitur, Arabibus emergere significat. Regnum obtinet in omnia, qua è mari emergunt.

De ceto explicat omnia. Veteres sensu litera- li c. 40. de Diabolo exponunt, quod videre est apud Ambros. l. 1. de pœnit. c. 13. Hieronym. in h. l. Au- gust. l. 2. de Genes. ad lit. c. 20. Gregorium M. lib. 32. c. 10. & seq. aliis non nisi allegorici Diabolo ap- plicantibus, quæ proprie de Elephanto loqui cen- sent. Similiter cap. 41. exponunt veteres quoad li- teram de Diabolo: quod vero sensu proprio & lite- rali de ceto, tanquam excellentissimo in aquis divi- næ potentiæ testimonio, agit: Neque tamen repre- hensionem merentur, qui hic etiam allegoriam ali- quam de Diabolo texunt: uti Es. 28, 1. Leviathan Diabolum designat. Quemadmodum mundus ma- ri, sic ille mundi Dominus maximo maris monstro comparatur, ob ferociam, quia non potest capi, aut ligari, aut ad servitutem cogi, aut oppugnari impune, nec non ob vim & potentiam infractam, quæ figu- ratur in ceti motu horribili, duritie inviolabili, effe- ctus terribili, negato pari: Tum ob membra Diaboli (Spiritualia) cutem nempe, quæ non facile detegi- tur, utpote hypocrisin, & mendacia, os hians, vel cu- piditatem perdendi, dentes horribiles (tentationes) Squamas (multitudinem concatenatam reprobo- rum) ignitos oculos, & nares (doctores falsos) cer- vicem duram (pertinaciam) & cor durum (immi- sericordiam) de quibus vid. B. Scultetus. Notamus solum hic Cocceji interpretationem, qui putat ver- bis hisce describi limitationem potentiæ Leviathan, & coercitionem ejus Deo facilem, ut sensus sit: Non est potestas ei super terram, licet robustissimus sit in mari, in sicco tamen nullam habet potestatem, cum terra data sit homini, ut in illa non timeat hæc mon- stra. Omne altum videt Deus, ipse est Rex super o- mnes filios ferociæ, non hunc tantum, sed & omnes fe- roces, & potentes potest coercere. Sed communis, & vulgata interpretatio simplicior. Neque habetur in textu vox Dei. Temere ergo ingeritur. Multas passim novas expositiones adfert Coccejus, quæ videri possint congruæ: Sed non raro alienæ sunt, ipsaque novitate sua non immerito suspectæ ha- bentur.

## 42:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLII.

Job, having humbly prayed, performs penance: he is preferred by the Lord to his friends, for whom he prays, and receiving double what he had lost, he dies full of days.

Vers. 1.

BUT JOB ANSWERING THE LORD, SAID] Acknowledging now that certain things had escaped him less than well-digested, and seeing that with such great wisdom of God appearing in all created things, nothing is done by Him without reason.

Latin:

CAPUT XLII.

Job humiliter deprecatus pœnitentiam agit: à Domino præfertur amicis, pro quibus orat, ac duplicia recipiens eorum, quæ amiserat, plenus dierum moritur.

Vers. 1.

RESPONDENS AVTEM JOB DOMINO, DIXIT] Agnoscens jam quædam sibi excidisse minus bene cocta vi- densque cum tanta Dei sapientia in omnibus rebus conditis appareat, nihil ab eo fieri absque ratione.

## 42:3
Vers. 3.

WHO IS THIS, THAT HIDETH COUNSEL WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE?] That is, who among men is so unskilled that he would dare to deny that all things are administered by the most wise counsel of God? He approves what God had said 38, 2.

THEREFORE I HAVE SPOKEN FOOLISHLY] 19, 6. & elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

QVIS EST ISTE, QVI CELAT CONSILIVM ABS- QVE SCIENTIA?] Id est, quis est hominum, qui tam im- peritus sit, ut negare audeat Dei consilio sapientissimo cuncta administrari? Approbat quod Deus dixerat 38, 2.

IDEO INSIPIENTER LOCVTVS SVM] 19, 6. & alibi.

## 42:5
Vers. 5.

WITH THE HEARING OF THE EAR I HAVE HEARD THEE] I know Thee more perfectly now from this revelation, like those who first heard a man's voice, and then behold him.

Eusebius, book 1 of the Demonstration of the Gospel, chapter 4, maintains that God was thus seen by Job in an assumed visible form: but Rabbi Moses Maimonides in More Nebuch. book 3, ch. 23, Gregory the Great, and Philip the Presbyter explain it as concerning the eyes of the mind.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

AVDITV AVRIS AVDIVI TE] Perfectius te jam co- gnosco ex hac revelatione, ut illi, qui hominis vocem primum audierunt, deinde eum conspiciunt.

Sic Deum assumta forma visibili Jobo conspe- ctum, Euseb. l. 1. de demonstr. Ev. cap. 4. statuit: Rabbi Moses Maimonides vero More Nebuch. l. 3. c. 23. Gregor. M. & Phil. Presbyt. de oculis mentis exponunt.

## 42:6
Vers. 6.

THEREFORE I REPREHEND MYSELF] I change my deed.

AND I DO PENANCE IN DUST AND ASHES] In dust and ashes, as those who are mourning are accustomed to do. This is the end of the metrical parts.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

IDCIRCO IPSE ME REPREHENDO] Muto factum.

ET AGO POENITENTIAM IN FAVILLA ET CINERE] In pulvere & cinere, ut lugentes solent. Hic est finis metricorum.

## 42:7
Vers. 17. IN THEE AND IN THY TWO FRIENDS] Elihu is not named here, just as he was not above at 2, 11, perhaps because he was a follower of one of the three.

BECAUSE YOU HAVE NOT SPOKEN what is right before me as my servant Job has] Job had spoken many true things, especially about his own life: but they were slandering an innocent man because of his present misfortune. AND OFFER A BURNT OFFERING FOR YOURSELVES] Namely through Job, whom I wish to be for you as a priest, as he is most dear to me. The Greeks explain the matter here paraphrastically: 'Take seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and he shall make a burnt offering for you.' The burnt offering pertains to this, that God's most free dominion over all things may be acknowledged. And the Hebrews think that this was the only kind of sacrifice before the law of Moses. Moreover, the number seven is dedicated to sacrifices, Leviticus 23:18. SO THAT FOLLY MAY NOT BE IMPUTED TO YOU] In the Hebrew: 'Lest I afflict you with ignominy': that is, with some prodigious punishment. The Greeks: 'For if it were not for him, I would have destroyed you.'

Latin:

Vers. 17. IN TE ET IN DVOS AMICOS TVOS] Eliu hic non nominatur, ut nec supra 2, 11. forte quod assecla esset alicujus trium.

QVONIAM NON ESTIS LOCVTI CORAM ME RECTVM VT SERVVS MEVS JOB] Job pleraque vera dixerat, maxime de vita sua: at illi ex praesente infortunio innocentem calumniabantur. ET OFFERTE HOLOCAUSTUM PRO VOBIS] Nempe per Jobum, quem ut mihi amicissimum vobis esse vo- lo pro Sacerdote. Graeci hic rem παραφρασικῶς explicant: λάβετε ἑπτὰ μόσχους καὶ ἑπτὰ κριοὺς, καὶ πορεύθητε πρὸς τὸν θεράποντά με Ἰὼβ, καὶ ποιήσει καύπωσιν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν. Holo- caustum eo pertinet, ut Dei dominium liberrimum in res omnes agnoscatur. Et id solum fuisse sacrificii genus ante legem Mosis putant Hebraei. Heptas autem sacrificiis dicata Levit. 23, 18. UT NON IMPUTETUR VOBIS STULTITIA] In He- braeo: Ne afficiam vos ignominia: id est, poena aliqua prodi- giosa. Graeci: εἰ μὴ γὰρ δι' αὐτὸν ἀπώλεσα ἂν ὑμᾶς.

## 42:9
Ver. 9.

AND THE LORD ACCEPTED THE FACE OF JOB] He heard him interceding for others: LXX 'and he took away their sin because of Job.' Job is here a figure of Christ. THE LORD ALSO TURNED TO THE REPENTANCE OF JOB] In the Hebrew: 'to the conversion of Job': That is, so that He might restore him to his former fortune. LXX 'and the Lord increased Job.' The change of Job's fortune is indicated: but mention is made of captivity, because he had been in the captivity and power of Satan by divine permission, from whose bonds he was freed. WHEN HE PRAYED FOR HIS FRIENDS] At that very time, God began to do that, when Job was pleading the cause of his friends before God. The LXX add: 'He forgave them their sin.' AND THE LORD ADDED ALL THINGS THAT WERE JOB'S DOUBLE] Understand this concerning possessions, not children, as appears below in verse 13. The Hebrews give the reason, because his former children also remained with him before God. Gregory Nazianzen gives this same reason in his Funeral Oration for Pulcheria. Bede and Philip the Presbyter [say this], because the former children were not lost, but were to be returned on the day of the restitution of all things.

Latin:

Verf. 9.

ET SUSCEPIT DOMINUS FACIEM JOB] Eum ex- audivit pro aliis deprecantem: LXX. καὶ ἔλυσε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν αὐτοῖς διὰ τὸν Ἰὼβ. Job hic figura Christi. DOMINUS QVOQVE CONVERSUS EST AD POE- NITENTIAM JOB] In Hebraeo: ad conversionem Iobi: Id est, ut eum restitueret in priorem fortunam. LXX. ὁ δὲ κύριος ηὔξησε τὸν Ἰὼβ. Indicatur mutatio fortunae Jobi: captivitatis autem mentio fit, quia fuerat in captivitate ac po- testate Satanae divina permissione, e cujus vinculis liberatus est. CUM ORARET ILLE PRO AMICIS SUIS] Eo ipso tempore, id facere coepit Deus, quo Job amicorum causam apud Deum agebat. Addunt LXX. ἀφῆκεν αὐτοῖς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν. ET ADDIDIT DOMINUS OMNIA QVAE FUE- RUNT JOB DUPLICIA] Hoc de possessionibus intellige, non de liberis, ut apparet infra 13. Causam reddunt Hebraei, quia & liberi priores ei manebant apud Deum. Hanc etiam causam dant Gregor. Nazianz. in Orat. in fun. Pulcher. Beda & Philip. Presbyter, quia priores liberi non amissi, sed in die restitutio- nis omnium reddendi erant.

## 42:11
Ver. 11.

AND THEY SHOOK THEIR HEAD OVER HIM] By that very gesture they showed how they grieved for the evils that had befallen him. AND THEY GAVE HIM EACH ONE EWE] He understands a coin struck with the sign of a sheep, as in Genesis 33:29 and Joshua 24:32. From this it appears how old the custom of 'erasmos' (a gift/contribution) is. AND ONE GOLDEN EARRING] So also Aquila and Theodotion. But Symmachus [translates it as] 'a shoulder-piece,' in which way the Hebrew word is clearly taken in Proverbs 11:22.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET MOVERUNT SUPER EUM CAPUT] Gestu ipso ostenderunt quam dolerent de malis quae ipsi obvenerant. ET DEDERUNT EI QVISQVE OVEM UNAM] Nummum intelligit ovis signo percussum ut Gen. 33, 29. & Jo- suae 24, 32. apparet hinc quam vetus sit mos ἐρασμοῦ. ET INAUREM AUREAM UNAM] Sic & Aquila & Theodotion. At Symmachus ἑπώμιον, quo modo vox He- braea manifeste sumitur Prov. 11, 22.

## 42:14
Ver. 14.

THE NAME OF THE ONE IS DAY] 'Day' to the Hebrews is happiness. That name is opposed to those shadows in which Job had complained he was wandering, Job 19:8 and elsewhere. THE NAME OF THE SECOND IS CASSIA] A sweet-smelling aroma. That name is opposed to the rot and stench, about which the same Job had complained, 7:5. AND THE NAME OF THE THIRD IS HORN OF ANTIMONY] By antimony, eyes become more beautiful, as we have said elsewhere. That name is opposed to the weeping with which Job's eyes had swollen, 16:17. 'Horn' signifies an abundance of antimony. These names were monuments to Job and his family, of how great a happiness God had restored them to from their miseries.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

NOMEN UNIUS DIEM] Dies Hebraeis est felicitas. Id nomen oppositum tenebris illis, in quibus versari se conque- stus erat Job 19, 8. & alibi. NOMEN SECVNDI CASSIAM] Optime olens aroma. Oppositum id nomen putredini & foetori, de quibus idem Job questus erat 7, 5. ET NOMEN TERTIAE CORNV STIBII] Stibio oculi pulchriores fiunt, ut diximus alibi. Id nomen oppo- situm fletui quo intumuerant oculi Jobi 16, 17. Cornu abun- dantiam stibii significat. Haec nomina monumenta erant Jobo Familiaeque ejus, ex quibus miseriis quantae felicitati eos Deus reddidisset.

## 42:15
Ver. 15. AND THEIR FATHER GAVE THEM AN INHERITANCE AMONG THEIR BROTHERS] Because of his immense wealth, he gave his daughters not just a little something for a dowry, but gave each one tenth-parts of the inheritance, contrary to custom. See Numbers 27:8.

Latin:

Vers. 15. DEDITQVE EIS PATER SVVS HAEREDI- TATEM INTER FRATRES EARUM] Ob ingentes di- vitias filiabus non paululum aliquid pro dote, sed de haereditate decimas cuique partes dedit, praeter morem. Vide Numer. XXVII, 8.

## 42:16
AND FULL OF DAYS] What follows here in the Greek codices is of little certain authority. The number of years is probably gathered from the 140 years granted to Job after his restitution. For since God returned everything to him double, it is likely that his former years were also doubled, and thus he was seventy years old when he was tempted, and consequently completed 210 years in living. The Appendix to Job among the Greeks, that Jobab was the great-grandson of Esau, the fifth from Abraham, King of Idumea, and lived in the borders of Idumea and Arabia, and that his friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, were each a King of his own dominion, is not in the Hebrew, nor in Aquila or Symmachus: and therefore it is of no authority.

And these [are] the annotations on the Grotius annotations to the book of Job. For it is not pleasing to cling to minute criticisms; nor to annotate everything where he has not grasped the sense of the Sacred text. That is the duty of interpreters and commentators. And Grotius has dealt quite skillfully with most words and phrases. Therefore, it was decided to retain his observations, though adding other interpretations here and there, when others seemed to explain them more conveniently. In the Index of verses, circumscribed by certain limits, we prepare defenses of the passages especially pertaining to the Articles of faith. Whoever desires a sufficiently convenient version and clear interpretation of the whole very difficult book, let him approach the Typical Analysis of our blessed Scultetus: which can here take the place of huge commentaries. For it surpasses in the felicity of its interpretation the prolixity of the laborious volumes of Pineda and others, to the reading of which one must bring judgment. For they abound with many errors and corruptions, like other commentaries of the Papist interpreters, and are stuffed with them. One may also approach the commentary on Job by Dr. Sebastian Schmidt, most recently published, whose learned version and interpretation from the signification of words and the coherence of the text (the best method of interpreting, which you would rightly prefer to the collation of many passages, as being often extraneous, and to the collection of the polysemy of words from other texts, which at least confuses the reader and often renders the uniquely true signification, proper to the passage at hand, doubtful, or involves it in diverse senses) was transmitted to me by the Author, after I had already finished this work of some sort a year and a half ago; [and] as I ran through it, it contributed a certain 'great addition' to these annotations here and there. We end here, and attribute praise to God alone.

Latin:

ET PLENUS DIERUM] Quae hic sequuntur in Graecis codicibus parum certae sunt fidei. Numerus annorum probabiliter colligitur e 140. annis post restitutionem Jobo concessis. Quum enim omnia duplicia ei rediderit Deus, vero affine est, etiam annos priores duplicatos, adeoque septuagenarium eum fuisse, cum tentare- tur, ac proinde 210. anno vivendo complevisse. Appendix Jobi apud Graecos, quod Jobab prone- pos Esavi, quintus ab Abraham Idumaeae Rex fuerit inque confinibus Idumaeae & Arabiae habitarit, ac amici ejus, Eliphas, Bildad & Sophar suae quisque ditionis Rex extiterint, in Ebraeo non habetur, nec apud Aquilam aut Symmachum: ideoque nullius fidei est.

Atque haec ad annotata Grotiana ad lib. Jo- bi. Non euim minutis Criticis inhaerere placet; Neque omnia illa, ubi sensum textus Sacri assecu- tus non est, annotare. Id interpretum, & commen- tatorum munus est. Et dextre satis in plerisque verbis & phrasibus versatus est Grotius. Ideo retinere placuit ejus observationes, additis tamen alicubi, cum alii commodius visi sunt exponere, aliis interpretationibus. In Elencho versuum, cer- tis finibus circumscripto, ac locorum cumprimis ad Articulos fidei spectantium vindicias paramus. Qui totius libri difficillimi versionem satis commo- dam, & interpretationem luculentam desiderat, B. Sculteti nostri Typicam Analysin adeat: quae ingen- tium commentariorum vicem hic praestare potest. Felicitate enim interpretationis superat prolixita- tem operosorum voluminum Pinedae, & aliorum, ad quae legenda judicium adferatur, oportet. Mul- tis enim erroribus, & corruptelis, ut alia Pontifi- ciorum Interpp. commenta, scatent, ac referta sunt. Adiri etiam poterit Dn. D. Sebastiani Schmidt com- mentarius in Jobum nuperrime editus, cujus eru- dita versio, & interpretatio e vocum significatione, ac textus cohaerentia (optima interpretandi ratione, quam merito praeferas multorum locorum collatio- ni, utpote saepius alienae, & πολυσημασίας vocum ex aliis textibus collectioni, quae confundit saltim lecto- rem & unice veram, ac loco, qui prae manibus est, propriam significationem saepe dubiam reddit, vel diversis sensibus involvit) mihi a Dn. Autore transmissa, postquam jam ante sesquiannum hanc qualemcunque operam absolveram, hisce annota- tis alicubi, cum eandem percurrerem, quoddam ἐπιβάλλον μέγ' contulit. Nos hic finimus, Deoque soli laudem tribuimus.

# Psalms

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
IN THE NAME OF JESUS ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD PSALMORUM LIBRUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Dedicatory Preface. To the Most Illustrious and Most Noble Lord, Lord Carl, Baron of Fries
DEDICATORY PREFACE. To the Most Illustrious and Most Noble Lord, Lord Carl, Baron of Friesen, Lord in Rotha and Geswitz, etc., Most Serene Elector of Saxony’s Chamberlain, and Most Excellent Councilor in the Privy Council. Now President of the Dresden High Court, and Most Eminent Director of Sacred Affairs throughout the Electorate. To my most gracious Lord, S. P. P. [Salus, Pax, Prosperitas - Health, Peace, Prosperity].

Most Illustrious and Most Noble Lord, most gracious Lord.

Concerning Saint Ignatius, whom it is believed the boy Jesus set before the Apostles as an example of faith and humility, some report that when his heart was cut open, the name of Jesus was found inscribed in golden letters, in individual sections. I would say more truly that the name of Jesus was inscribed upon the heart of David by the finger of the Holy Spirit, with a character indelible from the time of his conversion: inasmuch as he, having been confirmed concerning the Messiah of the God of Jacob above others, always had Jesus in his heart and frequently on his lips; and he repeated that mellifluous and beatific name, received as if by hand from his ancestors and especially from Jacob the Patriarch, more than seven times in the Psalms, with great joy of the Spirit and the highest desire for the saving advent. And when he most gravely exhorted all the kings and judges of the earth to devote themselves humbly to the Son of God with a kiss of faith and obedience, then indeed he himself, as an illustrious example, consecrated his whole self to Him, and in Him alone placed the trust of his heart and true blessedness. Therefore, nothing was earlier, nothing more ancient to him, than that his heart, full of JESUS, should belch forth a good word concerning this King and his Lord, and that his tongue, like the pen of a swift scribe, should be entirely dissolved into His praises. To proclaim the admirable person, the inestimable beauty, and the incomprehensible virtue of Him was his highest glory; to celebrate with hymns His most glorious kingdom and rule, the duties of His subjects, His most happy state, and the far most abundant and most desired array of His benefits and gifts was his highest pleasure. The love of DAVID, as Ignatius professed of himself, was the CRUCIFIED ONE: whose entire sufferings he depicted so graphically that Aurelius Cassiodorus rightly pronounced that it seemed to him a history written, not a prophecy. For he even recorded in the Psalms the words of the One hanging on the cross, by which He complained that He was forsaken by GOD, and the very last sigh of the One rendering up His soul to the Father, as if caught from His mouth under the cross: to which nothing similar is found in any of the Prophets. And this, without doubt, is the reason why Christ so frequently appealed to the testimonies of David, and why He demonstrated the necessity of His passion and resurrection to His disciples particularly from the book of Psalms; why also the holy quartet of Evangelists everywhere secured the faith of the Evangelical History with Davidic oracles; why the prince of the Apostles, St. Peter, not rarely brought them forward in his sermons and writings for the confirmation of faith; and why, finally, that athlete of Christ, taught by Him, anointed concerning Him, crucified with Him, glorious in Him (thus the Bishop of Hippo describes Paul), called upon the Jessean prophet, prophesying concerning Christ, more than twenty times for support. The pious ancients, following them, treated this Biblical epitome in such a way that they by no means neglected what our only Master taught—with the Rabbis of the Jews not denying it—to be the chief thing in the scrutiny of the Sacred Scriptures: Nor did they hesitate, at the Synod of Antioch, celebrated in the middle of the third century, to strike with anathema and smite Paul of Samosata, who contended that the Psalms sung in the glory of Christ should be removed from the midst.

Wherefore I believed that I also owed this entirely to the honor of my JESUS, that I should go to vindicate the Davidic Psalms, especially those that sing of JESUS, having followed the Blessed, after the great Luther, my predecessors, the Bugenhagens, Hunniuses, Gesners, and others, when I saw, not without astonishment, that all of them were being removed, so that they might no longer sound and celebrate JESUS. For to what end, finally, do Jewish glosses of this kind lead, when from the Prophetic oracles, clearer than the Sun, JESUS the Sun of righteousness is expunged, unless it be that in the end no faith remains for the ancients in the Messiah who suffered, died, and was resurrected for the sins of men, and no proof remains for Christians against the Jews from the Old Testament? It is truly to be lamented that a man of stupendous erudition, in both Ecclesiastical and profane antiquity as well versed as any other, when he applied his mind to illustrating Holy Scripture, in most classic testimonies, indulged more in Rabbinic inventions and Socinian-Remonstrant corruptions than he left room for the Christian Church's understanding and for the explanation of Christ himself and of the Apostles. It is to be lamented that that Hugo, great in deed and name, in his Annotations, which truly shine with every kind of learning, sometimes shed a certain light upon more obscure passages not concerning the faith and the mysteries of salvation, such as in historical matters and others to which something could be contributed from the philological storehouse, but in more illustrious passages concerning the faith and the very kernel of the faith, JESUS, he introduced darkness: furthermore, most things in the original text, whether from versions or from the Septuagint Interpreters. as they are called, or from the Vulgate Latin, concerning which not even the most ardent defenders of their authenticity in the Roman Church are sufficiently agreed, he has called into doubt, and the Hebrew truth, in the manner of the Papists, to whom he had entrusted his annotations to be reviewed, as testified by letters exchanged with the Jesuit Petavius, he dared to amend according to the norm of corrupted translations. Certainly, no hymn remains in the entire book of Psalms, by this Author, which remains proper to Christ, and sings of the same by design: all Prophetic Psalms are snatched away to all other things. I undertook to assert these with the more ready mind, the more generous the measure of the Spirit, above other sacred writers, by which it was established beyond doubt among the entire Church of Christ that David had known the mysteries of the Messiah, who was to come forth from his loins, who had even beheld the same in the form of a man of the most high GOD, or θεανθρώπως, and had shown himself to him in an illustrious vision prefiguring the future incarnation: especially when I saw that the previous vindications on the Pentateuch of Moses and the other historical books of the Old Testament, for the sake of asserting the integrity of the sources and the faith of the oracles, as well as the prophecies concerning Christ in their genuine sense, clearly handed down by the Holy Scriptures; clearly handed down; and hitherto holily propagated in the Church of Christ, modestly undertaken and dispatched, had not been ungrateful to the Church: as testified by theologians in most Academies, Leipzig, Jena, Giessen, Strasbourg, Rostock, Greifswald, and also in the principal ministries, Lübeck, Hamburg, Lüneburg, Celle, Brunswick, Danzig, Königsberg,

Wittenberg, the 8th day of May, in the year of our Lord 1661.

Address to the worshippers of the Holy Scriptures, the Psalm-lovers, greetings, Abraham Calovius.

The Synodical letters, which Eusebius in book 7 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 24, recounting, the Antiochene Fathers sent to Dionysius of Rome, to Maximus of Alexandria, and to the other bishops throughout the world concerning the causes of the excommunication of Samosatenus, claim that that Paul had removed the Psalms which were sung to the glory of Christ the Lord, as if they were the compositions of more recent men: Which, although it might seem to be said of the Psalms of the Christians, which the error of Artemon, his predecessor in that heresy, opposed, a certain excellent and very ancient author

and whom I ought to have named in the first place, of our Ephors in the illustrious Proto-Synedrium of Dresden, by their autographs and judgments. How much effort, however, has been worth the while in these vindications of the Psalms, I now likewise entrust to the Church of GOD. Which have grown a little, so that they had to be presented in a separate volume and a college of disputations: because the golden jewels of David (thus I designate the Prophetic Psalms, along with their author himself) did not deserve proletarian labor, but then the refutation itself, undertaken against him, who did not conduct the matter with a light arm; but relying on his talent, attempted to undermine from the lowest foundations what he strove to overthrow, seemed altogether to demand a slightly more accurate study. Therefore, I thought that I would consecrate David restored to himself, as I hope, that is, singing of JESUS again, to no one more rightly than to him whose heart, like David's, burns with the love of JESUS CRUCIFIED, and is entirely consecrated to his honor. Which, among other rarer and more illustrious documents of piety in such a high station, Your Illustrious Generosity recently demonstrated with a new and very excellent specimen, when you allowed the supreme care and direction of sacred matters throughout all the Electoral lands to be placed upon your shoulders: such care indeed primarily brought eternal and immortal glory to David. I ought now to congratulate you, most illustrious Baron, on this mind divinely given to you: but I adore with my whole heart our JESUS, who, as the supreme President of the Church, sitting at the right hand of the Father, endows his vicars, prelates, and ministers of the Church, that he may further fill your generous soul with the Davidic Spirit, that he may second all your counsels and actions with Davidic success, to the glory of his Name and the salvation of the entire Lutheran Church, and finally, that he may crown you, the PRESIDENT who will keep watch for the glory of the Name of JESUS and the salvation of the Church, purchased by the blood of JESUS, with Davidic glory and blessedness, and may he deign to grant all-encompassing blessing and glorious increases to your entire illustrious family, and especially to your firstborn Son, the LORD, DN. CHRISTIAN AUGUSTUS, happily following in the illustrious ancestral and paternal footsteps, now shining like a star in our Academy! Remaining of your most holy Name

Most humble worshipper, Abraham Calovius, D.

To the students of Sacred Theology. To the worshippers, and especially to the most learned in the LORD JESUS! Calovius, D.

but the ἀνώνυμος, in the same Eusebius, book 5, chapter 25: How many Psalms, how many canticles AB INITIO, written by faithful brethren, which celebrate and praise Christ the Word of GOD as God! Concerning which kind of Psalms Pliny the Younger also testified to the Emperor Trajan, book 10, Epistle 96, that indeed Christians were accustomed to meet on a stated day before dawn, and to sing a hymn to Christ as if to a god among themselves: Most, however, understand the Davidic Psalms, describing the Deity, advent, and benefits of Christ, which were a thorn in the eye to Samosatenus, just as the aforementioned anonymous author testifies concerning his predecessors, that with impious craftiness they fraudulently corrupted the simplicity of the divine scriptures, and laid irreligious hands upon the Holy Scriptures, boasting that they had amended them; some of them even simply denied the Law and the Prophets, in the extreme that Paul, the heretic of this impiety, translated and rejected the prophetic Psalms, which he saw were opposed to him, as if they were more recent. Although one may not doubt that the Psalms of the primitive Church in the century immediately following the departure of the Apostles, to which the aforementioned author refers, were composed after the manner of the Davidic Psalms, and were not alien to the mind of David, but that that flower of Christians devoutly celebrated the true God, the Messiah, with the Spirit of the son of Jesse.

But it is a matter to be seriously lamented that the spirit of Artemon and Samosatenus has revived not only in the Socinians, the champions of these heresies, but even in those who wish to be called worshippers of Christ the God-man, I mean Calvin and his accomplices: who, although they do not utterly reject the prophetic Psalms, nevertheless deprive them of their native and genuine sense in the passages which treat of the deity, advent, and office of Christ, as if they were the spirit and soul of the sayings, so that they seem to present a bloodless and empty skeleton, and neither exhibit Christ, nor should they any longer be considered prophetic. The blessed Luther complained of them in the previous century, in his Epistle to Eoban. Hess., that they bring Jewish darkness into the most clear light of the Psalms; Philip also complained, whose judgment Grotius values highly; for he is delighted by the very sweet nectar dripping from Melanchthon, as his own epigram testifies: 'It is a most inept class of men,' writes Philip to Eoban, 'who, led by a certain Jewish superstition, when they do not understand the figures nor notice the order of the sentences, often attach absurd interpretations, and truly, to speak in Greek, παρὰ τὸ μέλος [out of tune].' This complaint was repeated in the Anti-Pareus by the blessed Aegidius Hunnius concerning John Calvin, that he himself, chief among the Judaizers, had snatched the palm from the others in his age, which he demonstrated to Pareus so clearly that it was necessary for that champion of Calvin to be silenced. In Calvin's associates, our blessed Gesner likewise rebukes the same thing with righteous zeal in his Meditations on the Psalter. Geier, ch. 1, that they enervate the distinguished and brilliant oracles of the Psalms concerning Christ and his benefits in a plainly Jewish manner, and obscure with the shadows of types those things which, spoken without a type, are in themselves most clear, so that a pious mind cannot but shudder at such audacity of men, and groan vehemently. But indeed I do not know whether Hugo Grotius does not far surpass everyone in impiety in his Annotations, with which he has defiled rather than illustrated the book of Psalms, drunk not only with the spirit of Calvin or of Samosatenus and Artemon, but also so demented by the madness of the impious Jews that he perverts and overturns all the prophetic Psalms, which treat of Christ and his divine nature, advent, and benefits, by means of utterly detestable, crafty deceptions. He who did not deign to leave even a single Psalm to Christ the God-man alone: he twisted into a foreign sense, with remarkable deceit and craftiness, all of them universally, even those which the Apostles themselves interpreted concerning Christ, which they demonstrated could not be understood of any other than Christ, which Christ himself explained concerning himself, and with which he stopped the mouths of his fiercest adversaries, even the chief Rabbis of the Jews, by no means acquiescing in the interpretation of Christ or the Apostles, or even of the ancient Jews, but lending his ears to the more recent Rabbis, the implacable and utterly blinded enemies of Jesus of Nazareth, and yielding the palm to them. To the present matter I now bring only Psalm 110.

which, although he was compelled by the testimony of Christ and the ancient Jews to confess that it treats of the Messiah, he could not nevertheless restrain himself from perverting it in such a way that it might fit David perfectly, and that it is believed to describe not such a session at the right hand of God, which, according to the Apostle, cannot belong even to any of the angels, but only a secure rest under the confidence of divine aid: not an eternal priesthood, according to the order of Melchizedek, proper to the Messiah alone, but the perpetual ministry of David the just King; which kind of commenting, how pestiferous it is, cannot be explained by the judgment of the blessed Hunnius in a speech. For that not only inflicts the stings of most dangerous doubts upon the minds of men who are otherwise weak, but also renders the Jews more obstinate in the errors they have once conceived, while they see that their tricks, with which they disturb the limpid truth, do not displease even Christian interpreters. We ought to have given thanks entirely to the divine kindness, because through the Apostles, and our Savior himself, he brought the most clear light to the prophetic oracles: But these men labor with much effort to involve in darkness those things which the New Testament has made clear. Oh, admirable ingratitude, nay, detestable perversity!

Wherefore, since I have hitherto defended the Scripture of the Old Testament from the Grotian distortion by divine aid in two distinct Biblical Colleges, and indeed in the former I freed the Pentateuch of Moses from various corruptions through ten publicly held disputations: but in the latter I asserted the historical books, including also the history of holy Job, although it is believed to be written poetically, in six public disputations: it has been decided to purge the BOOK OF PSALMS in a special College (for that most excellent Biblical Enchiridion deserves that effort) with the help of Christ from the Grotian depravations, but especially the prophetic Psalms, which the prophet, the son of Jesse, confirmed by the Messiah of the God of Jacob, sang in the Spirit to the honor of Christ, and to restore them to their pristine splendor, having routed the glosses and Jewish commentaries of Grotius. For when Christ himself, as St. Luke reports, establishing his Passion and resurrection and the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world from the monuments of the Old Testament, assigned a special class to the testimonies of the Psalms, having instituted the demonstration first from Moses, then from the Psalms, and finally from the Prophets; we are not only assured, by the divine judgment of our Savior, that the Psalms exhibit all these things to us concerning Christ in a special way, but we also believe that we shall be doing no common service if we likewise bring forward, in a distinct collection and with somewhat more accurate work, those most significant testimonies which are contained in the book of Psalms. Which, therefore, we shall explain somewhat more fully, as for instance in about fifteen disputations, according to the greater or lesser scope within which each person may prefer his own Disputation to be circumscribed: intending to join with Grotius, for the sake of a clearer and richer index, the latest defender of Calvin, Andreas Rivetus, who, although he was otherwise a sharp adversary of Grotius in most matters, here, however, where Grotius chose the footsteps of the Judaizing Calvin, conspires in a friendly manner with Grotius (not otherwise than Pilate with Herod, when the matter was against Christ), though he was otherwise, and especially regarding that horrible absolute decree, extremely hostile to Calvin. Therefore, by the same effort, so that two birds may be killed with one stone, we shall weigh and discuss the glosses and tricks of Rivetus.

While I am writing these things, there offer themselves by chance the words of a certain excellent Doctor of Theology, whose name, on account of an old friendship, I spare here, before whose eyes such illusions of Rabbinic glosses, whether of Rivet or of other Calvinists, have cast such a cataract that not only does he seem to have been rendered doubtful concerning those interpolations, but he has also challenged another distinguished theologian of ours in this way: 'Whether the explanation of certain passages, which Calvin and others have interpreted from the Rabbis, and which have displeased one or another in our churches, are just as easily to be rejected, I hold to be a difficult disputation, and I cannot rashly judge of it. There are in England, Holland, and France Reformed [theologians] who are exceedingly learned and experienced in languages (Is there not a God in Israel?), many of whom would well like to take up the task of disputing with the Censor before Calvin regarding the explanation of certain difficult sayings of the Old Testament, and if his skin itches, he can just announce himself and warm the matter up again.' Which judgment, how pious, O Lords. The zeal of the predecessors, less than fair, as a defense of the Prophetic oracles, is less than religious, or is refuted by the alternating writings of B. Hunnius and Pareus. It is manifest, however, from this, how great a necessity lies upon us to expose such tricks and deceits, lest they impose upon students.

Indeed, with what great religious care the pious ancients investigated the Prophetic Psalms singing of Christ, with what great solicitude they labored to propagate the genuine sense concerning Christ, that excellent Epistle of St. Athanasius on the interpretation of the Psalms, which he wrote to Marcellinus, clearly teaches, not to mention others now. The same holy Bishop praises Marcellinus, who clung especially to the little book of Psalms and investigated the genuine sense with great contention: and he testifies that he himself is also carried toward the same book with great desire: and he brings forward, moreover, some well-industrious old man, who not only strongly commended the Code of Psalms to him as being worthy of special attention and observation above others, but also taught at length that the coming of the Messiah is treated everywhere in the Psalms, so that at one time the coming of God is predicted (e.g., Psalm 50), at another time Christ is described as the Son and Word of God (Psalm 2, Psalm 33), at another time as Messiah and God (Psalm 45), at another time the snares of the Jews against the Messiah (Psalm 11), at another time the condition of the death and crucifixion of Christ (Psalm 22), at another time the satisfaction of Christ (Psalm 69) and Redemption (Psalm 72), at another time his ascension (Psalm 47) and sitting at the right hand of God (Psalm 110), at another time the calling of the Gentiles (Psalm 47 and 72) is designated. And although each of the faithful can receive the remaining Psalms, which do not sing of Christ, as if the discourse there were about his own affairs, not another's, and he who hears, just like him who reads, is pricked in heart and thus is affected by the words of those odes as if they were his own, yet that God-taught old man professed that the reason for those Psalms where the prophecies of Christ are concerned is far different; inasmuch as they must be claimed for Christ ALONE, and thus every person ought to read them through with wonder and reverence. Athanasius approves this opinion of the venerable old man with his own vote and explains his mind concerning the Prophetic Psalms thus: 'When you wish to sing separately from the rest those things which pertain to Christ, you will find such things in every Prophetic Psalm, but especially in the 44th (Athanasius counts according to the Greeks here, and in the following) and 109th, in which his genuine birth from the Father and his coming in the flesh are indicated; Psalm 21 and 68, however, predict his divine cross, and what snares he endured for our sake, and the deceits of the Jews, and the malice, and the betrayal of Judas Iscariot. Furthermore, 22 and 49 and 71 demonstrate his kingdom and power of judging, and his second coming to us in the flesh. And 15 shows his carnal resurrection. The twenty-third and 46th, however, announce his ascension to the heavens. But when you read 93, 96, 97, 98, you will perceive the individual benefits conferred upon us by the virtue of his passion.' These things [are from] St. Athanasius, to whom other Fathers have devoted equal effort in asserting the Psalms concerning Christ, as have our own theologians from the time of B. Luther and with him; thus this shall be our greatest care in the Psalms, to vindicate for Christ—whom we are bound to investigate in the searching of the old Scripture, by Christ's own command—the prophecies which were sung concerning him.

We judge that there is no work more holy, none more useful and fruitful for the cultivators of Sacred Theology and especially for the psalm-lovers, none more necessary; wherefore we trust that those will be eager to undertake the same with us, to whom the accurate investigation of the sense of the Holy Spirit is a care and a concern, not so much the proletarian reading of this Biblical Epitome of the Psalms. Those, therefore, who desire to take on the roles of Respondents, either publicly or privately, and to exercise themselves in the ventilation of these most excellent matters in the Old Testament Code, are kindly asked to wish to profess their names to me this week. I will assign the disputations in such quantity as each may please: for some are accustomed to seek longer ones, others more concise: which will be left to the judgment of each. May the Lord JESUS be present, and by His Spirit, by which He predicted through David His passions and the glory that followed them, may He assert and vindicate the sense of the predictions and His own honor. Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Thy name be the glory.

Written at Wittenberg, the 3rd Sunday after the Feast of the Epiphany, in the Year of our Lord 1660.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO DEDICATORIA. PER-ILLUSTRI ET GENEROSISSIMO DOMINO, DOMINO CAROLO, LIBERO BARONI A Friesen/ DN. IN ROTHA, ET GESWITZ &c. SERENISS. SAXON. ELECTORI COMITI CUBICULARIO, ET IN SENATU INTIMIORI CONSILIARIO EXCELLENTISSIMO. NUNC PROTO-SYNEDRII DRESDENSIS PRÆSIDI, ET SACRORUM PER TERRAS ELECTORALES DIRECTORI EMINEN- TISSIMO. DOMINO MEO GRATIOSISSIMO S. P. P.

Per-Illustris & Generosissime Domine, Domine perquam gratiose.

DE Sancto IGNATIO, quem puerum admodum JESUS Apostolis in exem- plum fidei & humilitatis stitisse credi- tur, referunt nonnulli, quod cordi ejus, quum secaretur, nomen Jesu aureis literis, singulis sectionibus inscriptum, inventum fuerit. Verius ego dixerim, DAVIDIS cordi Jesu no- men digito Spiritus Sancti insculptum fuisse, cha- ractere, à conversione ejus, indelebili: utpote, qui de Messia DEI Jacob, præ aliis confirmatus, Jesum in corde semper, in ore frequenter habuit, nomenque etiam illud mellifluum, & beatificum à majoribus suis, & cumprimis à Jacobo Patriarcha veluti per manus acceptum, plusquam septenis vi- cibus in Psalmis, ingenti Spiritus lætitia, summo- que adventus salutiferi desiderio repetiit, & cum Reges, Judicesque terræ universos gravissime hor- tatus est, ut Filio DEI, osculo fidei, & obsequii se- se summisse devoveant, tum vero ipse, in illustre exemplum, totum illi se consecravit, & in eo cor- dis fiduciam, veramque beatitudinem unice collo- cavit. Idcirco nihil ei prius, nihil antiquius fuit, quam ut Cor, JESU plenum, de hoc Rege ac Do- mino suo verbum bonum eructaret, utque lingua, ceu calamus velocis scribæ, tota in laudes ejus sol- veretur. Hujus personam admirabilem, pulcri- tudinem inæstimabilem, virtutem incomprehen- sibilem deprædicare, summa ipsi gloria; Hujus re- gnum & regimen gloriosissimum, & subditorum officia, statumque felicissimum, & beneficiorum, donorumque apparatum longe uberrimum, & ex- optatissimum, hymnis celebrare, summa ipsi vo- luptas fuit. Amor DAVIDIS, quod de se professus Ignatius est, CRUCIFIXUS erat: cujus passiones universas tam graphice depinxit, ut historiam sibi scriptam videri, non Prophetiam Aurelius Cassio- dorus merito pronunciarit. Nam & verba pen- dentis in cruce, quibus se à DEO desertum esse que- stus est, ipsumque animam Patri reddentis supre- mum suspirium, velut ex ore ejus sub cruce exce- pta, in Psalmos retulit: quibus simile quid in nullo Prophetarum deprehenditur. Atque hæc fine du- bio, causa est, quod tam frequenter Christus ad Da- vidis testimonia provocarit, & è Psalmorum libro peculiariter discipulis suis passionis ac resurrectio- nis suæ necessitatem demonstrarit: quod item san- cta Evangelistarum quadriga oraculis Davidicis Historia Evangelicæ fidem passim conciliarit; quod Apostolorum primicerius S. Petrus non raro in concionibus, scriptisque suis ea in confirmatio- nem fidei adduxerit: Quod denique athleta ille Christi, doctus ab illo, unctus de illo, crucifixus cum illo, gloriosus in illo, (sic Paulum describit Hip- ponensis Episcopus) plusquam vicies Jessæum va- tem de Christo vaticinantem in subsidium vocarit. Quos secuti pii veteres Epitomen istam Biblicam ita tractarunt, ut quod præcipuum in literarum Sa- crarum scrutinio esse Magister Noster unicus, haud abnuentibus tum Judæorum Rabbinis, docuit, neu- tiquam negligerent: Neque dubitarunt, Paulum Samosatensem Psalmos in gloriam Christi decanta- tos, è medio tollere contendentem, in Synodo An- tiochena, medio seculo tertio celebrata, anathema- te ferire, ac percutere.

Quapropter honori JESU mei omnino id me quoque debere credidi, ut Psalmos Davidicos, eos imprimis, qui JESUM canunt, Beatos, post Mega- landrum Lutherum, Prædecessores, Bugenhagios, Hunnios, Gefneros, aliosque sequutus, vindicatum irem, cum non absque stupore vidi, universos illos tolli, ne JESUM amplius sonent, celebrentque. Quorsum enim denique Judaicæ ejusmodi glossæ expediunt, cum ex oraculis Propheticis, Sole clari- oribus, JESUS Sol justitiæ expungitur, nisi, ut nulla postremo in Messiam, pro peccatis hominum pas- sum, mortuum, ac resuscitatum, veteribus fides, nul- la Christianis adversus Judæos è Vet. Testamento relinquatur apodixis. Dolendum profecto, virum stupendæ eruditionis in utraque Ecclesiastica æque. ac prophana antiquitate, si quisquam alius, versatis- simum, quum animum ad illustrandam Scripturam S. applicaret, in plerisque testimoniis classicis, Rab- binis potius commentis, ac Sociniano-Remon- stranticis corruptelis indulsisse, quam Ecclesiæ- Christianæ sensui, Christique ipsius & Apostolo- rum explicationi locum reliquisse. Dolendum, Hugonem illum, re ac nomine magnum, Anno- tatis suis, omnigena sane doctrina fulgentibus, lo- cis quidem obscurioribus fidem ac mysteria sa- lutis non concernentibus, puta in historicis, aliis- que, ad quæ è penu Philologica aliquid conferri poterat, lucem quandam nonnunquam affudisse, illustrioribus vero fidem, nucleumque ipsum fidei, JESUM, attinentibus, caliginem induxisse: ad- hæc pleraque in textu primigenio, cum à versioni- bus, sive à Septuaginta Interpp. uti vocantur, sive à vulgata Latina, de quibus ne acerrimis qui- dem in Romana Ecclesia authentias earum propu- gnatoribus satis constat, discrepat, in dubium re- vocasse, veritatemque Ebraicam, more Papico- lis, quibus ille annotata sua recognoscenda, testi- bus literis cum Petavio Jesuita permutatis, commi- serat, solemni, ad normam corruptarum translatio- num emendare ausum fuisse. Nullus certe in uni- verso Psalmorum libro, per hunc Autorem, su- perat hymnus, qui Christo proprius maneat, & de eodem ex instituto canat: omnes Psalmi Prophe- tici ad alia omnia abripiuntur. Quos tanto prom- ptiori animo adserere aggressus sum, quanto lar- giori Spiritus mensura, præ aliis Scriptoribus sa- cris, Davidem mysteria Messiæ, è lumbis suis pro- dituri, qui eundem in forma hominis DEI excelsi, vel θεανθρώπως etiam aspexerat, eique illustri visi- one præludens futuræ incarnationi, sese exhibue- rat, cognovisse, penes universam Ecclesiam Chri- sti, extra dubium constitutum fuit: maxime, quum viderem, priores in Pentateuchum Mosis, libros- que Historicos cæteros Vet. Testamenti vindicias, pro adserenda fontium integritate, ac oraculorum fidei, nec non vaticiniorum de Christo germana mente, à S.S. luculenter tradita; & in Ecclesia Chri- sti sancte hactenus propagata modeste susceptas, at- que expeditas, Ecclesiæ non ingratas fuisse: testi- bus Theologorum in Academiis plerisque, Lipsi- ensi, Jenensi, Giessensi, Argentoratensi, Rostochi- ensi, Gryphiswaldensi, nec non in præcipuis mini- steriis, Lubeccensi, Hamburgensi, Luneburgensi, Cellensi, Brunsvicensi, Gedanensi, Regiomontano,

Wittebergæ die 8. Maj. Ann. Domini MDCLXI.

ΠροσΦώνησις ad S. S. LITERARUM CULTO τοῖς ΨαλμοΦίλοις Sal ABRAHAM C

Literæ Synodicæ, quas Eusebio lib. 7. Quæ excre- vere paululum, ut peculiari volumine, ac dispu- tationum Collegio exhibendæ fuerint: quia non proletariam operam merebantur aurea Davidis Clinodia (sic Psalmos Propheticos, cum ipso eo- rum autore, indigito) tum vero Elenchus ipse, ad- versus illum susceptus, qui non levi brachio rem egit; sed ingenio fretus, ex imis fundamentis sub- ruere tentavit, quæ evertere molitus est, studium paulo accuratius efflagitare omnino videbatur. DAVIDEM ergo sibi, ut spero, redditum, hoc est, JESUM iterum canentem, nemini rectius me consecraturum existimavi, quam illi, cujus cor, ad Davidis instar, JESU CRUCIFIXI amore flagrat, ejusdemque honori totum consecratum est. Quod inter alia pietatis, in tanto fastigio rariora, & illu- striora documenta, novo & peregregio specimine, Perillustris Tua Generositas demonstravit nuper, cum sacrorum curam & directionem, per Electo- rales terras universas, supremam humeris suis im- poni passa est: qualis cura Davidi profecto æter- nam & immortalem gloriam imprimis peperit. sed ἀνώνυμος, apud eundem Eusebium lib. 5. cap. 25. Quot sunt Psalmi, quot cantica AB INITIO, à fide- libus fratribus scripta, quæ Christum DEI verbum, tanquam Deum celebrant, ac laudant! De cujusmo- di Psalmis testatus etiam est Plinius Secundus ad Tra- janum Imperat. l. X. Epist. quod nempe soliti fuerint Christiani stato die ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo quasi Deo dicere secum invicem: Plerique ta- men intelligunt Psalmos Davidicos, Christi Deita- tem, adventum, ac beneficia describentes, quæ Sa- mosateno sudes fuere in oculis, quemadmodum de prædecessoribus ipsius Auctor prædictus Anonymus testatur, quod impia versutia simplicitatem divina- rum literarum fraudulenter corruperint, manusque irreligiosas Scripturis Sacris injecerint, gloriati, se eas- dem emendasse; nonnulli etiam eorum simpliciter le- gem & Prophetas negarint, in extremum impietatis ac perditionis barathrum prolapsi: unde mirum non fuerit, si Paulus ille impietatis istius hæres Psalmos Propheticos, quos sibi adversos videbat, ceu recen- tiores traduxerit ac reprobarit. Quamquam nec de eo dubitare liceat, quin Psalmi Ecclesiæ primitivæ proximo ab excessu Apostolorum Seculo, quos au- ctor prædictus respicit, ad Davidicorum Psalmo- rum instar compositi, nec à mente Davidis alieni fuerint, sed uno cum Isacide Spiritu Messiam verum Deum flos ille Christianorum devote celebrarint.

Id autem dolendum serio est, quod Artemonis & Samosateni Spiritus non in Socinianis modo, hære- seon istarum propugnatoribus, sed in iis etiam, qui Christi Θεανθρώπου cultores nuncupari volunt, Cal- vinum dico ejusque complices, revixerit: qui etsi Psal- mos Propheticos non rejiciant penitus, sensu tamen nativo, & genuino in locis, quæ de Christi Deitate, adventu & officio agunt, ceu Spiritu & anima dicto- rum, ita privant, ut exangue & inane sceleton re- ferre videantur, neque Christum exhibeant, aut Prophetici amplius haberi debeant. Questus est de iis superiori Seculo B. Lutherus, Epist. ad Eoban. Hess. quod tenebras Judaicas in lucem Psalmorum cla- rissimam invehant; questus & Philippus, cujus judi- cium magni facit Grotius; utpote quem prædulce juvat stillante Melanchthone nectar, teste ipsius Epi- grammate: Ineptissimum genus est, scribit Philippus ad Eoban. illorum, qui quadam Judaica superstitione adducti, glossematis Judæorum, cum figuras non in- telligant, nec sententiarum ordinem animadvertant, sæpe absurdas interpretationes, ac vere, ut Græce di- cam, παρὰ τὸ μέλος, affingunt. Quam querelam repetiit in Anti-Pareo altero B. Ægid. Hunnius de Joh. Calvino, quod ipse inter Judaizantes præcipuus palmam sua ætate cæteris præripuerit, quod πρὸς ὄμ- μα ita Pareo demonstravit, ut hyperaspisten illum Calvini obmutescere oportuerit. In Calvini Sociis idem pariter justo Zelo reprehendit B. Gesnerus no- ster Meditat. Psalter. Geier. c. 1. quod insignia & lu- culenta Psalmorum oracula de Christo ejusque beneficiis Judaico plane more enervent, typorumque umbris adeo obscurent, quæ absque typo dicta in se sunt clarissima, ut pia mens non possit non ad tantam hominum audaciam cohorrescere, & vehementer ingemiscere. Sed pro- fecto nescio, annon omnes impietate longe supe- ret Hugo Grotius in Annotatis, quibus Psalmorum librum fœdavit potius, quam illustravit, non Cal- vini modo, aut Samosateni & Artemonis Spiritu ebrius, sed impiorum etiam Judæorum vesania ita dementatus, ut Propheticos Psalmos universos, qui de Christo ejusque divina natura, adventu, ac benefi- ciis tractant, præstigiis veteratoriis prorsus dete- standis pervertat, atque evertat. Qui ne unicum qui- dem Psalmum Christo Θεανθρώπῳ soli relinquere dignatus est: omnes in universum, etiam quos ipsi- met Apostoli de Christo interpretati sunt, quos de- monstrarunt, non posse de alio, quam de Christo acci- pi, quos ipse Christus de sese exposuit, & quibus acerrimis adversariis præcipuis etiam Judæorum Rabbinis, ora obturavit, in alienum sensum insigni κυβείᾳ καὶ πανεργίᾳ detorsit, neutiquam Christi aut Apostolorum, ac ne Judæorum quidem veterum in- terpretationi acquiescens, sed recentioribus Rabbi- nis hostibus Jesu Nazareni ἀσπόνδοις, ac prorsus ex- cæcatis aures præbens, herbamque porrigens. In rem præsentem jam tantum adduco Psalmum 110.

quem etsi de Messia agere, testimonio Christi, ac an- tiquorum Judæorum convictus, fateri necessum habuerit, non potuit tamen sibi temperare, quin eundem ita perverteret, ut apprime Davidi conve- niat, neque jam sessionem ejusmodi ad dextram Dei, quæ ne ulli quidem Angelorum competere queat, teste Apostolo, sed solum securam quietem sub fidu- cia auxilii divini : non Sacerdotium æternum, secun- dum ordinem Melchisedeci, soli Messiæ proprium, sed ministerium perpetuum Davidis Regis justi describere credatur, quod commentandi genus quam sit pe- stiferum, judicio B. Hunnii, oratione satis explica- ri nequit : Id namque non modo periculosissimarum dubitationum stimulos mentibus infligit hominum alio- quin infirmorum, sed Judæos etiam in conceptis semel erroribus reddit obstinatiores, dum vident suas Stro- phas, quibus limpidam veritatem turbant, Christianis etiam interpretibus non displicere. Gratias omnino divinæ benignitati agere debebamus, quod per A- postolos, ipsumque Salvatorem nostrum Prophe- ticis oraculis clarissimam lucem intulerit : Sed isti multo conatu ea, quæ Novum Testamentum clara reddidit, tenebris involvere laborant. Proh admi- randam ingratudinem, imo detestandam perver- sitatem !

Quapropter quum hactenus duobus distinctis Collegiis Biblicis Scripturam Veteris Testamenti à Grotiana detorsione, ope divina, vindicarim, ac priori quidem Pentateuchum Mosis per decem Di- sputationes publice habitas, à variis corruptelis libe- rarim : Altero vero libros Historicos, inclusa etiam S. Jobi Historia, etsi Poetice, uti creditur, descri- pta, sex disputationibus publicis adseruerim : PSAL- MORUM LIBRUM peculiari Collegio (mere- tur enim eam operam præclarissimum illud Enchi- ridion Biblicum) repurgare σὺν παλάμᾳ τοῦ χριστοῦ constitutum est à depravationibus Grotianis, ma- xime tamen Psalmos Propheticos, quos vates Jessæus de Messia Dei Jacob confirmatus, in Spiritu, in ho- norem Christi decantavit, profligatis glossis & com- mentis Grotii Judaicis pristino nitori restituere. Quum enim Christus ipse, S. Luca perhibente, Pas- sionem & resurrectionem suam ac prædicationem Evangelii per universum orbem, è Veteris Te- stamenti monumentis adstruens, peculiarem clas- sem testimoniis Psalmorum assignarit, demonstra- tione primum è Mose, tum è Psalmis, denique è Pro- phetis instituta ; non certi modo, Salvatoris nostri divino judicio, reddimur, Psalmos ista omnia de Christo peculiariter nobis exhibere, sed operæ pretium non vulgare etiam nos facturos credimus, si pariter distincto collegio, atq; opera paulo accura- tiori testimonia illa maxime insignia, quæ in Psalmo- rum libro continentur, adferamus. Quod proinde aliquanto plenius, utputa XV. circiter disputationi- bus, prout majori minorive ambitu Disputationem quisque suam circumscribi maluerit, expediemus : cum Grotio, evidentioris ac uberioris Elenchi gra- tia, conjuncturi hyperaspisten Calvini novissimum Andream Rivetum, qui etsi de cætero in plerisque acris fuerit Grotii adversarius, hic tamen, ubi Cal- vini Judaizantis vestigia elegit Grotius, Calvino alias, & imprimis, ab horribile illud decretum absolu- tum, perquam infestus, amice cum Grotio (non se- cus atque Pilatus cum Herode, ubi adversus Chri- stum res erat,) conspirat. Glossmata ergo Riveti ac Strophas eadem opera, ut fidelia una, duo, quod agunt, dealbentur parietes, expendemus, ac discu- tiemus.

Dum hæc scribo, τυχόντως sese offerunt ver- ba eximii cujusdam Theologiæ Doctoris, cujus nomi- ni, ob veterem amicitiam, hic parco, cui tales glos- sematum Rabbinicorum sive Riveti, seu aliorum Calvinianorum offuciæ glaucomam ita fecere, ut non modo de παρεγχήμασι istis dubius videatur redditus, sed alium etiam insignem Theologum no- strum sic provocavit: Ob die Erklärung etlicher Sprüche, die Calvinus und andere aus den Rabbi- nen ausgeleget, und die einem oder dem andern in un- serer Kirchen mißgefallen haben, eben so leicht zu ver- werffen seyn, halt ich für eine schwere Disputation, und mag davon temere nicht urtheilen. Es sind in Engell-Holland und Franckreich aus der Massen ge- lehrte und in Sprachen erfahrne Reformirten (Nun- quid non Deus in Israel?) derer viel es wohl möchten mit Censore vor dem Calvino in Erklärung etlicher schwehren Sprüche Alten Testaments sonderlich zu disputiren auffnehmen, und daferne ihm die Haut jücket, kan er sich nur angeben, und die Sache wieder auffwärmen. Quod judicium, qua pium Dnn. Præ- decessorum Zelum, minus æquum, qua vindicias Propheticorum oraculorum, minus religiosum, vel examœbæis B. Hunnii, & Parei scriptis convinci- tur. Manifestum autem inde est, quanta nobis incumbat necessitas, tales præstigias & offucias, ne studiosis imponant, detegendi.

Equidem quanta religione pii veteres Psal- mos Propheticos Christum decantantes indaga- rint, quanta folicitudine sensum de Christo ger- manum propagare laborarint, egregia illa S. A- thanafii de interpretatione Psalmorum Epistola, quam ad Marcellinum perscripsit, ne alia nunc commemorem luculenter edocet. Laudat eadem S. Episcopus Marcellinum, libello potissimum Psal- morum inhærentem, magnaque contentione genui- num sensum indagantem: ac testatur, se etiam ma- gno desiderio in eundem librum ferri: senemque insu- per aliquem bene industrium adducit, qui non mo- do præclare sibi Psalmorum Codicem ceu præcipua attentione ac observatione præ aliis dignum vehemen- ter commendarit, verum etiam prolixe docue- rit, quod passim in Psalmis de Messiæ adventu aga- tur, ita ut modo adventus Dei prædicatur (ex. gr. Psalmo L.) modo Christus ut Filius & verbum Dei (Pfal. 2. Psal. 33.) modo ut Messias & Deus (Pfal. 45.) describatur, modo insidiæ Judæorum adversus Messiam (Pfal. 11.) modo conditio mortis & crucifixio Christi (Psalm. 22.) modo satisfactio Christi (Pfalm. 69.) & Redemtio (Psalm. 72.) modo ascensio ejus (Psalm. 47.) & sessio ad dextram Dei (Psalm. 110.) mo- do gentium vocatio (Pfalm. 47. & 72.) designetur. Et quum reliquos quidem Psalmos, qui de Christo non canunt, accipere ita quisque fidelium possit quasi ibi de rebus suis, non alienis sermo fieret, & is, qui audit, itidem ut ille, qui legit, compungatur, at- que sic afficiatur odarum illarum verbis, ac si sua ipsius propria essent: longe tamen aliam esse ratio- nem eorum Psalmorum, ubi de Vaticiniis Christi agitur, professus est senex ille θεοδίδακτος; ut- pote quos SOLI Christo vendicare, atque ita ad- mirabundus venerabundusque perlegere quisque de- beat. Quam venerandi senis sententiam calculo suo comprobat Athanasius ac de Psalmis Prophe- ticis ita mentem suam exponit: Cum vis seorsim à cæteris canere ea, quæ ad Christum spectant, in uno- quoque Psalmo Prophetico talia invenies, sed præ- sertim in XLIV. (Athanasius secundum Græcos numerat hic, & in seqq.) & CIX. quibus indicatur ejus ex Patre genuinus ortus, & in carne adven- tus, Psalm. 21. autem & 68. divinam ejus crucem præ- dicant, & quas insidias propter nos scleveraverit, Ju- dæorumque dolos, & malitiam, & proditionem Judæ Iscariotæ. Porro 22. & 49. & 71. regnum ejus & potestatem judicandi demonstrant, ejusque ad nos se- cundum in carne adventum. Et 15. ejus carnalem resurrectionem ostendit. Vigesimus autem tertius, & 46. annunciant ejus ad cælos ascensum. Cum autem 93.96.97.98. legeris, perspicere singula ejus in nos vir- tute passionis suæ collata beneficia. Hæc S. Athana- sius, cui uti in adserendis Propheticis de Christo Psalmis parilem navarunt operam alii Patres, nostri- que inde à B. Luthero & cum eodem Theologi, sic no- stra hæc in Psalmis potissima erit cura, Christo, quem in ἐρευνήσει veteris Scripturæ indagare, Christo ipso jubente, tenemur, vaticinia, quæ de ipso can- tata sunt, vindicare.

Qua opera nullam sanctiorem, nullam cultori- bus SS. Theologiæ & cumprimis τοῖς ψαλμοφίλοις magis utilem ac fructuosam, nullam magis necessa- riam esse arbitramur; quapropter alacres futuros in eadem nobiscum suscipienda, quibus non tam proletaria Epitomes hujus Biblicæ, Psalmorum le- ctio, quam accurata sensus Spiritus S. indagatio cu- ræ cordique est, confidimus. Qui ergo sive publice sive privatim Respondentium partes suscipere, atque ventilatione materiarum istarum in V. T. Codice præ- stantissimarum sese exercere discupiunt, nomina sua mihi hac septimana ut profiteri velint, amice rogan- tur. Assignabo disputationes ea quantitate, qua cuig; placuerit: Alii enim prolixiores, alii concisiores ex- petere solent: quod cujusvis arbitrio relinquetur. Ad- sit Dominus JESUS, & Spiritu suo, quo per Davi- dem passiones suas, & quæ illas sequuta gloriam præ- dixit, sensum prædictionum, honoremque suum adse- rat, vindicetque. Non nobis Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo sit gloria.
