## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of Grotius
PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

These odes are called David's, because he collected many ancient ones, and he himself, being skilled in psalmody, added many, or caused them to be added by suitable men. Moreover, it should not be doubted that many songs of later times were added, with Ezra adding them. For that Psalm 137 (I am now following the Hebrew numbers, not because it matters much, but because I began that way, and Jerome follows them in his version from

That the Hebrew) was written in the Babylonian exile: but that Psalm 126 and certain others were written at the return, it would be foolish to doubt. However, the distinction between these Psalms among themselves has not been the same for a long time. For example, the first Psalm in many copies was joined with the second. And so the ancient Greek Scholia on the second have: ἐν τῷ ἑβραϊκῷ συνημμένοι. And in Acts 13:33, for that which we have, ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ τῷ δευτέρῳ, many ancient books have πρώτῳ.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTII.

ODæ istæ Davidis dicuntur, quod is multas veteres collegerit, multas ipse, psallendi sciens, addiderit, aut per homines idoneos addi fecerit. Cæterum dubitari non debet, quin multa accesserint carmina posteriorum tem- porum, Esdra addente. Nam quin Psalmus CXXXVII. (Hebraicos numeros nunc sequor, non quod multum referat, sed quia ita incepi, & eos sequitur Hieronymus in versione ex

Hebræo) scriptus sit in exsilio Babylonico: Psalmus autem CXXVI. & alii quidam in reditu, stultum sit dubitare. Ho- rum autem Psalmorum inter se distinctio jam olim non ea- dem est. Exempli causa, primus Psalmus in multis exem- plaribus cum secundo cohæsit. Itaque vetera Scholia Græ- ca ad secundum habent: ἐν τῷ ἑβραϊκῷ συνημμένοι. Et Actor. 13,33. pro eo quod nos habemus, ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ τῷ δευτέρῳ, multi veteres libri habent πρώτῳ.

## 1:1 Introduction: To the Preface
TO THE PREFACE

Although not only Josephus and the ancient Rabbis agree greatly regarding David as the author of the Psalms, if Alesius is to be believed, but the opinion of those also seemed more credible to Augustine, book XVII of the City of God, chapter 14, who attribute all the Psalms to David, to which Cassiodorus adds his vote in the Preface to the Psalter, as do Ambrose, Chrysostom, Bede, and Euthymius, toward which Theodoret also leans: which Alexander Alesius defends quite sharply. Nevertheless, the opinion of others is deservedly preferred, who establish that some proceeded from other authors. This is the view not only of Origen, Eusebius, Hilary, and most of the moderns, but also of Jerome, in his Epistle to Sophronius, Vol. 3 of his Works, p. 78, where we testify that all the Psalms belong to those authors who are placed in the titles, namely David, Asaph, and Idithun, the sons of Korah, Heman, the Ezrahite, Moses, and Solomon, and the rest, whom Ezra included in the first volume. Following him, Isidore of Seville, in his book on Offices, teaches that the Psalter was written by ten Prophets: Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Heman, Ethan, Idithun, and the sons of Korah, Elkanah, Eleazar, Abiazab. Saint Athanasius names others as well, namely Haggai and Zechariah, whom he likewise counts among the authors of the Psalms; whose opinion is read thus in his Synopsis of Holy Scripture: Although this book of Psalms bears the inscription of David alone, there are nevertheless Psalms of many others in it, such as Asaph, Idithun, the sons of Korah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Heman the Israelite. There are also some that are commonly said by everyone at once, namely as many as have 'Hallelujah'. Therefore, Ezra gathered all these Psalms, by whomever they were spoken, into one book, which, because they are as it were the common Psalms of all whom it contains, is called the Book of Psalms, but is inscribed to David alone, for the reason that he was the first to receive from God the Spirit of psalmody, and was the first to compose and write Psalms, and he himself selected and instituted the aforementioned Psalmists from among the priests, and determined the station of their places and the order of melody and the time of morning and evening psalmody, and so arranged it that some stood with the temple open, others with it closed, some on the right, others on the left, and thus indeed sang psalms to God, and sang praise and hymns with their voices, while some preluded with confession and praise, the former on musical instruments, harps, nablums, and cymbals, the latter sounding forth on trumpets on high. Which opinion is not obscurely confirmed by 2 Chronicles 29, 30, when they were ordered to praise the Lord with the words or poems of David and Asaph the Levite. Since it is thus indicated that Asaph was no less an author of the Psalms than David. Therefore, just as 'Lidavid' in Psalm 3, 1 and in other Psalms is a mark of the author, whether it be rendered in the Genitive as in Habakkuk 3, 1 and 1 Samuel 14, 16 (the 'L' is the mark of the genitive, and is taken as such by grammarians in proper names): or in the Dative, which B. Walth. prefers in his 'Centuria Miscellanea' p. 521, as it is rendered by the LXX Interpreters, if it is explained as 'to David' by implication, understanding the Hymn to have been revealed or dictated by the Holy Spirit: so there is no reason for us to doubt that the same is noted in the inscriptions 'Leasaph' in Psalm 73 and following. However, regarding the sons of Korah, it is doubtful whether they are the authors of any Psalm: since it is not probable that one and the same Psalm was inspired into several, as Bonfrerius argues in his preface to Scripture S. chapter 7, page 26, also regarding Idithun and others, that there are no authors of the Psalms except these five: David, Asaph, Heman, the Ezrahite, and Ethan, and that of Moses there is only one, namely Psalm 90, of Ethan only one, 89, of Heman only one, 88, of Asaph twelve, namely 50, 73, and the ten following, and that all the remaining 135, whether they have an epigraph or are without an epigraph, seem to be ascribable to David.

But whoever the authors of the Psalms may be, it must not be doubted in any way that all were moved by the Holy Spirit, just as Asaph the Prophet is also explicitly named in the cited passage, 2 Chronicles 29, 30, and the same Asaph, as well as Heman and Iduthun, are said to have prophesied with harps, 1 Chronicles 25, 1. Therefore, it should not be judged, with Grotius, that just any men suitable for the composition of hymns were employed, but that they were 'theopneustos' (God-breathed) 2 Timothy 3, 16, and 'pheromenes hypo pneumatos hagiou' (borne along by the Holy Spirit) 2 Peter 1, 21. Nor did the Canonical books of the Old Testament, to which Christ himself refers the Psalms in Luke 24, whether in whole or in part, proceed from others than Prophets, divinely inspired, and by that name they are called prophetic.

Furthermore, that we ought to follow the order and distribution of the Psalms according to the Hebrew truth rather than the Latin translation is not ambiguous to us, who believe that one should not rashly depart from the Hebrew text, even in such distinctions. Moreover, that the first Psalm is to be distinguished from the second is confirmed not obscurely by the argument of each. Because in both it is most diverse. Therefore, the opinion of the ancients is to be preferred, which Jerome praises regarding Psalm 1: 'Some say this Psalm is as it were a preface of the Holy Spirit, and therefore has no title.' How excellently these things agree with the argument of the same, no one can be ignorant who, with B. Gesner leading the way in his meditation on the Psalter, chapter 14 and following, has weighed that the whole Psalter is occupied in explaining the spiritual blessedness of man.

Nor are we moved by the fact that some Codices in Acts 13, 33 have 'first' instead of 'second', because those are rarer, and among all of Beza's Codices only one had it so. Since, therefore, most Codices agree with the common distinction, which the argument of the psalms solidly establishes, one must by no means depart from it for the sake of a few Codices. The subject matter of the psalm certainly teaches sufficiently that the second psalm does not cohere with the first, but consists of a peculiar argument.

There are still to be added the interpreters who illustrated the Psalter with commentaries: such as from the ancients Arnobius the Younger in the year of Christ 445. Eusebius of Caesarea in the year 320. Eustathius of Antioch, and Theodoret of Heraclea in the year 340. Hilary of Poitiers, and Apollinaris in the year 360. Eusebius of Vercelli in the year 380. Gregory of Nyssa, and Didymus of Alexandria in the year 390. Theodore of Antioch in the year 420. Aurelius Augustine in the year 430. Epiphanius Scholasticus, author of the Greek catena, in the year 450. Peter of Edessa and Ninian, Bishop of the Picts, in the year 454. Aurelius Cassiodorus in the year 576. Leander in the year 590. Columbanus in the year 598. Smaragdus in the year 680. Remigius and Othfried in the year 880. Ambrose Ansbert in the year 890. Bruno of Würzburg in the year 1045. Lanfranc in the year 1060. Bruno the Carthusian in the year 1081. Honorius of Autun in the year 1120. Peter Lombard, Gilbert de la Porrée, and Rupert of Lincoln in the year 1140. Alexander of Chester in the year 1228. William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris, and Walter of Maguelone in the year 1230. Thomas Aquinas in the year 1274. Peter of Perpignan in the year 1300. Richard of Exeter, and Ludolph the Carthusian in the year 1330. Nicholas Gorran in the year 1390. Michael Angrian in the year 1396. (whose commentaries, under the title of an unknown author, later known as commonly Michael Ayguan, were published for the eighth time at Lyon in the year 1652, distributed into two volumes) Nicholas Trivet in the year 1400. Matthew the German in the year 1415. Peter Alan in the year 1416. Philip

The Chancellor of Paris in the year 1450. Johannes Mechlinius in the year 1460. Theodoricus Herpenius in the year 1476. Rudolphus Agricola in the year 1485. Gabriel Brebia in the year 1490. Johannes Picus Mirandula in the year 1494. Petrus Heren Hasius in the year 1496. Ludovicus Pictorius in the year 1510. Guilhelmus Gregorii in the year 1516. And these wrote on the entire Psalter before the Reformation of B. Luther. Those who followed them in the previous century are Felix Pratensis in the year 1520. Franciscus Titelmannus in the year 1530. Franciscus Puteanus in the year 1534. Henricus Lagen in the year 1535. Johannes Baptista Folengus, Hieronymus Varlemus Sylvius, as also Placidus Parmensis in the year 1550. Rainerus in the year 1554. Johannes de Turrecremata in the year 1560. Franciscus Visdominus in the year 1566. Genebrardus, Theologian of Paris, in the year 1587. Likewise Jansenius, and Robertus Bellarminus the Cardinal, and also Johannes Lorinus the Jesuit, of whom the latter prepared lengthy commentaries on the Psalms consisting of three volumes. To these must be added also Simon de Muis, Professor of the Hebrew language at Paris. Among our own, after the works of B. Luther, Johannes Bugenhagius of Pomerania and Salomo Gesnerus deserve praise in our Academy for their Arguments and summaries of the Psalms; in the University of Leipzig, Alexander Alesius, the blessed Lord Dr. Henricus Höpffnerus, and Lord Dr. Martinus Geier; in Tübingen, Erhardus Schnepfius; in Rostock, Dr. David Chytreus and Johann Tarnovius, who however commented only on some Psalms, and the latter on the first ten, as well as the Penitential and Passion Psalms: to these must be added the Homiletic works of the blessed Dr. Mörlinus, Nicol. Selneccerus, Joh. Arndtius, and Reinh. Backius. Among the Reformed, Johannes Calvinus, Wolfgangus Musculus, Henricus Mollerus, August. Marloratus, Coppenius, and Joh. Coccejus wrote on the Psalms. Joh. Vicarsus the Englishman published Decapla on the Psalms. Andreas Rivetus illustrated the Prophetic Psalms, etc.

Latin:

AD PRÆFATION

QUanquam non modo Josephus & Rabbi- ni veteres de autore Psalmorum Davi- de, si Alesio fides habenda, valde con- sentiant, sed & Augustino opinio eo- rum credibilior visa fuerit, l. XVII. de Civitate Dei cap. 14. qui omnes Psalmos Davidis operæ tribuunt, cui Cassiodorus calculum addit Præfat. Psalter. & Ambrosius ut & Chrysostomus, Beda & Euthymius, in quam etiam Theodoretes inclinat: quam propugnat Alex. Ales. satis acriter. Merito tamen præfertur aliorum sententia, qui nonnullos ab aliis autoribus profectos statuunt. Quæ non tantum Origenis, Eu- sebij, Hilarij, & recentiorum plerorumque, sed eti- am Hieronymi mens est, Epistola ad Sophroncum Tom. 3. Oper. p. m. 78. Psalmos omnes eorum testa- mur autorum qui ponuntur in titulis, David scilicet, Assaph, & Idithum, filiorum Core, Eman, Ezrahitæ, Moysi, & Salomonis, & reliquorum, quos Esdras pri- mo volumine comprehendit. Hunc sequutus Isidorus Hispalensis libro de Officiis Psalterium docet à de- cem Prophetis scriptum esse: Mose, Davide, Salomo- ne, Assapho, Eman, Ethan, Ithum & filiis Chore, El- cana, Eleazar, Abiazab. Sanctus Athanasius alios quoque nominat, Aggæum nempe & Zachariam, quos itidem annumerat Psalmorum autoribus; cu- jus hæc in Synopsi S. Scripturæ legitur sententia: Tametsi hic Psalmorum liber solius habeat Davidis in- scriptionem, multorum tamen aliorum quoque in illo sunt Psalmi, utpote Assaph, Idithum, filiorum Chore, Aggæi, Zachariæ, & Eman Israelitæ. Sunt etiam nonnulli, qui communiter ab omnibus semel sunt dicti, quotquot videlicet alleluja habent. Itaq; Esdras omnes hosce Psalmos à quibuscunque dictos uno complexus est libro, qui quidem quasi communes sint Psalmi omni- um quos continet, Psalmorum liber vocatur, soli ve- ro Davidi inscribitur, propterea quod ille primus Spi- ritum psallendi à Deo accepit, primusque Psalmos composuit & scripsit, & prædictos Psalmistas ipse ex sacerdotibus selegit ac instituit, stationemque locorum illis & ordinem melodiæ ac tempus psallendi matuti- num & vespertinum determinavit, & ita ordinavit, ut alii aperto, alii clauso templo, alii à dextris, alii à sini- stris starent, atque ita quidem Deo psallerent, laudem- que ac hymnum voce canerent, quidam vero confessio- nem ac laudem præluderent, illi in musicis instrumen- tis, citharis, nabliis, ac cymbalis, isti in tubis sublime personarent. Quæ sententia non obscure compro- batur 2. Paral. 29, 30. cum sermonibus, vel poemasi Davidis & Assaph Levitæ jussi sunt Dominum lauda- re. Siquidem ita non minus Assaphum, quam Da- videm Psalmorum autorem fuisse, indicatum sit. Ut ergo לדוד Psalm. 3, 1. & in aliis Psalmis nota est autoris sive in Genitivo reddatur ut Hab. 3, 1. 1. Sam. 14, 16. ל Nota genitivi est, & à Grammaticis in no- minibus propriis pro tali habetur: Sive in Dativo, quod mavult B. Walth. in centur miscell. p. 521. uti redditur à LXX. Interpp. si exponatur Davidi κατ' ὑπόνοιαν subintelligendo Hymnum esse à S. S. reve- latum, vel dictatum: ita idem in inscriptionibus לאסף notari Psalm. 73. & seqq. causa nulla est cur ambigamus. De filiis tamen Kore dubium est, an illi autores Psalmi alicujus sint: quum pluribus u- num eundemque Psalmum inspiratum esse haud sit probabile, ac disputat Bonfrerius in præloqv. ad Script. S. cap. 7. pag. 26. etiam de Idithun & aliis, quod autores Psalmorum nulli sint, nisi hi quinque, David, Assaph, Eman, Ezrahita & Ethan, & Mosis quidem unicum solum esse, Psalmum nimirum XC. Ethan unicum LXXXIX. Eman unicum LXXXVIII. Assaph duodecim nempe L. LXXIII. & decem sequentes, reliquos omnes 135. seu Epi- graphen habentes seu ἀνεπιγράφυς videri David adscribendos.

Sed quicunque tandem autores Psalmorum sint, nullatenus dubitandum est, omnes à Spiritu S. agi- tatos esse, quemadmodum etiam Assaph Propheta diserte nominatur loco laudato 2. Paral. 29, 30. & idem Assaph, nec non Heman & Iduthun in Cytharis prophetasse dicuntur 1. Paral. 25, 1. Non ergo homi- nes quoscunque ad hymnorum compositionem idoneos adhibitos fuisse, cum Grotio censendum, sed θεο- πνεύστης 2. Tim. 3, 16. & φερομένης ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε 2. Petr. 1, 21. Neque libri Canonici Vet. Testa- menti, ad quos refert Christus ipse Psalmos Luc. 24. sive integri sive ex parte, ab aliis, quam Pro- phetis, divinitus inspiratis, profecti sunt, atque eo nomine prophetici dicuntur.

Porro Psalmorum ordinem & distributionem juxta Ebraicam veritatem nos sectari potius debe- re, quam juxta Latinam translationem, haud am- biguum nobis est, qui non temere discedendum existimamus ab Ebræo textu, etiam in ejusmodi di- stinctionibus. Psalmum autem primum à secundo distinguendum esse non obscure argumentum utri- usque confirmat. Quod in utroque maxime diver- sum est. Ideo præferenda antiquorum sententia, quam laudat Hieronymus ad Psalm. 1. Quidam dicunt hunc Psalmum quasi præfationem esse Spiritus Sancti, & ideo titulum non habere. Quæ quam egregie ar- gumento ejusdem conveniant, ignorare non pote- rit, qui B. Gesnero in meditatione Psalterii cap. 14. & seqq. præeunte, expenderit totum Psalterium in explicanda spirituali hominis beatitudine occupari.

Neque vero nos movet, quod Codices aliqui A- ctor. 13, 33. pro τῷ δευτέρῳ habeant πρώτῳ, quia ra- riores illi, & inter omnes Bezæ Codices unus tan- tum ita habuit. Cum ergo plerique Codices com- muni distinctioni consentiant, quam argumentum psalmorum solide statuminat, ab ea nequaquam in gratiam paucorum Codicum discedendum est. Id certe materia psalmi satis docet, non cohærere psal- mum secundum primo, sed argumento peculiari constare.

Ale- xander Castriensis Anno 1228. Guilhelmus Alvernus Episcopus Parisiensis, & Galterus Magellensis An- no 1230. Thomas Aquinas Anno 1274. Petrus Perpi- nianus Anno 1300. Ricchardus Exestriensis, & Lu- dolphus Carthusianus Anno 1330. Nicolaus Gorranus Anno 1390. Michael Angrianus Anno 1396. (cujus commentarii sub titulo Autoris incogniti dehinc cogniti vulgo Michael. Ayguan. octavum Lugdu- ni Anno 1652. prodiere in duos Tomos distributi) Nicolaus Trivet Anno 1400. Matthæus Germanus Anno 1415. Petrus Alanus Anno 1416. Philippus

Cancellarius Parisiensis Anno 1450. Johannes Mech- linius Anno 1460. Theodoricus Herpenius Ann. 1476. Rudolphus Agricola Anno 1485. Gabriel Brebia Ann. 1490. Johannes Picus Mirandula Anno 1494. Quibus adden- dus & Simon de Muis Professor Ebrææ linguæ Pari- siensis. E nostris post B. Lutheri operationes in Psal- mos, & Argumenta & summas Psalmorum laudem merentur in nostra Academia Joh. Bugenhagius Po- meranus, & Salomo Gesnerus, in Lipsiensi Alexan- der Alesius, B. Dn. D. Henricus Höpffnerus, & Dn. D. Martinus Geier, in Tubingensi Erhardus Schne- pfius, in Rostochiensi D. ## 1:1 Argument
BOOK I. OF THE PSALMS. PSALM I. The Blessed man, and the miserable.

Vers. 1. BLESSED IS THE MAN. In Hebrew, the beatitudes of this man. LXX: μακάριος ὁ ἀνὴρ. See Tarnov. Exerc. Bibl. p. 761. Kimchi wishes to imply by the plural noun that not just one kind of good or prosperity is sufficient. The interjection of Coccejus, 'O blessed is he!', can hardly be approved, because the word אַשְׁרֵי occurs in other places where an interjection, adverb, or exclamation has no place. Michaël de Ayguan, however, explains the Psalm literally concerning the faithful, and allegorically concerning Christ. Alex. Alesius judges that it should be explained primarily and principally concerning Christ the head of the Church, and then concerning his members. But as the sense of Scripture is only one, so it is manifest from the whole Psalm that the blessedness of the Pious is described with an antithesis to the ungodly: which is done by the declaration of the subject, who the pious are, by negation and affirmation, and of the predicate; when his happiness is illustrated by the likeness of a good, fruit-bearing tree, with leaves that do not fall, convenient and beautiful, and by the prosperity of its works or fruits, and also from the contrary, that the ungodly, as chaff, destitute of root, sap, fruit, and all greenness, are dispersed by the wrath and power of the Lord, as if by the wind, and thus do not rise, nor stand in the judgment or the assembly of the righteous; with the addition of a confirmation: because God knows, with a knowledge of approval, the way of the righteous, which therefore does not perish, but succeeds happily and reaches its end, while the way of the ungodly, which He does not approve but detests, perishes at last with them. I pass over the fact that this first Psalm, according to some, contains the sum of the Law, and the second the sum of the Gospel, so that he who sees in the first that he can by no means keep the Law, may flee to the righteousness of the Gospel, which is situated in Christ, explained in the second Psalm: in which he is declared blessed who trusts in Christ, in the last verse, just as in the beginning of this one he is called blessed who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly. Compare the blessed Joh. Tarnovius on Psalm 1, as also the blessed Lord Dr. Jacob. Wellerus.

Vers. eod.

WHO HAS NOT WALKED IN THE COUNSEL OF THE UNGODLY. Three degrees of those living wickedly are described here: those who begin, those who persist, and those who now clearly acquiesce in an evil life. These past tenses, however, would be more correctly translated by the present: he walks, he stands, he sits.

It is a climax, as of the persons: 1. Of the wicked in mind. 2. Of sinners, whose impiety of heart breaks out into external action. 3. Of scoffers, who even glory in their malice: so also of the institutions of life, where there is attributed to them: 1. Counsel, by which wicked thoughts. 2. Way, by which the expression, progress, and continuation of impiety. 3. Seat, or chair of pestilence, by which the kingdom of malice and exultation in the same; and also of actions, as they are: 1. To walk, so that in any way they may attain the end which they have conceived in their mind. 2. To stand in the worst way, without any fear of God. 3. To sit, or to trust clearly in the chair of pestilence, and to exalt themselves in their malice, and to predominate.

Vers. eod.

IN THE CHAIR OF PESTILENCE) Aquila well: ἐν καθέδρᾳ χλευαστῶν. The לצים among the Hebrews are arrogant men to such a degree that they mock the pious.

Latin:

LIBER I. PSALMORUM. PSALM. I. Homo Beatus, & miser.

Vers. 1. BEATUS VIR. IN Ebr. Beatitudines istius viri. LXX. μακάριος ὁ ἀνὴρ. Vid. Tarnov. Exerc. Bibl. p. 761. Kimchi non unum tantum genus boni, aut prosperitatis suf- ficere innui voce plurali vult. Cocceji interjectio, ô beate illum! vix probari potest, quia τὸ אַשְׁרֵי in aliis locis occurrit, ubi interjectio, adverbium, vel exclamatio locum non habet. Exponit autem Psal- mum Michaël de Ayguan literaliter de fidelibus, al- legorice de Christo. Alex. Alesius primo & principa- liter de Christo capite Ecclesiæ, deinde de membris ejus exponendum esse censet. Sed uti sensus Scri- pturæ non est, nisi unicus, ita manifestum est è toto Psalmo Piorum beatitudinem cum ἀντιθέσει impio- rum eodem describi: Quod fit declaratione subje- cti, quinam pii sint, κατ’ ἄρσιν & θέσιν, & prædicati; cum felicitas ejus simili illustratur arboris bonæ, fru- giferæ, & foliis non defluentibus, commodæ, ac deco- ræ, & operum vel fructuum prosperitate, nec non à contrario, quod impii ut gluma, radice, succo, fru- ctu, omnique viriditate destituti, Domini ira, & po- tentia, ceu vento, dispellantur, adeoque non consur- gant, nec consistant in judicio, vel conventu justo- rum; addita confirmatione; quia Deus novit, no- titia approbationis, viam justorum, quæ proin- de non perit, sed feliciter succedit, & terminatur, impiorum via, quam non approbat, sed detestatur, cum ipsis tandem pereunte. Taceo, quod primus hic Psalmus juxta nonnullos summam legis, ac se- cundus summam Evangelii contineat, ut qui se le- gem haud posse servare in primo videt, ad justitiam Evangelii, quæ sita est in Christo, in Psalmo secun- do expositam confugiat: quo beatus prædicatur, qui in Christo confidit vers. ult. ut in hujus initio bea- tus dicitur, qui non abit in consilio impiorum. Conf. B. Joh. Tarnovius in Psalm. 1. ut & B. Dn. D. Jacob. Wellerus.

Vers. eod.

QVI NON ABIIT IN CONSILIO IMPIORVM Tres hic gradus describuntur male viventium, eorum qui incipiunt, eorum qui perstant, eorum qui plane jam in mala vita acquiescunt. Præterita autem hæc rectius per præsens vertentur: abit, stat, sedet.

Climax est, ut personarum 1. Improborum ani- mo. 2. Peccatorum, quorum impietas cordis in ex- ternum actum prorumpit. 3. Irrisorum, qui adhæc in malitia gloriantur: ita & vitæ institutorum, ubi tribuitur ipsis 1. Consilium, qua pravas cogitatio- nes. 2. Via, qua impietatis expressionem, progres- sum, & continuationem. 3. Sedes, seu cathedra pe- stilentiæ, qua regnum malitiæ, & exultationem in eadem; nec non actionum, ut sunt 1. Ambulare, ut quocunque modo finem, quem animo concepere, assequantur. 2. Consistere in via pessima, sine ullo Dei timore. 3. Sedere, seu confidere plane in cathe- dra pestilentiæ, suaque malitia sese efferre, ac præ- dominari.

Vers. eod.

IN CATHEDRA PESTILENTIÆ) Aquila optime: ἐν καθέδρᾳ χλευαστῶν. לצים apud Hebræos sunt homi- nes arrogantes eousque ut pios irrideant.

## 1:5
Verse 5.

THEREFORE THE UNGODLY SHALL NOT STAND IN THE JUDGMENT) Kimchi and the Hebrews infer strange things from this. The sense is, it will come to pass that they shall not lose their case when their life is examined without partiality. For קום means to subsist, as in Josh. 7:12, Nah. 1:6, Ezra 9:15, and it is often used in judicial matters, as σταθῆναι in Luke 21:36.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

IDEO NON SVRGENT IMPII IN JVDICIO) Mira hinc inferunt Kimchi, & Ebræi. Sensus est, futurum, ne causa cadant, ubi vita ipsorum fine affectu examinabitur. Nam קום est subsistere, ut Jos. 7, 12. Nah. 1, 6. Esdr. 9, 15. usurpaturque sæpe in re judiciali, ut σταθῆναι Luc. 21, 36.

## 1:6
Verse 6.

THE LORD KNOWETH THE WAY OF THE RIGHTEOUS) That is, He approves it.

THE WAY OF THE UNGODLY SHALL PERISH) That is, it will lead them to destruction.

Grotius deservedly leaves their portents to the Hebrews here: I wish he had not lent his ears to their ravings and inventions elsewhere! Rabbi David Kimchi thinks it is indicated that the ungodly will not rise again in the future: Menasse Ben Israel observes in Book 2 of 'On the Resurrection of the Dead', ch. 8, that Rabbi Saadia Gaon and Rabbi Moses Gerundensis deny the resurrection of the ungodly along with him. The passage of the aforementioned Saadia Gaon exists at Dan. 12: 'And those who shall not awake are those who forsake the Lord.' But Rabbi Menasse rightly proves the contrary from that passage: both because many are said to be resurrected, whereas the righteous are few; and especially because some of them are said to be resurrected unto shame. However, the sense of Grotius here is too general: It is certain that the ungodly lose their case and do not subsist when their life is examined without partiality. But by משפט, by antonomasia and absolutely, the divine Judgment is understood, and most especially the final one, which the Chaldean has openly expressed: 'therefore the wicked shall not be innocent in the Great Day.' And thus the Greek interpreters, Ambrose, Augustine, the Gloss, Lyranus, Jansenius, and Lorinus explain it as the final judgment, which is designated here by the emphatic or demonstrative ה, as the blessed Tarnovius observes. Concerning the judgment of God, the word קום is used in Is. 7:7, ch. 14:24, ch. 46:10. For the wicked do not stand in any judgment of God, whether that which God institutes here in the present life, or that which He will institute on the last day. Therefore, the ἀνάστασις or resurrection of the wicked is not denied, which is common to the pious and the impious, but the στάσις, the consistency, so to speak, because they will not be able to stand before the judge, Luke 21:35, nor will they have a place in the assembly of the righteous, as the Hiero-Psalmist teaches by way of ἐπεξήγησις; when the threshing floor is purged, they will be scattered like chaff and burned with unquenchable fire, Matt. 3:12. Thus Menasse from the Jews: the wicked shall not stand in judgment: that is, they will indeed rise again, but they will not stand: for that resurrection will not take place for their good and advantage, but for their most grievous punishment. This is correctly stated by R. Menasse; who, however, although he refutes certain trifles of his own people here, could not nevertheless abstain from them; for he reports in the same place a triple class of men to be resurrected, namely, that there are the righteous, the wicked, and the intermediate. The righteous are to rise again for their own advantage and good, so that they may receive the reward of virtue; the wicked for their own disadvantage and evil, so that they may be punished and miserably tormented in body and soul at the same time: but the intermediate are to rise again likewise for their own good: because they will indeed be punished for some time, but afterwards, having been made pure and immaculate, they will be received into the order of the good, so that they may enjoy equal happiness with them. Which are not only foreign to Holy Scripture, but are entirely opposed to it: For as there is no intermediate class between the faithful and the unfaithful, so there is no intermediate state and outcome for those who are to be resurrected, but according to Daniel, some will be awakened to eternal life, others to eternal disgrace: And, as is held here, the Lord knows and approves the way of the righteous, and will approve it in the last judgment, but the way of the wicked, i.e., whatever they themselves do, will finally perish with them, ch. 14:9, 10. Cf. Matt. 7:13, 23, ch. 25:46, John 5:29. Grotius also acknowledged this sense in his commentary on Luke 14:13, ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων. Christ seems here to have alluded to that of the first Psalm, οὐκ ἀναστήσονται ἐν βουλῇ δικαίων, where Symmachus has ἐν συνελεύσει δικαίων, others ἐν συλλόγῳ or συναγωγῇ.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NOVIT DOMINVS VIAM JVSTO RVM) Id est, ap- probar.

ITER IMPIORVM PERIBIT) Id est, in exitium eos ducet.

Merito Ebræis portenta sua hic relinquit Gro- tius: utinam & alias deliriis ac commentis eorum aures nullas præbuisset! R. David Kimchi putat id indicari; quod impii olim resurrecturi non sint: cum quo impiorum resurrectionem R. Saadia Ga- on, & R. Mosen Gerundensem negare Menasse Ben Israel observat lib. 2. de Resurr. mortuor. c. 8. Lo- cus prædicti Saadia Gaon extat ad Dan. 12. Et illi, qui non evigilabunt, sunt qui relinquunt Dominum. Sed ex eo loco R. Menasse recte contrarium pro- bat: tum quia multi dicuntur resuscitandi, justi au- tem pauci sunt: tum imprimis quia nonnulli eorum resuscitandi dicuntur in opprobrium. Sensus au- tem Grotii hic nimis generalis est: Certum est cau- sa cadere, non subsistere impios, cum vita eorum sine affectu examinatur. Sed per משפט κατ’ ἀν- τονομασίαν & absolute Judicium divinum, & maxi- me quidem novissimum intelligitur, quod aperte Chaldæus expressit, propterea non innocentes erunt improbi in Die magno: Atque ita interpp. Græci, Am- brosius, Augustinus, Glossa, Lyranus, Jansenius, Lori- nus de extremo judicio explicant, quod per ה Em- phaticum vel demonstrativum hic designari B. Tar- novius observat. De Judicio Dei verbum קום ad- hibetur Es. 7, 7. c. 14, 24. c. 46, 10. In nullo enim ju- dicio Dei consistunt impii, sive quod hic instituit Deus in præsente vita, seu quod in novissimo die in- stituet. Non ergo negatur impiorum ἀνάστασις ve resurrectio, quæ communis est piis & impiis, sed στάσις consistentia, ut ita dicam, quia coram judice stare non poterunt Luc. 21, 35. neque in cœtu justo- rum locum habituri sunt, ut per ἐπεξήγησιν doce Hiero-Psaltes; cum area purgabiur, instar paleæ dispergentur, & igne inextinguibili exurentur Matth 3, 12. Sic è Judæis Menasse: non consistent impii in judicio: id est, resurgent quidem, sed non consistent: quippe resurrectio illa non fiet eorum bono ac commo- do, sed ad gravissimam eorum pœnam. Hæc recte R. Menasse; qui vero utut nugas suorum quasdam hic refellat, ab illis tamen abstinere non potuit; tradit enim ibidem, hominum resuscitandorum triplicem classem, quod nempe sint probi, improbi, & interme- dii. Probi resurrecturi sint ad commodum ac bo- num suum, ut recipiant præmium virtutis; improbi ad incommodum & malum suum, ut corpore atque anima simul puniantur, ac misere crucientur: Inter- medii autem furrecturi itidem suo bono sint: quia punientur quidem aliquandiu, sed postea puri atque immaculati facti recipientur in ordinem bonorum, ut cum illis pari felicitate fruantur. Quæ à Scriptu- ra S. non aliena tantum sunt, sed ei prorsus adver- santur: Nam ut nullum intermedium genus inter fi- deles & infideles, ita nec status & exitus medius est resuscitandorum, sed teste Daniele, alii ad vitam æ- ternam excitabuntur, alii ad æternum opprobrium: Et, uti hic habetur, novit & approbat Dominus viam justorum, atque approbaturus est in judicio novissimo, impiorum autem iter, h. e. quicquid ipsi faciunt, tandem peribit cum ipsis, cap. 14, 9. 10. Conf. Matth. 7, 13. 23. cap. 25, 46. Joh. 5, 29. Agnovit hunc sensum & Grotius ad Luc. 14, 13. ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει τῶν δικαίων. Videtur hîc Christus allusisse ad illud Psal- mi primi ἐκ ἀναστήσονται ἐν βυλῇ δικαίων, ubi Sym- machus ἐν συνελεύσει δικαίων, alii ἐν συλλόγῳ aut συναγωγῇ.

## 2:1 Argument
PSALM II.

The Passion and Kingdom of the Son of the eternal God, who is the source of blessedness.

Verse 1. WHY DID THE GENTILES RAGE) The Philistines, Moabites, Sabaeans, Damascenes, Ammonites, Idumaeans, 2 Sam. 8 and 10. Their primary and manifest sense pertains to David, the mystical and more abstruse one to the Messiah, as David Kimchi acknowledges here, and Saadias Gaon to Daniel, in the way the Apostles took it.

Grotius owes the fabrication concerning the dual sense, the primary and manifest, as well as the mystical and more abstruse, primarily to the Papists: among whom Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, as well as Salianus here likewise, wishes to regard David as far as the literal sense is concerned, but Christ only as far as the mystical sense is concerned. He has this depravation here also from Calvin and his disciples Musculus, Tossanus, Paraeus, and others, to whom our author is otherwise sufficiently hostile: But because he saw that they approached more closely to the Jews here, he willingly added his vote to them. For it pleased him, especially in this and other Prophetic oracles, to defend the twisted and impious glosses of the rebels against Christ, or to offer them, proposed in a somewhat soft manner, to the unwary. Which was also done by Calvin, but with unhappy success, as our blessed Hunnius sufficiently showed in his 'Calvin the Judaizer' and his defense of the same against the Hyperaspistes David Pareus. For the modern Jews understand the present Psalm entirely concerning David according to the letter, and just as Grotius does, they explain everything concerning the affairs of David; that he, when he had been established as King and had chosen a royal seat for himself at his death, here expostulated with his enemies, whether already defeated or still rising up against him, the Philistines, Ammonites, and the like, and predicted that their attempts would be useless, because he was elected King by God, having received supreme power over his enemies, whose lands God had decreed to give to him as an inheritance. No egg is so similar to an egg as this gloss of the Hebrews is to the Grotian one. For even some of the Hebrews finally confess that certain things in this Psalm are applied mystically to the Messiah, or that David acted as a type of the Messiah in certain things, provided only that they maintain that the Psalm deals with David according to the letter. Some, however, among them refer the same to the times of Jehoshaphat, since many and powerful peoples formed a conspiracy against him, the children of Ammon, the children of Moab, and the inhabitants of Mount Seir with the Syrians, 2 Chronicles ch. 20. But because most all explain it concerning David, Grotius, Judaizing here in all things, preferred to follow the greater part of the Jews, but the more recent ones. Finally, it pleased our author here also to follow the footsteps of the Neo-Photinians, Enjedinus, and others, and in a like manner to deprave this most illustrious Psalm with them.

As we do not envy the advocate of the Jews and various heretics these masters, or accomplices, or clients, so it is certain that he here departs from the common and concordant explanation of the Fathers, which he otherwise commends as a rule of interpretation. For he will not easily produce any of the Fathers interpreting the text in that manner. And although they differ in certain points, e.g., that some explain the words, 'Today I have begotten thee,' differently, yet they agree in this, that that Psalm deals literally with our Messiah, just as also no one understands that voice: 'Thou art my son,' of David, but all understand it only of Christ. Which Andreas Rivetus does not deny in the school of the Calvinists, Comment. on the Decad of Psalms, on Ps. 2, p. 3: 'Almost all the orthodox Fathers accept and interpret simply and immediately of Christ whatever is said in this Psalm.' He adds, but for the sake of his Calvin, that not a few, especially of the MORE RECENT writers, interpret it of David and Christ, of whom the former was the type, the latter the truth. Of whom, however, NONE from antiquity, and from the more recent ones besides Calvin, Pellican, and Pareus, not easily ANYONE can be named. Although indeed Rivetus, a man of great name among his own, and a distinguished defender of his Calvin, would willingly yield the palm here also to Calvin; 'And certainly,' he says, 'it seems that David speaks in his own person, "But I have been constituted King by him," and what follows: Nor does it hinder the truth if those things which are cited from the Old Testament concerning Christ are understood literally to pertain first to someone who bore the figure and type of Christ; those things also seem to be understood more pleasantly and clearly concerning Christ, which we contemplate as having been first adumbrated in his type, but which we perceive to agree more truly and perfectly with Christ himself:' He could not, however, but, constrained by the light of truth, here abandon Calvin and his associates: 'I, however,' he says, 'easily descend into that opinion, on account of certain things which are held at the end of the Psalm, which pertain ONLY to Christ, that this Prophet sang this Psalm concerning Christ properly and by primary intention, if I may so speak.' With a wavering pen, Rivetus seems to have added this about 'primary intention.' For he knows well that there is not more than one sense of a single saying or sentence, and therefore that the Holy Spirit has only one intention in any oracle, if indeed Scripture ought not to be held as ambiguous, and like the Delphic oracles perplexed, and obscure. The things, therefore, which he subjoins, teach how eagerly he wished to help Calvin: although not without the type of his own kingdom, in which he saw the kingdom of Christ shadowed forth by many things, namely in the assault and contradiction of many kingdoms round about, the contradiction which the kingdom of Christ was to suffer first in Judea, and finally throughout the whole world from various peoples and Kings of the earth: in the expansion of his kingdom even to foreign nations, and his divine victory which he obtained over rebels, the propagation of the kingdom of Christ even to the extreme ends of the earth, and his power over rebels, which he will exercise over them especially on the last day. Here, therefore, David, having taken the occasion from the wicked attempts begun by his enemies, prophesied concerning the deliberations, studies, and attempts of all Anti-Christians against Christ and the Church, and predicted concerning the kingdom of Christ and its perpetual stability. Franc. Junius also has these in the same words in his parallels, from whom Rivetus received them. But even if all those things are true, they nevertheless do not help Calvin. For the question is not, on what occasion this prophecy was conceived? nor is the question whether certain things were predicted here, of which David bore the type, or whether in certain things which he predicted concerning Christ, the Holy Spirit represented the figure and type of David in his own time? But the question is concerning the sense of the Psalm and its words, and concerning the intention of the Holy Spirit; whether in this Psalm either all things, or at least some things, treat of David, and are to be understood of him, according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, and therefore properly? For there is only one sense, one mind and intention of the Holy Spirit in one place of Scripture; if it speaks of David and describes his affairs, it does not speak of Christ, nor can it be understood as such; if it speaks of Christ and predicts those things which he himself is about to do, it certainly ought not to be explained of David, whether you call it a primary or secondary intention, or proper or improper; or literal or mystical. Those distinctions and monstrosities are empty, devised to obscure the mind of the Holy Spirit and to help the Jews and Judaizers. The meaning of any given statement is not uncertain, nor ambiguous, but certain and constant, and therefore unique, the unique intention of the Holy Spirit, which is therefore proper to any given statement, and is accustomed to be called the literal sense, to be gathered from the preceding and following text. But that under that signified thing (not by the words, I say, but by that which the words signify and import) a type of future things is sometimes exhibited, or even something which in the Old Testament was typically shadowed forth elsewhere in another subject, is not new: but that is here irrelevant, where the inquiry is solely concerning the sense of the words of the Psalm, in which therefore Rivetus was forced to contradict his own Calvin, as he did the Jews, openly with Junius (for he made the latter's words his own): 'Some interpreters, however,' he says, 'doubt whether David speaks literally of himself and his kingdom in this Psalm? The Jews, subverting the doctrine concerning Christ as far as it can be done, contend that what is said in this Psalm ought simply to be accepted concerning David and his kingdom.' (Which Calvin also contends, Pareus, Tossanus, and others contend.) Which opinion is overturned not only by the argument of the Psalm itself, but also by the consequence and the order itself. For the argument pertains so manifestly to the kingdom of the Messiah that not even the most obstinate of the Jews can deny it: because God addresses his Son: he constitutes him Prophet, King, and Priest, attributes to him the inheritance of the whole world, assigns to him omnipotence, and commands worship, reverence, and fear, and finally faith in him, from all nations. Which things, I think, no one but a BLASPHEMER can understand of a mere man. The consequence of the statements also seems to be repugnant to this opinion, if, as pleases some, just as David proposed the sum of the law in the first Psalm, so he comprehends the doctrine of the Gospel and of faith in Christ in the second. And certainly among Christians there can be no doubt that this Psalm is to be understood of Christ the Savior, since the Apostles in various places have referred it to Christ, as is evident in Acts 4 and 13, Hebrews 1:5, Revelation 2 and 19. These are the words of Rivetus, and before him Junius. What of the fact that Rivetus proves against other Calvinists that this treats of Christ alone at verse 7, p. 18. Omitting also those of our own who accommodate this historically to David, and as a type of Christ, it will be a MATTER OF RELIGION for us to depart even a hair's breadth from the sense of Paul, whom arguments convince that this passage is to be accepted immediately and solely concerning Christ in its proper and genuine sense: 1. Taken from the circumstance of the place and persons, when in Acts 13 he referred that passage to Christ. For he was then in the synagogue, and was teaching among the Jews, to whom he would not have brought forward passages either controversial or difficult to accommodate as a place of confirmation; by which reasoning he would rather have confirmed them in error, unless it had been established among them at that time that this Psalm pertains properly to the Messiah. 2. From the opposition of the Son and the Angels. Because certainly the argumentation of Paul in Hebrews 1:9 would collapse entirely if these words could in any way be referred to another than Christ. These are again the words of Rivetus. Which are deservedly opposed to Calvin and Pareus. But Pareus himself, together with his Calvin, acknowledges that the last verse of this Psalm is to be understood of Christ alone. What stupor, therefore, what blindness and vertigo is it of both, that they interpret the seventh verse, equally august, of David and of Christ at the same time? when the connection of the text in no way admits such a distinction, that in verse 7 two Sons of God are understood, David and Christ, but in verses 11 and 12 only one Son, namely Christ alone: 'kiss the son: blessed are all who trust in him.' That is immovable and fixed, that the same and no other Son of God is insinuated and commended to us in both places. And these things concerning the Reformed. Many other Papists refute Salianus and Cornelius Jansenius: Cardinal Bellarmine in his explanation of the Psalms, page 5. For this WHOLE Psalm, he says, is a MOST MANIFEST prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ, and explained by the Apostles in Acts 4 and 13, and Hebrews 1 and 5, so that those who attempt to explain this Psalm LITERALLY of David seem to err ALTOGETHER. Jacobus Tirinus, when he had explained those words in verse 8, I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession, concerning the breadth of the Catholic Church, along with Eusebius, Didymus, Theodoret, and others, adds these things: Whence it is evident that this Psalm is to be expounded LITERALLY not of David, as the Rabbis and Salianus wish (for so ample an empire never fell to David), but of the Messiah, the Son of David. Thus the Holy Fathers and Doctors. Franc. Ribera in his Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, similarly rebukes Jansenius because he taught that the words of the Psalm apply to David as the type and to Christ as the antitype. With these, other Papists agree, including Menochius, whom Grotius is accustomed to value highly.

To Enjedinus the Neo-Photinian, who likewise contends with the Jews that the second Psalm speaks literally of David but spiritually of the Messiah, whom Schlichtingius also follows in his Disputation on the Holy Trinity against B. Meisner, page 429, perhaps Socinus himself might be opposed, who seems to accept this Psalm simply concerning Christ in his response given to Wujeckus, chapter 2, page 35. It is found written most frequently in the Old Testament, Christ or the anointed of Jehovah, that is, of that one God, even then when words are made concerning Christ our Lord himself, as in Psalm 2:2 and Psalm 132:17. The arguments also of Enjedinus, by which it is proved that these things are to be understood literally concerning David, they are so frivolous, and in part impious, that it is a wonder that anyone could have been moved to assent to them.

The first he draws from the authority of the Hebrews, which no sane person would rashly despise when interpreting the Scriptures, as well as from the consensus of certain Zwinglians: But who in his right mind would value the authority of the Hebrews so highly in those matters which concern Christ, that he would postpone the consensus of the Catholic Church for the sake of those ἀσπόνδȣς (implacable) enemies of Christ? Indeed, the authority of the Judaizing Zwinglians cannot here be held to be greater than the authority of the Jews themselves: inasmuch as others in the same school oppose them, just as the ancient Jews also agree with the Christians in the explanation of this Psalm, and oppose the interpretation of the more recent Jews.

The second, that the Psalm speaks of a past event, rests on a reed-like support, namely that present or past verbs are used. For who does not know that this is done in a manner most customary to the Prophets, for the sake of the certainty of predictions, and for a better representation of future things?

The third, that these things were never completed in Christ, is openly contradicted by the testimony of the Apostles in Acts 4. For that which they say was fulfilled in Pilate and Herod, the scoffer impiously mocks, saying that Pilate was not a King, that Herod did not rage against him, but that he (the profane man calls Christ so contemptuously) DESPISED THE MAN, that neither wanted to depose him from his throne; that Pilate was prepared to free him, and that Herod, when he had him in his power, dismissed him unharmed: that only the Jews were his enemies, but that their counsels against him were not in vain, but attained their desired end, that Jesus did not rule over the Jews or the Gentiles, nor did he cast off his bonds. What is it to speak against the Holy Spirit, if this is not? For thus the Apostle says in Acts 4:24, seqq. Lord, you are he who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them, who by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David your servant said: Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things? The Kings of the Earth stood by, and the Princes gathered together in one against the Lord and against his Christ! For they truly gathered together in this city against your Holy child Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod, and Pontius Pilate with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do what your hand and your counsel decreed to be done. What therefore is more certain than that the Apostles explain these things, which the Holy Spirit predicted concerning the raging and tumult of the Kings, as referring to the machinations undertaken against Christ by Herod, Pilate, and others? Whose counsels he impiously asserts attained their desired end, when the Holy Spirit predicted that they would be clearly in vain, and here also testified that they were in vain. For although they themselves killed the author of life, yet the Lord raised him up, and made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36, chapter 3:15, whose spiritual bonds are laws, and are attempted in vain to be broken and cast off by the impious.

The fourth and final argument of Enjedinus is that the words and sentences of the Psalm are accommodated to different persons and times, the beginning indeed to the Apostles and their persecution after the ascension of Christ, the middle to the resurrection and ascension of Christ, Acts 13, Heb. 5, the end partly to Christ already reigning, Apocal. 19:15, partly to the pious reigning in the future life. Resp. The beginning is explained concerning the raging against Christ when he was on earth, and especially at the time of his great passion, which is manifest both from the passage itself in Acts 4:24, and from a comparison of chapter 2:22, 23, chapter 3:15, 17, chapter 4:11, 12. Nor are the middle or the end explained concerning anyone other than Christ, even if his faithful are admitted to some communion of Christ's power, Apoc. 2:26. And how will it be taught from that interpretation made in the New Testament concerning Christ, that the present Psalm is not to be understood of Christ? Does it not rather clearly appear from that, that it deals entirely with Christ? For nowhere in the New Testament is it explained concerning David: always concerning Christ. But so much for Enjedinus.

To the modern Jews we oppose the more ancient ones. For that it was certain among the Hebrews even in the time of the Apostles that this Psalm deals properly and by the intention of the Holy Spirit with Christ, is manifest even from the fact that, writing to them, he affirms it as an ὁμολογούμενον (a thing agreed upon); and R. Solomon, and R. Aben-Esra, as well as Bereschith Rabba, in Genesis 49:10, who interpret it concerning the Messiah, are praised by Galatinus, lib. 3, de Cath. verit. arc. cap. 6, and by Helvicius, Elench. Judæor. 2, Class. 3, and others. Which was also done by R. Lusitanus in the Mittelburg Colloquy. In Bereschith Rabba, sect. 43, R. Jonathan is cited, God said to the three, ask: to Solomon in Gibeon, to Ahaz in Isa. 7, and to the Messiah in this place. Similar things are also cited from Seder Olam in Jalkuth to 1 Kings 3:5, Midrasch Tillim, and R. Saadia to Dan. 7:13. In Talmud Massech. Suca, cap. 5. and in Jalkuth to Psalm 2, our Masters taught that the holy and blessed God said to the Messiah, the son of David, ask whatever you wish, I will give it to you, because it is written, I will declare the decree to them. R. Obad. in this place, in this Psalm, makes mention of the days of Christ for converting the human race to the worship of God. And to the words, He shall mock them in his wrath: Christ shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, Isa. 11. To v. 12. To those who trust in him, and await redemption, Light arises. R. Aben-Esra to v. 11. Kiss the Son, who is the Messiah. Grotius himself granted us in his annotations to Matt. 22:41 the consensus of the Jews, namely that David Kimchi himself, and others with him, as also Trypho in Justin, interpret Psalm 2 concerning the Messiah. Nor do the Muhammadans deny that these things pertain to Christ. Phil. Guadagnolus praises the author of the Lexicon, saying thus: Then the word of the most high God to Jesus, to whom be the prayers of God and peace, and I have begotten thee, that is, I have nourished thee.

Now if we consider the text of the Psalm itself, with the application of a comparison of other passages and the interpretation of the New Testament, it is easily demonstrated against Grotius that it can in no way be explained as referring to David, but must be understood solely of the Messiah: first, from the designation of the Son. The Lord said to me: Thou art my Son. By which words it is treated of the Son of God, said in a singular way μονοτρόπως; for something peculiar and proper to this subject is explained here: and he is called the Son of God absolutely, both here and in verse 11, kiss the Son: and he is addressed as such by God himself: Thou art my Son: just as God says of Christ in Matthew 3 and 17, This is THAT Son of mine, as if God recalled us to this oracle of the Psalm. That name also is of such majesty, as it is claimed here for that anointed one of the Lord, that it suits Christ alone, and the Apostle testifies that it was never said to any of the Angels; and from this passage he demonstrates that Christ is the Son of GOD, ὁμοούσιον ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα τοῦ πατρὸς, Heb. 1:6, to which of the Angels did he say at any time, Thou art my Son: I have this day begotten thee? But if this had been said to David in the primary and literal sense, these words of the Apostle would be false, and there would be no strength in his argument, and no truth underlying the axiom.

Then from the eternal generation: Because the discourse here is about that Son who is Son not by creation, adoption, or constitution, but by generation, which is the communication of the same essence: and indeed by eternal generation, as the Orthodox Fathers commonly explain that היום. For since it concerns the generation of the Son, properly so called, begotten from the essence of the Father, that act must be eternal: through which the coeternal Son ὁμαιώνıῶ was begotten. And since that generation is laid as a foundation upon the eternal decree concerning the giving of the ends of the earth as an inheritance to this Son, it is necessary that that generation also be eternal. Therefore, this oracle is used to bring forward the eternal Deity and ὁμοıσίαν of the Son of God, Heb. 1, 6. and as the foundation of his eternal priesthood, Heb. 5, 5. Thirdly, from the title of Messiah. For he is called κατ’ ἀντονομασίαν the Messiah of the Lord: which name belongs absolutely and in an eminent sense to the only-begotten Son of God. Socinus himself admits, loc. cit., that the name of Christ, or the anointed of God, applies to Christ our Lord much more than to all others, and that this name has therefore become as it were his own. Therefore, the Rabbis also understand here that anointed of the Lord, of whom Isaiah 61, 1 speaks. The discourse is about that anointed one who is bound to the Lord Jehovah by a peculiar and indissoluble bond, so that their yoke is one, and the bonds are the same. But who is so bound, if not Christ our Lord? It concerns that Christ, against whom those who rage, always rage against God himself, and most vehemently provoke the wrath of God; against whom people and nations of every kind rise up; against whom every counsel is vain, whatever prudence and power may be employed. Isaiah 8. It concerns that Christ who was appointed King by God over his holy mountain Zion, in so far as that mountain is holy: which is proper to our only Lord Christ, that anointed one who is the holy of holies, Dan. 9, 25. and Psalm 110, 2. Is. 4, 2. ch. 9, 6. seqq. Jerem. 23, 6. Luke 1, 32.

Fourthly, from the amplitude of this dominion. It concerns that Lord who obtains the universal nations as an inheritance, and the ends of the earth as a possession, and thus the whole world. For it is said to him absolutely: ask of me, and I will give you the nations as an inheritance: Let there be no restriction. Whatever nations he asks for, he will have as an inheritance. And lest it be doubted that the same extends just as widely as the ends of the earth, it is added openly, and your possession the ends of the earth. Which can in no way be understood of David: but they are brought forward everywhere concerning the Messiah, Gen. 49, 8. Zech. 9, 10.

Fifthly, from the description of the government. You shall break them with a rod of iron, and like a potter's vessel. Which are said concerning the rebels. For David was not able to break all those who opposed him in such a way: many at times prevailed over him. This is predicated of Christ alone as the Lord of Lords, Rev. 19, who so claims this power for himself that in the other glorious life he will make us, as spiritual kings, participants in it in a certain way, Rev. 2, whence it is again clear that this is to be understood of Christ, not of David. As for the faithful subjects, grace and salvation are promised to them, therefore

We seek the sixth argument from the address to all kings and judges. For the Holy Spirit warns all magistrates, both the highest and the intermediate, all the kings and judges of the earth, that they should submit themselves to this Christ, as Lord of Lords and King of Kings, and that they should not strive to break asunder or cast off his bonds and yoke, which are the bonds and yoke of God himself (since all that is forbidden), but that they should submit themselves to the same, and give themselves to the same kiss of homage, faith, subjection, and adoration. For all are warned indefinitely, without distinction of places and times: just as all are commanded to serve Jehovah in every place and at every time, so also all are commanded to kiss his Son. That exhortation extends just as widely; indeed, it is the very same exhortation: serve the Lord in fear, kiss the Son, which the Vulgate renders, embrace discipline. Nor can these things be said of David, because David speaks here of another person, and commands the kings to kiss the Son, who therefore must be a person distinct from David. It concerns that Christ and King whom, when the kings and judges of the earth kiss, they serve the Lord himself, and whose veneration is of the exact same condition as the service which is rendered to the Lord our God. Whence now a seventh argument arises for us: From religious veneration: which is to be rendered to this anointed one. For it concerns that Son of God who is to be pursued with equal worship as Jehovah GOD the Father, and is ἰσότιμῶ to him, which uniquely befits Christ, John 5, 19. Serve the Lord, he says, in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling, kiss the Son, lest the Lord be angry. That kiss of subjection pertains equally to the spiritual and salutary understanding and instruction of kings, just as the religious service to be rendered to the Lord, and is held in equal estimation with it. Therefore, this exhortation is prefixed to both: And now, O kings, understand, be instructed, you who judge the earth.

The eighth is from divine threatening. For the worship and obedience of this anointed one, if neglected, is the cause of all destruction, even of Kings themselves, and judges, and indeed of all, whoever perish from the wrath of the Lord. It concerns him, therefore, on account of whom those who refuse to kiss the same with true faith are subjected to the wrath of God, and to eternal destruction. But the cause of the wrath of God, and of condemnation or eternal destruction, is infidelity, or that they do not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God, John 3:18, 36. For upon him who is unbelieving, the wrath of God remains. For just as here blessedness is ascribed to those who trust in the Son of God: so, conversely, destruction is adjudged to those who do not kiss the Son of GOD with true faith. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish in the way.

Ninth, from the honor of trust. For he, in whom the Holy Spirit commands us to place our trust, cannot be a ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (mere man), since the Holy Spirit pronounces a curse upon him who places his trust in a mere man, Jeremiah 17:5. Therefore, the Psalm cannot be understood of David, according to the primary and literal sense, but must necessarily and uniquely be accepted concerning the only-begotten Son of God. Inasmuch as he is the one in whom alone we are commanded to place our trust.

Tenth, from the promise of blessedness and salvation. Blessed are all who trust in him. Therefore, this discourse is about that Son of God, in whom is blessedness and salvation through faith in him, and in whom it is necessary to place trust, whoever wishes to be saved, in whom to believe is to be blessed. But who else is that, if not that only-begotten Son of God, in whom alone is our salvation through faith in him, which Scripture most clearly testifies in Acts 4:12, chapter 10:43, John 3:16, and elsewhere throughout.

Eleventh, from the distinction of the speaking person. For it is undoubted that this person who prophesies these things is David, and it is expressly stated in Acts 4: But the author of the Psalm speaks here in such a way, and so moderates the tenor of the entire Psalm, that it appears by no indication that he understands himself; rather, it is most manifest that he speaks of another person, whom he commands to be kissed and in whom he commands trust to be placed.

Twelfth, from the infallible explanation in the New Testament. For it is brought forward concerning Christ in the New Testament not only in a mystical sense, but in a native, proper, and directly intended sense by the Holy Spirit; indeed, it is brought forward in place of a proof, especially in Heb. 1:6. And indeed in such a way that it is declared and taught that this was said of no one else than Christ our Lord. How, therefore, would that Psalm have been said of David in a primary and proper sense? Paul also assumed this in Acts 13 as certain and indubitable, that this concerns Christ: and he testified that the foundation of His eternal Priesthood is fixed there, Heb. 5:5. Thus also Christ did not glorify Himself to become High Priest, but He who spoke to Him: You are My Son, today I have begotten You. Nor did the disciples understand it otherwise than that the Holy Spirit prophesied here concerning the only-begotten Son of God, and in this they placed the foundation and support of their boldness against the persecutions of enemies, Acts 4. Nor did the Apostle John understand it otherwise in Rev. 19, signifying that Christ is He who will rule with a rod of iron and will crush His enemies; not to mention that Christ Himself seems to look to this when, in Luke 18, He predicts that the Son of Man will be delivered to the Gentiles according to the oracles of the prophets: since no other prophetic oracle is easily found in which that conspiracy of the Gentiles and Jews against Christ was more significantly expressed than at the beginning of this Psalm.

Thirteenth, from the absurdity of the Grotian opinion. For who does not see how absurd it is to assign a type of the eternal generation of the Son of God, and how inconvenient it is to constitute the election of David as a type of that eternal generation? It has no analogy with the eternal generation; indeed, since a type is prior to the antitype, how is the election or elevation of David as King prior to the eternal generation of the Son of God? In vain, therefore, is it feigned that these things treat of David in an immediate and literal sense, and of Christ in a mystical sense: for the Apostolic demonstration, Heb. 1, does not permit us to doubt that they refer entirely to the eternal generation of the Son of God. Therefore, induced by these certainly invincible arguments, the Doctors of the Church have understood this Psalm concerning Christ our Lord with great consensus, according to its proper and literal sense, from whose unanimous interpretation one must never rashly depart, much less indeed when it rests upon such great reasons. What of the fact that Grotius himself, before he was fascinated by more recent Jews, in his annotations on the Evangelists, interpreted Psalm 2:8 concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of the Messiah, at Luke 24:47.

Verse of the same.

THE KINGS OF THE EARTH STOOD BY) Named in the history already mentioned, 2 Sam.

Latin:

PSALM. II.

Passio, & Regnum Filii Dei æterni, qui beatitu- dinis fons.

Vers. 1. QVARE FREMVERVNT GENTES) Phili- stini, Moabitæ, Sabæi, Damasceni, Ammonitæ, Idumæi, 2. Sam. 8. & 10. Sensus eorum primus & apertus ad Davidem pertinet, mysticus & abstrusior ad Messiam, ut hic agnoscit David Kimchi, & ad Danielem Saadias Gaon, quomodo sumsere Apostoli.

COmmentum de gemino sensu, primo & aper- to, nec non mystico & abstrusiori, Papistis im- primis debet Grotius: è quibus Cornelius Janse- nius Gandavensis Episcopus, ut & Salianus hic pari- ter, quod ad literalem sensum attinet, Davidem, Christum autem solum quoad mysticum sensum re- spici vult. Habet istam depravationem etiam hic à Calvino, & discipulis ejus Musculo, Tossano, Pa- ræo, & aliis, quibus alias satis infensus est Noster: Sed quia hic eos ad Judæos propius accedere vidit, calculum illis lubens adjecit. Placuit enim impri- mis tum in hoc, tum in aliis oraculis Propheticis, perduellium Christi Gloffemata contorta, atque im- pia tueri, vel μαλθακῶς quodammodo proposita incautis propinare. Quod etiam à Calvino factum, sed infelici successu, quemadmodum B. Hunnius noster in Calvino Judaizante, ejusdemque adversus Hyperaspistem Davidem Pareum defensione satis ostendit. Judæi enim moderni Psalmum præsentem quoad literam totum de Davide intelligunt, ac per- inde uti Grotius, de rebus Davidis omnia explicant; Eundem cum Rex esset constitutus, & in morte sua regiam sibi delegisset, hic expostulasse cum hostibus suis vel jam devictis, vel adhuc adversus se insurgen- tibus, Philistaeis, Ammonitis & similibus, ac praedice- re inutiles fore eorum conatus, quia à Deo sit in Re- gem electus, summa accepta in hostes potestate, quo- rum terras Deus ipsi in haereditatem dare decreverit. Non ovum ovo tam simile est, quam haec Ebraeo- rum glossa Grotianae. Nam & ex Ebraeis nonnulli fatentur denique quaedam in hoc Psalmo mystice ad Messiam applicari, vel gessisse in quibusdam Davi- dem typum Messiae, dum obtineant modo, quod se- cundum literam Psalmus de Davide agat. Quidam tamen ex illis ad Josaphati tempora eundem refe- runt, quandoquidem multi & potentes populi ad- versus ipsum conjurationem fecerint, filii Am- mon, filii Moab, & habitatores montis Seir cum Sy- ris 2. Chronic. cap. 20. Sed quia plerique omnes de Davide explicant, majorem partem Judaeorum, sed recentiorum sequi maluit, per omnia hic Judaizans Grotius. Denique insistere etiam hic placuit No- stro vestigiis Neo-Photinianorum, Enjedini, & alio- rum, parilique ratione Psalmum illustrissimum cum iisdem depravare.

Istos ergo seu Magistros, seu Complices, aut clientes, uti non invidemus Judaeorum & haeretico- rum variorum advocato, ita certum est, eundem à Patrum communi ac concordi explicatione, quam pro regula interpretationis alias commendat, hic re- cedere. Non enim facile producet ullum è Patri- bus ista ratione textum interpretantem. Et quam- vis discrepent in quibusdam v. g. quod verba, hodie genui Te, alii aliter explicent, in eo tamen consen- tiunt, quod Psalmus ille quoad literam de Messia nostro agat, uti etiam vocem illam: Tu es filius meus, nemo de Davide, omnes solum de Christo intelli- gunt. Quod non diffitetur in Calvinianorum Scho- la Andreas Rivetus comment. in Decad. Psalmor. ad Ps. 2. p. 3. Patres orthodoxi fere omnes de Christo simpliciter & immediate accipiunt, & interpretan- tur, quaecunque in hoc Psalmo dicuntur. Addit, sed in Calvini sui gratiam, non paucos praesertim RECEN- TIORUM de Davide & Christo, quorum ille typus fuit, hic veritas, interpretari. Quorum tamen ex antiquitate NULLUS, è recentioribus praeter Cal- vinum, Pelicanum, & Pareum non facile ULLUS nominari poterit. Quanquam vero Rivetus, vir magni inter suos nominis, & Calvini sui Hypera- spistes insignis hic etiam Calvino libenter herbam porrigere velit; Et certe, inquit, videtur David in sua persona dicere, ego autem constitutus sum Rex ab eo, & quae sequuntur: Neque etiam veritati officit, si quae de Christo sunt in V. Testam. citata, ad literam in- telligantur primo competere alicui, qui figuram & ty- pum Christi gesserit; videntur etiam jucundius & clarius ea de Christo intelligi, quae in ipsius typo prius adumbrata contemplamur, sed quae ipsi Christo verius & perfectius convenire cernimus: Non potuit ta- men, quin veritatis luce constrictus hic Calvinum & socios defereret: Ego tamen facile, inquit, in eam descendo sententiam, propter quaedam, quae in fine Psalmi habentur, quae Christo TANTUM competunt, Prophetam hunc Psalmum de Christo cecinisse pro- prie & primaria intentione, ut ita loquar; Tituban- te calamo hoc de primaria intentione addidisse Ri- vetus videtur. Novit enim probe, non esse unius dicti vel sententiae nisi unicum sensum, adeoque Spi- ritum S. unam tantum intentionem, in quovis ora- culo habere, siquidem non haberi debeat Scriptura ambigua, & instar oraculorum Delphicorum per- plexa, & obscura. Quæ ergo subjungit, docent, quam προθύμως juvare Calvinum voluerit : Quamvis non fine typo sui regni, in quo videbat Christi regnum per multa adumbrari, in oppugnatione scil. & contradictione multorum per circuitum regnorum, eam quam Christi regnum passurum erat contradictionem primum in Judæa, ac demum per universum orbem à variis populis ac Regibus terræ : In regni sui dilatatione etiam ad exteras gentes, suaq; quam de rebellibus obtinuit, divina victoria, propagationem regni Christi usq; ad extremos fines terræ, ejusque in rebelles potestatem, quam in novissimo potissimum die in illos exercebit. Hic igitur David occasione sumta ab hostium suorum improbis conatibus initis, de omnium Anti-Christianorum deliberationibus, studiis & conatibus adversus Christum & Ecclesiam prophetavit, & de Christi regno, & ejus perpetua stabilitate vaticinatus est. Quæ totidem verbis etiam habet Franc. Junius in parallelis, abs quo illa accepit Rivetus. Sed ut vera sint illa omnia, nihil tamen Calvinum juvant. Non enim quæritur, quanam occasione vaticinium hoc conceptum fuerit ? nec de eo quæstio est, an quædam hîc prædicta sint, quorum typum gesserit David, vel an in quibusdam quæ de Christo prædixit Spir. S. David figuram & typum repræsentarit suo tempore ? Sed de sensu Psalmi & verborum ejus, deque intentione Spiritus S. quæstio est; Anne in hoc Psalmo vel omnia, vel quædam saltem de Davide agant, ac de ipso intelligenda sint, secundum mentem Spiritus S. adeoque proprie ? Non enim nisi unus tantum sensus est, una mens & intentio Spiritus Sancti in uno Scripturæ loco ; Si de Davide loquatur, ejusque res describat, de Christo non loquitur, nec intelligi potest; si de Christo loquatur, ac prædicat ea, quæ acturus ipse sit, de Davide certe explicari non debet, sive primariam, sive secundariam dicas intentionem, sive propriam, sive impropriam; sive literalem, sive mysticam. Inanes sunt illæ distinctiones ac τερατολογίαι ad obfuscatam mentem Spiritus S. & juvandos Judæos ac Judaizantes excogitatæ. Non incerta est, nec ambigua, sed certa atque constans, adeoque unica dicti cujusvis sententia, unica Spiritus S. intentio, quæ proinde propria cuivis dicto est, ac literalis sensus dici consuevit, è textus antecedentibus & consequentibus colligendus. Sub re autem illa significata (non per verba, inquam, sed per id quod verba significant, & important) exhiberi quandoque typum rerum futurarum, vel etiam aliquid, quod in V. Test. typice alias in alio subjecto adumbratum fuit, novum non est : sed id hic ἄλλότριον, ubi unice de sensu verborum Psalmi disquiritur, in quo proinde Calvino suo, uti Judæis, palam cum Junio (hujus enim verba sua fecit) contradicere coactus fuit Rivetus : Dubitant tamen, inquit, Interpp. nonnulli, num in hoc Psalmo de se & regno suo David ad literam loquatur ? Judæi doctrinam de Christo, quoad ejus fieri potest, subvertentes, simpliciter quæ in hoc Psalmo dicuntur, de Davide & ejus regno contendunt accipi oportere. (Quod etiam contendit Calvinus, contendit Pareus, Tossanus & alii.) Quæ sententia non solum Psalmi ipsius argumento, verum etiam consequutione & ordine ipso evertitur. Nam argumentum tam manifeste ad regnum Messiæ pertinet, ut ne Judæorum quidem obstinatissimi id negare possint : quia Deus Filium suum compellat : Prophetam, Regem & Sacerdotem constituit, hæreditatem attribuit orbis totius, omnipotentiam assignat, omnibusque gentibus cultum, reverentiam & metum, ac denique fidem in ipsum imperat. Quæ omnia de homine puro puto nemo nisi BLASPHEMUS intelligere potest : Videtur etiam huic sententiæ repugnare consequutio di- Etorum, si quod nonnullis placet, ut in primo Psalmo David summam legis proposuit, sic in secundo Evan- gelii & fidei in Christum doctrinam comprehendit. Et certe apud Christianos dubium esse non potest, quod de Christo Salvatore sit intelligendus hic Psalmus, cum in variis locis Apostoli illum ad Christum retule- rint, ut patet Actor. 4. & 13. Ebr. 1, 5. Apoc. 2. & 19. Hæc Rivetus, & ante eum Junius. Quid quod Rive- tus de solo Christo hic agi contra alios Calvinianos probat ad v. 7. p. 18. Omissis etiam, qui ex nostris id ad David historice accommodant, atque tanquam ty- po Christi, RELIGIO nobis erit à sensu Pauli disce- dere vel latum unguem, quem proprio & germano sensu hunc locum de Christo immediate & solo acce- pisse convincunt argumenta: 1. à circumstantia loci & personarum desumtum, cum Actor. 13. ad Chri- stum locum illum retulit. Erat enim tunc in Synago- ga, & apud Judæos docebat, quibus locos aut contro- versos aut difficiles accommodatu non attulisset con- firmationis loco; qua ratione eos potius in errore con- firmasset, nisi apud eos tunc temporis constitisset, eum Psalmum proprie ad Messiam pertinere. 2. Ab op- positione filii & Angelorum. Quia certe argumenta- tio Pauli Ebr. 1, 9. omnino corrueret, si hæc verba ad alium, quam ad Christum possent quovis modo refer- ri. Hæc iterum Rivetus. Quæ merito Calvino & Pareo opponuntur. Sed & Pareus ipse una cum Calvino suo, agnoscit ultimum Psalmi hujus versum de solo Christo intelligendum esse. Quis ergo stupor, quæ cæcitas & vertigo utriusque est, ut versum se- ptimum, æque augustum, de Davide simul & de Christo interpretentur? quum συνάφεια textus nul- latenus talem distinctionem admittat, ut v. 7. duo intelligantur Filii Dei, David & Christus, v. 11. au- tem & 12. unus solum Filius, nempe Christus solus: osculamini filium: beati omnes, qui confidunt in eo. Ἀμετακίνητον & immotum illud est, eundem & non alium ullum Dei Filium utrobique nobis insinuari & commendari. Atque hæc de Reformatis. Salia- num & Cornelium Jansenium refutant alii plerique Papistæ: Cardinalis Bellarminus in explicatione Psalm. pag. 5. Etenim TOTUS hic Psalmus, inquit, Prophetia de regno Christi MANIFESTISSIMA & explicata ab Apostolis Actor. 4. & 13. Et Ebr. 1. & 5. ut OMNINO errare videantur, qui AD LITE- RAM de Davide Psalmum hunc explicare conantur. Jacobus Tirinus, ubi verba illa vers. 8. Dabo tibi gentes in hæreditatem, & populos usque ad terminos terræ, de amplitudine Ecclesiæ Catholicæ cum Euse- bio, Didymo, Theodoreto & aliis explicarat, hæc sub- jungit: Unde constat, hunc Psalmum AD LITE- RAM non de Davide, ut volunt Rabbini & Salia- nus (nam Davidi nunquam obtigit tam amplum im- perium,) sed de Messia Filio Davidis exponendum esse. Ita S. Patres & Doctores. Franc. Ribera in Epist. ad Hebr. cap. 1. reprehendit similiter Jansenium, quod docuerit verba Psalmi Davidi ut typo, Chri- sto, ut antitypo convenire. Quibus consonant alii è Pontificiis, etiam Menochius, quem magni facere solet Grotius.

Enjedino Neo - Photiniano, qui cum Judæis itidem contendit Psalmum secundum literaliter de Davide, spiritualiter vero de Messia loqui, quem etiam sequitur Schlichtingius Disp. de S. S. Trinita- te adversus B. Meisner. pag. 429. opponi fortassis poterit Socinus ipse, qui simpliciter de Christo Psal- mum hunc accipere videtur respons. Wujecko da- to cap. 2. p. 35. Frequentissime in Veteri Testamen- to scriptum invenitur, Christus sive unctus Jehovah, id est, unius illius Dei, tunc etiam cum de ipso Chri- sto Domino nostro verba fiunt, ut Psalm. 2, 2. & Psal. 132, 17. Argumenta etiam Enjedini, quibus pro- batum batum sit, literaliter hæc de Davide intelligenda es- se, adeo sunt frivola, & ex parte impia, ut mirum sit, quenquam illis ad assensum moveri potuisse.

Primum ab auctoritate Ebræorum petit, quam in Scripturis interpretandis nemo sanus temere contem- serit, ut & à Zwinglianorum quorundam consen- su: Sed quis sanus Ebræorum auctoritatem in illis, quæ de Christo agunt, tanti æstimabit, ut Catholi- cæ Ecclesiæ consensum propter hostes illos Christi ἀσπόνδȣς posthabeat? Zwinglianorum vero Judai- zantium auctoritas hic major ipsorum Judæorum auctoritate haberi non potest: utpote quibus alii in eadem Schola se opponunt, quemadmodum Ju- dæi quoque veteres in explicatione hujus Psalmi cum Christianis faciunt, ac recentiorum Judæo- rum interpretationi adversantur.

Alterum quod Psalmus de re transacta loquatur, ficulneo fulcro nititur, quod nempe verba præsentia vel præterita adhibeantur. Quis enim nescit, hoc fieri more Prophetis usitatissimo, ob prædictionum certitu- dinem, & ad meliorem rerum futurarum repræsen- tationem?

Tertium, quod in Christo hæc completa nunquam sint, Apostolorum testimonio Actor. 4. aperte reclamat.
