Psalmi nostri ab eodem de Davide explicari, qui geni- tus a Deo secundum ipsum dicitur (improprie) cum clare apparuit ejus electio, & Filius Dei appellatur, non certe naturalis & proprie dictus: fic enim Davidem ex essentia Dei genitum dicere oporte- bit; sed improprie & tralatitie. Sed missa Riveti & Calvini detorsione, nec non aliorum satis commo- da quidem, ac nativo verborum Hieropsaltis sensui minime adversa de demonstratione æternæ genera- tionis per resurrectionem Christi facta, interpreta- tione, simplicior & verbis Apostoli Act. 13, 23. ma- gis conveniens eorum explicatio est, qui de excita- tione & missione Christi ea intelligunt: Et nos vo- bis annunciamus eam, quæ ad Patres nostros repro- missio facta est, quoniam hanc Deus adimplevit Filiis nostris ἀναστήσας excitans Jesum, ficut & in Psalmo secundo scriptum est, Filius meus es, ego hodie genui te: quæ verba peculiariter citat Apostolus: quia istis verbis non tantum incipit decreti divini enar- ratio, de Messiæ regno, sed in loco illo ex professo, quod ajunt, docetur, ipsum Filium Dei futurum

Messiam, quæ est insignis illa repromissio Patribus, ipsique Davidi facta, ad quam auditores Judæos ut- pote notissimam remittit Apostolus, verbis solum quibusdam ex eadem prout fieri amat, adductis, personam Messiæ exhibendi designantibus, quæ ma- ximopere ipsis inculcanda erat; Siquidem non le- vi scandalo affecti fuerint Judæi, quod Christus se Filium Dei professus sit, illudque pro blasphemia ha- buerint Johan. 10. Adseruimus hanc explicationem plenius in Examine Libror. Crellii de uno Deo Pa- tre, quod habetur Tom. II. super Aug. Confession. vel Theolog. naturali & Revelat. pag. 1350.

Alterum quod attinet locum Ebr. 5, 5. sic & Christus non semetipsum clarificavit, ut Pontifex fie- ret, sed qui locutus est ad eum; Filius meus es tu: Ego hodie genui te: non innuitur eo, tum demum Filium DEI genitum esse, cum Pontifex factus est, sed, quod sæpius etiam Christus testatus est, ab ipso DEO Patre Christum accepisse hanc gloriam, & æternam generationem fundamentum esse glorifica- tionis istius, munerísᾶ Sacerdotalis æterni: Non hic de tempore, sed autore Pontificatus agitur: nec vero temporalis quædam generatio fundamentum esse potest æterni Pontificatus; nam ante jacta fun- damenta mundi Filius Dei munere Sacerdotali & intercessorio functus est, seque sponsorem, mediatorem & propitiatorem interposuit, in arcano S. S. Trini- tatis Concilio, ideo etiam ab origine mundi occisus dicitur agnus DEI Eph. 1. vers. 4. Apoc. 13. vers. 8.

## 2:7 Addition
To verse 7, let these things be added.

To the blessed Hülsemann, it seems that the Apostle proves the antecedent from the consequent in this way: because it is necessary for him who is the Son of God to be immortal, therefore the truth of the saying of the second Psalm, 'Thou art my Son, etc.,' had to be demonstrated to be consistent by the resurrection of the Son of God from the dead. For had this resurrection not followed, it would have been manifest that the dead subject was not the natural Son of God: for this is what the Pharisees and all the Jews of that sort, with whom Paul has business in this place, were inferring, as is evident from verses 15, 39, 42, etc. See the inference of the Jews in this form: 'He who is the natural Son of God does not die,' Matt 27:46, 47, Mark 14:61, Luke 22:20, John 19:7. This objection of the Jews is therefore resolved by the Apostle's allegation, Acts 13:33, by way of denial: that it is no obstacle to his being the Son of God that he dies voluntarily, provided he does not remain in death. For by the resurrection the truth of that saying of the Psalm is established: 'Thou art my Son, etc.'

Latin:

Ad vers. 7. hæc addantur.

B. Hülsemanno videtur Apostolus antecedens probare ex consequente hoc modo: quia eum, qui est Filius DEI, oportet esse immortalem, ideo veritatem dicti Psalmi secundi Filius meus es tu &c. sibi con- stare fuisse demonstrandum per resuscitationem Filii DEI ex mortuis. Hac enim suscitationem non sequu- ta manifestum fuisset subjectum mortuum non fuisse naturalem Dei Filium: hoc enim inferebant Pharisæi, omnesque Judæi, quales erant, cum quibus hoc loco Paulo negotium est, ut patet ex vers. 15. 39. 42. seq. vide Judæorum illationem sub hac forma: Qui Filius Dei naturalis est, non moritur Matth. 27. vers. 46. 47. Marc. 14, 61. Luc. 22, 20. Joh. 19, 7. Hæc igitur in- stantia Judæorum resolvitur allegatione Apostoli, Act. 13, 33. per inficiationem: non obstare, quo minus is sit Filius Dei, qui voluntarie moritur, dummodo in mor- te non maneat. Per suscitationem enim constare ve- ritatem dicto illi Psalmi: Filius meus es tu &c.

## 2:8
Verse 8.

I WILL GIVE YOU THE NATIONS AS YOUR INHERITANCE) As a property by Right of War. See the chapters already mentioned, 2 Sam. and Ps. 108.

That the discourse is not about David has already been proven by various arguments. Nor does this promise suit David. For it is a matter of a future event. Moreover, the raging and machinations of the peoples against David had already occurred, if verse 1 is to be understood concerning them: Why did the nations RAGE? It is a matter of such a giving, which has generation as its foundation. But the giving of the nations was not made to David, because he himself is the Son of GOD, and was begotten by GOD. It is a matter of an infinite and immense giving of authority and power, which extends to the peoples of the whole earth. For that, and the possession even to the ends of the earth, cannot be restricted by the small limits of certain neighboring nations of Palestine, but they extend as widely as the boundaries of the world, nor is the rule of the ends of the earth of infinite power. For the ends of the earth in the Scriptures denote the extremities of the globe, nay, they embrace the entire world; see Ps. 19:5, Rom. 10:18. (Conf. Rom. 15:19. Col. 1:23.) Psalm 22:28. Psalm 46:10. Psalm 70:14. Ps. 65:6. Zech. 9:10. Add that the inheritance of the nations brings in divine dominion over the nations, Psalm 47:9, requiring the adoration of all the families of the nations, Psalm 22:28, the service of all peoples, nations, and tongues, Dan. 7:14, Rev. 5:9, ch. 7:9, and is joined with the blessing of all the tribes of the earth, Psalm 72:17. It is a matter of a possession which falls to the Son by inheritance, not one which comes by right of war: for there is nothing here about the right of war, and those titles of possessions are distinct, the right of war, and sonship and generation. This King is born, because he has rule and possession by inheritance: but he is not made so by accident, as those who obtain possessions by right of war. GOD the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, Lord of all peoples, begat the Son as Lord likewise of the heavens and of the earth and of all peoples. By the same right by which the Father is Lord of the ends of the earth, by the same right also is the Son, who has all things, whatsoever the Father has, with the exception of the relation of the Son alone. Other Kings do not receive their regions, dominions, and peoples in respect to GOD by hereditary right, but as a fief for a short time, and when it has seemed good to God, they are compelled in turn to depart from their kingdom. But Christ possesses all nations by hereditary right, and indeed for all eternity, as in Dan. 2 and 7 this very distinction is explained at length and expressly. Which the blessed Gesner rightly pointed out. We shall speak of Psalm 108 next; for we believe this likewise to contain a prophecy concerning the Messiah. Mention is made of the nations, however, particularly because they were in the O.T. alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, but in the N.T. they were bound to become near through the blood of the Messiah Eph. 2, 12. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

DABO TIBI GENTES IN HÆREDITATEM TV- AM) In proprietatem ex Belli Jure. Vid. dicta jam capita 2. Sam. & Ps. 108.

Non esse Sermonem de Davide, jam proba- tum est variis argumentis. Neque hoc promissum convenit Davidi. Agitur enim de re futura. Fre- mitus autem & machinationes populorum adver- sus Davidem jam præcesserunt, si de illis v. 1. intelli- gatur: Quare FREMUERUNT gentes? Agi- tur de tali datione, quæ pro fundamento habet ge- nerationem. At datio gentium Davidi facta non est, quia ipse Filius DEI, & genitus est a DEO. Agitur de datione infinita & immensa ἐξουσίας, ac po- testatis, quæ ad populos universæ terræ se extendat. Non enim illa, & possessionem usᾷ ad fines terræ co- arctari possunt exiguis limitibus vicinarum qua- rundam Palæstinæ gentium, sed cum terminis mundi æque late patent, nec regimen finium terræ infinite potestatis est. Fines enim terræ in Scriptu- ris notant extremitates orbis, imo universum com- plectuntur orbem; vid. Ps. 19, 5. Rom. 10, 18. (Conf. Rom. 15. v. 19. Col. 1. vers. 23.) Psalm. 22. vers. 28. Psalm. 46. vers. 10. Psalm. 70. v. 14. Psal. 65. v. 6. Zach. 9. vers. 10. Adde quod hæreditas gentium, Dominium divinum in gentes inferat Psalm. 47, 9. adorationem universarum Familiarum gentium re- quirens Psal. 22, 28. servitutem omnium populorum, nationum & gentium Dan. 7. vers. 14. Apoc. 5. v. 9. cap. 7. vers. 9. & cum benedictione omnium tri- buum terræ conjunctum sit Psalm. 72, 17. Agitur de possessione, quæ hæreditario obtingit Filio, non quæ ex belli jure: nihil enim hic de jure belli, & di- stincti illi sunt possessionum tituli, jus belli, & filia- tio ac generatio. Rex hic natus est, quia regimen & possessionem habet hæreditario: non autem per accidens factus, uti qui jure belli possessiones conse- quuntur. DEUS Pater Dominus cœli & terræ, Dominus omnium populorum, Filium genuit Do- minum itidem cœli & terræ & populorum omnium. Quo jure Pater Dominus est finium terræ, eodem etiam jure Filius, qui habet omnia, quæcunq; habet Pater, sola Filii relatione excepta. Reliqui Reges suas regiones, ditiones, & populos respectu DEI non accipiunt hæreditario jure, sed tanquam feudum ad exiguum tempus, & cum Deo visum est, coguntur regno suo vicissim discedere. Sed Christus hæreditario jure omnes gentes possidet, & quidem in omnem æternitatem, ut Dan. 2. & 7. hoc ipsum discrimen prolixe & ex professo explicatur. Quod recte monuit B. Gesner. De Psal. 108. deinceps dicturi sumus; hunc enim itidem vaticinium de Messia complecti credimus. Gentium autem peculiariter fit mentio, quia fuerunt illæ in V. T. abalienatæ a conversatione Israelis, in N. T. autem debuerunt propinquæ fieri per sanguinem Messiæ Eph. 2, 12. 13.

## 2:9
Vers. 9. THOU SHALT RULE THEM WITH A ROD OF IRON) In the Hebrew: Thou shalt crush them with an iron rod, that is, with a sword.

That the discourse is not of a material sword, or of earthly and temporal power, but of a Spiritual sword and of divine, eternal, and infinite power, is manifest from the comparison of the parallel passage Apoc. 19. vers. 15. The sword is explained by the Spirit of the mouth of Christ, which is in place of all weapons, and suffices for crushing the enemies of the kingdom of Christ: By whose single word even in the height of exhaustion the enemies were prostrated John 18. vers. 6. Compare Isa. 11. vers. 4. 2. Thess. 2. vers. 8. Matth. 21. vers. 44. That this sword, which power, since it does not befit David, but Christ alone and only, it is again evident that the prophecy is to be understood not of David, but of Christ alone; of him who trod the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, and has on his garment and on his thigh a name written, King of kings and Lord of Lords Apoc. 19. vers. 15. 16. Which is also signified in Apoc. 12, when the pregnant woman brought forth a male child who was to rule all nations with an iron rod. As the Messiah will embrace those who are his inheritance with his grace, so he will shatter the enemies, of whom mention was made in vers. 1 and 2, with an iron rod, with his powerful word, which is like a two-edged sword Heb. 4. vers. 12. Eph. 6. vers. 17. Apoc. 1. vers. 6. with which he will strike all who rise up Isa. 11. vers. 4. Psalm 45. vers. 7. 8. and will dissipate them together with their opposing counsels, as vessels of potters which are broken with the greatest ease, Isa. 30, 12. and can be repaired by no art Jer. 19, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 9. REGES EOS IN VIRGA FERREA) In Hebræo: Conteres eas virga ferrea, id est gladio.

Non de materiali gladio, aut terrena & temporali potestate sermonem esse, sed de gladio Spirituali ac potestate divina æterna atque infinita, e collatione loci paralleli Apoc. 19. vers. 15. manifestum est. Explicatur gladius per Spiritum oris Christi, qui vice armorum omnium est, & ad conterendos hostes regni Christi sufficit: Cujus unico verbo etiam in summa exaninitione hostes prostrati sunt Joh. 18. vers. 6. Confer. Esa. 11. vers. 4. 2. Thess. 2. vers. 8. Matth. 21. vers. 44. Qui gladius, quæ potestas cum non conveniat Davidi, sed Christo soli, atque uni, iterum patet, non de Davide, sed de Christo unice vaticinium intelligendum esse; de eo qui calcavit torcular vini furoris iræ Dei omnipotentis, & habet in vestimento & in femore suo scriptum nomen, Rex regum & Dominus Dominantium Apoc. 19. vers. 15. 16. Quod etiam Apoc. 12. significatur, cum mulier prægnans peperit masculum recturum omnes gentes virga ferrea. Uti Messias illos, qui sunt hæreditas ipsius, gratia sua complectetur, ita hostes, qualium vers. 1. & 2. mentio facta diffringet virga ferrea, potente verbo suo, quod est instar ancipitis gladii Ebr. 4. vers. 12. Eph. 6. vers. 17. Apoc. 1. vers. 6. quo omnes insurgentes percutiet Esa. 11. vers. 4. Psalm. 45. vers. 7. 8. & dissipabit eos una cum consiliis adversariis, ut vasa figulorum quæ summa facilitate franguntur, Esa. 30, 12. & nulla arte reparari possunt Jer. 19, 12.

## 2:11
Vers. 11.

KISS THE SON) בר for בן is found in Chaldean and in Ezra 5, 1, 2. and often in the Chaldean paraphrasts: sometimes also בור. Thus in this place Aben-Ezra took it. Aquila, κατα φιλήσατε ἐκλεκτόν. For so it seems it should be read, instead of ἐκλεκτῶς. A kiss is a sign of subjection, or of homage. Thus Gen. 41, 40. ישק the Greeks translate he shall obey. This is what he says: you other neighboring Kings, terrified by the example of the slain Kings, come in time to a submissive covenant.

While he retains the Vulgate version elsewhere, here he substitutes another text in its place: For the Vulgate does not have KISS THE SON; but LAY HOLD OF DISCIPLINE. He also opposes to it, although the name is suppressed, along with the Hebrew truth, the Paraphrase of Aquila, and the explanation of R. Aben-Ezra. He could also have added R. Kimchi, Kasoenaki, and Midrash Tehillim, as well as more recent Christian interpreters, even Papists, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Vatablus. The LXX Interpreters, however, stand with the Chaldean on the side of the Vulgate version: but against the original text, to which Grotius here rightly adheres: whom Buxtorf defends from the suspicion of depravation, having been rashly accused by Ludov. Capellus, in Vind. Verit. Ebr. page 673. For בר nowhere in Scripture denotes discipline, nor can it be so rendered here, because of the word נשׁק; but it denotes the Son Prov. 31. vers. 32. Dan. 3. vers. 25. 31. chap. 5. vers. 22. And what will be the coherence, lay hold of discipline, lest he be angry? Does discipline get angry? But not only neighboring Kings, but all supreme and intermediate Magistrates, Kings and judges of the earth throughout the whole world are here warned. Nor is submission to a submissive covenant indicated by a kiss, but the worship of the first table, and religious worship, just as to kiss is accepted for the offering of divine honor 1 Kings 19. vers. 18. Job 31. vers. 27. For that religious veneration is included here is manifest, because it is subjoined to the servitude owed to God, as worship of the same kind (it meets the wrath and indignation of the divine vindictive justice, it includes religious trust, it is directed toward eternal blessedness, it is founded on the right of divine possession of the whole world, it befits the Son begotten from the substance of the Father, and the Messiah, who is so joined in worship with God the Father, as he is joined by enemies in opposing consultations, and is the common, or one, object of the raging of the enemies of the Church; since even the Jews, especially R. Aben-Ezra, confess that the words serve the Lord correspond to the words in vers. 2, against the Lord, but the words kiss the Son have reference to the words in vers. 2, against Christ. Add that the bonds and cords of God the Father and the Messiah are nothing other than the religious obedience owed to God and the Messiah according to divine laws, which, because the enemies refuse, it is commanded to them under grave threat. vers. 11. 12. Therefore the word kiss is rightly interpreted, as to the sense, by worship by Symmachus, Aben-Ezra, as also by Jerome. Nor indeed is the discourse of David, but of the Messiah our Lord, as noted before. It is David who exhorts Kiss the Son: he speaks therefore of another, not of himself: nay, since he himself, being devout, acquiesces in the bonds and cords of the Messiah and this Lord, which others break asunder, he excites others by his example to a like religious obedience.

Verse 13.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

OSCVLAMINI FILIVM) בר pro בן Chaldaïcum reperitur & Esdræ 5, 1, 2. & in paraphrastis Chaldæis sæpe: interdum & בור. Sic hoc loco sumpsit & Aben-Esdra. Aquila, κατα φιλήσατε ἐκλεκτόν. Ita enim legendum videtur, pro ἐκλεκτῶς. Osculum signum subjectionis, sive homagii. Sic Gen. 41, 40. ישק Græci vertunt ὑπακούσεται. Hoc est, quod dicit: vos alii vicini Reges interfectorum Regum exemplo territi, in tempore venite ad fœdus obsequiosum.

Quum vulgatam versionem retineat alias, hic ejus loco alium textum substituit: Vulgata enim non habet OSCULAMINI FILIUM; sed APPREHENDITE DISCIPLINAM. Opponit etiam eidem, licet suppresso nomine, cum Ebraica veritate Paraphrasin Aquilæ, & R. Aben-Esdræ explicationem. Poterat etiam addere R. Kimchi, Kasoenaki, & Midrasch Tehillim, ut & recentiores interpretes Christianos, etiam Pontificios, Pagninum, Ariæmontanum, Vatablum. LXX. tamen Interpretes cum Chaldæo a partibus vulgatæ versionis stant: sed invito textu originali, cui hic merito adhæret Grotius: quem temere accusatum a Ludov. Capello vindicat Buxtorffius a depravationis suspicione in vind. verit. Ebr. pag. 673. בר enim nullibi in Script. disciplinam notat, neq; hic ita red- di potest, ob verbum נשׁק; notat autem Filium Prov. 31. vers. 32. Dan. 3. vers. 25. 31. cap. 5. vers. 22. Et quæ erit cohærentia, apprehendite disciplinam, ne irascatur? Num disciplina irascitur? Non au- tem tantum vicini Reges, sed omnes Magistratus supremi & medii, Reges & judices terræ per univer- sum orbem hic commonentur. Neque per osculum tantum submissio ad fœdus obsequiosum sed cultus tabulæ primæ, ac religiosus indigitatur, uti osculari pro honoris divini oblatione 1. Reg. 19. vers. 18. Job. 31. vers. 27. accipitur. Comprehendi enim hic re- ligiosam venerationem, manifestum est, quia sub- juncta est servituti Deo debitæ, ceu cultus ejusdem generis (occurrit iræ & excandescentiæ divinæ vin- dicatricis justitiæ, includit fiduciam religiosam, di- recta est ad æternam beatitudinem, fundata est in jure divinæ possessionis universi terrarum orbis, convenit Filio e substantia Patris genito, & Messiæ, qui ita conjunctus est in cultu cum Deo Patre, uti ab hostibus conjunctus est in adversariis consulta- tionibus, & commune, vel unum cum eo fremitus hostium Ecclesiæ objectum est; siquidem & Judæi, imprimis R. Aben-Esdra fateantur, verba servite Domino respondere verbis vers. 2. adversus Domi- num, verba vero osculamini Filium respectum ha- bere ad verba vers. 2. adversus Christum. Adde, quod vincula & funes Dei Patris & Messiæ nihil aliud sint, quam religiosa obedientia Deo & Messiæ juxta leges divinas debita, quam quia detrectant hostes, sub gravi comminatione ea imperatur ipsis. vers. 11. 12. Ideo recte verbum osculamini inter- pretatur, quantum ad sensum, per adorate Symma- chus, Aben-Esra, ut & Hieronymus. Neque vero de Davide, sed de Messia Domino nostro sermonem esse, ante notatum. David est, qui hortatur Oscu- lamini Filium: de alio ergo loquitur non seipso: imo cum Messiæ ac Domini hujus vinculis & funi- bus, quos alii disrumpunt, ipse acquiescat devotus, alios suo exemplo ad parilem religiosam obedien- tiam excitat.

Vers. 13.

## 2:11 Addition
Verse 11.

SERVE THE LORD WITH FEAR, AND REJOICE UNTO HIM WITH TREMBLING.

What kind of trembling is to be understood here must be judged: 1. From the quality of the subject to whom the discourse is addressed, which are the kings and princes of the earth. 2. From the quality of the object about which the discourse is made, which is a greater and supreme prince, verses 7, 8. 3. From the impulsive cause for which one must tremble, which is explained in verse 9, and this admonition concerning the fear to be shown is inferred as a moral consequence from verse 9 by the particle ועתה and now, Jerome 'now therefore', 'and so': See 1 Chronicles 7, verse 7, Luke 11, verse 39.

1 Cor. 12:18. Heb. 11:16. Acts 7:34. 4. From the threatening of the punishment that is to follow in verse 10, when his wrath is kindled. 5. Finally, from the order of the position, because this trembling is placed before the kiss or the salutary acknowledgment of the Son. From all of which it is clear that the discourse here is properly about a pedagogical fear leading to the salutary acknowledgment of Christ, both on account of his power and his severity: not about doubt concerning the truth of present righteousness, as the blessed Hülsemann warns here.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

SERVITE DOMINO CUM TIMORE, ET EXULTATE EI CUM TREMORE.

Qualis tremor hic intelligatur, dijudicandum est: 1. Ex Qualitate Subjecti, ad quod sermo fit, quod sunt reges & principes terræ. 2. Ex Qualitate Objecti, de quo sermo fit, quod est princeps major, & summus. vers. 7. 8. 3. Ex causa impulsiva, ob quam tremendum sit: quæ exponitur vers. 9. & hæc admonitio de timore exhibendo tanquam consequens morale infer- tur ex versu 9. per particulam ועתה & nunc, Hieronymus nunc ergo, itaque: Vide 1. Paralipomen. 7. versu 7. Luc. 11. versu 39.

1. Cor. 12, 18. Ebr. 11, 16. Actor. 7, 34. 4. Ex com- minatione de subsecuturo supplicio vers. 10. quum exardescit ejus furor. 5. Denique ex ordine posi- tionis, quia hic tremor præmittitur osculo seu salutari agnitioni Filii. Ex quibus omnibus patet, de ti- more Pædagogico ad salutarem agnitionem Christi, cum ob potentiam, tum ob severitatem ejus hic pro- prie sermonem esse: non de dubitatione circa veri- tatem præsentis justitiæ, ut hic monet B. Hülseman- nus.

## 2:12
BLESSED ARE ALL WHO TRUST IN HIM) Who entrust themselves to the faith of this King (that is, of me). A truly perverse and impious Paraphrase. Perverse, because while David speaks of another in the third person, and as has been demonstrated, of the Son of God, the Messiah our Lord, in order that this may be twisted toward David himself, the pronoun of the third person is transformed into the pronoun of the second, which is to change squares into circles, and to mix heaven with earth. Impious, because he is pronounced cursed by the voice of the Lord who trusts in a mere man, Jer. 17. verse 5. Therefore, no less cursed is he who places trust in himself and commands others to trust: which is impious Sacrilege and idolatrous. But he is to be held most cursed and execrable who places the blessedness of all even in himself, if they trust in him. As trust is to be placed in God alone, so blessedness is to be sought in God alone: to trust in whom is true and sole salvation: that jejune gloss of the Jews, as if to trust were to entrust oneself to the faith of the King, is utterly unworthy of Christian commentaries and ears, confusing the duties of the second table with the offices of the first table, whence Calvin, although otherwise greatly Judaizing in the twisting of this Psalm, himself acknowledged that THESE cannot be referred to David except through enormous impiety, because hope and trust are to be placed in Christ alone, and not in David. From the Jews themselves R. Obad. on this passage explains these words thus: who trust in him: and await redemption, for them light arises. Rabbi also David Kimchi on this passage: some, he says, of the Rabboth explain this Psalm concerning Gog and Magog. And concerning the future Messiah, who will be the Lord's anointed; and this also is manifest. The discourse is not about temporal, but eternal blessedness, because it is opposed to eternal destruction, and the wrath of the Messiah, as Judge, Joh. 5, 21. 2. Thess. 1, 8. through which all must perish who refuse to kiss the same, who do not trust in the same, Joh. 3, 15. Apoc. 6, 16. 17. whom he himself will shatter with a rod of iron, as one who treads the winepress of the fury of God, Apoc. 19, 15. I pass over that the Interpreters observe the Hebrew אשרי is plural, embracing all blessednesses, just as true and eternal blessedness is a state made perfect by the aggregation of all goods which pertain to happiness, according to Boethius. Nor is any trust whatsoever designated here, but that by which we receive ourselves unto God, that we may be covered under the wings of his grace, just as chicks trust under the wings of hens, which is the emphasis of the word חסה, which is used concerning religious trust looking toward the first table. Conf. Ps. 57, 25. Esa. 25, 4. & Ps. 5. v. 12. 13. as also Psal. 11, 1. Ps. 17, 8. Ps. 91, 4. and also Ps. 34, 9. 37, 40. For the true cause of blessedness is Christ apprehended by faith, covering us with the shadow of his wings, Matth. 23, 47. outside of whom there is no blessedness. Act. 4, 12. Es. 45, 23.

Latin:

BEATI OMNES QVI CONFIDVNT IN EO) Qui fidei ejus Regis (id est, meæ) se permittunt. Vere perversa atque impia Paraphrasis. Per- versa, quia quum David de alio loquatur in tertia persona, & uti demonstratum est, de Filio Dei, Mes- sia Domino nostro, ut ad Davidem ipsum hoc detor- queatur, pronomen tertiæ personæ in pronomen secun- dæ transformatur, quod est mutare quadrata rotun- dis, cœlumq; terræ miscere. Impia, quia maledictus voce Domini pronunciatur, qui confidit in homine nudo Jer. 17. vers. 5. Non minus ergo maledictus, qui in se fiduciam collocare, ac confidere alios ju- bet: quod impium est Sacrilegium & idololatri- cum. Maxime autem maledictus & execrabilis habendus, qui in eo etiam beatitudinem ponat omnium, si in se confidant. Ut in solo Deo fiducia po- nenda, ita in Deo solo beatitudo quærenda est: cui confidere salus vera, atque unica est: Jejuna illa Judæorum glossa, quasi confidere sit fidei Regis se per- mittere, Christianis commentariis, & auribus pror- sus indigna est, confundens tabulæ secundæ munia, cum officiis tabulæ primæ, unde Calvinus, etsi de cætero in Psalmi hujus detorsione valde Judaizans, agnovit ipse, HÆC non nisi per enormem impieta- tem ad Davidem referri posse, quia in solo Christo, & non in Davide spes & fiducia collocanda. E Judæis ipsis R. Obad. in h. l. verba ista ita exponit: qui con- fidunt in eum: & expectant redemtionem, illis lux oritur. Rabbi etiam David Kimchi ad h. l. Non- nulli, inquit, ex Rabboth hunc Psalmum exponunt de Gog & Magog. & de Messia futuro, qui erit unctus Domini; & hoc etiam manifestum est. Non de temporali, sed æterna beatitudine sermo est, quia op- ponitur ea æterno interitui, & iræ Messiæ, ceu Judi- cis Joh. 5, 21. 2. Thess. 1, 8. per quam pereundum est omnibus, qui eundem osculari renuunt, qui eidem non confidunt Joh. 3, 15. Apoc. 6, 16. 17. quos ipse virga ferrea diffringet, utpote, qui calcat torcular vini furoris Dei Apoc. 19, 15. Taceo, quod obser- vent Interpp. Ebræum אשרי plurale beatitudines omnes complecti, quemadmodum vera & æterna beatitudo status est omnium bonorum aggreatione perfectus, quæ ad felicitatem pertinent, secundum Boëthium. Neque fiducia quæcunq; hic designatur, sed qua nos ad Deum recipimus, ut sub alis gratiæ ejus tegamur, quemadmodum pulli sub alis gallina- rum confidunt, quæ emphasis est vocis חסה quæ de fiducia religiosa ad tabulam primam spectante ad- hibetur. Conf. Ps. 57, 25. Esa. 25, 4. & Ps. 5. v. 12. 13. ut & Psal. 11, 1. Ps. 17, 8. Ps. 91, 4. nec non Ps. 34, 9. 37, 40. Vera enim beatitudinis causa Christus est fide apprehensus, umbra alarum nos tegens, Matth. 23, 47. extra quem nulla est beatitudo. Act. 4, 12. Es. 45, 23.

## 3:1 Argument
PSALM III. The trust of David as a fugitive because of Absalom.

A PSALM OF DAVID WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF ABSALOM HIS SON) Not that he said these things, but that he could have said such things at that mournful time 2. Sam. 15, 14.

The word מזמור introduces a song, consisting of numbers and caesuras composed with art, from זמר, he pruned, he sang, as Waser notes in Ps. 60. page 12. Cocceius wishes it to be said here that it is a poem fit for singing: and זמירו is used concerning every modulation of the voice, whether of an animal or an instrument. See Esa. 24. v. 16. Cant. 2, 12. For a song is made by the elevation and remission of the voice, at certain intervals, and differences of tones, through strophes and fit measures of melodies; which tempering of the voice to a certain law is like some precision and pruning. In לדוד the prefix is of the genitive, and a mark of the author as 1. Sam. 14, 16. Hab. 3, 1. Nothing, however, prevents one from saying that David composed this Psalm during his flight: which the words themselves imply. From which it is also evident that they hallucinate who say that it speaks first of Christ, secondly of David: nor that Cocceius's opinion deserves approval, because this Psalm fits Christ and his body, and Absalom represents both the priests and kings of the earth as enemies of Christ, and then the Anti-Christ, and commemorates the passions and death and resurrection of Christ at least in an enigma. For the inscription made by the Holy Spirit provides a completely different argument, to which one must acquiesce: which, as to sense, use, and accommodation to other things, we do not disapprove, provided that a SINGLE sense only be in the ford.

Vers. 1. WHY ARE THEY MULTIPLIED THAT TROUBLE ME?) How many do my enemies become? Those who follow Absalom. See 2. Sam. 15, 13.

Latin:

PSALMUS III. Fiducia Davidis ob Absolomum profugi.

PSALMVS DAVID CVM FVGERET A FACIE ABSALOM FILII SVI) Non quod hæc dixerit, sed quod talia dicere potuerit luctuoso illo tempore 2. Sam. 15, 14.

VOx מזמור canticum infert numeris, & cæsuris arte compositis constans, a זמר præscidit, cecinit, ut Waser. notat in Ps. 60. pag. 12. Coccejus hic dici vult carmen aptum ad canendum: & זמירו de omni vocis modulatione, sive animalis, sive instrumen- ti adhiberi. Vide Esa. 24. v. 16. Cant. 2, 12. Cantio- nem enim fieri vocis elevatione, & remissione, ad certa intervalla, & tonorum differentias, per stro- phas, & aptas modulorum mensuras; quæ vocis ad certam legem temperatio tanquam præcisio ali- qua & putatio est. In לדוד præfixum genitivi est, ac nota autoris ut 1. Sam. 14, 16. Hab. 3, 1. Nihil au- tem obstat, quo minus dicatur Davidem Psalmum hunc durante fuga composuisse: quod verba ipsa important. E quibus id constat etiam, hallucinari, qui dicunt eundem πρώτως de Christo, δευτέρως de Davide loqui: neq; Cocceji sententiam calculum mereri, quod Psalmus hic Christo & corpori ejus conveniat, & Absolom cum Sacerdotes ac Reges terræ hostes Christi tum Anti-Christum referat, ac Christi passiones & mortem atque resurrectionem saltim in ænigmate commemoret. Argumentum enim prorsus aliud ἐπιγραφή a S. S. facta submini- strat, cui acquiescendum: quod ad sensum, usum & accommodationem ad alia non improbamus, dum UNICUS solum sensus in vado sit.

Vers. 1. QVID MVLTIPLICATI SVNT QVI TRI- BVLANT ME?) Quam multi fiunt hostes mei? Qui Abso- lomum sequuntur. Vide 2. Sam. 15, 13.

## 3:2
Vers. 3. THEY SAY OF MY SOUL) They say of me.

Vers. 3. IN HIS GOD) Here follows in the Hebrew סלה, a mark which signifies that the song is to be intensified here, because it is now in sorrow, now in joy.

There are various opinions concerning this word, which occurs only in the Psalms and in the Canticle of Habakkuk, and in this one indeed three times, but in those it is read seventy-one times: The blessed Joh. Tarnovius reviewed ten of them at this place. But there are five principal ones. The first, which Grotius assumes here, seems to be that of the LXX Interpreters, who rendered it διάψαλμα, because a certain change is made in the musical melody at the place where it is found, just as Suidas explains that Greek word as ἐναλλαγὴν μέλος. Nor does R. David Kimchi in his Book of Roots dissent, deriving it from סלל, he exalted, he lifted up, because the elevation of the voice is indicated. Whence the Jews, in singing these places, used to lift up their voice together with their body. The same is the opinion of the interpreter of the Psalms, as noted by R. Aben-Ezra and R. Mordochai Nathan in the Chapter of Concordances. But the blessed Tarnovius observed that the grammatical form is repugnant to this etymology. The second is the explanation of R. Aben-Ezra, who explains it by כן הוא, so it is, and אמן, that is, truly; and thus also others declare it by the word Amen, and they prove that sense partly from the prayers of the Jews, partly from their Epitaphs, e.g., May his soul be bound in heaven, Sela. Thirdly, some explain it with the Targum of Jonathan as for ages, and always, with Aquila: and that it is so accepted, R. Mordochai notes in Ps. 84. יהללוך סלה they shall praise thee for ages of ages. Who also wishes this word to be used in this sense in the epitaphs of the Jews. Fourthly, some hold the same for a mark of a pause and of the attention of the mind, which opinion, in the judgment of the blessed Tarnovius, is the most likely of all, and agrees best with the derivation of this word, because סלה signifies he paved, so that it may be an indication of the voice to be laid down and remitted in singing, so that the preceding words, as exhibiting something singular and worthy of memory, may be considered all the better. To which opinion we also add our own approval. To this explanation also corresponds the meaning of the word סלה which Buxtorf noted in his Chaldaic-Talmudic Lexicon, that it is to estimate, to extol, to magnify: whence Zimri is called סלוא in Num. 25, verse 14, because he estimated the iniquities of his family. The explanation of those who understand by διάψαλμα a pausing of the voice also agrees. Finally, some, with Schindler in his Pentaglot Lexicon and Paul of Burgos, think the expression is an enclitic used only by poets, so that the number and modulation of the verse may be explained. Nor is the interpretation of those who wish it to signify properly τέλος, an end, repugnant, as the LXX interpreters are accustomed to render the word למנצח, and they interpreted the word כלה in Hab. 3, verse 12, so that the sense is that the song or rhythm is finished there, and a new one is to be begun, which pleases Ludovicus de Dieu in his animadversions on the O.T. at this place.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DICVNT ANIMÆ MEÆ) Dicunt de me.

Vers. 3. IN DEO EJVS) Hic sequitur in Hebræo סלה, nota, quæ cantum hic intendendum significat, quod modo in mœrore, modo in gaudio sit.

Variæ sunt de hac voce, quæ in Psalmis solum & in Cantico Abacuc occurrit, & in hoc quidem ter, in istis autem septuagies semel legitur, sententiæ: Decem earum recensuit B. Joh. Tarnovius ad b. l. Sed quinq; sunt præcipuæ. Prima, quam hic affu- mit Grotius, LXX. Interpretum videtur, qui reddi- dere διάψαλμα, quod Musicæ melodiæ eo quo repe- ritur loco, quædam mutatio fiat, uti vocem illam Græcam Suidas exponit ἐναλλαγὴν μέλος. Neque dissonat R. David Kimchi in lib. Radic. a סלל ex- altavit, elevavit, deducens, quod elevatio vocis in- dicetur. Unde Judæi in locis istis decantandis una cum corpore vocem attollebant. Eadem est interpre- tis Psalmorum, notante R. Aben - Ezra & R. Mar- dochai Nathanis in Capit. Concordant. sententia. Sed huic Etymo repugnare Grammaticam for- mam B. Tarnovius observavit. Altera est R. Aben- Ezræ explicatio, qui exponit per כן הוא ita est, & אמן id est, vere; atque ita etiam alii per vocem Amen declarant, eumque sensum probant partim e Judæo- rum precibus, partim ex eorum Epitaphiis, v. c. Ani- ma ejus sit ligata in cælo, Sela. Tertio exponunt non- nulli cum Tharg. Jonathan in secula, & semper, cum Aquila: atque ita accipi notat R. Mardochai in Psal. 84. יהללוך סלה laudabunt te in secula seculo- rum. Qui etiam hoc sensu in Epitaphiis Judæo- rum eam vocem usurpari vult. Quarto habent ean- dem nonnulli pro nota pausæ & attentionis animi, quæ sententia, judice B. Tarnovio, & omnium ma- xime verisimilis est, & derivationi hujus vocis con- gruit optime, quia סלה significat stravit, ut sit ster- nendæ & remittendæ vocis in cantu indicium, ut tan- to melius verba præcedentia, utpote singulare ali- quod & ἀξιομνημόνευτον exhibentia, considerentur. Cui sententiæ etiam nostrum adjicimus calculum. Huic explicationi congruit etiam significatio vocis סלה quam in Lexico Chaldaico-Talmudico Rabb. annotavit Buxtorfius, quod sit æstimare, extollere, magnificare: unde Zimri סלוא Num. 25. vers. 14. dictus, quod æstimarit iniquitates familiæ suæ. Con- sonat & eorum explicatio, qui per διάψαλμα pau- sationem vocis intelligunt. Postremo putant non- nulli cum Schindlero in Lexico Pentagl. & Paulo Burgensi dictionem esse enclyticam Poetis tantum usi- tatam, ut numerus & modulatio versus explicetur. Neque repugnat eorum interpretatio, qui proprie τέλος finem significare volunt, uti LXX. interpre- tes vocem למנצח reddere solent, & vocem כלה interpretati sunt Hab. 3. vers. 12. ut sensus sit, finiri ibi cantum aut rythmum, novumque esse inchoandum, quod placet Ludovico de Dieu in animadvers. in V. T. ad hunc locum.

## 3:4
Verse 5. FROM HIS HOLY MOUNT) From Zion, where the Ark was then.

Latin:

Vers 5. DE MONTE SANCTO SVO) De Sione, ubi tunc Arca.

## 3:5
Verse 6.

I SLEPT) I sleep secure, trusting in God.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

EGO DORMIVI) Dormio securus, Deo fidens.

## 3:7
Verse 8. YOU HAVE STRUCK ALL THOSE ADVERSE TO ME) Saul first, then his offspring, and their followers.

Verse 8. FOR YOU HAVE STRUCK ALL THOSE ADVERSE TO ME WITHOUT CAUSE.

In Hebrew it is לחי, jaw. Genebrard, in order to defend the Vulgate, says that this is put for לחינם by apocope, WITHOUT CAUSE. But rashly: for לחינם never occurs in Scripture, but either חנם simply, or אל-חנם, as in Ez. 6, v. 10. But לחי, jaw, is rightly retained, since the sense is perfectly consistent, you have struck all my enemies on the jaw; which the Chaldean and Syrian also express. Cornelius Jansenius also acknowledges in this place that it is read much more aptly as 'on the jaws' than 'without cause' with the LXX interpreters. For it is signified, he says, not only an ignominious striking on the jaw, but also a violent one, as if, namely, he had broken the teeth. To whom also Titelmann and Bellarmine agree.

Latin:

Vers. 8. TV PERCVSSISTI OMNES ADVERSAN- TES MIHI) Saulem primum, deinde progeniem ipsius, eo- rumque sectatores.

Vers. 8. QVONIAM TU PERGVSSISTI O- MNES ADVERSANTES MIHI SINE CAUSA.

In Ebr. est לחי maxilla. Genebrardus ut Vul- gatam tueatur, id pro לחינם per apocopen poni, SINE CAUSA, dicit. Sed temere: nam nuspiam לחינם in Script. occurrit, sed vel חנם simpliciter, vel אל-חנם, ut Ez. 6. v. 10. Recte autem לחי maxilla retinetur, quum sensus apprime sibi constet, percas- sisti omnes inimicos meos maxilla; quam etiam ex- primunt Chald. & Syrus. Agnoscit etiam Cornel. Jansenius in h. l. multo aptius legi in maxillis, quam sine causa cum LXX. Interpp. Significatur enim, in- quit, non solum ignominiosa in maxilla percussio, sed etiam vehemens, quasi scil. dentes confregerit. Cui ac- cedunt quoque Titelmannus, & Bellarminus.

## 3:8
Verse 9. SALVATION IS OF THE LORD AND UPON YOUR PEOPLE IS YOUR BLESSING.

The change of person seems to denote a plurality of divine persons. For he speaks of one person: Salvation is of the Lord, he addresses another: upon your people is your blessing: Athanasius and Theodoret accept it in the sense of a prayer, informatively, while Augustine and Cassiodorus take it as a statement of fact. Which seems more suitable: for the cause of the vow and prayer is rendered in verse 7, 'save me, my GOD'.

Latin:

Vers. 9. DOMINI EST SALUS ET SUPER POPULUM TUUM BENEDICTIO TUA.

Mutatio personæ pluralitatem personarum divinarum videtur notare. De alia enim persona loquitur: Domini est salus, aliam compellat, su- per populum tuum benedictio: Sensu precationis ac- cipiunt Athanasius, & Theodorets, informatorie vero August. & Cassiodorus. Qui convenientior vi- detur: nam causa redditur voti & orationis vers. 7. salvum me fac DEUS meus.

## 3:8 Addition
On Psalm 3, verse 9.

SALVATION IS OF THE LORD.

In the Hebrew it is a dative: Salvation is to the Lord, but the origin and cause are noted; the Lord is the fountain and author of all salvation, as in Revelation 7:10. Therefore the Vulgate rightly expressed the sense, as did the blessed Luther.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 3. v. 9.

DOMINI EST SALUS.

In Ebræo Dativus est: Domino est salus, sed notatur origo & causa, Dominus est salutis omnis fons, & autor, ut Apoc. 7, 10. Ideo recte sensum expreffit Vulgata, ut & B. Lutherus.

## 4:1 Argument
PSALM IV. A prayer to God, and an instruction for persecutors.

TO THE END, IN SONGS) Aquila, a follower of the origins, translates that לַמְנַצֵּחַ as τῷ νικοποιῷ ἐν ψαλμοῖς. But R. David Kimchi, if I am not mistaken, rightly says that he is called so who was the Prince in singing. There follows בִּנְגִינוֹת, that is, on those instruments which sound by striking. For there are others which sound by blowing.

B. Tarnovius has not poorly observed that that former word in general denotes an ἐργοδιώκτην (taskmaster) in 2 Chron. 2:18 and 34:13, whence here in particular it designates the prefect of organic music or the Symphoniac Choir, to whom the Psalms were handed over by David in 1 Chron. 16:4, as B. Luther noted. Not only R. David Kimchi favors this interpretation, but also Aben-Ezra and R. Salomo Kimchi, as well as R. Mardochai Nathan. That is indeed indicated particularly in the title of certain Psalms, because they were considered more distinguished than others, in which sense some also explain the Greek Interpreters' εἰς τέλος and the Vulgate's 'in finem', because such Psalms are to be sung perpetually or are more excellent and useful. To others, נִצּוּחַ is a species of praise by which the name of God is celebrated perpetually and indefinitely: or by which the strength of God, yielding to none and overcoming all, is sung. Which Ludovicus de Dieu proves from 1 Paral. 15:21. where among the various kinds of singers are also listed those who were appointed לְנַצֵּחַ, to handle that kind of praise by which the conquering virtue of God is extolled, as he himself explains, and he judges it to have been most prudently explained by the Vulgate; they sang an epinicion, that is, a song by which they celebrated the conquering God; nor do the LXX mean anything else when they render it τῷ ἐνισχύσαι, 'for strengthening'. Therefore, מְנַצֵּחַ according to him is the Cantor to whom it was enjoined to sing the Epinicion of God. But these opinions easily agree, since such a Cantor of divine praises was without doubt the prefect over the others: the former explanation, however, seems simpler and more expeditious. Augustine, from the Greek εἰς τὸ τέλος, extracted 'Christ the end of the law'. But in the Hebrew, it is not לַקֵּץ ('to the end'), as the Greek and Vulgate Latin rendered it, but לַמְנַצֵּחַ occurs: which denotes the conqueror, and is an epithet of the Master of Singers, on the musical instrument Neginoth: B. Hülsemann on Jer. 8:4. לַמְנַצֵּחַ is for continuing the song.

Latin:

PSALMUS IV. Precatio ad Deum, & informatio persequutorum.

IN FINEM IN CARMINIBVS) Illud לַמְנַצֵּחַ τῷ νι- κοποιῷ ἐν ψαλμοῖς vertit Aquila originum sectator. Sed R. David Kimchi recte ni fallor ita vocari ait eum, qui in cantu Princeps erat. Sequitur בִּנְגִינוֹת , id est, in iis instrumentis, quæ pulsu sonant. Nam sunt alia, quæ sonant flatu.

VOcem illam priorem in genere ἐργοδιώκτην notare 2. Chron. 2, 18. & 34, 13. non male ob- servavit B. Tarnovius, unde hic in specie præfectus Musicæ organicæ vel Chori Symphoniaci, cui tradi- ti Psalmi sunt a Davide 1. Chron. 16, 4 designatur, uti B. Lutherus annotavit. Favet interpretationi non tantum R. David Kimchi, sed etiam Aben- Ezra & R. Salomo Kimchi, ut & R. Mardochai Nathan. Id vero de quibusdam Psalmis peculia- riter in titulo indicatum est, quod illi præ aliis in- signiores haberentur, in quem sensum etiam non- nulli explicant Græcorum Interpp. εἰς τέλος & vul- gatæ, in finem, quod Psalmi ejusmodi perpetuo seu præstantiores & utiliores decantandi sint. Aliis נִצּוּחַ est species laudis, qua perpetuo & indefinenter no- men Dei celebratur: vel quo robur Dei nulli ce- dens, omnia superans decantatur. Quod probat Ludovicus de Dieu e 1. Paral. 15, 21. ubi inter varia Cantorum genera recensentur quoque qui consti- tuti erant לְנַצֵּחַ , ad illud laudum genus tractan- dum, quo vincens Dei virtus extollitur, uti ex- ponit ipse, ac prudentissime a vulgato expositum censet, canebant epinicion, id est, carmen, quo victorem Deum celebrabant; nec aliud LXX. velle cum reddunt τῷ ἐνισχύσαι ad roborandum. Pro- inde מְנַצֵּחַ secundum ipsum est Cantor, cui Epini- cion Dei decantare injunctum erat. Sed facile con- veniunt hæ sententiæ, siquidem talis Cantor lau- dum divinarum præfectus cæteris sine dubio fue- rit: Prior tamen explicatio simplicior, atque expe- ditior videtur. Augustinus e Græco εἰς τὸ τέλος exsculpsit Christum finem legis. Verum in Ebræo non לַקֵּץ in finem, ut Græcus & Vulgatus Latinus reddidere, sed לַמְנַצֵּחַ occurrit: quod vincentem notat, & epitheton est Magistri Cantorum, in Neginoth instrumento Musico: B. Hülsemanno ad Jer, 8, 4. לַמְנַצֵּחַ est ad continuandam cantionem.

## 4:2
Verse 3.

SONS OF MEN, HOW LONG WITH HEAVY HEART) From the Greek: ἕως πότε βαρυκάρδιοι. It appears they read in the Hebrew כְּבֵדֵי, 'your aggravation'. Thus also the Chaldean here. Those who are lazy and slothful to learn are said to aggravate their heart. The sense which is now in the Hebrew is such: 'How long do you labor to turn my glory into disgrace?'

Here Grotius imitated Cardinal Bellarmine, who likewise sought a laurel wreath in this cake of corruption by arguing against the Hebrew text in l. 2 de verb. DEI cap. 13, that scribes changed כ into כ: but Bellarmine contradicts himself, since in chapter 2 he proved with solid arguments that the Hebrew Bibles were not corrupted, and that the text did not have it otherwise in the time of Jerome than it has now, as Bellarmine himself admits; indeed, the Greek version, which the same chapter 6 demonstrates, is now very corrupted in many places, so that it is no longer safe to amend Hebrew texts from Greek Codices. The sense is also plain in the Hebrew: 'How long will my glory be into ignominy (will it be? which is the ellipsis of the substantive verb that is most frequent), wie lang soll meine Ehre geschändet werden? as B. Luther says. Nor is there any difficulty in the words, and the sequence and argument of the Psalm respond very well to that reading: ἀδελφίᾳ [in] the LXX Interpreters. or even the slips of the scribes who copied that version escape no one. Nor is it right to correct the sources from the versions.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

FILII HOMINVM VSQVE QVO GRAVI CORDE) Ex Græco: ἕως πότε βαρυκάρδιοι. Apparet eos legisse in Hebræo כְּבֵדֵי aggravatio vestra. Sic & Chaldæus hic. Aggravare cor suum dicuntur, qui pigri sunt & ignavi ad discendum. Sensus qui nunc est in Hebræo, talis est, Quousque gloriam meam in dedecus, supple vertere laboratis?

Imitatus est hic Grotius Cardinalem Bellar- minum, qui pariter in hoc mustaceo corruptionis arguendi textum Ebræum laureolam quæsivit l. 2. de verb. DEI cap. 13. quod librarii mutarint כ in כ: sed repugnat sibi ipsi Bellarminus, siquidem cap. 2. Argumentis solidis probarit, Biblia Ebræa corru- pta non esse, neque textus aliter habuerit tempore Hieronymi, quam nunc habet, fatente ipso Bellar- mino, imo versio Græca, quod idem cap. 6. demon- strat, valde nunc vitiata sit in pluribus locis, ut tu- tum jam non sit Ebraicos textus ex Græcis Codicibus emendare. Sensus etiam planus est in Ebræo: Quousque gloria mea in ignominiam (erit? quæ el- lipsis verbi substantivi est frequentissima) wie lang soll meine Ehre geschändet werden? ut B. Lutherus. Neque in verbis ulla difficultas est, & συνέχεια at- que argumentum Psalmi optime respondent isti le- ctioni: ἀδελφίᾳ LXX. Interpp. vel etiam lapsus li- brariorum descriptorum versionis istius neminem fugiunt. Neq; fas est e versionibus fontes corrigere.

## 4:3
Verse 4. HIS HOLY ONE) His Anointed.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SANCTVM SVVM) Vnctum.

## 4:3 Addition
On Psalm 4, verse 4.

THE LORD HATH WONDERFULLY SET APART HIS HOLY ONE.

The following clause teaches that this is to be understood concerning David: The Lord will hear me when I call unto him. And it is singular in the Hebrew, 'his holy one', as the Vulgate itself rendered it, and not plural: whence it is a wonder that the Papists, against the authority of the Vulgate and the sense of the text, strive to prove from this the miracles of the saints and the glory of the invocation of the same: since it is entirely a matter here of the grace and benefits with which he wonderfully affected David. Chrysostom, from the following words, rather proves that there is no need for intercessors to obtain the hearing of God.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 4. v. 4.

MIRIFICAVIT DOMINUS SAN- CTUM SUUM.

De Davide hoc intelligendum esse, comma sequens docet: Dominus exaudit me cum clamavero ad illum. Et singulare in Ebræo est Sanctum suum, ut vulgata ipsa reddidit, non vero plurale: unde mirum, quod Papistæ contra auctoritatem vulgatæ & sensum textus hinc miracula Sanctorum & glo- riam invocationis eorundem probare satagant: cum omnino de gratia & beneficiis, quibus Davidem mi- rabiliter affecit, hic agatur. Chrysostomus ex ver- bis sequentibus potius probat, opus non esse interces- soribus ad impetrandam exauditionem Dei.

## 4:4
Vers. 5. BE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT) It can be translated: Are you angry? but do not sin. It grieves you that I am destined for the kingdom: but see to it that you do not offend God out of that grief. Thus רגזו must be written, with the points of the Indicative.

But who gave Grotius the power to substitute other points at his own discretion? Is not the sense evident in itself, that one should be angry in such a way that we do not sin? For not every anger is a sin. And is not the Hebrew reading confirmed by the authority of the Apostle in Eph. 4:26, ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε. On which text Grotius annotated these things: I wonder that there are those who doubt whether this is from Psalm 4:5. For the LXX version has the same words there: ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε. Bellarmine explains it thus: He teaches that they should burn with a certain holy wrath, and resist depraved desires, and in that way avoid sin. Basil the Great, in his homily on anger: For this purpose anger was given to us by God, that it might be a goad to virtue. Gregory the Great to Leontius: From confession, anger in the punishment of the wicked ought to follow reason, not precede it, so that as if a handmaid of justice it may come behind, and not rush forward wantonly before the face. It is therefore understood either of the anger by which the King's enemies ought to be stirred up against themselves, i.e. be angry at your wicked deeds, as Augustine also explained; or hypothetically, i.e., If you are angry, do not sin, which sense is more consistent with the context and the Apostolic interpretation. Ambrose, book 1, On Duties, ch. 3: If we are angry, let us not bring forth evil speech from our mouth, lest we fall into guilt. See B. Gerhard on this passage.

Vers. same. WHAT YOU SAY IN YOUR HEARTS IN YOUR BEDS BE COMPUNCTIOUS) Better:

Think in your heart, in your bed, namely what you have done, and be silent: that is, do penance, as the Arab explains here. What he says, in your bed, agrees very well with that Pythagorean precept,

Do not admit sleep to your soft eyes until you have gone over each of the day's deeds three times: Where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty was left undone? Starting from the first, go through them, and afterwards, for the bad deeds, reproach yourself.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IRASCIMINI, ET NE PECCATE) Potest ver- ti: Irascimini? at ne peccate. Dolet vobis, quod ego regno destinor: sed videte ne ex eo dolore Deum offendatis. Ita רגזו scribendum erit, cum punctis Indicativi.

Ecquis vero potestatem dedit Grotio, pro arbitrio puncta alia substituendi? Annon sensus per se evidens est, ita irascendum esse, ne pecce- mus. Non enim omnis ira peccatum est. Et an- non firmata est lectio Ebræa auctoritate Apostoli Eph.4,26. ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε. Ad quem textum Grotius hæc annotavit: Miror esse, qui dubitent, an hoc sit ex Psalmo 4, 5. Nam versio LXX. ibi eadem habet verba: ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁ- μαρτάνετε. Bellarmin. ita explicat: Docet, ut sancta quadam iracundia exardescant, & resistant pravis desideriis, & eo modo peccatum vitent. Basilius M. orat. de ira: Ad hoc nobis data est ira a Deo, ut sit cos virtutis. Gregor. M. ad Leont. Ex conf. ira in vindi- cta malorum sequi debet rationem non præire, ut qua- si ancilla justitiæ post tergum veniat, & non lasciva ante faciem prorumpat. Accipitur ergo vel de ira qua Regis inimici in seipsos exstimulari debeant, q. d. irascimini super sceleribus vestris, uti etiam Augustinus exposuit; vel hypothetice, h. m. Si ira- scimini, nolite peccare, qui sensus convenientior est cum contextui. tum interpretationi Apostolicæ. Ambrof. l. 1. Offic. c. 3. Si irascimur, malum sermonem non proferamus de ore nostro, ne in culpam ruamus. Vid. B. Gerhard. in h. l.

## 4:4 Addition
Verse 5.

BE YE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.

It is a conditional expression: If you are angry, do not sin. For imperatives preceded by subsequent prohibitions are accustomed among the Hebrews to have the meaning of subjunctives or of the conditional IF. See Num. 24, 21. 22. From the parallel in Eph. 4, 26, it is to be gathered that what is hinted at is the difference between that disordered agitation which the faithful suffer against their will, and a voluntary and lingering agitation, so that if the former creeps upon us, we should take care that it does not degenerate into the latter, which Lorinus teaches from Cyril. Mollerus has warned that this admonition is not directed at the enemies of David, of whom he speaks in verse 3, but that the discourse is now turned toward his friends. In vain, therefore, do the Papists elicit from this that illicit concupiscence, devoid of plenary assent, is by no means a sin.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

IRASCIMINI, ET NOLITE PEC- CARE.

Conditionalis est locutio: Si irascimini, nolite peccare. Imperativi enim præmissi interdictis sequen- tibus solent apud Ebræos significationem subjunctivo- rum vel Conditionalis SI habere. Vid. Num. 24, 21. 22. Ex parallelo Eph. 4, 26. colligere est, quod in- nuatur diversitas commonitionis istius inordinatæ, quam fideles inviti patiuntur, & voluntariæ & moro- sæ commotionis, ut si illa nobis obrepar, caveamus, ne in hancce degeneret, quod Lorinus e Cyrillo do- cet. Non dirigi hanc monitionem ad hostes Davi- dis, de quibus vers. 3. sed converti jam sermonem ad amicos Mollerus monuit. Frustra ergo hinc Pa- pistæ concupiscentiam illicitam destitutam plenario as- sensu, nulla ratione peccatum esse, eliciunt.

## 5:1 Argument
PSALM V. A prayer for the divine inheritance, against the enemies of the Church.

TO THE END, FOR HER WHO OBTAINS THE INHERITANCE) What the first word לַמְנַצֵּחַ signifies has already been said. Regarding the second word הַנְּחִילוֹת, I find nothing more probable than what many Hebrews have said, that נחיל is the buzzing which bees emit, and that the musical instrument was named from the similarity of its sound. Also, to the Arabs, نحل is a bee.

Latin:

PSALMUS V. Oratio pro hæreditate divina, adversus hostes Ecclesiæ.

IN FINEM PRO EA QVÆ HÆREDITATEM CON- SEQVITVR) Vox prima לַמְנַצֵּחַ quid significet, dictum jam est. De altera voce הַנְּחִילוֹת nihil probabilius reperio, quam quod Hebræi complures dixere נחיל esse bombum quem edunt apes, & ex ejus soni similitudine dictum instru- mentum Musicum. Etiam Arabibus نحل est Apis.

## 5:4
Vers. 5. O LORD, LEAD ME IN THY JUSTICE) As if he were to say: this is the true worship which pleases Thee.

Grotius acknowledged that the Hebrew word הַנְּחִילוֹת is poorly expressed here by the Vulgate, which he, along with the Hebrews, takes to refer to a musical instrument. Thus also in Psalm 6:1, he abandoned the Vulgate interpretation concerning the octave, and preferred the Chaldean interpretation concerning the eight-stringed instrument: nor is he content with the initial translation of Psalm 7, שׁגָּיוֹן, but makes it the beginning of an ancient song with the Hebrews, to the melodies of which this ode was made: neither in Psalm 8, with the common title, 'for the winepresses,' yielding more to the Chaldean, as it seems, which has גתית for a musical instrument sought from the Philistines and the city of Gath; nor in the title of Psalm 9 and others: departing everywhere from the Vulgate when it pleases: whence he could by no means hold it for authentic with the Papists ought to marvel at, he nevertheless often corrects the Hebrew Codices to the norm of the Vulgate, and fashions new readings of the Hebrew text, congruent in some way with the Latin Vulgate or the Greek translation, and sells them as ancient and genuine. Which is a cacoethes [bad habit] of slandering the Hebrew truth, truly to be detested!

lectum [that it was read] is learned more correctly from Jerome's translation than from the Vulgate, because the former was translated from the Hebrew, not the latter. Bellarmine, concerning the author of the Vulgate in the Psalms, lib. 2 de verb. DEI cap. 9, has it thus: 'The Psalter of the Latin Vulgate edition is not that which St. Jerome translated from the Hebrew, nor that which he translated from the Greek version of the LXX interpreters. But that which he himself amended, translated by an ancient interpreter from the edition of St. Lucian the martyr.' And a little later: 'We say therefore that our Psalter is not that which Blessed Jerome translated from the Hebrew, and that is certain: for that exists in the works of Blessed Jerome, and almost everywhere dissents from ours, at least as regards the words. We add, neither is it that which he himself translated from the Hexapla of Origen, but that common one, which he amended twice: and that is proved from the Epistle to Sunia and Fretella;' for there he says that what is had, 'direct in thy sight my way,' has it otherwise among the LXX and all other interpretations, except the common and Vulgate. But our edition has it thus: 'Therefore our edition is that common and Vulgate one, and distinct from the pure interpretation of the LXX.' This Bellarmine from Jerome, whence it is evident that even the LXX interpreters had it otherwise in this place in Jerome's time, than either the Latin Vulgate version now has, or even the modern edition of the LXX interpreters itself consonant with it here. All other interpretations also had it otherwise then. Shall we therefore prefer one common and Vulgate version to all others, and to the Hebrew text itself? Shall we for the same reason correct the Hebrew text, which has all interpretations consenting, even the LXX interpreters, as it was had in Jerome's time? I add besides the Chaldean, Arnobius, Chrysostom, Dionysius the Carthusian, also certain Latin manuscripts noting Fr. Luca [Luke] to be consonant with the Hebrew: 'Direct before me thy way': which is not to be taken as Grotius perverts it, 'look upon me and my deeds,' but as Jerome explains: who says, 'The Prophet asks that the way of the Lord, which is straight in itself, may also be made straight for him. Grant that thy way, which is straight, may appear good and straight to me, lest I choose the broad way, which leads to destruction, Matt. 7, 13. Ps. 139, 24.' Concerning the various translations of Jerome in the Psalms, to illustrate those things which have been adduced from Bellarmine, one may compare Amama in Anti-Barb. Bibl. lib. 3. pag. 567.

vers. 5. FOR THOU ART NOT ONE WILLING INIQUITY.

GOD does not will iniquity, and therefore the error of the Calvinists is to be rejected, both of the crasser ones, who make God the cause of sin either physically or morally, and of those who today especially, after the Arminian controversies were stirred up in Belgium, assert that God wills sin indeed not as sin, but as it is a medium for declaring justice. Whom the Hieropsaltes [David] openly contradicts. For he who does not will sin, is neither the cause of sin, nor is he to be said to will sin in any respect: and not even as a medium of declaring justice. It is repugnant to the supreme goodness and justice of God to will what is evil in itself. Nor indeed is sin a medium of divine justice τῇ φύσει [by nature], but τῇ θέσει [by position/convention], not in itself, but by accident, just as evil customs are by accident the cause of good laws. And the justice of God toward man had been demonstrated when He forbade him the use of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, under the threat of death. There was therefore no need for sin to declare justice. But some object in vain that the word חפץ is 'to delight,' therefore it is only taught that God does not delight in sin, not that He does not will sin. For David teaches simply that God does not will it; which the context confirms; for he who so לא חפץ [does not will/delight in] sin, that he hates all who work iniquity, with whom the malignant does not dwell, nor do the unjust remain, he not only does not delight in sin, but absolutely does not will it, nay, he abominates sin. Add that חפץ generally denotes the will, and not delight, e.g., Jud. 13, 23. 'If the Lord were willing to kill us,' 1 Sam. 2, 25. 'God willed to kill them,' 1 Kings 21, 7. Ps. 115, 3. Is. 53, 10. Whence it is inferred that God in no way wills iniquity: not only that He does not delight in it, but that He also otherwise absolutely does not will it, nor does He will that evil be done, much less does He impel to evil.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DOMINE DEDV6 ME IN JVSTITIA TVA) Quasi dicat: hic verus est cultus qui tibi placet.

EBreæam vocem הַנְּחִילוֹת male a vulgata hic exprimi agnovit Grotius, quam cum Ebræis de instrumento Musico accipit. Ita etiam Psal- mo 6, 1. vulgatam interpretationem pro octava de- seruit, & Chaldæam interpretationem super octo- chordo prætulit: neque contentus est initiali Psal. 7. translatione, שׁגָּיוֹן sed initium cantici ve- teris facit cum Ebræis, ad cujus modulos hæc oda facta sit: neque Psal. 8. titulo vulgato, pro torcularibus, Chaldæo magis, ut videtur annuens, qui גתית pro instrumento musico a Philistæis & urbe Geth petito, habet; neque titulo Psalmi 9. aliorumque: passim discedens a vulgata, cum placet: unde eam pro authentica habere cum Papistis minime potuit. Et, quod mirari oportet, corrigit tamen sæpe Hebræos Codices ad normam vulgatæ, ac novas lectiones fingit Hebræi textus, Latinæ vulgatæ, aut Græcæ translationi utcunque congruas, easque pro antiquis & germanis venditat. Quod cacoethes est calumniandi Hebræam veritatem, vere detestandum!

lectum fuerit ex Hieronymi translatione rectius discitur, quam ex vulgata, quia illa ex Hebræo translata est, non hæc. Bellarminus de vulgatæ autore in Psalmis lib. 2. de verb. DEI cap. 9. ita habet: Psalterium vulgatæ editionis Latinæ non est illud, quod D. Hieronymus transtulit ex Hebræo, neque illud, quod transtulit ex versione Græca LXX. interpp. Sed illud, quod ipse emendavit, translatum ab antiquo interprete ex editione S. Luciani martyris. Et paulo post: Dicimus igitur Psalterium nostrum non esse illud, quod B. Hieronymus transtulit ex Hebræo, idque certum est: nam illud extat in operibus B. Hieronymi, & fere ubique dissentit a nostro, saltem quoad verba. Addimus, neque esse illud, quod ipse vertit ex Origenis Hexaplis, sed illud commune, quod bis emendavit: idque probatur ex Epistola ad Suniam & Fretellam; nam ibi dicit, quod habetur, dirige in conspectu tuo viam meam, aliter habere apud LXX. & omnes alias interpretationes, excepta communi & vulgata. At nostra editio ita habet: Igitur nostra editio est illa communis & vulgata, & a pura interpretatione LXX. distincta. Hæc Bellarminus ex Hieronymo, unde constat etiam LXX. interpp. aliter hoc loco habuisse Hieronymi tempore, quam vel versio Latina vulgata nunc habet, vel etiam ipsa moderna LXX. interpp. editio illi hic consona. Aliter etiam tum habuisse omnes alias interpretationes. Num ergo unam communem & vulgatam versionem aliis omnibus, textuique ipsi Hebræo præferemus? num ob eandem corrigemus textum Hebræum, qui omnes interpretationes habet consentientes, etiam LXX. Interpp. prout illa habebatur Hieronymi tempore? Addo præter Chaldæum, Arnobium, Chrysostomum, Dionysium Carthus. etiam manuscripta quædam Latina notante Fr. Luca Hebræo consonare: Dirige coram me viam tuam: quæ non ita accipienda, ut pervertit Grotius, respice ad me, meaque facta, sed ut explicat Hieronymus: qui, Postulat, inquit, Propheta, ut via Domini, quæ per se recta est, etiam sibi recta fiat. Da ut mihi quæ recta est, bona & recta videatur via tua, ne latam viam eligam, quæ ad exitium ducit, Matth. 7, 13. Psal.. 139, 24. De variis translationibus Hieronymi in Psalmos, ad ea, quæ ex Bellarmino adducta sunt, illustranda conferri potest Amama in Anti-Barb. Bibl. lib. 3. pag. 567.

vers. 5. QUONIAM NON VOLENS INIQUITATEM TU ES.

DEUS non vult iniquitatem, ideoque reprobandus Calvinianorum error, tum crassiorum, qui Deum peccati causam sive physicam sive moralem faciunt, tum eorum, qui hodie imprimis, post motas in Belgio controversias Arminianas, Deum peccatum quidem non ut peccatum, sed qua medium est declarandæ justitiæ, velle adserunt. Quibus Hieropsaltes palam contradicit. Qui enim non vult peccatum, is nec causa peccati est, nec peccatum quocunque respectu velle dicendus est: ac nequidem ceu medium justitiæ declarandæ. Repugnat id summæ Dei bonitati ac justitiæ, velle, quod malum est per se. Nec vero peccatum est medium divinæ justitiæ τῇ φύσει, sed τῇ θέσει, non per se, sed per accidens, uti mali mores per accidens causa sunt bonarum legum. Et demonstrata erat justitia Dei erga hominem, cum interdixit ei usui arboris cognitionis boni & mali, sub comminatione mortis. Non ergo opus erat peccato ad declarandam justitiam. Nequicquam autem excipiunt nonnulli, vocem חפץ esse delectari, solum ergo doceri, quod Deus non delectetur peccato, non quod peccatum non velit. Nam simpliciter docet David, Deum non velle, quod contextus confirmat; qui enim ita לא חפץ peccatum, ut odio habeat omnes, qui iniquitatem operantur, juxta quem non habitat malignus, neque permanent injusti, is non tantum non delectatur peccato, sed prorsus non vult, imo abominatur peccatum. Adde quod חפץ generaliter notet voluntatem, non autem delectationem, v. g. Jud. 13, 23. Si vellet Dominus occidere nos, 1. Sam. 2, 25. voluit Deus eos occidere, 1. Reg. 21, 7. Psal. 115, 3. Es. 53, 10. unde infertur, Deum nullo modo velle iniquitatem: non modo quod non delectetur eadem, sed quod etiam alias absolute eam non velit, nec malum fieri velit, nedum ad malum impellat.

## 5:8
Vers. 9. BECAUSE OF MY ENEMIES DIRECT IN THY SIGHT MY WAY] He reads לפניך דרכי as also the Greeks κατεύθυνον ἐνώπιόν σου τὴν ὁδόν μου. Make it so that I live that life which pleases thee, lest my enemies have anything to carp at. Similar below 27, 10. in our Hebrew is לפני דרכך, that is, 'look upon me and my deeds.' I would prefer that.

The Socinians gather from this that separated souls do nothing, nor do they remember or confess. But if these things are understood concerning temporal death and the sepulcher, they must be accepted in a qualified sense, because the deceased can be mindful of God, nor confess Him in the assembly of the Church, neither as to the soul nor as to the bodily members. But if eternal death and damnation, which is accustomed to be denoted by the word שאול, is understood, not every action, nor every memory or confession is taken away from souls after this life in hell. For the rich man confessed that he felt the pains of hell after death.

But from where is it established that the author of the Vulgate read otherwise than it is now read in the Hebrew? Grotius himself certainly admits that the Psalms were translated in the Vulgate not from the Hebrew, but from the Greek, noting these things at Psalm 7: 'My righteous help is from the Lord.' From the Greek, as ALMOST EVERYTHING in this version: for Jerome made another from the Hebrew, but that was not received into the churches. What then in the time of Jerome were the horrible [things] Luke 16, 24. But Eucharistic memory and confession of praise, because words of memory among the Hebrews denote not a bare recollection, but that which follows memory, and in this place memory joined with the celebration of divine benefits, or a grateful ἀνάμνησιν; and that a confession of praise is designated here is manifest.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PROPTER INIMICOS MEOS DIRIGE IN CONSPECTU TVO VIAM MEAM] Legit לפניך דרכי ut & Græci κατεύθυνον ἐνώπιόν σου τὴν ὁδόν μου. Fac ut eam vitam vivam, quæ tibi placet, ne quid habeant inimici mei, quod carpant. Simile infra 27, 10. in nostro Hebræo est לפני דרכך, id est, respice ad me, meaque facta. Ego illud præferam.

Colligunt inde Sociniani, animas separatas nihil agere, nec memorare, aut confiteri. At si de morte temporali ac sepulcro hæc intelligantur, secundum quid accipienda erunt, quod defuncti neque quoad animam, neq; quoad corporea membra memores Dei esse, eumq; confiteri in cœtu Ecclesiæ possint. Si vero mors æterna & damnatio, quæ voce שאול notari solet, intelligatur, animabus post hanc vitam in inferno non derogatur omnis actio, nec omnis memoria aut confessio. Epulo enim confitebatur dolores inferni se sentire post mortem

At unde constat vulgatæ autorem secus legisse, quam nunc legitur in Ebræo? Fatetur utique Grotius ipse Psalmos translatos esse in vulgata non ex Ebræo, sed ex Græco, ad Psal. 7. hæc annotans: Justum adjutorium meum a Domino. Ex Græco, ut PROPE OMNIA in hac versione: nam aliam ex Hebræo fecit Hieronymus, sed ea in Ecclessas recepta non est. Quid ergo Hieronymi tempore horribiles Lucæ 16, 24. Sed memoria Eucharisti- ca & confessio laudis, quia verba memoriæ apud Ebræos non nudam recordationem, fed id quod fequitur memoriam, & hoc loco memoriam con- junctam cum celebratione beneficiorum divinorum, vel gratam ἀνάμνησιν notant; ac confessionem lau- dis hic designari in propatulo est.

## 6:5 Addition
On Psalm 6, verse 6.

IN HELL WHO SHALL CONFESS TO THEE.

Bellarmino and Coton, in book 4 of his Institutions, chapter 1, are inept in supposing hypothetically here such a condition of the dead, that in hell, and also in purgatory, they might pray away their guilt: since there is no place for prayer there, Psalm 30, 10; Psalm 88, 11, and following.

Isa. 38. v. 18. And the Papist interpreters acknowledge this interrogation to be a pure negation, Cajetan, Eugubinus, Campensis, Jansenius, etc., and to this they apply the sentiment of Innocent III from Sir. 17:26, 'from the dead, confession perishes.' Whence it should rather be concluded that there is no intermediate state between temporal death and eternal salvation or damnation.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 6. v. 6.

IN INFERNO QUIS CONFITEBI- TUR TIBI.

Ineptus est Bellarminus, & Cotonus lib. 4. In- stitut. cap. 1. hypothetice hic supponi talem mortuo- rum conditionem, ut in inferno, in purgatorio etiam culpam deprecentur: quum ibi non sit locus deprecationis Psalm. 30, 10. Psalm. 88, 11. seqq.

Esa. 38. v. 18. Et Pontificii Interpp. agnoscunt hanc interrogationem esse puram negationem, Cajetan. Eugubinus, Campensis, Jansenius &c. eoque appli- cant Innocentii III. e Syr. 17, 26. sententiam, a mortuo perit confessio. Unde potius concludendum est, nullum esse statum intermedium inter mortem temporalem & salutem vel damnationem æternam.

## 6:7
Verse 8.

MY EYE IS TROUBLED BY REASON OF FURY) It has wasted away. Aquila [uses] ἠχλύωδη here. Thus also below 31, 11. The Hebrew word is taken, and is translated in the same way by Aquila.

I HAVE GROWN OLD AMONG ALL MY ENEMIES) In the Hebrew, sennit, namely the eye or the countenance.

It is credible to Bellarmine that the Hebrew reading has been changed, because in the word עתקה the Jod at the end has fallen out, and a ו has crept in in place of a ה, and the sense is that he has grown old (in his vices) among all his enemies, whether demons or men. But that sense is very twisted. For in the Hebrew all things are plain: Because of my oppressors my eye has grown old, and my face, having lost its pristine redness, has contracted wrinkles and old age, Prov. 17, 23. Thus this word also corresponds to the preceding one, which likewise is of the third person.

INVETERAVI INTER OMNES INIMICOS MEOS) In Hebræo, sennit, nempe oculus sive vultus.

Bellarmino credibile est Ebraicam lectionem immutatam esse, quod in voce עתקה Jod in fine exciderit, & ו loco ה irrepserit, ac sensus sit, quod consenuserit (in vitiis suis) inter omnes hostes suos, sive Dæmones, sive homines. Sed sensus ille val- de contortus est. In Ebræo enim plana sunt omnia: Propter oppressores meos consenuit oculus meus, ac facies mea amisso rubore pristino rugas, & senium contraxit, Prov. 17, 23. Sic respondet quoque hoc verbum præcedenti, quod itidem est tertiæ per- sonæ.

PRO VERBIS CHVSI FILII JEMINI) Melius: ob ver- ba, minacia scilicet. Chusus videtur fuisse aliquis ducum Saulis, cui mandatum fuit datum persequendi Davidis. Filii Iemini, id est, è tribu Benjaminis, ut 1. Sam. 22, 7.

## 7:3
Verse 4.

IF I HAVE DONE THIS) Which Saul's companions reproach me for. See 1 Sam. 24:10, ch. 25:10.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SI FECI ISTVD) Quod Saulis comites mihi expro- brant. Vide 1. Sam. 24, 10. c. 25, 10.

## 7:4
Verse 5.

IF I HAVE RENDERED TO THOSE REPAYING ME EVIL) Best thus: If I have rendered evil to him who had done it to me. For שלם in the sense of doing you may find in Isaiah 44:26, and thus the interpreters the Syrian and the Arab have taken it here.

Verse of the same.

MAY I FALL DESERVEDLY BY MY ENEMIES EMPTY) More correctly thus: And I oppressed him who was hostile to me without cause. For חלץ sometimes signifies to oppress, and thus the LXX in Job 36:15 translated חלץ עני as ἐξείλετο ἀσθενῆ. Nor did the Syrian take it otherwise here. The same sense was held by the changed guttural עלץ. And perhaps once it was written here ואלצה. It refers to the history which is in 1 Sam. 24 and 26.

He saw well that the Vulgate cannot be defended here, therefore he corrected the same. For what is this: May I fall deservedly by my enemies empty? And how can the verb חלץ be translated, I fall? Or the adverb ריקם be converted into a noun? But there is no need for that suspicion of a different reading ואלצה, because עלץ also means he oppressed. Although this verb can also be translated, to rescue: in this way: so far am I from having brought evil upon one who was at peace with me, that I even rescued him who was oppressing me without cause. For that verb signifies, as R. Nathan also notes, הצילה liberation.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

SI REDDIDI RETRIBUENTIBVS MIHI MALA) Optime sic: Si malum reddidi ei, qui mihi fecerat. Nam שלם sensu faciendi reperias apud Esaiam 44, 26. & ita hic cepere interpretes Syrus & Arabs.

Vers. eod.

DECIDAM MERITO AB INIMICIS MEIS INA- NIS) Rectius sic: Et oppressi eum, qui mihi infestus erat sine causa. Nam חלץ interdum significat opprimere, & ita LXX. Job. 36, 15. חלץ עני verterunt ἐξείλετο ἀσθενῆ. Neque ali- ter hic accepit Syrus. Eundem sensum habebat mutata gut- turali עלץ. Et forte olim hic scriptum fuerit ואלצה. Re- spicit historiam quæ est 1. Sam. 24. & 26.

VIdit probe vulgatum hic defendi non posse, ideo correxit eundem. Quid enim hoc est: Decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis? Et quo- modo verbum חלץ verti potest, decidit? aut ad- verbium ריקם converti in nomen? Non opus autem est ista suspicione diversæ lectionis ואלצה, quia עלץ etiam est oppressit. Quanquam hoc verbum etiam verti queat, eripere: hoc modo: tantum abest ut intulerim malum colenti pacem mecum, ut etiam eum qui me sine causa opprimebat, eripuerim. Significat enim verbum illud, notante R. Nathan etiam הצילה liberationem.

## 7:7
Verse 8.

AND ARISE O LORD MY GOD) He reads here אלי with a chirek, not with a patach under the lamed. The Greeks also read it thus: for they translate ἐξεγέρθητι κύριε Θεός μου. Nor did the Syrian or the Arab otherwise.

The Hebrew reading אלי fits the text well: Awake UNTO ME for judgment, or in the judgment which you have commanded. There is no need, therefore, that it be read: Awake O my God. Nor should the defect of the original text be concluded from the oversight of one interpreter, whom some others have followed. And whence that LORD? Did the interpreter also read יחוח in his text, which then fell out? If the Hebrew text is to be amended from the Latin interpretation, especially in the Psalms, it must be said that it teems with countless errors. Bellarmine himself confessed a little earlier that Jerome, who without doubt faithfully interpreted the Hebrew reading, almost everywhere differs from the Vulgate: in this very Psalm and present verse, when the Vulgate ought to have rendered, Lift yourself up against the indignations of those who straiten me, it rendered: Be exalted in the borders of my enemies: which therefore D. Tarnovius corrects here. Soon verse 12 exhibits a clearly contrary sense, with the addition of those words which do not appear in the archetype, which is not the part of an interpreter; God is a just judge, strong and patient, he is not angry every day. For in the Hebrew it is held thus, God is a just Judge, and God, who is angry daily. Bellarmine, to excuse the Vulgate, says that he read אל instead of אל, but he only betrays his ignorance: because אל is never constructed in the Holy tongue with a participle, but always with the future, and indeed then, when we are dissuading or deprecating.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET EXVRGE DOMINE DEVS MEVS) Legit hic אלי cum chirek, non cum patach sub lamed. Græci quoque sic legerunt: vertunt enim ἐξεγέρθητι κύριε Θεός με. Ne- aliter aut Syrus, aut Arabs.

Lectio Ebræa אלי textui probe congruit Evigila AD ME ad judicium, vel in judicio quod præcepisti. Non opus ergo, ut legatur: Evigil Deus meus. Neque ex παροράματι interpreti unius, quem secuti sunt alii nonnulli, vitium textus originalis concludendum. Et unde illud DOMI- NE? Num legit etiam interpres יחוח in suo tex- tu, quod deinde exciderit? Si ex interpretatione Latina, in Psalmis cumprimis, emendandus Ebræus textus, innumeris ipsum scatere erroribus dicen- dum erit. Ubique fere a vulgata discrepare Hiero- nymum, qui sine dubio fideliter interpretatus est lectionem Ebræam, paulo ante ipse Bellarminus fassus est: in hoc ipso Psalmo ac versu præsenti, quum reddere vulgata debuisset, Extolle te contra indignationes angustiantium me, reddidit: Exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum: quam proinde hic corrigit D. Tarnovius. Mox vers. 12. sensum plane contrarium exhibet, additis iis vocibus, quæ in ἀρχετύπῳ non comparent, quod non est interpre- tis; Deus judex justus, fortis & patiens, nunquam irascitur per singulos dies.
