In Ebræo enim ita ha- betur, Deus est justus Judex, & Deus, qui irascitur quotidie. Bellarm. ut excuset vulgatam, legisse אל pro אל ait, sed inscitiam tantum prodit: quia אל nunquam in lingua Sancta construitur cum Be- noni, sed semper cum futuro, & quidem tum, cum de- hortamur vel deprecamur.

## 7:8 Addition
On Psalm 7. v. 9. JUDGE ME O LORD ACCORDING TO MY RIGHTEOUSNESS,

It is not a discourse concerning the habitual righteousness of the person, as most Papists wish, but concerning the righteousness of a special cause, which David conducted with his slanderer, as Lorinus taught here, responding to Jerome and Chrysostom, who similarly abused this saying, as did the Pelagians.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 7. v. 9. JUDICA ME DOMINE SECUNDUM JUSTITIAM MEAM,

Non de justitia habituali personæ, ut Papistæ plerique volunt, sed de justitia causæ specialis sermo est, quam David cum calumniatore suo egit, ut Lo- rinus hic ex Hieronym. & Chrysost. Pelagianis, qui similiter abusi hoc dicto sunt, respondentibus, do- cuit.

## 7:10
Verse 11.

JUST IS MY HELP FROM THE LORD) From the Greek as almost everything in this version: for Jerome made another from the Hebrew, but that was not received into the Churches: δικαία ἡ βοήθεια μου παρὰ τῶ Θεοῦ. The Greeks transferred that 'just' here, when now in the Hebrew the preceding clause ends. The Syrian and the Arab also interpret מגני as my help. Therefore עבד which follows is for עלי, as also below 22:10 and elsewhere.

If in all places where the Vulgate has departed from the Hebrew, it is permitted to suspect a corruption of our Hebrew text, what then will be free from corruption? For Grotius himself now admits that almost ALL things were taken from the Greek in this version, and thus differ from the Hebrew, just as the Hebrew text also had it in the time of Jerome. But the matter is well: Grotius acknowledges that the Vulgate must not rarely be corrected in many places, and he himself corrects it, especially in the Psalms: as in this Psalm, verse 1. FOR THE WORDS OF CHUSI (better, he says, because of the words. And at verse 5. If I have rendered to those repaying me evils) best thus, if I have rendered evil to him who had done to me. I SHALL FALL DESERVEDLY BY MY ENEMIES IN VAIN. More correctly thus: & I oppressed him who was hostile to me without cause. And verse 15. BEHOLD HE HATH TRAVAILED WITH INJUSTICE, HE HATH CONCEIVED SORROW AND HATH BROUGHT FORTH INIQUITY. Better, Lo, he is in labor with vanity & he has conceived trouble & will bring forth empty things. All that labor will lack success. See. Job 15:35. Such are the emendations of the Vulgate in most of the Psalms that Grotius has instituted. What reason is there, therefore, why he should dream and suspect corruptions of the Hebrew text in other places of the Psalms? The Latin Vulgate was not made from the pure Greek text of the LXX interpreters; which we previously observed from Bellarmine, but from a certain common Greek text, concerning which Jerome writes in his Epistle to Sunia and Fretela at the beginning: Know that there is one edition, which Origen and Eusebius of Caesarea, and all Greek commentators call κοινή, that is, common, and vulgate, and by most it is now called Lucian's, and another of the seventy interpreters, which is found in the hexaplar codices. Therefore, the book of Psalms was not translated by Jerome, who was skilled in the Hebrew language, but by some other person: nor did it flow from the fountain of Hebrew truth, but was translated from the impure stream of the Greek version far more impurely: so that Whitaker rightly judged it could be said, contr. 1. on Scripture, chapter 6. that these are not the Davidic Psalms which the Papists in their sacred services frequently read and sing, but the errors of the Greek and Latin interpreter. Moreover, the barbarity of the translation renders them even more horrible: for such [barbarity] is detected in the Psalms, that they seem to have been turned into a reproach of the Latin language on purpose, as after our blessed Hunnius and Whitaker, Chamier shows, Tom. 1. Panstrat. 69. cap. 12. num. 12. See what we have observed in the Critico Sacro, page 606. That the Syrian and Arab followed the Vulgate is nothing against the genuineness of the Hebrew text: that they made a translation from the Hebrew or looked to the Hebrew text everywhere, as is proper, has not yet been proven. For it often happens that those who compare translations with the original text follow them in certain things, and depart from the former, whether led by their own judgment or perhaps doing something else. Let it therefore suffice to have observed these things here once. And why is the Chaldean, who translated from the Hebrew, not brought forward? Why is the reading of the same held in addition, and postponed to the more recent ones themselves? That just help must be referred to the preceding substantive, JUST GOD, not to the first word of the following verse: For among the Hebrews the adjective is always postponed to its substantive: מָגִנִּי is my shield: but not my help. My shield, that is, my protection and my defense is in God, or if you prefer, from God. There is absolutely no reason for correcting the Hebrew reading.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

JVSTVM ADJVTORIVM MEVM EST DOMINVS) Ex Græco ut prope omnia in hac versione: nam aliam ex Hebræo fecit Hieronymus, sed ea in Ecclesias recepta non est: δικαία ἡ βοήθεια με παρὰ τῶ Θεοῦ. Illud justum huc tran- stulere Græci, cum nunc in Hebræo comma præcedens fini- at. מגני adjutorium meum etiam Syrus & Arabs interpre- tantur. Ergo עבד quod sequitur est pro עלי, ut & infra 22, 10. & alibi.

Si in omnibus locis, quibus ab Ebræo abiit vulgatus, suspicari liceat corruptelam nostri Ebræi textus, quid tandem a corruptela liberum erit? Nam prope OMNIA a Græco in hac versione tran- sumta jam fatetur ipse Grotius, adeoque differre ab Ebræo, prout etiam Ebræus textus tempore Hieronymi habuit. Sed bene res habet: agnoscit Grotius haud raro corrigendum esse in multis vulgatum, eumque ipse corrigit, maxime in Psalmis: uti in hoc Psalmo vers. 1. PRO VERBIS CHUSI (melius, ait, ob verba. Et ad vers. 5. Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala) optime sic, si malum red- didi ei, qui mihi fecerat. DECIDAM MERITO AB INIMICIS MEIS INANIS. Rectius sic: & oppressi eum, qui mihi infestus erat sine causa. Et vers. 15. ECCE PARTURIIT INJUSTITIAM, CONCEPIT DOLOREM ET PEPERIT INI- QUITATEM. Melius, En parturit vanitatem & concepit enim molestiam & pariet inania. Successu carebit omnis ille labor. Vid. Job. 15, 35. Tales vulgatæ emendationes in Psalmis plerisque insti- tuit Grotius. Quid ergo causæ est, quod somniet ac suspicetur, in aliis Psalmorum locis, corrupte- las textus Hebraici? Non e Græco puro LXX. Interpp. textu facta est vulgata Latina; quod antea observavimus e Bellarmino, sed ex vulgato quo- dam Græco, quo de Hieronymus Epistola ad Suniam & Fretell. initio: Sciatis aliam esse editionem, quam Origenes & Cæsariensis Eusebius, omnesque Græci tractatores κοινὴν, id est, communem appellant, at- que vulgatam, & a plerisque nunc λυκιανός dicitur, alia septuaginta interpretum, quæ in ἑξαπλοῖς co- dicibus reperitur. Non ergo versus est Psalmorum liber ab Hieronymo Ebraicæ linguæ perito, sed ab alio quopiam: nec e fonte profluxit Ebraicæ veritatis, sed a rivo impuro Græcæ versionis traductus est longe impurius: ut vere dici posse censuerit Witakerus contr. 1. de Script. cap. 6. non esse hos Davidicos Psalmos, quos Papistæ in suis sa- cris lectitant atque cantitant, sed Græci Latinique interpretis errores. Quos insuper horridiores red- dit translationis barbaries: Ea quippe tanta in Psal- mis deprehenditur, ut illi videantur data opera versi in contumeliam Latini sermonis, ut post B. Hunnium nostrum & Witakerum, ostendit Cha- mier Tom. 1. Panstrat. 69. cap. 12. num. 12. Vide quæ observavimus in Critico Sacro pag. 606. Quod Syrus & Arabs sequuti sunt vulgatam, nihil contra γνησιότητα Ebræi textus: quos ex Ebræo translatio- nem fecisse aut Ebræum textum ubivis, ut par est, respexisse, nondum probatum est. Nam sæpe sit, ut qui conferunt cum textu originali translatio- nes, has in quibusdam sequantur, & ab illo abeant, seu judicio suo ducti, seu aliud forte agentes. Hæc ergo semel hic observasse sufficiat. Et cur non Chaldæus, qui ex Ebræo traduxit, adducitur? Cur ejusdem lectio insuper habetur, ac recentio- ribus ipsis postponitur? Illud justum adjutorium ad præcedens substantivum DEUS JUSTE, non ad sequentis versiculi primam vocem referendum est: Apud Ebræos enim adjectivum semper postpo- nitur suo substantivo: מָגִנִּי est clypeus meus : non au- tem adjutorium meum. Clypeus meus, id est, pro- tectio & defensio mea est in Deo, vel si malis, a Deo. Nulla omnino causa est corrigendi Ebræam le- ctionem.

## 7:11 Addition
v. 12. WILL HE BE ANGRY EVERY DAY.

In the Hebrew the sense is contrary, which the LXX, Jerome, and Chrysostom, just as the blessed Luther, render: and the context demands it; because it is a matter of the perpetual judgment of God against the slanderer, not of grace.

At the end of the eighth Psalm.

The blessed Hülsemann thinks the diminution by the angels should be explained by a voluntary privation, or subtraction of angelic ministry, concerning which see Matt. 4:11, ch. 26:63, Luke 22:43, because the Hebrew word in Piel in Eccles. 4:8, in which unique place it is still found, is used concerning privation, which is rendered ἐλαττονέω in Gen. 8:3, 5, where it concerns the privation or subtraction of the waters of the flood, which word the Apostle used in Heb. 2:7. Cocceius's paraphrase in the final words of Moses §. 1044 is perverse, and joined with a multiple sense of the word Elohim, and not consistent with orthodoxy: 'Lesser (by the state of emptying, not nature) than the Father, who had sent him. Lesser than the angels, to whom he was subjected, insofar as the law was given through angels; lesser than the princes, who are also called Gods, by whom he was also condemned in judgment.'

Latin:

vers. 12. NUMQUID IRASCETUR PER SINGU- LOS DIES.

In Ebr. contrarius est sensus, quem LXX. Hieronymus & Chrysostomus æque uti B. Lutherus reddunt: eumque poscit συνέχεια; quia agitur de judicio Dei perpetuo adversus calumniato- rem, non de gratia.

Ad finem Psalmi octavi.

B. Hülsemannus diminutionem ab Angelis de voluntaria privatione, seu subtractione ministerii an- gelici explicandam censet, de qua Matth. 4, 11. cap. 26, 63. Luc. 22, 43. quia verbum Ebræum in Piel Ec- cles. 4, 8. in quo unico adhuc loco reperitur, de pri- vatione adhibetur, quod ἐλαττονέω redditur Genes. 8, 3. 5. ubi de privatione vel subtractione aquarum diluvii agitur, quâ voce usus est Apostolus Ebr. 2, 7. Perversa, & cum multiplici sensu vocis Elo- him conjuncta, nec orthodoxiæ congrua est Coc- ceji in ultimis verbis Mosis §. 1044. Paraphrasis, Minor (statu exinanitionis, non natura) Patre, qui ipsum miserat. Minor Angelis, quibus subactus fuit, quatenus legi per angelos latæ; Minor principi- bus, qui etiam Dii appellantur, a quibus & judicio damnatus fuit.

## 7:14
Vers. 15. BEHOLD HE HATH TRAVAILED WITH INJUSTICE: HE HATH CONCEIVED SORROW AND HATH BROUGHT FORTH INIQUITY) Better: Behold he is in labor with vanity, for he has conceived trouble and will bring forth empty things. All that labor will lack success. See Job 15, 35.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ECCE PARTVRIIT INJVSTITIAM: CONCEPIT DOLOREM ET PEPERIT INIQVITATEM) Melius : En parturit vanitatem, concepit enim molestiam & pariet ina- nia. Successu carebit omnis ille labor. Vid. Job. 15, 35.

## 8:1 Argument
PSALM VIII. A prophecy concerning the emptying and exaltation of Christ.

Vers. 1. FOR THE WINEPRESSES) To be sung in the time of the vintage. But the Chaldean thinks that גִּתִּיתָא is a musical instrument, taken from the Philistines, whose city is Gath.

Thus it not obscurely supports the Chaldean, whose opinion also seems more convenient. Because in the Hebrew there is not עַל־הַגִּתּוֹת which denotes winepresses, but עַל־הַגִּתִּית whence, as in a similar construction after the word לַמְנַצֵּחַ a musical instrument is accustomed to be noted, it is likely that such a thing is also designated here. In the annotations to Heb. 2, 6, however, Grotius clings to the Vulgate, and observes that this Psalm was accustomed to be sung with joy in the vintages, which without doubt is for the sake of a preconceived opinion; as if in the literal sense there were talk here of Adam and his descendants, and those things which God bestowed upon them: but if it be rendered for the winepresses, blessed Luther teaches from Augustine, Tom. 2. Jenens. Lat. in this Psalm, that the ministry of the word concerning the passion and exaltation of Christ is conveniently understood. Who can be compared concerning this with blessed Gesner in this place. Nor indeed do we judge it worth the effort to cling to the diverse explanations of the Greek and Latin interpretation, inasmuch as it is erroneous, since all Hebrew codices agree here, and likewise read Psalm 81 and 84 עַל־הַגִּתִּית; whence those among the Papists who contend here that the Vulgate is more corrected are not to be heard: upon whom Polanus pours cold water in De legend. autor. fol. 328. We approve the Vulgate version in this place, with which the Greek agrees, which has ὑπὲρ τῶν ληνῶν. Whence the festivals were called Lenan by the Greeks. Those things which are brought forward by most concerning this inscription for the winepresses are certainly foreign, such as that this Psalm was sung in honor of God at the feast of tabernacles at the time of the vintage, as it seemed to Agellius and Bellarmine; or that the mysteries of the passion of Christ, whose blood was expressed as if in winepresses, are described, concerning which see Ambrose in Luke 8, Arnobius in this place. Jerome in Isaiah 10, or it is said for the winepresses because the Psalms are apt for expressing the wine of divine love from the hearts of men, as Bellarmine explains, or so that the passions of the martyrs are understood, as Remigius, Ludolphus, Titelmannus and others. For all those things are nothing to the purpose. But because the sum of the proclamation of the Evangelical ministry is contained here, this opinion does not fit badly, which through the winepress, with the Fathers Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Basil, Theodoret, Augustine, Eutychius, understands the ministry of the word in the vineyard of the Church, through which is expressed the most sweet doctrine gladdening the hearts of the faithful and inebriating them with the sweetness of heavenly goods, as Lindanus has in this place. Otherwise, these things do not agree with the Hebrew word. Which therefore others take as a patronymic, as if the Gittite people were designated, and the victory over Goliath, who was a Gittite, won by David were being sung, which argument William makes for the Psalm. Scepsius among Lorinus, and Maldonatus in Matthew 21, who says that David called himself an infant and a suckling through humility, from whose mouth, giving thanks for the defeated Goliath, God would have obtained great praise. But they were totally mistaken. For here it is sung of praise resounding through the whole earth, and not of David, but of Christ established over all the works of the hands of the Lord. Junius conjectures that the Gittite station of the ark of the covenant is looked to, and that the hymn was written at that time; but that is a too contorted exposition, which no one would have attained from that single word. Genebrardus understands a certain kind and manner of singing through the word Gitith, but does not know how to explain it: and therefore the more common opinion concerning a musical instrument, which had its origin in Gath of the Philistines, is deservedly retained, with Calvin clamoring in vain: if indeed in Jewish Antiquities more reliable faith is applied to the Chaldean Paraphrast, and when the word Lamnazeab, by means of the preposition על, is constructed with this word, and the noun מזמור follows, the sense will hardly be rendered more conveniently than in this way: To the victor (the one in charge of other musical matters) upon the Gittite instrument (whatever that may eventually have been) the present Psalm (or Song) of David is committed. Whence rightly blessed Luther: A Psalm of David to be sung on the Githith. And so also Osiander, the Vinariean Paraphrasts, Tarnovius; and from the Reformed, Musculus and Mollerus; then from the Papists also Lyranus, Eugubinus, Burgensis, Cajetanus, Vatablus, Eman. Saa, Lorinus and others. Franc. Lucas Burgensis reconciles both expositions according to the Hebrew and Greek text in this manner, that that musical instrument exhibited the form of a winepress. But whence he has that, it is not clear.

Latin:

PSALMUS VIII. Vaticinium de exinanitione, & exaltatione Christi.

Vers. 1. PRO TORCVLARIBVS) In tempore vindemiæ cantan- dum. Sed Chaldæus existimat גִּתִּיתָא esse instrumentum mu- sicum, petitum a Philistinis, quorum urbs Geth.

ITa non obscure suffragatur Chaldæo, cujus etiam sententia convenientior videtur. Quia in Ebræo non habetur עַל־הַגִּתּוֹת quod torcularia notat, sed עַל־הַגִּתִּית unde ut in simili constructione post vo- cem לַמְנַצֵּחַ instrumentum musicum notari solet, ta- le etiam hic designari verisimile est. In annotatis tamen ad Ebr. 2, 6. vulgatæ adhærescit Grotius, & observat, cantari solitum hunc Psalmum cum gau- dio in videmiis, quod sine dubio in gratiam præ- conceptæ opinionis sit; ac si sensu literali hic de Adamo & posteris ejus, & iis quæ Deus illis contu- lit, sermo esset: sed si reddatur pro torcularibus B. Lutherus ex Augustino docet Tom. 2. Jenens. Lat. in h. Psal. commode intelligi ministerium verbi de Christi passione & exaltatione. Qui de eo conferri poterit, cum B. Gesnero in h. l. Neque vero operæ precium judicamus inhærere diversis explicationi- bus interpretationis Græcæ & Latinæ, utpote quæ erronea est, quum omnes Ebræi Codd. hic consentiant, ac pariter Psalm. 81. & 84. עַל־הַגִּתִּית legant; unde audiendi non sunt, qui e Papistis hic vulgatam emendatiorem esse contendunt: quibus frigidam suffundit Polanus de legend. autor. fol. 328. Nos probamus h. l. vulgatam versionem, cum qua consentit Græca, quæ habet ὑπὲρ τῶν ληνῶν. unde Græcis dicta sunt Lenan festa. Aliena utique sunt, quæ de hac inscriptione pro torcularibus a pleris- que adferuntur, utpote quod Psalmus hic in festo tabernaculorum vindemiæ tempore in honorem Dei decantatus sit, uti Agellio & Bellarmino vi- fum; vel quod mysteria passionis Christi, cujus san- guis velut in torcularibus expressus, describantur, quo de vid. Ambros. in Luc. 8. Arnob. in h. l. Hie- ron. in Esa. 10. vel pro torcularibus dici, quod apti sint Psalmi ad exprimendum vinum divini amo- ris ex cordibus hominum, ut Bellarm. explicat, vel ut intelligantur passiones martyrum, ut Remigius, Ludolphus, Titelmannus & alii. Nam illa omnia ὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπη. Quia vero summa præconii mi- nisterii Evangelici hic continetur, sententia hæc non male congruit, quæ per torcular cum Patribus Origene, Eusebio, Athanasio, Basilio, Theodoreto, Augustino, Eutychio, ministerium verbi in vinea Ecclesiæ intelligit, per quod exprimitur doctrina svavissima corda fidelium lætificans & cælestium bonorum dulcedine inebrians, ut Lindanus in h. l. habet. Cæterum verbo Ebræo hæc non con- gruunt. Quod proinde alii ut Patronymicum ac- cipiunt, quasi populus Gethicus designaretur, & victoria de Goliatho, qui Githæus erat, a Davi- de reportata decantaretur, quod argumentum Psalmi facit Guilhel. Scepsius apud Lorinum, & Maldonatus in Matth. 21. qui Davidem ait, se per ταπείνωσιν infantem ac lactentem appellasse, ex cu- jus ore gratias pro devicto Goliath agentis, ma- gnam Deus laudem consequutus esset. Sed illi toto erant cælo. Nam hic de laude per univer- sam terram personante, nec de Davide, sed de Christo super omnia opera manuum Domini con- stituto canitur. Stationem Githæam arcæ fœderis respici, eoque tempore scriptum hymnum con- jectat Junius; sed nimis contorta ea expositio, quam nemo ex unica voce illa assecuturus erat. Ge- nebrardus certum genus & modum canendi per vocem Gitith intelligit, sed explicare non novit: ideoque merito retinetur sententia communior de instrumento Musico, quod originem in Gith Phili- stæorum habuerit, nequicquam obstrepente Calvi- no: siquidem in Antiquitatibus Judaicis Chaldæo Paraphrastæ tutior adhibeatur fides, ac cum vocem Lamnazeab mediante Præpositione על cum hac voce constructum sequatur nomen מזמור, sen- sus vix commodior reddetur, quam hoc modo: Vincenti (in Musicis cæteris præfecto) super in- strumento Gittæo (quodcunque illud tandem fue- rit) Psalmus (vel Canticum) Davidis præsens com- mittitur. Unde recte B. Lutherus: Ein Psalm Davids vorzusingen auf der Githith. Atque ita etiam Osiander, Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, Tarno- vius; & e Reformatis Musculus, ac Mollerus; tum e Papistis etiam Lyranus, Eugubinus, Burgensis, Cajetanus, Vatablus, Eman. Saa, Lorinus aliique. Conciliat utramque expositionem juxta Ebræum & Græcum textum Franc. Lucas Burgens. hoc pa- cto, quod instrumentum illud Musicum formam torcularis exhibuerit. Sed unde id habeat, non liquet.

## 8:2
Vers. 3.

OUT OF THE MOUTHS OF BABES AND SUCKLINGS THOU HAST PERFECTED PRAISE) From the wonderful structure of the breasts for nourishing infants with that food to which they were accustomed in the womb, which breasts infants draw upon without any teacher, for whom this is the beginning of 5οργῆς.

A wonderful gloss! The mouth of babes and sucklings is established by David as the efficient cause of divine praise: as the explicit words have it. For out of their mouth God perfects praise for Himself, by whom He Himself is praised and celebrated. And thus all, so far as I know, if you depart from the Judaizing Calvin, have hitherto understood it, Christian interpreters: nay, Christ Himself so understood it, Matt. 21, 16. Grotius on the contrary makes infants and sucklings the object, matter, argument, or reason for divine praises: not that infants celebrate God with their own mouth, but that others take from thence a cause for celebrating God, that they draw the breasts themselves without a Master, and that the breasts are wonderfully constituted for nourishing infants. In the sacred text there is nothing about breasts, nothing about their wonderful structure, nothing about the fact that infants have been accustomed to the nourishment of the breasts in the womb, nothing about the fact that they draw without any Master: he forces all these things upon the text. So that one ought to admire not an interpretation, but a remarkable στρεβλότητα and distortion. But if that man wished to be subtle in other matters, he certainly ought not to have exercised a versatile wit upon the sacred text. Moreover, he seems to be doing this very bad service to the Pelagians, Anabaptists, and Photinians, with whom he denies faith and the fruits of faith to infants; since the text clearly constitutes infants as heralds of divine praises, and it was declared by Christ concerning the boys singing Hosanna. Although many, and not wrongly in our judgment, wish to be understood by little ones and sucklings not only those who are such in years, but also those who are such in character, just as analogous names are wont to lead us to other things to which they are analogous: and that when one species is named, the others are understood together: Matt. 18:3, Mark 10:15, in simplicity similar to little children, but in minds adults and perfect, 1 Cor. 14:20, such as were the Apostles, Matt. 11:25, and whoever have allowed themselves to be given to drink, in the manner of infants, with the milk of the word, 1 Cor. 3:1, 1. Pet. 2:2, whence they observe that both the principal and instrumental cause, in the manifestation of the Gospel, is designated here. To which, in their own way, also pertained those who were shouting Hosanna. For they are called in Luke 19:37, 39, disciples of Christ: All the multitude of the Disciples began rejoicing to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen, saying: Blessed, etc. Therefore the Pharisees said to him: Master, rebuke your Disciples. To whom he himself said: If these should be silent, the stones will cry out. It is certain that they themselves were instruments of the divine praise to be propagated, which God is accustomed to confirm and propagate not only through ordinary ministers, but also extraordinarily through others. Thus, therefore, if infants as to years are understood in the Psalm, it is not undeservedly applied to those who were similar to infants: but if the Psalmist also metaphorically understands infants as to character, who are similar to children in simplicity, they are certainly included in those words among the heralds of God, or they themselves are supposed to be such, properly called infants: since others ought to become similar to them: such as this Prophet also foresaw and predicted that these future heralds would be, who would receive the Messiah. In Hebrew it is יסדת עז which in Matt. 21:16 is rendered κατηρτίσω αἶνον: because עז denotes not only strength, but also praise and glory, Ps. 118:14, and 29:1, and 96:7, Exod. 15:2, and that glory of God, which is due to Him on account of the redemption of Christ and the revelation of the Gospel, exhibits the infinite strength and power of God, which shines forth most in that matter and is manifested to the world. God therefore founded strength, and prepared for Himself praise and glory, when He sent His Son, and took care for that to be announced to the world, concerning which this Psalm prophesies, with Christ Himself as the undoubted interpreter. Grotius, however, also wished to gratify the Jews: who explain the present Psalm only concerning the natural works of God, against the aforementioned interpretation of Christ, which ought to be sacrosanct to all Christians. For he does not have that subtlety about the breasts from his own wit, but from Rabbinical ineptitudes, especially R. David Kimchi. Which, so that those who are accustomed to venerate the monstrous Grotian commentaries may admire them, it is helpful to bring forward: Out of the mouth of sucklings and infants; the beginning, he says, of the wonders in man, after he comes into the world, is in sucking, and just as man praises God on account of His works in heaven and on earth; so in his own body: therefore he says, you have founded strength, for just as the foundation of a building is the beginning, so sucking is the beginning of divine mercy, which made a hole in the udder, like a thin thread, not too wide, lest the milk should be dispersed without fruit, and lest too much should come at once; not too narrow, lest the lips of the infant should be burdened in sucking, and furthermore God placed the udders for man, IN THE PLACE OF INTELLIGENCE (The Rabbis have wisdom and intelligence in the breasts, not in the mind, or to speak more correctly, they carry it in the heel.) And not as in the rest of the creatures, therefore he says: you have founded strength; to show that all things come through divine strength, and not by chance, as the atheists, enemies of God, maintain, of whom he says, and he made the enemy and the avenger to be silent. You have founded strength. Since gradually after the speech of the mind the strength of the boy increases more and more. These are the Rabbinical mysteries, truly worthy of the applause of Grotius. Like lips have like lettuces. It is a wonder why he did not also add the rest from R. Kimchi and other Hebrews of similar bran: such as that which he says to the words; the works of your hands: Inferior and superior creatures also: up to this point he rules over them (man) because he understands the motions of the stars. To verse 9, who walk the paths of the sea (where the discourse is about fish) R. Kimchi notes that it concerns man, who through prudence passes through the seas in ships. To the words, the work of your hands, R. Aben-Ezra adds these things: The fingers are ten, and the spheres are ten, and therefore he says, the work of the fingers, in the manner of men: because it is known that the two great lights, and the five planets have seven mansions, and the eighth is on account of the great army of stars having motion from the East to the West, and the ninth is the starry heaven, and the tenth is the throne of glory. The author of Midrash Tillim is so inept: What is man (Abraham?) And the son of man? Isaac: You have made him a little lower than the Angels (Jacob Gen. 32. Hos. 12. where the exact opposite is held) You have crowned (Moses with the glory of a shining face,) you have given dominion (to Joshua, who had the dominion of the Sun.) under his feet (David Ps. 18. like the dust of the earth) Beasts of the field (like Daniel in the den of Lions) Birds of the heavens (Ravens fed Elijah) Fish of the sea (Jonah was in the bowels of the Leviathan) Passing through the paths of the sea (the Israelites in the Red Sea.) R. Solomon on that: A little lower than the Angels: he has it thus: Joshua the son of Nun was lower than Moses, who was called the God of Pharaoh, and Joshua had subjugated the whole land of Canaan, under his feet, sheep, oxen, &c. and Moses dried up the Red Sea, and Elijah raised the dead of the woman of Zarephath and the Shunammite, by which miracles they were a little lower than the Angels. But I have done with Rabbinical absurdities. From these masters, therefore, what sound thing can you expect? One must marvel at Rivet, that, captivated by the love of the trifles of his Calvin, he not only gave assent to those Jewish fictions here, but also labors to reconcile them with the citation of those words, out of the mouth of infants &c. made by Christ: But by what artifice will he reconcile things so disparate, nay, entirely contrary? For Christ, Matt. 21:16, applies them to the celebration which is made by the mouth of infants, effectively singing the praise of the Lord, or glorifying God: But Rivet, with the Rabbis, says that it is done not by infants, but by others, yet on account of the infants, when they see them sucking their mothers' milk, admiring the providence of God. Doubtless he thinks that Christ only accommodated the words of David in this way; as if he were arguing from a similar or equal case: If you ought to acknowledge the providence of God in the fact that he perfects his praise out of the mouth of babes, insofar as he wonderfully nourishes and protects them: Ought you not also to acknowledge the same providence from the fact that he causes his praise to be celebrated out of the mouth of these children and simple men in the keeping of the promises concerning the coming Messiah? But by what obscure indication did such an argumentation become known to Rivet: of which there is certainly neither a trace nor a footprint in Matthew? But then, could not any saying of the Old Testament be seized upon that testifies to divine providence, and be opposed to the Jews by a like reasoning, if that opposition has any weight? But who does not see that this is thus assumed as certain, which was by no means conceded by the Jews? Doubtless that was not in doubt, nor did it need any proof, let alone one so obscure and far-fetched, that it is a work of the providence of God if the Messiah or the promise concerning the Messiah is celebrated by simple people with a fulfilled eulogy: But that this reception and celebration of Christ had been specifically foretold by God, and that among other proofs the Messiah ought also to be recognized by the fact that he was to be received in such a way, that indeed had to be proved from the Scriptures, so that the mouths of the clamoring Jews might be stopped. Therefore Christ goes to prove that from the Davidic prediction. The objection of the adversaries teaches that. For it was not only a question of the fact that children or simple people were crying out, but also of what they were crying out, not only about the persons, but about the object of the acclamation, namely that they were singing Hosanna to the son of David. They were indignant, says Matthew, and said to him: Do you hear what these are saying? That this, therefore, was foretold by David, or at any rate is entirely consistent with the words of David, Christ teaches in the apology for his praisers: have you never read: Because out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise Matt. 21, 16. Who does not see here that by citing those words Christ proved that it was done rightly and in accordance with the prediction of the sacred psalmist, that he himself, as the Messiah, was received by such people, because, namely, at the time of the coming of the Messiah, and of the New Testament. God willed to prepare praise for himself specifically out of the mouth of infants, indeed because David had foretold, when he was about to deal with the emptying of Christ, that the name and glory of the Lord would be celebrated in all the earth, on account of the Messiah being sent, and his glorification and praise prepared especially also out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, a certain specimen of which was produced at the royal entry of Christ by children shouting Hosanna, which he defends by this Davidic prediction, even as to the manner and form of the words consistent with the prophecies of the Old Testament. Furthermore, if Christ had argued in such a way as Rivet wishes, would this not have been a begging of the question among the Jews, because he would have assumed as certain that he was the promised Messiah, and that the promises concerning the coming Messiah were fulfilled in him, which was by no means conceded by them? But when Christ appeals to the Scriptures, he never assumes that which is in question, but proves it from the Scriptures themselves, and brings forward those passages of the Old Testament which deal with the Messiah, and designate the criteria of the coming Messiah, which they could see or understand were being fulfilled in him: Which therefore was done here also. Besides, what would this have contributed to convincing or refuting the chief priests and scribes, that infants suck milk from breasts, and are thus wonderfully nourished, so that he would oppose this to them above all other words of scripture? Do you hear what these are saying? Have you not read, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, when they suck milk from breasts with their mouth, others take the matter and cause of praising GOD? They make the allegations of the hypostatic wisdom of God himself so inept, those who patronize Rabbinic absurdities! Finally, those things proceed from a false hypothesis, namely that the name of the Lord is celebrated here on account of the works of creation and conservation: Which, however, we have taught is preached on account of the work of redemption performed through Christ, to which he was presenting himself in Matthew 21 at his entry into Jerusalem: Indeed the Apostle himself testifies in Hebrews 2, 6. seq. as we shall show later. And here Rivet contradicts himself: For while he interprets the beginning of the Psalm concerning the glory of God shining forth through the works of creation and conservation: later he says that the glory to be celebrated in all the earth is predicted here, on account of the restoration of man, so that it is placed above the heavens themselves to that place of the blessed, into which Christ ascended, so that he might prepare dwellings for all his own, page 37. Because, namely, the Psalm sings thus; how great is your name in all the earth, you have set your glory above the heavens. In which words the supercelestial glory, which he explained to us in Christ, is regarded, asserts Junius, the predecessor of Rivet at the University of Leiden, in the argument of this Psalm: Rendering the words of verse 2 thus: Jehovah our Lord, how magnificent is your name in all the earth: You who set your supercelestial splendor. And in the notes he has this: The beginning or proposition of the praise is verse 2. Joined with exclamation and admiration; that God exhibits himself as praiseworthy to us, in infinite and supercelestial glory, in Christ Jesus. Not alien to this interpretation as far as the sense is concerned is the opinion of our blessed Tarnovius: who makes this the proposition of the Psalm; your name is magnificent in all the earth, especially in the time of the New Testament; and he says that this reason is annexed to it: because of giving your splendor (which is) above the heavens, or supercelestial, namely to man, that is, because you gave supercelestial glory, or communicated it to the human nature of Christ. He proves that this explanation of the proposition is consistent with the treatment in his Commentary on this Psalm. And the interpretation of the blessed Gesner also tends to this: that namely the meaning of the proposition is this: The proclamation of the Gospel concerning Christ is truly illustrious, magnificent, and stupendous. The magnificence and majesty of our Savior described therein is not only diffused throughout the whole world, but is also elevated above the heavens: which, with Blessed Jerome and Augustine, Blessed Luther interprets concerning the ascension of Christ above all heavens, Operat. on this Psalm, Vol. 2, Jena, fol. 87. I see, he says, that by this glory, or magnificence, or praise of God, almost everyone understands Christ the Son of God, who, having been taken up into heaven and sitting at the right hand of God, sent the Holy Spirit, who through the Apostles magnified the name of God in the whole world. And the opinion of these did not displease me either. The interpretation of others, however, I confess, is simpler: O Lord my God, the fame of your name is spread wonderfully in the whole earth, and your praise reaches even to the heavens, as Brentius explains: who rightly observes that David enunciates this little verse just as if he saw the Apostles before him, going about among the Jews as well as among the Gentiles, and illustrating by their preaching the glory of the name of God made manifest through Christ: Whence the Holy Spirit looks especially to the time when the Apostles carried the Gospel among all nations. So also Osiander: How great is your majesty, which becomes known everywhere in the world through the preaching of the Gospel. Because you have surely handed over the kingdom of heaven and earth to your Son Jesus Christ. You who set forth your praise even to the heavens, that is, your praise reaches from the earth even to the heavens: all things are full of your majesty, nor can anyone praise you worthily enough! It is also explained as meaning that the majesty of God, which the Gospel exhibits, may be preached not only in the whole earth by the faithful, but also in the heavens by the holy Angels themselves and the blessed Phil. 2, 10. Heb. 1, 6. that the earth and heaven, the Church militant and triumphant, may be filled with the praise of the name of God and his glory revealed in the Gospel. Conf. Ap. 5, 9. 12. 13. c. 12, 10. 12. Which interpretation I see is also approved by the blessed Gesner, and it seems here the simplest and most convenient. Whence it is again clear how jejune that Jewish gloss of the Calvinists is concerning the praise of God, which he prepared for himself from the fact that infants suck milk, and are nourished thereby, when far more eminent proofs of divine majesty in the whole earth, nay even in the heavens and in eternal life to be proclaimed, and to be celebrated by angels as well as men, are introduced here by the Psalmist.

Verse of the same.

BECAUSE OF THINE ENEMIES) To destroy, that is, to confound those enemies who deny that God exists, or that he cares for our affairs. The LXX here well: τοῦ καταλῦσαι τὸν ἐχθρόν. The same word Ezech. 30, 10. is translated ἀπολῶ.

AND THE AVENGER) Καὶ ἐκδικητὴν the Greeks, that is, the one who fights for you, as this word is translated in Esther 8, 13. Saul seems to be tacitly signified.

He likewise received this from R. Kimchi. Here therefore God perfects praise for himself out of the mouth of babes because of his enemies, i.e., according to Grotius, he wonderfully prepared breasts for infants, so that from that wonderful structure he might be known and praised to destroy the atheists, who deny God and divine providence. But since there is no doubt that the wisdom and goodness and providence of God shine forth in all the works of God, why should we understand the mouth of infants and the manner of sucking, and the breasts which they suck, to be designated here, so that atheists might be particularly convinced thereby? And how does the following name fit: Because of thine enemies AND THE AVENGER? How are atheists avengers? By this word Saul is tacitly designated, says Grotius. What connection, therefore, is there here, if the preceding words are taken as referring to infants sucking breasts as the object of divine praise? Although it does not appear by what reason Saul is introduced here, or how these things can be applied to Saul through the coherence of the text?

Latin:

Vers. 3.

EX ORE INFANTIVM ET LACTENTIVM PER- FECISTI LAVDEM) Ex mirabili structura mammarum ad alendos infantes eo alimento, cui in utero assveverunt, quas mammas sine ullo magistro attrahunt infantes, quibus id initium est 5οργῆς.

Mirabilis glossa! Infantum & lactentium os causa efficiens laudis divinæ constituitur a Davi- de: uti verba diserta habent. Ex ore enim illius lau- dem perficit sibi Deus, a quo ipse laudatur & cele- bratur. Atque ita omnes, quod sciam, si a Calvi- no Judaizante abeas, hactenus accepere interpretes Christiani: imo ita ipse Christus accepit Matth. 21, 16. Grotius contra infantium & lacten- tium objectum, materiam, argumentum vel ratio- nem facit laudum divinarum: quod non infantes ore suo celebrent Deum, sed quod alii inde Deum celebrandi causam sumant, quod mammas ipsi si- ne Magistro attrahant, quodque mammæ mirabi- liter ad infantes alendos constitutæ sint. In tex- tu sacro nihil de mammis, nihil de earum mirabi- li structura, nihil de eo, quod in utero assveverint alimento mammarum infantes, nihil de eo, quod sine ullo Magistro attrahant: omnia hæc ingerit textui. Ut non interpretationem, sed insignem στρεβλότητα ac detorsionem mirari oporteat. Sed homo ille argutus in aliis si esse voluit, in sacro certe textu versatile ingenium exercere non de- buit. Gratificari autem videtur operam istam pessimam Pelagianis, Anabaptistis & Photinianis, cum quibus infantibus fidem, fructusque fidei de- negat; quum textus luculenter infantes præcones laudum divinarum constituat, ac de pueris Hosian- na decantantibus a Christo declaratus fuerit. Quan- quam per parvulos & lactentes plerique, nec male nostro judicio, velint comprehendi non eos tan- tum, qui tales sunt τὰ ἔτη, sed etiam qui sunt τὰ ἤθη, uti solent nomina analoga ad alia, quibus sunt analoga, nos deducere: & nominata specie analo- ga una comprehendi cæteræ: Matth. 18, 3. Marc. 10, 15. simplicitate puerulis similes, mentibus vero adulti & perfecti 1. Corinth. 14, 20. quales fuere A- postoli Matth. 11, 25. & quicunque lacte verbi, mo- re infantum, se potari & ali passi sunt 1. Corinth. 3, 1. 1. Pet. 2, 2. unde & causam principalem & instru- mentalem, in Evangelii manifestatione, hic de- signari observant. Ad quam suo modo etiam per- tinebant illi, qui Hosianna acclamabant. Dicun- tur enim Luc. 19, 37. 39. discipuli Christi: Cæpe- runt omnes turbæ Discipulorum gaudentes laudare Deum voce magna super omnibus, quas viderant virtutibus, dicentes: Benedictus &c. Ideo Phari- sæi dixere ad illum: Magister increpa Discipulos tuos. Quibus ipse dixit: Si hi tacuerint, lapides clamabunt. Certum est, quod instrumenta ipsi fuerint propagandæ laudis divinæ, quam Deus non modo per ordinarios ministros, sed etiam ex- tra ordinem per alios solet firmare & propagare. Sic ergo si infantes quoad annos in Psalmo intelli- guntur, applicatur is non immerito iis, qui similes erant infantibus: Si vero Psaltes etiam Metapho- rice infantes intelligit τὰ ἤθη, qui simplicitate pue- ris similes sunt, verbis illis comprehenduntur uti- que inter præcones Dei, aut tales esse supponun- tur ipsimet proprie dicti infantes: quum iis cæte- ri similes fieri debeant: quales etiam futuros præ- cones istos, Messiam excepturos, prævidit, & præ- dixit hic Prophetha. In Ebræo est יסדת עז quod Matth. 21, 10. redditur κατηρτίσω αἶνον: quia עז non robur tantum notat, sed & laudem ac gloriam Psal. 118, 14. & 29, 1. & 96, 7. Exod. 15, 2. & glo- ria illa Dei, quæ ipsi debetur ob redemtionem Christi, & revelationem Evangelii, robur & po- tentiam Dei infinitam exhibet, quæ in illa maxime refulget, mundoque manifestatur. Fundavit er- go Deus robur, & paravit sibi laudem atque glo- riam, cum Filium suum misit, idque mundo an- nunciari curavit, de quo hic vaticinatur Psalmus, Christo ipso indubitato interprete. Gratificari autem voluit etiam Judæis Grotius: qui Psalmum præsentem de operibus tantum naturalibus Dei explicant, contra prædictam interpretationem Christi, quæ omnibus Christianis sacrosancta esse deber. Non enim argutiam illam de mammis ex suo habet ingenio, sed ex ineptiis Rabbinicis, cumprimis R. David Kimchi. Quas ut admiren- tur, qui portentosa Grotiana commenta venerari solent, adducere juvat: Ex ore lactentium infan- tum; initium, inquit, mirabilium in homine, post- quam venit in mundum, in sugendo est, & sicut ho- mo Deum laudat propter opera sua in cælo & in ter- ra; ita in corpore suo: idcirco dicit, fundavisti ro- bur, nam velut fundamentum ædificii initium est, ita sugere initium est divinæ misericordiæ, quæ fecit foramen in ubere, instar tenuis fili, non nimis la- tum, ne dispersum esset lac sine fructu, & ne nimium simul veniret; non angustum nimis, ne labia infan- tis in sugendo gravata essent, & porro pro homine DEUS ubera posuit, IN LOCO INTELLI- GENTIÆ (Rabbini sapientiam & intelligentiam in mammis habent, non in animo, vel ut rectius dicam, in calcaneo eam gestant.) Et non sicut in reliquis creaturis, idcirco ait: fundavisti robur; ut ostendat quod omnia per divinum robur veniant, & non fortuito, velut athei Dei inimici confirmant, de quibus dicit, & silere fecit inimicum & ultorem. Fundavisti robur. Quoniam gradatim post ser- monem animi pueri robore magis magisque auge- scit. Hæc sunt mysteria Rabbinica, digna pro- fecto Grotii plausu. Habent similes labra la- ctucas. Mirum, cur non reliqua etiam ex R. Kim- chi & aliis similis furfuris Ebræis adjecerit: utpo- te quod ille ad verba; opera manuum tuarum: In- feriores & superiores etiam creaturas: hucusque do- minatur in eas (homo) quod stellarum motiones in- telligit. Ad vers. 9. qui perambulant semitas maris (ubi de piscibus sermo est) R. Kimchi de homine agi notat, qui per prudentiam in navibus per maria transit. Ad verba, opus manuum tuarum R. Aben- Ezra hæc subjicit: Digiti sunt decem, & sphæræ sunt decem, ideoque more hominum dicit, opus digi- torum: quia notum est, quod duo magna lumina, & quinque planetæ habent septem mansiones, & octava est propter exercitum stellarum magnum habentem motum ab Oriente ad Occidentem, & nona est cœ- lum stellatum, & decima est thronus gloriæ. Autor Midrasch Tillim ita ineptit: Quid est homo (Abra- ham?) Et filius hominis? Isaac: Minorem fecisti An- gelis (Jacob Genes. 32. Hos. 12. ubi prorsus con- trarium habetur) Coronasti (Mosem cum gloria vultus splendentis,) dominium dedisti (Josuæ, quæ habuit Dominium Solis.) sub pedibus (Davidis Ps. 18. sicut pulvis terræ) Bestias agri (sicut Daniel in antro Leonum) Aves cælorum (Corvi alebant E- liam) Pisces maris (Jona fuit in visceribus Levia- than) Transeuntes semitas maris (Israelitæ in mare rubro.) R.Salomo ad illud: Minorem Angelis: ita ha- bet: Josua Filius Nun erat minor Mose, qui dictus est Deus Pharaonis, & Josua subjugarat totam ter- ram Canaan, sub pedibus ejus, oves, boves, &c. & Moses exsiccabat mare rubrum, & Elias resu- scitabat mortuos Sareptanæ & Sunamitidos, quibus miraculis paulo minores erant Angelis. Sed defi- no ineptiarum Rabbinicarum. Ab his ergo Ma- gistris quid expectes υγιές? Rivetum mirari oportet, quod amore affaniarum Calvini sui captus hic non tantum Judaicis illis commentis assensum præbuerit, sed ea etiam cum allegatio- ne verborum istorum, ex ore infantum &c. a Christo facta conciliare laboret: Quo vero artificio tam disparata, imo contraria prorsus conciliabit? Christus enim Matth. 21, 16. celebra- tioni ea applicat, quæ fit ore infantum, laudem Do- mini decantante, vel Deum glorificante effective: Quam vero non ab infantibus, sed ab aliis, in- fantum tamen causa, cum vident eos sugere lac matrum, Dei providentiam admirantibus, fieri, Rivetus cum Rabbinis ait. Nimirum accom- modasse Christum solum verba Davidis hoc pacto censet; quasi a simili vel pari argumentaretur: Si agnoscere debetis providentiam Dei in eo, quod laudem suam perficit ex ore lactentium, quatenus illos mi- rabiliter alit & tuetur: Nonne etiam agnoscere debe- tis eandem providentiam ex eo, quod ex ore istorum puerorum & simplicium hominum suam in pro- missis de Messia venturo servandis laudem celebrari curet? Sed quo vel obscuro indicio Riveto inno- tuit talis argumentatio: cujus certe nec vola, nec vestigium penes Matthæum? Tum vero, annon potuit ita quodcunque dictum Vet. Testamenti arripi, quod providentiam divinam testatur, atque parili ratione opponi Judæis, si ea oppositio ali- quid momenti habeat? At quis non videt, ita sup- poni hoc tanquam certum, quod a Judæis nullate- nus concedebatur? Nimirum dubium id non erat, neque probatione indigebat ulla, nedum tam ob- scura & longe petita, providentia Dei opus esse, si Messias vel promissio de Messia impleto elogio a sim- plicibus celebratur: Sed hanc Christi exceptionem ac celebrationem peculiariter a Deo prædictam fuisse, atque eo inter alia τεκμηρίῳ etiam Messiam agnosci debuisse, quod ita excipiendus fuerit, id vero e Scripturis probandum erat, ut obstrepen- tibus Judæis os obturaretur. Idcirco Christus id probatum it e prædictione Davidica. Docet id ob- jectio τῶν ἀντιπάλων. Non enim tantum, quod pueri vel simplices clament, sed etiam quid illi cla- ment, nen de personis solum, sed de objecto accla- mationis, quod nempe canerent Hosianna filio Da- vid, quæstio erat. Indignati sunt, inquit Mat- thæus, & dixerunt ei: Audis, quid isti dicunt? Id ergo a Davide prædictum esse, vel certe Davi- dis verbis prorsus consentaneum esse, Christus in apologia suorum elogistarum docet: utique nun- quam legistis: Quia ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem Matth. 21, 16. Quis hic non vi- det, verbis illis adductis probasse Christum, recte & juxta hieropsaltis prædictionem convenienter factum, quod tali gratulatione ipse, ceu Messias, & a talibus exceptus fuerit, quia scilicet tempore adventus Messiæ, ac Nov. Testament. Deus sibi laudem peculiariter parare ex ore infantum volue- rit, imo quia prædixerit David, cum de exinani- tione Christi acturus erat, in universa terra cele- bratum iri nomen & gloriam Domini, ob missum Messiam, ejusque glorificationem & laudem im- primis etiam ex ore infantum & lactentium para- tam, cujus specimen quoddam in ingressu Chri- sti regio a pueris Hosanna acclamantibus editum, etiam quoad modum & formam verborum Pro- phetiis Veteris Testamenti congruum, hac Da- vidica prædictione defendit. Porro si ita argu- mentatus fuisset Christus, uti vult Rivetus, nonne hæc fuisset penes Judæos petitio principii, quia as- sumsisset pro certo, se esse promissum Messiam, & in se promissiones impletas esse de venturo Messia, quod ab ipsis neutiquam concedebatur? At cum provocat Christus ad Scripturas, nunquam id as- sumit, quod in quæstione est, sed ex ipsis Scriptu- ris probat, atque loca ea adfert Vet. Testam. quæ de Messia agunt, ac κριτήρια venturi Messiæ desi- gnant, quæ in sese impleri videbant, vel intellige- re poterant: Quod proinde hic etiam factum. Ad- hæc quid antinuisset hoc ad convincendos vel re- darguendos principes sacerdotum & scribas, quod infantes lac sugant e mammillis, atque ita mirabi- liter alantur, ut hoc præ omnibus aliis scripturæ verbis iisdem opponeret? Audis, quid isti dicunt? Nonne legistis, ex ore infantum & lactentium, id est, cum ore suo lac sugunt e mammillis, alii sumunt ma- teriam & causam DEUM laudandi? Tam ine- ptas faciunt ipsius sapientiae hypostaticae Dei alle- gationes, qui ineptiis Rabbinicis patrocinantur! Denique procedunt ista ex falsa hypothesi, quod nempe hic nomen Domini ob opera creationis & conservationis celebretur: Quod vero ob opus redemtionis per Christum factae, ad quam se Matth. 21. ingressu Hierosolymitano sistebat, prae- dicari docuimus: Imo Apostolus ipse testatur Ebr. 2, 6. seq. uti postea ostendemus. Et contradicit hic sibi ipsi Rivetus: Nam quum initium Psalmi de gloria Dei per opera creationis & conservationis elucescente interpretetur: postea gloriam in uni- versa terra celebrandam hic praedici ait, ob repara- tionem hominis, ut ponatur super caelos ipsos ad lo- cum illum beatorum, in quem Christus ascendit, ut suis omnibus domicilia pararet, pag. 37. Quia scili- cet ita canit Psalmus; quam grande est nomen tuum in universa terra, posuisti gloriam tuam super caelos. Quibus in verbis supercaelestem gloriam, quam in Christo nobis explicavit, respici, asserit Junius, Praedecessor Riveti in Academia Lugdu- nensi, in argumento hujus Psalmi: Verba ver- sus 2. ita reddens: Jehovah Domine noster, quam magnificum est nomen tuum in universa terra: Qui exponis supercaelestem decorem tuum. Et in notis haec habet: Exordium sive propositio laudis est vers. 2. Conjuncta exclamatione & admiratione; Deum sese laudabilem nobis exhibere, infinita & su- percaelesti gloria, in Christo Jesu. A qua interpre- tatione non aliena est quantum ad sensum B. Tar- novii nostri sententia: qui propositionem Psalmi hanc facit; magnificum nomen tuum est in univer- sa terra, tempore praesertim Novi Testamenti; eique rationem istam annexam dicit: propter dare deco- rem tuum (qui est) super caelos, vel supercaelestem, nempe homini, hoc est, quod dedisti supercaelestem gloriam, seu communicasti humanae Christi naturae. Quam explicationem propositionis tractationi consentaneam esse probat in Comment. ad h. Psal. Atque eo etiam abit interpretatio B. Gesneri: quod nempe sententia propositionis haec sit: Concio Evan- gelii de Christo vere est illustris, magnifica & stu- penda. Magnificentia & majestas salvatoris nostri in eo descripta non modo per universum terrarum or- bem diffusa, sed & super caelos elevata est: quod cum B. Hieronymo & Augustino de ascensione Christi su- per omnes caelos interpretatur B. Lutherus operat. in hunc Psalm. Tom. 2. Jenens. fol. 87. Video, in- quit, ab omnibus ferme per hanc gloriam, seu magni- ficentiam, seu laudem Dei intelligi Christum Filium Dei, qui assumtus in caelum, sedensque ad dextram Dei Spiritum Sanct. misit, qui per Apostolos nomen Dei magnificavit in toto mundo. Et horum senten- tia mihi quoque non displicuit. Simplicior tamen, fateor, est aliorum interpretatio: Domine Deus meus, fama nominis tui spargitur mirabiliter in uni- versa terra, & laus tua pertingit usque ad caelos, uti exponit Brentius: qui recte observat, David hunc versiculum sic enunciare, perinde, ac si coram vide- ret Apostolos, tam inter Judaeos, quam inter gentes circumire, & gloriam nominis Dei per Christum patefactam, praedicatione sua illustrare: Unde Spirit. Sanct. respiciat maxime tempus, quo circumtulerint Apostoli Evangelium inter omnes gentes. Sic etiam Osiander: Quanta est majestas tua, quae passim in or- be terrarum per Evangelii praedicationem innotescit. Quod nimirum Filio tuo Jesu Christo tradideris re- gnum caeli & terrae. Qui edis laudem tuam usque ad caelos, id est, laus tua pertingit a terra ad caelos usque: omnia plena sunt tua majestate, neque quis- quam satis digne te laudare potest! Explicari etiam potest ita, quod majestas Dei, quam Evangelium ex- hibet, non solum in universa terra prædicetur a fide- libus, sed etiam in cœlis ab ipsis sanctis Angelis & bea- tis Phil. 2, 10. Ebr. 1, 6. quod repleantur laude nomi- nis Dei & gloria ejus in Evangelio patefacta, terra & cœlum, Ecclesia militans & triumphans. Conf. Ap. 5, 9. 12. 13. c. 12, 10. 12. Quam sententiam video etiam probare B. Gesnerum, atque ea videtur hic simplicis- sima & commodissima. Unde iterum patet, quam jejuna illa Judaica glossa Calvinianorum sit de laude Dei, quam sibi ex eo pararit, quod infantes lac su- gant, atque inde nutriantur, quum longe eminentio- ra majestatis divinæ documenta in universa terra, imo etiam in cœlis & in æterna vita deprædicandæ, & ab Angelis pariter atque hominibus celebrandæ, a Psalte hic introducantur.

Vers. eod.

PROPTER INIMICOS TVOS) Ad destruendos, id est, confundendos inimicos eos, qui negant Deum esse, aut res no- stras curare. LXX. hîc bene: τοῦ καταλῦσαι τὸν ἐχθρόν. Idem verbum Ezech. 30, 10. vertitur ἀπολῶ.

ET ULTOREM) Καὶ ἐκδικητὴν Græci, id est, τὸν πολε- μοῦντά σοι, ut hæc vox vertitur Esther. 8, 13. Videtur tacite Saul significari.

Hoc itidem a R. Kimchi accepit. Hic ergo Deus ex ore lactentium sibi perficit laudem propter ini- micos suos, h. e. secundum Grotium, mirabiliter in- fantibus paravit mammas, ut hinc cognoscatur ac lau- detur ex illa structura mirabili ad destruendos atheos, qui Deum & providentiam divinam negant. Sed quum in omnibus Dei operibus Dei sapientiam & bonitatem ac providentiam relucere dubium non sit, cur hic os infantium & modum sugendi, & mam- mas quas sugunt, designari intelligamus, ut inde pe- culiariter athei convincantur? Et quomodo quadrat sequens nomen: Propter inimicos tuos ET ULTO- REM? Quomodo athei ultores sunt? Voce hac taci- te Saul designari, ait Grotius. Quæ ergo hic συνέ- χεια, si præcedentia de infantibus mammas sugen- tibus ceu objecto laudis divinæ accipiantur? Quan- quam non appareat, qua ratione Saul hic ingeratur, aut quomodo per textus cohærentiam hæc Sauli applicari queant?

## 8:5
Verse 6.

THOU HAST MADE HIM A LITTLE LOWER THAN THE ANGELS) That is, you made him ruling over these lower things. For in the first state all things obeyed him of their own accord. That happiness lost through sin is restored through Christ: R. Judah and R. Jacob in the book Caphthor show that the Hebrews also hoped for this concerning the Messiah.

We see that Grotius explains this Psalm as referring to a mere man. Following the Jews, and Calvin and Pelican and Piscator, and also some Papists, especially Bellarmine, Genebrard, Tirinus, Menochius. But this Jewish depravation of an oracle most open and most august concerning Christ is altogether unworthy of Christians. This discourse is not about the whole human race, not about man in the state of integrity, not about the faithful in the state of reparation, but about a certain individual. What is man, that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man, that thou visitest him? It cannot be taken of Adam in the state of integrity. For he was not the Son of man in that way. Nor a miserable and wretched man, which the word אנוש indicates: Ps. 9, 21. Job 7, 1. But Christ is indicated, who is six hundred times in the New Testament called the Son of man, and in the Old Testament he was also so called, Dan. 7, 13. both because he is that promised seed, and because he is the son of a man, of a woman only, but not of two humans Gen. 3, 15. Gal. 4. v. 4. Furthermore, how and when was the name of the Lord more preached as admirable in the whole earth, or his magnificence elevated above the heaven, than in

the heavens by the work of redemption, in the advent of Christ, and the preaching of the Gospel through the whole world! O Lord our God, the sacred Psalmist exclaims deservedly in the proposition of the Psalm adorned with an exclamation and an address: How magnificent is thy name revealed in the Gospel in that great mystery of godliness 1 Tim. 3, 16. concerning God manifested in the flesh! Since it is his purpose to explain the mystery of the incarnation, emptying, and exaltation of the Son of God: which was to be preached in the New Testament in the whole earth, just as David foresaw it in the Spirit. Now that God perfected praise for himself out of the mouth of infants, which began to be fulfilled in those who received the advent of the Messiah with joyful acclamation, Christ himself, the infallible interpreter, taught Matt. 21, 16. which we know was completed more and more also through the Apostles and their successors. Which praise of God is to be firmly established on account of his enemies, both Jews and Gentiles, for the restraining of the unique שטן called by antonomasia, the Devil, who is so often called in the New Testament ὁ ἐχθρὸς & ὁ σατανᾶς. Cf. Job 1, 7. 1 Chr. 25, 1. Zech. 2, 2. Matt. 13, 39. Luke 10, 19. and the avenger of himself, by which name most understand the heretic precipitating himself and others into destruction, although Satan can again be understood; who, intending to avenge himself, has laid, and even now lays, most pernicious snares for the whole human race. Furthermore, what is there that can be preferred to the work of creation, except that which was done in our restoration? For I will see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded: that is, when I look upon those things which are truly admirable, and the chief among your works; when, especially in the night time most suitable for meditations, with the sun having departed below the horizon, I gaze upon the moon and the stars, I cannot but exclaim, what is man, that you are mindful of him, and the son of man, that you visit him? In what way will the Psalmist marvel more at the exaltation of the Son of man above all the works of the hands of the Lord, than at the very chief and highest works of the hands of the Lord in the visible machine of the world. To others, however, including B. Luther, Bugenhagen, Osiander, Gesner, and the Weimar paraphrasts, the allegorical sense is pleasing, so that by the moon the Church, Cant. 6, 9. Rev. 12, 11. by the stars, teachers and the faithful shining like stars in the world Rev. 1, 16. Phil. 2, 15. are understood, and by the name of the heavens and by the works of the fingers of God, the Church is likewise indicated, which is often wont to be called the kingdom of heaven, when it is estimated especially from its future glory, and its members, which are formed in regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, that finger of God, designated by the plural name of fingers on account of various gifts, Matt. 12, 18. Tit. 3, 5. 6. Which works are truly admirable on account of the beauty and splendor which they have from God; but far more illustrious and eminent by infinite parasangs is the glory which shines forth in Christ, exalted above all the works of the hands of God. But the former explanation is simpler, which is also approved by Brentius: for it is not easily permitted to depart from the propriety of words, and the works of the hands of the Lord seem to be compared here with him who has been established above all the works of the hands of the Lord, the glory which shines in them, and which is conspicuous in the Lord himself of all things. But that these things are to be understood of Christ, the Apostle testifies so clearly in Heb. 2, 5. seq. that it cannot be taught more clearly. Those, therefore, who explain it of anyone other than Christ contradict him to his face. And what is more certain from the very words of the Psalm than that both the emptying and the exaltation of Christ are described? For who is there of whom these things can be said in the present passage, you have made him lack a little מאלהים from God, or even from the Angels, except Christ, who for a little time was forsaken by God, and was made lower than the angels? It certainly cannot be said of Adam that he was made lower than the angels for a short time: for man was so created that what he was, he was not for a short time, but perpetually. Nor was he abandoned by God, but he himself abandoned God of his own accord.

Nor does that Rabbinical-Calvinian gloss of Grotius have any place: 'You have made him a little lower than the angels,' that is, you have made him ruling over these lower things. For the subject here is the κένωσις & ταπείνωσις, by which man and the Son of man was for a short time abandoned by God, or, as the Apostle interprets, made lower than the angels, whose Lord he was: Perversely, therefore, is that which speaks of humiliation explained in terms of the sublimity and excellence of man. But then the Rabbinical and Aristotelian fiction is presupposed, that the angels preside over superior things, for instance, the celestial spheres which they have devised, as the movers and directors of the same, but that man rules in the lower things. The Son of man, of whom there is speech, rules not only over the lower things, but also over the other things, and has power over all the works of the hands of the Lord: all things are subject to him: YOU HAVE SET him over the WORKS OF YOUR HANDS: by which are certainly comprehended also the heavens Ps. 102, 26. YOU HAVE PUT ALL THINGS under his feet. By which words the exaltation of the Son of man is now distinctly expressed κατ' ἀντίθεσιν; just as his emptying had been insinuated by the former. For these are openly opposites: to be cast down below the angels: and to be set over all things, and to have the angels themselves subject to him. For he who says 'all things' excludes nothing: nor is there any doubt that the angels are also contained among the works of the hands of God Ps. 103, 21. 22. But that terrestrial animals, birds, and swimming creatures are particularly expressed, it is to be believed that this is done so that we may know that his dominion extends itself even to those things which are outside the Church, and that the Messiah rules over them also (but in a far more eminent way), over which Adam presided in the state of integrity, so that he may in turn restore to us, his members, the dominion that was lost. Compare Gen. 1, 26. c. 3, 23. Rom. 14, 6. 14. 1. Cor. 8, 9. 10. 25. 26. Furthermore, when the sacred psalmist wonders, 'What is that afflicted and miserable man, that you are mindful of him,' that admiration looks to the fact that he, who was so cast down in his emptying, was subsequently crowned with such glory and honor that all things are subjected under his feet, and he himself is set as the supreme Lord over all.

But why many words? For we have here an interpreter superior to every exception, the Holy Spirit, who explains the present passage most openly concerning Christ, and interprets those words, 'you have made him a little lower than the angels,' not of a dominion slightly lower than angelic, but of his emptying, and declares that βραχύ τι Ebr. 2, 5. seq. not of a small degree of distance, but of a short time: For he says, God did not subject the world to come, of which we speak, to the angels (but to Christ). But one testified in a certain place, saying: 'What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the Son of man: that you visit him: ἠλάττωσας ἀυτὸν βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλες, δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας ἀυτὸν:' These are explained from the Psalm thus v. 9. 'But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor.' Who here does not see that τὸ ἠλάττωσαν ἀυτὸν is explained by τὸ πάθημα τῶ θα- νάτω, and that that ἐλάττωσιν is the very ταπεί- νωσιν καὶ κένωσιν of Christ, which is most conspicuous in his passion and death?

Again, the Apostolic interpretation proclaims with a clear voice that what the Psalmist sang concerning honor and glory can be understood of no one but Christ: For it must be understood of him who was crowned after the passion of death with glory and honor: to whom ALL THINGS are subject, without exception: (for in that, says the Apostle, that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him) to whom he also subjected the world to come, as that in which we shall see ALL THINGS subjected to him: For now, as the Apostle says, we do not yet see all things subjected to him. Which absolute and most Catholic universality the holy Apostle also urges 1. Cor. 15, 21. and he explains this Psalm again in the same place concerning Christ, teaching that the full complement will follow only then, when death, which is the last enemy, shall be subjected to him, which he concludes by the demonstration of the Spirit from this oracle will be subjected to Christ: If all things shall be subjected to him, it is necessary that death also be subjected to the same. 'The last enemy, death, shall be destroyed: FOR HE subjected ALL THINGS under his feet.' But when he says, 'ALL THINGS are subjected to him,' without doubt it is except him who subjected all things to him. He teaches, therefore, that nothing is excepted except the one God, who subjected all things to him: and that the subjection of all things will be most established and most fully fulfilled on the last day. Similarly, this passage is explained concerning Christ in Eph. 1. and indeed in such a way that his supreme and immense power over all things, and especially over the Church, is proved from it v. 20. Raising him from the dead, and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future. And he subjected all things under his feet. Which words are taken from our Psalm. We are therefore certain, by the interpretation of the Apostle, that by these ALL THINGS every principality and power, and angelic virtue and dominion are comprehended. Who now will any longer doubt that this oracle must be understood of Christ alone, and since the whole Psalm treats of one subject, that it must be explained of Christ alone? Compare here the Anti-Pareus of our Lord D. Hunnius, the other p. 344. seqq., by which the gloss of Grotius has already been overthrown in the Judaizing Calvin and the Hyperaspistes Pareus.

We note only that Grotius is inconsistent with himself. For here he explains the Psalmist's words solely concerning Adam in his first state. In his Annotations on Heb. 2:5, however, he explains them in the first obvious sense concerning Adam and HIS SEED (which did not live in that state of integrity), but in the mystical sense he takes them concerning Christ and his seed. There he says Adam was made a little lower than the angels because he has dominion only over inferior things, but here because of the condition of his body, and because he was made of clay like other living creatures. There he explains that word מעט only as A LITTLE, but here he says it signifies also in this same place FOR A SHORT TIME, and that the word is so taken in Hos. 1:4 and elsewhere. Now, to speak first of this latter explanation, it is by no means to be admitted that this passage has a double sense, literal or first obvious, and mystical: because that Popish hypothesis concerning a double sense of the same passage is utterly opposed to the perspicuity and certainty of Scripture: Nor can there be any discourse here about Adam, which is the second point, because Adam cannot be called the Son of man, nor do those things which are said here of the Son of man befit Adam: But they apply solely to Christ; on account of whom the name of God is celebrated in all the earth: of whom God also perfected praise for himself out of the mouth of babes: who was also full of misery, whereas Adam in his first state was devoid of miseries. Nor was Adam diminished below the angels for a time, but

Christ: for all things were subjected not to Adam, but to Christ alone under his feet: And who will admit that gloss: that Adam was a little lower than the angels by the condition of his body, crowned with honor and glory, because he was adorned with intellect and free will? Was Adam, before he was adorned with intellect and free will? just as the Son of man was ἐλαττώμενθν παρ᾿ ἀγγέλων, before he was crowned with glory? Were all things subjected to Adam, even the world to come, even the angelic dominions, powers, and virtues, just as all things are subjected to αὐτῷ, TO HIM, of whom the discourse here is, even if we do not yet see it fully? For as for the fact that we do not yet see all things subjected to HIM, that αὐτῷ, which Grotius understands of man considered generally, of Adam and his Seed, or his descendants, that is entirely repugnant to the Apostolic context, in which not even a tiny word of mention is made of Adam or his posterity, and that αὐτῷ refers itself openly to the preceding αὐτῦ you have subjected all things under the feet of HIM, which the Apostle accepts concerning Christ, whom he says is already established above all things, even if we do not yet see it now. And are those things not most poorly distorted, you have established him above the works of your hands, to Adam established over the herds and cattle? Since the works of the hands of the Lord extend so widely that they embrace even the angels, and τὴν οἰκυμένην τὴν μέλλεσαν, as the Apostle testifies, even if cattle and herds are also included under that general name, and for a certain reason are expressed particularly. Not a jot concerning Adam is with the Apostle, who explains all those things concerning Christ alone, and by the pronoun αὐτῷ understands one Christ (because he speaks of no other subject throughout the whole context): nay, he openly teaches that the Davidic Psalm cannot be understood except of Christ alone, or to speak more correctly, he supposes and assumes it among the Hebrews, as ὁμολογόμενον, that it must be accepted solely concerning him who, after a little time of ἐλάττωσιν below the angels, was established above ALL THINGS, and the angels themselves. Since this is completed in no one else but Christ, it must be understood solely of him. Imagine with Grotius that in the literal sense David spoke about Adam; how could the Hebrews have been convinced by that oracle? Would it not have been permissible to object that nothing sublime is expressed by those words, that Adam is described as made below the angels by the condition of his body, but adorned with intellect and will, established above the works of the hands of GOD, that is, the herds and cattle, all of which were subjected to him? What Grotius says, that it ought to be referred to Christ in a mystical sense, that is not to be conceded, because one saying has one sense, and it is most absurd for such disparate significations of the same words to obtain in the same saying, e.g., that Son of man should denote Christ, and at the same time denote Adam, who was the Son of no one but GOD, that מעט βραχύ τι should have one sense, as he himself speaks, and κατὰ πόδας another, and κατὰ τὸ ἀλληγορέμενον (which he says often happens, but could not prove by any example) should signify a little in that way, but in this way taken should signify for a little time, so that ἐλάττωσις should be understood both of the inferiority of the human species below the angels, as regards the body, and of the passion of the death of the Messiah; and that the discourse should be both of the dominion of Adam over inferior things (as he accepts it here) and of the emptying of Christ: so that the works of the hands of the Lord should be explained both of only inferior creatures concerning Adam, and again of superior ones, even the angels themselves, concerning Christ; and similarly that ALL those things should be explained of herds and cattle only, and not also at the same time of all things absolutely, even the world to come. Add that Grotius betakes himself in vain here to traditions, intending to prove from them that those things ought to be referred to Christ in a mystical sense, from the authority of the Hebrew wise men, who referred them in a mystical sense to the Messiah and his seed. For from where will he demonstrate those traditions? For if Grotius, Judaizing here, praises recent Rabbis, that does nothing for the Hebrews who lived in the Apostolic age: but from them he received the double sense of the same saying, literal and mystical; unless perhaps he defers that praise to the Papists, with whom this opinion is common among the Jews. Furthermore, if he sang of Adam in the state of integrity, how is it snatched away to the seed and posterity of Adam, which is bereft of primeval happiness: If of the Messiah, how is it drawn to the seed of the Messiah? Does this title, son of man, does that ἐλάττωσις βραχύ τι παρ᾽ ἀγγέλες made, does the establishment above the angels and the works of the hands of the Lord, does the subjection of ALL THINGS under their feet, and indeed of all things without exception, so that there is nothing not subjected, except him who subjected all things, belong to the faithful here? Furthermore, even if Adam is established as a type of Christ, or rather is compared with him, that is done in a disparate sense in Rom. 5:14, 1 Cor. 15:45, nor does it have anything in common with the Grotian type, of which there is neither a trace nor a footprint with the Apostle. As from Adam sin and condemnation, so on the contrary from Christ righteousness and justification, according to the Apostle: As we bear here the image of Adam: so we shall one day bear the image of the heavenly Adam, by the same Apostle as author. But from where will Grotius teach that Adam was a type of Christ in that the dominion over the things of the inferior world given to him was an image of the dominion which Christ has in the supreme world, that that which Adam, inferior by the condition of his body a little to the Angel (whose body, however, was not mortal, but immortal in the state of integrity, Wis. 1:13 and 2:23. Rom. 5, 12.) was an image of that, that for a short time Christ was made lower than the Angels in the passion of death: that that, which Adam was endowed with by intellect and free will, was an image of that, that Christ was crowned with the fullest knowledge of divine things, with a perfect will, and with admirable power, (just as the words, you have crowned him with glory and honor, which treat of immense and infinite glory, interpreted here by the Apostle in Eph. 1, 1. 2., and with other places of Scripture concurring, Dan. 7, 14. seqq., John 1, 14., ch. 5, 12. seqq., ch. 17, 3., Matt. 28, 19., etc., he perversely explains concerning finite glory) that that, which Adam was constituted over herds and cattle, was an image of that, that Christ had to be placed above the Angels: that that, which all things were subjected to Adam in a slight manner, was an image of that, that all things are absolutely subjected under the feet of Christ. Where, I beseech you, are these typical adumbrations explained in the Scriptures, or even lightly insinuated? And how was Adam in the state of integrity a type of Christ, who certainly would not have come if Adam had persisted in the state of integrity, and was not promised to him as a remedy except after the fall, as the Goel and Hyperaspistes of the human race against Satan. Therefore, no cause, no reason for a type existed before the fall. Types were added to the promise of the Messiah for the sake of illustration. But before sin, no promise of the Messiah existed, nor could it have a place. Now, since Grotius also makes the seed and descendants of Adam types of the seed of the Messiah, he involves himself in many absurdities: But there is no need for us to dissect all those things to the quick. He admits that that happiness of Adam, that he had dominion over inferior things, and that in the first state all things obeyed him spontaneously, was lost through sin: therefore, it did not have a place in his descendants.
