Therefore, in the annotations on Heb. 2, 6. τῆ ὑποθέσει

Declaring that dominion diminished by the fall, he says it was all but completely taken away, and he appeals to Cyril, Ep. to Calosarius against the Anthropomorphites, and Isidore, b. 3, Ep. 95. He admits that those words of the Psalm, 'You have put ALL things under his feet,' had no effect in Adam, nor in any of his descendants, except a slight one: and yet he wishes them to be understood of them, and says that sense is the FIRST obvious one; and he says that something greater lies hidden in them, namely, a mystical sense concerning the subjection of all creatures. But that sense does not lie hidden, or is not concealed in those words, but is immediately the first obvious one; since those words, 'He has put all things under him,' by themselves and according to the letter, imply the subjection of all creatures, and of all the works of the hands of God that exist, except that one who put all things under him, which the Apostle pronounces to be δῆλον MANIFEST from those words, 1 Cor. 15:27. Therefore, there is nothing slight in those words according to the first obvious sense, but such majesty is signified as does not fall to Adam, or any of his descendants, nor even to any Angel, but which is proper to the one Son of Man, the Messiah; so that it is δῆλον, entirely manifest, that the Psalm, which throughout its whole context deals with the same subject, cannot be explained except of the Messiah in the literal and first obvious sense. It must also be admitted that this is the only argumentative sense; from a typical, mystical, and allegorical sense, which is merely fictitious, such as that of Grotius, the Apostle could have concluded nothing.

Before we depart from here, the sophistries of Rivetus, by which he casts a cataract over the eyes of the unskilled for a gloss not unlike Calvin's, must be discussed. He himself had completely passed over the present Psalm, as also Psalm 118, when he illustrated the Decade of Prophetic Psalms concerning Evangelical mysteries with a commentary: from which it could be presumed that he did not consider those two Psalms as such: But in the second edition, instead of a Decade, he presented a Dodecade, which I note here because I cited the Decade somewhere, that is, the earlier edition. Moreover, if you look more deeply into the matter, he leaves little of the Prophetic or Evangelical mystery to our Psalm in his commentary, so that he seems to adorn it with that title for the sake of appearance only. He proposes his opinion thus in Vol. 2 of his works, in the Dodecade of Psalms, p. 32: that the Psalmist discourses with admiration concerning the benefits of God toward the human race, exalted by God above other sublunary creatures: But that he raised his mind, illuminated by the Prophetic Spirit, to Him in whom the grace granted to the human race ought to have shone most brightly, as in the head of all who were to become heirs of the earth and inhabitants of heaven. He denies, therefore, that he can follow the opinion of those who refer this whole Psalm immediately and properly, according to the first and literal sense, to Christ: and he joins those of his own sect who think that the primary subject is the magnitude of the glory of God, shining in the creation and preservation of all things, but especially in the procreation of men and the beneficence toward the human race, so that, however, the accumulation of all blessings is celebrated in the Messiah being exhibited in his own time: indeed he adds: that those who proceed otherwise are forced to invent alien interpretations, and to deviate from the sense of the letter, so that they may twist the words of the Prophet to their own thoughts. But what wonder is it that a disciple of Calvin should pronounce such things about those who follow the Apostle in explaining the Psalm, when Calvin, his master, judged no more mildly or religiously concerning the Apostle himself, namely, that he DEFLECTS what had been said in ANOTHER SENSE to his own purpose κατ’ ἐπεξεργασίαν. We have already clearly shown that we should accept the words of the Psalmist not according to our own thoughts, but according to the Apostolic interpretation, and that there is no need to depart from the sense of the letter to sustain it, but that it flows from the letter itself. We believe it is likewise evident from what has been said that that gloss of Rivetus deviates so much from the letter of the Prophet that it completely distorts his words to the depravity of Calvin, and openly contradicts even the Apostolic interpretation. For the discourse is most openly not about Adam, not about the whole human race, but about a certain individual, about the Son of Man, peculiarly so called in the Scriptures: nor is the exaltation of any other described than his: as one who alone was established OVER THE WORKS of the hands of the Lord, to whom alone ALL THINGS are subjected, who also alone, after he was made a little lower than the Angels for a short time, was crowned with that glory and honor, so that he was constituted Lord over all things. If anyone denies that these things speak universally of one subject, he will deny that the Sun shines at midday.

The text is too clear: which Rivetus presents thus: 'What is man, that You are mindful OF HIM, and the Son of man, that You visit HIM? For You have made HIM lack a little from the Angels, You have crowned HIM with glory and honor: You have made HIM rule over the works of your hands: You have put ALL THINGS under HIS feet.' The pronouns HIS and HIM powerfully convince that these things speak of one and the same subject, cohering in an inseparable connection. But how can it be said of the human race, so that you do not deviate from the sense of the letter, or twist the words of the Prophet, that it is constituted over all the WORKS of the hands of the Lord, that ALL THINGS are put under his feet, or that it is crowned with such glory and honor, after it had been diminished a little or for a short time below the Angels? How can the human race be understood by the term Son of man, or did Adam not belong to the human race, who certainly was not the Son of man, unless you assign a parent to Adam worse than the fabricator of the Pre-Adamites? But in this way, if the first parent is also to be included under the name of the Son of man, another parent must be assigned to him, and thus one would have to proceed to infinity, or it will be necessary to say that not all men are included under the name of the Son of man, or the whole human race, which God visited. And where did the Psalmist indicate even by a word that he is dealing here with Adam, or with the procreation of men, or with the human race? Where did he say that it was exalted above other sublunary creatures? It is a question of the exaltation of the Son of man: and that was done not only above sublunary creatures, but above ALL THINGS: because ALL THINGS were put under his feet, he was set over all the works of the hands of the Lord. By which also the heavens, as the work of the fingers of GOD, the sacred psalmist comprehends, and the Apostle protested that nothing at all is excepted here.

The Reformed twist themselves vehemently here, and turn themselves in all directions. Sometimes they refer these things to man in the state of integrity, who was crowned with glory and honor. Sometimes they understand man after the fall. Which opinion Rivetus chooses: because in the prior state man cannot be called mortal and miserable, which is denoted by the word אנוש, nor should the Prophet have spoken of him so abjectly in such great glory: because the first man, whose children we all are, could not be the Son of man, and because the mercy of God shines forth more in this, that He was willing to visit the human race, although fallen: But because he sees the Apostle, Heb. 2, v. 6, 1 Cor. 15, 27. interpreting [it] of Christ, soon from the whole human race, which he understands literally, Rivetus turns himself to the absolutely elect, who were given to the Son of God, that they might be his members, and further from these to the Son of God, made the son of man, to whom he says it is rightly and most appositely referred by the Apostle. But again he turns himself from the Son of God to the elect, and those things which concerning this one individual the Apostle interprets, he says must be referred to all the elect and faithful, who are considered in their head: so that Genebrard, having thus been carried from the species to the individual, has passed over, but on the condition that we return from that individual to the species, but considered in that head of the faithful. Behold the multiform Proteus! Behold the cyclic interpretation! And this they dare to peddle as the genuine interpretation of the purer Theology, as they call themselves, Doctors, because, forsooth, it is closer to the mind of Calvin, from which they do not easily allow themselves to be torn away. But if fallen man is understood, how are the elect substituted in his place? Is every fallen person elect? Have only the elect been visited by God? Again, let us imagine that those inconsistent things cohere: What is man, miserable, abject, fallen into sin, and subject to damnation? And, what is man, elect and predestined to eternal glory, or if you prefer, what is man, that you should wish to visit the elect? For Rivetus thinks that these alone are visited here, that is, restored: how does it now fit the Son of God, not aptly, but most aptly, whether it is said of miserable sinners or of the elect? Does he belong to miserable sinners, or is he among the elect? Which the latter seems at any rate to have pleased Rivetus; because he betakes himself from one individual (Christ) to all the elect; therefore it is necessary to establish Christ from the number of those whom God chose for eternal life from the human race fallen in sin, in whom he also says the grace granted to the human race shines MOST brightly, as in the head of all the blessed, from which he seems to leave it to be gathered that Christ was made a participant of the same grace (even if it shines MOST brightly in him) of which, indeed, the rest become participants from the human race, so that at least a difference of degrees intervenes: which to have recited these paradoxes is to have refuted them. But if Paul refers the Prophetic words most aptly to the Son of God, because it was done by him in such a way that he received the same things concerning the ONE Christ, to whom alone all things are subject, after he was made a little lower than the Angels for a short time (which he teaches the Psalmist sang concerning the son of man), what is more certain than that the Prophetic words concerning the Son of man must be accepted only concerning the one Son of God, and by no means can they be dragged to the entire human race, and not even to all the elect, except through a remarkable distortion? For whom shall we have as a better interpreter, Calvin or the Apostle Paul? Furthermore, since the Apostle takes that, you made him a little lower than the Angels, but crowned him with glory and honor, concerning the humiliation below the Angels for a short time in the passion and death of Christ, and also concerning his subsequent glorification: Rivetus interprets it not concerning a short time, but a small degree of distance, not concerning humiliation below the Angels and true emptying, but concerning a dignity closely approaching angelic dignity, which is attributed not to Christ alone, but to man in general: not concerning distinct states, as the Apostle does, namely the prior one of emptying and the subsequent one of exaltation, and thus not in an Antithetical sense concerning that little lower than the Angels and the CORONATION of glory and honor with the establishment over all things, even over the Angels: But exegetically he interprets it concerning the same state of man, who, namely, through gracious visitation, through the branch of righteousness Christ, has been raised to a dignity a little lower than angelic, and thus has been crowned with glory and honor, and established over all things: if this is not to pervert Scripture and to twist it into a completely contrary sense, I profess that I am entirely ignorant of what that would be.

Rivetus sees well that Paul stands in his way, but he tries in vain to reconcile the contradictory things, and to couple the Arctic pole with the Antarctic. The difficulty, he says, is found in this, that while the literal sense (according to the preconceived opinion of Calvin and Rivetus) refers that LITTLE, by which man was diminished from the angels, to the amplification of the glory of man, i.e., You have raised up weak man so that you have made him almost equal to the Angels, so that he differs little from them, the Apostle accommodates these words by bending them to the mediator Christ, even to his humiliation and death. For the sense of the latter is this: Although he was exalted above the Angels, he was nevertheless humbled for a short time, on account of the passion and death which he underwent. Therefore he refers that a little to time, not to quality or dignity. But what does he answer to this difficulty? He persists in his preconceived opinion, that the Prophet celebrates the goodness and mercy of God toward the human race corrupted by sin, subject to miseries, and despoiled of that dignity which it had received in the first creation (of which there is not even a jot in the Prophetic text, let alone in the Apostolic exegesis), of which God nevertheless had regard, while it was established in that state, so that he might restore it and raise it to its former or even better dignity (where, I beseech you, is there a word about that restoration in this Psalm, where is there even one iota about the raising of men to their former and better dignity? Who, therefore, is Rivetus to peddle these things as the literal sense?) And he attaches this sense to the Prophetic words: But I ask again and again, how can that be reconciled with the Apostolic exegesis? Rivetus answers: That the Apostle rightly places the foundation of that entire restoration in Christ, in whom human nature, although assumed in the likeness of sinful flesh, was after humiliation exalted in the head, and through the head will be exalted in the members, so that whatever is said about that Lord afterwards, may be considered in that second Adam first and in himself, to be communicated afterwards to others who are grafted into him, to the praise of the glorious grace of God, so that his glory may be magnified in the whole earth, and finally be placed above the heavens themselves, to that place of the blessed into which Christ ascended and prepared dwellings for all his own. But this is not only to correct the words of the Prophet, but also those of the Apostle. For the Apostle does not explain the FOUNDATION of the reparation of the human race, as it is described in the Psalm, but by bringing forward the very words of the Psalm, in place of proof, concerning the passion of Christ, or his humiliation for a short time, and the subsequent glorification of the same, and the subjection of all things under his feet, he proclaims with full cheeks, so to speak, that they are to be understood concerning that same thing. No one denies that the foundation of our reparation is to be placed in Christ. But that our reparation is treated according to the letter in the words of the Psalm, and that the Apostle does not designate the thing which the Psalmist treats, but only the foundation of the same, and that when the Psalm treats of the reparation of the human race, he indeed brings forward the words of the Psalm, but does not urge or press his words, or their genuine sense; that he only testifies that the foundation of that reparation is to be sought in Christ, this openly contradicts the Apostolic treatment: in which, if anywhere, the very words of the Psalmist are pressed and urged, and it is not inquired into, or explained, what the foundation of those things which the Psalmist sang might be, even if it is not touched upon by the Psalmist in his words. The Apostle establishes his first theme, which he intends to prove from the Psalm: namely, that God did not SUBJECT the world to come to Angels, but to Christ: then he brings forward as testimony the words of the Psalmist: But one testified in a certain place, saying: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the Son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the Angels: with glory and honor you have crowned him: and you have set him over the works of your hands, YOU HAVE SUBJECTED ALL THINGS under his feet. The reasoning of the inference is most clear, from the statement about all things: To whom ALL THINGS are subjected, it is necessary that the world to come should also be subjected to him. But to Christ, although he was made a little lower than the angels, all things have been subjected. Therefore, it is necessary that the world to come should also be subjected to Christ (not to angels, much less to men). He confirms the major proposition, pressing and urging the words of the Prophet, in this way: for in that he subjected ALL THINGS to him, he left nothing not subjected to him. And so that he may cut off every doubt, and teach that the truth stands in the Davidic prediction, he objects by way of ἀνθυποφορὰ (counter-objection), or at least anticipates it, for the sake of a clearer demonstration: But now we do not yet see ALL THINGS subjected TO HIM (he speaks of Christ, and indicates that the Psalmist spoke of him. For the same subject to which all the pronouns here refer is not different.) But him who was made βραχύ τι (a little) lower than the angels for a short time, we see JESUS, (thus he urges the words of the Prophet, and shows of whom they speak, namely of JESUS.) crowned with glory and honor through the suffering of death. He says this, therefore: We do not yet indeed see how that which the Psalmist predicted has been fulfilled, that ALL THINGS whatsoever are subjected to Christ (for that will be seen fully and openly in the other age, when even the last enemy, death, will be subjected to him, as the same Apostle testifies in 1 Cor. 15, v. 20), yet we see that it has been fulfilled according to the prophecy of the Prophet, and that Christ was made lower than the angels for a short time in his passion, and that afterwards he was crowned with honor and glory, whence we cannot doubt that it will also be fully fulfilled; so that we may indeed acknowledge that ALL THINGS are subjected to him, and therefore also the future world, which we shall openly see on the last day and in eternal life, as the Apostle testifies in the parallel passage 1 Cor. 15. Therefore, the Apostle does not only teach that the human nature of Christ was exalted after his humiliation, but he testifies that both that humiliation and the subsequent exaltation were delivered in the words of the Psalm; nay, he demonstrates from the same that the same thing, and that prophecy of his, obtained its fulfillment, he teaches. But nothing in those words of the Psalm, as they are adduced by the Apostle, is delivered concerning the whole human race, nothing concerning its humiliation below the angels, nothing concerning its exaltation to its former dignity, and nothing of the sort is taught by the Apostle to be delivered in them. And when Rivetus contends that in the literal sense the Prophet does not deal with Christ and his humiliation and exaltation, what remains but that he openly says that the Apostle, who refers the very words of the Psalmist to that, deviates from the literal sense and bends the words of the Psalmist, or rather distorts them to that of which they themselves do not speak? He certainly admits that the Apostle, by BENDING them to Christ the Mediator, accommodates them to his humiliation, because, forsooth, he saw that his Calvin did not shrink from this accusation, in Psalm. p. m. 40. When here the Prophet discourses on the excellence of men, and says that they approach near to God; the Apostle DRAWS it to the emptying of Christ. Likewise: That which the Apostle then treats concerning the BRIEF EMPTYING is not exegetical, but he DEFLECTS it κατ' ἐπεξεργασίαν (by way of further elaboration) to his own purpose, which had been said in ANOTHER SENSE. But this is not to accuse the Apostle, but the Holy Spirit himself: and to contradict himself no less openly than Him. For is this not an open contradiction: The Apostle refers these words of the Psalmist MOST APTLY to Christ: And, The Apostle BENDS the words of the Psalmist, or with Calvin, deflects them to his own purpose, which had been said in ANOTHER SENSE. But even in rendering the words of the Psalmist themselves in a paraphrastic sense, Rivetus contradicts himself: Let the paraphrastic sense of this passage be, he says, if after the consideration of that magnificent heavenly host we turn the eyes of our mind to contemplate human nature; What is man, that you deign to have any regard for him, so humble and abject, that you willed to visit him through that sprout, or the rising from on high sent to the earth? Yet he came, having assumed this weak nature of man, in which he was made lower than the angels (whom all the angels of God otherwise adore) because of the mortality to which he subjected himself, and the ignominious death which he suffered, for a little time; But a little later he was crowned with glory and honor, to last forever, as the head of those whom he makes participants of the same glory in himself, in whom alone that dominion resides, the fruit of which redounds to all the members of Christ, and will redound more fully. These things agree very well with those which follow, which ALL the Prophet saw by the Prophetic Spirit as if they were present, which were certainly to be in the future and were decreed and prepared by GOD from eternity. Thus far Rivetus. If this is the Paraphrastic sense of the words of the Prophet, agreeing very well also with those which follow, and he foresaw ALL those things here by the Prophetic Spirit, and therefore predicted them with these words (for it is not asked what he otherwise foresaw or predicted, but what has been predicted here), it is necessary that they all pertain to the literal sense (for this is the paraphrastic sense, agreeing very well with the preceding and following, delivered according to the foresight and suggestion of the Prophetic Spirit in the prophecies). Therefore, it must be false that, as regards the literal sense, the words of the Psalmist deal only with the restoration of the human race. False, that those words 'made a little lower than the angels' speak immediately of the excellence of the human race being a little lower than the angelic: because they assert that Christ was made lower than the angels for a little time. It is false that the words, 'thou hast crowned him with glory and honor,' treat of men in an immediate sense (as Calvinists are otherwise accustomed to establish a double sense, immediate and mediate), since they speak of the glory with which Christ was crowned after his humiliation. But where is it held in this Psalm that Christ, as head, had to attain that glory, and had to make the elect participants of it in himself? And, if that dominion of which the Psalmist sings resided with him alone, but its fruit redounds only to the faithful, it must be that Christ alone is that Lord of whom the Psalmist says: 'thou hast put all things under HIS feet'; and thus that the Psalm treats of him alone, even if the fruits of the dominion promised here to Christ redound to the faithful. Again, if by 'man' and 'son of man' in the literal and paraphrastic sense human nature or the human race is understood, which God deigns to visit, by what word then in the Psalm, by what name or verb is the 'branch' or 'dayspring from on high,' or the assumption of human nature indicated? And how is such a diverse subject introduced into a text which treats of one subject, of man and the son of man, and says he was made a little lower than the angels? If, therefore, this man is the human race, or man fallen into sin, how can Christ be understood by him? Thus, that paraphrastic sense of Rivet is in every way ἑαυτομαχεῖ [self-contradictory], so that it needs no further refutation.

It is helpful, however, for us to be spectators of this ἑαυτομαχίας [self-contradiction] of Rivet for a little while longer. For what will become of those words: you have crowned him with glory and honor? This was done, says Rivetus: through that dignity which God bestowed upon man, by which he set him over, and appointed him lord over all other creatures, namely the sublunar ones, according to the interpretation of God himself, who places man, once created, into the possession of all these things, Gen. 1, 24. Thus, therefore, he now explains it concerning the ψιλῶ ἀνθρώπῳ [mere man], the Lord established in the state of integrity, which, according to the paraphrastic sense of this passage, he had interpreted a little earlier with the Apostle concerning Christ crowned with glory after his humiliation. Thus, he now accepts the words of the Psalmist concerning man before the fall with Calvin: which, however, he had previously proven ought to be understood with others concerning man after the fall. Others (I report his words) do not think that man in the state of innocence can be called mortal and miserable, which we have taught is signified by the word Enos, nor that the Prophet ought to have spoken of him in such great glory and honor, and so abjectly. And certainly the Son of man, to whom THESE THINGS ARE ATTRIBUTED, could not be Adam the first man, whose sons we all are. TO US, therefore, as to some others, that later condition seems to be better understood, by which not only the goodness of God, but also his mercy toward men shines forth more, who willed to visit the fallen human race, however unworthy, through him whom he appointed from the very origin of the world as the redeemer of the whole human race. It therefore seems rightly a wonder that he willed nevertheless to raise such an abject creature, if you compare him with the heavenly ones, to that future dignity which he is about to describe later. If, therefore, he describes that dignity to which God willed to raise man, however mortal and miserable, fallen into sin, and thus unworthy, he is certainly not speaking of the dignity which he bestowed before that misery and

sin itself he bestowed. Furthermore, if they treat of the dignity of man, whether in the state of integrity or in the state of restoration, according to the letter, how does the Apostle not deviate from the sense of the letter when he accepts these things concerning Christ, and argues from that, that all things are subjected under his feet, so as to elicit from it also that the world to come and the Angels themselves are subjected to Christ? Rivetus does not approve, but refutes the opinion of those who say that these things are explained concerning Christ only in an allegorical sense, even if intended by the Holy Spirit: Since the Apostle, he says, was dealing with the Jews, although because of the knowledge of divine things in which he excelled, he could have brought forward a true and apt allegorical interpretation, yet it does not seem that he wished to force such a thing upon the Jews by his own authority; otherwise there would have been no need for argumentation and inference from the consideration of a universal proposition, but he would have simply professed, as he did elsewhere among the Galatians, that all these things are ἀλληγορύμενα [allegorized], as in Galatians 4, verse 24. Furthermore, there is nothing that proves that the dignity which he implanted in men at creation, and of which some traces also remain after sin, was a figure of that glory and honor to which God raised Christ, because man considered in general cannot be a type of Christ, who was himself also man, and to whom, as such, the description of human dignity pertained. Rivetus says these things very correctly against some of his accomplices. Therefore, he prefers another interpretation: Others, therefore, wish these things to have been attributed to Christ through a certain accommodation, by which, with the same words preserved, he wished to describe the dignity of Christ, and his dominion far above all those things which are attributed to men taken commonly. As if he had said, if these things were once said by the Prophet concerning man, because of that subjection of creatures which is common to the human race: Much better can these things, taken universally, be adapted to him who has been established as the head of men and Angels, etc. But there is no trace of that accommodation in the Apostle: who does not accommodate the words of David to another sense concerning the glory of Christ, but proves and demonstrates that glory of Christ from the oracle and words of David; for Rivetus confesses that he is arguing and inferring from the words of David. But if he were to argue in this way: If these things were once said universally concerning man, because of the subjection of only certain creatures, namely sublunar ones, then certainly all things will be universally subjected to Christ, with none excepted, would that not be a weak and inept argument? But if he infers, as Rivetus wishes him to infer, that these things taken universally can be much better adapted to him who has been established as the head of men and Angels, will this not be a mere αἴτησις τῇ ἐν ἀρχῇ [begging of the question]? For thus it is supposed that Christ presides over all things universally and is established above all things, even above the Angels, and above the world to come, when it is posited that this is brought out only by the words of the Psalm; whereas it does not suppose that here, nor could it suppose it without begging the question, as it was what the Apostle had taken upon himself to prove here, and which he proves entirely from the τῷ ῥητῷ [the literal text] of the words of the Psalmist. For he demonstrates with this axiom that they are not to be understood particularly concerning the subjection of certain creatures, as Rivetus wishes, when the Psalmist says, you have subjected all things under his feet, but must be understood universally and absolutely: for in the fact that he subjected ALL THINGS to him, he left nothing not subjected to him. Nor does he hint that the Psalmist is speaking of another, or that the words of the Psalmist accommodate themselves to another, but he persists most openly in that same subject, in that same Son of man, to whose feet he said all things were subjected in the words of the Psalm, verse 7, and teaches that all things are so subjected to him that nothing is left not subjected to him, verse 8, and names that Son of man JESUS, verse 9. The universal meaning of which words of David, which they infer according to the letter, the Apostle urges equally in 1 Cor. 15, 27. For he subjected all things under his feet. But when he says ALL THINGS are subjected to him, it is plain that these things are said, except for him who subjected all things to him. Where the Apostle also infers (which Rivetus does not deny here) that there is nothing, except God, which is not by right subjected to Christ here (by the force of the Davidic oracle), and which ought not in fact to be subjected. Now, indeed, had the Calvinists explained how, under that universality which the Apostle urges so solidly in those two passages in the words of David, all things are subjected to mere man, of whom they wish this Psalm to treat? Rivetus, because he saw himself pressed here, having abandoned the state of integrity of which he had said the Psalmist was treating, took refuge in the state of eternal blessedness, page 40, near the end of his explanation: For then, he says, in Christ and through Christ, ALL things except God are subjected to man, but he contradicts himself again in such a way, inasmuch as he had previously said that David was treating of that subjection of creatures which is common to the HUMAN RACE. Likewise, that this Psalm treats primarily and immediately of mere man, with respect to the present world, that is, of SUBLUNARY creatures. But now he takes them absolutely concerning the ELECT, and concerning ALL things except GOD. He also contradicts Scripture: which indeed urges the universal sense of the little word, but demonstrates that all things will be subjected to Christ alone in the next age, solely on account of Christ. And how will that ἀξίωμα of Christ be attributed to the elect, that all things, God excepted, are subject to them, without ἀποθέωσιν? Since the Apostle demonstrates that this is proper to Christ the θεανθρώπῳ alone, is it to be claimed for mere men? That, indeed, the Calvinists do not otherwise leave even to the human nature of Christ, so who is Rivetus to attribute it now to mere men? But enough of the deceits of Rivet. More sound are those things which his predecessor Francis Junius handed down in this place: who interprets it as Christ being made a little lower than the angels, through the passion of death, for a short time, but exalted to supercelestial and INFINITE (which epithet I would like others to note, Calvinists) glory. Although he errs in this, that he mixes in other men here, but otherwise than Rivet, and in inverted order, so that indeed through man and the son of man, Christ is understood in himself and through himself: but secondly Christ in us, and we in him: because the words of the Psalmist speak openly of only one Christ, and are explained in the N.T. Which has been shown thus far. It pleases me, however, to append the judgment of the great man Luther, not only because of this Psalm, but also because of other oracles of Scripture, in which some less wisely admit a double sense, namely the literal and the mystical, both intended by the Holy Spirit. There have not been wanting, he says in Vol. 2 of the Jena works on this Psalm, fol. 95, those who have tried to understand it concerning human nature compared to the angels. But we are compelled by the consequences to couple it with the preceding, and that in a unique and simple sense, therefore let us accept from all that which pleases and agrees, leaving the rest to their own authors. This verse explains the preceding one entirely, in which it was said that Christ is Enosh in the memory of the Lord, so that he who was despised by men might be visited by God. Therefore the sense is: You left him for a little time: But with great glory you took him up, by which you showed how you had not forgotten him, nor despised him, as in Psalm 22: For he has not despised, nor abhorred the prayer of the poor. For this Psalm speaks entirely of the passion of Christ, and the glory obtained through the passion: As the Apostle clearly says to the Hebrews 2: But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with honor and glory through the passion, etc. And 'a little' pertains not to dignity, but to time. For we had the same adverb in Psalm 2: When his wrath is kindled in a little while, that is, quickly and after a little time his wrath will be kindled. And absolutely nothing is being treated here concerning the substance, difference, or dignity of natures, but concerning the duration of the passion. Now the word 'you made lower,' because it did not render the Hebrew, sounds to us as if someone were to diminish him who is great, in the way that someone's power, dignity, or wealth is diminished; Johannes Reuchlin interprets it as 'failed,' 'was lacking,' 'was diminished.' As in 3 Kings 17: Neither shall the jar of oil be diminished. And below: Nor has the jar of oil been diminished. From which it is clear that it is signified in this place that Christ was forsaken by God, as one who ceased to protect him and was lacking to him, just as he cried out on the cross: Eli Eli Lama Sabachthani: For he understands this 'a little' as that very hour of which he said: But this is your hour, and the power of darkness. Therefore, when he was powerful in work and word up to this hour, suddenly and for a little time, namely for three days, he was diminished and deserted by God in this power, subjected to infirmity, and also to death and hell. And fol. 98, where he had said that some great Fathers are of the opinion that it treats of a mere man here, he adds: but Paul to the Hebrews (if by chance he denies that it is Paul's) strongly opposes it, but also 1 Cor. 15: he says, he puts all things under his feet. Since, however, it is necessary that there be one simple and constant sense of Scripture and the word of God, lest (as they say) we make a waxen nose of the Holy Scriptures, it is just that Paul's sense be preferred to the sense of all other Fathers, whether Ambrose, Augustine, or Jerome. All of which the great man [Luther] states gravely and solidly. We add the Confession of Johannes Cocceius, successor of Rivet in the Chair at Leiden, in the last chapter of Moses §. 1020. Whom to

Understand 'God properly crowned with glory and honor,' so that when he was for a little time lower than him who is and is called God, now he is no longer lower, honor and glory must be rendered to him, so that the name of God may be great in all the earth. THOSE interpreters SIN in this Psalm who think it treats of the first Adam (Calvin, Rivet, others), and think he is called a little lower than GOD, or the angels. Certainly the first man was not created a little lower than God, and after sin he was made now ENOSH, desperately miserable, both he himself and the sons of man, they descended even far below themselves, and did not retain dominion over all the works of God, much less that through man, the son of Adam, as such, the name of God should be great in all the earth. And it is entirely ABSURD not to oppose the 'diminution' (elattōsin) of v. 6, with the Apostle in Heb. 2:9, to the 'crowning with glory and honor.' Thus far Cocceius. And these things concerning the eighth Psalm.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

MINUISTI EUM PAULO MINUS AB ANGELIS) Id est, dominantem in res has inferiores eum fecisti. In primo enim statu omnia ei sponte parebant. Ea felicitas per pec- catum amissa per Christum redditur: id & Hebræos de Messia sperasse ostendunt R. Juda, & R. Jacob in lib. Caph- thor.

Videmus, quod Psalmum hunc de homine mero explicet Grotius. Judæos sequutus, & Cal- vinum ac Pelicanum & Piscatorem, nec non Pontifi- cios nonnullos, imprimis Bellarminum, Genebrardum, Tirinum, Menochium. Sed Judaica hæc depravatio oraculi de Christo apertissimi, augustissimi Christia- nis prorsus indigna est. Sermo hic non de univer- so genere humano, non de homine in statu integritatis, non de fidelibus in statu reparationis, sed de individuo certo. Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus, aut filius hominis, quoniam visitas eum? De Adam in statu in- tegritatis id capi non potest. Sic enim Filius hominis non erat. Nec homo miser & ærumnosus, quod vox אנוש indicat: Ps. 9, 21. Job. 7, 1. Indigitatur autem Christus, qui vel fexcenties in Nov. Test. Filius ho- minis dicitur, & in V. T. ita quoque appellatus est, Dan. 7, 13. tum quia est promissum illud semen, tum quod ipse hominis, mulieris tantum, non autem hominum duorum filius sit Gen. 3, 15. Gal. 4. v. 4. Porro quomodo & quando nomen Domini admi- rabile in terra universa magis prædicatum est, aut elevata magnificentia ejus super cœlum, quam in Tom. I. V. T.

cœlis opere redemtionis, in adventu Christi, & predica- tione Evangelii per terrarum orbem universum! Domine Deus noster exclamat Hieropsaltes merito in propositione Psalmi ἐκφωνήσει & προσφωνήσει exor- nata: Quam magnificum est nomen tuum in Evange- lio patefactum in magno illo pietatis mysterio 1. Tim. 3, 16. de Deo manifestato in carne! Siquidem proposi- tum ei sit mysterium incarnationis, exinanitionis & ex- altationis Filii Dei explicare: quod in Novo Testa- men. in universa terra deprædicandum erat, quem- admodum id in Spiritu David prævidit. Jam quod ex ore infantium Deus sibi perfecerit laudem, quod impleri cœperit in illis, qui adventum Messiæ læta acclamatione exceperunt, Christus ipse infallibilis interpres docuit Matth. 21, 16. quod per Apostolos quoque ac successores eorum magis magisqve com- pletum novimus. Quæ laus Dei firmiter fundenda est propter hostes ejus, cum Judæos, tum gentiles, ad compescendum שטן unicum κατὰ ἀντονομασίας di- ctum, Diabolum, qui ita sæpe in Nov. Testam. vo- catur, ὁ ἐχθρὸς & ὁ σατανᾶς. Conf. Job. 1, 7. 1. Chr. 25, 1. Zach. 2, 2. Matth. 13. 39. Luc. 10, 19. & ultorem sui, quo nomine plerique hæreticum seipsum & alios in exitium præcipitantem intelligunt, quamvis iterum Satanas intelligi possit; qui se ulturus toti generi humano struxit, atque etiamnum struit perniciosissi- fimas insidias. Ulterius quid est, quod operi crea- tionis præferri queat, nisi id quod in nostri repara- tione factum? Quoniam videbo cælos tuos, opera di- gitorum tuorum, Lunam & Stellas, quæ tu fundasti: hoc est, cum illa respicio, quæ vere admiranda sunt, ac præcipua in operibus tuis; cum tempore imprimis nocturno meditationibus aptissimo, sole sub hori- zontem digresso, Lunam & stellas intueor, non pos- sum, quin exclamem, quid est homo, quod memor es ejus, & filius hominis, quoniam visitas eum? Quo pa- cto mirabitur magis Psaltes exaltationem Filii homi- nis, super omnia opera manuum Domini, quam ipsa præcipua & summa manuum Domini opera in visi- bili orbis machina. Aliis tamen, etiam B. Luthe- ro, Bugenhagio, Osiandro, Gesnero, & Vinariensibus pa- raphrastis placet sensus allegoricus, ut per Lunam Ec- clesiam, Cant. 6, 9. Ap. 12, 11. per Stellas Doctores & fideles instar Syderum micantes in orbe Ap. 1, 16. Phil. 2, 15. intelligantur, atque cælorum nomine & per opera digitorum Dei pariter Ecclesia, quæ sæpe re- gnum cælorum, quando ex futura imprimis gloria æ- stimatur, vocari solet, ac membra ejusdem, indigi- tentur, quæ Spiritu Sancto, digito illo Dei, ob varia dona, plurali digitorum nomine designato, in rege- neratione & renovatione formantur Matth. 12, 18. Tit. 3, 5. 6. Quæ opera vere admiranda sunt ob de- corem ac splendorem, quem a Deo habent; Sed longe illustrior & infinitis parasangis eminentior est gloria, quæ in Christo effulget, exaltato super omnia opera manuum Dei. Sed simplicior est prior expli- catio, quæ etiam probata Brentio: neque enim fa- cile licet a proprietate verborum recedere, ac vi- dentur comparari hic opera manuum Domini cum illo, qui super omnia manuum Domini opera consti- tutus est, gloria quæ in illis elucet, & quæ in ipso Domino rerum omnium conspicua est. Hæc au- tem de Christo intelligenda esse tam luculenter testatur Apostolus Ebr. 2, 5. seq. ut non possit id doceri luculentius. Cui proinde in os contradi- cunt, qui de alio, quam de Christo explicant. Et quid ex ipsis verbis Psalmi certius, quam quod describa- tur Christi cum exinanitio, tum exaltatio? Quis e- nim est, de quo hæc præsenti loco dici queant, defice- re eum fecisti parum מאלהים a Deo, vel etiam ab Angelis, præter Christum, qui exiguo tempore dereli- ctus a Deo fuit, Angelisque inferior factus est? De A- damo dici utique non potest, quod exiguo tempore factus sit inferior Angelis: nam ita conditus est ho- mo, ut quod erat, non exiguo esset tempore, sed per- petuo. Nec derelictus ille a DEO fuit, sed ipse Deum dereliquit sponte.

Neque ullum locum habet glossa illa Rabbini- co-Calviniana Grotii: Minuisti eum paulo minus ab Angelis, id est, dominantem in res has inferiores eum fecisti. Nam agitur hic de κενώσει & ταπεινώσει, qua homo & Filius hominis ad exiguum tempus a Deo relictus, vel, uti Apostolus interpretatur, angelis, quorum Dominus fuerit, inferior factus sit: Perver- se itaque de sublimitate, & excellentia hominis ex- plicatur, quod de humiliatione loquitur. Tum ve- ro præsupponitur commentum Rabbinicum & Ari- stotelicum, quod Angeli rebus superioribus, puta cæle- stibus, quos illi excogitarunt, orbibus præsint, ceu motores & directores eorundem, homo vero in infe- rioribus dominetur. Dominatur non tantum in res inferiores Filius hominis, de quo sermo est, sed etiam in res cæteras, & in opera manuum Domini universa potestatem habet: omnia subjecta illi sunt: CONSTI- TUISTI eum super OPERA MANUUM TUA- RUM: quibus sane comprehenduntur etiam cæli Pf. 102, 26. OMNIA SUBJECISTI sub pedibus ejus. Quibus verbis distincte jam exprimitur Filii homi- nis exaltatio κατ' ἀντίθεσιν; ut prioribus insinuata fuerat ejusdem exinanitio. Nam hæc aperte sunt opposita: infra Angelos abjectum esse: & constitutum esse super omnia, Angelosque etiam ipsos sibi subjectos habere. Nam qui omnia dicit, nihil excludit: neque dubium est Angelos inter opera manuum Dei quo- que contineri Ps. 103, 21. 22. Quod autem pecu- liariter exprimantur animantia terrestria, volucria, natantia; id ideo fieri credendum est, ut sciamus Dominium ejus extendere sese etiam ad ea, quæ extra Ecclesiam sunt, & Messiam illis quoque domi- nari (sed longe eminentiori ratione,) quibus Adam in statu integritatis præerat, ut dominium amissum no- bis etiam, membris suis, vicissim restituat. Confer Gen. 1, 26. c. 3, 23. Rom. 14, 6. 14. 1. Cor. 8, 9. 10. 25. 26. Adhæc cum miratur Hieropsaltes, quid est homo ille afflictus & ærumnosus, quod memor es ejus, eo spectat illa admiratio, quod is, qui tam abjectus fuit in exi- nanitione, tanta gloria & honore deinceps coronatus sit, ut omnia sub pedibus ejus subjiciantur, omnibus- que ipse Dominus summus præficiatur.

Sed quid multis? Habemus enim hic inter- pretem omni exceptione superiorem Spiritum Sanctum, qui locum præsentem apertissime de Chri- sto explicat, & verba illa, minuisti eum paulo minus ab Angelis, non de Dominio paulum Angelico inferiori, sed de exinanitione ejus interpretatur, nec illud βραχύ τι Ebr. 2, 5. seq. de gradu distantiæ exiguo, sed de exiguo tempore declarat: Non enim, inquit, Angelis (sed Christo) subjecit Deus orbem terræ futu- rum, de quo loquimur. Testatus est autem in quo- dam loco quis, dicens: Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus, aut Filius hominis: quoniam visitas eum: ἠλάτ- τωσας ἀυτὸν βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλες, δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας ἀυτὸν: Hæc e Psalmo ita expli- cantur v. 9. τὸν δὲ βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλες ἠλατ- τωμένον βλέπομεν Ἰησῶν διὰ τὸ πάθημα τῶ θα- νάτω δοξῇ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφανωμένον. Quis hic non videt τὸ ἠλάττωσαν ἀυτὸν per τὸ πάθημα τῶ θα- νάτω exponi, & ἐλάττωσιν illam esse ipsam ταπεί- νωσιν καὶ κένωσιν Christi, quæ maxime in passione & morte ejusdem conspicua est?

Rursus quæ de honore & gloria cecinit Psaltes, non de alio, quam de Christo intelligi posse, inter- pretatio Apostolica λευκάδι φωνῆ proclamat: De eo enim intelligenda sunt, qui coronatus est post passio- nem mortis, gloria & honore: cui subjecta sunt O- MNIA, citra exceptionem: (in eo enim, inquit A- postolus, quod omnia ei subjecit, nihil dimisit, non sub- jectum ei) cui orbem futurum etiam subjecit, utpote, in quo videbimus OMNIA ei subjectum iri: Nunc enim, ut Apostolus ait, nec dum videmus omnia subjecta ei. Quam universalitatem absolutam & maxime Ca- tholicam urget etiam S. Apostolus 1. Cor. 15, 21. atque hunc Psalmum iterum ibidem explicat de Christo, docens, quod tum demum plenum complemen- tum sequuturum sit, cum mors, quæ hostis est novis- simus, ipsi subjicietur, quem Christo subjectum iri per demonstrationem Spiritus ex hoc oraculo con- cludit: Si omnia ei subjicientur, mortem etiam eidem subjici oportet. Novissima autem inimica destruetur mors: OMNIA ENIM subjecit sub pedibus ejus. Cum autem dicat, OMNIA subjecta sunt ei, sine dubio præ- ter eum, qui subjecit ei omnia. Docet ergo, nihil excipi præter unum Deum, qui ei omnia subjecit: ac in novissimo die maxime constiturum, & plenissime impletum iri subjectionem omnium. Similiter de Christo explicatur hic locus Eph. 1. & quidem ita, ut summa & immensa ejus potestas super omnia, & impri- mis super Ecclesiam inde probetur v. 20. Suscitans illum a mortuis, & constituens ad dextram suam in cæ- lestibus supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem, & omne nomen, quod no- minatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro. Et omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus. Quæ verba e Psal- mo nostro desumta sunt. Istis ergo OMNIBUS comprehendi omnem principatum & potestatem, & virtutem & dominationem Angelicam, interprete A- postolo certi sumus. Ecquis jam amplius dubitabit de solo Christo hoc oraculum intelligendum esse, & quum de uno subjecto totus agat Psalmus, de solo Christo eundem explicari debere? Conf. hic Dn. D. Hunnii nostri Anti-Pareus alter p. 344. seqq. quo in Calvino Judaizante ac Hyperaspiste Pareo glossa Grotii jam profligata est.

Notamus solum, quod sibi ipsi non constet Grotius. Hic enim unice de Adamo in primo sta- tu explicat Psaltis verba. In Annotatis vero ad Ebr. 2, 5. sensu primum obvio de Adamo & SEMINE E- JUS (quod in illo integritatis statu non vixit) ex- plicat, sensu vero mystico de Christo & semine ejus ac- cipit. Ibi Adamum pauxillum inferiorem Angelis factum dicit, quia dominium habet solum in res infe- riores, hic vero ob conditionem corporis, & quia ut cætera animantia de ludo factus. Ibi illud מעט tan- tum explicat PAUXILLUM, hic vero ait, signifi- care etiam id in hoc eodem loco AD TEMPUS EXI- GUUM, atque ita eam vocem sumi Ose. 1, 4. & alibi. Jam ut de posteriori hac explicatione primum dica- mus, neutiquam admittendum, dicti hujus gemi- num esse sensum: literalem, vel primum obvium, & mysticum: quia hypothesis ista Papistica, de gemino ejusdem dicti sensu perspicuitati ac certitudini Scri- pturæ penitus adversatur: Neque hic, quod alterum est, de Adamo sermo esse potest, quia Adam Filius hominis dici nequit, nec illa, quæ de Filio hominis hic dicuntur Adamo competunt: Sed unice Christo conveniunt; ob quem in universa terra celebratur nomen Dei: de quo ex ore lactentium etiam laudem sibi perfecit Deus: qui etiam ærumnosus fuit, quum A- dam in primo statu ærumnarum fuerit expers. Nec Adam ad tempus diminutus infra Angelos fuit, sed

Christus: nec Adamo, sed uni Christo omnia sub- dita sunt sub pedibus ejus: Et quis admittet illam glossam: Adamum pauxillum inferiorem Angelis corporis conditione, honore & gloria coronatum es- se, quia intellectu & voluntate libera ornatus fuit? Num Adam fuit, antequam intellectu & voluntate libera ornaretur? quemadmodum Filius hominis ἐλαττώμενθν παρ᾿ ἀγγέλων, fuit, priusquam gloria coronaretur? Num Adamo subjecta fuere omnia, etiam mundus futurus, etiam dominatio- nes, potestates, & virtutes Angelicæ, quemadmo- dum αὐτῷ, ILLI, de quo sermo hic est, subjecta sunt omnia, etsi id nondum plene videamus? Nam quod illud αὐτῷ nunc nondum videmus IPSI subjecta omnia, Grotius de homine generaliter consi- derato, de Adamo & Semine, vel posteris ejus intelligit, id repugnat prorsus contextui Apostolico, in quo ne uno verbulo Adami aut posteritatis ejus mentio facta, illudque αὐτῷ ad præcedens αὐτῦ omnia subjecisti sub pedes EJUS, se aperte refert, quod Apostolus accipit de Christo, quem supra omnia constitutum jam dicit, etsi nunc nondum id videamus. Et annon pessime illa detorquen- tur, constituisti eum supra opera manuum tuarum, ad Adamum super armenta & pecora constitutum? Si- quidem opera manuum Domini tam late pateant, ut Angelos etiam, ac τὴν οἰκυμένην τὴν μέλλεσαν complectantur, teste Apostolo, etsi pecora & ar- menta etiam comprehendantur sub isto generali nomine, ac certa de causa peculiariter expriman- tur. De Adamo ne apex penes Apostolum, qui ista omnia de uno Christo explicat, ac pronomine αὐτῷ unum Christum, (quia non nisi de uno subje- cto loquitur per totum contextum) intelligit:imo aperte docet, non posse nisi de Christo uno Psal- mum Davidicum intelligi, vel ut rectius dicam, supponit, atque assumit id penes Ebræos, velut ὁμολογόμενον, de eo unice accipiendum esse, qui post exigui temporis ἐλάττωσιν infra Angelos, supra OMNIA, ipsosque Angelos constitutus sit. Quod quum in nullo alio completum sit, nisi Christo, de illo unice intelligendum. Finge cum Grotio, sen- su literali Davidem de Adamo loquutum esse, quomo- do convinci oraculo isto potuissent Ebræi? annon excipere licuisset, nihil sublime illis verbis exprimi, Adamum describi corporis conditione infra Angelos fa- ctum, sed intellectu & voluntate ornatum supra opera manuum DEI, id est, armenta & pecora constitu- tum, quæ omnia ipsi subjecta fuerint? Quod Gro- tius dicit, sensu mystico referri id debere ad Christum, id neque concedendum, quia unius dicti unus est sensus, & perabsurdum est tam disparatas si- gnificationes earundem vocum in eodem dicto ob- tinere, v. g. ut Filius hominis Christum notet, ac simul notet Adamum, qui nullius nisi DEI Filius fuit, ut מעט βραχύ τι alium sensum, ut ipse lo- quitur habeat, κατὰ πόδας, alium κατὰ τὸ ἀλλη- γορέμενον (quod sæpe fieri ait, sed nullo exemplo probare potuit) illo modo sumtum significet pau- xillum, hoc vero modo sumtum significet ad tempus exiguum, ut ἐλάττωσις & de inferioritate humanæ speciei infra Angelos, quoad corpus, & de passione mor- tis Messiæ intelligatur; & tum de dominio Adami su- pra inferiora (uti hic accipit) tum de exinanitione Christi sermo sit: ut opera manuum Domini & de solis inferioribus creaturis de Adamo, & rursus de superioribus, etiam Angelis ipsis, de Christo expli- centur; ac similiter OMNIA illa de armentis ac pecoribus tantum, nec non simul de omnibus ab- solute, etiam mundo futuro. Adde quod frustra hic ad traditiones se recipiat Grotius, probaturus ex iisdem, quod sensu mystico referri debeant ista ad Christum, ab autoritate Hebræorum sapientum, qui ea retulerunt mystico sensu ad Messiam, & semen ejus. Unde enim demonstrabit traditiones illas? Nam si recentiores Rabbinos Grotius Judaizans hic laudet, nihil id ad Ebræos facit, qui Aposto- lica ætate vixere: ab illis autem accepit geminum ejusdem dicti sensum, literalem & mysticum; nisi forte laudem illam Papistis deferat, quibus cum Judæis communis est ista opinio. Porro si de A- damo cecinit in statu integritatis, quomodo id ad se- men & posteritatem Adami, quæ orbata felicitate pri- mæva est, abripitur: Si de Messia, quomodo ad se- men Messiæ trahitur? num fidelibus hic titulus, filius hominis, num illa ἐλάττωσις βραχύ τι παρ᾽ ἀγγέ- λες facta, num constitutio super angelos & opera manuum Domini, num subjectio OMNIUM sub pedibus eorum, & omnium quidem citra exceptio- nem, ut nihil non subjectum sit, præter illum, qui sub- jecit omnia, illis competit? Ulterius, etsi Adam typus constituatur Christi, vel potius cum ipso con- feratur, id tamen sensu disparato fit Rom. 5, 14. 1. Cor. 15, 45. nec quicquam cum Grotiano typo com- mercii habet, cujus penes Apostolum nec vola, nec vestigium. Ut ab Adamo peccatum & conde- mnatio, ita ex adverso a Christo Justitia & justifica- tio, secundum Apostolum: Uti gerimus hic ima- ginem Adami: ita portabimus olim cælestis Adami imaginem, autore eodem Apostolo. Sed unde docebit Grotius, quod Adam typus in eo Christi fuerit, quod dominium in res mundi inferio- ris ipsi datum, imago fuerit dominii ejus, quod in mundo supremo habet Christus, quod id, quod A- dam corporis conditione inferior pauxillum Angelo (cujus tamen corpus non mortale, sed immorta- le in statu integritatis fuit Sap. 1, 13. & 2, 23. Rom. 5, 12.) imago fuerit ejus, quod ad tempus exiguum Christus infra Angelos in passione mortis minor factus fuerit: quod id, quod Adamus intellectu & volun- tate libera ornatus fuit, imago extiterit ejus, quod Christus cognitione plenissima rerum divinarum, vo- luntate perfecta, potestate admirabili coronatus est, (quemadmodum verba, gloria & honore coro- nasti eum, quæ de immensa & infinita gloria agunt, interprete hic Ephes. 1, 1. 2. Apostolo, ac suffra- gantibus aliis Scripturæ locis Dan. 7, 14. seqq. Joh. 1, 14. cap. 5, 12. seqq. cap. 17, 3. Matth. 28, 19. &c. de finita gloria perverse explicat) quod id, quod Adam supra armenta & pecora constitutus fuit, ima- go fuerit ejus, quod Christus supra Angelos poni de- buit: quod id quod Adamo tenui modo subjecta omnia fuerint, imago fuerit ejus, quod Christo absolute omnia sub pedibus subjecta sint. Ubi, obsecro, hæ ty- picæ adumbrationes in Scripturis exponuntur, aut leviter saltim insinuantur? Et quomodo Adam in statu integritatis typus fuit Christi, qui utique non venisset, si Adam in statu integritatis perstitisset, nec nisi post lapsum ei in remedium promissus est, ut generis humani adversus Sathanam Goel, & Hyperaspistes. Nulla ergo typi ante lapsum causa, nulla ratio locum habuit. Typi Messiæ promissio- ni additi sunt, illustrandi gratia. Ante peccatum vero promissio Messiæ nulla extitit, nec locum ha- bere potuit. Jam cum semen & posteros Adami se- minis Messiæ typos etiam facit Grotius, absurditati- bus pluribus sese involvit: Sed non est, ut ista ad vivum resecemus omnia. Fatetur felicitatem il- lam Adami, quod dominatum in res inferiores habue- rit, eid, in statu primo omnia sponte paruerint, per pec- catum amissam esse: in posteris ergo ea locum non habuit. Proinde in annotatis Ebr. 2, 6. τῆ ὑποθέσει

δηλώων dominium illud per lapsum diminutum, tantum non plane ademtum dicit, & ad Cyrillum Ep. ad Calosarium cont. Anthropomorphitas, & Isidorum l. 3. Epist. 95. provocat. Fatetur, illa verba Psalmi subjecisti OMNIA sub pedibus ejus, nec in Adamo, nec in quoquam ex posteris ejus effectum habuisse nisi tenuem: & tamen de illis intelligi vult, eumque sensum PRIMUM obvium dicit; ac majus aliquid in illis latere ait, sensum nempe mysticum, de subjectione omnium creaturarum. At ille sensus non latet, aut occultatus est in illis verbis, sed primum statim obvius est; quum illa verba, subjecit illi omnia, per se & secundum literam inferant omnium creaturarum, & operum manuum Dei omnium quæ sunt, præter unum illum, qui subjecit ei omnia, subjectionem, quod δῆλον MANIFESTUM ex illis verbis esse, pronunciat Apostolus 1, Cor. 15, 27. Nihil ergo tenue illis verbis secundum sensum primum obvium, sed tanta majestas, quanta in Adamum, aut ullum ex posteris ejus non cadit, ac ne in Angelum quidem ullum, sed quæ uni Filio hominis Messiæ propria est, significatur; ut δῆλον manifestum omnino sit, non posse sensu literali, & primum obvio Psalmum, qui per totum contextum de eodem subjecto agit, nisi de Messia explicari. Quem solum etiam sensum argumentativum esse, fateri oportet; ex sensu typico, mystico, & allegorico, mere fictitio, qualis Grotii est, nihil concludere potuisset Apostolus.

Antequam hinc abeamus, Riveti etiam offuciæ, quibus pro glossa non absimili Calvini glaucomam facit imperitis, discutiendæ. Præterierat ipse prorsus Psalmum præsentem, ut & Psal. 118. cum Decadem Psalmorum Propheticorum de mysteriis Evangelicis commentario illustraret: unde præsumi poterat, quod duos illos Psalmos pro talibus non haberet: Sed in altera editione loco Decadis Dodecadem exhibuit, quod hic moneo, quia alicubi Decadem citavi, hoc est, priorem editionem. Cæterum si penitius rem introspicias, parum Prophetici, aut mysterii Evangelici Psalmo nostro relinquit in commentario suo, ut dicis causa tantum videatur eundem isto titulo ornare. Sententiam suam ita proponit Tom. 2. oper. in Dodec. Ps. p. 32. Psalten de beneficiis Dei erga genus humanum, a Deo supra alias creaturas sublunares exaltatum admirabundum disserere: Spiritu autem Prophetico illustratam mentem ad eum evexisse, in quo maxime elucere debuit generi humano præstita gratia, tanquam in capite omnium, qui hæredes terræ, & cœli incolæ fieri debuerunt. Negat proinde, se pedibus posse in eorum ire sententiam, qui totum hunc Psalmum immediate & proprie secundum primum & literalem sensum ad Christum referunt: suæque sectæ hominibus accedit, qui censent, primum agi de magnitudine gloriæ Dei, lucente in creatione & conservatione rerum omnium, sed maxime in hominum procreatione & beneficentia erga geng humanum, ita ut tamen cumulus omnium benedictionum in Messia exhibendo suo tempore celebretur: imo addit: qui aliter procedunt, eos cogi alienas interpretationes comminisci, & a sensu literæ deviare, ut verba Prophetæ torqueant ad suas cogitationes. Sed quid mirum Calvini discipulum ita pronunciare de illis, qui Apostolum in explicando Psalmo sequuntur, quum Calvinus Magister ejus de Apostolo ipso non mitius aut religiosius judicarit, quod nempe κατ’ ἐπεξεργασίαν ad suum institutum DEFLECTAT, quod ALIO SENSU dictum fuerat. Non juxta cogitationes proprias, sed secundum interpretationem Apostolicam nos verba Psaltis accipere, neque opus esse ad eam susti- stinendam, ut a literæ sensu discedamus, sed ex ipsa litera eundem fluere, jam luculenter oftendimus. Il- lam autem Riveti glossam ita a litera Prophetæ devia- re, ut verba ejusdem prorfus detorqueat ad Calvini depravationem, Apostolocæ etiam interpretationi palam contradicere, ex his, quæ dicta sunt, itidem constare arbitramur. Nam non de Adamo, non de humano genere universo, sed de certo individuo, de Fi- lio hominis, peculiariter ita in Scripturis dicto, aper- tissime sermo est: nec alterius describitur exaltatio, quam ejusdem: utpote qui solus SUPER OPERA manuum Domini constitutus, cui soli OMNIA subje- cta sunt, qui etiam solus, postquam exiguo tempore in- fra Angelos minoratus fuit, gloria & honore isto co- ronatus est, ut Dominus constitueretur super omnia. Quæ universa de uno subjecto loqui, si quis neget, Solem in meridie lucere negabit.

Textus nimis luculentus est: quem ita exhibet Rivetus: Quid est homo, quod recorderis EJUS, & Filius hominis, quod visites EUM? Siquidem deficere fecisti EUM paululum ab Angelis, gloria & decore co- ronasti EUM: Dominari fecisti EUM operibus manu- um tuarum: OMNIA posuisti sub pedibus EJUS. De uno atque eodem subjecto hæc, indivulso nexu co- hærentia, loqui pronomina EJUS & EUM potenter convincunt. Quomodo vero de genere humano id dici potest, ut non a sensu literæ devies, vel verba Pro- phetæ torqueas, quod constitutum id sit super OPERA manuum Domini universa, quod OMNIA sub pedibus ejus posita sint, aut quod tanta gloria & honore coro- natum id sit, postquam paululum vel exiguo tempore infra Angelos diminutum fuerit? Quomodo per Fi- lium hominis genus humanum intelligi potest, aut num Adam ad genus humanum non pertinebat, qui certe Filius hominis non erat, nisi Præ-Adamitarum fabricatore deterius Adamo parentem assignes. Sed ita parenti primo, si etiam Filii hominis nomine com- prehendatur, alius parens assignandus, & sic in infi- nitum procedendum fuerit, aut dicere oportebit, non comprehendi omnes homines nomine Filii ho- minis, seu totum genus humanum, quod visitavit Deus. Et ubi vel verbo Psaltes de Adami, aut de procreatione hominum, aut de genere humano hic sese agere indicavit? Ubi supra alias creaturas subluna- res id exaltatum dixit? De exaltatione Filii hominis agitur: Eaque facta non solum supra creaturas sub- lunares, sed super OMNIA: quia OMNIA pedibus ejus subjecta, super universa opera manuum Domini constitutus est. Quibus etiam cælos, ceu opus di- gitorum DEI comprehendit Hieropsaltes, ac nihil omnino hic excipi protestatus est Apostolus.

Vehementer hic se torquent Reformati, & in omnes partes se convertunt. Modo ad hominem hæc referunt in statu integritatis, qui gloria & hono- re coronatus fuerit. Modo hominem post lapsum intelligunt. Quam sententiam Rivetus eligit: quod in statu priori homo non possit dici mortalis & miser, quod voce אנוש notatur, neque tam abjecte debuerit in tanta gloria de eo loqui Prophetæ: quod Filius ho- minis esse non potuerit primus homo, cujus omnes filii sumus, quodque in eo etiam misericordia Dei magis eluceat, quod humanum genus, quamvis lapsum, visi- tare voluerit: Sed quia videt, Apostolum Ebr. 2. v. 6. 1. Cor. 15, 27. de Christo interpretari, mox a genere hu- mano universo, quod ad literam intelligit, se conver- tit Rivetus ad absolute electos, qui Filio Dei dati sunt, ut membra ejus sint, & porro ab his ad Filium Dei, fa- ctum hominis filium, ad quem recte & appositissime ab Apostolo referri, ait. Sed iterum sese a Filio Dei ad electos convertit, atque ea, quæ de hoc solo indi- viduo interpretatur Apostolus, ad omnes electos & fideles referenda dicit, qua in capite suo consideran- tur: Ut ita ferundum Genebrardum a specie ad indi- viduum transierit, sed ea lege, ut ab illo individuo ad speciem redeamus, sed in illo fidelium capite confide- ratam. En Protheum multiformem ! En inter- pretationem cyclicam ! Et hanc pro genuina ven- ditare audent purioris Theologiæ, uti se vocant, Doctores, quia scil. Calvini menti, a qua divelli non facile sese patiuntur, propinquior. Sed si homo lapsus intelligatur, quomodo electi ejus loco substituuntur, num omnis lapsus electus est ? num electi tantum visitati sunt a Deo ? Rursus finga- mus, ἀσύςατα illa cohærere: Quid est homo mi- ser, abjectus, in peccatum prolapsus, & damnationi obnoxius? Et, quid est homo electus & prædestinatus ad æternam gloriam, vel si mavis, quid est homo, ut visitare volueris electos? hos enim solos visitatos hic putat Rivetus, id est, reparatos: quomodo jam Fi- lio Dei non apposite, sed appositissime convenit, seu quod de miseris peccatoribus, seu quod de electis dicitur? num ad miseros peccatores ille pertinet, aut num inter electos est ? quod posterius videtur utique placuisse Riveto; quia ab uno individuo (Christo) ad omnes electos se confert; ideo Christum e nu- mero eorum, quos Deus ad vitam æternam e ge- nere humano in peccato prolapso elegit, consti- tui oportet, in quo etiam dicit MAXIME elucere gratiam generi humano præstitam, tanquam in capite omnium beatorum, unde colligendum relinquere videtur, ejusdem gratiæ Christum participem fa- ctum (etsi MAXIME in illo ea eluceat) cujus nem- pe reliqui participes fiunt e genere humano, ut gra- duum saltem intercedat differentia: quæ παράδοξα recitasse est refutasse. Si vero Paulus appositissime ad Filium Dei verba Prophetica refert, quod ita ab eodem factum, ut de UNO Christo eadem accepe- rit, cui soli subjecta sunt omnia, postquam exiguo tempore infra Angelos minoratus fuit (quod de filio hominis Psalten cecinisse docet) quid certius est, quam quod verba Prophetica de Filio hominis, non nisi de uno Filio Dei accipienda sint, neutiquam autem ad universum genus humanum, ac ne ad o- mnes quidem electos trahi possint, nisi per insignem ςρεβλότητα? Quem enim potiorem habebimus in- terpretem, Calvinum, an Paulum Apostolum ? Por- ro quum Apostolus illud, minorem eum fecisti pau- lisper Angelis, sed gloria & honore coronasti eum, de humiliatione infra Angelos ad exiguum tempus in pas- sione & morte Christi accipiat, nec non de subsequuta ejusdem glorificatione: Rivetus non de exiguo tem- pore, sed de exiguo distantiæ gradu, non de humilia- tione infra Angelos & vera exinanitione, sed de digni- tate proxime accedente ad angelicam dignitatem, quæ non soli Christo, sed homini in genere tribuatur: non de distinctis statibus, ut Apostolus, exinanitionis nempe prævio, & exaltationis subsequente, adeoque non sensu Antithetico illud modicum infra Angelos, & CORONATIONEM gloriæ & honoris cum constitu- tione supra omnia, etiam supra Angelos: Sed ἐξηγη- τικῶς de eodem statu hominis interpretatur, qui nem- pe per visitationem gratiosam, per germen justitiæ Christum, ad dignitatem paulo minorem Angelica eve- ctus, atque ita gloria & honore coronatus sit, & consti- tutus super omnia: quod si non sit Scripturam per- vertere, & in contrarium prorsus sensum detor- quere, quid illud sit me plane ignorare profi- teor.

Videt probe Rivetus, obstare sibi Paulum, sed frustra conciliare tentat τὰ ἀντιφατικὰ, & po- lum Arcticum antarctico copulare. Difficultas, in- quit, in eo reperitur, quod cum sensus literalis (juxta Calvini & Riveti præconceptam opinionem) MO- DICUM illud, quo homo ab angelis imminutus est ad gloriam hominis amplificandam referat, q. d. Tu hominem infirmum ita evexisti, ut fere æqualem An- gelis eum feceris, ut ab eis parum distet, Apostolus id ad mediatorem Christum inflectendo ad ejus humilia- tionem & mortem usque hæc verba accommodet. Sen- sus enim illius hic est: Quamvis supra Angelos fuerit exaltatus, ad modicum tamen tempus fuit humilia- tus, propter passionem & mortem, quam subiit. Ita- que illud βραχύ τι ad tempus refert, non ad qualita- tem, sive dignitatem. Quid vero respondet ad hanc difficultatem? Persistit in sua præconcepta o- pinatione, Prophetam celebrare bonitatem & miseri- cordiam Dei erga genus humanum per peccatum corru- ptum, miseriis obnoxium, & ea dignitate, quam in pri- ma creatione acceperat spoliatum (de quibus ne apex quidem in textu Prophetico, nedum in ἐξηγήσει Apostolica,) cujus nihilominus in illo statu constituti Deus rationem habuerit, ut illud repararet, ac ad pri- stinam imo meliorem dignitatem eveheret (ubi, obse- cro, de reparatione ista in hoc Psalmo verbum, ubi de evectione hominum ad pristinam & meliorem digni- tatem, vel Jota unum habetur? Qui ergo pro sensu literali ista venditat Rivetus?) Atque hunc sensum Propheticis verbis affingit: Sed quæro iterum ite- rumque, quomodo ille conciliari cum ἐξηγήσει Apostolica possit? Respondet Rivetus: Merito A- postolum fundamentum totius illius reparationis in Christo collocare, in quo humana natura, quamvis ad carnis peccati similitudinem assumta, post humiliatio- nem exaltata fuit in capite, & per caput exaltabitur in membris, ut quæcunque de Domino illo postea dicuntur, in secundo illo Adamo primo & in se considerentur, aliis postea, qui ei sunt insiti, communicanda, ad lau- dem gloriosæ gratiæ Dei, ut ejus gloria magnificetur in universa terra, & tandem ponatur super cælos ipsos, ad locum illum beatorum, in quem Christus ascendit, & suis omnibus domicilia paravit. Sed hoc est non corrigere tantum Prophetæ, sed etiam Apostoli verba. Non enim Apostolus FUNDA- MENTUM reparationis generis humani, ceu in Psalmo descriptæ exponit, sed verba ipsa Psalmi, probationis loco, de Christi passione, vel humi- liatione ad exiguum tempus, & sequuta ejusdem glorificatione, omniumque sub pedes ejus subje- ctione adducens, de eadem ea intelligenda esse, plenis, ut ita dicam, buccis prædicat. Nemo negat, fundamentum reparationis nostræ in Christo collocandum esse. Sed de reparatione nostra secun- dum literam in verbis Psalmi agi, Apostolum au- tem non rem illam, quam tractat Psaltes, sed fundamentum solum ejusdem designare, ac quum Psalmus agat de humani generis reparatione, ver- ba quidem Psalmi adducere, sed non urgere aut premere verba ejus, vel sensum eorum genuinum; testari solum, fundamentum istius reparationis in Christo quærendum esse, id aperte refragatur tracta- tioni Apostolicæ: in qua si uspiam, premuntur & ur- gentur ipsa verba Psaltis, non vero disquiritur, aut explicatur, quidnam eorum fundamentum sit, quæ Psaltes cecinit, etsi a Psalte in verbis ejus non attin- gatur. Constituit Apostolus primum thema suum, quod probatum it e Psalmo: quod nempe Christo, non Angelis SUBJECERIT Deus orbem futurum: tum adfert in testimonium verba Psaltis: Testatus est autem in quodam loco quis, dicens: Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus, aut Filius hominis, quoniam visi- tas eum? Minuisti eum paulisper infra Angelos: glo- ria & honore coronasti eum: & constıtuisti eum super opera manuum tuarum, OMNIA SUBJECISTI sub pedibus ejus. Ratio illationis luculentissima est, ex dicto de omni: Cui OMNIA subjiciuntur, illi etiam orbis terræ futurus subjiciatur, oportet. At Christo, etsi paulum infra Angelos minorato subjecta sunt omnia. Ergo etiam Christo (non Angelis, nedum hominibus) orbem terræ futurum subjici oportet. Majorem propositionem, verba Prophetæ premens & urgens, ita confirmat: in eo enim quod OMNIA ei subjecit, nihil dimisit non subjectum ei. Atque ut omne præscindat du- bium, ac prædictioni Davidicæ veritatem con- stare doceat, κατ' ἀνθυποφορὰν objicit, vel cer- te præoccupat, evidentioris demonstrationis gra- tia: Nunc autem necdum videmus OMNIA subjecta EI (de Christo loquitur, & de eo Psaltem loquu- tum esse, indicat. Idem enim subjectum omnia pronomina hic referunt non diversum.) Eum au- tem qui βραχύ τι exiguo tempore infra Angelos mi- noratus est, videmus JESUM, (ita verba urget Prophetæ, ac de quo loquantur, ostendit, nempe de JESU.) per passionem mortis gloria & honore co- ronatum. Id ergo dicit: Nondum utique vide- mus, quomodo illud impletum sit, quod prædi- xit Psaltes, quod OMNIA prorsus Christo sub- jecta sint (id enim in altero seculo plene ac palam videbitur, cum etiam novissimus hostis mors ei sub- jicietur, teste eodem Apostolo 1. Cor. 15. v. 20.) videmus tamen id impletum esse juxta Prophetæ vaticinium, & quod exiguo tempore Christus infra Angelos minoratus fuerit in passione, & quod post- ea honore & gloria coronatus sit, unde dubitare non possumus, plene etiam id impletum iri; ut nem- pe agnoscamus, OMNIA subjecta ei, adeoque e- tiam futurum terræ orbem, quod palam visuri su- mus in novissimo die & vita æterna, teste Apo- stolo in loco parallelo 1. Cor. 15. Non ergo tan- tum exaltatam humanam Christi naturam post hu- miliationem docet Apostolus, sed in Psalmi verbis illam cum humiliationem, tum subsequutam exal- tationem traditam esse testatur, imo ex iisdem de- monstrat eandem, ac vaticinium illud suum com- plementum obtinuisse, docet. Nihil autem in istis quidem Psalmi verbis, prout ab Apostolo addu- cuntur, de toto humano genere, nihil de ejusdem hu- miliatione infra Angelos, nihil de ejusdem exaltatio- ne ad pristinam dignitatem traditur, nihil tale in il- lis tradi ab Apostolo docetur. Et quum conten- dat Rivetus, in literali sensu Prophetam non agere de Christo, ejusque humiliatione & exaltatione, quid restat, quam ut aperte dicat, Apostolum, qui ipsissi- ma verba Psaltis eo refert, a literæ sensu deviare, & verba Psaltis inflectere vel potius eo detorquere, de quo ipsa non loquuntur; Admittit certe Apostolum ad Mediatorem Christum ea INFLECTENDO, ad ejus humiliationem accommodare, quia scil. vidit ab hoc ἐγκλήματι non abhorruisse Calvinum suum, in Psalm. p. m. 40. Quum hic de præstantia hominum disserat Propheta, & dicat eos ad Deum prope accede- re; Apostolus ad Christi exinanitionem TRAHIT. Item: Quod de BREVI EXINANITIONE deinde tractat Apostolus, non est exegeticum, sed κατ' ἐπε- ξεργασίαν ad suum institutum DEFLECTIT, quod ALIO SENSU dictum fuerat. Sed hoc est non A- postolum, sed ipsum etiam Spiritum S. criminari: ac sibi non minus quam ipsi palam contradicere. Nam annon aperta contradictio hæc: Apostolus AP- POSITISSIME ad Christum hæc verba Psaltis refert: Et, Apostolus INFLECTIT verba Psaltis, vel cum Calvino, ad institutum suum deflectit, quod ALIO SENSU dictum fuerat. Sed in ipsis etiam Psaltis verbis sensu paraphrastico reddendis con- tradicit sibi Rivetus: Sit ergo, inquit hujus loci sensus paraphrasticus, si post consideratio- nem magnifici illius exercitus cœlestis ad humanam naturam contemplandam oculos mentis convertamus; Quid est homo, quod ejus digneris rationem aliquam habere, tam humilis & abjecti, quod eum volueris visitare per germen illud, sive orientem ex alto in terras missum? Venit tamen ille, assumta hac in- firma hominis natura, in qua minor Angelis fa- ctus (quem alias adorant omnes Angeli Dei) pro- pter mortalitatem, cui se subjecit, & mortem igno- miniosam, quam passus est, ad modicum tempus; Sed paulo post gloria & honore fuit coronatus, in perpetuum duraturis, tanquam eorum caput, quos ejusdem gloriæ facit participes in seipso, penes quem solum dominium illud residet, cujus fructus ad omnia membra Christi redundat, & amplius redundabit. Hæc optime conveniunt ad ea, quæ sequuntur, quæ OMNIA Spiritu Prophetico tanquam præsentia vi- dit Propheta, quæ certo futura erant, & ab æter- no a DEO decreta & præparata. Hactenus Rive- tus. Si hic sensus Paraphrasticus est verborum Prophetæ, optime conveniens etiam illis quæ sequun- tur, & ea OMNIA Prophetico Spiritu hic prævidit, adeoque his verbis prædixit (non enim quid alias præviderit aut prædixerit, sed quid hic prædi- ctum sit, quæritur) oportet ea omnia ad sensum literalem (hic enim paraphrasticus est sensus, an- tecedentibus & consequentibus optime congruens, juxta prævisionem & suggestionem Spiritus Pro- phetici in vaticiniis traditus) pertinere. Falsum ergo esse oportet, quod quoad sensum literalem agatur in verbis Psaltis solum de generis humani reparatione. Falsum, quod illa verba paulisper minor factus Angelis de præstantia paulo minori An- gelica generis humani immediate loquantur: quia mi- norem Angelis fuisse Christum ad modicum tempus, asserunt. Falsum, quod verba, gloria & honore coronasti eum, de hominibus immediato sensu (ut alias Calviniani solent sensum geminum immedia- tum & mediatum constituere) agant, quum de glo- ria, qua post humiliationem Christus coronatus est, loquantur. Ubi autem in hoc Psalmo habetur, quod gloriam illam Christus tanquam caput con- sequi, ejusque participes electos in seipso facere debuerit? Et, si penes illum solum dominium il- lud, de quo Psaltes canit, resedit, fructus autem ejus ad fideles tantum redundat, oportet Chri- stum solum esse illum Dominum, de quo Psaltes: omnia subjecisti sub pedibus EJUS; adeoque de illo solo in Psalmo agi, etsi fructus promissi hic Christo dominii redundent ad fideles. Rursus si per ho- minem & Filium hominis sensu literali & paraphrasti- co humana natura, vel genus humanum intelligi- tur, quod visitare dignatur Deus, quo ergo in Psal- mo vocabulo, quo nomine vel verbo germen seu oriens ex alto, vel assumtio humanæ naturæ indica- tur? Et quomodo tam diversum subjectum inge- ritur textui, qui de uno subjecto, de homine, & Filio hominis agit, eumque infra Angelos paulisper minora- tum dicit? Si ergo hic homo est genus humanum, vel homo in peccatum prolapsus, quomodo intelligi per eum potest Christus? Ita undiquaque ἑαυτομαχεῖ sensus ille Riveti paraphrasticus, ut ulteriori confu- tatione non egeat.

Juvat tamen hujus ἑαυτομαχίας Riveti nos adhuc parumper Spectatores esse. Quid enim fiet illis: gloria & honore coronasti eum? Hoc factum est, inquit Rivetus: per eam dignitatem, quam Deus homini tribuit, qua eum præfecit, & dominatorem constituit super alias omnes creaturas, nempe sublu- nares, juxta interpretationem ipsius Dei, hominem creatum in harum omnium possessionem immittentis Gen. 1, 24. Sic ergo nunc de ψιλῶ ἀνθρώπῳ, Do- mino in statu integritatis constituto explicat, quod juxta sensum paraphrasticum hujus loci de Christo post humiliationem gloria coronato cum Apostolo in- terpretatus paulo ante erat. Sic de homine ante la- psum cum Calvino nunc verba Psaltis accipit: quæ vero antea de homine post lapsum cum aliis intelli- genda esse probarat. Alii (verba ejus refero) non putant hominem in statu innocentiæ posse dici morta- lem & miserum, quod voce Enos significatum do- cuimus, neque ita debuisse in tanta gloria & honore, & tam abjecte de eo loqui Prophetam. Et certe Filius hominis, cui HÆC TRIBUUNTUR, non potuit es- se Adam primus homo, cujus omnes Filii sumus. NOBIS ergo, ut aliis nonnullis, posterior illa condi- tio melius intelligi videtur, qua non tantum bonitas Dei, sed etiam misericordia erga homines magis elu- cet, qui humanum genus lapsum, quantumvis indi- gnum, voluit visitare, per eum, quem ab ipsa origi- ne mundi constituit redemtorem totius generis huma- ni. Id ergo jure mirum videtur, quod tam abjectam creaturam, si cum cœlestibus compares, voluerit nihilo- minus ad futuram illam dignitatem evehere, quam postea descripturus est. Si ergo dignitatem illam describit, ad quam hominem, utut mortalem & mise- rum, in peccatum prolapsum, adeoque indignum nihilominus invehere voluit Deus, utique non lo- quitur de dignitate, quam ante miseriam illam &

peccatum ipsum contulit.
