Porro si de dignitate hominis sive in statu integritatis, sive in statu re- parationis illa agant secundum literam, quomodo non deviat a sensu literæ Apostolus, cum ea de Christo accipit, & ex illo, quod omnia sub pedibus ejus subjecta, argumentatur, ut etiam inde eliciat, orbem futurum & Angelos ipsos Christo subjici? Non probat Rivetus, sed refellit eorum sententiam, qui de Christo sensu allegorico tantum, etsi a S. S. in- tento, dicunt ea explicari: Cum Apostolo, inquit, res essēt cum Judæis, quamvis pro ea, qua pollebat rerum divinarum cognitione, potuerit interpretationem alle- goricam veram & aptam proferre, non videtur tamen sua auctoritate talem voluisse Judæis obtrudere, alio- qui non opus fuisset argumentatione & illatione ex con- sideratione propositionis universalis, sed simpliciter, quod alias fecit apud Galatas, professus fuisset, hæc omnia esse ἀλληγορύμενα, ut Gal. 4. versu 24. Præ- terea nihil est quod evincat, eam, quam hominibus indidit, dignitatem in creatione, & cujus etiam non- nulla post peccatum restant vestigia, fuisse figuram gloriæ illius & honoris, ad quam Deus evexit Christum, quia homo in genere consideratus non potest esse Christi typus, qui & ipse homo fuit, & ad quem, qua talis, per- tinebat descriptio humanæ dignitatis. Hæc rectissi- me adversus nonnullos complices suos Rivetus. Aliud itaque interpretamentum præfert : Alii ergo volunt hæc Christo fuisse attributa per quandam accom- modationem, qua iisdem servatis verbis dignitatem Christi voluit describere, ejusque dominium longe supra ea omnia, quæ hominibus communiter sumtis tribuun- tur. Quasi dixisset, si hæc de homine olim dicta fue- runt a Propheta, propter eam creaturarum subjectio- nem, quæ generi humano communis est: Multo melius universaliter hæc sumta adaptari possunt ei, qui con- stitutus est caput hominum & Angelorum &c. Sed accommodationis istius nullum est in Apostolo ve- stigium: qui non accommodat verba Davidis ad alium sensum de Christi gloria, sed ex oraculo & verbis Davidis gloriam illam Christi probat & de- monstrat; argumentari enim illum, & inferre e ver- bis Davidis, fatetur Rivetus. Si vero isto modo argumentaretur: Si hæc de homine olim dicta univer- saliter, ob quarundam tantum creaturarum subluna- rium nempe, subjectionem, utique Christo universaliter omnia, nullis exceptis subjecta erunt, annon illa e- lumbis & inepta foret argumentatio? Quod si vero inferat, uti Rivetus eum inferre vult, multo melius universaliter hæc sumta adaptari ei possunt, qui con- stitutus est caput hominum & Angelorum, annon mera hæc erit αἴτησις τῇ ἐν ἀρχῇ? Nam ita sup- ponitur universaliter omnibus rebus præesse & super omnia constitutum esse Christum, etiam supra Ange- los, & supra orbem futurum, cum statuitur id efferri solum verbis Psalmi; quum tamen id hic non sup- ponat, nec citra petitionem principii supponere potuerit, utpote quod hic probandum sibi sumse- rat Apostolus, quodque omnino e τῷ ῥητῷ verbo- rum Psaltis probat. Nam ea non esse particulari- ter de quarundam creaturarum subjectione, ut vult Rivetus, intelligenda, cum Psaltes ait, omnia subjecisti pedibus ejus, sed universaliter & absolute intelligi debere, hoc axiomate demonstrat: in eo enim, quod OMNIA ei subjecit, nihil dimisit non subjectum ei. Neque vero de alio Psalten loqui, ad aliumq́; sese verba Psaltis accommodare, innuit, sed apertissime in eodem illo subjecto, in eodem Filio ho- minis, cujus pedibus omnia subjecta verbis Psalmi vers. 7. dixit, persistit, & omnia ei ita subjecta docet, ut nihil dimittatur non subjectum ei, vers. 8. illum- que Filium hominis JEsum nominet vers. 9. Quo- rum verborum Davidis universalem significatio- nem, quam secundum literam inferunt, urget pa- riter Apostolus 1. Cor. 15, 27. Nam omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus. Quum autem dicit OMNIA ei sub- jecta, palam est hæc dici, excepto eo, qui ei subjecit o- mnia. Ubi etiam infert Apostolus (quod hic non diffitetur Rivetus) nihil esse, excepto Deo, quod Chri- sto hic (vi oraculi Davidici) non sit subjectum jure, & quod de facto non debeat subjici. Jam vero edisse- rant Calviniani, quomodo sub ista universalitate, quam in verbis Davidis tam solide in binis istis lo- cis urget Apostolus, homini puro, de quo hunc Psalmum agere volunt, omnia subjecta sint? Rive- tus quia urgeri se hic vidit, relicto statu integritatis, de quo Psalten agere dixerat, ad statum æternæ bea- titudinis refugit pag. 40. circa finem explicationis suæ: Tunc enim, inquit, in Christo & per Christum, OMNIA præter Deum, subjiciuntur homini, sed ita deuuo contradicit sibi, utpote qui de ea creatura- rum subjectione, quæ GENERI HUMANO com- munis est, Davidem agere, antea dixit. Item, Psalmum hunc primo & immediate agere de homine puro, respectu mundi præsentis, id est, creatura- rum SUBLUNARIUM. Nunc autem de ELE- CTIS, ac de OMNIBUS præter DEUM absolute ea accipit. Contradicit etiam Scripturæ: quæ urget quidem universalem sensum voculæ, sed ob solum Christum, Christo uni subjecta iri in altero seculo omnia demonstrat. Et quomodo electis tribuetur illud ἀξίωμα Christi, quod ipsi subje- cta, excepto DEO, sint omnia, citra ἀποθέω- σιν? Quod Christo θεανθρώπῳ uni proprium esse demonstrat Apostolus, num hominibus meris vindicandum: Id utiq; ne humanæ quidem naturæ Christi alias relinquunt Calviniani, qui ergo nunc hominibus meris id tribuit Rivetus? Sed satis de offuciis Riveti. Saniora sunt, quæ antecessor e- jus Francifc. Junius in hoc loco tradidit: qui de Chri- sto minore facto Angelis, per passionem mortis, ad bre- ve tempus, sed exaltato ad supercœlestem & INFINI- TAM (quod epithetum velim alii notent Calvina- ni) gloriam, interpretatur. Quamvis in eo aber- ret, quod hic admisceat alios homines, sed secus, quam Rivetus, & inverso ordine, ut primo quidem per hominem & filium hominis intelligatur in se & per se Christus: secundo vero in nobis Christus, & nos in ipso: quia non nisi de uno Christo verba Psaltis & loquuntur aperte, & in N. T. explicantur. Quod hactenus ostensum. Placet autem subjungere Megalandri Lutheri judicium, non modo propter hunc Psalmum, sed etiam propter alia Scripturæ oracula, in quibus nonnulli minus φρονίμως gemi- num sensum admittunt, literalem nempe, & mysti- cum, utrumque a S. S. intentum. Non defuerunt, inquit Tom. 2. Jen. oper. in h. Psalm. fol. 95. qui de humana natura ad Angelos comparata conati sunt intelligere. Sed nos modo consequentia cogimur præ- cedentibus copulare, idque unico & simplici sensu, ideo ex omnibus quæ placent & congruunt, accipiamus, re- lictis cæteris apud suos. Explicat autem iste versus omnino præcedentem, in quo dictum est, Christum E- nos esse in memoria Domini, ut qui contemtus fuit ho- minibus, visitetur a Deo. Ideo sensus est: Dereliqui- sti eum parvulo tempore: Sed cum gloria magna su- scepisti eum, quo ostendisti, quam non fueris ejus obli- tus, nec eum despexeris, ut Psalm. 22. Quoniam non sprevit, neque despexit deprecationem pau- peris. Nam omnino de passione Christi hic Psalmus loquitur, & gloria per passionem obtenta: Ut clare Apostolus ad Ebr. 2. dicit: Eum autem, qui minora- tus est paulo minus ab Angelis, videmus JEsum per passionem honore & gloria coronatum &c. Et paulo minus non ad dignitatem, sed ad tempus per- tinet. Idem enim adverbium Psalm. 2. habuimus: Dum exarserit in brevi ira ejus, id est, cito & post modicum exardescet ira ejus. Et omnino nihil de substantia, differentia, dignitate naturarum hic agi- tur, sed de duratione passionis. Jam verbum minui- sti, quia non reddidit Ebraicum, nobis sonat, ac si eum, qui magnus est, quispiam imminuat, quomodo po- tentia, dignitas, opulentia alicujus minuitur, Johan- nes Reichlin. interpretatur, defecit, defuit, diminu- tum fuit. Ut 3. Reg. 17. Nec lecythus olei minue- tur. Et infra: Nec lecythus olei est imminutus. Ex quo patet, hoc loco significari, Christum derelictum a Deo, ut qui cesserit eum tueri, & ei defuerit, sicut in cruce clamavit: Eli Eli Lama Zabatani: Nam hoc paululum intelligit, scilicet horam illam, de qua dixit: Sed hæc est hora vestra, & potestas tenebrarum. Itaque cum ad hanc usque horam esset potens in ope- re & sermone, subito & parvulo tempore, nempe tri- duo minutus est, & desertus a Deo in hac potentia, sub- jectus infirmitati, & morti quoque & inferno. Et fol. 98. ubi dixerat, magnos aliquot Patres in ea sententia esse, quod de puro homine hic agatur, addit: verum fortiter obstat non modo ad Ebræos Paulus (si forte eam negat esse Pauli) sed & 1. Cor. 15. omnia, inquit, subjicit sub pedibus ejus. Cum autem Scriptura & verbi Dei oporteat esse unum simplicem, constantem- que sensum, ne (ut dicunt) Sacris literis cereum nasum faciamus, justum est, Pauli sensum præferri o- mnium aliorum Patrum sensui sive Ambrosii Augustini, Hieronymi. Quæ omnia graviter ac solide Megalander. Addimus Confessio- nem Johannis Cocceji successoris Riveti in Ca- thedra Lugdunensi in ult. Mofis §. 1020. Quem ad

Deus proprie coronavit gloria & honore intellige, ut cum ad parvum tempus fuerit minor eo, quod est & nominatur Deus, jam non fit minor, ei honor & gloria reddenda est, ut sit nomen Dei ingens in tota terra. PECCANT in hoc Psalmo interpretes ii, qui de primo Adamo (Calvinus, Rivetus, alii) eum agere putant, eumque existimant paulo minorem dici DEO, vel angelis. Certe homo primus haud paulo minor est conditus Deo, & post peccatum factus jam אנוש desperate miser, tum ipse, tum filii hominis, longe eti- am infra seipsos descenderunt, & non retinuerunt do- minium in omnia opera Dei, nedum ut per hominem filium Adami, qua talem, nomen Dei sit ingens in tota terra. Omninoque ABSURDUM est v. 6. ἐλάτ- τωσιν minorationem non opponere cum Apostolo Heb. 2,9. coronationi cum gloria & honore. Hactenus Coccejus. Atque hæc de octavo Psalmo.

## 9:1 Argument
PSALM IX.

Thanksgiving for the great enemy having been defeated.

Ver. 1.

TO THE END CONCERNING THE HIDDEN THINGS OF THE SON) More correctly: to the chief musician: concerning the death of Laban; that is, Nabal; for he wished to hide his name anagrammatically.

This is frivolous, nor is it in any way akin to the truth. For there is no example of such anagrams to be found in the Scriptures. Nor does the history of Nabal described in 1 Sam. 25 sufficiently agree with the argument of the Psalm. Which Grotius could have learned from his R. David Kimchi: Some, he says, say, concerning the death of Nabal, but this is far off. For this Psalm speaks of a great enemy of Israel, but Nabal did no injury to anyone except himself, because he was a miser. R. Solomon also warned of this: This is not correct, to transpose words; also in this Psalm there is no mention of Nabal. Therefore others explain it as 'concerning the death of Goliath,' which they wish to be noted by the word BEIN, because he is called ISH HABEINAYIM, the duelist, who came between the camps 1 Sam. 17:13, 14, which Dr. Tarnovius confirms with arguments in this place. Others more simply understand it concerning the death of Laban, because by that name one of the princes of the nations oppressing Israel was called, as R. Aben-Ezra wishes, or one King of the nations of the earth, as R. Obadiah has it: or Ben one of the Singers 1 Chron. 16, 18. You will see more opinions in Mr. Dr. Tarnovius, as well as in the decuples of the Englishman John Viccars. Some take it as one word עַלְמוּת rendering it youth, as Ps. 48, 15. And thus B. Luther vor die schöne Jugend: so that the particle ע was omitted for the sake of euphony: for youth, or upon the bright youth, by which they understand Christ's bride the Church. Thus it could be said that לַבֵּן is for that Son i.e. concerning the youth, which will be for that Son (by the emphatic He designated as the Son of God, that Son, promised to David). To which Aquila's translation νεανιότητος τɤ υἱɤ and the sixth edition νεανιότης contribute. And thus B. Luther rendered it in the year 1524 in his translation, and in the year 1525 Vol. III. Altenb. fol. 33. A Psalm of David to be sung highly concerning the youth of the Son, that is, concerning the martyrs of Christ the Son of God, which are his young, strong people through faith in death become quite perfect: where he delivered a succinct and nervous paraphrase of the whole Psalm: and Vol. II. Altenb. p. 671. Is a prophecy concerning the Youth, that is of the new children, and of the people of Christ, as also T. V. Altenb. f. 440. on the year 1530. It is a prophecy and doctrine of the Church, how she shall be saved from her persecutors, so that the tyrants perish, and the world remains, for God has a very wondrous way; through the slaughtered he slaughters the living, and through the martyrs he kills the tyrants. Previously indeed, namely in the year 1520, T. I. Altenb. fol. 666, he had rendered that word Almuth, hidden, because the article concerning the Church is hidden: but afterwards he preferred the aforementioned interpretation: in which manner also in the first explanation of the Psalter Bugenhagen interpreted it as beautiful youth, that is, of the faithful from the foundation of the world, citizens of the kingdom of the Messiah, because they are strong warriors with spiritual weapons, conquering by suffering, etc. although in the other exposition he varies the same, rendering it, upon the death (or secrets) of the son, that is, the faithful. But because not לַבֵּן but לָבָן denotes white or beautiful, the praised translation of B. Luther concerning the youth of that Son, of whom, namely, he had sung in Ps. 2, 7, approaches more closely: as Theodoret also noted that the Greeks Symmachus and Theodotion, along with Aquila, expound that word as Son: who likewise, like Augustine, understands the Son of God, and interprets it concerning the victory of Christ obtained in death. Our Gesner followed Luther, because it is taught here that the Church, although she is a tender and unarmed young girl, is nevertheless safe by the protection of Christ as her bridegroom: as also Selneccerus, Cramerus, etc. R. Solomon [interprets it] concerning the youth to be whitened to sins like snow from לִלְבֵּן. Others read עַלְמוּת concerning the secrets of the only-begotten Son, as Augustine: and the Arab concerning the mysteries of the Son, namely the resurrection of the kingdom and the destruction of the sons of disobedience. But in the Hebrew text there are two words, and the Vav Cholem is not present, but the Vau Schurek עַל־מוּת.

Latin:

PSALMUS IX.

Eucharistia pro devicto magno hoste.

Vers. 1.

IN FINEM PRO OCCVLTIS FILII) Rectius: prin- cipi cantorum: super morte Laban; id est, Nabal; voluit enim ἀναγραμματικῶς occultare nomen illius.

FRivolum hoc, nec ullo modo vero est affine. Anagrammatismorum enim talium nullum re- perire est in Scripturis exemplum. Neque satis congruit Historia Nabalis 1. Sam. 25. descripta cum argumento Psalmi. Quod ex suo R. David Kimchi didicisse poterat Grotius: Nonnulli, inquit ille, di- cunt, super mortem Nabalis, sed hoc procul est. Nam hic Psalmus de magno hoste Israelis loquitur, Nabal autem nullum injuria affecit, nisi seipsum, quia avarus erat. Id etiam monuit R. Salomo: Hoc non est re- ctum, transponere vocabula; etiam in hoc Psalmo non fit mentio Nabalis. Ideo exponunt alii, super mor- te Goliath, quam voce בֵּין inter notari volunt, quod vocetur אִישׁ הַבֵּינַיִם duellator, qui venit inter castra 1.Sam. 17, 13. 14. quod adducit R. David Kim- chi & R. Aben Ezra, argumentis confirmat Dn. D. Tarnovius in h. l. Alii simplicius de morte Laban, quod eo nomine unus ex principibus gentium oppri- mentibus Israelem nuncupatus fuerit, uti vult R. Aben-Ezra, vel Rex unus nationum terræ, uti habet R. Obad: vel Ben unus Cantorum 1. Chron, 16, 18. intelligatur. Plures sententias videbis apud Dn. D. Tarnovium, nec non in decuplis Johannis Vic- carsi Angli. Nonnulli pro una voce habent עַלְמוּת reddentes juventam, ut Ps. 48, 15. Atque ita B. Lutherus vor die schöne Jugend: ut particu- la ע euphoniæ causa omissa sit: pro juventute, vel super juventute candida, per quam intelligunt Christi sponsam Ecclesiam. Sic dici poterat לַבֵּן esse Filio illi h. m. de juventute, quæ Filio illi (per He emphaticum designato Filio Dei, Filio illi, Davidi promisso) erit. Quo facit Aquilæ translatio νεα- νιότητος τɤ υἱɤ & sexta editio νεανιότης. Atque ita reddidit B. Lutherus Ann. 1524. in translatione, & Anno 1525. Tom. III. Altenb. fol. 33. Ein Psalm Davids hochzusingen von der Jugend des Sohnes, das ist, von den Märtyrern Christi des Sohnes Gottes, welches sind seine junge, starcke Leute durch den Glauben im Tod recht völlig worden: ubi succin- ctam & nervosam tradidit Psalmi totius paraphrasin: & T. II. Altenb. p. 671. Ist eine Weissagung von der Jugend, das ist von den neuen Kindern, und von dem Volck Christi, ut & T. V. Altenb. f. 440. de Ann. 1530. Ist eine Prophecey und Lehre von der Kir- chen, wie sie von ihren Verfolgern soll errettet wer- den, also dass die Tyrannen untergehen, und die Welt bleibe, denn GOtt hat gar eine wunderliche Weise, durch die Erwürgeten erwürget er die Lebendigen, und durch die Märtyrer bringet er um die Tyrannen. Antea quidem, nempe anno 1520. T. I. Altenb. fol. 666. reddiderat vocem illam Almuth, verborgen, quod absconditus sit articulus de Ecclesia: sed post- modum prædictam interpretationem prætulit: quo pacto etiam in prima explicatione Psalterii Bugen- hagius per speciosam juventutem interpretatus est, h. e. de fidelibus a condito mundo, civibus regni Mesiæ, quod illi spiritualibus armis fortes sint bellatores, pa- tiendo vincentes, &c. etsi in altera expositione idem variet, reddens, super morte (vel occultis) filiique, h.e. fidelis. Quia vero non לַבֵּן sed לָבָן candidum vel speciosum notat, magis accedit laudata B. Lu- theri translatio de juventute Filii illius, de quo sc. Ps. 2, 7. cecinerat: uti etiam Græcos Symmachum, & Theodotionem cum Aquila per Filium vocem istam exponere monuit Theodoretius: qui pariter ut Au- gustin. Filium Dei intelligit, & de victoria Christi in morte obtenta interpretatur. Lutherum sequutus est Gesnerus noster, quod hic doceatur, Ecclesiam, quamvis tenella & inermis juvencula sit, tamen Christi præsidio ceu sponsi sui tutam esse: ut & Selneccerus, Cra- merus, &c. R. Salomo de juventute albificanda ad peccata sicut nix a לִלְבֵּן. Alii legunt עַלְמוּת de secretis Filii unigeniti, uti Augustinus: & Arabs de mysteriis Filii, utpote resurrectione regni & destru- ctione filiorum inobedientiæ. Sed in Ebræo textu duæ sunt voces, neque Vav Cholem habetur, sed Vau Schurek עַל־מוּת.

## 9:1 Addition
Toward the end of the notes on v. 1 of Ps. 9.

A general rule certainly concerning divine judgments from v. 8 to 14 does not allow these to be restricted to one certain history, whence the blessed Luther explained it concerning the vindication of the faithful from their enemies. But against Musculus and Mollerus, who urge the word Zion from v. 15, the blessed Hülsemann opposes this observation: Whenever the glory of God is said to be celebrated in Zion, it is most certain that the discourse is concerning a benefit pertaining to the whole Church. See Ps. 2:6, Ps. 14:7, Ps. 48:3, Ps. 50:3, Ps. 51:20, Ps. 65:2, Ps. 69:36, Ps. 102:14, 17. And the Jews themselves acknowledge in v. 9, 10 that the discourse is not concerning a peculiar but a universal judgment, see Galat. l. 7. c. 6. Menass. Ben Israel on the resurrection. Conf. Ps. 96:13, Ps. 98:10.

Latin:

Sub finem notarum ad v. 1. Ps. 9.

Generalis certe regula de judiciis divinis a v. 8. ad 14. non patitur ad unicam quandam historiam hæc restringi, unde B. Lutherus de vindicandis fide- libus ab hostibus exposuit. Musculo vero & Mollero vocem Sion urgentibus e v. 15. opponit B. Hülse- mannus hanc observationem: Quandocunque gloria Dei dicitur celebrata in Zion, certissimum est sermonem esse de beneficio pertinente ad totam Ecclesiam. Vid. Ps. 2, 6. Ps. 14, 7. Ps. 48, 3. Ps. 50, 3. Ps. 51, 20. Psal. 65, 2. Ps. 69, 36. Ps. 102, 14. 17. Et agnoscunt Ju- dei ipsi v. 9. 10. non de peculiari sed universali ju- dicio sermonem esse, vid. Galat. l. 7. c. 6. Menass. Ben Israel de resurrect. Conf. Ps. 96, 13. Ps. 98, 10.

## 9:16 Addition
v. 17. THE SINNER IS SNARED IN THE WORKS OF HIS OWN HANDS.

The Vulgate, with the LXX and the Syriac, omitted the word הגיון, which the blessed Luther in his commentary and marginal notes understands as 'the Word,' just as in Psalm 19:15, Psalm

92:4, it is taken concerning the study and meditation of the divine word, because the word of God is the means of destroying impiety and the cruelty of tyrants, Psalm 68:12, seq., 2 Cor. 10:5, 6. Not unsuitably, unless the inserted accent draws the final words 'Higgajon Sela' away from the former ones. Cocceius renders and explains it on p. 51: 'Meditation or study is underneath.' v. 17. Not rarely are nouns placed alone by ellipsis of the word 'is' or of a second added word. See Job 36:16, 18, Hos. 10:12. It can therefore be indicated: Jehovah being known, judgment being acted according to his word, the wicked man being implicated, there exists in the Church the study and meditation of the word of God and of sacred learning, from Psalm 1:2, with which Vatablus, Muis, Coppen, Junius, Tarnovius, and from the Hebrews Rashi agree: 'We will meditate on this, Sela.' Bellarmine himself thinks those words should not be neglected, rendering them, 'Meditation always,' because the judgments of God mentioned above are to be meditated upon assiduously and continually.

Latin:

Vers. 17. IN OPERIBUS MANUUM SUARUM COMPREHENSUS EST PECCATOR.

Prætermisit vulgatus cum LXX. & Syro vo- cem הגיון, quam B. Lutherus in Comment. & not. marginal. de Verbo intelligit, uti Psalm. 19, 15. Psal.

92,4. de studio verbi divini & meditatione accipitur, quia verbum Dei medium est destruendæ impieta- tis, & fævitiæ Tyrannorum Psalm. 68,12. seq. 2. Cor. 10,5.6. Non inconcinne, nisi interpositus accen- tus verba postrema Higgajon Sela a prioribus abstra- hat. Coccejus reddit & exponit p. 51. Meditatio sive studium subest. v. 17. Non raro ponuntur no- mina sola per ellipsin ש sive verbi est secundi adjecti. Vide Jobi 36,16.18. Hos.10, 12. Potest igitur indi- cari; Jehovah cognito, judicio secundum verbum ejus acto, improbo, implicito, in Ecclesia existere studium meditationemque verbi Dei & sacræ eruditionis, ex Psalm. 1, 2. cui consonant Vatablus, Muis, Coppen. Junius, Tarnovius, & ex Hebræis Rasche: Medita- bimur hoc, Sela. Bellarminus ipse verba illa non negligenda censet, reddens illa, Meditatio semper, quod judicia Dei supra dicta assidue ac jugiter me- ditanda sint.

## 9:17
Vers. 18.

LET SINNERS BE TURNED INTO HELL) Let them perish miserably. Mystically the Rabbis refer it to the punishments after this life.

Whence it will be proven that the Rabbis do not refer these things to that according to the letter, but only in a mystical sense. R. Solomon notes that R. Abarzabdi explains it thus: they shall be led away from Gehenna to judgment and from judgment they shall return to the lowest order of hell. R. David Kimchi: let them be turned into Gehenna, the Arab interpreter also goes there.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

CONVERTANTVR PECCATORES IN INFER NUM) Male pereant. Mystice ad pœnas post hanc vitam referunt Rabbini.

Unde probabitur, quod non secundum literam, sed mystico solum sensu eo hæc Rabbini referant. R. Salomo ita exponere R. Abarzabdi notat: abdu- centur de gehenna ad judicium & de judicio rever- tentur ad infimum inferni ordinem. R. David Kimchi: convertantur in gehennam, eo etiam abit Arabs interpres.

## 9:18
Vers. 19.

THE PATIENCE OF THE POOR SHALL NOT PERISH FOREVER) He well supplied the negative particle, which in the Hebrew is tacitly understood from the preceding.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

PATIENTIA PAUPERUM NON PERIBIT IN FI- NEM) Bene supplevit negativam particulam, quæ in He- bræo ex superioribus tacite intelligitur.

## 9:20
Vers. 21. APPOINT O LORD A LAWGIVER OVER THEM.

In the Hebrew it is: Place O Lord fear upon them. For מוֹרֶה is not present, which is derived from הוֹרָה he taught: but מוֹרָה fear from יָרֵא he feared. The sense is clear: Arise O Lord, and strike fear into them: so that Bellarmine complains in vain about the obscurity of the passage: He speaks of a terrible Doctor, who commands with authority. Many understand Christ by this Lawgiver, many the Anti-Christ. In a most obscure matter everyone abounds in his own sense. Which things arose from a bad version, and thus it is better to have approached the fountains rather than the streams.

Latin:

Vers. 21. CONSTITUE DOMINE LEGIS- LATOREM SUPER EOS.

In Ebræo est: Pone Domine timorem eis. Non enim habetur מוֹרֶה, quod ab הוֹרָה docuit de- rivatur: sed מוֹרָה timor a יָרֵא timuit. Sensus luculentus est: Surge Domine, & incute eis timorem: ut frustra queratur Bellarminus de obscuritate loci: Loquitur de Doctore terribili, qui cum imperio præci- pit. Multi per hunc Legislatorem intelligunt Chri- stum, multi Anti-Christum. In re obscurissima quis- que abundat suo sensu. Quæ e mala versione orta sunt, adeoque præstat fontes potius adiisse quam rivos.

## 9:20 Addition
Verse 21.

APPOINT, O LORD, A LAWGIVER OVER THEM.

The Hebrew word מורה is explained by some as Teacher, by others as terror. Whence, as Bellarmine notes, some understand Christ, others the Anti-Christ; he himself wishes Constantine and similar Emperors to be indicated: he permits, however, everyone to abound in his own sense IN A MOST OBSCURE MATTER. But the obscurity is not from the text, but from the variation of the interpreters. For the word מורה as it is read in the source denotes only terror, never Teacher, who is called מורה; therefore the Chaldean, Aquila, Theodotion, Jerome, Vatablus, Pagninus, the Belgian, Cocceius and others rendered it terror or fear: but the Vulgate's 'Lawgiver' is from the faulty translation of the seventy elders, which the Syrian also followed. Whence it is sufficiently clear, it is neither about Christ, nor about Christian Emperors: but neither about the Anti-Christ, whom who would believe David wished to entreat? these things are to be understood, but by the force of the context divine vengeance is desired against the impious, so that they may learn their own fragility, and no longer persecute the faithful, but desist and be converted as Brentius explained: to which sense Bugenhagius also recalls the Vulgate: Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver, that is, give them someone who may repress them, just as GOD always does, while He suppresses the pride of men by raising up some impious person far more powerful than them. Felix rendered it: Place, O Lord, a yoke upon them.

Furthermore, according to the Vulgate, the continuation of the ninth Psalm follows, but Cajetan, Eugubinus, and Montanus acknowledge that it is more correct for the Hebrew text to begin the new Psalm X, since this is not obscure from the argument.

Latin:

Versus 21.

CONSTITUE DOMINE LEGISLATO- REM SUPER EOS.

Vox Ebræa מורה a nonnullis Doctor expo- nitur, ab aliis terror. Unde notante Bellarmino alii Christum, alii Anti-Christum intelligunt; Ipse Constantinum, similesque Imperatores notari vult: permittit tamen quemque sensu suo abundare IN RE OBSCURISSIMA. At obscuritas non a textu, sed ab Interpp. variatione est. Vox enim מורה ut in fonte legitur terrorem tantum notat, nusquam Doctorem, qui מורה dicitur; Ideo Chald. Aqui- la, Theodot. Hieronymus, Vatablus, Pagninus, Bel- ga, Coccejus aliique terrorem vel timorem reddidere: Vulgarii vero Legislator est e vitiosa translatione LXX. senum, quam Syrus etiam sequutus est. Un- de satis liquet, nec de Christo, nec de Christianis Imperatoribus: sed neque de Anti- Christo, quem exorare Davidem voluisse ecquis credat? hæc in- telligenda esse, sed vi contextus vindictam divinam optari impiis, ut discant fragilitatem suam, nec am- plius persequantur fideles, sed desistant & conver- tantur ut Brentius exposuit: ad quem sensum revo- cat etiam Bugenhagius vulgatam: Constitue Domine legislatorem, id est, da eis aliquem, qui reprimat eos, sicut semper facit DEUS, dum superbiam hominum opprimit suscitato aliquo impio longe ipsis potentiore. Felix reddidit: Pone Domine jugum ipsis.

Sequitur porro juxta vulgatam continuatio Psalmi noni, sed rectius Ebræum textum Psalmum novum X. inchoare agnoscunt Cajetanus, Eugubi- nus, Montanus, quum id ex argumento haud obscu- rum sit.

## 10:3-4
Vers. 3. 4.

FOR THE SINNER IS PRAISED IN THE DESIRES OF HIS SOUL AND THE UNJUST MAN IS BLESSED,

Latin:

Vers. 3. 4.

QUONIAM LAVDATVR PECCATOR IN DESI- DERIIS ANIMÆ SVÆ ET INIQVVS BENEDICITVR,

## 10:3 Addition
Ps. 10. v. 3.

THE WICKED IS BLESSED.

The sense of the Vulgate is that the wicked are commended by others, because like rejoices in like. B. Luther: making gain, he has blessed himself. Felix connects it with the following: The wicked blesses him who blasphemes God, and Bugenhagius does not deny it. Musculus and Mollerus explain it as a curse, and Tarnovius easily agrees. B. Luther's opinion is to be preferred: because it is not expressed how the wicked is held by others, but how greatly he exalts himself. What kind of person he behaves as towards God is indicated afterwards. Cf. Isa. 3. verse 9.

Latin:

Psal. 10. v. 3.

INIQUUS BENEDICITUR.

Sensus Vulg. est ab aliis commendari iniquos, quod similis simili gaudeat. B. Lutherus: quæ- stum faciens sibi benedixit. Felix connectit cum sequentibus: Iniquus benedicit blasphemanti Deum, nec abnuit Bugenhagius. De maledictione ex- ponunt Musculus & Mollerus, facileque annuit Tarnovius. Præferenda B. Lutheri sententia: quia non, qualis ab aliis habeatur iniquus, sed quantopere se efferat, exprimitur. Qualem se erga Deum gerat postea indicatur. Conf. Esa. 3. vers. 9.

## 10:4
HE HAS PROVOKED THE LORD) It seems to me that it can best be translated thus: Because the impious man has boasted in his desires, and in the fulfillment (namely, of his desires) therefore he has cursed God, and he will provoke him. בָּרַךְ properly means to bless: but by antiphrasis, or euphemism, it is taken for to curse, as in Job 1. verse 5. II. chapter 2. verse 5. בָּצַע however is translated συντελεῖν in Proverbs 1. verse 19. Isaiah 10, verse 12. Jeremiah 6. v. 13. Lamentations 2, v. 17. Ezekiel 22. v. 12. 13.

Vers. 4.

THE SINNER ACCORDING TO THE MULTITUDE OF HIS WRATH WILL NOT SEEK, THERE IS NO GOD IN HIS SIGHT) Better: The sinner because of the pride of his countenance does not seek (supply God, from the following) nor is God in any of his thoughts.

Latin:

EXACERBAVIT DOMINUM) Optime videtur mihi sic posse verti: Quia gloriatus est impius in desideriis suis, & im- pletione (nempe desideriorum suorum) propterea maledixit Deo, & eum irritabit. בָּרַךְ proprie est benedicere: sed κατ' ἀντίφρασιν, aut εὐφημισμὸν sumitur pro maledicere, ut Job. 1. vers. 5. II. cap. 2. vers. 5. בָּצַע autem vertitur συντελεῖν Prov. 1. vers. 19. Esa. 10, vers. 12. Jer. 6. v. 13. Thren. 2, v. 17. Ezech. 22. v. 12. 13.

Vers. 4.

PECCATOR SECVNDVM MVLTITVDINEM IRÆ SVÆ NON QVÆRET, NON EST DEVS IN CON- SPECTU EJVS) Melius: Peccator ob superbiam vultus sui non quærit (supple Deum, ex sequentibus) neque Deus est in ulla cogitatione ejus.

## 11:1 Argument
PSALM XI. The justice of God is opposed to the weapons of the wicked.

Vers. 1.

Latin:

PSALMUS XI. Telis improborum Dei justitia obvertitur.

Vers. 1.

## 11:1 Addition
Towards the end of verse 1 of Psalm 11.

Concerning the aversion to solicitation toward heresy, Tertullian in Apology chapter 47, on prescription chapter 20, Augustine to Petilian chapter 7, accept; and the collation teaches that David is dealing with the subversion of true doctrine in verses 3 and 4, where it is indicated that the foundation of faith and piety is being destroyed, but the discourse is not about the overturning of political rule. Blessed Bugenhagen explains: Abandon the straight path which you seem to yourself to be following, abandon it like a sparrow, a timid animal, which flees even when no one is pursuing. Queen Elizabeth of England opposed this Psalm to Pius V, the Roman Pontiff, when he was soliciting her to defect to Roman superstition.

Latin:

Sub finem vers. 1. Psalm. 11.

De aversatione sollicitationis ad hæresin Tertull. in Apol. cap. 47. de præscript. cap. 20. Au- gust. ad lit. Petil. cap. 7, accipiunt; & de eversione veræ doctrinæ agere Davidem v. 3. & 4. collatio do- cet, ubi destrui fundamentum fidei & pietatis indi- catur, non vero de convulsione regiminis politici ser- mo est. B. Bugenhagius exponit: Desere viam rectam, quam tibi sequi videris, desere sicut passer, timidum animal, quod fugit etiam nemine persequen- te. Psalmum hunc Elisabetha Regina Angliæ op- posuit Pio V. R. P. ipsam ad defectionem ad Ro- manam superstitionem solicitanti.

## 11:2
IN THE LORD I TRUST, HOW DO YOU SAY TO MY SOUL] Better: I have trusted in God, what is it that you say to me? For it is a dialogue between David and his companions, such as in Horace book 3, ode 9.

Vers. the same.

MIGRATE TO THE MOUNTAIN LIKE A SPARROW) The friends are speaking. But this interpreter reads, and the Greeks whom he follows, נוּד וְהַר כְּצִפּוֹר, not as we now read .נוּדוּ הַרְכֶם צִפּוֹר But the argument from the version of the LXX interpreters is weak: since we do not have it complete and uncorrupted: and the Vulgate is indeed far more corrupt, nor was it translated from the Hebrew text itself. And who will pledge their word that the exemplar from which the translation of the LXX or Jerome was made was even uncorrupted, or that they translated it without error and oversight? There is certainly no reason to blame the Hebrew text here, which is the original and enjoys the privilege of divine providence, rather than those versions, since the sense there is plain, how do you say to my soul, that it should migrate to your mountain like a sparrow, as Arias Montanus explains. Which sense the explanation of Jerome also renders: How, he says, shall I migrate to YOUR MOUNTAINS, that is, to your pride?

Latin:

IN DOMINO CONFIDO, QVOMODO DICITIS ANIMÆ MEÆ] Melius: Deo confisus sum, quid est, quod mihi dicitis? Est enim Dialogus inter Davidem, & comites ejus, qualis in Horatio l. 3. ode 9.

Vers. eod.

TRANSMIGRA IN MONTEM VELVT PASSER) Amici loquuntur. Legit autem hic interpres, & Græci quos sequitur נוּד וְהַר כְּצִפּוֹר, non ut nos nunc legimus .נוּדוּ הַרְכֶם צִפּוֹר SEd argumentum e versione LXX. interpp. parum firmum est: siquidem eam integram & incorru- ptam non habeamus: Vulgata vero longe adhuc corruptior sit, neq; traducta ex ipso Ebræo textu. Et quis fidem interponet, quod vel incorruptum fuerit exemplar, unde LXX. aut Hieronymi translatio facta est, vel absq; errore ac παροράματι illi traduxerint? Nulla certe causa est, Ebræum potius textum, qui originalis est, & divinæ providentiæ privilegio gau- det, quam versiones istas hic arguendi, quum sensus ibi planus sit, quomodo dicitis animæ meæ, ut transmi- gret in montem vestrum sicut passer, ut exponit Aria- montanus. Quem etiam sensum reddit explicatio Hieronymi: Quomodo, inquit, ad VESTROS MON- TES, hoc est, ad vestram superbiam transmigrabo?

## 11:7
FOR THE LORD IS RIGHTEOUS, AND HATH LOVED RIGHTEOUSNESSES, HIS COUNTENANCE HATH BEHELD EQUITY.

Genebrardus renders it: their persons see the upright, and he notes here in the source a mystery of the plurality of persons, but the suffix וֹם is also sometimes taken singularly, as R. Kimchi in Michlol, and Aben-Ezra on this passage, and others from Job 22, 2; ch. 27, 13; Is. 44, 15; ch. 53, 8 observe. And the simplest sense is, the Lord is righteous, the upright loves righteousnesses, he shall see his face, as the Chaldean and some Rabbis in Gal. last book, ch. 6. Some oppose the Vulgate translation with the observation of Aben-Ezra, we do not find sight attributed to the face, but to the eyes. Coccejus gives another sense at Job 22, 2. The upright shall see their faces, that is, one another. But that is twisted. Ludovicus de Dieu, because of the Rebiæh accent, distinguishes and explains it thus: The Lord is righteous, the upright loves righteousnesses, their faces, or those of the wicked, shall see it. But that accent not rarely lacks the power of distinguishing in the book of Psalms. The sacred psalmist is occupied in celebrating God as the lover and rewarder of justice; and just as he had said that God proves himself just, to hate the impious, and to punish them v. 5. 6., so now he testifies concerning the fruit of the righteous, that God loves their righteousnesses, and they themselves see the face of God, h to be exhilarated by the gracious vision of the glorious face in time to come.

Latin:

QUONIAM JUSTUS DOMINUS, ET JUSTITIAS DILEXIT, ÆQUITATEM VIDIT VULTUS EJUS.

Genebrardus reddit: rectum vident personæ eo- rum, & notat hic in fonte mysterium pluralitatis per- sonarum, sed suffixum וֹם accipitur etiam quandoq; singulariter, ut R.Kimchi in Michlol, & Aben-Ezra ad h. l. aliique e Job. 22, 2. c. 27, 13. Es. 44, 15. c. 53, 8. ob- servant. Et simplicissimus est sensus, justus est Do- minus, justitias amat rectus, videbit faciem ejus, uti Chald. & Rabbini nonnulli apud Gal. l. ult. c. 6. Vul- gatæ translationi opponunt nonnulli observatio- nem Aben-Ezræ, non invenimus visum tribui faciei, sed oculis. Alium sensum reddit Coccejus ad Job. 22, 2. Recti videbunt facies suas, id est, se invicem. Sed ille contortus. Ludovicus de Dieu accentus Rebiæh causa ita distinguit & exponit: Justus est Dominus, justitias amat rectus, videbunt id facies eorum, sive impiorum. Sed accentus ille non raro distinguen- di vi caret in libro Psalmorum. In celebrando Deo justitiæ amatore & renumeratore occupatur Hiero- psaltes; & quemadmodum Deum probare justum, odisse impium, & suppliciis afficere v. 5. 6. dixerat ita nunc de fructu justorum testatur , quod Deus amet justitias eorum, ipsique Dei faciem videant, h gratiosa olim gloriosae faciei visione exhilarandi.

PSALM XII. The proven purity of the word of God is opposed to corruptions and hypocrites.

PSALMUS XII. Corruptelistiis & hypocritis opponitur verbi De probata puritas.

## 12:3
Ver. 4. MAY THE LORD DESTROY ALL DECEITFUL LIPS) The Syriac, lips of divisions: which interpretation the Hebrew word receives very well. And David seems to be dealing with those who had incited Absalom against him.

Latin:

Vers. 4. DISPERDAT DOMINUS UNIVERSA LA- BIA DOLOSA) Syrus, labia divisionum: quam interpre- tationem optime recipit vox Hebræa. Et videtur David agere de iis qui Absalomum contra se incitaverant.

## 12:7
Ver. 8. BECAUSE OF THE MISERY OF THE NEEDY, AND THE GROANING OF THE POOR, NOW I WILL ARISE.

The Papists wrongly distort this, as if the ancients could have obtained the coming of Christ by their own merits. There is nothing here about the coming of the incarnation. Nor about the pious in the New Testament. But it is treated indefinitely, whose misery and sighs are indeed a procatarctic cause, or rather an occasion of divine help, but they do not merit the same, nor can they be held as a cause properly so called of it, but some reason: much less a meritorious cause: just as the miseries and supplications of needy men move us to mercy, but they are not the cause of our mercy, nor do they merit the same.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PROPTER MISERIAM INOPUM, ET GEMITUM PAUPERUM NUNC EXUR- GAM.

PErperam hoc detorquent Papistæ, quasi veteres meritis suis adventum Christi consequi potue- rint. Nihil hic de adventu ἐνσαρκώσεως. Neque de piis in N. T. Sed indefinite agitur, quorum miseria & suspiria causa quidem προκαταρκτικὴ, vel occasio potius sunt opitulationis divinæ, non au- tem merentur eandem, nec causa proprie dicta illius haberi possunt, sed ratio aliqua: nedum causa meri- toria : quemadmodum miseriæ & supplicationes hominum egenorum movent nos ad misericor- diam, non vero causa nostræ misericordiæ sunt, nec merentur eandem.

## 12:8
Ver. 9. THE WICKED WALK IN A CIRCLE, ACCORDING TO THY HEIGHT THOU HAST MULTIPLIED THE SONS OF MEN] Certain Greeks better: when the lowest of the sons of men are exalted. Nothing is harsher than a base man when he rises to a height. But that happens most in civil discords. And in discord even the most base man obtains honor.

Latin:

Vers. 9. IN CIRCUITU IMPII AMBULANT, SECUNDUM ALTITUDINEM TUAM MULTIPLICASTI FILIOS HOMINUM] Melius Græci quidam: ὅταν ὑψωθῶσιν οἱ ἀντελεῖς τῶν υἱῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Asperius nihil est humili cum surgit in altum. Id autem maxime evenit in discordiis civilibus. Ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ ὁ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς.

## 13:1 Argument
PSALM XIII. The grace of God settles the anxiety concerning the forgetfulness of God.

Latin:

PSALMUS XIII. Anxietatem de oblivione Dei sistit Dei gratia.

## 13:6
Ver. 6. I WILL SING TO THE LORD WHO BESTOWS GOOD THINGS UPON ME) To him who has done good to me. So also the Syriac. The word גמר is translated by to do good also below 116, 7.

Ver. same. I WILL SING PSALMS TO THE NAME OF THE LORD MOST HIGH.

These words, because they do not occur in the Hebrew, Bellarmine thinks perhaps fell out by the length of time, but even if they are read in the Greek, and are explained by Theodoret and Euthymius just as by Jerome and Augustine, it is more certain that they were added to the Greek text than that they fell out of the Hebrew text. For those former words sufficiently teach that they are redundant, in which, according to the solemn custom in the Psalms, a distich, if we may call it so, was already complete: my heart will exult in thy salvation: I will sing to the Lord, who bestows good things upon me. Therefore this clause is not added so neatly, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord most high, which neither responds to the elegance of the Psalms, and savors of a tautology; Add finally that the system of accents proves that nothing is missing here, or has fallen out.

Latin:

Vers. 6. CANTABO DOMINO QUI BONA TRIBUIT MI- HI) Τῷ εὐεργετήσαντί με. Sic & Syrus. Verbum גמר per εὐεργετεῖν vertitur etiam infra 116, 7.

Vers. eod. PSALLAM NOMINI DOMINI ALTISSIMI.

Hæc verba, quia in Ebræo non occurrunt, diu- turnitate temporis fortasse excidisse Bellarm. putat, sed etiamsi ea in Græcis legantur, adeoque a Theod. & Eu- thymio pariter ac Hieron. & Augustino explicentur, certius est Græco textui addita esse quam ex Ebræo textu excidisse. Nam abundare illa priora satis docent, in quibus pro more in Psalmis solemni jam distichon, ut ita vocemus, completum fuit: exulta- bit cor meum in salutari tuo: cantabo Domino, qui bo- na tribuit mihi. Non ergo adeo concinne additur hæc clausula, & psallam nomini Domini altissimi, quæ nec elegantiæ Psalmorum respondet, & ταυτο- λογίαν sapit; Adde denique quod accentuum ratio nihil hic desiderari, aut excidisse, comprobet.

## 14:1 Argument
PSALM XIV. The malice of all men. The desire for the salvation of the Messiah.

Ver. 1. THE FOOL HATH SAID IN HIS HEART, THERE IS NO GOD) He calls them fools, in the Platonic manner, who are wicked, even if they seem to themselves to be very wise. But he wishes to say that the age is as depraved as it had been before the flood.

It seems to be gathered from this that it is not implanted by nature in the heart of all that God exists, but some observe that the word אָמַר (said) is to be explained as 'to will,' as in Ex. 2:14, 2 Sam. 2:16, 1 Kings 7:12, so that this is the sense: the impious man wishes, wills, and desires that there be no God who might see or punish perverse deeds; so that it is not so much the knowledge of the mind that is denied, as the affection of the heart and a perverse inclination that is designated. Others say that it is not the existence of God that is denied, but his providence. Moreover, we have warned in T. 2 in Aug. Confess. de notitia Dei natur. & revel. p. 171, from a comparison of Rom. 3:10, that the proclivity and inclination of man toward atheism in the state of sin is designated here, from which, however, the Θεογνωσία (knowledge of God) implanted by nature is not to be denied, since that vanity and perversity of the human heart can consist with implanted principles and the law of nature. Mr. Dr. Seb. Schmied. in the former Collegium, p. 80, says that this statement is merely legal: and therefore it is to be understood not that the impious man denies in total that God exists, but that there is only so much lacking in his heart for a perfect and firm acknowledgment of God that the rigor of the law rightly accuses him, as one denying that God exists, just as from the rigor of the law it is rightly said that whoever does not love God with his whole heart hates God.

Latin:

PSALMUS XIV. Malitia hominum omnium. Desiderium sa- lutis Messiæ.

Vers. 1. DIXIT INSIPIENS IN CORDE SUO, NON EST DEUS) Insipientes vocat, more Platonico, eos qui improbi sunt, etiamsi sapere sibi plurimum videantur. Vult autem dicere, sæculum esse tam depravatum quam fuerat ante di- luvium.

VIdetur hinc colligi, non esse omnium cordi natu- ra insitum, Deum esse, sed observant nonnulli vocem אָמַר dixit exponendum esse per velle ut Ex. 2,14. 2.Sam.2,16. 1.Reg. 7,12. ut hic sensus sit: optat impius,vult & desiderat,ne sit Deus,qui facta perver- sa videat,aut vindicet; ut non tam notitia mentis ne- getur, quam affectus cordis & inclinatio prava desi- gnetur. Alii dicunt non negari Dei existentiam, sed providentiam. Cæterum monuimus T. 2. in Aug. Confess. de notitia Dei natur. & revel. p. 171. e collatione Rom. 3, 10. proclivitatem hic & inclinatio- nem hominis in atheismum in statu peccati,designari, ex qua vero non neganda Θεογνωσία natura insita, quum vanitas & perversitas illa cordis humani con- sistere possit cum insitis principiis & lege naturæ. Dn. D. Seb. Schmied. in Colleg. priore p. 80. dicit, hoc dictum mere legale esse: adeoque ita intelligen- dum esse, non quod in totum neget impius Deum esse, sed quod tantum desit in corde ejus ad perfectam & fir- mam Dei agnitionem,ut rigor legis recte accuset, tan- quam negantem, quod Deus sit, quemadmodum ex ri- gore legis Deum odisse recte dicitur,quisquis non ex to- to corde amat Deum.

## 14:2
Verse 2.

THE LORD LOOKED DOWN FROM HEAVEN UPON THE CHILDREN OF MEN) From Gen. 6:5. Whence also, as regards the sense, what follows is taken.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DOMINUS DE COELO PROSPEXIT SUPER FI- LIOS HOMINUM) Ex Gen. 6, 5. Vnde & quoad sen- sum sumta quæ sequuntur.

## 14:3
Verse 3.

THERE IS NONE THAT DOETH GOOD, THERE IS NOT SO MUCH AS ONE) A hyperbole, which Paul also uses concerning the times before the Gospel was preached: which was the occasion why also what follows in Rom. 3, τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος (an open sepulchre) up to τ̄ ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν (of their eyes), have been inserted here into certain Greek, and likewise Latin, Arabic, and Ethiopic codices.

He explains the Psalm concerning the men of that age; he says, ad v. 1, that he wishes to say that the age was as depraved as it had been before the flood: therefore he cited Gen. 6:5. But just as the words are spoken generally, so from the very argument of the Psalm, and also from the Apostolic interpretation in Rom. 3, it is sufficiently clear that the nature and condition of men, such as it is after the fall, is described. Therefore, it is not about the corruption of actual sin only, but also about that which was brought about through original sin; it is not about the particular corruption of certain times and men, but about universal corruption, extending to all times and to all subjects, that is treated here. For the Psalmist speaks first indefinitely, but in a universal sense: They are corrupt, and have become abominable in their pursuits: that all are corrupt, and by their nature prone to detestable pursuits. Then he expresses the same thing negatively: There is none that doeth good: that there is no one who does any good, or can do any good by nature, inasmuch as it is only prone to evil, Gen. 6 and 8; afterwards he repeats the negative with emphasis, there is not so much as one: that not even one can be excepted from this common lot. Furthermore, as if to place the Catholic depravity before the eyes, he introduces God as if carefully looking around, whether even one can be found who either understands God, as is right, and has a just knowledge of God and divine things, or seeks God: who is neither corrupted in mind in perceiving spiritual things, nor in will in embracing those things which are good. The Lord looked down from heaven: upon whom? Upon certain men? by no means: but upon the whole human race: Upon the children of men, from the first parents: for the eyes of the Lord at every time behold the hearts, counsels, and deeds of all men universally: all things are open before his eyes, Heb. 4, verse 13, that he may see if there is any that understands, if there is any that seeks God. Thus everyone is found FOOLISH, saying in his heart, there is no God, that is, not understanding, not seeking God: so that this theme and argument of this Psalm is, just as this very treatment teaches. Furthermore, it defines the corruption of all universally, first by an affirmative proposition from the judgment of God himself, who surveys all with the eyes of his omniscience: all have turned aside, together they have become useless. Then by a negative proposition, and that doubled again: there is none who does good, not even one. Whence the Apostle Rom. 3, 10 brings these forward, to demonstrate that all men universally, as well Jews as Gentiles, are under sin and concludes all men under sin: just as by the voice of the law he concludes that the mouths of ALL universally are stopped, and the WHOLE WORLD is made ὑπόδικον, liable to GOD. Which universality is not accommodated, as the Scholastics call it, but absolute. For the voice of the law concludes all under sin Rom. 11, 31. Gal. 3, 22. And here the power of original sin is graphically described, namely that all have turned aside from God, ALL TOGETHER have become useless FOR GOOD. Therefore there is not one who does good, not even one; all by nature are inclined only to evil. Therefore from this Psalm also the Apostle infers in verses 22 and 23 that there is no διασολὴ or difference: that we have all sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God. Whence it is very manifest what ought to be held concerning the Grotian perversion, which he himself took from the Socinians: when around the third verse, THERE IS NONE WHO DOES GOOD, THERE IS NONE EVEN TO ONE, he feigns a hyperbole, both in this Davidic Psalm and in the Apostolic ἀποδείξει. A hyperbole, he says, which Paul also uses concerning the times before the Gospel was preached! For what is more evident than that Paul is not speaking only of the times before the Gospel was preached, but of the common state of all men, at all times? Since he demonstrates that all who are justified are justified only through the redemption of Christ: that no one is justified by the works of the law: and he uses this argument, that all have turned aside, all have become useless, all are condemned by the voice of the law, and the whole world is rendered liable to God. And with these also accords the votive conclusion of the Psalm, by which David sighs for, and vows the Redemption of the Messiah, through which alone the human race could be liberated from that, such, and so great a corruption: Who will give out of Zion salvation ישוע (from which word the Lord Jesus has his name) to Israel (he is called σωτήριον ἰσραὴλ Luke 2, 30.) when the Lord shall have turned back the (spiritual) captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice: (understand this of the Israel of God Gal. 6, 16. or of Israel according to the promise Rom. 9. verse 8.) such sighs we know the pious faithful in the O.T. expressed as a sacred desire for the Messiah, especially when they weighed or felt the gravity of sin, both original and actual. Thus therefore the same thing is treated here as by the Apostle Paul, so that the present Psalm has been most conveniently brought forward in Rom. 3. Whence Calvin himself, although he feigns that the confused and lost state of the Jews is described here, which Saul brought in when he had begun to rage openly: yet he confesses that he tacitly compares with the children of God whoever are not regenerated by the Spirit, but are carried by the bent of their own flesh: indeed he acknowledges that in Rom. 3 Paul is by no means disputing what the greater part of men is like, but whoever are carried and driven by their own nature: and he adds in his commentary on this very place, that we all, when we are born, bring this madness, which is described by David, and the stench of our whole life from the womb, and remain such, until God by his secret grace refashions us into new creatures. If that madness is described here, which we all bring from the womb, it is certain that this concerns original sin, common to all, not the prevarication which flourished under Saul. Thus therefore Calvin contradicts himself, and is forced to accede to the truth, convicted by its power.

But as for those things interposed against them, Their throat is an open sepulchre, they deal deceitfully with their tongues, the poison of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, their feet are swift to shed blood: Destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known, there is no fear of God before their eyes: although they do not belong to this Psalm, but have been added from different places of Scripture, by the words of the same in the Pauline allegation, whence they crept in here into the Greek, Latin, Arabic, and Ethiopic Codices of the Psalms, concerning which see Diatrib. 10. §. 35. they nevertheless contribute to explaining the power of original sin, according to the Apostle: inasmuch as it depraves man not only according to all the faculties of the soul, but also according to all the members and powers of the body from head to foot: the throat, the tongue, the lips, the feet, the eyes, the heart, the intellect, so that we do not know the way of peace; the will, so that the fear of God is not before our eyes, and all the counsels and actions of our heart; because in the ways of our counsels and actions there is nothing but destruction and misery: which, since they do not all apply to all, as regards actual transgression, but only as regards original concupiscence, which is said to have influence, and alas! has too much influence on sins of every kind, it is certain that the Apostle is not dealing with the former, but with the latter. Which is also to be believed concerning the sacred Psalmist: inasmuch as he must be occupied with the same argument: unless someone wishes to say that his words were brought forward by the Apostle beside the purpose.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

NON EST QVI FACIAT BONUM, NON EST US- QVE AD UNUM) Hyperbole, qua & Paulus de tempori- bus ante prædicatum Evangelium, utitur: quæ occasio fuit cur & quæ sequuntur Rom. 3. τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος usque ad τ̄ ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν, hic in quosdam codices Græcos, item Latinos, Arabicos, Æthiopicos inserta sint.

Explicat Psalmum de hominibus istius seculi; vult, inquit ad v. 1. dicere,seculum esse tam deprava- tum,quam fuerat ante diluvium: Ideo adduxit Gen. 6,5. Sed uti verba generaliter dicta sunt,fic ex ipso argumento Psalmi, nec non ex interpretatione A- postolica Rom. 3. satis liquet,ita naturam & condi- tionem hominum, qualis est post lapsum,describi. Non ergo de corruptipne peccati tantum actualis, sed de ea etiam,quæ per peccatum originale facta est; non de corruptione particulari certorum temporum & hominum: sed de corruptione universali,ad omnia tempora & ad omnia subjecta se extendente hic a- gitur. Nam loquitur Psaltes primum indefinite, sed sensu universali: Corrupti sunt, & abominabiles facti sunt in studiis suis: omnes corruptos esse,ac na- tura sua pronos ad detestanda studia. Tum nega- tive idem exprimit: Non est, qui faciat bonum: ne- minem dari, qui quid boni agat, aut agere possit per naturam, utpote quæ tantum ad malum prona est Gen. 6. & 8. postmodum repetit negativam cum ἐμφάσει,non est usque ad unum: quod ne unus qui- dem excipi possit ab hac communi sorte. Ulte- rius,ut ob oculos quasi ponat Catholicam deprava- tionem, Deum introducit velut accurate circum- spicientem, an vel unus inveniri possit, qui vel in- telligit Deum,uti par est, ac de Deo, & rebus divi- nis justam habeat notitiam, vel requirat Deum : qui aut mente corruptus non sit in Spiritualibus perci- piendis,aut voluntate in iis,quæ bona sunt, ample- ctendis. Dominus de cœlo prospexit : super quos? An super certos quosdam homines ? minime: sed super universum genus humanum: Super filios homi- num, inde a primis parentibus: nam oculi Do- mini omni tempore intuentur corda, consilia, & facta hominum omnium universa: omnia sunt aper- ta coram oculis ejus Ebr. 4. versu 13. ut videat, si est intelligens, si est reqvirens Deum. Ita nemo non invenitur INSIPJENS, in corde suo di- cens, non est Deus, hoc est, non intelligens, non requi- rens Deum: ut adeo istud thema & argumentum hu- jus Psalmi sit, quemadmodum ipsa haec tractatio e- docet. Porro universaliter tum propositione affir- mativa omnium corruptionem ex ipsius Dei judicio omnes oculis omniscientiae suae lustrantis definit: omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt. Tum propositione negativa, eaque geminata iterum: non est qui faciat bonum, nec est usque ad unum. Unde Apostolus Rom. 3, 10. haec adducit, ut demonstret o- mnes in universum homines, tam Judaeos, quam Ethnicos sub peccato esse omnesque homines sub peccato concludat: quemadmodum voce legis O- MNIBUS in universum ora obturari, TOTUM- QUE MUNDUM ὑπόδικον obnoxium fieri ΘΕΩ, concludit. Quae universalitas non accommoda est, uti Scholastici vocant, sed absoluta. Vox enim le- gis omnes concludit sub peccato Rom. 11, 31. Gal. 3, 22. Et graphice describitur hic vis peccati origi- nalis, quod nempe omnes declinaverint a Deo, O- MNES SIMUL inutiles facti sint AD BONUM. Proinde non sit, qui faciat bonum, ne unus quidem; omnes natura propensi sint tantum ad malum. Id- eo ex hoc etiam Psalmo infert Apostolus versu 22. 23. quod nulla sit διασολὴ vel differentia: quod o- mnes peccaverimus, & destituamur gloria Dei. Un- de manifestum oppido est, quid de perversione Grotiana haberi debeat, quam ipse a Socinianis sumsit: cum circa versum tertium, NON EST QUI FACIAT BONUM, NON EST USQUE AD UNUM, hyperbolen fingit, tum in hoc Davidi- co Psalmo, tum in Apostolica ἀποδείξει. Hyper- bole, inquit, qua & Paulus de temporibus ante praedi- catum Evangelium utitur! Quid enim evidentius, quam quod Paulus non loquatur solum de tempori- bus ante praedicatum Evangelium, sed de statu com- muni omnium hominum, omni tempore? Quum demonstret, omnes qui justificantur, non nisi per redemtionem Christi justificari: ex operibus legis justificari neminem: atque hoc argumento uta- tur, quod omnes declinaverint, omnes inutiles facti sint, omnes voce legis condemnentur, totusque mundus Deo reddatur obnoxius. Atque his consonat etiam Psalmi votiva conclusio, qua suspirat David, vovet- que Redemtionem Messiae, per quam unice ab illa, ta- li, ac tanta corruptione genus humanum liberari poterat: Quis dabit ex Sion salutare ישוע (a qua voce Dominus JEsus nomen habet) Israel (σωτή- ριον ἰσραὴλ vocatur Luc. 2, 30.) cum averterit Do- minus captivitatem (spiritualem) plebis suae, exulta- bit Jacob, & laetabitur Israel: (de Israele Dei id in- tellige Gal. 6, 16. vel de Israele secundum promissio- nem Rom. 9. versu 8.) qualia suspiria piis fideli- bus in V. T. desiderium sacrum Messiae expressisse, novimus, maxime, ubi peccati cum originalis tum actualis gravitatem expenderunt, aut senserunt. Sic ergo idem hic, quod ab Apostolo Paulo tracta- tum, ut convenientissime Psalmus praesens Rom. 3. adductus fuerit. Unde Calvinus ipse, tametsi fin- gat, confusum & perditum Judaeorum statum hic de- scribi, quem invexit Saul, quum palam furere caepis- set: Fatetur tamen, tacite conferre cum Dei filiis quicunque non sunt Spiritu regeniti, sed feruntur car- nis suae ingenio: imo agnoscit, Rom. 3. minime di- sputare Paulum, qualis sit major pars hominum, sed quicunque suapte natura feruntur & aguntur: ad- ditque comment. in hunc ipsum locum, nos omnes, quum nascimur, amentiam hanc, quae describitur a Davide, & totius vitae foetorem afferre ex utero, ta- lesque manere, donec arcana sua gratia Deus nos in no- vam vas creaturas refingat. Si amentia ea hic describi- tur, quam ex utero afferimus omnes, certum est, hic de originali peccato agi, omnibus communi, non de prævaricatione, quæ sub Saule viguit. Sic ergo sibi ipsi contradicit Calvinus, ac veritati, vi ejusdem con- victus, accedere cogitur.

Quod vero adversus illos interjectos, Sepul- crum patens est guttur eorum, linguis suis dolose agunt, venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum, quorum os maledi- ctione & amaritudine plenum est, veloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem: Contritio & infelicitas in viis eorum, & viam pacis non cognoverunt, non est ti- mor Dei ante oculos eorum: etsi illi non pertineant ad hunc Psalmum, sed ex diversis Scripturæ locis, ver- bis ejusdem in allegatione Paulina adjecta sint, unde huc irrepserunt in Græcos, Latinos, Arabicos, & Æ- thiopicos Psalmorum Codices, quo de vid. Diatrib. 10. §. 35. faciunt tamen ad explicandam vim origi- nalis peccati, penes Apostolum: utpote quod homi- nem non tantum secundum omnes animæ facultates, sed etiam secundum omnia membra, viresque corporis depravet a capite ad calcem: guttur, linguam, labia, pedes, oculos, cor, Intellectum, ut viam pacis non cogno- scamus; voluntatem, ut timor Dei non sit ante oculos nostros, & omnia cordis nostri consilia & actiones; quia in viis consiliorum & actionibus nostris non est nisi contritio & felicitas: quæ quum non conveniant omnia omnibus, quoad actualem transgressionem, sed solum quoad concupiscentiam originalem, quæ in- fluentiam habere dicitur, & eheu! nimis habet ad omnis generis peccata, non de illa, sed de hac Apostolum a- gere, certum est. Quod etiam de Hieropsalte cre- dendum: utpote quem circa idem argumentum oc- cupari oportet: nisi quis dicere velit, præter scopum verba ejus ab Apostolo adducta esse.

## 14:7
Vers. 7.

WHO WILL GIVE OUT OF ZION SALVATION TO ISRAEL?) That is, would that salvation might come to us out of Zion, from the ark of the Lord! Thus מי יתן is taken in Psal. 55. verse 6. Jerem. 9. verse 1. 2. Sam. 18, 33.

These are rightly understood in the optative sense. But although it may be admitted that there is an allusion here to the ark of the Lord, yet SALVATION was not expected from the ark of the Lord, but from heaven; whence it may be said that heaven was designated by Mount Zion: or, if you prefer, the Church: which was prefigured by Mount Zion, and is accustomed to be understood by that name; because that Salvation was to proceed from the Church and the people of God. Or, retaining the literal sense; from Zion, that is, Jerusalem, because the Messiah was established upon Mount Zion, Ps. 2:6, and the law was to go forth from Zion, Is. 2:3, as the blessed Gesner explained. Salvation is from the Jews, and not only from the Jews, that is, from the tribe of Judah, but from the family of David, whose city was called Zion. Therefore, salvation, or the promised Savior, was expected from Zion, the city of David. That is, from the stock of David, as Bellarmine explains. Moreover, by this name is understood either Jesus himself, who was to arise from the people of God, or the Salvation overflowing from him: for outside of him there is no salvation, Acts 4:12. To this pertains the fact that the faithful longed for the coming of the Messiah with a similar vow: as did the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. 49:18, 'I wait for ישועתך THY SALVATION, O Lord,' which passage the Jews themselves explained as referring to the Messiah, following the Jerusalem Targum: whose paraphrase is this: 'Our father Jacob said: My soul does not wait for the redemption of Gideon the son of Joash, which is temporary: nor for the redemption of Samson, who wrought a redemption: But for the redemption, of which you spoke in your word במברכך which is to be for your people, the children of Israel, that redemption my soul awaits. And the Targum Jonathan: I do not wait for the salvation of Gideon, son of Joash, which is a temporal salvation, nor the salvation of Samson, son of Manoah, which is a transitory salvation, but I wait for the salvation of the Messiah, the Son of David, who is to come to gather to himself the Children of Israel, for his redemption my soul longs. The same was the sigh and vow of David, Ps. 119:166. And thus also we read concerning the Messiah in Is. 25:9. This is Jehovah whom we wait for, we will exult and rejoice in his salvation בישועתו, which passage the Rabbis likewise understand concerning the times of the Messiah. Add Ps. 49:1, as also Ps. 118:14, Ex. 15:2, Is. 12:2. And what did the faithful have more in their vows than the advent of the Messiah, who is called the salvation of God, Luke 2:30, whose salvation and redemption all the faithful awaited, Luke 2:38, in whom they ought to have rejoiced and exulted more than in the advent of the Messiah? Is. 9:6, ch. 35:9, Zech. 2:10, ch. 9:9. What captivity is harder, from which they desired to be liberated, and in whose turning back they placed their salvation, than that from which we have been liberated through the Messiah, Zech. 9:11, Psalm 105:29, Psalm 68:29, Is. 49:9. From what captivity were all the tribes of Israel liberated, if not from the Spiritual one? Which liberation was performed by Christ. Here, however, Jacob and Israel are said to be liberated: concerning which Rabbi David Kimchi says: Jacob shall rejoice, that is, all the twelve tribes sprung from Jacob. This word Jacob shows that this Psalm is about the future, because all the tribes have not yet been gathered (as in Hos. 1, last verse); therefore the Rabbis understood it concerning the Messiah. To this contributes what is noted in Midrash Tillim, that morning and evening the Jews sigh for the advent of the Messiah, in the tenor of this vow, Save us, O God of our salvation. In which, regarding those words, salvation out of Zion, it is observed: all good things are from Zion: May he bless you from Zion: and out of Zion shone Is. 50. The Law out of Zion, Is. 2. He will strengthen you out of Zion, Psalm 20. Life out of Zion, Psalm 133. And Salvation. But why are all good things, Law or word, Light, Blessing, strength, life, Salvation out of Zion, unless because the Messiah is established in Zion, Psalm 2, verse 6, from whom, and in whom are ALL GOOD THINGS, Law, Light, blessing, strength, life, Salvation?

Verse of the same.

WHEN THE LORD SHALL TURN BACK THE CAPTIVITY OF HIS PEOPLE) Better: When God shall have brought back his returning people: that is, when he shall have caused us, put to flight by the force of Absalom, to return safely to Jerusalem.

Without cause he first corrects the vulgate version, with which other interpretations, the LXX, Jerome, and others agree: they render it thus: ἐν τῷ ἐπισρέψαι κύριον τὴν αἰχμάλωσιν τῶ λαῶ αὐτῶ. In Jerome there is the same translation as is held here in the vulgate: the Hieronymian commentary interprets the text thus: when the Lord shall turn back the captivity of his people through his own passion: since the Hebrew word שבות denotes captivity, and not indeed a returning one: Deut. 30, verse 3, Psalm 126:4, Jer. 48, last verse, Is. 29:14, Hos. 6, last verse, Am. 9:14. In vain, therefore, is this snatched away to a reduction from flight, into which they had been cast by Absalom: because the people of the Lord were not then captive. Nor does the gloss of Grotius in any way fit the context. Who treats of the universal apostasy of the human race, and seeks liberation from it, as being conjoined with dire servitude and captivity, Luke 1:71, Col. 1:13. By no word at all is mention made of Absalom here, nor is there anything in the whole Psalm that pertains peculiarly to him. Nor did that liberation from the force of Absalom come to the people from Zion or Jerusalem; for David was then an exile from Zion; Jerusalem was in the power of Absalom: Nor was the whole people of God put to flight by Absalom: Nor was that reduction conjoined with such joy, gladness, and exultation of Jacob and Israel, of all the tribes. But the turning back of the Spiritual captivity, all awaited with the highest desire with David in the Old Testament, and received with the highest joy and gladness in the New Testament. Which is also described in similar words, Am. 9:14. Cf. Acts 15:16. Similarly Is. 49:6, seqq., when it is predicted concerning Christ that he is to be the SALVATION of the Lord even to the end of the earth, it is attributed to him that he is to say to those who are bound and captive: go forth, v. 9. And Is. 61:1, he is said to be about to bring indulgence to the captives: Ps. 68:19, He shall lead captivity captive: Ps. 102:20, The Lord looked from heaven to the earth: to hear the groans of the prisoners: to loose the sons of the slain; that they may announce the name of the Lord in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem. But that gloss concerning the reduction from flight has been unheard of until now among Christians, nay even among the Jews, as being only recently devised by Grotius. Although, however, Jerome (or the commentary which is ascribed to him) and Augustine apply these things to the liberation of Israel according to the flesh, and the conversion which they awaited before the end of the world, you will not easily find Christian interpreters who deny that it looks to Spiritual liberation. Grotius ought to have consulted his own Jesuits here, Bellarmine, Lorinus, Genebrardus, Tirinus, Menochius, if he refused to lend his ears to others. Tirinus indeed notes that Origen, Theodoret, and Euthymius adapt this Psalm to Sennacherib and his legate Rabshakeh, 1 Kings 18, and that everything fits him perfectly: yet he makes the argument of the Psalm general of this kind: the multitude of atheists, impiety, and perverse fruits: and v. 7 he explains thus: Who shall give salvation: (in Hebrew salvation, in Greek the Savior, the Messiah or Christ) out of Zion, that is, out of the house and family of David, whose palace was in the citadel of Zion? Bellarmine proposes the argument of the Psalm thus: The argument is a deploring of corrupt human nature, such as is seen especially in infidels, in whom it has not yet begun to be healed by grace; but concerning the present verse he has this: This last verse prays to God for the swift advent of the Savior, who may liberate the human race from Diabolical captivity, in which were all those blinded and perverse ones, whose darkness and malice he had described throughout the whole Psalm. Genebrardus explains it thus; since all things are corrupt, would that the salvation promised to Israel might come forth from Sion, or the Savior of Israel, Jesus Christ! For he desires his coming from Sion, Isaiah 2, so that through him the depraved nature or the world might be restored. For the Apostle refers it not only to the Jews, but also to all men, Romans 3. Wherefore the Hebrews also interpret this verse concerning the days of the Messiah. Menochius the Jesuit indeed thinks this would happen after the Jews had returned from the captivities into which they were led away into Babylon and among the Assyrians: But when have all the Israelites returned? Therefore he soon adds a better paraphrase; or the sense is: When Christ has come, the Israelites will be freed from the captivity and servitude of vices and the devil, not only those who have Abraham as the author of their race by flesh, but also those who, from the nations, have been grafted into the stock of Abraham by communion of faith. And he proposes this argument of the chapter: He complains that all things are full of the wicked; desiring the coming of Christ, as if he would bring salvation to the good.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVIS DABIT EX SION SALVTARE ISRAEL?) Id est, utinam ex Sione, ab arca Domini, salus nobis obve- niat! Sic sumitur מי יתן Psal. 55. verf. 6. Jerem. 9. vers. 1. 2. Sam. 18, 33.

Recte hæc intelliguntur sensu optativo. Sed quamvis ad arcam Domini hic alludi, admitti possit, non tamen SALUTARE ab arca Domini, sed a cœlo expectabatur; unde dici potest, per montem Sion cœlum designatum: vel, si mavis, Ecclesiam: quæ per montem Sion figurata fuit, eoque nomine intelligi solet; Quia ex Ecclesia & populo Dei Salu- tare illud prodire debebat. Aut retento sensu lite- rali; e Sione, id est Hierosolyma, quia Messias super montem Sion constitutus est Psal. 2, 6. & ex Sion lex exire debuit, Es. 2,12. ut B. Gefnerus explicavit. Sa- lus ex Judæis est, nec solum ex Judæis, id est, ex tribu Juda, sed ex familia David, cujus civitas dicebatur Sion. Itaque expectabatur salus, sive Salvator pro- missus ex Sion, civitate David. Id est, ex stirpe David, ut exponit Bellarminus. Isto autem nomine vel Jesus ipse intelligitur e populo Dei oriturus, vel Sa- lus ab ipso redundans: extra ipsum enim nulla est sa- lus Act. 4,12. Quo pertinet, quod simili voto Mes- siæ adventum exoptarint fideles: utpote Patriarcha Jacob Gen. 49, 18. Expecto ישועתך SALUTARE TUUM Domine, quem locum ipsimet Judæi de Messia explicarunt, præeunte Targum Hierosolymi- tano: cujus hæc est παράφρασις: Dixit Pater noster Jacob: non expectat anima mea redemtionem Gideo- nis Filii Joasch, quæ temporaria: neque redemtionem Simsonis, qui redemtionem fecit: Sed redemtionem, de qua dixisti in verbo tuo במברכך quæ futura est populo tuo, filiis Israel, illam redemtionem ex- pectat anima mea. Et Targum Jonathan: Non ex- pecto salutare Gideonis, filii Joas, quæ est salus tempo- ralis, neque salutare Simson filii Manoah, quæ est salus transitoria, sed expecto salutare Messiæ, Filii David, qui venturus est ad accersendum sibi Filios Israel, ejus red- emtionem desiderat anima mea. Idem fuit suspirium & votum Davidis Psal. 119,166. Atque ita etiam de Messia legimus Es. 25, 9. Hic est Jehovah quem expe- ctamus, exultabimus & lætabimur de salute ejus בישועתו, quem locum de Messiæ temporibus iti- dem intelligunt Rabbini. Adde Ps. 49, 1. ut & Ps. 118, 14. Ex. 15, 2. Es. 12, 2. Et quid magis fideles in vo- tis habebant, quam adventum Messiæ, qui salutare Dei dicitur Luc. 2, 30. cujus salutem & redemtionem omnes fideles expectarunt Luc. 2, 38. in quo magis lætari & exultare debuerunt, quam in adventu Messiæ? Es. 9, 6. cap. 35, 9. Zach. 2, 10. c. 9, 9. Quænam est durior captivitas, ex qua liberari desiderarunt, & in cujus aversione salutem suam collocarunt, quam illa, e qua per Messiam liberati sumus Zach. 9, 11. Psalm. 105, 29. Psalm. 68, 29. Esa. 49, 9. Ex qua- nam captivitate omnes tribus Israel liberatæ, nisi e Spirituali? Quæ liberatio a Christo facta est. Hic autem Jacob & Israel liberari dicitur: quo de Rabbi David Kimchi: Jacob lætabitur, id est, omnes duode- cim tribus ex Jacob ortæ. Ostendit hæc vox Jacob, Psalmum hunc esse de futuro, quia omnes tribus non sunt adhuc congregati (ut in Hos. 1, ult.) de Messia er- go intellexere Rabbini. Quo facit, quod in Mi- drasch Tillim notatum, quod mane & vesperi suspi- rent Judæi adventum Messiæ, tenore hujus voti, Salva nos Deus salutis nostræ. In quo ad verba illa, ex Sione salutem, observatur: omnia bona esse ex Sion: Benedi- cat tibi ex Sione: & ex Sione luxit Esa. 50. Lex ex Sione Esa. 2. Corroborabit te ex Sione Psalm. 20. vita ex Sione Psalm. 133. & Salus. Cur autem bo- na omnia Lex vel verbum, Lux, Benedictio, ro- bur, vita, Salus ex Sione, nisi quia Messias in Sion con- stitutus est Psalm. 2. vers. 6. a quo, & in quo OMNIA BONA, Lex, Lux, benedictio, robur, vita, Sa- lus?

Vers. eod.

CVM AVERTERIT DOMINVS CAPTIVITATEM PLEBIS SVÆ) Melius: Cum reduxerit Deus reducem po- pulum suum: id est, cum nos vi Absolomi fugatos Hieroso- lyma salvos reverti fecerit.

Sine causa primum corrigit vulgatam versio- nem, cui aliæ interpretationes, LXX. Hieronymo, & aliorum consonant: illi sic reddunt ἐν τῷ ἐπισρέψαι κύριον τὴν αἰχμάλωσιν τῶ λαῶ αὐτῶ. In Hiero- nymo eadem, quæ in vulgata hic habetur translatio: Hieronymianus commentarius sic interpretatur tex- tum: cum averterit Dominus captivitatem plebis suæ per propriam passionem: siquidem vox Ebræa שבות captivitatem notet, non vero reducem: Deut. 30. vers. 3. Psalm. 126, 4. Jerem. 48, ult. Esa. 29, 14. Ose. 6, ult. Am. 9, 14. Nequicquam ergo abri- pitur hoc ad reductionem a fuga, in quam per Absolo- mum conjecti erant: quia populus Domini tum ca- ptivus non fuit. Neque contextui ullatenus con- gruit glossa Grotii. Qui agit de universali apostasia generis humani, & ab ea liberationem expetit, utpote cum dira servitute & captivitate conjuncta Luc. 1, 71. Col. 1, 13. Nullo utique verbo Absolomi hic facta est mentio, nec quicquam in toto Psalmo est, quod pe- culiariter ad ipsum spectet. Neque e Zione vel Hie- rosolyma illa a vi Absolomi liberatio populo obtigit; exulabat enim tum Sione David; erat Hierosolyma in potestate Absolom: Neque populus Dei univer- sus in fugam conjectus fuit ab Absalomo: Neque cum tanto gaudio, lætitia & exultatione Jacob & Israelis omnium tribuum conjuncta fuit illa redu- ctio. Aversionem autem captivitatis Spiritualis, & summo desiderio cum Davide omnes expectarunt in V. Test. & summo cum gaudio ac lætitia excepe- runt in N. T. Quæ etiam similibus verbis descri- bitur Am. 9, 14. Conf. Act. 15, 16. Similiter Es. 49, 6. seqq. cum de Christo prædicitur, quod futurus sit SALUS Domini usq, ad extremum terræ, tribuitur ipsi, quod dicturus sit his, qui vincti & captivi sunt: exite, v. 9. Et Es. 61, 1. allaturus dicitur captivis in- dulgentiam: Ps. 68, 19. Captivam ducet captivita- tem: Ps. 102, 29. Dominus de cælo in terram aspexit: ut audiret gemitus compeditorum: ut solveret filios inter- emtorum; ut annuncient in Sion nomen Domini, & lau- dem ejus in Jerusalem. Inaudita vero hactenus fuit inter Christianos glossa illa de reductione e fuga, imo etiam inter Judæos, utpote noviter demum excogi- tata a Grotio. Quanquam autem Hieronymus (vel qui ipsi adscribitur commentarius) & Augustinus ad liberationem Israelis secundum carnem, & conversio- nem, quam ante finem mundi expectarunt, hæc appli- cent, non tamen facile reperies Christianos inter- pretes, qui negant, liberationem Spiritualem respi- ci. Consulere hic debuisset Jesuitas suos Grotius, Bellarminum, Lorinum, Genebrardum, Tirinum, Me- nochium, si aliis aures præbere recusavit. Tirinus notat quidem Origenem, Theodoretum, & Euthymi- um adaptare hunc Psalmum Sennacheribo, ejusque Legato Rabsaci 1. Reg. 18. & optime quadrare in ipsum omnia: argumentum tamen Psalmi generale facit e- jusmodi: atheorum multitudo, impietas & perversi fructus: & v. 7. ita explicat: Quis dabit salutare: (Hebraïce salutem, Græce Salvatorem, Messiam seu Christum) ex Sion, id est, ex domo & familia Davidis, cujus palatium erat in arce Sion? Bellarminus argu- mentum Psalmi sic proponit: Argumentum est de- ploratio naturæ humanæ corruptæ, qualis præcipue cer- nitur in infidelibus, in quibus nondum cæpit sanari per gratiam; de versu vero præsente ita habet: Hic ver- siculus postremus orat Deum pro celeri adventu Salva- toris, qui liberet genus humanum a captivitate Diabo- lica, in qua erant omnes illi excæcati & perversi, quo- rum tenebras & malitiam toto Psalmo descripserat. Genebrardus ita exponit; cum omnia sint corrupta, utinam prodeat ex Sion salus Israeli promissa, vel Sal- vator Israelis JEsus Christus! Ejus enim adventum o- ptat ex Sion Esai. 2. ut per eum depravata natura vel mundus restituatur. Nam Apostolus non tantum ad Judæos, sed etiam ad omnes homines refert. Rom. 3. Quare & Ebræi versum istum interpretantur de diebus Messiæ. Menochius Jesuita putat quidem hoc even- turum, postquam ex captivitatibus quibus abducti sunt Judæi in Babylonem & in Assyrios, reversi fuerint: Sed quando omnes Israelitæ reversi sunt?
