Ideo melio- rem mox addit paraphrasin; vel sensus est: Cum Chri- stus venerit, vitiorum & dæmonis captivitate & servi- tute liberabuntur Israelitæ, non ii tantum, qui carne habent Abrahamum generis sui auctorem, sed ii etiam, qui ex gentibus fidei communione, in Abrahæ stipitem inserti sunt. Et argumentum capitis hoc proponit: Queritur quod impiorum plena sint omnia; Optans Christi adventum, velut bonis salutem allaturum.

## 15:1 Argument
PSALM 15.

A heavenly citizen.

Verse 1. LORD WHO SHALL DWELL IN THY TABERNACLE, OR WHO SHALL rest upon thy holy mountain?) In the royal Zion of David, where the ark was at that time.

If the question is only about the royal palace of David, it is necessary that only kings and the ministers of the palace be understood; for they alone occupy the palace. But here is a description of any faithful members of the Church. In that question, therefore, by the Tabernacle of the Lord, some, with Augustine and B. Gesner, understand the Church militant, which is a pilgrim in these lands, and by the holy mountain of the Lord, the heavenly Jerusalem, the seat of the blessed. But others think that by both names Heaven is described, because in the heavenly Jerusalem is the tabernacle of God not made with hands (Heb. 9, Apoc. 21), which is also called Mount Zion (Heb. 12, v. 12, and Apoc. 14); for the tabernacle was just as much a figure of the heavenly seat as Mount Zion was. This explanation also pleased Jerome. The Prophet asks, says Bellarmine, who is to dwell, that is, to possess a stable mansion in the heavenly tabernacle, or to rest on the summit of the highest mountain, in which all labor of ascent is finished, since there is nothing above it. For here on earth there can be neither a stable mansion nor true rest. So also the Rabbis themselves: R. David Kimchi: in the tabernacle, in the expanded heaven: R. Obad. Gaon: in the future sanctuary.

Latin:

PSALMUS XV.

Civis cælestis.

Vers. 1. DOMINE QVIS HABITABIT IN TA- BERNACULO TUO, AUT QVIS REQVIE- SCET IN MONTE SANCTO TVO) In Sione Regia Davidis, ubi tunc erat arca.

Si de Regia Davidis solum quæritur, neces- sum est solos Reges intelligi, & Regio ministros. illi enim soli occupant Regiam. At hic descri- ptio habetur quorumvis fidelium Ecclesiæ mem- brorum. In quæstione ergo illa per Taberna- culum Domini nonnulli cum Augustino & B. Ges- nero intelligunt Ecclesiam militantem, quæ pere- grinatur in his terris, per montem sanctum Domi- ni, cælestem Hierosolymam, beatorum sedem. Sed alii utroque nomine Cælum describi censent, quia in cælesti Hierosolyma est tabernaculum Dei non ma- nu factum Ebr. 9. Apoc. 21. quæ etiam mons Sion nuncupatur Ebr. 12. v. 12. & Apoc. 14. fuit enim ta- bernaculum æque ut mons Sion figura sedis cœle- stis. Quæ explicatio etiam placuit Hieronymo. Quærit Propheta, inquit Bellarminus, quis sit ha- bitaturus, id est, stabili mansione potiturus in taber- naculo cælesti, aut requieturus in vertice montis altis- simi, in quo finitur omnis labor ascensionis, cum supra illum nihil sit. Hic enim in terris neque stabilis man- sio neque vera quies esse potest. Sic etiam Rabbini ipsi: R. David. Kimchi: in tabernaculo, in cœlo ex- panso: R. Obad. Gaon: in sanctuario futuro.

## 15:2 Addition
To Psalm 15, verse 2.

HE WHO WALKS WITHOUT BLEMISH.

The word תמים does not denote perfection in every way, but is to be understood either comparatively with respect to others, as in Genesis 25, verse 27, or concerning the sincerity of a study striving toward perfection, Genesis 17, 1, or it must be restricted to innocence with respect to a certain vice, Genesis 20, verses 5 and 6, Psalm 101, verse 2, in which manner it here designates abstinence from those shameful acts about which it follows thereafter, such as from detraction, adulation, perjury, etc., or it must be explained concerning a sincere study of perfection. Campegius rendered it: to walk sincerely without pretense: but faith is also especially included, as in Genesis 17, verse 1, whence Blessed Bugenhagen excellently says on this passage, p. 74: He who conducts himself and lives without blemish, behold you have faith, which purifies hearts, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles, which absorbs all our sins in Christ. Whence is that: Blessed are the undefiled in the way. Otherwise, give me another who is undefiled. Hear Paul, who, when he had described our nature corrupted by sin in Romans chapter 7, and that believers still have remaining sin in the flesh, added in chapter 8: There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, etc. Here you certainly hear the one walking without blemish, not by his own virtue, but by the grace of Christ. It follows, and works righteousness. First, faith itself is the righteousness of GOD: and the work of GOD: For the just shall live by faith, and John 6. This is the work of GOD that you believe in him whom He sent. Then this faith goes forth and spends works of charity upon one's neighbor. For a tree that is good in itself cannot but produce both fruit and leaves at the opportune time. This is Bugenhagen. Compare Psalm 24, 4.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 15. v. 2.

QUI INGREDITUR SINE MACULA.

Vox תמים non perfectionem omnimodam notat, sed vel comparate intelligenda respectu a- liorum, ut Genes. 25. vers. 27. vel de sinceritate studii ad perfectionem contendentis Genes. 17, 1. vel restringenda ad innocentiam respectu certi vitii Genes. 20. versu 5. 6. Psalm. 101. versu 2. quo pa- cto hic abstinentiam ab illis flagitiis, de quibus deinceps sequitur, designat, utpote ab obtre- ctatione, adulatione, perjurio &c. vel de since- ro perfectionis studio explicandum. Campeusis reddidit: ambulare sincere absque fuco: sed impri- mis etiam fides comprehenditur, ut Gen. 17. v. 1. unde egregie B. Bugenhag. in hunc locum p. 74. Qui conversatur & vivit sine macula, Ecce habes fidem, quæ purificat corda, sicut dicit Pe- trus in Act. Apostolic. quæ absorbet omnia deli- cta nostra in Christo. Unde est illud: Beati immaculati in via. Alioqui da mihi alium qui sit immaculatus. Audi Paulum, qui cum ad Rom. c. 7. descripsisset nostram naturam pec- cato corruptam, & credentes adhuc habere re- liquum in carne peccatum, addidit cap. 8. Ni- hil nunc damnationis iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant &c. Hic audis certe ingredientem sine macula, non sua virtute, sed Christi gratia. Sequitur, & operatur justitiam. Primum ipsa fides est ju- stitia DEI: & opus DEI: Justus enim ex fide vivet, & Job. 6. Hoc est opus DEI ut creda- tis in eum, quem ille misit. Deinde hæc fides foris prodit & proximo impendit opera chari- tatis. Non enim potest arbor in se bona non producere in tempore oportuno & fructum & folia. Hæc Bugenhagius. Confer. Ps. 24, 4.

## 15:3
Vers. 3. AND HATH NOT TAKEN UP A REPROACH AGAINST HIS NEIGHBORS) ὀνειδισμὸν ὀυκ ἔλαβε ἐπὶ τοὺς ἔγγιστα ἀυτῡ: he has not taken it up, namely, into his mouth, as in Exod. 20, 7. But the Syrian reads חרם instead of חרפה, i.e., ἀνάθεμα.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET OPPROBRIUM NON ACCEPIT AD- VERSUS PROXIMOS SVOS) ὀνειδισμὸν ὀυκ ἔλαβε ἐπὶ τοὺς ἔγγιστα ἀυτῡ: non accepit nempe in os suum, ut Exod. 20, 7. At Syrus pro חרפה legit חרם, i. e. ἀνάθεμα.

## 15:4
Vers. 4. WHO SWEARETH TO HIS NEIGHBOR, AND DECEIVETH NOT) From the Greek: τῷ πλησίον ἀυτῡ. Others, who has sworn to afflict himself: that is, he has made a vow of fasting, and does not change it. For it is among the duties of the pious to fulfill such vows. Num. 30, v. 3. Deut. 21, v. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVI JVRAT PROXIMO SVO, ET NON DECIPIT) Ex Græco: τῷ πλησίον ἀυτῡ. Alii, qui juravit se affligere: id est, votum fecit jejunandi, & non mutat. Est enim inter piorum officia, vota talia persolvere. Num. 30. v. 3. Deut. 21. v. 21.

## 16:1 Argument
PSALM XVI.

A jewel concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ.

INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE) He translates it thus, which in Greek is στηλογραφία: understanding by title some small marble pillar, upon which David wished these sentences to be inscribed, as his own (Job 19, v. 24). For they read מכתב, not as we do מכתם, which in the Arabic word signifies hidden: that is, a thing worthy of being kept.

There is no reason why we should invent a different reading. As in many other things, so here the Greeks, whom the Vulgate followed, saw or interpreted poorly. For the fourth and fifth editions in Origen's Hexapla teach that מכתם was read in ancient times, which retained the word μαχθάμ. Nor does that interpretation fit. Some indeed wish the title inscribed on the cross of Christ to be noted, because it treats of the suffering, dying, and rising Christ. But how, then, and for that reason, would the title placed on the cross be understood here by the title? Such expositions are too arbitrary. The Hebrew reading, however, is excellent: provided that כתם denotes distinguished gold (Job 28, v. 16, 19; c. 31, v. 24; Ps. 45, v. 19; Cant. 5, v. 12; Prov. 25, v. 12; Is. 13, v. 12). Dan. 10, v. 15, whence most translate it as gold, or a golden ornament, which is commonly called a jewel: as Burgensis, a golden song: so that it may be indicated that such Psalms ought to be no less pleasing and acceptable to us than distinguished gold, or a golden jewel, and eminent above others, just as gold is among metals. R. Aben Ezra renders מכתם as more than pure gold. B. Luther elegantly: ein gülden Kleinoth. Rivetus agrees in his commentary on this place, and Ludov. de Dieu in his animadversions, p. 316, who observes that likewise in Arabic a new golden thing is inscribed. Ludov. Capellus argues here for a corruption of the Hebrew text on another ground: namely, that originally two words existed, מך תם, because Jerome rendered it humble and simple. But Joh. Buxtorff defended the Hebrew truth in his Vindic., p. 796.

DIXI DOMINO) He reads אָמַרְתְּ, as do the Greeks, not אָמַרְתְּ. But the Greeks read falsely, whom the Vulgate has followed. For it is certain from the Chaldean, David Kimchi, and R. Solomon, and especially from the Masora, that the Hebrew was as we now read it: see Drusius in his questions by Epistle, Ep. XXIX. And the sense of the same is convenient: my soul said, as R. Solomon explains. For thus there is greater emphasis: You have said, namely Jehovah, O my soul.

Latin:

PSALMUS XVI.

Clinodium de passione, & resurrectione Christi.

TITULI INSCRIPTIO) Ita vertit, quod in Græco est στηλογραφία: per titulum intelligens columellam aliquam marmoream, cui has sententias inscribi voluit David, ut suas Job. 19. v. 24. Legerunt enim מכתב, non ut nos מכתם, quod Arabica voce absconditum significat: id est, rem dignam servatu.

NOn est, cur diversam lectionem fingamus. Ut in aliis multis, ita hic male viderunt aut interpretati sunt Græci, quos sequutus est vulga- tus. Nam מכתם lectum fuisse olim quarta & quin- ta editio in Hexaplis Origenis docent, quæ reti- nuerunt vocem μαχθάμ. Neque congruit illa interpretatio. Nonnulli quidem volunt, titulum cruci Christi inscriptum notari, quia agitur de pati- ente, moriente, & resurgente Christo. Sed quomodo inde atque ideo titulus cruci impositus hic per titulum intelligetur? Nimis arbitrariæ sunt tales expositiones. Lectio autem Ebræa optime se habet: siquidem כתם notet aurum insigne Job. 28. v. 16. 19. c. 31. v. 24. Ps. 45. v. 19. Cant. 5. v. 12. Prov. 25. v. 12. Es. 13. v. 12. Dan. 10. v. 15. unde plerique per aurum reddunt, vel aureum ornamentum, quod vul- go Clinodium appellatur: ut Burgensis, aureolum carmen: ut indicetur tales Psalmos non minus gratos & acceptos nobis esse debere, quam insi- gne aurum, vel aureum clinodium, cæterisque emi- nens, sicut aurum inter metalla. R. Aben Ezra מכתם, reddit præ auro puro. B. Lutherus elegan- ter ein gülden Kleinoth. Annuit Rivetus in com- ment. ad h. l. & Ludov. de Dieu in anim. p. 316. qui observat pariter Arabica Alis aureolum novum in- scribi. Alia ratione corruptionis hic arguit Ebræ- um textum Ludov. Capellus: quod sc. prius duæ voces extiterint מך תם, quia Hieronymus reddi- dit humilis & simplicis. Sed vindicavit Ebræam veritatem Joh. Buxtorff. in vindic. p. 796.

Verf. 1. DIXI DOMINO) Legit אָמַרְתְּ, ut & Græci, non אָמַרְתְּ. Sed falso legere Græci, quos sequutus vulga- tus est. Sic enim habuisse Ebræum, uti nunc le- gimus, ex Chald. David. Kimchi, & R. Salomone constat, ac cumprimis ex Masora: vid. Drusius in quæsitis per Epist. Ep. XXIX. sensusque ejusdem commodus est: dixit anima mea, uti R. Salomo exponit. Sic enim major est emphasis: Dixisti sc. Jehovah o anima mea.

## 16:2
QVONIAM BONORUM MEORUM NON EGES) The sense is not bad: but you might translate it better and more coherently with what follows: Because my good is not with you, namely, stored up. You do not begrudge me the knowledge of saving things. You have עַל for apud in Gen. 18. v. 2, Exod. 14. v. 2, and elsewhere.

Before all things, it is necessary to be certain here about the subject. Grotius understands the Psalm to be about David according to the letter, here again Judaizing with Calvin. Therefore, at verse 5, The Lord is the portion of my inheritance: That kingdom has fallen to me, in which that true God is worshipped. And at 10, The historical sense (for a more sublime mystical one lies hidden, as in most Psalms) is this: although I am oppressed on all sides by Saul, yet I am certain from the promise of the kingdom made to me that he will not have the power to kill me. The question is therefore, whether this Psalm speaks of David according to the letter or the sense first obvious, as Grotius likes to speak elsewhere, and historically? For he perhaps would not deny that it treats of Christ in a mystical sense; even if he has not made mention of it here. But since it cannot be, as has often been warned, that a double sense of the same statement is established, and the literal is always uniquely intended by the Holy Spirit, it can be proven with most solid arguments that this is in no way about David, but uniquely about Christ according to the literal and proper sense. First indeed, because it speaks of the Holy One of the Lord: You will not give your Holy One to see corruption; Grotius interprets Your Holy One, that is, me. But nowhere does David call himself by such a sublime title, the Holy One of the Lord, but the eulogy, placed absolutely, is proper to the Holy One of Israel and the Holy of Holies, Christ, Is. 54, v. 5, Dan. 9, v. 24. Then, according to the literal sense, this discourse is about him who was not to see corruption. But David saw corruption: Therefore, it is certain that the discourse here is not about him. Than which demonstration nothing is firmer, nothing more evident, which not even the gates of hell will overturn. Since therefore that was fulfilled only in Christ, that he did not see corruption, it is concluded from this ἀναντιῤῥήτως that the discourse here according to the literal sense is about no one else than Christ. Thirdly, lest any doubt remain, we praise as a witness above all exception St. Peter, who proves by the same apodixis that this does not treat of David, but of Christ; because David saw corruption, and so he prophesied here by the Prophetic Spirit concerning the fruit of his loins, Acts 2, v. 23 seqq. From which Petrine demonstration both things are clearer than light, both that the words of the Psalm can in no way be accepted concerning David, as far as the literal and proper sense is concerned, and that they must be accepted uniquely concerning the Messiah according to the intention of the Prophetic Spirit. (4.) To St. Peter we join St. Paul, a divine witness of the same authority, who likewise convinces by that invincible argument that the prophecy must be understood concerning the resurrection of Christ, but can in no way be understood concerning David, because after he himself fell asleep, and was added to his fathers, he saw corruption: But he, whom GOD raised up, did not see corruption, Acts 13, verse 35 seqq. Therefore all Christian interpreters explain the Davidic oracle concerning Christ with the highest consensus; and then in the Syriac version the argument of the chapter is established concerning the resurrection of Christ; and the Arabic concerning the election of the Church, and the resurrection of Christ in Viccars; a certain document, that it is so understood by the Syrian and Christian Arabs as a Davidic prophecy. Which evidence of the matter compelled even Pareus, so that while he decided to defend his Calvin, who understood these things concerning David with the Jews, he was forced, having changed his position, to desert him and to confess it, in Calv. Orthod. p. 208. that the Apostles show that the prophecy of this Psalm speaks of Christ ALONE, and not of David, and he even supported this with arguments. The Apostles, says Pareus, do not allege (from the Psalm) everything, but only certain things, by which WITHOUT DOUBT (the Prophet) argued NOT CONCERNING HIMSELF, but concerning Christ, and his resurrection. That David says everything concerning himself is an error of the JEWS, refuted by Peter and Paul. But this is what Calvin and Grotius want, that David says everything concerning himself. They therefore foster the error of the Jews, already refuted by Peter and Paul. Add that Calvin himself in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles explained this prophecy concerning Christ, nay, he even acknowledges in his commentary on the Psalms that it was fulfilled in his person alone, although he twists it also to David (καθ᾽ ἑαυτομαχίαν): But as for what Peter in Acts 2, v. 30 and Paul in 13, 33 contend that this prophecy was fulfilled in HIS (Christ's) person ALONE, take it thus: that he was entirely and solidly exempted from the corruption of the grave, so that he may call his members gradually, and according to the measure of each, into his society. For when DAVID'S corpse was reduced to dust, they aptly conclude that he was not immune from corruption. Calvin indeed says that this does not prevent David from having rightly promised himself immunity from death, because Christ did not procure immortality by rising for himself privately, but for us all: But if the prophecy was fulfilled in the person of Christ alone, how can it be accepted concerning the person of David, as if he himself promised immunity from death, as far as the literal and proper sense of the words is concerned. For as for the rest, as far as it pertains to the fruit of the resurrection of Christ promised here, we can easily grant that David believed he would acquire for himself not indeed immunity from death (for he had to become subject to this) but a blessed resurrection and immortality by rising: That this is indicated by these words, however, you will not grant, 'You will not let your HOLY ONE see corruption,' and therefore that that holy one must be explained concerning David himself, we deny ἀποτόμως, induced here both by the evidence of the matter itself and by the authority of the explanation of the holy Apostles. More jejune, I add and more inept, is the gloss of Grotius, that namely the power of killing David was not to be Saul's. For there is no mention made here of Saul by any indication, but it is one thing far different not to see corruption, and another not to be killed; corruption follows death, and differs much from death and killing, nay, it is also one thing not to be left in hell, and another to be freed from the danger of death. Concerning which later. Nor do the Apostles explain concerning the immunity of David from bodily death, and liberation from Saul, but concerning the resurrection of Christ, which is most manifest in the cited places. Although indeed some wish certain things in the Psalm to be said concerning David himself, or concerning the Church, that namely David prayed here in his own person, or in the person of the Church, but finally rises to the head, Christ, to which Rivetus adds in his commentary on the Prophetic Psalms. nevertheless the whole συνέχεια teaches that everything is brought forth concerning only one subject, and therefore St. Peter in his sermon brought forward the very beginning of the Psalm, and almost the entire Psalm, and explained it concerning Christ, so that it might be clear that everything must be accepted concerning Christ, Acts 2. Nor is there anything in the Psalm that does not befit Christ, just as it has been demonstrated by our own, especially Dd. B. Luther, Tarnovius, and others. Concerning those words in verse 7, there might be a doubt, 'moreover my reins instructed me in the nights.' But they are solidly and learnedly explained by our Luther: Who are the reins of Christ, which either amend him, as Augustine reads, or rebuke him, as our own, or instruct him, as Jerome and the Hebrew? Unless it means that of the Apostle in Heb. 5: 'He learned obedience from the things which he suffered, and being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him.' And that in Matt. 26: 'The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.' Although however he was full of counsel, he nevertheless felt the nature of our weakness resisting his counsel, by which struggle he learned by experience to obey. Thus the reins of Christ, although holy and immaculate, nevertheless being weak, indeed shuddered at passion and death, when the weak nature desired more to live and fare well; yet this horror compelled the counsel to be more vigilant, and solicitous for those things which were of God. Similarly B. Brentius: 'He leads me with his Spirit in all my actions as well as my passions, so that my reins, or my thoughts, may not seduce me, but that I may walk straight in all his ways.'

Now since we are certain concerning the subject, that fabrication of Grotius, that the words brought from verse 2 have this meaning: 'you do not envy me the knowledge of saving things,' collapses by its own vanity. For that does not square with the subject, the person of the Messiah. The original words are thus: טוֹבָתִי בַל־עָלֶיךָ which you may render κατὰ πόδας thus: 'my good is not to you, or even to you': B. Luther understands them in this way: 'Whatever I have done and labored thus far, none of these redounds to you, O God, everything results for the benefit of men.' With which agree Brentius, Vatablus, Piscator, Drusius in Quæst. & Resp. lib. III. p. 72. Concerning which version see Prince Anhalt. GEORG. on this Psalm in his works, fol. 108. To this also seems to return the opinion of those who explain: 'My good, which I acquire by suffering, is not for your sake, but for the sake of men, whom I free from hell.' Nor do the LXX differ, as far as the sense is concerned, 'ὅτι τῶν ἀγαθῶν μου οὐ χρείαν ἔχεις.' Or the Vulgate; You do not need my goods, concerning which see B. Tarnov. in Psalm. Passion. in h. l. Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 617. Thus also R. David Kimchi from R. Joseph Kimchi: the good does not profit you, but it profits the Saints in the earth. The Syrian understood it interrogatively: Is my goodness not from You? that is, Without doubt it is from you: because the preposition עַל also sometimes signifies From. To which also returns the interpretation of the Chaldean, Symmachus, Jerome, Pagninus, it is not well for me without you. But the former explanation is to be preferred. Or certainly with B. Luther, in his German Version and explanation, these things will have to be taken thus: It is not well for me because of you, as Psalm 44 v. 13 אֵל is taken: Because of you we are killed, and Psalm 69 verse 8 I have sustained reproach because of you. But I will advise and hold that this is the meaning, for your sake I suffer, for your sake I do not have it well. But because the Maccaph connects the little word בַּל with the following one, and the Hebrew word does not sound like the adverb Well, but like the noun Good, we prefer to acquiesce to the other explanation of B. Luther. If, however, it should please one to assume the translation of Grotius, which is twin to that of Junius, there is no need for it to be explained concerning the knowledge of saving things. Junius explains it thus: you are not going to store up my good with you; that is, you will not withhold your blessings with you, but will liberally communicate them to me, and to the saints who are in the earth. This sense also can be rendered: my good is not hidden with you: whatever good I perform, or merit, it is not hidden in the secrets of GOD, but made manifest in the Gospel, for the sake of the salvation of men, especially to the saints, who are illuminated by the Holy Spirit, and are purified and saved by that faith Acts 15. verse 10. John 17. verse 17.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QVONIAM BONORUM MEORUM NON EGES) Sensus est non malus: sed melius & cohærentius cum, iisquæ sequuntur, vertas: Quia bonum meum non est apud te scil. reconditum. Non invides mihi cognitionem rerum saluta- rium. עַל pro apud habes Gen. 18. v. 2. Exod. 14. v. 2. & alibi.

Ante omnia de subjecto hic constare oportet. De Davide intelligit Psalmum Grotius secundum literam, hic iterum Judaizans cum Calvino. Ideo ad vers. 5. Dominus pars hæreditatis meæ: Id regnum mihi obtigit, in quo verus ille Deus colitur. Et ad 10. Sensus historicus (latet enim mysticus sublimior, ut in plerisque Psalmis) est hic: quanquam undiq; opprimor à Saule, tamen certus sum ex promissione regni mihi facta non fore ei potestatem me interficiendi. Quæ- ritur ergo, an Psalmus hic ad literam vel sensu pri- mum obvio, ut alias loqui amat Grotius, & historico de Davide loquatur? Sensu enim mystico de Chri- sto ipsum agere fortassis non negaverit; etsi hic mentionem non fecerit. Sed quum non possit, quod sæpe jam monitum, ejusdem dicti sensus ge- minus constitui, ac literalis unice intendatur sem- per à Spiritu S. hic nullatenus de Davide, sed uni- ce de Christo sermonem esse secundum sensum lite- ralem ac proprium solidissimis argumentis probari potest. Primo quidem, quia loquitur de Sancto Domini: Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptio- nem; Sanctum tuum, id est, me interpretatur Gro- tius. At nuspiam David se tam sublimi titulo San- ctum Domini vocat, sed elogium absolute positum Sancto Israelis & Sancto Sanctorum Christo pro- prium est, Es. 54, v. 5. Dan. 9. v. 24. Deinde se- cundum literalem sensum sermo hic est de eo, qui corruptionem videre non debuit. At David corru- ptionem vidit: Proinde de ipso hic sermonem non esse certum est. Qua ἀποδείξει nihil firmius, nihil evidentius est, quam nec ipsæ inferorum portæ evertent. Quum ergo id nonnisi in Christo im- pletum fuerit, quod corruptionem non viderit, ἀναντιῤῥήτως hinc concluditur, sermonem hic se- cundum literalem sensum de nullo alio esse, quam de Christo. Tertio ne ulla supersit dubietas, te- stem laudamus omni exceptione superiorem S. Petrum, qui eadem apodixi probat, non de Davi- de hic agi, sed de Christo; quia David corruptio- nem vidit, adeoq; Spiritu Prophetico hic de fructu lumborum suorum vaticinatus est Act. 2. v. 23. seqq. E qua demonstratione Petrina utrumque luce cla- rius constat, tum quod nullatenus de Davide acci- pi possint verba Psalmi, quoad sensum literalem & proprium, tum quod unice secundum intentionem Spiritus Prophetici de Messia illa accipi debeant. (4.) S. Petro adjungimus S. Paulum, ejusdem au- ctoritatis divinum testem, qui pariter isto invi- cto argumento convincit, de resurrectione Chri- sti vaticinium intelligendum esse, nullatenus autem de Davide intelligi posse, quia postquam ipse obdormivit, & ad Patres suos additus est, cor- ruptionem vidit: Is autem, quem DEUS resusci- tavit, non vidit corruptionem Act. 13. vers. 35. seqq. Ideo omnes Christiani Interpp. summo consensu explicant oraculum Davidicum de Christo; Atque inde in Syriaca versione argumentum capitis con- stituitur de resurrectione Christi; Et Arabica de electione Ecclesiae, & resurrectione Christi apud Vic- carsum; certo documento, quod ita intelligatur à Syris & Arabibus Christianis Prophetia Davi- dica. Quae rei evidentia coëgit etiam Pareum, ut dum Calvinum suum haec de Davide intelligen- tem cum Judaeis, tueri constituit, vice mutata ipsum deserere, ac fateri necessum habuerit, in Calv. Orthod. p. 208. Apostolos ostendere de SOLO Christo, & non de Davide loqui hujus Psalmi vatici- nium, idque etiam argumentis adstruxerit. Apo- stoli, inquit Pareus, non allegant (è Psalmo) omnia, sed quaedam tantum, quibus SINE DUBIO (Pro- pheta) NON DE SE, sed de Christo, ejusque resur- rectione disseruit. Omnia Davidem de se dicere JUDAEORUM est error, à Petro & Paulo refu- tatus. At hoc est, quod Calvinus ac Grotius vo- lunt, omnia Davidem de se dicere. Errorem ergo Judaeorum fovent, à Petro & Paulo jam refutatum. Adde quod Calvinus ipse in commentario Actor. Apostol. vaticinium hoc de Christo exposuerit, imo etiam in comment. Psalmor. in sola ejus perso- na impletum esse agnoscat, etsi ad Davidem etiam (καθ᾽ ἑαυτομαχίαν) id detorqueat: Quod autem Petrus Actor. 2. v. 30. & Paulus 13, 33. in SOLA ejus (Christi) persona impletum fuisse hoc vaticinium con- tendunt, sic accipe, ipsum à sepulchri corruptione fu- isse prorsus & solide exemtum, ut membra sua grada- tim, & pro cujusque mensura in societatem suam vo- cet. Nam quum DAVIDIS cadaver in pulverem redactum fuit, apte colligunt, ipsum a corruptione non fuisse immunem. Dicit quidem Calvinus, hoc non obstare, quin David jure sibi immunitatem à morte promiserit, quia Christus non sibi privatim resurgendo immortalitatem peperit, sed nobis omnibus: Sed si in sola Christi persona impletum vaticinium, quo- modo de persona Davidis id accipi potest, ac si ipse immunitatem à morte promiserit, quantum ad li- teralem & proprium verborum sensum. De cae- tero enim, quod ad fructum attinet resurrectionis Christi hic promissae, facile largiri possumus, quod crediderit David sibi non quidem immunitatem à morte (huic enim obnoxius fieri debuit) sed bea- tam resurrectionem, & immortalitatem resurgendo acquisiturus sit: Id tamen his verbis indicari, non dabis SANCTUM TUUM videre corruptionem, adeoque sanctum illum de ipso Davide explican- dum esse, hic cum rei ipsius evidentia, tum aucto- ritate explicationis S. Apostolorum inducti ἀπο- τόμως negamus. Magis jejuna, addo & magis in- epta est Grotii glossa, quod nempe Sauli potestas non sit futura interficiendi Davidem. Non enim de Saule ullo hic indicio mentio facta, at aliud longe est, non videre corruptionem, aliud non interfici; corruptio mortem sequitur, & à morte & interfe- ctione multum differt, imo aliud etiam est in in- ferno non relinqui, aliud ab mortis periculo liberari. Quo de postea. Neque de immunitate Davidis à morte corporali, & liberatione Saulis, sed de re- surrectione Christi explicant Apostoli, quod lo- cis laudatis manifestissimum est. Quanquam ve- ro nonnulli quaedam in Psalmo de Davide ipso di- cta velint, vel de Ecclesia, quod nempe hic orarit David in persona sua, aut in persona Ecclesiae, po- stremo vero ad caput Christum assurgat, quibus ac- cedit Rivetus in comment. Psalmor. Prophetic. tota tamen συνέχεια docet, non nisi de uno subjecto omnia efferri, atque ideo ipsum initium Psalmi, & universum pene Psalmum S. Petrus in concione sua adduxit, ac de Christo exposuit, ut constaret, omnia de Christo accipienda esse Actor. 2. neque quicquam est in Psalmo, quod Christo non conve- niat, quemadmodum à nostris cumprimis Dd. B. Luthero, Tarnovio, & aliis demonstratum est. De verbis illis vers. 7. dubium esse possit, insuper no- ctibus erudierunt me renes mei. Sed ea solide atque erudite explicantur à Luthero nostro: Qui sunt renes Christi, qui eum sive emendant, ut Augustinus legit, sive increpant, ut noster, sive erudiunt, ut Hiero- nymus & Ebræus? Nisi illud Apostoli Ebr. 5. velit. Didicit ex his, quæ passus est, obedientiam, & con- summatus, factus est omnibus obtemperantibus sibi causa salutis æternæ. Et illud Matth. 26. Spi- ritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma. Licet autem esset plenus consilio, sensit tamen reluctan- temei consilio naturam infirmitatis nostræ, qua lu- cta experimento didicit obedire. Ita renes Christi etsi sancti & immaculati, tamen infirmi exhorruerunt quidem passionem & mortem, cum magis vivere & be- ne habere cupivit infirma natura; Tamen hoc horro- re consilium cogebat magis vigilare, & solicitum esse pro iis, quæ Dei erant. Similiter B. Brentius: Ducit me Spiritu suo in omnibus tam actionibus, quam pas- sionibus meis, ne renes, seu cogitationes meæ seducant me, sed recta in omnibus viis ejus incedam.

Nunc cum de subjecto certi simus, commen- tum illud Grotii, quod verba è vers. 2. adducta hunc sensum habeant: non invides mihi cognitio- nem rerum salutarium; vanitate sua concidit. Id enim in subjectum, personam Messiæ non quadrat. Verba originalia ita habent: טוֹבָתִי בַל־עָלֶיךָ quæ κατὰ πόδας sic reddas: bonum meum non ad te, vel usq; ad te: B. Luther. intelligit ea hoc modo: Quicquid feci ac laboravi hactenus, horum nihil in te redundat Deus, omne in commodum hominum cedit. Cui consonant Brentius, Vatablus, Piscator, Dru- sius in quæst. & resp. lib. III. p. 72. De qua versio- ne vid. Princ. Anhalt. GEORG. in h. Ps. oper. suor. f. 108. Huc etiam eorum redire videtur sententia, qui explicant: Bonum meum, quod acquiro patiendo, non propter te, sed propter homines, quos ex inferno li- bero. Neque discrepant LXX, quoad sensum ὅτι τῶν ἀγαθῶν μꭣ ἐ χρείαν ἔχεις. Aut Vulgata; Bono- rum meorum non eges, de quo vid. B. Tarnov. in Psalm. Passion. in h. l. Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 617. Sic & R. David Kimchi è R. Joseph. Kimchio: bonum non prodest tibi, sed prodest Sanctis in ter- ra. Syrus interrogative intellexit: Bonitas mea non est à Te? id est, Sine dubio à te est: quia præ- positio עַל etiam quandoque significat Ex. Quo etiam redit interpretatio Chaldæi, Symmachi, Hieronymi, Pagnini, bene mihi non est sine te. Sed præferenda prior explicatio. Vel certe cum B. Luthero, in Versione & explicatione Ger- manica, accipienda hæc ita erunt: Non bene mihi (est) propter te, ut Psalm. 44. v. 13. אֵל sumitur: Propter te occisi sumus, & Psalm. 69. vers. 8. opprobrium propter te sustinui. Ich will aber zurathen und dafür halten, diss sey die Meynung, um deinet willen leide ich, um deinet willen hab ichs nicht gut. Sed quia Mac- caph voculam בַּל cum sequenti nectit, neque adverbialiter Bene, sed nominaliter vox Ebræa sonat Bonum, alteri explicationi B. Lutheri ac- quiescere malumus. Si tamen lubeat Grotii trans- lationem assumere, quæ gemina est Junianæ, o- pus non est, ut de cognitione rerum salutarium explicetur. Junius ita exponit: tu non es conditu- rus bonum meum penes te; id est, non cohibebis apud te benedictiones tuas, sed liberaliter eas mihi, & sanctis, qui sunt in terra, communicabis. Sen- sus etiam iste reddi potest: bonum meum non est apud te reconditum: quicquid ego boni præsto, aut promereor, non abfconditum est in occultis DEI, sed in Evangelio patefactum, Salutis hominum causa, sanctis præsertim, qui à Spiritu S. illuminantur, eaque fide purificantur & salvantur Actor. 15. vers. 10. Joh. 17. vers. 17.

## 16:4
Verse 4.

THEIR INFIRMITIES ARE MULTIPLIED) In the Hebrew: let the false gods of them be multiplied. By metonymy, that is, of the Syrians, Moabites, Ammonites. AFTERWARDS THEY HASTENED) Better: Let them eagerly follow an alien (supply God).

There is no reason why the Latin should be amended here in the former member: In the Hebrew, 'עצבים' is not found, which signifies idols: But 'עַצְבוֹת', which denotes sorrows or infirmities, and in the latter, the verb does not occur in Piel, 'מִהֲרוּ' which is, they hastened, or they eagerly followed: But in Cal, they endowed. The sense therefore is: The sorrows of them are multiplied, who endow another, that is, who choose another for themselves, to whom they may surrender themselves, to whom they may bring a dowry as if to a husband: because idolatry is spiritual whoredom. Conf. Ezek. 16. v. 31. Hos. 8, v. 10. Specifically, there is no reason why we should restrict to the idols of the Syrians, Moabites, Ammonites, what has been said in general about idols and idolatry.

Verse of the same.

I WILL NOT GATHER THEIR CONVENTICLES OF BLOOD] In the Hebrew: I will not offer their libations, which are of blood. For those nations used to drink the blood of sacrifices, often human blood too, as we said at Matt. 26. v. 28.

NOR WILL I BE MINDFUL OF THEIR NAMES BY MY LIPS) Of them, that is, of the false gods, of which he had treated above. See the law of Exodus 23. v. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

MVLTIPLICATÆ SVNT INFIRMITATES EO- RVM) In Hebræo: multiplicentur falsi Dii illorum. Δευ- τικῶς, id est, Syrorum, Moabitarum, Ammonitarum. POSTEA ACCELERAVERVNT) Melius: Alienum (supple Deum) cupidè sectentur.

Non est, cur Latinum hic in priori membro e- mendat: In Ebræo non habetur עצבים quod ido- la significat: Sed עַצְבוֹת quod notat dolores vel infirmitates, in altero vero verbum non occurrit in Piel, מִהֲרוּ quod est, accelerarunt, vel cupide sectati sunt: Sed in Cal dotarunt. Sensus ergo est: Mul- tiplicantur dolores eorum, qui alium dotant, hoc est, qui alium sibi eligunt, cui se dedant, cui dotem velut marito afferant: quia idololatria scortatio spiri- tualis est. Conf. Ezech. 16. v. 31. Hos. 8, v. 10. In spe- cie ad Syrorum, Moabitarum, Ammonitarum ido- la non est cur restringamus, quæ in genere de ido- lis & idololatria dicta sunt.

Vers. eod.

NON CONGREGABO CONVENTICVLA EO- RVM DE SANGVINIBVS] In Hebræo: non libabo libami- na eorum, quæ sunt de sanguine. Potabant enim gentes istæ sanguinem sacrificiorum, sæpe & humanum, ut diximus ad Matth. 26. v. 28.

NEC MEMOR ERO NOMINVM EORVM PER LABIA) Eorum, id est, falsorum Deorum, de quibus supra egerat. Vide legem Exodi 23. v. 13.

## 16:5
Verse 5. THE LORD IS THE PORTION OF MY INHERITANCE) That kingdom has fallen to me, in which that true God is worshipped.

Latin:

Vers. 5. DOMINVS PARS HÆREDITATIS MEÆ) Id regnum mihi obtigit, in quo verus ille Deus colitur.

## 16:6
Verse 6. THE LINES HAVE FALLEN TO ME IN EXCELLENT PLACES] The best land has fallen to me as if by lot.

He explains this solely of David: but it has been proven that it concerns Christ: Moreover, the Lord himself is called the portion of Christ's inheritance, just as God was the portion of the Levites in the Old Testament Num. 18. v. 20. both so that his Priesthood may be noted: and so that it may be designated that Christ, viewed according to his human nature, chose this portion for himself, and has his sole delight in the Lord. If it is also explained in the sense that Grotius wishes; it is understood that the kingdom has fallen to Christ, in which God is worshipped as his inheritance and peculiar possession: and in this way also the lines themselves will be said to have fallen in excellent places, or as Blessed Luther: 'Mir ist ein schön Erbtheil worden': For the Church, which is the kingdom of God, liberated from death, the power of the Devil, and hell, and selected from the unclean world, is a 'κειμήλιον' (treasure) to him, very precious. Conf. Ex. 19, 6. Deut. 7, 6. Tit. 2, 14. 1. Pet. 2, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 6. FVNES CECIDERVNT MIHI IN PRÆCLA- RIS] Optima terra mihi velut forte obtigit.

De Davide id unice explicat: sed probatum est, de Christo agi: Dicitur autem Dominus ipse pars hæreditatis Christi, uti Deus Levitarum fuit portio in Vet. Test. Num. 18. v. 20. tum ut Sacer- dotium ejus notetur: tum ut designetur, Christum secundum humanam naturam spectatum hanc portionem sibi elegisse, inque Domino unicam ob- lectationem habere. Si etiam eo sensu explicetur, quo vult Grotius; regnum Christo obtigisse intelli- getur, in quo Deus colatur in hæreditatem & peculi- um ipsius: atque hoc etiam pacto dicentur funiculi ipsi cecidisse in præclaris, vel ut B. Lutherus: Mir ist ein schön Erbtheil worden: Ecclesia enim, quæ re- gnum Dei ex morte, potestate Diaboli, & inferni li- berata, & ex mundo immundo selecta, κειμήλιον ipsi est valde pretiosum. Conf. Ex. 19, 6. Deut. 7, 6. Tit. 2, 14. 1. Petr. 2, 9.

## 16:9
Verse 9. AND MY TONGUE EXULTED) From the LXX, who seem to have read 'לשני' instead of 'כבודי', not without a slight difference, just as Luke also Acts 2, 26.

Again here, rashly and without sufficient cause, a different reading is invented. Who gave Grotius the power to change letters, nay, words, and to substitute others for others, with not a slight difference, as he himself admits? The LXX Elders did not always render word for word; which is manifest from very many places where they departed from the authentic text. But they expressed the sense well here, for which reason their translation is also praised by the Apostle in the New Testament, Acts 2. For since a man's tongue is his glory, as being the organ by which the glory of GOD is propagated, and from which his dignity is most perceived, as Blessed Luther has in the marginal gloss: 'Ehre, das ist meine Zunge, da ich GOtt mit ehre und preise' (Honor, that is my tongue, with which I honor and praise God), therefore it is so taken Gen. 49, 6. and in this place likewise, with the Holy Spirit approving in the N.T., glory is put for Tongue.

Verse of the same. MY FLESH SHALL REST IN HOPE) He rests: he consoles himself with good hope.

Not only is good hope noted in general, but that he rests IN HOPE: or rather that he is to have rest: for there is no need for an enallage of tenses. But this is pointed out, that in the hope of a glorious resurrection, and of not seeing corruption, the flesh is to rest: and therefore that hope is explained in the following verse: And thus the LXX κατασκηνώσει shall dwell (in the future) as in a tabernacle: Concerning which Rivetus: the burial of the just is a certain dwelling, and a house, in which the body rests until the resurrection. Thus also B. Luther interpreted it, Securely rests the flesh in the sepulchre, because it shall rise again. Indeed, some of the Rabbis, R. Isaac and R. David Kimchi, acknowledged here that immunity from corruption is hinted at, whom we shall cite later.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ET EXVLTAVIT LINGVA MEA) Ex LXX. qui videntur pro כבודי legisse non levi differentia לשני, quomodo & Lucas Act. 2, 26.

Iterum hic temere ac sine sufficienti causa fin- gitur diversa lectio. Quis Grotio potestatem dedit literas, imo voces permutandi, aliasque pro aliis, non levi, uti fatetur ipse, differentia substitu- endi? Non semper verbum verbo reddidere LXX. Seniores; quod ex plurimis locis, ubi à textu au- thentico discesserunt, manifestum est. Sensum autem hic bene expresserunt, ideo etiam ipsorum translatio in Nov. Test. ab Apostolo laudata Act. 2. Quum enim lingua hominis gloria ejus sit, ut- pote organum, quo DEI gloria propagatur, & ex quo dignitas ejus maxime perspicitur, uti B. Lu- therus in glossa marginali habet: Ehre, das ist meine Zunge, da ich GOtt mit ehre und preise, ideo sic accipitur Gen. 49, 6. atq; hoc in loco ita, appro- bante in N. T. Spiritu S. gloria pro Lingua posita.

Vers. eod. CARO MEA REQVIESCET IN SPE) Re- quiescit: solatur se bona spe.

Non tantum notatur in genere spes bona, sed quod IN SPE requiescat: vel potius requiem ha- bitura sit: non enim opus est enallage temporum. Id autem indigitatur, quod in spe resurrectionis glo- riosa, & non videnda corruptionis quietura sit caro: ideoque spes illa explicatur in versu subsequenti: Atque ita LXX. κατασκηνώσει commorabitur (in fu- turo) velut in tabernaculo: Quo de Rivetus: justi se- pultura est habitatio quædam, & domus, in qua cor- pus requiescit usque ad resurrectionem. Sic etiam B. Lutherus interpretatus est, Secura requiescit caro in sepulchro, quia resurget. Imo è Rabbinis non- nulli R. Isaac & R. David Kimchi agnovere hic immunitatem à corruptione innui, quos deinde adducemus.

## 16:10
Verse 10. BECAUSE THOU WILT NOT LEAVE MY SOUL IN HELL) My soul, for me, in Hebrew. שְׁאוֹל the sepulchre for death, the consequent for the antecedent. The historical sense (for a more sublime mystical one lies hidden, as in most Psalms) is this: although I am oppressed on all sides by Saul, yet I am certain from the promise of the kingdom made to me, that he will not have the power to kill me.

NEITHER WILT THOU GIVE THINE HOLY ONE TO SEE CORRUPTION] Thine holy one, that is, me. In this Hebrew word after ד the י is redundant, which the preceding Schæva also shows. To see corruption is to be corrupted. The LXX here οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθορὰν, as also Luke Acts 2:27, and no differently in 13:35. Thus Lamentations 4:20, בִּשְׁחִיתוֹתָם the LXX translate ἐν ταῖς διαφθοραῖς αὐτῶν. Thus also in Psalm 107, מִשְׁחִיתוֹתָם ἐκ τῶν διαφθορῶν αὐτῶν. And no differently Proverbs 28:10, Jeremiah 13:14, ch. 15:3, Ezekiel 19:4, ch. 21:31, Daniel 10:8, Hosea 13:9. The sense is the same as in the former member, in the manner of the Hebrews.

He understands it of David solely according to the literal sense, which he calls historical. He says indeed that a mystical sense lies hidden. But neither can a double sense of the same statement be established, nor if that could be admitted, would the mystical be indubitably certain, unless it were shown by the Holy Spirit Himself, who indeed in the Old Testament, where it might have been shown, cannot be demonstrated, whence it is left that the ancients by no means had their own more sublime sense of the divine oracles, although intended by GOD, which we have in the New Testament concerning the same. What then did the Prophetic oracles profit them? And who will believe that the Church for several centuries lacked the sense intended by GOD in most oracles concerning Christ, and that therefore they were hitherto useless to that Church, and to the faithful of those times, to whom they were revealed? But setting aside these general responses for the present, it is certain that this verse cannot be taken in the sense intended by the Holy Spirit, except concerning the Messiah: That the same cannot be understood of David according to the literal sense. I argue thus: Whose oracle's sense flowing from the words themselves and first obvious, implies immunity from corruption, that cannot be explained of David according to the first obvious and literal sense: for he without doubt saw corruption; But it must be understood of the Messiah, who alone is that Holy One, who did not see corruption. But the antecedent is true of this oracle, therefore the consequent also. Furthermore; That the oracle was fulfilled solely in Christ, not only do the two leaders of the Apostles, St. Peter and St. Paul, assert, denying at the same time, in express words, that it was fulfilled in David, but they also demonstrate apodictically from the very words of the oracle, and the sense flowing from them, that it is not to be understood, according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, of David, who saw corruption, and whose sepulchre was in Jerusalem, in which his body was preserved and made subject to corruption, but of the Messiah, and his immunity from corruption and resurrection; That it treats according to the literal and first obvious sense of the Messiah and not indeed of David, is indubitably certain: unless someone presumes to be wiser than the Apostles, or to contradict the same. Thus our opinion, which is common to all Christians, is vindicated. But what does our Judaizing Grotius say to this light of Apostolic interpretation and demonstration? On Acts 2:29, he annotates thus: He (the Apostle) does not deny that those words can in any way be understood of David, but neither so magnificently, nor so κατὰ κυριολογίαν (according to the literal sense), as of Jesus: whence it follows that he is the Messiah prefigured in David: David remains in the sepulcher, Jesus does not remain. But this is the very thing from which Peter proves that these things cannot be understood of David, but must be understood solely of Jesus, because they speak of him who does not remain in the sepulcher, nor did he see corruption. David, however, remained in the sepulcher, and saw corruption, Acts 13:46. The question is not whether a way can be devised by which those words might be able to fit David, but whether IN THIS PLACE, THEY ARE SAID IN ANY WAY of David? Peter proves that they are not, and cannot be accepted of him: because by the confession of all, David remained in the sepulcher: and Paul, Acts 13:46, because David saw corruption. But these words speak of him who did not see corruption, nor can they be accepted otherwise in this oracle. If they could, there would be no demonstration of Peter, no demonstration of Paul. For thus the Jews could have replied, that those words could be accepted in another sense, and explained of David. Which being granted, what force will remain for the demonstration? For the Jews will easily deny that they must be understood so magnificently, so κατὰ κυριολογίαν: nor, while Grotius's gloss stands, will the historical senses be able to be refuted.

Grotius objects at verse 25. That Peter rightly says that David spoke these things of Christ, Acts 2:25, because the Jews were persuaded that the affairs of David were types of the King Messiah. What follows has its sense in David, but more figurative. But God willed that the same things be fulfilled in the Messiah more κατὰ πόδας (literally/step by step), so that the people, a captious hunter of words, could not complain of anything. But these things are ἀσύστατα (inconsistent), nay, impious. Before, he established a historical sense concerning David; but he said that a mystical sense lay hidden under it: Now he explains these things κατὰ πόδας concerning the Messiah, that is, as he speaks elsewhere, in a more obvious sense, but in a more figurative sense concerning David. Grotius is therefore now forced to confess that these things were predicted more κατὰ κυριολογίαν καὶ κατὰ πόδας (literally and step by step) concerning Jesus, and fulfilled in him. But he still wishes them to be understood in some way concerning David also, and to have their sense in David as well, BUT MORE FIGURATIVELY, so that, for instance, he may gratify the Jews, nay, that he may destroy the strength of the Petrine and Pauline demonstration, and undermine it entirely. For once this hypothesis is admitted, that the words of the Psalm can be understood of David, the Jew will not be able to be compelled to believe they are also understood of Christ; because Grotius wishes them to be able to be understood of David in such a way that he believes they must also be accepted of David according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, whence it will be easy for the Jew to deny that any other sense besides this one concerning David must necessarily be admitted. That the affairs of David are types of the Messiah, ὀὐδὲν πρὸς διόνυσον (is nothing to the point): for this is not what is sought, whether in certain things David can be viewed as a type of the Messiah, but what is the sense of David's words and whether David sings of himself, or whether these things are of the Messiah according to the literal sense, or immediately intended by the Holy Spirit? For if he sings of the Messiah in this sense, it cannot and ought not to be explained of David: however much perhaps in that which is expressed by some words (though not as it is expressed here), David may have been a type of Christ: for the question is not about the figure of things, but about the sense of the words. If the Psalm speaks of David according to the literal sense, however much you may say that David was a type of Christ, and that those things are found more illustriously in him, it will nevertheless be κρινόμενον (a matter for judgment), and will need proof, that David precisely bore the type of the Messiah in those things, and when that has been most proven, it will still do nothing for the sense of those words. And how can such disparate and contrary senses underlie the same words according to the mind of the Holy Spirit in the same place, which Grotius has annotated here at verse 9, on Acts 2:26, ἔτι δὲ ἡ σάρξ μꙋ κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι. This, he says, David said, seeking hiding places from hiding places through fear of Saul: Christ before the cross and on the cross. Here he spoke of tranquil rest in the sepulcher with the hope of resurrection. There, of rest, or rather concealment in hiding places, which is restless, with the hope of escaping danger. Who will believe that such highly disparate things lie under the same words? Similarly verse 27, ὅτι ꙋκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μꙋ εἰς ᾅδꙋ: concerning David, he says, the sense is, you will not suffer me to be killed by Saul, 1 Sam. 22:1; concerning Christ, you will not leave me long under the kingdom of death. Which clearly import a contrary sense of the words. So that NOT TO RETAIN IN HELL is not to be permitted to be killed, or slaughtered: and conversely it is: not to be left long in death after being killed. Likewise in the other member ꙋδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σꙋ ἰδεῖν διαφθορὰν is you will not suffer me to be destroyed or killed while alive, and at the same time it is, you will not suffer me to remain in corruption while dead or lifeless. Which likewise require a clearly opposite meaning of the phrases. To verse 28, ἐγνώρισάς μοι ὁδꙋς ζωῆς (you have made known to me the ways of life), concerning David: you will take me out of these evils, which are compared to death: concerning Christ: you will take me out of death. There, the living is to be snatched from death; here, the dead is to be recalled from death to life. Behold again a contrary sense! Finally, Delights at your right hand even to the end, concerning David, I will rejoice relying on your help even to the end of life, namely when I shall be placed in the kingdom, as Grotius has in the annotations to the Psalm. πληρώσεις με εὐφροσύνης μετὰ τῶ προσώπꙋ σꙋ (you will fill me with gladness with your face), concerning David understand in the temple, as he has on Acts 2 concerning Christ in heaven. Concerning David, therefore, he understands a double joy, both secular and temporal assistance and the restoration of the kingdom, and spiritual, on account of the sight of the face in the temple: But concerning Christ, he wishes something far different to be designated: namely, heavenly and everlasting joy. At the right hand of GOD, therefore, for him is now in the temple, but now in heaven; even to the end for him is now even to the end of life, now for ever, or for ages of ages. Who will admit such desperate and contrary meanings of the same word or phrase in the same place? And what else does the Spirit of lying seek, than that divine truth be obscured, and most illustrious prophecies be rendered obscure, ambiguous, doubtful, and uncertain, like the Delphic oracles; which, when it has succeeded for him in such illustrious prophecies and sayings of Scripture, which were written with their own rays and most clearly explained in the N.T., it will be all over for the rest, and thus for the whole of Holy Scripture, nor will it be held as anything other than like a Lesbian Rule and a waxen nose, which is what he has done hitherto through the Papists.

But we must now examine in particular verse 10 of our Psalm, and the annotations of Grotius upon it: he states this historical sense: that Saul would not have the power to kill David: under which, because he says a mystical sense lies hidden, he undoubtedly understands by the historical sense the literal sense (for the mystical is usually opposed to this) and, as he is accustomed to speak elsewhere, the first and obvious one. But that literal or historical sense of Grotius is entirely lacking in any foundation, nor does it flow from the words of the text, indeed it could not easily have come into anyone's mind until now; he will certainly name no author for it. How then will it be held as the first and obvious sense? What of the fact that most of the words are thus twisted into a foreign meaning; I will not say that my soul here is wrongly by me explained, since the word for soul is not used here without a specific purpose; so that although through a Hebraism 'my soul' might be put for 'me', a singular regard must nevertheless be had for the soul as well: The word שׁאול is certainly twisted very badly if it is taken to denote death, which is nowhere in the Scriptures used for death or the power of killing: nor is it right to have recourse to figures, so that we might say the consequent is taken for the antecedent, the grave for death, when no necessity compels it. And what is this accepted concerning David, 'thou wilt not leave my soul in death,' unless you say that soul is put for body, (for the soul itself is immortal) and you wish it to be looked at in relation to the future resurrection, which is common to him with others? For those things differ as much as heaven and earth: 'Not to leave someone in death,' and 'not to permit someone to be killed.' He who is not to be left in death is understood to have been delivered into death beforehand: therefore it cannot be explained in a sense that is clearly contrary, concerning deliverance from the danger of death. Furthermore, since Grotius acknowledges that the latter clause is rightly translated thus, 'thou wilt not give thy holy one to see corruption,' how can it be the same as if you say, 'thou wilt not permit thy Holy One to be killed': for corruption is one thing, killing is another, therefore something specific is designated here, which although that Holy One is to be led down even into שׁאול and delivered into death, he is nevertheless not to be left in שׁאול, nor should he see corruption, and so that he may not see it, he is to be raised from the dead. Therefore, the Davidic phrase is twisted into a sense that is entirely contrary by a wicked and sacrilegious daring.

Now if we investigate the genuine meaning of both phrases, it is not the case that we should take as the same things those which, uttered distinctly and with emphasis, have something specific in reserve, and are proven to have it by the completion itself. The Messiah truly raises himself up, that he will not be moved, 'ich werde wol bleiben': as our Megalander says: and he testifies both to the joy of his heart, that is, his soul, and to the rest of his flesh, tranquil and secure in the hope of resurrection. 'Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoiced, moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope'; although indeed his soul was to be led down even into שׁאול, the hell, at the time of his passion and death, he trusts nevertheless that it will not be left in hell: although his flesh or body was to be delivered into death, he nevertheless consoles and sustains himself with that hope, in which even at the time of death the flesh itself is to rest securely, that God will not permit it to see corruption, since he himself is the Holy One, immune from all sin, through whom all sins must be expiated and all must be sanctified, Dan. 9. v. 24. nay, he is certain that GOD will make known to him the paths of life, not only as regards his soul, which is not to be left in hell, but also as regards his flesh, which is free from corruption: so that there he may be filled, in soul and body, with which he here endured immense sufferings, with the joy of the countenance of God, and may perceive the pleasures at the right hand of God forever. That 'thou wilt not leave my soul לשׁאול εἰς ἅδη (Act. 2. v. 28. 31.) even unto hell,' therefore, means this for him: although you are about to lead my soul into hell, which happened as often as he himself was tempted by the infernal power, and especially then before death in the agony of the garden, and on the cross, when he cried out that he was forsaken by GOD, for in both places he felt infernal pains, especially as regards his most holy soul, then after death, when he was led even into the place of hell or שׁאול; yet that his soul would by no means be left: for he was never to be left in the most grievous temptations and sufferings, which he had to sustain because of the sins of the world taken upon himself: which the negative phrases emphatically imply, as they affirm more vehemently: namely, that God will always be present to him with his help, even unto hell, even unto the sufferings of hell, and the place or שׁאול of the damned, so that he may always triumph over hell, by divine aid, both in the conflict with the infernal power, before death, and also when he will present himself to the infernal powers and the unbelieving in hell, and return from there as victor and triumpher. For that seems to be noted, says Dr. Tarnovius, that Christ would not be left to the extent that he would be in the power of the infernal ones, so that they could deal with him at their pleasure and detain him, which Peter also hints at in Acts 2:24, where, however, it is presupposed that he was in hell in the place of punishment, but without punishment, and he who in the very agony which he sustained in the garden felt infernal pains, and then cried out on the cross that he was forsaken by GOD, afterwards declared himself the victor of hell. The Weimar Paraphrasts explained it likewise: 'For you will not leave my soul (myself) in hell (to experience the same pain further) as happened before on the Mount of Olives and on the Cross, but you will let me triumph therein, and let my divine power, might, majesty, and the victory obtained be gloriously shown.' These are their words. Thus, therefore, all those things are comprised in that phrase by a certain reason: 'Thou wilt not leave my soul,' that is, with your omnipotent and most gracious help and aid you will be most present to me, and specifically to my soul EVEN UNTO HELL, even unto the infernal sufferings, or the state of the damned, when my soul is led down especially into hell. Cf. 1 Sam. 2:6, Ps. 18:5, Ps. 88:44 seqq., and even unto the very place of hell, or שׁאול of the damned, Ps. 31:18. Ps. 49:15, for Scripture is accustomed to include both the state and the שׁאול of the damned under the word שׁאול: but never, when it is explained by the word ᾅδης in the N.T., does it denote the grave: whence it can be much less admitted that the grave is put here for death. But since a double sense is so easily introduced, we judge that we must adhere to the former explanation. The opinion of Fr. Junius is clearly peculiar, who explains the whole Psalm concerning David. He, however, understands Christ by נפש, soul or life, as if to say, David: 'Thou wilt not leave my soul,' that is, Christ. But those things which deal with one subject are torn apart in this way. Nor is Christ ever called the soul of David, or of the faithful. And the continuity of the text and the analysis show that everything fits Christ. Therefore, the discourse is concerning the metaphorical descent of Christ into hell, as they call it, or concerning infernal sufferings, not concerning his real descent into hell, by the force of the context and the phraseology of the Holy Scriptures. Because (1.) He says his soul will not be left in hell, not himself: there is no reason, therefore, that we should posit a figure where no necessity compels it. Furthermore (2.) the soul is here distinguished from the flesh: rest is promised to the flesh, liberation from hell to the soul. But a real descent into hell was not made according to the soul alone, because having been made alive he descended in soul and body: therefore, the infernal pains of the soul are rather signified. (3.) Both things which were brought forward in v. 9 concerning joy and hope are distinctly confirmed here, joy indeed of the heart or soul to be perceived in those very most grievous sufferings, because God was not going to leave his soul in those very infernal pains. But the hope of rest (Acts 2. v. 26.) because he was not going to permit that his Holy One should see corruption. (4.) The phrase itself and the manner of speaking, you will not leave my soul in hell, sufficiently indicates that it is not a matter of the glorious descent of the triumphant CHRIST, but of the painful state of the suffering Christ. He who prays that he may not be abandoned in hell, and for that reason his soul rejoices and his tongue exults, because he is not to be abandoned in hell, sufficiently indicates that the state in hell, in which he is not to be abandoned, is not joyful, not glorious, but sad and painful, from which he desires to be freed. (5) That state in hell is treated here, which precedes the rest in the sepulcher. But Christ presented himself as a victor in hell after he had rested in the sepulcher; therefore, it is not about that state of the triumphant victor in hell, not about those things which pertain to the state of Christ's exaltation, but about the infernal passion and the state of humiliation that is treated. For the order of the words must be observed first of all: first he says that his soul will not be abandoned in hell: then, however, he confirms that he will not see corruption, and thus that his flesh will rest in hope: for he had to undergo and overcome the infernal passions before he was placed in the sepulcher, in which others see corruption, but he himself was not to see it. If the discourse were about a real descent into hell, the order would have to be inverted: in this way: you will not permit your holy one (in the sepulcher) to see corruption, but rather (having been brought to life) he will descend into hell, as a glorious victor over death, both soul and body being free from corruption. Blessed Hutterus agrees in the explanation of the Book of Concord, Art. 9, p. 977. Although most interpreters [take] that prayer of Psalm 16:10. You will not abandon my soul in hell, they accommodate to the descent of Christ into hell properly so called, yet it is confessed that they are mistaken in many ways: For what? Does not Christ pray there that God the Father might not be willing to abandon his soul in hell? Indeed. Furthermore; does not the descent of Christ properly so called pertain to the state of exaltation? Indeed. What then, I ask, and how absurd an interpretation of these words will emerge? Namely this: You will not abandon my soul in hell, that is, you will not permit that I should descend into hell, and there triumph over death, over the Devil, and over all infernal powers. That such a summary of prayer never entered Christ's mind is certain. Thus far Blessed Hutterus. Thummius urges this especially, that Christ is introduced as if humiliated, because he asks of the Father that he not be abandoned, which kind of petition cannot befit Christ in the state of exaltation. To which argument Hackspanius indeed tries to respond, that it is not new in the Old Testament that Christ is introduced through prosopopoeia as praying, and that in prosopopoeia not everything is to be measured by a standard: therefore, by this locution Christ is also introduced as if in a state of humiliation. But while he concedes this, how does he accept these things concerning a real majestic descent into hell? Certainly, he is nowhere introduced as praying in the state of majesty as if he were in the state of humiliation, not even in prosopopoeia. Meanwhile, these things are not to be understood with Smalcius against Franz, p. 21, concerning the common state of the dead, or with Arminius in Private Disputation 38, as if Christ were under the dominion of death. For he had already testified to the hope of the resurrection of his own body: but he was not under the dominion of death even in death itself, he who through death triumphed over death, and by dying conquered death, and obtained dominion.

The other member, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption, shines with its own light, you will not permit that your Holy One should feel and experience corruption after death, or rot in the sepulcher, and therefore you will preserve him, so that he may remain free from corruption, and you will gloriously raise him up from there. For to see in the Hebrew phrase is to experience, and it is accustomed to denote sensation or experience. The passages are everywhere obvious. Which sense R. David Kimchi could not deny among the Hebrews, even if he also explains it with Grotius in this way: My flesh will rest in hope: you will keep me alive from dangers: yet he adds, and after death I hope that the worm will not have power over me. Thus also R. Isaac in Midrash Tehillim: My flesh will dwell after death, because the worm did not have authority over it. But lest anyone object that the plural number is in the word חסדיך, which I remember being objected to me by some Judaizer at Königsberg: it must be observed that that Yod is not of the plural number, but is redundant, just as it is noted here in the Masora. Nor does Grotius deny this, in this Hebrew word after the Dalet the Yod abounds, which the preceding Sheva also shows. Therefore, the Jewish gloss of R. Lusitanus in the Middelburg Collection, f. 141, that the discourse is about the whole Jewish people, and their rescue from every kind of calamity, rests on no foundation; nor does it agree with the letter of the text concerning immunity from corruption; which the Apostles are the authors of designating with the Hebrew word along with the LXX interpreters, and Grotius acknowledges, and confirms with similar passages.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QVONIAM NON DERELINQVES ANI- MAM MEAM IN INFERNO) Animam meam, pro me, Hebraice. שְׁאוֹל sepulchrum pro morte, consequens pro antecedente. Sensus historicus (latet enim mysticus subli- mior, ut in plerisque Psalmis) est hic: quanquam undique opprimor a Saule, tamen certus sum ex promissione regni mihi facta, non fore ei potestatem me interficiendi.

NEC DABIS SANCTVM TVVM VIDERE COR- RVPTIONM] Sanctum tuum, id est, me. In hac voce He- bræa post ד abundat י quod & Schæva præcedens ostendit. Videre corruptionem est corrumpi. LXX. hic ὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σε ἰδεῖν διαφθορὰν, quomodo & Lucas Act. 2, 27. nec ali- ter 13, 35. Sic Thren. 4, 20. בִּשְׁחִיתוֹתָם vertunt LXX. ἐν ταῖς διαφθοραῖς αὐτῶν. Sic & Psalmo 107. מִשְׁחִיתוֹתָם ἐκ τῶν διαφθορῶν αὐτῶν. Nec aliter Prov. 28, 10. Jer. 13, 14. c. 15, 3. Ezech. 19, 4. c. 21, 31. Dan, 10, 8. Os. 13, 9. Sensus idem, qui in priore membro, more Hebræorum.

De Davide unice secundum sensum literalem, quem historicum vocat, intelligit. Mysticum qui- dem sensum latere ait. Sed nec potest ejusdem di- cti geminus statui sensus, nec si id admitti possit, mysticus indubitato certus esset, nisi à Spiritu S. ipso monstraretur, qui vero in Vet. Test. ubi mon- stratus sit, ostendi nequit, unde relinquitur, Ve- teres sensum suum sublimiorem, etsi à DEO inten- tum de oraculis divinis neutiquam habuisse, quem nos in Nov. Test. de iisdem habemus. Quid ergo ipsis profuere oracula Prophetica? Et quis credet, Ec- clesiam per aliquot secula sensu à DEO intento in plerisque oraculis de Christo caruisse, adeoque illa isti Ecclesiæ, & fidelibus istorum temporum, cui re- velata sunt, hactenus inutilia fuisse? Sed missis in præsenti generalibus his responsionibus, certum est, non posse hunc versum sensu à Spiritu S. inten- to accipi, nisi de Messia: Non posse eundem de Davide intelligi secundum sensum literalem. Ar- gumentor ita: Cujus oraculi sensus è verbis ipsis fluens & primum obvius, infert immunitatem à corruptione, id de Davide secundum sensum pri- mum obvium & literalem explicari non potest: is enim sine dubio vidit corruptionem; Sed de Mes- sia intelligendum est, qui solus est Sanctus ille, qui corruptionem non vidit. At de hoc oraculo verum est antecedens, E. & consequens. Porro; Quod oraculum unice in Christo impletum esse, non ad- serunt tantum Apostolorum Duumviri S. Petrus S. Paulus, negando simul, expressis verbis, id im- pletum esse in Davide, sed etiam ex verbis ipsis o- raculi, & sensu ex iisdem fluente apodictice de- monstrant, id intelligendum non esse, ex mente Spiritus Sancti de Davide, qui corruptionem vidit, & cujus sepulcrum Hierosolymis fuit, in quo cor- pus ejus asservatum ac corruptioni obnoxium fa- ctum, sed de Messia, ejusque immunitate à corru- ptione ac resurrectione; Id secundum sensum lite- ralem & primum obvium de Messia non vero de Davide, agere indubitato certum est: nisi quis sapientior esse præsumat Apostolis, aut iisdem contradicere. Ita nostra sententia evicta, quæ communis omnium est Christianorum. Quid vero ad hanc Apostolicæ interpretationis & demonstrationis lucem Judaizans noster Grotius? Ad Actor. 2. v. 29. hæc annotat: Non negat (A- post.) verba illa de Davide ullo modo posse intelligi, sed neq́ tam magnifice, neque tam κατὰ κυριολογίαν, quam de Jesu: unde sequitur, eum esse Messiam in Davide præfiguratum: David in sepulcro manet, Jesus non manet. At hoc est, ex quo probat Pe- trus de Davide hæc non posse intelligi, sed uni- ce de Jesu intelligenda esse, quia loquuntur de eo, qui in sepulcro non manet, nec corruptio- nem vidit. David autem in sepulcro mansit, vi- ditque corruptionem Actor. 13. v. 46. Non quæ- ritur, utrum excogitari possit modus, quo illa verba Davidi convenire queant, sed an HOC IN LOCO, ULLO MODO de Davide dicta sint? non esse, probat Petrus, nec de eo accipi posse: quia David omnium confessione in Sepulcro mansit: & Paulus Actor. 13. v. 46. quia David cor- ruptionem vidit. Hæc autem verba loquuntur de eo, qui non vidit corruptionem, neque aliter hoc in oraculo accipi possunt. Si possent, nulla foret Petri, nulla Pauli demonstratio. Sic enim excipe- re potuissent Judæi, verba illa posse alio sensu ac- cipi, & de Davide explicari. Quo concesso quæ vis remanebit demonstrationi? Nam tam magni- fice, tam κατὰ κυριολογίαν intelligi debere, facile negabunt Judæi: nec stante Grotii glossa sensus hi- storici convinci poterunt.

Excipit Grotius ad vers. 25. Recte dicere Pe- trum, hæc Davidem de Christo loquutum esse Actor. 2. v. 25. quia Judæis persuasum erat, res Davidis esse typos Regis Messiæ. Habent quæ sequuntur sensum suum in Davide, sed magis figuratum. Vo- luit autem Deus in Messia eadem impleri magis κατὰ πόδας, ne quid causari posset populus vocularum au- ceps. Sed hæc ἀσύσατα, imo impia sunt. Antea sensum historicum de Davide constituebat; sen- sum mysticum autem sub illo latere dicebat: Nunc κατὰ πόδας hæc de Messia explicat, hoc est, ut alias loquitur, sensu magis obvio, sensu autem ma- gis figurato de Davide. Fateri ergo jam cogitur Grotius, κατὰ κυριολογίαν καὶ κατὰ πόδας magis hæc de Jesu prædicta, & in ipso impleta esse. Sed ali- quo tamen modo de Davide etiam vult intelligi, & in Davide habere quoque sensum suum, SED MAGIS FIGURATUM, ut sc. Judæis gratificetur, imo ut robur demonstrationis Petrinæ ac Paulinæ de- struat, eamque universam subruat. Nam admissa semel hac hypothesi, quod verba Psalmi de Davi- de intelligi possint, non poterit Judæus cogi, de Christo etiam intelligi; quia Grotius ita posse de Davide intelligi vult, ut credat, de Davide ea et- iam ex mente S. S. accipienda esse, unde in proclivi erit Judæo negare, præter hunc de Davide sen- sum, alium necessario admittendum esse. Quod res Davidis typi sint Messiæ, ὀὐδὲν πρὸς διόνυσον: non enim hoc quæritur, anne in quibusdam David ut typus Messiæ spectari possit, sed quisnam sit verborum Davidis sensus & an David de se canat, an vero hæc de Messia secundum sensum literalem, vel immediate à Spiritu S. intentum? Nam si de Messia canat hoc sensu, non potest nec debet de Davide explicari: utut forte in eo, quod verbis nonnullis effertur, (non tamen qua hic effertur,) David etiam typus Christi fuerit: non enim de figura quæritur rerum, sed de sensu verborum. Si de Davide secundum sensum literalem loquatur Psalmus, utut dicas, Davidem typum fuisse Christi, in eo illa illustrius re- periri, κρινόμενον tamen id erit, ac probatione in- digebit, quod præcise in illis typum gesserit David Messiæ, & quum maxime id probatum fuerit, nil tamen ad sensum verborum istorum faciet. Et quomodo tam disparati atque contrarii sensus iisdem verbis ex mente Spiritus S. subesse possunt in eodem loco, quos hic annotavit Grotius vers. 9. ad Actor. 2. v. 26. ἔτι δὲ ἡ σάρξ μꙋ κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι. Hoc, inquit, Dixit David, Saulis metu latebras è latebris quærens: Christus ante crucem & in cruce. Hic dixit de quiete tranquilla in sepulcro cum spe resurrectionis. Ille de quiete, vel potius occultatione in latebris irrequieta, cum spe effugiendi periculi. Quæ maxime disparata quis credet sub iisdem verbis latere? Similiter vers. 27. ὅτι ꙋκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μꙋ εἰς ᾅδꙋ: de Davide, inquit, sensus, non patieris me interfici à Saule 1. Sam. 22. v. 1. de Christo, non relinquens me diu sub regno mortis. Quæ plane contrarium sensum verborum important. Ut NON RETINERE IN INFERNO sit non permitti interfici, vel internecioni: & vicissim sit: interfectum non diu relinqui in morte. Pariter in membro altero ꙋδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σꙋ ἰδεῖν διαφθορὰν sit non patieris me vivum perdi vel interfici, & simul sit, non patieris me mortuum vel exanimem in corruptione permanere. Quæ itidem plane oppositam phrasium significationem requirunt. Ad vers. 28. ἐγνώρισάς μοι ὁδꙋς ζωῆς, de Davide: eximes me his malis, quæ morti comparantur: de Christo: eximes me morte. Ibi vivus eripiendus è morte, hic mortuus à morte in vitam revocandus. En iterum sensum contrarium! Denique Delectationes in dextera tua usq́; ad finem, de Davide, gaudebo fretus auxilio tuo usq́; ad vitæ finem, nempe ubi in regno ero collocatus, ut habet Grotius in annotat. ad Psalm. πληρώσεις με εὐφροσύνης μετὰ τῶ προσώπꙋ σꙋ de Davide intellige in templo, ut ad Actor. 2. habet de Christo in cælo. De Davide ergo geminum gaudium intelligit tum seculare & temporalem opitulationem & regni restitutionem, tum spirituale, ob conspectum faciei in templo: De Christo vero longe aliud designari vult: gaudium nempe cæleste ac sempiternum. In dextera ergo DEI ipsi est jam in templo, jam vero in cælo; usque in finem ipsi est modo usque in finem vitæ, modo in æternum, vel in secula seculorum. Quis admittet tam disperatas ac contrarias ejusdem vocabuli aut phraseos in eodem loco significationes? Et quid aliud quærit Spiritus mendacii, quam ut divina veritas obfuscentur, ac illustrissima vaticinia obscura, ambigua, dubia, incerta reddantur, instar Delphicorum oraculorum; Quod ubi successerit eidem in tam illustribus vaticiniis & dictis Scripturæ, quæ ipsis solis radiis scripta, & luculentissime in N. T. explicata sunt, actum erit de reliquis, adeoque de tota Scriptura S. nec aliter ea quam instar Regulæ Lesbiæ, & nasi cerei, quod per Papistas hactenus egit, habebitur.

Sed dispiciendum jam in specie de vers. 10. Psalmi nostri, & annotatis Grotii ad eundem: Sensum historicum dicit hunc: non fore Sauli potestatem Davidem interficiendi: sub quo quia ait latere sensum mysticum, sine dubio per sensum historicum intelligit sensum literalem (huic enim opponi solet mysticus) & ut alias loqui solet primum obvium. At sensus ille literalis vel historicus Grotii omni prorsus caret fundamento, nec è verbis textus fluit, imo nec cuiquam facile in mentem hactenus venire potuit; nullum certe nominabit ejus auctorem. Quomodo ergo pro sensu primum obvio habebitur? Quid quod ita voces pleræque detorqueantur in alienam sententiam; Non dicam, quod animam meam hic perperam per me explicet, siquidem vox animæ non præter rem peculiariter usurpata sit; ut quanquam per Ebrais- mum animam meam pro me poneretur, respectus tamen singularis ad animam etiam habendus sit: Pessime certe torquetur vox שׁאול quasi mortem notet, quæ de morte vel interficiendi potestate nus- quam in Scripturis adhibetur: neque ad figuras re- currere fas est, ut consequens pro antecedente, sepul- crum pro morte sumi dicamus, quum nulla id cogat necessitas. Et quid hoc est de Davide acceptum, non derelinques animam meam in morte, nisi ani- mam pro corpore poni dicas, (anima enim ipsa im- mortalis est) & ad futuram resurrectionem, quæ ipsi cum aliis communis, respici velis? Nam ista toto cœlo discrepant: Non derelinquere aliquem in morte, & non permittere ut aliquis interficiatur.
