Qui non derelinquendus est in morte, in mor- tem prius traditus intelligitur: non ergo sensu plane contrario, de liberatione è mortis pericu- lo exponi potest. Porro quum agnoscat Gro- tius, recte ita verti posterius membrum, non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, quomo- do idem esse potest, ac si dicas, non permittes, ut Sanctus tuus interficiatur: nam aliud est corruptio, altud interfectio, ideo peculiare hic quid designa- tur, quod quamvis Sanctus ille usque in שׁאול de- ducendus ac in mortem tradendus, non tamen in שׁאול relinquendus sit, neque corruptionem videre debeat, adeoque ne eam videat, à morte resuscitandus sit. In sensum ergo prorsus contrarium detor- quetur phrasis Davidica ausu nefando & sacrilego.

Jam si utriusque phraseos mentem genuinam indagemus, non est, ut quæ distincte ac cum em- phasi prolata, peculiare quid in recessu habent, & habere ab complemento ipso comprobantur, pro iisdem accipiamus. Nimirum erigit sese Messias, se non commotum iri, ich werde wol blei- ben: uti Megalander noster: ac tum cordis sui, hoc est animæ lætitiam testatur, tum carnis requi- em, spe resurrectionis tranquillam & securam. Propter hoc lætatum est cor meum, & exultavit glo- ria mea, insuper & caro mea requiescet in spe; quan- quam vero anima ejus usq; in שׁאול infernum de- ducenda fuerit, tempore passionis & mortis, con- fidit tamen eam in inferno non derelictum iri: quam- vis caro ejus vel corpus in mortem tradendum, so- latur & sustentat tamen se illa spe, in qua etiam tempore mortis caro ipsa secure quietura est, quod non permissurus sit Deus, ut corruptionem vi- deat, siquidem ipse Sanctus sit, à peccato omni immunis, per quem peccata omnia expiari, o- mnesque sanctificari etiam debeant Dan. 9. v. 24. imo certus est, quod sibi DEUS notas facturus sit vias vitæ, sibi non quoad animam tantum, haud linquendam in inferno, sed etiam quoad carnem corruptionis expertem: ut ibi adimpleatur ani- ma & corpore, quibus hic passiones immensas exantlavit, lætitia vultus Dei, & delectationes in dextra Dei æternas percipiat. Illud ergo non es derelicturus animam meam לשׁאול εἰς ἅδη (Act. 2. v. 28. 31.) usque ad infernum, hoc sibi vult: quam- vis animam meam in infernum deducturus sis, quod factum, quoties ipse tentatus à potestate infernali fuit, & imprimis tum ante mortem in agonia hor- ti, & in cruce, cum à DEO se desertum excla- maret, utrobique enim dolores infernales sensit, maxime quoad animam sanctissimam, tum post mortem, quando in inferni etiam locum vel πῶς deductus; neutiquam tamen animam derelictam iri: nunquam enim in tentationibus & passioni- bus gravissimis, quas ob peccata mundi in se su- scepta sustinere debuit, ipse relinqui debuit: quod phrases negativæ emphaticè important, ut- pote quæ affirmant vehementius: Deum nempe ipsi semper auxilio suo adfuturum, usque in infer- num, usque ad inferni passiones, & locum vel נג in- fernale, ut triumphet semper de inferno, divina ope, tum in conflictu cum potestate infernali, ante mortem, tum etiam ubi infernalibus pote- statibus & incredulis sese in inferno sistet, atque inde victor & triumphator redeat. Id enim vi- detur notare, ait Dn. D. Tarnovius, Christum non derelictum iri eousque, ut in potestate inferorum sit, ut hi pro libitu cum illo agere, eumque detinere que- ant, quod etiam Petrus Actor. 2, 24. innuit, ubi ta- men præsupponitur, quod in inferno fuerit in loco pœnæ, sed sine pœna, & is qui in ipsa agonia, quam in horto sustinuit, infernales dolores sensit, & dein- de se à DEO derelictum esse in cruce clamavit, post- ea victorem inferni se declaraverit. Pariter ex- plicarunt Paraphrastæ Vinarienses: Denn du wirst meine Seele (mich selbst) nicht in der Höllen lassen (derselben Pein weiter zu erfahren) wie vor- hin geschehen am Oelberg und am Creutz, sondern du wirst mich darin triumphiren, und meine Gött- liche Krafft, Macht, Majestät, und erhaltenen Sieg herrlich erweisen lassen.) Hæc illi. Sic ergo certa ratione omnia illa comprehensa ista phrasi sunt: Non derelinques animam meam, id est, auxilio & ope tua omnipotenti ac gratiosissima præsentissimus eris mihi, & animæ peculiariter meæ USQUE AD IN- FERNUM, usque ad infernales passiones, vel statum damnatorum, cum in infernum præcipue anima mea deducitur. Conf. 1. Sam. 2. v. 6. Psal. 18. v. 5. Psal. 88. v. 44. seqq. & usque ad ipsum inferni locum, vel נג damnatorum Pf. 31. v. 18. Psal. 49. v. 15. utrum- que enim cum statum, tum נג damnatorum voce שאול comprehendere solet scriptura: nunquam autem cum per vocem ᾅδης in N. T. explicatur, Sepulcrum notat: unde multo minus admitti po- test, sepulcrum pro morte hic positum esse. Sed quum ita facile geminus sensus invehatur, prio- ri explicationi inhærendum censemus. Pecu- liaris plane est Fr. Junii sententia, qui totum Pfalmum de Davide explicat. Hic autem per נפש animam vel vitam Christum intelligit, q. d. David: Non relinques animam meam, id est, Chri- stum. Sed ita discerpuntur, quæ de uno subjecto agunt. Neque Christus uspiam vocatur anima Da- vidis, vel fidelium. Et Christo convenire omnia, συνέχεια textus & analysis docet. De Christi ergo descensu ad inferos, quem ita vocant, metaphorico, vel de passionibus infernalibus, non de descensu ejus ad inferos reali sermo est, vi contextus & phra- seologias S. S. Quia (1.) Animam suam dicit non relictum iri in inferno, non seipsum: non est ergo, quod figuram statuamus, ubi nulla cogit necessi- tas. Adhæc (2.) anima hic à carne distinguitur: carni requies, animæ liberatio ex inferno promit- titur. At descensus ad inferos realis non est fa- ctus secundum solam animam, quia ζωοποιηθεὶς de- scendit anima & corpore: ideo dolores animæ in- fernales potius significantur. (3.) Utrumque quod v. 9. de gaudio & spe adductum est, distincte hic confirmatur, gaudium quidem cordis vel animæ in ipsis passionibus gravissimis ideo perceptum iri, quia Deus animam ejus non relicturus erat in ipsis et- iam infernalibus doloribus. Spes vero quietis (Actor. 2. v. 26.) quia non permissurus erat, ut Sanctus ejus videret corruptionem. (4.) Phrasis ipsa & modus loquendi, non relinques animam me- am in inferno, satis indicat, non agi de descen- su triumphantis CHRISTI glorioso, sed de patientis Christi statu doloroso. Qui precatur, ne in inferno derelinquatur, & ob id lætatur ani- ma, & jubilat lingua, quod non relinquendus in inferno sit, satis indicat, statum in inferno, in quo non relinquendus, esse non lætum, non gloriosum, sed tristem, & dolorosum, è quo liberari desiderat. (5) De illo statu in inferno hic agitur, qui antece- dit quietem in sepulcro. At victorem Christus in inferno se stitit, postquam in sepulcro quieverat; non ergo de statu illo victoris triumphantis in in- ferno, non de iis, quæ ad statum exaltationis Chri- sti pertinent, sed de passione infernali, & statu exi- nanitionis agitur. Observandus enim imprimis or- do verborum: primum non derelictum iri animam suam in inferno dicit: deinde vero non visurum se corruptionem, adeoque in spe carnem suam quie- turam confirmat: Prius enim debebat passiones infernales subire & superare, antequam sepulcro conderetur, in quo alii corruptionem vident, ipse vero visurus non erat. Si de reali descensu ad in- feros sermo esset, ordo invertendus foret: hoc modo: non permittes sanctum tuum (in sepulcro) corruptionem videre, imo (vivificatus) in infernum descendet, ceu gloriosus victor mortis, & anima & corpore corruptionis experte. Annuit B. Hutte- rus in explic. libr. Concord. Art. 9. p. 977. Quan- quam plerique Interpp. precationem illam Psal. 16, 10. Non derelinques animam meam in inferno, ad de- scensum Christi ad inferos proprie sic dictum accom- modant, tamen multis modis eos falli in confesso est: Quid enim? annon ibi orat Christus, ut Deus Pa- ter animam suam in inferno derelinquere nolit? utique. Porro; annon descensus Christi proprie sic dictus pertinet ad statum exaltationis? utique. Quæ ergo, obsecro, & quam absurda emerget verborum istorum interpretatio? nempe isthæc: Non derelinques animam meam in inferno, hoc est, non permittes, ut ego descendam ad inferos, & ibi de morte, de Diabolo, deque potestatibus omnibus in- fernalibus triumphum agam. Quam precationis summam Christo nunquam in mentem venisse, certum est. Hactenus B. Hutterus. Thummius id imprimis urget, quod Christus introducatur, tan- quam exinanitus, quia petit à Patre, ne derelin- quatur, qualis petitio Christo in statu exaltationis convenire nequeat. Ad quod argumentum re- spondere quidem conatur Hackspanius, non esse novum in Vet. Test. ut Christus per prosopopœi- am introducatur, ut orans, in prosopopœia autem non esse omnia ad normam exigenda: hac locu- tione igitur Christum etiam quasi in statu exinani- tionis introduci. At dum hoc concedit, quo pa- cto de descensu ad inferos reali majestatico hæc accipit? Nuspiam certe ita orare in statu maje- statis, quasi in statu exinanitionis introducitur, ne in prosopopœia quidem. Interim non cum Smal- cio contr. Franz. p. 21. hæc intelligenda de statu mortuorum communi, aut cum Armin. in Disp. Priv. 38. quasi Christus fuerit sub Dominio mor- tis. Nam spem excitationis corporis sui jam an- te testatus erat: sub Domino autem mortis ne in ipsa quidem morte fuit, qui per mortem de morte triumphavit, & moriendo mortem vicit, atque Dominium obtinuit.

Alterum membrum, neq; dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, sua luce radiat, non permittes, ut Sanctus tuus corruptionem post mortem sentiat, & ex- periatur, aut in sepulcro putrescat, ideoque conservabis ipsum, ut expers corruptionis maneat, & gloriose inde resuscitabis. Videre enim phrasi Ebræa est experiri, ac sensum vel experientiam notare solet. Loca pas- sim sunt obvia. Quem sensum diffiteri non potuit inter Ebræos R. Dav. Kimchi. etsi enim cum Gro- tio etiam ita explicet: Caro mea requiescet in Spe: in vivis me servabis à periculis: addit tamen, & post mortem spero, quod vermis in me non habebit potesta- tem. Sic etiam R. Isaac in Midrasch Tillim: Caro mea habitabit post mortem, quia vermis non habuit ἐξού- σιαν in illam. Ne vero quis objiciat, quod pluralis nu- merus in voce חסדיך, quod à nonnemine Judaizante mihi Regiomonti objectum recordor: observan- dum, quod Jod illud non sit numeri pluralis, sed re- dundet, quemadmodum hic in Masora notatum est. Nec diffitetur id Grotius, in hac voce Hebræa post ד abundat י quod & Scheva præcedens ostendit. Glossa ergo Judaica R. Lusitani in Coll. Mittel- burg. f. 141. quod sermo sit de toto populo Judaico, & ereptione ex omnigena calamitate nullo fundamento nititur; neq; congruit literæ textus de immunitate à corruptione; quam voce Ebræa designari cum LXX. interpp. Apostoli autores sunt, & agnoscit Grotius, locisque similibus confirmat.

## 16:10
DELIGHTS AT YOUR RIGHT HAND EVEN TO THE END) I will rejoice, relying on your help until the end of life, namely when I shall have been placed in the kingdom.

It is false that these things were said about David: For the Holy Spirit openly testifies in Acts 2:25 that they were said about Christ: For David says concerning him, that is, with Grotius himself as interpreter, CONCERNING JESUS HIMSELF. Nor is there any reason why that more figurative sense, which Grotius himself calls such, should be admitted at Acts 2:25: since the same Grotius acknowledges that the prophecy was fulfilled in the Messiah more literally. I argue thus: That prophecy which God willed to be fulfilled in the Messiah is not to be explained concerning David; that which he willed to be fulfilled literally and properly, that ought not to be understood in a figurative sense. Because these are opposites, that the words of some saying are to be understood properly and are to be understood figuratively, that is, not properly, which therefore cannot have a place at the same time in the same words in the same saying. But God willed this prophecy to be fulfilled concerning the Messiah, and indeed literally and properly, which Grotius confesses. Therefore that is not to be explained concerning David, nor ought it to be understood in a figurative sense. Therefore, that opinion standing, and the explanation concerning Christ 'you have made known to me the ways of life,' that is, you will deliver me from death, you will recall me to life, which Grotius approves, the other cannot have a place, because he is to be delivered not from death, but only from those evils which are compared to death, and from dangers: which sense Grotius acknowledges to be more metaphorical and figurative. That explanation standing, that the words πληρώσεις με εὐφροσύνης μετὰ τῶ προσώπε σῦ speak concerning Christ, being refreshed in heaven by the sight of the face of God and eternal joys, which Grotius approves at Acts 2:28, it is certain that those words ought not to be explained concerning David, that he is to be filled with gladness in the temple of the Lord before the face of God. That explanation standing, that the Messiah is here said to be refreshed forever by delights at the right hand of God, everyone sees that that jejune gloss has no place, that David would rejoice when he had been established in his kingdom until the end of his life. Of which temporal joy David was not certain, namely that he would possess the kingdom until the end of his life, or that that joy would be perennial and perpetual for him. That was placed ἐν γόνασι θεῶ. Nor does this sense exhaust the magnificence of the words of the Psalm, concerning the way of life, the fullness of joy, before the face of God, and delights at the right hand of GOD lacking an end. Which import the blessedness of the future life not obscurely, inasmuch as it consists in the vision of the face of God, and will endure forever, as נצח properly denotes eternity, because eternity is as it were the victory of time,

This sentiment also demands continuity: for this is what the text means, not only that you will be present to me with your help in sorrows, and in the passions of Gehenna and the path into the underworld, nor only that you will preserve my body from corruption or putrefaction, but also that you will open for me the way to immortal life, and will raise me up to that blessed life, which will consist in the vision of God, and you will fill me with joy and perpetual delights at your right hand. Thus the right hand of God is opposed to the underworld, life to death, an immortal and incorruptible state to corruption, the abundance of joys to passions. And since until now no one has been able to find the ways by which a man might arrive from death to blessed life, Christ teaches that the ways of life have been uniquely demonstrated and revealed to him in reality, by which he himself has penetrated to blessed life, and others pass through to it, death having been overcome by his own death, and thus the way to eternal life has been opened. Nor did David rejoice so much on account of those temporal goods, or value them so highly: which he believed to be perishable, fleeting, and vain. While, however, we urge the κυριολογίαν [literal meaning] and the weight of words in this way, it is not to hunt for LITTLE WORDS, as Grotius quite impiously pronounces: but to search the scriptures, and to take care, lest the Prophecy of the Spirit be of private interpretation.

Latin:

DELECTATIONES IN DEXTERA TVA VSQVE IN FINEM) Gaudebo fretus auxilio tuo usque ad finem vi- tæ, nempe ubi in regno ero collocatus.

Falsum est, hæc de Davide dicta esse: Testatur enim palam Spir. S. Act. 2, 25. quod de Christo di- cta sint: Δαβὶδ γὰρ λέγει εἰς ἀυτόν, hoc est, interpre- te ipso Grotio, DE IPSO JESU. Neque est, quod sensus ille magis figuratus, quem ipse Grotius ita vocat, ad Act. 2, 25. admittatur: quum vaticinium in Messia magis κατὰ πόδας impletum agnoscat idem Groti- us. Argumentor ita: Quod vaticinium Deus in Mes- sia impleri voluit, id de Davide explicandum non est; quod impleri voluit κατὰ πόδας & κατὰ κυριο- λογίαν, id sensu figurato intelligi non debet. Quia opposita hæc sunt, verba dicti alicujus intelligenda esse proprie & figurate intelligenda ea esse, hoc est, non proprie, quæ proinde in eodem dicto simul locum habere in iisdem verbis non possunt. At Deus hoc vaticinium de Messia impleri voluit, & quidem κα- τὰ πόδας & κατὰ κυριολογίαν, quod fatetur Groti- us. Ergo id de Davide explicandum non est, nec sensu figurato intelligi debet. Stante ergo illa sen- tentia, & explicatione de Christo notas mihi fecisti vi- as vitæ, id est, eximes me morti, revocabis me in vitam, quam probat Grotius, non potest altera locum ha- bere, quod non ex morte, sed tantum ex iis malis, quæ morti comparantur, & è periculis eximendus sit: quem sensum magis Metaphoricum & figuratum esse agno- scit Grotius. Stante illa explicatione, quod verba πληρώσεις με εὐφροσύνης μετὰ τῶ προσώπε σῦ de Christo loquantur, in cœlo intuitu faciei Dei & gaudiis æternis reficiendo, quam approbat ad Act. 2, 28. Gro- tius, certum est, verba illa explicari non debere de Davide, quod in templo Domini implendus sit lætitia coram facie Dei. Stante illa explicatione, quod dele- ctationibus in dextra Dei in æternum recreandus hic dicatur Messias, nemo non videt, locum haud ha- bere jejunam illam glossam, quod gavisurus sit Da- vid, ubi in regno suo collocatus fuerit usque in finem vi- tæ. De quo gaudio temporali certus non fuit Da- vid, quod nempe usque ad finem vitæ regno potiturus sit, aut quod lætitia illa perennis ipsi, ac perpetua futura. Id erat ἐν γόνασι θεῶ positum. Nec exhau- rit hic sensus magnificentia verborum Psalmi, de via vitæ, gaudii plenitudine, coram facie Dei, & dele- ctationibus in dextra DEI fine carituris. Quæ beatitudinem futuræ vitæ haud obscure impor- tant, utpote quæ in visione faciei Dei consistit, & in æternum durabit, uti נצח æternitatem pro- prie notat, quia æternitas est quasi victoria temporis,

Hanc sententiam postulat etiam συνέχεια: id enim vult textus, non tantum auxilio tuo mihi præsto eris in doloribus, & passionibus gehennalibus & usœ́ in infer- num, neque solum conservabis corpus meum à corru- ptione vel putrefactione, sed etiam viam mihi aperies ad vitam immortalem, meque excitabis ad beatam il- lam vitam, quæ invisione Dei consistet, ac lætitia ac delectationibus perpetuis me replebis in dextra tua. Ita inferno opponitur dextra Dei, morti vita, corru- ptioni status immortalis & incorruptibilis, passioni- bus ubertas gaudiorum. Et cum hucusque nemo vias invenire potuerit, quibus à morte ad vitam beatam homo perveniat, Christus sibi unice reipsa demonstratas esse docet, ac patefactas vitæ vias, quibus & ipse ad beatam vitam penetrarint, & alii eo pertranseunt morte per mortem suam superata, & ita ad æternam vitam aperta via. Neque ob tem- poralia ista bona ita lætatus est David, aut tanti ea- dem fecit: quæ caduca, fluxa, & vana credidit. Dum autem κυριολογίαν & verborum pondera ita urgemus, non id est VOCULAS aucupari, uti Grotius satis impie pronunciat: sed ἐρευνᾷν τὰς γραφὰς, & præcavere, ne Prophetia Spiritus sit ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως.

## 16:11
Verse 11. YOU HAVE MADE KNOWN TO ME THE WAYS OF LIFE) You will make known, that is, you will show me the way by which I may be freed from these dangers.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NOTAS FECISTI MIHI VIAS VITÆ) No- tas facies, id est, ostendes mihi viam, qua liberer ab his periculis.

## 17:1 Argument
PSALM XVII.

The protection of innocence, and the heavenly reward.

Ver. 1. HEAR, O LORD, MY RIGHTEOUSNESS.

Some of the Papists themselves understand this concerning the justice of the cause, not of the person, which is explained in the following member, attend to my supplication, by which he commended his cause against his enemies to God, as Contarenus acknowledges in his book on justification, Jansenius, and Tirinus on Psalm 7. Others render it in the Genitive: Hear, O God of my righteousness, Ps. 4, v. 1. Perhaps it could not inappropriately be understood of CHRIST, our RIGHTEOUSNESS: Hear, O Lord, the Messiah praying for me, JUSTICE itself, Jerem. 23, 6, as one who intercedes for us, and in whose name it is necessary to ask, whoever wishes to be heard, Dan. 9, 17, John 16, 23.

Latin:

PSALMUS XVII.

Innocentiæ presidium, & cœleste præmium.

Vers. 1. EXAUDI DOMINE JUSTITIAM MEAM.

HOc de justitia causæ, non personæ, intelli- gunt nonnulli ex ipsis Pontificiis, quæ expli- catur sequenti membro, intende deprecationem meam, qua causam suam adversus inimicos Deo commendabat, ut agnoscit Contaren. libr. de justi- ficatione, Jansenius & Tirinus ad Psalm. 7. Alii reddunt in Genitivo: Audi Deus justitiæ Ps. 4. v. 1. Forsan non incommode de CHRISTO, JUSTI- TIA nostra intelligi poterit: Exaudi Domine Mes- siam pro me deprecantem, ipsammet JUSTITIAM, Jerem. 23, 6. utpote qui pro nobis interpellat, & in cujus nomine petere oportet, quicunque exau- diri volunt, Dan. 9, 17. Joh. 16, 23.

## 17:3
Ver. 3. AND INIQUITY IS NOT FOUND IN ME) They took that זָמֹּתִי not for a verb, but for a noun, and the Greeks connected it with the preceding, whom the Syrian and the Arab follow here. Thus זִמָּה is taken in Levit. 19, 29, where the Greeks translate it as iniquity.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET NON EST INVENTA IN ME INIQVI- TAS) Illud זָמֹּתִי non pro verbo, sed pro nomine sumserunt, & cum præcedentibus connexuere Græci, quos hîc sequitur & Syrus & Arabs. Sic sumitur זִמָּה Levit. 19, 29. ubi ἀνο- μίαν vertere Græci.

## 17:4
Ver. 4. I HAVE KEPT THE HARD WAYS) In the Hebrew: I have guarded against the paths of the robber. שָׁמַר for to guard against, as in Josh. 6, 18, and there is a deficiency of the little word מִן, as in Ruth 3, 2, 1 Kings 18, 32.

Bellarminus wishes that it had once been read פָּרֻץ a breach, i.e., the ways of a breach, that is, difficult, but he brings forward no parallel passage, nor does this phrase occur anywhere in that sense. However, the letter in the Hebrew source is plain: I have observed the ways of the breaker, I have observed where the breakers and violators of the law were tending, or also, as B. Luther rendered it, On the way of the murderer.

That robber is Satan, John 8, 44, against whose paths one must especially guard, of whom also verses 12 and 13 treat, as of a singular enemy, fierce as a lion, and as a lion's cub dwelling in hidden ambushes, by whom our enemies are instructed and armed with force and fraud: against whom the Lord rises up, that he may supplant him, and from whom he wishes to snatch the soul with his sword; Cf. 1 Pet. 5, 8, Psalm 45, 4, Is. 27, 1. To which enemy, called by way of excellence, are subordinated the men of the Lord's hand, the men of the world, Psalm 17, 14, who exalt themselves against the right hand of God, that is, the Messiah, v. 7, and are to be subdued by the hand of GOD, into which it is a fearful thing to fall, Heb. 10, v. 31. This is a periphrasis for the infidels, because they oppose themselves to the Messiah, and dare to speak against him, as they are designated by Enoch, Jude v. 15, just as in Ps. 118, v. 15 and 98, 1, the Messiah is called by David the right hand of God.

Latin:

Vers. 4. EGO CVSTODIVI VIAS DVRAS) In He- bræo: Cavi semitas latronis. שָׁמַר pro cavere, ut Jos. 6, 18. & est defectus voculæ מִן, ut Ruth. 3, 2. 1. Reg. 18, 32.

Bellarminus vult olim lectum fuisse פָּרֻץ ru- ptura, q. d. vias rupturæ, id est, difficiles, sed nul- lum adfert locum parallelum, nec uspiam hæc phrasis occurrit eo sensu. Litera autem in fonte Ebræo plana est: Ego observavi vias effractoris, observavi quo tenderent perfractores & perru- ptores legis, vel etiam, uti B. Lutherus reddidit, Auf dem Wege des Mörders.

Latro ille est Satanas Joh. 8, 44. à cujus semi- tis imprimis cavendum, de quo etiam vers. 12. 13. ceu de singulari hoste, leoni ferocia, & catulo leo- nis in abditis habitanti insidiis gemino agitur, à quo vi, & fraude instruuntur & armantur inimici no- stri: adversus quem exurgere Dominus, ut supplan- tet eum, & à quo animam eripere gladio suo velit; Conf. 1. Petr. 5, 8. Psalm. 45, 4. Es. 27, 1. Cui hosti κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν dicto subordinantur viri manus Domi- ni, viri sæculi, Psalm. 17, 14. qui se contra dextram Dei, id est Messiam v. 7. extollunt, & manu DEI subigendi sunt, in quam incidere horrendum est Ebr. 10. vers. 31. Est hæc περίφρασις infidelium, quod se Messiæ opponant, eique obloqui ausin, uti ab E- riocho designati sunt Jud. vers. 15. quemadmodum Pf. 118. v. 15. & 98, 1. Messias dextra Dei à Davide vocatur.

## 17:10
Ver. 10. THEY HAVE CLOSED UP THEIR FAT) The Arab and the Syrian explain: their fats have been condensed. I have seen one who would prefer it to be read סגרו, that is, they hold me bound with their rope.

Why does Grotius bring forward a reading not found in any Codex, and differing from the Vulgate, the Arabic, and the Syriac editions, unless it is to render the genuine reading doubtful, as far as lies in him? For he does not anonymously disapprove of its meaning: and where Grotius leaves the word חלבמו their fat, to which the verb סגרו they have closed up is added, i.e., they have become obese and fat, whence they speak with their mouth with pride. The satiety of carnal goods is the cause of insolence. Ps. 73, 7, Job 15, 27, ch. 21, 24, Deut. 32, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ADIPEM SVVM CONCLVSERVNT) Arabs & Syrus explicant: condensati sunt adipes eorum. Vidi qui mallet legi סגרו, id est, fune suo me sinctum tenent.

Cur lectionem nec in ullo Codice inventam, & à Vulgata, Arabis, & Syri editionibus discre- pantem adducit Grotius, nisi ut dubiam, quantum in ipso est, reddat lectionem germanam. Non enim improbat ἀνωνύμως illius mentem: & ubi relinquit Grotius vocem חלבמו adipem suum, cui additur verbum סגרו occluserunt h. e. obesi & opimi eva- serunt, unde ore suo loquuntur cum elatione. Sa- tietas bonorum carnalium est causa insolentiæ. Ps. 73, 7. Job. 15, 27. c. 21, 24. Deut. 32, 15.

## 17:13
Vers. 13. AND SUPPLANT HIM) The word כרע also signifies to take away, as appears in Psalm 78:31. For כרע is, among other things, to fall, as in Isaiah 65:12, and from there it is used for causing someone to fall.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET SVPPLANTA EVM) Verbum כרע et- iam tollere significat, ut apparet Psalm. 78, 31. Est enim כרע inter alia cadere, ut Esaiæ 65, 12. & inde usurpatur pro facere ut quis cadat.

## 17:14
Vers. 14. THEY ARE SATIATED WITH CHILDREN) From the Greek ἐχορτάσθησαν υἱῶν they abound in offspring. It happened through the fault of the scribes that instead of υἱῶν, υἱῶν or ὑείων crept in, which flowed also into the Arabic and Roman Psalter: and there is mention of this corrupt reading in Arnobius, Paulinus, and Augustine.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SATVRATI SVNT FILIIS) Ex Græco ἐχορ- τάσθησαν ὑῶν prole abundant. Vitio scriptorum factum est, ut pro ὑῶν irreperet ὑῶν aut ὑείων, quod & in Arabicum & in Romanum Psalterium fluxit: estque ejus corruptæ lectionis apud Arnobium, Paulinum & Augustinum mentio.

## 17:15
Vers. 17. BUT I IN RIGHTEOUSNESS SHALL APPEAR BEFORE THY FACE.

The Hebrew word אחזה ought to have been rendered in the Kal, not in the Niphal, because it is nowhere read as a passive, but the verb נראה is used in its place; therefore B. Luther more correctly [rendered it]: Ich will schauen dein Antlitz. Genebrard also wrongly concludes here that we shall see God because of works. For the Psalmist does not say because of righteousness, but in righteousness, as the Vulgate also rendered it, nor is that righteousness, in which we see the face of God, necessarily understood as the good works of this age, since it can be understood of the righteousness with which we are to be adorned in the other life, as the next verse seems to suggest that sense: Yet you may also understand it very well of imputed righteousness, which is the cause of the blessed vision of God. For the elect not only shine here with the righteousness of Christ, but also will shine hereafter with the same, which, just as it is imputed to them in this age by God in justification, so it will not cease to be imputed in the blessed age, for that imputation is eternal, nor are they only constituted righteous by the righteousness of Christ, but they are also saved by the same. Faith indeed ceases in the other life, as do the Word and the Sacraments, but the imputation of the righteousness of God, the remission or non-imputation of iniquities, remains eternally; therefore it is called eternal righteousness in Daniel 9:24. Christ is eternally OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS in Jeremiah 23:6. Therefore, the righteousness and innocence of Christ will shine in us in the other life, but in such a way that, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image, not successively from glory to glory, but simultaneously and perfectly: For that happens in the initial renewal in this life 2. Cor. 3:17, but there will be perfect illumination, perfect renewal, perfect righteousness, as much as falls to the elect. Therefore, the entire righteousness of the elect, both imputed and inherent, is understood as consummated, in which, being established before the face of God, the elect are to see the same by intuitive vision forever. Furthermore, most of our people conclude from such passages that we shall see God with bodily eyes. This does not please Hackspan; he denies that it can be done by any power that our eyes be elevated to see the essence of a stone, let alone God, but that this is the work of the intellect. But although it is the work of the intellect to know the essence, yet those who believe that we shall see Christ in glory do not deny that glorified bodies will be seen by glorified eyes with respect to the essence itself, and to that extent our people assert that we shall see God κατ' οἰκονομίαν, or according to his glorious manifestation to our very eyes glorified, although we cannot see the divine essence immediately with bodily eyes, because we shall see him, just as he is 1 John 3 v. 2, face to face 1 Cor. 13 v. 12. We reserve the mode for the other life. The thing itself, however, is not to be denied, nor is the power of GOD to be estimated by the measure of our reason, which can effect more ὑπὲρ περισσᾶ than we can understand Eph. 3 v. 20.

I SHALL BE SATISFIED WHEN THY GLORY SHALL APPEAR.

In the Hebrew it is: I shall be satisfied in awaking with thy image. Galatinus explains the image as Christ, which does not please Hackspan, for the reason that Christ is nowhere called the image of the Father in the Old Testament, and that men in the Old Testament rested in a confused knowledge of Christ, and did not have a distinct one. But this is far from the truth: for they believed in Christ the God-man Acts 15 v. 10, the Son of God, the same God with the Father, and thus ὁμοόσι- ον to him, in whom is the name of God Exod. 23 v. 20. It is not therefore unreasonable to seek Christ in the O.T. as the image of God, except for those who deny a distinct knowledge of Christ in the Old Testament. Meanwhile we acknowledge that the discourse is about the image of God that will shine forth in us, not that we are to see only an image and some likeness of God, and be satisfied with that, as it seemed to Hackspan, for David had previously testified his hope that he would see the face of God, not just some image of God, such as are the images which he thinks were forbidden by GOD Exod. 20 v. 4, which indeed the orthodox deny were forbidden simply, since idolatry, not image-making, was prohibited; but that we are to be satisfied (by the sight of the face of God) or with the goods of eternal life in awaking to the image or with the image of God, as Blessed Luther renders it: I will be satisfied when I awake after thy image, for the particle ב is sometimes understood: which opinion Blessed Luther did not change in his operations on the Psalms. But he rather amended that explanation of the operations in his version. For these were prior to the German translation, published in the year 1519. Nor does the Rebia accent prevent the words 'to awake' and 'in the likeness' from being joined, for Hackspan himself noted at Psalm 11 v. 8 that it does not always distinguish in the Psalms. And there is emphasis, even if it does distinguish in this place, I shall be satisfied, when I shall have awakened. But I shall awake in thy likeness. Such repetition is sometimes necessary in Scripture, as has been observed elsewhere. Therefore he had no cause to note the opinion of Blessed Gerhard, by which in Vol. 9 of his Commonplaces he proves from these words the restoration of the divine image in the other life: I shall see God when I shall have been made righteous, and I shall be satisfied, when I shall have awakened in thy primordial likeness. Bugenhagius, a supporter of Blessed Luther, praises Felix for rendering it thus: I shall be satisfied, when thy likeness shall arise, the likeness, he says, of GOD is man Genesis 1. But in the sin of Adam it was lost, which arises here indeed restored through the righteousness of faith, and grows while we proceed from faith to faith, but will be perfected with Christ in the final resurrection.

Latin:

Vers. 17. EGO AVTEM IN JVSTITIA APPAREBO CONSPECTVI TVO.

Ebr. vox אחזה reddenda erat in Kal, non in Niphal, quia nuspiam passivum legitur, sed ejus loco adhibetur verbum נראה; ideo rectius B. Luther. Ich will schauen dein Antlitz. Perperam et- iam hic Genebrard. colligit, nos propter opera Deum visuros. Non enim dicit Hiero-Psaltes propter ju- stitiam, sed in justitia, uti Vulg. etiam reddidit, ne- que illa justitia, in qua videmus Dei faciem, neces- sario de operibus bonis intelligitur hujus seculi, quum de justitia, qua ornandi sumus in altera vita, intelligi possit, uti comma alterum illum sensum ingerere videtur: Optime tamen etiam de justitia imputata intelligas, quæ causa est visionis Dei bea- tæ. Nam electi non tantum hic fulgent justitia Christi, sed etiam olim eadem fulsuri sunt, quæ uti imputata ipsis est in hoc seculo à Deo, in justi- ficatione, ita non desinet imputari in beato seculo, est enim imputatio illa æterna, nec tantum justi constituuntur justitia Christi, sed etiam salvantur eadem. Fides quidem cessat in altera vita ut & ver- bum & Sacramenta, sed imputatio justitiæ Dei, re- missio seu non imputatio iniquitatum æternum ma- net, ideo æterna dicitur justitia Dan. 9, 24. Christus in æternum est JVSTITIA NOSTRA Jer. 23, 6. Refulgebit ergo in altera vita in nobis justitia & innocentia Christi, sed ita ut revelata facie gloriam Domini intuentes in eandem imaginem simul transformemur non successive de gloria in gloriam, sed simul, & perfecte: Illud enim in inchoata reno- vatione in hac vita fit 2. Cor. 3, 17. ibi vero perfecta illuminatio erit, perfecta renovatio, perfecta justi- tia, quanta in electos cadit. Universa ergo justitia electorum cum imputata, tum inhæsiva consumma- ta intelligitur, in qua coram facie Dei constituti eandem visione intuitiva visuri sunt electi in æter- num. Porro colligunt Nostrates plerique è talibus locis, Deum oculis corporeis nos visuros. Non placet id Hackspanio, negat ulla potentia fieri posse, ut ocu- li nostri eleventur ad videndam essentiam lapidis, ne- dum Dei, sed id esse intellectus. At quamvis intelle- ctus sit essentiam cognoscere, tamen corpora glori- ficata quoad essentiam ipsam oculis glorificatis vi- sum iri, non negant, qui Christum nos visuros cre- dunt in gloria, & eatenus Deum nos visuros asse- runt nostrates κατ' οἰκονομίαν, vel secundum mani- festationem ejus gloriosam ipsis oculis nostris glorificatis, etsi essentiam divinam immediate ocu- lis corporeis videre nequeamus, quia videbimus eum, sicuti est 1. Joh. 3. v. 2. à facie ad faciem 1. Cor. 13. vers. 12. Modum reservamus in alteram vitam. Res ipsa tamen non neganda, nec modulo rationis nostræ æstimanda DEI potentia, quæ plus potest ὑπὲρ περισσᾶ efficere, quam nos intelligere Eph. 3. vers. 20.

SATIABOR CUM APPARUERIT GLO- RIA TUA.

In Ebræo est: Satiabor in evigilando imagine tua. Imaginem de Christo exponit Galatinus, quod non placet Hakspanio, ideo quod nuspiam Chri- stus in Vet. Testam. imago Patris dicatur, quodq; homines in Vet. Testam. in cognitione Christi confusa acquieverint, nec distinctam habuerint. Sed hoc à vero alienum est: nam crediderunt in Christum θεάνθρωπον Actor. 15. vers. 10. Filium Dei eundem cum Patre Deum, adeoque ei ὁμοόσι- ον, in quo est nomen Dei Exod. 23. vers. 20. Non ergo inconveniens quærere in V. T. Christum ut ima- ginem Dei, nisi illis qui denegant distinctam Chri- sti cognitionem in Vet. Testam. Interim agno- scimus de imagine Dei in nobis refulsura, sermo- nem esse, non quod imaginem solum, & similitudi- nem aliquam Dei visuri, eaque exsatiandi simus, ut Hackspanio visum, nam antea spem suam testatus erat David, quod faciem Dei, non imaginem so- lum aliquam Dei visurus sit, quales sunt imagines, quas à DEO interdictas putat Exod. 20. vers. 4. quas vero interdictas simpliciter orthodoxi alias negant, quum εἰδωλολατρεία non εἰκονοποιΐα pro- hibita sit; sed quod satiandi simus (aspectu faciei Dei) vel bonis vitæ æternæ in evigilando ad imaginem vel cum imagine Dei, ut B. Luther. reddit: Ich will fatt werden, wenn ich erwache nach deinem Bilde, particula enim ב subintelligitur quandoque: quam sententiam non mutavit B. Lutherus in operation. in Psalm. Sed illam operationum explicationem potius emendavit in versione. Hæ enim priores fuere translatione Germanica, editæ Anno 1519. Nec accentus Rebia prohibet, quo minus conjun- gantur verba evigilare in similitudine, nam eum non semper distinguere in Psalmis ad Psalm. 11. v. 8. notavit ipse Hackspanius. Et emphasis est, si ma- xime distinguat hoc loco, Satiabor, quando evigila- vero. Evigilabo autem in similitudine tua. Qualis repetitio nonnunquam in Script. ut alias observa- tum, necessaria est. Ideo non habuit causam B. Gerhardi sententiam notandi, qua T. 9. LL. CC. ex his verbis probat restitutionem imaginis divinæ in altera vita: Videbo Deum cum factus fuero ju- stus, & satiabor, quando evigilavero in similitudi- ne tua primæva. Bugenhagius parastates B. Luthe- ri laudat Felicem ita reddentem: Satiabor, dum surrexerit similitudo tua, similitudo, inquit, DEI est homo Genes. 1. Sed in peccato Adam perdita est, quæ surgit hic quidem reddita per justitiam fidei, & crescit dum pergimus ex fide in fidem, sed perficietur cum Christo in resurrectione novissima.

## 18:1 Argument
PSALM XVIII. God is my Rock, and my Salvation.

ON THE DAY THAT THE LORD DELIVERED HIM FROM THE HAND OF ALL HIS ENEMIES, AND FROM THE HAND OF SAUL) 2 Sam. 22.

Latin:

PSALMUS XVIII. Deus Petra, & Salus.

IN DIE QVA ERIPVIT EVM DOMINVS DE MA- NV OMNIVM INIMICORVM EJVS, ET DE MANV SAVL) 2. Sam. 22.

## 18:1 Addition
PSALM 18.

The conflict of Christ with the Devil and hell, and His victory, on account of which, after his Jewish enemies have been rejected, He receives that He will celebrate GOD among the nations.

TO THE END, TO THE SERVANT OF THE LORD, DAVID.

The Hebrews, and those who followed them, Calvin, Junius, Piscator, the Belgian Interpreters, Tossanus, etc., and among the Papists, Tirinus, Cornelius a Lapide, and others, explain the present Psalm concerning the enemies and victories of David: which is done by certain of our own, such as Blessed Gesner, Blessed Selneccer, the Vinarians, Blessed Backius, Blessed Boblius, and others, and among the ancients, Didymus, Theodoret, and Hesychius. The Hebrews, however, remain in the person of David: Christians, indeed, mystically apply to Christ those things which are said here about David as a type of Him, according to the letter, they think. But Saint Augustine, Blessed Luther, and especially Blessed Pomeranus, Blessed Brentius, and Blessed Schnepfius, and Blessed Osiander profess that the Psalm must be taken properly concerning Christ. To whose opinions we judge that one must entirely subscribe. How excellently Blessed Brentius has executed this above the others, from whom Osiander has almost repeated the summary in his Paraphrase. And among the Papists, Menochius indeed acknowledges that many things in this Psalm apply to Christ alone; but among the Reformed, Coccejus, although he thinks this Psalm treats of David, nevertheless acknowledges that the magnificence of the words exceeds his grasp BY MANY PARTS, and that there are CERTAIN THINGS which, if examined MORE EXACTLY & IN DETAIL, do not FIND in him a matter corresponding to the words in every respect, AND THAT THE SAME treats of THE MYSTICAL DAVID, so that all things are exhibited in him most excellently and most fully. B. Luther says that there are MANY things in this Psalm which compel one to understand it of Christ, although there are also many which compel one to understand it of David, in his Operationes on Psalm 29, Vol. III, Wittenberg Latin edition, fol. 374. and he professes that he wishes to follow Augustine, since it is safer that Christ himself should abound, rather than a Christian David, and it is easier to understand the figure from the truth; for which reason, however much he may say that David, while he gives thanks for his victories, at the same time weaves a prophecy in the person of Christ concerning the victories over sins, death, and the world, he nevertheless confesses that the WHOLE Psalm has the words of CHRIST rising again, and he understands the title in this way also: He who spoke to the Lord the words of this Canticle, that is, he who published this Canticle concerning the future Christ, and that on the day on which, having conquered all his enemies, he was enjoying a quiet life.

Nor can anyone who admits that some things in this Psalm are of Christ according to the letter determine otherwise than that the WHOLE Psalm is of the same: because it is one and the same person who speaks throughout the whole Psalm, without any indication of diversity, and violence must be done to the text if some things are understood of Christ, but others of another person, such as David. But to accept all things of both—of David according to the letter, and of Christ mystically—is to introduce a double sense into Scripture, which is most alien to the simplicity, perspicuity, and the proper certainty of the sense of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as David at that very time when he had conquered his enemies, and on that occasion had sung the present Psalm, which is indicated in the title, did not sing it of himself, but by the Prophetic Spirit sang of Christ, whose victories he was contemplating with a faithful mind on the occasion of his own, so that here it is not so much David speaking, who was only the instrument, as Christ through the mouth of David [singing of] his own infernal sufferings, or conflicts with the devil, death, and sin, and the deliverance by God the Father and to describe help and victory, because through him spoke the Strong One of Israel, the Ruler of men, the just ruler in the fear of God, as David speaks immediately after this Psalm was sung, 2 Samuel 23:3, since in the preceding chapter the same Psalm is exhibited, which it pleased the Holy Spirit to repeat in its entirety in the book of Psalms or by that name, so that He might render this most distinguished prophecy concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ, and concerning the calling of the Gentiles, commended to the Church, and might sail with its ἀσφαλεία [certainty] in matters of faith and for our consolation, which is above others most necessary. Which is said more safely than if it were established with Cocceius, who is very hesitant, that it is exhibited there, just as it was said by David first PERHAPS more in consideration of himself than by analogy, (in which, however, he previously acknowledged CERTAIN THINGS which do not find in David a matter responding in every way to the words,) here, as it is delivered to the Church, PERHAPS it pertains more to Christ than to the figure. And therefore the blessed Brentius rightly reproved that double sense, by which the literal sense is understood of David, but the allegorical and spiritual sense of Christ: and if we look more closely at this Psalm and consider it according to the Apostolic interpretation, he asserted and solidly confirmed that the literal sense or its letter applies TO NONE OTHER THAN CHRIST our Lord. Similarly Osiander in the argument of this Psalm: "Although David takes the occasion of composing this Psalm from his own calamities and deliverances: Yet because he himself was a type of Christ, in this Psalm he introduces Christ speaking. He gives thanks to the heavenly Father, because in his passion, cross, and death he was preserved miraculously and by divine Majesty unto a blessed resurrection and an eternal kingdom. And he describes that deliverance with many, and indeed clearly figurative, words. And he prophesies that the Jews are to be cast out from the kingdom of Christ, but the Gentiles are to be called in their place through the Gospel unto salvation. Osiander, however, warns very well with Brentius: But because the pious (being members of Christ) are exercised in this world by various afflictions and temptations, and are famously delivered by the Lord God: they themselves will also find in this Psalm formulas by which they may give thanks to the Lord God for the deliverance received." With whom our blessed Bugenhagius, in his commentary on this Psalm, judges it to be clearer than light that Christ is speaking here, and on page 91 he establishes this summary of the Psalm: "Christ gives thanks to God the Father, because he was heard in his greatest tribulation for such horrible miracles done for his sake, and was delivered with eternal joy from his most powerful enemies, and from death itself and the underworld, for the reason that the Father loved him, who was indeed immaculate, but humbled for our sake. And he brought me out, he says, into a broad place, he saved me, because he willed me, etc." Then he rejects the faithless flesh of the Jews and chooses the Gentiles who believe in him; "you have dilated," he says, "my steps, etc." The blessed Schnepfius says that the Son of God is speaking here, and is giving thanks to the Father for the benefits conferred upon him; but in those benefits lie the praises of God: in the benefit of deliverance from the highest dangers, the praise of divine clemency and majesty; in the benefit of the presence and vindication of the innocence of the Son of God, the praise of divine justice; in the benefit of the victory given to the Son, the praise of divine fortitude and of his mighty works; finally, in the benefit of the subjection of the Gentiles, the praise of divine liberality and beneficence.

However, this opinion is confirmed not indeed from the name of the servant of God in the title, which is Cocceius's argument, because there the ministerial author of the Psalm, David, is named, and not the Object, Christ; nor from the word למנצח [to the chief musician] because the Psalm was delivered for the perpetual use of the Church, which argument Cocceius also used: because that word occurs also in those Psalms which do not sound of Christ, such as Psalm 6:1, Ps. 51:1, and several others: nor from the word King of God alone, which there is no doubt fits David, nor from the fact that Christ is expressly included by the mention of David and his seed: because seed here is not taken μοναδικῶς [uniquely] of Christ. Other and invincible arguments are available, the strength of which Brentius especially exhibited. First, from the innocence and justice of the person who institutes the Eucharist here in verses 20, 21, 22, as it is absolute and perfect in every way. This boasting, says Brentius on page 85, concerning perfect innocence and justice before God, cannot fit David. For although David had a most just cause against Saul, and did not inflict any injury upon Saul, and could also boast of the justice which he had in the promised Messiah through faith, yet he had sin in his flesh, even in a most just cause, and the justice which he had through faith he did not have in his own works, but in Christ. Wherefore he truly and piously exclaims elsewhere: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified." And: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" The only-begotten Son of God alone, our Lord Jesus Christ, is of such innocence, purity, perfection, and holiness that he dares to profess truly and cheerfully before God that the Lord rewards him according to his justice, and renders to him according to the purity of his hands, because he keeps and perfectly fulfills all his judgments and statutes, namely his entire law. Secondly, from the subjection of the Gentiles in verse 43: "Thou shalt make me the head of the Gentiles: a people whom I have not known shall serve me": which indeed does not properly fit David, but Christ, who alone is the head, and as Isaiah says, the Light and salvation of the Gentiles, and to whom the Gentiles, having rejected the Jews, are called to acknowledge. The Truth itself expressed this to Cocceius on page 98 on this passage: "Thou hast set me as the head of the Gentiles," i.e., thou hast made me the prince of the Gentiles. See Ps. 2:8. You have made me Lord of all in every nation without distinction, that I may call them to my obedience according to the counsel of the Father, that I may preserve all whom He has given to me, that I may rule all for the increase and edification of my people, that I may judge all. Thirdly, from the Apostolic interpretation. Finally, says Brentius, Paul writing to the Romans ch. XV, recites from this Psalm a testimony concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the knowledge of Christ: The Gentiles, he says, shall glorify God for His mercy, as it is written: For this cause I will confess to Thee among the Gentiles, and will sing a Psalm to Thy name. These are not properly the words of David, but of Christ, which also testify that the whole Psalm, while recited by David, but dictated by the Spirit of God, is to be understood concerning Christ. Wherefore, since Paul expounds it concerning Christ, no other interpretation, not even that of an Angel, is to be acknowledged. This is Brentius. If anyone should say that these were adduced by Paul only in an allegorical or spiritual sense, the response is obvious, that a mystical sense distinct from the literal is nowhere in the Scripture of the New Testament adduced as a foundation in proving or demonstrating any matter, nor can it be adduced without begging the question: and the blessed Brentius already meets that objection: it is to be held by a most firm faith, he says on page 101, that the foundations of the articles of our religion, among which articles, including that one which concerns the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, are contained: they are not delivered by the Prophetic Scripture through allegories, but most of all through proper and most certain sayings, which are to be understood according to τὸ ῥητὸν or the letter. Since, therefore, Paul commemorates this Psalm, in the place of a foundation, concerning Christ and the calling of the Gentiles, let us not think that he is playing with allegory, but interpreting most properly. For although there is a place for allegories, after the foundations have been firmly laid, an example of which thing you have in the epistle to the Galatians ch. IV, nevertheless in laying foundations one must use proper testimonies. Which two latter arguments are also urged by the Blessed Pomeranus: the end of the Psalm shows that Christ is speaking here, you will deliver, he says, me from the contradictions of the people, you will constitute me as the head of the Gentiles. The people whom I have not known &c. And Paul in Rom. XV proves the mercy shown to the Gentiles from a verse of this Psalm, therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles O Lord and will sing to your name. So that those who are distorted about David because of the Hebrew title do nothing here, being ignorant that David in his own tribulations and liberations saw in the Spirit these things concerning Christ being troubled and being liberated, who was about to come forth from his loins, and to sit upon his seat, as Peter says in Acts II. Which thing also David himself says after this song in 1 Kings XXIII, in his last words, the Spirit, he says, of the Lord has spoken through me &c. More arguments can be sought from the whole context of the Psalm and the most lucid exposition of it by Brentius: But these easily suffice. To which also the Blessed Glassius agreed in his Exegetical notes on the Epistle for the 2nd Sunday of Advent, Vol. I. Exeg. p. 202.

Latin:

PSAL. XIIX.

Conflictus Christi cum Diabolo & in- ferno, ejusque victoria, ob quam Judæis inimicis suis reprobatis DEUM inter gentes se celebratu- rum recipit.

IN FINEM PUERO DOMINI DAVID.

PSalmum præsentem Hebræi, & qui eos sequuti Calvinus, Junius, Piscator, Belgici Interpp. Tossanus &c. e Pontificiis Tirinus, Cornelius a La- pide & alii, de Davidis hostibus, & victoriis expli- cant: quod a quibusdam nostratium sit, utpote B. Gesnero, B. Selneccero, Vinariensibus, B. Backio, B. Boblio aliisque, & e veteribus Didymo, Theodo- reto, & Hesychio. Ebræi tamen in persona Davidis subsistunt: Christiani vero mystice ad Christum ea applicant, quæ hic dicta de Davide tanquam typo ejusdem, secundum literam, putant. Sed de Chri- sto proprie accipiendum esse Psalmum S. Augusti- nus, B. Lutherus, & imprimis B. Pomeranus, B. Bren- tius, B. Schnepfius, B. Osiander profitentur. Quo- rum sententiæ omnino subscribendum censemus. Quam præclare exequutus præ cæteris est B. Brentius, ex quo summam in Paraphrasi fere repe- tiit Osiander. Et agnoscunt e Pontificiis quidem Menochius multa in hoc Psalmo soli Christo conve- nire; e Reformatis vero Coccejus etsi agere de Davide hunc Psalmum existimet, verborum tamen magnificentiam MULTIS PARTIBUS captum ejus exsuperare, QUÆDAM etiam, si EXACTIUS & SIGILLATIM examinentur non INVE- NIRE in ipso rem usquequaque verbis responden- tem, EUNDEMQUE agere de DAVIDE MYSTICO, ita ut omnia optime & plenissime in eo exhibeantur, agnoscit. B. Lutherus MULTA in hoc Psalmo esse, quæ de Christo, etsi multa etiam, quæ de Davide eum cogant intelligi, ait operatio- ne in Psalm. 29. Tom. III. Wittebergens. Latin. fol. 374. & Augustinum sequi se velle profitetur, cum tutius sit Christum ipsum, quam Christianum “ Davidem abundare, & ex veritate facilius sit fi- “ guram intelligere, quapropter utut dicat Davi- “ dem dum de victoriis suis gratias agit simul te- “ xere Prophetiam in persona Christi de pecca- “ torum, mortis, mundique victoriis, fatetur ta- “ men TOTUM Psalmum CHRISTI resur- “ gentis verba habere, atque ita etiam titulum in- “ telligit: Qui loquutus est Domino verba Can- “ tici hujus, id est, qui hoc Canticum edidit in “ Christum futurum, idque eo die, quo victis “ omnibus hostibus suis quieta vita frueretur. “

Neque aliter statuere potest, qui aliqua Christi esse secundum literam in hoc Psalmo admittit, quam TOTUM Psalmum ejusdem esse: quia una est eademque persona, quæ per totum Psal- mum loquitur, sine ullo indicio diversitatis, & vim fieri oportet textui, si quædam de Chri- sto intelligantur, alia vero de alia persona, ut- pote de Davide. De utroque autem omnia ac- cipere, de Davide secundum literam, de Christo mystice, est geminum sensum in Scripturam inve- here, quod a Scripturæ simplicitate, perspicui- tate, sensusque Spiritus Sancti propria certitudi- ne alienissimum est. Idcirco uti eo quidem tempore, quo hostes suos devicerat eaque occa- sione Psalmum præsentem, quod in titulo indi- catur, cecinerat David, non tamen de se, sed de Christo, cujus victorias suarum occasione mente fideli agitabat, Spiritu Prophetico decan- tavit, ut hic non tam Davidem loqui, qui or- ganon tantum fuit, quam Christum per os Davi- dis passiones suas infernales, vel conflictus cum dia- bolo, morte & peccato, & DEI Patris ereptionem & auxilium ac victoriam describere, quia per ipsum loquutus est Fortis Israel, Dominator homi- num, justus dominator in timore Dei, ut immedia- te post decantatum hunc Psalmum loquitur Da- vid 2. Samuel. XXIII, 3. quum præcedente capite idem Psalmus exhibeatur, quem repetere inte- grum in libro תהלים vel eo nomine placuit Spiritui S. ut hoc tam insigne vaticinium de passi- one ac resurrectione Christi, & de vocatione gentium Ecclesiæ commendatum redderet, ejusque ἀσφα- λείᾳ in materia fidei & consolationi nostræ præ aliis summe necessaria velificaretur. Quod tu- tius dicitur, quam si cum Coccejo valde tituban- te statuatur ibi exhiberi, prout à Davide primo FORTASSE inconsideratione sui MAGIS, quam analogi sit dictus, (in quo tamen QUÆDAM, quæ non inveniant in Davide rem usquequaque ver- bis respondentem, prius agnovit,) hic prout Ecclesiæ traditus, FORTASSE MAGIS ad Christum pertinens quam ad figuram. Ideoque beatus Brentius merito reprobavit geminum il- lum sensum, quo τὸ ῥητὸν de Davide, allegorico autem & spirituali sensu de Christo intelligitur: ac si Psalmum hunc pressius intueamur & confide- remus juxta Apostolicam interpretationem τὸ ῥητὸν seu literam ejus NONNISI IN CHRISTUM Do- minum nostrum competere asseruit, solideque con- firmavit. Similiter Osiander in argumento hu- jus Psalmi: "Etsi David à suis calamitatibus & "liberationibus occasionem accipit componen- "di hunc Psalmum: Tamen quia ipse typus erat "Christi, in hoc Psalmo inducit Christum lo- "quentem. Is agit Patri cœlesti gratias, quod in "passione, cruce & morte mirabiliter, & divi- "na Majestate ad beatam resurrectionem, & ad "regnum æternum sit conservatus. Eam vero "liberationem multis, & quidem plane figuratis "verbis describit. Et vaticinatur, quod Judæi "sint è regno Christi abjiciendi, Gentes vero in "eorum locum per Evangelion vocandæ ad salu- "tem. Monet tamen optime cum Brentio Osian- der: Quia vero pii (quippe membra Christi) variis & afflictionibus & tentationibus in hoc mundo exer- centur, & à Domino Deo præclare liberantur: in- venient & ipsi in hoc Psalmo formulas, quibus Do- mino Deo, pro accepta liberatione, gratias agant. Quibus ὁμοψήφως B. Bugenhagius noster, in com- mentar. in h. Psalm. luce CLARIUS esse censet, Christum hic loqui, & p. 91. summam Psalmi hanc "constituit Christus agit Deo patri, quod tam "horrendis pro se factis miraculis, in tribulatione "maxima exauditus sit, & cum gaudio æterno li- "beratus de inimicis fortissimis, ipsaque morte & "inferis, eo quod pater dilexerit eum immacula- "tum quidem, sed humiliatum propter nos. Et "eduxit, inquit, me in latitudinem, salvum me fe- "cit, quoniam voluit me &c. Deinde rejicit car- "nem infidelem Judæorum & elegit credentes sibi "gentes, dilatasti, inquit, gressus meos &c. B. "Schnepfius loqui hic Filium Dei ait, & Patri gratias "agere pro beneficiis in se collatis, in illis autem "beneficiis latere laudes Dei, in beneficio libera- "tionis ex summis periculis laudem divinæ cle- "mentiæ & majestatis, in beneficio præsentiæ & ul- "tionis innocentiæ Filii Dei laudem justitiæ divi- "næ, in beneficio victoriæ datæ Filio laudem for- "titudinis divinæ & rerum gestarum: in beneficio "denique subjectionis gentium laudem liberalita- "tis & beneficentiæ divinæ.

Confirmatur autem hæc sententia non quidem ex nomine servi Dei in titulo, quod Cocceji argu mentum, quia illic autor Psalm. ministerialis Da- vid non vero Objectum Christus ita nominatur; nec ex voce למנצח quod perpetuo usui Ecclesiæ tradi- tus sit Psalmus, quo argumento etiam usus est Coc- cejus: quia vox illa occurrit etiam in iis Psalmis, qui non sonant de Christo, utpote Psalm. 6, 1. Ps. 51, 1. & aliis plusculis: nec è sola voce Rex Dei, quam Davidi convenire nullum dubium est, nec inde quod mentione Davidis & seminis ejus expresse Chri- stus includatur: quia semen hic non accipitur μονα- δικῶς de Christo. Alia suppetunt eademque invi- cta argumenta: quorum nervum Brent. imprimis exhibuit. Primo ab innocentia & justitia personæ, quæ hic Eucharistiam instituit vers. 20. 21. 22. utpo- te quæ absoluta, omnibusque modis perfecta est. Hæc gloriatio, inquit Brentius p. 85. de perfecta in- nocentia & justitia coram Deo, non potest con- venire Davidi. Etsi enim David habuit justissi- mam causam contra Saulem, nec affecit Saulem ulla injuria, potuit etiam de justitia, quam habuit in promisso Messia per fidem, gloriari, tamen ha- buit peccatum in carne, etiam in causa justissima, & quam justitiam habuit per fidem, non habuit in operibus suis, sed in Christo. Quare vere & pie alias exclamat: Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Et: Si iniquitates observa- veris DOMINE, Domine quis sustinebit? Solus unigenitus Filius Dei, Dominus noster Jesus Christus, ea est innocentia, puritate, perfectio- ne & sanctitate, ut vere & alacriter coram Deo profiteri audeat, retribuere ipsi Dominum se- cundum justitiam suam, & reddere ipsi secun- dum puritatem manuum suarum, quia omnia ju- dicia & statuta ejus, universam videlicet legem ejus, servet ac perfecte impleat. Secundo à subje- ctione gentium vers. 43. Constitues me in caput gentium: populus quem non agnoscebam, obedit mihi: quod utig proprie non Davidi convenit, sed Christo, qui solus est caput, & ut Esaias ait, Lux & salus gentium, & ad quem agnoscendum vocatæ sunt, rejectis Judæis, gentes. Veritas ipsa hæc Coccejo expressit p. 98. ad h. l. Posuisti me in caput gentium, h. e. principem gentium me effecisti. Vi- de Ps. II, 8. Fecisti me Dominum omnium in qua- cunque gente absque discrimine, ut eos ad obedi- entiam meam vocem secundum consilium Patris, ut ex omnibus, quos dedit mihi, servem, ut omnes regam ad incrementum & ædificationem populi mei, ut omnes judicem. Tertio ab interpretatione Apostolica. Postremo, inquit Brentius, Paulus scribens ad Romanos c. XV. recitat ex hoc Psal- mo testimonium de vocatione gentium ad agniti- onem Christi: Gentes, inquit, pro misericordia glorificent Deum, sicut scriptum est: Propter hoc confitebor tibi in gentibus, & nomini tuo Psalmum dicam. Hæc non sunt proprie Davidis, sed Christi verba, quæ & testificantur universum Psalmum recitatore quidem Davide, dictatore autem Spiritu Dei, de Christo esse intelligendum. Quare, cum Paulus exponit eum de Christo, non est alia, ne Angeli quidem interpretatio agnoscen- da. Hæc Brentius. Si quis dicat allegorico vel spiri- tuali sensu hæc tantum adducta à Paulo, obvia est re- sponsio, quod sensus mysticus à literali diversus nu- spiam in Scriptura Nov. Testam. fundamenti loco in probanda vel demonstranda re aliqua adducatur, nec adduci, citra petitionem principii possit: & occurrit ei exceptioni jam B. Brentius: firmissima, inquit pag. 101. "fide tenendum est, quod fun- damenta articulorum religionis nostræ, inter „quos articulos etiam ille, qui est de abjectione „Judæorum, & vocatione Gentium, continetur: „non traduntur à Prophetica Scriptura allegoriis, „sed maxime omnium propriis & certissimis dictis, „quæ juxta τὸ ῥητὸν seu literam sunt intelligenda. „Cum igitur Paulus hunc Psalmum, fundamenti „loco, de Christo & vocatione gentium comme- „moret, non sentiamus eum allegoria ludere, sed „propriissime interpretari. Etsi enim suus est al- „legoriis locus, postquam fundamenta firmiter „jacta fuerint, cujus rei exemplum habes in epi- „stola ad Galatas cap. IV. tamen in ponendis fun- „damentis utendum est propriis testimoniis. Quæ duo posteriora argumenta etiam urgentur à B. Po- „merano: Christum hic loqui finis Psalmi ostendit, „eripies, inquit, me de contradictionibus populi, „constitues me in caput gentium. Populus quem „non cognovi &c. Et Paulus Rom. XV. miseri- „cordiam gentibus exhibitam probat ex versu hu- „jus Psalmi, propterea confitebor tibi in genti- „bus Domine & nomini tuo cantabo. Ut nihil „hic agant, qui propter titulum Hebraicum di- „storquentur de Davide, ignorantes, quod Da- „vid in suis tribulationibus & liberationibus vide- „rit in Spiritu hæc de Christo tribulando & libe- „rando, qui erat ex lumbis ejus egressurus, & ses- „surus super sedem ejus, ut dicit Petrus Actor. II. Id quod & ipse David post hoc canticum 1. Reg. „XXIII. in novissimis suis verbis dicit, Spiritus, in- „quit, Domini locutus est per me &c. Plura argu- menta è tota συνεχείᾳ Psalmi ejusdemque luculen- tissima expositione Brentiana peti possunt: Sed ista facile sufficiunt. Quibus etiam acquievit B. Glassius in not. Exeget. ad Epist. Dom. II. Advent. Tom. I. Exeg. p. 202.

## 18:1 Addition
Vers. 2. I WILL LOVE YOU O LORD.

Brentius places the exordium of the Psalm here, in which Christ, to capture the benevolence of God his Father, and to testify to his most certain and most firm readiness in liberating the afflicted, commemorates the sweetest epithets of GOD his Father. I WILL LOVE YOU. This word in this place signifies not an action, but an affection; they call it an interjection of praying or coaxing, in Latin: Amabo te; in German: Ach lieber. My strength. For in adversities, in death, in the horrors of hell, and in the wrath of God, there is nothing that preserves the afflicted more strongly and more powerfully than God himself. Deservedly, therefore, he reports the epithet of strength. My rock. For where will the afflicted stand more firmly and more stably than in the Lord his God? Justly, therefore, is the surname of rock attributed to him. My fortress, or my tower. So also Psalm XXXI. You are my strength and my refuge, or my tower. For in afflictions there is no asylum to which you may flee more safely than to the Lord our God. Schnepfius and Coccejus wish those words: I love You O Lord; to exhibit the proposition, and he who has it thus here: This whole verse is not read in 2 Samuel XXII. There is something magnificent in it, rightly to be claimed for Christ: from which David's modesty privately abstained. רחם is to love intimately and from the marrow with the movement of all the bowels. Either no word or this one can lead us into a suspicion of the love of Christ toward the Father. The words of verse 2, I will hope in him, rendered here by the LXX interpreters, ἐλπιῶ ἐπ’ αὐτὸν, are rendered in 1 Samuel XXII: ἐγὼ πεποιθὼς ἔσομαι ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, which Christ applied to himself in Isaiah VIII, 17, according to the LXX, and are brought forward concerning Christ in Hebrews II, 13, καὶ πάλιν ἐγὼ

ἔσομαι πεποιθὼς ἐπ' αὐτῷ. Some indeed wish them to be taken from Isaiah, with Drusius, others with Junius, from the place in Samuel, our parallel; but what forbids the Apostle from having looked to both? The text of Isaiah indeed: as concerning which Coccejus not badly says to this place of the Psalm: There seems to be a mimesis there of the complaint of the faithful disciples of God concerning the long delay of the mission of the promised Christ, verse 14. Which promise, since it was commonly a laughingstock or neglected, God had ordered to be sealed up for his disciples. For there is an open reasoning in that passage. Therefore, verse 18, those things are rightly subjected to that complaint of the pious: Behold I and the children &c. Which are the words of Christ as if coming onto the stage, but the word πάλιν seems to indicate that the Apostle simultaneously hinted at the words of David, and Coccejus thinks that the Apostle looks to his reception to God as to a rock, as one proving the same (though in a dissimilar way) dependence of Christ the man and the faithful upon God the Father in hope and trust in him. Concerning the title horn of my salvation, Brentius has it thus: Horn, in the Hebrew manner, signifies either the kingdom, because kings were anointed with balsam taken from a horn, or strength and power, because horned animals attack with their horns, as if they were weapons. Christ therefore calls God the horn of his salvation, that is, his kingdom or his saving power, because he preserved him royally, heroically, or powerfully in all adversities, and conferred upon him all salvation. Concerning the last epithet: My exaltation, he says, God did not simply save Christ his son in adversities, lest he perish, but also exalted him to the highest sublimity, and gave him a name above every name. Rightly, therefore, does Christ attribute to him the title of exaltation. But Brentius judges that the proposition is more correctly contained in these words of verse 3: Praising I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies: since verse 4 and following follows a narrative, in which the enemies are commemorated, from whose jaws he asks to be delivered and saved. In this form of a servant, he says concerning the SON of GOD, when he was already near to death, he prostrates himself before God his Father on the Mount of Olives, in the garden of Gethsemane, and says: Ah Lord, my rock, my fortress, the horn of my salvation, in such great straits and miseries of mine, to whom shall I flee, if not to you God the Father, my savior and my exalter? Thee therefore alone will I invoke, and that not simply, but with the highest praise of thy name, as one who ingenuously and from the heart professes that thou art of such truth and constancy in thy promises (than which praise, what can be said more excellent?) that as many as shall have invoked thee may be saved and delivered from their enemies. For let us not think that Christ, when he prayed in the garden of Gethsemane, said only those few words which the Evangelists recite: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, &c. These words indeed are an epitome and summary of the prayer of Christ: But if you weigh the matter properly, there is no doubt that, since the Evangelists testify that Christ prayed ἐκτενέστερον and even more intensely, while both the Apostles were falling asleep and he himself was sweating blood, he used those formulas of prayer which the Holy Spirit had already prescribed more or less a thousand years before through David his ancestor, in the catalogue of which this Psalm is also contained. Let us therefore place this Psalm among those prayers and supplications which Christ in the days of his flesh offered up with strong crying and tears (as the epistle to the Hebrews speaks) unto God the Father, who was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared. But he does not properly understand external and bodily enemies, such as were

Scribes and Pharisees. For although these and other impious men were incited by Satan to persecute Christ most virulently and cruelly, yet because neither is the kingdom of Christ of this world, nor did Christ come into this world as an external warrior: his enemies are properly to be understood as Satan, death, and hell, against whom he waged war in such a way that he brought back a victory far the most glorious of all, and most desired by us. The very narrative of Christ immediately subjoined teaches that these spiritual enemies are being designated.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DILIGAM TE DOMINE.

Exordium Psalmi hic ponit Brentius, in quo Christus ad captandam Dei Patris sui benevolentiam, & ad testificandam certissimam ac firmissimam prom- ptitudinem ejus in liberandis afflictis, commemorat dulcissima DEI patris sui epitheta. DILIGAM TE. Non est hoc loco vocabulum actionem, sed af- fectum significans; Interjectionem vocant precandi seu blandiendi, Latine: Amabo te; Germanice: Ach lieber. Fortitudo mea. In adversis enim, in morte, in horroribus inferni, & in ira Dei, nihil est, quod afflictum fortius & validius conservet, quam Deus ipse. Merito igitur reportat epitheton forti- tudinis. Petra mea. Ubi enim firmius & stabilius consistet afflictus, quam in Domino Deo suo? Juste igitur tribuitur ei cognomen petere. Arx mea, seu turris mea. Sic & Psalm. XXXI. Fortitudo mea & refugium, seu turris mea es tu. In afflictionibus enim non est asylum, ad quod tutius confugias, quam ad Dominum Deum nostrum. Propositionem autem verba illa: Diligo Te Domine; exhibere Schnepfius vult & Coccejus, qui hic ita habet: To- tus hic versus non legitur 2. Samuel. XXII. Magnifi- cum quippiam in eo est, Christo jure vindicandum: à quo privatim abstinuit Davidis modestia. רחם est intime ac medullitus cum motu omnium viscerum diligere. Vel nullum verbum vel hoc nos in suspi- cionem amoris Christi erga Patrem potest deducere. Verba vers. 2. Sperabo in eum, à LXX. interpp. hic reddita, ἐλπιῶ ἐπ’ αὐτὸν, 1. Samuel. XXII. redduntur: ἐγὼ πεποιθὼς ἔσομαι ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, quæ Christus de sese adhibuit Esa. VIII, 17. juxta τὺς ό. de Christo adducuntur Ebr. II, 13. καὶ πάλιν ἐγὼ

ἔσομαι πεποιθὼς ἐπ' αὐτῷ. Alii quidem ex E- saia deprompta volunt, cum Drusio, alii cum Junio, è loco Samuelis, nostro parallelo; sed quid vetat utrumque respexisle Apostolum? E- saiæ quidem textum: utpote de quo Coccejus non male ad hunc Psalmi locum: Videtur ibi esse mi- mesis querimoniæ fidelium discipulorum Dei de diu- turna dilatione missionis Christi promissæ vers. 14. Quam promissionem, quum vulgo esset risui aut neglectui, discipulis suis obsignari jusserat Deus. Est enim apertus in illa pericopa διαλογισμός. Er- go vers. 18. isti piorum querimoniæ rectè subjiciun- tur ista: Ecce ego & filii &c. Quæ sunt verba Christi tanquam prodeuntis in scenam, Davidis vero verba Apostolum simul innuisse vox πάλιν videtur indicare, & existimat Coccejus, rece- ptionem sui ad Deum tanquam ad rupem Apo- stolum respicere, utpote probantem eandem (li- cet dissimili modo) Christi hominis & fidelium à Deo Patre dependentiam in spe & fiducia in eum. De titulo cornu salutis meæ Brentius ita habet: Cornu more Hebræo, significat vel regnum, quod reges balsamo è cornu sumpto, ungebantur, vel vi- res & potentiam, quod animalia cornupeta gras- sentur cornibus suis, tanquam armis. Vocat igi- tur Christus Deum cornu salutis suæ, hoc est, re- gnum, seu potentiam suam salutarem, quod con- servaverit ipsum regie, heroice, seu potenter in omnibus adversis, & contulerit in ipsum omnem salutem. De postremo Epitheto: Exaltatio mea, Deus, inquit, non simpliciter servavit Christum filium suum in adversis, ne periret, sed etiam ex- altavit eum in summam sublimitatem, & dedit ei nomen super omne nomen. Recte igitur tribuit ei Christus titulum exaltationis. Propositionem ve- ro rectius in his verbis vers. 3. contineri censet Brentius: Laudans invocabo Dominum, & ab ini- micis meis servabor: quum vers. 4. seqq. sequa- tur narratio, in qua commemorantur inimici, è quorum faucibus se petit eripi, & servari. In hac servi forma, ait de Filio DEI, cum jam mor- ti vicinus esset, prosternit se coram Deo patre suo in monte Oliveti, in horto Gethsemane, & ait: Ah Domine, petra mea, arx mea, cornu salutis meæ, in tantis meis angustiis & ærumnis, ad quem con- fugiam, nisi ad te Deum Patrem, servatorem & exaltatorem meum? Te igitur solum invocabo, id- que non simpliciter, sed cum summa nominis tui laude, ut qui ingenue, & ex animo profitear, te tanta esse in promissis tuis veritate & constantia (qua laude, quid potest excellentius dici?) ut quotquot te invocaverint, ab inimicis suis serventur & libe- rentur. Non enim sentiamus Christum cum in hor- to Gethsemane oraret, pauca illa tantum verba, quæ Evangelistæ recitant, dixisse: Pater, si possibile est, transeat à me calix iste, &c. Hæc quidem verba epi- tome sunt & summa precationis Christi: Sed si rem probe expenderis, non est dubium, quin cum Evan- gelistæ testentur Christum ἐκτενέστερον adeoque tan- tisser orasse, dum & Apostoli obdormiscerent, & ipse sanguinem sudaret, usus sit iis precationis for- mulis, quas Spiritus S. jam ante mille plus minus an- nis, per Davidem atavum ejus præscripserat, in qua- rum catalogo etiam hic Psalmus continetur. Repo- namus igitur hunc Psalmum inter eas precationes & supplicationes, quas Christus in diebus carnis suæ cum valido clamore & lachrymis, (quemadmodum epistola ad Hebræos loquitur) apud Deum Patrem, qui poterat ipsum à morte servare, obtulit, & pro re- verentia exauditus est. Non autem Inimicos exter- nos & corporales proprie intelligit, quales fuerunt

Scribæ & Pharisæi. Etsi enim hi & alii impii ex- citati fuerunt à Satana, ut persequerentur Chri- stum virulentissime & crudelissime, tamen quia nec regnum Christi est de hoc mundo, nec Christus ve- nit in hunc mundum, ut externus bellator: inimi- ci ejus proprie intelligendi sunt, Satan, mors & in- fernus, contra quos ita belligeratus est, ut victo- riam longe omnium clarissimam, & nobis exopta- tissimam reportaverit. Hosce spirituales hostes designari ipsa Christi narratio immediate subjun- cta docet.

## 18:3 Addition
Verse 4.

THE SORROWS OF DEATH COMPASS ME, AND THE TORRENTS OF PERDITION TROUBLE ME.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

CIRCUMDANT ME DOLORES MOR- TIS, ET TORRENTES PERDITIONIS CONTURBANT ME.

## 18:4 Addition
Verse 5.

THE SORROWS OF HELL COMPASS ME, THE SNARES OF DEATH PREVENT ME.

Those enemies, therefore, are (1.) Death, of whose sorrows, or rather snares, by which he is compassed, he complains, through which the power and jurisdiction of death, by which it rules like a tyrant (Rom. 5), is designated. (2.) Satan, with the whole diabolical troop, which he designates by the Torrents of Belial or of perdition, just as the Holy Spirit said in Ephesians 5:12, πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας. Rushing torrents denote a great abundance and a terrible impetus. Just as the word for trouble occurs regarding the perturbation of an evil spirit in 1 Samuel 16:14: Osiander paraphrases it thus: Satan, by amplifying and exaggerating my sins and placing the wrath of God before my eyes, terrified me no differently than if someone sees himself suddenly and unexpectedly surrounded by a torrent, and nowhere does an escape lie open any longer: he thinks he is being suffocated at any moment. Hence those words of Christ in his passion: My soul is sorrowful even unto death. And My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? (3.) Hell, by whose sorrows or cords he says he was compassed. Whence in Psalm 16:10 he prayed, Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell. (4.) Sin, which is denoted by the nets of death: because we are ensnared by sins unto judgment and eternal condemnation, just as birds or wild beasts are by nets (Ecclesiastes 9:12), which are the snares of the devil (Psalm 91:3, 1 Timothy 6:11, 2 Timothy 2:26).

Latin:

Vers. 5.

DOLORES INFERNI CIRCUM- DANT ME, OCCUPANT ME LA- QUEI MORTIS.

Hostes ergo illi sunt (1.) Mors, de cujus dolo- ribus, vel potius laqueis, quibus circumdatus, queritur, per quos potentia & jurisdictio mor- tis, qua instar tyranni dominatur Rom. 5. designa- tur. (2.) Satanas, cum tota diabolica caterva, quam per Torrentes Belial seu perditionis desi- gnat, uti Ephes. V, 12. πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας dixit Spiritus Sanct. Torrentes irruentes copiam ma- gnam, & impetum terribilem denotant. Quem- admodum conturbationis verbum de mali Spiritus perturbatione 1. Samuel. XVI, 14. occurrit: Osian- der ita περιφράζει: Satan gravissimis suis tentatio- nibus amplificando & exaggerando peccata, & iram DEI ob oculos ponendo, non aliter me per- terruit, quam si quis videt, sese improviso & subi- taneo torrente circumventum, nusquam autem ef- fugium amplius patere: jam jamque suffocari se putet. Hinc illæ voces Christi in passione: Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Et Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti? (3.) Infernus, cujus doloribus vel funibus circumdatum sese fuis- se ait. Unde Psalm. XVI, 10. petiit, non derelin- ques animam meam in inferno. (4.) Peccatum, quod per retia mortis denotatur: quia peccatis irretimur ad judicium ad æternam condemnatio- nem, sicut aves aut feræ retibus Ecclesiast. IX, 12. quæ sunt laquei diaboli Psalm. XCI, 3. 1. Tim. VI, 11. 2. Tim. II, 26.

## 18:5
Ver. 6. THE SNARES OF DEATH PREVENTED ME) You would translate more correctly, they surrounded me. For קדמו is often to surround, as in Job 30:27, 2 Sam. 22:19. Thus what is יקדמני in Ps. 58, is the same as יסובבנו in Psalm 32.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PRÆOCCVPAVERVNT ME LAQVEI MORTIS) Rectius vertas, ambierunt me. Nam קדמו sæpe est circumdare, ut Jobi 30, 27. 2. Sam. 22, 19. Sic quod in Ps. 58. est יקדמני, idem est in Psalm. 32. יסובבנו.

## 18:6 Addition
Verse 7.

THE EARTH SHOOK AND TREMBLED.
